# Examen Theologicum Acroamaticum


## 1 Prolegomenon I: On Theology


### Question I. What is theology?

THEOLOGY is an eminent practical wisdom, teaching from the revealed word of God all things which are necessary for a sinful man, who is to attain eternal salvation, to know for true faith in Christ, and to do for the holiness of life ().

() Since it is evident that this definition explains specifically the theology 1) that is *ectypal*, from which is distinguished the *archetypal*, 2) of men, whose theology is different from that of the angels, 3) of those who are sinning, after their most sad defection from God, by which reason it is opposed to the theology, as it is commonly called, of paradise, in the state of integrity, 4) of wayfarers, whose theology differs from that which is called of the consummated, 5) revealed, which is distinguished from natural; therefore, it would have been consistent with the order of things if it had pleased the blessed Author to prefix a certain general definition, and all those divisions, concerning which he himself expounded thereafter, from question 7 up to 11. That which the blessed man himself seems to profess below, question 12. Then, as far as the definition itself is concerned, 1) for many reasons it seems to me that theology is more correctly called an efficacious, or practical, cognition than wisdom; certainly there was no need for this addition, "practical," if indeed no wisdom can exist unless it is practical, whereas cognition, or science, is rightly divided into theoretical and practical (see what the blessed Author himself will discuss thereafter, at question 13, inst. II and IV): 2) as for this, "from the revealed word of God," I judge it would have been said more plainly and more certainly: "consigned to letters, or, divine scripture." By this means we avoid every ambiguity that lies hidden in the words. Thus, indeed, the propriety of an accurate definition demands, as one of its chief requirements, that nothing in it be stated ambiguously. It is agreed among all that (α) FANATICAL men, indeed, despisers of scripture, interpret the revealed word of God either as the internal light which they invent, or as the immediate illumination which they fable to happen to a few select friends of God; (β) ROMAN CATHOLICS, however, besides the written word of God, feign some other thing, equally divinely revealed, namely, as they say, handed down by word of mouth. Few today are ignorant that the JEWS also posit a twofold word of God, partly the scriptures of the divine Prophets, partly the traditions which they call Mosaic, in almost the same manner in which Roman Catholics invent Apostolic traditions.

Q.

Etymology. Theology, by the force of the word, denotes λόγον περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ [a discourse concerning God], both as a speech, and primarily as a knowledge of God, or a habit of discoursing about God.

The assertion is proven: Theology is an abstract noun, derived from the concrete θεολόγος [theologian]. The word, λόγος [word/discourse], which constitutes the other part of the concrete, outside of composition signifies both an external speech of the mouth, namely an oration or dissertation; and an internal concept of the mind, or reason, or the dictate of reason: but within composition it denotes cognition or knowledge, so that a theologian is called one to whom ὁ λόγος περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ [the discourse concerning God] belongs by way of a scientific habit, just as one is called an astrologer who has acquired for himself knowledge of the motion of the stars, and excels in the habit of discoursing about the stars. Although the etymon of theology can be explained by λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ [discourse of God], as a speech or knowledge of God, because it is from God as the efficient cause; or by λόγον πρὸς τὸν θεόν [discourse toward God], as a speech leading to God, as the ultimate end: yet it is more correctly explained here as knowledge of God, as the primary object of theological consideration. For just as astrology is the knowledge of the stars, cosmology of the world, chronology of time, anthropology of man; so theology is the knowledge of God.

Q.

III. Is the word, theology, ἔγγραφος [written], or expressed in the sacred Code? The word, theology, κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν [according to the letter], does not exist in sacred scripture.

The concrete θεολόγος [theologian] is indeed seen in the epigraph of the Apocalypse of John; but that the same word was immediately inspired by the holy spirit is improbable. Proof. To those perusing the code of sacred oracles, it is evident that the word theology does not exist therein. The concrete θεολόγος [theologian] is read in the epigraph of the Apocalypse of John conceived in these words: Ἀποκάλυψις Ἰωάννη τοῦ θεολόγῳ [The Revelation of John the Theologian]. AUGUSTINE, tract. 36 on John, gives the reason for the denomination, because this apostle asserted the divinity of Christ with such emphasis as no one before him had. From which THEOPHYLACT calls him θεολογικώτατον [most theological]. The Complutensian exemplar has this inscription: Ἀποκάλυψις τοῦ ἁγίε Ἀποσόλε καὶ Εὐαγγελιστ Ἰωάννη τοῦ θεολόγῳ [The Revelation of the holy Apostle and Evangelist John the Theologian]. Which variation of the inscription leads us to conjecture that this epigraph is not θεόπνευστον [divinely inspired]; nor is it indeed consistent that John, being very modest, would have distinguished himself with the name of a holy apostle, as is held in the Complutensian exemplar.

Q.

IV. Who were the first to use the word, theology? The Gentiles used this word long before Christ was born, which the prelates of the primitive church transferred to express the true knowledge of God.

The word, theology, exists in PLATO, lib. 2 de republ., and ARISTOTLE, lib. 3 Metaph. cap. 4. CICERO, lib. 3 de natura Deorum: Theologians, he says, count three Jupiters. CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA, lib. 4 Stromat., calls it ἐπιδρομὴν τῆς θεολογίας [a running through of theology], which the Latins would call a theological course.

Latin:

THEOLOGIA est sapientia eminens practica, e verbo Dei revelato docens omnia, quae ad veram in Christum fidem cognitu, & ad sanctimoniam vitae factu necessaria sunt homini peccatori, aeternam salutem adepturo ().

() Quum evidens sit, hac definitione explicari speciatim theologiam 1) εκτυπον, a qua distinguitur αρχετυπος, 2) hominum, quorum alia est, ac angelorum theologia, 3) peccantium, post tristissimam illorum a Deo defectionem, qua ratione ei opponitur theologia, vt vulgo nominari solet, paradisiaca, in statu integritatis, 4) viatorum, quorum theologia differt ab ea, quae dicitur consummatorum, 5) revelatam, quae discernitur a naturali idcirco ordini rerum fuisset conveniens, si placuisset b. Auctori praemittere definitionem quamdam generalem, omnesque eas divisiones, de quibus deinceps ipse exposuit, quaest. 7. vsque ad 11. Id quod vir beatus ipse profiteri videtur infra, quaest. 12. Deinde, quod ad ipsam definitionem attinet, 1) multis de causis mihi videtur theologia rectius dici cognitio efficax, sive practica, quam sapientia, certe non opus erat hoc additamento, practica, si quidem nulla potest esse, nisi practica, sapientia, cognitio autem, sive scientia, recte dividitur in theoreticam, & practicam (vid. quae b. A. ipse differet deinceps, ad quaest. 13. inst. II. & IV.): 2) quantum ad hoc, ex verbo Dei revelato, planius equidem certiusque dictum fore arbitror: litteris consignato, seu, scriptura divina. Quo pacto omnem evitamus, quae in verbis latet, ambiguitatem. Ita nimirum postulat accuratae definitionis proprietas vna ex praecipuis, vt ne quidquam in ea sit ambigue dictum. Constat inter omnes, (α) FANATICOS quidem homines, scripturae contemtores, verbum Dei revelatum interpretari aut de lumine, quod illi comminiscuntur, interno, aut de immediata, quam paucis quibusdam & selectis Dei amicis contingere fabulantur, illuminatione; (β) ROMANO-CATHOLICOS autem, praeter scriptum Dei verbum, aliud quoddam fingere, aeque divinitus revelatum, quippe, vt aiunt, ore traditum. Pauci hodie nesciunt, etiam IVDAEOS statuere duplex Dei verbum, partim scripturas Vatum divinorum, partim traditiones, quas vocant Mosaicas, eumdem fere ad modum, quo Romano-Catholici traditiones comminiscuntur Apostolicas.

Quæst. II. Quid significat theologia?

Etymologia. Theologia, vi vocis, notat λόγον περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ, cum sermonem, tum in primis scientiam de Deo, vel habitum de Deo differendi.

Probatur assertum: Theologia est nomen abstractum, a concreto θεολόγος deductum. Vox, λόγος, quæ alteram concreti partem constituit, extra compositionem significat tum externum sermonem oris, nempe orationem, vel dissertationem; tum internum conceptum mentis, sive rationem, aut rationis dictamen: at intra compositionem notat cognitionem, sive scientiam, vt theologus dicatur, cui ὁ λόγος περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ per modum habitus scientifici inest, sicut astrologus appellatur, qui scientiam de motu astrorum sibi parauit, & habitu differendi de astris pollet. Quamuis ἔτυμον τῆς θεολογίας exponi possit per λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ, sermonem, siue scientiam Dei, quia est a Deo tanquam caussa efficiente; vel per λόγον πρὸς τὸν θεόν, per sermonem ducentem ad Deum, ut finem vltimum: Rectius tamen heic explicatur per scientiam de Deo, velut obiecto primario considerationis theologicæ. Quemadmodum enim astrologia est scientia de astris, cosmologia de mundo, chronologia de tempore, anthropologia de homine; ita theologia est scientia de Deo.

Quæst. III. Estne vox, theologia, ἔγγραφος, siue in Codice sacro expressa?

Vox, theologia, κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν, qua litteram, non extat in sacra scriptura.

Concretum θεολόγος cernitur quidem in epigraphe apocalypleos Ioannis; at eandem vocem immediate a spiritu sancto esse inspiratam, improbabile est. Prob. Euoluentibus sacrorum oraculorum codicem constat, vocem theologia in eodem non extare. Concretum θεολόγος legitur in epigraphe apocalypleos Ioannæ his verbis conceptæ: Ἀποκάλυψις Ἰωάννη τοῦ θεολόγῳ. Rationem denominationis reddit AVGVSTINVS tractat. 36. in Ioannem, quia hic apostolus diuinitatem Christi tanta cum emphasi, quanta ante eum nemo asseruit. Ex quo THEOPHYLACTVS eum vocat θεολογικώτατον. Exemplar Complutense hanc habet inscriptionem: Ἀποκάλυψις τοῦ ἁγίε Ἀποσόλε καὶ Εὐαγγελιστ Ἰωάννη τοῦ θεολόγῳ. Quæ variatio inscriptionis nos inducit, vt coniciamus isthanc epigraphen non esse θεόπνευστον; neque vero consentaneum est, Ioannem perquam modestum, seipsum apostoli sancti nomine insigniuisse, vt habetur in exemplari Complutensi.

Quæst. IV. Quinam primi voce, theologia, vsi sunt?

Gentiles dudum ante natum Christum hac voce vsi sunt, quam antistites primituæ ecclesiæ ad exprimendam veram de Deo scientiam transtulerunt.

Prob. Extat vox, theologia, apud PLATONEM lib. 2. de republ. & ARISTOTELEM lib. 3. Metaph. cap. 4. CICERO lib. 3. de natura Deorum: Theologi, ait, tres Ioues numerant. CLEMENS ALEXANDRINVS lib. 4. Stromat. vocat ἐπιδρομὴν τῆς θεολογίας, quam latini cursum theologicum dicerent.


### Q. V. Is there in the sacred scriptures a word equivalent to theology?

A word absolutely equivalent to theology is not read in sacred scripture, yet synonymous periphrases are given in it.

Proof. Theology is called the wisdom of God in a mystery, 1 Cor. II, 7. Hence by some it is called θεοσοφία [theosophy]. It is called ἔκθεσις τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ ὁδῦ [an exposition of the way of God], Acts XVIII, 26. Thence by the blessed DANNHAVER it is called ὁδοσοφία [way-wisdom]. Theologians are called θεοδίδακτοι [taught by God],

Latin:

Vox, theologiæ absolute æquipollens, in sacra scriptura non legitur, dantur tamen in eadem periphrases synonymicæ.

Prob. Vocatur theologia sapientia Dei in mysterio, 1 Cor. II, 7. Hinc a nonnullis appellatur θεοσοφία. Dicitur ἔκθεσις τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ ὁδῦ, expositio viæ domini, Act. XVIII, 26. Exinde a B. DANNHAVERO appellatur ὁδοσοφία. Theologi audiunt θεοδίδακτοι,


### Q. VI. In how many senses is the word, theology, accepted?

In a quadruple sense. (a) Most generally, for any doctrine concerning God, even if it be false, or mixed with errors. (b) Generally, for true theology, whether it be original, or participated, or of wayfarers, or of the blessed, or natural, or revealed. (c) Specially, for revealed theology, leading the wayfaring man to eternal salvation. (d) Most specially, for the doctrine concerning God one and three.

Prob. a. It was customary for the heathens to distinguish their own far-from-truth opinion about God into mythical, political, and physical theology, concerning which D. HILDEBRAND treats at length in theol. dogmat. p. 2, 3. But false theology is called theology καταχρηστικῶς (improperly) and abusively, being more properly called mateologia (vain-talk) from Tit. 1:10, or Pseudologia (false-speech) from 1 Tim. 4:2. Wherefore we shall reckon the same among the opposites of true theology.

Prob. b. Not a few authors have distinguished theology into archetypal and ectypal, of the way and of the fatherland, natural and revealed, who have looked to the etymology and force of the word theology, according to which it is the science of God and divine things. But, if we weigh the use of the word, neither God, nor angels, nor the blessed in heaven; nor men following nature as their guide, are called theologians. Wherefore that loose signification of theology does not rest so much on the common use of speaking, as on the derivation of the word, theology.

Prob. c. Revealed theology is accurately and strictly called theology, and those who have drawn it from the written word of God are by the consent of all called theologians.

Prob. d. The Fathers of the primitive church distinguished theology and oeconomy. Thus GREGORY NAZIANZEN says: "ἄλλος ἐϰὶ λόγος τῆς θεολογίας, ἤ τῆς φύσεως, ἄλλος τῆς οἰϰονομίας," the account of theology, or of nature, is one thing, the account of oeconomy is another, in B. CHEMNITIUS de duab. nat. in Christo fol. m. 44. By theology the prelates of the first church understood the knowledge of God one and three, the mystery of the incarnation, from Heb. 3:6. D. WILHELM LYSERUS seems to have imitated them, who in system. theolog. p. 22, divides theology into theology strictly so called, anthropology, and christology.

Latin:

Sensu quadruplici. (a) Generalissime, pro quauis de Deo doctrina, licet falsa, aut erroribus mixta sit. (b) Generaliter, pro theologia vera, siue ea originalis, siue participata, siue viatorum, siue beatorum, siue naturalis, siue reuelata sit. (c) Specialiter, pro theologia reuelata, hominem viatorem ad aeternam salutem perducente. (d) Specialissime, pro doctrina de Deo vno & trino.

Prob. a. Solemne fuit ethnicis, suam longe falsissimam de Deo opinionem distinguere in theologiam mythicam, politicam & physicam, de qua prolixe agit D. HILDEBRAND in theol. dogmat. p. 2. 3. Sed falsa theologia καταχρηστικῶς & abusiue dicitur theologia, vocanda potius mateologia ex Tit. 1, 10. aut Pseudologia ex 1. Tim. IV, 2. Quamobrem nos eandem oppositis verae theologiae accensebimus.

Prob. b. Haud pauci auctores distinxerunt theologiam in archetypam, & ectypam, viae & patriae, naturalem & reuelatam, qui respexerunt etymon & vim vocis theologiae, secundum quam est scientia de Deo & rebus diuinis. At, si vsum vocis pensitemus, neque Deus, neque angeli, aut beati in caelo; neque naturam ducem sequentes homines, theologi audiunt. Quare laxa illa theologiae significatio non tam nititur communi vsu loquendi, quam deriuatioue vocis, theologia.

Prob. c. Theologia reuelata accurate & stricte nuncupatur theologia, quam qui hauserunt ex verbo Dei scripto, omnium consensu theologi appellantur.

Prob. d. Patres primitiuae ecclesiae distinxerunt theologiam, & oeconomiam. Sic GREGORIVS NAZIANZENV S inquit: "ἄλλος ἐϰὶ λόγος τῆς θεολογίας, ἤ τῆς φύσεως, ἄλλος τῆς οἰϰονομίας, alia est ratio theologiae, aut naturae, alia oeconomiae, apud B. CHEMNITIVM de duab. nat. in Christo fol. m. 44. Per theologiam antistites primae ecclesiae intellexerunt notitiam de Deo vno & trino, mysterium incarnationis, ex Hebr. III, 6. Quos imitatus esse videtur D. WILHELM. LYSERVS, qui in system. theolog. p. 22. diuidit theologiam in theologiam stricte dictam, anthropologiam & christologiam.


### Q. VII

How is true theology distinguished? Into archetypal, or original, and ectypal, or participated. Archetypal is the knowledge which God has of Himself, and which in Him is the exemplar of another, to be communicated with intelligent creatures, theology. Ectypal is called the science of God and divine things communicated by God to intelligent creatures in imitation of His own theology, as an exemplar cause.

Obj. 1. Archetype properly is the first exemplar of an effect produced in imitation of itself, and by the force of the word it imports two things: 1. An exemplar, or form, which some effect imitates from the intention of the agent: 2. A negation of dependence on another exemplar cause; as archetypal theology by the force of the word is that which is the exemplar cause of another theology, and does not itself depend on another, as on an exemplar cause.

Obj. 2. Some theologians explain archetypal and ectypal theology a little differently. D. DANNHAV. in hodof. p. m. 12, says: The distinction of theology into ἀρχέτυπον (archetype) and ἔϰτυπον (ectype) ἔκτυπον (the copy), accepted in the schools, is not accurate in every respect. For neither can the most sublime theology, by which God naturally knows Himself, be an imitable exemplar for our theology: Rather, that idea which the divine mind conceives, in order that it might be expressed in the external word as a certain and free measure of revelation, is the archetypal theology.

D. SCHERZER supports this in system. p. 2.

We prove our assertion. (1) Man was created whole in the image of God. His image, however, consisted in the knowledge of God, conformable to divine wisdom. Therefore, its ἀρχέτυπον (archetype) was the infinite wisdom of God.

(2) Fallen man is renewed into knowledge according to the image of God, Col. III, 10. Therefore, its πρωτότυπον (prototype) is divine theosophy.

For the knowledge of God and divine things, which divine revelation generates in the intellect of wayfaring men, is called by the apostle an acknowledgment according to the image of God, for no other reason than that it is expressed in imitation of the knowledge which God has of Himself and of all divine things.

You say: (1) Our theology is not conformed to the infinite theosophy by which God knows Himself, but to the idea of the mind shining forth in the written word: Therefore, its πρωτότυπον (prototype) is not the infinite theosophy by which God knows Himself from eternity, but the idea of the divine mind expressed in the written word.

Resp. Archetypal theology, considered formally, does not exclude that idea expressed in the written word, but includes it. For archetypal theology is the knowledge which God has of Himself, conceived as the idea of a theology to be communicated with intelligent creatures; which idea is originally within the bosom of the deity, and representatively in Holy Scripture. Wherefore, by means of Holy Scripture, our theology is conformed to the archetypal theology of God.

You say: (2) God did not communicate theology to intelligent creatures in imitation of His own.

For it would follow that the theology which is in man after the fall is of infinite perfection, just as the knowledge God has of Himself is infinitely perfect.

Resp. I deny it.

Consequence. For it is not necessary that the ἔκτυπον (copy) be of the same perfection as the ἀρχέτυπον (archetype), but it suffices if it represents this in a certain way according to its own capacity.

This is evident from the example of the whole man, whose holiness was expressed according to the exemplar of divine holiness, yet it was not of the same perfection as the holiness of God.

Question. VIII. Does archetypal theology also belong to Christ the God-man?

Archetypal theology belongs to Christ essentially and by nature, insofar as He is the eternal God: it belongs to Him personally and by the communication of idioms, by virtue of the personal union, according to His human nature. From which it is also called the theology of union.

Proof. (1) Because in Christ dwells the whole fullness of the deity, Col. II, 9; in Him also dwells the whole fullness of archetypal theology.

(2) Because in Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, Col. II, 3, it is validly concluded that that theosophy, which is original and ἀρχέτυπον (archetypal), has been communicated to Him.

You say: Archetypal theology is incommunicable to a creature. The human nature of Christ is a creature.

Therefore.

The major premise is clear, since archetypal theology is the infinite and immense knowledge of God, by which God knows Himself, of which a creature is by no means capable. Resp. Distinguish between a mere creature, existing outside of God, and one deified, or hypostatically united with the deity.

To the former it is incommunicable; to the latter it is truly communicated for possession and use.

Question. IX.

Latin:

In archetypam, seu originalem, & ectypam, seu participatam. Archetypa est cognitio, quam Deus de seipso habet, & quae in ipso est exemplar alterius, cum creaturis intelligentibus communicanda, theologia. Ectypa dicitur scientia de Deo & rebus diuinis cum creaturis intelligentibus a Deo ad imitationem theologiae suae, velut causae exemplaris, communicata.

Obs. 1. Archetypum proprie est primum exemplar effectus ad sui imitationem producti, & vi vocis importat duo: 1. Exemplar, siue formam, quam effectus aliquis ex intentione agentis imitetur: 2. Negationem dependentiae ab alia exemplari causa; vt theologia archetypa vi vocis fit, quae alterius theologiae causa exemplaris est, & ab alia, velut a causa exemplari, ipsa non dependet.

Obs. 2. Nonnulli theologi paulo aliter theologiam archetypam & ectypam explicant. D. DANNHAV. in hodof. p. m. 12. inquit: Distinctio theologiae in ἀρχέτυπον & ἔϰτυπον ἔκτυπον, in scholis recepta, non est usque quaque accurata. Neque enim sublimissima theologia, qua Deus seipsum naturaliter cognoscit, nostrae theologiae potest esse exemplar imitabile: Potius idea illa, quam concipit mens diuina, ut in verbo externo exprimeretur certa & libera reuelationis mensura est archetypa theologia.

Suffragatur ipsi D. SCHERZER. in system. p. 2.

Probamus assertionem nostram. (1) Homo integer conditus erat ad imaginem Dei. Imago autem ipsius consistebat in cognitione Dei, sapientiae diuinae conformi. E. eius ἀρχέτυπον fuit infinita Dei sapientia.

(2) Homo lapsus renouatur in cognitionem secundum imaginem Dei, Col. III, 10. E. illius πρωτότυπον est theosophia diuina.

Nam cognitio Dei rerumque diuinarum, quam in hominum viatorum intellectu reuelatio diuina generat, dicitur ab apostolo agnitio iuxta imaginem Dei, non alia de caussa, quam quod ad imitationem cognitionis, quam Deus de se, omnibusque rebus diuinis habet, expressa est.

Dicist: (1) Theologia nostra non ad infinitam theosophiam, qua Deus seipsum cognoscit, sed ad ideam mentis, in verbo scripto relucentem, conformatur: E. eius πρωτότυπον non est infinita theosophia, qua Deus ab aeterno seipsum cognoscit, sed idea mentis diuinae, in verbo scripto expressa.

Resp. Theologia archetypa, considerata formaliter, ideam illam, in verbo scripto expressam, non excludit, sed includit. Nam theologia archetypa est cognitio, quam Deus de seipso habet, concepta ut idea communicandae cum creaturis intelligentibus theologiae; quae idea intra sinum deitatis est originaliter, in sacra scriptura est repraesentative. Quare, mediante sacra scriptura, nostra theologia ad archetypam Dei theologiam conformatur.

Dicist: (2) Deus ad imitationem suae non communicauit cum creaturis intelligentibus theologiam.

Sequeretur enim, theologiam, quae est in homine post lapsum, infinitae esse perfectionis, sicut cognitio Dei de seipso infinite perfecta est.

Resp. Neg.

Consequ. Neque enim necesse est, ut ἔκτυπον cum ἀρχετύπῳ eiusdem sit perfectionis, sed sufficit, si hoc certo modo pro captu suo repraesentet.

Patet hoc exemplo hominis integri, cuius sanctitas expressa erat ad sanctitatis diuinae exemplar, neque tamen eiusdem erat perfectionis cum sanctitate Dei.

Quaest. VIII. Num theologia ἀρχέτυπος competit etiam Christo θεανδρώπῳ?

Theologia archetypa competit Christo essentialiter & per naturam, quatenus aeternus Deus est: competit eidem personaliter & per communicationem idiomatum, vi vnionis personalis, secundum humanam naturam. Ex quo etiam theologia vnionis dicitur.

Prob. (1) Quia in Christo habitat tota plenitudo deitatis, Col. II, 9. in eodem etiam habitat tota plenitudo theologiae archetypae.

(2) Quia in Christo absconditi sunt omnes thesauri sapientiae & scientiae, Col. II, 3. valide colligitur, theosophiam illam, quae originalis & ἀρχέτυπος est, ipsi esse communicatam.

Dicist: Theologia archetypa creaturae est incommunicabilis. Humana Christi natura est creatura.

E.

Maior liquet, quoniam theologia archetypa est infinita & immensa scientia Dei, qua Deus seipsum cognoscit, cuius creatura minime capax est. Resp. Dist. inter creaturam meram, existentem extra Deum, & θεωθεῖσαν, siue hypostatice vnitam cum deitate.

Illi est incommunicabilis, huic ad possessionem & vsurpationem vere communicata est. sive hypostatice unitam cum deitate. Illi est incommunicabilis, huic ad possessionem & vfurpationem vere communicata est.

Quæft. IX.


### Question IX. How many kinds of theology are there, an image of human beings after the fall?

The theology of men after the fall is of one kind for the way, or for travelers, and of another for the fatherland, or for those who have attained. The former is of men, who in this world are journeying away from the Lord, and who know God imperfectly through certain means (a). The latter is of the blessed, who know God immediately and perfectly (b).

Observation. It is not relevant here to consider the ἔκτυπος (derived) theology of the human nature of Christ, of angels, and of whole men before the fall; because that doctrine pertains partly to the place concerning Christ, partly to the place concerning angels, and partly to the place concerning the image of God.

Proof a. 2 Cor. V, 6, 7. Therefore we are confident and knowing that while we dwell in the body, we are journeying away from the Lord, for we walk by faith, not by sight. The mind of the apostle is: since the Holy Spirit, who is the earnest of heavenly life, has been given to us, we do not lose heart, although the way of this life, hedged about as it were with the thorns of calamities, must be run by us not without many troubles, but we are of good courage as long as we dwell in the tent of this body, journeying away from the Lord, i.e., alienated from the beatific vision of God, and as it were absent abroad. For we spiritual travelers direct the course of our life and actions through the eye of faith, which is of τῶν μὴ βλεπομένων (things not seen), Hebr. XI, 1. But in the kingdom of glory we shall walk with Christ according to sight, that is, we shall have our Jesus visibly present, about to see him face to face, 1 Cor. XIII, 12; 1 John III, 2.

Proof b. from 1 Cor. XIII, 12. We see now through a mirror in a riddle, but then face to face: now I know in part, but then I shall know, even as I have been known. The apostle hints that the theology of travelers, compared with the theology of the blessed, is imperfect, not evident, and joined with the difficulty of learning. For just as those who look at the images of corporeal things in a mirror see them imperfectly: so in this life we obtain a certain thin knowledge of God and divine things, drawn from the revealed word, if it be compared to the far more perfect theosophy of eternal life. And as every riddle is a speech that is obscure, knotty, involved, and difficult to understand: so our theology, by reason of its object, is not evident, embracing most profound mysteries, and in this mortality very difficult to know. The theology of the fatherland, on the contrary, will be perfect, immediate, and intuitive. Just as God knows us most perfectly; so in the heavenly fatherland we in turn shall know God perfectly: he indeed with a divine and infinite perfection; but we not with an infinite one, but a finite one, and yet nonetheless complete in its own kind, as much indeed as can fall to a rational creature.

Latin:

Theologia hominum post lapsum alia est viæ, siue viatorum, alia est patriæ, siue comprehensorum. Illa est hominum, in hoc mundo a domino peregrinantium, & Deum per certa media imperfecte cognoscentium (a). Hæc est beatorum, Deum immediate & perfecte cognoscentium (b).

Obseru. Nil attinet hic considerare theologiam ἔκτυπον humanæ Christi naturæ, angelorum, & hominum integrorum ante lapsum; eo, quod doctrina ista partim ad locum de Christo, partim ad locum de angelis, partim ad locum de imagine Dei pertinet.

Prob. a. 2. Cor. V, 6. 7. Confidentes igitur (sumus) & scientes, quod dum habimus in corpore, peregrinemur a Domino, per fidem enim ambulamus, non per speciem. Mens apostoli est: quoniam spiritus sanctus, qui est arrhabo vitæ cælestis, nobis datus est, non despondemus animum, licet via huius vitæ, calamitatum quasi spinis obsæpta, nobis non sine multis molestiis sit decurrenda, sed bono animo sumus, quamdiu in tentorio huius corporis habitamus, a domino peregrinantes, i. e. a visione Dei beatifica alieni, & quasi peregre absentes. Etenim nos spirituales viatores dirigimus cursum vitæ & actionum nostrarum per oculum fidei, quæ est τῶν μὴ βλεπομένων, Hebr. XI, 1. In regno autem gloriæ ambulabimus cum Christo secundum speciem, hoc est, visibiliter præsentem Iesum nostrum habebimus, de facie ad faciem ipsum visuri, 1. Cor. XIII, 12. 1. Io. III, 2.

Prob. b. ex 1. Cor. XIII, 12. Videmus nunc per speculum in ænigmate, tunc vero a facie ad faciem: nunc cognosco ex parte, tunc vero cogniturus sum, sicut cognitus sum. Innuit apostolus, theologiam hominum viatorum, comparatam cum theologia beatorum, esse imperfectam, ineuidetem, & cum difficultate discendi coniunctam. Quemadmodum enim res corporeas imperfecte asspiciunt, qui earum imagines in speculo intuentur: ita in hac vita tenuem quandam de Deo & rebus diuinis cognitionem, ex verbo reuelato haustam consequimur, si ad longe perfectiorem vitæ æternæ theosophiam conferatur. Et vt omne ænigma est sermo obscurus, nodosus, inuolutus, intellectu difficilis: ita nostra theologia ratione obiecti est ineuidens, complectens mysteria profundissima, & in hac mortalitate cognitu difficillima. Theologia patriæ, contra, erit perfecta, immediata & intuitiua. Sicut Deus nos cognoscit perfectissime; ita in cælesti patria nos vicissim Deum perfecte cognoscemus: ille quidem perfectione diuina & infinita: nos vero non infinita, sed finita, atque nihilominus in suo genere completa, quanta quidem in creaturam rationalem cadere potest.


### Question X. The theology of the blessed is called the theology of the comprehenders, since the blessed have attained the desired goal of…

The theology of the blessed is called the theology of those who have attained, since the blessed have reached the desired goal of perfect knowledge concerning God.

Proof. The words of Paul gave occasion for this denomination, Phil. III, 12. Not that I have already apprehended, or am already made perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend (the Vulgate has: comprehend) that for which I am apprehended of Christ. The discourse of the apostle is concerning the saving knowledge of Christ. The pseudo-apostles arrogated to themselves a full knowledge of Christ, contending that it was enough that Christ was known, since no one is ignorant that Christ is the true Messiah, the expiator of past sins. Paul holds the opposite opinion to them, who, although he had known Jesus remarkably, yet denies that he had reached that goal of perfect knowledge, so that he was in need of no progress; but rather the apostle says that he will strive with all his might, so that he may embrace with his whole mind Jesus, who died and rose again for him, just as by

had been apprehended on the way to Damascus, that is, acknowledged, called, converted, and drawn into the way of salvation. From which it is plain that St. Paul did not speak directly of the θεογνωσία [knowledge of God] of the blessed: yet because he had asserted that he strives to apprehend Christ, i.e., to know Him perfectly, the scholastic doctors called the theology of the homeland the theology of the comprehenders, because the blessed know God perfectly.

Obs. (1) The comprehensive knowledge of God is taken in a broader sense, and sometimes in a stricter sense. The comprehensive knowledge of God, spoken of more broadly, is that by which God and whatever is in God, formally pertaining intrinsically to His essence and attributes, is known clearly, distinctly, and immediately. It is also called the theology of vision, because by its power the blessed know God, as He is in Himself, as clearly and distinctly as corporeal things are known when they fall into the eyes and are seen, the denomination being taken from the words of Christ: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God, Matt. V, 8. The comprehensive knowledge of God, spoken of more strictly, is that by which God is adequately known, and whatever is not only formally in God, but also virtually or eminently from Him, or whatever can be produced by God, or depend on Him in any way. Thus no creature comprehends God, who is plainly incomprehensible.

Obs. (2) Just as the theology of the blessed is called intuitive, because they know God immediately, as He is in Himself: so the theology of travelers is called abstractive, because they do not know God immediately in Himself, but mediately in another, namely, either in an effect, or in the revealed word, as in a mirror.

Latin:

Theologia beatorum vocatur theologia comprehensorum, quoniam beati desideratam perfectæ cognitionis de Deo metam consecuti sunt.

Prob. Occasionem huic denominationi dederunt verba Paullina, Phil. III, 12. Non quod iam apprehenderim, aut iam consummatus sim: persequor tamen, si etiam apprehendam (vulgata habet: comprehendam) in quo apprehensus a Christo sum. Sermo est apostolo de salutifera Christi cognitione. Pseudo-apostoli plenam Christi cognitionem sibi arrogabant, contendentes, satis esse, Christum cognitum, cum nemo nesciat, Christum esse verum Messiam, præteritorum peccatorum expiatorem. Quibus aduersam Paullus tenet sententiam, qui licet egregie cognouisset Iesum, negat tamen se eam perfectæ notitiæ metam attigisse, vt profectu nullo indigeat; sed potius se summa ope nixurum dicit apostolus, vt Iesum, pro se mortuum & resuscitatuin, tota mente complectatur, sicut a

Christo in via Damascena comprehensus, id est, agnitus, vocatus, conversus et in viam salutis pertractus erat. Ex quibus palam est, S. Paulum directe non locutum esse de θεογνωσία beatorum: quoniam tamen assuerat, se contendere, ut Christum comprehendant, i. e. perfecte cognoscat, doctores scholastici theologiam patriae vocarunt theologiam comprehensorum, eo quod beati Deum perfecte cognoscunt.

Obs. (1) Comprehensiva Dei scientia modo latiori, modo strictiori sensu accipitur. Latius dicta comprehensiva Dei scientia est, qua Deus et quidquid in Deo est, formaliter ad essentiam et attributa eius intrinsece pertinens, clare, distincte et immediate cognoscitur. Dicitur etiam theologia visionis, quod eius vi beati Deum, ut in se est, tam clare et distincte cognoscant, quam clare et distincte cognoscuntur res corporeae, cum in oculos incurrunt et videntur, denominatione desumta ex verbis Christi: Beati mundi corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt, Matth. V, 8. Strictius dicta comprehensiva Dei scientia est, qua adaequate cognoscitur Deus et quidquid non tantum in Deo est formaliter, sed etiam ab eo est virtualiter aut eminenter, sive quidquid a Deo produci, aut ullo modo dependere potest. Sic nulla creatura comprehendit Deum, plane incomprehensibilem.

Obs. (2) Sicut theologia beatorum vocatur intuitiva, quoniam Deum immediate, ut in se est, cognoscunt: ita theologia viatorum appellatur abstractiva, quia Deum non immediate in se cognoscunt, sed mediate in alio, nempe vel in effectu, vel in verbo revelato, tanquam speculo.


### Question XI. How many-fold is the theology of travelers?

The theology of travelers is twofold: natural and revealed. The former is that by which God becomes known both from innate notions and from the intuition of created things. The latter is the knowledge concerning God and divine things, which God communicates to men who are travelers, either through immediate revelation, or inspiration ; or through mediate revelation, or the divine word, consigned to letters .

Obs. (1) Natural theology will be treated more accurately below in the locus on God.

Obs. (2) It is called revealed theology, not from general revelation, or any manifestation whatsoever, through the utterances of God conspicuous in the kingdom of nature, concerning which Paul says in Rom. I, 19: Τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ, that which is known of God, is manifest in them. For God has manifested it to them; but from special revelation, by which things either not knowable by the guidance of nature are manifested, or things naturally knowable are declared in a supernatural way. Concerning this the Savior says: Matt. XI, 27. No one knows the Son, except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father, except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal Him.

Prob. a. God revealed, or inspired, theology immediately to the prophets in the Old Testament and the apostles in the New. For, as St. Peter testifies, 2 Ep. c. I, 21, holy men of God spoke being moved (φερόμενοι) by the Holy Spirit. Where note, (1) that the word φέρειν in the cited place does not signify to carry, but to act, to move, to impel, to moderate. For those things are called φερόμενα by the Greeks which are driven by a certain impetus. Whence φορὰ denotes an impetus. Compare CRAUSER'S Phosphorus p. 432. Moreover, that φορὰ embraces both the internal illumination of the mind and the suggestion of those things which are to be said or written, and the external motion, so that the tongue or the pen acted no less than the mind by that impulse, whatever it did; and not only were the matter or the things suggested, but also the words were placed into the mouth, or dictated to the pen, for the prophets and apostles by the Holy Spirit. See D. CALOVIUS in the illustrated Bibles on this passage f.

b. Because all scripture is θεόπνευστος, divinely inspired 2 Tim. III, 16. Through it, God and divine things are revealed to us for saving knowledge, worship, and use.

Latin:

Theologia viatorum est duplex, naturalis, et revelata. Illa est, qua Deus tum ex notitiis insitis, tum ex intuitu rerum creatarum innotescit. Haec est notitia de Deo et rebus divinis, quam Deus vel per immediatam revelationem, sive inspirationem ; vel per revelationem mediatam, seu verbum divinum, litteris consignatum, hominibus viatoribus communicat .

Obs. (1) De theologia naturali infra in loco de Deo accuratius agetur.

Obs. (2) Theologia revelata dicitur, non a revelatione generali, seu qualicunque manifestatione, per effata Dei in regno naturae conspicua, de qua Paullus Rom. I, 19. inquit: Τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ quod de Deo cognoscitur, manifestum est in ipsis. Deus enim ipsis manifestavit; sed a revelatione speciali, qua res vel ductu naturae non cognoscibiles manifestantur, vel naturaliter cognoscibiles supernaturali modo declarantur. De hac inquit salvator: Matth. XI, 27. Nemo cognoscit filium, nisi pater, neque patrem quisquam cognoscit, nisi filius, et cui filius voluerit revelare.

Prob. a. Prophetis in veteri, et apostolis in novo testamento Deus theologiam immediate revelavit, sive inspiravit. Nam teste S. Petro 2. Ep. c. I, 21. a Spiritu S. impulsi (φερόμενοι) locuti sunt sancti Dei viri. Vbi notes, (1) quod verbum φέρειν loco citato non significet portare, sed agere, mouere, impellere, moderari. Nam φερόμενα Graecis dicuntur, quae impetu quodam aguntur. Vnde φορὰ impetum notat. Confer CRAVSERI Phosphorum p. 432. Complectitur autem illa φορὰ tum illuminationem mentis internam et suggestionem eorum, quae dicenda vel scribenda sunt, tum externam motionem, vt non minus lingua vel calamus, quam animus impulsu isto egerit, quidquid egit; neque materia tantum vel res suggestae sint, sed etiam verba in os posita, vel dictata in calamum sint prophetis et apostolis a spiritu sancto. Vid. D. CALOVII in bibl. illustratis in h.l. f.

Prob. b. Quia tota scriptura est θεόπνευστος, divinitus inspirata 2 Tim. III, 16. eadem mediante, Deus & res divinae ad salutarem notitiam, cultum & usum nobis revelantur.


### Q. XII. In how many ways is revealed theology considered?

Revealed theology is considered (1) systematically, as it is a doctrine through which theologians are made: (2) habitually, insofar as it is a habit from which theologians are denominated.

Theology, viewed systematically and secondarily, is a doctrine concerning God, informing the wayfaring man from the divine word, concerning the true worship of God through Christ, unto eternal life. Theology, considered habitually and primarily, was defined above in the response to Q. 1, and is now to be weighed more exactly.

Latin:

Consideratur theologia revelata (1) systematice, prout est doctrina, per quam fiunt theologi: (2) habitualiter, quatenus est habitus, a quo theologi denominantur.

Theologia, systematice & secundario spectata, est doctrina de Deo, hominem viatorem, e verbo divino, de vero Dei per Christum cultu, ad vitam aeternam informans. Theologia, habitualiter & primario considerata, supra in responsione ad quaest. 1. est definita, nunc exactius ponderanda.


### Question XII. In how many ways is revealed theology considered?

Theology is wisdom, because it is an excellent science concerning God and divine things, which are most worthy and most difficult to be known . It is an eminent wisdom, since it is far superior to all human wisdom . It is a practical wisdom, because all its conclusions, if not formally, certainly virtually and ultimately tend toward practice.

Prob. a. Wisdom, considered generally, is an excellent science, which, since it deals with abstruse, arduous, and most excellent things, most diligently searches out the first and highest principles of its own forum, as D. Leichner defines in On True Good Philosophy , p. 16. One may also add the definition of wisdom which D. Calov provides in Divine Metaphysics , p. 147. Wisdom in common, considered precisely and abstractly, is a discursive habit joining together the knowledge of principles with the knowledge of conclusions, whatever those principles may be, whatever those conclusions may be . (He does indeed add τὸ θεωρητικὸν [the theoretical], saying: provided it rests ultimately in that cognition. But we judge that τὸ θεωρεῖν [theorizing], or resting ultimately in cognition, pertains to the material reasons of wisdom, not to its formal reason.) But theology is a discursive habit, which most diligently searches out the first principles of its own forum, and accurately demonstrates its conclusions from them, and treats of the sublime and arduous mysteries of faith. Therefore, theology is wisdom.

Prob. b. Theology is an eminent wisdom, because its principle is not per se and naturally evident, but exceeds the sphere of nature and reason, namely, divine revelation. With respect to which principle, revealed theology is called a θεόδοτος [God-given] habit, given divinely, not as if it were immediately infused, but because its principle is not human reason, but divine revelation. Therefore, revealed theology is called wisdom, coming from above, James III, 15. Wisdom of God in a mystery, and hidden, because it is full of difficult mysteries, and hidden from reason left to itself.

Prob. c.

That theology is a practical wisdom, is evident: (1) Because the intermediate end of theology is true faith in Christ, whose twofold energy is: internal, by which it apprehends Christ with his benefits; external, by which it brings forth good works, the fruits of righteousness. The ultimate end of theology is external blessedness, which consists not only in the intuitive knowledge of God, but also in the enjoyment of the same.

(2) Because theology is concerned with man not theoretically, insofar as he is the subject of demonstration: just as in physics affections are demonstrated concerning man; but insofar as he is the subject of operation, or in as much as the sinner is to be liberated from his misery, and transferred into a most blessed state.

(3) Because theology uses the most effective means of salvation, the word and sacraments, which are divinely ordained for promoting the practice of faith and piety.

(4) Because all the duties of the theologian are carried out for spiritual practice, whether he teaches the divine word, or dispenses the sacraments, or exhorts to the exercises of virtues, or calls away from the filthiness of vices, or soothes fearful consciences with divine consolation.

(5) Because St. Paul himself defines theology by the knowledge of the truth, which is according to godliness, .

Antithesis The antithesis is (1) of the ancient Scholastics, (2) of the modern Pontificians, who define theology, some by doctrine, some by theoretical habit, some by mixed habit, whose arguments we shall weigh.

(1) Theology is taught and learned.

Therefore, theology is doctrine or discipline. Resp.

Theology, considered systematically and secondarily, is taught and learned. Therefore, considered systematically and secondarily, it is doctrine or discipline: I concede.

But the question is concerning theology considered habitually and in the primary sense.

(2) Not all the requirements of wisdom belong to theology. For it is the mark of wisdom to be concerned with all things, to be most apt for teaching, to command inferior disciplines, to confirm conclusions from the first principles of knowing, and to establish certain orders of things. Resp.

(1) generally, I distinguish between eminent wisdom and common wisdom. Although not all the requirements of common wisdom belong to theology absolutely and simply, it suffices that they belong to theology analogically, as to an eminent wisdom.

(2) Specifically (a) theology teaches all things in the upper hemisphere, as metaphysics does in the lower hemisphere: it teaches all things that are contained in the law and the gospel: it teaches all things, because it generally considers the creator and creatures.

(b) Theology is most apt for teaching.

For it teaches from what principles the salvation of the sinner flows, and by what means he may become a partaker of salvation. (c) Theology, as a queen, commands inferior disciplines, bringing them together with the human intellect under the obedience of faith and taking captive every thought, .

From which it happens that true philosophy keeps itself within the sphere of the light of nature and its own object; but being humbly observant of theology, it is its faithful handmaid.

(d) Theology recalls its conclusions to the first principle: Whatever the first truth has revealed, that is infallibly certain.

(e) Those orders which you discover in the humble house of metaphysics, you will find the same, but far more sublime, in the vast kingdom of theology.

Metaphysics delivers the order of substances and accidents: Theology in just order delivers the distinction of law and gospel, of faith and good works. .

(3) Wisdom is a theoretical habit.

Theology is not a theoretical habit.

Therefore, theology is not wisdom. The major premise is established, since wisdom, intelligence, and science are commonly considered to be theoretical habits. R. I deny the major. For wisdom, considered in general and abstractly, is an excellent science concerning the most exalted things, tracing its conclusions back to the first principles of its own sphere, whether those principles be theoretical or practical. There is given a σοφία [wisdom], or moral φιλοσοφία [philosophy], which is without doubt practical. For the σοφίαν [wisdom] which the ancient Greeks called, Pythagoras, the author of the Italian sect, called φιλοσοφίαν [philosophy]. See LEICHN. de v. philosoph. bono, p. 30.

Latin:

Theologia est sapientia, quia est praecellens scientia de Deo & rebus divinis cognitu dignissimis difficillimisque . Est sapientia eminens, quoniam omni humana sapientia est longe superior . Est sapientia practica, quia omnes eius conclusiones si non formaliter, certe virtualiter & ultimato ad praxin tendunt.

Prob. a. Sapientia, generatim considerata, est praecellens scientia, quae cum agat de rebus abstrusis, arduis atque praestantissimis, prima & summa sui fori principia enixissime rimatur, definiente D. Leichnero de vera philosophia bona p. 16. Addere etiam licet definitionem sapientiae, quam tradit D. Calov. in metaphysica divina p. 147. Sapientia in communi, praecise & abstracte considerata, est habitus discursivus cum notitia principiorum simul conjungens notitiam conclusionum, quaecunque ea sint principia, quaecunque ea sint conclusiones . (Addit quidem τὸ θεωρητικὸν, inquiens: modo in ista cognitione ultimato sistatur. Sed τὸ θεωρεῖν, sive in cognitione ultimato conquiescere, nos censemus pertinere ad rationes sapientiae materiales, non ad eius rationem formalem.) Atqui theologia est habitus discursivus, qui prima sui fori principia enixissime rimatur, & ex iis conclusiones suas accurate demonstrat, atque de sublimibus & arduis fidei mysteriis agit. E. Theologia est sapientia.

Prob. b. Theologia est sapientia eminens, quia eius principium non est per se & naturaliter evidens, sed sphaeram naturae & rationis excedens, nempe revelatio divina. Respectu cuius principii theologia revelata dicitur habitus θεόδοτος, divinitus datus, non quasi sit immediate infusus, sed quia principium eius non est humana ratio, verum divina revelatio. Idcirco theologia revelata vocatur sapientia, superne veniens, Iac. III, 15. Sapientia Dei in mysterio, & abscondita, quia mysteriis arduis est plena, & rationi, sibi relictae, abscondita.

Prob. c.

Theologiam esse sapientiam practicam, patet: (1) Quia finis theologiae intermedius est vera in Christum fides, cuius duplex est ἐνέργεια: interna, qua Christum cum ipsius beneficiis apprehendit; externa, qua bona opera, fructus iustitiae, parit. Finis theologiae ultimus est externa beatitudo, quae non tantum in intuitiva Dei cognitione, sed etiam in eiusdem fruitione consistit.

(2) Quia theologia versatur circa hominem non theoretice, quatenus est subiectum demonstrationis: quemadmodum in physicis affectiones de homine demonstrantur; sed quatenus est subiectum operationis, seu in quantum peccator a miseria sua liberandus, & in statum beatissimum transferendus est.

(3) Quia theologia utitur efficacissimis salutis mediis, verbo & sacramentis, quae ad praxin fidei & pietatis promouendam diuinitus ordinata sunt.

(4) Quia omnia munia theologi spirituali praxi expediuntur, siue verbum diuinum doceat, siue sacramenta dispenset, siue ad virtutum exercitia cohortetur, siue a vitiorum turpitudine auocet, siue pauidas conscientias diuino solatio permulceat.

(5) Quia ipse S. Paullus theologiam definit per cognitionem veritatis, quae est secundum pietatem, .

Antithesis Antithesis est (1) antiquorum Scholasticorum, (2) hodiernorum Pontificiorum, quorum quidem per doctrinam, quidam per habitum theoreticum, quidam per habitum mixtum, theologiam definiunt, quorum argumenta expendemus.

(1) Theologia docetur & discitur.

E. Theologia est doctrina vel disciplina. Resp.

Theologia, systematice & secundario considerata, docetur & discitur. E. systematice & secundario considerata, est doctrina, vel disciplina: concedo.

At quaestio est de theologia habitualiter & sensu primario considerata.

(2) Non omnia requisita sapientiae conueniunt theologiae. Nam sapientiae est, versari circa omnia, esse ad docendum aptissimam, inferioribus disciplinis imperare, conclusiones e primis cognoscendi principiis confirmare, ac certos rerum ordines constituere. Resp.

(1) generatim dist. inter sapientiam eminentem, & vulgarem. Quamuis non omnia requisita vulgaris sapientiae theologiae absolute & simpliciter conueniant, sufficit, quod theologia, tanquam sapientiae eminenti, conueniant analogice.

(2) Speciatim (a) theologia omnia docet in hemisphaerio superiori, vti metaphysica in hemisphaerio inferiori: docet omnia, quae in lege & euangelio continentur: docet omnia, quia generatim considerat creatorem & creaturas.

(b) Theologia aptissima est ad docendum.

Docet enim, ex quibus principiis salus peccatoris fluat, & per quae media salutis compos fieri queat. (c) Theologia velut regina inferioribus disciplinis imperat, redigens easdem vna cum intellectu hominis sub obsequium fidei & captiuans πᾶν νόημα, .

Ex quo fit, vt vera philosophia sese contineat intra naturae luminis, obiectique proprii sphaeram; theologiae autem demisse obseruans, fidelisque ancilla sit.

(d) Theologia suas conclusiones ad primum reuocat principium: Quidquid veritas prima reuelauit, illud infallibiliter certum est.

(e) Quos ordines in humili casa metaphysices deprehendis, eosdem etiam, sed longe sublimiores reperies in latissimo regno theologiae.

Metaphysica tradit ordinem substantiarum & accidentium: Theologia iusto ordine tradit discrimen legis & euangelii, fidei & bonorum operum. .

(3) Sapientia est habitus theoreticus.

Theologia non est habitus theoreticus. E.

Theologia non est sapientia. Maior constat, quoniam sapientia, intelligentia & scientia vulgo censentur esse habitus theoretici. R. Neg. mai. Nam sapientia in communi & abstractive considerata est scientia eximia de rebus praestantissimis, conclusiones suas revocans ad prima fori sui principia, sive illa principia sint theoretica, sive practica. Datur σοφία, vel φιλοσοφία moralis, quae citra dubium practica est. Quam enim σοφίαν Graeci prisci vocarunt, Pythagoras Italicae sectae auctor φιλοσοφίαν appellauit. Vid. LEICHN. de v. philosoph. bono. p. 30.


### Question XII. In how many ways is revealed theology considered?: Instance I

Instance I.

If theology is a science, it is certainly not wisdom, since they are distinct habits. R. There is a distinction between wisdom and science, not real, but formal, since wisdom is a species of science, as man is an animal .

Instance II.

Practical wisdom seems to be an unusual way of speaking. I answer with the words of D. WILHELM LYSER, an accurate theologian, in System. p. 12, saying: "But if we wish to accommodate theology to Aristotelian habits, different opinions occur there. For some call it science on account of its certainty; others wisdom on account of its dignity; others intelligence on account of the knowledge of principles; others, and indeed the majority, call it practical wisdom, because it renders a man wise in such a way that he can also communicate it to others." Therefore, that manner of speaking is not unusual, but in the judgment of the blessed Lyser, it is used by most theologians. Compare DIAC. MARTIN, de constit. theol. p. 81 et seqq., and D. GERHARD, in the prooemio exeg. theolog. prefixed, p. 2.

Instance III.

Theology can be generically defined by prudence, which by the concession of all is a practical habit. R. Prudence is concerned with singulars and contingents, as Aristotle testifies in Book 1 of the Ethics, ch. VI. But theology is concerned with universals and necessaries. For it considers any sinner whatsoever in general, insofar as eternal salvation is to be conferred upon him through universal and necessary means.

Instance IV.

To avoid all difficulties, theology can be defined by a practical habit. R. By a practical habit, the nature of theology is not declared as much as is sufficient. For sometimes by a practical habit, according to the usage of speech, is understood that which is the proximate principle of practice or operation, and which, through prior deliberation in the particular, prescribes to the will what is fitting or not fitting to do here and now: sometimes by a practical habit is understood that which is a remote principle of practice, and which, through universal conclusions in general, prescribes what is fitting to do or not to do. In this latter sense, theology is indeed a practical habit; but a practical habit is a remote genus, by which the dignity of theology is not expressed as it ought to be. But if you define theology by practical wisdom, you immediately intimate that it deals with sublime and arduous matters, and is therefore a far more excellent habit.

4. Whatever discipline is occupied with the knowledge of God, that is not practical. But theology, etc. Therefore. The major is evident, because God does not fall under human practice, but is known by man only speculatively. R. (a) Distinguish between the general object of the consideration of theology, and the special object of operation. The former, and indeed the inadequate and primary one, is God; the latter is the sinner to be saved. (b) Distinguish between γνῶσιν [knowledge], or cognition, and θεωρίαν [theory], or speculation. Γνῶσις [knowledge] is partly theoretical, partly practical. We know God not speculatively, but practically, so that we may fix all our trust in Him, and be carried entirely into His love and worship.

5. In practical science all conclusions are practical. In theology not, etc. E. The minor is proved, because in theology there are given contemplative conclusions, e.g., God is good, omnipotent, etc. The world is created. There are given good and evil angels. R. Theological conclusions are either formally or virtually practical. Those are [formally practical] which formally and directly prescribe some operation pertaining to the worship of God, to the exercising of which man is obligated. e.g., God is to be invoked, the needy neighbor is to be relieved. Those are [virtually practical] which indeed do not formally prescribe an action pertaining to the worship of God; yet they do much within the scope of theology to infer practical conclusions. e.g., God is good. E. He is to be loved. The world is created. E. The creator is to be celebrated. There are given good angels as guardians of men. E. With them present, nothing evil is to be perpetrated. Learnedly says GERHARD in exeg. p. 2: All things which are treated in theology look to practice, if not immediately, yet directly, mediately, and indirectly.

6. Theology as archetype is speculative. E. And theology as ectype. The reason for the consequence is because the latter agrees with the former, as an image with its exemplar. R. Theology as archetype, considered formally, is practical; for it imports an act of the practical intellect, by which God conceives the knowledge of Himself as the form of another theology to be communicated with creatures.

7. A practical discipline considers what things are in our power (ἐφ' ἡμῖν). Theology is not, etc. E. The major is evident from ARISTOTLE, Lib. 1 ad Nicomach. c. 6. The minor is clear, because all theology depends upon the illumination of the Holy Spirit. Eph. 1, 17. R. Distinguish between a practical discipline that is human or common, and one that is divine or eminent. The object of the former are things in our power (τὰ ἐφ' ἡμῖν), of the latter are divine things (τὰ θεῖα), God and divine matters. 8. The formal end of theology, namely the beatific vision of God, is not practice: therefore revealed theology does not seem to be practical, since every habit has this appellation, by which it is called practical, from its end. R. The ultimate end of theology is not only the vision of the intellect, but also fruition, by which the will most fully perceives the goodness of God and is most abundantly satisfied. But that fruition is practice.

9. Theology is concerned with things to be believed and things to be done. E. It is a mixed habit, partly theoretical, partly practical. R. To believe does not mean to speculate, but to apply to oneself the grace of God obtained by the merit of Christ. There is given, therefore, a twofold practice, of faith and of piety. The former is the fiducial application of the grace of God founded in the merit of Christ and promised in the gospel. The latter is the study of good works, and it flows from the former, as a ray from the sun and a stream from the fountain.

Latin:

Instantia I.

Si theologia est scientia, vtique non est sapientia, cum sint distincti habitus. R. Datur discrimen inter sapientiam, & scientiam non reale, sed formale, quoniam sapientia est scientiae species, vt homo animalis .

Instantia II.

Sapientia practica videtur esse formula loquendi insolens. Respondeo verbis, D. WILHELMI LYSERI, accurati theologi, in System. p. 12. inquentis: Quod si theologiam ad habitus Aristotelicos accommodare velimus, ibi diuersae occurrunt sententiae. Alii enim scientiam propter certitudinem; alii sapientiam propter dignitatem; alii intelligentiam propter notitiam principiorum; alii & plerique sapientiam practicam dicunt, quia ita hominem reddit sapientem, vt aliis etiam eam communicare possit. Est ergo illa loquendi ratio non insolens, sed iudice b. Lyfero a plerisque theologis usurpata. Confer. DIAC. MARTINI de constit. theol. p. 81. & seqq. & D. GERHARD. in prooemio exeg. theolog. praefixo, p. 2.

Instantia III.

Potest theologia generice definiri per prudentiam, quae omnium concessu est habitus practicus. R. Prudentia versatur circa singularia & contingentia, teste Aristotele Libr. 1. Eth. c. VI. At theologia versatur circa vniuersalia & necessaria. Considerat enim, peccatorem quemcunque in genere, quatenus per media vniuersalia & necessaria in eundem aeterna salus conferenda est.

Instantia IV.

Ad euitandum omnes difficultates, theologia per habitum practicum definiri potest. R. Per habitum practicum natura theologiae non pro eo, ac satis est, declaratur. Nam interdum per habitum practicum ex vsu loquendi intelligitur, qui praxeos siue operationis principium propinquum est, & voluntati praeuia deliberatione in particulari, quae hic & nunc agere conueniat, aut non conueniat, praescribit: interdum per habitum practicum intelligitur, qui principium praxeos remotum est, & mediantibus conclusionibus vniuersalibus in genere, quae agere aut non agere conueniat, praescribit. Quo posteriori sensu theologia quidem habitus practicus est; at habitus practicus est genus remotum, quo dignitas theologiae non pro eo, ac decet, exprimitur. Sed si definieris theologiam per sapientiam practicam, confestim innuis, eam de rebus sublimibus & arduis agere, adeoque habitum longe praestantissimum esse.

4. Quaecunque disciplina occupata est in cognitione Dei, illa non est practica. Atqui theologia &c. E. Maior constat, quia Deus sub praxin humanam non cadit, sed ab homine speculatiue tantum cognoscitur. R. (a) Dist. inter obiectum generale considerationis theologiae, & inter obiectum speciale operationis. Illud & quidem inadaequatum ac primarium est Deus; hoc est peccator saluandus. (b) Dist. inter γνῶσιν, feu cognitionem, & θεωρίαν, seu speculationem. Γνῶσις partim theoretica, partim practica est. Cognoscimus nos Deum non speculatiue, sed practice, vt fiduciam omnem in eo defigamus, & in amorem cultumque eius toti feramur.

5. In scientia practica omnes conclusiones sunt practicae. In theologia non &c. E. Minor probatur, quia in theologia dantur conclusiones contemplabiles v. gr. Deus est bonus, omnipotens &c. Mundus est creatus. Dantur angeli boni & mali. R. Conclusiones theologicae sunt vel formaliter, vel virtualiter practicae. Illae sunt, quae formaliter ac directe praescribunt operationem aliquam ad cultum Dei pertinentem, ad quam exercendam homo obligatur. v. gr. Deus est invocandus, proximus egenus est sublevandus. Hae sunt, quae formaliter quidem non praescribunt actionem ad cultum Dei pertinentem; multum tamen faciunt intra ambitum theologiae ad inferendas conclusiones practicas. v. gr. Deus est bonus. E. Est amandus. Mundus est creatus. E. creator est celebrandus. Dantur angeli boni hominum custodes. E. illis praesentibus nil mali perpetrandum est. Scite inquit GERHARD. in exeg. p. 2. Omnia, quae in theologia tractantur, ad praxin spectant, si non immediate, directe tamen mediate & indirecte.

6. Theologia ἀρχέτυπος est speculativa. E. & theologia ἔκτυπος. Ratio consequentiae est, quia haec cum illa convenit, vt imago cum exemplari. R. Theologia ἀρχέτυπος formaliter considerata est practica; importat enim actum intellectus practicum, quo cognitionem sui Deus concipit, vt formam alterius cum creaturis communicandae theologiae.

7. Disciplina practica considerat, quae sunt ἐφ' ἡμῖν, in nostra potestate. Theologia non &c. E. Maior patet ex ARISTOT. Lib. 1. ad Nicomach. c. 6. Minor liquet, quia tota theologia pendet ab illuminatione spiritus sancti. Eph. 1, 17. R. Dist. inter disciplinam practicam humanam seu vulgarem, & diuinam seu eminentem. Illius obiectum sunt τὰ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, huius sunt τὰ θεῖα, Deus & res diuinae. 8. Theologiae finis formalis, nempe visio Dei beatifica non est praxis: Theologia igitur reuelata non videtur esse practica, cum omnis habitus hanc appellationem, quod practicus dicitur, habeat a fine. R. Theologiae finis vltimus non est tantum visio intellectus, sed & fruitio, qua voluntas bonitatem Dei plenissime percipit, & abundantissime satiatur. Sed illa fruitio est praxis.

9. Theologia versatur circa credenda & agenda. E. est habitus mixtus partim theoreticus, partim practicus. R. credere non significat speculari, sed gratiam Dei merito Christi conciliatam sibi applicare. Datur igitur duplex praxis, fidei & pietatis. Illa est fiducialis gratiae Dei in merito Christi fundatae, & in euangelio promissae applicatio. Haec est studium bonorum operum, & fluit ex illa, vt radius e sole & riuulus e fonte.


### Question XIV. Is theology an infused habit, or an acquired one?

Theology is not a habit immediately infused , but is a habit acquired, indeed by our acts, but elicited by the illumination of the Holy Spirit . Prob. a. Habits immediately infused are conferred in a moment, all at once. Thus the apostles in a moment were made theologians to speak the great works of God in various languages, when on the feast of Pentecost the Holy Spirit was poured out upon them. Acts II, 11. But this gift was extraordinary, the state of those times so requiring, in which the gospel was to be promulgated throughout the whole world. Prob. b. Today there is need of doctrine, meditation, and assiduous labor, so that the habit of theology may be acquired. Since, however, it is not drawn from the principles of reason, but rests entirely upon divine revelation, our intellect, being dim toward spiritual things, needs divine illumination so that it may know God and divine matters. On that account theology is called a God-given (θεόδοτος) habit, not not as if it were conferred upon us by God immediately without any study of our own, but because its principle is divinely given to us, and theology is acquired by the gracious illumination of the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

Theologia non est habitus immediate infusus , sed est habitus comparatus, nostris actibus quidem, sed illuminatione spiritus sancti elicitus . Prob. a. Habitus immediate infusi in momento toti simul conferuntur. Sic apostoli in momento effecti sunt theologi ad loquendum variis linguis magnalia Dei, cum in festo pentecostes Spiritus S. in eos effunderetur. Act. II, 11. Sed hoc donum erat extraordinarium, exigente sic illorum temporum statu, quo euangelium per totum terrarum orbem promulgandum erat. Prob. b. Hodie doctrina, meditatione & assiduo labore opus est, vt habitus theologiae acquiratur. Cum autem ille non hauriatur ex principiis rationis, sed totus reuelationi diuinae innitatur, intellectus noster ad spiritualia caligans illuminatione diuina indiget, vt Deum & res diuinas cognoscat. Id propter theologia dicitur habitus θεόδοτος, non quasi citra omne nostrum studium a Deo immediate nobis conferatur, sed quia tum principium eius divinitus nobis datum est, tum theologia gratiosa spiritus S. illuminatione comparatur.


### Q. XV. Who is the author of theology?

The author of theology is God (a) the Father (b), the Son (c), and the Holy Spirit (d).

Prob. a. Theology is wisdom coming from above. James 3:15. It is called coming from above because it descends from the Father of lights, i.e., of all light, whether it be the light of nature, or the light of grace, or the light of glory, James 1:17.

Prob. b. The God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, gives us the spirit of wisdom and revelation for the knowledge of Him. Eph. 1:17. God the Father sends the Holy Spirit into our hearts to that end, that He may imprint upon our minds the revealed wisdom by which God is known, i.e., theology.

Prob. c. No one knows the Father except the Son and he to whom the Son wills to reveal Him. Matt. 11:27. No one knows the Father comprehensively except the Son of God because of the ὁμοουσίαν (consubstantiality), and no one aspires to the revealed θεογνωσίαν (knowledge of God) unless his mind is illuminated by the revelation of the Son of God.

Prob. d. No one can call Christ Lord except by the Holy Spirit; 1 Cor. 12:3. No one acknowledges Christ the Lord, the foundation of all theology, and worships Him rightly, unless he is taught by the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

Auctor theologiae est Deus (a) pater (b), filius (c) & spiritus sanctus (d).

Prob. a. Theologia est sapientia superne veniens. Iac. III, 15. Dicitur superne veniens, quia descendit a patre luminum, i. e. omnis luminis, sive fit lumen naturae, sive lumen gratiae, sive lumen gloriae, Iac. I, 17.

Prob. b. Deus Domini nostri Iesu Christi, pater gloriae dat nobis spiritum sapientiae & revelationis ad agnitionem sui. Eph. I, 17. Deus pater eo fine mittit in corda nostra spiritum S. vt imprimat mentibus nostris sapientiam revelatam, qua Deus cognoscitur, i. e. theologiam.

Prob. c. Patrem nemo cognoscit, nisi filius & cui voluerit filius revelare. Matth. XI, 27. Nemo comprehensive cognoscit patrem, nisi filius Dei ob ὁμοουσίαν, & ad θεογνωσίαν revelatam nemo adspirat, nisi revelatione filii Dei mens eius illustretur.

Prob. d. Christum nemo potest dominum dicere sine spiritu sancto; 1 Cor. XII, 3. Christum dominum, totius theologiae fundamentum nemo agnoscit, & rite colit, nisi doceatur a spiritu sancto.


### Q. XVI. Of what does the whole system of theology consist?

The whole of theology, considered systematically, consists of theological truths, that is, of principles or conclusions, known from the supernatural revelation of God, or to be deduced.

Prob. Every theological truth is either demonstrating or to be demonstrated. A demonstrating truth is a proposition more known and more certain, from which another less known and doubtful thing is made known and proven, and it is called a principle in analytics; a truth to be demonstrated is a question, or conclusion, which, since it is not sufficiently clear or is called into doubt, must be made known and proven through an argument of demonstrations. Now, whatever is proposed in theology is either a question, and consequently a conclusion, or a principle of demonstrating.

Latin:

Tota theologia, systematice considerata, constat ex veritatibus theologicis, hoc est, ex principiis, aut conclusionibus, ex supernaturali Dei revelatione cognitis, aut deducendis.

Prob. Omnis veritas theologica vel est demonstrans, vel demonstranda. Veritas demonstrans est propositio notior & certior, e qua alia minus nota & dubia notificatur & evincitur, atque vocatur in analyticis principium; veritas demonstranda est quaestio, sive conclusio, quae cum vel non satis liquido constet, vel in dubium vocetur, per argumentum demonstrationum notificanda & evincenda est. Iam vero quidquid in theologia proponitur vel quaestio est, & consequenter conclusio, vel principium demonstrandi.


### Question XVI. Of what does the entire system of theology consist?

Theology generally considers God and divine things, insofar as they have been revealed by the First Truth to sinful man for believing and acting (a). Specifically, it teaches by what principles and means man as a wayfarer, corrupted by sin, is to be led to eternal salvation (b).

Prob. a. Whatever the entire scope of theology embraces, they are either things to be believed, as articles of faith: or things to be done, as good works, to which evil works, as things to be avoided, are opposed. Those things which are to be done and to be believed are the material object of theology, or the object of consideration; therefore, because the whole of theology is occupied in considering, explaining, and bringing these forward, and they are comprehended under the one name of the Christian religion. The formal object is sought from the revelation of the First Truth, or God most truthful. Wherefore, things to be believed and done are weighed in theology insofar as they have been revealed by God most truthful, or made manifest by the light of supernatural revelation, which for the present state of the church is Scripture θεόπνευστος, or divinely inspired, inasmuch as it testifies of itself, with the Holy Spirit concurring, through its inherent efficacy, and from which all theological assertions are deduced and confirmed.

Prob. b. The special object of theology (which in practical disciplines is also called the subject of operation) is man the sinner, insofar as he is to be saved eternally. For (1) in practical habits, of which class theology also is, the subject of operation is that into which, through certain principles and means, the ultimate end of the practical discipline itself is to be introduced. But man subject to sin is to be led to eternal salvation through certain principles and means. (2) Everything that is treated in theology can be recalled to the saving of man the sinner. For they either constitute man the sinner, or pertain to his end, namely eternal salvation, as principles of salvation and means, or the consequences of these. (3) This special object distinguishes theology revealed to us sinners (a) from paradisiacal theology, the object of which was man whole, or immune from sin. (b) From contemplative philosophy, in which the nature of man is viewed according to natural principles and inherent affections. (c) From practical philosophy, in which man is considered as to be made happy civilly. Only revealed theology considers man the sinner, to be led to eternal blessedness through supernatural principles and means.

Latin:

Theologia generatim considerat Deum, & res divinas, quatenus a prima veritate revelatae sunt homini peccatori ad credendum, & agendum (a). Speciatim docet, quibus principiis & mediis homo viator, peccato corruptus, ad aeternam salutem fit perducendus (b).

Prob. a. Quaecunque universus theologiae ambitus complectitur, vel sunt credenda, vt articuli fidei: vel sunt agenda, vt bona opera, quibus mala opera, vt fugienda, opponuntur. Quae agenda & credenda sunt, sunt obiectum theologiae materiale, sive obiectum considerationis; ideo quod tota theologia in iis considerandis, explicandis, afferendis occupatur, & vno religionis christianae nomine comprehenduntur. Obiectum formale petitur a revelatione veritatis primae, sive Dei veracissimi. Quamobrem credenda & agenda in theologia expenduntur, quatenus a Deo veracissimo sunt revelata, sive manifesta supernaturalis revelationis lumine, quod pro hodierno ecclesiae statu est scriptura θεόπνευστος, sive divinitus inspirata, quippe quae de seipsa, concurrente spiritu sancto, per insitam efficaciam testatur, & ex qua omnes assertiones theologicae deducuntur, & confirmantur.

Prob. b. Obiectum speciale theologiae (quod in disciplinis practicis etiam dicitur subiectum operationis) est homo peccator, quatenus aeternum salvandus. Etenim (1) in habitibus practicis, e quorum censu etiam est theologia, subiectum operationis est, in quod per certa principia & media ultimus ipsius disciplinae practicae finis introducendus est. Atqui homo peccato obnoxius per certa principia & media ad aeternam salutem perducendus est. (2) Ad hominem peccatorem salvandum omnia, quae in theologia tractantur, revocari possunt. Nam vel constituunt hominem peccatorem, vel ad eius finem, sive aeternam salutem pertinent, vt principia salutis & media, aut horum consequentia. (3) Distinguit hoc obiectum speciale theologiam nobis peccatoribus divinitus revelatam (a) a theologia paradisiaca, cuius obiectum erat homo integer, sive a peccato immutunis. (b) A philosophia contemplativa, in qua spectatur natura hominis secundum principia naturalia & affectiones insitas. (c) A philosophia practica, in qua consideratur homo civiliter beandus. Sola theologia revelata considerat hominem peccatorem, per principia & media supernaturalia ad aeternam beatitudinem perducendum.


### Quaest. XVIII. What is the end of theology, for the sake of which the theologian operates?

The ultimate objective end of theology is God, infinitely perfect and supremely good (a). The ultimate formal end is the beatific vision and fruition of God (b). The internal intermediate end is the leading of the sinner to saving faith (c). The external intermediate end is true faith in Christ (d). Which is followed by the holiness of life in an inseparable connection (e).

Prob. a. God, infinitely perfect and supremely good, most fully satisfies the appetite of man; since before his face is the fullness of joys, and pleasures at his right hand. Ps. 16: 11. And thus God is the objective end of theology; since he is that object to which the sinner is to be led by the theologian.

Prob. b. from Ps. 17: 15. But I in righteousness will behold thy face: I shall be satisfied, when I awake with thy likeness. The sacred psalmist joins satiety with the vision of God, because our appetite in the heavenly fatherland will perceive most solid joys from the intuition of the most glorious divine majesty, and thus will enjoy the supreme good according to its desire. This vision and fruition of God is called the formal end, because through it we enjoy, are satisfied by, and acquiesce in God, as the supreme good.

Prob. c. The internal end of theology is sought from the operation of the theologian, which is the leading of the sinner to saving faith: from which internal end the specific difference of theology is taken.

Prob. d. (1) Whatever is the intermediate end of Holy Scripture, the same is the intermediate end of theology. For just as Holy Scripture and theology have the same material and formal object: so also the end of both is one and the same. Since whatever Holy Scripture teaches under divine revelation: that theology teaches, explains, and defends under divine revelation, nor for any other end than that for which the things themselves, God revealing, were committed to writing, and to which they themselves tend by their own nature, or from the benevolent will of God revealing. But the intermediate end of Holy Scripture is faith resting on the merit of Christ. This is what two apostles teach, John and Paul: the former indeed in the evangelical history ch. 20: 31. Saying these things, these things were written, (a) The end of theology (a) God infinitely perfect and supremely good (b) The ultimate formal end (c) The internal intermediate end are, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life through His name. And here in 2 Tim. 2:15, where he bears witness to his Timothy, that from infancy he has known the scriptures, and adds: which are able to make you wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
