Both men, θεόπνευστοι [God-breathed], join eternal salvation and faith in Christ as two subordinate ends, and to the latter they attribute the nature of an intermediate end, and to the former that of the ultimate end.

(2) By the intermediate end of theology is understood that means of salvation by which we attain the ultimate end, or eternal blessedness. But we attain it through faith, which I show thus: By that means by which we miserable sinners are reconciled to God and receive the remission of sins, so that we have God as propitious, by that same means we attain eternal blessedness. But by true faith, leaning upon the merit of Christ, we are reconciled to God, etc. Therefore.

The major is confirmed by the royal Psalmist and Paul in Ps. 32:1-2 and Rom. 4:7-8: Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom God does not impute sin. The minor is established by the apostles Peter and Paul: the former in Acts 10:43: To Him all the prophets witness, that through His name, whoever believes in Him receives remission of sins: the latter in Rom.

3:24-25: We are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus: whom God set forth as a propitiation by faith in His blood. From which it is concluded that saving faith is the means of reconciliation with God, the intermediate end of theology strictly so called, as the organic cause of attaining eternal blessedness.

Prob. c. That faith, which has justified, exerts itself through consequent charity and the pursuit of good works, Paul teaches in Gal. 5:6: In Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love. Faith fixed upon the merit of Christ, which availed to justify the sinner, does not remain sterile or idle, but works through love, sanctifies the justified man, and restores in him the image of God. Whence love toward God and neighbor, the holiness of life, and the restoration of the divine image follow faith in Christ in an inseparable bond, and thus pertain to the consequences of the intermediate end of theology, but they are not causes of attaining eternal blessedness.

There are some authors who call holiness of life the concomitant intermediate end of theology, with D. JOH. MUSAEUS in Introduct. theol. p. 135, or the secondary end with D. HILDEBRAND in theol. dogmat. p. 21, or the non-causal intermediate end with D. BAIER in compend. theol. p. 39. With these we shall not litigate, since they confess that they take the end of theology in a broader sense.

Latin:

Finis theologiae ultimus obiectivus est Deus, infinite perfectus & summe bonus (a). Finis ultimus formalis est beatifica Dei visio & fruitio (b). Finis intermedius internus est perductio peccatoris ad fidem salvificam (c). Finis intermedius externus est vera in Christum fides (d). Quam indiuulso nexu sequitur sanctimonia vitae (e).

Prob. a. Deus infinite perfectus, & summe bonus appetitum hominis plenissime satiat; siquidem coram ipsius facie est satietas gaudiorum, & amoenitates ad dextram eius. Ps. XVI, 11. Adeoque Deus est finis theologiae obiectivus; quoniam est obiectum illud, ad quod a theologo perducendus est peccator.

Prob. b. ex Ps. XVII, 15. Ego vero iustitia videbo facies tuas: saturabor, cum evigilauero imagine tua. Coniungit hieropsaltes cum visione Dei satietatem, quia appetitus noster in patria coelesti solidissima percipiet gaudia ex intuitu maiestatis divinae gloriosissimae, atque adeo ex voto perfruetur summo bono. Quae visio & fruitio Dei beatifica vocatur finis formalis, quia per eam Deo, ceu summo bono, fruimur, satiamur & acquiescimus.

Prob. c. Finis internus theologiae petitur ab operatione theologi, quae est perductio peccatoris ad fidem salvificam: a quo fine interno sumitur differentia speciatim theologiae.

Prob. d. (1) Qui finis intermedius est sacrae scripturae, idem est finis intermedius theologiae. Quemadmodum enim sacra scriptura & theologia idem habent obiectum materiale & formale: ita & finis vtriusque vnus & idem est. Quippe quae sub diuina reuelatione docet S. scriptura: ea docet, explicat & defendit theologia sub reuelatione diuina, nec fine alio, quam quo res ipsae, deo reuelante, in litteras relatae sunt, & ad quem ipsaeinet suapte natura, siue ex Dei reuelantis beneuola voluntate tendunt. At finis intermedius S. scripturae est fides merito Christi innixa. Id quod docent duo apostoli, Ioannes & Paullus: ille quidem in historia euangelica cap. XX, 31. Haec inquiens, scripta sunt, Hæc inquiens, scripta sunt, ut credatis, Iesum esse Christum filium Dei, & ut credentes vitam habeatis per nomen ipsius. Hic vero in 2 Tim. II, 15. vbi Timotheo suo testimonium perhibet, quod ab infantia litteras nouerit, & subiungit: quæ te possunt sapientem reddere in salutem per fidem, quæ in Christo Iesu est. Ambo viri θεόπνευστοι salutem æternam & fidem in Christum, tanquam duos fines subordinatos, coniungunt, & huic, intermedii, illi vitimi finis rationem tribuunt.

(2) Per finem theologiæ medium intelligitur illud salutis medium, quo finem vltimum, seu æternam beatitudinem consequimur. Atqui consequimur eam per fidem, quod sic ostendo: Quo medio nos miseri peccatores Deo reconciliamur, & remissionem peccatorum accipimus, vt Deum habeamus propitium, eo medio æternam beatitudinem consequimur. Atqui vera fide, innixa merito Christi, Deo reconciliamur &c. Ergo.

Maiorem confirmant Psaltes regius & Paullus Ps. XXXII, 1. 2. Rom. IV, 7. 8. Beati, quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates, & quorum occultata sunt peccata. Beatus, cui non imputat Deus peccatum. Minorem stabiliunt Petrus & Paullus apostoli:

ille Act. X, 43. De Christo testimonium perhibent omnes prophetæ, quod remissionem peccatorum accipiat per nomen ipsius omnis, qui credit in ipsum: hic Rom. III, 24. 25. Iustificamur gratis gratia ipsius per redemptionem, quæ est in Christo Iesu: quem proposuit Deus propitiatorium per fidem in ipsius sanguine. E quibus conficitur, fidem saluificam esse medium reconciliationis cum Deo, stricte dictum finem medium theologiæ, velut caussam organicam consequendæ æternæ beatitudinis.

Prob. c. Fidem, quæ iustificauit, se exserere per consequentem charitatem, studiumque bonorum operum, docet Paullus Gal. V, 6. In Christo Iesu neque circumcisio quidquam valet, neque præputium, sed fides dilectionem operans. Fides defixa in Christi merito, quæ ad iustificandum peccatorem valuit, non manet sterilis aut otiosa, sed operatur per dilectionem, sanctificat hominem iustificatum, atque in eodem imaginem Dei instaurat. Vnde dilectio in Deum & proximum, vitæ sanctimonia & instauratio imaginis diuinæ fidem in Christum indiuideo nexu sequuntur, atque adeo ad consequentia finis intermedii theologiæ pertinent, sed non sunt caussæ consequendæ æternæ beatitudinis.

Sunt nonnulli auctores, qui sanctitatem vitæ vocant theologiæ finem medium concomitantem cum D. IO. MVSAEO in introduct. theol. p. 135. vel finem secundarium cum D. HILDEBRANDO in theol. dogmat. p. 21. vel finem intermedium non caussalem cum D. BAIERO in compend. theol. p. 39. Cum quibus non litigabimus, cum illi fateantur, se finem theologiæ in sensu latiori accipere.


### Q. XIX

Who is a theologian?

A theologian in the general sense is called a man instructed by the theological habit, by which he is rendered prompt to explain and defend heavenly truth (a). In a special and more excellent sense (*) a theologian is called a man reborn, offering an unmoved assent to the First Truth revealing the mysteries of faith, and leaning upon it with special trust, apt to teach others and to refute those who contradict (b). Prob. a.

(1) A theologian is so called from the theological habit, just as a logician is named from the logical habit. The apostle confirms this assertion of ours in Heb. 5:14, describing the theologian as one who by reason of habit has senses exercised to discern both good and evil.

(2) A theologian is said in a looser sense to be one who duly performs the office of a theologian by explaining, confirming, and defending theological truths, even if he is devoid of sincere holiness of will.

Prob. b. (1) In a more eminent sense, a theologian is said to be one who truly shows himself to be such as he ought to be according to the intention of the Holy Spirit. For if a civil orator is commonly described as a good man skilled in speaking aptly and ornately, whose moral virtues the most learned Mr. KIRCHMAIER recounts in his Synopsis orator. p. 36, why should a theologian not be defined as a man regenerated and renewed by the Holy Spirit, apt to teach and to refute those who contradict? For in a definition it is permitted to express the idea of a good and perfect theologian.

(2) Just as a bishop, so also a theologian must be irreproachable. Tit. I, 7.

(3) A regenerated theologian assents to the primary truth revealing itself more readily and more solidly than a privatively unregenerated theologian. For although the latter is not rarely endowed with a more distinguished knowledge of theological matters than the former, yet the regenerated one offers a special and fiducial assent to the word of the most truthful God, so that he rests in it entirely; but the hypocrite offers a general, not a special and fiducial, assent to the divine word. Compare D. QVENSTED. theol. didactico polem. part. IV. fol. 284.

Obs. An unregenerate person is a man devoid of true faith in Christ, and he is either negatively or privatively unregenerate. Negatively and simply unregenerate is he who has never been led to conceive faith in Christ, neither through baptism nor through the preaching of the gospel, such as is a Gentile, a Turk, a Tartar, a Jew, neither baptized nor regenerated through the proposition and explanation of the divine word. Privatively and in a certain respect unregenerate is he who was truly regenerated and endowed with saving faith, but through deliberate sins made shipwreck of his faith: who, by pretending to be truly regenerated, plays the hypocrite; he confesses that he knows God, but denies Him by his deeds. Tit. I, 16. Compare D. SONTAGII Fanaticism. pag. 37.

Quæst. XX. Is piety to be cultivated by a theologian with the utmost zeal?

A true theologian should cultivate piety with his whole heart, sincere and without guile.

Prob. D. HÜLSEMANN says excellently in his Method of Theological Study annexed to the method of preaching, p. 254: Piety toward God and neighbor is necessary above all in a future theologian, 1 Tim. IV, 7. 8. For this is the foundation upon which the whole structure must be imposed. If anyone wishes to do the will of my Father, he shall know of my doctrine, whether it be of God, are the words of Christ, Jo. VIII, 17. Conf. 1 Jo. II, 3. Sir. XXXII, 20. For it is not to be thought that theology is only a habit of the mind, or an apprehension of knowable things, such as the devils have; but that it is a practical habit, which ought to be used by the knower for the benefit of his own soul and the souls of others. Such a thing does not enter a malicious soul, and a body subject to sin. Sap. I, 4. Those who are to treat sacred things must be cleansed in heart and body from the filth of sins. Exod. XL, 12, 31. 32. For the word of God is a consuming fire to those who approach burning with the strange fire of desires. Lev. X, 1. 2. And such bells, sounding for others but not for themselves, 1 Cor. XIII, 1, have long since been cursed by God. Ps. L, 16. sqq. D. QVENSTED delivers similar things in his theolog. didact. tom. I. fol. 16. Those who are theologians in fact and in name, i. e., who are not only instructed in the theological habit, as such, but are at the same time regenerated, or faithful and pious, in them theology is not only from the Holy Spirit, but also with the Holy Spirit, and joined with his gracious indwelling.

Quæst. XXI. What kind of theological knowledge does a faithful and pious theologian have?

…The theological knowledge of a truly regenerated and renewed theologian is not merely literal, such as that of an unregenerate man, who through voluntary and reigning sins falls from the state of grace (a); but it is spiritual, applied to spiritual use, and joined with spiritual and pious movements of the heart (b).…

The distinction of theological knowledge into literal and spiritual is of no small importance, provided it is explained correctly.

Far be it from us to maintain with the fanatics that spiritual theological knowledge proceeds either from the immediate illumination of the Holy Spirit, or from the internal light of the soul, or from reminiscence, through introversion into the inner chambers of the soul, or that it only knows the mystical sense!

We know that the literal sense (logically so called) of biblical sayings is intended by the Holy Spirit directly and immediately through the θεοπνεύστοις (God-breathed) words.

For this reason, that knowledge is called literal theological knowledge which, in investigation, development, and cognition, is not transferred to the use intended by the Holy Spirit.

Spiritual theological knowledge is that by which the literal sense of biblical sayings is transferred to the use intended by the Holy Spirit, and produces spiritual and pious movements of the heart.

Proof a. Christ says: love your enemies Matt.

V, 44.

A theologian burning with hatred for his enemy perceives the literal sense of the Savior's words, but his knowledge is not translated into the living practice intended by Christ, nor is his heart affected by love for his enemy (which is a pious movement, or affection, of the heart).

His knowledge is therefore merely literal, of which Christ says in Luke

XII, 41.

The servant &c. Proof b.

Knowledge of divine things is called spiritual (1) by reason of its origin; because it is elicited from Holy Scripture through the full and perfect (for the state of this life) illumination of the Holy Spirit.

(2) By reason of its object, because it receives τὰ τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ Θεοῦ, which are the things of the Spirit of God.

1 Cor.

II, 14.

(3) By reason of its subject, because it is in a soul reborn through the Holy Spirit.

(4) By reason of its end, intended and obtained by the Holy Spirit, because it is translated to the use ordained by the Holy Spirit.

(5) By reason of the spiritual and pious movements of the heart, of which it is fruitful.

You say: Literal theological knowledge is also spiritual, since (1) its principle of knowing (the divine word) is spiritual.

(2) It proceeds from the imperfect illumination of the Holy Spirit, since the light of the Holy Spirit is joined in an individual connection with Holy Scripture.

From which SEB.

SCHMIDIUS in his later biblical collegium says p. 164. The animal man, considered absolutely, is such that he does not receive or grasp the things that are of the Spirit of God: meanwhile, the ψυχικὸς (natural man) can subjectively be spiritual, who understands something of those things which are of the Spirit of God, not indeed as such, but as already imperfectly illuminated by the Spirit of God.

(3) It is destined or ordained by the intention of the Holy Spirit for salutary use.

Response

Spiritual theological knowledge, contradistinguished from literal knowledge, is taken here in a stricter sense, as we have clearly shown.

But if anyone, because of the reasons adduced, wishes to call the literal knowledge of Holy Scripture spiritual in a broader sense, and κατά τι (in a certain way), according to something, or in a certain respect, we shall have no quarrel with him.

But the knowledge of divine things is called strictly and simply spiritual which is not only drawn from the word of God, but also arises from the full and perfect illumination of the Holy Spirit, sufficient for faith in Christ, and is not only destined for salutary use, but is also applied and translated in the very act.

This is joined with spiritual and pious movements of the heart, e.g., with trust in Christ, love and fear of God, charity toward one's neighbor, desire for heavenly goods; flight from sins, contempt for the vanities of this world, etc.

It is called by St. Paul σοφία καὶ σύνεσις πνευματική, spiritual wisdom and understanding Col.

I, 9.

To which may the candidate of theology, anticipated by the Holy Spirit, aspire and strive with the greatest contention of soul: for this is living θεογνωσία (knowledge of God), apprehending Christ, the life of the soul, and showing itself alive in practice: this is salutary in a complete second act, because it brings salvation to a soul anxiously panting for its sins and for divine grace: whence it is called γνῶσις τῆς σωτηρίας (knowledge of salvation) Luke

I, 77. which makes all believers before God θεοδιδάκτους (taught by God), and not And it makes not only wise, but also just. See Is. LIII, 11. Jer. IX, 23. 1 Cor. I, 30. John VI, 44, 47. This is practical and effective knowledge, consisting more in affection than in cognition, of which Paul says; 1 Cor. VIII, 2, 3. If anyone thinks he knows anything, he does not yet know anything as he ought to know: but if anyone loves God, he is known by Him. Conf. 1 John II, 4.

Latin:

XIX. Quis est theologus?

Theologus sensu generali dicitur homo instructus habitu theologico, quo promtus redditur ad veritatem cælestem explicandam & defendendam (a). Sensu speciali & excellentiori (*) theologus dicitur homo renatus, veritati primæ, mysteria fidei reuelanti, immotum præbens assensum, eique speciali fiducia innitens, aptus ad docendum alios, & ad redarguendum contradicentes (b). Prob. a.

(1) Ab habitu theologico dicitur theologus, sicut ab habitu logico nominatur logicus. Confirmat hoc nostrum assertum apostolus Hebr. V, 4. describens theologum, quod per habitum exercitatos sensus habeat ad diiudicationem boni & mali.

(2) Theologus sensu laxiori dicitur, qui munus theologi rite obit, veritates theologicas explicando, confirmando & defendendo, quamvis sincera voluntatis sanctitate destituatur.

Prob. b. (1) Eminentiori sensu theologus dicitur, qui re vera talem se præstat, qualis ex intentione spiritus sancti esse debet. Quod si enim orator civilis vulgo describitur, quod sit vir bonus apte ornateque dicendi peritus, cuius virtutes morales recenset doctiss. Dn. KIRCHMAIER. in synopsi orator. p. 36. quidni theologus definiatur per virum a spiritu S. regenitum, atque renovatum, aptum ad docendum, & ad redarguendum contra dicentes. Nam in definitione ideam boni & perfecti theologi exprimere fas est.

(2) Sicut episcopum, ita & theologum oportet esse irreprehensibilem. Tit. I, 7.

(3) Theologus renatus promtius & solidius primæ veritati revelanti assentitur, quam theologus privatiue irregenitus. Nam licet hic haud raro insigniori imbutus sit notitia rerum theologicarum, quam ille: attamen regenitus assensum specialem & fiducialem verbo Dei veracissimi præbet, vt eodem prorsus acquiescat: at hypocrita verbo diuino præstat assensum generalem, 'non specialem ac fiducialem. Confer D. QVENSTED. theol. didactico polem. part. IV. fol. 284.

Obs. Irregenitus est homo veræ in Christum fidei expers, estque vel negatiue, vel priuatiue irregenitus. Negatiue & simpliciter irregenitus est, qui nunquam ad fidem in Christum concipiendam, neque per baptismum, neque per prædicationem euangelii perductus est, qualis est Ethnicus; Turca, Tartarus, Judæus nec baptizatus, nec per propositionem & explicationem verbi diuini renatus. Priuatiue & secundum quid irregenitus est, qui fuit vere regeneratus, & salutifera fide donatus, per peccata autem proæretica fidei naufragium fecit: qui simulando se esse vere renatum, hypocritam agit: confitetur se Deum nosse, sed factis abnegat Tit. I, 16. Confer D. SONTAGII Fanaticism. pag. 37.

Quæst. XX. Estne theologo pietas summo studio colenda?

Verus theologus toto pectore colat pietatem sine fuco sinceram.

Prob. Præclare ait D. HÜLSEMANN. in methodo studii theologici methodo concionandi annexa p. 254. Necessaria est ante omnia in futuro theologo pietas erga Deum & proximum, 1 Tim. IV, 7. 8. Hæc enim est fundamentum, cui tota structura imponenda est. Si quis voluerit facere voluntatem patris mei, is cognoscet de doctrina mea, an sit ex Deo, sunt verba Christi Io. VIII, 17. Conf. 1 Io. II, 3. Sir. XXXII, 20. Nec enim putandum, theologiam esse tantum mentis habitum, seu apprehensionem rerum scibilium, qualem diaboli habent; sed esse habitum practicum, qui debeat a sciente ad suæ & aliarum animærum emolumentum adhiberi. Eiusmodi non ingreditur animam malignam, & corpus peccato subiectum. Sap. I, 4. Sacra tractaturos oportet corde & corpore a sorde peccatorum ablutos esse. Exod. XL, 12, 31. 32. Est enim verbum Dei ignis consumens eos, qui peregrino cupiditatum igne æstuantes accedunt. Leu. X, 1. 2. Atque eiusmodi tintinnabula aliis, non sibi ipsis sonantia, 1 Cor. XIII, 1. iam olim a Deo maledicta sunt. Ps. L, 16. sqq. Gemina his tradit D. QVENSTED. in theolog. didact. tom. I. fol. 16. Qui re & nomine theologi sunt, i. e. qui non tantum habitu theologico, vt sic, instructi, sed simul renati sunt, siue fideles & pii, in illis theologia non tantum a spiritu S. sed etiam cum spiritu S. est, & cum gratiosa eius inhabitatione coniuncta.

Quæst. XXI. Qualis est notitia theologica fidelis atque pii theologi?

Theologi vere renati atque renouati theologica notitia non est mere litteralis, qualis est hominis irregeniti, qui per peccata voluntaria & regnantia e statu gratiae excidit (a); sed est spiritualis, ad usum spiritualem applicata, & cum spiritualibus, piisque cordis motibus coniuncta (b).

Distinctio notitiae theologicae in literalem, & spiritualem, haud exigui est momenti, modo dextre explicetur.

Absit, vt statuamus cum fanaticis, notitiam theologicam spiritualem aut ex immediata spiritus S. illuminatione, aut ex interna animae luce, vel reminiscentia, per introuersionem in penetralia animae proficisci, aut eandem tantum sensum mysticum cognoscere!

Nouimus, sensum dictorum biblicorum literalem (logice ita dictum) verbis θεοπνεύστοις a spiritu S. proxime & immediate intendi.

Quam ob rem notitia theologica litteralis dicitur, quae in inuestigatione, euolutione & cognitione non ad usum a spiritu S. intentum transfertur.

Notitia theologica spiritualis est, quo sensus dictorum biblicorum litteralis ad usum a spiritu S. intentum transfertur, & spirituales piosque cordis motus parit.

Prob. a. Christus ait: diligite inimicos vestros Matth.

V, 44.

Theologus odio flagrans inimici sui, sensum litteralem verborum saluatoris perspicit, sed ipsius notitia ad viuam praxin a Christo intentam non traducitur, neque cor ipsius dilectione inimici (quae est pius cordis motus, vel affectus) afficitur.

Est itaque eiusdem notitia mere litteralis, de qua Christus inquit Luc.

XII, 41.

Seruus &c. Prob. b.

Notitia rerum diuinarum spiritualis dicitur (1) ratione originis; quia e S. scriptura per illuminationem spiritus S. plenam perfectamque (pro statu huius vitae) elicitur.

(2) Ratione obiecti, quia τὰ τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ Θεοῦ, quae sunt Spiritus Dei, suscipit.

1 Cor.

II, 14.

(3) Ratione subiecti, quia est in anima per spiritum S. renata.

(4) Ratione finis, a spiritu S. intenti & obtenti, ideo, quod ad usum a spiritu S. ordinatum traducitur.

(5) Ratione spiritualium & piorum cordis motuum, quorum facunda est.

Dicis: Notitia theologica litteralis etiam est spiritualis, quoniam (1) eius principium cognoscendi (verbum diuinum) spirituale est.

(2) Ex illuminatione spiritus S. imperfecta proficiscitur, cum lumen spiritus S. indiuiduo nexu cum S. scriptura coniunctum fit.

Ex quo SEB.

SCHMIDIVS in colleg. bibl. poster. inquit p. 164. Homo animalis absolute consideratus talis est, vt nihil suscipiat, vel capiat eorum, quae sunt Spiritus Dei: interim ψυχικὸς subiectiue potest esse spiritualis, qui aliquid intelligit eorum, quae sunt Spiritus Dei, non quidem qua talis, sed qua iam a spiritu Dei imperfecte illuminatus.

(3) Ex intentione spiritus S. ad usum salutarem destinata, vel ordinata est.

Resp.

Notitia theologia spiritualis, notitiae litterali contradistincta, sensu strictiori hic sumitur, sicut luculenter ostendimus.

Quod si quis, ob adductas rationes, notitiam S. scripturae litteralem sensu latiori, & κατά τι, secundum quid, vel certo respectu spiritualem appellare velit, cum illo nobis lis nulla erit.

At notitia rerum diuinarum stricte & simpliciter spiritualis dicitur, quae non tantum hauritur ex verbo Dei, sed etiam ex plena perfectaque Spiritus S. illuminatione, ad fidem in Christum sufficiente, oritur, & ad usum salutarem non tantum destinata est, sed & actu ipso applicatur & traducitur.

Haec coniuncta est cum spiritualibus & piis cordis motibus, v. gr. cum fiducia in Christum, amore & timore Dei, charitate proximi, desiderio bonorum coelestium; fuga peccatorum, contemptu vanitatum huius seculi &c.

Dicitur a S. Paulo σοφία καὶ σύνεσις πνευματική, sapientia & intelligentia spiritualis Col.

I, 9.

Ad quam candidatus theologiae, a spiritu S. praeuentus, summa animi contentione adspiret & connitatur: haec enim est θεογνωσία viua, Christum, vitam animae, apprehendens, & in praxi se viuam ostendens: haec est salutaris actu secundo completo, quia anima anxie de peccatis suis, & gratiani diuinam anhelanti salutem affert: vnde γνῶσις τῆς σωτηρίας dicitur Luc.

I, 77. quae coram Deo omnes credentes θεοδιδάκτους, & non & non tantum sapientes, sed etiam iustos facit. Vid. Es. LIII, 11. Ier. IX, 23. 1 Cor. I, 30. Io. VI, 44. 47. Hæc est notitia practica, & effectiua, magis in affectu, quam cognitione consistens, de qua Paullus ait; 1 Cor. VIII, 2. 3. Si quis videtur sibi scire aliquid, nondum quidquam scit, sicut decet cognoscere: sed si quis amat Deum, ac ipso cognitus est. Conf. 1 Io. II, 4.


### Q. XXII. What is the nature of the knowledge of God and divine things in the intellect of an unregenerate man, who has been imperfectly

The knowledge of God and divine mysteries in the intellect of an unregenerate man, imperfectly and as it were pedagogically illuminated by the Holy Spirit through the Holy Scripture, is not absolutely spiritual, but literal (a). Which literal knowledge is not natural or carnal, but supernatural (b), and can be considered and called spiritual in a certain way and in a certain respect (c).

The antithesis is (1) of the Schwenckfeldians and Weigelians, who maintain that all knowledge of God and divine things drawn from the Holy Scriptures, whether by a regenerate or an unregenerate man, is literal, natural, and carnal. For thus writes SCHWENCKFELD in his treatise on Holy Scripture, fol. 7: No one will draw the Spirit or spiritual wisdom from the dead letter, no one will obtain heavenly light from the Scripture, nor grasp the living truth from the image, just as no one can fetch heaven from the earth. WEIGEL in his Postilla, Part I, p. 130, says: The knowledge of Christ, or saving faith, is not a Christian human science, since they learn their faith from men, whereas it must be learned from God. (2) Of other mystics. For HOBURG in his mystical Postilla, Part II, p. 287, says: From outward conviction through the outward word follows only an outward faith, which he calls external faith, natural, Part I, p. 430. See that the Pentecostal Spirit comes upon you, that He may tinge your fleshly heart, that He may regenerate you; He can make your natural faith into a supernatural faith and trust. (3) Of the Quakers, who deny that spiritual knowledge of God is obtained from meditation on Holy Scripture. BARCLAY in his Apology to Thesis II, no. 1, p. 4, says: We distinguish between certain knowledge of God and uncertain: between spiritual science and literal: between the saving science of the heart and the empty and airy knowledge of the brain. We confess that the latter can be acquired in many ways; the former no one can attain except by the internal and immediate manifestation and revelation of the divine Spirit shining in the heart and illuminating the intellect. (4) Of the Socinians and Arminians, asserting that Holy Scripture can be understood unto salvation without the illumination of the Holy Spirit. Thus OSTOROD in his Institut. Germ., ch. I, fol. 3 and 4: We hold that all those err very grossly and dangerously who hold that the Holy Scripture cannot in any way work faith and obedience in man without preceding inward illumination and special revelation of the Holy Spirit. EPISCOPIUS on the perspicuity of Scripture, § 3, says: It is impossible that even any unregenerate person cannot perceive the sense of Scripture.

Εκθεσις.

Obs. I. An unregenerate man is also called ψυχικὸς, or animal, 1 Cor. II, 14, and is described by D. SEB. SCHMID in his Colleg. Bibl. posteriori, p. 176, as being one who is left to himself and nature: but a spiritual man is one who is not left to his nature, but has the help and grace of the Holy Spirit. II. The unregenerate, or animal man, according to the same Schmidius, is considered either absolutely and in general, or particularly and subjectively.

The unregenerate, or animal man, considered absolutely, grasps nothing of those things which are of the Spirit of God: meanwhile, he can be subjectively animal, who understands something of those things which are of the Spirit of God; not indeed as such, but as he has already been imperfectly illuminated by the Holy Spirit.

We are not speaking at present of the unregenerate man, insofar as he is such, or viewed according to natural powers, but considered according to the supernatural grace of the Holy Spirit, by which he has been imperfectly and, as it were, pedagogically illuminated.

By the grace of the Holy Spirit, however, we do not understand here indwelling grace, but assisting, preventing, preparing, and exciting grace.

Latin:

Notitia Dei, & mysteriorum diuinorum in intellectu hominis irregeniti, a spiritu sancto per sacram scripturam imperfecte & quasi pædagogice illuminati, non est absolute spiritualis, sed litteralis (a). Quæ notitiæ litteralis non est naturalis, aut carnalis, sed supernaturalis (b), & secundum quid, certoque respectu spiritualis, censeri dicique potest (c).

Antithesis est (1) Schwenckfeldianorum & Weigelianorum, statuentium, omnem de Deo, rebusque diuinis e sacris litteris tam ab homine renato, quam irregenito, haustam notitiam esse litteralem, naturalem, & carnalem. Sic enim scribit SCHWENCKFELDIVS in tractatu de sacra scriptura fol. 7. Es wird niemand aus den todten Buchstaben den Geist, noch geistliche Weisheit schöpfen, es wird niemand aus der Schrift das himmlische Licht erlangen, noch aus dem Bilde die lebendige Wahrheit fassen, gleichwie auch niemand aus der Erden kann den Himmel holen. WEIGELIVS in postilla P. I. p. 130. inquit: Christi Erkenntniß, oder seligmachender Glaube ist nicht eine christliche menschliche Wissenschaft, da sie ihren Glauben von den Menschen lernen, so er doch von Gott muß erlernet werden. (2) Aliorum mysticorum. Nam HOBVRGIVS in postilla mystica P. II p. 287. ait: Aus der äußern Ueberzeugung durchs äußere Wort folget nur ein äußerlicher Glaube, quam externam fidem vocat naturalem P. I. p. 430. Siehe, daß der Pfingst-Geist über dich komme, daß er dein fleischlich Herz tingire, dich wiedergebähre, der kann deinen natürlichen Glauben zu einem übernatürlichen Glauben und Vertrauen machen. (3) Quackerorum, negantium, spiritualem Dei cognitionem e S. scripturæ meditatione obtineri. BARCLAIVS in apol. ad Th. Wir halten dafür, daß alle die sehr gröblich und gefährlich irren, welche dafür halten, daß die heilige Schrift ohne vorhergehende innerliche Erleuchtung und sonderbare Offenbarung des heiligen Geistes auf keine Wege den Glauben und Gehorsam in den Menschen wirken könne. EPISCOPIVS de perspicuit. scripturæ §. 3. ait: Non potest non etiam irregenitus quilibet scripturæ sensum percipere.

Εκθεσις.

SCHMIDIO in colleg. bibl. posteriori p. 176. quod sit is, qui sibi & naturæ relictus est: Spiritualis autem, qui naturæ suæ relictus non est, sed spiritus sancti habet auxilium & gratiam. II. Non loquimur impraesentiarum de homine irregenito, quatenus tali, sive secundum vires naturales spectato, sed considerato secundum supernaturalem gratiam Spiritus sancti, qua imperfecte & quasi paedagogice illuminatus est.

Per gratiam autem Spiritus sancti non intelligimus hic gratiam inhabitantem, sed assistentem, praevenientem, praeparantem, & excitantem.

V. The distinction of the knowledge of things to be believed into literal and spiritual must be understood correctly.

For spiritual knowledge is not called by us that which is had from the immediate illumination of the Holy Spirit, or from an internal light immediately revealing, as fanatics imagine, or from a mystical sense, which some call spiritual; but that which is drawn from Holy Scripture concerning divine mysteries and is rightly applied according to the intention of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, literal theological knowledge is that by which a man knows God and divine mysteries from the sayings of Holy Scripture, rightly understood according to their true sense, even if he does not always apply this cognition to the salutary use intended by the Holy Spirit: spiritual knowledge, however, is the cognition of God and divine things drawn from the Holy Scriptures, applied to the use intended by the Holy Spirit, and joined with spiritual and pious movements of the heart.

The former is called by some theoretical, the latter practical.

Obs.

VI. Literal theological knowledge is either external, by which one considers the words of Scripture, insofar as they have an analogy with human words, according to the precepts of grammar and rhetoric, and investigates and extracts some sense of them from these: or internal, by which one duly weighs the words of Scripture as truly divine, and as docheia, receptacles, or vehicles of the mysteries of faith, and apprehends their true literal sense, conformable to the mind of the Holy Spirit, with a solid and certain concept.

We assert that supernatural grace is needed to obtain not the external, but the internal literal knowledge.

Let us hear D.

CALOVIUS vol.

X. Systema Theologicum p.

131. excellently, as is his custom, distinguishing: One must distinguish between the bare words themselves, outside of context, and the same viewed in context: between divine words, insofar as they are truly divine, and are docheia of spiritual things, and are theopneustos (God-breathed) divine sense: likewise between some sense of the words, and the true sense conformable to the mind of the Holy Spirit, or, as the blessed

HUNNIUS speaks, a solid and certain concept of the words of the Holy Spirit, which to the darkened and blinded intellect, such as that of the unregenerate outside the grace of the Holy Spirit

To wish to ascribe the grace of the Holy Spirit to this, what is it other than to attribute the vision of colors to a blind man? We do not deny that the literal, external knowledge of the sayings of Scripture can be attained by the natural powers of unregenerate reason, and therefore it is of no use to dispute at length about this.

Obs. VII. We are speaking not only of simple literal knowledge, but also of approbative knowledge, or of the historical and literal assent which an unregenerate man, imperfectly illuminated by the Holy Spirit, gives to the words of Holy Scripture—and indeed not an assent that is merely human, but one divinely persuaded. Cf. D. Hülsemann, *De auxiliis gratiæ*, p. 206.

Obs. VIII. The crux of the controversy turns on this: (a) Whether an unregenerate man, not insofar as he is such, but insofar as he is imperfectly illuminated by the Holy Spirit, possesses a spiritual knowledge of divine mysteries: (b) Whether internal literal knowledge is natural or supernatural: (c) Whether the same, in a certain respect, can be considered and called spiritual?

Confirmation.

Proof a. That the literal knowledge of things to be believed is not absolutely and simply spiritual in the intellect of an ungodly man is proved: (1) Because by the most accurate theologians, the spiritual knowledge of things to be believed is opposed to the literal; but opposites cannot be affirmed of one another. (2) The literal knowledge of God and divine things differs not a little from the spiritual. (a) Because the former proceeds from an imperfect illumination of the Holy Spirit, the latter from a perfect one sufficient for faith: the former is in a soul indeed anticipated by the Holy Spirit, but not yet perfectly regenerated; the latter is in a soul fully reborn, which lives in the faith of Christ, Gal. 2:20. (b) The former is indeed divinely ordained for a salutary use, but not yet brought into that use by a second act; the latter is applied to the use intended by the Holy Spirit. (c) The former produces some spiritual movements of the heart (e.g., compunction of soul, detestation of sin, sorrow for things committed, etc.), but not yet pious movements (of which kind there are none in an unregenerate man, since he is devoid of faith); the latter is joined with richer movements, both spiritual and truly pious, e.g., with trust in Christ, love and fear of God, charity toward one's neighbor, peace of conscience, spiritual joy, hope of divine aid, desire for heavenly goods, etc. From this it is also called affective knowledge, because it is fruitful in holy affections; likewise living, because it apprehends Christ, the life of the soul, and shows itself to be living in practice; and also salutary by a complete second act, because it brings salvation to a soul anxious about its sins and panting for divine grace. Whence it is called the "knowledge of salvation," Luke 1:77, which before God makes all believers *theodidaktoi* (taught by God), and not only wise, but also righteous, Isa. 53:11, Jer. 9:23, 1 Cor. 1:30.

The distinction between the literal and spiritual knowledge of things to be believed can be clearly perceived from a certain biblical saying. Paul says in Gal. 5:6: "In Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love." An unregenerate man, not of himself but from the illumination of the Holy Spirit, when he reads and meditates upon this oracle attentively, can know its true sense, which is conformable to the mind of the Holy Spirit, with a certain and solid conception; but because he does not apply it to the use intended by the Holy Spirit, so that he might truly believe and love God and his neighbor, his knowledge is not spiritual, but literal. Otherwise, if under the direction and special concurrence of the Holy Spirit the application to the due use were to follow, he would become truly reborn from being unregenerate.

Hic tendit ad regenerationem.

In praesenti quaeritur partim de irregenito privative tali, partim de eo, qui nunquam quidem renatus fuit, ad regenerationem tamen tendit.

V. Distinctio notitiae credendorum in litteralem, & spiritualem, dextre intelligenda est.

Neque enim spiritualis nobis dicitur notitia, quae habetur ex immediata illuminatione Spiritus sancti, vel ex lumine interno immediate revelante, quod fingunt fanatici, vel e sensu mystico, quem nonnulli spiritualem appellant; sed quae de mysteriis divinis e sacra scriptura hausta iuxta intentionem Spiritus S. recte applicatur.

Est itaque notitia theologica litteralis, qua homo Deum & mysteria divina e dictis sacrae scripturae, secundum verum eorum sensum recte intellectis, cognoscit, vt ut hanc cognitionem ad salutarem usum a Spiritu sancto intentum non semper applicet: spiritualis autem notitia est cognitio Dei & rerum divinarum e sacris litteris hausta, ad usum a Spiritu sancto intentum applicata, & cum spiritualibus, piisque cordis motibus coniuncta.

Illa a nonnullis theoretica, haec practica appellatur.

Obs.

VI. Notitia theologica litteralis est vel externa, qua quis verba scripturae, quatenus analogiam habent cum verbis humanis, iuxta praecepta grammaticae & rhetoricae considerat, atque sensum aliquem eorum ex his inuestigat & eruit: vel interna, qua quis verba scripturae tanquam vere divina, & mysteriorum fidei δοχεῖα, receptacula, vel vehicula, rite expendit, & eorum sensum litteralem verum, mentique Spiritus S. conformem solido certoque conceptu apprehendit.

Non ad externam, sed ad internam notitiam litteralem obtinendam supernaturali gratia opus esse, afferimus.

Audiamus D.

CALOVIVM tom.

X. system. theol. p.

131. praeclare, vt solet, differentem: Distinguendum est inter ipsa nuda verba in se, extra contextum, & inter eadem in contextu spectata: inter verba divina, in quantum vere divina, & δοχεῖα sunt rerum spiritualium, sensusque divini θεοπνεῦς: item inter aliquem verborum sensum, & inter verum, mentique Spiritus S. conformem sensum, vel, vt b.

HVNNIVS loquitur, solidum atque certum verborum Spiritus S. conceptum, quem intellectui tenebricoso & excaecato, qualis non renatorum extra Spiritus S. gratiam

S. gratiam est, adscribere velle, quid aliud est, quam cæco visionem colorum tribuere? Notitiam dictorum scripturæ litteralem externam viribus rationis irregenitæ naturalibus comparari posse, non imus infitias, adeoque nil attinet, de eadem prolixe disputare.

Obs. VII. Loquimur non tantum de notitia litterali simplici, sed etiam de notitia approbatiba, siue de assensu historico & litterali, quem homo irregenitus a Spiritu S. imperfecte illuminatus verbis S. scripturæ præbet, & quidem non de assensu humano, sed diuinitus persuaso. Conf. D. HÜLSEMANN. de auxiliis gratiæ p. 206.

Obs. VIII. Cardo controuersiæ in hoc vertitur: (a) Vtrum homo irregenitus, non quatenus talis, sed quatenus a Spiritu S. imperfecte illuminatus est, habeat notitiam mysteriorum diuinorum spiritualem: (b) Vtrum notitia litteralis interna sit naturalis, an supernaturalis: (c) An eadem certo respectu spiritualis censeri dicique possit?

Βεβαίωσις.

Prob. a. Notitiam credendorum litteralem in intellectu hominis impii non esse absolute & simpliciter spiritualem, probatur: (1) quia a theologis accuratissimis notitia credendorum spiritualis litterali opponitur; opposita autem de se affirmari nequeunt. (2) Notitia Dei rerumque diuinarum litteralis a spirituali haud parum differt. (a) Quia illa ex imperfecta, hæc ex perfecta, & a fidem sufficiente illuminatione Spiritus S. proficiscitur: illa est in anima a Spiritu S. quidem præuenta, sed nondum perfecte regenita: hæc est in anima plene renata, quæ viuit in fide Christi, Gal. II, 20. (b) Illa ad vsum salutarem quidem diuinitus est ordinata, sed nondum actu secundo ad eum traducta: hæc ad vsum a Spiritu S. intentum applicata. (c) Illa spirituales nonnullos cordis motus (v. gr. compunctionem animi, detestationem peccati, dolorem de admissis &c.) sed nondum pios motus, (cuiusmodi in homine irregenito, cum sit fidei expers, non dantur,) parit: Hæc coniuncta est cum vberioribus motibus, tum spiritualibus, tum vere piis, v. gr. cum fiducia in Christum, amore & timore Dei, charitate proximi, pace conscientiæ, gaudio spirituali, spe diuini auxilii, desiderio bonorum cælestium &c. Ex quo etiam dicitur notitia affectiua, quia sanctis affectibus fœcunda est: item viua, quia Christum vitam animæ apprehendit, & in ipsa praxi se viuam ostendit: nec non salutaris actu secundo completo; quia animæ anxiæ de peccatis suis, & gratiam diuinam anhelanti salutem affert. Vnde γνῶσις τῆς σωτηρίας dicitur, Luc. I, 77. quæ coram Deo omnes credentes θεοδιδάκτους, & non tantum sapientes, sed & iustos facit, Es. LIII, 11. Ier. IX, 23. 1 Cor. I, 30.

Discrimen notitiæ credendorum litteralis, & spiritualis, e dicto quodam biblico luculente perspicere licet. Paullus inquit Gal. V, 6. In Christo Iesu neque circumcisio aliquid valet, neque præputium, sed fides per charitatem operans. Homo irregenitus non ex se, sed ex illuminatione Spiritus S. hoc oraculum, cum illud attente legit & meditatur, eiusque verum atque menti Spiritus S. conformem sensum certo solidoque conceptu cognoscere potest; verum quia illud non applicat ad vsum a Spiritu S. intentum, vt vere credat, & Deum proximumque diligat, notitia eius non spiritualis, sed litteralis est. Ceterum si sub directione & speciali concursu Spiritus S. applicatio ad debitum vsum accederet, ex irregenito vere renatus fieret.


### Q. XXII. What is the nature of the knowledge of God and divine things in the intellect of an unregenerate man, who has been imperfectly: Proof b. Internal literal knowledge (there is no question regarding external) is…

Proof b. Internal literal knowledge (there is no question regarding external) is not natural, but

supernatural.

(1) By reason of its origin. For that knowledge whose principle of knowing is not the light of nature, but the light of supernatural revelation, is, by reason of its origin, supernatural. But the literal knowledge of God and divine things in the unregenerate, etc. Therefore. The major premise is clear; because knowledge is rightly distinguished according to the principles of knowing. For knowledge is called natural, is called that which is kindled from the light of nature: but supernatural knowledge is that which is obtained from the light of supernatural revelation.

But if an unregenerate man were to know the mysteries of faith from the principles of reason, then such knowledge would indeed be natural. If Keckermann could have demonstrated the mystery of the Trinity from logical and metaphysical principles, which he indeed attempted, the knowledge of such a stupendous mystery would have to be considered natural. But that his attempt was in vain, D. 10. Musaeus shows in Disput. 1, appended to the treatise on the use of the principles of reason.

(2) By reason of the object.

Whatever knowledge has an object, both material and formal, far superior or more sublime than the principles of reason, that cannot be obtained by the natural powers of the intellect. But internal literal knowledge, etc. Therefore.

The major premise is evident, because between the power of knowing and its object there must be a certain proportion or congruence, so that the latter may be reached by the former. Why cannot my eye see a spirit? The reason is: because there is no natural proportion between the faculty of seeing and an immaterial object.

The minor premise is proven: because the object of literal knowledge is the mysteries of faith. But what is a mystery, if not a dogma that transcends the grasp of reason left to itself? The formal object is special divine revelation.

For no one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father: he has explained him to us. John 1:18. No one knows the Father, except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him. Matt. 11:27. Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father, who is in heaven. Matt. 16:17.

You object: A distinction must be made between the understanding of words and of things. Literal knowledge is immediately and proximately concerned with the words of Scripture, taken from the customary use of speaking; which, therefore, the animal man can learn from usage without supernatural grace. Resp. External literal knowledge is concerned with the words of Scripture, insofar as they have an analogy with human words, for which supernatural grace is not necessarily required; but internal literal knowledge knows the words of Scripture insofar as they are truly divine, and δοχεῖα [vessels], or vehicles of divine things.

Latin:

Prob. b.

Notitia litteralis interna (de externa non est quæstio) non est naturalis, sed supernaturalis.

(1) Ratione originis. Nam cuius notitiæ principium cognoscendi non est lumen naturale, sed lumen supernaturalis reuelationis, illa, ratione originis, supernaturalis est. Atqui notitia litteralis Dei & rerum diuinarum in irregenito &c. Ergo. Maior liquet; quia cognitio secundum principia cognoscendi recte distinguitur. Nam notitia naturalis dicitur, quæ ex lumine naturæ accenditur: notitia vero supernaturalis est, quæ ex lumine supernaturalis revelationis obtinetur.

Quod si homo irregenitus ex principiis rationis mysteria fidei cognosceret, utique eiusmodi notitia foret naturalis. Si Keckermannus ex principiis logicis & metaphysicis mysterium Trinitatis demonstrare potuisset, quod quidem conabatur, tam stupendi mysterii cognitio naturalis censenda foret. At irritum fuisse eius conatum, ostendit D. 10. Mvsaevs in Disput. 1. adiuncta tractatui de usu principiorum rationis.

(2) Ratione obiecti.

Quæcunque notitia habet obiectum, tam materiale, quam formale, principiis rationis longe superius, aut sublimius, illa naturalibus intellectus viribus non potest obtineri. Atqui notitia litteralis interna &c. Ergo.

Maior constat, quia inter potentiam cognoscendi, & eius obiectum certa quædam esse debet proportio aut congruentia, ut hoc ab illa attingi possit. Cur oculus meus nequit videre spiritum? Ratio est; quia naturalem inter facultatem videndi, & obiectum immateriale, nulla datur proportio.

Minor probatur: quia obiectum notitiæ litteralis sunt mysteria fidei. Sed quid est mysterium, nisi dogma, captum rationis sibi relictæ transcendens? Obiectum formale est revelatio divina specialis.

Etenim Deum nemo vidit unquam, nisi vnigenitus filius, qui in sinu patris est: ille exposuit nobis. Io. I, 18. Patrem nemo cognoscit, nisi filius, & cui voluerit filius revelare. Matth. XI, 27. Caro & sanguis non tibi revelavit hoc, sed pater meus, qui est in cælis. Matth. XVI, 17.

Excipis: Distinguendum est inter intelligentiam verborum, & rerum. Notitia litteralis, immediate & proxime versatur circa verba scripturæ, ex consueto usu loquendi desumta; quæ proinde homo animalis ex usu citra gratiam supernaturalem addiscere potest. Resp. Notitia litteralis externa versatur circa verba scripturæ, quatenus analogiam habent cum verbis humanis, ad quam supernaturalis gratia non necessario requiritur; at notitia litteralis interna cognoscit verba scripturæ, quatenus sunt vere divina, & δοχεῖα, sive vehicula rerum divinarum.


### Q. XXII. What is the nature of the knowledge of God and divine things in the intellect of an unregenerate man, who has been imperfectly: Therefore, he who does not understand these, does not grasp their true meaning…

Therefore, he who does not understand these, does not grasp their true meaning either.

(3) We prove that internal literal knowledge is supernatural on account of the ἀδυναμίαν [inability], or impotence of the understanding subject, from the Pauline statement 1 Cor. 2:14. The animal man does not receive the things that are of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know them, because they are spiritually discerned.

The apostle teaches that the ψυχικὸν [natural/animal] man, who follows only the judgment of his own reason, does not δέχεσθαι [receive] τὰ τοῦ πνεύματος [the things of the Spirit], the divine mysteries, or the things of faith, which have been handed down by the Holy Spirit through the prophets and apostles, that is, he does not approve them by assent or by judging, since he cannot even γνῶναι [know], or understand them, and indeed for two reasons. The former is taken from the corruption of human nature; because the unregenerate man, as such, laughs at divine mysteries as μωρίαν [foolishness], i.e., as most absurd.

The latter is taken from the condition of divine mysteries, which far transcend the grasp of the animal man and do not admit a ψυχικὸν [natural] judge, because πνευματικῶς ἀνακρίνεται [they are spiritually discerned], i.e., they are judged by the power of the Spirit, or by the intellect illuminated by the Holy Spirit, and from principles dictated by the Holy Spirit. These things can be confirmed by an induction of biblical sayings containing divine mysteries. John says in his Gospel ch. 1:14, The Word was made flesh. Can the unregenerate man, left to himself, perceive the genuine meaning of these words intended by the Holy Spirit, and approve them with historical assent?

By no means. Paul says in Acts 20:28, God purchased the church with his own blood.

Is the animal man, by the powers of his own unilluminated reason, able to apprehend this stupendous mystery, which the apostle inculcates upon us? Truly μωρία αὐτῷ ἐστι [it is foolishness to him].

What? That not even the disciples of Christ, occupied with a preconceived opinion about an earthly kingdom of the Messiah, [the words of the Messiah's kingdom, the words]

Christ, concerning the passion and death of the Redeemer, now imminent, understood. Luke 18:31. Therefore, Christ, having been raised from the dead, opened their mind, that they might understand the scriptures. Luke 24:45. The sentiment of Christ is not obscure (these are the words of D. Hülsemann, De auxil. grat., p. 205) John 3:16: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life."

But that any pagan, from this, gathers a certain knowledge required for saving faith—that by God one must understand God the Father, by only begotten Son the Son begotten from the essence of the Father from eternity, by world all mortals whatsoever, by believing a fiduciary certainty in his merit, etc., and that he is necessarily compelled to understand this from the evidence of the object—is an anakolouthon (inconsequence).

However, when a Gentile subsequently reads, meditates, and compares parallel passages, in this reading, meditation, and collation, the Holy Spirit is effective and imprints the native character of this sentiment upon the reader.

(c) A veil of ignorance and prejudiced opinion is imposed upon the eyes of the mind of unregenerate men, which, unless it is removed by Christ, prevents the divine sense of the celestial oracles from being understood.

Latin:

Proinde qui has non intelligit, nec illorum verum sensum capit.

(3) Supernaturalem esse notitiam litteralem internam ob ἀδυναμίαν, sive impotentiam subiecti intelligentis, probamus ex effato Paullino 1 Cor. II, 14. Animalis homo non suscipit ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei; stultitia enim illi sunt, & non potest scire, quia spiritualiter diiudicantur.

Docet apostolus, hominem ψυχικὸν, qui iudicium rationis suæ tantum sequitur, τὰ τοῦ πνεύματος, mysteria divina, sive res fidei, quæ a Spiritu S. per prophetas & apostolos tradita sunt, & δέχεσθαι, non suscipere assensu, sive iudicando non approbare, cum ne ea quidem possit γνῶναι, sive intelligere, & quidem ob duas rationes. Prior sumitur a naturæ humanæ corruptione; quia homo irregenitus, quatenus talis, mysteria divina ridet velut μωρίαν, i. e. tanquam absurdissima.

Posterior desumitur a mysteriorum divinorum conditione, quæ captum hominis animalis longe transcendunt, & iudicem ψυχικὸν non admittunt, quia πνευματικῶς ἀνακρίνεται, spiritualiter diiudicantur, i. e. per virtutem spiritus, sive ab intellectu per Spiritum S. illuminato, & ex principiis a Spiritu S. dictatis diiudicantur. Confirmari hæc possunt inductione dictorum biblicorum, mysteria divina complectentium. Ioannes dicit in euangelio suo c. I, 14. Verbum caro factum est. Potestne homo irregenitus, sibi relictus, genuinum horum verborum sensum a Spiritu S. intentum perspicere, & assensu historico approbare?

Neutiquam. Paullus ait Act. XX, 28. Deus ecclesiam acquisivit, per proprium sanguinem.

An homo animalis rationis non illuminatæ viribus hoc mysterium stupendum, quod apostolus nobis inculcat, apprehendere valet? Profecto μωρία αὐτῷ ἐστι.

Quid? quod ne discipuli quidem Christi, præconcepta opinione de terreno Messiæ regno occupati, verba Meffiæ regno occupati, verba

Christi perquam luculenta de passione & morte redemptoris, iamiam imminente, intelligebant. Luc. XVIII, 31. Idcirco Christus e mortuis resuscitatus aperuit eorum mentem, vt scripturas intelligerent. Luc. XXIV, 45. Non obscura est sententia Christi (verba sunt D. HULSEMANNI de auxil. grat. p. 205.) Io. III, 16. Sic Deus dilexit mundum, vt filium suum unigenitum daret, vt omnis, qui credit in ipsum, non pereat, sed vitam aeternam habeat.

Sed quod notitia certa, & ad salutificam fidem requisita, quilibet paganus inde colligat, per Deum intelligendum esse Deum patrem, per filium unigenitum filium ex essentia patris genitum ab aeterno, per mundum omnes omnino mortales, per credere, fiducialem certitudinem in eius meritum &c. idque ex euidentia obiecti necessario cogatur intelligere, ἀνακόλουθον est.

Quum autem gentilis deinceps legit, meditatur, locos parallelos confert, in hac lectione, meditatione, collatione, & per hanc efficax est Spiritus S. & natiuum huius sententiae indolem legenti inprimit.

(c) Hominum irregenitorum oculis mentis velamen ignorantiae & praeiudicatae opinionis est impositum, quod, nisi a Christo remoueatur, impedit, quo minus sensus oraculorum coelestium diuinus intelligatur.


### Q. XXII. What is the nature of the knowledge of God and divine things in the intellect of an unregenerate man, who has been imperfectly: Paul teaches this in 2

Paul teaches this in 2

Cor. 3:14: "Their minds were blinded: for until this day remaineth the same vail untaken away in the reading of the old testament (which is done away in Christ)."

We conclude: Those upon whose eyes of the mind a veil is imposed do not perceive the literal sense of even the clearest words of Scripture without the supernatural grace of Christ. But the veil is imposed upon the eyes of the mind of both Jews and Gentiles, etc. Therefore. The major is proven, because just as for vision there is required both the perspicuity of the object and the removal of the veil, so for the understanding of the sacred letters, the perspicuity of the object is not sufficient, but there is simultaneously required the removal of prejudices and ignorance, effected by a certain divine power and supernatural grace.

(4) Literal knowledge is supernatural, on account of the inseparable conjunction of the Holy Spirit and Scripture. Hence the argument: If the internal literal knowledge of things to be believed is not supernatural, the Holy Spirit will not be perpetually and inseparably united with Holy Scripture. But the Holy Spirit is perpetually and inseparably united with Holy Scripture. Therefore, the internal literal knowledge of things to be believed is supernatural.

The consequence is evident; because the Holy Spirit, inseparably united with the divine Word, produces a supernatural effect.

But it is more certain than certain that the Holy Spirit is inseparably joined with Holy Scripture. For Christ says: "The words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life," John 6:63, because they are animated by spirit and life.

But the words which Christ spoke exist in Scripture. When the Apostle proposed what is now read in the Scriptures, he professed that he was bringing forth what the Holy Spirit teaches, 1 Cor. 2:13. If, however, when the Apostle taught Scripture, the Holy Spirit was teaching, it must be that a close union exists between the Holy Spirit and Scripture.

Therefore, when an unregenerate man attentively reads and meditates upon Holy Scripture, the Holy Spirit kindles a supernatural knowledge of the things to be believed in his intellect. (5) The literal knowledge of divine mysteries is supernatural, by reason of the end to which it is divinely ordained. For all knowledge of the sacred letters can make a man wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus, 2 Tim. 3:15, which end is undoubtedly supernatural.

Proof c. Although the knowledge of God and divine things is not absolutely spiritual (as has been shown above), it can nevertheless be called spiritual in a certain sense and respect: (a) by reason of the principle of knowing, because it flows from Scripture theopneustos (God-breathed), 2 Tim. 3:16. (b) By reason of the illuminating grace of the Holy Spirit, which... is inseparably joined with Scripture.

(c) By reason of the object, because it is concerned with ta tou pneumatos tou theou (the things of the Spirit of God), 1 Cor. 2:14.

(d) By reason of the end, because it is divinely ordained to spiritual faith, so that a man may be converted, regenerated, justified, is made, renewed, and saved, John 20:13. From which an argument arises: Whatever knowledge flows from a spiritual principle of knowing, is obtained from the illumination of the Holy Spirit, is occupied about a spiritual object, and is divinely ordained to a spiritual end; that is, in a secondary sense and in a certain respect, entirely spiritual. But the knowledge of things to be believed is literal, etc. Therefore. A. D. Johann Adam Osiander, a piously learned theologian, adds his vote, as they say, to us, who in his Collegium Theologicum, system part 4, p. 335, writes: Although the powers of assisting grace (whose effect is the literal knowledge of things to be believed) are new and spiritual; they are not, however, such, except in respect of the efficient cause, the divine intention, and the end to be attained, insofar as they proceed from the Holy Spirit and are directed to a spiritual end: although they do not yet constitute a man spiritually alive. Because literal knowledge does not yet constitute a sinful man spiritually alive, it is not called spiritual absolutely and simply. D.

Fecht holds the same opinion, whose words, most worthy of being remembered, are read in his manuscript Collegium: Something is called spiritual in two ways that which is from the acting spirit, although not everything that it intends through the action, it obtains. And thus every sense of Scripture, and its knowledge, is spiritual. Thus it is taken from John 6:63, where those words of Christ are also said to be spirit and life, which fall upon the unregenerate, v. 64. Which, indeed, although they are understood by him, and even approved by assent, yet are not transferred to the use of true conversion and piety. Then, that is called spiritual which has fully admitted the operation of the Holy Spirit, according to all His intention, and is therefore from the Holy Spirit both operatively and applicatively. And thus theologians have admitted a certain literal knowledge, i. e., one consisting in the sense of the letter, and not tending to its use and application, but another truly spiritual one, which, namely, has left room everywhere for the operating Spirit, in a sense, as is evident from the description itself, clearly different from the opinion of the fanatics. Διάλυσις (Resolution).

Latin:

Docet id Paullus 2

Cor. III, 14. Obdurati sunt sensus eorum: vsque enim hodiernum diem velamen super lectione veteris testamenti manet non reuelatum (quod in Christo abrogatur).

Colligimus: Quorum oculis mentis velamen est impositum, illi sensum literalem vel clarissimorum scripturae verborum non perspiciunt absque supernaturali gratia Christi. Atqui tam Iudaeorum, quam gentilium oculis mentis &c. E. Maior probatur, quia sicut ad visionem requiritur tum perspicuitas obiecti, tum remotio velaminis: ita ad intelligentiam sacrarum litterarum non sufficit perspicuitas obiecti, sed simul requiritur praeiudiciorum, & ignorantiae remotio, facta vi quadam diuina & gratia supernaturali.

(4) Notitia litteralis est supernaturalis, ob indiuiduam coniunctionem Spiritus S, & scripturae. Hinc arg. Si notitia credendorum litteralis interna non est supernaturalis, Spiritus S. cum scriptura sacra non erit perpetuo & indiulse vnitus. At Spiritus S. perpetuo & indiulse cum scriptura S. est vnitus. E. notitia credendorum litteralis interna est supernaturalis.

Consequentia est euidens; quia Spiritus S. cum verbo diuino indiulse vnitus effectum supernaturalem producit.

Certo autem certius est, Spiritum S. inseparabiliter coniunctum esse cum scriptura S. Nam Christus inquit: Verba mea, quae loquor vobis, spiritus & vita sunt, Io. VI, 63. quia spiritu & vita animata sunt.

At verba, quae Christus locutus est, in scriptura exstant. Apostolus cum, quae nunc in scripturis leguntur, suis proponeret, profitebatur, se afferre, quae Spiritus S. docet, 1 Cor. II, 13. Si autem, apostolo scripturam docente, Spiritus S. docebat, oportet arctam vnionem inter Spiritum S. & scripturam intercedere.

Proinde cum homo irregenitus scripturam sacram attente legit & meditatur, Spiritus sanctus supernaturalem credendorum notitiam in intellectu eius accendit. (5) Litteralis mysteriorum diuinorum notitia est, supernaturalis, ratione finis, ad quem diuinitus ordinata est. Nam omnis notitia sacrarum litterarum potest hominem sapientem reddere in salutem per fidem, quae in Christo Iesu est, 2 Tim. III, 15. qui finis haud dubie supernaturalis est.

Prob. c. Quamuis notitia Dei, rerumque diuinarum non fit absolute spiritualis (prout supra ostensum est) secundum quid tamen & certo respectu spiritualis dici potest (a) ratione principii cognoscendi, quia fluit e scriptura θεοπνεύστῳ, 2 Tim. III, 16. (b) Ratione gratiae illuminatricis Spiritus sancti, quae... cum scriptura indiulse coniuncta est.

(c) Ratione obiecti, quia versatur circa τὰ τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ θεοῦ, 1 Cor. II, 14.

(d) Ratione finis, quia ad fidem spiritualem diuinitus ordinatur, vt homo conuertatur, regeneretur, iustificetur, renouetur, & saluetur, Io. XX, 13. E quibus nascitur argumentum: Quae notitia e principio cognoscendi spirituali fluit, ex illuminatione Spiritus S. obtinetur, circa obiectum spirituale versatur, & ad finem spiritualem diuinitus ordinatur; illa secundum quid & certo respectu est omnino spiritualis. Atqui notitia credendorum litteralis &c. Ergo. Album, quod aiunt, calculum nobis adiicit D. IO. ADAM OSIANDER, theologus pie eruditus, qui in collegio theol. system part. IV. p. 335. scribit: Quanquam vires gratiae assistentis (cuius effectus est litteralis credendorum notitia) sint nouae & spirituales; non sunt tamen tales, nisi respectu efficientis causae, intentionis diuinae, & finis consequendi, quatenus scilicet a Spiritus S. proficiscuntur, & ad spiritualem finem diriguntur: quanquam nondum hominem spiritualiter uiuum constituunt. Quia notitia litteralis hominem peccatorem nondum spiritualiter uiuum constituit, non absolute & simpliciter spiritualis appellatur.

Eandem fouet sententiam D. FECHTIVS, cuius verba memoratu dignissima leguntur in collegio manuscripto: Spirituale aliquid dicitur dupliciter quod est a spiritu agente, quanquam non omne id, quod per actionem intendit, obtinente. Et ita omnis sensus scripturae, eiusque notitia est spiritualis. Ita sumitur Io. VI, 63. vbi dicuntur etiam illa verba Christi esse spiritus & vita, quae in irregenitum cadunt, v. 64. quae nimirum, quanquam ab eo intelligantur, & assensu etiam comprobentur, tamen ad vsum verae conuersionis & pietatis non transferuntur. Deinde spirituale dicitur, quod Spiritus S. operationem, secundum omnem intentionem ipsius, plane admisit, adeoque a Spiritu S. est & operatiue & applicatiue. Et ita quandam notitiam litteralem, h. e. in sensu litterae consistentem, neque ad vsum eius, & applicationem tendentem, aliam vero spiritualem, quae nempe Spiritui operanti ubique locum reliquit, admiserunt theologi, sensu, vt ex ipsa descriptione patescit, a fanaticorum opinione plane diuerso. Διάλυσις.


### Q. XXII. What is the nature of the knowledge of God and divine things in the intellect of an unregenerate man, who has been imperfectly: Those who dissent object

Those who dissent object

I. Literal knowledge cannot be called supernatural from a supernatural principle of knowing; because that principle (Holy Scripture) is outside of man. But from a principle that is outside of man, knowledge, which is in man, cannot derive its denomination. Resp. Every principle of knowing, considered formally, insofar as it is actually employed, is in the intellect, and therefore in man. For a principle of knowing is a universal proposition, prior and better known, suitable for demonstrating a thesis, as Leichner defines in his Synopsis veritatis apodicticae, p. 391. But whatever is known to man, that is in his intellect, and therefore in the man himself. And how will he who does not comprehend it with his mind elicit a certain conclusion from a biblical saying?

II. Knowledge that is occupied about a supernatural object cannot be called supernatural. For denomination does not come from the object; otherwise, the science that is occupied about silver would have to be called silvery; that which is occupied about gold, golden: which is absurd. Resp. In the denomination of a science, one must look not only to the material object, but to the formal. And so, just as the knowledge of silver, insofar as it is obvious to the senses, is called sensual: so the knowledge of God, insofar as it becomes known from supernatural revelation, is rightly called supernatural.

III. Whatever scripture is perspicuous, that can be easily understood without the supernatural light of divine grace. But Holy Scripture, etc. Therefore. Resp. I deny the major, and I argue by the same reasoning: Whatever is most bright is most shining, that can be seen by every eye. But the sun, etc. Therefore, the sun can be seen by every eye that is blind, closed, or covered by a veil. Since this is άτοπον (absurd), a distinction must be made between the perspicuity of the object and the capacity of the subject. Holy Scripture is in itself perspicuous; but through it the Holy Spirit removes the veil of ignoof ignorance, when the reader or hearer does not maliciously and morosely resist, but admits the illuminating grace.

IV. Hypocrites without supernatural grace know the literal sense of Holy Scripture. Resp. Hypocrites do not perceive the sense of Scripture from themselves, or from the natural powers of their own intellect, but from the grace of the Holy Spirit preventing, preparing, and exciting them—not as hypocrites (because hypocrisy presupposes knowledge of that thing which one pretends to approve, or pretends to disapprove), but as docile hearers or readers of the divine word: under which reading or hearing, the Holy Spirit is always efficacious, so that He may instill the true sense of His word.

V. Heretics, who are not illuminated by the Holy Spirit, understand Scripture. Resp. Heretics are considered either reduplicatively, insofar as they are heretics, or erring in the foundation of the faith: thus far they infer a sense of Scripture, they do not draw it out; they do not grasp the sense which the words of Scripture yield of themselves, but they attach to the biblical text a foreign sense, not analogous to it: or the same are viewed specifically, insofar as they are docile, and sometimes unearth the true sense of Scripture: thus the Holy Spirit does not deny them the grace that illuminates, as it were, pedagogically.

VI. Experience testifies that the nature of sacred speech is the same as that of common reason, since it is learned, understood, and treated by men in a human way in exactly the same manner.

Therefore, an unregenerate man, without assisting supernatural grace, can understand the literal sense of Scripture by the natural powers of his own genius. Resp. Distinguish between the literal external knowledge of things to be believed, and the internal.

It is not asked here whether sacred speech, insofar as it has an analogy or correspondence with other speeches, can be understood without assisting divine grace: for we grant this readily, and we give immortal thanks to God, thrice best, that He has handed down to us the articles of faith in clear speech, which bears a habit common with other speeches; otherwise, it would be of no use for converting unregenerate men. But this is what is asked: can an unregenerate man, from sacred speech, understand the very mysteries of faith and confirm them with solid assent without the assisting grace of the Holy Spirit? This is what we deny and utterly deny.

This we prove by examples. A virgin shall conceive and bear a son. It is clear speech, and analogous to other vulgar speeches.

For almost everyone knows what the word "virgin" signifies, and what "to conceive" and "to bear" mean. But the connection of that proposition, by which the highest mystery is contained, no one knows with solid conception, nor confirms with firm assent, unless the Holy Spirit, by illuminating grace, has illuminated his intellect and elevated it above natural powers.

Likewise: God was manifested in the flesh. What the words "God," "was manifested," "flesh" denote, escapes no one, since they are taken from common speech. But the ὁμολογουμένως μέγα μυστήριον (confessedly great mystery), which is exhibited by those words, no one understands, except the docile reader, whose intellect the Holy Spirit—who is inseparably joined with the divine word, and instills its true sense into readers who do not maliciously resist—bathes with supernatural light.

VII. Objection. A man possessing a sharp intellect, imbued with the humanities, and bestowing due effort in all disciplines—philosophy, medicine, and jurisprudence—can perceive even the most difficult things without the supernatural grace of the Holy Spirit. Why not also in theology? Resp. The reason is different.

For those things which are handed down in other disciplines, difficult at first glance, are not beyond the sphere of reason left to itself: but in theology, mysteries are proposed which so transcend the grasp of an unilluminated reason that they seem to it μωρία, i.e., foolishness, or most stupid and absurd.

Justin Martyr judged the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity to be ὑπὲρ νῦν, ὑπὲρ λόγον, καὶ ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν κατάληψιν (above mind, above reason, and above all comprehension). I would affirm the same concerning all the mysteries which revealed theology teaches.

But whatever is above intelis the comprehension of the intellect; this the intellect does not perceive, unless it be elevated beyond natural powers through divine grace.

VII. The knowledge of the simple apprehension of things, signified by the words of scripture, is natural, and falls even to unregenerate men, gentiles and pagans, who indeed are acquainted with the language in which Holy Scripture is recorded, and have knowledge of the force of the words to signify, and of the grammatical construction.

For it depends upon causes merely natural, namely, from the native force of the words, by which, as in any other speech spoken or written, so in Holy Scripture read, or proposed by the voice of a teacher, in a connatural way; through the intervention of the senses, they penetrate to the intellect; but being known in their force to signify, which they have from imposition, they move the intellect by their force to signify, again in a connatural way, to excite the species of the things of which they are signs, which pre-exist, and to coordinate them rightly.

Which species, by this very fact, that they pre-exist in the intellect before the words of scripture are perceived, are natural.

Resp. They are not natural intelligible species, which the revealed word of God inserts into minds, but they are supernatural; both by reason of their origin, impressed by the Holy Spirit through the supernatural word, so that they may be proportionate to the spiritual things which they represent to the intellect, and by reason of the celestial truths which they express, and by reason of the end intended by the Holy Spirit in the impression of them.

Nor do intelligible species concerning divine mysteries pre-exist in the intellect before the words of scripture are perceived.

What, I ask, intelligible species concerning the birth of the virgin, concerning the incarnation of the Word (τοῦ λόγου), concerning the one essence in three divine persons, pre-exists in the intellect before the words of scripture are perceived?

VIII. Most learned theologians, for example, HOEPFNER in his LL. theol. loc.

III. p. 13, DANNHAVER in his theol. conscient. part. II. p. 438, and others have asserted that the literal understanding of scripture can be obtained without special illumination. Resp.

Those theologians spoke of the external and superficial understanding of scripture, not of the solid literal knowledge of things to be believed, joined with assent.

This they attribute to the assisting divine grace.

We cite the witness D.

IOANN. ADAM. OSIANDER in his colleg. system. part. IV. p. 335, saying: The first degree of preventing and assisting grace is objective illumination in the preaching of the word, or strictly so called, with the application of the special object revealed through grace to the individual.

The second degree of the same is the inhibition and restraint of actual and natural repugnance.

The third, finally, is the dispensation of literal knowledge and historical assent to the gospel, not general trust in God, and the production of contrition through the mediation of the law.

Nor do we pass over D.

DANNHAVER, phaenom. IX, arguing clearly, as is his custom: All actual grace, otherwise called the aid of actual grace, which is not an infused habit, but a motion, impulse, drawing, opening, Apoc. 3, 20.

Act. 16, 14. Io. 6, 44. is (1) preventing and beginning, drawing, exciting, inviting, impelling, striking, by which it illuminates the intellect to the recognition and detestation of sin, and removes original repugnance, Eph. 5, 14.

Apoc. 3, 20. (2) operating, opening, which besides excitation, assent, desire, the powers of believing, effects the purpose of conversion, Luc. 8, 13. c.

13, 17. Act. 13, 48. c. 2, 37. and opens the heart, Act. 16, 14. to which, if man does not resist, follows grace;

(3) perfecting Phil. 1, 16.

Let us also hear D.

KOENIG in his theolog. positiva teaching thus: §. 503. seqq. Conversion happens successively, Marc. 4, 27.

28. and thence has its degrees, in the numbering and naming of which doctors vary greatly.

To us the first degree is, and is called that of beginning grace, etc.

This grace is otherwise called preventing, taking the term more strictly.

The second degree is that of preparing grace, etc.

The third degree is that of exciting grace, which is the universal dispensation of divine affection, by which the Holy Spirit produces in man the literal knowledge of things to be believed with historical assent, the supernatural powers of recognizing sin from the law, of assenting salutarily to the word of the gospel, and of believing in Christ, through the mediation of the word, of which this

is explained by D. Quensted explains in his System of Theology, part III, ch. VII, p. 45, and adds: The literal knowledge of the Gospel can in no way be had without grace, much less therefore can anyone assent to it historically.

We shall not bring forward more authors at present, but shall conclude with the words of the Formula of Concord, p. 657. Although human reason, or the natural intellect of man, has some obscure remaining spark of that knowledge, that God exists, and holds some small particle of the law: yet that reason is so ignorant, blind, and perverse, that even if the most ingenious and learned men in this world read or hear the Gospel concerning the Son of God and the divine promises of eternal salvation: yet they cannot perceive, understand, believe, and establish them to be true by their own powers.

Objection. Historical assent seems to be merely human, since divine assent belongs only to the regenerate.

Response. Historical assent is not human, because it rests not on the testimony of men, but immediately on the word divinely revealed.

That the regenerate, however, assent to the divine word with greater certainty is placed beyond all doubt.

IX. An unregenerate man perceives the grammatical and external sense, for which he does not need divine illumination, but he does not perceive the spiritual and internal sense.

For D. Quensted teaches that a distinction must be made between the grammatical and external sense, and the spiritual, internal, and divine sense of the divine word.
