The former is the formal aspect of the word of God, insofar as it is a word; the latter, insofar as it is the divine word: The former can be perceived even by any unregenerate person; the latter, however, only by an illuminated intellect.

D. Quensted, in the place cited, considers the divine word in two ways: (a) generally, and in a specificative sense, insofar as it denotes a word or speech, common with any other speech, whose individual words have their own meanings to be judged from the customary usage of speaking; (b) specifically, and in a reduplicative sense, insofar as it denotes the divine word, or the θεόπνευστον (God-breathed) medium of salvation, supernatural by reason of its essence, and endowed with supernatural power. The sense of the divine word considered generally and specificatively, as it is a word common with any other word, is that which the words produce in their proper and native meaning, even if it does not agree with the intention of the Holy Spirit.

It is otherwise called the sense of the letter. But the sense of the divine word viewed specifically and reduplicatively is that which the Holy Spirit immediately intends by the θεοπνεύστοις (God-breathed) words, and it is called logical and internal, in opposition to the grammatical and external; literal, in opposition to the mystical sense; spiritual and divine, because it is immediately intended by the Holy Spirit.

To know the grammatical and external sense, natural powers suffice: to perceive the literal internal, spiritual, and divine sense, there is need of the illumination of the Holy Spirit, whether that illumination be imperfect, of which the unregenerate is capable, or perfect, which the regenerate enjoys.

For D. Quensted does not by an illuminated man precisely understand the regenerate, although he opposes him to the unregenerate: since opposites are not always of equal breadth.

Beware, however, of understanding this author, in the place cited, to mean the mystical sense by the spiritual sense; because he teaches in express words that the mystical sense is called the sense of scripture ἀκύρως (improperly) and less accurately, fol. 130.

Furthermore, D. Quensted proves by very many arguments that there is one genuine literal and divine sense of a single biblical text intended by the Holy Spirit, fol. 132. Add that the sense of the words of scripture is one thing, and the knowledge of that sense impressed upon the mind of the reader is another.

Although the literal sense (logically speaking) is spiritual, i.e., the Holy Spirit's [sense] in the θεοπνεύστοις (God-breathed) words, yet the knowledge of that sense of scripture is either literal, and that both external and internal, or spiritual; for they are distinguished as the act of the mind and its object.

He who confuses these most distinct things does not teach clearly, but confusedly.

X. An unregenerate man, placed under assisting and knocking divine grace (e.g., a Jew or Gentile to be converted), cannot perceive the words of scripture with a solid concept and assent. ceive and approve; because he does not certainly believe the θεοπνευστίαν [theopneustia], or the divine origin of Scripture. And although this is proven by certain κριτήρια [criteria], those nevertheless produce only opinion and human faith.

Resp. The Jew certainly believes the θεοπνευστίαν [theopneustia] of the O.T., from which he can be convinced. But as for the converting of a Gentile, he is prepared and moved by external κριτηρίοις [criteria] to read and meditate upon Holy Scripture with study and desire. When he reads and meditates upon it attentively, he is convinced by internal κριτήρια [criteria], primarily the inherent efficacy of Holy Scripture, to acknowledge its divine origin. This being presupposed, and with the study of reading and meditating upon Scripture continued, he extracts, perceives, and with solid assent approves the genuine sense of the biblical sayings.

XI. The light of knowledge, kindled by divine illumination, is a light that is burning and warming the will toward trust in Christ and love toward God and neighbor. But the light of literal knowledge is not burning, nor warming, etc. Resp. (1) To the major: The light of knowledge kindled by divine illumination is burning and warming the will, unless some impediment is placed in its way. It not infrequently happens that the efficacy of a burning fire is hindered from immediately igniting wood, because it is too damp. (2) To the minor: The light of literal knowledge is not only shining, but also burning and warming, in that it immediately inflames the will toward the desire and purpose of conversion, and consequently toward the detestation of sin, toward faith in Christ, and toward the love of God and neighbor.

Latin:

Obiiciunt diffidentes I. Notitia litteralis a principio cognoscendi supernaturali non potest dici supernaturalis; quia illud principium (S. scriptura) est extra hominem.

Sed a principio, quod est extra hominem, notitia, quae est in homine, denominationem fortiri nequit. Resp. Omne principium cognoscendi formaliter consideratum, quatenus actu adhibetur, est in intellectu, adeoque in homine. Nam principium cognoscendi est propositio vniuersalis, prior & notior demonstrandae thesi idonea, definiente LEICHNERO in synopsi verit. apodicticae p. 391. Sed quicquid homini est notum, illud est in eius intellectu, adeoque in ipso homine. Et quomodo e dicto biblico eliciet conclusionem certam, qui illad mente non comprehendit?

II. Ab obiecto supernaturali, notitia, quae circa illud occupatur, supernaturalis dici nequit. Nam ab obiecto non fit denominatio; ceteroqui scientia, quae versatur circa argentum, argentea; quae occupatur circa aurum, aurea dicenda foret: quod est absurdum. Resp. In denominatione scientiae respiciendum est non tantum obiectum materiale, sed formale. Sicut itaque cognitio argenti, quatenus hoc sensibus obuium est, dicitur sensualis: ita cognitio Dei, quatenus e supernaturali reuelatione innotescit, recte dicitur supernaturalis.

III. Quaecunque scriptura est perspicua, illa absque supernaturali lumine gratiae diuinae facile intelligi potest. Atqui scriptura S. &c. Ergo. Resp. Neg. Maior, & eadem ratione argumentor: Quodcunque fidus est fulgidissimum, illud ab omni oculo potest videri. Atqui sol &c. E. Sol ab omni oculo caeco, clauso, velamine obtecto videri potest. Quod cum sit άτοπον, distinguendum est inter perspicuitatem obiecti, & capacitatem subiecti. Sacra scriptura in se est perspicua; at per eam Spiritus S. remouet velamen ignorantiae, quando lector, vel auditor, malitiose & morose non obnititur, sed gratiam illuminantem admittit.

IV. Hypocritae sine supernaturali gratia sensum S. scripturae litteralem cognoscunt. Resp. Hypocritae non ex se, aut naturalibus sui intellectus viribus, sed ex gratia Spiritus S. praeueniente, praeparante & excitante sensum scripturae perceperunt, non vt hypocritae (quia hypocrisis supponit notitiam eius rei, quam quis simulat, se probare, vel dissimulat improbare) sed vt dociles auditores, vel lectores verbi diuini: sub qua lectione, vel auditu Spiritus S. semper efficax est, vt verbi sui verum sensum instillet.

V. Haeretici, qui non illuminantur a Spiritu S. scripturam intelligunt. Resp. Haeretici considerantur vel reduplicatiue, quatenus sunt haeretici, vel errantes in fundamento fidei: hactenus sensum scripturae inferunt, non ex ea efferunt, non capiunt sensum, quem verba scripturae ex se fundunt, sed alienum, non analogum. textui biblico affingunt: vel iidem spectantur specificatiue, quatenus sunt dociles, & verum sensum scripturae aliquando eruunt: ita Spiritus S. gratiam quasi paedagogice illuminantem ipsis non denegat.

VI. Testatur experientia, eandem esse sermonis sacri rationem, quae est rationis communis, siquidem plane eodem modo addiscitur, intelligitur, & tractatur ab hominibus humane.

E. Homo irregenitus citra assistentem gratiam supernaturalem, viribus ingenii sui naturalibus sensum scripturae litteralem intelligere potest. Resp. Dist. inter notitiam credendorum litteralem externam, & internam.

Non quaeritur hic loci, an sermo facer, quatenus analogiam, aut conuenientiam habet cum sermonibus aliis, citra gratiam diuinam assistentem intelligi possit: hoc enim largimur faciles, & agimus Deo ter optimo gratias immortales, quod articulos fidei sermone perspicuo, qui communem cum aliis sermonibus habitum refert, nobis tradiderit; ceteroqui is hominibus irregenitis conuertendis nulli esset vsui. At hoc quaeritur: an homo irregenitus ex sermone sacro ipsa mysteria fidei citra assistentem Spiritus S. gratiam intelligere, & assensu solido comprobare possit? Hoc est, quod negamus & pernegamus.

Id quod exemplis probamus. Virgo concipiet & pariet filium. Est sermo perspicuus, aliisque sermonibus vulgaribus analogus.

Nam quid significet vox, virgo, quid concipere & parere, prope omnes norunt. At connexionem illius propositionis, qua summum continetur mysterium, nemo conceptu solido cognoscit, firmoque assensu comprobat, nisi Spiritus S., gratia illuminatrice, intellectum ipsius collustrauerit, & supra vires naturales eleuauerit.

Item: Deus est manifestatus in carne. Quid denotent voces, Deus, manifestatus est, caro, neminem fugit, siquidem ex vulgari sermone desumtae sunt. At ὁμολογουμένως μέγα μυστήριον, quod iis vocibus exhibetur, nemo intelligit, nisi lector docilis, cuius intellectum luce supernaturali perfundit Spiritus S., qui indiuulse coniunctus est cum verbo diuino, & huius verum sensum lectoribus malitiose non obsistentibus instillat.

VII. Instantia. Homo perspicaci pollens ingenio, humanioribus imbutus litteris, & debitam nauans operam in omnibus disciplinis, philosophia, medicina, iurisque prudentia, citra gratiam Spiritus sancti supernaturalem, difficillima quaeque percipere potest. Quidni etiam in theologia?

Resp. Dispar est ratio. Nam quae in aliis disciplinis traduntur prima fronte difficilia, non sunt vltra sphaeram rationis sibi relictae: at in theologia proponuntur mysteria, quae captum rationis non illuminatae adeo transcendunt, vt videantur ipsi μωρία, i. e. stultitia, vel stolidissima, & absurdissima.

Iustinus Martyr censuit mysterium SS. Trinitatis esse ὑπὲρ νῦν, ὑπὲρ λόγον, καὶ ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν κατάληψιν. Idem ego de omnibus mysteriis, quae theologia reuelata docet, affirmauerer.

Sed quicquid supra intellectus comprehensionem est, id intellectus non percipit, nisi per gratiam divinam ultra vires naturales elenetur.

VII. Notitia apprehensionis simplicis rerum, verbis scripturae significatarum, est naturalis, et cadit etiam in homines non renatos, gentiles et paganos, qui quidem linguae, qua scriptura S. consignata est, gnari sunt, et vocum vim significandi, constructionemque grammaticam cognitam habent.

Dependet enim ex causis mere naturalibus, nempe ex vi vocum nativa, qua, ut in alia quavis oratione voce prolata, aut scripta, ita in scriptura S. lecta, aut docentis voce proposita, modo connaturali; sensuum interventu, penetrant ad intellectum; cognitae autem in sua vi significandi, quam ex impositione habent, movent intellectum sua vi significandi, rursum modo connaturali, ad rerum, quarum signa sunt, species praeexistentes excitandas, et rite coordinandas.

Quae species hoc ipso, quod ante verba scripturae praecepta in intellectu praeexistunt, naturales sunt.

Resp. Non sunt naturales species intelligibiles, quas verbum Dei revelatum mentibus ingerit, sed sunt supernaturales; tum ratione originis a Spiritu S. per verbum supernaturale impressae, ut sint proportionatae rebus spiritualibus, quas intellectui repraesentant, tum ratione veritatum caelestium, quas exprimunt, tum ratione finis, a Spiritu S. in impressione illarum intenti.

Neque species intelligibiles de mysteriis divinis ante verba scripturae praecepta in intellectu praeexistunt.

Quae, quaeso, species intelligibiles de partu virginis, de incarnatione τοῦ λόγου, de una essentia in tribus divinis personis, ante percepta scripturae verba in intellectu praeexistit?

VIII. Doctissimi theologi, v. gr.

HOEPFNERVS LL. theol. loco III. p. 13. DANNHAVER. theol. conscient. part. II. p. 438. et alii asseruerunt, intelligentiam scripturae litteralem posse sine speciali illuminatione obtineri. Resp.

Locuti sunt theologi illi de intelligentia scripturae externa, et superficiaria, non de notitia credendorum litterali solida et cum assensu coniuncta.

Hanc gratiae divinae assistenti tribuunt.

Citamus testem D.

IOANN. ADAM. OSIANDR. in colleg. system. part. IV. p. 335. inquientem: Gradus primus gratiae praevenientis et assistentis est illuminatio obiectiva in verbi praedicatione, vel stricte sic dicta, cum obiecti specialis per gratiam revelati ad individuum applicatione.

Alter gradus eiusdem est actualis et naturalis repugnantiae inhibitio et refrenatio.

Tertius denique est dispensationis litteralis notitiae et historici assensus in evangelium, non generalis fiducia in Deum, et mediante lege contritionis productio.

Nec praeterimus D.

DANNHAVERVM phaenom. IX. praeclare, ut solet, disserentem: Omnis gratia actualis, alias auxilium gratiae attuale, quod non est habitus infusus, sed motus, pulsus, tractus, apertio, Apoc.

III, 20. Act. XVI, 14. Io. VI, 44. est (1) praeveniens ac incipiens, trahens, excitans, invitans, impellens, pulsans, quo intellectum illuminat ad agnitionem et detestationem peccati, repugnantiam originalem tollit, Eph.

V, 14. Apoc. III, 20. (2) operans, aperiens, quae praeter excitationem, assensum, desiderium, vires credendi, propositum conversionis efficit, Luc.

VIII, 13. c. XIII, 17. Act. XIII, 48. c. II, 37. ac cor aperit, Act. XVI, 14. cui, si homo non resistit, sequitur gratia; (3) perficiens Phil.

I, 16.

Audiamus etiam D.

KOENIGIVM in theolog. positiva sic docentem: §. 503. seqq. Conversio fit successive, Marc.

IV, 27. 28. indeque habet suos gradus, in quibus numerandis et nominandis admodum variant doctores.

Nobis primus gradus est, et dicitur gratiae incipientis etc.

Dicitur alias haec gratia praeveniens, strictius sumto termino.

Secundus gradus est gratiae praeparantis etc.

Tertius gradus est gratiae excitantis, quae est universalis divinae affectionis dispensatio, qua Spiritus S. in homine litteralem credendorum notitiam cum assensu historico, vires supernaturales agnoscendi peccatum ex lege, assentiendi salutariter verbo evangelii, et credendi in Christum, mediante verbo, producit, Fuius

hæc exponit D. QVENSTED. system. theolog. part. III. c. VII. p. 45. & addit: Evangelii litteralis cognitio nullo modo absque gratia haberi, multo minus ergo eidem historice quis assentiri potest.

Plures in præsenti non adducemus auctores, sed concludemus verbis Formulæ concordiæ p. 657. Etsi humana ratio, seu naturalis intellectus hominis obscuram aliquam notitiae illius scintillulam reliquam habet, quod sit Deus, & particulam aliquam legis tenet: tamen adeo ignorans, cæca & perversa est ratio illa, ut etiam si ingeniosissimi & doctissimi homines in hoc mundo evangelion de filio Dei, & promissiones divinas de æterna salute legant, vel audiant: tamen ea propriis viribus percipere, intelligere, credere, & vera esse statuere nequeant.

Instantia. Assensus historicus videtur tantum esse humanus, cum assensus divinus fit solum renatorum.

Resp. Assensus historicus non est humanus, quia non testimonio hominum, sed verbo divinitus revelato proxime innititur.

Renatos tamen maiori certitudine verbo divino assentiri, extra omnem dubitationis aleam positum est.

IX. Homo irregenitus sensum grammaticum & externum, ad quem divina illuminatione non indiget, non autem spiritualem & internum percipit.

Docet enim D. QVENSTED. distinguendum esse inter sensum grammaticum & externum, & inter sensum verbi divini spiritualem, internum & divinum. Ille formale est verbi Dei, quatenus verbum est; hic quatenus verbum divinum est: Ille a quovis etiam irregenito percipi potest; hic vero non nisi ab intellectu illuminato.

D. QVENSTED. l. c. verbum divinum considerat bifariam (a) generatim, & in sensu specificativo, quatenus notat verbum, aut sermonem, cum alio quocunque sermone communem, cuius singulæ voces habent suas significationes ex consueto loquendi usu diiudicandas; (b) speciatim, & in sensu reduplicativo, quatenus notat verbum divinum, sive θεόπνευστον salutis medium, ratione essentiæ supernaturale, vique supernaturali instructum. Verbi divini generatim & specificative considerati, prout est verbum cum quovis alio verbo commune, sensus est, quem voces in propria & nativa significatione gignunt, licet intentioni Spiritus S. non conveniat.

Dicitur alias sensus litteræ. Verbi autem divini speciatim & reduplicative spectati sensus est, quem Spiritus S. vocibus θεοπνεύστοις proxime intendit, diciturque logicus & internus, in oppositione ad grammaticum & externum; litteralis, in oppositione ad sensum mysticum; spiritualis & divinus, quia a Spiritu S. proxime intenditur.

Ad cognoscendum sensum grammaticum & externum sufficiunt vires naturales: ad percipiendum sensum litteralem internum, spiritualem & divinum, opus est illuminatione Spiritus S. sive illa illuminatio fit imperfecta, cuius capax est irregenitus, sive perfecta, qua gaudet renatus.

Neque enim D. QVENSTED. per illuminatum hominem præcise intelligit renatum, quamuis illum irregenito opponat: siquidem opposita non semper æqualis sunt latitudinis.

Caue autem, hunc auctorem l. c. per sensum spiritualem intelligere mysticum sensum; quia disertis verbis docet, sensum mysticum ἀκύρως, & minus accurate sensum scripturæ dici, fol. 130.

Ceterum vnius dicti biblici vnum esse sensum genuinum litteralem, & divinum a Spiritu S. intentum, plurimis argumentis condocefacit D. QVENSTED. fol. 132. Adiice, quod aliud fit sensus verborum scripturæ, aliud notitia de illo sensu, animo lectoris impressa.

Quamuis sensus litteralis (logice dictus) fit spiritualis, i. e. Spiritus S. verbis θεοπνεύστοις, notitia tamen de illo scripturæ sensu est vel litteralis, eaque tum externa, tum interna, vel spiritualis; quippe quæ distinguuntur, ut actus mentis, & ipsius obiectum.

Qui distinctissima hæc confundit, ille non perspicue, sed confuse docet.

X. Homo irregenitus, sub gratia divina assistente & pulsante constitutus (v. gr. Iudæus vel gentilis conuertendus) non potest solido conceptu & assensu verba scripturæ percipere & comprobare; quia non certo credit θεοπνευστίαν, fiue diuinam originem scripturæ. Et licet hæc per κριτήρια quædam probetur, illa tamen opinionem & fidem humanam tantum gignunt.

Resp. Iudæus θεοπνευστίαν V. T. e quo conuinci potest, certo credit, Quod autem attinet ad hominem gentilem conuertendum, ille κριτηρίοις externis præparatur & permouetur ad scripturam sacram cum studio & desiderio legendam & meditandam. Quam cum attente legit & meditatur, κριτηρίοις internis, in primis insita S. scripturæ efficacia, conuincitur ad agnoscendam diuinam eius originem. Hac præsupposita, & studio legendi ac meditandi scripturam continuato, genuinum dictorum biblicorum sensum eruit, percipit, & solido assensu comprobat.

XI. Lux notitiæ, per illuminationem diuinam accensa, est lux ardens, & calefaciens voluntatem ad fiduciam in Christum, & amorem in Deum & proximum. Atqui lux notitiæ litteralis non est ardens, neque calefaciens &c. Resp. (1) ad maiorem. Lux notitiæ per illuminationem diuinam accensa est ardens, & calefaciens voluntatem, nisi impedimentum aliquod ei obiciatur. Haud infrequenter vsu venit, vt ardentis ignis efficacia impediatur, quo minus lignum confestim accendat, ideo, quod iusto madidius est. (2) Ad minorem, Lux notitiæ litteralis non est tantum lucens, sed etiam ardens & calefaciens, eo quod voluntatem proxime inflammat ad desiderium & propositum conuersionis, & consequenter ad detestationem peccati, ad fidem in Christum, ad amorem Dei & proximi.


### Q. XXIII

How is theology, viewed according to the method of treatment, divided? Revealed theology, considered according to the method of treatment, is either exegetical, which is occupied with explaining the sayings of Scripture, or positive, which proposes to the assembly of learners certain theses taken from Scripture; and it is both didactic, which elucidates and confirms the articles of faith proposed in a becoming order, and moral, which hands down the precepts of morals; or it is historical, which recounts the history of the Church and explains how in it the doctrine of the Gospel was propagated by the orthodox, impugned by heretics, and defended both by councils and by faithful teachers by voice and writings. Obs.

Homiletics can be referred to exegetical theology, inasmuch as it also explains the biblical text, with special application added, so that the holy assembly may take salutary fruit from the exegesis of the biblical text. Catechetical theology is to be recalled to didactic theology, since the catechism is also a small system succinctly and clearly embracing things to be believed and things to be done. Casuistical theology, which resolves doubtful cases of conscience occurring regarding the morals of men, belongs to moral theology, as does politico-ecclesiastical theology, or that of ecclesiastical government, which is occupied with ecclesiastical discipline, visitation, synods, consistorial matters, etc.

Latin:

Theologia reuelata, qua modum tractandi considerata, est vel exegetica, quæ in explicandis scripturæ dictis occupatur, vel positiva, quæ discentium cœtui certas theses e scriptura sumtas proponit; estque tum didactica, quæ articulos fidei decenti ordine propositos enucleat & confirmat, tum moralis, quæ præcepta morum tradit; vel est historica, quæ historiam ecclesiæ recenset, & quomodo in ea doctrina euangelii ab orthodoxis propagata, ab hæreticis impugnata, & tam a conciliis, quam a fidelibus doctoribus voce & scriptis defensa sit, exponit.

Obs. Ad theologiam exegeticam referri potest homiletica, vtpote quæ etiam textum biblicum explicat, addita speciali applicatione, vt cœtus sacer e textus biblici exegesi salutarem fructum capiat. Ad theologiam didacticam reuocanda est theologia catechetica, cum etiam catechismus sit paruum systema succincte & perspicue complectens credenda & agenda. Ad theologiam moralem pertinet theologia casualis, quæ dubios conscientiæ casus circa mores hominum occurrentes enodat, & theologia politico-ecclesiastica, siue regiminis ecclesiastici, quæ versatur circa disciplinam ecclesiasticam, visitationem, synodos, consistorialia &c.


### Q. XXIV

By scholastic theology is understood either in a general sense systematic theology drawn from the revealed Word of God and accustomed to be taught in the schools of Christians, in which both the dogmas of faith are explained methodically digested with the precepts of morals, and arisen controversies are ventilated and decided, which I maintain ought to be diligently taught in higher and lower schools (a); or by scholastic theology is understood specifically the theology of those teachers who, not so much from the sacred letters as from the opinions of the fathers and the writings of the philosophers, primarily Aristotle, [derive] the dogmas of faith [from] the sacred, than from the opinions of the fathers, and the writings of the philosophers, primarily Aristotle, the dogmas

to explain the faith, and have attempted to raise curious questions, which I judge to be unnecessary for a cultivator of theology , although it may be useful for the refutation of popish errors .

Prob. a. In theological systems, the articles of faith derived from the sacred letters are proposed to man, a wayfarer corrupted by sins, in a neat order, the knowledge of which is necessary for a man about to attain eternal salvation. For this reason, the Christian church has long since used systems of theology. The Apostolic, Nicene, Constantinopolitan, Chalcedonian, and Athanasian Creeds are brief systems of theology. In the second century, JUSTIN wrote an exposition of the faith; in the third, Lactantius wrote books of divine institutions; in the fourth, ATHANASIUS wrote a synopsis of the whole scripture, CYRIL of Jerusalem a catechesis, GREGORY of Nazianzus on theology, as well as on the faith of the Nicene synod; in the fifth, AUGUSTINE wrote the Enchiridion; in the sixth, FULGENTIUS wrote on the faith to Peter the Deacon; in the eighth, JOHN OF DAMASCUS wrote on the orthodox faith: others I pass over in silence. Prob. b.

Lanfranc, in the eleventh century, laid a foundation for scholastic theology—gathered from the opinions of the fathers and the writings of philosophers—that was truly ruinous; upon this, in the twelfth century, Peter Lombard and Albert the Great built their own style of teaching, more curious than fruitful, whom others followed in a dense throng, vying with one another.

The orthodox church rightly and deservedly disapproves of that scholastic theology, because (1) having abandoned the principle of theology αὐτοῦ, or domestic, and that infallibly certain (the divine word), it gathers doubtful and by no means certain opinions from the fathers. (2) It mixes into theology the human writings of Aristotle, which are filled with many errors. (3) It affects thorny subtleties and raises curious, foolish, and unlearned questions, 2 Tim. II, 23. (4) It is split into various sects, by which the mind is not stabilized, but distracted. (5) It makes even the easiest things difficult to understand with barbaric and most inept terms. (6) It omits dogmas necessary to be believed and precepts necessary to be observed.

Prob. c. Since scholastic doctors possess significant authority in the Roman church, it is permitted to refute the errors of the papists from these same sources, which the most accurate theologians HÜLSEMANN, DORSCHAEUS, DANNHAVERUS, MUSAEUS, SCHERZERUS, and others have accomplished by the work itself. Indeed, Scotus suggests arguments against transubstantiation; Ockham, against the tyranny of the pope; Durandus, against the merits of works; Nicolaus de Orbellis, for the majesty of scripture against the innovators, etc. Conf. D. JOH. ADAM. OSIANDER, Theol. posit. acroamat. Part I, p. 67.

Latin:

Per theologiam scholasticam intelligitur vel sensu generali theologia systematica e verbo Dei reuelato hausta, & in scholis christianorum tradi sueta, in qua tum dogmata fidei cum præceptis morum methodice digesta explicantur, tum exortæ controuersiæ ventilantur, & deciduntur, quam in scholis superioribus & inferioribus sedulo docendam esse statuo (a); vel per theologiam scholasticam speciatim intelligitur theologia eorum doctorum, qui non tam e litteris sacris, quam sententiis patrum, & scriptis philosophorum, in primis Aristotelis, dogmata fidei sacris, quam fententiis patrum, & scriptis philosophorum, in primis Aristotelis, dogmata

fidei explicare, & curiosas quaestiones mouere conati sunt, quam cultori theologiae non necessariam esse censeo , quamuis utilis esse queat ad confutationem errorum pontificiorum .

Prob. a. In systematibus theologicis homini viatori peccatis corrupto articuli fidei e litteris sacris deducti concinno ordine proponuntur, quorum cognitio necessaria est homini aeternam salutem adepturo. Propterea ecclesia christiana iam dudum systematibus theologiae vsa est. Symbolum apostolicum, Nicenum, Constantinopolitanum, Chalcedonense, Athanasianum, sunt breuia theologiae systemata. Scripsit seculo II, IVSTINVS expositionem fidei, seculo III, Lactantius libros institutionum diuinarum, seculo IV, ATHANASIVS synopsin totius scripturae, CYRILLVS Hierosolymitanus catechesin, GREGORIVS Nazianzenus de theologia, item de fide Nicenae synodi, seculo V, AVGVSTINVS enchiridion, seculo VI, FVL GENTIVS de fide ad Petrum Diaconum, seculo VIII, IOANNES DAMASCENVS de fide orthodoxa: alios silentio praetereo.

Prob. b. Theologiae scholasticae e sententiis patrum & scriptis philosophorum congestae fundamentum sane quam ruinosum iecit Lanfrancus, seculo XI, cui seculo XII, Petrus Lombardus & Albertus magnus suum docendi genus, curiosum magis quam fructuosum, superstruxerunt, quos denso agmine certatim alii secuti sunt.

Ecclesia orthodoxa scholastica isthac theologia iure meritoque improbatur, quia (1) relicto theologiae principio αὐτοῦ, siue domestico, eoque infallibiliter certo (verbo diuino) e patribus colligit sententias dubias, minimeque certas. (2) Theologiae immiscet scripta Aristotelis humana multisque erroribus referta. (3) Spinosas affectat subtilitates, mouetque curiosas, stultas & ineruditas quaestiones, 2 Tim. III, 23. (4) In varias scinditur sectas, quibus animus non stabilitur, sed distrahitur. (5) Vocibus barbaris & ineptissimis facillima quaeque reddit intellectu difficilia. (6) Dogmata creditu & praecepta obseruatu necessaria omittit.

Prob. c. Cum in ecclesia romana doctores scholastici insigni polleant auctoritate, ex iisdem errores pontificiorum confutare licet, quod opere ipso praestiterunt theologi accuratissimi HÜLSEMANNVS, DORSCHAEVS, DANNHAVERVS, MVSAEVS, SCHERZERVS, & alii. Suggerit sane Scotus argumenta contra transubstantiationem, Occamus, contra pontificis tyrannidem, Durandus, contra operum merita, Nicolaus de Orbellis, pro scripturae maiestate contra nouatores &c. Conf. D. IOAN. ADAM. OSIANDRI theol. posit. acroamat. part. I. p. 67. Quæst. XXV.


### Q. XXV. What is your opinion concerning mystical theology?

Pure and orthodox mystical theology, drawn from the most limpid fountain of the divine word without the admixture of the filth of gentile philosophy, is most useful to the Christian church, and is comprised partly under didactic theology and partly under moral theology . However, impure and heterodox mystical theology does not benefit, but hinders, the truth to be established from heaven .

Nevertheless, the falsity of popish doctrine can be refuted to a certain extent from the same. Prob. a. Pure and orthodox mystical theology is biblical, inasmuch as it is sought solely from the divinely revealed word reduced into letters, for the present state of the church, to this end: that the human mind, withdrawn from earthly things, may know itself thoroughly, deny itself as known, place all confidence of salvation in Christ the mediator, be justified not by the merits of its own works but by the most precious merit of Christ, be betrothed to him, be united to the Holy Trinity, adorned with the image of God, burn with love of God and neighbor, continually commend itself to God the thrice-best by pious prayers, grow in faith and piety, enjoy the peace and joy of the Holy Spirit, and take a foretaste of heavenly blessedness.

Latin:

Theologia mystica pura & orthodoxa e limpidissimo verbi diuini fonte fine admixtis sordibus philosophiae gentilis hausta, ecclesia christiane est utilissima, & partim sub theologia didactica, partim sub theologia morali comprehenditur . Theologia autem mystica impura & heterodoxa veritati coelesti adstruenda non prodest, sed obest .

Falsitas tamen doctrinae pontificiae ex eadem quadantenus refelli potest . Prob. a. Theologia mystica pura & orthodoxa est biblica, quippe quae unice e verbo diuinitus reuelato & in litteras redacto pro hodierno statu ecclesiae eo fine petitur, vt mens humana a rebus terrenis abstracta seipsam penitus cognoscat, se cognitam abneget, omnem salutis fiduciam in Christo mediatore collocet, non propriorum operum meritis, sed pretiosissimo merito Christi iustificetur, eidem despondeatur, S. S. Triadi vniatur, imagine Dei exornetur, amore Dei & proximi flagret, piis precibus se Deo ter optimo iugiter commendet, fide ac pietate crescat, pace & gaudio Spiritus S. fruatur, & coelestis beatitudinis praegustum capiat.


### Q. XXVII

Conf. D. SONTAGII fanaticism. p. 88. D. VALENTINVS ERNESTVS LOESCHERVS exposed an epitome of orthodox mystical theology to the public light. Proof b. Impure mystical theology mixes the pagan philosophy of Hermes Trismegistus, Pythagoras, and Plato with biblical theology.

Not without reason, says M.

GVNTHER. in dissertation on the quietists §. 7. p. 14. The apostle Paul and the other apostles came, following the example of the Savior, not in the wisdom of words, but in simplicity, 1 Cor.

I. 17. lest their conversion be considered a human work. But to many, this simplicity was distasteful, and they looked back to the ancient philosophers of the Gentiles.

The philosophy of these men, confused with sacred dogmas, added two others to the simple theology unadulterated by ethnicism: the mystical and the scholastic, of which the one, by a certain holiness that strips the will of sins, and the other, by a subtlety that strips the intellect of ignorance, captivated the unwary into self-love. The former is a derivative of Platonic philosophy, the latter of Aristotelian.

(2) Mystical theology is the mother of spiritual pride.

For mystics, while contemplating, look down upon others with a high brow, and presume that they are progressing to such a degree of perfection that they are "christified" and "deified." Having detested this pride, LUTHER wrote considerately in tom. II. Ien. latin. fol. 53: "Everywhere, both from Italy and Germany, the commentaries of Dionysius on mystical theology are circulated, which is to say, mere incitements to a swelling and self-displaying knowledge."

And on Genesis chap. XIX. fol. 134: "Gerson wrote about the speculative life and adorns it with great titles; and the unskilled, when they read such things, embrace them as divine oracles."

But in truth, as the proverb says, the treasure is coals. Therefore, whether these vain speculators call you external or civil, let nothing move you.

Go, give thanks to God for the Word and these external things, and leave those bombastic speculations to others. Proof c. From impure mystical theology, such as that of the monks in the papacy, one may argue κατ’ ἄνθρωπον (according to man) against the merits of works, the opus operatum, the freedom of the will in spiritual matters, and the authority of the Roman pontiff.

Conf. D. LOESCHERI appendix I. to mystical theology p. 863. seqq. Question XXVI. By what means does a student of theology attain to a solid knowledge of divine things?

By three means: prayer (a), meditation (b), temptation (c).

Prayer begins the theological study, meditation continues it, temptation consolidates it. Proof a. from James

I, 5. If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all simply, and does not reproach: and it shall be given to him. Heavenly wisdom is drawn from the fountain of wisdom, God, who gives it ἁπλῶς (simply), i.e., candidly, not reproaching like the envious, but prompt to give to those who seek it with true confidence.

Proof b.

It is the theologian's duty to ἐρευνᾶν τὰς γραφάς (search the scriptures), John

V, 39.

Miners of metals investigate the innermost caverns of the earth so that they may possess the desired gold: the student of theology searches the rich veins of Holy Scripture so that he may seek for himself the precious gold of theosophy.

Conf.

Ps. I, 2. Proof c. from Sir.

XXXIV, 10. He who has not been tempted knows little.

No one weighs more deeply and knows more solidly the power, grace, wisdom, and truth of God than he who is frequently harassed by Satan and the world.

Question XXVII. What aids promote the meditation of the theologian?

Two aids promote the meditation of the theologian: (a) knowledge of the Hebrew and Greek languages, and (b) a moderate study of philosophy. Proof a.

The primary study of the theologian is biblical, because the sacred codex is as it were a treasury, from which the treasure of heavenly wisdom is sought.

The whole codex is divided into Testament: which are recorded in the Hebrew idiom, and of the New Testament, which are consigned in the Greek language.

For investigating the sense of the writings of the O. T. a knowledge of the Hebrew language is conducive: just as for understanding the N. T. a proficiency in the Greek language is required. Indeed, various versions of the Bible exist, yet the sources are necessary, (1) so that everyone, especially the learned, may be more certain that the sources are thus, and not otherwise; (2) so that concerning controversies that have arisen, one may pronounce his opinion with a firm conscience, which will never happen unless the sources are inspected; (3) because there will never be any version absolutely perfect in all respects; (4) because for a solid explanation of dogmas it is necessary to know the phrases of the sources.

Prob. b. Philosophy is a kind of cultivation of the mind, freeing it from innate rusticity, and preparing it to grasp more subtle things, and to vindicate true dogmas from the sophistries of adversaries. Philosophy provides significant utility (1) to exegetical theology. For certain biblical statements comprise mixed articles of faith, which become known not only from the light of supernatural revelation, but also to some extent from the light of reason, e.g., mixed articles are concerning God considered absolutely, concerning divine attributes, concerning creation and providence, concerning the parts of man, concerning the origin of the soul, concerning voluntary and involuntary sin, etc. (2) To polemical theology. For the enemies of truth strive to destroy the highest articles of faith from the principles of reason, e.g., the mystery of the Trinity, of the incarnation, of justification by the merit of Christ, of the Holy Supper, etc. The theologian, well-versed in philosophical disciplines, easily refutes these sophistries. Let us briefly and concisely survey the philosophical disciplines.

Modal philosophy, or logic, shows the theologian the method of arguing, demonstrating, defining, dividing, and methodically proposing theological dogmas.

Physics opens the book of nature, so that from creatures we may recognize the creator, from the series of natural things the governor. It also treats not a few things concerning place, concerning the soul, concerning the human intellect, the knowledge of which is profitable to the theologian.

Metaphysics teaches what is principle, cause, effect, necessary, contingent, eternal, independent, infinite, exemplar, image, substance, person, accident: which technical terms are scattered throughout all theological topics.

Moral philosophy elucidates both the law of nature and the principles of moral actions, from which prohairetic and involuntary sins are distinguished.

It is also useful for the cultivator of theology to touch upon the mathematical sciences. Astronomy is useful for knowing the stars, of which the sacred code makes mention: Chronology for calculating times: Geography for observing the journeys of the patriarchs, Israelites, prophets, Christ, and the apostles.

The knowledge of history commends itself by its fruits overflowing into the theologian. For the Old Testament is for the most part consigned in the manner of some historical writing. The New

The New Testament recounts the sayings and deeds of Christ and the apostles. If civil and ecclesiastical history be added to these, the knowledge of the Old and New Testament will be richer.

Latin:

Conf. D. SONTAGII fanaticism. p. 88. Theologiae mysticae orthodoxae epitomen publicae luci exposuit D. VALENTINVS ERNESTVS LOESCHERVS. Prob. b. Theologia mystica impura theologiae biblicae gentilem Hermetis, Trismegisti, Pythagorae, & Platonis philosophiam immiscet.

Haud ex vano inquit M.

GVNTHER. in dissertat. de quietistis §. 7. p. 14. Veniebant apostolus Paullus, & ceteri apostoli ad exemplum saluatoris non in sapientia, sed simplicitate verbi, 1 Cor.

I. 17. ne conuersio eorum humana censeretur opus. At multis haec simplicitas fordebat, & respiciebant ad veteres gentilium sapientes.

Horum philosophia, sacris dogmatibus confusa, simplici & ab ethnicismo non adulteratae theologiae duas alias apposuit, mysticam, & scholasticam, quarum altera sanctimonia quadam, quae voluntatem peccatis; altera subtilitate, quae intellectum inscitia exuat, in amorem sui rapuit incautos. Illa Platonica, haec Aristotelica philosophia tradux est.

(2) Theologia mystica est mater superbiae spiritualis.

Etenim mystici contemplantes alios alto supercilio despiciunt, & eo perfectionis se progredi autumant, vt christificentur & deificentur. Quam superbiam detestatus LVTHERVS considerate scripsit tom. II. Ien. latin. fol. 53. Passim circumferuntur tum ex Italia, tum Germania commentaria Dionysii super theologiam mysticam, hoc est, mera irritabula inflaturae & seipsam ostentaturae scientiae.

Et in Genesin cap. XIX. fol. 134. Gerson scripsit de vita speculatiua, ac ornat eam magnis titulis; ac imperiti, cum legunt talia, amplectuntur ea pro diuinis oraculis.

Sed reuera, ut in prouerbio dicitur, thesaurus carbones. Igitur seu externum, seu ciuilem te appellant vani speculatores isti, nihil te moueat.

Age tu Deo gratias pro verbo & externis istis, & relinque ampullosas istas speculationes aliis. Prob. c. Ex theologia mystica etiam impura, qualis est monachorum in papatu, κατ’ ἄνθρωπον argumentari licet aduersus operum merita, opus operatum, libertatem arbitrii in spiritualibus, & auctoritatem pontificis romani.

Conf. D. LOESCHERI appendicem I. theologiae mysticae p. 863. seqq. Quaest. XXVI. Quibus subleuatus mediis studiosus theologiae pertingit ad solidam rerum diuinarum cognitionem?

Tribus mediis, oratione (a), meditatione (b), tentatione (c).

Oratio studium theologicum inchoat, meditatio continuat, tentatio consolidat. Prob. a. ex Iac.

I, 5. Si quis vestrum indiget sapientia, petito a Deo, qui dat omnibus simpliciter, & non exprobrat: & dabitur ipsi. Depromitur sapientia coelestis ex fonte sapientiae, Deo, qui eam dat ἁπλῶς, i. e. candide, non inuidutorum more exprobrans, sed promptus ad dandum vera cum fiducia eam expetentibus.

Prob. b.

Theologi est ἐρευνᾶν τὰς γραφάς, Io.

V, 39.

Metallorum fossores intimas terrae cauernas peruestigant, vt desiderato potiantur auro: studiosus theologiae diuites sacrae scripturae venas rimatur, vt pretiosum theosophiae aurum sibi quaerat.

Conf.

Ps. I, 2. Prob. c. ex Sir.

XXXIV, 10. Qui non tentatus est, pauca scit.

Nemo penitius expendit, & solidius nouit Dei potentiam, gratiam, sapientiam & veritatem, quam crebro a satana & mundo diuexatus.

Quaest. XXVII. Quenam adminicula meditationem theologi promouent?

Duo adminicula meditationem theologi promouent (a), notitia hebraeae & graecae linguarum (b), moderatumque philosophiae studium. Prob. a.

Potissimum theologi studium est biblicum, quia sacer codex est quasi gazophylacium, e quo thesaurus sapientiae coelestis petitur.

Diuiditur totus codex in veteris testamenti: quae idiomate hebraeo, & noui testamenti, quae lingua graeca consignata sunt.

Ad indagandum sensum scriptorum V. T. conducit notitia linguae hebraeae: sicut ad intelligentiant N. T. requiritur peritia linguae graecae. Exstant quidem variae bibliorum versiones, fontes tamen necessarii sunt, (1) vt certior reddatur quilibet, praesertim litteratus, fontes ita habere, & non aliter; (2) vt de exortis controuersiis firma conscientia aliquis sententiam suam pronunciare possit, quod nunquam fiet, nisi fontibus inspectis; (3) quia nunquam ulla erit versio omnibus numeris absoluta; (4) quia ad dogmatum explicationem solidam necesse est cognosci phrases fontium.

Prob. b. Philosophia est quasi cultura quaedam animi, hunc liberans a connata rusticitate, eundemque praeparans ad capiendum res subtiliores, & ad vindicandum vera dogmata a strophis aduersariorum. Vtilitatem insignem praestat philosophia (1) theologiae exegeticae. Complectuntur enim quaedam dicta biblica articulos fidei mixtos, qui non tantum e lumine supernaturalis reuelationis, sed etiam quadantenus e lumine rationis innotescunt, v. gr. articuli mixti sunt de Deo absolute considerato, de attributis diuinis, de creatione & prouidentia, de partibus hominis, de origine animae, de peccato uoluntario & inuoluntario &c. (2) Theologiae polemicae. Nam hostes ueritatis a principiis rationis destruere nituntur summos fidei articulos v. gr. mysterium Trinitatis, incarnationis, iustificationis per meritum Christi, S. coenae &c. Quas ratiunculas theologus philosophicis disciplinis praecultus haud difficulter discutit. Liceat nobis breuiter atque strictim disciplinas philosophicas percurrere.

Philosophia modalis, siue logica, commonstrat theologo modum argumentandi, demonstrandi, definiendi, diuidendi, & methodice dogmata theologica proponendi.

Physica pandit librum naturae, vt ex creaturis creatorem, ex serie rerum naturalium gubernatorem agnoscamus. Tractat eadem haud pauca de loco, de anima, de intellectu humano, quorum notitia theologo proficua est.

Metaphysica docet, quid sit principium, caussa, effectus, necessarium, contingens, aeternum, independens, infinitum, exemplar, imago, substantia, persona, accidens: qui termini technici per omnes locos theologicos sparguntur.

Philosophia moralis, tum legem naturae, tum principia actionum moralium enucleat, e quibus peccata proaeretica & inuoluntaria dignoscuntur.

Mathematicae etiam attingere scientias e re est cultoris theologiae. Vtilis est astronomia ad cognoscendas stellas, quarum memoriam facer codex iniicit: Chronologia ad supputanda tempora: Geographia ad obseruanda itinera patriarcharum, Israelitarum, prophetarum, Christi & apostolorum.

Historiae notitia suis se fructibus in theologum redundantibus commendat. Nam uetus testamentum maiori ex parte per modum alicuius scripti historici consignatum est. Nouum

Novum testamentum dicta & facta Christi, atque apostolorum recenset. Quibus si accedat historia civilis & ecclesiastica, notitia veteris & novi testamenti erit uberior.


### Q. XXVIII. Is philosophy contrary to theology?

Philosophy is not contrary to, nor does it contradict, revealed theology. Proof. Philosophy is the science of truth. But just as truth does not contradict truth, so philosophical truth does not impugn theological truth.

You say I. Philosophy openly contradicts theology. For philosophy teaches that there are as many essences as there are persons; that nothing comes from nothing; that a virgin does not give birth. Theology teaches otherwise. Resp. Distinguish between true and apparent contradiction. The following statements are not truly contradictory: "As many as are the finite persons, so many are the essences," teaches philosophy: "three infinite persons are in one essence," asserts theology. "From nothing, nothing is made," by the powers of nature: "from nothing, something is made," by the immense power of God. "A virgin does not give birth," according to the ordinary course of nature: "the Virgin Mary gives birth," on account of the supernatural and extraordinary ἐπίλευσιν [overshadowing] of the Holy Spirit.

You say II. St. Paul warns in Col. 2:8: "See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deceit." Resp. The apostle is not speaking of true philosophy, which is according to Christ; but of false philosophy, which is not according to Christ, and which was sectarian, surviving in Paul's time in the schools of the Gentiles, which were frequented in Greece and Asia, and were worn out by use: such as the Platonic, Aristotelian, Epicurean, and Stoic, which the apostle calls empty and deceptive. And because the Jews, together with the pseudo-apostles, were mixing the tenets of the Greek philosophers with their own traditions, St. Paul adds, "according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world," which are external ceremonies, Gal. 4:9. Iacob. Mart. de constit. theol., p.m. 121, shows from the context that the apostle in that place is censuring the traditions and false opinions of the Pharisees, Essenes, and Sadducees concerning the law of God.

Latin:

Philosophia non contrariatur aut contradicit theologiae revelatae. Prob. Philosophia est scientia veritatis. At sicut verum vero non contradicit: ita veritas philosophica theologicam non impugnat.

Dicis I. Philosophia theologiae palam contradicit. Docet namque philosophia tot esse essentias, quot sunt personae; ex nihilo nihil fieri; virginem non parere. Secus docet theologia. Resp. Dist. inter contradictionem veram & apparentem. Sequentes enunciationes non sunt vere contradictoriae: Quot sunt personae finitae, tot sunt essentiae, docent te philosophia: tres personae infinitae sunt in vna essentia, afferente theologia. Ex nihilo nihil fit, viribus naturae: ex nihilo aliquid fit, immensa virtute Dei. Virgo non parit secundum ordinarium naturae cursum: Virgo Maria parit propter ἐπίλευσιν Spiritus S. supernaturalem & extraordinariam.

Dicis II. S. Paullus monet Col. II, 8. Videte, ne quis sit vos depraedans per philosophiam & vanam fraudem. Resp. Non est sermo apostolo de philosophia vera, quae est secundum Christum; sed de philosophia falsa, quae non est secundum Christum, & sectaria, superstite Paullo, in gentilium scholis, quae in Graecia & Asia frequentabantur, vsu trita: qualis erat Platonica, Aristotelica, Epicurea, Stoica, quam vanam & deceptricem apostolus appellat. Et quia Iudaei vna cum pseudo-apostolis philosophorum graecorum placita suis traditionibus immiscebant, addit S. Paullus, iuxta traditionem hominum, iuxta elementa mundi, quae sunt externae ceremoniae, Gal. IV, 9. Iacob. Mart. de constit. theol. p.m. 121. ex contextu ostendit, apostolum l. c. Pharisaeorum, Essenorum, & Sadducaeorum traditiones & falsas opiniones de lege Dei taxare.


### Q. XXIX. What is opposed to true theology?

Opposed to true theology is false theology, which is more correctly called mataeology [vain-theology] than theology. Such is ethnic, Turkish, Jewish, Samaritan, heretical, schismatic, syncretistic, and skeptical mataeology.

Ethnic mataeology is the knowledge of God implanted by the light of nature and indeed drawn from the inspection of creatures, but, because of the lack of revealed light, it is mixed with horrible darkness and changed into fables, Rom. 1:25. It was threefold: the mythical of the poets, the civil of the priests, and the physical in the schools of the philosophers. This last is closer to our natural theology. Yet, as it is found among the Gentile philosophers, it is defiled by grave errors.

Turkish or Mahometan mataeology is a false doctrine concerning God and divine things written by Mahomet, set forth in the Alcoran, and received by the Turks, who in a certain way acknowledge Christ, but blasphemously pervert his doctrine. Notes: (1) The author of the Alcoran was Mahomet the Ishmaelite, who lived in the 7th century, whose assistants were Sergius the Arian, John the Nestorian, and a certain Jew. (2) Mahomet concedes in the Alcoran that the Messiah has come, that he was born of a virgin, that Christ is a holy man and a great prophet. But he denies the deity of Christ, rejects the mystery of the Trinity, [claims] the Holy Spirit is a creature, and trifles that Christ is the soul of God. Furthermore, he urges circumcision, allows polygamy, and measures the happiness of eternal life by the pleasures of the flesh.

Jewish mataeology is a false doctrine concerning God, which is contained chiefly in the Talmud; it denies the coming of the Messiah, rejects the writings of the N.T., with various glosses distorts the oracles of the O.T., especially those concerning the H.S.

Trinitate & Messia agunt, impie depravat. They treat of the Trinity and the Messiah, [and] impiously pervert [them].

One must distinguish between the ancient theology of the Jews and the modern. The former was indeed divine, the latter is full of execrable blasphemies.

Mataologia samaritana is an erroneous opinion, connecting the doctrine of the Jews with the infidelity of the heathens. It takes its name from the Gentiles brought to Samaria, who both worshipped their own gods and judged that worship was to be rendered to the true God of Israel, mixing Gentilism with the Jewish religion.

Mataologia hæretica is a doctrine concerning God, [and] errors undermining the foundation of the faith. Note (a): αἵρεσις is derived from αἱρέω, I choose, and by the force of the word it is a certain choice including two acts: (1) an erroneous judgment of the intellect; for without the judgment of the intellect there is no choice: (2) an act of the will, by which one thing is preferred to another. For in heresy one opinion, but an erroneous one, is preferred to another, namely the true one. Heresy is therefore a voluntary error of the intellect, undermining a fundamental article of faith, asserted by one who professes himself to be a Christian. Note (b): Not every man erring concerning the foundation of the faith is called a heretic, but [only] the contumacious and one who is unwilling to be converted. Note (c): One never initiated into the sacraments of the Christians, erring in the foundation of the faith, is not called a heretic, but an infidel.

Mataologia schismatica is a false doctrine concerning God and divine things, by which indeed no article of faith is overturned, yet it strikes gravely at questions related to the faith, and the unity of the church is disturbed. It is said from σχίζω, which signifies I split or I separate, and thus schism by the force of the word signifies a splitting or separation. The word schism is taken either in a general sense or a special one. In the former sense heresy can also be called schism; in the latter sense it is called an error about the faith, not against the faith. Note I. Separation is either by infirmity and ignorance, or joined with pride. The former makes a weak brother, the latter properly makes a schismatic. II. Separation is made either from one or another person, or from the whole church. Paul and Barnabas separated themselves, Acts XV, 39, yet they were not schismatics. III. Separation is either just or unjust. Not the former, but the latter properly makes a schism. IV. Schism is considered either by reason of youthful age, or by reason of mature age, without reason of origin and progress. In the former way it is considered here; in the latter way it degenerates into heresy.

Mataologia syncretistica is an erroneous opinion, persuading a coalition of parties dissenting in the very doctrine of faith and morals, so that they may enter into fraternal and ecclesiastical concord, notwithstanding their dissent. Syncretism descends from σὺν and κρητίζω. PLUTARCH, περὶ τῆς Φιλαδελφίας, says: The Cretans, agitated by frequent seditions and civil wars, when enemies approached from without, entered into peace and society. ERASMUS, chiliad. I. adag. centur. I. p. 27, says: It was called syncretism by a Cretan proverb, as often as it happened that those who just before seemed the bitterest enemies were suddenly reduced to the highest concord, which frequently happens, especially if some common evil has befallen both. But such syncretism is introduced into the church badly. For the peace and concord of the Cretans was feigned, by which quarrels were not removed, but deferred; nor did it proceed from true charity, but only from fear of a common enemy and danger. But indeed it does not deserve the name of ecclesiastical concord, which is not sincere, proceeding from a pure love of truth, and which does not cut off or remove errors undermining the foundation of the faith, but nourishes and retains them.

Mataologia sceptica is that of the neutralists or libertines, who in matters of faith establish or define nothing certain, but either suspend their judgment, or embrace now this, now that, as occasion or necessity brings. The Arminians incline toward the most skeptical, who concerning the chief dogmas of the faith prefer to ἐπέχειν [withhold judgment] rather than to define anything certain.

Quest. XXX. How do theology and faith agree and differ? They agree, because (a) theology, as well as faith, is θεόδοτος [theodotos], or divinely bestowed. See above p. 11. (b) Both are drawn from the revealed word of God, and rest immovably upon it. (c) Both comprise the knowledge and assent of the intellect. (d) Both regard eternal salvation as the ultimate end of man.

They differ thus: (a) theology is a practical habit of the intellect; faith resides also in the will, if you consider trust. (b) Theology is the entire practical habit, including faith as a partial object, and indeed as an intermediate end. (c) From faith a man is called a believer, from theology a theologian. However, the number of believers is far greater than that of theologians.

For recognizing the true agreement of theology and faith, proof a. Theology is wisdom coming from above, Jas. III, 15, descending from the Father of lights. Jas. I, 17. Faith likewise is from God, whose gift it is said to be. Eph. II, 8. Therefore, both agree by reason of their author.

Proof b. The Holy Scriptures make a man wise, or a theologian. 2 Tim. III, 15. The same are written so that we may believe. John XX, 31. Therefore, theology and faith flow from one principle of knowing.

Proof c. Theology is defined by the knowledge of the truth. Tit. I, 1. The first degree of faith is by equal reason the knowledge of salvation. Luke I, 77. Therefore, the seat of both is the intellect.

Proof d. That the ultimate end of theology, no more than that of faith, is eternal salvation, Paul teaches when he writes to Timothy, Bishop of Ephesus, 2 Ep. c. III, 15: Because from infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures, which can make you wise unto salvation, through faith which is in Christ Jesus. Heavenly wisdom, i.e., theology and faith in Christ, regard one end.

To observe the distinction between faith and theology, proof a. Theology is the wisdom of God in a mystery, 1 Cor. II, 7. Faith, however, by reason of its ultimate degree, is hypostasis or trust. Heb. XI, 1. The latter is in the will, wisdom in the intellect.

Proof b. Theology is concerned with God and divine things, among which faith is counted: which together, if we look at the subject of theological operation, is an intermediate end of theology. Therefore, just as the whole that includes and the part that is included, the habit and its end, differ: so do theology and faith differ.

Proof c. A greater light of knowledge is required for theology than for faith. For faith, a simple and plain knowledge of heavenly truth suffices: but theology defends the truth when attacked, and settles controversies arising from canonical scripture.

Quest. XXXI. Is it the duty of every student of theology to make theological controversies known to himself? The study of theological controversies is most necessary for students aspiring to the higher offices of the church (a). It is right that those being moved to lower duties should acquire for themselves some knowledge of controversies (b).

Proof a. It befits a bishop τὰς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν [tas antilegontas elenchein], to refute those who contradict. Tit. I, 9. But one ignorant of theological controversies will stand poorly. b. It is incumbent upon every minister of the church to exhort the hearers entrusted to his skill, that they beware of false prophets.

Matt. VII, 15. Wherefore it is necessary that he know their false doctrine: he knows it, however, from theological controversies.

Furthermore, in even the most contemptible places, the occasion often arises that one must descend into a dispute, either with a certain sectarian or with a hearer seduced by others. Where the minister of the church will prostitute himself and his religion, who has not touched theological controversies even with a light arm.

Obs. I. The end of theological controversies is indeed to be desired, but in this militant church it is not to be expected.

For it is necessary that there be heresies among you (Christians), so that those who are approved may become manifest among you, says St. Paul, 1 Cor. XI, 19. The apostle speaks not of a necessity that is fatal, absolute, and of the consequent, but of a necessity that is hypothetical and of the consequence, assuming, of course, the craftiness of the devil, and the infirmity of men, ignorance of spiritual things, perversity, inconstancy, pride, and a proneness to novelties.

These are the causes of heresies that exist in the church until the consummation of this universe. Wherefore it is the duty of theologians, with the Holy Spirit as their guide, to arm themselves for the wars of the Lord.

Obs. II. Controversies that are useless, thorny, and sprung from the dominion of depraved affections, are unworthy of theological disquisition or laborious discussion.

S I G H. Thee, God the Father, sower of things and fountain of all good, thee, God the Son, sun of grace and justice, thee, Holy Spirit, sanctifier of the souls of the faithful, I humbly worship and beseech, that thou mayest suffuse our infirm minds with the light of heavenly grace, dispel the darkness of errors, hold up a torch for us to search out and find the truth in spiritual matters, so that our theology may be made conformable to the exemplar of thy wisdom, as far as it can be done in this weakness, supported by the most valid protection of the sacred scriptures, the light of faith, the guide of the way to heaven, the teacher of true piety, the expeller of vices!

Latin:

Verae theologiae opponitur theologia falsa, quae rectius mataeologia, quam theologia dicitur. Qualis est mataeologia ethnica, turcica, iudaica, samaritana, haeretica, schismatica, syncretistica, sceptica.

Mataeologia ethnica est notitia de Deo ex lumine naturae insita, & inspectione creaturarum quidem hausta, sed ob defectum luminis revelati horrendis mixta tenebris & in fabulas commutata, Rom. I, 25. Fuit triplex: mythica poetarum, civilis sacerdotum, & physica in scholis philosophorum. Haec vltima propius abest a nostra theologia naturali. Prout tamen apud gentiles philosophos deprehenditur, grauibus foedata est erroribus.

Mataeologia turcica seu mahometana est falsa doctrina de Deo & rebus diuinis a Mahomete conscripta, in alcorano exposita, & a turcis Christum quodammodo agnoscentibus, sed eiusdem doctrinam blaspheme deprauantibus, recepta. Notes (1) auctorem alcorani fuisse Mahometem Ismaelitam, qui vixit seculo VII. cuius paraftatae fuerunt Sergius Arianus, Ioannes Nestorianus, & Iudaeus quidam. (2) Concedit Mahometes in alcorano Messiam venisse, et virgine natum esse, Christum sanctum hominem esse, & prophetam magnum. At negat deitatem Christi, inficiatur mysterium Trinitatis, Spiritum S. creaturam, Christum animam Dei esse nugatur. Praeterea vrget circumcisionem, concedit polygamiam, vitae aeternae felicitatem voluptatibus carnis metitur.

Mataeologia iudaica est falsa de Deo doctrina, quae in talmude praecipue continetur, aduentum Messiae negat, scripta N. T. reprobat, variis commentis oracula V. T. inprimis quae de SS.

Trinitate & Messia agunt, impie depravat.

Distinguendum est inter priscam iudæorum theologiam & hodiernam. Illa vtique fuit diuina, hæc execrandis blasphemiis plena est.

Mataologia samaritana est opinio erronea, doctrinam iudæorum cum infidelitate ethnicorum connectens. Nomen habet a gentilibus Samariam traductis, qui & Deos suos colebant, & vero Deo Israelis cultum esse præstandum censebant, commiscentes gentilismum cum iudaica religione.

Mataologia hæretica est doctrina de Deo, erroribus, fundamentum fidei labefactantibus. Nota (a): αἵρεσις ab αἱρέω, eligo, deducitur, estque vi vocis electio quædam duos actus includens: (1) iudicium intellectus erroneum; nam sine iudicio intellectus non datur electio: (2) actum voluntatis, quo vnum alteri anteponitur. In hæresi enim vna sententia, sed erronea, alteri, nempe veræ, præfertur. Est igitur hæresis voluntarius intellectus error, articulum fidei fundamentalem labefactans, assertus ab eo, qui profitetur, se esse christianum. Nota (b): Non quilibet homo errans circa fundamentum fidei dicitur hæreticus, sed contumax & conuerti nescius. Nota (c): Sacris christianorum nunquam initiatus, errans in fundamento fidei, non vocatur hæreticus, sed infidelis.

Mataologia schismatica est falsa de Deo & rebus diuinis doctrina, qua non quidem articulus fidei conuellitur, in quæstiones tamen fidei agnatas grauiter impingitur, & vnitas ecclesiæ turbatur. Dicitur a σχίζω, quod significat scindo vel separo, adeoque schisma vi vocis significat scissionem vel separationem. Sumitur vox schisma vel sensu generali, vel speciali. Priori sensu etiam hæresis potest dici schisma, posteriori sensu dicitur error circa fidem, non aduersus fidem. Nota I. Separatio est vel infirmitate & ignorantia, vel cum superbia coniuncta. Illa infirmum fratrem, hæc proprie schismaticum facit. II. Separatio fit vel ab vna aut altera persona, vel ab integra ecclesia. Paullus & Barnabas se separarunt, Actor. XV, 39. non tamen fuerunt schismatici. III. Separatio est vel iusta, vel iniusta. Non illa, sed hæc proprie facit schisma. IV. Consideratur schisma vel ratione ætatis iuuenilis, vel ratione ætatis virilis, sine ratione ortus & progressus. Priori modo h.l. consideratur, posteriori modo degenerat in hæresin.

Mataologia syncretistica est opinio erronea, suadens coalitionem partium in ipsa fidei & morum doctrina dissidentium, vt fraternam & ecclesiasticam ineant concordiam, non obstante earum dissensu. Descendit syncretismus a σὺν & κρητίζω. PLVTARCHVS περὶ τῆς Φιλαδελφίας inquit: Cretenses crebris seditionibus bellisque ciuilibus agitati, extrinsecus aduentantibus hostibus, pacem & societatem iniuerunt. ERASMVS chiliad. I. adag. centur. I. p. 27. ait: Syncretismum Cretico prouerbio dicebatur, quoties fiebat, vt, qui modo videbantur hostes acerrimi, repente in summam concordiam redigerentur, id quod frequenter euenire solet, maxime si quod malum inciderit vtriusque commune. At male eiusimodi syncretismus in ecclesiam introducitur. Nam pax & concordia Cretensium erat simulata, qua lites non tollebantur, sed differebantur; neque proueniebat ex vera caritate, sed tantum ex metu communis hostis & periculi. At vero nomen ecclesiasticæ concordiæ non meretur, quæ non est sincera ex amore fuci puro profecta, & quæ errores fundamentum fidei conuellentes non resecat aut summovet, sed alit & retinet.

Mataologia sceptica est neutralium siue libertinorum, qui in rebus fidei nihil certi constituunt aut definiunt, sed vel sententiam suam suspendunt, vel modo hanc, modo illam amplectuntur, prout occasio vel necessitas fert. Inclinant in scepticissimum Arminiani, qui de præcipuis fidei dogmatibus malunt ἐπέχειν, quam certi quidquam definire.

Quæst. XXX. Quomodo theologia & fides conueniunt & differunt? Conueniunt, quia (a) tam theologia, quam fides est θεόδοτος, siue diuinitus collata. Vid. supra p. 11. (b) Vtraque ex verbo Dei reuelato hauritur, eidemque immote innititur. (c) Vtraque complectitur notitiam & assensum intellectus. (d) Vtraque respicit æternam salutem, vt finem hominis vltimum.

Differunt ita: (a) theologia est habitus practicus intellectus; fides etiam in voluntate, si spectes fiduciam, residet . (b) Theologia est totus habitus practicus, fidem, vt obiectum partiale, quin etiam vt finem medium, includens. (c) A fide homo denominatur fidelis, a theologia theologus. Longe amplior autem numerus fidelium, quam theologorum.

Ad veram conuenientiam theologiæ, & fidei cognoscendam, prob. a. Theologia est sapientia superne veniens, Iac. III, 15. descendens a patre luminum. Iac. I, 17. Fides itidem est a Deo, cuius donum dicitur. Eph. II, 8. Conuenit ergo vtraque ratione auctoris.

Prob. b. Sacræ litteræ reddunt hominem sapientem, siue theologum. 2 Tim. III, 15. Eædem scriptæ sunt, vt credamus. Io. XX, 31. E. theologia & fides fluunt ex vno principio cognoscendi.

Prob. c. Theologia definitur per cognitionem veritatis. Tit. I, 1. Fidei primus gradus pari ratione est cognitio salutis. Luc. I, 77. E. vtriusque sedes est intellectus.

Prob. d. Theologiæ non magis, quam fidei, vltimum finem esse æternam salutem, docet Paullus, cum ad Timotheum, episcopum Ephesinum, scribit 2 Ep. c. III, 15. Quia ab infantia sacras litteras nosti, quæ possunt te sapientem reddere in salutem, per fidem, quæ in Christo Iesu est. Sapientia cœlestis, i. e. theologia & fides in Christum, respiciunt vnum finem.

Ad obseruandum discrimen fidei, & theologiæ, prob. a. theologia est sapientia Dei in mysterio, 1 Cor. II, 7. Fides autem ratione vltimi gradus est hypostasis seu fiducia. Hebr. XI, 1. Hæc est in voluntate, sapientia in intellectu.

Prob. b. Theologia versatur circa Deum & res diuinas, e quarum censu est fides: Quæ insimul, si spectemus subiectum operationis theologicæ, est finis intermedius theologiæ. Idcirco, sicut differt totum includens & pars inclusa, habitus & eius finis: ita differunt theologia & fides.

Prob. c. Ad theologiam maius lumen cognitionis requiritur, quam ad fidem. Ad fidem sufficit simplex & plana veritatis cœlestis cognitio: at theologia veritatem oppugnatam defendit, & ex scriptura canonica exortas controuersias dirimit.

Quæst. XXXI. An cuiusuis studiosi theologiæ est, controuersias theologicas sibi cognitas reddere? Studium controuersiarum theologicarum maxime necessarium est studiosis adspirantibus ad sublimiora ecclesiæ officia (a). Admouendi muneribus inferioribus aliqualem controuersiarum notitiam sibi comparent, par est (b).

Prob. a. Episcopum decet τὰς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν, contradicentes redarguere. Tit. I, 9. Sed male stabit ignarus controuersiarum theologicarum. Prob. b. Cuilibet ecclesiae ministro incumbit auditores dexteritati suae concreditos cohortari, ut sibi caveant a falsis prophetis.

Matth. VII, 15. Quamobrem necesse est, ut eorum falsam doctrinam cognoscat: cognoscit autem ex controversiis theologicis.

Ceterum in locis etiam contemptissimis saepe occasio existit, ut vel cum sectario quodam, vel cum auditore ab aliis seducto in disputationem fit descendendum. Vbi seipsum & religionem suam prostituet minister ecclesiae, qui ne levi quidem brachio controversias theologicas attigit.

Obs. I. Controversiarum theologicarum finis optandus ille quidem, sed in hac militante ecclesia expectandus non est.

Oportet enim haereses inter vos (Christianos) esse, ut, qui probati, manifesti fiant inter vos, inquit S. Paullus, 1 Cor. XI, 19. Loquitur apostolus non de necessitate fatali, absoluta & consequentis, sed de necessitate hypothetica & consequentiae, supposita nimirum diaboli astutia, & hominum infirmitate, ignorantia rerum spiritualium, perversitate, inconstantia, superbia & pronitate in novitates.

Quae causae haeresium existunt in ecclesia usque ad consummationem huius universi. Quare theologorum est, se duce Spiritu S. armare ad bella domini.

Obs. II. Controversiae inutiles, spinosae, & exortae ex dominio pravorum affectuum, theologica disquisitione aut operosa discussione indignae sunt.

S V S P I R I V M. Te, Deus pater, sator rerum & fons omnium bonorum, te, Deus fili, sol gratiae & iustitiae, te, Spiritus S., sanctificator animarum fidelium, supplex veneror & obtestor, ut mentes nostras infermas coelesti gratiae luce perfundas, tenebras errorum discutias, ad veritatem in rebus spiritualibus indagandam & inveniendam facem nobis praeferas, quo nostra theologia exemplari sapientiae tuae, quoad eius in hac imbecillitate fieri potest, fit conformis, validissimo sacrarum litterarum praesidio subnixa, lux fidei, dux viae ad coelum, verae pietatis magistra, vitiorum expultrix!


### Q. XXIX. What is opposed to true theology?: Chapter II

CHAPTER II.

Latin:

CAPUT II.


## 2 Prolegomenon II: On Religion, the General Object of Theology

CONCERNING THE GENERAL OBJECT OF THEOLOGY, COMPREHENDED UNDER THE NAME OF THINGS TO BE BELIEVED AND THINGS TO BE DONE, OF THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION.

Q. I. What is the Christian religion?

Q. II. From whence is the word religion derived?

Some wish religion to be called from 'religando' (binding back) (a), others from 'relegendo' (re-reading) (b).

Prob. a. LACTANTIUS, book IV of the Divine Institutes, ch. 28, says: Bound by this bond of piety, we are bound back to God.

Whence religion itself received its name.

And ISIDORE, Origins, book VIII, ch. 11, says: It is called religion, because through it we bind back our souls to the one God for divine worship by a bond of serving. The Christian religion is the method of worshipping God, by true faith in Christ, and sincere charity toward God, oneself, and one's neighbor, so that the sinner, torn away from God, may be reconciled and reunited with God, renewed, and eternally saved.

You say: From religando (binding back) descends religatio, not religio, just as obligatio is deduced from obligando. R. According to BECHMANN in De originib. lat. linguae p. 609, among the ancients ligere, ligui meant the same as ligare does today: from this obsolete verb comes lictor.

R. According to BECHMANN in De originib. lat. linguae p. 609, among the ancients ligere, ligui meant the same as ligare does today: from this obsolete verb comes lictor. Proof b. CICERO, Book II, De natura deorum: "Those who would diligently retract and, as it were, re-read all things that pertain to the worship of God, were called religious from relegendo (re-reading/re-gathering): just as eligentes (choosing) from eligo, and intelligentes (understanding) from intelligendo." For in all these words there is the same force of reading as in religioso. AUGUSTINE, Book X, De civitate Dei c. 4, adds what they call a white stone to CICERO: "He himself is the fountain of our blessedness, he himself is the end of all desire. Choosing him, or rather re-choosing him (for we had lost him by neglecting him); re-choosing him, therefore—whence religion is said to be derived—we tend toward him by love." According to the former derivation, religion is an obligation to the true worship of God, or a principle binding man to duty and office. See D. SCHERZER, Brevic. theol. p. 7. According to the latter etymology, religion is the diligent treatment of those things which pertain to the worship of God. The former derivation pleases most theologians.

Latin:

DE OBIECTO THEOLOGIAE GENERALI, CREDENDIS ET AGENDIS, RELIGIONIS CHRISTIANAE NOMINE COMPREHENSIS.

Quaest. I. Quid est religio christiana?

Quaest. II. Vox religio unde deducitur?

Religionem alii a religando (a), alii a relegendo dictam volunt (b).

Prob. a. LACTANTIVS libr. IV. diuin. institut. c. 28. inquit: Hoc vinculo pietatis obstricti, Deo religati sumus.

Vnde ipsa religio nomen accepit. Et ISIDOR. origin. libr.

VIII. c. 11. ait; Religio appellata, quod per eam vni Deo religamus animas nostras ad cultum diuinum vinculo serviendi. Religio christiana est ratio colendi Deum, vera in Christum fide, & sincera in Deum, se, & proximum caritate, vt peccator, a Deo auulsus, cum Deo reconciliatus & redunitus, renouetur & aeternum saluetur.

Dicis: A religando descendit religatio, non, religio, sicut ab obligando deducitur obligatio. R. Censente BECHMANNO de originib. lat. linguæ p. m. 609. antiquis ligere, ligui, dictum idem fuit, quod hodie ligare: a quo obsoleto verbo est lictor.

Prob. b. CICERO lib. II. de nat. deor. Qui omnia, quæ ad cultum Dei pertinent, diligenter retractarent, & tanquam relegerent, sunt dicti religiosi a relegendo: ut eligentes ex eligo, ex intelligendo intelligentes. His enim verbis omnibus inest vis legendi eadem, quæ in religioso. Album, quod aiunt, calculum CICERONI adiicit AVGVSTINVS lib. X. de ciu. Dei c. 4. Ipse fons nostræ beatitudinis, ipse omnis appetitionis est finis. Hunc eligentes, vel potius relegentes (amiseramus enim negligentes); hunc ergo relegentes, vnde religio dicta perhibetur, ad eum dilectione tendimus. Secundum priorem deriuationem religio est ad verum Dei cultum obligatio, seu ratio hominem obligans ad debitum atque officium. Vid. D. SCHERZERI breuic. theol. p. 7. Secundum posteriorem etymologiam religio est diligens tractatio eorum, quæ ad cultum Dei pertinent. Prior deriuatio plerisque placet theologis.


### Q. III. How is religion called in Greek?

Among the Greeks, religion is called θρησκεία, εὐσέβεια, λατρεία.

Proof, James 1:27. Θρησκεία καθαρὰ καὶ ἀμίαντος, "Pure and undefiled religion before God and the Father is this: to visit the orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unspotted from the world." The name θρησκεία, as Plutarch, Suidas, and others observe, originated with the Thracians, inasmuch as Orpheus taught the Thracians the rites and ceremonies by which he thought God should be worshipped. Paul calls religion εὐσέβεια, 1 Tim. 4:8, ἡ εὐσέβεια πρὸς πάντα ὠφέλιμός ἐστι. "Godliness (religion) is profitable unto all things." On this passage Chrysostom notes that εὐσέβεια is "pure faith and upright life," homil. XII. in h. l. fol. 1581. It is named by the same apostle λογικὴ λατρεία, Rom. 12:1. The Vulgate version renders this into Latin as rationale obsequium (reasonable service), LUCAS OSIANDER as rationalem cultum (rational worship), SEBAST. SCHMID as cultum secundum verbum (worship according to the word). Let us listen to D. CALOVIUS commenting in h. l. fol. 203: Some prefer to say it is called λογικὴν with the Syriac interpreter, from λέγω Θεῦ, the word of God, because λατρεία must be instituted not according to the lead and norm of our reason, but according to the prescription and form of the word of God, if it is to please God, just as in 1 Pet. 2:2, according to them, λογικὸν γάλα is "verbal milk." This they observe against the Socinians, who, from this word, establish human reason as the rule of divine worship and religion. But because it alludes to Levitical sacrifices, it is better to say it is a hostia λογικὴν λατρείαν (a reasonable service sacrifice) with respect to the matter, because it is done not through the offering of cattle, but of our bodies, than with respect to the principle, whether efficient or directing.

Latin:

Græcis religio vocatur θρησκεία, εὐσέβεια, λατρεία.

Prob. Iac. I, 27. Θρησκεία καθαρὰ καὶ ἀμίαντος, religio pura & immaculata apud Deum & patrem hæc est: visitare orphanos & viduas in afflictione eorum, impollutum se ipsum seruare a mundo. Nomen θρησκεία, Plutarcho, Suida, aliisque obseruantibus, a Thracibus ortum est, siquidem Orpheus Thraces docuit ritus & ceremonias, quibus Deum coli censuit. Religionem Paullus vocat εὐσέβειαν, 1 Tim. IV, 8. ἡ εὐσέβεια πρὸς πάντα ὠφελιμός ἐςι. Pietas (religio) ad omnia vtilis est. Ad quem locum Chrysostomus notat, εὐσέβειαν εἶναι πίσιν καθαρὰν καὶ βίον ὀρθὸν, homil. XII. in h. l. fol 1581. Nominatur ab eodem apostolo λογικὴ λατρεία, Rom. XII, 1. Versio vulgata latine reddidit per rationale obsequium, LVCAS OSIANDER per rationalem cultum, SEBAST. SCHMIDIVS per cultum secundum verbum. Auscultemus D. CALOVIVM in h. l. fol. 203. commentantem: Nonnulli λογικὴν dici malunt cum Syro interprete, a λέγω Θεῦ, verbo Dei, quod non iuxta nostræ rationis ductum & normam, sed iuxta verbi Dei præscriptum & formam instituenda sit λατρεία, si Deo placere debeat, vti 1 Petr. II, 2. iuxta ipsos λογικὸν γάλα est lac verbale. Quod aduersus Socinianos obseruant, vtpote qui ex hac voce rationem humanam regulam cultus diuini & religionis constituunt, Sed quia alluditur ad sacrificia leuitica, præstat dici hostiam λογικὴν λατρείαν respectu materiæ, quod non per pecorum, sed corporum nostrorum oblationem fiat, quam ratione principii siue efficientis, siue dirigentis.


### Q. IV. In how many ways is the word religion taken?

Religion improperly denotes a false [worship], but properly the true principle of worshipping God: which today we call Christian, because by true faith in Christ we are redeemed to God.

Proof a. Paul, Col. 2:18, calls the worship of angels θρησκείαν τῶν ἀγγέλων. But the apostle disapproves of the religious worship of angels.

Proof b. The Christian religion is taken either μερικῶς, partially, or ὁλικῶς, totally. Taken μερικῶς, it designates πρώτως and primarily the immediate worship of God according to the first table of the law, Deut. 6:13; δευτέρως and secondarily the mediate worship of God, by which duties of charity are performed to one's neighbor, James 1:27.
