Taken ὁλικῶς and adequately, it embraces both faith in Christ and charity toward God, oneself, and one's neighbor.

V. What is the true religion?

True religion is that which is conformable to the divine word.

It is most ancient, approved also by the fathers of the O. T. (b), it illustrates the glory of God (c), it rightly teaches faith in Jesus, the author of salvation (d), it diligently inculcates the holiness of life (e), it calms the conscience (f), it procures εὐθανασίαν (a good death) (g).

Proof a. The word of God is truth. John XVII, 17.

Whatever religion corresponds to heavenly truth, that is true.

Proof b. By the same religion by which the fathers of the O. T. were saved, we also are saved, because there is one Lord, one faith, Eph. IV, 5.

We believe that we are saved through the grace of Jesus Christ, just as they, namely the fathers,

Acts XV, 11. Proof.

Proof (*) I fear, indeed, that a firm proof is not made from that statement.

That this word, κἀκεῖνοι (and they also), is more correctly referred to the disciples than to the fathers, clear arguments teach us: 1) The scope of the discourse; for there was absolutely no doubt concerning the salvation of the fathers, but all the controversy then was agitated concerning the difference between the Jews and the profane nations to be renewed in the age of the N. T., whether the method of obtaining salvation was different, or one and the same, v. 1-7, 9.

2) The coherence of the speech, and the force of the argumentation.

If this were the sentiment: We Jews trust that it will come to pass that we obtain blessedness in the same way as our ancestors: Therefore, do not impose upon the foreign disciples, now addicted to Christ, that yoke which our fathers were almost unable to sustain! What, I ask, is the connection? But in this manner: The grace of Jesus Christ today is one, and the common way of all, by which one goes to salvation: We therefore, born indeed of Jewish parents, are content with that one, and thus liberated from that hard burden, aspire to salvation: Therefore, much less is so heavy a yoke, with which they were never burdened, to be imposed upon others as if necessary for salvation. Only in this way do both the opposition and the argumentation hold. cf. the conclusion v. 17 & 19. In the conclusion, however, there should be neither more, nor less, nor anything other than what had been in the premises and the proof.

3) Consideration of the words. Χάρις (grace) in the N.

T. denotes antitypical grace, which is distinguished from the ritual and typical law, see John I, 17. And it is very significantly called the grace of Jesus Christ.

Through Christ, and his merits, and not otherwise, the approach to salvation has always been open, in the O. T. equally as in the N.

Testament. But through Jesus Christ we today obtain salvation, since this is the principal truth proper to the N. Testament, which distinguishes Christian doctrine from the Jewish; that Jesus of Nazareth, and no one else, becomes the Christ; in which way these words of his also ought to be understood, John XVI, 24.

4) The thing itself speaks.

For it was not permitted for the fathers of the Jews to become partakers of salvation unless they had holily observed the sacred ceremonies, insofar as those were shadows and images, designating the Christ who was to come. But the decree in that council of the Apostles looked precisely to this, that it might clearly appear that that typical worship had now ceased, and that which had been its first part, circumcision, had now been entirely abrogated. I pass over more.

Although, however, this statement does not seem to pertain to confirming the θεὸν (God): yet the thing itself is indeed most true, of the greatest moment, and must be constantly defended against the SOCINIANS.

For there are other statements proving it, among which one stands out above all, Heb. IX, 26: Otherwise Christ would have had to suffer often, from the foundations of the world being laid.

The nerve of the proof will be this: The sufferings and merits of Christ, the God-man (Heb.

I & II, 14.) have infinite force and efficacy: Therefore, by reason of their virtue and power they are always present, always valid: Therefore, once performed, they are held as always performed. Indeed, they pertain to the whole universality of men, from that time when sinful men existed: Therefore, they are valid no less before than after they were performed: Therefore, it was not necessary for Christ to suffer more often from the beginning of the world: That, however, would have been necessary, unless the future suffering of the ancestors, because of its infinite force, had always been estimated as present: Therefore, it could not happen that any of the mortals who ever lived before Christ was born and suffered could arrive at salvation otherwise than through his ransom and merits: Therefore, in the O. T. the way to salvation was the same as it is today in the N. T., the same necessity of saving faith on both sides, placed in Christ alone.

These also are clear, Acts

Acts XIII, 38. 39. Rom. IV, 6. 23. 24. 2 Cor. IV, 13.

c. 1 Cor. X, 31. Do all things for the glory of God. The glory of God is the ultimate goal, which true religion regards.

Prob. d. That the soul of religion is faith in Christ, is evident partly from this, that in Christ alone is eternal salvation found: For there is no salvation in any other: neither is there any other name given under heaven among men, whereby we must be saved, Acts IV, 12. partly from this, that faith, receiving Christ with his benefits, is, on our part, the only medium of salvation, since he who believes in Christ does not perish, but has eternal life. John III, 17.

Prob. e. Tit. II, 11. The saving grace of God has appeared to all men, instructing (παιδεύουσα) us, that we should deny ungodliness and worldly lusts, and live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present world. The scope of divine instruction (τῆς παιδείας), and of the Christian religion flowing from it, is to instill holiness of life, without which no one will see the Lord, Heb. XIII, 14. into sinners to be saved.

Prob. f. Rom. XV, 4. Whatever things were written, were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope. As the written word of God, so religion, drawn from it, fills the conscience with living solace, so that the religious man is not at all broken by adverse things, but is raised up by the hope of heavenly goods.

Prob. g. John VIII, 51. If anyone keeps my word, he shall not taste death forever. True religion teaches that Christians, keeping the word of God, will not taste the bitterness of death, but will exchange their temporal life, full of misery, for eternal rest, joy, and glory.

Q.

VI. Is the evangelical religion, which received its name from the ministry of Luther, true? Evangelical religion, purged by the ministry of Luther, is exactly agreeable to the divine word, approved by the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles, aiming universally at illustrating the glory of God, instilling true faith in Christ and holiness of life, tranquilizing the conscience, and procuring a good death (εὐθανασίαν): therefore it is true. The antecedent will be most clearly proven through all and each of the heads of theology.

The antithesis is of all those who differ from the Lutheran religion, whose arguments are:

I. The Lutheran religion is new. Therefore it is not true. R. The Lutheran religion is indeed renewed, but not new: since it is the same religion that was of the prophets and apostles.

II. The Lutheran religion is discordant. Therefore it is not true. R. The Lutheran religion is concordant in the fundamental articles of faith, although certain doctors may disagree in questions of faith that have arisen or in certain circumstances.

III. Lutherans are schismatics, because they impose upon themselves a distinctive name from Dr. Luther, just as the Corinthians 1 Cor. III, 4. R. The Lutheran religion is named from the minister and instrument of Luther

This truth, confirmed by the sayings of Holy Scripture, rests also upon certain principles, the chief of which are 1) the common nature of all men, and the corruption of nature: 2) the common damnation of all: 3) therefore, a necessary and common reconciliation and conjunction with God for all, if any recovery of lost salvation is to be hoped for, from whom all alike have fallen away: 4) the necessary vicarious obedience of a certain Sponsor and Reconciler, whose pledge, fulfilled in all its numbers and parts, would pertain equally to all.

Which, since 5) it is not, nor can be, except through the one God-man (θεάνθρωπον) (Rom. VIII, 3.): it follows that to no one could access to salvation ever have been open, in the Old Testament as well as in the New, except through that one God-man (θεάνθρωπον).

For where the reason is equal, there the consequence cannot but be equal.

See Rom. III, 23. 24. V, 18. 19. 1 Timoth. II, 4. 5. 6.

not of God, not as master and principal cause. The example of the Corinthians, however, is brought in irrelevantly, because the Corinthians agreed on the foundation of faith, and, led by love alone toward the teachers of the church, distinguished themselves by distinctive names. Lutherans allow themselves to be called by a distinctive name, taken from the ministry of Luther, in contrast to the Papists and others who dissent on the foundation of faith.

Latin:

Religio improprie notat falsam (a), proprie veram rationem colendi Deum: quam hodie christianam appellamus, quia vera in Christum fide cum Deo redunimur (b).

Prob. a. Paull. Col. II, 18. cultum angelorum vocat θρησκείαν τῶν ἀγγέλων. Sed apostolus religiosum angelorum cultum improbat.

Prob. b. Religio christiana sumitur vel μερικῶς, partialiter, vel ὁλικῶς, totaliter. Μερικῶς accepta designat πρώτως & primario cultum Dei immediatum secundum priorem tabulam legis, Deut. VI, 13. δευτέρως & secundario cultum Dei mediatum, quo officia caritatis proximo præstantur. Iac. I, 27. Ὁλικῶς & adæquate tum fidem in Christum, tum caritatem in Deum, se, & proximum complectitur.

V. Quanam est vera religio?

Vera religio est, quae verbo divino est conformis .

Antiquissima est, probata etiam patribus V. T. (b), gloriam Dei illustrat (c), fidem in Iesum salutis auctorem recte docet (d), sanctimoniam vitae sedulo inculcat (e), conscientiam tranquillat (f), εὐθανασίαν procurat (g).

Prob. a. Verbum Dei est veritas. Io. XVII, 17.

Quae religio caelesti veritati respondet, illa est vera.

Prob. b. Qua religione saluati sunt patres V. T. eadem et nos saluamur, quia vnus Dominus, vna fides, Eph. IV, 5.

Per gratiam Iesu Christi credimus saluari, quemadmodum et illi, scil. patres,

Act. XV, 11 . Prob.

Prob. (*) Vereor quidem, vt ex isto dicto firma efficiatur probatio.

Vocabulum hoc, κἀκεῖνοι, rectius ad μαθητάς, quam ad πατέρας, referri, luculenta nos docent argumenta: 1) Scopus orationis; nam de salute Patrum prorsus nulla erat dubitatio, sed controuersia tunc omnis agitabatur de differentia Iudaeorum, et profanarum gentium aetate N. T. renouandarum, vtrum diuersa esset, an vna eademque, salutis percipiendae ratio, v. 1-7. 9.

2) Coherentia sermonis, et vis argumentationis.

Si haec esset sententia: Nos Iudaei confidimus, fore, vt eodem nos modo, quo maiores nostri, beatitatem consequamur: E. nolite discipulis peregrinis, nunc Christo addictis, iugum imponere illud, cui sustinendo fere impares fuerunt Patres nostri! Quae, quaeso, connexio? Sed ad hunc modum: Gratia Iesu Christi hodie est vna, et communis omnium via, qua itur ad salutem: Nos igitur, Iudaicis quidem parentibus orti, ea vna contenti sumus, adeoque duro illo onere liberati, ad salutem adspiramus: E. multo minus aliis tam graue iugum, quo illi nunquam fuerunt onerati, imponendum est, tanquam ad salutem necessarium. Ita demum valet et oppositio, et argumentatio. conf. conclusio v. 17. & 19. In conclusione autem nec plus, nec minus esse debet, nec aliud quidpiam, quam fuerat in praemissis ac probatione.

3) Verborum consideratio. Χάρις in scriptura N.

F. denotat gratiam antitypicam, quae discernitur a lege rituali ac typica, vid. Ioan. I, 17. Et valde significanter dicitur χάρις Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.

Per Christum, eiusque promerita, nec aliter, aditus ad salutem semper patuit, in V. aeque, ac in N.

Foedere. Sed per Iesum Christum nos hodie salutem adipiscimur, quando quidem haec veritas principalis est N. Foederis propria, quae christianam doctrinam a iudaica distinguit; quod Iesus Nazarenus, et nemo alius, fit Christus; quem ad modum intelligi debent etiam haec ipsius verba, Ioann. XVI, 24.

4) Res ipsa loquitur.

Patribus enim Iudaeorum non licuit salutis fieri participes, nisi sancte obseruerant sacras ceremonias, quatenus illae erant vmbrae atque imagines, Christum venturum designantes. Atqui decretum in isto Apostolorum concilio prorsus eo spectabat, vt plane adpareret, cultum illum typicum nunc defuisse, et, quae prima eius pars fuerat, circumcisionem, nunc omnino abrogatam esse. Taceo plura.

Quamuis autem hoc effatum ad θεὸν confirmandam non pertinere videatur: ipsa tamen θεὸν est profecto verissima, maxime momenti, et aduersus S O C I N I A N O S constanter vindicanda.

Sunt enim alia dicta probantia, inter quae omnia vnum eminet illud, Hebr. IX, 26: Alioqui debuisset Christus saepe numero pati, inde a iactis mundi fundamentis.

Neruus probationis hic erit: Malorum perpetuo et promerita Christi, θεανθρώπης (Hebr.

I & II, 14.) infinitam habent vim atque efficacitatem: E. ratione virtutis ac potestatis suae semper sunt praesentia, semper valida: E. semel praestita, tamquam semper praestita habentur. Pertinent vero ea ad totam hominum vniuersitatem, inde ab eo tempore, quo exstiterunt homines peccatores: E. valent non minus ante, quam postquam praestita fuerunt: E. non fuit necesse, Christum ab initio mundi saepius pati: Id vero fuisset necessarium, nisi futura maiorum perpessio, propter vim suam infinitam, tamquam praesens semper fuisset aestimata: E. fieri non potuit, vt quisquam mortalium, qui ante Christum natum et passum vnquam vixerunt, aliter, ac per eius λύτρον ac promerita, ad salutem perueniret: E. in V. T. eadem fuit, quae hodieque in N. T. est, via ad salutem, eadem vtrimque necessitas fiduciae salutaris, in Christo vno posita.

Perspicua etiam haec sunt, Act.

Act. XIII, 38. 39. Rom. IV, 6. 23. 24. 2 Cor. IV, 13.

Prob. c. 1 Cor. X, 31. Omnia in gloriam Dei facite. Gloria Dei est meta vltima, quam vera respicit religio.

Prob. d. Animam religionis esse fidem in Christum, patet partim ex eo, quod in solo Christo aeterna salus inuenitur: Neque enim est in vllo alio salus: neque aliud nomen datum est sub caelo hominibus, in quo oporteat nos seruari, Act. IV, 12. partim ex eo, quod fides Christum cum ipsius beneficiis recipiens, ex parte nostri, vnicum salutis medium est, siquidem credens in Christum non perit, sed habet vitam aeternam. Ioh. III, 17.

Prob. e. Tit. II, 11. Apparuit gratia Dei salutaris omnibus hominibus, erudiens (παιδεύουσα) nos, vt abnegemus impietatem & mundanas concupiscentias, ac sobrie, iuste & pie viuamus in praesenti seculo. Scopus τῆς παιδείας diuinae, & ex hac manantis religionis christianae est, vt sanctimoniam vitae, sine qua nemo videbit dominum, Hebr. XIII, 14. peccatoribus saluandis instillet.

Prob. f. Rom. XV, 4. Quaecunque praescripta sunt, in nostram doctrinam praescripta sunt, vt per patientiam & consolationem scripturarum spem habeamus. Vt verbum Dei scriptum, ita religio, ex eo hausta, viuo solatio perfundit conscientiam, vt homo religiosus aduersis rebus minime frangatur, sed spe bonorum coelestium erigatur.

Prob. g. Io. VIII, 51. Si quis verbum meum seruauerit, non gustabit mortem in aeternum. Docet vera religio, christianos, verbum Dei seruantes, acerbitatem mortis non degustaturos, sed vitam temporalem miseriae plenam cum aeterna quiete, gaudio & gloria commutaturos esse.

Quaest. VI. Estne religio euangelica, quae a ministerio Lutheri cognomen accepit, vera?

Religio euangelica, ministerio Lutheri repurgata, verbo diuino ad amussim est consentanea, patriarchis, prophetis & apostolis probata, ad gloriam Dei illustrandam, veram in Christum fidem, & sanctitatem vitae instillandam, conscientiam tranquillandam, & εὐθανασίαν procurandam vniuersim collineans: ergo est vera. Antecedens per omnia & singula theologiae capita clarissime probabitur.

Antithesis est omnium a religione Lutherana diffidentium, quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Religio Lutherana est noua. E. non est vera. R. Religio Lutherana est quidem renouata, sed non noua: siquidem eadem est religio, quae fuit prophetarum & apostolorum.

II. Religio Lutherana est discors. E. non est vera. R. Religio Lutherana est concors in articulis fidei fundamentalibus, licet quidam doctores in quaestionibus fidei iuxta enatis aut circumstantiis quibusdam discrepent.

III. Lutherani sunt schismatici, quia nomen distinctiuum a D. Lutheri sibi imponunt, sicut Corinthii 1 Cor. III, 4. R. Lutherana religio dicitur a Lutheri ministro & organo Haec veritas dictis Scr.

S. confirmata, nititur etiam certis principiis, quorum praecipua sunt 1) communis omnium hominum natura, & naturae corruptio: 2) communis omnium damnatio: 3) necessaria igitur, & communis omnium, si qua salutis deperditae recuperatio speranda fit, reconciliatio coniunctioque cum Deo, a quo omnes pariter defciuerunt: 4) necessaria obedientia vicaria cuiusdam Sponsoris ac Reconciliatoris, cuius sponsio, omnibus suis numeris ac partibus expleta, ad omnes aequaliter pertineret.

Qui quum 5) non fit, nec esse possit, praeter vnum θεάνθρωπον (Rom. VIII, 3.): efficitur, vt nemini potuerit vnquam in V. T. aeque ac in N. T. nisi per vnum illum θεάνθρωπον, aditus ad salutem patere.

Vbi enim par est ratio, ibi par quoque non potest non esse consecutio.

Vid. Rom. III, 23. 24. V, 18. 19. 1 Timoth. II, 4. 5. 6.

Potestne homo in omni religione salvari? no Dei, non magistro & caussa principali. Exemplum autem Corinthiorum impertinenter adducitur, quia Corinthii in fundamento fidei consentiebant, & solo amore in doctores ecclesiæ adducti distinctiuis se nominibus insigniuerunt. Lutherani a Pontificiis, & aliis in fundamento fidei dissidentibus, nomine distinctiuo, a ministerio Lutheri petito, se vocari patiuntur.


### Question VII. Can a man be saved in every religion?

Since there is one foundation of the Christian religion (a), one gospel (b), one faith (c), the progenitor of love toward God and neighbor (d), it is validly concluded that there is only one Christian religion in which eternal salvation is sought and found. But so far is a false religion from being salutary to a man who is a wayfarer, that it is rather pestiferous to him (e).

Proof a. 1 Cor. III, 11. For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ. Jesus Christ is the foundation of the whole Christian religion: that religion which is rightly built upon this one foundation is true and salutary. More religions, and those contradictorily opposed to one another, cannot be built upon this one base of piety. For if they agree on the foundation, they are not more, but one religion.

Proof b. The principle from which genuine religion is drawn, if you look at faith in Christ, is the word of the gospel, which is one. For St. Paul says clearly in Gal. I, 8: If we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed. There is no gospel given other than that which was announced by Paul and his brethren, the rest of the apostles, from the hearing of which is faith, Rom. X, 17. The divine law, the norm of love toward God and neighbor, is also one and immutable, since it is a certain expression of the invariable divine justice. If, therefore, religion is derived from one true principle, it must certainly be that there is one true religion.

Proof c. Eph. IV, 5. One Lord, one faith. Just as there is one Lord, the redeemer of the human race and head of the church, namely Jesus Christ, who is the only way to heaven, John XIV, 6, so there is one faith, which like a spiritual bond unites the mystical members with the head, Christ. Therefore, it is called one faith, not by reason of the subjects, or believing men, but by reason of the object apprehended, since the faith of all men to be saved is directed toward one author of salvation. Paul says gravely in Gal. III, 26, 27: For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither bond nor free; there is neither male nor female; for ye are all one in Christ. Whoever are united in Christ through faith, theirs is one religion, of which faith is the principal part.

Proof d. Gal. V, 6. Faith worketh by love. Faith precedes, love follows. Faith works through love, as the soul through its faculties. Whoever, therefore, are united in faith, they love one God in Christ. Indeed, theirs is one heart and one soul, through reciprocal love. Acts IV, 32.

Proof e. Unless a religion, erroneous and heretical, were pestiferous, our Savior would not have commanded us to avoid false prophets. Matth. VII, 15. Paul would not have warned us to look out for them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which we have learned, and to avoid them. Rom. XVI, 17. John would not have called us away from their company with such singular zeal, saying: If there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, receive him not into your house, neither bid him God speed, 2 John V, 10. The apostle depicts a fundamental error in faith as a harmful gangrene, 1 Tim. II, 17. Their word will eat as doth a canker [gangrene]. As a gangrene creeps gradually further until it consumes the native heat, so error in faith gradually gains strength and propagates itself until it extinguishes the spiritual life by which we live in the faith of Christ, Gal. II, 20. What? Because A fundamental error will permeate saving faith itself. From which it follows that heretics depart from the faith, 1 Tim. IV, 1, and make shipwreck of it, 1 Tim. I, 19.

The antithesis is that of the Indifferentists, Libertines, Puccius, Weigelius, Arminius, and others, according to whose judgment a man can be saved in every religion, provided he strives for a holy life, with the added limitation, however, that a sinner can ordinarily be saved in the Christian religion, and extraordinarily in the Jewish, Mahometan, and ethnic religions. They rely upon the following arguments:

I. Just as there is one Catholic Christian church, so there is one Christian, Catholic, and principal religion: of which the particular sects are the Pontifical, Lutheran, Reformed, Socinian, etc., which, although they participate in the Catholic church, are nevertheless contaminated by particular blemishes and are not pure in every respect. Resp. 1. The Catholic Christian church is that which is built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, of which Jesus Christ is the cornerstone, through whom the whole structure, being fitly framed together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord, Eph. II, 20. In whatever religion those dogmas of faith and precepts of morals are handed down and inculcated which the prophets of old handed down in the O.T., that is Christian, Catholic, and undoubtedly true; which is not to be conceived as a universal idea existing nowhere outside the intellect, but is to be considered as it flourishes in a certain assembly of men embracing the true religion, which assembly of believers we call the church. (2) That the Lutheran religion is impure must be clearly demonstrated.

Objection I. It is not necessary that one should approach the visible church; it suffices that one be a Christian and a member of the invisible church. Resp. The true church is called visible and invisible according to a different mode of consideration. It is called visible when considered materially and subjectively as the assembly of men that meets the eye; it is called invisible when viewed both formally, by reason of its internal form or mystical union with the head, Christ—which spiritual union occurs through faith, Eph. III, 17—and comparatively, insofar as its splendor is obscured by the arising of persecutions or heresies; just as the Israelite church was obscured in the times of Elijah, so that this most sharp-sighted prophet could scarcely perceive its face, 1 Kings XIX, 18. But it is not absolutely and simply invisible, as Weigelius maintains (P. III. postill. fol. 91, 92). But where there is the pure preaching of the Word and the legitimate administration of the sacraments, there is the true visible church, and in this church the invisible, i.e., the little flock of truly believing and elect, to whom it has pleased the heavenly Father to give the kingdom, Luke XII, 32. Outside that true visible church of Christ, when rashly neglected, there is no salvation. For to this have been entrusted the τὰ λόγια τοῦ θεοῦ [oracles of God], Rom. III, 2. The Word and the sacraments are the efficacious means of grace and salvation, John III, 5; 1 John V, 8.

Objection II. If a true Christian were held captive in Turkey, he would be saved, even though he did not live in a pure church. Therefore, deduction or access to the church is not necessary for salvation. Resp. A true Christian captured by the Turks is not in the true church in body, indeed, yet he is in it in spirit, because he embraces with a sincere heart the heavenly truth which the true church of Christ guards and propagates.

II. If in the Pontifical religion there are true means of salvation, then eternal salvation is not sought and found in the Lutheran religion alone. But the former is true, as Luther concedes (tom. IV & VI, Altenburg). Therefore, the latter is also true. Resp. No religion is so corrupt that certain true dogmas, in themselves good and salutary, are not handed down in it. Conversely, in a false religion, many erroneous, harmful, spurious, and foreign things are contained; for example, in the Pontifical religion, human traditions are taught that are discordant with the divine Word, the infallible authority of the Roman Pontiff, the merits of the saints and their religious worship, trust in one's own works, the sacrificial mass, and the sacrament of the Supper under one kind—by which false dogmas true faith in Christ is neither generated nor nourished, but extinguished. But if a Pontifical adherent is saved, is saved, the salvation of the same is to be referred not to the pontifical religion, as such, but to the truth remaining in the papacy. For it is possible that a pontifical [Catholic], being seduced, having cast aside the trust in his own merits, may flee solely to the merit of Christ, and rest in the same: he is saved here, not as a pontifical, but as a faithful Christian.

Instantia III.

III. The foundation of the Christian religion is repentance and faith in Christ, which is taught in every religion of those men who profess themselves to be Christians. Therefore, in every religion of those who are distinguished by the name of Christians, salvation is given. The antecedent is proven, because the Savior himself, at the beginning of the New Testament, proposed this fundamental dogma to men to be saved, and seriously wills it: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. Matth. IV, 17. Repent, and believe the gospel. R. We grant readily that at the beginning of the New Testament men were warned to repent and to believe the gospel. But truly, many things are forgiven to beginners which are required of those who are proficient. For beginners, a summary or brief epitome of Christian doctrine suffices; for those who are proficient, a distinct knowledge of the fundamental articles of faith must be instilled. Those whom Christ anticipated with His grace, He prepared, informed, and illuminated more and more. This can be gathered both from many of the sermons of Christ and the apostles, and especially from the long discourse held before the people on the mount. Matth. V, VI, VII, chapter.

IV. The Apostle Peter seems to patronize indifferentism, Act. X, 34, saying: In truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons; but in every nation, he that feareth him and worketh righteousness is accepted with him. R. The apostle does not say: in every religion, but in every nation, he that feareth him and worketh righteousness is accepted with him. By which words he hints that no nation under heaven is absolutely excluded from converting and regenerating grace, provided that he ingenuously confesses that God has given repentance to the Gentiles. Act. X, 28. Therefore, Peter does not speak of Gentiles laboring under ethnic blindness, but of Gentiles admitting the means of grace and conceiving faith in Christ, which they testify and declare by fear toward God and works of righteousness.

V. Without the revealed word of God, not a few have been converted: which is evident from the example of the centurion Cornelius, Act. X, 2, who although he was a Gentile, was nevertheless religious, fearing God with all his house, beneficent toward the needy, and assiduous in prayers. The same is clear from the example of the oriental magi, Matth. II, 1, who were led to Christ without a preached word. Resp. (1) To the example of Cornelius. This man was religious not by reason of his Gentile origin, but by reason of his state, regenerated from the seed of the word, from which he had a general knowledge of the Messiah as the redeemer of the world, see Act. X, 36. A special application to a certain individual was lacking to him, namely to Jesus of Nazareth, whom he was to be more fully informed about by St. Peter so that he might recognize Him unto salvation. Resp. (2) To the example of the Persian magi. They recognized the Messiah from the writings of Daniel, to seek whom they were excited by a new star of unusual magnitude and brightness. That Daniel was educated in the school of the magi is evident from Dn. I, 6. On the occasion of which familiarity he undoubtedly instilled the doctrine concerning the Messiah to some. The same, c. II, 44. He explained several things to the Babylonian king concerning the kingdom of heaven at the future end without experience. To this is added, that not all Jews migrated back from Babylonia to Jerusalem, but many remained in those places, which had famous schools there. Confer. Act. II, 9. We add, that the sacred letters were rendered into Greek not without the provident care of the eternal Deity, and indeed in familiar speech. ...shared with the Gentiles. Here there were many good men, whom Scripture calls *eulabeis* [reverent/devout], who, although they were not circumcised, nevertheless unrolled the prophetic books and worshipped the God of Israel: which is read concerning the Ethiopian eunuch in Acts 8:28.

Latin:

Cum vnum sit fundamentum religionis christianæ (a), vnum euangelium (b), vna fides (c), caritatis in Deum & proximum genitrix (d), valide colligitur, vnam tantum esse religionem christianam, in qua æterna salus quæritur & inuenitur. Tantum autem abest, vt religio falsa homini viatori sit salutifera, vt potius eidem sit pestifera (e).

Prob. a. 1 Cor. III, 11. Fundamentum aliud nemo potest ponere, præter positum quod est, Iesus Christus. Fundamentum totius religionis christianæ est Iesus Christus: quæ religio huic vnico fundamento recte superstruitur, illa est vera & salutaris. Plures, eæque sibi contradictorie oppositæ religiones huic vni pietatis basi superædificari nequeunt. Nam si conueniunt in fundamento, non sunt plures, sed vna religio.

Prob. b. Principium, ex quo hauritur germana religio, si spectes fidem in Christum, est verbum euangelii, quod est vnum. Nam diferte inquit S. Paullus Gal. I, 8. Si nos, aut angelus e cælo euangelizaret vobis, præter id, quod euangelizauimus vobis, anathema sit. Non datur euangelium, præter id, quod a Paullo & ipsius fratribus, reliquis apostolis, est annunciatum, ex cuius auditu est fides, Rom. X, 17. Lex diuina, norma caritatis in Deum & proximum, etiam est vna eaque immutabilis, cum sit expressio quædam iustitiæ diuinæ inuariabilis. Quod si igitur religio ex vno vero principio depromitur, vtique vnam oportet esse veram religionem.

Prob. c. Eph. IV, 5. Vnus Dominus, vna fides. Sicut vnus est dominus redemtor generis humani & caput ecclesiæ, nempe Iesus Christus, qui est vnica in cælum via, Io. XIV, 6. ita vna est fides, quæ instar spiritualis vinculi membra mystica cum capite Christo vnit. Dicitur itaque vna fides, non ratione subiectorum, siue hominum credentium, sed ratione obiecti apprehensi, quoniam in vnum salutis auctorem fertur fides hominum omnium saluandorum. Grauiter inquit Paullus Gal. III, 26. 27. Quotquot in Christum baptizati sunt, Christum induerunt. Non est Iudæus, neque Græcus; non est seruus, neque liber; non est mas, neque fæmina; omnes enim vos vnus estis in Christo. Quicunque per fidem vniuntur in Christo, illorum vna est religio, cuius palmaria pars est fides.

Prob. d. Gal. V, 6. Fides per caritatem operatur. Præcedit fides, sequitur caritas. Operatur fides per caritatem, vt anima per suas facultates. Quicunque igitur vniuntur in fide, illi vnum Deum in Christo amant. Quin illorum vnum est cor, & vna anima, per amorem reciprocum. Act. IV, 32.

Prob. e. Nisi pestifera esset religio, erronea & hæretica, saluator noster non iussisset vitare falsos prophetas. Matth. VII, 15. Non monuisset Paullus, vt circumspiciamus eos, qui dissidia & scandala contra doctrinam, quam nos dicimus, faciunt, & declinemus ab iis. Rom. XVI, 17. Ioannes tam singulari studio ab illorum consortio nos non auocasset, inquiens: Si quis venit ad vos & hanc doctrinam non affert, ne suscipite illum in domum, neque salutem illi dicite, 2 Io. V, 10. Fundamentalem in fide errorem apostolus vt noxiam gangrænam depingit, 1 Tim. II, 17. Sermo eorum sicut gangræna pastum habebit. Vt gangræna sensim latius serpit, donec calorem natiuum absumat: ita error in fide paullatim inualescit, & propagatur, donec vitam spiritualem, qua in fide Christi viuimus, Gal. II, 20. exstinguat. Quid? quod error fundamentalis ipsam fidem salvificam perfundet. Ex quo fit, vt hæretici a fide discedant, 1 Tim. IV, 1. huiusque faciant naufragium, 1 Tim. I, 19.

Antithesis est Indifferentistarum, Libertinorum, Puccii, Weigelii, Arminii & aliorum, quibus arbitris homo in omni religione saluari potest, modo sanctimoniæ vitæ studeat, addita tamen limitatione, quod peccator ordinarie in religione christiana, extraordinarie in religione Iudaica, Mahometana, & ethnica feruari queat. Qui sequentibus innituntur argumentis:

I. Sicut vna est ecclesia christiana catholica, ita vna est religio christiana, catholica & principalis: cuius sectæ particulares sunt Pontificia, Lutherana, Reformata, Sociniana &c. quæ licet participent de ecclesia catholica, particularibus tamen næuis sunt contaminatæ, & non omni ex parte puræ. Resp. 1. Ecclesia christiana catholica est, quæ est superædificata super fundamento apostolorum & prophetarum, cuius est angularis Iesus Christus, per quem totum ædificium coagmentatum probe crescit in templum sanctum in Domino, Eph. II, 20. In quacunque religione illa dogmata fidei & præcepta morum traduntur atque inculcantur, quæ olim prophetæ in V. T. tradiderunt, illa est christiana, catholica, & haud dubie vera, quæ non concipienda est in idea vniuersali nullibi extra intellectum existente, sed consideranda est, prout viget in certo cœtu hominum, veram religionem amplectentium, quem credentium cœtum vocamus ecclesiam. (2) Lutheranam religionem impuram esse, liquido demonstrandum est.

Instantia I. Non necesse est, vt quis accedat ad ecclesiam visibilem, sufficit, quod sit christianus & membrum ecclesiæ inuisibilis. Resp. Ecclesia vera, diuerso considerandi modo visibilis, & inuisibilis audit. Visibilis dicitur considerata materialiter & subiectiue pro cœtu hominum, qui in oculos incurrit: inuisibilis vocatur, spectata tum formaliter, ratione formæ internæ, siue vnionis mysticæ cum capite Christo, quæ spiritualis vnio fit per fidem, Eph. III, 17. tum comparatiue, in quantum eius splendor exortis persecutionibûs, vel hærefibus obscuratur; sicut obfuscata erat ecclesia Israëlitica temporibus Eliæ, vt propheta hic oculatissimus illius faciem vix conspiceret, 1 Reg. XIX, 18. At non est absolute & simpliciter inuisibilis, vt statuit WEIGELIVS P. III. postill. fol. 91. 92. Sed vbi est pura verbi prædicatio & legitima sacramentorum administratio, ibi est vera ecclesia visibilis, & in hac ecclesia inuisibilis, i. e. paruus grex vere credentium & electorum, cui regnum dare patri cœlesti complacuit, Luc. XII, 32. Extra illam ecclesiam Christi veram visibilem temere neglectam non datur salus. Etenim huic concredita sunt τὰ λόγια τοῦ θεοῦ, Rom. III, 2. Verbum & sacramenta efficacia gratiæ & salutis media, Io. III, 5. 1Io. V, 8.

Instantia II. Si verus christianus in Turcia captiuus teneretur, saluaretur, licet non viueret in pura ecclesia. E. Deductio aut accessus ad ecclesiam non est necessarius ad salutem. R. Verus christianus a Turcis captus, non est corpore quidem, attamen animo in ecclesia vera, propterea, quod veritatem cœlestem, quam custodit & propagat vera Christi ecclesia, fincero animo amplectitur.

II. Si in religione pontificia dantur vera media salutis, non in vnica Lutheranorum religione æterna salus quæritur & inuenitur. Atqui prius verum est, concedente LVTHERO tom. IV. & VI. Altenburg. E. et posterius. R. Nulla religio adeo corrupta est, vt non quædam dogmata vera, per se bona & falutaria, in ea tradantur. Contra in religione falfa multa erronea, noxia, spuria & peregrina continentur, v. gr. docentur in religione pontificia traditiones humanæ, verbo diuino difformes, auctoritas pontificis romani infallibilis, merita sanctorum, & eorundem cultus religiosus, fiducia propriorum operum, sacrificium missaticum, sacramentum cœnæ sub vna specie, quibus dogmatibus falsis vera in Christum fides nec generatur, nec alitur, sed extinguitur. Quod si pontificius saluatur, salvatur, eiusdem salus accepta referenda est non religioni pontificiae, quatenus tali, sed veritati in papatu residuae. Fieri enim potest, ut pontificius seductus, abiecta propriorum meritorum fiducia, unice confugiat ad meritum Christi, & in eodem conquiescat: hic salvatur, non ut pontificius, sed ut fidelis christianus.

Instantia III. At pontificius ille ecclesiam Lutheranorum non ingreditur. R. Non ingreditur corpore quidem, at animo amplectitur dogmata illa salutifera, quae in religione Lutheranorum habentur. Non adit eorum externam societatem, cum illis tamen facit, si spectes internam animi consensionem.

III. Religionis christianae fundamentum est poenitentia & fides in Christum, quae docetur in omni religione illorum hominum, qui christianos se esse profitentur. E. in omni religione eorum, qui nomine christianorum insigniuntur, datur salus. Antecedens probatur, quia ipse salvator sub initium N. T. hominibus salvandis hoc fundamentale dogma proposuit, & serio vult: Poeniteat vos: appropinquauit enim regnum caelorum. Matth. IV, 17. Poenitentiam agite, & credite euangelio. R. Largimur faciles, sub initium N. T. monitos fuisse homines, vt poenitentiam agerent, vt crederent euangelio. At vero multa condonantur incipientibus, quae a proficientibus exiguntur. Incipientibus sufficit summa aut breuis epitome christianae doctrinae, proficientibus distincta articulorum fidei fundamentalium notitia instillanda est. Quos Christus gratia sua praeuenit, hos magis magisque praeparauit, informauit & illuminauit. Id quod cum ex pluribus Christi & apostolorum concionibus, tum inprimis ex prolixo sermone in monte ad populum habito colligere licet. Matth. V. VI. VII. capite.

IV. Apostolus Petrus indifferentismo patrocinari videtur, Act. X, 34. inquiens: In veritate deprehendo, quod non fit personarum acceptor Deus; sed in omni gente, qui timet ipsum & operatur iustitiam, acceptus illi est. R. non dicit apostolus: in omni religione, sed in omni gente, qui timet ipsum & operatur iustitiam, acceptus illi est. Quibus verbis innuit, nullam gentem sub caelo a gratia convertente, & regenerante absolute exclusam esse, siquidem ingenue fatetur, Deum gentibus dedisse poenitentiam. Act. X, 28. Non igitur loquitur Petrus de gentibus, qua caecitate ethnica laborantibus, sed de gentibus media gratiae admittentibus & fidem in Christum concipientibus, quam timore erga Deum & operibus iustitiae testantur atque declarant.

V. Sine verbo Dei revelato haud pauci conversi sunt: quod patet exemplo centurionis Cornelii, Act. X, 2. qui licet gentilis esset, attamen religiosus, timens Deum cum tota domo sua, beneficus erga egenos, assiduus in precibus erat. Liquet idem exemplo magorum orientalium, Matth. II, 1. qui fine verbo praedicato ad Christum perducti sunt. Resp. (1) Ad exemplum Cornelii. Erat hic vir religiosus non ratione originis gentilis, sed ratione status, regenitus ex semine verbi, ex quo habuit notitiam generalem de Messia tanquam redemptore mundi, vid. Act. X, 36. specialis ipsi deerat applicatio ad certum individuum, nempe ad Iesum Nazarenum, quem vt salutariter agnosceret, a S. Petro vberius informandus erat. Resp. (2) Ad exemplum magorum Persicorum. Agnouerunt hi Messiam e scriptis Danielis, ad quem quaerendum excitabantur per nouam stellam inusitatae magnitudinis & claritatis. Danielem in schola magorum educatum fuisse constat ex Dn. I, 6. Cuius familiaritatis occasione ipsam de Messia doctrinam haud dubie aliquibus instillauit. Idem c. II, 44. Regi Babylonico nonnulla exposuit de regno caeli futuro fine experte. His accedit, quod non omnes Iudaei a Babyloniis remigrauerint Hierosolymas, sed multi remanserint iis in locis, qui celebres illic scholas habuerunt. Confer. Act. II, 9. Addimus, sacras litteras non fine prouida aeterni Numinis cura graece fuisse redditas, atque adeo familiari sermone. mone cum gentilibus communicatas. Hic multi erant viri boni, quos scriptura εὐλαβεῖς appellat, qui licet non essent circumcisi, libros tamen euoluebant propheticos, & venerabantur Deum Israëlĭs: quod de eunucho Aethiope legitur Act. VIII, 28.


### Question VIII. Is the truth of the Christian religion to be judged by the external holiness of the men addicted to that religion?

The guileless holiness of men addicted to the Christian religion is a very notable testimony to the truth and efficacy of the Christian religion (a). But since hypocrisy not rarely puts on the appearance of external holiness, external holiness is not the principal, perpetual, and infallible mark of the true religion (b). But the truth of a religion is to be estimated principally and infallibly from its conformity with the revealed word of God (c).

Proof a. Above, in proof e to Question V, we showed that the scope of the *paideia*, or doctrine and religion of Christianity, is to inculcate in us a manner of living soberly, righteously, and godly, from the Epistle of Paul to Titus 2:11-12. And what the same apostle had taught there in verse 10 specifically, that it is the duty of servants to adorn the doctrine of our Savior God in all things: that can be said generally of all Christians, that it is their duty to adorn the doctrine of Jesus with the holiness of their lives, so that the Christian religion consists not so much in words as in deeds. For what religion has existed in the whole world that makes men truly pious, draws them away from vices, teaches them to trample upon earthly things, and commands and engenders virtues, besides the Christian? Whence, as witnessed by Dr. Johann Adam Osiander in *Theologia Positiva*, p. 76, Julian the Apostate ordered the priest of the idols to take care that the pagans should study virtue; for thus, he said, their cult would make progress, just as for that reason the Christian religion had had such great success. The same most celebrated theologian cites Justin Martyr in his second Apology speaking thus: "We who once delighted in debaucheries now love only chastity; we who used magic arts now consecrate ourselves to the good and eternal God; we who loved the fruits and revenues of money and possessions above all things now bring even what we have into a common stock and share with every needy person; we who were given to mutual hatreds and slaughters, and because of established custom did not share a common hearth with those who were of our own tribe, now, after the appearance of Christ, live together familiarly and pray for our enemies."

Proof b. If a life good in its outward appearance were an infallible sign of a true religion, all hypocrites would have the true religion; because they strive mightily that their external holiness may strike the eyes and ears of men. The Pharisees boasted of a singular holiness, as Christ testifies, Matthew 6:2 ff., Luke 18:11. Indeed, even while Paul was still alive, false teachers, who insinuated themselves into houses and captured silly women burdened with sins, had a form of godliness, 2 Timothy 3:5. And the worshippers of angels walked in "humility," Colossians 2:18. And the sheep's clothing of false prophets is, as it were, stitched together from continence, chastity, and fasting, according to the exposition of Jerome. See Calovius, *Biblia Illustrata* on this passage. Today, monks and Anabaptists hold before them an appearance of external holiness, whose religion is false.

Proof c. The truth of the Christian religion is to be estimated principally and infallibly from its conformity with divine revelation. Divine revelation, however, is held today in the writings of the prophets and apostles. Therefore, whatever religion acknowledges, observes, and perpetually follows Holy Scripture as an infallible principle, that religion submits itself to supernatural revelation and agrees with the mind of Jehovah, and is therefore true and divine, reflecting the nature of its principle.

Latin:

Expers fuci sanctitas hominum religioni christianae addictorum perquam insigne testimonium est veritatis & efficaciae religionis christianae (a). At cum hypocrisis externae sanctitatis speciem haud raro induat, externa sanctitas non est principalis, perpetua & infallibilis verae religionis nota (b). Sed veritas religionis principaliter & infallibiliter aestimanda ex conformitate eiusdem cum verbo Dei reuelato (c).

Prob. a. Supra in prob. e. ad q. V. ostendimus, τῆς παιδείας s. doctrinae & religionis christianae scopum esse, vt inculcet nobis modum sobrie, pie, ac iuste viuendi, ex epistola Paulli ad Tit. II, 11. 12. Et quod idem apostolus ibid. v. 10. docuerat in specie, seruorum esse, doctrinam seruatoris nostri Dei exornare in omnibus: id generatim de omnibus christianis dici potest, quod ipsorum sit, vitae sanctitate doctrinam Iesu exornare, vt non tam in dictis, quam in factis christiana religio consistat. Quae enim religio in toto terrarum orbe exstitit, quae homines vere pios reddat, a vitiis abstrahat, terrena calcare doceat, virtutes imperet & ingeneret, praeter christianam? Vnde teste D. IO. ADAMO OSIANDRO in theol. positiua p. 76. Iulianus apostata idolorum sacerdotem iussit curare, vt pagani virtuti studerent; sic enim illorum cultum progressus habiturum, quemadmodum ea de caussa tantos religio habuerit christiana. Adducit idem theologus celeberrimus Iustinum Martyrem in apologia secunda ita loquentem: Qui olim stupris delectabamur, nunc castitatem tantum amamus: qui magicis artibus vtebamur, bono & aeterno Deo nos consecramus: qui pecuniarum ac possessionum fructus atque prouentus prae rebus omnibus amabamus, nunc etiam ea, quae habemus, in commune conferimus, & cum indigentibus quibusque communicamus: qui odiis & caedibus mutuis inter nos grassabamur, & pro consuetudine recepta cum iis, qui tribules nostri erant, communem focum non habebamus, nunc post Christi apparitionem familiariter simul viuimus, & pro inimicis oramus.

Prob. b. Si vita extrinsecus bona infallibile signum verae religionis esset, omnes hypocritae veram haberent religionem; quia illi summopere annituntur, vt illorum sanctitas externa oculos auresque hominum incurrat. Pharisaei iactabant singularem sanctitatem, teste Christo, Matth. VI, 2. sq. Luc. XVIII, 11. Quin & superstite Paullo, doctores falsi, qui se insinuabant in domos, & captiuabant mulierculas oneratas peccatis, speciem pietatis habebant. 2 Tim. III, 5. Et angelolatrae incedebant ἐν ταπεινοφροσύνῃ, Col. II, 18. Et pseudoprophetarum vestimenta ouina consuta quasi sunt ex continentia, castitate ac ieiunio, iuxta expositionem Hieronymi. Vid. CALOVII bibl. illustr. in h. l. Hodiernum monachi & anabaptistae sanctitatis externae speciem prae se ferunt, quorum religio falsa est.

Prob. c. Veritas religionis christianae principaliter & infallibiliter ex conformitate eiusdem cum reuelatione diuina aestimanda est. Reuelatio autem diuina hodie habetur in scriptis prophetarum & apostolorum. Quaecunque igitur religio scripturam sacram velut principium infallibile agnoscit, obseruat & perpetuo sequitur, illa se submittit reuelationi supernaturali, mentique Iehouae congruit, adeoque vera & diuina est, referens naturam principii sui.


### Question IX

The religion of the Israelites in the Old Testament and of Christians in the New Testament is one, as regards substance.

Proof. (1) Generally, since the Israelites in the O. T. were justified and saved by faith in Christ no less than Christians in the N. T. St. Peter speaks with great emphasis concerning the justification of the Israelites by faith in Christ, Acts X, 43: To Him (Jesus) all the prophets bear witness, that through His name everyone who believes in Him receives remission of sins. You say: The prophets speak of the future, not of their own time; of the state of the Old, but not of the New Testament. I reply: Peter's words are unlimited and general. He implies that the Prophets, in those times in which they were survivors, did not prophesy, but bore witness to Jesus, that everyone who believes in Him receives remission of sins. Therefore he does not speak of the prophecy of future times, but of the testimony borne to the present Jesus, who was present morally, if you look at the divine promises, which presented the coming Jesus with all His benefits as present, and placed the efficacy of His merit before their eyes. Concerning the eternal salvation of the Israelites to be obtained through Christ, Peter discourses likewise excellently in Acts XV, 10. 11: Now therefore why do you test God, to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, just as they also. Obs. 1. By the yoke ἀβάςακτον, impossible to be borne, is understood not only the ceremonial law, but also the moral, as being βαρυτέρα i.e. heavier. Matt. XXIII, 23. It is indeed a matter of circumcision, but as obligating to universal obedience. Gal. V, 8. Obs. 2. When the apostle says: καθ’ ὃν τρόπον κᾀκεῖνοι, just as they also, by these same words he refers to the fathers, of whom he had made mention in this verse 11, not the disciples, of whom the discourse was in v. 10. This is validly gathered from the natural collocation of the words, which being preserved, the relative word looks to the proximate subject, not the remote (*).

Proof. (2) Specifically by the example of Abraham, whom he teaches was justified by faith, Rom. IV, 1. seqq. From which I argue: Abraham, the Father of all believers, as well of the uncircumcised as of the circumcised, no less of those who lived under the Old than who live under the New covenant, was justified and saved by faith in Christ. Therefore, all believers of all times are justified and saved by faith in Christ. You say: it is not permitted to conclude from one example to all men. I reply: The example concludes by virtue of parity or agreement with the rest. Therefore, from a singular proposition, a universal is validly inferred, because of the connection which is equally necessary everywhere. Now indeed all believers have obtained ἰσότιμον, i.e. an equally precious faith with Abraham, 2 Pet. I, 1. From which he is named the Father of all believers, uncircumcised and circumcised, Rom. IV, 11. 12. These things having been thus set forth, we form the perfect syllogism. By which faith Abraham, the father of all believers, as well of the uncircumcised as of the circumcised, was justified and saved, by the same faith all believers of the Old and New Testament are justified and saved. But Abraham was saved by faith in Christ. Therefore.

There is an antithesis of certain Papists, Socinians, Anabaptists, Schwenckfeldians, and Weigelians, who suppose that in the Old Testament faith in Christ was not necessary for a sinner to be saved, nor was the doctrine concerning the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity necessary for him to believe; whose arguments we shall weigh.

I. Christ the mediator did not exist in the times of the O.T. nor was his satisfaction then performed. Therefore, the Israelites could not believe in Christ the mediator. Resp. (1) Christ, as God, is indeed the father of eternity, Is. IX, 5. (2) The Israelites in the times of the O.T. believed that the Messiah was to be incarnated & sacrificed for the sins of the world. Who, although he was not present in the O.T. physically with respect to human nature, was nevertheless present morally. For this reason he is called the lamb slain from the foundation of the world, Apoc. XIII, 8. Indeed (1) by reason of the decree, (2) by reason of the promise, (3) by reason of typical representation in the sacrifices of the O.T., (4) by reason of the efficacy & fruit of the merit, which avails forward and backward.

II. That the Israelites in the O.T. did not believe in Christ, Paul seems to indicate, Gal. III, 23. Before faith came, we were kept under the law, shut up unto the faith which should afterwards be revealed. Resp. There are those who understand in the cited place 'faith' as that which is believed, or the doctrine of faith concerning Christ, which was revealed more clearly & abundantly in the New, than in the Old Testament. But B. LUTHER in his last commentary on Galatians, fol. 91, and with him D. CALOV. in his illustrated Bible on this passage, understand the words of Paul concerning the opposite state of any man under law and grace, in this sense: Before a man believes, the law must be imposed upon him, so that he may be shut up as if in a prison, restrained & saddened; but to the saddened one, the evangelical doctrine must be inculcated, so that, raised up by the promise of gratuitous mercy, he may flee to Christ, who is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth, Rom. X, 4.

III. That the righteousness of faith, fixed in the merit of Christ, was unknown to the Israelites in the O.T., the apostle seems to suggest, Rom. III, 21. Now without the law of God the righteousness is manifested, being witnessed by the law and the prophets, even the righteousness which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe. Resp. If the apostle had written: 'Now for the first time without the law the righteousness of God is manifested,' a certain nerve would be in the argument: but, with that word omitted, it is so enervated that it can be inverted: 'The righteousness of God which is now manifested without the law of God, but witnessed by the law and the prophets, was not unknown to the Israelites.' For now indeed it is manifested more clearly & abundantly, but it was witnessed long ago in the Mosaic Pentateuch and the prophetic writings, albeit with a lesser degree of clarity.

Latin:

Religio Israëlltarum in veteri, & Christianorum in nouo testamento, vna est, quoad substantiam.

Prob. (1) Generatim, quoniam Israëlitæ in V T. per fidem in Christum non minus, quam christiani in N. T. iustificati & saluati sunt. De iustificatione Israëlltarum per fidem in Christnm magna cum emphasl loquitur S. Petrus Actor. X, 43. Huic (Iesu) testimonium perhibent omnes prophetæ, quod remissionem peccatorum accipiat per nomen ipsius omnis, qui credit in ipsum. Dicis: Prophetæ loquuntur de futuro, non de suo tempore; de statu veteris, sed non noui testamenti. Resp. Verba Petri illimitata & generalia sunt. Innuit, Prophetas temporibus illis, quibus superstites fuerunt, non vaticinatos esse, sed testimonium Iesu perhibuisse, quod remissionem peccatorum accipiat omnis in ipsum credens. Non ergo loquitur de vaticinio futurorum temporum, sed de testimonio præsenti Iesu perhibito, qui præsens erat moraliter, si spectes promissiones diuinas, quæ venturum Iesum cum omnibus eius beneficiis præsentem sistebant, & meriti ipsius efficaciam ob oculos ponebant. De æterna salute Israëlltarum per Christum obtinenda præclare itidem disserit Petrus Act. XV, 10. 11. Nunc ergo quid tentatis Deum, ad ponendum iugum super ceruicem discipulorum, quod neque Patres nostri, neque nos valuimus portare? Sed per gratiam domini nostri Iesu Christi credimus (nos) saluari, quemadmodum etiam illi. Obs. 1. Per iugum ἀβάςακτον, portatu impossibile, intelligitur non tantum lex ceremonialis, sed & moralis, tanquam βαρυτέρα f. grauior. Matth. XXIII, 23. Agitur de circumcisione quidem, sed tanquam obligante ad vniuersalem obedientiam. Gal. V, 8. Obs. 2. Quando apostolus dicit: καθ’ ὃν τρόπον κᾀκεῖνοι, quemadmodum & illi, verbis iisdem respicit patres, quorum hoc versu 11. mentionem fecerat, non discipulos, de quibus v. 10. ipsi sermo erat. Id quod valide colligitur ex naturali verborum collocatione, qua seruata, vox relatiua subiectum proximum, non remotum spectat (*).

Prob. (2) Speciatim exemplo Abrahami, quem fide iustificatum esse docet Rom. IV, 1. seqq. Ex quo argumentor: Abraham, Pater omnium credentium, tam præputiatorum quam circumcisorum, non minus illorum, qui vixerunt sub veteri, quam qui viuunt sub nouo fœdere, fide in Christum iustificatus & saluatus est. E. Omnes credentes omnium temporum fide in Christum iustificantur & saluantur. Dicis: ab vno exemplo ad omnes homines concludere non licet. Resp. Exemplum concludit vi paritatis siue conuenientiæ cum reliquis. Proinde ex propositione singulari valide infertur vniuersalis, ob nexum pariter vbique necessarium. Iam vero omnes credentes cum Abrahamo ἰσότιμον, i. e. æque pretiosam fidem nacti sunt, 2 Petr. I, 1. Ex quo Pater omnium credentium, præputiatorum & circumcisorum, nominatur Rom. IV, 11. 12. Quibus ita præstitutis, perfectum formamus syllogismum. Per quam fidem Abraham, omnium credentium, tam præputiatorum, quam circumcisorum, pater, iustificatus & saluatus est, per eandem fidem omnes credentes veteris & noui testamenti iustificantur & saluantur. Atqui Abraham saluatus est per fidem in Christum. E.

Antithesis est quorundam Pontificiorum, Socinianorum, Anabaptistarum, Schwenckfeldianorum & Weigelianorum, qui autumant in vet. testamento peccatori saluando non necessariam fuisse fidem in Christum, neque ipsi creditu necessariam fuisse doctrinam de mysterio SS. Trinitatis; quorum ponderabimus argumenta.

I. Christus mediator non exstitit temporibus V. T. nec eius satisfactio tunc praestita est. E. Israelitae non potuerunt in Christum mediatorem credere. Resp. (1) Christus, qua Deus, est enim pater aeternitatis, Es. IX, 5. (2) Crediderunt Israelitae temporibus V. T. Messiam incarnandum & pro peccatis mundi immolandum. Qui quamvis in V. T. praesens non fuerit respectu humanae naturae physice, praesens tamen fuit moraliter. Id propter dicitur agnus occisus a fundatione mundi, Apoc. XIII, 8. Nimirum (1) ratione decreti, (2) ratione promissi, (3) ratione typicae repraesentationis in sacrificiis V.T. (4) ratione efficaciae & fructus meriti, quod valet antrorsum & retrorsum.

II. Israelitas in V. T. non credidisse in Christum, indicare videtur Paullus, Gal. III, 23. Antequam veniret fides, sub lege custodiebamur, conclusi sub fidem, quae revelanda erat. Resp. Sunt, qui intelligunt l. c. fidem, quae creditur, seu doctrinam fidei de Christo, quae luculentius & uberius revelata est in novo, quam veteri testamento. B. tamen LVTHERVS in comment. vlt. in Galat. fol. 91. & cum eo D. CALOV. in bibl. illustrat. in h. l. intelligunt verba Paulii de opposito cuiuscunque hominis statu sub lege & gratia, hoc sensu: Antequam homo credit, ipsi imponenda est lex, ut illa velut carcere concludatur, coërceatur & contristetur; contristato autem inculcanda est doctrina evangelica, ut promissione gratuitae misericordiae erectus confugiat ad Christum, qui est finis legis ad iustitiam omni credenti. Rom. X, 4.

III. Iustitiam fidei, in merito Christi defixae, incognitam fuisse Israelitis in V. T: innuere videtur apostolus, Rom. III, 21. Nunc sine lege Dei manifestata est iustitia, testificata a lege & prophetis, iustitia autem per fidem Iesu Christi in omnes & super omnes, qui credunt. Resp. Si apostolus scripsisset: Nunc primum sine lege iustitia Dei manifestata est, neruus quidam argumento inesset: at, illa voce omissa, adeo enerue est, ut inuerti queat: Quae iustitia Dei nunc sine lege Dei manifestata est, testificata autem a lege & prophetis, illa Israelitis non fuit incognita. Nam nunc quidem manifestata est clarius & uberius, testificata autem iamdudum est in pentateucho Mosaico & scriptis propheticis, quamuis minori claritatis gradu.


### Question X. Should men be compelled to embrace religion?

For the purpose of taking up religion, the human intellect, by the power of the divine word, and from arguments sought therefrom that are compelling, can be logically and internally compelled (a), but it neither can, nor ought to be compelled by political and external force to approve & embrace a religion which it judges to be false (b).

Prob. a. The intellect is a necessary power, which, all things required for acting being posited, cannot but act. For if truth is either most clear in itself, such as that of the most certain & evident principles; or is proved by the best consequences and clearly proposed to the human intellect: it is so constrained that it cannot deny internal assent. For just as, when a visible object is posited, illuminated by light at a proper distance, so that no defect subsists in the visual organ or eye, it is impossible that the eye should not see white and distinguish it from black, nor allow itself to be persuaded that a raven is white or a swan is black: so it cannot happen, if an object is clearly proposed to the intellect, that it should assent to the false and dissent from the true. Now, that the holy scripture is the infallible word of God can be most clearly demonstrated from certain criteria, in the first place from the efficacy of scripture. If therefore the intellect of man is convinced that Holy scripture is the word of God, it cannot but ratify everything which is either held in the sacred letters αὐτολεξεὶ, with terms defining them, or is deduced from it by an easy & manifest consequence, on account of the irrefragable authority of God speaking. (1) Because God alone is the King of minds, and He alone has dominion over consciences, as Gregory the Great speaks wisely in book 11, epistle 52. Therefore, as many as command religion to consciences encroach upon divine right.

(2) God is delighted by spontaneous, not coerced, religion. For which reason the royal prophet prophesies that the religion of Christians under the new covenant would be freely undertaken and practiced, Ps. CX, 3. Thy people (shall be a people) of willingness. The entire Psalm CX treats of Christ, cited by Christ himself Matth. XII, 44, by Peter Acts II, 34, by Paul 1 Cor. XV, 25, Hebr. I, 13. Namely, the sacred singer predicting that the Christian people will be eager and ready to worship the Messiah, to whom they will offer spiritual sacrifices not coerced by sword, club, or fire, but prompted by the internal impulse of the Holy Spirit.

(3) As the will, so religion cannot be coerced; since nothing is so voluntary as religion, from which if the mind is turned away, it is already removed, it is already nothing, in the judgment of Lactantius, book V, c. 19. (4) Faith, which is the chief part of the Christian religion, is born not from coercion, but from the hearing of the preached word, Rom. X, 17. Thus by the divine word Jonah converted the Ninevites, Peter three thousand souls on the day of Pentecost, Acts II, 41, Paul the Romans, Corinthians, Ephesians, etc.

Whose weapons were not carnal, but spiritual, 2

Cor. X, 4. Nor did they ever intend to lord it over the faith of their hearers, 2 Cor. X, 4. The antithesis is that of the Papists and the Muhammadans, who maintain that men must be coerced by sword and flames to embrace religion, and that heretics must be killed. Who strive to fortify their opinion with the following arguments.

I. The Savior himself says: Compel them to come in, Luke XIV, 23. Resp. Distinguish between logical or internal compulsion, and political or external, and violent, compulsion. In the place cited, it cannot be understood as political and violent compulsion. For the Savior compelled by the words brought forward, inviting the apostles, to whom ἀναγκασμὸς, or political compulsion, is denied, Matth. XX, 26: But it shall not be so among you. Wherefore the ministers of the church compel guests to enter by clearly proposing the word of Jehovah, by persuading and beseeching with arguments sought from it, not by threatening sword or wheel.

II. The magistrate is the guardian of both tables of the decalogue. Therefore it is also his duty to lead men to the true worship of God either by persuading or by using force. Resp. It is the magistrate's duty to lead not by force, but by the sinews of arguments, to external means, not immediately to the worship of God itself. That which is the duty of the theologian and pastor rather than the political magistrate. Therefore the Emperor Constantine was accustomed to say: You are bishops within the church, I am outside the church.

III. It is the magistrate's duty to deter citizens from idolatrous worship by proposing capital punishments. Which is clear from the divine command Deut. XII, 7, 8, 9, and the example of Jehu, who struck the Baalites with the sword, 2 Kings X, 35. Resp. in the O.

T. there exist express commands about killing idolaters; which we do not have in the N. T. regarding heretics. The commands of the Old Testament about killing idolaters were judicial, not moral. It is moral that the sincerity of religion must be preserved with the utmost zeal and defended from the corruptions of false prophets.

It is judicial and forensic that capital punishment must be inflicted upon idolaters, to which we are not bound in the N. T. For forensic laws have ceased in the N. T. But to us it has been said: Do you not know what manner of spirit you are of? For the Son of man is not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them, Luke

IX, 55, 56. Add that there is a huge difference between idolatry and heresy. In the former, malice opposed to natural light (which acknowledges that one God is to be worshipped) runs rampant; in the latter, blindness not grasping the supernatural mysteries of faith deserves pardon.

For the Savior says Matth. XIII, 30: Let both grow together (the tares with the wheat) until the harvest. The tares are the heretics, of whom he says heretics, of whom

the Lord says: Suffer them to grow because of the supernatural object of Faith, because of the greater sweetness and gentleness of the spirit of Zion compared to that of Sinai, because of the hope of future conversion. Take care, however, that the wheat does not perish through the cunning machinations of heretics. For the conviction of heretics through unanswerable arguments, the wheat does not perish, but is changed from tares into wheat. Augustine would surely have perished if he had proceeded with force and slaughter against the Manichaeans. Confer DANNHAU. Hodom. Sp. Pap. phantasm. VI. p. 1382.

IV. The magistrate does not bear the sword in vain, Rom. VIII, 4. And let him punish heretics, the disturbers of the church and public peace, with the sword drawn against them. Resp. The magistrate bears the sword against evil works, which are morally, civilly, and externally evil: heresy, because it is theologically evil and an error of the mind concerning spiritual matters, is not to be suppressed by a material sword, but by the spiritual sword of the divine word. But if indeed a heretic becomes a disturber of the peace and a manifest blasphemer, he is to be restrained by an afflictive bodily punishment, not as a simple heretic, but as a blasphemer and seditious person.

Latin:

Ad capessendam religionem intellectus humanus, vi verbi diuini, & ex eo petitis argumentis stringentibus, logice atque interne cogi potest (a), sed nec potest, nec debet vi ferri politice atque externe cogi ad approbandam & amplectendam religionem, quam falsam esse censet (b).

Prob. a. Intellectus est potentia necessaria, quae positis omnibus ad agendum requisitis, non potest non agere. Si enim veritas vel ipsa per se est clarissima, qualis est principiorum certissimorum & euidentissimorum; vel per optimas consequentias probata & perspicue proposita est intellectui humano: hic ita constringitur, ut assensum internum denegare nequeat. Sicut enim, posito obiecto visibili, luce illustrato in debita distantia, ita ut nullum subsit vitium in organo visuo sive oculo, impossibile est, quin oculus videat album & distinguat a nigro, nec sinat sibi persuaderi coruum esse album, cygnum esse nigrum: ita fieri non potest, si obiectum clare sit propositum intellectui, vt hic assentiatatur falso, dissentiat a vero. Iam vero sacram scripturam esse verbum Dei infallibile, clarissime demonstrari potest ex certis κριτηρίοις, in primis ex efficacia scripturae. Quod si itaque intellectus hominis convictus est, S. scripturam esse verbum Dei, non potest non omne, quod vel in sacris litteris habetur αὐτολεξεὶ, terminis terminantibus, vel ex ea per pronam & manifestam consequentiam deducitur, propter auctoritatem irrefragabilem Dei dicentis ratihabere. (1) Quia solus Deus mentium rex est, solusque in conscientias habet dominium, scite loquente Gregor. M. libr. 11. epist. 52. Involant igitur in ius divinum, quotquot religionem imperant conscientiis.

(2) Religione spontanea, non coacta Deus delectatur. Qua de causa propheta regius vaticinatur, religionem christianorum sub novo foedere libere susceptum & exercitum iri, Ps. CX, 3. Populus tuus (populus erit) promtitudinum. Totus Psalmus CX agit de Christo, citatus ab ipso Christo Matth. XII, 44. a Petro Act. II, 34. a Paullo 1 Cor. XV, 25. Hebr. I, 13. Nempe praedicente hieropsalte, populus christianus erit alacris & promptus ad colendum Messiam, cui sacrificia spiritualia offeret non coactus ferro, fuste, igne, sed interno Spiritus sancti impulsu instinctus.

(3) Vt voluntas, ita religio cogi nequit; quoniam nihil tam voluntarium est, quam religio, a qua si animus auersus est, iam sublata, iam nulla est, iudice Lactantio libr. V, c. 19. (4) Fides, quae religionis christianae pars praecipua est, nascitur non ex coactione, sed verbi praedicati auscultatione, Rom. X, 17. Sic verbo diuino Ionas Ninivitas, Petrus die pentecostes ter mille animas, Act. II, 41. Paullus Romanos, Corinthios, Ephesios, &c. conuerterunt.

Quorum arma non fuerunt carnalia, sed spiritualia, 2

Cor. X, 4. Neque iidem fidei auditorum dominari unquam intenderunt, 2 Cor. X, 4. Antitheis est Pontificiorum, & Muhammedanorum, statuentium, homines ad amplectendam religionem ferro & flammis cogendos, atque haereticos occidendos esse. Qui suam sententiam munire nituntur argumentis seqq.

I. Ipse saluator inquit: Compelle intrare, Luc. XIV, 23. Resp. Dist. inter compulsum logicum, siue internum, & politicum, siue externum, eumque violentum. Loco cit. non potest intelligi compulsus politicus & violentus. Compellauit enim verbis adductis saluator apostolos inuitantes, quibus ἀναγκασμὸς, siue compulsus politicus denegatus est, Matth. XX, 26: Vos autem non sic. Quare ministri ecclesiae hospites intrare compellunt, verbum Iehouae luculenter proponendo, petitis ex eo argumentis suadendo & obsecrando, non ferrum aut rotam minitando.

II. Magistratus est custos utriusque tabulae decalogi. Ergo eius quoque est homines adducere ad verum Dei cultum aut suadendo, aut adhibita vi cogendo. Resp. Magistratus est adducere non vi, sed argumentorum neruis ad externa media, non immediate ad ipsum Dei cultum. Id quod theologi & pastoris potius, quam magistratus politici est. Ideo Constantinus imperator dicere solitus est: Vos estis episcopi intra ecclesiam, ego extra ecclesiam.

III. Magistratus est, ciues a cultu idololatrico, propositis suppliciis capitalibus, deterrere. Quod patet ex mandato diuino Deuter. XII, 7. 8. 9. & exemplo Iehu, qui gladio percussit Baalitas, 2 Reg. X, 35. Resp. in V.

T. exstant mandata expressa de idololatris occidendis; quae in N. T. de haereticis non habemus. Mandata vet. testamenti de necandis idololatris erant iudicialia, non moralia. Morale est, sinceritatem religionis summo studio esse conferuandam & a corruptelis falsorum prophetarum vindicandam.

Iudiciale ac forense est, idololatris capitale supplicium esse irrogandum, ad quod in N. T. non obligamur. Cessarunt enim leges forenses in N. T. Nobis autem dictum est: Annon scitis, cuius Spiritus sitis vos? Filius enim hominis non venit ad perdendum animas hominum, sed ad seruandum, Luc.

IX, 55. 56. Adiice, quod ingens discrimen sit inter idololatriam, & haeresin. Ibi malitia lumini naturali (quod agnoscit unum Deum esse colendum) aduersa grassatur hic caecitas mysteria fidei supernaturalia non capiens veniam meretur.

Dicit enim saluator Matth. XIII, 30. Sinite vna crescere utraque (zizania cum tritico) usque ad messem. Zizania sunt haeretici, de quibus dicit hæretici, de quibus

dicit dominus: Sinite crescere ob Fidei obiectum supernaturale, ob spiritus Sionii præ Sinaitico maiorem suavitatem & lenitatem, ob spem futuræ conversionis. Cauete modo, ne hæreticorum callidis machinationibus triticum pereat. Ad conuictionem hæreticorum per argumenta inuicta non perit triticum, sed e lolio in triticum mutatur. Sane periisset Augustinus, si vi ac cæde in Manichæos animaduersum fuisset. Confer. D A N N H A V. Hodom. Sp. Pap. phantasm. VI. p. 1382.

IV. Magistratus gladium non gerit frustra, Rom. VIII, 4. E. puniat hæreticos ecclesiæ & pacis publicæ turbatores stricto in eos gladio. Resp. Magistratus gerit gladium aduersus mala opera, quæ moraliter, ciuiliter & externe mala sunt: hæresis, quia theologice mala & error mentis circa spiritualia est, non materiali, sed spirituali gladio verbi diuini opprimenda est. Quod si vero hæreticus fit turbator pacis & manifeste blasphemus, pœna corporis afflictiva coërcendus est, non vt hæreticus simplex, sed vt blasphemus & seditiosus.


### Q. XI. What things are comprehended under the name of the Christian religion?

Under the name of the Christian religion are comprehended things to be believed and things to be done by man as a wayfarer, corrupted by sins, who is to attain eternal salvation. Prob. Just as God is religiously worshipped by true faith and a sincere zeal for good works; so religion, which is the form or reason of worshipping God, embraces within its scope things to be believed and things to be done.

You say: That assertion, by which religion is said to embrace things to be believed and things to be done, does not seem to be accurate. For (1) things to be done are also things to be believed, in that they are divinely revealed. Whatever God has revealed must be believed. (2) Things to be believed also include practice, since faith is not a bare theory of the mind, but a practice of the heart. (3) A third member is omitted, namely things to be avoided, or to be omitted, such as sins. Resp. to I. We grant not unwillingly that things to be done are, in a looser sense, things to be believed because of divine revelation: But here things to be done are taken strictly, in so far as they are works to be directed to the glory of God, with faith shining before them: but things to be believed are mysteries to be received by the assent of faith. To II. Resp. The practice of faith differs from the practice of works. The former precedes in the order of nature, the latter follows; faith directs good works: Works are directed by the preceding acts of faith, knowledge and trust. To III. Resp. Under the name of things to be done, things to be avoided are also comprehended. For in practical disciplines, he who avoids sins is in a certain way said to act.

Obs. (1) Things to be believed are said in a threefold way: I. in a general sense. II. in a special sense. III. in a most special sense. In a general sense, those things are called things to be believed which have been revealed in the written word of God, e.g., physical, historical, moral, and supernatural things, whether they concern the eternal salvation of men or less. In a special sense, those things are called things to be believed which have been revealed in the word of God for the salvation of men, and are believed because of divine revelation, although they may be known in some way from the principles of reason. In a most special sense, mysteries are called things to be believed, which are superior to the grasp of reason, and are to be known for our salvation from divine revelation alone.

(2) Assertions, enunciations, or dogmatic theses formed from the word of God concerning things to be believed are called articles of faith by accepted usage of speech.

Latin:

Nomine religionis christianæ comprehenduntur credenda & agenda homini viatori, peccatis corrupto, æternam salutem adepturo. Prob. Sicut Deus religiose colitur vera fide, & sincero bonorum operum studio; ita religio, quæ est forma aut ratio colendi Deum, ambitu suo complectitur credenda & agenda.

Dicis: Assertio illa, qua religio dicitur complecti credenda & agenda, non videtur esse accurata. Nam (1) agenda etiam sunt credenda, eo quod diuinitus sunt reuelata. Quicquid Deus reuelauit, credendum est. (2) Credenda etiam includunt praxin, cum fides non fit nuda theoria mentis, sed praxis cordis. (3) Omittitur tertium membrum, nempe fugienda, siue omittenda, qualia sunt peccata. Resp. ad I. Largimur haud inuiti, agenda sensu laxiori credenda esse ob reuelationem diuinam: Sed heic stricte sumuntur agenda, in quantum sunt opera, prælucente fide ad gloriam Dei dirigenda: at credenda sunt mysteria assensu fidei recipienda. Ad II. Resp. Praxis fidei differt a praxi operum. Illa præcedit, ordine naturæ, hæc sequitur; fides bona opera dirigit: Opera a præuiis fidei actibus, notitia & fiducia, diriguntur. Ad III. Resp. Nomine agendorum comprehenduntur etiam fugienda. Nam in disciplinis practicis quodammodo agere dicitur, qui peccata fugit.

Obs. (1) Credenda trifariam dicuntur I. sensu generali. II. speciali. III. specialissimo. Sensu generali dicuntur credenda, quæ verbo Dei scripto reuelata sunt, v. gr. physica, historica, moralia, supernaturalia, siue respiciant hominum æternam salutem, siue minus. Sensu speciali credenda vocantur, quæ ob salutem hominum verbo Dei sunt reuelatæ, & creduntur ob reuelationem diuinam, quamuis ex principiis rationis quodammodo innotescant. Sensu specialissimo credenda appellantur mysteria, captu rationis superiora, & ex sola reuelatione diuina ad salutem nostram cognoscenda.

Obs. (2) Assertiones, enunciationes, vel theses dogmaticæ de credendis e verbo Dei formatæ, recepto loquendi vsu appellantur articuli fidei.


### Question XI. What is comprehended under the name of the Christian religion?

An article of faith is a part of the doctrine revealed in the written word of God, concerning God and divine things, proposed to the sinner who is to be saved for him to believe. Obs.
