(1) Article is said from 'artus' (joint), and this from 'arctando' (to bind together). It properly denotes the members of a body closely connected, just as the parts of the fingers cohere closely. By metaphor, the word article has been transferred to the parts of the doctrine of faith, joined by a most tight bond.

Latin:

Articulus fidei est pars doctrinæ verbo Dei scripto reuelatæ, de Deo & rebus diuinis, peccatori saluando ad credendum propositis. Obs. (1) Articulus dicitur ab artu, & hic ab arctando. Proprie notat membra corporis arcte connexa, sicut particulæ digitorum arcte cohærent. Per metaphoram vox articulus translata est ad partes doctrinæ fidei, arctissimo nexu coniunctas,


### Question XV

(2). By faith here is understood the faith which is believed, or the doctrine of faith, yet with respect to the faith by which it is believed, or the trust itself fixed in the merit of Christ.

Quest. XIII. In how many ways is an article of faith taken? Prob. Christian doctrine is distributed into chapters or theological topics, and the chapters are divided into certain theses. Both the chapters of the doctrine of faith and the theses of the chapters are called articles of faith; e.g., the theological topic concerning Christ is called an article of faith: and this proposition, "Christ, according to his flesh, sits at the right hand of God," is likewise named an article of faith.

Quest. XIV. What are the requirements of the articles of faith?

Prob. a. A true article of faith is said to be one that is conformable to divine revelation, which is held at this time in the Holy Scriptures; provided that it either exists expressly in them, or is elicited from them by invincible consequence. Prob. b. Every genuine article of faith respects the eternal salvation of men, either directly, insofar as it explains the principles and means of salvation; or indirectly, insofar as it is a dogma removing an impediment to salvation, so that we do not fall from the hope of eternal life. For not all and singular articles of faith imply an equal respect to eternal salvation; but some imply a proximate respect to salvation, others a remote one.

Prob. c. There is a neat harmony and a sweet concert, as it were, of the articles of faith. Hence faith is accustomed to be called one copulative and is compared to a chain connected from many links. Take away a link, and you have broken the chain: remove one article of faith, and you have disturbed the harmony of faith. Through this harmony, it cannot be that one article of faith is contradictorily opposed to another.

Prob. d. Just as that is called evident (in a stricter sense) which is known or investigated by the guidance of the light of nature (*): so that is inexevident which cannot be known or investigated from the light of nature, but from the supernatural light of divine revelation (). These things being duly observed, it must be established that some articles of faith are inexevident by reason of their material and formal object, and some are inexevident only by reason of their formal object.

Quest. XV. What is the object of the articles of faith? The object of the articles of faith are τὰ πιστὰ, or things to be believed. Things to be believed, however, are God and divine matters, insofar as they have been divinely revealed for the salvation of men. Obs.

(*) And indeed in such a way that we clearly and distinctly perceive its mode and reason: for there are many mysteries even in natural things, the causes and reasons of which we do not know sufficiently evidently, nor do we doubt the truth of the thing, although we are ignorant of the mode. see John III, 8. coll. Eccl. XI, 5. () So that we indeed know the thing, but that the thing can come to pass, known to God alone, no one can ever comprehend with mind and thought: wherefore they are called μυστήρια, above the mind, not only human, but also angelic, Phil. IV, 7. add. 1 Pet I, 12. Therefore, the distinction must be duly observed, though unknown to few, that there is one evidence of the thing, the mode of which we are ignorant of, and another of the revelation, which we know perspicuously.

An article of faith is taken either collectively or distributively. Collectively, it denotes an entire chapter of Christian doctrine: distributively, it designates any assertion or enunciation which constitutes a part of Christian doctrine.

For a true article of faith, it is required that it be revealed by the written word of God (a), that it respect the salvation of man (b), that it be closely connected with the remaining dogmas of faith (c), that it be inexevident (d).

From these it is evident that the material object of the articles of faith is God and divine things: the formal object of which is supernatural revelation divinely made and directed toward the salvation of men.

Quest. XVI. How are the articles of faith divided? The articles of faith, by reason of their object, are divided into pure and mixed: by reason of their relation or respect to the foundation of faith and salvation, they are divided into fundamental and non-fundamental.

Quest. XVII. Which are the mixed articles of faith, and which are the pure? The mixed articles of faith are called those parts of Christian doctrine concerning those divine things which are known to a certain extent from the light of nature, and are also believed from the supernatural light of divine revelation. The pure articles of faith are those parts of Christian doctrine concerning divine mysteries, which are superior to the grasp of human reason left to itself, yet are divinely revealed.

Proof a. The parts of Christian doctrine concerning the existence, power, and goodness of God, likewise concerning the creation, preservation, and government of the world, are true articles of faith. This we learn not only from Article I of the Apostolic Creed, but also from the testimony of Paul, Heb. XI, 6: Without faith it is impossible to please (God). For he who comes to God must believe that He is, and that He is a rewarder of those who seek Him. No one truly worships God by faith, no one approaches Him full of trust, unless he believes that there is an eternal, omnipotent, all-creating Numen, and that He takes care of human affairs, so that He wishes to render all the best things to those who worship Him.

Nevertheless, by the guidance of the light of nature, the existence, omnipotence, and providential care of God are made known, as Paul testifies in Rom. I, 19; Acts XIV, 17; ch. XVII, 24. From which it has come about that some authors have taken the opportunity to distinguish the articles of faith into pure and mixed.

You say: There are no mixed articles of faith, because we are not permitted to mix things that are of natural and supernatural light, just as it is not at all right for us to mix the highest with the lowest, or heaven with earth.

Resp. The distinction of the articles of faith into pure and mixed must be understood correctly. For no article of faith considered formally, insofar as it is an article of faith, is mixed; since all articles of faith depend on divine revelation, and thus, by reason of their formal object, are non-evident. However, they are distinguished into pure and mixed by reason of their material object. Namely, those divine things which are set forth in the articles of faith that they call mixed consist partly of reason and partly of supernatural revelation. They consist, I say, of the principles of reason less well, and less safely and fully, but from the revealed Word they are known far better, more certainly, and more fully for the salvation of man.

Add that certain circumstances concerning things knowable from both lights are of mere faith and revelation.

An example is the creation of this universe, completed within the hexaemeron. Not without reason does the apostle say: πίστει νοοῦμεν κατηρτίσθαι τοὺς αἰῶνας ῥήματι Θεοῦ. Heb. XI, 3.

Proof b. The pure articles of faith are occupied with explaining the mysteries of faith, which transcend the grasp of human reason left to itself. Μυστήριον is from μύειν, which means to have the eyes closed, to compress the mouth, and consequently to be silent. From μύειν is μύεσιν, which means to imbue someone with honorable doctrine. Μυεῖσθαι is the same as to be initiated into sacred rites. Ὁ μύστης is a man initiated into sacred rites, who either listens to others in silence and learns the sacred things; or who is so imbued with that knowledge of sacred things that he teaches the sacred things, to be heard with reverent silence.

See Phosphor. Crauferi p. 806. Τὸ μυστήριον, which descends from μύειν just as ὁ μύστης does, among profane authors [denotes] both every secret matter, not to be rashly uttered in speech, and especially sacred [rites]. ...the Eleusinian Ceres, enclosed in deep silence, denotes. Concerning these, consult, if you please, Alexandr. ab Alex. Book VI, D. G., ch. 19, p. 364 of the edition. In the Holy Scriptures, *mysteria* denote divine and supernatural things, which, left to themselves, are unknown and unevident to reason, yet have been divinely revealed for the sake of our salvation. Thus, the incarnation of the Son of God is called *ὁμολογουμένως μέγα μυστήριον*, confessedly a great mystery of godliness, 1 Tim. III, 16. The spiritual union of Christ with the church, Eph. V, 32. The calling of the Gentiles, Eph. III, 3. The conversion of the Jews to the faith of Christ, Rom. XI, 29. The transformation of those who shall be survivors on the last day, 1 Cor. XV, 51. The final liberation of the church, Apoc. X, 7, are called mysteries. By the Greek fathers, mysteries are specifically called sacraments, of which the sacred heralds are the stewards or dispensers, 1 Cor. IV, 1. Those parts of Christian doctrine that explain these mysteries are called pure articles of faith.

Question XVIII. Which articles of faith are fundamental? Fundamental articles of faith are those parts of Christian doctrine so necessary to be known that, if they are ignored, the foundation of faith is not salutarily apprehended or retained by a man; and if they are denied by him, it is, as far as it lies within him, undermined.

Question XIX. What is the foundation of faith and salvation? The foundation of faith is either real (or substantial) or dogmatic (or doctrinal). The substantial foundation of faith and salvation is Christ, insofar as He is the meritorious cause of obtaining from God the remission of sins and eternal life, promised in the Gospel to all who, through the efficacious influx of the Holy Spirit, believe in Him (a). The dogmatic foundation of faith and salvation is the complex of divinely revealed dogmas by which Christ, the substantial foundation of faith, and the principles and means of salvation necessarily connected with Him, are explained (b). Obs. I. A foundation is of the number of those things that imply a relation to something else. A foundation relates to the thing which it founds, and under which it is placed for the purpose of supporting it. It is defined by Dr. NICOL. HUNNIUS in *Διασκέψει de fundam.*, Diff. q. 1, ch. 1, p. 7: A foundation is that which in any structure is first, and underlies the whole structure, nor is it supported by anything else. By Dr. IO. MUSAEUS in *introduct. theol.*, p. 166, it is described thus: A foundation is that which in every thing is first, and which is the reason or cause why that which it founds is, or can be. Whence, in this place, *κατ' ἀναλογίαν* (by analogy), that which is first in justifying faith and the salvation of men is called the foundation of faith and salvation, and is the reason and cause why saving faith and the salvation of men itself is, or can be. Obs. II. Although faith and the salvation of man differ as two subordinate ends of theology, since faith is for the sake of the salvation of men, nevertheless the foundation of both is the same. For the saving faith of men rests upon the same thing as their salvation, since faith has from its foundation that it is saving, and the salvation of men depends upon the same. Wherefore, we deliberately join faith and the salvation of men together here from time to time. Obs. III. Some theologians add an organic foundation of faith, by which is understood Holy Scripture, considered as the fundamental principle of knowing the articles of faith. Concerning which, see the following chapter. Prob. a. From 1 Cor. III, 11: "For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Christ." St. Paul speaks of the foundation of the church, which he had compared to a well-cultivated field and an elegant building, v. 9. He had compared himself to a wise architect (ministerial... v. 10. He calls Christ the foundation of the building v. 10. For the whole church, which is the house of the living God, 1 Tim. III, 15. rests upon Christ, as upon an immovable rock, so that the gates of hell may not be able to overcome it. Matth. XVI, 18. But since the church is a gathering of faithful men and those to be saved, it is not invalidly inferred that Christ is also the foundation of faith and salvation.

For the faithful and those to be saved are built upon Christ as a foundation, insofar as they are faithful and to be saved, or, which amounts to the same thing, by reason of faith and salvation. St. Peter agrees, Acts IV, 11. 12. This Jesus Christ of Nazareth is the stone rejected by you builders, which has become the head of the corner. And there is no salvation in any other. Just as if he were to say: In the structure of salvation, Christ is that first thing from which salvation arises: for he is the reason and cause why saving faith, the remission of sins, and eternal salvation exist, or can exist.

Prob. b. From Eph. II, 20. Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, whose cornerstone is Jesus Christ. St. Paul is speaking of the dogmatic foundation of faith. For by the foundation of the apostles and prophets he implies the doctrine handed down by the apostles and prophets, both by living voice and by writings, since it is the immovable basis from which the structure of faith and salvation rises and is stabilized.

Furthermore, the apostle teaches that the ἀκρογωνιαῖον, or cornerstone, is Christ, intending to indicate that the prophetic and apostolic doctrine is a foundation in such a way that it itself rests upon Jesus Christ, as upon the lowest cornerstone and ultimate foundation, and the reason for the foundation ultimately returns to him. For just as a cornerstone, joining two walls, stands out, obvious and conspicuous to all: so Christ, connecting the prophetic and apostolic doctrine, stands out remarkably in it. Meanwhile, in an inseparable bond, the mercy of God the Father and the applying grace of the Holy Spirit cohere with Christ the foundation.

For the general and universal mercy of God placed Christ as the foundation. Is. XXVIII, 16. Jo. III, 16. But the special mercy of God, forgiving sins to believers, is founded upon the merit of Christ. For that God can forgive sins to sinners, while his immutable justice remains intact, and promises that he will forgive the same to believers, all that is from the merit and satisfaction of Christ, performed for the sins of the whole world.

Wherefore we, reconciled to God, do indeed glory in God, but through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation. Rom. V, 11. In whom all the promises of God are, ναὶ καὶ Ἀμήν.

2 Cor. I, 20. The applying grace of the Holy Spirit builds saving faith, which he gives and establishes through the word, upon Christ the foundation. For when the apostle had taught in Eph. II, 20 that Christ is the cornerstone of the prophetic and apostolic foundation, he adds in v. 22: Through whom you also are built together into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit. The mind of the apostle is: You Ephesians, Gentiles by origin, are built together with the Jews upon Christ, the cornerstone of all Christian doctrine, through the effective operation of the Holy Spirit, through whom you are converted and regenerated, so that God may dwell in you by his gracious presence.

From which it is concluded that the dogmatic foundation of faith is the catalog, series, and complex of all those dogmas by which the satisfaction and merit of Christ, the mercy of God the Father, and the gracious operation of the Holy Spirit are proposed and explained to the man to be saved for his belief.

Dicis Of one thing there is only one foundation. Therefore, there is not a double foundation, namely real and doctrinal. I answer: The substantial and dogmatic foundation of faith and salvation are not two adequately contradistinguished foundations, nor do they differ in reality, but according to our mode of conceiving them on account of different connotations.

For Christ is the foundation on the part of the thing: the doctrine concerning Christ is the foundation on the part of our knowledge. But the doctrine concerning Christ is nothing other than Christ known by the intellect, and proposed to others for knowing by the written or preached word. Therefore, the dogmatic and substantial foundations do not differ, except as doctrine and the object of doctrine, which finally taken together taken together constitute one foundation in reality, although our mind conceives it as twofold. Nor can one be torn away from the other, but our faith is so carried into the doctrine concerning Christ, that through the same believed doctrine it tends into Christ himself, signified or represented by the doctrine, and leans upon the same thus apprehended and believed, as upon a cornerstone.

Latin:

(2). Per fidem hic intelligitur fides, quæ creditur, feu doctrina fidei, cum respectu tamen ad fidem, qua creditur, fiue ipsam in merito Christi defixam fiduciam.

Quæst. XIII. Quot modis sumitur articulus fidei? Prob. Doctrina christiana distribuitur in capita siue locos theologicos, capita in theses certas diuiduntur. Tam capita doctrinæ fidei, quam capitum theses appellantur articuli fidei, v. gr. locus theologicus de Christo dicitur articulus fidei: & hæc propositio, Christus, qua carnem, sedet ad dextram Dei, itidem nominatur articulus fidei.

Quæst. XIV. Quæ sunt requisita articulorum fidei?

Prob. a. Articulus fidei verus dicitur, qui reuelationi diuinæ, quæ hoc tempore habetur in sacris litteris, conformis est; siquidem in iisdem vel diserte exstat, vel ex illis per inuictam consequentiam elicitur. Prob. b. Omnis genuinus fidei articulus æternam hominum salutem respicit vel directe, in quantum explicat principia & media salutis; vel indirecte, quatenus est dogma remouens impedimentum salutis, ne spe vitæ æternæ excidamus. Neque enim omnes & singuli articuli fidei æqualem important respectum ad salutem æternam; sed quidam inferunt respectum ad salutem proximum, quidam remotum.

Prob. c. Articulorum fidei concinna est harmonia & suauis quasi concentus. Proinde fides consueuit dici vna copulatiua & comparatur cum catena ex multis anfulis connexa. Tolle anfulam, & rupisti catenam: summoue vnum fidei articulum, & turbasti harmoniam fidei. Per hanc harmoniam fieri non potest, vt vnus articulus fidei alteri fit contradictorie oppositus.

Prob. d. Sicut euidens (sensu strictiori) dicitur, quod ductu luminis naturæ cognoscitur, aut inuestigatur (*): ita ineuidens est, quod non ex lumine naturæ, sed ex supernaturali lumine diuinæ reuelationis cognosci aut inuestigari potest (). Quibus probe obseruatis, statuendum est, quosdam articulos fidei esse ineuidentes ratione obiecti materialis & formalis, quosdam esse ineuidentes tantum ratione obiecti formalis.

Quæst. XV. Quodnam est obiectum articulorum fidei? Obiectum articulorum fidei sunt τὰ πιστὰ, siue credenda. Credenda autem sunt Deus & res diuinæ, quatenus ad salutem hominum diuinitus sunt reuelatæ. Obs.

(*) Et ita quidem, vt eius modum rationemque clare ac distincte percipiamus: Sunt enim in rebus etiam naturalibus multa arcana, quorum causas ac rationes non satis euidenter cognoscimus, nec vero dubitamus de rei veritate, quamuis modum ignoremus. vid. Ioann. III, 8. coll. Cohel. XI, 5. () Ita vt rem quidem sciamus, quod autem res fieri possit, Deo vni cognitum, mente & cogitatione complecti nemo vnquam valeat: quare dicuntur μυστήρια, supra mentem, nec humanam solum, sed etiam angelicam, Phil. IV, 7. add. 1 Pet I, 12. Idcirco probe obseruanda est distinctio, paucis quidem incognita, quod euidentia alia fit rei, cuius modum ignoramus, alia reuelationis, quam perspicue cognoscimus.

Articulus fidei accipitur vel collectiue, vel distributive. Collectiue notat integrum doctrinæ christianæ caput: distributive designat quamlibet assertionem siue enunciationem, quæ partem doctrinæ christianæ constituit.

Ad verum articulum fidei requiritur, vt verbo Dei scripto sit reuelatus (a), vt salutem hominis respiciat (b), vt cum reliquis fidei dogmatibus arcte sit connexus (c), vt fit ineuidens (d).

Ex his patescit, obiectum materiale articulorum fidei esse Deum & res diuinas: cuius obiecti formale est reuelatio supernaturalis diuinitus facta & directa ad hominum salutem.

Quaest. XVI. Quomodo diuiduntur articuli fidei? Articuli fidei ratione obiecti diuiduntur in puros & mixtos: ratione habitudinis siue respectus ad fundamentum fidei salutisque diuiduntur in fundamentales & non fundamentales.

Quaest. XVII. Quinam sunt articuli fidei mixti, quinam puri? Mixti dicuntur articuli fidei partes doctrinae christianae de illis rebus diuinis, quae tum ex lumine naturae quadantenus sciuntur, tum ex supernaturali lumine reuelationis diuinae creduntur . Articuli fidei puri sunt partes doctrinae christianae de mysteriis diuinis, captu rationis humanae sibi relictae superioribus, diuinitus tamen reuelatis .

Prob. a. Partes doctrinae christianae de existentia, potentia, bonitate Dei, item, de creatione, conseruatione & gubernatione mundi sunt veri articuli fidei. Id quod non tantum discimus ex articulo I. symboli apostolici, sed & ex testimonio Paulli, Hebr. XI, 6, Sine fide impossibile est placere (Deo). Credere enim oportet accedentem ad Deum, quod sit, & quaerentibus ipsum retributor mercedis fiat. Nemo vera Deum fide colet, nemo plenus fiducia ad eum accedet, nisi credat & esse Numen aeternum, omnipotens, omnificum, & curam agere rerum humanarum, ita vt se colentibus optima quaeque reddere velit.

Tamen & ductu luminis naturae existentia, omnipotentia, & prouida Dei cura innotescit, teste Paullo Rom. I, 19. Act. XIV, 17. c. XVII, 24. Ex quo factum est, vt nonnulli auctores ansam ceperint distinguendi articulos fidei in puros & mixtos.

Dicis: Non dantur articuli fidei mixti, quia, quae sunt luminis naturalis & supernaturalis, nobis miscere haud licet, perinde ac minime integrum nobis est summa imis, coelum terrae miscere.

Resp. Distinctio articulorum fidei in puros & mixtos dextre intelligenda est. Nam nullus articulus fidei formaliter consideratus, quatenus est articulus fidei, mixtus est; siquidem omnes articuli fidei pendentes a diuina reuelatione, adeoque ratione obiecti formalis, ineuidentes sunt. Distinguuntur autem in puros & mixtos, ratione obiecti materialis. Nempe res illae diuinae, quae articulis fidei, quos mixtos vocant, exponuntur, partim ex ratione, partim ex supernaturali reuelatione constant. Constant, inquam, ex principiis rationis minus bene, minusque tuto & plene, e verbo autem reuelato longe melius, certius & plenius innotescunt in salutem hominis.

Adiice, quod quaedam circumstantiae circa res, ex vtroque lumine cognoscibiles, merae fidei & reuelationis sint.

Exemplo fit creatio huius vniuersi, intra hexaëmeron consummata. Haud abs re inquit apostolus: πίστει νοοῦμεν κατηρτίσθαι τοὺς αἰῶνας ῥήματι Θεοῦ. Hebr. XI, 3.

Prob. b. Articuli fidei puri occupantur in explicandis mysteriis fidei, captum rationis humanae, sibi relictae, transcendentibus. Μυστήριον est ἀπὸ τοῦ μύειν, quod significat oculos habere clausos, os comprimere, & consequenter tacere. A μύειν est μύεσιν, quod significat, aliquem honesta doctrina imbuere. Μυεῖσθαι idem est, ac sacris initiari. Ὁ μύστης est homo sacris initiatus, qui vel cum silentio audit alios & sacra discit; vel qui ea sacrorum notitia imbutus est, vt sacra doceat, reuerenti cum silentio audiendus.

Vid. Phosphor. Crauferi p. 806. Τὸ μυστήριον, quod aeque, ac ὁ μύστης, ἀπὸ τοῦ μύειν descendit, apud profanos auctores cum rem omnem arcanam, sermone non temere enunciandam, tum in primis faera cra Cereris Eleusinia, alto silentio inclusa, notat. De quibus consule, si placet, Alexandr. ab Alex. L. VI. D. G. c. 19. p. m. 364. In sacris litteris μυστήρια notant res diuinas & supernaturales, quæ rationi sibi relictæ sunt ignotæ, ineuidentes, nostræ tamen salutis causa diuinitus reuelatæ. Quomodo incarnatio filii Dei vocatur ὁμολογουμένως μέγα μυστήριον, in confesso magnum pietatis mysterium, 1 Tim. III, 16. Vnio spiritualis Christi cum ecclesia, Eph. V, 32. Vocatio gentium, Eph. III, 3. Conuersio Iudæorum ad fidem Christi, Rom. XI, 29. Immutatio eorum, qui in die nouissimo superstites erunt, 1 Cor. XV, 51. Finalis liberatio ecclesiæ, Apoc. X, 7. mysteria appellantur. Græcis patribus specialiter mysteria dicuntur sacramenta, quorum œconomi siue dispensatores sunt præcones sacri, 1 Cor. IV, 1. Quæ partes doctrinæ christianæ mysteria illa explanant, audiunt articuli fidei puri.

Quæst. XVIII. Quinam articuli fidei sunt fundamentales? Articuli fidei fundamentales sunt partes doctrinæ christianæ, adeo necessariæ cognitu, vt, iis ignoratis, ab homine salutariter non apprehendatur, aut retineatur fundamentum fidei; negatis vero ab eodem, quantum in ipso, labefactetur.

Quæst. XIX. Quodnam est fundamentum fidei & salutis? Fundamentum fidei est vel reale, siue substantiale; vel dogmaticum, siue doctrinale. Fundamentum fidei & salutis substantiale est Christus, quatenus est caussa meritoria consequendæ a Deo remissionis peccatorum & vitæ æternæ, promissæ in euangelio omnibus, per efficacem Spiritus Sancti influxum in ipsum credentibus (a). Fundamentum fidei & salutis dogmaticum est complexus dogmatum diuinitus reuelatorum, quibus Christus fundamentum fidei substantiale, & cum eo necessario connexa principia mediaque salutis explicantur (b). Obs. I. Fundamentum est ex numero eorum, quæ inferunt respectum ad aliud. Respicit autem fundamentum rem, quam fundat, & cui sustentando substernitur. Definitur a D. NICOL. HVNNIO Διασκέψει de fundam. Diff. q. 1. c. 1. p. 7. Fundamentum est, quod in vnaquauis structura est primum, & toti structuræ substat, nec ab alio sustentatur. A D. IO. MVSAEO in introduct. theol. p. 166. describitur sic: Fundamentum est, quod in vnaquaque re est primum, quodque ratio vel caussa est, cur id, quod fundat, sit aut esse possit. Vnde h. l. κατ' ἀναλογίαν fundamentum fidei & salutis dicitur id, quod in fide iustifica, hominumque salute primum est, estque ratio & caussa, cur fides saluifica & salus ipsa hominum sit, aut esse possit. Obs. II. Quamuis fides, & salus hominis differant, vt duo fines theologiæ subordinati, siquidem fides est propter hominum salutem: attamen fundamentum vtriusque idem est. Nam cui salus, eidem fides saluifica hominum innititur, cum fides a suo fundamento habeat, quod saluifica est, & ab eodem salus hominum pendeat. Quare consulto heic fidem & salutem hominum subinde coniungimus. Obs. III. Additur a nonnullis theologis fundamentum fidei organicum, per quod intelligitur sacra scriptura, considerata vt fundamentale principium cognoscendi articulos fidei. De quo cap. sequenti. Prob. a. Ex 1 Cor. III, 11. Fundamentum aliud nemo ponere potest, præter positum, quod est Christus. Loquitur S. Paullus de fundamento ecclesiæ, quam cum agro bene culto & cum eleganti ædificio comparauerat v. 9. Seipsum contulerat sapienti architecto (ministeriali v. 10. Christum autem vocat fundamentum ædificii v. 10. Vniuersa enim ecclesia, quæ est domus Dei viuentis, 1 Tim. III, 15. Christo, ceu petra immobili, nititur, vt ne eandem portæ inferorum subigere valeant. Matth. XVI, 18. Cum autem ecclesia sit cœtus hominum fidelium & saluandorum, haud inualide colligitur, Christum etiam esse fundamentum fidei & salutis.

Fideles enim & saluandi fundamento Christo superstructi sunt, quatenus sunt fideles & saluandi, siue quod eodem redit, ratione fidei & salutis. Consentit S. Petrus Act. IV, 11. 12. Hic Iesus Christus Nazarenus est lapis reprobatus a vobis ædificantibus, qui factus est in caput anguli. Et non est in alio salus. Perinde ac si dicat: In structura salutis Christus est primum illud, a quo salus oritur: est enim ratio & caussa, cur fides saluifica, remissio peccatorum, & æterna salus fit, aut esse possit.

Prob. b. Ex Eph. II, 20. Superædificati super fundamento apostolorum & prophetarum, cuius lapis angularis est Iesus Christus. Sermo est S. Paulo de fundamento fidei dogmatico. Nam per fundamentum apostolorum & prophetarum innuit doctrinam, ab apostolis & prophetis, qua viua voce, qua scriptis traditam, quippe quæ est basis immobilis, a qua structura fidei salusque assurgit & stabilitur.

Ceterum docet apostolus ἀκρογωνιαῖον, siue lapidem angularem, esse Christum, indigitaturus, doctrinam propheticam & apostolicam ita esse fundamentum, vt & ipsa Iesu Christo, velut imo angulari lapide & fundamento vltimo, nitatur, & ratio fundamenti vltimo in eum redeat. Vt enim lapis angularis duos coagmentans parietes omnibus obuius & conspicuus prominet: ita Christus doctrinam propheticam & apostolicam connectens insigniter in eadem eminet. Indiuulso interim nexu misericordia Dei patris & gratia Spiritus S. applicatrix cum fundamento Christo cohæret.

Nam misericordia Dei generalis atque vniversalis Christum fundamentum posuit. Es. XXVIII, 16. Io. III, 16. Specialis autem Dei misericordia credentibus peccata remittens in merito Christi fundatur. Quod enim Deus peccatoribus, salua sua iustitia immutabili, peccata remittere potest, & eadem credentibus remissurum promittit, id omne est ex Christi merito & satisfactione, pro peccatis totius mundi præstita.

Quam ob rem nos Deo reconciliati gloriamur quidem in Deo, sed per dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, per quem nunc reconciliationem accepimus. Rom. V, 11. In quo omnes promissiones Dei sunt, ναὶ καὶ Ἀμήν.

2 Cor. I, 20. Gratia Spiritus Sancti applicatrix fidem saluificam, quam mediante verbo donat & statuminat, Christo fundamento superstruit. Nam cum Eph. II, 20. docuisset apostolus, Christum esse lapidem angularem fundamenti prophetici & apostolici, v. 22. addit: Per quem etiam vos vna ædificamini in habitaculum Dei in Spiritu. Mens apostoli est: Vos Ephesii, origine gentiles, vna cum iudæis ædificamini super Christo, lapide angulari totius doctrinæ christianæ, per efficacem operationem Spiritus S. per quem conuertimini & regeneramini, vt Deus præsentia sua gratiosa in vobis habitet.

E quibus conficitur, fundamentum fidei dogmaticum esse catalogum, seriem & complexum omnium illorum dogmatum, quibus satisfactio & meritum Christi, misericordia Dei patris, & gratiosa Spiritus S. operatio, homini saluando ad credendum proponuntur & explicantur.

Dicis Vnius rei vnum tantum est fundamentum. E. non datur duplex fundamentum, nempe reale & doctrinale. R. Fundamentum fidei salutisque substantiale, & dogmaticum, non sunt duo fundamenta adæquate contradistincta, neque differunt secundum rem, sed secundum nostrum concipiendi modum propter diuersa connotata.

Etenim Christus est fundamentum ex parte rei: doctrina de Christo est fundamentum ex parte nostræ cognitionis. Doctrina autem de Christo nihil est aliud, quam Christus intellectu cognitus, & aliis ad cognoscendum verbo scripto aut prædicato propositus. Non ergo differunt fundamentum dogmaticum, & substantiale, nisi vt doctrina, & doctrinæ obiectum, quæ demum iunctim sumta constituunt fundamentum reapfe vnum, quamuis mens nostra illud vt duplex concipiat. Neque etiam vnum ab altero potest diuelli, sed fides nostra ita fertur in doctrinam de Christo, vt per eandem creditam tendat in ipsum Christum, per doctrinam fignificatum aut repræsentatum, eidemque sic apprehenso & credito, velut imo lapidi angulari, innitatur.


### Q. XX. How are the fundamental articles of faith divided?

The fundamental articles of faith are divided into primary and secondary. The primary articles of faith are the principal parts of Christian doctrine, the distinct knowledge of which is so necessary for obtaining faith and salvation that, if they are ignored, neither can faith be generated or preserved, nor can eternal salvation be obtained. They are subdivided into constituent, antecedent, and consequent articles of faith. Constituent, or formal, articles of faith are those which explain the proximate causes of faith and salvation, and thus enter into the very causal definition of saving faith (a). Antecedent articles of faith are those by which the presuppositions of saving faith are set forth, which are so necessary that, if they do not pre-exist, the very foundation of faith does not exist (b). Consequent articles of faith are those which explain the consequences of saving faith: when these are posited, faith divinely conferred is confirmed, preserved, increases, and is exerted; when they are not posited, faith once kindled is extinguished and vanishes (c).

Proof a. The causal definition of saving faith can be conceived in the following words. Saving faith is a medium divinely conferred, by which a sinner, through the efficacious operation of the Holy Spirit, by means of the divine word, converted and regenerated, accepts the grace of God remitting sins, founded in the merit of Christ and promised in the Gospel, and applies it to himself with singular confidence, so that he may be justified and eternally saved. Whatever articles of faith enter into the given definition of saving faith are of the class of constituent, or formal, articles of faith. These we shall recount in decent order. I. It is concerning the triune God, the efficient cause of faith, righteousness, and salvation: although the conferring of the powers of believing is appropriated in the Holy Scriptures to the Holy Spirit, whom Paul calls the Spirit of faith, 2 Cor. IV, 13. II. It is concerning sin and the sinner, as he who is the remote material cause, in which faith is kindled. III. It is concerning the word of God, as a medium of grace and salvation, by means of which the sinner not maliciously resisting is converted and regenerated, just as the object of faith is offered. IV. It is concerning the conversion of the sinner, insofar as in the strictest sense it denotes the gracious action of God, by which He inhibits, breaks, and crushes the will and heart of man in the state of sin through the word of the law, so that he may seriously grieve and be saddened for his sins: the immediate effect of which is contrition. The contrite sinner is the proximate subject to whom faith is conferred. V. It is concerning regeneration, since it is the gracious action of the Holy Spirit, by which both the powers of believing and faith itself are conferred upon the contrite sinner. VI. It is concerning the justifying grace of God, the effect of which is the remission of sins and the imputed righteousness of Christ. VII. It is concerning Christ the mediator, and his satisfaction and merit, in which the justifying grace of God is founded. But the justifying grace of God, founded in the merit of Christ and promised in the Gospel, is the object of saving faith. VIII. It is concerning saving faith itself, insofar as it is ὄργανον ληπτικὸν, or a medium on the part of the converted and regenerated sinner, accepting the grace of God, the merit of Christ, and the evangelical promise with undoubted confidence, and singularly applying them: in which fiducial acceptance consists the form of faith. IX. It is concerning eternal salvation, as the ultimate end of saving faith.

…Obs. I. The enumerated constituent fundamental articles of faith can be comprehended in the following dogmatic thesis: God, moved by mercy toward the human race most prone to the fall, converts and regenerates all miserable sinners, not maliciously resisting, by the efficacious operation of the Holy Spirit, through His most efficacious word; and those reborn, on account of the satisfaction of Christ the mediator, offered by the evangelical promise, and accepted by true confidence of the heart, and singularly applied, justifies, and those justified He wills eternally He justifies, and those justified He wills to save eternally.

Upon this foundation rests man the wayfarer, corrupted by sin, about to obtain remission of sins and eternal salvation, and he subsumes and concludes in the following manner.

I am a most miserable sinner, not so resisting the operation of the Holy Spirit that I would not willingly admit His word, hear it devoutly, and meditate upon it assiduously; I seriously acknowledge, grieve for, and detest my committed sins; with undoubted confidence, given to me by the Holy Spirit, I accept the grace of God, forgiving sins on account of the satisfaction of Christ, and I apply it to myself individually.

Therefore I believe certainly that God forgives me my sins, imputes the righteousness of Christ, and is about to save me eternally.

The major premise contains the foundation itself of faith and salvation.

The minor premise is confirmed by conscience, and illuminated by the word of God.

The conclusion, therefore, resting upon the foundation of faith and salvation, is most certain.

Obf.

II. Although the mentioned articles of faith look most closely to the real foundation of salvation, namely Christ the mediator; yet they do not fully and completely fulfill the total and adequate dogmatic foundation of faith and salvation, but for the perfecting of it, and for the consolidating of it on the part of our knowledge, there are also required antecedent and consequent fundamental articles of faith.

This we learn from Heb. 6:1-2, where the apostle gravely says: Therefore leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection; not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God, of the doctrine of baptisms, and of laying on of hands, and of resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment.

From which words it is clearly known that the apostle reckons to the doctrinal foundation of faith not only divine dogmas concerning faith in God, concerning the conversion of the sinner, but also concerning baptism, and on account of the parity of reason, concerning the Holy Eucharist, concerning the ecclesiastical ministry, concerning the resurrection of the dead, and the final judgment .

Prob. b.

Before a sinner about to obtain eternal salvation can conceive justifying faith in Christ, it is necessary that he presuppose certain dogmas divinely revealed for the salvation of men.

Presupposition I is concerning the existence of God, most good, most powerful, most wise, and most true, the creator, preserver, and governor of this universe, the most benign rewarder of benefactors, and the most just avenger of evildoers.

This presupposition the apostle inculcates in Heb. 11:6.

He that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.

But if there were no God, there would be no mediator.

For Christ is the mediator of God and men.

1 Tim. 2:5.

II. In order to duly weigh the foul deformity of sin and the misery of the sinner, the image of God must be known beforehand, which shone most splendidly in the first-formed humans, and which, lost through the Adamic fall, deformed the sin of men to an immense degree.

III. To the word of God, considered as a means of grace and salvation, its divine authority and infallible truth must be presupposed: for unless it possessed this, it would not strike or penetrate the heart of the sinner with prevailing force to the detesting of sins, and to the conceiving of faith in Christ.

IV. To the dogma concerning the conversion of the sinner must be prefixed the part of Christian doctrine concerning the defect of free will in spiritual matters, so that the sinner, blinded and depraved, having acknowledged his misery, both innate and maliciously contracted, may surrender himself entirely to the grace of the Holy Spirit, who begins and perfects his conversion.

V. Regeneration is preceded by the calling to the church and to repentance, as well as by illumination through the law and the gospel.

VI. To the justifying grace of God is antecedent the heavenly doctrine concerning the universal benevolence of God, by which, having pity on all and singular sinners, He appointed a mediator, whose satisfaction for the sins of the whole world He decreed to accept graciously: and that miserable sinners might make this their own, He willed to confer faith upon all who do not maliciously resist, and for the obtaining of which He ordained most effective means, and proposed them to all men.

If this universal mercy of God did not pre-exist, neither faith in Christ, nor the remission of sins, nor eternal salvation would exist.

VII. For the knowing of Christ the mediator, there is pre-required the doctrine concerning the deity and humanity of Christ, and the personal union of the two natures in Christ, whereby He becomes true God and true man, and void of sin and the power of sinning: who, had He not been such, could not have expiated sins with His own blood.

Moreover, to the satisfaction and merit of Christ is immediately presupposed its sufficiency and universality, regarding the intention of applying it on the part of God, which is not indeed the proximate matter of trust, but the doctrine immediately underlying it: just as the universality of this underlies faith in the divine benevolence, from which it is manifest that the universality of merit follows.

It is indeed impossible that one who hopes for the grace of God on account of Christ's satisfaction should not consider whether that satisfaction is so abundant that he himself can possess it, or whether God even wills that he himself should enjoy it?

But in that very act, when one trusts in the divine goodness on account of the merit of Christ, it is not necessary that it should happen that he be simultaneously anxious in one concept about its universality or sufficiency, provided he has firmly and indubitably presupposed it: these are the words of the blessed Hülsemann in his dissertation on dogmas necessary to be believed for salvation, p. 491.

VIII. To the fiducial application of the merit of Christ shines forth the knowledge of Christ, and the assent given to the evangelical promise.

IX. The sinner believing that he, by the grace of God, on account of the satisfaction of Christ apprehended by true faith, will be a partaker of eternal salvation, presupposes the divine dogmas concerning death, insofar as it is a passage to eternal life, and concerning the resurrection of the dead and the final judgment.

Which parts of Christian doctrine, having been now recounted as presupposed by faith, are commonly called the fundamental articles of faith that are antecedent. Prob c. By the fundamental articles of faith that are consequent are explained those things to be believed which follow justifying faith, confirm and certify it a posteriori, preserve and increase it, exert and declare it.

Of whose number is I. the article of faith concerning the Word of God, as a means of grace and salvation. For although we have placed it above among the proximate causes of generating faith, yet its frequent meditation, hearing, and reading stabilizes and increases faith.

The apostle Peter teaches this, 1 Ep. c.

II, 1 . As newborn infants, desire the sincere milk of the word, that by it you may grow.

The Word of God is not only the seed by which faith is generated, 1 Petr. 1, 23 , but also the pure milk by which it is nourished, increased, and strengthened.

II. Concerning the sacrament of baptism.

Someone might perhaps reckon the doctrine concerning baptism among the constitutive fundamental articles of faith, because infants are regenerated by it, Io. III, 5 , and put on Christ, Gal. III, 27 .

But infants feel the efficacy of baptism rather than presuppose a knowledge of the efficacy of baptism, according to D. Kromayer in the proemium to his system, p. 9. Baptism of adults obligates and increases faith drawn from the Word of God, since it is today, like circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of faith.

Rom. IV, 11 .

III. Concerning the sacrament of the supper.

For it is that which was instituted by the Savior, so that in and with the bread it may certify to every recipient the true and substantial body of Christ, that body which he eats, as having been delivered for him unto death; the blood which he drinks as having been for him in particular & poured into the individual, by which he may adhere to his Savior with a firm and unshakable trust.

IV. Concerning the mystical union of the reborn soul with God, from which arises the confirmation of faith, and the sense of the same. The apostle speaks of the sense of faith, 2 Cor. XIII, 5: "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you?" In those in whom Jesus Christ graciously dwells, they know that they themselves are grafted into Christ through faith, while they examine and prove their faith by the purpose of living piously, by the peace of conscience, internal joy, and the living hope to which they have been reborn through the resurrection of Christ from the dead, 1 Pet. I, 3. But he who proves his faith by accurate examination has the sense and experience of it. Concerning the confirmation of faith, the same apostle says, 2 Cor. I, 22: "God hath sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts." God, by sending His Holy Spirit into our hearts, has confirmed faith, righteousness, and the hope of future inheritance.

V. Concerning renovation, or sanctification, the effects of which are good works, by which living faith is brought forth and shown: and by which, if they do not follow justifying faith, it is extinguished and vanishes. Concerning which St. James warns us, ch. II, 18, 20: "Show me thy faith without thy works." - "But wilt thou know, O vain man, that faith without works is dead?" As the presence of works demonstrates a posteriori the presence of justifying faith, so the absence of G. W. is an indication of dead faith.

VI. Concerning the church. For since Christ is the head and king of the church, about to defend the same, so that the gates of hell may not overcome it, Matt. XVI, 18, the trust of the reborn is greatly solidified, since they trust that they, as living members of the church under the rule and protection of Christ, will be defended from the snares of the devil and the allurements of the world, no less than from the raging and predominance of the flesh.

VII. Concerning the ecclesiastical ministry, the works of which the Holy Spirit uses to apply to man the benefits of grace and salvation. Wherefore the apostle graphically depicts the office of the ministers of the church, 1 Cor. IV, 1: "Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God." He who is to be held and accounted as a minister of God is to be esteemed by divine faith as a divine instrument, which the Holy Spirit uses to excite and confirm trust in Christ.

Latin:

Articuli fidei fundamentales diuiduntur in primarios, & secundarios. Articuli fidei primarii sunt præcipuæ partes doctrinæ christianæ, quarum distincta cognitio ad obtinendam fidem & salutem adeo necessaria est, vt, iis ignoratis, nec fides generari aut conferuari, nec æterna salus impetrari possit. Subdiuiduntur in articulos fidei constituentes, antecedentes, & consequentes. Articuli fidei constituentes, siue formales, sunt, qui proximas fidei salutisque caussas explicant, atque adeo ipsam caussalem fidei saluisicæ definitionem ingrediuntur (a). Antecedentes fidei articuli sunt, quibus exponuntur fidei saluisicæ præsupposita adeo necessaria, vt, iis non præexistentibus, ipsum fidei fundamentum non exsistat (b). Consequentes fidei articuli sunt, qui explanant fidei saluisicæ consequentia: quibus positis, fides diuinitus collata confirmatur, conferuatur, augescit & exseritur; non positis, fides accensa exstinguitur & euanescit (c).

Prob. a. Definitio caussalis fidei saluisicæ sequentibus verbis concipi potest. Fides saluisica est medium diuinitus collatum, quo peccator, efficaci Spiritus S. operatione, mediante verbo diuino, conuersus & renatus, gratiam Dei peccata remittentem, in merito Christi fundatam, & in euangelio promissam, acceptat, singularique cum fiducia sibi applicat, vt iustificetur & æternum saluetur. Quicunque articuli fidei datam definitionem fidei saluificæ ingrediuntur, sunt e censu articulorum fidei constitutiuorum, siue formalium. Quos ordine decenti percensebimus. I. Est de Deo triuno, caussa efficiente fidei, iustitiæ & salutis: quamuis collatio virium credendi in sacris litteris approprietur Spiritui sancto, quem Paullus appellat Spiritum fidei, 2 Cor. IV, 13. II. Est de peccato & peccatore, vtpote qui est caussa remota materialis, in qua fides accenditur. III. Est de verbo Dei, vt gratiæ & salutis medio, quo mediante peccator malitiose non obsistens conuertitur & regeneratur, iuxta atque obiectum fidei offertur. IV. Est de conuersione peccatoris, quatenus in sensu strictissimo notat actionem Dei gratiosam, qua voluntatem & cor hominis in medio peccati statu per verbum legis inhibet, frangitque ac conterit, vt de peccatis serio doleat ac contristetur: cuius immediatus effectus est contritio. Peccator contritus est subiectum proximum, cui fides confertur. V. Est de regeneratione, quippe quæ est actio Spiritus S. gratiosa, qua peccatori contrito tum vires credendi, tum ipsa fides conferuntur. VI. Est de gratia Dei iustificante, cuius effectus est remissio peccatorum & iustitia Christi imputata. VII. Est de Christo mediatore, eiusque satisfactione & merito, in quo gratia Dei iustificans fundatur. Gratia autem Dei iustificans in merito Christi fundata, & in euangelio promissa, est obiectum fidei saluisicæ. VIII. Est de ipsa fide saluisica, quatenus est ὄργανον ληπτικὸν, siue medium ex parte peccatoris conuersi & renati, gratiam Dei, meritum Christi, & promissionem euangelicam indubitata cum fiducia acceptans, & singulariter applicans: in qua acceptatione fiduciali consistit forma fidei. IX. Est de salute æterna, tanquam fine vltimo fidei saluisicæ.

Obs. I. Recensiti articuli fidei fundamentales constitutini sequenti thesi dogmatica comprehendi possunt: Deus, motus misericordia in genus humanum lapsu propensissima, omnes miseros peccatores, malitiose non obsistentes, efficaci operatione Spiritus Sancti, mediante verbo suo efficacissimo, convertit et regenerat, renatos, propter satisfactionem Christi mediatoris, evangelica promissione oblatam, et vera cordis fiducia acceptatam, atque singulariter applicatam, iustificat, iustificatos aeternum vult salvare.

Huic fundamento innititur homo viator peccato corruptus, remissionem peccatorum atque aeternam salutem adepturus, et sequenti ratione subsumit atque concludit.

Ego sum miserrimus peccator, Spiritus Sancti operationi adeo non obsistens, ut lubens potius verbum eius admittam, devotus audiam, assiduus mediter; peccata mea commissa serio agnosco, doleo, detestor; fiducia indubitata, a Spiritu Sancto mihi donata, gratiam Dei, peccata, ob satisfactionem Christi, condonantem, et evangelica promissione oblatam, accepto, et mihi in individuo applico.

Ergo certo credo, quod Deus mihi peccata mea remittat, iustitiam Christi imputet, et aeternum me fit salvaturus.

Maior continet ipsum fundamentum fidei et salutis.

Minorem confirmat conscientia, et verbo Dei illuminata.

Conclusio itaque, fundamento fidei et salutis subnixa, est certissima.

Obs.

II. Quamuis commemorati fidei articuli proxime respiciant fundamentum salutisque reale, nempe Christum mediatorem; non tamen totale et adaequatum fundamentum fidei salutisque dogmaticum plene planeque absolvunt, sed ad id confirmandum, et ex parte nostrae cognitionis consolidandum, requiruntur etiam articuli fidei fundamentales antecedentes, et consequentes.

Id quod discimus ex Hebr. Id quod discimus ex Hebr. VI, 1, 2. ubi apostolus grauiter inquit: Quapropter omittentes sermonem initii Christi ad perfectionem feramur, non iterum fundamentum iacentes poenitentiae ab operibus mortuis, et fidei in Deum, baptismorum doctrinae, impositionisque manuum, resurrectionisque mortuorum et iudicii aeterni.

E quibus verbis liquido innotescit, apostolum fundamento fidei doctrinali non tantum diuina dogmata de fide in Deum, de conuersione peccatoris, verum etiam de baptismo, et ob paritatem rationis de S. eucharistia, de ministerio ecclesiastico, de resurrectione mortuorum et extremo iudicio accensere .

Prob. b.

Priusquam peccator aeternam salutem adepturus iustificam in Christum concipiat fidem, dogmata quaedam diuinitus ad salutem hominum reuelata praesupponat, necesse est.

Praesuppositum I. est de existentia Dei optimi, potentissimi, sapientissimi et verissimi, creatoris, conseruatoris et gubernatoris huius vniuersi, benefactorum remuneratoris benignissimi, malefactorum vindicis iustissimi.

Hoc praesuppositum inculcat apostolus Hebr. Hoc praesuppositum inculcat apostolus Hebr. XI, 6.

Credere oportet accedentem ad Deum, quod fit, et quaerentibus ipsum retributor mercedis fiat.

Quod si non esset Deus, nullus esset mediator.

Nam Christus est mediator Dei et hominum.

1 Tim. II, 5.

II. Ad foedam peccati deformitatem et peccatoris miseriam rite ponderandam, praecognoscenda est imago Dei, quae splendidissime refulsit in protoplastis hominibus, eaque per lapsum Adamiticum amissa, peccatum hominum immane quantum deformauit.

III. Verbo Dei, considerato vt gratiae et salutis medio, praesupponenda est eius auctoritas diuina, et veritas infallibilis: qua nisi polleret, non vi praeualida cor peccatoris percelleret, aut penetraret ad detestandum peccata, & concipiendam fidem in Christum.

IV. Dogmati de conversione peccatoris praestituenda est pars doctrinae christianae de defectu liberi arbitrii in spiritualibus, vt peccator obcaecatus & deprauatus, agnita miseria connata & malitiose contracta, se totum permittat gratiae Spiritus Sancti, conuersionem incipienti & perficienti.

V. Regenerationem antecedit vocatio ad ecclesiam & poenitentiam, nec non illuminatio per legem & euangelium.

VI. Gratiae Dei iustificanti antestat doctrina coelestis de beneuolentia Dei vniuersali, qua misertus omnium & singulorum peccatorum destinauit mediatorem, cuius satisfactionem pro peccatis totius mundi gratiose acceptare decreuit: quam vt suam facerent miseri peccatores, omnibus malitiose non obsistentibus conferre voluit fidem, ad quam obtinendam efficacissima ordinauit, omnibusque hominibus proposuit, media.

Quae misericordia Dei vniuersalis nisi praexsisteret, nec fides in Christum, nec remissio peccatorum, nec aeterna salus exsisteret.

VII. Ad cognoscendum Christum mediatorem praerequiritur doctrina de deitate & humanitate Christi, atque vnione personali duarum naturarum in Christo, quod fit verus Deus & verus homo, & peccati, & potentiae peccandi expers: qui nisi fuisset, peccata sanguine suo expiare non potuisset.

Satisfactioni autem & merito Christi immediate praesupponitur eius sufficientia & vniuersalitas, quoad intentionem applicandi ex parte Dei, quae non est quidem proxima fiduciae materia, sed doctrina immediate substans: quemadmodum fidei in beneuolentiam diuinam substat huius vniuersalitas, ex qua meriti vniuersalitas sequi manifestum est.

Fieri quidem non potest, vt gratiam Dei propter Christi satisfactionem sperat, non cogitet, an illa satisfactio tam vber sit, vt ipse ea potiri possit, an Deus etiam velit, vt ipse ea fruatur? Sed eo ipso, quando quis bonitati diuinae ob meritum Christi confidit, non necessum est fieri, vt simul vno conceptu de vniuersalitate vel sufficientia sollicitus sit, modo firmiter & indubitato eam praesupposuerit: sunt verba b.

Hülsemanni in dissert. de dogmatibus ad salutem creditu necessariis, p. m. 491.

VIII. Fiduciali meriti Christi applicationi praelucet cognitio Christi, & assensus promissioni euangelicae praebitus.

IX. Peccator credens, se ex gratia Dei, propter satisfactionem Christi vera fide apprehensam, aeternae salutis compotem fore, praesupponit dogmata diuina de morte, quatenus est transitus ad aeternam vitam, de resurrectione mortuorum & iudicio extremo.

Quae partes doctrinae christianae iam recensita fidei praesupposita exponunt, communiter vocantur articuli fidei fundamentales antecedentes. Prob c. Articulis fidei fundamentalibus consequentibus explicantur ea credenda, quae fidem iustificantem consequuntur, firmant & a posteriori certificant, seruant & augent, exserunt & declarant.

E quorum censu est I. articulus fidei de verbo Dei, vt gratiae & salutis medio. Quamuis enim illud supra retulerimus inter causas proximas generandae fidei, crebra tamen eius meditatio, auscultatio & lectio fidem stabilit & auget.

Docet id apostolus Petrus, 1 Ep. c. II, 1 .

Tanquam modo geniti infantes verbale sincerum lac desiderate, vt per illud crescatis.

Verbum Dei non tantum est semen, quo fides generatur, 1 Petr. 1, 23 . sed & lac defecatum, quo illa nutritur, augetur & roboratur.

II. De sacramento baptismi.

Posset forte quispiam doctrinam de baptismo articulis fidei fundamentalibus constitutiuis accensere, quia infantes eodem regenerantur, Io. III, 5 . & Christum induunt, Gal. III, 27 .

At infantes efficaciam baptismi potius sentiunt, quam vt notitiam de baptismi efficacia praesupponant, centente D. Kromayero in system. proemio p. 9. Baptismus adultorum fidem ex verbo Dei hautam oblignant & auget, liquidem ad instar circumcisionis hodie figillum est iustitiae fidei.

Rom. IV, 11 .

III. De sacramento cenae.

Est enim illud a saluatore institutum, vt in & cum pane sumtum Christi verum & substantiale corpus quemuis sumentem certificet, illud corpus, quod edit, pro ipso esse in mortem traditum; quem bibit sanguinem pro ipso in singulari & in individuo fusum esse, quo firma & indvvlfa fiducia Salvatori suo adhaereat.

IV. De vnione mystica animae renatae cum Deo, ex qua oritur fidei confirmatio, & eiusdem sensus. De sensu fidei loquitur apostolus, 2 Cor. XIII, 5. Vos ipsos tentate, num sitis in fide, vos ipsos probate. Aut (num) non cognoscitis vos ipsos, quod Iesus Christus in vobis sit. In quibus Iesus Christus gratiose habitat, illi cognoscunt, seipsos Christo per fidem esse insitos, dum fidem suam tentant & probant ex proposito pie vivendi, ex pace conscientiae, gaudio interno, & spe viva, ad quam renati sunt, per resurrectionem Christi ex mortuis, 1 Petr. I, 3. Qui autem accurato examine probat fidem suam, huius sensum & experimentum habet. De confirmatione fidei idem inquit apostolus, 2 Cor. I, 22. Deus obsignavit nos, & dedit arrhabonem spiritus in cordibus nostris. Deus, misso suo Spiritu Sancto in corda nostra fidem, iustitiam & spem futurae hereditatis confirmavit.

V. De renovatione, sive sanctificatione, cuius effecta sunt bona opera, quibus viva fides profertur & ostenditur: & quibus non sequentibus fidem iustificam, haec exstinguitur & evanessit. De quo nos monet S. Iacobus, c. II, 18. 20: Ostende mihi fidem tuam ex operibus tuis. - Visne vero scire, o homo vane! quod fides sine operibus mortua sit? Vt praelentia operum a posteriori praesentiam fidei iustificantis demonstrat: ita absentia B. O. fidei mortuae est indicium.

VI. De ecclesia. Cum enim Christus sit caput & rex ecclesiae, defensurus eandem, ne portae inferorum ipsam opprimant, Matth. XVI, 18. fiducia renatorum maxime solidatur, quoniam confidunt, se tanquam viva ecclesiae membra sub regimine ac praesidio Christi, a diaboli insidiis, & mundi illecebris non minus, quam fremitu, atque praedominio carnis, defensum iri.

VII. De ministerio ecclesiastico, cuius opera Spiritus S. vtitur ad applicandum homini humanae gratiae & salutis. Quapropter apostolus graphice depingit officium ministrorum ecclesiae, 1 Cor. IV, 1. Sic nos reputet homo tanquam ministros Christi & oeconomos mysteriorum Dei. Qui habendus & reputandus est tanquam minister Dei, ille fide divina aestimandus est organum divinum, quo ad excitandam & confirmandam fiduciam in Christum Spiritus S. vtitur.


### Quest. XVI. Which articles of faith are secondary fundamental articles?

Secondary fundamental articles of faith are those whose simple ignorance does not hinder salvation; but whose obstinate denial or impugnation undermines the foundation of faith. Such are parts of Christian doctrine concerning the characteristic properties of the divine persons (a), concerning the communication of idioms in Christ (b), concerning original sin (c), concerning the decree of election in view of final faith (d), concerning the justification of the sinner by faith alone, excluding the merit of good works (e), etc.

Obs. I. Secondary articles are not so much entire heads of the doctrine of faith as they are parts and declarations of them. They are called articles of faith in a distributive sense, insofar as they are dogmas divinely revealed, coherent with the foundation of faith and salvation. They deserve and retain the name of fundamental articles because the denial of any secondary article necessarily and always imports an error indirectly opposing the foundation of faith and salvation, and by which, through consequence, the foundation itself, or something without which it cannot be safe, is destroyed.

Obs. II. Although the simple ignorance of secondary articles of faith does not hinder salvation, nevertheless, with all effort, it must be contended by the doctors of the church and of the schools, that Christians who are beginning may from time to time make greater progress in knowing the salutary dogmas. For thus it will come to pass, that they give a readier and stronger assent to the primary fundamental articles, of which the secondary articles are certain declarations. certain declarations.

Prob. a. Simpler men, initiated into the sacred rites of Christians, believe with simple faith in one God, who is and is called God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. They believe that the Father is one God, the Son of God another, and the Holy Spirit another, yet that there are not three Gods, but one true God, from whom all things are, are preserved, and are governed. But it happens not rarely that the same persons are ignorant of how a person differs from the essence? In what the personality of the Holy Spirit differs from the personality of the Son of God? Or who and what kind is the proper and distinguishing character of each? This most simple ignorance, devoid of opposing error, does not in itself condemn. But indeed, if anyone stubbornly denies the eternal generation of the Son of God from the Father, and the eternal procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, he will either not worship the Son of God and the Holy Spirit with the same religious cult with which God the Father is worshipped; or, with the Sabellians, he will confuse the three persons of the divinity, and consequently, as far as in him lies, will tear down the fundamental article concerning the one and triune God.

Prob. b. A reborn man of duller intellect believes in Christ as true God and true man, the one mediator between God and men: but he does not grasp with his mind how the divine nature communicated its properties to the assumed human nature, and appropriated the idioms of the latter to itself: that simple ignorance is not a hindrance to salvation. If, however, anyone contumaciously denies the communication of idioms, flowing from the personal union of the two natures of Christ, he will consequently impugn the fundamental doctrine of faith concerning the hypostatic union of the two natures.

Prob. c. For the conceiving of faith in Christ, the knowledge of original sin derived from Adam to his descendants is not simply required: (for a sinner can seriously acknowledge, mourn, and detest his sins, who does not understand the original stain, especially in an academic sense): yet it is required to prevent the contrary opinion, which is the persuasion of perfect holiness and the ability to fully keep the divine commands: by which if anyone is deceived, he does not arrive at a serious acknowledgment of sin and true contrition. Now the proximate subject, to which saving faith is conferred, is a contrite heart.

Prob. d. You may find among the assembly of Christians simpletons, firmly believing that they will obtain the remission of sins and eternal salvation from God out of unmerited grace, on account of the merit of Christ, yet thinking nothing of the eternal decree of election, made by God in view of final faith in Christ: simple ignorance of election will not condemn these; but a malicious denial imports this consequence, that God does not save men in time in view of persevering faith in Christ, because the decree and its execution correspond to each other accurately.

Prob. e. The justification of a converted sinner through faith in Christ is a constitutive fundamental article of faith. But it happens that a sinner, acknowledging and detesting his sins, places all his trust in Christ the mediator, to whose memory the exclusion of good works does not occur. Who would condemn him? But he who denies that a sinner is justified by faith in Christ alone strikes against the primary fundamental articles concerning the grace of God and the merit of Christ.

Obf. Denial is made either by a persistent seducer, or by one seduced out of mere ignorance and simplicity, denying some dogma of faith. The denial of the former destroys a primary article of faith, which the ignorance of the latter leaves unharmed. The reason is that the denial of a secondary article of faith does not oppose the foundation of faith except by consequence. But he who embraces that negative out of simplicity does not grasp the consequence. Therefore, that denial can stand with the foundation of faith. On the contrary, a persistent denial draws with it an error contrary to the foundation of faith.

Latin:

Articuli fidei fundamentales secundarii sunt, quorum simplex ignoratio non officit saluti; pertinax autem negatio vel impugnatio fundamentum fidei labefactat. Quales sunt partes doctrinae christianae de personarum divinarum proprietatibus characteristicis (a), de communicatione idiomatum in Christo (b), de peccato originis (c), de decreto electionis intuitu fidei finalis (d), de iustificatione peccatoris per solam fidem, excluso bonorum operum merito (e), &c.

Obs. I. Articuli secundarii non tam integra sunt capita doctrinae fidei, quam illorum partes & declarationes. Dicuntur articuli fidei sensu distributivo, quatenus sunt dogmata divinitus revelata, cum fundamento fidei & salutis cohaerentia. Merentur & retinent nomen articulorum fundamentalium, quia negatio alicuius articuli secundarii necessario & semper importat errorem, fundamento fidei & salutis indirecte adversantem, & quo per consequentiam ipsum fundamentum, vel aliquid, absque quo id saluum esse non potest, destruitur.

Obs. II. Quamvis simplex ignoratio articulorum fidei secundariorum non officiat saluti, omni tamen ope contendendum est doctoribus ecclesiae & scholarum, vt christiani incipientes subinde maiores in cognoscendis falutaribus dogmatibus progressus faciant. Sic enim futurum est, vt articulis fundamentalibus primariis, quorum declarationes quaedam sunt articuli secundarii, proniorem & validiorem assensum praebeant. quædam sunt articuli secundarii, proniorem & validiorem assensum præbeant.

Prob. a. Homines rudiores, sacris christianorum initiati, fide simplici credunt in Deum unum, qui est & vocatur Deus pater, filius & Spiritus S. Credunt alium esse Deum patrem, alium filium Dei, alium Spiritum sanctum, neque tamen esse tres Deos, sed unum verum Deum, a quo sunt, conferuantur & gubernantur omnia. At haud raro contingit, ut iidem ignorent, quomodo differat persona ab essentia? in quo differat personalitas Spiritus S. a personalitate filii Dei? seu quis & qualis sit vtriusque character proprius & discretivus? Quae simplicissima ignorantia, oppositi erroris expers, per se non damnat. Sed vero si quis praefracte neget aeternam generationem filii Dei a patre, & aeternam processionem Spiritus S. a patre & filio, is vel non eodem religioso cultu venerabitur filium Dei & Spiritum S. quo colitur Deus pater; vel cum Sabellianis tres diuinitatis personas confundet, & consequenter articulum fundamentalem de Deo vno & trino, quantum in ipso, conuellet.

Prob. b. Credit homo renatus hebetioris ingenii in Christum verum Deum, & verum hominem, vnum mediatorem Dei & hominum: sed mente non assequitur, quomodo natura diuina suas proprietates communicauerit assumtae humanae naturae, huiusque idiomata sibi appropriauerit: illa ignorantia simplex non obest saluti. Si quis autem contumaciter infitietur communicationem idiomatum, fluentem ex vnione personali duarum Christi naturarum, consequenter fundamentalem fidei doctrinam de vnione hypostatica duarum naturarum impugnabit.

Prob. c. Ad concipiendam fidem in Christum non simpliciter requiritur notitia peccati originalis ab Adamo in posteros deriuati: (potest enim peccator sua peccata serio agnoscere, lugere & detestari, qui labem originalem, praesertim acroamatice, non intelligit): requiritur tamen ad praecauendam opinionem contrariam, quae est persuasio perfectae sanctitatis, & facultatis diuina mandata plene seruandi: qua si quis fallitur, ad seriam agnitionem peccati, & veram contritionem non peruenit. Proximum autem subiectum, cui fides saluifica confertur, est cor contritum.

Prob. d. Inuenias in coetu christianorum idiotas, firme credentes, se a Deo ex gratia indebita, propter meritum Christi, remissionem peccatorum & aeternam salutem consecuturos esse, nil tamen cogitantes de aeterno electionis decreto, a Deo facto, intuitu finalis in Christum fidei: hos non damnabit simplex ignorantia electionis; sed malitiosa negatio hanc importat consequentiam, quod Deus in tempore homines non saluet intuitu fidei perseuerantis in Christum, propterea quod decretum & eius exsecutio sibi accurate respondent.

Prob. e. Iustificatio peccatoris conuersi per fidem in Christum est articulus fidei fundamentalis constituiuus. Sed contingit, ut peccator peccata agnoscens & detestans omnem fiduciam collocet in Christo mediatore, cuius memoriam non subeat exclusio bonorum operum. Quis hunc condemnaret? negans vero peccatorem sola in Christum fide iustificari, is impingit in articulos fundamentales primarios de gratia Dei & merito Christi.

Obs. Negatio fit vel a seductore pertinaci, vel a seducto ex mera ignorantia & simplicitate, aliquod dogma fidei infitiante. Prioris negatio destruit articulum fidei primarium, quem posterioris inscitia illaesum relinquit. Ratio est, quia negatio articuli fidei secundarii non aduersatur fundamento fidei, nisi per consequentiam. Consequentiam autem non capit, qui ex simplicitate illam negatiuam amplectitur. Ideo cum fundamento fidei illa negatio stare potest. Contra pertinax negatio comitem trahit errorem fundamento fidei contrarium.


### Quæst. XXII. Are all fundamental articles of faith comprehended autolexei or verbatim in Holy Scripture?

Some articles of faith are fundamental ῥητῶς, that is, in express words they are read in the sacred writings. Some διανοητικῶς & only according to the matter in sacred scripture are read in express words in the sacred writings (a). Some διανοητικῶς & only according to the matter in sacred scripture are contained, which are perceived from it through a manifest and immovable consequence (b).

Expressly we read it written, that there are three who testify in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one, 1 John

V, 7.

Christ being true man, 1 Tim.

II, 5. that the same is true God, 1 John

V, 21. one mediator of God and men, 1 Tim.

II, 5. the only-begotten Son of God, John

I, 14.

that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, John

XV, 26.

That all nations are to be baptized, Matt.

XXVIII, 19.

Proof b. Through a valid consequence we infer that God, one in essence, is three in persons, that God from eternity begat a Son of the same substance [ὁμοούσιον], that Christ is one person consisting of two natures, that the Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son of God, that infants are to be baptized, etc.

Quest.

XXIII.

Latin:

Quidam articuli fidei fundamentales ῥητῶς, siue disertis verbis in sacris litteris leguntur . Quidam διανοητικῶς & secundum rem tantum in sacra scriptura confiue disertis verbis in sacris litteris leguntur (a). Quidam διανοητικῶς & secundum rem tantum in sacra scriptura continentur, qui per manifestam & immotam consequentiam ex illa percipiuntur (b).

Expresse scriptum legimus, tres esse, qui testificantur in caelo, patrem, verbum & Spiritum sanctum, & hos tres esse vnum, 1 Io.

V, 7.

Christum verum esse hominem, 1 Tim.

II, 5. eumdem verum esse Deum, 1 Io.

V, 21. vnum mediatorem Dei & hominum, 1 Tim.

II, 5. filium Dei vnigenitum, Io.

I, 14.

Spiritum sanctum a patre procedere, Io.

XV, 26.

Omnes gentes esse baptizandas, Matth.

XXVIII, 19.

Prob. b. Per validam consequentiam inferimus, Deum, vnum essentia, personis esse trinum, Deum ab æterno genuisse filium ὁμοούσιον, Christum esse vnam personam e duabus constantem naturis, Spiritum sanctum etiam a filio Dei procedere, infantes esse baptizandos, &c.

Quæst.

XXIII.


### Question XXIII. Which articles of faith are non-fundamental?

Articles of faith that are non-fundamental are parts of Christian doctrine which can be ignored and denied without the loss of salvation.

Proof by examples.

It is established, that certain dogmas divinely revealed are debated on both sides. e.g., are the waters, divinely placed above the expanse, clouds, or are they waters above the heavens?

Was the world created in the spring time, or in the autumn?

Whether the first sin of the fallen angels was envy, or pride?

Will the destruction of the world be substantial, or accidental?

But if a sinner, about to attain eternal salvation, has ignored or denied the waters above the heavens, he neither falls from the hope of salvation, nor destroys the foundation of faith, since such questions or assertions do not touch upon it.

Observation. In these extra-fundamental dogmas let us conduct ourselves cautiously, and not rashly embrace error, lest we sin against the very revelation of God.

Above all, let us teach nothing against conscience and with the seduction of others, nor let us impinge upon any fundamental article of faith.

Question XXIV.

Are all articles of faith equally necessary to be known?

Latin:

Articuli fidei non fundamentales sunt partes doctrinæ christianæ, quæ citra iacturam salutis ignorari & negari possunt .

Prob. exemplis.

Constat, quædam dogmata divinitus reuelata in vtramque partem ventilari. v. g. sintne aquæ, divinitus locatæ supra expansum, nubes, an aquæ supra cœlestes?

Sitne mundus conditus tempore verno, an autumnali?

Vtrum primum peccatum angelorum lapsorum fuerit invidia, an superbia?

Sitne futurus mundi interitus substantialis, an accidentalis?

Quod si peccator æternam salutem adepturus aquas supra cœlestes ignorauerit, aut negauerit, nec spe salutis excidit, nec destruet fundamentum fidei, quippe quod eiusmodi quæstiones aut assertiones non attingunt.

Obseru. In his extrafundamentalibus dogmatibus caute versemur, neque temere amplectemur errorem, ne in ipsam reuelationem Dei peccemus.

In primis contra conscientiam & cum seductione aliorum nil doceamus, neque in vllum articulum fidei fundamentalem impingamus.

Quæstio XXIV.

Suntne omnes articuli fidei cognitu æque necessarii?


### Question XXIV. Are all articles of faith equally necessary to be known?

For those articles of faith which both enter into the very definition of saving faith and immediately underlie the generation of faith are most necessary to be believed for a man to be saved (a).

Of the remaining articles of faith, some are necessary to be believed positively and directly, others negatively and indirectly (b).

And if we trust in believers, the same measure of knowledge is not required of all and each (c).

Proof a.

Dogmas divinely revealed, by which the proximate causes of saving faith are explained, can neither be ignored nor denied by any man about to attain eternal salvation without the loss of eternal salvation; because they comprise the dogmatic foundation of faith, upon which the whole structure of faith and salvation rests.

Those things which must be immediately presupposed have the closest connection with the foundation of faith: the universal love of mankind [φιλανθρωπία] and grace of God, which destined and gave the mediator Christ, and is desirous of conferring faith upon all men; as well as the universality of the merit of Christ, so that a sinner, about to attain eternal life, may descend to himself under this universality, and may subsume from himself individually: God wills to have mercy on me, who has given me the ordinary means, so that by using them true faith may be conferred upon me, by which I may believe without any hesitation that Christ died for me, a most miserable sinner, so that I may not perish, but that through him I may enter into eternal life.

Prob. b. The remaining articles of faith are either primary, contributing not a little to strengthening and certifying faith in Christ, which are necessary to be believed positively and directly; or they are secondary, which are necessary to be known negatively and indirectly, since their denial by consequence undermines the foundation of faith.

Prob. c. The necessity of knowing the articles of faith seems to be limited to a certain extent on the part of the believing subjects, among whom some converted men are simpler, others more perspicacious, some infants, others adults, some hearers, others teachers and pastors. Who would demand that same degree of knowledge from a rustic that ought to be found in a learned man? Talents vary, since God himself dispenses and distributes them unequally, to one a greater measure of grace, to another a lesser. States also vary, so that a man may now be in a peaceful state, in which milk suffices for the nourishment of his faith; now in a turbulent state, where the devil is snarling, tyranny is growing strong, and heretics are spreading poisons, there is need of more solid food, greater safeguards, and more medicines. To this is added that some are converted while standing at the extreme rule of life; for some who are converted, a greater space of living and thinking has been left. To the former, the doctrine of faith is to be proposed in summary, that they may piously fall asleep in Christ the mediator; to the latter, the same is to be drawn out and explained more broadly, that they may grow in grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, 2 Pet. III, 18. Obs. The Holy Scriptures hand down the relation of dogmas to salvation partly under the express necessity of believing for salvation; partly implicitly and by consequence. When the Savior, John XVII, 3, says: This is eternal life, that they may know thee, the Father, the only true God, and whom thou hast sent, Jesus Christ, he expressly signifies that the dogma concerning the true God is so necessary to be believed for salvation, that eternal life, that is, the way and method of obtaining eternal life, consists in knowing and believing it.
