But the Holy Scriptures hand down the relation of dogmas to salvation implicitly and by consequence, while they reveal them, although not under an express necessity of believing; yet they propose and declare them in such a way that they cohere with the foundation of salvation, Jesus Christ, by a necessary bond, which can be understood and concluded by consequence from the very deeper consideration of those dogmas. For from the very consideration of them it will be evident that they ultimately aim at faith in Christ, and through faith at obtaining salvation, just as it is expressly said in John XX, 31: These are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.

Latin:

Nam qui articuli fidei tum ipsam saluificæ fidei definitionem ingrediuntur, tum generandæ fidei immediate substant, homini saluando creditu sunt maxime necessarii (a).

Reliquorum articulorum fidei quidam positiue & directe, quidam negatiue & indirecte creditu sunt necessarii (b).

Et si confidemus homines credentes, non eadem cognitionis mensura ab omnibus & singulis exigitur (c).

Prob. a.

Dogmata divinitus reuelata, quibus causæ proximæ fidei saluificæ explicantur, sine æternæ salutis dispendio neque ignorari, neque negari ab vllo homine æternam salutem adepturo possunt; quia complectuntur fundamentum fidei dogmaticum, cui tota fidei & salutis structura innititur.

Arctissimam cum fundamento fidei connexionem habent immediate præsupponenda: vniuersalis Dei φιλανθρωπία & gratia, quæ mediatorem Christum destinauit & dedit, atque cupida est conferendæ omnibus hominibus fidei; nec non vniuersalitas meriti Christi, vt peccator, adepturus vitam æternam, sub hac vniuersalitate ad se descendere, & de se in individuo subsumere queat: Deus vult mei misereri, qui mihi dedit ordinaria media, vt mihi illa vsurpanti vera conferatur fides, quo nil hæsitans credam, Christum pro me miserrimo peccatore esse mortuum, ne peream, sed vt per ipsum vitam æternam ingrediar.

Prob. b. Reliqui articuli fidei vel sunt primarii, haud parun facientes ad fidem in Christum fulciendam & certificandam, qui positive & directe creditu sunt necessarii; vel sunt secundarii, qui sunt negative & indirecte cognitu necessarii, quoniam illorum negatio per consequentiam fundamentum fidei labefactat.

Prob. c. Necessitas cognoscendi articulos fidei quadantenus limitanda videtur ex parte subiectorum credentium, e quibus alii homines conversi sunt simpliciores, alii perspicaciores, alii infantes, alii adulti, alii auditores, alii doctores & pastores. Ecquis exigat illum gradum notitiae a rustico, qui inveniri debet in litterato? Variant talenta, cum ipse Deus illa inaequaliter dispenset & distribuat, uni maiorem, alteri minorem gratiae mensuram. Variant etiam status, ut homo nunc sit in statu pacato, in quo ipsi lac sufficit ad fidei nutrimentum; nunc in statu turbulento, vbi ringente diabolo, invalescente tyrannide, spargentibus venena haereticis, solidiori cibo, maioribus praesidiis, & pluribus medicamentis opus est. Huc accedit, quod quidam convertantur stantes in extrema vitae regula; quibusdam conversis maius vivendi cogitandique spatium relictum sit. Illis doctrina fidei summatim proponenda est, ut pie in Christo mediatore obdormiscant; his eadem latius diducenda & explananda est, ut crescant in gratia & cognitione domini nostri & salvatoris Iesu Christi, 2 Petr. III, 18. Obs. Sacrae litterae habitudinem dogmatum ad salutem tradunt partim sub expressa necessitate credendi ad salutem; partim implicite & per consequentiam. Quando salvator, Io. XVII, 3. inquit: Haec est vita aeterna, ut cognoscant te, Pater, solum Deum verum, & quem misisti Iesum Christum, expresse significat, dogma de vero Deo ita esse creditu ad salutem necessarium, ut vita aeterna, hoc est, via & ratio consequendae vitae aeternae, in eo cognito & credito consistat. Implicite autem & per consequentiam tradunt sacrae scripturae habitudinem dogmatum ad salutem, dum ea, licet non sub expressa necessitate credendi, revelent; ita tamen proponunt & declarant, ut nexu necessario cum fundamento salutis Iesu Christo cohaerere, ex ipsa penitiori illorum dogmatum consideratione intelligi, & per consequentiam concludi possit. Ex ipsa enim illorum consideratione patebit, quod vltimo collineent ad fidem in Christum, & mediante fide ad salutem obtinendam, sicut Io. XX, 31. expresse dicitur: Haec scripta sunt, ut credatis, quod Iesus sit Christus filius Dei, & ut credentes vitam habeatis in nomine ipsius.


### Quaest. XXV. By what symbols of the Christian religion and of the articles of faith is the sum comprehended?

The sum of religion and of the articles of faith is contained in the older and more recent symbols. The older are the ecumenical, or universal, symbols, namely the Apostolic symbol (A), the Nicene (B), the Constantinopolitan (C), the Ephesian (D), the Chalcedonian (E), and the Athanasian (F). Obs.

Obs. (1) A symbol is called ἀπὸ τοῦ συμβάλλειν, from conferring, as if you were to say brought together from many. Among the Greeks, symbols were called tesserae, or signs, by which either soldiers in wars were distinguished from enemies (German: a field-sign, the watchword, the word); or which other men used in pacts and agreements, in place of tablets or written contracts. Compare Vossius, de symbolis, th. 9, 16, 17. Among Christians, therefore, symbols are confessions by which they go to testify both to their spiritual warfare, because they serve under the banner of King Christ against the devil and his associates, and to the pact entered into with God in baptism.

(2) The more prolix symbols, comprised in a decent order, are commonly called symbolic books, which are public confessions, by orthodox men in the name of the church concerning certain articles of faith ticles with the most serious counsel, so that the members of the orthodox church might be separated from the ignorance of infidels and from heretical depravity, and might be kept in a consenting profession of faith. A.

The Apostles' Creed is so called materially by reason of the dogmas which are contained in this symbol, and which agree precisely with the apostolic doctrine comprehended in the Holy Scriptures. But that it was signed by the apostles themselves in the very same words in which it is recited in the church today, cannot be clearly proven. For if it had been written by the apostles themselves after the miraculous outpouring of the Holy Spirit, before they went out into the world to preach the gospel of Christ, and had been delivered to the universal church as a universal epitome of things to be believed, surely Luke, the most diligent writer of the Acts of the Apostles, would not have passed over in silence a matter of such great moment and one more worthy of narration than all others. Who would believe that the Holy Spirit, who destined this symbol for the use of the Catholic Church, would have failed to make even the slightest mention of the symbol throughout the entire canon of Scripture? Meanwhile, we do not unwillingly receive that symbol, which is called apostolic because of the dogmas it embraces, and which is approved by the universal Christian church. We receive it, I say, not because it contains all things to be believed explicitly, adequately, and specifically. For certain fundamental articles of faith are passed over in silence in the Apostles' Creed. Nothing is explicitly taught in it concerning the universal benevolence of God, concerning the satisfaction and merit of Christ, concerning conversion and regeneration, concerning the mystical union of the reborn with God, concerning renewal, concerning sin and repentance, concerning the Word of God and the sacraments: although the apostle, in instructing catechumens, laid the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God, of the doctrine of baptisms, and of laying on of hands, and of the resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment. We receive it, therefore, because it is an epitome of many, but not all, articles of faith. B.

The Nicene Creed is named from Nicaea, a town of Bithynia, where in the year of Christ 325, under the presidency of the Emperor Constantine the Great, the first ecumenical council was held by 318 bishops against the heresy of Arius, who denied the true divinity of Christ. In this council, the gathered fathers declared the Apostles' Creed, having added a few dogmas, to be repeated.

C. The Constantinopolitan Creed receives its name from the most splendid city of Thrace, or Romania, Constantinople, where the second ecumenical council was celebrated against Macedonius, who had impugned the divinity of the Holy Spirit, in the year of Christ 383. There were present at it 150 bishops who, having repeated the Nicene Creed, added a few things concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit. D.

The Ephesine Creed, approved in the year of Christ 431 by 230 bishops, is completed by the 12 anathemas of Cyril against Nestorius. It obtained its name from Ephesus, a most famous city of Ionia. E.

The Chalcedonian Creed is named from Chalcedon, a city of Bithynia, and was subscribed to in the year of Christ 451 by 630 bishops against the Eutychian errors. F.

F. The Athanasian Creed is commonly so called, although it is very uncertain whether it was written by Athanasius himself in as many words as it is read in the church today, as D. CARPOZOVIUS judges in his Isagoge in libr. symbol., p. 72. This, however, is certain: that the symbol is very ancient, and that it holily embraces and defends the faith which Athanasius, surrounded by the most present dangers, strenuously defended against the Arians over the course of so many years, so that for this reason alone it can with every right be called Athanasian. It is numbered by some among the universal symbols by reason of its common approbation, since it was received with great consensus by the Roman, Constantinopolitan, Alexandrian, Bulgarian and other churches, as BARON. testifies, tom. III. annal. ad annum Christi CCCXC. DLIX. n. 11.

Latin:

Summa religionis & articulorum fidei continetur symbolis antiquioribus, & recentioribus. Antiquiora sunt symbola oecumenica, sive vniversalia, nempe symbolum apostolicum (A). Nicenum (B), Constantinopolitanum (C), Ephesinum (D), Chalcedonense (E), & Athanasianum (F).

Obs. (1) Symbolum dicitur ἀπὸ τοῦ συμβάλλειν, a conferendo, quasi dicas a multis collatum. Dicebantur autem Graecis symbola tesserae, vel signa, quibus vel milites in bellis dignoscebantur ab hostibus (German. ein Feld-Zeichen, die Losung, das Wort); vel quibus alii homines in pactis conuentisque, loco tabularum, vel syngrapharum, vtebantur. Confer voss. de symbolis, th. 9. 16. 17. Apud christianos igitur symbola sunt confessiones, quibus iidem tum militiam suam spiritualem, quod sub vexillo regis Christi aduersus diabolum & eius socios militent, tum pactum cum Deo in baptismo initum, testatum eunt.

Obs. (2) Prolixiora symbola decenti ordine comprehensa vulgo appellantur libri symbolici, qui sunt confessiones publicae, nomine ecclesiae ab orthodoxis viris de certis fidei articulis ticulis gravissimo consilio conscriptæ, vt membra ecclesiæ orthodoxæ ab infidelium ignorantia, & hæretica pravitate separentur, & in consentiente fidei professione contineantant.

A. Symbolum apostolicum ita dicitur materialiter ratione dogmatum, quæ isthoc symbolo continentur, & cum doctrina apostolica sacris litteris comprehensa ad amussim conspirant. Quod autem totidem verbis, quot hodie in ecclesia recitatur, ab ipsis apostolis consignatum sit, liquido probari nequit. Quod si enim ab ipsis apostolis post miraculosam Spiritus S. effusionem, antequam exierunt in terrarum orbem, prædicaturi evangelium Christi, gravissimo consilio conscriptum & universæ ecclesiæ traditum fuisset, ceu universalis credendorum epitome, utique Lucas, actorum apostolicorum scriptor diligentissimus, rem tanti momenti, & præ cæteris narratione dignissimam, silentio non involuisset. Ecquis credat, Spiritum sanctum, qui hoc symbolum in usum ecclesiæ catholicæ destinauerit, per totum scripturæ canonem ne minimam quidem symboli mentionem facturum fuisse? Haud inviti interim symbolum illud, quod ob dogmata, quæ complectitur, apostolicum audit, & ab universa ecclesia christiana comprobatur. recipimus. Recipimus, inquam, illud, non ideo, quod omnia credenda explicite, adæquate & specifice contineat. Nam quidam articuli fidei fundamentales in symbolo apostolico silentio prætereuntur. Nil explicite in illo traditur de benevolentia Dei universali, de satisfactione & merito Christi, de conversione & regeneratione, de vnione mystica renatorum cum Deo, de renouatione, de peccato & pœnitentia, de verbo Dei & sacramentis: cum tamen apostolus catechumenos informando fundamentum iecerit pœnitentiæ ab operibus mortuis, & fidei in Deum, baptismorum doctrinæ, impositionisque manuum, resurrectionisque mortuorum, & iudicii æterni. Recipimus ergo, quia est epitome multorum, sed non omnium, articulorum fidei.

B. Symbolum Nicenum dicitur a Nicea, Bithyniæ oppido, vbi anno Christi CCCXXV. præfide Constantino M. Imperatore, ab episcopis CCCXVIII. aduersus hæresin Arii, veram Christi diuinitatem negantis, concilium œcumenicum I. habitum est. In hoc concilio congregati patres symbolum apostolicum paucis adiectis dogmatibus, repetitum declararunt.

C. Symbolum Constantinopolitanum nomen accipit a splendidissima Thraciæ, siue Romaniæ, vrbe Constantinopoli, vbi concilium II. œcumenicum aduersus Macedonium, qui diuinitatem Spiritus S. impugnauerat, celebratum est, anno Christi CCCLXXXIII. Interfuerunt eidem episcopi CL. qui, symbolo Niceno repetito, pauca de diuinitate Spiritus S. inferuerunt.

D. Symbolum Ephesinum, anno Christi CCCCXXXI. ab episcopis CCXXX. approbatum, anathematismis XII. Cyrilli contra Nestorium absoluitur. Nomen obtinuit ab Epheso, clarissima Ioniæ vrbe.

E. Symbolum Chalcedonense dicitur a Chalcedone, vrbe Bithyniæ, estque anno Christi CCCCLI. aduersus errores Eutychianos ab episcopis DCXXX. subscriptum.

F. Symbolum Athanasianum vulgo ita nuncupatur, quamuis incertissimum sit, an tot verbis, quot hodie in ecclesia legitur, ab ipso Athanasio conscriptum sit, censente D. CARPOZOVIO in isagoge in libr. symbol. p. 72. Hoc interim certum est, symbolum illud esse perantiquum, & fidem, quam Athanasius, præsentissimis cinctus periculis, tot annorum decursu aduersus Arianos strenue defendit, sancte complecti ac tueri, vt vel ex hoc capite Athanasianum omni iure nominari possit. Annumeratur a nonnullis symbolis vniversalibus ratione communis approbationis, quoniam magno consensu a Romana, Constantinopolitana, Alexandrina, Bulgarica & aliis ecclesiis receptum fuit, teste BARON. tom. III. annal. ad annum Christi CCCXC. DLIX. n. 11.


### Q. XXVI. Which are the more recent symbols?

The more recent symbols of our churches are the Unaltered Augsburg Confession (a), the Apology of the Augsburg Confession (b), the Smalcald Articles (c), Luther’s Small and Large Catechisms (d), the Epitome of the XI articles, and also the Solid Declaration, which is specifically called the Formula of Concord (e). a.

The Unaltered Augsburg Confession was presented to Emperor Charles V in the year of Christ MDXXX at the most solemn diet of the Roman Empire at Augsburg. It is surnamed "unaltered" so that it may be distinguished from the "altered" version, which was interpolated by Philipp Melanchthon on his own authority and published at Wittenberg in the year MDXL. The Augsburg Confession comprises XXI doctrinal articles and VII chapters concerning abuses introduced into the church. b.

The Apology of the Augsburg Confession is that by which the confession itself was defended against the Papal confutation, which had been prepared at Augsburg, by the order of the Princes and Estates while the diet was still in session, with Philipp as the author. It was indeed offered to the Emperor, but was not received by him. It was printed at Wittenberg in the year MDXXXI. c.

The Smalcald Articles were written by the Blessed LUTHER in the year of Christ MDXXXVII, to be presented in the name of the Evangelical church to a council, if one were to be held. d.

Luther’s Small and Large Catechisms succinctly comprise and vigorously explain the chapters of Christian doctrine: they are to be esteemed very highly as a distinguished κειμήλιον [heirloom] and treasure of our church, which we consider to be, as it were, the bible of the laity. e.

The Formula of Concord is accepted in two ways: (α) generally and ὅλικῶς [wholly], for all the symbolic books of the Evangelical church gathered into one volume; (β) specifically and μερικῶς [partially], for the Epitome of the XI articles and their Solid Declaration, by which controversies that had arisen among the theologians addicted to the Augsburg Confession were settled. The authors were D. JACOB ANDREAE, D. MARTIN CHEMNITZ, D. ANDREAS MUSCULUS, D. DAVID CHYTRAEUS, D. NICHOLAS SELNECCER, and D. CHRISTOPHER CORNER. It was brought to light in the year MDLXXX.

Latin:

Recentiora nostrarum ecclesiarum symbola sunt Augustana confessio inuariata (a), Apologia Augustanae confessionis (b), Articuli Smalcaldici (c), Catechismus Lutheri minor & maior (d), Epitome articulorum XI, nec non solida declaratio, quae speciatim Formula concordiae appellatur (e).

a. Augustana confessio inuariata anno Christi MDXXX. Carolo V. Imperatori in solennissunis imperii Romani comitiis Augustae Vindelicorum exhibita est. Cognominatur inuariata, vt discernatur a variata, quae a Philippo Melanchthone proprio ausu interpolata, & anno MDXL. Wittebergae in lucem edita est. Complectitur Augustana confessio articulos XXI. doctrinales, & capita VII. de abusibus in ecclesiam inuectis.

b. Apologia Augustanae confessionis est, qua ipsa aduersus confutationem pontificiam, Augustae adornatam, iussu Principum & Statuum, durantibus comitiis, auctore Philippo defensa est. Oblata quidem est Caesari, sed ab eo non recepta. Typis impressa est Wittebergae anno MDXXXI.

c. Articuli Smalcaldici a b. LUTHERO sunt conscripti anno Christi MDXXVII. concilio, si quod futurum esset, nomine ecclesiae euangelicae exhibendi.

d. Catechismus Lutheri minor & maior capita doctrinae christianae succincte complectitur, & neruose explicat: permagni aestimandus, vt insigne κειμήλιον ac thesaurus ecclesiae nostrae, quem quasi biblia laicorum esse censemus.

e. Formula concordiae dupliciter accipitur, (α) generaliter & ὁλικῶς, pro omnibus libris symbolicis ecclesiae euangelicae in vnum volumen congestis; (β) specialiter & μερικῶς, pro epitome XI. articulorum, & solida eorum declaratione, de quibus inter theologos Augustanae confessioni addictos controuersiae exortae erant. Auctores fuerunt D. IACOBVS ANDREAE, D. MARTINVS CHEMNITIVS, D. ANDREAS MVSCVLVS, D. DAVID CHYTRAEVS, D. NICOLAVS SELNECCERVS, D. CHRISTOPHORVS CORNERVS. Prodiit in lucem anno MDLXXX.


### Q. XXVII. What is the distinction between Holy Scripture and the symbolic books?

Holy Scripture and the symbolic books differ (a).

Because 1) Holy Scripture is immediately inspired by God to the holy men of God, moved by the Holy Spirit: The symbolic books are sacred writings, composed by orthodox men, who were mediately endowed by God with the privilege of illumination (b).

2) Holy Scripture is αὐτόπιστος καὶ ἀναπόδεικτος [self-credible and indemonstrable], worthy of faith in itself, and not in need of a prior principle from which it might be demonstrated: The symbolic books are ἑπομένως ἀξιόπιστοι [consequently credible], that is, they deserve faith consequently, in that they are conformed to the revealed Word of God (c).

3) Holy Scripture possesses divine canonical authority, so that it is the infallible norm by which true dogmas of faith are distinguished from false ones: The symbolic books have ecclesiastical authority, and are respectively called a norm, namely, with respect to the external profession of faith, by which we testify to the unanimous consent of the church in the doctrine of faith (d). 4) Holy Scripture adequately contains all things to be believed and done: No symbolic book perfectly comprises all and singular dogmas of faith and precepts of morals.

Prob. a. When Paul says in 2 Tim. III, 16: πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευσος, "all scripture is inspired by God," he expresses with singular emphasis the θεοπνοήν [divine inspiration], or immediate divine inspiration. Explaining this, D. QUENSTEDT in his system, fol. 100, writes thus: θεοπνοή [divine inspiration] system. fol. 100, he writes thus:

The definition here does not denote the general concurrence of God with all creatures, nor the special or gracious [concurrence], by which God is present to all the faithful, but a most special and extraordinary concurrence, proper to the holy writers alone. Which comprises (1) ἔλλαμψιν, i.e., a certain supernatural and extraordinary illumination of the mind, which occurred like a flash and irradiation of some kind, and indeed not in the manner of a permanent habit, but of a transient act; (2) a peculiar mode, instinct, afflatus, impulse, and dictation of the Holy Spirit for writing this and nothing else. Add to these that even the individual words of the original Hebrew text in the Old, and the Greek in the New Testament, were dictated by the Holy Spirit into the pen. For if the individual words had not been suggested to the holy writers by θεοπνευσίαν [divine inspiration], Holy Scripture would not be properly, absolutely, and simply, but improperly and in a qualified sense, and at least regarding the concepts of the things signified, and could be called θεόπνευσος [divinely inspired], just as scripture translated by human effort into another language cannot be called properly, absolutely, and simply θεόπνευσος, because the formal words themselves, of which it consists, were not suggested by the Holy Spirit through inspiration, although it can be called θεόπνευσος in a qualified sense with the addition, namely, regarding the concepts of the things, once inspired in the holy writers, which are signified by the words of the version, as D. Musaeus rightly teaches.

In Introd. theol. p. 250: In which strictest sense no symbol of the church can be called θεόπνευσεν. For although orthodox men, illuminated by the Holy Spirit, conceived it in their mind and committed it to writing, they did not, however, write from a most special, extraordinary, and immediate inspiration of God, but were gifted and taught by God through ordinary and mediate illumination.

Nor were the individual words of the symbolic books dictated by the Holy Spirit into the pen, but with God assisting and directing, they themselves found the appropriate words and applied them to divine dogmas. *Prob. b.

Latin:

Sacra scriptura & libri symbolici differunt (a).

Quia 1) sacra scriptura est immediate inspirata a Deo sanctis Dei hominibus, a Spiritu sancto impulsis: Libri symbolici sunt scripta sacra, consignata a viris orthodoxis, mediate illuminationis priuilegio diuinitus donatis (b).

2) Sacra scriptura est αὐτόπιστος καὶ ἀναπόδεικτος, per se fide digna, neque indiga principii prioris, e quo demonstretur: Libri symbolici sunt ἑπομένως ἀξιόπιστοι, hoc est, consequenter merentur fidem, qua verbo Dei reuelato sunt conformes (c).

3) Sacra scriptura pollet diuina auctoritate canonica, vt sit norma infallibilis, qua vera fidei dogmata a falsis discernuntur: Libri symbolici habent auctoritatem ecclesiasticam, & respectiue dicuntur norma, nempe respectu externae fidei professionis, qua vnanimem ecclesiae in doctrina fidei consensum testamur (d). 4) Sacra scriptura adaequate continet omnia credenda, & agenda: Nullus liber symbolicus omnia & singula dogmata fidei praeceptaque morum perfecte complectitur.

Prob. a. Cum Paullus 2 Tim. III, 16. inquit: πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος, omnis scriptura a Deo est inspirata, singulari cum emphasi exprimit θεοπνοΐην, siue inspirationem diuinam immediatam. Quam explicaturus D. QVENSTEDIVS in system. fol. 100. ita scribit: Θεοπνοΐη

Deo. on non notat h. l. concursum Dei generalem cum omnibus creaturis, neque specialem seu gratiosum, quo adest Deus omnibus fidelibus, sed specialissimum plane & extraordinarium, solis sacris scriptoribus proprium concursum. qui complectitur (1) ἔλλαμψιν l. supernaturalem quandam & extraordinariam mentis illuminationem, quæ instar coruscationis & irradiationis alicuius fiebat, & quidem non ad modum habitus permanentis, sed actus transeuntis; (2) peculiarem modum, instinctum, afflatum, impulsum & dictamen Spiritus sancti ad hoc & non aliud scribendum. His adde, quod etiam singula verba textus primigenii hebræi in vetere, & græci in nouo testam. a Spiritu sancto in calamum dictata sint. Nam si verba singula non fuissent scriptoribus sacris suggesta per θεοπνευσίαν, scriptura sacra non proprie, non absolute & simpliciter, sed improprie & secundum quid, & quoad conceptus rerum significatarum saltem esset, dicique posset θεόπνευσος, perinde ut scriptura humano studio in aliam linguam translata proprie, absolute & simpliciter θεόπνευσος dici non potest, quia ipsa verba formalia, quibus constat, a Spiritu sancto per inspirationem suggesta non sunt, licet secundum quid cum apposito θεόπνευσος dici queat, nempe quoad conceptus rerum, scriptoribus sacris olim inspiratos, qui verbis versionis significantur, ut recte docet D.

MVSAEVS introd. theol. p. 250: Quo sensu strictissimo nullum ecclesiæ symbolum vocari potest θεόπνευσεν. Quamuis enim viri orthodoxi a Spiritu sancto illuminati illud mente conceperint, & in litteras retulerint, non tamen ex specialissima, extraordinaria & immediata inspiratione Dei scripserunt, sed ordinaria & mediata illuminatione a Deo fuerunt donati & edocti.

Neque iisdem singula-verba librorum symbolicorum a Spiritu sancto in calamum sunt dictata, sed assistente & dirigente Deo ipsi verba congrua inuenerunt, & dogmatibus diuinis applicarunt. *Prob. b.


### Q. XXVII. What is the distinction between Holy Scripture and the symbolic books?: The word of God revealed, and committed to writing, is not only the word of truth, Eph.* I, 13. but also truth itself, Io

The word of God revealed, and committed to writing, is not only the word of truth, Eph.* I, 13. but also truth itself, Io.

XVII, 17. and therefore it merits faith by itself and immediately. The symbols of the Church are deduced from the written word of God by consequence, and are conformed to it, and thus ἑπομένως [consequently] and by consequence procure faith for themselves.

D. Lobech does not speak ill in A. Confess. p. 16: We have faith in the Augsburg Confession, on account of Scripture, because it is built from it.

Prob. c. That Holy Scripture is the adequate norm of all those things which pertain to faith and morals is clearly evident, since it is explicitly called קו [line] or rule of them (the apostles), Ps. 19:5, κανὼν [canon], Gal. 6:16, Phil. 3:16. The name of norm or canon has obtained [usage] both for direction, because the truth of faith and the honesty of morals are directed according to it, and for correction, since the dogmas of faith and the precepts of morals come to be accurately examined by it, so that whatever agrees with it may be retained as right and pious; whatever dissents from it may be rejected as erroneous or impious.

No symbol of the church, however, is absolutely and simply the norm of faith and morals, but is called a norm in a qualified and relative sense, having regard to certain churches, which presuppose the truth and certainty of the symbols as proven from Scripture. For no symbolic book generates or prescribes faith, although faith already generated can be strengthened by it, and the external profession of faith can be determined by it for retaining the consensus of doctrine and avoiding dissensions.

Cf. Carpzov, Isagog. in libr. symbol. p. 6. By D. Quenstedt, a symbolic book is called a norma tesseralis [tessellated/token norm] and testimonial of public doctrine, which the church professes with great consensus, in System. fol. 46. Prob. d.

No symbolic book is an adequate catalog of all fundamental dogmas of faith, but according to the time and occasion in which the symbolic books were written, account was taken of those dogmas which were controversial and were most impugned. But Holy Scripture perfectly comprises whatever is necessary to be believed and done by a man about to attain eternal salvation. Which will be proven more fully and clearly below.

Dicis I.

The symbolic books are also called θεόπνευστοι (God-breathed) by theologians. For D. GEORG. MYLIVS in explicat. Aug. conf. p. 2 says: Because the Augustan confession rests upon the most firm foundation of the H.

Scriptures, we can and ought, with the best right, to call it θεόπνευστον . D. HVTTERVS in explicat. libri concordiae p. 1 writes: We constitute the primary author of the book of concord, or the αἴτιον κύριον (principal cause), not any man, whether theologian or politician: but God himself the Holy Spirit, the fountain and bestower of every good; so much so, that we do not hesitate in the least to call it θεόπνευστον, divinely inspired.

Resp. Paul, 2 Tim. III, 16, calls Scripture θεόπνευστον in the strictest sense, because both the concepts of things and the words of Scripture are immediately inspired by God.

But the aforementioned theologians call the symbolic books θεόπνευστοι in a broader sense, mediately. For D. MYLIVS renders a clear reason for this mediate θεοπνευστία (God-breathing), because it rests upon the most firm foundation of the H. Scriptures: and D. HVTTERVS, l. c., adds: with this distinction preserved, however, which intervenes between the holy scriptures and the symbolic or ecclesiastical writings.

This distinction he explains on page 4. Namely, in a broader sense, the symbolic books are called θεόπνευστοι by some authors (1) by reason of the object, since they contain and expound the word of God formerly immediately inspired to the prophets and apostles, and whatever is elicited from the word of God by manifest consequence.

Let us listen to our great CHEMNITIVS discoursing excellently on the symbols of the church, part III, loc. theol. fol. m. 235: (The ancients) indeed confirm their interpretations with the testimonies of the symbols of the ancient church: but those symbols are not something outside of, or against, Scripture, but are the very marrow of Scripture. (2)

By reason of mediate illumination: for we do not doubt that God by a special concurrence flowed into the minds of the faithful doctors who wrote the symbols of the church, illuminated their minds, and bent their wills, so that they conceived the most true and most wholesome dogmas in their minds and expressed them with the pen. Just as Job also says generally, ch. XXXII, 8: There is a spirit in men, and the inspiration of the Almighty gives understanding. The LXX rendered it: πνοὴ παντοκράτορός ἐστιν ἡ διδάσκουσα (the breath of the Almighty is that which teaches).

Specifically concerning the Nicene confession, ISIDORVS Pelusiota says, lib. IV, ep. 99: Divinely inspired, it handed down the truth of the dogmas.

Latin:

Verbum Dei reuelatum, & in litteras redactum, non est tantum verbum veritatis, Eph.* I, 13. sed etiam veritas ipsa, Io.

XVII, 17. adeoque per se & immediate meretur fidem. Symbola Ecclesiæ ex verbo Dei scripto per consequentiam deducuntur, & eidem conformantur, atque adeo ἑπομένως & consequenter fidem sibi conciliant.

Non male ait D. LOBECH. in A. Confess. p. 16. Confessioni Augustanæ fidem habemus, propter scripturam, quia ex ea exstructa est.

Prob. c. Sacram scripturam esse adæquatam normam eorum omnium, quæ ad fidem & mores pertinent, liquido constat, quoniam diserte dicitur קו linea vel regula eorum (apostolorum) Ps. XIX, 5. κανὼν, Gal. VI, 16. Phil. III, 16. Nomen normæ aut canonis obtinuit tum ob directionem, quia secundum eam veritas fidei & honestas morum dirigitur, tum ob correctionem, quoniam dogmata fidei & præcepta morum ad eam accurate examinanda veniunt, vt, quidquid cum ea consentit, tanquam rectum & pium retineatur; quidquid ab ea dissentit, velut erroneum aut impium reiiciatur.

Nullum autem symbolum ecclesiæ absolute & simpliciter est norma fidei & morum, sed dicitur norma secundum quid & respective, habito respectu ad ecclesias certas, quæ veritatem & certitudinem symbolorum ex scriptura probatam præsupponunt. Nullus enim liber symbolicus fidem gignit aut præscribit, quamuis fides iam genita ex ea possit roborari, & professio fidei externa per illum determinari ad retinendum doctrinæ consensum & vitanda dissidia.

Conf. CARPZOV. Isagog. in libr. symbol. pag. 6. D. QVENSTEDIO liber symbolicus vocatur norma tefferalis & testimonialis doctrinæ publicæ, quam ecclesia magno consensu profitetur, in system. fol. 46. Prob. d.

Nullus liber symbolicus est adæquatus catalogus omnium dogmatum fidei fundamentalium, sed pro ratione temporis & occasionis, qua libri symbolici scripti fuerunt, illorum dogmatum ratio fuit habita, quæ controuerfæ erant, & maxime impugnabantur. At S. scriptura perfecte complectitur, quidquid creditu factuque necessarium est homini æternam salutem adepturo. Id quod infra plenius & liquidius probabitur.

Dicis I.

Etiam libri symbolici a theologis nominantur θεόπνευστοι. Nam D. GEORG. MYLIVS in explicat. Aug. conf. p. 2. inquit: Quia August. confessio firmissimo scripturarum S. fundamento nititur, eam θεόπνευστον appellare iure optimo & possumus & debemus .

D. HVTTERVS in explicat. libri concordiae p. 1. scribit: Auctorem libri concordiae primarium, sive αἴτιον κύριον constituimus non hominem aliquem, sive theologum, sive politicum: sed ipsum Deum Spiritum sanctum, fontem & largitorem omnis boni; vsque adeo, vt θεόπνευστον, divinitus inspiratum, ipsum appellare minime dubitemus.

Resp. Paullus 2 Tim. III, 16. Scripturam nominat θεόπνευστον sensu strictissimo, quia & conceptus rerum, & verba scripturae, immediate a Deo sunt inspirata.

Memorati autem theologi libros symbolicos sensu latiori vocant mediate θεόπνευστους. Nam D. MYLIVS mediate θεοπνευστίας luculentam reddit rationem, quia firmissimo scripturarum S. fundamento nititur: & D. HVTTERVS l. c. addit: eo tamen seruato discrimine, quod scripturis sanctis, & scriptis symbolicis sive ecclesiasticis intercedit.

Id quod discrimen explicat pag. 4. Nimirum, sensu latiori, libri symbolici ab auctoribus nonnullis vocantur θεόπνευστοι (1) ratione obiecti, quoniam continent & exponunt verbum Dei prophetis & apostolis olim immediate inspiratum, & quidquid ex verbo Dei per manifestam consequentiam elicitur.

Auscultemus magnum nostrum CHEMNITIVM de symbolis ecclesiae egregie differentem part. III. loc. theol. fol. m. 235. Confirmant quidem (veteres) interpretationes suas testimoniis symbolorum veteris ecclesiae: sed illa symbola non sunt aliquid extra, aut contra scripturam, sed sunt ipsa medulla scripturae.

(2) Ratione mediatae illuminationis: neque enim dubitamus, quin Deus speciali concursu influxerit in mentes fidelium doctorum, qui symbola ecclesiae conscripserunt, mentes eorum illustrauerit, & voluntates ipsorum flexerit, vt verissima saluberrimaque dogmata mente conceperint, & calamo expresserint. Sicut & Iobus generatim inquit cap. XXXII, 8. Spiritus est in hominibus, & inspiratio omnipotentis dat intelligentiam. LXX, redderiderunt: πνοὴ παντοκράτορός ἐστιν ἡ διδάσκουσα.

Speciatim de confessione Nicena inquit ISIDORVS Pelusiota lib. IV. ep. 99. Diuinitus inspirata veritatem dogmatum tradidit.


### Q. XXVII. What is the distinction between Holy Scripture and the symbolic books?: Dicis II

Dicis II.

The symbolic writings are divine. *vid. CARPZOV. isagog. in libr. symbol. p. 3.* Therefore they possess divine canonical authority, and are simply the norm of things to be believed and done.

Resp. D. CARPZOV., l. c., expressly calls the symbols divine in a secondary sense, namely on account of the mediate origin which they owe to God. But it does not follow from this: Therefore, the symbols excel with divine canonical authority, and are absolutely the norm of faith and morals.

For to the norm of the doctrine of faith and morals, there is also required, on the part of the words, certainty and absolute infallibility, which excludes every danger of error. But infallibility and absolute certainty on the part of the words is not given, except from immediate dependence upon God inspired: which, however, has no place except in the original Hebrew and Greek text of holy Scripture. *Vid. D.

MVSAEI introduct. in theol. p. 540.* We do not deny, meanwhile, that the symbolic writings can be called divine in a sound sense, since they treat of God, are conformable to the divine word, and were written by the instinct of the Holy Spirit, nor are they destitute of the peculiar documents of divine providence governing them.

By common use of speaking, we call divine whatever is not only immediately, but also mediately of origin from God. For we know that Lactantius also wrote the books of the divine institutions.

Dicis III.

The symbolic books are human writings. Therefore, they are not even a norm respectively, namely under the respect of the external profession of faith in the consenting church.

Resp. A human writing is said to be such either by reason of its external form, or by reason of the matter which it embraces. The symbolic books, if you look at the external form and composition, are not immediately from God, but are from men: if you attend to the matter or doctrine which the symbolic books contain, that certainly is heavenly and divine: by whose intuition it is dangerous, whether with an added declaration the symbolic books to call human writings symbolic: since we do not call the calling to the ministry human, if special signs of the divine nod appear, but divine.

Ques. XXVIII. Can a man be bound by an oath to subscribe to symbolic books? To the doctrine of faith, which is contained in the symbols, no one who is not a member of that church which approves the symbolic books can be bound by an oath (a). But he who is a living member of the church, and intends to perform the public duty of teaching in it, can be obligated by the superior magistrate to a sworn subscription of books, even symbolic ones (b).

Proof a. An oath is provided for the confirmation of truth recognized and approved in the conscience. Therefore, no one is to be obligated by an oath to embrace a doctrine which he does not approve: for he would be compelled against his will to profess some dogma as true, which by the internal judgment of his mind he deems to be false.

Proof b. It pertains to the right of directing the external exercise of religion, which rests with the magistrate, to demand a sworn approval and subscription of symbolic books, so that he who is about to teach publicly in the church may be the more bound to the confession, explanation, and defense of the doctrine consenting to the public one. For we also read that the most pious princes of the Old Testament bound the people under a formula of covenant, so that they might amicably conspire in the harmonious observation and propagation of the Israelite religion. Known are the examples of Moses, Deut. XXXI, 10. & seqq. Joshua, c. XXIV, 25. Josiah, 2 Kings XXIII, 3.

You say I. Such an oath violates the liberty of consciences. Resp. The liberty of consciences would be violated if a man not approving the doctrine comprised in the symbols, and thus against his will, were compelled to a sworn subscription of symbolic books: but by swearing we only profess externally what we believe internally, knowing and willing.

You say II. The apostle warns 1 Thess. V, 19. Do not quench the Spirit. But it is quenched when the freer use of the gifts of the Holy Spirit is hindered by an exacted oath. Resp. Not the use, but the abuse of the gifts harmful to the church is hindered by the sworn subscription of symbols.

Ques. XXIX. Are symbolic books necessary? Symbolic books are necessary not absolutely (a), but hypothetically, for the state of the church, moved by most grave causes to publish symbols (b).

Proof a. There was a time when the church stood and flourished without written symbols. See D. CALOV. system. tom. I. pag. 247. & D. CARPZOV. isagoge in libr. symbol. p. 1136.

Proof b. Symbolic books are necessary by the necessity of expediency (1) to establish a solid, lasting, and firm concord in the church of God, so that a certain compendious form, and as it were a type approved by unanimous consent, may exist: in which the common doctrine, which the churches of the purer doctrine profess, collected from the word of God, may be contained. See Preface to the Solid Declaration of the Formula of Concord, p. 631. (2) To render an account of the Christian religion, if it is demanded by the magistrate. (3) To distinguish the true members of the church from its enemies, heretics, and schismatics. Conf. D. RECHENBERG. App. ad libr. symbol. p. 3.

Ques. XXX. Since the Christian religion consists not only of things to be believed, but also of things to be done: it is not without reason asked, what do we understand by things to be done? Things to be done are the works of the reborn, with the gracious concurrence of the Holy Spirit, to be performed according to the prescription of the divine law, from true faith in Christ, for the glory of God and the edification of the church.

Things to be done can also be defined as the duties of Christians, to be performed according to the norm of divine law from the powers of grace bestowed by the Holy Spirit, with true faith shining before, for the glory of God and the benefit of the neighbor.

Latin:

Dicis II.

Scripta symbolica sunt diuina. vid. CARPZOV. isagog. in libr. symbol. p. 3. Ergo pollent diuina auctoritate canonica, sunt simpliciter norma credendorum & agendorum.

Resp. D. CARPZOV. l. c. diserte vocat symbola secundo diuina, nempe ob originem mediatam, quam Deo debent.

At inde non sequitur: E. Symbola diuina auctoritate canonica eminent, & sunt absolute norma fidei & morum. Ad normam enim doctrinae fidei & morum, requiritur etiam ex parte verborum certitudo & infallibilitas absoluta, quae omne erroris periculum excludat. Infallibilitas vero & certitudo absoluta ex parte verborum non datur, nisi ex immediata dependentia a Deo inspirata: quae vero non locum habet, nisi in primigenio scripturae sacrae textu hebraeo & graeco.

Vid. D. MVSAEI introduct. in theol. p. 540. Non negamus interim posse scripta symbolica fano sensu vocari diuina, quoniam de Deo agunt, verbo diuino conformia, & instinctu Spiritus sancti conscripta sunt, nec peculiaribus prouidentiae diuinae gubernatricis documentis destituuntur.

Communi loquendi vsu diuinum appellamus, quidquid non tantum immediate, & mediate originis a Deo est. Nam & Lactantium libros diuinarum institutionum conscripsisse nouimus.

Dicis III.

Libri symbolici sunt scripta humana. E. ne respective quidem norma sunt, nempe sub respectu externae fidei professionis in ecclesia consentientis.

Resp. Scriptum humanum dicitur vel ratione externae formae, vel ratione materiae, quam complectitur. Libri symbolici, si respicias externam formam & compositionem, non immediate a Deo, sed ab hominibus sunt: si materiam aut doctrinam attendas, quam libri symbolici continent, illa certe caelestis & diuina est: cuius intuitu periculosum est, sive adiecta declaratione libros symbolicos humana scripta appellare: cum nec vocationem ad ministerium, si peculiaria diuini nutus signa appareant, humanam, sed diuinam vocemus.

Quaest. XXVIII. Potestne homo iuramento adstringi ad subscribendum libris symbolicis? Ad doctrinam fidei, quae symbolis continetur, nemo, qui non est membrum ecclesiae illius, quae libros symbolicos approbat, iuramento adstringi potest (a). Sed qui viuum ecclesiae membrum est, & in ea publico docendi munere perfungi cogitat, ad subscriptionem librorum, symbolicorum etiam, iuratam a magistratu superiori obligari potest (b).

Prob. a. Iuramentum praestatur ad confirmationem veritatis agnitae & in conscientia approbatae. Ergo nemo ad capessendam doctrinam, quam non approbat, iureiurando obligandus est: cogeretur enim inuitus ad profitendum aliquod dogma ceu verum, quod interno mentis iudicio falsum esse censet.

Prob. b. Ad ius dirigendi externum exercitium religionis, quod penes magistratum est, pertinet exigere iuratam librorum symbolicorum approbationem & subscriptionem, vt publice in ecclesia docturus eo magis obstringatur ad consentientem publicae doctrinae confessionem, explicationem & defensionem. Nam & piissimos veteris testamenti principes legimus, sub formula foederis populum obligasse, vt in harmonica religionis Israeliticae obseruatione & propagatione amice conspirarent. Nota sunt exempla Mosis, Deut. XXXI, 10. & seqq. Iosuae, c. XXIV, 25. Iosiae, 2 Reg. XXIII, 3.

Dicis I. Eiusmodi iuramentum libertatem conscientiarum violat. Resp. Violaretur libertas conscientiarum, si homo non approbans doctrinam symbolis comprehensam, atque adeo inuitus, ad iuratam librorum symbolicorum subscriptionem cogeretur: at nos iurando tantum externe profitemur, quod interne scientes & volentes credimus.

Dicis II. Monet apostolus 1 Thess. V, 19. Spiritum nolite extinguere. Extinguitur autem, cum liberior donorum Spiritus sancti vsus exacto iuramento impeditur. Resp. Non vsus, sed abusus donorum ecclesiae noxius, iurata symbolorum subscriptione, impeditur.

Quaest. XXIX. Suntne libri symbolici necessarii? Libri symbolici necessarii sunt non absolute (a), sed hypothetice, pro statu ecclesiae, grauissimis caussis ad edenda symbola permotae (b).

Prob. a. Fuit tempus, quo ecclesia stetit & viguit absque conscriptis symbolis. Vid. D. CALOV. system. tom. I. pag. 247. & D. CARPZOV. isagoge in libr. symbol. p. 1136.

Prob. b. Necessarii sunt libri symbolici necessitate expedientiae (1) ad solidam, diuturnam & firmam concordiam in ecclesia Dei constituendam, vt certa compendiaria forma, & quasi typus vnanimi consensu approbatus exstet: in quo communis doctrina, quam ecclesiae sincerioris doctrinae profitentur, e verbo Dei collecta contineatur. Vid. Praefat. sol. declar. F. Conc. p. 631. (2) Ad reddendam rationem religionis christianae, si a magistratu exigatur. (3) Ad dignoscendum vera ecclesiae membra ab eius hostibus, haereticis & schismaticis. Conf. D. RECHENBERG. App. ad libr. symbol. p. 3.

Quaest. XXX. Cum religio christiana non tantum constet credendis, sed & agendis: haud abs re quaeritur, quid per agenda intelligamus? Agenda sunt opera renatorum, gratiose concurrente Spiritu sancto, ad praescriptum legis diuinae, ex vera in Christum fide praestanda, in gloriam Dei & ecclesiae aedificationem.

Agenda etiam definiri possunt, quod sint officia christianorum, ad normam legis divinae ex viribus gratiae a Spiritu S. collatis, praelucente vera fide, facienda, in gloriam Dei & commodum proximi.


### Q. XXVII. What is the distinction between Holy Scripture and the symbolic books?: Quest. XXXI. What is opposed to true religion?

Quest. XXXI. What is opposed to true religion?

To true religion is opposed both false religion and atheism, or irreligion.

False religion is that by which either false gods are worshipped, or the true God is not truly worshipped .

Irreligion is that by which impious men hold all religion in contempt, so that, having denied the providence of God and his vindicatory justice, they take the boldness to perpetrate nothing without impunity and security .

Prob. a. The Gentiles worshipped false gods, who, since they were ignorant of the true God, partly worshipped men, renowned for memorable deeds, as gods, and partly attributed religious worship to other creatures.

Paul, about to sketch their idolatry, says in Rom. 1:23: They changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of a corruptible man, and of birds, and of four-footed beasts, and of creeping things.

The true God is not truly worshipped by various vain-talkers, who do not honor him in that manner by which he has revealed both himself and his will in his word: see their vain-talk sketched above on pp. 32, 33, 34.

Prob. b. Ps. 14:1. The fool has said in his heart: there is no God.

To such a point of madness does the impious man proceed, persisting in the state of sin, that, if he does not deny the existence, he certainly denies the providence and justice of God, wishing from his heart that there might exist no God who is omnipresent, omniscient, and the most just avenger of crimes.

SIGH.

Thee, O God, thrice best, thrice greatest, with sincere and never-failing vows we ask and beseech, that thou wouldst fill us all, joined by the covenant of the Christian religion, with thy most holy Spirit, fortify us with heavenly virtue, and instruct us with the gifts of grace, so that we may worship thee with our whole heart, burn with love for thee, and dedicate ourselves all to thee in perpetual obedience, and likewise express the sincerity of religion through pious works, and testify that our deeds correspond to our words.

Furthermore, do thou, most powerful governor of the church, restrain the petulance of the enemies of heavenly truth, break their wicked attempts, dissipate all their machines, so that true religion may not be crushed or utterly destroyed by them, but may endure safe and sound under thy protection, and may flourish, thrive, and triumph with most joyful growth!

Latin:

Quaest. XXXI. Quid opponitur verae religioni?

Verae religioni opponitur tum falsa religio, tum atheismus, sive irreligiositas.

Falsa religio est, qua vel falsi coluntur dii, vel verus Deus non vere colitur .

Irreligiositas est, qua homines impii religionem omnem despicatui ducunt, vt, abnegata providentia Dei & iustitia vindicativa, nihil non impune ac secure perpetrare frontem sumant .

Prob. a. Falsos Deos venerati sunt gentiles, qui cum verum ignorarent Deum, partim homines, memorandis factis inclytos, vt Deos coluerunt, partim cultum religiosum aliis creaturis tribuerunt.

Quorum idolatriam adumbraturus Paullus Rom. I, 23. inquit: Mutarunt gloriam incorruptibilis Dei in similitudinem imaginis corruptibilis hominis, & volatilium, & quadrupedum, & reptilium.

Verum Deum non vere colunt varii mataeologi, qui ipsum non ea ratione, qua in verbo suo & se & voluntatem suam patefecit, honorant: quorum mataeologiam supra p. 32. 33. 34. delineatam vide.

Prob. b. Ps. XIV, 1. Dixit stultus corde suo: non (est) Deus.

Eo vesaniae progreditur impius in statu peccati persistens, vt, si non existentiam, certe providentiam & iustitiam Dei abneget, optans ex animo, vt nullus exsistat Deus omnipraesens, omnisciens & iustissimus scelerum vindex.

SUSPIRIUM.

Te, Deus ter optime, ter maxime, ingenuis & nunquam defituris votis rogamus & obsecramus, vt nos omnes, christianae religionis foedere coniunctos, Spiritu tuo sanctissimo impleas, virtute coelesti munias, donis gratiae instruas, vt toto te colamus pectore, amore tui ardeamus, & nos cunctos in perpetuum tibi obsequium addicamus pariter atque sinceritatem religionis piis operibus exprimamus, & testemur, dictis nostris facta nostra respondere.

Ceterum tu, potentissime ecclesiae gubernator, hostium veritatis coelestis petulantiam compece, improbos conatus infringe, machinas omnes dissipa, vt vera religio ab iis non obteratur aut deleatur penitus, sed praesidio tuo farta tecta perennet, & incrementa laetissima floreat, vigeat, triumphet!


## 3 Prolegomenon III: On Holy Scripture, the Principle of Theology


### Quest. XXXI. What is opposed to true religion?


### Quest. I. What do you understand here by the name of principle?

By the name of principle is understood here the principle of knowing, and that incomplex, which is the fountain of complex theological principles, upon which our entire theology rests.

It is proven.

Quest. Since all theological truth is either demonstrating or to be demonstrated; and indeed, by the received usage of speech, the demonstrating truth is called a principle, and the truth to be demonstrated a conclusion: the laws of good method require that, at the threshold of theology, the incomplex principle be known beforehand, or the source and primordial element from which all reasons for proving are sought in universal theology.

Obs.

I. Theophrastus, in the presence of Alexander in the proemium to Book I of the Topics, defined the incomplex principle as that which is ἀρχή τις, ἢ στοιχεῖον ἀφ' ὧ̃ λαμβάνομεν τὰς περὶ ἕκασον ἀρχὰς, a certain principle or element from which we take the principles of each thing. It is commonly called the source of apodictic principles.

Obs.

II. A threefold source of apodictic principles is given. 1. The source of reason. 2. The source of experience. 3. The source of trustworthy authority. Philosophical and medical principles are derived from the source of reason and experience. Juridical principles flow from the source of imperial, royal, or principal authority, yet joined from time to time with the source of reason and experience.

Principles

of theology flow from the source of divine authority. Conf. D. LEICHNER'S Synopsis of True Apodictics, p. 392.

Obs.

III. A complex principle is a prior and better-known proposition, from which another, which is less known and comes into question, is validly proven. These complex principles are distinguished into primary and derived. Those are called primary which do not have a prior or superior principle from which their truth can be demonstrated. Otherwise, they are called principles κατ' ἐξοχήν (by excellence), because they never become conclusions. They are called by Aristotle, lib. 1. poster. c. 2, ἄμεσα, immediate, because they do not recognize a prior middle term: ἀναπόδεικτα, indemonstrable, viz., a priori: ἀνυπεύθυνα, infallible: αὐτόπισα, trustworthy in themselves: ἀναντίῤῥητα, placed beyond controversy. E.g., in metaphysics, the first principle is: it is impossible for the same thing to be and not to be at the same time. In physics, the first is: from nothing, nothing is naturally made. In ethics, the first is: moral good is to be loved, evil to be shunned. Derived principles are those which, with respect to the question to be demonstrated, are assumed as prior and better known, although they can be demonstrated from other principles and depend upon them. They are otherwise called mediate, because they have a superior middle term: they are also nicknamed in a special sense ἀποδεικτικὰ, i.e., demonstrable, in that their truth is demonstrable from prior principles. E.g., the ethical principle is: one must live chastely: which is demonstrated from this: one must live temperately. That same thing is proven because one must live honestly. Which is notified from the first moral principle: Good is to be loved: and thus a progression is made to the first ethical principle.

Quest. II. Upon what principle of knowing does theology rest?

Christian theology rests upon a most certain principle of knowing, namely divine revelation (a), and indeed, for the present state of the church, mediate divine revelation, comprised in the writings of the prophets and apostles (b). Whence the absolutely first complex principle of theology is: Whatever God has revealed is infallibly true. Its principle, secondary in a certain respect and for the present time, is: Whatever holy scripture teaches is infallibly certain (c).

Latin:

Nomine principii heic intelligitur principium cognoscendi, idque incomplexum, quod est fons principiorum theologicorum complexorum, quibus vniversa nostra nititur theologia.

Probatur.

Quaest. Cum omnis veritas theologica vel sit demonstrans, vel demonstranda; & quidem veritas demonstrans principium, demonstranda conclusio, recepto loquendi vsu, appelletur: leges bonæ methodi exigunt, vt in limine theologiæ præcognoscatur principium incomplexum, siue fons & primordiale elementum, ex quo omnes rationes probandi in vniuersa theologia petuntur.

Obs.

I. Theophrastus apud Alexandrum in proœm. super I. topic. principium incomplexum definiuit, quod sit ἀρχή τις, ἢ στοιχεῖον ἀφ' ὧ̃ λαμβάνομεν τὰς περὶ ἕκασον ἀρχὰς, principium quoddam seù elementum, ex quo principia cuiusque rei sumimus. Vocatur communiter fons principiorum apodicticorum.

Obs.

II. Triplex datur fons principiorum apodicticorum. 1. Fons rationis. 2. Fons experientiæ. 3. Fons auctoritatis fide dignæ. Principia philosophica & medica deriuantur ex fonte rationis & experientiæ. Principia iuridica fluunt ex fonte auctoritatis imperatoriæ, regiæ, principalis, iuncto tamen subinde fonte rationis & experientiæ.

Principia

theologica manant e fonte auctoritatis diuinæ. Conf. D. LEICHNERI synopsin veræ apodicticæ. p. 392.

Obs.

III. Principium complexum est propositio prior & notior, ex qua alia, quæ minus nota est, & in quæstionem venit, valide probatur. Quæ principia complexa distinguuntur in prima & orta. Prima dicuntur, quæ non habent principium prius aut superius, e quo eorum veritas demonstrari possit. Dicuntur ceteroquin principia κατ' ἐξοχήν, quia nunquam fiunt conclusiones. Vocantur ab Aristotele, lib. 1. poster. c. 2. ἄμεσα, immediata, quia medium terminum priorem non agnoscunt: ἀναπόδεικτα, indemonstrabilia, scil. a priori: ἀνυπεύθυνα, infallibilia: αὐτόπισα, per se fide digna: ἀναντίῤῥητα, extra controuersiam posita. V. gr. in metaphysicis principium primum est: impossibile est idem simul esse & non esse. In physicis primum est: ex nihilo naturaliter nihil fit. In ethicis primum est: bonum morale est amandum, malum fugiendum. Principia orta dicuntur, quæ, respectu demonstrandæ quæstionis, ceu priora & notiora assumuntur, quamuis ex aliis principiis demonstrari queant, & ab iis dependeant. Nuncupantur alias mediata, quia medium terminum superiorem habent: cognominantur etiam sensu speciali ἀποδεικτικὰ, i. e. demonstrabilia, eo quod veritas eorum, ex principiis prioribus est demonstrabilis. V. gr. Principium ethicum est: caste est viuendum: quod demonstratur ex hoc: temperanter est viuendum. Id ipsum probatur, quia honeste est viuendum. Quod notificatur ex principio morali primo: Bonum est amandum: atque adeo ad primum principium ethicum fit progressus.

Quæst. II. Quo principio cognoscendi nititur theologia?

Theologia christiana nititur principio cognoscendi certissimo, nempe reuelatione diuina (a), & quidem, pro hodierno ecclesiæ statu, reuelatione diuina mediata, scriptis prophetarum & apostolorum comprehensa (b). Vnde principium theologiæ complexum absolute primum est: Quidquid Deus reuelauit, infallibiliter verum est. Principium eiusdem secundum quid, & pro tempore præsenti, primum est: Quidquid sacra scriptura docet, infallibiliter certum est (c).


### Quest. I. What do you understand here by the name of principle?: Obs

Obs.

I. The discussion here is not about general revelation, or natural manifestation, by which God revealed Himself both through the light of nature implanted and through effects conspicuous in the realm of nature. See Rom. 1:19, ch. II:14, 15. But we are speaking of special and supernatural revelation, which is twofold, immediate and mediate. The Holy Spirit immediately illuminated the prophets and apostles, and suggested to them the concepts of things and words concerning the dogmas of faith and morals. Today God [reveals] Himself [and] reveals His will to the human race by means of the Word written by the prophets and apostles.

Obs. II. Divine revelation sometimes denotes, in the strictest sense which the very force of the word implies, the manifestation of things hidden and lying, as it were, under a certain veil. Sometimes, in a broader sense, it designates the manifestation of any things whatsoever—even those which can be known by the guidance of the light of nature—made by God in a supernatural manner. The latter signification, as the adequate one, holds place here.

Obs. III. Divine revelation was made πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως [in many parts and in many ways]. For one part was made mediately, through the intervention of the ministry of angels and men; another immediately, without the intervention of other persons. Thus God revealed Himself: I. Through an address of articulate voice formed in the air above the order of nature. That address was carried out by a sensible voice from God, appearing in a conspicuous form, or by another sensible sign testifying to His presence. Thus God appeared to the patriarchs in the form of a man. Gen. XVIII, 2; c. XIX, 1; c. XXII, 24. He spoke to Moses from the burning bush. Exod. XIX, 10, seqq. He spoke with Moses quite familiarly, or as Scripture says, mouth to mouth, as a friend speaks with a friend face to face. Num. XII, 6. II. Through a dream, when certain species were presented to those sleeping, with the external senses bound. Gen. XXVIII, 12; Dan. I, 1. III. Through an ἔκτασιν [ecstasy], when images of things were presented to the imagination of those awake, with the external operation of the senses ceasing. Ezech. I, 4; c. XXXVII, 1; Dan. X, 5. IV. God revealed some things to the priests through Urim and Thummim. Exod. XXVIII, 30; Lev. VIII, 8; Num. XXVII, 21. Now Urim and Thummim were twelve gems inserted into the breastplate of the priest, by which, when duly applied, God—having been appropriately asked by the high priest—gave answers concerning hidden things and uncertain events. D. PFEIFFER, dub. vexat. p. m. 276. V. Through internal inspiration, by which the Holy Spirit immediately infused some light of knowledge into the intellect of the prophets and apostles, while the operation of the senses remained. 2 Sam. XXIII, 2; 2 Tim. III, 16; 2 Petr. I, 20, 21. VI. The most illustrious divine revelation occurred in the N.T. through the Son of God, who appeared αὐτοπροσώπως [in His own person], i.e., in His own person manifested in the flesh, and announced the will of God. Jo. I, 18; Hebr. I, 1.

Proof a. That Christian theology is drawn from divine revelation, as from a fountain of theological principles, is evident from the fact that theology embraces within its scope the most sublime mysteries not at all demonstrable or knowable from the principles of reason, which become known only from the supernatural revelation of God; from which the apostle of the Gentiles, 1 Cor. II, 7, calls Christian theology "wisdom in a mystery," which the princes of this world do not acknowledge, v. 8, which God revealed through His Spirit, v. 10. Christian theology is full of the most profound mysteries, superior to the grasp of the princes of this world, revealed by God through the Holy Spirit. Therefore, it rests upon divine revelation as the most certain principle of knowing.

Proof b. For the present time and the current state of the church, it is clearly demonstrated that Holy Scripture, in which the ancient divine revelation made to the prophets and apostles is contained, is the proper, fundamental, and adequate principle for knowing God and divine things. I. From the words of St. John, ch. XX, 31: "These are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in His name." Whatever Scripture is divinely destined to that end, that all may believe in Christ through it to obtain eternal life, that must be a sufficient and saving principle of believing. But Holy Scripture, etc. Therefore.

II. From the Pauline statement, 2 Tim. III, 14, 15: "But continue thou in those things which thou hast learned, and which have been committed to thee, knowing of whom thou hast learned them; and that from infancy thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through the faith which is in Christ Jesus." From which we argue: That which

That which can make a wise man ready for salvation through faith in Christ, so that for that reason one must remain in it, is the sufficient principle of faith and theology. But Holy Scripture is such. Therefore.

III. From the saying of St. Paul, Rom. XV, 4: "For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope." From which arises the argument: That which is given for our learning, and such learning that we may have hope of future salvation, that is given so that it may be a sufficient principle of theological doctrine and saving faith. But Holy Scripture &c. Therefore.

IV. From the testimony of the same apostle, 2 Tim. III, 16. 17: "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: that the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly furnished unto all good works." Whatever scripture is so useful that it perfectly instructs a theologian in all parts of teaching, that is the fundamental and adequate principle of theology. But θεόπνευσος (God-breathed) scripture is so useful &c. Therefore. The major premise is evident, since that is the principle of theology from which a theologian draws all saving knowledge to perform the parts of his office. The minor premise is Paul's, who openly asserts that Holy Scripture provides so much utility to the man of God, or the teacher of the church, that through it he is rendered apt and thoroughly instructed for every work of teaching: whether he intends to teach others heavenly truth, or to convince the erring of their errors, or to imbue the ill-mannered with morals worthy of a Christian, or to add a spur to those running in the way of righteousness.

Prob. c. Although Holy Scripture, for the state of the present time, is the primary principle of knowing doctrine, it is not, however, absolutely and simply the primary principle, which is evident from the following syllogism: Whatever God has revealed is infallibly true. Whatever Holy Scripture teaches, that God has revealed (because it is θεόπνευσος, 2 Tim. III, 16). Therefore, whatever Holy Scripture teaches is infallibly true. In which syllogism scripture is the thing principled, and its infallible truth is derived from another middle term. Yet it is rightly called the primary principle of theology in a certain respect and in a certain regard, namely for the present state of the church, to which for the present time no other equal, let alone superior, principle of saving knowledge is to be considered. For after God willed that those things which are necessary to be known for salvation regarding revealed matters be comprised in certain books, with new revelations ceasing, the habit of theology relies upon those ancient revelations, which were made immediately to the prophets and apostles and committed to writing, as its sole and adequate principle. Cf. D. HILDEBRANDUS, Instit. theol. p. 48, and D. BAIERUS, in compend. theolog. p. 70.

Quæst. III. Is a new and immediate revelation at the present time an ordinary principle of Christian theology?

After the completion of the canon of scripture, there is no new and immediate divine revelation given which becomes a fundamental principle of knowing the doctrine of faith.

Prob. I. Because it has already been abundantly demonstrated by us that scripture, for the present state of the church, is the proper and adequate principle of saving knowledge, to which no other equal, let alone superior, is to be sought anywhere or expected.

II. St. Paul gravely warns in 1 Cor. IV, 6: μάθητε τὸ μὴ ὑπὲρ ἃ γέγραπται φρονεῖν. "That ye might learn in us not to think of men above that which is written": just as if he were saying, let none of you presume to be wise regarding divine matters above those things which God has revealed in the scriptures; since the apostle himself ingenuously and openly professes that he has said nothing beyond those things which are written in Moses and the prophets. Acts XXVI, 22.

III. That, after the canon of Scripture was established, new and immediate revelations do not occur to mortals, the Apostle teaches, Heb. I, 1. God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son. Revelations in the Old Testament occurred to the prophets πολυμερῶς (in many parts), by turns, degrees, and as it were parts; and also πολυτρόπως (in many ways), diversely, by the address of a voice formed in the air, by dream, by ecstatic vision, by immediate illumination: but the most illustrious and perfect manifestation of God and the divine will was made through the Son of God. He ἐξηγήσατο (hath declared) the gospel to us, explained it, and as a most learned exegete declared it plainly and clearly. John I, 18. Which evangelical doctrine was propagated by those who had heard the Lord Jesus, Heb. II, 3, so that we have no need of any new revelations.

IV. A theological principle must be infallibly certain. But new revelations are fallacious and exposed to the deceits of Satan; since this prince of darkness transforms himself into an angel of light, 2 Cor. XI, 14, and a corrupted imagination suggests to enthusiasts those things which they believe, through error, to have proceeded from God. Deut. XIII, 1. Jer. XIV, 14. ch. XXIII, 25, sq. The antithesis is that of the Enthusiasts, Anabaptists, Schwenkfeldians, Weigelians, and Quakers, who establish that heavenly wisdom is to be sought from the immediate revelation of the heavenly Father, from the internal information of Christ essentially united with them, from the magisterium of the Holy Spirit speaking and teaching within, from dreams and raptures, and from angelic colloquies, whose arguments are:

Latin:

Obs.

I. Non hic sermo est de reuelatione generali, siue manifestatione naturali, qua Deus se patefecit tum per lumen naturæ insitum, tum per effecta in regno naturæ conspicua. Vid. Rom. 1, 19. c. II, 14. 15. Sed loquimur de reuelatione speciali & supernaturali, quæ duplex est, immediata & mediata. Prophetas & apostolos Spiritus S. immediate illuminauit, iisdemque conceptus rerum & verborum de dogmatibus fidei & morum suggessit. Hodie Deus se fe & voluntatem fuam generi humano mediante verbo a prophetis & apoftolis fcripto revelat.

Obf. II. Reuelatio diuina interdum fenfu ftrictiffimo, quem ipfa vis vocis importat, notat rerum occultarum & fub quodam quafi velamine latentium manifeftationem. Interdum fenfu latiori defignat rerum quarumuis, etiam quæ ductu luminis naturæ cognofci poffunt, manifeftationem a Deo modo fupernaturali factam. Pofterior fignificatio, ceu adæquata, hic locum obtinet.

Obf. III. Reuelatio diuina πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως, multis vicibus, multisque modis, facta eft. Alia enim facta eft mediate, interueniente minifterio angelorum & hominum: alia immediate, absque interuentu aliarum perfonarum. Sic Deus fe reuelauit I. per alloquium vocis articulatæ in aëre fuper ordinem naturæ efformatæ. Alloquium illud peragebatur voce fenfibili a Deo, in confpicua forma apparente, vel per aliud fignum fenfibile fuam præfentiam teftante. Ita patriarchis Deus apparuit in forma hominis. Gen. XVIII, 2. c XIX, 1. c. XXII, 24. Ad Mofem locutus eft ex rubo ardente. Exod. XIX, 10. feqq. Cum Mofe locutus eft admodum familiariter, fiue vt fcriptura ait, ore ad os, vt amicus cum amico coram loquitur. Num. XII, 6. II. Per fomnium, cum fpecies quædam dormientibus, fenfibus externis ligatis, obiicerentur. Gen. XXVIII, 12. Dan. I, 1. III. Per ἔκτασιν, cum imagines rerum obiicerentur phantafiæ hominum vigilantium, externa fenfuum operatione ceffante. Ezech. I, 4 c. XXXVII, 1. Dan. X, 5. IV. Sacerdotibus Deus nonnulla reuelabat per Vrim & Thummim. Exod. XXVIII, 30. Leu. VIII, 8. Num. XXVII, 21. Erant autem Vrim & Thummim gemmæ duodecim pectorali facerdotis infertæ, quibus rite adhibitis, Deus, conuenienter a pontifice rogatus, de rebus occultis & incertis euentibus, refponfa dabat. D. PFEIFFER. dub. vexat. p. m. 276. V. Per internum afflatum, quo Spiritus S. intellectui prophetarum & apoftolorum, manente fenfuum operatione, lumen aliquod cognitionis immediate infundebat. 2 Sam. XXIII, 2. 2 Tim. III, 16. 2 Petr. I, 20. 21. VI. Illuftriffima reuelatio diuina contigit in N. T. per filium Dei, qui αὐτοπροσώπως, i. e. in perfona propria manifeftata in carne apparuit, & voluntatem Dei annuntiauit. Io. I, 18. Hebr. I, 1.

Prob. a. Theologiam Chriftianam ex reuelatione diuina, velut fonte principiorum theologicorum, hauriri, patet ex eo, quod theologia ambitu fuo complectitur myfteria fublimiffima ex principiis rationis minime demonftrabilia aut cognofcibilia, quæ non nifi ex fupernaturali Dei reuelatione innotefcunt; Ex quo gentium apoftolus 1 Cor. II, 7. theologiam chriftianam appellat fapientiam in myfterio, quam principes huius fæculi non agnofcunt, v. 8. quam Deus reuelauit per fpiritum fuum, v. 10. Theologia chriftiana myfteriis profundiffimis eft plena, captu principum huius fæculi fuperior, a Deo per Spiritum S. reuelata. Ergo nititur reuelatione diuina tanquam certiffimo cognofcendi, principio.

Prob. b. Pro tempore præfenti & hodierno ecclefiæ ftatu, S. fcripturam, in qua antiquæ reuelationis diuinæ, factæ prophetis & apoftolis, habentur, effe proprium, fundamentale & adæquatum principium cognofcendi Deum & res diuinas, liquido demonftratur. I. Ex S. Ioannis verbis cap. XX, 31. Hæc fcripta funt, vt credatis, quod Iefus fit Chriftus filius Dei, & vt credentes vitam habeatis in nomine ipfius. Quæcunque fcriptura eum in finem diuinitus deftinata eft, vt omnes per eam credant in Chriftum ad obtinendam vitam æternam, illam oportet effe principium credendi fufficiens & falutiferum. Atqui fcriptura S. &c. E.

II. Ex effato Paullino, 2 Tim. III, 14. 15. Tu vero mane in iis, quæ didicifti, & concredita tibi funt, fciens, a quo didiceris: Et quia ab infantia facras litteras nofti, quæ poffunt te fapientem reddere in falutem per fidem, quæ in Chrifto Iefu eft. Ex quo argumentamur:

Quod potest hominem sapientem reddere ad salutem per fidem in Christum, ita ut propterea in eo permanendum sit, illud est sufficiens principium fidei & theologiae. Atqui sacra scriptura talis est. E.

III. Ex dicto S. Paulli Rom. XV, 4. Quaecunque namque praescripta sunt, in nostram doctrinam praescripta sunt, ut per patientiam & consolationem scripturarum spem habeamus. Ex quo nascitur argumentum: Quod datur ad doctrinam nostram, eamque talem, qua spem futurae salutis habeamus, id datum est, ut sit sufficiens doctrinae theologicae fideique salutificae principium. Atqui scriptura S. &c. E.

IV. Ex eiusdem apostoli testimonio, 2 Tim. III, 16. 17. Omnis scriptura divinitus inspirata & utilis est ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad disciplinam, quae (fit) in iustitia, ut integer sit homo Dei ad omne opus bonum probe instructus. Quaecunque scriptura adeo utilis est, ut theologum ad omnes docendi partes perfecte instruat, illa est principium fundamentale & adaequatum theologiae. Atqui scriptura θεόπνευσος adeo utilis est &c. Ergo. Maior constat, quoniam illud est principium theologiae, ex quo theologus omnem salutarem notitiam ad partes muneris sui obeundas haurit. Minor est Paulli, qui aperte asserit, quod homini Dei, sive doctori ecclesiae, tantum utilitatis praestet S. scriptura, ut per eam ad omne opus docendi reddatur aptus & probe instructus: sive nitatur alios veritatem coelestem docere, sive errantes errorum convincere, sive male moratos moribus christiano dignis imbuere, sive currentibus in via iustitiae calcar addere meditetur.

Prob. c. Quamvis S. scriptura, pro praesentis temporis statu, fit principium cognoscendae doctrinae primum, non tamen absolute & simpliciter primum est principium, quod patet ex sequenti syllogismo: Quidquid Deus reuelauit, infallibiliter verum est. Quidquid S. scriptura docet, illud Deus reuelauit (quia est θεόπνευσος, 2 Tim. III, 16.) Ergo quidquid S. scriptura docet, infallibiliter verum est. In quo syllogismo scriptura est principiata, eiusque infallibilis veritas ex alio medio termino est educta. Recte tamen secundum quid, & certo respectu, nempe pro hodierno ecclesiae statu, dicitur primum theologiae principium, cui pro tempore praesenti nullum aliud par, nedum superius salutificae cognitionis principium censendum est. Postquam enim Deus ea, quae de rebus reuelatis ad salutem cognitu sunt necessaria, certis libris comprehendi voluit, desinentibus nouis reuelationibus, theologiae habitus antiquis illis, quae ad prophetas & apostolos immediate factae, in litteras relatae sunt, reuelationibus, tanquam principio vnico & adaequato, nititur. Conf. D. HILDEBRANDVS instit. theol. p. 48. & D. BAIERVS in compend. theolog. p. 70.

Quæst. III. Estne reuelatio noua & immediata tempore præsenti principium theologiæ christianæ ordinarium?

Post completum scripturae canonem nulla datur noua & immediata reuelatio diuina, quae fit fundamentale principium cognoscendi doctrinam fidei.

Prob. I. Quia abunde iam demonstratum a nobis est, scripturam, pro hodierno ecclesiae statu, esse proprium & adaequatum salutiferae cognitionis principium, cui nullum aliud par, nedum superius, sit quaerendum vllibi, aut exspectandum.

II. Grauiter monet S. Paullus 1 Cor. IV, 6. μάθητε τὸ μὴ ὑπὲρ ἃ γέγραπται φρονεῖν. Discatis non supra id, quod scriptum est, sapere: prorsus ac si dicat, nemo vestrum praesumat sapere de rebus diuinis super ea, quae Deus in scripturis reuelauit; siquidem ipse apostolus ingenue aperteque profitetur, se nihil dixisse extra ea, quæ scripta sunt in Mose & prophetis. Act. XXVI, 22.

III. Non obtingere mortalibus, post constitutum scripturæ canonem, nouas, easque immediatas reuelationes, docet apostolus Hebr. I, 1. Multis vicibus multisque modis olim Deus locutus patribus in prophetis: Vltimis hisce diebus locutus est nobis in filio. Reuelationes in Vet. Tettam. prophetis contigerunt πολυμερῶς per vices, gradus & quasi partes: nec non πολυτρόπως, diuersimode, per alloquium vocis in aëre formatæ, per somnium, per visionem ecstaticam, per immediatam illuminationem: illustrissima autem & perfectissima manifestatio Dei & voluntatis diuinæ facta est per filium Dei. Hic euangelium nobis ἐξηγήσατο, exposuit, & velut exegeta doctissimus plane ac dilucide declarauit. Io. I, 18. Quæ doctrina euangelica ab his, qui dominum Iesum audiuerant, propagata est, Hebr. II, 3. vt nullis reuelationibus nouis indigeamus.

IV. Principium theologicum oportet esse infallibiliter certum. Sed reuelationes nouæ sunt fallaces, & præstigiis fatanæ obnoxia; siquidem hic tenebrarum princeps se in angelum lucis transformat, 2 Cor. XI, 14. & corrupta phantasia enthusiastis ea fuggerit, quæ per errorem a Deo profecta esse credunt. Deut. XIII, 1. Ier. XIV, 14. c. XXIII, 25. sq. Antithefis est Enthusiastarum, Anabaptistarum, Schwenkfeldianorum, Weigelianorum, & Quakerorum, ex immediata patris cœlestis reuelatione, ex informatione interna Christi essentialiter cum ipsis vniti, ex magisterio Spiritus S. intus loquentis & docentis, ex somniis & raptibus, ex colloquiis angelicis, sapientiam cœlestem petendam esse statuentium, quorum argumenta sunt:


### Quest. I. What do you understand here by the name of principle?: Obs (continued)

I. St. John, 1 Ep. ch. II, 27, says: The anointing which ye have received of him abideth in you, and ye need not that (any man) teach you. Those who do not need external information, but are fully taught by the anointing remaining within the mind, are immediately illuminated and informed by God. But the regenerate, etc. Resp. That anointing commended by St. John is the Holy Spirit, the principal cause of faith, who informs us not immediately, but through the medium of the Word. 1 John II, 14. 1 Thess. II, 13. Rom. X, 17. Nor do we have need that anyone should teach us things new and different from those which the prophets and apostles have taught.

II. Joel II, 28. I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions. Resp.
