(1) St. Peter expressly refers the fulfillment of that promise to that time when the apostles visibly received the Holy Spirit. Acts II, 16. (2) The blessed Luther understands by prophecy, vision, and dreams simply the knowledge of God through Christ, which the Holy Spirit makes to shine through the word of the gospel. The prophet Joel speaks in the manner customary to the prophets, who were accustomed to adumbrate the state of the New Testament with figurative words, or those befitting the state of the Old Testament. And so the sense is: God, most rich in mercy, seriously intends to pour out the grace of the Holy Spirit in the New Testament upon all, so that they may know certainly and clearly those things which men of God once knew through prophets, dreams, and visions.

III. God in the N.T. instituted prophets, ennobled with the privilege of immediate illumination. Eph. IV, 11. 1 Cor. XII, 28. Resp. The Apostle speaks in the cited passages of the prophets of the N.T. to whom it was divinely granted to have the extraordinary gift of prophesying in the church being established; which, since it was temporal, did not remain perpetual in the church. For the gift of prophesying, or of speaking immediately by the spirit, just as the gift of healings and miracles, was therefore temporal, because for the church, at its beginning and in its as it were first infancy, it was necessary partly for preaching for the first time the mysteries of faith, which had been hidden from eternity; partly for make the better progress of the preaching of the same doctrine, to be promulgated more and more throughout the world, and to be embraced in every place.

Objection I.

Paul says, 1 Thess. 5:19-20: Do not quench the Spirit; do not despise prophecies, indicating that prophecies are never to be despised.

II. If God does not send prophets today immediately illuminated by the Holy Spirit, certainly the evangelical church in our times will be in a worse state than the church under the old covenant, which was to its great honor no less than its convenience, that God from time to time raised up prophets, instructed by the gift of immediate inspiration. Response. The happiness of the Christian church is to be estimated, not by the abundant harvest of prophets immediately illuminated, but by the gospel preached by Christ exhibited in the flesh, and propagated as widely as possible by the apostles, and, for the sake of ἀσφάλεια, or certainty of knowledge, reduced to writing.

Objection II.

IV. God promised to the faithful people in the New Testament immediate illumination, Jer. 31:33. I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it upon their hearts. Response. The law which God gave to his people to be read and heard, he gave and inscribed upon their hearts by the efficacious operation of the Holy Spirit, not separated from the reading and hearing of the law, but most closely joined with it.

V. Whoever the Spirit is in man, and remains, so that he may teach him all things, suggest all things to him, lead him into all truth, that Spirit reveals heavenly truth immediately to man. But the Holy Spirit &c. Therefore. The minor is clear from John 14:16. 17. 20. ch. 16:13. Response. From the intention of Christ speaking, those promises primarily and proximately regard instruction of the apostles for the function of the apostolic office, by which they were bound to serve by preaching the gospel to all nations. Matt. 28:19. Mark 16:15. Therefore, the disciples of Christ, since they were unrefined and illiterate, had to be fitted by the extraordinary benefit of immediate illumination for teaching all nations, and for communicating to men new revelations concerning the Messiah exhibited in the flesh, and concerning his office, and the other parts of Christian doctrine. Hence, just as not all believers were to be apostles, 1 Cor. 12:28, so the promises made to the apostles do not pertain to all in the same way: nor, if anything was promised to be conferred upon them immediately by Christ, is the same to be conferred upon individual believers.

VI. The Holy Spirit renders us more certain of the state of grace by an immediate testimony, concerning which St. Paul Rom. 8:16. The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God. Since this testimony is not rendered to external bodily ears, it is internal and immediate. Resp. The symmartyria (testimony together) of the Holy Spirit with our spirit is indeed internal, but not immediate. For the Holy Spirit, by means of the doctrine contained in the sacred scriptures, and perceived either through hearing or through reading, and retained in the mind, accomplishes this in the mind of man, so that it testifies not only concerning the truth of the doctrine itself, but also, when the mind of man reflects upon itself in the act of knowing, concerning the true and saving faith of man and the state of grace in which he lives.

VII. The Holy Spirit teaches the reborn man internally and immediately; which Nehemiah hints at, saying ch. 9:20, "You also gave your good Spirit to give them understanding." Resp. The Holy Spirit teaches the reborn man internally, but not immediately, which Nehemiah points out in the cited chapter, v. 30: "You drew out (wrath) over them for many years, and testified against them by your Spirit; by the hand of your prophets." If God testified against the Israelites by his Spirit, through the ministry of the prophets, it is easy to conclude that he instructed them not immediately by the Holy Spirit, but by means of the doctrine and information of Moses and the prophets.

VIII. In whomever the Spirit of God is, always placing words in his mouth, the Spirit of God teaches him immediately and perpetually. But the Spirit of God teaches the just immediately and perpetually. The minor is evident from Is. 59: 21. Jehovah says: "As for me: This (shall be) my covenant with them, says Jehovah: My Spirit, which is upon you, and my words, which I have put in your mouth, shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your offspring, says Jehovah; both now and forever." The major is certain, because the Spirit of God, dwelling in a just man and informing him in such a way that he places words in his mouth, teaches the man by immediate revelation. Resp. Jehovah promised that he would illuminate his people in the New Testament, but he did not express the mode, whether he would inform him immediately or mediately. Wherefore we maintain that Jehovah promised that he would place his words in the heart and mouth of the apostles by immediate illumination, and would communicate them to others desirous of learning by means of their preached sermon, or as related in letters.

IX. Sacred scripture does not contain all things necessary for a sinner to be saved, in knowledge and in deed. Therefore, sacred scripture is not the adequate principle of things to be believed and done. The antecedent is proven, because (I) from sacred scripture no one can know certainly and infallibly that he truly believes, and becomes an heir of eternal life. (II) A minister of the church does not clearly perceive from the sacred letters that his vocation to the ministry is legitimate. (III) The circumstances of actions, to be expedited here and now for the salvation of the neighbor, are not determined in the scriptures. All of which must be revealed immediately by the Holy Spirit to a faithful man aspiring to certain knowledge. Resp. to I. Every converted sinner knows with certainty from the sacred letters that he truly believes. This can be deduced at length, but this time we argue briefly:

He who receives the testimony of God, he seals that God is true, and thus truly believes, and reflecting upon himself, knows that he truly believes. But the converted sinner receives the testimony of God. Therefore the converted sinner truly believes, and reflecting upon himself, knows that he truly believes.

The major premise is revealed in the written word of God; for it is held in John 3:33. But it pertains to the definition of faith to accept the testimony or promise of God: it pertains to the certainty of knowledge to seal that God is true. For to seal signifies to establish something certainly and to hold it as valid.

We seal in the acts of common life those things which we wish to be certain and valid. The minor premise is of most certain knowledge, as Augustine speaks, lib. 13, c. 1. Everyone sees his own faith in himself, and holds it by most certain knowledge: the minor premise is confirmed in the following way.

When a converted sinner hears or reads the testimony of God concerning the gratuitous remission of sins, Isaiah 43:25, "I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins"; then he eagerly accepts that soul-comforting testimony of God, and seals it, or certainly establishes that this testimony of God, who is the primary truth, is most true. Why, therefore, should the converted sinner not know and believe from these letters that he truly believes?

Cf. Dannhaver in Hodosophia, p. 1361 et seq.

Ad II. The certainty of a vocation to the ecclesiastical ministry is not had from a new, peculiar, and immediate revelation of the Holy Spirit, but from a mediate revelation, comprised in the Holy Scripture. For Scripture teaches with what gifts a suitable minister of the church ought to be endowed, 1 Tim. 3:1 et seq. It teaches likewise that the church has the power of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, Matt.

16:18, and thus also the power of imposing the sacred ministry upon certain persons. If, therefore, a candidate for theology knows (the spirit of man knows what is in man, 1 Cor. 2:11) that he is divinely endowed with those gifts which Holy Scripture requires in the ministry of the church, and sees with his own eyes the letters of vocation present, conferred by some church having the right of calling, he is certain of his legitimate vocation to the ministry without a new and immediate revelation of the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

I. S. Ioannes 1 Ep. c. II, 27. inquit: Vnctio, quam accepistis ab illo, in vobis manet, & non opus habetis, vt (quis) doceat vos. Qui non indigent externa informatione, sed ab vnctione intra animum manente plene docentur, illi immediate a Deo illuminantur & informantur. Atqui renati &c. Resp. Vnctio illa a S. Ioanne commendata, est Spiritus sanctus, caussa principalis fidei, qui nos informat non immediate, sed mediante verbo. 1 Io. II, 14. 1 Thess. II, 13. Rom. X, 17. Neque opus habemus, vt quis nos doceat noua & diuersa ab his, quæ prophetæ & apostoli docuerunt.

II. Ioel. H, 28. Effundam de Spiritu meo super omnem carnem, & prophetabunt filii vestri filiæque: senes vestri somnia somniabunt, & iuuenes vestri visiones videbunt. Resp. (1) S. Petrus impletionem illius promissionis expresse refert ad illud tempus, quo apostoli visibiliter acceperunt Spiritum sanctum. Act. II, 16. (2) B. Lutherus per prophetiam, visionem & somnia simpliciter intelligit cognitionem Dei per Christum, quam Spiritus sanctus per verbum euangelii lucere facit. Loquitur autem propheta Ioel more prophetis vsitato, qui consueuerant statum noui testamenti verbis figuratis, aut statui Vet. testamenti conuenientibus, adumbrare. Adeoque sensus est: Deus misericordia ditissimus ferio intendit, gratiam Spiritus sancti in nouo testamento super omnes effundere, vt cognoscant ea certo & liquido, quæ olim per prophetas, somnia & visiones viri Dei cognoscebant.

III. Deus in N. T. instituit prophetas, immediatæ illuminationis priuilegio nobilitatos. Eph. IV, 11. 1 Cor. XII, 28. Resp. Loquitur apostolus locis citatis de prophetis N. T. quibus diuinitus concessum erat extraordinarium prophetandi donum in ecclesia constituenda; quod cum esset temporale, non mansit perpetuum in ecclesia. Nam donum prophetandi, siue per spiritum immediate loquendi, æque ac donum fanationum & miraculorum ideo erat temporarium, quod ecclesiæ, sub initium & in prima quasi infantia illius, necessarium erat partim ad mysteria fidei, quæ inde a seculis abscondita erant, primum prædicanda; partim ad faciliorem progressum praedicationis eiusdem doctrinae, magis magisque per orbem terrarum promulgandae, atque vbiuis locorum amplectendae. *Instantia

I. Paullus inquit, 1 Thess. V, 19. 20. Spiritum ne extinguite; prophetias ne spernite, indicans, nunquam prophetias esse contemnendas.*

Resp. Per Spiritum l. c. intelliguntur dona Spiritus sancti; per prophetiam interpretatio sacrae scripturae. Sed Spiritus sanctus donis sanctificantibus & administrantibus opulentissimus datur ex auditu fidei, Gal. III, 2. Et scriptura per scripturam explicanda est. Immediatae reuelationis, quae hodienum fidelibus obtingat, apostolus nullam facit mentionem. Instantia

II. Si Deus hodie non mittit prophetas immediate a Spiritu sancto illuminatos, certe in deteriori statu erit ecclesia euangelica nostris temporibus, quam ecclesia sub veteri foedere, cui permagno fuit decori non minus, quam commodo, quod Deus subinde excitauit prophetas, immediate inspirationis dono instructos. Resp. Ecclesiae christianae felicitas aestimanda est, non vberi prouentu prophetarum immediate illuminatorum, sed euangelio a Christo in carne exhibito praedicato, & ab apostolis quam latissime propagato, atque ob ἀσφάλειαν, siue certitudinem cognitionis, in litteras redacto.

Instantia III. Si Deus inde ab orbe condito se suamque voluntatem patriarchis & prophetis, euangelistis & apostolis immediate reuelauit, vtique hodienum se immediate sanctis hominibus reuelat. Atqui prius est verissimum. E. & posterius. Consequentia est clara, quia nos cum patriarchis & prophetis, euangelistis & apostolis vnius religionis foedere sumus coniuncti, & aeque pretiosam cum ipsis fidem nacti sumus, 2 Petr. I, 1. Sed vbi est vna religio & vna fides, ibi vnum est obiectum formale, nempe reuelatio diuina immediata. Resp. (1) Dist. inter tempora antegressa completum scripturae canonem, & hunc secuta. Priusquam absolueretur scripturae canon, Deus paucis hominibus sanctis, nempe patriarchis & prophetis, euangelistis & apostolis se immediate patefecit, ingenti autem hominum multitudini, interueniente virorum θεοπνεύστων ministerio, se manifestauit. Ex quo Noachus vocatur praeco iustitiae, 2 Petr. II, 5. Abrahamus praecepit liberis suis, vt custodirent viam domini, & facerent iustitiam & iudicium. Gen. XVIII, 19. Iacobus docuit familiam suam. Gen. XXXV, 2. (2) Vna est religio, vnaque fides, cuius obiectum formale est reuelatio diuina, siue illa fuerit mediata, siue immediata. Praescindit enim reuelatio ab ea, quae immediata, & quae mediata est: siquidem reuelare dicitur, qui res aliquas, aut sensa animi sui alteri manifestat; hoc autem non solum ille facit, qui immediate ad alium loquitur, sed & qui mediate, v. gr. per ministrum, nuntium, aut per amanuensem alteri, quod ipsum scire vult, patefacit: iam vero Deus partim immediate, partim mediate, se & decreta voluntatis suae patefecit. Id quod docet apostolus Hebr. I, 1. Multis vicibus, multisque modis Deus olim locutus est patribus in prophetis. Vbi duplex locutio, seu duplex reuelatio Dei occurrit, vna ad prophetas, quae immediata, altera per prophetas ad patres, quae mediata erat.

IV. Deus promisit populo fideli in N. Test. immediatam illuminationem, Ier. XXXI, 33. Dabo legem meam in interiora ipsorum, & super corda ipsorum scribam eam. Resp. Quam legem Deus populo suo dedit legendam, atque audiendam, eam dedit atque inscripsit in corda ipsius efficaci Spiritus sancti operatione, a lectione & auscultatione legis non seiuncta, sed cum ea arctissime coniuncta.

V. Quicunque Spiritus in homine est, & manet, vt illum omnia doceat, omnia ipsi suggerat, in omnem veritatem eundem ducat, ille veritatem caelestem immediate homini reuelat. Atqui Spiritus sanctus &c. Ergo. Minor liquet ex Io. XIV, 16. 17. 20. c. XVI, 13. Resp. Ex intentione Christi loquentis, promissiones illae primario & proxime respiciunt instructionem apostolorum ad functionem muneris apostolici, quo omnibus gentibus praedicando evangelium inferuire debuerunt. Matth. XXVIII, 19. Marc. XVI, 15. Idcirco discipuli Christi, cum essent rudes & illiterati, extraordinario immediatae... illuminationis beneficio aptandi erant ad docendas omnes gentes, & communicandas hominibus nouas reuelationes de exhibito in carne Messia, deque eius officio, & ceteris partibus doctrinae christianae. Proinde sicut non omnes fideles debebant esse apostoli, 1 Cor. XII, 28. sic non eodem modo ad omnes pertinent, quae apostolis factae sunt, promissiones: neque, si quid illis immediate conferendum a Christo fuit promissum, idem singulis fidelibus conferendum est.

VI. Spiritus S. nos certiores reddit status gratiae testimonio immediato, de quo S. Paulus Rom. VIII, 6. Ipse Spiritus testatur cum spiritu nostro, quod simus filii Dei. Quod testimonium cum non reddatur externis corporalibus auribus, internum & immediatum est. Resp. συμµαρτυρία Spiritus sancti cum spiritu nostro est quidem interna, sed non immediata. Nam Spiritus sanctus, mediante doctrina in sacris litteris contenta, eaque vel per auscultationem, vel per lectionem percepta, animoque retenta, hoc praestat in animo hominis, ut non solum de veritate ipsius doctrinae, verum etiam, cum animus hominis actu cognoscendi ad se ipsum reflectitur, de vera ac salutari hominis fide ac statu gratiae, in quo viuat, testetur.

VII. Spiritus sanctus hominem renatum interne & immediate docet; quod innuit Nehemias, inquiens cap. IX, 20. Spiritum quoque tuum bonum dedisti ad dandum iis intellectum. Resp. Spiritus sanctus interne hominem renatum docet, sed non immediate, id quod indigitat Nehemias capite citato v. 30. Protraxisti (iram) super iis annis multis, & testatus es contra eos per Spiritum tuum; per manum prophetarum tuorum. Si Deus testatus est contra Israëlitas per Spiritum suum, ministerio prophetarum, collectu proclive est, quod eos non immediate per Spiritum sanctum, sed mediante doctrina & informatione Mosis & prophetarum instruxerit.

VIII. In quocunque Spiritus Dei est, semper in ore eius verba ponens, illum Spiritus Dei docet immediate & perpetuo. Sed Spiritus Dei iustos docet immediate & perpetuo. Minor patet ex Es. LIX, 21. Inquit Iehouah: Me autem quod attinet: Hoc (erit) foedus meum cum illis, inquit Iehouah: Spiritus meus, qui super te, & verba mea, quae posui in os tuum, non recedent ex ore tuo, & ex ore feminis tui, inquit Iehouah; & nunc & usque in aeternum. Maior constat, quia Spiritus Dei habitans in homine iusto, eumque sic informans, vt verba in eius ore ponat, immediata reuelatione hominem docet. Resp. Promisit Iehouah se populum suum in nouo testamento illuminaturum esse, sed modum, an immediate, an mediate ipsum informaturus sit, non expressit. Quare statuimus, Iehouam promisisse, quod verba sua in corde & ore apostolorum per immediatam illuminationem positurus, & mediante illorum sermone praedicato, aut in literas relato, aliis discendi cupidis communicaturus sit.

IX. Sacra scriptura non omnia, cognitu & factu necessaria peccatori saluando, continet. Ergo sacra scriptura non est adaequatum credendorum & agendorum principium. Antecedens probatur, quia (I) ex sacra scriptura nemo certo & infallibiliter cognoscere potest, quod vere credat, & haeres vitae aeternae fit. (II) Minister ecclesiae ex sacris litteris non liquido perspicit, vocationem suam ad ministerium esse legitimam. (III) Circumstantiae actionum, hic & nunc in salutem proximi expediendarum, in scripturis non sunt determinatae. Quae omnia homini fideli, ad certam notitiam adspiranti, immediate a Spiritu sancto reuelanda sunt. Resp. ad I. Omnis peccator conuersus ex sacris litteris certo cognoscit, se vere credere. Potest hoc late deduci, sed hac vice breuiter argumentamur:

Qui accipit Dei testimonium, is obsignat, quod Deus verax sit, adeoque vere credit, & in se reflectens scit, se vere credere. Atqui peccator conuersus accipit testimonium Dei. Ergo peccator conuersus vere credit, & in seipsum reflectens, scit, se vere credere.

Maior verbo Dei scripto est reuelata; habetur enim Io. III, 33. Pertinet autem ad definitionem fidei, testimonium, siue promissionem Dei, acceptare: ad certitudinem cognitionis pertinet obsignare, quod Deus verax sit. Nam obsignare significat, aliquid certo statuere & ratum habere.

Obsignamus in actibus vitæ communis ea, quæ certa & rata esse volumus. Minor est certissimæ scientiæ, vt loquitur Avgustinvs lib. 13. c.

1. Suam quisque fidem in seipso videt, eamque tenet certissima scientia: Confirmatur minor sequenti modo. Quando peccator conuersus audit vel legit testimonium Dei de gratuita peccatorum remissione, Es. XLIII, 25. Ego, ego deleo iniquitates tuas propter me, & peccatorum tuorum non recordor; tunc illud solatiferum Dei testimonium auide acceptat, & obsignat, siue certo statuit, hoc testimonium Dei, qui prima est veritas, esse verissimum. Quidni igitur peccator conuersus ex hac litteris cognosceret & crederet, se vere credere?

Conf. Dannhaver. in hodosoph. p. 1361. seq.

Ad II. Certitudo vocationis ad ministerium ecclesiasticum non habetur ex noua, peculiari & immediata Spiritus S. reuelatione, sed ex reuelatione mediata, sacra scriptura comprehensa. Docet enim scriptura, quibus donis instructus esse debeat idoneus ecclesiæ minister, 1 Tim. III, 1 seq. Docet itidem, ecclesiam habere potestatem clauium cœlorum, Matth.

XVI, 18. adeoque & potestatem imponendi ministerium sacrum certis personis. Quod si itaque candidatus theologiæ sciat (nouit spiritus hominis, quid fit in homine, 1 Cor. II, 11.) se iis donis, quæ sacra scriptura in ministerio ecclesiæ requirit, diuinitus esse præditum, & litteras vocatorias ab ecclesia aliqua, ius vocandi habente, collatas, oculis suis videat præsentes, certus est legitimæ suæ ad ministerium vocationis absque noua & immediata Spiritus S. reuelatione.


### Quest. I. What do you understand here by the name of principle?: Ad III

Ad III.

Holy Scripture remains the adequate principle of things to be done, even though it does not apply or determine its universal precepts concerning the duties of Christians to the circumstances of actions. It is agreed among all that no universal rule applies itself. Therefore, the judgment of reason makes the application of the precepts of Scripture, divine grace concurring, which, having descended into the mind with the doctrine of Scripture, illuminates it.

X. Although for the state of the times new dogmas are not immediately revealed by the Holy Spirit, yet the interpretation of Scripture depends upon a peculiar and immediate illumination of the Holy Spirit. The apostle indicates this in 1 Cor. 2:14. "The natural man does not receive the things which (are) of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know them, because they are spiritually discerned." If the doctrine of Scripture, proper and principal, surpasses the capacity of human reason left to itself, it is necessary that a peculiar divine revelation precede, by which its sense may be notified.

Response:

The Holy Spirit, whose illuminating power is joined with Scripture in an individual bond, interprets Scripture by Scripture, and through the same reveals the will of God. XI. Literal knowledge of divine things is sought from the sacred letters, but the Holy Spirit immediately infuses into man an experimental and sensible knowledge of God. From which the peace of conscience and the internal joy of the soul is attributed to the Holy Spirit, Rom. 14:17.

Response: The immediate knowledge of God, which is otherwise called intuitive, is not of this life, but of the future life. But Holy Scripture, with the Holy Spirit concurring, illuminates, tranquilizes, and exhilarates the heart of man. The king of prophets sings excellently in Ps. 19:8. "The law of Jehovah (is) perfect, refreshing the soul: the testimony of Jehovah (is) firm, making the simple wise.

The mandates of Jehovah (are) right, gladdening the heart: the precept of Jehovah (is) pure, illuminating the eyes."

XII. That immediate revelations of God were not lacking with the apostles in the church, both the history of the times testifies, and orthodox theologians admit.

B. Luth.

Comment. in Joel, tom. IV. Ien. lat. p. 807. D. DAVID RVNG. in Gen. p. 1280. D. BALDVIN. in 1 Tim. IV. p. 251. & others.

Resp. Divine revelations concern either the doctrine of faith, or singular cases and events in ecclesiastical, political, or other matters.

The doctrine of faith rests entirely upon the word of God revealed and committed to writing.

But revelations concerning singular cases arise either from the full light of prophecy, or from certain sparks of prophetic light.

Theologians concede that after the passing of the apostles, in certain holy men, flashes or certain sparks of prophetic light have shone forth.

Which, the rarer they are, the more accurately they must be weighed, lest under the guise of divine revelations, the suggestions of the devil, or depraved fantasies, creep upon men greedy for novelty.

Q. IV. Is human reason a principle of theology?

Human reason either denotes the intellectual faculty of man, which, illuminated by the light of the divine word, is the receiving subject, or the one knowing theological truths, but it is not the fundamental principle from which the same are known Obs. 1.

Those are called organic principles which pertain to the instrumental disciplines, grammar, rhetoric, and logic.

Obs. 2. Some philosophical principles are absolutely and unlimitedly universal, which consist in an essential and simply necessary connection of terms, so that they can be shaken by no instance, nor even by Scripture. e.g. It is impossible for the same thing to be and not to be at the same time.

Whatever is, when it is, it must be.

Every spirit is immaterial, etc. Others are limited, and universal in a certain respect, which in a certain genus, by hypothesis, or according to the sphere of natural knowledge, are indeed true, yet admit of limitation, and can be infringed by a certain instance, if not sought from nature, certainly from Scripture . e.g. How many persons are there, (*) In most, however, there is need of right interpretation, and even universal principles are circumscribed by certain terms, which if neglected, they would not be greater than every exception.

E.g. This principle which is commonly called that of contradiction is indeed most true without any exception, provided we use all caution, lest we omit anything in discerning that which is openly, from that which seems to be, a contradiction.

I shall bring forward another example: The finite is not capable of the infinite.

This is certainly most true, if it is understood of comprehension and equation, not likewise of the closest conjunction and communion, as if the infinite could not receive the finite into itself, and communicate its own perfections with it.

() Nor can it be otherwise.

For it would be a manifest contradiction if any supernatural effect of God, to be known from nowhere else than divine revelation, were brought about by the powers of the nature of created things, and thus its reason could be explained from natural principles.

And those which are called particular philosophical principles are indeed general, and extend most widely without any exception; but only in that genus of things to which they pertain.

For among all

There are so many essences: Every human individual is a person in itself: Every begotten thing is a numerical essence, different from the begetter.

Proof a. Without the use of reason, we can neither perceive, nor confirm, nor defend theological dogmas against the sophistries of adversaries. Certainly, God revealed the wisdom of eternal salvation in His word not to brutes, but to men using sound reason, and He seriously enjoined upon them the mandate to read, hear, and meditate upon His word. Deut. 6:6; John 5:39. Therefore, intellect is required as the receiving subject or the apprehending instrument. For just as we see nothing without eyes and hear nothing without ears, so we understand nothing without reason. Meanwhile, however, human reason is not the source or primordial element from which the proper and proximate principles of faith are derived.

Proof b. Organic principles are employed as aids for acquiring theological habit, since without them neither the sense or meaning of words can be elicited (which is the task of grammar), nor figures and modes of speech weighed (which is the task of rhetoric), nor connections and consequences perceived, nor discourses formed (which is the task of logic).

Proof c. Those are called mixed articles of faith which consist not only of revelation but also of the light of nature; these are proved primarily and most safely up to the *plerophoria* (full assurance) of faith from Holy Scripture, and secondarily and less safely deduced from the principles of reason. Thus, philosophers proceed to prove the existence and attributes of God in metaphysics and pneumatics from the principles of reason.

Proof d. Reason left to itself knows nothing of the pure articles of faith, but is blind and dim-sighted regarding the mysteries of faith. The apostle of the Gentiles warns man of this spiritual blindness, 1 Cor. 2:14, saying: The natural man does not receive the things that are of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness to him; and he cannot know them, because they are spiritually discerned. It is to be observed here that the apostle’s argument is genuine. The former is taken from the congenital corruption of the human intellect after the fall. Whatever the natural man (not illuminated by the word of God) does not grasp, but rejects with a certain natural disgust as absurd, it is established that this is judged from the principles of reason; that there are some principles of the science of natural things, or physics, others of moral philosophy, others of civil prudence, and many even proper to mathematics; each one of which indeed obtains its force in its own kind, but cannot be accommodated to another kind of thing. But that which is far different from another is not immediately contrary to it, and by no means repugnant. What, therefore, do the adversaries of revealed doctrines do? They always make a *metabasis eis allo genos* (a transition to another genus) when they attack it with certain philosophical principles, and those particular ones at that. Therefore, one must go to meet them, both by limiting that principle and explaining its force and reason, and by opposing another, superior to it—namely, one that is absolutely universal; of which kind are logic and metaphysics. E.g., those who deny that the eternal Son of God is altogether equal to the Father abuse this principle: Every begetter cannot but be prior to the begotten in order and time. I reply: 1) by an explanation of this principle, which is entirely physical, limiting it thus: Every begetter whose nature is finite; for where there is a prior and a posterior, there is succession; where these are, there is a beginning, order, and series. 2) By the opposition of another, much greater and more certain principle, inasmuch as it contains the very nature and definition of the thing: Every generation, properly so called, is a communication of the same nature: Therefore, such as the nature of the begetter is, such cannot but be the communication and nature of the begotten. But God, and indeed the one God, is an infinite, necessary, and eternal being: Therefore, divine generation, if there is any (and revelation teaches us that there is), cannot but be equally infinite, necessary, and eternal: Therefore, he who is begotten of God cannot but be equal to the Father, and therefore neither posterior in order nor in time. The followers of Socinus, and all those to whom revealed dogmas seem contrary to reason, err vehemently in four ways. They are deceived in this: that they either confuse all reason with their own perception, or assume false hypotheses as true principles of reason, or usurp principles of reason that are indeed true but neither correctly understood nor rightly accommodated, or transfer particular principles to another genus of truths.

cannot be. But divine mysteries &c. Therefore. The latter is sought from the condition of the mysteries. Whatever is judged only spiritually (through the light of the Holy Spirit), that is not to be estimated or decided by the judgment of reason. But the mysteries of faith &c. Therefore. Proof of the same.

That philosophical principles can be rightly applied in theological discourses as ministerial and serving to complete a syllogism is shown in the following theological discourse. For if the truth of the human nature of Christ is to be proven against Marcion, the fundamental principle of theological demonstration is drawn from Holy Scripture. Christ has a human body and soul. Matt. XXVI, 27, 28. Luke XXIV, 39. Therefore Christ is true man. You say: Let the consequence or the connection of the antecedent and the consequent be proven. I prove the consequence by employing a principle of reason: Whoever has a human body and soul, he is a true man. Christ has a human body and soul. Therefore Christ is true man. In this discourse, the truth of the theological conclusion rests on the minor proposition taken from the revealed word of God, as the proper, fundamental, and primordial principle of demonstration. The major proposition is an absolutely universal principle of reason, and it concurs only as a common, secondary, and ministerial principle, flowing forth of its own accord, and superadded to complete the syllogism and to show the syllogistic δοκιμασίαν (testing). But it is not simply necessary always and everywhere to reduce a theological demonstration into a categorical and fully expressed syllogism. For syllogistic expression, where the other premise is highly evident, is indeed easy, but yet truly superfluous and tedious. Wherefore there is no doubt that a demonstrative argument can be proposed in an enthymematic, hypothetical, disjunctive, or even dilemmatic form, in the judgment of LEICHNER in his Synopsis vera apodictica, p. 365.

Latin:

Ad III.

Manet S. scriptura adæquatum agendorum principium, tametsi præcepta sua vniuersalia de officiis christianorum ad circumstantias actionum non applicet aut determinet, Constat inter omnes, nullam regulam vniuersalem se ipsam applicare. Applicationem itaque præceptorum scripturæ facit iudicium rationis, diuina gratia, quæ cum doctrina scripturæ ad animum demissa concurrit, illuminatum.

X. Quamuis pro statu temporis noua dogmata a Spiritu S. non immediata reuelentur, interpretatio tamen scripturæ pendet a peculiari & immediata Spiritus sancti illuminatione. Indicat id apostolus 1 Cor. II, 14. Animalis homo non suscipit ea, quæ (sunt) Spiritus Dei: Stultitia enim illi sunt, & non potest scire, quia spiritaliter diiudicantur. Si doctrina scripturæ propria & præcipua captum rationis humanæ sibi relicta superat, necesse est, vt præcedat peculiaris reuelatio diuina, qua eius sensus notificetur.

Resp.

Spiritus sanctus, cuius vis illuminatrix cum scriptura indiuiduo nexu coniuncta est, scripturam per scripturam interpretatur, & per eandem voluntatem Dei reuelat. XI. Litteralis rerum diuinarum notitia petitur e sacris litteris, sed cognitionem Dei experimentalem & sensibilem Spiritus S. immediate homini infundit. Ex quo pax conscientiæ & internum animæ gaudium Spiritui S. acceptum fertur, Rom. XIV, 17. Resp.

Immediata cognitio Dei, quæ ceteroquin intuitiua appellatur, non est huius, sed futuræ vitæ. Scriptura autem sacra, concurrente Spiritu sancto, cor hominis illuminat, tranquillat, exhilarat. Præclare canit rex prophetarum Ps. XIX, 8. Lex Iehouæ (est) perfecta, recreans animam: testimonium Iehouæ firmum (est), sapientem reddens simplicem.

Mandata Iehouæ recta (sunt), lætificantia cor: præceptum Iehouæ purum (est), illuminans oculos.

XII.

Reuelationes Dei immediatas non defuisse cum apostolis in ecclesia, tum historia temporum testatur, tum orthodoxi theologi fatentur. B. Lvth. Comment. in Ioel. tom.

IV. Ien. lat. p. 807. D. DAVID RVNG. in Gen. p. 1280. D. BALDVIN. in 1 Tim. IV. p. 251. & alii.

Resp. Revelationes divinae concernunt vel doctrinam fidei, vel casus & eventus singulares in ecclesiasticis, politicis aut aliis rebus.

Doctrina fidei verbo Dei revelato & in litteras relato in solidum nititur.

Revelationes autem de casibus singularibus oriuntur, vel ex pleno lumine prophetico, vel ex scintillis quibusdam luminis prophetici.

Concedunt theologi, post decessum apostolorum in quibusdam viris sanctis stricturas aut scintillas quasdam luminis prophetici emicuisse.

Quae, quo rariores sunt, eo accuratius ponderandae, ne sub specie revelationum divinarum suggestiones diaboli, aut prauae phantasiae, hominibus novitatis auidis obrepant.

Quaest. IV. Estne ratio humana principium theologiae?

Ratio humana vel notat facultatem hominis intellectiuam, quae collustrata lumine verbi diuini est subiectum recipiens, seu cognoscens veritates theologicas, sed non est principium fundamentale, ex quo eadem cognoscuntur

Obs. 1. Principia organica dicuntur, quae ad disciplinas instrumentales, grammaticam, rhetoricam & logicam pertinent.

Obs. 2. Principia philosophica alia sunt absolute & illimitate vniuersalia, quae constant nexu terminorum essentiali & simpliciter necessario, vt nulla instantia neque ex scriptura labefactari queant. v. gr. impossibile est, idem simul esse, & non esse.

Quidquid est, quando est, necesse est esse. Omnis spiritus est immaterialis &c. Alia sunt limitate, & secundum quid vniuersalia, quae in certo genere, ex hypothesi, aut secundum naturalis cognitionis sphaeram, vera quidem sunt, attamen limitationem admittunt, & instantia quadam, si non ex natura, certe ex scriptura petita, infringi possunt . v. gr.

Quot sunt personae, (*) In plerisque tamen omnibus opus est recta interpretatione, atque etiam vniuersalia principia certis quibusdam terminis circumscripta sunt, quibus neglectis non essent omni exceptione maiora.

V. g. Principium hoc quod vulgo dicitur contradictionis, est profecto sine vlla exceptione verissimum, dum modo omnem adhibeamus cautionem, ne quid praetermittamus in discernenda, quae aperte fit, ab ea, quae videatur esse, repugnantia.

Aliud proferam exemplum: Finitum non est capax infiniti.

Hoc sane certissimum est, si intelligatur de comprehensione atque exaequatione, non item de arctissima coniunctione & communione, quasi infinitum non posset finitum in se recipere, suasque cum illo perfectiones communicare.

() Nec potest aliter fieri.

Esset enim manifesta repugnantia, si quis Dei effectus supernaturalis, nec aliunde, quam ex diuina patefactione cognoscendus, ex viribus naturae rerum creatarum efficeretur, adeoque eius ratio ex principiis naturalibus explicari posset.

Et ea, quae particularia vocantur, principia philosophica, sunt quidem generalia, ac sine vlla exceptione latissime patent; sed duntaxat in eo rerum genere, ad quod illa pertinent.

Namque inter omnes

tot sunt essentiae: Omne individuum humanum per se est persona: Omne genitum numerica essentia, diversum est a generante.

Prob. a. Sine usu rationis dogmata theologica neque percipere, neque confirmare, neque a strophis adversariorum vindicare possumus. Certe non brutis, sed hominibus, sana ratione utentibus, Deus aeternae salutis sapientiam in verbo suo revelavit, & serio iis iniunxit mandato, ut verbum suum legerent, audirent, meditarentur. Deut. VI, 6. Io. V, 39. Requiritur itaque intellectus, ut subiectum recipiens, aut instrumentum apprehendens. Sicut enim sine oculis nihil videmus, sine auribus nihil audimus; ita sine ratione nihil intelligimus. Interim tamen ratio humana non est fons aut primodiale elementum, ex quo propria & proxima fidei principia deriventur.

Prob. b. Principia organica adhibentur, ut adminicula acquirendi habitus theologici, cum sine illis nec sensus aut significatio vocum erui (quod est grammaticae), nec figurae modique loquendi expendi (quod est rhetoricae), nec connexiones & consequentiae percipi, nec discursus formari (quod est logicae) possint.

Prob. c. Articuli fidei mixti vocantur, qui non solum ex revelatione, verum etiam ex lumine naturae constant; qui primario & tutissime usque ad πληροφορίαν fidei e scriptura S. probantur, secundario & minus tuto e principiis rationis deducuntur. Sic philosophi existentiam & attributa Dei in metaphysica & pneumatica ex principiis rationis probatum eunt.

Prob. d. De articulis fidei puris nihil novit ratio sibi relicta, sed ad mysteria fidei caecutit & caligat. Cuius caecitatis spiritualis gentium apostolus hominem admonet, 1 Cor. II, 14. inquiens: Animalis homo non suscipit ea, quae (sunt) Spiritus Dei: stultitia enim illi sunt; & non potest scire, quia spiritualiter diiudicantur. Observandum heic est genuinum apostoli argumentum. Prius a congenita intellectus humani post lapsum corruptione sumitur. Quidquid homo animalis (e verbo Dei non illuminatus) non capit, sed naturali quodam fastidio tanquam absurdum respuit, illud ex principiis rationis diiudicari constat, alia esse principia scientiae rerum naturalium, sive physica, alia philosophiae moralis, alia prudentiae civilis, multa etiam matheseos propria; quorum unum quodque omnino quidem in suo genere vim suam obtinet, nec vero ad aliud rerum genus potest adcommodari. Quod vero longe ab alio diversum est, id illi non continuo est contrarium, & neutiquam repugnat. Quid igitur agunt doctrinae revelatae adversarii? Semper illi faciunt μετάβασιν εἰς ἄλλο γένος, quando eam principiis quibusdam philosophicis, & iis quidem particularibus, impugnant. Itaque obviam illis eundum est, tum limitando id principium, eiusque vim ac rationem explicando; tum opponendo aliud, eo superius, nimirum prorsus universale; cuiusmodi sunt logica, & metaphysica. E. g. qui negant, aeternum Dei filium Patri omnino parem esse, illi abutuntur hoc principio: O. generans non potest non ordine ac tempore prius esse generato. Resp. 1) explicatione huius principii, quod omnino physicum est, ita limitandi: Omne generans, cuius natura finita est; nam ubi prius, & posterius est, ibi est successio; vbi haec, ibi initium, ordo ac series. 2) Oppositione alius cuiusdam, multo maioris & certioris, quippe quod ipsam rei naturam ac definitionem continet: O. generatio, proprie sic dicta, est eiusdem naturae communicatio: E qualis natura generantis est, talis non potest non esse eiusdem communicatio, & natura generati. Atqui Deus, & is quidem unus, est ens infinitum, necessarium, atque aeternum: E generatio divina, si qua est (esse autem eam, nos revelatio edocet) non potest non esse aeque infinita, necessaria atque aeterna: E. ex Deo genitus non potest non esse Patri aequalis, ideoque nec ordine, nec tempore, posterior. Socini adseclae, omnesque illi, quibus dogmata revelata videntur rationi contraria esse, vehementer errant quatuor modis. Falluntur in eo: quod aut rationem omnem cum sua perceptione confundunt, aut falsas hypotheses tamquam vera rationis principia adsumunt, aut principia rationis vera quidem, at nec recte intellecta, & male adcommoda, usurpant, aut principia particularia ad aliud veritatum genus transferunt.

eari nequit. Atqui mysteria divina &c. Ergo. Posterius petitur a conditione mysteriorum. Quaecunque non nisi spiritualiter (per lumen Spiritus S.) diiudicantur, illa iudicio rationis non sunt aestimanda aut decidenda. Atqui mysteria fidei &c. Ergo. Prob. e.

In discursibus theologicis principia philosophica velut ministerialia & ad integrandum syllogismum subservientia recte applicari posse, ostenditur sequenti discursu theologico. Quod si veritas humanae Christi naturae contra Marcionem probanda sit, ex S. scriptura fundamentale demonstrationis theologicae principium depromitur. Christus habet corpus & animam humanam. Matth. XXVI, 27. 28. Luc. XXIV, 39. Ergo Christus est verus homo. Dicis: Probetur consequentia sive connexio antecedentis & consequentis. Probo consequentiam adhibito rationis principio: Quicunque habet corpus & animam humanam, ille est verus homo. Christus habet corpus & animam humanam. Ergo Christus est verus homo. In hoc discursu nititur veritas conclusionis theologicae propositione minori e verbo Dei revelato petita, tanquam proprio, fundamentali & primordiali demonstrandi principio. Maior propositio est principium rationis absolute universale, & concurrit tantum ut principium commune, secundarium & ministeriale, sponte sua affluens, & superadditum ad integrandum syllogismum & ostendendam δοκιμασίαν syllogisticam. At non simpliciter necessarium est, semper & ubique demonstrationem theologicam in syllogismum categoricum & plene expressum redigere. Syllogistica enim expressio, vbi altera praemissa summe evidens est, facilis quidem, attamen supervacanea & taediosa vere est. Quare nullum dubium est, quin argumentum demonstrativum enthymematica, hypothetica, disiunctiva, vel dilemmatica etiam forma, proponi queat, iudice LEICHNERO in synopsi vera apodictica p. 365.


### Quest. I. What do you understand here by the name of principle?: Antithesis of the Socinians

Antithesis of the Socinians

Antithesis of the Socinians, who measure the mysteries of faith with the ten-foot pole of reason, whose arguments are: I. The Christian religion is a rational worship, Rom. XII, 1. Therefore, it must be judged from the principles of reason. Resp.

The Christian religion is called a rational worship, not by reason of the principle from which it is to be drawn as from a fountain, but by reason of the subjects, or rational men, who are addicted to the Christian religion. For just as in the O.T. ζῶα ἄλογα (irrational animals), animals lacking reason, were sacrificed to God: so in the N.T. men who are partakers of reason consecrate their bodies to God. It is therefore called by the apostle a rational worship, not that which is drawn from the fountain of reason, but which is the worship of rational men.

II. Paul defers the judgment concerning the doctrine of faith to the intellect of the Corinthians, 1 Cor. X, 15. I speak to those who understand, judge ye. Resp. The intellect of the Corinthians had been illuminated by the divine word. Wherefore the apostle permits them to judge, not from the principles of reason, which he commands to be taken captive, 2 Cor. X, 5, but from the revealed word of God, and that which is recorded in writing. He permits them, I say, a judgment not αὐτοκρατορικὸν (autocratic) or supreme, not κανονικὸν (normative) or standard, but δοκιμαστικὸν (discerning), discerning and ministerial.

See D. 10. ADAM OSIANDER in coll. system. part. I p. 143. III.

If reason does not grasp the mysteries of faith, what then will understand them? Resp. Illuminated reason grasps the mysteries of faith as a receiving subject and a knowing organ: but it is not the primordial and fundamental principle from which it is permitted to begin and construct a theological demonstration.

IV. Christ himself taught reasonably, as often as he used in teaching similarities and parables taken from reason. Resp. The Savior illustrated the mysteries of faith through sensible things, but he proved the same from Moses and the prophets, Luke

XXIV, 27, and deferred the normative judgment to Scripture alone, John V, 39, not to reason.

V. St. Paul demands from us in matters of faith a certain prudence, gravely admonishing, Do not become children, but in prudence be adults.

Prudence, however, is a habit active with right reason. Resp. The apostle is not speaking of worldly prudence, drawn from philosophical principles; but of spiritual [prudence], drawn from the fountain of Israel, the holy scripture.

VI. Just as reason judges of philosophical matters, so also of theological dogmas. For a philosophical truth is not contrary to a theological truth: and although in holy scripture there are many things above reason, yet nothing is against reason. For just as there cannot be a conflict between truth and truth: so neither can those things which right reason teaches be contrary [to them]. Resp. Although the mysteries of faith are not contrary to the principles of reason, yet one must not judge of them by these.

Medicine and jurisprudence are not contrary to each other: yet a physician does not show the method of curing a fever from the process of law, nor does a jurist seek from anatomy the method of settling forensic disputes. The art of painting and shoemaking do not fight among themselves, yet a shoemaker [should not go] beyond his shoe. Right reason, containing itself within the limits of its object, does not contradict the mysteries of faith; but it happens accidentally that corrupted reason, having gone beyond its sphere, enormous and unbridled, struggles against divine revelation.

VII. Every discourse is ultimately resolved into that principle: It is impossible for the same thing to be and not to be at the same time: which principle is of reason. And so, just as the final resolution is made into this: so the final judgment is deferred to reason.

Resp. That principle can be considered in two ways, as it is the common foundation of contradiction. As it is appropriated to divine things, and restricted to their nature. Although reason bears the formal judgment concerning the common foundation of contradiction: yet the real and normal judgment belongs to holy scripture, insofar as that foundation of contradiction is appropriated to divine things.

VIII. Evangelical doctors rarely use the principles of reason in theological syllogisms. Therefore they cannot accuse the Socinians of the abuse of reason. Resp. Evangelicals in theological syllogisms use principles of reason that are absolutely universal: the adversaries use particular principles, or at least those that are limitedly universal, and restricted to the sphere of nature or of finite being. Evangelicals use the principles of reason, not as proper to theology, but as common to many sciences; not as ministerial and quasi-instrumental, supplying aid for understanding and deducing a conclusion; not as primordial, from which the principle of demonstration is to be taken, but as superadded to show the syllogistic δοκιμασίαν (testing).

The adversaries, not attending to this, stubbornly oppose themselves to the mysteries of faith divinely revealed.

E.g. They impugn the mystery of the Trinity with this philosophical axiom: As many as are the persons, so many are the essences. They attack the mystery of the incarnation with this principle of reason: Every intelligent nature, and complete in being, is a person. They go about removing the substantial presence of the body of Christ from the sacrament of the supper with this lemma: Every natural body is in one determined place. Which principles of reason, since they are restricted to the sphere of nature and finite beings, are wrongly peddled as absolutely universal, nor are they applied to matters of mere faith without a μεταβάσει εἰς ἄλλο γένος (transition into another genus).

Reason is not the leader of theology, but the handmaid. Let the handmaid Hagar serve the mistress, let her not rule: let her, affecting rule, be eliminated from the sacred house.

Quest. V. Is the consensus of the fathers of the primitive church a principle of theology? The consensus of the fathers, who lived in the church of Christ in the first five centuries, whatever it may be able to have from their writings for the present time, is not an apodictic and fundamental principle of theology (a): nor is it accurately called a secondary principle of the Christian faith (b): nor, however, is it to be esteemed little, but greatly. It is to be highly esteemed, as a motive of credibility, a topical and probable principle of certain theological conclusions, and a notable testimony, that the ancient prelates of the Catholic Church understood and expounded the sayings of Holy Scripture in the same sense in which the modern Evangelical Church understands them ( ).

Obs. The principle of proving is divided (x) into apodictic and topical. The former produces science, or accurate and certain knowledge; the latter produces opinion or probable knowledge. (β) Into a principle *kata pragma* [according to the thing], or valid in itself for demonstrating a matter, and *kat' anthropon* [according to man], or valid with respect to the man, because it is conceded and approved by him.

It is proved a. I. Because Holy Scripture is the adequate principle of theology. See quest. II. prob. a.

II. Because the principle of theology must be *autopiston* [self-evident] and infallibly certain. But the fathers of the primitive Church were men not endowed with the privilege of infallibility, who, just as they were not exempt as individuals from the danger of erring, so as a whole they could deceive and be deceived in handing down the doctrine of the faith. Dr. Chemnitz demonstrates the errors of the fathers in his oration on the reading of the fathers, prefixed to his *Loci Theologici*, as does Dr. Gerhard in his *Confessio Catholica*, book 1, part II, chap. XIII, fol. 190. Nor do the fathers themselves deny this. For, as cited by Gerhard in the aforementioned place, Jerome writes in epistle 62 to Theophilus: "We must hold the apostles in one way, but the other writers of Scripture in another. Let us know that the former always speak the truth, but the latter, as men, err in certain things."

III. A universal consensus of the fathers of the Church exists nowhere. For (a) there were many churches throughout the world from the times of the apostles, whose teachers have not become known to us, nor do any testimonies exist concerning the doctrine handed down by them. (b) Before the controversies were stirred up, the fathers spoke more securely and harshly. (c) They differ immensely in interpreting the sayings of Holy Scripture. (d) Not a few of the writings of the fathers have been interpolated, castrated, and mutilated by the Papists.

IV. Every principle is prior to that which is principled. But the consensus of the fathers is not prior to, but posterior to, Christian theology. For after the apostles, for an entire century, not even one writer remains who wrote about all the dogmas of the faith. There exist, indeed, certain epistles which are attributed to Ignatius, but some of them, in the judgment of great men, are supposititious; others have been corrupted and mutilated by the wicked audacity of adversaries; those which are considered to be genuine can inform the reader about only a few articles of faith. There exist also certain writings of Justin, but most are spurious. For none are held to be genuine except the *Paraenetic Oration to the Greeks* and the *Dialogue with Trypho the Jew*. Whatever else was truly written by Justin has perished, so that nothing remains beyond the titles mentioned by Jerome and Eusebius. Irenaeus follows these, but regarding his writings, which were many, Erasmus in the previous century barely rescued from destruction and made public five books written against the Gnostics and Valentinians, and indeed in the Latin idiom, into which they were awkwardly translated from the Greek language in which they were written by the author. Tertullian not rarely deviates from the royal road and taught otherwise than the Church believed. Concerning whom Jerome, when pressed by his authority, said: "I answer nothing else about Tertullian than that he was not a man of the Church." See the above-cited oration of Chemnitz, fol. 3.

Prob. b. Although the consensus of the fathers of the primitive Church, such as it is held today in their writings, may be called a secondary principle of some theological conclusions in the same sense in which it is otherwise called a topical principle: it is not, speaking accurately, a secondary principle of the Christian faith. For the Christian faith is a divine and immovable faith. and the immovable hypostasis, Heb. XI, 1. Its principle, upon which it rests, can be nothing but divine and supernatural. But the consensus of the fathers, such as it is given for the state of the present time, is human. For no one will deny that the testimony of any father is human. But the testimonies of individuals gathered into one cannot be of a different kind than that which the individuals are when considered by themselves. For although the degree of authority increases to some extent on account of the multitude, the species of authority is not changed.

Prob. c. The consensus of the fathers of the primitive church, such as indeed survives today, contributes much weight to the interpretation of the sayings of Holy Scripture. Who, possessed of a sound mind, would not be moved to approve the interpretation of the Scriptures which the very ancient doctors of the primitive church, neighbors to the apostles, excellently instructed in the knowledge of divine things, and renowned for the holiness of their lives, commended to posterity in their writings?

The antithesis is that of the Papists, who urge the consensus of the fathers of the primitive church as an infallible principle of theology, whose arguments we shall weigh.

I. The consensus of the fathers, who lived and wrote in the first five centuries from the birth of the virgin, is the consensus of the catholic church, which is immune from error, for the reason that it is the church of the living God, στῦλος καὶ ἑδραίωμα τῆς ἀληθείας, the pillar and foundation of the truth, 1 Tim. III, 15. Resp. (α) The consensus of a few fathers of the church is not the consensus of the catholic church. (β) The consensus of the church is true because it agrees with Holy Scripture. Therefore, it is not a principle or a norm, but a principled or normed thing. (γ) It is called στῦλος, or pillar of the truth, not in an architectural sense, as if it were propping up the heavenly truth or sustaining it lest it fall headlong, but in a political sense. For just as in courts and before praetoria there stand pillars to which the laws and decrees of the magistrate are affixed: so the church is a public pillar to which the tablets of the divine word are affixed. The word ἑδραίωμα, however, properly denotes a seat, a chair, or a repository, because the church is as it were a seat or repository in which the heavenly truth is deposited. But by what cords, I ask, can it be extorted from the Pauline saying that the consensus of the fathers is a principle of theology (*)?

II. The fathers of the primitive church could not err, because by the power of divine promises the Holy Spirit led the fathers into all truth, Jo. XVI, 13. He remained with them perpetually, Jo. XIV, 16. Resp. The promises of the Savior πρώτως and primarily regard the apostles, whose minds the Holy Spirit illuminated immediately with the knowledge of heavenly doctrine, so that they would not err in the doctrine of faith. For that reason, the apostle asserts that the church is built upon the foundation of the apostles, Eph. II, 20. Δευτέρως and secondarily they can be accommodated to all doctors of the church, insofar as they follow the voice of the Holy Spirit. But it does not follow from this: Therefore, the doctors of the church are simply immune from the danger of erring.

III. From that which something is proved and known, that is a principle of knowing. Theological conclusions are proved from the consensus of the fathers. Therefore, the consensus of the fathers is a principle of theological conclusions.

Resp. (1) Distinguish between an apodictic principle and a topical one. If the major is understood concerning a topical principle, the whole argument is granted: if it is understood concerning an apodictic principle, the minor is denied.

For we argue from the consensus of the fathers (α) κατ’ ἄνθρωπον against the Papists, with whom the authority of the fathers carries the most weight: (β) κατὰ πρᾶγμα, since the universal consensus of the fathers the consensus of the primitive church fathers, such as can be given today, is not an invalid medium for interpreting the scriptures. But most validly, scripture is explained by scripture.

Latin:

Antithesis Socinianorum

Antithesis Socinianorum, mysteria fidei decempeda rationis dimetientium, quorum argumenta sunt. I. Religio Christiana est cultus rationalis, Rom. XII, 1. E. Ex principiis rationis diiudicanda est. Resp.

Religio christiana dicitur cultus rationalis, non ratione principii, ex quo, velut fonte, haurienda est; sed ratione subiectorum, sive hominum rationalium, qui religioni christianae sunt addicti. Sicut enim in V. T. ζῶα ἄλογα, animalia rationis expertia, Deo immolabantur: Sic in N. T. homines rationis participes corpora sua Deo consecrant. Appellatur igitur ab apostolo cultus rationalis, non qui ex rationis fonte depromitur, sed qui est cultus hominum rationalium.

II. Paullus Corinthiorum intellectui defert iudicium de doctrina fidei, 1 Cor. X, 15. Intelligentibus loquor, iudicate. Resp. Intellectus Corinthiorum verbo divino illuminatus erat. Quamobrem permittit illis apostolus, ut iudicent non ex principiis rationis, quam captiuare iubet, 2 Cor. X, 5. sed ex verbo Dei revelato, & in litteras relato. Permittit, inquam, illis iudicium non αὐτοκρατορικὸν, sive supremum, non κανονικὸν, sive normale, sed δοκιμαστικὸν, discretiuum & ministeriale.

Confer D. 10. ADAM OSIANDER in coll. system. part. I p. 143. III.

Si ratio non capit mysteria fidei, quid ergo illa intelliget? Resp. Ratio illuminata capit mysteria fidei vt subiectum recipiens & organon cognoscens: sed non est principium primordiale & fundamentale, ex quo ordiri & exstruere liceat demonstrationem theologicam.

IV. Christus ipse docuit rationabiliter, quotiescunque similibus & parabolis ex ratione desumtis in docendo vsus est. Resp. Mysteria fidei saluator per sensibilia illustrauit, sed ex Mose & prophetis, Luc.

XXIV, 27. eadem probauit, solique scripturae, Io. V, 39. non rationi, iudicium normale detulit.

V. S. Paullus exigit a nobis in rebus fidei prudentiam quandam, grauiter admonens, Ne sitis pueri, sed adulti prudentia.

Prudentia autem est habitus cum recta ratione actiuus. Resp. Loquitur apostolus non de prudentia mundana, depromta ex principiis philosophicis; sed spirituali, haustia ex fonte Israëlis, scriptura sacra.

VI. Sicut ratio iudicat de rebus philosophis, ita & de dogmatibus theologicis. Nam verum philosophicum non contrariatur vero theologico: & licet in sacra scriptura multa sint supra rationem, nil tamen contra rationem. Quemadmodum enim inter verum & verum non potest esse pugna: ita nec, quæ recta ratio docet, contraria esse possunt. Resp. Quamuis mysteria fidei non contrarierentur principiis rationis, non tamen ex his iudicandum est de illis.

Medicina & iurisprudentia sibi non contrariantur: neque tamen medicus ex processu iuris ostendit methodum curandi febrem, neque Ictus ex anatomia petit modum dirimendi lites forenses. Ars pictoria, & sutoria, non pugnant inter se, neque tamen sutor vltra crepidam. Ratio recta, continens se intra limites obiecti sui, non contradicit mysteriis fidei; per accidens autem fit, vt ratio corrupta, sphæram suam egressa, enormis & effrenata, reuelationi diuinæ obluctetur.

VII. Omnis discursus vltimo resoluitur in illud principium: Impossibile est, idem simul esse & non esse: quod principium est rationis. Vt itaque vltima in id fit resolutio: ita vltimum rationi defertur iudicium.

Resp. Principium illud duobus modis potest considerari, vt fit commune contradictionis fundamentum. Vt approprietur rebus diuinis, & ad earum naturam coarctetur. Quamuis ratio formale ferat iudicium, de communi contradictionis fundamento: iudicium tamen reale & normale competit sacræ scripturæ, quatenus illud contradictionis fundamentum rebus diuinis appropriatur.

VIII. Doctores euangelici haud raro vtuntur principiis rationis in syllogismis theologicis. Ergo Socinianos abusus rationis non possunt accusare. Resp. Euangelici in syllogismis theologicis vtuntur principiis rationis absolute vniuersalibus: aduersarii principiis particularibus, aut saltem limitate vniuersalibus, & ad sphæram naturæ aut entis finiti adstrictis, vtuntur. Euangelici vtuntur principiis rationis, non vt theologiæ propriis, sed multarum scientiarum communibus; non vt ministerialibus & quasi intrumentalibus, adiumentum intelligendi & deducendi conclusionem subministrantibus; non vt primordialibus, a quibus capiendum sit demonstrandi principium, sed vt supperadditis ad ostendendam δοκιμασίαν syllogisticam.

Id quod non attendentes aduersarii, mysteriis fidei diuinitus patefactis se præfracte opponunt.

V. g. Mysterium Trinitatis impugnant hoc axiomate philosophico: Quot sunt personæ, tot sunt essentiæ. Mysterium incarnationis adoriuntur hoc principio rationis: Omnis natura intelligens, & in essendo completa, est persona. Substantialem corporis Christi præsentiam e sacramento cœnæ sublatum eunt hoc lemmate: Omne corpus naturale est in vno determinato loco. Quæ principia rationis, cum adstricta sint ad naturæ & entium finitorum sphæram, perperam venditantur pro absolute vniuersalibus, neque sine μεταβάσει εἰς ἄλλο γένος ad res meræ fidei applicantur.

Est ratio non dux theologiæ, sed pedissequa. Seruiat ancilla Hagar dominæ, non imperet: imperium affectans æde sacra eliminetur.

Quæst. V. Estne consensus patrum primitiuæ ecclesiæ principium theologiæ? Consensus patrum, qui prioribus quinque seculis in ecclesia Christi vixerunt, qualiscunque ille ex scriptis ipsorum pro tempore præsenti habere potest, non est principium apodicticum & fundamentale theologiæ (a): neque accurate dicitur principium fidei christianæ secundarium (b): neque tamen parui ducendus, sed magni æstimandus est, vt motiuum credibilitatis, principium quarundam theologicarum conclusionum topicum & probabile, atque insigne testimonium, priscos ecclesiæ catholicæ antistites, dicta S. scripturæ eodem sensu, quo hodierna ecclesia euangelica intelligit, intellexisse & exposuisse ( ).

Obs. Principium probandi diuiditur (x) in apodicticum, & topicum. Illud scientiam, seu accuratam & certam notitiam, hoc opinionem seu notitiam verisimilem parit. (β) In principium κατὰ πρᾶγμα, fiue ad rem demonstrandam per se validum, & κατ' ἄνθρωπον fiue ad hominem, cuius respectu habetur validum, propterea, quod ab ipfo conceditur & approbatur.

Probatur a. I. Quia S. scriptura est principium theologiæ adæquatum. Vid. quæst. II. prob. a.

II. Quia principium theologiæ oportet esse αὐτόπιστον & infallibiliter certum. At patres primitiuæ ecclesiæ fuerunt homines priuilegio infallibilitatis non præditi, qui ficut finguli ab errandi periculo non fuerunt exemti, ita vniuersi in tradenda doctrina fidei fallere & falli potuerunt. Errata patrum commonstrat D. CHEMNIT. in orat. de lectione patrum loc. theol. præfixa, nec non D. GERHARD. in confess. cathol. libr. 1. part. II. cap. XIII. fol 190. Neque id diffitentur patres ipsi. Nam, citante Gerardo, loco allegato, Hieronymus scribit epist. 62. ad Theophyl.: Aliter habere debemus apostolos, aliter vero reliquos scripturæ tractatores. Illos sciamus semper vera dicere, istos vt homines in quibusdam errare.

III. Vniuersalis patrum ecclesiæ consensus nullibi datur. Nam (a) multæ per orbeim terrarum ecclesiæ ab apostolorum temporibus fuere, quarum tamen nec doctores nobis innotuerunt, neque de doctrina ab illis tradita vlla exstant testimonia. (b) Ante mota certamina patres fecurius & asperius sunt locuti. (c) In interpretandis dictis facræ scripturæ immane quantum discrepant. (d) Haud pauca patrum scripta a pontificiis funt interpolata, castrata & mutilata.

IV. Omne principium est prius principiato. At consensus patrum non est prior, sed posterior theològia christiana. Nam post apostolos per integrum seculum, ne vnus quidem superest scriptor, qui de omnibus fidei dogmatibus scripserit. Exstant quidem quædam, quæ Ignatio tribuuntur, epistolæ, sed earum nonnullæ fummorum virorum iudicio suppositiæ; aliæ aduerfariorum improbo ausu corruptæ ac mutilatæ sunt: quæ genuinæ esse existimantur, de paucis fidei articulis lectorem informare possunt. Exstant etiam quædam Iustini scripta, sed pleraque spuria sunt. Nulla enim habentur genuina, præter orationem paræneticam ad gentes, & colloquium cum Tryphone Iudæo. Quæ autem præterea a Iustino vere scripta sunt, perierunt, vt præter titulos ab Hieronymo & Eusebio memoratos nihil supersit. Hosce sequitur Irenæus, sed de eius scriptis, quæ multa fuere, Erasmus superiori seculo vix quinque aduerfus Gnosticos & Valentinianos conscriptos libros ab interitu vindicauit, & publici iuris fecit, & quidem latino idiomate, in quod e græca lingua, in qua ab auctore scripti, incommode translati sunt. Tertullianus haud raro a regia deflectit via, & aliter, quam ecclesia credidit, docuit. Ex quo Hieronymus, cum ipsius auctoritate vrgeretur, dixit: De Tertulliano aliud nihil respondeo, quam ecclesiæ hominem illum non fuisse. Vid. supra cit. orat. CHEMNIT. fol. 3.

Prob. b. Quamuis consensus patrum primitiuæ ecclesiæ, qualiscunque ille hodie in ipsorum scriptis habetur, vocari queat conclusionum nonnullarum theologicarum principium secundarium eodem sensu, quo alias appellatur principium topicum: non tamen accurate loquendo principium est fidei christianæ secundarium. Nam fides christiana est fides diuina & immota et immota hypostasis, Hebr. XI, 1. Cuius principium, cui innititur, non nisi divinum & supernaturale esse potest. At consensus patrum, qualiscunque pro statu temporis praesentis datur, humanus est. Nam cuiuslibet patris testimonium humanum esse nemo diffitebitur. At singulorum testimonia in unum collata non possunt esse alterius generis, quam cuius sunt singula per se considerata. Quamvis enim gradus auctoritatis quadantenus crescat propter multitudinem, non tamen mutatur auctoritatis species.

Prob. c. Consensus patrum primitivae ecclesiae, qualis quidem hodie superest, multum confert ponderis ad interpretationem dictorum sacrae scripturae. Ecquis sanae mentis compos non moueatur ad comprobandam interpretationem scripturarum, quam perantiqui ecclesiae primitivae doctores, apostolis vicini, rerum divinarum scientia apprime instructi, vitae sanctimonia inclyti, scriptis suis posteritati commendarunt?

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, consensum patrum primitivae ecclesiae, vt infallibile theologiae principium urgentium, quorum ponderabimus argumenta.

I. Consensus patrum, qui prioribus quinque seculis a partu virginis vixerunt & scripserunt, est consensus ecclesiae catholicae, quae ab errore immunis est, eo quod ecclesia Dei viventis est στῦλος καὶ ἑδραίωμα τῆς ἀληθείας, columna & fundamentum veritatis, 1 Tim. III, 15. Resp. (α) Consensus paucorum ecclesiae patrum non est consensus ecclesiae catholicae. (β) Consensus ecclesiae verus est, quoniam consentit cum sacra scriptura. Ergo non est principium, aut norma, sed principiatum aut normatum. (γ) Dicitur στῦλος, sive columna veritatis, non in sensu architectonico, perinde ac si veritatem coelestem suffulciat, aut, ne praeceps ruat, sustentet, sed in sensu politico. Vt enim in curiis & ante praetoria columnae exstant, ad quas leges & decreta magistratus appenduntur: ita ecclesia est columna publica, cui affixae sunt verbi divini tabulae. Vox ἑδραίωμα autem proprie notat sedem, sellam aut repositorium, quia ecclesia est quasi sedile aut repositorium, in quo veritas coelestis reposita est. At quibus, quaeso, fidiculis extorqueri potest ex dicto Paullino, consensum patrum esse principium theologiae (*)?

II. Patres ecclesiae primitivae errare nequiverunt, ideo quod vi promissionum divinarum Spiritus Sanctus duxit patres in omnem veritatem, Io. XVI, 13. Mansit cum illis perpetuo, Io. XIV, 16. Resp. Promissiones Salvatoris πρώτως & primario respiciunt apostolos, quorum mentes Spiritus sanctus cognitione doctrinae coelestis immediate illustravit, vt in doctrina fidei non errarent. Id propter apostolus asserit, super fundamentum apostolorum ecclesiam esse exstructam, Eph. II, 20. Δευτέρως & secundario accommodari possunt ad omnes doctores ecclesiae, quatenus vocem Spiritus sancti sequuntur. Sed exinde colligere non licet: Ergo doctores ecclesiae simpliciter immunes sunt ab errandi periculo.

III. Ex quo aliquid probatur & cognoscitur, illud est principium cognoscendi. Ex consensu patrum probantur conclusiones theologicae. Ergo consensus patrum est principium conclusionum theologicarum.

Resp. (1) Dist. inter principium apodicticum, & topicum. Si maior intelligatur de principio topico, conceditur totum argumentum: sin intelligatur de principio apodictico, negatur minor.

Nam e consensu patrum argumentamur (α) κατ’ ἄνθρωπον aduersus Pontificios, quos penes plurimum valet auctoritas patrum: (β) κατὰ πρᾶγμα, quoniam vniversalis patrum ecclesiae primitivae consensus, qualis ille hodie dari potest, non invalidum est medium interpretandi scripturas. At validissime scriptura per scripturam explicatur.


### On Holy Scripture, as the Proper and Adequate Principle for Knowing Theology


### Q. VI. What is holy scripture?

Holy scripture is the word of God, consigned to letters by prophets and apostles through divine inspiration, so that through it the sinner may be informed unto eternal salvation.

It is defined more fully. Holy scripture is the word of God, consigned to letters by prophets in the Hebrew Old Testament, and by apostles in the Greek idiom in the New Testament, through the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit, instructing the sinner so that he may conceive true faith in Christ, and being reconciled to God, may live holily, and at length attain eternal life by the benefit of God.

Obj. 1. Scripture is so called from the external act of writing, performed by holy amanuenses, with God directing; who, by carving the letters of the law on stone tablets, made the august beginning of scripture, Exod. XXXII, 16.

Obj. 2. It is called holy, since it has God as its author, whose holiness all creatures, and especially the angels, celebrate, Is. VI, 3. it is written by prophets and apostles, holy men of God, 2 Pet. I, 21. it embraces the holy mysteries of faith, the holy precepts of morals, the holy examples of pious men, and aims at the holiness of the sinner, John XVII, 17. nay, it is even consecrated to eternity by divine providence.

Obj. 3. Holy scripture is taken (α) generally & improperly, for all books existing in the biblical codex, whether they be canonical and θεόπνευστοι (God-breathed), or apocryphal, consigned by human study, containing holy things and useful for the edification of the church. (β) Specifically or specially & properly, for canonical books, written by the immediate influx of the Holy Spirit. In which special sense it denotes (1) formally the sense of the divine word, which is its internal form and as it were its soul; (2) materially it is taken for the letters, words, and books; (3) it is taken complexly, insofar as it embraces both the θεόπνευστον (God-breathed) sense, and the letters & words of which it consists. In which complex sense it is used here.

Obs. 4. Holy scripture is called otherwise by way of eminence, ἡ γραφή, scripture, John II, 22. αἱ γραφαὶ, scriptures, Matt. XXI, 42. αἱ γραφαὶ ἁγίαι, holy scriptures, Rom. I, 2. τὰ λόγια τοῦ θεοῦ, oracles of God, Rom. III, 2. ἱερὰ γράμματα, holy letters, 2 Tim. III, 15. סֵפֶר יְהוָה the book of the Lord, Is. XXXIV, 16. The fathers of the Greek church called them τὰ βιβλία, as if you would say books, or a volume of books, which, written by many in diverse places & times, are contained in one codex. Obs. 5. The word of God is viewed here as a principle of knowing, from which all things to be believed & done become known: below in part III it will be considered as a principle of acting, insofar as it is a medium of converting the sinner, of regenerating, justifying, & saving the same.

Latin:

Sacra scriptura est verbum Dei, a prophetis & apostolis ex inspiratione divina litteris consignatum, vt per illud peccator informetur ad aeternam salutem.

Vberius definitur. Sacra scriptura est verbum Dei, a prophetis in veteri testamento hebraeo, & in nouo testamento apostolis graeco idiomate, ex immediata Spiritus S. inspiratione litteris consignatum, peccatorem instruens, vt veram in Christum fidem concipiat, Deoque reconciliatus sancte viuat, ac tandem vitam aeternam beneficio Dei adipiscatur.

Obs. 1. Dicitur scriptura ab externo scribendi actu, praestito a sacris amanuensibus, dirigente Deo; qui litteras legis exarando in tabulis lapideis augustum scripturae fecit initium, Exod. XXXII, 16.

Obs. 2. Sacra dicitur, quoniam auctorem habet Deum, cuius sanctitatem cum omnes creaturae, tum inprimis angeli concelebrant, Es. VI, 3. a prophetis & apostolis, sanctis Dei viris, est conscripta, 2 Petr. I, 21. sancta fidei mysteria, sancta morum praecepta, sancta piorum hominum exempla complectitur, ad sanctitatem peccatoris collineat, Io. XVII, 17. quin a diuina etiam prouidentia aeternitati consecrata est.

Obs. 3. Sacra scriptura accipitur (α) γενικῶς & improprie, pro omnibus libris, in codice biblico exstantibus, siue sint canonici & θεόπνευστοι, siue apocryphi, studio humano consignati, continentes res sacras & ad aedificationem ecclesiae vtiles. (β) Εἰδικῶς siue specialiter & proprie, pro libris canonicis, immediato Spiritus S. influxu conscriptis. Quo sensu speciali notat (1) formaliter sensum verbi diuini, qui interna eius forma & quasi anima est; (2) materialiter accipitur pro litteris, vocibus, libris; (3) sumitur complexe, prout tum sensum θεόπνευστον, tum litteras & voces, e quibus constat, complectitur. Quo sensu complexo heic adhibetur.

Obs. 4. Sacra scriptura vocatur alias κατ' ἐξοχήν, ἡ γραφή, scriptura, Io. II, 22. αἱ γραφαὶ, scripturae, Matth. XXI, 42. αἱ γραφαὶ ἁγίαι, scripturae sanctae, Rom. I, 2. τὰ λόγια τοῦ θεοῦ, oracula Dei, Rom. III, 2. ἱερὰ γράμματα, sacrae litterae, 2 Tim. III, 15. סֵפֶר יְהוָה liber domini, Es. XXXIV, 16. Patres ecclesiae graecae appelliarunt τὰ βιβλία, quasi dicas libros, siue volumen librorum, qui multi diuersis locis & temporibus scripti, vno codice continentur. Obs. 5. Spectatur hic verbum Dei vt principium cognoscendi, ex quo omnia credenda & agenda innotescunt: infra parte III. considerabitur vt principium operandi, quatenus est medium conuertendi peccatorem, eumdem regenerandi, iustificandi & saluandi.


### Q. VII. Is holy scripture to be accurately defined by the word of God, which is living & efficacious for producing spiritual effects?

Holy scripture, speaking accurately, is the word of God, and that living & efficacious for producing spiritual effects. The antithesis is that of the Quakers, who opine that Holy Scripture is not the true and living word of God, but only a witness concerning the word of God and a dead letter. For thus AMESIUS left it written concerning false prophets on p. 9: They insist on the footsteps of the Baalites, who hold Scripture to be the true word of God. Thus also the Quakers trifle in the book which is inscribed: Der Stein, den die Bau-leute verworfen haben [The stone which the builders rejected], p. 2: "The Scripture was spoken of by the light, but it is not the Light, nor the Word, nor the Life, nor the Judge, nor the Rule, nor the Guide." And p. 4: "Christ is the Word, but the Scripture is not: He is the Light, and not the Scripture: He is the Teacher and Judge, but by no means the Scripture. The same is only a narrative of him, and a co-witness of our doctrine." FOXUS in XXVII. erroribus [27 errors] p. 30. n. 22. says: "Scripture is and remains a dead letter." PENNINGTON in via vitæ & mortis [the way of life and death] says p. 14: "Scripture is not the living word, which was given by God as a rule for Christians."

To these, other mystical theologians add their favorable vote.
