WEIGELIUS in his postil part III. p. 84: "Die Schrist ist ein todter Buchstab, und unkrästiges Wort, das allein in die lust schallet" [The Scripture is a dead letter, and an ineffective word, which only sounds into the air]. CHRISTIANUS HOBURGIUS in his mystical postil for the third day of the Nativity, p. 115:

"Die Schrist ist alt, kalt und todt Ding, das nur eitel Pharisaer machet" [The Scripture is an old, cold, and dead thing, which only makes vain Pharisees].

Exposition. Obs. I.

Holy Scripture is taken either materially, for the points, letters, and syllables of which it consists, or formally, for the theopneustos [God-breathed] sense, or finally complexly and completely, as it embraces both letters, syllables, and voices, as well as the theopneustos sense: the latter meaning is of this place. Obs. II.

The question is not, whether Scripture can be called the word of God metonymically or improperly?

but, whether it is accurately defined by the word of God?

Confirmation. Our assertion is proven. (I) The divinely inspired word is accurately defined by the divine word. But Holy Scripture is, etc. 2 Tim. III, 16. Therefore.

The major is clear, because just as the writing which a man dictates to another for the pen is rightly called human word committed to letters; so the writing inspired by God is most truly called the word of God committed to letters. (II) The prophetic word is accurately defined by the word of God effectively illuminating. But the Scripture of the Old Testament, etc. Therefore.

The major is proven; because God spoke through the mouth of the holy prophets. Luke I, 70. "The Spirit of Jehovah spoke in me, and his word was upon my tongue," says the royal prophet 2 Sam. XXIII, 2. "The Lord spoke by the hand of Isaiah," c. XV, 2. "The word of the Lord came to me," says Jeremiah c. I, 4. The minor is evident from 2 Peter I, 19: "We have a more sure prophetic word, to which you do well to pay attention, as to a light shining in a dark place, until the day dawns, and the morning star rises in your hearts."

Christians, while the apostle Peter was still alive, had the prophetic word committed to letters, and thus the Scripture of the Old Testament: since this is called a shining light, it cannot be a dead letter. (III) The oracles of God entrusted to the Jews are accurately called the words of God. (For oracles are words which God has spoken.) The Scriptures of the O.T. are the oracles entrusted to the Jews. Therefore. The minor is clear from the Pauline utterance, Rom. III, 1-2.

But, while Paul was living in these lands, the oracles of God, entrusted to the Jews, were contained in the prophetic writings. (IV) The word which the apostles preached, that is truly the word of God. But the word which the apostles wrote, they also preached. Therefore, the word which the apostles wrote is truly the word of God.

The major is clear from 1 Thess. II, 13.

"When you received the heard word of God, you accepted it not as the word of men, but as it is truly the word of God." The minor is confirmed.

From 1 John 1:3, 4, 5. "That which we have seen and heard, we announce to you: therefore we write these things to you." The divine word preached and written differ accidentally, not essentially. Dr. Dannhauer says excellently in Hodof. phæn. I, p. 29: "As Caesar does not differ from himself, even if he be represented by a painter on a map or by an engraver on bronze, so the word announced by mouth does not differ essentially from the written word.

(V) That by which word faith is conferred upon man for eternal salvation, that is most rightly defined as the word of God. And yet Holy Scripture is that word, &c. E. Paul confirms the major in Rom. 10:17: "Faith is from hearing, and hearing through the word of God." The truth of the minor is evident from the saying in John 20:31: "These things are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, and that believing you may have life in his name." Compare 2 Tim. 3:14, 15.

" (VI) Holy Scripture is the living word of God, Acts 7:38, 1 Pet. 1:23, Heb. 4:12; it is the word of life, Acts 5:20, Phil. 2:16; nay, life itself, John 6:63. Therefore, it is not a dead letter.

(VII) Holy Scripture regenerates and vivifies man. Therefore, it is the living and efficacious word of God. The reason for the consequence is that a dead letter cannot vivify; otherwise, the effect would be more excellent than its cause. The antecedent is clear from James 1:18: "It pleased God to beget us by the word of truth." Compare 1 Pet. 1:23. Dissolution.

Dissolution. I. Against us, the diffident argue: Christ is not Holy Scripture. Christ is the word of God, John 1:1. Therefore, the word of God is not Scripture. Resp. Distinguish between the word hypostaticum (hypostatic), or personal, and prophoricum (prophoric), or annunciative. We are speaking here of the latter, whereas John speaks of the personal word, which is Christ.

II. Whatever is a testimony concerning the word of God, and a declaration of it, is not the word of God itself. But Holy Scripture, etc. Therefore. The minor is proven because Scripture testifies of Christ as the word of God. Resp. (1) I deny the major and the minor. For the divine word is of such authority and efficacy that it testifies of itself. Furthermore, Scripture indeed testifies of Christ as the personal word, yet it is itself the annunciative word of God. (2) Holy Scripture is considered in two ways: (a) as a testimony, insofar as it testifies and declares what the salutary dogmas of the Christian religion are; (b) as an efficacious medium of grace and salvation, by which we are illuminated, converted, etc. The Weigelians and Quakers judge too crudely concerning Holy Scripture, deeming it to be only a witness.

III. External letters written on paper cannot act upon the soul and illuminate and regenerate it. If the Scriptures are external letters, etc. Therefore. Resp. External letters written on paper, and destitute of the theopneustos (God-breathed) sense and divine efficacy, cannot illuminate and regenerate the soul; but Holy Scripture is spirit and life, John 6:63; it is the seed of regeneration, 1 Pet. 1:23; it is a shining light, 2 Pet. 1:19.

IV. The true and living word of God is in us, Rom. 10:8. Holy Scripture is not in us. Therefore, etc. Resp. I deny the minor. For Holy Scripture is in us insofar as it is received by us; it is outside us insofar as it is proposed to us.

V. A sign of the divine word is not the word of God (for the sign and the signified differ). But Holy Scripture, etc. Therefore, etc. The minor is evident because Holy Scripture consists of letters and syllables, which are signs of the word. Resp. Holy Scripture, taken materially for letters and syllables, is a sign of the divine word, not semantikon (merely signifying), but metadotikon (imparting), exhibiting the theopneuston (God-breathed) sense, which is the formal element of Scripture; complexly, it is the written word of God, i.e., the sense expressed in divine letters dictated to the pen by the sacred amanuenses of the Spirit.

VI. Man is illuminated by Christ, John 1:9. E. not by Scripture. Resp. Man is illuminated by Christ, as the principal cause; he is illuminated by Scripture, as the intermediate cause.

Latin:

Sacra scriptura accurate loquendo est verbum Dei, idque viuum & efficax ad producendum effectus spirituales. Antithesis est Quakerorum, opinantium, S. scripturam non esse verum & vivum Dei verbum, sed tantum testem de verbo Dei & litteram mortuam. Sic enim scriptum reliquit AMESIVS de falsis prophetis p. 9. Baalitarum vestigiis insistunt, qui scripturam pro vero Dei verbo habent. Sic etiam nugantur Quakeri in libro, qui inscribitur: Der Stein, den die Bau-leute verworfen haben. p. 2. Die Schrist war gesprochen von dem licht, sie ist aber nicht das Licht, noch das Wort, noch das Leben, noch der Richter, noch die Regel, noch der Leit-Mann. & p. 4. Christus ist das Wort, die Schrist aber nicht: Er ist das Licht, und nicht die Schrist: Er ist der Lehrer und Richter, mit nichten aber die Schrist. Dieselbe ist nur eine Erzählung von ihm, und ein Mitzeuge unserer Lehre. FOXVS in XXVII. erroribus p. 30. n. 22. ait: Scriptura est manetque littera mortua. PENNINGTON in via vitæ & mortis inquit p. 14. Scriptura non est vivum verbum, quod a Deo pro regula christianorum datum est.

His & alii theolophi mystici album calculum adiiciunt. WEIGELIVS in postilla part. III. p. 84. Die Schrist ist ein todter Buchstab, und unkrästiges Wort, das allein in die lust schallet. CHRISTIANVS HOBVRGIVS in postilla mystica feria III. nativit. p. 115.

Die Schrist ist alt, kalt und todt Ding, das nur eitel Pharisaer machet.

Ἔκθεσις. Obs. I.

S. scriptura sumitur vel materialiter, pro apicibus, litteris & syllabis, e quibus constat, vel formaliter, pro sensu θεοπνεύστῳ, vel denique complexe & complete, prout tam litteras, syllabas & voces, quam sensum θεοπνευστον complectitur: postrema significatio huius est loci. Obs. II.

Non est quæstio, an scriptura metonymice, aut improprie, verbum Dei dici possit?

sed, an accurate per verbum Dei definiatur?

Βεβαίωσις. Probatur assertio nostra. (I) Verbum divinitus inspiratum accurate definitur per verbum divinum. Atqui S. scriptura est &c. 2 Tim. III, 16. Ergo.

Maior liquet, quia sicut scriptura, quam homo alteri in calamum dictat, recte dicitur verbum humanum in litteras relatum; ita scriptura a Deo inspirata verissime dicitur verbum Dei litteris consignatum. (II) Verbum propheticum accurate definitur per verbum Dei efficaciter illuminans. Atqui scriptura veteris testamenti &c. Ergo.

Maior probatur; quia Deus locutus est per os sanctorum prophetarum. Luc. I. 70. Spiritus Iehouæ locutus est in me, & sermo eius fuit super lingua mea, inquit propheta regius 2 Sam. XXIII, 2. Locutus est dominus per manum Elaiæ, c. VX, 2. Factum est verbum domini ad me, ait Ieremias c. I, 4. Minor patet ex 2 Petr. I, 19. Habemus firmius propheticum verbum, cui recte facitis, quod attenditis, tanquam lumini lucenti in loco tenebricoso, usque dum dies illucescat, & lucifer oriatur in cordibus vestris.

Christiani, superstite apostolo Petro, habebant verbum propheticum litteris consignatum, adeoque scripturam veteris testamenti: hoc cum dicatur lumen lucens, non potest esse littera mortua. (III) Eloquia Dei Iudæis concredita ἀκριβῶς dicuntur verba Dei. (Nam eloquia sunt verba, quæ Deus elocutus est.) Scripturæ V. T. sunt eloquia Iudæis concredita. Ergo. Minor claret effato Paullino, Rom. III, 11. 12.

At, vivente in his terris Paullo, eloquia Dei, Iudæis concredita, scriptis propheticis erant comprehensa. (IV) Quod verbum apostoli prædicarunt, illud reuera est verbum Dei. Sed quod verbum apostoli scripserunt, idem prædicarunt. E. Quod verbum apostoli scripserunt, reuera est verbum Dei.

Maior liquet ex 1 Thess. II, 13.

Cum accepistis verbum auditum Dei, suscepistis non ut verbum hominum, sed sicut est reuera verbum Dei. Minor confirmatur

ex 1 Io. 1, 3. 4. 5. Quod vidimus & audiuimus, annunciamus vobis: ideo hæc scribimus vobis. Verbum diuinum prædicatum & scriptum differunt accidentaliter, non essentialiter. Præclare inquit D. DANNHAV. in hodof. phæn. I. p. 29. Vt Cæsar a seipso non differt, repræsentetur licet a pictore in mappa, a chalcographo in ære: ita verbum ore annunciatum a verbo scripto non differt essentialiter.

(V) Per quod verbum confertur homini fides ad æternam salutem, illud rectissime definitur per verbum Dei. Atqui S. scriptura est illud verbum &c. E. Maiorem confirmat Paullus Rom. X, 17. Fides est ex auditu: auditus autem per verbum Dei. Minoris veritas patescit ex dicto Ioannæo c. XX, 31. Hæc scripta sunt, vt credatis, quod Iesus fit Christus, & vt credentes vitam habeatis in nomine ipsius. Confer 2 Tim. III, 14. 15.

(VI) Sacra scriptura est verbum Dei viuum, Act. VII, 38. 1 Petr. I, 23. Hebr. IV, 12. est verbum vitæ, Act. V, 20. Phil. II, 16. imo vita ipsa, Io. VI, 63. E. Non est littera mortua.

(VII) Sacra scriptura hominem regenerat & viuificat. E. Est verbum Dei viuum & efficax. Ratio consequentiæ est, quia littera mortua non potest viuificare; alias effectus præstantior foret sua causa. Antecedens liquet ex Iac. I, 18. Placuit Deo generare nos verbo veritatis. Confer 1 Petr. I, 23. Διάλυσις.

I. Contra nos diffidentes arguunt: Christus non est S. scriptura. Christus est verbum Dei, Io. I, 1. E. Verbum Dei non est scriptura. Resp. Dist. inter verbum ὑποσατικὸν, siue personale, & προφορικὸν, siue annunciatiuum. De hoc nobis iam sermo est, Ioannes autem loquitur de verbo personali, quod est Christus.

II. Quidquid est testimonium de verbo Dei, eiusque declaratio, illud non est ipsum verbum Dei. Atqui S. scriptura &c. E. Minor probatur, quia scriptura testatur de Christo, tanquam verbo Dei. Resp. (1) Neg. maior & minor. Nam verbum diuinum tantæ est auctoritatis & efficaciæ, vt de seipso testetur. Ad hæc scriptura de Christo tanquam verbo personali quidem testatur, ipsa tamen est verbum Dei enunciatiuum. (2) S. scriptura bifariam consideratur, (a) vt testimonium, quatenus testatur, & declarat, quænam sint salutifera religionis christianæ dogmata, (b) vt efficax gratiæ salutisque medium, quo illuminamur, conuertimur &c. Crude nimis Weigeliani & Quakeri iudicant de S. scriptura, censentes, eam tantum testem esse.

III. Litteræ externæ in charta scriptæ non possunt agere in animam, eamque illuminare atque regenerare. Si scripturæ sunt litteræ externæ &c. E. Resp. Litteræ externæ in charta scriptæ, & sensu θεοπνεύστῳ, atque efficacia diuina destitutæ, non possunt animam illuminare & regenerare: at S. scriptura est spiritus & vita, Io. VI, 63. est semen regenerationis, 1 Petr. I, 23. est lumen lucens, 2 Petr. I, 19.

IV. Verum & viuum Dei verbum est in nobis, Rom. X, 8. S. scriptura non est in nobis. E. cet. Resp. neg. min. Nam S. scriptura est in nobis, quatenus a nobis recipitur: est extra nos, quatenus nobis proponitur.

V. Signum verbi diuini non est verbum Dei (nam signum & signatum differunt). Atqui S. scriptura &c. E. cet. Minor constat, quia S. scriptura litteris & syllabis constat, quæ sunt signa verbi. Resp. S. scriptura sumta materialiter pro litteris & syllabis est signum verbi diuini, non σημαντικὸν, feu mere fignans, sed μεταδοτικὸν, exhibens sensum θεόπνευστον, qui est formale scripturæ: complexe est verbum Dei scriptum, i. e. sensus diuinis litteris a Spiritu amanuensibus sacris in calamum dictatis expressus.

VI. Illuminatur homo a Christo, Io. I, 9. E. non a scriptura. Resp. Illuminatur homo a Christo, vt causa principali: illuminatur a scriptura, vt causa intermedia.


### Q. VIII. What is understood by the name of the word of God in the definition of Holy Scripture?

In the definition of Holy Scripture, the word of God formally denotes the sentence of God, or the concept of the divine mind, concerning the salvation of men, manifested immediately to the prophets and apostles, and through their ministry, to the whole human race.

Prob. 1. Just as the matter and, as it were, the external bark of human writing are letters, syllables, voices, and periods, and the internal form and, as it were, the marrow is the sense of the man writing or dictating: so the matter from which the θεοπνεύστου (God-breathed) Scripture is made, are letters and voices divinely dictated: the form is the divine sense, which is the concept of the divine intellect, communicated to us concerning divine mysteries by writing, as far as suffices for salvation, as KOENIG defines in his positive theology, p. 12. Therefore, since the word of God is constituted in its being by this divine sense, and is distinguished from human speech, it is this which must be considered primarily in the definition of Holy Scripture.

2. St. Paul, 1 Cor. 2:16, explicitly calls the word of God the mind of Christ, saying: "But we have the mind of Christ." He speaks of the revealed mind of Christ, which the natural man does not grasp from the principles of reason. This the apostle hints at, when he asks in the words immediately preceding: "Who has known the mind of the Lord, that he might instruct him?" just as if he were saying: What natural man, not illuminated by the light of supernatural revelation, so knows the mind of the Lord that he can teach, confirm, and judge the spiritual man? But to us apostles, the mind of Christ has been revealed through the Holy Spirit, while the gospel of the Savior has been divinely inspired in us to the end that, through our ministry, the mind of the Savior might be made manifest to other men as well.

3. Just as divine speech formally consists in the manifestation of the divine concept (for God speaks when He declares His mind.

II. The word of God προφορικόν, consigned to letters, is not the concept of the divine mind itself, but a sign of it.

For written letters are signs of voices, voices are signs of the concept, and the concept is a sign of things, as Aristotle teaches in De Interpretatione, ch. 1. Resp. Our discourse is about the word of God προφορικόν considered not materially, with respect to the letters, syllables, and voices by which the divine sense is signified; but formally, by reason of the divine sense signified by written voices or those uttered by living voice.

In the former way of considering it, Holy Scripture is called the word of God only σημαντικῶς (significatively), significatively and improperly: but in the latter way, it is κυρίως (properly) and strictly the word of God, the wisdom of God, the mind of God. For just as a royal minister truly and with a certain emphasis asserts concerning the written mandate of his king: "This is the mind, sentence, and will of my king": whereas a just man would feel and say more precisely: "This is a sign of the sentence of my king": so we do not...

S. Scripture not by a verbal sign, but by the sentence of God made manifest in the writings of the prophets & apostles. Conf. D. SCHERTZER. in system, p. 6.

III. The divine sense is in H. Scripture: Therefore H. Scripture is not the divine sense itself. Resp. Just as I rightly say: God is in Christ, 2 Cor. V, 19. And Christ is true God, 1 John V, 20. So the divine sense is in H. Scripture, & nevertheless H. Scripture is the divine sense, concerning our salvation, expressed by the sacred amanuenses, and exhibited to men to be saved.

Latin:

In definitione sacrae scripturae verbum Dei formaliter notat sententiam Dei, sive conceptum mentis divinae, de salute hominum immediate prophetis & apostolis, atque mediante eorum ministerio, universo generi humano manifestatum.

Prob. 1. Quemadmodum scripti humani materia & externus quasi cortex sunt litterae, syllabae, voces & periodi, forma interna & quasi medulla est sensus hominis scribentis aut dictantis: ita scripturae θεοπνεύστου materia ex qua, sunt litterae & voces divinitus dictatae: forma est sensus divinus, qui est conceptus divini intellectus, de mysteriis divinis scriptione nobis communicatus, quantum ad salutem sufficit, definiente KOENIGIO in theol. positiva p. 12. Idcirco cum sensu isthoc divino verbum Dei in esse suo constituatur, & a verbo humano distinguatur, ipse praecipue considerandus venit in definitione S. scripturae.

2. S. Paullus 1 Cor. II, 16. verbum Dei diserte appellat mentem Christi, inquiens: nos vero mentem Christi habemus. Loquitur de mente Christi revelata, quam homo animalis ex principiis rationis non capit. Quod innuit apostolus, cum verbis proxime praecedentibus interrogat: Quis novit mentem domini, qui confirmatus fit ipsum? prorsus ac si dicat: Ecquis homo animalis, supernaturalis revelationis lumine non collustratus, ita novit mentem domini, vt hominem spiritualem docere, confirmare & diiudicare queat? Nobis vero apostolis per Spiritum sanctum mens Christi est revelata, dum evangelium Salvatoris nobis divinitus est inspiratum eo fine, vt nostro ministerio etiam aliis hominibus mens Salvatoris patefiat.

3. Sicut locutio divina formaliter consistit in manifestatione conceptus divini (dicit enim Deus, cum mentem suam declarat.

II. Verbum Dei προφορικόν, litteris consignatum, non est ipse conceptus mentis divinae, sed eiusdem signum.

Litterae enim scriptae sunt signa vocum, voces vero conceptum, & conceptus rerum, docente Aristotele περὶ ἑρμην. c. 1. Resp. Sermo nobis est de verbo Dei προφορικόν considerato non materialiter, respectu litterarum, syllabarum & vocum, quibus sensus divinus significatur; sed formaliter, ratione sensus divini vocibus scriptis, vel viva voce prolatis, significati.

Priori considerandi modo S. scriptura dicitur verbum Dei saltim σημαντικῶς, significative & improprie: posteriori vero ratione, κυρίως & proprie est verbum Dei, sapientia Dei, mens Dei. Sicut enim minister regius de scripto regis sui mandato vere & cum emphasi quadam asserit: haec est mens, sententia & voluntas regis mei: iusto autem exilius sentiret ac diceret: hoc est signum sententiae regis mei: ita nos non dedefinus

S. scripturam per signum verbale, sed per sententiam Dei scriptis prophetarum & apostolorum patefactam. Conf. D. SCHERTZER. in system, p. 6.

III. Sensus divinus est in S. scriptura: Ergo S. scriptura non est ipse sensus divinus. Resp. Sicut recte dico: Deus est in Christo, 2 Cor. V, 19. Et Christus est verus Deus, 1 Io. V, 20. Ita sensus divinus est in S. scriptura, & nihilo tamen minus S. scriptura est sensus divinus, de salute nostra, ab amanuensibus sacris expressus, & hominibus salvandis exhibitus.


### IX. What is the principal cause of Holy Scripture?

The principal cause of Holy Scripture is the triune God , the Father , the Son of God , and the Holy Spirit .

Prob. a. Prob. a. That God is the author of Holy Scripture is abundantly clear from the fact that He not only made an august beginning of writing, by inscribing the most holy law on stone tablets with His own finger, Exod. XXXI, 18, but also inspired the entire canonical scripture of both the Old and New Testaments to the sacred amanuenses. For this reason, the whole scripture is called θεόπνευστος, or divinely inspired, 2 Tim. III, 16.

Prob. b. That God the Father is the fountain of the revealed divine word, the apostle inculcates to us. Hebr. I, 1. 2. At sundry times and in divers manners, God spoke in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son.

By God the apostle understands God the Father, since He is said to have spoken in the Son. (β)

The same differs concerning the λόγῳ προφορικῷ, or the external word of God; for God is said to have spoken to the fathers in the prophets. Therefore, a twofold divine locution is to be noted, immediate & mediate. Immediately, God the Father spoke in the hearts of the prophets, in whom, as in dedicated temples, He graciously dwelt, and revealed to them the concept of His mind concerning the restoration of human salvation: mediately He spoke to the fathers, i.e., the ancestors of the Hebrews, through the intervention of the work of the prophets. (γ)

The apostle hints both at the diversity of times in which the divine revelations were made, and at the various modes of revealing, of which above.

In the first place (δ) he shows that in the last times, namely the times of the New Testament, God the Father manifested Himself in the Son, the greatest of the prophets, Deut. XVIII, 5. But just as the prophets taught the people partly by the proclamation of the voice, partly by published monuments of letters: so God the Father is the author of the external word, both preached and written. Prob. c.

That the Son of God is the principal cause of the divine word, and its omniscient interpreter, the Savior Himself went to indicate, John I, 18. No man hath seen God at any time: the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he ἐξηγήσατο, hath declared [explained] him unto us. The sense is: Neither angel nor any man has perceived the counsels of God the Father Most High as equally as the only begotten Son of the Father, who, since He is in His bosom, that is, co-essential, most dear, and conscious of all the mysteries which are as it were stored in the bosom of God, has explained His decrees concerning the procuring of our salvation, as the most learned exegete of all, so that no one has done so more clearly. Prob. d.

Prob. d. That the revelation of the divine word is attributed to the Holy Spirit κατ' ἰδιοποίησιν, and by a certain appropriation, is evident from 2 Pet. I, 21. Prophecy came not in old time by the will of man, but holy men of God spake as they were φερόμενοι, moved [impelled], by the Holy Spirit. By these words St. Peter teaches that prophecy, that is, the prophetic sermon v. 19, is not a human invention; since holy men of God, namely the prophets, sanctified and consecrated to their office, and likewise conspicuous for the holiness of an irreproachable life, spoke, not moved by their own will, as those are wont to do who indulge in their own inventions; but impelled, illuminated, ennobled with the gift of interpreting, and with the privilege of infallibility, by the Holy Spirit. For ἡ φορὰ denotes both the impulse to speak & write, and the illumination of the Holy Spirit: which δύναμις ἑρμηνευτική follows. to write, and the illumination of the Holy Spirit: which δύναμις ἑρμηνευτική follows.

tian, the faculty of interpreting, by which most sublime mysteries are clearly unfolded, and also the gift of infallibility, so that they might be immune from the danger of erring. What S. Peter asserts concerning the prophets of the Old Testament, the same S. Paul asserts concerning the apostles of the New Testament, 1 Cor. II, 12. 13. We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit which is from God (is), that we may know the things that are given to us by God: which things also we speak, not in the learned words of human wisdom, but in the learned words of the Holy Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual. The apostles did not receive the deceitful spirit of the world; whether you understand the demon, by whom the Pythonics were once agitated; or the human spirit, entirely occupied in attaining worldly wisdom; but the most holy, most true, most wise Spirit, proceeding from God the Father and the Son, so that they might most clearly know the benefits obtained by the merit of Christ, and most widely diffused throughout the whole human race: which they spoke in words not composed by art, not bound by the flowers of rhetoricians, but simple, but grave, and those immediately suggested by the Holy Spirit, so that they might accommodate a spiritual kind of speaking to explaining spiritual dogmas. Moreover, as the preached word of God, so also the written word owes its origin to the Holy Spirit. This is evident no less from the testimony of Peter than from the suffrage of Paul cited above. For the former speaks of the προφητεία τῆς γραφῆς, of the prophetic word committed to writing, v. 21. But the latter openly appeals to scripture, v. 9. The reason is at hand; because the preached and written word of God do not differ really, but as to their formal internal notion they are the same.

Q.

X. What impelled God to instruct men by sacred letters? Internally, most intense mercy impelled God to impart the written word to the human race (a): externally, the extreme misery of men (b). Prob. a.

He has made known to us the mystery of His will according to His good pleasure, which He purposed in Himself, says S. Paul concerning the gospel revealed to us, Eph. I, 9. The gospel is nothing other than the manifestation of the mystery of the divine will, concerning the redemption of the human race and the gratuitous remission of sins through Christ, v. 7. Since this salutary manifestation of so great a mystery is referred to τῇ εὐδοκίᾳ, or the divine good pleasure; it is not invalidly gathered that God, bound by no necessity, provoked by no merits of our works, but led by mere benevolence and mercy, was moved to reveal the ministry of saving men through Christ, and to procure its writing, so that believing in Christ they might have life in His name, Io. XX, 31. You say: God indeed revealed the gospel, and took care for it to be consigned to letters out of grace; but He did not command the law to be written for the same cause; since it is the letter that kills, 2 Cor. III, 6. Working wrath, Rom. IV, 15. Resp. 1) God gave the law out of grace, as a rule of holy life. For the royal psalmist commemorates that God testified to His special benevolence by this most signal pledge of love toward the Israelite people, because He announced His words to Jacob, His statutes and His judgments to Israel; although He did not deign to favor the Gentiles with the same degree of favor in the O. T., Ps. CXLVII, 9. 2) The law is called the letter that kills and works wrath, not of itself, but accidentally, by the fault of men, who perversely transgress it, to whom it denounces the wrath of God and death: but of itself the law is good and holy.

Rom. VII, 10. Prob. b. The animal man, as long as he wanders in these lands, destitute of the wayfaring light of the divine word, walks through pathless deserts, and does not know the way of the Lord, Sap. V, 7. Wherefore God, being propitious, having pitied the lot of the sinner, lights a lamp to his feet, His word, and a light to his path, Ps. CXIX, 105. Which word of His, God preserved and propagated by the tradition of the living voice, without the aid of scripture, for over 2500 years. See the chronology prefixed to the illustrated Bible of Dr. CALOVII, fol. 38. But as the innumerable multitude of men increased and the span of human life was diminished, God commanded that the principal heads of the divine revelations be comprehended in writings, so that aid might be provided for the weakness of human memory through the support of Holy Scripture, the treachery of heretics might be suppressed, and corruptions, creeping in through a tradition of the living voice less trustworthy, might be turned away.

Cf. D. GERHARD, in Exeg. fol. 15.

Latin:

Causa principalis sacræ scripturæ est Deus triunus , pater , filius Dei , & Spiritus sanctus .

Prob. a. Deum esse auctorem sacræ scripturæ, affatim liquet ex eo, quod non tantum augustum scribendi fecit initium, legem sanctissimam in tabulis lapideis digito suo exarando, Exod. XXXI, 18. sed & universam scripturam canonicam tam veteris, quam novi testamenti amanuensibus sacris inspiravit. Id propter tota scriptura dicitur θεόπνευστος, sive divinitus inspirata, 2 Tim. III, 16.

Prob. b. Deum patrem esse fontem verbi divini revelati, nobis inculcat apostolus. Hebr. I, 1. 2. Multis vicibus, multisque modis, olim Deus locutus est patribus in prophetis, ultimis hisce diebus locutus nos est in filio.

Obs. (α) Per Deum apostolus intelligit Deum Patrem, quippe qui dicitur locutus esse in filio. (β)

Differt idem de λόγῳ προφορικῷ, sive verbo Dei externo; nam dicitur Deus esse locutus patribus in prophetis. Idcirco notanda est duplex locutio divina, immediata & mediata. Immediate Deus pater locutus est in cordibus prophetarum, in quibus, velut dedicatis templis, gratiose habitavit, iisdemque conceptum mentis suæ de reparanda hominum salute revelavit: mediate locutus est patribus, i. e. maioribus hebræorum, interveniente prophetarum opera. (γ)

Innuit apostolus tum diversitatem temporum, quibus divinæ factæ sunt revelationes, tum varios revelandi modos, de quibus supra.

In primis (δ) ostendit, ultimis temporibus, scilicet temporibus novi testamenti, Deum patrem se manifestasse in filio, prophetarum maximo, Deut. XVIII, 5. Quemadmodum autem prophetæ partim præconio vocis, partim editis litterarum monumentis, populum docuerunt: ita Deus pater verbi externi, tam prædicati, quam scripti, auctor est.

Prob. c. Filium Dei esse causam principalem verbi divini, eiusque interpretem omniscium, ipsemet saluator indicatum iuit, Io. I, 18. Deum nemo vidit unquam: vnigenitus filius, qui in sinu patris est, ille ἐξηγήσατο, exposuit nobis. Sensus est: Consilia Dei patris altissimi neque angelus, neque homo vllus peruidit æque, ac filius patris vigenitus, qui cum sit in sinu eius, hoc est, coëssentialis, charissimus & conscius omnium arcanorum, quæ in sinu Dei quasi reposita sunt, ipsius decreta de procuranda salute nostra, velut exegeta omnium longe doctissimus sic exposuit, vt nemo clarius.

Prob. d. Verbi diuini reuelationem Spiritui sancto κατ' ἰδιοποίησιν, & per quandam appropriationem tribui, patet ex 2 Petr. I, 21. Non voluntate hominum allata est olim prophetia, sed a Spiritu sancto φερόμενοι, impulsi, locuti sunt sancti Dei homines. Docet his verbis S. Petrus, prophetiam, id est, sermonem propheticum v. 19. non esse inuentum humanum; quum sancti Dei homines, nempe prophetæ, ad munus suum sanctificati & consecrati, pariter atque vitæ inculpatæ sanctitate conspicui, locuti sint, non moti proprio arbitrio, vt solent, qui suis indulgent inuentis; sed a Spiritu sancto impulsi, illuminati, dono interpretandi, & priuilegio infallibilitatis nobilitati. Nam ἡ φορὰ tum impulsum ad loquendum & scribendum, tum illuminationem Spiritus sancti notat: quam consequitur δύναμις ἑρμηνευτική. scribendum, tum illuminationem Spiritus sancti notat: quam consequitur δύναμις ἑρμηνευτική.

tian, facultas interpretandi, qua mysteria sublimissima perspicue enuclearant, nec non donum infallibilitatis, vt ab errandi periculo fuerint immunes. Quod de prophetis veteris testamenti S. Petrus, idem de apostolis noui testamenti S. Paullus asserit, 1 Cor. II, 12. 13. Nos non accepimus spiritum mundi, sed Spiritum, qui ex Deo (est), vt sciamus ea, quæ a Deo donata sunt nobis: quæ etiam loquimur non doctis humanæ sapientiæ verbis, sed doctis Spiritus sancti, spiritualibus spiritualia componentes. Non acceperunt apostoli fallacem mundi spiritum; siue intelligas dæmonem, quo agitabantur olim Pythonici; siue spiritum humanum in assequenda sapientia mundana totum occupatum; sed Spiritum sanctissimum, verissimum, sapientissimum, ex Deo patre & filio procedentem, vt liquidissime scirent beneficia merito Christi parta, & in vniuersum humanum genus latissime diffusa: quæ elocuti sunt verbis non arte compositis, non rhetorum flosculis illigatis, sed simplicibus, sed grauibus, iisque a Spiritu sancto immediate suggestis, vt dogmatibus spiritualibus explanandis spirituale dicendi genus accommodarent. Ceterum vt verbum Dei prædicatum, ita & verbum scriptum, Spiritui sancto suam debet originem. Id quod non minus ex testimonio Petri, quam suffragio Paulli supra citato elucet. Nam ille loquitur de προφητεία τῆς γραφῆς, de verbo prophetico in litteras relato, v. 21. Hic autem aperte ad scripturam prouocat, v. 9. Ratio est in promptu; quia verbum Dei prædicatum & scriptum non differunt realiter, sed quoad formale internum idem sunt.

Quæst. X. Quid impulit Deum ad instruendum homines sacris litteris?

Interne impulit Deum, ad impertiendum generi humano verbum scriptum, misericordia intensissima (a): externe, miseria hominum extrema (b).

Prob. a. Notum fecit nobis mysterium voluntatis suæ iuxta beneplacitum suum, quod proposuit in seipso, inquit de euangelio nobis reuelato S. Paullus, Eph. I, 9. Euangelium nil aliud est, quam patefactio mysterii voluntatis diuinæ, de redemptione generi humani & gratuita remissione peccatorum per Christum, v. 7. Quæ salutifera tanti mysterii patefactio cum accepta referatur τῇ εὐδοκίᾳ, siue beneplacito diuino; haud inualide colligitur, Deum nulla necessitate adstrictum, nullis operum nostrorum meritis prouocatum, sed mera beneuolentia & misericordia adductum esse ad ministerium de seruandis per Christum hominibus reuelandum, & eiusque scriptionem procurandam, vt credentes in Christum vitam habeant in nomine ipsius, Io. XX, 31. Dicis: Deus euangelium quidem reuelauit, litterisque consignari curauit ex gratia; sed non eadem de caussa scribi iussit legem; quippe quæ est littera occidens, 2 Cor. III, 6. Iram operans, Rom. IV, 15. Resp. 1) Deus ex gratia dedit legem, sanctæ regulam vitæ. Commemorat enim psaltes regius, Deum specialem beneuolentiam testatum esse hoc perinsigni amoris pignore in populum Israëliticum, quod verba sua Iacobo, statuta sua & iudicia sua Israëli annuntiauerit; cum tamen gentes eodem fanoris gradu in V. T. non dignatus sit, Ps. CXLVII, 9. 2) Lex dicitur littera occidens & iram operans, non per se, sed per accidens, culpa hominum, eam proterue transgredientium, quibus iram Dei mortemque denuntiat: per se autem lex bona & sancta est. Rom. VII, 10.

Prob. b. Homo animalis, quamdiu in his terris peregrinatur, destitutus luce viali verbi diuini, perambulat deserta inuia, viam vero domini non cognoscit, Sap. V, 7. Quare Deus propitius, vicem peccatoris miseratus, accendit lucernam pedibus ipsius verbum suum, & lucem semitæ eius, Ps. CXIX, 105. Quod verbum suum Deus, viuæ vocis traditione, sine scripturæ adminiculo, conferuatum propagauit vltra 2500. annos. Vide chronologiam D. CALOVII bibliis illustratis præfixam. fol. 38. At inualescente innumeralibili hominum multitudine, & imminuto vitæ humanæ spatio, Deus primaria diuinarum reuelationum capita scriptis comprehendi iussit, vt memoriæ humanæ imbecillitati sacræ scripturæ subsidio consuleretur, perfidia hæreticorum reprimeretur, & corruptelæ, traditione vivæ vocis minus fida irrepentes, auerterentur.

Conf. D. GERHARD, in Exeg. fol. 15.


### Q. XI. What is the less principal cause of Holy Scripture?

The efficient, less principal, and ministerial cause of Holy Scripture were the holy men of God , prophets under the Old and apostles under the New Testament , who, with the Holy Spirit inspiring them, applied their hand to the pen and adorned Scripture in diverse places and times.

Prob. a. The amanuenses, by whose ministry the Holy Spirit was used in recording the sacred letters, are called by the apostle Peter with singular emphasis the holy men of God, 2 Ep. I, 21. Who, just as they were otherwise holy both by the imputed holiness of Christ and by the holiness of morals inherent in them: so they were peculiarly and immediately called to this by God, set apart, consecrated, and instructed with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, so that they might commit divine revelations to writing.

Prob. b. The prophets were the holy men of God who, before the Messiah was exhibited in the flesh, composed the Scripture of the Old Testament: most of whom performed the public prophetic office. You should observe that in the class of writers of the Old Testament are also contained David, Solomon, and Daniel, who did not perform the public office of teaching in the Israelite church: Wherefore it must either be said that the sacred writers of the Old Testament are denominated prophets by synecdoche from the more important part, because most of them sustained the public office of teaching in the church; or in a broader sense, by prophet is to be understood any writer of the Old Testament who is θεόπνευστος (God-breathed). Concerning the prophets, St. Peter affirms that they spoke (and wrote) impelled by the Holy Spirit, 2 Ep. I, 21. Prob. c.

What the apostles saw and heard, they not only announced by living voice, but also wrote, so that our joy might be complete, 1 Jn. I, 4. They wrote the same, not in the learned words of human wisdom, but in the learned words of the Holy Spirit, 1 Cor. II, 13. But by the name of apostles are here designated the holy men of God who, after Christ was born, adorned the Scripture of the New Testament: although not all were from the college of the apostles, chosen by Christ before the ascension to teach all nations of the elect; but were numbered among the apostles after Christ was taken up into heaven, such as were Matthias (whose writings, however, we do not have) and Paul. Indeed, in a broader sense, apostolic men are also called apostles here, being next to the apostles in office and dignity, such as were Mark and Luke, the evangelists. Which broader meaning of the word apostle is not unusual. For Paul, Rom. XVI, 7, calls Andronicus and Junia notable among the apostles, and Phil. II, 25, calls Epaphroditus the Philippian an apostle.

Obj. By some theologians, the writers of the New Testament are distinguished into apostles and evangelists. But that distinction is not adequate, so that no evangelist is an apostle, nor any apostle (strictly so called) an evangelist. For Matthew and John were not only evangelists, but also apostles strictly so called.

Latin:

Causa efficiens minus principalis atque ministerialis scripturæ sacræ fuerunt sancti Dei homines , prophetæ sub veteri & apostoli sub nouo testamento , qui, Spiritu sancto inspirante, manum calamo admouerunt, scripturamque locis & temporibus diuersis adornarunt.

Prob. a. Amanuenses, quorum ministerio Spiritus S. vsus est in consignandis sacris litteris, ab apostolo Petro singulari cum emphasi appellantur sancti Dei homines, 2 Ep. I, 21. Qui, sicut alias sancti fuerunt tum sanctitate Christi imputata, tum sanctitate morum inhærente: ita peculiariter atque immediate a Deo ad id vocati, segregati, consecrati & donis Spiritus S. instructi fuerunt, vt reuelationes diuinas in litteras referrent.

Prob. b. Prophetæ fuerunt sancti Dei homines, qui ante Messiam in carne exhibitum scripturam veteris testamenti concinnarunt: quorum plerique publico munere prophetico functi sunt. Obserues, quod in classe scriptorum veteris testamenti contineantur etiam Dauid, Salomon & Daniel, qui publicum docendi munus in ecclesia Israëlitica non obierunt: Quare vel dicendum est, scriptores sacros veteris testamenti denominari prophetas per synecdochen a parte potiori, eo quod plerique eorum publicum docendi officium in ecclesia sustinuerunt; vel laxiori sensu per prophetam intelligendus est quilibet scriptor veteris testamenti θεόπνευστος. De prophetis affirmat S. Petrus, quod locuti sint (& scripserint) impulsi a Spiritu S. 2 Ep. I, 21.

Prob. c. Quæ apostoli viderunt, & audierunt, illa non tantum viua voce annuntiarunt, sed & scripserunt, vt gaudium nostrum sit completum, 1 Io. I, 4. Scripserunt iidem non doctis sapientiæ humanæ verbis, sed doctis Spiritus S. 1 Cor. II, 13. Apostolorum autem nomine hic designantur sancti Dei homines, qui post natum Christum scripturam noui testamenti adornarunt: quamuis non omnes fuerint e collegio apostolorum, a Christo ante ascensionem ad docendum omnes gentes electorum; sed post Christum in cælos euectum apostolis annumerati sint, quales fuerunt Matthias (cuius tamen scripta non habemus) & Paullus. Quin & apostoli sensu latiori hic nuncupantur viri apostolici, apostolis munere ac dignitate proximi, quales fuerunt Marcus, & Lucas, euangelistæ. Quæ laxior significatio vocis apostoli non est insolita. Nam Paullus Rom. XVI, 7. Andronicum & Iuniam insignes inter apostolos, & Phil. II, 25. Epaphroditum Philippensum apostolum appellat.

Obs. A nonnullis theologis scriptores noui testamenti in apostolos & euangelistas distinguuntur. At vero distinctio illa non est adæquata, vt nullus euangelista sit apostolus, nec vllus apostolus (stricte dictus) euangelista. Nam Matthæus, & Ioannes non solum euangelistæ, sed & apostoli stricte dicti fuerunt.


### Q. XII. Did the sacred amanuenses write by the command of God?

That an express command to write was given divinely to certain sacred amanuenses, Scripture openly testifies

Prob. a. By the express command of God, they were stirred to write: Moses, Exodus 17:14, Deuteronomy 31:19; Isaiah 8:1, 30:8; Jeremiah 36:2; Habakkuk 2:2; John, Revelation 1:11, etc.

Twelve times in the Apocalypse we read that a special mandate for writing was given to John by God. Proof b.

(1) From the general mandate of Christ, Matt. XXVIII, 19: Go, teach all nations. Nations are taught not only by living voice, but also by writings. Therefore, the apostles had a general mandate to teach either by proclamation or by the writing of the divine word. They had a mandate to teach all nations even of subsequent times until the extreme old age of the world (as is evident from the annexed promise, v. 20). But the apostles could not teach the nations of subsequent times by living voice without writing. Therefore, the mandate of writing is also included under the general mandate of teaching.

(2) From the impulse of the Holy Spirit, which St. Peter teaches in 2 Epist. I, 21: Prophecy was not brought by the will of men, but holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit. Whatever prophecy was not brought by the will of men, but by the impulse of the Holy Spirit, that was published by the will and command of God. But προφητεία τῆς γραφῆς, written prophecy (cf. v. 20), was not brought by the will of men, but by the impulse of the Holy Spirit. Therefore. You say: An internal impulse of the Holy Spirit is one thing, an external mandate is another.

It happens not rarely that someone is impelled to write who is not commanded. Resp. The internal impulse of the divine Spirit is an internal mandate equivalent to an external mandate. The impulse of a master urging a servant to write is a mandate of great weight. But the Holy Spirit is true God and the supreme master.

(3) From the divine inspiration of the sacred letters, which St. Paul inculcates in 2 Tim. III, 16: All scripture is divinely inspired. Whoever dictates to someone the things and words to be written, he directly commands the amanuensis, who is subject to him, to write. But God dictated to the prophets as well as to the apostles, etc. Therefore.

(4) From the apostolic office, in which those holy men were legates of God, 2 Cor. V, 20. Legates are bound to the mandate of their prince. Peter, a legate of God, did not sustain preaching the gospel to the nations without a divine mandate: Therefore, much less did he dare to write an epistle, not being commanded by God. See.

Acts X, 19, 26.

Antithesis. The antithesis is that of the Papists, who deny that the evangelists and apostles wrote by divine mandate; they rely on the following arguments.

I. If it had been the intention of Christ and the apostles to narrow and restrict the word of God to scripture, Christ would have first commanded a matter of such importance. But that command is read nowhere. Resp.

1. He certainly commanded it generally, when he ordered the apostles to teach, Matt. XXVIII, 19. We are taught equally by scripture and by living voice. 2. Just as the apostle John was instructed and excited by a special mandate to write: so it is easy to conjecture that the remaining apostles did not undertake the arduous province of writing without a divine mandate; otherwise they would have incurred the same crime that a secretary commits by writing a document to citizens without the order of his prince.

II.

If the apostles received a general mandate to write from God, it was necessary for all the apostles to write. But not all the apostles wrote. Therefore, they did not receive a general mandate to write. Resp. The general mandate to teach was given divinely to the whole college of apostles; some of whom, impelled by the Holy Spirit, taught both by voice and by writings; others taught only by the proclamation of the living voice, who nevertheless approved the writings of others with their votes, and referred their hearers to the same.

III. Whoever wrote incidentally, when an occasion was offered, or when a particular necessity was pressing, they did not write by divine mandate. But the apostles, etc. Therefore. The major premise is evident, because a minister commanded by his master to write does not draft letters incidentally. The minor is proven: the apostles were impelled to write by various occasions.

St. Matthew, as witnessed by EUSEBIUS, book 3 of his history.

chap.

Quest.

Quest. 24. He took the occasion for writing the gospel from the fact that, after the gospel had been preached to the Gentiles, thinking of his departure, he judged it good and useful to leave some memorial of his teaching to those from whom he was departing, and this after many years had elapsed since the passion of the Lord. The same author in book II, chapter 15, says that St. Mark was not incited to write by his own motion or by the command of Peter, but solely by the request and solicitation of the Romans. Dealing with Luke in book 3, chapter 24, he testifies that he was stimulated to apply his hand to the pen because not a few were thrusting themselves forward to write many things which they did not know, so that he might gradually oppose the splendor of truth to the creeping uncertain and doubtful things. Add that he learned the better part of those things which he wrote by hearing and tradition. As regards John, the same author testifies that he did not write until he was burdened by the years of extreme old age, and this when he was urged by the bishops of Asia to refute the heresy of the Ebionites. Resp. The occasion and other motives for writing were not fortuitous, or encountered by the apostles by accident, but were offered to them by the peculiar providence of God, by which they were made more certain of the will of God, by which they were invited to write. To this is added that, although they wrote some things to private individuals out of occasion or particular necessity, all things were nevertheless divinely directed to the common benefit of the catholic church. Wherefore the will and command of God remains the principal impulsive cause; occasion and necessity are secondary motives, which are not to be opposed to the divine command, but subordinated to it, and composed with it.

IV. If the apostles had wished to commit their doctrine to writing by divine command on purpose, they would certainly have committed a catechism to writing. But they did not commit this to writing. Therefore. The consequence is clear, because a catechism is an epitome of things to be believed and things to be done, necessary to be known for a sinner tending toward salvation. Resp. The consequence is null. For it was not necessary that the apostles should commit a catechism to writing, in which things to be believed and done would be comprehended. For those things are comprehended by the historical revelation of those things which Jesus and the apostles taught and did, as well as by the epistles of holy men, from which it was easy to extract and methodically arrange a catechism.

Quest. XIII. What is the matter from which [is] holy scripture?

The matter from which holy scripture consists are the letters, syllables, voices, phrases, periods, and canonical books both of the old testament, which were written before the Messiah was manifested in the flesh, and of the new testament, which were committed to writing after Christ was born.

Prob. This is common to holy scripture with other writings, that it is said to consist of letters, syllables, and words, as if of matter. Although matter does not belong to it univocally or properly speaking; for this belongs only to substances composed of matter and form; but holy scripture is one by aggregation: nevertheless, we attribute to it matter from which, analogically.

Quest. IV. What is the matter about which holy scripture is concerned?

The matter about which holy scripture is concerned is either general or special. The special and primary matter are the dogmas of faith and the precepts of morals (a). The general matter are all things which are contained in the canonical writings of the prophets and apostles (b).

Prob. a. By the dogmas of faith, things to be believed, and by the precepts of morals, things to be done are explained to the sinner to be saved, and thus holy scripture is primarily concerned about them.

b. Contained in Holy Scripture are historical, chronological, genealogical, astronomical, physical, and political matters; which, although they are not simply necessary for salvation to be known; are nevertheless divinely revealed, because the knowledge of them contributes not a little to interpreting Holy Scripture and illustrating the dogmas of faith and the precepts of morals.

Latin:

Quibusdam amanuensibus sacris expressum mandatum ad scribendum diuinitus datum fuisse, aperte testatur scriptura (a): ex eadem valide colligimus, reliquos volente & iubente Deo scripsisse (b).

Prob. a. Expresso Dei mandato ad scribendum excitati sunt Moses, Exod. XVII, 14. Deut. XXXI, 19. Esaias, VIII, 1. XXX, 2, Ieremias, XXXVI, 2. Habacuc, II, 2. Ioannes, Apoc. I, 11. &c.

Duodecies in Apocalypsi legimus, speciale ad scribendum mandatum, Ioanni a Deo datum esse. Prob. b.

(1) Ex mandato Christi generali, Matth. XXVIII, 19. Euntes docete omnes gentes. Docentur gentes non tantum viva voce, sed et scriptis. Habuerunt igitur apostoli mandatum generale docendi aut praeconio, aut scriptione verbi divini. Habuerunt mandatum docendi omnes gentes etiam sequentium temporum usque ad extremam mundi senectam (prout constat ex annexa promissione v. 20.). Sed gentes sequentium temporum apostoli viva voce absque scripto docere nequiverunt. E. Sub mandato docendi generali etiam mandatum scribendi comprehenditur.

(2) Ex impulsu Spiritus sancti, quem docet S. Petrus 2 Epist. I, 21. Non voluntate hominum allata est prophetia, sed a Spiritu S. impulsi locuti sunt sancti Dei homines. Quaecunque prophetia non allata voluntate hominum, sed impulsu Spiritus sancti, illa volente et iubente Deo edita est. Atqui προφητεία τῆς γραφῆς, prophetia scripta (conf. v. 20.) non est allata voluntate hominum, sed impulsu Spiritus S. Ergo. Dicis: Aliud est internus Spiritus S. impulsus, aliud externum mandatum.

Haud raro contingit, vt aliquis ad scribendum impellatur, qui non iubetur. Resp. Internus Spiritus divini impulsus est mandatum internum aequipollens mandato externo. Impulsus domini instigantis ministrum ad scribendum est mandatum magni ponderis. Atqui Spiritus S. est verus Deus et summus dominus.

(3) Ex divina sacrarum litterarum inspiratione, quam inculcat S. Paullus 2 Tim. III, 16. Omnis scriptura divinitus inspirata est. Quicunque alicui dictat res et verba scribenda, ille amanuensem, sibi subiectum, directe iubet scribere. Atqui Deus tam prophetis, quam apostolis dictavit etc. Ergo.

(4) Ex munere apostolico, in quo sancti illi viri fuerunt legati Dei, 2 Cor. V, 20. Legati ad mandatum principis adstricti sunt. Petrus legatus Dei absque mandato divino evangelium praedicare gentibus non sustinuit: Ergo minus epistolam conscribere, a Deo non iussus, ausus est. Vid.

Act. X, 19, 26.

Antithesis Antithesis est Pontificiorum, negantium, euangelistas et apostolos ex mandato divino scripsisse; qui sequentibus innituntur argumentis.

I. Si Christo et apostolis fuisset propositum verbum Dei coarctandi et restringendi ad scripturam, in primis rem tanti momenti Christus praecepisset. Sed nullibi id praeceptum legitur. Resp.

1. Vtique praecepit generatim, quando apostolos iussit docere, Matth. XXVIII, 19. Docemur aeque scriptura, ac viva voce. 2. Sicut apostolus Ioannes speciali mandato ad scribendum instructus et excitatus est: ita coniectu proclive est, reliquos apostolos arduam scribendi provinciam non subiisse sine mandato divino; caeteroquin idem incurrissent crimen, quod fecretarius iniussu principis sui diploma ad ciues scribendos admittit.

II.

Si apostoli a Deo acceperunt generale ad scribendum mandatum, oportuit omnes apostolos scribere. Sed non omnes apostoli scripserunt. E. non acceperunt generale ad scribendum mandatum. Resp. Mandatum docendi generale divinitus datum est toti apostolorum collegio; quorum quidam impellente Spiritu sancto tam voce, quam scriptis; quidam tantum praeconio vivae vocis docuerunt, qui tamen aliorum scripta suffragiis suis comprobarunt, et ad eadem auditores suos remiserunt.

III. Quicunque scripserunt incidenter, oblata occasione, aut particulari urgente necessitate, illi non scripserunt ex mandato divino. Sed apostoli &c. E. Maior constat, quia minister iussus a domino scribere, non exarat litteras incidenter. Minor probatur: apostoli variis occasionibus ad scribendum impulsi sunt.

S. Matthæus, teste EVSEBIO lib. 3. histor.

cap.

Quaest.

Quaest. 24. occasionem scribendi euangelii sumsit ex eo, quod post euangelium prædicatum gentibus, de discessu cogitans, bonum & vtile iudicauit, aliquod doctrinæ suæ memoriale relinquere iis, a quibus discedebat, idque post multos annos a passione domini elapsos. Idem auctor lib. II. cap. 15. ait, S. Marcum non proprio motu, vel ex Petri mandato ad scribendum incitatum fuisse, sed rogatu & sollicitatione sola Romanorum. De Luca agens lib. 3. cap. 24. testatur, vt calamo manum admoueret, stimulatum fuisse, quia non pauci se ingerebant ad scribendum multa, quæ nesciebant, vt sensim serpentibus incertis & dubiis veritatis splendorem opponeret. Adde, quod meliorem partem eorum, quæ scripsit, auditione & traditione didicerit. Ad Ioannem quod attinet, testatur idem, ipsum non scripsisse prius, quam extremæ senectutis annis grauaretur, idque cum vrgeretur ab Asiæ episcopis ad refutandam Ebionitarum hæresin. Resp. Occasio & alia motiua ad scribendum non fuerunt fortuita, aut per accidens apostolis obiecta, sed peculiari Dei prouidentia ipsis oblata, quibus de voluntate Dei, qua ad scribendum inuitabantur, certiores reddebantur. Huc accedit, quod, quamuis ex occasione, aut necessitate particulari, ad priuatos nonnulla scriberent, omnia tamen ad commune commodum ecclesiæ catholicæ diuinitus dirigerentur. Quamobrem manet voluntas ac mandatum Dei caussa impulsiua principalis; occasio & necessitas sunt motiua secundaria, quæ mandato diuino non sunt opponenda, sed subordinanda, & cum eo componenda.

IV. Si apostoli ad mandatum diuinum ex professo suam doctrinam litteris mandare voluissent, vtique catechismum litteris consignassent. Sed hunc non consignarunt. Ergo. Consequentia patet, quia catechismus est epitome credendorum & agendorum, peccatori ad salutem tendenti cognitu necessariorum. Resp. Consequentia nulla est. Neque enim necesse erat, vt apostoli catechismum consignarent, quo credenda & agenda comprehenderentur. Comprehensa enim illa sunt historica reuelatione eorum, quæ Iesus & apostoli docuerunt & fecerunt, nec non epistolis virorum sanctorum, e quibus catechismum excerpere & methodice concinnare facile erat.

Quæst. XIII. Quæ est materia, ex qua, sacræ scripturæ?

Materia, ex qua sacra scriptura constat, sunt litteræ, syllabæ, voces, phrases, periodi & libri canonici tam veteris testamenti, qui ante Messiam in carne manifestatum scripti, quam noui testamenti, qui post natum Christum consignati sunt.

Prob. Hoc commune est sacræ scripturæ cum aliis scriptis, vt ex litteris, syllabis & verbis, velut materia, constare dicatur. Quamuis illi non competat materia vniuoce aut proprie dicta; nam hæc conuenit tantum substantiis ex materia & forma compositis; sacra scriptura autem est vnum per aggregationem: attamen ei materiam, ex qua, analogice tribuimus.

Quæst. IV. Quæ est materia, circa quam sacra scriptura versatur?

Materia, circa quam sacra scriptura versatur, est vel generalis, vel specialis. Materia specialis & primaria sunt dogmata fidei & præcepta morum (a). Materia generalis sunt res omnes, quæ in scriptis canonicis prophetarum & apostolorum continentur (b).

Prob. a. Dogmatibus fidei credenda, præceptis morum agenda peccatori saluando exponuntur, adeoque circa illa sacra scriptura primario versatur.

Prob. b. Continentur in S. scriptura res historicae, chronologicae, genealogicae, astronomicae, physicae & politicae; quae licet cognitu ad salutem non sint simpliciter necessariae; sunt tamen divinitus revelatae, quia illarum notitia ad interpretandam sacram scripturam & illustranda dogmata fidei morumque praecepta haud parum facit.


### Q. XV. What is the form of Holy Scripture?

The internal form of Holy Scripture is the sense θεόπνευστος (divinely inspired), expressed by words dictated by the Holy Spirit .

Prob. a. Of every word, as much that which is spoken by mouth as that which is committed to letters, the form is the sense, or the power of signifying. Wherefore if Scripture is considered generally, as it is written word, its internal form, and that a generic one, is the sense, or the signification of the words and phrases which the holy men of God used in adorning Holy Scripture. Prob. b.

If Holy Scripture is viewed specifically, as the word of God, its internal form is the divine sense; for this reason, that through this, as a reason a priori, Holy Scripture is constituted in its specific being, and is distinguished from any human writing whatsoever. See above Q. VII. Prob. c.

Since by θεοπνευσία (divine inspiration), or the immediate dictation of the Holy Spirit, the concepts of both things and words were suggested to the sacred amanuenses: the sense θεόπνευστος (divinely inspired), expressed by words dictated by the Holy Spirit, completes the adequate internal form of Holy Scripture. For by this πρεσδιορισμῷ (qualification), or addition, Holy Scripture is distinguished not only from the writings of other men, kings, princes, philosophers, etc., but also from versions of Holy Scripture prepared by human study; for these, if they are conformable to the original text, indeed represent the divine sense and convey it to us: but they are distant from Scripture viewed in the original text by as great an interval as Scripture αὐτόπιστος (self-credible), to which faith is owed of itself, is distant from Scripture, to which faith is not owed of itself, but only on account of another original one to which it is exactly conformable; or Scripture that is norming, and that which is normed; Scripture, to which it is repugnant that it should have been false, and Scripture, to which it is not repugnant that falsehood should underlie it. Confer D. M V S A E V S in introduct. in theol. p. 271.

Latin:

Forma sacrae scripturae interna est sensus θεόπνευστος , vocibus a Spiritu sancto dictatis expressus .

Prob. a. Omnis verbi tam ore prolati, quam in litteras relati, forma est sensus, sive vis significandi. Quamobrem si scriptura consideretur generatim, prout est verbum scriptum, forma eius interna, eaque generica, est sensus, sive significatio vocum & phrasium, quibus sancti Dei homines in adornanda sacra scriptura usi sunt.

Prob. b. Si sacra scriptura spectetur speciatim, ut verbum Dei, forma illius interna est sensus divinus; propterea, quod per hunc, velut rationem a priori, scriptura sacra in esse suo specifico constituitur, & a quovis scripto humano distinguitur. Vid. supra quaest.

VII. Prob. c. Quoniam τῇ θεοπνευσίᾳ, sive immediato Spiritus sancti dictamine, conceptus tam rerum, quam vocum, amanuensibus sacris suggesti sunt: formam internam adaequatam sacrae scripturae absolvit sensus θεόπνευστος, verbis a Spiritu sancto dictatis expressus. Nam hoc πρεσδιορισμῷ, sive additamento, sacra scriptura distinguitur non tantum a scriptis aliorum hominum, regum, principum, philosophorum &c. sed etiam a versionibus sacrae scripturae studio humano concinnatis; quippe quae, si conformes sint textui originali, sensum quidem divinum repraesentant, nobisque ingerunt: at a scriptura in textu primigenio spectata tanto distant intervallo, quanto distat scriptura αὐτόπιστος, cui per se debetur fides, a scriptura, cui per se non creditur, sed tantum propter aliam primigeniam, cui exacte conformis est; vel scriptura normans, & normata; scriptura, cui repugnat fuisse falsum, & scriptura, cui falsum subesse non repugnat. Confer. D. M V S A E V S in introduct. in theol. p. 271.


### Q. XVI. Are the concepts of all things which are contained in the sacred writings divinely inspired?

The concepts of all things which are contained in the sacred writings were immediately inspired into the prophets and apostles by the Holy Spirit.

Prob. 1. From the Pauline utterance 2 Tim. III, 16. πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευσος, all Scripture is divinely inspired. Obs. (α) It is understood not indeterminately of any Scripture, but ἱερὰ (holy), as is evident from v. 15. (β) Θεοπνοὴ (divine breathing) or θεοπνευσία (divine inspiration) denotes both the antecedent divine motion, or the peculiar impulse of the will to write, and the immediate illumination, by which the intellect of the sacred writer is illuminated by the supernatural, and therefore extraordinary, light of divine grace, and the concepts of the things to be written are themselves immediately suggested by the Holy Spirit. This θεοπνευσία (divine inspiration), or divine inspiration, differs from divine governance. For by the latter it is only ensured that nothing is written which is not true, becoming, and congruous; but by the former, the concepts of the things to be written are suggested by the dictating Holy Spirit. The latter can provide an infallible Holy Scripture, but not θεόπνευσος (divinely inspired). From which we argue: If only the mysteries of faith, which are contained in the sacred writings, depend on divine inspiration, but the rest, which are knowable by the guidance of the light of nature, depend only on divine direction, the whole of Holy Scripture is not θεόπνευσος (divinely inspired). But, with the testimony of According to Paul, the entire Holy Scripture is divinely inspired. Therefore, not only the mysteries of faith, but also the remaining things knowable by the guidance of the light of nature, which are contained in the sacred letters, have been divinely suggested and inspired.

II. From the promise of Christ, John XIV, 26. "The Holy Spirit will teach you all things and will bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you." The Savior, now about to depart to the Father, promises the Holy Spirit to the apostles, who would most fully imbue their minds with heavenly doctrine, and would recall to their minds everything heard from Christ, whether not yet sufficiently understood or consigned to oblivion, so that, with this internal teacher as guide and president, they might either transmit by living voice or consign to writing all things necessary to be known.

From which it follows that the concepts of all things described by the apostles were immediately infused into them by the Holy Spirit.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, Socinians, and Arminians, according to whose mind the mysteries of faith were indeed divinely inspired to the sacred amanuenses; but things of lighter moment, knowable from the light of nature, were indeed directed by divine governance while they were being written, so that they might be reported from truth, but were not divinely inspired. We shall weigh their arguments.

I. Whatever the prophets and apostles knew by natural reason or experimental knowledge, they did not need divine revelation to know. But historical, natural, moral, etc. [things are such]. Therefore. The major premise is evident, because what one knows from the light of reason, one does not need the supernatural light of revelation to know.

Resp. 1. Under the name of revelation lies a certain ambiguity that must now be unfolded.

Revelation is taken sometimes more narrowly, sometimes more broadly. In the narrower sense, it denotes the supernatural manifestation of latent and occult things. For to reveal, in Greek ἀποκαλύπτειν, by the force of its origin, is to uncover and manifest things that are hidden and, as it were, lying under a certain veil.

See 1 Cor. II, 10;

Gal. I, 12; Matt. XI, 25. In the broader sense, revelation is taken for the manifestation of any things whatsoever, even those that can be known by the guidance of the light of nature, provided it is done in a supernatural way.

In the former sense, the whole argument is conceded; in the latter, the major premise is denied.

2. Things that were known to the sacred writers are considered either absolutely and in themselves, or respectively, insofar as they were to be written by the will of God. In the former way, they were known to the sacred writers even before [the act of writing], but not in the latter way. For although the sacred amanuenses had known certain things that were described by them before the act of writing, yet it was not known to them by themselves whether those things were to be described by the will of God, with what circumstances, in what order, and with what words they were to be committed to letters.

It not infrequently happens that we dictate to an amanuensis things and words not at all unknown to him; nor is it his place, however, to add or subtract anything, but to depend entirely upon the mouth of the dictator: thus also the sacred amanuenses recorded nothing in letters except what was suggested by the Holy Spirit.

II. There are found in Scripture things of lighter moment hardly worthy of being referred to divine revelation, e.g., the staff of Jacob, Gen. XXXII, 10; the cloak of Paul, 2 Tim. IV, 13.

Resp. Whatever things, even the least, God deemed worthy of creation, He judged not unworthy of supernatural revelation. Meanwhile, no one reverently worshiping God will consider anything in the Scriptures as light or vile which has been inserted into them by the most wise counsel of God.

III. Many impious deeds are recounted in Holy Scripture which could not have been divinely inspired.

Resp. Those impious deeds are reported from truth; but they are not approved as good. Their historical narration is divinely inspired not for imitation, but for avoidance.

IV. Whoever confesses, and not the Lord, that he asserts something, he by this very fact confesses that not all things are inspired by the Lord.

But the apostle of the Gentiles, 1 Cor. VII, 12.

Resp. Distinguish between a general or implicit assertion and a special or explicit one. Paul confesses that the Lord did not explicitly assert or ordain anything concerning the perpetual cohabitation of a faithful husband with an unfaithful wife, and vice versa: but what is contained generally and implicitly therein, Gen. II, 24; Matt. XIX, 16, that very thing the apostle directs and applies specifically and explicitly to the present case; he points this out when he says: "But to the rest I say, not the Lord." V. Whoever as an amanuensis received the deeds he describes from men as eyewitnesses (αὐτόπταις), he did not receive them from divine inspiration. But Luke, the sacred amanuensis, etc., Luke I, 3. Therefore. Resp. The deeds that Luke received from human witnesses before describing them were divinely inspired into him in the very act of writing, so that he might write in decent order, with appropriate words, and with the necessary circumstances for knowledge added, without lapse of memory or any error. VI. John XIX, 35 says that he writes what he saw, not what was revealed to him. He appeals, therefore, in his written testimony about Jesus, not to divine inspiration, but to the sense of his eyes. Resp. John appeals as an eyewitness to sight, not to exclude divine inspiration, but to establish it. For he alleges the word of God revealed and recorded in letters both by Moses, Exod. XII, 46, and by the prophet Zechariah, ch. XII, 10. Here the testimony of the Holy Spirit and the apostles concurs, of which the author of our salvation says: "The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me. And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning." John XV, 26, 27. The apostles bore witness, moved by the Holy Spirit, 2 Pet. I, 21. VII. For things seen by the apostles to be truly described, divine assistance and governance sufficed, preserving the sacred amanuenses from error, and there seems to have been no need for divine inspiration. Resp. Holy Scripture is a certain homogeneous whole, and thus it was not consigned partly by divine inspiration and partly by divine direction; but πᾶσα γραφὴ ἱερά, the entire Holy Scripture, as much as there is of it, is called θεόπνευσος by the apostle. It is called θεόπνευσος, however, not from mere assistance, governance, or direction, but from divine dictation, suggestion, and inspiration. Observe that we are speaking of mere governance; otherwise, we do not entirely exclude divine governance, but we join it with θεοπνευσίᾳ. See DANNHAV. in hodof. p. 36. Quest. XVII. Are even the individual words, of which Holy Scripture consists, divinely inspired?. All and individual words that are read in the sacred code were inspired by the Holy Spirit to the prophets and apostles and dictated to the pen. Prob. I. Whatever Scripture is entirely θεόπνευσος, of that not only the sense or the things signified, but also the words, as signs of things, are divinely inspired. But Holy Scripture is, 2 Tim. III, 16. Therefore. The major premise is evident, because (1) the apostle does not simply say: "Every word of God is θεόπνευσος": for someone might in this way take the divine word formally for the divine sense: but he says: πᾶσα γραφὴ, "all Scripture": which denotes not precisely the divine sense, but also the written words. (2) The apostle does not say πάντα γεγραμμένα θεόπνευσα, but πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευσος, to indicate that not only the things contained in Holy Scripture were divinely revealed, but also that the words themselves were dictated to the pen by the Holy Spirit. (3) The apostle speaks of that Scripture which Timothy had read as a boy, and which, having been made a bishop, he assiduously pondered and explained to his hearers. But he read and explained Holy Scripture as it consists not only of things, but also of written words. Therefore, the entire Holy Scripture, as it consists not only of things but also of written words, is divinely inspired. vice versa, [he] had asserted or sanctioned nothing explicitly: but what is contained in it generally and implicitly, Gen. II, 24; Matt. XIX, 16, that very thing the apostle directs and applies specifically and explicitly to the present case; he points this out when he says: "But to the rest I say, not the Lord."

V. Whoever as an amanuensis received the deeds which he describes from men, as eyewitnesses (αὐτόπταις), he did not receive the same from divine inspiration. But Luke, a holy amanuensis, etc., Luke I, 3. Therefore. Resp. The deeds which Luke received from human witnesses before describing them were divinely inspired in him at the very act of writing, so that he might write in a decent order, with appropriate words, and with the necessary circumstances for knowledge added, without any lapse of memory or any error.

VI. John XIX, 35 says that he writes what he has seen, not what was revealed to him. He appeals, therefore, in his written testimony about Jesus, not to divine inspiration, but to the sense of his eyes. Resp. John appeals to sight as an eyewitness, not to exclude divine inspiration, but to establish it. For he alleges the word of God revealed and committed to writing both by Moses, Exod. XII, 46, and by the prophet Zechariah, ch. XII, 10. Here the testimony of the Holy Spirit and of the apostles concurs, of which the author of our salvation says: "The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will testify of me. And you also will testify, because you have been with me from the beginning." John XV, 26, 27. The apostles testified, moved by the Holy Spirit, 2 Pet. I, 21.

VII. In order for the things seen by the apostles to be truly described, divine assistance and governance sufficed, preserving the holy amanuenses from error, and there seems to have been no need for divine inspiration. Resp. Holy Scripture is a certain homogeneous whole, and thus it was not consigned partly by divine inspiration and partly by divine direction; but πᾶσα γραφὴ ἱερά, the whole Holy Scripture, as much as there is of it, is called θεόπνευσος by the apostle. It is called θεόπνευσος, however, not from mere assistance, governance, or direction, but from divine dictation, suggestion, and inspiration. Observe that we are speaking of mere governance: otherwise, we do not entirely exclude divine governance, but we join it with θεοπνευσίᾳ. See DANNHAV. in hodof. p. 36.

Latin:

conceptus omnium rerum, quae in sacris litteris habentur, divinitus inspirati? Conceptus omnium rerum, quae in sacris litteris habentur, prophetis & apostolis a Spiritu sancto immediate inspirati sunt.

Prob. 1. Ab effato Paulino 2 Tim. III, 16. πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευσος, omnis scriptura divinitus est inspirata. Obs. (α) Intelligitur non indeterminate quaevis scriptura, sed ἱερὰ, sancta, vt patet ex v. 15. (β) Θεοπνοὴ sive θεοπνευσία notat, tum antecedentem motum divinum, sive peculiarem impulsum voluntatis ad scribendum, tum immediatam illuminationem, qua intellectus scriptoris sacri supernaturali, eoque extraordinario, lumine gratiae divinae collustratur, & conceptus rerum scribendarum ipsa Spiritu sancto immediate suggeruntur. Differt haec θεοπνευσία, sive inspiratio divina, a gubernatione divina. Nam hac tantum cauetur, ne quidquam scribatur, quod non fit ex vero, decoro, congruo; illa autem a dictante Spiritu sancto conceptus rerum scribendarum suggeruntur. Illa praestare potest scripturam sacram infallibilem, sed non θεόπνευσy. Ex quo argumentamur: Si tantum mysteria fidei, quae in sacris litteris habentur, a divina inspiratione, reliqua autem, ductu luminis naturae cognoscibilia, tantum a directione divina pendent, tota sacra scriptura non est θεόπνευσος. At, teste Paulo, tota sacra scriptura est divinitus inspirata. E, non tantum mysteria fidei, sed & reliqua ductu luminis naturæ cognoscibilia, quæ in sacris litteris habentur, divinitus suggesta & inspirata sunt.

II. A promisso Christi Io. XIV, 26. Spiritus sanctus docebit vos omnia & commonefaciet vos de omnibus, quæ dixi vobis. Promittit saluator, iamiam abiturus ad patrem, apostolis Spiritum sanctum, qui mentes ipsorum doctrina cœlesti plenissime imbuturus, & omnia audita a Christo, siue nondum satis intellecta, siue obliuioni tradita, ipsis in mentem fit reuocaturus, vt, duce & præfide hoc interno doctore, omnia cognitu necessaria, vel viua voce traderent gentibus, vel scriptis consignarent.

Ex quo consequitur, conceptus omnium rerum ab apostolis descriptarum, ipsis immediate a Spiritu sancto fuisse inditos.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, Socinianorum, & Arminianorum, ex quorum mente mysteria quidem fidei amanuensibus sacris divinitus sunt inspirata: res autem leuioris momenti, e lumine naturæ cognoscibiles, a gubernatione quidem diuina, cum scriberentur, fuerunt directæ, vt ex vero referrentur, sed non divinitus inspiratæ. Quorum argumenta pensitabimus.

I. Quæcunque naturali ratione, vel experimentali notitia, sciuerunt prophetæ & apostoli, ad ea cognoscenda non indiguerunt reuelatione diuina. Sed historica, naturalia, moralia &c. Ergo. Maior constat, quia, quod quis cognoscit e lumine rationis, ad illud sciendum non indiget supernaturali lumine reuelationis.

Resp. 1. Sub nomine reuelationis latet quædam ambiguitas iam euoluenda.

Sumitur reuelatio modo angustius, modo latius. Sensu angustiori notat rerum latentium & occultarum manifestationem supernaturalem. Reuelare enim, Græce ἀποκαλύπτειν, vi originis est occulta, & quasi sub velamine quadam latentia, retegere & manifestare.

Vid. 1 Cor. II, 10.

Gal. I, 12. Matth. XI, 25. Latiori significatu reuelatio sumitur pro rerum quarumuis, etiam quæ ductu luminis naturæ cognosci possunt, manifestatione, modo supernaturali facta.

Priori sensu conceditur totum argumentum, posteriori negatur maior.

2. Res, quæ scriptoribus sacris fuerunt notæ, considerantur vel absolute & in se, vel respectiue, quatenus ex voluntate Dei fuerunt scribendæ. Priori modo iam ante scriptoribus sacris fuerunt cognitæ, non vero posteriori modo. Tametfi enim amanuenses sacri res quasdam, quæ ab ipsis descriptæ sunt, habuerint cognitas ante actum scriptionis, per se tamen ipsis non fuit cognitum, an res illæ ex voluntate Dei essent describendæ, quibus circumstantiis, quo ordine, & quibus verbis essent litteris mandandæ.
