Haud raro vfu venit, vt amanuensi dictemus res & verba, ipsi minime ignota; neque tamen ipsius est, quidquam addere, aut detrahere, sed ab ore dictantis in solidum pendere: sic & amanuenses sacri nil, nisi a Spiritu sancto suggestum, in litteras retulerunt.

II. Inueniuntur in scriptura res leuioris momenti vix dignæ, quæ reuelationi diuinæ acceptæ referantur, v. gr. baculus Iacobi, Gen. XXXII, 10. penula Pauli 2 Tim. IV, 13.

Resp. Quas res, vel minimas, Deus creatione dignas censuit, eas non indignas supernaturali reuelatione iudicauit. Nemo interim Deum reuerenter colens in scripturis pro leui aut vili habebit, quod sapientissimo Dei consilio ipsis est insertum.

III. Multa facta impia in S. scriptura recensentur, quæ non potuerunt divinitus esse inspirata.

Resp. Facta illa impia referuntur ex vero: at non, vt bona, approbantur. Historica eorum narratio divinitus est inspirata non ad imitationem, sed ad euitationem.

IV. Quicunque fatetur, & non Dominum, aliquid affeuerare, ille hoc ipso fatetur, non omnia a Domino esse inspirata.

Atqui gentium apostolus, 1 Cor. VII, 12. Resp.

Dist. inter affeuerationem generalem, siue implicitam, & specialem, siue explicitam. Fatetur Paullus, Dominum de perpetua cohabitatione mariti fidelis cum vxore infideli, & vice versa, nihil explicite assuerasse aut sanxisse: sed quod generatim et implicite in ea continetur, Gen. II, 24. Matth. XIX, 16. id ipsum apostolus speciatim et explicite ad praesentem casum dirigit et applicat; id indigitat, cum inquit: reliquis vero ego dico, non Dominus.

V. Quicunque amanuensis res gestas, quas describit, accepit ab hominibus, tanquam testibus αὐτόπταις, ille non accepit easdem ex divina inspiratione. Atqui Lucas, amanuensis facer [sic] et c. Luc. I, 3. Ergo. Resp. Quas res gestas Lucas ante descriptionem earundem accepit a testibus humanis, in ipso scriptionis actu divinitus ipsi sunt inspiratae, ut decenti ordine, convenientibus verbis, et adiectis cognitu necessariis circumstantiis, sine lapsu memoriae aut errore ullo, scriberet.

VI. Ioannes XIX, 35. dicit, se scribere, quae viderit, non quae ipsi revelata fuerint. Provocat ergo in suo de Iesu testimonio scripto non ad inspirationem divinam, sed ad sensum oculorum. Resp. Provocat Ioannes, ut oculatus testis ad visum, non ut inspirationem divinam excludat, sed ut eam stabiliat. Allegat enim verbum Dei revelatum et in litteras relatum tum a Mose Exod. XII, 46. tum a propheta Zacharia c. XII, 10. Concurrit hic testimonium Spiritus S. et apostolorum, de quo salutis nostrae auctor inquit: Spiritus veritatis, qui ex patre exit, ille testabitur de me. Etiam vos testabimini, quia ab initio mecum estis. Io. XV, 26. 27. Testati sunt apostoli acti a Spiritu sancto, 2 Petr. I, 21.

VII. Vt res ab apostolis visae vere describerentur, suffecit divina assistentia et gubernatio, praeferuans amanuenses sacros ab errore, neque opus videtur fuisse divina inspiratione. Resp. S. scriptura est totum quoddam homogeneum, adeoque non alia ex parte divina inspiratione, alia ex parte divina directione consignata est; sed πᾶσα γραφὴ ἱερά, tota scriptura sancta, quanta quanta est, ab apostolo vocatur θεόπνευσος. Dicitur autem θεόπνευσος, non a mera assistentia, gubernatione aut directione, sed a divina dictatione, suggestione et inspiratione. Obferues, quod loquamur de mera gubernatione: ceteroqui gubernationem divinam non prorsus excludimus, sed cum θεοπνευσίᾳ coniungimus. Vid. DANNHAV. in hodof. p. 36.


### Q. XVI. Are the concepts of all things which are contained in the sacred writings divinely inspired?: 36. Question XVII. Are the individual words, of which Holy Scripture consists, also divinely inspired?

36. Question XVII. Are the individual words, of which Holy Scripture consists, also divinely inspired?

All and individual words, which are read in the sacred code, were inspired by the Holy Spirit to the prophets and apostles and dictated to the pen.

Proof I. Whatever scripture is entirely θεόπνευσος, of that not only the sense or the signified things, but also the voices [words], as signs of things, are divinely inspired.

But Holy Scripture, 2 Tim. III, 16. Therefore. The major premise is certain, because (1) the apostle does not simply say: "Every word of God is θεόπνευσος": for someone might in this way take the divine word formally for the divine sense: but he says: πᾶσα γραφὴ, "all scripture": which denotes not precisely the divine sense, but also the written voices. (2) The apostle does not say πάντα γεγραμμένα θεόπνευσα, but πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευσος, to indicate that not only the things contained in Holy Scripture were divinely revealed, but also that the very voices were dictated to the pen by the Holy Spirit. (3) The apostle speaks of that scripture which Timothy had read as a boy, and which, having been made a bishop, he diligently perused and explained to his hearers. But he read and explained Holy Scripture as it consists not only of things, but also of written voices. Therefore, the whole of Holy Scripture, as it consists not only of things, but also of written voices, is divinely inspired. II. Whatever has proceeded not from human will, as a principle, but from the special impulse of the Holy Spirit, that whole thing, composed of words and things, is of divine origin. But Holy Scripture is conceived in the Hebrew and Greek idiom, etc. Therefore.

The major premise is clear, since that is called human invention or writing which proceeds from human will. The minor premise is proved from 2 Pet. 1:20-21. "No prophecy of scripture is of ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως, private interpretation: for prophecy was not brought in old time by the will of men: but holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit." Objection (1): The apostle Peter denies that the prophecy of scripture is of private interpretation, on this foundation, because it was not brought or proceeded from human will, but from the impulse of the Holy Spirit.

But Holy Scripture must be interpreted as it is composed of words and things. Therefore, no word of written prophecy proceeds from human judgment, but from divine inspiration.

(2) Holy men of God are said to have spoken as moved by the Holy Spirit. Therefore, not only the things, but ἡ λαλιὰ, the speech, or the words of the apostles, as uttered by mouth, so also written, have proceeded from the divine Spirit: for by λαλιὰν, both diction and writing are denoted indifferently (since they do not differ in reality) by virtue of the saying in Acts 3:24. (3) Although St. Peter primarily speaks of the prophecy of the Old Testament, vindicating it for an immediate divine origin, yet by a ready and good consequence it is elicited from this Petrine statement that the scripture of the New Testament is consigned by divine inspiration as much regarding the words as regarding the things themselves. Which consequence will be the more lucid, the more accurately the following argument is weighed.

III. Whatever words the apostles uttered by living voice in their apostolic office, and consigned to letters, the Holy Spirit taught them. But the apostles uttered by living voice and consigned to letters the words existing in the code of the New Testament in their apostolic office. Therefore.

The major premise is Paul's, 1 Cor. 2:12-13. "We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit which is of God, that we might know the things that are freely given to us of God: which things also we speak, not in the words which man's wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Spirit teacheth." See above, quest. VIII, prob. c. The minor premise is clear in itself.

For example, the words existing in the epistle to the Romans are the words of Paul reduced to writing, and they are plainly conformable to the words which Paul spoke by mouth in his apostolic office, on account of the most exact harmony of the divine word uttered by mouth and related into letters. IV. God immediately taught Moses the words to be written. Exod. 34:27-28. Afterward Jehovah said to Moses: "Write thou these words: for after the mouth (tenor) of these words I have made a covenant with thee and with Israel." By these words to be written, some interpreters understand precisely the words of the decalogue, others the entire precepts of the Mosaic law, moral, Levitical, and forensic. See D. Calov, in System. Theolog., vol. I, p. 564. But the words which Moses had to write by divine command, God himself had immediately taught him.

Compare v. 10 and ch. 19:3, following. What is the case of the Mosaic law, is in this part the reason for other divine writings. Therefore, it is so frequently inculcated in scripture: "The word of the Lord: thus said the Lord," so that it may be indicated that these words are not of human, but of divine origin.

V. If all and singular the words which the sacred amanuenses use in scripture are not divinely inspired: (1) there will be no distinction between the original text and versions adorned by human study; provided these are conformable to the authentic text, since these also express a sense that is θεόπνευστον (God-breathed), but not in words that are θεοπνεύστοις (God-breathed); (2) nor will the emphasis, force, or value of the words of the authentic text need to be elucidated with singular applied care: Which things are ἀτοπώτατα (most absurd), no more wicked to say than to think.

The antithesis is that of Erasmus, Suarez, Episcopius, Beza, Vorstius, and others who deny that the individual words of Holy Scripture were divinely inspired in the prophets and apostles: who argue: 1. If all and individual words of Holy Scripture were inspired by the one Spirit of God, there would be one manner of speaking for all the sacred amanuenses, one and the same style. But their style is very diverse. Therefore, not all and individual words of Holy Scripture were divinely inspired in them. The consequence of the major premise is proven, because one author forms one style. The antecedent is evident: for Isaiah, born in an illustrious place and educated in a court, wrote more elegantly; Amos, a herdsman, more humbly; Luke, polished in Greek letters, more elegantly.

Resp. (1) It happens among humans that one secular author, illustrious for the praise of his genius and eloquence, founds a varied manner of speaking. Certainly, Cicero expressed and cultivated a grand, a middle, and a humble style in speaking and writing. The same thing happens in divine matters.

St. John composed his gospel, epistles, and apocalypse with a diverse manner of diction, moved by the diversity of the subject matter, to which the style had to be adapted. For the Johannine gospel sets forth the divinity of Christ with the gravity of its words, the epistles the nourishment of charity with the sweetness of their diction, the apocalypse the fates of the church with a character familiar to the prophets, nowhere without a notable mark of θεοπνευστία (divine inspiration).

The Holy Spirit gives to each to speak as He Himself wills. Acts II, 4. (3) The style of the O. & N. T. is uniform, as regards substance: although, as regards the accidental conformation of style, the Holy Spirit, by a singular συγκατάβασις (condescension), lowered Himself to the geniuses, studies, and nations of the θεοπνεύστων (divinely inspired) men: just as in a musical organ the substance of the song, the harmony, and the tone is one; but the Spirit, who blows into the pipes, adapts Himself to the pipes, some sharper, some flatter.

Conf. DANNHAU. in hodosoph. p. 58.

II. That whose knowledge sacred writers acquired for themselves by daily use and custom was not divinely revealed to them. But the knowledge of the words and the manner of speaking by which Holy Scripture is consigned, the sacred writers acquired for themselves by daily use and custom. Therefore. The major premise is certain, because revelation is the manifestation of the unknown, which lies hidden under a kind of veil. The minor premise is evident, because the sacred amanuenses used words taken from the common mode of speaking, which they learned by associating familiarly with prudent men.

Resp. 1. An ambiguity lies under the name of revelation, unfolded in the previous question. I now add a necessary distinction between revelation and divine inspiration. Revelation, strictly speaking by the force of its origin, is the manifestation of the unknown; inspiration, however, is the action of the Holy Spirit by which the actual knowledge of things is infused into the created intellect, prescinding from prior knowledge and ignorance.

(2) We do not maintain that all and individual words were divinely inspired in the prophets and apostles for the sake of knowing, but for the sake of writing. For some words, unknown to the prophets and apostles before the act of writing, the Holy Spirit first revealed to them: but others, assumed from common usage of speech, He appropriated to Himself and applied to divine things. But He dictated all and individual words to the sacred pen, whether they were previously known to them or less so: just as it happens daily that those who dictate letters to an amanuensis use words taken from common usage of speech, the force and meaning of which was long known to him.

You say: The divine inspiration of words known from common usage of speech does not seem to have been necessary, but superfluous. Resp. It was necessary to properly express the mind of the Holy Spirit. For it was not free for the prophets and apostles to cast the divine sense into those words which they might choose at their own discretion; but it was their duty to cling to and depend upon the mouth of the dictating Holy Spirit, so that they might consign Holy Scripture to this pleasing and approved order and context of words, by which it might turn out to be entirely conformed to the mind of the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

Quaest. XVII. Num etiam verba singula, e quibus sacra scriptura constat, divinitus inspirata sunt?

Omnia et singula verba, quae in sacro codice leguntur, a Spiritu sancto prophetis et apostolis inspirata, et in calamum dictata sunt.

Prob. I. Quaecunque scriptura tota est θεόπνευσος, illius non tantum sensus aut res significatae, sed et voces, tanquam signa rerum, divinitus sunt inspiratae.

Atqui scriptura sacra, 2 Tim. III, 16. Ergo. Maior constat, quia (1) apostolus non simpliciter dicit: Omne verbum Dei est θεόπνευσος: posset enim quispiam hac ratione verbum divinum formaliter accipere pro sensu divino: sed dicit: πᾶσα γραφὴ, omnis scriptura: quae non praecise sensum divinum, sed et voces scriptas notat. (2) Non ait apostolus πάντα γεγραμμένα θεόπνευσα, sed πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευσος, vt indicet non tantum res, in sacra scriptura contentas, esse divinitus revelatas, sed et ipsas voces a Spiritu S. in calamum esse dictatas. (3) De illa scriptura loquitur apostolus, quam Timotheus puer legerat, et quam episcopus creatus assidue voluebat, atque auditoribus suis explicabat. At legebat et explicabat scripturam S. prout constat non tantum rebus, sed et vocibus scriptis. Ergo tota scriptura sacra, prout constat, non tantum rebus, sed et vocibus scriptis divinitus inspirata est. II. Quidquid profectum est non ex voluntate humana, ut principio, sed speciali Spiritus sancti impulsu, id totum, ex verbis et rebus conflatum, divinae est originis. Atqui scriptura S. hebraeo et graeco idiomate concepta et c. Ergo.

Maior liquet, quoniam id inuentum aut scriptum humanum vocatur, quod ex voluntate humana proficiscitur. Minor probatur ex 2 Petr. I, 20. 21. Omnis prophetia scripturae non est ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως, propriae interpretationis: non enim voluntate hominum allata est olim prophetia: sed a Spiritu S. impulsi locuti sunt sancti Dei homines.

Obs. (1) Negat apostolus Petrus prophetiam scripturae esse propriae interpretationis, ex hoc fundamento, quia non ex voluntate humana allata, aut profecta est, sed ex impulsu Spiritus S. At interpretanda est sacra scriptura, prout ex vocibus et rebus conflata est. Ergo nulla vox prophetiae scriptae ex humano provenit arbitrio, sed ex inspiratione diuina.

(2) Dicuntur sancti Dei homines esse locuti impulsi a Spiritu S. Ergo non tantum res, sed ἡ λαλιὰ, loquela, siue verba apostolorum, vt ore prolata, ita quoque scripta, a Spiritu diuino sunt profecta: nam per λαλιὰν indifferenter tum dictio, tum scriptio notatur (cum non differant realiter) vi dicti Act. III, 24. (3) Quamuis S. Petrus primario loquatur de prophetia veteris testamenti, immediatae origini diuinae eam vindicando, per pronam tamen bonamque consequentiam ex Petrino hoc effato elicitur, scripturam noui testamenti tam quoad voces, quam quoad res ipsas ex inspiratione diuina consignatam esse. Quae consequentia eo luculentior erit, quo accuratius sequens ponderabitur argumentum.

III. Quae verba apostoli in munere apostolico viua voce protulerunt, litterisque consignarunt, ea ipsos docuit Spiritus sanctus. Atqui verba exstantia in codice noui testamenti apostoli in munere apostolico viua voce protulerunt, litterisque consignarunt. Ergo.

Maior est Paulli 1 Cor. II, 12. 13. Nos non accepimus spiritum mundi, sed Spiritum, qui ex Deo (est) vt sciamus ea, quae a Deo donata sunt nobis: quae etiam loquimur non doctis humanae sapientiae verbis, sed doctis Spiritus S. Vid. supra quaest. VIII. prob. c. Minor per se clara est. v. gr.

Verba exstantia in epistola ad Romanos sunt verba Paulli in litteras redacta, eaque plane conformia sunt verbis, quae in munere suo apostolico Paullus ore prolocutus est, ob exactissimam harmoniam verbi diuini ore prolati, et in litteras relati. IV. Mosen verba scribenda Deus immediate docuit. Exod. XXXIV, 27. 28. Post dixit Iehouah ad Mosen: scribe tibi verba haec: quia super ore (tenore) verborum horum pepigi tecum foedus, et cum Israele. Per verba haec scribenda quidam interpretes intelligunt praecise verba decalogi, alii vniuersa praecepta legis Mosaicae moralis, leuiticae et forensis. Vid. D. CALOV. in system. theolog. tom. I. p. 564. Quae verba autem Moses ex mandato diuino scribere debebat, ipsum Deus immediate docuerat.

Confer v. 10. et c. XIX, 3. sequ. Quae legis Mosaicae, ea hac in parte aliorum scriptorum diuinorum est ratio. Ideo tam frequenter in scriptura inculcatur illud: Verbum domini: haec dixit dominus, vt indicetur, haec verba non humanae, sed diuinae originis esse.

V. Si voces omnes et singulae, quibus amanuenses sacri in scriptura vtuntur, diuinitus inspiratae non sunt: (1) nullum erit discrimen textus originalis, et versionum studio humano adornatarum; modo haec textui authentico sint conformes, cum et haec sensum exprimant θεόπνευστον, sed non verbis θεοπνεύστοις; (2) neque emphasis, vis aut valor vocum textus authentici, singulari adhibita cura enucleandus erit: Quae sunt ἀτοπώτατα, dictu non magis quam cogitatu nefaria.

Antithesis est Erasmi, Suarezii, Episcopii, Bezae, Vorstii & aliorum negantium, singula verba S. scripturae prophetis atque apostolis divinitus inspirata esse: qui argumentantur: 1. Si omnia & singula verba sacrae scripturae ab uno Dei Spiritu essent inspirata, unum esset omnium amanuensium sacrorum dicendi genus, unus idemque stilus. At illorum stilus est longe diversissimus. Ergo non omnia & singula sacrae scripturae verba illis divinitus sunt inspirata. Consequentia maioris probatur, quia unus auctor unum efformat stilum. Antecedens patet: nam Esaias illustri loco natus, & in aula educatus, nitidius, Amos bubulcus, humilius, Lucas graecis litteris perpolitus, elegantius scripsit.

Resp. (1) Contingit in humanis, ut unus auctor profanus ingenii & eloquentiae laude praeclarus varium fundat dicendi genus. Certe Cicero grandem, mediocrem, humilem stilum dicendo scribendoque expressit & excoluit. Idem usu venit in divinis.

S. Ioannes diverso dictionis genere evangelium, epistolas, & apocalypsin contexit, motus diversitate argumenti, cui stilus attemperandus erat. Etenim evangelium Ioanneum divinitatem Christi verborum gravitate, epistolae caritatis fomenta dictionis suavitate, apocalypsis fata ecclesiae charactere prophetis familiari, exponit, nullibi absque insigni τῆς θεοπνευστίας nota.

Spiritus sanctus unicuique dat eloqui, prout ipse vult. Act. II, 4. (3) Stilus V. & N. T. uniformis est, qua substantiam: quanquam, quoad accidentalem stili conformationem, singulari συγκαταβάσει Spiritus S. se demiserit ad ingenia, studia, nationesque virorum θεοπνεύστων: sicut in organo musico substantia cantici, harmoniae, toni una est; fistulis autem aliis acutioribus, aliis obtusioribus, se Spiritus, qui inflat tibias, accommodat.

Conf. DANNHAU. in hodosoph. p. 58.

II. Cuius notitiam scriptores sacri quotidiano usu & consuetudine sibi compararunt, illud divinitus ipsis non est revelatum. Atqui notitiam verborum & generis dicendi, quibus sacra scriptura est consignata, scriptores sacri quotidiano usu & consuetudine sibi compararunt. Ergo. Maior constat, quia revelatio est manifestatio ignoti, quod sub quodam quasi velamine latet. Minor patet, quia amanuenses sacri vti sunt verbis ex vitato loquendi modo assumtis, quae familiariter versando cum prudentibus hominibus condidicerunt.

Resp. 1. Latet ambiguitas sub nomine revelationis, quaestione superiori evoluta. Addo iam necessariam distinctionem inter revelationem & inspirationem divinam. Revelatio, vi originis stricte dicta, est manifestatio ignoti; inspiratio vero est actio Spiritus sancti, qua actualis rerum cognitio intellectui creato infunditur, praescindendo a praevia notitia & ignorantia.

(2) Non statuimus verba omnia & singula prophetis atque apostolis divinitus inspirata esse ad sciendum, sed ad scribendum. Quaedam enim verba prophetis & apostolis ante scriptionis actum ignota, Spiritus S. ipsis primum revelavit: quaedam vero ex communi loquendi usu assumta sibi appropriauit, & rebus divinis applicauit. At omnia & singula verba sacris in calamum dictavit, sive antea ipsis fuerint nota, sive minus: sicut quotidie contingit, ut, qui epistolas amanuensi in calamum dictitant, utantur verbis, desumtis ex communi loquendi usu, quorum vis ac significatio ipsi dudum fuit nota.

Dicis: Verborum ex communi loquendi usu notorum inspiratio divina non videtur fuisse necessaria, sed superflua. Resp. Fuit necessaria ad mentem Spiritus S. rite exprimendam. Neque enim liberum fuit prophetis & apostolis, sensum divinum in ea coniicere verba, quae ipsi pro arbitratu suo eligerent; sed ipsorum erat haerere & pendere ab ore dictantis Spiritus sancti, vt huic grato & probato verborum ordine & contextu scripturam sacram consignarent, quo ea menti Spiritus sancti evaderet prorsus conformis. sancti euaderet prorsus conformis.


### XVIII. Did divine inspiration preserve the sacred amanuenses from all error?

Divine inspiration, by which the things and words to be spoken, no less than those to be written, were immediately suggested to the prophets and apostles by the Holy Spirit, rendered them immune from all error both in the preaching and in the consigning of the divine word.

Proof. I. Whatever has proceeded immediately from God, the primary truth, must be most true. But the whole of Holy Scripture, etc. 2 Tim. III, 16. Therefore.

II. The word of God, preached by the prophets and committed to writing, is called λόγος βεβαιότερος, a more firm word, 2 Pet. I, 19. Καὶ ἔχομεν βεβαιότερον τὸν προφητικὸν λόγον. We have also a more firm prophetic word. The apostle compares the Scripture of the Old Testament with the voice of the Father brought from heaven, v. 17. 18. and asserts the former to be firmer than the latter, not simply—for nothing can be firmer than the voice of the Father heard from heaven—but insofar as the latter was confirmed by the testimony of Peter. The prophetic word is therefore firmer than the testimony of Peter, given concerning the voice of the heavenly Father, with respect to the Jews converted to Christ. Firmer and more certain than these was the prophetic word [compared] to the apostolic testimony concerning the voice of the Father heard from heaven (*). For the authority of the prophetic word had been corroborated by the length of time and the consensus of the ancients; the authority of the apostolic testimony concerning the voice of the heavenly Father, however, was more recent, and not yet proven by the calculation of so many Jews. Wherefore, since the prophetic word becomes firmer than the voice of the heavenly Father insofar as that [voice] is brought forward by Petrine attestation, it is concluded that it is most firm and infallible, preached and written by prophets who were incapable of deceiving or being deceived.

III. The Spirit of truth led the apostles into all truth, by virtue of Christ’s promise, John XVI, 12. The Holy Spirit was the most faithful guide of the apostles, who led them just as a mother leads a child, or a χειραγωγὸς leads a blind man, by taking him by the hand, and brought them into the way of truth, so that they never erred in proposing and explaining the doctrine of faith.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians and Arminians, who posit that the sacred writers sometimes lapsed in memory and erred slightly; as well as that of the Copernican and Cartesian philosophers, who assert that Holy Scripture sometimes accommodates itself to the erroneous opinion of the vulgar: let us weigh their stronger arguments.

I. Peter erred, not walking uprightly according to the truth of the gospel, Gal. II, 14. Resp. Peter did not err in the doctrine of faith, but in a certain special act: for he erred out of ὀρθοποδῶν not walking straight in the way of life or morals; and thus the sin of Peter was a fault not of preaching, but of conduct, in the judgment of TERTULLIAN.

II. John erred, being about to worship the angel. Apoc. XIX, 10. Resp. John erred in the person, whom he thought to be an uncreated angel; he did not err in the preaching or the consignation of the divine word.

III. Matthew erred c. XXVII, 9. alleging Jeremiah instead of Zechariah; which words cited by him concerning the weighing of thirty silver coins are read in Zechariah c. XI, 12. Resp. The words of Matthew are: Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremiah the prophet saying. Concerning the writing of Jeremiah nothing is held in the text. Whatever therefore Jeremiah said, Zechariah his disciple wrote.

IV. Luke erred c. III, 36. when he wrote that Sala was the son of Kainan; when nevertheless, by the testimony of Moses Gen. XI, 12. he was the son of Arphaxad. Resp. That Kainan is ὑποβολιμαῖος supposititious or surreptitious; since by some writer of the book, from whom many copies flowed, the name of Kainan was replaced in this verse 36 from the penultimate clause of this chapter by some error, through wrongly inspecting the archetype or the hallucination of the dictator. In the most ancient copies Kainan is not read in v. 36. See HVG. GROT. in this place & confer D. CALOV. bibl. illustr. fol. 571.

V. Paul erred Hebr. XI, 21. by citing the erroneous version of the LXX interpreters: προσεκύνησεν ἐπὶ τὸ ἄκρον τῆς ῥάβδου αὐτοῦ, he worshipped (Jacob) upon the top of his staff; when nevertheless Moses testifies Gen. XLVII, 31. that he worshipped upon the head of the bed. Resp. Paul does not contradict Moses: for both assert that Israel bowed himself, about to show political reverence to Joseph (or according to the mind of other interpreters, about to worship God himself most humbly) Paul points out the place of Moses, the instrument by which he supported himself, being infirm, namely the staff of Joseph.

You say: Paul followed the LXX interpreters, who, having hallucinated in the translation of the word מִטָּה, when they read מִטָּה, translated staff instead of bed. Resp. Paul did not approve and express the license of the LXX interpreters in translating, but the thing itself truly done, that Jacob bowed himself upon the head of the bed, supported by the staff of Joseph (if with some it is read αὐτοῦ with the rough breathing, he leaned upon his own staff). See D. PFEIF. dub. vexat. p. 221. confer D. CALOV. bibl. illustr. in the place cited at Hebrews c. XI, 21. fol. 1360. add D. VAREN. in Gen. decad XII. loc. V. p. 569.

VI. Stephen seems to have erred twice: I. when he recounts that Joseph brought Jacob into Egypt, and his whole kindred in 75 souls (consisting) Act. VII, 14. when nevertheless Moses counts only 70. Gen. XLVI, 27. II. When the same asserts that Abraham bought the sepulcher for a price of silver from the sons of Emor (sons) of Sichem, Act. VII, 16. which not Abraham, but his grandson Jacob bought, Gen. XXXIII, 19. Resp. to I. Stephen begins the number from one point, Moses covers the catalog from another. For the latter does not count the wives of Jacob: for he writes distinctly Gen. XLVI, 26. 27. All the soul coming with Jacob into Egypt who came out of his thigh besides the wives of the sons of Jacob: all (I say) the soul are sixty and six. But the sons of Joseph, who were born to him in Egypt, two souls: (whence) all the soul of the house of Jacob, who came into Egypt, seventy (if indeed Jacob the root, the family & Joseph are added). But Stephen enumerates all who were summoned by Joseph with Jacob into Egypt, to whom certainly the wives of Jacob are to be reckoned; to whom if you add from the household the handmaids or servants, the number 75 is easily completed. Moses therefore recounts the descendants of Jacob, Stephen recounts his retinue. To II. The Latin Vulgate interpreter wrongly translates the Greek words of Stephen, which D. SEBAST. SCHMID rendered more accurately in bibl. latiz. (partly) & (partly) they are placed in the monument, which Abraham had bought for a price of silver, besides (that) of the sons of Emor, (which is of Sichem). Stephen brings forward that some fathers were buried with Jacob in the field of Ephron, bought by Abraham, Gen. XXIII, 17, and some with Joseph at Sichem, Jos. XXIV, 32.

Consult GLASSIUS in philolog. sacr. book III. tract. 2. can. 2. p. 503.

VII. The prophet Isaiah is commanded to write with the pen of a man, i.e., popularly according to the erroneous opinion of men, because most men judge only according to external appearances.

Is. VIII, 1. Resp.

Isaiah is commanded to write with the pen of a man not precisely by accommodation to the vulgar custom of speaking, especially if erroneous, or by deformity from the divine sense; but by accommodation to public use, and thus he is commanded to write with the pen of a man, i.e., as men are accustomed, on some paper or open leaf, clearly, with distinct characters, so that anyone may be able to read & understand. VIII. If the apostles themselves accommodated themselves to the opinion of the newly converted Jews, and granted them the observance of circumcision: which nevertheless through Christ in the N.

T. has been abrogated (see Acts XVI. Gal. V, 2. 3.): it follows much more that the Holy Spirit, in those things in which error is not joined with the danger of salvation, accommodated himself to the opinion of common men, until this world, in which we know only in part, through a glass & in a riddle, is buried. But the former is true: therefore the latter.

Resp.

Resp. 1. Circumcision, abrogated and permitted for a time, is poorly compared with an erroneous locution. For circumcision is a rite, considered absolutely, apart from a divine command or prohibition, an adiaphoron, intrinsically including no notion of either goodness or foulness: but with a divine command added, it became morally good; with a divine prohibition added, morally evil. But an erroneous locution intrinsically includes turpitude, and from God, who is the primary truth, it can in no way proceed.

2. To grant circumcision for a time speaks only of a permissive act; by the permission of the rite of circumcision, it is rendered neither good nor evil, nor is it appropriated to the one permitting. But to deliver something according to the erroneous opinion of the vulgar is a positive act, which, when reduced to God, manifestly argues that He is the cause of the error itself.

Conf. D. 10.

Latin:

Inspiratio divina, qua res & verba dicenda non minus, quam scribenda, prophetis atque apostolis a Spiritu sancto immediate suggesta sunt, ipsos ab omni errore immunes praestitit tam in praedicatione, quam in consignatione verbi diuini.

Prob. I. Quidquid a Deo, prima veritate, immediate profectum est, illud oportet esse verissimum. Atqui tota scriptura sacra &c. 2 Tim. III, 16. Ergo.

II. Verbum Dei, a prophetis praedicatum & litteris mandatum, vocatur λόγος βεβαιότερος, verbum firmius, 2 Petr. I, 19. Καὶ ἔχομεν βεβαιότερον τὸν προφητικὸν λόγον. Habemus etiam firmius propheticum verbum. Confert apostolus scripturam vet. testamenti cum voce patris de caelo delata, v. 17. 18. & illam hac firmiorem asserit non simpliciter: nihil enim firmius esse potest voce patris de caelo audita: sed quatenus illa testimonio Petri confirmata erat. Firmius itaque est verbum propheticum testimonio Petri, de voce patris coelestis perhibito, respectu Iudaeorum ad Christum conversorum. His firmius & certius erat verbum propheticum testimonio apostolico de voce patris, e caelo audita (*). Nam verbi prophetici auctoritas temporis diuturnitate, maiorumque consensu corroborata erat: Auctoritas vero testimonii apostolici de voce patris coelestis erat recentior, nec dum tot Iudaeorum calculo comprobata. Quare, cum verbum propheticum firmius fit voce patris coelestis, quatenus illa attestatione Petrina est asserta, conficitur, illud esse firmissimum & infallibile, praedicatum & scriptum a prophetis, fallere & falli nesciis.

III. Apostolos Spiritus veritatis in omnem veritatem duxit, vi promissionis Christi, Io. XVI, 12. Fuit Spiritus S. fidelissimus apostolorum hodegeta, qui ipsos perinde ac mater puellum, aut χειραγωγὸς caecum, iniecta manu, ducit, in viam veritatis perduxit, vt in doctrina fidei proponenda & explicanda nunquam erraverint.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, & Arminianorum, statuentium, scriptores sacros interdum memoria lapsos leuiter errasse; nec non philosophorum Copernicanorum, & Cartesianorum, afferentium, scripturam sacram se interdum accommodare ad erroneam vulgi opinionem: quorum potiora expendamus argumenta.

I. Errauit Petrus, non recto pede incedens iuxta veritatem euangelii, Gal. II, 14. Resp. Non errauit Petrus in doctrina fidei, sed in speciali quodani facto: nam errauit ex ὀρθοποδῶν non recte ambulans in via vitae aut morum; adeoque peccatum Petri fuit vitium non praedicationis, sed conversationis, iudice TERTULLIANO.

II. Errauit Ioannes, angelum adoraturus. Apoc. XIX, 10. Resp. Errauit Ioannes in persona, quam angelum increatum esse putauit; non errauit in praedicatione, aut consignatione verbi diuini.

III. Errauit Matthaeus c. XXVII, 9. allegans Ieremiam pro Zacharia; quae verba ab ipso citata de appendendis triginta nummis argenteis leguntur apud Zachariam c. XI, 12. Resp. Verba Matthaei sunt: Tunc impletum est, quod dictum est per Ieremiam prophetam dicentem. De scriptione Ieremiae nihil habetur in textu. Quidquid igitur Ieremias dixit, Zacharias ipsius discipulus scripsit.

IV. Errauit Luc. c. III, 36. cum scripsit, quod Sala fuerit filius Kainanis; cum tamen teste Mose Gen. XI, 12. fuerit filius Arphachsadi. Resp. Kainan ille ὑποβολιμαῖος supposititius aut irreptitius est; siquidem a scriptore aliquo libri, vnde multa exemplaria fluxerunt, ex penultimo huius capitis commate nomen Kainanis hoc v. 36. errore quodam repositum est, perperam inspecto archetypo, aut dictantis hallucinatione. In antiquissimis exemplaribus Kainan v. 36. non legitur. Vid. HVG. GROT. in h. l. & conf. D. CALOV. bibl. illustr. fol. 571.

V. Errauit Paullus Hebr. XI, 21. citando versionem LXX. interpretum erroneam: προσεκύνησεν ἐπὶ τὸ ἄκρον τῆς ῥάβδου αὐτοῦ, adorauit (Iacobus) super summo baculo ipsius; cum tamen Moses testetur Gen. XLVII, 31. quod adorauit super caput lecti. Resp. Paullus Mosi non contradicit: nam vterque asserit, quod Israel se inclinauerit, reuerentiam politicam Iosepho exhibiturus (aut ex aliorum interpretum mente Deum ipsum humillime adoraturus) Mosis locum, Paullus instrumentum, quo se infirmum sustinuerit, nempe scipionem Iosephi, indigitat.

Dicis: Paullus secutus est LXX. interpretes, qui, hallucinati in translatione vocis מִטָּה, cum legerint מִטָּה, baculum pro lecto transtulerunt. Resp. Paullus non licentiam LXX. interpretum in vertendo, sed rem ipsam vere factam approbauit & expressit, quod Iacobus se inclinauerit super caput lecti, subnixus scipione Iosephi (si cum nonnullis legatur αὐτοῦ cum spiritu aspero, propria innixus fuit baculo). Vid. D. PFEIF. dub. vexat. p. 221. confer D. CALOV. bibl. illustr. in locum citatum ad Hebraeos c. XI, 21. fol. 1360. adde D. VAREN. in Gen. decad XII. loc. V. p. 569.

VI. Bis errasse videtur Stephanus I. cum recenset, Iosephum transtulisse Iacobum in Aegyptum, & totam cognationem ipsius in animabus 75. (consistentem) Act. VII, 14. cum tamen Moses tantum numeret 70. Gen. XLVI, 27. II. Cum idem asserit, quod Abraham pretio argenti emerit sepulcrum a filiis Emor (filii) Sichem, Act. VII, 16. quod non Abraham, sed eius nepos Iacobus coëmit, Gen. XXXIII, 19. Resp. ad I. aliam Stephanus init numerum, aliam catalogum texit Moses. Nam hic vxores Iacobi non connumerat: diserte enim scribit Gen. XLVI, 26. 27. Omnis anima veniens cum Iacobo in Aegyptum egressi femur eius praeter vxores filiorum Iacobi: omnis (inquam) anima sunt sexaginta & sex. Filii autem Iosephi, qui nati ipsi sunt in Aegypto, animae duae: (vnde) omnis anima domus Iacobi, qui venit in Aegyptum, septuaginta (si nempe Iacobus stirps, familiae & Iosephus addantur). Stephanus autem enumerat omnes, qui a Iosepho accersiti sunt cum Iacobo in Aegyptum, quibus vtique vxores Iacobi accensendae sunt; quibus si ex famulitio addas ancillas aut seruos, facile completur numerus 75. Moses igitur posteros Iacobi, Stephanus huius comitatum recenset. Ad II. vulgatus interpres latinus verba graeca Stephani male vertit, quae accuratius reddidit D. SEBAST. SCHMIDIVS in bibl. latiz. (partim) & (partim) positi sunt in monumento, quod emerat Abrahamus pretio argenti, praeter (illud) filiorum Emor, (quod Sichemi est). Affert Stephanus, quosdam patres cum Iacobo in agro Ephronis, emto ab Abrahamo, Gen. XXIII, 17. quosdam cum Iosepho Sichemi, Ios. XXV, 52. sepultos esse.

Confer GLASSIVS in philolog. sacr. libr. III. tract. 2. can. 2. p. 503.

VII. Iesaias propheta iubetur scribere stilo hominis, i. e. populariter ad opinionem hominum erroneam, propterea quod plerique homines secundum externas tantum apparentias iudicant.

Es. VIII, 1. Resp.

Iubetur Iesaias scribere stilo hominis non praecise per contemperationem ad vulgarem loquendi consuetudinem, in primis erroneam, aut difformitatem a sensu divino; sed per accommodationem ad usum publicum, adeoque iubetur scribere stilo hominis, i. e. ut homines solent, in charta aliqua vel folio patenti, perspicue, insignibus characteribus, ut quilibet possit legere & intelligere. VIII. Si ipsi apostoli opinioni Iudaeorum noviter conversorum se accommodaverunt, iisque observationem concesserunt circumcisionis: quae tamen per Christum in N.

T. est abrogata (vid. Act. XVI. Gal. V, 2. 3.): sequitur multo magis Spiritum sanctum in iis, in quibus error cum periculo salutis non coniunctus est, opinioni vulgarium se attemperasse hominum, donec mundus hic, in quo cognoscimus tantum ex parte, per speculum & aenigma, sepeliatur. At prius est verum: E. & posterius.

Resp.

Resp. 1. Circumcisio abrogata, & ad tempus permissa, male comparatur cum locutione erronea. Nam circumcisio est ritus, absolute, citra mandatum aut interdictum divinum, consideratus, adiaphorus, intrinsece nullam nec bonitatis, nec foeditatis rationem includens: accedente autem mandato divino, factus est moraliter bonus; accedente interdictio divino, moraliter malus. At locutio erronea intrinsece includit turpitudinem, & a Deo, prima veritas est, nullo modo prouenire potest.

2. Concedere circumcisionem ad tempus, dicit solum actum permissivum; permissione ritus circumcisionis nec bonus, nec malus redditur, nec appropriatur permittenti. At tradere aliquid secundum opinionem vulgi erroneam, est actus positivus, qui, in Deum reductus, eum ipsius erroris caussam esse manifesto arguit.

Conf. D. 10.


### XVIII. Did divine inspiration preserve the sacred amanuenses from all error?: Adam

ADAM.

OSIANDR. colleg. systemat. part. 1. p. 75. Question XIX. How manifold is the sense of any biblical saying? The sense of a biblical saying is a simple literal sense, and that formal, it is one, which the Holy Spirit intends to express immediately by θεοπνεύστοις (God-breathed) words.

Obs. I. One simple biblical saying is called one proposition, consisting of one subject & predicate. But if diverse subjects & predicates are present in conglomerated & connected biblical sayings, a double sense emerges, for the reason that it is not one, but a double biblical saying. e.g.

The prophet Joel, chapter II, 13, gravely exhorts: Rend your hearts, and do not rend your garments. Here a double biblical saying is present: Repentant sinners should rend their hearts. Repentant sinners should not rend their garments. The former is understood in a metaphorical sense; the latter in a literal sense.

Obs. II. The literal sense is so called either grammatically or logically.

The grammatical literal sense is that which words join in their proper & native signification, even if it does not at all conform to the intention of the speaker. It is more correctly called the sense of the letter than the literal sense. The literal sense of Holy Scripture is called logical, which the Holy Spirit himself, by θεοπνεύστοις words, whether they be proper or affected by some trope, immediately intends.

See KOENIG. in theolog. positiu. p. 12. How the sense of the letter & the literal sense (logically taken) differ, is easily made clear by the following biblical sayings.

Luke XIII, 32. Herod is called a fox. Matt. V, 29. 30. the Savior commands to pluck out the right eye, and to amputate the right hand, if these members have scandalized us.

Ps. XCI, 13. he says if these members have scandalized us. Ps. XCI, 13.

says the Holy Spirit through the hierophant: You shall tread upon the lion and the adder: you shall trample the young lion and the dragon. These heavenly oracles cohere poorly according to the sense of the letter, but excellently according to the literal sense.

Obf. III. The literal sense is divided into the proper sense and the figurative, or tropical, sense.

The proper sense is that which the Holy Spirit intends by words taken in their native signification. e.g. God is Spirit, John 4:24. The figurative, or tropical, sense is that which is intended immediately by the Holy Spirit, with the words affected by some trope. e.g. God is our shield, and our reward very great. Gen.

15:1. Obs. IV. One sense of a biblical saying is formal, or immediate, another is virtual, or mediate.

That is the one which is intended immediately by the Holy Spirit by the θεοπνεύστοις (God-breathed) words, and is known from them by themselves without any inference. e.g. You shall have no other God before my face. Exod. 20: 3. The formal sense is: I, the true God, alone am to be religiously worshipped by you, O man. The virtual sense is that which is elicited from the formal sense by inference. e.g. From the biblical saying already cited I elicit various mediate senses: Angels are not to be religiously worshipped: St. Mary is not to be adored: Sculptures and images are not to be invoked: No man, Prince, King, Caesar, is to be loved and feared as the true God: Mammon is not to be served: Our trust is not to be fixed in our wisdom, justice, strength, arms: Our belly should not be our God. We maintain that of one biblical saying there is one formal sense, from which various virtual and mediate senses can be deduced. Obs.

Latin:

ADAM.

OSIANDR. colleg. systemat. part. 1. p. 75. Quaest. XIX. Quotuplex est sensus alicuius dicti biblici? Sensus dicti biblici simplex sensus litteralis, isque formalis, unus est, quem Spiritus S. verbis θεοπνεύστοις immediate exprimere intendit.

Obs. I. Vnum dictum biblicum simplex dicitur una propositio, constans uno subiecto & praedicato. Quod si dictis biblicis conglomeratis & connexis diversa subiecta & praedicata adsint, duplex emergit sensus, ideo, quod non unum, sed duplex dictum biblicum est. v. gr.

Propheta Ioël cap. II, 13. grauiter cohortatur: Scindite corda, & ne scindite vestes. Hic duplex adest dictum biblicum: Peccatores resipiscentes scindant corda sua. Peccatores resipiscentes non scindant vestes suas. Prior intelligitur sensu metaphorico; posterior sensu proprio.

Obs. II. Sensus litteralis vel grammatice, vel logice ita dicitur.

Sensus litteralis grammaticus est, quem verba in propria & nativa sua significatione iungunt, etiamsi intentioni dicentis minime congruat. Dicitur rectius sensus litterae, quam litteralis. Logice sensus litteralis S. scripturae dicitur, quem Spiritus S. ipse verbis θεοπνεύστοις, sive ea propria sint, sive tropo aliquo affecta, proxime intendit.

Vid. KOENIG. in theolog. positiu. p. 12. Quomodo sensus litterae & litteralis (logice sumus) discrepent, et sequentibus dictis biblicis facile patescit.

Luc. XIII, 32. Herodes vocatur vulpes. Matth. V, 29. 30. iubet saluator dextrum eruere oculum, dextramque amputare manum, si haec membra nos scandalizauerint.

Ps. XCI, 13. inquit si hæc membra nos scandalizauerint. Ps. XCI, 13.

inquit Spiritus Sanctus per hierophanten: Super leonem et aspidem calcabis: conculcabis leonem iuuenem et draconem. Quae oracula coelestia secundum sensum litterae male, secundum sensum litteralem optime cohaerent.

Obs. III. Sensus litteralis, diuiditur in sensum proprium, et figuratum, seu tropicum.

Sensus proprius est, quem verbis sumtis in natiua sua significatione Spiritus Sanctus intendit. v. gr. Deus est Spiritus, Io. IV, 24. Sensus figuratus, siue tropicus est, qui proxime intenditur a Spiritu Sancto, verbis tropo aliquo affectis. v. gr. Deus est clypeus noster, et merces nostra multa valde. Gen. XV, 1.

Obs. IV. Sensus dicti biblici alius formalis, siue immediatus, alius virtualis, siue mediatus est.

Ille est, qui a Spiritu Sancto immediate intenditur verbis θεοπνεύστοις, et ex illis per se citra ullam consequentiam cognoscitur. v. gr. Non erit tibi Deus alius ante facies meas. Exod. XX, 3. Sensus formalis est: Ego verus Deus solus a te, o homo, religiose colendus sum. Virtualis, qui e sensu formali per consequentiam elicitur. v. gr. Ex dicto biblico iam citato varios elicio sensus mediatos: Angeli non sunt religiose colendi: S. Maria non est adoranda: Sculptilia et imagines non sunt inuocandae: Nullus homo, Princeps, Rex, Caesar, perseque amandus ac timendus est, ac verus Deus: Mammonae non est seruiendum: Fiducia nostra non est defigenda in nostra sapientia, iustitia, robore, armis: Venter noster non sit Deus noster. Statuimus unius dicti biblici vnum esse sensum formalem, e quo per consequentiam varii sensus virtuales et mediati deduci possunt. *Obs.


### XVIII. Did divine inspiration preserve the sacred amanuenses from all error?: V. The sense of a biblical saying is commonly divided into literal and mystical. The literal sense, logically spoken of above in Obs

V. The sense of a biblical saying is commonly divided into literal and mystical. The literal sense, logically spoken of above in Obs.

II. has been defined. The mystical sense is called that which is not signified immediately by the θεοπνεύστα (God-breathed) words, but which flows and is deduced from the thing signified by the θεοπνεύστοις words. However, it is called improperly, loosely, and abusively the sense of a biblical saying, since it is not the immediate sense of the θεοπνεύστων (God-breathed) words; but because God, through the thing or fact described by the same words, wished to set another thing or another fact before the eyes and minds of men to be considered. More accurately, therefore, it is called the literal sense's accommodation, or mystical application, rather than the mystical sense of scripture, e.g. Jonah 2:1. the prophet Jonah is said to have been three days and nights in the belly of the whale: there the literal sense is that which was immediately intended by God, which the words carry before them and immediately produce; but when this entire history or event is transferred to signify Christ's stay in the sepulcher for three days and nights, Matt. 12:30, a new sense does not arise from it, but only an accommodation and application of that history to signify that Christ would be in the sepulcher for so many days and nights (even though the days and nights were not complete, but their beginning and end are understood). Confer D. QVENSTED. in systemat. theol. fol 134.

VI. The mystical sense, loosely so called, is divided by the Papists into the allegorical, tropological, and anagogical sense.

The allegorical sense is when the words of scripture, beyond the literal sense, signify something in the N.T. that pertains to Christ or the church of Christ. The tropological, or moral, sense is when words or facts are referred to signify something that as it pertains to morals. The anagogical sense is when words or deeds are referred to the signification of eternal life. For example, Jerusalem in the literal sense denotes the city of Palestine; in the allegorical sense, the church militant on earth; in the anagogical sense, the church triumphant in heaven. These diverse senses of Holy Scripture are comprehended in the following distinction: The letter teaches deeds; what you believe, allegory; Moral, what you do; what you hope for, anagogy.

But indeed, the papistical distinction of the mystical sense is not altogether accurate. (1) Because all three species of the mystical sense, enumerated by the papists, are comprehended under allegory. (2) The moral sense is wrongly called tropological, because morals are not called τρόποι, but ἤθη. (3) Elevation in Greek is not called ἀναγωγία (which word denotes a lack of discipline, or a dissolute life) but ἀναγωγή.

Obs. VII. Orthodox theologians distinguish the mystical sense into typical, allegorical, and parabolic. The typical sense (as defined by D. Glassius, lib. II. part. I. tract. II. Sect. II. p. 289.) is when, under external deeds or prophetic visions, hidden things, whether present or future, are figured, and especially when the deeds of the O.T. prefigure or shadow forth the deeds of the N.T. The typical sense is sub-distinguished by D. Glassius, l. c., into prophetic and historical. The type of the prophet, or the prophetic type, is that which divinely inspired prophets frequently use in their discourses, which are partly admonitory and partly vaticinatory. Namely, when they figure and signify hidden things, whether present or future, by external symbols through the Holy Spirit. It consists, however, in prophetic and typical 1. actions, 2. visions. The typical actions of the prophecies are when, by those things which the prophets performed outwardly by divine command, something mystical and hidden is shadowed forth. For example, Isaiah c. XX, 2, he walks naked, i.e., stripped of his prophetic garment, to shadow forth the slaughter of the Egyptians and Ethiopians. Visions are offered either to those sleeping or to those waking. Typical visions offered to those sleeping are through dreams divinely sent, insofar as they are wrapped in figures and types, e.g., the dream of Jacob concerning the ladder reaching from earth to heaven, Gen. XXVIII, 12. For its typical application, see John I, 15. Typical visions offered to those waking have some added interpretation of the type, the explanation of which must be elicited from the συναφείᾳ (connection) and the circumstances of the text. For example, the prophet Jeremiah saw two baskets of figs, good and bad. The former basket, full of good figs, prefigured the restoration of the Israelite church; the latter signified the deportation of Zedekiah and the Jewish people: which interpretation is had in Jer. XXIV, v. 5, 6, 7, 8. The type of history, or the historical type, is the mystical sense of Scripture by which the deeds of the O.T. prefigure the deeds of the N.T. that are done or to be done. For example, the paschal lamb was a type of Christ. Concerning the paschal lamb, Jehovah says, Exod. XII, 46, "You shall not break a bone in it." Which words, in the literal sense, are understood solely of the paschal lamb, to be slaughtered and eaten by the Israelites: by typical accommodation to Christ, prefigured by the paschal lamb, they are applied, John XIX, 36. The allegorical sense is when the history of Scripture, truly performed, is referred to some mystery, or spiritual doctrine, by the intention of the Holy Spirit. For example, the Creator strictly forbade cruelty toward brutes, especially toward working oxen: whose interdict may be read in Deut. XXV, 4, "You shall not muzzle the ox when it treads out the grain." In the literal sense, this biblical saying is understood of no other than the ox treading out grain: allegorically, the same is applied to the minister of the church, laboring intently for the salvation of men, 1 Cor. IX, 9. The parabolic sense is when some matter, as if done, is aptly feigned and narrated, and referred to signify something else spiritual. Thus it is known to no one not initiated into the Christian sacraments that there is a parable concerning the father of a household, who went out at first light to hire laborers for his vineyard. Matth. XX, 1. sqq.

Matt. XX, 1, sqq. Obs. VIII. Mystical accommodation is either innate or applied. The former is that which Holy Scripture itself either expressly shows or insinuates to a certain extent: The latter is that which Holy Scripture itself does not show, but which has been devised by the doctors of the church. If this is offered, not without probable foundation sought from the literal sense, and analogous to the faith, it is accepted by us not unwillingly; but if it has been extorted, destitute of probable foundation, and deflecting from the analogy of faith, it is repudiated.

That the formal literal sense of every single simple biblical saying, intended by the Holy Spirit, is not double, but one, is proven.

I. From the efficient cause of Holy Scripture, God, who, since He is most truthful, best, and most wise, does not play with ambiguities, as that spirit Loxias [the oblique/ambiguous one], who, when consulted by Pyrrhus, plotting treachery against the Romans, answered ambiguously: I say that you, descendant of Aeacus, the Romans can conquer. The impostor deluded with the double sense of the oracle: but every biblical saying exhibits a single divine literal sense.

II. From the nature of sense and signification. The form of Holy Scripture is one. But the literal sense is the form of Holy Scripture, and as it were its soul. Therefore the literal sense of Holy Scripture is one.

III. From the truth of Holy Scripture. Whatever is true is one. (It cannot be true in more than one way.) But the sense of Holy Scripture is true. Therefore it is one.

IV. From the perspicuity of Holy Scripture, which is so clear that even an infant may attain its sense. We have the example of Timothy, commended by St. Paul, because from infancy he had known the sacred letters. 2 Tim. III, 15. But Scripture, if implicated in various senses, wraps itself in its own obscurity, and distracts the mind of the reader.

V. From the end of Holy Scripture, which is to make wise, or to make the unskilled and little ones wise, Ps. XIX, 8. 2 Tim. III, 15. The multiple sense of any saying does not make a man wise, but erring: for it begets equivocation, the fertile mother of errors.

VI. From the absurd. If Holy Scripture were to sustain many, and those in one place, in one proposition, different senses: no firm argument could be sought from it: it would be a trumpet giving an uncertain sound, and thus useless, 1 Cor. XIV, 7. it would not be a constant rule of faith and morals.

There is an antithesis of the Papists and the Socinians, who maintain that there can be multiple literal senses of one biblical saying; who, to fortify their own opinion, bring forward not a few biblical sayings which, in their mind, possess a double sense, divinely intended.

I. Joel II, 13. Rend your heart, and not your garments. Resp. This biblical saying is not one proposition, but by virtue double. We are speaking of one simple biblical saying.

See Obj. 1. II. That saying: Exod. XX, 3. You shall have no other Gods before me, begets many senses. Resp. It begets one formal, or immediate sense, from which virtual and mediate senses are elicited by consequence.

III. There are biblical sayings in which both the literal and the mystical sense are intended by God. e.g. Exod. XII, 46. You shall not break a bone of it. Deut. XXV, 4. Which are explained by the Holy Spirit Himself in a mystical sense, John XIX, 36. 1 Cor. IX, 9. Resp. The mystical sense is more correctly called an accommodation, or application of a biblical saying, than its sense, since it is not intended by the Holy Spirit through the God-breathed words, but through the thing or fact, pointed out by the God-breathed words, it is applied by the Holy Spirit to another thing, or another fact, on account of analogy, or some convenience.

We are speaking of the sense intended by the divine words, not of the mystical accommodation of things or... facts. IV. The words of Hosea c. XI, 1. When Israel was a child, then I loved him: and out of Egypt I called my son, are to be accepted in a double sense.

1. In the literal sense concerning the Israelite people, from the from Egyptian servitude liberated. 2. In the mystical sense concerning Christ departing into Egypt and returning, Resp. 1) Nothing would be taken from our opinion if we were to say that those words are understood in the literal sense concerning the Israelite people, whose migration out of Egypt is applied mystically to the return of Christ from Egypt. 2) The words of Hosea: Out of Egypt I have called my son, are not to be taken mystically, but literally and immediately, concerning Christ in this way: When Israel was a נער [boy], i. e., rude, precipitous in his actions, and shaking off the yoke; yet I loved him so much that for his sake I called my son Jesus out of Egypt, that he might instruct the ignorant, correct the petulant, and amend and strengthen the precipitous with heavenly doctrine.

V. The words of Ps. II, 7. Today I have begotten thee, have a triple sense: for they are explained concerning the eternal generation of the Son of God, Hebr. I, 5. concerning the resurrection of Christ, Acts XIII, 33. Concerning his priesthood, Hebr. V, 5. Resp. The words of Ps. II, 7 cited are rightly explained concerning the eternal generation of the Son of God, Hebr. I, 33. it treats of the resuscitation of Christ from the dead, but that Greek word: ἀναστήσας is the same as exciting, exhibiting, bringing forward. The sense therefore is: God the Father, mindful of his promise, excited, sent, and exhibited to the Jews his Son begotten from eternity, whom he had addressed in Ps. II: Thou art my son: Today I have begotten thee. It treats of the resurrection of Christ from the dead v. 34. Hebr. V, 5. The person is described by whom Christ was called to the priesthood. That person is God the Father, the fountain and origin of the Son, from whom, as he received his essence through eternal generation, so he received the honor of the great priesthood at the appointed time. From which it is evident that the words of Psalm II, Today I have begotten thee, have only one signification, and retain it everywhere.

VI. The words of Is. LIII, 4. He hath borne our infirmities, are explained in 1 Pet. II, 25 concerning sins, and in Matt. VIII, 17 concerning bodily diseases. Resp. Christ bore all diseases generally, of body and soul: for he bore sins, and their punishments, from the reckoning of which are diseases. By removing therefore diseases, or punishments, he demonstrated a posteriori that he bears and expiates the sins of the world.

VII. That memorable prophecy of Jehovah, 2 Sam. VII, 14. When thy days be fulfilled, and thou shalt sleep with thy fathers, I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son: is understood as much of Solomon as of Christ. Resp. This whole prophecy is to be understood in the literal sense concerning the Messiah; because I. it treats here of the seed to be excited from the bowels of David, after the times of David: therefore not of Solomon, who after David had fulfilled his fate was neither born nor placed on the royal throne. II. Nor was the throne of his kingdom established for Solomon forever, but for the Messiah v. 13. III. David answers: This is the law of man, who is the Lord God, designating Christ the θεάνθρωπον [God-man]. IV. St. Paul testifies that this oracle was published concerning Christ, Hebr. I, 5. You say I. Not all the predicates of this prophecy belong to the Messiah. For it treats of the builder of the house of the Lord, who is Solomon. Resp. The house of the Lord does not denote the material temple of Solomon, but the spiritual house, namely the church, whose architect is Christ. The reason is, because a house is understood that is as perpetual as the kingdom of this seed of David is eternal. You say II. It treats of the building of that temple in the divine response, concerning which there had been discussion in the counsel of David, which without doubt according to the mind of David was material. Resp. The divine response is partly negative, partly affirmative. Negatively the Lord answers: Shalt thou build me a house to dwell in? Therefore the Lord does not desire... a material temple. Affirmatively the same answers by inversion: Jehovah (God the Father) has announced to thee, that Jehovah (God the Son, because the Lord speaks of the Lord) will make thee a house. Which words contain a πρότασιν [proposition] & and the sum of what follows; as it indicates that David was not to build a house for the Lord, but the Lord was to build a spiritual house and an eternal kingdom for David: which spiritual house and eternal kingdom is the church, the house of the living God, 1 Tim. III, 15. which Christ built, Matth. XVI, 18. the kingdom of Christ, of which there will be no end. Luc. I, 33.

You say III. The Lord speaks of a person who was not immune from a propensity to sin. For he says in v. 14. "If he commits iniquity, I will chastise him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men." Reply. The Lord speaks (α) not of inherent sin, by which the Messiah was never infected, but of imputed sin; because he willingly took upon himself the sins of the whole world to be atoned for, 1 Io. II, 2. Which the sacred scripture graphically delineates, speaking of Christ as if he himself had sinned. Ps. XL, 13. Ps. XXXI, 15. Ps. LXIX, 6. (β) Of Christ's satisfactory passion.

You say IV. This prophecy, combined with a most sweet promise, is explained concerning Solomon by David himself, 1 Paral. XXII, 9. and also applied to himself by Solomon, 1 Reg. V, 5. c. VIII, 17. 2 Paral. VI, 7. Reply. The cited passages are not parallel to the prophecy we have already discussed. For that promise in 1 Paral. XXII, 9. which the other passages refer to, is later in time than our prophecy. That one speaks of a son to be born to David; this one of a seed to be raised up long after David's death: that one speaks of a material house and the temple in Jerusalem; this one speaks of a spiritual house and an eternal kingdom, and is repeated in 1 Paral. XVII, 11. seqq.

VIII. The words of Ierem. XXXI, 15. "A voice was heard in Rama (indeed), lamentation, bitter weeping: Rachel weeping for her children," are understood of the Benjaminites being led into captivity. But Matth. II, 18. they are explained of Herod's infanticide, and the lamentation of the Bethlehemite mothers. Reply. The lamentation of the Benjaminites (some of whom are also designated as Jews, united with them since the division of the Israelite kingdom, 1 Reg. XXII, 20.) heard because of their abduction into captivity, of which the Holy Spirit never explains that lamentation, is not understood in the cited passage; but Rachel weeping is introduced by prosopopoeia because of the Herodian infanticide, to signify that Herod's tyranny would rage even to the borders of Benjamin, and that in those confines, where Rachel closed her eyes and was buried, her posterity would be killed with detestable cruelty. Rachel's tomb, moreover, stood in the field of Bethlehem, Gen. XXXV, 19. Therefore, there is not a double meaning in the cited passage.

IX. Io. VI, 50. Caiaphas says: "It is expedient for us that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish." But he did not say this of himself; but being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus would die for that nation. Reply. The biblical saying already cited has one intention, intended by the Holy Spirit; namely, that it would be for the good of the entire human race if Christ were to suffer death to avert its eternal destruction, notwithstanding that Caiaphas conceived another meaning in his mind. For our discussion is not about the human meaning of the biblical saying, but the divine, which Caiaphas did not understand, but only lent his mouth to the Holy Spirit in uttering the prophecy, as did Balaam, and prophesied without understanding the prophecy.

X. When Moses in Deut. XXXII, 1. exclaims: "Hear, O heavens; for I will speak, and let the earth hear the words of my mouth": by "heavens," according to Cocceius, angels, aerial and ethereal heavens can be understood; because scripture uses the word "heaven" in all those significations. Reply. α) Distinguish between words taken separately and conjointly in the whole phrase. If words are taken separately, they can be explained in various senses; if they are taken conjointly, the speaker's purpose must be considered, and the antecedents must be carefully compared with the consequents: by which method they produce one sense. β) It is one thing for a word to be able to be explained in a different sense, and another for it to have to be explained in a varying sense. Luther: "Ein anders ist: es kann also heißen; Ein anders: es muß also heißen."

In the cited passage, we understand metonymically by 'heavens', the angels, witnesses of divine deeds in the heaven of glory; by 'earth', men, the inhabitants of the world.

Latin:

V. Diuiditur vulgo sensus dicti biblici in litteralem, et mysticum.* Sensus litteralis logice dictus supra Obs.

II. definitus est. Sensus mysticus dicitur, qui non significatur proxime per verba θεοπνεύστα, sed qui ex re, verbis θεοπνεύστοις significata, fluit atque deducitur. Dicitur autem ἀκύρως, παχυλῶς, improprie et abusiue, sensus dicti biblici, cum non sit immediatus sensus verborum θεοπνεύστων; sed quia Deus per rem, aut factum, verbis iisdem descriptum, aliam rem, aut aliud factum, oculis mentibusque hominum considerandum sistere voluit. Accuratius itaque vocatur sensus litteralis accommodatio, siue applicatio mystica, quam sensus scripturae mysticus, v. gr. Ionae II, 1. propheta Ionas dicitur fuisse tribus diebus et noctibus in ventre ceti: ibi sensus litteralis a Deo proxime intentus est, quem verba prae se ferunt, et immediate gignunt; quando vero integra haec historia siue res gesta transfertur ad significandam Christi per tres dies et noctes mansionem in sepulcro, Matth. XII, 30. non oritur inde nouus sensus, sed tantum illius historiae accommodatio et applicatio ad significandum Christum tot dies et noctes (licet non fuerint completi dies ac noctes, sed earum initium et finis intelligatur) in sepulcro futurum esse. Confer. D. QVENSTED. in systemat. theol. fol 134.

Obs. VI. Παχυλῶς dictus sensus mysticus a pontificiis diuiditur in sensum allegoricum, tropologicum et anagogicum.

Sensus allegoricus est, cum verba scripturae praeter litteralem sensum significant aliquid in N. T. quod ad Christum, vel ecclesiam Christi, pertinet. Tropologicus, siue moralis, est, cum verba, aut facta, referuntur ad significandum aliquid, quod pertinet ad mores. Anagogicus est, cum verba, aut facta, referuntur ad significandam vitam aeternam. v. gr. Hierosolyma sensu litterali notat urbem Palaestinae; sensu allegorico ecclesiam militantem in terris; sensu anagogico ecclesiam triumphantem in coelis. Comprehenduntur hi diversi sacrae scripturae sensus sequenti distinctio: Littera gesta docet; quod credas, allegoria; Moralis, quid agas; quid speres, anagogia.

At vero papistica sensus mystici distinctio non usque adeo accurata est. (1) Quia omnes tres species sensus mystici, a pontificiis recensitae, sub allegoria comprehenduntur. (2) Sensus moralis male dicitur tropologicus, quia mores non vocantur τρόποι, sed ἤθη. (3) Elevatio graece non vocatur ἀναγωγία (quae vox notat defectum disciplinae, vel vitam dissolutam) sed ἀναγωγή.

Obl. VII. Theologi orthodoxi distinguunt sensum mysticum in typicum, allegoricum & parabolicum. Sensus typicus (definiente D. Glassio lib. II. part. I. tract. II. Sect. II. p. 289.) est, quando sub externis factis seu propheticis visionibus, res occultae, sive praesentes, sive futurae, figurantur, & praesertim quando res gestae V. T. praesignificant seu adumbrant res gestas N. T. Subdistinguitur sensus typicus a D. Glassio l. c. in propheticum, & historicum. Typus prophetae seu propheticus est, quo prophetae divinitus inspirati suis in concionibus partim commonitoriis, partim vaticinatoriis crebro utuntur. Quando videlicet symbolis externis res occultas, sive praesentes, sive futuras, per Spiritum S. figurant & significant. Consistit autem in propheticis ac typicis, 1. actionibus, 2. visionibus. Actiones prophetiarum typicae sunt, quando iis, quae exterius-divino mandato prophetae peragebant, mysticum aliquod & occultum adumbratur. v. gr. Esaias c. XX, 2. nudus, i. e. veste sua prophetica exutus incedit, ad adumbrandam cladem Aegyptiorum & Aethiopum. Visiones oblatae sunt vel dormientibus, vel vigilantibus. Visiones typicae dormientibus oblatae sunt per somnia divinitus immissa, quatenus figuris & typis sunt involuta, e. g. Somnium Iacobi de scala, a terra ad coelum pertingente, Gen. XXVIII, 12. Applicationem eius typicam vid. Io. I, 15. Visiones typicae, vigilantibus oblatae, quaedam habent additam interpretationem typi, quarum explicatio ex συναφείᾳ & circumstantiis textus eruenda est. v. gr. propheta Ieremias vidit duas corbes ficuum bonarum & malarum. Prior corbis plena bonis ficubus praefigurauit ecclesiae Israeliticae instaurationem; posterior significauit Zedekiae & populi iudaici deportationem: quae interpretatio habetur Ier. XXIV. v. 5. 6. 7. 8. Typus historiae, seu historicus, est sensus scripturae mysticus, quo res gestae V. T. praefigurant res gestas aut gerendas N. T. v. gr. Agnus paschalis erat typus Christi. De agno paschali inquit Iehouah, Exod. XII, 46. Os ne frangetis in eo. Quae verba sensu litterali unice de agno paschali, ab Israelitis mactando & comedendo, intelliguntur: typica accommodatione ad Christum, agno paschali praefiguratum, applicantur, Io. XIX, 36. Sensus allegoricus est, quando historia scripturae, vere gesta, ad mysterium quoddam, sive spiritualem doctrinam, ex intentione Spiritus S. refertur. v. gr. Saevitia in bruta, inprimis in boues laborantes, feuere vetuit creator: cuius interdictum legere licet Deut. XXV, 4. Non obturabis os bouis, cum triturat. Sensu litterali hoc dictum biblicum de nullo alio, quam de boue triturante, intelligitur: allegorice idem applicatur ad ministrum ecclesiae, in salutem hominum impense laborantem, 1 Cor. IX, 9. Sensus parabolicus est, quando res aliqua, vt gesta, apposite fingitur & narratur, atque ad aliud spirituale designandum refertur. Sic nemini non christianorum sacris initiato constat parabola de patrefamilias, qui exiuit summo diluculo ad conducendum operarios in vineam suam. Matth. XX, 1. sqq.

Obl. VIII. Accommodatio mystica est vel innata, vel illata. Illa est, quam ipsa sacra scriptura vel expresse ostendit, vel quadantenus insinuat: Haec est, quam ipsa sacra scriptura non ostendit, sed quae a doctoribus ecclesiae excogitata est. Quae si fuerit oblata, non sine probabili fundamento e sensu litterali petita, fideique analoga, a nobis haud invitis acceptatur; sin fuerit extorta, probabili fundamento destituta, et ab analogia fidei deflectens, repudiatur.

Vnius cuiusque dicti biblici simplicis sensum litteralem formalem a Spiritu S. intentum non duplicem, sed vnum esse, probatur.

I. A causa S. scripturae efficiente, Deo, qui cum sit veracissimus, optimus, et sapientissimus, non ludit amphiboliis, vt spiritus ille λoξίας, qui consultus a Pyrrho, Romanis insidias molienti, ambigue respondit: Aio te, Aeacida, Romanos vincere posse. Illusit impostor gemino oraculi sensu: at quodlibet dictum biblicum vnicum exhibet sensum litteralem diuinum.

II. A natura sensus et significationis. Forma sacrae scripturae est vna. Atqui sensus litteralis est forma sacrae scripturae, et eius quasi anima. Ergo sensus litteralis sacrae scripturae est vnus.

III. A S. scripturae veritate. Quidquid est verum, est vnum. (Plus vno verum esse nequit.) Atqui sensus S. scripturae est verus. Ergo est vnus.

IV. A S. scripturae perspicuitate, quae adeo lucida est, vt vel infans eius sensum assequatur. Exemplo nobis est Timotheus, commendatus a S. Paulo, quod ab infantia sacras litteras nouerit. 2 Tim. III, 15. At scriptura, variis implicita sensibus, sua se obscuritate inuoluit, legentisque animum distrahit.

V. A S. scripturae fine, qui est σοφίσαι, seu imperitos et paruulos sapientes reddere, Ps. XIX, 8. 2 Tim. III, 15. Sensus alicuius dicti multiplex non reddit hominem sapientem, sed errantem: parit enim aequivocationem, fecundam errorum genetricem.

VI. Ab absurdo. Si S. scriptura multos, eosque in vno loco, in vna propositione, diuersos sustineret sensus: nullum firmum ex ea peteretur argumentum: esset tuba, incertum reddens sonum, adeoque inutilis, 1 Cor. XIV, 7. non foret constans fidei morumque regula.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, et Socinianorum, statuentium, vnius dicti biblici plures posse esse sensus litterales; qui, suam munituri opinionem, haud pauca adducunt dicta biblica, quae ex eorum mente pollent duplici sensu, diuinitus intento.

I. Ioelis II, 13. Scindite cor vestrum, et non vestimenta vestra. Resp. Dictum hoc biblicum non vna propositio, sed virtute duplex. Nobis sermo est de vno dicto biblico simplici.

Vid. Obf. 1. II. Dictum illud: Exod. XX, 3. Non habebis Deos alienos coram me, multos gignit sensus, Resp. Gignit vnum sensum formalem, siue immediatum, ex quo sensus virtuales et mediati per consequentiam eliciuntur.

III. Dantur dicta biblica, in quibus tam sensus litteralis, quam mysticus, a Deo intentus est. v. gr. Exod. XII, 46. Os non confringetis in eo. Deut. XXV, 4. Quae ab ipso Spiritu sancto sensu mystico explicantur, Io. XIX, 36. 1 Cor. IX, 9. Resp. Sensus mysticus rectius vocatur accomodatio, siue applicatio dicti biblici, quam eius sensus, siquidem a Spiritu sancto non per verba θεόπνευστα intenditur, sed per rem aut factum, verbis θεόπνευστοις indigitatum, ad aliam rem, aut aliud factum, ob analogiam, aut qualemcunque conuenientiam, a Spiritu sancto applicatur.

Nos loquimur de sensu per verba diuina intento, non... de accomodatione rerum, aut factorum mystica. IV. Verba Hoseae c. XI, 1. Quum puer (esset) Israël, tum delexi eum: et ex Aegypto vocaui filium meum, duplici sensu accipienda sunt. 1.

Litterali sensu de populo Israëlico, e fer-e servitute Aegyptiaca liberato. 2. Sensu mystico de Christo in Aegyptum secedente & redeunte, Resp. 1) Nihil nostræ sententiæ decederet, si diceremus, verba illa sensu litterali intelligi de populo Israëlitico, cuius ex Aegypto remigratio,... ad reditum Christi ex Aegypto mystice applicetur. 2) Verba Hoseæ: Ex Aegypto vocaui filium meum, non mystice, sed ad litteram & immediate, de Christo accipienda sunt hoc modo: Cum Israël נער puer i. e. rudis, præcipitans in actionibus suis, & excutiens iugum esset; adeo tamen ipsum dilexi, vt illius gratia filium meum Iesum euocauerim ex Aegypto, quo inscium erudiat, petulantem corrigat, præcipitantem doctrina cœlesti emendet ac firmet.

V. Verba Ps. II, 7. Ego hodie genui te, triplicem habent sensum: explicantur enim de æterna filii Dei generatione, Hebr. I, 5. de resurrectione Christi, Actor. XIII, 33. De sacerdotio ipsius, Hebr. V, 5. Resp. Verba Ps. II, 7. citata recte exponuntur de æterna filii Dei generatione, Hebr. I, 33. de Christi resuscitatione a mortuis agitur, sed græcum illud: ἀναστήσας idem est, quod excitans, exhibens, adducens. Sensus igitur est: Deus pater, memor promissionis suæ, excitauit, misit & exhibuit Iudæis filium suum ab æterno genitum, quem compellauerat Ps. II. Filius meus es tu: Ego hodie genui te. De resurrectione Christi a mortuis agitur v. 34. Hebr. V, 5. Describitur persona, a qua Christus ad sacerdotium vocatus est. Persona illa est Deus pater, fons & origo filii, a quo, vt essentiam per æternam generationem, ita honorem sacerdotii magni, tempore constituto accepit. Ex quibus elucet, quod verba Psalmi II. Ego hodie genui te, non nisi unam habeant significationem, eamque vbique retineant.

VI. Verba Es. LIII, 4. Languores nostros portauit, 1 Petr. II, 25. de peccatis, Matth. VIII, 17. de morbis corporis exponuntur. Resp. Christus portauit generatim omnes morbos, corporis & animæ: portauit enim peccata, & eorum pœnas, e quarum censu sunt morbi. Summouendo igitur morbos, seu pœnas, a posteriori demonstravit, se portare & expiare peccata mundi.

VII. Memorabile illud vaticinium Iehouæ, 2 Sam. VII, 14. Cum complebuntur dies tui, & cubueris cum patribus tuis, erigam semen tuum post te, quod exibit ex visceribus tuis, & firmum faciam regnum eius. Ego ero illi in patrem, & ille erit mihi in filium: tam de Salomone, quam de Christo intelligitur. Resp. Totum hoc vaticinium sensu litterali intelligendum est de Messia; quia I. hic agitur de semine excitando ex visceribus Dauidis, post Dauidis tempora: non ergo de Salomone, qui post Dauidem fato functum neque natus, neque in folio regio collocatus est. II. Neque Salomoni thronus regni eius stabilitus est in æternum, sed Messiæ v. 13. III. Dauid respondet: Hæc est lex hominis, qui est Dominus Deus, designans Christum θεάνθρωπον. IV. S. Paullus hoc oraculum de Christo editum esse testatur Hebr. I, 5. Dicis I. Non omnia prædicata huius vaticinii competunt Messiæ. Nam de conditore domus domini agitur, qui est Salomon. Resp. Domus domini non notat templum materiale Salomonem, sed domum spiritualem, nempe ecclesiam, cuius architectus est Christus. Ratio est, quia intelligitur domus æque perpetua, ac regnum huius feminis Dauidis æternum. Dicis II. De illius templi ædificatione agitur in responso diuino, de quo in consilio Dauidis actum erat, quod fine dubio ex mente Dauidis fuit materiale. Resp. Diuina responsio est partim negatiua, partim affirmatiua. Negatiue respondet Dominus: Num tu ædificabis domum, vt habitem? Non ergo desiderat... dominus templum materiale. Affirmatiue respondet idem per inuerfionem: Annuntiauit tibi Iehouah (Deus pater), quod tibi domum facturus sit Iehouah (Deus filius, quia Dominus loquitur de Domino). Quæ verba continent πρότασιν & summam eorum, quæ fequuntur; vtpote quibus indicatur, quod non Dauid dominominum exstruere debebat, sed dominus Dauidi domum spiritualem & regnum æternum conditurus erat: quæ domus spiritualis, & quod regnum æternum est ecclesia, domus Dei viuentis, 1 Tim. III, 15. quam Christus condidit, Matth. XVI, 18. regnum Christi, cuius non erit finis. Luc. I, 33.
