Dicis III. De ea perfona loquitur dominus, quæ a proclivitate ad peccandum non fuit immunis. Nam inquit v. 14. Qui quum prauum quid fecerit, castigabo eum baculo hominum, & plagis filiorum hominis. Resp. Loquitur dominus (α) non de peccato inhærente, quippe quo Messias nunquam fuit infectus, sed de peccato imputato; ideo quod peccata totius mundi expianda lubens in fe fuscepit, 1 Io. II, 2. Quæ graphice delineatura sacra scriptura perinde loquitur de Christo, ac fi ipse peccauerit. Pf. XL, 13. Pf. XXXI, 15. Pf. LXIX, 6. (β) De paffione Christi fatisfactoria.

Dicis IV. Hoc vaticinium cum dulcissima promissione coniunctum exponitur de Salomone ab ipso Dauide, 1 Paral. XXII, 9. nec non a Salomone sibi ipsi applicatur, 1 Reg. V, 5. c. VIII, 17. 2 Paral. VI, 7. Resp. Loca citata non sunt parallela vaticinio, de quo iam egimus. Nam ista promissio 1 Paral. XXII, 9. quam cætera loca respiciunt, tempore est posterior nostro vaticinio. Illa de filio Dauidi nascituro; hoc de femine excitando longe post fata Dauidis: illa de domo materiali & templo Hierofolymitano; hoc de domo spirituali & regno æterno agit, atque repetitur 1 Paral. XVII, 11. feqq.

VIII. Verba Ierem. XXXI, 15. Vox in Rama (quidem) audita est, planctus, fletus amaritudinum: Rachel est deplorans fuper filiis suis, intelliguntur de Beniaminitis in captiuitatem adducendis. Sed Matth. II, 18. exponuntur de infanticidio Herodis, & lamentatione matrum Bethlehemiticarum. Resp. Non intelligitur 1. c. planctus Beniaminitarum (quorum nonnine etiam designantur Iudæi, inde a scissione regni Ifraëlitici cum illis coniuncti, 1 Reg. XXII, 20.) auditus ob abductionem in captiuitatem, de qua Spiritus S. illum planctum nunquam exponit; sed ob infanticidium Herodianum Rachel plorans introducitur per propofopeiam, quo defignetur, vsque in fines Beniamin tyrannidem Herodis fæuituram, & in illis confiniis, vbi Rachel oculos clausit & sepulta est, posteritatem eiusdem detestabili truculentia interemptum iri. Rachelis autem sepulcrum exstabat in agro Bethlehemitico, Gen. XXXV, 19. Non ergo geminus l. c. datur sensus.

IX. Io. VI, 50. Caiphas inquit: Expedit nobis, vt vnus homo moriatur pro populo, & non tota gens intereat. Hoc autem a fe ipso non dixit; sed cum facerdos magnus illius anni effet, prophetauit, quod Iefus moriturus esset pro gente (illa). Resp. Dicti biblici iam citati vnus est huius intentus, a Spiritu S. intentus; nempe e re fore vniuerfi generis humani, fi ad huius interitum æternum auertendum Christus mortem oppeteret, non obstante, quod Caiphas alium sensum mente sua conceperit. Neque enim fermo nobis est de sensu dicti biblici humano, sed diuino, quem Caiphas non intellexit, sed in edendo vaticinio os tantum Spiritui S. præbuit, vt aliæa Bileami, & fine prophetiæ intellectu vaticinatus est.

X. Quando Mofes Deut. XXXII, 1. exclamar: Auscultate cæli; loquar enim, audiatque terra fermones oris mei: per cælos, censente Coccëio, intelligi poffunt angeli, cæli aërii & ætherii; quia scriptura vocem cælum, in omnibus illis significationibus vfurpat. Resp. α) Diſt. inter vocabula fumta feorfim, & coniunctim in tota phrafi. Si vocabula fumantur feorfim, sensu vario poffunt exponi, fi fumantur coniunctim, scopus dicentis respiciendus, & antecedentia cum confeq. n'ibus accurate sunt conferenda: qua ratione vnum pariunt sensum. β) Aliud est, vocabulum posse sensu differenti exponi, & aliud, sensu variante explicandum esse. Lutherus: Ein anders ist: es kann also heißen; Ein anders: es muß also heißen.

Loco citato metonymice per cælos, angelos, testes factorum divinorum in cælo gloriæ, per terram, homines, orbem terrarum incolentes, intelligimus.


### XVIII. Did divine inspiration preserve the sacred amanuenses from all error?: XI. Whatever is the word of God, it is fruitful in many senses.... But holy scripture is [the word of God] &c. Therefore. The major is…

XI. Whatever is the word of God, it is fruitful in many senses.... But holy scripture is [the word of God] &c. Therefore. The major is evident, because the word of God is a concept of the divine mind.

But God can express infinite things in one mental concept. Resp. I deny the major.

To the proof we say that God adorned holy scripture, not according to the measure of His own intellect, but according to His most benign will, and thus with a quantity pleasing to Himself, so that He might condescend by a convenient συγκατάβασις (condescension) to the capacity of our intellect. For since God speaks in holy scripture not for His own sake, but for ours, i. e., to aid and direct the concepts of our intellect, He did not express multiple senses in individual passages: otherwise it would not aid our intellect, but overwhelm it.

XII. Interpreters of holy scripture often elicit a manifold sense from one biblical saying. e. g.

When the Holy Spirit exhorts through the psalmist, Ps. II, 12. נַשְּׁקוּ־בַר, those words can be expounded in a fourfold sense, analogous to the faith. 1) adore the son. 2) adore purely. 3) kiss the wheat. 4) apprehend discipline.

Resp. α) Distinguish between the sense of holy scripture that is brought in and that which is innate. Interpreters, since they do not always attain the mind of the Lord, bring various senses to one biblical saying: although only one is as it were innate, and intended by the Holy Spirit. β) Although the Hebrew word נַשְּׁקוּ־בַר denotes son, wheat, pure (but never doctrine or instruction) if taken separately; yet here, taken conjunctively in the whole phrase, it must be explained according to the scope of the speaker, and the collation of the preceding and following [verses]. The scope of the second Psalm is the religious veneration of the Messiah.

The reasons are most pregnant, because He is the king anointed by God the Father, and established upon the most holy mount Zion, i. e., the church, v. 6. the catholic king, v. 8. the omnipotent king, v. 9. a hostile conspiracy against Him stands in the way of the religious veneration of the Messiah, v. 1. 2. and the contempt of His religion, v. 3. which obstacles must be removed.

The mode of worshipping the Messiah is inculcated in the immediately preceding v. 11. namely, that He must be served in fear, joined with spiritual joy: in the following [verses] confidence is commended to be placed in this divine, catholic, and omnipotent king. These things being weighed, there is no doubt that the Hebrew words נַשְּׁקוּ־בַר should be rendered: kiss the son, i. e., worship the only-begotten Son of God, the greatest king, full of confidence, love, joy, fear, and submission, in the rite of those who, about to venerate most powerful kings, kiss their hands. Other senses brought to this biblical saying by interpreters, although they may be analogous to the faith, are not, however, analogous to the text.

Latin:

XI. Quidquid est verbum Dei, illud multis sensibus est fœcundum. Atqui sacra scriptura &c.... Ergo. Maior patet, quia verbum Dei est conceptus mentis divinæ. Deus autem uno conceptu mentali infinita exprimere potest.

Resp. neg. maiorem.

Ad probationem dicimus, quod Deus sacram scripturam adornaverit, non secundum mensuram intellectus sui, sed secundum voluntatem suam benignissimam, adeoque quantitate sibi complacente, ut commoda συγκαταβάσει ad captum intellectus nostri condescenderet. Cum enim Deus in sacra scriptura loquatur non sui, sed nostri gratia, i. e. ad iuvandos dirigendosque intellectus nostri conceptus, singulis locis non expressit sensus plures: ceteroqui non iuvaret intellectum nostrum, sed obrueret.

XII. Interpretes sacræ scripturæ sæpenumero ex uno dicto biblico multiplicem eruunt sensum. v. gr.

Quando Spiritus sanctus per hieropsalten cohortatur, Ps. II, 12. נַשְּׁקוּ־בַר verba illa quadruplici sensu, fidei analogo, exponi possunt. 1) adorate filium. 2) adorate pure. 3) osculamini triticum. 4) apprehendite disciplinam.

Resp. α) Dist. inter sensum sacræ scripturæ illatum & innatum. Interpretes, cum mentem Domini non assequantur semper, varios sensus uni dicto biblico inferunt: quamvis ipsi unus tantum sit quasi innatus, & a Spiritu sancto intentus. β) Quamvis vox hebræa נַשְּׁקוּ־בַר notet filium, triticum, purum (at nunquam doctrinam aut institutionem) si sumatur seorsim; hic tamen coniunctim sumta in tota phrasi, secundum scopum dicentis, atque collationem antecedentium & consequentium explicanda est. Scopus Psalmi secundi est religiosa veneratio Messiæ.

Rationes prægnantissimæ sunt, quia est rex unctus a Deo patre, & constitutus super montem sanctissimum Sionem, i. e. ecclesiam, v. 6. rex catholicus, v. 8. rex omnipotens, v. 9. religiose Messiæ venerationi obstat hostilis adversus eum conspiratio, v. 1. 2. & eius religionis contemptus, v. 3. quæ obstacula removenda sunt.

Modus colendi Messiam inculcatur in proxime præcedenti v. 11. nimirum, quod ei serviendum sit in timore, cum spirituali gaudio coniuncto: in consequentibus commendatur fiducia in hoc rege divino, catholico & omnipotente, collocanda. Quibus pensitatis, nullum est dubium, quin verba hebræa נַשְּׁקוּ־בַר reddenda sint: osculamini filium, i. e. Christum unigenitum Dei filium, regem maximum, pleni fiduciæ, amoris, gaudii, timoris & obsequii submisse colite, ritu eorum, qui reges potentissimos veneraturi, ipsorum manus osculantur. Sensus alii huic dicto biblico ab interpretibus illati quamvis sint analogi fidei, non tamen sunt analogi textui.


### Quæst. XX. What is the external form of Holy Scripture?

The external form of Holy Scripture is the style, the character of the speech, and the idiom; and that is Hebrew in the Old Testament ; except for a few certain particles, which, as the occasion required, were recorded in the Chaldean idiom

Prob. b. A Chaldean pericope is found in the codex of the Old Testament, Jer. 10, 11. Containing the response of the Jews to the Chaldeans: and almost entire chapters in books written after the Babylonian captivity: namely in the book of Ezra from ch. 4, 8. up to ch. 6, 19. and from ch. 7, 10. up to verse 27. Letters written by the Chaldeans and to the Chaldeans are commemorated: and also in the book of Daniel from ch. 2. up to ch. 8. where the Babylonian king's account of a dream, consultation, acts, visions, and some writings are composed in the Chaldean style.

Prob. c. The New Testament is consigned in the Greek idiom. For since, besides the Jews, Gentiles also, differing in languages and dialects, were to be enticed to the Christian faith through the preaching of the Gospel, the New Testament was written in the Greek language quite appropriately; because this was most well-known at that time not only to the Jews, but also to the Gentiles everywhere, and thus most convenient for the propagation of evangelical doctrine.

Latin:

Quæ est forma S. scripturæ externa? Forma S. scripturæ externa est stilus, sermonis character & idioma; idque hebræum in veteri testamento ; exceptis paucis quibusdam particulis, quæ, occasione sic ferente, chaldaico idiomate consignatæ sunt

Prob. b. Invenitur in codice veteris testamenti pericope chaldaica, Ierem. X, 11. Iudæorum ad Chaldæos responsum continens: & integra pene capita in libris post captivitatem Babylonicam scriptis: nempe in libro Esdræ a c. IV, 8. vsque ad c. VI, 19. & a c. VII, 10. vsque ad versum 27. litteræ a Chaldæis & ad Chaldæos scriptæ commemorantur: nec non in libro Danielis a cap. II. vsque ad cap. VIII. vbi regis Babylonici relatio somnii, consultatio, acta, visiones & scripta nonnulla stilo chaldaico contexta sunt.

Prob. c. Nov. Testam. idiomate græco consignatum est. Cum enim præter Iudæos, etiam gentiles, linguis & dialectis differentes, per prædicationem euangelii ad fidem christianam alliciendi essent, congrue admodum lingua græca scriptum est novum testamentum; quia hæc non solum Iudæis illo tempore, verum gentilibus etiam vndiquaque erat notissima, adeoque ad propagationem doctrinæ euangelicæ conuenientissima.


### Question XXI. Is the style of Holy Scripture, especially of the New Testament, uneducated, filled with barbarisms and solecisms?

The style of Holy Scripture, as much of the Old as of the New Testament, is grave and worthy of divine majesty, defiled by no grammatical vice, no barbarism or solecism.

Obj. 1. An unlearned style is crude, rustic, and destitute of accurate connection and every ornament.

Obj. 2. The Stoics, according to Diogenes Laertius lib. VIII, and Suidas following him, define a barbarism as that which is made ἐκ τῶν κακῶν λέξις παρὰ τὸ ἔθος τῶν εὐδοκιμέντων ἑλλήνων, a vicious expression contrary to the custom of the illustrious Greeks. A solecism, however, to the same Suidas is ὁ λέγες ἀκαταλλήλως συντεταγμένος, speech incongruously constructed. To Donatus, a solecism is a vice committed in the context of the parts of speech against the rule of

Prob. I. The style of the most wise God is not to be called idiotic, nor defiled by barbarisms or solecisms. But the style of Holy Scripture is the style of the most wise God. Therefore. The major is evident, because to God, the giver of languages and the most wise artificer of speech, no vice of speech can be imputed without the great mark of blasphemy and impiety. The minor is proved from Matt. 10, 19. 20 Take no thought how or what you shall speak: for it shall be given you in that hour what you ought to speak. For it is not you that speak, but the Spirit of your Father which speaks in you. But if the Holy Spirit inspired the apostles in extemporaneous apologies not only τὸ τί, the thing itself, but also τὸ πῶς, the manner of speaking: much more did He suggest to them the manner of writing words that were decorous and suitable for expressing things; inasmuch as they were to endure for many centuries by the will of God.

II. Crude and ignorant men write a vicious style. But the prophets were not crude and ignorant. Therefore. The major is clear, because, in the opinion of Quintilian, a solecism is a name for ignorance and crudity. The minor is evident, since the prophets and apostles were men moved and illuminated by the Holy Spirit, 2 Pet. 1, 21. to whom the Spirit inspired both the things and the words to be written, 2 Tim. 3, 16.

There is an antithesis from Erasmus, Vorstius, Salmasius, and others, who think too abjectly of the style of Holy Scripture, and assert that it is unlearned and defiled by barbarisms and solecisms: whose stronger arguments are:

I. The apostles were men ἀγράμματοι καὶ ἰδιῶται, unlearned and crude, Acts 4, 13. Therefore they wrote an unlearned and crude style. R. The apostles in the cited place are called unlearned and idiots antecedently, i.e., before they had been endowed with power from on high, Luke 24, 49. because they had not been cultivated in the disciplines of the philosophers or the Pharisees: but they were not unlearned and idiots consequently, i.e., after rudeness of language was taken away by the fire of the Holy Spirit, so that they spoke in their own dialect (Act. II, 6) to the men of most diverse languages who were present.

Instantia The Apostle Paul, illuminated by the Holy Spirit, calls himself an idiot (2 Cor. XI, 6). Εἰ δὲ καὶ ἰδιώτης τῷ λόγῳ, ἀλλ’ ἐν τῇ γνώσει. But if I am indeed an idiot (unskilled, rude) in speech, yet not in knowledge. Resp. α) The apostle is arguing in the place cited κατ’ ἄνθρωπον: for he is not speaking categorically, but hypothetically, i.e., according to a hypothetical concession based on the opinion of the pseudo-apostles and the Corinthians adhering to them, as if he were saying: Be it that, to the boastful judges (λεγ:δαιδάλεις), I am an idiot, or rude in speech; yet the worthiness of the knowledge of divine mysteries, proper to prophets and apostles, compensates for the defect of my simple oration. β) The apostle denies himself the glory of a polished, curled, and rhetorical-school-derived oration, which is often soft and effeminate; yet he did not lack a masculine eloquence, heavy with the weight of thoughts, full of divine energy, so that the Spirit might draw the souls of men to Christ, not entice them with the blandishments of speech in the manner of flatterers.

II. Whoever uses Hebraisms in Greek writings, their writings are barbarous. But, etc. Therefore. The major premise is evident, because foreign words, such as Hebrew ones, used in the Greek language, and also the Hebraic idioms sprinkled into the Attic language, make it barbarous. The minor is evident both from Hebrew and Chaldean-Syriac words: Korban, Thalita, Racha, Manna, Halleluia, Hosianna, Mammona, etc., and from the formulas of constructing speech, proper to the Hebrews, in which the Scripture of the N. T. abounds. Resp. (α) The major is not universal: for by the same retained form of arguing, someone might conclude: Whoever uses Grecisms in Latin writings, their writings are barbarous. But CICERO, VIRGILIUS, HORATIUS, etc. Therefore. (β)

A foreign word received by usage, sometimes when necessity urges, sometimes when elegance persuades, we use without the vice of barbarism. (γ) Barbarism is not introduced when a lower language receives formulas of speech from a higher, more excellent, and more ancient one (such as Hebrew is), and transfers them into its own use. (δ) It pleased the Holy Spirit, in order to show the harmony of the O. & N. T., to propagate the mysteries of the faith with the same style and thread of speech. Wherefore it is no wonder that the property of the Hebrew language, as the first, spreads itself through both the O. and N. T., and flows into the biblical Grecism. Whence that which is considered barbarous in the Greek language of the Attics is not to be held as barbarous in the biblical, Hebrew-Greek language.

III. There is in the N. T. speech written incongruously: Therefore a solecism. The antecedent is evident from (Luc. XXII, 26) ἐν τῷ αἵματι ἐκχυνόμενον: it should have been said congruously: ἐκχυνομένῳ. Resp. The Greek words are to be explained by ellipsis: ὃ ἐστὶν ἐκχυνόμενον. D. DANNHAV. warns excellently in Hodof. Phaen. I. p. 42. What a profane person would call a solecism, a Christian would more rightly call this figure grammar, syllepsis, ellipsis, enallage: for far be it that we should impute κακίαν, or foulness, as Fabius calls it, to the Holy Spirit.

IV. SALMASIUS objects in his commentary on the Hellenistic language, p. 260, that certain Fathers of the church called the apostles ἰδιώτας, ἀγροίκους, ἀμαθεῖς, ἀγραμμάτους, idiots, rustics, unskilled in speaking, illiterate, whose diction becomes ἀγροικιτομένη, σολοικίζουσα, βαρβαρίζουσα & ἰδιωτική. Resp. (1) Not all the Fathers feel so abjectly about the apostolic style, but they ingenuously and openly confess its gravity. (2) Certain Fathers spoke from the hypothesis of the Gentile sophists, whom they did not wish to refute on this very point, but by conceding this, that the apostolic style is idiot and unpolished, they refuted this objection by another reason, partly by preferring the simplicity of biblical eloquence to the pomp of words, the allurements of rhetoricians, and the affected kind of speaking of the sophists; partly, leaving the nature of the style, by appealing to the very majesty of the things contained in the Holy Scripture, and by this very argument, as a stronger battering ram, they [refuted] them.

Hence ORIGEN, Book

IV, On First Principles, ch.

I: If the books of the New Testament had been written by rhetorical art or philosophical cunning to entice men to believe, without doubt our faith would be thought to consist in the art of words and in human wisdom, and not in the power of God.

AMBROSE, Epistle

LXIV: Although the writers of the divine books did not write according to art, but according to grace, which is above all art: yet those who have written about art have found art in their writings.

AUGUSTINE, Book

IV, On Christian Doctrine, ch. VI: Just as there is a certain eloquence that better befits a youthful age, and there is one that befits an old age: and it is no longer to be called eloquence if it does not suit the person speaking: so there is a certain kind that befits men of the highest authority and who are clearly divine.

These things the apostles spoke: nor does any other befit them, nor does this befit others: for it is suitable to them: but to others, the more humble it seems, the more highly it transcends, not by vanity, but by solidity.

CHRYSOSTOM feels magnificently about the eloquence of Paul, Book IV, On the Priesthood:

One should not look for the lightness of Socrates, the swelling of Demosthenes, the dignity of Thucydides, the height of Plato, or the ornament of foreign eloquence in St. Paul: yet there is not lacking in him a bare and simple speech, which has the meaning of the greatest things, and confirms all things most robustly: from which ornament of his, which is greatest and of the highest praise, he is not to be stripped.

Latin:

Stilus sacræ scripturæ, tam veteris, quam N. T. est gravis & dignus maiestate diuina, nullo vitio grammatico, nullo barbarismo aut solæcismo fœdatus.

Obs. 1. Stilus idioticus est rudis, agrestis, accurata connexione & omni ornamento destitutus.

Obs. 2. Barbarismum Stoici apud Diogenem Laërtium lib. VIII. & ex eo Suidas definiunt, quod fit ἐκ τῶν κακῶν λέξις παρὰ τὸ ἔθος τῶν εὐδοκιμέντων ἑλλήνων, vitiosa dictio præter consuetudinem clarorum græcorum. Solæcismus vero eidem Suidæ est ὁ λέγες ἀκαταλλήλως συντεταγμένος, oratio incongrue constructa. Donato solæcismus est vitium in contextu partium orationis contra regulam artis commissum.

Prob. I. Stilus Dei sapientissimi neque idioticus, neque barbarismis aut solæcismis obfutus dicendus est. Atqui stilus sacræ scripturæ est stilus Dei sapientissimi. Ergo. Maior patet, quia Deo, linguarum datori, sermonisque artifici sapientissimo, non fine grandi blasphemiæ atque impietatis nota vitium sermonis imputari potest. Minor probatur ex Matth X, 19. 20 Ne solliciti estote, quomodo & quid locuturi sitis: dabitur enim vobis illa hora, quid loqui debeatis. Non enim vos estis, qui loquimini, sed Spiritus patris, qui loquitur in vobis. Quod si Spiritus S. apostolis in apologiis extemporalibus non solum τὸ τί, rem ipsam, sed etiam τὸ πῶς, modum loquendi, inspirauit: multo magis ipsis fugessit modum scribendi verba decora & rebus exprimendis conuenientia; vtpote quæ ex voluntate Dei multis seculis perennare debebant.

II. Stilum vitiosum scribunt rudes & ignorantes. Sed prophetæ non fuerunt rudes & ignorantes. Ergo. Maior liquet, quia, censente Quintiliano, solæcismus est nomen ignorantiæ & ruditatis. Minor patet, quoniam prophetæ & apostoli fuerunt viri a Spiritu S. agitati & illuminati, 2 Petr. I, 21. quibus Spiritus & res & verba scribenda inspirauit, 2 Tim. III, 16.

Antithesis est Erasmi, Vorstii, Salmasii, & aliorum, nimis abiecte de stilo sacræ scripturæ sentientium, eumque idioticum, barbarismis & solæcismis obitum esse, asserentium: quorum potiora sunt argumenta:

I. Apostoli fuerunt viri ἀγράμματοι καὶ ἰδιῶται, indocti & rudes, Act. IV, 13. Ergo scripserunt stilum idioticum & rudem. R. Apostoli l. c. dicuntur indocti & idiotæ antecedenter, i. e. priusquam virtute ex alto induti fuerant, Luc. XXIV, 49. quoniam nec philosophorum, nec pharilæorum disciplinis exculti erant: at non erant indocti & idiotæ consequenter, i. e. postquam ruditas linguae per ignem Spiritus S. fuit sublata, adeo, vt locuti fuerint ἰδίᾳ διαλέκτῳ ad diuersissimarum linguarum homines praesentes, Act. II, 6.

Instantia: Apostolus Paulus, a Spiritu S. illuminatus, se idiotam appellat 2 Cor. XI, 6. Εἰ δὲ καὶ ἰδιώτης τῷ λόγῳ, ἀλλ’ ἐν τῇ γνώσει. Quod si vero etiam idiota (imperitus, rudis) sum sermone, non tamen notitia. Resp. α) Discurrit apostolus l. c. κατ’ ἄνθρωπον: neque enim loquitur categorice, sed hypothetice, f. ad concessionem hypotheticam ex opinione pseudo-apostolorum & Corinthiorum iis adhaerescentium, quasi dicat: Esto, quod iudicibus thrasonibus λεγ:δαιδάλεις sim idiota, siue rudis sermone; simplicis tamen meae orationis defectum compensat digna prophetis & apostolis mysteriorum diuinorum scientia. β) Derogat sibi apostolus gloriam orationis fucatae, calamistratae, e scholis rhetorum petitae, quae saepe mollis & effoeminata est; non tamen ipsi defuit eloquentia mascula, sententiarum pondere grauis, plena diuina ἐνεργείᾳ, vt si Spiritus animos hominum ad Christum raperet, non adulatorum ritu sermonis blanditiis alliceret.

II. Quicunque in scriptis graecis vtuntur hebraismis, illorum scripta sunt barbara. Atqui &c. Ergo. Maior constat, quia vocabula peregrina, qualia sunt hebraea, usurpata in lingua graeca, nec non hebraeorum idiotismi aspersi linguae atticae, hanc efficiunt barbaram. Minor patet tum ex vocibus hebraeis, & chaldaeo-syriacis: Korban, Thalita, Racha, Manna, Halleluia, Hosianna, Mammona &c. tum ex formulis orationem construendi, hebraeorum propriis, quibus scriptura N. T. abundat. Resp. (α) Maior non est vniuersalis: nam eadem retenta argumentandi forma quispiam concluderet: Quicunque in scriptis latinis vtuntur graecismis, illorum scripta sunt barbara. Atqui CICERO, VIRGILIUS, HORATIUS &c. Ergo. (β)

Voce peregrina vsu recepta, modo urgente necessitate, modo fuadente venustate, fine vitio barbarismi vtimur. (γ) Non inducitur barbarismus, quando lingua inferior a superiori, praestantiori & antiquiori (qualis est hebraea) formulas loquendi mutuo accipit, & in vsum suum transfert. (δ) Placuit Spiritui S. ad ostendendam harmoniam V. & N. T. eodem stilo filoque sermonis mysteria fidei propagare. Quare nil mirum, quod proprietas linguae hebraeae, tanquam primae, se tam per V. quam N. T. diffundat, & in graecismum biblicum dimanet. Vnde barbarum habendum non est in lingua biblica, hebraeo-graeca, quidquid barbarum censetur in lingua graeca Atticorum.

III. Datur in N. T. oratio incongrue scripta: Ergo soloecismus. Antecedens patet ex Luc. XXII, 26. ἐν τῷ αἵματι ἐκχυνόμενον: congrue dicendum erat: ἐκχυνομένῳ. Resp. Verba graeca explicanda sunt per ellipsin: ὃ ἐστὶν ἐκχυνόμενον. Praeclare monet D. DANNHAV. in Hodof. Phaen. I. p. 42. Quem soloecismum vocaret profanus, hanc figuram christianus rectius dixerit grammaticam, syllepsin, ellipsin, enallagen: absit enim, vt Spiritui sancto κακίαν, aut faeditatem, vt appellat Fabius, imputemus.

IV. Obiicit SALMASIUS comm. de lingua hellenist. p. 260. Patres quosdam ecclesiae appellasse apostolos ἰδιώτας, ἀγροίκους, ἀμαθεῖς, ἀγραμμάτους, idiotas, rusticos, dicendi imperitos, illitteratos, quorum dictio fit ἀγροικιτομένη, σολοικίζουσα, βαρβαρίζουσα & ἰδιωτική. Resp. (1) Non omnes patres tam abiecte sentiunt de stilo apostolico, sed illius gravitatem ingenue aperteque fatentur. (2) Quidam patres locuti sunt ex hypothesi gentilium sophistarum, quos redarguere quoad hoc ipsum punctum noluerunt, sed conceflo hoc, quod filus apostolicus fit idiotus & impolitus, alia ratione obiectionem hanc confutarunt, partim simplicitatem eloquentiae biblicae verborum pompae, lenociniis rhetorum, & sophistarum affectato dicendi generi praeferendo; partim, indole fili relicta, ad ipsam maiestatem rerum in scriptura sacra contentarum prouocando, & hoc ipso argumento, vt fortiori ariete, ipsos de-belbellando.

Hinc ORIGENES L.

IV. περὶ ἀρχῶν c.

I. Si vel arte rhetorica, vel philosophica calliditate conscripti libri novi testamenti ad credendum illicerent homines: fine dubio fides nostra putaretur in verborum arte consistere atque in sapientia humana, & non in virtute Dei.

AMBROSIVS epist.

LXIV. scriptores divinorum librorum quamvis non secundum artem scripserint, sed secundum gratiam, quæ super omnem artem est: ii tamen, qui de arte scripserunt, eorum scriptis artem invenerunt.

AVGVSTINVS lib.

IV. de doctr. christ. c. VI. Sicut est quædam eloquentia, quæ magis ætatem iuvenilem decet; est, quæ senilem: nec iam dicenda est eloquentia, si personæ non congruat eloquentis: ita est quædam, quæ viros summa auctoritate dignissimos, planeque divinos decet.

Hæc illi (apostoli) locuti sunt: nec ipsos decet alia, nec alios ipsa: ipsis enim congruit: aliis autem quanto videtur humilior, tanto altius non ventositate, sed soliditate transcendit.

De eloquentia Paulli magnifice sentit CHRYSOSTOMVS

L. IV. de sacerdot. Non requirenda in S. Paullo levitas Socratis, tumor Demosthenis, dignitas Thucydidis, Platonis altitudo, eloquentiæ peregrinæ ornatus: non deest autem in ipso nuda ac simplex oratio, quæ sententiam habet rerum maximarum, omniaque robustissime confirmat: quo ornatu suo maximo & laude summa spoliandus non est.


### Question XXII

For the benefit of which men were the sacred scriptures destined and written? For all men, possessing the full use of reason, and capable of the external word, the sacred scriptures were destined and written, so that it may be permitted and expedient for clerics and laics, the learned and unlearned, men and women to read them attentively and meditate upon them devoutly .

Proof a. The end for whom, or the subject of Holy Scripture, for whose salvation the most merciful God destined his word revealed and committed to writing, is every man, corrupted by sin, to be saved by a serious divine intention.

For God himself inscribed this law in stone tablets with letters, and handed it to Moses, not so that he might keep it shut up in a chest, as a divine deposit proper to himself, but so that he might communicate it to the people of God, and declare it as a great prophet.

This we gather from Exodus XXIV, 12: Afterward Jehovah said to Moses, ascend to me into the mountain, and be there: for I will give you tablets of stone, and the law and the commandment, which I will write to teach them.

And not only was Moses, or another prophet, bound to teach others the law written by Jehovah, but also the father of a family was bound to inculcate the same to his children and his household: which he seriously enjoined upon Jehovah himself, Deut. VI, 6 seq.: Let all these words, which I (am) commanding you today, be upon your heart: and you shall sharpen them for your children, and you shall speak of them, when you sit in your house, and when you walk in the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.

Indeed, you shall bind them as a sign upon your hand, and they shall be frontlets between your eyes, and you shall write them upon the doorposts of your house and upon your gates.

The crasser Jews understand the cited words each literally; therefore they make for themselves phylacteries of the head and hands, and bind them at the time of prayers to their forehead and left arm, thinking that in this way they have satisfied the divine command well.

See D. PFEIFFER, Sacred Antiquities, decade II, position I, p. 29. But indeed some of these are more correctly explained by metaphor.

Doubtless God commends in these words to the Israelites a faithful custody of the law, so that they may have it assiduously in heart, mouth, and deed. In the heart, as a most precious treasure never to be buried in oblivion; in the mouth, as the chief subject of daily conversation to be instituted with children; in deed, as a norm of obedience to be rendered to God.

Hence JEROME in ch.

23 of Matthew: The precepts shall be in your hand, so that they may be fulfilled: before your eyes, so that you may meditate upon them day and night.

Thus the law written by God was destined for doctors, fathers of families, their children, household, and consequently for all men.

Latin:

Omnium hominum, pleno rationis usu pollentium, & verbi externi capacium, sacræ litteræ destinata & conscriptæ sunt, vt eas attente legere, deuoteque meditari liceat & expediat clericis & laicis, doctis & indoctis, viris & fœminis .

Prob. a. S. scripturæ finis cui, sive subiectum, cuius saluti procurandæ Deus misericordissimus verbum suum revelatum, litterisque mandatum destinavit, est omnis homo, peccato corruptus, ex feria intentione divina saluandus.

Hanc enim legem Deus ipse in tabulis lapideis litteris exaravit, Mosi tradidit, non vt eam in cista concludam, velut depositum divinum sibi proprium, asseruaret, sed vt eam populo Dei communicaret, & velut magnus propheta declararet.

Id quod colligimus ex Exod. XXIV, 12. Post dixit Iehouah ad Mosen, ascende ad me in montem, & esto ibi: dabo enim tibi tabulas lapidis, & legem & præceptum, quæ scribam ad docendum eos.

Neque tantum Moses, aut alius propheta, scriptam a Iehouah legem docere alios, sed & paterfamilias eandem liberis atque domesticis suis inculcare tenebatur: quod serio ipsi Iehouah iniunxit, Deut. VI, 6. seq. Sint omnia verba hæc, quæ ego (sum) præcipiens tibi hodie, super corde tuo: & acuas ea filiis tuis, loquarisque de iis, quum fœderis in domo tua, & quum iueris in via, & quum cubueris, & quum surrexeris.

Immo alliges ea in signum super manum tuam, ac sint infrontalia inter oculos tuos, scribasque ea super postes domus tuæ & in portis tuis.

Iudæi crassiores verba citata singula ad litteram intelligunt; ideo sibi phylacteria capitis & manuum conficiunt, eaque tempore precum fronti & sinistro brachio alligant, putantes se hoc modo mandato divino belle satisfecisse.

Vid. D. PFEIF. antiquit. sacr. decad. II. posit. I, p. 29. At vero nonnulla ex iis rectius per metaphoram explincantur.

Nimirum commendat his verbis Deus Israëlitis fidelem legis custodiam, vt eam assidue habeant in corde, ore, & opere. In corde, vt pretiosissimum thesaurum nunquam oblivione sepeliendum; in ore, vt præcipuum argumentum quotidiani colloquii cum filiis instituendi; in opere, vt normam obsequii Deo præstandi.

Hinc HIERONYMVS in cap.

23. Matth. Præcepta erunt in manu tua, vt compleantur: ante oculos tuos, vt die ac nocte mediteris in iis.

Fuit itaque lex a Deo scripta destinata doctoribus, patribusfamilias, horum liberis, domesticis, & consequenter omnibus hominibus.

Prob. a. S. ſcripturæ finis cui, siue fubiectum, cuius saluti procurandæ Deus mifericordissimus verbum suum reuelatum, litterisque mandatum destinaut, est omnis homo, pecrato corruptus, ex feria intentione diuina saluandus. VI, 6. feq. Sint omnia verba hæc, quæ ego (fun) præcipiens tibi hodie, fuper corde tuo: & acuas eafiliis tuis, loquarisque de iis, quum federis in domo tua, & quum iueris invia, & quum cubueris, & quum surrexeris. ### Question XXII: To God, who dispenses all things, to those subject to Him

To God, who dispenses all things, to those subject to Him.

The word of the Gospel is likewise written for all who will believe in Christ, for the attainment of eternal life.

Jn. XX, 31. The Apostles wrote their epistles to whole churches & to all the called, Rom.

I, 7. to all the holy brethren, 1 Thess. V, 2. to fathers, to young men, to little children, 1 Jn. II, 13. so that the word of God may dwell richly among all with all wisdom. Col. III, 16. I. From the destination of Scripture.

Those for whose salvation the Holy Scripture is divinely destined, to them it is to be read. But the Holy Scripture is divinely destined for the salvation of all, as we have now clearly shown. Therefore. By a general divine mandate, by which the reading of Holy Scripture is enjoined upon all men, as much in the Old as in the New Testament.

Clearly the Holy Spirit speaks through the mouth of the prophet Isaiah ch. XXXIV, 16. Seek out from the book of Jehovah and read. By the book of Jehovah is understood the Mosaic Scripture, which, on account of its antiquity, is called κατ' ἐξοχὴν [by way of excellence] the book of the Lord.

To read this book of the Lord, the prophet exhorts the promiscuous multitude, intending to indicate that Holy Scripture is a fountain closed to no one, but open to all for a salutary draught.

Nor less clear is the mandate of the Savior, Jn. V, 39. Search the scriptures, for you think that in them you have eternal life: and they testify of me. Obs. α) The verb ἐρευνᾶτε, search, transferred either from hunters tracking wild beasts in the woods with the greatest zeal, or from miners seeking gold in the caverns of the earth with the most intense care, is not of the indicative, but of the imperative mood: for Christ does not here praise the Jews as diligent readers of the sacred code, but rebukes them because they did not read the scriptures in the way they ought, and thus exhorts them to apply greater diligence. β) The verb δοκεῖτε, you think, does not denote the uncertain opinion of a wavering mind, but a certain & well-founded dogma, to be believed with certain faith. γ) We have eternal life in Holy Scripture as a revelation & testimony, because it testifies of eternal life and its causes and the manner of attaining it, and instructs us.

Wherefore this sense emerges: Search more skillfully than you have hitherto done the gold-mine of the Holy Scriptures; because you believe with certain faith that in them you have a doctrine more precious than gold concerning eternal life, and the causes and means of obtaining it.

But they testify of me, as the meritorious cause of salvation.

Wherefore you ought to have come to me, so that through me you might attain eternal life.

But since you refuse to come to me—which is your blindness—that is a most clear indication that you have not read the scriptures with the industry you ought.

III. From a special mandate, by which kings of the O.T. were commanded to read Scripture, Deut. XVII. 18. 19. But kings, according to the mind of the papists, are reckoned among the laity. IV.

From divine commendation.

Commended generally are all readers of Holy Scripture, Ps. I, 2. Apoc. I, 3. Specifically praised is Timothy, because from infancy he aspired to the knowledge of sacred letters, 2 Tim. III, 15. The Beroeans, Jews, εὐγενέστεροι, more noble, than the Thessalonian Jews: who received the word with all readiness, daily searching the scriptures, whether these things were so, which Paul had taught.

Acts XVII, 11. V. From the end & effect of Holy Scripture, which is information unto salvation, 2 Tim. III, 16. Therefore, let everyone who is to be informed unto salvation read it diligently, and devoutly meditate upon it.

The antithesis is that of the papists, who keep most of the laity from the reading of sacred letters, with the reading of them permitted to very few; who rely on the following arguments.

I. Whatever reading is dangerous & inconvenient, that is to be prohibited. (). () It is worthy of note in this first of all: that this... opposition, if it had any validity, would surely accomplish more than the adversaries themselves wish. This, indeed, is the most valid refutation of all, if we can oppose the same argumentation to any opponent, so that the weakness of the convention

And yet the reading of the Bibles, which is done by the laity, etc. Therefore. The minor premise is proven, because dangers to faith and morals threaten the layman reading the Bibles. From the reading of the Bibles such a rich harvest of heresies has sprouted: just as falls and vices, commemorated in the Bibles, easily provoke the laity to imitation. For if a layman reads in Scripture about the incest of Tamar, 2 Sam. XIII, 14; about the fornicating wife taken by the prophet Hosea, ch. I, 2; about the Israelites taking away the goods of the Egyptians by theft, Exod. XII, 36; and many such things contained in the Scriptures: he slips into that opinion, and [thinks] it is permitted for him to commit similar crimes. Resp. (1) The minor premise is so false that it can be inverted: namely, from the omission of attentive reading and devout meditation of Holy Scripture, heresies and vices are born. CHRYSOSTOM says excellently in the preface to Romans: Infinite evils have germinated from the ignorance of the Scriptures: hence the great plague of heresies has arisen; hence a life lived negligently. (2) Whatever reading is in itself dangerous and inconvenient, that is to be prohibited. But the reading of the books is in itself salutary; it is inconvenient by accident and through the fault of the readers, while they do not use Scripture rightly, but basely abuse it: for the occasion of erring is not offered to those reading Scripture, but is taken by them; scandal is not given, but received. If scandal were given to the readers of Scripture, God would not have done rightly in having ordered such things to be written, and thus He would be the author of evil in Himself; which is blasphemous to say. (3) Let those reading the Bibles attend to the scope of the Holy Spirit, namely that vices are recounted in the Scriptures for caution, avoidance, and the amendment of life, not for imitation. For rarely are atrocious crimes commemorated in them, without the punishments divinely inflicted upon the delinquents being added thereafter. For which reason, let the readers of the Bibles not apprehend the deed of Tamar as legitimate, since it was disapproved by God; nor the deed of Hosea as evil, since it was good; inasmuch as the prophet himself did not commit fornication, but by the will of Jehovah he took a harlot as a wife, to shadow forth the spiritual whoredom of the people; nor the deed of the Israelites as theft; since they took with them the wages due, justly adjudged by God, the supreme Lord of all goods, to the people of Israel for so many labors exhausted in Egypt.

II. Whatever reading produces no fruit for the laity, is to be prohibited to them. And yet the reading of the Bibles, etc. Therefore. The minor premise is proven, because Holy Scripture is difficult to understand: hence, since it is not understood by the laity, it is read by them without fruit.

Resp. (1) to the major premise. Whatever reading is fruitless for all readers, that is to be prohibited to them. But the reading of the sacred letters is so far from being devoid of fruit for all the laity, that it makes the simple wise. Ps. XIX, 8. Just as, therefore, the scattering of seed into a field is not to be prohibited: even though the seed scattered into a stony field, and one overgrown with thorns, bears no fruit: so the reading of Holy Scripture is to be forbidden to no one; however much the mind is blinded, obstinate, and imbued with depraved preconceived opinions, may derive no fruit from the reading of the sacred book. Furthermore, is the preaching of the divine word, and the hearing of it, also to be prohibited for not a few hearers because it is little fruitful? Therefore, is that also to be prohibited? to the minor premise. Holy Scripture, in the handing down of the articles of faith and the precepts of morals, is not obscure, but is a light illuminating the eyes. Ps. XIX, 9.

Latin:

Deo, cuncta dispensanti, subiectis.

Verbum euangelii itidem scriptum est omnibus in Christum credituris ad consequendam vitam aeternam.

Io. XX, 31. Apostoli epistolas suas scripserunt integris ecclesiis & omnibus vocatis, Rom.

I, 7. omnibus fratribus sanctis, 1 Thess. V, 2. patribus, adolescentibus, puerulis, 1 Io. II, 13. vt verbum Dei inter omnes cum omni sapientia opulenter habitet. Col. III, 16. I. A destinatione scripturae.

Quorum saluti procurandae S. scriptura diuinitus est destinata, illis est legenda. Atqui omnium saluti procurandae S. scriptura diuinitus est destinata, vt iam luculenter ostendimus. Ergo. mandato diuino generali, quo lectio S. scripturae omnibus hominibus iniungitur tam in veteri, quam in nouo testamento.

Clare loquitur Spiritus S. per os prophetae Isaiae c. XXXIV, 16. Quaerite desuper libro Iehouae & legite. Per librum Iehouae intelligitur scriptura Mosaica, quae ob antiquitatem κατ' ἐξοχὴν dicitur liber domini.

Ad hunc librum domini legendum promiscuae multitudinem cohortatur propheta indicaturus, S. scripturam esse fontem nemini clausum, sed omnibus ad salutarem haustum patentem.

Neque minus clarum est mandatum Saluatoris, Io. V, 39. Scrutamini scripturas, quia vos existimatis, quod in iis vitam aeternam habeatis: atque illae testantur de me. Obs. α) Verbum ἐρευνᾶτε, scrutamini, vel a venatoribus feras in siluis summo studio indagantibus, vel a fossoribus metallorum, in cauernis terrae aurum cura intensissima quaerentibus, transumtum, non est indicatiui, sed imperatiui modi: neque enim Christus hic laudat Iudaeos, vt sedulos sacri codicis lectores, sed eos reprehendit, quod scripturas non eo, quo debebant, modo legerint, adeoque hortatur, vt maiorem diligentiam adhibeant. β) Verbum δοκεῖτε, existimatis, non notat opinionem incertam fluctuantis animi, sed certum & bene fundatum dogma, certa fide credendum. γ) Habemus vitam aeternam in sacra scriptura tanquam reuelatione & testimonio, quia de vita aeterna, eiusque caussis & consequendi modo testatur, nosque erudit.

Quare hic emergit sensus: Rimamini solertius, quam adhuc fecistis, aurifodinam S. scripturarum; quia certa fide creditis, quod in illis habeatis auro potiorem doctrinam de vita aeterna, eiusque obtinenda caussis & mediis.

Atqui illae testantur de me, vt caussa salutis meritoria.

Quare debebatis ad me venire, vt per me vitam aeternam consequamini.

At cum recusetis, quae vestra est caecitas, ad me venire, id luculentissimo indicio est, vos non ea, qua debebatis, industria scripturas legisse.

III. A mandato speciali, quo imperatum est regibus V. T. scripturam legere, Deut. XVII. 18. 19. Reges autem ex pontificiorum mente laicis accenfentur. IV.

A diuina commendatione.

Commendantur generatim omnes Lectores S. scripturae, Ps. I, 2. Apoc. I, 3. Speciatim laudatur Timotheus, quod ab infantia ad notitiam sacrarum litterarum adspirauerit, 2 Tim. III, 15. Berrhoënses, Iudaei, εὐγενέστεροι, generofiores, Iudaeis Thessalonicenfibus: qui acceperunt verbum cum omni promtitudine, quotidie scrutantes scripturas, num se haberent haec ita, quae Paullus docuerat.

Act. XVII, 11. V. A fine & effectu S. scripturae, qui est informatio ad salutem, 2 Tim. III, 16. Ergo omnis ad salutem informandus eam sedulo legat, deuoteque meditetur.

Antithesis est pontificiorum, qui plerosque laicos a lectione sacrarum litterarum arcent, paucissimis lectione earum permissa; qui sequentibus innituntur argumentis.

I. Quaecunque lectio est periculosa & incommoda, illa est prohibenda. (*). (*) Notatione dignum est hoc in primis: quod haec... oppositio, si quid valeret illa, plus profecto efficeret, quam ipsi volunt aduersarii. Haec nimirum est omnium validissima refutatio, si cui opponenti eamdem nos argumentationem opponere possimus, vt conuentionis infirmitatem

Atqui lectio bibliorum, quæ fit a laicis &c. Ergo. Minor probatur, quia laico legenti biblia pericula fidei & morum imminent. Ex lectione bibliorum tam vber hæresium seges pullulauit : iuxta atque lapsus & vitia, in bibliis commemorata, laicos facile ad imitationem prouocant. Nam si laicus in scriptura legit de incestu Thamaridis, 2 Sam. XIII, 14. de vxore fornicaria ducta a propheta Hosea, c. I, 2. de Israëlitus per furtum bona Ægyptiorum auferentibus, Exod. XII, 36. & eiusmodi plura in scripturis contenta: in eam prolabitur opinionem, & sibi licere similia patrare facinora. Resp. (1) Minor adeo falsa est, vt inuerti queat: nempe ex omissione attentæ lectionis & deuotæ meditationis S. scripturæ hæreses & vitia nascuntur. Eximie inquit CHRYSOSTOMUS in præfat. ad roman. Infinita mala germinarunt ab ignorantia scripturarum: hinc magna hæresium pestis exorta est; hinc vita negligenter acta. (2) Quæcunque lectio per se est periculosa & incommoda, illa est prohibenda. At lectio librorum per se est salutaris; per accidens & vitio legentium est incommoda, dum illi scriptura non recte vtuntur, sed turpiter abutuntur: neque enim occasio errandi legentibus scripturam præbetur, sed ab ipsis sumitur, scandalum non datur, sed accipitur. Si lectoribus scripturæ scandalum daretur, non recte fecisset Deus, quod talia scribi iussisset, adeoque per se foret auctor mali; quod dictu blasphemum est. (3) Legentes biblia attendant scopum Spiritus sancti, nimirum quod vitia in scripturis recenseantur ad cautionem, euitationem, vitæque emendationem, non ad imitationem. Raro quippe atrocia commemorantur in iisdem scelera, quin insecuta supplicia delinquentibus diuinitus irrogata subiungantur. Quam ob rem lectores bibliorum non apprehendant factum Thamaris, vt legitimum, quippe a Deo est improbatum; neque factum Hoseæ vt malum, cum illud fuerit bonum; siquidem non fornicatus est propheta ipse, sed ex voluntate, Iehouæ scortatricem duxit vxorem, ad adumbrandam scortationem populi spiritualem; neque factum Israëlitarum, vt furtum; cum tulerint secum mercedem debitam, a Deo, supremo omnium bonorum domino, pro tot laboribus in Ægypto exantlatis Israëlitarum genti iuste adiudicatam.

II. Quæcunque lectio laicis nullum parit fructum, iisdem est prohibenda. Atqui lectio blibliorum &c. Ergo. Minor probatur, quia S. scriptura est intellectu difficilis: hinc cum a laicis non intelligatur, sine fructu ab illis legitur.

Resp. (1) ad maiorem. Quæcunque lectio omnibus legentibus est infructuosa, illa ipfis est prohibenda. At lectio sacrarum litterarum adeo non expers est frugis omnibus laicis, vt sapientes reddat simplices. Ps. XIX, 8. Quemadmodum igitur sparsio seminis in agrum non prohibenda est: tametsi semen sparsum in agrum petrosum, & spinis obsitum, nullum ferat fructum: ita lectio S. scripturæ nemini est interdicenda; vtut mens occæcata, obstinata & præconceptis opinionibus pravis imbuta, e lectione sacri codicis nullum capiat fructum. Quin prædicatio etiam verbi divini, eiusque auscultatio haud paucis auditoribus parum frugifera est. Ergone & illa prohibenda est? ad minorem. S. scriptura in tradendis articulis fidei, morumque præceptis non obscura, sed lux est illuminans oculos. Ps. XIX, 9.


### Question XXII: III. It is the duty of the laity to seek the law from the mouth of the priest

III. It is the duty of the laity to seek the law from the mouth of the priest.

Therefore, it is not for them to handle the divine law with their hands. Resp. To read the divine law and to seek it from the mouth of the priest are not opposites, but are subordinate and compatible. Meanwhile, we descend more readily, more joyfully, and more eagerly into the assent of those things which we ourselves read.

IV. Judgment concerning matters of faith, revealed in the written word of God, pertains to the clergy.

Let the laity observe that trite saying: let the cobbler not go beyond his last. Resp. Distinguish between the judgment that is prophetic, or exegetical, which belongs to the public interpreters of the sacred letters; and that which is discretive, by which all things are tested, and the good is held fast. This, in its own way, belongs to the laity; it is their duty to test the spirits, whether they are from God, 1 Ioh. IV, 1. to beware of false prophets, Matth. VII, 15. to test all things, and to hold fast the good. 1 Thess. V, 21. Wherefore, they have need of discretive judgment.

V. Whoever are dogs and swine, to them the holy word of God is not to be communicated, Matth. VII, 6. But the laity, etc. Therefore. Resp. By dogs and swine are not understood all the laity; but the impious, the epicureans, the blasphemers, the stubbornly wicked, who wallow in the mire of carnal pleasures, like swine; and like dogs, have cast off all shame. To these, the sacraments are not to be offered, as long as they remain beasts, dogs, and swine. On the contrary, there are given the docile laity, who mourn and detest their sins, and pant for the grace of God and the righteousness of Christ: to these, the streams of the sacred letters are open.

VI. For the laity, catechesis suffices: images suffice, which are the bibles of the laity.

Resp. The catechesis of the laity is fashioned from the sacred letters, which, when they have learned, let them grow in the knowledge of Jesus Christ by reading the bibles, 2 Petr. III, 18. For this reason, let them apply effort, that the word of Christ may dwell in them richly. Col. III, 16. Since images are not to be tolerated in temples unless they have a foundation in the scriptures, they do not exclude these, but move the laity to the reading of the sacred book.

VII. You may find not a few laity to whom it is not given to read or understand Holy Scripture, such as infants and the blind.

Therefore, it is not permitted for all men to read through the sacred book. Resp. The end for which Holy Scripture is destined is every man possessing the full use of reason, and capable of the divine word reduced to letters. Since infants have not yet reached the full use of reason, they enjoy the grace of God in the covenant, and in the progress of time are imbued with catechetical precepts: as for the blind, the less they are able to read, the more diligently and frequently let them hear the divine word.

Latin:

III. Laicorum est, legem ex ore sacerdotis requirere.

Ergo eundem non est, legem divinam manibus terere. Resp. Legem divinam legere, & ex ore sacerdotis requirere, non sunt opposita, sed subordinata & compossibilia. Promtius interim, lætius & excitius descendimus in assensum eorum, quæ nos ipsi legimus.

IV. Iudicium de rebus fidei, verbo Dei scripto revelatis, pertinet ad clericos.

Laici obferuent tritum illud: ne sutor vltra crepidam. Resp. Dist. inter iudicium προφητικὸν, sive exegeticum, quod competit publicis sacrarum litterarum interpretibus; & δοκιμαστικὸν, sive discretivum, quo omnia probantur, & bonum tenetur. Hoc suo modo competit laicis; horum est probare spiritus, num ex Deo sint, 1 Ioh. IV, 1. cauere sibi a pseudoprophetis, Matth. VII, 15. omnia probare, & bonum tenere. 1 Thess. V, 21. Quare ipsis opus est iudicio discretivo.

V. Quicunque sunt canes & porci, illis sanctum Dei verbum non est communicandum, Matth. VII, 6. Atqui laici &c. Ergo. Resp. Per canes & porcos non intelliguntur omnes laici; sed empectæ, epicuræi, blasphemi, præfracte impii, qui in cœno carnalium voluptatum, more porcorum, volutantur; & ad instar canum omnem pudorem exuerunt. His sacramenta non sunt offerenda, quamdiu bestiæ, canes & porci manent. Dantur contra laici dociles, peccata sua lugentes & detestantes, gratiam Dei & iustitiam Christi anhelantes: his fluenta sacrarum litterarum patent.

VI. Laicis sufficit catechesis: sufficiunt imagines, quæ sunt laicorum biblia.

Resp. Laicorum catechesis e sacris litteris concinnata est, quam ubi didicerint, legendis bibliis crescant in cognitione Iesu Christi, 2 Petr. III, 18. Id propter operam nauent, ut verbum Christi in ipsis habitet opulenter. Col. III, 16. Imagines cum non sint tolerandæ in templis, nisi fundamentum habeant in scripturis, has non excludunt, sed laicos ad lectionem sacri codicis permovent.

VII. Inuenias haud paucos laicos, quibus nec legere, nec intelligere S. scripturam datum est, quales sunt infantes & cœci.

Non igitur omnibus hominibus permissum est sacrum perlegere codicem. Resp. Finis, cui destinata est scriptura S. est omnis homo pleno rationis usu pollens, & verbi divini in litteras redacti capax. Cum infantes ad plenum rationis usum nondum pertigerunt, gratia Dei fœderati perfruuntur, & progressu temporis præceptis catecheticis imbuuntur: Cœci, quo minus legere possunt, hoc diligentius & crebrius verbum divinum auscultent.


### Question XXIII. What is the end for whose sake Holy Scripture was adorned by the inspiration of God?

The end, for the sake of which the word of God has been related in letters, is to be observed both with respect to God and with respect to men. With respect to God, the end of Holy Scripture is the salutary knowledge and veneration of the divine majesty (a). The ultimate end with respect to men is eternal life. The general intermediate end is true faith in Christ (b), which is accompanied by holiness of life (c). The special intermediate end of Scripture, with respect to the ministers of the church, is instruction that is didascalic, elenchtic, epanorthotic, paedeutic, and paracletic (d).

Prob. a. Without the shining torch of Holy Scripture, we do not know God as our salvation requires. The human eye does not behold the sun without the light of the sun: nor does the human mind salutarily acknowledge God without the light of the divine word. The king of prophets hints at this very thing, Ps. 119:18. Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things from your law: as if he were about to say; Remove, I beseech you, most merciful God, the veil of ignorance innate to the eyes of my mind: so that I may know with salutary effect, esteem most highly, and praise with a full mouth, your wisdom shining in the mirror of your word, your admirable and inexhaustible goodness, your most ardent love, your most constant truth, your immense power, your stupendous works, and your tremendous mysteries.

Prob. b. These things are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ the Son of God; and that believing you may have life in his name, John 20:31. By which golden words the theologian John submits to our minds to be considered the intermediate end of the Scriptures, which is faith in Christ, and the ultimate, which is eternal life: consequently he asserts that all these things, which Christ taught and did, were written to this end, that men as wayfarers, corrupted by sins, might be reconciled with God through faith in Christ, drawn from the Scriptures, and obtain eternal life.

Prob. c. Faith in Christ is followed by an inseparable bond of holiness of life, with which the Holy Spirit adorns the sinner, reconciled with God, by means of Holy Scripture. The Savior teaches this in John 17:17. Sanctify them in your truth: your word is truth. The word of truth, impressed and implanted in the heart of the sinner by the Holy Spirit, sanctifies him, frees him from the dominion and stains of sin, and restores the image of God in him. Wherefore holiness of life is the end of Holy Scripture accompanying faith in Christ.

Prob. d. The ends of Holy Scripture considered specifically in relation to the ministry of the church are recounted in 2 Tim. 3:16. All scripture inspired by God is also useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for training; which (is) in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work. Ministers of the church are rendered by Holy Scripture apt and suitable for teaching the truth, for reproving falsehood, for correcting distorted morals, for directing honest morals, so that those who have begun to live well may strenuously run the path of a just and pious life. Which things look to this, that the doctor of the church, who presides over the people in the name of God, may be perfectly instructed by the sacred letters to duly perform all the works of the sacred ministry.

Obs. Although the apostle of the Gentiles in the cited place made no mention of paracletic information, for the sake of which Scripture is said to be consigned in Rom. 15:4, nevertheless παράκλησις can in some way be included under διδασκαλία, or doctrine; insofar as Holy Scripture teaches that the cross of Christians both takes its origin from a propitious God and is directed by the same to an optimal end.

Latin:

Finis, cuius gratia verbum Dei in litteras est relatum, obseruandus est tum respectu Dei, tum respectu hominum. Respectu Dei finis sacræ scripturæ est salutifera agnitio & veneratio maiestatis divinæ (a). Finis ultimus respectu hominum est vita æterna. Finis intermedius generalis est vera in Christum fides (b), quam comitatur sanctimonia vitæ (c). Finis intermedius specialis scripturæ, respectu ministrorum ecclesiæ, est informatio didascalica, elenchtica, epanorthotica, pædeutica, & paracletica (d).

Prob. a. Sine prælucente sacræ scripturæ face non pro eo, ac salutis nostræ interest, Deum cognoscimus. Solem absque lumine solis oculus hominis haud intuetur: nec Deum absque lumine verbi diuini mens humana salutariter agnoscit. Innuit hoc ipsum rex prophetarum, Psal. CXIX, 18. Reuela oculos meos, vt videam mirabilia e lege tua: quasi dicturus; Detrahe, obsecro, Deus misericordissime, connatum mentis meæ oculis velamen ignorantiæ: vt relucentem in speculo verbi tui sapientiam tuam admirandam, bonitatem inexhaustam, amorem ardentissimum, veritatem constantissimam, potentiam immensam, opera stupenda, mysteria tua tremenda salutari cum effectu cognoscam, maximi æstimem, plenoque ore collaudem.

Prob. b. Hæc scripta sunt, vt credatis, quod Iesus sit Christus filius Dei; & vt credentes vitam habeatis in nomine ipsius, Io. XX, 31. Quibus aureis verbis theologus Ioannes mentibus nostris subiicit considerandum finem scripturarum intermedium, qui est fides in Christum, & vltimum, qui est vita æterna: proinde asserit, omnia hæc, quæ Christus docuit & fecit, eum in finem esse scripta, vt homines viatores, peccatis corrupti, per fidem in Christum, haustam ex scripturis, reconcilientur cum Deo, & vitam æternam consequantur.

Prob. c. Fidem in Christum indiuulso nexu sequitur sanctimonia vitæ, qua Spiritus S. peccatorem, cum Deo reconciliatum, exornat, mediante S. scriptura. Docet hoc Saluator Io. XVII, 17. Sanctifica illos in veritate tua: verbum tuum veritas est. Verbum veritatis, per Spiritum S. impressum ac insitum cordi peccatoris, eundem sanctificat, a dominio maculisque peccati liberat, & imaginem Dei in ipso instaurat. Quare sanctitas vitæ est finis S. scripturæ concomitans fidem in Christum.

Prob. d. Fines S. scripturæ speciatim considerati in ordine ad ministerium ecclesiæ recensentur 2 Tim. III, 16. Omnis scriptura diuinitus inspirata, etiam vtilis est ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad disciplinam; quæ (sit) in iustitia, vt integer sit homo Dei, ad omne bonum opus probe instructus. Ministri ecclesiæ per scripturam S. redduntur apti & idonei ad docendam veritatem, ad redarguendam falsitatem, ad corrigendum mores distortos, ad dirigendum mores honestos, vt qui bene viuere cœpere, tramitem vitæ iustæ atque piæ strenue decurrant. Quæ eo spectant, vt doctor ecclesiæ, qui nomine Dei populo præest, sacris litteris perfecte instruatur ad omnia opera ministerii sacri rite peragenda.

Obs. Quamuis gentium apostolus l. c. nullam iniecerit mentionem informationis paraclæticæ, cuius caussa scriptura consignata dicitur Rom. XV, 3. παράκλησις tamen quodammodo sub διδασκαλίἀ, siue doctrina, comprehendi potest (*); quatenus S. scriptura docet, crucem christianorum tum originem ducere a Deo propitio, tum ad finem optimum ab eodem dirigi.


### Question XXIV. What are the affections or properties of Holy Scripture?

The more important affections of Holy Scripture are: I. Its authority, II. Perspicuity, III. Perfection or sufficiency, IV. Efficacy.

Latin:

Affectiones S. scripturæ potiores sunt: I. Eius auctoritas, II. Perspicuitas, III. Perfectio siue sufficientia, IV. Efficacia.


### Question XXV. What is the authority of Holy Scripture?

The authority of Holy Scripture is its eminent dignity, communicated to it by God, the most truthful and omnipotent author, clearly known and so highly esteemed by men that it moves their intellect to assent, their will to obedience, discerns the true from the false, the good from the evil, and judges the controversies of faith that have arisen.

Observation I. Authority in general is the dignity of an author, who completes some thing rightly and without defect, known by others, and esteemed as is fitting. Therefore, two things are required for authority: (1) the perfection of the author, (2) the knowledge and estimation of others. For the dignity of an author is not called authority unless it becomes known to others for decent estimation. For example, a king unknown excels in royal majesty, but when surrounded by his retinue and appearing before his subjects with scepter and crown, he possesses authority.

Observation II. The authority which belongs to an author from himself, primarily and originally, belongs to a writing published by the author dependently, participatively, and by communication. Hence, the more perfect, truthful, and powerful an author is held to be by others, the more significant is the authority of the writing adorned by him.

Observation III. The authority of God, moving and obliging us to faith and obedience through Scripture, consists both in His truthfulness, by which, because of His infinite wisdom and goodness, He neither wishes nor is able to deceive or be deceived; and in His supreme right and power of ruling, by which He prescribes to men a norm of believing and acting. Therefore, since Holy Scripture shines with the same authority with which God shines independently and originally, but dependently and participatively, it is easily understood that the authority of Holy Scripture is founded (1) on its infallible truth, by which it moves the human intellect to grant assent to biblical statements; which the Greeks call ἀξιοπισίαν; (2) on the power of obliging the wills of men to render obedience to the commands contained in the sacred code, to which corresponds the Greek word ἐξοσία or the power of commanding. Generally, however, the authority of Scripture, both moving to assent and obliging to obedience, is called in Greek αὐθεντία: just as among jurists, those instruments and writings are called authentic which have certain and just authority, so that they can oblige to assent or even to obedience.

Observation IV. The knowledge and estimation of men, by which the authenticity of Scripture is truly recognized and decently esteemed, is not a constitutive part of the authority of Holy Scripture, nor its foundation; but only a necessary condition on the part of men, whose minds are to be moved to faith and obedience through the dignity of Scripture, which is known and esteemed. It is clear, therefore, that the authority of Scripture is not its absolute property, but relative, referred to men who recognize and highly esteem it. The dignity of Scripture, considered absolutely, is called its majesty; but viewed relatively, insofar as it is recognized by all men and esteemed as is proper, it is called its authority.

Latin:

Auctoritas S. scripturæ est eminens illius dignitas, a Deo auctore veracissimo & omnipotente ipsi communicata, luculenter cognita tantique æstimata ab hominibus, vt horum intellectum ad assensum, voluntatem ad obsequium permoveat, verum a falso, bonum a malo discernat, & exortas fidei controuersias diiudicet.

Obs. I. Auctoritas in genere est dignitas auctoris, rem aliquam recte & sine defectu perficientis, ab aliis cognita, & pro eo, ac decet, æstimata. Duo igitur requiruntur ad auctoritatem (1) perfectio auctoris, (2) aliorum cognitio & æstimatio. Neque enim dignitas auctoris vocatur auctoritas, nisi aliis ad decentem æstimationem innotescat. v. gr. Rex incognitus eminet regia maiestate, sed stipatus satellitio, & coram sibi subiectis cum sceptro & corona apparens, pollet auctoritate.

Obs. II. Quæ auctoritas competit auctori ex se, primo & originaliter: illa scripto ab auctore edito conuenit dependenter, participatiue & per communicationem. Hinc quo perfectior, veracior & potentior auctor ab aliis habetur, eo insignior est auctoritas scripti ab eo adornati.

Obs. III. Auctoritas Dei, per scripturam ad fidem & obsequium nos permouentis, atque obligantis, consistit tum in veracitate eius, qua ob infinitam sapientiam & bonitatem nec fallere, nec falli vult, aut potest; tum in summo iure dominandique potestate, qua hominibus normam credendi & agendi præscribit. Quare cum eadem auctoritate, qua Deus refulget independenter & originaliter, S. scriptura resplendescat dependenter & participatiue, ex facili intelligitur, quod auctoritas S. scripturæ fundetur (1) in veritate eius infallibili, qua intellectum hominis mouet ad assensum dictis biblicis præbendum; quam Græci vocant ἀξιοπισίαν; (2) in potestate obligandi voluntates hominum ad obsequium, mandatis in sacro codice con entis præstandum, cui respondet vox græca ἐξοσία siue potestas imperandi. Generatim autem auctoritas scripturæ tam ad assensum mouens, quam ad obsequium obligans, græce αὐθεντία dicitur: prout apud ICtos authentica instrumenta & scripta dicuntur, quæ certam & iustam habent auctoritatem, vt ad assensum, vel etiam ad obsequium obligare possint.

Obs. IV. Cognitio & æstimatio hominum, qua authentia scripturæ vere agnoscitur & decenter æstimatur, non est pars constitutiua auctoritatis sacræ scripturæ, neque eius fundamentum; sed tantum conditio necessaria ex parte hominum, quorum animi per dignitatem scripturæ cognitam & æstimatam, ad fidem & obsequium mouendi sunt. Patet ergo, quod auctoritas scripturæ non sit proprietas eius absoluta, sed respectiua, ad homines, eandem agnoscentes & magni æstimantes, relata. Dignitas scripturæ, absolute considerata, vocatur eius maiestas; sed relatiue spectata, quatenus ab omnibus hominibus agnoscitur, &, prout par est, æstimatur, appellatur eius auctoritas.


### Question XXVI. How manifold is the authority of Holy Scripture?

The authority of Holy Scripture, as regards the thing itself, is one (a): according to our mode of conceiving, it is distinguished into the causative of faith and the canonical. The former is that by which Scripture generates and confirms the assent of things to be believed in the intellect of man: the latter is that by which both the authentic Scripture is distinguished from other writings and versions, and the true is distinguished from the false (b).

Proof a. The authority of Scripture is one, by reason of its origin and internal form; for it proceeded from one most truthful God through the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit, and received the dignity and power equally to elicit faith and to discern the true from the false. Proof b. Holy Scripture is considered partly as the principle of knowing and the formal object of faith and revealed theology, and partly as the norm for discerning writings, by which the words and concepts of things that are θεόπνευστα [God-breathed] are distinguished from other writings, and the true is distinguished from the false. In the former mode, it is used in any language to generate faith in the intellect of an unbeliever and to confirm it in the mind of a believer; in which respect it is called the causative or motive [principle] of faith: in the latter mode, it is used only in the original text to distinguish from θεοπνεύστῳ [God-breathed] Scripture any version, symbolic books, and all writings that deal with matters of faith and morals. Cf. D. Musaeus in introduct. in theol. p. 295.

Latin:

Auctoritas sacræ scripturæ, quoad rem, vna est (a): secundum nostrum concipiendi modum, distinguitur in caussatiuam fidei & canonicam. Illa est, qua scriptura assensum credendorum in intellectu hominis generat & confirmat: hæcest, qua tum scriptura authentica ab aliis scripturis, & versionibus, tum verum a falso dignoscitur (b).

Prob. a. Vna est auctoritas scripturae, ratione originis & formae internae; ab uno quippe Deo veracissimo per immediatam Spiritus S. inspirationem profecta, dignitatem & vim accepit pariter eliciendi fidem, ac discernendi verum a falso. Prob. b. Consideratur sacra scriptura partim vt principium cognoscendi, & obiectum formale fidei ac theologiae revelatae, partim vt norma discernendi scripta, qua verba rerumque conceptus θεόπνευστα, a scriptis aliis, atque dignoscendi verum a falso. Priori modo adhibetur in quacunque lingua ad fidem in intellectu hominis infidelis generandam, & in animo hominis fidelis confirmandam; quo respectu vocatur causatiua, aut motiua fidei: posteriori modo adhibetur tantum in textu primigenio ad dignoscendum a scriptura θεοπνεύστῳ versionem, libros symbolicos, scriptaque omnia, quae de rebus fidei ac morum agunt. Confer. D. Mvsaevs in introduct. in theol. p. 295.


### Question XXVII. Whence does sacred scripture have its authority?

Holy Scripture owes its authority to God, its author (a). It is known and estimated by the equal consideration of the minds of the authors by men, who properly consider the following two principles of the certainty of H. S., the former of which is: Whatever Scripture is recorded by the inspiration of God, that is certainly and infallibly true (b): the latter is: Holy Scripture is recorded by the inspiration of God (c).

Proof a. Just as the authority of any writing depends upon the perfection, veracity, and power of the author by whom it was composed, whether by writing or by dictating: so Holy Scripture has obtained its authority, both causative of faith and canonical, from God alone, its most wise, best, most truthful, and most powerful author. Proof b. This principle: Whatever Scripture is recorded by the inspiration of God, that is certainly and infallibly true, is evident, accessible to every sane intellect, and known from the very terms once grasped. For as no darkness comes from the sun, so no falsehoods proceed from God, the primary truth: but whatever God, who is ignorant of deceiving and being deceived, says, reveals, and dictates as if into the pen to his amanuenses: that is absolutely true, to which it is simply repugnant for falsehood to be present.

Proof c. This principle: Holy Scripture, both of the Old and New Testament, is recorded by the inspiration of God, is for true Christians the first principle, αὐτόπιστον [self-evident], worthy in itself, most clear, most firm, ἀναπόδεικτον [indemonstrable], not needing demonstration a priori, to which they adhere with unshaken faith: but that [principle] is rejected by atheists and Epicureans, called into doubt by tempted Christians, and received by human faith by hypocrites and beginning Christians who pass from the camps of the Gentiles into the camps of the Christians. Wherefore it behooves and becomes the theologian to consolidate that principle with not-invalid arguments a posteriori, so that atheists may be confounded, the scruples of tempted Christians concerning the authority of Scripture, injected by the devil and their own flesh, may be uprooted, and hypocrites and beginning Christians may be so convinced that they firmly embrace it.

We confess, meanwhile, that certain arguments proving the divine origin of the Scriptures only generate human faith, so that Gentiles to be converted may be prepared to a certain extent; [and that] certain arguments produce divine faith. Hence it happens that these proving arguments are divided into topical and apodictic. Topical are those that induce, move, and persuade, the effect of which is opinion, which is probable and joined with the fear of the opposite: apodictic are those that compel, constrain, and thoroughly move, the effect of which is knowledge, which is certain and devoid of the fear of the opposite.

Latin:

S. scriptura suam auctoritatem debet auctori Deo (a). Cognoscitur & aequa Origo auctorum animorum pensitatione aestimatur ab hominibus, sequentia duo principia certitatis S. S. ma probe considerantibus, quorum prius est: Quaecunque scriptura, inspirante Deo, consignata est, illa certo & infallibiliter vera est (b): posterius est: Scriptura sacra, Deo inspirante, consignata est (c).

Prob. a. Sicut vniuscuiusque scripti auctoritas pendet a perfectione, veracitate & potestate auctoris, quo litteras exarante, aut dictante concinnatum est: ita sacra scriptura suam auctoritatem, tam causatiuam fidei, quam canonicam, nacta est a solo Deo, auctore suo sapientissimo, optimo, veracissimo & potentissimo. Prob. b. Principium hoc: Quaecunque scriptura, inspirante Deo, consignata est, illa certo & infallibiliter vera est, euidens est, omnique fano intellectui peruium & ex ipsis terminis apprehensis notum. Vt enim a sole nullae tenebrae, ita a Deo, veritate prima, nulla mendacia proficiscuntur: sed quidquid Deus, fallere & falli nescius, dicit, revelat, suisque amanuentibus quasi in calamum dictat: id absolute verum est, cui subesse falsum simpliciter repugnat.

Prob. c. Hoc principium: Sacra scriptura tam veteris, quam noui testamenti, Deo inspirante, consignata est, veris christianis est principium primum, αὐτόπιστον, per se dignum, liquidissimum, firmissimum, ἀναπόδεικτον, demonstrationis a priori haud indigens, cui fide iminota adhaerescunt: at reiicitur illud ab atheis & epicuraeis, vocatur in dubium a christianis tentatis, fide humana recipitur ab hypocritis & christianis incipientibus, qui e castris gentilium transeunt in castra christianorum. Quare theologum decet & oportet principium illud haud inualidis a posteriori consolidare argumentis, vt athei confundantur, christiani tentatis scrupuli de auctoritate scripturae, a diabolo propriaque carne iniecti, euellantur, hypocritae & incipientes christiani ita conuincantur, vt illud firmiter suscipiant.

Fatemur interim, quaedam argumenta, originem diuinam scripturarum probantia, tantum gignere fidem humanam, vt gentiles conuertendi quadantenus praeparentur; quaedam argumenta parere fidem diuinam. Exinde fit, vt argumenta haec probantia diuidantur in topica, & apodictica. Topica sunt inducentia, mouentia, suadentia, quorum effectus est opinio, quae probabilis & cum formidine oppositi coniuncta est: apodictica sunt cogentia, stringentia, & perinouentia, quorum effectus est scientia, quae certa & formidinis oppositi expers est.


### Question XXVIII. By what arguments is the divine origin of the Holy Scriptures proven?

The arguments by which the divinity of Holy Scripture is proven arise from *criteria*, or clear indications of divine origin, by which the Holy Scriptures are distinguished: which *criteria* are commonly divided into external and internal. The former are assumed from outside of Scripture from other sources; the latter are sought from the intrinsic nature of Holy Scripture and its properties.

Latin:

Argumenta, quibus diuinitas sacræ scripturæ probatur, nascuntur ex κριτηρίοις siue luculentis indiciis diuinæ originis, qua sacræ litteræ eminent: quæ κριτήρια communiter distinguuntur in externa, & interna. Illa extra scripturam aliunde assumuntur: hæc ex intrinseca scripturæ sacræ natura, eiusque proprietatibus petuntur.


### Question XXIX. By what external *criteria* is the divine origin of the Scriptures made known?

The external *criteria*, which make known the immediate dependence of the Holy Scriptures upon God, are: (a) the antiquity of Scripture; (b) the singular light of the sacred amanuenses, and their zeal for knowledge and truth; (c) the clarity of the miracles by which the celestial doctrine of the Scriptures is confirmed; (d) the consenting testimony of the Church, diffused throughout the whole world, concerning the divinity of Holy Scripture; (e) the constancy of the martyrs; (f) the testimonies of other peoples borne to the doctrine contained in the sacred code; (g) the successful and sudden propagation of Christian doctrine throughout the whole world, and its admirable preservation amidst so many persecutions; (h) the most grave punishments inflicted upon the contemners and persecutors of the divine word.

Proof a. The divine origin of Holy Scripture is argued by (1) The antiquity of the doctrine, in that the Holy Scriptures accurately set forth the origin of this universe, the beginnings of time and their continuous series, the foundations of the Church, of the polity, of the economy, the first rudiments of the arts, the cradle of sin, the protoevangelium, and the beginning of the written law made by God. (2) The antiquity of the ministerial cause. For Moses, the most ancient writer, precedes all the historians, philosophers, orators, and poets of the Gentiles. Before any book became famous, there existed the ocean of wisdom, the Pentateuch. (3) The antiquity of the external form; for the Scripture of the Old Testament was conceived in the Hebrew language, which, as it is the simplest, so it is the first. But the more ancient a thing is, the truer, more excellent, and more divine it is. We argue: That Scripture which is most ancient is most true and most divine. But Holy Scripture is most ancient. Therefore, Holy Scripture is most true and most divine.

Proof b.
