There are two things which render the sacred amanuenses *axiōpistous* (worthy of belief) and commend their writings as divine: 1) Their extraordinary knowledge of the things to be handed down. 2) Their sincere love of truth, without the pursuit of passions or partisanship. Their incomparable knowledge shines forth partly from the fact that they taught, by living voice and by writings, the mysteries of faith which exceed the grasp of reason left to itself; which could not have become known to them except by divine inspiration; and partly because they proposed dogmas knowable from the light of nature more fully and more certainly than philosophers did from the principles of reason; even though, before their extraordinary illumination, most of them were unlearned in the disciplines. They openly testified to their love of truth; since they preached and wrote the divine word, void of exorbitant passions. For they were neither terrified by the most present dangers, nor inflamed by the desire for gain, nor did they pursue the shadow of vain glory, nor hunt for popular favor, nor flatter any mortal. They did not cover their own vices or those of their kin with silence, nor did they cloak them, as Gentile writers are wont to do, but they ingenuously confessed them. Thus, Moses did not suppress his own lack of faith at the waters of contradiction, nor the impious murmuring of his sister, nor the horrible idolomania of his brother Aaron. Jonah did not disguise his own disobedience, his unjust desire for the destruction of the Ninevites, however much they were repenting, nor his immoderate impatience. King David, moreover, so published his own crimes that he even gave them to others to be sung, which [are] not obscure. are obscure indications of a mind without guile.

Latin:

Κριτήρια externa, sacrarum litterarum immediatam a Deo dependentiam notificantia, sunt (a) scripturæ antiquitas; (b) Amanuensium sacrorum singulare lumen, notitiæ veritatisque studium; (c) Miraculorum, quibus doctrina cœlestis scripturarum firmatur, claritas; (d) Ecclesiæ, per vniuersum terrarum orbem diffusæ, consentiens testimonium de diuinitate sacræ scripturæ; (e) Martyrum constantia; (f) Testimonia reliquorum populorum perhibita doctrinæ in sacro codice contentæ; (g) Doctrinæ christianæ felix & subita per totum terrarum orbem propagatio, eiusque admiranda inter tot persecutiones conseruatio; (h) inflicta contemtoribus & persecutoribus verbi diuini pœnæ grauissimæ.

Prob. a. S. scripturæ diuinam originem arguit (1) Antiquitas doctrinæ, eo quod sacræ litteræ originem huius vniuersi, initia temporum, eorumque continuatam seriem, primordia ecclesiæ, politiæ, œconomiæ, prima rudimenta artium, peccati incunabula, proteuangelium, legis scriptæ a Deo factum exordium, accurate exponunt. (2) Antiquitas causæ ministerialium. Mofes enim, antiquissimus scriptor, omnes gentilium historicorum, philosophorum, oratores & poëtas anteuertit. Priusquam vllus inclaresceret liber, exsistit sapientia oceanus, pentateuchus. (3) Antiquitas formæ externæ; concepta quippe est scriptura veteris testamenti lingua hebræa; quæ vt simplicissima, ita prima est. At quo quid antiquius, eo verius, præstabilius & diuinius est. Argumentamur: Quæ scriptura antiquissima est, illa est verissima atque diuinissima. Atqui scriptura S. est antiquissima. Ergo scriptura S. est verissima atque diuinissima.

Prob. b. Duo sunt, quæ amanuenses sacros ἀξιοπίστους reddunt, eorumque scripta, vt diuina, commendant: 1) Scientia rerum tradendarum eximia. 2) Amor veritatis sine affectuum partiumque studio fincerus. Incomparabilis eorum scientia partim ex eo effulgefcit, quod mysteria fidei, captum rationis fibi relictæ excedentia, viua voce & fcriptis docuerunt; quæ ipfis non, nifi ex infpiratione diuina, innotefcere potuerunt; partim quod dogmata e lumine naturæ cognofcibilia plenius certiusque, quam philofophi ex rationis principiis propofuerunt; cum tamen ante extraordinariam illuminationem plerique eorum fuerint difciplinarum rudes. Amorem veritatis aperte teftati funt; quoniam prædicarant & fcripferunt verbum diuinum, affectibus exorbitantibus vacui. Neque enim præfentiffimis periculis funt exanimati, neque cupiditate lucri inflammati, neque vinbram vanæ gloriæ fectati, neque auram popularem aucupati, neque vlli mortalium affentati. Sua fuorumque vitia non texerunt filentio aut palliarunt, vt folent fcriptores gentiles, fed ingenue faffi funt. Sic Mofes neque fuam ad aquas contradictionis diffidentiam, neque impium fororis murmur, neque horribilem fratris Aaronis idolomaniam fuppreffit. Ionas fuam inobedientiam, iniquum defiderium exitii Niniuitarum, quantutnuis refipifcentium, immoderatam impatientiam non diffimulauit. Rex Dauid autem fua crimina adeo propalauit, vt ea aliis etiam cantanda dederit, quæ haud obfcura obscura sunt animi fine fuco candidi indicia.


### Question XXIX. By what external *criteria* is the divine origin of the Scriptures made known?: We argue: Whatever scripture is adorned by men divinely illuminated and most upright, that is of divine origin

We argue: Whatever scripture is adorned by men divinely illuminated and most upright, that is of divine origin.

But the Holy Scripture is such, &c. Therefore. Prob. c. Miracles are effects of infinite divine power, rare and unusual, produced above the order of the whole created nature. God alone performs them. Which miracles the Creator and Arbiter of things destined for the mission of his ambassadors and for the confirmation of doctrine.

For which reason God, when sending Moses, extraordinarily, both to the Israelite people and to Pharaoh, the king of the Egyptians, first instructed him with miracles, by which he might prove his divine mission, and might win faith for himself in the words he was to speak in God's name, before he sent him. Christ himself, being asked by the disciples of John whether he was the true Messiah promised to the fathers and sought with many sighs, appealed to the miracles performed by himself. The apostles, going forth, preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed.

Dicis Even false prophets are said to perform signs and wonders.

The Egyptian magicians emulated Moses in producing signs and portents. I answer: Distinguish between marvels and true miracles.

The false prophets performed אותות signs, and מופתים wonders, or portents, which produced a certain admiration in ignorant men, but they did not perform מופתים miracles, properly and strictly so called. For although all miracles are signs and wonders, yet not all signs and wonders are true miracles. They agree in this very thing, that they are rare and unusual effects; they differ in that miracles strictly so called are effects of infinite divine power, rare and unusual, produced above the order of the whole created nature; but the signs and wonders performed by false prophets are either deceptions and diabolical delusions, or indeed real effects, but by the help of the devil through natural causes, disposed in a way unusual in nature, and agitated most swiftly.

The magicians emulated Moses the wonder-worker, but with unhappy success: for they were finally forced to confess that the miracles of Moses were performed by the finger of God, i.e., by divine power. Wherefore we argue: Whose scripture's doctrine is confirmed by miracles performed by the finger of God, that has not mere men, but God himself as its author. But the doctrine of Holy Scripture is such, &c. Therefore. Prob. d. The Israelite Church of the Old Testament, just as the Christian Church of the New, as much the one contemporary with the prophets and apostles, which saw these holy men of God and frequently feasted its eyes upon their αὐτόγραφα (autographs), as the one that succeeded them, spread far and wide throughout the whole world, comprising the flower of men most learned in doctrine and most adorned in the honesty of their lives, testifies with wondrous consent that the prophetic and apostolic writings have God himself as their author, who is best, greatest, most wise, and most truthful.

Who could believe that so many thousands of men, dispersed most widely, conspired in a single lie or error, by which a human writing might be held to be divine? Whoever would oppose himself to such a huge cloud of witnesses would be just as absurd as one who, about to call into doubt the faith of all writers and literature in general, would debate whether some Cicero or Aristotle ever lived: or whether Rome or America exists in the world.

Therefore this argument remains firm: Of whose scripture's divine origin an innumerable multitude of men living in the bosom of the Catholic Church testifies, to that scripture faith must be given. But of the divine origin of Holy Scripture it is testified, &c. Therefore. Prob. e.

The martyrs testified to the immediate dependence of the Holy Scriptures upon God not only by words, but also sealed their testimony, as it were, with their shed blood. For such an unusual strength of mind was divinely bestowed upon them, that they preferred to endure the most exquisite tortures and to meet the most bitter death with a cheerful spirit, rather than to recede even a hair's breadth from that doctrine which Holy Scripture hands down.

For this, the most pious martyrs endured most immense pains most pious of both sexes, of all ages, in every place, as often as by the permission of God the storms of persecution have been stirred up in the Church of Christ. Not without astonishment do we read in NICEPHORUS, lib. VIII. hist. c. VI. that, when persecution arose under Diocletian and Maximian, most cruel tyrants, at Nicomedia, among twenty thousand and more Christians of all sexes, ages, and stations, who had gathered in the temple to celebrate the birthday of the Lord, not even one was found who, fearing death at the voice of the herald—that he who wished to live should go out of the temple and burn incense on the nearby altar of Jupiter, otherwise, if he did not do this, he would be burned together with the house itself—preferred his life to death, and went out of the temple. But rather, there was one voice of all: We are all Christians, we believe in one and the same only God and King, Christ, and we are all prepared to offer sacrifice to Him and to His Father and to the Holy Spirit. This is a memorable example, that the martyrs, through the Holy Spirit dwelling in their hearts, were most fully persuaded of the truth of the doctrine contained in the Holy Scriptures, and were excited and raised up to an intrepid confession of the same.

Whence arises the argument: For which doctrine the most religious martyrs of every sex, of every age, in every place, when persecutions arose, underwent most bitter tortures and a most ignominious death cheerfully and gladly, the same have testified, not by words only, but by the very deed itself, that it proceeded from God, the primary truth.

But they did so for the doctrine in Holy Scripture, the most religious martyrs, etc. Therefore.

Prob. f. Peoples alien to the sacred rites of the Christians, and their mortal enemies, have borne a most honorable testimony to Holy Scripture.

I will say nothing of the Jews, whom Augustine in Ps. XL. calls our capsarii [book-bearers], who carry the codex for us who study: since they acknowledge the θεοπνευστίαν [divine inspiration] of the Old Testament, and can be convinced from the same that the New Testament, because of the harmony of both, was consigned by the inspiration of God. The Turks have excerpted many things from the Holy Scriptures, and have translated them into their Alcoran.

The Gentiles have partly commended the monuments of men who were θεοπνεύστων [divinely inspired]: As Longinus, the teacher of the philosopher Porphyry, who in his book on (*) There is indeed much strength in this argumentation: But two things are to be properly observed.

First, in the history of the Martyrs, things truly done must be accurately distinguished from fictitious and invented fables, since many are counted as Martyrs who were not even men at all. But while we must take care not to increase their number, we must no less take care not to diminish it, as DODWELL erred in his dissertation on the paucity of Martyrs.

Secondly, as far as the definition is concerned, the nature and character of those who are to be proclaimed Martyrs by their own merit must be explored, since many have been ψευδομάρτυρες [false martyrs]. Namely, a Martyr, strictly so called, is a man of integrity of life and pure from wickedness, who so professes the truth divinely revealed, which he himself has known sufficiently and confirmed with the firmest assent, that for its sake he himself endures all injuries and most grievous vexations with a brave and constant mind.

There are, therefore, four properties by which a Martyr, worthy of his name, is distinguished from any Pseudomartyr: 1) Confession of the truth, and indeed of that which is to be learned from divine revelation, John XV, 27. & XVI, 13.

He who wanders in error, and dares to defend it with most stubborn zeal even unto death, is to be judged clearly unworthy of the name of Martyr, as are very many ψευδομάρτυρες [false martyrs] among all nations, blinded by superstition. 2) Sufficient and certain knowledge of that truth, so that when questioned he may be able to give to everyone a reason for the doctrine which he himself constantly professes, 1 Pet. III, 15.

3) A sincere purpose, that he may endure all calamities for the sake of the truth itself: for it can happen that one may indeed profess the truth, but not for the sake of the truth, but rather with a far different mind, not so much from a zeal for propagating the truth as for the pursuit of his own glory, Phil. I, 12-15.

4) Constancy, and fortitude of mind, which is indeed at a very long interval distant from rash audacity.

To precipitate oneself into dangers which, while the truth is safe, could have been avoided, is of rashness; but those dangers which we cannot avoid otherwise than by the denial or dissimulation of the truth, to undergo and sustain them (ὑπομονεῖν [to endure]), that is finally true constancy.

Matt. X, 16. 17. coll. with v. 32.

Regarding the sublime, he says that Moses is to be compared with Homer: Moses was a legislator of the Jews of no common sort; inasmuch as he made the power of the Divine known in accordance with its dignity, and declared it immediately at the beginning of the prologue of his laws, writing: God said: Let there be Light! and it was: Let there be earth! and it was: and also Amelius, the Platonic philosopher, who accepts the beginning of the Johannine Gospel as consonant with the principles of Plato: they partly transferred sacred histories into their own writings. For one pursuing these matters at length, see Jo. Adam Osiander, *Theologiae Positivae Acroamaticae*, p. 294, and compare Grotius, *De Veritate Religionis Christianae*, Book IV. Hence, an opportunity is given to us for arguing: That scripture which the chief enemies of the Christian church have esteemed so highly—that the Jews have received the writings of the prophets, with whom the monuments of the apostles most amicably conspire, as *theopneustos* (divinely inspired); that the Turks have inserted many things taken from them into their Alcoran; that the Gentiles have commended the same, and have supplemented their own histories from them—that scripture is of divine origin, it is reasonable to agree. But the chief enemies of the church have esteemed sacred scripture so highly, etc. Therefore.

Proof g. Christian doctrine, communicated divinely, by the efficacy of a lightning bolt suddenly drew many myriads of men into its assent. At one sermon of Peter, three thousand souls were converted, Acts 2:42; at another sermon of this apostle, the number of believers grew to five thousand, Acts 4:4. Apostolic doctrine, having crossed the borders of the land of Palestine, quickly pervaded very many regions, as St. Paul testifies that in his own times it had gone out into all the earth, and unto the ends of the world, Rom. 10:18. Against this, the Jews struggled with vain effort, blinded by an inveterate error concerning the earthly kingdom of the Messiah; the pagans, fascinated by idolomania; tyrants, threatening iron, the wheel, and fire to the sincere propagators of the divine word, who were equipped neither with arms, nor with feigned eloquence, nor with the apparatus of human learning. This sudden propagation of apostolic doctrine was followed by its admirable preservation amidst immense persecutions. The world and the underworld conspired against the gospel of Christ; men and demons raged; but with no success. For sacred scripture, like the palm tree, always emerged superior and remained impregnable, so that it is permissible to say: If this counsel or this work were of men, it would be dissolved: but because it is of God, it cannot be dissolved. Acts 5:38. We argue: Whatever doctrine, like a lightning bolt, has suddenly drawn human minds into its assent, has suddenly pervaded very many provinces, and has remained impregnable against the machinations of the devil and the world: that was not invented by men, but proceeded from God himself. But the doctrine comprised in the sacred letters, etc. Therefore.

Proof h. God, the most just avenger of his word, has inflicted the most severe punishments upon the enemies of the Bible. Antiochus, having burned many copies of the sacred code, 1 Maccab. 1:56, was struck by a divine, incurable plague, 2 Maccab. 9:5. The orator Theopompus and the tragedian Theodectes, when they had handled the sacred Bibles with impure hands—the former, because he wished to excerpt certain things for mockery, was seized in his mind; the latter, because he had applied them to a drama, was deprived of the light of his eyes. Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book XII. Herod the Ascalonite, a most truculent enemy of the gospel of Christ, was eaten by worms. Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book XV, ch. 16. Julian the Apostate, a great hater of sacred scripture, surrounded in the Persian war and wounded by an arrow, when he had scattered his gushing blood into the air, with the added impious voice: "You have conquered, Galilean!" breathed out his impure soul. Theodoret, Book III, ch. 20. When Diocletian and Maximian had consigned to the flames the scriptures extorted by force from the Christians, the fire was suddenly extinguished, and copious hail fell from heaven, so that all the elements seemed to have conspired, as if sworn, for the authority of the sacred books. See Bonfrerius in *Praeloquia Pentateuchi*, fol. 20. From these is born the argument: That scripture whose contempt has been avenged by the most harsh punishments sent by God is not a human invention, but a divine gift. But sacred scripture, etc. Therefore.

Observation. We have premised these external criteria because the minds of infidel men are prepared by them for sacred scripture, to be read with study and a desire to learn, and to be meditated upon. For since the entire race of the Gentiles, atheists, and Epicureans does not believe that Holy Scripture has proceeded from God, they scarcely deign to read it. Wherefore it is necessary that, first of all, through the adduced external criteria, or, as others call them, signs and motives of credibility, the infidels be moved so that they may judge it not improbable that Holy Scripture derives its origin from God, and thus begin to esteem, read, and meditate upon it. For thus, through the criteria of divinely inspired Scripture, they will be moved more and more to apply faith to it, and through the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit, the immovable plerophoria or fiducial assent, by which we adhere to Scripture, will be kindled, fostered, and confirmed.

Latin:

Argumentamur: Quaecunque scriptura adornata est a viris divinitus illuminatis & integerrimis, illa divina est originis.

Atqui scriptura S. &c. Ergo. Prob. c. Miracula sunt effectus infinitae potentiae divinae, rari & insoliti, supra ordinem totius naturae creatae producti. Facit ea Deus solus. Quae miracula rerum fator & arbiter legatorum suorum missione & doctrinae confirmandae destinavit.

Quam ob rem Deus Mosen, extra ordinem cum ad populum Israeliticum, tum ad Pharaonem, Aegyptiorum regem, mittendum, miraculis prius instruebat, quibus divinam suam missionem probaret, verbisque suis Dei nomine faciendis fidem sibi conciliaret, quam eundem mitteret. Christus ipse quaesitus a discipulis Ioannis, an verus patribus promissus, multisque suspiriis expetitus Messias esset, provocavit ad miracula a se edita. Apostoli exeuntes praedicarunt ubique, domino cooperante & verbum confirmante per subsequentia signa.

Dicis Etiam pseudoprophetae dicuntur facere signa & prodigia.

Magi Aegyptiaci Mosen in edendis signis & portentis aemulati sunt, Resp.

Dist. inter mirabilia, & vera miracula. Fecerunt pseudoprophetae אותות signa, & מופתים prodigia, sive portenta, quae admirationem quandam imperitis hominibus pepererunt, sed non fecerunt מופתים miracula, proprie & stricte sic dicta. Quamvis enim omnia miracula sint signa & prodigia, non tamen omnia signa & prodigia sunt vera miracula. Conveniunt hoc ipso, quod sint effectus rari & insoliti; differunt, quod miracula stricte dicta sint effectus infinitae potentiae divinae rari & insoliti, supra ordinem totius naturae creatae producti; at signa & prodigia facta a pseudoprophetis, vel sunt praestigia & delusiones diabolicae, vel reales quidem effectus, sed ope diaboli per causas naturales, modo in natura inusitato dispositas, celerrimeque agitatas.

Magi aemulati sunt Mosen thaumaturgum, sed successu infelici: coacti enim tandem sunt fateri, miracula Mosis patrari digito Dei, i. e. virtute divina. Quare argumentamur: Cuiuscunque scripturae doctrina miraculis digito Dei patratis confirmata est, illa non nudos homines, sed ipsum Deum habet auctorem. Atqui S. scripturae doctrina &c. Ergo. Prob. d. Ecclesia Israelitica veteris, pariter atque christiana novi testamenti, tam coaeva prophetis atque apostolis, quae hos sanctos Dei homines vidit, & αὐτόγραφα eorum crebro oculis usurpavit, quam succedanea, per totum terrarum orbem longe lateque diffusa, complexa florem hominum doctrina excultissimorum, vitaeque honestate ornatissimorum, miro consensu testatur, scripta prophetica & apostolica ipsum Deum habere auctorem optimum, maximum, sapientissimum, veracissimum.

Ecquis credat tot millia hominum latissime dispersorum conspirasse in unum mendacium aut errorem, quo scriptum humanum habeatur divinum? Qui tam ingenti testium nubi se opponeret, perinde absurdus foret, ac qui omnium in universum scriptorum ac litterarum fidem in dubium vocaturus ambigeret, an vixerit Cicero aliquis, aut Aristoteles: an exstet in mundo Roma, aut America.

Proinde firmum manet hoc argumentum: De cuius scripturae origine divina testatur innumerabilis copia hominum in gremio ecclesiae catholicae viventium, illi scripturae fides est habenda. Atqui de origine divina scripturae sacrae testatur &c. Ergo. Prob. e.

Immediatam sacrarum litterarum dependentiam a Deo martyres non verbis tantum testati sunt, sed & testimonium suum fuso sanguine quasi obsignarunt. Tam inusitatum enim animi robur divinitus ipsis fuit collatum, ut exquisitissimos sustinere cruciatus, mortemque acerbissimam alacri obire animo, quam vel latum unguem a doctrina illa, quam S. scriptura tradit, recedere maluerint.

Pro hac dolores immanissimos pertulerunt martyres piissimi utriusque sexus, omnium aetatum, ubivis locorum, quotiescunque permissu Dei persecutionum procellae in ecclesia Christi excitatae sunt. Non sine stupore legimus apud NICEPHORUM lib. VIII. histor. c. VI. quod, exorta persecutione sub Diocletiano & Maximiano, tyrannis dirissimis, Nicomedia, inter vicies mille & plures omnium sexuum, aetatum & statuum christianos, qui in templo ad celebrandum natalem domini convenerant, ne unus quidem inventus sit, qui mortem veritus ad praeconis vocem, vt, qui vivere vellet, et in templo exiret, & in proxima ara Iouis thura adoleret, alioqui, nisi hoc fecisset, una cum domo ipsa conflagraturus, vitam suam morti praetulerit, & templo egressus fit. Quin potius omnium una vox fuit: Omnes christiani sumus, unum eumque solum Deum & regem credimus Christum, & ipsi patrique eius & Spiritui sancto sacrificare, atque nos omnes una offerre parati sumus. Id quod memorabili est exemplo, martyres, per Spiritum S. in cordibus ipsorum habitantem, de veritate doctrinae sacris litteris comprehensae fuisse maxime persuasos, & ad intrepidam eiusdem confessionem excitatos atque erectos.

Vnde nascitur argumentum: Pro qua doctrina martyres religiosissimi omnis sexus, omnis aetatis, ubivis locorum, coortis persecutionibus, cruciatus acerbissimos, mortemque ignominiosissimam alacres & laete subiverunt, illam non verbis tantum, sed & opere ipso testati sunt iidem, a Deo veritate prima esse profectam.

Atqui pro doctrina in S. scriptura martyres religiosissimi &c. Ergo.

Prob. f. Populi alieni a sacris christianorum, eorumque hostes capitales, perquam honorificum sacrae scripturae testimonium perhibuerunt.

Nil dicam de Iudaeis, quos Augustinus in Ps. XL. nostros appellat capsarios, qui nobis studentibus codicem portant: cum hi τὴν θεοπνευστίαν veteris testamenti agnoscant, & ex eodem convinci possint, novum testamentum, ob utrinsque harmoniam, inspirante Deo esse consignatum. Turcae multa e sacris litteris excerpserunt, & in alcoranum suum transtulerunt.

Gentiles monumenta virorum θεοπνεύστων partim commendarunt: Vt Longinus, Porphyrii philosophi praeceptor, qui libro περὶ (*) Multum quidem roboris in hac argumentatione inest: Sed duo sunt probe observanda.

Primum in historia Martyrum res vere gestae accurate discernendae sunt a fictis & commentitiis fabellis, quando quidem multi numerantur Martyres, qui ne homines quidem unquam fuerunt. Dum vero cavendum nobis est, ne eorum numerum augeamus, non minus est providendum, ne eum minuamus, quem ad modum DODWELLUS erravit, in sua de paucitate Martyrum commentatione.

Deinde, quod ad definitionem attinet, exploranda est natura atque indoles eorum, qui suo merito Martyres praedicandi sunt, quum multi fuerint ψευδομάρτυρες. Scilicet Martyr, ex proprie ita dictus, est homo integer vitae scelerisque purus, qui veritatem divinitus patefactam, quam ipse satis cognitam ac firmissima adfensione comprobauit, ita profitetur, vt propter eam omnes ipse iniurias grauissimasque vexationes forti & constante animo sustineat.

Sunt igitur quatuor proprietates, quibus Martyr, suo nomine dignus, a quouis Pseudomartyre distinguitur: 1) Confessio veritatis, & eius quidem, quae ex diuina reuelatione discenda est, Ioann. XV, 27. & XVI, 13.

Qui in errore versatur, eumque pertinacissimo studio ad mortem vsque tueri audet, is nomine Μάρτυρος plane indignus est iudicandus, vt sunt ψευδομάρτυρες permulti inter omnes gentes, superstitione obcaecatas. 2) Sufficiens & certa illius veritatis cognitio, ut interrogatus valeat cuique rationem reddere doctrinae, quam constans ipse profitetur, 1 Petr.

III, 15. 3) Sincerum propositum, vt pro veritate ipsa omnes calamitates perferat: fieri enim potest, vt quis veritatem quidem profiteatur, at non propter veritatem, immo vero longe alia mente, non tam veritatis propagandae studio, quam suae gloriae aucupio, Phil.

I, 12-15. 4) Constantia, ac fortitudo animi, quae longissimo sane intervallo distat a temeraria audacia.

In pericula, quae, salua quidem veritate, euitari poterant, se ipsum praecipitare, temeritatis est; ea vero pericula, quae non aliter, quam veritatis aut negatione, aut dissimulatione, subterfugere queamus, subire ac sustinere (ὑπομονεῖν), ea demum vera constantia est.

Matth. X, 16. 17. coll. cum v. 32.

περὶ ὕψες Mosen cum Homero comparandum inquit: Mofes Iudæorum legislator fuit haud vulgaris; quandoquidem Numinis potentiam pro dignitate notam fecerit, declaraueritque statim initio proœmii legum suarum, scribens: Dixit Deus: Fiat Lux! & facta est: Fiat terra! & facta est: nec non Amelius, Platonicus philosophus, qui euangelii Ioannæi exordium vt consonum Platonis principiis recipit: partim historias sacras in scripta sua transtulerunt. Fuse hæc prosequentem vide IO. ADAM. OSIANDR. in theol. posit. acroamat. p. 294. & conf. GROTIVM de verit. relig. christ. lib. IV. Hinc nobis datur ansa argumentandi: Quam scripturam capitales ecclesiæ christianæ hostes tanti æstimarunt, vt Iudæi scripta prophetarum, quibuscum monumenta apostolorum amicissime conspirant, tanquam θεόπνευστα receperint, Turcæ ex iis multa sublecta alcorano suo inseruerint, gentiles eadem commendarint, & ex ipsis historias suas suppleuerint, illam scripturam diuinæ esse originis, vero consentaneum est. Atqui scripturam sacram capitales ecclesiæ hostes tanti æstimarunt &c. Ergo.

Prob. g. Doctrina christiana, diuinitus communicata, sua efficacia ritu fulminis multas hominum myriadas derepente in sui assensum pertraxit. Ad vnam concionem Petri conuersæ sunt ter mille animæ, Act. II, 42. ad alteram huius apostoli concionem credentium numerus ad quinquies mille excreuit, Act. IV, 4. Doctrina apostolica, limites terræ Palæstinæ egressa, celeriter plurimas peruafit regiones, vt S. Paullus testetur, suis eam temporibus exiisse in omnem terram, & in fines orbis terrarum. Rom. X, 18. Cui irrito conatu obluctati sunt Iudæi, inueterato errore de regno Messiæ terreno occæcati: pagani, idolomania fascinati: tyranni, ferrum, rotam, ignem minitati sinceris verbi diuini propagatoribus, neque armis, neque fucata eloquentia, neque apparatu doctrinæ humanæ instructis. Quam subitam doctrinæ apostolicæ propagationem secuta est illius inter immanes persecutiones admiranda conseruatio. Conspirarunt aduersus euangelium Christi orbis & orcus, fremuerunt homines & dæmones; sed nullo successu. Sacra enim scriptura, instar palmæ, semper euasit superior, & perstitit inexpugnabilis, vt dicere liceat: Si ex hominibus esset consilium hoc, aut opus, dissolueretur: quia autem ex Deo est, dissolui non potest. Act. V, 38. Argumentamur: Quæcunque doctrina, fulminis instar, derepente mentes humanas in sui assensum pertraxit, plurimas prouincias subito peruasit, aduersus machinas diaboli & mundi perstitit inexpugnabilis: illa non ab hominibus inuenta, sed a Deo ipso profecta est. Atqui doctrina sacris litteris comprehensa &c. Ergo.

Prob. h. Deus iustissimus verbi sui vindex pœnas longe grauissimas bibliorum hostibus irrogauit. Antiochus, combustis plurimis sacri codicis exemplaribus, 1 Maccab. I, 56. plaga insanabili diuinitus percussus est. 2 Maccab. IX, 5. Theopompus orator, & Theodectes tragœdus, cum impuris manibus sacra biblia contrectassent, ille, quod quædam ad ludibrium excerpere voluerit, mente captus; hic vero, quod ad drama adhibuisset, oculorum lumine orbatus est. IOSEPH. libr. XII. antiqu. Iudaic. Herodes Ascalonita, hostis euangelii Christi truculentissimus, a vermibus erosus est. IOSEPH. libr. XV. antiqu. Iudaic. c. 16. Iulianus apostata, osor maximus sacræ scripturæ, bello Persico circumuentus & sagitta vulneratus, cum erumpentem sanguinem in aërem sparsisset, addita impia voce: Vicisti Galilæe! impuram animam efflauit. THEODORET. lib. III. c. 20. Cum Diocletianus, & Maximianus, vi extortas a christianis scripturas flammis addixissent, ignis subito exstinctus est, & grando copiosa de cœlo decidit, vt omnia elementa pro sacrorum librorum auctoritate conspirare velut coniurata viderentur. v. BONFRERIVS in præloqu. pentat. fol. 20. Nascitur ex his argumentum: Cuius scripturæ contemptus immissis a Deo pœnis asperrimis vindicatus est, illa non est inuentum humanum, sed donum diuinum. Atqui scriptura sacra &c. Ergo.

Obs. Κριτήρια externa præmisimus ideo, quod animi hominum infidelium conuertendorum iisdem præparantur ad scripturam sacram, cum studio & desiderio discendi legendam atque meditandam. Cum enim vniversa gentilium, atheorum, & epicuraeorum gens non credat sacram scripturam a Deo esse profectam, eam legere vix dignatur. Quare necesse est, vt primo omnium per adducta externa κριτήρια, siue, vt alii vocant, signa & motiua credibilitatis, infideles moueantur, vt non improbabile esse censeant, sacram scripturam a Deo ducere originem, atque adeo eam aestimare, legere & meditari incipiant. Sic enim per κριτήρια scripturae diuinitus inspiratae ad fidem eidem adhibendam magis magisque permouebuntur, & per internum Spiritus sancti testimonium immota πληροφορία siue assensus fiducialis, quo scripturae adhaerescimus, accendetur, fouebitur, confirmabitur.


### Question XXX. What are the internal criteria by which the divine origin of sacred literature becomes known?

What are the internal criteria from which the divine origin of the sacred letters becomes known? The criteria or internal indications from which the theopneustia of the sacred letters is revealed are: (a) The majesty of God testifying of Himself in the sacred code; (b) The simplicity and gravity of the biblical style; (c) The sublimity of the divine mysteries which Scripture unfolds; (d) The truth of all biblical assertions; (e) The holiness of the precepts comprised in the sacred letters; (f) The sufficiency of Holy Scripture for salvation.

Obs.

These internal criteria, collected into one bundle and taken conjointly, provide a more valid argument (just as united strength is always stronger) than if they were taken separately and individually: therefore we shall later gather them into one syllogism.

Proof, a. The sacred amanuenses gravely assert that they bring forth and utter the word of God Himself from His dictation. This is evident from the prophetic formulas: Thus says the Lord, Is. 1:2. The word of Jehovah came to me, Jer. 2:4. What is more? They not rarely introduce God Himself speaking, e.g., Exod. 20:1, 2, 3. Then God spoke all these words, saying: I am Jehovah thy God, etc. Since, therefore, God testifies of Himself in the sacred letters, that divine testimony must be approved with ready assent.

You say: In the Alcoran, God and the angel Gabriel are sometimes introduced speaking and testifying that the things handed down in that book are true and divine. Resp. The internal criteria taken conjointly conclude validly. (α) Join the majesty of God, testifying of Himself in Scripture, with the truth of all biblical assertions, and you have a firm argument for the theopneustia of Holy Scripture. (β) Who would not notice in the Alcoran the claws of the devil appearing through lies and a thieving blade? Who would not notice a lymphatic spirit of vertigo in its paradoxes? as D A N N H A V. wittily says in Hodoph. Phaenom. I, p. 45.

Proof, b. The biblical style is worthy of divine majesty, since it is simple and grave. It is simple because it is not smeared with the paint of human eloquence, not singed with the curling-irons of words to capture the minds of the vulgar, but is chaste and full of virtue. The apostle of the Gentiles agrees, saying: My speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, 1 Cor. 2:4. It is grave because by the same Holy Spirit, things to be believed, even the most sublime, are proposed without demonstration; but things to be done and omitted are commanded and prohibited to the highest and lowest with remarkable authority. Thus God gives laws to every man, of whatever status or sex he may be: Thou shalt not kill: Thou shalt not commit adultery: Thou shalt not steal: Which style, simple and grave, is most worthy of the supreme Arbiter of all things. A certain atheist of brazen brow opposes us, according to whose mind the style of Holy Scripture is not worthy of even a good human writer, let alone the most wise God. He strives to deceive us when he writes 1) That Holy Scripture is confused and mixed, which is evident to one inspecting the Proverbs of Solomon, in which, he says, it is not unusual for things of every kind to be mixed and confused like a hodgepodge even in a single chapter. things of a kind to be mixed and confused like a hodgepodge.

Resp.

1) The atheist argues from the particular to the universal, and thus incorrectly: Various things are mixed together in proverbs without a certain method. Therefore, the whole Holy Scripture is confused.

2) That book of Solomon is not occupied with explaining any determined subject matter, but contains maxims of every kind, and brief and rounded sentences about various things, in the listing of which a certain method is not required. 2) He writes that scripture is placed without connection, e.g., ch.

Latin:

Kριτήρια siue indicia interna, e quibus sacrarum litterarum θεοπνευσία patescit, sunt (a) Dei de se ipso in sacro codice testantis maiestas; (b) Stili biblici simplicitas & grauitas; (c) Mysteriorum diuinorum, quae scriptura pandit, sublimitas; (d) Omnium assertionum biblicarum veritas; (e) Praeceptorum sacris litteris comprehensorum sanctitas; (f) Sacrae scripturae ad salutem sufficientia.

Obs.

Kριτήρια haec interna in vnum fasciculum collecta, & coniunctim sumta validius suppeditant argumentum (sicut vis vnita semper fortior est), quam si sumantur seorfim & sigillatim: idcirco eadem postea in vnum conglobaturi sumus syllogismum.

Prob, a. Amanuenses sacri grauiter asseuerant, se ipsius Dei verbum e dictamine illius proferre & eloqui. Id quod patet e formulis propheticis: Sic dicit Dominus, Es. I, 2. Factum est verbum Iehouae ad me, Ier. II, 4. Quid? quod Deum ipsum loquentem introducunt haud raro, v. gr. Exod. XX, 1. 2. 3. Deinde locutus est Deus omnia verba haec dicendo: ego sum Iehouah Deus tuus &c. Cum igitur Deus in sacris litteris de ipso testetur, testimonium illud diuinum prono assensu comprobandum est.

Dicis: In alcorano aliquoties Deus, & angelus Gabriel, introducuntur loquentes & testificantes ea, quae traduntur in isto libro, esse vera & diuina. Resp. κριτήρια interna coniunctim sumta valide concludunt. (α) Coniunge maiestatem Dei, de se ipso in scriptura testantis, cum veritate omnium assertionum biblicarum, & firmum habetis τῆς θεοπνευσίας S. scripturae argumentum. (β) Quis non animaduertat in alcorano vngues diaboli per mendacia & acinacem latrocinantem apparentes? Quis non spiritum vertiginis lymphaticum in paradoxis? argute inquit D A N N H A V. in hodofoph. phaenom. I. p. 45.

Prob, b. Stilus biblicus maiestate diuina dignus est, cum sit simplex granis. Simplex est, quia non fuco eloquentiae humanae illitus, non verborum calamistris inustus ad captandum animos vulgi, fed castus, virtutisque plenus est. Concine inquit gentium apostolus: Sermo meus & praeconium meum non fuit in persuaforiis sapientiae humanae verbis: sed in demonstratione spiritus & virtutis, 1 Cor. II, 4. Grauis est, quia eodem a Spiritu S. credenda vel sublimitima sine demonstratione proponuntur; agenda autem & omittenda summis & imis insigni cum auctoritate praecipiuntur, & prohibentur. Sic Deus omni homini, cuiuscunque status aut sexus fit, fert leges: Non occides: Non moechaberis: Non furtum facies: Qui stilus simplex & grauis fummo rerum arbitro perquam dignus est. Obnititur nobis atheus quidam perfrictae frontis, ex cuius mente stilus S. scripturae ne bono quidem scriptore humano, nedum...Deo sapientissimo dignus fit. Fucum nobis facere nititur, dum scribit 1) Sacram scripturam esse confusam & commixtam, quod pateat inspicienti prouerbia Salomonis, in quibus, dicit, non insolens esse, in vno etiam capite omnis generis res ad instar farraginis commisceri & confundi.

Resp.

1) Argumentatur atheus a particulari ad universale, adeoque perperam: Sine certa methodo commiscentur variæ res in prouerbiis. Ergo tota S. scriptura est confusa.

2) Liber ille Salomonis non occupatur in determinata aliqua materia explicanda, sed continet omnis generis gnomas, breuesque ac rotundas de rebus variis sententias, in quibus recensendis certa methodus non requiritur. 2) Scribit, scripturam positam esse fine connexione, v. gr. c.


### Question XXX. What are the internal criteria by which the divine origin of sacred literature becomes known?: II. of Habakkuk, and indeed, v

II. of Habakkuk, and indeed, v.

1. does not cohere with the last verse of chapter I.

Resp.

Again the atheist argues from the particular, and because of the stupor of his mind, he does not notice the connection between chapters I and II of Habakkuk.

For in chapter I, the prophet had prophesied about the tyranny of the Chaldeans, by which they were about to rage against the Israelite people, and he had urged God with most ardent prayers to restrain the enemy and avert punishments from His people, or at least to mitigate them.

Chapter

II indicates that he is awaiting a divine response to his prayers and complaints: to the one waiting, a promise is given concerning the coming Messiah to refresh the afflicted people. These cohere clearly, provided that it is introduced with SEBAST.

SCHMIDT v. 1. ch.

II. of Habakkuk the particle (nevertheless). 3) He writes that the sacred codex was written without any color of words.

He cites ch.

V and VIII

of the Apocalypse, where he says that all verses begin with the particle "And."

Resp.

(1) The style of the Holy Spirit is not painted with the color of words, such as that of some rhetorician; but it is heavy with the weight of sentences, such as that of a master eminent in authority. (2) The particle "And" is repeated many times in the Latin Vulgate version, not in the Latin translation of SEBAST.

SCHMIDT, which is more accurate. The Greek καὶ sustains various meanings.

4) The bibliomastix writes that the order of sentences in the Bibles is often inverted, e.g.,

Luke

XX, 35, where eternal life is placed before the resurrection of the dead, an order which, however, Christians themselves reject.

Resp. (1) If the truth of the resurrection of the dead and eternal life is established, it matters little whether the one or the other is placed first; since in popular usage of speech we are not precisely bound to the order of things. (2) In the cited passage, the order of things is not inverted.

For the words of the text are: "But those who shall be accounted worthy to attain that age, and the resurrection from the dead." To be accounted worthy of that age extends more broadly than to be accounted worthy of the resurrection from the dead. For in the number of those who are accounted worthy of that age are also included the pious, whom the last day will find alive: as those who will not die, so they will not rise again.

But by the order of nature, the more general precede, the more specific follow.

5) The same man writes that some things in Holy Scripture are placed without sense, e.g.,

Eph.

II, 1.

"And you, who were dead in trespasses and sins": likewise John

VIII, 25. "the beginning, because I speak to you": Resp.

Eph.

II, 1. the word "he raised" is omitted by ellipsis, which if it is repeated from verse 20 of chapter I, the sense is plain: "And you also (he raised) when you were dead in trespasses and sins," John

VIII, 25. HUGO GROTIUS seems to have expressed the sense conveniently: "This is the first thing, which I also say to you: this very thing, which I said I am at this very time, that is, the light of the world." For v. 26 the Savior says: "I have many things to say and to judge concerning you": just as if he were saying: "Concerning myself I say only this, which I have said: but concerning you I could say many things to mark you."

Latin:

II. Habacuci, & quidem, v.

1. non cohærere cum vers. vltimo capitis I.

Resp.

Rursus argumentatur atheus a particulari, & præ stupore mentis non animaduertit connexionem c. I. & II. Habacuci.

Nam in capite I. propheta vaticinatus erat de Chaldæorum tyrannide, qua sæuituri essent in populum Israëliticum, Deumque precibus ardentissimis follicitauerat, vt hostem compesceret, pœnasque auerteret a populo suo; aut certe mitigaret.

Cap.

II. indicat se exspectare ad preces & querelas suas responsum diuinum: exspectanti datur promissio de venturo Messia ad recreandum populum afflictum. Quæ luculenter cohærent, modo inferatur cum SEBAST.

SCHMIDIO v. 1. c.

II. Habacuci particula (veruntamen). 3) Scribit, codicem sacrum conscriptum esse fine omni verborum colore.

Adducit cap.

V. & VIII.

Apocal. vbi ait, omnes versus a particula Et incipere.

Resp.

(1) Stilus Spiritus S. non est verborum colore pictus, qualis est rhetoris alicuius; sed est sententiarum pondere grauis, qualis est domini auctoritate eminentis. (2) Particula Et repetitur multoties in vulgata versione latina, non in translatione latina SEBAST.

SCHMIDII, quæ accuratior est. Græcum καὶ varias sustinet significationes.

4) Scribit bibliomastix, sententiarum ordinem in bibliis sæpe inuerti, v. gr.

Luc.

XX, 35. vbi vita æterna resurrectioni mortuorum præponitur, quem tamen ordinem ipsi christiani reiiciunt.

Resp. (1) Si de veritate resurrectionis mortuorum & vitæ æternæ constet, parum refert, hæc an illa præponatur; siquidem in populari loquendi vsu ad ordinem rerum præcise non adstringimur. (2) Loco citato rerum ordo non est inuersus.

Nam verba textus sunt: Qui vero digni habebuntur, vt seculum alterum consequantur, & resurrectionem ex mortuis. Dignum haberi seculo altero latius patet, quam dignum haberi resurrectione ex mortuis. Nam in numero eorum, qui habentur digni seculo altero, comprehenduntur etiam pii, quos extrema dies viuos deprehendet: vt qui non morientur, ita non resurgent.

Sed ordine naturæ præcedunt generaliora, sequuntur specialiora.

5) Scribit idem, nonnulla in S. scriptura posita esse fine sensu, v. gr.

Eph.

II, 1.

Atque vos, qui eratis mortui in lapsibus & peccatis: item Io.

VIII, 25. principium, quia vobis dico: Resp.

Eph.

II, 1. verbum suscitauit per ellipsin omissum est, quod si e versu 20. capitis I. repetatur, sensus planus est: Atque vos etiam (suscitauit) cum essetis mortui in lapsibus & peccatis, Io.

VIII, 25. sensum commode expressisse videtur HVGO GROTIVS: primum hoc sum, quod & dico vobis: hoc ipsum, quod me hoc ipso tempore esse dixi, id est lux mundi. Nam v. 26. inquit Saluator: Multa habeo de vobis loqui & iudicare: perinde ac si dicat: De me hoc tantum dico, quod dixi: de vobis autem multa possem dicere ad vos notandos.


### Question XXX. What are the internal criteria by which the divine origin of sacred literature becomes known?: 6) The author writes that some things in the scriptures are said without reason, as Ex XX, 18, where the…

6) The author writes that some things in the scriptures are said without reason, as Ex.

XX, 18, where the people are said to have seen the sound of trumpets, which, however, they heard, and Job

XXII, 6, where Job is said to have stripped clothes from the naked.

Resp. The Hebrew word רָאָה is not always referred to sight, but often in general denotes sensory cognition, by which something is perceived by the sense.

BUXTORF observed in the cited place in his Hebrew lexicon, p. 785, that the word רָאָה, "he saw," is also used of the mind and other senses, and signifies to experience, to notice, to perceive, to enjoy.

The words in Job are to be understood are in the divided sense: You have stripped garments from those who were previously clothed in garments, and now walk naked.

Prob. c. Holy Scripture everywhere hands down dogmas that are impervious and hidden to human reason, left to itself, which are called mysteries. Such are the dogmas concerning the trinity of divine persons in one divine essence, concerning the two natures and the unity of the person of Christ, concerning the redemption of the human race through the passion and death of Christ, concerning the justification of the sinner through faith in Christ, concerning the resurrection of the dead, concerning beatitude consisting on the part of the soul in the beatific vision and fruition of God, and on the part of the body in its clarification, etc. Since all these things far exceed the grasp of human reason by their sublimity, they could not have been devised by men, but became known from the supernatural revelation of God. This is what St. Paul openly confesses when, dealing with divine mysteries in 1 Cor. II, 7 sqq., he says in v. 10: But to us God has revealed them through His Spirit. Whatever Scripture, however, contains those sublime mysteries, which could not become known to men except by God revealing them, and could not be committed to writing by them except by God inspiring them, that is consigned by the inspiration of God. There is no reason for the enemies of Christian doctrine, who attempt to measure the articles of faith with the measuring rod of reason, to object that these same dogmas or mysteries conflict with right reason: for below in its proper place, with God as our guide and leader, we shall demonstrate that these same mysteries are indeed superior to the light of reason, but do not conflict with it, nor involve a contradiction.

Prob. d. The truth of biblical assertions can be shown: I. By an induction of all the articles of faith revealed in the sacred letters and proposed to man about to attain eternal salvation; some of which are mixed, some pure. Holy Scripture hands down mixed articles of faith, if you look at the matter proposed, in accordance with the principles of reason; but if you regard the manner of proposing, it inculcates them much more simply, certainly, and perfectly than human reason, investigated from its own principles, inculcates the same dogmas. See above prolegom. II. p. 50. As for pure articles of faith, just as human reason cannot know them from its own principles, so it cannot convict them of falsehood from those same principles. II. From the wondrous harmony of the Old with the New Testament, of Moses and the prophets with Christ and the apostles. Everything in the biblical body conspires: everything sounds together far more sweetly than diverse sounds in any musical instrument. Looking at this admirable conception of the sacred letters, Zechariah says that God has spoken through the mouth, not mouths, of the prophets. Luc. I, 79. Paul presented the Scripture of the O.T. under the aspect of one, not many books. Hebr. V, 7. The alleged contradiction is apparent, not true. But indeed, that so many writers, most dissimilar in talent and character, separated by the longest intervals of place and time, deprived of the opportunity of comparing the thoughts of their minds, should have conspired so egregiously in one opinion on a matter so grave and sublime, concerning the religion and salvation of all men, is a clear argument that Holy Scripture depends immediately on God as the one author, and he most truthful. III. From the fulfillment of the prophecies contained in Holy Scripture. Scripture abounds with prophecies about future contingent events, to happen after many centuries from the free will of God and men; some of which we shall recount. There are read in the O.T. prophecies concerning the Messiah, the redeemer of the human race, Gen. III, 15, and in very many other places: concerning the servitude of the Israelites in Egypt, and their liberation, Gen. XV, 13, 14: concerning the Babylonian captivity of the Jewish people, and the restoration of Jerusalem, Es. XXXIX, 6, seq. Ier. XVI, 13, seq.: concerning the second destruction of the city of Jerusalem, never to be repaired, Dan. IX, 26: concerning the blinding and rejection of the Jewish people, Es. VI, 9: concerning the …supreme empires of the world, and their vicissitudes, Dan. II, 38, sqq. c. VII, 4, c. VIII, 3: concerning the calling of the Gentiles to the church, Es. LX, 3, and concerning innumerable other things, which, besides God and the holy men of God to whom God revealed them, no one could foresee or predict. Concerning the fulfillments of those prophecies, both the entire Scripture of the N.T. and the very experience testifies more than enough. But is it not permissible to gather from this that Scripture, full of prophecies concerning future contingent events, which after many centuries would come to pass from the free will of God and men, confirmed by the event itself, was composed with God as its author, dictating to the sacred amanuenses?…

Prob. e. By the calculation of all men who think rightly, Holy Scripture is held to be holy, whose precepts are conformed exactly to the eternal law of God. For every rule of holiness is the eternal and immutable law of God, consisting of two tables. The former directs man to the true knowledge and sincere worship of God. The latter directs man to lead a life toward himself and his neighbor that is sober and just. On both sides, prophetic and apostolic Scripture is holy; because it prescribes to man the most exact conformity of internal and external movements of the soul with the law of God, such as no book of Scripture, in which the religion of any nation is delineated and contained, prescribes. On the part of the first table, it directs man to a worship of God that is perfect in every way, according to that: You shall love Iehouah your God with all your heart, and with all your soul; and with all your strength. Deut. VI, 5. On the part of the second table, it prescribes and demands charity toward one's neighbor that is most pure and without blemish, according to that: You shall love your neighbor as yourself, Levit. XIX, 18. where under the name of neighbor even an enemy is included, Matth. V, 44. Conversely, it prohibits all inordinate movements of concupiscence, even those that are indeliberate, which confuse or overturn the judgment of reason and the will. Exod. XX, 14. Rom. VII, 7. For which reason Holy Scripture requires greater holiness in man than human reason, by the power of the law implanted in it, demands for this state of corrupted nature. For the latter subsists in whatever external acts there may be, and also in the deliberate acts of virtues pertaining to the first and second tables of the law, but it does not exclude or prohibit the indeliberate movements of concupiscence, distrust, and hatred. But that Scripture which teaches a more perfect and holy religion than human reason, by the power of the law implanted in it, for this state of corrupted nature, does not have men, but God, as its author.

Prob. f. That doctrine fully and clearly demonstrates the way of salvation, which accurately hands down how a sinner is to be reconciled to God who has been offended. But there is no doctrine given under heaven that hands down the manner of the reconciliation of the sinner with God, who has been offended by sins, as certainly and clearly as that which is contained in the sacred letters. This asserts that we have been reconciled to God through the death of Christ, when we were enemies, and being justified by his blood, are saved from wrath. Rom. V, 9. From which it follows that the doctrine contained in the sacred letters is to be attributed not to human reason, but to divine revelation.

We shall combine the internal κρɩτήρɩα (criteria) clearly notifying the divine inspiration of the sacred letters into one syllogism: Whatever Scripture is conspicuous by the majesty of God, speaking of himself therein, adorned with a style that is simple, grave, and thus worthy of the supreme arbiter of things, full of mysteries far exceeding the grasp of reason, fortified by the perpetual harmony of amanuenses separated by very long times and places, which is most true in its dogmas of faith and prophecies, most holy in its precepts of morals, and sufficient for demonstrating the way of salvation, it is certain that it proceeded immediately from God.

But prophetic and apostolic Scripture [is such], etc. Therefore. The major is certain, because so many indications of divinity never fall upon writings devised by men.

We have demonstrated the minor above. The antithesis is that of the Papists, having brought forward criteria firmly proving the divine origin of Scripture; whose arguments we shall weigh on the balance of truth.

I. Whatever κρɩτήρɩα (criteria) produce human opinion and faith, those do not firmly prove the divine origin of H. Scripture. But the κρɩτήρɩα brought forward by the Lutherans [produce human opinion and faith], etc.

Therefore. The major [is that criteria] etc. Therefore. The major consists in this, because opinion and human faith is an infirm knowledge, a weak assent, joined with the fear of the opposite.

Some Lutherans concede the minor, namely D.

Musaeus in introd. in theol. p. 305, and D. Quenstedt in system. theol. part. I. c. IV. fol. 98. I respond:

Latin:

6) Scribit auctor, quædam in scripturis dici fine ratione, vt Ex.

XX, 18. vbi populus dicitur vidisse sonitum tubarum, quem tamen audierunt, & Iob.

XXII, 6. vbi Iobus dicitur nudis exuisse vestes.

Resp. Verbum hebræum רָאָה non semper ad visum refertur, sed fæpe in genere notat cognitionem sensualem, qua aliquid sensu percipitur.

Obseruauit c. l. BVXTORF. in lexico hebr. p.m. 785. quod verbum רָאָה, vidit, fit etiam animi & aliorum sensuum, atque significet experiri, animaduertere, percipere, frui.

Verba apud Iobum intelligenda sunt in sensu diuiso: Tu illis, qui antea vestibus erant induti, & iam nudi incedunt, vestimenta exuisti.

Prob. c. Sacra scriptura passim locorum tradit dogmata, humanæ rationi, sibi relictæ, imperuia & abscondita, quæ mysteria vocantur. Qualia sunt dogmata de trinitate personarum diuinarum in vna essentia diuina, de duabus naturis & vnitate personæ Christi, de redemtione generis humani per passionem & mortem Christi, de iustificatione peccatoris per fidem in Christum, de resurrectione mortuorum, de beatitudine ex parte animæ in visione & fruitione Dei beatifica, ex parte corporis vero in illius clarificatione consistente &c. Quæ omnia cum humanæ rationis captum sublimitate sua longissime excedant, non potuerunt ab hominibus excogitari, sed ex supernaturali Dei reuelatione innotuerunt. Id quod aperte fatetur S. Paullus, quando 1 Cor. II, 7. sqq. de mysteriis diuinis agens, inquit v. 10. Nobis vero Deus reuelauit per Spiritum suum. Quæcunque scriptura autem continet ea sublimia mysteria, quæ non nisi reuelante Deo hominibus innotescore, & ab iis in litteras referri potuerunt, illa inspirante Deo consignata est. Non est, quod doctrinæ christianæ hostes, qui articulos fidei rationis decempeda dimetiri conantur, obuertant, cum recta ratione eadem dogmata aut mysteria pugnare: infra enim suo loco, Deo auspice & præside, demonstraturi sumus, eadem mysteria lumine rationis esse quidem superiora, sed eidem non repugnare, neque contradictionem inuoluere.

Prob. d. Veritas assertionum biblicarum ostendi potest: I. Per inductionem omnium articulorum fidei in sacris litteris reuelatorum, & homini æternam salutem adepturo propositorum; quorum quidam mixti, quidam puri sunt. Articulos fidei mixtos sacra scriptura tradit, si rem propositam spectes, principiis rationis conuenienter; sin modum respicias proponendi, multo simplicius, certius & perfectius, quam eadem dogmata ratio humana e suis principiis inuestigata inculcat. Vide supra prolegom. II. p. 50. Articulos fidei puros, vt ratio humana e suis principiis cognoscere nequit; ita ex ipsis falsitatis conuincere non potest. II. Ex mira harmonia veteris cum nouo testamento, Mosis & prophetarum cum Christo & apostolis. Conspirant omnia in corpore biblico: concinunt cuncta longe suauius, quam in quocunque organo musico soni diuersi. Quem admirandum sacrarum litterarum couceptum respiciens Zacharias dicit, Deum locutum esse per os, non ora, prophetarum. Luc. I, 79. Paullus scripturam V. T. sub ratione vnius, non plurium librorum, exhibuit. Hebr. V, 7. Quæ prætenditur contradictio, apparens est, non vera. At vero scriptores tam multos, ingenio moribusque dissimillimos, locorum & temporum interuallis longissime seiunctos, occasione conferendi sensa animi destitutos, in materia tam graui & sublimi, religionem & salutem omnium hominum concernente, in vnam sententiam tam egregie conspirasse, id luculento argumento est, sacram scripturam immediate a Deo auctore vno, eoque veracissimo, dependere. III. Ex complemento vaticiniorum in sacra scriptura contentorum. Abundat scriptura vaticiniis de futuris contingentibus, post multa secula ex libera Dei hominumque voluntate euenturis; quorum nonnulla recensebimus. Leguntur in V. T. vaticinia de Messia redemtore generis humani, Gen. III, 15. & aliis locis longe plurimis: de Israëlitarum seruitute in Aegypto, eorumque liberatione, Gen. XV, 13. 14. de populi Iudaici captiuitate Babylonica, & Solymorum restauratione, Es. XXXIX, 6. sequ. Ier. XVI, 13. seq. de altero excidio vrbis Hierosolymæ nunquam reparandæ, Dan. IX, 26. de excæcatione & reiectione populi Iudaici, Es. VI, 9. de summis mundi imperiis, eorumque vicissitudinibus, Dan. II, 38. sqq. c. VII, 4. c. VIII, 3. de vocatione gentium ad ecclesiam, Es. LX, 3. & de rebus aliis innumeris, quas præter Deum & sanctos Dei viros, quibus eas Deus reuelauit, nemo præscire aut prædicere potuit. De complementis istorum vaticiniorum tam scriptura N. T. vniuersa, quam ipsa experientia satis superque testatur. At nonne hinc colligere licet, scripturam plenam vaticiniis de futuris contingentibus, post multa secula ex libera Dei hominumque voluntate euenturis, ipso euentu comprobatis, auctore Deo, eam amanuensibus sacris dictante, esse concinnatam?

Prob. e. Omnium hominum recte sentientium calculo sancta habetur scriptura, cuius præcepta æternæ Dei legi ad amussim sunt conformia. Etenim omnis sanctitatis regula infallibilis est lex Dei æterna & immutabilis, duabus constans tabulis. Prior ordinat hominem ad veram agnitionem & sincerum cultum Dei. Posterior dirigit hominem ad vitam erga se, & proximum, sobrie iusteque traducendam. Ex vtraque parte scriptura prophetica & apostolica sancta est; quia præscribit homini exactissimam motuum animi internorum & externorum conformitatem cum lege Dei, qualem nullus scripturæ codex, quo alicuius gentis religio delineata contineatur, præscribit. Ex parte tabulæ primæ dirigit hominem ad cultum Dei, vndiquaque perfectum, iuxta illud: Diliges Iehouam Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, & ex tota anima tua; & ex omnibus viribus tuis. Deut. VI, 5. Ex parte tabulæ secundæ præscribit & exigit caritatem in proximum sine næuo purissimam, iuxta illud: Diliges proximum tuum, sicut teipsum, Leuit. XIX, 18. vbi sub nomine proximi etiam inimicus comprehenditur, Matth. V, 44. Contra prohibet omnes inordinatos concupiscentiæ motus, etiam indeliberatos, qui rationis iudicium ac voluntatem confusiorem aut euertunt. Exod. XX, 14. Rom. VII, 7. Quam ob rem maiorem requirit S. scriptura sanctitatem in homine, quam pro hoc naturæ corruptæ statu ratio humana vi legis insitæ ab eodem exigit. Hæc enim subsistit in qualibuscunque actibus externis, nec non internis virtutum ad primam & secundam legis tabulam pertinentium actibus deliberatis, indeliberatos vero concupiscentiæ, diffidentiæ, odii, motus non excludit, aut prohibet. At illa scriptura, quæ perfectiorem & sanctiorem docet religionem, quam ratio humana vi legis sibi insitæ, pro hoc naturæ corruptæ statu, ea non homines, sed Deum habet auctorem.

Prob. f. Illa doctrina plene & liquido commonstrat viam salutis, quæ accurate tradit, quomodo peccator Deo offenso reconciliandus sit. At nulla sub cœlo datur doctrina, quæ modum reconciliationis peccatoris cum Deo, peccatis offenso, tam certo & liquido tradat, quam quæ sacris litteris comprehensa est. Hæc asserit, nos reconciliatos esse Deo per mortem Christi, cum inimici essemus, & sanguine illius iustificatos seruari ab ira. Rom. V, 9. Ex quo consequitur, doctrinam sacris litteris comprehensam non rationi humanæ, sed reuelationi diuinæ acceptam referendam esse.

Kρɩτήρɩα interna inspirationem diuinam-sacrarum litterarum liquido notificantia in vnum compingemus syllogismum: Quæcunque scriptura maiestate Dei, de seipso in illa loquentis, est conspicua, stilo simplici, graui, adeoque summo rerum arbitro digno, adornata, mysteriis captum rationis longissime excedentibus plena, perpetua amanuensium multis temporibus & locis longissime seiunctorum harmonia munita, qua dogmata fidei & vaticinia verissima, qua præcepta morum sanctissima, & ad commonstrandam salutis viam sufficiens, illam a Deo immediate profectam esse, certum est.

Atqui scriptura prophetica, & apostolica &c. Ergo. Maior est certa, quia in scripta, ab hominibus excogitata, tot diuinitatis indicia nunquam cadunt.

Minorem supra demonstrauimus. Antithesis est pontificiorum, adductis criteriis diuinam scripturæ originem firmiter probantium; quorum argumenta ad veritatis lancem expendemus.

I. Quæcunque κρɩτήρɩα opinionem & fidem humanam pariunt, illa non firmiter probant originem diuinam S. scripturæ. Atqui adducta a Lutheranis κρɩτήρɩα &c. Ergo.

Maior κριτήρια &c. Ergo. Maior constat, quia opinio & fides humana est notitia infirma, assensus debilis, cum formidine oppositi coniunctus.

Minorem concedunt nonnulli Lutherani, nominatim D.

Mvsaevs in introd. in theol. p. 305. D. Qvensted. in system. theol. part. I. c. IV. fol. 98. Resp.


### Question XXX. What are the internal criteria by which the divine origin of sacred literature becomes known?: Distinguish between external and internal κριτήρια (criteria). External κριτήρια concerning the θεοπνευσία…

Distinguish between external and internal κριτήρια (criteria). External κριτήρια concerning the θεοπνευσία (divine inspiration) of Holy Scripture.

Lutheran doctors teach by a certain consensus that external κριτήρια concerning the θεοπνευσία of Holy Scripture beget only opinion or human faith. However, whether internal κριτήρια beget human or divine faith, the same men depart into different opinions.

For D.

J. A. Osiander in colleg. theol. system. P. p. 106, sharply contends that internal κριτήρια produce divine faith. The most celebrated theologian argues: That which is the same with the divine word generates the same faith as the divine word.

But the contained abstruse dogmas, divine prophecies, and most holy precepts are identified with the divine word. Therefore. And how should an abstruse dogma with some supreme mystery of religion not beget a faith greater than human? How should prophecies and oracles not generate divine faith? How should most holy precepts not demand a most holy mind? Κριτήρια are employed either to confirm the languid faith of a tempted brother, or to convert an infidel man.

Theologians do not deny that internal κριτήρια can be applied to a tempted Christian to consolidate an infirm faith.

The most learned Musaeus writes not badly in introduct. theol. p.

456: Certain signs and motives are so constituted that, where they are properly weighed by a mind willing to learn, through attentive consideration and meditation of themselves they can move the intellect of man into a supernatural assent: of which kind are, for example, the truth of the Scripture of Christian doctrine pure from all error: its harmony and exact agreement in all its parts: the truth of prophecies proved by the event itself, etc. which, as they do not really differ from Holy Scripture itself and the doctrine contained in it (for the truth of Scripture does not really differ from true Scripture; and the agreement of Christian doctrine or Holy Scripture in all its parts, as to the thing itself, is nothing other than the parts of Scripture or doctrine agreeing among themselves): so while they are constituted in act through the reading or meditation of Scripture itself, or through the hearing and explanation of the doctrine contained in it, and are applied to the human intellect to manifest the divine origin of Holy Scripture, they can simultaneously exert themselves, and do exert themselves by their own divine virtue, in which they are powerful, to kindle an assent to themselves and a supernatural, divine faith; unless perhaps an obstacle is placed inwardly by man against the grace of the Holy Spirit; and its operation is checked. But in order to convert infidels, signs and motives of credibility do not behave otherwise than as motives generating human faith, or an opinion concerning the divine origin of the sacred doctrine of Scripture.

Which, viewed individually, although perhaps one may possess greater power than another to move the minds of men, yet taken together, since they conspire from every side toward the divine origin of Holy Scripture and the Christian religion, and cry out as if with one mouth that it was not invented by men, but revealed to the human race by God himself, they generate a certain knowledge, superior to every other, whether human faith or opinion.

But there is no need for these circumlocutions if, with D.

Osiander, we simply maintain that the internal κριτήρια of Holy Scripture procure a certain assent and divine faith; although there are degrees of certainty, since one is absolute and supreme, another intermediate, another lowest. See

Leichner, synops. verae apodict. page 415. The internal testimony of the Holy Spirit procures the supreme certainty of assent to Holy Scripture.

Latin:

Dist. inter κριτήρια externa, & interna. Κριτήρια externa de θεοπνευσίᾳ S.

Scripturae gignere tantum opinionem aut fidem humanam, consensu quodam docent Lutherani doctores. Vtrum autem κριτήρια interna humanam, an diuinam generent fidem, iidem in diuersum abeunt.

Etenim D.

10. AD. Osiander in colleg. theol. system. P. p. 106. acriter contendit, κριτήρια interna parere fidem diuinam. Argumentatur theologus celeberrimus: Quod est idem cum verbo diuino, illud eandem fidem generat, quam verbum diuinum.

Atqui contenta dogmata abstrusa, vaticinia diuina, praecepta sanctissima identificantur verbo diuino. Ergo. Et quomodo dogma abstrusum cum aliquo summo mysterio religionis non gignat fidem maiorem, quam humanam? Quomodo vaticinia & oracula non generent fidem diuinam? Quomodo praecepta sanctissima non depofcant mentem sanctissimam? Κριτήρια adhibentur vel ad confirmandam fidem languidam fratris tentati, vel ad conuertendum hominem infidelem.

Non diffitentur theologi, quin christiano tentato κριτήρια interna applicari possint ad consolidandam fidem infirmam.

Haud male scribit doctissimus Mvsaevs in introduct. theol. p.

456. Quaedam signa & motiua ita comparata sunt, vt, vbi animo discendi probe expendantur, per attentam sui considerationem ac meditationem intellectum hominis in assensum supernaturalem permouere possint: cuiusmodi sunt v. gr. veritas scripturae doctrinae christianae ab omni errore pura: eius harmonia & exacta consensio in omnibus suis partibus: veritas vaticiniorum ipso euentu comprobata &c. quae vt ab ipsa scriptura S. & contenta in illa doctrina realiter non differunt: (nam veritas scripturae a scriptura vera realiter non differt; & consensio doctrinae christianae aut scripturae S. in omnibus suis partibus, quoad rem nihil aliud est, quam partes scripturae aut doctrinae inter se consentientes): ita dum per lectionem aut meditationem scripturae ipsius, vel per praedicationem & explicationem doctrinae in ea comprehensae auditu perceptam in actu constituuntur, hominisque intellectui ad diuinam scripturae S. originem manifestandam applicantur, simul sese exserere possunt, exseruntque sese sua diuina, quae pollent, virtute ad fui assensum supernaturalem fidemque diuinam accendendam; nisi ab homine forsan gratiae Spiritus S. interius ponatur obex; eiusque operatio sufflaminetur. In ordine vero ad conuertendos infideles signa & motiua credibilitatis se aliter non habent, quam vt motiua fidem humanam, aut opinionem de diuina scripturae doctrinae sacrae origine generantia.

Quae singulatim spectata, licet forsan vnum altero maiori polleat vi hominum animos commouendi, iunctim tamen sumta, cum vndique in diuinam scripturae S. religionisque christianae originem conspirent, eamque non ab hominibus inuentam, sed ab ipsomet Deo mortalium generi patefactam esse, vno quasi ore clament, generant cognitionem certam, omnique alia, siue humana fide, siue opinione superiorem.

At his ambagibus non opus est, si cum D.

Osiandro simpliciter statuamus, κριτήρια interna S. scripturae conciliare assensum certum & fidem diuinam; quamuis dentur gradus certitudinis, siquidem alia est absoluta & summa, alia media, alia ima. Vid.

Leichn. synops. verae apodict. pag. 415. Summam assensus certitudinem S. scripturae conciliat internum Spiritus S. testimonium.


### Question XXX. What are the internal criteria by which the divine origin of sacred literature becomes known?: II. Κριτήρια are either the same as Holy Scripture, or different from it

II. Κριτήρια are either the same as Holy Scripture, or different from it.

If the same, they cannot prove its θεοπνευσία, otherwise the same would be proved by the same: If different, they will not beget divine faith; since the unique principle of conceiving faith is Holy Scripture.

Therefore κριτήρια are not suitable for proving the divine origin of Scripture.

I respond: Κριτήρια are the same as Holy Scripture really, or on the part of the thing, but they differ from it formally, or on the part of the concept.

They will beget divine faith, because they coincide really with Holy Scripture: they prove the divine scrip-coincide: they prove the divine the divine origin of Scripture, who differ from it formally: just as the divine attributes are the same as the divinity on the part of the thing, they differ on the part of the concept, and hence they signify the divinity of the Word.

III. To believe on account of an argument is at least human faith, not divine: acquired, not infused.

E.

E. Criteria do not beget divine faith.

Resp. To believe on account of a topical argument, derived from the testimony of a man, is human faith; I concede.

To believe on account of an argument, derived from internal criteria, is to believe on account of a topical argument; I deny.

For that is apodictic, begetting not human faith, which is uncertain and slippery, but a solid and certain assent.

Certainly the apostles everywhere propose arguments for this or that conclusion, which a Christian embraces by divine faith.

See 1 IV.

If the individual internal criteria are weighed accurately, they do not seem to be so valid as to move a man to provide a solid assent to the sacred letters.

For I.

For I. The external divine attestation, brought forward by a prophet or apostle in these and similar words: The Word of the Lord came to me: I received from the Lord: consists in phrases and formulas of speaking, which can provide nothing but a probable argument and generate an opinion or human faith.

II. The style of H.

II. The style of H. Scripture is not uniform, but now more humble, now more sublime.

Therefore a certain indication of the divinity of Scripture cannot be taken from it.

III. Mysteries exceeding the grasp of reason are neither read everywhere in all biblical books; since historical and moral matters, knowable from ocular inspection and the leading of the light of nature, are inserted throughout; nor are they detected only in biblical books, but also in Josephus, Philo, and the Augsburg Confession.

What is more? That the same thing often retards the conversion of pagans, the more they recede from reason.

IV. The truth of dogmas and prophecies does not certainly argue for the divine origin of Scripture: for pagan and Christian writers also teach true things.

Prophecies and oracles are read throughout in the writings of the nations, e.g.

Latin:

II. Κριτήρια aut sunt eadem cum S. scriptura, aut ab ea diuersa.

Si eadem, non possunt eiusdem θεοπνευσίαν probare, ceteroqui idem per idem probaretur: Sin diuersa, non gignent fidem diuinam; cum vnicum concipiendae fidei principium sit S. scriptura.

Ergo κριτήρια non sunt idoneae ad probandam diuinam scripturae originem.

Resp. Κριτήρια cum S. scriptura sunt eadem realiter, siue ex parte rei, differunt ab ea formaliter, siue ex parte conceptus.

Fidem diuinam gignent, quia realiter cum S. scriptura coincidunt: probant diuinam scriptura coincidunt: probant diuinam vinam scripturae originem, qui ab ea formaliter differunt: sicut attributa divina ex parte rei cum divinitate sunt eadem, differunt ex parte conceptus, & hinc divinitatem τοῦ λόγου notificant.

III. Credere propter argumentum, est fides saltem humana, non divina: acquisita, non infusa.

E.

E. Criteria non gignunt fidem divinam.

Resp. Credere propter argumentum topicum, a testimonio hominis petitum, est fides humana; concedo.

Credere propter argumentum, a criteriis internis petitum, est credere propter argumentum topicum; nego.

Est enim illud apodicticum, non fidem humanam, quae incerta & lubrica est, sed solidum certumque assensum gignens.

Certe apostoli passim argumenta proponunt huius vel illius conclusionis, quam fide divina amplectitur christianus.

Vide 1 IV.

Si accurate ponderentur singula κριτήρια interna, non videntur esse adeo valida, ut hominem ad assensum solidum sacris litteris praebendum permoueant.

Nam I.

Nam I. Attestatio divina externa, adducta a propheta aut apostolo his, similibusque verbis: Verbum Dei factum est ad me: A domino accepi: consistit in phrasibus & formulis loquendi, quae non nisi argumentum probabile praebere, & opinionem, vel fidem humanam generare possunt.

II. Stilus S.

II. Stilus S. Scripturae non est uniformis, sed modo humilior, modo sublimior.

Ergo ab illo certum divinitatis scripturae indicium sumi nequit.

III. Mysteria captum rationis excedentia neque leguntur vbiuis in omnibus libris biblicis; cum inferta sint passim historica & moralia ex oculari inspectione & ductu luminis naturae cognoscibilia; neque in solis deprehenduntur libris biblicis, sed etiam Iosepho, Philone, Augustana confessione.

Quid? quod eadem conversionem paganorum retardat hoc saepius, quo magis a ratione recedunt.

IV. Veritas dogmatum & vaticiniorum non certo arguit divinam scripturae originem: nam vera docent etiam scriptores gentiles & christiani.

Vaticinia & oracula leguntur passim in scriptis gentium, v. gr.


### Question XXX. What are the internal criteria by which the divine origin of sacred literature becomes known?: Of the Sibyls

Of the Sibyls.

Furthermore, it is not unusual for a certain author to be consistent with himself everywhere and to observe a harmony of dogmas.

V. Plato, Cicero, and Seneca also gave holy precepts.

VI. Naturalists, whose writings are not God-breathed, also show the way to eternal salvation.

Therefore the adduced criteria do not procure an immovable assent to Holy Scripture, since they do not demonstrate its divine origin.

Resp. to I. The external attestation of God speaking about Himself in Scripture consists indeed of phrases, but dictated by the Holy Spirit, under which the weight of things lies; and it is joined with the truth of dogmas and prophecies.

Therefore it does not produce human faith, but divine.

By the confession of all , the effect or consequence of divine testimony is divine faith.

To II.

To II. The biblical style is uniform, as to substance, in both bodies of the Testament, so that it may be held as one mouth of all God-breathed men, Luke

I, 70. although as to the accidental conformation of the style, it is both tempered to the nature of the various materials about which it was necessary to write, and accommodated by the most free condescension of the Holy Spirit to the talents, studies, and familiar manner of speaking of the amanuenses.

Conf. D A N N H A V. hodof. phaenom.

I. p.

I. p. 58. Care is taken, however, that nothing should be lacking to the divine majesty.

Worthy indeed is the simple and grave Son everywhere by the majesty of God in Scripture.

For neither is it of man, but of God alone, to oblige all men without exception to have faith in Himself, while bringing no demonstration, or to render obedience to Himself, while commanding or forbidding without persuasive reasons.

To III.
