To III. Although not in all, yet in most biblical books, mysteries superior to the grasp of reason are read, which are sometimes also linked to historical matters.

Mysteries are held in the sacred code originally, in others derivatively derived from writings. Josephus and Philo, Jews, derived from the source of the scriptures, but with a turbulent guidance: Philo, in particular, often deviated from the truth of mysteries to the tenets of Platonic philosophy.

The more sublime the mysteries, the more they are admired by pagans. From this it follows that by marveling, they are induced to read the scripture, and by the illuminating Holy Spirit, to understand it, by which progress of time they are converted.

To IV. The writings of gentile authors abound in errors; those of Christians are true only insofar as they conform to the norm of truth of the sacred scriptures.

Prophecies concerning future contingent events, depending on the free will of God and men, when proven by their fulfillment, outside of the revealed word of God and committed to writing, are of no consequence. Contingent events, depending on the free will of God and men, will find no fulfillment; only God knows them, Ef. XLVI, 9. and XXVIII, 9.

The prophecies read in the writings of the gentiles were either doubtful, conceived in words mostly obscure, ambiguous, and adapted to various meanings, or foreseen by mere conjectures and causes.

Furthermore, it happens that one author is consistent with himself in writing; but that so many authors, so different in genius, places, times, wrote with such consensus about matters of faith, about mysteries superior to the grasp of reason, so that one never contradicted the other, is to be attributed to the one and only Holy Spirit, who suggested the words and concepts of things.

To V. So far is it from the truth that Plato, Cicero, Seneca, and other pagan authors gave holy precepts concerning the true worship of God, that, when they knew God, they did not glorify Him as God, or give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened; and while they claimed to be wise, they became fools.

Rom. I, 21. 22. For God desires to be worshipped not according to the arbitrary will of men, but according to the prescription of His will, which He has revealed in His word.

To this is added that, since ethnic writers were ignorant of original sin, they did not prohibit the evil, indeliberate movements of the soul, which precede the judgment of the intellect and the consent of the will, and thus did not teach perfect holiness.

To VI. Naturalists, from the principles of reason, do not attain the means of reconciling the sinner with God, who has been offended by sins.

From an offended God, not reconciled, no salvation is to be expected. The only reconciler, the only way to heaven, is Christus.

Naturalists, deviating from this path of salvation, open the way to hell, and enter it when opened. Therefore, it remains fixed and unmovable that κειρήγεια, mentioned above, are proper to the sacred scripture alone, and strongly prove its immediate dependence on God.

Latin:

Sibyllarum.

Praeterea non est insolens, auctorem quendam sibi ubique constare, & harmoniam dogmatum observare.

V. Praecepta sancta dederunt etiam Plato, Cicero, Seneca.

VI. Viam ad perennem salutem commonstrant quoque Naturalistae, quorum scripta non sunt θεόπνευσα.

Ergo adducta κριτήρια non conciliant sacrae scripturae immotum assensum, cum eius divinam originem non demonstrent.

Resp. ad I. Attestatio externa Dei de seipso in scriptura loquentis constat quidem phrasibus, sed dictatis a Spiritu sancto, quibus rerum pondera subsunt; & coniuncta est cum veritate dogmatum atque vaticiniorum.

Proinde non parit fidem humanam, sed divinam.

Omni um confessione testimonii divini effectus aut consequens est fides divina.

Ad II.

Ad II. Stilus biblicus uniformis est, quoad substantiam, in vtroque testamenti corpore, vt vnum os omnium virorum θεπνεύσων habeatur, Luc.

I, 70. quanquam quoad accidentalem stili conformationem, tum attemperatus sit variarum materiarum, de quibus scribendum erat, indoli, tum liberrima Spiritus sancti συγκαταβάσει accommodatus amanuensium ingeniis, studiis, familiari dicendi generi.

Conf. D A N N H A V. hodof. phaenom.

I. p.

I. p. 58. Cautum tamen est, ne maiestati divinae quidquam decederet.

Dignus quippe ubique est filius simplex & grauis scripturae maiestate Dei.

Neque enim hominis, sed solius Dei est obligare homines sine exceptione omnes ad fidem sibi, fine demonstratione afferenti, habendam, vel ad obsequium sibi, absque rationibus persuasoriis praecipienti, aut prohibenti, praestandum.

Ad III.

Ad III. Quamuis non in omnibus, in plerisque tamen libris biblicis leguntur mysteria captu rationis superiora, quae interdum etiam historicis innexa sunt.

Habentur mysteria in sacro codice originaliter, in aliis feriscriptis derivativæ. Derivaruæ ex fonte bibliorum Iofephus & Philo, Iudæi, at ductu turbido: in primis Philo a veritate mysteriorum ad placita philofophiæ Platonicæ aliquotiès deflexit.

Quo sublimiora sunt mysteria, eo magis a paganis in admirationem rapiuntur. Ex quo fit, vt mirando inducantur ad scripturam legendam, & illuminante Spiritu S. intelligendam, quo progressu temporis conuertantur.

Ad IV. Scripta auctorum gentilium scatent erroribus; christianorum in tantum sunt vera, in quantum sacræ scripturæ veritatis normæ conformia sunt.

Vaticinia de rebus futuris contingentibus, ex libera Dei hominumque voluntate pendentibus, cum complemento comprobata, extra verbum Dei reuelatum & litteris mandatum nullius contingentia, ex libera Dei hominumque voluntate pendentia, nullum complementum suum nactura, solus nouit Deus, Ef. XLVI, 9. & XXVIII, 9.

Quæ vaticinia in scriptis gentilium leguntur, vel fuerunt dubia, verbis plerumque obscuris, ambiguis, & ad diuerfos sensus reddendos conformatis, concepta, vel per meras coniecturas & caussas prospecta.

Præterea vfu venit, vt vnius auctor in scribendo sibi constet; at quod auctores tam multi, tam differentes ingenijs, locis, temporibus, de rebus fidei, de mysteriis captu rationis fuperioribus, tanto confenfu scripserint, vt alter alteri nunquam contradixerit, id vni & soli Spiritui sancto, verba & rerum conceptus suggerenti, tribuendum est.

Ad V. tantum abest, vt Plato, Cicero, Seneca & alii auctores ethnici, sancta de derint præcepta de vero cultu Dei, vt, cum cognoscerent Deum, non vt Deum glorificauerint, aut gratias egerint, sed vani facti sint in cogitationibus suis, & obscuratum fit infipiens eor eorum; atque dum dixerunt fe sapientes esse, stulti facti sint.

Rom, I, 21. 22. Etenim coli vult Deus non pro arbitratu hominum, sed ex præscripto voluntatis suæ, quam in verbo suo patefecit.

Huc accedit, quod, cum scriptores ethnici peccatum originis ignorauerint, prauos motus animi indeliberatos, qui iudicium intellectûs & confenfum voluntatis anteuertunt, non prohibuerint, atque adeo perfectam sanctitatem non docuerint.

Ad VI. Naturalifæ ex principiis rationis non assequuntur rationem reconciliandi peccatoris cum Deo, peccatis offenso.

A Deo offenso, nec reconciliato, nulla falus exspectanda est. Vnicus reconciliator, vnica ad cælum via Christus est.

Deflectentes ab hac via salutis Naturalistæ viam ad orcum aperiunt, apertam ingrediuntur. Quare fixum & immotum manet, κειρήγεια, supra memorata, soli sacræ scripturæ esse propria, eiusque immediatam a Deo dependentiam valide probare.


### Question XXXI. What is the principal and ultimate reason for knowing and believing with divine faith the divine origin of sacred scripture?

The internal testimony of the Holy Spirit, certifying and sealing the human heart concerning the Θεοπνευσία of the sacred letters, is the principal and ultimate reason for knowing and believing with divine faith the divine origin of S. scripture.

Latin:

Testimonium internum Spiritus sancti, cor humanum de Θεοπνευσία sacrarum litterarum certificans & obsignans, est præcipua & vltima ratio cognoscendi diuinaque fide credendi diuinam S. scripturæ originem.


### Question XXXII. What is understood here by the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit?

that this written word, and that which we read, hear, and believe from the scriptures, is true and divine, is the sole authority of God both externally revealing, and internally sealing in our hearts and convincing the conscience: not the veracity, or presumption of the veracity of the ministerial cause, of the present church, or of the present teacher, proposing that to us here and now: nor conformity with human intellect or sense: nor the notorious consensus of the church. Obf.

II. The internal testimony of the Holy Spirit concerning the authenticity of Holy Scripture coincides, as to the thing itself, with the efficacy of Holy Scripture viewed in its second act; insofar as Holy Scripture, attentively read and deeply pondered, illuminates the human intellect so that it clearly recognizes the θεοπνευστίαν (divine inspiration) of the scriptures, and draws and allures its will into consent: The Holy Spirit works the same through the word of God properly used. For the effective power, which we attribute to the word of God in producing the effect of illumination, conversion, renovation, and confirmation, is truly divine, Rom. 1:16. Nor does it differ, as to the thing itself, from that which is of the Holy Spirit working in the hearts of men, although there is a disparity in the mode of possessing this power, inasmuch as it belongs to the Holy Spirit of himself, and from himself, as the principal cause: but to the word participatively, as an organic cause. For which reason Holy Scripture, when read, or proposed by the voice of a teacher, explained, and perceived by hearing, with the efficacy divinely communicated to it, moves the intellect of man to a supernatural assent of its dependence upon God revealing, by itself indeed immediately, without any other revelation, or any motive of credibility, but with the supernatural concurrence of the Holy Spirit. From which it is concluded that the unmoved and fiduciary assent, by which the divine origin of the scriptures is believed, depends both upon the scripture itself, and upon the Holy Spirit himself, concurring with it as a formal motive, and thus upon both simultaneously and conjointly, but from neither separately and apart. Obf.

III. The whole sacrosanct Trinity testifies most powerfully concerning the authenticity of Holy Scripture; terminatively the Holy Spirit. Hence it happens that faith, by which the divine inspiration of the scriptures is believed, is sometimes attributed in the sacred letters to the power of God, and by theologians to the supernatural concurrence of God. Prob. I. from 1 John 5:6.

Prob. I. from 1 John 5:6. The Spirit testifies, that the Spirit is truth. By the word 'Spirit' placed in the subject we understand the Holy Spirit, the third person of the Trinity; both because this word, placed absolutely, without a restricting condition, as an analogous term, is deservedly accepted in its more famous meaning; and because it is presented at once in the following verse 7 under the notion of a person, and indeed the third in the Trinity, with the added epithet, when it is said τὸ πνεῦμα ἄγιον (the Holy Spirit), to whom, no less than to the Father and the Son, the heavenly testimony is ascribed in the same place: but by 'Spirit' in the predicate we understand the word of God, or scripture, the word 'Spirit' being taken metonymically; because otherwise the word of God is also called Spirit and life, John 6:63. The particle ὅτι (that) is not causal, but determinative, so that the sense is: The Holy Spirit testifies that the doctrine of the Spirit is truth, i. e., most true, when he works inwardly through the doctrine revealed by himself in the hearts of men, knocks at them, draws and moves them, so that they believe it to have proceeded from God, or to be truly divine. Hence v. 10 John adds: He who believes in the Son has the testimony in himself: he who does not believe God, has made him a liar: because he has not believed the testimony which God has testified concerning his Son. He is said to have the testimony of God in himself who believes; because the faith, by which one believes in the Son of God, is an effect of the Holy Spirit, who works through the doctrine revealed by himself in the heart of the believer, and produces the assent of faith. From whom therefore man has it, that he believe with divine faith that the doctrine revealed by the Holy Spirit is truth, i. e., most true, that is the principal and ultimate reason for knowing, with divine power of believing, the authority of Holy Scripture. But from the testimony of the Holy Spirit, whereby he testifies in the hearts of men that the doctrine of the Spirit is most true, man, man has, that he believes by divine faith, that the doctrine revealed by God is truth, i.e., most true. Therefore, the testimony of the Holy Spirit, by which He testifies in the hearts of men that the doctrine revealed by Himself is truth, i.e., most true, is the principal and ultimate reason for knowing and believing by divine faith the authority of Holy Scripture.

II. From 1 Thess. 1:5. 6. Our gospel was not among you in word only, but also with power and in the Holy Spirit and with much assurance, as you know what kind of men we were among you for your sake. And you became followers of us and of the Lord, having received the word in much affliction with joy of the Holy Spirit. That gospel which Paul had preached to the Thessalonians with singular presence of mind, amidst most grievous afflictions and dangers to life, they had received with great joy excited in their souls by the Holy Spirit, because the gospel of Paul was not a naked, empty, and fruitless speech, but a speech joined with the power of the Holy Spirit, who had illuminated them, converted them, and endowed them with faith. Wherefore the primary reason moving a man to receive the gospel of Christ as truly divine is the power of the Holy Spirit, united in an inseparable bond with the word of God read or heard.

III. We subjoin a notable statement of the same apostle from 1 Thess. 2:13. For this reason we also thank God without ceasing, because when you received the word of hearing of God from us (namely the word), you accepted it, not (as) the word of men, but, as it is in truth, (as) the word of God, which also worked in you who believe. Here Paul expressly ascribes to God working in the Thessalonians that they received the sermon of the apostles, not as the word of men, but as the word of God. But to receive the word from the mouth of the apostles as the word of God is to receive that word as having proceeded from God, or preached by God’s suggestion or inspiration. Now, one and the same is the reason for Scripture being divinely inspired, and for the doctrine preached by the apostles from divine inspiration. For although an accidental difference intervenes, in that the former consists of voices consigned to writing, while the latter consists of those uttered by mouth; yet one and the same is the force moving the intellect to assent. For which reason, just as the Thessalonians were moved by the supernatural operation of God to believe that the sermon of the apostles was not of men, but of God the author: so even now the hearts of men are moved by the supernatural operation of God to believe that Holy Scripture is truly divine, or proceeded from God. We argue: By the same motive that the Thessalonians were moved to believe that the word of the apostles was truly the word of God, by the same are men even now moved to believe that Holy Scripture proceeded from God and is truly divine. But the Thessalonians were moved to believe that the word of the apostles was the word of God by God Himself acting in them through the very word preached, and testifying of the divinity of the word. Therefore, even now, believers are moved to believe that Holy Scripture proceeded from God and is truly divine, by God Himself testifying in the hearts of men through it.

IV. As often as the divine word of the law and the gospel is attentively read or heard, a teachable man truly feels its heart-turning power, and gathers that God is speaking with him from the internal acts and supernatural motions of the heart. Those acts are, on the part of the intellect, the arising of the light of supernatural cognition and an inspired holy thought: on the part of the will, they are spiritual motions: sorrow for sins, a desire for learning and progressing, pious affection toward God who reveals, a sweet inclination to command the intellect—already illuminated by some spiritual light—to give unshaken assent to the things to be believed, and spiritual joy. These acts of the intellect and motions of the will, excited by the Holy Spirit through the word of the law and the gospel in the hearts of readers or hearers, are more clearly known from certain biblical examples. At the first sermon of the apostle Peter, which he delivered on the feast of Pentecost to the Jews who had crucified Christ, the hearers, as Luke relates in Acts II, 37, κατενύγησαν τῇ καρδίᾳ, were pricked in heart. Which pricking of heart this without doubt brought about, on the part of the intellect, the recognition of sin, and also a holy thought, inspired by means of the Word of God, concerning the death and resurrection of Christ: on the part of the will, however, that compunction of heart undoubtedly imported most bitter sorrow concerning the most atrocious sin, perpetrated against Christ, joined with a certain inclination of the will toward Christ, and a desire of obtaining eternal salvation. Therefore they said to Peter and the other apostles: "What shall we do, men and brethren?" In the eunuch of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, from the passage of Is.

LIII, 7. 8, which he was reading, having been more fully explained to him by Philip from other places of Scripture, there shone forth on the part of the intellect only the light of saving knowledge, and on the part of the will there arose such affection and readiness, that with a prone will he both professed his faith in Christ, and asked that baptism be administered to him: "See, water," he said to Philip, "what hinders me from being baptized?" But when Philip said: "If you believe with all your heart, it is allowed": he answered: "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God": and he was baptized.

Acts VIII, 36. 37. In Lydia, a seller of purple, through the word preached by Paul, both a holy thought and a pious desire (both are indicated by the opening of her heart) were inspired by God, so that, led by a desire of learning, she attended to those things which were said by Paul, and having been converted, she received baptism.

Acts XVI, 14. seq. The Thessalonians received the word of God in much affliction with joy of the Holy Spirit, 1 Thess. I, 6. Which supernatural acts of the intellect and motions of the will, by the power of the flowing dependence upon God, incline the intellect to offer assent to the divine word, more validly than the living voice of a man worthy of faith, recounting a thing difficult to believe, moves the intellect to the assent of a thing done. For just as they were excited by the Holy Spirit through the word of the law and gospel: so they argue God to be their author; just as every other effect testifies concerning its cause.

Antithesis The Antithesis is 1. Of the Papists, some of whom traduce that Spirit, by whose infallible testimony we say the divine authority of Scripture is established for us, by the name of a private Spirit, and thus they deride the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit as a human fabrication. 2. Of the Socinians, who, since they maintain that the divine origin of Holy Scripture cannot be infallibly demonstrated, silently pass over the attestation of the Holy Spirit.

3. Of the Arminians, who deny that the testimony of the Holy Spirit is necessary for it to be understood that Scripture is of divine origin. Whose arguments we shall weigh. 1. 1. Whatever opinion introduces enthusiasts into the church, that is not to be approved. But the opinion of the Lutherans, maintaining that the divine authority of the sacred writings becomes known through the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit, introduces enthusiasts into the church.

Therefore, etc. Resp. Distinguish between the attestation of the Holy Spirit concerning the divinity of the sacred writings, which is done through immediate illumination, and that which is done through mediate illumination. Enthusiasts boast of immediate illuminations of the Holy Spirit; but it is the constant opinion of the Lutherans that the Holy Spirit testifies concerning the divinity of Scripture through the mediate illumination of the mind, which for the state of the present time is done by the written Word of God.

Instance Instance: The Lutherans say that they do not receive illumination from a gathering of men, such as the church is. Therefore they receive illumination immediately from the Holy Spirit. Resp. The Lutherans exclude the personal medium of a human gathering, not the real medium of the divine word reduced to letters. 2. 2. Where this is posited, a sophistic circle is committed, that is not an efficacious argument. But, the sealing of the Holy Spirit being posited as a medium of the demonstration of the divinity of Scripture, a sophistic circle is committed.

Therefore. The major is posited beyond controversy, because a sophistic circle is a begging of the question running backward. The minor is evident from the nature of a circle. For if I ask: whence do you know that Scripture is divine? The Lutherans answer: because the Holy Spirit in each one through Scripture testifies and seals this. But if I ask: whence do you prove that that Spirit is divine? The same answer: because Scripture testifies that he is divine, and the sealing of that is infallible. Resp. 1). Lutherans do not appeal to a private spirit; rather, the Spirit who seals the authority of the divine word is the Holy Spirit, common to all the faithful. 2) Distinguish between a sophistic circle and a demonstrative regress. In a sophistic circle, the unknown is proved by the equally unknown; but in a demonstrative regress, we proceed from a confused cognition to a distinct one. Namely, the divine dignity of Scripture is proved by the supernatural effect of the Holy Spirit, effectively working, illuminating, converting, regenerating, and renewing through Scripture. But if you ask: Is that Spirit divine, or malignant? Then from the effect, which is divine and salutary, we regress to prove that the Spirit testifying inwardly concerning the divine origin of Scripture is divine, most holy, and best.

3. Whatever testimony no one has in himself unless he is converted and reborn, that does not beget a solid assent to be offered to Scripture as truly divine. But no one has the testimony of the Holy Spirit in himself unless he is converted and reborn. Therefore. The major is proved, because the testimony, begetting assent, must necessarily precede faith. But a converted and reborn man already has faith; therefore, the testimony of the Holy Spirit follows and seals his faith. The minor is evident from 1 John V, 10: He who believes in the Son has the testimony in himself. Resp. The attestation of the Holy Spirit is considered either in relation to men who are converted and reborn, or in relation to those men who are on the way to conversion and regeneration. The internal testimony of the Holy Spirit seals, confirms, and enriches the faith of converted and reborn men concerning the divinity of Scripture. But the effective attestation and operation of the Holy Spirit through the word of God read or heard knocks at, opens, and illuminates the hearts of men who are on the way to conversion, and kindles faith in them. Let Lydia, the seller of purple, be an example to us, Acts XVI, 14, who, when she began to listen to the word of Paul, was not yet converted and reborn, but was on the way to conversion: to her the Holy Spirit was knocking at her heart, opening it, removing all the wild beasts of ignorance, all the barriers of innate malice, so that she might attend to those things which were spoken by Paul, and make greater progress in the knowledge of spiritual things, until a full assent of faith was obtained.

4. The internal testimony of the Holy Spirit does not seem to be a valid reason moving an unbelieving man to believe that the prophetic and apostolic writings depend immediately on God. For if you say: The Holy Spirit testifies in my heart that these writings were consigned by the inspiration of God: the unbeliever will deny that the Holy Spirit testifies this in your heart, and thus by this motive you will not convince him. D. Kromayer responds aptly to this objection in his theol. positivo-polem. p. 20. This internal testimony, although it may not avail πρὸς ἕτερον [toward another], i.e., for convincing another (e.g., "You ought to believe that this writing is θεόπνευστον [God-breathed], because I am convinced in my heart that the matter is not otherwise"), it does, however, avail πρὸς ἑαυτὸν [toward oneself], i.e., for convincing oneself, who feels the testimony of the Holy Spirit concerning this matter in his heart. For just as while we live, we experience by the very act that we live; while we believe, we experience that we believe: so while the Holy Spirit confirms heavenly truth in us, while He works through the word and testifies inwardly concerning the word, then we similarly experience by the very act that He is working and testifying.

Latin:

dum, quod hoc verbum scriptum, & id, quod ex bibliis legimus, audimus, credimus, fit verum ac divinum, est sola auctoritas Dei tum externe revelantis, tum interne, sive in cordibus nostris obsignantis & conscientiam convincentis: non veracitas, vel præsumtio de veracitate causæ ministerialis, præsentis ecclesiæ, vel præsentis doctoris, hic & nunc illud nobis proponentis: neque conformitas cum intellectu aut sensu humano: neque consensus notorius ecclesiæ.

Obs. II. Internum Spiritus sancti testimonium de authentia sacræ scripturæ coincidit, quoad rem, cum efficacia sacræ scripturæ in actu secundo spectata; quatenus nempe sacra scriptura attente lecta, & intime penfitata, intellectum hominis illuminat, vt θεοπνευστίαν scripturarum clare cognoscat, & voluntatem eius in consensum trahit & allicit: Idem operatur Spiritus sanctus per verbum Dei decenter usurpatum. Etenim vis effectiva, quam verbo Dei in producendo effectu illuminationis, conversionis, renovationis & confirmationis tribuimus, vere divina est, Rom. I, 16. nec differt, quoad rem, quæ Spiritus sancti operantis in cordibus hominum est, quanquam disparitas fit in modo habendi hanc vim, utpote quæ spiritui sancto ex se, & a se, seu causæ principali: verbo autem participative, vt causæ organicæ, competit. Quam ob rem sacra scriptura lecta, vel voce docentis proposita, explicata, audituque percepta, efficacia divinitus sibi communicata, movet hominis intellectum ad assensum supernaturalem suæ a Deo revelante dependentiæ, per se immediate quidem, citra aliam revelationem, aut vllum motivum credibilitatis, sed cum concursu supernaturali Spiritus S. E quibus conficitur, quod immotus & fiducialis assensus, quo divina scripturarum creditur origo, dependeat & ab ipsa scriptura, & ab ipso Spiritu Sancto, cum ea concurrente, velut motivo formali, atque adeo ab vtroque simul & coniunctim, a neutro autem seorsim & separatim.

Obs. III. De authentia sacræ scripturæ potentissime testatur tota sacrosancta Trinitas; terminative Spiritus sanctus. Exinde fit, vt fides, qua divina scripturarum creditur inspiratio, in sacris litteris interdum potentiæ Dei, a theologis concurrui Dei supernaturali, tribuatur.

Prob. I. ex 1 Io. V, 6. Spiritus testatur, quod Spiritus veritas est. Per vocem Spiritus in subiecto positam intelligimus Spiritum S. tertiam Trinitatis personam; tum quia hæc vox, absolute posita, citra conditionem restringentem, tanquam analoga, merito accipitur in significato suo famosiori; tum quia coessetim in sequenti versiculo 7. sistitur sub ratione personæ, & quidem tertiæ in Trinitate, addito epitheto, cum dicitur τὸ πνεῦμα ἄγιον, cui haud secus, ac patri & filio, testimonium cœleste ibidem adscribitur: per Spiritum autem in prædicato intelligimus verbum Dei, sive scripturam, vocabulo Spiritus metonymice accepto; quia alias verbum Dei quoque dicitur Spiritus & vita, Io. VI, 63. Particula ὅτι non est causalis, sed determinativa, vt sensus fit: Spiritus S. testatur, quod doctrina Spiritus fit veritas, h. e. verissima, quando interius per doctrinam, a se patefactam, in hominum cordibus operatur, ea pulsat, trahit & movet, vt eam a Deo profectam, sive vere divinam esse credant. Hinc v 10. subiungit Ioannes: Qui credit in filium, habet testimonium in seipso: qui non credit Deo, mendacem fecit illum: quia non credidit testimonio, quod Deus testificatus est de filio suo. Dicitur testimonium Dei habere in seipso, qui credit; quia fides, qua creditur in filium Dei, est effectus Spiritus sancti, qui per doctrinam, a se patefactam, in corde credentis operatur, & fidei assensum efficit. A quo ergo homo habet, vt fide divina credat, doctrinam a Spiritu S. patefactam esse veritatem, i. e. verissimam, illa est ratio principalis & vltima cognoscendi divinæ virtute credendi scripturæ S. auctoritatem. Sed a Spiritus S. testimonio, quo testificatur in hominum cordibus, doctrinam Spiritus esse verissimam, mam, habet homo, quod credit fide diuina, doctrinam a Deo patefactam esse veritatem, h. e. verissimam. Ergo testimonium Spiritus sancti, quo testificatur in cordibus hominum, doctrinam a se patefactam esse veritatem, h. e. verissimam, est ratio principalis & vltima cognoscendi diuinaque fide credendi auctoritatem S. scripturae.

II. Ex 1 Thess. I, 5. 6. Euangelium nostrum non tantum fuit apud vos in verbo, sed etiam cum virtute & in Spiritu S. & in confidentia loquendi multa, sicut scitis, quales fuerimus apud vos propter vos. Vos vero imitatores nostri fuistis, & Domini, dum accepistis verbum in afflictione multa cum gaudio Spiritus S. Quod euangelium Paullus Thessalonicæ singulari animi præsentia prædicauerat, id Thessalonicenses inter afflictiones grauissimas, vitæque discrimina receperant magno cum gaudio in animis eorum a Spiritu S. excitato, propterea quod euangelium Paulli non erat sermo nudus, inanis, frugisque expers, sed sermo coniunctus cum virtute Spiritus sancti, qui ipsos illuminauerat, conuerterat, & fide donauerat. Quare præcipua ratio mouens hominem ad recipiendum euangelium Christi, vt vere diuinum, est virtus Spiritus sancti, cum verbo Dei lecto vel audito indiuiduo nexu vnita.

III. Subiungimus insigne effatum eiusdem apostoli ex 1 Thess. II, 13. Propterea etiam nos gratias agimus Deo indefinenter, quod quum accepistis a nobis verbum auditus Dei (nimirum verbum) suscepistis, non (vt) verbum hominum, sed, sicut est reuera, (vt) verbum Dei, qui & operatus est in vobis credentibus. Hic Paullus diserte adscribit Deo in Thessalonicentibus operanti, quod acceperint apostolorum sermonem, non vt verbum hominum, sed vt verbum Dei. Accipere autem verbum ex ore apostolorum, vt verbum Dei, est, id accipere verbum a Deo profectum, siue ex Dei suggestione, aut inspiratione, prædicatum. Est autem par ratio scripturæ diuinitus inspiratæ, & doctrinæ ab apostolis ex diuina inspiratione prædicatæ. Quamuis enim accidentalis intercedat differentia; in quantum illa vocibus scripto consignatis, hæc ore prolatis constat; attamen vna eademque est vis mouens intellectum ad assensum. Quam ob rem sicut Thessalonicenses ex supernaturali Dei operatione mouebantur ad credendum, sermonem apostolorum non esse hominum, sed auctoris Dei: ita etiamnum hominum corda mouentur ex supernaturali Dei operatione ad credendum, scripturam S. esse vere diuinam, siue a Deo profectam. Argumentamur: Quo motiuo Thessalonicenses mouebantur ad credendum, verbum apostolorum esse vere verbum Dei, eodem etiamnum homines mouentur ad credendum, S. scripturam esse a Deo profectam atque vere diuinam. Atqui Thessalonicenses mouebantur ad credendum, verbum apostolorum esse verbum Dei, ab ipfomet Deo per ipsum verbum prædicatum in ipsis agente, & de diuinitate verbi testificante. Ergo etiamnum credentes mouentur ad credendum, scripturam S. esse a Deo profectam, & vere diuinam, ab ipsomet Deo per ipsam in hominum cordibus testificante.

IV. Quotiescunque attente legitur, vel auscultatur diuinum legis & euangelii verbum, huius vim verticordiam homo docilis vere sentit, & Deum secum loqui colligit ex internis cordis actibus & motibus supernaturalibus. Sunt illi actus ex parte intellectus, oborta lux cognitionis supernaturalis, & inspirata cogitatio sancta: ex parte voluntatis, spirituales motus sunt: dolor de peccatis, desiderium discendi & proficiendi, pia affectio erga Deum reuelantem, suauis inclinatio ad imperandum intellectui, iam luce aliqua spirituali collustrato, immotum assensum credendorum, gaudium spirituale. Qui actus intellectus motusque voluntatis, a Spiritu S. per verbum legis & euangelii in cordibus legentium, vel auscultantium, excitati, luculentius cognoscuntur e' quibusdam exemplis biblicis. Ad primam apostoli Petri concionem, quam habuit in festo pentecostes Iudæis crucifixoribus Christi, auditores, referente Luca Act. II, 37. κατενύγησαν τῇ καρδίᾳ, compuncti sunt corde. Quæ compunctio cordis citra dubium inferebat ex parte intellectus agnitionem peccati, nec non cogitationem sanctam, mediante verbo Dei inspiratam, de morte & resurrectione Christi: ex parte autem voluntatis compunctio illa cordis haud dubie importabat dolorem acerbissimum de atrocissimo peccato, in Christum perpetrato, cum voluntatis quadam inclinatione in Christum, & desiderio æternam salutem obtinendi, coniunctum. Idcirco dicebant ad Petrum & ceteros apostolos: Quid faciemus, viri fratres?

Eunucho Candacis, reginæ Æthiopum, ex loco Es. LIII, 7. 8. quem legebat, a Philippo ex aliis scripturæ locis ipsi vberius declarato, ex parte intellectus tantum affulgebat lucis notitiæ salutaris, & ex parte voluntatis tanta oriebatur affectio & promtitudo, vt prona voluntate & suam fidem in Christum profiteretur, & baptismum sibi administrari peteret: Ecce aqua, inquiens ad Philippum, quid prohibet me baptizari?

Dicenti autem Philippo: Si credis ex toto corde, licet: respondebat: Credo filium Dei esse Iesum Christum: & baptizatus est. Act. VIII, 36. 37. Lydia, purpurarum venditrici, per verbum a Paullo prædicatum simul & cogitatio sancta & pium desiderium (vtrumque apertione cordis eius indicatur) a Deo inspiratum est, vt desiderio discendi ducta attenderet his, quæ dicebantur a Paullo, & conversa baptismum susciperet. Act. XVI, 14. seq.

Thessalonicenses verbum Dei susceperunt in afflictione multa cum gaudio Spiritus sancti, 1 Thess. I, 6. Qui actus intellectus motusque voluntatis supernaturales, vi fluxæ a Deo dependentiæ, intellectum ad assensum verbo diuino præbendum inclinant validius, quam viua vox viri fide digni, rem creditu difficilem commemorantis, intellectum in assensum rei gestæ mouet. Sicut enim a Spiritu S. per verbum legis & euangelii sunt excitati: ita Deum fui arguunt auctorem; sicut alias omnis effectus testatur de sua causa.

Antithesis Antithesis est 1. Pontificiorum, quorum nonnulli Spiritum illum, cuius infallibili testimonio scripturæ diuinam auctoritatem nobis constare dicimus, priuati Spiritus nomine traducunt, atque adeo internum Spiritus S. testimonium, vt hominum commentum, rident. 2. Socinianorum, qui cum statuant, diuinam S. scripturæ originem infallibiliter non posse demonstrari, attestationem Spiritus S. tacite prætereunt.

3. Arminianorum negantium, testimonium Spiritus S. ad id necessarium esse, vt scripturam diuinæ esse originis intelligatur. Quorum argumenta ponderabimus. 1. 1. Quæcunque sententia enthusiastarum inuehit in ecclesiam, illa non est approbanda. Atqui sententia Lutheranorum, statuentium, auctoritatem diuinam sacrarum litterarum innotescere per internum Spiritus S. testimonium inuehit enthusiastarum in ecclesiam.

Ergo &c. Resp. Dist. inter attestationem Spiritus S. de diuinitate sacrarum litterarum, quæ fit per illuminationem immediatam, & quæ fit per illuminationem mediatam. Immediatas illuminationes Spiritus S. iactant enthusiastæ; at Lutheranorum constans sententia est, Spiritum S. testari de diuinitate scripturæ per illuminationem mentis mediatam, quæ pro statu temporis præsentis fit verbo Dei scripto. Instantia

Instantia: Lutherani dicunt, se non accipere illuminationem a cœtu hominum, qualis est ecclesia. Ergo immediate accipiunt illuminationem a Spiritu sancto. Resp. Lutherani excludunt medium personale cœtus humani, non medium reale verbi diuini in litteras redacti. 2. 2. Quo posito, committitur circulus sophisticus, illud non est argumentum efficax. Atqui, posita obsignatione Spiritus sancti, vt medio demonstrationis diuinitatis scripturæ, committitur circulus sophisticus.

E. Maior extra controuersiam posita est, quia circulus sophisticus est petitio principii retrocurrens. Minor constat ex natura circuli. Si enim quæram: vnde scis, scripturam esse diuinam? Respondent Lutherani: quia Spiritus S. in vnoquoque per scripturam hoc testatur & obsignat. Si autem quæram: vnde probas, Spiritum illum esse diuinum? Respondent iidem: quia scriptura testatur, illum esse diuinum, & obsignationem illius esse infallibilem. Resp. 1). Lutherani non provocant ad spiritum privatum; verum Spiritus, qui obsignat verbi divini auctoritatem, est Spiritus S. communis omnibus fidelibus. 2) Dist. inter circulum sophisticum, & regressum demonstrativum. In circulo sophistico probatur ignotum per aeque ignotum; in regressu vero demonstrativo a cognitione confusa ad distinctam procedimus. Nempe scripturae dignitas divina probatur per effectum supernaturalem Spiritus sancti, per scripturam efficaciter operantis, illuminantis, convertentis, regenerantis, renouantis. Si autem quaeras: Estne ille Spiritus divinus, an malignus? Tunc ab effectu, qui est divinus & salutaris, regredimur ad probandum, Spiritum interius testantem de divina scripturae origine, esse divinum, sanctissimum & optimum.

3. Quodcunque testimonium nemo in se habet, nisi fit conversus & renatus, illud non gignit assensum solidum scripturae, vt vere divinae, praebendum. Atqui testimonium Spiritus S. nemo in se habet, nisi fit conversus & renatus. E. Maior probatur, quia testimonium, gignens assensum, fidem praecedat necesse est. At homo conversus & renatus fidem iam habet; ideoque testimonium Spiritus S. fidem eius sequitur & obsignat. Minor patet ex 1 Io. V, 10. Qui credit in filium, habet testimonium in seipso. Resp. Attestatio Spiritus S. consideratur vel in ordine ad homines conversos & renatos, vel in ordine ad illos homines, qui sunt in via ad conversionem & regenerationem. Conversorum & renatorum hominum fidem de divinitate scripturae testimonium internum Spiritus S. obsignat, confirmat & locupletat. Sed corda hominum, qui sunt in via ad conversionem, efficax Spiritus S. attestatio & operatio per verbum Dei lectum vel auditum pulsat, aperit, illuminat, fidemque in illis accendit. Exemplo nobis esto Lydia, purpurarum venditrix, Act. XV, 4. quae cum inciperet auscultare verbum Pauli, nondum erat conversa & renata, erat autem in via ad conversionem: huic Spiritus S. cor pulsabat, aperiebat, omnes feras ignorantiae, omnia repagula connatae malitiae summouebat, et attenderet iis, quae a Paulo dicebantur, & maiores progressus in cognitione rerum spiritualium faceret, vsque dum assensus fidei plenus obtineretur.

4. Testimonium internum Spiritus S. non videtur esse valida ratio movens hominem infidelem, vt credat, scripta prophetica & apostolica immediate a Deo dependere. Nam si tu dicas: Spiritus S. testatur in corde meo, haec scripta, inspirante Deo, esse consignata: negabit infidelis, Spiritum S. hoc in corde tuo testari, adeoque hoc motino ipsum non convinces. Respondet apposite ad hanc obiectionem D. Kromayer. in theol. positivo-polem. p. 20. Hoc testimonium internum licet non valeat πρὸς ἕτερον, i. e. ad convincendum alium, (v. gr. Tu credere debes, hoc scriptum esse θεόπνευστον, quia ego in corde meo convictus sum, rem aliter se non habere) valet tamen πρὸς ἑαυτὸν, i. e. ad convincendum se ipsum, qui Spiritus S. testimonium hac de re sentit in corde suo. Vt enim dum vivimus, nos vivere; dum credimus, nos credere actu ipso experimur: ita dum Spiritus S. veritatem caelestem in nobis confirmat, dum per verbum operatur, & de verbo intus testificatur, tum eum operari & testificari similiter actu ipso experimur.


### Quest. XXXIII. Does the authority of Holy Scripture depend on the authority of the church?

The authority of Holy Scripture does not depend on the church by reason of the divine and most eminent dignity in which it excels , nor does it need the testimony of the church by reason of cognition, as the primary and ultimate reason for knowing the divine authority of Scripture , nor as a unique and absolutely necessary argument .

Prob. a. (1) All authority of any writing depends on its author. The church is not the author of Holy Scripture. Therefore, the authority of Holy Scripture does not depend on the church. (2) Whatever is subject to divinely inspired Scripture by a natural and necessary order possesses less authority than divinely inspired Scripture, and therefore cannot confer authority upon it.

But the church, etc. Therefore. The major premise is clear once the terms are grasped. The minor is proved, because just as the law of a prince shines with greater authority than the subjects bound to that law: so the dignity of the divine word outweighs the dignity of the church. It would have gone badly for the Israelites in the time of Moses if they had wished to be superior to the θεοπνεύστῳ (theopneust/divinely inspired) word or the divine law: or if they had wished to say that the priests and Levites conferred authority upon the divine law, when rather the law, as it constituted the priests, so it procured authority for them.

Proof b.

That the primary and ultimate reason for knowing and believing by divine faith the divine authority of the Holy Scriptures is the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit, or, which is the same thing, the efficacy of Holy Scripture, with the Holy Spirit concurring and working in our souls, was shown in the preceding question.

The same is confirmed if we accurately weigh the nature of the church.

For the church is viewed either as a multitude of men spread far and wide throughout the globe, consenting in divine worship: or it is viewed as a multitude of the faithful built by Christ, and constituted the pillar and ground of the truth. Viewed in this latter way, the authority of the church depends upon the authority of Scripture itself, and is posterior to it. However, it is repugnant that the authority of Scripture should depend, as we say, upon the authority of the church, and yet the authority of the church not be known to us except from the authority of Scripture, already previously known.

Viewed in the former way, the authority of the church is merely human, placed in this, that it is not probable that such a great multitude of men, testifying concerning the authority of Scripture—that it truly and immediately proceeded from God—could conspire in one lie, and in testifying could have been deceived or have deceived.

It is well to observe here that the force of the testimony rendered to the divine authority of Scripture by the church does not become magisterial, but ministerial, for the reason that the church is not the mistress, but the handmaid of Scripture; not the mother, but the daughter; not the author, but the guardian, witness, and interpreter; not the judge, but the index and vindicator.

This can be illustrated by the example of the Samaritan woman, mention of whom is made in John 4:7.

She, having conversed with Jesus, from his most efficacious words and the wondrous knowledge of divine and hidden things, the rays of which the Savior was at that time most clearly pouring forth from himself, gathered that Jesus was not only a prophet, but the Messiah himself. see v. 19, 20.

Wherefore, full of joy, she entered the city of Samaria, and invited its citizens, and as it were led them by the hand to see and hear Christ. v. 29.

Many of whom believed in Jesus because of the word of the woman, confirming that Jesus was the Christ. v. 39.

But when they had seen Jesus no less with their eyes than they had received his sermon with attentive ears, many more of them believed because of his own word, and said to the woman: because we no longer believe because of your speech: for we ourselves have heard and know that this is indeed the Savior of the world, Christ. v. 42.

The prior faith of the Samaritans, arising from the word of the woman, was opinion: the posterior, born from the word of Christ, was knowledge, i.e., accurate and certain cognition.

By a like reason, the church testifies to Scripture by its authority, proposes it, and entices and leads men to read it.

Who, when they have attentively read, or heard the Scripture explained by the voice of a teacher, do not believe in Scripture because of the testimony of the church, but believe in Scripture by divine faith because of Scripture itself, insofar as it, with the Holy Spirit concurring, exerts its heart-turning force, illuminates the intellect of the reader or listener, and bends the will into the obedience of faith, so that a full and indubitable assent is offered to Scripture.

Proof c. The testimony of the church is indeed a notable motive of credibility, by which we are led to know and to believe by human faith the divinity of Scripture, but it is not a motive of Scripture, but is not a motive. one, nor absolutely necessary.

It is not the only one, because there are given many κριτήρια καὶ γνωρίσματα, signs & motives, whose moving power is the same as that of the church: such as the antiquity of the scripture, the clarity of the miracles by which it was confirmed: the constancy of the martyrs, who shed their own blood for the authority of the scripture: the sudden propagation of the doctrine which the scripture hands down, and its admirable preservation amidst so many persecutions: the confession of the enemies of the church, and the punishments divinely inflicted upon the persecutors and contemners of the scripture.

What is more?

The internal κριτήρια of the divinity of scripture, such as the majesty of God testifying of Himself in the sacred code, the singularity of the style, the truth of the dogmas and prophecies, and the holiness of the precepts, possess a greater moving power than the testimony of the church.

The testimony of the church is not absolutely necessary for believing the divine authority of the S. [Scripture], because without the attestation of the church the authority of the scripture can be recognized, and has often been recognized.

For the word of God, both as preached and as written, by its own divine efficacy, which it exerts in converting men with the concurring Holy Spirit, betrays its own divine origin, without the testimony of the church being added.

This is what examples, both biblical and others, prove.

When the man of God Shemaiah said to the army of Rehoboam, about to contend with Jeroboam concerning the Israelite kingdom, by the instinct and illumination of God: Thus said Jehovah: you shall not go up, nor fight with your brothers, the sons of Israel: return every man to his house; for this word has been done by me: they obeyed therefore the word of Jehovah, and returned to go according to the word of Jehovah. 1 Kings XII, 24. When the prophet Jonah preached in the city of Nineveh, and said: Yet forty days (there are), and Nineveh shall be overthrown: the men of Nineveh believed in God; and therefore they proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth from the greatest of them, even to the least.

Jon. III, 4. 5. Behold the stupendous efficacy of the divine word!

By which, like a most penetrating lightning bolt, the holy men of God, Shemaiah and Jonah, instructed by no testimony of the church, struck a huge multitude of men, and moved them to the obedience of faith.

More examples from sacred and profane histories could be brought forward, if there were need.

The example of the Christian Gerson, a converted Jew, is worthy of mention.

He describes the occasion and manner of his conversion in D. Calxtus in the tract on the authority of scripture p. 36, in the following words: A certain poor Christian woman, my neighbor, gave me as a pledge a copy of the German New Testament of the converted Luther: to whom I gave eight shillings in exchange, so that I might earn interest in my own way, and meanwhile peruse the book; not indeed that I doubted the truth of the Jewish religion, or believed any article of the Christian faith to be right, but so that I might know what that so greatly efficacious error was, which seduced so many myriads of souls, and cast them headlong into destruction.

Therefore, in the presence of my two relatives, Lazarus and Simeon, I read the whole thing through, not without blasphemies.

Meanwhile, however, my heart was struck; and when I had noticed that the evangelists, and the apostles, and Christ himself so often appealed to the Old Testament, and repeatedly brought forward passages from it one after another: I was enticed to read it again, and indeed secretly, with no one knowing, not even my wife, and to compare the passages brought forward with the very text of the Old Testament.

When I did this, such a light shone upon me, that on that account I owe eternal thanks to God.

More examples of those who, having fallen by some chance into the reading of the sacred letters, perceived an incredible movement of the soul, and were most fully persuaded of their divinity, are recounted by D.

Dorscheus in theol. Zachar. part. II. disp. I. §. 53. Antithesis The Antithesis is that of the Papists, some of whom establish that the authority of the H. scripture, as to the thing itself, depends upon the authority of the church; others assert that the authority of the scripture becomes known to us from the testimony of the church, as an argument either unique or principal, who rely upon the following arguments. I. Whatever, like a solid column, supports and strengthens the truth of Scripture, its authority depends upon that.

But the Church, like a solid column, supports and strengthens the truth of Scripture. Therefore. The major is evident: For just as the strength of a building depends upon its columns, so the valid authority of Scripture depends upon the column and foundation of truth.

The minor is clear from 1 Tim.

3:15, where the Church is called by the Apostle στῦλος καὶ ἑδραίωμα τῆς ἀληθείας, the pillar and ground of the truth. Resp.

1) D.

SEBAST. SCHMID explains the words of Paul very conveniently in colleg. bibl. post. p. 301, whose opinion is that, 1. by the name στῦλος καὶ ἑδραίωμα, reference is made to the columns which were in Solomon’s temple, 1 Kings 7:15; 2 Chron. 3:17, just as it is commonly established that by its name the temple of Solomon is intended.

The function of those columns, however, was not to support anything, but they were in themselves a distinguished work and an ornament of the temple. Whence there is no need for us to say that the Church is called a column because it carries and supports something.

That 2) the Church is called the column and foundation of truth passively: partly because it has been built and erected by heavenly truth; partly because the same truth dwells in it, and the Church believes and professes it, insofar as it is indeed true.

The cited author proves his interpretation from the scope, because the Apostle exhorts Timothy to conduct himself in the Ephesian Church according to the divine word, by this argument, that the Church is made the column of truth, built by it, and to be further built up through it.

Whence the Church is not considered by reason of the office which it performs for the truth, but by reason of the edification through the ecclesiastical ministry, and thus passively as to be built up into a column and foundation of truth, so that, having been built up by the truth, it may firmly hold it.

This interpretation is confirmed by a similar appellation in the context.

Just as in this very place the Church is called οἶκος θεοῦ ζῶντος, the house of the living God, because it has been built by God, and God dwells firmly joined in it: so it is called the column and foundation of truth, because it is built by the truth, and holds the truth dwelling within itself.

3) Some theologians distinguish between the column of truth spoken of in an architectural sense and in a political sense.

For just as in courthouses and before praetoria there stand columns to which the laws and decrees of the magistrate are attached: so the Church is called στῦλος, insofar as the tablets of the divine word are attached and affixed to it as to a public column.

The word ἑδραίωμα, however, does not primarily denote a foundation, as the Vulgate rendered it, or a foundation (which the Greeks call θεμέλιον), but a seat, a chair, a repository, because the Church is made as it were a seat or sacred repository, in which the truth is deposited.

In the architectural sense, however, the Church is not absolutely and primarily called the column and foundation of truth, as if it so strengthens and supports heavenly truth just as a column supports a building; since this very column is supported and strengthened by heavenly truth, as that which is the base and foundation of this column and support; but only respectively, secondarily, and organically, insofar as it stabilizes or supports the truth by testifying to it, proposing it, professing it, interpreting it, guarding it, and defending it, not by conferring authority upon heavenly truth, or by generating divine faith.

Confer D.

GERHARD in loc. de eccles. p. 804; D. CALOV in system. theol. tom.

I. p. 418.

Latin:

Auctoritas S. scripturae neque ratione divinae & eminentissimae dignitatis, qua pollet, ab ecclesia dependet , neque ratione cognitionis indiget testimonio ecclesiae, vt ratione praecipua & vltima cognoscendi divinam scripturae auctoritatem , neque vt argumento vnico & absolute necessario .

Prob. a. (1) Omnis auctoritas alicuius scripturae dependet ab auctore. Ecclesia non est auctor S. scripturae. Ergo ab ecclesia auctoritas S. scripturae non dependet. (2) Quidquid naturali & necessario ordine subiectum est verbo divinitus inspirato, illud minori pollet auctoritate, quam verbum divinitus inspiratum, atque adeo non potest illi conferre auctoritatem.

Atqui ecclesia &c. Ergo. Maior apprehensis terminis clara est. Minor probatur, quia ut lex principis maiori fulget auctoritate, quam subditi illi legi adstricti: ita verbi divini dignitas dignitati ecclesiae praeponderat. Israëlitis male cessisset tempore Mosis, si voluissent esse superiores verbo θεοπνεύστῳ aut lege divina: aut si voluissent dicere, sacerdotes & levitas legi divinae auctoritatem contulisse, cum potius lex, ut sacerdotes constituit, ita ipsis auctoritatem conciliauit.

Prob. b.

Praecipuam & ultimam rationem cognoscendi, divinaque fide credendi divinam auctoritatem sacrarum litterarum, esse internum Spiritus S. testimonium, sive, quod idem est, efficaciam S. scripturae, concurrente Spiritu S. in animis nostris, operosam, praecedente quaestione ostensum est.

Confirmatur idem, si naturam ecclesiae accurate expendamus.

Ecclesia enim vel spectatur ut hominum multitudo longe lateque per terrarum orbem diffusa, in cultu divino consentiens: vel spectatur ut multitudo fidelium a Christo aedificata, & constituta columna & stabilimentum veritatis. Hoc posteriori modo spectata ecclesiae auctoritas dependet ab ipsa scripturae auctoritate, estque ea posterior. Repugnat autem, auctoritatem scripturae dependere, quod nos, ab auctoritate ecclesiae, & tamen auctoritatem ecclesiae non innotescere nobis, nisi ex auctoritate scripturae, iam prius cognita.

Priori modo spectata ecclesiae auctoritas est mere humana, in eo posita, quod probabile non sit, tantam hominum multitudinem de auctoritate scripturae, quod vere & immediate a Deo profecta sit, testificantem, in unum mendacium conspirare, & in testificando falli aut fallere potuisse.

Probe hic obseruandum est, quod vis testimonii, perhibiti divinae auctoritati scripturae ab ecclesia, non fit magisterialis, sed ministerialis, propterea, quod ecclesia non est magistra, sed ministra scripturae; non mater, sed filia; non auctor, sed custos, testis & interpres; non iudex, sed index & vindex.

Illustrari hoc potest exemplo mulieris Samaritanae, cuius mentio fit Io.

IV, 7. Haec, collocuta cum Iesu, ex verbis eius efficacissimis, & miranda rerum divinarum & occultarum scientia, cuius radios Saluator id temporis clarissime ex se fundebat, colligebat, Iesum esse prophetam haud tantum, sed & ipsum Messiam. vid. v. 19. 20.

Quare gaudii plena ingressa urbem Samariam, eius ciues inuitabat, & manu quasi ducebat ad videndum & audiendum Christum. v. 29.

Quorum multi crediderunt in Iesum propter verbum mulieris, confirmantis Iesum esse Christum. v. 39.

At cum Iesum non oculis minus conspexissent, quam pronis auribus sermonem ipsius accepissent, eorum multo plures crediderunt propter verbum ipsius, mulierique dixerunt: quia non amplius propter loquelam tuam credimus: ipsi enim audiuimus & scimus, quod hic fit vere saluator mundi Christus. v. 42.

Prior Samaritanorum fides, orta ex verbo mulieris, erat opinio: posterior, nata ex verbo Christi, erat scientia, i. e. accurata & certa notitia.

Pari ratione ecclesiae auctoritate scriptura testatur, hanc proponit, & ad ipsam legendam homines allicit atque inducit.

Qui vbi attente legerunt, vel voce docentis explicatam audierunt scripturam, non credunt scripturae propter testimonium ecclesiae, sed credunt scripturae fide diuina propter ipsam scripturam, quatenus illa concurrente Spiritu sancto vim suam verticordiam exserit, intellectum legentis vel auscultantis illuminat, & voluntatem in obsequium fidei flectit, vt plenus & indubitatus scripturae assensus praebeatur.

Prob. c. Testimonium ecclesiae est quidem insigne motiuum credibilitatis, quo inducimur ad cognoscendam humanaque fide credendam diuinitatem scripturae, sed non est motiuum. vum vnicum, neque absolute necessarium.

Vnicum non est, quia dantur plura κριτήρια καὶ γνωρίσματα, signa & motiua, quorum eadem est vis mouens, quæ est ecclesiæ: qualia sunt scripturæ antiquitas, miraculorum, quibus confirmata est, claritas: martyrum, qui pro auctoritate scripturæ sanguinem suum fuderunt, constantia: subita doctrinæ, quam scriptura tradit, propagatio, & admiranda eius inter tot persecutiones conseruatio: hostium ecclesiæ confessio, & pœnæ diuinitus immissæ persecutoribus & contemtoribus scripturæ.

Quid? quod κριτήρια diuinitatis scripturæ interna, qualia sunt Dei de seipso in sacro codice testantis maiestas, stili singularitas, dogmatum & vaticiniorum veritas, præceptorumque sanctitas, maiori pollent vi mouente, quam ecclesiæ testimonium.

Absolute necessarium non est testimonium ecclesiæ ad credendam S. auctoritatem diuinam, quia sine testificatione ecclesiæ scripturæ auctoritas agnosci potest, & sæpe agnita est.

Etenim verbum Dei, qua prædicatum, qua scriptum, diuina sua efficacia, quam concurrente Spiritu S. in conuertendis hominibus exserit, diuinam suam prodit originem, non accedente testimonio ecclesiæ.

Id quod exempla, tum biblica, tum alia, comprobant.

Cum vir Dei Schemaia exercitui Rehabeami, cum Ieroboamo de regno Israëlitico decertaturo, ex instinctu & illuminatione Dei diceret: Sic dixit Iehouah: non ascendetis, neque pugnabitis cum fratribus vestris, filiis Israëlis: reuertimini vir in domum suam; quia a me factum est verbum hoc: obediuerunt itaque verbo Iehouæ, & reuersi sunt ad abeundum iuxta verbum Iehouæ.

1 Reg. XII, 24. Cum propheta Ionas concionaretur in vrbe Ninine, & diceret: Adhuc quadraginta dies (sunt), post Ninine euertetur: crediderant viri Ninines in Deum; ideoque proclamarunt ieiunium, indueruntque saccos a maximo eorum, vsque ad minimum.

Ion. III, 4. 5. En stupendam efficaciam verbi diuini! quo, velut fulmine penetrantissimo, sancti Dei viri, Schemaia & Ionas, nullo testimonio ecclesiæ instructi, ingentem hominum multitudinem perculerunt, & ad obedientiam fidei permouerunt.

Exempla plura ex historiis sacris & profanis adduci possent, si opus foret.

Exemplum Christiani Gersonis, Iudæi conuersi, memoratu dignum est.

Hic occasionem & modum conuersionis suæ apud D.

Calxtvm in tract. de auctoritate scripturæ p. 36. sequentibus verbis describit: Paupercula quædam christiana fœmina, vicina mea, tradebat pignori mihi codicem noui testamenti germanici a Lutheri conuersi: cui ego mutuos dabam octo solidos, vt vsuram meo more lucrarer, & librum interim euoluerem; non quidem quod de veritate iudaicæ religionis dubitarem, aut vllum christianæ fidei articulum rectum crederem, sed vt cognoscerem, quisnam ille tantopere efficax error, qui tot animarum myriadas seduceret, & in exitium præcipites daret. Præsentibus igitur meis duobus affinibus, Lazaro, & Simeone, totum perlegi non sine blasphemiis.

Interim vero cor meum percellebatur; & cum animaduertissem, euangelistas, & apostolos, & Christum ipsum toties ad vetus testamentum prouocare, & subinde loca ex eo alia post alia adducere: illectus fui, vt denuo legerem, & clanculum quidem, nemine conscio, ne quidem vxore mea, & vt loca adducta cum ipso veteris testamenti textu contenderem.

Quod vbi feci, tanta mihi lux illuxit, vt eo nomine æternas Deo debeam gratias.

Plura exempla eorum, qui casu quodam in sacrarum litterarum lectionem delapsi incredibilem animi motum persenserunt, & de diuinitate illarum plenissime persuasi fuerunt, recenset D.

Dorschevs in theol.

Zachar. part. II. disp. I. §. 53. Antithesis Antithesis est Pontificiorum, quorum quidam statuunt, auctoritatem S. scripturæ, quoad rem, secundum se ab ecclesiæ auctoritate dependere; alii asserunt, auctoritatem scripturæ nobis e testimonio ecclesiæ, ceu argumento aut vnico, aut præcipuo innotescere, qui sequentibus argumentis innituntur. I. A quaecunque, velut solida columna, veritas scripturae suffulcitur & firmatur, ab eo auctoritas eius dependet.

Sed ab ecclesia, velut solida columna, veritas scripturae suffulcitur & firmatur. Ergo. Maior patet: Sicut enim aedificii robur pendet a columnis: ita valida scripturae auctoritas pendet a columna & firmamento veritatis.

Minor liquet ex 1 Tim.

III, 15. vbi ecclesia ab apostolo vocatur στῦλος καὶ ἑδραίωμα τῆς ἀληθείας, columna & stabilimentum veritatis. Resp.

1) Verba Pauli percommode exponit D.

SEBAST. SCHMID. in colleg. bibl. post. p. 301. cuius sententia est, quod 1. nomine στῦλος καὶ ἑδραίωματος respiciatur ad columnas, quae in templo Salomonaeo fuerunt, 1 Reg. VII, 1er. LII. quemadmodum nomine eius respici templum Salomonum communiter statuunt.

Istarum autem columnarum officium non erat, vt aliquid sustentarent, sed per se insigne opus fuerunt & templi ornamentum. Vnde non opus, vt ecclesiam columnam dicamus appellari, quod aliquid portet ac sustentet.

Quod 2) columna & firmamentum veritatis dicatur ecclesia passive: partim quod a veritate caelesti exstructa & erecta sit; partim quod eadem veritas in illa habitet, eamque ecclesia credit & profitetur, quatenus quidem vera est.

Probat laudatus auctor interpretationem suam a scopo, quia hortatur apostolus Timotheum, vt in ecclesia Ephesina secundum verbum divinum conversetur, argumento hoc, quod ecclesia fit columna veritatis, ab ea exstructa, & per eam porro exaedificanda.

Vnde ecclesia non consideratur ratione officii, quod praestat veritati, sed ratione aedificationis per ministerium ecclesiasticum, adeoque passive vt exaedificanda in columnam & firmamentum veritatis, vt exstructa per veritatem, hanc firmiter teneat.

Confirmatur haec interpretatio a simili in contextu appellatione.

Quemadmodum hoc ipso loco ecclesia dicitur οἶκος θεοῦ ζῶντος, domus Dei viui, quod a Deo exstructa sit, & Deus in ea firmiter coagmentata habitet: sic columna & firmamentum veritatis vocatur, quod a veritate exstruatur, & veritatem in se habitantem teneat.

3) Distinguunt nonnulli theologi inter columnam veritatis dictam in sensu architectonico, & politico.

Vt enim in curiis & ante praetoria columnae exstant, ad quas leges & decreta magistratus appenduntur: sic ecclesia vocatur στῦλος, quatenus ad illam ceu columnam publicam appensae & affixae sunt verbi diuini tabulae.

Vox ἑδραίωμα vero non firmamentum primo denotat, vti vulgata reddidit, vel fundamentum (quod θεμέλιον vocant graeci) sed sedem, sellam, repositorium, quod ecclesia fit quasi sedile aut repositorium sacrum, in quo deposita fit veritas.

In sensu vero architectonico ecclesia absolute & primario non vocatur columna & firmamentum veritatis; perinde, ac si veritatem caelestem ita firmet & fulciat, sicut columna aedificium sustentat; siquidem haec ipsa columna a veritate caelesti sustentatur & firmatur, vtpote quae huius columnae & fulcimenti basis est & fundamentum; sed tantum respective, secundario & organice, quatenus stabilit, vel suffulcit veritatem, eam testando, proponendo, profitendo, interpretando, custodiendo, defendendo, non auctoritatem veritati caelesti conferendo, vel fidem diuinam gignendo.

Confer, D.

GERHARD. in loc. de eccles. p. 804.

D. CALOV. in system. theol. tom. I. p. 418.


### Quest. XXXIII. Does the authority of Holy Scripture depend on the authority of the church?: (*). II

(*). II.

Whatever testimony is divine and infallible, that generates divine faith.

But the testimony of the Church concerning the θεοπνευσία (divine inspiration) of Holy Scripture is, etc. Therefore.

The minor is proved, because the Church is led by the Holy Spirit into all truth, John 16:13.

Wherefore the testimony of the Church concerning the authenticity of the Holy Scriptures, as it proceeds from the Spirit of truth, so it is to be believed by divine faith- (*) But we have another explanation, as we noted above at question 5, page 73. must be believed. Resp. From the intention of Christ speaking, that promise primarily and proximately regards the instruction of the apostles for the function of the apostolic office, by which they were bound to serve all nations by preaching the word of truth. The promise was fulfilled on the day of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit immediately illuminated the hearts of the apostles with the knowledge of heavenly doctrine, so that they might not err in the doctrine of faith. Secondarily, that promise can be accommodated to the universal church, which, in so far as it follows the guidance of the Holy Spirit, does not err, but is infallible. But in this way, infallibility will redound principally to the Holy Spirit Himself, who inhabits and directs it.

III. The church is older than Scripture. Therefore, Scripture, as far as we are concerned, has its authority from the church. Resp. Distinguish between the material and the formal of Holy Scripture. The material is the words committed to writing by the prophets and apostles: the formal is the sense comprising the dogmas divinely revealed. The church is older than Scripture if you look at its material; it is not older if you consider the formal of Scripture, for the reason that it was collected and built up through the dogmas divinely revealed.

Instance: God communicated His word to the protoplasts, when the church was already constituted. Therefore, the church is older than the divine word, even as to its formal. Resp. Our discussion is not about the first humans in the state of innocence (although it has not yet been proven that Adam and Eve were a church, properly so called; cf. ADAMI OSANDRI colleg. system. theol. part. I. p. 90.) but about the Christian church, which was built up through the first protevangelium, and propagated through the word preached by the prophets and apostles, and reduced to writing.

IV. The Papists object to us that worn-out saying of AUGUSTINE: I would not believe the Gospel, unless the authority of the church moved me. Resp. 1. Augustine speaks of himself as an individual, and does not prescribe a rule of believing the authority of Scripture for everyone. Wherefore it is wrongly inferred: Augustine did not believe the Gospel unless the testimony of the church intervened. Therefore, the case is the same for all believers. 2. He speaks of himself, not as he was then a Christian and bishop, but as he had been when he was being led from Manichaeism to the orthodox religion; he says, namely, that he would not have believed (using an African phrase familiar to him, for credidissem [I would have believed]) unless he had first been moved by the authority of the church. 3. The testimony of the church can be the first medium of believing by reason of order, although it is not the first, much less the only, medium in the efficacy of proving. For which reason, the mind of Augustine is not that he believed with divine faith and immovable assent that Holy Scripture proceeded from God because of the authority of the church, but he speaks of a motive of credibility, by which he was moved and induced to read Holy Scripture, as if he were going to say: If I had not been induced by the authority and testimony of the church to read Scripture, I would not have believed, that is, I would neither have read the Scripture, nor would it have worked assent in me: but after I attentively read the Scripture, it, with the Holy Spirit concurring, testified of itself in my heart by its own illuminating power, so that I certainly believe that it depends immediately on God.

V. Whoever cannot believe without a preacher, they cannot believe without the church testifying. But, men cannot &c. Therefore. The major is evident, because every preacher is a member of the church. The minor is proved from Rom. 10: 14. Resp. Distinguish between the proclamation of the divine word and the testimony of the church concerning the divine word. The former generates divine faith; the latter produces human faith. And although the preacher is necessary, nevertheless one does not believe on account of the authority of the preacher or of the one proposing, but on account of the authority of the word preached.

Latin:

(*). II.

Quodcunque testimonium est diuinum & infallibile, illud generat fidem diuinam.

Atqui testimonium ecclesiae de θεοπνευσίᾳ sacrae scripturae est &c. Ergo.

Minor probatur, quia ecclesia ducitur a Spiritu sancto in omnem veritatem, Io.

XVI, 13. Quare testimonium ecclesiae de authentia sacrarum litterarum, vt a Spiritu veritatis proficiscitur, ita fide diuina creden- (*) Sed aliam habemus explanationem, quem credendum est. Resp. Ex intentione Christi loquentis promissio illa primario & proxime respicit instructionem apostolorum ad functionem muneris apostolici, quo omnibus gentibus, praedicando verbum veritatis, inferuire debuerunt. Impleta est promissio in die pentecostes, vbi Spiritus sanctus corda apostolorum cognitione doctrinae coelestis immediate illuminauit, vt in doctrina fidei ne errarent. Secundario illa promissio accommodari potest ad vniuersam ecclesiam, quae, in quantum Spiritus sancti ductum sequitur, non errat, sed infallibilis est. Sed ita infallibilitas principaliter sese refundet in ipsum Spiritum sanctum inhabitantem & dirigentem.

III. Ecclesia est antiquior scriptura. Ergo scriptura, quoad nos, ab ecclesia habet auctoritatem. Resp. Dist. inter materiale, & formale sacrae scripturae. Materiale sunt verba a prophetis & apostolis litteris mandata: Formale est sensus complectens dogmata diuinitus reuelata. Ecclesia scriptura antiquior est, si huius materiale spectes; non est antiquior, si pensites formale scripturae, ideo, quod per dogmata diuinitus reuelata collecta & exstructa est.

Instantia Communicauit Deus verbum suum protoplastis, cum ecclesia iam constituta esset. Ergo ecclesia verbo diuino, etiam qua formale ipsius, antiquior est. Resp. Sermo nobis est non de hominibus primis in statu innocentiae (quamuis nondum euictum sit, quod Adamus & Eua in statu integritatis fuerint ecclesia, proprie dicta; conf. ADAMI OSANDRI colleg. system. theol. part. I. p. 90.) sed de ecclesia christiana, quae per proteuangelium primum exstructa, & per verbum a prophetis & apostolis praedicatum, inque litteras redactum, propagata est.

IV. Obiiciunt nobis Pontificii tritum illud AVGVSTINI: Euangelio non crederem, nisi ecclesiae me moueret auctoritas. Resp. 1. Augustinus loquitur de se in individuo, non autem praescribit omnibus regulam credendi auctoritatem scripturae. Quare male infertur: Augustinus non credidit euangelio, nisi interueniente ecclesiae testimonio. Ergo omnium credentium par est ratio. 2. Loquitur de se, non qualis tum erat christianus & episcopus, sed qualis fuerat, cum a Manichaeismo ad orthodoxam religionem deduceretur, se nempe haud crediturum fuisse, dicit, phrasi Africana sibi familiari vsus, pro credidissem) nisi primum ecclesiae auctoritate commotus fuisset. 3. Potest ecclesiae testimonium ordinis ratione primum esse credendi medium, licet probandi efficacia non sit primum, nedum vnicum. Quam ob rem mens Augustini non est, quod ob auctoritatem ecclesiae fide diuina & immoto assensu crediderit, scripturam sacram esse a Deo profectam, sed loquitur de motiuo credibilitatis, quo motus & inductus fuerit ad legendam scripturam sacram, quasi dicturus: Si ecclesiae auctoritate & testimonio non inductus fuissem ad legendam scripturam, non credidissem, id est, nec legissem scripturam, nec ipsa in me assensum operata fuisset: postquam vero scripturam attente legi, ipsa, concurrente Spiritu sancto, vi sua illuminatrice de se testata est in corde meo, vt certo credam, eam immediate a Deo dependere.

V. Quicunque non possunt credere sine praedicante, illi non possunt credere sine ecclesia testificante. Atqui, homines non possunt &c. Ergo. Maior patet, quia omnis praedicans est membrum ecclesiae. Minor probatur ex Rom. 10, 14. Resp. Dist. inter praeconium verbi diuini, & testimonium ecclesiae de verbo diuino. Illud generat fidem diuinam, hoc parit fidem humanam. Et licet necessarius sit praedicans, non tamen creditur propter auctoritatem praedicantis aut proponentis, sed propter auctoritatem verbi praedicati.


### Quest. XXXIV. What is

the canonical authority of Holy Scripture, or the normative authority of faith and morals? The canonical authority of Holy Scripture is the most eminent dignity of Scripture, by which it is an infallible and adequate norm, both in respect of its sense and of its divinely inspired idiom, to which all things that must be believed and done by man, who is to attain eternal salvation, must be brought, all controversies of faith must be settled, and all other writings must be judged.

Obs. I. The causative authority of faith differs from the canonical authority of Holy Scripture (a) in that Scripture generates faith through its θεόπνευστον (God-breathed) sense, or heavenly doctrine, which sense of Scripture is one and the same, and remains so, whether it be expressed in the original idiom of Scripture or in some version conformable to the original text. Therefore, the illuminating power, joined to the sense of Scripture, exerts itself effectively to generate faith not only through the original Scripture, but also through a version of Scripture, provided the version be perspicuous and conformable to the authentic text: such is the biblical version of the Blessed Luther, which faithful men use in our churches; which, when read or perceived by hearing, is as effective for causing the assent of faith as if they had read the Hebrew text of the Old Testament and the Greek of the New, or had heard it proposed and explained by the voice of a teacher, although the words of that version are not immediately inspired by God. But in order for Scripture to avail with canonical authority, it is necessary that not only the sense, but also the words, should have proceeded immediately from God. For to a canon, or norm of doctrine and morals, there is required also, on the part of the words, absolute certainty and infallibility, which is not given except in the original text of Holy Scripture, since it depends immediately on God who inspires it. Versions have been compiled by the study of men, who in translating Scripture could suffer and err in something human. (b) Holy Scripture exerts its canonical authority most especially when a controversy arises concerning the truth of doctrine, and the truth is to be confirmed, but falsehood is to be refuted: however, Scripture exerts its motive authority of faith whenever either infidels are to be converted to the Christian faith, or the weak faith of the faithful is to be confirmed.

Obs. II. The word canon denotes a rule or norm, and is defined by Varinus: Κανών ἐστι μέτρον ἀδιάψευστον πᾶσαν πρόσθεσιν καὶ ἀφαίρεσιν μηδαμῶς ἐπιδεχόμενον (A canon is an infallible measure, admitting in no way any addition or subtraction). A norm is an infallible measure, admitting no addition or subtraction. Properly, it is an instrument for measuring quantity. Analogically, the word canon, or norm, has been transferred to laws, which are called the norm of life; and to the principles of disciplines, which are the norm of dogmas; and to the principle of theology, Scripture, which is called the norm of things to be believed and done. Conf. D. CALOV. metaphys. diuin. p. m. 655.

Obs. III. The norm of cognition performs a twofold function, directive and corrective. For it directs the cognition of the human mind, so that it may keep itself within the bounds of truth, and it corrects errors, since the straight is the norm of itself and of the crooked. Therefore, Holy Scripture is called a canon, or norm, partly on account of direction; because according to it the truth of faith and the honesty of morals are directed: partly on account of correction; since controversies of faith are examined by it, and whatever is right and pious is retained; whatever is erroneous and impious is rejected.

Obs. IV. However, the word canon is taken by Christian writers in three ways: 1) Generally for every writing or book which has some force of a rule. In which general sense the decrees of the pontiffs, and the pontifical law itself, arranged in a certain order, is called canonical, or regular; for this reason, that on account of the authority of the pontiff those who are subject to his jurisdiction are bound to follow it as it were a rule. 2) Specifically for every book contained in the biblical codex; therefore because it contributes to the edification of readers, and in this respect is a certain rule, which the faithful follow for their own edification. In this sense, Augustine, in book XVIII of *The City of God*, ch. 36, counts the books of the Maccabees, Tobit, Wisdom, and others as canonical; even though the Jewish church never held them in the canon. 3) Most specially as a divine, entirely certain, and infallible rule of faith and morals, to which it is utterly repugnant that anything false should underlie it: in this most special sense, the authority of Scripture is called canonical; because Holy Scripture is an infallible rule of things to be believed and things to be done, depending immediately upon God, and communicated by Him to men, so that those things which conform to it may be admitted, and those which differ may be rejected.
