That Holy Scripture is the rule of faith and morals is proven because it is explicitly called קו, a line, a rule, a plumb line, in Ps. XIX, where the Hebrew word קו is found. Now, קו is either the measuring cord of workmen or geometers, Jer. XXXI, 38; Lam. II, 8; 2 Chron. IV, 2; or the plumb line of architects, Job XXXVIII, 5; Is. XLIV, 13; or the line of writing, Is. XXVIII, 10, as noted by GEIER in Ps. XIX, p. 317. The Greek word κανὼν is read in Gal. VI, 16: καὶ ὅσοι τῷ κανόνι τέτῳ σοιχήσουσιν, εἰρήνη ἐπ' αὐτὲς καὶ ἔλεος, "and as many as walk by this rule, peace (shall be) upon them and mercy." By "canon" in the cited passage, according to Paul's intention, is primarily and directly understood the heavenly doctrine which the Apostle embraced in the Epistle to the Galatians, concerning justification, spiritual liberty, and the new creature. But since the nature of all θεοπνεύστων (God-breathed) writings is the same, we conclude from the truth that the entire θεοπνεύστων Scripture is an infallible canon, or rule, for truly believing and piously living. Cf. Phil. III, 16. Certainly, Scripture is very appropriately called a canon. For the church is a mystical building, whose cornerstone is Christ: the architects are the teachers, who use Scripture as a norm to erect the spiritual house and to build up doctrine. Hence, BASIL, book 1 against Eunomius, calls Scripture the canon of rectitude and the norm of truth. CYRIL, book IV of his dialogues, calls it the straight and perfect canon of faith. CHRYSOSTOM, homily 13 on 2 Corinthians: "We have the most exact balance and gnomon and rule, the assertion of the divine laws. And therefore I pray and beseech you that you leave behind what seems right to this one or that one, and inquire about all these things from the Scriptures." AUGUSTINE, book 11 against the Donatists, ch. 6: "Let us bring to the examination not deceitful scales, where we weigh what we want and how we want, saying according to our own whim: this is heavy, this is light; but let us bring the divine balance from the Holy Scriptures as if from the Lord's testaments, and let us weigh in it what is heavier—or rather, let us not weigh, but recognize what has been weighed by the Lord." Cf. D. CALOV, in *Systema Theologicum*, vol. I, p. 475.

Latin:

Auctoritas sacrae scripturae canonica est eminentissima scripturae dignitas, qua illa tam ratione sensus, quam idiomatis diuinitus inspirati, infallibilis & adaequata norma est, ad quam omnia, homini aeternam salutem adepturo credenda & agenda, sunt exigenda, omnes controuersiae fidei dirimendae, & omnia alia scripta diiudicanda.

Obs. I. Auctoritas causatiua fidei ab auctoritate sacrae scripturae canonica differt (a) quod scriptura fidem generat per sensum θεόπνευστον, siue doctrinam caelestem, qui sensus scripturae vnus & idem est, ac manet, siue idiomate scripturae primigenio, siue versione aliqua, textui originali conformi, exprimatur. Ideo vis illuminatrix, scripturae sensui coniuncta, ad generandam fidem non tantum per scripturam primigeniam, sed & per versionem scripturae se efficaciter exserit, modo versio perspicua sit & textui authentico conformis: qualis est versio biblica B. Lutheri, qua vtuntur homines fideles in nostris ecclesiis; quae lecta, vel auditu percepta, tam efficax est ad causandum assensum fidei, quam si textum hebraeum veteris & graecum N. T. legissent, vel voce docentis propositum & explicatum audiuissent, quamuis verba illius versionis a Deo immediate non sint inspirata. At vero vt scriptura valeat auctoritate canonica, non tantum sensum, sed & verba a Deo immediate profecta esse oportet. Ad canonem enim, siue normam doctrinae & morum, requiritur etiam ex parte verborum certitudo & infallibilitas absoluta, quae non datur nisi in primigenio scripturae sacrae textu, quippe qui a Deo inspirante immediate dependet. Versiones concinnatae sunt studio hominum, qui in transferenda scriptura aliquid humani pati & errare potuerunt. (b) Sacra scriptura suam potissimum exserit auctoritatem canonicam, quando de veritate doctrinae exoritur controuersia, & veritas confirmanda, falsitas vero confutanda est: auctoritatem vero motiuam fidei exserit scriptura, quotiescunque vel infideles ad fidem christianam conuertendi sunt, vel fidelium infirma fides confirmanda est.

Obs. II. Vox canon notat regulam, vel normam, & definitur a Varino: Κανών ἐστι μέτρον ἀδιάψευστον πᾶσαν πρόσθεσιν καὶ ἀφαίρεσιν μηδαμῶς ἐπιδεχόμενον. Norma est mensura infallibilis, nullam additionem vel detractionem admittens. Proprie est instrumentum mensurandae quantitatis. Analogice vox canon, vel norma, translata est ad leges, quae dicuntur norma vitae; & disciplinarum principia, quae norma dogmatum sunt; & ad principium theologiae, scripturam, quae norma credendorum & agendorum salutatur. Conf. D. CALOV. metaphys. diuin. p. m. 655.

Obs. III. Norma cognitionis duplici fungitur munere, directiuo, & correctiuo. Dirigit enim cognitionem humanae mentis, vt intra metas veritatis se contineat, & corrigit errores, siquidem rectum est norma sui & obliqui. Dicitur itaque scriptura sacra canon, sine norma, partim ob directionem; quia secundum eam veritas fidei & honestas morum dirigitur: partim ob correctionem; quoniam controuersiae fidei ad eam examinantur, & quidquid rectum piumque est, retinetur; quidquid erroneum impiumque est, reiicitur.

Obs. IV. Accipitur autem hic vox, canon, a scriptoribus christianis tribus modis: 1) generaliter pro omni scripto aut libro, qui vim aliquam regulae habet. Quo generali sensu decreta pontificum, & ius ipsum pontificium, certo ordine digestum, dicitur canonicum, siue regulare; propterea, quod ob auctoritatem pontificis illud velut regulam sequi tenentur, qui eius iurisdictioni subiecti sunt. 2) Specialiter pro omni libro, qui in codice biblico continetur; ideo quod ad legentium aedificationem facit, & hoc intuitu quaedam regula est, quam fideles ad sui ædificationem fequuntur. Quo fenfu Auguftinus libr. XVIII. de C. D. c. 36. libros Maccabæorum, Tobiæ, Sapientiæ, & alios, canonicis accenfet; tametfi eos ecclefia iudaica in canone nunquam habuerit. 3) Specialiffime pro regula fidei & morum diuina, prorfus certa & infallibili, cui falfum fubeffe plane repugnat: quo fenfu fpecialiffimo auctoritas fcripturæ dicitur canonica; quia fcriptura facra eft infallibilis credendorum & agendorum regula, a Deo immediate dependens, & ab eodem hominibus communicata, vt, quæ illi congruunt, admittantur, quæ difcrepant, reiiciantur.

Sacram fcripturam effe regulam fidei & morum, probatur, quia differte appellatur קו linea, regula, amuffis, Pf. XIX. vbi vox hebræa קו habetur. Eft autem קו vel funis menforius opificum aut geometrarum, Ier. XXXI, 38. Thren. II, 8. 2 Paral. IV, 2. vel amuffis architectorum, Iob. XXXVIII, 5. Ef. XLIV, 13. vel linea fcripturæ, Ef. XXVIII, 10. annotante GEIERO in Pf. XIX. p. 317. Vox græca κανὼν legitur Gal. VI, 16. καὶ ὅσοι τῷ κανόνι τέτῳ σοιχήσουσιν, εἰρήνη ἐπ' αὐτὲς καὶ ἔλεος, & quotquot canone hoc incedunt, pax (erit) fuper eos & mifericordia. Per canonem l. c. ex intentione Pauli primo & proxime intelligitur doctrina cœleftis, quam epiftola ad Galatas apoftolus complexus eft, de iuftificatione, de libertate fpirituali, de noua creatura. At cum fcriptorum θεοπνεύσων eadem fit ratio, ex vero colligimus, totam fcripturam θεοπνεύσων effe infallibilem canonem, fiue regulam vere credendi & pie viuendi. Confer. Phil. III, 16. Certe fcriptura percommode canon appellatur. Nam ecclefia eft ædificium myfticum, cuius lapis angularis eft Chriftus: Architecti funt doctores, qui vtuntur fcriptura, velut norma, ad domum fpiritualem erigendam, & doctrinam exftruendam. Exinde BASILIVS lib. 1. contra Eunom. fcripturam appellat canonem recti & normam veritatis. CYRILL. lib. IV. dial. canonem fidei rectum & perfectum vocat. Ideoque oro & obfecro vos, vt relinquatis, quid huic aut illi vi„deatur, deque hiis a fcripturis omnia inquiratis. AVGVSTIN. l. 11. c. donatift. c. 6. ### Quest. XXXIV. What is: Question XXXV. Whence is the authority of Holy Canonical Scripture known to us?

Question XXXV. Whence is the authority of Holy Canonical Scripture known to us?

For the canonical authority of Holy Scripture, an infallible certainty is required, both of the doctrine and of the words of the divinely inspired Scripture: absolute certainty of the words is not given except in the original idiom. The canonical authority of Scripture, considered with respect to doctrine, is known both from external and internal criteria, and especially from the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit, through Scripture attentively read or perceived by hearing from the mouth of a teacher, illuminating the minds of men (a). But the canonical authority of Scripture, considered with respect to the original idiom, or the authentic Hebrew text in the Old Testament and the Greek in the New, is distinctly recognized indeed by the testimony of the primitive church (b), but not by that alone (c).

…Proof a. By the same signs and arguments by which the divine origin of the Holy Scriptures is notified to us, by those same signs is the authority of canonical Scripture, viewed with respect to doctrine, notified to us. For Holy Scripture is an infallible canon, or norm, of faith and morals for this reason: because it derives its immediate origin from God, and was destined by the same for canonical use. Wherefore, since the κριτήρια adduced above certify to us that the sense or doctrine of Holy Scripture proceeded immediately from God, it is of no use to prove the canonical authority of Scripture at length here, if you look at the doctrine of the canon. But it is otherwise with the original idiom of the Old and New Testaments. For the Holy Spirit… bears internal testimony to those who attentively meditate upon the heavenly doctrine, announced by some version, whether it be Latin or German, that it is from God, although the words of the version are from men, who could be deceived and deceive. Thus also most κριτήρια, both external and internal, distinctly signify the sense, not the idiom of Scripture. Prob. b. When it is asked: Was the Gospel of Matthew written first in Greek or in Hebrew? that question is not dogmatic, but historical. For it is a question of fact, falling into the senses, concerning which the canonical writers themselves, by word of mouth, by the subscription of their hand, and by the tradition of the autographs; and the autographs themselves, delivered to the church and preserved in it with the greatest care, testified as to the sense. The witness of this sensible fact is the primitive church, which, while the writers were living in the flesh, campaigned under the banner of Christ on earth, and received their αὐτόγραφα from their hands; and likewise the subsequent church, which flourished in the times immediately following, when the αὐτόγραφα of the canonical books still survived, were worn by hands, and were seen by the eyes of readers as to the idiom in which they were inscribed. However, the more recent church cannot testify of itself concerning the canonical authority of Holy Scripture; but if it wishes to testify, it is necessary that it recur to the primitive and subsequent church, and borrow from it the testimony of the authentic text. Thus we seek the testimony of the Hebrew idiom in the Old Testament from the Jewish church, and of the original Greek text in the New Testament from the primitive Christian church. Prob. c. We willingly accept the testimony of the primitive church, but not that alone. We join to it the testimony of Scripture, its long-lasting preservation for the salutary use of men, and the quality of the style. (1) That the Old Testament was inscribed in the Hebrew style, we gather from Rom. III, 2, where Paul explicitly writes: that the oracles of God were entrusted to the Jews. From this Pauline utterance we argue: Whatever oracles were entrusted to the Jews, so that through them they might be made wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus, those were entrusted to them in the Hebrew idiom. But the oracles of God are contained in the sacred code of the Old Testament, etc. Therefore. The major premise is certain, because by no oracles, no sayings, can a man or a whole nation be made wise unto salvation, unless the words or oracles are proposed to the man or nation in a familiar and vernacular idiom, which that nation understands, and can thus apply to itself for salutary use. The minor premise is clear from the cited Pauline saying, Rom. III, 2, compared with the utterance of the same apostle, 2 Tim. III, 15. We apply the testimony of Paul to the Greek language of the New Testament, and we probably conclude: Whatever oracles were entrusted to all nations, so that through them they might be made wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus, those were entrusted to them in the Greek language. But the oracles of Christ and the apostles are contained in the sacred code of the New Testament, etc. Therefore. The connection of the major premise is shown. Just as God and the prophets entrusted their oracles to the Jews in a language vernacular to them, which all Jews understood, namely Hebrew: so Christ and the apostles entrusted their oracles to all nations, most widely diffused throughout the whole world, in a most common language, and most known to all nations, namely Greek, so that through it all nations might be made wise unto salvation. Cicero says gravely in the Oration for the poet Archias: Greek is read among almost all nations, Latin is contained within its own boundaries, which are indeed small. (2) If a controversy arises concerning the original idiom of some sacred amanuensis, it cannot always be solidly resolved without the application of other arguments. This is evident from the question concerning the primitive idiom of the Gospel of Matthew, it is debated: was it originally composed in Hebrew, or in Greek? For HUGO GROTIUS, in his preface to the Gospel of Matthew, reports that pious antiquity teaches with the greatest consensus that the πρωτότυπον [original] of the Gospel of Matthew was Hebrew. To this opinion he brings PAPIAS, IRENAEUS, ORIGEN, PANTAENUS, JEROME, & EPIPHANIUS. Nevertheless, GROTIUS praises the Greek version, which is frequented today, saying: I deem it impious to doubt the authority and fidelity of the Greek version received from the very beginning of Christianity. D. CALOVIUS, contending against this for the authenticity of the Greek text, goes to refute HUGO GROTIUS with an argument taken from divine providence, in Bibl. Illustrat. tom. I. on the New Testament, fol. 140. “GROTIUS says that one must not doubt the authority & fidelity of the Greek version of Matthew: but if we do not have the πρωτότυπον [original] itself preserved by divine providence, which was divinely destined for the canonical use of the church, how shall we be able to be certain, by faith, of the fidelity and authority of the translation, or of its perennial and uncorrupted preservation? We believe that the Word of God will not perish, and that not even an iota or a tittle of it can perish; we securely place our faith in the word of Christ, but we have no promise concerning the preservation of translations.” Furthermore, HOTTINGER, Systemat. Theol. lib. 1. loc. 3., cited by CALOVIUS, urges this, that an authentic Hebrew Gospel of Matthew exists nowhere: but that the original text itself should have perished is repugnant to divine providence.

(3) But if anyone possesses such keenness of intellect, and is so imbued with the knowledge of the Hebrew and Greek languages, that he knows how to deeply inspect and meditate upon the Hebrew text of the Old, and the Greek text of the New Testament, he will believe without any hesitation that both idioms are original, authentic, and proceeded immediately from God inspiring them.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, who assert that the canonical authority of Holy Scripture depends solely, as far as we are concerned, upon the authority and testimony of the church; their arguments are:

Latin:

Quæft. XXXV. Vnde innotefcit nobis auctoritas facræ fcripturæ canonicæ?

Ad auctoritatem facræ fcripturæ canonicam requiritur infallibilis certitudo tam doctrinæ, quam verborum fcripturæ diuinitus infpiratæ: certitudo abfoluta verborum non datur, nifi in idiomate primigenio. Auctoritas fcripturæ canonica confiderata ratione doctrinæ, cum ex κριτηρίοις externis & internis, tum præfertim ex interno teftimonio Spiritus fancti, per fcripturam attente lectam, vel ex ore docentis auditu perceptam, mentes hominum illuminantis innotefcit (a). At confiderata fcripturæ auctoritas canonica ratione idiomatis primigenii, fiue textus authentici hebræi in veteri, & græci in nouo teftamento, teftimonio quidem ecclefiæ primitiuæ (b), fed non folo (c), diftincte cognofcitur.

Prob. a. Quibus indiciis & argumentis diuina facrarum litterarum origo, iisdem auctoritas fcripturæ canonicæ, ratione doctrinæ fpectata, nobis notificatur. Nam ideo S. fcriptura infallibilis fidei morumque canon, fiue norma eft, quia a Deo immediatam ducit orioriginem, & ab eodem in vsum canonicum destinata est. Quare cum supra adducta κριτήρια nos certificent, sensum, vel doctrinam S. scripturæ inmediate a Deo esse profectam, canonicam scripturæ auctoritatem hic prolixe probare nil attinet, si spectes doctrinam canonis. At cum idiomate primigenio veteris & noui testamenti aliter comparatum est. Nam Spiritus S. attente meditantibus doctrinam cœlestem, versione quadam, latina, an germanica sit, enuntiatam, testimonium internum perhibet, illam esse a Deo, cum tamen verba versionis sint ab hominibus, qui falli & fallere potuerunt. Sic & pleraque κριτήρια tam externa, quam interna, sensum, non idioma scripturæ distincte notificant. Prob. b. Quando quæritur: Estne euangelium Matthæi græce, an hebraice primum scriptum? quæstio illa non dogmatica, sed historica est. Est enim quæstio facti, in sensus incurrentis, de quo & scriptores canonici ipsi ore, subscriptione manus, & traditione autographorum; & ipsa autographa ecclesiæ tradita, inque ea summo studio asseruata, ad sensum testabantur. Huius facti sensibilis testis est ecclesia primitiua, quæ scriptoribus in carne viuentibus sub vexillo Christi in terris militauit, eorumque αὐτόγραφα ab illorum manibus accepit; nec non ecclesia subsequens, quæ temporibus proxime sequentibus, cum ipsa librorum canonicorum αὐτόγραφα adhuc superessent, manibus tererentur, oculisque legentium, quo essent idiomate consignata, conspicerentur, floruit. Ecclesia autem recentior de canonica scripturæ S. auctoritate testari per se non potest; sed si testari velit, necesse est, vt ad ecclesiam primitiuam atque subsequentem recurrat, & ab ea testimonium textus authentici mutuo sumat. Sic ab ecclesia iudaica hebræi idiomatis in veteri, & ab ecclesia christiana primitiua textus originalis græci in nouo testamento testimonium petimus. Prob. c. Lubentes acceptamus testimonium ecclesiæ primitiuæ, sed non solum illud. Adiungimus ei testimonium scripturæ, diuturnam conseruationem in vsum hominum salutarem, & stili qualitatem. (1) Vetus testamentum stilo hebraico consignatum esse, colligimus ex Rom. III, 2. vbi Paullus diserte scribit: Iudæis oracula Dei concredita esse. Ex quo effato Paullino argumentamur: Quæcunque oracula Iudæis concredita sunt, vt per ea sapientes redderentur in salutem per fidem, quæ est in Christo Iesu, illa ipsis concredita sunt idiomate hebræo. Atqui, oracula Dei in sacro codice veteris testamenti comprehensa &c. Ergo. Maior constat, quia per nulla oracula, nulla dicta, homo, aut tota natio sapiens reddi potest in salutem, nisi verba vel oracula proponantur homini, vel nationi, idiomate familiari & vernaculo, quod illa natio intelligit, atque adeo sibi ad salutarem vsum applicare potest. Minor liquet ex citato dicto Paullino, Rom. III, 2. collato cum effato eiusdem apostoli, 2 Tim. III, 15. Applicamus testimonium Paulli ad linguam græcam noui testamenti, & probabiliter colligimus: Quæcunque oracula concredita sunt omnibus gentibus, vt per ea sapientes redderentur in salutem per fidem, quæ est in Christo Iesu, ea lingua græca illis concredita funt. Atqui, oracula Christi & apostolorum in sacro codice noui testamenti comprehensa &c. Ergo. Maioris connexio ostenditur. Quemadmodum Deus & prophetæ oracula sua concrediderunt Iudæis lingua ipsis vernacula, quam omnes Iudæi intelligebant, nempe hebræa: ita Christus & apostoli sua oracula concrediderunt omnibus gentibus per totum terrarum orbem latissime diffusis lingua vulgatissima, omnibusque gentibus notissima, nempe græca, vt per eam omnes gentes sapientes redderentur ad salutem. Grauiter inquit CICERO in Orat pro Archia poëta: Græca leguntur in omnibus fere gentibus, latina suis finibus, exiguis sane, continentur. (2) Si controuersia exoriatur de idiomate primigenio alicuius amanuensis sacri, illa non semper solide dirimi potest citra coadhibita alia argumenta. Id quod patescit ex quæstione de primitiuo euangelii Matthæi idiomate ventilata: sitne illud primitus hebraice, an græce consignatum? Nam HVGO GROTIVS in præloquio in euangelium Matthæi refert, piam antiquitatem maxima consensione docere πρωτότυπον euangelii Matthæi fuisse hebraicum. In quam sententiam adducit PAPIAM, IRENAEVM, ORIGENEM, PANTAENVM, HIERONYMVM, & EPIPHANIVM. Nihilominus collaudat GROTIVS versionem græcam, quæ hodie frequentatur, inquiens: De versionis græcæ ab ipso christianisini initio receptæ auctoritate ac fide dubitare, nefas arbitror. D. CALOVIVS contra dimicans pro authentia textus græci HVG. GROTIVM refutatum it argumento petito a prouidentia diuina, in bibl. illustrat. tom. I. in nouum testamentum fol. 140. „GROTIVS non dubitandum esse dicit de versionis græcæ „Matthæi auctoritate & fide: sed si non habemus ipsum πρωτότυπον diuina prouidentia con„seruatum, quod in vsum canonicum ecclesiæ destinatum erat diuinitus, quomodo certi esse „poterimus, siue de fide & auctoritate translationis, siue de conseruatione eiusdem perenni & „intemerata? Verbum Dei non periturum credimus, ac ne iota quidem, vel apicem eius interire „posse, verbo Christi secure fidem adhibemus, sed de translationum conseruatione nullam „promissionem habemus.„ Quin etiam HOTTINGERVS systemat. theol. lib. 1. loc. 3. citante CALOVIO, vrget hoc, quod nuspiam exstet hebraicum euangelium Matthæi authenticum: Periisse autem ipsum textum originalem prouidentiæ diuinæ repugnet.

(3) Quod si quis èa polleat ingenii acie, eaque cognitione hebrææ & græcæ linguarum imbutus sit, vt textum hebræum veteris, & græcum noui testamenti penitus inspicere & meditari sciat, absque vlla hæsitatione crediturus est, vtrumque idioma esse originale, authenticum, immediate a Deo inspirante profectum. Fidem ipsi faciet vtriusque stili conformitas, simplicitas, grauitas, & singularis verborum emphasiss.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum asserentium, auctoritatem S. scripturæ canonicam quoad nos vnice dependere ab auctoritate & testimonio ecclesiæ; quorum argumenta sunt:


### Quest. XXXIV. What is: 1. The church has the power of constituting the canon

1. The church has the power of constituting the canon.

Therefore, the canon of Scripture depends upon the church. Resp. The canon of Scripture denotes either the canonical books, or the catalog or number of the canonical books. The church historically recounts this. But the catalog of canonical books is not an article of faith. Many have been imbued with true faith and saved who were ignorant of this catalog or number of canonical books.

2. Nowhere in Holy Scripture does it exist which books are canonical. Therefore, the testimony of the church is a condition without which the canonical authority of the biblical books cannot be known. Resp. The canonical books are Holy Scripture itself, which testifies to its own authority by its inherent efficacy, with the Holy Spirit concurring, working in our hearts, just as the sun testifies of itself by its rays, and fire by its heat.

3. The church alone testifies concerning the primitive idiom of Holy Scripture. Therefore, the canonical authority of Holy Scripture regarding the primitive idiom depends upon the church as far as we are concerned. Resp. The church testifies concerning the primitive idiom of Holy Scripture, not just any church, but the primitive one; but not the church alone. See the proof in ch.

4. Nowhere in the sacred code does it exist: This book is truly the Gospel of Matthew: this epistle is truly Paul’s. Perhaps it might happen that someone would propose a false epistle to me, and assert that this very one is a Pauline epistle. Therefore, so that I may not be deceived, I have need of the testimony of the church. Resp. Distinguish between the historical and dogmatic question. The question: Is the Gospel of Matthew Matthew’s? is historical, for resolving which the testimony of the church must be entirely admitted; but the question: Is the Gospel of Matthew a canonical writing? is a dogmatic question, to be decided from the internal and external κριτηρίοις [criteria] of the canonical writers.

Latin:

1. Ecclesia habet potestatem constituendi

canonem. E. Canon scripturæ ab ecclesia dependet. Resp. Canon scripturæ vel notat libros canonicos, vel catalogum siue numerum librorum canonicorum. Hunc ecclesia historice recenset. Sed catalogus librorum canonicorum non est articulus fidei. Multi vera sunt imbuti fide & saluati, qui catalogum siue numerum librorum canonicorum hunc ignorarunt.

2. Nullibi exstat in sacra scriptura, quinam libri sint canonici. Ergo ecclesiæ testimonium est conditio, sine qua non cognosci potest canonica librorum biblicorum auctoritas. Resp. Libri canonici sunt ipsa S. scriptura, quæ testatur de sua auctoritate insita sua efficacia, concurrente Spiritu sancto, in cordibus nostris operosa, haud secus ac sol radiis suis, ignis calore suo de seipso testatur.

3. De idiomate primitiuo S. scripturæ sola testatur ecclesia. Ergo canonica S. scripturæ auctoritas ratione idiomatis primitiui ab ecclesia quoad nos dependet. Resp. De idiomate primitiuo S. scripturæ testatur ecclesia non qualislibet, sed primitiua; at non sola. Vid. probat. c.

4. Nullibi in sacro codice exstat: Hic liber vere est euangelium Matthæi: hæc epistola vere est Paulli. Fortean contingeret, vt mihi quispiam falsam proponeret epistolam, & assereret, hanc ipsam esse epistolam Paullinam. Quare ne decipiar, testimonio ecclesiæ mihi opus est. Resp. Dist. inter quæstionem historicam & dogmaticam. Quæstio: An euangelium Matthæi sit Matthæi? est historica; ad quam resoluendam testimonium ecclesiæ omnino admittendum est: sed quæstio: an euangelium Matthæi sit scriptum canonicum? est quæstio dogmatica decidenda ex internis & externis κριτηρίοις scriptorum canonicorum.


### XXXVI. How are the biblical books divided?

Biblical books are divided into canonical and apocryphal (*). Canonical books are those whose doctrine and individual words were recorded by prophets and apostles from the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit, inasmuch as they were communicated by God to the church and received by it, so that they might be an infallible rule of faith and morals for saving man.

Latin:

Libri biblici diuiduntur in canonicos & apocryphos (*). Libri canonici sunt, quorum & doctrina & verba singula ex immediata Spiritus sancti inspiratione a prophetis & apostolis sunt consignata, quippe ecclesiæ a Deo sunt communicati, & ab ea recepti, vt essent homini saluando infallibilis regula fidei & morum.


### XXXVII. How are the canonical books divided?

Some canonical books are of the Old, others of the New Testament. The former are those which, from the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit, were written before Christ was born by prophets in the Hebrew language, entrusted to the Israelite church, and received by it, so that they might be an infallible norm of things to be believed and done. The latter are those which, from the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit, were recorded by the apostles in the Greek language, entrusted to the Christian church, and received by it, so that they might be a perpetual rule of faith and life.

Obs. I. Biblical books can be divided (α) by reason of the ministerial cause into prophetic and apostolic, from Eph. II, 20; (β) by reason of time into books of the Old and New Testament; (γ) by reason of form and normative use into canonical and apocryphal. The last distinction is most worthy of note.

Obs. II. The canonical books of the Old Testament agree with the canonical books of the New Testament (α) by reason of the principal cause, God, from whom they proceeded, 2 Pet. I, 21; 2 Tim. III, 16; (β) by reason of the primary object, which is Christ, John V, 39; Acts X, 43; (γ) by reason of canonical use, Luke XVI, 29; 2 Tim. III, 15, 16.

Obs. III. The canonical books of the Old and New Testament differ (α) by reason of the ministerial cause. For the books of the Old Testament were written by prophets predicting the coming Messiah: the books of the N.T. were recorded by apostles testifying of Christ exhibited in the flesh. (β) By reason of the subject that received them. The books of the O.T. were entrusted to the Israelite church, Rom. III, 2; the books of the N.T. were entrusted to the Christian church gathered from all nations, John XX, 31. Yet the Christian church also received the canonical books of the O.T. because of the most beautiful harmony of the prophetic and apostolic writings, their remarkable utility, and especially because of the command of Christ, John V, 39. (γ) By reason of idiom: because the books of the O.T. were written in the Hebrew language (and in certain parts in Chaldean, which is a dialect of it), which the Jews understood as their vernacular: the books of the N.T. were written in the Greek language, as the most known and most used in that age. (δ) By reason of perspicuity, in that the N.T. is clearer than the Old Testament. There is a disparity regarding the degrees of perspicuity; but not a diversity regarding the object of revelation, as if other things necessary to be believed were explicitly handed down here than there; since faith is the same in both places.

Eph. IV, 16. Q. XXXVIII. How many kinds of canonical books of the Old Testament are there?

Of the canonical books of the Old Testament, some are legal, some historical, some dogmatic, some prophetic. The legal are the Pentateuch, or the five books of Moses, namely Genesis, having 50 chapters.

Exodus, 40 chapters. Leviticus, 27 chapters. Numbers, 36 chapters. And Deuteronomy, 34 chapters. The historical are the book of Joshua, having 24 chapters. Judges, 21 chapters. Ruth, 4 chapters. First Samuel, 31 chapters. Second Samuel, 24 chapters. First Kings, 22 chapters. Second Kings, 25 chapters. First Paralipomenon, or Chronicles, 30 chapters. Second Paralipomenon, 36 chapters. The book of Ezra, 10 chapters. Nehemiah, 8 chapters. Esther, 10 chapters.

The dogmatic (which are also called poetical) are the book of Job, 42 chapters. The Book of Psalms, 150. The three books of Solomon: Proverbs, 31 chapters. Ecclesiastes, 12 chapters.

Song of Songs, 8 chapters. The prophetic are those of the prophets, some of whom are called major, who produced more extensive works; some minor, who produced more concise ones. The major are four: Isaiah, having 66 chapters. Jeremiah, 52 chapters, to whom also belong the Lamentations, 5 chapters. Ezekiel, 48 chapters. Daniel, 12 chapters. The minor are twelve: Hosea, 14 chapters. Joel, 3 chapters. Amos, 9 chapters. Obadiah, 1 chapter. Jonah, 4 chapters. Micah, 7 chapters. Nahum, 3 chapters. Habakkuk, 3 chapters. Zephaniah, 3 chapters. Haggai, 2 chapters. Zechariah, 14 chapters. Malachi, 4 chapters.

Latin:

Libri canonici alii sunt veteris, alii noui testamenti. Illi sunt, qui ex immediata Spiritus sancti inspiratione ante Christum natum a prophetis lingua hebræa conscripti, ecclesiæ Israëliticæ commendati, & ab ea recepti sunt, vt essent infallibilis norma credendorum & agendorum. Hi sunt, qui ex immediata Spiritus sancti inspiratione ab apostolis sermone græco consignati ecclesiæ christianæ commendati, & ab ea recepti sunt, vt perpetua sint regula fidei & vitæ.

Obs. I. Possunt libri biblici (α) ratione caussæ ministerialis diuidi in propheticos & apostolicos, ex Eph. II, 20. (β) ratione temporis in libros veteris & noui testamenti: (γ) ratione formæ & vsus normalis in canonicos & apocryphos. Vltima distinctio notatu dignissima est.

Obs. II. Conueniunt libri canonici vet. testamenti cum libris canonicis noui testamenti (α) ratione caussæ principalis Dei, a quo profecti, 2 Petr. I, 21. 2 Tim. III, 16. (β) ratione obiecti primarii, quod est Christus, Io. V, 39. Act. X, 43. (γ) ratione vsus canonici. Luc. XVI, 29. 2 Tim. III, 15. 16.

Obs. III. Differunt libri canonici veteris & noui testamenti (α) ratione caussæ ministerialis. Nam libri vet. testam. conscripti sunt a prophetis venturum Messiam prædicentibus: libri N. T. consignati sunt ab apostolis, de Christo in carne exhibito testantibus. (β) Ratione subiecti, quod illos recepit. Libri V. T. concrediti sunt ecclesiæ Israëliticæ, Rom. III, 2. libri N. T. commendati sunt ecclesiæ christianæ ex omnibus gentibus collectæ, Io. XX, 31. Recepit tamen etiam ecclesia christiana libros canonicos V. T. ob pulcherrimam harmoniam scriptorum propheticorum & apostolicorum, insignem eorum vtilitatem, & inprimis ob mandatum Christi, Io. V, 39. (γ) Ratione idiomatis: quia libri V. T. scripti sunt lingua hebraica (& in particulis quibusdam chaldaica, quæ illius est dialectus), quam ceu vernaculam Iudæi intelligebant: libri N. T. scripti sunt lingua græca, ceu notissima & vsitatissima ea ætate. (δ) Ratione perspicuitatis, eo quod N. T. clarius est veteri testamento. Est disparitas, quoad gradus perspicuitatis; non autem diuersitas, quoad obiectum reuelationis, quasi hic alia creditu necessaria explicite tradita essent, quam illic; quum fides vtrobique eadem sit.

Eph. IV, 16. Quaest. XXXVIII. Quotuplices sunt libri canonici veteris testamenti?

Librorum canonicorum veteris testamenti alii sunt legales, alii historici, alii dogmatici, alii prophetici. Legales sunt pentateuchus, sive quinque libri Mosis, nempe Genesis, habens capita

L. Exodus, cap. XL. Leviticus, cap. XXVII. Numeri, cap. XXXVI. & Deuteronomium, cap. XXXIV. Historici sunt liber Iosuae, habens capita XXIV. Iudicum, cap. XXI. Ruth, cap. IV. prior Samuelis, cap. XXXI. posterior Samuelis, cap. XXIV. prior Regum, cap. XXII. posterior Regum, cap. XXV. prior Paralipomenon, sive Chronicorum, cap. XXX. posterior Paralipomenon, cap. XXXVI. Liber Esdrae, cap. X. Nehemiae, cap. VIII. Esther,

cap. X. Dogmatici (qui etiam poetici dicuntur) sunt liber Iobi, cap. XLII. Liber Psalmorum, CL. Tres libri Salomonis: Proverbia, cap. XXXI. Ecclesiastes, cap. XII. Canticum canticorum,

cap. XII. Prophetici sunt prophetarum, quorum quidam dicuntur maiores, qui prolixiora ediderunt opera; quidam minores, qui arctiora ediderunt. Maiores sunt quatuor: Esaias, habens capita LXVI. Ieremias, cap. LII. cuius etiam sunt Threni, cap. V. Ezechiel, cap. LXII. Daniel, cap. XII. Minores sunt duodecim: Hoseas, cap. XIV. Ioel, cap. III. Amos, cap. IX. Obadias, cap. I. Ionas, cap. IV. Micheas, cap. VII. Nahum, cap. III. Habacuc, cap. IV. Zephanias, cap. III. Haggaeus, cap. II. Zacharias, cap. XIV. Malachias,


### Q. XXXIX. How are the canonical books of the New Testament divided?

The canonical books of the New Testament are distinguished into historical, dogmatic, and prophetic. The historical books describe either the life and deeds of Christ, namely the four evangelists: Matthew, consisting of 28 chapters.

Mark, 16 chapters. Luke, 24 chapters. John, 21 chapters. Or the life and deeds of the apostles, namely the Acts of the Apostles, 28 chapters. The dogmatic, or doctrinal, are the epistles written by the apostles.

The epistles of Paul are 14: to the Romans, 16 chapters. First to the Corinthians, 16 chapters. Second to the Corinthians, 13 chapters. To the Galatians, 6 chapters. To the Ephesians, 6 chapters. To the Philippians, 4 chapters. To the Colossians, 4 chapters. First to the Thessalonians, 5 chapters. Second to the Thessalonians, 3 chapters. First to Timothy, 6 chapters. Second to Timothy, 4 chapters. One to Titus, 3 chapters. One to Philemon, 1 chapter. To the Hebrews, 13 chapters. The epistles of Peter are two: the first having 5 chapters, the second, 3 chapters. The epistles of John are three: the first having 5 chapters, the second 1 chapter, the third 1 chapter. There is one epistle of James, having 5 chapters. There is one epistle of Jude, 1 chapter. Finally, the prophetic book is the Apocalypse of John, which is completed in 22 chapters.

Obs. The books of the New Testament are distinguished by some into πρωτοκανονικοὺς (protocanonical), concerning whose authority there has never been any doubt, and δευτεροκανονικοὺς (deuterocanonical), whose authority has been called into doubt by some particular churches. Of this order are the latter epistle of Peter, the second and third of John, the epistle to the Hebrews, James, Jude, and the Apocalypse. There are those who maintain that the pious ancients doubted not so much of their canonical authority as of their secondary authors. See D. HILDEBRAND, in instit. theol. p. 68. But since today all evangelical doctors assign divine authority to these deuterocanonical books, there seems to be no need at all for this distinction.

Latin:

Libri canonici novi testamenti distinguuntur in historicos, dogmaticos & propheticum. Libri historici describunt vel vitam & res gestas Christi, vtpote quatuor euangelistae: Matthaeus, constans ex capitibus

XXVIII. Marcus, cap. XVI. Lucas, cap. XXIV. Ioannes, cap. XXI. vel vitam & res gestas apostolorum, nempe Acta apostolica, cap. XXVIII. Dogmatici, sive doctrinales, sunt epistolae ab apostolis scriptae.

Epistolae Paulli sunt XIV. ad Romanos, cap. XVI. prior ad Corinthios, cap. XVI. posterior ad Corinthios, cap. XIII. ad Galatas, cap. VI. ad Ephesios, cap. VI. ad Philippenses, cap. IV. ad Colossenses, cap. IV. prior ad Thessalonicenses, cap. V. posterior ad Thess. cap. III. prior ad Tim. cap. VI. posterior ad Timotheum, cap. IV. vna ad Titum, cap. III. vna ad Philemonem, cap. I. ad Hebraeos, cap. XIII. Epistolae Petri sunt duae: prior habens cap. V. posterior, cap. III. Epistola Ioannis sunt tres: prima habens cap. V. altera cap. I. tertia cap. I. vna est epistola Iacobi, habens cap. V. vna est epistola Iudae, cap. I. Liber denique propheticus est apocalypsis Ioannis, quae capitibus XXII. absoluitur.

Obs. Libri novi testamenti a nonnullis distinguuntur in πρωτοκανονικοὺς, de quorum auctoritate nunquam est dubitatum, & δευτεροκανονικοὺς, quorum auctoritas a nonnullis ecclesiis particularibus in dubium vocata est. Huius ordinis sunt posterior epistola Petri, secunda & tertia Ioannis, epistola ad Hebræos, Iacobi, Iudæ, Apocalypsis. Sunt, qui statuunt, pios veteres non tam de canonica eorum auctoritate, quam de illorum auctoribus secundariis dubitasse. Vid. D. HILDEBRAND. in instit. theol. p. 68. At cum hodie evangelici doctores omnes deuterocanonicis istis divinam auctoritatem assignent, distinctione isthac minime opus esse videtur.


### Quæst. XL. Which books are apocryphal?

Apocryphal books are those which exist in the codex, indeed, but not in the biblical canon, and were not written by the immediate inspiration of God; and thus they are read publicly and usefully in the church not for the proof of articles of faith, but for the edification of morals; and they are either entire books, or parts and appendices of the sacred books. Entire books are either historical or didactic. The historical are Tobias, having 14 chapters; Judith, ch. 16; Baruch, ch. 5; the first of Maccabees, ch. 16; the second of Maccabees, ch. 15; the third of Maccabees, ch. 7; the third book of Esdras, ch. 9; the fourth book of Esdras, ch. 16. The didactic are the book of Wisdom, having 19 chapters; Ecclesiasticus or Siracides, ch. 51. Appendices of the books are the epistle of Jeremiah annexed to Baruch, ch. 1; additions to Daniel, ch. 3; the Supplement to Esther, ch. 7; the Prayer of Manasseh, ch. 1.

Obs. I. Apocryphal books are called ἀπὸ τῦ ἀποκρύπτειν (from hiding), from hiding or concealing, because their hidden origin was not clear to those by whose testimony the authority of the true scriptures has reached us, AUGUSTINE, book 2, against Faustus, ch. 1. Their origin is said to be hidden because it can be proven by no criterion, by no clear indication, nor by any certain argument, that they were immediately inspired by the Holy Spirit. Rather, it can be shown that they are not of immediate divine origin, because 1) the canonical books of the Old Testament were written in the Hebrew idiom: but the apocryphal books appeared in the Greek language. 2) The canonical books of the Old Testament bear witness to the coming Messiah, Acts 10:43, but none of the apocryphal books testify anything about the coming Messiah. 3) The θεόπνευσοι (God-breathed) authors were so immune from error that they were even exempt from the danger of erring: on the contrary, the writers of the apocryphal books feared for themselves regarding errors, and pray for pardon for them. Siracides does this in the prologue, and the author of the book of 2 Maccabees, ch. 15:39. Indeed, not insignificant errors are noted in them. In the book of Tobias, there is the lie of the angel, ch. 5:18, ch. 11:3; superstition, ch. 6:8. The book of Wisdom clearly treats things that are from Platonic philosophy. And although it has the title of Solomon, it is nevertheless Philo's. It uses a style of speaking that savors of Plato's philosophy, in the opinion of IO. ADAM OSIANDER, in collect. system. theol. part 1, p. 119. An error is noted in it, ch. 16:21, compared with Exod. 16:31, Num. 11:8. In the book of Judith, ch. 9:2, the deed of Simeon is approved as praiseworthy, which, however, Jacob himself on his deathbed accused as a disgrace, Gen. 49:5. The second book of Maccabees, ch. 14:42, 43, 46, commends the αὐτοχειρίαν (suicide) of Razias, etc. 4) The canon of the Old Testament contains 22 books, according to JOSEPHUS, book 1, against Apion, as many as there are letters of the Hebrew alphabet. This canon is tripartite, divided into the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa: which partition was known even then in the time of Christ, and was approved by Him, Luke 14:44. In which

In the tripartition of the Jews, the books of Tobias, Wisdom, Judith, etc., are not found (*). 5) The primitive Christian church reviews and approves the biblical canon of the Old Testament in the same manner, order, and number as our church. For the Synod of Laodicea, gathered around the year of Christ 364 from various provinces of Asia, defends in every respect the biblical canon which we hold. From the most ancient fathers, MELITO, Bishop of Sardis, having traveled to the East around the year of Christ 150 for the sake of investigating this matter, could not discover a canon other than ours, as EUSEBIUS reports in H. E. book IV, chapter XXV. ORIGEN in the proem to the Psalms and JEROME in the galeated prologue subscribe to Melito, as do other Greek and Latin fathers. Cf. HILDEBRAND in instit. theol. p. 65.

Objection II There are also other apocryphal writings which come under this name, because they are to be utterly hidden, and not to be read publicly in the church to the people, since they are fabulous, absurd, and impious; such as the gospel of Peter, of Thomas, of Nicodemus, the apocalypse of Peter, the acts of Paul, the shepherd of Hermas, etc. See EUSEB. lib. III. H.E.

cap. III. * Antithesis is of the Papists, who maintain that the book of Tobit, Wisdom, Sirach, etc., are to be numbered among the canonical books; who wish to fortify their opinion with the following arguments: I. The books of the Maccabees are received by the Jews themselves. Therefore they are canonical. Resp. The books of the Maccabees are received by the Jews as historical, not as θεόπνευστοι (divinely inspired). II. Those books from which the dogmas of faith are proven are canonical. From the book of Wisdom, etc. Therefore. The minor premise is clear, because the immortality of the first man is proven from Wis. II, 24. The envy of the devil brought death into the world. Resp. Distinguish between an apodictic and a topical proof. This can be sought from the apocryphal books, which is added to apodictic arguments for the sake of superabundant illustration. The immortality of the first man is proven apodictically from Gen. II, 17. Rom. V, 12. *

III. The book of Wisdom is cited in the N.T. by Paul in Rom. XI, 34. 1 Cor. II, 16. Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Which words are read in Wis. IX, 13. Therefore the book of Wisdom is canonical. Resp. 1) A mere allegation does not make a book canonical. The writings of Aratus are cited in Acts XVII, 18. Of Menander in 1 Cor. XV, 33. Of Epimenides in Tit. I, 12. Who would dare to call those canonical? 2) The words of Paul are taken from Isa. XL, 7.

IV. Whoever as a writer of the Old Testament has testified of Jesus, he was endowed with a prophetic spirit, and his writing is canonical. But Sirach, etc. Therefore. The major premise is established from Acts X, 43. The minor is evident from c. XLIII, 25 of Sirach, where this author uses the following words: At his word the wind blows, and by his thought he calmed the abyss, and the Lord Jesus planted it. Resp. No light error has been committed in the Latin Vulgate version: concerning which HUGO GROTIUS says in the place cited: you may understand from this passage how much the scribes err through ignorance or a perverse zeal for religion. For some have written: καὶ ἐφύτευσεν αὐτὴν Ἰησοῦς, which also crept into certain Latin copies: and the Lord Jesus planted it. The words of the Greek text are these: Sir. XLIII, 27. Ἐν λογισμῷ αὐτοῦ ἐκόπασεν ἄβυσσον καὶ ἐφύτευσεν ἐν αὐτῇ νήσους, by his word he made the abyss quiet, and planted islands in it. It is clear, therefore, that for νήσους (islands), it was written by some through error: Ἰησοῦς (Jesus).

V. The Papists object that the biblical canon of the books of the O.T. received by the Roman church is most ancient. For this canon is held in the Council of Trent, Sess. IV, and the fathers of that council received it by tradition from Pope Eugenius, in the Council of Florence, as can be seen in BARTH. CARANZA in his Summa Conciliorum. Again, Eugenius received it from Pope Gelasius in the Roman Council, as is evident from Vol. II of the councils, in the decree of Gelasius near the end. Again, Gelasius from Augustine, lib. II, de doctrin. christ. cap. VIII, and Augustine from the Council of Carthage III, which some call the fifth, others the sixth. Finally, the fathers of this council from Innocent, epist. III, to Exup. cap. VII. Now Innocent lived in the year of Christ 402. From that time of the primitive church, therefore, down to us, that same canon of scripture has persisted through continuous tradition, which the Papists now hold and embrace. Resp. From this discourse of the Papists it is gathered that they cannot produce any witness of their opinion from the first four centuries of the primitive church, since it is established that Innocent I, pontiff, lived in the fifth century. But truly if the Papists were going to prove their canon from antiquity, it would have to be traced back to the Israelitish church, contemporary with the prophets, which saw their autographs, and approved and received them as θεόπνευσα (divinely inspired). To this is added that in that discourse of the Papists many things are partly uncertain, partly false. For we reject the decree of the Council of Trent; seeing that in it the Roman pontiff is actor, accused party, and judge.

was: nor does the Council of Florence possess authority; inasmuch as it was celebrated only in the 15th century by Eugenius, who had been deposed from pontifical authority by the decree of the Council of Basel. The Roman Council under Gelasius is too distant from the Council of Florence, namely by nearly ten centuries, so that the continuation of that canon is seen to be openly gap-ridden. The Council of Carthage has an older one, namely the Laodicean, which fights for our canon. It is furthermore false that the pontifical canon was defined at the Council of Florence. Only Bartholomaeus Caranza affirms this; Surius does not have it, nor Carolinus, nor the tomes of the councils; Antoninus himself, Archbishop of Florence, who was σύγχρονος (contemporary) to that council, approves our canon.

VI. The Papists distinguish between the canon of the Jews and of the Christians, pretending that the controversial books are not indeed in the canon of the Jews, yet they are in that of the Christians, who, on account of the assistance of the Holy Spirit, which was promised to the church, could add them to the canonical ones. Resp. Christians neither can nor ought to accept other prophetic books than those which they received from the Jews, to whom they were entrusted, Rom. III, 2. The Christian church does not make canonical books, but only testifies concerning them. The assistance of the Holy Spirit was promised to the church not absolutely, but hypothetically, insofar as it does not deflect from the means through which the Holy Spirit operates.

Latin:

Libri apocryphi sunt, qui in codice quidem, sed non in canone biblico exstant, neque immediato Dei afflatu scripti sunt; adeoque non ad articulorum fidei probationem, sed ad morum ædificationem in ecclesia publice & utiliter leguntur; suntque vel libri integri, vel partes & appendices librorum sacrorum. Libri integri vel sunt historici, vel didactici. Historici sunt Tobias, habens capita XIV. Iudith, cap. XVI. Baruch, cap. V. primus Maccabæorum, cap. XVI. secundus Maccabæorum, cap. XV. tertius Maccabæorum, cap. VII. Liber tertius Esdræ, cap. IX. Liber IV. Esdræ, cap. XVI. Didactici sunt liber sapientiæ, habens capita XIX. Ecclesiasticus vel Siracides, cap. LI. Appendices librorum sunt epistola Ieremiæ Baruch annexa cap. I. additamenta ad Danielem, cap. III. Supplementum Esther, cap. VII. Oratio Manassis, cap. I.

Obs. I. Libri apocryphi dicuntur ἀπὸ τῦ ἀποκρύπτειν, ab occultando, vel abscondendo, propterea quod occulta eorum origo non claruit illis, quorum testificatione verarum scripturarum auctoritas ad nos pervenit, AVGUSTIN. libr. II. contr. Faust. cap. 1. Occulta eorum dicitur origo, quia nullo κριτηρίῳ, nullo luculento indicio ant certo argumento probari potest, illos immediate a Spiritu S. inspiratos esse. Quin potius ostendi potest, eos non esse originis divinæ immediatæ, quia 1) libri canonici veteris testamenti hebræo idiomate sunt scripti: at libri apocryphi prodierunt sermone græco. 2) Libri canonici vet. testam. venturo Messiæ testimonium perhibent, Act. X, 43 at librorum apocryphorum nullus quidquam de Messia venturo testatur. 3) Auctores θεόπνευσοι ab errore adeo immunes fuerunt, vt etiam errandi periculo fuerint exemti: contra scriptores librorum apocryphorum metuerunt sibi ab erratis, eorumque veniam precantur. Facit hoc Siracides in prologo, & auctor libr. 2 Maccab. c. XV. 39. Quin haud exigui in iis errores notantur. In libro Tobiæ habetur mendacium angeli c. V, 18. c. XI, 3. superstitio c. VI, 8. Liber sapientiæ plane tractat ea, quæ sunt ex philosophia Platonica. Et licet habeat titulum Salomonis, tamen est Philonis. Utitur dicendi genere tali, quod Platonis sapit philosophiam, censente IO. ADAM. OSIANDR. in collect. system. theol. part. I p. 119. Notatur in ipso error c. XVI, 21. collat. cum Exod. XVI, 31. Num. XI, 8. In libro Iudith c. IX, 2. factum Simeonis tanquam laudabile approbatur, quod tamen ipse Iacobus moribundus probri incusavit, Gen. XLIX, 5. Liber II. Maccab. c. XIV, 42. 43. 46. commendat αὐτοχειρίαν Rhaziæ &c. 4) Canon vet. testam. libros XXII. teste IOSEPHO libr. 1. contra Appionem continet, quot sunt alphabeti Hebræorum litteræ. Tripartito est hic canon, in legem, prophetas & hagiographa divisus: quæ partitio iam tum Christi tempore nota, sic & ab eodem approbata fuit, Luc. XIV, 44. In qua

Iudæorum tripartitione non inueniuntur libri Tobiæ, Sapientiæ, Iudithæ &c. (*). 5) Primitiua ecclesia christiana canonem biblicum vet. testam. eodem modo, ordine & numero, quo nostra ecclesia, recenset & approbat. Etenim synodus Laodicena, circa annum Christi 364. ex diuersis Asiæ prouinciis collecta, canonem biblicum, quem nos tenemus, per omnia tuetur. Ex antiquissimis patribus MELITO Sardicensis Episcopus circa annum Christi 150. huius rei scifcitandæ caussa in orientem profectus, alium a nostro canonem indagare non potuit, referente EVSEBIO lib. IV. H. E. cap. XXV. Subscribunt Melitoni ORIGENES in proœm. Psalm. & HIERONYMVS in prologo galeato, nec non alii græci & latini patres. Conf. HILDEBRAND. in instit theol. p. 65.

*Obiectio II Sunt & alia scripta apocrypha, quæ hoc nomine veniunt, quod prorsus sunt abscondenda, nec in ecclesia populo prælegenda, cum sint fabulosa, absurda, impia; qualia sunt euangelium Petri, Thomæ, Nicodemi, apocalypsis Petri, acta Paulli, pastor Hermæ &c. Vid. EVSEB. lib. III. H.E.

cap. III. .* Antithesis est Pontificiorum statuentium, librum Tobiæ, Sapientiæ, Siracidæ &c. libris canonicis annumerandos esse; qui suam opinionem sequentibus munitam volunt argumentis: I. Libri Maccabæorum ab ipsis Iudæis recipiuntur. Ergo sunt canonici. Resp. Libri Maccabæorum recipiuntur a Iudæis vt historici, non vt θεόπνευστοι. II. Ex quibus libris dogmata fidei probantur, illi sunt canonici. Ex libro Sapientiæ &c. Ergo. Minor liquet, quia immortalitas primi hominis probatur ex Sap. II, 24. Inuidia diaboli mors intrauit in mundum. Resp. Dist. inter probationem apodicticam & topicam. Hæc ex libris apocryphis peti potest, quæ argumentis apodicticis ex abundanti illustrationis ergo adiicitur. Apodictice primi hominis immortalitas probatur ex Gen. II, 17. Rom. V, 12. *

III. Liber sapientiæ citatur in Nou.* Test. a Paullo Rom. XI, 34. 1 Cor. II, 16. Quis mentem domini cognouit? Aut quis illi fuit a consiliis? Quæ verba leguntur Sap. IX, 13. Ergo liber sapientiæ est canonicus. Resp. 1) Nuda allegatio non facit librum canonicum. Citantur scripta Arati Act. XVII, 18. Menandri 1 Cor. XV, 33. Epimenidis Tit. I, 12. Ecquis ausit illa appellare canonica? 2) Verba Paulli depromta sunt ex Es. XL, 7.

8. IV. Quicunque scriptor veteris testamenti testatus est de Iesu, ille spiritu prophetico fuit donatus, illiusque scriptum est canonicum. Atqui Siracides &c. Ergo. Maior constat ex Act. X, 43. Minor patet ex c. XLIII, 25. Siracidæ, vbi hic auctor sequentibus vtitur verbis: In sermone eius fluit ventus, & cogitatione sua placauit abyssum, & plantauit illam dominus Iesus. Resp. Haud leuis commissus est error in vulgata versione latina: de quo HVGO GROTIVS in hunc locum citatum: quantum peccent scribæ per ignorantiam aut studium peruersum religionis, ex hoc loco intelligas. Quidam enim scripsere: καὶ ἐφύτευσεν αὐτὴν Ἰησοῦς, quod & in quadam exemplaria latina irrepsit: & plantauit illam dominus Iesus. Verba textus græci hæc sunt: Sir. XLIII, 27. Ἐν λογισμῷ αὐτοῦ ἐκόπασεν ἄβυσσον καὶ ἐφύτευσεν ἐν αὐτῇ νήσους, oratione sua quiescere fecit abyssum, & plantauit in ea insulas. Patet ergo, pro νήσους, insulas, scriptum esse ab aliquibus per errorem: Ἰησοῦς.

V. Obiiciunt Pontificii, canonem biblicum librorum V. T. ab ecclesia Romana receptum esse antiquissimum. Nam hic canon habetur in concilio Tridentino Sess. IV. & patres illius concilii acceperunt illum per traditionem ab Eugenio Papa, in concilio Florentino, vt videre est apud BARTH. CARANZAM. in summa conciliorum. Rursum Eugenius accepit illum a Gelasio Papa in concilio Romano, vt patet ex II. tom. concil. in decr. Gelas. circa finem. Iterum Gelasius ab Augustino lib. II. de doctrin. christ. cap. VIII. & Augustinus a concilio Carthag. III. quod alii quintum, alii sextum vocant. Denique patres huius concilii ab Innocentio epist. III. ad Exup. cap. VII. Vixit autem Innocentius anno C. 402. Ab illo igitur tempore primitiuæ ecclesiæ ad nos vsque per continuam traditionem perfeuerat idem ille scripturæ canon, quem pontificii nunc tenent & amplectuntur. Resp. Ex hoc discursu pontificiorum colligitur, ipsos non posse ex prioribus seculis IV. primitiuæ ecclesiæ vllum testem suæ sententiæ producere, cum constet, Innocentium I. pontificem vixisse seculo V. At vero si ex antiquitate probaturi essent pontificii canonem suum, repetendus ille foret ab ecclesia Isrælitica prophetis coæua, quæ illorum vidit autographa, eaque vt θεόπνευσα approbauit & recepit. Huc accedit, quod in illo discursu pontificiorum multa sint partim incerta, partim falsa. Reiicimus enim decretum concilii Tridentini; quippe in quo pontifex Romanus actor, reus & iudex.

fuit: neque concilium Florentinum auctoritate pollet; utpote quod seculo demum XV. celebratum est ab Eugenio, qui decreto concilii Basileensis a pontificali auctoritate deiectus erat. Concilium Romanum sub Gelasio nimis distat a concilio Florentino, decem scil. prope seculis, ut continuatio istius canonis aperte videatur hiulca. Concilium Carthaginense antiquius habet, nempe Laodicenum, quod pro nostro militat canone. Falsum est insuper in concilio Florentino definitum esse canonem pontificium. Solus Bartholomaeus Caranza hoc affirmat; non habet Surius, non Carolinus, non tomi conciliorum; ipse Antonius, Archiepiscopus Florentinus, concilio illi σύγχρονος, nostrum canonem probat.

VI. Distinguunt Pontificii inter canonem Iudaeorum & christianorum, praetendentes libros controversos non quidem esse in canone Iudaeorum, attamen christianorum, qui propter assistentiam Spiritus sancti, quae promissa est ecclesiae, eos addere canonicis potuit. Resp. Christiani nec possunt, nec debent alios libros propheticos acceptare, quam quos acceperunt a Iudaeis, quibus illi sunt concrediti, Rom. III, 2. Ecclesia christiana libros canonicos non facit, sed tantum de iis testatur. Assistentia Spiritus sancti promissa est ecclesiae non absolute, sed hypothetice, quatenus a mediis, per quae Spiritus sanctus operatur, non deflectit.


### Q. XLI. Is the biblical canon so perfect without defect that no canonical book has perished?

The biblical canon persists so entire and uninjured to this very day, that not even one book divinely destined for the normal use of faith and morals, and received by the primitive church, has perished.

Prob. I. Divine providence has so watched over the θεοπνεύστοις (God-breathed) and canonical books that it has not allowed even a dot of the law to perish, Matt. V, 17. Therefore, much less has it permitted entire books to perish.

II. John the Theologian closed and sealed the entire canon, so that under the penalty of eternal damnation nothing can be added or diminished.

Rev. XXII, 19. III. The church would not have been a diligent and faithful treasurer and guardian of the deposit entrusted to it, if it had not cautiously ensured that all canonical books were propagated to posterity uninjured and entire.

The antithesis is that of the Papists asserting that certain canonical books have perished.

For in their opinion there perished I. The Book of Enoch, of which St. Jude makes mention in his epistle v. 14.

II. The Book of the Wars of the Lord. Num. XXI, 14.

III. The Book of the Just. Josh. X, 13. 2 Sam. I, 18.

IV. The Book of the Judgment of the Kingdom. 1 Sam. X, 25.

V. The Book of Solomon. 1 Kings IV, 32.

VI. The Book of the Words of the Days of Solomon. 1 Kings XI, 41. likewise the Book of the Words of the Days of Judah and Israel. 1 Kings XIV, 19.

VII. The books of the prophets Nathan and Gad. 1 Chron. XXIX, 26.

VIII. The Lamentations of Jeremiah for King Josiah. 2 Chron. XXXV, 25.

IX. The first epistle to the Corinthians. 1 Cor. V, 9. For the apostle says: I wrote to you in an epistle, not to associate with fornicators.

not to associate with fornicators. X. The Epistle to the Laodiceans. Col. IV, 16.

Resp. a) In general, by distinguishing between sacred and canonical books. Not all sacred books were written for the purpose of constituting a perpetual canon of faith and morals, and these could perish by God’s permission: but canonical books were divinely destined as a perpetual canon of things to be believed and done and were commended to the church, and these could not perish through divine providence.

Those books which the Papists deem to be lost either were not canonical, or, if they were in the canon, we deny that they have perished, but judge that they exist to this day in the biblical canon under other names.

Resp. b) In particular, to I. St. Jude makes mention of the prophecy of Enoch, but does not assert that it was committed to writing. It became known, therefore, to this apostle from the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

To II. The Book of the Wars of the Lord was not a prophetic or canonical book, but a political one, in which the wars of the Lord waged by the Israelites were described; which were described by the Israelites; which perished without the diminution of the biblical canon.

To III. By the book of Jasher (ספר הישר), some understand a political book concerning law and duty; others understand a book of forensic annals, which perished while the biblical canon remained intact.

To IV. The book of the acts of the kingdom is held in 1 Sam.

VIII. But if it were different from this, it was never in the canon.

To V. Solomon is said to have spoken 3,000 proverbs.

By these proverbs are understood the proverbs of Solomon, which either all, or the better part, exist today. If anyone should contend that there are other proverbs than those which survive, we say that they were never in the canon: just as Solomon’s proverbs concerning physical things were never inserted into the biblical canon.

To VI. The book of the words of the days of Judah and Israel was either the book of chronicles, or it was never received into the canon (*).

To VII. Nathan and Gad recorded the books of Samuel and Kings.

To VIII. In the cited place, mention is made of Jeremiah’s lamentation for King Josiah; but it is not asserted that it was committed to writing.

To IX. The apostle says: "Εγραψα ὑμῖν ἐν τῇ ἐπιστολῇ, I wrote to you in this letter: it is therefore understood as this very first letter.

To X. It is not said to have been written and sent πρὸς τοὺς ἐν Λαοδικείᾳ (to those in Laodicea), but written ἐν Λαοδικείᾳ (in Laodicea), which is the first to Timothy, whose subscription is: "Εγράφη ἀπὸ Λαοδικείας () (Written from Laodicea).

Question XLII. Is the biblical canon, or the authentic Hebrew text in the Old Testament and the Greek in the New Testament, preserved pure and uncorrupted?

With the provident care of God watching over it, the biblical canon has been preserved so intact and pure in all and every word (a), that neither the malice of the Jews has caused the Hebrew text of the O.

T. to be depraved (b), nor the treachery of heretics the Greek text of the N. T. to be falsified (c), nor the negligence or ignorance of copyists the original text to be corrupted in all copies (d). Proof a.

From the words of Christ, Matt. V, 18: "For amen I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, one iota or one tittle shall not pass from the law, until all be fulfilled." Regarding the words of the Savior, we observe 1) the occasion.

The Jews were accusing Christ as if He were abolishing the law: but Christ protests that He did not come to abolish, but to fulfill the law. Therefore, as certain as it is that the law was not abolished by Christ, so intact does the integrity of the scripture remain. 2) Christ’s assertion; who gravely asserted that no apex, no iota could perish.

Therefore, neither the letters, the smallest of which among the Hebrews is the iota, nor the vowel points, which are called κεραῖαι (horns) or tittles, can perish. Cf.

D. CALOV. in bibl. illustr. in h. l. fol. 187. 3) The comparison of scripture with heaven and earth.

The vast structure of heaven and earth will be dissolved before there will be any place for a universal corruption of the sacred letters.

turus. 4) The certainty of the fulfillment of the entire Scripture. From which the following argument is sought: If it cannot be certain to us concerning the fulfillment of the divine word, unless the Holy Scripture is integral, it is necessary that it be kept integral. But the former is true. Therefore, also the latter. 5) The reason of divine providence; which is the foundation of the assertion of Christ, for if the word of God were not preserved integral, neither could the church stand, which rests upon the foundation of the prophets and apostles, Eph. II, 20.

Prob. b. The Jews could not, nor did they wish to, corrupt the Hebrew text. That they could not is gathered both from the dispersion of the Jews throughout the whole world, and from the huge multitude of biblical codices described in various places, and transported most widely through very many provinces. For how could the Jews, dispersed through the most remote intervals of lands, have been able to meet and conspire to deprave so many thousands of biblical copies everywhere encountered in this universe of things? Nor did the Jews wish to corrupt the Hebrew text, whether you look at the times before Christ was born, or count the centuries after Christ was exhibited in the flesh. That they did not wish to be forgers of the Scriptures before Christ was born is clear from the fact that they are commended as depositaries of good faith, to whom τὰ λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ were entrusted, Rom. III, 2. From then it happened that Christ and the apostles urged us to the assiduous scrutiny of the prophetic Scripture, Jo. V, 39. Luc. XVI, 29. Act. XV, 21. 1 Tim. IV, 13. and from it proved the heavenly doctrine; who surely would never have kept silent about a falsification of the Hebrew text undertaken by the Jews. Nor did the Jews wish to corrupt the Hebrew codices after Christ was born. This is evident from the oracles concerning the Messiah published in the O.T., still unharmed today. If the Jews had taken up the plan of falsifying the Hebrew codex, they would certainly have attacked the prophecies concerning Christ with a headlong rush, and would have either stolen them from the Hebrew codex, or at least interpolated them. But the prophecies concerning Christ are still read today in the Hebrew codex in the same words in which they are cited by Christ and the apostles. Therefore, the Jews never intended in their minds to deprave the Hebrew text of the Old Testament. PHILO testifies in the book on the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, and from him EUSEBIUS lib. 3. H. E. cap. X. that up to his own times, through a space of more than two thousand years, not even a word had ever been changed in the law of the Hebrews, and that any Jew would rather die a hundred times than suffer the law to be changed in anything.

Prob. c. 1) That the Greek text of the New Testament has not been corrupted by the perfidy of heretics is evident from the fact that the church is built equally upon the foundation of the apostles and upon the foundation of the prophets, at Eph. II, 20. but just as the foundation of the prophets, so also that of the apostles is firm and solid. But it would not be firm if the apostolic writings were corrupted; nor would the Greek Scripture of the New Testament be an infallible rule of faith if it were falsified. 2) Because the industry of catholic doctors stood against the perfidy of heretics, never allowing the corruption of the sacred text.

Prob. d. Amanuenses, copyists, or librarians could not deprave all Hebrew copies by a universal corruption, the Masora averting universal corruption, which, as defined by BUXTORF in Tiberias cap. II. p. 6. is a critical doctrine ingeniously invented by the ancient wise men of the Hebrews concerning the Hebrew text of Holy Scripture, by which its verses, words, and letters are counted, and every variety of them is noted, and indicated in their own places with the recitation of individual verses, so that its constant and genuine reading may be preserved, and eternally protected from all change or corruption, and validly fortified. Nor could copyists adulterate all Greek copies. For the Christian church, which is στύλος καὶ ἑδραίωμα τῆς ἀληθείας, the pillar and seat of truth, 1 Tim. III, 15. has cherished and nourished in its bosom, again and again, men most learned in Greek, who fixed all their care and effort on vindicating the divine text from creeping errors or corruptions.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, with whom the Socinians, Arminians, and Anabaptists partly side, asserting that the Hebrew and Greek text has suffered various corruptions, and that for this reason we should by no means appeal to the turbidly flowing fountains; they rely on the following arguments:

I. Certain things seem to be missing in the Hebrew text, e.g., Exod. II, 22. For the historical account of the other son of Moses is missing, which is found in the LXX Interpreters, the Vulgate version, and also the German version of Luther here in these words: He also begat another, and called his name Eliezer, saying: The God of my father has helped me, and delivered me from the hand of Pharaoh. Resp. α) Cajetan admits that this verse is superfluous, the Louvainists mark it with an asterisk, Robert Stephanus rejects it, Dr. Luther inserted it only in parentheses. β) The Greek and Latin versions are not the rule of authentic truth in the Hebrew text. For judgment should not be made of the fountain from the rivulets, but on the contrary, judgment should rather be made of the rivulets from the fountain. γ) The Hebrew text has that verse in a suitable place, Exod. XVIII, 4. For Gerson, the son of Moses, had preceded his brother Eliezer by many years, during which years the Israelites looked to God, and God in turn to them: but Eliezer was born toward the end of those years, and was still ἀπερίτμητος, uncircumcised; when Moses was preparing himself for the return to Egypt.

See GERH. in exeg. §. 332. and conf. D. GLASS. in Phil. S. lib. 1. tract. I. p. m. 54. II. The Jews in Ps.

XXII, 17 read כארי, as a lion, although the Greek interpreters of the LXX have the word ὤρυξαν, the Latin Vulgate: They dug my hands and my feet.

It is probable that the Jews corrupted this text for this reason, so that the prophecy concerning the crucifixion of Christ might not exist in the O.T.

Resp. The word כארי is genuine and free from any fault, and can most conveniently be explained by the participle: digging, as Dr. Sebast. Schmid renders it in his Latin translation of the Bible.

2. with Golius: he cast down digging with a spear) then from the compound word כור, which denotes a crucible or metallic furnace, which can not inconveniently be derived from digging. Furthermore, from כור analogically in the Benoni participle becomes plural כורים by epenthesis כארים, conf. Ezech. XXVIII, 24. Zach. XIV, 10. Whence by apocope כארי, as it is said לרי for לרים 2 Reg. II, 4. 19. Therefore כארי is a Benoni plural participle, for כורים having undergone epenthesis of N and apocope, to be explained: digging.

Confer. D. PFEIFER in dub. vex. p. m. 673. III.

Ps. XIX, 5. קו is read, their line, although St. Paul Rom. X, 18, following the LXX viral version, has φθόγγος αὐτῶν, their sound. Resp. The Hieropsalmist understands by line a sonorous line, or that tract through which sound is heard. For v. 4 it is expressly said קולם their voice, and in this verse ἐπεξηγητικῶς is added מליהם their words. Accordingly, the line is understood as that through which the voice is conceived to pass, be carried, and heard; which is as it were a vehicle of the voice to the ears. For which reason it is the same in sense, whether it is said that the voice itself passes, or that the line carrying the voice is extended. St. Paul looked to the sense, and cited the LXX viral version not as authentic, but because it was then most customary and accepted.

IV. Es. IX, 6 it is read in the Hebrew text, יקרא he shall call, but the Vulgate has, he shall be called; as if formerly in the fountain it had been, יקרא he shall be called. Resp. The word יקרא is to be rendered impersonally: and one shall call. A suitable nominative can also be added, i.e., Every faithful person shall call. Confer. GLASSIUS in philol.

S. lib. III. tract. III. can. XXIII. p. m. 594.

Jer. XXIII, 6. it is read: יקרא he shall call him, which in the Vulgate is rendered: they shall call him, as if formerly in the fountain it had been: יקראוה they shall call him. Resp. It should likewise be rendered impersonally: one shall call him. A suitable nominative can also be added, i.e., Every faithful person shall call him.

VI. In the conflagration of the temple and city of Jerusalem stirred up by the Chaldeans, all the biblical books were consumed by fire; which Ezra, inspired by the divine Spirit, restored and dictated to five men; by whom it was often erred, with Ezra dictating most rapidly, see book IV of Ezra, ch. XIV, 14 ff. Resp. The book of Ezra, from which the proof is sought, is in the highest degree apocryphal. We are not therefore moved by its testimony to believe that all biblical copies perished in the fire. For the vigilant care of the eternal deity stands in the way (α), which most wisely took care that not one iota or apex should perish from the divine word, Matt. V, 18. (β) The multitude of biblical copies. (γ) The testimony of Daniel, who read the scriptures during the Babylonian captivity. Dan. IX, 2. (δ) The purity of the Hebrew codex. Ezra would have dictated the codex in the language then in use among the people of God, namely, Chaldean, or mixed from the idiom of the Chaldeans and Hebrews: yet a codex written in the purest Hebrew language exists. The Hebrew canon was preserved, while Antiochus raged, who strove earnestly that all the books of the Hebrews should be burned, 1 Maccab. I, 56. How much more in the Babylonian captivity? since the Chaldeans did not progress to that degree of cruelty to which Antiochus had been carried away.

VII. 1 Cor. XV, 47. in the Greek text it is read: Ὁ δεύτερος ἄνθρωπος ὁ Κύριος ἐξ οὐρανοῦ: But in the Vulgate it is read: The second man from heaven is heavenly. The Greek text seems to have been depraved by the Marcionites, who denied the human nature of Christ. Resp. The Latin version seems to favor the Marcionites more than the Greek text. Certainly the antithesis of earthly and Lord is stronger than of earthly and heavenly; since there are many heavenly created things; but he is called Lord, who holds supreme authority over all. The Syriac and Arabic versions agree with the Greek text.

VIII. Rom. XII, 11. in the Greek text it is read: Καιρῷ δουλεύοντες, although in the Latin version it is read: Serving the Lord, just as if it were written: Κυρίῳ δουλεύοντες. Resp. Both readings are analogous to the faith; yet the connection of the text shows that it should be read: Καιρῷ δουλεύοντες, because in Paul's judgment one must rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep, and thus regard for the time must be had.

IX. In the Greek codex that heavenly oracle concerning the three persons of the divinity is not contained. 1 John V, 7. There are three that bear witness in heaven &c. Resp. That this heavenly oracle concerning the three persons of the deity exists in the most ancient Greek codices, D. CALOV. clearly demonstrates in his illustrated Bible on this passage, fol. 1664.

X. To the Lord's Prayer, as an appendix, is added that clause, Matt. VI, 13. οὗ ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία &c. which is not contained in the Latin version. Resp. (α) That doxology is found in the most ancient Greek codices. It is read in the Syriac, Arabic, Persian, and Ethiopic versions. (β) The Latins omitted it, as it appears, by error, because it is not contained in Luke. But the Latin version cannot prejudice the Greek canon. Quæst.

Latin:

Canon biblicus adeo integer & illaesus in hunc usque diem persistit, vt nevnus quidem liber in vsum normalem fidei & morum diuinitus destinatus, & ab ecclesia primitiua receptus, perierit.

Prob. I. Prouidentia diuina adeo aduigilauit libris θεοπνεύστοις & canonicis, vt nec apicem legis interire passa sit, Matth. V, 17. Ergo multo minus permisit, vt integri libri perirent.

II. Ioannes theologus canonem vniuersum clausit atque obsignauit, ita vt sub aeterna damnationis poena nil addi aut diminui possit.

Apoc. XXII, 19. III. Ecclesia non fuisset fedula atque fidelis thesauraria & custos depositi sibi conerediti, si non caute accurasset, vt omnes libri canonici illaesi & integri ad posteros propagarentur.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum asserentium, quosdam libros canonicos interiisse.

Nam ex mente illorum periit I. Liber Henochi, cuius mentionem iniicit S. Iudas epistola sua v. 14.

II. Liber bellorum domini. Num. XXI, 14.

III. Liber iustorum. Ios. X, 13. 2 Sam. I, 18.

IV. Liber iudicii regni. 1 Sam. X, 25.

V. Liber Salomonis. 1 Reg. IV, 32.

VI Liber verborum dierum Salomonis. 1 Reg. XI, 41. item Liber sermonum dierum Iudae & Israelis. 1 Reg. XIV, 19.

VII. Libri prophetarum Nathanis & Gath. 1 Paral. XXIX, 26.

VIII. Lamentationes Ieremiae propter Iosiam regem. 2 Par. XXXV, 25.

IX. Epistola ad Corinthios prima. 1 Cor. V, 9. Dicit enim apostolus: scripsi verbis in epistola, ne commisceamini cum scortatoribus.

X. Epistola Laodicensium. Col. IV, 16.

Resp. a) In genere distinguendo inter libros sacros & canonicos. Non omnes libri sacri eum in finem scripti fuerunt, vt perpetuum fidei morumque canonem constituerent, qui permittente Deo perire potuerunt: libri autem canonici in perpetuum credendorum & agendorum canonem diuinitus destinati & ecclesiae commendati fuerunt, qui per prouidentiam diuinam intercidere nequinerunt.

Quos libros deperditos esse autumant pontificii, illi vel non fuerunt canonici, vel, si fuerint in canone, eos periisse negamus, sed in canone biblico sub aliis nominibus hodienum exstare arbitramur.

Resp. b) In specie ad I. S. Iudas mentionem iniicit prophetiae Henochi, sed non asserit, eam fuisse in litteras relatam. Innotuit igitur apostolo huic ex immediata Spiritus S. inspiratione.

Ad II. Liber bellorum domini non fuit liber propheticus aut canonicus, sed politicus, quo bella domini ab Israelitis gesta descripta fuerunt; qui Israëlitis gesta descripta fuerunt; qui fine imminutione canonis biblici interiit.

Ad III. Per ספר הישר librum recti, nonnulli librum politicum de iure & officio; nonnulli librum annalium forensium intelligunt, qui interiit falvo canone biblico.

Ad IV. Liber iudicii regni habetur 1 Sam.

VIII. Quod si diuersus ab hoc fuerit, nunquam fuit in canone.

Ad V. Salomo dicitur elocutus fuisse 3000. sententias.

Per has sententias intelliguntur prouerbia Salomonis, quæ vel omnia, vel pars potior hodienum exstant. Si quis contenderit, esse alias ab his, quæ supersunt, sententias; dicimus, eas nunquam fuisse in canone: sicut sententiæ Salomonis de rebus physicis canoni biblico nunquam fuerunt insertæ.

Ad VI. Liber sermonum dierum Iudæ & Israëlis aut fuit liber chronicorum, aut nunquam in canonem fuit receptus (*).

Ad VII. Nathan & Gath consignarunt libros Samuelis & Regum.

Ad VIII. Loco citato mentio fit lamentationis Ieremiæ propter regem Iosiam; sed eam litteris mandatam fuisse, non asseritur.

Ad IX. Dicit apostolus: "Εγραψα ὑμῖν ἐν τῇ ἐπιστολῇ, scripsi vobis in hac epistola: intelligitur itaque ipsa hæc prior epistola.

Ad X. Non dicitur scripta ac missa πρὸς τοὺς ἐν Λαοδικείᾳ, sed scripta ἐν Λαοδικείᾳ, quæ est prior ad Tim. cuius subscriptio est: "Εγράφη ἀπὸ Λαοδικείας ().

Quæst. XLII. Estne canon biblicus, siue textus authenticus hebræus in veteri, & græcus in nouo testamento, purus & incorruptus conferuatus?
