Aduigilante prouida Dei cura canon biblicus in verbis omnibus & singulis adeo illibatus & purus conferuatus est (a), vt neque Iudæorum malitia textus hebraicus V.

T. fit deprauatus (b), neque textus græcus N. T. hæreticorum perfidia falsatus (c), neque descriptorum incuria, aut inscitia textus originalis, in omnibus exemplis corruptus fit (d). Prob. a.

Ex verbis Christi Matth. V, 18. Amen enim dico vobis, vsque dum prætereat cœlum & terra, iota vnum, aut vnum corniculum non præteribit de lege, donec omnia fiant. Circa verba Saluatoris obseruamus 1) occasionem.

Iudæi Christum arguebant, quasi legem tolleret: Christus vero protestatur, se non venisse ad soluendum, sed implendum legem. Quam certum igitur est, legem a Christo non esse sublatam, tam illæsa perstat scripturæ integritas. 2) Christi assertionem; qui grauiter assuerat, quod nullus apex, nullum iota perire queat.

Ergo nec litteræ, quarum minima apud hebræos est iota, neque puncta vocalia, quæ κεραῖαι siue cornicula dicuntur, perire possunt. Confer.

D. CALOV. in bibl. illustr. in h. l. fol. 187. 3) Comparationem scripturæ cum cœlo & terra.

Prius dissoluetur ingens cœli terræque compages, quam vniuersali corruptelæ sacrarum litterarum locus sit futurus.

turus. 4) Impletionis vniuersæ scripturæ certitudinem. E qua sequens petitur argumentum: Si constare nobis non potest de impletione verbi diuini, nisi S. scriptura sit integra, necesse est eam integram seruari. Atqui verum est prius. Ergo & posterius. 5) Diuinæ prouidentiæ rationem; quæ fundamentum assertionis Christi est, si enim verbum Dei non conseruaretur integrum, nec ecclesia stare posset, quæ fundamento prophetarum & apostolorum nititur, Eph. II, 20.

Prob. b. Iudæi textum hebræum corrumpere nec potuerunt, nec voluerunt. Quod non potuerint, colligitur tum ex Iudæorum per totum orbem dispersione, tum ex ingenti multitudine codicum biblicorum variis locis descriptorum, & latissime per plurimas prouincias transportatorum. Quomodo enim Iudæi, per remotissima terrarum interualla dispersi, convenire & conspirare potuerunt ad deprauandum tot millia exemplarium biblicorum in hac rerum vniuersitate vbique obuiorum? Nec voluerunt Iudæi textum hebræum corrumpere, siue spectes tempora ante natum Christum, siue numeres secula post Christum in carne exhibitum. Quod noluerint esse falsarii scripturarum ante Christum natum, liquet ex eo, quod commendantur vt bonæ fidei depositarii, quibus τὰ λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ concredita fuerint, Rom. III, 2. Exinde factum est, vt Christus & apostoli ad assiduum scripturæ propheticæ scrutinium nos exstimulauerint, Io. V, 39. Luc. XVI, 29. Act. XV, 21. 1 Tim. IV, 13. & ex ea doctrinam cœlestem probauerint; qui sane falsationem textus hebræi susceptam a Iudæis nunquam reticuissent. Neque voluerunt Iudæi post Christum natum codices hebræos corrumpere. Id quod patet ex oraculis de Messia in V. T. editis, hodienum illæsis. Si Iudæi cepissent consilium falfandi codicem hebræum, vtique præcipiti impetu adorti fuissent vaticinia de Christo, eaque ex codice hebræo vel surripuissent, vel saltem interpolassent. Atqui vaticinia de Christo vsque adhuc in codice hebræo iisdem verbis leguntur, quibus a Christo & apostolis citantur. Ergo Iudæi nunquam animis intenderunt, textum hebræum veteris testamenti deprauare. Testantur PHILO libro de egressu filiorum Israëlis ex Ægypto, & ex eo EVSEBIVS lib. 3. H. E. cap. X. vsque ad sua tempora per spatium amplius quam duorum millium annorum ne verbum quidem fuisse vnquam in lege Hebræorum mutatum, & quemlibet Iudæum centies potius moriturum, quam vt pateretur legem in aliquo mutari.

Prob. c. 1) Textum græcum noui testamenti perfidia hæreticorum non esse corruptum constat ex eo, quod ecclesia peræque super fundamentum apostolorum, ac super fundamentum prophetarum exstructa est, ad Eph. II, 20. at sicut fundamentum prophetarum, ita & apostolorum firmum & solidum est. Non esset autem firmum, si scripta apostolica essent corrupta; neque scriptura græca noui testamenti foret infallibilis fidei norma, si esset falsata. 2) Quia perfidiæ hæreticorum obstitit doctorum catholicorum industria, textus sacri corruptionem nunquam permissura.

Prob. d. Non potuerunt amanuenses, descriptores aut librarii vniuersali corruptione omnia exemplaria hebraica deprauare, auertente corruptelam vniuersalem Masora, quæ, definiente BVXTORFIO in Tiberiade cap. II. p. 6. est doctrina critica a priscis hebræorum sapientibus circa textum hebræum S. scripturæ ingeniose inuenta, qua versus, voces & litteræ eius numeratæ, omnisque ipsarum varietas notata, & suis locis cum singulorum versuum recitatione indicata est, vt constans & genuina eius lectio conseruetur, & ab omni mutatione aut corruptione æternum præseruetur, valideque præmuniatur. Neque potuerunt descriptores omnia exemplaria græca adulterare. Etenim ecclesia christiana, quæ est στύλος καὶ ἑδραίωμα τῆς ἀληθείας, columna & sedes veritatis, 1 Tim. III, 15. viros græce doctissimos in sinu suo vsque & vsque fouit & aluit, qui in textu diuino ab irrepentibus mendis aut corruptelis vindicando omnem curam & operam fixerunt.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, quibuscum ex parte faciunt Sociniani, Arminiani & Anabaptistae, asserentium, textum hebraeum & graecum varias esse passum corruptelas, atque id propter nobis minime provocandum esse ad fontes turbide fluentes; qui sequentibus innituntur argumentis:

I. Videntur quaedam deesse in textu hebraeo, v. gr. Exod. II, 22. Omissa est enim historica relatio de altero filio Mosis, quae in LXX. Interpretum, vulgataque versione, nec non versione germanica Lutheri habetur hic verbis: Alium quoque genuit, & vocavit nomen eius Eliezer, dicens: Deus patris mei auxiliatus est mihi, & liberavit me de manu Pharaonis. Resp. α) Caietanus fatetur, hunc versum esse supervacuum, Louanienses eum asterisco notant, Robertus Stephanus ipsum reiicit, D. Lutherus per parenthesin tantum inferuit. β) Graeca & latina versiones non sunt regula authenticae veritatis in textu hebraeo. Ex rivulis enim non est faciendum iudicium de fonte, sed contra ex fonte potius iudicandum est de rivulis. γ) Hebraeus textus versum illum habet competente loco, Exod. XVIII, 4. Gerson enim Mosis filius multis annis praecesserat Eliezerem fratrem, quibus annis Israëlitae respexerunt ad Deum, & ad illos vicissim Deus: Eliezer vero sub finem annorum illorum natus est, & adhuc fuit ἀπερίτμητος, incircumcisus; cum sese Moses ad reuersionem in Aegyptum accingeret.

Vid. GERH. in exeg. §. 332. & conf. D. GLASS. in Phil. S. libr. 1. tract. I. p. m. 54. II.

Iudaei Ps. XXII, 17. legunt כארי, sicut leo, cum tamen LXX. interpretes graeci habeant verbum ὤρυξαν, latina vulgata: Foderunt manus meas & pedes meos.

Iudaeos hunc textum ideo depraualle verisimile est, ne exstaret in V. T. vaticinium de crucifixione Christi.

Resp. Vox כארי est genuina & ab omni mendo immunis, atque commodissime exponi potest per participium: fodientes, vti reddit D. Sebast. Schmid. in latina bibliorum translatione. Est enim a radice כור (quae quidem in sacro codice non inuenitur, attamen facile restitui potest tum e radibus collectaneis כרה & קור, tum e radice Arab. כור vel כאר) (unde in coni.

2. apud Golium: deturbauit fodiens hasta) tum e voce coniugata כור, quae notat catinum vel fornacem metallicam, quae ab effodiendo non incommode potest. Porro e כור analogice in participio Benoni fit plural. כורים per epenthesin כארים, conf. Ezech. XXVIII, 24. Zach. XIV, 10. Vnde per apocopen כארי, vti dicitur לרי pro לרים 2 Reg. II, 4. 19. Itaque כארי est participium Benoni plurale, pro כורים facta epenthesi N & apocope, exponendum: fodientes.

Confer. D. PFEIFER in dub. vex. p. m. 673. III.

Ps. XIX, 5. habetur קו linea eorum, cum tamen S. Paullus Rom. X, 18. LXX. viralem secutus habeat, φθόγγος αὐτῶν, sonus eorum. Resp. Hieropsaltes per lineam intelligit lineam fonoram, siue tractum illum, per quem sonus auditur. Nam v. 4. expresse dicitur קולם vox eorum, & hoc versu ἐπεξηγητικῶς additur מליהם verba eorum. Proinde linea intelligitur, per quam vox concipitur transire, deferri & audiri; quae quasi vehiculum vocis est ad aures. Quam ob rem in sensu idem est, siue dicatur vox ipsa transire, siue linea vocem deferens extendi. Respexit S. Paullus sensum, & citavit LXX. viralem versionem non vt authenticam, sed quia tunc vsitatissima & receptissima erat.

IV. Es. IX, 6. legitur in textu hebraeo, יקרא vocabit, sed vulgata habet, vocabitur; quasi olim in fonte fuerit, יקרא vocabitur. Resp. Vox יקרא impersonaliter reddenda est: und man wird nennen. Potest etiam addi nominatiuus conueniens, h. m. Vocabit fidelis quisque. Confer, GLASSIVS in philol.

S. lib. III. tract. III. can. XXIII. p. m. 594. V.

Ier. XXIII, 6. legitur: יקרא vocabit eum, quod in vulgata redditur: vocabunt eum, quasi in fonte esset: יקראוה vocabunt eum. Resp. Reddi itidem debet impersonaliter: man wird ihn nennen. Addi potest nominatiuus conueniens: fidelis quisque vocabit eum.

VI. In conflagratione templi & vrbis Hierosolymæ a Chaldæis excita, libri biblici omnes igne absumti sunt; quos diuino Spiritu afflatus Esdra restituit, & in calamum dictauit viris quinque; a quibus sæpius erratum est, celerrime dictante Esdra, vid. libr. IV. Esdræ cap. XIV, 14. seqq. Resp. Liber Esdræ, e quo probatio petitur, in summo gradu apocryphus est. Non igitur ipsius testimonio adducimur, vt credamus, omnia exemplaria biblica igne periisse. Obstat enim (α) peruigil æterni numinis cura, quæ sapientissime cauit, ne iota vel apex vnus de verbo diuino periret, Matth. V, 18. (β) Exemplarium biblicorum multitudo. (γ) Testimonium Danielis, qui sub captiuitate Babylonica scripturas legit. Dan. IX, 2. (δ) Codicis hebræi puritas. Dictasset vtique Esdra codicem lingua tunc in populo Dei vsitata, scil. chaldaica, vel mixta ex Chaldæorum & Hebræorum idiomate: cum tamen lingua purissima hebraica conscriptus codex exstet. Conferuatus est canon hebræus, sæuiente Antiocho, qui enixe allaborauit, vt libri Hebræorum omnes comburerentur, 1 Maccab. I, 56. Quanto magis in captiuitate Babylonica? cum Chaldæi non eo sæuitiæ, quo abreptus erat Antiochus, progressi sint.

VII. 1 Cor. XV, 47. in textu græco legitur: Ὁ δεύτερος ἄνθρωπος ὁ Κύριος ἐξ οὐρανοῦ: In vulgata autem legitur: Secundus homo de cœlo cœlestis. Textus græcus a Marcionitis deprauatus videtur, qui humanam Christi naturam negarunt. Resp. Latina versio magis, quam textus græcus Marcionitis fauere videtur. Certe fortior est antithesis terreni & domini, quam terreni & cœlestis; cum multæ sint res cœlestes creatæ; dominus autem dicatur, qui summum in omnes imperium obtinet. Consentiunt cum textu græco syriaca & arabica versiones.

VIII. Rom. XII, 11. in textu græco legitur: Καιρῷ δουλεύοντες, cum tamen in versione latina legatur: Domino seruientes, perinde, ac si scriptum fit: Κυρίῳ δουλεύοντες. Resp. Vtraque lectio est analoga fidei; attamen connexio textus ostendit, legendum esse: Καιρῷ δουλεύοντες, quia iudice Paulo cum gaudentibus gaudendum, cum flentibus flendum, adeo que temporis ratio habenda est.

IX. In codice græco non habetur cœleste illud oraculum de tribus diuinitatis personis. 1 Io. V, 7. Tres sunt, qui testantur in cœlo &c. Resp. Quod hoc oraculum cœleste de tribus deitatis personis in antiquissimis codicibus græcis exstet, luculenter demonstrat D. CALOV. in bibl. illustrat. in h. l. fol. 1664.

X. Orationi dominicæ velut appendix adiicitur clausula illa, Matth. VI, 13. οὗ ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία &c. quæ non habetur in versione latina. Resp. (α) inuenitur illa δοξολογία in vetustissimis græcis codicibus. Legitur in syriaca, arabica, persica & æthiopica versionibus. (β) Latini omiserunt, vt apparet, ex errore, quia apud Lucam non habetur. Non potest autem versio latina canoni græco præiudicare.


### XLIII. Are the vowel points coeval with the letters of the Hebrews?

Prob. I. Because no language can be without vowels. Therefore neither can the Hebrew language. The antecedent is manifest. For vowels are so called from voice, because they vivify and as it were animate it. From which vowels are called the souls of words. But who would believe that the prophets handed down to us a scripture destitute of life?

You say: Vowels have always existed coeval with the letters of the Hebrews as to value, but not as to figures; inasmuch as they were added to the sacred text by the Masoretes. Resp. We are speaking of written speech: whatever does not exist in this, is of no value. The value of vowels without figures is thus The vowel points in the biblical codex of the Old Testament are coeval with the Hebrew consonants.

it does not help the interpreters, that because of the absence of the points such an ambiguous reading existed for the interpreters, so that one read it thus, another otherwise, as each was able to attain by conjecture.

2. From the testimony of Christ, asserting in Matt. V, 18 that not one iota, nor one apex shall perish from the law. By which words he joins both the letter and the most minute point. Therefore, in the time of Christ, vowel points visibly present existed, appended to the letters.

3. From the perfection of Scripture, which is so absolute that it rejects not more of a diminution than an addition, Deut. IV, 2. But according to the hypothesis concerning the points, added by the Rabbis, it must necessarily be established that some human addition has accrued to the divinely inspired Scripture.

4. From the Masoretic notes. The Masoretes weighed the existing vowels, and passed judgment upon them. Therefore, the Masoretes did not invent or devise the vowel points.

5. From the absurd consequences. If the vowel points of the Hebrew letters were not coeval, for many centuries the Scripture of the Old Testament was ambiguous and obscure. For in the absence of points, letters can be read in various ways. The LXX interpreters erred gravely in translating the Hebrew text, because, in the opinion of many, they were destitute of a pointed codex.

There is an antithesis both of the Papists and of the Critics, Rabbi Elias Levita, Grotius, Erpenius, Ludovicus Capellus, Walton, and others: whose stronger arguments are:

I. That which the LXX interpreters did not use, did not exist at that time. But, the LXX interpreters did not use a pointed codex. Therefore, a pointed codex did not exist then. The major premise is proven, because the LXX interpreters were men of integrity of life, excelling in age and prudence of the laws, as Aristeas testifies on p. 31, invited by King Ptolemy with most ample rewards for an accurate and consistent interpretation of the divine law; who would undoubtedly have had vowel points appended to the letters, if at that time vowel points had been appended to the letters.

The minor premise can be proven at length; but for this occasion we shall only adduce Gen. XLVII, 31, where the Hebrew text has: וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל עַל-רֹאשׁ הַמִּטָּה. They rendered it: Καὶ προσεκύνησεν Ἰσραὴλ ἐπὶ τὸ ἄκρον τοῦ ῥάβδος αὐτοῦ. The Hebrew words are rendered in Latin: then Israel bowed himself upon the head of the bed. The Greek words, which Paul cited in Heb. XI, 21, are expressed in Latin: and worshipped upon the top of his staff. This translation of the LXX interpreters is a not obscure indication that they lacked a pointed codex. For the Hebrew word מִטָּה, according to the different placement of the vowel points, denotes both a bed and a staff: a bed, if you write מִטָּה; a staff, if you write מַטֶּה.

Since, however, in all pointed codices it is constantly read as מִטָּה to designate a bed, and nevertheless the LXX translated this Hebrew word as ῥάβδος (staff), it is easy to conclude that they had in their hands a Hebrew codex marked with no points.

Resp. 1) The argument is drawn invalidly from the version of the LXX Greek interpreters.

For there are grave authors who maintain that the ancient version of the LXX interpreters has perished entirely, among whose number are Pagninus, Ussher, Drusius, and others: others think that the ancient version of the LXX indeed survives, but not flowing purely, but rather corrupted in many ways. Worthy of mention are the words of Cardinal BELLARMINE, l. II. de verbo Dei cap. VI. fol. m. 82. "I think it probable that that version of the LXX interpreters survives, but so corrupted and vitiated that it seems to be something else entirely."

I add our own D. PFEIFFER, writing gravely on vexed doubts, p. 41. Which is not to be taken as if no pointed exemplars existed in the age of the LXX interpreters, or that they did not have such; but because they sometimes neglected the points present out of zeal, which the Talmudists also do from a perverse hypothesis concerning various literal senses nesting in the text itself (the points being changed a little).

What? If we say that that version proceeded from men who were unreliable, yet not from the LXX interpreters, since the version which circulates under their name is so interpolated that you can now scarcely pronounce what is undoubtedly from them, and what is not.

Latin:

Prob. I. Quia nulla lingua vocalibus potest carere. Ergo nec lingua hebræa. Antecedens manifestum est. Nam vocales a voce dicuntur, quod hanc viuificent & quasi animent. Ex quo vocales dicuntur animæ vocum. Quis vero credet prophetas scripturam nobis tradidisse vita destitutam?

Dicis: Vocales semper litteris Hebræorum exstiterunt coæuæ quod valorem, sed non quod figuras; vtpote quæ a Maforetis textui sacro adiectæ sint. Resp. Loquimur nos de sermone scripto: quidquid in hoc non exsistit, non valet. Valor vocalium sine figuris adeo Puncta vocalia in codice biblico veteris testamenti consonantibus hebraicis sunt coæua.

nil iuvat interpretes, vt propter absentiam punctorum tam ambigua lectio exstiterit interpretibus, vt alius sic, alius aliter legerit, prout unusquisque coniectura assequi potuit.

2. E testimonio Christi, afferentis Matth. V, 18. non periturum de lege iota unum, nec apicem unum. Quibus verbis & litteram & punctum minutissimum coniungit. Ergo tempore Christi visibiliter præsentis puncta vocalia exstiterunt litteris adscripta.

3. A scripturæ perfectione, quæ adeo absoluta est, vt non diminutionem magis, quam augmentum respuat, Deut. IV, 2. At iuxta hypothesin de punctis, a Rabbinis adiectis, necessario statuendum erit, aliquod augmentum humanum scripturæ divinitus inspiratæ accessisse.

4. A notis Masoreticis. Masoretæ vocales exstantes ponderarunt, & de illis iudicium tulerunt. Ergo Masoretæ puncta vocalia non inuenerunt aut excogitarunt.

5. A consequentibus absurdis. Si puncta vocalia litteræ Hebræorum non fuerunt coæua, per multa secula scriptura veteris testamenti fuit flexiloqua & obscura. Absentibus enim punctis litteræ vario possunt legi modo. Grauiter errarunt LXX. interpretes in transferendo textu hebræo, quia codice punctato ex multorum sententia destituti fuerunt.

Antithesis est tum Pontificiorum, tum Criticorum, Rabbi Eliæ Leuitæ, Grotii, Erpenii, Ludouici Capelli, Waltoni, & aliorum: quorum potiora sunt argumenta:

I. Quo non sunt usi LXX. interpretes, id tunc temporis non exstitit. Atqui, codice punctato LXX. interpretes usi non sunt. Ergo codex punctatus tunc non exstitit. Maior probatur, quia LXX. interpretes erant viri honestate vitæ, senio & prudentia legum præstantes, teste Aristea p. m. 31. amplissimis muneribus ad accuratam & consentientem legis diuinæ interpretationem a rege Ptolemæo inuitati; qui haud dubie puncta vocalia litteris adscripta fuissent, si tunc temporis puncta vocalia litteris adscripta fuissent.

Minor prolixe probari potest; sed hac vice tantum adducemus Gen. XLVII, 31. vbi textus hebræus habet: וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל עַל-רֹאשׁ הַמִּטָּה. reddiderunt: Καὶ προσεκύνησεν Ἰσραὴλ ἐπὶ τὸ ἄκρον τοῦ ῥάβδος αὐτοῦ. Verba hebræa latine redduntur: tum incuruauit se Israël super caput lecti. Verba græca, quæ citauit Paullus Hebr. XI, 21. latine exprimuntur: & adorauit super summo baculi ipsius. Hæc translatio LXX. interpretum haud obscuro est indicio, ipsos caruisse codice punctato. Nam vox Hebræa מִטָּה pro diuerso punctorum vocalium positu & lectum & baculum notat: lectum, si scribas, מִטָּה;

baculum, si scribas, מַטֶּה. Cum autem in omnibus codicibus punctatis constanter legatur מִטָּה ad designandum lectum, & nihilominus LXX. transtulerint hanc vocem hebræam per ῥάβδον, proclive collectu est, illos manibus triuissis codicem hebræum nullis punctis insignitum.

Resp. 1) A versione LXX. græcorum interpretum inualidum petitur argumentum.

Sunt enim auctores graues, qui statuunt antiquam versionem LXX. interpretum penitus interiisse, e quorum censu sunt Pagninus, Vsserius, Drusius, & alii: alii censent, superesse quidem antiquam versionem LXX. sed non pure fluentem, verum multis modis turbatam. Memoratu digna sunt verba Cardinalis BELLARMINI l. II. de verbo Dei cap. VI. fol. m. 82. Probabile censeo, illam versionem LXX. interpretum superesse, sed adeo corruptam & vitiatam, vt omnino alia esse videatur.

Addo nostrum D. PFEIFFERVM, in dubiis vexatis grauiter scribentem p. 41. Quod non ita accipiendum, quasi LXX. interpretum ætate nulla punctata exemplaria exstiterint, vel illi talia non habuerint; sed quia nonnunquam puncta præsentia studio neglexerunt, quod & Talmudici faciunt e praua hypothesi de variis sensibus literalibus ipso textu (mutatis paullulum punctis) nidulantibus.

Quid? si dicamus istam versionem profectam esse ab hominibus ἀνεξβεαίοις, non tamen a LXX. interpretibus, cum versio, quæ sub ipsorum nomine circumfertur, adeo fit interpolata, vt ægre iam pronuntiare queas, quid indubitato ab iis fit, quid minus.


### XLIII. Are the vowel points coeval with the letters of the Hebrews?: 2) D

2) D.

WASMUTHUS otherwise brings forward the causes of the discrepancy of that version from the Hebrew text: namely, that the LXX used a paraphrastic liberty, being little concerned about the words, and strove only to express a convenient sense; that their translation was made primarily from the Samaritan codex; that pointed codices were rarer at that time because of the greater difficulty of writing; or even if pointed codices could perhaps have been had, they nevertheless held that more abstruse doctrine of points and accents then as a part of the oral law received from Moses, which they deemed it a sin to divulge to foreigners and Gentiles.

See WASMUTH in Vindiciae Hebraicae, L., p. 116. II. The current volume of the law, unpointed, is held in the highest esteem among the Jews, which they preserve with the utmost religion in their synagogues, nor do they present it to be seen by the people without a sacred horror.

By which they wish to shadow forth that the primeval Pentateuch of Moses was likewise destitute of vowels. I answer with the words of WASMUTH, l. c., p.

135: This custom was introduced among the Jews only from that time from which, through the discovered צרופים (tserufim) or manifold balistic combinations, the abuse of the Kabbalah and the perverse study of distorting Scripture into various senses arose. This is manifestly detected from these words of R.

Bechai on Num. XI, 5: "For this reason we were commanded not to point the book of the law."

By whom they were commanded, he does not add: but he subjoins the reason, (not this, that Moses also wrote the law thus, but) because a pointed word admits of only a single sense; but with an unpointed word, a man can understand and find many, and those admirable and excellent senses.

III. Vowel points are not absolutely necessary for those reading a Hebrew codex, provided they accurately observe the construction and the servile letters.

In other languages, the variation of conjugating and declining resides principally in the vowels, but in the Hebrew language it depends on the servile letters. Wherefore it is consistent that the Israelites read the prophetic writings without points. I answer: 1. Although vowel points are not absolutely necessary for reading some Hebrew writing, they nevertheless contribute not a little to the certainty and perspicuity of Holy Scripture.

For when the points are removed, the Hebrew text is rendered liable to ambiguity and obscurity. For example, if דבר is written, by this Hebrew word can be understood: my pestilence, my word, my words, and in the construct state, words.

But if vowel points are added, that ambiguity immediately expires. Q.

XLIV. Does the power of judging belong to Holy Scripture?

The power of judging belongs to Holy Scripture, both insofar as it is the voice of the supreme judge, the Holy Spirit, who speaks through Scripture, judges all controversies through it, and pronounces His sentence (a), and insofar as it is the primary and adequate norm, which the inferior judge is bound to regard and attentively observe in discerning the true from the false, the good from the evil (b).

Obs. 1. Theologians distinguish between a judge judging autokratorikos (by sovereign authority), kanonikos (canonically), and diakonikos (ministerially).

The judge autokratorikos, the supreme, absolute, and independent judge of all controversies of faith, is the triune God—Father, Son, and idiopoietikos, or by appropriation, the Holy Spirit. The judge kanonikos, or organikos, directive and instrumental, is Holy Scripture.

The judge diakonikos, or ministerial, is either public, namely the ecclesiastical ministry, to which belongs the prophetikon or exegetical judgment of interpreting Holy Scripture: or private, namely any man illuminated and reborn through the Word of God, to whom belongs the dokimastikon or discretive judgment.

1 Cor.

X, 15. 1 Thess.

V, 19. Obs.

2. The word "judge" in a stricter sense denotes the person judging: taken in a broader sense, it also includes the voice of the judge and the norm which he regards in judging.

In which sense ARISTOTLE said, Nicomachean Ethics, Bk. 5, ch.

IV: "To go to a judge is to go to justice."

For a judge seems to be nothing other than justice animate.

And CICERO, De Legibus, Bk.

III: "The law is a mute magistrate, just as a magistrate is a speaking law." Hence D. DORSCHEUS in Thomas Confessor Veritatis, p. 29, says: "Holy Scripture judges as a canonical judge, and through it the Holy Spirit as the hypostatic judge." Obs. 3. Holy Scripture judges directive, as a canon and norm which the inferior judge is bound to regard, and to confirm by it the sentence which he pronounces concerning an arisen controversy of faith. In this sense Holy Scripture is called a canonical, normal, and directive judge, which directs the inferior judge, namely the minister of the church and any reborn man, like a norm and rule, lest he err in judging. Definitively, because as the voice of the supreme judge it composes litigating parties, defines doubts of religion, and settles controversies. Effectively, insofar as Holy Scripture is the most efficacious organon, medium, and sword of the Holy Spirit, by which He penetrates the heart of man, subdues the ferocious mind, and convinces the consciences of the litigating parties. Obs. 4. Although the canonical authority of Holy Scripture has been clearly proven above, here nevertheless the duty lies upon us of demonstrating that Holy Scripture is the primary and adequate norm for deciding controversies. For although the oi ex enantias (those on the contrary side) concede that Holy Scripture is a norm of things to be believed and done, they nevertheless deny that Holy Scripture is a universal, total, and primary norm. Prob. a. (1) Whoever is the author of Holy Scripture, he judges best of all concerning its sense and all dogmas contained in it. But God, etc. 2 Tim. III, 16. Therefore. (2) Whoever convicts the world of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment, he is the supreme judge in spiritual matters. But the Holy Spirit, etc. John XVI, 8. Therefore. (3) Whoever was the judge of controversies at the time of the nascent Christian church in the apostolic council, he is the supreme judge in all councils today. But the Holy Spirit speaking through the Scriptures, etc. Therefore. The minor is proven from Acts XV, 28, where the apostles pronounce the definitive sentence of the apostolic council with the following words: "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us." The ministerial judges in the apostolic council were the apostles and the presbyters of the church of Jerusalem, and other pious men. Acts XV, 6, 22, 23. The supreme judge was the Holy Spirit speaking through the Scriptures. For James confirmed Peter's suffrage from the prophetic oracles alone, saying: "And to this the words of the prophets agree: as it is written (Amos IX, 11)." The Holy Spirit therefore judged in the apostolic council through prophetic Scripture: this was the voice of the supreme judge, the Holy Spirit. (4) If God, the supreme judge, concludes men under sin through Scripture, then Scripture is the voice of the supreme judge, through which men are convicted of sin. But the former is undoubtedly true, therefore the latter also. The antecedent is evident from a collation of the Pauline sayings, Rom. XI, 32 and Gal. III, 22. For God is said to conclude all men into unbelief, that He may have mercy on all. Rom. XI, 32. It is likewise affirmed of Scripture that it concludes all under sin, that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe. Gal. III, 22. Let us hear the interpreter CALOVIUS in Biblia Illustrata on Rom. XI, 32, fol. 201: "God concludes all under apeitheia (disobedience), not energetikos, by working or effecting unbelief; but elenktikos, by arguing, convicting, and condemning: not aitiatikos, or causally; but dikastikos and judicially, by which voice of the law, or legal and judiciary sentence, all men are argued guilty, convicted of sin, and condemned on account of sin, and as if cast into prison, and held captive as eternal slaves of condemnation." Deut. XXVII, 26. (5) Christ Himself assigns the role of judge to His word, John XII, 48: "He who rejects me, and does not receive my words, has one who judges him: the word that I have spoken, that will judge him in the last day." By the same reason that the word of Christ will judge in the last day, it judges in this age. a mute magistrate, just as a magistrate is a speaking law. Hence D. DORSCHEVS in Thomas, confessor of the truth, p. 29, says: Holy Scripture judges as a canonical judge, and through it the Holy Spirit as a hypostatic judge.

2) D.

WASMVTHVS alias affert causas discrepantiae illius versionis a textu hebraeo: nempe quod LXX. usi libertate paraphrastica, de verbis parum solliciti, sensum tantum commodum exprimere annixi sint; quod translatio illorum potissimum facta sit e codice samaritano; quod rariores tunc exstiterint punctati codices ob maiorem scriptionis difficultatem; vel etiamsi haberi forte potuerint punctati codices, nihilominus illam punctorum & accentuum abstrusiorem doctrinam habuerint tunc quasi partem legis oralis a Mose acceptae, quam exteris & gentibus propalare nefas duxere.

Vid. WASMVTH. in vindic. hebr. L. p. 116. II. Hodiernum volumen legis non punctatum apud Iudaeos in summo est pretio, quod summa religione in suis asseruant synagogis, nec sine sacro horrore populo conspiciendum praebent.

Quo adumbratum ipsi volunt primaevum Mosis pentateuchum vocalibus item destitutum. Respondeo verbis WASMVTHI l. c. p.

135. Introducta est haec consuetudo apud Iudaeos ab eo demum tempore, ex quo per repertas צרופים seu multiplices combinationes balifticas, cabalae abusus ac perversum studium detorquendi scripturam in varios sensus exstitit. id quod manifesto deprehenditur ex his R.

Bechai ad Num. XI, 5. Hac de causa iussi fumus non punctare librum legis.

A quo iussi sint, non addit: caussam vero subiicit, (non hanc, quod Mofes quoque legem sic scripserit, sed) quia non nisi unicum vox punctata admittit sensum; voce vero non punctata, potest homo intelligere & invenire multos, eosque admirandos & eximios sensus.

III. Puncta vocalia non absolute necessaria sunt codicem hebraeum legentibus, modo accurate observent constructionem & litteras serviles.

In aliis linguis coniugandi & declinandi variatio principaliter in vocalibus haeret, sed in lingua hebraea pendet a litteris servilibus. Quare vero consentaneum est, Israelitas scripta prophetica sine punctis legisse. Resp. 1. quamuis puncta vocalia non absolute necessaria sint ad legendum scriptum aliquod hebraeum, haud parum tamen faciunt ad certitudinem & perspicuitatem S. scripturae.

Sublatis enim punctis, textus hebraeus ambiguitati & obscuritati obnoxius redditur. v. gr. Si scribatur דבר per hanc vocem hebraeam intelligi potest: pestis mea, verbum meum, verba mea, & in regimine, verba.

Sed si adduntur puncta vocalia, illa ambiguitas protinus exspirat.

Quaest. XLIV. Competitne S. scripturae potestas iudicandi?

Potestas iudicandi competit S. scripturae, tum quatenus est vox summi iudicis Spiritus sancti, qui per scripturam loquitur, per eam omnes controversias diiudicat, & sententiam suam pronuntiat (a), tum quatenus est norma primaria & adxequata, quam iudex inferior in discernendo vero a falso, bono a malo, respicere & attente observare tenetur (b).

Obs. 1. Distinguunt theologi inter iudicem iudicantem αὐτοκρατορικῶς, κανονικῶς, καὶ διακονικῶς.

Iudex αὐτοκρατορικῶς summus, absolutus & independens omnium controversiarum fidei est Deus triunus pater, filius, & ἰδιοποιητικῶς, sive per appropriationem, Spiritus S. Iudex κανονικῶς, vel ὀργανικῶς, directivus & instrumentalis est S. scriptura.

Iudex διακονικῶς, sive ministerialis, est vel publicus nempe ministerium ecclesiasticum, cui competit iudicium πρεφητικὸν, sive exegeticum S. scripturam interpretandi: vel privatus, nempe quilibet homo per verbum Dei illuminatus & renatus, cui competit iudicium δοκιμαστικὸν, sive discretivum.

1 Cor.

X, 15. 1 Thess.

V, 19. Obs.

2. Vox iudex in sensu strictiori notat personam iudicantem: sensu latiori accepta etiam vocem iudicis, & normam, quam in iudicando respicit, complectitur.

Quo sensu dixit ARISTOTELES L.

5. ad Nicomach. c. IV.

Adire ad iudicem est adire ad ius. Iudex enim nihil videtur aliud esse, quam ius animatum.

Et CICERO libr.

The ministerial judges in the apostolic council were the apostles and the presbyters of the Jerusalem church, and other pious men. Acts XV, 6, 22, 23. The supreme judge was the Holy Spirit speaking through the scriptures. For James was confirming Peter’s vote from the prophetic oracles alone, saying: And to this the words of the prophets agree: as it is written (Amos IX, 11). The Holy Spirit therefore judged in the apostolic council through prophetic scripture: this was the voice of the supreme judge, the Holy Spirit.

(4) If God, the supreme judge, shuts men up under sin through scripture, then certainly scripture is the voice of the supreme judge, through which men are convicted of sin. But the former is undoubtedly true, therefore the latter is as well. The antecedent is clear from a comparison of the Pauline sayings. Rom. XI, 32, and Gal. III, 22. For God is said to shut up all men into unbelief, that he may have mercy on all.

Rom. XI, 32. It is likewise affirmed of scripture, that it shuts up all things under sin; that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to them that believe.

Gal. III, 22. Let us hear the interpreter CALOVIVS in Biblia illustrata on Rom. XI, 32, fol. 201. God shuts up all under ἀπειθεία [disobedience], not ἐνεργητικῶς [actively], by working or effecting unbelief; but ἐλεγκτικῶς [convictingly], by arguing, convincing, and condemning: not αἰτιατικῶς [causally], or by way of cause; but δικαστικῶς [judicially], by which voice of the law, or of the legal and judicial sentence, all men are argued guilty, are convicted of sin, and are condemned on account of sin, and are as it were cast into prison, and held captive as slaves of eternal condemnation.

Deut. XXVII, 26. (5) Christ himself assigns the role of judge to his word, Jo. XII, 48. He that rejecteth me, and receiveth not my words, hath one that judgeth him: the word that I have spoken, the same shall judge him in the last day. By the same reason that the word of Christ will judge in the last day, it judges in this age.

But he will judge on the last day by convicting the consciences of sinners: Therefore he holds the same judicial power in this age.

It is evident that Holy Scripture is the adequate and primary norm, according to which all dogmas of faith and precepts of morals are to be judged.

1. From the Pauline utterance, Gal. VI, 16. As many as walk by this rule, peace (shall be) upon them, and mercy, and upon the Israel of God. It was shown above that this apostolic dictum is rightly understood of Holy Scripture, of which this epistle written to the Galatians exhibits to us a compendium. Now we argue: Whatever word suffices for obtaining grace from God and peace for all who run the right path of faith and piety, that is the adequate norm of things to be believed and done. But the word of God revealed, and related by the prophets and apostles into writings, is such, etc. Therefore.

2. From the prophetic oracle, Is. VIII, 19. 20. But when they shall say to you: seek the pythons and soothsayers that hiss and mutter: (I answer) Shall not a people seek their God? for the living, the dead? (Wherefore) (let them seek) the law and the testimony: which if they shall not speak according to this word: truly there shall be no morning (for them). Obj. (1) The scope of the prophet was to warn the pious against the superstition and idolatry of those who went to consult pythons and soothsayers about doubtful matters. The prophet seriously dissuades the people of God from this superstition, having taken an argument from law and equity: Shall not a people seek their God? as if he were to say: Is it not just that every people should consult their own God, whom they are persuaded to know future things? The prophet illustrates his argument by the contrary, saying: Shall we consult the dead for the living? i.e., Is it not wicked and absurd to consult the dead (whether you understand idols or the shades of the departed) for the salvation of the living, who know nothing and can help nothing? (2) The prophet concludes: Wherefore let them seek the law and the testimony. The law and the testimony is the Mosaic law and the entire Scripture, in which God could be consulted, so that the sense is: If you wish to be certain about doubtful cases and uncertain future events, do not go to pythons and diviners, but to the law and the testimony, in which you have clearly what you ought to do and what you ought to omit, so that you may be able to expect salutary outcomes with certainty. (3) The prophet adds a commination: If they shall not speak according to this word, i.e., if your teachers or fathers have not sent the people to the law and the testimony of God, and the people have not obeyed: then there shall be no morning for that people, or the light of that salutary wisdom, and the good and happiness proceeding thence, whether temporal or spiritual. From the words of the prophet thus explained we argue: To whatever alone the whole people is sent and is obliged in resolving doubts concerning salvation, that is the unique and adequate norm, according to which all doubts raised concerning the salvation of man are to be examined and resolved. But to the Mosaic law and the testimony of Scripture, etc. Therefore. The minor can be more fully confirmed by the words of Abraham, with which he instructed the rich glutton: They have Moses and the prophets, let them hear them, Luke XVI, 29. just as if he said: the Mosaic and prophetic Scripture is the adequate rule for penance to be duly performed.

3. From the apostolic testimony, with which Timothy is adorned, 2 Tim. III, 15. 16. which see explained above. For it is easily applied to the norm of things to be believed and done, provided that in place of the principle of adequate theology, the adequate norm of faith and morals is substituted.

4. That which alone was held by Christ, the apostles, and other saints as the norm of controversies of faith, that even now is the only norm of faith, and that a primary one. But Holy Scripture is that, &c. Therefore. The major is clear, because no other than that which was employed by Christ, the apostles, and other saints as the norm of controversies can be employed today. For just as in the time of Christ and of the apostles, and in our own time, the same things are to be believed and done: so also the same norm is to be employed. The minor is proved by the example of Christ, disputing with the Pharisees and Sadducees from Scripture, Matth. XIX. and referring the Jews to Scripture. Io. V, 39. The same is evident from the example of the apostles.

Acts XXV, 22, where Paul asserts that he said nothing beyond the prophets and Moses.

The antithesis is 1. Of the Papists, who opine that holy scripture is a partial norm of the controversies of faith, but not the judge. 2. Of the Socinians, who deny that holy scripture is the sole rule of faith. 3. Of the Arminians, who concede that holy scripture is the norm of the controversies of faith, but not the judge effectively judging. 4. Of the Quakers, who deny that holy scripture is the primary and universal norm of faith and morals; for they posit it to be the dictate of the spirit speaking or revealing immediately to the internal part of every man; although they concede that holy scripture is a partial, subordinate, secondary, and declaratory norm. Their stronger arguments are the following.

1. The norm of faith is not its judge. But holy scripture is the norm of faith. Therefore. Resp. (1) The norm of faith is not its autocratical and personal judge; I concede: but truly it is the canonical and directive judge of faith. (2) Holy scripture is not only the norm which an inferior index respects, but it is also the voice of the superior judge, the Holy Spirit, by which through holy scripture He settles controversies of religion that have arisen.

2. If holy scripture is not a personal judge, it will not be a judge properly so called. But if it is not a judge properly so called, it will not judge properly and truly. Resp. If in a stricter sense a judge is called a judging person, we admit that holy scripture is not a judge properly, but improperly so (by grammatical, not rhetorical, impropriety). Nor yet for this reason must it be said that holy scripture does not judge truly. For whatever power of judging belongs to the Holy Spirit originally, that belongs to holy scripture participatively; therefore, because the voice of the supreme judge is convincing to the conscience, while it exhibits the sentence of the Holy Spirit as clearly and perspicuously as the sentence written for the tribunal, handed down by a visible judge to the litigating parties, is the voice of a visible judge.

3. Whoever judges truly can compel the disobedient to obedience. (Otherwise a judgment without the execution of the passed sentence will be a bell without a clapper.) But holy scripture cannot compel the disobedient to obedience (because very many spurn the judgment of holy scripture). Therefore holy scripture does not judge truly. Resp. By distinguishing between the external coercion of bodies, and the internal coercion of minds, or consciences. Scripture does not compel bodies, but convinces minds and consciences, that they may submit themselves to heavenly truth; which you will obtain by no political machinations, being more likely to make a hypocrite than a believer. Nor is there reason for you to object that not a few spurn the judgment of holy scripture; which they would not do if scripture judged coercively. For it is certain that very many scoffers hold the judgment of Christ with the highest force and power of the judge in contempt. Holy scripture compels not violently, but supernaturally; not by irresistible force, but by resistible.

4. Whoever is the judge of the controversies of faith, he condemns heretics, so that they may confess that the sentence has been passed against them. But the Holy Spirit speaking through holy scripture does not so condemn heretics. Therefore the Holy Spirit speaking through holy scripture is not the judge of the controversies of faith. I respond by denying the major, and by distinguishing between the internal and external word, between the internal sense of the heart, and the external confession of the mouth. The Holy Spirit speaking through holy scripture condemns heretics, so that they may feel in their heart that the sentence has been passed against them; although they do not confess with the mouth that they have been convicted. Add, that the Holy Spirit condemns heretics not nominatim and individually, but generically and fundamentally, by supplying the general foundation of the condemnatory sentence, according to that, John III, 18: He who does not believe has already been judged.

5. A judge properly so called must be visible, who can be seen and heard by all who are to be judged. The Holy Spirit speaking through the scriptures is not visible. Therefore. Resp. I deny the major, because visibility is not an essential and universal requirement of a judge, but an accidental and particular one. For a judge does not judge insofar as he is visible, but insofar as he is intelligible, or insofar as he issues a sentence which can be perceived. Visibility is required more of an inferior than of a superior judge. Thus the Roman pontiff publishes his judgment not immediately, but mediately through heralds, legates, and bulls, where however the pope himself is not seen.

6. Whatever norm is universal for things to be believed and done, it has existed at all times. But Holy Scripture has not existed at all times. Therefore. The major is evident, because a norm that directs the faith and morals not of all, but only of some people at some time, is not universal, but at least particular. The minor is clear, because Holy Scripture did not exist in the times of the patriarchs. Resp. Holy Scripture is called a universal norm not by reason of time, nor by reason of the subject, or the people using that norm, but by reason of the object, because it directs all dogmas of faith within the limits of truth, and all precepts of morals within the boundaries of holiness, and distinguishes them from all false dogmas and all defiled and imperfect precepts of morals.

Instance. Just as the faith of the patriarchs and ours is one: so there ought to be one principle of faith, one norm of things to be believed. Resp. Just as the faith of the patriarchs and ours is one: so there is one principle for generating faith, namely the revealed word of God: but the mode of administering divine revelation is different. For God immediately inspired His word to the patriarchs, and granted them the privilege of longevity, so that they might hand down the heavenly doctrine by living voice, without writing, as if by hand to their descendants; but because the imagination of the human heart is evil, the purity of the word was not faithfully preserved through traditions of the living voice, but was corrupted and adulterated, nay, finally completely lost. Wherefore God in the time of Moses established and showed another method of teaching, so that, namely, by writings approved and confirmed by divine authority and testimony, the purity of the heavenly doctrine might be propagated and preserved: lest, from questions or controversies arising concerning the old, genuine, and pure doctrine of the patriarchs, new and peculiar revelations should always have to be sought and expected: as our CHEMNIT. excellently warns in exam. concil. Trid. de origine & vsu verbi diuini fol. m. 8.

Latin:

Obs.

3. S. Scriptura iudicatat directiue, tanquam canon & norma, quam iudex inferior respicere, eique in iudicando sententiam suam, quam de exorta controuersia fidei pronuntiat, confirmare tenetur. Hoc sensu S. Scriptura dicitur iudex canonicus, normalis & directiuus, qui iudicem inferiorem, nempe ministrum ecclesiae & quemlibet hominem renatum, ne in iudicando aberret, instar normae & amussis dirigit. Definitiue, quia tanquam vox supremi iudicis litigantes partes componit, dubia religionis definit, & controuersias dirimit. Effectiue, quatenus S. scriptura est efficacissimum ὄργανον, medium & gladius Spiritus sancti, quo cor hominis penetrat, animum ferocientem subigit, & partium litigantium conscientias conuincit.

Obs.

4. Quamuis supra luculenter probata sit canonica S. scripturae auctoritas: hic tamen nobis incumbit debitum demonstrandi, S. scripturam esse normam decidendarum controuersiarum primariam & adaequatam.

Quamuis enim oi ἐξ ἐναντίας concedant, S. scripturam esse normam credendorum & agendorum, negant tamen S. scripturam esse normam vniuersalem, totalem & primariam.

Prob. a. (1) Quicunque est auctor scripturae sacrae, is de illius sensu omnibusque in ea contentis dogmatibus omnium optime iudicat. Atqui Deus &c. 2 Tim. III, 16. Ergo.

(2) Quicunque arguit mundum de peccato, de iustitia & iudicio, ille est summus iudex in rebus spiritualibus. Atqui Spiritus S. &c. Io. XVI, 8. Ergo.

(3) Quicunque fuit iudex controuersiarum tempore nascentis ecclesiae christianae in concilio apostolico, ille hodienum in omnibus conciliis est summus iudex. Atqui Spiritus S. per scripturas loquens &c. Ergo. Minor prob. ex Act. XV, 28. vbi sententiam decifiuam concilii apostolici, sequentibus verbis pronuntiant apostoli: Visum est Spiritui sancto, & nobis.

Iudices ministeriales in concilio apostolico erant apostoli & presbyteri ecclesiae Hierosolymitanae, aliique pii viri. Act. XV, 6. 22. 23. Supremus iudex erat Spiritus S. loquens per scripturas. Nam Iacobus Petri suffragium comprobabat ex solis oraculis propheticis, dicens: Et huic consentiunt verba prophetarum: sicut scriptum est (Amos IX, 11.) Iudicauit ergo Spiritus S. in concilio apostolico per scripturam propheticam: haec erat vox supremi iudicis Spiritus S.

(4) Si Deus supremus iudex per scripturam homines concludit sub peccato, vtique scriptura vox est summi iudicis, per quam homines peccati conuincuntur. Atqui prius indubitato verum est, Ergo & posterius. Antecedens patet ex collatione dictorum Paullinorum. Rom. XI, 32. & Gal. III, 22. Deus enim dicitur omnes concludere homines in infidelitatem, vt omnium misereatur.

Rom. XI, 32. De scriptura itidem affirmatur, quod omnia concludat sub peccatum; vt promissio ex fide Iesu Christi detur credentibus.

Gal. III, 22. Audiamus interpretem CALOVIVM in bibl. illustr. ad Rom. XI, 32. fol. 201. Concludit Deus omnes sub ἀπειθεία, non ἐνεργητικῶς, operando seu efficiendo incredulitatem; sed ἐλεγκτικῶς, arguendo, conuincendo & condemnando: non αἰτιατικῶς, seu causaliter; sed δικαστικῶς & iudicialiter, qua voce legis, seu legalis ac iudiciariae sententiae, rei arguuntur omnes homines, conuincuntur de peccato, & condemnantur ob peccatum, ac velut in carcerem compinguntur, captiuique detinentur aeterna condemnationis mancipia.

Deut. XXVII, 26. (5) Christus ipse verbo suo partes iudicis assignat, Io. XII, 48. Qui spernit me, & non accipit verba mea, habet, qui iudicet ipsum: verbum, quod locutus sum, illud iudicabit illum in extremo die. Qua ratione verbum Christi iudicabit in extremo die, eadem iudicat in hoc seculo.

Sed iudicabit in extremo die conscientias peccatorum conuincendo: Ergo eandem potestatem iudicialem in hoc seculo obtinet.

Prob. b. S. scripturam esse normam adaequatam & primariam, iuxta quam omnia fidei dogmata morumque praecepta sint diiudicanda, patet.

1. Ex effato Paullino, Gal. VI, 16. Quotquot canone hoc incedunt, pax (erit) super eos, & misericordia, & super Israelem Dei. Supra ostensum est, hoc dictum apostolicum recte intelligi de scriptura sacra, cuius compendium nobis exhibet haec ad Galatas scripta epistola. Iam argumentamur: Quodcunque verbum sufficit ad gratiam a Deo ac pacem obtinendam omnibus rectam viam fidei pietatisque decurrentibus, illud est norma adaequata credendorum & agendorum. Atqui verbum Dei reuelatum, & a prophetis atque apostolis in litteras relatum, est &c. Ergo.

2. Ex oraculo prophetico Es. VIII, 19. 20. Quando vero dixerint ad vos: quaerite pythones & hariolos sibilantes & mussitantes: (respondeo) Annon populus Deum suum quaeret? pro viuisne mortuos? (Quare) legem & testimonium (quaeret): quod si non dixerint iuxta verbum hoc: profecto non (erit) vlli aurora. Obs. (1) Scopus prophetae erat, praemunire pios a superstitione & idololatria illorum, qui de rebus dubiis consultum ibant pythones & hariolos. Serio dehortatur propheta populum Dei ab hac superstitione, petito argumento a iure & aequo: Annon populus Deum suum quaeret? quasi dicat: Annon aequum est, vt quisque populus consulat Deum suum, quem futura praenosse persuasum est, Illustrat propheta argumentum suum contrario, dicens: Num pro viuis ad mortuos? q. d. Nonne iniquum & absurdum est, pro salute viuorum consulere mortuos (siue intelligas idola, siue manes defunctorum) qui nil sciunt, nil iuuare possunt? (2) Concludit propheta: Quare legem & testimonium quaeret. Lex & testimonium est lex Mosaica & vniuersa scriptura, in qua Deus consuli potuit, vt sensus fit: Si vultis certi esse de casibus dubiis, & incertis euentibus futuris, nolite abire ad pythones & diuinatores, sed ad legem & testimonium, in quibus clare habetis, quid facere, quid omittere debeatis, vt salutares euentus exspectare certo possitis. (3) Subiungit propheta comminationem: Si non dixerint verbum hoc, i. e. si doctores, vel patres vestri, non ablegauerint populum ad legem & testimonium Dei, & populus non obedierit: tum non erit populo illi aurora, siue lux illius sapientiae salutaris, & inde prouenientis boni atque felicitatis, siue temporalis, siue spiritualis. Ex verbis prophetae sic explicatis argumentamur: Ad quodcunque solum ablegatur vniuersus populus & obligatur in soluendis dubiis circa salutem, illud est vnica & adaequata norma, iuxta quam omnia de salute hominis mota dubia examinanda & soluenda sunt. Atqui ad legem Mosaicam & testimonium scripturae &c. Ergo. Minor vberius confirmari potest verbis Abrahami, quibus instruebat diuitem epulonem: Habent Mosen & prophetas, audiant illos, Luc. XVI, 29. prorsus ac si diceret: adaequata poenitentiae rite agenda regula est scriptura Mosaica & prophetica.

3. E testimonio apostolico; quo ornatur Timotheus 2 Tim. III, 15. 16. quod explicatum vid. superius. Ad normam enim credendorum & agendorum facile applicatur, modo loco principii theologiae adaequati substituatur norma fidei & morum adaequata.

4. Quod solum a Christo, apostolis, aliisque sanctis pro norma controuersiarum fidei fuit habitum, id etiamnum solum est norma fidei, eaque primaria. Atqui sacra scriptura est id, &c. Ergo. Maior clara est, quia non alia, quam quae a Christo, apostolis, & aliis sanctis norma controuersiarum fuit adhibita, hodie adhiberi potest. Sicut enim tempore Christi & apostolorum, & nostro tempore eadem sunt credenda & agenda: ita quoque eadem norma est adhibenda. Minor probatur exemplo Christi, cum Pharisaeis & Sadducaeis ex scriptura disputantis, Matth. XIX. & Iudaeos ad scripturam remittentis. Io. V, 39. Idem patet exemplo apostolorum.

Act. XXV, 22. vbi Paullus extra prophetas & Mosen se nihil dixisse asserit. Similiter Stephanus Act. VI. vnice ex scripturis disputat. Beroenses quotidie scrutati sunt scripturas, num se haberent hæc ita, quæ Paullus docebat. Act. XVII, 11.

Antithesis est 1. Pontificiorum opinantium, sacram scripturam esse normam controuersiarum fidei partialem, sed non iudicem. 2. Socinianorum negantium, sacram scripturam esse vnicam regulam fidei. 3. Arminianorum concedentium, S. scripturam esse normam controuersiarum fidei, sed non iudicem effective iudicantem. 4. Quakerorum, infitiantium, S. scripturam esse normam fidei & morum primariam & vniuersalem; quippe quam statuunt esse dictamen spiritus immediate loquentis aut reuelantis cuique hominum internum; quamuis concedant, sacram scripturam esse normam partialem, subordinatam, secundariam & declaratoriam. Potiora eorum argumenta sunt sequentia.

1. Norma fidei non est eius iudex. Atqui S. scriptura est norma fidei. Ergo. Resp. (1) Norma fidei non est iudex eius αὐτοκρατορικὸς & personalis; concedo: at vero est iudex fidei κανονικὸς & directiuus. (2) Sacra scriptura non tantum est norma, quam index inferior respicit, sed est etiam vox iudicis superioris Spiritus sancti, qua per scripturam S. controuersias de religione exortas dirimit.

2. Si S. scriptura non est iudex personalis, non erit iudex proprie talis. Sed si non est iudex proprie talis, non proprie & vere iudicabit. Resp. Si sensu strictiori iudex dicatur persona iudicans, fatemur sacram scripturam non esse iudicem proprie, sed improprie talem (improprietate grammatica, non rhetorica). Neque tamen hac de causa dicendum est, quod S. scriptura non vere iudicet. Etenim quæ potestas iudicandi Spiritui sancto competit originaliter, illa conuenit S. scripturæ participatiue; ideo, quod vox summi iudicis est conscientiam conuincens, dum Spiritus sancti sententiam tam clare & perspicue exhibet, quam certo sententia pro tribunali, visibili iudice scripta & partibus litigantibus tradita, iudicis visibilis vox est.

3. Quicunque vere iudicat, immorigeros cogere potest ad obedientiam. (Ceteroqui iudicium sine executione latæ sententiæ erit campana sine pistillo.) Atqui S. scriptura non potest cogere immorigeros ad obedientiam (quia plurimi iudicium S. scripturæ aspernantur). Ergo S. scriptura non vere iudicat. Resp. Distinguendo inter coactionem externam corporum, & internam mentium, siue conscientiarum. Scriptura non cogit corpora, sed conuincit mentes & conscientias, vt veritati cœlesti se submittant; quod nullis impetrabis machinis politicis, facilius hypocritam facturus, quam fidelem. Neque est, quod obuertas, haud paucos iudicium S. scripturæ aspernari; quod non facerent, si scriptura iudicaret coactine. Etenim constat, plurimos empæctas iudicium Christi summa cum vi & potestate iudicantis contemtim habere. Cogit S. scriptura non violenter, sed supernaturaliter; non per vim irresistibilem, sed resistibilem.

4. Quicunque est iudex controuersiarum fidei, ille condemnat hæreticos, vt fateantur sententiam contra se esse latam. Atqui Spiritus S. per scripturam S. loquens non ita condemnat hæreticos. Ergo Spiritus S. per scripturam S. loquens non est iudex controuersiarum fidei. Respondeo negando maiorem, & distinguendo inter λόγον ἔσω καὶ ἔξω, inter sensum internum cordis, & confessionem externam oris. Spiritus S. per scripturam S. loquens condemnat hæreticos, vt in corde sentiant sententiam contra se esse latam; licet ore non fateantur, se esse conuictos. Adiice, quod Spiritus S. hæreticos condemnet non nominatim & indiuidualiter, sed generatim & fundamentaliter, generale fundamentum sententiæ condemnatoriæ suppeditando, iuxta illud Io. III, 18: Qui non credit, iam iudicatus est.

5. Iudex proprie dictus debet esse visibilis, qui ab omnibus iudicandis videri & audiri queat. Spiritus S. per scripturas loquens non est visibilis. Ergo. Resp. Neg. maior, quia visibilitas non est iudicis requisitum essentiale & universale, sed accidentale & particulare. Neque enim iudicat iudex, quatenus est visibilis, sed quatenus est intelligibilis, sive quatenus sententiam edit, quae percipi potest. Visibilitas magis ab inferiori, quam superiori iudice requiritur. Sic pontifex Romanus suum iudicium publicat non immediate, sed mediate per praecones, legatos, bullas, vbi tamen ipse papa non videtur.

6. Quaecunque norma est universalis credendorum & agendorum, illa omni exstitit tempore. Sed S. scriptura non exstitit omni tempore. Ergo. Maior constat, quia norma non omni, sed quodam tantum tempore dirigens fidem moresque non omnium, sed quorundam tantum hominum, non est universalis, sed saltim particularis. Minor clara est, quia S. scriptura temporibus patriarcharum non exstitit. Resp. S. scriptura dicitur norma universalis non ratione temporis, neque ratione subiecti, sive hominum, ea norma utentium, sed ratione obiecti, quia omnia dogmata fidei intra veritatis limites, omnia praecepta morum intra sanctitatis cancellos dirigit, & ab omnibus falsis dogmatibus, omnibusque inquinatis & imperfectis morum praeceptis discernit.

Instantia. Sicut una est fides patriarcharum & nostra: ita oportet esse unum fidei principium, unam credendorum normam. Resp. Sicut fides patriarcharum & nostra est una: ita unum est generandae fidei principium, nempe verbum Dei revelatum: sed modus administrandae revelationis diuinae diversus est. Nam patriarchis Deus verbum suum immediate inspirauit, iisque priuilegium longaeuitatis concessit, vt doctrinam coelestem, viua voce, sine scripto, quasi per manus traderent posteris; sed quia figmentum cordis humani malum est, puritas verbi per traditiones viuae vocis non fideliter fuit conseruata, sed corrupta & adulterata, imo tandem plane amissa. Quamobrem Deus tempore Mosis aliam docendi rationem constituit & ostendit, vt scilicet scriptis diuina auctoritate & testimonio approbatis & confirmatis puritas doctrinae coelestis propagaretur, & conseruaretur: ne quaestionibus, aut controuersiis, de veteri genuina & pura patriarcharum doctrina exortis, semper & quaerendae, & expectandae essent nouae & peculiares reuelationes: vti egregie monet noster CHEMNIT. in exam. concil. Trid. de origine & vsu verbi diuini fol. m. 8.


### XLIII. Are the vowel points coeval with the letters of the Hebrews?: 8. 7. A universal canon of things to be believed and done is infallible. The canon of Holy Scripture is not infallible. Therefore the canon…

8. 7. A universal canon of things to be believed and done is infallible. The canon of Holy Scripture is not infallible. Therefore the canon of Holy Scripture is not a universal canon of things to be believed and done.

The major radiates with its own light. The minor is proven, because 1. the church constitutes the canon of the scriptures, whose testimony is human and fallible. 2. Certain councils, namely the Third Council of Carthage, the Florentine, and the Tridentine, broadened the biblical canon and inserted more books, such as the book of Wisdom, Tobit, and the Maccabees, into the biblical canon: certain councils narrowed the canon of scripture and did not receive the mentioned books into the canon, namely the Council of Laodicea and the Sixth Constantinopolitan. All of which argue for the fallibility of the canon of scripture. Resp. a) The biblical canon denotes 1) the rule of faith and morals. 2) The catalog or series of canonical books. The church does not constitute the canon of faith as a mistress or judge, but as a minister, index, and interpreter, it historically reviewed the catalog of canonical books and declared it by its own testimony. Which testimony, although it is human, does not on that account detract from the infallibility of the biblical canon, just as the human testimony of the Samaritan woman rendered to Christ took nothing away from His divine majesty and infallible truth. 3) The disagreement of councils concerning the number of canonical books is more verbal than real. For one must distinguish between the canon taken broadly and loosely, as the canon of ecclesiastical reading, for whatever kind of edification of morals; and the canon taken strictly and properly, as the canon for the confirmation of faith. Augustine the third Council of Carthage, likewise Gelasius & Innocentius, Roman Pontiffs, in a looser signification called all books that are usefully read in the church for the amendment of morals "canonical," distinguishing them from those "apocryphal" books which, full of trifles & lies, are to be hidden & rejected. most ancient fathers, Melito, Origen, Eusebius, Jerome in his "prologue galeatus," & others, in a stricter sense called those books "canonical" which were immediately, in terms of words & concepts, inspired by the Holy Spirit to the prophets & apostles, and thus possess infallible canonical authority to separate truth from falsehood, and piety from impiety.

8. If Holy Scripture is an infallible rule of faith & morals, it will have that normative power either in the autographs or in the apographs. But not in the autographs of the prophets & apostles; since these do not survive in the church today. Nor in the apographs; since we are not certain whether they agree in all respects with the autographs, given that there are many variant readings. Response: The divine authority that is originally in the autographs of the prophets & apostles is radically the same in the apographs faithfully transcribed from them; because they contain not only the divine sense, but also those very words which the Holy Spirit inspired & dictated to Moses, the prophets & apostles: just as the autographs of the constitutions & recesses of the Holy Roman Empire, the Constitutio Criminalis Carolina, the Instrument of Peace, etc., which are preserved in the archives of the Arch-Chancellor of the German Empire, the Elector of Mainz, have never been seen by us, indeed, by many states of the empire; nevertheless, the authority of the apographs, printed by the will & command of the emperor, is so great that they are held to be the very decrees of the German Empire, & disputes arising in the empire are decided by them. The αὐτόγραφα καὶ πρωτότυπα [autographs and originals] of the prophets did not exist in the time of Christ & the apostles, who nevertheless appealed to their apographs, & commended their reading to us, which they would never have done unless they had recognized their infallible truth. Nor can variant readings render the canonical authority of scripture doubtful; because it is easy to investigate & gather the genuine reading from the coherence of the text.

9. Every rule is clear & sufficient for proving doctrines. But Holy Scripture is not clear, but obscure in many places; nor is it sufficient for proving the doctrines of faith; otherwise, so many books on cases of conscience would not have been written. Response: That Holy Scripture is clear in those things necessary for man's instruction in faith & life, tending towards salvation, and that it sufficiently transmits the main points of the Christian religion, will be proven below.

10. Every rule is continuous. Holy Scripture is not continuous. Therefore, Holy Scripture is not a rule. The minor premise is proven because Holy Scripture is not perpetually occupied with explaining or confirming doctrines of faith & precepts of morals, but inserts into them chronological, genealogical, astronomical, physical, etc. matters. Response: Every architectural rule is continuous; I grant that. For a dogmatic rule, it is sufficient that everything it transmits refers to a single end, either by way of definition & confirmation, or by way of illustration. The chronological, genealogical, astronomical, physical matters found in the sacred writings contribute not a little both to interpreting scripture itself & to illustrating the precepts of faith & morals.

11. Although Holy Scripture can be called a rule of faith, it is not a primary, but a secondary, subordinate & declaratory rule; since the principal rule is the immediate light or dictate of the Holy Spirit speaking in the heart of the reborn person, teaching him, & suggesting to him what is necessary to know & do. Response: To call Holy Scripture, which is the word not of men, but of God himself, 1 Thess. II, 13. the power of God, Rom. I, 16. the mind of Christ, 1 Cor. II, 16. Spirit & life, Io. VI, 63. the seed of our regeneration, 1 Petr. I, 23. a secondary, subordinate & merely declaratory rule of what is to be believed & done, is a matter of conscience for us.

Latin:

7. Canon universalis credendorum & agendorum est infallibilis. Canon sacrae scripturae non est infallibilis. Ergo canon sacrae scripturae non est universalis credendorum & agendorum canon.

Maior sua radiat luce. Minor probatur, quia 1. canonem scripturarum constituit ecclesia, cuius testimonium est humanum & fallibile. 2. Canonem biblicum quaedam concilia, nimirum Carthaginense III. Florentinum & Tridentinum laxarunt, pluresque libros, vtpote librum Sapientiae, Tobiae, Maccabaeorum, canoni biblico inferuerunt: quaedam concilia canonem scripturae coarctarunt, memoratosque libros in canonem non receperunt, nempe concilium Laodicenum & Constantinopolitanum VI. Quae omnia fallibilitatem canonis scripturae arguunt. Resp. a) Canon biblicus notat 1) regulam fidei & morum. 2) Catalogum siue seriem librorum canonicorum. Ecclesia non vt magistra aut iudex canonem fidei constituit, sed vt ministra, index, interpres, catalogum librorum canonicorum historice recensuit, & testimonio suo declarauit. Quod testimonium quamuis humanum sit, infallibilitati canonis biblici perinde non derogat, ac testimonium humanum mulieris Samaritanae Christo perhibitum diuinae ipsius maiestati & infallibili veritati nil detrahebat. 3) Dissensus conciliorum de numero librorum canonicorum magis verbalis, quam realis est. Distinguendum enim est inter canonem παχυλῶς & late sumtum, pro canone ecclesiasticae lectionis, ob qualemcunque morum aedificationem; & canonem stricte & proprie acceptum, pro canone fidei confirmationis. Augustinus concilium Carthaginense tertium, item Gelasius & Innocentius, Pontifices Romani, laxiore fignificatione omnes libros, qui vtiliter ad emendationem morum in ecclesia leguntur, vocarunt canonicos, quibus contradistinxerunt illos libros apocryphos, qui nugis & mendaciis pleni abscondendi & reiiciendi sunt. Contra concilium Laodicenum, & Constantinopolitanum VI. iuxta atque antiquissimi patres, Melito, Origenes, Eusebius, Hieronymus in prologo galeato, & alii, sensu strictiori illos libros vocarunt canonicos, qui immediate, qua verba & rerum conceptus, prophetis & apostolis sunt inspirati a Spiritu S. atque adeo infallibili pollent auctoritate canonica, verum a falfo, pium ab impio segregandi.

8. Si S. scriptura infallibilis norma est fidei & morum, vel in autographis, vel in apographis illam vim normandi habebit. At non in autographis prophetarum & apostolorum; cum illa hodie in ecclesia non supersint. Nec in apographis; cum certo nobis non constet, an illa per omnia confentiant autographis, siquidem plurimæ dantur lectiones variantes. Resp. Quæ auctoritas diuina est in autographis prophetarum & apostolorum originaliter; eadem radicaliter est in apographis fideliter ex illis transscriptis; eo quod continent non tantum sensum diuinum, sed etiam illa ipsa verba, quæ Spiritus S. Mofi, prophetis & apostolis inspirauit atque dictauit: sicut autographa constitutionum ac recessuum imperii Romano-Germanici, constitutionis Carolinæ, instrumenti pacis &c. quæ asseruantur in tabulario archi-cancellarii imperii Germanici, electoris Moguntini, a nobis, imo etiam a plurimis imperii statibus nunquam sunt vifa; apographorum tamen, ex voluntate & mandato imperatoris typis impressorum, tanta est auctoritas, vt ea pro ipfis Imperii Germanici decretis habeantur, & exorte in imperio lites ex illis decidantur. Αὐτόγραφα καὶ πρωτότυπα prophetarum non exstabant tempore Christi & apostololorum, qui tamen ad illorum apographa prouocarunt, eorumque lectionem nobis commendarunt, nunquam id facturi, nisi infallibilem eorum veritatem agnouissent. Neque variantes lectiones dubiam reddere poffunt auctoritatem canonicam scripturæ; propterea quod genuinam lectionem e cohærentia textus indagare & colligere procliue est.

9. Omnis norma est perspicua & fufficiens dogmatibus probandis. Atqui, S. scriptura non est perspicua, sed multis locis obscura; neque fufficiens est dogmatibus fidei probandis; ceteroqui tot libri de cafibus conscientiæ non essent conscripti. Resp. Sacram scripturam in his, quæ ad fidei & vitæ informationem necessaria sunt homini ad salutem tendenti, esse perspicuam, & summa religionis christianæ capita fufficienter tradere, infra probabitur.

10. Omnis norma est continua. S. scriptura non est continua. Ergo S. scriptura non est norma. Minor probatur, quia S. scriptura non perpetuo occupata est in explicandis aut confirmandis dogmatibus fidei & præceptis morum, verum inferit iisdem chronologica, genealogica, astronomica, phyfica &c. Resp. Omnis norma architectonica est continua; concedo. Ad normam dogmaticam fufficit, quod omnia, quæ tradit, referat ad vnuum finem, vel per modum definitionis & confirmationis, vel per modum illustrationis. Quæ in sacris litteris habentur chronologica, genealogica, astronomica, phyfica, & ad interpretandam ipfam scripturam, & illustranda fidei morumque præcepta haud parum faciunt.

11. Quamuis S. scriptura dici possit norma fidei, non tamen primaria, sed fecundaria, subordinata & declaratoria est norma; siquidem norma principalis est immediatum lumen aut dictamen Spiritus S. in corde hominis renati loquentis, ipsum docentis, & cognitu factuque necessaria ipsi suggerentis. Resp. S. scripturam, quæ est verbum non hominum, sed ipfius Dei, 1 Theff. II, 13. potentia Dei, Rom. I, 16. mens Christi, 1 Cor. II, 16. Spiritus & vita, Io. VI, 63. femen nostræ regenerationis, 1 Petr. I, 23. normam credendorum & agendorum appellare secundariam, subordinatam & tantum declaratoriam, nobis est religio.


### XLIII. Are the vowel points coeval with the letters of the Hebrews?: Against the immediate

Against the immediate

PART I. T

that an immediate light or dictation of the Holy Spirit, after the completion of the canon of Scripture, is indeed feigned, but in reality is not given, has been clearly shown above.

Latin:

Contra immePARS I.

T

diatum lumen aut dictamen Spiritus S. post completum scripturae canonem fingi quidem, sed reuera non dari, supra luculenter ostensum est.


### Q. XLV. Is there a visible judge of controversies of faith in the church?

A visible judge is said generally to be any discerning judge who, by employing the judgment of the intellect, distinguishes the true from the false. In this general sense, all laymen instructed with the aids for explaining the Holy Scriptures and treating theological controversies , especially all doctors of the church, whose duty it is to vindicate the purity of the faith from corruptions and to refute those who contradict , and all synods and councils, which are gathered for the most part from bishops and doctors of the churches, are judges of controversies of faith . But a visible judge, specifically and strictly so called—namely, an authoritative and decisive one, who pronounces judgment by authority and, by the force of the authority in which he excels, obliges the litigants so that they acquiesce in the sentence passed by him without further inquiry—is not given in the church after the canon of the Scriptures has been established .

Proof a. That a dogmatic discerning judgment of faith resides with every reborn man according to the measure of the Spirit is clear from the honorable testimony of St. Paul, with which he adorns the faithful man, 1 Cor. II, 15: "The spiritual man judges all things; yet he himself is judged by no one." By the spiritual man is not understood the Roman Pontiff, since he did not yet exist while Paul was alive, nor only the pastors of the churches, but every man illuminated, converted, and reborn by the Holy Spirit, who has the mind of Christ and understands the sense of the Holy Scripture. He judges—that is, perceives through the light of faith—all things which Christ has revealed in His gospel and which are necessary to be known for the worship of God and eternal salvation, and distinguishes them from the inventions of men. But the reborn man is not judged by the animal man, who is ignorant of the sacred letters; that is, he cannot be convicted of error. For the animal man relies on the principles of reason; but the spiritual man follows Scripture as his guide. But what is reason in sacred matters, if not delirium? 2) The same is evident from the general exhortation of Paul, who addresses all the Corinthians, 1 Cor. X, 15: "Judge for yourselves what I say"; and likewise the Thessalonians, 1 Thess. V, 21: "Test all things; hold fast what is good." 3) The same is gathered from the scrutiny of Holy Scripture, which is commended to all men to be saved. For the Savior, John V, 39, invites all indiscriminately to the diligent reading of Scripture when He says: "Search the scriptures." To those to whom it is not only permitted but also seriously enjoined to read and search the Scriptures, it belongs to weigh with an accurate balance of mind all dogmas of faith and precepts of morals, whether they are consonant or dissonant with Holy Scripture. But that scrutiny of the Scriptures is enjoined not only upon the clergy, but also upon the laity. The Bereans proved this by their example, searching the Scriptures daily to see if those things which Paul had preached concerning the passion, death, and resurrection of Jesus were so. Acts XVII, 11.

Proof b. Every doctor of the church ought to rightly divide the word of truth. 2 Tim. II, 15. He himself must be "holding fast the faithful word as he has been taught, that he may be able, by sound doctrine, both to exhort and convict those who contradict." We argue: To whom it belongs to rightly divide the word of truth, to exhort the unskilled in sound doctrine, and to refute those who contradict, to him belongs the judgment of the dogmas of faith, whether δοκιμαστικὸν (discerning), or ἐξηγητικὸν (interpretative), or ἐλεγκτικὸν (vindictive).

Prob. c. From the acts of the Council of Jerusalem, Acts XV. In which council the judge, ἀνυπεύθυνος [unaccountable] & infallible, was the Holy Spirit. "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit," say the apostles, Acts XV, 28. The interpreters of the divine judgment were the θεόπνευστοι [God-breathed/inspired] apostles, led into all truth by the Holy Spirit. "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us," say the apostles. The presbyters of the church of Jerusalem, and other pious men, were not only witnesses of the business treated by apostolic authority, but also examiners of the Antiochene cause and ministerial judges. Then "it seemed good to the apostles and presbyters with the whole church," Acts XV, 22, 23, who having consulted unanimously, cast their votes and decided, v. 25. "It seemed good to us, being assembled unanimously." Therefore, the decisions of councils are of great utility regarding the consensus of doctrine and external order; but they do not bind the conscience unless they are conformable to the norm of the divine word. For they are not praetorian edicts, but the counsels of wise men and the responses of the prudent, to be highly esteemed by fair judges of spiritual matters.

Prob. d. (1) After the completed canon of Holy Scripture, there are not given θεόπνευστοι [inspired] men, or those instructed by the privilege of immediate divine inspiration. Therefore, after the completed canon of Holy Scripture, there is not given in the church a visible judge immune from the danger of error. (2) Dictatorial authority in matters of faith neither God nor the church has granted to any mortal. For if God had granted it, Scripture would testify to such a pinnacle of dignity; or it would send us off to one αὐτόπιστον [self-credible] bishop. But it neither testifies to this, nor does it dispatch us to a universal visible judge in the church. That the church granted to one bishop the authority of deciding all controversies of faith does not appear from ecclesiastical antiquity: nor does the church possess such powers that it could transfer the gift of infallibility to one bishop.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, who posit that the Roman Pope, viewed as the universal doctor of the church and pronouncing his sentence ex cathedra, is the infallible judge of controversies of faith; although, in their view, the Roman Pontiff can err as a private person and a particular doctor.
