They consider the Pope to pronounce sentence ex cathedra, if (α) he pronounces it with a general council; (β) outside a general council, after due diligence, he pronounces sentence, having employed as aids the common rules of faith, which they constitute in the sacred scriptures, apostolic traditions, approved councils, and the consensus of the fathers.

The stronger arguments of the Papists are the following.

I. In the O.T., all legal controversies that were of greater moment were defined and settled by the high priest, and indeed with irrefragable authority, Deut. XVII, 8. Therefore, in the N.T. also, all controversies of faith are to be settled and defined by the Roman Pontiff with irrefragable authority. Resp. The consequence falters. For (1) in the Old Testament, the high priest was instituted by God, and the power which he used in judging was expressly conferred upon him and the Levites and priests by God. But the Roman Pontiff is not constituted by God as the high priest of the universal church, nor was the judicial power, which he arrogates to himself above other bishops, granted to him by God. (2) The controversies, for which a judge was constituted in Deut. XVII, 8, were not controversies of faith, but controversies that arose between brothers, and more difficult practical cases, and that judgment was "between blood and blood, between leprosy and leprosy; between plea and plea," as Deut. XVII, 8 clearly says. But it is not permitted to argue from the legal controversies of the Israelites to the controversies of faith in the N.T. church. (3) The antecedent is also false. For the judicial power in Deut. XVII, 8 was not conferred precisely upon the high priest, but granted to the whole college, constituted of several persons. That judgment consisted in a college both of Levites and priests, over whom the high priest presided, and of the political judge and the elders of the people. The political judge, at that time when the people of Israel was governed not by kings but by judges, was highest magistrate of the Israelite people: in the time of the kings, however, it was he whom the king had designated, so that he might be present at the judgment as a political judge in his own name and place. The high priest was not infallible in judging.

For he had to be directed by the norm of the law, Deut. 17:11. But every norm regulates him who is fallible. And the supreme pontiff erred most gravely in condemning the most innocent Christ.

II. For deciding civil questions, a visible authoritative judge is necessary.

Therefore, also for questions of faith.

Resp.

The Papists conclude wrongly from political judgment to ecclesiastical judgment, from the decision of civil questions to the decision of controversies of faith. In civil matters, the will of the prince is the supreme rule of decision, in whose judgment the litigating parties are bound to acquiesce on account of the supreme authority and power which he holds in the republic. In matters of faith, however, there is no mortal man given to whose will and arbitration they are subject: for matters of faith depend on God alone revealing, and on his revelation contained in the Holy Scriptures. Most vain, therefore, is he who arrogates divine power to himself.

III. If there is no visible judge in the church who decides controversies of faith with public and infallible authority, there will be no end to disputing.

Resp.

Theological controversies either concern fundamental articles of faith, or non-fundamental ones: Fundamental articles of faith are contained in Scripture either αὐτολεξεὶ (word for word) and in express terms, and those unambiguous, or are deduced by good and proximate consequence from clear sayings of Scripture. Controversies arising from these can easily be ended, provided the state of the controversy is accurately formed and observed, and the arguments of both parties are weighed by pious, learned, and truth-loving men according to the norm of Scripture. That they are not yet ended happens by accident, and arises either from preconceived opinions, or from party zeal and malice of will.

Controversies, however, concerning non-fundamental articles of faith can be ventilated ἄνω καὶ κάτω (up and down), back and forth, without loss of salvation, provided we are solicitous to take care that we do not rashly embrace error and sin against divine revelation itself.

Conf. supra quaest. 23, prob. 2.

IV. Peter was the first Roman Pontiff and was infallible.

Therefore, his successors are infallible.

The antecedent is proved 1) from Matt. 16:18: Thou art Peter: and upon this same rock I will build my church. Hence arises the argument: Upon whom the church is built, he must be infallible.

But the church is built upon Peter. Therefore, Peter must be infallible. 2) From Luke 22:32, where Christ addresses Peter with these words: But I have prayed (in the first place) for thee, that thy faith fail not.

Resp. to 1) by denying the consequence.

For the argument is not valid: Peter was infallible: Therefore the Roman Pontiffs are infallible. For it is uncertain that Peter was the Roman Pontiff: more uncertain that the Roman pontiffs are the legitimate successors of Peter: most uncertain that the infallibility of Peter is necessarily transferred and as it were derived into his successors.

For a personal privilege does not necessarily pass to descendants; otherwise all the kings who succeeded David would have been immediately illuminated by God, just as King David was struck by the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

Furthermore, the cited words of Christ are to be understood not of Peter's person, primacy, or privilege of infallibility, but of the confession and doctrine of Peter.

For this apostle had delivered a very distinguished confession about Christ, when he had said: Thou art that Christ, the Son of the living God, Matt. 16:16. The Savior answered: Blessed art thou, Simon Bar-Jona, for flesh and blood hath not revealed (this) unto thee, but my Father, which is in heaven.

Nay, indeed, I say unto thee; thou art Peter: and upon this same rock I will build my church.

Christ does not say: thou art Peter, and upon thee Peter I will build my church, but with the name changed he says: Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build. Therefore, Peter is one thing, the rock is another.

Some of the most ancient fathers understand by the rock the apo-

stolic doctrine of Peter concerning Christ (*), some [interpret] Christ himself, preached or celebrated by the doctrine of Peter (as of other apostles). Both expositions come to almost the same thing. For the apostolic doctrine concerning Christ, and Christ preached by apostolic doctrine, do not differ according to the thing, but according to our mode of conceiving. Christ is the substantial foundation of the church; the doctrine concerning Christ is the dogmatic foundation of the church.

Instantia I. When Christ in John XXI, 17 said to Peter: 'feed my sheep', he granted infallibility and the government of the church without error to Peter, and to his successors, namely the Roman pontiffs. Resp. I deny the consequence. For to feed the sheep of Christ belongs to all pastors of the church. The apostle of the gentiles gravely addresses all the presbyters of the Ephesian church: 'The Holy Spirit hath placed you bishops to feed the church of God.' Acts XX, 28.

Instantia II. Just as there was one supreme pastor of the Old Testament, Eccles. XII, 11, so there ought to be one supreme pastor of the New Testament. Resp. The one pastor, and he the supreme one, is the triune God, and by appropriation the Son of God, who is called Ἀρχιποίμην, 1 Pet. II, 25. Quest.

Latin:

Iudex visibilis dicitur generaliter omnis iudex discretiuus, qui adhibito iudicio intellectus verum a falso dignoscit. Quo sensu generali omnes laici adminiculis ad explicandas S. scripturas & tractandas controuersias theologicas instructi , in primis omnes doctores ecclesiae, quorum est puritatem fidei a corruptelis vindicare & contradicentes redarguere , omnes synodi & concilia, quae ex episcopis & ecclesiarum doctoribus maximam partem congregantur, iudices controuersiarum fidei sunt . Sed iudex visibilis specialiter & stricte dictus, nempe auctoritativus & decisiuus, qui pro auctoritate ferat sententiam, & vi auctoritatis, qua pollet, litigantes obliget, vt in lata a se sententia citra vlteriorem inquisitionem acquiescant, post constitutum scripturarum canonem in ecclesia non datur .

Prob. a. Iudicium discretiuum dogmaticum fidei esse penes omnem hominem renatum pro mensura spiritus, liquet ex honorifico testimonio S. Pauli, quo hominem fidelem ornat, 1 Cor. II, 15. Spiritualis diiudicat quidem omnia; ipse vero a nemine diiudicatur. Per hominem spiritualem non intelligitur Pontifex Romanus, quippe qui viuo Paulo nondum erat, neque soli ecclesiarum pastores, sed omnis homo a Spiritu S. illuminatus, conuersus & renatus, qui mentem Christi habet & sensum S. scripturae intelligit. Ille omnia, quae Christus in euangelio suo patefecit, & quae ad cultum Dei aeternamque salutem cognitu necessaria sunt, diiudicat, i. e. per lumen fidei perspicit, eaque ab hominum commentis discernit. Renatus autem ab homine animali, sacrarum litterarum rudi, non diiudicatur, hoc est, erroris conuinci non potest. Etenim homo animalis principiis rationis innititur; spiritualis autem ducem scripturam sequitur. At quid ratio in sacris, nisi deliratio, rebus? 2) Patet idem ex adhortatione generali Pauli compellantis omnes Corinthios, 1 Cor. X, 15. Iudicate vos, quod dico; nec non Thessalonicenses, 1 Thess. V, 21. Omnia probate, quod bonum est, tenete. 3) Colligitur idem ex scrutinio sacrae scripturae, omnibus hominibus saluandis commendato. Saluator enim Io. V, 39. omnes promiscue inuitat ad sedulam lectionem scripturae, cum ait: scrutamini scripturas. Quibus permissum non tantum, sed & serio iniunctum est, legere & scrutari scripturas, illorum est, accurata mentis lance expendere omnia dogmata fidei & praecepta morum, sint ne consentanea, an dissentanea sacrae scripturae. Atqui non tantum clericis, sed laicis etiam illud scrutinium scripturarum iniunctum est. Exemplo suo id comprobarunt Beroenses, singulis diebus scrutati scripturas, num haberent haec ita, quae Paulus de passione, morte & resurrectione Iesu praedicauerat. Act. XVII, 11.

Prob. b. Omnem ecclesiae doctorem oportet recte secare verbum veritatis. 2 Tim. II, 15. Oportet ipsum tenacem esse eius, qui (est) secundum doctrinam, fidelis sermonis, vt potens sit etiam adhortari in doctrina sana, & contradicentes arguere. Argumentamur: Cuius est, verbum veritatis recte secare, imperitos in sana doctrina adhortari, & contradicentes redarguere, illi competit iudicium dogmatum fidei tum δοκιμαστικὸν siue discretiuum, tum ἐξηγητικὸν siue interpretatiuum, tum ἐλεγκτικὸν siue vindicatiuum.

Prob. c. Ex actis concilii Hierosolymitani Act. XV. In quo concilio iudex ἀνυπεύθυνος & infallibilis fuit Spiritus sanctus. Visum est Spiritui sancto, inquiunt apostoli Actor. XV, 28. Iudicii diuini interpretes fuerunt apostoli θεόπνευστοι, in omnem veritatem a Spiritu sancto ducti. Visum est Spiritui sancto, & nobis, aiunt apostoli. Presbyteri ecclesiæ Hierosolymitanæ, aliique pii viri non testes solum fuerunt negotii apostolica auctoritate tractati, sed etiam cognitores causæ Antiochenæ & iudices ministeriales. Tunc visum est apostolis & presbyteris cum tota ecclesia, Act. XV, 22. 23. qui vnanimiter consultarant, suffragia tulerunt & deciderunt, v. 25. Visum est nobis vnanimiter congregatis. Sunt itaque conciliorum decisiones, quoad consensum doctrinæ & externum ordinem, magnæ vtilitatis; at non obligant conscientiam, nisi conformes sint normæ verbi diuini. Neque enim sunt edicta prætoria, sed sapientum consilia & prudentum responsa, æquis rerum spiritualium æstimatoribus magni-facienda.

Prob. d. (1) Post completum S. scripturæ canonem non dantur viri θεόπνευστοι, siue priuilegio immediatæ diuinæ inspirationis instructi. Ergo post completum S. scripturæ canonem non datur in ecclesia visibilis iudex ab errandi periculo immunis. (2) Auctoritatem dictatoriam in rebus fidei neque Deus, neque ecclesia vlli mortalium concessit. Si enim concesserit Deus, scriptura de tanto dignitatis fastigio testaretur; aut ad vnum episcopum αὐτόπιστον nos ablegaret. Sed neque de eo testatur, neque ad vniuersalem in ecclesia iudicem visibilem nos amandat. Quod ecclesia vni episcopo concesserit auctoritatem decidendi omnes controuersias fidei, ex antiquitate ecclesiastica non constat: neque ecclesia iis pollet viribus, vt donum infallibilitatis in vnum episcopum transferre queat.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, statuentium, Papam Romanum, spectatum vt vniuersalem ecclesiæ doctorem & pronuntiantem sententiam suam ex cathedra, esse iudicem controuersiarum fidei infallibilem; licet ex mente illorum Pontifex Romanus errare possit, vt persona priuata & doctor particularis. Ex cathedra autem Papam pronuntiare sententiam censent, si (α) cum generali concilio eam pronuntiet; (β) extra concilium generale, præuia debita diligentia, sententiam pronuntiet, adhibitis in subsidium regulis fidei communibus, quas constituunt in scripturis sacris, traditionibus apostolicis, conciliis approbatis, & consensu patrum.

Argumenta potiora Pontificiorum sunt sequentia.

I. In V. T. omnes controuersiæ legales, quæ erant maioris momenti, a summo sacerdote definitæ & diremtæ sunt, & quidem auctoritate irrefragabili, Deut. XVII, 8. Ergo in N. T. etiam omnes fidei controuersiæ a Pontifice Romano auctoritate irrefragabili dirimendæ & definiendæ sunt. Resp. Vacillat consequentia. Nam (1) in vet. testam. summus sacerdos erat a Deo institutus, & potestas, qua in iudicando vtebatur, erat ipsi & leuitis ac sacerdotibus a Deo expresse collata. Sed Pontifex Romanus non est a Deo constitutus summus ecclesiæ vniuersæ sacerdos, nec potestas iudiciaria, quam sibi præ aliis episcopis arrogat, a Deo ipsi concessa est. (2) Controuersiæ, quarum iudex Deut. XVII, 8. constitutus est, non erant controuersiæ fidei, sed controuersiæ inter fratres ortæ, & casus practici difficiliores, eratque iudicium illud inter sanguinem & sanguinem, lepram & lepram; caussam & caussam, vt Deut. XVII, 8. clare dicitur. Sed a controuersiis legalibus Israëlitarum ad controuersias fidei in ecclesia N. T. argumentari non licet. (3) Antecedens etiam falsum est. Nam iudicaria potestas Deut. XVII, 8. non præcise sacerdoti summo collata, sed toti collegio, ex pluribus personis constituto, concessa erat. Constabat illud iudicium collegium tum ex leuitis & sacerdotibus, quibus præsidebat summus sacerdos, tum ex iudice politico & senioribus populi, Iudex ille politicus, eo tempore, quo populus Israëliticus non per reges, fed per iudices regebatur, erat summus populi Israelitici magistratus: tempore regum vero is, quem rex designauerat, vt velut iudex politicus suo nomine & loco iudicio interesset. Sacerdos summus non erat in iudicando infallibilis.

Etenim dirigendus erat a norma legis Deut. XVII, 11. Sed omnis norma normat eum, qui est fallibilis. Et summus pontifex Christum innocentissimum condemnando grauissime errauit.

II. Ad quaestiones ciuiles decidendas necessarius est iudex visibilis auctoritatiuus.

Ergo & quaestiones fidei.

Resp.

Perperam concludunt pontificii a iudicio politico ad iudicium ecclesiasticum, a decisione quaestionum ciuilium ad decisionem controuersiarum fidei. In ciuilibus voluntas principis est suprema decidendi ratio, in cuius sententia partes litigantes acquiescere tenentur ob summam auctoritatem & potestatem, qua in republica eminet. In rebus fidei autem nemo mortalium datur, cuius voluntati & arbitrio illae subsint: dependent enim res fidei a solo Deo reuelante, eiusque reuelatione in sacris litteris comprehensa. Vanissimus igitur est, qui diuinam sibi potestatem arrogat.

III. Si non datur iudex visibilis in ecclesia, qui auctoritate publica & infallibili controuersias fidei decidat, nullus controuertendi finis erit.

Resp.

Controuersiae theologicae vel concernunt articulos fidei fundamentales, vel non fundamentales: Articuli fidei fundamentales vel αὐτολεξεὶ & conceptis verbis, iisque non ambiguis in scriptura continentur, vel per bonam proximamque consequentiam e claris scripturae dictis deducuntur. De his exortae controuersiae facile possunt finiri, modo status controuersiae accurate formetur & obseruetur, iuxtaque argumenta vtriusque partis a viris piis, doctis & veritatis amantibus ad normam scripturae expendantur. Quod nondum finiantur, fit ex accidente, & prouenit, vel ex praeconceptis opinionibus, vel ex studio partium & malitia voluntatis.

Controuersiae vero de articulis fidei non fundamentalibus citra dispendium salutis ἄνω καὶ κάτω, vltro citroque, ventilari possunt, modo follicite caeuamus, ne temere errorem amplectentes in ipsam reuelationem diuinam peccemus.

Conf. supra quaest. XXIII. prob. II.

IV. Petrus primus Romus Pontifex fuit infallibilis.

E. & successores eius sunt infallibiles.

Antecedens probatur 1) ex Matth. XVI, 18: Tu es Petrus: & super hanc eandem petram aedificabo ecclesiam meam. Hinc nascitur argumentum: Super quem aedificata est ecclesia, illum oportet esse infallibilem. Atqui super Petrum aedificata est ecclesia. E. Petrum oportet esse infallibilem.

2) Ex Luc. XXII, 32. vbi Christus Petrus his compellat verbis: Ego vero oraui (in primis) prote, vt non desinat fides tua.

Resp. ad 1) negando consequentiam. Neque enim argumentum licet: Petrus fuit infallibilis: Ergo Pontifices Romani sunt infallibiles.

Incertum enim est, Petrum fuisse Pontificem Romanum: incertius, pontifices Romanos esse legitimos Petri successores: incertissimum, infallibilitatem Petri necessario transferri & quasi deriuari in successores.

Nam priuilegium personale non necessario in posteros transit; alioqui omnes reges, qui Dauidi successerunt, fuissent immediate a Deo illuminati, sicut rex Dauid immediato Spiritus sancti afflatu perculsus erat. De cetero verba citata Christi non de Petri persona, primatu aut priuilegio infallibilitatis, sed de confessione & doctrina Petri intelligenda sunt. Etenim hic apostolus perquam insignem confessionem de Christo ediderat, cum dixisset: Tu es Christus ille, filius Dei viuentis, Matth.

XVI, 16. Respondebat Saluator: Beatus es Simon, fili Iona, quia caro & sanguis non reuelauit tibi (hoc) sed pater meus, qui est in caelis.

Quin immo vero ego tibi dico; tu es Petrus: & super hanc eandem petram aedificabo ecclesiam meam.

Non dicit Christus: tu es Petrus, & super te Petro aedificabo ecclesiam meam, sed mutato nomine inquit: Tues Petrus, & super hanc petram aedificabo.

Aliud igitur est Petrus, aliud petra.

Antiquissimorum patrum nonnulli per petram intelligunt apostolicam

Petri doctrinam de Christo (*), nonnulli ipsum Christum, doctrina Petri (vt aliorum apostolorum) prædicatum aut celebratum. Vtraque expositio prope eodem recidit. Nam doctrina apostolica de Christo, & Christus apostolica doctrina prædicatus, non differunt secundum rem, sed secundum nostrum concipiendi modum. Christus est fundamentum ecclesiæ substantiale, doctrina de Christo est fundamentum ecclesiæ dogmaticum. Vid. supra pag. 47. Quæst. XIX. Prob. II. Resp. ad 2) verba Christi oraui pro te, ne fides tua deficiat! non intelligenda sunt absolute de immunitate ab omni defectu fidei; amisit enim Petrus fidem, ter Christum abnegando; sed de immunitate a finali fidei amissione, vt sensus sit: pro te, Simon Petre, rouaui, ne finaliter fidem amittas, ne in finali incredulitate persistas, & æterna salute excidas.

Instantia I. Cum Christus Io. XXI, 17. ad Petrum dixit: pasce oues meas, infallibilitatem & regimen ecclesiæ sine errore Petro, eiusque successoribus, nempe pontificibus Romanis concessit. Resp. Neg. conseq. Nam pascere oues Christi est omnium pastorum ecclesiæ. Grauiter gentium apostolus omnes ecclesiæ Ephesinæ presbyteros alloquitur: Spiritus sanctus vos posuit episcopos ad pascendum ecclesiam Dei. Actor. XX, 28.

Instantia II. Sicut vnus erat pastor summus vet. testam. Eccles. XII, 11. ita debet esse vnus pastor summus noui testamenti. Resp. Pastor vnus, isque summus, est Deus triunus, & per appropriationem filius Dei, qui dicitur Ἀρχιποίμην, 1 Petr. II, 25. Quæst.


### Quest. XLVI. Is holy scripture an evident and perspicuous principle of Christian theology?

Holy scripture proposes the dogmas of faith and the precepts of morals, necessary for men who are to attain eternal salvation, in a clear manner and in words so perspicuous that it can be easily understood by a man who is teachable, attentive, free from preconceived opinions, and knowledgeable in the idiom in which he reads scripture.

Obs. I. One must distinguish between the perspicuity of words and the evidence (strictly so called) of things. The principal things contained in the sacred letters are non-evident; for they are mysteries which can be known neither by immediately apprehended terms, nor from other naturally evident principles. Hence holy scripture is called clear not by reason of the things, but of the words; because non-evident things can also be proposed in clear and perspicuous words.

Obs. II. The perspicuity of H. scripture is gradual; since it is greater in the N. than in the O. T.: and in the N. T. some sayings are clearer, some less clear, which are to be explained and illustrated from the clearer ones. But in those things which are necessary to be believed and done for men to be saved, H. scripture is sufficiently plain and perspicuous.

Obs. III. The perspicuity of H. scripture is not absolute, but ordered; since for understanding it, the order divinely instituted must be accurately observed. For there is required 1) invocation of God, the father of lights. 2) Knowledge of the idiom in which H. scripture is read, whether in the source or in a version. 3) Attentive consideration of phrases, of the scope, of the antecedents and consequents. 4) The casting off of preconceived opinions and depraved affections, of ambition, hatred, envy, audacity, etc. Whoever does not implore the help of God who illuminates, nor is attentive, nor free from preconceived opinions and inordinate affections, nor is acquainted with the idiom in which scripture is proposed to be read, he is not a suitable subject, or one disposed to investigate and grasp the sense of the divine word.

Our assertion is proven. I. From the wisdom and goodness of the author of Holy Scripture, who is God.

Since He is most wise, He could, and since He is most good, He wished to enunciate the senses of His mind clearly.

Hence He Himself says: Deut. XXX, 11. This commandment, which I (am) commanding you today, is not wonderful before you, nor is it far off. It is not in heaven (that you should say): who will ascend for us into heaven, and take it for us, and make us hear it, that we may do it? Nor is it beyond the sea, (that you should say): who will cross the sea for us, and take it for us, and make us hear it? But the word is very near to you, in your mouth, and in your heart, that you may do it.

Regarding this celestial oracle, observe that by the divine commandment, given by Moses to the Israelite people, one should not understand precisely the word of the law, but also the word of the gospel, as Paul teaches, Rom.

X, 6. This is the word of faith, which we preach. 2) That not only is the proximity of place signified, when it is said: it is not far off, but it is near to you.

For since Moses, on the day he said these things, had commanded them this commandment, and set it before them, it was manifest that it was near by reason of place, and there was no need to say: it is not far off, it is very near to you. But it is also understood as the distance and proximity of knowledge and evangelical fulfillment: where distance is the impossibility of knowing and fulfilling; as if it were said: It is not wonderful before you, or so difficult that you cannot understand and fulfill it: proximity, however, is the ease of knowing and fulfilling.

3) This knowledge and fulfillment consists in the confession of the mouth, and the faith of the heart: which Paul makes manifest in Rom. X, 8.

9. 10. Where indeed 4) Confession of the mouth requires knowledge of the words and the sense: for there is no true confession of that which is not understood.

Thus, of a parrot that might utter the apostolic symbol by chattering, no one would say that it is making a confession of the Christian faith. But the faith of the heart 5) adds to the external confession internal knowledge, assent, and trust.

Therefore 6) both the knowledge and sense of the commandment is easy, and the assent and trust of the heart is no less easy: not that 7) a man can do all these things from the powers of nature, but from the powers of the promise: but the promise here is evangelical, Rom.

X, 6. clearly made, not finally to be desired and expected from heaven or from places beyond the sea.

II. From the description of Holy Scripture. For this is described by Peter as a lamp or light shining in a dark place, 2 Pet.

I, 19. compare Ps. CXIX, 105. But if Holy Scripture is a light shining in a dark place, it is necessary that it shine forth with inherent clarity.

It is not for you to say that Holy Scripture is called a light, not because it is easy to understand, but because it illuminates the mind once understood.

For this is just as if you were to say: The sun is bright not because it pours forth light from itself, but because, when it is seen, it illuminates the eyes. III.

From the end for which Holy Scripture is to be proposed. For it is to be proposed to the learned and the unlearned, to adults and to little children, who are capable of reading scripture.

The apostles wrote their epistles to all the called saints, Rom.

I, 9. to fathers, to little children, to adolescents, 1 John II, 13. Wisely says JEROME on Ps.

LXXXVI. The apostles and prophets wrote not for a few, but for the whole people, so that all might understand.

But that scripture, which is obvious and exposed to all, must be so lucid that it brings wisdom even to little children.

Ps. XIX, 8. IV.

From the end for the sake of which the sacred letters were consigned. Which end the apostle of the gentiles excellently inculcates, 2 Tim.

III, 15. 16. Because from infancy you have known the sacred letters, which can make you wise unto salvation through the faith which is in Christ Jesus.

(For) all scripture is divinely inspired is also useful for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction, which (is) in righteousness: that the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly furnished unto all good works.

The sacred letters, with Paul as teacher, are adorned to this end, that they may abundantly instruct the man of God, or the minister of the church, so that he himself may clearly know the heavenly doctrine, and may conveniently instill it in others, refute false doctrine, correct distorted morals, and instruct men concerning righteousness, both begun and consummated, so that they may be rendered wise unto salvation, which is in Christ Jesus. But none of these things can be duly and prosperously accomplished, unless scripture uses clear words, so that the minister of the church may evidently know what things contribute to doctrine, reproof, correction, and a certain momentum.

The apostle adds a paracletic use in Rom. XV, 4. Whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope. But unless the fountain of scripture becomes clear, no one will draw living comfort from it.

V. From the principal parts of scripture, the law and the gospel.

The divine law is proposed in Exod. XX. and the gospel in John III, 16. in clear words. Therefore scripture is clear; for the denomination is made from the more powerful part.

Latin:

Sacra scriptura dogmata fidei morumque præcepta, cognitu factuque hominibus æternam salutem adepturis necessaria, modo luculento verbisque adeo perspicuis proponit, vt ab homine docili, attento, præconceptis opinionibus vacuo, & idiomatis, quo scripturam legit, gnaro, facile intelligi queat.

Obs. I. Distinguendum est inter perspicuitatem verborum, & euidentiam (stricte dictam) rerum. Res præcipuæ, in sacris litteris comprehensæ, sunt ineuidentes; sunt enim mysteria, quæ nec immediate apprehensis terminis, nec ex aliis naturaliter euidentibus principiis cognosci possunt. Proinde clara dicitur scriptura sacra non ratione rerum, sed verborum; quia res ineuidentes etiam claris & perspicuis verbis proponi possunt.

Obs. II. Perspicuitas S. scripturæ est gradualis; quippe quæ maior in N. quam V. T. est: & in N. T. quædam dicta sunt clariora, quædam minus clara, quæ ex clarioribus explicanda & illustranda sunt. In iis autem, quæ hominibus saluandis creditu factuque necessaria sunt, satis liquida & perspicua est S. scriptura.

Obs. III. Perspicuitas S. scripturæ non est absoluta, sed ordinata; siquidem ad eam intelligendam ordo diuinitus institutus accurate obseruandus est. Requiritur enim 1) inuocatio Dei, patris luminum. 2) Notitia idiomatis, quo S. scriptura legitur, siue in fonte, siue in versione. 3) Attenta consideratio phrasium, scopi, antecedentium & consequentium. 4) Depulsio præconceptarum opinionum & prauorum affectuum, ambitionis, odii, inuidiæ, audaciæ &c. Quotusquisque neque auxilium Dei illuminantis implorat, neque attentus, neque liber a praeconceptis opinionibus & inordinatis affectibus, neque gnarus est idiomatis, quo scriptura legenda proponitur, ille non est subiectum idoneum, aut dispositum ad indagandum & capiendum sensum verbi diuini.

Assertio nostra prob. I. A sapientia & bonitate auctoris S. scripturae, qui est Deus.

Hic cum sapientissimus fit, potuit, &, cum optimus fit, voluit sensa mentis suae perspicue enuntiare.

Hinc ipse inquit: Deut. XXX, 11. Praeceptum, hoc, quod ego (sum) praecipiens tibi hodie, non est mirabile prae te, neque longinquum illud. Non in caelo illud (vt dicas) dicendo: quis ascendet nobis in caelum, & accipiet illud nobis, facietque audire nos illud, vt faciamus illud? Neque est trans mare, (vt dicas) dicendo: quis transibit nobis ad transmare, & accipiet nobis illud, & audire nos faciat illud? Sed propinquum apud te est valde verbum in ore tuo, & in corde tuo, vt facias illud.

Circa hoc oraculum celeste obferues quod per praeceptum diuinum, a Mose populo Israelitico datum, non intelligatur praecise verbum legis, sed & verbum euangelii, docente Paulo, Rom.

X, 6. Hoc est verbum fidei, quod praedicamus. 2) Quod non tantum significetur propinquitas loci, quum dicitur: non est longinquum, sed est propinquum apud te.

Nam cum Moses eo die, quo haec dixit, praeceperit illis praeceptum hoc, & coram proposuerit, manifestum fuit, quod ratione loci propinquum esset, nec opus erat dicere: non est longinquum, propinquum est tibi valde. Sed intelligitur etiam longinquitas & propinquitas cognitionis & euangelicae impletionis: vbi longinquitas est impossibilitas cognoscendi & implendi; ac si diceretur: Non est mirabile prae te, seu adeo difficile, vt non possis intelligere & implere: propinquitas autem est facilitas cognoscendi & implendi.

3) Cognitio & impletio haec consistit in confessione oris, & fide cordis: quod manifestum facit Paullus Rom, X, 8.

9. 10. Vbi sane 4) Confessio oris requirit notitiam verborum & sensus: nulla enim est confessio vera eius, quod non intelligitur.

Ita de psittaco, qui symbolum apostolicum garriendo proferat, nemo dixerit, quod confessionem christianae fidei edat. Fides autem cordis 5) addit confessioni externae notitiam internam, assensum & fiduciam.

Itaque 6) tum notitia & sensus praecepti facilis est, tum assensus & fiducia cordis non minus facilis est: non quod 7) omnia isthaec possit homo facere ex viribus naturae, sed ex viribus promissionis: promissio autem hic est euangelica, Rom.

X, 6. clare facta, non e caelo demum aut locis transmarinis desideranda & expectanda.

II. A descriptione sacrae scripturae. Haec enim describitur a Petro per λύχνον siue lumen lucens in loco caliginoso, 2 Petr.

I, 19. confer. Ps. CXIX, 105. Quod si autem sacra scriptura lumen est lucens in loco caliginoso, necesse est, eam insita claritate resplendescere.

Non est, quod dicas, sacram scripturam dici lumen, non quia intellectu facilis est, sed quia intellecta mentem illustrat.

Nam hoc perinde est, ac si diceres: Sol est lucidus non ideo, quod lucem ex se fundit, sed quia, cum visus est, oculos illuminat. III.

A fine, cui sacra scriptura proponenda. Proponenda autem illa est doctis & indoctis, adultis & paruulis, lectionis scripturae capacibus.

Scripserunt apostoli suas epistolas omnibus vocatis sanctis, Rom.

I, 9. patribus, paruulis, adolescentibus, 1 Io. II, 13. Scite inquit HIERONYMUS in Ps.

LXXXVI. Apostoli & prophetae non paucis, sed vniuerso populo scripserunt, vt omnes intelligerent.

Sed illam scripturam, quae omnibus obuia & exposita est, oportet esse adeo dilucidam, vt sapientiam etiam afferat paruulis.

Ps. XIX, 8. IV.

A fine, cuius gratia sacrae litterae sunt consignatae. Quem finem egregie inculcat gentium apostolus, 2 Tim.

III, 15. 16. Quia ab infantia sacras litteras nosti, quae possunt te sapientem reddere in salutem per fidem, quae in Christo Iesu est.

(Nam) omnis scriptura diuinitus inspirata etiam utilis est ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad disciplinam, quae (fit) in iustitia: ut integer sit homo Dei, ad omne opus bonum instructus.

Sacrae litterae, docente Paulo, ea fini adornatae sunt, ut hominem Dei, sive ministrum ecclesiae abunde instruant, quo caelestem doctrinam et ipse liquido cognoscat, et aliis commode instillet, falsam doctrinam redarguat, distortos mores corrigat, hominesque de iustitia tum inchoata, tum consummata, erudiat, ut sapientes reddantur in salutem, quae est in Christo Iesu. At nihil horum rite prospereque expediri potest, nisi scriptura perspicuis utatur verbis, ut minister ecclesiae evidenter cognoscat, quae ad doctrinam, redargutionem, correctionem, momentum quoddam conferant.

Addit apostolus usum paracleticum Rom. XV, 4. Quaecunque praescripta sunt, in nostram salutem praescripta sunt, ut per patientiam et consolationem scripturarum spem habeamus. At nisi fons scripturae fit liquidus, nemo ex eo vivum hauriet solamen.

V. A praecipuis scripturae partibus, lege et euangelio.

Lex diuina Exod. XX. et euangelium, Io. III, 16. luculentis verbis proponitur. Ergo scriptura est perspicua; nam a potiori fit denominatio.


### Quest. XLVI. Is holy scripture an evident and perspicuous principle of Christian theology?: VI. From the absurdities accompanying the contrary opinion

VI. From the absurdities accompanying the contrary opinion.

If sacred scripture is not clear: α) the celestial oracles will not differ from the oracles of Apollo; since both are equivocal, and involved in perplexing senses, so that they do not so much teach as distract the mind, or render it suspended. β) Sacred scripture will be useless; not otherwise than a letter is of no use, which is composed in words so intricate that it deceives the sharpness of the intellect. γ) An apology will not be lacking to the infidels against the final judgment, that they could not attain the will of God from scripture so obscure. δ) The Holy Spirit will not be a good teacher. For it is the mark of a good teacher to deliver his dogmas clearly and distinctly, and to condescend with prudent accommodation to the capacity of the learners.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, Weigelians, and Socinians, who deny the perspicuity of scripture; who rely on the following arguments (*): I. What-. (*)

Regarding the state of the controversy, it must be carefully observed that five distinctions pertain to it. 1) Obscurity must be accurately distinguished from difficulty. For that is called obscure, for the investigation of which we have no sufficient means, so that no one is able to attain the mind of the author, even if one has applied the greatest diligence (which is that which is δυσνόητον, 2 Pet. III, 16.). 2) Obscurity is one thing of things, another of words. Divine things, which are called mysteries, far surpass all the limits of finite reason, and therefore no one will ever be able to perceive the manner in which they are performed, Phil. IV, 7. But the words, however, by which those arcane truths are signified, are sufficiently clear. Who is there who does not understand this saying, John III, 16? Who indeed is there who would investigate such a great and immense matter with all thought? 3) We concede the obscurity of words, but not of the text. Words, viewed separately and outside of coherence, are often and much obscure, since they are ambiguous, nay, they possess many significations. But all ambiguity is removed if they are considered in context, and also if truly parallel passages are diligently compared. E.g. Zech. III, 9. it is asked, what is עין. The word עין denotes in one place an eye, in another it designates a fountain. But nevertheless, the context itself first determines the power of the word in this place; for the dual is never used of fountains, but always of eyes. Then in another saying, very similar to this, ch. IV, 10. is added, מעין, as that which is fitting not to fountains but to eyes; see also Rev. V, 6. 4) The obscurity, or rather difficulty, of scripture we deny; of certain parts we affirm it. For what lies hidden in one place is manifest in another. 5) Objective obscurity inheres in no words, but, if there is any, it is certainly subjective in the mind of the interpreter. Which difference scripture itself indicates 2 Corinth. IV, 3. 4. 2 Pet. III, 16. Luke XVIII, 31. 32, 33. XXIV, 32. compared with v. 45. from which verse of either I. Whatever contains most abstruse things, and things removed from all reason, that is without doubt obscure. But, holy scripture contains &c. Therefore. The major premise is evident, because that is perspicuous which is suitable and proportionate to the intellect: conversely, that is obscure which is very far removed from the intellect. Resp. Whatever contains most abstruse things, that is obscure, as regards the real object; I concede: as regards the proposition of the object through words, I deny. For just as things most easy to the intellect can be obscured by words: so things most difficult can be proposed in most clear words. And for that reason God uses the medium of letters, so that whatever we do not attain by investigating with nature as our guide, we may clearly know that through scripture revealing it. Jo. XX, 31.

II. If holy scripture could be understood without an interpreter, commentaries would not be necessary. But commentaries are necessary for the understanding of scripture (otherwise so many huge volumes of commentaries would not be written with the greatest labor on the sacred code). Therefore holy scripture cannot be understood without an interpreter. Resp. Commentaries are necessary not by absolute necessity, for being simply, but by hypothetical necessity, for well-being. The first Christians understood scripture before any commentaries were written, with the light of scripture alone irradiating their minds, and the Holy Spirit working in their hearts. Therefore commentaries are not necessary for all and individual men for the simple understanding of scripture, but partly for easier, more intense, and more accurate knowledge; partly for showing the application and salutary use, and for promoting the edification of faithful souls to a greater degree. But it does not follow from that: Therefore holy scripture is obscure. For the catechism and other most clear writings are drawn out by commentaries, and applied to living practice.

III. The disciples of Emmaus could not understand Moses and the prophets prophesying about Christ, but they were in need of the explanation of Christ, Luc. XXIV, 25. Therefore holy scripture is obscure. Resp. α) The disciples of Emmaus were in need of the explanation of Christ not because of the obscurity of scripture, but because of the folly and slowness of their heart, occupied by a preconceived opinion about an earthly kingdom of the Messiah. But just as the sun remains bright, even if bats and owls are blinded by its splendor, and blind men do not see it at all: so holy scripture remains perspicuous, even if a man, blinded by the spell of prejudice, does not notice its clarity. β) The disciples of Emmaus understood the clear words of Moses and the prophets, but they were ignorant of what underlying thing, or conceived person, they were about. Therefore Christ applied the words of Moses and the prophets to himself. For that reason the evangelist says v. 27. And beginning from Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the scriptures, the things which concerned himself. γ) Interpretation argues for the infirmity of the human intellect and the profundity of the mysteries, not the obscurity of holy scripture. For interpretation is sought from scripture itself; indeed, it shines with such clarity that it reveals the sense of the recorded words by itself through itself.

Instance: The entire college of Christ's disciples did not attain the sense of Christ's words concerning his near-impending passion and death. Luc. XVIII, 34. Therefore holy scripture cannot be understood without an interpreter. Resp. The disciples, infatuated by the prejudice of an earthly kingdom, and occupied by more vehement affections, namely fear and sadness, born from the announced death of Jesus, did not foresee with the eyes of their mind the final cause of Christ's passion, and the salutary fruit to be taken from it: but the words of Christ were so liquid that even a seven-year-old boy could have grasped their sense.

That eunuch Acts VIII, 32, did not understand the prophecy of Isaiah concerning Christ until it was explained to him by Philip. Therefore, Scripture, unless it is explained by teachers, is obscure. Resp. That eunuch was inexperienced in the Christian religion, unrefined, and a proselyte, from whose unrefined state it is wrongly inferred that Holy Scripture is obscure; just as if someone were to conclude: An infant can neither read nor understand the words of the catechism: Therefore, the words of the catechism are obscure. 2) The eunuch understood the words of Isaiah, but he was ignorant of what person they denoted, and how and when they were actually fulfilled. Therefore, the things contained in the prophecy were not evident to him, but the words were clear enough. 3) The question concerning the perspicuity of Holy Scripture is ventilated between us and the Papists for the present time, insofar as Scripture consists of the completed canon of the books of the Old and New Testaments. The light of the New Testament had not shone upon the eunuch, whence he did not grasp the substance and fulfillment of the prophetic oracle. However, the prophecy of Isaiah is elucidated in John I, 29; 2 Peter II, 24, 25.

V. King David Psalm CXIX, 18, asked God: Give me understanding, and I will search thy law. Therefore, without the special concurrence of God, he did not understand Scripture. Resp. 1. We posit the perspicuity of Holy Scripture as ordered, not absolute. 2. We distinguish between the literal and the saving knowledge of God. God established this order, that man, intending to understand Holy Scripture with saving fruit, should implore divine aid. 3. David’s prayer argues not for the obscurity of Scripture, but for the profundity of divine mysteries and the weakness of the human intellect: for he does not ask that light be poured upon the divine law, but upon him-self un-

VI. St. Peter testifies 2 Epist. c. III, 16, that in the Epistles of St. Paul there are certain δυσνόητα, things difficult to understand, which the unlearned and unstable twist. Resp. α) Not badly does LORINUS, a Papist, say: That, ἐν οἷς, in which, is not referred to the epistles, but to those things which are treated in the epistles. For the pronoun οἷς is not a pronoun of the feminine gender, of which the noun ἐπιστολῶν is. Therefore, the obscurity of the Pauline epistles is not noted here, but the non-evidence of the things contained in them. β) If certain things in the Pauline epistles are δυσνόητα, that is, difficult to understand, the rest will be εὐνόητα, easy to understand. γ) They are δυσνόητα to the unlearned, the unstable, and the torturers of the divine word: yet they are understood according to the state of the wayfarer by docile, attentive readers who modestly search the sense of Scripture.

VII. From whatever principle the enigmatic knowledge of God is drawn, that principle must be obscure. But the enigmatic knowledge of God is drawn from Scripture as the principle of theology. Therefore, Holy Scripture must be obscure. The major premise is certain, because such as the derived thing is, such is the principle: enigmatic knowledge flows from an obscure principle. The minor premise is proved from 1 Cor. XIII, 12: We see now through a glass in a riddle, but then face to face. Resp. The words of the Apostle are to be understood comparatively, because the comparison of the state of grace and glory is instituted by the same. For the theological knowledge of wayfaring men, compared with the beatific vision of God which the blessed enjoy in the heavenly fatherland, is imperfect, and thus comparatively enigmatic, specular, and obscure. But that knowledge of God which is comparatively imperfect and obscure is clear enough for the state of this life; since it suffices for obtaining salvation. Wherefore, just as it does not follow: I see the image of a thing more obscurely in a mirror than when I behold it as it is in itself: Therefore the mirror is obscure: so it does not follow: Not so clear is the knowledge of God and divine things here through Scripture as it will be in heaven, where we shall see God face to face: therefore Holy Scripture is obscure.

VIII. Holy Scripture is like a book closed and sealed. Therefore, without the key of interpretation it cannot be understood. The antecedent is proved from Dan. XII, 4: But thou, Daniel, close the words, and seal the book until the time of the end. Resp. 1. The prophecy of Daniel is a part of Scripture, not Scripture as a whole. We concede that Holy Scripture is in certain places less clear, but in tra-

regarding the dogmas of faith and the precepts of morals, we assert that the same is sufficiently perspicuous according to the state of life. 2. For the present time, a question is ventilated between us and the Papists: Whether Holy Scripture, as it now consists of the books of the Old and New Testaments, with the canon completed, becomes clear and perspicuous. Thus, neither is the prophecy of Daniel obscure. For Daniel is commanded by the angel to shut up the words and seal the book even to the time of end; many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased. The angel therefore implies that the prophecy of Daniel is to be sealed not simply and for all times, but until the time divinely appointed, when many, taught by experience, shall understand it from the event.

IX. Every credible thing according to the Lutherans must be perspicuous. But the whole of Scripture, down to the smallest apex, according to the Lutherans, must be perspicuous. Resp. 1) "Credible" is said in two ways: a) generally, on account of the authority of the speaker; b) specifically, because it is a dogma of faith and a precept of morals necessary for a man to be saved, both to be known and to be done. There are in Holy Scripture chronological, onomastic, astronomical, etc., matters which, without detriment to salvation, are safely ignored. Wherefore we limit the major: every credible dogma of faith and precept of morals, according to the Lutherans, must be perspicuous; I grant it: but the whole of Scripture, down to the smallest apex, is a credible dogma of faith and precept of morals; I deny it. 2) The Lutherans assert that the clarity of Holy Scripture is gradual, and that less clear biblical sayings are to be illustrated by clearer ones.

X. If the words of Holy Scripture were perspicuous, the most serious dispute concerning the genuine sense of the words of the Holy Supper: "This is my body," would long since have been settled. But that dispute is not yet settled. Therefore, the words of Scripture are not perspicuous. Resp. The words of the Holy Supper are most clear, but the underlying subject matter is most sublime; which, since the diffident cannot attain to it by reason, they flee to tropes. From which it has come to pass that that dispute has been protracted for so many years, not without great detriment to the Evangelical Church.

XI. The words of Holy Scripture cannot be perspicuous (1) because there are many amphibolies in Holy Scripture, (2) many hysterologies, (3) many tropes and figures, (4) many antilogies or apparent contradictions, (5) many parables, (6) in the original Hebrew and Greek text, hapax legomena [voces monadicae], subject to diverse interpretations. From which an obscure kind of speech cannot but arise. Resp. (a) Generally. We do not deny that in certain places of Holy Scripture less clarity is detected: but we urge this, that in those things which are necessary to be believed and done by a man who is a traveler aspiring to eternal salvation, Holy Scripture is sufficiently perspicuous. (b) Specifically to (1): Amphibolies vanish into perspicuous speech if both the scope of the speaker and parallel passages are accurately weighed. To (2): although in Scripture an ὕστερον πρότερον [hysteron proteron] is sometimes committed, yet the true order of biblical histories is elicited partly from the circumstances of the text, partly from the inspection of parallel passages, as is especially wont to be done in composing a harmony of the Evangelists. To (3): tropes and figures are not shadows, but lights of speech. To (4): apparent contradictions are easily reconciled by a prudent collation of the places that seem to conflict, having observed the laws of contradiction. To (5): most parables were explained by Christ: but when the Savior did not explain them, He wished the minds of the hearers and readers to be excited to a greater investigation of the hidden kernel. To (6): hapax legomena occurring in the sacred code, with so many versions and so many commentaries now extant, have long since been explained. Moreover, AUGUSTINE, about to render the reason why God did not will all and every biblical saying to be expressed with an equal degree of clarity, de doctrina Christ. lib. II. cap. VII., says: Magnificently and salubriously has the Holy Spirit so modulated the Holy Scriptures, that in more open places He might meet hunger, but in more obscure ones might wipe away distaste. For almost nothing is elicited from the more obscure passages which may not be found said most plainly elsewhere.

Latin:

VI. Ab absurdis sententiam contrariam concomitantibus.

Si sacra scriptura non est perspicua: α) oracula caelestia non discrepabunt ab oraculis Apollinis; cum utraque sint aequivoca, et perplexis sensibus involuta, ut non tam doceant, quam animum distrahant, aut suspensum reddant. β) Sacra scriptura erit inutilis; haud secus, ac epistola nulli est usui, quae verbis adeo intricatis est consignata, ut aciem intellectus fallat. γ) Infidelibus non defutura est apologia contra extremum iudicium consequuturus, se e scriptura adeo obscura non potuisse voluntatem Dei assequi. δ) Spiritus S. non erit bonus doctor. Nam boni doctoris est, sua dogmata clare et distincte tradere, et prudenti attemperatione ad captum discentium condescendere.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, Weigelianorum et Socinianorum, perspicuitatem scripturae negantium; qui seqq. innituntur argumentis (): I. Quid- ()

Ad statum controversiae, probe observandum, pertinent quinque distinctiones. 1) Obscuritas accurate distinguenda est a difficultate. Etenim obscurum dicitur, ad quod pervestigandum nulla nobis sunt media sufficientia, ut nemo valeat mentem auctoris assequi, etiam si quis maximam adhibuerit diligentiam (id quod est δυσνόητον, 2 Petr. III, 16.). 2) Obscuritas alia est rerum, alia verborum. Divinae res, quae appellantur mysteria, finitae rationis terminos longe omnes superant, ideoque modum, quo illae peragantur, nemo unquam poterit perspicere, Phil. IV, 7. At verba tamen, quibus arcanae illae veritates significantur, satis sunt perspicua. Quotus quisque non intelligit hoc dictum, Ioan. III, 16. Quis vero est, qui rem tantam atque immensam omni cogitatione percontetur? 3) Obscuritatem verborum concedimus, non item textus. Verba, seorsum et extra cohaerentiam spectata, saepe multumque obscura sunt, quando quidem sunt ambigua, immo plures obtinent significationes. Omnis autem tollitur ambiguitas, si in contextu considerentur, locis etiam, vere parallelis, diligenter comparatis. V. g. Zachar. III, 9. quaeritur, quid fit עין. Vox עין denotat alicubi oculum, alibi fontem designat. Verum tamen primum contextus ipse determinat vocis hoc in loco potestatem; nam dualis nunquam de fontibus, semper de oculis usurpatur. Deinde in alio dicto, huic fimillimo, cap. IV, 10. additur, מעין, utpote quod non fontibus, sed oculis convenit, vid. et Apoc. V, 6. 4) Obscuritatem, sive potius difficultatem scripturae, negamus; partium quarumdam, affirmamus. Quod enim uno in loco latet, id in altero patet. 5) Obscuritas obiectiva in verbis nulla inest, sed, si qua est, certe est subiectiva in mente interpretis. Quam differentiam scriptura ipsa indicat 2 Corinth. IV, 3. 4. 2 Petr. III, 16. Luc. XVIII, 31. 32, 33. XXIV, 32. coll. cum v. 45. ex cuius vtriusque versus I. Quidquid continet res abstrusissimas, & ab omni ratione remotas, id procul dubio est obscurum. Atqui, sacra scriptura continet &c. Ergo. Maior constat, quia id perspicuum est, quod conueniens & proportionatum est intellectui: contra obscurum est, quod ab intellectu valde remotum est. Resp. Quidquid continet res abstrusissimas, illud est obscurum, quoad obiectum reale; concedo: quoad obiecti propositionem per verba, nego. Sicut enim res intellectu facillimæ verbis possunt obscurari: ita res difficillimæ verbis liquidissimis proponi queunt. Et propterea vtitur Deus medio litterarum, vt quidquid natura duce inuestigando non consequimur, id scriptura reuelante clare cognoscamus. Io. XX, 31.

II. Si sacra scriptura sine interprete posset intelligi, non essent necessarii commentarii. Atqui necessarii sunt commentarii ad intelligentiam scripturæ (ceteroqui tot ingentia commentariorum volumina labore maximo in sacrum codicem non scriberentur). Ergo sacra scriptura sine interprete non potest intelligi. Resp. Commentarii sunt necessarii non necessitate absoluta, ad esse simpliciter, sed necessitate hypothetica, ad bene esse. Primi christiani intellexerunt scripturam ante vllos conscriptos commentarios, sola scripturæ luce irradiante animos, & Spiritu sancto operante in illorum cordibus. Non itaque commentarii necessarii sunt omnibus & singulis hominibus ad simplicem scripturæ intelligentiam, sed partim ad cognitionem faciliorem, intensiorem & accuratiorem; partim ad applicationem & vsum salutarem ostendendum, atque ædificationem fidelium animarum in maius prouehendam. Sed inde non sequitur: Ergo sacra scriptura est obscura. Nam catechismus aliaque scripta clarissima commentariis diducuntur, & ad viuam praxin applicantur.

III. Discipuli Emauntici non potuerunt intelligere Mosen & prophetas de Christo vaticinantes, sed indiguere explicatione Christi, Luc. XXIV, 25. Ergo sacra scriptura est obscura. Resp. α) Indiguerant discipuli Emauntici explicatione Christi non ob scripturæ obscuritatem, sed ob amentiam & tarditatem cordis, præconcepta opinione de regno Messiæ terreno occupati. Sicut autem sol lucidus manet, licet vespertiliones & noctuæ ad eius splendorem caligent, & homines cæci eum plane non videant: ita scriptura sacra manet perspicua, tametsi homo, fascino præiudicii occæcatus, eius claritatem non animaduertat. β) Discipuli Emauntici clara verba Mosis & prophetarum intellexerunt, sed de qua re substrata, aut persona concepta essent, ignorarunt. Applicauit itaque Christus verba Mosis & prophetarum ad semetipsum. Propterea inquit euangelista v. 27. Incipiens porro a Mose & omnibus prophetis, interpretatus est illis in omnibus scripturis, quæ ad ipsum pertinebant. γ) Interpretatio arguit intellectus humani infirmitatem & mysteriorum profunditatem, non sacræ scripturæ obscuritatem. Petitur enim interpretatio ex ipsa scriptura; quippe quæ ea fulget claritate, vt ipsa per se ipsam sensum verborum consignatorum pandat.

Instantia: Vniuersum discipulorum Christi collegium non assequebatur sensum verborum Christi de prope instanti passione & morte. Luc. XVIII, 34. Ergo sacra scriptura sine interprete intelligi nequit. Resp. Discipuli infatuati præiudicio regni terrestris, & occupati affectibus vehementioribus, nempe metu & tristitia, natis e prænuntiata Iesu morte, passionis Christi caussam finalem, & hinc capiendum salutarem fructum oculis mentis non peruidebant: verba autem Christi adeo liquida erant, vt vel septennis puer eorum sensum capere potuisset.

Eunuchus ille Act. VIII, 32. non intellexit vaticinium Iesaiae de Christo, donec a Philippo ipsi explanaretur. Ergo scriptura, nisi explicetur a doctoribus, obscura est. Resp. Eunuchus ille erat religionis christianae imperitus, rudis & proselytus, a cuius ruditate ad obscuritatem S. scripturae perperam colligitur; perinde, ac si quis concluderet: Infans verba catechismi nec legere, nec intelligere potest: Ergo verba catechismi sunt obscura. 2) Verba Iesaiae intelligebat Eunuchus, sed quam personam notarent, quomodo & quando reapse impleta essent, ignorabat. Idcirco res in vaticinio contentae erant ipsi ineuvidentes, verba autem satis clara. 3) Quaestio de perspicuitate sacrae scripturae nos inter, & pontificios, ventilatur pro tempore praesenti, in quantum scriptura ex veteris & noui test. libris completo canone constat. Eunucho lux noui testamenti non affulserat, vnde vaticinii prophetici rem substantam & complementum non capiebat. Enucleatur autem prophetia Iesaiae Io. I, 29. 2 Petr. II; 24. 25.

V. Rex Dauid Psalm. CXIX, 18. rogauit Deum: Da mihi intellectum, & scrutabor legem tuam. Ergo fine concursu Dei speciali scripturam non intellexit. Resp. 1. Statuimus nos perspicuitatem sacrae scripturae ordinatam, non absolutam. 2. Distinguimus inter notitiam Dei litteralem & salutarem. Hunc ordinem Deus constituit, vt homo salutari cum fructu sacram scripturam intellecturus, auxilium diuinum imploret. 3. Precatio Dauidis non scripturae obscuritatem, sed mysteriorum diuinorum profunditatem, & humani intellectus imbecillitatem arguit: neque enim petit, legi diuinae, sed sibi lucem a Deo affundi.

VI. Testatur S. Petrus 2 Epist. c. III, 16. quod in Epistolis S. Paulli sint quaedam δυσνόητα, intellectu difficilia, quae indocti & instabiles detorquent. Resp. α) Non male LORINVS, pontificius, inquit: Non refertur illud, ἐν οἷς, in quibus, ad epistolas, sed ad ea, de quibus in epistolis tractatur. Nam pronomen οἷς non est pronomen foeminini generis, cuius est nomen ἐπιστολῶν. Non ergo notatur hic epistolarum Paullinarum obscuritas, sed rerum in iis contentarum ineuvidentia. β) Si quaedam in epistolis Paullinis sunt δυσνόητα, fine intellectu difficilia, reliqua erunt εὐνόητα, intellectu facilia. γ) Sunt δυσνόητα indoctis, instabilibus, verbi diuini tortoribus: intelliguntur tamen pro statu viae a docilibus, attentis & sensum scripturae modeste scrutantibus lectoribus.

VII. Ex quo principio hauritur cognitio Dei enigmatica, illud principium oportet esse obscurum. Atqui ex scriptura velut principio theologiae hauritur cognitio Dei enigmatica. Ergo sacram scripturam oportet esse obscuram. Maior constat, quia quale est principiatum, tale est principium: cognitio enigmatica fluit ex principio obscuro. Minor probatur ex 1 Cor. XIII, 12. Videmus nunc per speculum in enigmate, tunc vero a facie ad faciem. Resp. Verba Apostoli intelligenda sunt comparate, quia ab eodem instituitur collatio status gratiae & gloriae. Nam hominum viatorum notitia theologica, comparata cum visione Dei beatifica, qua gaudent beati in patria coelesti, est imperfecta, atque adeo comparate enigmatica, specularis & obscura. Sed quae notitia Dei comparata est imperfecta & obscura, pro statu huius vitae est satis clara; cum ad obtinendum salutem sufficiat. Quain ob rem vti non sequitur: obscurius video imaginem rei in speculo, quam, cum intueor, qualis est in seipsa: Ergo speculum est obscurum: ita non sequitur: Non tam clara est cognitio Dei & rerum diuinarum hic per scripturam, quam futura est in coelo, vbi videbimus Deum a facie ad faciem: ergo scriptura sacra est obscura.

VIII. S. scriptura est velut liber clausus & signatus. Ergo fine claue interpretationis non potest intelligi. Antecedens probatur ex Dan. XII, 4. Tu vero Daniel occlude verba, & obsigna librum vsque ad tempus finis. Resp. 1. Prophetia Danielis est pars scripturae, non scriptura tota. Concedimus S. scripturam in quibusdam esse locis minus claram, sed in tra-

dendis dogmatibus fidei morumque praeceptis eandem pro statu vitae satis esse perspicuam asserimus. 2. Pro tempore praesenti nos inter & Pontificios ventilatur quaestio: An scriptura sacra, prout nunc constat ex libris vet. & novi testamenti, canone completo, fit clara & perspicua. Sic nec prophetia Danielis obscura est. Iubetur enim ab angelo Daniel occludere verba & obsignare librum usque ad tempus finis, percurrent (enim) multi, & multiplicabitur scientia. Innuit igitur angelus, prophetiam Danielis esse obsignandam non simpliciter & omnibus temporibus, sed usque ad tempus divinitus statutum, quo multi experientia edocti ex eventu eam intellecturi sint.

IX. Omne credibile secundum Lutheranos debet esse perspicuum. Atqui tota scriptura usque ad minimum apicem secundum Lutheranos debet esse perspicua. Resp. 1) Credibile bifariam dicitur: a) generatim ob auctoritatem dicentis; b) speciatim, quia est dogma fidei & praeceptum morum homini saluando cognitu factuque necessarium. Dantur in S. scriptura chronologica, onomastica, astronomica &c. quae citra dispendium salutis tute ignorantur. Quare limitamus maiorem: omne credibile dogma fidei, morumque praeceptum, secundum Lutheranos debet esse perspicuum; concedo: atqui tota scriptura usque ad minimum apicem est credibile dogma fidei morumque praeceptum; nego. 2) Asserunt Lutherani, claritatem S. scripturae esse gradualem, & dicta biblica minus clara ex clarioribus esse illustranda.

X. Si verba S. scripturae essent perspicua, lis gravissima de genuino sensu verborum sacrae coenae: hoc est corpus meum, iam dudum esset sopita. Atqui, lis illa nondum est sopita. Ergo verba scripturae non sunt perspicua. Resp. Verba sacrae coenae sunt clarissima, sed res substrata est sublimissima; quam cum ratione assequi nequeant diffidentes, ad tropos confugiunt. Ex quo factum est, vt lis illa non fine grandi ecclesiae evangelicae detrimento tot annos sit protracta.

XI. Verba S. scripturae non possunt esse perspicua (1) quia dantur multae in scriptura S. amphiboliae, (2) multae hysterologiae, (3) multi tropi & figurae, (4) multae antilogiae sive contradictiones apparentes, (5) multae parabolae, (6) in textu primigenio hebraeo & graeco voces monadicae, diversis interpretationibus obnoxiae. E quibus non potest non obscurum dicendi genus subnasci. Resp. (a) Generatim. Non diffitemur, in quibusdam locis sacrae scripturae minorem claritatem deprehendi: sed hoc urgemus, in his, quae creditu factuque necessaria sunt homini viatori ad aeternam salutem adspiranti, sacram scripturam satis esse perspicuam. (b) Speciatim ad (1): Amphiboliae abeunt in sermonem perspicuum, si & scopus dicentis & dicta parallela accurate pensitentur. Ad (2): quamvis in scriptura interdum committatur ὕστερον πρότερον, verus tamen historiarum biblicarum ordo partim ex circumstantiis textus, partim ex inspectione locorum parallelorum, vt praesertim fieri solet in concinnanda evangelistarum harmonia, eruitur. Ad (3): tropi & figurae non sunt tenebrae, sed lumina orationis. Ad (4): contradictiones apparentes e locorum, in speciem pugnantium, prudenti collatione, observatis contradictionis legibus, facile conciliantur. Ad (5): parabolae pleraeque expositae sunt a Christo: quando autem easdem Salvator non explanavit, animos audientium & legentium ad maiorem indagationem nuclei latentis excitatos voluit. Ad (6): voces monadicae occurrentes in sacro codice, exstantibus tot versionibus, tot commentariis iam dudum sunt explicatae. Ceterum causam, cur Deus non omnia & singula dicta biblica pari claritatis gradu expressa voluerit, redditurus AUGUSTINUS, de doctrina Christ. lib. II. cap. VII. inquit: Magnifice & salubriter Spiritus S. ita Scripturas S. modificavit, vt locis apertioribus fami occurreret, obscurioribus autem fastidia detergeret. Nihil enim fere de obscurioribus eruitur, quod non planissime dictum alibi reperiatur.


### Question XLVII. Is Holy Scripture so perspicuous that an unregenerate man can grasp its true sense without the illumination of the Holy…

Is Holy Scripture so perspicuous that an unregenerate man can grasp its true sense without the illumination of the Holy Spirit?

An unregenerate man, by placing an impediment in the way of the illuminating grace of the Holy Spirit, does not grasp the true sense of the sacred writings .

But the Holy Spirit illuminates the docile unregenerate man, who reads Holy Scripture attentively or hears it proposed by the voice of a teacher, through Scripture itself, so that he may perceive the genuine sense of the divine word, and rightly apply what has been perceived to salutary effects .

Objection 1.

Holy Scripture is said to be perspicuous in itself, or objectively, in relation to readers, or subjectively.

In itself, Holy Scripture is clear, even if no mortal were to read or understand it; just as the sun is luminous in itself, even if no eye beholds it.

In relation to readers or hearers, however, its perspicuity is not absolute or irresistible, such that no impediment can be placed against it, but it is ordered, requiring a subject that is capable and not resistant.

The sun illuminates every eye, but not the blind one, not the closed one, not the one covered by a veil, not the one hidden in a prison or a deep cell: Thus, Holy Scripture possesses such clarity that it can illuminate every human intellect; yet it does not illuminate the intellect of a man who resists, or who is covered by the veil of prejudice.

Objection 2.

An unregenerate man is either docile and corrigible, or indocile and incorrigible.

A docile unregenerate man is one who does not reject Holy Scripture, but admits it, reads it attentively, meditates upon it, is not occupied by prejudice, inordinate affections, or the cares of this world, and possesses a moderate judgment.

An indocile unregenerate man is one who either refuses to read Holy Scripture or to hear it proposed by the voice of a teacher; or if he reads, he does not meditate attentively, he maliciously closes the eyes of his mind to the illuminating grace of the Holy Spirit, he pertinaciously clings to preconceived opinions, and, enslaved by depraved affections, or by reason of age, is unfit to read and understand Scripture.

Objection 3.

The illuminating grace of the Holy Spirit, which is also called preparing grace, precedes the converting and regenerating grace of God in the order of nature, and is an action of the Holy Spirit that is not instantaneous or momentary, but successive and gradual; which the excellent Dr.

Fechtius explains accurately in his theological dissertation on the order and mode of divine grace, in aphorism IX, saying: Illuminating grace, whether of the mind or the will of man, does not flow into man immediately, does not complete illumination in one moment, does not work in man irresistibly, but acts by degrees, by turns, and by many and repeated acts, and thus disposes and prepares man through the passage of time to admit the greater light of truth by and by; so much so that, if he rejects the first degree of illumination, he denies himself the second; for it cannot have a place without the first.

Objection 4.

Distinguish between the sense of Holy Scripture considered in itself and formally, and the sense of Scripture rightly applied according to the intention of the Holy Spirit.

A docile unregenerate man grasps the sense of Holy Scripture considered formally by the preventing and preparing grace of the Holy Spirit; but unless the converting and regenerating grace of the Holy Spirit is added, he does not rightly apply the sense of Scripture according to the intention of the Holy Spirit to the grasping of sorrow for sins and the conceiving of faith in Christ.

The distinction of other theologians comes to nearly the same thing, between the external or literal knowledge of Holy Scripture, when one perceives its sense from the words of Scripture: and the internal or salutary knowledge, when one understands those things which Scripture delivers, so as to transfer them to salutary effects.

A docile unregenerate man, prepared by the illuminating grace of the Holy Spirit, can attain to the external and literal knowledge of Holy Scripture; but unless he is converted and regenerated by the Holy Spirit, he does not attain to the internal and salutary knowledge of Scripture.

You say: I. A man illuminated by the Holy Spirit is regenerate, but not unregenerate. Resp. An unregenerate man tending toward the state of regeneration is truly illuminated by the Holy Spirit through Scripture in many things, before he fully and savingly conceives faith. You say:

II. The literal knowledge of Scripture is also saving, because it is drawn from the word of salvation and divinely ordained for saving operations. Resp. The literal knowledge of Scripture is saving in a certain sense and in a certain respect, namely by reason of its principle and divine intention; but that knowledge is called simply saving which is joined with saving operations and spiritual movements of the heart.

Prob. a. From the Pauline utterance 1 Cor. II, 13. 14. We speak not in words taught by human wisdom, but in those taught by the Holy Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual. But the natural man does not receive the things that are of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness to him; and he cannot know them, because they are spiritually discerned. (a) The Apostle embraces both the words and the things of Holy Scripture in this remarkable utterance.

He asserts that the words of Scripture were taught by the Holy Spirit and dictated to the prophets and apostles, so that a divine and spiritual manner of speaking might be accommodated to divine and spiritual things. The things of Scripture are τὰ τὲ πνεύματος τῦ Θεῦ, all things revealed by the Holy Spirit, as well the small as the great, as well the sublime as the less sublime, specifically divine mysteries transcending the grasp of reason, insofar as they are proposed in spiritual words.

Cf. D. SEB. SCHMID. in colleg. bibl. post. p. 167. (b) The man ψυχικός, i.e., natural, is opposed by the Apostle to the πνευματικῷ, i.e., spiritual.

D. AEGID. HVNNIVS defines both in this place: The natural man is he who is led only by and relies upon the judgment of reason, which is the supreme faculty of the human soul: The spiritual man, however, is he who is ruled by the Holy Spirit through the word. D. SEB. SCHMID describes both in the same place: The natural man is he who is left to himself and his own nature: The spiritual man, however, is he who is not left to his own nature, but has the help and grace of the Holy Spirit. D.

SCHMID observes that the natural man is considered either absolutely and in general, or in particular and subjectively. The natural man considered absolutely grasps nothing of those things which are of the Spirit of God: meanwhile, one can be subjectively natural who understands something of those things which are of the Spirit of God; not indeed as such, but insofar as he is imperfectly illuminated by the Holy Spirit. (c) The Apostle denies that the natural man δέχεσθαι, receives, γνῶναι, knows, διακρίνεσθαι, discerns divine mysteries. Δέχεσθαι, to receive, is otherwise used of a guest who is not repelled, but admitted; to whom the door is opened, who is led into the house and treated well.

Matt. X, 14. 40. 41. Thus, the reception of spiritual things occurs when the intellect apprehends and assents, the will chooses and approves, and the affections conceive them within themselves. The beginning of this reception, when done in a legitimate manner, is made by the intellect; so that, when the intellect does not grasp, the will and affections also cannot rightly admit. Whence the Apostle argues most excellently: The natural man does not accept, or admit, the things that are of the Spirit of God: because they are foolishness to him, and he cannot γνῶναι, understand. But if he cannot understand: much less will the will and affections admit. (d) The Apostle attaches a twofold reason to his assertion.

He takes the former from the natural disgust of blind reason, which repudiates divine mysteries, saying: μωρία γὰρ αὐτῷ ἐσι, καὶ ὀ δύναται γνῶναι, for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand, just as if he were to say: The natural man, relying only on the protection of reason, disdains, turns away from, and laughs at divine dogmas as false, absurd, and stupid: and therefore, from natural powers and the principles of reason, left to himself, he cannot know them. He takes the latter from the condition of divine mysteries; which are so sublime that no one, unless illuminated by the Holy Spirit, can discern them. The Apostle therefore says: ὅτι πνευματικῶς ἀνακρίνεται, because they are spiritually discerned, indicating that no one, destitute of the supernatural light of the Holy Spirit, can pass an uncorrupted judgment on matters of faith.

Having clearly expounded the Pauline utterance, we argue: I. No one correctly understands whatever words the Holy Spirit has taught, who has never listened to the heavenly teacher, the Holy Spirit, speaking in the Scriptures. But the Holy Spirit has taught the words of Holy Scripture. Therefore.

The major premise is illustrated from the place of comparisons. Just as no one understands human words who has never heard humans: so no one grasps the words of the Holy Spirit who has never entered His school.

It is confirmed by experience: Who among the unregenerate Gentiles, placed outside the first pulse of assisting grace, could understand this saying from himself, John 1: "In the beginning was the Word: and the Word was made flesh"?

If I should ask a Gentile: what does the apostle understand by "the Word"? what does "made flesh" signify?

Latin:

Estne S. scriptura adeo perspicua, ut eiusdem verum sensum homo irregenitus sine illuminatione Spiritus S. capere queat?

Homo irregenitus, gratiae Spiritus sancti illuminanti impedimentum obiiciens, verum sacrarum litterarum sensum non capit .

At hominem irregenitum docilem, attente legentem scripturam sacram, vel hanc voce docentis propositam audientem, Spiritus sanctus per ipsam scripturam illuminat, vt genuinum verbi diuini sensum percipiat, perceptumque ad salutares effectus recte applicet .

Obiectio 1.

Perspicua dicitur S. scriptura in se, siue obiective, in ordine ad lectores, siue subjective.

In se S. scriptura est dilucida, si vel maxime nemo mortalium eam legat aut intelligat; sicut sol in se lucidus est, licet nullus oculus eum intueatur.

In ordine vero ad lectores vel auditores, eius perspicuitas non est absoluta, aut irresistibilis, vt nullum ei impedimentum obiici queat, sed ordinata, requirens subiectum capax & non repugnans.

Sol illustrat omnem oculum, sed non caecum, non clausum, non velamine obiectum, non latentem in carcere vel ima cella: Ita sacra scriptura ea pollet claritate, vt omnem intellectum humanum illuminare possit; at non illuminat intellectum hominis obsistentem, aut velamine praeiudicii obductum.

Obiectio 2.

Homo irregenitus vel est docilis & corrigibilis, vel indocilis & incorrigibilis.

Homo irregenitus docilis est, qui S. scripturam non reiicit, sed admittit, attente legit, meditatur, neque praeiudicio, neque affectibus inordinatis, aut curis huius seculi occupatus est, & mediocri pollet iudicio.

Homo irregenitus indocilis est, qui vel S. scripturam legere, aut docentis voce propositam audire recusat; vel si legit, non attente meditatur, ad illuminantem Spiritus S. gratiam oculos mentis malitiose occludit, praeconceptis opinionibus pertinaciter inhaeret, & prauis affectibus mancipatus, aut per aetatem ad legendam & intelligendam scripturam inidoneus est.

Obiectio 3.

Gratia Spiritus S. illuminans, quae etiam praeparans vocatur, gratiam Dei conuertentem & regenerantem ordine naturae praecedit, estque actio Spiritus S. non instantanea siue momentanea, sed successiva & gradualis; quam accurate explicat excell.

D. Fechtivs in dissertat. theol. de ordine modoque gratiae diuinae, aphorismo IX. inquiens: Gratia illuminans siue mentem, siue voluntatem hominis, non immediate in hominem illabitur, non vno momento illuminationem absoluit, non irresistibiliter in homine operatur, sed agit per gradus, per vices, & plures & repetitos actus, hominemque adeo temporis successu disponit & praeparat ad maiorem subinde veritatis lucem admittendam; adeo, vt, si primum illuminationis gradum repellat, alterum ipsi deneget; quippe qui sine primo locum habere non potest.

Obiectio 4.

Dist. inter sensum S. scripturae in se & formaliter consideratum, & inter sensum scripturae iuxta intentionem Spiritus S. recte applicatum.

Homo irregenitus docilis sensum S. scripturae formaliter consideratum capit ex gratia Spiritus S. praeueniente & praeparante; at nisi accedat gratia Spiritus sancti conuertens & regenerans, sensum scripturae iuxta intentionem Spiritus S. non recte applicat ad capiendum dolorem de peccatis, & concipiendam fidem in Christum.

Prope eodem recidit aliorum theologorum distinctio inter notitiam S. scripturae externam, siue litteralem, cum quis ex verbis scripturae sensum eius percipit: & internam siue salutarem, cum quis ea, quae scriptura tradit, intelligit, vt ad salutares effectus eadem transferat.

Homo irregenitus docilis, gratia Spiritus S. illuminanti praeparatus pertingere potest ad notitiam S. scripturae externam & litteralem; at nisi a Spiritu S. conuertatur & regeneretur, non assequitur notitiam S. scripturae internam & salutarem. scripturæ internam & salutarem.

Dicis: I. Homo illuminatus a Spiritu sancto est renatus, non autem irregenitus. Resp. Homo irregenitus ad statum regenerationis tendens, a Spiritu sancto per scripturam in plurimis vere illuminatur, antequam fidem plene & salutariter concipiat. Dicis:

II. Notitia scripturae litteralis est etiam salutaris, quia e verbo salutis hausta & ad salutares operationes divinitus ordinata est. Resp. Notitia scripturae litteralis secundum quid & certo respectu salutaris est, nempe ratione principii & intentionis divinae; at simpliciter salutaris dicitur notitia, quae cum salutaribus operationibus & spiritualibus cordis motibus coniuncta est.

Prob. a. Ex effato Paullino 1 Cor. II, 13. 14. Loquimur non doctis sapientia humanae verbis, sed doctis Spiritus sancti, spiritualibus spiritualia componentes. Animalis autem homo non suscipit ea, quae (sunt) Spiritus Dei: stultitia enim illi sunt; & non potest scire, quia spiritualiter diiudicantur. (a) Apostolus tam verba, quam res sacrae scripturae insigni hoc eloquio complectitur.
