Verba scripturae a Spiritu S. docta & prophetis atque apostolis dictata esse asserit, vt rebus divinis & spiritualibus divinum ac spirituale dicendi genus accommodaretur. Res scripturae sunt τὰ τὲ πνεύματος τῦ Θεῦ omnia a Spiritu S. revelata, tam parua, quam magna, tam sublimia, quam minus sublimia, speciatim divina mysteria captum rationis transcendentia, quatenus verbis spiritualibus proponuntur.

Conf. D. SEB. SCHMID. in colleg. bibl. post. p. 167. (b) Homo ψυχικός f. animalis ab apostolo opponitur πνευματικῷ f. spirituali.

Virumque definit D. AEGID. HVNNIVS in h. l. Animalis homo est, qui tantum ducitur ac nititur iudicio rationis, quae animae humanae suprema facultas est: Spiritualis autem, qui Spiritu S. regitur per verbum D. SEB. SCHMID. utramque l. c. describit: Homo animalis est, qui sibi & naturae suae relictus est: Spiritualis autem, qui sua natura relictus non est, sed Spiritus S. habet auxilium & gratiam. Observant D.

SCHMID, quod homo animalis consideretur vel absolute & in genere, vel in particulari & subiective. Homo animalis absolute consideratus nihil eorum capit, quae sunt Spiritus Dei: interim potest esse subiective animalis, qui aliquid intelligit eorum, quae sunt Spiritus Dei; non quidem qua talis, sed quam a Spiritu sancto imperfecte illuminatus est. (c) Negat apostolus, hominem animalem δέχεσθαι, suscipere, γνῶναι, cognoscere, διακρίνεσθαι, diiudicare mysteria divina. Δέχεσθαι, suscipere, alias usurpatur de hospite, qui non repellitur, sed admittitur; cui ianua aperitur, qui intra domum ducitur & bene tractatur.

Matth. X, 14. 40. 41. Ita susceptio rerum spiritualium est, quando intellectus apprehendit & assentitur, voluntas eligit & approbat, & affectus intra se concipiunt. Cuius susceptionis legitimo modo factae initium fit ab intellectu; ita vt, quando intellectus non capit, voluntas & affectus etiam non possint rite admittere. Vnde optime argumentatur apostolus: Animalis homo non acceptat, seu admittit ea, quae sunt Spiritus Dei: quia stultitia illi sunt, & non potest γνῶναι, intelligere. Quod si non potest intelligere: multo minus voluntas & affectus admittent. (d) Apostolus geminam assertioni suae annectit rationem.

Priorem sumit a naturali fastidio caecae rationis divina mysteria repudiantis, inquiens: μωρία γὰρ αὐτῷ ἐσι, καὶ ὀ δύναται γνῶναι, stultitia illi sunt, & non potest intelligere, perinde ac si dicat: Homo animalis, rationis tantum praesidio nitens, divina dogmata fastidit, aversatur & ridet, vt falsa, absurda, stolida: ideoque ex viribus naturalibus & principiis rationis, sibi relicta, ea cognoscere nequit. Posteriorem sumit a conditione mysteriorum divinorum; quae adeo sublimia sunt, vt nemo, nisi illuminatus, a Spiritu S. diiudicare queat. Dicit itaque apostolus: ὅτι πνευματικῶς ἀνακρίνεται, quia spiritualiter diiudicantur, indigitatus, neminem, destitutum supernaturali lumine Spiritus sancti, de rebus fidei incorruptum ferre iudicium.

Effato Paullino luculenter exposito argumentamur: I. Quaecunque verba docuit Spiritus S. illa nemo recte intelligit, qui doctorem coelestem Spiritum S. in scripturis loquentem nunquam auscultauit. Atqui, verba S. scripturae docuit Spiritus S. Ergo.

Maior illustratur ex loco comparatorum. Sicut verba humana nemo intelligit, qui homines nunquam audiuit: ita verba Spiritus S. nemo capit, qui huius scholam nunquam intrauit.

Comprobatur ab experientia: Eequis gentilium irregenitorum, & extra primum assistentis gratiae pulsum positorum, poterit hoc dictum ex se intelligere, Io I. In principio erat verbum: & verbum caro factum est?

Si quaeram e gentili: quid intelligit apostolus per verbum? quid significat: caro factum?


### Question XLVII. Is Holy Scripture so perspicuous that an unregenerate man can grasp its true sense without the illumination of the Holy…: He will hesitate, astonished, and finally will profess his ignorance

He will hesitate, astonished, and finally will profess his ignorance.

We argue II. Whoever relies only on the protection of reason, he neither receives, nor understands, nor correctly judges divine mysteries, but repudiates them as absurd. But the unregenerate man, destitute of all light of the Holy Spirit, etc.

Therefore. The major premise is Paul’s own, and is confirmed by the examples (1) of the ancient Israelites, of whose blinding Moses complains, Deut. 29:3-4: "Your eyes have seen those great signs and wonders: yet Jehovah has not given you a heart to know."

The divine word had been revealed to Israel, backed by stupendous miracles; yet they did not know it, because by supreme malice and obstinacy they had hindered the supernatural illumination of Jehovah.

(2) Of the Jews in the times of the N.T., concerning whom St. Paul says, 2 Cor. 3:15: "Even to this day, when Moses is read, a veil lies upon their heart."

The Jews diligently read the writings of Moses, but they do not understand them, a veil of malicious blindness being placed upon their hearts, which no one can remove except the Holy Spirit, to whose illuminating grace they place an obstacle.

(3) Of the Pharisees and scribes in the Jewish synagogue.

It was their custom to turn the codex of heavenly oracles with an assiduous hand, Acts 15; and they were professedly teachers of the law and masters of the Scriptures, Matt. 23:2; Rom. 2:19; yet they are pronounced by Christ to be blind and leaders of the blind, Matt. 15:14. (4) Of the disciples of Christ, occupied with a preconceived opinion about an earthly kingdom of the Messiah; to whom Christ had preached in words surely clear enough about his passion and death now imminent, Luke 18:31. But they understood none of these things, and this word was hidden from them, so that they did not know what was being said.

The disciples perceived the simple words, "passion," "death," what they denoted, but they did not grasp the entire propositions, and how such predicates agreed with the subject, with a full concept of the mind and a solid assent.

Prob. b. (1) To the unregenerate man who is teachable, admitting the word of God and correctly applying it, the Holy Spirit opens the eyes of the mind and illuminates them with divine light. This we learn from the sincere prayer of St. Paul, Eph. 1:17, in which he prays that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give us the Spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of Him, the eyes of the mind being illuminated. The Holy Spirit is called by the apostle the Spirit of wisdom, because to all who attentively read and intimately meditate upon the Scriptures, He gives and increases the knowledge of God and divine things: the same Spirit is called the Spirit of revelation not only because He revealed the divine will in the word of God, but also because He draws away the veil innate to hearts, for attaining the sense of Scripture: for which end the Holy Spirit also gives illuminated eyes of the mind.

For just as to discern the light of the sun, vigorous, pure, and open eyes are required: so to understand Holy Scripture, there is need of eyes illuminated by the Holy Spirit.

(2) The king-prophet worships God as a suppliant: "Reveal my eyes, that I may see the wondrous things from your law," Ps.

119:18. Long since he had prepared for himself a literal knowledge of the divine word by reading the Scriptures; but in earnest prayers he desires more abundantly the light of the Holy Spirit and an increase of fuller knowledge, so that with a revealed face he may behold the stupendous works and most sublime mysteries of God may behold, and thoroughly know, and may apply the same knowledge more and more to salutary effects, to repentance, to faith, to the pursuit of good works.

(3) The examples of the disciples of Christ confirm the same, to whom the Lord Jesus himself opened their mind, that they might understand the scriptures, Luke XXIV, 45. The minds of the apostles had been obstructed by the bars of preconceived opinions concerning an earthly kingdom of the Messiah: therefore the words of the Savior, concerning his own passion and death, passed by the disciples, who were thinking of everything else concerning Christ. But the Lord, externally proposing what was written concerning him in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms, by an internal supernatural operation removed the bars of prejudice concerning a worldly kingdom, irradiated the mind of the disciples with spiritual light, and instructed them with the gift τῆς ἑρμηνείας (of interpretation). Lydia, the seller of purple in the city of the Thyatirians, Acts XVI, 14, whose heart the Lord opened, that she might attend to those things which were spoken by Paul. The heart of Lydia had been closed as if by the bolts of blindness and ignorance; which, while Paul was preaching the word of God, the concurring Holy Spirit unbolted, by injecting such a thought into the heart of Lydia, and by exciting in her will a spiritual desire, by which she was stimulated to greater attention, and to attaining from the preaching of Paul a salutary knowledge of divine things. From which it is evident that a special light of the Holy Spirit, and a divine power of persuading to a solid knowledge of the sacred letters, and to rendering a firm assent to them, is required.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians and Arminians, who assert that Holy Scripture is so clear that there is no need for a special light of divine grace for its understanding; the stronger arguments of whom are the following.

I. Whatever scripture is perspicuous, that can be easily understood without the supernatural light of divine grace. But Holy Scripture, etc. Therefore. Resp. Holy Scripture is in itself lucid and clear, but this clarity is ordered toward this grace, which furthermore is not irresistible or irrefragable; since a malicious obstacle or veil can be placed before the eyes of the mind, so that they do not see the clarity of scripture. Wherefore, just as it would be wrongly concluded: The sun is most bright: therefore it illuminates a blind eye, one closed or covered with a veil; so the adversaries conclude badly: Holy Scripture is most clear: therefore its sense is perceived by an unregenerate man, indocile, a rebel, an enemy of grace, a hater and contemner of celestial truth. Consider, says the apostle of the Gentiles, 2 Cor. IV, 3. 4. If our gospel is hidden, it is hidden in those who are perishing; in whom the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, that the illumination of the gospel of the glory of Christ might not shine upon them. The apostle teaches that the gospel, perspicuous in itself, is κεκαλυμμένον (veiled), covered or hidden by accident, by the fault of men laboring under blindness, not only connate, which is common to all, but also adventitious and voluntarily contracted, and permitted by the judgment of God, when pertinacity, corroborated by Satan, is added. 2 Pet. I, 9. 1 John II, 9.

II. The words of the prophets and apostles are taken from the customary use of speaking, the power of signifying which an animal man can learn without supernatural grace. Resp. The words of the prophets and apostles are considered either outside the context, or in the context of a biblical proposition. In the former way, they have an analogy with human words, and can be understood by an unregenerate person without the supernatural grace of the Holy Spirit: but if they are viewed in context, insofar as they are accommodated to the mysteries of faith, and are as it were their δοχεῖα (vessels), receptacles or vehicles, and truly divine words, without the prevenient and preparing grace of the Holy Spirit, a solid conception concerning them, conformable to the mind of the Holy Spirit, cannot be formed. It is illustrated by example. What it is to exalt, what it is to draw, every unregenerate gentile man knows, Turk, Tartar, Jew. But truly if I should propose to him for consideration the oracle of Christ, John XII, 32. And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto myself, he will not understand the utterance of the Savior, unless his understanding, cultivated beforehand by the Holy Spirit, be illuminated.

III. Hypocrites, destitute of the light of the Holy Spirit, understand Holy Scripture. Resp. (1) The knowledge of hypocrites, which they have sought from the reading of the sacred letters, is external and literal, not internal, effectively saving, and (strictly speaking) spiritual, i.e., joined with spiritual motions, contrition, faith, and the love of God. The reason is because hypocrites do not apply the literal sense of Scripture to a living practice and a saving use. (2) The literal knowledge of hypocrites is imperfect and pedagogical, apart from the illumination of the Holy Spirit.

IV. Heretics, without the illumination of the Holy Spirit, attain the sense of Scripture, and from it dispute against the orthodox. When heretics are considered reduplicatively, insofar as they are heretics, i.e., erring in the foundation of faith, they infer a sense of Scripture, they do not bring it out from it; they do not grasp the sense which the words of Scripture pour forth of themselves, but they affix to it a foreign one, not analogous to the text itself.

V. The Devil, not capable of supernatural light, understands Scripture, since he cited its words in Matt. IV, 6. Resp. The Devil is not the subject for whose benefit Holy Scripture is configured; and therefore the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is prevenient, does not assist him, inasmuch as it intends the salvation of man. Whatever the evil spirit has snatched from divine things out of the sacred letters, he has stolen it all as if from foreign coffers, not pertaining to himself. Nor, however, did he attain the genuine sense of Scripture in the cited passage, but he nefariously perverted its words and twisted them into a foreign sense.

VI. If an unregenerate man cannot understand Holy Scripture without supernatural light, he is not to be punished for unbelief. But he is to be punished for unbelief. Therefore, an unregenerate man can understand Scripture without the supernatural light of the Holy Spirit. The consequence of the major premise is proven, because the Holy Spirit has denied to the unregenerate man the supernatural light without which he cannot conceive faith. Resp. The Holy Spirit denies supernatural light to no one absolutely, but imparts it to every reader or hearer of the divine word, provided he does not morosely resist His operation, or hinder the supernatural illumination by a veil of blindness voluntarily contracted. Therefore, the unregenerate is punished not for the light of the Holy Spirit not admitted, but petulantly rejected.

VII. The illuminating grace of the Holy Spirit is either perpetually joined with Holy Scripture, or it is separated from it. If it is perpetually joined, all men reading Scripture are equally illuminated, converted, and regenerated. If it is said to be separated, enthusiasm is brought into the church with, as it were, full sails. Resp. 1) The illuminating grace of the Holy Spirit is indeed perpetually joined with Holy Scripture, but it does not illuminate unregenerate, indocile, and perseveringly struggling persons. Nor does it illuminate in a moment, but by turns and degrees. He who repels the first degree of illumination does not receive the second, which is superior. In order for a man to be converted and regenerated, there is required a previous illumination of the Holy Spirit continued through many repeated acts, which, in the order of nature, is followed by the divine converting grace, which works contrition, and the regenerating grace, which confers the powers of believing. Aptly says D. SCHERZER in Breuiar. Hulsein. enucleato p. 57. The supernatural grace of the Holy Spirit is joined to the divine word, the hearing of which kindles faith, Rom. X, 17, and is by no means to be separated from it: to which we do not deny that another gracious operation of the Holy Spirit, who has already slipped into the heart by means of the word, approaches for that end. 2) We do not introduce enthusiasm into the church by the fact that we assert that the Holy Spirit, for the state of the present time, illuminates the minds of men, not ἀμέσως, immediately, but ἐμμέσως, mediately, through Holy Scripture itself.

Latin:

Haerebit attonitus, & tandem suam ignorantiam profitebitur.

Argumentamur II. Quicunque tantum praesidio rationis nititur, ille mysteria diuina neque suscipit, neque intelligit, neque recte diiudicat, sed vt absurda repudiat. Atqui homo irregenitus omni lumine Spiritus S. destitutus &c.

Ergo. Maior est ipsius Paulli, & comprobatur exemplis (1) antiquorum Israelitarum, de quorum excoecatione conqueritur Moses Deut. XXIX, 3. 4. Viderunt oculi tui signa & prodigia magna illa: non tamen dedit Iehouah vobis cor ad cognoscendum.

Reuelatum erat Israelis verbum diuinum stupendis miraculis flipatum; at non cognoscebant illud, quia summa malitia & obstinatione supernaturalem Iehouae illuminationem impediuerant.

(2) Iudaeorum temporibus N. T. superflutum, de quibus S. Paullus inquit 2 Cor. III, 15. Vsque hodie, quando legitur Moses, velamen super corde eorum iacet.

Iudaei assidue legunt scripta Mosis, sed ea non intelligunt, velamine malitiosae coecitatis cordibus ipsorum imposito, quod nemo nisi Spiritus sanctus tollere potest, cuius gratiae illuminanti obstaculum ponunt.

(3) Pharisaeorum & scribarum in synagoga Iudaica.

His moris erat assidua manu versare oraculorum coelestium codicem, Act. XV. erantque ex professo legis doctores ac scripturarum magistri, Matth. XXIII, 2. Rom. II, 19. coeci tamen & coecorum duces a Christo pronuntiantur, Matth. XV, 14. (4) Discipulorum Christi praeconcepta opinione de terreno Messiae regno occupatorum; quibus Christus verbis sane quam luculentis de passione & morte sua iamiam imminente praedicauerat, Luc. XVIII, 31. Sed illi nihil horum intellexerunt, eratque verbum hoc absconditum illis, vt nescirent, quae dicebantur.

Discipuli simplicia verba, passio, mors, quid notarent, percipiebant, sed integras propositiones, & quomodo praedicata eiusmodi subiecto conuenirent, pleno mentis conceptu, folidoque assensu non complectebantur.

Prob. b. (1) Homini irregenito docili, verbum Dei admittenti & recte adhibenti, Spiritus S. oculos mentis aperit, diuina luce collustrat. Id quod discimus ex ingenuo S. Paulli voto, Eph. I, 17. quo precatur, vt Deus domini nostri Iesu Christi, pater gloriae, det nobis Spiritum sapientiae, & reuelationis in cognitionem sui, illuminatos oculos mentis. Spiritus sanctus appellatur apostolo Spiritus sapientiae, quia omnibus, scripturas attente legentibus intimeque meditantibus, cognitionem Dei rerumque diuinarum donat & auget: dicitur idem Spiritus reuelationis non tantum ideo, quod voluntatem diuinam verbo Dei reuelauit, sed etiam propterea, quod connatum cordibus velamen detrahit, ad assequendum sensum scripturae: quo fine Spiritus S. etiam illuminatos dat oculos mentis.

Vt enim ad cernendum lumen folis vegeti, puri & aperti requiruntur oculi: ita ad intelligendam S. scripturam opus est oculis a Spiritu S. illuminatis.

(2) Rex propheta Deum supplex veneratur: reuela oculos meos, vt videam mirabilia tua e lege tua, Pf.

CXIX, 18. Iam dudum ille litteralem... verbi diuini notitiam sibi legentibus scripturis parauerat; at vero conceptis votis feriis exoptat vberius Spiritus S. lumen & plenioris cognitionis augmentum, vt facie reuelata stupenda Dei opera & mysteria sublimissima intueatur, penitusque cognoscat, atque eandem cognitionem ad salutares effectus, ad poenitentiam, ad fidem, ad studium bonorum operum magis magisque applicet.

(3) Comprobant idem exempla discipulorum Christi, quibus ipse Dominus Iesus aperuit mentem, vt intelligerent scripturas, Luc. XXIV, 45. Obstructae erant mentes apostolorum repagulis praeconceptarum opinionum de regno Messiae terreno: proinde verba Salvatoris, de passione & morte ipsius, discipulos, omnia alia de Christo cogitantes, praeteribant. At dominus externe proponens, quae scripta erant de ipso in lege Mosis, prophetis & psalmis, interna operatione supernaturali repagula praeiudicii de regno mundano remouebat, mentem discipulorum lumine spirituali irradiabat, & dono τῆς ἑρμηνείας instruebat. Lydiae purpurae venditricis in ciuitate Thyatirorum, Act. XVI, 14. cuius dominus aperuit cor, vt attenderet iis, quae a Paulo dicebantur. Occlusum erat Lydiae caecitatis & ignorantiae quasi feris; quas, praedicante verbum Dei Paulo, concurrens Spiritus S. reuellebat, cogitationem tantam cordi Lydiae immittendo, & excitando in voluntate illius spirituale desiderium, quo ad maiorem attentionem, & assequendam e predicatione Paulli salutarem rerum diuinarum cognitionem stimulabatur. E quibus dispalescit, speciale Spiritus S. lumen, & diuinam vim persuadendi ad solidam sacrarum litterarum notitiam, firmumque iis praestandum assensum requiri.

Antithesis est Socinianorum & Arminianorum afferentium, S. scripturam adeo claram esse, vt ad eius intelligentiam speciali gratiae diuinae lumine opus non sit; quorum potiora argumenta sunt sequentia.

I. Quaecunque scriptura est perspicua, illa sine supernaturali gratiae diuinae lumine facile intelligi potest. Atqui S. scriptura &c. Ergo. Resp. S. scriptura in se est dilucida & clara, sed haec claritas est ordinata ad hanc gratiam, quae praeterea non est irresistibilis aut irrefragabilis; siquidem oculis mentis malitiosus obex aut velamen obiici potest, vt ne claritatem scripturae videant. Quamobrem sicut perperam concluderetur: Sol est fulgidissimus: ergo illuminat oculum caecum, clausum, velo obtectum; ita male concludunt aduersarii: S. scriptura est clarissima: ergo eius sensum percipit homo irregenitus indocilis, empecta, hostis gratiae, osor & contemtor veritatis coelestis. Considerate inquit gentium apostolus, 2 Cor. IV, 3. 4. Si absconditum est euangelium nostrum, in iis, qui pereunt, est absconditum; in quibus Deus seculi huius excaecauit sensus infidelium, vt non splendeat illis illuminatio euangelii gloriae Christi. Docet apostolus, euangelium, per se perspicuum, esse κεκαλυμμένον, tectum vel opertum per accidens, culpa hominum laborantium caecitate, non tantum connata, quae omnibus communis est, sed etiam adscititia & voluntarie contracta, ac permissa iudicio Dei, cum accedit pertinacia, a Satana corroborata. 2 Petr. I, 9. 1 Io. II, 9.

II. Verba prophetarum & apostolorum ex consueto loquendi vsu desumta sunt, quorum vim significandi homo animalis citra gratiam supernaturalem addiscere potest. Resp. Verba prophetarum & apostolorum considerantur vel extra contextum, vel in contextu propositionis biblicae. Priori modo analogiam habent cum verbis humanis, & ab irregenito citra supernaturalem Spiritus S. gratiam intelligi possunt: at si spectentur in contextu, quatenus accommodantur mysteriis fidei, & eorum quasi δοχεῖα, receptacula aut vehicula, & verba vere diuina sunt, citra praeuenientem & praeparantem Spiritus S. gratiam, solidus de ipsis conceptus, conformis menti Spiritus sancti, formari nequit. Illustratur exemplo. Quid sit exaltare, quid trahere, nouit omnis homo irregenitus gentilis, Turca, Tartarus, Iudaeus. At vero si proponerem ipsi considerandum oraculum Christi, Io. XII, 32. Ego vero si exaltatus fuero e terra, omnes traham ad me ipsum, effatum Salvatoris non intelliget, nisi intellectus eius a Spiritu S. praecultus illustretur.

III. Hypocritæ destituti lumine Spiritus S. sacram scripturam intelligunt. Resp. (1) Notitia hypocritarum, quam e lectione sacrarum litterarum quæsiverunt, est externa & litteralis, non interna effectiue salutaris, & (stricte loquendo) spiritualis, i. e. cum spiritualibus motibus, contritione, fide, amore Dei coniuncta. Ratio est, quia hypocritæ sensum scripturæ litteralem ad viuam praxin & salutarem vsum non applicant. (2) Notitia litteralis hypocritarum est ab illuminatione Spiritus sancti imperfecta & pædagogica.

IV. Hæretici sine illuminatione Spiritus S. sensum scripturæ assequuntur, & ex illa aduersus orthodoxos disputant. Hæretici cum considerantur reduplicatiue, quatenus sunt hæretici, i. e. errantes in fundamento fidei, sensum scripturæ inferunt, non ex ea efferunt, non capiunt sensum, quem verba scripturæ ex se fundunt, sed alienum, non analogum textui ipsi affingunt.

V. Diabolus non capax luminis supernaturalis intelligit scripturam, quippe cuius verba citauit Matth. IV, 6. Resp. Diabolus non est subiectum, cuius commodo scriptura S. est configuata; ideoque gratia Spiritus S. præueniens ipsi non assistit, vtpote quæ salutem hominis intendit. Quidquid cacodæmon de rebus diuinis e sacris litteris arripuit, id omne velut ex alienis scriniis, ad se non pertinentibus, furatus est. Neque tamen assecutus est sensum genuinum scripturæ loco citato, sed illius verba nefarie peruertit, & in peregrinum sensum detorsit.

VI. Si homo irregenitus sacram scripturam sine lumine supernaturali intelligere nequit, ob incredulitatem non est puniendus. Sed ob incredulitatem puniendus est. Ergo homo irregenitus sine lumine supernaturali Spiritus S. scripturam intelligere potest. Consequentia maioris probatur, quia Spiritus S. homini irregenito lumen supernaturale, sine quo fidem concipere nequit, denegauit. Resp. Spiritus S. lumen supernaturale nemini denegat absolute, sed omni lectori vel auditori verbi diuini impertitur, modo eius operationi morose non obsistat, aut supernaturalem illuminationem obiecto velamine cæcitatis voluntarie contractæ non impediat. Punitur igitur irregenitus ob lumen Spiritus S. non admissum, sed petulanter reiectum.

VII. Gratia Spiritus S. illuminans aut perpetuo coniuncta est cum scriptura sacra, aut ab ea separata est. Si perpetuo coniuncta est, omnes homines scripturam legentes pariter illuminantur, conuertuntur, regenerantur. Si separata esse dicitur, enthusiasmus in ecclesiam plenis quasi velis inuehitur. Resp. 1) Gratia Spiritus S. illuminans quidem perpetuo coniuncta est cum scriptura sacra, sed non illuminat irregenitos indociles & perseueranter obluctantes. Neque illuminat in momento, sed per vices & gradus. Qui primum illuminationis gradum repellit, alterum eumque superiorem non accipit. Vt homo conuertatur & regeneretur, requiritur præuia illuminatio Spiritus S. per multos actus repetitos continuata, quam ordine naturæ gratia diuina conuertens, quæ contritionem operatur, & regenerans, quæ vires credendi confert, subsequitur. Apposite inquit D. SCHERZER. in breuiar. Hulsein. enucleato p. 57. Supernaturalis gratia Spiritus S. verbo diuino, cuius auditus fidem accendit, Rom. X, 17. est coniuncta, nequaquam vero ab eo separanda: cui aliam gratiosam Spiritus sancti, qui iam mediante verbo in cor illapsus est, operationem ad eum finem accedere non negamus. 2) Enthusiasmum in ecclesiam non introducimus, eo quod asserimus Spiritum S. pro statu præsentis temporis illuminare mentes hominum, non ἀμέσως, immediate, sed ἐμμέσως, mediate, per ipsammet scripturam S.


### Question XLVIII. Is scripture to be explained by scripture?

Sacred Scripture is the fundamental principle , from which one illuminated by the Holy Spirit, the supreme & infallible interpreter of the sacred letters , an inferior interpreter, whether public or private , can accurately investigate, certainly elicit, and perspicuously declare the genuine sense of biblical sayings through legitimate means of interpretation . Obs.

I. Πρώτως (Primarily) & fundamentally, the interpretation of Scripture is called an analytical act, by which the genuine sense of some biblical saying that is less clear and more difficult to understand is accurately investigated, demonstratively elicited, and rendered clear. Δευτέρως (Secondarily), the interpretation of Scripture is called the demonstration of the true sense, comprehended in a most clear and easily understood biblical saying, by which it is either vindicated from the distortions of heterodox persons, or accommodated to salutary use. Obs.

II. When we assert that Scripture is to be explained by Scripture, then in the subject, by "Scripture" is understood some prophetic or apostolic utterance, less clear or controversial, to be explained by interpretation: in the predicate, by "Scripture" are understood the clearer utterances of the prophets & apostles; inasmuch as they are accustomed to explain Scripture from that part which, at first glance, seems more obscure. Obs.

Obs. III. When we teach that Scripture is to be explained by Scripture, we remove immediate divine revelation, upon which we do not rely in expounding the sacred letters, since that is not given in the Church after the canon of Scripture has been established. Human reason. For although this is the receiving subject and the organ knowing the sense of Scripture, it is nevertheless not the fundamental principle, from which as from a fountain a solid exposition of Scripture is to be drawn, nor an infallible rule, to which the interpretation of the sacred letters is to be directed, examined, and discerned from ψευδερμηνείᾳ (false interpretation). They deceive and are deceived who subject those things which are above reason to reason. For faith is not to be led captive under the obedience of reason, but reason under the obedience of faith. 2 Cor. X, 5. All human writings, all commentaries of the doctors of the Church, both of the more ancient (who come under the venerable name of the Fathers) and of the more recent: whose writings we use as external, probable, and not-to-be-despised aids for interpreting; but we do not rely upon them as a fundamental principle or an infallible norm for expounding the Scriptures.

IV. Scripture explains itself either in act or in potency. It explains itself in act when it immediately subjoins an explanation to its sayings, as when in John II, 21, it immediately adds of what temple Christ had spoken, namely, of the temple of His body. It explains itself in potency when it provides the means of interpreting Scripture: the original text, the antecedents and consequents, the scope of the speaker, parallel passages, and the analogy of faith. Prob. a.

I. From the perspicuity of Sacred Scripture. Every perspicuous writing pours forth its sense from itself, and imparts and notifies the same to attentive readers. But Sacred Scripture is perspicuous. Therefore. The major is evident. For just as an epistle, not woven with obscure or ambiguous words, pours forth a certain sense from itself and instills it into the attentive reader; just as a decree of a prince intimates his will through perspicuous words; just as a father's testament exposes the sentiments of a fatherly mind: so, since Scripture is nothing other than an epistle of the Almighty to His creature, a promulgation of legal and evangelical will, a certain testament, 2 Cor. III, 6-14, it surely brings a clear sense to readers and openly intimates the will of the testator. The minor is clear from the perspicuity of Scripture demonstrated above.

II. Concerning the end of the sacred letters, which is σοφίσαι, to make men wise unto salvation through faith, which is in Christ Jesus. Whatever scripture is consigned to that end, that it may render a man wise unto salvation through faith, fixed in Christ Jesus, it opens the sense comprehended under the words, and promptly insinuates it into the minds of the readers. But sacred scripture &c. The major is evident, because scripture, from which, when attentively considered, a certain sense cannot be elicited, renders the reader not so much wise, as doubting and erring.

III. Concerning the property of the interpretation of scripture. Every interpretation of faith is analogous, or consentaneous, and must be sought from sacred scripture itself. Every solid interpretation of the sacred letters &c. The major is clear, since, defining it, D. Io. Adam Osiander in Theolog. posit. p. 334 says: the analogy of faith is the harmony of biblical sayings, or it is a type of doctrine, superstructed upon clear and perspicuous testimonies of scripture; which cannot dissent, because the spirit of the prophets and of men θεοπνεύστων (divinely inspired) is one and without any dissonance; which in the Latin churches in the time of TERTULLIAN was called the rule of faith. According to the definition of D. CALOVIIUS, the analogy of faith is the conformity of the doctrine of faith, clearly expounded in the sacred scriptures; which has been done in those places especially where each doctrine has its proper seat, in Bibl. illustr. in Rom. VII. fol. 207. If, therefore, the doctrine of faith is collected and constructed from perspicuous testimonies of scripture, certainly every interpretation, consentaneous to faith, must rest upon the foundation of sacred scripture. The minor is Paul's, Rom. XII, 6. Having prophecy, (let them have it) according to the analogy of faith. By prophets, the interpreters of scripture, and by prophecy, the interpretation of scripture is understood. Conf. 1 Cor. XV, 1-3. 1 Thess. V, 20. 1 Tim. IV, 14. () ()

Indeed, I join myself to those to whom the meaning of this saying seems to be otherwise. Namely 1) as regards προφητείαν (prophecy), these things must be considered: First, it could hardly be demonstrated by any clear example that the interpretation of the sacred letters is designated by that name. Then, with no necessity pressing us, it is not permitted for us to deflect from the signification of the word, if not perpetual, then certainly most customary. In most places, and I dare contend, in all, προφήτης (prophet) denotes an extraordinary person, namely that Doctor who, by divine instinct and inspiration, reveals arcane things and specifically predicts future events. Finally, it is certain that προφητείαν (prophecy), properly and customarily so called, was necessary for the beginning of the N.T. church, and was not only divinely given to the Apostolic assembly, but also in other places, adjacent to this, 1 Corinth. XII, 28. XIV, 1. sqq., is expressly numbered among the extraordinary and miraculous gifts. 2) As for ἀναλογίαν (analogy), the whole series of words teaches us that PAUL understands by that name the same thing which he had said a little before, v. 3, μέτρον πίστεως (measure of faith). Furthermore, it is certain that 1) the complex, consensus, and agreement of the fundamental doctrines of faith can be rightly called ἀναλογίαν πίστεως (analogy of faith). For ἀναλογία (analogy) is generally a proportion, which is seen specifically either in the measure of things compared and aptly joined, or in the coherence of truths, all connected and fitted among themselves. It is also clear that 2) the coherence of the principal dogmas of faith, the ὑποτύπωσιν τῶν ὑγιαινόντων λόγων (pattern of sound words), is the unique principle of the interpretation of divine scripture, and it must be assumed in such a way that nothing, entirely alien to it, or plainly contrary to it, should ever be thought to be a true interpretation. This indeed right reason so demands. Would anyone not interpret falsely, if he expounded the words of some Philosopher far otherwise than agreeably with the principles which he himself laid down? And certainly very great weight belongs to the argument which proceeds from the lesser to the greater: If in human writings no prudent author is ever believed to have sensed anything adverse to the principal parts of his doctrine, connected among themselves: much less does so unjust a suspicion fall upon the divine letters. It can happen, and often comes to pass, that a man, though wise, yet mutable, or at some time forgetful of what he has been, contradicts himself. God, on the contrary, is always the same, never failing to be consistent with himself, devoid both of all mutation and of all error. Therefore it can never come to pass that that sense becomes the true sense of even one word of God which does not accord excellently with the principal parts of the doctrine divinely revealed. I add this one thing: The principal dogmas of faith exist in places, as in many others, so especially in classical ones, in which there is the greatest perspicuity of words.

E. Of the analogy

is: Let those who are interpreters of Scripture take pains that the interpretation be analogous to faith, i.e., that it agrees with the fundamental articles of faith, or with the principal chapters of the Christian faith, collected from the most lucid testimonies of Scripture.

IV. From the contrary. Whatever Scripture is therefore not ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως, of proper interpretation, because it was not brought by the will of men, the interpretation of that Scripture is not to be taken from the judgment of men based on principles of reason, but from Scripture itself, as a divine principle.

But, prophetic Scripture, etc. Therefore. The major and minor are evident from the utterance of Peter in 2 Epist. c. 1, 20, 21. Every prophecy of Scripture is not of proper interpretation; for prophecy was not brought of old by the will of men. By prophecy, in the cited place, some understand by hypallage prophetic Scripture, others the interpretation of Scripture; who differ only in the manner of speaking; because materially prophetic Scripture and its sense and interpretation are the same.

The apostle argues: Whatever Scripture does not depend on human judgment or a principle of reason, but on the impulse and illumination of the Holy Spirit, that is not to be explained according to human judgment from a principle of supernatural revelation. (For those things which are above reason and the powers of free will cannot be judged or expounded by reason). But prophetic Scripture does not depend on the judgment of human reason, but on the impulse and illumination of the Holy Spirit. Therefore.

You say: The Petrine passage militates for the Papists against the Protestants: For if Holy Scripture is not ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως, of proper or private interpretation, it follows that it is of public and ecclesiastical interpretation, and that the same must be explained by the spirit of the church, not by a private spirit. I reply: Proper interpretation here is not opposed to public human interpretation, but to divine interpretation, or to the dictation and mind of the Holy Spirit speaking in and through Scripture. Hence every interpretation of Holy Scripture not drawn from the fountain of Scripture, but taken from one's own bosom, proceeding from one's own brain, fashioned according to human whim, and discordant with the mind of the Holy Spirit, is ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως, or proper interpretation. Wisely says our D. WILHELMVS LYSERVS in system. p. 95. Let there be fathers, let there be councils, let there be pontiffs; if they do not bring forth an interpretation from Scripture, but bring into it preconceived opinions, it is ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως, or private interpretation. What is objected concerning the private spirit does not touch us in the least; because we, aided by divine grace, strive that our interpretation of Scripture may be conformable to the mind of the Holy Spirit, who is not a private spirit, but common to all the regenerate. Whatever is brought forth outside of Scripture against articles of faith, that is produced by a private spirit.

Latin:

Sacra scriptura est principium fundamentale , ex quo illuminatus a Spiritu S. summo & infallibili sacrarum litterarum interprete , interpres inferior, publicus , an priuatus fuerit , genuinum dictorum biblicorum sensum per legitima interpretandi media accurate inuestigare, certe eruere, & perspicue declarare potest.

Obs. I. Πρώτως & primario dicitur interpretatio scripturae actus analyticus, quo alicuius dicti biblici minus clari & intellectu difficilioris genuinus sensus accurate inuestigatur, demonstratiue eruitur, & ad liquidum redigitur. Δευτέρως secundario dicitur interpretatio scripturae veri sensus, in dicto biblico clarissimo & intellectu facillimo comprehensi, demonstratio, qua is vel a detorsionibus heterodoxorum vindicatur, vel ad salutarem vsum accommodatur.

Obs. II. Quando asserimus scripturam per scripturam esse explicandam, tunc in subiecto, per scripturam intelligitur aliquod effatum propheticum, aut apostolicum, minus clarum, aut controversum, interpretatione explanandum: in praedicato, per scripturam intelliguntur eloquia prophetarum & apostolorum clariora; quippe quae solent explicare scripturam ex parte illa, quae primo intuitu obscurior videtur.

Obs. III. Quando docemus scripturam per scripturam esse explicandam remotum imus immediatam reuelationem diuinam, qua in exponendis sacris litteris non nitimur, cum illa post constitutum scripturae canonem in ecclesia non detur. Rationem humanam. Quamuis enim haec sit subiectum recipiens & organon cognoscens sensum scripturae, non tamen est principium fundamentale, ex quo velut fonte haurienda solida expositio scripturae, neque infallibilis regula, ad quam interpretatio sacrarum litterarum dirigenda, examinanda & a ψευδερμηνείᾳ discernenda sit. Fallunt & falluntur, qui ea, quae supra rationem sunt, rationi subiiciunt. Neque enim fides sub obsequium rationis, sed ratio sub obsequium fidei captiuanda est. 2 Cor. X, 5. Omnia scripta humana, omnes commentarios doctorum ecclesiae tam antiquiorum (qui venerando Patrum nomine veniunt), quam recentiorum: quorum scriptis vtimur, vt adminiculis interpretandi externis, probabilibus, non contemnendis; at non nitimur iisdem, vt principio fundamentali, aut infallibili exponendi scripturas norma.

Obs. IV. Scriptura seipsam explicat vel actu, vel potentia. Semet ipsam actu explicat, cum statim dictis explicationem subiungit, vtpote cum Io. II, 21. confestim addit, de quo templo Christus fuerit locutus, nempe de templo corporis sui. Potentia seipsam explicat, cum suppeditat media scripturae interpretandi, textum originalem, antecedentia & consequentia, scopum dicentis, loca parallela, fidei analogiam.

Prob. a. I. a perspicuitate sacrae scripturae. Omnis scriptura perspicua suum de se fundit sensum, eundemque attentis lectoribus impertit atque notificat. Atqui sacra scriptura est perspicua. Ergo. Maior constat. Vt enim epistola, non obscuris, aut ambiguis verbis contexta, sensum de se fundit certum, lectorique attento instillat; vt decretum principis per verba perspicua ipsius voluntatem intimat; vt testamentum patris sensa animi paterni exponit: ita cum scriptura nihil aliud sit, quam epistola omnipotentis ad suam creaturam, promulgatio legalis & euangelicae voluntatis, testamentum quoddam, 2 Cor. III, 6-14. Tenfum vtique liquidum ingerit lectoribus, & voluntatem testatoris aperte intimat. Minor liquet ex supra demonstrata perspicuitate scripturae.

II. A fine sacrarum litterarum, qui est σοφίσαι, sapientes reddere homines ad salutem per fidem, quae in Christo Iesu est. Quaecunque scriptura eo fine est consignata, vt hominem sapientem reddat ad salutem per fidem, defixam in Christo Iesu, illa sensum sub verbis comprehensum aperit, & mentibus legentium prompte insinuat. Atqui sacra scriptura &c. Maior patet, quia scriptura, ex qua, attente considerata, certus erui nequit sensus, lectorem non tam sapientem, quam dubitantem errantemque reddit.

III. A proprietate interpretationis scripturae. Omnis interpretatio fidei analoga, siue consentanea, ex ipsa scriptura sacra est petenda. Omnis solida sacrarum litterarum interpretatio &c. Maior liquet, quoniam definiente D. Io. Adam. Osiandro in Theolog. posit. p. 334. Analogia fidei est harmonia dictorum biblicorum, siue est typus doctrinae, claris & perspicuis testimoniis scripturae superstructus; quae dissentire nequeunt, eo quod prophetarum & virorum θεοπνεύστων vnum est oc citra vllam dissonantiam, quae in ecclesiis latinis tempore TERTULLIANI vocata fuit regula fidei. Secundum definitionem D. CALOVII analogia fidei est conformitas doctrinae fidei, scripturis sacris luculenter exposita; quod in iis inprimis locis, vbi quaeque doctrina propriam habet sedem, factum est, in Bibl. illustr. in Rom. VII. fol. 207. Quod si igitur doctrina fidei ex perspicuis scripturae testimoniis collecta & exstructa est, certe omnis interpretatio, fidei consentanea, scripturae sacrae fundamento inniti debet. Minor est Pauli Rom. XII, 6. Habentes prophetiam, secundum analogiam fidei (habeant). Per prophetas, scripturae interpretes, & per prophetiam, scripturae interpretatio intelliguntur. Conf. 1 Cor. XV, 1-3. 1 Thess. V, 20. 1 Tim. IV, 14. (*) (*)

Equidem me eis adiungo, quibus alia videtur esse huius dicti sententia. Scilicet 1) quod ad προφητείαν attinet, haec sunt consideranda; Primum luculento exemplo vix vllo demonstrari poterit, eo nomine designari interpretationem sacrarum litterarum. Deinde, nulla nos vrgente necessitate, non licet nobis deflectere a significatione vocis, si non perpetua, certe vsitatissima. Plerisque in locis, & contendere ausim, in omnibus, προφήτης personam extraordinariam denotat, nimirum eius Doctoris, qui diuino instinctu adflatuque arcanas res patefacit, & sigillatim futuros euentus praenuntiat. Denique constat, προφητείαν, proprie vsitateque ita dictam, ad auspicium ecclesiae N. T. necessariam, non solum coetui Apostolico diuinitus datam fuisse, verum etiam in aliis locis, huic finitimis, 1 Corinth. XII, 28. XIV, 1. sqq. diserte in donis extraordinariis ac miraculosis numerari. 2) Quantum ad ἀναλογίαν, tota verborum series nos docet, PAVLLUM eo nomine intelligere id idem, quod paullo ante, v. 3. dixerat μέτρον πίστεως. Caeteroquin certum est, 1) complexionem, consensum concentumque fundamentalium fidei doctrinarum recte omnino vocari posse ἀναλογίαν πίστεως. Etenim ἀναλογία generatim est proportio, quae speciatim cernitur siue in mensura rerum comparatarum apteque coniunctarum, siue in cohaerentia veritatum, omnium inter se connexarum atque aptarum. Perspicuum est etiam 2) principalium fidei dogmatum cohaerentiam, ὑποτύπωσιν τῶν ὑγιαινόντων λόγων, esse vnicum principium interpretationis scripturae diuinae, illudque ita adsumendum, vt nihil, ab eo prorsus alienum, aut plane ei contrarium, vnquam putandum sit pro vera interpretatione. Id profecto recta ratio ita postulat. An ne falso interpretaretur, si quis Philosophi cuiusdam verba multo aliter explicaret, ac principiis, quae ipse posuit, conuenienter? Et plurimum sane valet, quae a minori ad maius procedit, argumentatio: Si in scriptis humanis prudens auctor nullus vnquam creditur aliquid sensisse, doctrinae suae principalibus partibus, inter se connexis, aduersarium: multo minus in diuinas litteras tam iniusta cadit suspicio. Fieri potest, & saepe vsu venit, vt homo, quamuis sapiens, tamen mutabilis, aut fui aliquando immemor, sibi ipse repugnet. Deus, contra, semper idem est, nunquam non sibi constans, omnis & mutationis, & erroris expers. Non potest igitur vnquam fieri, vt vel vnius verbi diuini vera fit ea sententia, quae non optime congruat cum praecipuis partibus doctrinae, diuinitus reuelatae. Addo hoc vnum: Principalia fidei dogmatum exstant in locis vt multis aliis, sic potissimum classicis, in quibus maxima inest verborum perspicuitas.

E. Analogiae gruenest:

Qui sunt interpretes scripturae, operam dent, ut interpretatio sit analoga fidei, h. e. congruat cum fundamentalibus fidei articulis, sive cum principalibus christianae fidei capitibus, ex luculentissimis scripturae testimoniis collectis. *

IV. A contrario.* Quaecunque scriptura ideo non est ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως, propriae interpretationis, quia voluntate hominum non est allata, illius scripturae interpretatio non arbitrio hominum ex principiis rationis, sed ex ipsa scriptura, tanquam principio divino, desumenda est.

Atqui, scriptura prophetica &c. Ergo. Maior & minor patet ex effato Petri no 2 Epist. c. 1, 20. 21. Omnis prophetia scripturae non propriae interpretatonis fit; non enim voluntate hominum allata est olim prophetia. Per prophetiam l. c. nonnulli intelligunt per hypallagen scripturam propheticam, nonnulli interpretationem scripturae; qui tantum modo loquendi differunt; quia materialiter idem sunt scriptura prophetica, eiusque sensus & interpretatio. Vid. D. CALOVIVS in bibl. illustr. fol. 1546.

Argumentatur est apostolus: Quaecunque scriptura non ab arbitrio humano aut principio rationis dependet, sed ab impulsu & illuminatione Spiritus S. illa non pro arbitrio humano ex principio supernaturalis revelationis explicanda est. (Nam quae sunt supra rationem & vires liberi arbitrii, illa ex ratione nequeunt diiudicari, aut exponi). Atqui scriptura prophetica non ab arbitrio humanae rationis, sed ab impulsu & illuminatione Spiritus sancti dependet. Ergo.

Dicis: Locus Petrinus militat pro Pontificiis contra Protestantes: Quod si enim scriptura sacra non est ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως, propriae, sive privatae interpretationis, consequens est, eam esse interpretationis publicae & ecclesiasticae, eandemque explicandam esse a spiritu ecclesiae, non a spiritu privato. Resp. Propria interpretatio hic non opponitur interpretationi hominum publicae, sed interpretationi divinae, sive dictamini & menti Spiritus S. in scriptura & per scripturam loquentis. Proinde omnis interpretatio S. scripturae non hausta ex fonte scripturae, sed sumta ex proprio sinu, profecta ex proprio cerebro, conficta pro arbitratu humano, difformis menti Spiritus sancti, est ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως, sive propria interpretatio. Scite inquit noster D. WILHELMVS LYSERVS in system. p. 95. Sint patres, sint concilia, sint pontifices; si non ex scriptura interpretationem efferunt, sed in eam per praeconceptas opiniones inferunt, ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως, seu privata interpretatio est. Quae de spiritu privato obiiciuntur, nos minime tangunt; eo quod nos gratia divina adiuti nitimur, ut nostra interpretatio scripturae conformis sit menti Spiritus sancti, qui non spiritus privatus, sed omnibus renatis communis est. Contra quidquid in articulis fidei extra scripturam profertur, illud proficitur a spiritu privato.


### Question XLVIII. Is scripture to be explained by scripture?: V. From the inseparable union of the internal sense with the external letter of Scripture

V. From the inseparable union of the internal sense with the external letter of Scripture.

For there are two things in Scripture, the written words, and the sense included in them. The words are as it were the scabbard, the sense is the very sword of the Spirit, as BELLARMINE admits, lib. IV. de verbo Dei cap. IV. §. 7. fol. 171. To which Gordon Huntlaeus assents, as cited by D. GERHARD in confess. cathol. lib. II. art. I. c. III. fol. 420. The letter alone without the true sense cannot be called properly and truly the word of God, just as neither is a body without a soul truly and properly called a man.

Those, therefore, who despoil the letter of its true sense, do just as those who [do] properly explain Holy Scripture, that is, to interpret more difficult passages conveniently by the most clear passages, and indeed by dogmatic and principal ones. But that is likewise most agreeable to reason. Therefore it is evident how unjustly our adversaries act toward us, when they, indeed, demand that this rule, that Scripture is to be explained by Scripture, is a circle, than which there is no baser vice in argumentation. Furthermore, few are ignorant of the distinction, but also the conjunction, of both analogies, both of faith and of Scripture. The former exists in certain places of Scripture, namely the dogmatic and principal ones; the latter in all, of whatever argument they may be, and this is wont to be signified by the name of both context and parallelism. The former constitutes the sole principle of suitable interpretation; the latter pertains to the rules and means.

who deprive man of soul and life. If, therefore, the θεόπνευσος (God-breathed) sense is in the letters and words of Holy Scripture, as the sword in the sheath, the soul in the body; nowhere else but in the letters and words of the same Scripture is its genuine sense to be sought and found.

VI. From the absurd.

If the true sense of Scripture cannot be drawn from Scripture itself, but must be inferred from elsewhere, Scripture will be a) an inanimate skeleton, or a mute statue, to be animated by the voice of the church; whereas the word of God is living and active. Heb. IV, 12. b) It will not be clear and lucid, but filled with darkness; whereas Holy Scripture is a light shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in our hearts. 2 Pet. I, 19. c) It will be of an inferior condition to human writings; for all princes, jurists, philosophers, and orators declare their mind by their own writings: but from the opinion of the dissenters it follows that God has so involved His Scripture, through which He willed men to be informed unto salvation, that, even with pious prayers poured out and every diligence exerted, we cannot attain to the discovery of its genuine sense. d) It will be useless.

For that which is written cannot be understood, as it is neglected, being devoid of fruit. e) Nothing will be solid in theology; since its every innermost moment resides in the demonstration of the true sense of scripture.

Prob. b. Whoever is the author of Scripture, he is the best and authentic interpreter of the same. But the Holy Spirit, etc. Therefore. The major is clear, since everyone is the best interpreter of his own words. The minor is established by 2 Pet. I, 21: moved by the Holy Spirit, holy men of God spoke. We argue further: if the Holy Spirit interprets Scripture best, He explains it either by immediate or by mediate revelation. Not by immediate revelation; as that which has no place in the church after the completion of the canon of Scripture.

Therefore, through mediate revelation comprised in Holy Scripture.

Prob. c. A public interpreter is one who, equipped with sufficient gifts and legitimately called, that for the edification of those in the solemn assembly of the faithful, either by living voice or by writings published into the light, may expound the sense of Scripture dug out by accurate investigation. This public interpretation of Scripture has been divinely committed to the ecclesiastical ministry. For it befits an episcopus to be διδακτικόν, apt to teach, 1 Tim. III, 2. καὶ ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν, and to refute those who contradict. Tit. I, 9. The public office of teaching, moreover, embraces both the explication of the Scriptures and their application to salutary use. Both are sought from Scripture itself, as from a ταμιείῳ, or most abundant treasury.

For all Scripture is divinely inspired and is useful for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.

Prob. d. A private interpreter is every man imbued with a preliminary knowledge of the rudiments of heavenly doctrine, possessed of moderate judgment, and skilled in the language in which he reads the Scripture; who investigates the sense of the heavenly oracles for the confirmation of his own faith, or even for the edification of others, and declares it in private houses. That the interpretation of the sacred letters has been divinely permitted to him is evident: 1) Because Christ commends to all men journeying toward eternal life τὸ ἐρευνᾶν, to search the scriptures. John V, 39. Private men would not be commanded to search Holy Scripture, as a rich gold mine, unless it were divinely given to them to dig out the gold, or as the deep sea, unless to draw out the pearl, or as a most spacious forest, unless to hunt the morning stag, or, that I may say it more clearly, unless to inquire into the sense of the Holy Spirit. 2) Because private men are permitted the discerning judgment concerning matters of faith. I speak as to intelligent men: judge ye yourselves what I say. 1 Cor. X, 15. Those who understand the words of the apostles so accurately that they can render judgment concerning them, that they are truly divine, are not denied the faculty of attaining to and declaring the sense of the divine word. 3) In vain would the Bereans have searched the scriptures daily whether those things which Paul preached were so, unless the judgment concerning the sense of Scripture had belonged to them. is the faculty of attaining to and declaring the sense of the divine word. 3) In vain would the Bereans have feigned daily searching of the scriptures, whether those things which Paul preached.

they would be so, unless God had granted them the gift of διακρίσεως καὶ δοκιμασίας, of discernment and probation, to distinguish the genuine sense of Scripture from the foreign and externally imposed one.

Prob. e. Sacred Scripture interprets itself, by providing certain means of interpretation. These hermeneutical means are comprised by some theologians for the sake of brevity under two precepts. 1) The habit and construction of biblical words and phrases according to the custom of the holy language must be diligently considered. 2) From the antecedents and consequents, from the occasion, scope, impulsive cause, and circumstances, the mind of the speaker is to be investigated. D. FRANZIVS has deduced and illustrated these laws of interpretation more fully in his tract. de interpret. script. p. 5. 6. sqq. D. GLASSIVS in philol. sacra L. II. P. II. p. 352. seqq. Conf. D. BAYER in comp. theol. p. 271. But by other theologians, the means of interpreting the Scriptures are taken in such breadth that they also embrace within their scope the conditions required in an interpreter of Scripture and the external aids, by which the literal sense once found is secondarily confirmed and applied to salutary fruits. Wherefore, for the sake of easier doctrine, we shall distinguish hermeneutical means into antecedent, formal, and consequent.

Antecedent hermeneutical means are the requirements in an interpreter of the sacred letters, especially the more learned one, the aids by which he is instructed and rendered fit to inquire into, elicit, and explain the true sense of the sacred letters.

I. The chief hermeneutical aid is the illumination of the Holy Spirit, to be sought from God by pious prayers. For a prophet is given through the Holy Spirit, 1 Cor. XII, 10. By the same are given the eyes of the mind illuminated, Eph. I, 18. But God gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask, Luc. XI, 3. and confers wisdom through prayers to those asking for it, Iac. I, 5. Wherefore, to the interpretation of Scripture, an ardent prayer is always to be prefixed, that the Holy Spirit himself may teach us; not through immediate illumination, which is no longer to be expected; but mediately through Scripture, where the Holy Spirit has deposited his sense.

II. The previous knowledge of the fundamental articles of faith, since their uniform agreement is commended by St. Paul, i.e., the analogy of faith, which is never not to be observed by the sacred hermeneut. Rom. XII, 6.

III. A solid knowledge of the Hebrew and Greek languages. For in these languages the Holy Spirit has spoken through the prophets and apostles: in these languages the canonical Scripture was adorned, and by the provident care of God has reached us preserved. An interpreter ignorant of these original languages is forced to see with others' eyes, to hear with others' ears, and to consult and follow the brain of another. Wherefore, for an interpreter who is to understand the sacred letters solidly, usefully, and perfectly (according to the state of the way) and to explain them to others, for the full apprehension of the efficacy and δεινότητος (power) latent in the bark of the words, and also for vindicating the true sense of Scripture from the distortions of the heterodox, the study of the Greek and Hebrew languages is extremely necessary.

IV. The ancillary apparatus of the liberal arts, both instrumental and principal. Hebrew and Greek grammar teaches the idioms of the Hebrews and Greeks: rhetoric inculcates the method of explaining tropical and figurative locutions: logic demonstrates the method of eliciting the consequent from the antecedent. Philosophical disciplines especially conduce to the distinct explanation both of the mixed articles of faith and of physical and moral matters, of which mention is made in the sacred letters. Nay, they also serve the sacred hermeneut for the richer illustration (from the similar, the contrary, etc.) of matters of pure faith which Scripture hands down: they serve, I say, they do not direct him as a norm.

V. A burning love of truth, as well as the proposed desire and genuine study of inquiring into and clearly narrating the sense of any biblical text. For to handle the eloquence of Scripture without an ingenuous study and desire for the truth, to be drawn from its own fountain, is often more than enough to handle the same without understanding and without the effort of tranquilizing one's own conscience and that of others. Meanwhile, we learn by experience that the study of truth, having applied as it were a brake, delays preconceived erroneous opinions. For indeed, by indulging in these one imposes a foreign sense upon Scripture, and does not draw out the divine sense from it. HILARY says most beautifully in Book I of De Trinitate: "The best reader is he who expects the understanding of the things said from the things themselves, rather than imposing it upon them, and who brings back [the meaning] rather than bringing it in; nor does he force that to seem contained in the words which he had presumed should be understood before the reading." VI. Diligent and frequently repeated reading of Holy Scripture, and intimate meditation upon it, joined at times with solidly learned interpreters. For the reader, turning over the book of the sacred oracles again and again, in the progress of time becomes accustomed to readily understanding the phrases of Scripture, and renders the style of the Holy Spirit familiar to himself.

The formal hermeneutical media are the internal and proximate aids for correctly performing interpretation, supplied by Holy Scripture itself, by which the intimate viscera of the biblical text are searched, so that its internal sense, conformable to the mind of the Holy Spirit, may be investigated, elicited, and reduced to clarity. Such internal and proximate media of interpreting are: I. A solicitous scrutiny of individual words and connected phrases which are held in the original text. For since words are symbols of things and, as it were, the resting places of the internal sense, the power of signifying and the emphasis of individual words must be weighed, and the native signification must be distinguished from the tropical, or transferred. D. GLASSIUS’s Sacred Rhetoric elucidates the tropes occurring in sacred writings. Lexicons and concordances teach the native signification. If a word is polysēmos, or of diverse signification, then both the connection of the text and parallel passages will supply a determined signification analogous to the text; to which lexicons, concordances, paraphrases, and versions will provide assistance. Connected phrases are to be explained according to the idioms of the Greeks and Hebrews, with the grammar of D. GLASSIUS acting as a torch.

II. An attentive consideration of the scope which the Holy Spirit intends in the biblical text. Paul says gravely to the leaders of the people in 1 Tim. 1:6-7: "From which some astochēsantes, wandering away, have turned aside to vain talk, desiring to be teachers of the law, while they understand neither what they say nor the things about which they affirm." In the word astochēsantes, wandering away, CHRYSOSTOM, OECUMENIUS, and others have noted that the metaphor is taken from unskilled archers who, in shooting arrows, do not hit the set mark. For those shooting, a certain scope is predefined; if they deflect from it, they strike the air and expose themselves to the mockery of all: so those who wish to be teachers of the law, and turn their minds away from charity and its companion, or guide, unfeigned faith—from the scope of the law—wander away shamefully. Lest the same befall the interpreter of Holy Scripture, it is right that he, about to expound the biblical text, should gaze with unswerving eyes upon the scope intended by the Holy Spirit. The principal scope of Holy Scripture is the glory of God, Ps. 119: 18. The intermediate scope is the didactic, elenchtic, epanorthotic, paedeutic, and paracletic information of man unto salvation, 2 Tim. 3:16. Therefore, that interpretation of Scripture is not legitimate which derogates from the praise of God’s holiness, goodness, justice, and power, just as it undermines the pursuit of piety and obstructs the fountains of consolation.

III. A diligent and circumspect weighing of the whole context, the antecedents, and the consequents. Both the order and the circumstances in the text of the discourse must be weighed. Sometimes the members of prophetic and apostolic discourse cohere in a lucid order, as if in a concatenated series, so that one flows from another, or can be deduced. To the interpreter who skillfully attends to this synapheia and connection of the biblical text, a compendious way lies open for eliciting its true sense. JEROME teaches this in Matt. 25: "I always advise the prudent reader that he should not acquiesce in superstitious interpretations, and what is said comatice [in a disconnected manner] according to the whim of those inventing them, but should consider the prior, middle, and subsequent parts, and connect for himself all things that are written: for from the antecedents and consequents the true sense is gathered." To which AUGUSTINE adds his vote in Tract 70 on John: "The words of the Gospel are rightly understood if they are found to have concord with the things above."

For the preceding must agree with the following, when truth speaks. CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA, Strom. 7, complains that heretics pluck certain things from the sacred letters, οὐχ ὡς τὸ φῶς καὶ τὸ σῶμα τῆς προφητείας ὑπαγορεύει, not as the context (the web of speech) and the body of prophecy requires. IRENÆUS, book I, ch. 2, pours out the same complaints about the Valentinians who distort the scriptures. They leap over καὶ τὸν εἰρμὸν τῶν γραφῶν, the sequence of the scriptures, and as much as lies in them, they dissolve the members of the speech. For they transfer and transform: and, while they make one thing out of another, they deceive many with wisdom poorly compacted from the sayings of the Lord, which they accommodate to their own error. The circumstances of persons, occasion and moving cause, time and place, inserted into the context, shed no small light on biblical sayings; LYRA in ch. XVIII of Deuteronomy cites the saying of HILARY: the understanding of sayings must be taken from the causes of the speaker. Concerning the circumstance of time, AUGUSTINE says in sermon XVI on the words of the Lord: Distinguish the times, and the scripture will agree.

Latin:

V. Ab inseparabili unione sensus interni cum externa scripturae littera.

Duo enim sunt in scriptura, voces scriptae, & sensus in eis inclusus. Voces sunt quasi vagina, sensus est ipse gladius spiritus, fatente BELLARM. lib. IV. de verbo Dei cap. IV. §. 7. fol. 171. Cui adstipulatur Gordonus Huntlaeus citante D. GERHARD. in confess. cathol. lib. II. art. I. c. III. fol. 420. Sola littera fine vero sensu proprie & vere verbum Dei dici non potest, sicut neque corpus sine anima vere ac proprie dicitur homo.

Illi igitur, qui litteram vero sensu spoliant, perinde faciunt, ac illi, qui gruenter explanare scripturam sacram, hoc est, loca difficiliora interpretari convenienter locis clarissimis, & quidem dogmaticis ac praecipuis. Atqui id itidem rationi maxime consentaneum est. E. patet, quam inique nobiscum agant aduersarii, quando illi quidem hanc regulam, scriptura per scripturam explananda est, postulant circuli, quo nullum turpius est vitium in argumentatione. De caetero, pauci nesciunt distinctionem, sed & coniunctionem, vtriusque analogiae, tum fidei, tum scripturae. Illa exstat in quibusdam scripturae locis, quippe dogmaticis ac principalibus; haec in omnibus, cuiuscunque sint argumenti, atque haec nomine tum contextus, tum parallelismi significari solet. Illa constituit principium unicum idoneae interpretationis; hac ad regulas ac media pertinet.

qui hominem anima & vita priuant. Quod si igitur sensus θεόπνευσος in litteris & vocibus S. scripturae est, vt gladius in vagina, anima in corpore; nullibi nisi in litteris & vocibus scripturae eiusdem genuinus sensus quaerendus & inueniendus est.

VI. Ex absurdo.

Si scripturae verus sensus non potest ex ipsa scriptura erui, sed aliunde debet inferri, scriptura erit a) inanimo sceleton, aut statua muta, per ecclesiae vocem animanda; cum tamen sermo Dei sit viuus & efficax. Hebr. IV, 12. b) Non erit clara & dilucida, sed tenebris impleta; cum tamen scriptura S. fit lumen lucens in loco tenebricoso, vsque dum dies illucescat, & lucifer oriatur in cordibus nostris. 2 Petr. I, 19. c) Erit inferioris conditionis, quam scripta humana; nam omnes principes, ICti, philosophi, oratores, scriptis suis mentem suam declarant: at ex sententia diffidentium confecquitur, Deum scripturam suam, per quam homines ad salutem informatos voluit, sic inuoluisse, vt, fusis piis precibus omnique expromta diligentia, germanum eius sensum indagando assequi nequeamus. d) Erit inutilis.

Nam quod scriptum non potest intelligi, vt frugis expers negligitur. e) Nihil solidum erit in theologia; quippe cuius penitissimum omne momentum in demonstratione veri scripturae sensus residet.

Prob. b. Quicunque est auctor scripturae, ille eiusdem optimus & authenticus est interpres. Atqui Spiritus S. &c. Ergo. Maior liquet, quoniam vnusquisque optimus est interpres verborum suorum. Minor constat 2 Petr. I, 21. a Spiritu S. impulsi locuti sunt sancti Dei homines. Argumentamur porro: si Spiritus S. scripturam optime interpretatur, eandem vel per reuelationem immediatam, vel per mediatam exponit. Non per reuelationem immediatam; vtpote quae post completum scripturae canonem in ecclesia locum non habet.

Ergo per reuelationem mediatam in S. scriptura comprehensam.

Prob. c. Publicus hermeneuta est, qui sufficientibus donis instructus & legitime vocatus est, vt in aedificationem illorum in solemni fidelium caetu vel viua voce, vel editis in lucem scriptis sensum scripturae accurata inuestigatione erutum exponat. Publica isthaec scripturae interpretatio ministerio ecclesiastico diuinitus est commissa. Episcopum enim decet esse διδακτικόν, aptum ad docendum, 1 Tim. III, 2. καὶ ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν, & contradicentes arguere. Tit. I, 9. Complectitur autem publicum docendi munus tum scripturarum explicationem, tum earum ad salutarem vsum applicationem. Vtraque ex ipsa scriptura, velut ταμιείῳ, aut locupletissimo aerario, petitur.

Omnis enim scriptura diuinitus inspirata vtilis est ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad disciplinam, vt integer sit homo Dei, ad omne opus bonum probe instructus. 2 Tim. III, 16, 17.

Prob. d. Interpres priuatus est omnis homo rudimentorum doctrinae caelestis praecognitione imbutus, mediocri pollens iudicio, & idiomatis, in quo scripturam legit, gnarus; qui ad propriae fidei confirmationem, vel etiam aliorum aedificationem, sensum oraculorum caelestium inuestigat, & in aedibus priuatis declarat. Huic diuinitus permissam esse sacrarum litterarum interpretationem, patet: 1) Quia Christus omnibus hominibus viatoribus ad vitam aeternam tendentibus commendat τὸ ἐρευνᾶν, scrutari scripturas. Io. V, 39. Non iuberentur homines priuati scrutari sacram scripturam, tanquam diuitem aurifodinam, nisi aurum effodere, vel tanquam mare profundum, nisi margaritam extrahere, vel tanquam syluam amplissimam, nisi ceruam matutinam indagare, aut vt clarius dicam, nisi sensum Spiritus sancti inquirere, ipsis diuinitus datum foret. 2) Quia hominibus priuatis permittitur discretiuum de rebus fidei iudicium. Tanquam intelligentibus loquor: vos ipsi iudicate, quod dico. 1 Cor. X, 15. Qui verba apostolorum adeo accurate intelligunt, vt de iisdem, quod vere diuina sint, iudicium ferre queant, illis non denegata est facultas verbi diuini sententiam assequendi & enuntiandi. 3) Frustra Beroënses singulis diebus scrutati fuissent scripturas, an ea, quae Paullus praedicabat, ita se haberent, nisi iudicium de sensu scripturae ipsis competisset. est facultas verbi diuini sententiam assequendi & enuntiandi. 3) Frustra Beroënses fingulis diebus scrutati fuissent scripturas, an ea, quæ Paullus prædicabat.

ita se haberent, nisi Deus donum διακρίσεως καὶ δοκιμασίας, discretionis & probationis, ipsis indulsisset, ad discernendum scripturae sensum genuinum a peregrino & forinsecus illato.

Prob. e. Scriptura sacra seipsam interpretatur, certa interpretandi media suppeditando. Quae media hermeneutica a nonnullis theologis brevitatis causa duobus comprehenduntur praeceptis. 1) Vocum, phrasiumque biblicarum habitus & constructio iuxta consuetudinem linguae sanctae diligenter sunt consideranda. 2) Ex antecedentibus & consequentibus, ex occasione, scopo, causa impulsiva & circumstantiis mens loquentis est investiganda. Has interpretandi leges fulius diduxit & illustravit D. FRANZIVS in tract. de interpret. script. p. 5. 6. sqq. D. GLASSIVS in philol. sacra L. II. P. II. p. 352. seqq. Conf. D. BAYER in comp. theol. p. 271. Ab aliis autem theologis media interpretandi scripturas ea latitudine sumuntur; vt ambitu suo complectantur etiam requisitas in interprete scripturae conditiones & adminicula externa, quibus inuentus sensus litteralis secundario confirmatur, & ad salutares fructus applicatur. Quamobrem facilioris doctrinae causa media hermeneutica distinguemus in antecedentia, formalia, & consequentia.

Media hermeneutica antecedentia sunt requisita in interprete sacrarum litterarum, praesertim doctiori, subsidia, quibus ille instruitur & idoneus redditur ad verum sacrarum litterarum sensum inquirendum, eliciendum & explanandum.

I. Palmarium subsidium hermeneuticum est illuminatio Spiritus sancti, piis precibus a Deo expetenda. Propheta enim datur per Spiritum sanctum, 1 Cor. XII, 10. ab eodem donantur oculi mentis illuminati, Eph. I, 18. Dat autem Deus Spiritum S. petentibus, Luc. XI, 3. ac sapientiam confert per preces ipsam postulantibus, Iac. I, 5. Quare interpretationi scripturae & vsque praemittenda est ardens precatio, vt Spiritus S. nos ipse doceat; non per immediatam illuminationem, quae non amplius exspectanda; sed mediate per scripturam, vbi Spir. S. sensum suum deposuit.

II. Prauia articulorum fidei fundamentalium cognitio, quippe quorum vniformis concentus est commendata a S. Paullo, analogia sc. fidei, hermeneutae sacro nunquam non obferuanda. Rom. XII, 6.

III. Solida hebraeae & graecae linguarum notitia. His namque linguis locutus est Spiritus S. per prophetas & apostolos: his linguis scriptura canonica adornata, & prouida Dei cura ad nos conseruata peruenit. Rudis harum linguarum originalium interpres alienis oculis videre, alienis auribus audire, alterius cerebrum consulere & sequi cogitur. Quocirca interpreti, solide, vtiliter & perfecte (pro statu viae) sacras litteras intellecturo, aliisque exposituro, ad plenam efficaciae & δεινότητος in verborum cortice latentis apprehensionem, nec non ad vindicandum verum scripturae sensum ab heterodoxorum detortionibus, perquam necessarium est graecae & hebraeae linguarum studium.

IV. Apparatus ancillaris artium liberalium tam instrumentalium, quam principalium. Idiotismos hebraeorum & graecorum docet grammatica hebraea & graeca: modum explicandi tropicas & figuratas locutiones inculcat rhetorica: modum eliciendi consequens ex antecedente demonstrat logica. Disciplinae philosophicae inprimis conducunt ad distinctam explicationem tum articulorum fidei mixtorum, tum rerum physicarum & moralium, quarum in sacris litteris fit mentio. Quin & ad vberiorem rerum merae fidei, quas scriptura tradit, illustrationem (a simili, contrario &c.) hermeneutae sacro inferuiunt: inferuiunt, inquam, non normae instar ipsum dirigunt.

V. Flagrans veritatis amor, iuxta atque desiderium propositum & studium genuinum alicuius textus biblici sensum exquirendi & perspicue enarrandi. Versare enim eloquia scripturae absque ingenuo veritatis, e fonte suo hauriendae, studio & desiderio, plus satis saepe est versare eadem absque intellectu, & conatu suam aliorumque conscientiam tranquillandi. Experimento interim discimus, veritatis studium, iniecto quasi sufflamine, remorari praeconceptas opiniones erroneas. Etenim his indulgens, scripturae alienum sensum infert, non sensum divinum ex ea effert. Bellissime inquit HILARIVS in libr. I. de trin. Optimus lector est, qui dictorum intelligentiam exspectet ex dictis potius, quam imponat, & retulerit magis, quam attulerit; neque cogat id videri dictis contineri, quod ante lectionem praesumpserit intelligendum. VI. Sedula & crebro repetita lectio S. scripturae, illiusque intima meditatio, iunctis interdum solide doctis interpretibus. Nam lector, iterum iterumque voluens sacrorum oraculorum codicem, progressu temporis phrasibus scripturae prompte intelligendis assuescit, stilumque Spiritus S. sibi familiarem reddit. Exegetis interpretum ante ἐξεργασίαν, sive actum interpretationis, cum scripturae lectione coniuncta, & aequa animi lance expensa, χειραγωγία sive manuductio est, ad sensum scripturae sagaci indagine inquirendum.

Media hermeneutica formalia sunt interna & proxima interpretationis dextre perficiendae subsidia, ab ipsa scriptura S. suppeditata, quibus intima textus biblici viscera perquiruntur, ut internus ipsius sensus menti Spiritus S. conformis investigetur, eruatur, & ad liquidum redigatur. Qualia media interpretandi interna & proxima sunt: I. Sollicitum vocum singularum, phrasiumque coniunctarum, quae habentur in textu originali, scrutinium. Cum enim voces sint rerum symbola, & interni sensus quasi cubilia, singularum vocum vis significandi & emphasis ponderanda, atque significatio natiua a tropica, sive translata, discernenda est. Tropos in sacris occurrentes enucleat rhetorica sacra D. GLASSII. Natiuam significationem docent lexica & concordantiae. Si vox πολύσημος, sive diversae fuerit significationis, determinatam & textui analogam significationem suppeditabit tum connexio textus, tum loca parallela: quibus adiumentum praestabunt lexica, concordantiae, paraphrases & versiones. Phrases coniunctae secundum idiotismos graecorum & hebraeorum explicandae sunt, facem praeferente grammatica D. GLASSII.

II. Attenta scopi, quem Spiritus sanctus in textu biblico intendit, consideratio. Deductoribus populi grauiter inquit Paullus 1 Tim. I, 6. 7: A quibus nonnulli ἀστοχήσαντες, aberrantes, auersi sunt ad vaniloquium, dum volunt esse legis doctores, quum tamen non intelligant, neque quae dicunt, neque circa quae asseuerant. In voce ἀστοχήσαντες, aberrantes, metaphoram sumtam esse ab imperitis sagittariis, sagittas emittendo scopum praefixum non attingentibus, notarunt CHRYSOSTOMVS, OECVMENIVS, & alii. Sagittantibus certus praefinitus est scopus; a quo si deflectant, aerem feriunt, omniumque ludibriis se exponunt: ita qui volunt esse doctores legis, & mentes suas auertant a caritate eiusque comite, aut duce, intemerata fide, a scopo legis, turpiter aberrant. Ne idem interpreti sacrae scripturae obtingat, par est, vt ille expositurus textum biblicum, scopum intentum a Spiritu sancto irretortis oculis intueatur. Scopus principalis sacrae scripturae est gloria Dei, Psal. CXIX, 18. Scopus intermedius est hominis informatio didactica, elenchtica, epanorthotica, paedeutica & paracletica ad salutem, 2 Tim. III, 16. Proinde non est legitima scripturae interpretatio, quae Deo laudem sanctitatis, bonitatis, iustitiae & potentiae derogat, iuxta atque studium pietatis labefactat, & fontes solatii obstruit.

III. Diligens & circumspecta totius contextus, antecedentium & consequentium pensitatio. Pensitandus est in textu orationis tum ordo, tum circumstantiae.
