Interdum membra orationis propheticae & apostolicae ordine lucido, quasi concatenata serie, cohaerent, vt vnum ex alio fluat, aut deduci possit. Quam συνάφειαν & connexionem textus biblici solerter attendenti interpreti patet via compendiaria ad verum ipsius sensum enucleandum. Docet id HIERONYMVS in Matth. XXV. c. Prudentem semper admoneo lectorem, vt non superstitiosis acquiescat interpretationibus, & quae comatice dicuntur pro fingentium arbitrio, sed confideret priora, media & sequentia, & nectat sibi vniuersa, quae scripta sunt: ex antecedentibus enim & consequentibus verus sensus colligitur. Cui album calculum adiicit AVGVSTINVS tract. 70, in Io. Verba euangelii recte intelliguntur, si cum superioribus reperiantur habere concordiam. si cum superioribus reperiuntur habere concordiam.

convenire enim debent praecedentia consequentibus, quando veritas loquitur. CLEMENS ALEXANDR. Strom. 7. conqueritur, haereticos e sacris litteris decerpere quaedam, οὐχ ὡς τὸ φῶς καὶ τὸ σῶμα τῆς προφητείας ὑπαγορεύει. non ut contextus (tela orationis) et corpus prophetiae requirit. Easdem querelas de Valentinianis scripturas detorquentibus effundit IRENÆVS lbr. I. cap. 2. Transiliunt καὶ τὸν εἰρμὸν τῶν γραφῶν et seriem scripturarum, et quantum in ipsis, dissoluunt membra orationis. Transferunt enim et transformant: et, dum aliud ex alio faciunt, multos fallunt sapientia male compacta ex dictis Domini, quae errori suo accommodant. Inserta contextui circumstantiae personarum, occasionis et causae mouentis, temporis et loci, haud parum lucis dictis biblicis affundunt, LYRANVS in cap. XVIII. Deuter. allegat dictum HILARII: intelligentia dictorum ex causis sumenda est dicentis. De circumstantia temporis inquit AVGVSTINVS sermon. XVI. de verbis Domini. Distribue tempora, et concordabit scriptura.


### Question XLVIII. Is scripture to be explained by scripture?: IV. The perpetual observation of the analogy of faith

IV. The perpetual observation of the analogy of faith.

We showed above that the analogy of faith is the conformity of the doctrine of faith, or the uniform agreement of the fundamental articles of faith handed down in the clear sayings of scripture. For the dogmas of faith and the precepts of morals have their own seats in the sacred letters, in which they are treated not incidentally or by the way, but directly, accurately, and professedly, and are proposed in clear words; which dogmas of faith the Christian church comprehends summarily in its symbols. Therefore, every interpretation of a biblical saying must be considered weak, insofar as it is obscure and repugnant to the clear eloquence of scripture, or to a fundamental article of faith contained in the symbolic books of the Christian church.

V. The assiduous collation of parallel places of scripture.

For the now-mentioned analogy of faith requires that the more obscure and fewer things be explained by the clearer and more numerous ones, and by which they gain some light. AUGUSTINE, book II of Christian Doctrine, ch. 9, recommends the collation of parallel places. Let examples be taken from the more manifest to illustrate more obscure locutions, and let certain testimonies of sure sentences remove doubt about uncertain ones. Parallel sayings, which deal with the same matter or the same dogma of faith, are some parallel as to phrase, others as to the sentence or the thing itself. The same phrase, which the Holy Spirit uses in Isa. 6:10, 'Make fat the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes and hear with their ears, and their heart understand and be converted, that it may be healed for itself,' you will see repeated six times in the N.T.: Matt. 13:14, Mark 4:12, Luke 8:10, John 12:40, Acts 28:26, Rom. 11:8. Although in that repetition, either for the sake of exegesis or brevity, some variation may occur.

As to the thing, or the sentence, parallel sayings are Gen. 3:15, 'The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent,' and 1 John 3:8, 'For this the Son of God appeared, that he might dissolve the works of the devil.' Therefore, let the hermeneut carefully consider: 1) whether the sayings are parallel as to phrase or as to sentence; 2) let him beware lest heterogeneous things be sold as parallel or homogeneous places; 3) let him provide that darkness not be poured upon the clearer sayings of scripture by the less clear.

For it is the mark of a good interpreter to reduce the sense of an obscure saying to the clear; conversely, to render a clear saying obscure by a twisted explanation is the mark of a malicious calumniator.

Latin:

IV. Perpetuae analogiae fidei obseruatio.

Supra ostendimus, analogiam fidei esse conformationem doctrinae fidei, seu vniformem concentum articulorum fidei fundamentalium claris scripturae dictis traditorum. Habent enim dogmata fidei morumque praecepta in sacris litteris proprias sedes, in quibus non incidenter aut obiter, sed directe, accurate et ex professo tractantur, verbisque proponuntur perspicuis; quae fidei dogmata ecclesia christiana in suis symbolis summatim comprehendit. Sublestam igitur oportet esse omnem interpretationem dicti biblici, quatenus obscuri, repugnantem claro scripturae eloquio, aut articulo fidei fundamentali in libris symbolicis ecclesiae christianae contento.

V. Assidua locorum scripturae parallelorum collatio.

Requirat enim iam memorata analogia fidei, vt obscuriora et pauciora explicentur clarioribus et pluribus, et quibus lucem aliquam sortiuntur. Commendat locorum parallelorum collationem AVGVSTINVS lib. II. doctr. christ. cap. 9. Ad obscuriores locutiones illustrandas de manifestioribus sumantur exempla, et quaedam certarum sententiarum testimonia dubitationem de incertis auferant. Dicta parallela, quae de eadem materia, siue de eodem fidei dogmate agunt, alia parallela sunt, quoad phrasin, alia, quoad sententiam, seu rem ipsam. Eandem phrasin, qua Spiritus sanctus vtitur Ies. VI, 10. Impingua cor populi huius, et aures eius aggraua, ac oculos eius obline, ne forte videat oculis suis et auribus suis audiat, et cor eius intelligat conuertaturque, ut sanetur sibi, sexies repetitam videbis in N. T. Matth. XIII, 14. Marc. IV, 12. Luc. VIII, 10. Io. XII, 40. Act. XXVIII, 26. Rom. XI, 8. Quamuis in illa repetitione vel exegeseos, vel breuitatis causa, quaedam variatio occurrat.

Quoad rem, siue sententiam, dicta parallela sunt Gen. III, 25. Semen mulieris conteret caput serpentis, et I Io. III, 8. In hoc apparuit filius Dei, ut dissoluat opera diaboli. Sedulo itaque consideret hermeneuta: 1) sintne dicta parallela, qua phrasin, an qua sententiam; 2) caueat, ne pro locis parallelis, siue homogeneis, venditentur heterogenea; 3) prouideat, ne dictis scripturae clarioribus e minus claris offundantur tenebrae.

Boni namque interpretis est sensum dicti obscurioris redigere ad liquidum: ex aduerso dictum liquidum contorta explicatione reddere obscuram, malitiosi calumniatoris est.


### Question XLVIII. Is scripture to be explained by scripture?: VI. The proper and native signification of biblical words and phrases must be constantly retained, unless the highest necessity presses the…

VI. The proper and native signification of biblical words and phrases must be constantly retained, unless the highest necessity presses the interpreter to descend to a figurative sense of the words.

A theological canon is to be observed here: one must persist in the proper and customary signification of words, as long as neither the analogy of faith, nor clearer parallel places of scripture, nor the antecedents and consequents in the context, or the scope of the speaker, or other circumstances, most openly repugn the proper signification of the words. This rule is founded on the natural reason of understanding, by which we are commanded to attend to that sense which all conceive according to the common use and signification of words; otherwise, no certainty of our understanding will be given.

Most rightly says B. LUTHER, in the book on the Babylonian Captivity, p. 277: 'No force is to be done to divine words, neither by man, nor by an angel;'

but as far as possible, they are to be kept in their simplest signification: and unless a manifest circumstance compels it, they are not to be taken outside of grammar, lest an opportunity be given to adversaries to evade the whole of Scripture.

The mediate hermeneutical consequences are the aids of interpretation, which the hermeneut uses after the act of interpretation to confirm the literal sense of Scripture, or to acquire a salutary knowledge of Scripture. These are two: I. Commentaries of the ancients and recent doctors of the church, whose exegetical labor we use as an external aid to interpretation, not relying upon it as a divine principle. Our B. Gerhard says excellently in Exeg. L. de scriptura S. fol. m. 204: God is not to be thought to have conferred upon us the testimonies of prior antiquity in vain, but that they might be a certain aid for investigating the meaning of Scripture, and that, the true meaning having been perceived from the sacred letters, the minds of the pious might be more confirmed. Wherefore the interpreter of Scripture uses the commentaries of the doctors of the church 1) before the act of interpretation, insofar as they lead him by the hand to elicit the true sense of a biblical saying. 2) after the ἐξεργασίαν (elaboration) of the interpretation, to confirm the meaning of this or that prophetic or apostolic oracle, already drawn beforehand from the very fountain of Scripture.

II. The serious application of the literal sense to a salutary, and indeed manifold, use. The public interpreter of Scripture, under the guidance of Paul, 2 Tim. III, 16, transfers the literal sense of the divine utterances a) to διδασκαλίαν (teaching), to consolidate true doctrine, b) to ἔλεγχον (reproof), to refute the false dogmas of heretics, c) to ἐπανόρθωσιν (correction), to correct the depravity of morals, d) to παιδείαν (training), to promote the study of piety, e) to παράκλησιν (encouragement), to instill all the most present comforts into anxious minds. The private interpreter of Scripture applies the literal sense of the heavenly oracles, investigated and found by assiduous reading, to his own edification and that of his neighbor, and thus to the exercises of repentance, faith, and piety, so that by reading the sacred letters he may learn and become accustomed to recognize his sins more deeply, to mourn them more bitterly, to detest them more gravely, to preserve, increase, and stabilize more diligently the faith conceived in Christ, to love, fear, and venerate God more intensely, to deny himself, to keep a sober and chaste mind, and to love his neighbor more validly. This application produces a salutary knowledge of Holy Scripture.

The antithesis is 1) of the Papists, who establish that the true understanding of Scripture must be sought from the consensus of the fathers and councils, and especially from the Roman Pontiff, whose authority in explaining the Scriptures is made supreme and infallible. 2) of the Socinians, who think that reason, or innate and cultivated philosophical principles and axioms, contributes most to the interpretation of Scripture. 3) of the Quakers and Enthusiasts, who desire a new and immediate revelation of the Holy Spirit for the ἑρμηνείαν (interpretation) of a more obscure biblical saying: whose arguments we shall weigh.

I. If Scripture were explained by Scripture, the same would be explained by the same, which seems to be absurd. Resp. 1) To explain the same by the same, considered in a different way or respect, is not absurd. Indeed, a prince's diploma is explained by the same diploma, a father's testament by the same testament: just as the light of the sun notifies itself and offers itself to be seen. 2) The different way of considering consists in this, that a biblical saying is explained according to the antecedents and consequents, which differ to some extent from it: or if it is proposed in the vernacular language, its sense is drawn from the original language. 3) When we assert that Scripture is to be explained by Scripture, then in the subject, by Scripture is understood a divine utterance less clear: in the predicate, an effatum of the Holy Spirit more clear. But there is required a natural rule of understanding, that the more obscure things be explained by the clearer.

II. Whatever Scripture interprets by itself, that is not to be interpreted by the doctors of the church: But according to the mind of the protestant doctors, sacred Scripture interprets itself, Therefore. Resp. 1) Whatever Scripture interprets by itself, that is not necessarily to be interpreted; I concede. For Holy Scripture delivers the dogmas of faith and the precepts of morals necessary for man to be saved so clearly and perspicuously that the interpretations of the doctors of the Church are not simply necessary. Yet those are useful for an easier and richer understanding of Scripture, and also for showing the application of the literal sense to practice and salutary use, and thus for the edification of the faithful. 2) Scripture interprets itself not always in act, but in potency, by supplying certain means of interpreting, which the doctors of the Church employ, so that what seem more difficult to understand may receive some light from easier and plainer things.

Latin:

VI. Constanter retinenda vocum phrasiumque biblicarum propria et natiua significatio, nisi summa interpretem premat necessitas descendendi ad sensum verborum figuratum.

Obseruandus heic est canon theologicus: in propria et vsitata significatione verborum persistendum est, quamdiu neque analogia fidei, neque loca scripturae parallela clariora, neque antecedentia et consequentia in contexto, scopusue dicentis, aut aliae circumstantiae propriae vocum significationi apertissime repugnant. Fundatur haec regula in naturali ratione intelligendi, qua iubemur ad eum attendere sensum, quem secundum communem verborum vsum et significationem omnes concipiunt; alioqui enim nulla dabitur intelligentiae nostrae certitudo.

Rectissime inquit B. LVTHER, in libr. de captiu. Babyl. p. 277. Verbis diuinis non est vlla vis facienda, neque per hominem, neque per angelum;

sed quantum fieri potest, in simplicissima significatione servanda sunt: et nisi manifesta circumstantia cogat, extra grammaticam accipienda non sunt, ne detur adversariis occasio eludendi totam scripturam.

Media hermeneutica consequentia sunt interpretandi subsidia, quibus hermeneuta facer post actum interpretationis utitur ad sensum scripturae litteralem confirmandum, vel ad salutarem scripturae notitiam acquirendam. Sunt haec duo: I. Commentarii veterum et recentium ecclesiae doctorum, quorum labore exegetico utimur, ut adminiculo interpretandi externo, non nitimur ut principio divino. Praeclare ait noster B. Gerhard. in exeg. L. de scriptura S. fol. m. 204. non frustra prioris antiquitatis testimonia nobis conferuasse existimandus est Deus, sed ut essent quoddam adminiculum ad scripturae sententiam investigandam, et ut perspecta vera sententia ex sacris litteris piorum animi magis confirmentur. Quocirca utitur interpres scripturae commentariis doctorum ecclesiae 1) ante actum interpretationis, quatenus ad verum dicti biblici sensum eliciendum ipsum manuducunt. 2) post ἐξεργασίαν interpretationis, ad confirmandam sententiam huius vel illius oraculi prophetici, aut apostolici, iam ante ex ipso scripturae fonte haustam.

II. Seria sensus litteralis ad usum salutarem, eumque multiplicem, applicatio. Publicus scripturae interpres, ductu Pauli, 2 Tim. III, 16. sensum litterale eloquiorum divinorum transfert a) ad διδασκαλίαν, ad veram doctrinam consolidandam, b) ad ἔλεγχον, ad falsa haereticorum dogmata confutanda, c) ad ἐπανόρθωσιν, ad pravitatem morum corrigendam, d) ad παιδείαν, ad studium pietatis promovendum, e) ad παράκλησιν, ad praesentissima quaeque solatia, anxiis mentibus instillanda. Privatus scripturae interpres sensum litteralem oraculorum coelestium assidua lectione investigatum et inuentum applicat ad propriam proximique aedificationem, atque adeo ad exercitia poenitentiae, fidei et pietatis, vt legendis sacris litteris peccata sua penitius agnoscere, acerbius lugere, grauius detestari, fidem in Christum conceptam diligentius conferuare, augere, stabilire, Deum impensius amare, timere, venerari, seipsum abnegare, sobriam castamque seruare mentem, proximum validius diligere discat et consuescat. Quae applicatio parit salutarem scripturae sacrae notitiam.

Antithesis est 1) Pontificiorum statuentium, veram scripturae intelligentiam petendam esse e consensu patrum, et conciliis, inprimis a Pontifice Romano, cuius in scripturis explicandis summa et infallibilis fit auctoritas. 2) Socinianorum, qui rationem, sive principia et axiomata philosophica innata et exculta putant vel maxime facere ad interpretationem scripturae. 3) Quakerorum et Enthusiastarum, qui ad ἑρμηνείαν dicti biblici obscurioris novam et immediatam desiderant Spiritus S. revelationem: quorum argumenta ponderabimus.

I. Si scriptura per scripturam explicaretur, idem explicaretur per idem, quod videtur esse absurdum. Resp. 1) Idem per idem, diverso consideratum modo, aut respectu, explicare, non est absurdum. Sane diploma principis per idem diploma, testamentum patris per idem testamentum exponitur: sicut lumen solis ipsum notificat, et conspiciendum praebet. 2) Diversus considerandi modus consistit in hoc, quod dictum biblicum explanatur secundum antecedentia et consequentia, quae ab ipso quadantenus differunt: vel si proponatur in lingua vernacula, sensus eius eruitur e lingua originali. 3) Quando asserimus, scripturam per scripturam esse explicandam, tunc in subiecto, per scripturam intelligitur eloquium divinum minus clarum: in praedicato, effatum Spiritus S. clarius. Requiritur autem naturalis intelligendi ratio, ut obscuriora explicentur per clariora.

II. Quaecunque scriptura seipsam interpretatur, illa a doctoribus ecclesiae non est interpretanda: Atqui ex mente doctorum protestantium scriptura sacra seipsam interpretatur, Ergo. Resp. 1) Quaecunque scriptura seipsam interpretatur, illa a doctoribus ecclesiae non neccessario est interpretanda; concedo. Nam sacra scriptura dogmata fidei morumque praecepta homini saluando cognitu necessaria adeo clare & perspicue tradit, vt interpretamenta doctorum ecclesiae non simpliciter sint necessaria. Sunt autem illa utilia ad intelligentiam scripturae faciliorem & uberiorem, nec non ad ostendendam applicationem sensus litteralis ad praxin & usum salutarem, atque adeo ad aedificationem fidelium. 2) Scriptura seipsam interpretatur non semper actu, sed potentia, suppeditando certa interpretandi media, quae doctores ecclesiae adhibent, vt, quae videntur intellectu difficiliora, ex facilioribus & planioribus lucem aliquam accedat.


### Question XLVIII. Is scripture to be explained by scripture?: III. The hermeneutical means, brought forward above, are human and probable. Therefore, through them the sense of Scripture is not elicited…

III. The hermeneutical means, brought forward above, are human and probable. Therefore, through them the sense of Scripture is not elicited certainly and infallibly.

Resp. The formal hermeneutical means are not human, nor probable, but most certain. For the clearer sayings, from which less clear ones are elucidated, are divine sayings: the antecedents and consequents are the pronouncements of the Holy Spirit: the Hebrew and Greek words are δοχεῖα, receptacles, and as it were the chambers of the divine sense: the analogy of faith has the Holy Spirit as its author. Therefore, the hermeneutical means are aids for interpreting that are not human, but divine, not extrinsic to Scripture, but intrinsic, although their use comes to them externally from men.

IV. Whatever Scripture has proceeded from the Holy Spirit, that must be interpreted by the Holy Spirit, and not by the doctors of the Church.

But Holy Scripture, etc. Therefore. Resp. By distinguishing between the principal interpreter of Holy Scripture and the ministerial one. The former is the Holy Spirit, the latter is the doctor of the Church, following the leading of the Holy Spirit speaking in Scripture and through Scripture. His ministry in declaring the Scriptures does not exclude the Holy Spirit, but rather requires from him the τὸ ἐρευνᾶν, to search the Scriptures, John 5:39, the τὸ προσέχειν, to pay attention to the prophetic word, 2 Pet. 1:19, the τὸ διδάσκειν, to teach the sacred letters, 1 Tim. 3:2.

V. Whatever common means of interpreting are held by heretics teaching false things, through them the true sense of Scripture cannot be elicited.

But the means of interpreting brought forward above are common to heretics. Therefore. Resp. 1) The Papists conclude against themselves. For the interpreters of Scripture, addicted to the Papal religion, use the aforementioned means. Therefore, neither can they elicit the true sense of Scripture. 2) We deny the major. For it is certain that Holy Scripture itself is common to the orthodox and the heterodox, to true Christians and hypocrites: which nevertheless remains a true medium for illuminating, converting, regenerating, and renewing men corrupted by sin. 3) It is no wonder that hermeneutical means are common to heretics. For from them, as from common and mutually conceded means of interpreting, they can be convicted of their errors, and at length, with the Holy Spirit concurring, be converted. 4) Distinguish between the abuse and the legitimate use of hermeneutical means. Heretics abuse hermeneutical means to cloak preconceived opinions which they force upon the Scriptures.

VI. The hermeneutical means, reviewed above, cannot be employed everywhere.

Therefore, through the same means the sense of Scripture cannot always and everywhere be investigated and found. For the collation of antecedents and consequents finds no place where the discourse is not continuous, as in the Proverbs of Solomon, or where the order is inverted by ὕστερολογίαν. The collation of parallel passages brings no utility for expounding monadical words, which are read only once in Scripture. Nor is the scrutiny of words, phrases, and style a catholic medium for interpreting the Scriptures; since the biblical style is diverse. For those born in the court speak one way, like Isaiah: another way, those who came forth from the sheepfold, like Amos.

Resp. 1) The hermeneutical means are to be employed not distributively, but conjunctively. If one cannot be applied, let us use another. 2) When the discourse is not continuous; let the sources be inspected, every word be scrutinized, and the whole phrase be considered, let parallel passages be compared, let the analogy of faith be observed, nor without a most urgent cause one should depart from the literal and proper sense: and the way will be opened to finding the sense of discourse that is not continuous.

The signification of monadic words is to be sought from the derivation of the word, and that of others from paraphrase and lexicons. Ὑσερολογίαι (Hysterologies) are reduced to order, provided the circumstances are accurately weighed.

Finally, the biblical style is uniform as to substance, but diverse as to accidental conformation.

Latin:

III. Media hermeneutica, supra adducta, sunt humana & probabilia. - Ergo per ea sensus scripturae non certo & infallibiliter elicitur.

Resp. Media hermeneutica formalia non sunt humana, neque probabilia, sed certissima. Nam dicta clariora, ex quibus minus clara dilucidantur, sunt dicta diuina: Antecedentia & consequentia sunt pronunciata Spiritus sancti: Voces hebraeae & graecae sunt δοχεῖα, receptacula, & quasi cubilia sensus diuini: Analogia fidei auctorem habet Spiritum S. Ergo media hermeneutica sunt subsidia interpretandi non humana, sed diuina, scripturae non extrinseca, sed intrinseca, quamuis eorum usus forinsecus ab hominibus accedat.

IV. Quaecunque scriptura profecta est a Spiritu sancto, illa interpretanda est a Spiritu sancto, & non a doctoribus ecclesiae.

Atqui scriptura S. &c. Ergo. Resp. Distinguendo inter interpretem S. scripturae principalem, & ministerialem. Ille est Spiritus sanctus, hic est doctor ecclesiae, ductum Spiritus S. in scriptura & per scripturam loquentis, sequens. Huius ministerium in declarandis scripturis Spiritum S. adeo non excludit, vt potius ab eo τὸ ἐρευνᾶν, scrutari scripturas, Io. V, 39. τὸ προσέχειν, attendere verbo prophetico, 2 Petr. I, 19. τὸ διδάσκειν, docere sacras litteras, 1 Tim. III, 2. requirat.

V. Quaecunque media interpretandi communia sunt haereticis falsa docentibus, per illa verus scripturae sensus erui nequit.

Atqui media interpretandi supra adducta communia sunt haereticis. Ergo. Resp. 1) Concludunt Pontificii aduersus seipsos. Nam interpretes scripturae, Pontificiae religioni addicti, supra memoratis mediis utuntur. Ergo neque illi verum scripturae sensum eruere queunt. 2) Negamus maiorem. Constat enim, ipsam Scripturam S. communem esse orthodoxis & heterodoxis, veris Christianis & hypocritis: quae nihilo tamen minus manet verum medium homines peccato corruptos illuminandi, conuertendi, regenerandi & renouandi. 3) Nihil mirum est, media hermeneutica haereticis esse communia. Nam ex illis, velut communibus & vtrinque concessis interpretandi mediis, errorum suorum conuinci, & tandem concurrente Spiritu S. conuerti possunt. 4) Dist. inter abusum, & legitimum usum mediorum hermeneuticorum. Haeretici abutuntur mediis hermeneuticis ad palliandum praeconceptas opiniones, quas scripturae inferunt.

VI. Media hermeneutica, supra recensita, non vbique possunt adhiberi.

Ergo per eadem sensus scripturae non semper & vbique inuestigari & inueniri potest. Nam collatio antecedentium & consequentium locum non inuenit, vbi datur oratio non continua, vt in prouerbiis Salomonis, vel vbi per ὕστερολογίαν ordo inuerfus est. Collatio locorum parallelorum nil utilitatis confert ad exponenda vocabula monadica, quae semel in scriptura tantum leguntur. Neque scrutinium vocum, phrasium & stili medium interpretandi scripturas catholicum est; cum stilus biblicus diuersus sit. Aliter quippe loquuntur in aula nati, vt Iesaias: aliter, qui prodierunt e caula, vt Amosus.

Resp. 1) Media hermeneutica non diuisim, sed coniunctim adhibenda sunt. Si vnum applicari nequit, vtamur alio. 2) Quando oratio non continua est; inspiciantur fontes, peruestigetur vox quaelibet, & tota phrasis consideretur, conferantur loca parallela, obseruetur analogia fidei, neque fine vrgentissima causa recedatur a sensu litterali ac proprio: & patebit via ad inveniendum orationis non continuae sensum.

Significatio vocabulorum monadicorum ex derivatione vocis, aliorum paraphrasi & lexicis petenda est. Ὑσερολογίαι rediguntur in ordinem, modo circumstantiae accurate expendantur.

Stilus denique biblicus uniformis est, qua substantiam, diversus, qua accidentalem conformationem.


### Question XLVIII. Is scripture to be explained by scripture?: See above, qu XVII. in the antithesis

See above, qu.

XVII. in the antithesis.

VII. The safest means of interpreting the scriptures is the consensus of the Fathers, who relied upon the same means of interpretation.

Resp. We venerate with a grateful mind, and receive with a grateful hand, the consensus of the Fathers interpreting the sacred code, such as it is and as great as it is given in the church today, as an external, guiding, attesting, and confirming means of interpreting the scriptures; but we do not receive it as a divine, fundamental, and infallible principle from which, as from a most limpid fountain, the true sense of the heavenly oracles is to be drawn.

For we see that most of them dissent as much as possible in explaining the divine utterances, not rarely depart from themselves, introduce a sense that is ἀσύμφωνον, or incongruous, into the scriptures, and use a style of speaking so obscure and perplexed that their writings stand in need of new light and a new interpreter.

What is more? That very few of the most ancient knew Hebrew, and of the Latins, Greek, and thus were necessarily destitute of a certain hermeneutical medium.

VIII. The Protestant churches consult poorly by permitting the interpretation of Holy Scripture to plebeian men and idiots of both sexes, whose interpretation is ἰδία ἐπίλυσις, a proper or private exposition, disapproved by the apostle Peter, 2 Epist. ch.

I, 20.

Resp.

By distinguishing between private interpretation and the interpretation of a private man.

When a private man piously meditates on Holy Scripture for his own immediate edification, and investigates and unfolds its internal sense by comparing antecedents and consequents, and observing the scope of the speaker, that interpretation is not private or proper, since it is sought from a divine principle that is obvious and exposed to all.

Conversely, when a hundred bishops and a hundred councils, from principles of reason, human authority, and preconceived opinions, introduce a sense of scripture that is deformed from the intention of the Holy Spirit, then it is ἰδία ἐπίλυσις, a proper and private exposition, since it is fabricated according to human whim and ingenuity.

Furthermore, we do not permit plebeian men to interpret the scriptures in a solemn assembly of the faithful.

It suffices for plebeian men, who attentively and devoutly turn the pages of the sacred code, that scripture by itself unfolds and exhibits the sense of the Holy Spirit, so that it is permitted to them to apprehend the same and apply it to salvation.

Objection: The interpretation of scripture is numbered among the singular gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are not granted to all plebeians, 1 Cor. XII, 10 and XIV, 25. Resp.

In 1 Cor.

XII, 10, the apostle commemorates extraordinary gifts, bestowed in a peculiar manner and measure upon the teachers of the primitive church at the beginning of the nascent Christian church, of whom some were distinguished by these gifts, others by those.

For the apostle writes: "to another, kinds of tongues; to another, the interpretation of tongues (are given)" .

On which words D.

CALOV. in *Bibl.

Illustrat.* fol. 380, comments thus:

There were those who spoke in tongues, yet could not conveniently interpret what they were saying. And conversely, there were those who had the gift of interpreting what others uttered in a foreign tongue, and were not so much instructed to teach as to interpret those things which were taught by others.

To which gift of interpretation, in later centuries, the office of those who are called professors of languages succeeded.

In 1 Cor.

XIV, 26, Paul deals with public interpretation, which takes place in a solemn assembly of the faithful.

The words of the apostle are, v. 27, 28:

"But let one interpret: but if there be no interpreter, let him keep silence in the church, and let him speak to himself and to God."

We do not posit that extraordinary gifts of interpreting the scriptures were given by the Holy Spirit to plebeian men, nor do we permit public interpretation to them in the church, but we assert from the truth that to all men, even of the lowest condition, who read the sacred letters attentively, who are acquainted with the idiom in which they read them, and who diligently consider the context, divinely given to be, to attain the genuine sense of the said biblical proposition, and, occasion offering, to expound it to others in private houses for salutary edification.

Latin:

Vid supra qu.

XVII. in antith.

VII. Tutissimum scripturas interpretandi medium est consensus Patrum, qui iisdem interpretandi mediis innixi sunt.

Resp. Consensum Patrum, sacrum codicem interpretantium, qualis & quantus ille hodie in ecclesia datur, grata mente veneramur, grata manu recipimus, vt medium interpretandi scripturas externum, manuducens, attestans, confirmans; at non recipimus vt principium divinum, fundamentale & infallibile, ex quo velut fonte limpidissimo verus oraculorum caelestium sensus hauriendus sit.

Videmus enim plerosque in exponendis eloquiis divinis quam maxime dissentire, haud raro a seipsis abire, sensum ἀσύμφωνον, sive incongruum, scripturis inferre, dicendique genere adeo obscuro & perplexo vti, vt scripta eorum nova luce, novo interprete indigeant.

Quid? quod paucissimi ex antiquissimis hebraice, ex latinis graece sciuerint, adeoque necessario quodam medio hermeneutico destituti fuerint.

VIII. Male consulunt ecclesiae protestantes, permittendo interpretationem sacrae scripturae hominibus plebeiis & idiotis vtriusque sexus, quorum interpretatio est ἰδία ἐπίλυσις, propria sive privata expositio, improbata ab apostolo Petro 2 Epist. c.

I, 20.

Resp.

Distinguendo inter interpretationem privatam, & inter interpretationem hominis priuati.

Quando homo priuatus ad suam proxime aedificationem sacram scripturam pie meditatur, eiusque internum sensum, collatis antecedentibus & consequentibus, obseruatoque scopo dicentis inuestigat & enucleat, illa interpretatio non privata aut propria est, cum e principio diuino omnibus obuio expositoque petita sint.

Contra cum centum episcopi, & centum concilia, ex principiis rationis, auctoritate humana, & praeconceptis opinionibus, scripturae sensum difformem intentioni Spiritus S. inferunt, tunc ἰδία ἐπίλυσις, propria & privata expositio est, cum pro lubitu humano ingenio conficta fit.

Ceterum non permittimus hominibus plebeiis, in solenni fidelium coetu scripturas interpretari.

Sufficit hominibus plebeiis, attente & devote sacrum codicem voluentibus, quod scriptura per seipsam sensum Spiritus sancti pandat & exhibeat, vt eundem apprehendere & ad salutem applicare ipsis liceat.

Inflantia: Interpretatio scripturae numeratur inter dona Spiritus S. singularia, quae non omnibus plebeiis concessa sunt, 1 Cor.

XII, 10. & XIV, 25. Resp. 1 Cor.

XII, 10. commemorat apostolus dona extraordinaria, sub exordium nascentis ecclesiae christianae peculiari modo & mensura in doctores ecclesiae primitivae collata, quorum alii his, alii aliis donis claruere.

Scribit enim apostolus; alii vero genera linguarum, alii vero interpretatio linguarum (data sunt) .

In quae verba D.

CALOV. in bibl. illustrat. fol.

380. ita commentatur: Fuere, qui linguis loquebantur, nec tamen ea, quae dicerent, interpretari commode poterant.

Et vicissim fuerunt, qui donum habebant interpretandi ea, quae alii lingua peregrina proferebant, nec tam ad docendum instructi erant, quam ad interpretandum ea, quae ab aliis docebantur.

Cui interpretationis dono posterioribus seculis officium eorum, qui professores linguarum vocantur, successit.

1 Cor.

XIV, 26, Paullus de publica interpretatione, quae fit in solemni fidelium caetu, agit.

Verba apostoli sunt, v. 27. 28.

Vnus autem interpretetur: si vero non fit interpres, taceto in ecclesia, sibi ipsi vero loquatur & Deo.

Non statuimus, extraordinaria interpretandi scripturas dona a Spiritu S. data esse hominibus plebeiis, neque publicam interpretationem in ecclesia ipsis permittimus, sed ex vero afferimus, omnibus hominibus vel infimae conditionis sacras litteras attente legentibus, gnaris idiomatis, in quo eas legunt, contextum sedulo considerantibus, diuinitus. datum esse, propositi dicti biblici sensum genuinum assequi, & occasione ferente, aliis in privatis ædibus ad salutarem ædificationem exponere.


### Question XLIX. Is it permissible and advisable to translate the ancient Hebrew language and the Greek of the New Testament into vernacular…

The most holy word of God from the Hebrew source of the Old [Testament], and the Greek of the New Testament, is not only lawful to be transferred into vernacular languages and those known to the common people for the salutary knowledge of the laity, but it is also greatly expedient .

Obs. 1.

A vernacular language is called that which is familiar, maternal, and commonly known to any nation. nota. Obs. 2. The question is not only about the right of translating the original languages of the Old and New Testaments into vernaculars, but also about the utility and hypothetical necessity of versions.

Prob. a. I. Whatever is preached in languages familiar to all nations, nothing prohibits that from being written in vernacular languages and those known to the common people. But the great works of God are preached in languages familiar to all nations. Therefore. The major premise is certain, because the word preached and the word written do not differ in reality. If, therefore, nothing detracted from the majesty of the divine word by its preaching done in various languages known to the common people: what will a writing that is polyglot (πολύγλωττος), or adorned in various vernacular languages, detract? The minor is evident from Acts 2:11, where the evangelist Luke commemorates that the apostles on the day of Pentecost spoke the great works of God in various languages. In which most narrow feast of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit dedicated the languages of all nations and consecrated them for the propagation of the glory of God and the salvation of men, so that they might be as liquid channels through which streams of divine grace, flowing from sacred fountains, might run down into the minds of men for the obtaining of eternal salvation. BELLARMINE impugns the major proposition, in book II of De Verbo Dei , ch. 16, fol. 123, holding that it is wrongly concluded from the preaching of the divine word to its writing. The Cardinal's words are: If the consequence from preaching to writing is good, why did the apostles write only in Greek, when they preached in so many languages? Therefore, the word of God is rightly preached in the vulgar tongue, because preaching contains an explanation which all easily grasp: but when it is written, it is written nakedly, and is not grasped by all. Resp. (1) BELLARMINE changes the state of the controversy. For we are speaking of versions, he of the original canon, which, since it was Greek, could be transferred by the churches to which the apostolic speech arrived into the languages vernacular to each church. The reason, however, why the apostles wrote everything in Greek is this, because at that time the Greek language was the most common of all, as M. TULLIUS testifies in his oration pro Archia Poëta , saying: Greek is read among all nations: Latin is contained within its own truly narrow boundaries. (2) Holy Scripture explains itself either in act or in potency, by providing certain means of interpretation.

II. The perpetual practice of the church confirms the same. For Moses and the prophets wrote their books in the language vernacular to the Israelites, Deut. 31: 11. When after the return from the Babylonian captivity the pure Hebrew language was no longer vernacular to the Israelites, but mixed with the Chaldean idiom, the Chaldean paraphrase brought help. Whence a triple Targum came forth: Babylonian, Onkelos, and Jerusalem. When under the empire of the Greeks the Greek language became known to almost all nations, under the auspices of Ptolemy, King of Egypt, by LXXII elders sent from Judea, the books of the Old Testament were translated into the Greek tongue [*]. The evangelists and apostles wrote the books of the New Testament in the Greek tongue, which was [known] to almost all nations at that time common to the age. Since, on account of the vastness of the Roman Empire, the Latin language began to be familiar to many nations, various Latin versions followed. Since the Gospel was being propagated to all nations, and every language began to praise the Lord, very many vernacular translations accompanied the evangelical light. This is testified to by THEODORE, book V, De curandis graecis affectionibus, vol. II. The Hebrew books were not only converted into the Greek idiom, but also into the Roman language, Egyptian, Persian, Indian, Armenian, Scythian, and even Sarmatian, and, to say it once, into all the languages which nations use to this day. AUGUSTINE agrees, book II, De doctrina christiana, ch. V. Divine Scripture, having proceeded from one language, diffused far and wide through the various languages of interpreters, became known to the nations for their salvation.

Prob, b. from I Cor. XIV, 6, 7, 8, 9, 14. Now indeed, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what will I profit you, unless I speak to you either by revelation, or by prophecy, or by doctrine? Certainly (as regards) inanimate things giving sound, whether it be a pipe (or) a harp: unless a distinction is given to the sounds, how will it be known what is played by the pipe, what by the harp? For even if a trumpet gives an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself for battle? So also you, unless you utter a speech by a significant tongue, how will it be known what is said? For you will be speaking into the air. - - - For if I pray in a tongue, my Spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful. The Apostle shows, I. that all divine offices (to which pertain preaching, reading & meditation of the divine word, pious prayers, spiritual canticles, the administration of the sacraments) performed in a foreign language, which the assembly of faithful souls does not understand, lack saving fruit.

For just as musical instruments, whether they be harps or trumpets, which do not emit a distinct sound, are of no use: so all preaching & reading of the divine word, which is done in an exotic language, all public prayers, which are recited in the church in a language unknown to the common people, are void of saving fruit. Whence we argue: In whatever language the people are skilled, in that they perform divine offices with saving fruit.

But it is skilled not in the Hebrew, Greek, or Latin language, but in the vernacular. Therefore, the people do not perform divine offices (to which pertains the reading of Sacred Scripture) in the Hebrew, Greek, or Latin language, but in the vernacular language with saving fruit.

Latin:

Sanctissimum Dei verbum e fonte hebræo veteris, & græco noui testamenti, in linguas vernaculas & vulgo notas ad salutarem laicorum notitiam transferre non licet tantum , sed magnopere etiam expedit .

Obs.

1. Lingua vernacula dicitur, quæ cuius nationi est familiaris, materna, & vulgo nota. Obs. 2. Non tantum quæritur de iure vertendi linguas originales veteris & noui testamenti in vernaculas, sed etiam de versionum utilitate, & necessitate hypothetica.

Prob. a. I. Quæcunque prædicantur linguis omnibus nationibus familiaribus, illa linguis vernaculis & vulgo notis scribi nihil prohibet. Atqui magnalia Dei prædicantur linguis omnibus nationibus familiaribus. Ergo. Maior constat, quia verbum prædicatum, & scriptum, non differunt realiter. Quod si igitur maiestati verbi diuini nihil detraxit eiusdem prædicatio variis linguis vulgo notis facta: quid detrahet scriptio πολύγλωττος, seu variis adornata linguis vernaculis? Minor patet ex Act. II, 11. vbi euangelista Lucas commemorat, apostolos in die pentecostes locutos esse variis linguis magnalia Dei. In quo angustissimo pentecostes festo Spiritus S. omnium gentium linguas dedicauit, & propagandæ gloriæ Dei salutique hominum consecravit, vt essent liquidi quasi canales, per quos ex sacris fontibus fluentes riui gratiæ diuinæ ad obtinendam æternam salutem in hominum animos decurrerent. Impugnat maiorem propositionem BELLARMIN. libr. II. de verbo Dei, cap. 16. fol. 123. ratum, a prædicatione verbi diuini ad eius scriptionem perperam concludi. Verba Cardinalis sunt: Si bona est consequentia a prædicatione ad scripturam, cur apostoli solum scripserunt græce, cum prædicauerint tam multis linguis? Ideo verbum Dei recte prædicatur lingua vulgari, quia prædicatio explanationem continet, quam omnes facile capiunt: At cum scribitur, nudum scribitur, nec ab omnibus capitur. Relp. (1) Mutat BELLARM. statum controuersiæ. Nam nos loquimur de versionibus, ille de canone primigenio, qui cum græcus fuerit, poterat ab ecclesiis, ad quas sermo apostolicus peruenit, in linguas cuilibet ecclesiæ vernaculas transfundi. Ratio autem, cur apostoli omnia græce scripserunt, hæc est, quia tunc lingua græca erat omnium communissima, vt M. TVLLIVS testatur in orat. pro Archia Poëta, inquiens: Græcæ leguntur in omnibus gentibus: Latina suis finibus exiguis sane continentur. (2) S. scriptura seipsam explicat vel actu, vel potentia, certa interpretandi media suppeditando.

II. Confirmat idem perpetua ecclesiæ praxis. Nam Moses & prophetæ scripserunt libros suos lingua Israëlitus vernacula, Deut. XXXI, 11. Cum post reditum ex captiuitate Babylonia pura lingua hebræa non amplius esset Israëlitus vernacula, sed chaldaico idiomate permixta, chaldaica paraphrasis opem tulit. Vnde triplex Targum prodiit Babylonicum, Onkelosi, & Hierosolymitanum. Cum sub imperio græcorum lingua græca omnibus fere gentibus innotesceret, auspiciis Ptolemæi, regis Ægyptii a LXXII. senioribus ex Iudæa missis libri vet. testamenti in græcum sermonem fuerunt translati [*]. Euangelistæ & apostoli libros N. T. scripserunt lingua græca, quæ fuit omnibus fere gentibus eo tempore communis. (e) Cum propter Romani imperii amplitudinem lingua latina multis gentibus inciperet esse familiaris, secutae sunt variae versiones latinae. (f) Cum evangelium ad omnes gentes propagaretur, & omnis lingua inciperet laudare dominum, lucem evangelicam comitatae sunt translationes vernaculae quam plurimae. Id quod testatur THEODORVS libr. V. de curand. graec. affect. tom. II. Hebraici libri non modo in graecum idioma conuersi sunt, sed in romanam quoque linguam, aegyptiacam, persicam, indicam, armeniacam, scythicam, atque adeo fauromaticam, semelque ut dicam, in linguas omnes, quibus ad hanc diem nationes utuntur. Consentit AVGVSTINVS libr. II. de doctrin. christ. c. V. Scriptura diuina, ab una lingua profecta, per varias interpretum linguas longe lateque diffusa gentibus innotuit ad salutem.

Prob, b. ex I Cor. XIV, 6. 7. 8. 9. 14. Iam vero, fratres, si veniam ad vos linguis loquens, quid vobis profum, nisi vobis loquar vel per reuelationem, vel per prophetiam, vel per doctrinam? Vtique (quod ad) inanimata sonum edentia, siue fistula (fuerit) siue cithara: nisi discrimen sonis reddatur, quomodo cognoscetur, quid fistula canatur, quid cithara? Etiam si namque obscuram etiam vocem tuba dederit, quis parabit se ad bellum? Sic etiam vos, nisi per linguam significantem sermonem edideritis, quomodo cognoscetur, quod dicitur? Eritis enim in aerem loquentes. - - - Si namque orauero lingua, Spiritus meus orat, mens vero mea infrugifera est. Ostendit apostolus, I. omnia officia diuina (ad quae pertinent praedicatio, lectio & meditatio verbi diuini, piae preces, cantica spiritualia, dispensatio sacramentorum) peracta lingua peregrina, quam coetus animarum fidelium haud intelligit, salutari carere fructu.

Sicut enim instrumenta musica, citharae fuerint, an tubae, quae distinctum non edunt sonum, nulli sunt vsui: ita omnis praedicatio & lectio verbi diuini, quae fit lingua exotica, omnes preces publicae, quae in ecclesia recitantur lingua promiscuae plebi ignota, salutifero vacant fructu. Vnde argumentamur: Quamcunque linguam populus callet, in ea salutari cum fructu officia diuina peragit.

Atqui non linguam hebraeam, graecam, aut latinam, sed vernaculam callet. Ergo non in lingua hebraea, graeca, aut latina, sed in lingua vernacula officia diuina (ad quae pertinet lectio scripturae sacrae) populus salutari cum fructu peragit.


### Question XLIX. Is it permissible and advisable to translate the ancient Hebrew language and the Greek of the New Testament into vernacular…: II. Whoever are commanded to search the Scriptures, to them the Scripture must…

II. Whoever are commanded to search the Scriptures, to them the Scripture must be proposed in the vernacular language.

But all men, as travelers tending toward eternal life, are commanded by Christ to search the Scriptures, John V, 39. Therefore. The major premise is certain, because the searching of an unknown Scripture, whose meaning cannot be investigated or grasped, is vain & void.

III. Most worthy to be imprinted on the memory is the exhortation of Paul, Col.

III, 16, saying: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom: teaching & admonishing yourselves in psalms & hymns & spiritual canticles, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.

The Apostle excites the laity to the reading & meditation of the divine word related in letters, and admonishes them that they should grant it a fixed seat in the church, and in the innermost recesses of the mind, so that, like a most welcome guest received kindly into a house, it may be rendered domestic, familiar & most well-known to them. Nor without emphasis does the Apostle add: let it dwell πλŋσίως, richly in all wisdom: Just as if he were to say: not only a particle of Scripture, but the whole must be turned over, meditated upon, and fixed in the mind by repeated turns; to the end that it may be treated prudently, piously and rightly understood, and accommodated to living practice, so that you may mutually admonish and edify one another through psalms; the word of God becomes so familiar to you that from it you may compose hymns & spiritual canticles to be sung not only with the mouth, or a sonorous voice, but also with the most joyful affection of the heart, giving praises to the immortal God for the benefits conferred upon you. But how will the word of Christ dwell abundantly in the minds of the laity; how will it be treated by them prudently; or what material for mutual edification through psalms will it provide, unless it be read in the vernacular language most known to all?

The antithesis is that of the Papists, some of whom disapprove of all translation into vulgar languages; others concede it, but contend sharply that it is not the business of the church for the laity to read Scripture in the vernacular language, and to perform sacred rites in the same.

Their stronger arguments are: I. In the times of Ezra, Holy Scripture was not read to the Israelites in the vernacular language.

Therefore, it is not to be read in the vernacular today.

The antecedent is proven because the Israelites, after the lapse of 70 years during which they were in Babylon among the Chaldeans, had forgotten their own language, namely Hebrew, and had learned Chaldean, which was then familiar or vulgar to them, which is evident from Nehem.

VIII, 8: when the book of the law of the Lord was read to the people, Nehemiah, Ezra, and the Levites interpreted it; otherwise the people would not have understood it. Resp.

(1) The adversaries do not deny that for a long tract of time before Ezra, the Bible was read to the people in a language known to the vulgar, namely Hebrew.

Wherefore it is our duty to follow the custom of the flourishing Israelite church rather than the declining one.

(2) We are not led to believe that the Israelites, within the course of 70 years, had completely unlearned the Hebrew language, of which Chaldean is a dialect, since many fathers were still surviving.

If they had forgotten it, with what fruit could Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, the last prophets, have preached or written in Hebrew?

(3) It is customary for exegetes to interpret even the clearest biblical sayings by drawing them out more fully and applying them to use, so that the minds of readers or hearers may be imbued with their saving knowledge.

II. To this day, Jews in the synagogues read the Scriptures in Hebrew, even though at this time the Hebrew language is vulgar to no nation.

Resp.

The Jews make the Hebrew language familiar to themselves from childhood, and thus it is still in a way vernacular to them.

Therefore, the Jews read in Hebrew because they understand Hebrew and honor the original language: they would not read if they did not understand.

III. The Apostles wrote their epistles to peoples not in the language that was vernacular to them, but in the Greek language.

Paul wrote to the Romans not in the Roman or Latin idiom: Peter and James wrote to the Hebrews dispersed throughout the world not in the Hebrew, but in the Greek language.

Therefore, the Bible is not to be translated into the vernacular language today.

Resp.

(1) The Apostles wrote in Greek because at that time the Greek language was the most common.

Therefore, because in Germany the German language is the most common of all, Scripture is to be read in German.

(2) Paul wrote to the Romans not only those born in Rome or endowed with Roman citizenship, but all who dwelt in Rome, whether they were Greeks, or Italians, or Jews converted to Christ, who knew Greek.

IV. The unity of the church must be preserved: Therefore, by one language which all understand.

Resp.

Therefore, the unity of the German church must be preserved by the German language, which all Germans understand.

Latin:

II. Quicunque iubentur scrutari scripturas, illis scripturae lingua vernacula proponendae.

Atqui omnes homines viatores ad vitam aeternam tendentes iubentur a Christo scrutari scripturas, Io. V, 39. Ergo. Maior constat, quia vanum & irritum est scrutinium scripturae ignotae, cuius sensus inuestigari, aut capi nequit.

III. Dignissima est, quae memori imprimatur menti, adhortatio Paulli

Col. III, 16. inquitientis: Verbum Christi habitet in vobis opulenter in omni sapientia: docentes & admonentes vos ipsos & hymnis & canticis spiritualibus, cum gratia canentes in cordibus vestris domino.

Excitat apostolus laicos ad lectionem & meditationem verbi diuini in litteras relati, eosque admonet, vt fixam ipsi concedant sedem in ecclesia, intimisque animi penetralibus, quo, instar hospitis exoptatissimi in aedes comiter recepti, ipsis reddatur domesticum, familiare & notissimum. Neque sine emphasi addit apostolus: habitet πλŋσίως, opulenter in omni sapientia: Perinde, ac si dicat: non modo particula scripturae, sed tota etiam repetitis vicibus voluenda, meditanda, mentique infigenda est; quo fine tractetur prudenter, pie recteque intelligatur, & ad viuam praxin accommodetur, vt vos mutuo commonefaciatis & aedificetis per psalmos; adeo familiare vobis fit verbum Dei, vt ex eo componatis hymnos & cantica spiritualia recinendum non ore tantum, aut sonora voce, sed & laetissimo cordis affectu, Deo immortali pro collatis in vos beneficiis laudes. At quomodo habitabit verbum Christi in laicorum animis affluenter; quomodo tractabitur ab ipsis prudenter; aut quam materiam mutuae aedificationis per psalmos praebebit, nisi legatur in lingua vernacula omnibus notissima?

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, quorum quidam omnem translationem in linguas vulgares improbant; quidam eam concedunt, sed acriter contendunt, non esse e re ecclesiae, ut laici in lingua vernacula scripturam legant, & in eadem sacra peragant. Quorum potiora sunt argumenta:

I. Temporibus Esdrae lingua vernacula Israelitis S. scriptura non est praelecta.

Ergo nec hodie lingua vernacula praelegenda est. Antecedens probatur, quia Israelitae elapsis LXX. annis, quibus fuerunt Babyloniae inter Chaldaeos, obliti erant linguam propriam fine hebraeam, & chaldaicam didicerant, quae ipsis tunc familiaris aut vulgaris erat, quod patet ex Nehem.

VIII, 8. cum legeretur populo liber legis domini hebraice scriptus, Nehemias, Esdras & Levitae eum interpretabantur, alioqui populus eum non intellexisset. Resp.

(1) Adversarii non diffitentur, ante Esdram longo temporum tractu biblia lingua vulgo nota, nempe hebraea, populo fuisse praelecta.

Quare nostrum est, sequi potius consuetudinem ecclesiae Israeliticae florentis, quam inclinantis.

(2) Non inducimur, ut credamus, Israelitas intra decursum LXX. annorum linguam hebraeam, cuius dialectus est chaldaica, penitus dedidicisse, cum multi patres essent superstites.

Si eam obliti fuissent, quo fructu Haggaeus, Zacharias & Malachias, prophetarum ultimi, potuissent hebraice concionari aut scribere?

(3) Solemne est exegetis, dicta biblica vel clarissima interpretari fusius ea diducendo, & ad usum applicando, ut mentes lectorum, vel auditorum, salutifera eorum notitia imbuantur.

II. Vsque ad hanc diem in synagogis Iudaei scripturas hebraice legunt, cum tamen nulli nationi hoc tempore lingua hebraica sit vulgaris.

Resp.

Iudaei a pueris hebraicam linguam sibi reddunt familiarem, adeoque adhuc ipsis quodammodo vernacula est.

Legunt igitur Iudaei hebraice, quia hebraice intelligunt, & linguam originalem honorant: non lecturi, si non intelligerent.

III. Apostoli scripserunt epistolas suas populis non ea lingua, quae ipsis erat vernacula, sed lingua graeca.

Paullus scripsit ad Romanos non idiomate romano, sive latino: Petrus & Iacobus scripserunt Hebraeis per terrarum orbem dispersis non hebraica, sed graeca lingua.

Ergo nec hodie biblia in linguam vernaculam transferenda sunt.

Resp.

(1) Apostoli scripserunt graece, quia id temporis lingua graeca erat communissima.

Ergo, quia in Germania lingua germanica est omnium communissima, scriptura germanice est legenda.

(2) Scripsit Paullus ad Romanos non solos Romae natos, aut Romana ciuitate donatos, sed omnes Romae habitantes, sive fuerint Graeci, siue Itali, siue Iudaei ad Christum conuersi, qui graece sciebant.

IV. Seruanda est ecclesiae vnitas: Ergo per vnam linguam, quam omnes intelligunt.

Resp.

Seruanda igitur est ecclesiae germanicae vnitas per linguam germanicam, quam omnes Germani intelligunt.


### Question XLIX. Is it permissible and advisable to translate the ancient Hebrew language and the Greek of the New Testament into vernacular…: Instance I

Instance I.

The discussion is about the Catholic church, whose unity must be preserved by the Latin language, which all nations understand.

Resp.

Neither is the Roman church Catholic, because it is not spread throughout the whole world: Nor does the Latin language extend to all nations; and what portion of the West and North is skilled in it?

Instance II.

Yet all learned men understand the Latin language.

Resp.

It is the duty not only of learned men, but also of any common people whatsoever, to search the Scriptures, John V, 39, which they would search in vain in an exotic language.

Instance III.

But councils cannot be instituted except in a common language, because not all parts have the gift of tongues.

Resp.

(1) Councils are extraordinary and rare assemblies, to which ordinary, frequent, and almost daily assemblies of the faithful ought not to be accommodated.

(2) Let fathers be called to councils who have the gift of tongues: or let place be given to interpreters, whose use there was in the Council of Ephesus, in which the Latin letters of Celestine were translated into the Greek idiom. Ephesino vfus fuit, in quo litteræ Cœleftini latinæ in græcum idioma translatæ funt.

Conf. D.

DANNHAV.

Hodomor. pap. parte prior. pag. 209.

V. Which-

must not be translated. The vernacular language changes every century. Therefore. Resp. Neither does the whole language change every century, nor is the understanding of Scripture disturbed by a slight change. But if it were to happen that the vernacular language varied as the centuries passed, even the translation could be varied without danger to the doctrine of the faith: just as ancient monuments, inscribed in monastic letters, have been interpolated with a recent and customary form of writing without any danger to the faith.

VI. Let us be content with the three most excellent languages, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, which the cross of Christ honored.

Resp. Pilate ordered the title of the cross of Christ to be expressed in three languages, so that the peoples who were present in Jerusalem, Jews, Greeks, and Latins, might read it: he would have written it in German too, had Germans been present. However, the excellence of a language here is to be judged by nothing other than its use, as far as we are concerned: for all languages have been sanctified by the divine Spirit, Acts II, 11. A golden sword is more excellent than an iron one; yet the soldier prefers to use the latter in battle.

VII. There is no perfect version, immune from all errors. Therefore, one should not have recourse to versions.

Resp. (1) Therefore, neither should the Papists take refuge in the Vulgate version, which many admit has errors, but they should look to the sources themselves, namely the Hebrew and Greek text. (2) Divine providence has most wisely watched over the versions of Holy Scripture, so that they would not be corrupted in such a way that you could not draw from them what is sufficient for saving information.

Latin:

Instantia I.

Sermo est de ecclesia catholica, cuius vnitas conferuanda est per linguam latinam, quam omnes gentes intelligunt.

Resp.

Neque ecclesia Romana catholica est, quia non per totum terrarum orbem diffusa: Neque latinam linguam omnes gentes exulat; & quota pars occidentis, atque septentrionis eam callet?

Instantia II.

Omnes tamen viri eruditi linguam latinam intelligunt.

Resp.

Non virorum tantum eruditorum, sed etiam quorumuis hominum plebeiorum est, scrutari scripturas, Io.

V, 39. quas scrutarentur frustra in lingua exotica.

Instantia III.

Sed concilia non possunt institui, nisi lingua communi, quia non omnes partes habent donum linguarum.

Resp.

(1) Concilia sunt conuentus extraordinarii, & rari, quibus non debent conuentus fidelium ordinarii, frequentes & pene quotidiani accomodari.

(2) Vocentur ad concilia patres, qui habent donum linguarum: vel detur locus interpretibus, quorum in concilio Ephesino vsus fuit, in quo litterae Caelestini latinae in graecum idioma translatae sunt. Ephesino vfus fuit, in quo litteræ Cœleftini latinæ in græcum idioma translatæ sunt.

Conf.

D.

DANNHAV.

Hodomor. pap. parte prior. pag. 209.

V. Quæ-

non est transferenda. Lingua vernacula singulis seculis mutatur. Ergo. Resp. Neque singulis seculis mutatur tota lingua, neque leui mutatione intelligentia scripturae turbatur. Quod si autem contingeret, vt vertentibus pluribus seculis lingua vernacula variaret, etiam translatio citra periculum doctrinae fidei posset variari: sicut monimenta vetera, monasticis litteris exarata, recenti ac vsitata scribendi forma interpolata sunt citra vllum fidei periculum.

VI. Simus contenti tribus linguis praestantissimis, hebraea, graeca, latina, quas crux Christi honorauit.

Resp. Pilatus titulum crucis Christi tribus linguis exprimi iussit, vt populi, qui aderant Hierosolymis, Iudaei, Graeci & Latini eum legerent: scripturus, si adfuisent germani, etiam germanice. Praestantia autem linguae hic non aliunde, quam ex vsu, quoad nos, aestimanda est: sunt enim omnes linguae a spiritu diuino sanctificatae, Actor. II, 11. Praestantior est gladius aureus ferreo; hoc tamen vti mauult miles in acie.

VII. Non datur versio perfecta, ab omnibus erroribus immunis. Ergo non recurrendum est ad versiones.

Resp. (1) Ergo nec Pontificii confugiant ad versionem vulgatam, plurimis fatentem mendis, sed inspiciant ipsos fontes, nempe textum hebraeum & graecum. (2) Sapientissime aduigilauit prouidentia diuina versionibus sacrae scripturae, ne sic corrumperentur, vt non inde haurias, quod satis est ad salutiferam informationem.


### Question XLIX. Is it permissible and advisable to translate the ancient Hebrew language and the Greek of the New Testament into vernacular…: Quest. L. Is Holy Scripture so perfect that it fully and sufficiently contains…

Quest. L. Is Holy Scripture so perfect that it fully and sufficiently contains all dogmas of faith and precepts of morals?

Holy Scripture is perfect with a final perfection, so that there are no dogmas of faith and precepts of morals, necessary to be believed and done by man as a traveler tending toward eternal salvation, which are not contained in it either ῥητῶς, explicitly, as to the letter, or διανοητικῶς, implicitly, as to the matter and meaning.

Obs. I. Holy Scripture is perfect (a) by reason of its matter; since no book θεόπνευστος (divinely inspired), included in the perpetual canon of faith, has perished. (β) By reason of its form, in that no error has crept into the authentic text through the negligence or perfidy of scribes. (γ) By reason of its end; since it sufficiently delivers all dogmas of faith and precepts of morals to man who is to attain eternal salvation. From which this final perfection is called by some theologians the sufficiency of Holy Scripture. See D. CALOV. in system. theol. vol. I. p. 609. AUGUSTINE speaks skillfully about this sufficiency of Scripture in tract. XLIX. on John c. 11. Those things were chosen to be written which seemed sufficient for the salvation of believers (*).

Obs. II. When we assert that holy scripture is sufficient for salvation, (1) we remove every other principle required for obtaining eternal salvation, whether it be called tradition, or the consensus of ecclesiastical antiquity, or the decree of the Roman Pontiff; (2) we imply that holy scripture is sufficient both for proving the dogmas of faith and for refuting the false dogmas of heretics.

Obs. III. Certain fundamental articles of faith are contained in the holy scriptures ῥητῶς αὐτολεξεὶ, explicitly, according to the letter, in express words and defining terms: but certain other articles of faith are held in holy scripture διανοητικῶς, κατὰ τὸ πρᾶγμα, according to the matter and meaning, so that they can be deduced from holy scripture by a ready, proximate, manifest, and necessary consequence. Thus the whole apostolic creed, as to its matter, is contained in the scriptures, although not in the same words or in the same series of articles (*).

That holy scripture is perfect with a final perfection, is proved I. from the classic passage Deut. IV, 2. You shall not add to this word, which I (am) commanding you: nor shall you diminish from it, that you may observe the commandments of Jehovah your God, which I (am) commanding you. God forbids through Moses the addition of new dogmas, different from the Mosaic pentateuch: the same forbids the diminution of Mosaic doctrine, by which anyone might dare to take anything away from it, as if it were not (α) proceeded from God through Moses, (β) as if it were not canonical, pertaining to the norm of the church. Let us be permitted to compare with this Mosaic oracle the parallel utterance of the apostle John, Apoc. XXII, 18. 19. For I testify to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book, if anyone shall add to these things, God will add (*) God [will add] upon him the plagues written in this book. And if any man shall take away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God shall take away his part out of the book of life, and out of the holy city, and from the things which are written in this book.

We refer the words of John by right and merit to the entire Holy Scripture; because the apostle by this memorable saying fortified the entire sacred codex as if with a seal, testifying most clearly that the entire Holy Scripture is so consummate and perfect that nothing is to be added to it, or taken away from it.

We argue: That to which nothing is to be added, or taken away, is perfect. But to Holy Scripture [nothing is to be added, etc.]. Therefore. The major premise is clear, because that is perfect to which nothing is lacking, and to which nothing ought to be added.

The Papists object: that Moses speaks of the word of God handed down by living voice; of the Pentateuch of Moses, which admitted the addition of many books; of the addition of dogmas contrary to and repugnant to Mosaic doctrine; that the Apostle John prohibits the corruption of the book of the Apocalypse, but does not prohibit that other books be written, or other dogmas be handed down.

Resp. to I. To every word which Moses commands, he wills that nothing be added, nothing taken away from it. But the written word of Moses is every word which he commanded. Therefore.

To II. In the Pentateuch of Moses the sum of the doctrine of faith and morals is contained; to which the prophets and apostles did not add new and diverse dogmas, but explained the same dogmas in more words, and showed their completion.

To III. An addition is not of contraries, since by them the former is abolished and destroyed, but of diverse things, to which place is granted to the former, but something is superadded to it as if it were imperfect.

To IV. The words of John are to be understood as much of the entire canonical scripture as of the Apocalypse; since all canonical books, dictated by the same spirit, possess the same authority, and all are directed to the same end, eternal salvation, which end is not given to be attained except by divine manifestation: for obtaining this, Holy Scripture alone suffices, and therefore it needs no addition, nor is it to be diminished by any subtraction.

II. From the most clear saying of St. Paul, 2 Tim. III, 15. 16. Because from infancy thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith, which is in Christ Jesus. (For) all scripture divinely inspired is also profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction, which (is) in righteousness: that the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly furnished unto all good works.

Latin:

Quaest. L. Estne sacra scriptura adeo perfecta, vt omnia fidei dogmata morumque praecepta plene & sufficienter contineat?

Sacra scriptura perfecta est perfectione finali, vt nulla dentur fidei dogmata morumque praecepta, homini viatori ad aeternam salutem tendenti creditu factuque necessaria, quae in ipsa non contineantur vel ῥητῶς, explicite, qua litteram, vel διανοητικῶς, implicite, qua rem & sententiam.

Obs. I. Sacra scriptura perfecta est (a) ratione materiae; quoniam nullus liber θεόπνευστος, relatus in perpetuum fidei canonem, intercidit. (β) Ratione formae, eo quod nullus error in textum authenticum negligentia aut perfidia amanuensium irrepsit. (γ) Ratione finis; quoniam omnia fidei dogmata, morumque praecepta, homini aeternam salutem adepturo sufficienter tradit. Ex quo haec perfectio finalis a nonnullis theologis sufficientia sacrae scripturae appellatur. Vid. D. CALOV. in system. theol. tom. I. p. 609. Scite de hac sufficientia scripturae loquitur AVGVSTINVS tract. XLIX. in Io. c. 11. Electa sunt, quae scriberentur, quae saluti credentium sufficere videbantur (*).

Obs. II. Quando asserimus, sacram scripturam ad salutem sufficere, (1) remotumimus omne comprincipium, ad obtinendam aeternam salutem requisitum, sive illud vocetur traditio, sive consensus antiquitatis ecclesiasticae, sive decretum Pontificis Romani; (2) innuimus, sacram scripturam sufficere tum ad probanda dogmata fidei, tum ad confutanda falsa dogmata haereticorum.

Obs. III. Quidam articuli fidei fundamentales continentur in sacris litteris ῥητῶς αὐτολεξεὶ, explicite, qua litteram, disertis verbis & terminis terminantibus: quidam autem articuli fidei habentur in sacra scriptura διανοητικῶς, κατὰ τὸ πρᾶγμα, qua rem & sententiam, vt per consequentiam pronam, proximam, manifestam & necessariam e sacra scriptura deduci possint. Sic totum symbolum apostolicum, quod rem, in scripturis continetur, licet non iisdem verbis, aut eadem articulorum serie (*).

Sacram scripturam perfectam esse perfectione finali, prob. I. ex loco classico Deut. IV, 2. Non addetis ad verbum hoc, quod ego (sum) praecipiens vobis: neque diminuetis de eo, vt observetis praecepta Iehovae Dei vestri, quae ego (sum) praecipiens vobis. Prohibet Deus per Mosen additionem novorum dogmatum, a pentateucho Mosaico diversorum: prohibet idem diminutionem doctrinae Mosaicae, qua quis ausit quidquam demere de illa, quasi non sit (α) a Deo per Mosen profectum, (β) quasi non sit canonicum ad normam ecclesiae pertinens. Conferre nobis liceat cum hoc oraculo Mosaico effatum apostoli Ioannis parallelum Apoc. XXII, 18. 19. Contestor enim omni, qui audit verba prophetiae libri huius, si quis addiderit ad haec, addet Deus super eum plagas scriptas in libro hoc. Et si quis abstulerit de verbis libri prophetiae huius, auferet Deus partem eius de libro vitae & ex urbe sancta, & eorum, quae scripta sunt in libro hoc.

Verba Ioannis iure meritoque ad universam scripturam S. referimus; quia apostolus memorabili hoc dicto universum sacrum codicem velut sigillo communivit, luculentissime testatus, universam sacram scripturam adeo consummatam & perfectam esse, vt ei nihil addendum, vel demendum sit.

Argumentamur: Cui scripturae nihil est addendum, vel detrahendum, illa est perfecta. Atqui scripturae S. &c. Ergo. Maior liquet, quia illud est perfectum, cui nihil deest, & cui nihil addi debet.

Excipiunt Pontificii loqui Mosen de verbo Dei viva voce tradito; de pentateucho Mosis, qui additionem multorum librorum admisit; de additione dogmatum contrariorum doctrinae Mosaicae repugnantium; Apostolum Ioannem prohibere corruptionem libri apocalyptici, non autem prohibere, ne alii libri scribantur, aut alia dogmata tradantur.

Resp. ad I. Ad omne verbum, quod Moses praecipit, nihil vult addi, nihil ipsi adimi. Atqui scriptum verbum Mosis est omne verbum, quod ille praecepit. Ergo.

Ad II. In pentateucho Mosis summa doctrinae fidei & morum continetur; cui prophetae & apostoli non addiderunt nova & diversa dogmata, sed eadem dogmata pluribus verbis explicarunt, eorumque complementum ostenderunt.

Ad III. Additio non est contrariorum, quippe quibus prius aboletur & destruitur, sed diversorum, quibus priori locus conceditur, sed ei velut imperfecto aliquid superadditur.

Ad IV. Verba Ioannis tam de universa scriptura canonica, quam de apocalypsi accipienda sunt; siquidem omnes libri canonici, ab eodem spiritu dictati, eadem auctoritate pollent, & omnes ad eundem finem, aeternam salutem, directi sunt, quem finem non nisi divina manifestatione consequi datur: ad hunc obtinendum sufficit sola scriptura sacra, adeoque nulla additione indiget, nulla detractione imminuenda est.

II. Ex effato S. Paulli clarissimo 2 Tim. III, 15. 16. Quia ab infantia sacras litteras nosti, quae possunt te sapientem reddere in salutem per fidem, quae in Christo Iesu est. (Nam) omnis scriptura divinitus inspirata etiam utilis est ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad disciplinam, quae (fit) in iustitia: vt integer sit homo Dei ad omne bonum opus probe instructus.


### Question XLIX. Is it permissible and advisable to translate the ancient Hebrew language and the Greek of the New Testament into vernacular…: From this apostolic saying a triple argument is born

From this apostolic saying a triple argument is born:

I. Whatever scripture can make a man wise unto salvation through faith in Christ, that is finally perfect. But scripture divinely inspired, etc. Therefore.

II. Whatever scripture is profitable for all ecclesiastical functions, that is perfect. But scripture divinely inspired, etc. Therefore.

III. Whatever scripture renders the ministry of the church, upon which many things lie ἐν γνώσει καὶ τάξει, in knowledge and administration of office, than the faithful hearer, perfect, that abounds in final perfection. But Holy Scripture, etc. Therefore.

The Papists object: That the term πᾶσα γραφὴ is said not collectively, but distributively, because individual parts of scripture are θεόπνευστοι (divinely inspired), which nevertheless are not so perfect that they reject addition. That the apostle speaks of the scripture of the Old Testament, which admitted the addition of the N. T. That this saying treats not of perfection, but of utility.

Resp. to I. The apostle speaks of the entire scripture, which both by reason of the whole biblical canon, and by reason of the parts, is θεόπνευστος καὶ ὠφέλιμος, divinely inspired and profitable, serving the four uses mentioned by the apostle: nor is there any part of scripture which, if not for all these uses, yet conduces to some use, and rejects an addition which is made by human authority.

To II. If the scripture of the Old Testament contributes much moment to producing those four uses: certainly the scripture of the N. T. will contribute more, which was added not by way of a partial norm, but by way of a clearer light.

To III. This saying treats of that utility of Holy Scripture which renders the man of God perfect.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, who maintain that the word of God is not perfect with a final perfection, but that unwritten traditions must be added to it. They rely, I., on the testimony of John, Jo. XXI, 25. There are also many other things which Jesus did: which, if they were written every one, the world would not contain them. Resp. Distinguish between the sayings and the deeds of Christ, and between the necessary articles of Christian doctrine. Not all those things, but these, have been consigned to the Holy Scriptures.

II. They bring forward the testimony of Christ, Jo. XVI, 12. I have yet many things to say unto you; but ye cannot bear them now. Resp. The Savior is not speaking of new dogmas different from those which He had delivered to them, but of a richer explanation and a fuller knowledge of the doctrine of Christ.

For He adds v. 13. When the Spirit of truth is come, ὁδηγήσει ὑμᾶς, He will guide you into all truth. The meaning is: I have more things to say to you, but you do not grasp them at this time, both because of preconceived opinions and because of the excessive grief of your minds.

Wherefore I shall reserve those things for the future miraculous outpouring of the Holy Spirit, who will more fully illustrate all the dogmas delivered by me, and will explain them to you more clearly.

III. That Holy Scripture does not contain all things necessary for belief has been demonstrated by the Papists, by bringing forward certain things to be believed that are not comprised in the Holy Scriptures.

I. According to their view, no remedy is indicated in the Old Testament for females, by which they might be freed from original sin.

II. Nowhere in Holy Scripture is the biblical canon designated.

III. Nothing is held in Scripture concerning infant baptism.

IV. The arduous article concerning the Most Holy

Latin:

Nascitur ex hoc dicto apostolico triplex argumentum:

I. Quaecunque scriptura hominem potest sapientem reddere in salutem per fidem in Christum, illa finaliter est perfecta. Atqui scriptura divinitus inspirata &c. Ergo.

II. Quaecunque scriptura utilis est ad omnes functiones ecclesiasticas, illa est perfecta. Atqui scriptura divinitus inspirata &c. Ergo.

III. Quaecunque scriptura ministerium ecclesiae, cui plura incumbunt ἐν γνώσει καὶ τάξει, in cognitione & officii administratione, quam auditori fideli, perfectum reddit, illa abundat perfectione finali. Atqui scriptura sacra &c. Ergo.

Excipiunt Pontificii: Vocem πᾶσα γραφὴ dici non collective, sed distributive, quia singulae partes scripturae sunt θεόπνευστοι, quae tamen non sunt adeo perfectae, vt additionem respuant. Loqui apostolum de scriptura vet. testam. quod admisit additionem N. T. Agere hoc dictum non de perfectione, sed de vtilitate.

Resp. ad I. Loquitur apostolus de universa scriptura, quae tum ratione totius canonis biblici, tum ratione partium est θεόπνευστος καὶ ὠφέλιμος, divinitus inspirata & vtilis, faciens ad quatuor ab apostolo memoratos vfus: neque vlla pars scripturae est, quae si non ad omnes istos vfus, ad aliquem tamen vsum conducit, & additionem, quae fit auctoritate humana, respuit.

Ad II. Si scriptura vet. testam. multum momenti confert ad pariendos quatuor illos vfus: certe plus conferet scriptura N. T. quae addita est non per modum normae partialis, sed per modum lucis clarioris.

Ad III. Agit hoc dictum de illa vtilitate sacrae scripturae, quae hominem Dei reddit perfectum.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum statuentium, verbum Dei non esse perfectum perfectione finali, sed ei addendas esse traditiones non scriptas. Nituntur I. testimonio Ioannis, Io. XXI, 25.
