Sunt & alia multa, quae fecit Iesus: quae si scriberentur omnia, mundus non caperet. Resp. dist. inter dicta & facta Christi, & inter necessaria doctrinae christianae capita. Non illa omnia, sed haec sacris litteris consignata sunt.

II. Adducunt testimonium Christi Io. XVI, 12. Adhuc multa habeo dicere vobis; sed non potestis ferre nunc. Resp. Non loquitur salvator de dogmatibus novis & diversis ab his, quae ipsis tradiderat, sed de uberiori explicatione & pleniori cognitione doctrinae Christi.

Addit enim v. 13. Quum venerit spiritus veritatis, ὁδηγήσει ὑμᾶς, ducet vos in omnem veritatem. Sensus est: Sunt mihi plura vobis dicenda, sed vos illa tum ob praeconceptas opiniones, tum ob nimium animi moerorem hac vice non capitis.

Quare referuabo illa ad futuram effusionem miraculosam Spiritus S. qui omnia a me tradita dogmata plenius illustrabit, & luculentius vobis exponet .

III. Quod S. scriptura non omnia creditu necessaria contineat, demonstratum cunt Pontificii, adductis quibusdam credendis, in sacris litteris non comprehensis.

I. Ex mente illorum non indicatur in veteri testamento remedium pro foemellis, quo a peccato originali sint liberatae.

II. Nuspiam in S. scriptura designatur canon biblicus.

III. Nil habetur in scriptura de paedobaptismo.

IV. Arduus de SS.


### Question XLIX. Is it permissible and advisable to translate the ancient Hebrew language and the Greek of the New Testament into vernacular…: Trinity is not clearly delivered in Holy Scripture V. The number of the…

Trinity is not clearly delivered in Holy Scripture.

V. The number of the sacraments is not found in it.

VI. Nothing is read in it concerning the sacrifices of the Old Testament expiating sins by the virtue of the passion and death of Christ.

VII. Scripture nowhere defines that Mary, the Mother of God, remained a virgin forever.

Resp. to I.

A bodily and external remedy for females was not necessary in the Old Testament. It suffices that they were born of circumcised fathers. That the sacrament of circumcision was lacking to them was compensated for by faith, which embraced the divine promise: I will be a God to thy females, Gen.

XVII, 7. Which promise was applied to the female sex through the prayers of parents, through sacrifices and offerings. To II. The biblical canon either formally denotes the catalog of biblical books, or materially designates the canonical books themselves.

The catalog of biblical books, since it is a historical review, is not an article of faith necessary for salvation to be known. But the divinity of the canonical books is known from their efficacious and heart-bending power, communicated to them by the concurring Holy Spirit.

To III. Although this proposition does not exist ῥητῶς (expressly) in Scripture: infants are to be baptized, it is nevertheless elicited by valid consequence from that: All nations are to be baptized, Matth. XXVIII, 29.

To IV. The mystery of the Most Holy Trinity is delivered sufficiently clearly in the Scriptures, 1 Jo. V, 7.

To V. The septenary number of the sacraments has as its author Peter Lombard, not the Holy Spirit: and therefore it is sought in the scriptures in vain. The binary number of the sacraments will be clearly proven by us below from the sacred letters. To VI. That the sacrifices of the Jews signified the death of Christ, we read clearly in the scripture of the new testament, Gal. III, 24. Heb. VIII, 5. c. IX, 9. To VII. The perpetual virginity of Mary, after she had brought forth Christ, is not an article of faith, precisely necessary to be believed for salvation; it is gathered, however, probably from scripture, because her care was entrusted by Christ to John, Jo. XIX, 26. If she had had more sons besides Jesus, they would have taken charge of their mother. Epiphanius collected more arguments from the sacred code, Haer. LXXVIII.

Latin:

Trinitate articulus in S. scriptura perspicue non traditur.

V. Non invenitur in ea numerus sacramentorum.

VI. Nil legitur in ipsa de sacrificiis vet. testam. expiantibus peccata, virtute passionis & mortis Christi.

VII. Nusquam definit scriptura Mariam Deiparam semper mansisse virginem.

Resp. ad I.

Remedium corporale & externum foemellis in vet. testam. non fuit necessarium. Sufficit, quod a patribus circumcisis natae fuerint. Quod ipsis defuit sacramentum circumcisionis, id compensavit fides amplexa promissionem divinam: Ero Deus feminis tui, Gen.

XVII, 7. Quae promissio per preces parentum, per sacrificia & oblationes foemineo sexui fuit applicata . Ad II. canon biblicus vel formaliter notat catalogum librorum biblicorum, vel materialiter designat ipsos libros canonicos.

Catalogus librorum biblicorum, cum sit historica recensio, non est articulus fidei ad salutem cognitu necessarius. Divinitas autem librorum canonicorum cognoscitur ex eorum efficaci & corda flectente vi, a concurrente Spiritu S. ipsis communicata.

Ad III. licet non ῥητῶς exstet in scriptura haec propositio: infantes sunt baptizandi, per validam tamen consequentiam ex illa: Omnes gentes sunt baptizandae, Matth. XXVIII, 29. elicitur.

Ad IV. mysterium SS. Trinitatis satis perspicue traditur in scripturis, 1 Io. V, 7 .

Ad V. numerus septenarius sacramentorum auctorem habet Petrum Lombardum, non Spiritum sanctum: ideoque frustra in scripturis quaeritur. Numerus binarius sacramentorum a nobis infra ex sacris litteris luculenter probabitur. Ad VI. sacrificia Iudaeorum significasse mortem Christi, clare legimus in scriptura noui testamenti, Gal. III, 24. Hebr. VIII, 5. c. IX, 9. Ad VII. perpetua virginitas Mariae, postquam ea Christum peperit, non est articulus fidei, creditu praecise necessarius ad salutem; colligitur tamen probabiliter e scriptura, quia eius cura a Christo demandata est Ioanni, Io. XIX, 26. Si plures praeter Iesum habuisset filios; hi matris rationem duxissent. Plura argumenta e sacro codice collegit Epiphanius, Haeres. LXXVIII.


### Question LI. Whether unwritten traditions are to be added to the written word of God, and received with an equal affection of piety?

Unwritten traditions are neither to be added to the divine word , nor are they to be received with the same equal affection of piety . Obs.

I. The word tradition, derived from tradendo (handing over), in the broadest sense denotes any act by which something is transferred to another and given, as it were, from hand to hand.

In the present sense, however, it denotes in a stricter way the act of informing, by which a certain doctrine is handed down and inculcated to someone.

Obs. II. Just as the names of actions are otherwise often transferred to objects: so here the word tradition is taken either actively, or passively, or objectively. Taken actively, it signifies the active and pedagogical institution by which some doctrine, pertaining to faith, morals, or external discipline, is instilled into someone. Confer. DANNHAV. hodom. prior. Pap. phantasm. I. p. 224. Taken passively, it designates the doctrine handed down.

Obs. III. Tradition, taken passively for the doctrine handed down, denotes either generally any doctrine whatsoever handed down by Christ and the apostles, whether it was later comprised in writing or not. In which meaning the vulgar interpreter used the word tradition, Acts VI, 14, for the law of Moses, which was comprised in writing, and 2 Thess. II, 15, Paul calls παράδοσιν (tradition) the doctrine handed down by him both by word and by writing; or specifically, as it is contradistinguished from doctrines handed down through scripture, and is the same as doctrine handed down by voice only, not written. Which is the latter meaning of this place.

Obs. IV. Since, however, something is said to be contained in the scriptures either expressly and ῥητῶς (verbally), or implicitly, διανοητικῶς (intellectually) and by consequence: tradition also, contradistinguished from scripture, can be taken either for doctrine which is not written expressly and in so many words by the prophets and apostles, but handed down and propagated by voice, although it is contained implicitly and as to the matter in the scriptures: or for doctrine which is contained neither in express words nor as to the matter in the scriptures, but has been handed down by voice only, and preserved in the church by continuous succession. In the former sense, the apostolic symbol is sometimes called by the name of tradition by the fathers. Confer. D. CHEMNITIUS in exam. conc. Trident. de traditionibus fol. 63, where he alleges Irenaeus and Tertullian, who, reciting almost word for word those articles of faith which the apostolic symbol embraces, appeal to apostolic tradition, on account of certain heretics who either rejected the scriptures, or depraved them, or complained that they were insufficient; although the apostolic symbol is entirely contained, as to the matter, in the scriptures, even if not in the same words and the same series of articles. For Irenaeus himself also, lib. III. IV. V., proves and confirms those articles of faith from scripture at length. Thus Origen and Augustine call infant baptism apostolic tradition. Confer. CHEMNITIUS l.c. fol. 69, whom however they prove and establish with manifest testimonies of scripture. In the present controversy there intervenes between us and the Papists a dispute concerning traditions in the latter sense accepted, namely concerning doctrine handed down orally from Christ and the apostles, which is contained in the scriptures neither as to the matter nor as to the very words, but has been preserved in the church by continuous succession.

Latin:

Traditiones non scriptae neque verbo diuino addendae , neque cum eodem pari pietatis affectu suscipiendae sunt . Obs.

I. Vox traditio, a tradendo deducta, sensu latissimo notat quemuis actum, quo quippiam ad alterum transfertur & de manu ad manum quasi datur.

In praesenti vero sensu strictiori notat actum informandi, quo doctrina quaedam alicui traditur & inculcatur.

Obs. II. Quemadmodum alias nomina actionum saepe ad obiecta transferuntur: ita hic vox traditio sumitur vel actiue, vel passiue siue obiectiue. Actiue sumta significat institutionem actiuam & paedagogicam, qua doctrina aliqua pars, ad fidem, mores aut externam disciplinam pertinens, alicui instillatur. Confer. DANNHAV. hodom. prior. Pap. phantasm. I. p. 224. Passiue accepta designat doctrinam traditam.

Obs. III. Traditio, passiue sumta pro doctrina tradita, notat vel generatim doctrinam quamlibet a Christo & apostolis traditam, siue scripto postea comprehensa fuerit, siue minus. Quo significatu vulgatus interpres traditionis voce vsus est, Actor. VI, 14. pro lege Mosis, quae scripto comprehensa erat, & 2 Thess. II, 15. Paullus παράδοσιν traditionem vocat doctrinam cum sermone, tum scripto a se traditam; vel speciatim, prout doctrinae per scripturam traditae contradistinguitur, & idem est, quod doctrina voce tantum tradita, non scripta. Quae posterior significatio huius loci est.

Obs. IV. Cum vero in scripturis aliquid contineri dicatur vel expresse & ῥητῶς, vel implicite, διανοητικῶς & per consequentiam: traditio etiam, scripturae contradistincta, accipi potest vel pro doctrina, quae expresse & totidem verbis a prophetis & apostolis scripta non est, sed voce tradita & propagata, quamuis implicite & quoad rem in scripturis contineatur: vel pro doctrina, quae nec verbis expressis, nec quoad rem in scripturis continetur, sed voce tantum tradita, & continua successione in ecclesia conseruata est. Priori sensu symbolum apostolicum a patribus quandoque traditionis nomine appellatur. Confer. D. CHEMNITIVS in exam. conc. Trident. de traditionibus fol. 63. vbi allegat Irenaeum & Tertullianum, qui recitantes ad verbum ferme illos articulos fidei, quos symbolum apostolicum complectitur, ad traditionem apostolicam prouocant, propter haereticos quosdam, qui scripturas vel reiiciebant, vel deprauabant, vel conquerebant insufficientes esse; cum tamen symbolum apostolicum totum, quoad rem, contineatur in scripturis, licet non iisdem verbis & eadem articulorum serie. Nam & ipse IRENAEVS lib. III. IV. V. illos fidei articulos ex scriptura prolixe probat & confirmat. Sic ORIGENES & AVGVSTINVS paedobaptismum vocant traditionem apostolicam. Conf, CHEMNITIVM l.c. fol. 69. quem tamen iidem probant & stabiliunt manifestis scripturae testimoniis. In praesenti controuerfia nobis intercedit cum Pontificiis de traditionibus in posteriori significatu acposteriori significatu posteriori significatu acceptis, nempe de doctrina a Christo & apostolis oretenus tradita, quæ nec quoad rem, nec quoad ipsa verba, in scripturis contineatur, continua autem successione in ecclesia conservata sit.


### Question LI. Whether unwritten traditions are to be added to the written word of God, and received with an equal affection of piety?: Obs

Obs.

V. Orthodox theologians distinguish the traditions of the church into ritual, historical, exegetical, testimonial, and dogmatic.

Ritual traditions concern ceremonies and rites, e.g., concerning feast days, concerning triple immersion or aspersion in the act of baptism, etc. By historical traditions are enumerated the canonical books of Holy Scripture, kept by the church through an uninterrupted series of times and a certain succession of connection, and faithfully transmitted to posterity; the milder and harsher fates of the church are also commemorated, as well as the struggles stirred up in the church concerning certain articles of faith. By exegetical traditions it is shown in what sense the doctors of the primitive church explained this or that biblical saying. By testimonial traditions is exhibited the consensus of ecclesiastical antiquity, which provides clear testimony to the truth of the articles of faith. Dogmatic traditions are dogmas of faith and morals; which are said by adversaries to be contained in the scriptures neither in express words, nor implicitly and as to the matter, yet handed down by word of mouth from Christ and the apostles, and preserved in the church by continuous succession. Such dogmatic traditions are the dogmas concerning the invocation of saints, the worship of images, the celibacy of priests, the choice of foods, the sacrifice of the mass, concerning the sacraments of penance, confirmation, orders, matrimony, and extreme unction, communion under one species, purgatory, and indulgences.

There is a controversy between us and the Papists concerning dogmatic traditions.

For we do not disapprove of all ritual traditions of the church, provided the theological rule observed by D. Chemnitius in Exam. Conc. Trid. fol. 75 be observed. Ceremonies in the church should be indifferent in kind, few in number, and should be pious and useful for edification, order, and decorum: they should have free observances outside the case of scandal, so that according to the reason of edification, time, place, and persons, they may be instituted, changed, and abrogated.

We admit the historical tradition concerning the canon of scripture as an argument, not infallible, but probable.

We receive exegetical traditions with a grateful mind, if indeed the interpretation of the fathers does not differ from the phrase of scripture, the propriety of the words, the context, and the analogy of faith.

We value the testimonial tradition highly, and we confess with Chemnitius (l.c. fol. 71) that we differ from those who invent opinions which have no testimony of any time in the church: as Servetus, Campanus, the Anabaptists, and others have done. We also feel that no dogma in the church is to be received that is new and repugnant to all antiquity.

The question is ventilated concerning dogmatic traditions, concerning the very dogmas of faith and the precepts of morals, which are neither proposed in express words in Holy Scripture, nor can be deduced and constructed from it by forced consequence.

Latin:

Obs.

V. Distinguunt theologi orthodoxi traditiones ecclesiæ in rituales, historicas, exegeticas, testificatorias & dogmaticas.

Traditiones rituales concernunt cærimonias & ritus, v. g. de diebus festis, de trina immersione vel aspersione in actu baptismali &c. Traditionibus historicis recensentur libri canonici S. scripturæ, non interrupta serie temporum & certa connexionis successione ab ecclesia custoditi, & fideliter ad posteros transmissi; commemorantur etiam fata ecclesiæ mitiora & asperiora, nec non certamina de quibusdam articulis fidei in ecclesia mota. Traditionibus exegeticis ostenditur, quo sensu doctores primitivæ ecclesiæ hoc vel illud dictum biblicum exposuerint. Traditionibus testificatoriis exhibetur consensus antiquitatis ecclesiasticæ, quæ veritati articulorum fidei luculentum perhibet testimonium. Traditiones dogmaticæ sunt dogmata fidei & morum; quæ nec expressis verbis, nec implicite & quoad rem in scripturis continentur, viva tamen voce a Christo & apostolis tradita, & continua successione in ecclesia conservata ab adversariis dicuntur. Eiusmodi traditiones dogmaticæ sunt dogmata de invocatione sanctorum, cultu imaginum, cœlibatu sacerdotum, delectu ciborum, sacrificio missæ, de sacramentis pœnitentiæ, confirmationis, ordinis, matrimonii & extremæ vnctionis, communione sub vna specie, purgatorio & indulgentiis.

Controuertitur nos inter, & Pontificios, de traditionibus dogmaticis.

Neque enim improbamus omnes traditiones ecclesiæ rituales, modo obseruetur regula theologica, obseruata a D. CHEMNITIO in exam. conc. Trid. fol. 75. Cærimoniæ in ecclesia sint genere indifferentes, numero paucæ, sint piæ & vtiles ad ædificationem, ordinem & decorum: habeant extra casum scandali liberas obseruationes, vt pro ratione ædificationis, temporis, loci, & personarum, institui, mutari & abrogari possint.

Admittimus traditionem historicam de canone scripturæ, vt argumentum, non infallibile, sed probabile.

Traditiones exegeticas grata mente recipimus, si nempe interpretatio patrum a scripturæ phrasi, verborum proprietate, contextu & analogia fidei non discrepet.

Traditionem testificatoriariam magni facimus, & fatemur cum CHEMNITIO l. c. fol. 71. nos ab illis dissentire, qui fingunt opiniones, quæ nulla habent testimonia vllius temporis in ecclesia: sicut fecerunt SERVETVS, CAMPANVS, ANABAPTISTÆ & alii. Sentimus etiam, nullum dogma in ecclesia nouum, & cum tota antiquitate pugnans recipiendum.

Ventilatur quæstio de traditionibus dogmaticis, concernentibus ipsa fidei dogmata morumque præcepta, quæ neque disertis verbis in S. scriptura proponuntur, neque per inuitam consequentiam ex eadem deduci & adstrui possunt.


### Question LI. Whether unwritten traditions are to be added to the written word of God, and received with an equal affection of piety?: Obs

Obs.

VI. That we may look more deeply into the mind of the Papists, it must be properly observed that they distinguish unwritten traditions 1) by reason of their authors, 2) by reason of their matter.

By reason of authors, the traditions of the Old Testament are divided into Mosaic and Pharisaic.

The former are said to derive their origin from Moses and the prophets, the latter from the Pharisees. The traditions of the N.T. are divided by the Papists into divine, apostolic, and ecclesiastical.

Those are called divine by them which were received from Christ himself, while teaching the apostles, and are nowhere found in divine letters. Such are those which pertain to the matter and form of the sacraments.

For we have few things concerning these in divine letters, and yet it is certain that the essence of the sacraments could not have been instituted except by Christ. For that reason the apostle, 1 Cor.

11:23, speaking of the sacrament of the eucharist, said: For I received from the Lord that which I also delivered to you. Apostolic traditions are called those which were instituted by the apostles, yet not without the assistance of the Holy Spirit, and nevertheless do not exist written in their epistles: such as the fast of Lent, and the four temof times, and many other things. Ecclesiastical traditions are called certain ancient customs, begun either by prelates or by the peoples, which gradually, by the tacit consent of the peoples, obtained the force of law.

By reason of their subject matter, traditions are divided by the Pontificians into traditions of faith and traditions of morals; which in turn are either perpetual or temporal, and either universal or particular, necessary or free.

A tradition of faith is that the Blessed

Mary was always a virgin, that there are only four gospels, etc.

A tradition pertaining to morals is that the sign of the cross is to be painted on the forehead, that fasts or feasts are to be celebrated on certain days, etc.

A perpetual tradition is one that is instituted so that it may always be kept; as in the examples given: A temporal one is that which is instituted for a certain time, such as the observation of certain legal ceremonies: which were to be kept until the full promulgation of the gospel, so that the church might more easily coalesce from Jews and Gentiles.

A universal tradition is that which is handed down to be kept by the whole church, such as the observation of Easter, Pentecost, and similar great feasts: a particular one is that which is handed down to only one or several churches, such as was the fast of the Sabbath in the time of Augustine, which Peter had handed down to the Roman church, and was kept by it alone and certain others, as Augustine teaches in epist. 86. to Casulanus.

A necessary tradition is that which is handed down in the form of a precept, such as the celebration of Easter after the fourteenth moon of March: a free one is that which is handed down in the form of a counsel, such as the sprinkling of holy water and the like.

Concerning these, see BELLARM. book on the word of God, chap.

II. fol.

163.

Prob. a. That unwritten dogmatic tradition is not to be added to Holy Scripture as a principle of faith necessary for salvation to be believed, is evident

I. from the perfection and sufficiency of Scripture.

For the word of God, consigned to writing, is so perfect and sufficient for salvation that by human authority no new dogma, heterogeneous or different from those things which are written, is to be added, as Moses testifies Deut.

IV, 2. chap.

XIII, 1. and John Apoc.

XXII, 18.

Cf. the preceding question.

The consequence is manifest; because that is perfect which lacks no substantial supplement (*).

II. From the divine interdict most holily observed by St. Paul: That you may learn not to be wise above that which is written.

1 Cor.

IV, 6.

Whence it happened that Paul said nothing beyond those things which Moses and (*) In the principal passage, 2 Tim.

III, 16. there are many nerves of proof.

It must be considered, 1) that the written word is commended, and indeed as the means for obtaining salvation, and that the only one, inasmuch as it is the only one that PAUL praises, in which he also bids his Timothy to remain entirely, v. 14. But that in which one must remain and persist cannot but be so perfect and sufficient that we may acquiesce in it, lest we require anything further.

O. The means, uniquely commended, must necessarily be sufficient: If sufficient, therefore perfect.

2) That Scripture is said to make a man perfect, and especially a minister of the church.

For that name, ἄνθρωπος θεῦ (man of God), just as the Hebrew, אִישׁ אֱלֹהִים, denotes him who performs the office of teaching divinely mandated to him, cf.

2 Pet.

I, 21.

From which a double argumentation is made.

One: The effect cannot be nobler than its cause, uniquely named, and as great as is the end for the sake of which a thing is so and not otherwise, so great also cannot but be the very constitution of the thing.

E. Holy Scripture is perfect and altogether sufficient.

The other: If Holy Scripture is so perfect and sufficient that it supplies to the minister of the church all things useful for the function of his office, why should it not much more suffice for the members of the church?

3) That those things, the perfect knowledge of which is to be drawn from divine writings, are called doctrines, both concerning things to be believed and the refutation of errors opposed to them (διδασκαλία καὶ ἔλεγχος), and concerning things to be done (παιδεία καὶ ἐπανόρθωσις).

But besides these there is nothing that pertains to the end of Scripture: E. Scripture is altogether sufficient for the proposed end.

4) That not only are all genera of saving truths enumerated, πρὸς διδασκαλίαν, etc. v. 17. but also specifically an affirmation is added concerning every good work, v. 17. E. Holy Scripture is perfect and sufficient not only in general, but also in specific, so that it may teach us individual truths to be referred to any genus whatsoever, with none omitted.

prophets have spoken. Acts XXVI, 22. Just as Peter wished to say οὐδὲν ἄτερ γραφῶν [nothing without the scriptures], as testified by CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA, Stromat. book VI. III. From divine commendation. If we or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel to you, besides that which we have preached to you, let him be anathema, Gal. I, 8. Since the Holy Spirit threatens the thunderbolt of anathema against one preaching a gospel besides that which was preached by Paul and the remaining apostles, one must provide with the utmost caution that no principle of faith be added to the gospel preached and written by the apostles which is not contained in the apostolic writings.

You say: I. The apostle does not speak of the written word alone, but of every word, whether written or handed down. For he does not say: If anyone shall preach a gospel besides that which we have written, but besides that which we have preached.

I reply: Paul speaks in general of the word preached by him. But he preached nothing outside of that which was written by Moses and the prophets. Acts XXVI, 22. Whatever he preached, that he also wrote. 2 Cor. I, 13; c. XIII, 2. He wrote that gospel which he had preached to the Galatians.

You say: II. The Greek particle παρὰ signifies "against," Acts XVIII, 13. Therefore the apostle prohibits not new or different dogmas, but those contrary to the preached gospel. I reply: The particle παρὰ often signifies "besides." Compare the notable passage 1 Cor. III, 11. In the Vulgate version, which is authentic for the Papists, the Latin "praeter" [besides] is found here. Indeed, the apostle himself even renders it by ἕτερον, "another," "different," v. 6. For which reason, just as that minister sins not only who issues a diploma in the name of a prince that is repugnant to his statutes, but also he who promulgates something besides those statutes which is different and alien from the wisdom and counsel of the prince: so that minister of the church sins not only who proposes dogmas of faith repugnant to the gospel of Christ preached by the apostles, but also he who proposes dogmas different and alien from the gospel of Christ.

Proof b. Whatever is to be received with that affection of piety with which the written word of God is received, that must be most certain and infallible, so that it may be able to beget divine faith, and be believed by divine faith, Rom. XV, 4. Luke wrote ἀκριβῶς καὶ δι' ἀσφάλειαν [accurately and for certainty]. c. I, 3, 4. Paul wrote δι' ἀσφαλὲς [for certainty], for greater certainty. Phil. III, 1. But whence can we be infallibly certain concerning unwritten traditions that they are from God? Is it from scripture? But they are not written. Is it from the testimony of the church? But this itself is not infallible, since its authority, being human, cannot beget divine faith. Nay, the adversaries have never even proven their traditions from the testimony of the more ancient church.

But if we examine more deeply the origin of unwritten traditions, they flowed from Pharisaism.

It is established concerning the Pharisees, partly from scripture, partly from Josephus and others, that besides the written word they held many traditions alien to the word of God, and rejected by Christ himself. Matt. XV, 2, 3, and following. JOSEPHUS, book XIII of the Antiquities of the Jews, c. 18: "Now," he says, "it must be indicated that the Pharisees have handed down to the people many constitutions received from the fathers by hand, which are not written among the Mosaic laws." And for this reason the Sadducees derogated from their authority, saying that only those things ought to be kept which are contained in writing: and hence a great controversy arose between the two.

The Papists distinguish between Mosaic and Pharisaic traditions, opining that Christ rejected Pharisaic traditions indeed, but not Mosaic ones: but in vain. For they cannot prove that Moses handed down dogmas which were not consigned to letters, but preserved by the faithful memory of posterity. Christ never refers us to Mosaic traditions, but to the scriptures.

John V, 39. The antithesis is that of the Papists, who establish that unwritten divine and apostolic traditions are to be received with an equal affection of piety as the written word of God. They rely on the following arguments:

I. Traditions are commended everywhere in the sacred scriptures, Exod. XIII, 8. Deuter. XXXII, 7. Iudic. V, 13. Resp. In the cited places, tradition is understood actively, or the act of handing down, informing, catechizing; it is commonly called instruction, which is done by word of mouth, the foundation of which is sacred scripture.

Concerning this there is no controversy: but there is controversy concerning tradition taken passively or objectively, insofar as by it is understood dogma handed down orally and not contained in the sacred scriptures, nor deducible from them by necessary consequence.

II. The doctors of the primitive church called the apostolic symbol and infant baptism traditions, as CHEMNITIUS admits in exam. conc. Trid. fol. 63. and 69. But we retain the apostolic symbol and infant baptism. Therefore we retain unwritten traditions. Resp. The doctors of the primitive church used the name of tradition in a looser sense; because by it they understood all doctrine concerning God and divine things, which κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν, according to the letter and express words, is not contained in the scriptures: today the controversy is ventilated concerning unwritten traditions so-called in a stricter sense, which are held neither as to the very words, nor as to the matter and meaning in the divine scriptures.

III. Paul refers us to traditions, 2 Thess. II, 15. Stand, brethren, and hold the traditions, which you have been taught, whether by word, or by our epistle. Resp. The Apostle speaks of doctrine, the same in respect of substance, but handed down in a different way; as it was proposed to the members of the church both by word of mouth and by writings.

The disjunctive particle εἴτε does not disjoin the dogmas handed down, but the different modes of handing them down. For before the canon of scripture was completed, men θεόπνευστοι (divinely inspired), handed down many things by voice, which they later committed to writing. Today, with the biblical canon completed, it is not right to have recourse to unwritten traditions.

IV. Paul commends traditions to Timothy, 1 Tim. VI, 20. O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust (the doctrine handed down by word of mouth). By the deposit, the Pontificians do not understand the written word, which does not seem to need anxious custody, since it is easily kept in its cases. Resp. By the name of deposit is understood not tradition, but the whole celestial doctrine, first handed down to Timothy the disciple by the teacher Paul by word of mouth from Moses and the prophets, Act. XXVI, 22. and later committed to writing. For the deposit of doctrine is not opposed by Paul to S. Scripture as traditions are opposed to it, but (as is evident from v. 21.) to profane novelties of words and oppositions of science falsely so called. Wherefore the mind of the apostle is: O Timothy, keep the celestial doctrine, handed down to thee both by word of mouth and by writings: avoid with the greatest zeal sophistical disputations, by which evangelical doctrine is rendered doubtful to the simpler sort.

V. Paul attributes much to unwritten traditions, 1 Cor. XI, 23. I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you. He concludes the same chapter with these words: the rest will I set in order when I come. Resp. Paul in the cited chapter v. 23. understands written tradition: for he treats of the institution of the Lord's supper, which was written not only here by Paul, but also by the three evangelists. But the apostolic arrangement, which is mentioned in v. 34. pertains to ceremonies and rites, useful for edification in the church. But here our discourse is not about ceremonies, which can be learned from ritual traditions, but about dogmas of faith and precepts of morals, necessary for man to be saved in belief and practice, which are learned solely from the written word.

VI. That there are unwritten traditions in the church is hinted at by John chap. XXI, 25. But there are also many other things which Jesus did, which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written. Resp. We concede that not all things which Christ said or did were written by the evangelists; but we deny that anything of those things which are necessary for faith and morals was omitted by them. CYRILLUS says excellently, book XII on John, last chapter: Not all things which the Lord did have been written down, but those things which, in writing, for morals as well as which they thought sufficient for dogmas. And no less skillfully says AUGUSTINE Tract. XLIX. in John c. 11. Those things were chosen to be written, which seemed sufficient for the salvation of believers (*).

VII. John confirms unwritten traditions in 2 Ep. 12. 13. & 3 Ep. 13. 14. Having many things to write unto you, I would not write with paper and ink: but I trust to come unto you, and speak face to face, that our joy may be full.

1) John is not speaking of the whole of Scripture, but of this very epistle of his, in which he did not write everything to the chosen lady. 2) What kind of things those are, which John denies he wished to write by letter, no one will easily guess. 3) If the adversaries will clearly show that those things which John handed down to the chosen lady were dogmas of faith and precepts of morals, we will take it upon ourselves to demonstrate, from the written word, each one of all those things which are necessary.

VIII. The tradition of the church seems necessary both for proving the divine origin of Holy Scripture and for eliciting its genuine meaning.

Res. The divine origin of Scripture is known both from external and internal sources, but especially from the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit.

We willingly accept the testimony of the church concerning the divinity of Scripture, as a significant argument, but not as the only, principal, and absolutely necessary one.

We seek and find the true meaning of Scripture in Scripture itself, just as a sword is found in its sheath, a pearl in its shell, and a soul in the body.

The consensus of the fathers, interpreting some biblical saying, is received by us as an external hermeneutical aid, guiding and secondarily confirming, not as a fundamental principle, nor as an infallible norm of interpretation ().

Quest. (*) Allow me to add these two things: 1) If we compare these words, John XXI, 25, with those whose meaning is the same, XX, 30 & 31, John openly and plainly professes that those things which have been written are sufficient for faith and salvation: 2) Do the Roman Catholics have all the deeds of Christ, which his Legates did not commit to memory, received from the Elders? How great, I ask, and how full of miracles must such a tradition be, which in its scope embraces all those things which, if they had been committed to writing, not even the world itself could have contained! ()

To accomplish this business, an argument ad hominem will contribute not a little, and that indeed a twofold one. 1) The dissenters say, in the Council of Trent, sess. IV, decr. 1, that they receive traditions preserved by continuous succession in the Catholic church. But where on earth is that continuous succession in those cases in which the Roman church has manifestly defected from ancient institution, and that by a perpetual, uninterrupted series? Examples are clearer than the sun, these two especially: namely, the institution of the Holy Supper and concerning the chalice in the most holy feast. Let them therefore produce the tradition and the continued succession, since they cannot produce even one witness speaking from all of antiquity, through the first XII centuries. Behold their own confession, l. c. sess. XXI, cap. 1 & 2. 2) The Greek and Oriental church likewise received traditions, as a norm of things to be believed and done. Among their number are some, very different from those which the Romanists venerate, namely in those controversies in which the Greek church departs far from the Roman. Which therefore is the true tradition? That which is kept in the Greek church? Or this, which the Roman Catholics think should be cultivated with the highest observance? What then is this continuous succession, of which the Romanists boast so much? What finally? They do not fear to put this forward: that Holy Scripture is very uncertain, ambiguous, and highly doubtful. But why? Because, they say, heretics flee to Scripture and distort it to their own private opinions. Is that therefore uncertain, to which those who err, no less than those who think rightly, appeal? If this consequence is valid, it follows that traditions are likewise uncertain, if indeed heretics, whom they themselves count among the Greeks, are accustomed to appeal to Apostolic traditions. What they have answered us, the same will be returned to them.

Latin:

Obs.

VI. Vt mentem Pontificiorum penitius inspiciamus, probe obseruandum est, quod illi traditiones non scriptas distinguunt 1) ratione auctorum, 2) ratione materiæ.

Ratione auctorum diuiduntur traditiones veteris testamenti in Mosaicas & Pharisæicas.

Illæ a Mose & prophetis, hæ a Pharisæis originem ducere dicuntur. Traditiones N.

T. a Pontificiis diuiduntur in diuinas, apostolicas & ecclesiasticas. Diuinæ ab ipsis dicuntur, quæ acceptæ sunt ab ipso Christo, apostolos docente, & nusquam in diuinis litteris inueniuntur.

Tales sunt, quæ ad materiam & formam sacramentorum pertinent. Pauca enim de his habemus in diuinis litteris, & tamen certum est, sacramentorum essentiam non potuisse, nisi a Christo, institui.

Propterea enim apostolus 1 Cor. XI, 23. loquens de sacramento eucharistiæ dicebat: Ego enim accepi a domino, quod etiam tradidi vobis. Apostolicæ traditiones dicuntur illæ, quæ ab apostolis institutæ sunt, non tamen sine assistentia Spiritus sancti, & nihilominus non extant scriptæ in eorum epistolis: quale est ieiunium quadragesimæ, & quatuor temporum, & multa alia. Ecclesiasticae traditiones dicuntur consuetudines quaedam antiquae, vel a praelatis, vel a populis inchoatae, quae paulatim tacito consensu populorum vim legis obtinuerunt.

Ratione materiae diuiduntur traditiones a Pontificiis in traditiones de fide, & traditiones de moribus; quae rursum aut sunt perpetuae, aut temporales, & vel vniuersales, vel particulares, necessariae, vel liberae.

Traditio de fide est, quod B.

Maria semper fuerit virgo, quod quatuor sint tantum evangelia &c.

Traditio ad mores pertinens est, quod signum crucis in fronte pingendum sit, quod certis diebus ieiunia aut festa celebranda &c.

Traditio perpetua est, quae instituitur, vt semper feruetur; vt in exemplis positis: Temporalis est, quae instituitur ad certum tempus, vt obferuatio legalium quarundam caerimoniarum: quae feruandae erant vsque ad plenam euangelii promulgationem, vt facilius ecclesia ex Iudaeis & gentibus coalesceret.

Traditio vniuersalis est, quae toti ecclesiae feruanda traditur, qualis est paschatis, pentecostes & similium magnorum festorum obferuatio: particularis est, quae traditur vni tantum aut pluribus ecclesiis, qualis erat tempore Augustini ieiunium sabbati, quod Petrus Romanae ecclesiae tradiderat, & ab ea sola, & quibusdam aliis seruabatur, vt Augustinus docet epist. 86. ad Calu.

Traditio necessaria est, quae traditur in forma praecepti, vt celebratio paschae post decimam quartam lunam Martii: libera est, quae traditur in forma consilii, vt aspersio aquae lustralis & similia.

De his vide BELLARM. libr. de verbo Dei cap.

II. fol.

163.

Prob. a. Traditionem non-scriptam dogmaticam S. scripturae non esse addendam, vt principium fidei, ad salutem creditu necessarium, patet

I. ex perfectione & sufficientia scripturae.

Verbum enim Dei, litteris consignatum, adeo perfectum & ad salutem sufficiens est, vt humana auctoritate nullum nouum, heterogeneum, siue diuersum ab his, quae scripta sunt, dogma addendum sit, teste Mose Deut.

IV, 2. c.

XIII, 1. & Ioanne Apoc.

XXII, 18.

Conf. quaest. praecedentem.

Consequentia est manifesta; quia illud perfectum est, quod nullo substantiali supplemento indiget (*).

II. Ab interdicto diuino a S. Paullo sanctissime obseruato: Discatis, non supra id, quod scriptum est, sapere.

1 Cor.

IV, 6.

Vnde factum, vt Paullus nihil praeter ea dixerit, quae Moses & (*) In loco praecipuo, 2 ad Tim.

III, 16. plures insunt nerui probationis.

Considerandum est, 1) quod verbum scriptum commendatur, & quidem vt medium ad salutem obtinendam, idque vnicum, vtpote quod solum PAVLLVS laudat, in quo etiam totum manere Timotheum suum iubet, v. 14. Id vero, in quo permanendum est, ac persistendum, non potest non tam perfectum ac sufficiens esse, vt in eo acquiescamus, ne quid vltra requiramus.

O. medium, vnice commendatum, necesse est, vt fit sufficiens: Si sufficiens, ergo perfectum.

2) Quod scriptura dicitur, perfectum efficere hominem, in primisque ministrum ecclesiae.

Nomen enim illud, ἄνθρωπος θεῦ, quem ad modum hebraicum, אִישׁ אֱלֹהִים, eum denotat, qui munere docendi diuinitus sibi mandato fungitur, conf.

2 Pet.

I, 21.

Ex quo duplicata efficitur argumentatio.

Vna: Effectus non potest esse nobilior sua causa, vnice nominata, & quantus est finis, propter quem res ita, nec aliter est, tanta quoque non potest non esse ipsa rei constitutio.

E. scriptura S. est perfecta atque omnino sufficiens.

Altera: Si scriptura S. ita perfecta ac sufficiens est, vt ministro ecclesiae suppeditet omnia, ad functionem muneris sui vtilia, quidni ea multo magis sufficiat membris ecclesiae?

3) Quod res illae, quarum perfecta cognitio ac scriptis diuinis haurienda est, dicuntur doctrinae, tum de credendis, & his oppositis erroribus refutandis (διδασκαλία καὶ ἔλεγχος), tum de agendis (παιδεία καὶ ἐπανόρθωσις).

Atqui praeter ea nihil est, quod ad finem scripturae pertineat: E. scriptura ad finem propositum omnino est sufficiens.

4) Quod non modo genera veritatum salutarium omnia numerantur, πρὸς διδασκαλίαν, κ. τ. λ. v. 17. sed etiam speciatim adfeueratio adiungitur de vno quoque opere bono, v. 17. E. scriptura S. perfecta ac sufficiens est non solum in genere, verum etiam in specie, vt singulas veritates, ad quoduis genus referendas, nulla demta, nos edoceat.

prophetæ locuti sunt. Act. XXVI, 22. Sicut Petrus οὐδὲν ἄτερ γραφῶν teste CLEMENTE ALEXANDR. Stromat. libr. VI. dicere voluit. III. A commendatione diuina. Si nos aut angelus e cælo euangelizaret vobis, præter id, quod euangelizauimus vobis, anathema fit, Gal. I, 8. Cum Spiritus S. anathematis fulmen interminetur prædicanti euangelium præter id, quod prædicatum est a Paullo & reliquis apostolis, summa cautione prouidendum est, ne euangelio ab apostolis prædicato & scripto vllum principium fidei addatur, quod scriptis apostolicis non est comprehensum.

Dicis: I. Non loquitur apostolus de solo verbo scripto, sed de omni verbo, siue scripto, siue tradito. Neque enim inquit: Si quis euangelizauerit, præter id, quod scripsimus, sed præter id, quod euangelizauimus.

Resp. Loquitur Paullus in genere de verbo a se prædicato. At nihil prædicauit extra id, quod a Mose & prophetis scriptum est. Act. XXVI, 22. Quidquid prædicauit, id etiam scripsit. 2 Cor. I, 13. c. XIII, 2. Scripsit illud euangelium, quod Galatis prædicauerat.

Dicis: II. Particula græca παρὰ fignificat, contra, Act. XVIII, 13. Prohibet itaque apostolus non dogmata noua aut diuerfa, sed contraria euangelio prædicato. Resp. Particula παρὰ sæpe fignificat, præter. Confer locum infignem 1 Cor. III, 11. In vulgata verfione, quæ Pontificiis est authentica, habetur hic latinum, præter. Quin ipse etiam apostolus reddit per ἕτερον, aliud, diuerfum v. 6. Quam ob rem sicut non solum is peccat minister, qui nomine principis diploima edit, quod repugnat eius statutis, sed & qui præter illa statuta aliquid promulgat, quod a sapientia & consilio principis diuerfum atque alienum est: ita non solum ille peccat minister ecclesiæ, qui proponit dogmata fidei euangelio Christi ab apostolis prædicato repugnantia, sed & qui proponit dogmata ab euangelio Christi diuerfa & aliena.

Prob. b. Quidquid eo pietatis affectu suscipiendum est, quo suscipitur verbum Dei scriptum, illud oportet esse certissimum ac infallibile, vt fidem diuinam gignere possit, ac fide diuina credatur, Rom. XV, 4. Scripsit Lucas ἀκριβῶς καὶ δι' ἀσφάλειαν. c. I, 3. 4. Scripsit Paullus δι' ἀσφαλὲς, ob maiorem certitudinem. Phil. III, 1. Vnde vero de traditionibus non scriptis infallibiliter certi esse possumus, quod illæ sint a Deo?

Num e scriptura? At non sunt scriptæ. Num ex testimonio ecclesiæ? At hoc ipsum infallibile non est, quippe cuius auctoritas cum fit humana, fidem diuinam gignere nequit. Quinimmo ne quidem ex antiquioris ecclesiæ testimonio aduersarii suas traditiones vnquam probarunt. Quod fi altius rimemur originem traditionum non scriptarum, manarunt illæ e Pharisaismo.

De Pharifæis constat partim e scriptura, partim ex Iofepho & aliis, quod præter verbum scriptum multas habuerint traditiones a verbo Dei alienas, & ab ipso Christo reiectas. Math. XV, 2. 3. & feqq. IOSEPHVS libr. XIII. antiquit. Iud. c. 18. Nunc, inquit, indicandum est, quod multas constitutiones a maioribus per manus acceptas Pharifæi tradiderint populo, quæ non sunt scriptæ inter leges Mosaicas. Et ideo Sadducæi his auctoritatem derogarunt, dicentes, oportere eas tantum feruari, quæ scripto continentur: atque hinc magna inter vtrosque exorta est controuerfia.

Distinguunt Pontificii inter traditiones Mosaicas, & Pharisaicas, opinantes, Christum pharisaicas quidem, sed non Mosaicas traditiones reiecisse: at frustra. Nam probare nequeunt, Mofen tradidisse dogmata, quæ litteris non sint consignata, sed fideli posterorum memoria conferuata. Christus nos nunquam remittit ad traditiones Mosaicas, sed ad scripturas.

Io. V, 39. Antithefis est Pontificiorum statuentium, traditiones non scriptas diuinas & apostolicas pari pietatis affectu cum verbo Dei scripto suscipiendas esse. Nituntur fequentibus argumentis:

I. Traditiones passim in sacris litteris commendantur, Exod. XIII, 8. Deuter. XXXII, 7. Iudic. V, 13. Resp. In locis citatis intelligitur traditio active, sive actus tradendi, informandi, catechizandi; vocatur communiter institutio, quae fit viva voce, cuius fundamentum est sacra scriptura.

De hac nulla est controversia: sed controvertitur de traditione passive sive obiective sumta, quatenus per illam intelligitur dogma oretenus traditum et sacris litteris non comprehensum, neque ex illis per necessariam consequentiam deducibile.

II. Doctores primitivae ecclesiae symbolum apostolicum et paedobaptismum vocarunt traditiones, fatente CHEMNITIO in exam. conc. Trid. fol. 63. et 69. Sed retinemus symbolum apostolicum et paedobaptismum. Ergo retinemus traditiones non scriptas. Resp. Doctores primitivae ecclesiae sensu laxiori traditionis nomine usi sunt; quia per eam intellexerunt omnem doctrinam de Deo et rebus divinis, quae κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν, qua litteram et expressa verba, in scripturis non continetur: ventilatur hodie controversia de traditionibus non scriptis sensu strictiori ita dictis, quae neque qua ipsa verba, neque qua rem et sententiam in divinis litteris habentur.

III. Paullus nos remittit ad traditiones, 2 Thess. II, 15. State, fratres, et tenete traditiones, quas edocti estis, sive per verbum, sive per epistolam nostram. Resp. Apostolus loquitur de doctrina, ratione substantiae eadem, sed diversimode tradita; utpote quae tum viva voce, tum scriptis, membris ecclesiae proponebatur.

Particula disiunctiva εἴτε non disiungit dogmata tradita, sed diversos tradendi modos. Priusquam enim canon scripturae absolueretur, viri θεόπνευστοι, multa tradebant voce, quae postea in litteras referebant. Hodie, completo canone biblico, ad traditiones non scriptas confugere non est integrum.

IV. Paullus commendat Timotheo traditiones, 1 Tim. VI, 20. O Timothee, depositum (doctrinam viva voce traditam) custodi. Per depositum non intelligunt Pontificii verbum scriptum, quod anxia custodia non videtur indigere, cum illud in thecis suis facile retineatur. Resp. Depositi nomine intelligitur non traditio, sed tota doctrina coelestis, Timotheo discipulo a doctore Paullo primum viva voce tradita ex Mose et prophetis, Act. XXVI, 22. et in litteras postea relata. Depositum enim doctrinae a Paullo non opponitur script. S. ut ei opponuntur traditiones, sed (ut patet e v. 21.) profanis vocum inanitatibus et falso nominatae scientiae. Quare mens apostoli est: O Timothee, doctrinam coelestem, et viva voce, et scriptis tibi traditam, custodi: contra summo studio vita disputationes sophisticales, quibus doctrina evangelica simplicioribus redditur dubia.

V. Paullus multum tribuit traditionibus non scriptis, 1 Cor. XI, 23. Ego accepi a domino, quae tradidi vobis. Concludit idem caput his verbis: cetera, cum venero, disponam. Resp. Paullus in capite citato v. 23. intelligit traditionem scriptam: agit namque de institutione coenae dominicae, quae non tantum hic a Paullo, sed et a tribus euangelistis scripta fuit. Dispositio autem apostolica, cuius fit mentio v. 34. pertinet ad caerimonias et ritus, ad aedificationem in ecclesia utiles. At vero nobis hic sermo est non de caerimoniis, quae ex traditionibus ritualibus condisci possunt, sed de dogmatibus fidei morumque praeceptis, homini saluando creditu factuque necessariis, quae unice e verbo scripto addiscuntur.

VI. Dari in ecclesia traditiones non scriptas innuit Ioannes cap. XXI, 25. Sunt vero etiam alia multa, quae fecit Iesus, quae si scriberentur singula, nec ipsum arbitror mundum capturum eos, qui scriberentur, libros. Resp. Concedimus, non esse omnia, quae Christus dixit aut fecit, ab euangelistis scripta, sed negamus aliquid eorum, quae ad fidem et mores sunt necessaria, esse ab illis praetermissum. Praeclare inquit CYRILLUS libr. XII. in Ioann. cap. ult. Non omnia, quae dominus fecit, conscripta sunt, sed quae scribentes, tam ad mores, quam ad dogmata putarunt sufficere. Nec minus scite ait AUGUSTINUS Tract. XLIX. in Ioann. c. 11. Electa sunt, quae scriberentur, quae saluti credentium sufficere videbantur (*).

VII. Comprobat Ioannes traditiones non scriptas Ep. II, 12. 13. & Ep. III, 13. 14. Cum multa habeam, quae vobis scriberem: non volui per chartam & atramentum (scribere). Sed spero, venturum me ad vos, & ore ad os locuturum, ut gaudium nostrum sit impletum.

1) Non loquitur Ioannes de universa scriptura, sed de hac ipsa sua epistola, in qua electa foeminæ non omnia scripsit. 2) Cuiusmodi sint illa, quæ negat Ioannes se per litteras scribere voluisse, nemo facile divinabit. 3) Si aduertarii perspicue ostendent, ea, quæ Ioannes cretenus electæ foeminæ tradidit, fuisse dogmata fidei morumque præcepta, omnibus quæ necessaria, recipiemus in nos, singula ex verbo scripto demonstrare.

VIII. Traditio ecclesiæ necessaria videtur tum ad probandam sacræ scripturæ divinam originem, tum ad genuinum eius sensum eruendum.

Res. Divina scripturæ origo cum ex externis & internis, tum præcipue ex interno testimonio Spiritus S. innotescit.

Testimonium ecclesiæ de divinitate scripturæ lubentes acceptamus, vt argumentum insigne, sed non vnicum, præcipuum & absolute necessarium.

Verum scripturæ sensum quærimus & invenimus in ipsa scriptura, sicut gladius in vagina, margarita in concha, anima in corpore invenitur.

Confentens patrum, dictum aliquod biblicum interpretantium, expositio a nobis recipitur vt adminiculum hermeneuticum externum, manuducens & secundario confirmans, non vt principium fundamentale, neque vt infallibilis interpretandi norma ().

Quæst. (*) Addere mihi liceat hæc duo: 1) Si hæc verba, Io. XXI, 25. conferamus cum illis, quorum eadem est sententia, XX, 30. & 31. aperte palamque Ioannes profitetur, ea, quæ scripta sunt, sufficere ad fidem & salutem: 2) Habent ne Romano-Catholici res Christi gestas omnes, quas eius Legati memoriæ non prodiderunt, a Maioribus acceptas? Quantam, quæso, & quam plenam miraculorum oportet esse traditionem eiusmodi, quæ suo ambitu complectitur eas res ad vnam omnes, quas, si litteris fuissent consignatæ, ne mundus quidem, comprehenfurus fuisset! ()

Ad conficiendum hoc negotium haud parum conferet argumentatio κατ’ ἄνθρωπον, & ea quidem duplex. 1) Dicunt differentes, in Concil. Trid. sess. IV. decr. 1. se recipere traditiones continua successione in ecclesia catholica conferuatas. Vbinam vero terrarum est illa successio continua in iis causis, in quibus ecclesia Romana manifesto defecit ab antiqua institutione, eaque perpetua, non interrupta serie? Exempla sunt, sole clariora, hæc duo potissimum: institutione Sc. S. & de calice in sanctissimo epulo. Proterant igitur traditionem, & successionem continuatam, quum ne vnum quidem producere valeant testem loquentem ex tota antiquitate, per priora XII. sæcula. En ipsorum confessionem, l. c. sess. XXI. cap. 1. & 2. 2) Græca atque orientalis ecclesia similiter traditiones valde suscepit, velut normam credendorum atque agendorum. Earum in numero sunt quædam, multum diversæ ab his, quas Romanenses venerantur, nimirum in illis controversiis, in quibus græca ecclesia longe a romana discedit. Vtra igitur est vera traditio? Illa ne, quæ in græca ecclesia seruatur? an hæc, quam Romano-catholici summa obferuantia colendam arbitrantur? Quænam adeo continua successio, de qua tantopere se iactant Romanenses? Quid tandem? Non verentur, hoc præ se ferre: Scripturam S. admodum incertam esse, ambiguam valdeque dubiam. Quare autem? Propterea, inquiunt, quod hæretici ad scripturam confugiunt, eamque ad sua animi sensa detorquent. Estne igitur hoc incertum, ad quod errantes non minus, quam recte sentientes, prouocant? Si hæc valet consequentia: efficitur, vt traditiones itidem sint incertæ, si quidem hæretici, quibus ipsi Græcos adnumerant, ad Apostolicas traditiones prouocare solent. Quod nobis responderunt, id idem sibi redditum habebunt.


### Q. LII

What is the efficacy of Holy Scripture? The efficacy of Holy Scripture is a supernatural power, communicated to it by God himself, by which it not only reveals and exhibits the will of God, and persuades one to render obedience to it, but also, by divine ordination, as a most valid medium, it converts, regenerates, renews, and saves men corrupted by sins, with the Holy Spirit concurring.

Obj. The arduous and salutary doctrine concerning the efficacy of Holy Scripture is to be delivered professedly in Part III of Theology, where we must treat of the means of grace and salvation, among which is the Word of God: let it suffice to have tasted of it here.

Latin:

Quae est efficacia sacrae scripturae? Efficacia sacrae scripturae est vis supernaturalis, ipsi a Deo communicata, qua illa non tantum revelat & exhibet voluntatem Dei, atque huic praestandum obsequium suadet, sed etiam ex ordinatione divina ut medium validissimum homines peccatis corruptos, concurrente Spiritu sancto, convertit, regenerat, renovat & salvat.

Obs. Ardua & salutifera de efficacia sacrae scripturae doctrina ex professo tradenda est parte III. Theol. ubi agendum est de mediis gratiae & salutis, e quorum censu est verbum Dei: hic eam praelibasse sufficiat.


### Q. LIII

Is Holy Scripture necessary to be known by all who aspire to eternal salvation? Holy Scripture is the principle of faith and morals, necessary not by an absolute necessity (a), but by a hypothetical one (b).

Holy Scripture is necessary not only by the necessity of command (c), but also of means (d), and therefore Scripture, both of the Old (e) and New Testament, is to be attentively read, or at least devoutly listened to when proposed by the voice of a teacher, and most deeply pondered by all men who are to attain eternal life, to whom no invincible impediment is opposed.

Prob. a. That Holy Scripture is not necessary by absolute necessity is evident, because there was a time when the Holy Scriptures did not exist, namely from Adam to Moses.

It happens that there is no abundance of them to be read, if, for instance, a Christian is carried off into the captivity of the Turks, Tartars, or other barbarians.

It may happen that, with Mars raging, there are no schools, no opportunities by which a boy or girl may be imbued with the knowledge of reading.

Moreover, it happens not rarely that a man is by nature impotent, such as a blind man, an infant, etc., to whom no law is set, because the kingdom of grace presupposes the kingdom of power.

Conf. DANNHAV. hodof. phaenom. I. p. 87. Prob. b.

The hypothetical necessity of Holy Scripture shines forth both from divine ordination and from the need of men.

For by the benefit of Scripture, the Church, extending most widely, is to be preserved until the end of the age: the enticements of corruptions and errors are to be averted, the infirmity of human memory is to be relieved, and the certainty of faith is to be established.

For the Word of God was written for the sake of ἀσφάλειαν [certainty], for the sake of greater certainty; Luke 1:

3. Prob. c. That the Holy Scriptures were consigned by divine command, both external and internal, we have clearly shown above in

Q. XII, p. 80, 81. Prob. d.

From John 20: 31. These are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.

St. John teaches that Holy Scripture is a medium, divinely ordained, for kindling faith in Christ and obtaining eternal life.

Prob. e. From the command of Christ, John 5:

39. Search the scriptures, for you think that in them you have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me. The Lord Jesus speaks of the Scripture of the Old Testament (for the writings of the apostles did not exist at that time) and commands that men, tending toward eternal salvation, should diligently search the writings of Moses and the prophets.

For which reason the Scripture of the Old Testament is to be read: 1) On account of the command of Christ: 2) On account of the foundation of the Christian faith, which is that Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah, and the meritorious cause of eternal salvation (*). 3) On account of the clearer understanding of the writings of the New Testament, in in which the scriptures of the Old Testament are most frequently cited: 4) On account of the refutation of the Jews, Acts XVIII, 28: 5) On account of our solid hope & consolation, Rom.

XV, 4. *Antithesis The antithesis is 1) of the Papists, who maintain that Holy Scripture is not so necessary that the church can be without it.

2) Of the Schwenkfeldians & Weigelians, to whom Holy Scripture is a dead letter; hence they refer their disciples to the internal natural word & to immediate revelations. 3) Of the Socinians, who deny the necessity of the Holy Scripture of the O.T.; the stronger of their arguments are:

I. The ancient church from Adam to Moses was preserved without the written word of God. Therefore, without it, the modern church can be propagated.

Resp. The condition of those times, in which the patriarchal church flourished, and of the following times is different. For the patriarchs were μακρόβιοι [long-lived], i. e. long-lived, so that they prolonged their lives to almost a thousand years. Men also were fewer then, and frequent immediate divine revelations occurred. Consequently, at that time, the heavenly doctrine could be conveniently transmitted by word of mouth from long-lived fathers, immediately illuminated, to the assembly of believers, which was not so large. But indeed, with the increase of the human race and the shortening of the course of human life, God himself made a majestic beginning of writing, and commanded his word to be recorded διὰ τὸ ἀσφαλὲς [for the sake of security], to establish the certainty of our faith, Phil.

III, 1.

II. From Moses to Christ, for two thousand years, scriptures indeed existed, yet they were only those of the Jews, while the remaining nations, among whom not a few had the true religion, used only unwritten tradition. For that many men, besides the Israelites, truly believed in God, Job & his friends testify.

Resp. It is false that religious people situated outside the camp of Israel lacked the written word: the contrary is clear from the example of the Eunuch, Acts VIII.

Add the Babylonian captivity, and the dispersion of the Israelites, who carried the scriptures with them.

Consider also thoroughly the Greek version of the Bible, most widely propagated among many nations. III.

In the very people of God, although scriptures existed, the Jews nevertheless used tradition more than scripture, as is evident from Exod. XIII, 8.

Resp. In the cited passage, active tradition is understood, i. e. the act of handing down, preaching & catechizing, with dependence on the written law as a norm. IV.

Up to the time of Ezra, the scriptures were not reduced to order so that they could be conveniently read, but were held dispersed in various papers, and sometimes, through the negligence of the priests, were not found for a long time, 2 Kings XXII, 8. Resp. Ezra indeed reduced the books of Moses & the prophets into order and one system; but the Israelites had the books themselves written down successively.

And although the public copy was kept rather negligently by the priests, the laity, however, read their own private copies within their own walls.

Furthermore, it is wrongly inferred: Before Ezra there was not the same order of prophetic writings that exists today: Therefore scripture is not necessary. For the sacred letters were not so confused & disordered that they could not be read.

V. It differs from the old in that in the O. [Testament] there are prophecies, in the N. [Testament] the fulfillments of the same, which, if they are referred to one sum, all appear joined in Jesus of Nazareth, 2 Corinth. I, 20. so that not even the least thing is contained in the whole Christian religion which was not foretold in the O.T., Acts XXVI,

22. since finally it is certain that 3) a fulfillment without a prophecy, to which it entirely corresponds, can neither be understood nor held as true: it is clear how necessary it is that the New Testament be perpetually compared with the old. V. Various heresies have arisen from Holy Scripture: Therefore it would have been better if it did not exist.

Resp.

Heresies arise not from Scripture, but from the distortion of Scripture.

Nay, rather, Holy Scripture is the means of repelling heresies.

The New Testament is to be inscribed not so much on paper as on the heart, "You are a letter of Christ, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God." Resp.

These things are not opposed, but consistent.

For Scripture is necessary for this reason, that when it is attentively read, properly known, and rightly applied, the New Testament may be inscribed upon our hearts, since that inscription does not happen immediately, but mediately.

VII. The reading of the Old Testament does not seem necessary today, because the promises of eternal life are not contained in it.

For that reason, Christ is called the mediator of a better testament, which has been established upon better promises. Resp.

In the cited passage, the Old and New Testament are not taken for the books of the O. and N.

T., but for the legal covenant, which is called the Old Testament, and the evangelical, which is called the New Testament.

Its promises are said to be better not by reason of the good promised, but by reason of the condition required.

For the Old Testament, or legal covenant, indeed promises eternal life, but under the condition of perfect obedience, which after the fall is impossible for us. The New Testament, however, or evangelical covenant, promises eternal life under the condition of faith, which is conferred upon all who admit the means of grace.

Add that the evangelical promises are superior to the legal ones by reason of efficacy; because the law only promises life to the obedient, but does not confer the strength to obey.

The Gospel, however, not only promises eternal life to those who believe, but also bestows the strength to believe.

Quest. LIV. To what practical uses is the meditation of Scripture to be applied?

The practical uses to which the reading and meditation of Scripture are to be transferred concern both faith and life, or the morals of men. Faith is considered in various ways, according as it is to be generated, preserved, or defended.

Faith is to be generated in the souls of unbelievers; to those who attentively read Holy Scripture, this very thing is the seed of regeneration and of kindling faith. For believers in a tranquil state, faith is to be preserved; it is nourished by the written Word of God as if by the purest milk, and is strengthened as if by solid food. In a turbulent or afflicted state, Holy Scripture is to be defended against the assault of the devil, the perfidy of heretics, the afflictions of the world, and the allurements of the flesh, as the sword of the Holy Spirit, with which, like Christ, we defeat the devil and his satellites. What is more?

For afflicted Christians, Holy Scripture is a storehouse of all vivifying consolation.

"Whatever things were written before were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the Scriptures might have hope." A life worthy of Christians is to be directed and conformed to the rule of Scripture, that they may live εὐσεβῶς, godly, toward God, σωφρόνως, temperately, toward themselves, δικαίως, justly, toward their neighbor. Therefore, he who is about to read the Holy Scriptures with salutary fruit should properly attend to which utterances of the Holy Spirit make for supporting faith, and which for passing a life piously, soberly, and justly, and should inscribe them most deeply upon the tablets of his heart.

Latin:

Estne sacra scriptura omnibus ad aeternam salutem adspirantibus cognitu necessaria? Sacra scriptura est principium fidei & morum necessarium, necessitate non absoluta (a), sed hypothetica (b).

Necessaria est sacra scriptura necessitate non solum mandati (c), sed & medii (d), adeoque scriptura tam veteris (e), quam novi testamenti attente legenda, vel saltem voce docentis proposita devote auscultanda, penitissimeque pensitanda est omnibus hominibus aeternam vitam adepturis, quibus invincibile non obiicitur impedimentum.

Prob. a. Quod S. scriptura non sit necessaria necessitate absoluta, patet, quia fuit tempus, quo sacrae litterae non fuerunt, nempe ab Adamo ad Mosen.

Contingit, ut earum legendarum non sit copia, si scilicet christianus abripiatur in captivitatem Turcarum, Tartarorum, aut aliorum barbarorum.

Potest fieri, vt, saeviente Marte, nullae sint scholae, nullae occasiones, quibus puer, aut puella, notitia lectionis imbuatur.

Quinimmo accidit haud raro, vt homo per naturam fit impotens, vtpote caecus, infans &c. cui lex nulla est posita, quia regnum gratiae supponit regnum potentiae.

Conf. DANNHAV. hodof. phaenom. I. p. 87.

Prob. b. Hypothetica S. scripturae necessitas tum ex ordinatione divina, tum ex indigentia hominum elucescit.

Beneficio namque scripturae ecclesia latissime patens ad consummationem seculi est conferuanda: corruptelarum illecebrae & errores sunt avertendi, infirmitas memoriae humanae sublevanda, fideique certitudo stabilienda est.

Scriptum quippe est verbum Dei ἀσφάλειαν, propter maiorem certitudinem; Luc.

I, 3. Prob. c. Mandato divino externo, & interno, consignatas esse sacras litteras, perspicue ostendimus supra quaest.

XII. p. 80.

81. Prob. d. ex Io. XX, 31. Haec scripta sunt, vt credatis, quod Iesus sit Christus, filius Dei, & vt credentes vitam habeatis in nomine ipsius.

Docet S. Ioannes, S. scripturam esse medium, diuinitus ordinatum, ad accendendam fidem in Christum, & consequendam vitam aeternam.

Prob. e. Ex mandato Christi Io.

V, 39. Scrutamini scripturas, quia vos existimatis, quod in iis vitam aeternam habeatis: atqui illae sunt, quae testantur de me. Loquitur dominus Iesus de scriptura veteris testamenti, (neque enim eo tempore scripta apostolorum extabant) & praecipit, vt homines, ad aeternam salutem tendentes, scripta Mosis & prophetarum sedulo scrutentur.

Quam ob rem legenda est scriptura vet. testam. 1) Ob mandatum Christi: 2) Ob christianae fidei fundamentum, quod est, Iesum Nazarenum esse Messiam, & aeternae salutis caussam meritariam (*). 3) Ob planiorem intelligentiam scriptorum noui testamenti, in quibus scripta veteris testamenti frequentissime adducuntur: 4) Ob elenchum Judaeorum, Act. XVIII, 28: 5) Ob solidam spem & solatium nostrum, Rom.

XV, 4. Antithesis Antithesis est 1) Pontificiorum, statuentium, S. scripturam non adeo necessariam esse, quin ea carere possit ecclesia.

2) Schwenkfeldianorum & Weigelianorum, quibus S. scriptura est littera mortua; hinc ad verbum internum naturale & ad immediatas revelationes discipulos suos remittunt. 3) Socinianorum, necessitatem S. scripturae V. T. infitiantium; quorum potiora sunt argumenta:

I. Vetus ecclesia ab Adamo ad Mosen conservata est sine verbo Dei scripto. Ergo sine eodem ecclesia hodierna propagari potest.

Resp. Dispar est ratio temporum illorum, quibus floruit ecclesia patriarchalis, & sequentium temporum. Patriarchae enim erant μακρόβιοι, i. e. longaevi, ut ad mille propemodum annos vitam produxerint. Homines etiam tunc erant pauciores, & crebrae fiebant divinae revelationes immediatae. Proinde id temporis doctrina caelestis a longaevis patribus, immediate illuminatis, ad coetum credentium, non adeo magnum, viva voce transmitti commode potuit. At vero aucto mortalium genere, & imminuto vitae humanae curriculo, Deus ipse augustum scribendi fecit initium, verbumque suum consignari iussit διὰ τὸ ἀσφαλὲς, ad stabiliendam fidei nostrae certitudinem, Phil.

III, 1.

II. A Mose usque ad Christum per duo annorum millia exstiterunt quidem scripturae, ex tamen solae erant Judaeorum, reliquae autem gentes, in quibus haud paucis vera erat religio, sola traditione non scripta utebantur. Vere enim in Deum credidisse, praeter Israëlitas, homines bene multos, testantur Iobus & eius amici.

Resp. Falsum est, religiosos extra castra Israëlis constitutos caruisse verbo scripto: contrarium liquet exemplo Eunuchi, Act. VIII.

Adde captivitatem Babylonicam, & dispersionem Israëlitarum, scripturas secum advehentium.

Penitus etiam considera versionem bibliorum graecam, inter gentes plurimas latissime propagatam. III.

In ipso populo Dei etsi scripturae extarent, magis tamen utebantur Judaei traditione, quam scriptura, ut patet ex Exod. XIII, 8.

Resp. Loco citato intelligitur traditio activa, i. e. actus tradendi, praedicandi & catechizandi, cum dependentia a lege scripta, tanquam norma. IV.

Vsque ad tempus Esdrae scripturae non redactae fuerunt in ordinem, ut commode legi potuerint, sed dispersae in variis chartis habebantur, & aliquando ex negligentia sacerdotum longo tempore non inventae, 2 Reg. XXII, 8. Resp. Libros Mosis & prophetarum Esdras redegit quidem in ordinem vnumque systema; sed ipsos libros successive conscriptos habuerunt Israëlitae.

Et licet publicum exemplar negligentius asservatum fit a sacerdotibus, laici tamen, priuatos inter parietes, peculiaria sua legerunt exemplaria.

Praeterea perperam colligitur: Ante Esdram non idem ordo fuit scriptorum propheticorum, qui hodie est: Ergo scriptura non est necessaria. Neque enim ita confusae & conturbatae fuerunt sacrae litterae, vt legi nequiuerint.

V. Ex veteri in eo differat, quod in V. sint vaticinia, in N. eorundem complementa, quae, si ad vnam summam referantur, omnia in Iesu Nazareno coniuncta adpareant, 2 Corinth. I, 20. vt adeo ne quidem minimum in tota religione Christiana contineatur, quod non fuerit in V.T. praenuntiatum, Act. XXVI,

22. quum denique certum fit, 3) complementum fine vaticinatione, cui illud omnino respondet, neque intelligi posse, neque pro vero haberi: perspicuum est, quam fit necesse, vt nouum Test. cum antiquo perpetue conferatur. V. Ex S. scriptura variae exortae sunt haereses: Ergo satius fuisset, si non exstaret.

Resp.

Haereses oriuntur non ex scriptura, sed e detorsione scripturae.

Quin potius S. scriptura medium est repellendarum haeresium.

Novum testamentum non tam chartae, quam cordi inscribendum est, Estis epistola Christi scripta non atramento, sed Spiritu Dei vivi.

Resp.

Haec non sunt opposita, sed consentanea.

Ideo enim scriptura est necessaria, vt illa attente lecta, probe cognita, & recte applicata, novum testamentum cordibus nostris inscribatur, cum illa inscriptio non fiat immediate, sed mediate.

VII. Lectio veteris testamenti hodie non videtur necessaria, quia in eo non habentur promissiones vitae aeternae.

Ea de causa Christus dicitur melioris testamenti mediator, quod super melioribus promissionibus sancitum est. Resp.

Loco citato vetus & novum testamentum non accipitur pro libris V. & N.

T. sed pro foedere legali, quod vetus, & euangelico, quod novum testamentum appellatur.

Huius promissiones meliores dicuntur non ratione boni promissi, sed ratione conditionis requisitae.

Nam vetus testamentum, sive foedus legale, promittit quidem vitam aeternam, sed sub conditione perfectae obedientiae, quae post lapsum nobis impossibilis est, Novum vero testamentum, sive foedus euangelicum promittit vitam aeternam sub conditione fidei, quae omnibus media gratiae admittentibus confertur.

Adiice, quod promissiones euangelicae praestant legalibus ratione efficaciae; quia lex solum promittit obedientibus vitam, sed vires obediendi non confert.

Euangelium vero non solum credentibus vitam aeternam pollicetur, sed etiam vires credendi largitur.

Quast. LIV. Ad quos usus practicos applicanda est meditatio scripturae?

Usus practici, ad quos transferenda est lectio & meditatio scripturae, concernunt tum fidem, tum vitam, sive mores hominum. Fides diversimode consideratur, prout nempe vel generanda, vel confervanda, vel defendenda est.

Fides generanda est in animis infidelium; quibus attente legentibus sacram scripturam, haec ipsa est semen regenerationis & accendendae fidei, Fidelibus in statu tranquillo confervanda fides verbo Dei scripto, velut purissimo lacte nutritur, velut cibo solido corroboratur, In statu turbulento, sive afflicto, ab insultu diaboli, haereticorum perfidia, afflictionibus mundi, carnisque illecebris defendenda est scriptura sacra, tanquam gladio Spiritus sancti, quo, instar Christi, diabolum eiusque satellites profligamus. Quid? quod christianis afflictis sacra scriptura est promptuarium omnis consolationis vivificae.

Quaecunque praescripta sunt, in nostram doctrinam praescripta sunt, vt per patientiam & consolationem scripturarum spem habeamus. Vita christianis digna dirigenda & conformanda est ad regulam scripturae, vt vivant εὐσεβῶς, pie, erga Deum, σωφρόνως, temperanter, erga seipsos, δικαίως, iuste, erga proximum. Quocirca lecturus salutari cum fructu sacras litteras, probe attendat, quae eloquia Spiritus S. ad fidem fulciendam, quae ad vitam pie, sobrie & iuste transigendam faciant, eaque tabulis cordis sui penitissime inscribat.


### Q. LV. How is the Holy Scripture to be read, so that we may attain the aforementioned uses?

The Holy Scriptures are transferred to salutary uses if we read them piously and with the imploring of divine aid, so that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give us the Spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of Him, and the eyes of our mind enlightened, Eph. 1:17-18. Attentively and with singular reverence, so that we may know not only theoretically that the Holy Scripture is the Word of God, but also practically, and with a solid assent of faith, receive this true Word of God. For the Holy Scripture is a letter of the omnipotent God to His creature, in which the words of God sound, and the heart of God is learned, as Gregory the Great says, Book IV, ep. 84. Accurately, so that with diligent inquiry we may search the Scriptures, John 5:39, and investigate their genuine meaning. Assiduously, so that we may meditate on the law of God day and night, Ps. 1:2. Obediently, so that we may be not only readers or hearers, but also doers of the Word, James 2:22.

Latin:

Transferuntur sacrae litterae ad salutares usus, si eas legamus pie & cum imploratione auxilii diuini, vt Deus domini nostri Iesu Christi, pater gloriae, det nobis Spiritum sapientiae & reuelationis in cognitionem sui & illuminatos oculos mentis, Eph. I, 17. 18. Attente & singulari cum reuerentia, vt non tantum theoretice cognoscamus, sacram scripturam esse verbum Dei, sed & practice, & solido fidei assensu, verum hoc verbum Dei recipiamus. Est enim sacra scriptura epistola omnipotentis Dei ad creaturam suam, in qua verba Dei sonant, & cor Dei discitur, dicente Gregorio M. L. IV, ep. 84. Accurate, vt solicita indagine scrutemur scripturas, Io. V, 39. earumque genuinum sensum inuestigemus. Assidue, vt diu noctuque in lege Dei meditemur, Ps. I, 2. Obedienter, vt non tantum lectores vel auditores, sed etiam factores verbi simus. Iac. II, 22.


### Q. LVI. How is the mind of man to be confirmed in the divinity of Scripture?

To a weak brother, doubting the divine origin of the Scriptures, arguments taken from external κριτήρια (criteria), or motives of credibility, are to be proposed, so that he may be induced to read the Holy Scripture piously, attentively, and accurately. If he does this, he will be moved, both by internal κριτήρια (criteria) and especially by the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit, to believe in the immediate dependence of the Holy Scriptures upon God.

Latin:

Fratri infirmo, de diuina scripturarum origine dubitanti, proponenda sunt argumenta petita a κριτηρίοις externis, siue motiuis credibilitatis, vt inducatur ad scripturam sacram pie, attente, accurateque legendam. Quod si fecerit, cum κριτηρίοις internis, tum inprimis testimonio Spiritus S. interno, permouebitur ad credendam immediatam sacrarum litterarum a Deo dependentiam.


### Q. LVII. How are those to be raised up who grieve and mourn because they have received little or no fruit from the Holy Scripture, though

They are to be excited to pious prayers, by which the more abundant grace of the Holy Spirit is obtained. The sacred psalmist shines before us with a most praiseworthy example, Ps. 119:18, 34, sighing: Reveal my eyes, that I may see the wonders from Thy law. Make me to understand, that I may keep Thy law, and observe it with my whole heart. They are to be admonished to inquire into their own life and morals, and to renounce more serious sins, if they are indulging in any, and to extricate themselves from the cares of this world by which they have been ensnared. These are the thorns by which the seed of the divine Word is suffocated, Luke 8:14.
