Intent upon sacred meditations, they should await the hour of divine sweetness, until they taste it from the most free dispensation of God. Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you disquieted within me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise Him; the salvation of my countenance (He) and my God, says the King-prophet, Ps. 42:12.

Latin:

Sunt illi excitandi ad pias preces, quibus copofior Spiritus S. gratia impetratur. Praelucet nobis perquam laudabili exemplo hieropsaltes, Ps. CXIX, 18. 34. suspirans: Reuela oculos meos, vt videam mirabilia e lege tua. Intelligere fac me, vt custodiam legem tuam, & obseruem eam toto corde. Admonendi sunt, vt inquirant in vitam moresque suos, & peccatis grauioribus, si quibus indulgent, nuntium remittant, curisque huius seculi, quibus irretiui fuerunt, se expediant. Hae sunt spinae, quibus semen verbi diuini suffocatur. Luc. VIII, 14. Meditationibus sacris intenti expectent horam suauitatis diuinae, donec hanc ex dispensatione Dei liberrima degustent. Quid incuruas te, anima mea, & quid tumultuaris super me? Expecta Deum, quia adhuc confitebor illi; salutes facierum mearum (ille) & Deus meus, inquit Rex propheta, Ps. XLII, 12.


### Q. LVIII. How are those to be roused who read the Holy Bible unwillingly?

(1) The divine command must be inculcated upon them, Deut. 6:7-8; John 5:39. (2) The example of Martha and Mary must be urged, Luke 10:40 ff. (3) The goodness and wisdom of God must be shown to them to shine forth in the Holy Scripture as in a most limpid mirror, Matt. 11:25-26. (4) The most abundant utility of Scripture must be commended to them, 2 Tim. 3:16. Of what goods are they deprived who sleep in such slothful laziness that they never, or only unwillingly, wear out the holy book with their hands. On the contrary, they are entangled in the foulest errors and many evils, Matt. 22:29. You err, not knowing the Scriptures.

SIGH.

S I G H.

With the most ardent prayers, I beseech Thee, O God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, Father of glory, that Thou wouldst give us, out of grace provoked by no merits of our own, the Spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of Thee, and enlightened eyes of the mind for the saving understanding of Thy word, comprised in the prophetic and apostolic writings!

We kiss the Scripture, signed by Thy inspiration. It is our love, our delight, our spiritual treasury, our storehouse, full of every consolation. Thy Scripture is a most luminous epistle, sent to us from heaven, in which Thy words resound, from which Thy heart is learned. Thou hast opened Thy heart burning with love, O supreme Arbiter of things, in Thy divine letters Thou hast laid bare Thy mind, Thou hast revealed Thy counsel concerning the raising up of the fallen sinner, and leading him into the heavenly fatherland, if he does not unwillingly admit the aids of Thy grace. Supply, O most merciful God, spiritual strengths to us, that we may follow Thy counsel promptly, that we may be intent upon the nod of Thy will, that we may imprint Thy word upon the tablets of our hearts, and express it in good deeds, and finally at some time be drawn by Thee to Thee!

Latin:

(1) Inculcandum est illis mandatum diuinum, Deut. VI, 7. 8. Io. V, 39. (2) Vrgendum est exemplum Marthae & Mariae, Luc. X, 40. seqq. (3) Oftendendum illis est, bonitatem & sapientiam Dei in sacra scriptura, velut speculo limpidissimo, relucere, Matth. XI, 25. 26. (4) Commendanda illis est vtilitas scripturae vberrima, 2 Tim. III, 16. Quibus bonis priuantur, qui tam supinae indormiscunt ignauiae, vt vel nunquam, vel inuiti sacrum codicem manibus terant. Contra iidem foedissimis erroribus plurimisque malis implicantur. Matth. XXII, 29. Erratis nescientes scripturas.

SVSPIRIVM.

S V S P I R I V M.

Calidissimis precibus a te, Deus, pater domini nostri Iesu Christi, pater gloriae, efflagito, vt des nobis ex gratia, nullis nostris meritis prouocata, Spiritum sapientiae & reuelationis in cognitionem tui, & illuminatos oculos mentis ad salutarem intelligentiam verbi tui, scriptis propheticis & apostolicis comprehensi!

Exosculamur scripturam, te inspirante consignatam. Est illa noster amor, nostrae deliciae, nostrum spirituale aerarium, nostrum penu, plenum omnis solatii. Scriptura tua est epistola luculentissima, de caelo ad nos missa, in qua verba tua sonant, ex qua cor tuum discitur. Flagrans amore cor tuum aperuisti, summe rerum arbiter, in diuinis tuis litteris patefecisti mentem tuam, reuelasti consilium tuum de peccatore lapso erigendo, & in patriam caelestem perducendo, si subsidia gratiae tuae non inuitus admittat. Suffice, o Deus misericordissime, nobis vires spirituales, vt consilium tuum sequamur promti, ad nutum voluntatis tuae simus intenti, verbum tuum & tabulis cordium imprimamus, & bonis factis exprimamus, atque tandem aliquando per te ad te trahamur!


## 4 Concerning God

CHAPTER I.

CONCERNING GOD.

Quest. I. In what manner of consideration is God treated here? He is treated here as the objective end of theology. Proved.

Since theology is a practical science, first of all its end must be treated. But since the end of theology is twofold—one indeed objective, which is God, infinitely perfect and supremely good; the other formal, which is the beatific vision and enjoyment of God—therefore the objective end of theology, namely God, most fully satisfying the appetite of man, must be considered first.

Quest. II. What is understood by the name of God? By the name of God is understood the first being, which is from itself and the cause of all other things; and which preserves and governs all things. Proved.

All men who are wayfarers experience in themselves that they do not conceive, or cannot conceive, God otherwise than in relation to created things, as the first being, which is from itself and the cause of all other beings, and preserves and governs all things; or as the most excellent being of all, than which nothing better or more perfect can be or be thought. Pressed by calamity, the Gentiles implored the help of God, and named Him the best and greatest: conscious of evil in themselves, they dreaded Him as a most just and powerful judge: reasoning that there is nothing prior to God, nothing more excellent.

Quest. III. Does it behoove man to strive with the greatest effort to know God? It is necessary for man to expend much labor in attaining the knowledge of God (1) on account of the dignity of the knowledge of God (a).

On account of its greatest utility (b).

Proved a. From the divine oracle Jer. 9:22, 23. Thus said Jehovah: let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the strong man glory in his strength, neither let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, to understand and know Me, that I (am) Jehovah, doing mercy, justice, and judgment in the earth.

By as much as eternal things excel native things, and immortal things excel perishable things: by so much is the true knowledge of God to be preferred to all other sciences.

Learnedly says HIERONYM.

Hieronymus in epitaph. nepot. Without knowledge of his creator, every man is a beast. And excellently Hilarius, book VIII. de Trinit. He does not know how to be wise, who does not know God.

Prob. b. This is eternal life, that they may know you the only true God, and whom you have sent, Jesus Christ, says the Truth itself, John XVII, 3. Since the true knowledge of the true God, as Christ testifies, becomes the cause of eternal life, and as it were a mother bringing forth everlasting salvation, it becomes most commendable to us all.

Latin:

CAPVT I.

DE DEO.

Quæst. I. Quo considerandi modo hic de Deo agitur? Agitur hic de Deo vt fine obiectiuo theologiae. Prob.

Cum theologia sit scientia practica, primo omnium de eius fine agendum est. Cum autem finis theologiae sit duplex, vnus quidem obiectiuus, qui est Deus infinite perfectus & summe bonus, alter vero formalis, qui est visio & fruitio Dei beatifica; ideo finis theologiae obiectiuus, nempe Deus, appetitum hominis plenissime fatians, primum considerandus est.

Quæst. II. Quid intelligitur nomine Dei? Nomine Dei intelligitur ens primum, quod a se & ceterorum causa est; quodque omnia conferuat & gubernat. Prob.

Experiuntur in se homines viatores omnes, quod Deum non aliter concipiant, aut concipere possint, quam in ordine ad res creatas, vt ens primum, quod a se & ceterorum entium omnium causa est, & omnia conferuat ac gubernat; vel vt ens omnium excellentissimum, quo nihil melius, nihil perfectius esse, aut cogitari potest. Pressi calamitate gentiles implorarunt opem Dei, eumque nominarunt optimum maximum: male sibi conscii reformidarunt ipsum, vt iudicem iustissimum & potentissimum: rati Deo nihil esse prius, nihil praestantius.

Quæst. III. Num hominem summa ope niti decet, vt Deum cognoscat? Oportet hominem assequendae notitiae Dei plurimum operae impendere (1) ob τῆς θεογνωσίας dignitatem (a).

Ob maximam eiusdem vtilitatem (b).

Prob a. Ex oraculo diuino Ier. IX, 22. 23. Sic dixit Iehouah: ne glorietur sapiens de sapientia sua, neque glorietur fortis de fortitudine sua, neque glorietur diues de diuitiis suis; sed de hoc glorietur, qui gloriatur, intelligere & nosse me, quod ego (sum) Iehouah, faciens misericordiam, iustitiam & iudicium in terra.

Quanto aeterna natiuis, immortalia caducis antecellunt: tanto vera Dei cognitio omnibus aliis scientiis est anteponenda. scientiis est anteponenda.

Scite inquit HIERONYM.

Hieron. in epitaph. nepot. Absque notitia sui creatoris omnis homo pecus est. Et praeclare Hilarius, libr. VIII. de Trinit. Nescit sapere, qui Deum nescit.

Prob. b. Haec est vita aeterna, ut cognoscant te solum verum Deum, et quem misisti, Iesum Christum, inquit ipsa veritas, Io. XVII, 3. Cum vera veri Dei cognitio, teste Christo, fit causa vitae aeternae, et quasi mater sempiternam salutem pariens, eadem nobis omnibus fit commendatissima.


### Q. IV. Whence is the knowledge of God (theognosia), or the knowledge of God, sought?

The knowledge of God is sought both from the light of nature, or reason, and from the light of revelation. From which the knowledge of God (theognosia) is commonly distinguished into natural and revealed. The former is pedagogical, the latter is saving.

Latin:

Notitia Dei petitur tum ex lumine naturae, sive rationis, tum ex lumine revelationis. Ex quo θεογνωσία in naturalem et revelatam communiter distinguitur. Illa paedagogica, haec salutifera est.


### Q. V. What is natural knowledge of God?

Natural knowledge of God is that by which man, from principles known by nature, knows the existence, essence, attributes, and actions of God to a certain extent: It is divided into innate and acquired. Innate natural knowledge of God is a perfection, congenital to man as a wayfarer and analogous to a habit, by which the human intellect, aided by the truth of propositions about God that are self-evident, perceives them by their terms, without discursive reasoning, and gives them undoubted assent . Acquired natural knowledge of God is that which is obtained both from the testimony of others and from the contemplation of creatures through discursive reasoning .

Obs. I. By the light of nature By the light of nature are understood here the principles of nature and reason, upon which the natural knowledge of God rests as upon a reason for knowing; which have obtained the name of light, because they are to the intellect a reason for knowing other things, and they relate to it as light, which, joined to colors, is to the visual power a reason for seeing and knowing colors, relates to the visual power. Wisely says Phil. Melanchthon in erot. dial. p. m. 234. as light is stored in the eyes for discerning bodies: so light in the mind are innate notions, by which we are advanced to some knowledge of God.

Obs. II. Principles of nature and reason Principles of nature and reason, from which God is known to a certain extent, are otherwise called innate notions, also common notions about God, and are certain as it were ruins or remnants of the divine image, about which Augustine discourses excellently in book I. de spirit. et lit. c. XXVIII. The image of God in the human soul has not been so worn away by the stain of earthly affections, that no extreme outlines of it have remained; whence it can deservedly be said that the impious, even in the very impiety of their life, do some things of the law, or are wise.

Obs. III. Principles of nature and reason Principles of nature and reason, from which God is in some way made known, are either theoretical or practical. Theoretical are: God is, God is one, true, good, omnipotent, most just, etc. God is the preserver and governor of this universe. The practical principle is: God is to be worshipped.

Prob. a. (1) Innate natural knowledge of God. Innate knowledge of God is gathered from the apostolic utterance, Rom. II, 14. For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law (written by Moses), do by nature those things which are of the law: these, although they do not have (that) law, are a law unto themselves. (Indeed) who show the work of the law (not the letter) written in their hearts, while their conscience bears witness to them, and their thoughts accuse or even excuse them among themselves.

We argue: Whoever naturally do those things which are of the law, and by this very fact show that the work of the law is written in their hearts, with their conscience convicting them, they by this very fact testify that the knowledge of God, as the rewarder of good and the avenger of evil, is naturally innate. But, the Gentiles not having the external law, etc. Therefore.

The major premise is established, because (α) those who naturally do the things that are of the law, the law of nature is in them, which they observe as a norm in acting. (β) If that law is written in the hearts of men, since it is not written through regeneration, it must be that it was written through creation, and that it has survived from creation and is innate. Moreover, the knowledge and worship of God pertains to the written law, as the chief part of the natural law. For not only the commandment about loving one's neighbor, but also about worshipping God, pertains to the law of nature. (γ) He who is convicted by his conscience of things done well or ill, necessarily presupposes a first judge having dominion over consciences, and a supreme legislator forbidding and punishing evil, and commanding and rewarding good.

(2) The consensus of all the gentiles is added. For, in the judgment of M. TULLIUS, book I of the Tusculan Disputations, no nation is so savage, no one among all so monstrous, that his mind has not been imbued with an opinion of the Gods. Many hold perverse views about the Gods; for that is usually brought about by corrupt custom. Yet all judge that there is a divine power and nature. Nor indeed is this effected by the conversation or consensus of men: the opinion has not been confirmed by institutions, nor by laws. But in every matter the agreement of all nations must be considered the law of nature. And in book II On the Nature of the Gods the orator says: it is innate to all, and as it were engraved on the mind, that there are Gods.

It is therefore established τὸ εἰ ἔστι, that is, the true existence of the innate knowledge concerning God; but τὸ τί ἔστι, that is, its definitive account, is not so clear. From this it comes about that it is defined in various ways even by orthodox theologians. For some wish it defined by a proximate faculty, others by a disposition, others by a habit, others by a perfection, or light congenital to the human intellect and analogous to a habit.

Let us listen to D. MUSAEUS accurately distinguishing about innate knowledge of God in his Introduction to Theology, p. 80. Modern theologians do not assert that an actual knowledge of God, or its impressed species, exists in man before the use of reason. Indeed, there are those who expressly deny it. Nor are there wanting those who reject its impressed species. Whatever, therefore, it is that, in their opinion, can be said to be in the intellect by nature, or to be innate to it, it must return to a certain inborn perfection, or light of the intellect, aided by which it perceives the truth of common notions about God, once the terms are grasped, immediately and without discourse. And in this they almost agree; although some call that innate perfection a habit, others something analogous to a habit, and some call it an imperfect habit and a disposition. And whoever adds to this the instinct inculcated by the ancient Fathers, innate to man by nature, which adds weight to the intellect, and which, together with that innate perfection, determines it to assent to other common notions about God, and especially to that which is about His existence, immediately and without discourse, will, in our judgment, have strayed not at all from the truth.

We, rejecting the false judgments of others, believe that innate knowledge of God is not a habit in the strict sense; since that consists in impressed species well coordinated and disposed among themselves. But neither the species of creation nor of creatures are properly impressed upon us by nature. Indeed, experience testifies that we conceive of God in no other way than in relation to created things, as the first being, which is from itself, and is the cause of all other things, preserving and governing all creatures. We do not, however, deny that innate knowledge of God is a certain perfection, innate to man as a wayfarer and analogous to a habit. Which analogy consists in the following. (1) Just as the image of God in the protoplast humans was a habit: so the remaining parts of it, to which pertains the law of nature, declaring that God is to be worshipped, in some manner approach its nature; since homogeneous parts are of the same nature as the whole. (2) Just as a habit is a certain perfection superadded to nature, facilitating it for operation: so also natural knowledge of God is superadded to the cognitive faculty, inclining it to apprehend God in whatever manner. (3) Just as a habit is with difficulty movable: so deeply does this natural knowledge inhere in the soul, nor can it be entirely eradicated.

For which reason HENR. NICOLAI, tract. de notit. natural. cap. II. p. 26, does not contradict us, saying: The word habit is taken either in the philosophical rigor, for a firm and stable quality superimposed upon a power, rendering the subject easy and prompt to act; or the word habit is taken more generally for any disposition whatsoever, from which, if it be perfected by labor, a habit can be made and arise; and thus, generally, natural knowledges can be said to be present by way of a habit; because that luminous disposition remains in the intellect, by which, with nature as a guide, one can see the truth, and if one investigates it dexterously, one can, in the success of time, bring it forth into a habit.

Nor does LEICHNER in synopsi vera apod. pag. 398 dissent entirely. Natural knowledges are present to an intellect ignorant of terms, not indeed by an explicit act, nor even habitually, yet according to a natural disposition and proclivity.

(2) For those who look upon creatures with applied care, a threefold path lies open for acquiring knowledge of God: (a) The path of causality, by which we know the first efficient cause from effects, the creator from creatures, and the best, most powerful, and most wise preserver and governor from the most ornate and wise governance of this universe.

The argument here is taken from a most evident axiom: The effect testifies concerning the cause, and its perfection.

(b) The path of eminence, by which, whatever we discover to be most perfect in creatures, we attribute to God in a most eminent way by the force of a principle most known by nature: Whatever is in the effect, pre-exists in the cause.

From which we conclude that all perfections which are in creatures are in the creator either formally or eminently.

Prob. b.

Latin:

Notitia Dei naturalis est, qua homo ex principiis, natura notis, exsistentiam, essentiam, attributa et actiones Dei quadantenus cognoscit: Diuiditur in insitam, et acquisitam. Notitia Dei naturalis insita est perfectio, homini viatori congenita et habitu analoga, qua intellectus humanus adiutus veritatem euidentium de Deo propositionum, apprehendis earum terminis, citra discursum perspicit, iisdemque indubitatum assensum praebet . Notitia Dei naturalis acquisita est, quae tum ex aliorum testificatione, tum ex creaturarum intuitu per discursum comparatur .

Obs. I. Per lumen naturae Per lumen naturae heic intelliguntur principia naturae et rationis, quibus notitia Dei naturalis, velut rationi cognoscendi innititur; quae luminis appellationem fortita sunt, quod intellectui sunt ratio cognoscendi res alias, et ad eum se habent, vt lumen, quod coloribus coniunctum potentiae visivae est ratio videndi et cognoscendi colores, ad potentiam visivam se habet. Scite inquit Phil. Melanchthon in erot. dial. p. m. 234. vt lumen in oculis conditum est ad cernenda corpora: ita lumen in mente sunt notitiae innatae, quibus prouehimur ad qualemcunque notitiam Dei.

Obs. II. Principia naturae et rationis Principia naturae et rationis, e quibus Deus quadantenus cognoscitur, dicuntur alias notitiae innatae, item communes de Deo notiones, et sunt quaedam quasi rudera aut reliquiae imaginis divinae, de quibus praeclare disserit Augustinus libr. I. de spirit. et lit. c. XXVIII. Non vsque adeo in anima humana imago Dei terrenorum affectuum labe detrita est, ut nulla in ea velut lineamenta extrema remanserint; vnde merito dici possit, impios etiam in ipsa impietate vitae suae facere aliqua legis, vel sapere.

Obs. III. Principia naturae et rationis Principia naturae et rationis, e quibus Deus quodammodo innotescit, sunt vel theoretica, vel practica. Theoretica sunt: Deus est, Deus est vnus, verus, bonus, omnipotens, iustissimus et c. Deus est conseruator et gubernator huius vniuersi. Principium practicum est: Deus est colendus.

Prob. a. (1) Notitia Dei naturalis insita Notitia Dei insita colligitur ex effato apostolico, Rom. II, 14. Quando namque gentes, quae legem (Mosis scriptam) non habent, natura ea, quae legis sunt, faciunt: hi licet legem (istam) non habeant, sibi ipsis sunt lex. (Quippe) qui demonstrant opus legis (non litteram) scriptum in cordibus suis, dum illis testimonium perhibet conscientia illorum, et inter sese cogitationes accusant, vel etiam excusant.

Argumentamur: Quicunque naturaliter faciunt ea, quae sunt legis, et hoc ipso ostendunt, opus legis inscriptum esse cordibus suis conuincente eos conscientia, illi hoc ipso testantur, notitiam de Deo, tanquam boni remuneratore et mali vindice, naturaliter esse insitam. Atqui, gentiles legem externam non habentes et c. Ergo.

Maior constat, quia (α) qui naturaliter faciunt ea, quæ sunt legis, illis lex natura inest, quam velut normam in agendo observant. (β) Si ista lex scripta est in cordibus hominum, quum non per regenerationem inscripta fit, oportet eam per creationem inscriptam, atque adhuc e creatione superstitem atque connatam esse. Pertinet autem ad legem inscriptam notitia & cultus Dei, tanquam pars legis naturalis præcipua. Neque enim tantum præceptum de diligendo proximo, sed etiam de colendo Deo ad legem naturæ spectat. (γ) Qui convincitur a conscientia de bene vel male actis, is necessario supponit primum iudicem dominium habentem in conscientias, & legislatorem summum mala vetantem & punientem, bona præcipientem & remunerantem.

(2) Accedit gentilium omnium consensus. Neque enim, iudice M. TVLLIO libr. I. Tusculan. quæst. ulla gens tam fera, nemo omnium tam immanis est, cuius mentem non imbuerit Deorum opinio. Multi de Deis prava sentiunt; id enim vitioso more effici solet. Omnes tamen esse vim & naturam divinam arbitrantur. Nec vero id collocutio hominum, aut consensus efficit: non institutis opinio est confirmata, non legibus. Omni autem in re consensio omnium gentium lex naturæ putanda est. Et libr. II. de natur. Deor. orator inquit: omnibus innatum est, & animo quasi insculptum, esse Deos.

Constat itaque τὸ εἰ ἔστι, sive existentia vera notitiæ de Deo innatæ; at τὸ τί ἔστι, sive eius definitiva ratio, non adeo liquida est. Ex quo fit, ut a theologis etiam orthodoxis diversimode definiatur. Alii enim eam per facultatem propinquam, alii per dispositionem, alii per habitum, alii per perfectionem, aut lucem intellectui humano congenitam & habitui analogam, definitam volunt.

Auscultemus D. MVSAEVM de notitia Dei insita accurate differentem in introduct. in theol. p. 80. Non afferunt theologi moderni, ante rationis usum homini inesse cognitionem Dei actualem, sive eius speciem impressam. Quin inveniuntur, qui id diserte negant. Neque desunt, qui eius speciem impressam inficiantur. Quicquid ergo est, quod ex illorum mente intellectui natura inesse, sive ei connatum dici possit, necesse est, vt redeat ad ingenitam quandam perfectionem, sive lucem intellectus, qua adiutus veritatem communium de Deo notionum, apprehensis terminis, statim citra discursum perspiciat. Atque in hoc fere conveniunt; licet perfectionem illam innatam alii habitum, alii quidpiam habitui analogum, nonnulli habitum imperfectum & dispositionem appellent. Cui qui addiderit inculcatum a Patribus priscis instinctum, natura homini insitum, qui intellectui pondus superaddat, eumque una cum illa ipsi innata perfectione qualicunque ad assensum, tum aliarum communium de Deo notionum, tum eius inprimis, quæ est de existentia ipsius, immediate & citra discursum præbendum determinet, a vero nihil, nostro quidem iudicio, aberraverit.

Nos, falsis aliorum iudiciis, censemus, notitiam Dei insitam non esse habitum exquisite dictum; quippe qui consistit in speciebus impressis inter se bene coordinatis ac dispositis. At nec creationis, nec creaturarum species proprie nobis sunt natura impressæ. Sane experientia teste Deum non aliter concipimus, quam in ordine ad res creatas, vt ens primum, quod a se, & ceterorum causa est, omnes creaturas conservans & gubernans. Non tamen diffitemur, notitiam Dei insitam esse perfectionem quandam, homini viatori congenitam & habitui analogam. Quæ analogia consistit in sequentibus. (1) Sicut imago Dei in hominibus protoplastis fuit habitus: ita reliquæ eiusdem, ad quas pertinet lex naturæ, Deum colendum esse dictitans, ad ipsius naturam quodammodo accedunt; cum partes homogeneæ sint eiusdem naturæ cum toto. (2) Sicut habitus est quædam perfectio superaddita naturæ, eam facilitans ad operationem: ita quoque notitia Dei naturalis superaddita est facultati cognoscitivæ, illam inclinans ad apprehendendum quocunque modo Deum. (3) Sicut habitus est difficulter mobilis: ita profunde inhaeret ista notitia naturalis animae, nec penitus eradicari potest.

Quam ob rem nobis non contradicit HENR. NICOLAI, tract. de notit. natural. cap. II. p. 26. inquiens: Vox habitus sumitur vel in rigore philosophico, pro firma & stabili qualitate potentiae superiecta, facile & promptum reddente subiectum ad operandum; vel vox habitus generalius accipitur pro qualicunque dispositione, ex qua, si elaborando perficiatur, habitus fieri & exsurgere queat; & sic generaliter per modum habitus notitiae naturales inesse dici possunt; quia ista dispositio luminosa in intellectu superest, qua veritatem duce natura quis videre, & si eam dextre investiget, in habitum eam successu temporis protollere possit.

Neque plane dissentit LEICHNER. in synopsi vera apod. pag. 398. Naturales notitiae terminorum ignaro intellectui non quidem actu expresso, nedum habitualiter, secundum dispositionem tamen naturalemque proclivitatem insunt.

(2) Creaturas adhibita cura intuentibus triplex patet via ad notitiam Dei acquirendam: (a) Via causalitatis, qua ex effectis causam efficientem primam, e creaturis creatorem, ex ornatissima sapientissimaque huius universi gubernatione conservatorem & gubernatorem optimum, potentissimum & sapientissimum cognoscimus.

Argumentum hic petitur ab axiomate euidentissimo: Effectus testatur de causa, eiusque perfectione.

(b) Via eminentiae, qua, quidquid in creaturis maxime perfectum deprehendimus, Deo modo eminentissimo tribuimus vi principii natura notissimi: Quidquid est in effectu, praexistit in causa.

Ex quo colligimus, omnes perfectiones, quae sunt in creaturis, esse in creatore vel formaliter, vel eminenter.

Prob. b.


### Q. V. What is natural knowledge of God?: (1) That natural knowledge of God is acquired from the testimony of others, experience itself speaks of all day long

(1) That natural knowledge of God is acquired from the testimony of others, experience itself speaks of all day long.

For Christian, Turkish, Tartar, and Gentile parents instill the name and knowledge of God into their children from their tenderest years: they invoke God daily, both great and small: they swear by God: they appeal to God as witness and judge, etc.

By this more frequent mention of the divine name in daily life, natural knowledge of God is acquired, and once acquired, it is confirmed.

ON THE NATURAL KNOWLEDGE OF GOD. Namely, there shine forth in creatures certain perfections, absolute and simply such, which in their formal concept involve no imperfection, but are better than the creatures themselves.

If we observe in men, the most excellent of visible creatures, the power of understanding and willing, wisdom, goodness, justice, etc. Which perfections are in God formally, and indeed in a most excellent manner.

(c) The way of negation, by which we remove from God whatever implies imperfection in creatures, and attribute to Him the opposite perfection, according to the principle of nature obvious to all: What is supremely perfect, in it there is no defect .

Relying on this principle of nature, we call God independent, infinite, incorporeal, immense, immortal, incomprehensible.

For to depend on another, to be included by certain limits, to bear a corporeal mass, to be terminated by a commensurate space, to be subject to mortality, and to be adequately comprehended by the human intellect, are imperfections of creatures, repugnant to the infinite perfection of the Creator, and therefore to be removed from Him as far as possible.

To this threefold way of knowing God from the contemplation of creatures, the prophets and apostles in their Θεοπνεύσοις (God-breathed) writings point their finger, as it were, in many places where they speak of the natural knowledge of God.

The way of causality is pressed by the king-prophet, Ps.

XIX, 2, singing: The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the work of his hands .

With which words the most pious king opens the school of nature, in which all men are instructed concerning the glory of the artificer of nature.

The heavens declare the glory of God , not by the proclamation of an articulate voice, but by the artifice of the work: just as every work praises the artificer, and every effect testifies concerning the cause, and its perfection.

D. GEIER comments not badly on *Ps.

XIX, 2.

By prosopopoeia, speech is attributed to the heavens, insofar as they objectively perform the same thing that a speaker of articulate words otherwise performs: for they inform and convince the observer that their architect is most good, most wise, most powerful*.

The same way of causality is shown to us by St. Paul, Rom.

I, 19.

20. τὸ γνωστὸν τᾶ Θεᾶ, that which is known of God, is manifest in them: for God has manifested it to them .

For the invisible things of him (even) from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the works; and his eternal power and deity: so that they are without excuse.

Concerning this apostolic utterance, observe: (1) that the apostle speaks generally of all men, who are subject to the divine wrath on account of impiety and unrighteousness, as is evident from v. 18. (2) that by the invisible things he does not understand those hidden mysteries of which Christ speaks in Matt.

XIII, 35, but, as the context teaches, the invisible power and divinity, which become known from the contemplation of creatures.

(3) By ποιήματα Socinus wishes the miracles of Christ to be understood; but he errs and is deceived.

For τὰ ποιήματα in the sacred letters never denote miraculous actions, nor were miracles performed by Christ from the origin of the world; nor does the apostle express a special medium of knowing God, such as the miracles of Christ are, but a general medium of knowing, which could lead even idolatrous nations to the knowledge of God, such as the works effected by the Creator.

(4) Ἀπὸ κτίσεως τᾶ κόσμε , in the opinion of most, is the same as ἐκ κτίσεως , and therefore does not denote the beginning of time, but the medium of knowing: just as in Matt.

VII, 16, the Savior says: ἀπὸ τῶν καρπῶν , by their fruits you shall know them.

The Savior says: ἀπὸ τῶν καρπῶν, by their fruits you shall know them.

Grant, however, that the beginning of time is understood, then the sense will be: From the beginning of creatures, God could be known from his works.

We learn from this classic passage that it is possible to know by the natural light of reason (a) the existence of God, (b) the eternal power of God, (c) his invisibility and spirituality, (d) the creation of this universe, (e) the glory of God which is to be perpetually proclaimed.

The apostle insists on the same way in the sermon at Lystra, Acts

XIV, 17. *God did not leave himself without witness, doing good, giving us rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness.

The apostle inculcates the catholic testimony of divinity; by which God did not leave himself ἀμάρτυρον, declared by no testimony, even to the Gentiles, who were destitute of the testimony of the revealed word: The manner of testimony, that God rendered his goodness attested bythe benefits bestowed on all nations, by sending rains from heaven, and by granting fruitful seasons for the sustenance and recreation of man. Wherefore, as fruits testify to the nobility of the tree; so the benefits of God are the most evident testimonies, from the knowledge of which we ascend to the knowledge of the most exuberant divine goodness.

Latin:

(1) Notitiam Dei naturalem acquiri ex aliorum testificatione

, ipsa experientia toto velut die loquitur.

Nam parentes christiani, turcae, tartari, gentiles, liberis suis a teneris unguiculis nomen ac notitiam Dei instillant: Deum quotidie & magni & parui invocant: per Deum iurant: prouocant ad Deum tanquam testem & iudicem &c.

Qua crebriori nominis diuini mentione in vita quotidiana notitia Dei naturalis acquiritur, acquisita confirmatur.

Neimpe relucent in creaturis quædam perfectiones absolute & simpliciter tales, quæ in suo conceptu formali nullam inuoluunt imperfectionem, sed sunt meliores, quam creaturæ ipsæ.

Si animaduertimus in hominibus, creaturarum visibilium præstantissimis, potentiam intelligendi & volendi, sapientiam, bonitatem, iustitiam, &c. Quæ perfectiones Deo formaliter, & quidem modo excellentiffimo insunt.

(c) Via negationis, qua a Deo remouemus, quidquid in creaturis imperfectionem implicat, eique oppositam perfectionem attribuimus, iuxta principium naturæ omnibus obuiam: Quod summe perfectum est, ei nullus inest defectus.

Hoc principio naturæ subnixi Deum vocamus independentem, infinitum, incorporeum, immensum, immortalem, incomprehensibilem.

Nam dependere ab alio, certis includi finibus, corpoream gerere molem, commensurato terminari spatio, mortalitati subiacere, & ab humano intellectu adæquate comprehendi, sunt imperfectiones creaturarum, infinitæ creatoris perfectioni repugnantes, adeoque ab eodem longissime remouendæ.

Ad triplicem hanc viam, cognoscendi Deum e contemplatione creaturarum, prophetæ & apostoli in scriptis suis Θεοπνεύσοις passim locorum, vbi de naturali Dei cognitione loquuntur, digitum quasi intendunt.

Viam caussalitatis premitt rex propheta, Ps.

XIX, 2. canens: Cæli enumerant gloriam Dei, & opus manuum eius annuntiat firmamentum.

Quibus verbis rex piissimus scholam naturæ aperit, in qua omnes homines instruuntur de gloria opificis naturæ.

Cæli enumerant gloriam Dei, non vocis articulatæ præconio, sed operis artificio: sicut omne opus laudat artificem, & omnis effectus testatur de caussa, eiusque perfectione.

Haud male commentatur D. GEIER. in *Ps.

XIX, 2.

Per profopopœiam cælis tribuitur sermo, quatenus nimirum obiectiue idem præstant, quod alias præstat loquens verba articulata: informant enim ac conuincunt intuentem, quod ipforum architectus fit optimus, sapientissimus, potentissimus*.

Eandem caussalitatis viam nobis commonstrat S.

Paullus Rom. I, 19.

20. τὸ γνωστὸν τᾶ Θεᾶ, quod notum Dei, manifestum est in ipsis: Deus enim ipsis manifestauit.

Nam inuisibilia ipsis (etiam) a creatione mundi operibus intellecta perspiciuntur; æternaque ipsius potentia & deitas: adeo vt sint inexcusabiles.

Circa hoc eloquium apostolicum obferues: (1) quod apostolus loquatur generatim de omnibus hominibus, ob impietatem & iniustitiam iræ diuinæ obnoxiis, vt patet e v. 18. (2) quod idem per inuisibilia non intelligat abscondita illa mysteria, de quibus Christus loquitur Matth.

XIII, 35. sed, docente contextu, inuifibilem potentiam & diuinitatem, quæ e contemplatione creaturarum innotescunt.

(3) Per ποιήματα miracula Christi intellecta vult Socinus; sed fallit & fallitur.

Nam τὰ ποιήματα in sacris litteris nunquam notant actiones miraculosas, neque miracula ab origine mundi a Christo sunt facta; neque exprimitur ab apostolo medium cognoscendi Deum speciale, quale sunt miracula Christi, sed medium cognoscendi generale, quod etiam gentes idololatrix deditas ad notitam Dei adducere potuit, quale sunt opera a creatore effecta.

(4) Ἀπὸ κτίσεως τᾶ κόσμε, plurimorum ex sententia idem est, quod ἐκ κτίσεως, adeoque non notat initium temporis, sed medium cognoscendi: sicut Matth.

VII, 16.

Saluator inquit: ἀπὸ τῶν καρπῶν, ex fructibus eorum cognoscetis eos.

Fac tamen, intelligi initium temporis, tum sensus erit: Inde ab initio creaturarum Deus ex operibus potuit cognosci.

Discinus ex hoc dicto classico, naturali rationis lumine cognosci posse (a) existentiam Dei, (b) potentiam Dei æternam, (c) eius inuisibilitatem & spiritualitatem, (d) creationem huius vniuerfi, (e) gloriam Dei perpetuo deprædicandam.

Eidem viæ insistit apostolus in concione Lystrenfi, Act.

XIV, 17. *Deus non fine testimoniis seipsum reliquit, benefaciens, cœlitus nobis pluvias dans, et tempora frugifera, implens cibo et lætitia corda nostra.

Inculcat apostolus catholicum divinitatis testimonium; qua etiam gentibus, destitutis testimonio verbi revelati, Deus se non reliquit ἀμάρτυρον, nullo testimonio declaratum: Testificationis modum, quod Deus bonitatem suam collatis in omnes gentes beneficiis testatam reddiderit, pluvias de cœlo mittendo, et tempora frugifera largiendo in sustentationem et recreationem hominis. Quam ob rem, ut fructus de nobilitate arboris testantur; ita beneficia Dei sunt luculentissima testimonia, e quorum cognitione assurgimus ad notitiam bonitatis divinæ exuberantissimæ.


### Q. V. What is natural knowledge of God?: The hieropsaltes indicates the way of eminence

The hieropsaltes indicates the way of eminence,

Ps. XCIV, 9. He who plants the ear, shall he not hear?

If (he is) the one who forms the eye, shall he not see? The man of God concludes: God planted the ear in man to hear, and formed the eye in him to see.

Therefore, he himself also hears and sees. No other reason for the consequence can be given than that the perfections of effects, if not formally, yet eminently, and through something more perfect, must pre-exist in the cause.

We conclude, imitating the author of the psalms: God gave man understanding, bestowed wisdom, granted freedom of will, conferred the power of acting.

Therefore, God understands in the most perfect way, is wise, and acts most freely and powerfully. Saint Paul combines the way of negation with the way of causality and eminence in his Areopagitic sermon, Acts XVII, 22. 23. 24. 25. Standing in the midst of the Areopagus, the apostle said:

Men of Athens! I perceive that in all things you are too superstitious.

For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription: TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you.

God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands; neither is worshipped with men's hands, as though he needed any thing: for he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things.

The Areopagite apostle, who had erected an altar τῷ ἀγνώστῳ, to the unknown God, and worshipped him in a temple made with hands, intending to lead them to the knowledge of the true God, convinces them by concluding from effect to cause, from the fabric of the world to its Lord, and by showing that the author of life lives most blessedly, and the giver of all good things suffers from no lack of good, as if he had said: You must worship, O Athenians, who are too superstitious, the true and living God.

He is the true God, who, by creating heaven and earth, has abundantly testified that he is the best, most powerful, and wisest Lord of this universe.

He is living, who, by granting life, breath, and all the necessities of life to all living beings, clearly shows that he lives a most blessed life, free from all defect.

But the Lord of this universe is circumscribed by no place, bound by no necessary temple, since he is immense, infinite, and incomprehensible.

And the author of life and of all good things is in need of no ministry that would be useful to him, since he, abounding in his own riches, is αὐταρκέστατος.

The antithesis is of certain Scholastics who deny this proposition: God is, by himself, known to us.

Latin:

Viam eminentiæ indigitat hieropsaltes,

Ps. XCIV, 9. Qui plantat aurem, nonne audiet?

Si (est) formans oculum, num non spectabit? Concludit vir Dei: Deus plantavit in homine aurem ad audiendum, et formavit in eo oculum ad videndum.

Ergo ipse etiam audit et videt. Ratio consequentiæ alia dari nequit, quam quod perfectiones effectuum, si non formaliter, tamen eminenter, et per aliquid perfectius in causa præexistere oporteat.

Imitatur psalmorum auctorem concludimus: Deus homini dedit intellectum, donavit sapientiam, indulsit libertatem arbitrii, contulit vim agendi.

Ergo Deus modo perfectissimo intelligit, sapit, liberrime potentissimeque agit. Viam negationis cum via causalitatis et eminentiæ conjungit S. Paullus in concione Areopagitica, Act. XVII, 22. 23. 24.

25. Constitutus in medio Areopago apostolus dixit: Viri Athenienses! per omnia superstitiosiores vos video.

Transiens enim et circumspiciens cultus vestros, inveni etiam altare, in quo inscriptum est: Ignoto Deo. Quem ergo ignorantes colitis; eum ego annuntio vobis.

Deus, qui fecit mundum, et omnia, quæ in illo, hic cum cœli et terræ dominus fit, non in manu factis templis habitat; neque a manibus hominum colitur, quasi ullius rei indigeat: quia ipse dat omnibus vitam, et spiritum et omnia.

Apostolus Areopagita, qui τῷ ἀγνώστῳ, Deo ignoto, altare extruxerant, eundemque in templo manu facto colebant, ad veri Dei notitiam perducturus, eosdem convincit, ab effectu ad causam, a fabrica mundi ad eius dominum concludendo, et ostendendo, auctorem vitæ vivere beatissime, et datorem omnium bonorum nullius boni defectu laborare, perinde ac si dixisset: Colendus est vobis, o Athenienses nimis quam superstitiosi, verus et vivus Deus.

Verus Deus est, qui fabricando cœlum et terram, se optimum, potentissimum, atque sapientissimum dominum huius universi esse, abunde testatus est.

Vivus est, qui, omnibus animantibus vitam, halitum, omniaque vitæ subsidia concedendo, se vitam sane quam beatissimam omnisque defectus expertem agere, non obscure ostendit.

At dominus huius universi nullo loco circumscriptus, nullo templo necessario alligatus est, cum sit immensus, infinitus et incomprehensibilis.

Et auctor vitæ omniumque bonorum, nullius ministerii, quod ipsi sit usui, est indigus, cum ipse suis pollens opibus fit αὐταρκέστατος.

Antithesis est Scholasticorum quorundam, negantium hanc propositionem: Deus est, per se nobis esse notam.


### Q. V. What is natural knowledge of God?: 2) Of the Socinians, some of whom deny both acquired and innate natural knowledge of God, and some only innate knowledge of God

2) Of the Socinians, some of whom deny both acquired and innate natural knowledge of God, and some only innate knowledge of God.

3) Of the Cartesians who assert that the idea of God, representing his existence, is innate in us.

These rely on the following arguments.

I. Nothing is in the intellect that was not first in the senses.

Therefore, there is no innate natural knowledge of God.

The reason for the consequence is that God, who is the purest spirit, falls under no sense. Reply:

That much-repeated statement is not universal.

For in the intellect of Adam in his integrity, there was a habit of concreated wisdom, not drawn from sensual observation.

After the fall, remnants of the divine image remained, which do not depend on the senses.

Wherefore, that axiom is to be understood of uncomplex intelligible species, which after the fall are not naturally im pressed on the intellect, but are held by the benefit of abstraction, but not concerning concreated and connate habits, which are present in the intellect before abstraction. Therefore, before sensory perception, there is nothing in the intellect regarding the ideal representation of things: yet there is something in the intellect regarding habitual knowledge.

Instance I. This opinion seems to overturn itself. For no habit, no habitual knowledge is given before the impressed species of things, since, as experience testifies, the species of things firmly impressed upon the intellect and well coordinated and disposed constitute a habit. For example, a physicist has transmitted the species of natural things from objects to his intellect through the intervention of the senses, and has firmly impressed them upon it, and thus has acquired for himself habitual knowledge of natural things. Resp. The term habit is taken either specially, and in philosophical rigor, for a quality of a power naturally superadded by firm impression, for the promptness of acts: we do not deny that impressed species are required for this habit strictly so called: or it is taken analogically, for a certain perfection of the human cognitive power superadded, in the manner of a habit inhering deeply in the intellect: and inclining the same to recognize the truth. There is indeed not given after the fall in the human intellect a species or innate idea representing the essence of God: yet there is given in the same a certain connate light, by which the truth of common notions about God is perceived without discourse: there is given an inclination implanted in the human intellect, by which it is inclined to readily provide assent to evident propositions about God. D. CALOVIUS supports us in tom. II. system. theol. p. 80, writing thus: Natural knowledge of God is not properly called habitual, or a habit, but κατ’ ἀναλογίαν, and thus it is recognized as an imperfect habit, or a disposition, which is a way to a habit. Although therefore knowledge about God is not present in man before the use and exercise of reason, as far as an expressed species and some idea conceived by the mind: we do not think it should be denied that there is given in man either a disposition, or something analogous to a habit, namely some τελείωσιν of the intellectual power in man, remaining after the fall, by whose benefit man can know God to some extent without a teacher.

Instance II. Man does not by nature understand the truth of the most common propositions about God before their terms are explained to him. Therefore, the most common propositions about God are not known to man by nature. The reason for the consequence is because the knowledge of propositions depends on the knowledge of terms. If these are ignored, the propositions themselves are ignored. The antecedent is clear, since the terms of these propositions: God is; God is best, greatest; God is the creator of the world, are not known by nature. Resp. If the terms of common notions about God were known to man by nature, without any discourse, or information from others, the knowledge of God would be actual, not habitual. For this implies nothing other than a perfection, a light, and a certain inclination, innate to the human intellect, by which the intellect, aided, discerns the truth of evident propositions about God as soon as their terms are explained and apprehended, and approves them with ready assent.

II. The opinion of divinity is from faith. Heb. XI, 6. Therefore it is not natural. Resp. These are not opposites. God is known from nature: He is savingly believed from sacred scripture: just as the distinction between just and unjust is established both from nature and from scripture.

III. The world did not know God in its wisdom. 1 Cor. I, 21. Resp. The world did not know God by special and saving knowledge, yet it knew Him by general and pedagogical knowledge.

IV. The natural man does not receive the things that (are) of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness to him; and he cannot know them, because they are spiritually discerned, 1 Cor. II, 14. Resp. The apostle speaks of the mysteries of faith transcending the grasp of reason left to itself, and manifested to us for our salvation by the supernatural revelation of God; which we frankly admit become known to us only from the light of scripture. V. Gentiles served those who by nature are not Gods. Gal. IV, 8. Therefore they did not know the true God.

Resp. Distinguish between simple cognition, by which a gentile man knows God: and cognition applied to a certain object, namely the true God. All gentiles formed for themselves this concept of God, that He is the first and most excellent being, by whom all created things are conserved and governed; but they did not rightly apply that concept. They knew this major proposition by the guidance of the light of nature: The true God is to be worshipped religiously. But they formed the minor proposition badly: heaven, the sun, Jupiter, etc., is the true God. Therefore Heaven, the sun, Jupiter, etc., is to be worshipped religiously.

VI. Whoever says in his heart: there is no God: in them there is no natural knowledge of God. But the impious, etc. Ps. XIV, 1. Therefore.

Resp. 1) The sacred psalmist speaks of the affection of a malicious heart. The impious man wishes, wills, and desires that there be no God, who might see and punish wicked deeds. Therefore, one must distinguish between a simple ignorance of God and a malicious denial of Him. For however there may be those who, stirred by the affection of a malicious heart, deny that God exists, they are not entirely ignorant of Him. Peter denied Christ, whom he did not ignore.

2) He speaks of those who deny the providence of God more than His existence. For impious men conduct themselves in life and morals just as if God, the inspector of morals, were nowhere. Tit. I, 10.

VII. If natural knowledge of God were implanted in man as a wayfarer, there would be no atheists. But there are atheists, as Paul testifies, Eph. II, 12. The consequence of the major is clear, because whatever is naturally implanted adheres necessarily and immutably.

Resp. 1) Men are called atheists either absolutely and simply because of a defect of general knowledge of God; or comparatively and in a certain respect, because of a defect of special and saving knowledge of God. Gentiles before the preaching of the gospel were atheists comparatively and in a certain respect, because they did not know God savingly in Christ. Yet there was in them a general knowledge of God, which by divine intention ought to have been a leading to further inquiry and knowledge of God, which is had in the church.

2) Some atheists are such not speculatively, but practically, who deny God by their deeds. VIII. Experience testifies that there have not only been those who denied the existence of God, but also those who have impugned it with arguments; the procession of whom is led by Julius Caesar Vaninus, the Caesar of atheists, with XII disciples, spreading atheism through Gaul, an Italian by nation, burned at Toulouse. Therefore there are atheists not only practically, but also speculatively such.

Resp. Such speculative atheists can exist not by nature, but through the just desertion of God and the blinding of the devil; not through a total eradication of the light of nature, as regards habit, but through suffocation, as regards act and exercise; not through the whole space of life and permanently, but only through a certain passing paroxysm, for some time. For the law of nature does not suffer that a settled and firm opinion should adhere to anyone, that there is no God. For although the mind of an impious man is as if lulled into a lethargy, so that he does not think about God: yet no one can be found in whom conscience does not eventually vindicate itself, and even in death itself accuse him of the neglected God.

Cf. Hülsem. breuiar. enucl. cap. II. p. 87. IX.

If

IX. If the knowledge of God were innate in humans, it would certainly be found the same among all people. But many humans are found who have no sense of divinity at all, such as in the New World, Brazil, etc.

Resp. 1) Crellius, Book I, On God, ch. V, p. 47, does not stray far from the truth, saying: Although there may be found peoples in some of whom no opinion of divinity seems to have existed, yet far more have been found in whom an opinion of divinity has existed, even if they were otherwise barbarians and alien to the cultivation of humanity. Furthermore, histories testify that those nations, in whom an opinion of divinity existed, nevertheless have someone whom they fear and, lest he harm them, revere. This is more than enough for us here. For this is also a trace of divinity and religion, even if twisted in the opposite direction. M. T. Cicero saw this long ago, writing excellently in Book I De Legibus: "There is no nation so untamed, nor so savage, that it does not think it must have a God, even if it does not know what kind of God it is fitting to have." Among the Indians and Brazilians, not obscure traces of a recognized Divinity are perceived. For they admit the immortality of the soul, they turn pale at thunder, which they call a trumpet, they have priests, and they celebrate annual assemblies. Some sacrifice to an evil spirit, some to the sun and moon, as Lerio teaches in De nauig. Brasil., ch. XVI. However, I approve of distinguishing here between the natural knowledge of God and its application to the proper object. The barbarians indeed err gravely, offering divine worship to the sun, moon, and demons; yet by that very act they betray an instinct innate to nature and a propensity toward worshipping God. *

Latin:

2) Socinianorum, quorum nonnulli notitiam Dei naturalem tam acquisitam, quam insitam, nonnulli tantum infitam notitiam Dei, infitiantur.

3) Cartesianorum statuentium, ideam Dei, existentiam ipsius repræsentantem, nobis ingenitam esse.

Qui sequentibus innituntur argumentis.

I. Nihil est in intellectu, quin prius fuerit in sensu.

Ergo non datur notitia Dei naturalis infita.

Ratio consequentiæ est, quia Deus, qui spiritus purissimus est, sub nullum cadit sensum.

Resp. Πολυθρύλλητον illud non esse universale.

Nam in intellectu Adami integri erat habitus sapientiæ concreatæ, non ex sensuali observatione haustæ.

Post lapsum remanferunt reliquiæ imaginis divinæ, quæ non pendent a sensibus.

Quamobrem axioma illud intelligendum est de speciebus intelligibilibus incomplexis, quæ post lapsum intellectui natura impressæ pressæ non sunt, sed habentur beneficio abstractionis, non autem de habitibus concreatis & connatas, qui ante abstractionem intellectui insunt. Proinde ante sensualem perceptionem nihil est in intellectu quoad idealem rerum repræsentationem: est tamen aliquid in intellectu, quoad notitiam habitualem.

Instantia I. Hæc sententia videtur seipsam euertere. Nam nullus habitus, nulla habitualis notitia datur, ante species rerum impressas, cum, experientia teste, habitum constituant species rerum firmiter intellectui impressæ, & bene coordinatæ, atque dispositæ. v. gr. Physicus rerum naturalium species interuentu sensuum ab obiectis transmisit ad intellectum suum, eique firmiter impressit, atque adeo habitualem rerum naturalium notitiam sibi comparauit. Resp. Vox habitus sumitur vel specialiter, & in rigore philosophico, pro qualitate potentiæ naturali firma impressione superaddita, ad actus promtitudinem: ad hunc habitum stricte dictum species requiri impressas, non diffitemur: vel sumitur analogice, pro perfectione quadam potentiæ hominis cognoscitiuæ superaddita, per modum habitus profunde intellectui inhaerente: eundemque ad veritatem agnoscendam inclinante. Non datur quidem post lapsum in intellectu humano species vel idea congenita essentiam Dei repræsentans: datur tamen in eodem lux quædam connata, qua veritas communium de Deo notionum citra discursum perspicitur: datur insita humano intellectui procliuitas, qua ad assensum, euidentibus de Deo propositionibus promte præbendum, inclinatur. Adstipulatur nobis D. CALOVIVS tom. II. system. theol. p. 80. ita scribens: Naturalis Dei notitia non proprie habitualis, aut habitus dicitur, sed κατ’ ἀναλογίαν, adeoque imperfectus habitus, vel dispositio agnoscitur, quæ via est ad habitum. Quanquam ergo non insit homini notitia de Deo ante rationis vsum & exercitium, quantum ad speciem expressam & ideam aliquam mente conceptam: non tamen negandum arbitramur, in homine dari siue dispositionem aliquam, siue quoddam analogum habitui, aliquam nempe τελείωσιν potentiæ intellectualis in homine, post lapsum reliquam, cuius beneficio homo Deum quantenus cognoscere possit sine magistro.

Instantia II. Communissimarum de Deo propositionum veritatem homo natura non intelligit prius, quam ipsi termini earum explicentur. Ergo communissimæ de Deo propositiones homini natura non sunt notæ. Ratio consequentiæ est, quia cognitio propositionum pendet a cognitione terminorum. His ignoratis ipsæ propositiones ignorantur. Antecedens liquet, quoniam harum propositionum: Deus est; Deus est optimus, maximus; Deus est creator mundi, termini natura non sunt noti. Resp. Si termini communium de Deo notionum natura homini noti essent, citra vllum discursum, ant aliorum informationem, no-. titia Dei insita esset actualis, non habitualis. Hæc enim nihil aliud infert, quam perfectionem, lucem & procliuitatem quandam, intellectui humano ingenitam, qua intellectus adiutus veritatem euidentium de Deo propositionum, simulatque termini earum explicati & apprehensi sunt, cernit, easque prono assensu approbat.

II. Diuinitatis opinio est ex fide. Hebr. XI, 6. E. non est naturalis. Resp. Hæc non sunt opposita. Deus ex natura scitur: ex scriptura sacra salutariter creditur: sicut discrimen iusti & iniusti tam ex natura, quam ex scriptura constat.

III. Mundus Deum in sapientia sua non cognouit. 1 Cor. I, 21. Resp. Mundus Deum non cognouit notitia speciali & salutari, cognouit tamen eundem notitia generali & paedagogica.

IV. Animalis homo non suscipit ea, quae (sunt) Spiritus Dei: stultitia enim illi sunt; & non potest scire, quia spiritualiter diiudicantur, 1 Cor. II, 14. Relp. Loquitur apostolus de mysteriis fidei captum rationis sibi relictæ transcendentibus, & supernaturali Dei reuelatione ad salutem nostram nobis manifestatis; quæ tantum e lumine scripturæ nobis innotescere ingenue fatemur. V. Gentiles servierunt iis, qui natura non sunt Dii. Gal. IV, 8. Ergo verum Deum non cognoverunt.

Resp. Dist. inter cognitionem simplicem, qua homo gentilis Deum cognoscit: & inter cognitionem applicatam ad certum obiectum, sive verum Deum. Omnes gentiles formarunt sibi hunc conceptum de Deo, quod sit ens primum & excellentissimum, a quo omnia creata conservantur & gubernantur; sed illum conceptum non rite applicarunt. Hanc propositionem maiorem ductu luminis naturæ cognoverunt: Verus Deus est religiose colendus. Sed male formarunt propositionem minorem: cœlum, sol, Iupiter &c. est verus Deus. Ergo Cœlum, sol, Iupiter &c. est religiose colendus.

VI. Quicunque dicunt in corde suo: non est Deus: in illis non est notitia Dei naturalis. Atqui impii &c. Ps. XIV, 1. Ergo.

Resp. 1) Loquitur hieropsaltes de malitiosi cordis affectu. Optat impius, vult & desiderat, ne sit Deus, qui facta nefanda videat & vindicet. Distinguendum itaque est inter simplicem Dei ignorationem & malitiosam eius abnegationem. Utut enim sint, qui concitati malitiosi cordis affectu Deum esse negent, non tamen penitus ignorant. Abnegavit Petrus Christum, quem non ignoravit.

2) Loquitur de illis, qui providentiam Dei magis, quam ipsius existentiam negant. Ita enim se gerunt in vita & moribus homines impii, perinde ac si morum inspector Deus nullibi esset. Tit. I, 10.

VII. Si notitia Dei naturalis homini viatori esset insita, non darentur athei. Sed dantur athei, teste Paulo Eph. II, 12. Consequentia maioris patet, quia quidquid naturaliter insitum est, necessario & immutabiliter inhæret.

Resp. 1) Homines dicuntur athei vel absolute & simpliciter ob defectum generalis notitiæ Dei; vel comparate & secundum quid, ob defectum notitiæ Dei specialis & salvificæ. Gentiles ante prædicationem evangelii fuerunt athei comparate & secundum quid, ideo quod Deum in Christo salvater non cognoverunt. Fuit tamen in illis notitia Dei generalis, quæ ex intentione divina ipsis debebat esse manuductio ad ulteriorem inquisitionem & cognitionem Dei, quæ habetur in ecclesia.

2) Quidam athei non speculative, sed practice tales sunt, qui factis suis Deum abnegant. VIII. Experientia testatur, non solum fuisse, qui existentiam Dei abnegaverint, sed & qui argumentis illam impugnaverint; quorum agmen ducit Iulius Cæsar Vaninus, atheorum Cæsar, cum XII. discipulis, per Galliam atheismum spargentibus, natione Italus, Tolosæ combustus. Ergo dantur athei non tantum practice, sed & speculative tales.

Resp. Possunt dari athei speculative tales non per naturam, sed per iustam Dei desertionem & diaboli excæcationem; non per totalem eradicationem luminis naturæ, quoad habitum, sed per suffocationem, quoad actum & exercitium; non per totum vitæ spatium & permanenter, sed tantum per quendam paroxysmum transeuntem, ad aliquod tempus. Neque enim lex naturæ patitur, ut rata & firma sententia alicui inhæreat, non esse Deum. Quanquam enim mens hominis impii lethargo quasi sopiatur, vt de Deo non cogitet: nullus tamen potest dari, in quo tandem conscientia se non vindicet, & vel in ipsa morte neglecti Dei ipsum accuset.

Conf. Hülsem. breuiar. enucl. cap. II. p. 87. IX.

Si

IX. Si notitia Dei hominibus esset insita, vtique apud omnes homines eadem inueniretur. At multi reperiuntur homines, qui nullum penitus sensum diuinatis habent, vt in nouo orbe, Brasilia &c.

Resp. 1) Haud a vero aberrat Crellius L. I. de Deo c. V. p. 47. inquiens: Licet reperiri sint populi, in quorum aliquibus nulla propemodum videatur exstitisse de diuinitate opinio: tamen longe plures fuerunt reperti, in quibus diuinitatis opinio exstitit, licet alias barbari essent, & ab humanitatis cultu alieni. Deinde testantur historiae, eas nihilo minus gentes, in quibus diuinitatis opinio exstitit, habere aliquem, quem metuant, & ne noceat, reuereantur. Id quod nobis hic plusquam satis est. Est enim & hoc diuinitatis ac religionis, quanquam in contrarium detortum, vestigium. Vidit id dudum M. T. Cicero lib. I. de legib. praeclare scribens: Nulla gens est neque tam immansueta, neque tam fera, quae non, etiamsi ignoret, qualem habere Deum deceat, tamen habendum putet. Apud Indos & Brasilianos haud obscura cernuntur vestigia agniti Numinis. Animae enim immortalitatem admittunt, ad tonitrua, quae tubam vocant, pallent, sacerdotes habent, & conuentus annuos celebrant. Quidam cacodaemoni, quidam soli & lunae sacrificant, docente Lerio de nauig. Brasil. c. XVI. Probo autem hic distinguendum est inter notitiam Dei naturalem, & eius applicationem ad debitum obiectum. Grauiter quidem errant barbari, deferentes cultum diuinum soli, lunae, daemonibus: eo ipso tamen produnt insitum naturae instinctum & propensionem ad colendum Deum. *


### Q. V. What is natural knowledge of God?: X. The Cartesians argue: * If no idea or image representing the essence of God were innate to the human intellect, God could in no way be…

X. The Cartesians argue: * If no idea or image representing the essence of God were innate to the human intellect, God could in no way be known by man from the light of nature.

But God is known by man from the light of nature. Therefore, an idea or image representing the essence of God is innate to man. The consequence of the major premise is proven, because God is an infinite Spirit, devoid of all matter, who cannot be known from the intuition and contemplation of creatures. For between the finite and the infinite, and between spirit and sensible body, there is no proportion, no correspondence.

But when one thing is to be known from another, it is necessary that a certain correspondence intervene between both. Resp. 1) After the loss of wisdom created in the protoplasts, there are no innate ideas, images, or simple intelligible species in the human intellect representing the essence of things to be known, but impressed species of things are transmitted from objects through the senses and the phantasm to the intellect. To which that trite saying points: "There is nothing in the intellect that was not first in the sense." Wherefore the idea representing the essence of God, innate to the human intellect, is a vain dream of the Cartesians. 2) Although God, considered in Himself and His essence, is an infinite spirit, devoid of all matter accessible to the senses, the effects of God, however, are exposed to the senses. Wherefore our intellect, through the species of sensible effects produced by God, transmitted to it by the intervention of the senses and phantasms, is determined to elicit acts of knowing which represent God and His perfections to a certain extent, by means of discourse and through consequence, resting on this principle, most known by nature: "The effect testifies to the cause and its perfection." 3) There is no proportion between the finite and the infinite by way of mathematical commensuration, yet there is a certain correspondence between creator and creature, such as exists between cause and effect, between the signified and the sign.

For the effects produced by God are signs and, as it were, traces representing the goodness, power, and wisdom of God.

most wickedly desires that there be no God, the investigator and avenger of vices: therefore, he also most easily persuades himself that there is none. This is what it means to say in the heart, Ps. XIV, 1. For by the name of heart, Scripture designates not only thoughts, but also and especially pleasures and desires, and that these are also signified in this very place is apparent from the entire series of words. VI. Is natural knowledge of God true? Natural knowledge of God, viewed in itself, is true, as much regarding its principles as regarding the conclusions which are deduced from the principles by manifest consequence.

Proof a. Paul explicitly testifies in Rom. 1:18 that all men considered outside of Christ, among whose number are also the Gentiles, hold down the truth in unrighteousness. The apostle gives the reason why the wrath of God is revealed against the impiety and unrighteousness of all men: because the truth is known to all, if not from the book of Scripture, certainly from the book of nature, which they indeed hold down in unrighteousness. They hold down, as if captive, the true knowledge of God, lest it exert its power. They hold down the truth in unrighteousness; because the justice of God requires that innate knowledge of God be rightly used. For they were implanted by God for this reason, that we might not neglect to seek God, nor remain in impiety or unrighteousness.

Acts 17:27. Proof b. The principles are most true and most certain: God is, God is one, true, good, most wise, most powerful. God is the creator, preserver, and governor of this universe.

Proof c. Practical conclusions flow spontaneously from common notions about God through discourse. For example: God is good, and the author of every good: Therefore God is to be loved above all. God is most wise: Therefore He is to be venerated. He is most just: Therefore He is to be feared. He is most good and most powerful: Therefore trust is to be placed in Him, and His help is to be implored in all harsh circumstances.

Antithesis was once that of Matthias Flacius, Daniel Hofmann, and others, according to whose opinion natural knowledge of God is fallacious and full of many errors, of which their stronger arguments are: I. Whatever knowledge does not recognize the true God, that is false. But by natural knowledge the true God is not recognized. Therefore natural knowledge of God is false. The major premise is certain, because true cognition is conformed to the object being known, it is equal. The minor premise is clear, because the true God is one in essence and three in persons, whom no one recognizes from the principles of nature.

Response Whatever knowledge recognizes neither the true God nor anything about the true God, that is false; I concede this. But although by natural knowledge of God the true God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, is not distinctly recognized, nevertheless something about the true God—namely His existence, goodness, wisdom, justice, etc.—is apprehended, which cognition, although it is inadequate and confused, is nevertheless not false.

Instance: Jews and Muhammadans are said for this reason not to recognize and invoke the true God, because they do not recognize and invoke God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Response: Jews and Muhammadans not only are ignorant of, but also deny the Holy Trinity; nor do they only conceive of God under a confused being as omnipotent and wise, but they also positively add a contrary concept, restricting the essence of God, conceived confusedly, to one person, and thus they adore an idol, or a figment of their own heart.

II. Because all men by nature are foolish, they deny God. Ps. 14:1. Rom. 3:10. Therefore their natural knowledge of God is full of errors.

Response Natural knowledge of God, viewed in itself, is true, to which imperfection and a proclivity toward errors adheres accidentally, and does not take away its truth; since indeed the Gentiles also hold it down in unrighteousness, Rom. 1:18.

Question VII. Is natural theognosy useful? Natural theognosy promises a threefold utility, namely pedagogical, insofar as it leads man to seek that assembly in which the true God of Israel manifested itself (a): didactic, because it contributes not a little to illustrating the revealed knowledge of God, if it is used soberly (b); paedeutic, for directing morals and external discipline in the church, and outside the same (c). Proof a. Paul in the Areopagite discourse, Acts XVII, 24, warns the Gentiles to seek the Lord, if they might grope for Him and find Him. Just as groping is an obscure knowledge (the blind are accustomed to grope with their hands, cf. Is. LIX, 10): so finding is a full knowledge, and perfect according to the condition of travelers, which is not had except from supernatural light.

Let them seek therefore the Gentiles God, that they may not only grope, or know God confusedly from works running into the senses, but may fully find Him in supernatural revelation, which divine grace denies to no one. Proof b.

Whatever natural theology teaches concerning the divine attributes, infinity, independence, eternity, simplicity, etc., is not rejected in revealed theology, but is used soberly, so that judgment is by no means deferred to reason. Proof c.

Natural knowledge of God contributes to the celebration of God, as David testifies, Ps. XIX, 1, and Paul, Rom. I, 21.

The law of nature prescribes certain things concerning the worship of God and the love of neighbor, Rom. II, 15.

Latin:

X. Cartesiani argumentantur:.* Si nulla idea aut imago essentiam Dei repraesentans intellectui humano esset ingenita, Deus ab homine nullo modo ex lumine naturae cognosci posset.

Sed cognoscitur Deus ab homine ex lumine naturae. Ergo idea aut imago essentiam Dei repraesentans homini est ingenita. Consequentia maioris probatur, quia Deus est Spiritus infinitus, omnis materiae expers, qui ex intuitu & contemplatione creaturarum cognosci nequit. Nam finiti ad infinitum, & spiritus ad corpus sensibile, nulla datur proportio, nulla conuenientia.

Quando autem unum ex altero cognoscendum est, inter vtrumque conuenientia quaedam intercedat, necesse est. Resp. 1) Post concreatae hominibus protoplastis sapientiae iacturam non dantur in intellectu humano ideae, imagines aut species intelligibiles simplices, cognoscendarum rerum essentiam repraesentantes, congenitae, sed species rerum impressae transmittuntur ab obiectis per sensus & phantasma ad intellectum. Quo collineat tritum illud: Nihil est in intellectu, quin prius fuerit in sensu. Quare idea essentiam Dei repraesentans, intellectui humano congenita, fuaue est Cartesianorum somnium. 2) Quamuis Deus, in se & essentia sua consideratus, fit spiritus infinitus, omnis materiae sensibus obviae expers, effectus tamen Dei sensibus expositi sunt. Quocirca intellectus noster per species effectuum sensibilium, a Deo productorum, interuentu sensuum & phantasmatum ad se transmissas, determinatur ad actus cognoscendi eliciendos, qui Deum eiusque perfectiones quadantenus repraesentant, mediante discursu & per consequentiam, nixam hoc principio, natura notissimo: Effectus testatur de causa, eiusque perfectione, 3) Finiti ad infinitum non datur proportio ratione mathematicae commensurationis, datur tamen qualiscunque conuenientia inter creatorem & creaturam, qualis est inter caussam & effectum, inter signatum & signum.

Nam effectus a Deo producti sunt signa & quasi vestigia, bonitatem, potentiam & sapientiam Dei repraesentantia. sunt signa & quasi vestigia, bonitatem, potentiam & sapientiam Dei repræsentantia.

mentissime exoptat nullum esse Deum, vitiorum investigatorem atque vltorem: proinde & facillime sibi persuadet, nullum esse. Id quod est, corde dicere, Ps. XIV, 1. Cordis enim nomine scriptura non cogitationes solum, sed & vel maxime voluptates ac desideria nuncupat, atque ea etiam in hoc ipso loco significari, ex integra verborum ferie adparet. VI. Estne notitia Dei naturalis vera? Notitia Dei naturalis in se spectata est vera, tam quoad principia, quam quoad conclusiones, quae e principiis per manifestam consequentiam deducuntur.

Prob. a. Paullus diserte testatur Rom. I, 18. quod omnes homines extra Christum considerati, e quorum censu etiam sunt gentiles, veritatem in iniustitia detineant. Reddit apostolus caussam, cur ira Dei super hominum quorumuis impietatem & iniustitiam reveletur, quia omnibus nota est veritas, si non e scripturae, certe naturae libro, quam vero in iniustitia detinent. Detinent, quasi captiuam, veram de Deo notitiam, ne vim suam exserat. Detinent veritatem in iniustitia; quia ius Dei requirit, vt recte vsurpentur innatae de Deo notitiae. Ideo enim a Deo sunt inditae, vt Deum quaerere non negligamus, neque in impietate aut iniustitia permaneamus.

Act. XVII, 27. Prob. b. Principia verissima & certissima sunt: Deus est, Deus est vnus, verus, bonus, sapientissimus, potentissimus. Deus est creator, conseruator & gubernator huius vniuersi.

Prob. c. Conclusiones practicae & communibus de Deo notionibus vltro fluunt per discursum. v. gr. Deus est bonus, & omnis boni auctor: Ergo Deus maxime amandus est. Deus est sapientissimus: Ergo est venerandus. Est iustissimus: Ergo timendus. Est optimus & potentissimus: Ergo fiducia in eo est collocanda, eiusque auxilium in omnibus casibus asperis est implorandum.

Antithesis fuit olim Matthiae Flacii, Danielis Hofmanni & aliorum, ex quorum sententia notitia Dei naturalis est fallax & multorum plena errorum, quorum potiora sunt argumenta: I. Quacunque notitia non agnoscitur verus Deus, illa est falsa. Sed notitia naturali non agnoscitur verus Deus. Ergo notitia Dei naturalis est falsa. Maior constat, quia vera cognitio obiecto cognoscendo conformetur, par est. Minor patet, quia verus Deus est vnus in essentia, & trinus in personis, quem nemo e principiis naturae cognoscit.

Resp. Quacunque notitia neque verus Deus, neque aliquid de vero Deo cognoscitur, illa est falsa; concedo. At notitia Dei naturali licet non distincte agnoscatur verus Deus, Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanctus, aliquid tamen de vero Deo, nempe eius existentia, bonitas, sapientia, iustitia &c. apprehenditur, quae cognitio licet sit inadaequata & confusa, non tamen est falsa.

Instantia: Iudaei & Mahometani ideo dicuntur non agnoscere & inuocare verum Deum, quia non agnoscunt & inuocant Deum Patrem, Filium & Spiritum sanctum. Resp. Iudaei & Mahometani non tantum ignorant, sed & negant S. S. Trinitatem; neque tantum concipiunt Deum sub esse confuso vt omnipotentem & sapientem, verum etiam positiue addunt conceptum contrarium, restringentem essentiam Dei confuse conceptam ad vnam personam, atque adeo idolum, siue figmentum cordis sui adorant.

II. Quia omnes homines natura sunt stulti, Deum negant. Ps. XIV, 1. Rom. III, 10. E. naturalis eorum notitia de Deo est errorum plena.

Resp. Notitia Dei naturalis spectata in se est vera, cui imperfectio & procliuitas ad errores per accidens adhaerescit, neque eius veritatem tollit; quippe quam etiam gentiles in iniustitia detinent, Rom. I, 18.

Quaest. VII. Estne θεογνωσία naturalis utilis? Θεογνωσία naturalis triplicem pollicetur vtilitatem, nempe paedagogicam, quatenus inducit hominem ad quaerendum coetum illum, in quo verus Deus Israëlis se manifestavit (a): didacticam, quia ad notitiam Dei revelatam illustrandam haud parum facit, si sobrie adhibeatur (b); paedeuticam, ad dirigendos mores & externam disciplinam in ecclesia, & extra eandem (c). Prob. a. Paullus in concione Areopagitica Act. XVII, 24. monet gentiles, ut quaerant dominum, si omnino palpent & inveniant. Sicut palpatio est cognitio obscura (palpare solent manibus caeci, conf. Ies. LIX, 10.): ita inventio est cognitio plena, & pro conditione viatorum perfecta, quae non nisi ex supernaturali lumine habetur.

Quaerant ergo gentiles Deum, vt non tantum palpent, aut ex operibus in sensus incurrentibus Deum confuse cognoscant, sed in supernaturali revelatione, quam gratia divina nemini denegat, plene inveniant. Prob. b.

Quidquid theologia naturalis de attributis divinis, infinitate, independentia, aeternitate, simplicitate &c. docet, in theologia revelata non reiicitur, sed sobrie adhibetur, vt rationi iudicium minime deferatur. Prob. c.

Facit notitia Dei naturalis ad celebrationem Dei, teste Dauide, Ps. XIX, 1. ac Paullo, Rom. I, 21.

Lex naturae praescribit quaedam de cultu Dei & amore proximi, Rom. II, 15.


### Q. V. What is natural knowledge of God?: Question VIII. Is the natural knowledge of God so perfect that it suffices for obtaining eternal salvation?

Question.

VIII. Is the natural knowledge of God so perfect that it suffices for obtaining eternal salvation?

The natural knowledge of God does not attain that peak of perfection so that it suffices for a man who is a traveler to obtain eternal salvation, but it is lacking, mutilated, and nothing for salvation. Proof.
