I. Christ is not apprehended by natural knowledge of God, outside of whom there is no salvation.

Acts IV, 12.

II. Not nature, but Holy Scripture is the principle of saving faith, Rom. X, 14.

But, he who does not believe, is condemned. Mark XVI, 16.

III. By the law of Moses eternal salvation is obtained by no one, Gal. III, 11.

Therefore much less by the law of nature, which is far inferior and weaker than the Mosaic law. IV. The Gentiles, even supposing a natural knowledge of God, are said to be alienated from the life which is in God, Eph.

IV, 18. Not to know God (savingly), Gal.

IV, 8. nay, to be without God. Eph. II, 12.

The antithesis is that of Puccius, Zwingli, Herbert, Curcellaeus, Pelagius, and certain scholastics, who are of the opinion that the natural knowledge of God is sufficient for salvation.

Edward Herbert of Cherbury, an English Baron, thinks that those things which are necessary for men are contained in five articles sought from the common providence of God.

Namely it must be believed I. That there is some supreme Deity.

II. That this supreme Deity is to be worshipped.

Virtue, joined with piety, is the chief part of divine worship. IV.

That one must repent of sins. V.

That there is a reward and punishment, both in this life and after this life.

Response.

Although by the guidance of the light of nature it can be known that there is some Deity, which is most to be worshipped, yet the manner of worshipping is not known from the principles of nature in this state of sin, in which we often offend God. Unless, therefore, satisfaction has been made for sins, by which the angry God is reconciled, we can neither place trust in God, nor sincerely love the same, nor perform works approved by Him.

Nor are sins expiated by repentance, because this indeed concerns the sinner, who detests and as it were retracts the committed sins; but by the same, satisfaction is not made to God, the supreme judge who has been offended.

Nor even in a civil court is a defendant [acquitted] by sorrow alone, by which willed, sins never to have been committed, he satisfies the magistrate whose law he violated.

Since, therefore, natural theognosy does not teach the manner in which God, when angry, can be satisfied, its doctrine is insufficient and is nothing for salvation. Add that, with nature as a guide, piety pure of dross does not consist for man; for it has as its author the Holy Spirit inhabiting the heart, it proceeds from faith in Christ the satisfier, and is to be directed toward the glory of the true God.

You say: The goodness of God is so great that it looks to repentance without the intervention of satisfaction, which goodness of God becomes known from the light of nature.

I respond: Although God is most good, he is nevertheless also supremely just, and a most grave avenger of sinners who oppose his most holy law, and that by the power of his immutable justice.

For which reason, unless satisfaction is made to divine justice, the goodness of God, which does not abolish divine justice, cannot be so known from the light of nature that the remission of sins and eternal salvation can be expected from it.

Quæst. IX. Is there in the human soul some internal, universal, substantial, and saving light, revealing all things necessary for salvation immediately and objectively, so that every man, turning himself to it, can be illuminated and saved by it?

With immediate revelations having ceased after the completion of the canon of Holy Scripture , there is not in the human soul an internal, universal , substantial , and saving light ; revealing all things necessary for salvation immediately and objectively , so that every man can be illuminated and saved by it .

In vain, therefore, is that fictitious light adorned with various honorary titles .

Antithesis 1) Of the Platonic philosophers, who maintain that some light was infused into the souls of men when they were first created, by which, being illuminated, they were able to know God and divine things.

MARSILIO FICINO, the Platonist, teaches this clearly in his commentary on Plato's Symposium, oration 4, chapter 2.

Men, that is, the souls of men, were once—that is, when they were created by God—whole, and were adorned with two lights, innate and infused: so that they might behold things equal and inferior with the innate, and superior things with the infused.

They wished to make themselves equal to God; they turned themselves back to the single innate light. Here they were divided. They lost the infused splendor when they turned themselves to the innate alone, and immediately fell into bodies. Furthermore, the Platonists add that that light has been lost only to the extent that it is indeed obscured, but not entirely extinguished; since a recollection of it is given, provided the mind, purified or abstracted from the senses and affections, turns itself into its innermost center, and with its powers gathered into itself is carried upward, seeks celestial and divine things, and strives to return to its own principle.

Three things, therefore, are required for receiving the light: κάθαρσις (purification), ἐπιστροφὴ εἰς ἑαυτὸν (turning back into oneself), and ἄνοδος (ascent), concerning which see SCHEFF. in phil.

Ital. c. IX. p. 75 ff. and compare MARSIL.

FICIN. Comm. in conuiu. Platonis, who says: But as for those things which are above nature, thinking that there is need of a more sublime light, they prepare themselves by a certain most exact purification of the soul so that the divine light may shine upon them again. 2) Of the Mystics, who insist on the footsteps of the Platonists.

Let us listen to WEIGEL, part II of his postil, p.

61, who differentiates thus: That is certain, we must be taught by the Holy Spirit, by the anointing in us (so he calls the internal light), otherwise everything is in vain that one teaches outwardly, and he writes: we must all be taught by God: knowledge must well up from within into the present, and not be carried in from a book; for that does not hold water: we see well what those accomplish in theology who deny the internal testimonies of the Holy Spirit in every single person.

We are all gifted with this Spirit, with this anointing, only that we must turn inward and learn from him: thus we shall be more learned than all our teachers, as David was: whoever can listen to him much, can also experience much. At one time this spirit promoted a peasant to a doctor.

Upon this dictation of the Holy Spirit speaking immediately in the heart, which they also call the internal light, the Quakers have built their entire matxology [vain discourse]. For they assert that God reveals Himself and His will through some internal light, which becomes the vehicle of God and His celestial and invisible organ.

Concerning which BARCLAY writes in apol. th. 6. p. 86. That light is the vehicle of God, in which God and Christ always dwell, and from which they cannot be separated, and which, as it obtains a place in the heart and is joined with it, Christ is formed and arises.

Latin:

Quaest.

VIII. Estne notitia Dei naturalis adeo perfecta, vt ad obtinendam aeternam salutem sufficiat?

Non assequitur notitia Dei naturalis eum perfectionis apicem, vt homini viatori ad obtinendam salutem aeternam sufficiat, sed manca, mutila & ad salutem nulla est. Prob.

I. Notitia Dei naturali non apprehenditur Christus, extra quem non est salus.

Act. IV, 12.

II. Non natura, sed scriptura S. est principium fidei salutiferae, Rom. X, 14.

At, qui non credit, damnatur. Marc. XVI, 16.

III. Per legem Mosis nemini aeterna salus obtingit, Gal. III, 11.

Ergo multo minus per legem naturae, quae lege Mosaica est longe inferior & infirmior. IV. Gentiles, supposita etiam notitia Dei naturali, dicuntur alienati a vita, quae est in Deo, Eph.

IV, 18. Deum non cognoscere (salutariter), Gal.

IV, 8. immo absque Deo esse. Eph. II, 12.

Antithesis est Puccii, Zwinglii, Herberti, Curcellaei, Pelagii, & quorundam scholastici, opinantium, naturalem Dei notitiam ad salutem esse sufficientem.

Eduardus Herbert de Cherbury, Baro Anglus, putat ea, quae hominibus sunt necessaria, quinque articulis e communi providentia Dei petitis contineri.

Nempe credendum est I. Esse aliquod supremum Numen.

II. Supremum illud Numen esse colendum.

Virtutem, cum pietate coniunctam, praecipuam esse partem cultus divini. IV.

Resipiscendum esse a peccatis. V.

Dari praemium & poenam, tum in hac vita, tum post hanc vitam.

Resp.

Etsi ductu luminis naturae cognosci possit, esse aliquot Numen, quod maxime colendum sit, modus tamen colendi e principiis naturae non innotescit in hoc statu peccati, quo Deum saepe offendimus. Nisi itaque praestita fit satisfactio pro peccatis, qua Deus iratus reconcilietur, neque fiduciam in Deo collocare, neque eundem fincere amare, neque opera ipsi probata praestare possumus.

Neque expiantur peccata poenitentia, quia haec concernit quidem peccantem, qui commissa peccata detestatur & quasi retractat; sed eadem non satisfit Deo, summo iudici offenso.

Neque in foro quidem civili reus per solum dolorem, quo vellet, peccata nunquam esse perpetrata, magistratui, cuius legem violauit, satisfacit.

Quum itaque θεογνωσία naturalis non doceat modum, quo Deo irato satisfieri queat, eius doctrina insufficiens, & ad salutem nulla est. Adhice, quod duce natura non constat homini pietas fuci pura; quippe quæ auctorem habet Spiritum S. corda inhabitantem, proficiscitur ex fide in satisfactorem Christum, atque dirigenda est in gloriam veri Dei.

Dicis: Tanta est bonitas Dei, vt pœnitentiam adspectet, sine interuentu satisfactionis, quæ bonitas Dei ex lumine naturæ innotescit.

Resp. Licet Deus sit maxime bonus, est tamen etiam summe iustus, & peccatorum sanctissimæ legi suæ aduersantium vindex grauissimus, idque ex vi immutabilis suæ iustitiæ.

Quam ob rem nisi iustitiæ diuinæ fiat satis, bonitas Dei, quæ iustitiam diuinam non tollit, e lumine naturæ ita cognosci non potest, vt ab ea expectari queat remissio peccatorum & salus æterna.

Quæst. IX. Daturne in anima humana aliquod lumen internum, vniuersale, substantiale, & salutiferum, omnes res ad salutem necessarias immediate & obiective reuelans, vt omnis homo, se ad illud conuertens, eodem illuminari & saluari queat?

Cessantibus post completum scripturæ sanctæ canonem reuelationibus immediatis , non datur in anima humana lumen internum vniuersale , substantiale , & salutiferum ; omnes res ad salutem necessarias immediate & obiective reuelans , vt omnis homo per illud illuminari & saluari queat .

Frustra itaque fictitium illud lumen variis titulis honorariis insignitur .

Antithesis 1) Philosophorum Platonicorum, statuentium, animabus hominum primum creatis infusum esse aliquod lumen, quo illustratæ Deum & res diuinas cognoscere potuerint.

Perspicue illud docet MARSILIVS FICINVS, Platonicus in comm. in conuiu.

Platon. orat. 4. c. 2. Homines i. e. hominum animæ quondam, i. e. quando a Deo creantur, integræ sunt, duobus sunt ornatæ luminibus, ingenito & infuso: vt ingenito æqualia & inferiora, infuso superiora conspicerent.

Deo æquare se voluerunt, ad vnicum lumen ingenitum se reflexerunt. Hic diuisæ sunt. Splendorem infusum amiserunt, quando ad solum ingenitum sunt conuersæ, statimque in corpora cecidere. Ceterum addunt Platonici, lumen illud hactenus esse amissum, vt quidem offuscatum, non autem penitus extinctum sit; siquidem eius detur reminiscentia, modo mens purgata, siue abstracta a sensibus & affectibus, se conuertat in intimum suum centrum, & collectis in se viribus sursum feratur, cœlestia diuinaque petat, & ad ipsum principium suum reuerti studeat.

Tria ergo requiruntur ad recipiendum lumen, κάθαρσις, ἐπιστροφὴ εἰς ἑαυτὸν, καὶ ἄνοδος, de quibus vid.

SCHEFF. in phil. Ital. c. IX. p. 75. seqq. & confer.

MARSIL. FICIN. Comm. in conuiu. Platonis, inquinientem: Ad ea vero, quæ supra naturam sunt, sublimiore lumine opus esse putantes, exactissima quadam animæ purgatioe ita se præparant, vt diuina lux iterum illis effulgeat. 2) Mysticorum, vestigiis Platonicorum insistentium.

Auscultemus WEIGELIVM part.

II. postillæ p. 61. ita differentem: Das ist gewiß, wir müssen von dem heiligen Geiste, von der Salbung in uns (ita vocat lumen internum) gelehret werden, sonst ist alles umsonst, was man auswendig lehrt, und schreibet: wir müssen alle von Gott gelehret werden: von innen muß heraus quellen die Erkenntniß in den Gegenwart, und nicht vom Buche hinein getragen werden; denn dasselbige hält nicht den Stich: wir sehen wohl, was selbe ausrichten in der Theologia, die da leugnen die innere Zeugnuisse des heiligen Geistes in einem jedweden.

Wir sind alle begabet mit diesem Geiste, mit dieser Salbung, allein daß wir einkehren, und von ihm lernen: so werden wir mit dem David gelehrter, denn alle unsere lehrer: wer ihm viel zuhören kann, der kann auch viel erfahren. Stunde promoveret dieser Geist einen Bauren zu einem Doctor.

Huic dictamini Spiritus S. immediate in corde loquentis, quod etiam lumen internum vocant, Quakeri totam suam matxologiam superstruxerunt. Asserunt enim, Deum se & voluntatem suam revelare per lumen aliquod internum, quod fit vehiculum Dei, eiusque coeleste ac invisibile organum.

De quo scribit BARCLAIVS in apol. th. 6. p. 86. Illud lumen est Dei vehiculum, in quo Deus & Christus semper habitant, & a quo separari nequeunt, & quod prout locum in corde obtinet, cumque eo coniungitur, Christus formatur & oritur.


### Q. V. What is natural knowledge of God?: E K T H E S I S [Exposition]

E K T H E S I S [Exposition]

Obs. I.

Here one must accurately distinguish between natural and supernatural light. We do not deny that there is given in the soul of man a natural internal light, by which the essence, attributes, and actions of God are known to a certain extent, concerning which the apostle of the gentiles treats in Rom. II, 14.

But that light of nature is maimed, mutilated, and useless for salvation, since Christ is not apprehended by natural knowledge of God, outside of whom there is no salvation, Acts IV, 12. But the Quakers opine that, besides natural light, there is also given in every man some supernatural light, concerning which ROBERT BARCLAY discourses in apol. ad thes. 5. & 6. n. 16. p.

88. Just as God created two great lights to govern the external world, the sun and the moon, the greater light to rule the day, the lesser to rule the night: so He gave to men the spiritual light of His Son and divine light to govern him in spiritual things: and the light of reason to govern him in natural things. Obs.

II. Our churches teach that there is given in reborn men the light of faith, kindled by means of the divine word reduced to writing, from Matth.

V, 16. Act. XXVI, 18. But the Quakers think that spiritual light exists not only in the reborn, but also in the unregenerate, infused immediately into all men by the Holy Spirit, although it shines more clearly in one man and less clearly in another.

God has given to each one some measure of saving, sufficient, and supernatural light, says BARCLAY l. c. p.

84. The light of faith is an accident; but the Quakers believe the internal light to be a real and spiritual substance, which the soul of man can feel and apprehend, in the judgment of BARCLAY l. c. p.

84. Obs. III. We are not speaking here of general revelation, or natural manifestation, by which God has revealed Himself both through the light of nature implanted within, and through effects conspicuous in the realm of nature.

See Rom.

I, 19. c.

II, 14. 15. But we are speaking of special and supernatural revelation, which is either mediate or immediate.

The latter is that by which God reveals Himself without an external written or preached word: the former is that by which God declares Himself and His will through an external written or preached word. The internal light is said to be immediately revealing, or immediately teaching.

Obs. IV. The internal light is said to reveal objectively, in opposition to subjective illumination.

For thus BARCLAY writes in apol. p. 22: The Holy Spirit today not only breathes and leads on the part of the subject, by illuminating the intellect to believe the truth objectively declared in scripture, but also by presenting that truth objectively, or as an object. Where one must properly distinguish between the material and formal object of faith.

The material object is the thing that is believed: The formal object is the cause, or formal reason for believing, or it is that to which one believes primarily, and because of which one believes other things. e.g. A true Christian believes in the triune God, insofar as He has revealed Himself by means of the external word. From which it is clear that for a true Christian the material object of faith is the triune God, the formal object is mediate revelation.

The Quaker, however, believes in God insofar as He has revealed Himself immediately through the internal light, i.e., without the concurrence of Holy Scripture. To the Quaker, therefore, the material object of faith is God, the formal object the formal object is immediate revelation. For this reason, according to the opinion of the Quakers, the inner light reveals God immediately and objectively, because without an external medium, without Holy Scripture, it manifests, represents, and sets God before the minds of men as the object of faith.

Obs. V. The Quakers distinguish the inner light with various honorary titles or equivalent terms. For it is called by them Christ in us, the internal Christ, the Holy Spirit speaking immediately in the heart, or the dictation of the Spirit speaking in the heart, the seed of the kingdom, the seed of regeneration, the communion of the Spirit, the manifestation of the Spirit, the light teaching immediately, the light illuminating all men, the anointing teaching all things, the light of conscience, the great mystery, the light of the gospel, the lamb of God, the divine aura, the divine tincture, etc. They maintain that these names signify the same thing, distinguished only by operations and manifestations.

Latin:

Ε Κ Θ Ε Σ Ι Σ

Obs. I.

Accurate hic distinguendum est inter lumen naturale, & supernaturale. Non imus infitias, dari in anima hominis lumen internum naturale, quo essentia, attributa & actiones Dei quadantenus cognoscuntur, de quo agit gentium apostolus Rom. II, 14.

At istud lumen naturae est mancum, mutilum, & ad salutem nullum, cum notitia Dei naturali non apprehendatur Christus, extra quem non est salus, Act. IV, 12. At Quakeri opinantur, praeter lumen naturale dari etiam in omni homine aliquod supernaturale, de quo ROBERTVS BARCLAIVS disserit apol. ad thes. 5. & 6. n. 16. p.

88. Sicut Deus duo magna luminaria creavit ad externum orbem gubernandum, solem & lunam, maius lumen ad diem, minus ad noctem regendam: ita hominibus dedit lumen filii sui spirituale & divinum lumen ad gubernandum in rebus spiritualibus: & lumen rationis ad gubernandum illum in rebus naturalibus. Obs.

II. Docent ecclesiae nostrae, dari in hominibus renatis lumen fidei, mediante verbo divino in litteras redacto accensum, ex Matth.

V, 16. Act. XXVI, 18. At Quakeri censent, non tantum in renatis, sed & irregenitis exsistere lumen spirituale, a Spiritu S. omnibus hominibus immediate infusum, quamuis in uno homine clarius, in altero minus clare luceat.

Deus unicuique dedit mensuram aliquam salutiferi, sufficientis, & supernaturalis luminis, ait BARCLAIVS l. c. p.

84. Lumen fidei est accidens; at Quakeri credunt, lumen internum esse realem & spiritualem substantiam, quam anima hominis sentire & apprehendere potest, iudice BARCLAIO l. c. p.

84. Obs. III. Non heic sermo est de revelatione generali, seu manifestatione naturali, qua Deus se patefecit tum per lumen naturae insitum, tum per effecta in regno naturae conspicua.

Vid. Rom.

I, 19. c.

II, 14. 15. Sed loquimur de revelatione speciali & supernaturali, quae est vel mediata, vel immediata.

Haec est, qua Deus absque verbo externo scripto aut praedicato se patefecit: illa est, qua Deus se & voluntatem suam declarat per verbum externum scriptum, aut praedicatum. Lumen internum dicitur immediate revelans, vel immediate docens.

Obs. IV. Lumen internum dicitur obiective revelare, in oppositione ad illuminationem subiectiuam.

Ita enim BARCLAIVS in apol. p. 22. scribit: Spiritus sanctus hodie non solum afflat, & ducit ex parte subiecti, illuminando intellectum ad credendam veritatem, in scriptura obiective declaratam, sed etiam praesentando eam veritatem obiective, sive tanquam obiectum. Vbi probe distinguendum est inter obiectum fidei materiale, & formale.

Obiectum materiale est res, quae creditur: Obiectum formale est causa, aut ratio formalis credendi, siue est id, cui primo, & propter hoc aliis creditur. v. gr. Verus christianus credit in Deum triunum, quatenus mediante verbo externo se revelavit. Ex quo patet, vero christiano obiectum fidei materiale esse Deum triunum, obiectum formale esse revelationem mediatam.

Quakerus autem credit in Deum, quatenus per lumen internum immediate, i. e. non concurrente S. scriptura, se revelavit. Quakero itaque obiectum fidei materiale est Deus, obiectum formale est revelatio immediata. Quam ob rem Quakerorum de sententia lumen internum Deum immediate & obiective revelat, quia sine medio externo, sine S. scriptura, Deum, tanquam obiectum fidei, manifestat, repraesentat, & mentibus hominum obiicit.

Obs. V. Quakeri lumen internum variis titulis honorariis, vel vocibus aequipollentibus insigniunt. Appellatur enim ab ipsis Christus in nobis, Christus internus, Spiritus S. immediate in corde loquens, vel dictamen Spiritus in corde loquentis, semen regni, semen regenerationis, communio Spiritus, manifestatio Spiritus, lumen immediate docens, lux omnes homines illuminans, unctio omnia docens, lumen conscientiae, mysterium magnum, lumen euangelii, agnus Dei, aura diuina, tinctura diuina, &c. Statuunt, ista nomina idem significare, operationibus & manifestationibus tantum distingui.


### Q. V. What is natural knowledge of God?: B E B a I Ω Σ I Σ [confirmation]

B E B A I Ω Σ I Σ [CONFIRMATION]

Prob. a. After divine immediate revelations have ceased, there is not given in all men an inner light, immediately revealing God and divine things, which is necessary for a man to be saved for saving knowledge, or for saving faith. But after the completion of the canon of Scripture they ceased, etc. Therefore. The major is clear, because when the end (immediate revelation) ceases, the medium by which it ought to be obtained (the inner light immediately revealing) ceases.

Minor problem (1) from the apostolic oracle, Heb. 1:1. "God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son." From this apostolic utterance, a twofold argument arises for us: The first is: Whoever closed and sealed all modes of immediate revelations (made *polytropos* [in many ways]) with his own revelation, after his time immediate revelations ceased entirely. But the Son of God did this in these last days, as the text holds. Therefore. The second is: Whoever added the final limit of immediate revelation to all the turns and intervals of revelations (made *polymeros* [in many parts]), he finished, closed, and sealed immediate revelations. But the Son of God, as the apostle teaches in the cited text, [did this to] all, etc. Therefore.

(2) From the divine command of Christ: for he, being about to be taken up into heaven and about to instruct the apostles as the common teachers of the world, said, Matt. 28:20: Teach them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you. If immediate revelations were given after the completion of Scripture, the Savior would certainly have commended these to the apostles before his ascension into heaven. But he did not commend these, but commanded them to inform men who are to be saved so that they might observe all things that Christ commanded them: which commands of Christ were committed to writing, John 20:31. But if Christ had said: teach men to observe all things whatsoever shall be immediately revealed to you inwardly: the apostles would certainly have used this method of teaching: turn yourselves, O men, about to obtain eternal salvation, into your hearts, and apply them to the inner light that teaches immediately. But in truth they never and nowhere used this method of teaching. For this reason, at the present time, immediate revelations are not given, and thus the inner light, immediately revealing, is indeed imagined, but by no reason is proved.

(3) From the prophetic oracle of Daniel, ch. 9:24. The vision and prophecy shall be sealed, when the most holy shall be anointed. From which we gather: Whose office it was to seal the vision and prophecy by revealing all things necessary to be known for salvation, he consummated and sealed the immediate revelations pertaining to our salvation. But it was the office of the Messiah speaking in the last times, and... etc. Therefore. The major is clear, because the vision and prophecy is an immediate revelation, which whoever fulfills is said to seal. The minor is evident from the cited prophetic oracle, to which add the testimony of the Samaritan woman, speaking according to the common opinion of the Jews:

John IV, 25. When the Messiah shall come, he will tell us all things. Which Christ in fact performed. For all things, he says, which I have heard from my Father, I have made known to you, John XV, 15.

(4) From the Pauline testimony, 1 Cor. IV, 6. μάθητε τὸ μὴ ὑπὲρ ὃ ...γέγραπται φρονεῖν, that you may learn not to think beyond that which is written. Those who ought not to think about divine matters beyond that which is written, it is not for them to expect immediate revelations. But men who are to attain eternal salvation &c. Therefore.

You say: The words of Paul are to be understood as regarding the avoidance of ambition, so that the sense may be: that you may learn, lest anyone think more ambitiously beyond that which is written. Resp. (a) The words of Paul are set down indeterminately and generally, by which false teachers are warned not to presume to think beyond those things which God has revealed in the scriptures. (b) False teachers, who today boast of immediate revelations, are the most ambitious of all.

(5) If an immediate revelation were given today, Christ and the apostles, and indeed the prophets, would have referred us to observe, expect, and receive an internal light, revealing immediately. But in truth they never refer us to this, but frequently commend to us the reading and meditation of the Holy Scripture. How gravely Christ exhorts us, John V, 39. Search the scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life, and they testify of me. But if an internal light existed, infused into our hearts and teaching immediately, Christ would undoubtedly have said: Search the light existing in the innermost recesses of your hearts, because you think that in it you have eternal life. And it testifies of me. But this the author of our salvation said neither in the cited passage, nor anywhere else. Wherefore the light infused into the minds of all men, and teaching the mysteries of faith immediately, is a chimera, a being of reason, and a figment of the brain.

The Quakers object, to whom this oracle of Christ is a thorn in the eye: (1) That Christ is not speaking in the imperative, as if he were commanding them to search the scripture, but in the indicative, rebuking the Jews because they search. (2) That the opinion of the Pharisees, that they have eternal life in the scripture, was erroneous. Whence Christ said: ὑμεῖς δοκεῖτε, you think, not approving this opinion, but simply reporting it. (3) That the searching of the scripture hindered the Jews from coming to Christ. Resp. to (1): Both the nature of the Greek language and the context teach that the imperative holds entirely now: otherwise Christ would have said: ὑμεῖς ἐρευνᾶτε καὶ δοκεῖτε. For the idiom of the Greek language does not allow that when two verbs are joined in the indicative mood, the pronoun ὑμεῖς be prefixed to the latter, but not to the former. The most learned interpreters have observed this, Chrysostom, Augustine, Theophylact, Euthymius, Lyranus, the Carthusian, Maldonatus, and others, whom the Syriac version supports, which rendered it, בצו, search, inquire. Furthermore, although the sense and use of the passage is not entirely perverted if it is read in the indicative, without doubt there is greater emphasis in the imperative. Moreover, it is not credible that the common people of the Jews, with whom Christ is dealing here, applied such diligence in reading the scripture that it could be said of them in general, ἐρευνᾶτε, you search the scriptures. The Pharisees and scribes themselves, as can be evident from many places of scripture, were men of supine negligence in investigating and not even casually reading the scriptures, let alone the common people. The Jews therefore deserved to be rebuked rather for not reading the scripture than for reading it too much. And how would he rebuke the readers of scripture, who are commended elsewhere for this study, 2 Pet. I, 19. To (2): the word δοκεῖτε does not denote an uncertain and ill-founded opinion, but a certain and well-founded dogma: δοκεῖτε, i.e., you hold it as a dogma, you regard it as a divine dogma, you believe it with certain faith. Thus Paul, when he says: δοκῶ δὲ κἀγὼ, I think also I myself, that I have the spirit of God, certainly does not say an uncertain opinion, but a certainty of mind, or that which he knew and held with certain faith. To (3): Not the searching of the scriptures, but rather the searching of the scriptures, but rat omission, or neglect of due scrutiny, i.e., of a more diligent, more accurate, and more perspicacious one, by which the scope of scripture was to be perceived, hindered the Jews, so that they did not come to Christ, or believe in him.

The apostles refer us to the external light of Holy Scripture, Peter 2 Ep. c. I, 19. We have a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place. Peter speaks of the prophetic word, which holy men of God spoke by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, v. 21, and which is preserved in scripture for perpetual use, 2 Tim. II, 16. And he says that it is more sure than immediate revelation, not absolutely, but respectively, in respect of the apostolic testimony concerning the voice of the Father brought from heaven, and in respect of the readers or hearers.

Now the apostle exhorts us to attentive meditation on the prophetic word.

For προσέχειν signifies to read scripture, and to meditate attentively.

Which meditation on the divine word, reduced to writing, Paul also urges 1 Thess. V, 27. I charge you by the Lord, that this epistle be read unto all the holy brethren.

Confer 2 Tim. II, 14, 15. Moreover, the prophets also referred the Israelites to the assiduous meditation of Holy Scripture.

Thus God commands the Israelite king through Moses, that he should write for himself a copy of the law, that it be with him, and that he read therein all the days of his life, Deut. XVII, 18. The same is commanded to the Israelite leader Joshua, Jos. I, 7. Thus also God commanded to read the written law to the whole people, Deut. XXXI, 11. When all Israel shall come to appear before Jehovah, thy God, in the place which he shall choose, thou shalt read this law before all Israel in their ears.

Joshua exhorts the Israelites c. XXIII, 6. Be ye therefore very courageous to keep and to do all that is written in the book of the law of Moses.

Isaiah earnestly exhorts c. XXXIV, 16. Seek ye out of the book of Jehovah, and read.

Abraham sends the brothers of the rich glutton to Moses and the prophets. They have Moses and the Prophets: let them hear them.

Luc. XVI, 29. He does not say: they have an internal light, teaching immediately: let them apply themselves to that.

( 6) For a man who is a wayfarer, tending toward eternal salvation, there is no need for an internal light revealing immediately: because Holy Scripture manifests God and divine things sufficiently fully and perspicuously, and thus is a sufficient principle of saving faith.

Which is clearly demonstrated: (a) From the words of St. John c. XX, 31. These are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name.

Whatever scripture is divinely destined to that end, that all may through it believe in Jesus, to obtain eternal life, it reveals the way of salvation so fully and plainly, that a man who is a wayfarer does not need immediate revelation.

But Holy Scripture does so, etc. Therefore.

( b) From the Pauline dictum Rom. XV, 4. Whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.

Since this divine word is given for our learning, and such a one, from which we may have the hope of salvation, it is given to that end, that we may draw from it as much of saving knowledge as is sufficient for obtaining salvation.

But Holy Scripture does so, etc. Therefore.

(c) From the testimony of the same apostle 2 Tim. III, 14, 15, 16.

Continue thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of, knowing of whom thou hast learned them; and that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.

For all scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness.

From this classic dictum we gather two things: (1) Holy Scripture can generally make every man wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus, so that one must persist in its saving doctrine: (2) The same specifically instructs the theologian perfectly for all parts of teaching.

Therefore, Holy Scripture reveals things necessary to be known for salvation sufficiently fully and perspicuously, so that for a man who is a wayfarer there is no need at all for an internal light, revealing immediately. That there is no universal internal light given, is manifest, because the Gentiles, to whom the external word of God has not become known, are described by Paul as being darkness, Eph.

V, 8. i. e. most dark, or immersed in the densest darkness of ignorance and vices; whom the apostle in ch. IV, 18. graphically depicts as being darkened in mind, existing alienated from the life of God, because of the ignorance that is in them, because of the hardening of the heart; and also dead in sins, Eph. II, 1. without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants, having no hope of the promise, and atheists in the world. Eph. II, 12. We argue: (1) Whosoever are men immersed in the densest darkness of ignorance, darkened in mind, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, without Christ, having no hope of the promise, atheists, and dead in sins, in them there is no supernatural light given, which reveals God and divine things to them immediately and objectively. The major is clearer than the sun. For darkness is opposed to light by the apostle l. c. those darkened in mind are destitute of light: those alienated from the life of God do not have the Holy Spirit speaking in the heart: those who are without Christ, in them there is no internal light, which is called the vehicle of Christ: atheists lack the anointing that teaches all things: in the dead there is not even a spark of light.

Hence I kiss the words of the FORM. CONCORD. p. 662. Before man is illuminated, converted, regenerated, and drawn by the Holy Spirit, he can, of himself and by his own natural powers, in spiritual things and toward his own conversion or regeneration, initiate, perform, or cooperate in nothing: and no more than a stone, a trunk, or clay.

And p. 670. It has seemed good to God through this medium, namely through his holy word, when it is heard being preached, or is read, and through the legitimate use of the sacraments, to call men to eternal salvation, to draw them to himself, to convert, regenerate, and sanctify them.

Quakers object: Paul testifies in Rom.

II, 14. 15. that the Gentiles have the law of nature inscribed; because they demonstrate the work of the law written in their hearts. But the law of nature inscribed is an internal light revealing immediately. Resp. The law inscribed in hearts by nature, by reason of its proximate origin, is natural, which does not reveal the mysteries of the faith; otherwise they would not be mysteries.

Now it is evident to us that the internal light of the Quakers is not spiritual, or supernatural, but natural.

Wherefore not without cause does D. BAIERVS in dissert. V. de norma doctrinæ §. 19. judge that Naturalism lies hidden in Quakerism.

We proceed therefore by arguing: (2) Whatever light is in all men from birth, that is natural.

But the internal light of the Mystics and Quakers is in all men from birth. Therefore. The major is so firm that it cannot be infringed by any instance, and it is confirmed by this, that the work of generation is most natural, by which no supernatural gift is propagated, or spread to descendants.

For properly speaking, a supernatural gift is called that which is not in nature from its first origin, but is superadded by God from special grace to supply its imperfection.

(3) In the hearts of those men who are without Christ, no light shines except natural light.

But the Gentiles, to whom the external word of God has not become known, are without Christ, Eph. II, 13. Therefore. (4) Whatever light, after the completed canon of Holy Scripture, is not kindled in the hearts of men by the external word of God, that is either natural light, or the ignis fatuus of the devil.

But the light of the Quakers &c. Therefore.

Prob. c. (1) Internal light, revealing immediately, cannot be a substance.

For it would be a substance either complete or incomplete. But it is not a complete substance, because it is not the whole man; nor is it a part of man, because it is neither the body nor the soul of man.

Latin:

B E B A I Ω Σ I Σ

Prob. a. Postquam cessauerunt reuelationes diuinae immediatae, non datur in omnibus hominibus lumen internum, Deum, & res diuinas immediate reuelans, quo homini saluando opus fit ad salutarem cognitionem, seu ad fidem saluificam. Atqui post completum scripturae canonem cessarunt &c. Ergo. Maior liquet, quia cessante fine, (reuelatione immediata), cessat medium, quo is obtineri debeat (lumen internum immediate reuelans).

Minor prob. (1) ex oraculo apostolico, Hebr. I, 1. Multis vicibus, multisque modis olim Deus locutus patribus in prophetis; vltimis hisce diebus locutus est nobis in filio. Ex hoc eloquio apostolico geminum nobis nascitur argumentum: Prius est: Quicunque omnes reuelationum immediatarum modos (πολυτρόπως factos) sua reuelatione clausit & obsignauit, post eius tempora reuelationes immediatae omnino defierunt. At filius Dei vltimis his temporibus id praestitit, vt textus habet. Ergo. Posterius est: Quicunque omnibus reuelationum vicibus & interuallis (πολυμερῶς factis) vltimum reuelationis immediatae terminum adiecit, ille reuelationes immediatas finiuit, clausit, & obsignauit. Atqui filius Dei, docente apostolo in citato textu, omnibus &c. Ergo.

(2) E diuino Christi mandato: quippe qui iamiam in coelum subuecturus, & apostolos communes mundi doctores instructurus, dicebat, Matth. XXVIII, 20: Docete eos seruare omnia, quaecunque mandaui vobis. Si darentur post completum scripturam reuelationes immediatae, vtique has Saluator ante ascensionem in coelum apostolis commendasset. At has non commendauit, sed praecepit illis, sic informare homines saluandos, vt seruarent omnia, quae Christus ipsis mandauit: quae mandata Christi in litteras, sacras relata sunt, Io. XX, 31. Quodsi Christus dixisset: docete homines seruare omnia, quaecunque intrinsecus immediate vobis reuelabuntur: vtique apostoli hac docendi methodo vsi fuissent: conuertite vos, o homines, aeternam salutem adepturi, in corda vestra, eaque applicate ad lumen internum immediate docens. At vero hac docendi methodo nunquam & nusquam vsi sunt. Quam ob rem tempore praesenti non dantur reuelationes immediatae, atque adeo lumen internum, immediate reuelans, fingitur quidem, sed nulla ratione probatur. (3) Ex oraculo prophetico Danielis, cap. IX, 24. Obsignabitur visio & prophetia, cum ungetur sanctus sanctorum.

Ex quo colligimus: Cuiuscunque officium erat, oblignare visionem & prophetiam, omnia ad salutem cognitu necessaria reuelando, is reuelationes immediatas ad salutem nostram pertinentes consummauit & obsignauit. At Messiae vltimis temporibus loquentis officium erat, &...c. Ergo. Maior claret, quia visio & prophetia est reuelatio immediata, quam qui implet, obsignare dicitur. Minor patet ex oraculo prophetico citato, cui adde testimonium mulieris Samaritanae ex communi Iudaeorum fententia loquentis:

Io. IV, 25. Quando Messias venerit, nobis annuntiabit omnia. Quod Christus reapse praestitit. Nam omnia, inquit, quae audiui a patre meo, nota feci vobis, Io. XV, 15.

(4) E testimonio Paullino, 1 Cor. IV, 6. μάθητε τὸ μὴ ὑπὲρ ὃ ...γέγραπται φρονεῖν, discatis non supra id, quod scriptum est, sapere. Qui non debent de rebus diuinis sapere supra id, quod scriptum est, illorum non est immediatas expectare reuelationes. Atqui homines aeternam salutem adepturi &c. Ergo.

Dicis: Verba Paulli intelligenda sunt de vitanda ambitione, vt sensus sit: discatis, ne quis supra id, quod scriptum est, se sentiat ambitiosius. Resp. (a) Verba Paulli indeterminate & generatim posita sunt, quibus monentur falsi doctores, ne sapere praesumant supra ea, quae Deus in scripturis reuelauit. (b) Falsi doctores, qui hodie iactant reuelationes immediatas, sunt omnium ambitiosissimi.

(5) Si daretur hodieum immediata reuelatio, Christus & apostoli, quin & prophetae, ad obseruandum, expectandum & recipiendum lumen internum, immediate reuelans, nos ablegassent. At vero nunquam ad hoc nos ablegant, sed frequenter nobis commendant lectionem & meditationem sacrae scripturae. Quam grauiter nos adhortatur Christus, Io. V, 39. Scrutamini scripturas, quia vos existimatis, quod in iis vitam aeternam habeatis, Atqui illa testantur de me. Quod si exsisteret lumen internum cordibus nostris infusum, & immediate docens, haud dubie Christus dixisset: Scrutamini lumen in intimis vestrorum cordium penetralibus existens, quia existimatis, quod in vitam aeternam habeatis. Atqui illud testatur de me. At hoc salutis nostrae assertor nec loco citato, nec vllibi dixit. Quare lumen omnium hominum mentibus infusum, & mysteria fidei immediate docens, est chimera, ens rationis & figmentum cerebrinum.

Excipiunt Quakeri, quibus hoc oraculum Christi fudes in oculis est: (1) Christum non in imperatiuo loqui, quasi scripturam iubeat scrutari, sed in indicatiuo, reprehendendo Iudaeos, quod scrutentur. (2) Opinionem Pharisaeorum, quod vitam aeternam in scriptura habeant, fuisse erroneam. Vnde Christus dixerit: ὑμεῖς δοκεῖτε, vos putatis, opinionem hanc non aprobando, sed simpliciter referendo. (3) Scrutinium scripturae Iudaeos impediuisse, quo minus ad Christum venerint. Resp. ad (1): Tam indoles graecae linguae, quam contextus docet, imperatiuum omnino nunc obtinere: ceteroqui Christus dixisset: ὑμεῖς ἐρευνᾶτε καὶ δοκεῖτε. Neque enim idiotismus graecae linguae patitur, vt cum duo verba indicatiuo modo coniunguntur, posteriori, non autem priori, pronomen ὑμεῖς praefigatur. Id obseruarunt doctissimi interpretes, Chrysostomus, Augustinus, Theophylactus, Euthymius, Lyranus, Carthusianus, Maldonatus, & alii, quibus suffragatur versio Syriaca, quae reddidit, בצו, scrutamini, inquirite. Deinde, quanquam non plane peruertatur sensus & vsus loci, si in indicatiuo legatur, fine dubio tamen maior emphasis est in imperatiuo. Insuper non est credibile, quod vulgus Iudaeorum, cum quo hic Christus agit, tantam in legenda scriptura diligentiam adhibuerit, vt in vniuersum de illis dici potuerit, ἐρευνᾶτε, peruestigatis scripturas. Ipsi fere Pharisaei & scribae, vt ex multis scripturae locis patere potest, homines fuerunt supinae negligentiae in inuestigandis, & non obiter legendis scripturis, nedum vulgus. Merebantur itaque Iudaei increpari potius, quod non legerent scripturam, quam quod nimium legerent. Et quomodo reprehenderent scripturae lectores, qui alibi ab hoc studio commendantur, 2 Petr. I, 19. Ad (2): verbum δοκεῖτε non notat incertam & male fundatam opinionem, sed certum & bene fundatum dogma: δοκεῖτε, h. e. tanquam dogma tenetis, pro dogmate diuino habetis, certa fide creditis. Sic Paullus, cum dicit: δοκῶ δὲ κἀγὼ, existimo etiam ego, quod spiritum Dei habeam, vtique non incertam dicit opinionem, sed animi certitudinem, seu id, quod certa fide sciebat & tenebat. Ad (3): Non scrutinium scripturarum, sed vel scrutinium scripturarum, sed vel omissio, vel neglectus scrutinii debiti, i. e. diligentioris, accuratioris, & perspicacioris, quo scripturae scopus perspiciendus erat, Iudaeos impedivit, quo minus ad Christum venirent, sive in ipsum crederent.

Ad externum S. scripturae lumen nos ablegant apostoli, Petrus 2 Ep. c. I, 19. Habemus firmius propheticum verbum: cui, recte facitis, quod attenditis, tanquam lumini lucenti in loco tenebroso. Loquitur Petrus de verbo prophetico, quod ex afflatu Spiritus S. locuti sunt sancti Dei homines, v. 21. & quod in scriptura ad perpetuum usum asseruatur, 2 Tim. II, 16. idque firmius esse revelatione immediata dicit, non absolute, sed respective, respectu testimonii apostolici de voce patris coelitus delata, & respectu lectorum, vel auditorum.

Iam apostolus nos adhortatur ad attentam verbi prophetici meditationem.

Nam προσέχειν significat scripturam legere, & attente meditari.

Quam meditationem verbi diuini, in litteras redacti, vrget etiam Paullus 1 Thess. V, 27. Adiuro vos per dominum, legi epistolam omnibus sanctis fratribus.

Confer 2 Tim. II, 14. 15. Quin etiam prophetae ad assiduam S. scripturae meditationem Israelitas ablegarunt.

Sic Deus per Mosen praecipit regi Israelitico, vt scribat sibi exemplar legis, vt fit cum ipso, legatque in eo omnibus diebus vitae suae, Deut. XVII, 18. Idem duci Israelitico Iosuae praecipitur, Ios. I, 7. Sic & Deus iussit, legem scriptam vniuerso populo praelegere, Deut. XXXI, 11. Quum venerit omnis Israel ad comparendum coram Iehouah, Deo tuo, in loco, quem elegerit, praleges legem hanc coram omni Israele in auribus eorum.

Iosua compellat Israelitas c. XXIII, 6. Confirmate modo vos valde, ad custodiendum & faciendum omne, quod scriptum est in libro legis Mosis.

Iesaias ferio cohortatur c. XXXIV, 16. Quaerite desuper libro Iehouae, & legite.

Abrahamus fratres diuitis epulonis remittit ad Mosen & prophetas. Habent Mosen & Prophetas: audiunto illos.

Luc. XVI, 29. Non dicit: habent lumen internum, immediate docens: ad illud se applicanto.

( 6) Homini viatori, ad aeternam salutem tendenti, non opus est lumine interno immediate revelante: quia Deum & res diuinas S. scriptura satis plene & perspicue manifestat, atque adeo principium fidei saluificae sufficiens est.

Id quod liquido demonstratur: (a) E verbis S. Ioannis c. XX, 31. Haec scripta sunt, vt credatis, quod Iesus sit Christus, filius Dei, & vt credentes vitam habeatis in nomine ipsius.

Quaecunque scriptura eum in finem diuinitus destinata est, vt omnes per eam credant in Iesum, ad obtinendam vitam aeternam, illa viam salutis adeo plene & plane reuelat, vt homo viator reuelatione immediata non indigeat.

Atqui scriptura S. &c. Ergo.

( b) Ex effato Paullino Rom. XV, 4. Quaecunque praescripta sunt, in nostram doctrinam praescripta sunt, vt per patientiam & consolationem scripturarum spem habeamus.

Quod verbum diuinum datum est ad doctrinam nostram, eamque talem, ex qua spem salutis habeamus, id eo fine datum est, vt ex eo tantum notitiae salutaris hauriamus, quantum ad salutem obtinendam satis est.

Atqui scriptura S. &c. Ergo.

(c) E testimonio eiusdem apostoli 2 Tim. III, 14. 15. 16. Mane in iis, quae didicisti, & credita tibi sunt, sciens, a quo didiceris.

Et quia ab infantia sacras litteras nosti, quae possunt te sapientem reddere in salutem per fidem, quae in Christo Iesu est.

Nam omnis scriptura diuinitus inspirata etiam vtilis est ad doctrinam, ad redarguitionem, ad correctionem, ad disciplinam in iustitia.

Ex hoc dicto classico duo colligimus: (1) S. scriptura generatim omnem hominem sapientem reddere potest ad salutem per fidem, quae in Christo Iesu est, vt in doctrina ipsius salutifera persistendum sit: (2) Eadem speciatim theologum ad omnes docendi partes perfecte instruit.

E. S. scriptura satis plene & perspicue res ad salutem cognitu necessarias reuelat, vt homini viatori lumine interno, immediate reuelante, minime opus sit. Quod non detur internum lumen vniversale, manifestum est, quia gentiles, quibus verbum Dei externum haud innotuit, a Paulo describuntur, quod sint tenebræ, Eph.

V, 8. i. e. tenebricosissimi, vel densissimis ignorantiæ & vitiorum tenebris immersi; quos apostolus cap. IV, 18. graphice depingit, quod sint obscurati mente, existentes abalienati a vita Dei, propter ignorantiam, quæ in illis, propter obdurationem cordis; nec non in peccatis mortui, Eph. II, 1. sine Christo, abalienati a politia Israëlis, & peregrini testamentorum, promissionis nullam spem habentes, & athei in mundo. Eph. II, 12. Arguimus: (1) Quicunque homines sunt densissimis ignorantiæ tenebris immersi, mente obscurati, abalienati a vita Dei propter ignorantiam, quæ in illis est, sine Christo, nullam spem promissionis habentes, athei, & in peccatis mortui, in illis non datur lumen supernaturale, quod Deum & res diuinas ipsis immediate & obiectiue reuelat. Maior sole clarior est. Nam tenebræ opponuntur luci ab apostolo l. c. obscurati mente destituuntur lumine: abalienati a vita Dei non habent Spiritum S. in corde loquentem: qui sunt sine Christo, in illis non est lumen internum, quod dicitur vehiculum Christi: athei carent vnctione omnia docente: in mortuis nec scintilla lucis est.

Proinde ex osculor verba FORM. CONCORD. p. 662. Antequam homo per Spiritum S. illuminatur, conuertitur, regeneratur & trahitur, ex sese, & propriis naturalibus suis viribus, in rebus spiritualibus & ad conuersionem aut regenerationem suam nihil inchoare, operari, aut cooperari potest: nec plus, quam lapis, truncus aut limus.

Et p. 670. Visum est Deo per hoc medium, nimirum per sanctum verbum suum, cum id vel prædicari auditur, vel legitur, & per sacramentorum legitimum vsum, homines ad æternam salutem vocare, ad se trahere, conuertere, regenerare & sanctificare.

Excipiunt Quakeri: Testatur Paulus Rom.

II, 14. 15. gentes habere legem natura insertam; quia demonstrant opus legis scriptum in cordibus suis. Atqui lex natura inserta est lumen internum immediate reuelans. Resp. Lex cordibus natura inserta ratione proximæ originis est naturalis, quæ mysteria fidei non reuelat; ceteroqui non forent mysteria.

Iam nobis patescit, lumen internum Quakerorum non esse spirituale, aut supernaturale, sed naturale.

Quare haud ex vano censet D. BAIERVS in dissert. V. de norma doctrinæ §. 19. Naturalismum in Quakerismo latere.

Pergimus itaque argumentando: (2) Quodcunque lumen omnibus hominibus a natiuitate est, illud est naturale.

Atqui lumen internum Mysticorum & Quakerorum omnibus hominibus a natiuitate inest. E. Maior adeo firma est, vt nulla instantia infringi queat, & confirmatur ex eo, quod opus generationis naturalissimum est, quo nullum donum supernaturale propagatur, aut in posteros diffunditur.

Nam proprie loquendo donum supernaturale dicitur, quod naturæ a prima ipsius origine non inest, sed ad imperfectionem eius supplendam a Deo ex speciali gratia superadditur.

(3) In cordibus hominum illorum, qui sunt sine Christo, nullum lumen, nisi naturale, lucet.

Sed gentiles, quibus verbum Dei externum non innotuit, sunt sine Christo, Eph. II, 13. E. (4) Quodcunque lumen post completum scripturæ S. canonem in cordibus hominum non accenditur per verbum Dei externum, illud est aut lumen naturale, aut ignis diaboli fatuus.

Atqui lumen Quakerorum &c. E.

Prob. c. (1) Lumen internum, immediate reuelans, non potest esse substantia.

Nam foret substantia vel completa, vel incompleta. At non est substantia completa, quia non est totus homo; neque est pars hominis, quia neque corpus, neque anima hominis est.


### Q. V. What is natural knowledge of God?: (2) Whatever is in another, as in a subject, that is not a substance

(2) Whatever is in another, as in a subject, that is not a substance. But the internal light, etc. Therefore. The minor is proven because the internal light is in man not as his part, nor can it exist without him. The Quakers object: that this light can also subsist outside of man. Resp. Let them show, therefore, where it subsists outside of man, in heaven, under heaven, or above heaven.

(3) The internal light receives more and less, as Barclay does not deny in his Apol. p.

35. Therefore, it is not a substance.

Proof d. We are going to demonstrate, by a single but invincible argument, that the internal light revealing immediately is not salvific. Whatever light does not manifest to us Jesus Christ, the author, assertor, and vindicator of salvation, that is not salvific. But the immediate internal light of the Mystics and Quakers does not manifest to us Jesus Christ, the author, assertor, and vindicator of our salvation. Therefore, it is not salvific.

The major possesses invincible strength, because outside of Christ there is no salvation. Acts IV, 12. This is eternal life, that they may know you the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent, John XVII, 12. He who believes in the Son has eternal life: but he who does not believe the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him. The minor is clear, because the Gentiles, to whom the external word of God has not become known, are without Christ, Eph. II, 13. i.e., they do not acknowledge Christ.

To this argument, by which the Quakers are struck as if by lightning, they respond in various ways.

Some contend that explicit knowledge of Jesus Christ, who suffered and died for us, is not necessary for salvation: Others assert that many men have known Christ to whom the external word of God never became known, among whom they count not only the patriarchs, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, etc., but also the Sibyls and Hermes Trismegistus, to whom Christ was revealed without scripture. Resp.

(1) That explicit knowledge of Christ who suffered and died for us is most necessary for obtaining eternal salvation, the cited biblical sayings clearly show. We therefore detest the dogma of the Quakers, to which they would never have fallen if they believed that Christ was revealed through their light without scripture, as judged by D. SCHELWIG in Quakerismo confutato, Artic. I. §.

26. p. 167. (2) Distinguish between the times preceding the completed canon of scripture, and those following it.

Before the canon of scripture was completed, God sometimes revealed Himself immediately to a few holy men, namely the patriarchs and prophets; but to a huge multitude of men, He manifested Himself through the ministry of θεοπνεύστων (God-breathed) men. From which Noah is called a preacher of righteousness, 2 Pet. II, 5. Abraham commanded his children that they should keep the way of the Lord, and do justice and judgment. Gen. XVIII, 19. Jacob taught his family, Gen. XXXV, 2. Yet the patriarchs did not attain to the saving knowledge of God by internal revelation alone, without external means.

For the word of the Gospel concerning the seed of the woman, who would crush the head of the serpent, was for that reason revealed to the protoplasts not only to their minds, but also to their ears, so that they might propagate it by teaching to their descendants. Conf. Gen. III, 15. & IV, 26. Abraham also was informed by God by an external word concerning the seed, in whom not more to him than to the rest of the Gentiles was blessing to be given, Gen. XII, 3. which word he transmitted to his sons.

Gen. XVIII. (3) That the writings of the Sibyls and Hermes Trismegistus are supposititious, and gathered by heretics, is shown by M. COLBERG in Christianismo Platonico Hermetico Part I. c. I. p. 100. & c.

V. p. 208. Proof e. That the internal light, revealing immediately, does not manifest all things necessary to be known for salvation, is proven (1) because it does not reveal Christ the author of salvation, which we have already shown. (2) It does not notify the mysteries of faith; for they are hidden dogmas, and so sublime that they transcend the sphere of natural light by a very long way, nor do they become known except from special divine revelation, cease, which, upon the completion of the canon of scripture, has ordinarily been mediated.

We have proven above, however, that the internal light, in those things which it truly manifests, is the natural light, but in those things which it seems to reveal falsely, it is the devil’s will-o'-the-wisp.

(3) But if the entire economy of salvation could be learned from the internal light, teaching immediately all things necessary to be known for salvation, we earnestly ask those who disagree to provide clear reasons why God commanded the patriarchs to preach the external word? Why God sent prophets to teach the Israelite people? Why He raised up a great prophet and placed His word in his mouth? Why Christ brought the gospel from the bosom of the Father and preached it Himself with His honeyed mouth? Why the apostles went into the whole world to propagate the gospel of Christ far and wide, both by voice and by writings? Why even today pastors and teachers are divinely given for the edification of the body of Christ? Why they themselves teach in their assemblies? Why they have brought forth catechetical books and other writings into the light, if the internal light teaches immediately all things necessary for salvation?

The adversaries object that the preaching of the external word testifies to the internal light, and declares and manifests it.

Resp.

If the internal light is a true light, it will declare and manifest itself: but if it cannot accomplish this, it is truly a miserable light, having more darkness than splendor.

Moreover, an account will have to be rendered someday.

The Quaker's account before the divine tribunal, because they have thought so abjectly and contemptuously of the divine scripture; which we know to be θεόπνευστον (God-breathed), spirit and life, the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth.

Prob. f.

(1) Not the internal light, but the external word of God is the effective medium by which we are called to the church, illuminated, converted, regenerated, justified, renewed, preserved, and saved.

Latin:

(2) Quidquid est in alio, tanquam in subiecto, illud non est substantia. Atqui lumen internum &c. E. Minor prob. quia lumen internum est in homine non tanquam eius pars, neque sine illo esse potest. Excipiunt Quakeri: hoc lumen posse etiam extra hominem subsistere. Resp. Monstrent igitur, vbi extra hominem subsistat, in caelo, sub caelo, aut supra caelum.

(3) Lumen internum recipit magis & minus, non diffitente Barclaio in apol. p.

35. E. non est substantia.

Prob. d. Lumen internum immediate reuelans non esse salutiferum, vnico argumento, sed inuicto, demonstratum imus. Quodcunque lumen nobis non manifestat Iesum Christum, salutis auctorem, assertorem & vindicem, illud non est salutiferum. Atqui lumen internum immediatum Mysticorum & Quakerorum non manifestat nobis Iesum Christum, salutis nostrae auctorem, assertorem & vindicem. E. non est salutiferum.

Maior pollet robore inuicto, quia extra Christum non est salus. Act. IV, 12. Haec est vita aeterna, vt cognoscant te solum verum Deum, & quem misisti Iesum Christum, Io. XVII, 12. Qui credit in filium, habet vitam aeternam: qui vero non credit filio, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super illo. Minor claret, quia gentiles, quibus verbum Dei externum non innotuit, sunt fine Christo, Eph. II, 13. i. e. Christum non agnoscunt.

Ad hoc argumentum, quo velut fulmine percutiuntur Quakeri, diuerfimode respondent.

Alii contendunt, explicitam Iesu Christi, pro nobis passi & mortui, notitiam ad salutem non esse necessariam: Alii afferunt, multos homines cognouisse Christum, quibus verbum Dei externum nunquam innotuit, quos inter recensent non tantum patriarchas, Enochum, Noachum, Abrahamum &c. sed etiam Sibyllas & Hermetem Trismegistum, quibus absque scriptura Christus fit reuelatus.

Resp. (1) Explicitam Christi pro nobis passi & mortui notitiam ad aeternam salutem consequendam esse quam maxime necessariam, adducta dicta biblica luculenter ostendunt. Detestamur itaque dogma Quakerorum, ad quod nunquam fuissent delapsi, si per lumen suum, absque scriptura, Christum reuelari crederent, iudice D. SCHELWIGIO in Quakerismo confutato, Artic. I. §. 26. p.

167. (2) Dist. inter tempora antegressa completum scripturae canonem, & hunc secuta.

Priusquam absolueretur scripturae canon, Deus paucis hominibus sanctis, nempe patriarchis & prophetis se immediate quandoque patefecit; ingenti autem hominum multitudini, interueniente virorum θεοπνεύστων ministerio, se manifestauit. Ex quo Noachus vocatur praeco iustitiae, 2 Petr. II, 5. Abrahamus praecepit liberis suis, vt custodirent viam domini, & facerent iustitiam & iudicium. Gen. XIIX, 19. Iacobus docuit familiam suam, Gen. XXXV, 2. Neque tamen patriarchae ad salutarem Dei scientiam pertigerunt sola interna reuelatione, absque externis modis.

Nam verbum euangelii de semine mulieris, caput serpentis contrituro, ea de caussa protoplastorum non animis tantum, sed & auribus reuelabatur, vt ad posteros docendo propagarent. Conf. Gen. III, 15. & IV, 26. Abrahamus quoque a Deo informabatur verbo externo de semine, in quo non magis, ipsi quam reliquis gentilibus, benedicendum erat, Gen. XII, 3. quod verbum ad filios transmittebat. Gen. XIIX. (3) Scripta Sibyllarum & Hermetis Trismegisti supposita esse, & ab haereticis congesta, commonstrat M.

COLBERG. in christianismo Platonico Hermetico Part. I. c. I. p. 100. & c.

V. p. 208. Prob. e. Lumen internum, immediate reuelans, non omnia ad salutem cognitu necessaria manifestare, prob. (1) quia non reuelat Christum salutis auctorem, quod iam ostendimus. (2) Non notificat mysteria fidei; quippe quae sunt dogmata recondita, & adeo sublimia, vt sphaeram luminis naturalis longissime transcendant, nec nisi ex speciali reuelatione diuina innotescant, tescant, quae, completo scripturae canone, ordinarie mediata est.

Lumen internum autem in iis, quae vere manifestat, lumen naturale, in iis autem, quae falso revelare videtur, ignem diaboli fatuum esse, supra probatum dedimus.

(3) Quod si ex lumine interno, omnia ad salutem cognitu necessaria immediate docente, tota oeconomia salutis condisci posset, enixe rogamus diffidentes, ut luculentas reddant causas, cur Deus patriarchis praedicationem verbi externi mandaverit? cur Deus prophetas miserit ad docendum populum Israeliticum? cur suscitauerit prophetam magnum, & verbum suum in os ipsius posuerit? cur Christus e sinu patris evangelium protulerit, & ore suo mellifluo ipsemet praedicaverit? cur apostoli iuerint in vniuersum orbem ad evangelium Christi, qua voce, qua scriptis, longe lateque propagandum? cur hodienum diuinitus dantur pastores & doctores ad aedificationem corporis Christi? cur ipsi in conuentibus suis doceant? cur libros catecheticos, & alia scripta in lucem emiserint, si lumen internum omnia ad salutem necessaria immediate docet?

Excipiunt aduersarii, praedicationem verbi externi testari de lumine interno, idque declarare ac manifestare.

Resp.

Si lumen internum est verum lumen, seipsum declarabit & manifestabit: si hoc autem praestare nequit, profecto miserum est lumen, plus caliginis, quam splendoris habens.

Ceterum reddenda erit aliquando.

Quakeri ratio coram tribunali diuino, quod de scriptura diuina tam abiecte atque contemtim senserint; quippe quam nouimus esse θεόπνευστον , spiritum & vitam , potentiam Dei ad salutem omni credenti .

Prob. f.

(1) Non lumen internum, sed verbum Dei externum est efficax medium, quo ad ecclesiam vocamur , illuminamur , conuertimur , regeneramur , iustificamur , renouamur , conferuamur , saluamur .


### Q. V. What is natural knowledge of God?: (2) The internal light is not a true medium of salvation, but the devil’s will-o'-the-wisp; for by it the Quakers are enormously deceived…

(2) The internal light is not a true medium of salvation, but the devil’s will-o'-the-wisp; for by it the Quakers are enormously deceived and scatter so many false dogmas.

For it is false that there is a supernatural light in the Gentiles: it is false that a sinful man can be saved without explicit knowledge of Christ: it is false that there are not three persons in the one essence of God: it is false that Christ did not assume His flesh from Mary and her blood, but brought it from heaven: it is false that a converted sinner is justified without the imputed righteousness of Christ, etc.

Wherefore we must constantly persevere in this, that God does not wish to deal with us otherwise than through the vocal word and the sacraments, and that whatever is boasted of as spirit without the word and sacraments is the devil himself, as LUTHER rightly says, art.

Smalcald. p.

333. Prob. g.

In vain is the internal light adorned with great titles by the Quakers; because we have most clearly demonstrated that it is a non-entity.

But to distinguish a non-entity with honorary titles is very foolish.

In vain (1) is it called Christ in us.

For in that place Paul deals with Christ having suffered and been crucified for us, in whose blood we have the remission of sins.

Whether these things can be said of the internal light, let the Quakers judge, if there is any grain of salt in them.

(2) The Holy Spirit teaching all things.

For He is the third person of the divinity, which certainly is not the internal light.

For that is eternal, this begins with man.

(3) The seed of the kingdom.

By which is understood the external word of God, which is heard, and therefore, so that it may be heard, is preached.

(4) The seed of regeneration.

For that seed is the external word, which is evangelized among us.

(5) The communion of the spirit.

For in that place

Paul teaches that Christians have received one and the same spirit of Christ, which communion of the spirit ought to incite them to foster concord. They received, however, the Holy Spirit from the communion in the gospel, of which the apostle had made mention above in ch.

I, 5. (6) The manifestation of the Spirit, which is given to each one for the profit, 1 Cor.

XII, 7. For the manifestation of the Spirit, which pertains to the profit of the church, is made through the γραφὴν θεόπνευστον [God-breathed scripture], which is useful for doctrine &c.

2 Tim. III, 16. (7) The anointing that teaches all things, 1 Io.

II, 20. For by this is understood the Holy Spirit, who is true God. But the internal light is not God, and therefore the l. c. [loco citato - in the cited place] cannot be understood [as such].

D I S S O L U T I O N

Dissidents try to prove the internally teaching light, 1 from Io.

I, 9. He was the true light, which illuminates every man coming into this world. They think that in the l. c. it is not Christ for us that is understood, but Christ in us.

For the former did not illuminate all, but the latter is found in all, and therefore illuminates all who turn into themselves, wait for, observe, and receive immediate illumination in silence. Resp: 1) There is only one Christ, one mediator of God and men.

1 Tim. II, 4. 2) The cited words are understood of the person of Christ, who calls himself the light of the world, Io.

VIII, 12. by reason of the prophetic office, which he performed by preaching the divine word, and performs to this day by sending pastors and teachers into the church. 3) We distinguish with our D.

Hülsemann between intentional and actual illumination. Chrysostom explains the words of the Evangelist regarding intentional illumination.

Christ illuminates every man through the preaching of the word, as much as is in him. But if any do not wish to direct the eyes of their mind to the rays of this light, they have remained in darkness not from the nature of the light, but from their own malice.

Cyril, however, and Augustine wish for actual illumination to be understood in a reduplicative sense: Christ illuminates every man who is illuminated by the preaching of the word. But none of the interpreters explained the Johannine statement regarding an internal supernatural light.

Conf. D. Hülsemann. de auxiliis gratiae [on the aids of grace] p. 89. & 118. II.

The adversaries bring forward the saying of Christ Io. XII, 35. Yet a little while is the light with you: walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you.

The Quakers deny that the person of Christ is noted here, relying on the following argument: That which, when removed, would have caused the Jews to lose the time of believing, is not the person of Christ. But the light, of which John makes mention, being removed, the Jews &c.

The major premise is evident, because they could believe in Christ, and many believed in him for salvation, just as today all true Christians believe in him, even though his person is removed.

Resp. 1) The person of Christ is entirely understood, and it is indicated that the Jews, with Christ visibly present, teaching, and confirming his doctrine with miracles, had the most convenient opportunity for believing: whereas, once he was lifted onto the cross and taken up into heaven, no one would teach them with such a remarkable degree of love and candor.

2) We note the gross error of the Quakers, who posit that, with the visible presence removed, the person of Christ is removed. Which base opinion is repugnant both to heavenly truth, Matth.

XXVIII, 20. and to the Quakers' own hypothesis, asserting that the internal light is never separated from God and Christ, but where that is, there also God and Christ are involved and veiled within it. III. The λόγος ἔμφυτος [implanted word] can save a man, Iac.

I, 21. The internally teaching light is the λόγος ἔμφυτος, i. e. the implanted word. Therefore.

Resp. The λόγος ἔμφυτος is the external word, preached or read, which is called the λόγος ἔμφυτος, because it is implanted into the hearts of men through external preaching, just as natural external seed is cast into the furrows of the earth. IV.

That word which is in the man himself, that is internal. But the illuminating and regenerating word is in the man himself.

Therefore. The major premise is evident, because just as the external word is that which is outside the man: so the internal word is that which is in the man.

The minor premise is proved from Rom. X, 8. X, 8. The word is near you, in your mouth, and in your heart: see Col. III, 16. Let the word of Christ dwell in you abundantly. Resp. 1) The external word becomes internal when it is received by the heart of the listener or reader. For the divine word is external by reason of writing and preaching: yet it is also internal by reason of subjective adherence, insofar as it is received by the heart and adheres to it. Just as philosophical doctrine is external insofar as it is proposed by the teacher to the student: yet it is internal insofar as it is received by the student.

2) Paul, Rom. X, 8, expressly adds: This is the word of faith, which we preach, intending to point out that he is speaking about the external word.

V. In whom Christ is, in them is an internal light teaching immediately. But in men &c. Therefore. The major premise is self-evident, because Christ is the true light, John VIII, 12. The minor is clear from Col. I, 27. Christ is in you. Conf. 2 Cor. XIII, 5. Gal. IV, 19. Resp. 1) Christ, as a gracious presence, is not in all men: but the internal light revealing immediately is said by the adversaries to be in all. 2) Christ is in those who keep his word, John XIV, 23, and thus he teaches man not immediately, but mediately.

VI. In whom the kingdom of Christ is, in them is a supernatural light. But in men &c. Therefore. The major premise is established, because a supernatural light is required to know the kingdom of Christ. The minor is clear from Luke XVII, 21. The kingdom of God ἐντὸς ὑμῶν ἐστι, is within you. From which WEIGELIUS gathers in the book gnōthi seauton p. 52, that the kingdom of grace is in all men by nature, and does not come to them only through the preaching of the word; since it had already been in the Pharisees, albeit infidels.

Resp. The Savior teaches that the kingdom of God is not to be expected from elsewhere outside Judea, Is. II, 3, but is already in the bosom of the Jewish nation. For Christ and his disciples were preaching the kingdom of God, Matt. IV, 17, although it was not in individual Jews: because the Pharisees here are considered not in themselves, and by themselves alone, but gathered as it were into one body with the rest. 2) Grant that the kingdom of God was within the hearts of the Pharisees, by reason of knowledge, yet they had not obtained that knowledge of the kingdom of grace from an internal natural or supernatural light, but from the external word preached within the Jews.

VII. In whose hearts God is manifested, in them is an internal light. But in the hearts of the Gentiles &c. Therefore. The major premise is established, because that is called light which manifests something. The minor is proved from Rom. I, 19. τὸ γνωστὸν τῇ θεῷ φανερόν ἐστιν ἐν αὐτοῖς, whatever is known about God is manifest in them: for God has manifested it to them.

Resp. In whose hearts God is manifested, in them is an internal supernatural light; I deny it. For there is also given a natural light, from which God and divine things are known to a certain extent. The context teaches that Paul is speaking in the aforementioned place about the natural knowledge of God. But that does not suffice for salvation.

VIII. Immediate revelations are given. Therefore, today an internal light revealing immediately is given. The antecedent is proved by this argument: Those who even now receive the Spirit of God, so that they may know what things are of God, they even now receive immediate revelations. But all Christian believers &c. Therefore. The major premise is established, because the Holy Spirit is the spirit of wisdom and revelation, Eph. I, 17. The minor is clear from 1 Cor. II, 11. Resp. I deny the major. For where the spirit of wisdom and revelation is, there is divine revelation, either mediate or immediate. Immediate revelation happened long ago to the prophets and apostles; today all true Christians enjoy mediate revelation, who receive the Spirit of God in an orderly way through baptism, John

III, 5, and through the written or preached word, John VI, 63, Acts X, 44. Furthermore, the other arguments by which those of the opposite side strive to establish immediate revelations have been answered above, proleg.

III. qu. 3.

Latin:

(2) Lumen internum non est verum salutis medium, sed ignis diaboli fatuus; quippe quo Quakeri enormiter decepti, tot falsa dogmata spargunt.

Nam falsum est, in gentilibus esse lumen supernaturale: falsum est, hominem peccatorem sine explicita Christi notitia saluari: falsum est, in vnica Dei essentia non esse tres personas: falsum est, Christum carnem suam non ex Maria, eiusdemque sanguine assumpsisse, sed ex caelo attulisse: falsum est, peccatorem conuersum absque imputata Christi iustitia iustificari &c.

Quare in hoc nobis est constanter perseuerandum, quod Deus non velit nobiscum aliter agere, nisi per vocale verbum & sacramenta, & quod, quicquid sine verbo & sacramentis iactatur vt spiritus, sit ipse diabolus, recte ait LUTHERUS artic.

Frustra lumen internum a Quakeris magnis titulis ornatur; quia liquidissime demonstrauimus, illud esse nonens.

At nonens titulis honorariis insignire, perineptum est.

Frustra (1) vocatur Christus in nobis .

2 Tim. III, 16. (7) Unctio omnia docens, 1 Io.

Nam ille non omnes illuminauit, hic autem reperitur in omnibus, adeoque omnes illuminat, qui in seipsos introuertuntur, illuminationem immediatam cum silentio exspectant, obseruant, & recipiunt. Resp: 1) Vnus tantum est Christus, vnus mediator Dei & hominum.

1 Tim. II, 4. 2) Verba citata intelliguntur de persona Christi, qui se ipsum vocat lucem mundi, Io.

VIII, 12. ratione muneris prophetici, quo functus est, verbum diuinum praedicando, & hodienum fungitur, pastores atque doctores in ecclesiam mittendo. 3) Distinguimus cum nostro D.

Hülsemanno inter illuminationem intentionalem, & actualem. Chrysostomus verba Euangelistae exponit de illuminatione intentionali.

Christus per praedicationem verbi illuminat omnem hominem, quantum in ipso est. Si qui autem ad huius lucis radios, mentis oculos dirigere noluerint, non ex luminis natura, sed ex malitia sua in tenebris perfliterunt.

Cyrillus vero, & Augustinus intellectam volunt illuminationem actualem in sensu reduplicatiuo: Christus praedicatione verbi omnem hominem illuminat, qui illuminatur. At nemo interpretum dictum Ioanneum de lumine interno supernaturali exposuit.

Conf. D. Hülsemann. de auxiliis gratiae p. 89. & 118. II.

Adducunt aduersarii effatum Christi Io. XII, 35. Adhuc breue tempus vobiscum est: ambulate, quousque lucem habetis: ne tenebrae vos apprehendant.

Hic personam Christi notari negant Quakeri, nixi sequenti argumento: Quo remoto Iudaei tempus credendi amisissent, illud non est persona Christi. Sed lumine, cuius Ioannes meminit, remoto, Iudaei &c.

E. Maior patet, quia potuerunt in Christum credere, & multi ad salutem in ipsum crediderunt, sicut hodie omnes veri christiani in ipsum credunt, licet ipsius persona fit remota.

2) Notamus crassum Quakerorum errorem, statuentium, remota visibili praesentia, Christi personam remotam esse. Quae sublesta opinio repugnat tum veritati coelesti, Matth.

XXVIII, 20. tum propriae Quakerorum hypothesi, afferentium, lumen internum nunquam separari a Deo & Christo, sed vbi illud est, ibi etiam Deum & Christum in illo inuolutum & velatum esse. III. Λόγος ἔμφυτος potest hominem saluare, Iac.

I, 21. Lumen internum immediate docens est λόγος ἔμφυτος, i. e. verbum insitum. E.

Resp. Λόγος ἔμφυτος est verbum externum, praedicatum vel lectum, quod dicitur λόγος ἔμφυτος, quia per externam praedicationem cordibus hominum inseritur, sicut semen naturale externum sulcis terrae inicitur. IV.

Quod verbum in ipso est homine, illud est internum. Atqui verbum illuminans & regenerans in ipso est homine.

Etenim verbum divinum est externum, ratione scriptionis & prædicationis: idem tamen etiam est internum, ratione subiectivæ inhæsionis, quatenus a corde recipitur, eidemque inhæret. Sicut doctrina philosophica, est externa, quatenus a præceptore discipulo proponitur: eadem tamen interna est, quatenus a discipulo recipitur.

2) Paullus Rom. X, 8. expreffe addit: Hoc est verbum fidei, quod prædicamus, indigitaturus, se de verbo externo loqui.

Christus est in vobis. Conf. 2 Cor. XIII, 5. Gal. IV, 19. Resp. 1) Christus, qua præsentiam gratiosam, non est in omnibus hominibus: at lumen internum immediate revelans, ab aduersariis dicitur esse in omnibus. 2) Christus est in iis, qui verbum eius feruant, Io. XIV, 23. adeoque non immediate, sed mediate hominem docet.
