XVII, 21. Regnum Dei ἐντὸς ὑμῶν ἐστι, intra vos est. Ex quo colligit WEIGELIVS in libro γνῶθι σεαυτόν p. 52. Regnum gratiæ omnibus hominibus inesse per naturam, nec demum per verbi prædicationem in eos venire; siquidem illud iamdudum fuerit in Pharisæis, licet infidelibus.

Resp. Docet Saluator, regnum Dei non esse aliunde extra Iudæam exspectandum, Es. II, 3. sed iam esse in sinu gentis iudaicæ. Nam Christus & discipuli eius prædicabant regnum Dei, Matth. IV, 17. licet non esset in singulis Iudæis: quia Pharisæi hic considerantur non in se, ad per se soli, sed in vnum quasi corpus cum reliquis collecti. 2) Fac, regnum Dei fuisse intra corda Pharisæorum, ratione cognitionis, non tamen illam notitiam regni gratiæ ex lumine interno naturali, vel supernaturali, sed ex verbo externo intra Iudæos prædicato consecuti erant.

VII. In quorum cordibus manifestatur Deus, in illis est lumen internum. Atqui in cordibus gentiliuin &c. E. Maior constat, quia lumen dicitur, quod aliquid manifestat. Minor prob. ex Rom. I, 19. τὸ γνωστὸν τῇ θεῷ φανερόν ἐστιν ἐν αὐτοῖς, quidquid de Deo cognoscitur, manifestum est in ipsis: Deus enim ipsis manifestauit.

Resp. In quorum cordibus manifestatur Deus, in illis est lumen internum supernaturale; nego. Nam datur etiam lumen naturale, e quo Deus & res divinæ quadantenus cognoscuntur. De notitia Dei naturali Paullum l. c. loqui, docet contextus. At illa ad salutem non sufficit.

VIII. Dantur revelationes immediatæ. E. Hodienum datur lumen internum immediate revelans. Antecedens probatur hoc argumento: Qui etiamnum accipiunt Spiritum Dei, vt sciant, quæ sunt Dei, illi etiamnum accipiunt revelationes immediatas. Atqui omnes fideles christiani &c. F. Maior constat, quia Spiritus S. est spiritus sapientiæ & reuelationis. Eph. I, 17. Minor liquet ex 1 Cor. II, 11. Resp. Neg. maior. Nam vbi est spiritus sapientiæ & reuelationis, ibi est reuelatio diuina, vel mediata, vel immediata. Immediata olim contigit prophetis & apostolis; mediata hodie gaudent omnes veri christiani, qui Spirituna Dei ordinate per baptismum, Io.

III, 5. & per verbum scriptum, aut prædicatum, Io. VI, 63. Act. X, 44. accipiunt. Ceterum ad reliqua argumenta, quibus oi ἐξ ἐναντίας revelationes immediatas stabilire nituntur, responsum est supra, proleg.

III. qu. 3.


### Q. V. What is natural knowledge of God?: Q. X

Q. X.

What is the revealed knowledge of God? The revealed knowledge of God is that which is drawn in the church from supernatural divine revelation, comprised in the written Word, concerning the triune God, and is sufficient for eternal salvation.

The revealed knowledge of God differs from natural knowledge 1) By reason of the principle, which here is not nature, or a creature, but Holy Scripture. 2) By reason of the object: because, even though some things are also known by the light of nature, which the revealed θεογνωσία (theognosia) embraces, this nevertheless contains many things unknown to nature, such as concerning the divine persons, and concerning the evangelical will. 3) By reason of the knowing subject. Revealed knowledge of God is proper to the church; natural knowledge is common to all men. 4) By reason of the end. The revealed knowledge of God is salvific, John XVII, 3. But the natural knowledge of God is not sufficient for salvation, but only pedagogical; because its end, intended by the Creator in itself, is χειραγωγία (cheiragōgia), leading man to think and inquire about the assembly in which the true God of Israel dwells. Acts XVII, 27. Its accidental end, however, or outcome, resulting from the abuse of innate knowledge, is ἀναπολόγησις (anapologēsis), inexcusability, Rom. I, 20.

Latin:

Quaest. X. Quae est notitia Dei revelata?

Notitia Dei revelata est, quae est supernaturali revelatione divina, verbo scripto comprehensa, de Deo unitrino in ecclesia hauritur, & ad aeternam salutem sufficit. Obs.

Notitia Dei revelata differt a notitia naturali 1) ratione principii, quod hic non est natura, vel creatura, sed S. scriptura. 2) Ratione obiecti: quia, etsi nonnulla etiam lumine naturae sint nota, quae revelata θεογνωσία complectitur, haec tamen multa continet natura ignota, vtpote de personis divinis, de voluntate evangelica. 3) Ratione subiecti cognoscentis. Notitia Dei revelata ecclesiae propria, naturalis omnibus hominibus est communis. 4) Ratione finis. Notitia Dei revelata est salutifera, Io. XVII, 3. At notitia Dei naturalis, non est ad salutem sufficiens, sed tantum paedagogica; quia eius finis per se intentus a creatore est χειραγωγία, inducens hominem ad cogitandum & inquirendum de coetu, in quo verus Deus Israëlis habitat. Act. XVII, 27. Accidentalis autem eius finis, sive eventus, ex abusu notitiarum innatarum resultans, est ἀναπολόγησις, inexcusabilitas, Rom.


### Q. XI. Is the contemplation of God and divine things, which is said to occur either without species and discourse, or through new species

The contemplation of God and divine things, for the state of this life, neither occurs without species (a), nor without discourse (b), nor through new species divinely infused (c), nor is it to be preferred to the meditation of the divine Word (d). The antithesis is that of the Mystics, insisting on the footsteps of PLATO, who placed the highest good in the contemplation of God & divine things. See Theol. Myst. BALTHAS. KOEPKENII Part. I. c. I. p. 46. The Mystics, however, distinguish between meditation, & contemplation: which distinction D. MICHAEL DE MOLINOS explains and inculcates in the preface of the Manuductio spiritualis, admonition I. & II. p. 19. & seqq. Meditation is properly called that when the intellect considers the mysteries of our holy faith with attention, in order to know the truth of them, by discoursing upon the particular chapters of the same, and weighing the circumstances, and stirring up affections in the will. Contemplation, however, as THOMAS defines it, is a sincere, sweet, and quiet intuition of eternal truth, without discourse or reflection. It is otherwise called the prayer of faith, the prayer of quiet, interior recollection. They distinguish contemplation into acquired and infused. Acquired contemplation is otherwise called active and imperfect, and is that which can be obtained by our diligence, yet with divine grace assisting us, while we recollect our powers or faculties and senses, and prepare ourselves for all that God might will. Infused contemplation is passive and perfect, in which (as St. Teresa says) God speaks to man, suspending his intellect, interrupting his thought, and draws the word (as it is said) from his mouth, so that, even if he should wish ever so much, he is yet scarcely, and indeed not even scarcely, able to speak. He understands without the noise of words; the divine master instructs him, suspending his powers, which would then harm rather than help if they were to operate. They themselves rejoice, but how they rejoice, they do not understand. The soul burns with love, but how it burns, it does not perceive. It knows that it is enjoying Him whom it loves, but how it enjoys Him, it does not know: it sufficiently perceives that this enjoyment is not that to which the intellect aspires. The will embraces Him, nor does it understand how. p. 33. The same author brings forward the testimony of Bonaventure in these words: St. Bonaventure teaches that no thing is to be thought about, not even concerning God Himself, when imperfection occurs, by holding forms, images and species, however subtle they may be made, both of will and goodness, trinity and unity, even of the divine essence itself: when-unity, even of the divine essence itself: indeed all those species and images, although they may appear God-like, are nevertheless not God himself, who does not admit of any image or form.

One ought not, says the Saint, think there of things concerning creatures, nor of angels, nor of the trinity, because this wisdom must arise through the affections of desires, not through prior meditation.

He relates here that one should think of absolutely nothing concerning creatures, nor of angels, nor of God himself, because that wisdom and perfection is not generated through subtle meditation, but through desire and the affection of the will. p.

56. MOLINOS requires in the mystical contemplator a knowledge of God and divine things that is not distinct, but confused: Interior recollection is faith and silence in the presence of God.

Thence you ought to acquire the habit of recollecting yourself in his presence, with a certain most loving attention, so that he who gives himself to God, and unites with him with reverence, humility, and submission, beholding him within yourself, in the innermost end of your soul without form, species, mode, or figure, by an intuition and general knowledge of faith full of love and obscure, without any distinction of perfection or attribute. p.

93. & p. 95. Faith ought to be pure, without images and species, simple, without discourses, and universal, without reflection on distinct things.

Wherefore he judges that contemplation is not performed through the second operation of the mind, which is judgment; nor through the third, which is discourse; but through the first and principal operation of the intellect, namely through simple apprehension, illuminated by holy faith and aided by the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

To this Molinos we shall add the opinions of other Mystics concerning contemplation.

BARTHOLOMEW OF THE MARTYRS writes in his compendium of spiritual doctrine: If you ask what that darkness is, which contemplatives assert to be the supreme and ultimate goal to which our intellect can arrive on the way in the contemplation of the Lord (understand, however, without a special infused light), know that there are three degrees of divine knowledge.

The first is called discourse or meditation, when anyone contemplates divine perfections, or the attributes of the Lord, such as power, wisdom, and goodness, and proceeds from one to the others.

The second degree is called simple intelligence, when our intellect is so simply fixed on God and the divine essence that it considers nothing else besides God; but since this intellection, although simple, brings with it a positive concept of God, even if it does not regard any special attribute of his, and it is held by all for certain that all positive concepts which the frailty of our intellect can fashion concerning God are imperfect, and cannot fully suffice for true knowledge of God; but they are certain media between God and our intellect: therefore a third, still more sublime degree of divine knowledge is found, to which we arrive when our intellect entirely suspends both the acts and the concepts which it formed concerning God in meditation; or which it receives in the simple intellection of the divine essence, and then it is submerged in a certain ignorance, in which it confesses that it cannot sufficiently understand what the Lord is: and it is said to remain in darkness, which is the highest goal of all to which our intellect, while we live, can ascend.

Whence Dionysius writes that the best knowledge of God is this ignorance.

Wherefore the calamity of this life is deservedly to be deplored, whose highest happiness consists in this very ignorance and darkness of God, when yet the clear knowledge of the Lord alone exists as the highest beatitude.

What is denoted by that darkness, the author himself explains l. c.: The intellect, existing in that darkness, does not remain entirely idle, but since it expels all positive concepts, it remains in a certain negative concept far more perfect than them, namely, incomprehensible, inconceivable, unintelligible.

He therefore deems him happy who enters the darkness with Moses.

Among the principal cultivators of mystical theology is counted Cardinal RICHELIEU, who in his treatise on the perfection of the Christian differs in the following manner: In order that those (species of mental prayer) may be better understood, four different means by which men can attain knowledge of God seem to me to be proposed.

I.) The first is common to philosophers and Christians, and depends on the senses and the vision of creatures, from whose existence the first cause, which is God, is necessarily inferred.

By this means it is discerned that there is truly one first principle of all things; but what it is, is unknown, and by that pact, certain of its existence, certain of its existence, ty, we remain ignorant of the essence.

II.) The second is particular to Christians, who by faith attain and believe many things which do not fall into the senses, and which even at first glance are repugnant to reason, and also which in their judgment seem entirely impossible, whence faith is called by the Apostle the evidence of things not seen.

By this second means, not only is it known that God exists, but also what He is like: although we are in no way able to conceive clearly what His essence and perfections are.

III.) The third is special to certain souls, which God desires to raise to a peculiar degree of sublimity, by granting them a foretaste of the celestial happiness of the blessed, although not by the same reason and way by which they enjoy those things.

This happens in two ways: First, through the infusion of intelligible species, which are not expressed by the senses, but are formed expressly by God in the human mind, so that this agent, independently of sensible species, which it borrows from the eyes, ears, and other senses, may recognize its Creator more perfectly than it is accustomed to do through ideas produced by revelation regarding created things, which must be imperfect, because of the distance between the created and the uncreated, the defect and limits of the one, and the perfection and infinity of the other.

Such species infused by God are called by contemplatives Deiform and Deific, because they correspond more with the knowledge of the saints, who are united to God through God Himself in heaven, than with the knowledge of men, who on earth are not commonly carried to God, except through species drawn from sensible things.

The other mode, by which this effect is produced, consists not in the creation of a new form, species, or image, but only in the infusion of extraordinary light bestowed by God upon the soul, so that it may know Him better than usual, so efficacious that His essence, previously conceived imperfectly because of a lack of clarity, is then better perceived, even through the very same species by which the human mind was previously occupied in knowing Him.

The truth of this kind can be apprehended by the example of one who, not having enough from a single torch of light to perceive an image hidden in the dark, perceives it much more perfectly when illuminated by three or four torches.

IV.) The fourth means of knowing God is so much more varied and singular, in that it grants not only that the happiness of the blessed may be foretasted even here, but also that one may enjoy it in the same way that they enjoy it in heaven, i.e., to behold God through the light of glory, with this only difference, that in heaven the happiness and the mode of enjoying it are perpetual; but in these lower realms both are transient and momentary.

Such were the visions of Moses and divine Paul; the former the first doctor of the Jews, the latter of the Christians.

MAXIMILIAN SANDAEUS, no mean mystic, in his Theol.

Myst.

Book I, commentary XIV, exercise 1, disq. 1 & 3, calls this infused and passive contemplation supereminent.

The mystic enjoys it when God communicates a fuller influx of intellectual light, either through the emission or infusion of certain new species, suitable for the most excellent knowledge of God, so that they may represent God most clearly and accurately, or through a certain peculiar and most accommodating disposition, connection, complication, or ordering of pre-existing species.

For they are sometimes caught up in an admirable way to the interior of the darkness, and there, as if in the sight of God, who is essentially light, they receive new and unusual illuminations: the will also so burns and seethes that it seems to leap forth by a certain impulse and to be transformed and deified.

The mode by which such supereminent contemplation occurs, SANDAEUS delineates in the following way: Mystics describe it obscurely, yet I shall say, as best I can, in their sense, in my own words most clearly.

The contemplative soul is admitted to the divine darkness, since in it there is an intellectual and an affective part: the former, which is also the intelligence, beholds the Beloved in a certain way, but the intuition is so obscure that in beholding it does not behold.

And so it is considered to lie before the door or the inner sanctum of the dark dwelling, and there with crying, groaning, and sighing, with vows and repeated supplication, it asks that the face so often desired be manifested to it.

While it pants to see this, the affective part, which is the will, is caught up to the darkness of the indwelling God, to a most intimate meeting, while the intelligence remains outside.

Wherefore it is elevated by charity tative elevation of God above the understanding.

There, the will, having been established, begins by a certain new covenant to be borne toward God through a most intense affection, to be loved by Him as a bride, to love Him as the beloved, to be embraced by His arms, to be deemed worthy of a kiss, to be joined to God in an ineffable manner, to be transfused into Him, to flow out, to be transformed—in a single word, to be deified—not by a change of substance, but by a conversion of affection and most intense love; thus the will, united to God, conceives, tastes, and enjoys its beloved. Then, indeed, the understanding itself is also called to the supreme inner sanctuaries, and enters as it were into the holy of holies of a dark temple; it struggles through the densest cloud of incomprehensibility, is led to the very throne of majesty, is illuminated with new splendors, and although every veil is not withdrawn from the face of the divinity, yet it is borne toward God, who is surrounded by inaccessible light, with such an unswerving gaze that there seems to fall between it and the face of the beloved only the thinnest curtain of translucent linen or lamp-paper. This is that contemplation of the highest degree, sought by the vows of so many mystics, celebrated by so many encomiums, wrapped in the coverings of so many unknown names, designated by the symbols of so many varied things, expressed or shadowed forth by so many images, so often described, so often invoked by affection, voice, and tears. It is of no use to bring forward more mystical authors, since from the four cited, it is permitted to us to perceive clearly the opinion of the mystics concerning contemplation.

Latin:

Contemplatio Dei, rerumque divinarum, pro statu huius vitae, neque fit fine specie (a), neque fine discursu (b), neque per novas species divinitus immissas (c), neque eadem meditationi verbi divini praeferenda est (d). Antithesis est Mysticorum, insistentium vestigiis PLATONIS, qui summum bonum in contemplatione Dei & rerum divinarum collocavit. Vid. Theol. Myst. BALTHAS. KOEPKENII Part. I. c. I. p. 46. Distinguunt autem Mystici inter meditationem, & contemplationem: quam distinctionem exponit & inculcat D. MICHAEL DE MOLINOS in prooemio manuduct. spirit. monito I. & II. p. 19. & seqq. Meditatio proprie vocatur, quando intellectus mysteria sanctae nostrae fidei cum attentione considerat, ut veritatem eorum cognoscat, differendo de particularibus eorundem capitibus, ac ponderando circumstantias, ac ciendos in voluntate affectus. Contemplatio autem, definiente THOMA, est intuitio sincera, suavis, & quieta aeternae veritatis, sine discursu, aut reflexione. Vocatur alias oratio fidei, oratio quietis, recollectio interior. Contemplationem distinguunt in acquisitam, & infusam. Contemplatio acquisita dicitur alias activa & imperfecta, & est illa, quae nostra obtineri diligentia potest, adiuvante tamen nos gratia divina, dum potentias seu facultates nostras, sensusque recolligimus, nosque ad omne id, quod Deus voluerit, praeparamus. Contemplatio infusa est passiva & perfecta, in qua (dicente S. Theresia) Deus ad hominem loquitur, suspendens ipsius intellectum, interrumpens eius cogitationem, verbumque (vt dicitur) ex ore depromit, vt, si vel maxime velit, tamen vix, ac ne vix quidem, loqui valeat. Intelligit absque strepitu verborum, instruit ipsum divinus magister suspendens ipsius potentias, quod tunc nocerent potius, quam iuvarent, si operarentur. Gaudent ipsae, sed quomodo gaudeant, non intelligunt. Ardet anima amore, sed quomodo ardeat, non percipit. Cognoscit, quod fruatur eo, quem amat, sed quomodo eo fruatur, nescit: satis percipit, quod ea fruitio non fit, ad quam intellectus aspiret. Voluntas illum amplectitur, nec intelligit, quomodo. p. 33. Adducit idem testim. Bonaventurae his verbis: Docet S. Bonaventura nullam rem cogitandam esse, ne quidem de ipso Deo, cum imperfectio fit, tenere formas, imagines ac species, quam etiam fiat subtiles, tam voluntatis, quam bonitatis, trinitatis & unitatis, ipsius etiam essentia divina: quandovnitatis, ipsius etiam essentiæ diuinæ: quandoquidem omnes illae species ac imagines, quanquam Deiformes videantur, ipsae tamen non sunt Deus, qui non admittit imaginem, aut formam ullam.

Non ibi, dicit Sanctus, oportet cogitare res de creaturis, nec de angelis, nec de trinitate, quia haec sapientia per affectus desideriorum, non per meditationem praeuiam habet confurgere.

Refert hic plane nihil cogitare de creaturis, nec de angelis, nec de ipso Deo, quia ista sapientia & perfectio non generatur per subtilem meditationem, sed per desiderium & affectum voluntatis. p.

56. Notitiam Dei & rerum diuinarum requirit MOLINOSVS in contemplatore mystico non distinctam, sed confusam: Recollectio interior est fides & silentium in praesentia Dei.

Inde debes habitum acquirere, recolligendi te in eius praesentia, amantissima quadam attentione, ut qui se Deo dedat, & cum eo vniat cum reuerentia, humilitate ac submissione, intuens ipsum intra te, in intimo animae tuae fine forma, specie, modo aut figura, intuitione ac generali notitia fidei amoris plenae & obscurae, absque vlla distinctione perfectionis, aut attributi. p.

93. & p. 95. Fidem oportet esse puram, absque imaginibus ac specie, simplicem, absque discursibus, & vniuersalem, absque reflexione rerum distinctarum.

Quamobrem arbitratur, contemplationem non fieri per secundam mentis operationem, quae est iudicium; nec per tertiam, quae est discursus; sed per primam ac principem intellectus operationem, nempe per simplicem apprehensionem, sancta fide illuminatam, & adiutam Spiritus S. donis.

Huic Molinosio aliorum Mysticorum de contemplatione sententias adiiciemus.

BARTHOLOMAEVS DE MARTYRIBVS in compendio spiritualis doctrinae scribit: Si queras, quid sit caligo illa, quam contemplantes afferunt esse supremam ac vltimam metam, ad quam intellectus noster in via peruenire potest in contemplatione Domini (intellige tamen absque speciali lumine infuso), scito, tres esse gradus diuinae cognitionis.

Primus dicitur discursus aut meditatio, cum diuinas perfectiones quilibet contemplatur, seu domini attributa, ut potentiam, sapientiam & bonitatem, & ex vna in ceteras progreditur.

Secundus gradus dicitur simplex intelligentia, cum intellectus noster ita simpliciter in Deo, & diuina essentia figitur, ut nihil aliud praeter Deum consideret; sed cum haec intellectio, quamuis simplex, secum afferat conceptum de Deo positiuum, licet non respiciat aliquod speciale eius attributum, ac id ab omnibus pro certo habeatur, conceptus omnes positiuos, quos de Deo fingere intellectus nostri fragilitas potest, esse imperfectos, nec plene posse ad veram Dei cognitionem sufficere; at sunt media quaedam inter Deum & intellectum nostrum: ideo tertius sublimior adhuc reperitur cognitionis diuinae gradus, ad quem tunc peruenimus, cum intellectus noster omnino suspendit tam actus, quam conceptus, quos de Deo in meditatione formauit; vel quos in simplici diuinae essentiae intellectione recipit, & tunc in quadam ignoratione demergitur, in qua fatetur, se non satis intelligere posse, quid sit Dominus: & dicitur manere in caligine, quae est altissima meta omnium, ad quas intellectus noster, dum viuimus, ascendere potest.

Vnde scribit Dionysius, optimam de Deo scientiam esse hanc ignorantiam.

Quapropter merito deploranda est huius vitae calamitas, cuius summa felicitas in ipsa ignorantia atque Dei caligine consistit, cum tamen sola Domini clara cognitio summa existat beatitudo.

Quid per illam caliginem denotetur, ipse auctor l. c. exponit: Intellectus in ea exsistens caligine, non omnino manet otiosus, sed cum expellat omnes positiuos conceptus, manet in quodam negatiuo conceptu longe illis perfectiori, videlicet incomprehensibili, inconceptibili, inintelligibili.

Felicem igitur censet eum, qui cum Mose caliginem intrat.

Praecipuis theologiae mysticae cultoribus accensetur Cardinalis RICHELIEV, qui in tractatu de perfectione Christiani sequenti ratione disserit: Vt illae (species orationis mentalis) melius intelligantur, diuersa quatuor media, quibus Dei notitiam consequi possunt homines, proponenda mihi videntur.

I.) Primum philosophis at christiani est commune, & a sensibus ac visione creaturarum pendet, ex quarum existentia, prima causa, quae Deus est, necessario infertur.

Hoc medio omnium rerum vnum reuera primum principium dari, cernitur; sed quale fit, ignoratur, atque eo patto, certi de eius existentia pacto, certi de eius existentia, tia, remanemus ignari de essentia.

II.) Alterum christianis particulare est, qui fide multa assequuntur, & credunt, quae non in sensum cadunt, & quae etiam prima fronte rationi repugnant, nec non quae eorum iudicio penitus impossibilia videntur, unde fides ab apostolo vocatur argumentum non apparentium.

Hoc secundo medio non solum Deus esse cognoscitur, sed etiam qualis fit: quamuis illius essentia, perfectiones quas sint, euidenter concipere minime valemus.

III.) Tertium quibusdam animabus speciale est, quas ad peculiarem gradum sublimitatis Deus efferre cupit, felicitatem beatorum caelestem eis quadantenus praegustandam tribuendo, licet non eadem ratione ac via, qua illi ista perfruuntur.

Quod bifariam contingit: Primo per infusionem specierum intelligibilium, quae a sensibus non exprimuntur, sed a Deo expresse in hominis mente formantur, vt hic agens independenter a sensibilibus speciebus, quas ab oculis, auribus, aliisque sensibus mutuatur, perfectius agnoscat creatorem suum, quam soleat per ideas, reuelatione ad creata facta productas, quas imperfectas esse, necesse est, ob distantiam inter creatum & increatum, defectum ac limites vnius, & perfectionem atque infinitatem alterius.

Eiusmodi a Deo infusae species vocantur a contemplatiuis Deiformes & Deificae, quod magis conueniant cum notitia sanctorum, qui Deo per Deum ipsum in caelis vniuntur, quam cum hominum cognitione, qui ad Deum in terris communiter non feruntur, nisi per species a rebus sensibilibus eductas.

Alter modus, quo producitur iste effectus, consistit non in creatione nouae formae, speciei vel imaginis, sed tantum in infusione luminis extraordinarii a Deo collati animae, vt solito melius eam cognoscat, adeo efficacis, vt eius essentia eadem, ante concepta imperfecte ob defectum claritatis, tunc melius perspiciatur, licet per easmet species, per quas mens humana prius circa ipsum cognoscendum versabatur.

Veritas eiusmodi apprehendi potest eius exemplo, qui ex vnica face luminis satis non habens, vt in obscuro latentem imaginem perspiciat, multo perfectius eam conspicit, cum tribus, aut quatuor facibus circumlustratur.

IV.) Quartum Deum cognoscendi medium eo varius ac singularius est, quo non solum beatorum felicitatem etiam hic praelibandam concedit, sed & illa frui eadem via, qua illi in caelo ipsa perfruuntur, h.e. Deum intueri, per lumen gloriae, cum hoc duntaxat discrimine, quod in caelo felicitas, modusque ea fruendi perpetua sint; in his vero inferioribus vtraque transeuntia & momentanea.

Tales Mosis & diui Paulli fuere visiones; illius primi Iudaeorum doctoris, alterius christianorum.

Infusam & passiuam contemplationem MAXIMILIANVS SANDAEVS, mysticorum haud strenuus, in theol. myst.

L.I commentat. XIV. exercit.

1. disq. 1 & 3. appellat supereminentem.

qua gaudet mysticus, cum Deus pleniorem luminis intellectualis influxum communicat, siue per immissionem, aut infusionem nouarum quarundam specierum, ad notitiam Dei excellentissimam idonearum, vt Deum clarissime accuratissimeque repraesentent, siue per peculiarem quandam & accomodatissimam dispositionem, connexionem, complicationem, seu ordinationem specierum prae-habitarum.

Siquidem rapiuntur nonnunquam admirando quodam modo ad interiora caliginis, ibique tanquam in conspectu Dei, qui essentialiter lux est, illuminationes nouas & inusitatas recipiunt: voluntas quoque ita ardet & exaestuat, ut impetu quodam exilire videatur & transformari & deificari.

Modum, quo eiusmodi contemplatio supereminens fiat, sequenti ratione SANDAEVS delineat: Mystici fat obscure depromunt, dicam tamen, quam possum, ipsorum sensu, meis verbis clarissime.

Admissa anima contemplatiua ad caliginem, diuinam, cum in ea fit pars intellectiua & affectiua: illa, quae & intelligentia intuetur quodammodo dilectum, sed est intuitus tam obscurus, vt intuendo non intueatur.

Itaque iacere censetur ante domicilii tenebrosi ianuam vel adyta, ibique clamore, genitu & suspiriis, votis & repetita supplicatione postulare, manifestari sibi desideratam toties faciem.

Ad quam videndam dum anhelat, rapitur pars affectiua quae & voluntas, ad inhabitantis Dei caliginem, familiarissimum congressum, foris consistente intelligentia.

Quocirca eleuatur per charitatium tativam Dei sublevationem supra intelligentiam.

Ibi constituta voluntas incipit novo quodam pacto per incitatissimum affectum in Deum ferri, ab illo amari, ut sponsa, illum amare, ut dilectum, ab illo ulnis stringi, osculo dignari, ineffabili ratione Deo coniungi, in eum transfundi, diffluere, transformari, unico verbo, deificari, non substantiae immutatione, sed affectus & amoris intensissimi conversione, sic dilectum suum concipit, gustat, eoque fruitur voluntas unita Deo. Tum vero & intelligentia ipsa ad suprema vocatur adyta, ac veluti sancta sanctorum caliginosi templi ingreditur, per densissimam incomprehensibilitatis nubem enititur, ad ipsum maiestatis thronum ducitur, novis splendoribus illustratur, & quamvis velum omne a divinitatis vultu non subducatur: tamen ita irretorto in Deum, luce inaccessibili circumdatum, obtutu fertur, ut non nisi tenuissima ex carbaso translucente, aut lucernali papyro cortina inter ipsam & dilecti faciem, intercadere videatur. Haec est illa altissimi gradus contemplatio, tot mysticornm votis expetita, tot celebrata encomiis, tot nominum ignotissimorum obvoluta involucris, tot rerum variarum designata symbolis, tot expressa vel adumbrata imaginibus, toties descripta, toties affectu, voce, lacrimis advocata. Plures auctores mysticos adducere nil attinet, cum ex quatuor citatis, sententiam mysticornm de contemplatione liquido perspicere nobis liceat.


### Q. XI. Is the contemplation of God and divine things, which is said to occur either without species and discourse, or through new species: Ε Κ Θ Ε Σ Ι Σ (exposition)

Ε Κ Θ Ε Σ Ι Σ (EXPOSITION)

Obs. I. By contemplation (in German, die Beschauung oder Beschaulichkeit) the mystics do not understand speculation, which consists in and rests upon the mere cognition of an object.

For there are two ways, according to MOLINOS, Manuductio spiritualis, Book III, ch. XVIII, p. 373, which lead to the knowledge of God: one is remote, the other proximate. The first is called speculation; the second, contemplation. The learned, who follow scientific speculation and the sweetness of sensible discourses, ascend in this way, as they are able, to God, so that by this aid they may be able to love Him; but none of those who follow this way, which is called scholastic, arrives by it alone to the mystical way, nor to the excellence of union, transformation, simplicity, light, peace, tranquility, and love, as he who is led by divine grace through the mystical way to contemplation arrives at the experience of it.

Obs. II. Evangelical doctors do not wish for every contemplation of God and spiritual things to be rejected. For regenerate men, who have learned from the words of Scripture the true opinion concerning God and divine things, and have given their assent to it—while this knowledge and assent remain, and the intelligible species having thus been retained in their mind—then look upon the things themselves, which, these things being supposed, they behold just as they are exhibited to the intellect through intelligible species; and abstaining from carnal desires, they let themselves down into the deep contemplation and admiration of spiritual things; and those things which are contained generally in the Scriptures, they, descending under these to themselves, perceive some spiritual sense of the divine goodness, whereby the soul is sweetly affected and finds rest.

Cf. D. BAIERUS in Dissertatio de praegustu vitae aeternae, § 58, p. 52. Obs. III. It is asked at present: whether the contemplation of God occurs 1) without any species, either taken from created things or impressed upon the mind from the reading and hearing of the external divine word, 2) without discourse, 3) through new species divinely infused, or through an extraordinary light? 4) whether contemplation is to be preferred to divine meditation? Β Ε Β Α Ι Ω Σ Ι Σ (CONFIRMATION)

Prob. a. That the contemplation of God and divine things in this mortal life does not occur without an impressed species, we demonstrate clearly:

1) From the assertion of Paul, 1 Cor. XIII, 12. We see now through a glass in a dark manner, but then I shall know, even as I am known. The apostle opposes τὸ βλέπειν δι' ἐσόπτρου, to see through a glass, to τὸ βλέπειν πρόσωπον πρὸς πρόσωπον, to see face to face: of which the former, taken from a mirror, which presents to those looking into it not the thing itself, but its image, transferred to designate the knowledge of God and divine things, is the same as to know God, and those things which are of God, not in themselves, but as it were in an image, by means of signs and impressed species: which indeed are either taken from created things, or occur and inhere in the intellect through internal inspiration, or through an external word, whether of the living voice or of writing, by which God and divine things are represented to the human intellect; but the latter, or τὸ to see face to face, just as, speaking properly, it is the same as to discern the thing itself, without any image of it intervening, which, sustaining the place of the thing itself, is presented to our eye; so, transferred to the knowledge of God, it is the same as to know God through himself immediately, and without an impressed species. Therefore, by the force of the opposition between that which now is, and will at some time be abolished; and that which now is not, but will be at last after this life, when the imperfection of this life is abolished, it is necessarily gathered that the immediate and intuitive contemplation of God, by which God is discerned without an image of himself, is so reserved for the future life, that it has absolutely no place in this life. And since the apostle includes even himself in the number of those who know not face to face, but through a glass in a dark manner: with what face is a more sublime knowledge of God in this life attributed to any believers whatsoever? Is there any mortal who can be carried to such a height that he may reach the measure of Paul? says GREGORY NAZIANZEN, Orat. 29. From these premises we weave our argument: Whatever contemplation is so reserved for the future life, that not even the apostles were capable of it in this life, no mortal attributes that to himself without a notable mark of rashness and impiety. But the immediate and intuitive contemplation of God, which occurs without any impressed species, is so reserved for the future life, etc. Therefore. 2)

You say: Supereminent contemplation is intermediate between the abstractive and intuitive knowledge of God; because it occurs through a supernatural light, actually infused, and new species divinely infused. I reply: Paul denies that there is an intermediate knowledge of God between the abstractive, which occurs through an impressed species, and the intuitive, which occurs without a species. St. John supports him, 1 Ep. c. III, 2. Dearly beloved, we are now the sons of God, and it hath not yet appeared what we shall be; but we know that when he shall appear, we shall be like to him, because we shall see him as he is. To see God, as he is, denotes the intuitive knowledge of God, which occurs without an intervening image or species. But when the apostle says that this has not yet appeared, he says at the same time that the contemplation which occurs without a species has not yet happened to anyone in this life.

But the contemplation of the mystics, which occurs without an impressed species, is confused and obscure. Therefore, true Christians rightly and deservedly condemn it.

The major is evident, because the ἐπίγνωσις (knowledge) of true Christians is clear and distinct, it is ἐπίγνωσις, solid knowledge, Col. I, 9. It is πληροφορία τῆς συνέσεως (full assurance of understanding), firm persuasion of the intellect, Col. II, 2. It is the duty of true Christians to grow in grace and in the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, 2 Tim. III, 18.

The minor is clear, because MOLINOS confesses that, even if the intellect of the contemplator does not know distinctly by discourse, images and considerations, he nevertheless understands and knows through a dark, general and confused faith, in the proœmium of the manuduct. spirit., p. 17. The contemplation of the mystics is so murky that DIONYSIUS writes, as attested by PETER OF ALEXANDRIA, in compendio spiritualis doctrinæ, P. II, c. II, that this ignorance is the best knowledge of God. But in sacred Scripture ἄγνοια, or ignorance, is opposed to true faith, Act. XVII, 30. Eph. IV, 10. Indeed, I would dare to say that the contemplation of the pseudo-mystics is of the greatest ruin to the entire Christian religion. For not only heretics, but also Turks, Tartars, and Gentiles know God obscurely, confusedly, & indistinctly. For which reason that confused θεογνωσίας [knowledge of God] removes the distinction between true and false religion, and opens the way to skepticism and universal syncretism with heretics, Jews, Turks, and Gentiles.

Cf. D. ANDREAS KÜHNIVS, Contemplation on the Quietism of the Mystics , ch. II, p. 89.

(3) Every true contemplation of the human intellect, as long as the soul dwells in this mortal body, occurs through the conversion of the intellect to phantasms, or to sensible species, from which the human intellect abstracts, elicits, and purifies intelligible species.

From which FRANCISCVS SVAREZ, Tom. II. de Relig. l. 2. c. 14, concludes that it is naturally impossible for a man in this life to be rapt into the true contemplation of God through the intellect, while cooperating nothing at all through the senses, neither external nor internal.

Therefore, the human intellect does not contemplate God without sensible or intelligible species, unless it is separated from the body by death, or abstracted from the use of external senses by ecstasy. The most expert of the mystics seem to me to have acknowledged this. BARTHOLOMAEVS DE MARTYRIBVS, in his Compendium of Spiritual Doctrine , says: Mystical theology is nothing other than ecstatic love, having attained a pure intelligence of the spirit, purified from the clouds of phantasms. MICHAEL DE MOLINOS reckons ecstasy, rapture, liquefaction, swooning, etc., among the degrees of contemplation, p. 358.

Cardinal RICHELIEV, de perfect. christ. c. XXXII, says: The first and more significant effect of this sublime contemplation is ecstasy. Nay, this Cardinal calls supereminent contemplation rapture here, ch.

XXXIV. Rapture is the translation of any thing to a state either contrary to its nature or at least superior to it. Thus, a stone lifted upward, etc. Whence, since God, leading the soul away from its accustomed mode of operating through the imagination, elevates it to behold His majesty without reflection and without discourse, either in intelligible species which He fixes by industry, or in the divine essence itself, it ought to be judged as rapt, insofar as it acts above itself and in a mode by no means proper to its nature. From these things it is concluded that the contemplation of the pseudo-mystics, which they say they obtain without any phantasm, is to be valued no more than an ecstasy, through which the human soul is transferred from a natural state into a preternatural one. For ecstasy, as defined by RICHELIEV, is a state of the soul operating in a mode exceeding ordinary sensible and intellectual functions.

(4) The human intellect cannot know God better than through the images in Holy Scripture representing God to us as a most powerful Lord and King, a most just Judge, a most benign Father, a most merciful Redeemer of the human race, a most effective Sanctifier and Paraclete, etc. Through these images or species, God is known more rightly, more clearly, and more perfectly than without them.

You say: We know God more perfectly (in the opinion of DIONYSIUS) through negations than through affirmations. We think more highly of God, knowing that He is incomprehensible and superior to all our grasp, than by conceiving Him under some image according to our crude intellect. Therefore, greater esteem and love will be generated from that confused, obscure, and negative mode than from any other sensible and distinct one; because the former is proper to God, the latter is common to creatures, and therefore imperfect.

I respond: (I) We acknowledge, admire, and most highly esteem God as incomprehensible. But the love of God is not founded upon His incomprehensibility as a negative term, but upon His goodness as a positive term; because nothing is desirable and lovable unless it is good.

(II) God is Lord, King, Father, Redeemer, Sanctifier; He is likewise just, good, wise, and merciful properly, and these predicates are said of God more properly than of men, since they belong to God πρώτως [primarily], or primarily, but to creatures only δευτέρως [secondarily], secondarily.

Latin:

Ε Κ Θ Ε Σ Ι Σ

Obs. I. Per contemplationem (Germanice die Beschauung oder Beschaulichkeit) non intelligunt mystici speculationem, in mera cognitione obiecti consistentem & acquiescentem.

Duae enim viae sunt, censente MOLINOSIO libr. III. manuduct. spirit. c. XVIII. p. 373. quae ad cognitionem Dei deducunt: una est remota, altera proxima. Prima vocatur speculatio; secunda, contemplatio.

Docti, qui sequuntur scientificam speculationem ac dulcedinem fentibilium discursuum, ascendunt hoc modo, quod possunt, ad Deum, vt hoc adminiculo amare ipsum possint; sed nemo eorum, qui hanc viam sequuntur, quae vocatur scholastica, pervenit ea sola ad viam mysticam, neque ad excellentiam unionis, transformationis, simplicitatis, lucis, pacis, tranquillitatis, & amoris, vti pervenit ad eius experientiam is, qui deducitur divina gratia per viam mysticam ad contemplationem. Obs. II. Doctores evangelici non omnem contemplationem Dei, & rerum spiritualium reiectam volunt.

Nam homines renati, qui ex verbis scripturae veram de Deo ac rebus divinis sententiam didicerunt, eique assensum commodarunt, stante hac notitia & assensu, retentisque adeo in mente sua speciebus intelligibilibus, deinde res ipsas respiciunt, quas, his suppositis, prout intellectui per species intelligibiles sunt exhibitae, intuentur, & abstinentes a carnalibus desideriis in profundum rerum spiritualium contemplationem, & admirationem se demittunt, & quae in scripturis generaliter continentur, ipsi sub istis ad se descendentes, sensum aliquem spiritualem bonitatis divinae percipiunt, quod animus suaviter afficitur & acquiescit. Conf. D. BAIERVS in dissertat. de praegustu vitae aeternae §. 58. p. 52. Obs. III. Quaeritur impraesentiarum: an contemplatio Dei fiat 1) fine omni specie, vel a rebus creatis desumta, vel ex lectione & auditu verbi diuini externi menti impressis, 2) fine discursu, 3) per nouas species diuinitus immissas, aut per extraordinarium lumen?

4) an contemplatio meditationi diuinæ præferenda fit? Β Ε Β Α Ι Ω Σ Ι Σ Prob. a. Contemplationem Dei rerum diuinarum in hac vita mortali non fieri fine specie impressa, luculenter demonstramus: specie impressa, luculenter demonstramus:

1) Ex assertione Paulina 1 Cor. XIII, 12. Videmus nunc per speculum in ænigmate, tunc vero cognoscam, quemadmodum & cognitus sum. Opponit apostolus τὸ βλέπειν δι' ἐσόπτρου, videre per speculum, τῷ βλέπειν πρόσωπον πρὸς πρόσωπον, videre facie ad faciem: quorum illud, desumtum a speculo, quod non rem ipsam, sed imaginem eius intuentibus obiicit, ad cognitionem Dei & rerum divinarum designandam translatum, idem est, ac cognoscere Deum, & ea, quæ sunt Dei, non in se, sed velut imagine, mediantibus signis ac speciebus impressis: quæ quidem vel a rebus creatis desumtæ sunt, vel per inspirationem internam, vel per verbum externum, seu vivæ vocis, seu scripti, quo Deus & res divinæ intellectui hominis repræsentantur, obtingunt, & intellectui inhærent; posterius autem, seu τὸ videre a facie ad faciem, sicut proprie loquendo idem est, ac rem ipsam, non intercedente aliqua eius imagine, quæ vicem rei ipsius sustinens, oculo nostro obiiciatur, cernere; ita ad cognitionem Dei translatum, idem est, ac Deum per se immediate, & absque specie impressa cognoscere. Itaque vi oppositionis inter id, quod nunc est, atque aliquando abolebitur; & id, quod nunc non est, sed tunc demum post hanc vitam, abolita imperfectione huius vitæ, futurum est, necessario colligitur, contemplationem Dei immediatam & intuitiuam, qua Deus sine imagine sui cernitur, ita reseruatam esse futuræ vitæ, vt prorsus locum non habeat in hac vita. Cumque apostolus seipsum etiam eorum numero comprehendat, qui non de facie ad faciem, sed per speculum in ænigmate cognoscunt: qua fronte fidelibus quibuslibet sublimior in hac vita cognitio Dei tribuitur? An quisquam est mortalium, qui ad eam sublimitatem efferri possit, vt ad Paulli mensuram perueniat? ait GREGORIVS NAZIANZENVS, Orat. 29. Ex his præstitutis nectimus argumentum: Quæcunque contemplatio sic reseruata est futuræ vitæ, vt ne apostoli quidem illius fuerint in hac vita capaces, illam nemo mortalium sine insigni temeritatis & impietatis nota sibi tribuit. Atqui contemplatio Dei immediata & intuitiua, quæ sine omni fit impressa specie, sic reseruata est futuræ vitæ &c. Ergo. 2)

Dicis: Contemplatio supereminens est media inter cognitionem Dei abstractiuam, & intuitiuam; quia fit per lumen supernaturale, actualiter infusum, & nouas species diuinitus immissas. Resp. Paullus negat, dari mediam cognitionem Dei inter abstractiuam, quæ fit per impressam speciem, & intuitiuam, quæ fit sine specie. Suffragatur ipsi S. Ioannes, 1 Ep. c. III, 2. Charissimi, nunc filii Dei sumus, sed nondum apparuit, quid futuri simus; scimus autem, quod cum apparuerit, similes ei erimus, quoniam videbimus eum, sicut est. Videre Deum, sicut est, notat cognitionem Dei intuitiuam, quæ fit sine intercedente imagine, aut specie. Quando autem apostolus dicit, hoc nunc nondum apparuisse, simul dicit, contemplationem, quæ fit sine specie, nondum in hac vita cuiquam obtigisse.

3) Quæcunque cognitio Dei est confusa & obscura, illam veri christiani iure meritoque contemnunt. Atqui contemplatio mysticorum, quæ fit sine impressa specie, est confusa & obscura. Ergo veri christiani eam iure meritoque contemnunt.

Maior constat, quia ἐπίγνωσις verorum christianorum est liquida & distincta, est ἐπίγνωσις, solida cognitio, Col. I, 9. est πληροφορία τῆς συνέσεως, firma persuasio intelligentiæ, Col. II, 2. Verorum christianorum est, crescere in gratia & cognitione domini nostri & saluatoris Iesu Christi, 2 Tim. III, 18.

Minor claret, quia MOLINOSIVS fatetur, quod, etiamsi intellectus contemplatoris non cognoscat distincte per discursum, imagines & considerationes, intelligat nihilominus & cognoscat per fidem obscuram, generalem & confusam, in proœm. manuduct. spirit. p. 17. Contemplatio mysticorum adeo caliginosa est, vt DIONYSIVS scribat, optimam de Deo scientiam esse hanc ignorantiam, teste PETRO A MARTYRIBVS, in compendio spiritualis doctrinæ, P. II, c. II. In sacris litteris autem ἄγνοια, seu ignorantia, veræ fidei opponitur, Act. XVII, 30. Eph. IV, 10. Profecto ausim dicere, contemplationem pseudo-mysticorum universae christianae religioni summae esse perniciei. Etenim obscure, confuse & indistincte Deum cognoscunt non tantum haeretici, sed & Turcae, Tartari, gentiles. Quam ob rem confusa illa θεογνωσίας summouet discrimen inter religionem veram, & falsam, & pandit viam ad scepticismum, & universalem syncretismum cum haereticis, Iudaeis, Turcis & gentilibus.

Conf. D. ANDREAS KÜHNIVS de mysticorum Quietismo contemplatio c. II. p. 89.

(3) Omnis vera intellectus humani contemplatio, quoad anima in hoc mortali corpore degit, fit per conversionem intellectus ad phantasmata, sive ad species sensibiles, a quibus intellectus humanus abstrahit, elicit, & depurat species intelligibiles.

Ex quo colligit FRANCISCVS SVAREZ, Tom. II. de Relig. l. 2. c. 14. naturaliter fieri non posse, vt homo in hac vita rapiatur ad veram Dei contemplationem per intellectum, nihil omnino cooperando per sensum, neque externum, neque internum.

Non itaque contemplatur intellectus humanus Deum sine speciebus sensibilibus, aut intelligibilibus, nisi per mortem separetur a corpore, vel per ecstasin ab usu sensuum externorum abstrahatur. Mysticorum peritissimi id agnouisse mihi videntur. BARTHOLOMAEVS DE MARTYRIBVS in comp. doctrinae spiritualis inquit: Theologia mystica nihil aliud est, quam amor ecstaticus, consecutus puram spiritus intelligentiam, a nubibus phantasmatum depuratam. MICHAEL DE MOLINOS gradibus contemplationis accenset ecstasin, raptum, liquefactionem, deliquium &c. p. 358.

Cardinalis RICHELIEV de perfect. christ. c. XXXII. ait: Primus atque insignior effectus excelsae huius contemplationis ecstasis est. Quin immo supereminentem contemplationem hic Cardinalis raptum vocat, cap. XXXIV.

Raptus est cuiusuis rei translatio ad statum, vel naturae suae contrarium, vel saltem eo superiorem. Sic lapis sursum eleuatus &c. Vnde cum Deus animam a modo solito operandi per imaginationem educens, eam ad maiestatem suam conspiciendam sine reflexione, & sine discursu, vel in speciebus intelligibilibus, quas figit ex industria, vel in propria essentia diuina extollit, rapta illa censeri debet, quatenus supra se, & modo naturae suae minime proprio agit. Ex his conficitur, contemplationem pseudo-mysticorum, quam sibi sine omni phantasmate obtingere dicunt, non pluris esse aestimandam, quam ecstasin, per quam anima humana e statu naturali in praeternaturalem transfertur. Nam ecstasis, definiente RICHELIEV, est status animae operantis, modo excedente functiones ordinarias sensibiles & intellectuales.

(4) Intellectus humanus Deum melius cognoscere nequit, quam per imagines in S. scriptura Deum nobis repraesentantes, vt dominum & regem potentissimum, iudicem iustissimum, patrem benignissimum, redemptorem generis humani misericordissimum, sanctificatorem & paracletum efficacissimum &c.

Per has imagines aut species Deus rectius, clarius & perfectius, quam fine illis cognoscitur. Dicis: Perfectius (censente DIONYSIO) Deum cognoscimus per negationes, quam per affirmationes. Altius de Deo sentimus, cognoscentes, quod fit incomprehensibilis, & omni nostro captu superior, quam sub imagine quadam eum concipientes secundum rudem nostrum intellectum. Itaque maior aestimatio & amor gignetur ex isto modo confuso, obscuro & negativo, quam ex omni alio sensibili & distincto; quia ille Deo proprius, hic creaturis communis, adeoque imperfectus est.

Resp. (I) Deum incomprehensibilem agnoscimus, admiramur, maximeque aestimamus. At amor Dei non fundatur in ipsius incomprehensibilitate, tanquam termino negativo, sed in bonitate, tanquam termino positivo; quia nihil est appetibile, & amabile, nisi fit bonum.

(II) Deus est dominus, rex, Pater, redemptor, sanctificator, idem est iustus, bonus, sapiens, misericors proprie, & dicuntur haec praedicata de Deo magis proprie, quam de hominibus, siquidem Deo πρώτως, sive primario, creaturis vero tantum δευτέρως, secundario, competunt.


### Q. XI. Is the contemplation of God and divine things, which is said to occur either without species and discourse, or through new species: (5) The contemplation of the mystics introduces no small number of absurdities

(5) The contemplation of the mystics introduces no small number of absurdities. For since it is said that it occurs without any impressed species, BONAVENTURA maintains that no thing is to be thought of, not even God himself, since it is an imperfection to hold forms, images, and species, however subtle they may be, of the will, of goodness, of the trinity and unity, and even of the divine essence itself: since all those species and images, although they may seem God-like, are nevertheless not God himself, who does not admit any image or form.

From this absurd assertion it follows that God is not to be invoked in the Lord's Prayer as a heavenly father, not to be feared as lord and judge, and not to be loved as the highest good.

Which images or positive concepts, although they may not represent God adequately and fully, do so nevertheless inadequately and truly; since, if they do not represent the whole of God, they do represent something of God.

DIONYSIUS, however, uses insolent and clearly monstrous ways of speaking, c.

V. theol. myst., saying: God is not one, nor wise, nor wisdom, nor virtue, nor omnipotent, etc.

Who would not detest those ineptitudes, shall I say, or blasphemies?

(6) Paul seriously exhorts Timothy: ὑποτύπωσιν ἔχε ὑγιαινόντων λόγων, hold the form of sound words, which you have heard from me, in faith and love, which is in Christ Jesus, 2 Tim.

I, 13. The Vulgate [translates] Ὑποτύπωσιν as "form," HUGO GROTIUS as "a pattern fixed in the mind," others have rendered it "image" and "delineation."

Whose duty it is never not to have the form of sound words in faith and love, it is theirs not to contemplate God without any species or image.

But it is the duty of the faithful teachers of the church never not to have the form of sound words in faith and love.

Therefore,

Prob. b.

(1) True and salutary contemplation of God and divine things is directed toward the practice of the will, and thus occurs through discourse and practical syllogism, if not formal and fully expressed, certainly virtual and implicit, if not verbal, certainly mental.

For the true contemplator, with fixed eyes of the mind, beholds and weighs the independent, infinite, and immense essence of God, and concludes with himself: Therefore the majesty of God is to be admired: he contemplates the most exuberant goodness of God, and concludes: Therefore God is to be loved: nay, he even adds a more specific practical conclusion: Therefore God is to be loved by me also: he contemplates the wisdom and power of God, and reasons: Therefore God is also to be venerated.

A true contemplator, if anyone, was the apostle John, who, when he had turned the eyes of his mind to the love of God with which he embraces us mortals, concludes: Let us love him, because he first loved us, 1 John

IV, 19. You may find very many such virtual discourses in the monuments of the prophets and apostles.

To what good would the contemplations of God, thrice best and thrice greatest, be, unless they elicited spiritual and pious motions in our souls through discourse?

(2) The mystical contemplatives, thinking that contemplation occurs through the first operation of the mind, or simple apprehension, do not consider with themselves with how much infirmity our intellect labors, if you look at simple apprehension, which is necessary for beholding the essences of things, about which let us hear the philosopher of most refined judgment, D.

LEICHNER, lib. I. de vera philosophiae bono, cap. XIV. p.

150. Which original flaw, if considered philosophically, consists in this, that the intellect of man by its very nature is entirely NAKED (according to Aristotle, with respect to all actual knowledge), or (according to the mind of Plato, with respect to the notions they call innate) is a BLANK SLATE, with nothing of science actually inscribed, nor can anything be inscribed, except through sensory perception, and hence further by means of reasoning.

By both of which ways, indeed, the first operation of the mind (the simple apprehension of essences) in itself, or intrinsically, can by no means be perfected, nor can it ever be imbued with any intellectual species that represent the very essences of things, however much in the meantime vicarious sensible species and nodded complex concepts (predicatively and argumentatively) may provide assistance; otherwise, indeed, than they provide assistance; otherwise, indeed, than things had with the innocent first man, since his mind was not such a naked or erased tablet, which held nothing inscribed, unless what it had first received through prior sense or the discourse of reason, but shone with the ideas and images of essences impressed from the concreated light (like a living mirror), so that from this, even by simple intuition (without affirmation and negation, and without discourse), he truly perceived or contemplated the same; otherwise, indeed, he would have been just as blind and miserable as we are today.

Therefore, the entire power of our intellect, and the faculty of knowing, and all vigor resides in composition and division (affirmation and negation), and likewise in argumentation, partly resting on the first principles of any science, which are most known per se, and partly on the induction and experience of particulars, and as far as that light extends to both, penetrating the complex truth of things as the occasion arises scientifically.

These things having been established, I deny that the contemplation of God and divine things is uniquely achieved through the first operation of the mind; I deny that it is a simple intuition of God without judgment and discourse.

Prob. c. However, we utterly disapprove of and reject the passive, infused, and supereminent contemplation of the mystics, which occurs through the emission of new species (which are not revealed), or the infusion of extraordinary light.

For (1) Paul exhorts us 1 Cor. IV, 6. μάθητε τὸ μὴ ὑπὲρ ἃ γέγραπται, φρονεῖν, learn not to be wise above that which is written. They are not content with the species revealed in the word of God, but expect new ones. The light of Holy Scripture seems to them impure and too meager, and therefore they burn with a desire for extraordinary light: but by that very fact they slide into enthusiasm.

For thus are enthusiasts delineated in the Smalcald Articles, art. VIII, p. 351: In those things which concern the vocal and external word, it must be constantly held that God grants His Spirit or grace to no one, except through the word and with the external and preceding word, so that we may thus fortify ourselves against the enthusiasts, that is, the Spirits who boast that they have the Spirit before the word and without the word.

(2) For the teachers of truth, striving for sincere piety, the sufficient light of the prophetic and apostolic word shines forth, which the apostle Peter commends 2 Ep. I, 19. Indeed, the author of salvation himself gravely warns, John XXXI. Ἐὰν ὑμεῖς μείνητε ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τῷ ἐμῷ, ἀληθῶς μαθηταί μου ἐσέ. If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples. Conversely, if anyone teaches otherwise, and does not accede to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the doctrine which is according to godliness, he is puffed up, knowing nothing.

1 Tim. VI, 3, 4. (3) The mystics, by the supereminent contemplation which they boast of, pervert the order of the faculties of the soul, namely, of the intellect and the faculty, thinking that the will of the contemplator is snatched to the darkness of the indwelling God, to a familiar congress, while the intelligence stands outside, and is thus elevated through the charitable uplifting of God above intelligence.

But indeed, it is known to everyone that axiom: Nothing is willed, unless it is previously known. And that pronouncement of AUGUSTINE: As much as you know, so much do you love, is most conformable to the truth. (4) To the assertion of Cardinal RICHELIEV, saying that some reborn persons, exceptionally dear to God, are carried by singular divine grace to a peculiar degree of sublimity, so that they behold God through the light of glory on earth, just as the blessed in heaven, with this difference only, that in heaven the happiness and the mode of enjoying it are perpetual, while in these lower ones both are passing and momentary, we do not at all give our approval.

For by this assertion the state of wayfarers and the blessed is confounded. For the former now see God through a glass in a dark manner: but the latter face to face. The former know in part: but the latter perfectly.

1 Cor. XIII, 12. It has not yet been manifested to the former what they shall be: but the latter are like God, and see him as he is, 1 John III, 3. The former, while they dwell in the body, are pilgrims from the Lord; because they walk by faith, not by sight, appearance. These, while they wander away from the body, dwell with God, 2 Cor. V, 6. 7. 8. In this kingdom of grace, they are considered blessed who do not see, and yet believe. John XX, 29. Proof: (1) Meditation on the divine word produces a saving and beatific knowledge of God and divine things. Therefore, contemplation cannot produce a more perfect ἐπίγνωσιν (full knowledge) than meditation. The consequence is solid, because in this life a greater and more perfect knowledge of God and divine things cannot be given than that which leads us to eternal beatitude.

The antecedent is evident from very many biblical sayings. King David declares him blessed who meditates on the law of God day and night, Ps. I, 2. Christ pronounces those blessed who hear the word of God and keep it, Luke XI, 28. James exhorts c. I, 21: In meekness receive the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.

(2) From assiduous and attentive meditation on the divine word is born a distinct knowledge of God, of the divine persons, of the attributes and actions of God, and of the principles and means of salvation. From contemplation, however, proceeds a confused, obscure, and general knowledge, as witnessed by MOLINOS, monit. I. n. 7. p. 17. But knowledge, the more distinct it is, the more perfect it is. For confusion in any matter is an imperfection, while distinction is a perfection, especially in knowledge. For this reason, Protestant doctors, moved by weighty causes, consider meditation on the divine word superior to the contemplation of the mystics, although they do not reject all contemplation.

Latin:

(5) Haud exigua absurda infert contemplatio mysticorum. Cum enim dicatur fine omni impressa specie fieri, BONAVENTVRA statuit, nullam rem cogitandam esse, ne quidem de ipso Deo, cum imperfectio sit, tenere formas, imagines ac species, quam etiam sint subtiles tam voluntatis, quam bonitatis, trinitatis & unitatis, ipsius etiam essentiae diuinae: quandoquidem omnes illae species ac imagines, quanquam deiformes videantur, ipsae tamen non sunt Deus, qui non admittit imaginem, aut formam ullam.

Ex hoc absurdo asserto consequitur, Deum oratione dominica non esse inuocandum, vt patrem caelestem, non timendum, vt dominum & iudicem, non amandum, vt summum bonum.

Quae imagines aut conceptus positivi licet Deum non repraesentent adaequate & plene, attamen inadaequate & vere; siquidem non totum Deum, aliquid Dei tamen repraesentent.

Insolentibus autem, & plane monstrosis loquendi rationibus vtitur DIONYSIVS c.

V. theol. myst. inquies: Deus non est vnus, neque sapiens, neque sapientia, nec virtus, nec omnipotens &c.

Ecquis illas ineptias, dicam, an blasphemias, non detestetur?

(6) Paullus Timotheum serio cohortatur: ὑποτύπωσιν ἔχε ὑγιαινόντων λόγων, formam habe sanorum verborum, quae a me audiuisti, in fide & caritate, quae est in Christo Iesu, 2 Tim.

I, 13. Ὑποτύπωσιν vulgatus formam, HVGO GROTIVS exemplar in animo fixum, alii imaginem & delineationem reddiderunt.

Quorum est, formam sanorum verborum in fide & caritate nunquam non habere, illorum est, non absque omni specie, aut imagine, Deum contemplari.

Atqui fidelium doctorum ecclesiae est, formam sanorum verborum in fide & caritate nunquam non habere.

Ergo,

Prob. b.

(1) Vera & salutaris contemplatio Dei, rerumque diuinarum, dirigitur ad praxin voluntatis, adeoque fit per discursum & syllogismum practicum, si non formalem & plene expressum, certe virtualem & implicitum, si non verbalem, certe mentalem.

Nam verus contemplator fixis mentis oculis intuetur atque expendit essentiam Dei independentem, infinitam & immensam, atque secum colligit: Ergo maiestas Dei est admiranda: contemplatur bonitatem Dei exuberantissimam, & concludit: Ergo Deus est amandus: quin & specialiorem addit conclusionem practicam: Ergo & mihi Deus est amandus: contemplatur sapientiam & potentiam Dei, & ratiocinatur: Ergo & Deus est venerandus.

Verus contemplator, si quis alius, fuit Ioannes apostolus, qui cum oculos mentis conuertisset in dilectionem Dei, qua nos mortales complectitur, concludit: Nos diligamus eum, quia ipse prior dilexit nos, 1 Io.

IV, 19. Eiusmodi discursus virtuales longe plurimos in monumentis prophetarum & apostolorum inuenias.

Eccui bono forent contemplationes Dei ter optimi, ter maximi, nisi spirituales piosque motus in animis nostris elicerent per discursum?

(2) Mystici contemplatiui arbitrantes, contemplationem fieri per primam mentis operationem, siue simplicem apprehensionem, secum non reputant, quanta aegritudine laboret intellectus noster, si spectes simplicem apprehensionem, ad intuendas rerum essentias necessariam, de qua accurate differentem audiamus philosophum limatissimi iudicii, D.

LEICHNERVM lib. I. de vera philosophiae bono, cap. XIV. p.

150. Quae quidem originalis labes, si philosophice consideretur, in eo consistit, quod iam intellectus hominis natura sua prorsus NVDA (iuxta Aristotelem, respectuque actualis omnis notitiae), vel (ad mentem Platonis, respectuque notitiarum, quas innatas vocant) RASA TABVLA est, nihil scientiae actu inscriptum, sed nec inscribi quidquam potest, nisi sensuali perceptione, & hinc porro ratiocinatione mediante.

Qua vtraque sane via, prima mentis operatio (simplex essentiarum apprehensio) in sese, siue intrinsecus, haudquaquam perfici, nec ullis vnquam imbui potest intellectualibus speciebus, quae ipsas rerum essentias repraesentent, quales etiam cumque interim vicariae species sensibiles, nutuatique conceptus complexi, (praedicatiue & argumentatiue) suppetias ferant; secus vtique, ac suppetias ferant; secus utique, ac res habuit cum innocente adhuc primo homine, quippe cuius animus haud ita nuda, vel rasa fuit tabula, quæ nihil tenuerit inscriptum, nisi quod prævio sensu, vel rationis discursu primum acceperit, sed ex concreato lumine impressis (velut vivum speculum) splenduit essentiarum ideis & imaginibus, ita ut hinc simplici quoque intuitu (citra affirmationem & negationem, citraque discursum) easdem vere pernosceret, seu contemplaretur; alioqui namque æque profecto cæcus atque miser fuisset, ac nos hodieque.

Universa igitur ingenii nostri virtus, sciendique facultas, ac vigor omnis residet in compositione & divisione (affirmatione & negatione), itemque argumentatione, partim primis & κατ’ αὐτὸ notissimis cuiuslibet scientiæ principiis, partim singularium inductioni & experientiæ innitentibus, & quousque utrumque id lumen patet, complexam rerum veritatem pro re nata ἐπιστημονικῶς penetrantibus.

Quibus præstitutis, nego, contemplationem Dei rerumque divinarum unice fieri per primam mentis operationem; nego, eam esse simplicem Dei intuitum sine iudicio & discursu.

Prob. c. Contemplationem autem mysticorum passivam, infusam & supereminentem, quæ fit per immissionem novarum specierum (quæ non sunt revelatæ), aut infusionem luminis extraordinarii penitus improbamus & auferamur.

Nam (1) Paullus nos adhortatur 1 Cor. IV, 6. μάθητε τὸ μὴ ὑπὲρ ἃ γέγραπται, φρονεῖν, discatis, non supra id, quod scriptum est, sapere. Non contenti sunt speciebus in verbo Dei revelatis, sed novas expectant. Lumen S. scripturæ illis impurum, nimisque exile videtur, ideoque flagrant desiderio luminis extraordinarii: at eo ipso in enthusiasmum prolabuntur.

Sic namque enthusiaste artic. VIII. Smalcaldico p. 351. delineantur: In his, quæ vocale & externum verbum concernunt, constanter tenendum est, Deum nemini spiritum vel gratiam suam largiri, nisi per verbum & cum verbo externo & præcedente, vt ita præmuniamus nos aduersum enthusiastas, id est, Spiritus, qui iactitant, se ante verbum, & sine verbo, Spiritum habere.

(2) Doctoribus veritatis, sinceræque pietatis fatagentibus, sufficiens lumen verbi prophetici & apostolici prælucet, quod commendat apostolus Petrus 2 Ep. I, 19. Quin ipse etiam salutis auctor grauiter monet, Io. XXXI. Ἐὰν ὑμεῖς μείνητε ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τῷ ἐμῷ, ἀληθῶς μαθηταί μου ἐσέ. Si vos manseritis in sermone meo, veri discipuli mei estis. Contra, si quis aliter docet, & non accedit sanis sermonibus domini nostri Iesu Christi, & doctrina, quæ secundum pietatem est, is inflatus est, nihil sciens.

1 Tim. VI, 3. 4. (3) Mystici contemplatione supereminente, quam iactant, peruertunt ordinem facultatum animæ, sc. intellectus & facultatis, arbitrantes, voluntatem contemplatoris rapi ad Dei inhabitantis caliginem, familiarem congressum, foris consistente intelligentia, atque adeo elenari per caritatiuum Dei subleuationem supra intelligentiam.

At vero nemini non constat illud axioma: Nihil volitum, quin præcognitum. Et illud AVGVSTINI pronuntiatum: Quantum cognoscis, tantum diligis, quam maxime conforme est veritati. (4) Assertioni Cardinalis RICHELIEV, dicentis, nonnullos renatos, Deo eximie caros, singulari gratia diuina ad peculiarem sublimitatis gradum efferri, vt Deum intueantur per lumen gloriæ in terra, perinde ac beati in cælo, cum hoc duntaxat discrimine, quod in cælo felicitas modusque ea fruendi perpetua sint, in his vero inferioribus vtraque transeuntia & momentanea, album calculum minime adjicimus.

Hac quippe assertione status viatorum & beatorum confunditur. Nam illi nunc vident Deum per speculum in ænigmate: hi vero facie ad faciem. Illi cognoscunt ex parte: hi vero perfecte.

1 Cor. XIII, 12. Illis nondum manifestatum est, quid futuri sint: hi autem Deo sunt similes, & vident eum, sicut est, 1 Io. III, 3. Illi, dum habitant in corpore, peregrinantur a domino; quia per fidem ambulant, non per Speciem. Hi, dum peregrinantur e corpore, habitant apud Deum, 2 Cor. V, 6. 7. 8. In hoc regno gratiæ beati censentur, qui non vident, & tamen credunt. Io. XX, 29. Prob. d. (1) Meditatio verbi diuini parit notitiam Dei, rerumque diuinarum salutiferam & beatificam. E. Contemplatio meditatione perfectiorem ἐπίγνωσιν gignere nequit. Consequentia est solida, quia in hac vita maior & perfectior Dei, rerumque diuinarum notitia dari nequit, quam quæ ad æternam beatitudinem nos perducit. Antecedens e plurimis dictis biblicis patescit.

Rex Dauid eum beatum prædicat, qui in lege Dei meditatur diu noctuque, Ps. I, 2. Christus beatos pronuntiat, qui verbum Dei audiunt & custodiunt, Luc. XI, 28. Iacobus hortatur c. I, 21. In mansuetudine recipite implantatum verbum, quod potest saluas facere animas vestras.

(2) Ex assidua & attenta verbi diuini meditatione nascitur cognitio distincta Dei, personarumque diuinarum, attributorum & actionum Dei, principiorum & mediorum salutis. E contemplatione autem proficiscitur cognitio confusa, obscura & generalis, teste MOLINOSIO, monit. I. n. 7. p. 17. At cognitio, quo magis est distincta, eo perfectior est. Confusio enim in quacunque re imperfectionis est, distinctio perfectionis, in cognitione præcipue. Quam ob rem doctores protestantes grauibus moti caussis, meditationem verbi diuini contemplatione mysticorum potiorem ducunt, quamuis non omnem reiiciant contemplationem.


### Q. XI. Is the contemplation of God and divine things, which is said to occur either without species and discourse, or through new species: D I S S O L U T I O N

D I S S O L U T I O N

The mystics opine I. That experimental knowledge, which Paul calls αἴσθησιν, sense or experience, and distinguishes from ἐπιγνώσει, or cognition, Phil. I, 9, flows from and is drawn from contemplation. Resp.

(1) That αἴσθησιν denotes the sense or internal experience of grace, love, and divine goodness, is open to everyone. This sense of divine grace is also called the taste of goodness. Ps. XXXIV, 9, the Psalmist says: Taste and see how good Jehovah is. Where both to taste and to see denotes an experimental and sensible knowledge of divine goodness.

We subscribe to D. GEIER, who interprets the Davidic words concisely: טעם taste, i.e., ponder and experience with singular delight. The metaphor is drawn from the external animal sense to the internal intellect of man, and thus to taste is the same as to understand, to experience, to enjoy, as in Proverbs XXXI, 15. טעם and see, i.e., know abundantly and in many ways. Again, the metaphor is transferred from sensual knowledge to intellectual knowledge, in such a way that vision designates a more accurate knowledge of some thing: for sight is also more accurate than the other senses. Indeed, to see is sometimes the same as to enjoy the thing known at the same time. Cf. Eccl. I, 16. Ps. IV, 7. 13. For this reason, both to taste and to see denotes experimental knowledge, because in civil life we take an experiment of some thing no more through the taste of the tongue than the sight of the eyes.

We note at the same time the error of the mystics who establish that to taste designates practice, and to see designates theory, and from this conclude that practice in mystical theology precedes theory. But truly, the practice of the will is blind, which is not preceded by the distinct knowledge of the intellect.

(2) Not only literal knowledge about God and divine things, but also experimental knowledge, is drawn from the word of God reduced to letters. This we learn (a) from the Petrine statement, 1 Ep. c. II, 2. 3. As newborn infants, desire the sincere milk of the word, that you may grow by it; if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is gracious. Peter implies that we taste and feel the goodness of God in the sweetest milk of the gospel; for it presents to us the sweetness of the Lord to be tasted.

(b) From the Pauline utterance; since the apostle Paul joins the taste of the divine word and the taste of the powers of the world to come most closely, Hebr. VI, 5, saying: They have tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come; for the reason that the evangelical word not only [presents] celestial joys reveals to us objectively, but also effectively works in us righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit, Rom. XIV, 17. (3) That genuine contemplation, by which reborn men, according to intelligible species, gaze upon the grace of God with fixed eyes of the mind, and embrace it with singular trust, brings nothing of moment to the experimental knowledge of God, we do not deny. It is certain, however, that τὴν αἴσθησιν (the perception) does not occur without intelligible species, impressed upon the intellect by means of the external word.

II. Whoever tastes God dwelling in their hearts, they know Him immediately (without the concurrent external word of God). But true contemplatives, etc. The major is evident, because man can perceive everything that is in his heart, provided he descends into himself, without an external medium, and thus immediately. For the things of a man, the spirit of man which is in him knows, 1 Cor. II, 11. The minor is proven, because God dwells in the reborn, 1 Cor. III, 16. The same taste the goodness of God, Ps. XXXIV, 9. Resp. Whoever tastes God dwelling in their hearts, and are illuminated by the light of glory, they know God immediately; I concede. But in this life the illuminating grace of the Holy Spirit informs and illuminates us through the prophetic and apostolic word, 2 Petr. I, 19; 2 Cor. IV, 6; and thus we taste God not immediately, but in the milk of the Gospel.

III. Whoever tastes the powers of the age to come, they must be illuminated by the light of glory, so that they may be able to behold God immediately. But pious contemplatives, etc. E. The major is clear, because the powers of the age to come are joys which in these lands neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor have they descended into the heart of man, 1 Cor. II, 7. Wherefore, for their perception, the light of glory is required. The minor is clear from Heb. VI, 5. Resp. By the powers of the age to come, following D. SEBAST. SCHMIDIUS, comm. in h. l. p. 605, we understand righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit, in which the kingdom of God consists, Rom. XIV, 17. They are called δυνάμεις (powers), because God also singularly exercises His power within us in these; which δυνάμεις are common to the kingdom of grace and glory, although the degree of perception in the other life will be far more excellent. Indeed, peace and joy, and even begun righteousness, are most true goods, nor are they different in substance in this life than they are in the future life. But why, you ask, did the apostle not rather say the powers of this age, than of the age to come? Resp. The most powerful reason is that the apostle was about to teach that certain charisms, or goods of eternal life, are conferred even in this life in a certain degree upon those who are illuminated and have tasted the Gospel of Christ by true faith: it would have been permitted for them to attain the most perfect degree if they had persevered in faith. For this taste of faith, the light of glory is not required, but the light of grace suffices (*). Objection I. By this opinion, the blessedness of grace and glory differs only in degree; which is known to be false, because the γνῶσις (knowledge) of this life will be abolished in heaven, 1 Cor. XIII, 8. Now, perfect knowledge, differing only by degrees from imperfection, does not abolish it, but perfects it: just as a greater light does not remove a lesser, but increases it.

Resp. The blessedness of grace and glory differs with respect to certain charisms, or gifts common to this and the future life: it differs but the blessedness of glory differs from the blessedness of grace even in species, especially by reason of the beatific vision, which is the basis and most excellent good of eternal life.

For we see now through a glass in a riddle, but then face to face, 1 Cor. XIII. But speculative, abstractive, and mediate knowledge differs from facial, intuitive, and immediate knowledge, not in degree, but in species.

II. Instance II.
