Besides the common foretaste of eternal life, which is of faith tasting the goodness of God in the gospel, there is also given a proper and rarer foretaste of future blessedness, which the ancients called a rare little hour and a brief little delay; and which happens as if it were a divine kiss, bestowed in a moment, or a most sweet odor quickly affecting, quickly failing, and it consists in a certain more sublime joy, concerning which the Blessed Israel Mvrschelivs treats in his Aurora or Foretaste of Eternal Life p.

72. Cf. the Apologetic Script of the Tripolitan Ministry part 1. p. 333. and D. Baier’s Dissertation on the Foretaste of Eternal Life §. 60. Which rarer foretaste seems to infer an immediate and intuitive knowledge of God.

Resp. The foretaste of eternal life has certain degrees, according to which it can be distinguished into greater and lesser.

And although some men, especially the dying, have a more abundant sense or taste of certain gifts of eternal life; yet it is not to be denied that it happens through faith, which owes its origin to the gospel. Rom. X, 17. But the taste of faith does not infer an immediate knowledge of God.

III. III. God operates and concurs immediately with secondary causes in the kingdom of nature; why should He not also operate immediately in pious contemplators, who are in the kingdom of grace.

Resp. There is one immediacy of the operating subject, and another of the excluded operative medium. Just as God in the kingdom of nature concurs immediately, or proximately, with generating parents, yet not with the exclusion of the confluence of the parents and their fecund seed: so God in the kingdom of grace operates immediately and proximately in pious contemplators, not with the exclusion of the external word, as the ordinary medium of grace and faith.

IV. IV. King David, contemplating the divine goodness, says Psalm.

LXXXV, 9. I will hear what God speaks in me.

E. A pious man in contemplation hears God speaking in him immediately.

Resp. The words of the original text are poorly rendered in the Vulgate version, since they should have been translated thus: I will hear what Jehovah will speak: for He will speak peace to His people, and to His saints. Where it is not a matter of an internal and immediate address of God, but of the external word of promise, by which God promises peace, i.e., all prosperous things, to His people through the preaching of the prophets.

V. V. Whoever, as a bridegroom, speaks alone with a bride alone, he speaks with her immediately.

But God, as a bridegroom, speaks alone with the reborn soul, the spiritual bride, alone. E. The minor is proved from Hos.

II, 14. Therefore behold, I will persuade her, and lead her into the desert, and speak upon (to) her heart.

By which words God indicates that He is about to lead the pious soul into solitude, so that He may speak alone with her alone, and reveal Himself to her immediately. Resp.

The matter in the cited place concerns the gathering of the church in the N. T., to which, as it wanders, God wishes to persuade it to return to the way: He wishes to lead it into solitude, i.e., to segregate it from the impious lovers of the world: He wishes to speak to her heart (others translate: to her heart), i.e., He wishes to address and console her kindly through the gospel, which is full of comfort. For to speak to the heart, or upon the heart, signifies to comfort someone through gentle words, see Gen.

XXXIV, 2. Wherefore neither the major nor the minor of the argument stands on a firm foot.

For (a) a bridegroom speaking alone with a bride alone does not always speak with her immediately (with the external medium excluded), but sometimes by letter. Thus God today speaks with the soul through Scripture.

Paul Hebr. I, 1. says: At sundry times and in divers manners God spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets: hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son.

From which we argue: That locution with the soul which the Son of God finished, consummated, and sealed in these last times, that is no longer to be expected. But an immediate locution &c.

Therefore. God, leading the church into the wilderness, speaks upon the heart, or to her heart, not always alone, but through his ministers.

VI. Christ spoke immediately with the contemplative Mary of Bethany. Even today Christ speaks immediately with contemplatives. R. Mary of Bethany was not so much a contemplative as a meditatrix; for she heard the word of Christ, who, having visibly dwelt in these lands, spoke αὐτοπροσώπως (in person) with men; but being taken up into heaven, he speaks until the last day with the reborn through the mouth of the prophets and apostles,

VII. Paul seems to treat of the intuitive knowledge of God, saying: But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord. From which words the Mystics and Quakers gather: Those who with open face behold the glory of the Lord, they know God immediately and intuitively. But the reborn, etc. Therefore. The major is evident, because to behold the glory of God with open face is the same as to behold the essence of God. Resp. 1) I deny the major. For in the source is the Greek word κατοπτρίζεσθαι, which properly signifies to see something in a mirror, and thus denotes a specular, or abstractive, knowledge, not a facial, or intuitive, one. 2) The apostle does not say that we behold the revealed face of God, but that with open face we behold the glory of God as in a mirror. Indeed, he opposes the faithful Christians to the blinded Jews, upon whom a veil of ignorance is imposed, so that they might not understand that the end of the law and the fulfillment of the types and prophecies is Christ; but concerning himself and the faithful men of the New Testament, he asserts that with unveiled face they behold the glory of Christ shining in the mirror of the gospel: which knowledge is certainly mediate.

VIII. In the Holy Scriptures there are examples of those who saw God immediately. For Paul, caught up into the third heaven, saw the Lord, which vision cannot be mediate; because Paul was caught up into the third heaven, where the angels behold God immediately. So also Stephen, looking into heaven, saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. Resp. 1) Generally. It has happened to no man in this life to behold God immediately, except to Christ the θεανθρώπῳ (God-man). No man hath seen the Father, save he which is of the Father: he hath seen him, Cf. John 1, 18. 1 Tim. 6, 16. 2) Specifically. Paul did not see the essence of God in his ecstatic rapture; otherwise he would not have said: No man hath seen God, 1 Tim. 6, 16. (Now the epistle to Timothy was written after the epistle to the Corinthians) but he saw Christ in his glorious body, who revealed himself to him in an extraordinary way. The same must be said of Stephen, who saw the glory of God, i.e., a certain brightness, by which the majesty of God was represented: as the glory of God is understood, Luke 2, 9. He saw Jesus appearing in an immortal body and an august form.

IX. Mystics, intending to prove their dark contemplation, claim that they enter into the darkness with Moses, when, having expelled positive concepts, they remain in a negative concept, namely, incomprehensible, inconceptible, and unintelligible. Resp. The mystics are not slightly deceived. For Mount Sinai was surrounded and covered by smoke, which was the cause of the thick darkness, but the mystics, interpreting that darkness allegorically, understand by it the incomprehensibility of God. But it is agreed among all that an allegory is not argumentative, nor is a negative concept of itself quieting, since it satisfies neither the aspiration of the intellect nor the desire of the will. For pure negation is non-being, but mixed negation is founded upon affirmation, and presupposes it, as the victor GELENIUS says, P. I. dec. 8. art. 6. p. 8. Therefore the intellect rests not in negation, but in affirmation, while the will is borne toward the good, which is positive.

Let the mystics therefore be gone with their dark

THEOL. PART. I. CAP. I. DE DEO. contemplation! True disciples of Christ, by meditating on the revealed word of God, seek and find the knowledge of salvation.

Question XII. What does the revealed knowledge of God encompass? The revealed knowledge of God encompasses 1. the existence of God, 2. the essence and attributes of God, 3. the divine persons, 4. the divine actions and works.

Question XIII. Is the existence of God to be assumed here as known by the light of nature? The existence of God.

Since the knowledge of God drawn from the fount of reason is confused, weak, and languid: for the generation of undoubted faith (a), and the solid refutation of atheists (b), the existence of God must be demonstrated more fully and clearly here from supernatural revelation, as contained in the sacred scriptures (c).

Proof a. The principal article of faith is, that God exists: as it is the foundation upon which all others rest. For he that comes to God must believe that He is, and that He is a rewarder of them that diligently seek Him, as the apostle teaches, Hebr. XI, 6. But undoubted faith is generated from the seed of the divine word.

Io. XVII, 20. Proof b. Although atheists can be refuted from the principles of nature and reason: nevertheless, in order that they may believe by faith that God exists, the word of God committed to writing certainly deserves to be called to aid. For faith is not kindled except by the light of the divinely revealed word.

Rom. X, 14. Proof c. From the fount of Holy Scripture, through which a solid demonstration is drawn, by which the existence of God is proven.

For 1) generally all and singular letters of the divine written word speak of God's existence ; clearly the whole scripture is θεόπνευσος, consigned by God's inspiration, 2 Tim. III, 16. But what scripture is divinely inspired, that proves God to be its author. 2) *Specifically, the existence of God is gathered a) from the names attributed to God in the authentic writings of the prophets and apostles*; b) from the divine attributes, which, since they belong to God alone per se, cannot exist unless God Himself exists ; c) *from the works of God, which are the creation, the preservation of the whole world, especially the governance of the church described in the sacred scriptures, stupendous miracles, benefits bestowed on the pious, punishments inflicted on the impious, prophecies confirmed by events*. All these things, since they testify most clearly to the existence of God, must be most deeply impressed upon our minds, and opposed to our doubts about God no less than to the impiety of atheists, who deny God ; since it happens that even pious people, tossed by the heat of temptations, may have doubts about whether God exists.

Latin:

Δ Ι Α Λ Υ Σ Ι Σ

Mystici opinantur I. Notitiam experimentalem, quam Paullus vocat αἴσθησιν, sensum siue experientiam, & distinguit ab ἐπιγνώσει, siue cognitione, Phil. I, 9. e contemplatione fluere & hauriri.

Resp. (1) αἴσθησιν sensum siue experientiam internam gratiæ, amoris & bonitatis diuinæ denotare, nemini non apertum est. Vocatur hic sensus gratiæ diuinæ etiam gustus bonitatis. Ps. XXXIV, 9. ait Psalmista: Gustate & videte, quam bonus sit Iehouah. Vbi tam gustare, quam videre, notat experimentalem & sensibilem cognitionem bonitatis diuinæ.

Subscribimus D. GEIERO, verba Dauidica concinne interpretanti: טעם gustate, i.e. singulari cum oblectatione perpendite ac experimini. Metaphora ducitur ab externo animali sensu ad internum hominis intellectum, adeoque gustare idem est, quod intelligere, experiri, frui, ceu Prouerb. XXXI, 15. טעם & videte, h. e. abunde & multifariam cognoscite. Iterum a cognitione sensuali transfertur metaphora ad cognitionem intellectualem, ita quidem, ut visio designet cognitionem alicuius rei accuratiorem: nam etiam visus præ reliquis sensibus est accuratior. Immo videre idem quandoque est, ac frui simul re cognita.

Conf. Cohel. I, 16. Ps. IV, 7. 13. Quam ob rem tam gustare, quam videre denotat notitiam experimentalem, eo quod in vita ciuili experimentum alicuius rei capimus non magis per gustum linguæ, quam visum oculorum. Notamus insimul errorem mysticorum statuentium, gustare, praxin; videre, theoriam designare, atque ex hoc colligentium, praxin in theologia mystica præcedere theoriam. At profecto cæca est praxis voluntatis, quam non distincta præcedit cognitio intellectus.

(2) Non tantum notitia de Deo & rebus diuinis litteralis, sed etiam experimentalis, e verbo Dei in litteras redacto hauritur. Id quod discimus (a) ex effato Petrino, 1 Ep. c. II, 2. 3. Tanquam modo geniti infantes, verbale sincerum lac desiderate, ut per illud crescatis; siquidem gustastis, quod benignus sit Dominus. Innuit Petrus, nos gustare & sentire bonitatem Dei in dulcissimo lacte euangelii; quippe quod suauitatem domini degustandam nobis exhibet.

(b) Ex eloquio Paullino; siquidem apostolus Paullus gustum verbi diuini, & gustum virtutum futuri seculi arctissime coniungit, Hebr. VI, 5. inquien: Bonum gustarunt Dei verbum, virtutesque futuri sæculi; ideo quod verbum euangelicum non tantum gaudia cœlestia nobis obiective revelat, sed etiam effective in nobis operatur iustitiam, pacem et gaudium in Spiritu S. Rom. XIV, 17. (3) Genuinam contemplationem, qua homines renati iuxta species intelligibiles gratiam Dei fixis mentis oculis intuentur, eamque singulari fiducia amplectuntur, nihil momenti afferre ad notitiam Dei experimentalem, non negamus. Certum tamen est, τὴν αἴσθησιν non fieri sine speciebus intelligibilibus, mediante verbo externo intellectui impressis.

II. Quicunque Deum in cordibus suis habitantem gustant, illi ipsum immediate (absque concurrente verbo Dei externo) cognoscunt. Atqui veri contemplatores &c. E. Maior est evidens, quia homo omne id, quod in corde suo est, modo in se descendat, citra externum medium, adeoque immediate, perspicere potest. Nam quae sunt hominis, novit Spiritus hominis, qui in ipso est, 1 Cor. II, 11. Minor probatur, quia Deus in renatis habitat, 1 Cor. III, 16. iidem bonitatem Dei degustant, Ps. XXXIV, 9. Resp. Quicunque Deum in cordibus suis habitantem gustant, et lumine gloriae collustrantur, illi immediate Deum cognoscunt; concedo. At in hac vita Spiritus S. gratia illuminatrix nos informat et illuminat per verbum propheticum et apostolicum, 2 Petr. I, 19. 2 Cor. IV, 6. adeoque gustamus Deum non immediate, sed in lacte evangelii.

III. Quicunque gustant virtutes futuri saeculi, illos oportet lumine gloriae collustratos esse, ut Deum immediate intueri queant. At pii contemplatores &c. E. Maior patet, quia virtutes futuri saeculi sunt gaudia, quae in his terris nec oculus vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis descenderunt. 1 Cor. II, 7. Quare ad earum perceptionem requiritur lumen gloriae. Minor claret ex Hebr. VI, 5. Resp. Per virtutes futuri saeculi, praeunte D. SEBAST. SCHMIDIO, comm. in h. l. p. 605. intelligimus iustitiam, pacem et gaudium in Spiritu S. in quibus regnum Dei consistit. Rom. XIV, 17. dicuntur δυνάμεις virtutes, propterea quod singulariter Deus quoque in his suam virtutem intra nos exercet; quae δυνάμεις regno gratiae et gloriae communes sunt, licet gradus perceptionis in altera vita longe excellentior futurus sit. Sane pax, gaudiumque, quin et iustitia inchoata, verissima bona sunt, nec ratione substantiae alia in hac, quam in futura vita sunt. Sed quare, inquis, apostolus non potius dixit virtutes huius saeculi, quam futuri saeculi? Resp. Potissima ratio est, quia apostolus docturus fuit, quaedam charismata, sive bona-vitae aeternae, etiam in hac vita conferri in certo gradu iis, qui sunt illuminati, et evangelium Christi gustarunt vera fide: gradum perfectissimum iisdem licuisset consequi, si in fide perseverassent. Ad hunc gustum fidei non requiritur lumen gloriae, sed sufficit lumen gratiae (*). Inflantia I. Per istam sententiam beatitudo gratiae et gloriae tantum gradu differt; quod falsum esse constat, quia γνῶσις huius vitae in caelo abolebitur, 1 Cor. XIII, 8. Iam vero cognitio perfecta, gradibus tantum differens ab imperfectione, hanc non abolet, sed perficit: sicut maius lumen minus non tollit, sed auget.

Resp. Beatitudo gratiae et gloriae differt respectu quorundam charismatum, sive donorum huic et futurae vitae communium: differt autem beatitudo gloriae a beatitudine gratiae etiam specie, inprimis ratione visionis beatificae, quae vitae aeternae basis & praestantissimum bonum est.

Videmus enim nunc per speculum in aenigmate, tunc autem a facie ad faciem, 1 Cor. XIII. At cognitio specularis, abstractiva & mediata, a faciali, intuitiva & immediata, non gradu, sed specie differt.

II. Instantia II.

Praeter communem vitae aeternae praegustum, qui est fidei in euangelio bonitatem Dei degustantis, datur etiam proprius & rarior praegustus futurae beatitudinis, quem veteres vocarunt raram horulam & breuem morulam; quique fit quasi osculum diuinum, momento illatum, aut suauissimus odor cito afficiens, cito deficiens, & consistat in gaudio quodam sublimiore, de quo agit B.

Israel Mvrschelivs in aurora siue praegustu vitae aeternae p. 72. Conf. Ministerii Tripolitani script. apol. part. 1. p. 333. & D. Baieri Dissert. de praegustu vitae aeternae §. 60. Qui praegustus rarior videtur inferre immediatam & intuitiuam Dei cognitionem.

Resp. Praegustus vitae aeternae certos habet gradus, secundum quos distingui potest in maiorem & minorem.

Et quamuis nonnulli homines, inprimis moribundi, abundantiorem quorundam donorum vitae aeternae sensum aut gustum habeant; non tamen negandum est, eum fieri per fidem, quae suam originem debet euangelio. Rom. X, 17. At gustus fidei non infert immediatam Dei cognitionem.

III. III. Deus immediate operatur & concurrit cum causis secundis in regno naturae; quidni etiam immediate operetur in piis contemplatoribus, qui sunt in regno gratiae.

Resp. Alia immediatio est subiecti operantis, alia est exclusi medii operatiui. Sicut Deus in regno naturae cum parentibus generantibus immediate, siue proxime concurrit, non autem excluso parenteum confluxu, eorumque faecundo semine: ita Deus in regno gratiae immediate & proxime operatur in piis contemplantibus, non excluso verbo externo, tanquam ordinario gratiae fatusque medio.

IV. IV. Rex Dauid contemplans bonitatem diuinam, dicit Psalm.

LXXXV, 9. Audiam, quid Deus in me loquatur.

E. Homo pius in contemplatione audit Deum in se immediate loquentem.

Resp. Verba textus originalis in vulgata versione male reddita sunt, cum sic essent vertenda: Audiam, quod locuturus sit Iehouah: nam loquetur pacem ad populum suum, & ad sanctos suos. Vbi non agitur de interno & immediato alloquio Dei, sed de externo verbo promissionis, quo Deus per conciones prophetarum populo suo pacem, i.e. prospera quaeque, promittit.

V. V. Quicunque sponsus solus cum sponsa sola loquitur, is immediate cum ea colloquitur.

Atqui Deus, tanquam sponsus, solus cum anima renata, spirituali sponsa, sola loquitur. E.

Minor probatur ex Hos. II, 14. Propterea ecce, ego persuadens illi, & deducam illam in desertum, & loquar super (ad) cor illius.

Quibus verbis Deus indicat, se ducturum esse animam piam in solitudinem, vt solus cum sola loquatur, & se eidem immediate reuelet. Resp.

Agitur l. c. de collectione ecclesiae in N. T. cui erranti Deus vult persuadere, vt redeat in viam: vult eam deducere in solitudinem, i.e. segregare ab impiis mundi amatoribus: vult fuer eius cor (alii reddunt: ad cor illius) loqui, i.e. vult eam comiter alloqui & consolari per euangelium, quod est plenum solatii.

Nam loqui ad cor, vel super cor, significat per verba blanda aliquem solari, vid. Gen. XXXIV, 2. Quare nec maior, nec minor argumenti firmo stat talo.

Nam (a) sponsus solus cum sola sponsa loquens, non semper cum ea loquitur immediate (excluso medio externo), sed interdum per epistolam. Ita Deus hodie loquitur cum anima per scripturam.

Paullus Hebr. I, 1. dicit: Multis vicibus, multisque modis olim Deus locutus patribus in prophetis: vltimis diebus hisce locutus est nobis in filio.

Ex quo arguimus: Quam locutionem cum anima filius Dei vltimis temporibus finiuit, consummauit, & obsignauit, illa non amplius est exspectanda. Atqui locutionem immediatam &c.

Ergo. Deus deducens ecclesiam in desertum, loquitur super cor, siue ad cor illius non semper solus, sed per ministros suos.

VI. Christus cum contemplatrice Maria Bethaniensi immediate locutus est. Hodienum Christus cum contemplatoribus immediate loquitur. R. Maria Bethaniensis non tam contemplatrix, quam meditatrix fuit: audiuit enim verbum Christi, qui visibiliter versatus in his terris, αὐτοπροσώπως collocutus est cum hominibus; at evectus in coelum vsque ad diem extremum cum renatis loquitur per os prophetarum & apostolorum,

VII. De intuitiua Dei cognitione agere videtur Paullus inquiens: Nos autem omnes reuelata facie gloriam domini introspicientes, in eandem imaginem transformamur a gloria in gloriam, tanquam a domini Spiritu. E quibus verbis colligunt Mystici & Quakeri: Qui reuelata facie gloriam domini introspiciunt, illi cognoscunt Deum immediate & intuitiue. Atqui renati &c. Ergo. Maior patet, quia reuelata facie gloriam Dei introspiciere idem est, quod essentiam Dei intueri. Resp. 1) Neg. maior. Nam in fonte habetur græcum verbum κατοπτρίζεσθαι, quod proprie significat aliquid in speculo videre, adeoque notat cognitionem specularem, seu abstractiuam, non facialem, seu intuitiuam. 2) Non dicit apostolus, quod reuelatam Dei faciem intueamur, sed quod reuelata facie gloriam Dei velut in speculo introspiciamus. Nimirum opponit fideles christianos occæcatis Iudæis, quibus velamen ignorantiæ impositum est, vt ne intelligant finem legis & complementum typorum ac vaticiniorum esse Christum; de se autem & hominibus fidelibus N. T. asserit, quod facie retecta introspiciant in gloriam Christi in speculo euangelii relucentem: quæ cognitio vtique mediata est.

VIII. In sacris litteris prostant exempla eorum, qui Deum immediate viderunt. Nam Paullus raptus in cœlum tertium, vidit Dominum, Quæ visio non potest esse mediata; quia Paullus raptus est in cœlum tertium, vbi angeli Deum immediate intuentur. Sic & Stephanus, intuens in cœlum, vidit gloriam Dei, & Iesum stantem a dextris Dei, Resp. 1) generatim. Nulli hominum in hac vita contigit, immediate intueri Deum, nisi Christo θεανθρώπῳ. Nemo vidit patrem, nisi qui apud patrem est: hic vidit ipsum, Conf. Io. I, 18. 1 Tim. VI, 16. 2) Speciatim. Non vidit Paullus in raptu suo ecstatico essentiam Dei; alioqui non dixisset: Deum vidit nullus hominum, 1 Tim. VI, 16. (Scripta autem est epistola ad Timotheum post epist. ad Corinthios) sed vidit Christum in corpore ipsius glorioso, qui modo extraordinario se ipsi reuelauit. Idem dicendum est de Stephano, qui vidit gloriam Dei, i. e. fulgorem quendam, quo maiestas Dei repræsentabatur: prout gloria Dei accipitur, Luc. II, 9. Vidit Iesum in corpore immortali formaque augusta apparentem.

IX. Mystici, probaturi caliginosam suam contemplationem, afferunt, se cum Mose intrare in caliginem, quando expulsis conceptibus positiuis, manent in conceptu negatiuo, videlicet incomprehensibili, inconceptibili, & intelligibili. Resp. Haud leuiter desipiunt mystici. Etenim mons Sinai fumo circumdatus & obtectus erat, qui spissæ caliginis caussa erat, Mystici autem caliginem illam allegorice exponentes intelligunt per eam incomprehensibilitatem Dei. At vero constat inter omnes, allegoriam non esse argumentatiuam, nec conceptum negatiuum per se quietificum, cum nec adspirationi intellectus, nec desiderio voluntatis satisfaciat. Nam pura negatio est nonens, mixta autem negatio fundatur super affirmatione, eamque præsupponit, dicente victore GELENIO P. I. dec. 8. art. 6. p. 8. Conquiescit itaque intellectus non in negatione, sed in affirmatione, Voluntas autem fertur in bonum, quod est positiuum.

Valeant igitur mystici cum caliginosa sua

contemplatione! Veri Chriſti diſcipuli, meditando verbum Dei reuelatum, ſcientiam ſalutis quærunt & inueniunt.

Quæſt. XII. *Quænam complectitur notitia Dei reuelata?* Notitia Dei reuelata complectitur 1. exiſtentiam Dei, 2. eſſentiam & attributa Dei, 3. perſonas diuinas, 4. actiones & opera diuina.

Quæſt. XIII. *An exiſtentia Dei hic ſupponenda eſt, vt nota & lumine naturæ?* Exiſtentia Dei.

Cum hauſta e fonte rationis notitia Dei fit confuſa, debilis & languida: ad indubitatæ fidei generationem (a), ſolidamque atheorum confutationem (b), ex ſupernaturali reuelatione, in ſacris litteris comprehenſa, exiſtentia Dei plenius & liquidiùs hic demonſtranda eſt (c).

Prob. a. Princeps fidei articulus eſt, eſſe Deum: vtpote cui, ceu fundamento, ceteri omnes innituntur. Credere enim oportet accedentem ad Deum, quod fit, & quærentibus ipſum retributor mercis fiat, docente apoſtolo, Hebr. XI, 6. Indubitata autem fides e ſemine verbi diuini generatur.

Io. XVII, 20. Prob. b. Quamuis-athei ex principiis naturæ & rationis confutari queant: attamen vt fide credant, eſſe Deum, in ſubſidium vocari omnino meretur verbum Dei in litteras redactum. Neque enim accenditur fides, niſi ex lumine verbi diuinitus reuelati.

Rom. X, 14. Prob. c. Ex fonte S. ſcripturæ, per quam ſolida hauritur demonſtratio, qua exiſtentia Dei euincitur.

Nam 1) generatim omnes & ſingulæ verbi diuini ſcripti litteræ loquuntur efſe Deum; liquidem tota ſcriptura eſt θεόπνευσος, inſpirante Deo conſignata, 2 Tim. III, 16. Sed quæ ſcriptura diuinitus eſt inſpirata, illa Deum arguit auctorem. 2) *Speciatim colligitur exſiſtentia Dei a) ex nominibus, quæ Deo in authenticis prophetarum & apoſtolorum ſcriptis tribuuntur*; b) ex attributis diuinis, quæ cum ſoli Deo per ſe conueniunt, eſſe nequeunt, niſi ſit ipſe Deus; c) *ex operibus Dei, quæ ſunt creatio, conſeruatio totius mundi, in primis eccleſiæ gubernatio in ſacris litteris deſcripta, miracula ſtupenda, beneficia in pios collata, ſupplicia impiis irrogata, vaticinia euentibus comprobata*. Quæ omnia, cum de exiſtentia Dei ſane quam luculenter teſtentur, mentibus noſtris penitiſſime infigenda ſunt, & dubitationibus de Deo noſtris non minus, quam atheorum, Deum negantium, impietati opponenda; cum contingat, vt etiam piis, æſtu tentationum iactatis, oboriatur dubitatio, an ſit Deus.


### Question XIV. By what names is God designated by the prophets in the Old Testament?

Divine Hebrew names. The names by which God is designated by the prophets in the Old Testament, some express the very essence of God, such as יהוה (a), יה (b), אהיה (c); some name God from power, such as אל (d), and שדי (e); some from dominion, such as אדון (f) and ארכי (g); some from religious worship, such as אלה (h), and אלהים (i).

Proof a. The most sacred name יהוה descends immediately from the verb היה, 'was, existed'. It is expressed in Greek by S. Ioannes as ὁ ὤν, καὶ ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος, 'who is, and who was, and who is to come'. Apoc. I, 8. It is rendered by IVNIVS as αὐτοών, by SCALIGER as αὐτότατος, by b. WALTHER as αὐτοϋπαρκτος, in Latin, 'essentiator', or as d. VARENIVS renders it, 'essentians'. Vid. *Decad. V. in Exod. p.99. By this name is noted 1) divine independent essence, because God is from Himself and not from another; 2) the immutability and eternity of the divine essence: What is mutable does not necessarily exist: but God is an eternal and necessary being, which cannot not be; 3) the divine essence-

the eminence of being. Creatures, in the judgment of PLATO, have more of non-being than of being. For example, a man has one being, namely, human; he lacks infinite other beings, such as angelic, stony, sidereal, etc. God, however, as He is the fountain and origin of all essence, so He contains all being within Himself, either eminently, or virtually and effectively. Whence, by DAMASCENE, lib. I, *de fide orthodoxa*, c. 2, He is called πέλαγος τῆς οὐσίας ἄπειρον καὶ ἀόριστον, an infinite and interminable sea of essence.

4) The constancy of divine promises. To this may be referred the passage in Exodus VI, 3, where God says: I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as בְּאֵל שַׁדָּי (God Almighty), but by my name Jehovah I did not make myself known to them. These words cannot be understood absolutely: for Abraham invoked the name Jehovah (Gen. XIII, 4). But they are to be understood respectively, namely, with respect to the complement by which a promise receives its existence. God declared His power to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, that He could stand by His promises (for He had promised them the hereditary possession and full dominion of the land of Canaan); but they had not yet experienced the complement of the promise, by which God gives being to His words. Intending to indicate this, God says that He had not yet made Himself known to them by the name Jehovah.

This name, the tetragrammaton, consisting of four letters, is the proper name of God, grammatically and logically. Grammatically, because all the requirements of a proper name belong to it entirely. For a) from the beginning it has the initial *yod*, the preformative letter of a proper name. b) It is devoid of the plural number. c) It never assumes the emphatic *he* at the beginning. d) It receives no suffix. e) It is never placed in the construct state. The *arnegis* (denial) of this last property of a proper name seems to be contradicted by Ps. XXIV, 10, צְבָאוֹת יְהוָה, where the name יְהוָה governs the name after it, and thus is placed in the construct state. Resp. Before this name *Zebaoth*, one must supply from other passages אֱלֹהֵי (God). Thus, this complete phrase is found in Ps. XXXIX, 9; Jer. XV, 6; Hos. XII, 6; Amos III, 13. Wherefore, in this elliptical formula of speech, it is not the name יְהוָה that is placed in the construct state, but that word which is understood between the name Jehovah and Zebaoth. (*)

Logically, the name יְהוָה is proper because, in the nominative case, standing alone, outside of composition, and without an added restrictive ending, it applies to no one except the eternal God alone, and thus is incommunicable to creatures. This is evident a) from etymology. For it descends from הָיָה (to be), to represent the independent, immutable, and eternal essence of God. b) Because all creatures and all idols are excluded from the participation of this name. Is. XLII, 8: I am Jehovah; that is my name: my glory I will not give to another. Ps. LXXXIII, 19: Let them acknowledge that you (are), by your name Jehovah, alone; the most high over all the earth.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, who contend that the name יְהוָה is also attributed to creatures in the Holy Scriptures. To strengthen their opinion, they argue:

1. Whatever name is attributed to idols, that is not the proper name of God. But the name יְהוָה, etc. Therefore. The minor is proven from Exod. XXXII, 5: Tomorrow shall be a feast to Jehovah, i.e., to the golden calf. Resp. Distinguish between the general concept of God, who is called Jehovah, and the special application of that concept. Aaron had a true concept of Jehovah, but he applied it wrongly. The sense of Aaron was that, through that idol, divine worship could ultimately be referred to the supreme deity.

2. The name יְהוָה is attributed to angels, Gen. XVI, 8, 9; Exod. III, 2; Mal. III, 1. Resp. The cited passages, and others twin to them, are to be understood not of created angels, but of the uncreated angel, the Son of God. This is evident from the predicates which are affirmed of that angel in the text. Through the angel, who The one who appeared to Hagar in Gen. XVI cannot be understood as a created angel, because in v. 10 he addresses Hagar thus: I will multiply your seed, so that it cannot be numbered for the multitude. Surely this multiplication of the woman and her descendants presupposes omnipotence, and can in no way be attributed to a created angel.

Neither was the angel who appeared to Moses in the burning bush a created angel, because he explicitly calls himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, v. 6. Which denomination belongs to God alone.

By the angel of the covenant, however, Mal. III, 1, no one can be understood except Christ; seeing as he was to confirm the new covenant with his own blood.

You say: The name Jehovah can be attributed to a created angel, insofar as he performs the office of an envoy. For it is permitted for an envoy to assume the name of the one sending him.

Resp. John the Baptist was an envoy of Christ, and yet he denied that he was Christ. The envoy of Caesar does not dare to say: I am Leopold, Emperor of the Romans.

3. The name יהוה is attributed to men, Deuter. XIX, 17. They shall stand before Jehovah, before the priests and judges.

Resp. By Jehovah, priests and judges are not understood, but these are subordinated to God as instrumental causes to the principal cause.

Cf. 2 Paral. XIX, 6.

4. Certain inanimate creatures are honored with the name Jehovah. 1) The altar erected by Moses, Exod. XVII, 15. 2) The ark of the covenant, Num. X, 35. 3) Mount Moriah, Gen. XXII, 24. 4) Jerusalem, Ezech. XLVIII, 35.

Latin:

* Nomina diuina hebraica. Nomina, quibus Deus a prophetis in vet. teſtamento inſignitur, quædam ipſam exprimunt eſſentiam Dei, vt יהוה (a), יה (b), אהיה (c); quædam Deum a potentia, vt אל (d), & שדי (e); quædam a dominio, vt אדון (f) & ארכי (g); quædam a cultu religioſo, vt אלה (h), & אלהים (i) denominant.

Prob. a. Sacroſanctum nomen יהוה immediate deſcendit a verbo היה fuit, exſtitit. Exprimitu græce a S. Ioanne ὁ ὤν, καὶ ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος, qui eſt, & qui fuit, & qui venturus eſt. Apoc. I, 8. Redditur a IVNIO αὐτοών, a SCALIGERO, αὐτότατος, a b. WALTHERO αὐτοϋπαρκτος, latine, eſſentiator, vel vt reddit d. VARENIVS, eſſentians. Vid. *Decad. V. in Exod. p.99. Notatur hoc nomine 1) eſſentia diuina independentia, quia Deus eſt a ſe & non ab alio; 2) eſſentiæ diuinæ immutabilitas & æternitas: Quod mutabile eſt, non neceſſario exſiſtit: Deus autem eſt ens æternum & neceſſarium, quod non poteſt non eſſe; 3) *eſſentiæ divi-

vinæ eminentia. Creaturæ, iudice PLATONE, habent plus non entis, quam entis. v.gr. Homo habet vnum esse, nempe humanum; desunt ei infinita esse alia, vt esse angelicum, lapideum, sidereum &c. Deus autem sicut omnis essentiæ fons & origo est: ita omnia esse in se continet vel eminenter, vel virtualiter & effectiue. Ex quo a DAMASCENO libr. I. orthod. fid. c. 2. vocatur πέλαγος τῆς οὐσίας ἄπειρον καὶ ἀόρισον, mare essentiæ infinitum ac interminabile.

4) Promissionum diuinarum constantia. Huc referri potest locus Exod. VI, 3. vbi Deus dicit: Innotui Abrahamo, Isaaco & Iacobo בְּאֵל שַׁדָּי in Deo omnipotente, sed in nomine meo Iehouah ipsis non innotui. Verba hæc absolute intelligi nequeunt: nam Abraham inuocauit nomen Iehouah: Gen. XIII, 4. Sed intelligenda sunt respective, nempe respectu complementi, quo promissio suam existentiam accipit. Abrahamo, Isaaco & Iacobo declarauit Deus potentiam suam, quod posset stare promissis (promiferat autem ipsis hereditariam terræ Canaan possessionem plenumque dominium ); sed illi promissionis complementum, quo Deus verbis suis dat esse, nondum erant experti. Id indicaturus Deus dicit, quod ipsis in nomine Iehouah nondum innotuerit.

Nomen hoc τετραγράμματον, quatuor constans litteris, est nomen Dei proprium grammatice & logice. Grammatice, quia omnia requisita nominis proprii ipsi ex asse conueniunt. Nam a) ab initio habet iod initiale, litteram præformatiuam nominis proprii. b) Destituitur numero plurali. c) Nunquam ab initio assumit ה emphaticum. d) Nullum recipit suffixum. e) Nunquam ponitur in regimine. Huic vltimo nominis proprii ἄρνησῳ ob-stare videtur Ps. XXIV, 10. צְבָאוֹת יְהוָה vbi nomen יְהוָה post fe regit nomen, adeoque in regimine ponitur. Resp. Ante hoc nomen Zebaoth supplendum est ex aliis locis אֱלֹהֵי Deus. Sic integra habetur hæc locutio Ps. XXXIX, 9. Ier. XV, 6. Hos. XII, 6. Amos III, 13. Quamobrem in hac elliptica formula loquendi non nomen יְהוָה ponitur in regimine, sed illa vox, quæ inter nomen Iehouah & Zebaoth subintelligitur. (*)

Logice nomen יְהוָה proprium est, quia in casu recto solitarie, extra compositionem & fine addito restringente positum nemini competit, nisi foli Deo æterno, adeoque creaturis in-municabile est. Id quod patet a) ex etymologia. Descendit enim ab הָיָה fuit, ad repræsentandam independentem, immutabilem & æternam essentiam Dei. b) Quia a participatione huius nominis omnes creaturæ, omnia idola excluduntur. Es. XLII, 8. Ego sum Iehouah; illud est nomen meum: gloriam meam alteri non dabo. Ps. LXXXIII, 19. Agnoscant, quod tu (sis) nomine tuo Iehouah solus; altissimus supra omnem terram.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, contendentium nomen יְהוָה in sacris litteris etiam creaturis tribui. Opinionem suam firmaturi argumentantur:

1. Quodcunque nomen tribuitur idolis, illud non est nomen Dei proprium. Sed nomen יְהוָה &c. Ergo. Minor probatur ex Exod. XXXII, 5. Cras erit solennitas Iehouæ, i. e. vituli aurei. Resp. Distingu. inter conceptum de Deo, qui dicitur Iehouah, generalem, & illius conceptus applicationem specialem. Habuit Aaron conceptum de Iehouah verum, sed eundem male applicauit. Sensus Aaronis erat, per idolum illud cultum diuinum vltimo referri posse ad supremum numen.

2. Nomen יְהוָה tribuitur angelis, Gen. XVI, 8. 9. Exod. III, 2. Mal. III, 1. Resp. Loca citata, & iis gemina alia, intelligenda sunt non de angelis creatis, sed de angelo increato, filio Dei. Id quod patet ex prædicatis, quæ de angelo illo in textu affirmantur. Per angelum, qui Hagari apparuit Gen. XVI. non potest intelligi angelus creatus, quia v. 10. ita alloquitur Hagarem: Multiplicabo semen tuum, ut non possit numerari præ multitudine. Sane hæc multiplicatio feminis & posterorum præsupponit omnipotentiam, & angelo creato tribui nullo modo potest.

Neque angelus, qui Mosi apparuit in rubo ardente, fuit angelus creatus, quia se diserte vocat Deum Abrahami, Isaaci & Iacobi. v. 6. Quæ denominatio soli Deo competit.

Per angelum fœderis autem Mal. III, 1. intelligi nemo, nisi Christus, potest; quippe qui sanguine suo novum fœdus confirmaturus erat.

Dicis: Angelo creato nomen Iehouah tribui potest, quatenus munere legati perfungitur. Nam legato legantis nomen assumere licet.

Resp. Ioannes Baptista erat legatus Christi, & tamen negabat, se esse Christum. Legatus Cæsaris non audet dicere: Ego Leopoldus Romanorum imperator.

3. Nomen יהוה tribuitur hominibus, Deuter. XIX, 17. Stabunt ante Iehouam, ante sacerdotes & iudices.

Resp. Per Iehouam non intelliguntur sacerdotes & iudices, sed hi tanquam causæ instrumentales subordinantur Deo, vt causæ principali.

Conf. 2 Paral. XIX, 6.

4. Nomine Iehouah honorantur quædam creaturæ inanimatæ. 1) Altare a Mose erectum, Exod. XVII, 15. 2) Arca fœderis, Num. X, 35. 3) Mons Moria, Gen. XXII, 24. 4) Hierosolyma, Ezech. XLVIII, 35.


### Question XIV. By what names is God designated by the prophets in the Old Testament?: Resp. α) in general

Resp. α) in general.

A consequence from compound to divided does not hold. For a word entering into a composition signifies one thing, and placed outside of a composition, another.

Thus, Constantine is one thing, Constantinople another; Theophilus is one thing. The name יהוה placed solitarily, with an ending added, or outside of a composition, always denotes the divine essence.

In the cited places, the name τετραγράμματον is placed with an added noun, verb, or adverb.

Resp. β) in particular to 1) The name יהוה with the noun נסי

Ex. XVII, 15 denotes the protection of God, of which the altar was an erected perpetual memorial.

To 2) There is no strength in the consequence: When the ark was setting out, Moses said: Arise, Jehovah: Therefore, he called the ark Jehovah. When an army is setting out, a commander can say: Arise, Jehovah, and scatter our enemies. Who, unless he were out of his mind, would conclude: The commander called the army Jehovah?

To 3) Mount Moriah is not called Jehovah absolutely, but The Lord will provide. Mount Moriah was to be a memorial sign of divine providence, not Jehovah himself.

To 4) There is no sequence. The Lord is there. Therefore, the city of Jerusalem is called the Lord or Jehovah.

Just as if you were to conclude: Lycurgus is in Sparta. Therefore, Sparta is Lycurgus.

Objection, Jerusalem is called: יהוה צדקנו the Lord our righteousness. Jerem. XXXIII, 16.

Resp. The words of the text are: In those days Judah shall be saved, and Jerusalem shall dwell securely: and this is (his name) which they shall call her: Jehovah our righteousness.

It is clear from the text that they will call not that Jerusalem, but לה i.e., to Jerusalem. The sense is: This is the name of the offspring of David, which they shall call, i.e., name, announce, preach to Jerusalem: Jehovah our righteousness. This is a title of the Messiah, not of Jerusalem.

Cf. Jer. XXIII, 6.

5. If the name Jehovah is incommunicable, it cannot be communicated to the Son of God and the Holy Spirit. But it is communicated, etc.

Therefore.

Therefore. Resp. The name Jehovah is said to be incommunicable to creatures existing outside of God, not to divine persons. Objection, Therefore the name Jehovah cannot be attributed to the human nature of Christ.

Resp. The human nature of Christ does not exist outside of God, but is entirely in the throne of the deity.

Prob. b. The divine name יה agrees with the name יהוה and is significant of the independent and immutable divine essence. It is rendered by the LXX as κύριος, by THEODOT. as τὸ ὄν, or being. It occurs mostly in hymns, and is used as the proper name of God. Ps.

LXVIII, 5.

Sing to God, praise his name, extol him who rides upon the clouds, by Iah is his name.

To some, this name appears contracted from the name Iehouah, by syncope with the two middle letters cast out: to others, it is held to be shortened with the two preceding letters retained, since the former, the He in the tetragrammaton, becomes mappikated or mobile, not the latter. But the opinion of those who judge it to be primitive is to be preferred here, because it is joined with the name Iehouah .

Prob. d. The name אֵל denotes the divine essence with a connotation of infinite power. For אֵל is אֱלֹהַ, which signifies strength or fortitude. It is applied to the true and living God, when it occurs in the singular, and absolutely without any diminishing or alienating condition, and indeed it is taken substantively and concretely. Who is אֵל, besides Iehouah? . The Socinians think it is a common noun, and object: 1) Daniel XI, 36. God is אֵל אֵלִים.

Resp. אֵלִים is a plural, which is used of strong men and the gods of the nations; but אֵל placed in the singular denotes the supreme Numen. 2) אֵל placed in the singular in Ezekiel XX, 11 does not denote the supreme Numen. Resp. In the cited passage, אֵל is placed with an addition, and is taken adjectivally for the most robust among the nations. Prob. e. שַׁדַּי likewise denotes the divine essence with a connotation of infinite power. For it is derived, in the opinion of the most learned philologists, from the root שָׁדַד, he devastated, and by the rite of lightning he permeated or penetrated. It is attributed to God , so that by this name is expressed the divine omnipotence, by which he permeates all things, and alone, according to his pleasure, can destroy and reduce to nothing all things which he has made. In which sense it is rendered by the LXX interpreters as παντοκράτωρ, by AQUILA as ἄλκιμος, by ABEN ESRA as חָקִיק, by SEB. SCHMIDT it is explained as the thunderer; by b. LUTHER and the Jews in the German translation it is turned as allmächtig (almighty). Nor is this derivation destitute of reasons. For α) The Dagesh in the middle letter ד indicates not obscurely that this word draws its origin from a geminated Aiin verb. β) In the cognate Arabic language, שַׁדִּי is valid. γ) To express the infinite power of God, אֵל is added as an ἐξηγητικόν (explanatory term). δ) The prophets seem to regard this origin of the word . There are, however, those who derive this divine name from שַׁד, a breast, adding a very pious reason for the etymology, that just as a mother feeds and sustains her infant, God graciously feeds and sustains us. There are others who wish this divine name to be derived from the relative pronoun ש and דַּי, which word denotes sufficiency, because God is sufficient to himself and lacks nothing. Hence he is called in Greek αὐταρκής, or by the Platonic phrase ἀνενδεής. We acquiesce in the first derivation given. Conf. D. PFEIF. diff. Philolog. VIII. de nominibus diuinis.

Proof f. אדון denotes the divine essence with a connotation of divine sustenance and lordship.

For it is derived from אדון [foundation], and thus by the force of the word it denotes the sustainer, the preserver, and the lord of all things. It is applied to the independent and eternal God when 1) it is placed absolutely, and is limited by nothing restrictive.

2) When it is uttered with the demonstrative ה.

3) When it is placed with an additive that dilates, amplifies, and extends to a universal subject.

4) When it occurs doubled, as Adon Adonim, Deut.

X, 17. 5) When in the same case such attributes are connected [to it] which can belong to no one except Jehovah.

Cf. D. DORSCHEUS, Pentadec. dissert. theolog., disp. XII, § 34. Proof g.

The name אדני, of the same origin as אדון, sustains the same meaning, and denotes the sustainer and ruler of this universe.

This name is with a Kamez at the end, and that a native one, not arising from a pause, and is proper to God.

For it is never placed in the construct state, nowhere has the emphatic ה prefixed, admits no suffixes, and is always uttered in the same manner with a singular verb or adjective: which are the criteria of a proper name.

There are those who wish its form to be plural with a suffix of the first person; others prefer it to be simply plural after the form of גובי [locusts], Nah.

III, 17; שרי [princes], Jud. V, 15; חלונות [windows], Jer. XXI, 14. Wherefore, since this divine name is of the plural number, an argument for the plurality of the divine persons can be taken from it.

Cf. D. CALOVIUS, in System. theol., tom. II, p. 125. Proof h.

Some derive the divine name אלה from the Hebrew root אלה [he swore, he cursed]; either because one must swear by the name of God alone, or because God alone can effectively bless and curse.

But the mappiq ה seems to stand in the way of this origination; for the same reason we do not accept the derivation from אלה; since a mappiq ה can never be servile or Heemantic.

The princes of philologists, ERPENIUS, AMAMA, LUDOVICUS DE DIEV, GLASSIUS, PFEIFERUS, establish its root as אלה, today unused among the Hebrews, but most visited among the Arabs, to whom אלה is to serve, to worship, and, according to the nature of the object, to adore.

Therefore, this most august name designates God as religiously to be served and adored, or as D.

VARENIUS explains more fully, it denotes the highest [being] of infinite divine majesty, to be trembled at and venerated by angels, men, and all creatures whatsoever. See Dec. I. in Gen., p. 10. Placed absolutely, it is claimed for the true God alone, never for creatures or idols, unless an express limitation is made, as in Dan.

XI, 39, where mention is made of אלה [a god] of a foreign [god]. Otherwise, the name remains proper to the independent and eternal God.

Who is אלה, besides Jehovah?

Ps. XVIII, 32, where an affirmative interrogation introduces a categorical negative enunciation. Proof i.

The personal name אלהים, arising from the singular אלה, is likewise significant of divine majesty to be religiously venerated, implying a plurality of persons.

This is the first name of God in the sacred letters, and is read in the very beginning of Scripture, Gen. I, 1, to which finally in ch. II, 4, the name Jehovah is joined.

Indeed, the Jews are authors everywhere of the idea that the word Elohim denotes a judge, and many Christians, both ancient and modern, follow them: certainly without any foundation, except that the Jews seek an escape so that they are not forced to concede the mystery of a plurality of persons in God.

For they can prove neither from the origin of the word nor from the usage of the language that the word Elohim in its proper sense designates a judge.

For no place in Scripture can be shown anywhere where it treats of a created judge or judges by design, and the name Eloah or Elohim is attributed to them simply.

The consequence is inept: Elohim is transferred to judges by a trope.

Therefore, it properly signifies a judge. Therefore it properly signifies a judge. For also the name of Achilles is tropically attributed to a strong man, and yet it does not follow: ... Therefore it denotes per se a strong man.

Cf. D. SCHMID, colleg. bibl. prins p. 115. Relying on the origin of the word, which we gave above, and on the usage of the language, we establish that the word אלהים is placed properly and perpetually without any alienating or diminishing condition. to designate God as religiously to be worshipped & adored, under the notation of a plurality of persons. This is what Moses intimates, Deut. IV, 35. Know that Jehovah himself becomes Elohim, and there is no more (anyone) besides him, i.e., Jehovah alone is the God religiously to be venerated. Metaphorically & κατ’ ἀναλογίαν (by analogy), on account of a certain similarity of honor with God, angels, Ps. VIII, 6. cf. Heb. I, 6, and also magistrates, Ps. LXXXII, 6, are called Elohim. Μιμητικῶς & κατὰ δόξαν (mimetically & according to opinion), the false gods or demigods of the heathens, because the Gentiles worshipped them in the place of the true God, are expressed by the name Elohim. Exod. XXIII, 24. c. XXXII, 4.

Meanwhile, it remains fixed and established that the divine name אלהים is plural not only in formation and termination, but also in sense and signification, and thus implies a plurality of persons indefinitely—not precisely the Trinity—or at least imports a certain respect toward the same. We grant credence to this assertion because 1) the word Elohim has its own regular singular number of the same signification and frequent use. But every word of the plural number, whose singular signifying the same thing is in use, signifies a certain plurality beyond enallage. 2) Because the name Elohim is constructed with both a noun and a verb in the plural. See Gen. XX, 13. ch. XXV, 7. Josh. XXIV, 19. 2 Sam. VII, 33. Ps. LVIII, 12. 3) Because several Elohim are introduced consulting or speaking together, Gen. I, 26. Let us make man in our image. For which reason no one in the Hebrew language speaks of himself as one person.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, who deny that a plurality of divine persons is inferred by the word Elohim, to whom some Papists also accede, whose arguments are: I. The name Elohim is constructed with a verb of the singular number in the very frontispiece of Scripture ברא אלהים . Therefore, it does not infer a plurality of persons.

Resp. 1) It is also constructed with a plural verb to express plurality. 2) There is no Jew who does not marvel at the unusual construction of this name, as witnessed by HORNBECK, Disp. V. antiqu. Iudaic. "If this had not been written in the word, it would not have been permitted to say: Bara Elohim," says R. Hunna in GERHARD, in exegef. loc. III. §. 115. 3) The name Elohim is constructed with a singular verb to signify the unity of the divine essence and the plurality of persons; otherwise, no reason can be given why Moses used the plural name Elohim in the work of creation, when it is not lacking a singular number. It can be very conveniently explained: Each of the persons created in the deity common to one and three persons. Confer VAREN. decad. I, in Gen. p. 15.

You say: I. The name Elohim is a name of dominion, and thus is used in the plural number to amplify the honor of God; yet in a singular sense. Resp. The name Eloah is not a name of dominion, but of glory, expressing in itself the highest honor of adoration. Therefore, to use its plural number to amplify the honor of God is of no avail.

You say: II. God speaks of himself in the number of the multitude after the manner of magnates, Gen. I, 26. Resp. 1) The style of magnates speaking of themselves in the plural number with authority is alien to the very simple Hebrew style. There exist in the sacred letters rescripts and mandates of kings speaking of themselves in the singular number. See Ezra VII, 13. Dan. IV, 3. c. VI, 20. 2) Magnates speak of themselves in the plural number to signify that they decree something by the votes or assistance of counselors and nobles. But there is no one who is a counselor to God, Is. XL, 13. 3) Princes who speak of themselves in the plural never, however, express their own proper or appellative name in the plural. For they do not say: We Leopoldi, Emperors of the Romans, command; but: We, Leopoldus, Emperor. But God also expresses his name in the plural, where it is said: Jehovah Elohim. 4) If it had pleased God, in order to declare his majesty, to speak of himself in the plural, either always, or for the most part, or certainly in the promulgation of the Sinaitic law, to speak in the plu-of the Sinaitic law in the plural.

he had spoken in the plural. But the contrary is evident from Exod. XX, 2. Nay rather, God considers the unity of his essence as his highest praise. Is. XLIV, 6. and elsewhere passim.

III. You say: The words Gen. I, 1. ברא אלהים, are to be explained from the idiom of the Hebrew language, and indeed from the analogy of Adon, Baal, etc., by an enallage of number, where the plural is used for the singular. That senior servant Gen. XXIV, 9. calls Abraham אדני. Potiphar is called אדני of Joseph, Gen. XXXIX, 20. Joseph is called אדני of the land, Gen. XLII, 30. Schemer is called אדני of the mount of Samaria. 1 Kings XVI, 24. Resp. 1) From the noun אדון, which denotes a lord, to אלה, which designates religious worship, an invalid argument is drawn. 2) The Jews themselves do not deny that in the cited places a certain respect of plurality is introduced, the foundation of which they place in a plurality of virtues and honors. 3) Although in the cited places one is clearly named, who is primarily regarded, yet more are understood. Gen. XXIV, 9. Isaac, the son of Abraham, is connoted. Gen. XXXIX, 20. not only Potiphar is understood, but at the same time also Pharaoh, whose eunuch Potiphar was. Gen. XLII, 30. Joseph's officials are connoted, or even Pharaoh himself: The man, the lords of the land, spoke, i.e., each one of the lords of the land. 1 Kings XVI, 24. the mount of Samaria did not have one, but many lords in order, and perhaps those very ones who made up the family of Schemer, whence the name for the mount; and therefore they are called lords of the mount of Samaria not without relation either to predecessors, or to kinsmen, and by equal right of birth.

II. The name Elohim is said of one God, Deut. VI, 4. Therefore it introduces no plurality.

Resp. The name Elohim is said of God, who is one, but not insofar as he is one, but insofar as he consists of several persons. In the cited place אלהינו יהוה denotes the unity of the divine essence, and the plurality of the divine persons.

III. If there are several Elohim, there are several gods. But there are not several gods. Therefore. The consequence is evident, because Elohim is rendered in Latin as Deus.

Resp. The Latin noun, Deus, is an essential divine name: but the Hebrew, Elohim, is a personal divine name. It is wrongly concluded from a personal name to an essential one. There is no Latin name given that corresponds fully to the Hebrew Elohim.

IV. Moses is called Aaron's Elohim Exod. IV, 16.

Resp. Moses is not called Aaron's Elohim absolutely and in the nominative case, but לאלהים in the place of God, or for God, because he interpreted the will of the true and triune God to Aaron.

V. The name Elohim does not always introduce plurality, because it is used 1) of one idol, Jud. XVI, 23. Exod. XXXII, 4. 2) of one angel; Jud. XIII, 22. 3) of the person of God the Father alone, Ps. XLV, 8.

Resp. To 1): An idol is not called Elohim, except in the confused relation of an idolatrous concept to that which in reality is more. For idolaters worship their idol just as if it were the true God, who is one in essence, and three in persons. e.g. Dagon for the Philistines κατὰ δόξαν & μιμητικῶς (according to opinion and imitatively) was the same as the triune God was for the Israelites. Which is also the reason why the Israelites spoke in the plural number about the calf: These are thy Elohim! Exod. XXXII, 4. because they represented by the same Elohim, who had liberated the Israelites from Egypt. To 2): The angel, whom Manoah saw, was not a created angel, but uncreated, namely the Son of God, because he is called Jehovah, who accepted the burnt offering, v. 23. To 3): When the word Elohim is used of one divine person, it is signified that that one person is from the number of several, or that that divine person is not God solitarily, but one together with the other two persons, toward which there obtains a perpetual respect. Conf. D. GERHARD. exeg. loc. III. p. 365.

VI. If Elohim, by force of the number, insinuates plurality into minds, the Holy Spirit is his own spirit. But the Holy Spirit is not his own spirit. Therefore Elohim does not, by force of the number, insinuate plurality into minds.

Consequence The major premise is proven, because that plurality is a trinity, which the Holy Spirit constitutes together with God the Father and the Son.

Resp.

From the word Elohim we prove a plurality of persons indefinitely, not precisely or determinately a trinity.

It suffices, that the plural noun Elohim signifies many, and that formally: but that this plurality is a trinity, which is of persons in one essence in number, that is added to the signification of the name Elohim materially.

Nor is it necessary that a word signifying many should always be taken for many jointly; especially where one of those many persons is distinguished from the rest.

Therefore we most firmly assert that the Holy Spirit is not the spirit of himself, but the spirit of the Father and the Son.

Quest. XV. By what names is He distinguished by the apostles in the New Testament?

The Greek names, by which God is distinguished by the apostles in the N.

T. are Θεὸς (a), Κύριος (b), Δεσπότης (c).

Latin:

Resp. α) in genere.

A compositis ad diuisa non valet consequentia. Nam aliud significat vox ingressa compositionem, aliud posita extra compositionem.

Sic aliud est Constantinus, aliud Constantinopolis; aliud est Theophilus. Nomen יהוה positum solitarie, fine addito, siue extra compositionem, semper notat essentiam diuinam.

Locis citatis ponitur nomen τετραγράμματον cum addito nomine, verbo aut aduerbio.

Resp. β) in specie ad 1) Nomen יהוה cum nomine נסי

Ex. XVII, 15. notat protectionem Dei, cuius perpetuum memoriale erat erectum altare.

Ad 2) Nihil nerui inest consequentia: Proficiscente arca, dixit Moses: Surge Iehouah: E. arcam vocauit Iehouam. Proficisceute exercitu, dicere potest imperator: Surge Iehouah, & disperge inimicos nostros. Ecquis, nisi mentis impos, colligeret: Imperator exercitum vocauit Iehouam?

Ad 3) Mons Moria non absolute dicitur Iehouah, sed Dominus prouidebit. Debebat mons Moria esse signum memoriale prouidentiæ diuinæ, non ipse Iehouah.

Ad 4) Nulla est sequela. Dominus est ibi. E. vrbs Hierosolyma vocatur dominus aut Iehouah.

Perinde ac si colligas: Lycurgus est Spartæ. Ergo Sparta est Lycurgus.

Instantia, Hierosolyma vocatur: יהוה צדקנו dominus iustitia nostra. Ierem. XXXIII, 16.

Resp. Verba textus sunt: In diebus illis seruabitur Iuda, & Hierosolyma habitabit secura: hoc autem est (nomen eius) quod vocabunt illi: Iehouah iustitia nostra.

Patet e textu, quod vocaturi sint non illam Hierosolymam, sed לה scil. Hierosolymæ. Sensus est: Hoc est nomen germinis Dauidis, quod vocabunt i. e. nuncupabunt, annunciabunt, prædicabunt Hierosolymæ: Iehouah iustitia nostra. Est hic titulus Messiæ, non Hierosolymæ.

Conf. Ier. XXIII, 6.

5. Si nomen Iehouah est incommunicabile, non potest filio Dei & Spiritui S. communicari. Sed communicatur &c.

E.

E. Resp. Dicitur nomen Iehouah incommunicabile creaturis extra Deum, existentibus, non personis diuinis. Instantia, Ergo nomen Iehouah non potest humanæ Christi naturæ tribui.

Resp. Humana Christi natura non existit extra Deum, sed in thronum deitatis cuncta est.

Prob. b. Nomen diuinum יה conuenit cum nomine יהוה & est significatiuum essentiæ diuinæ independentis & immutabilis. Redditur a LXX. κύριος, a THEODOT. per τὸ ὄν, siue ens. Occurrit potissimum in hymnis, & adhibetur vt nomen Dei proprium. Ps.

LXVIII, 5.

Cantate Deo, laudate nomen eius, extollite equitantem super nubibus, per Iah nomen ipsius. Quibusdam videtur hoc nomen contractum ex nomine Iehouah, per syncopen eiectis duabus litteris mediis: aliis habetur decurtatum retentis duabus litteris anterioribus, cum prius, He in tetragrammato mappikatum siue mobile fit, non posterius. At præferenda hic videtur illorum sententia, qui primitiuum id esse censent, quia cum nomine Iehouah coniungitur .

Prob. c. Nomen אֶהְיֶה est nomen diuinum peculiare a Iehouah non tam sensu, quam forma & signandi modo diuersum. Deus ipse hoc nomine se insigniuit . cum Mosen in Ægyptum mittere vellet, iubebat, vt diceret Israëlitus: Eieh misit me ad vos. Vox hæc alias primæ personæ est futuri ab הָיָה fuit. Sed migrauit illud futurum in nomen: construitur enim vt nomen nominatiui casus, præcedens verbum & constituens subiectum orationis. Græce redditur a LXX. interpretibus, ὤν, ab Hieronymo latine, Eriturus. Potest concipi vt nomen essentialissimum & propriissimum Dei, non modo ab aliis denominati (quod peculiariter importare videtur אֶהְיֶה); sed et denominantis seipsum, sub notione radicali summi & in actus specialissimi complemento operantis entis, censentibus D. VARENIO . D. PFEIFERO . Designat essentiæ diuinæ independentem immutabilitatem, induuisibilem æternitatem, fœderis ac gratiæ firmitatem, promissionum diuinarum certissimam veritatem.

Prob. d. Nomen אֵל notat essentiam diuinam cum connotatione potentiæ infinitæ. Nam אֵל est אֱלֹהַ, quod significat robur aut fortitudinem. Adhibetur de vero & viuo Deo, cum in singulari occurrit, & absolute sine conditione diminuente vel alienante & quidem substantiue ac concretiue sumitur. Quis est אֵל, præter Iehouam? . Sociniani putant esse nomen commune, & obiiciunt 1) Daniel. XI, 36. Deus est אֵל אֵלִים.

Resp. אֵלִים est plurale, quod de hominibus fortibus & diis gentium usurpatur; sed אֵל in singulari positum notat supremum Numen. 2) אֵל in singulari positum Ezechiel. XX, 11. non notat supremum Numen. Resp. Loco citato אֵל ponitur cum addito, & sumitur adiectiue pro robustissimo inter gentes. Prob. e. שַׁדַּי itidem notat essentiam diuinam cum connotatione potentiæ infinitæ. Deriuatur enim doctissimorum philologorum de sententia a radice שָׁדַד vastauit, & ritu fulminis permeauit aut penetrauit. Tribuitur Deo . adeo, vt hoc nomine exprimatur diuina omnipotentia, qua res cunctas permeat, & solus pro lubitu omnia, quæ fecit, destruere & in nihilum redigere potest. Quo sensu a LXX. interpretibus . redditur παντοκράτωρ, . ab A Q V I L A, ἄλκιμος, ab ABEN ESRA חָקִיק, a SEB. SCHMIDIO fulminator explicatur; a b. LVTHERO & Iudæis in translatione germanica allmächtig vertitur. Neque hæc originatio rationibus destituitur. Nam α) Dages in media littera ד haud obscure indicat, vocem hanc a verbo geminato Aiin originem ducere. β) In lingua cognata Arabica שַׁדִּי est validus. γ) Ad exprimendam potentiam Dei infinitam additur אֵל ἐξηγητικόν. δ) Hanc vocis originem respicere videntur prophetæ . Sunt tamen, qui hoc nomen diuinum deducunt a שַׁד, mamma, perquam piam addentes etymi rationem, quod non secus ac mater infantem suum, Deus nos gratiose alat & sustentet. Sunt alii, qui hoc nomen diuinum deriuatum volunt a ש pronómine relatiuo & דַּי, quæ vox sufficientiam notat, quia Deus est sibi sufficiens, & nullius indiget. Hinc græce αὐταρκής, vel phrasi Platonica ἀνενδεής vocatur. Nos data prima deriuatioue acquieicimus. Conf. D. PFEIF. . deriuatione acquiescimus. Conf. D. PFEIF. diff. Philolog. VIII. de nominibus diuinis.

Prob. f. אדון notat essentiam divinam cum connotatione sustentationis & dominii divini.

Derivatur enim ab אדון fundamento, adeoque vi vocis notat sustentatorem, conservatorem & omnium rerum dominum. Adhibetur de Deo independente & æterno, quando 1) absolute ponitur, & nullo restringente limitatur.

2) Quando effertur cum ה demonstrativo.

3) Quando positum est cum additamento dilatante, ampliante & ad universale subjectum extendente.

4) Quando geminatum occurrit, ut Adon Adonim Deuter.

X, 17. 5) Quando in casu eodem talia connectuntur attributa, quæ nemini, nisi Iehouah, convenire possunt.

Conf. D. DORSCHEI pentadec. dissert. theolog. disp. XII. §. 34. Prob. g.

Nomen אדני, eandem cum אדון eiusdem fit originis, sustinet significationem, & notat sustentatorem & rectorem huius universi.

Est hoc nomen cum Kamez in fine, eoque nativo, non ex pausa oriundo, Deo proprium.

Neque enim unquam ponitur in regimine, nuspiam ה emphaticum præfixum habet, suffixa nulla admittit, ac semper eadem ratione cum verbo vel adiectivo singulari effertur: quæ sunt κριτήρια nominis proprii.

Sunt, qui eius formam volunt esse pluralem cum suffixo primæ personæ: alii malunt esse simpliciter pluralem ad formam גובי locustæ Nah.

III, 17. שרי principes Iud. V, 15. חלונות fenestræ Ier. XXI, 14. Quamobrem cum hoc nomen divinum pluralis fit numeri, ab eodem argumentum pluralitatis personarum divinarum desumi potest.

Conf. D. CALOV. in system. theol. tom. II. p. 125. Prob. h.

Nomen divinum אלה nonnulli deducunt a radice Hebraica אלה iurauit, exsecratus est; vel quod per folius Dei nomen fit iurandum, vel quod solus Deus possit effective benedicere & maledicere.

At huic originationi obftare videtur ה mappikatum; eadem de caussa derivationem ab אלה non recipimus; cum ה mappikatum nunquam possit esse servile, aut Heemanticum.

Philologorum principes ERPENIVS, AMAMA, LVDOVICVS DE DIEV, GLASSIVS, PFEIFERVS, radicem eius constituunt אלה, hodie inusitatam apud Hebræos, sed visitatissimam apud Arabes, quibus אלה est servire, colere, &, pro ratione obiecti, adorare.

Proinde designat augustissimum hoc nomen Deum religiose colendum & adorandum, sive ut plenius explicat D.

VARENIVS, notat summum Dei infinitæ maiestatis, angelis, hominibus, omnibusque omnino creaturis tremendæ & venerandæ. Vid. Dec. I. in Gen. p. 10. Absolute positum soli vero Deo vindicatur, nunquam vel creaturis, vel idolis, nisi expressa fiat limitatio, vt Dan.

XI, 39. vbi fit mentio אלה Dei alieni. Ceteroqui manet nomen Deo independenti & æterno proprium.

Quis אלה, præter Iehouah?

Pl. XVIII, 32. vbi interrogatio affirmativa infert enunciationem categoricam negantem. Prob. i.

Nomen personale אלהים ortum a singulari אלה itidem est significativum maiestatis divinæ religiose venerandæ, pluralitatem personarum inferens.

Est hoc primum Dei in sacris litteris nomen, legiturque in ipso scripturæ exordio, Gen. I, 1. cui demum c. II, 4. nomen Iehouah iungitur.

Equidem Iudæi auctores sunt passim, quasi vox Elohim iudicem denotet, & sequuntur eos multi ex christianis veteres & recentiores: nullo sane fundamento; nisi quod Iudæi effugium quærunt, ne mysterium plurimum in Deo personarum concedere cogantur.

Nam vocem Elohim sensu proprio designare iudicem, neque ex origine vocis, neque ex usu linguæ valide probare possunt.

Nullus quippe vsquam locus scripturæ monstrari potest, quo de iudice aut iudicibus creatis ex instituto agitur, & nomen Eloah vel Elohim illis tribuitur simpliciter.

Inepta est consequentia: Elohim ad iudices per tropum transfertur.

Ergo proprie iudicem significat. Nam & nomen Achillis viro forti tropice tribuitur, neque tamen sequitur: ...Ergo per se virum fortem denotat.

Conf. D. SCHMID. colleg. bibl. prins p. 115. Nos origine vocis, quam supra dedimus, & vsu linguæ freti statuimus, vocem אלהים proprie, & perpetuo sine conditione alienante aut diminuente positam designare Deum religiose colendum & adorandum, sub notatione pluralitatis personarum. Id quod innuit Moses, Deut IV, 35. Scias, quod Iehouah ipse fit Elohim, nec amplius (quispiam) præter ipsum, q. d. solus Iehouah est Deus religiose venerandus. Metaphorice & κατ’ ἀναλογίαν ob quandam honoris similitudinem cum Deo, angeli, Ps. VIII, 6. collat. Hebr. I, 6. nec non magistratus, Ps. LXXXII, 6. Elohim appellantur. Μιμητικῶς & κατὰ δόξαν falsi ethnicorum dii siue deastri, quia gentiles eos loco veri Dei colebant, nomine Elohim exprimuntur. Exod. XXIII, 24. c. XXXII, 4.

Fixum interim ratumque manet, nomen diuinum אלהים non tantum formatione & terminatione, sed etiam sensu & significatione esse plurale, atque adeo pluralitatem personarum indefinite talem, non præcise trinitatem, inferre, aut certe ad eandem respectum quendam importare. Assertioni fidem damus, quia 1) vox Elohim singularem suum numerum regularem eiusdem significationis, frequentisque usus habet. At omnis vox numeri pluralis, cuius singularis eiusdem rei significatiuus in usu, extra enallagen significat quandam pluralitatem. 2) Quia nomen Elohim & cum nomine & cum verbo plurali construitur. Vid. Gen. XX, 13. cap. XXV, 7. Ios. XXIV, 19. 2 Sam. VII, 33. Ps. LVIII, 12. 3) Quia plures Elohim consultantes aut colloquentes introducuntur, Gen. I, 26. Faciamus hominem in imagine nostra. Qua ratione nemo in hebræa lingua de se vt vna persona loquitur.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, negantium, voce Elohim pluralitatem personarum diuinarum inferri, quibus et Pontificiis nonnulli accedunt, quorum argumenta sunt: I. Nomen Elohim construitur cum verbo numeri singularis in ipso frontispicio scripturæ ברא אלהים . Ergo non infert pluralitatem personarum.

Resp. 1) Construitur etiam cum verbo plurali ad exprimendam pluralitatem. 2) Non est Iudæus, qui non insolitam huius nominis constructionem miretur, teste HORNBECK, Disp. V. antiqu. Iudaic. Nisi hic sermo fuisset scriptus, non licuisset dicere: Bara Elohim, inquit R. Hunna apud GERHARD. in exeges. loc. III. §. 115. 3) Construitur nomen Elohim cum verbo singulari ad significandum essentiæ diuinæ vnitatem & personarum pluralitatem; ceteroqui ratio dari nequit, cur Moses nomine plurali Elohim in opere creationis sit vsus, cum illud numero singulari non desfituatur. Percommode exponi potest: Vnaquæque personarum creauit in vna & tribus personis communi deitate. Confer VAREN. decad. I, in Gen. p. 15.

Dicis: I. Nomen Elohim est nomen dominii, adeoque ad amplificandum honorem Dei in numero quidem plurali; sensu tamen singulari adhibetur. Resp. Nomen Eloah non est nomen dominii, sed gloriæ, per se summum adorationis honorem exprimens. Ergo numerum eius pluralem ad amplificandum honorem Dei adhibere, nil attinet.

Dicis: II. Deus de se magnatum more in numero multitudinis loquitur, Gen. I. 26. Resp. 1) Stilus magnatum de se in numero multitudinis singularis cum auctoritate loquentium a stilo hebræo simplicissimo alienus est. Exstant in sacris litteris rescripta & mandata regum de se in numero singulari loquentium. Vid, Efræ VII, 13. Dan. IV, 3. c. VI, 20. 2) Magnates de se in numero multitudinis loquuntur, vt significent, se consiliariorum & optimatum suffragiis aut adminiculis aliquid decernere. At Deo nemo est a consiliis Es. XL, 13. 3) Principes, qui de se in plurali loquuntur, nunquam tamen nomen suum proprium aut appellatiuum in plurali exprimunt. Neque enim dicunt: Nos Leopoldi, Imperatores Romanorum, mandamus; sed: Nos, Leopoldus, Imperator. At Deus quoque suum nomen in plurali exprimit, vbi dicitur: Iehouah Elohim. 4) Si Deo placuisset ad declarandam maiestatem suam de se in plurali loqui, vel semper, vel vt plurimum, vel certe in promulgatione legis Sinaiticæ in pluSinaiticae in plurali loqui.

plurali locutus esset. At contrarium patet ex Exod. XX, 2. Quin potius Deus essentiae unitatem sibi summae laudi ducit. Es. XLIV, 6. & alibi passim.

III. Dicis: Verba Gen. I, 1. ברא אלהים, ex idiotismo linguae hebraeae, & quidem ex analogia Adon, Baal &c. per enallagen numeri, ubi pluralis pro singulari usurpatur, explicanda sunt. Servus ille senior Gen. XXIV, 9. Abrahamum vocat אדני. Potiphar dicitur אדני Iosephi, Gen. XXXIX, 20. Iosephus dicitur אדני terrae, Gen. XLII, 30. Schemer vocatur אדני montis Schomronis. 1 Reg. XVI, 24. Resp. 1) A nomine אדון, quod notat dominum, ad אלה, quod cultum religiosum designat, inualidum petitur argumentum. 2) Ipsi Iudaei in locis citatis respectum quendam pluralitatis inferri, non negant, cuius fundamentum in pluralitate virtutum & honorum ponunt. 3) Quamuis in locis citatis diserte unus, qui primo respicitur, nominetur, plures tamen intelliguntur. Gen. XXIV, 9. connotatur Isaac, filius Abrahami. Gen. XXXIX, 20. non intelligitur solus Potiphar, sed simul etiam Pharao, cuius Eunuchus fuit Potiphar. Gen. XLII, 30. connotant Iosephi officiales, vel ipse etiam Pharao: Locutus est vir, domini terrae, i. e. unusquisque ex dominis terrae. 1 Reg. XVI, 24. mons Schomron non unum, sed multos ordine habuit dominos, & forfitan illos ipsos, qui Schemeri faciebant familiam, unde monti nomen; nec proinde sine relatione vel ad antecessores, vel ad cognatos, parique iure nascendi, montis Schomronis domini dicuntur.

II. Nomen Elohim dicitur de uno Deo, Deut. VI, 4. Ergo nullam infert pluralitatem.

Resp. Nomen Elohim dicitur de Deo, qui unus est, sed non quatenus unus est, verum quatenus pluribus constat personis. Loco citato אלהינו יהוה essentiae diuinae unitatem, personarum diuinarum pluralitatem denotat.

III. Si plures sunt Elohim, plures sunt dii. Sed non sunt plures dii. Ergo. Consequentia patet, quia Elohim latine redditur Deus.

Resp. Nomen latinum, Deus, est nomen diuinum essentiale: at hebraeum, Elohim, est nomen diuinum personale. A nomine personali ad essentiale perperam concluditur. Nullum datur nomen latinum, quod hebraeo Elohim ex asse respondeat.

IV. Moses dicitur Aaronis Elohim Exod. IV, 16.

Resp. Moses non dicitur absolute & in casu recto Aaronis Elohim, sed לאלהים loco Dei, vel pro Deo, quia Aaroni voluntatem Dei veri & triunius interpretabatur.

V. Nomen Elohim non semper infert pluralitatem, quia usurpatur 1) de uno idolo, Iud. XVI, 23. Exod. XXXII, 4. 2) de uno angelo; Iud. XIII, 22. 3) de sola Dei patris persona, Pl. XLV, 8.

Resp. Ad 1): Idolum non dicitur Elohim, nisi in confusa relatione conceptus idololatrici ad id, quod reuera est plures. Perinde enim colunt idololatrae suum idolum, ac si fit verus Deus, qui unus est essentia, trinus personis. v. gr. Dagon Philistaeis κατὰ δόξαν & μιμητικῶς idem fuit, qui Israëlitis Deus triunus. Quae etiam causa est, quod plurali numero de vitulo dixerint Israëlitae: Hi sunt Elohim tui! Exod. XXXII, 4. quod repraesentarint eodem Elohim, qui Israëlitas liberarant ex Aegypto. Ad 2): Angelus, quem vidit Manoah, non fuit angelus creatus, sed increatus, nempe filius Dei, quia vocatur Jehovah, qui holocaustum suscepit, v. 23. Ad 3): Quando vox Elohim de una persona diuina usurpatur, significatur, quod una illa persona fit ex numero plurium, siue quod illa persona diuina non fit solitarie Deus, sed una cum reliquis duabus personis, ad quas perpetuum obtinet respectum. Conf. D. GERHARD. exeg. loc. III. p. 365.

VI. Si Elohim vi numeri pluralitatem mentibus insinuat, Spiritus S. sui ipsius spiritus est. Sed Spiritus S. non est sui ipsius spiritus. Ergo Elohim vi numeri pluralitatem mentibus ininsinuat.

Consequentia maioris probatur, quia pluralitas illa est trinitas, quam vna cum Deo patre & filio constituit Spiritus S.

Resp.

Ex voce Elohim probamus pluralitatem personarum indefinite, non præcise, aut determinate trinitatem.

Sufficit, nomen plurale Elohim plures significare, idque formaliter: quod autem illa pluralitas sit trinitas, quod fit personarum in vna numero essentia, id nominis Elohim significationi accedit materialiter.

Neque necesse est, vt vox plures significans semper pro pluribus coniunctim sumatur; maxime vbi vna ex istis pluribus persona reliquis contradistinguitur.

Quocirca firmissime afferimus, Spiritum S. non sui ipsius, sed patris & filii spiritum esse.

Quæst. XV. Quibus nominibus ab apostolis in nouo testamento insignitur?

Nomina græca, quibus Deus ab apostolis in N.

T. insignitur, sunt Θεὸς (a), Κύριος (b), Δεσπότης (c).


### Question XIV. By what names is God designated by the prophets in the Old Testament?: Obs

Obs.

I. Some wish the name Θεὸς to be derived from θέω, I run, because He permeates or penetrates all things: others from αἴθω, I burn, because He becomes as it were a consuming fire (of vices), Deut.

IV, 24: others from θεάομαι, I contemplate, because God sees and completes all things: others from θέω, I place, because God placed, made, prepared, and founded all things: others ἀπὸ τοῦ δέος, from fear, because God is to be feared above all things: others from the Hebrew שדי, sufficiency, because God is αὐταρκέστατος, in need of nothing, but most perfectly sufficient unto Himself: which allusive derivations we indeed admit, but we judge the word itself to be rather primitive, not otherwise than the Latin word, Deus.

Allusions can be given more easily than the true reasons for denominations.

Obs.

II. In three ways, as BASIL THE GREAT teaches in ep.

141. to the Caesareans, the name God is used.

(1) Κατ' οὐσίαν, according to essence, the supreme and eternal One is called God.

(2) Κατὰ χάριν, according to grace, those are called gods to whom some divine office has been committed, such as magistrates, Ps.

LXXXII, 6.

(3) Κατὰ ψεῦδος, according to falsehood, those who sell themselves or desire to be sold as God, such as idols and the god of this world, 2 Cor.

IV, 4.

Indeed, the word God κυρίως and properly denotes the independent God, who is from Himself, and from whom are all other things: μεταφορικῶς and because of a certain similarity with God in such a nature, it is said of gods by such dignity and office. Μιμητικῶς and by catachresis, because of the vain and erroneous opinion of men, idols and the devil have obtained the appellation of God.

Prob. a.

The name Θεὸς, whether placed absolutely or distinguished by divine attributes and operations, is significative of the independent divine essence, is clear (1) from the common concept of all nations; for when the word God is heard, they immediately conceive of the first being, which is from itself, and the cause of all other things.

(2) Θεότης, Col.

II, 9. and θειότης, Rom.

I, 20. primarily designate the divine nature and essence.

Therefore Θεὸς primarily denotes Him who has the divine nature.

(3) Holy Scripture distinguishes between Θεὸν φύσει, or by nature, and Θεὸς λεγομένους, those called gods, not by reality or nature, such.

1 Cor.

VIII, 5.

Gal.

IV, 8.

Therefore the name Θεὸς primarily denotes God as such by nature.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians who, in order to elude the arguments taken from the divine names by which Christ is distinguished in the Holy Scriptures, establish that the name Θεὸς is significative of power or dignity rather than of divine essence, who argue, fortified in their assertion: 1.

Moses is called the God of Aaron because of the granted power, Exod.

IV, 16.

And the name God is not a name of essence, but of power.

Resp.

God addresses Moses thus: You shall be to him (Aaron) as God.

Just as a viceroy is never simply called king: so he who is as God is not absolutely called God.

We assert that the word, God, placed absolutely and without a diminishing condition, designates the supreme and independent God.
