2. Angels Ps. VIII, 6, as well as judges or magistrates Ps. LXXXII, v. 1, 6, bear the name of God, who are not gods by nature. Therefore, God is not always a name of nature, but also of power. Resp. (1) Angels and magistrates are indeed called Elohim in the plural number; since there are many θεοὶ λεγόμενοι, gods by name; but no judge or magistrate, no created angel is called Eloah, or God, in the singular number absolutely. (2) Magistrates and angels are called gods metaphorically; he is called God properly who has an independent essence.

3. The magistrate obtains the name of God either truly or falsely. Not falsely; because thus idols, Acts VII, 43, the devil, 2 Cor. IV, 4, the belly, Phil. III, 19, have obtained the name of God from the false opinion of men. Therefore, the magistrate is truly honored with the name of God on account of a likeness to God that is not fictitious, but true. I answer with the words of GERHARD in Exeg. loc. III, fol. 228. Distinguish between these phrases: to be the true God, and to be truly called God. To be the true God belongs to the one and eternal God alone, who is such by nature and essence; because every thing is called true from its own nature and essence. Thus, true gold, true man is said, from the true essence of gold and man. CYRIL, lib. XII, thesaur. cap. 13: If Christ is the true God; substantially, not by participation, this very thing is, just as a creature. But he who is the true God is God by nature. But to be truly called God belongs also to men, who on account of a likeness and a certain participation of divinity are improperly called by that name; for there it is a question only of the truth of words taken metaphorically. Thus, the apostles are truly called the light of the world, the salt of the earth; because although they are called light improperly and metaphorically: yet, because they truly perform that spiritually which light, salt, etc., do corporally, therefore they are truly so called. By the same reasoning, magistrates, judges, etc., are called gods, and are truly so called, because they are so called on account of the participation of a divine office, meanwhile they are not that true God who is such by nature and essence.

4. Therefore God is called El Elohim, Ps. L, 1, Elohe Elohim, Deut. X, 17, because the word God also signifies him who has sublime power from the one God. Resp. (1) The Greek word, θεός, and the Hebrew names אֵל and אֱלֹהִים are not in every respect synonymous and equipollent. For El denotes God the strong, Elohim God to be worshipped under the notion of the plurality of persons. The Greek θεός simply designates him who has a divine nature. Hence, from the Hebrew divine names, El and Elohim, to the Greek θεός, one concludes invalidly. (2) The eternal and independent God is called the God of gods, of those spoken of both metaphorically and catachrestically, not only on account of greater power, but also on account of independence and eternity; because God is prior to all gods by name (such as magistrates), and putative gods (such as the idols of the nations), and also on account of greater wisdom, goodness, truth &c. wisdom, goodness, truth &c.

Objection I. It cannot be denied that magistrates are metaphorically called gods on account of dignity and power. Therefore, God is also properly so called on account of dignity and power; otherwise there would be no foundation for the metaphor. Resp. From a metaphorical signification to a proper one is concluded wrongly. For a metaphor arises from a likeness that is not absolute, but respective. Wherefore, although magistrates are metaphorically called gods, in respect of power communicated by God, yet the true and highest God is properly and primarily called God, on account of his divine nature and essence, of which power is a consequence according to our mode of conceiving.

Prob. b. The divine name κύριος is derived ἀπὸ τοῦ κύρεος, which word designates authority, right, or dominion. It is used in the N.T. of the true God, in the place of the divine names of the old testament Iehouah, El, Adonai. Thus the Saviour repeats from Deut. VI, 4 that memorable saying: Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, κύριος εἷς ἐστί, the Lord is one, Marc. XII, 29. It must therefore be rightly observed that the name κύριος placed in the N.T. absolutely, without restricting conditions, imports a most eminent dominion, suitable to God alone.

Prov. c. The word Δεσπότης properly signifies a master, (*) and is used in the N.T. regarding God, Luke 2:29, Acts 4:24, 2 Tim. 2:21, 2 Pet. 2:1, Jude v. 4. The reason for the denomination is because God most powerfully and wisely presides over the world, which He created, and governs it as a most spacious house, fortified with supreme authority.

Latin:

Obs.

I. Nomen Θεὸς deriuatum volunt alii a θέω curro, quod omnia permeet aut penetret: alii ab αἴθω uro, quod fit quasi ignis consumens (vitia), Deut.

IV, 24: alii a θεάομαι, contemplor, quod Deus omnia videat & completur: alii a θέω pono, quia Deus omnia posuit, fecit, parauit, fundauit: alii ἀπὸ τοῦ δέος a metu, quia Deus super omnia timendus est: alii ab Hebræo שדי sufficientia, quia Deus est αὐταρκέστατος, nullius indigus, sed sibi ipsi perfectissime sufficiens: quas derivationes allusiuas admittimus quidem, vocem autem ipsam potius primitiuam esse censemus, haud secus ac vocem latinam, Deus.

Allusiones facilius dari possunt, quam veræ denominationes rationes.

Obs.

II. Tribus modis, docente BASILIO M. ep.

141. ad Cæsar. nomen Deus vsurpatur.

(1) Κατ' οὐσίαν secundum essentiam dicitur summus & æternus, Deus.

(2) Κατὰ χάριν secundum gratiam vocantur dii, quibus diuinum aliquod officium commissum est, vt magistratus, Ps.

LXXXII, 6.

(3) Κατὰ ψεῦδος secundum mendacium, qui se pro Deo venditant aut venditari cupiunt, vt idola & Deus huius mundi, 2 Cor.

IV, 4.

Nempe vox Deus κυρίως & proprie notat Deum independentem, qui est a se, & a quo sunt omnia alia: μεταφορικῶς & ob similitudinem quandam cum Deo natura tali, dicitur de diis dignitate & officio talibus. Μιμητικῶς & per catachresin, ob vanam & erroneam hominum opinionem, idola & diabolus appellationem Dei fortita sunt.

Prob. a.

Nomen Θεὸς vel absolute positum, vel insignitum attributis & operationibus diuinis, esse significatiuum essentiæ diuinæ independentis, patet (1) ex communi conceptu gentium omnium; quippe quæ audita voce, Deus, protinus concipiunt ens primum, quod est a se, & ceterorum omnium caussa.

(2) Θεότης, Col.

II, 9. & θειότης, Rom.

I, 20. primo designat naturam & essentiam diuinam.

Ergo Θεὸς primo notat eum, qui naturam diuinam habet.

(3) Scriptura S. distinguit inter Θεὸν φύσει, seu natura, & Θεὸς λεγομένους, Deos nomine, non re, aut natura, tales.

1 Cor.

VIII, 5.

Gal.

IV, 8.

Ergo nomen Θεὸς primo notat Deum natura talem.

Antithesis est Socinianorum qui, vt eludant argumenta petita a nominibus diuinis, quibus Christus in sacris litteris insignitur, statuunt nomen Θεὸς potestatis, aut dignitatis potius, quam essentiæ diuinæ esse significatiuum, qui suam assertionem muniti arguunt: 1.

Moses dicitur Deus Aaronis ob concessam potestatem, Exod.

IV, 16.

E nomen Deus non est nomen essentiæ, sed potestatis.

Resp.

Deus Mosen ita compellat: Tu fis illi (Aaroni) pro Deo.

Sicut prorex nunquam simpliciter vocatur rex: ita qui pro Deo est, non absolute appellatur Deus.

Nos afferimus vocem, Deus, absolute & sine conditione imminuente positam, designare Deum summum & independentem. absolute & fine conditione imminuente positam, designare Deum summum & independentem.

2. Angeli Ps. VIII, 6. nec non iudices aut magistratus Ps. LXXXII, v. 1. 6. nomen Dei sustinent, qui natura non sunt dii. Ergo Deus non semper est nomen naturae, sed etiam potestatis. Resp. (1) Angeli & magistratus in numero quidem multitudinis dicuntur Elohim; cum multi sint θεοὶ λεγόμενοι, dii nuncupatiui; sed nullus iudex aut magistratus, nullus angelus creatus in numero singulari absolute appellatur Eloah, aut Deus. (2) Magistratus & angeli vocantur dii metaphorice; proprie Deus vocatur, qui habet essentiam independentem.

3. Magistratus nomen Dei obtinet aut vere, aut falso. Non falso; quia sic idola , Act. VII, 43. diabolus , 2 Cor. IV, 4. venter , Phil. III, 19. ex falsa hominum opinione nomen Dei fortita sunt. Ergo magistratus nomine Dei vere honoratur ob similitudinem cum Deo non fictam, sed veram. Respondeo verbis GERHARDI in exeg. loc. III. fol. 228. Dist. inter has phrases, esse verum Deum, & vere dici Deum. Esse verum Deum competit solo uni & aeterno Deo, qui per naturam & essentiam talis est; quia unaquaeque res dicitur vera, a sua natura & essentia. Sic verum aurum, verum homo dicitur, a vera auri & hominis essentia. CYRILLVS lib. XII. thesaur. cap. 13. Si Christus verus Deus est; substantialiter, non participatione, hoc ipsum est, sicut creatura. Qui autem verus Deus est, natura Deus est. Sed vere dici Deum competit etiam hominibus, qui propter similitudinem & participationem quandam diuinitatis eo nomine improprie appellantur; ibi enim agitur duntaxat de veritate vocum metaphorice acceptarum. Sic apostoli vere dicuntur lux mundi, sal terrae; quia etsi improprie & metaphorice dicuntur lux: tamen, quia vere illud praestant spiritualiter, quod lux, sal &c. faciunt corporaliter, ideo vere sic dicuntur. Pari ratione magistratus, iudices &c. dicuntur dii, & vere sic dicuntur, quia propter participationem diuini officii sic dicuntur, interim non sunt verus ille Deus, qui natura & essentia talis est.

4. Ideo Deus dicitur El Elohim , Ps. L, 1. Elohe Elohim , Deut. X, 17. quia vox Deus etiam significat eum, qui sublimem potentiam ab uno Deo habet. Resp. (1) Graeca vox, θεός, & hebraea nomina אֵל & אֱלֹהִים non sunt omni ex parte synonymica & aequipollentia. Nam El notat Deum fortem, Elohim Deum colendum sub notione pluralitatis personarum. Graecum θεός simpliciter designat eum, qui habet naturam diuinam. Proinde a nominibus diuinis hebraeis, El & Elohim, ad graecum θεός inualide concluditur. (2) Deus aeternus & independens vocatur Deus deorum, tam metaphorice, quam catachrestice dictorum, non tantum ob maiorem potestatem, sed etiam propter independentiam & aeternitatem; quia Deus prior est omnibus diis nuncupatiuis (quales sunt magistratus), & putatiuis (quales sunt idola gentium), nec non ob maiorem sapientiam, bonitatem, veritatem &c. sapientiam, bonitatem, veritatem &c.

Instantia I. Negari nequit, magistratus metaphorice dici Deos ob dignitatem & potestatem. E. Etiam Deus proprie ita dicitur ob dignitatem & potestatem; ceteroqui nullum foret metaphoræ fundamentum. Resp. A significatione metaphorica ad propriam male concluditur. Metaphora enim oritur e similitudine non absoluta, sed respectiua. Quamobrem licet magistratus metaphorice dicantur dii, respectu potestatis a Deo communicatæ, verus tamen & summus Deus proprie & primo Deus dicitur, ob naturam & essentiam diuinam, cuius consequens nostro concipiendi modo est potestas diuina.

Prob. b. Nomen diuinum κύριος deducitur ἀπὸ τοῦ κύρεος, quæ vox auctoritatem, ius aut dominium designat. Adhibetur in N. T. de vero Deo, loco nominum diuinorum vet. testam. Iehouah, El, Adonai. Sic Saluator ex Deut. VI, 4. repetit memorabile illud dictum: Audi Israel, Dominus, Deus noster, κύριος εἷς ἐσὶ, Dominus vnus est, Marc. XII, 29. Probe itaque obferuandum est, quod nomen κύριος in N. T. positum absolute fine conditionibus restringentibus eminentissimum importet dominium, soli Deo conueniens.

Prov. c. Nomen Δεσπότης proprie herum significat, (*) & usurpatur in N. T. de Deo Luc. 11, 29. Act. IV, 2. Tim. II, 21. 2 Petr. II, 1. Iud. v. 4. Ratio denominationis est, quia Deus mundo, quem condidit, potentissime sapientissimeque praeest, & eundem velut domum amplissimam summa munitus auctoritate gubernat.


### Q. XXI. What is God?

God is an independent Spirit.

More fully defined. God is an independent spiritual essence of three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Obs. 1. The given description of God is not a logically perfect definition. For (1) a logical definition strictly so-called consists of genus and difference. But in God, nothing is found that has the nature of genus and difference. For a genus behaves by way of passive potency, which can be perfected. But nothing perfectible falls into the most perfect God. Nor does a difference include the species which it constitutes, nor the genus of that species: as can be illustrated by the example of rationality; for that is neither man nor animal. But there is nothing in God that is not God Himself. (2) A logical definition is perfect for those things which are in the categories. But God is in no category. For He is not a genus; since He is not said of many species of gods: Nor is He a species; because a species is multipliable through many individuals, but it is repugnant for there to be many Gods: Nor is He an individual, because this immediately lies under a most specific species. But Spirit is immediately predicated of God, which is not a most specific species; since it has some species under itself, namely, finite Spirit. It is clear, therefore, that God is directly in no category.

Obs. 2. An imperfect description, which consists of a common and proper concept, and is reciprocal with its definiendum, can define God. For God agrees with creatures in this, that He is an essence subsisting through itself, immaterial, which we call Spirit. He differs from creatures; because He does not receive His being from another, as creatures do, but has it from Himself, and is therefore independent.

Obs. 3. In natural theology, God is defined by Spirit independent, or subsisting from Himself. That God is Spirit is known to some extent from the light of nature. For (1) the first Being existing from itself, which is the cause of all other things, cannot be a body, consisting of matter and form. For in order for matter and form to be united and composed into one body, an efficient cause is required to compose the matter and form. But for God, there is no prior efficient cause. (2) Matter behaves by way of perfectible passive potency: form by way of perfecting act. But into God, who is purest act and perfection itself, no perfectible passive potency falls. (3) If God were corporeal, He would not be infinite. For a body cannot be infinite. (4) Since God is both invisible and most wise, the preserver and governor of all things, reason concludes that God is Spirit. That God is independent is also known in a certain way by the guidance of the light of nature. For looking upon [the world] we admire

the structure of this universe, we easily gather that the world is not from itself, but from some first cause, since in efficient causes there is no progress to infinity. That first cause, however, depending on no prior cause, is God.

Obf. 4. Revealed theology, from divine revelation comprised in the Holy Scriptures, proves far more solidly that God is an independent Spirit; it adds, moreover, the mention of the three persons of the divinity; without which there is no complete definition of the true God; for the reason that he is not the true God who is not one in essence and three in persons. D. CALOV. says gravely in tom. II. system. theol. p. 182. Those who do not add the mention of the three persons in the description of God, do not make it genuine or complete at all; since without them it is not yet established who the true God is. Ethnics and pagans do not have the true God, not acknowledging God as three in persons; nor do the Mahometans, denying the mystery of the H. Trinity; nor the modern Jews, nor the Samosatenians, Arians, Photinians, and other Anti-Trinitarians, denying three persons in the divine essence.

Obf. 5. That God is essence, we have the clearest testimony in Exod. III, 14. where to Moses asking about the name of God, He Himself answered in these words: I am who I am. Similarly Apocal. I, 8. God is called ὁ ὤν, who was, and who is to come. Since therefore God attributes to Himself a name from being, it is validly inferred that the essence of God is most perfect, most simple, and most pure; on account of which purity and simplicity of essence, God is His own deity and essence.

Latin:

Deus est Spiritus independens.

Vberius definitur. Deus est essentia spiritualis independens trium personarum, Patris, Filii, & Spiritus sancti.

Obs. 1. Data descriptio Dei non est logice perfecta definitio. Nam (1) definitio logica rigorose dicta constat genere & differentia. At in Deo nihil invenitur, quod generis & differentiae rationem habeat. Genus quippe se habet per modum potentiae passivae, quae perfici potest. Sed nullum perfectibile in Deum perfectissimum cadit. Differentia neque includit speciem, quam constituit, neque genus illius speciei: quemadmodum exemplo rationalitatis illustrari potest; ea enim nec homo, nec animal est. At nihil est in Deo, quod non sit ipse Deus. (2) Definitio logica perfecta est earum rerum, quae sunt in praedicamentis. Atqui Deus in nullo est praedicamento. Neque enim est genus; quoniam non dicitur de multis speciebus Deorum: Neque enim species; quia species est multiplicabilis per plura individua, repugnat autem plures esse Deos: Neque est individuum, quia hoc immediate subiacet speciei specialissimae. At de Deo immediate praedicatur Spiritus, qui species specialissima non est; cum sub se habeat aliquam speciem, nempe Spiritum finitum. Patet ergo, quod Deus directe in nullo sit praedicamento.

Obs. 2. Descriptio imperfecta, quae constat conceptu communi & proprio, atque cum definito suo reciprocatur, Deus definiri potest. Conuenit enim Deus cum creaturis in hoc, quod est essentia per se subsistens immaterialis, quam vocamus Spiritum. Differt a creaturis; quia esse suum non ab alio accipit, vt creaturae, sed a se habet, adeoque independens est.

Obs. 3. In theologia naturali Deus definitur per Spiritum independentem, siue a se subsistentem. Deum Spiritum esse, e lumine naturae quadantenus innotescit. Nam (1) Ens primum a se existens, quod est caussa ceterorum omnium, non potest esse corpus, constans ex materia & forma. Nam vt materia & forma ad vnum corpus vniantur & componantur, praerequiritur caussa efficiens materiam, & formam componens. At Deo nulla datur caussa efficiens prior. (2) Materia se habet per modum potentiae passivae perfectibilis: forma per modum actus perficientis. At in Deum, qui est purissimus actus & ipsa perfectio, nulla potentia passiva perfectibilis cadit. 3) Si Deus corporeus esset, non foret infinitus. Neque enim corpus infinitum esse potest. (4) Cum Deus & inuisibilis, & sapientissimus, rerum omnium conferuator & gubernator sit, ratio colligit, Deum esse Spiritum. Quod Deus independens sit, etiam quodammodo constat ductu luminis naturae. Adspicientes enim admiram

randam huius vniversi structuram, facile colligimus, mundum non esse a seipso, sed a causa aliqua prima, cum in causis efficientibus non detur progressus in infinitum. Illa autem causa prima, a nulla priori causa dependens, est Deus.

Obs. 4. Theologia revelata e revelatione divina, in sacris litteris comprehensa, longe solidius probat, Deum esse Spiritum independentem; addit autem mentionem trium personarum divinitatis; sine qua non est completa definitio veri Dei; propterea quod verus Deus non est, qui non est unus essentia & trinus personis. Graviter inquit D. CALOV. in tom. II. system. theol. p. 182. Qui non addunt mentionem trium personarum in descriptione Dei, eam nequaquam genuinam aut completam filunt; quum sine iisdem nondum constet, quisnam fit verus Deus. Non habent verum Deum ethnici & pagani, Deum in personis trinum haud agnoscentes; non Mahometani, S. S. Trinitatis mysterium infitiantes; non Iudaei moderni, non Samosateniani, Ariani, Photiniani, aliique Anti-Trinitarii, tres personas in essentia divina negantes.

Obs. 5. Quod Deus sit essentia, clarissimum habemus testimonium Exod. III, 14. vbi quaerenti Mosi de nomine Dei, ipse respondit his verbis: Ego sum, qui sum. Similiter Apocal. I, 8. Deus appellatur ὁ ὤν, qui erat, & qui futurus est. Cum igitur Deus sibi ipsi ab essendo nomen tribuat, valide infertur, essentiam Dei esse perfectissimam, simplicissimam & purissimam; propter quam essentiae puritatem & simplicitatem Deus est ipsa sua deitas & essentia.


### Q. XXI. What is God?: Quaest. XVII. Is God a Spirit devoid of all corporeal mass? God is a most pure and most simple Spirit, devoid of all matter, of all corporeal mass

Quaest. XVII. Is God a Spirit devoid of all corporeal mass?

God is a most pure and most simple Spirit, devoid of all matter, of all corporeal mass.

Prob. 1. Because the most explicit sentence of Holy Scripture is: God (is) Spirit: Therefore those who worship Him must worship in Spirit and truth. Jo. IV, 24. Obf. In that proposition: πνεῦμα ὁ θεὸς, God is the subject, and Spirit the predicate; Because (1) The article is accustomed to be placed not before the predicate, but the subject, and thus placed from the beginning of the proposition. (2) Because πνεῦμα extends more widely than θεὸς. For indeed everything that is God is Spirit, but not every Spirit is God; since angels and the human soul are spirits, yet not God. That, however, which is wider, sustains the nature of the predicate; that which is narrower, the nature of the subject. From which it follows that God is devoid of corporeal mass. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones. Luc. XXIV, 39.

Because God is invisible, Deut. IV, 12. and the same is most wise, Prov. III, 19. it is gathered that He is a Spirit, free from all corporeal concretion.

3. Because those are argued of idolatry who attributed to God the likeness of a corruptible man. Rom. I, 23.

The antithesis is that of the Audaeans, or Anthropomorphites, who attributed a human body to God; as also Crellius, Vorstius, and others, establishing that God is called Spirit, not only as angels and souls are, but also as air and other bodies similar to this are called spirits. They rely on frequent arguments: 1. In Holy Scripture, corporeal members—hands, arms, eyes, ears, feet, etc.—are attributed to God in many places. Therefore God is corporeal. Resp. These things are said of God ἀνθρωποπαθῶς, in a human manner, and are to be understood θεοπρεπῶς, i.e., in a manner becoming to God. By the arms of God is understood omnipotence, by hands operation, by eyes omniscience, by feet the omnipresence of God.

2. God is seen. Therefore God is not a Spirit. The reason for the consequence is because a Spirit is invisible. The antecedent is clear from Exod. XXXIV, 5. Ef. VI, 1.

Resp. God was seen

not in essence, but in an external symbol, or an assumed corporeal form. AUGUSTINE says wisely in Ep. CXII: God, who is invisible by the proper nature of his deity, could be seen, and appeared through an assumed creature, or by the arrangement of some assumed visible matter.

3. He in whose image man is created is corporeal. Man is created in the image of God. Therefore, God is corporeal. The major premise is certain, because an image agrees with its exemplar, or prototype. The minor premise is evident from Gen. I, 26. Response: The image of God was primarily or principally situated in the soul, namely in the cognition of the intellect and the holiness of the will. Col. III, 19. Secondarily and subsequently in the immortality of the body. But the whole man was not like God by reason of corporeal mass or external figure, but by reason of immortality.

4. Certain Fathers, among whom is TERTULL. in the book de incarnat. c. XI, attributed a body of some kind to God. Response: The holy fathers did not understand "body" in the proper sense, by which it denotes a material, quantitative, and divisible substance, but they took the word "body" in a catachrestic sense, insofar as it designates a true and solid substance, opposed to an empty phantom and likewise to a shadowy accident.

Latin:

Quaest. XVII. Estne Deus Spiritus omnis corporeae molis expers?

Deus est Spiritus purissimus & simplicissimus, omnis materiae, omnis corporeae molis expers.

Prob. 1. Quia disertissima sacrae scripturae sententia est: Spiritus (est) Deus: Ideo eos, qui adorant ipsum, in Spiritu & veritate oportet adorare. Io. IV, 24. Obs. In propositione illa: πνεῦμα ὁ θεὸς, Deus est subiectum, & Spiritus praedicatum; Quia (1) Articulus non praedicato, sed subiecto solet praeponi, adeoque poni ab initio propositionis. (2) Quia πνεῦμα latius patet, quam θεὸς. Nam omne quidem, quod Deus est, Spiritus est, sed non omnis Spiritus est Deus; cum angeli & anima humana sint Spiritus, nec tamen Deus. Illud autem, quod latius est, sustinet rationem praedicati; quod angustius, rationem subiecti. Ex quo consequitur, Deum corporeae molis expertem esse. Nam Spiritus carnem & ossa non habet. Luc. XXIV, 39.

2. Quia Deus est invisibilis, Deut. IV, 12. idemque sapientissimus, Prou. III, 19. colligitur, eum esse Spiritum, omni concretione corporea liberum.

3. Quia idololatriae arguuntur, qui similitudinem corruptibilis hominis Deo tribuerunt. Rom. I, 23.

Antithesis est Audaeanorum, sive Anthropomorphitarum, qui Deo corpus humanum tribuerunt; nec non Crellii, Vorstii & aliorum, statuentium, Deum dici Spiritum, non modo vti angeli & animae, sed etiam vt aër, ac alia corpora, huic similia, spiritus dicuntur. Innituntur frequentibus argumentis: 1. Deo in sacra scriptura passim locorum tribuuntur membra corporea, manus, brachia, oculi, aures, pedes &c. Ergo Deus est corporeus. Resp. Dicuntur haec de Deo ἀνθρωποπαθῶς, more humano, & intelligenda sunt θεοπρεπῶς, i. e. conuenienter Deo. Per brachia Dei omnipotentia, per manus operatio, per oculos omniscientia, per pedes omnipraesentia Dei intelligitur.

2. Deus est visus. Ergo Deus non est Spiritus. Ratio consequentiae est, quia Spiritus est invisibilis. Antecedens liquet ex Exod. XXXIV, 5. Es. VI, 1. Resp.

Deus visus est

non in essentia, sed in externo symbolo, sive assumta forma corporea. Scite inquit AVGVSTINVS Ep. CXII. Deus, qui per propriam deitatis naturam invisibilis est, videri potuit, atque apparuit per assumtam creaturam, vel dispositione alicuius materiae conspicabilis assumtae.

3. Ad cuius imaginem homo est conditus, ille est corporeus. Ad imaginem Dei homo est conditus. Ergo Deus est corporeus. Maior constat, quia imago cum suo exemplari, sive prototypo convenit. Minor patet ex Gen. I, 26. Resp. Imago Dei πρῶτως sive primario sita fuit in anima, nempe in cognitione intellectus, & sanctitate voluntatis. Col. III, 19. Δευτέρως & secundario in immortalitate corporis. Non autem ratione corporeae molis aut figurae externae Deo similis fuit homo integer, sed ratione immortalitatis.

4. Patres quidam, e quorum censu est TERTVLL. libr. de incarnat. c. XI. Deo corpus, quoddam tribuerunt. Resp. Sancti patres corpus intellexerunt non in sensu proprio, quo notat substantiam materialem, quantam, divisibilem, sed fumerunt τὸ corpus in sensu catachrestico, quatenus designat substantiam veram & solidam, inani phantasmati, itemque vmbratili accidenti oppositam.


### Q. XXI. What is God?: Question XVIII. How are Spirit, substance, being, and essence predicated of God and creatures?

Question XVIII. How are Spirit, substance, being, and essence predicated of God and creatures?

When Spirit, substance, being, and essence are predicated of God and creatures, that predication is not improper and equivocal, but proper, yet not univocal, but analogical, according to the analogy of intrinsic attribution.

Proof a. Whatever things are said only equivocally, only their name is common, but the definition of the name is different. But not only the name of being, essence, substance, and Spirit, but the thing itself, signified by the name, belongs to the Creator and to creatures. Therefore. The major premise is clear from the definition of equivocal terms; the minor is shown inductively. E.g., Man truly is, a stone has its own essence, a lion exists in itself, every angel is a Spirit. THOMAS AQUINAS accurately concludes in P.I. q. 13. art. 5: If these things were predicated equivocally of God and creatures, nothing could be known about God from creatures, but one would always fall into the fallacy of equivocation. And this is as much against the philosopher, who proves many things demonstratively about God, as it is against the apostle, Rom. I, 17.

Proof b. Whatever names are indeed common to many, yet in such a way that one of those of which they are said participates in them primarily and independently, while the others participate in them secondarily, on account of dependence; those are predicated analogically and unequally. But being and essence, substance and Spirit, are common to the Creator and the creature, yet in such a way that God participates in them primarily and independently, while creatures participate in them secondarily on account of dependence.

The major premise is clear from the definition of analogical terms. The minor is certain, because God is an independent being, substance, and Spirit; but all creatures depend on God.

The antithesis is (1) of the Platonists and some Scholastics asserting that being and essence, substance and Spirit are predicated equivocally of God and creatures; (2) of the Scotists maintaining that those predicates are said univocally and equally of God and creatures.

The stronger of their arguments are: 1. Between things where an infinite distance is given, a common concept cannot be formed of them. But such is the distance between God and creatures, etc. Therefore. Response: I limit the major premise. Between things where an infinite negative distance is given, such that absolutely no agreement intervenes between them (such as is between being and nothing), a common concept cannot be formed of them; I concede this. But between God and creatures there is an infinite positive distance; because God surpasses creatures infinitely in most eminent perfection.

surpasses. From this, however, it is gathered that it is not permitted [to say] that they do not agree in any perfection or any common concept; for since God, supremely good and perfect, is communicative of Himself, He has communicated some rivulets of His goodness, some rays of His perfection, to creatures, so that they might agree in a certain perfection, in an unequal manner. Instantia The Holy Spirit testifies in the sacred scriptures that creatures, when compared with God, are as nothing, Is. XL, 17. All nations (are) as nothing before Him (God), less than nothing, and are reputed as vanity to Him. Resp.

Those comparative expressions are not destructive, but attenuative. Essential perfection is not taken away by them, but the most eminent prerogative and majesty of the Creator before creatures is indicated. 2.

Whoever maintains that the name יהוה is incommunicable to creatures, they must also maintain that 'being' is incommunicable to creatures. For יהוה, which draws its origin from 'being', walks in step with 'being'. But the Lutherans &c. [do this]. Therefore. Resp.

The name יהוה denotes the essence of God as independent and immutable; which, when considered as essence in general, does not walk in step [with it]. 3. Whatever at some time was not, and at some time cannot be, that is to be numbered among non-entities rather than entities. But every creature &c. Therefore. Resp.

I distinguish between past, present, and future. In past time, at some point, there was no creature; in future time, at some point, it may not be; since it can be annihilated by the absolute omnipotence of God. But in the present time, in which it exists, it is necessarily a being. There are certain creatures which in the present time move, live, praise God, [and] certain in the heaven of glory behold His face. Who, being in possession of reason, would call them non-entities? 4. From the first being, a prior 'being' cannot be abstracted, common to God and creatures. But God is the first being. Resp.

I distinguish between priority of predication, or of our concepts, and real priority. 'Being', abstracted from God and creatures, is said to be prior not really, but according to our mode of conceiving. 5. Scotists argue: Whatever concept inferiors participate in equally, that is univocal. But inferiors participate in the concept of being equally. Therefore. The major is manifest in itself. The minor is proven, because we conceive being universally; as truly existing. But God truly exists; and the creature truly exists. In this most abstract concept, no inequality is detected, but inequality is given in the inferiors, not in being considered universally. Resp.

The inequality, which founds the analogy, is not to be understood by reason of the common and abstract concept, but by reason of the mode of participating in that common concept; which unequal mode of participating arises from dependence. Namely, creatures participate in the nature of being in a posterior and more equitable manner, because their whole essence, and every perfection, depends on the Creator. But God is being, substance, and Spirit in a most eminent manner, inasmuch as He is not only existing from Himself, but is also the first cause and author, preserver, and governor of other beings. Quaest. XIX. Is independence the quidditative, contracting, and quasi-differential concept of God? The differential concept of God is independence. But independence primarily belongs to God, and is the root of all attributes which are said of God.

Therefore. The major is evident, because every difference primarily belongs to the thing which it constitutes, and is the root of all properties. The minor radiates with its own light, since all the attributes of God acknowledge the independence of God as their root, in our mode of conceiving. e.g. God is therefore infinite, because His essence does not depend on another, by whom it could be limited. God is eternal, because He is independent, consequently He neither has a beginning from another, nor can He be destroyed. &c.

2. By that through which a creature is first constituted in the being of a creature, by its opposite God is constituted in the being of the first deity. But a creature is first constituted in the being of a creature through dependence. Therefore, God is first constituted in the being of deity through independence.

The antithesis is of certain Theologians, for whom the first contracting concept of God seems to be either infinity, or intellectual life, whose principal arguments are:

I. That through which the divine nature according to its own formal reason is first constituted in its own being, and is distinguished from any finite nature, that is the first quidditative concept of God. But through infinity &c. Therefore. Resp. Deny the minor, because independence is prior to infinity. For independence denies the origin of the divine essence, infinity denies its end. But just as origin is prior to end: so according to our mode of conceiving, independence is prior to infinity.

II. Whatever embraces every other reason in God, by which being posited nothing is lacking to the perfection of divinity, that has the reason of a quidditatively determining concept. But infinity &c. Therefore. Resp. Limit the major. Whatever in the first mode of conceiving embraces every other reason in God, by which being posited nothing is lacking to the perfection of divinity, that has the reason of a quidditatively determining concept. Thus the minor is denied. For he who conceives God, in the first moment of consideration, conceives Him as a being existing from Himself; in the second moment he notices that, since God is from Himself, limits or ends can be placed upon Him by no one.

III. If all the attributal perfections of God are infinite, by reason of the identity which they have with the divine essence, the essence of God will be formally infinite, and God will be formally constituted in the being of deity through infinity. But the former is true. Therefore the latter. Resp. Deny the consequence of the major. For the same argument can be formed concerning eternity, simplicity &c. If all the attributal perfections of God are eternal, by reason of the identity which they have with the divine essence, the essence of God will be formally eternal, and God will be formally constituted in the being of deity through eternity.

IV. Whatever is a mode of the divine essence is not its differential concept. But independence &c. Therefore. The major is evident, since a mode indeed affects a thing, but does not first distinguish it. The minor is clear, because in metaphysics independent and dependent are numbered among the modes of being. Resp. Distinguish between an efficient mode and a contracting mode. Independence is a contracting mode, because it contracts the common concept, namely the spiritual essence of God, first constitutes it, distinguishes it from creatures, and pours forth the remaining perfections of God from itself. Instance: But independence is a negative term, positing or importing no perfection. Resp. Independence formally and as a mode of signifying is a negative term: materially and as a mode of being, it denotes the highest perfection of God.

V. Independence acknowledges a perfection prior to itself in God. Therefore it is not the first quidditative concept of God. The antecedent is proved, because independence presupposes the intellectual life of God. Resp. Independence does not presuppose life, except as it presupposes spiritual essence: which pertains to the common concept of God. But if by life is understood the eternal life of God, certainly this presupposes the independence of God; since God is conceived as independent before He is conceived as eternally living.

Latin:

Quæst. XVIII. Quomodo Spiritus, substantia, ens & essentia, de Deo & creaturis prædicantur?

Quando Spiritus, substantia, ens & essentia, de Deo & creaturis prædicantur, prædicatio illa non est impropria & aequivoca , sed propria, neque tamen univoca, sed analogica, iuxta analogiam attributionis intrinsecae .

Prob. a. Quaecunque aequivoce tantum dicuntur, eorum solum nomen commune est, ratio autem nominis diversa. At creatori & creaturis non tantum nomen entis, essentiae, substantiae & Spiritus, sed res ipsa, nomine significata, convenit. Ergo. Maior ex definitione aequivocorum liquet; Minor ostenditur inductive. v. g. Homo vere est, lapis suam habet essentiam, leo per se existit, omnis angelus est Spiritus. Accurate colligit THOMAS AQVINAS P.I. q. 13. art. 5. Si aequivoce ista praedicarentur de Deo, & creaturis, nihil posset de Deo ex creaturis cognosci, sed semper incideret fallacia aequivocationis. Et hoc est tam contra philosophum, qui multa demonstrative de Deo probat, quam etiam contra apostolum, Rom. I, 17.

Prob. b. Quaecunque nomina pluribus quidem sunt communia, ita tamen, ut unum eorum, de quibus dicuntur, participet ea per prius & independenter, cetera autem participent ea per posterius, propter dependentiam; illa praedicantur analogice & inaequaliter. Sed ens & essentia, substantia & Spiritus, sunt communia creatori & creaturae, ita tamen, ut Deus ea participet per prius & independenter, creaturae ea participent per posterius propter dependentiam.

Maior est clara e definitione analogorum. Minor constat, quia Deus est ens, substantia, Spiritus independens; creaturae autem omnes a Deo dependent.

Antithesis est (1) Platonicorum & nonnullorum Scholasticorum asserentium, ens & essentiam, substantiam & Spiritum de Deo & creaturis aequivoce praedicari; (2) Scotistarum statuentium, praedicata illa de Deo atque creaturis univoce & aequaliter dici.

Illorum potiora sunt argumenta: 1. Inter quae infinita datur distantia, de illis conceptus communis formari nequit. At qui inter Deum & creaturas &c. Ergo. Resp. Limit. maior. Inter quae datur distantia infinita negativa, ut plane inter ea nulla intercedat convenientia, (qualis est inter ens, & nihil) de illis conceptus communis formari nequit; concedo. At inter Deum & creaturas datur distantia infinita positiva; quia Deus perfectione eminentissima creaturas infinities exsuperat.

Exinde autem colligitur non licet, quod nulla perfectione, nulloque conceptu communi conveniant; cum enim Deus, summe bonus & perfectus, sui sit communicativus, nonnullos rivulos suae bonitatis, nonnullos radios suae perfectionis creaturis communicavit, ut quadam perfectione, modo inaequali, conveniant. Instantia Spiritus S. in sacris litteris testatur, creaturas, cum Deo comparatas, esse instar nihili, Es. XL, 17. Omnes gentes (sunt) sicut nihil erga ipsum (Deum) minus, quam nihil, & inane reputantur illi. Resp.

Comparativae illae locutiones non sunt destructivae, sed extenuativae. Non tollitur illis perfectio essentialis, sed eminentissima creatoris prae creaturis praerogativa & maiestas indicatur. 2.

Quicunque statuunt, nomen יהוה esse incommunicabile creaturis, illos oportet etiam statuere, ens esse creaturis incommunicabile. Nam יהוה, quod ab essendo ducit originem, cum ente pari passu ambulat. Atqui Lutherani &c. Ergo. Resp.

Nomen יהוה notat essentiam Dei independentem & immutabilem; quae cum essentia generatim considerata pari passu non ambulat. 3. Quidquid aliquando non fuit, & aliquando esse non potest, illud non-entibus potius, quam entibus annumerandum est. Atqui omnis creatura &c. Ergo. Resp.

Disting. inter praeterita, praesentia, & futura. Tempore praeterito aliquando non fuit creatura, tempore futuro etiam aliquando esse non potest; cum absoluta Dei omnipotentia annihilari queat. At tempore praesenti, quo exsistit, necessario est ens. Dantur quaedam creaturae, quae tempore praesenti moventur, vivunt, laudant Deum, quaedam in caelo gloriae faciem eius intuentur. Ecquis rationis compos eas non-entia appellaret? 4. Ab ente primo non potest abstrahi ens prius, commune Deo & creaturis. Sed Deus est ens primum. Resp.

Dist. inter prioritatem praedicationis, seu conceptuum nostrorum, & prioritatem realem. Ens, a Deo & creaturis abstractum, prius dicitur non realiter, sed secundum nostrum concipiendi modum. 5. Scotistae argumentantur: Quemcunque conceptum inferiora participant aequaliter, il est univocus. Atqui conceptum entis inferiora participant aequaliter. Ergo. Maior per se manifesta est. Minor probatur, quia concipimus ens universaliter; ut reuera exsistens. Sed Deus reuera exsistit; & creatura reuera exsistit. In hoc conceptu abstractissimo non deprehenditur ulla inaequalitas, sed inaequalitas datur in inferioribus, non in ente universaliter considerato. Resp.

Inaequalitas, quae fundat analogiam, non intelligenda est ratione conceptus communis & abstracti, sed ratione modi participandi illum conceptum communem; qui modus participandi inaequalis ex dependentia oritur. Nempe creaturae per posterius & aequiori ratione de natura entis participant, quia tota earum essentia, omnisque perfectio a creatur. dependent. Deus autem eminentissima ratione est ens, substantia & Spiritus, quippe qui non tantum est a se exsistens, sed etiam ceterorum entium causa prima & auctor, conservator & gubernator. Quaest. XIX. Estne independentia conceptus Dei quidditativus, contrahens, & quasi differentialis? Conceptus Dei differentialis est independentia. Prob.

I. Ille conceptus Dei contrahens & differentialis est, qui primo Deo competit, & radix est omnium attributorum, quae de Deo dicuntur. Atqui independentia primo Deo competit, & radix est omnium attributorum, quae deo dicuntur. Ergo. Maior constat, quia omnis differentia primo rei, quam constituit, competit, & radix est omnium proprietatum. Minor sue radiat luce, quoniam attributa Dei omnia independentiam Dei quasi radicem, nostro concipiendi modo, agnoscunt. v.gr. Deus ideo est infinitus, quia eius essentia non dependet ab alio, a quo finiri possit. Deus est aeternus, quia independens est, consequenter ab alio neque principium habet, neque destrui potest. &c.

2. Per quod creatura in esse creaturae primo constituitur, per eius oppositum Deus esse in primo deitatis constituitur. Atqui creatura per dependentiam in esse creaturae primo constituitur. Ergo Deus per independentiam in esse deitatis primo constituitur.

Antithesis est quorundam Theologorum, quibus conceptus Dei primus contrahens videtur esse vel infinitudo, vel vita intellectualis, quorum praecipua sunt argumenta:

I. Per quod diuina natura secundum propriam rationem formalem constituitur primo in esse proprio, & a natura quauis finita distinguitur, illud est conceptus primus quidditatinus Dei. Atqui per infinitudinem &c. E. Resp. Neg. minorem, quia independentia infinitudine prior est. Nam independentia originem essentiae diuinae, infinitudo eius finem negat. Sicut autem origo prior est fine: ita secundum nostrum concipiendi modum independentia prior est infinitate.

II. Quidquid complectitur omnem aliam rationem in Deo, qua posita nihil deest diuinitatis perfectioni, illud habet rationem conceptus, quidditatiue determinantis. Atqui infinitudo &c. E. Resp. Limit. maiorem. Quidquid primo concipiendi modo complectitur omnem aliam rationem in Deo, qua posita nihil deest diuinitatis perfectioni, illud habet rationem conceptus quidditatiue determinantis. Sic negatur minor. Nam qui Deum concipit, primo considerandi momento, eum concipit, vt ens a se existens; secundo momento animaduertis, quoniam Deus est a se, ipsi limites aut fines a nemine poni posse.

III. Si omnes attributales Dei perfectiones infinitae sunt, ratione identitatis, quam habent cum essentia diuina, essentia Dei erit formaliter infinita, & Deus in esse deitatis formaliter constituetur per infinitudinem. Atqui prius verum est. Ergo & posterius. Resp. Neg. Consequentiam maioris. Nam idem argumentum formari potest de aeternitate, simplicitate &c. Si omnes attributales Dei perfectiones sunt aeternae, ratione identitatis, quam habent cum essentia diuina, essentia Dei formaliter erit aeterna, & Deus in esse deitatis formaliter constituetur per aeternitatem.

IV. Quidquid est modus essentiae diuinae, non est eius conceptus differentialis. Sed independentia &c. E. Maior constat, quoniam modus rem quidem afficit, sed non primo distinguit. Minor patet, quia in metaphysicis independens, & dependens, modis entis connumeratur. Resp. dist. inter modum efficientem, & contrahentem. Independentia est modus contrahens, quia conceptum communem, nempe spiritualem Dei essentiam, contrahit, primo constituit, a creaturis distinguit, & reliquas Dei perfectiones ex se fundit. Instantia: Sed independentia est terminus negatiuus, nullam ponens aut importans perfectionem. Resp. Independentia formaliter & qua modum significandi, est terminus negatiuus: materialiter & qua modum essendi, notat summam Dei perfectionem.

V. Independentia se priorem agnoscit perfectionem in Deo. E. Non est primus Dei conceptus quidditatiuus. Antecedens probatur, quia independentia praesupponit vitam Dei intellectualem. Resp. Independentia non supponit vitam, nisi qua supponit spiritualem essentiam: quae ad conceptum Dei communem pertinet. Si autem per vitam intelligatur vita aeterna Dei, vtique haec independentiam Dei supponit; quum Deus independens prius concipiatur, quam aeternum viuens. æternum viuens.


### Q. XXI. What is God?: Whence is the independence of God proved?

Whence is the independence of God proved?

The independence of God can be proved both from scripture (a), and from nature (b).

Whence is the independence of God proved?

The independence of God can be proved both from scripture, and from nature.

Prob. a. 1) Isa. XLIV, 6. Thus said Jehovah: I am the first and I am the last, and besides me there is no God. Cf. Isa. XLI, 4. Rev. I, 17. But he who is first does not acknowledge a prior, from whom he might depend as if from a cause. 2) When God says: Exod. III, 14. I am who I am, he indicates that he does not exist from another, but from himself, and thus, that his nature involves necessary and immutable existence .

Prob. b. In nature all dependent beings are traced back to a first and independent being, lest there be a progression to infinity, which nature abhors.

Latin:

Quæft. XX. Vnde probatur independentia Dei?

Independentia Dei tum ex scriptura (a), tum ex natura (b) probari potest.

Quaest. XX. Vnde probatur independentia Dei?

Independentia Dei tum ex scriptura , tum ex natura probari potest.

Prob. a. 1) Es. XLIV, 6. Sic dixit Iehouah: Ego primus & ego nouissimus, & præter me non est Deus. Conf. Es. XLI, 4. Apoc. I, 17. Qui autem primus est, non agnoscit priorem, a quo velut causa dependeat. 2) Cum Deus dicit: Exod. III, 14. Sum, qui sum, indicat, se non exsistere ab alio, verum a se ipso, atque ita, vt eius natura exsistentiam necessariam & immutabilem inuoluat .

Prob. b. In natura omnia entia dependentia ad ens primum & independens reuocantur, ne detur progressus in infinitum, a quo natura abhorret.


### Of the Divine Attributes. Quest. XXI. What are the attributes of God?

Attributes of God are the perfections of God, which follow the divine essence by our mode of conceiving in and of themselves, and are predicated of God paronymously .

Obj. 1. The attributes of God are called perfections, because they declare the essence of God most perfectly.

Obj. 2. Essence is otherwise called the first concept of a thing, than which none is prior, but which is the root of other concepts. Thus, for example, God is first conceived to be an independent being.

tributes of God are called secondary concepts, because they follow the primary concept of God by themselves, and flow from it spontaneously as it were. They are also called inadequate concepts: because they do not express the whole essence of God, on account of His infinite perfection, but set forth something of God. Obs.

3. Attributes are predicated of God paronymously and in the concrete, insofar as they are considered formally. Thus, for example, He is called immense, eternal in the concrete. But in an identical sense God can be called immensity, eternity, etc., since the attributes do not differ from the divine essence really, but only in our order of conceiving. Obs.

4. Some perfections are such simply, others after a fashion. The former imply no imperfection, such as being wise, true, good, etc., which are formally in God; otherwise God would not be absolutely perfect: for nothing of perfection is lacking to the absolutely perfect. The latter involve certain imperfections, and belong to God eminently or virtually; insofar as He has something more excellent than them, and by virtue encompasses them, and can exercise their acts by Himself, for example, to reason, to hear, to see, etc.

Latin:

Attributa Dei sunt perfectiones Dei, quæ essentiam diuinam nostro concipiendi modo per se consequuntur, & de Deo paronymice prædicantur .

Obi. 1. Attributa Dei dicuntur perfectiones, quia essentiam Dei perfectissime declarant .

Obi. 2. Essentia alias dicitur primus rei conceptus, quo nullus est prior, sed qui radix est ceterorum conceptuum. Sic v. gr. Deus primo concipitur esse ens independens.

tributa Dei vocantur conceptus secundi, quia primum Dei conceptum per se consequuntur, & ex eo vltro quasi fluunt. Appellantur etiam conceptus inaedequati: quia totam essentiam Dei, ob infinitam eius perfectionem, non exprimunt, sed aliquid Dei exponunt. Obs.

3. Attributa de Deo praedicantur paronymice & in concreto, quatenus formaliter considerantur. Sic v. gr. dicitur immensus, aeternus in concreto. In sensu autem identico Deus potest dici immensitas, aeternitas &c. quoniam attributa ab essentia diuina non differunt realiter, sed tantum nostro concipiendi ordine. Obs.

4. Perfectiones aliae sunt simpliciter, aliae secundum quid tales. Illae nullam implicant imperfectionem, vt esse sapientem, verum, bonum &c. quae sunt formaliter in Deo; alioqui Deus non foret absolute perfectus: nam absolute perfecto nihil perfectionis deest. Hae quasdam inuoluunt imperfectiones, & eminenter aut virtualiter Deo conueniunt; quatenus habet aliquid iis excellentius, & virtute easdem complectitur, actusque earum per se ipsum exercere potest, v. gr. ratiocinari, audire, videre &c.


### Q. XXII

Are the divine attributes accidents? The divine attributes are not accidents. Prob. I. Because God is most perfect, into whom, just as no imperfection, so no accident falls. For this cannot even be conceived without imperfection; since every accident exists dependently upon a substance.

II. If an accident were to inhere in God as in a subject, He would be composed of subject and accident. But God is in no way composed, but most simple.

You say: 1. Every property is an accident. The divine attributes are properties of God. Therefore. Resp. Every predicamental property, and one spoken of in the strict sense, is an accident. But the divine attributes are not predicamental properties, but transcendental, since they transcend the classes of the predicaments with their eminence, and do not differ from the divine essence really, but only formally. They are called properties analogically, since they follow the essence of God according to our concept of reason, are predicated of the same paronymously, and are reciprocal with it.

You say: 2. Certain divine attributes are affections, for example, love, mercy, etc. But affections are accidents. Resp. Certain affections are spoken of concerning God figuratively, improperly, and anthropopathically (ἀνθρωποπαθῶς), for example, desire, sadness, repentance, etc. Certain ones are predicated primarily of God, secondarily of creatures: which, although they may be accidents in creatures, are not so in God. For the names of affections must be purged of imperfections, and that which remains pure and perfect must be attributed to God.

Q. XXIII.

How are the divine attributes distinguished from the divine essence and from one another? The divine attributes are distinguished from the divine essence, and from one another, not nominally, nor really, but formally, according to our mode of conceiving, not without a certain foundation of distinction.

Prob. a. The divine attributes bring about distinct concepts. Therefore they differ by more than nominally.

Gregory of Nyssa says shrewdly in book XII against Eunomius, intending to lead him to an absurdity: If you are asked what is signified by the name of judge, interpret your mind by answering: or if it should be necessary to give an account of justice, the name of incorporeal is ready for you to answer. But what does incorruptibility signify? You will say it is entirely the same as mercy, or what the notion of judge carries before it. In the same way also let all things pass into one another individually; just as no peculiar signification separates one from another. But if Eunomius declares these things as a legislator: why does Scripture in vain call the divine nature by various names when they name God judge, just, strong, patient, true, merciful, and other things of that kind? nant? If no name is understood in any proper notation, but all are mixed in a confusion of significations, it is a vain labor to use many appellations for the same thing, since no difference of signification distinguishes the names from one another.

Prob. b, I. The divine essence is most simple, devoid of all real composition. But it would not be most simple if the divine attributes differed really from the essence of God and from one another. For the essence of God would be composed of those many essential predicates, or those positive concepts, distinct from one another by the nature of the thing. II. The essence of God is independent and infinite, being supremely perfect, containing all perfections simply within itself. But if the divine essence differed really from the divine attributes, it would be perfected by them, and thus would not be supremely perfect. III. In the divine, all things are one, where no opposition of relation stands in the way. But the divine attributes are not relatively opposed either to the divine essence or to each other. Therefore, the divine attributes are the same as the divine essence, because the individual attributes imply the divine essence itself and represent it by an inadequate concept.

Prob. c. The foundation of the distinction by which the divine attributes are distinguished from the essence of God and from one another is provided to our intellect by diverse extrinsic connotations. 1) Diverse effects, e.g., divine mercy saves, divine justice damns. Therefore, they differ. 2) The agreement of the perfections of creatures with the perfections of God; which are first in the Creator, second in the creatures. E.g., goodness, wisdom, power differ really as they are in creatures, but formally in the Creator. 3) The negations of imperfections which are detected in creatures. E.g., dependence and death differ in creatures on the part of the thing: independence and immortality differ in God on the part of our concept. However, when we assert that the mercy and justice, the wisdom and goodness of God do not differ really in the Creator as they do in creatures, but only formally, the foundation of our assertion is the supreme simplicity and perfection of God, through which it is not permitted to distinguish the divine attributes really from the divine essence and from one another. For although certain divine attributes produce really distinct operations and bring forth diverse effects, the attributes themselves remain simply one; because even from a simple power, with respect to distant subjects, a diverse operation proceeds, and not always does one effect result. This is clearly evident from the heat of the sun, which hardens clay and melts butter. Furthermore, although certain divine attributes negate really distinct imperfections, yet because this is done solely on account of the imperfection of our intellect, really distinct perfections are not on that account affirmed in God. Moreover, although certain attributes belong both to the Creator and to creatures, that agreement does not introduce a real distinction; because they are not in the Creator and in creatures in the same way. In the former they are eminently, in the latter perfectly. For God is merciful and just, good and wise by His essence: creatures are merciful and just, good and wise by qualities that differ really from their essence.

The antithesis is that of some Scholastics, primarily the Scotists, who maintain that the divine attributes are distinguished by the nature of the thing: they fortify their opinion with the following arguments: I. Whatever things have contrary effects differ really. Certain divine attributes have contrary effects. Therefore. Resp. 1) The major premise is not universal. For one cause not rarely produces diverse effects. 2) Diverse effects for the most part acknowledge diverse principles in creatures, in which substance differs from qualities, and one quality from another; but not in God, who by one and most simple essence not only is whatever He is, but also produces all things which He does. II. Whatever things differ in definitions differ really. The divine attributes differ in definitions. Therefore. The major premise shines with its own light; because of one thing one definition is given; but diverse definitions of differing things are formed. The minor premise is clear, because wisdom is defined in one way, and the omnipotence of God in another. Resp. Definitions are either of things, as they are in themselves, or as they are conceived by us. If they are defined as they are in themselves, the wisdom and omnipotence of God do not have diverse definitions, but are God himself, wise and omnipotent; however, something else must be said if they are defined as they are conceived by us.

3. Whatever cannot be predicated of one another are really distinct. But the divine attributes cannot, etc. Therefore. The major premise is evident, because things that agree with one another are mutually affirmed of each other: as Peter and man, man and animal. The minor premise is clear, because the mercy of God is not his justice; nor is the justice of God the divine essence itself. Resp. Distinguish between the formal sense and the identical sense. If the mercy and justice of God are considered in the identical sense, as they are ταὐτὸ [the same] in God, they are one and the same, and that proposition is true: The mercy of God is the justice of God. But if they are viewed in the formal sense, as they are in our concepts, that proposition is false: the mercy of God is the justice of God. For the mercy and justice of God, on account of the distinct effects they produce, are represented by distinct inadequate concepts. Predication, however, follows the concept of the mind; for as we understand, so we name and predicate; since names are symbols of concepts.

Objection: If the divine attributes are not in God as we conceive them, but in another way, they are falsely attributed to God: for when that which is most perfect is conceived with imperfection, there must be an error in that concept. Resp. Something is said to be conceived with imperfection in two ways: 1) regarding the object, when the thing itself is conceived as imperfect. And thus, whoever conceives God with any imperfection errs; for He is devoid of imperfection: 2) Regarding the mode, when only the mode of conceiving is imperfect, or when the thing is not conceived as imperfect, but only imperfectly: and in this way God, who is most perfect, is conceived with imperfection; and that without any error.

4. Whatever can be separated are really distinct. But the divine attributes, etc. Therefore. The major premise is clear in itself, because the most evident sign of a real distinction is the separation of one from another. The minor premise is proven, because the human nature of Christ is rightly called omniscient, but not eternal. Therefore, eternity can be separated from divine knowledge. Resp. The communication of divine attributes is considered either regarding possession. (Thus all divine attributes are communicated to the flesh of Christ; since the whole fullness of the divinity dwells in Christ as in its own temple, Col. II, 9.) or it is considered regarding denomination and usurpation. (Thus not all divine attributes, but only those are communicated to the flesh of Christ which are required for fulfilling the mediatorial office, namely ἐνεργητικὰ [active], or operative.)

Latin:

Suntne attributa diuina accidentia? Attributa diuina non sunt accidentia. Prob. I. Quia Deus est perfectissimus, in quem vt nulla imperfectio, ita nullum cadit accidens. Hoc enim sine imperfectione ne quidem concipi potest; cum omne accidens dependenter a substantia existat.

II. Si Deo tanquam subiecto accidens inhaereret, foret compositus ex subiecto & accidente. At Deus nullo modo est compositus, sed simplicissimus.

Dicis: 1. Omne proprium est accidens. Attributa diuina sunt propria Dei. E. Resp. Omne proprium praedicamentale, & in rigore dictum, est accidens. At diuina attributa non sunt propria praedicamentalia, sed transcendentalia, cum eminentia sua classes praedicamentorum transcedant, neque ab essentia diuina realiter, sed formaliter tantum differant. Dicuntur propria analogice, quoniam essentiam Dei iuxta nostrum rationis conceptum consequuntur, de eadem paronymice praedicantur, & cum illa reciprocantur.

Dicis: 2. Quaedam attributa diuina sunt affectus, v. gr. amor, misericordia &c. Sed affectus sunt accidentia. Resp. Quidam affectus dicuntur de Deo figurate, improprie, & ἀνθρωποπαθῶς, v. gr. desiderium, tristitia, poenitentia &c. Quidam praedicantur primo de Deo, secundo de creaturis: qui licet in creaturis sint accidentia, non tamen in Deo. Repurganda enim sunt nomina affectuum ab imperfectionibus, & id, quod remanet purum ac perfectum, Deo tribuendum.

Quaest. XXIII.

Quomodo attributa diuina ab essentia diuina & a se inuicem distinguuntur? Attributa diuina ab essentia diuina, & a se inuicem, distinguuntur non nominaliter, neque realiter, sed formaliter, secundum nostrum concipiendi modum, non fine certo distinctionis fundamento .

Prob. a. Attributa diuina distinctos inferunt conceptus. Ergo plus, quam nominaliter differunt.

Argute inquit GREGOR. NYSSENVS lib. XII. contra Eunomium, hunc ad absurdum deducturus: Si interrogeris, quid iudicis nomine significetur, ingenium interpretare respondendo: aut si iustitiae rationem reddere oporteat, in promptu tibi fit ad respondendum incorporei nomen. Quid autem incorruptibilitas significat? Idem quod misericordia, omnino dices, aut quod iudicis notio prae se fert. Ad eundem modum etiam sigillatim omnia in se inuicem transeant; Sicut nulla peculiaris significatio alterum ab altero secernat. Quod si haec Eunomius tanquam legislator aliquit edicit: cur scriptura frustra diuinam naturam variis nominibus appellant cum Deum iudicem, iustum, fortem, patientem, verum, misericordem & id genus alia nominant? nant? Si nullum nomen in propria aliqua notione intelligitur, sed omnia significationum confusione miscentur, inanis est labor, multas de eodem appellationes usurpare, cum nulla significationis differentia a se invicem nomina distinguat.

Prob. b. I. Essentia diuina est simplicissima, omnis realis compositionis expers. At non foret simplicissima, si attributa diuina ab essentia Dei, & a se inuicem realiter differrent. Componeretur enim essentia Dei ex multis illis prædicatis essentialibus, siue conceptibus politiuis, ex natura rei inter se distinctis. II. Essentia Dei independens & infinita est summe perfecta omnes perfectiones simpliciter in se continens. At si essentia diuina ab attributis diuinis realiter differret, per hæc illa perficeretur, adeoque summe perfecta non foret. III. In diuinis omnia sunt vnum, vbi non obuiat relationis oppositio. Sed attributa diuina neque essentiæ diuinæ, neque sibi inuicem relatiue opponuntur. Ergo attributa diuina sunt eadem, quia singula attributa implicant ipsam essentiam diuinam, eamque inadequato conceptu repræsentant.

Prob. c. Fundamentum distinctionis, qua attributa diuina ab essentia Dei, & a se inuicem, distinguuntur, intellectui nostro præbent diuersa connotata extrinseca. 1) Diuersi effectus, v. gr. misericordia diuina saluat, iustitia diuina damnat. E. Differunt: 2) Conuenientia perfectionum creaturarum cum perfectionibus diuinis; quæ primo sunt in creatore, secundo in creaturis. v. gr. Bonitas, sapientia, potentia vt in creaturis realiter, ita in creatore formaliter differunt. 3) Negationes imperfectionum, quæ deprehenduntur in creaturis. v. gr. Dependentia & mors in creaturis differunt ex parte rei: independentia & immortalitas differunt in Deo ex parte nostri conceptus. Quando autem afferimus, misericordiam & iustitiam, sapientiam & bonitatem Dei non perinde in creatore, ac in creaturis, differre realiter, sed tantum formale fundamentum est summe Dei simplicitatis & perfectio, per quam attributa diuina ab essentia diuina & a se inuicem realiter distinguere non licet. Quamuis enim quædam attributa diuina realiter distinctas edant operationes, diuersosque producant effectus: ipsa tamen attributa simpliciter vnum manent; quia etiam a simplici virtute, respectu distinctorum subiectotum, diuersa procedit operatio, nec semper vnus prouenit effectus. Id quod liquido constat e calore solis, lutum indurante, & butyrum liquefaciente. Deinde quamuis per quædam attributa diuina realiter distinctæ imperfectiones negentur: tamen quia id fit solum propter imperfectionem intellectus nostri, realiter ob id distinctæ perfectiones in Deo non affirmantur. Præterea licet quædam attributa & Creatori, & creaturis conueniant: non tamen illa conuenientia reale infert discrimen; quia non eodem modo sunt in Creatore, & in creaturis. In illo sunt eminenter, in his perfecte. Deus quippe per essentiam sum est misericors & iustus, bonus & sapiens: creaturæ sunt misericordes & iustæ, bonæ & sapientes, per qualitates, ab essentia realiter differentes.

Antithesis est nonnullorum Scholasticorum, in primis Scotistarum, statuentium, attributa diuina ex natura rei distingui: qui suam opinionem sequentibus muniunt argumentis: I. Quæcunque contrarios habent effectus, differunt realiter. Quædam attributa diuina habent contrarios effectus. E. Resp. 1) Maior non est vniuersalis. Nam vna causa diuersos haud raro producit effectus. 2) Diuersi effectus plerumque diuersa agnoscunt principia in creaturis, in quibus substantia a qualitatibus, & vna qualitas ab altera differt; sed non in Deo, qui per vnam & simplicissimam essentiam non solum est, quidquid est, sed omnia etiam efficit, quæ agit. 2. Quæcunque differunt definitionibus, realiter differunt. Attributa diuina differunt definitionibus. E. Maior sua radiat luce; quia vnius rei vna datur definitio; diuersæ autem definitiones de rebus differentibus formantur. Minor est clara, quia aliter sapientia, aliter omnipotentia Dei definitur. Resp. Definitiones sunt vel rerum, prout in se sunt, vel prout a nobis concipiuntur. Si definiantur, prout in se sunt, sapientia & omnipotentia Dei, non habent diversas definitiones, sed sunt ipse Deus sapiens, & omnipotens; aliud tamen dicendum est, si definiantur, prout a nobis concipiuntur.

3. Quaecunque non possunt de se invicem praedicari, illa sunt realiter distincta. Sed attributa divina non possunt &c. Ergo. Maior constat, quia, quae inter se conveniunt, de se mutuo affirmantur: vt Petrus & homo, homo & animal. Minor liquet, quia misericordia Dei non est ipsius iustitia; neque iustitia Dei est ipsa essentia divina. Resp. Dist. inter sensum formalem, & identicum. Si misericordia & iustitia Dei considerentur in sensu identico, prout in Deo ταὐτὸ, unum idemque sunt, propositio illa vera est: Misericordia Dei est iustitia Dei. At si spectentur in sensu formali, prout in nostris sunt conceptibus, falsa est propositio illa: misericordia Dei est iustitia Dei. Nam misericordia & iustitia Dei, ob distinctos, quos edunt, effectus, distinctis conceptibus inadequatis repraesentantur. Praedicatio autem sequitur conceptum mentis; vt enim intelligimus, sic nominamus & praedicamus; cum nomina sint symbola conceptuum.

Instantia: Si attributa divina non ita sunt in Deo, vt nos ea concipimus, sed alio modo, falso illa Deo tribuuntur: quando enim cum imperfectione concipitur, quod perfectissimum est, oportet errorem in conceptu illo esse. Resp. Dupliciter aliquid dicitur concipi cum imperfectione: 1) quoad obiectum, cum res ipsa concipitur vt imperfecta. Et sic errat, quisquis cum vlla imperfectione Deum concipit; imperfectionis enim ille expers est: 2) Quoad modum, cum modus tantum concipiendi imperfectus est, siue cum non concipitur res vt imperfecta, sed tantummodo imperfecte: & hoc pacto Deus, qui perfectissimus est, cum imperfectione concipitur; idque fine vllo errore.

4. Quaecunque possunt separari, sunt realiter distincta. Sed attributa divina &c. E. Maior per se clara est, quia luculentissimum indicium distinctionis realis est separatio vnius ab alio. Minor probatur, quia humana Christi natura recte dicitur omniscia, sed non aeterna. Separari itaque potest aeternitas a scientia diuina. Resp. Communicatio attributorum diuinorum consideratur, vel quoad possessionem. (Sic carni Christi omnia attributa diuina sunt communicata; cum tota plenitudo diuinitatis in Christo velut proprio templo habitet, Col. II, 9.) vel consideratur quoad denominationem & vsurpationem. (Sic non omnia attributa diuina, sed ea tantum carni Christi communicata sunt, quae requiruntur ad obeundum officium mediatorium, nempe ἐνεργητικὰ, siue operantia.)


### Q. XXIV. How are the divine attributes divided?

The divine attributes are divided (1) into negative and positive. The former are those by which imperfections, which are found in creatures, are removed from God. The latter are those by which perfections are simply affirmed of God. (2) Into ἀνενέργητα [inactive], quiescent, or immanent, which are ordered to the divine essence absolutely and in itself, without respect to operation, and thus to no act: and into ἐνεργητικὰ [active], or operative and outwardly exerting, which describe the divine essence respectively, with respect to operation, and thus are known to be ordered to certain acts.

Obj. 1. The negative divine attributes are infinity, immensity, immortality, immutability, incomprehensibility, invisibility; which are considered, partly formally, partly materially or fun fundamentally.

In the former way, they only deny and remove a certain imperfection from God; in the latter way, they connote a certain positive perfection of God.

Thus, when I say: God is immutable; I indeed deny that God is subject to any change, but in such a way that I connote that He is most constant both in being and in willing.

Objection 2.

The quiescent, or immanent, attributes of God are also called absolute; because they declare the divine essence absolutely, without respect to operation, and they are: Unity, simplicity, truth, goodness, infinity, eternity, immutability, immortality, immensity, incomprehensibility, invisibility, blessedness, and the majesty of God.

Objection 3.

The operative attributes of God are also called respective; because they introduce a respect to ἐνέργειαν [energy/operation], or divine act, and they are life, omniscience, omniwisdom, omnipotence, grace, justice, truth, and the omnipresence of God.

Latin:

Attributa diuina diuiduntur (1) in negatiua, & positiua. Illa sunt, quibus a Deo imperfectiones, quae reperiuntur in creaturis, remouentur. Haec sunt, quibus perfectiones simpliciter de Deo affirmantur. (2) In ἀνενέργητα, quiescentia, seu immanentia, quae essentiam diuinam absolute & in se, contra respectum ad operationem, atque adeo ad nullum actum ordinantur: ἐνεργητικὰ, seu operantia & ad extra se exserentia, quae essentiam diuinam describunt respective, respectu operationis, atque adeo ad certos actus ordinata esse cognoscuntur.

Obs. 1. Attributa diuina negatiua sunt infinitas, immensitas, immortalitas, immutabilitas, incomprehensibilitas, inuisibilitas; quae considerantur, partim formaliter, partim materialiter seu fundamentaliter.

Priori modo tantum negant et removent imperfectionem quandam a Deo: posteriori modo positivam quandam perfectionem Dei connotant.

Sic cum dico: Deus est immutabilis; nego quidem Deum esse ulli mutationi obnoxium, sed ita, ut connotem, illum esse tam in essendo, quam volendo constantissimum.

Obiectio 2.

Attributa Dei quiescentia, sive immanentia, dicuntur etiam absoluta; quia essentiam divinam declarant absolute, citra respectum ad operationem, et sunt: Unitas, simplicitas, veritas, bonitas, infinitas, aeternitas, immutabilitas, immortalitas, immensitas, incomprehensibilitas, invisibilitas, beatitudo, et maiestas Dei.

Obiectio 3.

Attributa Dei operativa vocantur etiam respectiva; eo quod respectum inferunt ἐνέργειαν, aut actum divinum, et sunt vita, omniscientia, omnisapientia, omnipotentia, gratia, iustitia, veritas, omnipraesentia Dei.


### On the Absolute, or Immanent, Attributes of God

Question XXV.

What is the unity of God?

Objection.

God is said to be one, not in species, but in number; because He is a most singular being, not only undivided in Himself, but also indivisible, on account of the supreme simplicity of the divine essence; because in God there is no composition given.

Some Fathers prefer to say that God is one by simplicity of existence, or by perfection, rather than by number; see those cited by D.

Calov, Syst. tom. II. p. 278.

But a distinction must be made between predicamental number and transcendental number.

Predicamental number is discrete quantity, which does not befit God; but transcendental number is the difference of singular things.

God is said to be one not only absolutely and internally, but also exclusively and externally, because He is the only God.

He is unique not only in act, like species monadically, the sun, the moon, etc., which are called species for this reason, that although no more individuals are given in act, it is not repugnant that more suns or moons could be given: but it is simply repugnant to the divine essence that more individuals of the same kind be given, to which it might be communicated through its own multiplication, since nothing is as repugnant to deity as a plurality of essence.

The unity of God is proved both from nature and from Scripture.

The latter teaches the unity of God, 1) assertively, Deut.

VI, 4: Hear, O Israel, Iehouah our God (is) Iehouah one.

Moses, about to exhort the Israelites to love God with all their heart, with all their soul, and with all their strength, renders the reason, because God is one, the only treasure of the heart, the only spouse of the soul, the one cause of all human powers, to whom by the most equitable right the heart, soul, and all powers are to be devoted.

2) Negatively, Know that Iehouah Himself is God, and there is no one else besides Him.

Deut. IV, 35. 3) Exclusively, Let all the kingdoms of the earth know that Thou art Iehouah God.

2 Kings XIX, 19.

Following the guidance of the light of nature, we gather the unity of God 1) from independence; because all dependent beings are traced back to one, which is the a [from], and from whom are all things.

2) From infinity; because two infinite beings cannot be posited without contradiction.

For as two beings are circumscribed by a certain number, so they differ by a certain limit of essence.

3) From the most eminent perfection of God.

Two most perfect beings cannot exist; because one would possess a perfection that the other would lack; otherwise they would not differ.

4) From the omnipotent government of this universe.

If there were several gods, no-

The unity of God is an attribute of God by which we conceive the divine essence as most singular, not only undivided, but also indivisible, and incommunicable through any multiplication of itself. none of them would be omnipotent. For if one were to create something, and were to strive to preserve what was created, another would either be able to destroy his work, or would not be able. If he could, the other would be impotent and weak; for he would not possess such power that he would be able to preserve and protect the work which he had founded. If he could not destroy the other's work, he would not be omnipotent, and therefore not the true God either. Wherefore it can by no means come to pass that there be two omnipotent rulers of the world. Οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη, εἷς κοίρανος ἔστω. 5) From the love of God incommunicable to many. The true God is to be loved above all things. But he who is not one cannot be loved above all things (*).

The antithesis is 1) Of the Gentiles, who wandered most foully from the way of salvation by worshipping many gods. 2) Of the ancient heretics, among whom in the 1st century were the Valentinians, who established thirty αἰῶνας, or ages of generation, in God, and invented gods generating, being born, and marrying. In the 2nd and 3rd centuries, the Cerdonians and Marcionites, who blasphemously asserted that one God is the creator of the world of the O.T., and another God is the father of Christ of the N.T.; that the former is just and cruel, but the latter is merciful, clement, and good. In the 3rd century, the Manichaeans, who established two first principles of all things, coeternal but diverse among themselves, namely the good, which they called God, light, and the evil, which they called the devil, darkness: concerning whom EPIPHANIUS Haeres. LXVI. (**). 3) The Socinians, opining that one true God is supreme, another subordinate; that one is independent, the other dependent. Their principal arguments are:

I. God is a name of power. Therefore, he who possesses true power (e.g., an angel, a magistrate) is the true God. Resp. The name God formally designates him who possesses the divine nature, of which power and dominion are a consequence, as we have demonstrated above.
