Certainly, if neither the Greek name, θεὸς, nor the Latin, Deus, denoted the divine essence and nature, then neither in the Greek nor in the Latin language would a divine name signifying the divine nature be given, which seems altogether absurd.

II. The magistrate is said to be God either truly or falsely. Not falsely: for the idols of the nations and the devil are falsely called gods due to the erroneous opinion of men. Therefore truly, and with a true and not fictitious likeness to God. But he who is truly called God, he is the true God. Resp. 1) The magistrate is not called God in the singular number, but judges and magistrates are named gods in the plural number. For there are many gods λεγόμενοι (so-called), titular, such only by participation in the name, not in the divine essence. 2) It is one thing to be truly called God in a figurative and metaphorical sense, and another to be truly God in a proper and native signification. In a metaphorical sense, magistrates are truly called gods: but the true God is he who possesses an independent and infinite nature.

III. Christ is the true God and yet at the same time made God, Therefore, one true God is independent, who is not made, and another true God is dependent, who is made. Resp. St. Peter does not say that God the Father made Christ God, but that he made Jesus, the son of Mary, Lord and Christ, i.e., that he exalted him to the use of the fullest dominion and royal power by his exaltation to his right hand. For although Christ received τὴν κτῆσιν, or the possession of royal dignity, according to his human nature from the hypostatic union, yet by his exaltation to the right hand of God he was made Lord and Christ, as to the χρῆσιν, or the fullest and incessant usurpation of divine omnipotence in governing this universe, especially in gathering and defending the church as the kingdom of grace. For the word χριστὸς here denotes the king of the people of God, as observed by H. GROTIUS in this place.

Latin:

Quaestio XXV.

Quae est unitas Dei?

Obiectio.

Unus dicitur Deus, non specie, sed numero; quia est ens singularissimum, non tantum in se indivisum, sed et indivisibile, ob summam essentiae divinae simplicitatem; quia in Deo nulla datur compositio.

Patres nonnulli malunt Deum dicere unum, existentiae simplicitate, aut perfectione, quam numero, quos citatos vide a D.

Calov. syst. tom. II. p. 278.

Sed distinguendum est inter numerum praedicamentalem, et transcendentalem.

Numerus praedicamentalis est quantitas discreta, non conveniens Deo; sed numerus transcendentalis est differentia rerum singularium.

Unus dicitur Deus non tantum absolute et interne, sed etiam exclusive et externe, quia est Deus unicus.

Unicus est non tantum actu, ut species monadice, sol, luna etc. quae dicuntur species propterea, quod licet non plura actu dentur individua, non tamen repugnat, plures dari soles, vel lunas: at essentiae divinae simpliciter repugnat, plura eiusdem dari individua, quibus communicetur per sui multiplicationem, cum nihil aeque pugnet cum deitate, quam essentiae pluralitas.

Unitas Dei probatur tum ex natura, tum ex scriptura.

Haec docet unitatem Dei, 1) assertive, Deut.

VI, 4. Audi Israel, Iehouah Deus noster (est) Iehouah unus.

Cohortaturus Moses Israelitas ad amandum Deum toto corde, tota anima, et ex omnibus viribus, rationem reddit, quia unus est Deus, unicus cordis thesaurus, unicus animae sponsus, una causa omnium virium humanarum, cui iure aequissimo cor, anima, omnesque vires devovendae sunt.

2) Negative, Scias, quod Iehouah ipse fit Deus, nec amplius (quisquam) praeter illum.

Deut. IV, 35. 3) Exclusive, Cognoscant omnia regna terrae, quod tu sis Iehouah Deus.

2 Reg. XIX, 19.

Ductum luminis naturae sequentes unitatem Dei colligimus 1) ex independentia; quia omnia entia dependentia revocantur ad unum, quod est a, et a quo sunt omnia.

2) Ex infinitate; quia duo entia infinita sine contradictione statui nequeunt.

Duo enim entia ut certo numero circumscribuntur, ita certo essentiae limite differunt.

3) Ex eminentissima Dei perfectione.

Duo perfectissima esse nequeunt; quia uni adesset perfectio, quae alteri deesset; ceteroqui non differrent.

4) Ab omnipotenti regimine huius universi.

Si plures essent dii,

Unitas Dei est attributum Dei, quo essentiam divinam singularissimam non indivisam tantum, sed et indivisibilem, atque per quandam sui multiplicationem incommunicabilem, concipimus. nullus ex iis foret omnipotens. Quod si enim vnus aliquid crearet, creatumque conseruare niteretur, alter vel posset opus eius destruere, vel non posset. Si posset, alter foret impotens & imbecillis; neque enim ea polleret vi, vt opus, quod condiderat, conseruare & protegere valeret. Si non posset alterius opus destruere, non esset omnipotens, adeoque nec verus Deus. Quare nullo pacto fieri potest, vt duo sint omnipotentes mundi rectores. Οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη, εἷς κοίρανος ἔστω. 5) Ex amore Dei pluribus incommunicabili. Verus Deus super omnia diligendus est. At non potest super omnia diligi, qui non est vnus (*).

Antithesis est 1) Gentilium, qui a via salutis foedissime aberrarunt multos colendo Deos. 2) Priscorum hæreticorum, quos inter sæculo I. fuerunt Valentiniani, qui triginta αἰῶνας, siue sæcula generationis, in Deo statuerunt, & Deos generantes, nascentes, nubentesque commenti sunt. Sæculo II. & III. Cerdoniani & Marcionitæ, Deum alium V. T. mundi creatorem, alium Deum N. T. patrem Christi; illum iustum & sæuum, hunc autem misericordem, clementem & bonum esse, blaspheme asseruerunt. Sæculo III. Manichæi, qui duo rerum omnium principia prima statuerunt coæterna, sed inter se diuersa, nempe bonum, quod vocarunt Deum, lucem, & malum, quod vocarunt diabolum, tenebras: de quibus EPIPHANIVS Hæres. LXVI. (**). 3) Sociniani opinantes, Deum verum alium summum, alium subordinatum; alium independentem, alium dependentem esse. Quorum praecipua sunt argumenta:

I. Deus est nomen potestatis. Ergo veram habens potestatem (v. gr. angelus, magistratus) verus Deus est. Resp. Nomen Deus formaliter designat eum, qui habet naturam divinam, cuius consequens est potestas & imperium, ut supra demonstravimus. Sane si neque graecum nomen, θεὸς, neque latinum, Deus, essentiam ac naturam divinam denotaret, neque in graeca, neque in latina lingua nomen divinum significativum naturae divinae daretur, quod perquam absurdum videtur.

II. Magistratus aut vere, aut falso dicitur Deus. Non falso: nam idola gentium & diabolus falso dicuntur dii ob erroneam hominum opinionem. Ergo vere, & veram & non fictam similitudinem cum Deo. Sed qui vere vocatur Deus, ille est verus Deus. Resp. 1) Magistratus non in numero singulari vocatur Deus, sed iudices & magistratus in numero multitudinis nominantur dii. Multi enim sunt dii λεγόμενοι, nuncupativi, sola nominis, non essentiae divinae participatione tales, 2) Aliud est vere dici Deum sensu figurato & metaphorico, aliud est vere esse Deum significatione propria & nativa. Sensu metaphorico magistratus vere dicuntur dii: sed verus Deus est, qui habet naturam independentem & infinitam.

III. Christus est verus Deus & tamen simul Deus factus, Ergo alius Deus verus est independens, qui non est factus, alius verus Deus dependens, qui est factus. Resp. S. Petrus non dicit, quod Deus pater Christum fecerit Deum, sed quod Iesum filium Mariae fecerit dominum & Christum, i. e. quod ad usum plenissimi dominii & regiae potestatis eum euexerit per exaltationem ad dextram suam. Quamuis enim Christus τὴν κτῆσιν, siue possessionem dignitatis regiae, secundum humanam naturam acceperit ex vnione hypostatica, per euectionem tamen ad dextram Dei factus est dominus & Christus, qua χρῆσιν, seu plenissimam & incessantem vsurpationem divinae omnipotentiae in gubernando hoc vniuerso, inprimis in colligenda & defendenda ecclesia tanquam regno gratiae. Etenim vox χριστὸς hic notat regem populi Dei, observante H V G. G R O T I O in h. l.


### Quest. XXVI. What is the simplicity of God?

The simplicity of God is a divine attribute, by which the essence of God is devoid of all composition.

Prob. I. From the divine names Jehovah, Eieh Ascher Eieh, Which divine names, as they draw their origin from being (effendo), so they infer and signify the most absolute simplicity of the divine essence, that nothing happens in God except to be, and that God is his own being.

II. From abstract predicates. That is a most simple being, of which predicates are verified in the abstract: because this has a simple mode of signifying. But concerning God, etc. That this is being, and contains a manifest contradiction in itself, we easily understand when we reason thus: Evil is mixed with good in one world, and thus in every single man. Therefore, either two contrary gods have consented in one counsel and decree, and have worked with joined forces in creating one effect; or one of them; and indeed that good one, was not able to prevent the other from rendering the effect of the former depraved and mutilated in its very nature and constitution. Both are certainly of such a kind that nothing more absurd could be conceived. This is to abolish all independence and supreme perfection of God, and thus God himself.

The minor is proven, because God not only has life in Himself, but is also life itself. So does God love, that He becomes charity itself.

You say: Abstract expressions do not always imply the simplicity of essence: for Paul also addresses the Ephesians, that they are light in the Lord, R. Abstract expressions are either absolute, or limited by restricting and diminishing conditions. God is called light absolutely, but the Ephesians are called light in the Lord with an added restriction, and thus dependently upon the illuminating grace of God.

III. From the spirituality of God.

Whoever is the highest and most perfect spirit, his essence is simple. But God is, etc. Therefore. The major is evident, because spirit is contrasted with body, which is composite. The minor is clear from

You say: Angels are spirits, and nevertheless are composed of essence and accidents.

Resp. 1) From the spirituality of God we gather that He is not composed of matter and form, and integral parts. 2) The reason for God and for angels is different. He is the highest and most perfect spirit, into whom no accident can fall: Angels are inferior and more imperfect spirits.

IV. From the independence of God.

Where composition is given, there is given something prior, which joins and composes the things to be composed. But God is the first and independent being, not acknowledging a prior cause by which He could be composed. *

Latin:

Simplicitas Dei est attributum divinum, quo essentia Dei omnis compositionis expers est.

Prob. I. Ex nominibus divinis Iehouah, Eieh Ascher Eieh, Quae nomina divina, vt ab essendo trahunt originem, ita absolutissimam essentiae divinae simplicitatem inferunt atque significant, quod nihil in Deo fit, nisi esse, & quod Deus sit ipse esse suum.

II. Ex praedicatis abstractivis. Illud est ens simplicissimum, de quo verificantur praedicata in abstracto: quia hoc simplicem habet significandi modum. Atqui de Deo &c. Enim esse, & manifestam in se repugnantiam continere, facile intelligimus, cum ita ratiocinamur: Bono malum adnistum est in uno mundo, atque adeo in uno quoque homine. E. aut duo dii contrarii, aeternis consiliis ac decretis in unum consenserunt, & coniunctis viribus operati sunt in uno effectu creando; aut alteruter eorum; & bonus quidem ille, non valuit prohibere alterum, quo minus hic illius effectum, in ipsa eius natura & constitutione perficienda, deprauatum mutilatumque efficeret. Vtrumque sane est eiusmodi, quo nihil cogitari queat absurdius. Hoc est, tollere omnem Dei independentiam ac summam perfectionem, atque adeo ipsum Deum.

Minor probatur, quia Deus non tantum in se ipso habet vitam, sed est etiam ipsa vita. Ita diligit Deus, ut fit ipsa caritas.

Dicis: Abstractivae locutiones non semper inferunt simplicitatem essentiae: nam et Ephesios compellat Paullus, quod sint lux in domino, R. Abstractivae vel sunt absolutae, vel per conditiones restringentes et diminuentes limitatae. Deus absolute dicitur lux, sed Ephesii cum addita restrictione vocantur lux in domino, adeoque dependenter a gratia Dei illuminante.

III. Ex spiritualitate Dei.

Quicunque est spiritus summus et perfectissimus, illius essentia est simplex. Atqui Deus etc. Ergo. Maior patet, quia spiritus contradistinguitur corpori, quod est compositum. Minor liquet ex

Dicis: Angeli sunt spiritus, et nihilominus compositi ex essentia et accidentibus.

Resp. 1) Ex spiritualitate Dei colligimus, ipsum non esse compositum ex materia et forma, partibusque integrantibus. 2) Dispar est ratio Dei et angelorum. Ille est spiritus summus et perfectissimus, in quem non cadit accidens: Angeli sunt spiritus inferiores et imperfectiores.

IV. Ex independentia Dei.

Vbi datur compositio, ibi datur aliquid prius, quod componenda coniungit et componit. At Deus est ens primum et independens, non agnoscens caussam priorem, a qua componi queat. *


### Quest. XXVI. What is the simplicity of God?: V. From the perfection of God

V. From the perfection of God.

For the simpler a thing is, the more perfect it is.

VI. From the immutability of God.

In every composition there are diverse principles, which, just as they come together, can in turn be divided, and thus bring about change. But God is not subject to any change.

VII. By induction, by removing all and singular compositions from God.

Physical composition from matter and form, and quantitative parts, is alien to God. For that composition belongs to natural bodies: but God is a most pure spirit. Nor is logical composition from genus and species, from subject and accident, to be attributed to God. For the genus behaves like potency; the difference like act; but God is most pure act. The genus is multipliable into many species; the species is multipliable into many individuals: but nothing is as repugnant to God as plurality; since He is most singularly one. Moreover, accidental composition brings about imperfection. Nor does metaphysical composition from essence and existence befit God. For our intellect conceives through essence a thing actually existing, but which was at one time possible; but through existence, an act of existing superadded to the essence. But it is not permitted to conceive of God as possible; because He is a necessary being, of whose essence it is to exist necessarily. Nor from nature and suppositum, or essence and subsistence. For every composition is in its own way founded in the ratio of potency, or if the parts do not regard one another as act and potency, they nevertheless tend toward the integrity, increase, and perfection of the whole. But in God both the act of essence and of subsistence is independent of omnipotence and most pure, since neither exists in potency to the other. Therefore, the act of essence and subsistence makes no composition in God.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, Vorstius, Burgersdicius, and others, who maintain that God is not devoid of all composition: who confirm their opinion with the following arguments.

I. In that in which a distinction of reason has a place, in that a composition of reason finds a place.

But in God, etc. Therefore. The major is certain, because distinction presupposes composition. The minor is evident, because attributes are distinguished from the divine essence by reason.

Resp. I deny the major. For the fact that many concepts of God are given; that a distinction of reason can be admitted; that the very divine essence provides the foundation: all of this is not from a prior composition, but from the most eminent perfection of God. For since God is a sea of innumerable perfections, he therefore provides the foundation, now under this, now under that perfection, for considering God inadequately, and for distinguishing one perfection from another. But it is compared far differently with composition; since it always involves imperfection.

Conf. D. Osiander, coll. system, P. I. p. 272.

II. Whatever essence consists of three persons, that is composite. The divine essence &c. Therefore.

Resp. Whatever essence consists of three essentially distinct persons, that is composite; I concede. The divine essence consists of three essentially distinct persons; I deny. The three persons of the divinity differ indeed really, on account of real oppositions, yet they do not differ essentially, because they do not have a diverse essence, but the same.

Latin:

V. Ex perfectione Dei.

Nam quo quid simplicius, eo perfectius.*

VI. Ex immutabilitate Dei.

In omni compositione sunt diversa principia, quae uti coeunt, ita vicissim dividi possunt, adeoque mutationem inferunt. At Deus nulli mutationi est obnoxius.

VII. Per inductionem, omnes et singulas compositiones a Deo remouendo.

Aliena est a Deo compositio physica ex materia et forma, partibusque quantitativis. Est enim compositio illa corporum naturalium: at Deus est spiritus purissimus. Neque attribuenda est Deo compositio logica ex genere et specie, ex subiecto et accidente. Nam genus se habet instar potentiae; differentia instar actus; at Deus purissimus est actus. Genus est multiplicabile in plures species; species multiplicabilis est in plura individua: Deo autem nihil peraeque repugnat, ac pluralitas; cum sit singularissime unus. Accidentalis autem compositio imperfectionem infert. Neque conuenit Deo compositio metaphysica ex essentia et existentia. Nam intellectus noster concipit per essentiam, rem actu quidem existentem, sed quae aliquando fuit possibilis; per existentiam autem, actum existendi essentiae superadditum. At Deum ut possibilem concipere non licet; quia est ens necessarium, de cuius essentia est, necessario exsistere. Neque ex natura et supposito, siue essentia et subsistentia. Nam omnis compositio suo modo fundatur in ratione potentiae, aut si partes non respiciant se inuicem ut actus et potentia, tendunt tamen ad integritatem, augmentum et perfectionem totius. Sed in Deo vterque actus essentiae et subsistentiae ab omnipotentia independens et purissimus est, cum neuter exsistat in potentia ad alterum. Ergo actus essentiae et subsistentiae nullam in Deo facit compositionem.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, Vorstii, Burgersdicii et aliorum statuentium, Deum non omnis compositionis esse expertem: qui sequentibus argumentis suam opinionem firmatur cunt.

I. In quo locum habet distinctio rationis, in eo compositio rationis locum inuenit.

Atqui in Deo etc. Ergo. Maior constat, quia distinctio compositionem supponit. Minor patet, quia attributa ab essentia diuina ratione distinguuntur.

Resp. neg. maiorem. Quod enim dentur multi conceptus de Deo; quod distinctio rationis admitti possit; quod ipsa esfentia divina fundamentum praebeat: id omne est non a praevia compositione, sed ab eminentissima Dei perfectione. Quia enim Deus est pelagus innumerabilium perfectionum, ideo praebet ille fundamentum nunc sub hac, nunc sub illa perfectione, Deum inadæquate considerandi, unamque perfectionem ab alia distinguendi. Sed longe aliter comparatum est cum compositione; quippe quæ semper involuit imperfectionem.

Conf. D. Osiander, coll. system, P. I. p. 272.

II. Quæcunque essentia constat tribus personis, illa est composita. Essentia divina &c. Ergo.

Resp. Quæcunque essentia constat tribus personis essentialiter distinctis, illa est composita; concedo. Essentia divina constat tribus personis essentialiter distinctis; nego. Tres personæ divinitatis differunt quidem realiter, propter reales oppositiones, non tamen differunt essentialiter, quia non habent essentiam diversam, sed eandem.


### Quest. XXVI. What is the simplicity of God?: Instantia I

Instantia I.

But because the persons differ really, they are really composed.

Resp. Distinction is one thing, composition is another. The former is a sign of perfection, the latter is a sign of imperfection. The former denotes the diversity of extremes, the latter their union.

Instantia II.

Union also pertains to the three persons of the deity; because they are united in one essence.

Resp. They are not united strictly speaking; because for a true union diverse substances are required. But the three divine persons have one essence, or substance.

Furthermore, in a true union one of the united things behaves by way of potency, the other by way of act. Thus in man, who is really composite, the soul has the notion of perfecting act, matter is like perfectible potency. Since these things cannot be said of the divine persons, it is truly gathered that they are not, strictly speaking, united.

Instantia III.

The three divine persons are either united, or they are not. If the former; composition will be given, because union. If the latter; the divine persons will be diverse by reason of essence, and thus a triple essence will have to be admitted.

Resp. The divine persons are neither united, nor diverse by reason of essence, but by reason of essence they are one.

III. In that in which essence and real relation are given, in that is given real composition. But in God &c. Therefore.

The major is evident, because a relation adds to the essence a peculiar respect, with which it is composed. The minor is clear, because in divine matters, as scripture testifies, there is given one who is really father, and who is really called son. Therefore there must be given in God a real paternity and a real filiation, which are relations.

Resp. The hypostatic relation does not inhere in God as an accident of the divine essence, nor does it really differ from it. Therefore it does not make a real composition: it indeed distinguishes one person from another, but it does not compose.

But in God accidents are given.

Therefore. The minor is proven, because in God there are decrees, which are accidents.

Resp. I deny the minor; because decrees in God are not in a more imperfect mode, but eminently, i. e. the divine decrees are not accidents, but the divine essence itself decreeing.

Instantia I. The divine essence is one. The decrees of God are not one, but many.

Therefore the decrees of God are not the divine essence itself.

Resp. The decrees of God, considered in themselves, without order to objects, or connoted things, are the divine essence itself decreeing; viewed in order to diverse connoted things, or objects, they are many outside of God.

There is given, therefore, a multitude of divine decrees, not on the part of God, or in God, but on the part of the connoted things, or objects.

Instantia II. Decrees are effects of the divine will.

Latin:

Instantia I.

Sed quia personæ differunt realiter, realiter componuntur.

Resp. Aliud est distinctio, aliud compositio. Illa est signum perfectionis, hæc est signum imperfectionis. Illa notat extremorum diversitatem, hæc eorundem unionem.

Instantia II.

Unio competit etiam tribus personis deitatis; quia uniuntur in una essentia.

Resp. Non uniuntur stricte loquendo; quia ad veram unionem diversæ requiruntur substantiæ. Sed tres personæ divinæ unam habent essentiam, sive substantiam.

Deinde in vera unione unum vnitorum se habet per modum potentiæ, alterum per modum actus. Sic in homine, realiter composito, anima habet rationem actus perficientis, materia est instar potentiæ perfectibilis. Quæ cum dici nequeant de personis divinis, ex vero colligitur, illas non esse stricte loquendo unitas.

Instantia III.

Tres personæ divinæ aut sunt unitæ, aut non. Si prius; dabitur compositio, quia unio. Si posterius; personæ divinæ ratione essentiæ erunt diversæ, adeoque triplex admittenda erit essentia.

Resp. Personæ divinæ neque sunt unitæ, neque ratione essentiæ diversæ, sed ratione essentiæ sunt unum.

III. In quo datur essentia & relatio realis, in illo datur compositio realis. Atqui in Deo &c. Ergo.

Maior constat, quia relatio essentiæ addit peculiarem respectum, cum quo illa componitur. Minor liquet, quia in divinis, scriptura teste, datur, qui realiter est pater, & qui realiter dicitur filius. Dari ergo oportet in Deo realem paternitatem & realem filiationem, quæ sunt relationes.

Resp. Relatio hypostatica in Deo non inhæret, ut accidens essentiæ divinæ, neque ab hac realiter differt. Ergo realem non facit compositionem: distinguit quidem unam personam ab altera, sed non componit.

IV. In quo dantur accidentia, ille est compositus. Atqui in Deo dantur accidentia.

Ergo. Minor probatur, quia in Deo sunt decreta, quæ sunt accidentia.

Resp. neg. minorem; quia decreta in Deo non sunt imperfectiori modo, sed eminenter, i. e. decreta divina non sunt accidentia, sed ipsa essentia divina decernens.

Instantia I. Essentia divina est una. Decreta Dei non sunt una, sed multa.

Ergo decreta Dei non sunt ipsa essentia divina.

Resp. Decreta Dei, considerata in se, fine ordine ad obiecta, sive connotata, sunt ipsa essentia divina decernens; spectata in ordine ad diversa connotata, sive obiecta, sunt multa extra Deum.

Datur itaque multitudo decretorum divinorum, non ex parte Dei, aut in Deo, sed ex parte connotatorum, aut obiectorum.

Instantia II. Decreta sunt effectus voluntatis divinæ.


### Quest. XXVI. What is the simplicity of God?: Therefore they are not the divine essence itself

Therefore they are not the divine essence itself.

Resp. Divine decrees are not effects, but immanent acts of the divine will, which, existing within the end of the deity, are the divine essence itself perpetually active.

For to be within God, and to be able to act, do not differ.

Instant III. The divine essence is necessary. The divine decree is not necessary. Therefore. Resp. The divine decree is considered either by reason of the principle according to existence in God, or by reason of the term, insofar as it is terminated toward creatures. Divine decrees are free with respect to the free termination toward created objects: they are necessary insofar as they are intrinsic to God; for He decrees not by any accident, but immediately through His own essence . Instant IV. Divine decrees include a relation to creatures.

The divine essence does not, etc. Therefore. Resp. (α) Divine omnipotence also includes a relation to creatures, and notwithstanding this, it is the same as the divine essence. (β) Distinguish between a real relation and a relation of reason. In the same sense that the divine decree includes a relation of reason toward the outside, in that same sense the divine essence decreeing includes such a relation; although it is certain that creatures are referred more to God than God is to creatures.

V. God swears by His soul. Jer. LI, 14. Amos VI, 8. Therefore God is composite.

Resp. God, speaking properly, does not have a soul; and therefore He is said to swear by His soul, while He swears by Himself. VI. BURGERSDIJCK, the Batavian philosopher, argues: Wherever one thing is made from those things which are distinct, there some composition arises. Therefore in God there is some composition. Resp. Holy Scripture does not say that the three divine persons become one, but that they are one. 1 John V, 7. Moreover, they are one, not as a composite, but as most simple; since one divine person does not relate to another by way of passive and perfectible potency. But for true composition it is required that the component parts relate to one another, as perfectible potency and perfecting act. Instance: Passive generation is attributed to the Son of God. Therefore passive potency falls into Him. Resp. The generation of the Son of God is called passive, not because passive potency, or passion properly so-called, real or physical, falls into the Son of God, but because in the lack of another convenient word, necessity commands us to use this in so sublime a mystery. It is called passive generation grammatically, because He is said not to generate, but to be generated; although it is a most pure act, bringing in no composition, namely the most pure emanation of the λόγος from the Father.

Latin:

Ergo non sunt ipsa essentia divina.

Resp. Decreta divina non sunt effectus, sed actus immanentes voluntatis divinæ, qui, intra finem deitatis exsistentes, sunt ipsa essentia divina perpetuo actuosa.

Nam intra Deum esse, & posse operari, non differunt.

Instant. III. Essentia divina est necessaria. Decretum divinum non est necessarium. Ergo. Resp. Decretum divinum consideratur, vel ratione principii secundum existentiam in Deo, vel ratione termini, quatenus terminatur ad creaturas. Libera sunt decreta divina, quoad liberam terminationem ad obiecta creata: necessaria sunt, in quantum intrinseca sunt Deo; quippe qui non per accidens aliquod, sed immediate per suammet essentiam decernit . Instant. IV. Decreta divina includunt respectum ad creaturas.

Essentia divina non &c. Ergo. Resp. (α) Omnipotentia divina etiam includit respectum ad creaturas, & hoc non obstante eadem est cum essentia divina. (β) Disting. inter respectum realem, & rationis. Quo sensu decretum divinum ad extra respectum rationis includit, eodem sensu eiusmodi respectum includit essentia divina decernens; quamvis certum sit, quod creaturæ magis referantur ad Deum, quam Deus ad creaturas.

V. Deus iurat per animam suam. Ierem. LI, 14. Amos VI, 8. Ergo Deus est compositus.

Resp. Deus proprie loquendo non habet animam; ideoque iurare dicitur per animam, dum iurat per seipsum. VI. BURGERSDICIVS, philosophus Batavus, argumentatur: Ubicunque ex iis, quæ distincta sunt, fit unum, ibi oritur aliqua compositio. Ergo in Deo datur aliqua compositio. Resp. Sacra scriptura non dicit, quod tres personæ divinæ fiant unum, sed quod sint unum. 1 Io. V, 7. Sunt autem unum non compositum, sed simplicissimum; cum una persona divina ad alteram se non habeat per modum potentiæ passivæ & perfectibilis. Ad veram compositionem autem requiritur, ut partes componentes se invicem respiciant, ut potentia perfectibilis, & actus perficiens. Instantia: Filio Dei tribuitur generatio passiva. Ergo in illum cadit potentia passiva. Resp. Generatio filii Dei appellatur passiva, non quod potentia passiva, aut passio proprie dicta, realis, aut physica, in filium Dei cadat, sed quod in defectu alius vocis commodæ hanc in tam sublimi mysterio usurpare necessitas nos iubeat. Vocatur generatio passiva grammatice, quia non generare, sed generari dicitur; quamvis sit actus purissimus, nullam inferens compositionem, nempe purissima emanatio τοῦ λόγου ex patre.


### Quæst. XXVII. What is the truth of God?

The truth of God is the conformity of the divine essence with the divine intellect. Obf. I. The sense of the definition is: The truth of God is that by which He is truly such as He is known by Himself to be in His own nature and essence.

Obf. II. God is true both κατ' ἔσω (inwardly), or simply and in Himself, because He is true God by essence and the primary truth: and κατ' ἔξω (outwardly), because He is true in words, promises, and threats. Therefore, both essential and moral truth belong to God. Here our discourse is concerning the essential truth of God . Obf. Obs. III. Truth is of two kinds: one primary and independent, the other derived and dependent. The former is the conformity of the divine essence with the speculative and knowing intellect of God; the latter is that by which a created being corresponds with the practical and measuring intellect of God. God, therefore, is true both entitatively and independently; indeed, God is *autaletheia* [self-truth], the primary, supreme, and independent truth. He is also true exemplarily, insofar as He Himself is the archetype, idea, and norm of all truth that exists in creatures. Created things, therefore, are true only insofar as they correspond with the idea in the divine mind.

Essential truth of God.

I. From the prophetic oracle, Jer. X, 10. אֱלֹהִים אֱמֶת יהוה. The Vulgate renders it: The Lord God is true: Pagninus: The Lord God is truth. Seb. Schmidius: Jehovah (is) God (in) truth. Observe, therefore, that God is called by the prophet not only true, but truth itself, not in respect of faithfulness, because God cannot deceive, but in respect of His very essence, in that He is not a fictitious God, as the idols of the nations are mere figments, but is the true God by an independent essence, eternally living, and governing all things.

Wherefore the prophet distinguishes the true God from idols v. 8, 9, and in v. 10 adds: He is the living God and the king of the age (eternal).

II. From the apostolic utterance, 1 John V, 20, 21. We know, indeed, that the Son of God has come, and has given us a mind, that we may know the true One: and we are in the true One, in His Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life. Little children, keep yourselves from idols, Amen.

That this treats of the supreme God, who possesses a true divine and independent essence, is clear from the context, because (1) absolutely and in the nominative case He is called ὁ ἀληθινὸς θεός, that true God. But there is no true God except one who enjoys true deity, and thus a true divine essence; just as there is no true man except one who consists of true humanity, that is, a true human nature. (2) Because this true God is opposed to idols. But He is not opposed to idols and τοῖς μὴ φύσει ᾖ θεοῖς, to those who are not gods by nature, as the true God, unless He is God τῇ φύσει, by nature, and thus that one supreme God. (3) Because that true God is called eternal life, i. e., the author of eternal life.

It is evident from this apostolic utterance that both the eternal Father and the co-eternal Son are the true God. For when St. John asserts that the Son of God has come, and has given us a mind, that we may know the true One (God), he indicates that God the Father is the true God, because he immediately adds: And we are in the true One, in His Son Jesus Christ, so that he may distinguish the person of the Father, who is the true God, and at the same time indicate that the Son of God is also the true God. For this reason, he adds the most memorable words: This is the true God and eternal life.

Which words are undoubtedly to be understood of Christ. For (a) the demonstrative pronoun ὃτος ordinarily refers to and demonstrates the name immediately preceding, which here is Jesus Christ. (b) It is peculiar to John to call Christ eternal life, partly in this same epistle, ch. I, 1, ch. V, 12, 13, partly in the Gospel, ch. I, 4, ch. XI, 25, ch. XIV, 6. (c) If the demonstrative pronoun ὃτος were said to refer to the more remote name, τὸν ἀληθινὸν, a very inept tautology would emerge.

20. & 21. II. The truth of God in the intellect is the agreement of thoughts with the object, whether it exists truly or is truly possible, insofar as it is possible.

It does not fall to God to err, nor to be ignorant. Job X, 7. Acts XV, 18. Sirach XXIII, 28.

III. The truth of God in the will is the agreement of every efficacious decree and purpose with the reasons properly known and judged in the intellect. Rom. XI, 33.

IV. The truth of God in deeds is the agreement of actions with a purpose and decree, consonant with right principles and moving arguments, Ps. XXV, 10, in which place the ways of the Lord are proclaimed to be goodness and truth; but the ways are works, or actions, as means most apt for the purpose.

Cf. Ps. XXXIII, 4, in the source & Eph. I, 11.

V. The truth of God in words, which is usually called veracity, is the agreement of all words with right thought and the sentiment of the mind, and with the efficacious decree and purpose of the will, Num. XXIII, 19. 1 Sam. XV, 29. Tit. I, 2. Heb. VI, 18.

This is discerned 1) in doctrines, John XVII, 17.

2) in predictions, promises, as also in comminations. Num. XXIII, 19.

tologia: This is the true God, the true God. It remains therefore settled and fixed, that God the Father, as well as the Son of God, is truly God by nature. The apostle did not exclude the Holy Spirit, because in the same chapter, verse 7, he had asserted that the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit are one.

Latin:

Veritas Dei est conformitas essentiæ divinæ cum intellectu divino. Obs. I. Sensus definitionis est; Veritas Dei est, qua reuera talis est, qualis in sua natura & essentia esse a seipso cognoscitur.

Obs. II. Verus est Deus tum κατ' ἔσω, sive simpliciter & in se, quia ipse per essentiam verus Deus & prima veritas est: tum κατ' ἔξω, quia in verbis, promissionibus & minis verus est. Proinde competit Deo tam essentialis, quam moralis veritas. De veritate Dei essentiali hic nobis sermo est . Obs. Obs. III. Veritas alia est prima & independens, alia orta & dependens. Illa est conformitas essentiae divinae cum intellectu Dei speculativo & cognoscente: haec est, qua ens creatum congruit cum intellectu Dei practico & mensurante. Verus itaque Deus est tum entitative & independenter; quin immo Deus est αὐταλήθεια, prima, summa & independens veritas: tum exemplariter, quatenus ipse archetypum, idea & norma omnis veri est, quod datur in creaturis. Res igitur creatae hactenus sunt verae, quatenus cum idea in mente divina congruunt.

Veritas Dei essentialis prob.

I. ex oraculo prophetico, Ier. X, 10. אֱלֹהִים אֱמֶת יהוה. Vulgata reddit: Dominus Deus est verus: Pagninus: Dominus Deus est veritas. Seb. Schmidius: Iehouah (est) Deus (in) veritate. Observes igitur, quod Deus a propheta non modo verus, sed & ipsa veritas vocetur, non respectu fidelitatis, quod Deus fallere nequit, sed respectu ipsius essentiae, eo quod non est Deus fictus, sicut idola gentium mera sunt figmenta, sed est Deus verus per essentiam independentem, aeternum viventem, & omnia gubernantem.

Quapropter propheta verum Deum discernit ab idolis v. 8. 9. & v. 10. addit: Ille Deus vivus & rex seculi (sempiternus).

II. Ex effato apostolico, 1 Io. V, 20. 21. Scimus vero, quod filius Dei venerit, & dederit nobis mentem, ut cognoscamus verum: & simus in vero, in filio ipsius Iesu Christo. Hic est verus Deus & vita aeterna. Filioli, cavete vobis ab idolis, Amen.

Quod hic agatur de Deo summo, qui veram essentiam divinam & independentem habet, e contextu liquet, quia (1) absolute & in casu recto dicitur ὁ ἀληθινὸς θεός, verus ille Deus. At verus Deus non est, nisi qui vera deitate, adeoque vera divina essentia gaudet; ut verus homo non est, nisi qui vera humanitate, hoc est, vera humana natura constat. (2) Quia verus hic Deus opponitur idolis. At idolis & τοῖς μὴ φύσει ᾖ θεοῖς, his, qui natura dii non sunt, non opponitur ut verus Deus, nisi qui τῇ φύσει, natura, Deus est, adeoque unus ille summus Deus.

(3) Quia verus ille Deus vocatur vita aeterna, i. e. auctor vitae aeternae. Patet ex hoc eloquio apostolico, tam patrem aeternum, quam filium coaeternum, verum esse Deum. Nam quando S. Ioannes asserit, quod filius Dei venerit, & dederit nobis mentem, ut cognoscamus verum (Deum), indigitat, Deum patrem esse verum Deum, quia confestim addit: Et sumus in vero, in filio ipsius Iesu Christo, ut distinguat personam patris, qui est verus Deus, & simul indicet, filium Dei quoque esse verum Deum. Id propter verba memoratu dignissima annectit: Hic est verus Deus & vita aeterna.

Quae verba haud dubie de Christo intelligenda sunt. Nam (a) pronomen demonstrativum ὃτος ordinarie respicit & demonstrat nomen proxime praecedens, quod hic est Iesus Christus. (b) Peculiare est Ioanni, Christum vocare vitam aeternam, partim in hac eadem epistola, cap. I, 1. cap. V. 12. 13. partim in euangelio, cap. I, 4. cap. XI, 25. cap. XIV, 6. (c) Si pronomen demonstrativum ὃτος dicatur respicere remotius nomen, τὸν ἀληθινὸν, perquam inepta emergeret tautologia.

20. & 21. II. Veritas Dei in intellectu, est convenientia cogitationum cum obiecto, sive vere existente, sive vere possibili, quoad est possibile.

Non cadit in Deum, errare, neque ignorare. Iob. X, 7. Act.

XV, 18. Sirac. XXIII, 28. III. Veritas Dei in voluntate est convenientia decreti ac propositi efficacis cuiusque, cum rationibus in intellectu probe cognitis ac iudicatis. Rom. XI, 33.

IV. Veritas Dei in factis, est convenientia actionum cum proposito ac decreto, rectis principiis argumentisque mouentibus consentaneo, Ps. XXV, 10. quo in loco viae Domini praedicantur, quod sint bonitas ac veritas; viae autem sunt opera, sive actiones, tanquam media, ad propositum aptissima.

Conf. Ps. XXXIII, 4. in font & Ephes. I, 11.

V. Veritas Dei in dictis, quae singulatim vocari solet veracitas, est convenientia verborum omnium, cum recta cogitatione animique sententia, & efficaci voluntatis decreto ac proposito, Num. XXIII. 19. 1 Sam. XV, 29. Tit. I, 2. Hebr. VI, 18.

Haec cernitur 1) in doctrinis, Io. XVII, 17. 2) in praedictionibus, promissionibus, vt & comminationibus.

Num. XXIII, 19.

tologia: Hic verus ille Deus est verus Deus. Ratum igitur fixumque manet, tam Deum patrem, quam filium Dei, esse verum natura Deum. Spiritum S. non exclusit apostolus, quia eodem c. V, 7. assuererat, patrem, verbum & Spiritum S. esse unum.


### Q. XXVIII. What is the goodness of God?

The goodness of God is the conformity of the divine essence with the divine will.

Obs. I. The sense of the definition is: The goodness of God is that by which the divine essence is so pleased with the will of God that it loves it as the most perfect and most lovable good in an ineffable manner, and is most sweetly delighted and rests in it.

Obs. II. The goodness of God is in one sense essential, which we have already defined; in another sense it is moral, by which God is devoid of every moral vice, and is called the holiness of God.

Obs. III. Transcendental goodness is in one sense original, in another participated. The former is that by which God is good independently and by essence: the latter is that by which creatures are good dependently and by participation.

The goodness of God is proved from the speech of Christ, who addressed a certain Pharisee, who had called him a good teacher, as follows: Why do you call me good? No one is good except one, God. Matth. XIX, 17. By these words the Savior was endeavoring to convince of error the young man, who had been instructed in the Pharisaic schools, who believed that Christ was a mere man, and who was indeed seeking the way to obtain eternal life, but was fascinated by the perverse opinion that he could obtain it by his own poneros (works), or by his own deeds, intending to argue with the following reasoning: You cannot by equal right call him most singularly good whom you do not believe to be the true God, the author of eternal life. But you do not believe that I am the true God: Therefore, you can by no right call me most singularly good. Now, God is called most singularly good because (1) He is good originally and independently: creatures are good dependently and participatively, in that they participate in the goodness of God by way of a certain assimilation. (2) Efficiently, because God is the fountain and origin of every good. (3) Exemplarily, because the goodness of God is the idea and measure of all goodness that is in creatures. (4) Finally, because He is the simply supreme good, toward which, as the ultimate end, whatever is good tends. The Greeks beautifully called God agathon, autagathon, panariston; the Latins, thrice best; the Germans, Gott, as if Gut.

Since, therefore, God is the first and supreme good, it follows: (a) That God is the most communicative of all good. The communication of divine goodness is either free or necessary. The latter has a place in personal actions. Thus, God the Father communicates the whole essence to the Son by begetting, John V, 26, and the Father and the Son communicate the same essence in number to the Holy Spirit by breathing, John XVI, 14. The former concerns creatures, to whom God communicates Himself freely, either through creation, conservation, concurrence, and universal presence, Acts XIV, 17, or through grace, 1 John III, 1, or through glory, 1 Peter V, 10, Rom. VIII, 30, or through the incarnation of the Son, John III, 16. (b) That God is a fruible good, to whom we adhere with love for His own sake; we do not enjoy the world and other things, but use them, and refer their use to God as the ultimate end.

Quest. XXIX. What is the holiness of God? The holiness of God is the divine attribute by which the essence of God is most pure, most upright, and devoid of every moral vice (). Prob. ()

If we ask in general: what is holiness? It is the separation of a certain thing, its distance from the rest, with distinguished preeminence and excellence. That, indeed, is the power of the words, qadosh and

*) If we ask in general: what is holiness? It is the separation of a certain thing, distinct from the rest, with distinguished preeminence and excellence. That, indeed, is the power of the words, qadosh and God. hagios

Proof. From the song of the most pious Hannah, 1 Sam. II, 2. There is no holy one like Jehovah. No intelligent creature, no angel, no man reborn in the kingdom of grace, no blessed soul in the kingdom of glory, attains that pinnacle of holiness by which God, thrice most holy, excels. For (1) God is holy independently and by essence: creatures dependently, and by a quality superadded to their essence: (2) Immutably; since the holiness of God cannot, like that of a creature, fail or undergo change. For with the Father of lights there is no transmutation, or shadow of turning. James I, 17. The natural sun rises, sets, returns, and has its παραλλάξεις [variations]: but God, the sun of holiness, is ἀπαράλλακτος [unchanging], always the same, superior to every conversion of light and darkness, shining with immutable holiness. (3) Efficiently, because He is the author of all holiness, 1 Thess. V, 23. (4) Exemplarily, since the holiness of God is the exemplar of all holiness, which the holy children of God should perpetually contemplate and imitate. Which imitation the heavenly Father demands of them, Lev. XI, 44. I am Jehovah your God: Therefore you shall sanctify yourselves, and you shall be holy, because I am holy. Cf. Lev. XIX, 2. 1 Pet. I, 16. The holiness of the reborn corresponds to divine holiness in likeness, not in equality. (5) Objectively, because the holiness of God is to be holily acknowledged and celebrated by us. The head of our prayers is: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name! Most sweetly the choir of angels sings in harmony: Holy, holy, holy Jehovah Zebaoth! Is. VI, 3.

Latin:

Bonitas Dei est conformitas essentiae divinae cum voluntate divina.

Obs. I. Sensus definitionis est: Bonitas Dei est, qua essentia divina voluntati Dei adeo complacet, ut ipsam, tanquam perfectissimum & maxime amabile bonum, modo ineffabili amet, eademque suavissime delectetur & acquiescat.

Obs. II. Bonitas Dei alia est essentialis, quam iam definivimus; alia est moralis, qua Deus omnis vitii moralis expers est, & vocatur sanctitas Dei.

Obs. III. Bonitas transcendentalis alia est originalis, alia participata. Illa est, qua Deus independenter & per essentiam bonus est: Haec est, qua creaturae dependenter & per participationem bonae sunt.

Bonitas Dei probatur ex eloquio Christi, Pharisaeum quendam, qui ipsum bonum vocaverat magistrum, ita alloquentis: cur me dicis bonum? nullus bonus est, nisi unus Deus. Matth. XIX, 17. Quibus verbis Salvator iuvenem in scholis Pharisaicis informatum, credentem, Christum esse merum hominem, & de ratione consequendi vitam aeternam quidem quaerentem, sed perversa opinione, quod πονηρος sua, sive propriis operibus eam consequi posset, fascinatum, erroris convincere nitebatur, sequenti ratione argumentaturus: Quem non credis verum esse Deum, auctorem vitae aeternae, illum non potes aequo iure vocare singularissime bonum. Atqui non credis, me esse verum Deum: Ergo nullo iure me potes vocare singularissime bonum. Dicitur autem Deus singularissime bonus, quia (1) originaliter & independenter bonus est: creaturae bonae sunt dependenter & participative, in quantum per modum assimilationis cuiusdam de bonitate Dei participant. (2) Efficienter, quia Deus omnis boni fons & origo est. (3) Exemplariter, quia bonitas Dei idea & mensura est omnis bonitatis, quae est in creaturis. (4) Finaliter, quia est bonum simpliciter summum, ad quod tanquam finem ultimum, quidquid boni est, tendit. Pulcre Graeci Deum ἀγαθὸν, αὐταγαθὸν, πανάρισον, latini ter optimum, Germani Gott, quasi Gut, appellarunt.

Cum itaque Deus sit primum & summum bonum, consequitur: (a) Deum esse bonum omnium maxime communicativum. Communicatio autem bonitatis divinae est vel libera, vel necessaria. Posterior locum habet in actionibus personalibus. Sic Deus pater filio totam essentiam gignendo communicat, Io. V, 26. et pater & filius eandem numero essentiam spirando communicant Spiritui sancto, Io. XVI, 14 Prior respicit creaturas, quibus Deus sese communicat libere, vel per creationem, conservationem, concursum & praesentiam universalem, Act. XIV, 17. vel per gratiam, 1 Io. III, 1. vel per gloriam, 1 Petr. V, 10. Rom. VIII, 30. vel per incarnationem filii, Io. III, 16. (b) Deum esse bonum fruibile, cui propter ipsum amore inhaeremus; mundo & aliis rebus non fruimur, sed utimur, earumque usum ad Deum ceu ultimum finem referimus.

Quaest. XXIX. Quae est sanctitas Dei? Sanctitas Dei est attributum divinum, quo essentia Dei purissima, rectissima & omnis vitii moralis expers est (*). Prob. (*)

Si quaeramus in universum: quid sit sanctitas? Est separatio rei cuiusdam, a reliquis distantia, cum insigni praestantia atque excellentia. Ea nimirum est potestas verborum, קדש &

Prob. Ex cantico piissimæ Hannæ 1 Sam. II, 2. Non est sanctus, sicut Iehouah. Nulla creatura intelligens, nullus angelus, nullus homo renatus in regno gratiæ, nulla anima beata in regno gloriæ, eum assequitur sanctitatis apicem, quo eminet Deus ter sanctissimus. Nam (1) Deus sanctus est independenter & per essentiam: creaturæ dependenter, & per qualitatem essentiæ superadditam: (2) Immutabiliter; siquidem sanctitas Dei haud perinde, ac creaturæ, deficere, aut vicissitudinem subire potest. Nam apud patrem luminum non est transmutatio, aut conuersionis (vel) vmbra. Iac. I, 17. Sol naturalis oritur, occidit, recidit, suasque habet παραλλάξεις: at Deus, sol sanctitatis, est ἀπαράλλακτος, semper idem, omni conuersione lucis & tenebrarum superior, incommutabili refulgens sanctitate. (3) Efficienter, quia omnis sanctitatis auctor est, 1 Thess. V, 23. (4) Exemplariter, quoniam sanctitas Dei est exemplar omnis sanctitatis, quod sancti Dei filii perpetuo intueantur & imitentur. Quam imitationem pater cœlestis ab ipsis exigit, Leu. XI, 44. Ego Iehouah Deus vester: Ideo sanctificabitis vos, eritisque sancti, quia ego sanctus. Conf. Leu. XIX, 2. 1 Petr. I, 16. Renatorum sanctitas respondet sanctitati diuinæ similitudine, non æqualitate. (5) Obiectiue, quia sanctitas Dei sancte a nobis est agnoscenda & celebranda. Precum nostrarum caput est: Pater noster, qui es in cœlis, sanctificetur nomen tuum! Suauissime concinit angelorum chorus: Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus Iehouah Zebaoth! Es. VI, 3.


### Q. XXVIII. What is the goodness of God?: Question XXX. What is the infinity of God?

Question XXX. What is the infinity of God?

Infinity is a divine attribute, through which the essence and perfections of God have no limits.

Proof. I. From Ps. CXLV, 3. Great is Jehovah, and greatly to be praised, and of his greatness there is no searching. The Vulgate indeed rendered it: of his greatness there is no end: but the Hebrew word חקר properly denotes scrutiny, or investigation. The king of prophets proclaims the greatness of God, and understands not the greatness of mass; which, since it has matter as its root, does not fall upon God; but the greatness of perfection. Therefore the sense is: All labor is spent in vain, which is expended in circumscribing the essence and setting limits to the divine perfection. For no one by searching will find an end where the majesty of Jehovah ceases and fails. Therefore the essence and perfection of God is absolutely infinite, because His greatness is unsearchable.

II. From the independence of God. Whatever essence is independent, it acknowledges no cause from which it could be enclosed by limits. But the divine essence is independent. Therefore.

III. From the absolute perfection of God. Whoever is of such perfection that he is the purest act, excluding all passive potency, he does not suffer that limits be placed upon his essence and perfection. But God, etc. Therefore.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians and Arminians, some of whom doubt the infinity of God, some deny it, to whom Vorstius is added. We shall consider their stronger arguments.

ON THE INFINITY OF GOD. 247

I. That which nature abhors is nowhere given. But nature abhors the infinite: Therefore the infinite is nowhere given, and consequently God is not infinite. Resp. Nature abhors the infinite that is such by reason of quantitative extension, not that which is infinite by reason of essence and perfection.

II. Whoever can be seen is not infinite, because he is terminated by sight. But God &c. Therefore. The minor is proved, because God has often been seen by men who are wayfarers, Is. VI, 1. Dan. VII, 13. In the heavenly fatherland we shall see God face to face. I Cor. XIII, 12. Resp. God was seen by men who are wayfarers not in essence, but in the economy of manifestation; but how we shall see Him in the fatherland, the heavenly school will teach.

III. Whoever is absolutely infinite is not knowable. God is knowable. Therefore God is not infinite. The major is proved, because between a knowing faculty and a knowable object there must indeed be a proportion; which is not given between the infinite and the finite. Resp. Distinguish between mathematical proportion in being and intentional proportion in knowing. Although between a finite intellect and the infinite God there is no mathematical proportion in being, there is nevertheless an intentional proportion in knowing; which, although it may not be adequate, it suffices that we know the infinite God insofar as He has manifested Himself to us.

IV. The power of God is not infinite: Therefore neither is the essence of God. The antecedent is proved, because the power of God does not extend to impossibilities. Resp. For the infinity of divine power it is not required that it extend to impossibilities: for it suffices that it extends to infinite possibilities. No power is concerned with the impossible, since this regards only the possible.

V. If God is an infinite good, there will be no evil in the nature of things. The consequent is false. Therefore the antecedent also. The consequence of the major is proved; because if one of the opposites is infinite, it will utterly destroy the other opposite, on account of its infinity. Resp. I deny the consequence. For this alone follows, that just as God is infinitely good: so there is no evil in God. Indeed, infinite goodness in God excludes all evil from Him.

VI. If God is of infinite perfection, all creatures will be equally perfect. The consequent is false. Therefore the antecedent also. The consequence of the major is proved, because a creature is said to be more or less perfect according to how much more or less it is distant from the perfection of God. But if the perfection of God is infinite, all the perfections of creatures will be infinitely distant from it, and thus equally so. Now, if all the perfections of creatures are equally distant from the perfection of the creator, they will be equal. Resp. The perfections of creatures are judged not only from the general distance from the infinite perfection of God, but also from the more or fewer degrees of perfection which each creature receives from God: with respect to which degrees one creature approaches closer to God than another.

VII. God is "this something" (hoc aliquid). Therefore He is not actually infinite. The reason for the consequence is that τὸ τί, "this something," is singular, distinguished by a certain peculiar perfection which is not given in others. But whatever is of infinite perfection contains all perfections in itself, and thus cannot be distinguished from others. Resp. It is not repugnant to be "this something" and yet contain all perfections in oneself. For by infinity itself God is distinguished from creatures, and He contains some of their perfections formally, and some eminently, or virtually, in Himself. *

VIII. God is defined.* Therefore He is not infinite. The consequence is proved, because definition is derived from "finishing" (finire), and thus denotes the boundaries of an essence. Resp. The consequence is denied. For a definition, or logical description, which is called ὁρισμὸς τῆς οὐσίας (definition of essence), is one thing, because it presents the nature of a thing to our mind; but a description of an essence made by certain ends and limits, by which a finite being is physically defined, is another. physically, or metaphysically, and is opposed to the infinite being. God is indeed described logically, but he is not defined physically.

XXXI. What is the eternity of God? Eternity is the interminable and permanent duration of the divine essence. Obs. The word eternity is πολύσημος [polysemous], sustaining diverse significations.

(1) It denotes a temporary duration, not interrupted in the course of many years, which is also called periodic eternity. Thus circumcision is called an eternal covenant, Gen. XVII, 13. (2) The word eternity designates a duration which indeed has a beginning, but not an end, in the way that the life of the blessed and the death of the damned is called eternal; which eternity is not absolute, but restricted and limited. (3) It denotes absolute eternity, i. e., an interminable duration, devoid of beginning and end, as well as permanent, or continuous, which excludes all succession of present, past, and future whatsoever.

Three things, therefore, must be proven: (a) That God is eternal: (b) That the divine eternity has neither beginning nor end: (c) That absolute eternity excludes all succession or vicissitude of time. Prob. a.

(1) Because God in scripture is called אֵל עוֹלָם, God of eternity, Gen. XXI, 33. cf. Is. XL, 28. inhabiting eternity, Is. LVII, 15. αἰώνιος θεός, Rom. XVI, 26. βασιλεὺς τῶν αἰώνων, king of the ages incorruptible, 1 Tim. I, 17.

(2) Whoever is not eternal, at some time was not. But God was not at some time not. Therefore God is eternal. The minor is evident, because he who at some time was not, was produced by another. But God was not produced by another, because he is the first and independent being.

Prob. b. (1) God is called the first and the last, Is. LXI, 4. the beginning and the end, Apoc. XXI, 6. Alpha and Omega, Apoc. I, 8.

The mercy of God is said to endure from eternity to eternity, Ps. CIII, 17. (2) That God, from the part before, is interminable, Moses teaches Ps. XC, 2. Before the mountains were born, and the earth and the world were formed; and from eternity to eternity thou (art) God. That he lacks an end, the sacred singer asserts Ps.

CII, 28. Thy years shall not be consumed. Prob. c.

That absolute eternity is permanent, or continuous, is clearly evident (1) because eternity, since it is a divine attribute, is in respect of the thing God himself, who is not changed, Mal. III, 6. with whom there is no shadow of transmutation or conversion, Jas. I, 17. Therefore eternity is not subject to the mutation of times.

(2) A thousand years could not be like one day, Ps. XC, 5. 2 Pet. III, 8. if the eternity of God were successive.

(3) The whole duration of God is the perpetual הַיּוֹם, today, without a νῦν [now] and an immobile and immutable instant, Ps. II, 7. From which BOETHIUS, book V of the Consolation of Philosophy, prose VI, defines eternity as the interminable life's whole at once, and perfect possession. Eternity is said to be whole at once, not by reason of parts, since it has none, but to deny the succession of moments.

There is an antithesis of the Socinians, to whom Vorstius in most things assents, who maintain, 1) not only that God is eternal, 2) that eternity is successive, and therefore consists in the flux of prior and posterior: who rely on the following arguments: I. I. Whoever dwells eternally, he has a coeternal dwelling.

But God &c.

Is.

LVII, 5.

Therefore, I answer with the words of AUGUSTINE Ps. CXXII.

Someone says: Before God made the saints, where did He dwell?

God dwelt in Himself, He dwelt with Himself, and God is with Himself.

Objection: God is said to inhabit light inaccessible 1 Tim.

VI, 26.

Therefore a certain light, surrounding God, was coeternal to Him.

Resp.

The inaccessible light is the incomprehensible majesty of God.

But the majesty of God is God Himself.

From which God Himself is called light 1 Jn.

I, 6.

II. Whatever is not made, that is eternal.

Time is not made.

Therefore time is eternal.

The major premise is evident; because whatever is not made, that is uncreated.

But an uncreated being is eternal.

The minor premise is proven; because if time were made, the present would also have been made.

But if the present had been made, it would have been made in the present, and thus there would have been time before time, and a process into infinity would occur.

Resp.

Creation, by reason of its term, is a substantial action, and thus terminates in the creation of a substance, not an accident; such as time is.

Meanwhile, present time was created together with the first body, and began to exist with the same.

III. Every duration has a before and an after, and thus parts succeeding one another.

But eternity is a duration.

Therefore.

Resp.

I distinguish between a defectible duration, which has parts succeeding one another, and an indefectible one, which, as the thing itself, is the divine essence itself, devoid of all parts.

IV. Whatever duration is not like a moment, that is not indivisible into differences of time.

But eternity is not like a moment.

Therefore.

The major premise is certain, since a moment is indivisible into differences of time.

Resp. I distinguish between a fixed moment and a flowing one, or standing and flowing.

Eternity is conceived as a moment; since it is indivisible, and is conceived as a whole simultaneously as a standing or fixed moment; because it does not have parts succeeding one another.

You say: whatever lasts for a moment is not constant.

Resp.

Eternity lasts not in one, but in every moment.

V. Whatever duration contains all differences of time within itself, that is not permanent.

But eternity &c.

Therefore.

The minor premise is proven because the eternal God is described as being ὁ ὢν, καὶ ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος, who is, and who was, and who is to come, Rev.

I, 4.

Resp.

1) Eternity contains all times within itself not formally, by admitting the succession of prior and posterior within itself, but eminently, or by excess; because it is not constituted by times, but exceeds and transcends them, although it coexists with them.

2) S.

St. John indeed describes the eternal God through differences of time, anthropopathically, in a human manner, because the Holy Spirit accommodates Himself to the grasp of men, who can hardly conceive of any duration without parts succeeding one another: however, the words of scripture are to be understood theoprepically, in a manner befitting God.

Confer.

Ps.

XC, 5.

2 Pet.

III, 8.

3) If the differences of time described by John are taken collectively, the continuity or permanence of the divine duration is delineated by that phrase of scripture.

For whatever being is whole simultaneously in the present, past, and future, that has a continuous duration.

VI. If eternity is whole simultaneously, and coexists with all differences of time, namely present, past, and future, all these differences of time will coexist with one another, and there will be no distinction of time.

The latter is false.

Therefore the former is too.

The consequence of the major premise is proven; because if eternity as a whole simultaneously coexists with all differences of time, and these coexist with the whole of eternity, they certainly meet in the point of eternity, and thus are coeternal and perpetually coexist.

Resp.

I deny the consequence.

For the whole of eternity coexists with all differences of time not jointly, but divisively, or taken separately, e.g.

The whole of eternity simultaneously coexists with the present day. but divisively, or taken separately, e.g.

The whole of eternity simultaneously coexists

today, and will coexist with tomorrow. But from this it is not permitted to infer that today and tomorrow coexist. For just as the whole heaven coexisted with Abraham, the whole likewise with Isaac, the whole also with Jacob, and the whole with their descendants; yet it does not follow from this that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob coexisted with one another: so it does not follow, because the differences of times meet in the point of eternity; therefore they meet with one another. Certainly lines meet in the center, and yet they differ in the periphery: the center is at rest, with the lines drawn successively.

VII. If the eternity of God exists wholly at any given moment, everything that does not exist at a moment will be eternal. The consequent is false. Therefore the antecedent is also. The reason for the consequence is that in this respect it agrees with eternity, that it exists at a moment. Resp. I distinguish between that which coexists with eternity adequately and commensurably, and that which coexists inadequately and in a more imperfect mode. Whatever exists at one moment, that coexists with eternity, but inadequately; for this exists wholly at once at every moment.

VIII. If in eternity there is no given prior or posterior, at the same moment that God created the world, he would destroy it. The latter is absurd. Therefore there is a prior. Resp. God created the world not in eternity, but in time, in which there is a flow of prior and posterior.

Instance: When the world was first being created, there was no time, but eternity. Resp. When the world was being created, time did not pre-exist, but coexisted, since it was co-created with the world, and began to be with the first origin.

IX. The space of time during which the eternal God has endured, that has passed: and that during which he will endure, that has not yet come. Therefore there is a prior and posterior in the eternity of God. Resp. Those vicissitudes of prior time are in our intellect, which we consider eternity according to coexistence with the differences of time, but they are not in God, who is devoid of all vicissitude or mutation .

Latin:

Quæst. XXX. Quæ est infinitas Dei?

Infinitas est attributum diuinum, per quod essentia & perfectiones Dei nullos habent terminos.

Prob. I. e Ps. CXLV, 3. Magnus (est) Iehouah, & laudabilis valde, & magnitudinis eius non (est) inuestigatio. Vulgata quidem reddidit: magnitudinis eius non est finis: at vox hebræa חקר proprie scrutationem, aut peruestigationem notat. Magnitudinem Dei deprædicat rex prophetarum, & intelligit non magnitudinem molis; quæ cum radicem habeat materiam, in Deum non cadit; sed magnitudinem perfectionis. Proinde sensus est: Frustra insumitur omnis labor, qui circumscribendæ essentiæ, figendisque perfectioni diuinæ limitibus impenditur. Nemo quippe scrutando inueniet finem, vbi desinat deficiatque maiestas Iehouæ. Est itaque essentia & perfectio Dei absolute infinita, quia magnitudo eius est imperuestigabilis.

II. Ex independentia Dei. Quæcunque essentia est independens, illa nullam agnoscit caussam, a qua finibus includi queat. Atqui essentia diuina est independens. Ergo.

III. Ex absoluta Dei perfectione. Quicunque tantæ perfectionis est, vt purissimus sit actus, omnem excludens potentiam passiuam, ille non patitur, vt essentiæ & perfectioni suæ ponantur limites. Atqui Deus &c. Ergo.

Antithesis est Socinianorum & Arminianorum, quorum nonnulli de infinitate Dei dubitant, nonnulli eandem negant, quibus accedit Vorstius. Potiora eorundem argumenta considerabimus.

DE INFINITATE DEI. 247

I. A quo abhorret natura, illud nullibi datur. Atqui ab infinito abhorret natura: Ergo infinitum nullibi datur, & consequenter nec Deus est infinitus. Resp. Natura abhorret ab infinito, quod tale est ratione quantitatiuae extensionis, non ab eo, quod est infinitum ratione essentiae & perfectionis.

II. Quicunque potest videri, ille non est infinitus, quia terminatur visu. Atqui Deus &c. Ergo. Minor probatur, quia Deus ab hominibus viatoribus saepe est visus, Es. VI, 1. Dan. VII, 13. In patria coelesti Deum a facie ad faciem visuri sumus. I Cor. XIII, 12. Resp. Visus est Deus ab hominibus viatoribus non in essentia, sed in manifestationis oeconomia; quomodo autem in patria ipsum visuri fimus, schola coelestis docebit.

III. Quicunque absolute infinitus est, ille non est cognoscibilis. Deus est cognoscibilis. Ergo Deus non est infinitus. Maior probatur, quia inter facultatem cognoscentem & obiectum cognoscibile debet quidem esse proportio; quae inter infinitum, & finitum non datur. Resp. dist. inter proportionem mathematicam in essendo, & intentionalem in cognoscendo. Quamuis inter intellectum finitum, & Deum infinitum non detur proportio mathematica in essendo, datur tamen proportio intentionalis in cognoscendo; quae licet non sit adaequata, sufficit tamen, quod in tantum Deum infinitum cognoscamus, in quantum se nobis manifestauit.

IV. Potentia Dei non est infinita: Ergo nec essentia Dei. Antecedens probatur, quia potentia Dei non extendit ad impossibilia. Resp. Ad infinitatem potentiae diuinae non requiritur, vt se extendat ad impossibilia: sufficit enim, quod se ad infinita possibilia extendat. Circa impossibile non versatur vlla potentia, cum haec possibile tantum respiciat.

V. Si Deus est bonum infinitum, nullum erit malum in rerum natura. Consequens est falsum. Ergo & antecedens, Consequentia maioris probatur; quia si vnum oppositorum est infinitum, alterum oppositum penitus destruet, ob infinitatem suam. Resp. neg. consequentiam. Hoc enim solum sequitur, quod sicut Deus infinite bonus est: ita in Deo non fit vllum malum. Infinita quippe bonitas in Deo omne ab ipso malum excludit.

VI. Si Deus infinitae est perfectionis, omnes creaturae erunt aequaliter perfectae. Consequens est falsum. E. & antecedens. Consequentia maioris probatur, quia creatura dicitur magis vel minus perfecta, prout magis vel minus distat a perfectione Dei. Sed si perfectio Dei est infinita, omnes perfectiones creaturarum ab ea distabunt infinite, atque adeo aequaliter. Iam vero si omnes perfectiones creaturarum aequaliter distant a perfectione creatoris, erunt aequales. Resp. Perfectiones creaturarum non tantum diiudicantur ex generali distantia ab infinita perfectione Dei, sed etiam e pluribus vel paucioribus gradibus perfectionis, quos quaelibet creatura a Deo accipit: quorum graduum respectu vna creatura propius ad Deum accedit, quam altera.

VII. Deus est hoc aliquid. Ergo non est actu infinitus. Ratio consequentiae est, quia τὸ τί, hoc aliquid, est singulare, peculiari quadam perfectione, quae non datur in aliis, distinctum. At quidquid est infinitae perfectionis, omnes in se continet perfectiones, adeoque ab aliis distingui nequit. Resp. Non repugnat, esse hoc aliquid, & tamen omnes in se continere perfectiones. Nam per ipsam infinitudinem Deus distinguitur a creaturis, earumque perfectiones nonnullas formaliter, nonnullas eminenter, seu virtualiter, in se continet. *

VIII. Deus definitur.* Ergo non est infinitus. Consequentia probatur, quia definitio a finiendo derivatur, adeoque fines essentiae notat. Resp. Negatur consequ. Aliud enim est definitio, seu descriptio logica, quae ὁρισμὸς τῆς οὐσίας dicitur, quod sistat naturam rei menti nostrae; aliud vero essentiae certis finibus & limitibus facta descriptio, qua ens finitum dicitur physice. aut metaphysice, & enti infinito opponitur. Deus logice quidem describitur, sed physice non definitur.

XXXI. Quae est aeternitas Dei? Aeternitas est interminabilis & permanens essentiae divinae duratio. Obs. Vox aeternitas est πολύσημος, diversas sustinens significationes.

(1) Notat temporariam durationem, multorum annorum decursu non interruptam, quae etiam vocatur aeternitas periodica. Sic circumcisio appellatur foedus aeternum, Gen. XVII, 13. (2) Designat vox aeternitas durationem, quae quidem initium, non autem finem habet, quomodo beatorum vita & damnatorum mors aeterna dicitur; quae aeternitas non absoluta, sed restricta & limitata est. (3) Notat aeternitatem absolutam, i. e. durationem interminabilem, principii & finis expertem, iuxta atque permanentem, sive continuam, quae omnem omnino successionem praesentis, praeteriti, & futuri excludit.

Tria itaque probanda sunt: (a) Deum esse aeternum: (b) Aeternitatis divinae neque initium, neque finem esse: (c) Aeternitatem absolutam omnem successionem aut vicissitudinem temporis excludere. Prob. a.

(1) Quia Deus in scriptura vocatur אֵל עוֹלָם, Deus aeternitatis, Gen. XXI, 33. conf. Es. XL, 28. aeternum habitans, Es. LVII, 15. αἰώνιος θεός, Rom. XVI, 26. βασιλεὺς τῶν αἰώνων, rex saeculorum incorruptibilis, 1 Tim. I, 17.

(2) Quicunque non est aeternus, aliquando non fuit. Atqui Deus non aliquando non fuit. Ergo Deus est aeternus. Minor patet, quia qui aliquando non fuit, ab alio est productus. Sed Deus ab alio non est productus, quia est ens primum & independens.

Prob. b. (1) Deus vocatur primus & novissimus, Es. LXI, 4. principium & finis, Apoc. XXI, 6. A & Ω, Apoc. I, 8.

Misericordia Dei dicitur durare ab aeterno in aeternum. Ps. CIII, 17. (2) Quod Deus, a parte ante, sit interminabilis, docet Moses Ps. XC, 2. Antequam montes nati sunt, & formata est terra & orbis; & ab aeterno usque in aeternum tu (es) Deus.

Quod careat fine, asserit Hieropsaltes Ps. CII, 28. Anni tui non consumentur.

Prob. c. Aeternitatem absolutam esse permanentem, sive continuam, liquido constat (1) quia aeternitas, cum sit attributum divinum, ex parte rei est ipse Deus, qui non mutatur, Mal. III, 6. apud quem non est transmutationis aut conversionis vmbra, Iac. I, 17.

Ergo aeternitas temporum mutationi non est obnoxia. (2) Mille anni non possent esse instar vnius diei, Ps. XC, 5. 2 Petr.

III, 8. si aeternitas Dei foret successiva. (3) Tota Dei duratio, est perpetuum הַיּוֹם, hodie, sine νῦν ac instans immobile & immutabile, Ps. II, 7. Ex quo BOETIVS libr.

V. de consol. philosoph. prof. VI. definituit aeternitatem, quod sit interminabilis vitae tota simul, & perfecta possessio. Dicitur aeternitas tota simul, non ratione partium, quippe quas non habet, sed ad negandam successionem momentorum. Antithesis est Socinianorum, quibus in plerisque adstipulatur Vorstius, statuentium, 1) non solum Deum aeternum esse, 2) aeternitatem esse successivam, atque adeo constare fluxu prioris & posterioris: qui sequentibus innituntur argumentis: I. I. Quicunque aeternum habitat, ille habet coaeternum domicilium.

Atqui Deus &c.

Es.

LVII, 5.

Ergo, Respondeo verbis AVGVSTINI Ps. CXXII.

Dicit aliquis: Antequam Deus faceret sanctos, ubi habitabat?

In se habitabat Deus, apud se habitabat, & apud se est Deus.

Instantia Deus dicitur inhabitare lucem inaccessibilem 1 Tim.

VI, 26.

Ergo lux quaedam, circumfusa Deo, coeterna ipsi fuit.

Resp.

Lux inaccessibilis est incomprehensibilis Dei maiestas.

At maiestas Dei est ipse Deus.

Ex quo Deus ipse lux dicitur 1 Io.

I, 6.

II. Quodcunque non est factum, illud est aeternum.

Tempus non est factum.

Ergo tempus est aeternum.

Maior patet; quia quidquid non est factum, illud est increatum.

Sed ens increatum est aeternum.

Minor probatur; quia si tempus esset factum, etiam praesens esset factum.

Si autem praesens fuisset factum, factum fuisset in praesenti, & sic fuisset tempus ante tempus, fieretque processus in infinitum.

Resp.

Creatio ratione termini est actio substantialis, adeoque terminatur ad creationem substantiae, non accidentis; quale est tempus.

Tempus interim praesens cum primo corpore concreatum est, & cum eodem esse incepit.

III. Omnis duratio habet prius & posterius, adeoque partes sibi succedentes.

Atqui aeternitas est duratio.

Ergo.

Resp.

Distinguo inter durationem defectibilem, quae partes sibi succedentes habet, & indefectibilem, quae, qua rem ipsam, est ipsa essentia diuina, omnium partium expers.

IV. Quaecunque duratio non est instar momenti, illa non est indiuisibilis in temporum differentias.

Atqui aeternitas non est instar momenti.

Ergo.

Maior constat, quoniam momentum est indiuisibile in temporum differentias.

Resp. dist. inter momentum fixum, & fluxum, siue stans, & fluens.

Concipitur aeternitas vt momentum; quoniam est indiuisibilis, & tota simul concipitur vt momentum stans, siue fixum; quia non habet partes, sibi succedentes.

Dicis: quidquid momento durat, non est constans.

Resp.

Aeternitas non vno, sed omni momento durat.

V. Quaecunque duratio omnes temporis differentias in se continet, illa non est permanens.

Atqui aeternitas &c.

Ergo.

Minor prob. quia aeternus Deus describitur, quod sit ὁ ὢν, καὶ ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος, qui est, & qui erat, & qui venturus est, Apoc.

I, 4.

Resp.

1) Aeternitas omnia tempora in se continet non formaliter, successionem prioris & posterioris in se adinittendo, sed eminenter, siue per excessum; quia ex temporibus non constituitur, sed ea excedit & supergreditur, quamuis iisdem coexixtat.

2) S.

S. Ioannes describit quidem aeternum Deum per temporis differentias, ἀνθρωποπαθῶς, more humano, propterea, quod Spiritus S. se accommodat ad captum hominum, qui vix possunt ullam concipere durationem, sine partibus, sibi succedentibus: intelligenda autem sunt verba scripturae θεοπρεπῶς, modo Deo conuenienti.

Confer.

Ps.

XC, 5.

2 Petr.

III, 8.

3) Si descriptae a Ioanne temporis differentiae sumantur collectiue, continuitas, siue permanentia durationis diuinae, ea scripturae phrasi delineatur.

Nam quodcunque ens totum simul est in praesenti, praeterito & futuro, illud habet durationem continuam.

VI. Si aeternitas est tota simul, & coexistit omnibus temporum differentiis, nempe praesenti, praeterito & futuro, omnes hae temporum differentiae sibi coexistent, neque ullum temporis discrimen erit.

Posterius est falsum.

Ergo & prius.

Consequentia maioris probatur; quia si aeternitas tota simul coexistit omnibus temporis differentiis, & hae toti aeternitati coexistunt, vtique in puncto aeternitatis coeunt, adeoque coaeternae sunt & perpetuo coexistunt.

Resp.

Neg. consequ.

Nam tota aeternitas coexistit omnibus temporum differentiis non coniunctim, sed diuisim, siue seorsim sumtis, v. gr.

Aeternitas tota simul coexistit hodierno. sed diuisim, siue seorsim sumtis, v. gr.

Æternitas tota simul coëxistit

hodierno die, & coëxistet crastino. At exinde inferre non licet, hodiernum & crastinum diem coëxistere. Nam sicut totum cœlum coëxtitit Abrahamo, totum itidem Isaaco, totum quoque Iacobo, totum eorum posteris; neque tamen ex eo sequitur, Abrahamum, Isaacum & Iacobum sibi coëxtitisse: ita non sequitur, quia temporum differentiæ in puncto æternitatis coëunt; ergo inuicem coëunt. Certe lineæ coëunt in centro, & tamen differunt in peripheria: centrum quiescit, lineis successiue ductis.

VII. Si æternitas Dei quouis momento tota existit, omne, quod non momento existit, æternum erit. Consequens est falsum. Ergo & antecedens. Ratio consequentiæ est, quia hac in parte cum æternitate conuenit, quod in momento existat. Resp. Dist. inter id, quod adæquate & commensurabiliter æternitati coëxistit, & quod coëxistit inadæquate & imperfectiori modo. Quidquid existit vno momento, illud coëxistit æternitati, sed inadæquate; hæc enim tota simul existit omni momento.
