VIII. Si in æternitate non datur prius aut posterius, eodem momento, quo Deus mundum condidit, eundem destruet. Posterius est absurdum. Ergo est prius. Resp. Deus condidit mundum non in æternitate, sed in tempore, in quo datur fluxus prioris & posterioris.

Instantia: Cum mundus primum conderetur, non erat tempus, sed æternitas. Resp. Cum mundus conderetur, non præexistebat, sed coëxistebat tempus, siquidem cum mundo est concreatum, & cum prima origine esse incepit.

IX. Quo temporis spatio Deus æternus durauit, illud præteriit: & quo durabit, illud nondum venit. Ergo datur in æternitate Dei prius & posterius. Resp. Illæ vicissitudines prioris temporis sunt in nostro intellectu, quæ æternitatem secundum coëxistentiam ad temporis differentias consideramus, sed non sunt in Deo, omnis vicissitudinis, aut mutationis experte .


### Q. XXVIII. What is the goodness of God?: What is the immensity of God?

What is the immensity of God? Immensity is a divine attribute, according to which the essence of God cannot be circumscribed by any limits of place, but is understood to exist everywhere. Obs.

I. God is called immense not locally, because He is not contained by any spaces of places; but illocally, as He is within all things, but not included; outside all things, but not excluded, as ISIDORE says in book

I. sent. de S.B. cap. II.

God is called immense not extensively, as air is extended most widely: not inclusively, as the heaven includes sublunary bodies: not commixtively, as in the atmosphere things are mixed with air: not diffusively, through a diffusion conformable to a body, just as the sea is diffused most widely (although it is explained by some theologians through the diffusion of the divine essence, conformable to a spirit. See OSIANDER in colleg. system. part. I. p. 329.) but through an interminable ubiquity.

Obs.

II. The immediate consequence of divine immensity is the power of being present illocally to all places whatsoever; which belongs to God by way of an essential attribute from eternity.

The remote consequence, however, is actual omnipresence, by which God is actually present to all creatures. Obs. III. Divine immensity and the power of being present (which is also called the majesty of omnipresence) differ: 1) As antecedent and consequent: 2) The immensity of God is a negative attribute, the majesty of omnipresence is an affirmative attribute.

3) Immensity is an ἀνενεργητικόν (non-active) attribute, the majesty of omnipresence is an ἐνεργητικόν (active) attribute. 4) Immensity flows from the spirituality and infinity of God according to our mode of conceiving: the power of being present everywhere emanates from the immensity and omnipotence of God. Obs. IV. Divine immensity and actual omnipresence differ.

1) Immensity is a divine attribute: actual omnipresence is the effect of certain divine attributes (immensity, the power of being present, omnipotence, and the most free divine will). 2) Immensity is an absolute property: omnipresence, however, involves a relation to creatures, to whom God is present. 3) Immensity formally introduces no operation: omnipresence, however, is always operative. 4) Immensity is eternal, actual omnipresence began at that time when heaven and earth were first created. 5) Immensity is one: omnipresence, however, has many degrees and modes: 6) Immensity is absolutely necessary: omnipresence is free, and not necessary except by hypothesis, viz., once creatures have been posited, to each of which God is present as long as He wills.

For if God were to command creatures to fall back into nothingness, He would not be present to them. 7) Omnipresence is restricted to creatures which are contained by the compass of this world: Immensity extends itself beyond the world, beyond the highest heaven, and infinitely.

Conf. D. CALOV. system. tom. II. p. 613.

Prob. The immensity of God 1) from the royal utterance of Solomon, 1 Kings VIII, 27. For will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold! the heavens and the heavens of heavens do not contain thee: much less this house which I have built.

From which we argue: He whom neither the earth nor the heavens of heavens contain, he is absolutely immense. But God [is such], etc. Therefore. The major is evident, because by the phrase of Scripture "earth and heaven," whenever they are joined, they designate the entire machinery of the world. Whatever truly exists, and is not contained by the machinery of the world, but exceeds the circuit of the heaven, that is absolutely immense. VORSTIUS objects 1) That this saying does not validly confirm the immensity of God; for the reason that King Solomon asks: Will God indeed dwell on the earth?

Which interrogation has the force of denying, and thus Solomon denies that God dwells on the earth. But if God does not dwell on the earth, He is not everywhere, and if He is not everywhere, He is not absolutely immense. 2) The Hebrew word יכלכל does not mean: they contain or comprehend, but they will sustain.

Luther himself rendered it in German:

provides: to provide, and thus it is not immensity, but the all-sufficiency or blessedness of God that is expressed by that word. Resp. to I. God does not dwell upon the earth locally, so as to be contained by it. To II. The primary signification of the root is to contain or to comprehend. Cf. 1 Kings 8:27, which the same word retains here, since it is evident from the preceding and following context that the discourse is about the indwelling or habitation of God. Therefore, the wisest of kings pointed out that not even the vast structure of the world is equal to containing God.

2) From the spirituality and infinity of God. No infinite spirit can be defined by the limits of places or any "where." But God is a spirit, John 4:24, and infinite, Ps. 145:3. The major premise is proved, because 1) only a quantitative body is circumscribed by the limits of places, but no spirit, neither created nor uncreated, is so circumscribed. 2) Created spirits are in a determinable "where," and thus a definitive one, because of the finitude of their essence. But since the spiritual essence of God is infinite and interminable, His "whereness" (vbietas) is also interminable; for it is, in reality, the same as the divine essence.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, some of whom deny the immensity of God entirely, while others doubt it. Since their arguments are so constructed that they strike properly and directly at the divine omnipresence, we shall consider them below, where we are to treat of the presence of God.

Latin:

Quæ est immensitas Dei? Immensitas est attributum divinum, secundum quod essentia Dei nullis locorum terminis circumscribi potest, sed ubique exsistere intelligitur. Obs.

I. Immensus dicitur Deus non localiter, quia nullis locorum spatiis continetur; sed illocaliter, vt fit intra omnia, sed non inclusus, extra omnia, sed non exclusus, dicente ISIDORO libr.

I. sent. de S.B. cap. II.

Immensus dicitur Deus non extense, vt aër latissime extenditur: non inclusive, vt cœlum corpora sublunaria includit: non commixtive, vt in atmosphæra aëri sunt commixta: non diffuse, per diffusionem corpori conformem, sicut mare latissime diffunditur (quamuis a nonnullis theologis explicetur per diffusionem essentiæ divinæ, spiritui conformem. Vid. OSIANDER in colleg. system. part. I. p. 329.) sed per vbietatem interminabilem.

Obs.

II. Consequens immediatum immensitatis divinæ est potentia illocaliter adessendi omnibus omnino vbi; quæ Deo competit per modum attributi essentialis ab æterno.

Consequens vero remotum est actualis omnipræsentia, qua Deus omnibus creaturis actu adest. Obs. III. Differunt immensitas divina, & potentia adessendi (quæ etiam maiestas omnipræsentiæ vocatur): 1) Vt antecedens & consequens: 2) Immensitas Dei est attributum negativum, maiestas omnipræsentiæ est attributum affirmativum.

3) Immensitas est attributum ἀνενεργητικόν, maiestas omnipræsentiæ est attributum ἐνεργητικόν. 4) Immensitas ex spiritualitate & infinitate Dei secundum nostrum concipiendi modum fluit: potentia vbique adessendi ex immensitate & omnipotentia Dei emanat. Obs. IV. Immensitas divina, & actualis omnipræsentia, differunt.

1) Immensitas est attributum divinum: actualis omnipræsentia est certorum attributorum divinorum (immensitatis, potentiæ adessendi, omnipotentiæ, liberrimæque voluntatis divinæ) effectus. 2) Immensitas est proprietas absoluta: omnipræsentia vero involuit respectum ad creaturas, quibus Deus præsto est. 3) Immensitas formaliter nullam infert operationem: omnipræsentia autem semper est operosa. 4) Immensitas est æterna, omnipræsentia actualis cœpit eo tempore, quo cœlum & terra primitus sunt condita. 5) Immensitas est vna: omnipræsentia autem plures sunt gradus & modi: 6) Immensitas est absolute necessaria: omnipræsentia est libera, & non nisi ex hypothesi, scil. positis iam creaturis, necessaria, quarum singulis Deus adest, quamdiu vult.

Nam si Deus iuberet creaturas recidere in nihilum, illis non esset præsens. 7) Omnipræsentia restringitur ad creaturas, quæ huius mundi complexu continentur: Immensitas vltra mundum, vltra supremum cœlum & infinitum sese porrigit.

Conf. D. CALOV. system. tom. II. p. 613.

Prob. Immensitas Dei 1) ex effato regio Salomonis, 1 Reg. VIII, 27. Num enim reuera habitabit Deus super terra? En! cœli & cœli cœlorum non comprehendunt te: multo minus domus hæc, quam ædificaui.

Ex quo argumentamur: Quem neque terra, neque cœli cœlorum comprehendunt, ille est absolute immensus. Atqui Deum &c. Ergo. Maior patet, quia phrasi scripturæ terra & cœlum, quotiescunque coniunguntur, designant vniuersam mundi machinam. Quidquid reuera exsistit, neque mundi machina continetur, sed ambitum cœli excedit, illud absolute immensum est. Excipit VORSTIVS 1) Dictum hoc non valide confirmare immensitatem Dei; propterea, quod rex Salomo interrogat: Num reuera Deus habitabit super terram?

Quæ interrogatio habet vim negandi, adeoque negat Salomo, Deum habitare super terram. Sed si Deus non habitat super terram, non est vbique, & si non est vbique, non est absolute immensus. 2) Vox hebræa יכלכל non significat: continent aut comprehendunt, sed sustentabunt.

Ipse Lutherus germanice reddidit:

versorgen, adeoque non immensitas, sed omnisufficientia, aut beatitudo Dei, ea voce exprimitur. Resp. ad I. Deus non habitat super terram localiter, vt ab ea comprehendatur. Ad II. Primaria significatio radicis est continere, aut comprehendere. Conf. 1 Reg. VII, 26. quam eadem vox heic retinet, quoniam ex antecedentibus & consequentibus patescit, quod de incolatu aut habitatione Dei sermo sit. Idcirco regum sapientissimus indigitatum iuit, ne vastam quidem mundi compagem comprehendendo Deo parem esse.

2) Ex spiritualitate & infinitate Dei. Nullus spiritus infinitus locorum, aut vllius vbi terminis definiri potest. Atqui Deus est spiritus, Io. IV, 24. infinitus, Ps. CXLV, 3. Maior probatur, quia 1) locorum terminis solum corpus quantum, nullus autem spiritus neque creatus, neque increatus, circumscribitur. 2) Spiritus creati sunt in vbi determinabili; eoque definitiuo ob essentiae finitudinem. At cum essentia Dei spiritualis sit infinita, & interminabilis, etiam vbietas eius est interminabilis; quippe quae cum essentia diuina, quoad rem, eadem est.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, quorum quidam immensitatem Dei penitus infitiantur, quidam ea dubitant. Cum argumenta eorum ita comparata sint, vt proprie & directe omnipraesentiam diuinam impugnent; eadem infra, vbi de praesentia Dei acturi sumus, considerabimus.


### Q. XXXIII. What is the immutability of God?

Immutability is an attribute of God, by which He is subject to no change, neither physical nor moral.

Obs. I. Physical change, according to Aristotle, is fourfold: a) It occurs according to substance, such as generation, which happens from non-being to being, and corruption, which happens from being to non-being. b) According to quantity, such as augmentation, by which a body is made larger, and diminution, by which it is made smaller. c) According to quality, such as alteration, by which a quality is introduced and corrupted, e.g., cooling. d) According to place, such as local motion.

II. Moral change is that by which a will is changed in the executing, omitting, or inverting of its decrees.

Proof a. God is not physically changed as to substance, because He is from Himself, and cannot be destroyed by another. "You are the same, and your years will not fail," says the sacred psalmist, Ps. 102: 28. Nor as to quantity, for its root is matter. But God is a spirit devoid of all matter, John 4:24. Nor as to quality; for since this is an accident, it does not fall upon the most perfect God. St. James says wisely: ch. 1:17, "With the Father of lights there is no variation or shadow of turning." Nor as to local motion; because God, being immense, is not included by any limits of places, but fills heaven and earth with His presence, Jer. 23:24.

Proof b. God is not morally changed; because a change of will arises either from inconstancy, or from ignorance, or from an inability to act. But from the most perfect God, all inconstancy is far removed, all ignorance from the omniscient, and all inability to act from the omnipotent. Therefore, the purpose of the divine will remains valid, fixed, and invariable: "I, Jehovah, do not change," says the most truthful God. Mal. 3:6. The antithesis is that of the Socinians, who assert the mutability of the divine will, relying on the following arguments:

I. Whoever repents of a deed is changed. But God repents of a deed. Therefore. The major is certain; because by repentance a prior decree of the will is retracted; the minor is proved from Gen. 6:6, 1 Sam. 15:11. Resp. Repentance is not predicated of God properly, insofar as it is sorrow of mind over deeds committed out of a defect of knowledge or power; but anthropopathōs, improperly and with respect to us; because repentance, when attributed to God, designates either the denunciation and execution of divine judgment, which befalls the impious, or the declaration of mercy toward converted sinners. Therefore, change occurs not in God, but in the objects, namely in creatures placed outside of God, in sinners who are converted, or not converted.

Instance: God retracts the decree of his will, Jonah 3:10. Therefore, repentance is said of God not ἀνθρωποπαθῶς (anthropopathically), figuratively or improperly, but truly and properly. Response: God does not retract or revoke the decree of his will, but establishes and confirms it. The reason is: because the sentence of the decree is conditional, not absolute, although the external form, or the manner in which the decree is conceived, may at first glance appear absolute. Thus, God is said to be led to repentance when he does not execute a conditional threat or promise, because the annexed condition has not been fulfilled.

II. Every free will is mutable. The will of God is free. Therefore. The major is proved because a free will is changeable toward opposites. Response: I deny the major. For liberty is one thing; mutability is another. The former is opposed to necessity, the latter to constancy. The former is a perfection, the latter an imperfection, since it argues for the inconstancy of the will. The will of God is called free, not because it is changeable toward opposites, but because it is freely terminated toward objects.

III. God can either suspend a free act, or not. If the former; then that act will be mutable. If the latter; God will be a being acting not freely, but necessarily. The consequence of the major is proved; because between contradictories there is no third. The first member is proved; because when a certain act is suspended, and afterwards is performed, there is given some delay, according to which it is permissible to say that that act does not exist. The latter member is proved; because whatever act cannot be suspended, that is necessary. Response: It is falsely objected that one act is elicited after another in God, for the reason that in God, by reason of time, there is no 'before' or 'after'. For that any act is suspended, that happens with connotation to a creature, and so it can be admitted only of an extrinsic act. But the intrinsic act of God is neither suspended, nor can it be suspended, and so immutability remains in divine acts, in so far as they are identified with the divine essence.

IV. God, in justifying a sinner, becomes propitious from being angry. Therefore he is changed. Response: God is not changed in himself by justifying a repentant sinner, but the change is in the objects and effects: just as the sun remains the same, although to a healthy eye it becomes lovely, to a wounded eye harsh and troublesome.

V. Whoever becomes creating from not creating, he is changed. But God has become creating from not creating. Therefore God is changed. The major is proved; because change is concerned with an act and its negation. Response: I deny the major, because all change happens in the creature, not in the creator. Therefore creation is said of God by extrinsic denomination; for although it is done by the Creator, it is not terminated in the Creator, but in creatures.

VI. Whoever intrinsically unites a creature to himself, he is changed. But the Son of God, etc. Therefore. The major is evident; because to be changed is the same as to be otherwise. The minor is certain: because the ὁ λόγος ἄσαρκος (Word without flesh) through the incarnation intrinsically united human nature to himself, so that he might become ἔνσαρκος (enfleshed). Response: Whoever intrinsically unites a creature to himself, by way of a subject, that of a passively receiving one, he is changed. Thus, with the major limited, the minor is denied. The ὁ λόγος (Word) did not unite human nature to himself as a suffering subject, but only terminates the same, not indeed by mere sustentation, but by the communication of the infinite hypostasis. He who terminates a thing is not changed, but he who suffers.

Latin:

Immutabilitas est attributum Dei, per quod ille nulli, neque physicae , neque moralis mutationi obnoxius est.

Obs. I. Mutatio physica, censente Aristotele, est quadruplex: a) Fit ea secundum substantiam, vt generatio, quae fit a non esse ad esse, & corruptio, quae fit ab esse ad non esse. b) Secundum quantitatem, vt augmentatio, qua corpus redditur maius, & diminutio, qua illud fit minus. c) Secundum qualitatem, vt alteratio, qua qualitas introducitur & corrumpitur, v. gr. frigefactio. d) Secundum locum, vt motus localis.

Obs. II. Mutatio moralis est, qua voluntas in decretis suis exsequendis, omittendis, aut invertendis mutatur.

Prob. a. Deus physice non mutatur, qua substantiam, quia est a seipso, & ab alio derui nequit. Tu idem es, & anni tui non deficient, inquit hieropsaltes Ps. CII, 28. nec qua quantitatem, quippe cuius radix est materia. At Deus est spiritus omnis materiae expers. Io. IV, 24. Nec qua qualitatem; haec enim cum sit accidens, in Deum perfectissimum non cadit. Scite ait S. Iacobus: c. I, 17. Apud patrem luminum non est transmutatio, aut conuersionis (vel) vmbra. Nec qua motum localem; quia Deus immensus nullis locorum terminis includitur, sed praesentia sua coelum & terram implet. Ier. XXIII, 24.

Prob. b. Moraliter Deus non mutatur; quia mutatio voluntatis vel ex inconstantia, vel ex ignorantia, vel ex agendi impotentia prouenit. At vero a Deo perfectissimo omnis inconstantia, ab omniscio omnis ignorantia, ab omnipotente omnis agendi impotentia longissime abest. Manet ergo propositum voluntatis diuinae ratum, fixum & inuariabile: Ego Iehouah, nec mutor, inquit Deus verissimus. Mal. III, 6. Antithesis est Socinianorum, mutabilitatem voluntatis diuinae afferentium, fretorum sequentibus argumentis.

I. Quem poenitet facti, ille mutatur. Atqui Deum poenitet facti. Ergo. Maior constat; quia poenitentia prius voluntatis decretum retractatur; Minor prob. ex Gen. VI, 6. 1 Sam. XV, 11. Resp. Poenitentia de Deo non dicitur proprie, quatenus est dolor animi de factis, ex defectu scientiae aut potentiae commissis; sed ἀνθρωποπαθῶς, improprie & respectu nostri; quia poenitentia, Deo attributa, designat vel denuntiationem et executionem iudicii divini, quae contingit impiis, vel declarationem misericordiae erga peccatores conversos. Proinde contingit mutatio non in Deo, se in obiectis, nempe in creaturis extra Deum positis, in peccatoribus conversis, aut non conversis.

Instantia: Deus decretum voluntatis retractat, Ionae III, 10. Ergo poenitentia de Deo dicitur non ἀνθρωποπαθῶς, figurate aut improprie, sed vere et proprie. Resp. Deus decretum voluntatis non retractat aut revocat, sed stabilit et confirmat. Ratio est: quia sententia decreti est conditionata, non absoluta, licet externa forma, sive modus, quo decretum conceptum est, prima fronte absolutus videatur. Dicitur itaque Deus poenitentia duci, quando comminationem aut promissionem conditionatam non exsequitur, eo quod annexa conditio non est adimpleta.

II. Omnis voluntas libera est mutabilis. Voluntas Dei est libera. Ergo. Maior prob. quia voluntas libera est vertibilis ad opposita. Resp. Neg. mai. Aliud enim est libertas; aliud mutabilitas. Illa necessitati, haec constantiae opponitur. Illa est perfectio, haec imperfectio, cum arguat inconstantiam voluntatis. Dicitur voluntas Dei libera, non quia est vertibilis ad opposita, sed quia libere ad obiecta terminatur.

III. Deus aut potest suspendere liberum actum, aut non. Si prius; tunc actus ille erit mutabilis. Si posterius; Deus erit ens non libere, sed necessario agens. Consequentia maioris probatur; quia contradictoria non datur tertium. Prius membrum probatur; quia quando actus quidam suspenditur, et postea perficitur, datur aliqua mora, secundum quam dicere licet, illum actum non esse. Posterius membrum probatur; quia quicunque actus non potest suspendi, ille est necessarius. Resp. Falso opponitur, unum actum post alium in Deo elici, eo quod in Deo ratione temporis non datur prius, aut posterius. Quod enim actus aliquis suspendatur, id fit cum connotatione ad creaturam, adeoque de actu extrinseco tantum admitti potest. Actus autem Dei intrinsecus nec suspenditur, nec suspendi potest, adeoque manet immutabilitas in actibus divinis, in quantum essentiae divinae identificantur.

IV. Deus, iustificans peccatorem, ex irato fit propitius. Ergo mutatur. Resp. Deus in se non mutatur, peccatorem poenitentem iustificando, sed mutatio est in obiectis et effectis: sicut sol idem manet, quamvis oculo sano fit amabilis, oculo sauciato asper et infestus.

V. Quicunque fit ex non creante creans, ille mutatur. Sed Deus factus est ex non creante creans. Ergo Deus mutatus est. Maior probatur; quia mutatio versatur inter actum, et eius negationem. Resp. Neg. maiorem, quia omnis mutatio fit in creatura, non in creatore. Dicitur itaque creatio de Deo per denominationem extrinsecam; licet enim fit a Creatore, non tamen in Creatore, sed creaturis terminatur.

VI. Quicunque sibi intrinsece uniuit creaturam, ille mutatus est. Atqui filius Dei et cetera. Ergo. Maior patet; quia mutari idem est, ac aliter se habere. Minor constat: quia ὁ λόγος ἄσαρκος per incarnationem sibi intrinsece uniuit humanam naturam, ut fieret ἔνσαρκος. Resp. Quicunque sibi intrinsece uniuit creaturam, per modum subiecti, illam patrie recipientis, ille mutatur. Sic limitata maiori negatur minor. Ὁ λόγος non uniuit sibi humanam naturam, ut subiectum patiens, sed eandem tantum terminat, non quidem per nudam sustentationem, sed per hypostasis infinitae communicationem. Non mutatur, qui rem terminat, sed qui patitur.


### Q. XXXIV. What is the immortality of God?

Immortality is a divine attribute, by which it is simply repugnant for God to die.

Proved from 1 Tim. VI, 16. God alone has immortality, God alone is called immortal, because 1) he is immortal not by the will or grace of another, but by his own nature, which is devoid of all corruption. Enoch and Elijah did not die, by the special grace of God; although otherwise, by the force of their nature, they were mortal. 2) God alone is immortal independently and by essence; angels and our souls are immortal dependently and by participation, since they refer their immortality as received from God.

Latin:

Immortalitas est attributum diuinum, quo Deo simpliciter repugnat mori.

Prob. ex 1 Tim. VI, 16. Solus Deus habet immortalitatem, Solus Deus immortalis dicitur, quia 1) non alterius voluntate aut gratia, sed suapte natura, omnis corruptionis experte, immortalis est. Enochus & Elias non sunt mortui, ex speciali Dei gratia; quamuis cæteroquin vi naturæ suæ fuerint mortales. 2) Solus Deus est immortalis independenter, & per essentiam, angeli & animæ nostræ sunt immortales dependenter & per participationem, cum immortalitatem suam Deo acceptam referant.


### Q. XXXV. What is the incomprehensibility of God?

Incomprehensibility is a divine attribute, by which the essence of God cannot be adequately known by any creature.

Proved 1) From the testimony of Scripture, Ps. CXLV, 3. Great is Jehovah, and greatly to be praised; and of his greatness there is no searching. Since the greatness of God is unsearchable, we conclude that his essence is incomprehensible.

2) From the light of reason. For comprehensive knowledge, such an exact proportion of the knowing faculty to the knowable object is required that there is as much perfection in the knowing intellect as there is in the knowable object. But there is no proportion given between finite intellects and the infinite God, since the intellect of creatures (angels, men) is infinitely surpassed by the perfection of God.

You say: The blessed are called "comprehenders," Phil. III, 12. Therefore their *theoria* (contemplation) is comprehensive. Cf. KÖNIG, *theol. positiu.* p. 3. Response: The intuitive knowledge of God by the blessed is also called comprehensive, taking this word in a broader sense. See above p. 6, qu. 5, prol. I.

Latin:

Incomprehensibilitas est attributum diuinum, quo essentia Dei a nulla creatura adæquate cognosci potest.

Prob. 1) Ex testimonio scripturæ, Pf. CXLV, 3. Magnus est Iehouah, & laudabilis valde; & magnitudinis eius non (est) inuestigatio. Cum magnitudo Dei sit imperuestigabilis, essentiam eius incomprehensibilem esse, colligimus.

2) Ex lumine rationis. Ad cognitionem comprehensiuam tam exacta requiritur proportio facultatis cognoscentis ad obiectum cognoscibile, vt tanta sit perfectio in intellectu cognoscente, quanta est in obiecto cognoscibili. Sed intellectus finiti ad Deum infinitum nulla datur proportio, cum intellectus creaturarum (angelorum, hominum) infinities a perfectione Dei superetur.

Dicis: Beati dicuntur comprehensores, Phil. III, 12. Ergo illorum θεωρία est comprehensiua. Conf. KÖNIG. theol. positiu. p. 3. Resp: Beatorum notitia Dei intuitiua vocatur etiam comprehensiua, latius sumta hac voce. Vid. supra p. 6. qu. 5. prol. I.


### I. Q. XXXVI. What is the invisibility of God?

Invisibility is a divine attribute, according to which the divine essence cannot be seen by the natural faculty of bodily eyes.

Proved from the heavenly oracle Exod. XXXIII, 20. You shall not be able to see my face; for man shall not see me and live—v. 23. you shall see my back parts. By these words God openly declares that his essence and majesty (which is indicated by the name of "face") cannot be discerned by bodily eyes. The added reason indicates that man, as long as he is in this life, which is subject to material changes, cannot gaze upon the essence of God. Whether, however, in the heavenly life we shall see the divine essence with glorified bodily eyes, we neither stubbornly deny nor assert as apodictic, but rather judge it to be reserved for future experience. Meanwhile, we see his "back parts," while the works and benefits of God are daily obvious to our eyes.

You say: God was often seen, Exod. XXXIV, 5; Is. VI, 1. Response: With AUGUSTINE, ep. XI. God was seen by the fathers through the assumption of some visible arrangement of matter, while his invisibility remained intact.

Question XXXVII. What is the blessedness of God?

Blessedness is a divine attribute, through which God is not only free from all evils, but also abounds most cumulatively in all goods, and is most fully sufficient unto himself.

Prob. St. Paul calls God μακάριον, blessed, 1 Tim. 1:11; 6:15. The blessedness of God consists in the lack of all evils, 2) in the abundance of all good things, 3) in the most pleasant sense of Himself. From these redounds the communication of blessedness, which God pours out copiously upon the faithful. For God is indeed essential blessedness itself, and the fountain and spring of all blessedness.

Latin:

Inuisibilitas est attributum diuinum, secundum quod essentia diuina naturali oculorum corporeorum facultate conspici nequit.

Prob. Ex oraculo cœlesti Exod. XXXIII, 20. Non poteris videre facies meas; quia non videbit me homo, viuetque - v. 23. videbis posteriora mea. Quibus verbis Deus aperte denunciat, essentiam & maiestatem suam (quæ nomine faciei indicatur) corporeis non posse cerni oculis. Ratio addita indigitat, non posse hominem, quamdiu in hac est vita, quæ materialibus subdita est mutationibus, essentiam Dei intueri. An vero in vita cœlesti essentiam diuinam oculis corporis glorificatis visuri simus, nec præfracte negamus, nec vt apodicticum afferimus, fed futuræ potius experientiæ referuandum censemus. Videmus interim posteriora eius, dum opera & beneficia Dei quotidie oculis nostris sunt obuia.

Dicis. Deus fæpe est visus, Exod. XXXIV, 5. Ef. VI, 1. Resp. Cum AVGVSTINO ep. XI. Visus est Deus patribus alicuius conspicabilis materiæ dispositione assumta, salua sua inuisibilitate.

Quæst. XXXVII. Quæ est beatitudo Dei?

Beatitudo est attributum diuinum, per quod Deus non tantum ab omnibus malis liber est, sed etiam omnibus bonis cumulatissime affluit, fibique ipsi plenissime sufficit.

Prob. S. Paulus Deum appellat μακάριον beatum, 1 Tim. I, 11. c. VI, 15. Consistit beatitudo Dei in omnium malorum carentia, 2) in bonorum omnium affluentia, 3) in iucundissimo fui ipsius sensu. E quibus redundat communicatio beatitudinis, quam Deus in fideles copiose effundit. Est quippe Deus & ipsa essentialis beatitudo, & omnis beatitudinis fons & scaturigo.


### Q. XXXVIII. What is the majesty of God?

The majesty of God is a divine attribute, from which God is not only called glorious, but also religious worship is owed to Him alone.

Prob. Because of His most eminent majesty, He is called by St. Stephen the God of glory, Acts 7:2; by the royal prophet, the most high, Ps. 7:18; by Moses, the great and terrible God, Deut. 7:21, whose glory the whole earth is full of, Is. 6:3. Therefore God is glorious, not only because of the benefits with which He heaps upon us, but also because of the incomparable perfection of the divine nature, wisdom, power, and goodness. For sound reason dictates that honor is appropriate to everyone according to the excellence of their nature. God is glorious, not only because of His greatest glory, but also because it is incommunicable. My glory I will not give to another, says Jehovah, Is. 42:8.

Latin:

Maiestas Dei est attributum divinum, ex quo Deus non tantum dicitur gloriosus, sed etiam ipsi soli cultus religiosus debetur.

Prob. Ob maiestatem eminentissimam a St. Stephano vocatur Deus gloriae Act. VII, 2. a propheta regio altissimus, Ps. VII, 18. a Mose Deus magnus & formidabilis, Deut. VII, 21. cuius gloria omnis terra plena est. Es. VI, 3. Gloriosus itaque est Deus, non tantum propter beneficia, quibus nos cumulat, sed & ob incomparabilem naturae divinae perfectionem, sapientiam, potentiam, bonitatem. Etenim sana ratio dictitat, cuilibet competere honorem secundum excellentiam naturae. Gloriosus est Deus, non tantum propter gloriam maximam, sed & incommunicabilem. Gloriam meam alteri non dabo, inquit Iehouah, Es. XLII, 8.


### Of the Operative Divine Attributes, Which Signify Both the Origin of Acting and the Mode of Acting

Obs. According to our mode of conceiving, the life of God is the principle signifying the origin of acting: the remaining divine attributes, which refer to ἐνέργειαν (energy/activity), designate the divine mode of acting.

Latin:

Obs. Secundum nostrum concipiendi modum, vita Dei est principium insinuans agendi originem: reliqua attributa divina, quae ad ἐνέργειαν referunt, modum agendi divinum designant.


### Q. XXXIX. What is the life of God?

Life is a property essential to God, through which the essence of God demonstrates itself to be always active. Obs.

I. God lives a life that is not vegetative, as plants: nor sensitive, as brutes; but intellectual, and that not imperfect, as men who are wayfarers, nor finite, as angels, but infinite and most perfect.

Obs. II. The intellectual life of God is viewed either in first act, or in second act. In first act it is the intellect and will itself: in second act it is intellection and volition, which, however, in God are not actions really produced, but are only conceived by way of actions.

The life of God is proved, because 1) God in Holy Scripture is called living, Jer. 10:10: the Lord God is truth, the living God. 2) God is said to swear by His life, Ezek. 33:1. 3) God is called life itself, John 14:16. And eternal life, 1 John 5:20. 4) God is the fountain of life, Ps. 36:10; Acts 17:28.

Latin:

Vita est proprietas Deo essentialis, per quam essentia Dei se semper actuosam demonstrat.

Obs. I. Viuit Deus vitam non vegetabilem, vt plantae: nec sensitivam, vt bruta; sed intellectualem, eamque non imperfectam, vt homines viatores, neque finitam, vt angeli, sed infinitam & perfectissimam.

Obs. II. Vita Dei intellectualis spectatur vel in actu primo, vel in actu secundo. In actu primo est ipse intellectus & voluntas: in actu secundo est intellectio & volitio, quae tamen in Deo non sunt actiones realiter productae, sed tantum per modum actionum concipiuntur.

Probatur vita Dei, quia 1) Deus in S. scriptura dicitur vivus, Ier. X, 10: dominus Deus veritas est, Deus vivus. 2) Deus dicitur iurare per vitam suam, Ezech. XXXIII, 1. 3) Deus vocatur ipsa vita, Io. XIV, 16. Et vita aeterna, 1 Io. V, 20. 4) Est Deus fons vitae, Ps. XXXVI, 10. Act. XVII, 28.


### Q. XL. What is the intellect of God?

The intellect of God is the essence of God itself, insofar as it is conceived by us by way of an intellectual power. Obs.

I. The intellect of God is called the divine essence itself; for just as God is a most simple being, and is not composed of many things: so His intellect does not really differ from His essence.

Obj. II. In intelligent creatures, intellect and intellection differ in point of reality as potency and act. In God, intellect and intellection are distinguished not in point of reality, but in point of our concept: for we conceive the intellect of God as the first act, and the intellection or cognition of God as the second act.

The divine intellect is proven from divine omniscience and omni-wisdom.

Q. XLI. What is the omniscience of God?

Omniscience is a divine attribute ἐνεργητικὸν (energetic), by which God knows all things that are, have been, will be, or can be in any way, by one simple act, immediately and most perfectly.

Prov. I. Because Jehovah is a God of knowledge; 1 Sam. II, 3. that is, possessing all knowledge. God knows all things, 1 John III, 20. No creature is invisible (not appearing) before Him: but all things are naked and circumcised, laid bare. Heb. IV, 13.

II. God alone knows the heart of all the children of men, 1 Kings VIII, 39. He Himself tests the hearts and reins, Ps. VII, 10. Hence He is called καρδιογνώστης (knower of hearts), Acts XV, 7.

III. That God also knows future contingencies is proven (1) from the royal utterance of David: Ps. CXXXIX, 2. You have understood my thought from afar, i.e., before it arises in my heart.

(2) Because by this very thing the true God is distinguished from idols; that He foreknows and predicts even future contingencies, Isa. XLI, 21. Bring forward (O Gentiles) your case, says Jehovah; bring your strong ones (idols), says the King of Jacob. Let them bring and announce to you those things that are happening; the former things, what they were, indicate, that we may set them to our heart, and know their posterity, or make us hear things to come: indicate signs for the future, that we may know that you are Gods. From this divine discourse we learn that he is not the true God who neither foreknows nor predicts future contingencies. (3) Numerous examples confirm the same. The repentance of the Tyrians and Sidonians, as well as the betrayal of David, were only futuribles, yet God was not ignorant of them, Matt. XI, 21. 1 Sam. XXIII, 12. God predicted many future contingencies determinately, even evils, which He Himself was not about to effect, but at least to permit, e.g.,

the hardening of Pharaoh, Exod. III, 19. The betrayal of Judas, Ps. XLI, 10. John XIII, 8. The passion of Christ, Ps. XXII. Isa. LIII. The fall of Peter, Matt. XXVI, 34. The impiety of men toward the end of the world, Luke XXI, 20. The advent and duration of the Anti-Christ, 2 Thess. II, 7.

Obs. I. The primary object of the divine science is God Himself, who adequately, and thus comprehensively, knows His own essence, His perfections, hypostases, and actions, John III, 11. 1 Cor. II, 10. The secondary object is all things that are outside of God, have been, or can be in any way, whether they be good or evil.

Obj. II. By reason of mode, the knowledge of God is (1) continuous and eternal, but not successive or variable; because God knows all things by one simple intuition; for He does not discourse or reason by gathering the unknown from the known, since all things are most known to God, Heb. IV, 13. (2) Immediate, because God does not need intelligible species. We humans understand through species, or images, which, abstracted from things perceived by sense, are impressed upon the mind like seals upon wax. Through such species God does not understand; because He is the most simple being without any passive potency: therefore He cannot receive images as something suffering, and have knowledge arising from an extrinsic principle. We need intelligible species to unite and approximate the absent object to the knowing intellect: but to God all things are most present; wherefore He does not need representative species.

Obj. III. The knowledge of God is distinguished (1) into general and special. General knowledge extends to all things, and the causes of things, even to sins. By special knowledge are known onthen the elect.

For God has known from eternity who are finally to believe in Christ, and whom He has chosen for life. Those whom He foreknew, He also predestined, Rom. VIII, 29.

(2) The knowledge of God is distinguished into simple, approbative, and permissive knowledge. Simple knowledge, or that of bare awareness, is that by which God knows all things speculatively. Approbative knowledge is that by which He knows good things; permissive, that by which He knows evil things.

(3) The knowledge of God is distinguished into natural, free, and middle knowledge. Natural knowledge, which is also called the knowledge of simple intelligence, is that by which God knows possible things, as they are possible. The free knowledge of God, which is also called the knowledge of vision, is that by which God knows all things that are, have been, or are absolutely to be, whether they be necessary or contingent. Middle knowledge is said to be that by which God knows those things which are to be under a condition, i.e., which are not absolutely to be, yet would be to be if this or that condition were fulfilled; although, due to the failure of that condition, they often do not come to pass.

For this distinction, most common in the schools, to be understood more soundly, a knowledge of the terms is necessary. Namely, it is called natural knowledge because it is necessary: for "natural" is here opposed to "free." For just as possible things are necessarily such, so the knowledge of God, by which He Himself knows things as they are possible, is necessary or natural, so that God cannot not know possible things as they are possible. The same is called the knowledge of simple intelligence because it precedes every decree of the divine will. It is also called abstractive knowledge, because it is made as if abstracted from created things.

But indeed the knowledge of God, by which He knows what are, have been, and are absolutely to be, is termed free, because by reason of the creatures it is not absolutely necessary, but only from the position of an object present or future. The same is called the knowledge of vision, or intuitive, because God beholds the actual existence of things. Middle knowledge, however, by which God knows things conditionally to be, is distinguished from the natural and free knowledge of God by the formal reason of the object: for the former knows possible things, the latter absolutely future things, and middle knowledge knows things to be under a condition; from which, by the same reason of the object, it is called hypothetical or conditional.

These things having been premised, we prove the middle knowledge of God by the following argument. God, besides possible and absolutely future things, also knows those things which are to be under a condition. Therefore, in God, besides natural and free knowledge, there is also middle or conditional knowledge. The reason for the consequence is that middle knowledge is distinguished from the natural and free knowledge of God by a peculiar formal object.

The antecedent is proved by certain examples taken from Holy Scripture. (1) From 1 Sam. XXIII, 5. sqq., where David consulted the Lord whether, if he remained in the city of Keilah, Saul would come: and if Saul besieged the city, whether the men of Keilah would deliver him up? To both, the Lord answered: Saul will come, and they will deliver you up. When, however, David fled from that city, neither did Saul come, nor did the men of Keilah deliver up David. God therefore foretold, and thus foreknew, that which was to be not absolutely, but upon a hypothesis.

(2) From Matth. XI, 21. Where the Savior says: If the miracles which were performed in you (Chorazin) had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. Christ, as true God, foreknew the future repentance of the Sidonians and Tyrians under a condition, namely, if such stupendous miracles had reached their senses.

(3) Without the presupposed middle knowledge of God, election from foreseen faith cannot be conveniently explained; since God wills men to be saved not absolutely, but under the condition of persevering faith.

Antithesis The antithesis is (1) of the Socinians, who deny that God certainly knows future contingent things. (2) Of certain theologians among the Reformed and our own, who deny the middle knowledge of God.

Arguments of the Socinians (1) Whoever knows things as they are, he does not have certain knowledge of contingent things.

But God, etc. Therefore. The major is evident; because true cognition is analogous to the object.

From this it follows that no certain and determined knowledge corresponds to a contingently future thing. Resp. Future contingents can be viewed in two ways: (1) insofar as they can be produced and not produced, be and not be, by their cause; in which respect they are called contingent: (2) insofar as they will certainly be produced by their cause, which is about to determine itself freely to production; in which sense they are called future.

Future contingents are presented to the infinite knowledge of God from eternity to be known, just as they are about to exist or not exist determinately through their free causes.

Instance: Future contingents are not from eternity.

Therefore, they could not have been known by God from eternity.

Resp. Future contingents are not from eternity as regards real or actual being: yet they are from eternity as regards objective or intelligible being with respect to the divine intellect.

For the determinate truth of future contingents, it is not required that the contingents themselves exist actually and in reality; for thus they would not be future, but present; nor that their causes be actually in the nature of things: but it suffices that they themselves, together with their causes, were so presented to the infinite knowledge of God from eternity, that they were about to exist determinately in time through their causes.

(2) If this is posited, the contingency of things or the liberty of human will is removed; that is not to be affirmed concerning God.

But if a determinate knowledge of future contingents is posited, all contingency of things and liberty of human will is removed.

E.

The minor is proved; because if God infallibly foreknows all things, all things will happen necessarily: if they happened otherwise, the knowledge of God would be deceived.

Latin:

Intellectus Dei est ipsa essentia Dei, quatenus a nobis concipitur per modum potentiae intellectivae. Obs.

I. Intellectus Dei dicitur ipsa essentia divina; sicut enim Deus est ens simplicissimum, nec componitur ex pluribus: ita intellectus eius ab essentia realiter non differt.

Obs. II. In creaturis intelligentibus intellectus & intellectio differunt ex parte rei vt potentia & actio. In Deo intellectus & intellectio non ex parte rei, sed ex parte conceptus nostri distinguuntur: Concipimus quippe intellectum Dei, vt actum primum, intellectionem siue cognitionem Dei, vt actum secundum.

Probatur intellectus diuinus ex omniscientia, & omnisapientia diuina.

Quæst. XLI. Quæ est omniscientia Dei?

Omniscientia est attributum diuinum ἐνεργητικὸν, quo Deus omnia, quæ sunt, fuerunt, erunt, aut vlla ratione esse possunt, vno simplici actu immediate & perfectissime cognoscit.

Prob. I. Quia Iehouah est Deus scientiarum; 1 Sam. II, 3. id est, omnem scientiam possidens. Deus cognoscit omnia, 1 Io. III, 20. Nulla creatura est inuisibilis (non apparens) coram ipso: omnia vero nuda, & circumcisa nudata. Hebr. IV, 13.

II. Deus solus nouit cor omnium filiorum hominis, 1 Reg. VIII, 39. Ipse probat corda & renes, Ps. VII, 10. Hinc dicitur καρδιογνώστης, Act. XV, 7.

III. Deum cognoscere etiam futura contingentia, probatur (1) ex effato regio Dauidis: Ps. CXXXIX, 2. Intellexisti cogitationem meam e longinquo, i.e. antequam in corde meo exoriatur.

(2) Quia hoc ipso verus Deus ab idolis distinguitur; quod futura etiam contingentia præscit & prædicit, Es. XLI, 21. Adferte (gentiles) litem vestram, dicit Iehouah; adducite robora (idola) vestra, dicit rex Iacobi. Adducant & annuntient vobis ea quæ contingunt; priora, quæ fuerint illa, indicate, vt ponamus ad cor nostrum, & sciamus posteritatem eorum, aut ventura audire facite nos: indicate signa in futurum, vt sciamus, quod Dii vos (sitis). Ex hoc eloquio diuino discimus, illum non esse verum Deum, qui futura contingentia nec præscit, nec prædicit. (3) Confirmant idem plurima exempla. Tyriorum ac Sidoniorum pœnitentia, pariter atque traditio Dauidis, futuribilia tantum erant, neque tamen Deus illa ignorabat, Matth. XI, 21. 1 Sam. XXIII, 12. Prædixit Deus multa futura contingentia determinate, etiam mala, quæ ipse effecturus non erat, sed saltem permissurus, v. gr.

Indurationem Pharaonis, Exod. III, 19. Proditionem Iudæ, Ps. LXI, 10. Io. XIII, 8. Passionem Christi, Ps. XXII. Es. LIII. Lapsum Petri, Matth. XXVI, 34. Impietatem hominum sub finem mundi, Luc. XXI, 20. Aduentum & durationem Anti-Christi, 2 Thess. II, 7.

Obs. I. Obiectum scientiæ diuinæ primarium est Deus ipse, qui adæquate, atque adeo comprehensiue cognoscit suam essentiam, suas perfectiones, hypostases, actiones, Io. III, 11. 1 Cor. II, 10. Obiectum secundarium sunt omnia, quæ extra Deum sunt, fuerunt aut vlla ratione esse possunt, siue sint bonæ, siue malæ.

Obs. II. Ratione modi scientia Dei est (1) continua & æterna, non autem successiua, aut variabilis; quia Deus vno simplici intuitu cognoscit omnia; neque enim discurrit aut ratiocinatur colligendo ex notis ignotum, siquidem Deo sunt omnia notissima, Hebr. IV, 13. (2) Immediata, quia Deus speciebus intelligibilibus non indiget. Nos homines intelligimus per species, siue imagines, quæ a rebus sensu perceptis abstractæ imprimuntur animo, tanquam sigilla ceræ. Per eiusmodi species Deus non intelligit; quia est simplicissimum ens absque vlla potentia passiua: proinde non potest recipere imagines, vt quiddam patiens, & habere scientiam ab extrinseco principio ortam. Nos indigemus speciebus intelligibilibus, vt obiectum absens intellectui cognoscenti vniant & approximent: Deo autem omnia sunt præsentissima; quapropter non indiget speciebus repræsentatiuis.

Obs. III. Scientia Dei distinguitur (1) in generalem & specialem. Generalis se extendit ad omnes res, rerumque causas, etiam ad peccata. Scientia speciali cognoscuntur tantum electi.

Novit enim Deus ab aeterno, qui finaliter in Christum sint credituri, & quos ad vitam elegerit. Quos praecognovit, hos praedestinavit, Rom. VIII, 29.

(2) Distinguitur scientia Dei in scientiam simplicem, approbativam & permissivam. Scientia simplex, sive nudae notitiae, est, qua Deus omnia speculative cognoscit. Scientia approbativa est, qua bona: permissiva, qua mala cognoscit.

(3) Distinguitur scientia Dei in naturalem, liberam & mediam. Scientia naturalis, quae etiam scientia simplicis intelligentiae audit, est, qua Deus res possibiles, vt sunt possibiles, cognoscit. Scientia Dei libera, quae etiam scientia visionis appellatur, est, qua Deus cognoscit omnia, quae sunt, fuerunt aut absolute futura sunt, sive illa sint necessaria, sive contingentia. Scientia media dicitur, qua Deus cognoscit ea, quae sub conditione futura sunt, i. e. quae absolute futura non sunt, essent tamen futura, si haec vel ista conditio adimpleretur; quamvis ob defectum istius conditionis saepe non eueniant.

Ad hanc distinctionem, in scholis usu tritissimam, solidius intelligendam, necessaria est cognitio terminorum. Nempe naturalis scientia dicitur, quia est necessaria: Naturale quippe hic opponitur libero. Nam sicut res possibiles necessario sunt tales: Ita scientia Dei, qua ipse res, vt possibiles, cognoscit, necessaria sive naturalis est, vt non possit non Deus possibilia, vt sunt possibilia, cognoscere. Vocatur eadem scientia simplicis intelligentiae, quia omne decretum voluntatis divinae antecedit. Appellatur etiam scientia abstractiva, quod fit a rebus creatis quasi abstracta.

At vero scientia Dei, qua quae sunt, fuerunt, & absolute futura sunt, cognoscit, libera nuncupatur, quia ratione creaturarum non est absolute necessaria, sed solum ex positione obiecti praesentis, aut futuri. Dicitur eadem scientia visionis, sive intuitiva, quia Deus intuetur actualem rerum exsistentiam. Scientia autem media, qua Deus conditionate futura cognoscit, per rationem formalem obiecti distinguitur a scientia Dei naturali & libera: nam illa possibilia, haec absolute futura, scientia media sub conditione futura cognoscit; ex quo eadem ratione obiecti hypothetica, sive conditionata appellatur.

Quibus praemissis, scientiam Dei mediam sequenti argumento probamus. Deus praeter possibilia, & absolute futura, cognoscit etiam ea, quae sub conditione futura sunt. Ergo in Deo praeter scientiam naturalem & liberam etiam est media, sive conditionata. Ratio consequentiae est, quia scientia media, peculiari obiecto formali, a scientia Dei naturali & libera distinguitur.

Antecedens probatur e quibusdam exemplis, petitis e sacra scriptura. (1) Ex 1 Sam. XXIII, 5. sqq. vbi Dauid consuluit dominum, an, si maneret in ciuitate Kegila, venturus esset Saul: & si obsideret Saul ciuitatem, an Kegilae essent ipsum tradituri? ad vtrumque respondit dominus: Et Saul veniet, & hi tradent te. Cum autem Dauid e ciuitate ista profugeret, nec Saul venit, nec Kegilae Dauidem tradiderunt. Praedixit igitur, atque adeo praesciuit Deus id, quod non absolute, sed ex hypothesi futurum erat.

(2) Ex Matth. XI, 21. Vbi Salvator inquit: Si in Tyro & Sidone facta fuissent miracula, quae edita sunt in vobis (Coracis), olim in sacco & cinere poenitentiam egissent. Praesciuit Christus, tanquam verus Deus, Sidoniorum & Tyriorum poenitentiam futuram sub conditione, si scilicet tam stupenda miracula eorum sensus incurrissent.

(3) Sine praesupposita scientia Dei media, electio ex praeuisa fide commode explicari nequit; cum Deus homines non absolute, sed sub conditione perseverantis fidei, velit faluos fieri.

Antithesis Antithesis est (1) Socinianorum negantium, Deum futura contingentia certo cognoscere. (2) Quorundam e reformatis & nostratibus theologis, scientiam Dei mediam infitiantium.

Argumenta Socinianorum (1) Quicunque cognoscit res, vt sunt, ille non habet rerum contingentium certam scientiam.

Atqui Deus &c. Ergo. Maior constat; quia vera cognitio obiecto est analoga.

Exinde fit, vt rei contingenter futurae nulla respondeat certa & determinata notitia. Resp. Futura contingentia bifariam spectari possunt: (1) quatenus a causa sua possunt produci, & non produci, esse, & non esse; quo respectu vocantur contingentia: (2) quatenus a causa sua, ad productionem libere se determinatura, certo producentur; quo sensu dicuntur futura.

Futura contingentia ab aeterno infinitae Dei scientiae cognoscenda obiiciuntur, prout illa per suas causas liberas determinate exstitura, aut non exstitura sunt.

Instantia: Futura contingentia non sunt ab aeterno.

Ergo non potuerunt ab aeterno a Deo cognosci.

Resp. Futura contingentia non sunt ab aeterno, quoad esse reale, sive actuale: sunt tamen ab aeterno, quoad esse obiectum, sive intelligibile respectu intellectus diuini.

Ad determinatam futurorum contingentium veritatem non requiritur, ut vel ipsa contingentia actu & reipsa exsistant; sic enim non essent futura, sed praesentia; vel ut eorum causae actu sint in rerum natura: sed sufficit, quod ipsa, una cum causis suis, infinitae Dei scientiae ita ab aeterno fuerint obiecta, vt in tempore per suas causas determinate exstitura erant.

(2) Quo posito, tollitur rerum contingentia, aut libertas humani arbitrii, illud de Deo non est affirmandum.

Sed posita determinata futurorum contingentium scientia, tollitur omnis rerum contingentia, libertasque arbitrii humani.

E.

Minor probatur; quia si Deus omnia infallibiliter praescit, omnia euenient necessario: si aliter euenirent, scientia Dei falleretur.


### Q. XL. What is the intellect of God?: R

R.

The foreknowledge of God does not impose a necessity of existing upon things; because it is not the cause of things, neither proximate nor remote.

Not proximate; because otherwise all foreknown things would be necessary, and sin itself would have God as its author.

Not remote; for things are not future because God foreknows them; but because they are future, it cannot be that God does not foreknow them.

The foreknowledge of God is an effect, not that the thing happens thus; but to see that it happens thus.

Therefore, just as a physician does not impose a necessity of dying upon a sick man whom he foresees will die shortly: so God, foreseeing future contingents, does not impose upon them a necessity of existing.

We distinguish meanwhile between the necessity of the consequent and of the consequence, or absolute and hypothetical.

Because God foreknew future contingents, they are not necessarily future by a necessity of the consequent and absolute, which cannot consist with the contingency of things; although they are necessarily future by a necessity of the consequence and hypothetical, which does not remove the contingency of things and liberty: just as Sempronius runs freely, even if it is necessary that he run, posited that you see him running, and your sight does not deceive you.

(3) Once a determinate knowledge of future contingents is admitted in God, many places of Holy Scripture can neither be solidly understood nor rightly understood; such as (a) Gen.

VI, 6, where Moses asserts that it repented God that He had made men.

Therefore, He did not foreknow the future impiety of men.

(b) Gen.

XXII, 12.

Now I know that you fear the Lord.

Therefore, it seems God did not previously know the piety of Abraham thoroughly.

(c) Num.

XIV, 23, where God says that He swore that He would bring the Israelites into the land of Canaan, and yet because of their sins He would not do so.

But no one swears that he will do something which he foreknew he would not do.

(d) Gen.

XVIII, 21, where God says: I will go down and see whether they have done according to the cry that has come to me.

Therefore, God did not foreknow that cry.

Resp. to (a): Repentance, when it is attributed to men, imports two things: first, an internal motion of the mind, or sorrow: then, a decree concerning destroying that which has been done, or concerning not committing it anymore.

Repentance is attributed to God not by reason of the former; because no sorrow, no motion of the mind falls upon God on account of immutability.

Repentance therefore belongs to God by reason of the latter, namely by reason of the decree concerning destroying that which has been done.

Such a decree does not remove foreknowledge, for nothing prevents one from having foreknown something which he has decreed foreknowledge, for nothing prevents one from having foreknown something which he has decreed

to destroy. Ad (b): The knowledge of God is considered in a twofold way: now as knowledge of the future, now as proof of a fact. In the former way God knows all things from eternity, Act. XV, 18. In the latter way God approves certain deeds, and clearly declares them to be approved by Him. Thus God says to Abraham: Now I know, i.e., now, when you have wished to sacrifice your son, by the evidence and the greatest experiment of piety I have known, and have approved, that you fear the Lord. But the piety of Abraham was already most known to God before. Vid. Gen. XIIX, 19. Ad (c): The promise concerning the introduction of the Israelites into the land of Canaan was not absolute, but conditional, if they would render obedience to divine commands. But to the disobedient, God had never promised or sworn the introduction into the land of Canaan. Ad (d): When the Lord is said to have descended to know, it is said figuratively and anthropopathically (ἀνθρωποπαθῶς), to be explained judicially and exemplarily, after the example of judges, whom it behooves to know before they decide. Conf. DANN H. Hodof. p. 223.

The middle knowledge of God is attacked by the following arguments.

I. If the knowledge of God is adequately and sufficiently distinguished into natural and free knowledge, no necessity urges us to constitute a third knowledge of God, which might be called middle. But the former is true. Therefore, also the latter. The antecedent is proved: because just as between being and non-being no medium is given: so between the natural and free knowledge of God, middle knowledge does not lie. For the object of the natural knowledge of God is every possible thing, under which is comprehended also non-being, i.e., that which does not exist in act. The object of the free knowledge of God is every being existing in act in some difference of time. Wherefore no object remains left over to be known by the middle knowledge of God. Resp. By denying that the distinction of divine knowledge into natural and free is adequate. For the former concerns possibles, insofar as they are such, the latter concerns absolute futures. There remain the futures, conditionally such. Rightly, therefore, it is called middle knowledge, because its object lies between things, viewed precisely under the notion of possibility, and things absolutely future.

Instantia 1. Conditions opposed to the middle knowledge of God are either future or not future. If they are not future, they pertain to the object of the natural knowledge of God. For this embraces all possibles, even those which will never be future. If they are future, they pertain to the object of the free divine knowledge; for this considers all things which are, have been, and will be. Resp. Conditions opposed to the middle knowledge of God are neither absolutely future, nor simply not future, but are indifferent to future existence and non-existence. For sometimes they are fulfilled, sometimes they fail. The reason is because they have a connection with the effect that is not necessary, but contingent, and therefore they can be and can not be.

Instantia 2. Conditionally future things, the condition failing, remain in the sphere of possibles, and so are known by God by the knowledge of simple intelligence. Resp. There is no small difference between possibles and conditionally future things, as is revealed even from the tradition of David, future under this condition, if he should remain in the city of Keilah, I Sam. XXIII. The words of the Lord certainly mean more, when He said: And Saul will come, and they will deliver you; than if He had said: It is possible that Saul may come, and the Keilites may deliver you themselves. The tradition of David was then (so to speak) a futurible, not merely a possible. For Saul had taken counsel to oppress David unawares: the Keilites had conspired by previous deliberation in the betrayal of David: God had decreed to permit the betrayal and oppression of David, if he should remain in the city of Keilah. But concerning possibles never existing, neither does God form a decree, nor do prudent men deliberate. Although therefore conditionally future things, which are never brought into act, agree with possibles materially and in part: nevertheless they do not agree formally and in all respects.

II. The knowledge which is called middle is conditional. But no knowledge of God is conditional. Therefore, no knowledge of God is middle. The major premise is clear; because by the received usage of speaking, middle knowledge is called conditional. See HILDEBRANDI institut. theol. p. 105. The minor is proved; because God knows all things absolutely. For just as He knows successive things without the succession of His own cognition: so also He knows conditional things without a condition which might affect the divine intellect. Resp. The middle knowledge of God is called conditional not subjectively, as if God knew something conditionally, but it is conditional objectively, because it is knowledge of future conditional things.

III. Whatever knowledge relies upon a predetermining decree, that is not to be affirmed of God. But middle knowledge &c. Therefore. The major is proved; because a predetermining decree destroys the liberty of the human will. The minor is evident; because God by middle knowledge foreknows those things which are future under a condition. But since that condition has a contingent connection with the effect, it can be and can not be. Wherefore, in order that it may be fulfilled, it must be predetermined by the efficacious decree of God. Resp. The middle knowledge of God does not rely upon a predetermining decree, but is joined with the hypothetical decree of God, which, since it is not irresistible, does not predetermine free causes in acting.

IV. Whatever things are foreknown by God are known by Him determinately. But things future under a condition are not known determinately. Therefore. The minor is proved; because things future conditionally are not of determinate truth, but are indifferent to future existence and non-existence. Resp. I deny the minor. To the proof we say that things future conditionally, just as future contingent things, are considered in two ways: (1) Insofar as their cause behaves itself indifferently toward either of the opposites, namely toward the fulfillment and the non-fulfillment of the condition. (2) Insofar as their cause is about to determine itself to one of the opposites. God foreknows whither the human will is about to incline and determine itself. To this point looks the response of D. CALOV: The object of middle knowledge is indeed indifferent, but not as an object or formally, but only materially. For what is objected to divine knowledge is certain and determinate, since the knowledge of God is not doubtful and indeterminate. Conf. D. CALOV. tom. II. syst p. 523. & synops. contr. p. 107.

Latin:

R.

Praescientia Dei non imponit rebus necessitatem existendi; quia non est causa rerum, neque proxima, neque remota.

Non proxima; quia ceteroqui res omnes praescitae forent necessariae, & ipsum peccatum Deum haberet auctorem.

Non remota; neque enim ideo res futurae sunt, quia Deus praescit; sed quia futurae sunt, fieri non potest, quin Deus eas praesciat.

Praescientia diuinae effectus est, non vt res ita fiat; sed videre, quod ita fiat.

Proinde sicut medicus aegroto, quem breui moriturum praevidet, non imponit necessitatem moriendi: ita Deus, praeuidens futura contingentia, non imponit illis necessitatem existendi.

Distinguimus interim inter necessitatem consequentis, & consequentiae, sive absolutam & hypotheticam.

Quia Deus futura contingentia praenouit, illa non necessario futura sunt necessitate consequentis & absoluta, quae cum contingentia rerum consistere nequit; quamuis necessario futura sint necessitate consequentiae & hypothetica, quae contingentiam rerum & libertatem non tollit: perinde ac Sempronius libere currit, etiamsi necesse sit illum currere, posito quod tu illum currentem videas, nec tuus te visus fallat.

(3) Admissa in Deo determinata futurorum contingentium notitia, multa sacrae scripturae loca nec solide intelligi, nec dextre intelligi possunt; qualia sunt (a) Gen.

VI, 6. vbi Moses asserit, Deum paenituisse, quod homines fecerit.

Ergo futuram hominum impietatem non praesciuit.

(b) Gen.

XXII, 12.

Nunc cognoui, quod timeas dominum.

Ergo videtur Deus antea pietatem Abrahami non penitus cognouisse.

(c) Num.

XIV, 23. vbi Deus ait, se iurasse, quod Israelitas in terram Canaan introducturus esset, & tamen propter peccata se id facturum non esse.

Sed nemo iurat se aliquid facturum esse, quod praesciuit, se non esse facturum.

(d) Gen.

XIIX, 21, vbi Deus inquit: Descendam & videbo, num fecerint homines secundum clamorem, qui ad me venit.

Ergo Deus illum clamorem non praenouit.

Resp. ad (a): Paenitentia cum tribuitur hominibus, duo importat: primum internum animi motum, siue dolorem: deinde decretum de destruendo eo, quod factum est, aut de eo non amplius committendo.

Tribuitur paenitentia Deo non ratione prioris; quia in Deum ob immutabilitatem nullus dolor, nullus animi motus cadit.

Competit igitur paenitentia Deo ratione posterioris, nempe ratione decreti de destruendo eo, quod factum est.

Eiusmodi decretum non tollit praescientiam, Nihil enim obstat, quo minus aliquis praescuerit aliquid, quod decreuit præfcientiam, Nihil enim obstat, quo minus aliquis præfciuerit aliquid, quod decreuit

destruere. Ad (b): Scientia Dei duplici ratione consideratur: iam vt notitia futuri, iam vt probatio facti. Priori modo Deus omnia nouit ab æterno, Act. XV, 18. Posteriori modo facta quædam Deus approbat, eaque sibi probari luculenter declarat. Ita Deus ad Abrahamum ait: Nunc cognoui, i. e. nunc, cum filium tuum immolare voluisti, ex indicio atque experimento pietatis maximo cognoui, atque probaui, te dominum timere. Ceterum pietas Abrahami iam ante Deo erat notissima. Vid, Gen. XIIX, 19. Ad (c): Promissio de introductione Israëlitarum in terram Canaan non fuit absoluta, sed conditionata, si mandatis diuinis obedientiam præstarent. At immorigeris introductionem in terram Canaan nunquam Deus promiserat, aut iurauerat. Ad (d): Cum dominus descendisse dicitur ad sciendum, id figurate & ἀνθρωποπαθῶς dicitur, explicandum iudicialiter & exemplariter, ad exemplum iudicum, quos cognoscere prius oportet, quam decernere. Conf. DANN H. Hodof. p. 223.

Scientia Dei media sequentibus oppugnatur argumentis.

I. Si scientia Dei adæquate & sufficienter distinguitur in scientiam naturalem, & liberam, nulla nos vrget necessitas constituendi scientiam Dei tertiam, quæ vocetur media. At prius verum est. E. & posterius. Probatur antecedens: quia sicut inter ens, & non ens, nullum datur medium: ita inter scientiam Dei naturalem, & liberam, non interiacet scientia media. Nam obiectum scientiæ Dei naturalis est omne possibile, sub quo comprehenditur etiam non ens, i. e. actu non existens. Obiectum scientiæ Dei naturalis est omne ens actu existens in aliqua temporis differentia. Quare nullum manet obiectum residuum, scientia Dei media cognoscendum. Resp. negando, distinctionem scientiæ diuinæ in naturalem, & liberam, esse adæquatam. Nam illa circa possibilia, quatenus talia, hæc circa absolute futura versatur. Residua manent futura, conditionate talia. Recte igitur vocatur scientia media, propterea, quod obiectum eius inter res, sub ratione possibilitatis præcise spectatas, & res absolute futuras, interiacet.

Instantia 1. Conditiones oppositæ scientiæ Dei mediæ, vel sunt futuræ, vel non futuræ. Si non sunt futuræ, spectant ad obiectum scientiæ Dei naturalis. Hæc enim complectitur omnia possibilia, etiam ea, quæ nunquam futura sunt. Si sunt futuræ; pertinent ad obiectum scientiæ diuinæ liberæ; hæc enim considerat omnia, quæ sunt, fuerunt, erunt. Resp. Conditiones appositæ scientiæ Dei mediæ neque absolute futuræ, neque simpliciter non futuræ, sed indifferentes sunt ad futuram existentiam, & non existentiam. Nonnunquam enim implentur, nonnunquam deficiunt. Ratio est, quia connexionem habent cum effectu non necessariam, sed contingentem, adeoque esse, & non esse possunt.

Instantia 2. Conditionate futura, deficiente conditione, manent in sphæra possibilium, adeoque cognoscuntur a Deo scientia simplicis intelligentiæ. Resp. Haud exiguum discrimen est inter possibilia, & conditionate futura, vti vel ex traditione Dauidis futura sub hac conditione, si in ciuitate Kegila maneret, patescit, I Sam. XXIII. Plus sane important verba domini, dum dixit: Et Saul veniet, & hi tradent te; quam si dixisset: Fieri potest, vt Saul veniat, & Kegilitæ te ipsi tradant. Traditio Dauidis tum erat (vt ita dicam) futuribilis, non mere possibilis. Saul quippe ceperat consilium Dauidem inopinantem opprimendi: Kegilitæ præuia deliberatione conspirauerant in traditionem Dauidis: Deus decreuerat traditionem & oppressionem Dauidis permittere, si commoraretur in ciuitate Kegila. At de possibilibus nunquam exstitutis neque Deus format decretum, neque prudentes consultant homines. Quamuis igitur conditionate futura, quæ nunquam in actum traducuntur, cum possibilibus conueniant materialiter & ex parte: non tamen formaliter & per omnia conueniunt.

II. Scientia, quæ vocatur media, est conditionata. At nulla scientia Dei est conditionata. E. nulla scientia Dei est media. Maior est clara; quia recepto loquendi vsu scientia media appellatur conditionata. Vid. HILDEBRANDI institut. theol. p. 105. Minor probatur; quia Deus omnia cognoscit absolute. Vti enim nouit successiua absque successione suæ cognitionis: ita quoque nouit conditionata absque conditione, quæ afficiat intellectum diuinum. Resp. Scientia Dei media dicitur conditionata non subiectiue, quasi Deus aliquid conditionaliter cognoscat, sed est conditionata obiectiue, quia est scientia futurorum conditionatorum.

III. Quæcunque scientia nititur decreto prædeterminante, illa de Deo non est affirmanda. Atqui scientia media &c. Ergo. Maior probatur; quia decretum prædeterminans conuellit libertatem voluntatis humanæ. Minor constat; quia Deus scientia media præscit ea, quæ sub conditione futura sunt. Cum autem conditio illa cum effectu connexionem habeat contingentem, esse, & non esse potest. Quare vt impleatur, efficaci Dei decreto prædeterminanda est. Resp. Scientia Dei media non nititur decreto prædeterminante, sed coniuncta est cum decreto Dei hypothetico, quod cum non sit irrestibile, caussas in agendo liberas non prædeterminat.

IV. Quæcunque a Deo præsciuntur, ab ipso determinate cognoscuntur. Atqui sub conditione futura determinate non cognoscuntur. E. Minor probatur; quia conditionate futura non sunt determinatæ veritatis, sed sunt indifferentia ad futurum existentiam & non existentiam. Resp. neg. minor. Ad probationem dicimus, quod conditionate futura, perinde ac futura contingentia, bifariam considerentur: (1) quatenus eorum caussa se indifferenter habet ad vtrumque oppositorum, nempe ad impletionem, & non-impletionem conditionis. (2) Quatenus eorum caussa ad vnum oppositorum se determinatura est. Præscit Deus, quorsum voluntas humana inclinatura & se determinatura sit. Huc spectat responsio D. CALOVII: Indifferens quidem est obiectum scientiæ mediæ, sed non qua obiectum seu formaliter, sed tantum materialiter. Nam quod obiicitur scientiæ diuinæ, certum est ac determinatum, cum scientia Dei non sit dubia & indeterminata. Conf. D. CALOV. tom. II. syst p. 523. & synops. contr. p. 107.


### Question XLII. What is the wisdom of God?

Wisdom is a divine attribute ἐνεργητικὸν, through which God by most high counsel created, preserved, disposed, and ordered all things to certain ends, so that the divine glory might be illustrated and the salvation of men promoted.

Obs. The wisdom of God, although as to the thing it is the same as the knowledge of God, nevertheless imports more than knowledge. For besides knowledge it also imports the most exquisite counsel of God and the admirable disposition of all things, says D. FRIDEM. BECHMAN. in instit. theol. p. 120. Conf. D. BAYERI comp. theol. p. 212. (*)

Prob. I. From the Holy Scriptures. St. Paul, 1 Tim. I, 17, calls God alone wise. God alone is wise by essence from Himself, immutably and most perfectly. The Apostle marvels at the abyss of divine wisdom, Rom. XI, 33. The wisdom of God shines forth especially from the work of redemption, in which God, great in counsel, Jer. XXXII, 19 , discovered an admirable tempering of justice and mercy, so that the wisdom of God, hidden from the ages, is most highly to be praised. 1 Cor. II, 7.

II. The wisdom of God is known from the light of nature by way of causality, to those contemplating the most orderly system of the world. From which the most pious of kings sings: How many are your works, Jehovah; (which) you have made all in wisdom. Ps. CIV, 24. By way of eminence. Angels and men are wise: God is all-wise and wisdom itself.

Latin:

Sapientia est attributum diuinum ἐνεργητικὸν, per quod Deus altissimo consilio omnia condidit, conseruat, disponit, & ad certos fines ordinat, vt gloria diuina illustretur, & salus hominum promoueatur.

Obs. Sapientia Dei, licet, quod rem, idem sit, ac scientia Dei, plus tamen importat, quam scientia. Nam præter scientiam importat etiam consilium Dei exquisitissimum, & admirandam rerum omnium dispositionem, inquit D. FRIDEM. BECHMAN. in instit. theol. p. 120. Conf. D. BAYERI comp. theol. p. 212. (*)

Prob. I. E sacris litteris. S. Paullus 1 Tim. I, 17. solum Deum vocat sapientem. Solus Deus est sapiens per essentiam a seipso, immutabiliter & perfectissime. Apostolus abyssum sapientiae divinae miratur Rom. XI, 33. Elucescit inprimis sapientia Dei ex opere redemptionis, in quo Deus, magnus consilio, Ier. XXIII, 19. admirandum iustitiae & misericordiae temperamentum adinvenit, vt excelffime laudanda sit sapientia Dei, a saeculis abscondita. 1 Cor. II, 7.

II. Innotescit sapientia Dei e lumine naturae per viam causalitatis, ordinatissimum mundi systema intuentibus. Ex quo canit regum piissimus: Quam multa sunt opera tua, Iehouah; (quae) omnia in sapientia fecisti. Ps. CIV, 24. Per viam eminentiae. Sapientes sunt angeli & homines: Deus est omniens & sapientia ipsa.


### Question XLIII. What is the will of God?

The will of God is the divine essence itself, insofar as it is conceived by way of a power desiring the good, known by the intellect, and turning away from evil.

Obs. 1. Will is spoken of in three ways: it denotes τὸ θελητικὸν (the volitive), the power of willing. Thus it is used in Eph. I, 11: God works all things according to the decree of his will. τὴν θέλησιν (the volition), the act of willing or volition, which the sacred psalmist expresses in Ps. CXV, 3: Our God, who is in the heavens, does all things that he wills. τὸ θελητὸν (the volitum), the willed object. Thus Paul takes it in 1 Thess. IV, 3: This is the will of God, your sanctification. The last meaning does not belong here: the first two are of this place.

Obs. 2. The essence of God, and his will, and the act of willing, or volition, do not differ in God really, but only formally, or according to our mode of conceiving. For God does not will anything through a faculty superadded to the divine essence, or through an act really produced; for these are accidents, most alien to the perfection and simplicity of God; but through his essence. Therefore, the will of God is the divine essence, conceived with the connotation of an inclination toward the good.

Obs. 3. The object of the divine will is only the good, and that not φαινομένως (phenomenally), but ἀληθῶς (truly), not apparently, but truly such; because God does not will evil, nor can he will it, being supremely good. Ps. V, 5. Moreover, the good, about which the will of God is concerned, is twofold: one supreme, which is God himself: the other derived: which are created things. From which it follows that God himself is the primary object of his will, and creatures are the secondary object. God wills himself primarily, as the ultimate end, and all other things for his own sake. Prov. XVI, 4.

God desires and loves his own essence and goodness, not with the desire of longing, which is an affection for having that which is not yet present: but with the desire of complacency, which denotes acquiescence in the good that is possessed.

Proof. The will of God from the testimonies of Scripture, observ. I. adduced above. From the light of reason. For the will follows the intellect, since these two faculties never exist separately. In man, the will is a perfection that excels the brutes: Therefore, the will in God is in a most eminent mode. God created creatures freely; but liberty is an attribute of the will.

Latin:

Voluntas Dei est ipsa essentia divina, quatenus concipitur per modum potentiae, bonum, ab intellectu cognitum, appetentis, & malum auersantis.

Obs. 1. Voluntas dicitur tribus modis: notat τὸ θελητικὸν, potentiam volendi. Sic vsurpatur Eph. I, 11. Deus omnia operatur, secundum decretum voluntatis suae. τὴν θέλησιν, actum volendi seu volitionem, quam exprimit hieropsaltes Ps. CXV, 3. Deus noster, qui in caelis, (est) omnia, quae vult, facit. τὸ θελητὸν obiectum volitum. Ita accipit Paullus 1 Thess. IV, 3. Haec est voluntas Dei, sanctificatio vestra. Postrema significatio huc non pertinet: duae priores sunt huius loci.

Obs. 2. Essentia Dei, ipsiusque voluntas, & actus volendi, seu volitio, in Deo non differunt realiter, sed tantum formaliter, sive secundum nostrum concipiendi modum. Neque enim Deus aliquid vult per facultatem essentiae divinae superadditam, aut per actum realiter productum; haec enim sunt accidentia, perfectione & simplicitate Dei alienissima; sed per suam essentiam. Est itaque voluntas Dei essentia divina, concepta cum connotatione inclinationis ad bonum.

Obs. 3. Obiectum voluntatis divinae est tantum bonum, idque non φαινομένως, sed ἀληθῶς, non apparenter, sed vere tale; quia Deus malum non vult, nec velle potest, quippe summe bonus. Ps. V, 5. Est autem bonum, circa quod versatur voluntas Dei, aliud summum, quod est Deus ipse: aliud ortum: quod sunt res creatae. Ex quo consequitur, Deum ipsum voluntatis suae obiectum primarium, creaturas obiectum secundarium. Deus se vult primario, vt finem vltimum, reliqua omnia propter se ipsum. Prou. XVI, 4. se ipsum. Prou. XVI, 4.
