Suam ipsius essentiam & bonitatem appetit & amat Deus, non appetitu desiderii, qui est affectus habendi id, quod nondum adest: sed appetitu complacentiae, qui notat acquiescentiam in bono, quod habetur.

Prob. Voluntas Dei e testimoniis scripturae, obseru. I. supra adductis. Ex lumine rationis. Nam intellectum sequitur voluntas, cum hae duae facultates nunquam seorsum exsistant. In homine voluntas est perfectio, quae brutis antecellit: Ergo voluntas in Deo est modo eminentissimo. Condidit Deus creaturas libere; libertas autem est attributum voluntatis.


### Question XLIV. How is the will of God distinguished?

The will of God is distinguished into natural and free. The former is that by which God wills and loves himself, as the highest good, by nature, so that he cannot not will and love himself: the latter is that by which God wills all things outside himself in such a way that he can also not will them. Into secret and revealed. The former is that by which God wills many things which are not necessary for us to know, and has not willed to reveal: the latter is that by which he has willed to explain candidly to us in his word those things which make for our salvation. Into absolute and conditional. The former is that by which God wills something without condition: the latter is that by which God wills something under a certain condition. Into absolute and ordained. The former is that by which God wills something to be brought about by his absolute power, or not bound to secondary causes: the latter is that by which God wills something to be brought about by his ordained power, bound to secondary causes and a certain order of means instituted by himself. Into antecedent and consequent. The former is that by which God wills something, without regard to a cause or condition foreseen on the part of creatures: the latter is that by which God wills something, with regard to a condition which he himself requires on the part of creatures. There also occurs a distinction of the divine will into the will of sign and of good pleasure. The former is when God shows by a certain sign that he wills or does not will something: the latter is the internal act of the will, by which God wills the good and turns away from evil.

God wills and loves himself necessarily; because in him every notion of good appears, without any defect. When the will loves something, so that it could not love it, or even pursue it with hatred: this happens because either some evil or some imperfection is proposed to the will in that object, on account of which the will ceases from love and is moved to the opposite act, namely, hatred. But indeed, no evil, no imperfection falls into God, and therefore no cause can be rendered why God would or could not love himself, or pursue himself with hatred. But God wills creatures freely, so that he could also not will them. For he does not need the comfort of creatures, since he is αὐταρκέστατος (self-sufficient), most fully sufficient to himself. From which God is said to work all things according to the counsel of his will, Eph. 1:11, and to distribute his gifts as he wills, 1 Cor. 12:11.

You say: 1. The necessity of willing and loving himself seems to be a certain imperfection in God, both because it is similar to the mode of operating of natural agents, which is imperfect, and also, [they] perish, even an unhappy day, prepared for the wicked man. There are indeed other things which pertain to the proofs mentioned, namely all those of such a kind which testify that God turns and directs all things to his own glory, e.g., Ps. 19:2, 9:17, 11:36, Col. 1:16.

also, because liberty is a greater perfection than necessity. Resp. There is a threefold necessity in acting. One is violent, which is from an intrinsic source. Another is natural, which indeed is from an intrinsic source, but inanimate, or at least irrational. Both are imperfect. The third is natural, vital, and supremely voluntary. This is a great perfection. And such a necessity of willing and loving exists in God with respect to the highest and infinite good. Indeed, this necessity is more perfect than the opposite liberty.

Dicis: 2. The natural will, by the very fact that it is necessary, is not will properly so called; for the will ought to be free. Resp. The will of God, considered in itself and radically, is the divine essence itself. But just as this is necessary, so also is the will of God. But if it is considered objectively: by reason of an extrinsic object, namely creatures, it is most free.

Dicis: 3. If God necessarily wills and loves himself, he necessarily also wills creatures; because he himself is the end of creatures; and he who necessarily wills the end, necessarily wills also the means leading to the end. Resp. I deny the consequence. For creatures do not have the nature of means, which are simply necessary for the ultimate end. For God, if the creature did not exist, would be most blessed.

4. Liberty of choice brings in a certain mutability, or flexibility of the will, since it consists in a difference toward either of the opposites, and therefore it cannot be attributed to the immutable God. Resp. Liberty of choice does not bring in mutability of the will, but the election of different things, with the prior light of directing knowledge: which belongs to God in a most perfect way.

Prob. b. That there is in God a hidden and a revealed will, scripture teaches: The former, Prov. 25:2. It is the glory of God to conceal a word: but the glory of kings to search out a word, and Rom. 11:33, where Paul exclaims: O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! how inscrutable are his judgments! and his ways past finding out! for who has known the mind of the Lord? or who has been his counselor? The latter, however, when the prophet king says, Ps. 147:19-20. He declares his words to Jacob, his statutes and his judgments to Israel. He has not done so to any nation, nor have they known his judgments. The apostle supports this, Eph. 1:9. He makes known to us the mystery of his will according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in himself.

Here it must be observed that the secret will of God and the revealed will do not concern the same object, but rather a different one. For whatever is hidden in the secret will of God, that, as such, is not the object of the revealed will. And therefore, no conflict is to be imagined here, as if God willed one thing by His secret will and another by His revealed will. For thus the wills of God would be contrary, nor would the revealed will of God be indubitable and infallible.

Prob. c. The absolute will of God is shown to us by the most pious king, Ps. CXV, 3. Our God, who is in the heavens, does all that He wills. And Jehovah Himself says: My counsel shall stand, and I will do My will. Is. XLVI, 10. By a conditional will, God wills that we be heaped with many blessings. Hence He promises His blessing, under the condition of sincere obedience, Deut. XXVIII, 1 sqq. If you will obey the voice of Jehovah, your God, you shall be blessed in the city, and blessed in the field. Thus God wills all men to be saved under the condition of faith persevering in Christ, 1 Tim. II, 4. Jn. III, 36.

You say: I. If God wills all men to be saved, under the condition of persevering faith, He either wills that condition to come to pass, or He does not. If He does not will it, He will be frustrated in His end, which is alien to divine wisdom: if He wills it, all men will believe. For what God wills, He does, Ps. CXV, 3. Resp. God wills that condition to come to pass, but not by a precise, peremptory, and irresistible will, but rather by an ordered will, by which He has certainly dispensed the means: whoever rightly uses these, to them are divinely suggested the powers to fulfill that condition.

You say: II. An inefficacious will is not to be attributed to God. A conditional will is inefficacious. Therefore. The major is proved; because the will of God is omnipotent. The minor is evident, since a conditional will is not always fulfilled. Resp. A conditional will is efficacious by reason of its intention: although the event does not always respond to it. For God seriously intends the end (e.g., the salvation of men) to be obtained through the most valid means which He has ordained. Also, a conditional will is always fulfilled, the condition being posited. For by the very fact that it is called conditional, it does not tend toward the end except through the positing of the condition.

Instance: Thus God will be frustrated in His end, since that condition is not always fulfilled. Resp. The general end, namely the glory of His goodness and offered grace, God always obtains: the special end, which redounds to the benefit of man, the man himself hinders by petulantly rejecting the offered means by which the prefixed condition is translated into act.

You say: III. Whatever will presupposes a condition in man, that depends on, or is determined by, the will of man. But the will of God does not depend on, nor is it determined by, the will of man. But the will of God presupposes no condition in man. Resp. I deny the major; because dependence is from causes. The presupposed condition is not the cause, nor the norm of the divine will, but pertains to the order freely constituted by God.

You say: IV. Nothing is prior to the divine will. Therefore it presupposes no condition in man. Resp. Nothing is prior to the divine will, by reason of real existence; although God most wisely pre-established that condition, and regards that reason a priori in conferring the effect out of mere grace.

Prob. d. When the will of God is distinguished into absolute and ordered, then the absolute will is called [such] from law, order, or the course of nature, or of secondary causes. Thus God willed, when Joshua was contending with impious enemies, that the sun should stand still in the midst of heaven, Josh. X, 13. But the ordered will receives its name from the order which, since God has constituted it out of inscrutable wisdom, He applies Himself to the same in acting out of mere grace. Thus God in the kingdom of nature wills the life of men to be preserved through certain foods and nourishment: in the kingdom of grace He wills to save men through the Word and sacraments, as the most efficacious means of grace and salvation. Whence it is simultaneously clear, conditional and ordained will, do not entirely coincide, although at first glance it might seem so.

By the conditional will, God wills to save men, if they believe; by the ordained will, He wills that they believe, i.e., that from the means of grace, rightly used, they may conceive and establish faith . Prob. e. We shall confirm the distinction of the divine will into antecedent and consequent below, and defend it against objections.

Prob. f. The distinction of the divine will into the will of sign and of good pleasure is found both among the scholastics and among our own theologians.

LOMBARD used it (I Sent. dist. XLV, cap. III, et seqq.), THOMAS (in I, quæst. XIX, artic. XII), B. BALTHASAR MEISNER (anthropol. disp. XII, quæst. I), GERHARD (exeg. libr. de Deo § 269), and others.

Regarding this distinction, you will observe a) that the will of sign, taken formally and abstractively, is not properly will, but is only called so by extrinsic denomination, because of its relation to the will of good pleasure, of which it is a sign .

The will of good pleasure, however, denotes the act itself of the divine will, by which He wills something. Whence it is clear that this distinction is only analogical, since the will of sign is called will improperly, and the will of good pleasure properly. b) Under the name of the will of good pleasure, the scholastics include not only the will to do good, but also the permission of the reprobation of the infidels and the decree of their damnation.

But since the word εὐδοκία, or good pleasure, is extended more broadly than this way of signifying justly allows, D. HENR. MÜLLER (in theol. scholast. p. 137) distinguishes the divine will into the will of sign and of pleasure. He subdistinguishes the will of pleasure into the will of good pleasure, of permission, and of punishment. The former is that by which God is inclined to do good to the pious: the latter is that by which God permits infidels to fall into sins, and finally to be delivered into a reprobate sense: the third is that by which God wills the impious to be punished.

The will of sign, however, is when God shows by a certain sign that He wills or does not will something: which sign they make fivefold: precept, prohibition, counsel, permission, and operation, according to the most celebrated verse of DURANDUS: He commands and prohibits, permits, counsels, fulfills. c) That there is a perpetual harmony between the will of sign and the will of good pleasure, we prove 1) from the nature of the sign and the signified.

The will of sign is nothing else is nothing other than an external sign of the internal will. Just as, therefore, every true sign is referred to its signified, and represents it, but does not indicate something different from or opposite to it: so the will of the sign truly notifies the will of the divine good pleasure, but does not manifest anything contrary to this. 2) From the truthfulness & holiness of God. He who utters one thing with his mouth and suppresses another in his heart acts the hypocrite. This does not befit a truthful man, nor an honest man: much less the most truthful God. 3) From the unity of the divine will. There are not given in God contrary or contradictory wills. But if God were to command in His word all men to repent, to believe in Christ, to pursue a life of piety; and yet by His secret good pleasure He did not will those things to be done by all: the will of the sign would be contrary or contradictorily opposed to the internal good pleasure. 4) From the consequent absurdity. If God does not always will what He testifies by the will of the sign that He wills, it is all over for the truth of Scripture. For although Holy Scripture clearly asserts what God wills to be done by us: yet we must always doubt whether the assertions of Holy Scripture truly agree with the internal good pleasure of the divine will.

BEZA, ZANCHIUS, PISCATOR, and others, relying on the following arguments, impugn the harmony of the will of the sign and the will of the divine good pleasure.

I. God signified by His word to Abraham that he should slaughter his son, and yet He did not will that slaughter with an internal affection, Gen. XXII, 11. Therefore, the will of the sign does not always agree with the will of the divine good pleasure. Resp. God did not say one thing to Abraham with His mouth and feel another within His mind, but He only willed this, that he should offer his son as a burnt offering. When Abraham performed this, the exploratory precept was fulfilled. But that God was going to compensate for the sacrifice in another way was unknown to Abraham. For it was a πειραστικὴ action, in which the whole will of God does not shine forth immediately. But God manifested the way of salvation most openly.

II. God announced the death of Hezekiah, Is. XXXVIII, 1. seqq., which, however, He did not will. Resp. Just as God had denounced death to Hezekiah: so he had to die entirely, if you attend to the ordained decree of God, conformable to the course of nature; his life was preserved for the praying Hezekiah for XV years, by the decrees of an extraordinary privilege. God indeed established the order of nature, yet He reserved for Himself the freedom of acting outside, or above, this established order.

III. God threatened the Ninevites with destruction, Jon. III, 2. And yet He did not bring that threat to execution. Therefore, the will of the sign did not accord with the will of the good pleasure. Resp. Distinguish between the absolute and the conditional will: the latter includes 'if' and 'unless'. God willed to destroy the Ninevites, unless they repented. The threat is understood with the exception of repentance.

IV. God commanded Pharaoh the dismissal of the Israelite people, and yet He hardened his heart, Exod. VII, 2. 3. Therefore, the will of the sign was not conformable to the will of the divine good pleasure. Resp. The precept given to Pharaoh about dismissing the people was most serious. For God willed from the heart that Pharaoh should dismiss the people. But when he resisted the divine will, God, in punishment for his preceding sins, hardened him by a just judgment, by permitting that he who did not allow himself to be softened, left to himself, should remain hard to his own destruction.

Latin:

Voluntas Dei distinguitur in naturalem, & liberam. Illa est, qua Deus seipsum, ceu summum bonum, per naturam ita vult & amat, vt non possit non seipsum velle & amare: haec est, qua Deus omnia extra se ita vult, vt possit eadem non velle. In arcanam, & reuelatam. Illa est, qua Deus multa vult, quae scitu nobis non sunt necessaria, reuelare noluit: haec est, qua verbo suo candide exponere nobis voluit ea, quae ad nostram salutem faciunt. In absolutam, & conditionatam. Illa est, qua Deus aliquid vult sine conditione: haec est, qua Deus aliquid vult sub certa conditione. In absolutam, & ordinatam. Illa est, qua Deus vult aliquid efficiendum potentia sua absoluta, seu ad causas secundas non alligata: haec est, qua Deus vult aliquid efficiendum potentia ordinata, ad causas secundas certumque mediorum ordinem, a se institutum, alligata. In antecedentem, & consequentem. Illa est, qua Deus aliquid vult, non habita ratione causae vel conditionis ex parte creaturarum praeuisae: haec est, qua Deus aliquid vult, habita ratione conditionis, quam ipse ex parte creaturarum requirit. Occurrit etiam distinctio voluntatis diuinae in voluntatem signi, & beneplaciti. Illa est, cum Deus certo signo ostendit, se aliquid velle, aut nolle: haec est internus actus voluntatis, quo Deus bonum vult, & malum auersatur.

Prob. a. Deus seipsum vult & amat necessario; quia in ipso omnis ratio boni, fine vllo defectu, apparet. Quando voluntas aliquid amat, vt illud possit non amare, vel etiam odio prosequi: id ideo fit, quia voluntati in obiecto illo vel malum aliquod, vel aliqua imperfectio proponitur, propter quam voluntas cessat ab amore, & ad oppositum actum, odium scilicet, mouetur. At vero in Deum nullum malum, nulla imperfectio cadit, adeo que nulla potest reddi causa, cur Deus seipsum non diligere, vel odio prosequi velit, aut possit. Creaturas autem Deus vult libere, vt etiam possit eas non velle. Neque enim indiget conforto creaturarum, cum fit αὐταρκέστατος, sibi ipsi plenissime sufficiens. Ex quo Deus omnia secundum consilium voluntatis suae operari, Eph. I, 11. & dona sua, prout vult, distribuere dicitur, 1 Cor. XII, 11.

Dicis: 1. Necessitas volendi & amandi seipsum, videtur quaedam in Deo, esse imperfectio, tum quia similis est modo operandi agentium naturalium, qui imperfectus est, tum etiam, deant, etiam infelix dies, improbo homini paratus. Sunt vero alia, quae pertinent, dieta probantia, nimirum omnia eiusmodi, quae testantur, Deum vniuersas res vertere ac dirigere ad suam gloriam, c. g. Ps. XIX, 2. IX, 17. XI, 36. Col. I, 16.

etiam, quia libertas est maior perfectio, quam necessitas. Resp. Triplex est necessitas in agendo. Una violenta, quae est ab intrinseco. Altera naturalis, quae quidem est ab intrinseco, sed inanimata, vel saltem irrationalis. Utraque est imperfecta. Tertia est naturalis, vitalis & summe voluntaria. Haec magna perfectio est. Et talis necessitas volendi atque amandi est in Deo respectu summi & infiniti boni. Immo haec necessitas est perfectior, quam libertas opposita.

Dicis: 2. Voluntas naturalis eo ipso, quod est necessaria, non est voluntas proprie dicta; nam voluntas debet esse libera. Resp. Voluntas Dei in se & radicaliter spectata est ipsa essentia divina. Sicut autem haec est necessaria, ita & voluntas Dei. At si consideretur obiective: ratione obiecti extrinseci, nempe creaturarum, liberrima est.

Dicis: 3. Si Deus seipsum necessario vult & amat, necessario etiam vult creaturas; quia ipse est finis creaturarum; qui autem necessario vult finem, necessario vult etiam media ad finem ducentia. Resp. Neg. consequ. Creaturae enim non habent rationem mediorum, ad finem ultimum simpliciter necessariorum. Deus quippe non exsistente creatura foret beatissimus.

Dicis: 4. Libertas arbitrii infert quandam mutabilitatem, aut flexibilitatem voluntatis, cum consistat in differentia ad utrumque oppositorum, adeoque Deo immutabili tribui nequit. Resp. Libertas arbitrii non infert mutabilitatem voluntatis, sed electionem rerum diversarum, cum praevio lumine scientiae dirigentis: quae Deo modo perfectissimo competit. *

Prob. b. Dari in Deo voluntatem arcanam, & revelatam, docet scriptura:.* Illam quidem, Prou. XXV, 2. Gloria Dei est occultare verbum: sed gloria regum investigare verbum, & Rom. XI, 33. ubi Paullus exclamat: O profunditatem divitiarum & sapientiae & cognitionis Dei! quam inscrutabilia sunt iudicia eius! & impervestigabiles viae eius! quis enim cognovit mentem domini? aut quis consiliarius eius fuit? Hanc vero, dum propheta rex inquit, Ps. CXLVII, 19. 20. Annuntiat verba sua Iacobo, statuta sua & iudicia Israëli. Non facit sic ulli genti, nec iudicia eius noverunt. Suffragatur apostolus, Eph. I, 9. Notum facit nobis mysterium voluntatis suae iuxta beneplacitum suum, quod proposuit in seipso.

hic observandum est voluntatem Dei arcanam, & revelatam, non versari circa idem, sed circa diversum obiectum. Quidquid enim reconditum est in arcana Dei voluntate, id qua tale revelatae voluntatis obiectum non est. Ideoque nulla pugna heic fingenda est, quasi aliud Deus velit arcana voluntate, aliud revelata. Sic enim contrariae essent Dei voluntates, nec revelata Dei voluntas indubia & infallibilis foret.

Prob. c. Absoluta Dei voluntas nobis ostenditur a rege piissimo, Ps. CXV, 3. Deus noster, qui in caelis (est), omnia, quae vult, facit. Et ipse Iehouah inquit: Consilium meum stabit, & voluntatem meam faciam. Es. XLVI, 10. Voluntate conditionata Deus nos plurimis bonis vult cumulatos. Exinde promittit benedictionem suam, sub conditione sincerae obedientiae, Deut. XXVIII, 1. sqq. Si obedueris voci Iehouah, Dei tui, benedictus tu in urbe (eris), & benedictus tu in agro. Sic Deus omnes homines vult salvos fieri sub conditione perseverantis in Christum fidei, 1 Tim. II, 4. Io. III, 36.

Dicis: I. Si Deus omnes homines vult salvos fieri, sub conditione perseverantis fidei, vel vult eam conditionem evenire, vel non vult. Si non vult, frustrabitur fine suo, quod a sapientia divina est alienum: si vult, omnes homines credent. Nam quae Deus vult, facit, Ps. CXV, 3. Resp. Deus vult illam conditionem evenire, sed non voluntate praecisa, peremptoria & irresistibili, verum ordinata, qua certe dispensavit media: quicunque his rite utuntur, illis divinitus suggeruntur vires ad conditionem illam implendam.

Dicis: II. Voluntas inefficax Deo non est tribuenda. Voluntas conditionata est inefficax. Ergo. Maior probatur; quia voluntas Dei est omnipotens. Minor constat, quoniam voluntas conditionata non semper impletur. Resp. Voluntas conditionata est efficax ratione intentionis: quamuis illi non semper respondeat eventus. Serio quippe Deus intendit finem (v. gr. salutem hominum) per validissima media, quae ordinavit, obtinendum. Semper etiam impletur voluntas conditionata, posita conditione. Nam eo ipso, quod conditionata dicitur, non tendit in finem, nisi per conditionis positionem.

Instantia: Sic Deus frustrabitur fine suo, cum illa conditio non semper impletur. Resp. Finem generalem, nempe gloriam bonitatis & oblatae gratiae, Deus semper obtinet: finem specialem, qui in commodum hominis cedit, ipse homo impedit, oblata media, quibus praefixa conditio in actum traducitur, petulanter reiiciendo.

Dicis: III. Quaecunque voluntas praesupponit conditionem in homine, illa ab hominis voluntate dependet, aut determinatur. At voluntas Dei ab hominis voluntate non dependet, neque determinatur. At voluntas Dei in homine nullam conditionem praesupponit. Resp. Neg. maiorem; quia dependentia est a causis. Conditio praesupposita non est causa, neque norma voluntatis divinae, sed pertinet ad ordinem, a Deo libere constitutum.

Dicis: IV. Voluntate divina nil prius est. Ergo illa nullam in homine conditionem praesupponit. Resp. Voluntate divina nil prius est, ratione realis existentiae; quamuis conditionem illam Deus sapientissime praestituerit, eamque rationem a priori in effectu conferendo ex mera gratia respiciat.

Prob. d. Quando voluntas Dei distinguitur in absolutam, & ordinatam, tunc voluntas absoluta dicitur a lege, ordine aut cursu naturae, seu causarum secundarum. Sic voluit Deus, confligente Iosua cum hostibus impiis, solem stare in medio caeli, Ios. X, 13. Voluntas autem ordinata nomen accipit ab ordine, quem cum Deus ex inscrutabili sapientia constituerit, eidem in agendo ex mera gratia se applicat. Sic Deus in regno naturae vitam hominum vult conferuatam per certos cibos & alimenta: in regno gratiae homines salvare vult per verbum & sacramenta, tanquam efficacissima gratiae salutisque media. Vnde simul patet, voluntatem conditionatam, & ordinatam, non omnino coincidere, licet primo intuitu ita videri possit.

Voluntate conditionata Deus homines vult saluare, si credant; voluntate ordinata vult, ut credant, i. e: vt ex mediis gratiæ, recte vsurpatis, fidem concipiant & stabiliant . Prob. e. Distinctionem voluntatis diuinæ in antecedentem, & consequentem infra confirmabimus & ab obiectionibus vindicabimus.

Prob. f. Distinctio voluntatis diuinæ in voluntatem signi, & beneplaciti, inuenitur tum apud scholasticos, tum apud nostrates theologos.

Vsurpauit eandem LOMBARDVS I. sent. dist. XLV. cap. III. seqq. THOMAS in I. quæst. XIX. artic. XII. b. BALTHAS. MEISNERVS anthropol. disp. XII. quæst. I. GERHARD. exeg. libr. de Deo §. 269. & alii.

Circa quam distinctionem obseruabis a) quod voluntas signi, formaliter & abstractiue sumta, proprie non fit voluntas, sed tantum per extrinsecam denominationem ita dicatur, propter habitudinem ad voluntatem beneplaciti, cuius signum est .

Voluntas autem beneplaciti denotat actum ipsum diuinæ voluntatis, quo aliquid vult. Vnde patet, hanc distinctionem tantum esse analogicam, cum voluntas signi improprie, voluntas beneplaciti proprie voluntas dicatur. b) Scholastici nomine voluntatis beneplaciti complectuntur non tantum voluntatem benefaciendi, sed & permissionem reprobationis infidelium & eorum damnationis decretum.

Cum autem vox εὐδοκία, siue beneplacitum, iusto latius hoc significandi modo extendatur, D. HENR. MVLLERVS in theol. scholast. p. 137. voluntatem diuinam distinguit in voluntatem signi & placiti. Voluntatem placiti subdistinguit in voluntatem beneplaciti, permissionis & punitionis. Ista est, qua Deus ad benefaciendum piis propendet: illa est, qua Deus permittit, vt infideles in peccata prolabantur, & tandem in sensum reprobum tradantur: hæc est, qua Deus impios vult punitos.

Voluntas autem signi est, cum Deus certo signo ostendit, se aliquid velle, aut nolle: quale signum quintuplex faciunt: præceptum, prohibitum consilium, permissionem, & operationem, secundum decantatissimum DVRANDI versiculum: Præcipit ac prohibet, permittit, consulit, implet. c) Perpetuam esse harmoniam voluntatis signi, & voluntatis beneplaciti, probamus 1) a natura signi & signati.

Voluntas signi nihil aliud est, quam externum signum voluntatis internæ. Sicut igitur omne verum signum refertur ad suum signatum, idque repræsentat, non autem diuersum ab hoc, aut oppositum indicat: ita voluntas signi vere notificat voluntatem beneplaciti diuini, non autem huic contrarium manifestat. 2) A veracitate & sanctitate Dei. Qui aliud ore promit, aliud corde premit, hypocritam agit. Non hominem veracem, non virum honestum id decet: multo minus Deum veracissimum. 3) A diuinæ voluntatis vnitate. Non dantur in Deo voluntates contrariæ, aut contradictoriæ. Si autem Deus verbo suo præciperet omnibus hominibus pœnitentiam agere, in Christum credere, pietatem vitæ sectari; neque tamen arcano beneplacito vellet ea ab omnibus fieri: voluntas signi interno beneplacito contraria, aut contradictorie opposita foret. 4) A consequente absurdo. Si, quæ voluntate signi Deus se velle testatur, non semper vult, actum est de veritate scripturæ. Nam quamuis S. scriptura liquido asserat, quid Deus a nobis fieri velit: semper tamen dubitandum nobis erit, an assertiones S. scripturæ cum interno voluntatis diuinæ beneplacito vere consentiant.

Harmoniam voluntatis signi & voluntatis beneplaciti diuini BEZA, ZANCHIVS, PISCATOR, & alii, sequentibus innixi argumentis impugnant.

I. Deus verbo suo significauit Abrahamo, vt mactaret filium suum, neque tamen illam mactationem interno voluit affectu, Gen. XXII, 11. Ergo voluntas signi non semper consentit cum voluntate beneplaciti diuini. Resp. Deus Abrahamo non aliud ore dicebat, aliud intra mentem sentiebat, sed tantum hoc volebat, vt filium suum offerret in holocaustum. Cum hoc præstitit Abrahamus, præceptum exploratiuum fuit expletum. Quod autem Deus alia ratione sacrificium compensaturus esset, Abrahamo erat ignotum. Erat enim actio πειραστικὴ, in qua tota Dei voluntas non e vestigio illucesceit. Sed viam salutis Deus apertissime manifestauit.

II. Deus annuntiauit mortem Hiskiæ, Es. XXXVIII, 1. seqq. quam tamen noluit. Resp. Sicut Deus Hiskiæ mortem denuntiauerat: ita ipsi omnino moriendum erat, si attendas decretum Dei ordinatum, cursui naturæ conforme: conseruabatur vita precanti Hiskiæ XV. annos, decreta priuilegii extraordinarii. Deus quidem ordinem naturæ constituit, reseruauit tamen sibi libertatem agendi, extra, vel supra hunc ordinem constitutum.

III. Deus comminatus est Niniuites internecionem. Ion. III, 2. Neque tamen illam comminationem exsecutioni dedit. Ergo voluntas signi non concordauit cum voluntate beneplaciti. Resp. dist. inter voluntatem absolutam & conditionatam: hæc complectitur si, & nisi. Voluit Deus perdere Niniuitas, nisi resipiscerent. Comminatio intelligitur cum exceptione pœnitentiæ.

IV. Præcepit Deus Pharaoni dimissionem populi Israëlitici, & tamen cor ipsius induravit. Exod. VII, 2. 3. Ergo voluntas signi non fuit conformis voluntati beneplaciti diuini. Resp. Præceptum Pharaoni datum de dimittendo populo maxime fuit serium. Ex animo enim volebat Deus, vt Pharao populum dimitteret. At cum hic voluntati diuinæ reluctaretur, Deus in pœnam antegressorum peccatorum eum iusto iudicio indurauit permittendo, vt ille, qui se emolliri non patiebatur, sibi permissus durus maneret in propriam perniciem.


### Quæst. XLV. What is the grace of God?

The grace of God is a divine ἐνεργητικὸν attribute, by which God loves both all creatures, and especially intelligent creatures, angels and men, and is inclined to do good to them.

Obs. I. The affection of God, benevolently inclined toward creatures, is distinguished by various names according to the reason of the different things connoted. For insofar as it is provoked by no merit, it is called grace; for it is opposed to merits, Rom. XI, 6. (*); in so far as He wills some good to be communicated to creatures, it is called love, charity, affection, John III, 16. For to love signifies to will good to someone, as THOMAS P. I. Q. 20. art. 2. judges. In so far as He promotes the conveniences of creatures by conferred benefits, it is named benignity, in Greek χρησότης, ἀπὸ τᾶ χρησε̃, from useful. Tit. III, 4. In so far as He is moved by the sight of misery to dispel it, it is called mercy. Tit. III, 5. These are the same in God, they are distinguished by us by reason of objects and effects.

Obs. II. The grace of God, benevolently inclined toward all creatures, is proved from Ps. XXXIII, 5. The earth is full of the grace of God. In the source it is חֶסֶד, which is rendered: benignity, grace, mercy. D. GEIERUS rendered it by grace, by which God imparts benefits to all creatures that are in the whole world of lands. For this reason, here it is understood in the most general sense as all grace of creation, preservation, cooperation, redemption, sanctification, salvation.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, who deny that mercy is an essential attribute of God, who rely on the following arguments:

I. Whatever does not perpetually belong to God is not an essential attribute of God. But mercy does not perpetually belong to God. Therefore. The minor is proved; because there is no place for mercy where there is no misery. But this did not afflict man in the state of innocence. Resp. Distinguish between the first and second act of mercy, or between the attribute of mercy and its exercise. The attribute of mercy always belongs to God; the misery of man provides the occasion for the exercise of mercy.

II. If God were by nature merciful, He would punish no sin. But God punishes sin. Therefore, God is not by nature merciful. The consequence of the major is proved; because He does nothing against those things which naturally inhere in God, for example, He does nothing against His wisdom, holiness, or truthfulness. But if God were to punish sin, He would act against natural mercy. Resp. Distinguish between absolute mercy and ordered mercy, or that tempered by justice. The mercy of God is not absolute, excluding all satisfaction, but always regards justice as its inseparable companion. Therefore, by punishing sin, God does nothing at all against His essential mercy, since He neither punishes unmercifully (**), nor forgives unjustly; but He wisely tempers justice with mercy.

III. He upon whom the compassion of the heart does not fall, upon him mercy does not fall. But it does not fall upon God, etc. Therefore. The major is evident; because mercy is a compassion in our heart for the misery of another, as AUGUSTINE defines in book XIX of The City of God, ch. V. The minor is proved; because God is the purest act, devoid of all passion. Resp. Distinguish between the precise or formal reason of mercy and its material or determined reasons. Mercy, viewed precisely and formally, denotes grace toward the needy or favor toward the miserable. In this way, mercy truly and really exists in God; although it is in Him eminently, i.e., in a most excellent and perfect manner. Viewed materially and determinately, mercy involves some imperfections, because 1) in man it is an accident; 2) it includes compassion of the heart and a certain sadness. In this way, mercy does not exist in God as an imperfection.

Latin:

Gratia Dei est attributum diuinum ἐνεργητικὸν, quo Deus cum creaturas omnes, tum in primis creaturas intelligentes, angelos & homines, amat, & ad benefaciendum iisdem propendet.

Obs. I. Affectus Dei, in creaturas beneuole propensus, pro ratione diuersorum connotatorum diuersis insignitur nominibus. Nam quatenus nullo prouocatus est merito, vocatur gratia; quippe quæ meritis opponitur, Rom. XI, 6. (*); quatenus creaturis vult bonum aliquod communicatum, dicitur amor, caritas, dilectio, Io. III, 16. nam amare significat velle alicui bonum, censente THOMA P. I. Q. 20. art. 2. quatenus collatis beneficiis commoda creaturarum promouet, nuncupatur benignitas, græce χρησότης, ἀπὸ τᾶ χρησε̃, ab vtili. Tit. III, 4. quatenus intuitu miseriæ mouetur ad eam depellendam, appellatur misericordia. Tit. III, 5. Sunt hæc in Deo ταυτὸ, distinguuntur a nobis ratione obiectorum, & effectorum.

Obs. II. Probatur gratia Dei, in omnes creaturas beneuole propensa, e Ps. XXXIII, 5. Gratia Dei plena est terra. In fonte est חֶסֶד, quæ redditur: benignitas, gratia, misericordia. D. GEIERVS reddidit per gratiam, qua Deus omnibus creaturis, quæ sunt in vniuerso terrarum orbe, beneficia impertitur. Quam ob rem hic sensu generalissimo intelligitur omnis gratia creationis, conseruationis, cooperationis, redemtionis, sanctificationis, saluationis.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, negantium, misericordiam esse attributum Dei essentiale, qui nituntur sequentibus argumentis:

I. Quidquid Deo non perpetuo competit, non est attributum Dei essentiale. Atqui misericordia Deo perpetuo non competit. Ergo. Minor probatur; quia misericordiæ non est locus, vbi nulla est miseria. Sed hæc in statu innocentiæ hominem non affligebat. Resp. dist. inter actum primum & secundum misericordiæ, siue inter attributum misericordiæ, & eius exercitium. Attributum misericordiæ Deo semper competit; exercitio misericordiæ occasionem præbet hominis miseria.

II. Si Deus natura misericors esset, nullum peccatum puniret. At Deus punit peccatum. E. Deus natura non est misericors. Consequ. maioris probatur; quia contra ea, quæ naturaliter Deo insunt, ipse nihil agit, v. gr. nihil agit contra sapientiam, sanctitatem, veracitatem suam. Sed si Deus peccatuin puniret, contra naturalem misericordiam ageret. Resp. dist. inter misericordiam absolutam, & ordinatam, siue iustitia temperatam. Misericordia Dei non est absoluta, omnem satisfactionem excludens, sed iustitiam velut indiuiduam comitem semper respicit. Propterea Deus peccatum puniendo contra essentialem suam misericordiam nil quidquam agit, siquidem nec immisericorditer punit (**), nec iniuste condonat; sed sapienter iustitiam cum misericordia temperat.

III. In quem non cadit cordis compassio, in illum non cadit misericordia. Atqui in Deum non &c. E. Maior constat; quia misericordia est alienæ miseriæ in corde nostro compassio, definiente AVGVSTINO libr. XIX. de ciu. Dei, c. V. Minor probatur; quia Deus est actus purissimus, omnis passionis expers. Resp. dist. inter rationem præcisam, seu formalem misericordiæ, & inter rationes eius materiales, seu determinatas. Misericordia præcise & formaliter spectata notat gratiam erga egenum, seu fauorem erga miserum. Hac ratione misericordia Deo vere & realiter inest; quamuis in eo sit eminenter, i. e. modo excellentissimo & perfectissimo. Materialiter & determinate spectata misericordia nonnullas inuoluit imperfectiones, quia 1) in homine est accidens; 2) includit compassionem cordis & quandam tristitiam. Hoc modo imperfectioni misericordia non est in Deo.


### Question XLVI. What is the justice of God?

The justice of God is a divine ἐνεργητικὸν attribute, by the power of which God wills and does all things that are conformable to His eternal law, (a) prescribes suitable laws to creatures, (b) fulfills promises made to men, (c) rewards the good (d) and punishes the impious (e).

Obs. I. By the justice of God here is not understood the justice from God, by which He justifies us; which is twofold (*), evangelical, consisting in the remission of sins and the imputation of the justice of Christ, Rom. III, 22: and legal, consisting in conformity with the law, which is begun in this life, and will be consummated only in the future life: but here justice is predicated of God, insofar as it is an essential property in God.

Obs. II. The justice of God is in one sense universal, which is the rectitude of the immutable divine will, by which God wills, approves, and does all things that are good and right, conformably to His eternal law; which coincides with the holiness of God: in another sense it is particular, which is exercised toward creatures by the most righteous government of them, and the retribution of good and evil.

Obs. III. The justice of God, which is exercised toward creatures, is in one sense dispositive, in another compensative. The former is that by which God governs the life of intelligent creatures (angels and men) by laws given to them that are suitable. The latter is either remunerative, by which God is moved to confer rewards upon the pious; or vindicative, by which God is moved to inflict punishments upon the impious.

Obs. IV. Commutative justice (by which one thing is equalized to another, mine to yours, good to good, damage to damage) cannot intervene between God and fallen man, whether placed outside or inside the state of grace. The reason is: because fallen man can merit nothing that could be exchanged out of justice for a divine reward and the relaxation of punishment. Between God, however, and man in his integrity, commutative justice could have intervened by virtue of a special divine covenant. For man persisting in the state of integrity could perform as much as divine justice required in relation to the obligation of giving, not of adequately meriting. But with the covenant and special obligation of God set aside, commutative justice cannot intervene between any created act and uncreated goodness; because there can be no equality, or proportion, or obligation by itself; but on the part of God there is always an infinite excess, and the most noble act of a creature is nothing but finite. Between God and Christ the satisfier, there is perfect commutative justice, because the merit and satisfaction of Christ for the sins of the whole world is of infinite value and preciousness. Distributive justice between God and man would have found a place in the state of integrity, if, supposing the equality of the divine image and the inequality of operations, without sin, the promise of God had intervened, that He willed to distribute degrees of glory among men according to the proportion of their operations. However, as for the fact that after the fall unequal degrees of glory are given to the faithful in eternal life, according to the measure of their works, that happens properly and strictly speaking not from distributive justice, even supposing the divine promise, but from grace and mercy. For in distributive justice, labors are not only the measure, which is regarded in distribution, but at the same time the cause and reason, moving by its own dignity to distribute in such a way, and not otherwise. But the labors of the pious cannot be such a cause and reason; because they do not attain a perfection conformable to the divine law in every respect; nay, they are reprobable by divine justice on account of their sinful contamination, which is εὐπερίςατος. Speaking absolutely, therefore, between God and fallen men, neither commutative nor distributive justice is given, because man receives more of a reward than he has labored for, whether actively or passively. Rom. VIII, 18. 2 Cor. IV, 17. Conf. D. DORSCH. theol. Zachar. part. II. fol. 163. & D. SCHERZ. in syst. p. 50.

Prob. a. Ps. XCII, 16. Righteous is Jehovah my rock, and there is no perversity in him. The royal prophet describes the righteousness of the divine will with affirmative and negative words, intending to indicate that not even a trace of injustice is to be found in God.

Prob. b. Since God is a most righteous legislator, whose law is perfect, and whose commandments are right, Ps. XIX, 8. by the force of his dispositive justice, he instructs intelligent creatures with suitable laws.

Prob. c. Es. XLV, 23. Jehovah says: Righteousness has gone out from my mouth, a word that will not be revoked. To fulfill promises is indeed a matter of truthfulness and faithfulness; but since truthfulness is contained under universal justice, and is the foundation of particular justice, it comes under the name of justice in the Holy Scriptures. It is called by theologians the justice of promise. Vid. GERH. exeg. loc. II. fol. 299.

Prob. d. Rom. II, 5. 6. 7. It is referred to δικαιοκρισίαν or righteous judgment, which God is about to render to everyone according to his works: to those indeed who, according to patience in well-doing, seek glory and honor and incorruptibility, eternal life. And 2 Thess. I, 6. 7. It is said to be righteous before God to render relief to those who are afflicted. By which words remunerative justice is indicated, founded in the goodness and promises of God. Whence to man, in order toward God, no right belongs; by the force of which the Lord should owe man any good thing, but God crowns his own good things in us. For whatever good is in us is from God's grace, Dan. IX, 18. For which reason remunerative justice, speaking properly, is not commutative or distributive justice, but is only called justice by a certain analogy.

Prob. e. Holy Scripture most clearly teaches the vindicatory justice of God. For 1) God judges the impious according to his justice. Righteous (are) you, O Jehovah; and your judgments are right, Ps. CXIX, 137. Δικαίωμα is the righteous judgment of God, that those who do such things are worthy of death, Rom. I, 32. To τῇ δικαιοκρισίᾳ, the righteous judgment, it is attributed to render to everyone according to his works, affliction and anguish of soul to the one working evil. Rom. II, 5. 6. 9. The day of the final judgment will take place in justice, Act. XVII, 31. 2) The infliction of punishments is ascribed to the ἀνταποδοτικῇ, or retributive, justice of God, 2 Thess. I, 6. It is righteous before God to repay affliction to those who afflict. 3) The condemnation of the impious is called righteous. Rom. III, 8. 4) That the punishment of our sins, which God took from Christ, according to the prophet Isaiah c. LIII, 5, is a proof of divine justice, Paul testifies in Rom. III, 25: God set forth Christ Jesus as a propitiation, through faith in his blood, for the demonstration of his justice. From which apostolic oracle we argue: Whoever, by inflicting the punishment of a bloody death, demonstrates his justice, in him vindicatory justice has a place. But God, by inflicting the punishment of a bloody death on Christ &c. Therefore. The major is proved: where someone proceeds through justice to the point of afflicting even to blood, there indeed vindicatory justice has …a place; as is evident from the example of the magistrate, who punishes the wicked with death. That this vindicatory justice in God is essential and necessary, not arbitrary, is evident: α) because God is eminent in natural holiness, so that he does not will sins, but hates them, Ps. V, 5. Therefore there is given in God a certain vindicatory justice, belonging to him by essence: β) because without He never absolves the guilty, Exod. XXXIV, 7. and He abominates those who justify the wicked, Prov. XVII, 15. Therefore, He is moved by natural justice to punish sins: γ) The Δικαίωμα of God, that those who do evil are worthy of death, is known by nature, Rom. I, 32. Therefore, this justice of God is not voluntary, but natural. For those things which are of the free divine will are not made known by nature. (*).

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, who deny that vindicatory justice is an essential attribute of God; (**) whose stronger arguments are: I. Every essential attribute of God belongs to God from eternity. Vindicatory justice does not belong to God from eternity. Therefore. The minor is proven: because from eternity there did not exist creatures upon whom God could exercise justice. Resp. Distinguish between the justice of God considered radically and formally. The justice of God considered radically is the will to punish sins, belonging to God from eternity. Formally, it is something relative, and it exercises its acts only in time, and only upon the hypothesis of a rational creature.

II. No property of God has a contrary property in God. The justice of God has a contrary property in God. Therefore. The minor is clear; since mercy, which pardons sins, is contrary to punitive justice. Resp. 1) The justice and mercy of God are not contrary to each other, although the effects of these divine attributes differ. For opposite effects can proceed from one principle. Thus, the same sun melts butter and hardens mud. 2) Opposites are understood regarding the same subject and object, insofar as it is the same. Divine mercy and justice are not concerned with the same object, insofar as it is the same. For justice is concerned with the sinner, as such, who is viewed by reason of the sins by which God has been injured, without respect to satisfaction. But mercy is concerned with the sinner under the aspect of satisfaction, or insofar as he has the satisfaction of Christ for his sins, by which God is moved to mercy. Hence, mercy pardons the sins of the faithful; but justice condemns the unfaithful, because they did not avert the wrath merited by their sins through the apprehension of the satisfaction of Christ. III. Whatever is a natural attribute of God is not overcome by another divine attribute. Divine justice is overcome by the mercy of God. Therefore. The major premise is evident, because every divine attribute, on the part of the thing itself, is the divine essence itself. Just as this is not overcome by itself, so one essential attribute is not surpassed by another. The minor premise is proved because God shows mercy more often and more quickly than He punishes; for He is slow to anger, Exod. XXX, 6. To show mercy is His own proper work, to afflict is a strange work. Is. XXVIII, 21. Response: One attribute is not overcome by another if viewed intrinsically, insofar as it is in God; yet the external effects of one divine attribute are seen to be more numerous than those of another attribute. God shows mercy more often and more quickly than He punishes, because the world has been reconciled to God through Christ, and by His antecedent will He wills all to be saved, to show mercy to all; but those who reject this grace offered in Christ, He punishes finally by His consequent will.

IV. If vindicatory justice were naturally in God, He would always punish sin. But He does not always punish sin. Therefore. Response: God would always punish sin, had not the most sufficient merit of Christ intervened, by which God is moved to forgive sins. For God punishes sin either in the sinner himself or in the sinner's sponsor, Christ; he who applies His satisfactory passion to himself by true faith removes the punishments merited for sins.

V. God punishes when and where He wills. Therefore His punitive justice is not natural, but free. Response: God punishes when He wills; but it does not follow: Therefore He does not punish according to natural justice. For the consequence from the freedom of the act, for the here and now, to the freedom of the principle is not valid. The act and exercise, for the here and now, are of the free will of God; from which God can defer punishments at will. But the principle, the natural justice of God, is necessary. Thus creation is free, but the power of creating in God is natural and necessary.

VI. Punishing sins is attributed in the Holy Scriptures not to justice, but to wrath or severity. Rom. II, 5. chap. XI, 22. Indeed, it is attributed to justice when God forgives sins. 1 John I, 9. Rom. III, 26. Response: 1) The infliction of punishments is referred to δικαιοκρισίαν, or the just judgment of God. Rom. II, 5-9. But when severity, wrath, indignation, fury, and vengeance are opposed to divine mercy, they are placed by metonymy of the sign for the vindicatory justice of God, and they presuppose it. 2) Δίκαιος, 1 John I, 9, is explained by πιστὸς, and thus denotes that God most faithfully fulfills His promises. But here the dispute is about the punitive justice of God. 3) Rom. III, 25. Paul deals with justice founded in blood, or that which demands a bloody death. Which is indeed vindicatory justice, which the judge exercises by inflicting the punishment of a bloody death upon the sources. There is no reason for you to object that Luther rendered these words: So that He might present the righteousness that avails before God. Luther renders the consequent for the antecedent, because that imputative righteousness is none other than that which was exacted in Christ through vindicatory justice.

VII. If God is just, why is it well with the wicked and ill with the good? Response: Look to the end, since it is indeed well with the wicked and ill with the good for a time, but not finally. For it will be well with the good in the end, and ill with the wicked, if not in this life, then in the other. Add that it ought never to be ill with the perfectly good; but we are not perfectly good.

Latin:

Iustitia Dei est attributum diuinum ἐνεργητικὸν, vi cuius Deus omnia, quæ æternæ suæ legi sunt conformia, vult & agit, (a) creaturis conuenientes leges præscribit, (b) promissa facta hominibus implet, (c) bonos remuneratur (d) & impios punit (e).

Obs. I. Per iustitiam Dei hic non intelligitur iustitia a Deo, qua nos iustificat; quæ duplex est (*), euangelica, consistens in remissione peccatorum & imputatione iustitiæ Christi, Rom. III, 22: et legalis, consistens in conformitate cum lege, quæ in hac vita est inchoata, in futura demum vita erit consummata: sed hic iustitia prædicatur de Deo, quatenus est proprietas in Deo essentialis.

Obs. II. Iustitia Dei alia est vniuersalis, quæ est immutabilis voluntatis diuinæ rectitudo, qua Deus omnia, quæ bona & recta sunt, æternæ suæ legi conformiter vult, approbat & agit; quæ cum sanctitate Dei coincidit: alia est particularis, quæ exercetur erga creaturas rectissima earum gubernatione, & boni atque mali retributione.

Obs. III. Iustitia Dei, quæ exercetur erga creaturas, alia est dispositiva, alia compensatiua. Illa est, qua Deus vitam creaturarum intelligentium (angelorum & hominum) convenientibus ipsis datis legibus gubernat. Hæc est vel remuneratiua, qua Deus mouetur ad præmia piis conferenda; vel vindicatiua, qua Deus mouetur ad pœnas impiis infligendas.

Obs. IV. Iustitia commutatiua (qua res rei, meum tuo, bonum bono, damnum damno æquat) inter Deum, & hominem lapsum, siue extra, siue intra statum gratiæ positum, intercedere non potest. Ratio est; quia homo lapsus nil mereri potest, quod cum præmio diuino & relaxatione pœnæ permutari ex iustitia queat. Inter Deum autem, & hominem integrum, ex speciali diuino fœdere iustitia commutatiua intercedere potuit. Tantum enim homo persistens in statu integritatis præstare potuit, quantum diuina iustitia in ordine ad obligationem dandi, non adæquate promerendi, requisiuit. At secluso fœdere & speciali obligatione Dei, inter nullum actum creatum, & bonitatem increatam, intercedere potest iustitia commutatiua; quia nulla per se potest esse æqualitas, aut proportio aut obligatio; sed ex parte Dei semper datur infinitus excessus, & creaturæ actus nobilissimus non nisi finitus est. Inter Deum, & Christum satisfactorem, datur perfecta iustitia commutatiua, quia meritum & satisfactio Christi pro peccatis totius mundi est infiniti valoris & pretiositatis. Iustitia distributiua inter Deum, & hominem, locum inuenisset, in statu integritatis, si supposita æqualitate imaginis diuinæ, & inæqualitate operationum, sine peccato, interuenisset promissio Dei, quod velit gradus gloriæ iuxta proportionem operationum inter homines distribuere. Quanto autem post lapsum fidelibus gradus gloriæ inæquales in vita æterna dantur, secundum mensuram operum, illud fit proprie & stricte loquendo non ex iustitia distributiua, etiam supposita promissione diuina, sed ex gratia & misericordia. Nam in iustitia distributiua labores non sunt mensura tantum, quæ respicitur in distributione, sed simul caussa & ratio, sua dignitate mouens ad taliter, & non aliter distribuendum. At labores piorum sancti talis caussa & ratio esse nequeunt; quia non assequuntur perfectionem legi diuinæ ex asse conformem, immo ex iustitia diuina sunt reprobabiles ob peccaminosam, quæ εὐπερίςατος est, contaminationem. Absolute igitur loquendo inter Deum, & homines lapsos, neque commutatiua, neque distributiva datur iustitia, quia plus præmii accipit homo, quam laborauit, siue actiue, siue passiue. Rom. VIII, 18. 2 Cor. IV, 17. Conf. D. DORSCH. theol. Zachar. part. II. fol. 163. & D. SCHERZ. in syst. p. 50.

Prob. a. Ps. XCII, 16. Rectus est Iehouah petra mea, & peruersitas non est in eo. Regius propheta verbis affirmatiuis & negatiuis describit rectitudinem voluntatis diuinæ, indicaturus, ne vestigium quidem iniustitiæ in Deo deprehendi.

Prob. b. Cum Deus sit legislator iustissimus, cuius lex est perfecta, & mandata sunt recta, Ps. XIX, 8. vi iustitiæ suæ dispositiuæ, creaturas intelligentes conuenientibus instruit legibus.

Prob. c. Es. XLV, 23. inquit Iehouah: Exiuit ex ore meo iustitia, verbum. quod non reuocabitur. Implere promissa, veracitatis quidem ac fidelitatis est; At cum veracitas sub iustitia vniuersali contineatur, & iustitiæ particularis fundamentum sit, in sacris litteris iustitiæ nomine venit. Vocatur a theologis iustitia promissionis. Vid. GERH. exeg. loc. II. fol. 299.

Prob. d. Rom. II, 5. 6. 7. Ad δικαιοκρισίαν seu iustum iudicium refertur, quod Deus redditurus est vnicuique, secundum opera ipsius: iis quidem, qui iuxta patientiam boni operis gloriam & honorem & incorruptibilitatem quærunt, vitam æternam. Et 2 Thess. I, 6. 7. Iustum esse dicitur apud Deum, reddere his, qui affliguntur, relaxationem. Quibus verbis indigitatur iustitia remuneratiua, fundata in bonitate & promissionibus Dei. Vnde homini, in ordine ad Deum, nullum ius competit; cuius vi dominus homini aliquid boni debeat, sed sua in nobis bona Deus coronat. Quidquid enim boni in nobis est, ex Dei gratia est, Dan. IX, 18. Quam ob rem iustitia remuneratiua proprie loquendo non est iustitia commutatiua aut distributiua, sed tantum per quandam analogiam iustitia appellatur.

Prob. e. Iustitiam Dei vindicatiuam clarissime docet S. Scriptura. Nam 1) Deus iudicat impios secundum iustitiam suam. Iustus (es) tu Iehouah; & recta iudicia tua Ps. CXIX, 137. Δικαίωμα iustum Dei iudicium est, quod qui eiusmodi faciunt, digni morte sint, Rom. I, 32. τῇ δικαιοκρισίᾳ, iusto iudicio tribuitur, reddere vnicuique secundum opera ipsius, afflictionem & angustiam animæ, malum operanti. Rom. II, 5. 6. 9. Dies extremi iudicii fiet in iustitia, Act. XVII, 31. 2) Irrogatio pœnarum iustitiæ diuinæ ἀνταποδοτικῇ, s. retributiuæ, adscribitur 2 Thess. I, 6. Iustum est apud Deum, retribuere affligentibus afflictionem. 3) Impiorum condemnatio dicitur iusta. Rom. III, 8. 4) Pœnam peccatorum nostrorum, quam Deus a Christo sumsit, secundum prophetam Iesaiam c. LIII, 5. documentum iustitiæ diuinæ esse, testatur Paullus Rom. III, 25: Christum Iesum proposuit Deus propitiatorium, per fidem in ipsius sanguine, in demonstrationem iustitiæ suæ. Ex quo oraculo apostolico argumentamur: Quicunque infligendo pœnam mortis cruentæ, iustitiam suam demonstrat, in illo iustitia vindicatiua locum habet. Atqui Deus infligendo Christo pœnam mortis cruentæ &c. Ergo. Maior probatur: vbi aliquis per iustitiam eo vsque procedit, vt ad sanguinem affligat, ibi sane locum habet iustitia vindicatiua; vt patet exemplo magistratus, qui morte punit malos. Quam iustitiam vindicatiuam in Deo essentialem ac necessariam, non arbitrariam esse, patet: α) quia Deus naturali eminet sanctitate, vt peccata non velit, sed oderit, Ps. V, 5. Ergo datur in Deo iustitia: quædam vindicatiua, per essentiam ipsi competens: β) quia citra satisfactionem nocentem nunquam absoluit, Exod. XXXIV, 7. & homines impium iustificantes abominatur, Prou. XVII, 15. Ergo naturali iustitia mouetur ad puniendum peccata: γ) Δικαίωμα Dei, quod mala facientes digni sint morte, natura notum est, Rom. I, 32. Ergo ius istud Dei non voluntarium, sed naturale est. Quæ enim liberæ voluntatis diuinæ sunt, ex natura non innotescunt. (*).

Antithesis est Socinianorum, negantium, iustitiam vindicatiuam esse attributum Dei essentiale; (**) quorum potiora sunt argumenta: I. Omne attributum Dei essentiale competit Deo ab æterno. Iustitia vindicatiua non competit Deo ab æterno. Ergo. Minor prob. quoniam ab æterno non extiterunt creaturæ, in quas Deus iustitiam exercere potuit. Resp. dist. inter iustitiam Dei radicaliter, & formaliter consideratam. Iustitia Dei radicaliter considerata est voluntas puniendi peccata, Deo ab æterno competens. Formaliter est aliquid relatiuum, atque actus suos exercet non nisi in tempore, non nisi ex hypothesi creaturæ rationalis.

II. Nulla proprietas Dei habet in Deo contrariam proprietatem. Iustitia Dei habet in Deo contrariam proprietatem. Ergo. Minor liquet; quoniam iustitiæ punitiuæ contrariatur misericordia, peccata condonans. Resp. 1) Iustitia & misericordia Dei sibi non contrariantur, licet effectus horum attributorum diuinorum differant. Nam oppositi effectus ab vno principio possunt proficisci. Sic idem sol butyrum liquefacit, & lutum indurat. 2) Opposita intelliguntur de eodem subiecto & obiecto, quatenus est idem. Misericordia, & iustitia diuina, non versatur circa obiectum idem, quatenus est idem. Nam iustitia versatur circa peccatorem, qua talem, qui spectatur ratione peccatorum, quibus læsus est Deus, sine respectu ad satisfactionem. Misericordia vero versatur circa peccatorem sub ratione satisfactionis, seu quatenus pro peccatis suis habet satisfactionem Christi, qua Deus ad misericordiam mouetur. Hinc misericordia condonat peccata fidelibus; iustitia autem damnat infideles, quod iram peccatis promeritam non auerterint apprehensione satisfactionis Christi, III. Quidquid est attributum Dei naturale, ab alio attributo diuino non vincitur. Iustitia diuina vincitur a misericordia Dei. E. Maior constat, quia omne attributum diuinum ex parte rei est ipsa essentia diuina. Sicut haec a seipsa non vincitur: ita nec vnum attributum essentiale ab altero superatur. Minor prob. quia Deus saepius & celerius miseretur, quam punit; est enim tardus ad iram, Exod. XXX, 6. Misereri est ipsius proprium, affligere alienum opus. Es. XXVIII, 21. Resp. Vnum attributum non vincitur ab altero, si spectetur intrinsece, quatenus est in Deo: effectus tamen externi vnius attributi diuini plures, quam alterius attributi conspiciuntur. Saepius & celerius Deus miseretur, quam punit; quia mundus Deo per Christum reconciliatus est, & voluntate antecedente omnes vult saluos fieri, omnium misereri; repudiantes autem hanc in Christo oblatam gratiam punit demum voluntate consequente.

IV. Si Deo naturaliter inesset iustitia vindicatiua, semper peccatum puniret. Atqui peccatum non semper punit. Ergo. Resp. Deus semper puniret peccatum, nisi interuenisset sufficientissimum Christi meritum, quo Deus ad condonandum peccata permouetur. Punit enim Deus peccatum vel in ipso peccante, vel in peccantis sponsore, Christo; cuius passionem satisfactoriam qui vera sibi fide applicat, poenas peccatorum promeritas amolitur.

V. Deus punit, quando & vbi vult. Ergo iustitia ipsius punitiua non est naturalis, sed libera. Resp. Punit Deus, quando vult; sed non sequitur: Ergo non punit secundum iustitiam naturalem. A libertate enim actus, pro hic & nunc, ad libertatem principii non valet consequentia. Actus & exercitium, pro hic & nunc, sunt liberae voluntatis Dei; ex quo Deus poenas pro lubitu differre potest. Sed principium, naturalis Dei iustitia, est necessarium. Ita creatio est libera, potentia autem creandi in Deo naturalis & necessaria est.

VI. Punire peccata, in sacris litteris non iustitiae, sed irae, vel seueritati tribuitur. Rom. II, 5. cap. XI, 22. Immo iustitiae attribuitur, cum Deus peccata condonat. 1 Io. I, 9. Rom. III, 26. Resp. 1) Ad δικαιοκρισίαν, siue iustum Dei iudicium, refertur irrogatio poenarum. Rom. II, 5-9. Quando vero seueritas, ira, indignatio, furor, vindicta, misericordiae diuinae opponuntur, per metonymiam signi pro iustitia Dei vindicatiua ponuntur, eamque praesupponunt. 2) Δίκαιος, 1 Io. I, 9. per πιστὸς exponitur, atque adeo notat, Deum promissa sua fidelissime implere. At hic controuertitur de iustitia Dei punitiua. 3) Rom. III, 25. Paullus agit de iustitia fundata in sanguine, seu quae exigit mortem cruentam. Quae sane est iustitia vindicatiua, quam exercet iudex mortis cruentae poenam fontibus irrogans. Non est, quod obuertas, Lutherum haec verba reddidisse: Damit er darbiete die Gerechtigkeit, die vor GOtt gilt. Lutherus reddit consequens pro antecedente, quia illa iustitia imputatiua nulla alia est, quam quae exacta fuit in Christo per iustitiam vindicatiuam.

VII. Si Deus iustus est, cur malis bene, & bonis male est? Resp. Respice finem, siquidem malis quidem bene, & bonis male est ad tempus, sed non finaliter. Bonis enim tandem bene, & malis male erit, si non in hac, tamen in altera vita. Adiice, quod perfecte bonis nunquam debeat esse male; sed nos non sumus perfecte boni.


### Quæst. XLVII. What is the veracity of God?

Veracity is a divine ἐνεργητικὸν attribute, by which God, in speaking the truth, is constant in keeping His promises and fulfilling His threats.

Obs. 1. The truth of God in being differs from truth in speaking. The former is an absolute or quiescent attribute; the latter is a relative or operative attribute.

2. By this attribute, both hypocrisy and every false speech are removed from God.

Prob. 1. Num. XXIII, 19. Balaam says: God is not a man, that he should lie: neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good? God had placed these words into the mouth of Balaam, so that he might express the truthfulness of God as clearly as possible by them. Moreover, the most truthful God is compared with fallacious men. Men are prone to lying, because they are often deceived not only on account of the weakness of their intellect, but they also deceive most frequently on account of the inconstancy of their will. God, however, because he possesses infinite knowledge, is never deceived: and because the infinite constancy of his will stands out, he never deceives.

2. Hebr. VI, 18. the apostle says: It is impossible for God to lie. God is able to do all things by effecting them, but nothing by failing. Since lying is an enormous defect, it is beneath the object of divine power.

Latin:

Veracitas est attributum diuinum ἐνεργητικὸν, quo Deus dicendo vero in seruandis promissis & implendis comminationibus suis constans est.

Obs. 1. Veritas Dei in essendo a veritate in dicendo differt. Illa est attributum absolutum, siue quiescens, haec attributum respectiuum siue operans

2. Hoc attributo remouetur a Deo tum hypocrisis, tum omne falsiloquium.

Prob. 1. Num. XXIII, 19. inquit Bileamus: Non vir (est) Deus, ut mentiatur: aut filius hominis, ut pœniteat: num ille dixerit, & non fecerit? aut locutus fuerit, & non stabiliuerit illud? Verba hæc Deus in os Bileami posuerat, vt iisdem veracitatem Dei quam luculentissime exprimeret. Confertur autem Deus veracissimus cum hominibus fallacibus. Homines ad mendacium sunt proclives, propterea, quod non tantum ob intellectus infirmitatem fæpe falluntur, sed ob voluntatis etiam inconstantiam frequentissime fallunt. Deus vero, quia infinita scientia pollet, nunquam fallitur: & quia infinita voluntatis constantia eminet, nunquam fallit.

2. Hebr. VI, 18. inquit apostolus: Impossibile est, Deum mentiri. Deus omnia potest efficiendo, nil autem deficiendo. Mendacium cum sit enormis defectus, obiecta potentiæ diuinæ inferius est.


### Quest. XLVIII. What is the power of God?

Power, or the omnipotence of God, is a divine attribute, active (ἐνεργητικὸν), by which God is able to effect everything that is possible to be done; and it imports no imperfection in God. Obs.

I. God is called omnipotent from active power. For since God is the most pure and most perfect act, he is devoid of passive omnipotence.

Obs. II. Obs. II. The attribute of omnipotence belongs to God not accidentally, but essentially, not dependently, but independently, not mutably, but immutably, not in a qualified sense, but absolutely, so that His power is not finite or measured, but infinite and immense with respect to objects; because those things which God can perform are infinite. By reason of the mode of acting; since God never acts so intensely and effectively that He could not act more intensely and effectively. Obs.

Obs. III. A distinction must be made between the ordained and the absolute power of God. The ordained is that by which God acts conveniently to His decree and the order established by Himself. That order is twofold, of nature and of grace. The former is that by which God operates according to the laws of nature established by Himself, e.g., God can preserve the natural life of man through corporal nourishment. The latter is that by which God, through supernatural means established by Himself, can illuminate, convert, regenerate, justify, renew, and save sinful man. The absolute power of God is that which belongs to God according to Himself, and is not determined by any prior thing or law. The ordained divine power can be resisted, since the influx of secondary causes, with which God concurs, and of the means through which He operates, can be hindered. But the absolute divine power cannot be resisted; for otherwise the power of a finite creature would prevail over the infinite power of God. By His absolute power God can cause a virgin to give birth, the sun to stand still, iron to float, etc. Obs.

Obs. IV. Those things are called possible which, if they were to happen, involve no contradiction, neither on the part of the agent, God, nor on the part of the thing produced: e.g., if it were possible that God could lie, or sin in any way, He would not be the most holy God. For to be most holy and yet to sin implies a contradiction. But if God were to make today yesterday, a contradiction would be involved on the part of the thing produced. For to be yesterday and today at the same time brings in a contradiction. Obs.

Obs. V. Obs. V. The norm for judging a contradiction is not the human intellect, but the divine. Things often seem contradictory to us which are not. Whence God can ὑπερεκπερισσοῦ (superabundantly) do beyond those things which we understand, Eph. III, 20. Generally, indeed, most assert that God cannot do contradictory things (although THOMAS P. I. quæst. 25. art. 3. thinks it is more theologically stated that such things cannot be done, rather than that God cannot do them; since they do not argue a defect of power in God, but in the class of possibles they do not exist due to a defect of entity; since they can in no way exist): however, it is not permitted for us to determine all those things that are truly contradictory in particular, because we do not perfectly know what the essence of each thing is. Just as a fool does not judge what all wise men are able to perform: Nor does a brute grasp all things that are within the power of man: Nor does man attain to the powers in which angels excel: So much the less does our intellect know what is impossible to God. This, meanwhile, is certain: that those things which God has asserted in His word that He will do do not bring in a contradiction, which do not overturn the essence of a thing clearly known to us. Obs.

Obs. VI. A distinction must be made between the possibles of nature and nature itself. The impossibles of nature are those which surpass the customary course of nature. Thus nature cannot cause an ass to speak, or water to turn into wine. The impossibles of nature are those which, if they were to happen, would involve a manifest contradiction. These, because they are simply impossible, fall under no power, and therefore not even under the power of God Himself: Just as the simply invisible falls under no power of sight.

Prob. The Omnipotence of God I. Prob. The Omnipotence of God I. From the light of revelation. For in the sacred writings 1) God is expressly called omnipotent, Gen. XVII, 1. שדי q. d. God the destroyer, who can lay waste all things and reduce them to nothing, just as He created all things out of nothing. He is called κύριος παντοκράτωρ the Lord omnipotent 2 Cor. VI, 18. 2) The Holy Spirit affirms that with God all things are possible, Matth. XIX, 26. 3) The same divine Spirit denies that any word (any thing) is impossible with God, Luc. I, 37.

II. From the light of reason, and indeed 1) from the perfection of God. Every perfection belongs to God in the most excellent way. But power in acting is a perfection. Therefore. 2) From the effects. Whoever created the world, preserves and governs the created, he is omnipotent. But God, etc. Therefore. Antithesis

Antithesis was I. Of the Gentiles, among whom is PLINY lib. II. nat. hist. c. VII. GALEN lib. II. de usu part. c. XIV. who denied that God could do all things. II. Of the Socinians, (to whom Vorstius accedes) who deny the infinity of divine power. They attempt to deceive us with the following arguments.

I. God cannot sin, lie, be deceived, die, be conquered, condemn the innocent, or dismiss the sinner unpunished without satisfaction. Therefore God is not omnipotent. Resp. These predicates infer a contradiction on the part of God the agent; for they are repugnant to his most eminent perfection. If God could do those things, he would not be God, he would not be the most perfect being. God cannot sin, because he is most holy: not be deceived, because most wise: not lie, because most truthful: not die, because eternal: not be conquered, because infinitely powerful: not condemn the innocent, or dismiss the guilty unpunished, because he is most just.

II. God cannot walk, eat, sleep, etc., which creatures can perform. Therefore God cannot do all things that are absolutely possible. Resp. (1) God certainly does, by his immense power, that creatures walk, eat, sleep, and thus the motion of creatures, and his sleep, proceeds from the power of God. 2) God does not exercise those acts immediately in himself, because they are joined with manifold imperfection. Walking is done with the feet of the body, and introduces passive power and change of place. Eating food requires bodily limbs, and argues the indigence and passive power of creatures. Sleep, however, arises from weariness, and indicates a certain weakness. Hence it is clear that these predicates are repugnant to spirituality, immutability, beatitude, and divine omnipotence.

III. God cannot make contradictory things true, he cannot make the done undone, or make yesterday today, or make a deflowered virgin pure and chaste. Therefore God is not omnipotent. Resp. (1) It is simply not possible that both contradictory propositions be true. But whatever is simply impossible falls under no power. ARMANDUS DE BELLO VISU says excellently: Instantia Instantia. If God cannot do any impossible thing, his power will be limited, not absolute. Resp. God can do things impossible to nature, but not things impossible by nature. Since these are simply impossible, they are inferior to active omnipotence, and thus place no limits on divine omnipotence.

IV. God cannot make a creature infinitely more perfect or better than he has made. Therefore he is not omnipotent. Resp. (1) Distinguish between a creature considered by reason of essential and accidental goodness, or perfection. (2) Distinguish between a thing that remains the same in number, and one that is changed so that it becomes another essence in number. God cannot make a thing infinitely better in goodness or essential perfection if it must remain the same in number. For the essences of things are like numbers, to which, if they must remain the same, nothing can be added or taken away. A tree, as long as it remains a tree, cannot become a man; although from a tree, if it were no longer to remain a tree, God could make a man.

Accidentally, however, and indeed in infinite ways, God can make a thing better or more perfect; since He can add to it a degree of magnitude, and to this a degree of multitude, and to this another degree of accidental perfection, to infinity.

V. God cannot make God.

Resp. It implies a contradiction to be God and yet to have been made. For the true God is the first being, independent, existing of Himself, not made by another.

VI. The effects of divine power (namely, creatures) are finite.

Therefore, divine power is also finite; for such as the effect is, such is the cause.

Resp. Distinguish between a univocal effect and an equivocal one. Divine effects are equivocal; therefore, they are not of the same nature as God. But it is not permitted to argue from the quality of an equivocal effect to the quality of the cause.

Divine power is infinite insofar as it is considered in itself; for thus it is the very infinite essence of God: insofar as it is viewed in relation to objects and the mode of acting.

See observation above.

II. VII.

VII. Whoever cannot bring all possible things into act, he is not omnipotent. But God cannot, etc. Therefore.

The minor premise is proven because thus no possible thing would remain.

Resp. God produces all possible things into act separately, or one by one, not collectively and simultaneously, so that no possible thing remains. For the infinity of divine power does not consist in this, that He makes every possible thing at once and together.

Latin:

Potentia, siue omnipotentia Dei, est attributum diuinum ἐνεργητικὸν, quo Deus efficere potest omne, quod fieri possibile est; & in Deo nullam importat imperfectionem. Obs.

I. Deus dicitur omnipotens a potentia actiua. Cum enim Deus sit actus purissimus & perfectissimus, omnipotentia passiua expers est.

Obs. II. Obs. II. Attributum omnipotentiæ competit Deo non accidentaliter, sed essentialiter, non dependenter, sed independenter, non mutabiliter, sed immutabiliter, non secundum quid, sed absolute, ut potentia eius non sit finita aut dimensa, sed infinita ac immensa respectu obiectorum; quia infinita sunt, quæ Deus præstare potest. Ratione modi agendi; cum Deus nunquam tam intense & efficaciter agat, quin possit intensius & efficacius operari. Obs.

III. Obs. III. Distinguendum est inter potentiam Dei ordinatam, & absolutam. Ordinata est, qua Deus agit convenienter suo decreto, & ordini a semet constituto. Ordo ille duplex est, naturæ & gratiæ. Ille est, quo Deus secundum leges naturæ, a se positas, operatur v. gr. Deus potest vitam hominis naturalem conservare per alimenta corporalia. Hic est, quo Deus per media supernaturalia, a semet constituta, hominem peccatorem illuminare, convertere, regenerare, iustificare, renovare, salvare potest. Potentia Dei absoluta est, quæ Deo secundum se convenit, nec prævio aliquo aut lege determinata est. Potentiæ divinæ ordinatæ resisti potest, cum causarum secundarum, quibuscum Deus concurrit, & mediorum, per quæ operatur, influxus impediri queat. Potentiæ autem divinæ absolutæ obsisti nequit; alias enim potentia creaturæ finita infinitæ Dei potentiæ prævaleret. Potentia absoluta Deus facere potest, ut virgo pariat, sol stet, ferrum natet &c. Obs.

IV. Obs. IV. Possibilia dicuntur, quæ, si fiant, nullam involuunt contradictionem, neque ex parte agentis Dei, neque ex parte rei productæ: v. gr. Si fieri posset, ut Deus mentiretur, aut ulla ratione peccaret, non foret Deus sanctissimus. Nam esse sanctissimum, & tamen peccare, contradictionem implicat. Si autem Deus ex hesterno hodiernum faceret diem, involueretur contradictio ex parte rei productæ. Nam esse simul hesternum & hodiernum diem, contradictionem infert. Obs.

V. Obs. V. Norma diiudicandæ contradictionis non est intellectus humanus, sed divinus. Nobis contradictoria sæpe videntur, quæ non sunt. Vnde Deus potest ὑπερεκπερισσοῦ superabundanter facere vltra ea, quæ intelligimus, Eph. III, 20. Generatim quidem plerique asserunt, Deum non posse facere contradictoria (quamquam THOMAS P. I. quæst. 25. art. 3. putet, magis theologice dici, talia non posse fieri, quam Deum ea facere non posse; quum non arguant defectum potentiæ in Deo, sed in genere possibilium non sint ob defectum entitatis; quippe quæ nullo pacto esse queunt): non licet autem nobis omnia illa vere contradictoria in particulari determinare, eo, quod non perfecte cognoscimus, quæ cuiusque rei sit essentia. Sicut stultus non diiudicat, quid omnes præstare valeant sapientes: Neque brutum capit omnia, quæ sunt penes hominem: Neque homo assequitur, quibus polleant viribus angeli: Ita multo minus intellectus noster cognoscit, quid sit Deo impossibile.
