Hoc interim certum est, non inferre contradictionem, quæ Deus in verbo suo afferuit, se facturum esse , quæ essentiam rei a nobis liquido cognitam non evertunt. Obs.

VI. Obs. VI. Distinguendum est inter possibilia naturæ & natura. Impossibilia naturæ sunt, quæ usitatum naturæ cursum superant. Sic natura efficere nequit, ut asina loquatur, aqua in vinum abeat. Impossibilia natura sunt, quæ manifestam, si fiant, contradictionem involuunt. Hæc, quia simpliciter sunt impossibilia, sub nullam, adeoque nec ipsius Dei potentiam cadunt: Sicut simpliciter invisibile sub nullam cadit potentiam visiuam.

Prob. Omnipotentia Dei I. Prob. Omnipotentia Dei I. Ex lumine reuelationis. In sacris enim litteris 1) Deus diserte vocatur omnipotens, Gen. XVII, 1. שדי q. d. Deus vastator, qui omnia vastare & in nihilum redigere potest, sicut ex nihilo omnia condidit. Dicitur κύριος παντοκράτωρ Dominus omnipotens 2 Cor. VI, 18. 2) Spiritus S. affirmat, apud Deum omnia esse possibilia, Matth. XIX, 26. 3) Negat idem spiritus divinus, apud Deum impossibile esse ullum verbum (vllam rem) Luc. I, 37.

II. Ex lumine rationis, & quidem 1) a perfectione Dei. Omnis perfectio Deo modo excellentissimo competit. Atqui potentia in operando est perfectio. Ergo. 2) Ab effectis. Quicunque mundum creavit, creatum conservat & gubernat, ille est omnipotens. Atqui Deus &c. Ergo. Antithesis

Antithesis fuit I. Gentilium, quos inter est PLINIVS lib. II. nat. hist. c. VII. GALENVS lib. II. de usu part. c. XIV. qui negarant, Deum omnia facere posse. II. Socinianorum, (quibus accedit Vorstius) infinitatem potentiæ divinæ infitiantium. Conantur illi fucum nobis facere sequentibus argumentis.

I. Deus non potest peccare, mentiri, falli, mori, vinci, innocentem damnare, peccatorem sine satisfactione dimittere impunitum. Ergo Deus non est omnipotens. Resp. Hæc prædicata inferunt contradictionem ex parte Dei agentis; quippe cuius eminentissimæ perfectioni repugnant. Si illa Deus posset, non foret Deus, non ens perfectissimum. Non potest Deus peccare, quia est sanctissimus: non falli, quia sapientissimus: non mentiri, quia veracissimus: non mori, quia æternus: non vinci, quia infinite potens: non damnare innocentem, aut nocentem dimittere impunitum, quia est iustissimus.

II. Deus non potest ambulare, edere, dormire &c. quod præstare possunt creaturæ. Ergo Deus non potest facere omnia absolute possibilia. Resp. (1) utique Deus facit immensa sua potentia, vt creaturæ ambulent, edant, dormiant, atque adeo creaturarum motus, eius somnus a potentia Dei proficiscitur. 2) Actus illos Deus immediate in seipso non exercet, quia cum multiplici imperfectione sunt coniuncti. Ambulatio fit pedibus corporis, & infert potentiam passivam atque mutationem loci. Manducatio cibi requirit membra corporea, & arguit creaturarum indigentiam atque potentiam passivam. Somnus autem oritur ex lassitudine, & imbecillitatem quandam indicat. Proinde patet, hæc prædicata spiritualitati, immutabilitati, beatitudini, & omnipotentiæ divinæ repugnare.

III. Deus non potest contradictoria vera efficere, non potest factum infectum, hesternum diem hodiernum reddere, stupratam puram castamque efficere virginem. E. Deus non est omnipotens. Resp. (1) Simpliciter non possibile est, vt utraque contradictoria propositio sit vera. Sed quidquid simpliciter impossibile est, sub nullam cadit potentiam. Eximie inquit ARMANDVS DE BELLO VISV Instantia Instantia. Si Deus non potest facere ullum impossibile, potentia eius erit limitata, non absoluta. Resp. Deus potest facere impossibilia naturæ, sed non impossibilia natura. Hæc cum sint simpliciter impossibilia, omnipotentia activa sunt inferiora, atque adeo omnipotentiæ divinæ nullos ponunt limites.

IV. Deus non potest facere creaturam infinite perfectiorem aut meliorem, quam fecit. Ergo non est omnipotens. Resp. (1) dist. inter creaturam consideratam ratione essentialis, & accidentalis bonitatis, seu perfectionis. (2) Dist. inter rem, quæ manet eadem numero, & quæ mutatur, ut fiat alia numero essentia. Deus non potest facere rem bonitate aut perfectione essentiali infinite meliorem, si debeat manere eadem numero. Nam essentiæ rerum sunt sicut numeri, quibus, si iidem manere debeant, nihil addi aut demi potest. Arbor, quamdiu manet arbor, non potest fieri homo; quamuis ex arbore, si non amplius maneret arbor, Deus facere possit hominem.

Accidentaliter tamen, & quidem infinitis, meliorem aut perfectiorem Deus rem facere potest; siquidem ipsi gradum magnitudinis, & huic gradum multitudinis, & alium huic gradum perfectionis accidentalis in infinitum addere potest.

V. Deus non potest facere Deum.

Resp. Contradictionem implicat, esse Deum, & tamen factum. Verus enim Deus est ens primum, independens, a se existens, non factum ab alio.

VI. Effectus potentiæ diuinæ (nempe creaturæ) sunt finiti.

Ergo & potentia diuina est finita; nam qualis est effectus, talis est causa.

Resp. Dist. inter effectum vniuocum, & æquiuocum. Effectus diuini sunt æquiuoci; ideo quod non sunt eiusdem naturæ cum Deo. At a qualitate effectus æquiuoci ad qualitatem causæ argumentari non licet.

Potentia diuina est infinita, quatenus consideratur in se; sic enim est ipsa essentia infinita Dei: quatenus spectatur in ordine ad obiecta & modum agendi.

Vid. supra obseru.

II. VII.

VII. Quicunque non omnia possibilia potest in actum traducere, ille non est omnipotens. Atqui Deus non potest &c. Ergo.

Min. prob. quia sic nullum remaneret possibile.

Resp. Deus omnia possibilia in actum producit diuisim, siue sigillatim, non collectiue & simul, vt nullum possibile remaneat. Neque enim in hoc consistit infinitas potentiæ diuinæ, vt simul & semel faciat quamcunque rem possibilem.


### Quest. XLVIII. What is the power of God?: It is sufficient that no possible thing can be named which God is not able to produce

It is sufficient that no possible thing can be named which God is not able to produce.

VIII. Whatever is exceeded by some divine attribute, that cannot be infinite. But divine power is exceeded by some divine attribute, namely, by divine knowledge. Therefore.

The major premise is evident; because in infinity the ratio of the exceeding and the exceeded has no place, but mere parity dominates. The minor is clear; because God knows more things, namely, sins, natural defects, and other things, which He cannot do.

Resp.

Resp. The power of God is considered in two ways: (α) κατ' ἔσω (inwardly), or intrinsically, according to its entity; insofar as it is identified with the very essence of God; thus it is not exceeded by the knowledge of God, but is infinite just as that is. (β) κατ' ἔξω (outwardly), extrinsically, regarding objects; thus power is exceeded by the knowledge of God regarding the number of objects; because more things fall under the knowledge than the power of God: not regarding the proportion of objects; because as the knowledge of God extends itself to all knowable things, so divine power extends itself to all possible things.

IX. Christ, true God, could not do miracles in His own country, Mark. 5. Therefore, divine power is not immense.

Resp. Christ could do miracles in His own country by absolute power, but not by ordained power, the miraculous force being retarded, not by ἀδυναμίᾳ (impotence), or a defect of power in Himself, but by ἀπιστίᾳ (unbelief) or a defect of faith in the people.

Question XLIX.

What is the omnipresence of God?

Omnipresence of God is a divine attribute ἐνεργητικὸν (active), by the power of which God is present to all creatures not only by the proximity of substance, but also by efficacious operation. Omnipresence of God.

Obs. I. There is one presence of God that is universal, another special, another singular.

By universal presence, which is also called the presence of power, God is present to all creatures. Special presence is twofold: the presence of grace and of glory.

By the presence of grace, God is present to believers in this life. By the presence of glory, God is present to angels and blessed men in heaven.

The singular and hypostatic presence is that through which the whole fullness of the deity dwells in Christ bodily, Col. II, 9.

Obs. II. The degrees of divine presence follow one another mutually, such that the later ones always presuppose and prerequire the earlier degrees, but not vice versa. Thus, the presence of grace presupposes divine omnipresence: the presence of glory includes in a certain way, or prerequires, the presence of grace. And finally, the presence of the hypostatic union presupposes and prerequires in its own way the presence of glory, as also the presence of grace, and indeed even the universal presence or that of power.

Latin:

Sufficit, quod nullum possibile nominari queat, quod Deus producere non valeat.

VIII. Quidquid exceditur ab aliquo attributo diuino, id non potest esse infinitum. Atqui potentia diuina exceditur ab aliquo attributo diuino, nempe a scientia diuina. Ergo.

Maior constat; quia in infinitate ratio excedentis & excessi locum non habet, sed mera dominatur paritas. Minor liquet; quia Deus plura scit, nempe peccata, defectus naturales, & alia, quæ facere non potest.

Resp.

Resp. Potentia Dei dupliciter consideratur (α) κατ' ἔσω, siue intrinsece, secundum suam entitatem; in quantum cum ipsa essentia Dei identificatur; sic non exceditur a scientia Dei, sed perinde, ac illa, infinita est. (β) κατ' ἔξω, extrinsece, quoad obiecta; sic exceditur potentia a scientia Dei, quoad numerum obiectorum; quia plura sub scientiam, quam potentiam Dei cadunt: non quoad proportionem obiectorum; quia vt se extendit scientia Dei ad omnia scibilia, ita potentia diuina se extendit ad omnia possibilia.

IX. Christus, verus Deus, non potuit in patria sua miracula facere, Marc. 5. Ergo potentia diuina non est immensa.

Resp. Poterat Christus in patria sua miracula facere potentia absoluta, sed non ordinata, vim miraculosam retardante, non ἀδυναμίᾳ, siue defectu potentiæ in se ipso, sed ἀπιστίᾳ siue defectu fidei in hominibus.

Quæst. XLIX.

Quæ est omnipræsentia Dei?

Omnipræsentia Dei est attributum diuinum ἐνεργητικὸν, vi cuius Deus non tanOmnipræsentia Dei. sum substantia propinquitate , sed etiam efficaci operatione omnibus creaturis adest .

Obs. I. Præsentia Dei alia est vniuersalis, alia specialis, alia singularis.

Præsentia vniuersali, quæ etiam vocatur, præsentia potentiæ, Deus omnibus creaturis adest. Præsentia specialis duplex est, præsentia gratiæ & gloriæ.

Præsentia gratiæ Deus adest credentibus in hac vita. Præsentia gloriæ Deus adest angelis & beatis hominibus in cœlo.

Præsentia singularis & hypostatica est, per quam tota plenitudo deitatis habitat in Christo corporaliter, Col. II, 9.

Obs. II. Gradus praesentiae divinae se mutuo consequuntur, ut posteriores semper praesupponant ac praerequirant priores gradus, non autem vice versa. Sic praesentia gratiae praesupponit divinam omnipraesentiam: praesentia gloriae includit certa ratione, vel praerequirit gratiae praesentiam. Ac denique praesentia unionis hypostaticae supponit ac praerequirit suo modo praesentiam gloriae, ut & praesentiam gratiae, immo & praesentiam vniversalem seu potentiae.


### Quest. XLVIII. What is the power of God?: Obs. III

Obs. III.

Divine presence in the biblical style, and in a complex sense, implies two things: (1) ἀδιαστασίαν [adiastasian], or the substantial presence of God to creatures.

(2) ἐνέργειαν [energeian], or efficacious operation. Therefore, two things must be proven here: (a) That God is present everywhere by reason of substance. (b) That for a full and accurate definition of divine presence, the efficacious operation of God, or the definitive part, is also required, with Holy Scripture shining as the light.

Prob. a. (1) From Jer. XXIII, 23-24. "Am I a God at hand, saith Jehovah, and not a God afar off? Can any hide himself in secret places, that I shall not see him? saith Jehovah. Do not I fill heaven and earth? saith Jehovah." Concerning this prophetic oracle, observe (a) the prefix ב in the nouns מקרוב and מרחוק makes the construction of the substantives to be expressed in Latin by the genitive, as observed by BUXTORF in his Thesaurus, lib. II, c. III, p. 365, and SEB. SCHMID in Colleg. Bibl., the former, p. 97. And since the locution is elliptical, Buxtorf supplies the noun מקום place, i.e., "Am I a God of a near place?" And thus also: "Am I a God of a far place?" Rightly indeed. For thus God is also called the God of heaven and earth, Gen. XXIV, 3. Unless you prefer to understand "of a thing," i.e., "Am I a God of that thing which is near," etc. Obs. (b) Near and remote places, or near and remote things, are called such with respect had to a certain mode of divine presence, according to which God is said to be somewhere. Nor does it seem that there should be any doubt here about the fact that the Lord refers to heaven, which is otherwise called in Scripture, and has always been held by all peoples to be, the dwelling place of God. By those false prophets against whom the Lord here acts, it was also held as the same. Therefore, with respect to heaven and with respect to the mode of presence by which God is in the heavens, places are called near and remote. But since God is in heaven by reason of substance, He is also substantially present to places near to and remote from heaven. Obs. (c) When the Lord says: "Do not I fill heaven and earth?" the proper meaning of the verb "to fill" must be retained. Something is said to be filled by something when it so penetrates and possesses all things that nothing remains empty, nothing in which the thing that fills does not exist. We argue: Whoever is the God not only of a near place, but also of the most remote, filling heaven and earth, he is omnipresent by reason of his substance.

But God, etc. Therefore. (2) From Ps. CXXXIX, 7-8. "Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy face? If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou (art there)." Obs. By the spirit of God is to be understood the Holy Spirit; by the face of God, the tremendous majesty of God, or as D. GEIERUS judges, Commentar. in h. l. , p. 1208, the Son of God, who is the image of the Father and the character of his substance, Col. I, 15; Heb. I, 3, is understood. An argument is born for us: Whoever is so in the heavens and in hell that no one can escape his spirit and his face, he is substantially omnipresent. But God is, etc. Therefore. Prob. b. That divine omnipresence must be defined complexly through an operative presence, we show by the following argument: By whatever reason Holy Scripture defines divine omnipresence, by that same reason it must be defined by us. But Holy Scripture defines divine omnipresence complexly through the substantial presence of God to creatures and at the same time most efficacious operation. Therefore. The minor is proven; because in Holy Scripture no mode of divine presence is found defined without operation included. For (1) the universal presence, that God fills heaven and earth, by the phrase of Scripture, denotes not a bare presence of God, but the most powerful preservation and government of creatures: for St. Paul, about to delineate this, says in Acts XVII, 27: The Lord exists not far from each one of us. For in him we live, and move, and are. We live in God, as an infant in the maternal womb, in which it is vivified: we move in him, as ships in the ocean, by which they are sustained: we are in him, as light in the air, with which it is united.

(2) By gracious presence God inhabits the faithful, renewing, consoling, and protecting them. Lev. XXVI, 12. 2 Cor. VI, 16. Ps. XCI, 15. (3) By glorious presence God is present to the angels and the blessed, glorifying and exhilarating them. Ps. XVI, 11. Rev. XXI, 3. Wherefore, since every divine presence is connected with a certain operation, we define the same complexly as an operative presence.

The antithesis is (1) of the Socinians (to whom Vorstius assents) denying the substantial omnipresence of God.

(2) Of certain theologians, among whom are also the Tubingensians, denying that the efficacious operation of God enters into the definition of divine presence.

Latin:

Obs. III.

Praesentia divina stylo biblico, & sensu complexo, duo infert (1) ἀδιαστασίαν sive substantialem adessentiam Dei ad creaturas.

(2) ἐνέργειαν, sive efficacem operationem. Duo itaque probanda hic sunt: (a) Deum ratione substantiae ubique adesse. (b) Ad plenam & accuratam praesentiae divinae definitionem etiam efficacem Dei operationem, seu partem definitiuam, praelucente S. scriptura requiri.

Prob. a. (1) Ex Ierem. XXIII, 23-24. Num Deus eius, quod e propinquo est, ego sum, inquit Iehouah; & non Deus eius, quod e longinquo est? Num abscondetur vir in latibulis, & ego non videbo cum? inquit Iehouah. Nonne caelum & terram ego impleo? inquit Iehouah. Circa hoc oraculum propheticum observes (a) praefixum ב in nominibus מקרוב & מרחוק efficere constructionem substantivorum latine per genitivum exprimendam, observantibus BUXTORF. in thesauro lib. II, c. III. p. 365. & SEB. SCHMID. in colleg. bibl. priori p. 97. Et cum elliptica sit locutio, Buxtorff supplet nomen מקום loci q. d. Num Deus loci propinqui ego sum? Et sic etiam: Num Deus loci longinqui ego sum? Recte sane. Ita enim Deus etiam dicitur Deus caeli & terrae. Gen. XXIV, 3. Nisi malueris subaudire rei q. d. Num Deus ego eius rei, quae prope est &c. Obs. (b) Loca propinqua & remota, aut res propinquae & remotae, dicuntur tales, respectu habito ad certum divinae praesentiae modum, iuxta quem Deus alicubi esse dicitur. Nec videtur hic dubitandum de hoc, quod Dominus respiciat caelum, quod alias in scriptura dicitur, & ab omnibus populis semper habitum est habitaculum Dei. Ab iis falsis prophetis, contra quos Dominus hic agit, pro eodem quoque habebatur. Respectu caeli itaque & respectu modi praesentiae, quo Deus in caelis est, loca propinqua & remota appellantur. Cum autem Deus in caelo fit ratione substantiae, etiam locis caelo propinquis & ab eo remotis substantialiter adest. Obs. (c) Quando Dominus dicit: Nonne caelum & terram ego impleo? propria significatio verbi, implere, retinenda est. Dicitur aliquid ab aliquo impleri, quando ita omnia illius penetrat & possidet, vt nihil remaneat vacuum, nihil, in quo non fit res, quae implet. Argumentamur: Quicunque est Deus non tantum loci proximi, sed etiam remotissimi, implens caelum & terram, ille est omnipraesens ratione substantiae suae.

Atqui Deus &c. Ergo. (2) Ex Ps. CXXXIX, 7-8. Quo abiero a spiritu tuo? & quo a facie tua auolauero? Si ascendero in caelos, ibi tu: aut sternam (in) inferno, ecce tu (hic). Obs. Per spiritum Dei intelligendus est Spiritus sanctus; Per faciem Dei, maiestas Dei tremenda, vel vt D. GEIERVS censet, commentar. in h. l. p. 1208. Filius Dei, qui est imago patris & character substantiae eius, Col. I, 15. Hebr. I, 3. intelligitur. Nascitur nobis argumentum: Quicunque ita in caelis & in inferno est, vt spiritum & faciem eius nemo effugere queat, ille substantialiter omnipraesens est. Atqui Deus &c. Ergo. Prob. b. Omnipraesentiam divinam complexe per adessentiam operosam definiendam esse, sequenti argumento ostendimus: Quacunque ratione sacra scriptura omnipraesentiam divinam definit, eadem ratione nobis definienda est. Atqui sacra scriptura omnipraesentiam divinam complexe definit per adessentiam Dei ad creaturas substantialem, & operationem simul efficacissimam, Ergo. Minor probatur; quia in scriptura sacra non reperitur vllus praesentiae divinae modus, sine inclusa operatione definitus. Nam (1) Praesentia vniversalis, qua Deus cælum & terram implet, phrasi scripturæ non nudam Dei adessentiam, sed potentissimam creaturarum conseruationem & gubernationem notat: quippe quam S. Paullus delineaturus, ait Act. XVII, 27: Dominus non procul ab vnoquoque nostrum existit. In ipso enim viuimus, mouemur & sumus. Viuimus in Deo, vt infans in vtero materno, in quo viuificatur: mouemur in ipso, vt naues in oceano, a quo sustentantur: sumus in ipso, vt lux in aëre, cum quo vnitur.

(2) Præsentia gratiosa Deus fideles inhabitat, eos renouando, consolando, protegendo. Leu. XXVI, 12. 2 Cor. VI, 16. Ps. XCI, 15. (3) Præsentia gloriosa Deus angelis & beatis adest, eos glorificando & exhilarando. Ps. XVI, 11. Apoc. XXI, 3. Quam ob rem cum omnis præsentia diuina cum operatione quadam connexa sit, eandem complexe per adessentiam operosam definimus.

Antithesis est (1) Socinianorum (quibus adstipulatur Vorstius) negantium omnipræsentiam Dei substantialem.

(2) Quorundam theologorum, e quibus etiam sunt Tubingenses, infitiantium, efficacem Dei operationem præsentiæ diuinæ definitionem ingredi.


### Quest. XLVIII. What is the power of God?: The Socinians impugn our assertion with the following arguments

The Socinians impugn our assertion with the following arguments.

I. If God by reason of substance filled heaven and earth, he would be in the most sordid places. But the latter seems to be absurd. Therefore also the former.

Resp. Sordid places do not stain God; because bodies indeed, but not spirits, are contaminated by sordid things. Created spirits, namely angels and souls, and also the light of the sun, are present to physically sordid things and yet are not defiled. God is offended by things morally base (the sins of men), not physically sordid.

Instance: God commanded that everything sordid be removed from the camp of the Israelites. Num. V, 28. Deut. XXII, 10. R. God did not command that on account of a fear of the defilement of the divine essence, but so that he might commend to the Israelites the most accurate pursuit of moral purity through the way of symbolic observation, and also provide for the health of the Israelites.

II. If God were substantially omnipresent, he would be present to the devils. The latter is absurd. Therefore also the former.

Resp. God is present to the devils by a general presence, or presence of power; otherwise he would not be present to the good angels struggling with the devils, Jude v. 9, indeed God would not even have been present to Christ when he was tempted and carried by the devil. Matt. IV.

The adversaries admitting that God is present to the devils by reason of power, knowledge, and providence: why then not by reason of substance; which does not really differ from the divine attributes. III. Whoever is immense and excluded by no place, he is mixed with created things. But God is not mixed with created things.

Resp. Presence formally does not signify mixture, but non-distance. Angels are present to lions, yet they are not mixed with them. God, the purest act, excluding all passive potency, is not mixable.

IV. Whoever dwells in heaven, does not dwell on earth. God, etc. Therefore.

The minor is evident from Ps. II, 4. Resp. God dwells in heaven not only, not exclusively, but also fills the earth, Jer. XXIII, 24.

He dwells in us. John XIV, 17. God is in heaven by presence of glory, because he most lucidly manifests his glory to the angels and blessed men in heaven: He is nevertheless also on earth by presence of grace and power: everywhere by essence. [*]

For 1) that no determination of place or dwelling is to be attributed to God, it stands plainly written in 1 Kings VIII, 27: 2) God is said to be higher than all the heavens, Job XI, 8. 3) to be in heaven and earth at once, Isaiah LVII, 15. 4) to fill heaven and earth, that is, to be circumscribed by no boundaries of places, Jer. XXIII, 24. Nor so much presence.

V. Those praying stretch their hands toward heaven, and lift up their eyes and hearts on high. They do this because God is substantially only in heaven.

Resp. We stretch our hands toward heaven so that, venerating the majesty of God, we may think of nothing but sublime things, and thus lift our mind from earthly to heavenly things. So that we may seek heavenly goods, testifying that our citizenship (πολίτευμα), the desire for which we are held by, is in heaven, Phil.

III, 20. VI. Whoever changes place, by ascending and descending, he is not immense or substantially omnipresent.

But God &c. Gen. XI, 7. Resp. God descends not by reason of essence, but by reason of manifestation .

However, he does not change place, because he is not in a place locally or circumscriptively. VII. If God were whole in the entire world, and whole in every speck of dust, it would follow that he would be at once finite and infinite, equal and unequal to the same thing, greater and smaller than himself.

The latter is absurd. Therefore also the former. Resp. I deny the consequence.

Because God is not some physical whole of essence, or integral; composed of parts, but is a perfectional whole, which, having supreme perfection without parts, is said to be a whole. Confer, CALOVIUS, metaph. diu. part. gen. p. 520. God is present everywhere as a whole, because he is indivisible (ἀμέριστος), or a most simple spirit, devoid of all parts, he is present everywhere, not circumscriptively or occupatively, but repletively.

Therefore he is whole in a speck of dust, without inclusion from within, without exclusion from without.

If the whole soul is in the whole body, and whole in every part of the body: why would God, a spirit, and a most simple act, not be whole in the whole world, and whole in every part of the world? God is infinite, not by reason of quantitative extension, but by reason of essence and perfection.

While he is present to finite things, his essence is not rendered finite: just as his essence does not become temporal by coexisting with temporal things. Equality is an affection of quantity, not befitting angels, much less God, the most pure spirit. No one is said to be greater or smaller than himself, but is said to be greater than others, insofar as he is compared with them by reason of quantity. VIII. If God were omnipresent to all parts of the world, outside and inside, above and below, before and after, to the right and to the left, it would follow that all parts of the world, however separated, would also be most conjoined.

The latter is absurd. Therefore also the former. The major consequence is proven; because things which are joined to the same third thing according to the same respect, are also joined among themselves with respect to that third, or in order to that third, but not absolutely. India has the present God no less than Germany; but for that reason those regions, situated very far apart, are not absolutely conjoined.

Quæst. L. What practical uses will you extract from the description of God and his attributes?

From the description of God and the divine attributes, most abundant uses, both paraenetic, by which the majesty of God is designated by this manner of speaking: to be in heaven, to dwell, to sit. For heaven in the sacred scriptures, spoken improperly, is a sign of altitude, as earth is of humility. see related notions Ps. CIII, 19. CXV, 3. we are stimulated to exercises of piety; then one may extract paracletic [consolatory] passages, which contribute no small amount to the tranquility of the soul.

I. God is Spirit. John IV, 24. Therefore a) let us worship Him in Spirit and truth; let us walk according to the Spirit.

Rom. VIII, 7. b) Since our soul is a spirit, it is not tranquilized in adverse circumstances except by spiritual consolation.

My soul, (be) silent only toward God: for from Him (will be) my salvation. Ps. LXII, 2.

II. God is the first and independent being, from whom all creatures depend. Let us therefore depend entirely a) on the divine will expressed in the Holy Scriptures.

I have cleaved to your testimonies, says the royal prophet Ps. CXIX, 31. b) Those who depend on God are supported by Him, lest they perish.

My soul cleaves to you; but your right hand sustains me. Ps. LXIII, 9.

III. God is one. a) Therefore let us worship this one Lord our God, and serve Him alone. Matt. IV, 10. b) This one is the treasure of our heart, better than all the treasures of the world.

Let us trample upon the riches of this age; the one treasure of the heart suffices.

IV. God is simple; therefore a) let us love simplicity, fleeing all deceit and hypocrisy worse than a dog or a snake.

Let us pray with David: May simplicity and your uprightness, O Christ, govern me. Ps. XXV, 21. b) Jehovah keeps the simple: when they are brought low, He saves them.

Ps. CXVI, 6.

V. God is true. Therefore let us a) truly acknowledge and worship Him from the word of truth. b) Let us repeatedly reflect with ourselves that eternal life is situated in that one true God.

John XVII, 3.

VI. God is good. Therefore a) He is to be loved. But if we love derived, imperfect, fragile good: how much more the original, archetypal, eternal good?

No one is good, except God alone. Matt. XIX, 17. b) To those who love God, all things work together for good Rom.

VIII, 28.

Hence we do not fear to die (I speak with St. AMBROSE), because we have a good Lord.

VII. God is holy. Wherefore a) let us imitate the most holy Father.

Be holy, for I am holy, the Lord your God. Lev. XIX. b) To the holy children of God nothing good is lacking, provided they strenuously continue to worship God holily.

Fear Jehovah, you His holy ones; for there is no lack for those who fear Him. Ps. XXXIV, 10.

VIII. God is infinite. Therefore let us most humbly a) acknowledge our own imperfection, who, when compared with God, who is infinitely perfect, were nothing, and are worth nothing.

All nations are as nothing before Him, they are reckoned by Him as less than nothing, and vanity, Is. XL, 17. b) As the essence of God is infinite: so His mercy is bounded by no end.

This I will recall to my heart: therefore I will hope: that the mercies of Jehovah are not finished; that His compassions are not consumed.

Lam. III, 21.

IX. God is eternal. Therefore, with most ardent desire, let us aspire away from fleeting and perishable goods a) to Him who alone dwells in eternity.

Is. LVII, 15.

Let us ascend from earth to heaven, from shadow to truth, from time to eternity, from creatures to God, the creator and king of the ages. 1 Tim. I, 17. b) With the devil raging, and the world pressing upon us, let us lift up our minds with the hope of eternal glory.

For the momentary lightness of our affliction works for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all excellence; because we do not look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal. 2 Cor. IV, 17.

X. God is immense, substantially present everywhere. Therefore let us solicitously beware a) lest we commit works of darkness in hidden corners.

Shall a man be hidden (from me) in secret places, so that I do not see him, says Jehovah, Jer. XXIII, 24.

Wisely says AUGUSTINE in Ps. I, 6: God is all eye, because He sees all things: He is all ear, because He hears all things: He is all hand, because He works all things: He is all foot, because He is present everywhere. b) Walking

through the dark valley of death, let us say with David: Though I walk in the valley of the shadow of death: I will fear no evil: for thou, Jehovah, wilt be with me.

XI. God is Immutable. a) Therefore, let our mutable will adhere to the immutable goodness and will of God, so that it may be established and confirmed in the good. b) Since the gifts and calling of God are without repentance, Rom. 11, 28, let us most firmly conclude that God will never change the favorable affection He has toward us, provided that we ourselves do not allow ourselves to be overcome by the lusts of the flesh and to be torn away from God.

XII. God is Immortal. For which reason a) let us fix all our trust, all our hope, in the immortal God. He who loves transitory things perishes with transitory things. But hope, relying on God, rests upon an immortal, immovable foundation. b) Our immortal soul is not satisfied, does not rest, except in the immortal God.

Ps. 18, 15. XIII. God is Invisible and Incomprehensible. Therefore a) let us acknowledge and celebrate with a grateful heart and mouth that He has come forth from the secret seat of His majesty, and has revealed Himself to us both through the creation of the world and through the preaching of the Word. b) This becomes a most effective consolation to us travelers, that although we now see God in a riddle according to the state of this life: in the heavenly fatherland we shall see Him face to face.

XIV. God is Most Glorious. Wherefore a) let us refer all our undertakings, words, and deeds to the glory of God, as the ultimate goal, 1 Cor. 10, 21. b) Let the afflicted children of God glory in the Lord, Jer. 9, 23, expecting from Him the riches of heavenly glory, Eph. 1.

XV. God is Most Blessed. Let us therefore seek a) everlasting blessedness not in creatures, but in the Creator, the source and author of solid blessedness. Most elegantly AUGUSTINE, De spir. et anim. c. 63: God is the supreme good, sufficient unto Himself for all things, needing nothing, of whom all things have need, that they may exist and be well. Let afflicted Christians in this world soothe their minds with the foretaste of heavenly blessedness; for it is divinely given to them to taste the powers of the age to come, Heb. 6, 5.

XVI. God Lives. He lives an intellectual life by seeing through and directing all things with a most sharp intellect; by commanding all things with a most free will. Let us therefore live a) also a divine life after the example of Enoch, Gen. 4, 24. Let us live by the will of God, not by the lusts of men, 1 Pet. 4, 2. b) It is a most present consolation to us that God does not delight in the death of the sinner, but wills that he, repenting, may live eternally with Him, Ezek. 33, 11.

XVII. God is Omniscient and Omnisapient. And therefore a) let us flee all hypocrisy, since God does not look only at external deeds, but also searches the hearts and reins, Ps. 7, 10. b) Let us not lose heart when destitute of human aid. For the heavenly Father knows all things of which we have need, Matt. 6, 32. He sees the affliction of His people, Exod. 3, 7.

XVIII. God is Benign and Merciful. Therefore a) let the care of the miserable also touch us. Be ye merciful, as your Father also is merciful, says Christ, Luke 6, 36. b) Conscious of even the gravest sins, let us not despair with Cain and Judas, but with contrite hearts let us call upon the throne of divine mercy, repeating that Davidic prayer: Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy great mercy, Ps. 51, 1. Moreover, to all the afflicted, the mercy of God is a sweet harbor of the soul and an anchor of hope, Isa. 54, 7.

XIX. God is Most Just. Let us therefore live a) also justly ourselves, Tit. 2, 12, by observing divine laws, by harming no one, by rendering to each his own, and by standing by promises and covenants. b) Oppressed by the unjust censures or judgments of others, let us repeatedly consider with ourselves that God will bring a just cause into the light. Mich. 7, 9.

Accordingly a) let us follow the truth after the example of our heavenly Father. Speak every man truth with his neighbor, says the prophet Zechariah, ch. 8, 16. b) I live God is Omnipotent. Far be it, therefore, that we should attempt to measure the infinite power of God with the a) yardstick of our reason!

For God can do more than abundantly above those things that we understand, Eph. III, 20. Rather, let us acknowledge that the glory of most humble obedience is left to us, 1

Petr. V, 6. b) In every necessity, the omnipotent hand of God, which is able to change all things, Ps.

LXXVII, 11. sustains and refreshes us. Father, all things are possible unto thee.

Marc. XIV, 36. XXII. God is Omnipresent. Therefore a) let us cleanse our souls from all filth, that God may dwell in us.

He who prepares the house of his mind for God must wipe away the filth of evil work, says GREGORY the Great in homily XXX on the Gospels. b) Surrounded by dangerous peril, let us be comforted by the most present help of God.

For God has promised us his helping presence.

Es. XLIII, 2. 3. Ps.

XCI, 14. 15. (). SIGH. () But before we depart from here, the divine Reserved things must be considered with great attention of mind.

For in those perfections of God which have been communicated in some way to finite things, especially to intelligent ones, there are none that agree with the infinite nature of God, which God has reserved as proper to himself.

That we may begin from the beginning: In every thing, that which is supreme, and which pertains entirely to infinity and independence, cannot but always be the property of God alone.

They are therefore Reserved.

I. Divine Knowledge Divine knowledge, which is generally comprehended under the name of Omniscience, specifically 1) the most perfect knowledge of God himself and of all secret counsels, Iob.

XV, 8. Ies.

XL, 13. Matth. XI, 27. Rom. XI, 34. 1 Cor. II, 10, 11. 2) Knowledge of the whole of nature, for he himself is the one effector and moderator of all things.

Ps.

CXXXIX, 1. 3. 4. Hebr. IV, 13. 3) Knowledge of all things that are superior to all the powers of nature; for God alone is able to perform miracles.

4) Knowledge of souls, 1 Reg. VIII, 39. Act. I, 24. and that indeed (α) immediate, as it is wont to be said, with no intervening manifestation or declaration by signs, Ps.

CXXXIX, 1. 3. 4. Ioan. II, 25. (β) certain, not probable, which force the word ידע possesses, (γ) universal and perpetual, without any exception of either men, 1

Reg. VIII, 39. Act. I, 24. or of the thoughts and motions of the mind, of the hiding places and recesses in souls, of counsels even the most clandestine and of which man himself is not conscious, Ps.

CXXXIX, 2. 4. 23. Finally 5) foreknowledge, and indeed of all those things which are (α) most remote, whence so many predictions about future events, to be expected only after many centuries, (β) most minute, not only of the period of time, but also of the point and moment, Act.

I, 7. (γ) Future contingencies.

Ies. XLI, 22. 23. XLIII, 8. 9. XLIV, 7. 1 Sam.

Latin:

Sociniani sequentibus nostram assertionem argumentis impugnant.

I. Si Deus ratione substantiæ cælum & terram impleret, esset in locis sordidissimis. Sed posterius videtur esse absurdum. Ergo & prius.

Resp. Loca sordida non maculant Deum; quia corpora quidem, non autem spiritus rebus sordidis contaminantur. Spiritus creati, nempe angeli & animæ, nec non lumen solis rebus physice sordidis adsunt neque tamen fœdantur. Deus rebus moraliter turpibus (flagitiis hominum) non physice sordidis offenditur.

Instantia: Præcepit Deus, vt ex castris Israëlitarum omne sordidum amoueretur. Num. V, 28. Deut. XXII, 10. R. Non præcepit illud Deus, propter inquinationis essentiæ diuinæ metum, sed vt tum per viam symbolicæ obseruationis Israëlitarum accuratissimum moralis puritatis studium commendaret, tum sanitati Israëlitarum consuleret.

II. Si Deus substantialiter esset omnipræsens, adesset diabolis. Posterior est absurdum. Ergo & prius.

Resp. Deus præsentia generali, siue præsentia potentiæ diabolis adest; alioqui non præsto foret angelis bonis luctantibus cum diabolis, Iud. v. 9. immo ne Christo quidem Deus fuisset præsens, cum tentatus & portatus est a diabolo. Matth. IV.

Fatentibus aduersariis Deus adest diabolis ratione potentiæ, scientiæ & prouidentiæ: quidni ergo ratione substantiæ; quæ ab attributis diuinis realiter non differt. III. Quicunque immensus & nullo loco exclusus est, ille cum rebus creatis est permixtus. Atqui Deus cum rebus creatis non est permixtus.

Resp. Præsentia formaliter non dicit permixtionem, sed indistantiam. Angeli præsentes sunt leonibus, neque tamen iis permiscentur. Deus, actus purissimus, omnem potentiam passiuam excludens, non est permiscibilis.

IV. Quicunque habitat in cælo, non habitat in terra. Deus &c. Ergo.

Minor constat e Ps. II, 4. Resp. Deus habitat in cælo non tantum, non exclusive, sed etiam terram implet, Ier. XXIII, 24.

Habitat in nobis. Io. XIV, 17. Deus est in cælo præsentia gloriæ, quia angelis & beatis hominibus in cælo suam gloriam lucidissime manifestat: Est tamen etiam in terris præsentia gratiæ, & potentiæ: vbique per essentiam. [] [] Sunt potissimum quatuor argumenta, ex quibus elucet, non proprie dictum esse, cum Deus dicitur in cælo esse, immo habitare.

Nam 1) Determinationem loci & habitationem nullam Deo tribuendam esse, aperte scriptum exstat 1 Reg. VIII, 27: 2) superior cælis omnibus Deus dicitur, Iobi XI, 8. 3) in cælo & terra simul esse, Iesaiæ LVII, 15. 4) cælum & terram implere, hoc est, nullis locorum terminis circumscriptum esse, Ierem. XXIII, 24. Nec tam præsentia.

V. Precantes manus suas in caelum tendunt, & oculos atque corda sua sursum attollunt. Quod faciunt ideo, quod Deus substantialiter tantum est in caelo.

Resp. Precantes manus nostras ad caelum tendimus vt maiestatem Dei venerantes, non nisi sublimia cogitemus, atque adeo mentem a terrenis ad caelestia elevemus. Vt caelestia bona quaeramus, testantes πολιτευμα nostrum, cuius desiderio tenemur, esse in caelo, Phil.

III, 20. VI. Quicunque locum mutat, adscendendo & descendendo, ille non est immensus aut substantialiter omnipraesens.

Atqui Deus &c. Gen. XI, 7. Resp. Deus descendit non ratione essentiae, sed ratione manifestationis .

Locum autem non mutat, quia localiter, aut circumscriptive non est in loco. VII. Si Deus totus esset in vniverso mundo, & totus in quolibet puluifculo, sequeretur, quod simul finitas & infinitus, eidem rei aequalis & inaequalis, seipso maior & minor esset.

Posterius est absurdum. Ergo & prius. Resp. neg. consequ. Quia Deus non est aliquod totum physicum essentiae, aut integrale; ex partibus compositum, sed est totum perfectionale, quod, summam habens perfectionem sine partibus, totum esse dicitur.

Confer, CALOVII metaph. diu. part. gen. p. 520. Deus vbique totus adest, quia ἀμέριστος, siue spiritus simplicissimus, omnium partium expers, vbique adest, non circumscriptive aut occupatiue, sed repletive.

Totus ergo est in puluifculo, sine inclusione ab intra, sine exclusione ab extra. Si tota anima est in toto corpore, & tota in qualibet parte corporis: quidni Deus, spiritus, & actus simplicissimus, totus foret in toto mundo, & totus in qualibet parte mundi? Deus infinitus est, non ratione quantitiuae extensionis, sed ratione essentiae & perfectionis.

Dum rebus finitis adest, essentia eius finita non redditur: sicut essentia eius non fit temporaria rebus temporalibus coëxistendo. Aequalitas est affectio quantitatis, non angelis, nedum Deo, spiritui purissimo, conueniens. Nemo se ipso maior aut minor dicitur, sed maior dicitur aliis, quatenus cum iis ratione quantitatis comparatur.

VIII. Si Deus omnibus mundi partibus esset omnipraesens, extra & intra, supra & infra, ante & post, ad dextram & sinistram, sequeretur, quod omnes partes mundi seiunctissimae, etiam forent coniunctissimae.

Posterius est absurdum. Ergo & prius. Consequ. mai. probatur; quia quae eidem secundum idem iunguntur, etiam inter se iuncta sunt respectu illius tertii, siue in ordine ad illud tertium, non autem absolute. India non minus atque Germania Deum praesentem habet; sed ideo non absolute coniunctae sunt regiones illae longissime dissitae.

Quæst. L. Quos usus practicos e descriptione Dei & attributis excerpes? E descriptione Dei & attributis diuinis usus vberrimos, tum paraeneticos, quibus sentia, quam maiestas Dei designatur hac dicendi ratione: in caelo esse, habitare, sedere.

Caelum enim in sacris litteris, improprie dictum, est signum altitudinis, vt terra humilitatis. vid. notiones connexae Ps. CIII, 19. CXV, 3. bus ad exercitia pietatis exstimulamur; tum paracleticos, qui ad tranquillitatem animi haud parum momenti conferunt, excerpere licet.

I. Deus est Spiritus. Ioh. IV, 24. Ergo a) in Spiritu & veritate eum adoremus; ambulemus secundum Spiritum.

Rom. VIII, 7. b) Cum anima nostra sit Spiritus, rebus in adversis non nisi solatio spirituali tranquillatur.

Tantummodo erga Deum silentium (esto tibi) anima mea: ab illo enim (erit) salus mea. Ps. LXII, 2.

II. Deus est ens primum & independens, a quo omnes creaturae dependent. Pendeamus ergo toti a) a voluntate diuina sacris litteris expressa.

Adhaesi testimoniis tuis, inquit propheta regius Ps. CXIX, 31. b) Qui a Deo pendent, ab ipso, ne pessum eant, suffulciuntur.

Adhaeret tibi anima mea; me autem sustentat dextra tua. Ps. LXIII, 9.

III. Vnus est Deus. a) Vnum igitur hunc dominum Deum nostrum adoremus, & ipsi soli seruiamus. Matth. IV, 10. b) Vnus hic cordis nostri thesaurus est omnibus mundi thesauris potior.

Calcemus diuitias huius saeculi; sufficit vnicus cordis thesaurus.

IV. Simplex est Deus; ideo a) amemus simplicitatem, omnem dolum & hypocrisiam cane peius & angue fugientes.

Precemur cum Dauide: Simplicitas rectumque tuum me, Christe, gubernet. Ps. XXV, 21. b) Simplices custodit Iehouah: quum atteruntur, tum illos seruat.

Ps. CXVI, 6.

V. Verus est Deus. Hunc igitur a) e verbo veritatis vere agnoscamus & colamus. b) In vno illo vero Deum vitam aeternam sitam esse, subinde nobiscum reputemus.

Io. XVII, 3.

VI. Bonus est Deus. Ergo a) amandus. Quod si amamus bonum deriuatum, imperfectum, fragile: quanto magis bonum originale, archetypum, aeternum?

Nemo bonus, nisi solus Deus. Matth. XIX, 17. b) Diligentibus Deum omnia cooperantur in bonum Rom.

IIX, 28.

Hinc mori non timemus (cum S. AMBROSIO loquor), quia bonum Dominum habemus.

VII. Sanctus est Deus. Quare a) imitemur patrem sanctissimum.

Estote sancti, quia ego sanctus, dominus Deus vester. Leuit. XIX. b) Sanctis Dei filiis nil boni deest, modo Deum sancte colere strenue pergant.

Timete Iehouah sancti illius; quia non est defectus timentibus ipsum. Ps. XXXIV, 10.

VIII. Infinitus est Deus. Humillime igitur a) nostram agnoscamus imperfectionem, qui, cum Deo, infinite perfecto, comparati, nil fuimus, nil valemus.

Omnes gentes sunt sicut nihil erga ipsum, minus quam nihil, & inane reputantur illi, Es. XL, 17. b) Vt infinita est essentia Dei: ita misericordia eius nullo fine terminatur.

Hoc reuocabo ad cor meum: ideo sperabo: misericordia Iehouae quod non finitae sint; quod non consumtae miserationes eius.

Thren. III, 21.

22. IX. Eternus est Deus. Contentis igitur bonis fluxis & caducis desiderio flagrantissimo a) adspiremus ad eum, qui solus habitat in aeternum.

Es. LVII, 15.

Adscendamus a terra in coelum, ab vmbra ad veritatem, a tempore ad aeternitatem, a creaturis ad Deum, saeculorum conditorem & regem. 1 Tim. I, 17. b) Fremente diabolo, & premente nos mundo, erigamus mentes nostras spe aeternae gloriae.

Nam momentanea leuitas afflictionis nostrae iuxta excellentiam in excellentiam aeternum pondus gloriae operatur nobis; eo, quod nos non spectamus ad ea, quae videntur, sed ad ea, quae non videntur: quae enim videntur, temporaria sunt; quae vero non videntur, aeternae. 2 Cor. IV, 17.

18. X. Immensus est Deus, vbique substantialiter praesens. Sollicite igitur caueamus a) ne opera tenebrarum in abstrusis committamus angulis.

Num occultabitur (a me) vir in latibulis, vt ego non videam eum, dictum Iehouae, Ierem. XXIII, 24.

Scite inquit AVGVSTIN. in Ps. I, 6. Deus totus oculus est, quia omnia videt: totus auris est, quia omnia audit: totus manus est, quia omnia operatur: totus pes est, quia vbique praesens est. b) Ambulantes

per obscuram mortis vallem, dicamus cum Dauide: Cum ambulauero in valle vmbrofitatis: non timebo mihi malum: quoniam tu, Iehouah, mecum eris. Ps. XXIII, 15.

XI. Immutabilis est Deus. a) Mutabilis itaque voluntas nostra immutabili bonitati ac voluntati diuinae adhaereat, vt in bono solidetur & confirmetur. b) Cum ἀμεταμέλητα fine poenitentia sint dona & vocatio Dei, Rom. XI, 28. firmissime statuamus, Deum pronum sum in nos affectum nunquam mutaturum esse, modo ipsi nos a cupiditatibus carnis vinci, & a Deo auelli non patiamur.

XII. Immortalis est Deus. Quam ob rem a) in Deo immortali omnem fiduciam, omnem spem nostram defigamus. Qui transitoria amat, cum transitoriis interit. At spes, confisa Deo, immortali, immobili nititur fundamento. b) Anima nostra immortalis non satiatur, non quiescit, nisi in Deo immortali. Ps. XVIII, 15.

XIII. Inuisibilis & incomprehensibilis est Deus. Ergo a) grato corde & ore cognoscamus atque celebremus, quod ex arcana suae maiestatis sede prodierit, & tum per mundi creationem, tum per verbi praedicationem se nobis reuelauerit. b) Hoc nobis viatoribus efficacissimo, fit solatio, quod licet nunc pro statu vitae in aenigmate Deum videamus: in patria coelesti a facie ad faciem ipsum visuri simus. 1 Cor. XV, 28.

XIV. Gloriosissimus est Deus. Quo circa a) omnia nostra coepta, dicta, facta ad gloriam Dei, ceu scopum vltimum, referamus, 1 Cor. X, 21. b) Afflicti Dei filii glorientur in domino Ier. IX, 23. exspectantes ab ipso diuitias coelestis gloriae, Eph. I.

XV. Beatissimus est Deus. Quaeramus igitur a) perennem beatitudinem non in creaturis, sed in creatore, solidae beatitudinis fonte & auctore. Perquam eleganter AVGVSTIN. de spir. & anim. c. LXIII. Deus est summum bonum, sibi ad omnia sufficiens, nullo indigens, quo omnia indigent, vt sint & bene sint. Afflicti in hoc mundo christiani mentes suas permulceant praegustu coelestis beatitudinis; diuinitus quippe ipsis datur, gustare virtutes futuri saeculi, Hebr. VI, 5.

III. Divine Goodness For there is none good but God, Matth. XIX, 17. namely, to use terms received by usage, 1) independently, 2) excellently, as being the supreme good and the one most excellent of all, 3) causally, since all good things proceed from one God, Iac.

I, 17. 4) constantly, without any mutability, ibid. We offer thanks to you, O eternal God, for having come forth from the secret seat of your majesty and revealed yourself to us, both with the stupendous works in the kingdom of nature and especially through your revealed word. Enlightened and illuminated, therefore, by the light of your grace, we acknowledge you as the most holy Spirit, and we worship you in Spirit and in truth. We acknowledge you as perpetually living, and we ardently desire to live for you now. We stand in awe of you, the omniscient and avenging eye, seeing all things. We entrust our whole selves to you, the all-wise, and to your counsel and will. We acknowledge you as most benevolent, and as we recall your benefits with a grateful memory, so we proclaim them with a grateful mouth. We implore you, the most merciful, and troubled by the remembrance of our sins, we flee as suppliants to the sacred altar of your mercy. We acknowledge you as most powerful, and we submit ourselves most humbly to your right hand, which dispenses all things. We revere you as most present, and we dedicate the temples of our hearts to your gracious indwelling. Remain in us, Lord, so that we may remain in you eternally!

Immortales tibi, o Deus aeterne, agimus gratias, quod ex arcana maiestatis tuae sede prodiens cum stupendis in regno naturae operibus, tum praecipue verbo tuo revelato te nobis patefeceris. Praenenti igitur & collustrati lumine gratiae tuae, agnoscimus te Spiritum sanctissimum, & in Spiritu atque veritate adoramus. Agnoscimus te perpetuo viventem, & tibi iam vivere ardenter desideramus. Te omniscium, & vindicem oculum, tuum omnia videntem reformidamus. Tibi omnifapienti, & consilio atque arbitrio tuo nos totos permittimus. Te misericordissimum imploramus, & peccatorum nostrorum recordatione turbati, ad sacram misericordiae tuae aram supplices confugimus. Agnoscimus te potentissimum, & dextrae tuae, cuncta dispenfanti, nos humillime subiicimus. Te praesentissimum reveremur, & templa cordium nostrorum ad gratiosam inhabitationem tibi dedicamus. Mane in nobis, domine, vt aeternum in te maneamus!

## 5 On the Highest Mystery of the Holy Trinity


### On the Supreme Mystery of the Most Holy

MYSTERY OF THE HOLY TRINITY.

Quest. I. How should the mystery of the Trinity be proposed and inculcated most simply and clearly to the unlearned common people?

The most august mystery of the venerable Trinity is handed down to the unlearned in the simplest and clearest way, let it show 1) that God is one. 2) That the one God is the Father, IV. Of divine truth, and specifically of that which is usually called veracity: 1) Universality, without any exception, Josh. XXIII, 14. 2 Kings X, 10. Luke XVIII, 31. Acts III, 21: 2) Necessity, so that God cannot even ever deceive, Num. XXIII, 19. 1 Sam. XV, 29. Heb. VI, 18. V. Of divine power, and authority, since God is all-powerful, παντοκράτωρ (almighty), 2 Cor. VI, 18. Rev. IV, 8. μόνος δυνατής (the only powerful one), Ps. LXII, 12. 1 Tim. VI, 15. Therefore, the proper and reserved attributes of this must be considered.

(α) By reason of things, or Objects: In the power of the one God is 1) the mind of every human, Matt. X, 28. to whom belongs the right (α) of binding the conscience, Rom. II, 15. XIII, 5. 1 Pet. II, 19. (β) of remitting sins, and indeed by his own authority, Mark II, 7: 2) both kinds of fortune, as being the highest and ultimate in any action, Gen. XXXIX, 3. Deut. XXX, 9. Ps. CXXVII, 1. 2. Eccles. IX, 11: 3) heaven no less than the whole earth, Ps. CXV, 16. CXXXV, 6. Dan. IV, 32: 4) the church, Eph. I, 22: 5) every Magistrate, with no exception even for the highest Rulers, Dan. II, 21. Rom. XIII, 1. 2. 1 Tim. VI, 15: 6) the life and death of mortals, to the one of all, Ps. XC, 3. Isa. XXXVIII, 1. 5: 7) judgment, and that supreme, and thus common, Gen. XVIII, 25. Ps. LIX, 14: 8) the universal nature of things, Ps. LXXXIII, 19. so that God alone is also able to effect miracles, much greater than the forces of nature, Ex. XV, 11. Ps. LXXII, 18. (β) By reason of the mode: God, and he indeed one, is able to do all things 1) by his own will, or, as is commonly said, independently, so that he has all power and authority in himself, not given to him by another, (β) so that no one can ever resist God, (γ) so that he himself is never bound to render an account of his deeds to anyone (all these three notions are contained in the one saying, Daniel IV, 32.): 2) immediately, provided he wills and commands, Ps. XXXIII, 9. Rev. IV, 11. so that he can even effect all things where there was nothing before, Rom. IV, 17: 3) infinitely, so that there was no beginning of power, nor is there any end, Dan. IV, 31. VI, 26: 4) perfectly, so that nothing at all is lacking, Gen. I, 31. Isa. XL, 26. I judge this doctrine concerning divine reserved attributes to be one of the most important.

For this will be of very great use hereafter, since it will bring the greatest momentum to proving the supreme divinity of both Christ and the Holy Spirit. For if we can demonstrate that Scripture asserts all those things which are proper to God, without any exception, to Christ and the Holy Spirit no less than to the Father: it will follow that we should not doubt that both Christ and the Holy Spirit are entirely equal to the Father, and thus the supreme God, which will be evident from what is to be said below.

Father, Son & Holy Spirit. 3) That the Father is one, the Son another, the Holy Spirit another. 4) That the Father eternally begets the Son, the Son is eternally begotten by the Father, the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father & the Son.

Latin:

TRINITATIS MYSTERIO.

Quæst. I. Quomodo rudi plebi mysterium Trinitatis simplicissime & planissime proponendum & inculcandum est?

Augustissimum venerandae Trinitatis mysterium modo simplicissimo & planissimo idiotis traditur, ostendat 1) quod Deus sit unus. 2) Quod unus Deus sit Pater, IV. Veritatis divinae, & sigillatim eius, quae dici solet veracitas: 1) Universitas, sine ulla exceptione, Ios. XXIII, 14. 2 Reg. X, 10. Luc. XVIII, 31. Act. III, 21: 2) Necessitas, vt Deus ne possit quidem unquam fallere, Num. XXIII, 19. 1 Sam. XV, 29. Hebr. VI, 18. V. Potentiae divinae, & potestatis, quum Deus sit omnia valens, παντοκράτωρ, 2 Corinth. VI, 18. Apoc. IV, 8. μόνος δυνατής, Ps. LXII, 12. 1 Tim. VI, 15. Huius igitur propria ac referuata consideranda sunt.

(α) ratione rerum, sive Obiectorum: In potestate unius Dei est 1) animus hominis cuiusque, Matth. X, 28. quorum spectat ius (α) obligandi conscientiam, Rom. II, 15. XIII, 5. 1 Petr. II, 19. (β) remittendi peccata, & sua quidem auctoritate, Marc. II, 7: 2) fortuna utraque, vtpote summum atque extremum in quavis actione, Gen. XXXIX, 3. Deut. XXX, 9. Ps. CXXVII, 1. 2. Cohel IX, 11: 3) caelum non minus, quam terra universa, Ps. CXV, 16. CXXXV, 6. Dan. IV, 32: 4) ecclesia, Eph. I, 22: 5) Magistratus quisque, summorum quoque Imperantium nullo excepto, Dan. II, 21. Rom. XIII, 1. 2. 1 Tim. VI, 15: 6) vita & mors mortalium, ad vnum omnium, Ps. XC, 3. Ies. XXXVIII, 1. 5: 7) iudicium, idque supremum, atque adeo commune, Gen. XVIII, 25. Ps. LIX, 14: 8) universa rerum natura, Ps. LXXXIII, 19. vt Deus etiam solus valeat miracula, naturae viribus multo maiora, efficere, Ex, XV, 11. Ps. LXXII, 18. (β) Ratione modi: Deus, & is quidem unus, valet omnia agere 1) suo arbitrio, seu, vt vulgo dicitur, independenter, vt potentiam omnem potestatemque in se ipse habeat, non sibi datam ab alio, (β) vt nemo unquam possit Deo repugnare, (γ) vt rationem factorum nemini unquam reddere ipse teneatur (omnes hae tres notiones continentur in vnodicto, Daniel. IV, 32.): 2) immediate, dum modo velit & iubeat, Ps. XXXHI, 9. Apoc. IV, 11. vt adeo possit efficere omnia, vbi nihil fuit antea, Rom. IV, 17: 3) infinite, vt nullam fuerit potentiae initium, nullus etiam fit terminus, Dan. IV, 31. VI, 26: 4) perfecte, vt quid minimum desit, Gen. I, 31. Ies. XL, 26. Hanc de reservatis divinis doctrinam, vnam ex praecipuis esse arbitror.

Haec enim deinceps permagno usui erit, quum immo maximum momentum adferet ad probandam & Christi, & Spiritus sancti, summam divinitatem. Quod si enim demonstrare poterimus, scripturam ea, quae Dei propria sunt, omnia, sine vlla exceptione, Christo ac Spiritui sancto non minus, quam Patri, adserere: consequens erit, vt non dubitemus, quin & Christus, & Spiritus S. Patri omnino aequalis sit, atque adeo summus Deus, Id quod ex infra dicendis constabit.

Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. 3) Quod alius fit Pater, alius Filius, alius Spiritus S. 4) Quod Pater in aeternum generet Filium, Filius ab aeterno a Patre fit genitus, Spiritus S. a Patre & Filio procedat.


### Quest. II. Why does the church use terms in explaining the mystery of the Trinity that do not exist in the letter of Holy Scripture?

In handing down the sublime and arduous article of faith concerning the most holy Trinity, the Church uses certain terms which do not exist ῥητῶς, or in the letter, in Holy Scripture, yet they are deduced from it by good and ready consequence, and are employed both to refute ἑτεροδοξίαν, or false doctrine, and to declare ὀρθοδοξίαν, or heavenly truth .

Prob. a. The enemies of heavenly truth spoke the same things as the Catholic Church, but did not think the same things, as witnessed by IRENAEUS in the preface to book I. Therefore, the Church was compelled to uncover the deceit of the adversaries by using terms that do not exist in the letter of Holy Scripture, yet do not differ from it in sense. For when the Church taught that there are three in whose name we are baptized, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; Sabellius, intending to corrupt the dogma of the Church with ψευδερμηνεία, or false interpretation, said that those three were not distinct by real discrimination, but that one and the same person was called now Father, now Son, now Holy Spirit. Therefore, so that the orthodoxy of this article might remain unimpaired, the Church began to call those three, three distinct persons. When the Church taught that the Father and the Son are one (John 10:30); Arius said that the Father and the Son are one by consent and will, just as it is said of believers that they are one heart (Acts 4:32). Therefore, so that orthodoxy might stand unshaken, the Church began to teach that the Son is ὁμοούσιον to the Father. Cf. D. GERHARD, Exeg. book III, fol. 334.

Prob. b. The most sublime mystery of the Trinity is briefly proposed and vigorously explained by terms received by the Church: for they cannot be twisted into a foreign sense by the enemies of heavenly truth.

Latin:

Ecclesia in tradendo sublimi & arduo articulo fidei de sacrosancta Trinitate utitur vocibus quibusdam, quae ῥητῶς, sive qua litteram, non exstant in sacra scriptura, per bonam tamen & pronam consequentiam ex eadem deducuntur, & adhibentur tum ad confutandam ἑτεροδοξίαν, sive fallam doctrinam, tum ad declarandam ὀρθοδοξίαν, seu veritatem coelestem .

Prob. a. Hostes veritatis coelestis cum ecclesia catholica idem loquebantur, sed non idem sentiebant, teste IRENAEO in praefat. libr. I. Quare coacta est ecclesia ad detegendum adversariorum fucum usurpare terminos, qua litteram in sacra scriptura non exstantes, neque tamen ab ea qua sensum discrepantes. Cum enim ecclesia doceret, tres esse, in quorum nomine baptizamur, Patrem, Filium & Spiritum sanctum; Sabellius dogmia ecclesiae ψευδερμηνεία, falsa interpretatione, depravaturus dicebat, tres illos non esse reali discrimine distinctos, sed unam eandemque personam modo vocari Patrem, modo Filium, modo Spiritum S. Proinde ut orthodoxia huius articuli illibata maneret, ecclesia illos tres vocare coepit tres distinctas personas. Cum ecclesia doceret, Patrem & Filium esse unum Io. X, 30; Arius dicebat, Patrem & Filium esse unum consensu & voluntate, sicut credentium dicitur unum cor, Act. IV, 32. Quare ut orthodoxia flaret, inconcussa, ecclesia docere coepit Filium esse ὁμοούσιον Patri. Conf. D. GERHARD. exeg. libr. III. fol. 334.

Prob. b. Sublimissimum mysterium Trinitatis breviter proponitur, & nervose explicatur vocibus ab ecclesia receptis: quippe quae non possunt in peregrinum sensum ab hostibus veritatis coelestis detorqueri.


### Quest. III. What are those terms by which the mystery of the Trinity is briefly proposed and vigorously explained by the Church?

Ecclesiastical terms, by which the mystery of the Trinity is briefly and vigorously proposed, are trinity, essence, person, hypostasis, hypostatic character, personal notion, personal act, ὁμοούσιος, περιχώρησις; the meaning of which must be elucidated here, and their foundations shown from the sacred writings, before we proceed to prove this sublime article of faith.

Latin:

Voces ecclesiasticae, quibus mysterium Trinitatis breviter & nervose proponitur, sunt trinitas, essentia, persona, hypostasis, character hypostaticus, notio personalis, actus personalis, ὁμοούσιος, περιχώρησις; quarum significatio hic enucleanda, earumque fundamenta e sacris litteris ostendenda sunt prius, quam sublimem hunc fidei articulum probatum eamus.


### Quest. IV. What does the term, Trinity, denote?

Trinity, in the ecclesiastical custom of speaking, here denotes the ternary number of divine persons. Obs.

I. There are those who wish Trinity to be so called as if it were a trinity of three; but wrongly. For rightly, with ATHANASIUS, we venerate unity in Trinity and Trinity in unity. But who has ever said: We venerate the unity of three in unity? Obs.

II. There is a great difference between trine and triple. Trine is that which, being one in essence, has three modes of subsisting: Triple is that which is composed of three. We call God trine, but we are forbidden by the Christian religion to call Him triple. It is more correctly called in German die Dreyeinigkeit than die Dreyfaltigkeit.

Prob. The word "Trinity" is drawn from the fountains of Israel; since its concrete form is read in 1 John V, 7: "These three are one." Since, therefore, Holy Scripture uses the concrete, why should it not be permitted to infer the abstract from it, just as we infer "unity" from "one"?

Quest. V. What do you understand by the essence of God? The essence of God is the spiritual and independent nature of God, common to the three divine persons, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Prob. 1) In general, they define essence as that which is first conceived in a thing, without which the thing cannot exist, and which is the foundation and cause of the other things that are in the same thing, from THOMAS, De ente et essentia, ch. 1, and 7 Metaphysics, sect. 5. Since, therefore, we first conceive spirituality and independence in God—as these are, in our mode of understanding, the principle and foundation from which the divine attributes flow—we deliberately describe the essence of God through the spiritual and independent nature of God: moreover, the divine attributes are ταὐτὸ [the same], likewise common to the three persons of the divinity.

For the Father is omnipotent, the Son is omnipotent, the Holy Spirit is omnipotent: and yet not three omnipotents, but one omnipotent, says ATHANASIUS in his creed.

2) The word οὐσία [essence] is not indeed found in express letters in Holy Scripture; yet it is elicited from it by an easy consequence. For a) God in the O.T. is called הָיָה [He who is/the Essentiator]: therefore He has an essence, and one that is independent, infinite, and immutable. b) In the N.T. God is named ὁ ὤν [He who is], Apoc. I, 8. From whom is οὐσία or essence. c) A synonym for the divine essence is Φύσις θεία [divine nature], of which St. Peter makes mention in 2 Epist. ch. I, 4. Essence, nature, and form of God, according to the holy fathers, is the same, says DAMASCENUS, Isagog. ch.

I. Quest. VI. What is a person? A person, viewed materially or concretely, is an intelligent suppositum. A suppositum, indeed, is an ὑφιστάμενον [that which stands under] or a singular, incommunicable subsistent, not sustained by another. But considered formally or abstractly, a person is the independent and incommunicable subsistence of a singular, complete, and intelligent substance.

Obs. We define 1) a person, viewed concretely, by a suppositum, i.e., a singular subsistent. There are those who define it by a singular substance; but less accurately. For a person, considered in the concrete sense, is not a substance, but an ὑφιστάμενον, a singular subsistent, which consists of substance and the ultimate mode of subsisting. When CRELLIUS, a Socinian, defined a person by substance, D. SCHERZERUS replied: You define a person falsely. In place of substance, it is a subsistent that must be posited, in Colleg. Anti-Sociniano, p. 264. And the Augsburg confessors in Article I say: We use the name of person in the signification in which ecclesiastical writers have used it in this cause, so that it signifies not a part or a quality in another, but that which properly subsists.

But since the subsisting of substances happens, it follows that no accident is a person. 2) Every person is a singular subsistent. Therefore, universals are not persons, since, when considered formally, they are not outside the intellect. We call a person a singular ὑφιστάμενον, because this imports a logical relation to the most specific species, which is predicated of the individual.

But God is not predicated by way of species of the divine persons, nor do these differ by numerically diverse essences, just as individuals do. 3) Every person is an intelligent suppositum. This stone, this tree, this horse are indeed called supposita, but not persons, because they are destitute of intellect.

4) Every person subsists incommunicably, i.e., the subsistence of one person cannot be communicated to another person, because each person obtains its own and ultimate act of subsisting, so as to be further terminated by another person.

Latin:

Trinitas, ecclesiastica loquendi consuetudine, hic notat ternarium personarum divinarum numerum.

Obs. I. Sunt qui Trinitatem dictam volunt, quasi trium unitatem; at male. Recte enim, cum ATHANASIO, unitatem in Trinitate & Trinitatem in unitate veneramur. At quis vnquam dixit: Trium unitatem in unitate veneramur?

Obs. II. Magnum est discrimen inter trinum, & triplex. Trinum est, quod, in essentia unum, tres habet subsistendi modos: Triplex est, quod e tribus est compositum. Trinum Deum dicimus, sed triplicem dicere christiana religione prohibemur. Rectius Germanice vocatur die Dreyeinigkeit, quam die Dreyfaltigkeit.

Prob. Hausta est vox, Trinitas, e fontibus Israëlis; siquidem eius concretum legitur, 1 Ioh. V, 7. Hi tres unum sunt. Cum ergò S. scriptura usurpet concretum: quidni exinde colligere liceat abstractum: pèrinde ac ex vno colligimus vnitatem?

Quaest. V. Quid intelligis per essentiam Dei? Essentia Dei est natura Dei spiritualis & independens, tribus personis diuinis, Patri, Filio, & Spiritui sancto, communis. Prob. 1) In genere definiunt essentiam, quod fit id, quod primo in re concipitur, sine quo res esse non potest, estque fundamentum & causa ceterorum, quae sunt in eadem re, ex THOMA de ente & essentia c. 1. & 7. metaphys. sect. 5. Cum itaque in Deo primo concipiamus spiritualitatem & independentiam; quippe quae nostro intelligendi modo est principium & fundamentum, e quo attributa diuina fluunt: consulto describimus essentiam Dei per naturam Dei spiritualem & independentem: Attributa autem diuina sunt ταὐτὸ, pariter tribus diuinitatis personis communia.

Nam omnipotens Pater, omnipotens Filius, omnipotens Spiritus sanctus: Et tamen non tres omnipotentes, sed vnus omnipotens, inquit in symbolo suo ATHANASIVS.

2) Vox οὐσία essentia non quidem expressis litteris habetur in sacra scriptura; attamen per facilem consequentiam ex illa elicitur. Etenim a) Deus in V. T. appellatur הָיָה essentiator: ergo habet essentiam, eamque independentem, infinitam & immutabilem. b) In N. T. Deus nominatur ὁ ὤν, Apoc. I, 8. A quo est οὐσία siue essentia. c) Synonymum essentiae diuinae est Φύσις θεία, natura diuina, cuius meminit S. Petrus 2 epist. c. I, 4. Essentia, natura, & forma Dei, iuxta sanctos patres, idem est, ait DAMASCENVS isagog. c.

I. Quaest. VI. Quid est persona? Persona materialiter s. concretiue spectata est suppositum intelligens. Suppositum vero est ὑφιστάμενον s. subsistens singulare, incommunicabile, non sustentatum ab alio. At formaliter, siue abstractiue, considerata persona est substantiae singularis, completae, & intelligentis independens & incommunicabilis subsistentia.

Obs. Definimus 1) personam, concretiue spectatam, per suppositum, i. e. subsistens singulare. Sunt, qui eam definiunt per substantiam singularem; at minus accurate. Nam persona, sensu concretiuo considerata, non est substantia, sed ὑφιστάμενον, subsistens singulare, quod substantia & vltimo subsistendi modo constat. Cum CRELLIVS, Socinianus personam definiret per substantiam, respondebat D. SCHERZERVS: Falso definis personam. Substantiae loco subsistens subsistendu[m] est, in colleg. Anti-Sociniano p. 264. Et confessores Augustani articulo I. dicunt: Nomine personae vtimur ea significatione, qua vsi sunt in hac causa scriptores ecclesiastici, vt significet non partem aut qualitatem in alio, sed quod proprie subsistit.

Cum autem subsistere substantiarum fit, consequitur, nullum accidens esse personam. 2) Omnis persona est subsistens singulare. Proinde vniversalia non sunt personae, cum formaliter considerata non sint extra intellectum. Vocamus personam ὑφιστάμενον singulare, quia hoc importat logicum ad speciem specialissimam, quae de indiuiduo praedicatur.

At Deus non praedicatur per modum speciei de personis diuinis, neque hae essentiis numero diuersis, pèrinde, ac indiuidua, differunt. 3) Omnis persona est suppositum intelligens. Hic lapis, haec arbor, hic equus, dicuntur quidem supposita, sed non personae, quia intellectu-destituuntur.

4) Omnis persona subsistit incommunicabiliter, i. e. vnius personae subsistentia non potest alii personae communicari, eo, quod vnaquaeque persona proprium & vltimatum subsistendi actum obtinet, vt ab alia persona vlterius terminari.


### Q. VIII

cannot.

5) Every person subsists independently of another united thing, as if it were a support. For this reason, the human nature of Christ is not called a person, because it is united with the Word (τῷ λόγῳ), by whom it is terminated in subsisting.

Quest. VII. What do you understand by hypostasis? Hypostasis (ὑπόστασις), no differently than person, abstractly denotes the incommunicable mode of subsisting of a complete singular substance: concretely, it is the same as that which subsists (ὑφισάμενον) or a suppositum.

Obs. I. The Holy Fathers, as DAMASCENUS testifies in Dial. cap. XXVI, called hypostasis and person the same thing. However, person differs from hypostasis in this very fact, that hypostasis is common to intellectual nature and that which lacks reason: person is said only of intellectual nature.

Obs. II. The formal and abstractive signification of both person and hypostasis has a place when three persons, or hypostases, are asserted in one divine essence. For by this assertion of the Catholic Church, three relative and incommunicable modes of subsisting of one divine essence are indicated, and are called by the Greeks modes of existence (τρόποι ὑπάρξεως); since to each person its own proper mode of subsisting corresponds; for the Father subsists unbegottenly (ἀγεννήτως), the Son begottenly (γεννητῶς), the Holy Spirit proceedingly (ἐκπορεύτως).

Proof. Although the word person, in the signification in which it is used here by the Church, is not read [in Scripture], nevertheless, since the Greek Fathers called that which the Latins called person a hypostasis; it is incumbent upon us to derive the name of hypostasis (ὑποτάσεως) from the Holy Scriptures.

The word hypostasis (ὑπόστασις) is found in Heb. 1:3, where the Son of God is called the image of the hypostasis of the Father (χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποτάσεως τοῦ πατρὸς). There are those who deny that hypostasis is used by the Apostle in the ecclesiastical sense, to denote the person of the Father.

But our GERHARD rightly advises that the name of person is taken either materially and concretely, for a suppositum having essence; or formally and precisely, so that it is distinguished from essence, and becomes the same as personality. In the former sense, the Son of God is called the image of the person of the Father, but not in the latter sense. An image immediately regards the person; because an image, as such, is a relative term, [and] mediately regards the essence; in that the Son of God is the substantial image of the Father, not only to imperfection, but to the most perfect.

The correlate of an image is indeed a person; but the foundation, by reason of which the Son is called the image of the Father, is the essence of the Father communicated to the Son through eternal generation. To which LUTHER referred when he rendered it in German: das Ebenbild seines Wesens (the image of his essence).

For he indicated the essence marked by the hypostatic character of the Father. The divine essence, viewed absolutely, cannot be understood by hypostasis (ὑπόστασις) in this apostolic passage: because the same essence is in the Father and the Son.

Moreover, an image is not an image of itself, but of another. See

AUGUSTINE, Book VII, De Trinitate, ch. 1. Conf.

GERHARD, Exeg. loc. III, fol. 342, and D. CALOVIUS, Systema, vol. III, p. 98.

Quest. VIII. What is denoted by the name of hypostatic character? A hypostatic character, or personal property, is a relation founded in a personal act, constituting a person in the being of a certain person, and bringing about a distinction from another person through real relative opposition.

Quest. IX. How many hypostatic characters or personal properties are there? The hypostatic characters of the divine persons are three: paternity, filiation, and passive spiration, or procession, strictly so called.

Proof. Paternity is a relation founded in active generation, constituting God the Father in the being of Father, and, through the relative opposition which exists between paternity and filiation, bringing about a real distinction between God the Father and the Son. Let the same judgment be formed. with filiation, and passive spiration.

The term, hypostatic character, without doubt draws its origin from Heb. 1:3, where the Son of God is called, as we indicated above, the character, or image of the Father's hypostasis, in that he refers to the person of the Father, as regards essence. Hence it has come about that every relation, by which one divine person refers to or looks toward another, is called a hypostatic character, or personal property.

Obf. The proximate foundation of a hypostatic relation is a personal act; which, since it founds the relation, and does not differ from it in reality, is not rarely called by theologians a hypostatic character, or personal property. Thus the active generation of God the Father, and the passive generation of the Son of God, is a hypostatic character. Certainly, by the consensus of all, the personal property of the Holy Spirit is expressed by the name of passive spiration, or procession.

Q. Q. X. What are personal notions? Personal notions are the means of knowing the divine persons, and of distinguishing them ad intra; of which some are συστατικαὶ (constitutive), or constitutive of any person, in the being of such a person; some are σημαντικαὶ (significative), or significative, which indeed notify the divine persons, and indicate their distinction, but constitute no person in the being of such a person.

Obf. Constitutive personal notions coincide with hypostatic characters, or personal properties; which, if they are counted among the personal notions, five personal notions are numbered: inascibility and paternity in the Father, spiration in the Father and Son, filiation in the Son, and procession in the Holy Spirit. But truly, insofar as personal notions are taken more strictly as σημαντικαὶ ἢ θεωρισικαὶ (significative or theoretical), i.e., only significative and notificative, distinct from personal properties, there are only two personal notions: inascibility and active spiration. For ἀγεννησία (unbegottenness) or inascibility indeed notifies God the Father and indicates that he derives his origin from no other person; but it does not constitute him in the being of Father, and therefore it is not his hypostatic character, but a personal notion. Active spiration, since it is common to God the Father and the Son, is not a property, but a personal notion.

Q. XI. Which are the personal acts? Personal acts are those which are terminated within the divine essence toward a certain person, and whose principle of acting is not the divine essence common to the three persons, but one, or two persons; and they are two, generation and spiration.

Obf. I. Personal acts are also called works ad intra, concerning which that well-worn theological axiom is true: works ad intra are personal and divided, i.e., not common to all persons of the divinity; if indeed a work, proper to one person, does not belong to another, relatively opposed person.

Obf. II. Generation no less than spiration, viewed by reason of the principle from which it emanates, is called active, and by reason of the term which it produces, passive, speaking grammatically; although on the part of God the eternal, most pure, and passionless birth of the Word (τοῦ λόγου) is an emanation from the Father, but the procession of the Holy Spirit is an emanation of the same from the Father and the Son; since passive potency does not fall into God.

Q. XII. What does the word ὁμοούσιος mean? The Greek word ὁμοούσιος is rendered in Latin as coessentialis or consubstantialis, and denotes that the three persons of the divinity are of one and the same essence.

Proof. The Greek word ὁμοούσιος is derived from ὁμῶς, one or together, and ὀσία, essence, and indicates that the Son of God and the Holy Spirit are of the same essence as God the Father and are coeternal.

It is deduced from those sayings of Scripture which testify that two or three persons, expressly named, are one.
