Christ says John X, 30. I and the Father are one.

St. John says: These three are one, 1 ep.

V, 7. Aptly says AUGUSTINE, tract. 97 on John. Against the impiety of the Arian heretics, the fathers established a new name, ὁμοούσιον, but they did not signify a new thing by such a name; for this is what is called homousion, which is: I and the Father are one, namely, of one and the same substance.

God the Father and the Son are one, not indeed by unity of person, nor of will and concord alone, but by essence, not specifically, but most singularly one.

This is gathered 1) from the scope.

Christ proves that no one can snatch the sheep from his hand, because he and the Father are one; that whatever power the Father has, the Son has the same. Imagine, if the discourse were only about unity of concord, by the same consequence you could infer that no one could be snatched from the hand of John or Peter. 2) From the manner of speaking θεοπρεπῶς (in a manner befitting God) about divine things.

From which we conclude in this manner: The one will of the Father is the one essence of the Father (for divine attributes are the same as the essence of God). But Christ's will is that one will of the Father. Therefore, Christ's will is the very essence of the Father. These things being properly considered, the Council of Nicaea asserted τὴν ὁμοούσιον, i.e., the most singular unity of essence, in the three divine persons, and defended it against the Arians.

To them, ὁμοούσια was so hateful that they would have preferred to have ὁμοιούσιον thrust upon the church.

From this it happened that the entire Christian world was divided by only a single letter. Yet that single letter represents no light, but a great distinction between the Catholic and Arian dogma; by which, through ὁμοούσιαν, the Son of God is designated by Catholics as independent, eternal, and supreme God with the Father, and through ὁμοιούσιαν, he is designated by the Arians as a creature similar to the Creator, but infinitely distant from the Creator in terms of essence.

Furthermore, EPIPHANIUS warns in the Ancoratus that συνέσιον is one thing, αὐτοέσιον another, and ὁμοούσιον another. Συνέσιον denotes specific unity of essence, just as all men have one common essence: αὐτοέσιον signifies one person in one essence, manifesting itself through diverse properties and operations: But ὁμοούσιον denotes numerical unity of essence, with a distinction of persons.

Excellent says AMBROSE Book III. de fide c. VII. We rightly call the Son of God homousion to the Father; because by that word both the distinction of persons and the unity of nature are signified.

Conf. D. CHEMNIT. in loc. theol. de tribus person. diuin. fol. m. 48.

Q. XIII. What does the word περιχώρησις mean? Περιχώρησις is rendered in Latin as immeatio, circumcessio, immanentia, and denotes the eternal and intimate indwelling of one divine person in another.

Obs.

Obs. I. The word περιχώρησις is not biblical, but ecclesiastical, used by DAMASCENE in book I of the Orthodox Faith, c. 19. It is distinguished by theologians into essential and personal. The former is the most singular indwelling of one divine person in another: The latter is the intimate and ineffable interpenetration by which the divinity intimately permeates, inhabits, and perfects the human nature assumed by the Word.

We are concerned here with the essential περιχώρησις of the divine persons; which is founded on the words of Christ in John.

XIV, 11. Believe me that I am in the Father, and the Father in me.

Conf. John XVII, 21. Indeed, the essential περιχώρησις of the divine persons causes the Father to be in the Son, the Son in the Father, and the Holy Spirit in both.

Latin:

nequeat.

5) Omnis persona subsistit independenter ab alio vnito, tanquam sustentante. Quam ob rem humana Christi natura non appellatur persona, quia vnita est cum τῷ λόγῳ, a quo in subsistendo terminatur.

Quaest. VII. Quid intelligis per hypostasin? Ὑπόστασις haud secus, ac persona, abstractiue notat substantiae singularis completae incommunicabilem subsistendi rationem: concretiue idem est, quod ὑφισάμενον siue suppositum.

Obs. I. Sancti Patres, teste DAMASCENO dial. cap. XXVI. hypostasin, & personam, idem vocarunt. Differt tamen persona ab hypostasi hoc ipso, quod hypostasis communis est naturae intellectuali, & rationis experti: persona tantum de natura intellectuali dicitur.

Obs. II. Formalis & abstractiua tam personae, quam hypostasis, significatio tum locum habet, cum tres personae, aut hypostases, in vna essentia diuina afferuntur. Nam isthac assertione ecclesiae catholicae, tres subsistendi rationes relatiuae, exque incommunicabiles, vnius essentiae diuinae indigitantur, & a Graecis τρόποι ὑπάρξεως, modi subsistendi appellantur: cum cuius personae proprius subsistendi modus conueniat; subsistit quippe Pater ἀγεννήτως, filius γεννητῶς, Spiritus S. ἐκπορεύτως.

Prob. Quamuis vox persona ea significatione, qua hic ab ecclesia vsurpatur, non legatur, attamen cum graeci patres hypostasin appellatarint, quam latini personam vocarunt; nomen ὑποτάσεως e sacris litteris deducere nobis incumbit.

Inuenitur vox ὑπόστασις Hebr. I, 3. vbi filius Dei dicitur χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποτάσεως τοῦ πατρὸς, imago hypostatis patris. Sunt, qui negant hypostasin sensu ecclesiastico ab apostolo vsurpari, vt patris personam denotet.

Sed recte monet noster GERHARDVS, nomen personae sumi vel materialiter & concretiue, pro supposito essentiam habente; vel formaliter & praecise; vt distinguatur ab essentia, & idem fit, quod personalitas. Priori sensu filius Dei dicitur imago personae patris, non autem sensu posteriori. Imago immediate respicit personam; quia imago, qua talis, est vocabulum relatiuum, mediate respicit essentiam; eo quod filius Dei non modo imperfectioni, sed perfectissimo est substantialis imago patris.

Correlatum imaginis quidem est persona; sed fundamentum, ratione cuius filius dicitur imago patris, est essentia Patris per aeternam generationem filio communicata. Quo respexit LVTHERVS, cum reddidit germanice das Eberbild seines Wesens.

Indigtauit enim essentiam charactere hypostatico patris insignitam. Essentia diuina, absolute spectata, in hoc loco apostolico per ὑπόστασιν intelligi nequit: quia eadem essentia in patre & filio est.

Imago autem non est fui ipsius imago, sed alterius. Vid.

AVGVSTINVS lib. VII. de trinit. c. 1. Conf.

GERHARDI exeg. loc. III. fol. 342. & D. CALOVII systema tom. III. p. 98.

Quaest. VIII. Quid notatur nomine characteris hypostatici? Character hypostaticus, siue proprietas personalis, est relatio in actu personali fundata, personam in esse certae personae constituens, & per oppositionem relatiuam realem ab alia persona distinctionem inferens.

Quaest. IX. Quot sunt characteres hypostatici siue proprietates personales? Characteres hypostatici personarum diuinarum sunt tres, paternitas, filiatio & spiratio passiua, siue processio, stricte dicta.

Prob. Paternitas est relatio fundata in generatione actiua, Deum patrem in esse patris constituens, & per oppositionem relatiuam, quae inter paternitatem & filiationem intercedit, realem distinctionem inter Deum patrem, & filium inferens. Idem formetur iudicium. de filiatione, et spiratione passiva.

Vox, character hypostaticus, dubio procul originem trahit ex Hebr. I, 3. vbi filius Dei dicitur, vt supra indicavimus, character, sive imago hypostasis patris, eo, quod personam patris, quoad essentiam, refert. Exinde factum, vt inditum omnis relatio, qua una persona divina aliam refert, aut respicit, vocetur character hypostaticus, aut proprietas personalis.

Obs. Fundamentum proximum relationis hypostaticae est actus personalis; qui cum relationem fundet; nec ab ea realiter differat, haud raro a theologis character hypostaticus, aut proprietas personalis appellatur. Sic generatio activa Dei patris, generatio passiva filii Dei character hypostaticus est. Certe omnium consensu nomine spirationis passivae, aut processionis proprietas personalis Spiritus S. exprimitur.

Quaest. X. Quid sunt notiones personales? Notiones personales sunt rationes cognoscendi personas divinas, easque ad intra distinguendi; quarum quaedam sunt συστατικαὶ, seu constitutivae cuiuslibet personae, in esse talis personae; quaedam sunt σημαντικαὶ, seu significativae, quae personas divinas quidem notificant, earumque distinctionem indicant, sed nullam personam in esse talis personae constituunt.

Obs. Notiones personales constitutivae cum characteribus hypostaticis, seu proprietatibus personalibus, coincidunt; quae, si connumerentur notionibus personalibus, numerantur notiones personales quinque, inascibilitas et paternitas in patre, spiratio in patre et filio, filiatio in filio, processio in Spiritu S. At vero quatenus notiones personales strictius sumtunt σημαντικαὶ ἢ θεωρισικαὶ, i. e. tantum significativae et notificativae, a proprietatibus personalibus distinctae, duae tantum sunt notiones personales; inascibilitas et spiratio activa. Nam ἀγεννησία seu inascibilitas notificat quidem Deum patrem et indicat, ipsum a nulla alia persona ducere originem; at non constituit illum in esse patris, adeoque non ipsius character hypostaticus, sed notio personalis est. Spiratio activa, cum communis sit Deo patri et filio, non proprietas, sed notio personalis est.

Quaest. XI. Quinam sunt actus personales? Actus personales sunt, qui intra essentiam divinam terminantur ad certam personam, et quorum principium agendi non essentia divina tribus personis communis, sed una, vel duae sunt personae; suntque duo, generatio et spiratio.

Obs. I. Actus personales vocantur etiam opera ad intra, de quibus tritum illud axioma theologicum verum est: opera ad intra personalia sunt divisa, i. e. non omnibus personis divinitatis communia; si quidem opus, uni personae proprium, alteri, relative oppositae, non convenit.

Obs. II. Generatio non minus, ac spiratio, spectata ratione principii, a quo emanat, activa, ratione termini, quem producit, passiva appellatur, grammatice loquendo; quamvis ex parte Dei natiuitas τοῦ λόγου aeterna, purissima, omnisque passionis expers, fit emanatio a patre, processio autem Spiritus S. emanatio eiusdem a patre et filio fit; cum in Deum non cadat potentia passiva.

Actus perſonales sunt, qui intra effentiam diuinam terminantur ad certam perfonam, & quorum principium agendi non effentia diuina tribus perſonis communis, sed vna, vel duæ sunt perſona; fintque duo, generatio & spiratio. Obf. I. Actus perſonales vocantur etiam opera ad intra, de quibus tritum illud axioma theologicum verun est: opera ad intra perſonalia sunt diuifa, i. e. non omnibus perſonis diuinitatis communia; fi quidem opus, vni perſonæ proprium, alteri, relatiue oppofitæ, non conuenit. Obf. II. Generatio non minus, ac ſpiratio, ſpectata ratione principii, a quo emanat, altina, ratione termini, quem producit, paſſiua appellatur, graminatice loquendo; quainuis. ex parte Dei natiuitas τε λόγο xterna, puriffuna, omnisque paffionis expers, fit emanatio a patre, proceſſio autem Spiritus S. emanatio eiusdem a patre & filio fit; cuun in Dennon cadat potentia paffiua.

Notiones perſonales sunt rationes cognoscendi perſonas diuinas, easque ad intra distinguendi; quarum quædam sunt συςατικαί, feu constitutiuæ cuiuslibet perſonæ, in eſſe talis perſonæ; quædam sunt σημαντικαί, feu fignificatiuæ, quæ perſonas diuinas quidem notificant, earumque distinctionem indicant, sed nullam perſonam in eſſe talis perſonæ constituunt. Obf. Notiones perſonales constitutiuce cinn characteribus hypoſtaticis, feu proprietatibus perſonalibus, coincidunt; quæ, fi connumerentur notionibus perſonalibus, numerantur notiones perſonales quinque, innascibilitas & paternitas in patre, spiratio in patre & filio, filiatio infilio, proceffio in Spiritu S. At vero quatenus notiones perſonales stristius fumta, tantumfunt σημαντικαὶ ἢ θεωριτικαὶ, i. e, tantun fignificatine & notificatiuæ, a proprietatibus perſonalibus diſtinctæ, duæ tantum sunt notiones perſonales, innascibilitas & spiratio affiua. Nain ἀγεννησία ſcu insascibilitas notificat quidem Deum patrem & indicat, ipfiun a nulla alia perſona ducere originem; at non constituit illun in eſſe patris, adeoque non ipfius character hypostaticus, sed notio perſonalis est. Spiratio actina, cum communis fit Deo patri & filio, non proprietas, sed notio perfonalis est. De notionibus perſonalibus accurate egerunt, D. 10. ADAM. OSIAND. in colleg. system. part. I. p. 408. D. BAYER. in compend. theol. P. 251. D. BREITHAVPT. in instit. theol. p. 35.

Quæst. XII. Quid significat vox ὁμοούσιος? Vox graeca ὁμοούσιος latine redditur coessentialis, vel consubstantialis, & denotat, tres diuinitatis personas esse vnius eiusdemque essentiae.

Prob. Deriuatur vox Graeca ὁμοούσιος ab ὁμῶς, vna, vel simul, & ὀσία essentia, atque indicat, filium Dei & Spiritum S. cum Deo patre esse eiusdem essentiae & coaeternum.

Deducitur ex illis dictis scripturae, quae duas, tresue personas, nominatim expressas, vnum esse testantur.

Christus ait Io. X, 30. Ego & pater vnum sumus.

S. Ioannes inquit: Hi tres vnum sunt, 1 ep.

V, 7. Apposite inquit AVGVSTINVS tractat. 97. in Ioan. Aduersus impietatem Arianorum haereticorum nouum nomen patres ὁμοούσιον condiderunt, sed non rem nouam tali nomine signauerunt; hoc enim vocatur homousion, quod est: Ego & pater vnum sumus, videlicet vnius eiusdemque substantiae.

Deus pater & filius vnum sunt, non vnitate quidem personae, nec solius voluntatis & concordiae, sed essentia, non specifice, sed fingularissime vnius.

Id quod colligitur 1) ex scopo.

Probat Christus, neminem posse oues e manu sua rapere, quod ipse & pater vnum sint; quod quam potentiam habeat pater, eandem & filius. Finge, de vnitate concordiae solum esse sermonem, eadem consequentia posses inferre, nec e manu Ioannis, aut Petri, aliquem posse eripi. 2) Ex modo loquendi θεοπρεπῶς de diuinis.

Ex quo hunc in modum concludimus: Vna voluntas patris est vna essentia patris (sunt enim attributa diuina cum essentia Dei ταὐτό). Atqui Christi voluntas est illa vna patris voluntas. E. Christi voluntas est ipsa essentia patris. Quibus probe consideratis, concilium Nicaenum τὴν ὁμεούσιον, i. e. vnitatem essentiae singularissimam, in tribus personis diuinis asseruit, & defendit aduersus Arianos.

His adeo exosa fuit ὁμοούσια, vt fuunt ὁμοιούσιον ecclesiae obtrusum mallen.

Exinde factum, vt vniuersus christianus orbis vnica tantum littera distraheretur. Neque tamen vnica illa littera leue, sed grande discrimen dogmatis catholici, & Ariani repraesentat; quam per ὁμοούσιαν filius Dei independens, aeternus & summus cum patre Deus a catholicis, per ὁμοιούσιαν creatura creatori similis, sed essentiae ratione infinitum a creatore distans, ab Arianis designaretur.

Ceterum monet EPIPHANIVS in Ancorato, aliud esse συνέσιον, aliud αὐτοέσιον, aliud ὁμοούσιον. Συνέσιον notat vnitatem essentiae specificam, prout omnium hominum vna est communis essentia: αὐτοέσιον significat in vna essentia vnam personam, diuersis proprietatibus & operationibus se exferentem: Ομοούσιον vero denotat vnitatem essentiae numericam, cum distinctione personarum.

Praeclare inquit AMBROSIVS Libr. III. de fide c. VII. Recte homousion patri filium Dei dicimus; quia verbo illo & personarum distinctio, & naturae vnitas significatur.

Conf. D. CHEMNIT. in loc. theol. de tribus person. diuin. fol. m. 48.

Quaest. XIII. Quid significat vox περιχώρησις? Περιχώρησις latine redditur immeatio, circumcessio, immanentia, & notat aeternam atque intimam vnius personae diuinae in alia immanentiam.

Obs.

Obs. I. Vox περιχώρησις non est biblica, sed ecclesiastica, vsurpata a DAMASCENO libr. I. orth. fid. c. 19. Distinguitur a theologis in essentialem, & personalem. Illa est singularissima immanentia vnius personae diuinae in alia: Haec est intima eaque ineffabilis immeatio, qua diuinitas τῷ λόγῳ alluntam humanam intime permeat, inhabitat, & perficit.

De essentiali περιχώρησις personarum diuinarum in praesenti nobis sermo est; quae fundatur in verbis Christi Io.

XIV, 11. Credite mihi, quod ego in me, & pater in me sit.

Conf. Io. XVII, 21. Nimirum περιχώρησις essentialis personarum diuinarum facit, vt Pater sit in Filio, Filius in Patre, & Spiritus S. in vtroque.


### Quæst. XIV. The Holy Scripture proposes the number of the divine persons in two ways. (1) It teaches their plurality indefinitely or…

Obf. II. Having clarified the ecclesiastical terms by which the most august mystery of the H. Trinity is commonly proposed in the church, the truth of this mystery must now be demonstrated. Since, therefore, the most singular unity of the divine essence has been clearly proven above, it will be worth the effort at present to show clearly that both the plurality of the divine persons indefinitely, and their trinity determinately, are most openly taught by the Holy Spirit in the divine scriptures.

Quæst. XIV.

The Holy Scripture proposes the number of the divine persons in two ways. (1) It teaches their plurality indefinitely or indeterminately. (2) It expresses the trinity of the divine persons definitely or determinately.

Obf. I. To those who are more unlearned, who are to be imbued with catechetical doctrine, it is not the indefinite plurality of the divine persons, but their determinate trinity that must be proposed and inculcated at the first step by the faithful catechist, by virtue of the divine mandate in Matt. XXVIII, 19, by which the prelates of the church are commanded to teach the nations and to baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit: but in a disputation with adversaries, one acting as a respondent, against the objected unity of one person in the divine essence in the first conflict (the end of which is to confound the adversary and to convict his antithesis of falsehood), may defend the indefinite plurality of the divine persons; in the second action, or the progress of the disputation, he should confirm the catholic truth, namely, that there are neither more nor fewer divine persons than three, and that they are that one true and supreme God. See HÜLSEMANN, Breviar. enucleat. p. 128.

Obf. II. The indefinite plurality of the divine persons is proposed more frequently in the Old Testament; even though their determinate trinity is not merely tacitly or obscurely insinuated there; but in the New Testament, testimonies of the indefinite plurality of the divine persons occur more rarely, while those of the H. Trinity occur more frequently and clearly than in the Old Testament.

Latin:

Obf. II. Enucleatis vocibus ecclesiasticis, quibus augustissimum mysterium S. S. Trinitatis in ecclesia communiter proponitur, iam demonstranda est mysterii huius veritas. Cum itaque singularissima essentiæ divinæ vnitas supra luculenter probata sit: in præsentiarum operæ pretium erit, vt tum indefinite pluralitatem personarum divinarum, tum determinate earum trinitatem a Spiritu S. in divinis litteris apertissime doceri, liquido ostendamus.

Quæst. XIV. Quot modis sacra scriptura veteris, & noui testamenti, numerum personarum divinarum proponit?

Sacra scriptura numerum personarum divinarum duobus modis proponit. (1) Indefinite siue indeterminate earum pluralitatem docet. (2) Definite seu determinate personarum divinarum trinitatem exprimit.

Obf. I. Rudioribus, doctrina catechetica imbuendis, a fideli catecheta non indefinita personarum divinarum pluralitas, sed determinata earum trinitas et vestigio proponenda & inculcanda est, vi mandati divini Matth. XXVIII, 19. quo iubentur antistites ecclesiæ gentes docere & baptizare in nomine patris, filii & Spiritus sancti: in disputatione vero cum aduersariis respondentis vices gerens, contra obiectam vnitatem vnius personæ in essentia divina in conflictu primo (cuius finis est aduersarium confundere, ipsius antithesin falsitatis conuincere) defendere potest indefinitam personarum divinarum pluralitatem; in actione altera, seu disputationis progressu confirmet veritatem catholicam, scilicet non plures, nec pauciores personas divinas, quam tres esse, easque vnum illum verum ac summum esse Deum. Vid. in HÜLSEMANN. breuiar. enucleat. p. 128.

Obf. II. Indefinita personarum divinarum pluralitas in veteri testamento frequentius proposita est; etiamsi neque determinata earum trinitas ibi tacite aut obscure solum insinuata sit; in nouo autem testamento rariora indefinitæ pluralitatis personarum divinarum, frequentiora vero & clariora, quam in vet. testamento S. S. Trinitatis occurrunt testimonia.


### Quæst. XV

The arguments by which the indefinite plurality of the divine persons is proven shall be drawn from the clear testimonies of the Holy Scripture; of which some vindicate distinct divine actions for distinct persons (a), others attribute common conversations and common works to several divine persons in the number of a multitude (b), others make manifest mention of a plurality of divine persons (c), and others express the plurality of the divine persons with nouns of the plural number (d).

Prob. a. The Son of God is begotten by God, Ps. II, 7. God is anointed by God, Ps. XLV, 8. Jehovah is sent by Jehovah, Is. XLVIII, 16. The Lord is exalted to the right hand by the Lord, Ps. CX, 1. We argue: Wherever a God begetting and begotten, anointing and anointed, sending and sent, exalting and exalted is introduced: there several divine persons are introduced. But in the sacred letters, a God begetting and a God begotten, etc., is introduced. Therefore.

Prob. b. (1) From Gen. I, 26... And Elohim said (by distribution, each one of the Elohim, or the divine persons said to one another, exciting and consulting themselves): Let us make man in our image and after our likeness. We argue: where there are several

Latin:

Argumenta, quibus indefinita personarum divinarum pluralitas probatur, petentur a luculentis sacræ scripturæ testimoniis; quorum alia distinctas actiones divinas distinctis personis vindicant (a), alia communia colloquia & communia opera pluribus personis divinis in numero multitudinis attribuunt (b), alia manifestam plurimi personarum divinarum mentionem faciunt (c), alia pluralitatem personarum divinarum nominibus plurali numeri exprimunt (d).

Prob. a. Filius Dei a Deo gignitur Ps. II, 7. Deus a Deo vngitur Ps. XLV, 8. Iehouah a Iehouah mittitur. Es. XLVIII, 16. Dominus a domino ad dextram exaltatur, Ps. CX, 1. Argumentamur: Vbicunque introducitur Deus gignens, & genitus, vngens, & vnctus, mittens, & missus, exaltans, & exaltatus: ibi introducuntur plures personæ divinæ. Atqui in sacris litteris introducitur Deus gignens & Deus genitus &c. Ergo.

Prob. b. (1) Ex Gen. I, 26.... Et dixit Elohim (per distributionem, vnusquisque ex Elohim, aut personæ divinæ dixerunt ad se inuicem, se excitando & consultando) faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostram & ad similitudinem nostram. Arguimus: vbi sunt plures


### Question XVI. How will you prove the determined Trinity of the divine persons?

speaking and consulting, there are several persons. But, in the divinity there are several speaking and consulting. Therefore, in the divinity there are several persons.

You say: I. God speaks of himself in the manner of princes in the plural number for the sake of honor. Resp. No king or prince speaks of himself alone in the Holy Scriptures in the Hebrew language, which is most simple and devoid of all pretense, in the plural number. In other languages, indeed, princes speaking of themselves use the plural number, but they signify that they are decreeing something with the assistance of counselors and nobles; which cannot be said of the all-wise God.

You say: II. God spoke with, or consulted with, the angels. Resp. Angels were never admitted into the Council of God: Is. XL, 13. Nor could they concur in the work of creation, which is of infinite power: nor were men created in the image of angels, but in the image of God.

Proof. The same from Gen. XI, 7. Jehovah said: come! let us descend & let us confuse the languages there. Adversaries object that God joined the angels to himself in the confusion of languages; but in vain. For the confusion of languages belongs to God alone, who possesses such incomparable power that he can act immediately upon the minds of men, instill other concepts and other thoughts into them, and obliterate the memory of a language previously very well known.

Proof c. From Gen. III, 22. Jehovah God said (to himself:) Behold, man was like one of us (divine persons) knowing good & evil (& yet he sinned). Whoever compares one to many by reason of the order of knowledge, he designates several persons. But God, speaking of himself, compares one man to many by reason of the order of knowledge. Therefore God designates several persons.

(2) Illustrious is the passage Is. VI, 8. where Adonai says: Whom shall I send, & who will go for us? He who says: us, he does not imply himself as one (person) but others with himself, and thus several. Proof d. We demonstrated above that the divine name אלהים is plural not only in termination, but also in signification.

This divine name is constructed (1) with a plural verb Gen. XX, 13. where Abraham says: It came to pass, when Elohim caused me to wander from my father's house. Since there is only one God, by Elohim constructed with a plural verb we cannot understand several divine persons.

Conf. Gen. XXXV, 7. 2 Sam. VII, 23. (2) It is constructed with a plural adjective. Thus by Joshua c. XXIV, 19. they are called אלהים קדשים, holy divine persons.

You say: Elohim is also constructed with a singular verb. Gen. I, 1. ברא אלהים. Resp. It is constructed with a singular verb to indicate the mystery of several persons in one essence of God.

Question. XVI. How will you prove the determined Trinity of the divine persons? The determined Trinity of the divine persons is proved by undoubted testimonies of Holy Scripture; some of which exhibit all three persons of the divinity together: some distinctly teach that not only the eternal Father, but also the Son of the eternal Father, as well as the Holy Spirit, is the true and supreme God.

Both

a class of testimonies concerning the most holy Trinity is taken both from the apostolic writings of the New Testament and from the prophetic monuments of the Old Testament.

Obj. A distinction must be made here between the order of divine revelation and the method of demonstration. The latter proceeds in such a way that we begin from the clearer things and progress to the less clear: the former observes the series of times. Since here the Trinity of the divine persons must be demonstrated by us against the enemies of heavenly truth, we attend to the method of demonstrating, and we place the testimonies of the N. T. before the testimonies of the V. T. as being clearer, in which a lesser degree of clarity is observed.

Latin:

colloquentes & consultantes, ibi sunt plures personae. Atqui, in diuinitate sunt plures colloquentes & consultantes. Ergo in diuinitate sunt plures personae.

Dicis: I. Deus de se more principum in numero multitudinis loquitur honoris causa. Resp. Nullus rex aut princeps de se solo in sacris litteris lingua hebraea simplicissima, omnis que fuci experte, loquitur in numero multitudinis. In aliis quidem linguis principes de se loquentes numero plurali utuntur, sed significant, se consiliariorum ac procerum adminiculis aliquid decernere; quod de Deo omnisapiente dici nequit.

Dicis: II. Deus collocutus est, aut consultauit cum angelis. Resp. Angeli nunquam adhibiti sunt in Consilium Dei: Es. XL, 13. neque iidem ad opus creationis, quod infinitae virtutis est, concurrere potuerunt: neque homines ad imaginem angelorum, sed ad imaginem Dei conditi sunt.

Prob. Idem Ex Gen. XI, 7. Dixit Iehouah: agite! descendamus & confundamus ibi labia. Excipiunt aduersarii, Deum in confusione linguarum angelos sibi adiunxisse; sed frustra. Nam confusio linguarum solius est Dei, qui ea pollet vi incomparabili, vt immediate in hominum animos agere, illis alios conceptus, alias cogitationes inferere & linguae prius notissimae memoriam oblitterare queat .

Prob. c. Ex Gen. III, 22. Dixit Iehouah Deus (apud se:) Ecce homo fuit sicut vnus ex nobis (personis diuinis) sciendo bonum & malum (& tamen peccauit). Quicunque vnum pluribus fuit ordinis ratione scientiae confert, ille plures designat personas. Atqui Deus, de se loquens; vnum hominem pluribus fuit ordinis ratione scientiae confert. Ergo Deus plures designat personas .

(2) Illustris est locus Es. VI, 8. vbi Adonai inquit: Quem mittam, & quis iturus est nobis? Qui dicit: nobis, ille se non vnum (persona) sed secum alios, adeoque plures innuit. Prob. d. אלהים nomen diuinum non tantum terminatione, sed & significatione plurale esse, supra demonstrauimus.

Construitur hoc nomen diuinum (1) cum verbo plurali Gen. XX, 13. vbi Abrahamus ait: Factum vero est, quum discedere me facerent Elohim a domo patris mei. Cum vnus tantum sit Deus, per Elohim constructum cum verbo plurali non possumus plures personas diuinas intelligere.

Conf. Gen. XXXV, 7. 2 Sam. VII, 23. (2) Construitur cum adiectiuo plurali. Sic a Iosua c. XXIV, 19. dicuntur אלהים קדשים, perfonæ diuinæ sanctae.

Dicis: construitur Elohim etiam cum verbo singulari. Gen. I, 1. ברא אלהים. Resp. Construitur cum verbo singulari, ad indicandum mysterium plurium in vna Dei essentia personarum.

Quæst. XVI. Quomodo determinatam personarum diuinarum Trinitatem probabis? Determinata personarum diuinarum Trinitas probatur indubitatis sacrae scripturae testimoniis; quorum quaedam coniunctim exhibent omnes tres diuinitatis personas: quaedam distincte docent, non aeternum tantum Patrem, sed etiam Filium aeterni patris, vt & Spiritum S. esse verum & summum Deum.

Vtraque

testimoniorum de sacrosancta Trinitate classis tum e scriptis apostolicis novi test. tum e monumentis propheticis vet. test. desumitur.

Obi. Distinguendum hic est inter ordinem patefactionis divinae, & methodum demonstrationis. Haec ita procedit, ut a clarioribus ordiamur, & ad minus clara progrediamur: ille seriem temporum observat. Quum hic nobis adversus hostes veritatis caelestis demonstranda sit personarum divinarum trinitas, methodum demonstrandi attendentes testimonia N. T. ut clariora, praemittimus testimoniis V. T. in quibus gradus claritatis minor animadvertitur.


### Quest. XVII. What are the testimonies of the New Testament by which the Trinity of the divine persons is exhibited conjointly?

The testimonies of the N. T. by which the Trinity of the divine persons is proposed conjointly, clearly set forth our regeneration through baptism , the θεοφάνεια or apparition of the divine persons , the incarnation of the Son of God , the mission of the Holy Spirit , the gracious indwelling of God in us , the divine operation in the church and its ministry , the religious veneration of God , and the apostolic assertion concerning the ὁμοουσία of the divine persons , so that we may be imbued with the saving knowledge of the most holy Trinity.

Prob. a. Christ, now about to ascend into heaven, prescribed the solemn form of administering baptism to his disciples, Matt. 28:19. Go therefore μαθητεύσατε, make disciples (for me) of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. From this classic dictum we demonstrate (1) The Deity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. (2) Their personal distinction. (3) The ὁμοουσίαν, i.e., one essence, of the divine persons. We argue: He in whose name we are baptized is the true and supreme God. We are baptized in the name of God the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is the true and supreme God. The major premise is evident; because we are baptized in the name of him who instituted baptism, the medium of grace and salvation. But God alone, the fountain of grace and author of salvation, instituted baptism. Add that we are baptized in the name of him in whom we are bound to believe and whom we are bound to invoke; for by the sacrament of baptism we are bound to the profession of faith, the worship, and the obedience of him who is the author of baptism. Therefore baptism is called the interrogation of a good conscience toward God, 1 Pet. 3:21. We must believe as we have been baptized, as we believe, says BASIL M. ep. 78. Furthermore, those who are baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit must believe that there are three divine persons. But all nations are baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Therefore. The major premise is clear; because without any doubt the Father and the Son differ as distinct persons. But in the same way that the Son is distinguished from the Father in the words of the institution of baptism, so the Holy Spirit is distinguished from the Father and the Son, as the series of the text shows. But the Son is distinguished from the Father as a person. Therefore the Holy Spirit is also distinguished from the Father and the Son as a person. Moreover, the Holy Spirit is not only proposed in this place as other than the Father and the Son, but is also joined with these divine persons in the administration of baptism, and the same name, the same authority to institute baptism, the same majesty of adoration, and the same power of regenerating, which belongs to the Father and the Son, is attributed to him. Therefore the H. S. is a divine person. Certainly it is absurd and contrary to the usage of speech for the same name to be applied to persons and to a non-person. Finally, we prove the ὁμοουσίαν of the divine persons; because we are not baptized into names, but into the name of the Father, Son, and H. S., that we may be bound to acknowledge and venerable the same name, the same authority, majesty, holiness, grace and power, and indeed the same essence of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

The Socinians object (1)1. To be baptized into the name of someone is not an indication of deity, since one can also be baptized into a human; thus the Israelites were baptized into Moses, as Paul testifies 1 Cor. 10: 1. Response (a)2. It is one thing to be baptized into someone, another to be baptized into the name of someone. The former can be explained ministerially, the latter only authoritatively. (b)3. One must distinguish between baptism properly so called, which is the washing of regeneration and the sacrament of the New Testament, and typical or metaphorical baptism. Baptism, properly so called, cannot be administered in the name of any man: but the baptism of the Israelites into Moses was typical, by which they were obligated to show faith and obedience to Moses, the servant of God, so that they might pass through the Red Sea under the cloud, with Moses leading: just as we are obligated by the baptism of regeneration to place our trust in God the Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

They object (2)4. It is not new, in matters of no less importance than baptism, for things and persons not pertaining to His essence to be joined to God. Thus 1 Sam. 12:18, the people are said to have feared Jehovah and Samuel. Exod. 14:31, where the Israelites are said to have believed in God and Moses. Eph. 6:10, Paul says: be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might, where Paul, along with the Lord, who is a person, joins the power of God, which is not a person, but a divine attribute.

Resp. (1) The examples brought forward are dissimilar and inappropriate. For God and Moses are joined as lord and servant, principal and instrumental cause, by reason of their concurrence toward some certain third thing, which pertains to God and the creature (not equally, but in a different way). But to dispense baptism into the name of someone belongs to no creature. 1 Cor. 1:13. Let the adversaries bring forward an example from the Holy Scriptures where God and man, by a single and simultaneous command, and equal authority, have instituted a new sacrament, and offer them grass. (2) A non-person is never joined to persons in authoritative communion (which happens here, where one name is attributed to three) of a divinely ordained means of salvation. Paul indeed says: be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might, but he does not attribute one name to the Lord and His power. To be baptized into the name of a divine attribute, or even of a divine breath, is unheard of in the Scriptures and inappropriate.

Proof b. A most illustrious theophany or divine apparition occurred at the baptism conferred upon Christ, the administration of which is described in Matt. 3:16, Mark 1:10, Luke 3:22. Concerning this theophany we observe (1) three names. For He whose voice is heard from heaven is called the Father. 2 Pet. 1:17. He who stands on the bank of the Jordan is called the Son, Matt. 3:17. He who descends in the form of a dove is called the Holy Spirit, Luke 3:22. (2) Three distinct symbols of manifestation, while the Father appears by voice, the Son in body, the Spirit as a bird. (3) Three distinct acts: the Father crying from heaven, the Son standing in the Jordan, the Holy Spirit descending in the form of a dove. (4) The common deity of the three persons. For the Father, crying from heaven, is undoubtedly the true God; to whom the Son is coessential, since He is not an adopted, but the natural Son of God; inasmuch as He is emphatically called by the doubled Greek article ὁ υἱὸς ὁ ἀγαπητὸς, that Son, that beloved one, in whom all εὐδοκία, the complacency of God, resides and rests. But every natural son has the same essence with his father; the same, I say, in species among humans, the same in number in divine things. The Spirit, who descends in the form of a dove, cannot be a creature; inasmuch as He came upon Christ for this reason, that He might fill and anoint Him, qua man, with gifts, so that He might preach liberty to the captives and release to the prisoners, Isa. 61:3 [sic]; who also afterwards led Christ into the desert. Matt. 4:1. Therefore that Spirit is the true God.

With these things premised, we argue: By as many names, external symbols, and distinct acts as God manifested Himself in the baptism of Christ, so many are there in diin the divinity of the person. Yet by three names, three external symbols, and three distinct acts, God manifested Himself in the baptism of Christ. Therefore, there are three persons in the divinity.

The Socinians, intending to cut the nerve of this argument, object: (1) that no theophany occurred in the baptism of Christ, since nothing was seen except Christ and the Holy Spirit, but only a divine voice was heard: (2) that the Holy Spirit did not appear in the form of a dove, but only descended from on high upon Christ with force and sound like a dove: (3) that the form of a dove no more argues that the Holy Spirit is a person than the tongues of fire, which were many, were many persons: (4) that external symbols, since they were separated, imply three persons not only really, but also essentially distinct; for those which are loc

Resp. to 1) That God the Father manifested Himself with an audible voice is clear (a) from the correlate, which is the Son; for He cried out: This is my beloved Son.

(b) From the assertion of Peter, 2 Epist. ch.

1, 17, where he says of Christ: He received honor and glory from God the Father, so that a voice was brought by the magnificent glory: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.

To 2): The adverb ὡσεὶ (as) denotes not a manner of descending similar to the flight of a dove, but a columbine form; for the dove was seen and remained upon Him, Jo.

Latin:

Testimonia N. T. quibus personarum divinarum trinitas coniunctim proponitur, nostram per baptismum regenerationem , θεοφάνειαν sive apparitionem personarum divinarum , incarnationem Filii Dei , missionem Spiritus S. , gratiosam Dei in nobis inhabitationem , divinam in ecclesia eiusque ministerio operationem , religiosam Dei venerationem , apostolicam de ὁμοουσία personarum divinarum assertionem perspicue exponunt, ut salutari sacrosanctae Trinitatis notitia imbuamur.

Prob. a. Christus, iam iam in coelum ascensurus, solemnem administrandi baptismi formam discipulis suis praescripsit, Matth. XXIX, 19. Euntes ergo μαθητεύσατε, discipulos facite (mihi) omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomen Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus sancti. Ex hoc dicto classico demonstramus (1) Deitatem Patris, Filii & Spiritus sancti. (2) Eorum distinctionem personalem. (3) Personarum divinarum ὁμοουσίαν, f. unam essentiam. Argumentamur: In cuius nomen baptizamur, ille est verus & summus Deus. In nomen Dei Patris & Filii, & Spiritus sancti baptizamur. E. Deus Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanctus est verus & summus Deus. Maior constat; quia in illius nomen baptizamur, qui baptismum, gratiae salutisque medium, instituit. At solus Deus, fons gratiae & auctor salutis, baptismum instituit. Adiice, quod in illius nomen baptizemur, in quem credere & quem invocare tenemur; nam sacramento baptismi ad fidei professionem, cultum & obsequium illius, qui auctor est baptismi, adstringimur. Ideo baptismus dicitur interrogatio bonae conscientiae ad Deum 1 Petr. III, 21. Oportet nos credere, ut baptizati sumus, ut credimus, ait BASIL. M. ep. LXXIIX. Deinde, qui baptizantur in nomen Patris, Filii & Spiritus sancti, illos oportet credere, tres esse personas divinas. Atqui omnes gentes baptizantur in nomen Patris, Filii & Spiritus sancti. Ergo. Maior liquet; quia citra omne dubium Pater & Filius differunt, ut distinctae personae. At quomodo distinguitur Filius a Patre in verbis institutionis baptismi: eodem modo distinguitur Spiritus sanctus a Patre & Filio, ut ostendit textus series. Atqui Filius a Patre distinguitur, ut persona. Ergo etiam Spiritus sanctus a Patre & Filio, ut persona distinguitur. Praeterea Spiritus sanctus non tantum hoc loco proponitur ut alius a Patre & Filio, sed etiam cum his personis divinis in administratione baptismi coniungitur, idem nomen, eadem auctoritas baptismum instituendi, eadem maiestas adorationis, eadem vis regenerandi, quae Patri & Filio competit, ipsi tribuatur. E. Spiritus S. est persona divina. Certe absurdum & vsui loquendi adversum est, idem nomen apponi personis, & non-personae. Oμοουσίαν denique personarum divinarum probamus; quia non baptizamur in nomina, sed in nomen Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. vt obligemur ad agnoscendum & venerandum idem nomen, eandem auctoritatem, maiestatem, sanctitatem, gratiam & potentiam, atque adeo eandem essentiam Patris, Filii & Spiritus S.

Excipiunt Sociniani (1)1. In nomen alicuius baptizari non esse indicium deitatis, cum etiam in hominem aliquis possit baptizari; sic Israëlitas baptizatos esse in Mosen teste Paulo 1 Cor. X, 1. Resp. (a) Aliud est baptizari in aliquem, aliud baptizari in nomen alicuius. Illud ministerialiter, hoc non nisi auctoritative exponi potest. (b) Distinguendum est inter baptismum proprie sic dictum, qui est lauacrum regenerationis & sacramentum N. T. & inter baptismum typicum, seu metaphoricum. Baptismus, proprie dictus, in nullius hominis nomen potest administrari: Israëlitarum autem baptismus in Mosen erat typicus, quo obligabantur ad fidem & obsequium Mosi, seruo Dei, praestandum, vt sub nube promti transirent mare rubrum, Mose praeunte: sicut nos baptismo regenerationis obligamur ad fiduciam in Deo Patre, Filio & Spiritu S. collocandam.

Excipiunt (2)4. Non esse nouum, in rebus non minoris momenti, quam est baptismus, coniungi Deo res & personas, non pertinentes ad eius essentiam. Sic 1 Sam. XII, 18. populus dicitur timuisse Iehouam & Samuelem. Exod. XIV, 31. vbi Israëlitae dicuntur credidisse Deo & Mosi. Eph. VI, 10. dicit Paullus: confortamini in Domino & in robore potentiae illius, vbi Paullus cum domino, qui est persona, coniungit potentiam Dei, quae non est persona, sed attributum diuinum.

Resp. (1) Exempla adducta sunt dissimilia & inconuenientia. Nam Deus & Moses coniunguntur vt dominus & seruus, causa principalis & instrumentalis, ratione concursus ad certum aliquod tertium, quod Deo & creaturae (non aequaliter, sed diuersa ratione) conuenit. At dispensare baptismum in nomen alicuius, nulli creaturae competit. 1 Cor. I, 13. Proferant aduersarii ex sacris litteris exemplum, quod Deus & homo vnico, eoque simultaneo mandato, & aequali auctoritate, nouum sacramentum instituerint, & porrigenus illis herbam. (2) Nunquam personis coniungitur non-persona in communione auctoritativa (quod h.l. fit, vbi vnum nomen tribus tribuitur,) diuinitus ordinati medii salutis. Dicit quidem Paullus: confortamini in Domino & robore potentiae illius, fed non vnum nomen Domino & eius potentiae attribuit. In nomen attributi diuini, vel etiam halitus diuini, baptizari, inauditum in sacris & inconueniens est.

Prob. b. Illustrissima θεοφάνεια seu apparitio diuina contigit in baptismo, Christo collati, administratione, quae describitur Matth. III, 16. Marc. I, 10. Luc. III, 22. Circa hanc θεοφάνειαν obseruamus (1) tria nomina. Es enim, cuius vox e caelo auditur, vocatur Pater. 2 Petr. I, 17. Qui in ripa Iordanis stat, vocatur Filius Matth. III, 17. Qui in specie columbae descendit, appellatur Spiritus S. Luc. III, 22. (2) Tria distincta manifestationis symbola, dum apparet Pater voce, Natus corpore, Flamen aue. (3) Tres distinctos actus, Patris de caelo clamantis, Filii in Iordane stantis, Spiritus S. in specie columbae descendentis. (4) Communem trium personarum deitatem. Nam Pater, de caelo clamans, haud dubie est verus Deus; cui Filius coëssentialis est, cum non sit adoptiuus, fed naturalis Dei filius; quippe qui geminato articulo graeco emphatice dicitur ὁ υἱὸς ὁ ἀγαπητὸς, ille filius, ille dilectus, in quo omnis εὐδοκία, complacentia Dei residet & acquiescit. Sed omnis filius naturalis cum patre habet essentiam eandem; eandem, inquam, specie in humanis, numero eandem in diuinis. Spiritus, qui in specie columbae descendit, non potest esse creatura; quippe qui ideo venit super Christum, vt eundem, qua homo est, donis impleret & vngeret, quo captiuis libertatem, & vinctis dimissionem praedicaret, Es. LXI, 3. qui etiam postea Christum in desertum egit. Matth. IV, 1. Ergo Spiritus ille verus est Deus.

Quibus praemissis argumentamur: Quot nominibus, externis symbolis, atque distinctis actibus, Deus in baptismo Christi se manifestauit, tot sunt in divinitate personae. Atqui tribus nominibus, tribus externis symbolis, tribus distinctis actibus, Deus in baptismo Christi se manifestavit. Ergo tres sunt in divinitate personae.

Sociniani, nervum huius argumenti incisuri, excipiunt (1) nullam contigisse θεοφάνειαν in baptismo Christi, cum praeter Christum & Spiritum S. nihil conspectum, sed tantum divina vox audita fuerit: (2) Spiritum S. non apparuisse in specie columbae, sed tantum ad instar columbae ex alto in Christum cum impetu sonituque descendisse: (3) Speciem columbae non magis arguere, Spiritum S. esse personam, quam linguae igneae, quae multae fuerunt, personas fuisse multas: (4) Symbola externa, cum separata fuerint, inferre tres personas non realiter tantum, sed etiam essentialiter distinctas; nam quae loc

Resp. ad 1) Deum patrem voce audibili se manifestasse, patet (a) ex correlato, quod est filius; clamavit enim: Hic est filius meus dilectus.

(b) Ex assertione Petri 2 Epist. c.

1, 17. vbi de Christo ait: Accepit a Deo patre honorem & gloriam, ita ut vox delata sit a magnifica gloria: Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi complacuit.

Ad 2): Adverbium ὡσεὶ non modum descendendi similem volatu columbino, sed formam columbinam notat; visa est enim columba & mansit super ipso Io.


### Quest. XVII. What are the testimonies of the New Testament by which the Trinity of the divine persons is exhibited conjointly?: I, 32

I, 32.

The Holy Spirit descended in bodily form, as a dove, witness Luke III, 22. To 3): We establish the personality of the Holy Spirit from this theophany: Whoever assumes a bodily form, appeared in it, and descended visibly, he is a ὑφιστάμενον (subsistent) subject, and since he is of an intellectual nature, a person.

But the Holy Spirit, etc. Therefore.

That He is a person distinct from the Father and the Son is clear from the fact that not the Father, not the Son, but the Holy Spirit alone assumes the columbine form.

The example taken from the multitude of tongues of fire, from Acts II, is disparate.

For the Holy Spirit occupied those many tongues with the same form of fire. Wherefore there was not a different, but one symbol of the same Spirit, dispersed through many tongues.

But indeed in Matt. III, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinctly named. By one external symbol the Father, by another the Son, by another the Holy Spirit manifests Himself, and according to the diversity of the symbol, different acts are produced by them.

To 4): From the separation of external signs to the separation of the signified, the consequence does not hold.

Although external symbols might be separated and essentially distinguished; yet the divine persons are neither separated nor essentially distinguished; inasmuch as they are one.

1 John V, 7. The symbolic manifestation of the Trinity brings about a personal, not an essential, distinction.

Prob. c. The incarnation of the Son of God leads us to the recognition of the Holy Trinity; which the angel announces to St. Mary, and declares in Luke I, 35.

The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God.

The incarnation of the Word flows from the common hand, as it were, of the Trinity, if you look at its principle; but it terminates only in the person of the Son of God (just as three virgins place a crown upon one of their number).

Conf. D. DANNH. in hodof. phaen. II. p. 185. Wherefore the angel commemorates all three persons of the divinity, calls God the Father the Most High, who sent the Son into the flesh, Gal.

IV, 4. He calls the Son of God the power of the Most High; who overshadowed Mary in a mysterious and ineffable way, filling the temple of His body in the womb of Mary with all the fullness of the divinity: just as God once filled the Solomonic temple, 1 Kings VIII, 11, through ἐπισκιασμὸν (overshadowing); but the Holy Spirit, as the angel predicted, shall come upon Mary; stirring up the drops of blood, sanctifying them, and forming from them the body of Christ.

Therefore, pious antiquity derived proof of the Trinity from the incarnation of the Word.

Beautifully says RUFINUS in the exposition of the creed: See the simple Trinity working together!

The Holy Spirit is said to come, and the power of the Most High to overshadow. But who is the power of the Most High, if not Christ Himself, who is the power and strength of God? Whose power is this? The Most High's. Therefore the Most High is present, the power of the Most High is present, the Holy Spirit is present. We argue: Whoever from the revealed word of God acknowledge that the incarnation of the Son of God is the work of the Father,

the Son, and the Holy Spirit, they cannot but believe in the Trinity of divine persons. But all Christians, etc. Therefore.

The Socinians object: (1) That only God the Father is called the Most High by the angel: (2) That Christ calls himself the Son of God because of his singular conception by the Holy Spirit. (3) That the Holy Spirit is called the power of the Most High, and therefore is not God the Most High himself, nor even a person, since power is not a person. Response to 1): God the Father is indeed called the Most High, but not exclusively, since Christ is also distinguished by the name of the Most High. Luke 1:76. To 2): The angel does not say that Christ is called the Son of God because of his singular conception by the Holy Spirit, but because of the overshadowing of the power of the Most High. For the conclusive conjunction διὸ, therefore, immediately refers to the words immediately preceding: the power of the Most High will overshadow you, so that the sense is: because the Son of God, the consubstantial power of the Father, overshadowed Mary, by assuming flesh in her womb and uniting it to himself: therefore, what is born of Mary will be called the Son of God. Certainly, if Christ is called the Son of God because he was conceived by the Holy Spirit, it would follow that the Holy Spirit himself is the father of Christ; which we are forbidden by the Christian religion to say. To 3): It is not the Holy Spirit, but the Son of God, who is called the power of the Most High, since Paul also calls Christ the power of God. 1 Cor. 1:24. There is no reason for you to object that power is not a person; for Reuben was also called the power of his father; Gen. 49:3, who was a true person.

Proof d. We seek a not invalid proof of the Most Holy Trinity from the mission of the Holy Spirit, which is described John 14:16. I will ask the Father, that he may give you another paraclete, that he may remain with you forever. In the same chapter v. 26. But the paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things. John 15:26. But when the paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who goes forth (proceeds) from the Father ἐκπορεύεται, he will testify of me. Cf. Gal. 4:6. We use these testimonies both for the deity of the Son of God, and especially to demonstrate the personality of the Holy Spirit: since both are impugned by adversaries with great effort.

To which end we argue: (1) He who is not true God with the Father, equal to him in unity of essence, does not have the right of sending the Holy Spirit. But the Son of God has the right of sending the Holy Spirit. Therefore, the Son is true God with the Father, equal to him in unity of essence. The major premise is evident; because in the opinion of the adversaries, the Holy Spirit is the power and efficacy of God. But no one can send the power and efficacy of God, unless he himself is God. (2) The Holy Spirit is described by Christ as a paraclete, as another paraclete, as the spirit of truth, teaching all things, who proceeds from the Father, and is sent in the name of the Son: whom the Son also sends from the Father. Therefore, the Holy Spirit is a divine person distinct from the Father and the Son. The reasoning of the consequence is not at all obscure; since all those predicates belong only to a true person, and likewise imply a personal distinction.

The Socinians object: (1) That Christ obtains by prayers from the Father that he may be able to send the Holy Spirit; and that he is not his source or fountain, and therefore not equal to him from whom he is derived. (2) Nor can the Holy Spirit be equal to him from whom he proceeds and is given. Response to 1): The intercession of a person does not in itself argue for inequality; since an equal can intercede with an equal, or even a greater with a lesser, a prince with a companion, for a third party. But Christ, as man, asks the Father for the sending of the Holy Spirit, while indeed, as God, he has by nature the right of sending. Nor indeed is the Father alone the source and fountain of the Holy Spirit, but also the Son of God; since from him, as wisdom, so also the essence of the Holy Spirit is received. John 16:14, 15. To 2): It is not permitted to infer inequality from the fact that the Holy Spirit proceeds from and is given by the Father and the Son, but only to gather origin and order in the Most Holy Trinity from the same.

Proof e. The mystery of the Trinity is made known from the gracious indwelling of the triune God in the faithful, which the Savior promises John 14:23. If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will make our abode with him. He teaches the same Paul 1 Cor. III, 6. Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? From these divine utterances we argue: Whoever dwells in believers, as in consecrated temples, he is the true God. But the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit dwell in believers, as in consecrated temples. Therefore. The major premise shines with its own light. You are the temple of the living God, says Paul 2 Cor. VI, 16. Cf. Levit. XXVI, 22. Excellent is the statement of CYRIL, L. XXXIV, Thesaurus: No creature, nor any created thing, is said to dwell as God in a temple.

The dissenters object: (1) According to the opinion of the Lutherans, Christ also, even according to the assumed human nature, which is not God, dwells in the pious: (2) From the indwelling of the Holy Spirit in believers it does not follow that the Holy Spirit is a divine person; since God dwells in the saints through His Spirit, as if through His virtue. Resp. to I. The human nature of Christ is viewed not in itself, but in the personal union, insofar as it has been assumed into the hypostasis τῆς λόγου [of the Word], it has been raised into the fellowship of the Holy Trinity. To II. The deity of the Holy Spirit is invincibly asserted from His gracious indwelling in the pious. For He Himself, whose temple the Corinthians are said to be, is expressly called God, and He, as Paul testifies, is the Spirit of God. Nor do we read anywhere in the Holy Scriptures that God dwells in us through the Holy Spirit as if through His virtue, but just as God the Father and the Son, as divine persons, dwell in the pious: So we rightly conclude that the Holy Spirit, dwelling in them, is also a divine person.

Prob. f. The Trinity of the divine persons is known from the divine operation of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit in the church; which the apostle teaches 1 Cor. XII, 3. 4. 5. 6. I make known to you, that no one, speaking in the Spirit of God, says Jesus is anathema: And no one can say Jesus is Lord, except in the Holy Spirit. Now there are diversities of gifts; but the same Spirit. And there are diversities of ministries: but there is one God, who works all things in all. There are those who take v. 4-6 concerning the person of the Holy Spirit, and judge that He comes under the name of one Spirit, one Lord, one God. But truly, since the apostle wishes to recall the Corinthians to the adequate object of Christian worship and faith, which is the triune God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and by one Lord understands the same whom he had called κύριον 'Ιησοῦν [Lord Jesus] in v. 3, and by one God designates the same of whom he had spoken in v. 3, likewise naming the Spirit of God: we doubt not that all three persons of the divinity are exhibited by the apostle jointly in the l. c. [loco citato]. Namely, to the Holy Spirit are assigned χαρίσματα [gifts], spiritual gifts, both ministering and sanctifying, according to the third article of the Apostolic Creed: διακονίαι [ministries] in the church are attributed to Christ, the Lord and Archbishop of the church: ἐνεργήματα [operations] are claimed for God the Father, from whom originally is every faculty of working. Cf. D. CALOV. in bibl. illustrat. in h. l. fol. 378. We argue: From whom all gifts, all ministries, all operations in the church depend, he is the true God. But from God the Father, the Son, and the Spirit, etc. Therefore.

The Socinians object (1) Although divine gifts and operations are ascribed to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, it cannot be inferred, however, that they are of the same essence: (2) The Lord and the Spirit are here clearly distinguished from the one God, so that the name of Lord signifies something less than the name of God; the Holy Spirit, however, since He is distinguished from God, denotes only the virtue of God. Resp. to (1): All divine gifts and works proceed from God, whose essence is only one. To (2): The heavenly Father is indeed called God, but not exclusively. For just as Christ the Lord, and the Holy Spirit do not exclude God the Father from dominion and from fellowship of spiritual nature: so neither does God the Father exclude Christ and the Holy Spirit from the unity of the divine essence. Nor is Christ a subordinate lord, but the supreme Lord, Lord of lords, Apoc. XIX, 16. Nor is the Holy Spirit a virtue of God ἀνυπόστατος [without hypostasis], destitute of proper personality, but ἐνυπόστατος [with hypostasis], understanding a suppositum, or true divine person; since indeed the same Spirit works and distributes to each one as he wills, 1 Cor. XII, 11.

Prob. g. The trinity of the divine persons is made manifest from the apostolic vow in 2 Cor. XIII, 13. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit (be) with you all! Amen! Obs. The Apostle in this final vow placed the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ in the first position, not to invert the order among the divine persons, but to set forth the substantial foundation of faith and salvation, which is Christ, 1 Cor. III, 11, the leader and perfecter of faith, Heb. XII, 2, by whose merit both the love of the Father and the communion of the Holy Spirit have been obtained for the fallen human race. Wherefore the Apostle understands the special love of the Father, and the active communion of the Holy Spirit; for he is the one who makes us partakers of the grace of Christ and the love of the Father. From this apostolic vow arises the argument: He whose love, grace, and communion we pray for ourselves and others in pious vows and sighs, he is the one and true God. But we pray for the love of the Father, the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the communion of the Holy Spirit for ourselves and others. Therefore, the heavenly Father, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit are the one and true God.

The adversaries object: 1) It is one thing to wish that the communion of the Holy Spirit be with all, another to invoke the Holy Spirit: 2) The name κοινωνίας, of communion, is not taken actively, but passively, so that it is understood concerning the gifts of the Holy Spirit communicated to us, which do not sustain the name of a person: 3) Only the Father is designated by the name of God κατ' ἐξοχήν (by way of eminence). Resp. to I. The apostolic vow is a votive invocation of the Most Holy Trinity. The Father and the Son are joined to the Holy Spirit. Therefore, just as we invoke them, so we also invoke him. To II. In the same way that we pray for love from the Father and grace from Christ, we pray for κοινωνίαν (communion) from the Holy Spirit. But we pray for the active love and grace of Jesus Christ. Therefore, we also seek the active communion of the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit communicates himself to us with his gifts, which he distributes as a divine person, as he wills, 1 Cor. XII, 11. To III. The heavenly Father is designated by the name of God in the apostolic vow: Because he is the fountain of divinity: By which very fact the origin and order of the divine persons is inferred, not the eminence or prerogative of the Father, since the essence of the divine persons is one and the same, and their majesty and glory are one and the same.

Prob. h. The apostolic assertion concerning the ὁμοουσίᾳ (consubstantiality) of the divine persons is read in 1 John V, 7. There are three who testify in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one. The scope of St. John in chapter V, 1 of the epistle was to teach: that Jesus of Nazareth, born of the Virgin Mary, is that Christ, or the Messiah, promised in the O.T. and exhibited in the N.T. v. 1. is the true Son of God v. 5. and the savior of the world, who by most perfect obedience and most full satisfaction acquired for us sinners the victory of the world v. 4. and eternal life v. 11.

The apostle, intending to confirm this doctrine of the greatest importance, brings forward three heavenly witnesses, just as well as three earthly witnesses.

Concerning the heavenly witnesses he says: v. 7. There are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, and the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one.

Latin:

I, 32.

Descendit Spiritus sanctus corporali specie, quasi columba, teste Luc. III, 22. Ad 3): Personalitatem Spiritus S. ex hac θεοφανείᾳ stabilimus: Quicunque formam corpoream assumit, in ea apparuit, visibiliterque descendit, ille est ὑφιστάμενον suppositum, & cum intellectualis sit natura, persona.

Atqui Spiritus S. &c. E.

Quod distincta sit a Patre & Filio persona, liquet ex eo, quod non Pater, non Filius, sed solus Spiritus S. formam columbinam assumit.

Exemplum petitum a multitudine linguarum ignearum, ex Act. II. dispar est.

Nam multas illas linguas Spiritus S. eadem forma ignis occupavit. Quare ibi non diversum, sed unum symbolum eiusdem Spiritus, fuit dispersum per multas linguas.

At vero Matth. III. distincte nominatur Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. Alio symbolo externo Pater, alio Filius, alio Spiritus S. se manifestat, & pro diversitate symboli ab iisdem diversi eduntur actus.

Ad 4): A separatione signorum externorum, ad separationem signati, non valet consequ.

Quamvis symbola externa separarentur & essentialiter distinguerentur; personae tamen divinae nec separantur, nec essentialiter distinguuntur; quippe quae unum sunt.

1 Io. V, 7. Symbolica Trinitatis manifestatio personale, non essentiale discrimen infert.

Prob. c. Ad agnitionem S. S. Trinitatis nos perducit incarnatio filii Dei; quam angelus annuntiat S. Mariae, & declarat Luc. I, 35.

Spiritus S. veniet super te, & virtus altissimi adumbrabit te: ideo etiam, quod nascetur ex te sanctum, vocabitur filius Dei.

Incarnatio τοῦ λόγου fluit a communi quasi Trinitatis manu, si spectes eius principium; terminatur autem ad solam personam filii Dei (perinde, ac tres virgines uni ex numero suo imponunt coronam).

Conf. D. DANNH. in hodof. phaen. II. p. 185. Quare angelus omnes tres divinitatis personas commemorat, Deum patrem vocat altissimum, qui Filium in carnem misit Gal.

IV, 4. Filium Dei appellat virtutem altissimi; qui obumbravit Mariam arcano & ineffabili modo, in vtero Mariae templum corporis sui omni divinitatis plenitudine implendo: sicut olim Deus templum Salomonaeum 1 Reg. IIX, 11. per ἐπισκιασμὸν, sive obumbrationem replevit; Spiritus S. autem, praedicente angelo, veniet super Mariam; guttulas sanguineas excitando, sanctificando, & ex iis corpus Christi efformando.

Idcirco pia antiquitas ex incarnatione τοῦ λόγου documentum Trinitatis desumsit.

Pulchre inquit RVFFINVS in expos. symboli: Vide cooperantem simplicem trinitatem!

Spiritus S. venire dicitur, & virtus Altissimi obumbrare. Qui est autem virtus altissimi, nisi ipse Christus, qui est Dei virtus & potentia? Cuius haec est virtus? Altissimi. Adest ergo Altissimus, adest virtus Altissimi, adest Spiritus S. Nos argumentamur: Quicunque ex verbo Dei revelato agnoscunt, incarnationem filii Dei esse opus Patris,

Filii, et Spiritus S. illi non possunt non credere personarum divinarum Trinitatem. Atqui omnes christiani etc. Ergo.

Excipiunt Sociniani: (1) Solum Deum Patrem ab angelo vocari altissimum: (2) Christum dicere filium Dei ob singularem conceptionem e Spiritu S. (3) Spiritum S. nuncupari virtutem Altissimi, adeoque non esse ipsum Deum altissimum, ac ne personam quidem, cum virtus non sit persona. Resp. ad 1): Deus Pater dicitur quidem altissimus, sed non exclusive, cum nomine altissimi etiam Christus insigniatur. Luc. I, 76. Ad 2): Angelus non dicit, Christum vocari filium Dei ob singularem eius conceptionem a Spiritu S. sed propter obumbrationem virtutis Altissimi. Nam coniunctio conclusiva διὸ, ideo, immediate respicit verba proxime antegressa: virtus Altissimi obumbrabit te, vt sensus sit: quia Filius Dei, virtus Patris consubstantialis, obumbravit Mariam, in vtero eius carnem assumendo, sibique vniendo: ideo, quod nascetur ex Maria, vocabitur filius Dei. Certe si Christus propterea vocatur filius Dei, quod a Spiritu S. conceptus est, sequetur, ipsum Spiritum S. esse patrem Christi; quod dicere religione christiana prohibemur. Ad 3): Non Spiritus S. sed Filius Dei vocatur virtus Altissimi, cum et Paullus Christum appellet virtutem Dei. 1 Cor. I, 24. Non est, quod obvertas; virtutem non esse personam; nam et Ruben dicebatur virtus patris sui; Gen. XLIX, 3. qui vera erat persona.

Prob. d. Documentum S.S. Trinitatis haud inualidum petimus a missione Spiritus S. quae deseribitur Io. XIV, 16. Ego rogabo patrem, vt alium paracletum det vobis, vt maneat vobiscum in aeternum. Eodem capite v. 26. Paracletus autem Spiritus S. quem mittit Pater in nomine meo, ille docebit vos omnia Io. XV, 26. Quando vero venerit paracletus, quem ego missurus sum vobis a Patre, Spiritus veritatis, qui ex Patre ἐκπορεύεται exit (procedit) ille testabitur de me. Conf. Gal. IV, 6. Vtimur his testimoniis cum ad deitatem filii Dei, tum inprimis ad personalitatem Spiritus S. demonstrandam: quum vtraque ab aduersariis magno conatu impugnetur.

Quem in finem argumentamur: (1) Qui non est verus cum patre Deus, essentiae vnitate eidem aequalis, non habet ius inittendi Spiritum sanctum. At filius Dei habet ius mittendi Spiritum S. Ergo Filius est verus cum Patre Deus, essentiae vnitate eidem aequalis. Maior constat; quia ex mente aduersariorum Spiritus S. est virtus et efficacia Dei, At virtutem et efficaciam Dei nemo potest mittere, nisi ipse sit Deus. (2) Spiritus S. describitur a Christo vt paracletus, vt paracletus alius, vt spiritus veritatis, omnia docens, qui a Patre procedit, et in nomine Filii mittitur: quem mittit etiam a Patre Filius. Ergo Spiritus S. est persona divina a Patre et Filio distincta. Ratio consequentiae minime obscura est; cum omnia illa praedicata non nisi verae personae conueniant, pariter atque personalem distinctionem inferant.

Excipiunt Sociniani: (1) Christum precibus impetrare a Patre, vt Spiritum S. mittere queat; neque esse eius fontem aut scaturiginem, adeoque non aequalem illi, a quo derivatur. (2) Neque Spiritum S. posse aequari illi, a quo proficiscitur et donatur. Resp. ad 1): Intercessio personae inaequalitatem per se non arguit; cum aequalis apud aequalem, immo maior apud minorem, princeps apud comitem, pro tertio quodam intercedere queat. Christus autem, qua homo, rogat Patrem pro mittendo Spiritu S. cum quidem, qua Deus, ius mittendi natura obtineat. Neque vero fons et scaturigo Spiritus S. solus est Pater, sed etiam Filius Dei; quippe a quo, vt sapientiam, sic essentiam Spiritus S. accipit. Io. XVI, 14. 15. Ad 2): Non licet inferre inaequalitatem ex eo, quod Spiritus S. a Patre et Filio proficiscitur atque donatur, sed tantum originem et ordinem in S.S. Trinitate ex eodem colligere est.

Prob. e. Innotescit mysterium Trinitatis ex gratiosa Dei trinunius in fidelibus inhabitatione, quam promittit Saluator Io. XIV, 23. Si quis dilexerit me, verbum meum seruabit, et pater meus diliget illum, et mansionem apud illum faciemus. Docet eandem Paullus 1 Cor. III, 6. Nonne scitis, quod templum Dei fitis, & Spiritus Dei habitet in vobis? Ex his eloquiis divinis arguimus: Quicunque in fidelibus, velut consecratis templis, habitat, ille est verus Deus. Atqui Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. in fidelibus, velut consecratis templis, habitat. Ergo. Maior sua radiat luce. Vos templum Dei viventis, inquit Paullus 2 Cor. VI, 16. Conf. Levit. XXVI, 22. Praeclare ait CYRILLUS L. XXXIV. thesaur. Nulla creatura, neque factum aliquod, tanquam Deus in templo habitare dicitur.

Excipiunt diffidentes: (1) Ex sententia Lutheranorum, Christum etiam secundum assumtam humanam naturam, quae non est Deus, in piis habitare: (2) Ex inhabitatione Spiritus S. in fidelibus non sequi, Spiritum S. esse personam divinam; cum Deus in sanctis habitet per Spiritum suum, tanquam per virtutem suam. Resp. ad I. Humana natura Christi spectata non in se, sed in unione personali, quatenus assumta est in hypostasin τῆς λόγου, in consortium SS. Trinitatis euecta est. Ad II. Deitas Spiritus S. ex inhabitatione eius gratiosa in piis invicte afferitur. Nam ille ipse, cuius templum dicuntur Corinthii, diserte vocatur Deus, is vero, teste Paulo, Spiritus Dei est. Neque vllibi in sacris litteris scriptum legimus, Deum habitare in nobis per Spiritum S. tanquam per virtutem suam, sed sicut Deus Pater & Filius, tanquam personae divinae, habitant in piis: Ita & Spiritum S. in ipsis habitantem, personam divinam esse, recte concludimus.

Prob. f. Cognoscitur personarum divinarum Trinitas ex operatione divina Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. in ecclesia; quam docet apostolus 1 Cor. XII, 3. 4. 5. 6. Notum vobis facio, quod nemo, in Spiritu Dei loquens, dicat anathema Iesum: Et nemo possit dicere dominum Iesum, nisi in Spiritu S. Divisiones tamen donorum sunt; idem tamen spiritus. Et divisiones ministeriorum sunt: unus tamen est Deus, qui operatur omnia in omnibus. Sunt, qui v. 4-6. de persona Spiritus S. accipiunt, & hunc nomine unius Spiritus, vnius Domini, vnius Dei venire censent. At vero cum apostolus Corinthios ad adaequatum cultus & fidei christianae obiectum, quod est trinunus Deus Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. reuocatos velit, & per vnum dominum eundem, quem v. 3. κύριον 'Ιησοῦν appellauerat, intelligat, atque per vnum Deum eundem, de quo v. 3. itidem nominato Spiritu Dei, locutus erat, designet: Omnes tres diuinitatis personas ab apostolo coniunctim l. c. exhiberi, nulli dubitamus. Nempe Spiritui S. χαρίσματα, dona spiritualia, cum ministerantia, tum sanctificantia, secundum tertium symboli apostolici articulum assignantur: διακονίαι, ministeria, in ecclesia Christo, domino & archiepiscopo ecclesiae, tribuuntur: ἐνεργήματα, operationes, Dei Patri, a quo originaliter est omnis operandi facultas, vindicantur. Conf. D. CALOV. in bibl. illustrat. in h. l. fol. 378. Nos argumentamur: A quo omnia dona, omnia ministeria, omnes operationes in ecclesia dependent, ille est verus Deus. Atqui a Deo Patre, Filio & Spiritu &c. Ergo.

Excipiunt Sociniani (1) Licet Patri, Filio & Spiritu S. diuina dona & operationes adscribantur, inferri tamen non posse, quod sint eiusdem essentiae: (2) Dominum & Spiritum hic clare a Deo vno discerni, ita, vt nomen Domini aliquid minus, quam nomen Dei significet; Spiritus S. autem, cum a Deo distinguatur, virtutem solum Dei denotet. Resp. ad (1): Omnia dona & opera diuina proficiscuntur a Deo, cuius vna tantum est essentia. Ad (2): Pater caelestis dicitur Deus quidem, sed non exclusive. Sicut enim Christus dominus, & Spiritus S. non excludunt Deum Patrem a dominio & communione spiritualis naturae: ita nec Deus Pater excludit Christum & Spiritum S. ab vnitate essentiae diuinae. Neque Christus est dominus subordinatus, sed dominus summus, dominus dominorum, Apoc. XIX, 16. Neque Spiritus S. est virtus Dei ἀνυπόστατος, propria personalitate destituta, sed ἐνυπόστατος, suppositum intelligens, seu vera persona diuina; siquidem idem Spiritus operatur & distribuit unicuique, sicut vult, 1 Cor. XII, 11. At operationes sunt suppositorum .

Prob. g. Patescit personarum divinarum trinitas ex voto apostolico 2 Cor. XIII, 13. Gratia Domini Iesu Christi & amor Dei, & communicatio sancti Spiritus (fit) cum omnibus vobis! Amen! Obs. Apostolus in hoc voto finali primo loco posuit gratiam domini Iesu Christi, non ut ordinem inter personas divinas inverteret, sed ut praestitueret fundamentum fidei salutisque substantiale, quod est Christus, 1 Cor. III, 11. dux & consummator fidei, Hebr. XII, 2. cuius merito & caritas Patris & communicatio Spiritus S. lapso generi humano parta est. Quare intelligit Apostolus caritatem Patris specialem, & actuam Spiritus S. communicationem; quippe qui nos participes facit gratiae Christi & caritatis Patris. Ex hoc voto apostolico nascitur argumentum: Cuius caritatem, gratiam & communicationem piis votis atque suspiriis nobis & aliis precamur, ille est unus & verus Deus. Atqui caritatem Patris, gratiam domini Iesu Christi, & communicationem Spiritus S. nobis & aliis precamur. Ergo Pater caelestis, dominus Iesus Christus, & Spiritus S. sunt unus & verus Deus .

Excipiunt adversarii: 1) Aliud esse, optare, vt communicatio Spiritus S. fit cum omnibus, aliud Spiritum S. invocare: 2) Nomen κοινωνίας, communicationis, non accipi active, sed passive, vt intelligatur de donis Spiritus S. nobiscum communicatis, quae nomen personae non sustinent: 3) Solum Patrem κατ' ἐξοχήν Dei nomine designari. Resp. ad I. Votum apostolicum est votiva invocatio SS. Trinitatis. Coniunguntur Spiritui S. Pater & Filius. Ergo sicut hos, ita illum etiam invocamus. Ad II. Quo pacto a Patre amorem, a Christo gratiam, eodem a Spiritu S. κοινωνίαν precamur. At amorem & gratiam Iesu Christi actuam precamur. Ergo & actuam communicationem Spiritus S. expetimus. Communicat Spiritus S. seipsum nobis cum donis suis, quae distribuit, vt persona divina, sicut vult, 1 Cor. XII, 11. Ad III. Pater caelestis in voto apostolico nomine Dei designatur: Quia est fons divinitatis: Quo ipso origo & ordo personarum divinarum, non eminentia aut praerogativa patris infertur, cum personarum divinarum una eademque sit essentia, una eademque maiestas & gloria.

Prob. h. Apostolica de ὁμοουσίᾳ personarum divinarum assertio legitur 1 Io. V, 7. Tres sunt, qui testificantur in caelo, Pater, verbum & Spiritus S. & hi tres unum sunt. Scopus S. Ioannis erat in cap. V, 1. epistolae docere: Iesum Nazarenum, ex Maria virgine natum, esse Christum, sive Messiam, in V. T. promissum, & in N. T. exhibitum v. 1. verum Dei Filium v. 5. & salvatorem mundi, qui perfectissima obedientia & satisfactione plenissima victoriam mundi v. 4. & vitam aeternam v. 11. nobis peccatoribus acquisivit.

Doctrinam hanc maximi momenti apostolus confirmaturus, adducit tres testes coelestes, pariter atque tres testes terrestres.

De testibus coelestibus inquit: v. 7. Tres sunt, qui testificantur in caelo, Pater, & verbum, & Spiritus S. & hi tres unum sunt.


### Concerning this classic dictum let us observe: 1) The divine majesty of the heavenly witnesses

For those three witnesses are said to be in heavenly and divine glory: Just as our Father, whom we worship daily, is in heaven, Matt. VI, 9.

They are therefore three heavenly witnesses, divine witnesses 2) The unity of the divine essence.

For John says: and these three are one. He does not say: They are one in sentiment, but they are one.

He implies therefore the unity of essence, or ὁμοουσίαν [consubstantiality], the consequence of which is the unity of consent.

3) The trinity of the divine persons; for the apostle says: These three are one.

Here, therefore, is held a trinity, not in the abstract, but in the concrete. For we easily gather: If three divine witnesses are one, in one divinity there is given a trinity of persons.

For the apostle understands witnesses properly so called, living, intelligent, subsisting by themselves, such as are the Father & the Son; to which personal witnesses when the Holy Spirit is added as a third witness, he cannot but be a true person.

4) The name and personal property of each person.

S. John calls the first witness the Father, whose hypostatic character is paternity, founded in the eternal generation of the son.

He calls the second witness λόγον, or the Word, on account of the eternal generation from the Father, just as the internal word is generated in the mind, without real mutation of the conceiver: so also the Son of God is generated by the Father immutably, within the divine essence.

The third witness he names the Holy Spirit, whose personal property is passive spiration, from which the Spirit is denominated.

5) The order of the divine persons, founded in the origin of the mode of possessing the divine essence.

For the first witness is the Father, because he is from no one, neither generated, nor proceeding. The second witness is ὁ λόγος, or the Son of God, because he is generated from the Father; the third witness is the Holy Spirit, because he proceeds from the Father & the Son.

With these premises we conclude: Whoever asserts that three divine witnesses are one, he teaches that in one divine essence there are three distinct persons.
