But S. John asserts &c. Therefore.

The Socinians object: 1) that this text is supposititious, since it is not read in the Syriac version, nor in the ancient Latin versions, nor in the first German version of Luther 2) It does not follow; as many as are the witnesses, so many are the persons.

For in the following verse the Spirit, water and blood are called three witnesses, and yet they are not three persons. 3) That the apostle is dealing with a unity not of essence, but of consent; because otherwise it would follow that the spirit in the ministry, the water in baptism, the blood in the supper, agree in one essence; since unity is attributed to them also by the apostle.

Resp. to 1): This text is not supposititious.

For although in some codices of the bibles it was expunged or erased by the Arians; yet it is read in the most approved Greek copies, in the most ancient British codex, in the Complutensian, Basle, and Antwerp editions, in the Vatican copy, in the bibles of Robert Stephanus, and in very many others. It was adduced by ATHANASIUS in his disputation against Arius, and was not rejected or called into doubt by him: It was alleged by the Ante-Nicene fathers; it was found in all Greek codices in the time of Jerome, who accused the Latin translators of infidelity, because they omitted the testimony of the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, by which the catholic faith is most strengthened, and the one divine essence of the Father & the Son & the Holy Spirit is proven.

Conf.

D. GERHARD. in disp. acad. p. 1293. sqq.

D. CALOV. in bibl. illustrat. in h. l. fol. 1664.

D. SCHERZ. in colleg. Anti-Socin. p. 162. sqq.

It cannot be omitted without a hiatus in this chapter V.

of John. For John, intending to prove that Jesus of Nazareth is the Christ, the Son of God and the Savior of the world, brings forward witnesses partly heavenly, part. partly earthly, and connects them by the copulative conjunction καὶ in v. 8. But if the three heavenly ones were omitted, the primary ones would be passed over, and the cohesion of the text would be disturbed.

To 2): I distinguish between a witness properly and figuratively so called. When John asserts that there are three witnesses in heaven, he speaks of witnesses properly so called; which is evident from the fact that the Father is certainly a testifying person, the Son is a testifying person, as the Socinians themselves acknowledge. What, therefore, prevents the Holy Spirit from also being a testifying person? But if the Holy Spirit were only a virtue, not three, but only two witnesses would emerge in the heavens.

But in the following v. 8, the discourse is about witnesses spoken of improperly and figuratively; because that whole verse speaks of things, not of persons. To 3): The earthly witnesses εἰς τὸ ἕν εἰσὶ are into one, i. e., they tend toward one goal, so that they may bear concordant testimony to Christ the Savior of the world, just as they have been divinely ordained for the salvation, procured by the merit of Christ, to be offered, conferred, and sealed, as means and seals of grace.

But indeed the heavenly witnesses ἓν εἰσὶ are one, i. e., they are of one essence. This we prove a) because these witnesses are divine; for they are in heaven, i. e., in heavenly and divine glory: their testimony is called divine v. 9. The Word (substantial) and the Holy Spirit are immediately joined with God the Father in testifying, and are said to be one with Him.

Therefore, just as the Father is true God: so also ὁ λόγος is true God, and the Holy Spirit is true God. But since there are not three gods, not three divine essences; it is necessarily inferred that the three witnesses agree in one essence, but are distinguished by personal distinction. b) We appeal to the parallel passage, Jo.

X. That unity is urged here by St. John, which is intimated by Christ Himself in Jo. X, 30, saying: I and the Father are one. But the Father and the Son are said to be one in that place in such a way that not only consensus, but the unity of essence is evidently concluded.

For Christ posits that unity as the foundation of His insuperable power and the impossible snatching of the sheep from His hand.

But unless the unity of power, and consequently of essence, is granted, there will be no force of proof in the argument.

For the apostles were also a certain one, by unity of consensus with the Father: but who would say that no one could have snatched the sheep of Christ from their hand? c) As the Holy Spirit, whom most Socinians posit to be the essential virtue of God, does not differ essentially from the Father: so neither does ὁ λόγος, or the Son of God, who is one with the Father and the Holy Spirit. d) If only the unity of consensus had been indicated by John, he could have brought forward far more witnesses in heaven.

For the angels, Moses, and Elijah bore witness in agreement with Christ, as is evident from the angelic apparitions and the transfiguration of Christ. e) If the Word and the Holy Spirit are one with the Father by reason of consensus and will: they are also one with Him in essence; because the will of God does not differ really from the divine essence. Wherefore, just as in our mode of conceiving, the will follows the essence of God: so the unity of the divine essence is followed by the unity of consensus.

For which reason, just as the will follows the essence of God in our way of conceiving it, so the unity of divine consensus follows the unity of the divine essence.

Latin:

Nam dicuntur tres illi testes esse in coelesti divinaque gloria: Sicut Pater noster, quem quotidie adoramus, est in coelis, Matth. VI, 9.

Sunt igitur tres testes coelestes, testes divini 2) Essentiae divinae unitatem.

Dicit enim Ioannes: & hi tres unum sunt. Non dicit: Unum sentiunt, sed unum sunt.

Innuit igitur unitatem essentiae, seu ὁμοουσίαν, cuius consequens est unitas consensus.

3) Personarum divinarum trinitatem; nam dicit apostolus: Hi tres unum sunt.

Habetur ergo hic trinitas, non in abstracto, sed in concreto. Ex facili enim colligimus: Si tres testes divini sunt unum, in una divinitate personarum datur trinitas.

Intelligit quippe apostolus testes proprie dictos, vivos, intelligentes, per se subsistentes, quales sunt Pater & Filius; quibus testibus personalibus cum adiungatur Spiritus S. vt testis tertius, non potest non vera esse persona.

4) Cuiusque personae nomen & proprietatem personalem.

S. Ioannes primum testem appellat Patrem, cuius character hypostaticus est paternitas, fundata in aeterna generatione filii.

Secundum testem vocat λόγον, seu verbum, propter aeternam a patre generationem, Sicut enim verbum internum in mente generatur, sine reali mutatione concipientis: ita etiam filius Dei a Patre genitus est immutabiliter, intra essentiam divinam.

Tertium testem nuncupat Spiritum S. cuius proprietas personalis est spiratio passiva, a qua Spiritus denominatur.

5) Ordinem personarum divinarum, fundatum in origine modi habendi essentiam divinam.

Nam primus testis est Pater, quia est a nullo neque genitus, neque procedens. Secundus testis ὁ λόγος, sive Filius Dei, quia est a Patre genitus; tertius testis est Spiritus sanctus, quia a Patre & Filio procedit.

Quibus praemissis concludimus: Quicunque asserit, tres testes divinos esse unum, ille docet in una essentia divina esse tres distinctas personas.

Atqui S: Ioannes asserit &c. Ergo.

Excipiunt Sociniani: 1) hunc textum esse supposititium, cum non legatur in versione Syriaca, neque in versionibus antiquis latinis, neque in versione prima germanica Lutheri 2) Non sequi; quot sunt testes, tot sunt personae.

Nam versu sequenti Spiritus, aqua & sanguis dicuntur tres testes, neque tamen tres sunt personae. 3) Apostolum agere de unitate non essentiae, sed consensus; quia alias secuturum fit, spiritum in ministerio, aquam in baptismo, sanguinem in coena, convenire in una essentia; cum & illis unitas apostolo tribuatur.

Resp. ad 1): Non est hic textus supposititius.

Quamvis enim in quibusdam bibliorum codicibus ab Arianis expunctus aut erasus fit; legitur tamen in exemplaribus graecis probatissimis, in codice Britannico vetustissimo, in editione Complutensi, Basileensi, Antverpiana, in exemplari Vaticano, in bibliis Roberti Stephani, & aliis, longe plurimis. Adductus est ab ATHANASIO in disputatione contra Arium, nec ab hoc reiectus, aut in dubium vocatus: Allegatus est a patribus Ante-Nicenis; inuentus est in omnibus codicibus graecis tempore Hieronymi, qui translatores latinos infidelitatis accusavit, quod Patris, verbique, ac Spiritus S. testimonium omiserint, quo maxime fides catholica roboratur, & Patris & Filii & Spiritus S. una divinitatis essentia comprobatur.

Conf.

D. GERHARD. in disp. acad. p. 1293. sqq.

D. CALOV. in bibl. illustrat. in h. l. fol. 1664.

D. SCHERZ. in colleg. Anti-Socin. p. 162. sqq.

Nequit omitti sine hiatu huius capitis V.

Ioannae. Probaturus enim Ioannes, Iesum Nazarenum esse Christum, Filium Dei & Salvatorem mundi, testes adducit partim coelestes, par. partim terrestres, eosque per coniunctionem copulativam καὶ v. 8. connectit. Omissis vero tribus cœlestibus, prætermitterentur primarii, & cohæsio textus turbaretur.

Ad 2): Distinguo. inter testem proprie & figurate sic dictum. Cum Ioannes affert, tres esse testes in cœlo, loquitur de testibus proprie sic dictis; quod patet ex eo, quia vtique Pater est persona testans, Filius est persona testans, agnoscentibus ipsis Socinianis. Quid igitur obstat, quo minus Spiritus S. quoque fit persona testans? Quod si Spiritus S. solum esset virtus, non tres, sed duo tantum emergerent testes in cœlis.

At in sequenti v. 8. de testibus improprie & figurate dictis fermo est; quia totus ille verficulus de rebus, non de personis loquitur. Ad 3): Testes terrestres εἰς τὸ ἕν εἰσὶ sunt in vnum, i. e. in vnum tendunt scopum, vt concors perhibeant testimonium Christo saluatori mundi, pariter atque ad salutem, merito Christi partam, offerendam, conferendam & obsignandam, diuinitus ordinata sunt, vt media & sigilla gratiæ.

Ac vero testes cœlestes ἓν εἰσὶ vnum sunt, i. e. vnius sunt essentiæ. Id quod probamus a) quia hi testes sunt diuini; sunt enim in cœlo, i. e. in cœlesti & diuina gloria: testimonium eorum vocatur diuinum v. 9. Verbum (substantiale) & Spiritus S. cum Deo Patre in testando immediate coniunguntur, & cum illo vnum esse dicuntur.

Ergo sicut Pater est verus Deus: Ita & ὁ λόγος est verus Deus, & Spiritus S. est verus Deus. At cum non sint tres dii, non tres essentiæ diuinæ; necessario infertur, tres testes conuenire in vno essentia, distingui autem distinctione personali. b) Prouocamus ad locum parallelum, Io.

X. Ea vnitas hic vrgetur a S. Ioanne, quæ intimatur ab ipso Christo Io. X, 30. dicente: Ego & Pater vnum sumus. At Pater & Filius in isto loco ita vnum esse dicuntur, vt non tantum consensu, sed essentiæ vnitas euidenter concludatur.

Ponit enim Christus istam vnitatem pro fundamento insuperabilis suæ potentiæ, & impossibilis ereptionis ouium ex manu sua.

At nisi concedatur vnitas potentiæ, & consequenter essentiæ, nulla vis probandi in argumento erit.

Nam etiam apostoli fuerunt vnum quid, vnitate consenfus cum Patre: Quis autem diceret neminem ex manu illorum rapere potuisse oues Christi? c) Vti Spiritus S. quem plerique Sociniani virtutem Dei essentialem esse statuunt, non differt essentialiter a Patre: Ita nec ὁ λόγος, siue Filius Dei, qui cum Patre & Spiritu S. vnum est. d) Si a Ioanne tantum vnitas consensus indicata fuisset, longe plures in cœlo testes adducere potuisset.

Nam angeli, Mofes & Elias consentientia Christo testimoniis perhibuerunt, vt ex apparitionibus angelicis & transfiguratione Christi constat. e) Si Verbum & Spiritus S. vnum sunt cum Patre ratione consensus & voluntatis: Vnum quoque cum ipso sunt in essentia; quia voluntas Dei ab essentia diuina non differt realiter.

Quam ob rem sicut nostro concipiendo modo essentiam Dei sequitur voluntas: ita vnitatem essentiæ diuinæ consequitur vnitas consensus.


### Q. XVIII. What are the testimonies of the O.t. by which the Trinity of divine persons is exhibited conjointly?

The testimonies of the O.T.

by which the Trinity of divine persons is taught conjointly are taken from the creation of the world (a), the leading of the Israelites out of Egypt (b), the predicted mission and anointing of the Messiah (c), the solemn blessing of the priests (d), and the angelic trisagion (e).

Proof a. From Gen. I, 1. 2. 3. In the beginning Elohim created the heaven and the earth. The earth, indeed, was made waste and void, and darkness... was upon the face of the abyss. Then indeed the Spirit of God moved itself over the face of the waters: and God said: let there be light, and there was light.

That this passage is among the chief ones of the O.T. which treat of the mystery of the H. Trinity, appears even from the fact that without doubt the phrase of Ps. XXXIII, 6 is deduced from it: By the Word of Jehovah were the heavens made, and all the host of them by the Spirit of his mouth. But who indeed would deny that John c. I, 1, 2, 3 looked hither with these words: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word: this was in the beginning with God: all things were made by him, and without him was not anything made that was made.

Obs. 1) Moses, about to describe the first work of God, says: He created ברא, which is a noun plural not only in termination, but also in signification, constructed with the singular verb ברא, it signifies a work common to many, or an action, q. d. he created, who are God. See the annotations of D. SEB. SCHMID in Gen. p. 2. 2) God, about to create light, said: let there be light. God saying is God the Father, by virtue of the contradistinction of the Word, through whom he said, and the Holy Spirit, in whom he moved himself with the Word, through whom he was about to speak, over the waters. 3) God the Father said by commanding, according to Ps. XXXIII, 9. He said, and it was done: He commanded, and it stood fast. Therefore, the saying of God denotes the word of command, so that it nevertheless 4) connotes or prenotes the hypostatic word, or substantial word. This we prove a) from the infallible interpretation of John c. I, 1, 2, 3. From which passage we conclude thus: That Word was in the beginning of creation with God the Father, through whom all things were made. But the Word subsisting by itself, which is true God, was in the beginning of creation with God the Father. Therefore, the Word subsisting by itself is that Word through whom all things were made. b) From the testimony of Solomon, who attributes to the wisdom of God (hypostatic, the eternal Son of God, the author and fountain of all wisdom) the same things which Moses here attributes to the Word of God, Prov. VIII, 22 sqq. c) From the consideration of the thing itself. For just as in man the external word of the mouth presupposes the internal word of the mind, and internal wisdom: so the word of divine command does not occur without the hypostatic Word, not without substantial wisdom, the eternal Son of God, since the Father does not work without the Son, Io. V, 17. d) When Moses in verse 2 says: But then the Spirit of God moved himself over the faces of the waters, by the Spirit of God is indicated the third person of the divinity, whom King David calls the Spirit of the divine mouth, Ps. XXXIII, 6. By the motion of the Spirit of God we understand his most eminent motion to create light, since in verse 2 the latter hemistich in the Hebrew codex coheres most tightly with the infrequent verse 3, so that here emerges the sense: And in this his Spirit, moving himself over the waters, God the Father said through his internal Word, the Son, this spoken (prophoric) saying: Let there be light. Conf. the annotations of D. SCHMID in Gen. p. 4. These things being premised, we argue: Whatever work is common to many divine persons, and is performed by God saying through his internal Word, in the Spirit of his mouth, from that work the trinity of the divine persons is made known. But the work of creation is common to many divine persons, and is performed &c. Therefore.

Latin:

Testimonia

V. T. quibus personarum diuinarum Trinitas coniunctim docetur, desumuntur a creatione mundi (a), eductione Israëlitarum ex Aegypto (b), prædicta missione & vnctione Messiæ (c), benedictione sacerdotum solemni (d), & trifagio angelico (e). Prob. a.

Ex Gen. I, 1. 2. 3. In principio creauit Elohim cœlum & terram. Terra nimirum facta est vasta & inanis, & tenebræ... fuerunt super faciem abyssi. Tum vero Spiritus Dei mouebat se super faciebus aquarum: & dixit Deus: fiat lux & facta lux.

Hunc locum esse inter præcipuos V. T. qui de mysterio SS. Trinitatis agunt, vel inde apparet, quia procul dubio phrasis Ps. XXXIII, 6. inde deducta est: Verbo Iehouae caeli facti sunt, & Spiritu oris eius omnis exercitus eorum. Quis vero etiam negauerit, Ioannem c. I, 1. 2. 3. huc respexisse hisce verbis: In principio erat Verbum, & Verbum erat... apud Deum, & Deus erat Verbum: hoc erat in principio apud Deum: omnia per ipsum facta sunt, & sine ipso factum est nihil, quod factum est.

Obs. 1) Descripturus Moses primum Dei opus inquit: Creauit ברא, quod nomen plurale non tantum terminatione, sed & significatione, cum verbo singulari ברא constructum, plurium commune opus, seu actionem significat, q. d. creauit, qui Deus sunt. Vid. annotat. D. SEB. SCHMID. in Gen. p. 2. 2) Deus creaturus lumen dixit: fiat lux. Deus dicens, est Deus Pater, vi contradistinctionis Verbi, per quod dixit, & Spiritus S. in quo se cum Verbo, per quod dicturus erat, super aquis inouit. 3) Dixit Deus Pater praecipiendo, iuxta Ps. XXXIII, 9. Ille dixit, & factum est: Ipse praecepit, & adstitit. Notat igitur dicere Dei verbum mandati, vt tamen 4) verbum ὑποστατικὸν, siue substantiale, connotet, aut praenotet. Id quod probamus a) ex infallibili interpretatione Ioannis c. I, 1. 2. 3. Ex quo loco ita concludimus: Illud verbum erat in principio creationis apud Deum Patrem, per quod omnia facta sunt. Atqui Verbum per se subsistens, quod verum Deus est, erat in principio creationis apud Deum Patrem. Ergo verbum, per se subsistens, est illud verbum, per quod omnia facta sunt. b) E testimonio Salomonis, qui sapientiae Dei (hypostaticae, aeterno Dei Filio, sapientiae omnis auctori atque scaturigini) eadem tribuit, quae hic Moses verbo Dei, Prou. VIII, 22. sqq. c) Ex ipsius rei consideratione. Sicut enim in homine verbum externum oris supponit verbum internum mentis, internamque sapientiam: ita verbum mandati diuini non fit sine verbo hypostatico, non sine sapientia substantiali, aeterno Dei Filio, cum Pater non operetur absque Filio, Io. V, 17. d) Quando Moses versu 2. inquit: Tum vero Spiritus Dei mouebat se super faciebus aquarum, per Spiritum Dei indigitatur tertia diuinitatis persona, quam rex Dauid vocat Spiritum oris diuini, Ps. XXXIII, 6. Per motum Spiritus Dei intelligimus ipsius motum eminentissimum ad creandum lucem, cum versu 2. hemistichium posterius in codice Hebraeo arctissime cum infrequenti versu 3. cohaereat, vt hic emergat sensus: Et in hoc Spiritu suo, se super aquis mouente, dixit Deus Pater per verbum suum internum, Filium, dictum hoc προφορικὸν: Fiat lux. Conf. annotat. D. SCHMID. in Gen. p. 4. Quibus praemissis argumentamur: Quodcunque opus commune est plurium personarum diuinarum, & perficitur a Deo dicente per Verbum suum internum, in Spiritu oris sui, ex illo opere innotescit personarum diuinarum trinitas. Atqui opus creationis est commune pluribus personis diuinis, & perficitur &c. Ergo.


### Q. XVIII. What are the testimonies of the O.t. by which the Trinity of divine persons is exhibited conjointly?: Socinians object: The Word of God in the work of creation denotes the divine command

Socinians object: The Word of God in the work of creation denotes the divine command.

2) The Spirit of God, who moved himself over the faces of the waters, designates air, or wind. 3) Neither the Word, nor the Spirit of God, are persons. Resp. to I. The word of divine command is not to be thought of here without the hypostatic Word; since without him nothing was made. Io. I, 3. To II. Neither air, nor wind, was there on the first day of creation; nor did God employ wind for the creation of light, or associate any creature. And why is it called the wind of God rather than the heaven of God, the earth of God &c. To III. Since creation, a most noble action, is ascribed to the Word and Spirit of God, personality cannot be denied to them; for they are actions of supposita.

Proof b. The leading out of the Israelites from Egypt testifies to the trinity of the divine persons. God the Father led the Israelites out of Egypt through an angel ἐδηγὸν, or leader, Exod. XIV, 19, whom the ancient Rabbis called מטטרון Metatron, that is, the guide or leader of the way. He is not a created angel, but uncreated, namely the Son of God. For he is called 1) expressly יהוה, which is the proper name of God, and incommunicable to creatures. Ex. XIV, 24. 2) He is called the angel of the face, who saves the people. Concerning this angel, God says: my name is in him, by which his glory, majesty, essence, or divine nature is denoted. 4) To this angel is attributed the judicial power of taking notice of the disobedient. Beware of his face, and hear his voice; and do not provoke him: for he will not endure your transgression. 5) Divine works are assigned to him, which are singular custody on the way, going before, and also the introduction of the Israelites into the land of Canaan, 6) Religious veneration, due only to God, is to be shown to this angel. Hear his voice, says Jehovah, such honor as is nowhere read to have been offered to any created angel. For which reason, by the angel who was the leader of the Israelite people, we understand the Son of God, who led the Israelites, and was tempted by them. To this is added that God the Father led his people out of Egypt through the Holy Spirit. For the Israelites are said in the desert to have rebelled and provoked the Spirit of the holiness of Jehovah. From these arises the argument: He who led the Israelites out of Egypt is the true, eternal, and supreme God. But God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, etc. Therefore. Prob. c.

We gather the Trinity of divine persons from the mission and anointing of the Messiah, concerning which those words, worthy of perennial memory, deserve to be noted in particular, Now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit. He who speaks here is not the prophet Isaiah, as the Jews and Photinians wish, but the Messiah: since Christ himself made the words immediately preceding: I have not spoken in secret from the beginning, his own. He who speaks here is called the first and the last the founder of the earth the redeemer Therefore, in this prophetic oracle are expressed the Lord sent, Christ the redeemer; the Lord sending, God the Father, to whom in the sacred scriptures the mission of the Son is attributed in many places; and the Spirit of the Lord, who anointed and sent Christ according to the flesh, The Spirit of Adonai Jehovah is upon me: Jehovah has anointed me, to evangelize the poor he has sent me. Conf. From the truth, therefore, we argue: Wherever God sent, God sending, and his Spirit are introduced, there three persons of the divinity are expressed. But in the prophetic oracle of Isaiah, etc. Therefore. Prob. d.

The mystery of the Trinity shines forth from the priestly blessing. Jehovah will bless you, and keep you: Jehovah will make his faces shine upon you and will have mercy on you: Jehovah will lift up his faces upon you, and will set peace for you. From this solemn blessing, the Trinity of divine persons is gathered: (1) Because the name Jehovah had to be recited not twice, not four times or more, but three times in this blessing. Which threefold repetition of the name Jehovah, since it is not without a mystery, nor can a solid reason for the same be brought from scripture if you depart from the mystery of the Holy Trinity, there is no doubt that the Trinity of divine persons was designated here: since no apex in such a succinct and vigorous blessing is made in vain. (2) Because twice three benefits are desired and vowed to the people of God. God the Father is invoked as the fountain of blessing, and the author of the custody of soul and body. That custody denotes divine preservation and protection; which benefits pertain to the first article of the apostolic faith. The Son of God is invoked as the light of the nations, and the throne of grace. calling us, illuminating, converting, regenerating, justifying, renewing, and endowing us with the internal peace of conscience. For the Holy Spirit is the paraclete, tranquilizing the conscience. To this priestly blessing we annex the royal blessing of David, Let God bless us: our God; let God bless us, that all the ends of the earth may fear him. The word God is repeated three times not in vain, but to notify God as one in essence, three in persons. We conclude: Whomever the prelates of the church invoke in the solemn blessing as the author of all corporal and spiritual benefits, which are prayed for by the sacred assembly, spiritual benefits, which are prayed for by the sacred assembly, pray, he is one and true God. But the leaders of the church invoke God as three in persons, etc. Therefore.

Prob. e. The angelic trisagion, or the Seraphic δοξολογία (doxology), which is read in Isaiah VI, 3, teaches us the Trinity of divine persons: Holy, holy, holy Jehovah, Zebaoth: the fullness of all the earth (is) his glory.

The Jews and Socinians object 1) That God deliberated with the angels about sending a messenger, when he said v. 8: Who will go for us? 2) That something is often called three times, even if in reality it is only one, not three. Thus hypocrites cry: This is the temple of the Lord, this is the temple of the Lord, this is the temple of the Lord. Jer. VII, 4. Compare Jer. XXII, 29. Ezek. XXI, 27. 3) That the triple repetition of the word "holy" is done either to demonstrate the perfection of divine holiness, or for the sake of the constancy of an asseveration. We respond to I. God, being all-wise, never deliberates with angels. Who is a counselor to God? Is. XL, 13: To II. We do not argue from the mere repetition of the word "holy," but we observe that God himself in chapter VI, 8 of Isaiah revealed the plurality of divine persons, and therefore when the Seraphim by crying out repeat three times: holy, holy, holy, Jehovah, Zebaoth, we assert that the determined Trinity of several divine persons is indicated. We have cited the previous guides or irrefragable witnesses of our assertion, John, ch. XII, 41, and Paul, Acts XXVIII, 25. To III. A triple repetition is an index of perfection, because a most perfect being is threefold. For the first in every genus is the measure of the rest. Furthermore, there was no reason why the Seraphim should go to confirm the holiness of God with constant asseveration, since there is no doubt about it. Constant asseveration is opposed to stirred-up doubts.

Latin:

Excipiunt Sociniani: Verbum Dei in opere creationis notare mandatum diuinum.

2) Spiritum Dei, qui se mouit super faciebus aquarum, designare aerem, aut ventum. 3) Nec verbum, nec Spiritum Dei, esse personas. Resp. ad I. Non cogitandum hic est verbum mandati diuini, sine verbo hypostatico; quippe sine quo nihil factum est. Io. I, 3. Ad II. Nec aer, nec ventus, primo creationis die erat; neque Deus ad creationem lucis adhibuit ventum, aut vllam adfciuit creaturam. Et cur ventus Dei potius dicitur, quam caelum Dei, terra Dei &c. Ad III. Cum creatio, actio nobilissima, adscribatur verbo & spiritui Dei, personalitas ipsis denegari nequit; sunt enim actiones suppositorum.

Prob. b. De personarum diuinarum trinitate testatur eductio Israëlitarum ex Aegypto. Eduxit Deus Pater Israëlitas ex Aegypto per angelum ἐδηγὸν, siue ductorem, Exod. XIV, 19. quem veteres Rabbini appellauerunt מטטרון Metatron, metatorem aut ducem viae. Ille non est angelus creatus, sed increatus, nempe Filius Dei. Dicitur enim 1) diserte יהוה, quod est nomen Dei proprium, & creaturis incommunicabile. Ex. XIV, 24. 2) Vocatur angelus faciei, qui saluat populum. De hoc angelo dicit Deus: nomen meum est in illo, quo gloria, maiestas, essentia seu natura diuina denotatur. 4) Tribuitur huic angelo potestas iudiciaria animaduertendi in inobedientes. Caueto tibi a faciebus eius, & audi vocem eius; nec exacerba eum: quia non sustinebit praeuaricationem vestram. 5) Assignantur ipsi opera diuina, quae sunt custodia singularis in via, praeessio, nec non introductio Israelitarum in terram Canaan, 6) Exhibenda est huic angelo religiosa, solique Deo debita veneratio. Audi vocem eius, inquit Iehouah, qualis honor nuspiam angelo vlli creato delatus legitur. Quam ob rem per angelum ductorem populi Israelitici intelligimus Filium Dei, qui duxit Israelitas, & ab iis tentatus fuit. His accedit, quod Deus pater duxerit populum suum ex Aegypto per Spiritum S. Nam dicuntur Israelitae in deserto rebellasse & exacerbasse Spiritum sanctitatis Iehouah. Ex his nascitur argumentum: Qui Israelitas eduxit ex Aegypto, ille est verus, aeternus & summus Deus. Atqui Deus Pater, Filius, & Spiritus S. &c. Ergo. Prob. c.

Trinitatem personarum diuinarum colligimus ex missione & vnctione Messiae, de qua notari in primis merentur verba illa, perenni memoria digna, Nunc Dominus misit me, & Spiritus eius. Qui hic loquitur, non est propheta Iesaias, vt volunt Iudaei & Photiniani, sed Messias: siquidem Christus ipse verba proxime praecedentia: ab initio non in occulto locutus sum, sua fecit. Qui hic loquitur, vocatur primus & nouissimus fundator terrae redemtor Exprimitur itaque in hoc oraculo prophetico Dominus missus, Christus redemtor; Dominus mittens, Deus Pater, cui in sacris litteris passim locorum missio Filii tribuitur; & Spiritus Domini, qui Christum secundum carnem vnxit & misit, Spiritus Adonai Iehouah super me: vnxit Iehouah me, ad euangelizandum pauperibus misit me. Conf. Ex vero igitur arguimus: Vbicunque introducuntur Deus missus, Deus mittens, & Spiritus eius, ibi exprimuntur tres diuinitatis personae. Atqui in oraculo prophetico Iesaiae &c. Ergo. Prob. d.

Illucescit mysterium Trinitatis ex benedictione sacerdotali. Benedicet tibi Iehouah, & custodiet te: illuminabit Iehouah facies suas super te & miserebitur tui: tollet Iehouah facies suas super te, & ponet tibi pacem. Colligitur ex hac solemni benedictione diuinarum personarum Trinitas: (1) Quia nomen Iehouah non bis, non quater aut pluries, sed ter in hac benedictione recitandum fuit. Quae trina nominis Iehouah repetitio, quum mysterio non careat, neque solida eiusdem ratio, si a mysterio S. S. Trinitatis abeas, e scriptura adduci queat, dubitandum non est, personarum diuinarum Trinitatem hic designatam fuisse: siquidem nullus apex in eiusmodi succincta & neruosa benedictione superuacaneus fit. (2) Quia bis tria beneficia exoptantur & populo Dei vouentur. Inuocatur Deus Pater, vt fons benedictionis, & auctor custodiae animae corporisque. Custodia illa notat conseruationem & protectionem diuinam; quae beneficia ad primum fidei apostolicae articulum pertinent. Inuocatur filius Dei, vt lux gentium, & thronus gratiae. nos vocans, illuminans, conuertens, regenerans, iustificans, renouans & interna pace conscientiae nos donans. Est enim Spiritus S. paracletus, conscientiam tranquillans. Cui benedictioni sacerdotali annectimus benedictionem regiam Dauidis, Benedicat nobis Deus: Deus noster; benedicat nobis Deus, vt timeant ipsum omnes fines terrae. Vox Deus ter repetitur non frustra, sed ad notificandum Deum essentia vnum, personis trinum. Colligimus: Quemcunque in solemni benedictione antistites ecclesiae inuocant, vt auctorem omnium corporalium & spiritualium beneficiorum, quae coetui sacro apprecantur, spiritualium beneficiorum, quæ cætui facro apprecantur, precantur, ille est unus & verus Deus. Atqui Deum in personis trinum antistites ecclesiæ invocant, &c. Ergo.

Prob. e. Trinitatem personarum divinarum nos docet trisagium angelicum, sive δοξολογία Seraphica, quæ legitur Es. VI, 3. Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus Iehouah, Zebaoth: plenitudo omnis terræ (est) gloria eius. Quem concelebrarunt Seraphiin, non est una persona, sed plures. Concinentibus enim Seraphim mox audiuit propheta vocem Adonai dicentis: Quem mittam, & quis iturus est nobis? Cui dixit propheta: Ecceme! mitte me. Loquitur Deus de seipso pluraliter, ad docendam pluralitatem personarum divinarum. Quod plures illæ personæ determinate tres sint, colligimus ex eo, quod chorus Seraphicus ter τὸ sanctus repetit; cuius trinæ repetitionis idonea causa nulla alia dari potest, quam determinata plurium personarum divinarum trinitas. Cui nostræ assertioni haud parum roboris accedit ex infallibili expositione N. T. siquidem præsens locus propheticus in nouo testamento de distinctis diuinitatis personis exponitur. Vidit enim Iesaias gloriam filii Dei, & de ipso locutus est teste S. Ioanne cap. XII, 41. Spiritus S. ibi locutus est per Iesaiam prophetam ad patres, teste Paulo Act. XXII, 25. Quibus præsuppositis argumentamur: In quocunque scripturæ loco Deus ipse pluralitatem personarum divinarum reuelauit, eodem loco, cum Deus ter sanctus a choro angelico nuncupatur, personarum divinarum Trinitas indigitatur hoc certius, quo clarius ille locus alibi in sacris litteris de distinctis diuinitatis personis exponitur. Atqui in præsenti loco vel capite Iesaiæ Deus ipse pluralitatem personarum divinarum reuelauit, eodemque loco Deus ter sanctus a choro angelico nuncupatur: Ergo in hoc loco, vel capite Iesaiæ, personarum divinarum Trinitas indigitatur hoc certius, quo clarius hic locus alibi in sacris litteris de distinctis diuinitatis personis exponitur.

Excipiunt Iudæi & Sociniani 1) Deum deliberasse cum angelis de mittendo nuntio, cum dixit v. 8. Quis ibit nobis? 2) Sæpe ter appellari rem aliquam, etsi reuera vna tantum sit, non trina. Sic clamant hypocritæ: Hic est templum domini, hic est templum domini, hic est templum domini. Ier. VII, 4. Confer. Ier. XXII, 29. Ezech. XXI, 27. 3) Trinam repetitionem τὸ sanctus vel ad perfectionem sanctitatis divinæ demonstrandam, vel ob asseuerationis constantiam fieri. Resp. ad I. Deus omnisapiens cum angelis nunquam deliberat. Quis Deo est a consiliis? Es. XL, 13: Ad II. Nos non ex nuda repetitione τὸ sanctus argumentamur, sed obseruamus, Deum ipsummet cap. VI, 8. Iesaiæ pluralitatem personarum divinarum reuelasse, adeoque cum Seraphim clamando ter repetunt: sanctus, sanctus, sanctus, Iehouah, Zebaoth, determinatam plurium personarum divinarum Trinitatem indigitari asserimus. Assertionis nostræ præuios duces, aut irrefragabiles testes citauimus, Ioannem, cap. XII, 41. & Paullum, Act. XXVIII, 25. Ad III. Trina repetitio perfectionis index est, eo quod ens perfectissimum trinum est. Primum enim in vnoquoque genere est mensura reliquorum. Ceterum nil causæ erat, cur Seraphim constanti asseueratione sanctitatem Dei confirmatum irent, cum de ea nullum sit dubium. Constans asseueratio motis dubiis opponitur.


### Q. XIX. By what arguments is the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit distinctly proved?

The arguments by which the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is solidly confirmed are sought from the divine names, attributes, actions, and religious worship owed to God alone.

…Obs. The general and invincible argument is: If the same names, attributes, works, and glory truly divine, which belong to God the Father, insofar as he is considered absolutely as true God, are attributed in the sacred letters to the Son of God and to the Holy Spirit, it is necessary that the Son of God and the Holy Spirit one with God the Father, to be the true and highest God, or as the church speaks, that in one divine essence there are three distinct persons, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The antecedent is true. Therefore also the consequent. That we may validly fortify the truth of the antecedent, we must treat distinctly in the present of the three persons of the divinity. (*).

OF GOD THE FATHER.

Ques. XX. Who is God the Father?

God the Father is the first person of the divinity, neither begotten, nor proceeding, but from eternity begetting the substantial Son, his image, and with the Son from eternity breathing forth the Holy Spirit.

He is described more fully.

God the Father is the first person of the divinity, neither begotten, nor proceeding, but from eternity begetting the substantial Son, his image, and with the Son from eternity breathing forth the Holy Spirit, creating, preserving, and governing all things, sending the Son the redeemer and the Holy Spirit the sanctifier of the human race.

Obs. In the former succinct and vigorous description, God the Father is described 1) by order, that he is the first person of the divinity; 2) by personal notion, that God the Father is ἀγέννητος, unoriginated, neither begotten, nor proceeding from another. 3) By personal acts, the eternal generation of the Son, and the eternal spiration of the Holy Spirit. In the active generation of the Son is founded paternity, the personal property of the Father. Through active spiration, the Father and the Son, although not between themselves, are nevertheless distinguished from the Holy Spirit. The latter, fuller definition annexes to the notion and personal property of God the Father his works ad extra, and benefits relative to the church. See D. CHEMNIT. loc. theol. fol. m. 44.

Ques. XXI. How is the name of Father taken here?

The name of Father is not taken here ὀσιωδῶς, or essentially, but ὑποσατικῶς or personally.

Proof. The name of Father, taken essentially, does not belong to the first person of the divinity alone, but to all divine persons equally; since, taken in this sense, it carries a respect to creatures, of whom God is called Father both on account of creation; as angels are called sons of God, Job XXXVIII, 7. and on account of regeneration and adoption; as men converted and reborn by the merit of Christ, apprehended by faith, have obtained this ἐξυσίαν, power, or dignity, that they might become sons of God, John I, 12. But taken personally, the name of Father is proper of the first divine person, and implies a relation to the consubstantial Son, whom He begat from His own essence as the image of Himself, of whom He is declared to be ἴδιος πατήρ, His own proper Father. John 5:18.

Latin:

Argumenta, quibus distincte diuinitas Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. solide confirmatur, petuntur a diuinis nominibus, attributis, actionibus, & cultu religioso soli Deo debito.

Obs. Argumentum generale idque inuictum est: Si eadem nomina, attributa, opera, & gloria vere diuina, qua Deo Patri, quatenus absolute vt verus Deus consideratur, competunt, in sacris litteris Filio Dei & Spiritui S. attribuuntur, necesse est, Filium Dei & Spiritum sanctum ctum cum Deo Patre vnum, verum & fummum Deum esse, siue vt ecclesia loquitur, in vna essentia diuina tres esse distinctas personas, Patrem, Filium & Spiritum sanctum. Antecedens est verum. Ergo & consequens. Vt antecedentis veritatem valide muniamus, de tribus diuinitatis personis distincte in præsenti nobis agendum est. (*).

DE DEO PATRE.

Quæst. XX. Quis est Deus Pater?

Deus Pater est prima diuinitatis persona, nec genita, nec procedens, sed ab æterno gignens Filium substantialem, sui imaginem, & cum Filio ab æterno spirans Spiritum sanctum.

Vberius describitur.

Deus Pater est prima diuinitatis persona, nec genita, nec procedens, sed ab æterno gignens Filium substantialem, sui imaginem, & cum Filio ab æterno spirans Spiritum S. creans, conseruans & gubernans omnia, mittens Filium redemtorem & Spiritum S. sanctificatorem generis humani.

Obs. Priori descriptione succincta & neruosa Deus Pater describitur 1) ab ordine, quod sit prima diuinitatis persona; 2) a notione personali, quod Deus Pater sit ἀγέννητος inoriginatus, nec genitus, nec procedens ab alio. 3) Ab actibus personalibus, æterna generatione Filii, & æterna spiratione Spiritus S. In generatione actiua Filii fundatur paternitas, proprietas Patris personalis. Per spirationem actiuam Pater & Filius, licet non inter se, a Spiritu S. tamen distinguuntur. Posterior definitio vberior notioni & proprietati Dei Patris personali annectit ipsius opera ad extra, & beneficia relatiue ad ecclesiam. Vid. D. CHEMNIT. loc. theol. fol. m. 44.

Quæst. XXI. Quomodo nomen Patris hic accipitur?

Nomen Patris hic non accipitur ὀσιωδῶς, seu essentialiter, sed ὑποσατικῶς seu personaliter.

Prob. Nomen Patris, essentialiter sumtum, non soli primæ personæ diuinitatis, sed omnibus personis diuinis ex æquo conuenit; siquidem hoc sensu acceptum, respectum infert ad creaturas, quarum Deus Pater dicitur tum ob creationem; quomodo angeli audiunt Filii Dei, Iob. XXXVIII, 7. tum ob regenerationem & adoptionem; quomodo homines conversi & renati ex merito Christi, fide apprehenso, hanc ἐξυσίαν, potestatem, vel dignitatem nacti sunt, vt fiant Filii Dei, Io. I, 12. At personaliter acceptum nomen Patris proprium est primæ personæ divinæ, & infert respectum ad Filium consubstantialem, quem ex essentia sua genuit imaginem sui, cuius ἴδιος πατήρ, proprius Pater, perhibetur. Io. V, 18.


### Q. XXII. Why is God the Father called the first person of the Godhead?

God the Father is called the first person of the Godhead not by reason of the divine essence, nor with respect to time, nor on account of a prerogative of dignity; but by reason of origin and order.

Proof: God the Father is termed the first person of the Godhead not by reason of the essence of the nature; for the Son and the Holy Spirit have the same essence that the Father has: nor by reason of time; since the three divine persons are coeternal: nor by reason of dignity; because in the Trinity there is nothing greater or lesser, as Athanasius teaches in his creed; but by reason of origin and order.

By reason of origin, God the Father is the first divine person; because He is unoriginated, neither begotten, nor proceeding from another. The Son and the Holy Spirit originate from God the Father, and the Son indeed as the second person from the Father alone, but the Holy Spirit as the third person from the Father and the Son together. Whence God the Father is called by Athanasius against Sabellius ῥίζα καὶ πηγὴ τοῦ υἱοῦ καὶ τοῦ πνεύματος, the root and fountain of the Son and of the Spirit, as cited by DANHAV. in hodof. phæn. III. p. 230. God the Father is also the first person of the Godhead by reason of order, or natural enumeration, founded in origin, or the emanation of one person from another, and observed in the solemn formula of baptism, Matt. 28:19, and repeated by John, 1 Epist. ch. 5:7.

Latin:

Deus Pater dicitur prima persona deitatis non ratione essentiæ divinæ, neque respectu temporis, neque ob dignitatis prærogativam; sed ratione originis & ordinis.

Prob. Deus Pater nuncupatur prima persona divinitatis non ratione essentiæ naturæ; qui eandem essentiam habet Filius & Spiritus S. quam habet Pater: neque ratione temporis; quoniam tres personæ divinæ sunt coæternæ: neque ratione dignitatis; quia in Trinitate nihil maius aut minus est, docente Athanasio in symbolo suo; sed ratione originis & ordinis.

Ratione originis Deus Pater est prima persona divina; quia est inoriginatus, nec genitus, nec procedens ab alio. Filius & Spiritus S. a Deo Patre oriuntur, & Filius quidem ut secunda persona a Patre solum, Spiritus S. vero ut tertia persona a Patre simul & a Filio. Ex quo Deus Pater ab Athanasio contra Sabell. appellatur ῥίζα καὶ πηγὴ τοῦ υἱοῦ καὶ τοῦ πνεύματος, radix & fons Filii & Spiritus, citante DANHAV. in hodof. phæn. III. p. 230. Est etiam Deus Pater prima divinitatis persona ratione ordinis, seu naturalis enumerationis, fundatæ in origine, seu emanatione vnius personæ ab alia, & obseruatæ in solemni formula baptismi, Matth, XXVIII, 19. atque repetitæ a Ioanne, 1 epist. c. V, 7.


### Q. XXIII. By what arguments is the divinity of God the Father proved?

The divinity of the eternal Father is demonstrated by (1) Divine names: (2) Attributes proper to the true God alone: (3) Works truly and merely divine, both ad intra and ad extra: (4) Religious worship competent to God alone.

Obs. The demonstration of the divinity of the heavenly Father can be deduced most fully from innumerable sayings of Holy Scripture: But since no one who receives the sacred writings as infallible doubts the same, we shall supersede a more prolix demonstration, and shall adduce only one apostolic saying, embracing the four already mentioned classes of arguments, from 1 Pet. 1:3. "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to His abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a living hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead." This apostolic oracle exhibits to us (1) an ὀνομασικόν [nominal] argument, taken from divine names. For God the Father is expressly called God by the apostle Peter, and is called the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who can be none other than the supreme God. (2) This apostolic statement contains an ἰδιωματικόν [idiomatic] argument, taken from a divine attribute. Abundant mercy is attributed to God the Father, which is a property of the true God. (3) It embraces an ἐνεργητικόν [active] argument, drawn from a divine action. For God the Father is said to regenerate us. Regeneration is a divine action. (4) This classic saying comprises a λατρευτικόν [cultual] argument, taken from religious worship. For the apostle says: Blessed be God the Father! God the Father is worshipped and celebrated by the apostle as the fountain and source of all blessing, regeneration, and eternal inheritance. Therefore God the Father is the true and supreme God. But this scope of proving might perhaps seem superfluous here. For if God the Father is not God, there will be no God in the world, since He is the fountain of divinity. Q. XXIV. Whence is the distinct personality of God the Father known? That God the Father is a person distinct from the Son of God and the Holy Spirit is evident from the denomination and personal property (a); from the personal acts ad intra, and their manifestation (b); from the action ad extra, appropriate to God the Father (c).

Prob. a. God the Father is named the proper Father of the Son (John 5:8), and thus on account of the properly so-called paternity founded in the true and essential generation.

But the Father, generating the Son from his own substance, is a person distinct from him. Prob. b. Just as God the Father is personally distinguished from the Son by active generation, so is he distinguished from the Holy Spirit by active spiration. Which personal distinction is also made manifest by the mission of the Son for the work of redemption, and the mission of the Holy Spirit for the work of sanctification.

For the sender and the sent differ as distinct persons. Prob. c. Since God the Father created this universe through his Son, as substantial wisdom (Prov. 8:30) and the hypostatic Word (John 1:3), by the Spirit of his mouth (Ps. 33:6), it is gathered that he is a true person, and one distinct from the Son and the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

Divinitatem æterni Patris demonstrant (1) Nomina divina: (2) Attributa soli vero Deo propria: (3) Opera vere & mere divina, cum ad intra, tum ad extra: (4) Cultus religiosus soli Deo competens.

Obs. Potest demonstratio divinitatis Patris cœlestis ex innumeris S. scripturæ dictis fusissime deduci: At cum de eadem nemo, qui sacras litteras vt infallibiles recipit, dubitet, prolixiori demonstratione supersedebimus, & vnum tantum dictum apostolicum, complectens quatuor iam memoratas argumentorum classes, adducemus ex 1 Petr. I, 3. Benedictus Deus & Pater domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui iuxta multam suam misericordiam regenerauit nos in spem viuam per resurrectionem Iesu Christi ex mortuis. Exhibet nobis hoc oraculum apostolicum (1) argumentum ὀνομασικόν, petitum a nominibus divinis. Nam Deus Pater ab apostolo Petro diserte dicitur Deus, dicitur Pater domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui non nisi summus Deus esse potest. (2) Continet hoc effatum apostolicum argumentum ἰδιωματικόν, sumtum ab attributo divino. Attribuitur Deo Patri multa misericordia, quæ est proprietas veri Dei. (3) Complectitur argumentum ἐνεργητικόν, depromtum ab actione divina. Deus enim Pater dicitur nos regenerare. Regeneratio est actio divina. (4) Comprehendit hoc dictum classicum argumentum λατρευτικόν, sumtum a cultu religioso. Dicit enim apostolus: Benedictus fit Deus Pater! Colitur & celebratur Deus Pater ab apostolo, vt fons & scaturigo omnis benedictionis, regenerationis & æternæ hæreditatis. Ergo Deus Pater est verus & summus Deus. Sed hic probandi ambitus superuacaneus forte videri queat. Nam si Deus Pater non est Deus, nullus erit Deus in mundo, cum fit fons divinitatis. Quæst. XXIV. Vnde distincta Dei Patris personalitas innotescit? Deum patrem distinctam a Filio Dei & Spiritu S. personam esse, constat ex denominatione atque proprietate personali (a); ex actibus ad intra personalibus, eorumque manifestatione (b); ex actione ad extra, Deo Patri appropriata (c).

Prob. a. Deus Pater nominatur proprius Filii Pater Io. V, 8. adeoque ob proprie dictam paternitatem in vera & essentiali generatione fundatam.

Sed Pater, de substantia sua generans Filium, ab hoc distincta persona est. Prob. b. Sicut Deus Pater per activam generationem a Filio: ita per spirationem activam a Spiritu S. personaliter distinguitur. Quae distinctio personalis ex missione Filii ad redemptionis, & missione Spiritus S. ad opus sanctificationis, etiam patescit.

Mittens enim & missus differunt ut distinctae personae. Prob. c. Cum Deus Pater hoc universum per Filium suum, tanquam sapientiam substantialem, Prou. VIII, 30. & verbum hypostaticum, Io. I, 3. in Spiritu oris sui, Ps. XXXIII, 6. condiderit, eundem esse personam veram, eamque distinctam a Filio & Spiritu S., colligitur.


### Q. XXV. What is the personal property of God the Father?

The hypostatic character, or personal property, of God the Father is paternity, founded in the active generation of the only-begotten Son. Prob. By paternity, God the Father is not only distinguished from the remaining divine persons, but is also constituted in the being of the Father.

Therefore, paternity is the hypostatic character of the Father. Obj. Since the proximate foundation of paternity is the active generation of the Son, on account of which God the Father is properly called Father, by some theologians the hypostatic character of the Father is held to be active generation, especially for the reason that this does not differ in reality from paternity.

Dannhav. Hodof. Phaen. III, p. 186).

Latin:

Character hypostaticus, sive proprietas personalis Dei Patris est paternitas, fundata in generatione activa Filii unigeniti. Prob. Paternitate Deus Pater non tantum a reliquis personis divinis distinguitur, sed etiam in esse Patris constituitur.

Ergo paternitas est character hypostaticus Patris. Obs. Cum paternitatis fundamentum proximum sit generatio activa Filii, propter quam Deus Pater proprie Pater dicitur, a nonnullis theologis character hypostaticus Patris perhibetur esse generatio activa, vel maxime ideo, quod haec a paternitate reapse non differt.

Con. DANNHAV. hodof. phæn. III. p. 186.


### Q. XXVI. What are the notions of God the Father?

The personal notions of God the Father are ἀγεννησία (unbegottenness), and the active spiration of the Holy Spirit . Prob. a. A personal notion, strictly so-called, insofar as it is distinguished from the hypostatic character, notifies a person and distinguishes him from another person, but does not constitute him in the being of such a person. Yet ἀγεννησία does not formally constitute the Father in the being of the Father; for he is called Father on account of the eternal generation of the Son, whom he regards as his correlate. ἀγεννησία, however, does not of itself imply such a relation, and thus it is not a characteristic property, but only a notional one, merely notifying.

For since ἀγεννησία, as is usually done, is explained in such a way that it denotes the negation of all origin, God the Father is called ἀγέννητος, i.e., inoriginate, because he has his origin from no one, neither by generation nor by spiration. But the Holy Spirit is sometimes called ἀγέννητος, because he derives his origin from the Father and the Son, not by generation, but by spiration. In the same sense, God the Father is properly said to be from himself, because he is from no one else; likewise αὐτόθεος (God of himself), not that the Father alone is from himself, or possesses αὐτοσίαν (self-existence), i.e., an independent and uncreated essence, alone; but that he alone is God from himself, and does not have from another the αὐτοσίαν, the independent essence by which Jehovah is, as the Son and the Holy Spirit do. (Conf. Conf. D. CALOV. in System. Theol. Tom. III, p. 192.

The active spiration of the Holy Spirit is called an act and a personal notion according to the different way of considering it. It is called a personal act because through it the Holy Spirit is produced. It is called a personal notion because through it God the Father is known as a person distinct from the Holy Spirit. Yet it is not a personal property of God the Father, since it is common to the Father and the Son; nor does God the Father become Father on account of the spiration of the Holy Spirit, but on account of the generation of the Son.

Latin:

Notiones personales Dei Patris sunt ἀγεννησία (a), & spiratio activa Spiritus S. (b). Prob. a. Notio personalis, stricte dicta, quatenus characteri hypostatico contradistinguitur, notificat personam, eamque ab alia persona distinguit, sed non in esse talis personae constituit. Atqui ἀγεννησία non formaliter constituit Patrem in esse Patris; quippe qui Pater dicitur propter aeternam generationem Filii, quem ceu correlatum suum respicit. ἀγεννησία autem per se non infert eiusmodi relationem, adeoque non est proprietas χαρακτηριστική, sed tantum notio γνωριστική, mere notificans.

Cum enim ἀγεννησία, ut plerumque fieri assolet, sic exponitur, ut denotet negationem omnis originis, Deus Pater vocatur ἀγέννητος, i. e. inoriginatus, eo quod neque per generationem, neque per spirationem, originem ab alio habet. Spiritus S. autem quandoque dominatur ἀγέννητος, quia non per generationem, sed per spirationem, originem a Patre & Filio ducit. Probe eodem sensu dicitur Deus Pater esse a seipso, quia est a nullo alio; item αὐτόθεος, non quod solus Pater sit a seipso, vel αὐτοσίαν, i. e. essentiam independentem & increatam solus obtineat; sed quod solus sit a seipso Deus, ac αὐτοσίαν essentiam independentem, per quam Iehouah est, non habet ab alio, ut Filius & Spiritus S. Conf. D. CALOV. in system. theol. tom. III. p. 192.

Prob. b. Spiratio activa Spiritus S. pro diverso considerandi modo, actus, & notio personalis vocatur. Actus personalis dicitur, quia per eam Spiritus S. producitur. Notio personalis appellatur, quoniam per eandem Deus Pater, vt distincta a Spiritu S. persona cognoscitur. Neque tamen proprietas Dei Patris personalis est; cum communis sit Patri & Filio; neque Deus Pater ob spirationem Spiritus S. sed ob generationem Filii Pater fit.


### Q. XXVII. What are the personal acts of God the Father?

The personal acts of God the Father are the generation of the Son, and the active spiration of the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

Actus personales Dei Patris sunt generatio Filii, & spiratio Spiritus S. activa.


### Q. XXVIII. What is the active generation of God the Father?

The active generation of God the Father is a personal act ad intra, by which God the Father, by the communication of one and the same essence in number, [generates] the Son, the image of himself, from eternity truly and properly; yet in a hyperphysical and unsearchable manner, he begets. Obs. This hyperphysical generation will be proved below, where the passive generation of the Word (τῦ λόγυ) will come to be considered.

Latin:

Generatio Dei Patris activa est actus divinus ad intra personalis, quo Deus Pater unius eiusdemque numero essentiae communicatione Filium, imaginem sui ab æterno vere proprieque; modo tamen hyperphysico ac impervestigabili, gignit. Obs. Hyperphysica hæc generatio probabitur infra, vbi generatio τῦ λόγυ passiva consideranda veniet.


### Q. XXIX. What is active spiration?

Active spiration is an internal personal divine act, by which God the eternal Father, with the eternal Son, by the communication of one and the same essence in number, produces the Holy Spirit, the common breath of both, in one indivisible and eternal act, in a hyperphysical and ineffable manner.

Latin:

Spiratio activa est actus divinus ad intra personalis, quo Deus Pater æternus cum Filio æterno, vnius eiusdemque numero essentiæ communicatione, Spiritum sanctum, commune vtriusque spiraculum, vno actu indivisibili & æterno, modo hyperphysico & ineffabili, producit.


### Q. XXX. What is the consequence of generation and active spiration, by which it is manifested?

Active mission follows active generation and spiration, by which God the Father sent the Son the redeemer, and together with the Son, the Holy Spirit the sanctifier of the human race in time .

Prob. a. John 3:17. God sent his Son into the world, not that he might judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him. By which words the scope of the mission of the Son of God is designated negatively; not that he might judge, i.e., condemn the world positively, that the world might be saved through him, that is, that it might be advanced through means divinely ordained from darkness to light, from sin to justice, from death to life.

Prob. b. John 15:26. When the paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness of me. God the Father and the Son send the Holy Spirit; because he proceeds from him.

The temporal mission is a mark and argument a posteriori of the eternal procession.

The Father sends the Holy Spirit in the name of Christ, i.e., on account of the merit and intercession of the Savior, John 14:26. God the Son sends the Holy Spirit from the Father; since as he has essence, so he has power from the Father, that he may send the Holy Spirit.

Obs. This active mission is not local or separative, since local separation is repugnant to the intimate identity and infinite presence of the divine persons; but it is illocal and manifestative: nor is it illative of inequality, because it happens through voluntary consent, not through command.

Latin:

Actiuam generationem & spirationem consequitur missio activa, qua Deus Pater Filium redemtorem, & vna cum Filio Spiritum S. sanctificatorem generis humani in tempore misit .

Prob. a. Io. III, 17. Misit Deus Filium suum in mundum, non, vt iudicet mundum, sed vt saluetur mundus per ipsum. Quibus verbis scopus missionis Filii Dei designatur remotiue; non vt iudicet i. e. condemnet mundum positiue, vt mundus per ipsum saluetur, hoc est, per media diuinitus ordinata a tenebris ad lucem, a peccato ad iustitiam, a morte ad vitam prouehatur.

Prob. b. Io. XV, 26. Quando venerit paracletus, quem ego missurus sum vobis a Patre, Spiritus veritatis, qui a Patre procedit, ille testabitur de me. Spiritum S. mittunt Deus Pater & Filius; quia ab illo procedit.

Missio temporalis est nota & argumentum a posteriori processionis æternæ.

Mittit Pater Spiritum S. in nomine Christi i. e. ob meritum & intercessionem saluatoris, Io. XIV, 26. Filius Deus mittit Spiritum S. a Patre; quoniam vt essentiam, ita potentiam a Patre habet, vt Spiritum S. mittat. Obs.

Missio hæc activa non est localis aut separatiua, cum separatio localis intimæ personarum diuinæ identitati & infinitæ præsentiæ repugnet; sed illocalis & manifestatiua: neque est illatiua inæqualitatis, quia fit per voluntarium consensum, non per imperium.


### Q. XXXI. What divine action ad extra is peculiarly vindicated to God the Father?

In the sacred scriptures, and in the apostolic symbol, creation, which is the first divine operation ad extra, is ascribed to God the Father, as the first person of the divinity, through a certain singular appropriation.

Prob. God the Father created this universe by speaking through the substantial Word in the Spirit of his mouth, Gen. 1:1. Ps. 33:6. John 1:3. Therefore, the work of creation is vindicated to God the Father not exclusively, as if the Son of God and the Holy Spirit were entirely excluded from that first action: nor in an excellent manner (ἐξοχικῶς), as if God the Father were the principal cause, but the Son the instrument of creation: because the unity of essence, which is the principle of operations ad extra, is repugnant to this; but God the Father is said to have created through the Son in the Holy Spirit appropriatively and relatively, to designate the order of the divine persons, saving the unity of action and of the power of acting.

The same judgment is to be formed concerning conservation, which is continuous creation, and the government of this universe.

Latin:

In sacris litteris, & symbolo apostolico, Deo Patri, vt primæ diuinitatis personæ, creatio, quæ est prima operatio diuina ad extra, per singularem quandam appropriationem adscribitur.

Prob. Hoc vniuersum Deus Pater dicendo per Verbum substantiale in Spiritu oris sui creauit, Gen. I, 1. Ps. XXXIII, 6. Io. I, 3. Vindicatur itaque opus creationis Deo Patri non exclusive, quasi Filius Dei & Spiritus S. a prima ista actione penitus fuerint exclusi: neque ἐξοχικῶς modo excellentiori, vt Deus Pater causa principalis, Filius autem instrumentum fit creationis: quia repugnat vnitas essentiæ, quæ principium est operationum ad extra; sed appropriatiue & relatiue Deus Pater per Filium in Spiritu Sancto creasse dicitur, ad designandum personarum diuinarum ordinem, salua actionis & virtutis agendi vnitate.

Idem formetur iudicium de conseruatione, quæ est continua creatio, & gubernatio huius vniuersi.


### Of God the Son

XXXII. Who is the Son of God?

The Son of God is the second person of the divinity, begotten from the essence of the Father from eternity, who with God the Father breathes forth the Holy Spirit from eternity. He is described more fully. The Son of God is the second person of the divinity, begotten from eternity by the Father, of the same essence and majesty as the Father; who with the Father breathes forth the Holy Spirit from eternity and in the fullness of time assumed a human nature into His own hypostasis, that He might redeem and save the human race. Obs.

By the former description, brief indeed but vigorous, the Son of God is described (1) by order, in that He is the second person of the divinity; because He is not from Himself, but from the Father. (2) By origin, which He derives from the Father through eternal generation, in which, viewed passively or terminatively, is founded the filiation, the hypostatic character of the Son of God. (3) By personal notion, namely the active breathing forth of the Holy Spirit, so that the Son of God may be distinguished not only from the Father, but also from the Holy Spirit; since He Himself breathes Him forth with the Father. The latter description, somewhat more prolix, adds to the former (a) the incarnation of the Son of God, by which He manifested Himself externally. God was manifested in the flesh, says Paul, 1 Tim. III, 16. Mention of this is made here, for the reason that the human nature now pertains to the integrity of the person of the Son of God, after He assumed the same into the unity of His person. (b) The external operation, which is appropriated to the Son of God, and is the redemption of the human race, the end of which is the eternal salvation of men. Q. XXXIII. How is the name Son of God taken here? The name Son of God is not taken here improperly, but properly, so as to designate a son begotten from the substance of the father. Prob.

Angels are called sons of God improperly (1) on account of a certain likeness of divine wisdom and holiness which shines forth in them, Job XXXVIII, 7. From which God embraces them, as sons, with singular love. (2) Magistrates, on account of an analogy or a certain convenience with God, by reason of office, Ps. LXXXII, 6. (3) The faithful, on account of spiritual regeneration, Jo. I, 13, and adoption to the inheritance of eternal life, Rom. VIII, 16, Gal. IV, 5. (4) The blessed, on account of the glorious fruition of adoption, Luc. XX, 36. But the second person of the H. Trinity is called the Son of God on account of a true, proper, and essential generation, by which the very essence, which is that of the begetting Father, is perfectly communicated to the begotten Son, so that the Son becomes consubstantial with God the Father. Hence He is called the Son of God's own, Rom. VIII, 32, and the only-begotten, Jo. I, 14, existing in the bosom of the Father, Jo. I, 18, the image of the invisible God and the firstborn of every creature, Col. I, 15, the brightness of glory and the express image of the person of the Father, Hebr. I, 3. Q. XXXIV. By what arguments is the true and eternal divinity of the Son of God proved? The true and eternal divinity of the Son of God is confirmed by arguments ὀνοματικοῖς (nominal), drawn from divine names (a); ἰδιωματικοῖς (idiomatic), drawn from attributes proper to the true God alone (b); ἐνεργητικοῖς (energetic), taken from the personal and essential acts of God (a); λατρευτικοῖς (latreutic), sought from the acts of God that are personal and essential (a); λατρευτικοῖς, de-

[and] from the religious worship owed to God alone (d). To which add an accurate collation of the Old and New Testaments (e).

Proof a. There are very many places in Holy Scripture in which the Son of God is distinguished by divine names, both essential and personal, from which we shall select a few, and those the clearer ones. Thus, the divinity of the Son of God is shown

Latin:

XXXII. Quis est Filius Dei?

Filius Dei est secunda divinitatis persona, ex essentia Patris ab aeterno genita, quae cum Deo Patre ab aeterno spirat Spiritum sanctum. Uberius describitur. Filius Dei est secunda divinitatis persona, ab aeterno a Patre genita, eiusdem cum Patre essentiae & maiestatis; quae cum Patre ab aeterno spirat Spiritum S. & in plenitudine temporis humanam naturam in propriam hypostasin assumsit, vt humanum genus redimeret & saluaret. Obs.

Priori descriptione brevi quidem, sed nervosa, describitur Filius Dei (1) ab ordine, quod fit secunda persona divinitatis; quia non est a seipso, sed a Patre. (2) Ab origine, quam ducit a patre per aeternam generationem, in qua, passive seu terminative spectata, fundatur filiatio, character hypostaticus Filii Dei. (3) A notione personali, nempe activa spiratione Spiritus S. vt distinguatur Filius Dei non a Patre solum, sed etiam a Spiritu sancto; quippe quem ipse cum Patre spirat. Posterior descriptio, aliquanto prolixior, priori addit (a) incarnationem Filii Dei, qua se externe manifestavit. Deus manifestatus est in carne, inquit Paullus 1 Tim. III, 16. Cuius mentio hic fit, ideo quod humana natura iam ad integritatem personae Filii Dei spectat, postquam is eandem in suae personae unitatem assumsit. (b) Operationem externam, quae Filio Dei appropriatur, estque redemtio generis humani, cuius finis est aeterna hominum salus. Quaest. XXXIII. Quomodo nomen Filii Dei hic accipitur? Nomen Filii Dei hic non sumitur improprie, sed proprie, vt designet filium de substantia patris genitum. Prob.

Improprie Filii Dei dicuntur (1) angeli, ob similitudinem quandam sapientiae & sanctitatis divinae, quae in iisdem relucet, Iob. XXXVIII, 7. Ex quo ipsos, vt filios, Deus singulari amore complectitur. (2) Magistratus, ob analogiam aut convenientiam quandam cum Deo, ratione officii, Ps. LXXXII, 6. (3) Fideles, ob spiritualem regenerationem, Io. I, 13. & adoptionem ad hereditatem vitae aeternae, Rom. VIII, 16. Gal. IV, 5. (4) Beati, ob gloriosam adoptionis fruitionem, Luc. XX, 36. At secunda SS. Trinitatis persona vocatur Filius Dei ob veram, propriamque, ac essentialem generationem, qua ipsa essentia, quae est Patris generantis, Filio genito perfecte est communicata, vt fit Filius Deo Patri consubstantialis. Exinde Filius Dei proprius Rom. VIII, 32. & unigenitus, Io. I, 14. existens in sinu Patris, Io. I, 18. imago Dei invisibilis & primogenitus omnis creaturae, Col. I, 15. splendor gloriae & character personae patris, Hebr. I, 3. appellatur. Quaest. XXXIV. Quibus argumentis vera & aeterna divinitas Filii Dei probatur? Vera & aeterna divinitas Filii Dei firmatur argumentis ὀνοματικοῖς, depromtis a nominibus divinis (a); ἰδιωματικοῖς, haustis ex attributis soli vero Deo propriis (b); ἐνεργητικοῖς, sumtis ab actibus Dei personalibus & essentialibus (a); λατρευτικοῖς, petitis fumtis ab actibus Dei personalibus & essentialibus (a); λατρευτικοῖς, pe-

titis a cultu religiofo foli Deo debito (d). Quibus adde accuratam V. & N. T. collationem (e).

Prob. a. Plurima funt S. fcripturæ loca, in quibus Filius Dei nominibus diuinis, tam effentialibus, quam perfonalibus infignitur, e quibus nos pauca, eaque clariora, feligemus. Oftenditur itaque diuinitas Filii Dei


### Of God the Son: I. From essential divine names

I. From essential divine names.

In the Old Testament, Christ, the branch of David, is called Jehovah, our righteousness, Jer. XXIII, 6. He is called Jehovah, whom Jehovah anointed, upon whom is the Spirit of the Lord, Is. LXI, 1. 8. He is called Adonai, sitting upon a throne high and lifted up, religiously honored by the Seraphim, Is. VI, 1. 2. 3. cf. with John XII, 41. No creature is called Jehovah and Adonai. In the New Testament, the Son of God (1) is called God absolutely, without any limiting or alienating condition. The Word was God, says John, ch. I, 1. Whom Thomas, about to issue a sincere confession, addresses with great confidence: My Lord, and my God, John XX, 28. Which words were directed not to God the Father, but to the Lord Jesus. For Thomas answered and said to him (Jesus, who, having shown the scars of his hands and side, had said: be not faithless, but believing): My Lord, and my God. Nor are these words merely of one exclaiming or admiring, but of Thomas confessing; for Christ immediately adds: Because you have seen me, you have believed. (2) To the divine names are added words by which the incarnate Son of God is designated. Thus Paul, Acts XX, 28, says: God purchased the church with his own blood. Where by God, who purchased the church with his own blood, none other than the Son of God is understood. The same apostle says 1 Tim. III, 16: God was manifested in the flesh, [meaning] the Son of God; inasmuch as he who was made flesh, John I, 14, was made a partaker of flesh and blood, Heb. II, 14, and came in the flesh, 1 John IV, 2. 3. (3) To the divine names are annexed epithets by which the supreme God is indicated. For (a) Christ is named by St. John the true God and eternal life, 1 John V, 20-22. And we know that the Son of God has come, and has given us an understanding, that we may know the true one: And we are in the true one, in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life. Where (α) the position of the words (because the demonstrative pronoun οὗτος, "this," ordinarily refers to and demonstrates the immediately preceding noun), (β) the scope of the apostle, dealing with Christ as the principal theme of this epistle, see 1 John I, 2, (γ) the absurdity of a tautology (if it be referred to the Father), (δ) the epithet of eternal life, so proper to Christ that you would not easily read it attributed to any other person, all cry out that the truth of the deity is asserted of Christ. Cf. DANNH. hodof. phæn. III. p. 233. (b) By St. Paul the Son of God is called the great God, Tit. II, 13. Looking for the blessed hope, and the appearing of the glory of the great God. Concerning this apostolic statement we observe: (α) The name of the great God is claimed for the one and only supreme God. Which the prophet Daniel teaches, ch. II, 45: The great God has made known to the king what shall come to pass hereafter. (β) By the words, τοῦ μεγάλου θεοῦ καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, one and the same subject is designated, namely Jesus Christ: since only one Greek article is employed, which denotes nothing but one subject, according to the property of the Greek language; just as the apostle treats of that God whose ἐπιφάνεια, appearing for judgment, is expected: which appearing for judgment is attributed only to the Son of God, 2 Thess. II, 8. 1 Tim. VI, 14. 2 Tim. IV, 1. Nor does the interposed conjunction καὶ, "and," stand in the way; since it often couples two nouns to one subject. Cf. 1 Pet. I, 3. (c) By the same apostle Christ is called God over all blessed for ever, Rom. IX, 5. Whose are the fathers, and of whom is Christ, according to the flesh, who is over all God blessed for ever, Amen! From these it is clear that Christ is the supreme God; since those words of the apostle express a periphrasis of the supreme God. Cf. Rom. I, 25. The Socinians, wishing to evade this illustrious statement, object (1): the words those words, ὁ ὢν ἐπὶ πάντων θεὸς, are not to be referred to Christ, but are a doxological exclamation, by which God the Father is celebrated: And therefore after the words, κατὰ σάρκα, a period should be written, which is accustomed to be omitted by many scribes. (2) Ἐπὶ πάντων, signifies, over all, namely men, not over all things. Resp.

To 1): The Socinian punctuation is opposed by (a) all Greek copies: (b) The scope of the apostle, which is to exalt the dignity of the Jewish race; which, that he may successfully perform, he teaches that Christ, born of the fathers of the Jews, is not only man, but also God, blessed over all: (c) The limitation added, according to the flesh; for which there would be no need, if Christ were only man: (d) The context: The doxological exclamation, which is feigned by the adversaries, coheres neither with the preceding words, nor with the following.

Not with the preceding; because the apostle had testified his sympathy towards the Jews, v. 2. and had wished to be anathema for his brethren, v. 3. whose glory he is about to describe, v. 4. among other things he commemorates, that from their fathers Christ is made according to the flesh. Who therefore would the apostle abruptly jump to a doxology? He grieves, he wishes, he does not congratulate. He extols the dignity of the Jews, not that he may celebrate God, but that he may exaggerate the causes of his own grief.

Nor with the following; for how do those things cohere? I wished to be anathema for my brethren &c. Of whom is Christ according to the flesh. Who is over all God, be blessed for ever, Amen! Not so, however, that the word of God has fallen away? Certainly no connection, or coherence of the text appears.

To 2): If even the words, ἐπὶ πάντων, were rendered, over all, yet the divinity of Christ would not be diminished; for he is not only over all men, but also all creatures.

Iehouah is high over all the earth, greatly exalted over all Gods: whom all the angels of God shall adore. Ps. XCVII, 9. Conf. Hebr. I, 6.

With these things premised we argue: Whoever in the O. T. is called Iehouah & Adonai, and in the N. T. not only absolutely God, but also true, great, God blessed over all, he is the highest and by nature God. But Christ &c. Therefore.

Nor does the name Κύριος, Lord, often corresponding in the N. T. to the name יהוה, which in the O. T. is vindicated for the true God alone, provide us with an invalid argument for the divinity of Christ. For he is called (1) Κύριος ἐξ οὐρανοῦ, Lord from heaven.

1 Cor. XV, 47. Which, since it cannot be said of him by reason of human nature; there must be a more sublime, and divine nature in him, according to which he is made Lord from heaven. (2) He is called Lord of all, Acts X, 36. and thus Lord of heaven and earth, which is a description of the true God.

Matt. XI, 15. (3) Lord of lords & King of kings, Apoc. XVII, 14. chap. XIX, 16. which denomination it is clear from 1 Tim. VI, 15 is proper to the true God alone. We may therefore conclude for ourselves: The Lord from heaven, the Lord of lords, & the King of kings is the highest God.

But Christ &c. Therefore (*).

II. Of personal divine names. Christ is called in the holy scriptures (1) The proper Son of God, Rom.

VIII, 32. having God as his proper Father. Io. V, 18. But he would not be the proper Son of God, if he were of a different nature from the Father.

For it is of the formal notion of a properly called son, that he be of the same essence as the Father.

Latin:

I. E nominibus diuinis effentialibus.

In V. T. Chriftus, germen Dauidis, appellatur Iehouah, iuftitia noftra, Ier. XXIII, 6. Vocatur Iehouah, quem vnxit Iehouah, fuper quo eft Spiritus Domini, Ef. LXI, 1. 8. Dicitur Adonai, fedens fuper throno alto & elato, a Seraphim religiofe honoratus. Ef. VI, 1. 2. 3. coll. cum Io. XII, 41. Nulla creatura dicitur Iehouah & Adonai. In N. T. Filius Dei (1) abfolute, fine vlla conditione limitante, aut alienante appellatur Deus. Deus erat verbum, inquit Io. cap. I, 1. Quem Thoinas, finceram editurus confeffionem, magna cum fiducia compellat: Domine mi, & Deus mi, Io. XX, 28. Quæ verba non ad Deum Patrem, fed ad Dominum Iefum directa fuerunt. Nam Thomas refpondit & dixit ipfi (Iefu, qui oftenfis cicatricibus manuum & lateris dixerat: non efto incredulus, fed credulus): Domine mi, & Deus mi. Neque funt hæc verba tantum exclamantis, aut admirantis, fed confitentis Thomæ; confeftim enim fubiicit Chriftus: Quia vidifti me, credidifti. (2) Nominibus diuinis adduntur verba, quibus Filius Dei incarnatus defignatur. Sic Paullus Act. XX, 28. inquit: Deus ecclefiam acquifiuit per proprium fanguinem. Vbi per Deum, qui fanguine proprio ecclefiam acquifiuit, non nifi Filius Dei intelligitur. Idem apoftolus ait 1 Tim. III, 16. Deus in carne manifeftatus eft Filius Dei; vtpote qui caro factus Io. I, 14. carnis & fanguinis particeps factus eft. Hebr. II, 14. & in carne venit. 1 Io. IV, 2. 3. (3) Nominibus diuinis annectuntur epitheta, quibus fummus Deus indigitatur. Nam (a) Chriftus a S. Joanne nominatur verus Deus & vita æterna. 1 Jo. V, 20-22. Scimus vero, quod Filius Dei venerit, & dederit nobis mentem, vt cognofcamus verum: Et fimus in vero, in Filio Iefu Chrifto. Hic eft verus Deus & vita æterna. Vbi (α) fitus vocum (quia pronomen demonftratiuum ὃρος, hic ordinarie refpicit & demonftrat nomen immediate antecedens) (β) fcopus apoftoli, de Chrifto, vt principali huius epiftolæ themate agendi. Vid. 1 Jo. I, 2. (γ) Tautologiæ (fi ad patrem referatur) abfurditas, (δ) epitheton vitæ æternæ, Chrifto fic proprium, vt nulli alii perfonæ facile tributum legas, adeoque omnia clamant, veritatem deitatis Chrifto adferi. Conf. DANNH. hodof. phæn. III. p. 233. (b) A S. Paullo Filius Dei vocatur magnus Deus. Tit. II, 13. Exfpectantes beatam fpem, & apparitionem gloriæ magni Dei. Circa hoc effatum apoftolicum obferuamus: (α) Nomen magni Dei vni & foli fummo Deo vindicari. Quod docet propheta Daniel cap. II, 45. Deus magnus notum fecit regi id, quod futurum eft pofthac. (β) Vocibus, τοῦ μεγάλου θεοῦ καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, vnum idemque fubiectum, nimirum Iefum Chriftum defignari: cum vnicus tantum adhibeatur articulus græcus, qui non nifi vnum fubiectum denotat, fecundum græcæ linguæ proprietatem; iuxta atque de illo Deo agat apoftolus, cuius ἐπιφάνεια, apparitio ad iudicium exfpectatur: quæ apparitio ad iudicium foli Filii Dei tribuitur. 2 Theff.
