II, 8. 1 Tim. VI, 14. 2 Tim. IV, 1. Neque obftat interpofita coniunctio καὶ, &; fiquidem illa fæpe duo nomina ad vnum fubiectum copulat. Conf. 1 Petr. I, 3. (c) Ab eodem apoftolo Chriftus nuncupatur Deus fuper omnia benedictus in fecula. Rom. IX, 5. Quorum funt Patres, & ex quibus eft Chriftus, quantum ad carnem, qui eft fuper omnia Deus benedictus in fæcula, Amen! Ex his liquet, Chriftum effe fummum Deum; cum illa verba apoftoli periphrafin fummi Dei exprimant. Conf. Rom. I, 25. Illuftre hoc dictum elufuri Sociniani excipiunt (1): verba illa, ὁ ὢν ἐπὶ πάντων θεὸς, non referenda esse ad Christum, sed esse exclamationem δοξολογικὴν, qua celebretur Deus Pater: Et ideo post voces, κατὰ σάρκα, scribendum esse punctum, a multis librariis omitti solitum. (2) Ἐπὶ πάντων, significare, super omnes, scil. homines, non super omnia. Resp.

Ad 1): Interpunctioni Socinianæ aduersantur (a) omnia exemplaria græca: (b) Scopus apostoli, qui est gentis Iudaicæ dignitatem euchere; quod vt feliciter præstet, docet, Christum & Iudæorum patribus ortum non tantum hominem, sed & Deum, super omnia benedictum esse: (c) Limitatio adiecta, secundum carnem; qua non opus foret; si Christus tantum homo esset: (d) Contextus: Exclamatio δοξολογικὴ, quæ ab aduersariis fingitur, neque cum verbis antecedentibus, neque cum sequentibus cohæret.

Non cum antecedentibus; quia apostolus contestatus erat suam συμπάθειαν erga Iudæos, v. 2. & optauerat anathema esse pro fratribus, v. 3. quorum descripturus gloriam, v. 4. inter alia commemorat, quod ex eorum patribus fit Christus secundum carnem. Qui igitur apostolus ex abrupto ad δοξολογίαν transiliret? Dolet, optat, non gratulatur. Euchit Iudæorum dignitatem, non, vt Deum celebret, sed doloris sui caussas exaggeret.

Neque cum sequentibus; quomodo enim illa cohærent? Optabam esse anathema pro fratribus &c. Ex quibus est Christus secundum carnem. Qui est super omnia Deus, sit benedictus in sæcula, Amen! Non ita tamen, quod exciderit verbum Dei? Certe nulla συναφεια, aut cohælio textus apparet.

Ad 2): Si vel maxime verba, ἐπὶ πάντων, redderentur, super omnes, non tamen imminueretur diuinitas Christi; est enim non tantum super omnes homines, sed cunctas etiam creaturas.

Est Iehouah altus super omnem terram, valde exaltatus super omnes Deos: quem omnes angeli Dei adoranto. Psal. XCVII, 9. Conf. Hebr. I, 6.

Quibus præmissis argumentamur: Quicunque in V. T. Iehouah & Adonai, in N. T. non solum absolute Deus, sed etiam verus, magnus, super omnia benedictus Deus appellatur, ille est summus & natura Deus. Atqui Filius &c.

Ergo. Neque nomen Κύριος, Dominus, fæpe respondens in N. T. nomini יהוה, quod in V. T. soli vero Deo vindicatur, inualidum pro diuinitate Christi nobis suppeditat argumentum.

Vocatur enim (1) Κύριος ἐξ οὐρανοῦ, Dominus e cælo. 1 Cor. XV, 47. Quod cum ratione humanæ naturæ de ipso dici nequeat; sublimiorem in illo, & diuinam naturam esse oportet, iuxta quam fit dominus e cælo.

(2) Dicitur omnium Dominus, Act. X, 36. adeoque Dominus cœli & terræ, quæ est descriptio veri Dei. Matth. XI, 15. (3) Dominus dominorum & Rex regum, Apoc. XVII, 14. cap. XIX, 16. quam denominationem soli vero Deo propriam esse ex 1 Tim. VI, 15. liquet.

Colligere itaque nobis licet: Dominus e cælo, Dominus dominorum, & Rex regum est summus Deus. Atqui Christus &c. Ergo (*).

II. E nominibus diuinis personalibus.

Vocatur Christus in sacris litteris (1) Filius Dei proprius, Rom. VIII, 32. habens Deum Patrem proprium. Io. V, 18. At proprius Dei Filius non esset, si diuersæ a patre esset naturæ.

Est enim de ratione formali proprie dicti filii, vt fit eiusdem cum Patre essentiæ.


### Of God the Son: (2) The only-begotten Son from the Father, John 1

(2) The only-begotten Son from the Father, John 1. I, 14.

The name of the only-begotten Son in the entire sacred code never denotes anyone other than Him who alone is born from the substance of the Father (*).

(3) The Son existing in the bosom of the Father, John I, 18. which is said of Him metaphorically indeed and anthropopathically: yet it insinuates the innermost secret of the paternal love and nature, in which the Son always is, as AMBROSE has it in his book on the blessing of the Patriarchs, sermon 17. A kinship of substance, proximity, knowledge and power equal to the Father, as CHRYSOSTOM has it in this place; because He is made consubstantial with the Father, intimately beloved, conscious of the Father’s heart and all mysteries, inseparable from the Father, as Augustine and others explain: whom see cited by D. CALOVIUS in System. theol. vol. III, p. 554.

(4) The firstborn Son, Heb.

I, 6. The firstborn of every creature; because in Him all things were created, Coloss. I, 15. 16. He is not called πρωτόκτισος (first-created); who also Himself is made from the census of creatures, but πρωτότοκος (firstborn), the firstborn of all creatures, and their creator; because in Him all things were created, visible and invisible, whether in heaven or on earth: v. 16. The apostle therefore implies that the Son of God was begotten from eternity, before anything was created.

(5) The Son superior to the angels, Heb.

I, 5. For to which of the angels did He ever say: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. The apostle, having brought forward the testimony of Psalm II, 7, teaches that Christ is the Son of God not by creation, nor because of a concession of power, as angels are called sons of God, Job XXXVIII, 7, but by a far more eminent reason, which exceeds the condition and strength of all angels by a great distance. But since there is nothing more eminent above the angels, except God, as far as nature or essence is concerned, the Son of God must be of the divine nature, and thus, since there is only one God by nature, He is of the same nature and essence with God the Father.

(6) The Son equal to God the Father.

John XV, 17. 18. Jesus answered them: My Father is working until now, and I am working. Therefore the Jews sought the more to kill Jesus, because He not only had broken the Sabbath, but also said that God was His own Father, making Himself equal with God. From those words of Christ: My Father is working now, and I am working, the Jews concluded that Christ was making Himself equal to God. So far was Christ from disapproving of that mode of concluding, that He rather confirmed it, saying: whatever the Father does, these things the Son also does likewise (ὁμοίως), intending to indicate that He, together with the Father, performs the same works, as in essence, so in power.

Having established these things, we conclude: The proper Son of God, only-begotten from the Father, existing in His bosom, the firstborn of every creature, superior to the angels and equal to God, is God true and supreme by nature, ὁμοούσιος or consubstantial with God the Father. But Christ is the proper Son of God, etc. Therefore.

Prob. b: The divinity of the Son of God is validly proven from the divine attributes, which are assigned to Him in the Holy Scriptures no differently than to God the Father. I. ETERNAL

The Son of God.

Paul pointed out His eternity, saying, Col. I, 17. The Son of God is πρὸ πάντων, before all things, and all things consist in Him.

He who is prior to all visible and invisible creatures, which are preserved by His providence, is the eternal and independent God.

By the testimony of the same apostle, Jesus Christ is yesterday, today, the same and forever, Hebr. XIII, 8. By which words, embracing all differences of time, not a finite, but an infinite duration, not time, but eternity, which eminently embraces all durations, is described.

St. John supports this, who gravely says in chap. I, 1.

In the beginning was the Word, understanding the hypostatic Word, namely the Son begotten of the Father. v. 14. In this beginning, in which the universe of things began to be created, He was already then.

John does not say: In the beginning the Word was made, or began to be, but was, i.e., He was prior to every beginning: For neither is the beginning of creation, or of the restoration of men, precisely determined here, but it is called a beginning absolutely and simply.

For whatever beginning you posit, the Word (ὁ λόγος) did not begin to be at that same point, but was already then: He anticipated every beginning of times that can be conceived by the mind, every beginning of divine works.

Therefore, although these things are rightly compared with the Mosaic words: In the beginning God created heaven and earth; yet here τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ is taken more absolutely, and signifies the same as before all things.

Which the apostle, intending to indicate, says: The Word was with God, when there was nothing but God, nothing but mere eternity.

Nor was He with God as a creature, created before all other creatures, but as God.

That Word (λόγος), God, was in the beginning with God (the Father), so that neither did He exist before the Word (λόγος), but the Word (λόγος) coexisted with Him from eternity.

All things were made through the Word (τὸν λόγον) v. 3. Therefore He was before all things that were made; for the craftsman, through whom things are made, is prior to the things made.

The world was made through Him v. 10. Therefore He was before the creation of the world.

God created the ages through this Word (λόγῳ), Ebr. I, 2. Therefore He was before the ages, and thus from eternity.

Nor does St. John delineate the eternity of the Son of God less graphically in Apoc. I, 8. where he introduces Him speaking: I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, says the Lord, He who is, and who was, and who is to come. Just as the first letter of the Greek alphabet is Alpha, the last Omega: so Christ is the beginning, without a beginning of time, and the end, without an end: He is the first, because before Him there is nothing: He is the last, because after Him there is nothing: He is interminable from the side before, and from the side after.

Cf. Is. XLI, 4. chap. XLIV, 6. chap. XLVIII, 12. This Lord is, was, and is to come, because His eternity coexists with all differences of time, remaining indivisible in itself .

Latin:

(2) Filius vnigenitus a Patre Io. I, 14.

Nomen filii vnigeniti in vniuerso sacro codice nunquam alium, quam qui solus e substantia Patris natus est, denotat (*).

(3) Filius existens in sinu Patris, Io. I, 18. quod de ipso metaphorice quidem & ἀνθρωποπαθῶς dicitur: insinuatur tamen intimum paternae caritatis & naturae secretum, in quo semper est Filius, vt habet AMBROSIVS lib. de bened. Patriarch. serm. 17. Substantiae cognatio, propinquitas, par patri cognitio & potestas, vt habet CHRYSOST. in h.l. quod fit patri consubstantialis, intime dilectus, paterni pectoris & arcanorum omnium conscius, a Patre ἀχώριστος, vt Augustinus & alii exponunt: quos vide citatos a D. CALOVIO in system. theol. tom. III. p. 554.

(4) Filius primogenitus, Hebr.

I, 6. Primogenitus omnis creaturae; quia in ipso creata sunt omnia, Coloss. I, 15. 16. Non vocatur πρωτόκτισος primo creatus; qui & ipse e censu creaturarum fit, sed πρωτότοκος, primogenitus omnium creaturarum, earumque creator; quia in ipso creata sunt omnia, visibilia & inuisibilia quae in caelis, & quae super terra: v. 16. Innuit igitur apostolus, Filium Dei ab aeterno, antequam quidquam crearetur, esse genitum.

(5) Filius angelis superior, Hebr.

I, 5. Cui enim dixit angelorum: Filius meus es tu; ego hodie genui te. Apostolus adducto Psalm II, 7. testimonio docet, Christum esse Filium Dei non per creationem, nec propter potestatis concessionem, vt angeli audiunt Filii Dei Iob. XXXVIII, 7. sed longe eminentiore ratione, quae conditionem & fortem omnium angelorum longissime excedit. Quum vero supra angelos nihil eminentius sit, praeter Deum, quantum ad naturam, vel essentiam, Filium Dei diuinae naturae esse oportet, adeoque cum non nisi vnus fit natura Deus, eiusdem naturae & essentiae cum Deo Patre.

(6) Filius Deo Patri aequalis.

Io. XV, 17. 18. Iesus respondit illis: Pater meus vsque nunc operatur: ideo etiam ego operor. Propterea itaque quaerebant magis Iesum Iudaei interficere, quod non tantum sabbatum soluisset sed etiam Patrem proprium dixisset Deum, aequalem se ipsum faciens Deo. Iudaei ex illis verbis Christi: Pater meus nunc operatur, ideo etiam ego operor, concludebant, Christum seipsum Deo aequalem facere. Tantum aberat, vt Christus illum concludendi modum improbaret, vt potius eundem firmaret, inquiens: quae Pater facit, haec etiam Filius ὁμοίως similiter facit, indicaturus, se vna eamque, vt essentia, ita virtute, cum Patre eadem opera expedire.

Quibus praestitutis concludimus: Filius Dei proprius, vnigenitus a Patre, in huius sinu existens, primogenitus omnis creaturae, angelis superior & Deo aequalis, est Deus natura verus & summus, Deo Patri ὁμοούσιος sine consubstantialis. Atqui Christus est Filius Dei proprius &c. Ergo.

Prob. b: Divinitas Filii Dei ex attributis divinis, quae ipsi haud secus, ac Deo patri, in sacris litteris assignantur, valide evincitur. I. AETERNVS

Filius Dei.

Cuius aeternitatem indigitatum iuit Paullus, inquiens, Col. I, 17. Filius Dei est πρὸ πάντων, ante omnia, & omnia in ipso consistunt.

Qui prior est omnibus creaturis visibilibus & invisibilibus, quae ipsius prouidentia conseruantur, is aeternus & independens Deus est.

Teste eodem apostolo, Iesus Christus est heri, hodie, idem & in saecula, Hebr. XIII, 8. Quibus vocibus, omnes temporis differentias complectentibus, non finita, sed infinita duratio, non tempus, sed aeternitas, quae omnes durationes eminenter complectitur, describitur.

Suffragatur S. Ioannes, qui grauiter inquit cap. I, 1.

In principio erat verbum, intelligens verbum hypostaticum, nempe filium vnigenitum a Patre. v. 14. Hic in principio, quo rerum vniuersitas creari coepit, iam tum erat.

Non dicit Ioannes: In principio verbum factum est, aut esse coepit, sed erat, q. d. omni principio prius erat: Neque enim praecise hic principium creationis, aut restaurationis hominum determinatur, sed absolute & simpliciter dicitur principium.

Quodcunque enim ponas principium, non eodem demum esse coepit, sed iam tum erat ὁ λόγος: omne principium temporum, quod mente concipi potest, omne principium operum diuinorum anteuertebat.

Idcirco quamuis recte conferantur haec cum verbis Mosaicis: In principio creauit Deus caelum & terram; hic tamen absolutius τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ sumitur, & idem valet, atque ante omnia.

Quod indicaturus apostolus ait: Verbum erat apud Deum, cum nil, nisi Deus, nil, nisi mera aeternitas esset.

Neque erat apud Deum vt creatura, ante omnes alias creaturas condita, sed vt Deus.

Ille λόγος, Deus, in principio erat apud Deum (Patrem), vt neque hic exstiterit ante λόγον, sed λόγος ei ab aeterno coexstiterit.

Omnia per τὸν λόγον facta sunt v. 3. Ergo fuit ante omnia, quae facta sunt; opifex enim, per quem res fiunt, rebus factis prior est.

Mundus per ipsum factus est v. 10. Ergo fuit ante creationem mundi.

Saecula per hunc λόγον Deus condidit, Ebr. I, 2. Ergo fuit ante saecula, atque adeo ab aeterno.

Neque minus graphice aeternitatem Filii Dei delineat S. Ioannes Apoc. I, 8. vbi ipsum loquentem introducit: Ego sum Alpha & Omega, principium & finis, inquit Dominus, is, qui est, & qui fuit, & qui venturus est. Sicut graeci alphabeti prima littera est Alpha, vltima Omega: ita Christus est principium, fine principio temporis, & finis, fine fine: est primus, quia ante ipsum nihil: est nouissimus, quia post ipsum nihil: a parte ante, & a parte post interminabilis est.

Conf. Es. XLI, 4. cap. XLIV, 6. cap. XLVIII, 12. Hic Dominus est, fuit & venturus est, quia ipsius aeternitas omnibus temporis differentiis coexistit, ipsa in se indiuisibilis manens .


### Of God the Son: II. Immense & Omnipresent

II. IMMENSE & OMNIPRESENT

He is immense; because He is in the immense bosom of the Father Io.

I, 18 . He is omnipresent; because, where two or three are gathered in His name, there he is in the midst of them.

Matt. XVIII, 20. He is with us all days even unto the consummation of the world.

Matt. XXVIII, 20. III. IMMUTABLE. You are the same, and your years shall not fail.

Ps. CII, 28. That these words are to be understood of the Son of God, Paul teaches in Hebr.

I, 12. IV. MOST HOLY; inasmuch as the prophet Daniel calls him the holy of holies, ch. IX, 24. *V. OMNIPOTENT.* The Son of God himself says: I am παντοκράτωρ (the Almighty).

Apoc. I, 8. No one shall snatch my sheep from my hand, Jo.

X, 28. Therefore the power of Christ surpasses every finite power.

VI. OMNISCIENT. Lord, you know all things, says Peter, Jo.

XXI, 17. Christ knows what is in man.

Jo. II, 25. VII.

VII. MOST BLESSED &amp; αὐταρκέστατος (most self-sufficient); for he has all things that the Father has, Jo. XVI, 15.

VIII. MOST GLORIOUS; for he is the Lord of glory, 1 Cor.

VIII, 8. He had glory with the Father before the world was, Jo.

XVII, 5. From these it is gathered: Whoever is eternal, immense, omnipresent, immutable, most holy, omnipotent, omniscient, most blessed, and most glorious, he is the supreme and true God by nature.

But Christ, etc. Therefore. The major premise is certain; because to whom divine attributes belong, to him the divine essence itself belongs; since the former do not differ from the latter in reality. Proved: above all heavens, he was superior to all heavens, and filled all things: Therefore, according to his divine nature, when the human had not yet existed.

Many sayings of this kind point to this, which testify that Christ came from above, and for that reason is far superior to all, John.

III, 31. That Christ was with God before the foundations of the world were laid, Jo. I, 2. That Christ descended from heaven, yet in such a way that he himself is still always in heaven, Jo.

III, 13. that he came forth from the Father, Jo.

XVI, 28; but nevertheless is perpetually in the Father, Jo. XIV, 10.

11. For just as God, who fills heaven and earth, is sometimes said to have descended, namely when he manifested himself in some singular way: in the same way Christ, eternal and immense, descending from the heavens, showed himself to us, manifested in the flesh.

I will complete the argumentation of these sayings, Eph.

IV, 10. Jo.

III, 13. with that, Job XI, 8. where the holy man assigns the heights of the heavens to God alone, and from there draws an argument for the immense knowledge of all things that is in God, v. 7. So likewise Christ, intending to assure Nicodemus that he knows the τὰ ἐπουράνια (heavenly things), brings forward this reason: that he himself has always been in heaven, nay, even higher than all heavens, Eph. IV, 10.

Hebr. VII, 26.

With these reasons collected, that rapture of Christ into heaven, which the Socinians speak of so barbarously, and which they were forced to invent, serving their own preconceived opinion, is stripped of all protection.

I.

Knowledge of the divine, specifically 1) the most perfect knowledge of God himself, for in the same way that the Father knows the Son, the Son in turn knows the Father, Matt.

XI, 27. Jo.

I, 18. &amp; VI, 46. in which place indeed there is a threefold nerve of proof, if indeed this knowledge of God the Father, which Christ claims for himself, (α) is denied to all others, add.

1 Tim. VI, 16: (β) is opposed to that knowledge which is acquired through divine doctrine and instruction, v. 45: (γ) is derived from the intimate union of the Son with the Father, ὁ ὢν παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ (who is with God). 2) Knowledge of the entire nature, Jo.

XXI, 17. Hebr.

IV, 13. the word, αὐτὰ (them), pertains to what follows, πρὸς ὃν ἡμῖν ὁ λόγος (with whom we have to do), but it is not the Father, but the Son, concerning whom it was Paul's intention to set forth the discourse in these letters, v. 14. 3) Knowledge of supernatural things, as they are called, Jo.

XVI, 30. and this is to be compared with those things which we shall discuss next concerning the power, in which Christ excels, of performing any miracles whatsoever. 4) Knowledge of souls, and that indeed (α) immediate, without any testimony or sign, Jo.

II, 24. &amp; 26. (β) The true divinity of Christ is demonstrated by divine acts, both personal and essential, which are attributed to Him in the divine Scriptures. The personal acts of the Son of God are the eternal spiration and the temporal mission of the Holy Spirit. 26. (β) certain, not probable, which is the power of the word, ᾄδω, John 1:47, 48. (γ) universal and perpetual, John 21:17. Peter concludes from the universal to the singular, and especially in Rev. 2:23, where the number of the multitude, πᾶσαι ἐκκλησίαι, is coupled with the number of unity, ἕκαστος, that is, to know the thoughts of all and of each one by searching.

That Christ speaks thus of Himself is abundantly clear from v. 18, as also from the continuation of the discourse up to v. 28.

Indeed, the very manner of speaking is entirely that which befits the one God, 1 Kings 8:39; add Jer.

11:20, where likewise the power of judging is closely joined with the investigation of things and hearts.

Finally, 5) Foreknowledge, and indeed (α) of the most remote events, Luke 21:25 sqq. and more often in the revelation of John; (β) of the most minute, among the number of which is also the point of time, and even the opportunity (which indeed pertains more to wisdom than to knowledge), John 13:1, 17:1; (γ) of future contingents, John 18:4: even of those things which would have happened, given a certain condition (that which they have called middle knowledge in God), John 6:15.

II. Of divine Wisdom: 1) The choice of always the best, wherefore Christ is named no less than the Father, both κατ’ ἐξοχήν (by way of eminence) and in the abstract, the very wisdom of God, Luke 7:34, 35, 11:29, coll. with Matt. 23:34.

2) Infinite amplitude, without any exception, πάντες θησαυροὶ τῆς σοφίας (all the treasures of wisdom), Col. 2:3. 3) Supreme authority, or, as is commonly said, independence, for Christ is endowed with that wisdom (α) which no one taught Him, 1 Cor. 2:16; add Rom.

11:34; (β) which He Himself confers upon others, and (γ) which no one is able to resist, Luke 21:15.

4) Immense depth, 1 Cor. 2:16, coll. with Rom.

11:34, Eph. 3:8; add Rom.

11:33. III. Of divine Goodness:

1) independently, John 3:31, 16:15: 2) excellently, by which reason Christ is called good κατ’ ἐξοχήν, John 10:11:

3) causally, John 10:10; add Ps. 23:1, 6, and especially notable is that which is said of Christ, 2 Cor.

12:9. 4) Constantly, so that neither any change nor mutability falls upon Him, Heb.

1:11, 12; thus, indeed, Paul interprets the words of David concerning the Son of God.

But in that place, Matt. 19:16, 17, Christ institutes a disputation κατ’ ἄνθρωπον (according to man), against him who denied the glory of divinity to Him.

By what right, He says, or with what mind, do you indeed call Me good, when you are unwilling to confess that I am God? An example, most similar to this, we see in Matt.

22:43, 45.

Who would have thought that Christ denied Himself to be the Lord of David? But this was His intention, that the adversaries might explain how they could reconcile that with their false opinion.

IV. Of divine Truth, which is accustomed to be called veracity: 1) Universality, without any exception, John 3:31, 32, 33.

2) Necessity, so that Christ is ignorant of how to deceive.

For thus He Himself attributes immutability to His words, Luke 21:33; add Ps.

119:96. For which reason He Himself is named κατ’ ἐξοχήν, ὁ ἀμήν, καὶ ὁ ἀληθινός (the Amen, and the true one), Rev.

3:7, 14, and the truth itself, John 14:6.

Therefore, Christ also swears by Himself, and Paul confirms his own pronouncements by an oath through Christ; concerning which argument it will be necessary to discourse below.

V. Of divine Power, and thus of authority.

General sayings exist in John 16:19, Phil.

3:21, Ps. 8:7, so that nothing is excepted, except God, 1

Cor. 15:27.

Specifically (δ) by reason of things, or objects; In the power of Christ, equally as in that of the Father, are: 1) the soul of every single man, and its empire has two parts: (α) the right of binding the conscience, Rom.

14:1, 10; (β) the right of remitting sins, and indeed in His own name, Matt.

9:6, just as the Legates also performed their duty in the name of Him, equally as that of the Father, having been commanded to them, both in remitting sins, 2 Cor. 2:10, and in retaining them, 1 Cor.

5:4, 5. 2) directing fortune, Mark 16:20, Rom.

15:18: 3) heaven and earth, and all created things, Rev.

5:13: 4) the Church, Col. 1:18, the foundation of whose supreme power is not only liberation, v. 14, but also creation and conservation, v. 16, 17, Heb. 3:3, 4, and to this looks the right of instituting sacraments:

5) the Magistrate, and thus the supreme Rulers, Ps.

2:9, 110:1, and therefore this name, King of kings, Lord of lords, which is truly proper to the supreme Deity (1 Tim. 6:15, 16), is attributed to Christ no less than to the Father, Rev.

17:14, 19:16, compare with the preceding v. 11-15 and the following v. 17. 6) the right of life and death, restricted by no limits, Rom.

14:7, 8, 9, in which place there are four things worthy of note From which it is argued: He who together with God the Father breathes forth from eternity, and in time sends the Holy Spirit, is true God, or co-essential with God the Father. But the Son of God, etc. Therefore. The major is clear; because the Holy Spirit, who is eternal God, can be breathed forth and sent only by the true and eternal God. We shall provide proof for the minor below.

The essential divine acts, which are claimed for the Son of God in the Holy Scriptures, viewed generally, are the same as those of God the Father; considered specifically, they are the acts of divine power, omniscience, mercy, and justice(). The identity of the essential operations of God the Father and the Son is made manifest from John 5:19. What things the Father does, these also the Son does likewise.

By which words Christ teaches that absolutely all things which the Father does are his own works, and he claims for himself both the identity of the works and the same manner of working. To these add John 10:37-38. If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me. But if I do, even if you do not believe me, believe the works, that you may know and believe that the Father is in me, and I in him. most worthy: (α) the name, κύριος, by which it is clear that Christ is signified, v. 9; (β) the sign of universality, θεὸς ἡμῶν (γ) the locution is exactly the same as that which is used of God the Father, Luke 20:38. πάντες αὐτῷ ζῶσιν (δ) the conjunction of this predicate with other indications of supreme divinity, v. 10, 11. add, Isa. 45:21-24, to which prophecy the Apostle clearly looked.

### Of God the Son: II. Immense & Omnipresent (continued)

But it is also relevant to say this, which Christ pronounces concerning his own life, John 2:19, 10:18.

7) The right of judging the whole world, Rom. 14:10, 11. (8) The right over the whole nature of things, so that he himself can perform miracles, superior to all the forces of nature, whatever and in whatever way he wills; concerning which I shall explain a little later.

(α) By reason of the mode, namely 1) independently; for Christ, (α) as he has life in himself, John 5:26 (see page 234*), so also he has all power of acting, if he wills, and whatever he wills, John 5:21, Matt.

8:2, 3 (but it behooves those who are inferior to God to speak in a much different way, James 4:15);

(β) no one is able to resist him, 1 Cor.

15:25; (γ) he owes an account to no one, he himself is the supreme judge of all: 2) immediately, with one word, and by his own sufficient will, Matt.

8:8. 3) infinitely, Rev.

5:12, 13, in which place there is a threefold nerve of proof, (α) ἰσχὺς καὶ κράτος, without any determination, (β) eternal power, and that (γ) attributed to the Son equally as to the Father, v. 13.

Add Dan. 7:13, 14, Luke 1:33, cf. with Dan. 4:31, where the same thing is predicated in the same words concerning the most high God: 4) perfectly, Matt. 28:18, Phil. 3:21, 4:13.

(*) Works that are strictly divine, namely both those which God himself performs, and not through some minister, and in every way that is becoming to God alone (page 301*). Behold! A general statement, John 5:19.

Specifically (א) Those actions, and indeed all those which God alone performs, with no one ministering, are 1) The creation of the whole world, as also its preservation, both of which are attributed to Christ, Col.

1:16 & 17, John 1:3 (we learn from Heb.

1:10, 3:3, 4 that the particle διά, in this place, as sometimes elsewhere, denotes the efficient cause): 2) The new creation, Heb. 3:1-4.

3) The mission of the ministers of the church, John 20:21, and clearly so, as it is attributed to the Father, Gal.

1:1: 4) The efficacy of the means of grace, Rom.

15:18, Heb. 4:12 (for who is he, from whose mouth the word is brought forth like a two-edged sword? namely Christ, Rev. 1:16, 2:12, 16:

5) The recalling of all the dead to life, John 5:21.

(ב) In the very way that uniquely becomes God, 1) To act by his own will, in his own name, and by his own authority, in the manner of the Father, John 5:21, Luke 4:36, 7:14, Matt. 8:3, 4.

No one sent divinely, not even an angel, has ever dared this. All, if they attempted anything, did it under divine auspices, always appealing to the will and authority of God.

The one greatest prophet of all, Moses, always calls God the effector of such great things, says that God did this, but that he himself lent his hands to God, Ex.

4:22, 23,

7:16, 14:21, 24. He never dared to say: I will do this, thus I will, thus I command, in the manner that Christ, and he indeed alone, did not hesitate to speak. 2) To confer the power of performing divine things, and the greatest of all things, upon others, Matt.

16:19, Luke 9:1, John 20:21, Eph. 4:10, so that his legates might conduct his business in his own name, and rely upon his own will and authority, Luke 9:54, Mark 16:17, Acts 3:6, coll. with v. 12.

3) To perform miracles with the intention that he might manifest his own glory, John 2:11, 5:11, 5:23.

And yet all things must be referred and directed only to the glory of the supreme Deity.

I (am) in the Father. The Savior shows not obscurely that from the communion of works, the communion of essence is to be inferred. Wherefore we conclude: He who does the same divine works which the eternal Father does, and works with him in the same manner of acting, he is of one essence with the heavenly Father. But Christ &c. Therefore.

The acts of divine power are 1) The creation of this universe, ποίησις τῶν πάντων, John 1:3, Col. 1:16, so that not only are all things said to be produced through him (just as through the Father, certainly not as a less principal cause, but as a principal one, Paul says he was called, Gal. 1:1), but also in the nominative case he himself is said to have created all things, Heb. 1:10, from Ps. 102:26, Thou in the beginnings, O Lord, hast founded the earth, and the works of thy hands are the heavens. 2) The preservation and government of this universe. For the Son of God carries all things by the word of his power, Heb. 1:3, he carries all things by preserving and governing: he carries all things by the word of his power, i.e., by his most powerful command and authority. From which Paul asserts that all things consist in him, Col. 1:17, namely, so that they do not fall apart or collapse. 3) The performance of miracles. True miracles, αὐτοκρατορικῶς, by his own virtue, God alone performs. Ps. 72:18, Ps. 136:4. For true miracles are rare and unusual effects, beyond the order of the whole created nature, produced by God. Christ performed a) true miracles, to which he appealed as witnesses of his divine mission, greater than any exception. Matt. 11:5: b) singular and ἀμίμητα, of which AUGUSTINE commemorates three, tom. II, epist. III. To be born of a virgin, to rise from the dead, to ascend into heaven: if anyone thinks this is little for God, I do not know what more he expects. c) αὐτοκρατορικῶς, by a virtue not adventitious or precarious, but primitive and independently flowing, from which as a fountain the grace of miracles flowed into other wonder-workers. Matt. 10:1, Acts 3:6; d) for his own glory, John 2:11.

The acts of divine grace are 1) Redemption, which is indeed a truly divine action. For God acquired the church through his own blood. Acts 20:28. 2) The gathering, preservation, government, and defense of the church; for he gathered it as the king of Zion, Ps. 2:6, through the word and sacraments. Mark 16:15, Matt. 28:19, ch. 26:26, which he also protects against the gates of hell. Matt. 16:18. The gates of hell are vices, heresies, and persecutions stirred up by the devil against the church. 3) Salvation, which is indeed a divine work. I (am) Jehovah, and besides me there is no savior. Is. 43:11. But Jesus is the Savior, who saves his people from their sins. Matt. 1:21.

The acts of omniscience are 1) The prediction of future events. Future contingencies, which depend on the will of God or of men, God alone knows and predicts certainly and infallibly. Is. 43:9. Christ predicted future events. Matt. 24:15, John 2:18. Prophets indeed also predicted future events, but enlightened by the Spirit of Christ, 1 Pet. 1:11. 2) Καρδιογνωσία, the scrutiny of human hearts, which belongs to God alone, 1 Kings 8:29, Jer. 17:10, pertains to Christ, who says of himself in Rev. 2:23, I am he who searches the reins and hearts.

The acts of divine justice are 1) The resurrection of the dead, which is a truly divine action, Rom. 4:17, 2 Cor. 1:9, and is attributed to Christ, Job 19:26, John 6:39. 2) The universal judgment, John 5:22, for which infinite knowledge, power, and majesty are required, and therefore it is claimed for God alone, Gen. 18:25. From the divine actions taken together arises the argument: Whoever created this universe, preserves and governs what is created: performs true miracles by his own virtue for his own glory; redeemed the whole fallen human race: gathered, protects, and saves the church through the word and sacraments: infallibly knows and predicts future contingencies, and searches the hearts of men: raises the dead, and exercises universal judgment upon all men, he is the supreme and true God by nature. But Christ &c. Therefore.

…Prob. d. The divinity of Christ is also solidly established from divine worship. God denies that he will give his glory to another, Is. 42:8. But to Christ is claimed 1) in general, divine worship. for all are commanded to honor the Son, καθὼς just as they honor the Father, John 5:23. 2) Specifically, all men are commanded a) to be baptized in the name of the Son of God, equally as in the name of God the Father and the Holy Spirit, Matt. 28:19; b) to believe in Christ just as in God the Father. Believe in God, and believe in me, John 14:1; c) to worship Christ religiously, Ps. 45:12; Isa. 45:24; Rom. 14:11; Phil. 2:10; d)… Rom. 14:11; Phil. 2:10; d) to celebrate God the Father and the Son with equal honor. To him who sits upon the throne and to the Lamb (be) blessing, and honor, and glory, and power for ever and ever, Rev. 5:13.

This argument will be: Whosoever men are commanded to honor, just as they honor the Father, to be baptized into and to believe in, to worship religiously, and to celebrate equally as the Father, he is the supreme God, of the same essence and majesty as the heavenly Father. But the Son of God is [such a one], etc. Therefore (*).

Prob. (*) Religious worship is that by which one looks to the properties and supreme perfections of God. This is to be rendered to Christ, and indeed all its parts, so that nothing remains that is proper and peculiar to the Father.

1) Saving trust, which our forefathers in the Apol. Aug. Conf. p. 69, 88, rightly call λατρείαν and the highest worship of God, of which let us consider (α) the object, which is the merits of Christ (what and how great? Certainly so great that they are able to reconcile God to the whole world, and the world in turn to God, 2 Cor. 5:19, 20, which declares the infinite power of the merits of Christ: the liberation of one soul, let alone all, consists of a price which must be valued more than the universe of things, Matt. 16:26); (β) the mode and true manner in which it ought to be done, so that we prefer Christ, the supremely good, to all things, Phil. 3:8, 9; (γ) the effect, namely, righteousness availing before God, and the forgiveness of all sins, Acts 10:43; 1 Tim. 1:15, 16, indeed eternal salvation, John 3:16; (δ) the foundation upon which it rests, which is the word of Christ, inasmuch as he knows not how to be deceived or to deceive, John 8:51; (ε) the adjunct, namely this, that the trust to be placed in Christ is tightly coupled with that which we ought to place in the Father, John 14:1.

2) Hope, the most certain expectation of all future goods, John 10:11; 14:13, 14, and finally of everlasting blessedness, John 10:28, and indeed in such a way that the foundation of this hope is the immense power of Christ, Phil. 3:20, 21, so that its effect is also αὐτάρκεια, 2 Cor. 12:9, 10; Phil. 4:11, 12, 13.

3) Love that overcomes all things, both goods to be sought, Luke 14:26, cf. with Matt. 10:37, 39; 19:29, and evils to be feared, 2 Cor. 12: 10. Both kinds are treated in Rom. 8:37, 38, 39, in which place ὕψωμα are honors and pleasures, βάθος are dangers and calamities.

4) Obedience, and that indeed most perfect, without any exception of either duties, John 15:10, or men, Ps. 2:8, 10. We are admonished to avoid opposition against Christ and temptation, entirely the same as that by which God was once violated, 1 Cor. 10:9, add. Exod. 17:2, 7; Num. 21:5, 6; Deut. 6:16.

5) Covenant, and that indeed by which we profess our conscience to be bound and obligated to God, 1 Pet. 3:21; Matt. 28:19.

6) The greatest religion of swearing an oath, inasmuch as by it we profess the supreme knowledge, and especially the καρδιογνωσίαν (heart-knowledge), and justice, and power, which God possesses, Deut. 17:13; 10:20; Heb. 6:13, 16.

Therefore these three documents are to be noted: (α) Paul swears by Christ no less than by the Father, Rom. 9:1; 2 Cor. 11:10; 2 Tim. 4:1. (β) Paul adjures Timothy by Christ equally as by the Father, 1 Tim. 6:13. (γ) Christ swears by himself, which is a judgment that there is no one superior to him, Heb. 6:16. He swears, however, in that manner, Isa. 45:23. That these are the words of Christ appears both from the whole series of the discourse and from the interpretation, Rom. 14:10, 11; Phil. 2:10. Nor should that be passed over, Isa. 65:16. אמן is Christ, Rev. 3:14. The reason lies at hand, 2 Cor. 1:20 & John 1:17. From this it is understood, (α) why Christ, and he alone, and often, made use of this formula of speaking, ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, doubtless thus swearing by himself, (β) for what cause he usually employed that assertion doubled, for ἀμὴν, ἀμὴν in that prophecy, as it is in Isaiah, both the repetition of the word אמן exists, and the signification of two things, of which indeed one is an oath, but the other,

Prob. e. An accurate comparison of the sayings of the O. and N. T. provides us with the most certain arguments for strengthening the divinity of Christ. For example: Let the argument be: He whom the Israelites tempted in the desert besides Moses is the true and eternal God, Num. XXI, 5. 6. But Christ is he whom the Israelites &c. 1 Cor. X, 9. Therefore, Christ is the true God. Similarly: He who ascended on high, led captivity captive, received gifts for man, is God, Ps. LXVIII, 19. But Christ &c. Eph. IV, 8. Therefore. By the same reasoning compare Ps. CX, 1. and Hebr. I, 10. Mal. III, 1. with Matth. XI, 10. Is. XL, 3. with Matth. III, 3.

The antithesis is of all Antitrinitarians, among whom today the most hostile enemies of the divinity of Christ are the Socinians; the Arminians, however, deny that Christ is truly called ἀυτόθεον. Their arguments are of two orders. 1) They attempt to prove that only the heavenly Father is the supreme God. From which they conclude that Christ is not the supreme, but a subordinate God. 2) They directly attack the supreme divinity of Christ. The arguments of the first class are.

I. Whoever is called the only true God by Christ, besides him there is no supreme God. But God the Father &c. Therefore. The major is clear; because an exclusive particle of the subject excludes all other subjects from the participation of the same predicate. The minor is evident from Jo. XVII, 2. where the Savior says: This is eternal life, that they may know thee the only true God, and whom thou hast sent, Jesus Christ. Where the Father is called the only true God. Resp. The particle, only, is not added to the subject, which (as to the meaning) is the Father, but to the predicate, which is that true God: and thus the words of Christ do not imply this, that the Father alone is that true God, but that the Father is that only true God, or he, who alone is the true God. Notwithstanding which, the Son of God is also the true God, as is expressly said 1 Jo. V, 20. This (the Son) is that true God. For the verb, ἗ιναι, seems to have been omitted by ellipsis, or insinuated by the article, τὸν, so that the complete sense here may be: This is eternal life, that they may know, thee, Father, to be that true God, nedictio. Therefore Christ saying, ἀμὴν λέγω, and again ἀμὴν λέγω, first swears by himself, then also says well to us, by himself likewise.

7) Prayer, and indeed both its kinds: a) Adoration, by which we venerate the majesty of God and his infinite excellence. Conf. Rom. XIV, 11. with that Is. XLV, 23. 24. where Christ is considered as יהוה. There is certainly very much weight in this saying, Apoc. V, 13. 14. in which the nerve of the proof is fourfold: (α) the eternal continuation of praise, which is a certain part of supreme religion, εἰς τὸς ἀιῶνας τῶν ἀιώνων, (b) the common duty of all created things πᾶν κτίσμα, ὅ ἐστιν ἐν τῷ ὀρανῷ κ. τ. λ. so that not even the angels are excepted, Hebr. I, 6. of whom, however, none venerates Christ as his liberator, Hebr. II, 16. Therefore as his Creator, and Preserver, Hebr. I, 10; (γ) the joining of words most significantly, ἡ ἐυλογία, καὶ ἡ τιμὴ, καὶ ἡ δόξα, καὶ τὸ κράτος, so that nothing is left, which pertains to supreme veneration, (δ) the conjunction of the Son with the Father, as being worthy of equal honor, τῷ καθημένῳ ἐπὶ τῶ θρόνω, καὶ τῷ ἀρνίῳ. What remains, reserved for the Father alone? Absolutely nothing. b) Supplication, or, as it is commonly called, Invocation, by which we implore the kindness of God, and seek the benefits to be conferred upon us divinely. But that supplication, which is to be decreed to the one supreme God, ought to be common and perpetual, Rom. X, 13. 14. Common, and, what is usually called universal, is named for a fourfold reason, which always looks to the divine properties and perfections, and therefore is religious worship (by definition). It is indeed a universality (α) of places, the reason for which is the immense presence and knowledge of God, (β) of times, to this pertains the eternity of God and immutability, (γ) of those praying, the foundation of this is the knowledge of the supreme empire of God, because all depend on the will of one God, (δ) of things to be sought, this rests on the consideration of the infinite in God both of power, and of authority, and of goodness, Eph. III, 20. But to Christ no less than to the Father is attributed this universality of supplication, by reason of (α) all places, Matth. XVIII, 20. 1 Cor. I, 2. (β) all times, Thess. I, 11. & 12. (γ) all those praying, Rom. X, 13. 14. coll. with v. 9. 10. 11. 12 (δ) things and benefits, partly the bestowal of every good, Io. XIV, 13. add. Ps. XXXVII, 5. where this is said to be proper to God, יהוה יעשׂה partly the liberation and freedom from all evil, 2 Tim. IV, 18. That Christ is Κύριον, both the context declares, v. 1. 8. 22. and the perpetual habit of Paul's speech, see 1 Cor. VIII, 6. And when it is added; and, whom you sent, Jesus Christ, it must be repeated from the preceding in this way: And, whom you sent, Jesus Christ, to be that only true God; so that thus the Father and the Son may be said to be that only true God.

Latin:

11. add, Ies. XLV, 21-24. ad quam vaticinationem manifesto respexit Apostolus. Sed & hoc dicere attinet, quod de sua vita Christus pronuntiat, Io. II, 19. X, 18.

7) Ius orbem terrarum vniuersum iudicandi, Rom. XIV, 10. 11. (8) Ius in vniuersam rerum naturam, vt possit ipse miracula, viribus naturæ omnibus superiora, quæcunque & quocunque modo velit, efficere; de quo paullo post exponam.

(α) Ratione modi, nimirum 1) independenter; Christus enim, (α) vt vitam in se ipse habet, Io. V, 26. (vid. pag. 234.*) sic omnem quoque potestatem agendi, si velit, & quidquid velit, Io. V, 21.

Matth. VIII, 2. 3.

(omnes vero eos, qui Deo inferiores sunt, multo aliter decet loqui, Iac. IV, 15.); (β) nemo ipsi valet resistere, 1 Cor.

XV, 25.; (γ) nemini rationem reddere debet, ipse summus omnium iudex: 2) immediate, vno verbo, & sua voluntate sufficiente, Matth. VIII, 8.

3) infinite, Apoc. V, 12.

13. quo in loco triplex inest neruus probationis, (α) ἰσχὺς καὶ κράτος, fine vlla determinatione, (β) æterna potentia, eaque (γ) Filio æque, ac Patri tributa, v. 13.

Add. Dan. VII, 13. 14. Luc. I, 33. conf. cum Dan. IV, 31. vbi id idem, iisdem verbis, de Deo altissimo prædicatur: 4) perfecte, Matth. XXVIII, 18.

Phil. III, 21. IV, 13. (*) Opera prorsus diuina, scilicet tum ea, omnia, quæ Deus ipse, nec per ministrum quemdam, peragit, tum omni eo modo, qui Deo vni est conueniens (pag. 301.*) En! dictum generale, Io. V, 19.

Speciatim (א) Illæ actiones, & omnes quidem illæ, quas Deus ipse solus, nemine ministrante, perficit, sunt 1) Creatio mundi vniuersi, vt & conseruatio, quæ vtraque Christo adferitur, Col.

I, 16. & 17. Io.

I, 3. (voculam, διά, hoc in loco, vt alibi interdum, caussam efficientem denotare, discimus ex Hebr. I, 10. III, 3. 4.): 2) Creatio noua, Hebr. III, 1-4.

3) Missio ministrorum ecclesiæ, Io. XX, 21. & plane ita, vt Patri ea tribuitur, Gal.

I, 1.: 4) Efficacitas mediorum gratiæ, Rom. XV, 18.

Hebr. IV, 12. (quis enim est ille, ex cuius ore profertur verbum tamquam gladius anceps? quippe Christus, Apoc. I, 16.

II, 12. 16: 5) Mortuorum omnium ad vitam reuocatio, Io. V, 21.

(ב) Eo prorsus modo, qui Deum vnice decet, 1) Agere suo arbitrio, suo nomine, suaque auctoritate, quem ad modum pater, Ioan. V, 21. Luc. IV, 36. VII, 14. Matth. VIII, 3.

4. Id nemo diuinitus missus, ac ne angelus quidem, vnquam ausus est. Omnes si quid moliti sunt, fecerunt illud auspiciis diuinis, semper ad Dei arbitrium atque auctoritatem prouocantes.

Vates vnus omnium maximus, Moses, semper Deum tantarum rerum effectorem adpellat, Deum, ait, hoc effecisse, se autem Deo manus suas commodasse, Ex. IV, 22. 23.

VII, 16. XIV, 21.

24. Nunquam ausus est dicere: Ego hoc faciam, sic volo, sic iubeo, quem ad modum Christus, & is quidem vnus, loqui non dubitauit. 2) Potestatem, res diuinas, omniumque maximas peragendi, in alias conferre, Matth. XVI, 19.

Luc. IX, 1. Io. XX, 21. Eph. IV, 10. vt eius Legati ipsius nomine rem suam gererent, ipsius arbitrio atque auctoritate niterentur, Luc.

IX, 54. Marc. XVI, 17. Act. III, 6. coll. cum v. 12. 3) Miracula facere ea mente, vt suam ipse gloriam patefaceret, Io. II, 11.

V, 11. V, 23. Atqui omnia ad gloriam fummi Numinis tantum referenda sunt, ac dirigenda.

ego in Patre (sum). Haud obscure ostendit Saluator, ex communione operum, communionem essentiæ esse colligendam. Quare concludimus: Qui eadem opera diuina, quæ æternus Pater facit, eodemque agendi modo cum ipso operatur, is vnius cum Patre cœlesti essentiæ est. Atqui Christus &c. Ergo.

Actus potentiæ diuinæ sunt 1) Creatio huius vniuersi, ποίησις τῶν πάντων, Io. I, 3. Col. I, 16. ita vt non solum per ipsum omnia producta dicantur (prout per Patrem, non certe vt caufsam minus principalem, sed principalem, Paullus se vocatum esse dicit Gal. I, 1.), verum etiam in casu recto ipse creasse omnia dicatur, Hebr. I, 10. ex Ps. CH, 26. Tu in principiis, Domine, terram fundasti, & opera manuum tuarum sunt cœli. 2) Conseruatio & gubernatio huius vniuersi. Etenim Filius Dei omnia portat verbo potentiæ suæ. Hebr. I, 3. portat omnia conseruando & gubernando: portat omnia verbo potentiæ suæ, i. e. iussu atque imperio suo potentissimo. Ex quo Paullus asserit omnia in ipso consistere, Col. I, 17. scilicet ne diffluant aut concidant. 3) Miraculorum effectio. Vera miracula αὐτοκρατορικῶς, propria virtute, solus Deus patrat. Ps. LXXII, 18. Ps. CXXXVI, 4. Sunt enim vera miracula effectus rari & insoliti, præter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ, a Deo producti. Edidit Christus a) vera miracula, ad quæ velut testes suæ missionis diuinæ omni exceptione maiores prouocauit. Matth. XI, 5.: b) singularia & ἀμίμητα, quorum tria commemorat AVGVSTINVS tom. II. epist. III. Nasci de virgine, a mortuis resurgere, in cælum ascendere: hoc Deo qui parum putat, quid plus exspectet, ignoro. c) αὐτοκρατορικῶς virtute non aduentitia aut precaria, sed primitiua & independenter fluente, ex qua velut fonte gratia miraculorum in alios thaumaturgos dimanauit. Matth. X, 1. Act. III, 6.; d) in suimet gloriam, Io. II, 11.

Actus gratiæ diuinæ sunt, 1) Redemtio, quæ sane actio vere diuina est. Nam Deus ecclesiam acquisiuit per proprium sanguinem. Act. XX, 28. 2) Ecclesiæ collectio, conseruatio, gubernatio & defensio; quippe quam velut rex Sionis Ps. II, 6. congregauit per verbum & sacramenta. Marc. XVI, 15. Matth. XXVIII, 19. cap. XXVI, 26. quam etiam aduersus portas inferorum protegit. Matth. XVI, 18. Portæ inferorum sunt vitia, hæreses, persecutiones a diabolo aduersus ecclesiam concitatæ. 3) Saluatio, quæ sane diuinum opus est. Ego (sum) Iehouah, & præter me non est saluator. Es. XLIII, 11. At Iesus est Saluator, qui saluat populum suum a peccatis eorum. Matth. I, 21.

Actus omniscientiæ sunt 1) futurorum prædictio. Futura contingentia, quæ a voluntate Dei aut hominum dependent, solus Deus certo & infallibiliter prænouit & prædicit. Es. XLIII, 9. Christus futura prædixit. Matth. XXIV, 15. Io. II, 18. Prædixerunt quidem etiam prophetæ futura, sed illustrati a Spiritu Christi 1 Petr. II, 11. 2) Καρδιογνωσία, scrutinium cordium humanorum, quod solius Dei est, 1 Reg. VIII, 29. Ier. XVII, 10. competit Christo, qui de seipso inquit Apoc. II, 23. Ego sum, qui scrutatur renes & corda.

Actus iustitiæ diuinæ sunt 1) mortuorum resuscitatio, quæ actio vere diuina est, Rom. IV, 17. 2 Cor. I, 9. & tribuitur Christo, Iob. XIX, 26. Io. VI, 39. 2) Vniuersale iudicium, Io. V, 22. ad quod infinita scientia, potentia & maiestas requiritur, ideoque vindicatur vni Deo, Gen. XVIII, 25. Ex actionibus diuinis simul sumtis nascitur argumentum: Quicunque hoc vniuersum creauit, creatum conseruat & gubernat: vera miracula propria virtute in suimet gloriam patrat; vniuersum genus humanum lapsum redemit: ecclesiam per verbum & sacramenta collegit, protegit & saluat: futura contingentia infallibiliter prænouit & prædicit, cordaque hominum scrutatur: mortuos resuscitat, & vniuersale iudicium in omnes homines exercet, is est summus & verus natura Deus. Atqui Christus &c. Ergo.

Prob. d. e cultu etiam diuino solide adstruitur diuinitas Christi. Negat Deus se gloriam suam alteri daturum, Es. XLII, 8. Christo autem vindicatur 1) in genere cultus diuinus. IuIubentur enim omnes honorare Filium, καθὼς sicut honorant patrem, Io. V, 23. 2) In specie iubentur omnes homines a) in nomen Filii Dei, peraeque, ac in nomen Dei Patris & Spiritus S. baptizari, Matth. XXVIII, 19.; b) in Christum perinde, ac in Deum Patrem credere. Credite in Deum, & credite in me, Io. XIV, 1.; c) Christum religiose adorare, Ps. XLV, 12. Ef. XLV, 24. Rom. XIV, 11. Phil. II, 10.; d) aequali honore celebrare Deum Patrem & Filium. Sedenti super throno & agno (fit) benedictio, & honor & gloria, & robur in saecula saeculorum, Apoc. V, 13.

Argumentum hoc erit: Quemcunque honorare iubentur homines, sicut Patrem honorant, in ipsum baptizari & credere, eundem religiose adorare, & aeque, ac Patrem celebrare, ille est summus Deus, eiusdem cum Patre caelesti essentiae & maiestatis. Atqui Filium Dei &c. Ergo (*).

Prob. (*) Cultus religiosus est ille, quo ad proprietates Dei perfectionesque summas respicitur. Is Christo deferendus, atque adeo omnes eius partes, vt nihil supersit, Patris proprium ac praecipuum.

1) Fiducia salutaris, quum Maiores nostri in Apol. Aug. Conf. p. 69. 88. recte appellant λατρείαν & summum Dei cultum, cuius consideremus (α) obiectum, quod sunt promerita Christi (quae & quanta? Tanta certe, vt Deum mundo vniverso, & mundum vicissim Deo, reconciliare valeant, 2 Cor. V, 19. 20. id quod infinitam vim meritorum Christi declarat: vnius animi liberatio, nedum omnium, constat pretio, quod pluris faciendum est, quam rerum vniversitas, Matth. XVI, 26.); (β) modum, veramque rationem, qua fieri oportet, vt Christum, summe bonum, rebus omnibus anteferamus, Phil. III, 8. 9.; (γ) effectum, nempe iustitiam, coram Deo valituram, omniumque peccatorum veniam, Act. X, 43. 1 Tim. I, 15. 16. immo aeternam salutem, Ioan. III, 16.; (δ) fundamentum, quo ea nititur, quod est verbum Christi, vtpote falli ac fallere nescit, Ioan. VIII, 51.; (ε) adiunctum, nempe hoc, quod fiducia, in Christo collocanda, arcte copulatur cum ea, quam in Patre ponere debemus, Ioan. XIV, 1.

2) Spes, certissima exspectatio futurorum bonorum omnium, Ioan. X, 11. XIV, 13. 14. sempiterna tandem beatitatis, Ioan. X, 28. & ita quidem, vt huius spei fundamentum sit immensa Christi potentia, Phil. III, 20. 21. vt etiam effectus sit αὐτάρκεια, 2 Cor. XII, 9. 10. Phil. IV, 11. 12. 13.

3) Amor vincens omnia, tam bona expetenda, Luc. XIV, 26. coll. cum Matth. X, 37. 39. XIX, 29. quam mala pertimescenda, 2 Corinth. XII, 10. De vtroque genere agitur Rom. VIII, 37. 38. 39. quo in loco ὕψωμα sunt honores ac voluptates, βάθος sunt pericula & calamitates.

4) Obedientia, & ea quidem omnino perfectissima, fine vlla exceptione aut officiorum, Ioan. XV, 10. aut hominum, Ps. II, 8. 10. Admonemur de evitanda repugnantia aduersus Christum ac tentatione, prorsus eadem, qua Deus quondam violatus fuit, 1 Cor. X, 9. add. Exod. XVII, 2. 7. Num. XXI, 5. 6. Deut. VI, 16.

5) Pactio, & ea quidem, qua nostram Deo conscientiam obstrictam devinctamque profitemur, 1 Petr. III, 21. Matth. XXVIII, 19.

6) Iurisurandi maxima profecto religio, vtpote qua profitemur summam, qua Deus valet, & scientiam, in primisque καρδιογνωσίαν, & iustitiam, & potestatem, Deut. XVII, 13. X, 20. Hebr. VI, 13. 16.

Notanda sunt igitur tria haec documenta: (α) Paullus iurat per Christum non minus, quam per Patrem, Rom. IX, 1. 2 Cor. XI, 10. 2 Tim. IV, 1. (β) Paullus adiurat Timotheum per Christum aeque, ac per Patrem, 1 Tim. VI, 13. (γ) Christus per se ipse iurat, id quod iudicio est, nullum esse ipso superiorem, Hebr. VI, 16. Iurat autem eo modo, Ief. XLV, 23. Haec Christi verba esse, tum ex tota orationis ferie adparet, tum ex interpretatione Rom. XIV, 10. 11. Phil. II, 10. Nec praetermittendum est illud, Ief. LXV, 16. אמן est Christus, Apoc. III, 14. Ratio est in promptu, 2 Cor. I, 20. & Io. I, 17. Ex quo intelligitur, (α) quare Christus, & solus, & saepe numero, hanc vsurpauerit dicendi formulam, ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ita nimirum per se ipse iurans, (β) qua de caussa geminatam plerumque adhibuerit istam adseuerationem, ἀμὴν, ἀμὴν namque in illa vaticinatione, vt est apud Iesaiam, & iteratio vocis, אמן, exstat, & significatio duarum rerum, quarum quidem vna est, iusiurandum, altera vero,

Prob. e. Accurata collatio dictorum V. & N. T. certissima nobis suppeditat argumenta ad firmandam diuinitatem Christi. v. gr. Sit argumentum: Quem Israëlitæ præter Mosen in deserto tentarunt, est verus atque æternus Deus, Num. XXI, 5. 6. Atqui Christus est is, quem Israëlitæ &c. 1 Cor. X, 9. E. Christus est verus Deus. Similiter: Qui ascendit in altum, captiuam duxit captiuitatem, accepit dona pro homine, est Deus, Pf. LXVIII, 19. Atqui Christus &c. Eph. IV, 8. Ergo. Pari ratione confer. Pf. CX, 1. & Hebr. I, 10. Mal. III, 1. cum Matth. XI, 10. Es. XL, 3. cum Matth. III, 3.

Antithesis est omnium Antitrinitariorum, quos inter hodie infensissimi diuinitatis Christi hostes sunt Sociniani; Arminiani autem negant, Christum vere dici ἀυτόθεον. Argumenta eorum duplicis sunt ordinis. 1) Probatum eunt, solum Patrem cœlestem esse summum Deum. Vnde colligunt, Christum non summum, sed subordinatum esse Deum. 2) Directe summam Christi diuinitatem impugnant. Argumenta prioris classis sunt.

I. Quicunque a Christo solus verus Deus dicitur, præter eum non datur summus Deus. Atqui Deus Pater &c. E. Maior liquet; quia particula exclusiua subiecti omnia alia subiecta a participatione eiusdem prædicati excludit. Minor patet ex Jo. XVII, 2. vbi Saluator inquit: Hæc est vita æterna, vt cognoscant te solum verum Deum, &, quem misisti, Jesum Christum. Vbi solus Pater verus Deus dicitur. Resp. Particula, solus, non est addita subiecto, quod (qua sententiam) est Pater, sed prædicato, quod est verus ille Deus: adeoque verba Christi non hoc important, quod solus Pater sit verus ille Deus, sed quod Pater sit ille solus verus Deus, siue ille, qui solus verus Deus est. Quo non obstante filius Dei etiam verus Deus est, sicut expresse dicitur 1 Jo. V, 20. Hic (Filius) est verus ille Deus. Videtur enim verbum, ἗ιναι, per ellipsin esse omissum, aut per articulum, τὸν, insinuatum, vt sensus completus hic sit: Hæc est vita æterna, vt cognoscant, te, Pater, esse illum verum Deum, nedictio. Itaque Christus dicens, ἀμὴν λέγω, atque iterum ἀμὴν λέγω, primum iurat per se ipse, deinde & bene nobis dicit, per se itidem ipse.

7) Precatio, & eius quidem vtrumque genus: a) Adoratio, qua maiestatem Dei infinitamque excellentiam veneramur. Conf. Rom. XIV, 11. cum illo Ies. XLV, 23. 24. vbi Christus consideratur vt יהוה. Plurimum sane ponderis in hoc inest dicto, Apoc. V, 13. 14. in quo nervus probationis est quadruplex: (α) æterna laudis continuatio, quæ est pars quædam summæ religionis, εἰς τὸς ἀιῶνας τῶν ἀιώνων, (b) commune omnium rerum creatarum officium πᾶν κτίσμα, ὅ ἐστιν ἐν τῷ ὀρανῷ κ. τ. λ. vt ne angeli quidem excepti sint, Hebr. I, 6. quorum tamen nullus Christum veneratur vt suum liberatorem, Hebr. II, 16. E. vt Creatorem suum, & Conseruatorem, Hebr. I, 10; (γ) coagmentatio verborum maxime significans, ἡ ἐυλογία, καὶ ἡ τιμὴ, καὶ ἡ δόξα, καὶ τὸ κράτος, vt nihil sit reliquum, quod ad summam venerationem pertineat, (δ) coniunctio Filii cum Patre, vtpote pari honore digni, τῷ καθημένῳ ἐπὶ τῶ θρόνω, καὶ τῷ ἀρνίῳ. Quid superest, soli Patri reseruatum? Omnino nihil. b) Supplicatio, siue, vt vulgo dicitur, Inuocatio, qua benignitatem Dei imploramus, ac beneficia, diuinitus in nos conferenda, expetimus. Ea autem, quæ summo Deo vni decernenda est, supplicatio debet esse communis ac perpetua, Rom. X, 13. 14. Communis, &, quæ dici solet vniuerfalis, nominatur quadruplici ratione, quæ semper ad proprietates perfectionesque diuinas respicitur, ideoque est cultus religiosus (per definit.) Est nimirum vniuersitas (α) locorum, cuius ratio est immensa Dei præsentia ac scientia, (β) temporum, ad hanc pertinet æternitas Dei atque immutabilitas, (γ) supplicantium, huius fundamentum est cognitio summi Dei imperii, quod omnes ex Dei vnius arbitrio pendeant, (δ) rerum expetendarum, hæc nititur consideratione infinita in Deo & potentia, potestatisque, & bonitatis, Eph. III, 20 Atqui Christo non minus, quam Patri, tribuitur hæc supplicationis vniuersitas, ratione (α) locorum omnium, Matth. XVIII, 20. 1 Cor. I, 2. (β) temporum omnium, Thess. I, 11. & 12. (γ) supplicantium omnium, Rom. X, 13. 14. coll. cum v. 9. 10. 11. 12 (δ) rerum ac beneficiorum, partim largitio omnis boni, Io. XIV, 13. add. Pf. XXXVII, 5. vbi hoc dicitur Dei proprium, יהוה יעשׂה partim liberatio vacuitasque omnis mali, 2 Tim. IV, 18. Κύριον esse Christum, tum contextus declarat, v. 1. 8. 22. tum perpetua Paulli consuetudo sermonis, vid. 1 Cor. VIII, 6. & cum additur; &, quem misisti, Iesum Christum, praedicatum ex praecedentibus repetendum est hoc modo: Et, quem misisti, Iesum Christum, esse illum solum verum Deum; vt ita Pater & Filius dicantur esse ille solus verus Deus.


### Of God the Son: II. 1

II. 1

Cor. VIII, 6.

Paul says: To us however there is one (only true) God, the father from whom are all things, and we in him: And one (true) Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him.

Where Paul calls only the Father God.

Resp.

1) The apostle does not say: Only the Father is God; but thus: to us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things. One God is opposed not to the divine persons, but to the so-called gods, v. 5. who are so called either metaphorically and by analogy, as angels and magistrates, or catachrestically, and according to opinion, as the idols of the gentiles.

2) If from the fact that the Father is called one God, it were permitted to conclude that Christ is not one God: by the same reasoning from the fact that Christ is called one Lord, it would have to be inferred that God the Father is not one Lord. Thus the Father would be God, who would not be the Lord of all, and Christ would be Lord, who would be only a so-called god, by name, not by nature God.

Which are most alien to the Christian religion.

For the Father is Lord of heaven and earth, Matt. XI, 25. and Christ is true God, 1 John V, 20.

Objection: Christ is subordinated to God by the apostle: because from God are all things, through Christ all things are said to be.

'From' designates the principal cause, 'through' the less principal cause.

Resp.

The particles, 'from' and 'through', do not designate inequality, but the order of the divine persons.

Nor does the particle, 'through', always denote a less principal cause.

For from God, and through God are all things, Rom.

XI, 36. Through the Father are all things, Heb. II, 10. III.

Eph.

IV, 6. Paul says: One God and Father of all.

Where one God, and Father, signify the same subject. Therefore the one does not extend more broadly than the other, nor is anyone else that one God, than the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Resp.

1) If Father, and God, are equally broad here; the name of Father is not taken here personally, but essentially.

Which meaning is established from the fact that he is called Father of all. When it is taken personally, it precisely imports the relation to the only-begotten Son Christ.

But one God, as he is the father of all, is the whole Holy Trinity. Whence it may be conceded that one God, and Father of all, extend equally broadly here.

2) If it should even be posited that the name of Father is taken here personally, yet one God is not opposed to the Son of God; since he is true God, 1 John V, 20. but is opposed to creatures, and false gods.

Objection: But one God is openly distinguished from one Lord, and one Spirit, v. 4. 5.

Therefore the Father is God, Christ is Lord, and the Spirit is our Sanctifier.

Resp.

…The adversaries wrongly oppose one God, one Lord, one Spirit by reason of essence: and that against the mind of Paul, who distinguishes them by reason of person, and of the actions which are appropriated to them: Otherwise it would follow that the Father is not the Spirit, because there is one Spirit v. 4. nor that he himself is the Lord because there is one Lord v. 5. But that is false, see John IV, 24. That too is false, see Matthew XI, 25. IV. The Father alone knows the day and the extreme hour. Therefore, the Father alone is the true God. The reasoning of the consequence is evident: Because omniscience, to which the knowledge of the extreme day pertains, is an attribute of the true God. The antecedent is made clear from Mark XIII, 32. Of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels who are in heaven, XIII, 32. Of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels who are in heaven, nor the son himself, but the father alone. Resp. The particle 'alone' here excludes creatures from the participation of the foreknowledge of the extreme day, and the Son himself, as man in the state of emptying, in which he had voluntarily abdicated the universal and incessant exercise of divine omniscience; but it does not exclude the Holy Spirit and the Son, as God; since he knows all things, John XXI, 17. V. Whoever is distinguished by the name of God from the Son and the Holy Spirit, he alone is the supreme God. But God the Father &c. Therefore. The minor is clear from 1 Cor. XII, 6. There is one God, who works all things in all. The Son is called Lord v. 5. The Holy Spirit is absolutely called spirit v. 4. But the Father alone is called God. Resp. In the cited place the name of God is taken ὑποσατικῶς, personally, and διακριτικῶς, distinctively, because he is distinguished from the Son and the Holy Spirit as the first person of the divinity, so that nevertheless ὁσιωδῶς, essentially, the Son, as also the Holy Spirit, are also that same God, working all things in all. VI. Whoever is that God, between whom and men Christ is the mediator; he alone is the supreme God. But Christ is the mediator between God the Father and men. E. The minor is evident from 1 Tim. II, 5. Resp. By God in the cited place is understood the triune God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Instance: If in the cited place by God is understood the triune God, Christ will be the mediator of himself, although the mediator is clearly distinguished from God. Resp. 1) Christ is not the whole SS. Trinity, although he is one of the SS. Trinity. 2) Christ is not the mediator of himself, insofar as he is one with the Father and the Holy Spirit, the offended God, but insofar as he is θεάνθρωπος, solving the offense, according to that: God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not imputing their sins to them, 2 Cor. V, 19. 3) The mediator is distinguished from God by reason of person and office, not by reason of divine essence. VII. If the Father alone sits on the throne of divine majesty, he alone is the supreme God. The antecedent is true. Therefore also the consequent. The reason for the consequence is; because the supreme God occupies the highest throne of divine majesty. The antecedent is proved from Dan. VII, 9. Apoc. IV, 5. Resp. a) In general: Parabolic theology is not argumentative. b) In particular: From the vision of the Father alone on the throne to the negation of the divinity of the Son does not follow, etc. For an apparition is of free termination, and thus can be of one or more persons. Although God is three in persons, he can nevertheless in some vision be represented not as three, but as one because of the unity of essence, power, glory and majesty. Christ says of himself: I sat down with my Father in his throne, Apoc. III, 21. (*). VIII. Whoever is alone ἀυτόθεος, he alone is the supreme God. But God the Father &c. Therefore. The major is evident; because ἀυτόθεος is he who is God from himself. To be from himself is proper to the supreme God. The minor is clear, because God the Father received his essence from no one, he is truly called ἀυτόθεος, i.e. God existing from himself. Resp. The Greek word ἀυτόθεος is not biblical, but ecclesiastical, used first by ORIGEN tom. II. in John fol. 272. citing HÜLSEMANN in breu.

p. 137. We could safely abstain from this word. But truly, since dissenters impugn the divinity of Christ from this ecclesiastical word, its force of meaning must be accurately weighed. Since αὐτός means 'itself' and θεός means 'God', the ecclesiastical term αὐτόθεος can be explained in two ways, so as to denote a) him who is God by himself, or in himself. Thus the Son of God (as also the Holy Spirit) is αὐτόθεος, God by himself, or in himself. For just as the Father has life in himself: so also he has given to the Son to have life in himself, John 5:26. b) So as to designate him who is God from himself. But just as being from oneself either signifies the negation of dependence on another, as an efficient cause, or the negation of all origin and personal procession: so αὐτόθεος is called God from himself as an independent God. In which sense the Son of God is rightly called αὐτόθεος; because he is a being, just as the Father is, independent. For to depend signifies to be from another, as an efficient cause, in a diversity of nature. But the Father in divine matters is not the cause of the Son, but only a non-causal principle through eternal generation: nor is there a diversity of nature between the Father and the Son, but a most singular unity. αὐτόθεος is called God unoriginated. Thus only the Father is αὐτόθεος, God from himself, i. e., having origin from no one. The Son, through generation from the Father, and the Holy Spirit, through procession from the Father and the Son, have the communicated divine essence. Nor yet is the supreme divinity of the Son or the Holy Spirit rightly impugned by this. For to be from oneself is proper to the supreme God, insofar as it denies causal dependence on another; but insofar as it denies all origin or personal procession, it is the notion γνωριστικὴ (distinctive) of the first divine person. It remains, therefore, fixed and settled that the Son of God is αὐτόθεος, who is God from himself and in himself, because Jehovah is independent and eternal. Nor was EPIPHANIUS wrong when he called the Son of God αὐτοτέλειον καὶ αὐτόθεον (self-perfect and self-God). Haer.

LXIX. Instantia I The Fathers of the Council of Nicaea called the Son God from God, and thus denied that he is αὐτόθεος, God from himself. Resp. By the very fact that the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea said God from God, they indicated that he is from the Father not by way of dependence, as creatures are, but by way of origin and ὁμοοσίας (consubstantiality), otherwise they would not have called him God from God. The same men accepted the word 'God' not essentially, but personally. Conf. 2 Cor. 13:13, 1 Tim. 3:16.

Conf. 2 Cor. 13:13, 1 Tim. 3:16. Instantia II God the Father seems to be God κατ' ἐξοχὴν (by preeminence), because he is a) the fountain of deity; b) because the reason of the giver is stronger than that of the receiver; just as if a king were to give power equal to his own in the kingdom to his son. Resp. The fountain and principle, before the principled, has ἐξοχὴν (preeminence) or prerogative, if it be distinguished from this essentially. But the three divine persons are of one singular essence, and thus of one excellence and majesty.

Instantia III It could not be inappropriately distinguished between an axiom ὑποστατικὸν (hypostatic), or personal, and φυσικὸν (physical) or natural. Although the Son of God possesses the same majesty with the heavenly Father, if you look at the same divine nature; yet by reason of person he seems a prior, more worthy, and more eminent God. Which personal eminence of the Father some doctors of the primitive church asserted, according to DIONYS. PETAV. L. II. de trinitat cap. II. §. XI. Resp. 'Eξοχὴ (preeminence), excellence, and majesty of God is a divine essential attribute, not personal. Hence where a diversity of ἐξοχῆς (preeminence), ἀξιώματος (dignity) and worthiness is asserted; there a diversity of essence is believed. And where there is a prerogative, there is inequality. But the Son (the same must be thought of the Holy Spirit) is ὁμοούσιος (consubstantial) with the Father, John 10:30. equal, John 5:18. having all things which the Father has, John 16:15. We do not imitate the 'Ακυρολογίαν (empty talk) of the Fathers.

Latin:

II. 1

Cor. VIII, 6. inquit Paullus: Nobis tamen unus (tantum verus) Deus est, pater ex quo omnia, & nos in ipsum: Et unus (verus) Dominus Iesus Christus, per quem omnia, & nos per ipsum.

Vbi Paullus solum Patrem Deum appellat.

Resp.

1) Non dicit apostolus: Solus Pater est Deus; sed ita: nobis unus est Deus, Pater, ex quo omnia.

Vnus Deus opponitur non personis diuinis, sed θεοῖς λεγομένοις, v. 5. qui ita dicuntur vel metaphorice & κατ' ἀναλογίαν, vt angeli & magistratus, vel catachrestice, & κατὰ δόξαν, vt idola gentium.

2) Si ex eo, quod Pater dicitur unus Deus, colligere liceret, Christum non esse unum Deum: pari ratione ex eo, quod Christus dicitur unus dominus, inferendum esset, Deum Patrem non esse unum Dominum.

Foret itaque Pater Deus, qui non esset omnium Dominus, & Christus foret Dominus, qui tantum θεὸς λεγόμενος, nomine, non natura esset Deus. Quae a religione christiana sunt alienissima.

Nam Pater est Dominus caeli & terrae, Matth.

XI, 25. & Christus est verus Deus, 1 Io. V, 20.

Instantia: Christus Deo ab apostolo subordinatur: quia ex Deo omnia, per Christum omnia esse dicuntur.

Ex, caussam principalem, per, caussam minus principalem designant.

Resp.

Particulae, ex, & per, non inaequalitatem, sed ordinem personarum diuinarum designant.

Neque particula, per, semper caussam minus principalem notat.

Nam ex Deo, & per Deum sunt omnia, Rom.

XI, 36. Per Patrem sunt omnia. Hebr. II, 10.

III. Eph. IV, 6. inquit Paullus: Vnus Deus & Pater omnium.

Vbi Deus unus, & Pater, idem subiectum significant. Ergo alterum altero latius non patet, nec quisquam alius est Deus ille unus, quam Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi.

Resp.

1) Si Pater, & Deus, aeque late hic patent; nomen patris hic non sumitur personaliter, sed essentialiter.

Quae significatio stabilitur ex eo, quod dicitur Pater omnium. Personaliter cum accipitur, praecise importat relationem ad Filium vnigenitum Christum.

At Deus unus, prout est pater omnium, est tota SS. Trinitas.

Vnde Deum vnum, & Patrem omnium, patere hic aeque late, concedi potest.

2) Si vel maxime ponatur, nomen Patris hic sumi personaliter, non tamen unus Deus opponitur Filio Dei; quippe qui verus Deus est, 1 Io.

V, 20. sed opponitur creaturis, falsisque diis. Instantia: Sed unus Deus aperte distinguitur ab vno Domino, & vno Spiritu, v. 4. 5.

Ergo Pater Deus, Christus Dominus, & Sanctificator noster Spiritus est.

Resp. Aduersarii male opponunt vnum Deum, vnum Dominum, vnum Spiritum ratione essentiae: idque praeter mentem Paulli, qui eos distinguit ratione personae, & actionum, quae eis appropriantur: Alias sequeretur, Patrem non esse Spiritum, quia unus est Spiritus v. 4. nec ipsum esse Dominum, num, quia vnus Dominus v. 5. At falsum est illud, vid. Io. IV, 24. Falsum & istud, vid. Matth. XI, 25. IV. Solus Pater nouit diem & horam extremam. Ergo solus Pater est verus Deus. Ratio consequentiá est euidens: Quia omniscientia, ad quam pertinet notitia diei extremi, est attributum veri Dei. Antecedens patescit ex Marc. XIII, 32. De die illo ac hora nemo scit, ne angeli quidem, qui in cœlo sunt, nec ipse filius, sed solus pater. Resp. Particula solus hic a participatione præscientiæ extremi diei excludit creaturas, & ipsum Filium, qua hominem in statu exinanitionis, in quo vniuersali & incessanti exercitio omniscientiæ diuinæ se sponte abdicauerat; non autem excludit Spiritum S. & Filium, qua Deum; quippe qui nouit omnia, Io. XXI, 17. V. Quicunque nomine Dei a Filio & Spiritu S. distinguitur, is solus est summus Deus. Atqui Deus Pater &c. Ergo. Minor liquet ex 1 Cor. XII, 6. Vnus est Deus, qui operatur omnia in omnibus. Filius vocatur dominus v. 5. Spiritus S. absolute dicitur spiritus v. 4. Sed solus Pater appellatur Deus. Resp. Loco citato nomen Dei accipitur ὑποσατικῶς, personaliter, & διακριτικῶς, discretiue, quod distinguatur a Filio & Spiritu S. tanquam prima diuinitatis persona, vt nihilominus ὁσιωδῶς, essentialiter, Filius, vt & Spiritus S. etiam sint idem ille Deus, operans omnia in omnibus. VI. Quicunque est Deus ille, inter quem & homines Christus mediator est; ille solus est summus Deus. Atqui inter Deum Patrem & homines Christus mediator est. E. Minor constat ex 1 Tim. II, 5. Resp. Per Deum l. c. intelligitur Deus triunus, Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. Instantia: Si l. c. per Deum intelligitur Deus triunus, Christus sui ipsius mediator erit, cum tamen mediator a Deo manifesto distinguatur. Resp. 1) Christus non est tota SS. Trinitas, quamuis vnus sit e SS. Trinitate. 2) Christus non est mediator sui ipsius, quatenus est vnus cum Patre & Spiritu S. Deus offensus, sed quatenus est θεάνθρωπος offensam soluens, iuxta illud: Deus erat in Christo mundum sibi reconcilians, non imputans illis peccata, 2 Cor. V, 19. 3) Distinguitur mediator a Deo ratione personæ & officii, non ratione essentiæ diuinæ. VII. Si solus Pater sedet in throno maiestatis diuinæ, ipse solus summus Deus est. Antecedens est verum. Ergo & consequens. Ratio consequentiæ est; quia summus Deus celsissimum maiestatis diuinæ thronum obtinet. Antecedens probatur ex Dan. VII, 9. Apoc. IV, 5. Resp. a) In genere: Theologia parabolica non est argumentatiua. b) In specie: A solius Patris visione in throno ad negationem diuinitatis Filii non v. c. Apparitio enim liberæ est terminationis, adeoque vnius pluriumue personarum esse potest. Quamuis Deus in personis trinus sit, potest tamen in aliqua visione non vt trinus, sed tanquam vnus repræsentari ob vnitatem essentiæ, potentiæ, gloriæ & maiestatis. Christus de seipso dicit: Consedi cum Patre meo in throno ipsius, Apoc. III, 21. (*). VIII. Quicunque solus est ἀυτόθεος, is solus est summus Deus. Atqui Deus Pater &c. Ergo. Maior constat; quia ἀυτόθεος est, qui a seipso Deus est. Esse a seipso summi Dei proprium est. Minor liquet, quia Deus Pater a nullo essentiam suam accepit, vere dicitur ἀυτόθεος, i. e. Deus a se ipso existens. Resp. Vox græca ἀυτόθεος non est biblica, sed ecclesiastica, vsurpata primum ab ORIGENE tom. II. in Ioan. fol. 272. citante HÜLSEMANNO in breu.

p. 137. Possemus ab hac voce tuto abstinere. At vero cum dissidentes ex hac voce ecclesiastica deitatem Christi impugnent, eius vis significandi accurate pensitanda est. Cum αὐτὸς ipsum, θεὸς Deum significet, terminus ecclesiasticus αὐτόθεος bifariam exponi potest, vt notet a) eum, qui seipso, aut in seipso Deus est. Sic Filius Dei (vt & Spiritus S.) est αὐτόθεος seipso, aut in seipso Deus. Sicut enim Pater vitam habet in seipso: ita & Filio dedit vitam habere in seipso, Io. V, 26. b) Vt designet eum, qui a seipso Deus est. Sicut autem esse a seipso, vel dicit negationem dependentiæ ab alio, tanquam causa efficiente, vel negationem omnis originis & processionis personalis: ita αὐτόθεος Deus a seipso dicitur Deus independens. Quo sensu Filius Dei recte dicitur αὐτόθεος; quia ens est, æque ac Pater, independens. Dependere enim significat esse ab alio, tanquam causa efficiente, in diversitate naturæ. At Pater in diuinis non est causa Filii, sed tantum principium non causale per æternam generationem: nec inter Patrem & Filium est diversitas naturæ, sed vnitas singularissima. αὐτόθεος vocatur Deus inoriginatus. Sic solus Pater est αὐτόθεος Deus a seipso, i. e. a nullo habens originem. Filius per generationem, a Patre, Spiritus S. per processionem, a Patre & Filio communicatam essentiam diuinam habet. Neque tamen eo recte impugnatur summa diuinitas Filii aut Spiritus S. Nam esse a seipso est proprium summi Dei, quatenus negat dependentiam causalem ab alio; at quatenus negat omnem originem aut processionem personalem, notio γνωριστικὴ primæ personæ diuinæ est. Ratum igitur fixumque manet, Filium Dei esse αὐτόθεον, qui a seipso & in seipso Deus est, quia Iehouah independens & æternus est. Neque falsus fuit EPIPHANIVS, cum Filium Dei appellauit αὐτοτέλειον καὶ αὐτόθεον. Hæres.

LXIX. Instantia I Patres concilii Nicæni vocarunt Filium Deum de Deo, adeoque negarunt, illum esse αὐτόθεον, Deum a se ipso. Resp. Eo ipso, quo Patres concilii Nicæni dixerunt Deum de Deo, indigitarunt, illum esse a Patre non per modum dependentiæ, vt sunt creaturæ, sed per modum originis, & ὁμοοσίας, alias non vocassent eum Deum de Deo.
