Acceperunt iidem vocem, Deus, non essentialiter, sed personaliter. Conf. 2 Cor. XIII, 13. 1 Tim. III, 16.

Instantia II Deus Pater videtur esse Deus κατ' ἐξοχὴν, quia est a) fons deitatis; b) quia potior est ratio dantis, quam accipientis; veluti, si rex parem sibi potestatem in regno det filio. Resp. Fons & principium præ principiato habet ἐξοχὴν excellentiam, aut prærogatiuam, si ab hoc essentialiter distinguatur. At tres personæ diuinæ sunt vnius essentiæ singularis, adeoque vnius excellentiæ & maiestatis.

Instantia III Haud incongrue distingui posset inter axioma ὑποστατικὸν, siue personale, & φυσικὸν siue naturale. Quamuis Filius Dei cum Patre cœlesti eadem polleat maiestate, si spectes eandem naturam diuinam; attamen ratione personæ prior, dignior & eminentior Deus videtur. Quam eminentiam personalem Patris asseruerunt nonnulli doctores primitiuæ ecclesiæ apud DIONYS. PETAV. L. II. de trinitat cap. II. §. XI. Resp. 'Eξοχὴ, excellentia & maiestas Dei est attributum diuinum essentiale, non personale. Hinc vbi diuersitas ἐξοχῆς, ἀξιώματος & dignitatis asseritur; ibi diuersitas essentiæ creditur. Et vbi prærogatiua est, ibi est inæqualitas. At Filius (idem sentiendum de Spiritu S.) est Patri ὁμοούσιος Io. X, 30. æqualis Io. V, 18. habens omnia, quæ Pater habet, Io. XVI, 15. 'Ακυρολογίαν Patrum non imitamur.


### Of God the Son: Argumenta posterioris classis by which they directly impugn the supreme divinity of the Son of God, are the following: 1

Argumenta posterioris classis by which they directly impugn the supreme divinity of the Son of God, are the following: 1.

Whoever is distinguished from the supreme God is not the supreme God. But Christ, etc. E. The minor is proved from John 1:2. Where the hypostatic Word, which is Christ, is said to have been with God. Resp. Christ is distinguished from God the Father by reason of person and office, not by reason of divine essence.

Objection I: It is necessary that the substance of the Father be one thing, and that of the Son another. Resp. It suffices that they are two persons.

Objection II: The Son is posterior to the Father in time, and therefore of a different essence from him. Resp. The Son is posterior to the Father in time in human affairs, not in divine. For in human affairs the Son is born in time, and has a nature different in number than the Father. But the Son of God is begotten from eternity, and has the same essence in number with the Father.

II. The supreme God can do all things of himself. The Son of God cannot &c. Therefore. The major is evident; because the supreme God is as he is from himself: so from himself he has the force and most free power of acting. The minor is proved from John 5:19. The Son can do nothing of himself, unless he sees the Father doing it. Resp. 1) That phrase: to do of himself, can be taken in a double sense: one, so that it imports simply the negation of all origin whatsoever, so that the sense becomes: that supreme God can do all things of himself, so that he acknowledges no origin at all, from which he might have the power and knowledge of acting. In the other, so that to do of himself imports the negation of dependence in acting upon another superior cause, and the sense becomes: that supreme God can do all things of himself, that is, independently of another superior cause. In the former sense the major proposition is not universally true, but proceeds only concerning the Father. In the latter sense the minor is denied. When therefore Christ says: Can the Son do anything of himself, unless he sees the Father doing it? then his words are to be taken in the former sense, not in the latter, and their meaning is: the Son, as he is from the Father through eternal generation, and receives from the Father the same power and knowledge of acting that the Father has; so he can do nothing of himself, and apart from the Father, but whatever he does, he does simultaneously with the Father. 2) Nor is his supreme divinity rightly impugned from the words of Christ: unless he sees the Father doing it. For the Son does not do nothing unless he sees the Father doing it, as a disciple, but as the Son: but if as the Son, he certainly has that concurrence of operation not through information, but through eternal generation. Since therefore the divine essence and knowledge are identified; it follows that he who receives the essence from the Father through generation, also receives knowledge from the same. Consequently, the Son can do nothing of himself because of the unity of both power and knowledge with the Father: which unity is an argument for the divine ὁμοουσίας (consubstantiality).

III. Whoever is sent by God, he is not the supreme God. But the Son of God &c. Therefore. The major is evident; because a superior sends an inferior. The minor is proved from John 3:17. Resp. The Son of God was sent by the Father not by command, but with consent. But a mission which occurs with consent does not imply the right of a superior. For a friend can send a friend of the same dignity.

IV. Whoever does not come of himself, is not the supreme God. Christ did not come of himself. Therefore. The major is evident; for the reason that the arrival of him who does not come of himself depends upon another. The minor is proved from John 7:28, ch. 8:42. Resp. In the cited places Christ, as the God-man (Θεάνθρωπος), speaks of his arrival to the prophetic office, to which he did not come of himself, by arrogating to himself the office of prophet against the will of the Father, or by thrusting himself into the office, but he was sent by the Father by that mission which occurs with consent.

Objection I: The supreme God does nothing by an alien will. Resp. Nor does the Son of God do anything by an alien will: for the will of the Father is the will of the Son.

Objection II: Christ denies that he came to do his own will, John 5:30. Resp. The words of Christ are to be understood not in the divided sense, but in the composite sense, with the exclusive particle, only, understood. Christ came, not that he might do only his own will, but that he might do the will of himself and of the Father, since the same will is made of both.

Objection III: Christ subjects his own will to the Father. Matthew 26:39. Resp. Christ subjects to the Father his human will, which indeed is not contrary to the divine will, yet is distinct from it.

V. If Christ were the supreme God, He could seek His own glory. But He did not seek His own glory. Therefore. The consequence of the major is clear; because to God supreme honor and supreme glory belong. The minor is proved from John 8:50. Response: 1) Christ in the cited passage speaks not from His own sense, but from the sense of His adversaries. For the Jews were slandering Him, that He was seeking glory with a certain arrogance. But Christ denies that He, stimulating vain ambition, was hunting for glory. 2) The words of Christ can also be taken in a composite or conjunctive sense, with the exclusive particle understood, i.e., alone. As if to say: I do not seek my glory alone, but my Father seeks it, since the glory of both is one and common.

VI. The supreme God is κατ' ἐξοχὴν (by preeminence) good. Christ is not, etc. Therefore. The minor is proved from the words of Christ, Matthew 19:17. Why do you call me good? No one is good except one, God. Response: The words of Christ contain a response κατ' ἄνθρωπον (according to man), by which Christ answers according to the mind of the questioning youth, who had called Christ good in no other sense than he would have called any other teacher who had not been sent by God. Intending to correct this man, Christ answers: Why do you call me good, whom you believe to be neither God nor sent by God? No one is good by essence except one, God: nor does he deserve to be called a teacher who is not sent by God. Wherefore, either stop calling me good, or believe that I am the θεάνθρωπον (God-man), true God, and a true teacher sent by God.

VII. Christ is not the first author of His own doctrine. Therefore He is not the supreme God. The antecedent is evident from John 7:16. My doctrine is not mine, but His who sent me. Response: The sense of Christ's words is: My doctrine is not only mine, but also the Father's; whom the Jews were separating from the Son, and were judging Christ to be a mere man, who ought to have learned letters like others. Intending to answer these, He shows His doctrine to be plainly divine, not drawn from the instruction of teachers.

VIII. The supreme God is the ultimate scope of faith, and its principal object. But Christ is not, etc. Therefore. The minor is proved from the words of Christ, John 12:44. He who believes in me, does not believe in me, but in Him who sent me. Response: The sense is: He who believes in me, does not only believe in me, but also in Him who sent me.

IX. The Father is greater than Christ, John 14:28. Therefore Christ is not the greatest God. Response: The Father is greater than Christ as the emptied man, or viewed in the state of exinanition. But Christ, as God, is equal to the Father, John 5:18, and is ὁμοούσιος (consubstantial), John 10:30.

X. God the Father is called the God and head of Christ, John 20:17, 1 Cor. 11:3. Therefore Christ is not the supreme God. Response: In the cited passages, it is a matter of Christ as man.

XI. Christ is of God, 1 Cor. 3:23. Therefore God is lesser. Response: Christ is said to be of God, either as man; or if He be said to be of God absolutely and simply, it must be taken by reason of generation, mission, and destination to an office; which also befit Christ, as the second person, because of His origin from the Father. In whichever way He is said to be of God, nothing will be lost from His eternal deity thereby.

XII. He in whose power and will all things are not, he is not the supreme God. All things are not in the power of Christ. Therefore. The minor is proved from Matthew 20:23. To sit at my right hand and my left is not mine to give, except to those for whom it has been given by the Father. Response: By the cited words, Christ does not derogate from Himself the power of giving a prerogative in the kingdom of grace or glory, but only limits the object. For the genuine sense is: To sit at the right and left is not mine to give (to others), except to those for whom it has been prepared. But thus neither does the Father bestow any prerogative in His kingdom on others than those on whom He has decreed from eternity to bestow it.

XIII. Objection: But Christ says that He would give according to the will of the Father. Response: The will of the Father and of Christ is one. For as the Father raises the dead and quickens them: so also the Son quickens whom He wills. John 5:21.

XIII. All things are given to Christ by the Father. Therefore He is not the supreme God, to whom nothing can be given; the antecedent is proved from John 3:35, 5:22. Response: By the giving kat' eso [inwardly], or through eternal generation, the divinity of Christ is not diminished: but the giving kat' exo [outwardly], or temporal, pertains to Christ according to His humanity.

XIV. Christ received commands from the Father, John 10:18, 12:49, and obeyed God, Rom. 5:19, Phil. 2:8. Therefore He is not the supreme God. Response: Christ, not as God, but as man, assuming the form of a servant, received commands from the Father and obeyed Him.

XV. If Christ were the supreme God, He would certainly have glorified Himself, so that He might become a high priest. But He did not glorify Himself, Heb. 5: 5. Therefore. Response: From a statement in a qualified sense to a statement in an unqualified sense is a fallacy.

In the cited passage, it is not denied unqualifiedly that Christ glorified Himself, but it is only denied that Christ glorified Himself in the way that autokletoi [self-called ones] glorify themselves, who, not sent by God, thrust themselves into offices and take the honor of the office to themselves by their own daring: whereas Christ was indeed called and glorified by the Father so that He might become a high priest, although the glorification of Himself, which was from the Father, was also from Himself, as God. XVI. The supreme God does not hand over His kingdom to another, by laying it down and abdicating His right to rule. Christ will hand over the kingdom to the Father, by laying it down and abdicating His right. Therefore Christ is not the supreme God. The minor premise is clear from 1 Cor. 15: 24. Response: That the supreme God, as such, hands over His kingdom to no one, is true.

But the theanthropos [God-man], or supreme God, manifested in the flesh, will hand over the kingdom to the Father, by ceasing from a certain form of government administered through the Word and sacraments, not by laying down royal power; since it is established from the Scriptures that the kingdom of Christ is eternal, Dan. 7:14, Luke 1:33.

Latin:

Argumenta posterioris classis quibus summam diuinitatem Filii Dei directe impugnant, sunt sequentia: 1.

Quicunque a summo Deo distinguitur, is non est summus Deus. Atqui Christus &c. E. Minor prob. ex Io. I, 2. Vbi Verbum hypostaticum, quod est Christus, dicitur fuisse apud Deum. Resp. Christus a Deo Patre distinguitur ratione personæ, & officii, non ratione essentiæ diuinæ.

Instantia I: Necesse est, ut alia sit substantia Patris, alia Filii. Resp. Sufficit, quod duae sint personae.

Instantia II: Filius est Patre posterior tempore, adeoque diversae ab hoc essentiae. Resp. Filius in humanis, non in divinis, Patre posterior est tempore. In humanis enim Filius natus est in tempore, aliamque numero habet naturam, quam Pater. At Filius Dei genitus est ab aeterno, eandemque numero essentiam cum Patre habet.

II. Summus Deus potest omnia a seipso facere. Filius Dei non potest &c. Ergo. Major est evidens; quia summus Deus ut a seipso est: ita a se ipso habet vim & potestatem liberimam agendi. Minor prob. ex Io. V, 19. Non potest Filius facere a se quidquam, nisi quod viderit Patrem facere. Resp. 1) Phrasis illa: a se ipso facere, potest duplici sensu accipi, uno, vt importet simpliciter negationem omnis plane originis, ita vt sensus fit: Deus ille summus omnia a se facere potest, vt nullam prorsus agnoscat originem, vnde potentiam & scientiam operandi habeat. Altero, vt a se facere importet negationem dependentiae in operando ab alia superiori causa, & sensus fit: Deus ille summus omnia a se ipso, id est, independenter ab alia superiori causa, facere potest. Priori sensu maior propositio non est vniuersaliter vera, sed de solo Patre procedit. Posteriori sensu negatur minor. Quando itaque Christus dicit: Num potest a se Filius quidquam facere, nisi quod viderit Patrem facere? tum in priori sensu accipienda sunt illius verba, non in posteriori, estque illorum mens: Filius, vt per aeternam generationem a Patre est, & eandem operandi potentiam & scientiam, quam Pater habet, a Patre accipit; ita nihil facere potest a se, & seorsum a Patre, sed quidquid facit, simul cum Patre facit. 2) Neque ex Verbis Christi: nisi quod viderit Patrem facere, summa illius diuinitas recte impugnatur. Non enim Filius nihil facere, nisi viderit Patrem facientem, ut discipulus, sed ut Filius: Si autem ut Filius, sane habet illam operationis concurrentiam non per informationem, sed per aeternam generationem. Cum itaque essentia & scientia diuina identificentur; consequitur, ut qui essentiam accipit a Patre per generationem, ab eodem quoque accipiat scientiam. Proinde Filius nihil facere potest a seipso ob vnitatem tum potentiae, tum scientiae, cum Patre: quae vnitas ὁμοουσίας diuinae argumentum est.

III. Quicunque missus est a Deo, is non est summus Deus. At Filius Dei &c. E. Major patet; quia superior mittit inferiorem. Minor probatur ex Io. III, 17. Resp. Missus est Filius Dei a Patre non per imperium, sed cum consensu. At missio, quae fit cum consensu, non infert ius superioris. Amicus enim amicum eiusdem dignitatis mittere potest.

IV. Quicunque a se ipso non venit, summus Deus non est. Christus a se ipso non venit. Ergo. Major est evidens; ideo, quod aduentus illius, qui a seipso non venit, ab alio dependet. Minor prob. ex Io. VII, 28. c. VIII, 42. Resp. Locis citatis loquitur Christus Θεάνθρωπος de aduentu suo ad officium propheticum, ad quod non venit a seipso, contra voluntatem Patris munus prophetae sibi arrogando, aut in officium se ingerendo, sed missus est a Patre missione illa, quae fit cum consensu.

Instantia I: Summus Deus nihil facit voluntate aliena. Resp. Nec Filius Dei quidquam facit voluntate aliena: voluntas enim Patris est voluntas Filii.

Instantia II: Christus negat, se venisse, vt voluntatem suam faceret, Io. V, 30. Resp. Verba Christi intelligenda sunt non in sensu opposito, sed composito, subintellecta particula exclusiva, tantum. Christus venit, non vt tantum suam, sed vt suam patrisque voluntatem faceret, cum vtriusque eadem fit voluntas.

Instantia III: Christus voluntatem suam Patri subiicit. Matth. XXVI, 39. Resp. Christus subiicit patri voluntatem suam humanam, quae quidem non est contraria voluntati divinae, ab eadem tamen diuersa.

V. Si Christus esset summus Deus, suam posset quaerere gloriam. At non quaesivit gloriam suam. E. Maioris consequentia est clara; quia Deo summus honor, summa gloria competit. Minor prob. ex Io. VIII, 50. Resp. 1) Christus l. c. loquitur non ex suo, sed adversariorum suorum sensu. Iudaei enim calumniabantur, eum rex arrogantia quadem quaerere gloriam. At negat Christus, se vana stimulantem ambitione aucupari gloriam. 2) Possunt verba Christi etiam accipi sensu composito, vel coniunctivo, subintellecta particula exclusiva, solus q. d. Ego non quaero gloriam meam solus, sed Pater meus quaerit eam, cum utriusque una & communis sit gloria.

VI. Supremus Deus est κατ' ἐξοχὴν bonus. Christus non est &c. E. Minor probatur ex verbis Christi, Matth. XIX, 17. Cur me dicis bonum? nullus bonus est, nisi unus Deus. Resp. Verba Christi continent responsionem κατ' ἄνθρωπον, qua Christus respondet secundum mentem interrogantis iuvenis, qui Christum non alio sensu bonum appellaverat, quam appellasset quemuis alium magister, qui a Deo non esset missus. Hunc correcturus Christus respondet: Cur me vocas bonum, quem nec Deum, nec a Deo missum esse credis? Nullus bonus est per essentiam, nisi unus Deus: nec dici meretur magister, qui a Deo non est missus. Quare aut define me vocare bonum, aut crede, me esse θεάνθρωπον, verum Deum, & verum doctorem a Deo missum.

VII. Christus non est primus doctrinae suae auctor. Ergo non est supremus Deus. Antecedens constat ex Io. VII, 16. Mea doctrina non est mea, sed eius, qui misit me. Resp. Sensus verborum Christi est: Doctrina mea non est tantum mea, sed & Patris; quem Iudaei a Filio separabant, Christumque nudum hominem esse, qui instar aliorum litteras discere debuisset, arbitrabantur. His responsurus, ostendit doctrinam suam esse plane divinam, non haustam ex informatione praeceptorum.

VIII. Deus summus est ultimus fidei scopus, eiusque obiectum principale. Sed Christus non est &c. E. Minor probatur ex verbis Christi, Io. XII, 44. Qui in me credit, non in me credit, sed in eum, qui misit me. Resp. Sensus est: Qui in me credit, non tantum in me credit, sed etiam in eum, qui misit me.

IX. Pater Christo maior est, Io. XIV, 28. Ergo Christus non est Deus maximus. Resp. Pater Christo homine exinanito, sive in statu exinanitionis spectato maior est. At Christus, qua Deus, Patri aequalis, Io. V, 18. & ὁμοούσιος est, Io. X, 30.

X. Deus Pater dicitur Deus & caput Christi, Io. XX, 17. 1 Cor. XI, 3. E. Christus non est summus Deus. Resp. In locis citatis agitur de Christo, qua homine.

XI. Christus est Dei, 1 Cor. III, 23. Ergo Deus minor est. Resp. Christus dicitur esse Dei, vel qua homo; vel si absolute & simpliciter Dei esse dicatur, ratione generationis, missionis & destinationis ad officium id accipiendum erit; quae conveniunt etiam Christo, ut secundae personae, ob eius originem a Patre. Vtro modo dicatur Dei esse, eterne ipsius deitati nihil inde decedet.

XII. In cuius potestate & arbitrio non sunt omnia, ille non est summus Deus. In potestate Christi non sunt omnia. E. Minor probatur ex Matth. XX, 23. Sedere ad dextram meam, & sinistram meam, non meum est dare, nisi iis, quibus datum est a Patre. Resp. Verbis citatis non derogat Christus sibi potentiam dandi praerogativam in regno gratiae, aut gloriae, sed obiectum tantum limitat. Sensus enim genuinus est: Sedere ad dextram & sinistram non est meum dare (aliis), nisi iis, quibus id paratum est. At sic nec Pater aliis, quam quibus ab aeterno dare decrevit, ullam praerogativam in regno suo largitur.

XIII. Instantia: Sed Christus ad Patris fui arbitrium se daturum esse, dicit. Resp. Arbitrium Patris & Christi, est unum. Quemadmodum enim Pater suscitat mortuos & vivificat: ita etiam Filius, quos vult, vivificat. Io. V, 21. viuificat. Io. V, 21.

Omnia Christo a Patre sunt data. Ergo non est summus Deus, cui dari nihil potest, antecedens prob. ex Io. III, 35. c. V, 22. Resp. Datione κατ' ἔσω, siue per aeternam generationem, diuinitas Christi non imminuitur: Datio autem κατ' ἔξω, siue temporalis Christo secundum humanitatem competit.

XIV. Christus mandata a Patre accepit, Io. X, 18. c. XII, 49. & obediuit Deo, Rom. V, 19. Phil. II, 8. Ergo non est summus Deus. Resp. Christus non qua Deus, sed qua homo, affluenta forma ferui, mandata a Patre accepit, & eidem obediuit.

XV. Si Christus summus Deus esset, vtique seipsum glorificasset, vt pontifex fieret. Sed se ipsum non glorificauit, Hebr. V, 5. E. Resp. A dicto secundum quid, ad dictum simpliciter non v. c.

In loco citato non negatur simpliciter, Christum se ipsum glorificasse, sed negatur tantum, Christum se glorificasse eo modo, quo se glorificant αὐτόκλητοι, qui non missi a Deo, sese in officia ingerunt, & muneris honorem proprio ausu sibi sumunt: cum Christus vtique a Patre vocatus & glorificatus fit, vt pontifex fieret, licet glorificatio sui, quae a Patre ipsius erat, esset etiam ab ipsomet, vt Deo. XVI. Deus summus alteri regnum non tradit, id deponendo & iure ad imperandum se abdicando. Christus Patri tradet regnum, id deponendo & iure se abdicando. Ergo Christus non est summus Deus. Minor liquet ex 1 Cor. XV, 24. Resp. Deum summum, qua talem, regnum suum nemini tradere, verum est.

At θεάνθρωπος, siue Deus summus, in carne manifestatus, tradet Patri regnum, cessando a certa regiminis per Verbum & sacramenta administrati forma, non potestatem regiam deponendo; cum constet e scripturis regnum Christi esse aeternum, Dan. VII, 14. Luc. I, 33.


### Q. XXV. Whence is the true and distinct personality of the Son of God known?

That the Son of God is a true person, and one distinct from God the Father and the Holy Spirit, is evident from the personal denomination and property (a), from the personal act ad intra and its manifesting sign (b), and from the action ad extra, appropriated to the Son of God (c).

Prob. a. Christ is called the proper Son of God, Rom. 8:32, and therefore on account of a properly so-called filiation, founded in passive generation, which is manifested by passive mission to the work of redemption. Now, that the Son, begotten from the substance of the Father, sent by Him to a certain office, is a true and distinct person from the Father, is evident.

Prob. b. Just as the Son of God is personally distinguished from the Father by passive generation, so He is distinguished from the Holy Spirit by active spiration: which personal distinction becomes more fully clear from the mission of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, the spirating and the spirated, the sender and the sent, differ as distinct persons.

Prob. c. To the Son of God is appropriated the redemption of the human race: which, although by reason of principle, ordination, and application it is common to the whole Most Holy Trinity, yet terminatively, by reason of merit and acquisition, it is proper to the Son of God: where something singular occurs. For the Son of God did not only appropriate this work ad extra to Himself externally, but also internally, in the unity of His person He assumed human nature, and communicated His own subsistence to it, so that in and with human nature He might complete the work of redemption; which cannot be said of the other persons of the divinity. For neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit communicated their subsistence to the human nature of Christ; nor do they have proper flesh and blood in such a way that through it they could have perfected the redemption of the human race.

Quest. XXXVI. What is the hypostatic character of the Son of God?

The hypostatic character, or personal property of the Son of God, is filiation, founded in eternal generation, viewed passively or terminatively, which is also called eternal birth.

Proof. Divine, and indeed proper, filiation belongs to the eternal Son of God, by which he is not only distinguished from God the Father and the Holy Spirit, but is also constituted in the being of the Son.

Obs. Since the proximate foundation of divine filiation is eternal birth, this is called by some theologians the hypostatic character of the Son of God, most especially because filiation and the eternal birth of God do not differ on the part of the thing.

Quest. XXXVII. What is the passive generation of the Son of God?

Passive generation, or eternal birth, is that by which the Son of God is produced by the eternal Father, as his substantial image, by the communication of one and the same essence, truly and properly, yet in a hyperphysical and unsearchable manner.

Obs. The active generation of the Father and the passive generation of the Son of God are not two generations, but one generation, which is called active by reason of the principle, and passive by reason of the term grammatically, since the Son of God is said not to generate, but to be generated; yet it is not passive really and physically, as if a real passion fell upon the Son of God; his supreme perfection, simplicity, and immutability do not admit of this.

Latin:

Filium Dei veram, eamque distinctam a Deo Patre & Spiritu S. personam esse, constat ex denominatione atque proprietate personali (a), ex actu ad intra personali, eiusque nota manifestatiua (b), & ex actione ad extra, Filio Dei appropriata (c).

Prob. a. Christus vocatur Filius Dei proprius, Rom. VIII, 32. adeoque ob proprie dictam filiationem, fundatam in generatione passiua, quae missione passiua ad opus redemptionis manifestatur. Iam autem Filium genitum e substantia Patris, ab hoc ad certum munus missum, veram atque distinctam a Patre personam esse, euidens est.

Prob. b. Sicut Filius Dei a Patre per generationem passiuam, ita per spirationem actiuam a Spiritu S. personaliter distinguitur: quae distinctio personalis ex missione Spiritus S. vberius inclarescit. Sane spirans & spiratus, mittens & missus, differunt, vt distinctae personae.

Prob. c. Appropriatur Filio Dei redemtio generis humani: quae licet ratione principii, ordinationis & applicationis toti SS. Trinitati communis fit: terminatiue tamen, ratione meriti & acquisitionis, propria est Filio Dei: vbi aliquid singulare occurrit. Etenim Filius Dei hoc opus ad extra non tantum externe sibi appropriauit, sed etiam interne, in vnitatem suae personae assumsit humanam naturam, & huic subsistentiam suam communicauit, vt in & cum humana natura opus redemptionis absolueret; quod de aliis diuinitatis personis dici nequit. Nec enim vel Pater, vel Spiritus S. suam subsistentiam humanae Christi naturae communicarunt; nec ita propriam carnem & sanguinem habent, vt per illam generis humani redemptionem perficere potuerint.

Quæst. XXXVI. Quis est character hypostaticus Filii Dei?

Character hypostaticus, seu proprietas personalis Filii Dei, est filiatio, fundata in æterna generatione, passiue, seu terminatiue spectata, quæ etiam æterna nativitas vocatur.

Prob. Diuina, eaque propria, filiatio competit æterno Filio Dei, per quam non tantum a Deo Patre & Spiritu S. distinguitur, sed etiam in esse Filii constituitur.

Obs. Cum fundamentum proximum diuinæ filiationis sit æterna natiuitas, hæc a nonnullis theologis character hypostaticus Filii Dei appellatur, vel maxime ideo, quod filiatio, & æterna Dei natiuitas, ex parte rei non differunt.

Quæst. XXXVII. Quid est generatio Filii Dei passiua?

Generatio passiua, seu æterna natiuitas est, qua Filius Dei a Patre æterno, vt substantialis ipsius imago, vnius eiusdemque essentiæ communicatione vere & proprie, modo tamen hyperphysico & imperuestigabili producitur.

Obs. Generatio actiua Patris, & passiua Filii Dei, non sunt duæ generationes, sed vna generatio, quæ ratione principii, actiua; ratione termini, passiua vocatur grammatice, quoniam Filius Dei non generare, sed generari dicitur; non autem passiua est realiter & physice, quasi realis passio in Filium Dei cadat; hanc non admittit summa ipsius perfectio, simplicitas & immutabilitas.


### Q. XXV. Whence is the true and distinct personality of the Son of God known?: Quest. XXXVIII. What kind of generation is the generation of the Son of God?

Quest. XXXVIII. What kind of generation is the generation of the Son of God?

The generation of the Son of God is not improper, metaphorical, or accidental, but proper, true, and substantial (a); it is not physical, but hyperphysical (b); not temporal, but eternal (c); not external, but internal (d); not voluntary, but natural and necessary (e).

Proof. a. We learn that the generation of the Son of God is not metaphorical or accidental (such as the regeneration of sinful men), but proper and substantial, from Ps. II, 7, where God the Father addresses his Son with the sweetest words: Thou art my Son: this day have I begotten thee. From which words we form an argument. To whomever Jehovah said: Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee, he is produced by a true, proper, and substantial generation from the Father Jehovah. But Jehovah said to the second person of the divinity, etc. Therefore. The major is proved (1) from the true definition of a Son. A Son, properly so called, is he who is born from the substance of the Father, and has an essence with the Father that is either the same in species (as in human affairs), or the same in number (as in divine affairs). But Christ is the proper Son of God, Rom. VIII, 32. But he would not be the proper Son of God if his generation were improper or metaphorical: The only-begotten Son is from the Father, John I, 14. The name of only-begotten Son in the entire canonical scripture never denotes anyone other than him who alone is born from the substance of the Father. The Socinians object that the most beloved son is called only-begotten, just as Solomon is יָחִיד, unique, Prov. IV, 3, just as Isaac is called not only יָחִיד Gen. XXII, 22, but also μονογενὴς, only-begotten, Hebr. XI, 17, to whom, however, there was a brother, Ishmael. Resp. Solomon is indeed called unique, but not only-begotten; but Isaac was properly only-begotten. For although he had a brother, Ishmael, he was nevertheless only-begotten with respect to that marriage which was between Abraham and Sarah. (2) From the true definition of generation. Generation is formally an action by which the generator, in producing …the generated, communicates his essence to the latter, so that he may be his image. But God the Father, in producing his Son, communicated his essence to him, so that he might be his image. For (a) The word יָלַד, which is found in Ps. II, 7, as often as it is used in the sacred writings concerning a person producing a person, absolutely and without a diminishing addition, designates a substantial production. (b) Christ himself says: As the Father hath life in himself: so also he hath given to the Son to have life in himself.…

God the Father by eternal generation gave to the Son his own life: Therefore also his own essence; since this does not differ really from that.

(c) The Son of God is the image of the invisible God,

Col. 1:15. Every image implies both an origin and an expression from an exemplar, and a correspondence with the same, so that it may represent it. The Son of God is therefore the substantial image of the Father; because he has his origin from God the Father by eternal generation, and corresponds with the same by reason of a most singular essence, being personally distinct from him.

The apostle teaches the same more fully, when the Son of God in Heb.

1:3 is called by him ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ, the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person (God the Father). Ἀπαύγασμα properly signifies an effulgence, a refulgence, or a resplendence emitted from a light, and in the New Testament it is used only in this place. The author of the book of Wisdom, ch. 7:26, calls wisdom ἀπαύγασμα φωτὸς ἀϊδίου, the brightness of eternal light. But the glory of the Father is the most glorious and adorable essence of God the Father.

The apostle therefore intimates by this phrase that the Son of God is begotten by the most glorious Father not freely, or by will and counsel, but naturally, necessarily, continuously, from eternity, without any mutation of the begetter or the begotten, and that he coexists inseparably with the Father; just as the light of the sun naturally, necessarily, continuously, and coevally with the sun, and inseparable from it, emanates from the sun without any mutation: and yet the Son is distinct from the Father, as a ray is distinct from the sun. To which the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea looked, when they called the Son of God light of light.

Furthermore, as every son is the image of his father: So the Son of God is the character of the hypostasis, taken concretely, namely of the person of the Father, or of the divine essence, determined by the subsistence of the Father. But χαρακτὴρ denotes an image not vibrating, fleeting, or evanescent, but express, constant, and perfect.

Wherefore by this word the apostle asserts that the Son of God is the express, most perfect, and eternal image of God, by which the Father is represented to the life, so that the Father being seen in the Son, the Father is seen, John 14:9. The minor of this argument is evident; because the whole of Ps.

2 contains a most manifest prophecy concerning the kingdom of Christ, expounded and applied by the apostles, Peter, Acts 4:25. Paul, Acts 13:33. Heb. 1:5, ch. 5:5. John, Apoc. 2:27, ch. 19:15. Prob. b.

That the generation of the Son of God is not physical, or common, but hyperphysical and most eminent, is evident from the fact that this generation procures for the Son of God a majesty far superior to angelic eminence, as the apostle teaches, Heb. 1:5: To which of the angels said he at any time: Thou art my Son: this day have I begotten thee? Majesty, superior to angelic eminence, is truly divine. The generation of the Son of God is therefore truly divine, to be cut off from all imperfections adhering to physical generation, such as are: the dependence of the generated upon the generator, priority and posteriority of duration, mutation and transition from non-being to being, multiplication of numerical essence, propagation by transmission, etc. Prob. c.

The eternity of the generation of the Son of God is proved (I) from Ps. 2:6-7, in which the generative act, in our mode of conceiving, is described as prior to the divine decree concerning the inauguration of this King Messiah. But the divine decree is certainly eternal. Therefore the act of generation, conceptually prior to that decree, is eternal.

Next, that act of generation produces an infinite, omnipotent, omnipresent, and adorable person, v. 9 seqq. But such an act is not temporal, but eternal. Finally, that act of generation is described by the word "today," which, used of an internal divine act, such generation is nothing but a divine "today," and thus excludes the flux of time, prescinds from past and future, and denotes a perpetual "now," or a day of immutable eternity.

For where a day is neither begun by the end of yesterday, nor terminated by the beginning of tomorrow, it is always "today," i.e., it is eternity itself, as judged by AUGUSTINE, tom. III, in Enchirid. ad Laurent. cap. 49.

The adversaries object: (1) that "today" signifies a certain day, which is clearly contrary to eternity: (2) that God the Father addresses the Son in the past tense: "I have begotten thee," to indicate that that generation has already passed. To I. "Today" does not always designate a determined day in the Holy Scriptures, but a continuous time, as Psalm XCV, 7.

"Today if ye will hear his voice," i.e., always, as long as it is called today, Heb. III, 13; or a long course of time, as Gen. XXII, 14.

Whence it is said "today, in the mount of Jehovah it shall be seen." Moreover, the day itself denotes eternity, Is.

XLIII, 13. "Even from the day I am," i.e., from eternity; because one day is with the Lord as a thousand years.

2 Pet. III, 8. & 18. To II.

The generation of the Son of God is expressed in the past tense, not as if it had passed or ceased, but because the Son of God was most certainly and most perfectly begotten before the ages.

GREGORY NAZIANZEN says excellently, orat.

III. de theol. "Neither does God the Father beget in such a way that He has not yet perfectly begotten; nor did He beget the Son in such a way that He ceased to beget."

For those things have a place only in those things which are subject to the changes of time: the birth in God is true, but perfect; for the Son is always being born, yet is perfect.

(II) From Prov.

VIII, 22-24. "Jehovah possessed me, the beginning of his way; before his works, from the time (it is) from eternity I was poured out from the beginning, from the antiquities of the earth."

"When there were no depths, I was brought forth."

That this passage is not to be explained concerning the essential wisdom of God, or a divine attribute, but concerning the hypostatic or personal wisdom of God, namely the Son of God, D.

CALOV. in bibl. illustrat. in h. l. fol. 1147. seqq. shows at length. We, studying brevity, observe (1) that the Son of God is also called the wisdom of God in the N.

T. "We preach Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God," 1 Cor.

I, 24. Conf.

Matt. XI, 19. Luke VII, 35. (2) That Wisdom testifies of herself in Solomon: חוללתי "I was brought forth" (that חול signifies the act of conception and generation is clear from Ps.

LI, 7. Job

XV, 7. Is. LI, 2.) by which word the hypostatic character of the Son of God is expressed: "I was brought forth," he says, "from the beginning, from the antiquities of the earth, when there were no depths": by which words his ante-secular and eternal pre-existence is insinuated; which is indicated more clearly when the hypostatic wisdom says of herself: "Jehovah possessed me" (by generation, conf.

Gen. IV, 1.) "the beginning of his way; before his works from the time (it is)"; where we understand "beginning" not as material, but as effective and architectural. These things being established, we argue: Whatever wisdom is begotten and possessed by God before all his works, from the time He himself is, that generation is eternal.

But the Son of God is that wisdom, etc. Therefore.

(III) From Mic.

V, 2. "His goings forth are from of old, from the days of eternity." The prophet speaks of the ruler of Israel, or of Christ, conf.

Matt. III, 7. John VII, 42. However, "goings forth" are designated not merely as manifestations, insofar as the Son of God went forth to the holy Fathers Adam, Noah, etc., and revealed himself to them in familiar speech; but generatively; just as that word is sometimes taken, Gen.

XVII, 6. c. XXV, 26.

Jud. VIII, 30. "Goings forth" are said in the plural, not that a double birth, eternal and temporal, is insinuated; for both the determination of eternity and the absurdity of an idle repetition stand against this; since the temporal going forth is dealt with in the former member; but to note the eminence of the eternal birth; for it is customary for the Hebrews to state in the plural what is sublime, and a constant emanation: just as we call the emanation of a fountain "springs," because water constantly springs forth. From these we conclude: Whose generative goings forth are from of old, from the days of eternity, he is begotten from eternity.

But the goings forth of the ruler of Israel, etc. Therefore.

Prob. d.

That the generation of the Son of God is not external or transient, but intimate and immanent, is clear: because God the Father did not produce his Son outwardly, but begat him within his own essence: nor is the Son separated from the Father, as happens elsewhere, but remains in the bosom of the Father, John

I, 18: nor is the Son only in the Father, but the Father also is in the Son, through intimate, mutual communion.

and mutual circuminsession.

Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father in me? Io. XIV, 10. This immanent generation is illustrated by the fact that the Son of God is called wisdom, Prov. VIII, 24. and ὁ λόγος, or the Word, which in the beginning was with God, Io. I, 2. For as the internal word and wisdom flows from the mind as from a principle, and remains in the mind as a certain offspring and daughter of the mind: so the Son of God is begotten by the Father, and remains in the Father.

Prob. e. For if the generation of the Son of God were elicited and free through an act of the will, and not necessary or natural, the Son would not be equal to the Father and ὁμοούσιος; for the latter exists necessarily, and cannot not be. DAMASCENE aptly says in L. I. O. F. c. 8: γέννησις ἐστιν ἔργον Φύσεως, κτίσις ἔργον θελήσεως (Generation is a work of nature, creation is a work of will). It is well to observe here that God the Father, not compelled, and yet not by the counsel of a free will preceding the generation, but by the necessity of nature, though entirely removed from all coercion, begat the Son by a most perfect generation.

Antithesis is of the Socinians who deny the eternal generation of the Son of God; (2) who seek other foundations for divine filiation. The arguments by which they impugn the eternal and substantial generation of the Son of God are the following:

I. God the Father begat the Son either existing or not existing. If the Son always existed, he could not be begotten; because generation proceeds from non-being to being. But if he did not exist, the Son of God is not eternal. Resp. God the Father begets the Son as always existing, always emanating from the Father, just as a ray always flows from the sun. Physical and temporal generation proceeds from non-being to being, since it is subject to the mutation of natural bodies, but not so hyperphysical and eternal generation, since it is of a necessary being, superior to all mutation. Instance: To be from eternity, and to be begotten from eternity, are contradictory, and cannot stand together. Resp. They are not contradictory. For a contradiction exists between the same terms. But here a significant distinction of terms appears. For to be from eternity denotes the essence itself: to be begotten from eternity denotes the mode of having the essence from eternity. Hence the contradiction vanishes.

II. Whatever is eternal, in it there is no place for prior and posterior. In every generation there is a place for prior and posterior. Therefore no generation is eternal. The major is evident, because eternity is a perpetual νῦν (now), excluding all succession of prior and posterior. The minor is proved: because every generated thing is posterior to the generator. Resp. Every physically generated thing is posterior to the generator; I concede. But the Son of God is supernaturally begotten. Instance: Supernatural generation seems to be improper, because it destroys the formal notion of true generation. Resp. The formal notion of generation consists in the communication of the same essence; which supernatural generation does not destroy. It is called hyperphysical because it is most eminent, transcending by far all the imperfections of physical generation.

III. The Son of God is either always being begotten, or at some time ceases to be begotten. If he is always being begotten, he never attains perfection: because that which is still being generated, has not yet reached the term of generation. is affected. But if it is defined as being begotten, there will be some change in God from being to non-being. Resp. He is always being begotten, but without time. From which no imperfection arises. Those things which are still being begotten in time have not yet obtained the limit of perfection. But eternal generation is not to be estimated from temporal generation. God the Father always begets perfectly, the Son of God is always begotten perfect.

Latin:

Quæst. XXXVIII. Qualis est generatio Filii Dei?

Generatio Filii Dei non est impropria, metaphorica aut accidentalis, sed propria, vera & substantialis (a); non physica, sed hyperphysica est (b); non temporalis, sed æterna (c); non externa, sed intima (d); non voluntaria, sed naturalis & necessaria (e) est.

Prob. a. Generationem Filii Dei non metaphoricam, aut accidentalem (qualis est hominum peccatorum regeneratio), sed propriam & substantialem esse, discimus ex Ps. II, 7. vbi Deus Pater Filium suum verbis compellat dulcissimis: Filius meus (es) tu: ego hodie genui te. E quibus verbis formamus argumentum. Ad quemcunque dixit Iehouah: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te, is vera, propria & substantiali generatione a Patre Iehouah est productus. Atqui ad secundam personam diuinitatis dixit Iehouah &c. Ergo. Maior probatur (1) ex vera ratione Filii. Filius, proprie dictus est, qui e substantia Patris prognatus est, & vel specie eandem (vt in humanis), vel numero eandem (vt in diuinis) cum Patre essentiam habet. Christus autem est Filius Dei proprius, Rom. VIII, 32. At non foret Filius Dei proprius, si eius generatio impropria, aut metaphorica esset: Filius vnigenitus est a Patre, Io. I, 14. Filii vnigeniti nomen in vniuersa scriptura canonica nunquam notat alium, quam eum, qui solus e substantia Patris natus est. Excipiunt Sociniani, vnigenitum dici filium dilectissimum, sicut Salomo יָחִיד, vnicus, Prou. IV, 3. vt & Isaac non tantum יָחִיד Gen. XXII, 22. sed & μονογενὴς, vnigenitus, Hebr. XI, 17. appellatur, cui tamen fuit frater Ismaël. Resp. Salomo dicitur quidem vnicus, sed non vnigenitus; Isaac autem proprie fuit vnigenitus. Licet enim fratrem habuerit Ismaëlem, vnigenitus tamen fuit respectu illius coniugii, quod fuit inter Abrahamum & Saram. (2) Ex vera ratione generationis. Generatio formaliter est actio, qua generans producendo generatum, huic suam communicat essentiam, vt sit ipsius imago. Atqui Deus Pater, producendo Filium suum, huic suam communicauit essentiam, vt sit ipsius imago. Nam (a) Verbum יָלַד, quod habetur Ps. II, 7. quotiescunque in sacris litteris de persona, producente personam, absolute & sine additamento diminuente vsurpatur, substantialem designat productionem. (b) Christus ipse inquit: Quemadmodum Pater vitam habet in seipso: ita etiam Filio dedit vitam habere in seipso.

Deus Pater per æternam generationem dedit Filio suam vitam: Ergo & suam essentiam; cum hæc ab illa realiter non differat.

(c) Filius Dei est imago Dei invisibilis,

Col. I, 15. Omnis imago importat tum originem & expressionem ab exemplari, tum convenientiam cum eodem, vt illud repræsentet. Est itaque Filius Dei imago Patris substantialis; quia a Deo Patre originem per æternam generationem habet, & cum eodem ratione essentiæ singularissimæ conuenit, personaliter ab ipso distinctus.

Idem plenius docet apostolus, cum Filius Dei Hebr.

I, 3. ab eodem appellatur ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ, splendor gloriæ, & character personæ ipsius (Dei Patris). Ἀπαύγασμα proprie significat effulgentiam, relucentiam, aut resplendescentiam a luce editam, & in N. T. non nisi in h. l. vfurpatur. Auctor libri Sap. c. VII, 26. vocat sapientiam ἀπαύγασμα φωτὸς ἀϊδίου, splendorem lucis æternæ. Gloria Patris autem est essentia Dei Patris gloriosissima & adorabilis.

Innuit igitur apostolus hac phrasi, Filium Dei a Patre gloriosissimo gigni non libere, aut voluntate consilioque, sed naturaliter, necessario, continuo, ab æterno, sine vlla gignentis genitique mutatione, eundemque Patri inseparabiliter coexsistere; sicut lumen solis naturaliter, necessario, continuo, & soli coæuum, atque ab ipso inseparabile, sine vlla mutatione, e sole emanat: Filiumque tamen a Patre distinctum esse, vt radius a sole distinctus est. Quo respexerunt Patres concilii Nicæni, cum vocarunt Filium Dei lumen de lumine.

Ceterum, vt omnis Filius est imago sui Patris: Ita Filius Dei est character hypostaseos, concretive acceptæ, nempe personæ Patris, seu essentiæ diuinæ, subsistentia Patris determinatæ. Notat autem χαρακτὴρ imaginem non vibraticam, fugacem aut euanidam, sed expressam, constantem & perfectam.

Quare hac voce apostolus affert, Filium Dei esse imaginem Dei expressam, perfectissimam & æternam, qua ad viuum repræsentatur Pater, vt viso Filio videatur Pater, Io. XIV, 9. Minor huius argumenti patet; quia totus Ps.

II. manifestissimam continet prophetiam de regno Christi, expositam & applicatam ab apostolis, Petro, Actor. IV, 25. Paullo, Actor. XIII, 33. Hebr. I, 5. c. V, 5. Ioanne, Apoc. II, 27. c. XIX, 15.

Prob. b. Generationem Filii Dei non esse physicam, aut vulgarem, sed hyperphysicam & eminentissimam, constat ex eo, quod hæc generatio conciliat Filio Dei maiestatem, eminentia angelica longe superiorem, docente apostolo, Hebr. I, 5: Cui dixit vnquam angelorum: Filius meus es tu: Ego hodie genui te? Maiestas, eminentia angelica superior, vere diuina est. Est igitur generatio Filii Dei vere diuina, resecanda ab omnibus imperfectionibus, generationi physicæ adhærentibus, quales sunt: dependentia generati a generante, prioritas & posterioritas durationis, mutatio & transitus a non esse ad esse, multiplicatio essentiæ numericæ, propagatio per traducem, &c.

Prob. c. Æternitas generationis Filii Dei probatur (I) e Ps. II. 6. 7. in quo actus generatiuus, nostro concipiendi modo, prior describitur decreto diuino de inauguratione huius regis Messiæ. At decretum diuinum vtique æternum est. Ergo actus generationis, decreto illo conceptibiliter prior, est æternus.

Deinde actus ille generationis producit personam infinitam, omnipotentem, omnipræsentem & adorabilem, v. 9. seqq. At talis actus non temporalis, sed æternus est. Describitur denique actus ille generationis per τὸ hodie, quod vfurpatum de actu diuino interno, qualis generatio non nisi diuinum hodie est, adeoque excludit fluxum temporis, præscindit a præterito & futuro, atque notat perpetuum νῦν, siue diem immutabilis æternitatis.

Vbi enim dies nec hesterni fine inchoatur, nec initio crastini terminatur, semper hodiernus est, i. e. ipsa est æternitas, iudice AVGVSTINO tom. III. in enchirid. ad Laurent. cap. 49.

Excipiunt aduersarii: (1) τὸ hodie certum intimare diem, quod aeternitati plane contrarium est: (2) Deum Patrem alloqui in praeterito Filium: Ego genui te, vt indicet, illam generationem iam praeteriisse. Ad I. τὸ hodie non semper in sacris litteris designat diem determinatum, sed tempus continuum, vt Psalm XCV, 7.

Hodie si vocem Domini audieritis , e. semper, quamdiu hodie vocatur, Hebr. III, 13; aut longum temporis decursum, vt Gen. XXII, 14.

Vnde dicitur hodie, in monte Iehovah videbitur. Quin & dies ipsam notat aeternitatem, Es.

XLIII, 13. Etiam ex quo dies est: Ego sum, i.e. ab aeterno; quia una dies apud Dominum, sicut mille anni.

2 Petr. III, 8. & 18. Ad II.

Generatio Filii Dei exprimitur in praeterito, non quasi praeterierit, aut desierit, sed quia Filius Dei ante saecula certissime non minus, quam perfectissime genitus est.

Praeclare ait GREGOR. NAZIANZEN. orat.

III. de theol. Nec Deus Pater ita generat, vt nondum perfecte generarit; neque ita generauit Filium, ut generare desierit.

Illa enim locum habent in iis duntaxat, quae temporum mutationibus sunt obnoxia: vera in Deo est natiuitas, sed perfecta; semper enim Filius nascitur, sed perfectus.

(II) E Prou.

IIX, 22-24. Iehouah possedit me, principium viae suae; ante opera eius, ex quo (est) ab aeterno inuncta (effusa) sum a principio, ab antiquitatibus terrae.

Cum nondum essent abyssi, genita sum.

Hunc locum non de sapientia Dei essentiali, aut attributo diuino, sed de sapientia Dei hypostatica seu personali, nempe Filio Dei exponendum esse, prolixe ostendit D.

CALOV. in bibl. illustrat. in h. l. fol. 1147. seqq. Nos breuitati studentes, obseruamus (1) Filium Dei etiam in N.

T. sapientiam Dei vocari. Praedicamus Christum, Dei virtutem & Dei sapientiam, 1 Cor.

I, 24. Conf.

Matth. XI, 19. Luc. VII, 35. (2) Sapientiam apud Salomonem de se ipsa testari: חוללתי genita sum (הח actum conceptionis & generationis, significare, liquet e Ps.

LI, 7. Iob.

XV, 7. Es. LI, 2.) qua voce character hypostaticus Filii Dei exprimitur: Genita sum, inquit, a principio, ab antiquitatibus terrae, cum nondum essent abyssi: quibus verbis eius praeexistentia ante-saecularis & aeterna insinuatur; quae clarius indigitatur, cum sapientia hypostatica de seipsa inquit: Iehouah possedit me (per generationem, conf.

Gen. IV, 1.) principium viae suae; ante opera eius ex quo (est); vbi intelligimus principium non materiale, sed effectiuum & architectonicum. Quibus praestitutis argumentamur: Quae sapientia est genita & possessa a Deo ante omnia eius opera, ex quo ipse est, illius generatio est aeterna.

Atqui Filius Dei est illa sapientia &c. Ergo.

(III) Ex Mich.

V, 2. eius egressiones sunt ab antiquo, a diebus aeternitatis. Loquitur propheta de dominatore Israëlis, siue de Christo, conf.

Matth. III, 7. Io. VII, 42. Egressiones autem designantur non nude patefactiuae, quatenus Filius Dei ad sanctos Patres Adamum, Noachum &c. egressus, se illis familiari sermone patefecit; sed generatiue; quemadmodum illa vox aliquoties accipitur, Gen.

XVII, 6. c. XXV, 26.

Iud. VIII, 30. Egressiones dicuntur in plurali, non quod duplex natiuitas, aeterna, & temporalis insinuetur; obstat enim & aeternitatis determinatio, & absurdum otiosae repetitionis; cum de egressione temporali in priori membro fit actum; sed ad notandam aeternae natiuitatis eminentiam; Hebraeis enim, quae sublimia sunt, pluraliter enuntiare solemne est, & iugem emanationem: sicut fontis emanationem vocamus scaturigines, quia iugiter aqua scaturit. Ex his colligimus: Cuius egressiones generatiuae sunt ab antiquo, a diebus aeternitatis, ille ab aeterno genitus est.

Atqui egressiones dominatoris Israëlis &c. Ergo.

Prob. d.

Generationem Filii Dei non esse externam, aut transeuntem, sed intimam & immanentem, patet: quia Deus Pater Filium suum non ad extra produxit, sed intra essentiam suam genuit: nec a Patre separatur Filius, vt alias fit, sed in sinu Patris manet, Io.

I, 18: nec Filius tantum in Patre est, sed Pater etiam in Filio est, per intimam communionem. est, per intimam communionem, mutuam

mutuamque περιχώρησιν.

Non credis, quod ego in Patre & Pater in me est. Io. XIV, 10. Illustratur immanens hæc generatio ex eo, quod Filius Dei sapientia, Prou. IIX, 24. & ὁ λόγος, siue Verbum, quod initio erat apud Deum Io. I, 2. appellatur. Nam vt verbum internum & sapientia a mente velut principio redundat, & in mente manet, vt proles quædam & filia mentis: ita Filius Dei a Patre gignitur, & in Patre manet.

Prob. e. Quod si generatio Filii Dei, per actum voluntatis elicita & libera, non autem necessaria aut naturalis esset, non foret Filius Patri æqualis & ὁμοούσιος; nam hic existit necessario, & non potest non esse. Concinne ait DAMASC. L. I. O. F. c. 8. γέννησις ἐστιν ἔργον Φύσεως, κτίσις ἔργον θελήσεως. Probe hic obseruandum, quod Deus Pater non coactus, nec tamen consilio liberæ voluntatis generationem præcedentis, sed necessitate naturæ, ab omni tamen coactione penitus remota, generatione perfectissima Filium genuerit.

Antithesis est Socinianorum æternam Filii Dei generationem negantium; (2) alia filiationis diuinæ fundamenta conquirentium. Argumenta, quibus æternam & substantialem Filii Dei generationem impugnant, sunt sequentia:

I. Deus Pater genuit Filium aut existentem, aut non existentem. Si semper Filius exstitit, gigni non potuit; eo quod generatio progreditur a non esse, ad esse. Si autem non exstitit, Filius Dei non est æternus. Resp. Gignit Deus Pater Filium semper existentem, semper emanantem a Patre, sicut radius semper fluit ex sole. Physica & temporalis generatio progreditur a non esse ad esse, cum sit corporum naturalium mutationi obnoxiorum, non autem generatio hyperphysica & æterna, quippe quæ est entis necessarii, omni mutatione superioris. Instantia: Esse ab æterno, & genitum esse ab æterno, sunt contradictoria, quæ simul stare nequeunt. Resp. Non sunt contradictoria. Nam contradictio versatur inter eosdem terminos. At hic insignis terminorum distinctio apparet. Nam esse ab æterno notat ipsam essentiam: genitum esse ab æterno, notat modum habendi essentiam ab æterno. Hinc contradictio exspirat.

II. Quidquid est æternum, in illo prius & posterius locum non habet. In omni generatione prius & posterius locum habet. Ergo nulla generatio est æterna. Maior constat, quia æternitas est perpetuum νῦν, omnem successionem prioris & posterioris excludens. Minor probatur: quia omnis generatus est posterior generante. Resp. Omnis physice generatus posterior est generante; concedo. At Filius Dei supernaturaliter genitus est. Instantia: Generatio supernaturalis videtur esse impropria, quia rationem formalem veræ generationis destruit. Resp. Formalis ratio generationis consistit in communicatione eiusdem essentiæ; quam supernaturalis generatio non destruit. Dicitur hyperphysica, quia est eminentissima, omnes imperfectiones generationis physicæ longissime transcendens.

III. Filius Dei aut semper gignitur, aut aliquando definit gigni. Si semper gignitur, nunquam perfectionem assequitur: quia quod adhuc generatur, id nondum generationis terminum est affectum. Si autem definit gigni, erit aliqua mutatio in Deo ab esse, ad non esse. Resp. Semper gignitur, sed sine tempore. Ex quo nulla oritur imperfectio. Quae in tempore adhuc gignuntur, perfectionis terminum nondum obtinuerunt. At generatio aeterna non est aestimanda ex generatione temporali. Deus Pater semper generat perfecte, Filius Dei semper generatur perfectus.


### Q. XXV. Whence is the true and distinct personality of the Son of God known?: IV. Whoever is by nature and necessarily most simple, he cannot beget another like unto himself

IV. Whoever is by nature and necessarily most simple, he cannot beget another like unto himself.

But God &c. Therefore. The major is proved; because God is most perfect; but there can be only one who is most perfect. Resp. Distinguish between immanent generation, or kat' eso (inwardly), and transient, or kat' exo (outwardly). In transient generation, indeed, the essence of the begetter is always one, and that of the begotten another. But it is far otherwise with immanent generation, in which the multiplication of essence has no place; since divine immanent generation is the communication of the same singular essence.

Instance I. That immanent generation either takes place without essence, or with essence. If without essence; it will not be a communication of essence. If with essence; the essence of the begetter will be one, and that of the begotten another. Resp. It does not take place without essence, nor yet with the multiplication of essence; because it is a communication of the same essence in number.

Instance II. If it is a communication of the same singular essence, the same will beget itself. Resp. Deny the consequence. Because there is indeed one essence, but the persons of the begetter and the begotten are distinct.

Instance III. God the Father begets either the essence of the Son, or his person. If he begets the essence of the Son, the essence of the Father will be one, and that of the Son another. If he begets only the person, the person could be the essence, which is absurd. Resp. Generation is of the person, as to the term, because actions belong to supposita. Meanwhile, since generation formally is nothing other than the communication of the same essence; God the Father is rightly said to beget from his own essence; nor yet is a diverse essence of the begetter and the begotten necessarily inferred.

V. If Christ is begotten from the essence of the Father, he is begotten either from a part of it, or from the whole essence.

Not from a part of it; because it is indivisible. Nor from the whole essence; because otherwise the Father would cease to be the Father. Resp. This argument is so invalid that it does not even hold true in natural things. For the whole soul of the son is propagated from the whole soul of the father, and yet this remains whole. A lamp is lit from a lamp, without the diminution of the latter.

VI. God the Father either necessarily begets, or freely.

Not necessarily; since God can be compelled by no one. Nor freely; because thus the Son of God could not be. Therefore, God the Father does not beget the Son at all. Resp. A fallacy of equivocation is committed. For there is one necessity of coercion, another is the necessity of immutability and nature. God the Father freely begat the Son, if you look at freedom from coercion; yet he begat necessarily, if you look at the necessity of immutability and nature.

Latin:

IV. Quicunque natura & necessario simplicissimus est, ille non potest alium sibi similem generare.

Atqui Deus &c. Ergo. Maior probatur; quia Deus est perfectissimus; perfectissimus autem non nisi unus esse potest. Resp. Dist. inter generationem immanentem, seu κατ' ἔσω, & transeuntem, seu κατ' ἔξω. In generatione transeunte quidem semper alia est essentia gignentis, alia geniti. Longe aliter autem comparatum est cum generatione immanente, in qua locum non habet essentiae multiplicatio; quoniam generatio immanens diuina est eiusdem essentiae singularis communicatio.

Instantia I. Generatio illa immanens vel fit sine essentia, vel cum essentia. Si sine essentia; non erit communicatio essentiae. Si cum essentia; alia erit essentia gignentis, alia geniti. Resp. Non fit sine essentia, neque tamen cum multiplicatione essentiae; quia est communicatio eiusdem numero essentiae.

Instantia II. Si est communicatio eiusdem singularis essentiae, idem seipsum generabit. Resp. Neg. conseq. Quia una quidem essentia est, sed sunt distinctae generantis & geniti personae.

Instantia III. Deus Pater generat vel essentiam Filii, vel eiusdem personam. Si generat essentiam Filii, alia erit essentia Patris, alia Filii. Si personam tantum generat, persona poterit esse essentia, quod est absurdum. Resp. Generatio est personae, quoad terminum, quia actiones sunt suppositorum. Interim cum generatio formaliter nihil aliud fit, quam eiusdem essentiae communicatio; recte Deus Pater ex essentia sua generare dicitur; nec tamen genitoris, & geniti essentia diuersa necessario infertur.

V. Si Christus ex essentia Patris genitus est, aut ex parte eius, aut ex tota essentia genitus est.

Non ex parte eius; quia est indiuisibilis. Neque ex tota essentia; quia ceteroqui Pater defineret esse Pater. Resp. Hoc argumentum adeo inualidum est, vt ne in naturalibus quidem semper valeat. Nam anima tota filii propagatur a tota anima patris, & haec tamen tota manet. Lychnus a lychno accenditur, sine huius diminutione.

VI. Deus Pater aut necessario generat, aut libere.

Non necessario; quoniam Deus a nemine cogi potest. Nec libere; quia sic Filius Dei posset non esse. E. Deus Pater Filium plane non generat. Resp. Committitur fallacia aequivocationis. Alia namque est necessitas coactionis, alia est necessitas immutabilitatis & naturae. Deus Pater libere genuit Filium, si respicias libertatem a coactione; genuit tamen necessario, si spectes necessitatem immutabilitatis & naturae.


### Q. XXV. Whence is the true and distinct personality of the Son of God known?: VII. If Christ is begotten from the essence of the Father, he will be begotten from his own essence and consequently from himself, because…

VII. If Christ is begotten from the essence of the Father, he will be begotten from his own essence and consequently from himself, because he is of the same essence in number with the Father.

But no one can be begotten by himself. Therefore the Son of God is not begotten from the essence of the Father. Resp. The Son of God is said to be begotten from the essence of the Father, because God the Father communicated his essence to the Son. But from this it is wrongly inferred: Therefore the Son of God is begotten from himself. For although the divine essence is the same, common to the whole Trinity, if viewed absolutely: yet the foundation of generation is not the divine essence viewed absolutely, but considered relatively, insofar as... it is marked with the hypostatic character of the Father.

VIII. If God the Father, by begetting the Son, communicated to him the same essence in number, he cannot be called the image of God the Father.

But the Son is called the image of God the Father. Therefore God the Father, by generating the Son, He did not communicate the same essence in number to Him. The consequence of the major premise is manifest; because no image is of the same essence in number with that of which it is an image.

Resp. In the order of creatures, no image is of the same essence in number with that of which it is an image. But because of the infinity of the divine essence, it comes to pass that one divine person is the image of another; and yet is of the same essence with it.

Instance:

Thus the same will be the image of itself. Resp. I deny the consequence. Because the Son of God is personally distinguished from the Father.

The arguments by which adversaries strive to construct other foundations for divine sonship are the following. I.

They posit that Christ is called the Son of God because of His miraculous conception by the Holy Spirit, concerning which the angel says in Luke 1:35: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Highest will overshadow you: therefore also that which is born of you will be called the Son of God."

Resp. The angel does not assert that Christ is called the Son of God because of His singular conception by the Holy Spirit, but because of the overshadowing of the power of the Highest, which is Christ (1 Cor. 1:24). Therefore the sense is: because the Son of God will fill the womb of Mary with a singular presence and in an unsearchable manner, and will unite to Himself in it the flesh formed by the Holy Spirit, therefore also that which will be born of Mary will be called the Son of God.

Instance: Thus there will be two Sons of God, one because of the eternal generation from the Father, the other because of the incarnation of the λόγος (Word). Resp. Because the hypostasis of the Son of God is one in number, therefore also there is one Son of God; and although the reasons for sonship are distinct, they do not constitute two Sons of God; because they do not produce two persons.

II. They opine that Christ is the Son of God because of His sanctification and mission into the world; because the Savior Himself gives this reason for His sonship in John 10:34-36:

"Is it not written in your law: I said, You are gods?

(Ps. 82:6). If He called them gods, to whom the word of God came, and the scripture cannot be broken: do you say of Him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, 'You blaspheme,' because I said, 'I am the Son of God'?"

Resp. By "sanctification" in the cited passage is understood the essential communication of divine holiness through eternal generation.

For just as those to whom the word of God came are gods and sons of God not through the communication of the divine nature, but through the bestowal of dignity outside of God and the essence of God, and thus are adoptive sons of God and nominal gods: so He whom the Father sanctified is God and the Son of God through the communication of the divine essence, such that He who was sent into the world to redeem and sanctify men was sufficient through the communicated divine holiness.

Christ mentions this sanctification, or holiness communicated through eternal generation, because He wished to indicate the principle of our sanctification.

Cf.

D.

SCHMID in coll. bibl. post. p. 55.

III. They judge that Christ is the Son of God because of His resuscitation to immortal life.

For Paul says in Rom.

1:2-4.

"Which gospel He promised before... concerning His Son, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, but demonstrated to be the Son of God in power (omnipotent) according to the Spirit of holiness by the resurrection of the dead."

Resp. Christ is said by the apostle to be ὁρισθεὶς, demonstrated or declared to be the omnipotent Son of God, because He raised Himself from the dead through the Spirit of sanctification, that is, through His own divine nature; which resuscitation is an argument a posteriori effectively demonstrating the divine sonship of Jesus Christ.

They add the saying of Paul in Acts

13:32-

33: "We declare to you glad tidings—that promise which was made to the fathers, God has fulfilled this to their children, in that He raised up Jesus: as it is also written in the second Psalm: 'You are My Son, today I have begotten You.'"

Resp. The apostle does not speak here of the resuscitation of Christ from the dead, but of the raising up of the Messiah from the seed of David, whose most eminent person he is about to describe, and he brings forward the words of Ps.

2 to show that the Messiah is not a mere man, but the only-begotten and eternal Son of God.

The apostle deals with the resuscitation from the dead in verse 35.

Objection: But why is Christ called the firstborn from the dead, Col. 1:18, Apoc. 1:5, if not because he is the Son of God by reason of the resurrection? Response: Christ is called the firstborn from the dead because his resurrection was the cause and consecrator of our resurrection (which is a certain kind of παλιγγενεσία, regeneration). IV. Some suppose that Christ is the Son of God by reason of his exaltation to dominion and the high priesthood. They rely on the apostolic saying in Heb. 5:5: So also Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest, but he who said to him: You are my Son, today I have begotten you. Response: By the words of the apostle, not the cause of divine filiation, but the legitimate and divine calling of Christ to the priesthood is expressed. Christ was not from the family of Aaron, nor even from the tribe of Levi, which alone was priestly, but from the royal family of Judah. Therefore, a scruple could have been cast into the minds of the Hebrews concerning the authority of Christ's priesthood. Lest any place be left for this, the apostle says: Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest, but he who said to him: You are my Son, today I have begotten you. That is to say, no one is more worthy of the priestly office than Christ; because he is the only-begotten Son from the Father; from whom he received his priesthood by vocation, just as he received his essence by eternal generation. Certainly, the firstborn Son is a priest by right of birth in the house of his Father. Wherefore the authority of Christ's priesthood is greatest, as its author is the eternal Father of Jesus Christ.

Latin:

VII. Si Christus ex essentia Patris est genitus, ex sua essentia & consequenter ex seipso erit genitus, quia eiusdem numero essentiae cum Patre est.

At non potest quisquam a seipso gigni, Ergo Filius Dei non ex essentia Patris genitus est. Resp. Filius Dei dicitur ex essentia Patris genitus, quia Deus Pater Filio suam essentiam communicauit. At exinde perperam infertur: Ergo Filius Dei ex seipso genitus est. Nam quamuis eadem sit essentia diuina toti Trinitati communis, si spectetur absolute: attamen fundamentum generationis non est essentia diuina absolute, sed relative considerata, quatenus... charactere hypostatico Patris est insignita.

VIII. Si Deus Pater generando Filium eandem numero essentiam ipsi communicauit, non potest hic Dei, Patris dici imago.

At dicitur Filius imago Dei Patris. Ergo Deus Pater, generando Filium, eandem numero essentiam ipsi non communicauit. Consequentia maioris est manifesta; quia nulla imago est eiusdem numero essentiae cum eo, cuius est imago.

Resp. In ordine creaturarum nulla imago est eiusdem numero essentiae... cum eo, cuius est imago. At propter infinitatem essentiae diuinae fit, vt vna persona diuina sit imago alterius; & tamen eiusdem essentiae cum ea.

Instantia: Sic idem sui ipsius erit imago.

Resp. Neg. consequ. Quia Filius Dei a Patre personaliter distinguitur.

Argumenta, quibus aduersarii alia fundamenta filiationis diuinae adstruere nituntur, sunt sequentia. I.

Statuunt Christum dici Filium Dei ob miraculosam a Spiritu S. conceptionem, de qua angelus Luc. 1, 35. Spiritus S. veniet super te, & virtus altissimi obumbrabit te: ideo etiam, quod nascitur ex te, vocabitur Filius Dei.

Resp. Non asserit angelus, Christum dici Filium Dei ob singularem eius conceptionem e Spiritu S. sed propter obumbrationem virtutis altissimi, quae est Christus 1 Cor. 1, 24. Proinde sensus est; quia Filius Dei vterum Mariae praesentia singulari & modo imperuestigabili implebit, carnemque a Spiritu S. formatam in eo sibi vniet, ideo & quod nascetur ex Maria, vocabitur Filius Dei.

Instantia: Sic erunt duo Filii Dei, vnus propter aeternam generationem a Patre, alter ob incarnationem τοῦ λόγου. Resp. Quia hypostasis Filii Dei est numero vna, ideo etiam vnus est Filius Dei & licet distincte sint rationes filiationis, non tamen duo constituunt Filios Dei; quia duas non conficiunt personas.

II. Opinantur, Christum esse Filium Dei ob sanctificationem & missionem in mundum; quia ipse Saluator hanc filiationis suae rationem reddit 10.

X, 34-36. Nonne scriptum est in lege vestra: Ego dixi: Dii estis?

(Ps. LXXXII, 6.) Si eos dixit Deos, ad quos verbum Dei factum est, & non potest solui scriptura: quem Pater sanctificauit & misit in mundum vos dicitis: blasphemas; quod dixi: Filius Dei sum!

Resp. Per sanctificationem l. c. intelligitur essentialis diuinae sanctitatis communicatio per aeternam generationem.

Quemadmodum enim illi, ad quos verbum Dei factum est, sunt dii & filii Dei non per diuinae naturae communicationem, sed per collationem dignitatis extra Deum, Deique essentiam, adeoque filii Dei adoptiui & dii nominales: ita is, quem Pater sanctificauit est Deus & Filius Dei per essentiae diuinae communicationem, ita vt sufficiens esset per communicatam diuinam sanctitatem, qui mundum mitteretur ad redimendum & sanctificandum homines.

Meminit Christus huius sanctificationis, seu communicatae per aeternam generationem sanctitatis, quia principium nostrae sanctitatis indicare voluit.

Conf.

D.

SCHMID. in coll. bibl. post. p. 55.

III. Censent, Christum esse Filium Dei ob resuscitationem ad vitam immortalem.

Nam Paullus inquit Rom.

1, 2-4.

Quod euangelium prius promisit --- de Filio suo, nato ex semine Dauidis secundum carnem, demonstrato autem, quod Filius Dei in potentia (omnipotens) secundum Spiritum sanctitatis ex resurrectione mortuorum.

Resp. Dicitur ab apostolo Christus ὁρισθεὶς, demonstratus seu declaratus omnipotens Filius Dei, quia seipsum per Spiritum sanctificationis, hoc est, per naturam suam diuinam ex mortuis resuscitauit; quae resuscitatio est argumentum a posteriori efficaciter demonstrans filiationem diuinam Iesu Christi.

Addunt dictum Paulli Act.

XIII, 32.

33. Nos vobis euangelizamus promissionem ad Patres factam, quod hanc Deus implenerit filiis eorum nobis excitans Iesum: Sicut etiam in Psalmo secundo scriptum est: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te.

R. Non loquitur hic apostolus de resuscitatione Christi ex mortuis, sed de excitatione Messiae e semine Dauidis, cuius personam eminentissimam descripturus, adducit verba Ps.

II. vt ostendat, Messiam non esse nudum hominem, sed vnigenitum & aeternum Filium Dei.

De resuscitatione ex mortuis agit apostolus v.

Instantia: Sed quare dicitur Christus primogenitus ex mortuis, Col. I, 18. Apoc. I, 5. nisi quia Filius Dei est ob resurrectionem? Resp. Christus dicitur primogenitus ex mortuis, quia illius resurrectio nostræ resurrectionis, (quæ est quædam quasi παλιγγενεσία, regeneratio,) causa et consecratrix fuit. IV. Autumant, Christum esse Filium Dei ob exaltationem ad imperium et summum sacerdotium. Nituntur dicto apostolico Hebr. V, 5. Sic et Christus non seipsum glorificauit, vt fieret sacerdos princeps, sed is, qui dixit ad ipsum: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. R. Verbis apostoli non causa filiationis diuinæ, sed legitima et diuina Christi vocatio ad sacerdotium exprimitur. Non erat Christus ex familia Aaronis, ac ne quidem e tribu Leui, quæ sola sacerdotalis erat, sed ex regia Iudæ familia. Poterat itaque Hebræorum animis de auctoritate sacerdotii Christi scrupulus inuici. Cui ne relinqueretur locus, inquit apostolus: Christus non seipsum glorificauit, vt fieret sacerdos princeps, sed is, qui dixit ad eum: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. q.d. Christo nemo dignior est munere sacerdotali; eo quod vnigenitus a Patre Filius est; a quo vt essentiam per æternam generationem, ita sacerdotium per vocationem accepit. Certe Filius primogenitus iure natiuitatis in domo Patris fui sacerdos est. Quare auctoritas sacerdotii Christi est maxima, vtpote cuius auctor est æternus Iesu Christi Pater.


### Q. XXV. Whence is the true and distinct personality of the Son of God known?: Question XXXIX

Question XXXIX.

What is the consequence of eternal generation? The passive mission of the Son of God into the flesh.

Objection: We shall provide the proof and explanation of this passive mission of the Son of God below.

Latin:

Quæst. XXXIX. Quodnam est consequens natiuitatis æternæ?

Missio passiua Filii Dei in carnem.

Obs. Probationem et explicationem huius passiuae missionis Filii Dei dabimus infra.


### Question XLI. What is the consequence of active spiration?

The personal act of the Son of God is the spiration of the Holy Spirit, by which the Son of God, together with the Father, produces the third person of the divinity—the common spiraculum of both—by the communication of the same essence in number in an ineffable manner.

Objection: This act is at once the personal notion of the Word; for it signifies the second person of the divinity, distinguishes the same from the third person, and relates to this relation: but it is not the personal property of the Son of God, because it is common to the Father and the Son, nor does it constitute him in the being of the Son.

Question XLI.

What is the consequence of active spiration? The active mission of the Holy Spirit, by which the Son of God, together with God the Father, sends the Holy Spirit for the work of sanctification. Proof: From John 15:26.

But when the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father. Christians must struggle with no small, but a great misery, to which Christ opposes a greater comfort, the Holy Spirit, whom he calls the Paraclete, i.e., the Comforter. Christ is to send him by a mission not through command, but through most free consent. He is to send the same from the Father, not only with the Father consenting and sending at the same time, but also by communicating to the Son the power of sending the Holy Spirit through eternal generation.

Quæst. XLII. Which external action is appropriated to the Son of God? The redemption of the human race. Proved from Gal. IV, 4.
