When the fullness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons of God.

Where note a) that our Redeemer is the Son of God and the Son of man, and thus the God-man (θεάνθρωπον), b) sent by the Father; which mission is a consequence of substantial generation, not implying inequality, not local, not separative, but manifestative and most free. c) That those redeemed are men who were under the law: by whom are understood not only the Jews, who lived under the ceremonial law, but all men who have been, or shall be, all debtors to the law. d) That the redemption of Christ is called ἐξαγορασμός (buying back); by which word is noted a redemption not metaphorical, but true, satisfactory, and meritorious, which is accomplished by the payment of a price. e) That the final cause of redemption is twofold, namely 1) liberation from the law, insofar as it curses, compels, and presses with the burden of ceremonies.

The Redeemer liberated us from the law, while he submitted himself to the law, of which he was Lord, 2) Adoption as sons of God, with every right and privilege that accompanies adoption.

Latin:

Actus personalis Filii Dei est spiratio Spiritus sancti, qua Filius Dei vna cum Patre tertiam diuinitatis personam, commune vtriusque spiraculum, eiusdem numero essentiae communicatione modo ineffabili producit.

Obs. Hic actus τῷ λόγῳ simul eiusdem notio personalis est; quippe quæ secundam diuinitatis personam notificat, eandem a tertia persona distinguit, et ad hanc relationem infert: at non est proprietas Filii Dei personalis, quia communis est Patri et Filio, neque hunc in esse Filii constituit.

Quæst. XLI. Quodnam est consequens spirationis actuae?

Missio actua Spiritus sancti, qua Filius Dei vna cum Deo Patre Spiritum S. ad opus sanctificationis mittit.

Prob. e Io. XV, 26. Quando vero venerit paracletus, quem ego missurus vobis sum a Patre, Conflictandum est christianis cum miseria non exigua, sed magna, cui Christus maius solamen Spiritus S. quem paracletum, i. e. consolatorem vocat, opponit. Hunc missurus est Christus missione non per imperium, sed liberrimum consensum. Missurus est eundem a Patre, non tantum consentiente et simul mittente, sed et facultatem mittendi Spiritum S. Filio per æternam generationem communicante.

Quæst. XLII. Quæ actio externa Filio Dei appropriatur? Redemtio generis humani. Prob. ex Gal. IV, 4. Quando venit plenitudo temporis, misit Deus Filium suum natum ex muliere, factum sub lege, ut eos, qui sub lege erant, redimeret, ut adoptionem filiorum Dei acciperemus.

Vbi obs. a) Redemtorem nostrum esse Filium Dei & Filium hominis, adeo que θεάνθρωπον, b) missum a Patre; quæ missio est aliquod consequens substantialis generationis, non illatiua inæqualitatis, non localis, non separatiua, sed manifestatiua & liberrima. c) Redemtos esse homines, qui sub lege erant: per quos non tantum intelliguntur Iudæi, qui sub lege cæremoniali viuebant, sed omnes homines, qui fuerunt, aut erunt, omnes debitores legis. d) Redemtionem Christi vocari ἐξαγορασμόν; qua voce notatur redemtio non metaphorica, sed vera, satisfactoria & meritoria, quæ fit persoluto pretio. e) Causam finalem redemtionis esse geminam, nempe 1) liberationem a lege, quatenus illa maledicit, cogit, & onere cæremoniarum premit.

Liberauit nos redemtor a lege, dum seipsum legi submisit, cuius Dominus erat, 2) Adoptionem in filios Dei, cum omni iure & priuilegio, quod adoptionem comitatur.


### Of the Holy Spirit

XLIII. Who is the Holy Spirit? The Holy Spirit is the third person of the divinity, not begotten, but eternally proceeding from the Father and the Son. It is defined more fully.

The Holy Spirit is the third person of the divinity, of the same essence with the Father and the Son, who eternally proceeds from the Father and the Son, and is sent by both in time to sanctify the hearts of those to be saved.

Quæst. XLIV. Why is he called Spirit? He is called Spirit not so much from spirituality, as from breathing (spirando). Proved. Spiritual essence is common to all three persons of the divinity; but passive spiration is proper to the Holy Spirit. He is therefore called Spirit, because he is eternally breathed by the Father and the Son in an ineffable manner, or the omnipotent breath.

Job.

XXXIII, 4. Quæst. XLV. Why is he denominated holy? The third person of the divinity is called holy not only because of the holiness of his essence, but also because of the work of sanctification, which is appropriated to him.

Proved. The Holy Spirit has the most holy divine essence in common with God the Father and the Son; but the Holy Scripture and the Apostolic Creed appropriate the work of sanctification to the Holy Spirit.

I am a minister of Jesus Christ among the Gentiles, sacrificing the gospel of God, that the offering of the Gentiles might be acceptable, being sanctified by the Holy Spirit, says Paul in Rom.

XV, 16. Quæst. XLVI. How do you prove the Holy Spirit to be a true person, distinct from the Father and the Son? The true personality of the Holy Spirit is proved from the definition of a person (a) and from acts proper to a true person (b).

But that the Holy Spirit is a person distinct from the Father and the Son is known from the order of the divine persons (c), the hypostatic character and its manifestative mark (d), the action ad extra appropriated to the Holy Spirit (e), and the theophany at the Jordan (f).

Prob. a. A person is defined as that which is ὑφιστάμενον, or an intelligent supposit endowed with free will. The Holy Spirit subsists by himself; because he is the paraclete, who cannot be conceived even by the mind without an ultimate subsistence. He is intelligent; for he is called the spirit of intelligence, searching the deep things of God, He is endowed with free will; since he distributes gifts to each one as he wills, Therefore he is a true person.

Prob. b. Actions proper to persons are predicated of the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit speaks through the mouth of holy men, He convicts, teaches, announces, He consoles and testifies, He appoints bishops over the church, He commands ministers to be set apart for himself, Which actions can belong to none but a true person.

Prob. c. The Holy Spirit is joined with God the Father in the business of salvation, and is enumerated as a third person. For we are baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Cf. Where he is called the third heavenly witness. Therefore the Holy Spirit is both a true person and distinct from the Father and the Son.

Prob. d. The Holy Spirit is breathed by the Father and the Son, or proceeds, and is sent, But the breather and the breathed, the sender and the sent, are distinct persons.

Prob. e. The work of sanctification is appropriated to the Holy Spirit, to which also pertains the consolation of the afflicted. But the Holy Spirit is the paraclete, or comforter, distinct from Christ. I will ask the Father, that he may give you another paraclete.

Prob. f. When Christ was being baptized in the Jordan, the Father appeared by a voice, the Son in body, the Spirit as a bird. To assume a visible and corporeal form for a time, to descend in it from heaven, to appear in the likeness of a dove, to come and remain upon Christ, as they argue a person, so they can in no way be applied to an accident, a quality, or a breath. Furthermore, since the Holy Spirit, having assumed a distinct symbol of manifestation, has produced distinct acts, we truly conclude that he is a person distinct from the Father and the Son.

Antithesis is that of the Socinians, who maintain that the Holy Spirit is not a person, but the virtue of God, sanctifying us, and that it is ἀνυπόστατον, i.e., that which lacks its own subsistence, but exists in God in the manner in which mercy, justice, and other attributes are in God: their stronger arguments are:

I. The virtue of God is not a person; because it is an essential attribute of God. The Holy Spirit is the virtue of God, Therefore. Resp. 1) The Holy Spirit is nowhere in the sacred scriptures called a virtue. In the cited passage, the efficacy or efficacious operation of the Holy Spirit is understood. 2) Distinguish between a virtue that is ἀνυπόστατον, lacking subsistence, and one that is ἀνυπόστατον, enjoying its own subsistence, through which an active and living person is understood. Christ is the virtue of God, and yet a true person Reuben was the first virtue of Jacob, (*). II. Spi- (*): There are altogether three kinds of sayings by which we fight and conquer, that the Holy Spirit is not the virtue of God. 1) There are statements of such a kind by which the Holy Spirit is distinguished from the virtue of God, 2 Cor. 6:6-7, and also from the internal efficacy of God in the mind of man, Eph. 3:16, 20. 2) There are others by which he is distinguished from his own virtue and efficacy, Acts 1:8, 1 Cor. 12:11: all things (gifts, v. 4) are effects, energies; the one generating these effects is virtue and efficacy. What then will the Spirit be? What is the sense: Divine virtue exerts its own virtue, or efficacy, in these effects? see also Rom. 15:13 & 19. 3) There are enunciations by which such excellent powers are attributed to the Holy Spirit that they cannot flow into men, nor ever be communicated with any created thing, namely, most profound intelligence, 1 Cor. 2:10-11, and a secret mind, which no one is able to perceive, except one God, Rom. 8:26-27.

The Holy Spirit is a gift . Therefore, He is not a person. Response: Children are gifts , and yet they are persons.

III. The Holy Spirit is a pledge. Therefore, He is not a person. Response: The Holy Spirit is called a pledge and a seal metaphorically, just as children are commonly called the pledges of their parents. Zerubbabel is called a signet ring, and yet he was a person.

IV. A person is incommunicable. The Holy Spirit is not incommunicable . Therefore, the Holy Spirit is not a person. Response: The Holy Spirit is incommunicable by reason of His ultimate subsistence; but He is communicable by reason of His gracious presence and saving efficacy.

V. No person is in another. The Holy Spirit is in God the Father. Therefore, He is not a person. Response: An infant is in a pregnant mother, yet is nonetheless a true person. God the Father is in the Son, and the Son is in the Father, with the personality of each preserved.

VI. If the Holy Spirit were a person, Christ would more rightly be called the Son of the Holy Spirit than the Son of God the Father. The latter is absurd. Therefore, the former is as well. The consequence of the major premise is proven; because Christ is said to be conceived not by the Father, but by the Holy Spirit. Response: The consequence is denied. Christ is conceived by the Holy Spirit not as a generating principle, but as an exciting and sanctifying one, from which no filiation arises.

VII. No person is extinguished. But the Holy Spirit is extinguished. Response: In the cited passage, the name 'Holy Spirit' is not taken ὑποστατικῶς (hypostatically), personally, for the person of the Holy Spirit, but ἐνεργητικῶς (energetically), metonymically and effectively, for the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

XLIII. Quis est Spiritus sanctus? Spiritus sanctus est tertia diuinitatis persona, non genita, sed ab æterno procedens a Patre & Filio. Vberius definitur.

Spiritus S. est tertia diuinitatis persona, eiusdem cum Patre & Filio essentiæ, quæ ab æterno procedit a Patre & Filio, & ab vtroque in tempore mittitur ad sanctificandum corda hominum saluandorum.

Quæst. XLIV. Quare dicitur Spiritus? Spiritus vocatur non tam a spiritualitate, quam a spirando. Prob. Essentia spiritualis communis est omnibus tribus diuinitatis personis; at spiratio passiua propria est Spiritus S. Vocatur itaque Spiritus, quia a Patre & Filio modo ineffabili ab æterno spiratur, seu spiraculum omnipotens.

Iob.

XXXIII, 4. Quæst. XLV. Quare denominatur sanctus? Sancta dicitur tertia diuinitatis persona non tantum ob sanctitatem essentiæ, sed & ob opus sanctificationis, quod ipsi appropriatur.

Prob. Diuinam essentiam sanctissimam Spiritus S. cum Deo Patre & Filio communem habet; opus autem sanctificationis scriptura sacra & symbolum apostolicum Spiritui S. appropriant.

Ego sum minister Iesu Christi inter gentes, sacrificans euangelium Dei, vt fit oblatio gentium peraccepta, sanctificata in Spiritu S. inquit Paullus Rom.

XV, 16. Quæst. XLVI. Quomodo probas Spiritum S. esse veram, & distinctam a Patre & Filio personam? Vera personalitas Spiritus S. ex definitione personæ (a) & actibus veræ personæ propriis (b) probatur.

Quod autem Spiritus S. distincta a Patre & Filio sit persona, ex ordine personarum diuinarum (c), charactere hypostatico, eiusque nota manifestatiua (d), actione ad extra Spiritui S. appropriata (e), & θεοφανείᾳ, Iordanica (f) innotescit.

Prob. a. Persona definitur, quod sit ὑφιστάμενον, sive suppositum intelligens & libera voluntate præditum. Spiritus S. per se subsistit; quia est paracletus, qui fine subsistentia ultimata ne mente quidem concipi potest. Est intelligens; dicitur quippe spiritus intelligentiæ, scrutans profunda Dei, Est libera voluntate præditus; quoniam dona unicuique distribuit, sicut vult, Ergo est vera persona.

Prob. b. Prædicantur de Spiritu S. actiones personarum propriæ. Nam Spiritus S. loquitur per os sanctorum virorum, Arguit, docet, annuntiat, Consolatur & testatur, Præficit ecclesiæ episcopos, Jubet ministros sibi segregari, Quæ actiones non nisi veræ personæ convenire possunt.

Prob. c. Spiritus S. in negotio salutis cum Deo Patre coniungitur, & vt tertia persona enumeratur. Baptizamur enim in nomen Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. Conf. Vbi tertius testis cœlestis appellatur. Ergo Spiritus S. & vera & distincta a Patre filioque persona est.

Prob. d. Spiritus S. a Patre & Filio spiratur, sive procedit, & mittitur, At spirans & spiratus, mittens & missus, sunt distinctæ personæ.

Prob. e. Appropriatur Spiritui S. opus sanctificationis, ad quod pertinet etiam consolatio afflictorum. At Spiritus S. est paracletus, sive consolator a Christo distinctus. Rogabo Patrem, vt alium paracletum det vobis.

Prob. f. Cum Christus baptizaretur in Jordane, apparuit Pater voce, Natus corpore, Flamen ave. Formam visibilem & corporalem ad tempus assumere, in eadem de cœlo descendere, specie columbina apparere, super Christum venire & manere, vti personam arguunt, ita accidenti, qualitati & flatui nullo modo applicari possunt. Cæterum cum Spiritus S. assumto manifestationis symbolo distincto, distinctos ediderit actus, eundem distinctam a Patre & Filio esse personam, ex vero colligimus.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, statuentium, Spiritum S. non esse personam, sed virtutem Dei, nos sanctificantem, eamque ἀνυπόστατον, i. e. quæ propria subsistentia careat, existat autem in Deo eum in modum, quo misericordia, iustitia, & alia attributa sunt in Deo: quorum potiora sunt argumenta:

I. Virtus Dei non est persona; quia est attributum Dei essentiale. Spiritus S. est virtus Dei, Ergo. Resp. 1) Spiritus S. nullibi in sacris litteris vocatur virtus. Loco citato efficacia, seu efficax operatio Spiritus S. intelligitur. 2) Dist. inter virtutem ἀνυπόστατον, subsistentia carentem, & ἀνυπόστατον, propria subsistentia gaudentem, per quam persona agilis & viuda intelligitur. Christus est virtus Dei, & tamen vera persona Ruben erat Jacobi prima virtus, (*). II. Spi- (*):

Spiritus S. est donum . E. non est persona. Resp. Liberi sunt dona . & tamen personæ.

III. Spiritus S. est pignus . E. non est persona. Resp. Spiritus S. metaphorice dicitur pignus & sigillum, sicut liberi pignora vulgo appellantur. Serubabel dicitur annulus signatorius . Et tamen fuit persona.

IV. Persona est incommunicabilis. Spiritus S. non est incommunicabilis . Ergo Spiritus S. non est persona. Resp. Spiritus S. est incommunicabilis, ratione subsistentiæ ultimatæ; communicabilis autem est ratione gratiosæ præsentiæ & salutaris efficaciæ.

V. Nulla persona est in alia. Spiritus S. est in Deo Patre. Ergo non est persona. Resp. Infans est in matre gravida, nihilo tamen minus est vera persona. Deus pater est in Filio, & Filius in Patre, salua vtriusque personalitate .

VI. Si Spiritus S. persona esset, Christus rectius diceretur Filius Spiritus sancti, quam Filius Dei Patris. Posterius est absurdum. Ergo & prius. Consequentia maioris probatur; quia Christus dicitur conceptus non a Patre, sed a Spiritu S. Resp. Negatur consequentia. Conceptus est Christus a Spiritu S. non tanquam principio generante, sed excitante & sanctificante, vnde nulla oritur filiatio.

VII. Nulla persona exstinguitur. Sed Spiritus S. exstinguitur . Resp. Locitato nomen Spiritus S. non sumitur ὑποστατικῶς personaliter, pro persona Spiritus sancti, sed ἐνεργητικῶς, metonymice & effectiue pro donis Spiritus S.


### Q. XLVII: By what arguments is the divinity of the Holy Spirit demonstrated?

The divinity of the Holy Spirit is demonstrated by arguments ὀνομασικοῖς (nominal), taken from divine names (a), ἰδιωματικοῖς (idiomatic), drawn from divine attributes (b), ἐνεργητικῶς (energetic), taken from operations belonging to God alone (c), λατρευτικοῖς (latreutic), taken from the supreme worship owed to God (d). To these add the accurate collation of the sayings of the Old and New Testaments (e).

Prob. a. 1) Peter says that He, to whom Ananias had lied—besides the apostles, and in the first place—or had dared to foist his lie as truth, is the Holy Spirit: but soon in v. 4 he calls Him God Himself. From which we argue: He to whom Ananias lied, besides the apostles and in the first place, is the true God. But the Holy Spirit [is He], etc. Therefore. 2) Paul says that the faithful are the temple of God by this, that the Spirit of God dwells in them as in temples. He indicates, therefore, that the Holy Spirit is God. 3) King David says: The Spirit of Jehovah spoke in me, and His word (was) upon my tongue. The God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spoke to me. Whom King David had previously called the Spirit of Jehovah, he afterwards calls the God of Israel (*).

Prob. b. Divine idioms are predicated of the Holy Spirit. For He is called 1) eternal. Concerning whom Isaiah says: Who has helped the spirit of the Lord, when He weighed the mass of the earth? Therefore, the Holy Spirit, when the earth was first created, was already then: Which Moses also by his testimony proves, Gen. I, 2. Moreover, everything before the world is eternal by the style of scripture. 2) Omnipresent. Whither shall I go from thy spirit? The sacred psalmist asks. 3) Omniscient: For the Spirit of God searches even the deep things of God, i.e. he penetrates the mysteries of God, unsearchable to any creature. 4) Omnipotent. For he is called the spirit of power, of whom it is said, power from on high, if not synonymously; yet paronymously, Luc. XXIV, 49. You shall be endued with power from on high. Which words Christ himself explains: you shall receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you. 5) ἐξοχῶς or excellently good. Let thy good Spirit lead me in the land of uprightness. 6) Most true. For he is the spirit of truth leading us into all truth. 7) Most glorious; because he is the spirit of glory, resting upon us. 8) To God the Father and the Son ὁμοούσιος, or consubstantial. There are three heavenly witnesses, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one. These things being premised, we argue. Whoever is eternal, omnipresent, omniscient, omnipotent, most good, most true, most glorious, consubstantial with God the Father and the Son, he is the true and supreme God. But the Holy Spirit is, &c. Therefore (*). Prob. c.

The divinity of the Holy Spirit is confirmed from the divine works, which in the sacred scriptures are attributed to the Holy Spirit. Namely 1) works of power, such as creation, . (*) Since immutability is undoubtedly to be numbered among the natural properties of God , this also is in the Holy Spirit .

The word, αὐτὸ, can here designate nothing else than perpetuity, void of all mutability; for 1) it is distinguished from that word, 2) it is opposed to variety, just as τὸ ἐν is to multitude, . E denotes that which is contrary to variation and mutation; 3) it is attributed to the Holy Spirit equally as to the Father, 4) it is explained in Hebr. I, 12. as signifying the opposite of mutability, and corresponding to the Hebrew, הוּא, always the same, . But as regards the divine perfections, from those reserved as proper to them, and indeed all of them, with none removed, the supreme divinity of the Holy Spirit shines forth clearer than light .

For they are reserved to him no less than to God the Father I. Of divine knowledge: 1) the most perfect knowledge of God himself, and of all the secret counsels of God, . 2) The knowledge of the whole nature of things, and also 3) of those things which far surpass all the powers of nature, . and therefore miracles are ascribed to him: 4) The knowledge of minds, . nay even that . especially to pertain to the Holy Spirit, appears from this, that the power of appointing ministers of the church is attributed to him, .

5) The foreknowledge of future events, and of contingent things, and of the most remote, and of the smallest, for his are the predictions and prophecies concerning things long after to be, and also concerning definite times, . II. Of divine wisdom: 1) The choice of that which is never not the best; wherefore he is called κατ' ἐξοχὴν the Spirit of wisdom and understanding: 2) Amplitude, without any exception, . 3) Independence; for he himself possesses that wisdom, (α) which no one taught him, . (β) which he also teaches us, and (γ) which no one can resist, . where the foolishness of the Spirit is said plainly thus, as the foolishness of God, . This saying is also very notable, . E. The Holy Spirit is of more value, than that renewed men can both ask of God and understand, which is proper to God, .

III. Of divine truth: 1) Universality, . and for that reason he is called κατ' ἐξοχὴν the Spirit of truth: 2) Necessity, so that his testimony is most certain, upon which our whole faith rests, in divine matters, and in those pertaining to our eternal salvation, .

IV. Of divine power, and authority; for the Holy Spirit 1) alone can effect 2) all things, and indeed 3) independently; whenever it pleases him, 4) immediately, namely miracles, 5) perfectly, so that nothing is lacking, which pertains to the common salvation of men, especially indeed of their souls.

All these things are contained in this one saying, .

Preservation, Job XXXIII, 4. Ps. CIV, 30. Performance of miracles, Luke I, 35. Matt. XII, 28. Acts X, 38. 2) Works of grace, which pertain either to the redemption or to the sanctification of the human race. To redemption pertains the mission of the redeemer regarding his humanity. Isa. XLVIII, 16. Anointing, Ps. XLV, 8. Isa. LXI, 1. 1 John III, 34. Acts X, 38. Instruction, Isa. XI, 2. Direction, Matt. IV, 1. To sanctification (taken broadly) pertain the calling and preaching of the word, which is called the ministry of the Spirit, 2 Cor. III, 6. (The Holy Spirit calls and ordains bishops preaching the divine word, Acts XX, 28. He speaks through them, Matt. X, 20.) Illumination, 2 Cor. III, 28. Regeneration, John III, 5. Justification, 1 Cor. VI, 35. Gracious indwelling, 1 Cor. III, 16. Renewal, Tit. III, 5. Gal. V, 22. Glorification, Eph. I, 14. 3) Works of justice, namely, the conviction of the world, John XVI, 8. Withdrawal of the word, done out of just judgment, Acts XVI, 6. Resurrection of the dead, Rom. VIII, 11. From these arises an argument: He who performs truly divine works is the true God. But the Holy Spirit, etc. Therefore. Proof d. The divinity of the Holy Spirit is established from the religious worship which is owed to Him. For 1) we are baptized into the name of the Holy Spirit just as into the name of the Father and of the Son. Matt. XXIII, 19. But baptism implies the worship of faith and invocation. Which BASIL teaches excellently in epistle 78. We must be baptized as we have received: But we must believe as we are baptized: But we must glorify, as we believe, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. 2) Our hearts are temples of the Holy Spirit. 1 Cor. VI, 19. Whoever dwells in pious hearts as in His own temples, He is God to be glorified by us (1 Cor. VI, 19. 20.) But the Holy Spirit dwells, etc. Therefore. 3) The angels adore the Holy Spirit, Isa. VI, 3. compared with Acts XXVII, 26. 29 King David invoked [Him] Ps. CXLIII, 10. Paul 2 Cor. XIII, 13. John Rev. I, 4. (*) Proof e. An accurate comparison of the sayings of the Old and New Testament Scripture provides us with the firmest arguments for the deity of the Holy Spirit in the following manner: He who spoke to Isaiah, and ordered him to go to the people, etc. Isa. VI, 9. He is the true and supreme God. But the Holy Spirit is He who spoke to Isaiah according to Acts XXVIII, 25. Therefore the Holy Spirit is the true God. He who spoke through the prophets is Jehovah, Isa. I, 2. Ezek. I, 3. But the Holy Spirit spoke through the prophets, 1 Pet. I, 11. 2 Pet. I, 21. Thus compare 2 Sam. XXIII, 2. with Acts I, 16. The antithesis was once that of the Macedonians, but today it is that of the Socinians, who deny that the Holy Spirit is the supreme God, whose stronger arguments are the following: I. The Holy Spirit is nowhere in the sacred writings called God. Therefore He is not the true God. Resp. The Holy Spirit is indeed called God. Acts V, 3. 4. 1 Cor. III, 16. 17. 2 Sam. XXIII, 2. 3.

Objection 1. But this proposition: The Holy Spirit is God, which the Evangelicals bring forward, does not explicitly exist in the Holy Scriptures. Resp. 1) Neither that proposition: The Holy Spirit is the virtue of God, which Socinus attempts to defend; nor that thesis: The Holy Spirit is a quality intermediate between the virtue of God and the effects in man, which Crellius strives to maintain, is read expressly in Holy Scripture. 2) We show that the Holy Spirit is expressly called God in the Holy Scriptures by easy and manifest consequence. When in 1 Cor. 3:16–17 believers are called the temple of God, for the reason that the Spirit of God dwells in them; it necessarily follows that the Holy Spirit is God Himself, from whom believers have this, that they are called the temple of God. This argument will be: He by whom, as the indweller, believers are called temples of God, is expressly called God (compare this with the statement in 2 Cor. 6:16): But believers are called temples of God by the indwelling Holy Spirit (cf. 1 Cor. 6:19–20). Therefore, the Holy Spirit is expressly called God. Pious antiquity used this argument most extensively against the Pneumatomachi. Hence Theophylact on 1 Cor. 3:16: "If we are the temple of God, because the Holy Spirit dwells in us. Therefore, the Holy Spirit is God." And Athanasius in Dialogue III on the Trinity, Vol. II of his Works: "Every temple of God is a temple of the Holy Spirit." Objection 2.

Objection 2. But the Holy Spirit l.c. [in the place cited], as also elsewhere in Holy Scripture, Isa. 63:10, Joel 2:28, Matt. 3:16, is distinguished from God (for He is called the Spirit of God): Therefore He is not God Himself. For things that are distinguished are not the same. Resp. The Spirit is distinguished from God not essentially, but personally. For when it is said "the Spirit of God," then the word "God" is not taken ousiodōs [οὐσιωδῶς], or essentially, but hypostatikōs [ὑποστατικῶς], or personally; and from the distinction of the Holy Spirit from God, thus accepted, it is not correctly inferred that He is not God, but this only follows: that He is a person other than that divine person from whom He is distinguished.

Latin:

Diuinitas Spiritus sancti demonstratur argumentis ὀνομασικοῖς, petitis a nominibus diuinis (a), ἰδιωματικοῖς, haustis ex attributis diuinis (b), ἐνεργητικῶς, depromtis ab operationibus Deo soli conuenientibus (c), λατρευτικοῖς, sumtis a cultu summo Deo debito (d). Quibus adde accuratam dictorum V. & N. T. collationem (e).

Prob. a. 1) Petrus eum, cui Ananias præter apostolos, atque in primis mentitus, seu mendacium suum pro vero obtrudere ausus fuerat, Spiritum S. esse dicit: mox autem v. 4. Deum ipsum appellat. Ex quo argumentamur: Cui præter apostolos atque in primis mentitus est Ananias, is est verus Deus. Atqui Spiritus S. &c. Ergo. 2) Paullus fideles dicit esse templum Dei per hoc, quod Spiritus Dei in ipsis, tanquam in templis, habitet. Indicat ergo Spiritum S. esse Deum. 3) Rex Dauid inquit: Spiritus Iehouæ locutus est in me, & sermo eius (fuit) super lingua mea. Dixit Deus Israëlis, mihi locuta est petra Israëlis. Quem antea rex Dauid vocauerat spiritum Iehouæ, postea Deum Israëlis appellat (*).

Prob. b. Prædicantur de Spiritu S. idiomata diuina. Dicitur enim 1) æternus. De quo Esaias inquit: Quis adiuvit spiritum domini, cum appendit molem terræ? Ergo Spiritus S. cum terra primum crearetur, iam tum erat: Id quod Moses etiam testimonio suo comprobat, Gen. I, 2. Est autem omne antemundanum stilo scripturae aeternum . 2) Omnipraesens. Quo ibo a spiritu tuo? Interrogat hieropsaltes . 3) Omnisciens: Spiritus enim Dei scrutatur etiam profunda Dei . i. e. penetrat arcana Dei nulli creaturae pervestigabilia. 4) Omnipotens. Vocatur enim spiritus potentiae, . de quo dicitur virtus ex alto, si non synonymice; attamen paronymice, Luc. XXIV, 49. Vos induemini virtute ex alto. Quae verba Christus ipse exponit . accipietis virtutem supervenientis Spiritus S. super vos. 5) ἐξοχῶς seu excellenter bonus. Spiritus tuus bonus ducat me in terra rectitudinis, . 6) Verissimus. Est quippe spiritus veritatis ducens nos in omnem veritatem, . 7) Gloriosissimus; quia est spiritus gloriae, super nobis requiescens. . 8) Deo Patri & Filio ὁμοούσιος, sive consubstantialis. Tres testes coelestes, Pater, verbum & Spiritus S. sunt unum, . Quibus praemissis argumentamur. Quicunque est aeternus, omnipraesens, omniscius, omnipotens, optimus, verissimus, gloriosissimus, Deo Patri & Filio consubstantialis, ille est verus & summus Deus. Atqui Spiritus S. &c. Ergo (*). *Prob. c.

Confirmatur diuinitas Spiritus S. ex operibus diuinis, quae in sacris litteris Spiritui S. tribuuntur. Nempe 1) opera potentiae, qualia sunt creatio, .* (*) Quum in proprietatibus Dei naturalibus haud dubie numeranda sit immutabilitas , etiam haec est in Spiritu S. .

Vocabulum, αὐτὸ, hic nihil potest designare aliud, quam perpetuitatem, omnis mutabilitatis expertem; namque 1) discernitur ab illa voce, 2) opponitur varietati, sicut τὸ ἐν multitudini, . E denotat id, quod variationi ac mutationi contrarium est; 3) tribuitur Spiritui S. aeque, ac Patri, 4) explicatur Hebr. I, 12. quod significet oppositum mutabilitati, & respondeat hebraico, הוּא, semper idem, . Sed quod ad perfectiones diuinas attinet, ex harum propriis reservatis, & quidem vniuersis, nullo demto, luce clarius elucet Spiritus sancti summa diuinitas .

Ipsius enim non minus, quam Dei Patris, sunt reservata I. Scientia diuinae: 1) perfectissima Dei ipsius, omniumque arcanorum Dei consiliorum, cognitio, . 2) Natura rerum vniversa, atque etiam 3) eorum, quae natura vires longe omnes superant, scientia, . ideoque miracula ipsi adfignantur: 4) Animorum cognitio, . immo & illud, . praesertim ad Spiritum S. pertinere, adparet ex eo, quod potestas constituendi ministros ecclesiae ipsi tribuitur, .

5) Praescientia futurorum euentuum, & contingentium, & remotissimorum, & minimorum, ipsius enim sunt praedictiones & vaticinationes de rebus, longe post futuris, atque etiam de temporibus definitis, . II. Sapientiae diuinae: 1) Electio nunquam non optimi; quocirca dicitur κατ' ἐξοχὴν Spiritus sapientiae atque intelligentiae: 2) Amplitudo, fine vlla exceptione, . 3) Independentia; ea enim ipse valet sapientia, (α) quam nemo eum docuit, . (β) quam & ipse nos docet, & (γ) cui nemo potest resistere, . ubi μωρία τῶν τῦ πνεύματος dicitur plane sic, ut μωρία τῦ Θεῦ, . Valde etiam notabile est hoc dictum, . E. Spiritus S. plus valet, quam renouati homines & petere a Deo possunt & intelligere, id quod est Dei proprium, .

III. Veritatis diuinae: 1) Vniversitas, . eamque ob causam dicitur κατ' ἐξοχὴν Spiritus veritatis: 2) Necessitas, vt certissimum sit ipsius testimonium, quo tota nititur fides nostra, in rebus diuinis, & ad nostram salutem aeternam spectantibus, .

IV. Potentiae diuinae, ac potestatis; namque Spiritus S. 1) vnus potest efficere 2) omnia, & quidem 3) independenter; vcumque ipsi placuerit, 4) immediate, nimirum miracula, 5) perfecte, vt nihil desit, quod ad communem hominum salutem, praecipue vero animorum, pertineat.

Haec vniuersa continentur in vno hoc dicto, .

Conferuatio, Job. XXXIII, 4. Pf. CIV, 30. Miraculorum patratio, Luc. I, 35. Matth. XII, 28. Act. X, 38. 2) Opera gratiæ, quæ vel ad redemptionem, vel ad sanctificationem generis humani spectant. Ad redemptionem pertinent redemtoris quoad humanitatem missio. Es. XLVIII, 16. Vnctio, Pf. XLV, 8. Es. LXI, 1. 1 Io. III, 34. Act. X, 38. Instructio, Es. XI, 2. Directio, Matth. IV, 1. Ad sanctificationem (late sumtam) pertinent vocatio & prædicatio verbi, quæ dicitur ministerium Spiritus, 2 Cor. III, 6. (Spiritus S. vocat & ordinat episcopos verbum diuinum prædicantes, Act. XX, 28. Loquitur per eos, Matth. X, 20.) Illuminatio, 2 Cor. III, 28. Regeneratio, Io. III, 5. Iustificatio, 1 Cor. VI, 35. Gratiosæ inhabitatio, 1 Cor. III, 16. Renouatio, Tit. III, 5. Gal. V, 22. Glorificatio, Eph. I, 14. 3) Opera iustitiæ, nempe, mundi redargutio, Io. XVI, 8. Verbi subtractio ex iusto iudicio facta, Act. XVI, 6. Mortuorum resuscitatio, Rom. VIII, 11. Nascitur ex his argumentum: Qui opera vere diuina efficit, is est verus Deus. Atqui Spiritus S. &c. Ergo. Prob. d. Stabilitur diuinitas Spiritus S. e cultu religioso, qui illi debetur. Nam 1) in nomen Spiritus S. æque ac in nomen Patris & Filii baptizamur. Matth. XXIII, 19. Baptismus autem infert cultum fidei & inuocationis. Quod præclare docet BASIL. in epist. 78. Baptizari nos oportet, sicut accepimus: Credere autem sicut baptizamur: Glorificare autem, sicut credimus, Patrem, Filium & Spiritum S. 2) Corda nostra sunt templa Spiritus S. 1 Cor. VI, 19. Quicunque habitat in cordibus piis tanquam templis suis, ille est Deus a nobis glorificandus (1 Cor. VI, 19. 20.) Atqui Spiritus S. habitat &c. Ergo. 3) Spiritum S. adorant angeli Es. VI, 3. collat. cum Act. XXVII, 26. 29 Inuocarunt rex Dauid Pf. CXLIII, 10. Paullus 2 Cor. XIII, 13. Ioannes Apoc. I, 4. (*) Prob. e. Accurata collatio dictorum scripturæ V. & N. T. firmissima pro deitate Spiritus S. nobis suppeditat argumenta sequenti modo: Qui locutus est ad Esaiam, & iussit eum ire ad populum &c. Es. VI, 9. Is est verus ac summus Deus. Sed Spiritus S. est is, qui locutus est ad Esaiam iuxta Act. XXVIII, 25. Ergo Spiritus S. est verus Deus. Qui locutus est per prophetas, est Iehouah, Es. I, 2. Ezech. I, 3. Sed Spiritus S. locutus est per prophetas, 1 Pet. I, 11. 2 Petr. I, 21. Sic conf. 2 Sam. XXIII, 2. cum Act. I, 16. Antithesis olim fuit Macedonianorum, hodie autem est Socinianorum, negantium Spiritum S. esse sumunum Deum, quorum argumenta potiora sunt sequentia: I. Spiritus sanctus nullibi in sacris litteris dicitur Deus. Ergo non est verus Deus. Resp. Spiritus S. vtique Deus dicitur. Act. V, 3. 4. 1 Cor. III, 16. 17. 2 Sam. XXIII, 2. 3.

Instantia 1. Sed haec propositio: Spiritus S. est Deus, quam afferunt Evangelici, in sacris litteris diserte non exstat. Resp. 1) Neque ista propositio: Spiritus S. est virtus Dei, quam defendere conatur Socinus; neque illa thesis: Spiritus S. est qualitas intermedia inter virtutem Dei, et effectus in homine, quam tueri nititur Crellius, expresse in scriptura S. legitur. 2) Spiritum S. in sacris litteris expresse vocari Deum, per consequentiam facilem et manifestam ostendimus. Quando 1 Cor. III, 16. 17. credentes dicuntur templum Dei, ideo, quod Spiritus Dei in illis habitat; necessario sequitur, quod Spiritus S. fit ipse Deus, a quo credentes hoc habent, quod templum Dei vocentur. Argumentum hoc erit: A quo, tanquam inhabitante, credentes dicuntur templa Dei, is expresse vocatur Deus, (confer cum hoc dicto 2 Cor. VI, 16.): Atqui a Spiritu S. inhabitante credentes dicuntur templa Dei (conf. 1 Cor. VI, 19. 20.) Ergo Spiritus S. expresse vocatur Deus. Pia antiquitas contra Pneumatomachos hoc argumentum quam maxime visit. Hinc Theophylactus in 1 Cor. III, 16. Si Dei templum nos sumus, quia in nobis inhabitat Spiritus S. Ergo Spiritus S. est Deus. Et Athanasius in dialogo III. de Trinitat. tom. II. Oper. Omne templum Dei templum Spiritus S. est. Instantia 2.

Sed Spiritus S. l. c. vt et alibi in S. scriptura, Es. LXIII, 10. Joel. II, 28. Matth. III, 16. a Deo distinguitur (dicitur enim spiritus Dei): Ergo non est ipse Deus. Nam quae distinguuntur, non sunt idem. Resp. Spiritus distinguitur a Deo non essentialiter, sed personaliter. Nam quando dicitur spiritus Dei, tunc vox Dei non sumitur ουσιωδῶς, seu essentialiter, sed ὑποστατικῶς, seu personaliter; et distinctione Spiritus S. a Deo, sic accepto, minus recte infertur, eum non esse Deum, sed hoc saltim sequitur, eum esse personam aliam ab illa persona divina, a qua distinguitur.


### Q. XLVII: By what arguments is the divinity of the Holy Spirit demonstrated? (continued)

II. The Most High God is eternal. The Holy Spirit is not eternal. Therefore. The minor is proved: 1) John 7:39: "The Holy Spirit was not yet, because Jesus was not yet glorified." 2) From Acts 19:2: Those baptized by John did not know that there was a Holy Spirit. Resp. to I. The words of the text are to be understood concerning the miraculous mission and visible effusion of the Holy Spirit, by which the apostles were instructed with extraordinary gifts on the day of Pentecost, so that the sense is: the Holy Spirit was not yet visibly poured out upon the apostles, because Christ had not yet been taken up into heaven. To II. In the place cited, the discourse is not about the essence of the Holy Spirit itself, but about the miraculous gifts of the Holy Spirit, which flourished at the beginning of the nascent church: for Paul had inquired about these in v. 2, and had conferred these through the laying on of hands in v. 6. How otherwise could the Holy Spirit, who is so often inculcated in the Scriptures of the Old Testament, Gen. 1:2, Ps. 33:6, etc., have been unknown to the Jews or proselytes? Indeed, the Baptist himself publicly professes the doctrine concerning the Holy Spirit, Matt. 3:11, John 1:32.

III. Whoever receives essence from God is not the Most High God. But the Holy Spirit, etc. Therefore. The major is certain: because the Most High God is Jehovah, or the Essentiator [the one who gives essence]. But he who receives essence from another is an essentiated being, and thus not Jehovah. The minor is clear from John 15:16. Resp. Whoever receives essence from God a) dependently, as from an efficient cause, b) numerically different, he is not the Most High God. The Holy Spirit indeed proceeds from the Father and the Son as the principle of origin, not as from an efficient cause, and He receives not a numerically different, but the same essence.

IV. Whoever is sent by the Father and the Son of God is not the Most High God. But the Holy Spirit, John 15:26, cf. 14:26, cf. 16:7. Therefore. Resp. Whoever is sent by the Father and the Son with an imperious mission is not the Most High God, this I concede. But the Holy Spirit is sent with the most free consent, and His mission is nothing other than a temporal manifestation of His origin, or eternal procession from the Father and the Son.

V. The most high God, whatever He speaks, speaks from Himself. The Holy Spirit does not, &c. Jo. XVI, 13. Therefore. Resp. The phrase: to speak from Himself, can be taken in a double sense. First: that it may imply simply the negation of all origin, so that the sense is: The most high God speaks all things from Himself, so that He acknowledges no origin at all, from which He might have the power and knowledge of speaking. Second: that to speak from Himself may imply the negation of dependence in speaking upon another and superior cause, so that the sense is: The most high God, whatever He speaks, speaks from Himself, i.e., He speaks independently of any other superior cause. In the former sense the major proposition is not universal, but is true only of God the Father; for the Father alone is not from another; thus He does not hear, or receive from another, what He speaks, but speaks from Himself. But if the major is taken in the latter sense, it will indeed be universally true, but the minor will be denied by us. For when Christ says: The Spirit of truth shall not speak from Himself, but whatever He shall hear, He shall speak, then those words are to be taken in the former, not in the latter sense, so that their meaning is: The Holy Spirit, as He receives His essence by procession from the Father and the Son, so He receives the power and knowledge of speaking, so that He speaks nothing from Himself; but whatever He speaks, He speaks simultaneously with God the Father and the Son. The venerable Bede agrees with us, who, as cited by D. Calovius in bibl. illustrat. in h. l. fol. 801, explains the words of Christ thus: The Spirit does not speak from Himself, that is, by the communion of the Father and the Son: for the Spirit is not different, nor apart from the equals; but whatever He shall hear, He shall speak; He shall hear, namely, through the unity of substance and the property of knowledge: from whom He has essence, from Him certainly also knowledge, from Him therefore hearing, which is nothing else than knowledge. For which reason the words of Christ denote not ignorance or dependence, but the identity of doctrine and essence, and the order of eternal procession.

VI. The most high God is omniscient. The Holy Spirit does not, &c. Therefore. The minor is proved from I Cor. XI, 10. The Holy Spirit searches τὰ βάθη, i.e., the deep things of God: To search signifies to inquire into those things which are unknown. Resp. From divine searching, or omniscience, to human searching, or ignorance, the consequence does not hold. For the Holy Spirit does not search, as men do, by gathering unknown things from known things through successive reasoning, but by penetrating and inspecting the intimate and most secret counsels and decrees of God by a simple intuition. He searches in such a way that He knows the things that are of God, I Cor. II, 11. Thus God is said to search the reins and hearts, Ps. VII, 10. Jer. XI, 20, by knowing them most intimately.

VII. The most high God is given to no one, is obtained by no one through prayers, is possessed by no one. But the Holy Spirit is given to men, is obtained by them through prayers, is possessed by the same. Therefore, the Holy Spirit is not the most high God. The major is evident; because whatever is given, and obtained by prayers, is in the power of the giver: but whatever is possessed, is in the power of the possessor. Both are most alien to the majesty of the most high God. The minor is proved from Luc. XI, 13. Jo. VII, 39. c. XIV, 16. 17. Act. V, 32. c. XV, 8. &c. Resp. (1) By way of objection: The Son of God is true God, and yet He is given to us. Es. IX, 6. Jo. III, 16. We have God the Father as dwelling in us (Jo. XIV, 23.), we obtain Him by prayers. (2) For a gift, it is not required that it be in the power of superiority of him who gives; for the power of origin suffices. And one can give himself to another. For the Son of God gave Himself, Galat. II, 20. Eph. V, 25, not made superior by Himself. (3) God is possessed by us not indeed by a possession of authority, which infers the right and power of the possessor; but nevertheless by a communicative possession, by which we have God Himself graciously present and indwelling. Whence He is called our reward, Gen. XV, 1. our portion, Psal. LXXIII, 26. (4) Concerning the passages alleged, it must be …observed that the primary signification, in which the name of the Holy Spirit is taken ὑποστατικῶς, i.e., for the person, must be distinguished from the secondary signification, in which it is taken ἐνεργητικῶς, or for the gifts. For Luc. XI, 13. means gifts, as is evident from Matth. VII, 11.; Jo. VII, 39. the visible outpouring; Act. XV, 8. the visible gift are understood. Jo. XIV, 16. Act. V, 32. concerning the person of the Holy Spirit is indeed being discussed, but neither by the intercession of Christ, nor by the giving of the Father, is anything detracted from the deity of the Holy Spirit. For He is given by the Father and the Son; because He proceeds from both from eternity, and is sent in time. VIII. Whoever is not commanded in Holy Scripture to be worshipped, he is not the true God. But the Holy… Spirit is not commanded in Holy Scripture to be worshipped. Therefore. Resp. (1) There is no strength in the major proposition. For because we believe that the Holy Spirit is the supreme God, it is evident of itself and by itself that the Holy Spirit is to be worshipped, even if no precept or example concerning His religious veneration were expressed in the sacred scriptures. For he who is commanded to worship God is commanded to worship the Holy Spirit. (2) That the minor is false is evident from the proof of IX. If the Holy Spirit were God, ὁμοούσιος to the Father and the Son, He would know both the Father and the Son. But He knows neither the Father nor the Son. Therefore. The antecedent is proved from Matt. XI, 27. No one knows the Son, except the Father: nor does anyone know the Father, except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal Him. Where the Holy Spirit is excluded from the knowledge of the Father and the Son. Resp. Exclusive and exceptive particles, added to one divine person, do not exclude other divine persons, but creatures. That the Holy Spirit indeed knows the Father and the Son without the revelation of another is evident from 1 Cor. II, 11. Jo. XIV, 26. X. The supreme God is not divisible. The Holy Spirit is divisible (conf. 1 Jo. IV, 13. Act. II, 18. Hebr. II, 4. Num. XI, 17. etc.) Therefore. Resp. In the cited places the name of the Holy Spirit is taken metonymically and effectively, for the gifts of the Holy Spirit. But from the division of gifts to the division of the essence of the Holy Spirit the consequence is not valid; there is one Holy Spirit and He is indivisible, but there are divisions and partitions of charisms, 1 Cor. XII, 4. 7. XI. The Holy Spirit is the virtue of God, that is to say, that which proceeds from God, and flowing into men sanctifies them, consecrates them, and produces various and admirable effects in them, which is accustomed to be called divine inspiration. Luke XXIV, 49. 1 Cor. II, 4. 5. But the virtue of God cannot be the supreme God or a divine person. Resp. (1) Above we showed the infirmity of this argument. (2) No virtue of God is ἀνυπόστατος, which behaves by way of a divine attribute, is the Paraclete, another from Christ, the third heavenly witness, distinct from the Father and the Son: no virtue of God is said to proceed from the Father and the Son, and to be sent by both. Which predicates agree with the Holy Spirit. Jo. XIV, 16. c. XVI, 7. 1 Jo. V, 7. Therefore He is a divine person, ὁμοούσιος to God the Father and the Son. XII. The supreme God is not poured out. The Holy Spirit is poured out. Therefore. The major is clear. For who would say that any person, let alone the supreme God, is poured out into men? The minor is proved from Is. XLIV, 3. Ez. XXXIX, 29. Joel II, 28. 29. Resp. The intimate communication of the Holy Spirit to produce gracious effects is signified metaphorically by the name of effusion. What is there in this meaning that cannot be attributed to the supreme God? Is not the supreme good communicative of itself and as it were diffusive? Cannot God the Father, since He is a living fountain, pour Himself out, so that His grace may irrigate us? Jer. II, 13. Rom. V, 5. You say: The Holy Spirit does not pour Himself out, but is passively poured out, which is below the majesty of the supreme God. Resp. The active communication of the Holy Spirit is wished for by Paul, 2 Cor. XIII, 13. And by the same apostle, 1 Cor. XII, 4. 11. The Holy Spirit is proposed not only as poured out, but also as pouring out both Himself and the divisions of gifts. But He is said to be poured out by the Father and the Son, because He proceeds from both from eternity, and is sent in time. XIII. Whoever is omitted when the Father and the Son are commemorated in many places of scripture, where the sanctification and salvation of man is discussed, he is not the supreme God. But the Holy Spirit etc. Therefore. The minor is proved from the ep. of Jude v. 2. 1 Cor. VIII, 6. 7. R. I deny the major, which, if it were solid, should be formed thus: Whoever is nowhere in Holy Scripture called God, nor is ever commemorated with divine persons, or joined in the business of salvation, is not the supreme God. But the Holy Spirit is often called God in the sacred scriptures, and is often commemorated with the mentioned divine persons. Luke III, 22. Matt. XXIX, 19. 1 Jo. V, 7. 1 Petr. I, 2. and in other places.

Latin:

II. Summus Deus est aeternus. Spiritus S. non est aeternus. Ergo. Minor prob. 1) Io. VII, 39. Nondum erat Spiritus sanctus, quia Iesus nondum glorificatus erat. 2) Ex Act. XIX, 2. Baptizati a Ioanne nescierunt esse Spiritum S. Resp. ad I. Verba textus intelligenda sunt de miranda missione et visibili effusione Spiritus sancti, qua apostoli in die pentecostes donis extraordinariis instructi sunt, vt sensus sit: nondum erat Spiritus S. visibiliter effusus super apostolos, quia Christus in coelum nondum evectus erat. Ad II. Loco citato sermo est non de ipsa Spiritus S. essentia, sed de miraculosis Spiritus S. donis, quae initio nascentis ecclesiae vigebant: de his enim Paulus quaesuerat v. 2. et haec per manuum impositionem contulerat v. 6. Quomodo alias Iudaeis, vel proselytis ignotus potuit esse Spiritus S. qui toties in scripturis V. T. inculcatur, Gen. I, 2. Ps. XXXIII, 6. et c.? Quin ipse etiam baptista doctrinam de Spiritu S. publice profitetur Matth. III, 11. Io. I, 32.

III. Quicunque essentiam accipit a Deo, is non est summus Deus. Atqui Spiritus S. et c. Ergo. Maior constat: quia summus Deus est Jehouah, sive essentiator. At, qui ab alio essentiam accipit, est essentiatus, adeoque non Jehouah. Minor liquet ex Io. XV, 16. Resp. Quicunque essentiam accipit a Deo a) dependenter, tanquam a causa efficiente, b) numero diversam, is non est summus Deus. Spiritus S. procedit quidem a Patre et Filio vt principio originis, non vt a causa efficiente, neque numero diversam, sed eandem essentiam accipit.

IV. Qui a Patre et Filio Dei mittitur, is non est summus Deus. Atqui Spiritus S. Jo. XV, 26. c. XIV, 26. c. XVI, 7. Ergo. Resp. Quicunque a Patre et Filio mittitur missione imperiosa, is non est summus Deus, concedo. At Spiritus S. mittitur cum liberrimo consensu, eiusque missio nihil aliud est, quam temporalis manifestatio originis, sive processionis aeternae a Patre et Filio.

V. Deus summus, quidquid loquitur, a se ipso loquitur. Spiritus S. non &c. Jo. XVI, 13. Ergo. Resp. Phrasis: a se ipso loqui, duplici potest sensu accipi. Vno: vt importet simpliciter negationem omnis originis, ita vt sensus sit: Deus summus omnia a se ipso loquitur, vt nullam prorsus agnoscat originem, vnde potentiam & scientiam loquendi habeat. Altero: vt a se loqui, importet negationem dependentiae in loquendo ab alia & superiori causa, vt sensus fit: Deus summus quidquid loquitur, a se ipso loquitur, i. e. independenter ab alia superiori causa loquitur. Priori sensu maior propositio non est vniuersalis, sed de solo Deo Patre vera est; solus enim Pater vti non ab alio est; ita non audit, vel accipit ab alio, quid loquatur, sed a seipso loquitur. Sin posteri-ori sensu maior accipiatur, illa quidem vniuersaliter vera erit, sed minor a nobis negabitur. Quando enim Christus dicit: Spiritus veritatis non loquetur a se ipso, sed quaecunque audierit, loquitur, tum in priori, non in posteriori sensu verba illa accipienda sunt, vt eorum mens sit: Spiritus S. vt per processionem a Patre & Filio essentiam, ita loquendi potentiam & scientiam accipit, vt nihil loquatur a se ipso; sed quidquid loquitur, simul cum Deo Patre & Filio loquitur. Facit nobiscum venerabilis Beda, qui, citante D. Calovio in bibl. illustrat. in h. l. fol. 801. verba Christi ita exponit: Non loquitur spiritus a semet ipso, hoc est, Patris & Filii communione: neque enim diuersus, ac a paritibus est spiritus; sed quaecunque audiet, loquetur; audiet videlicet per vnitatem substantiae & proprietatem scientiae: a quo illi essentia, ab illo vtique & scientia, ab illo igitur audientia, quae nihil aliud est, quam scientia. Quam ob rem verba Christi non ignorantiam aut dependentiam, sed doctrinae & essentiae identitatem, ordinemque aeternae processionis denotant.

VI. Summus Deus est omnisciens. Spiritus S. non &c. Ergo. Minor. prob. ex I Cor. XI, 10. Spiritus S. scrutatur τὰ βάθη, i. profunda Dei: Scrutari significat inquirere in ea, quae sunt incognita. Resp. A scrutinio diuino, siue omniscientiae, ad scrutinium humanum, siue ignorantiae, non valet consequentia. Nam scrutatur Spiritus S. non, vt homines, ignota e notis per discursum successiue colligendo, sed intima secretissimaque consilia & decreta Dei simplici intuitu penetrando & inspiciendo. Sic scrutatur, vt nouerit ea, quae sunt Dei, I Cor. II, 11. Sic Deus dicitur scrutari renes & corda, Ps. VII, 10. Ier. XI, 20. ea penitissime cognoscendo.

VII. Summus Deus nemini donatur, a nemine precibus impetratur, a nemine possidetur. At Spiritus S. hominibus donatur, ab illis precibus impetratur, ab iisdem possidetur. E. Spiritus S. non est summus Deus. Maior patet; quia quidquid donatur, precibusque impetratur, est in potestate donantis: quidquid autem possidetur, est in potestate possidentis. Vtrunque a maiestate summi Dei alienissimum est. Minor prob. ex Luc. XI, 13. Jo. VII, 39. c. XIV, 16. 17. Act. V, 32. c. XV, 8. &c. Resp. (1) Per instantiam: Filius Dei est verus Deus, & tamen nobis datur. Es. IX, 6. Jo. III, 16. Deum Patrem, vt habitantem in nobis (Jo. XIV, 23.) habemus, precibus impetramus. (2) Ad donum non requiritur, vt fit in potestate superioritatis eius. qui donat; sufficit enim potestas originis. Et potest quis se ipsum donare alteri. Filius enim Dei se ipsum donauit, Galat. II, 20. Eph. V, 25. se ipso non factus superior. (3) Possidetur a nobis Deus non quidem possessione auctoritativa, quae ius & potestatem possidentis infert; attamen possessione communicativa, qua Deum ipsum gratiose praesentem & inhabitantem habemus. Vnde nostra merces, Gen. XV, 1. nostra portio, Psal. LXXIII, 26. appellatur. (4) Circa loca allegata obseruandum, quod significatio primaria, qua ὑποστατικῶς, siue pro persona sumitur, a significatione secundaria, qua ἐνεργητικῶς, feu pro donis accipitur nomen Spiritus sancti, distinguendum sit. Nam Luc. XI, 13. dona, vt ex Matth. VII, 11. patet, Jo. VII, 39. effusio visibilis, Act. XV, 8. donum visibile intelliguntur. Jo. XIV, 16. Act. V, 32. de de persona Spiritus S. agitur quidem, sed neque intercessione Christi, neque datione Patris, deitati Spiritus S. quidquam derogatur. Nam datur a Patre & Filio; quia ab vtroque procedit ab æterno, & in tempore mittitur. VIII. Quicunque non iubetur in S. scriptura adorari, is non est verus Deus. Atqui Spiritus S. non iubetur in S. scriptura adorari. E. Resp. (1) Nihil roboris inest maiori propositioni. Nam quia cuicimus, Spiritum S. esse Deum summum, vltro & per se patet, Spiritum S. esse adorandum, licet de religiosa ipsius veneratione nullum præceptum, aut exemplum in sacris litteris expressum esset. Etenim qui iubetur adorare Deum, iubetur adorare Spiritum sanctum. (2) Minorem falsam esse, patet ex prob. d. IX. Si Spiritus S. esset Deus, Patri & Filio ὁμοούσιος, & Patrem & Filium nosset. Sed neque Patrem, neque filium nouit. Ergo. Antecedens prob. ex Matth. XI, 27. Nemo nouit Filium, nisi Pater: neque Patrem nouit quisquam, nisi Filius, & cui voluerit Filius reuelare. Vbi Spiritus S. a cognitione Patris & Filii excluditur, Resp. Particulæ exclusiuæ & exceptiuæ, vni personæ diuinæ additæ, non excludunt alias personas diuinas, sed creaturas. Spiritum S. vero nosse Patrem & Filium sine reuelatione alterius, patet ex 1 Cor. II, 11. Jo. XIV, 26. X. Deus summus non est partibilis. Spiritus S. est partibilis (conf. 1 Jo. IV, 13. Act. II, 18. Hebr. II, 4. Num. XI, 17. &c.) Ergo. Resp. Locis citatis nomen Spiritus S. sumitur metonymice & effectiue, pro donis Spiritus S. Sed a diuisione donorum ad diuisionem essentiæ Spiritus S. non valet consequentia; Vnus est Spiritus S. & impartibilis, diuisiones autem & partitiones charismatum sunt, 1 Cor. XII, 4. 7. XI. Spiritus S. est virtus Dei, ea nimirum, quæ a Deo procedit, atque in homines manans eos sanctificat, consecrat, & varias atque admirabiles in iis effectus parit, quæ afflatus diuinus appellari solet. Luc. XXIV, 49. 1 Cor. II, 4. 5. Dei autem virtus summus Deus aut persona diuina esse nequit. Resp. (1) Supra infirmitatem huius argumenti ostendimus. (2) Nulla virtus Dei ἀνυπόστατος, quæ per modum attributi diuini se habeat, est paracletus, a Christo alius, testis cœlestis tertius, a Patre & Filio distinctus: nulla virtus Dei a Patre & Filio procedere, & ab vtroque mitti dicitur. Quæ prædicata conueniunt Spiritui S. Jo. XIV, 16. c. XVI, 7. 1 Jo. V, 7. Ergo est persona diuina, Deo Patri & Filio ὁμοούσιος. XII. Summus Deus non effunditur. Spiritus S. effunditur. Ergo. Maior liquet. Quis enim dixerit, personam aliquam, nedum summum Deum in homines effundi? Minor prob. ex Es. XLIV, 3. Ez. XXXIX, 29. Joel. II, 28. 29. Resp. Intima Spiritus S. communicatio ad effectus gratiosos producendos nomine effusionis metaphorice significatur. Quid in hoc significatu est, quod Deo summo tribui nequeat? Nonne summum bonum est sui communicatiuum & quasi diffusiuum? Nonne Deus pater, cum sit fons viuus, se effundere potest, vt ipsius gratia irrigeinur? Jer. II, 13. Rom. V, 5. Dicis: Spir. S. non se effundit, sed passiue effunditur, quod infra maiestatem summi Dei est. Resp. Actiui Spir. S. communicatio a Paullo exoptatur, 2 Cor. XIII, 13. Et ab eodem apostolo, 1 Cor. XII, 4. 11. Spir. S. proponitur non tantum vt effusus, sed & vt effundens tum seipsum, tum diuisiones donorum. Effundi autem dicitur a Patre & Filio, quia ab vtroque procedit ab æterno, & in tempore mittitur. XIII. Quicunque commemorato Patre & Filio in plurimis locis scripturæ, vbi de sanctificatione & saluatione hominis agitur, omittitur, is non est summus Deus. Atqui Spir. S. &c. E. Minor prob. ex ep. Iudæ v. 2. 1 Cor. VIII, 6.7. R. Neg. mai. quæ, si solida foret, sic formanda esset: Quicunque nullibi in sacra scriptura dicitur Deus, nec cum personis diuinis unquam commemoratur, aut in negotio salutis coniungitur, non est summus Deus. At Spir. S. sæpe in sacris litteris dicitur Deus, & memoratis personis diuinis sæpe commemoratur Luc. III, 22. Matth. XXIX, 19. 1 Jo. V, 7. 1 Petr. I, 2. & locis aliis.


### Q. XLVIII. Who is the hypostatic character of the Holy Spirit?

The hypostatic character, or personal property of the Holy Spirit, is passive spiration, or the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son. Proof. Passive spiration belongs solely to the Holy Spirit, distinguishes Him from the Father and the Son, and constitutes Him in the being of the Spirit. Therefore, it is the personal property of the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

Character hypostaticus, seu proprietas personalis Spiritus S. est spiratio passiva, seu processio Spiritus S. a Patre & Filio. Prob. Spiratio passiva soli competit Spiritui sancto, hunc a Patre & Filio distinguit, & in esse Spiritus constituit. Ergo est proprietas personalis Spiritus sancti.


### Q. XLIX. What is passive spiration, or the procession of the Holy Spirit?

Procession, or passive spiration, is the eternal origin of the Holy Spirit, by which He Himself, within the bosom of the deity from the Father and the Son, by the communication of one and the same essence in number, is produced as the common spiracle of both.

Obj. 1. It is called passive spiration, not physically, as if it implied a passive power or imperfection; but grammatically, because the Holy Spirit is said not to breathe, but to be breathed. Nor are active and passive spiration two spirations, but it is one and the same spiration, which by reason of the principle breathing and producing is called active spiration, and by reason of the term produced is called passive. Otherwise, the emanation of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son is most pure.

Obj. 2. Spiration is understood here not as external, such as was the breathing of Christ upon the disciples (John 20:20), but internal and immanent, since it takes place within the very bosom of the deity; not transitory and evanescent, such as that of breathing men, but eternal and permanent; because the Holy Spirit proceeds from eternity, or the spiracle of the Almighty (Job 33:4) and the Spirit of the mouth of the Lord (Ps. 33:6); not an accidental, but a substantial spiration: for an accident does not fall upon God, nor can the Holy Spirit, or the divine person and substance, be produced by an accidental act.

Latin:

Processio, sive spiratio passiva, est æterna Spiritus S. origo, qua ipse intra sinum deitatis a Patre & Filio, unius eiusdemque numero essentiæ communicatione, vt commune utriusque spiraculum producitur.

Obs. 1. Dicitur spiratio passiva, non physice, quasi inferat potentiam passivam, aut imperfectionem; sed grammatice, quia Spiritus S. non spirare, sed spirari dicitur. Neque spiratio activa & passiva sunt duæ spirationes, sed est una eademque spiratio, quæ ratione principii spirantis & producentis, spiratio activa, ratione termini producti, passiva vocatur. Ceteroqui purissima est emanatio Spiritus S. a Patre & Filio.

Obs. 2. Intelligitur hic spiratio non externa, qualis erat insufflatio Christi ad discipulos Jo. XX, 20. sed interna & immanens, cum fiat intra ipsum deitatis sinum; non transitoria & evanescentis, qualis est hominum spirantium, sed æterna & permanens; quia Spiritus S. ab æterno procedit, seu spiraculum omnipotentis Job. XXXIII, 4. & Spiritus oris Domini Ps. XXXIII, 6; non spiratio accidentalis, sed substantialis: in Deum enim non cadit accidens, neque Spiritus S. seu persona & substantia divina, actu accidentali produci potest.


### Q. L. How will you prove that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and from the Son?

That the Holy Spirit proceeds from God the Father, Holy Scripture teaches (a) literally and in express words. That He proceeds from the Son of God is validly gathered from the denomination of the Spirit of the Son (b), the ὁμοοσία (consubstantiality) of the Father and the Son (c), the reception of omniscience from the Son (d), the apocalyptic vision of the river proceeding from the throne of the Lamb (e), the mission of the Holy Spirit by the Son (f), the breathing of Christ upon the disciples (g), and the order and distinction of the divine persons (h).

Proof a. The words of Christ are clear, (John 15:26): When the Comforter shall come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds (ἐκπορεύεται) from the Father, He shall testify of me. The Savior speaks of the eternal and internal procession of the Holy Spirit, by which He Himself receives essence from the Father, not of a temporal and external mission for the work of sanctification, of which the Socinians wish this classic passage to be understood, but wrongly. For (1) mission is openly distinguished from procession. Whom I will send unto you from the Father, who proceeds from the Father. (2) Mission is said to occur in the future time, procession in the present time, so that we may understand the discourse to be not of a temporal mission, but of the eternal emanation of the Holy Spirit. For eternity is the νῦν (now) most present and immovable. (3) The scope of Christ was to bring forward the authority of a heavenly witness, namely, that the testimony of the Holy Spirit is irrefragable and greater than any exception, since He proceeds from the Father Himself, and searches and looks into His τὰ βάθη (depths). (4) The origin of the Holy Spirit is designated in parallel passages by the word ἐκπορεύεσθαι, (Dan. 7:10), (Rev. 22:1).

Obj. To this express assertion of Holy Scripture concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father, other arguments can be added, namely (1) that the Holy Spirit is from God, (1 Cor. 2:12). (2) That He is the Spirit

of the Father, Matt. X, 20. The Spirit of the mouth of the Lord, Ps. XXXIII, 6. The breath of the Almighty, Job XXXIII, 4. Therefore, because He is breathed by the Father, and proceeds from His mouth as the breath of the same, yet in a divine and ineffable manner.

(3) Because He is sent by the Father, John XIV, 26. Temporal mission is a sign of eternal procession. The Father alone is not read to be sent, because He has His origin from no one.

Prob. b. In the same way that the Holy Spirit is called the Spirit of the Father, Matt. X, 20, in the same way He is called the Spirit of the Son, Gal. IV, 6; the Spirit of Christ, Rom. VIII, 9; the Spirit of the lips of Christ, Isa. XI, 4; the Spirit of the mouth of Christ, 2 Thess. II, 8; because as He is breathed by the Father, so He is breathed by the Son of God in an ineffable manner, and proceeds from His mouth like a divine breath.

Prob. c. All things that the Father has are mine: For this reason I said; that He shall take of mine, and shall announce it to you, John XVI, 15. From which words of Christ not only the consubstantiality (ὁμοουσία) of the Father and the Son, but the origination of the Holy Spirit from the Son is gathered. For whatever is said of the Father, this must be said entirely of the Son, except for this very thing, that He is the Father, says CYRIL in the Thesaurus. We argue: Whoever has all things that God the Father has, except for fatherhood alone, he has the power of breathing the Holy Spirit. But the Son of God [has all things] etc. Therefore.

Prob. d. John XVI, 13, 14. When that Spirit of truth shall come, He will lead you into all truth. For He shall not speak of Himself, but whatever He shall hear, He shall speak, and He shall announce to you the things to come. He shall glorify me: because He shall receive of mine, and shall announce it to you. From whom the Spirit of truth receives the knowledge of speaking and announcing future things, from Him He receives His essence. But [He receives it] from the Son of God etc. Therefore. The major premise is evident; because in the Holy Spirit, essence and knowledge are the same. The knowledge of future things is divine and eternal, which, on the part of the thing, is the divine essence itself. You say: If the discourse had been about the reception of knowledge through eternal procession by Christ, He would not have used a verb of future time, but of present or past. I answer with the words of AUGUSTINE in Tract. XCIX on John. Let it not disturb you that a verb of future time is used: For it is not said, whatever He heard, or whatever He hears, but whatever He shall hear, He shall speak; for that hearing is eternal, because the knowledge is eternal. Moreover, in that which is eternal, without beginning and end, whatever verb of time is placed, whether of the past, or of the present, or of the future, it is not placed falsely. Christ used a verb of future time, because He was speaking about the reception under the relation of announcement, which at that time was still future, as is evident from verse 14.

Prob. e. Apoc. XXII, 1. Furthermore, He showed me a pure river of water of life, bright as crystal, proceeding (ἐκπορευόμενον ἐκ τοῦ θρόνου Θεοῦ καὶ ἀρνός), going out from the throne of God and of the Lamb. Where note: (1) That by the throne of God and of the Lamb is understood the essence of God the Father and the Son, marked with the hypostatic character, insofar as it is most glorious and majestic. (2) That by the river is understood the Holy Spirit, the phrase of Scripture teaches, which is accustomed to describe the Holy Spirit thus by water, by which we are refreshed, Isa. XLIV, 2. John IV, 10; ch. VII, 38, 39. (3) The word proceeding (ἐκπορευόμενον), to proceed or to go out, is appropriated by John to the Holy Spirit. John XV, 26. (4) Since this river is said to go out from the throne of God and of the Lamb, the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son is indicated. These things having been premised, we argue: Whoever proceeds like a river from the throne not only of the Father, but also of the Lamb, i.e., of the Son of God, he proceeds from both. But the Holy Spirit &c. Therefore.

Prob. f. The Holy Spirit is sent equally from the Son and from the Father, John XV, 26. & c. XVI, 26. Temporal mission, since it is of a divine person, presupposes eternal origination and procession from that person by whom He is sent. A divine person is not sent in time except from Him from whom He eternally proceeds. Hence the argument: The principle of the mission of a divine person in time is the principle of His origination in eternity. But the Son of God is one with God the Father the principle mission of the Holy Spirit in time. Therefore, the Son of God is, together with God the Father, the principle of the origin of the Holy Spirit in eternity.

You say: The Holy Spirit with respect to the Son of God is the principle of the mission in time, Is. 61:1. but not the principle of his origin in eternity. Response: Christ was sent by the Holy Spirit as man, not as God. We are speaking of the mission of the divine persons, insofar as they are divine. Prob. g. John 20:22. Saying this, he breathed, and said to them: receive the Holy Spirit. From which words Augustine, Book 4 of the Trinity, ch. 19, gathers the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son of God: We cannot say that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son, nor is the same Holy Spirit called the spirit of the Father and of the Son in vain. Nor do I see what else he could have wished to signify, when breathing into the face of the disciples he says: Receive the Holy Spirit. For that breath was not corporeal, proceeding from the body with the corporeal sense of touching, it was not the substance of the Holy Spirit, but a demonstration through a fitting signification that the Holy Spirit proceeds not only from the Father, but also from the Son. Prob. h. If the Holy Spirit did not also proceed from the Son, then he would not be really distinguished from him. For every distinction in God arises from relations founded in origin. Otherwise the order of the persons in the Most Holy Trinity would expire. For no reason can be given why the Son is the second, and the Holy Spirit the third person of the Trinity, if there is no order of origin. Finally, this absurdity would follow, that the Son of God does not have his own spirit.

There is an antithesis of (1) the Nestorians, (2) the recent Greeks, denying that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son of God, (3) the Socinians, maintaining that the procession of the Holy Spirit is his temporal mission, (4) the Weigelians, asserting that the Holy Spirit proceeded from the Father alone before the birth of Christ, but after the ascension of Christ proceeds also from the Son; who impugn the orthodox opinion with the following arguments.

I. Holy Scripture testifies that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, John 15:26. it does not assert the same concerning the Son of God. Response: The words of Christ in the cited place are not to be understood exclusively. For he does not say that the spirit of truth proceeds from the Father alone; but when the Savior says: Whom I will send to you from the Father, he implies that the Holy Spirit also proceeds from himself. For a divine person is not sent in time, except by him from whom he proceeds eternally. Add this argument: The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, either as such, or insofar as he has the Son as co-essential. If the former, the Holy Spirit will be the Son; because he who proceeds from the Father as such, proceeds to the image of him from whom he proceeds. If the latter; therefore he proceeds from both.

II. Whoever communicates essence to someone, generates the same. The Son of God does not generate the Holy Spirit. Therefore, the Son of God does not communicate essence to the Holy Spirit. The major premise is evident; because generation is formally the communication of essence. Response: I deny the major. For the formal notion of generation is not completed by the communication of essence alone, but by the communication of essence to the image of the producer. The procession of the Holy Spirit indeed denotes the communication of essence; but not to the image of the producer, but so that he becomes the common breath of the Father and the Son.

III. God the Father is either a sufficient principle of spiration, or he is not. If the former; he will not need the help of the Son: if the latter; imperfection will fall upon God the Father. Response: 1) By counter-instance: God the Father is either a sufficient principle of creation, or he is not. If the former; he does not need the help of the Son of God and of the Holy Spirit, if the latter, imperfection will fall upon God the Father the creator. (2) There is one force of spirating in the Father and the Son. Wherefore God the Father in the spiration of the Holy Spirit does not need the help of the Son of God on account of imperfection, but the Son of God concurs to the Spiration of the Holy Spirit on account of the identity of spirative virtue.

IV. Whoever is not the fountain and root of deity, from him the Holy Spirit does not emanate. (For a river emanates from its fountain.) But the Son of God does not &c. Therefore. The minor premise is proved by the fact that he alone

God the Father is the fountain and root of deity, as ATHANASIUS says in DANNH. in hodof. p. 230. Resp. The Father is called the fountain of deity because he is unoriginated, and because both the Son and the Holy Spirit derive their origin from him. In this strictest sense, it is clear that the Son of God is not the fountain of deity. But if by fountain one understands the principle of origin, nothing prevents calling the Son of God the fountain of the procession of the Holy Spirit.

V. If the Holy Spirit proceeded from the Son, it would follow that the Son is more similar to the Father than the Holy Spirit is. The latter is absurd. Therefore, the former is as well. The consequence of the major premise is proven; because, if the Son breathed the Holy Spirit with the Father, not only by reason of essence, but also by reason of the breathing virtue, he would be similar to the Father; a virtue of which the Holy Spirit is destitute. The absurdity of the latter is evident; because the divine persons are of the same majesty, just as they are of the same essence. Resp. Similarity in divine matters is considered not according to relations, but according to essence, and therefore the consequence of the major premise is null.

VI. If the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, namely from the Father and the Son, he either proceeds by one and simple procession, or by a double procession. If by one; a contraction of persons follows; for the Father and the Son are contracted into one breathing person, and the Holy Spirit will be another person, namely the breathed one, and thus the Holy Trinity will be torn apart. If by double; the Holy Spirit will be doubled, or composed; for a double action brings about a double term. Resp. (a) The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son by one procession; yet it does not follow that both are contracted into one person; because the Father and the Son agree in the same essence, but are distinguished by a distinct hypostatic character: But breathing is not a character constitutive of a person, but a personal notion γνωρισικὴ, or merely notificatory, common to God the Father and the Son on account of the common power of breathing. (b) The three persons of the divinity created the world without any contraction of persons.

Instance: One spirit cannot proceed from two persons, since individual persons have their own proper spirit. Resp. One spirit does not proceed from two persons that are essentially different. But God the Father and the Son have the same essence, and the same virtue of breathing, and stand as one principle.

VII. The ancient doctors asserted that the Holy Spirit is from the Father through the Son. See CHEMNIT. loc. theol. f. m. 102. Resp. The preposition, through, is used by the ancient fathers only for the sake of order, not for the sake of inequality or diversity of principle. Namely, they taught that the Holy Spirit is from the Father through the Son, so that the property of each person might be preserved; because the Son, by being born from the Father, has this, that the Spirit proceeds from him: but the Father has this from no one, but from himself. But the ancients did not deny that the Son of God is a principle of the procession of the Holy Spirit.

Instance: If the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son, so that the latter is equally a principle of origin as the former; the Holy Spirit will proceed mediately from God the Father, and immediately from the Son of God, and thus the Holy Spirit will be more closely joined and more familiar to the Son than to the Father. Resp. The Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Father ἐμμέσως, or mediately, by the intervention of the Son; for in this way he would indeed be closer to one person than to the other: but he proceeds ἀμέσως, immediately, from both as if from one essential fountain. For just as the Father and the Son are one in essence: so in producing one and the same consubstantial spirit they are one essential principle: yet in such a way that the Father has that breathing faculty from himself, while the Son receives it through an ineffable generation from the Father.

Latin:

Spiritum sanctum a Deo Patre procedere, αὐτολεξεὶ & disertis verbis docet sacra scriptura (a). Eundem procedere a Filio Dei, ex denominatione Spiritus Filii (b), ὁμοοσία Patris & Filii (c), acceptione omniscientiæ a Filio (d), visione apocalyptica fluuii de throno agni procedentis (e), missione Spiritus S. a Filio (f), insufflatione Christi ad discipulos facta (g), ordine & distinctione personarum divinarum (h), valide colligitur.

Prob. a. Perspicua sunt verba Christi, Jo. XV, 26. Quando venerit paracletus, quem ego missurus sum vobis a Patre, spiritus veritatis, qui ex Patre ἐκπορεύεται procedit, ille testabitur de me. Loquitur Salvator de processione Spiritus S. æterna & interna, qua ipse essentiam a patre accipit, non de missione temporali & externa ad opus sanctificationis, de qua hunc locum classicum intellectum volunt Sociniani, sed male. Nam (1) missio a processione aperte distinguitur. Quem ego missurus vobis sum a Patre, qui ex patre procedit. (2) Missio tempore futuro, processio tempore præsenti fieri dicitur, ut non de temporali missione, sed de æterna emanatione Spiritus S. sermonem esse intelligamus. Nam æternitas est νῦν præsentissimum & immobile. (3) Scopus Christi erat, adserere cœlestis testis auctoritatem, nempe testimonium Spiritus S. esse irrefragabile & omni exceptione maius, cum ex ipso patre procedat, eiusque τὰ βάθη, seu profunda scrutetur & introspiciat. (4) Designatur origo Spiritus S. in locis parallelis per verbum ἐκπορεύεσθαι, Dan. VII, 10. Apoc. XXII, 1.
