Obs. Huic disertæ assertioni S. scripturæ de processione Spiritus S. a Patre addi possunt alia argumenta, nempe (1) quod Spiritus S. sit ex Deo, 1 Cor. II, 12. (2) Quod sit Spiritus

Patris, Matth. X, 20. Spiritus oris Domini. Ps. XXXIII, 6. Spiraculum omnipotentis Job. XXXIII, 4. ideo, quod a Patre spiratur, atque ex ore ipsius ceu spiraculum eiusdem procedit, modo tamen divino & ineffabili.

(3) Quia a Patre mittitur, Jo. XIV, 26. Missio temporalis est nota processionis aeternae. Solus pater non legitur missus, quia a nullo habet originem.

Prob. b. Quo modo Spiritus S. dicitur spiritus Patris, Matth. X, 20. eodem modo dicitur spiritus Filii, Gal. IV, 6. spiritus Christi, Rom. VIII, 9. spiritus labiorum Christi, Es. XI, 4. spiritus oris Christi, 2 Thess. II, 8. quia vt a Patre, ita a Filio Dei modo ineffabili spiratus, & ex ore ipsius velut halitus divinus procedit.

Prob. c. Omnia, quaecunque Pater habet, mea sunt: Propter hoc dixi; quod de meo accepturus sit, & vobis annuntiaturus, Jo. XVI, 15. Ex quibus verbis Christi non tantum ὁμοουσία Patris & Filii, sed originatio Spiritus S. a Filio colligitur. Quidquid enim de Patre dicitur, hoc omnino de Filio dici debet, praeter hoc ipsum, quod est Pater, inquit CYRILL. in thesaur. Nos argumentamur: Quicunque omnia habet, quae Deus Pater, excepta sola paternitate, ille habet vim spirandi Spiritum S. Atqui Filius Dei &c. Ergo.

Prob. d. Jo. XVI, 13. 14. Quando venerit ille spiritus veritatis, ducet vos in omnem veritatem. Non enim loquetur a seipso, sed quaecunque audiverit, loquetur, etiamque futura annuntiabit vobis. Ille me glorificabit: quia ex meo accipiet, & annuntiabit vobis. A quo spiritus veritatis accipit scientiam loquendi & annuntiandi futura, ab eodem accipit essentiam. Atqui a Filio Dei &c. Ergo. Maior constat; quia in Spiritu S. essentia & scientia idem sunt. Notitia rerum futurarum est divina & aeterna, quae ex parte rei est ipsa essentia divina. Dicis: Si de acceptione scientiae per aeternam processionem Christo fuisset sermo, non adhibuisset verbum futuri temporis, sed praesentis, vel praeteriti. Respondeo verbis AVGVSTINI in tract. XCIX. in Ioan. Nec moueat, quod verbum futuri temporis positum est: Non enim dictum est, quaecunque audivit, aut quaecunque audit, sed quaecunque audiet, loquetur; illa quippe audientia sempiterna est, quia sempiterna est scientia. In eo autem, quod sempiterni, fine initio & fine, cuiuslibet temporis verbum ponatur, sive praeteriti, sive praesentis, sive futuri, non mendaciter ponitur. Adhibuit autem Christus verbum futuri temporis, quia loquebatur de acceptione sub relatione annuntiationis, quae tunc temporis adhuc futura erat, vt patet ex vers. 14.

Prob. e. Apoc. XXII, 1. Praeterea ostendit mihi purum fluvium aquae vitae, splendidum sicut crystallum, ἐκπορευόμενον ἐκ τοῦ θρόνου Θεοῦ καὶ ἀρνός, exeuntem e throno Dei & agni. Vbi obs. (1) Quod per thronum Dei & agni intelligatur essentia Dei Patris & Filii, charactere hypostatico insignita, quatenus illa gloriosissima & maiestatica est. (2) Per fluvium intelligi Spiritum S. docet phrasis scripturae, quae solet Spiritum S. ita describere per aquam, qua reficimur, Es. XLIV, 2. Jo. IV, 10. c. VII, 38. 39. (3) Verbum ἐκπορευόμενον procedere vel exire, a Joanne appropriatur spiritui S. Jo. XV, 26. (4) Cum hic fluvius dicatur exire a throno Dei & agni, processio spiritus S. a Patre & Filio indigitatur. Quibus praemissis, argumentamur: Quicunque instar fluminis procedit a throno non tantum patris, sed & agni, h.e. Filii Dei, is procedit ab vtroque. Atqui spiritus S. &c. Ergo.

Prob. f. Spiritus S. aeque a Filio, ac a patre mittitur, Jo. XV, 26. & c. XVI, 26. Missio autem temporalis, cum sit personae divinae, prae-supponit aeternam originem & processionem ab illa persona, a qua mittitur. Non mittitur persona divina in tempore, nisi ab ea, a qua aeternum procedit. Vnde argumentum: Principium missionis personae divinae in tempore, est principium originis eiusdem in aeternitate. Atqui Filius Dei est vna cum Deo Patre principium missionis Spiritus S. in tempore. E. Filius Dei est, una cum Deo Patre, principium originis Spiritus S. in aeternitate.

Dicis: Spiritus S. respectu Filii Dei est principium missionis in tempore, Es. LXI, 1. neque tamen principium originis eiusdem in aeternitate. Resp. Christus missus est a spiritu S. qua homo, non qua Deus. Nos loquimur de missione personarum divinarum, quatenus sunt divinae. Prob. g. Jo. XX, 22. Hoc dicens inspiravit, & dixit illis: accipite Spiritum S. Ex quibus verbis AVGVSTIN. L. IV. de trinit. c. 19. processionem Spiritus S. a Filio Dei colligit: Non possumus dicere, quod Spiritus S. a Filio non procedat, neque frustra idem Spiritus & Patris & Filii spiritus dicitur. Nec video, quid aliud significare voluerit, cum sufflans in faciem discipulorum ait: Accipite Spiritum S. Neque enim flatus ille corporeus, cum sensu corporali ter tangendi procedens ex corpore, substantia Spiritus S. fuit, sed demonstratio per congruam significationem non tantum a Patre, sed & a Filio procedere Spiritum S. Prob. h. Si Spiritus S. non procederet quoque a Filio, tum ab eo realiter non distingueretur. Omnis enim distinctio in Deo oritur ex relationibus fundatis in origine. Quin ratio ordinis personarum in SS. Trinitate exspiraret. Neque enim reddi poterit ratio, cur Filius secunda, & Spiritus S. tertia fit Trinitatis persona, si ordo originis nullus. Sequeretur denique hoc absurdum, Filium Dei non habere proprium spiritum.

Antithesis est (1) Nestorianorum, (2) Recentiorum Graecorum, negantium Spiritum S. a Filio Dei procedere, (3) Socinianorum, statuentium, processionem spiritus sancti esse eiusdem missionem temporalem, (4) Weigelianorum, afferentium, Spiritum S. ante natiuitatem Christi a solo patre processisse, post ascensionem vero Christi etiam a Filio procedere; qui sequentibus orthodoxam sententiam impugnant argumentis.

I. Scriptura sacra testatur, Spiritum S. procedere a Patre, Jo. XV, 26. idem non asserit de Filio Dei. Resp. Non exclusive verba Christi loco citato intelligenda sunt. Neque enim dicit, spiritum veritatis a solo Patre procedere; sed dum ait Saluator: Quem ego mittam vobis a Patre, Spiritum S. quoque ex se procedere innuit. Non enim mittitur persona divina in tempore, nisi ab ea, a qua aeternum procedit. Adiice hoc argumentum: Procedit spiritus S. a Patre, aut qua tali, aut quatenus Filium habet coessentialem. Si prius, Spiritus S. erit Filius; quia qui a Patre, quatenus tali procedit, ille procedit ad imaginem eius, a quo procedit. Si posterius; ergo ab vtroque procedit.

II. Quicunque alicui communicat essentiam, is eundem generat. Filius Dei Spiritum S. non generat. E. Filius Dei spiritui S. essentiam non communicat. Maior constat; quia generation formaliter est communicatio essentiae. Resp. Neg. mai. Nam generationis ratio formalis non absoluitur sola communicatione essentiae, sed communicatione essentiae ad imaginem producentis. Processio spiritus S. notat quidem communicationem essentiae; verum non ad imaginem producentis, sed vt fit patris filiique commune spiraculum.

III. Deus Pater aut est sufficiens spirationis principium, aut non. Si prius; non indigebit auxilio Filii: sin posterius; imperfectio cadet in Deum patrem. Resp. 1) Per instantiam: Deus pater aut est sufficiens creationis principium, aut non. Si prius; non indiget auxilio Filii Dei & Spiritus S. sin posterius, cadet imperfectio in Deum Patrem creatorem. (2) Vna est vis spirandi in Patre & Filio. Quare Deus Pater in spiratione Spiritus S. non indiget auxilio Filii Dei ob imperfectionem, sed Filius Dei concurrit ad Spirationem Spiritus sancti ob identitatem virtutis spiratiuae.

IV. Quicunque non est fons & radix deitatis, ab eo Spiritus sanctus non emanat. (Fluvius enim emanat e fonte suo.) Atqui Filius Dei non &c. Ergo. Minor prob. qua solus

Deus Pater est fons & radix deitatis, dicente ATHANASIO apud DANNH. in hodof. p. 230. Resp. Fons deitatis dicitur pater, quia est inoriginatus, & quia tam Filius, quam Spiritus sanctus ab eo ducit originem. Quo sensu strictissimo Filium Dei non esse fontem deitatis, in aprico est. At si per fontem intelligatur principium originis, nil vetat filium Dei vocare fontem processionis Spiritus sancti.

V. Si Spiritus sanctus procederet a Filio, sequeretur, Filium esse similiorem patri, quam Spiritum sanctum. Posterius est absurdum. E. & prius. Consequentia maioris probatur; quia, si Filius spiraret Spiritum sanctum cum Patre, non tantum ratione essentiæ, sed & ratione virtutis spiratiuæ, Patri foret similis; qua virtute Spiritus sanctus destituitur. Posterioris absurditas patet; quia personæ diuinæ eiusdem, vt essentiæ, ita maiestatis sunt. Resp. Similitudo in divinis attenditur non secundum relationes, sed secundum essentiam, adeoque consequentia maioris est nulla.

VI. Si Spiritus sanctus ab vtroque nempe a Patre & Filio procedit, aut procedit processione vna & simplici, aut processione duplici. Si vna; sequitur personarum contractio; contrahentur enim Pater & Filius ad vnam personam spirantem, & Spiritus sanctus erit persona altera, nempe spirata, atque adeo conuelletur SS. Trinitas. Si duplici; Spiritus sanctus duplicabitur, aut componetur; duplex enim actio duplicem infert terminum. Resp. (a) Spiritus sanctus procedit a Patre & Filio vna processione; neque tamen sequitur vtriusque contractio ad vnam personam; quia Pater & Filius conueniunt eadem essentia, distinguuntur autem distincto charactere hypostatico: At spiratio non est character personæ constitutiuus, sed notio personalis γνωρισικὴ, seu tantum notificatiua Deo Patri & Filio communis ob communem vim spirandi. (b) Tres personæ diuinitatis crearunt mundum circa vllam personarum contractionem.

Instantia: A duabus personis vnus spiritus prodire nequit, cum singulæ personæ proprium habeant spiritum. Resp. A duabus personis, essentialiter diuersis, non prodit vnus spiritus. At Deus Pater & Filius habent eandem essentiam, eandemque virtutem spirandi, & stant pro principio vno.

VII. Veteres doctores asseruerunt, Spiritum sanctum esse a Patre per Filium. Vid. CHEMNIT. loc. theol. f. m. 102. Resp. Præpositio, per, ab antiquis patribus ordinis tantum caussa, non inæqualitatis aut diuersitatis principii ergo adhibetur. Nempe docuerunt, spiritum sanctum esse a Patre per Filium, vt cuiusque personæ proprietas seruetur; quia Filius nascendo a Patre hoc habet, quod de ipso Spiritus procedat: Pater vero id a nullo, sed a seipso habet. At non negarunt veteres, filium Dei esse principium processionis Spiritus sancti.

Instantia: Si Spiritus sanctus a Patre per Filium procedit, vt hic peræque, ac ille sit principium originis; Spiritus sanctus a Deo Patre mediate, a Filio Dei immediate procedet, adeoque Spiritus sanctus coniunctior & familiarior erit Filio, quam Patri. Resp. Spiritus sanctus non procedit a Patre ἐμμέσως, seu mediate, interuentu scilicet Filii; hac ratione vtique vni personæ esset propinquior, quam alteri: sed procedit ἀμέσως, immediate, ab vtroque velut ex vno fonte essentiali. Vt enim essentia sunt vnum Pater & Filius: ita in producendo vno eodemque spiritu consubstantiali sunt vnum principium essentiale: ita tamen, vt Pater illam facultatem spiratiuam a seipso habeat, Filius autem per ineffabilem a Patre generationem accipiat.


### Question LI. Is the generation of the Son of God effected by the divine intellect, and the procession of the Holy Spirit by the divine will?

Neither is the generation of the Son of God effected by the divine intellect, nor the procession of the Holy Spirit by the divine will, but by the most eminent fecundity of the divine nature, marked by a certain hypostatic character.

Proof. I. Because the divine intellect and will are common to the three persons of the Godhead. Wherefore, if the generation of the Son of God were effected by the intellect, and the spiration by the will, this absurdity would follow: that the Son, by understanding or thinking, would generate another son, and the Holy Spirit, by willing, would produce another holy spirit. You say: The discussion is not about absolute divine intellection, but about the relative intellection of the Father, and the relative volition of the Father and the Son. Resp. By this distinction, new labyrinths are opened. For whence does it come that the Father’s intellection is fecund, but the intellection of the Son of God is not? Whence does it come that the Father’s volition in the production of the Spirit is common to the Son of God, but the intellection is not?

II. True and proper filiation does not acknowledge the diffusion of the intellect as its principle, but the fecundity or communicability of nature. Since, therefore, ὁ λόγος is the proper Son of God, Rom. 8:32, his origin is to be attributed not to the intellect, but to the fecundity of the divine essence, which is in the Father and the Son.

III. If God the Father and the Son breathe the Holy Spirit by willing, they certainly breathe freely, and can choose not to breathe, and thus the spiration of the Holy Spirit would be a free action, and not necessary or natural. But if the Holy Spirit is not breathed necessarily from the divine nature itself, he is not God, ὁμοούσιος (consubstantial) with the Father and the Son. For the true God exists necessarily and cannot not be.

IV. If the Holy Spirit proceeds by volition, but the Son of God is generated by intellection, the Holy Spirit will not be equal to the Son of God. The latter is absurd. Therefore, the former is also. The consequence of the major is proved; because volition is always less noble than intellection. The antithesis is that of the Scholastics and Jesuits, according to whose opinion the Son of God is generated by the intellect of God the Father, and the Holy Spirit is breathed by the will of the Father and the Son. Their stronger arguments are: I. Whoever is the son of the father’s word, he is begotten by the father’s intellect. But the Son of God is the λόγος, or word of the father, John 1:1. Therefore. The major is proved: because the internal word regards the intellect, by which it is begotten. Resp. (1) I deny the major. For the son can be called the word, for the reason that he expounds the will of the father. (2) Distinguish between the created and uncreated λόγος. The created λόγος indeed regards the intellect as its proximate and formal principle; because man cannot produce a word unless the intellect intervenes as an intermediate faculty; which is a matter of human imperfection. But the uncreated λόγος is produced immediately by the divine nature. (3) The Son of God is called the word of the father to indicate the spirituality of the divine generation, not to express the formality of the principle. As a concept is produced by the mind, so the Son of God is produced by the Father immaterially and ἀπαθῶς (as BASIL says, Homily XVI), without passion and corruption. A concept of the mind remains thus from the mind: so the son is from the father, and never is he not remaining in the father. From which it does not follow that God the Father begat the son insofar as, by intuiting and considering himself, he conceived and begat an image of himself. Certainly, filiation is founded in the communication of the same nature, not in the thought of the intellect.

II. Whoever in sacred scripture is called the love of the Father and the Son, he proceeds from the divine will; but the Holy Spirit etc. Therefore. The major is evident; because the principle of love is the will. The minor is clear from Rom. 5:5, 1 John 4:6. Resp. In the cited passages the Holy Spirit is not called love of the Father; but in Rom. V, 5, the love of God (by which God loves us) is said to have been poured out, i.e., most abundantly declared through the Holy Spirit. The triune God is called charity, 1 John IV, 16. But who would gather from that, that the Holy Spirit is the love of the Father & ...the Son?

III. The productive action of the Son & the Holy Spirit is either transient, or immanent. Not transient; otherwise its terminus would be outside of God, & it would be either creation, or preservation, or cooperation. But if it is immanent; it will be through intellect & will. For no immanent action in a spiritual nature exists apart from intellect & volition, as is evident from the soul & the angelic nature. Resp. The productive action of the Son of God & the Holy Spirit is indeed immanent, but personal, which is immediately founded in the divine essence, marked by a certain hypostatic character.

IV. If the Son of God is not generated through the intellect of the Father, nor the Holy Spirit breathed through the will of the Father & the Son, there will be no distinction between the generation of the Son, & the procession of the Holy Spirit. But there is a distinction of generation, & procession. Therefore, the former occurs through the intellect, the latter through the will. Resp. We frankly confess that the distinction of the eternal generation τῷ λόγῳ [by the Word] & the procession of the Holy Spirit in this infirmity of life can neither be exactly known by us, nor fully explained. However, generation differs from procession, not in that the former occurs through the divine intellect, the latter through the divine will: But (a) the Son of God is generated by the Father alone; the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father & the Son. (b) The Son is generated by the Father, as his image; the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father & the Son, as the common spiraculum [breath] of both. (c) The production of the Son of God is the first divine production, diffusing itself into another person with further fecundity: the production of the Holy Spirit is the final divine production (immanent), in which the communicability of the divine nature rests within the bosom of the deity. Conf. D. OSIANDER in colleg. system. theol. part. I. p. 450.

Latin:

Neque generatio Filii Dei fit per intellectum divinum, neque processio Spiritus S. per voluntatem divinam, sed per eminentissimam foecunditatem naturae divinae, certo charactere hypostatico notatae.

Prob. I. Quia intellectus et voluntas divina sunt communes tribus divinitatis personis. Quare si generatio Filii Dei per intellectum, et spiratio per voluntatem fieret, sequeretur hoc absurdum, quod filius intelligendo, aut cogitando, aut alium filium generaret, et Spiritus sanctus volendo alium spiritum sanctum produceret. Dicis: Non de intellectione divina absoluta, sed de intellectione Patris, et volitione Patris et Filii relativa sermo est. Resp. Hac distinctione novi labyrinthi aperiuntur. Nam unde fit, ut Patris intellectio fit foecunda, non item intellectio Filii Dei? Unde fit, ut volitio Patris in productione Spiritus sit communis Filio Dei, non item intellectio?

II. Vera et propria filiatio pro principio non agnoscit intellectus diffusionem, sed foecunditatem, seu communicabilitatem naturae. Cum itaque ὁ λόγος sit Filius Dei proprius, Rom. IIX, 32. illius origo tribuenda est non intellectui, sed foecunditati essentiae divinae, quae est in Patre et Filio.

III. Si Deus Pater et Filius spirant Spiritum sanctum volendo, utique spirant libere, et possunt non spirare, atque adeo spiratio Spiritus sancti erit actio libera, et non necessaria, aut naturalis. Si autem Spiritus sanctus non spiratur necessario ex ipsa natura divina, non est Deus, Patri et Filio ὁμοούσιος. Nam verus Deus existit necessario et non potest non esse.

IV. Si Spiritus sanctus procedit per volitionem, Filius Dei autem generatur per intellectionem, Spiritus sanctus Filio Dei non erit aequalis. Posterius est absurdum. E. et prius. Consequentia maioris probatur; quia volitio semper ignobilior est intellectione. Antithesis est Scholasticorum et Jesuitarum, quorum de sententia Filius Dei per intellectum Dei Patris generatur, et Spiritus sanctus per voluntatem Patris et Filii spiratur. Horum argumenta potiora sunt: I. Quicunque filius est verbum patris, ille per intellectum patris est genitus. Atqui filius Dei est λόγος, seu verbum patris, Jo. I, 1. Ergo. Maior probatur: quia verbum internum respicit intellectum, a quo gignitur. Resp. (1) Neg. maiorem. Nam filius potest vocari verbum, ideo, quod voluntatem patris exponit. (2) Dist. inter λόγον creatum, et increatum. λόγος creatus quidem respicit intellectum, tanquam principium proximum et formale; quia homo non potest producere verbum, nisi interveniente intellectu, tanquam facultate intermedia; id quod imperfectionis humanae est. At λόγος increatus immediate a natura divina producitur. (3) Filius Dei dicitur verbum patris ad indicandam generationis divinae spiritualitatem, non ad exprimendum principii formalitatem. Vt conceptus a mente, sic filius Dei a patre producitur inmaterialiter et ἀπαθῶς (dicente BASIL. Homil. XVI.) sine passione et corruptione. Conceptus mentis ita a mente manet: sic filius a patre est, et nunquam non in patre permanet. Ex quo non sequitur, Deum patrem genuisse filium, quatenus sefe intuens et considerans, imaginem sui conceperit ac genuerit. Sane filiatio in communicatione eiusdem naturae, non in cogitatione intellectus fundatur.

II. Quicunque in sacra scriptura dicitur amor Patris et Filii, is procedit a voluntate divina; Atqui Spiritus sanctus etc. Ergo. Maior patet; quia principium amoris est voluntas. Minor liquet ex Rom. V, 5. 1 Jo. IV, 6. Resp. Locis citatis Spiritus sanctus non vocatur amor patris; sed Rom. V, 5. dicitur dilectio Dei (qua Deus nos diligit) effusa, i. e. uberrime declarata esse per Spiritum sanctum. Deus triunus nuncupatur caritas, 1 Jo. IV, 16. Sed quis exinde colligeret, Spiritum sanctum esse amorem Patris & ...Filii?

III. Actio productiva Filii & Spiritus sancti aut est transiens, aut immanens. Non transiens; ceteroqui terminus eius foret extra Deum, & esset vel creatio, vel conservatio, vel cooperatio. Si autem est immanens; erit per intellectum & voluntatem. Nulla enim actio immanens in natura spirituali est præter intellectum & volitionem, ut patet ex anima & natura angelica. Resp. Actio productiva filii Dei & Spiritus S. est quidem immanens, sed personalis, quæ immediate fundatur in essentia divina, certo charactere hypostatico notata.

IV. Si filius Dei non generatur per intellectum patris, nec Spiritus S. spiratur per voluntatem patris & filii, nullum erit discrimen generationis filii, & processionis Spiritus sancti. At est discrimen generationis, & processionis. E. illa fit per intellectum, hæc per voluntatem. Resp. Ingenue fatemur, discrimen æternæ generationis τῷ λόγῳ & processionis Spiritus sancti in hac vitæ infirmitate a nobis neque exacte posse cognosci, neque plene explicari. Differt autem generatio a processione, non eo, quod illa per intellectum, hæc per voluntatem divinain fiat: Sed (a) generatur filius Dei a solo patre; procedit Spiritus S. a Patre & Filio. (b) Generatur Filius a Patre, vt eiusdem imago; procedit Spiritus S. a Patre & Filio, vt commune vtriusque spiraculum. (c) Productio filii Dei est productio divina prima, vlteriori fœcunditate se in aliam personam diffundens: productio Spiritus S. est productio divina vltima (immanens), in qua communicabilitas naturæ divinæ intra sinum deitatis conquiescit. Conf. D. OSIANDER in colleg. system. theol. part. I. p. 450.


### Q. LII. What is the consequence of the procession of the Holy Spirit, by which it is manifested a posteriori?

The eternal procession of the Holy Spirit is manifested by the temporal mission of the Holy Spirit, which occurs from the Father & the Son.

Prob. God the Father sends the Holy Spirit in the name of the Son, John XIV, 26. The Son, however, sends the Holy Spirit from the Father, John XV, 26. Therefore, the power of sending the Holy Spirit is common to God the Father & the Son; which God the Father has from himself, the Son received from the Father through eternal generation.

Furthermore, the mission of the Holy Spirit is either visible, or invisible. It is visible, by which the Holy Spirit is so given & communicated, that he manifests his presence through some symbol, accessible to human senses. In this visible manner the mission of the Holy Spirit took place at the baptism of Christ, when he descended in the form of a dove upon Christ, Matt. III, 16, and also at the feast of Pentecost, when he came upon the apostles in the form of tongues of fire, Acts II, 3. Moreover, it is sometimes called the visible outpouring of the Holy Spirit, by which he suddenly reveals his presence through rare & unusual effects; such as occurred to the converted Gentiles in the house of Cornelius the centurion, Acts X, 45. For they began immediately to speak in various tongues, & to celebrate God. But the visible mission of the Holy Spirit is that which he [performs] through a certain singular οἰκονομίαν [economy], or divine dispensation. The invisible mission of the Holy Spirit is that by which he is ordinarily sent into the hearts of penitent sinners through the Word & sacraments, & his gifts are communicated to them. Gal. IV, 6. 1 Cor. XII, 2.

XII, 2. Furthermore, some gifts of the Holy Spirit are sanctifying, others ministering. Sanctifying are those which are conferred upon the sinful man, so that he may become & remain just & holy; such as are: illumination Eph. I, 18. Conversion, Ezek. XXXVI, 27. Regeneration, John III, 16. Justification, 1 Cor. VI, 11. Adoption, Rom. VIII, 15. Mystical union, 1 Cor. III, 16. Renewal, Tit. III, 4. Virtues worthy of a Christian, which are the fruits of the Holy Spirit, Gal. V, 22. Certification of eternal salvation, Eph.

I, 14. Ministering are, which which are distributed for the administration of the public office in the church according to the measure of divine grace, 1 Cor. XII, 8-10.

Latin:

Processio Spiritus S. æterna manifestatur missione Spiritus S. temporali, quæ fit a Patre & Filio.

Prob. Deus Pater mittit Spiritum S. in nomine Filii Jo. XIV, 26. Filius autem mittit Spiritum sanctum a Patre Jo. XV, 26. Est igitur potestas mittendi Spiritum sanctum Deo Patri & Filio communis; quam Deus pater habet aseipso, filius a patre per æternam generationem accepit.

Ceterum missio Spiritus S. est vel visibilis, vel invisibilis. Visibilis est, qua Spiritus S. ita datur & communicatur, vt per symbolum aliquod, sensibus humanis obvium, præsentiam suam manifestet. Quo visibili modo facta est missio Spiritus S. in baptismo Christi, cum descendit in specie columbæ super Christum, Matth. III, 16. nec non in festo pentecostes, cum in forma linguarum ignearum super apostolos venit, Act. II, 3. Dicitur præterea quandoque effusio visibilis Spiritus S. qua is per effectus raros & insolitos suam præsentiam subito prodit; qualis contigit conuersis gentibus in ædibus Cornelii centurionis, Act. X, 45. Cœperunt enim illico variis linguis loqui, & Deum concelebrare. Est autem missio visibilis Spiritus S. quæ is per singularem quandam οἰκονομίαν, seu dispensationem divinam. Invisibilis missio Spiritus S. est, qua is ordinarie per verbum & sacramenta in corda pœnitentium peccatorum mittitur, & ipsius dona iisdem communicantur. Gal. IV, 6. 1 Cor. XII, 2.

Ceterum sunt dona Spiritus S. alia sanctificantia, alia ministrantia. Sanctificantia sunt, quæ homini peccatori, ut iustus & sanctus fiat & maneat, conferuntur; qualia sunt: illuminatio Eph. I, 18. Conuersio, Ezech. XXXVI, 27. Regeneratio, Jo. III, 16. Iustificatio, 1 Cor. VI, 11. Adoptio, Rom. VIII, 15. Vnio mystica, 1 Cor. III, 16. Renouatio, Tit. III, 4. Virtutes christiano dignæ, quæ sunt fructus Spiritus S. Gal. V, 22. Aeternæ salutis certificatio, Eph. I, 14.

Ministrantia sunt, quæ quae ad officii publici in ecclesia obeundi administrationem secundum mensuram gratiae divinae distribuuntur, 1 Cor. XII, 8-10.


### Quest. LIII

Is the Holy Spirit sent only with respect to gifts and gracious operation, or indeed also as to his hypostasis? Not only are the gifts of the Holy Spirit communicated to the faithful, but the person of the Holy Spirit himself is sent by God the Father and the Son into their hearts, so that he is present to the pious more closely, both by reason of his substance and by reason of his ἐνέργεια or gracious operation, than to the impious.

Proved I. from Gal. IV, 6: God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying: Abba, Father! Here the apostle indeed distinguishes the operation of the Holy Spirit, by which he excites in us prayers flowing from filial confidence, from the person of the Holy Spirit himself, but he does not tear them apart. For he teaches that God the Father sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, who effects pious prayers in us.

II. From the προαγωνίως (pre-agonizing/farewell) discourse of Christ, John XIV, 16: I will ask the Father, that he may give you another παράκλητον (Comforter), that he may remain with you forever; the Spirit of truth. And v. 26: But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, (ἐκεῖνος) he will teach you all things and remind you of all things which I have said to you: Which words of Christ cannot be explained as referring only to the gifts of the Holy Spirit: For the Holy Spirit has distinct personal names.

For he is called the Paraclete, which is a personal name. 1 John II, 1. He is called ἄλλος παράκλητος (another Comforter). Gifts are not distinguished from the Father and the Son as ἄλλος (another). He is described as a catholic (universal) teacher of truth: For he is called the Spirit of truth, who is to teach all things. This cannot be asserted of the gifts of the Holy Spirit alone.

III. From 1 Cor. VI, 19: Do you not know that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you? And 1 Cor. III, 16: The Spirit of God dwells in you. A temple is said to be for God, and indwelling is of a person, not of gifts, which are not said to dwell, but to be present.

You say I. The Holy Spirit is omnipresent: how then does he become present through mission? Resp. The Holy Spirit is omnipresent by a universal presence. Ps. CXXXIX, 7. But he deigns to be with the faithful by a special presence. Which special presence is a more intimate and secret conjunction of the Holy Spirit with the faithful for singular gracious effects.

You say II. The infinity and immensity of the Holy Spirit seems to stand in the way of this more intimate conjunction of the Holy Spirit with the faithful. For he who is infinite and immense is absent from no place, from no creature, but is most present to it. Resp. The infinity and immensity of the Holy Spirit did not prevent him from being joined more closely to that dove, in which he descended visibly upon Christ at his baptism, than to other creatures. Indeed, the ὁ λόγος (Word), though infinite and immense, dwells more closely in his own assumed flesh, and indeed σωματικῶς (bodily), Col. II, 9, than in other pious men. Therefore, by reason of the immensity of the Holy Spirit that more intimate conjunction is not hindered.

Latin:

Mittitur-ne Spiritus S. tantum quoad dona & gratiosam operationem, an vero etiam qua hypostasin? Non tantum dona Spiritus S. fidelibus communicantur, sed & ipsa Spiritus S. persona in corda ipsorum a Deo Patre & Filio mittitur, vt tam ratione substantiae, quam ratione ἐνεργείας sive gratiosae operationis propius adsit piis, quam impiis.

Prob. I. ex Gal. IV, 6: Misit Deus Spiritum Filii sui in corda vestra clamantem: Abba Pater! Hic apostolus operationem Spiritus sancti qua in nobis preces, e filiali fiducia manantes, excitat, ab ipsa persona Spiritus sancti distinguit quidem, at non divellit. Docet enim Deum Patrem Spiritum Filii sui in corda nostra misisse, qui pias in nobis preces efficit.

II. E concione προαγωνίως Christi Io. XIV, 16. Ego rogabo Patrem, vt alium παρακλητον det vobis, vt maneat vobiscum in aeternum; Spiritum veritatis. Et v. 26. Paracletus autem Spiritus S. quem mittit Pater in nomine meo, (ἐκεῖνος) ille vos docebit omnia & commonefaciet vos de omnibus, quae dixi vobis: Quae verba Christi de solis donis Spiritus S. explicari nequeunt: Nam Spiritus S. distincta habet nomina personalia.

Vocatur enim paracletus, quod nomen personale est. 1 Io. II, 1. Vocatur ἄλλος παράκλητος. Dona non distinguuntur a Patre & Filio, vt ἄλλος. Describitur vt doctor veritatis catholicus: Nam appellatur Spiritus veritatis, qui docturus sit omnia. Id quod de solis donis Spiritus S. afferri nequit.

III. E 1 Cor. VII, 19. Annon scitis, quod corpus vestrum templum sancti Spiritus, qui in vobis est? Et 1 Cor. III, 16. Spiritus Dei habitat in vobis. Templum dicatur Deo, & inhabitatio est personae, non donorum, quae non dicuntur inhabitare, sed inesse.

Dicis I. Spiritus S. est omnipraesens: quomodo igitur per missionem fit praesens? Resp. Spiritus S. est omnipraesens praesentia universali. Ps. CXXXIX, 7. At praesentia speciali dignatur fideles. Quae praesentia specialis est intimior & secretior Spiritus S. coniunctio cum fidelibus ad effectus singulares gratiosos.

Dicis II. Infinitas & immensitas Spiritus S. huic intimiori coniunctioni Spiritus sancti cum fidelibus obstare videtur. Nam qui infinitus & immensus est, a nullo loco, a nulla creatura abest, sed ei praesentissimus est. Resp. Infinitas & immensitas Spiritus S. non obstabat, quo minus is propius iungeretur columbae illi, in qua descendebat visibiliter super Christum in huius baptismo, quam aliis creaturis. Quin ὁ λόγος etiam infinitus & immensus, proximus habitat in assumta carne propria & quidem σωματικῶς, Col. II, 9. quam in aliis hominibus piis. E. immensitate Spiritus S. intimior illa coniunctio non impeditur.


### Quest. LIV

Which divine action ad extra is proper to the Holy Spirit? The sanctification of the sinful man.

Proved. Sanctification is indeed a divine action ad extra, and therefore undivided or common to all three persons of the Godhead, from which it is also attributed to God the Father, John XVII, 17, and to the Son of God, Heb. IX, 14: but in the Holy Scriptures and the Apostolic Creed, it is appropriated to the Holy Spirit as an external mark of distinction, so that he himself is said to sanctify us terminatively. Namely, God the Father sanctifies us, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit. This is what Paul teaches in Rom. XV, 16: I am a minister of Jesus Christ among the Gentiles, sacrificing the gospel of God, that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified in the Holy Spirit. Paul, by preaching the gospel, showed that unique [thing] to all.

the sacrifice of the Lamb of God, the ἱλασμὸν, or propitiation, which most fully expiated the sins of the whole world, into which Lamb of God the nations, previously unclean, believing and cleansed, sanctified, and made most acceptable to God as offered victims through faith by the working of the Holy Spirit, have been brought. The Holy Spirit therefore sanctifies not instrumentally or ministerially, but principally; since He is openly distinguished from the minister Paul. He sanctifies through the ministry of the word, which is called the διακονία, or ministry of the Spirit, 2 Cor. III, 8, by calling, illuminating, converting, regenerating, justifying, inhabiting, renewing, establishing, and saving fallen men.

Latin:

Quae actio divina ad extra Spiritui S. propria est? Sanctificatio hominis peccatoris.

Prob. Est quidem sanctificatio actio divina ad extra, adeoque indivisa seu communis omnibus tribus divinitatis personis, ex quo etiam Deo Patri, Io. XVII, 17. & Filio Dei, Hebr. IX, 14. tribuitur: at Spiritui S. in sacris litteris & symbolo apostolico, velut externa discretionis nota appropriatur, ut ipse nos terminative sanctificare dicatur. Nimirum sanctificat nos Deus Pater, per Filium, in Spiritu S. Id quod docet Paullus Rom. XV, 16. Ego sum minister Iesu Christi inter gentes sacrificans evangelium Dei, vt fit oblatio gentium peraccepta, sanctificata in Spiritu S. Paullus, praedicando evangelium, ostendebat omnibus illud vnicum.

THEOL. PART. I. CAP. II. DE MYST. TRIN. 344 agni Dei sacrificium ἱλασμὸν, seu propitiatorium, quod totius mundi peccata plenissime expiauit, in quem agnum Dei credentes gentes, prius immundæ, per fidem operante Spiritu S. mundatæ, sanctificatæ & Deo peracceptæ hostiæ oblatæ sunt. Sanctificat itaque Spiritus S. non instrumentaliter, aut ministerialiter, sed principaliter; siquidem aperte a ministro Paullo distinguitur. Sanctificat per ministerium verbi, quod διακονία, seu ministerium Spiritus appellatur, 2 Cor. III, 8. homines lapsos vocando, illuminando, conuertendo, regenerando, iustificando, inhabitando, renouando, stabiliendo, saluando.


### Quest. LV

Can the mystery of the Trinity be demonstrated or refuted from the principles of reason? The truth of the supreme mystery of the Trinity can neither be established nor destroyed from the principles of reason.

Proof. That the mystery of the Trinity is known in its entirety from the divinely revealed word, as its ὀικείῳ or proper principle, and that it is altogether more sublime than any natural grasp, light, or sphere of reason, the Savior Himself teaches, Matt. XI, 27: No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal Him. But if we know neither the Son of God without the kindness of the revealing Father, nor God the Father without the revelation of the Son; it follows that the knowledge of the Most Holy Trinity, as Justin Martyr says, is ὑπὲρ νοῦν, ὑπὲρ λόγον, καὶ ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν κατάληψιν, i.e., it transcends the principles of reason by a great distance, and depends solely upon supernatural revelation.

Wherefore it can and ought to be neither demonstrated nor impugned by reason. Objection. Without reason, the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity cannot be known. Therefore, the dictate of reason must be heeded here. Resp. Without reason, as a receiving subject and knowing organ, we do not apprehend the mystery of the Trinity: We do not know it by reason, as a norm and judge: Just as we do not speak without a tongue, yet we do not use it as the judge of speech.

The antithesis is 1) of the Scholastics and Keckermann, according to whose opinion the mystery of the Trinity can be demonstrated from the principles of reason. 2) Of the Socinians, who attempt to impugn the truth of the supreme article of faith concerning the unity of the divine essence and the Trinity of persons with arguments sought from the light of reason. The little arguments of the Scholastics are as follows:

The little arguments of the Scholastics are as follows: I. Whoever is good from eternity has communicated his goodness from eternity. (For every good is communicative of itself.) But God, etc. Therefore. Furthermore: If God communicated His goodness from eternity; He either communicated it to creatures or to divine persons. Not to creatures; because these did not exist from eternity. Therefore to divine persons.

Resp. If this argument were objected to a pagan philosopher, he would resolve it with no trouble. Namely: The good is communicative of itself, not as a mother, fruitful with offspring, communicates nature to this through generation, but as the sun communicates itself to the world, not by bringing forth a new sun, but by imparting its rays to the world.

II. Supreme blessedness seems to require society and friendship. But God has this without the need of creatures; since they are not co-eternal with God. Friendship, however, cannot consist without a distinction of persons. Resp. A pagan philosopher will reply that God is αὐταρκέστατον, most content in Himself, and does not need a friend.

III. In that essence in which there is a perfect intellect, reflected upon itself, and a perfect will, inclined toward itself, in that essence there is a begotten image and a spirit proceeding by the impulse of the will. But in the divine essence, etc. Therefore. Resp. Neither intellection nor volition is productive of a person. Angels possess an intellect reflected upon itself and a will inclined toward itself, yet they do not produce persons. Add that God knows all things through His essence, and not through species or images. See above p. 258.

IV. The mystery of the Trinity is either conformable or difformable to reason. If it is difformable to reason, it is false. For whatever is against reason cannot be true, because reason has God as its author, from whom nothing but truth can proceed. Therefore it is conformable to reason, and thus demonstrable from its own principles. Response: The mystery of the Trinity is difformable to reason, when left to itself, not in such a way that it is against reason, but above reason.

V. Theologians demonstrate the truth of the mystery of the Trinity through similarities taken from nature, see DANNHAU. hodosoph. p. 276. Response: Those similarities are not adequate, but inadequate, by which that most sublime mystery is in some way shadowed forth, but not proved. VI. Certain philosophers, especially the Platonists, acknowledged the Trinity of divine persons. Response: Those philosophers transferred some things into their writings from the monuments of the Israelite church, but interpolated and corrupted by most vain inventions.

The arguments of the Socinians drawn from the principles of reason, by which they impugn the mystery of the Trinity, are the following: I. As many as are the persons, so many are the essences. But there are three divine persons. Therefore there are also three divine essences. The conclusion is absurd, the absurdity of which arises not from the major proposition, since that is known from the light of nature: Therefore from the minor. Response: 1) The absurdity of the conclusion arises from the major proposition, which is not universally true. For when persons are multiplied, it is not necessary that essences be multiplied. The reason is at hand: because a person, considered abstractively and formally, is a mode of essence; but that there can be many modes of one essence, there is no doubt. For example, we note in Peter the mode of subsistence, presence, duration, position, habit, while the unity of Peter's essence remains. 2) As many as are finite and separate persons, so many are the essences; I concede. But the divine persons are both infinite and are one, 1 John V, 7, so that one person is in another, John XIV, 11. Consequently, it must be attributed to the infinite perfection of God that in one divine essence there are three distinct persons, enjoying mutual περιχωρήσις; which infinite divine perfection it is forbidden to measure by rules taken from creatures.

II. Whatever dogma implies a manifest contradiction, that is truly not consistent. But the dogma concerning the Trinity of persons in the unity of the divine essence implies a manifest contradiction. Therefore. The major is evident: because two contradictories cannot be true at the same time. The minor is proven; because the dogma concerning the Trinity implies that God is one and not one, trine and not trine; by which very thing a manifest contradiction is involved. Response: A contradiction is the affirmation and negation of the same thing concerning the same thing, insofar as it is the same. But when we say that God is one and not one, trine and not trine, then the same thing is not affirmed and denied of the same thing according to the same respect; but unity is affirmed of God according to essence, and denied of the same according to modes of subsisting; or personalities: the trinity is affirmed of God according to personalities, and denied of the same according to essence. You say: A divine person is the divine essence itself. Response: A divine person is ambiguously called the divine essence. For it can 1) have the sense that a divine person in the nominative case is the divine essence, 2) that a divine person in the oblique case connotes the divine essence. In the former sense the assertion is false. For a person taken concretely and materially is an ὑφιστάμενον or an intelligent supposit, which consists of essence and subsistence: the same, taken abstractively and formally, is a mode of essence, which is called in Greek ἀνυπαρξία, and in Latin incommunicable subsistence. In the latter sense the assertion is indeed true. But just as we do not call John's humanity his person; so neither is a divine person in the nominative case accurately called the divine essence itself.

III. If a person formally is a mode of subsisting, God the Father, Son & Holy Spirit will be three modes. The consequent is absurd. Therefore also the antecedent. The absurdity of the consequent is evident; because a mode is a non-being. But who would call God the Father, Son & Holy Spirit non-beings attempt to call?

Resp. I deny the consequence of the major; because God the Father, Son & Holy Spirit are concretes, which besides personality itself connote the divine essence: but a person formally considered is a mode of subsisting, or an ultimate subsistence.

Nor is a mode of subsisting a non-entity; for since it modifies and determines us, it must be something of an entity, materially implying the essence itself.

IV.

No singular is communicable to many.

The divine essence is singular.

It is not communicable from many persons.

Resp. No singular is communicable to many inferiors differing in number; I concede.

For thus universals, namely genera & species, are communicated to inferiors, so that they are essentially multiplied in them.

Yet a singular can be communicable to many in another way.

Thus one and the same prince in number is divinely communicated to many citizens, one pastor to many listeners.

Resp. One singular essence cannot be common to many finite and separately existing persons.

But it is far otherwise with infinite persons, one of whom is in another; these, as Holy Scripture teaches, are one, 1 John.

V, 7. And yet the three divine persons are the same to a third, namely, the divine essence.

Therefore the three divine persons are the same among themselves, and do not differ in any way.

Resp. Whatever things are the same to one third incommunicable thing, those are simply and adequately the same among themselves, e.g.

The promised Messiah, and Jesus of Nazareth; the apostle of the Gentiles, and Paul.

But whatever things are the same to one third communicable thing, identity does not intervene between them, except by reason of that common third.

E.g.

A horse and a man agree in a common generic concept, which is animal, saving the specific difference.

John and James agree in a common specific concept, which is man, saving the numerical difference.

Since therefore the divine essence is communicable to three persons, those persons indeed agree in one common essence, but while the personal distinction remains.

VI. The Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God.

Therefore there are three Gods. Resp.

There is no strength in the consequence; because one may not say: The Father is God, as to essence, distinct from another, who is the supreme God.

Therefore it is wrongly concluded from an indeterminate and common middle term, in which the three divine persons agree.

By similar reasoning someone might perhaps collect: Solomon the king is a man, Solomon the husband is a man, Solomon the father is a man: Therefore Solomon the king, husband, and father are three men.

Objection: Why then do the defenders of the Trinity conclude thus:

The Father is a person, the Son is a person, the Holy Spirit is a person.

And there are three persons?

They conclude correctly thus; because they conclude from a determined and distinctive middle term.

For as to personality, the Father, Son & Holy Spirit are distinguished.

VII. There are three infinite persons: Therefore there are three infinite entities, which is absurd. Resp.

I deny the consequence.

For a person formally and in the nominative case does not denote the entity itself, but something of an entity, namely a certain mode of its existing, which is called ultimate subsistence.

VIII.

God is one and three in persons: Every divine person is God: Therefore every divine person is three in persons. Resp.

1) The major is not distributively universal, because one may not say: Everyone who is one God is three in persons.

2) There are four terms in this sophism because of the varied supposition, which in the major is simple, in the minor is personal.

A similar sophism is: An animal is both rational and irrational: Every Socinian is an animal: Therefore every Socinian is both rational and irrational.

IX.

Three really distinct divine persons are three Gods.

But God the Father, Son & Holy Spirit are three really distinct divine persons.

Therefore.

Therefore God the Father, Son & Holy Spirit There are three Gods. Resp. Three divine persons, really and essentially distinct, are three Gods, I concede. But God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are indeed three persons, really distinct on account of relative oppositions, but they are not distinguished by reason of essence; since they have this in common.

X. In whomever the whole essence of God is, in him the whole Trinity is. But in any divine person, etc. Therefore. Resp. In whom the whole essence of God is under all three modes of subsisting, in him the whole Trinity is, I concede. But one divine person has the essence of God not under three, but one mode of subsisting. For God the Father subsists ἀγεννήτως, the Son of God γεννήτως, the Holy Spirit ἐκπορεύτως.

XI. The true God is to be invoked through a mediator. God, one in essence and three in persons, is not to be invoked through a mediator. Therefore. Resp. The major is particular in the second figure. For not everyone who is the true God is to be invoked through a mediator; since the mediator himself is the true God, who is not invoked through a mediator as someone different from himself (as the adversaries understand it). Although the minor is not to be conceded either; because to invoke through a mediator is to seek a hearing on account of the merit of the mediator: Which certainly can be alleged in the invocation of the Most Holy Trinity. See D. CALOV. System. tom. III. qu. III. p. 114.

XII. The divine essence is the Father: The divine essence is the Son: Therefore the Son is the Father. Resp. 1) Neither the major nor the minor is universal; because I cannot say: Everything that is the divine essence is the Father. 2) The conclusion is to be inferred thus: Therefore a certain one, who is the Son, is the Father (namely, in a different respect).

XIII. If the divine essence is distinguished from the divine persons, there will be a quaternity in God (namely 1. Essence 2. Father 3. Son 4. Holy Spirit). The consequent is absurd; therefore the antecedent is as well. Resp. If the divine essence is really distinguished from the persons, there will be a quaternity in God, I concede. But the divine essence is not really distinguished from the divine persons, but only by an eminent reason, or a reasoned one.

XIV. Whoever consists of three persons is composite. God is not composite. Therefore. Resp. We have satisfied this argument above.

Latin:

Veritas summi mysterii Trinitatis ex principiis rationis neque adstrui, neque destrui potest.

Prob. Mysterium Trinitatis in solidum e verbo diuinitus reuelato, velut ὀικείῳ seu proprio principio, cognosci, omnique adeo naturali rationis captu, lumine, sphæra prorsus sublimius esse, docet ipse Saluator, Matth. XI, 27. Nemo cognoscit Filium, nisi Pater, neque Patrem quisquam cognoscit, nisi Filius, & cui voluerit Filius reuelare. Quod si neque Filium Dei sine reuelantis Patris benignitate, neque Deum Patrem sine reuelatione Filii cognoscimus; consequitur, cognitionem SS. Trinitatis, dicente Iustino Martyre, esse ὑπὲρ νοῦν, ὑπὲρ λόγον, καὶ ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν κατάληψιν, i. e. principia rationis longissime transcendere, & a supernaturali reuelatione vnice pendere. Quare ex ratione neque demonstrari, neque impugnari potest, ac debet.

Dicis Sine ratione mysterium SS. Trinitatis cognosci nequit. E. rationis dictamen hic attendendum est. Resp. Sine ratione, vt subiecto recipiente, & organo cognoscente, mysterium Trinitatis non apprehendimus: Cognoscimus illud sine ratione, vt norma & iudice: Sicut sine lingua non loquimur, ea tamen vt iudice sermonis non vtimur.

Antithesis est 1) Scholasticorum, & Keckermanni, quorum de sententia mysterium Trinitatis ex principiis rationis demonstrari potest. 2) Socinianorum, qui argumentis, e lumine rationis petitis, veritatem summi fidei articuli de vnitate essentiæ diuinæ & Trinitate personarum impugnare conantur.

Scholasticorum ratiunculæ sunt sequentes: I. Quicunque ab æterno bonus est, ab æterno suam bonitatem communicauit. (Nam omne bonum est sui communicatiuum.) Atqui Deus &c. Ergo. Porro: Si Deus ab æterno suam bonitatem communicauit; aut creaturis eam communicauit, aut personis diuinis. Non creaturis; quia hæ ab æterno non exstiterunt. Ergo personis diuinis.

Resp. Si hoc argumentum obiiceretur philosopho gentili, nullo negotio illud refolueret. Nimirum; Bonum est sui communicatiuum, non vt mater, fœcunda prolis, per generationem huic naturam communicat, sed vt fol mundo se communicat, non nouum pariendo solem, sed radios suos mundo impertiendo.

II. Summa beatitudo societatem & amicitiam requirere videtur. Atqui Deus hanc habet sine indigentia creaturarum; quippe quæ Deo non sunt coæternæ. Amicitia autem sine distinctione personarum consistere nequit. Resp. Philosophus gentilis reponet, Deum αὐταρκέστατον, seipso maxime contentum, amico non indigere.

III. In qua essentia est intellectus perfectus, reflexus in seipsum, & perfecta voluntas, in seipsum propensa, in illa essentia est imago genita, & spiritus impetu voluntatis procedens. Atqui in essentia diuina &c. E. Resp. Neque intellectio, neque volitio est productiua personæ. Angeli pollent intellectu in seipsum reflexo, & voluntate in seipsam propensa, neque tamen personas producunt. Adiice, quod Deus omnia cognoscat per essentiam suam, non autem per species aut imagines. Vid. supra p. 258.

IV. Mysterium Trinitatis aut est conforme, aut difforme rationi. Si est difforme rationi, falsum est. Quidquid enim contra rationem est, ideo non potest esse verum, quod ratio auctorem habet Deum, a quo non nisi verum provenire potest. Ergo est conforme rationi, adeoque ex ipsius principiis demonstrabile. Resp. Mysterium Trinitatis est rationi, sibi relictae, difforme, non ut sit contra rationem, sed supra rationem.

V. Theologi veritatem mysterii Trinitatis ostendunt per similia e natura petita, vid. DANNHAU. hodosoph. p. 276. Resp. Similia illa non sunt adaequata, sed inadæquata, quibus sublimissimum illud mysterium quodammodo adumbratur, sed non probatur. VI. Philosophi quidam, inprimis Platonici, Trinitatem personarum divinarum agnoverunt. Resp. Philosophi illi in scripta sua nonnulla transtulerunt ex monumentis ecclesiae Israeliticae, sed vanissimis commentis interpolata & corrupta.

Socinianorum argumenta ex principiis rationis hausta, quibus mysterium Trinitatis impugnant, sunt sequentia: I. Quot sunt personae, tot sunt essentiae. Sed tres sunt personae divinae. Ergo & tres sunt essentiae divinae. Conclusio est absurda, cuius absurditas provenit non ex maiori propositione, quippe quae e lumine naturae innotescit: Ergo ex minori. Resp. 1) Absurditas conclusionis oritur ex maiori propositione, quae universaliter vera non est. Nam multiplicatis personis non est necesse multiplicari essentias. Ratio est in promptu: quia persona abstractive & formaliter considerata est modus essentiae; at plures posse unius essentiae esse modos, dubium nullum est. V. gr. notamus in Petro modum subsistentiae, praesentiae, durationis, situs, habitus, salva manente unitate essentiae Petri. 2) Quot sunt personae finitae & separatae, tot sunt essentiae; concedo. At personae divinae tum infinitae, tum unum sunt, 1 Io. V, 7. ita ut una persona sit in alia, Io. XIV, 11. Proinde infinitae Dei perfectioni tribuendum est, quod in una essentia divina sint tres distinctae personae, mutua gaudentes περιχωρήσει; quam infinitam perfectionem divinam regulis, a creaturis desumtis, metiri, nefas est.

II. Quodcunque dogma manifestam implicat contradictionem, id vero non est consentaneum. Atqui dogma de Trinitate personarum in unitate essentiae divinae manifestam implicat contradictionem. Ergo. Maior constat: quia duo contradictoria simul vera esse nequeunt. Minor probatur; quia dogma de Trinitate infert, Deum esse unum, & non unum, trinum, & non trinum; quo ipso manifesta involuitur contradictio. Resp. Contradictio est affirmatio & negatio eiusdem de eodem, quatenus idem. Quando autem dicimus, Deum esse unum & non unum, trinum & non trinum, tunc idem de eodem non affirmatur & negatur secundum idem; sed unitas de Deo affirmatur secundum essentiam, negatur de eodem secundum modos subsistendi; seu personalitates: trinitas affirmatur de Deo secundum personalitates, negatur de eodem secundum essentiam. Dicis: Persona divina est ipsa essentia divina. Resp. Persona divina ambigue dicitur essentia divina. Potest enim 1) sensus esse, personam divinam in casu recto esse essentiam divinam, 2) personam divinam in casu obliquo essentiam divinam connotare. Priori sensu assertio est falsa. Nam persona sumta concrete & materialiter est ὑφιστάμενον sive suppositum intelligens, quod ex essentia & subsistentia constat: eadem, sumta abstractive & formaliter, est essentiae modus, qui graece, ἀνυπαρξία, latine, subsistentia incommunicabilis, vocatur. In sensu posteriori assertio quidem vera est. At sicut personam Ioannis non vocamus ipsius humanitatem; ita nec persona divina in casu recto accurate dicitur ipsa essentia divina.

III. Si persona formaliter est subsistendi modus, Deus Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. erunt tres modi. Consequens est absurdum. Ergo & antecedens. Absurditas consequentis patet; quia modus est non ens. At quis Deum Patrem, Filium & Spiritum S. non entia appellare pellare conaretur?

Resp. Negat. consequ. maioris; quia Deus Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. sunt concreta, quæ præter personalitatem ipsam essentiam diuinam connotant: at persona formaliter considerata est modus subsistendi, seu subsistentia vltimata.

Neque modus subsistendi non ens est; cum enim nos modificet ac determinet, oportet eum aliquid entis esse, essentiam ipsam materialiter implicans.

IV.

Nullum singulare pluribus est communicabile.

Essentia diuina est singularis.

E pluribus personis non est communicabilis.

Resp. Nullum singulare pluribus inferioribus numero differentibus est communicabile; concedo.

Nam sic vniuersalia, nempe genera & species; communicantur inferioribus, vt in iisdem essentialiter multiplicentur.

Potest tamen singulare alia ratione pluribus esse communicabile.

Sic vnus idemque numero princeps pluribus ciuibus, vnus pastor pluribus auditoribus diuinitus communicatur.

Resp. Vna essentia singularis non potest esse communis pluribus personis finitis & seorsum existentibus.

At longe aliter comparatum est cum personis infinitis, quarum vna est in alia; hæ, docente scriptura S. vnum sunt, 1 Io.

V, 7. Atqui tres personæ diuinæ sunt eadem vni tertio, nempe, essentiæ diuinæ.

Ergo tres personæ diuinæ inter se sunt eadem, neque vlla ratione differunt.

Resp. Quæcunque sunt eadem vni tertio incommunicabili, ea inter se simpliciter & adæquate eadem sunt, v. gr.

Messias promissus, & Iesus Nazarenus; gentium apostolus, & Paullus.

At quæcunque sunt eadem vni tertio communicabili, iis non intercedit identitas, nisi ratione illius tertii communis.

V. gr.

Equus & homo conueniunt in conceptu communi generico, qui est animal, salua differentia specifica.

Ioannes & Iacobus conueniunt in conceptu communi specifico, qui est homo, salua differentia numerica.

Cum itaque essentia diuina tribus personis communicabilis sit, personæ illæ in vna essentia communi quidem conueniunt, sed salua manente distinctione personali.

VI. Pater est Deus, Filius est Deus, Spiritus S. est Deus.

Ergo tres sunt Dii. Resp.

Nihil neruorum inest consequentiae; quia dicere non licet: Pater est Deus, qua essentiam, ab alio, qui summus Deus est, distinctus.

Perperam ergo concluditur ex medio termino indeterminato & communi, in quo tres personæ diuinæ conueniunt.

Simili ratione quispiam forte colligeret: Salomo rex est homo, Salomo maritus est homo, Salomo pater est homo: Ergo Salomo rex, maritus, & pater, sunt tres homines.

Instantia Quare igitur defensores Trinitatis sic concludunt:

Pater est persona, Filius est persona, Spiritus S. est persona.

E tres sunt personæ?

Recte illi sic colligunt; quia concludunt e medio termino determinato & distinctiuo.

Qua personalitatem enim, distinguuntur Pater, Filius & Spiritus S.

VII. Sunt tres personæ infinitæ: Ergo sunt tria entia infinita, quod ἄτοπον. Resp.

Neg. consequ.

Nam persona formaliter & in casu recto non notat ipsum ens, sed aliquid entis, nempe eius quendam modum existendi, qui subsistentia vltimata dicitur.

VIII.

Deus vnus est trinus in personis: Quælibet persona diuina est Deus: Ergo quælibet persona diuina est trina in personis. Resp.

1) Maior non est distributiue vniuersalis, quia dicere non licet: Omnis ille, qui est vnus Deus, est trinus in personis.

2) Sunt quatuor termini in hoc sophismate ob variatam suppositionem, quæ in maiori simplex, in minori personalis est.

Simile sophisma est: Animal est tum rationale, tum irrationale: Omnis Socinianus est animal: Ergo omnis Socinianus tum rationalis, tum irrationalis est.

IX.

Tres personæ diuinæ realiter distinctæ sunt tres Dii.

Atqui Deus Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. sunt tres personæ diuinæ realiter distinctæ.

E.

E. Deus Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. sunt sunt tres Dij. Resp. Tres personæ diuinæ, realiter & essentialiter distinctæ, sunt tres Dii, concedo. At Deus Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. sunt quidem tres personæ, ob relatiuas oppositiones realiter distinctæ, non autem distinguuntur ratione essentiæ; quippe quam cominunem habent.

X. In quocunque est tota essentia Dei, in illo tota est Trinitas. Atqui in qualibet persona diuina &c. E. Resp. In quo est tota essentia Dei sub omnibus tribus subsistendi modis, in illo est tota Trinitas, concedo. At vna persona diuina habet essentiam Dei non sub tribus, sed vno subsistendi modo. Subsistit enim Deus Pater ἀγεννήτως, Filius Dei γεννήτως, Spiritus S. ἐκπορεύτως.

XI. Verus Deus est inuocandus per mediatorem. Vnus in essentia, & trinus in personis Deus, non est inuocandus per mediatorem. Ergo. Resp. Maior est particularis in secunda figura. Non enim, quicunque verus Deus est, inuocandus est per mediatorem; siquidem & ipse mediator verus Deus est, qui per mediatorem, ceu diuersum abs se (vti aduersarii intelligunt) non inuocatur. Quanquam neque minor concedenda sit; quia per mediatorem inuocare, est propter meritum mediatoris exauditionem petere: Quod vtique allegari posse in SS. Trinitatis inuocatione, certum est. Vid. D. CALOV. System. tom. III. qu. III. p. 114.

XII. Essentia diuina est Pater: Essentia diuina est Filius: Ergo Filius est Pater. Resp. 1) Neque maior, neque minor vniuersalis est; quia non possum dicere: Omne id, quod est essentia diuina, est Pater. 2) Conclusio ita inferenda est: Ergo quidam, qui est Filius, est Pater (scil. diuerso respectu.)

XIII. Si essentia diuina a personis diuinis distinguitur, erit in Deo quaternitas (nempe 1. Essentia 2. Pater 3. Filius 4. Spiritus S.) Consequens est absurdum; E. & antecedens. Resp. Si essentia diuina a personis distinguitur realiter, erit in Deo quaternitas, concedo. At essentia diuina a personis diuinis non distinguitur realiter, sed tantum ratione eminente, seu ratiocinata.

XIV. Quicunque constat e tribus personis, is est compositus. Deus non est compositus. Ergo. Resp. Huic argumento satisfecimus supra.


### Q. LVI. Is the mystery of the Trinity necessary to be believed by all who are to be saved?

The mystery of the Most Holy Trinity is necessary to be believed by all men who are to be saved in the Old (a) and New Testament (b), as much by the necessity of a divine precept as by the necessity of a means, divinely ordained for obtaining salvation (c).

Prob. a. When God was promulgating the decalogue, he was inculcating this precept to the Israelites. Exod. XX, 2. I am Jehovah your God; who led you out of the land of Egypt from the house of servants: you shall have no other God before my face. But that the triune God led the Israelites out of Egypt, we have clearly shown above. Furthermore, God was saying in the same place, v. 10. 11. The seventh day shall be a sabbath to Jehovah, your God --- Because in six days Jehovah made heaven and earth. The Creator of heaven and earth is God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Gen. I, 1. 2. Ps. XXXIII, 6.

Prob. b. In the N. T. all who are to be saved are commanded to be baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Matth. XXVIII, 9. Therefore all who are to be saved are obligated by divine precept to acknowledge and worship God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Prob. c. 1) This is eternal life, that they may know you the only true God, and whom you sent, Jesus Christ Io. XVII, 3. Just as eternal life consists in the vision and everlasting fruition of the Most Holy Trinity: so the means and way of obtaining eternal life is the saving knowledge of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

2) No atheist is saved: He who does not honor the triune God is an atheist: Therefore. The minor is proved both from Io. V, 32. He who does not honor the Son, does not honor the Father: and from 1 Io. II, 23.

Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father either. But whoever acknowledges neither God the Father nor the Son of God is an atheist. Concerning which ATHANASIUS in his creed gravely says: Whosoever will be saved, before all things it is necessary that he hold the catholic faith; which faith except every one do keep whole and undefiled, without doubt he shall perish everlastingly. And the catholic faith is this, that we worship one God in trinity, and trinity in unity.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, Arminians, and certain Papists, who deny that the mystery of the Trinity is necessary to be believed by all who are to be saved; whose arguments are:

I. The H. Trinity does not exist in Holy Scripture. Therefore, it is not necessarily to be believed by all.

Resp. We have in the Holy Scriptures three witnesses, who are one, 1 John V, 7. Although the abstract, Trinity, does not exist in Holy Scripture ῥητῶς (expressly), it suffices that τὸ πρᾶγμα (the thing), or the reality itself, is clearly made known from the heavenly oracles.

II. To whomever the mystery of the Trinity is necessary to be known, to them the distinction between essence and person must be known. But not all men know that distinction. Therefore.

Resp. The supreme dogma of the Christian faith concerning three persons in one divine essence is necessary to be known by all, not insofar as it is proposed in ecclesiastical terms, but simply in the phrases of Scripture. Furthermore, we teach the unlearned the distinction of essence and person most plainly; namely, that the essence is common to all three persons of the divinity: but a person is incommunicable to another person.

III. Infants do not believe in the H. Trinity, because they are utterly ignorant of the distinction of essence and divine persons, and yet they are saved. Therefore, the mystery of the Trinity is not necessary to be believed by all.

Resp. Infants are baptized into God the Father, Son, and H. Spirit, and therefore, by the illuminating H. Spirit, they believe in the triune God, with a faith not indeed discursive or reflex, yet simple and direct, in a manner inexplicable to us.

IV. If the mystery of the Trinity was known in the O. T., it was known either implicitly or explicitly. If the former; the Jews did not have a distinct knowledge of the divine persons, and so this mystery cannot be proven from passages of the O. T. If the latter; the distinction of the O. and N. T. will be removed, although it is certain that the mystery of the Trinity is proposed more clearly in the N. than in the O. T.

Resp. The Jews of the O. T. explicitly knew the triune God, but explicit knowledge has its degrees; for it is clearer under the new covenant, and was less clear under the old.

V. Whoever were kept under the law for the faith to come, they did not have explicit faith in the H. Trinity. But the Israelites in the O. T. &c. Gal. III, 23.

Resp. 1) By faith in the cited passage, some understand the doctrine concerning Christ exhibited, which was to be revealed in the N. Testament. Meanwhile, the Fathers under the O. T. had faith in the Messiah who was to come. 2) B. Luther understands saving faith, and distinguishes not between the times of the O. and N. Testament, but between the different states of man, who lives either in a state of anxiety under the law, or in a state of grace, or faith. We are all kept and restrained under the law unto the acknowledgment of sins, until we are raised up and refreshed by faith in Christ.

VI. The Israelites in the O. T. did not worship the Father in the name of Christ. Therefore, they did not explicitly know the mystery of the Trinity.

Resp. I deny the antecedent. Daniel sought to be heard by the Lord for the Lord's sake, ch. IX, 17. i.e., for Christ's sake.

Objection. But Christ says: Hitherto have ye asked nothing in my name. John XVI, 24.

Resp. By the name of Christ in the cited passage, as LUTHER explains, is understood all that which Christ performed for us in his mediatorial office, to which pertains the passion, death, burial, resurrection, &c., which at the time when Christ was using the cited words, had not yet been accomplished, but were soon to be accomplished.

VII. Modern Jews do not acknowledge the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity. Resp. Modern Jews are blinded and hardened; the Jews of the O.T. were teachable. To argue from the latter to the former is wrong.

Latin:

Mysterium SS. Trinitatis omnibus hominibus saluandis in veteri (a) & nouo testamento (b) creditu necessarium est, tam necessitate præcepti diuini, quam necessitate medii, ad salutem consequendam diuinitus ordinati (c).

Prob. a. Cum Deus decalogum promulgaret, hoc præceptum Israëlitis inculcabat. Exod. XX, 2. Ego sum Iehouah Deus tuus; qui eduxi te e terra Ægypti e domo seruorum: non erit tibi Deus alius ante facies meas. At Deum trinum Israëlitas ex Ægypto eduxisse, supra liquido ostendimus. Præterea dicebat Deus ibidem, v. 10. 11. Dies septimus sabbatum esto Iehouæ, Deo tuo --- Quia sex diebus fecit Iehouah cælum & terram. Creator cæli & terræ est Deus Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. Gen. I, 1. 2. Ps. XXXIII, 6.

Prob. b. In N. T. iubentur omnes saluandi baptizari in nomine Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. Matth. XXVIII, 9. Ergo præcepto diuino obligantur omnes saluandi ad agnoscendum & colendum Deum Patrem, Filium & Spiritum S.

Prob. c. 1) Hæc est vita æterna, vt cognoscant te solum verum Deum, & quem misisti, Iesum Christum Io. XVII, 3. Vt in SS. Trinitatis visione & fruitione sempiterna consistit vita æterna: ita medium & via consequendi vitam æternam est salutifera cognitio Dei Patris, Filii & Spiritus S.

2) Nullus atheus saluatur: Deum trinunum non honorans est atheus: Ergo. Minor probatur tum ex Io. V, 32. Qui Filium non honorat, non honorat Patrem: tum ex 1 Io. II, 23.

Omnis, qui negat Filium, neque Patrem habet. At qui neque Deum Patrem, neque Filium Dei agnoscit, is atheus est. Ex quo ATHANASIVS in symbolo suo grauiter inquit: Quicunque vult saluus esse, ante omnia opus est, vt teneat catholicam fidem; quam nisi quisque integram, inuiolatamque seruauerit, absque dubio in aeternum peribit. Fides autem catholica haec est, vt vnum Deum in trinitate, & trinitatem in vnitate veneremur.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, Arminianorum, & quorundam Pontificiorum, negantium, mysterium Trinitatis omnibus saluandis creditu esse necessarium; quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Non exstat SS. Trinitas in scriptura sacra. Ergo non omnibus necessario credenda est.

Resp. Habemus in sacris litteris tres testes, qui vnum sunt, 1 Jo. V, 7. Licet abstractum, Trinitas, non exstet in sacra scriptura ῥητῶς, sufficit, τὸ πρᾶγμα, siue rem ipsam, ex oraculis coelestibus clare innotescere.

II. Quibuscunque mysterium Trinitatis est cognitu necessarium, illis cognoscendum est discrimen inter essentiam & personam. Atqui non omnes homines cognoscunt illud discrimen. Ergo.

Resp. Summum fidei Christianae dogma de tribus personis in vna essentia diuina omnibus cognitu necessarium est, non quatenus terminis ecclesiasticis, sed phrasibus scripturae simpliciter proponitur. Ceterum idiotis discrimen essentiae & personae planissime tradimus; quod videlicet essentia fit communis omnibus tribus diuinitatis personis: persona autem incommunicabilis fit alteri personae.

III. Infantes non credunt SS. Trinitatem, quia discrimen essentiae & personarum diuinarum penitus ignorant, & tamen saluantur. Ergo mysterium Trinitatis non omnibus creditu est necessarium.

Resp. Infantes baptizantur in Deum Patrem, Filium & Spiritum S., ideoque illuminante Spiritu S. in Deum trinum credunt, fide non quidem discursiua, aut reflexa, attamen simplici & directa, modo nobis inexplicabili.

IV. Si mysterium Trinit. in V. T. cognitum fuit, vel implicite vel explicite fuit cognitum. Si prius; Iudaei non habuerunt distinctam notitiam personarum diuinarum, adeo que e locis V. T. probari hoc mysterium nequit. Si posterius; tolletur discrimen V. & N. T. cum tamen constet, mysterium Trinitatis clarius in N. quam V. T. esse propositum.

Resp. Iudaei V. T. explicite cognouerunt Deum trinum, sed explicita cognitio suos habet gradus; clarior enim est sub nouo foedere, minus clara sub veteri fuit.

V. Quicunque custoditi fuerunt sub lege in futuram fidem, illi fidem explicitam in SS. Trinitatem non habuerunt. Atqui Israëlitæ in V. T. &c. Gal. III, 23.

Resp. 1) Per fidem l. c. nonnulli intelligunt doctrinam de Christo exhibito, quæ in N. Test. erat reuelanda. Habuerunt interim Patres sub V. T. fidem in Messiam venturum. 2) B. Lutherus intelligit fidem saluificam, & distinguit non inter tempora V. & N. Test., sed inter diuersos flatus hominis, qui viuit vel in statu anxietatis sub lege, vel in statu gratiæ, seu fidei. Nos omnes custodimur & coërcemur sub lege in agnitionem peccatorum, donec fide in Christum erigamur & reficiamur.

VI. Israëlitæ in V. T. non adorauerunt Patrem in nomine Christi. E. mysterium Trinitatis explicite non cognouerunt.

Resp. Neg. anteced. Daniel expetiit exaudiri a Domino propter Dominum, c. IX, 17. i. e. propter Christum.

Instantia. Sed Christus dicit: Hactenus in nomine meo non petiistis. Io. XVI, 24.

Resp. Per nomen Christi l. c. explicante LVTHERO, intelligitur omne illud, quod Christus in officio suo mediatorio pro nobis præstitit, quo pertinet passio, mors, sepultura, resurrectio &c. quæ id temporis, quo Christus verbis citatis vtebatur, nondum erant peracta, sed propediem peragenda.

VII. Hodierni Iudaei mysterium SS. Trinitatis non agnoscunt. Resp. Hodierni Iudaei sunt excoecati & indurati, Iudaei V. T. erant dociles. Ab illis ad hos argumentari, nefas est.


### Q. LVII. Does the human nature of Christ also pertain to the Most Holy Trinity?

The human nature of Christ, by means of the personal union with the Word (τῷ λόγῳ), pertains to the Most Holy Trinity. Proof. By whatever reason the human nature of Christ pertains to the Word (τὸν λόγον), by that same reason it pertains to the Most Holy Trinity. But by means of the personal union it pertains to the Word (τὸν λόγον). Therefore, by means of the personal union it pertains to the Most Holy Trinity.

The minor premise is established from John 1:14, 1 Tim. 3:16. Antithesis also of the Papists, who deny that the human nature of Christ has been elevated into the fellowship of the Most Holy Trinity. They rely on the following arguments: I. In the Most Holy Trinity there is the Father, the Son of God, and the Holy Spirit. But the human nature of Christ is not the Father, the Son of God, and the Holy Spirit. Therefore. The Son of God manifested in the flesh consists of the divine and human nature.

II. If the human nature pertains to the Trinity, an equalization of the divine and human nature will occur. The consequent is absurd. Therefore, the antecedent is also. Resp. No equalization of natures occurs. For the human nature of Christ does not pertain to the Trinity essentially, immediately, and of itself, but only mediately and by the grace of the personal union.

Latin:

Humana Christi natura, mediante personali cum τῷ λόγῳ unione, ad SS. Trinitatem pertinet. Prob. Qua ratione humana Christi natura pertinet ad τὸν λόγον, eadem ratione pertinet ad SS. Trinitatem. At mediante unione personali pertinet ad τὸν λόγον. E. mediante unione personali pertinet ad SS. Trinitatem.

Minor constat e Io. I, 14. 1 Tim. III, 16. Antithesis et Pontificiorum, negantium, humanam Christi naturam in consortium SS. Trinitatis evectam esse. Nituntur sequentibus argumentis: I. In SS. Trinitate est Pater, Filius Dei & Spiritus S. Atqui humana Christi natura non est Pater, Filius Dei & Spiritus S. Ergo. Filius Dei in carne manifestatus constat ex natura divina & humana.

II. Si natura humana ad Trinitatem pertinet, fiet exaequatio naturae divinae & humanae. Consequens est absurdum. E. & antecedens. Resp. Non fit exaequatio naturarum. Neque enim humana Christi natura essentialiter, immediate & per se, sed tantum mediate & per unionis personalis gratiam ad Trinitatem pertinet.


### Q. LVIII. How are those to be instructed who cannot grasp the doctrine concerning the Most Holy Trinity?

To these, the mystery of the Trinity is to be explained most simply by the phrases of Scripture.

Proof. Holy Scripture teaches most plainly that God is one, Deut. 6: 4. That this one God, in whose name we are baptized, is the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, Matt. 28: 19. That the Father is one, the Son of God another, the Holy Spirit another, John 14:16. That the Son of God is begotten of the Father, Ps. 2:7. That the Holy Spirit proceeds from God the Father and the Son from eternity, John 15:26. Furthermore, the Apostle admonishes that reason must be taken captive into the obedience of Christ, 2 Cor. 10:5.

Latin:

His mysterium Trinitatis phrasibus scripturae simplicissime explicandum est.

Prob. Sacra scriptura planissime docet, Deum esse unum, Deut. VI, 4. Deum illum unum, in cuius nomen baptizamur, esse Patrem, Filium & Spiritum S. Matth. XXIIX, 19. Alium esse Patrem, alium Filium Dei, alium Spiritum S. Io. XIV, 16. Filium Dei esse a Patre genitum. Ps. II, 7. Spiritum S. a Deo Patre & Filio ab aeterno procedere, Jo. XV, 26. De cetero rationem captiuandam esse sub obsequium Christi, monet apostolus 2 Cor. X, 5.


### Q. LIX. Does one who worships one person of the Godhead worship the Most Holy Trinity itself?

When one person of the Godhead is worshipped, the whole Most Holy Trinity is worshipped.

Proof. The three persons of the Godhead are ὁμοούσιοι (homoousioi) or consubstantial, John 14:10, 1 John 5:7. Therefore, by prayers directed to one person, we do not exclude the others, but we withdraw our mind from creatures and everything that is not God; however, for the sake of the concept of distinction, we direct our prayers to the divine persons.

Latin:

Adorata una divinitatis persona tota SS. Trinitas adoratur.

Prob. Tres divinitatis personae sunt ὁμοούσιοι siue consubstantiales, Jo. XIV, 10. 1 Jo. V, 7. Non igitur precibus ad unam personam directis, reliquas excludimus, sed abstrahimus mentem a creaturis & omni eo, quod non est Deus, distinctionis autem conceptus causa preces nostras ad personas divinas dirigimus.


### Q. LX. What practical uses will you extract from the doctrine concerning the Most Holy Trinity?
