The practical uses to be derived from the mystery of the Trinity concern partly the confidence of our heart , and partly the declaring of our love toward God and neighbor .

Proof. a. Nothing so equally raises and supports the confidence of our heart as the love of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For God the Father loved us sinners, guilty of eternal death, by sending the Son as mediator into the flesh, and by benevolently accepting the satisfaction rendered by Him for our sins. The Son of God loved us by putting on our flesh, by paying in it the penalties of our sins, and by procuring eternal salvation for us. The Holy Spirit loved us by offering and conferring upon us, through the Word and Sacraments, the salvation procured by the Son of God. O love without example! O grace without measure! Supported by this, we pour out prayers full of confidence to the Triune God, and promise ourselves from Him every best blessing.

Proof. b. AUGUSTINE says excellently in his Manual, ch. XIX: God the Father is love: God the Son is charity: the Holy Spirit is the love of the Father and the Son: this love and this charity require something similar in us, namely, love, by which we may be associated and joined to Him as if by a certain affinity of consanguinity.

Thee, fount of divinity and creator of the world, eternal Father; thee, neither posterior nor lesser than the Father, savior and preserver of the human race, eternal Son; thee, who proceedest from both, in majesty inferior to neither, sanctifier of the souls of the faithful, Holy Spirit, as devoutly as can be, I pray, venerate, and beseech, that with the same grace by which you have anticipated us miserable sinners, you may accompany and follow us perpetually, so that in the light of your revelation, we may clearly see, sincerely love, and constantly worship our light and sun.

Forgive, O Father! the sins of your repenting children: adorn, O God the Son! them with the garment of your justice; inhabit and fill them, O Holy Spirit! with your gifts, so that they may live soberly, justly, and piously in the present age, awaiting the blessed life in the kingdom of glory.

Latin:

Usus practici e mysterio Trinitatis deriuandi concernunt partim fiduciam cordis nostri , partim caritatem nostram erga Deum & proximum declarandam .

Prob. a. Nihil peraeque fiduciam cordis nostri erigit & fulcit, atque caritas Dei Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. Amauit quippe nos peccatores, aeterna mortis reos, Deus Pater, Filium mediatorem in carnem mittendo, & ipsius pro nostris peccatis praestitam satisfactionem beneuole acceptando. Amauit nos Filius Dei carnem nostram induendo, in ea poenas peccatorum nostrorum luendo, aeternamque salutem nobis pariendo. Amauit nos Spiritus S. partam a Filio Dei salutem per verbum & sacramenta nobis offerendo & conferendo. O caritas sine exemplo! O gratia sine mensura! Hac subnixi, preces fiduciae plenas ad Deum trinum fundimus, & salutem berriima quaeque ab eodem nobis promittimus.

Prob. b. Praeclare inquit AVGVSTINVS in Manuali c. XIX. Deus Pater caritas est: Deus Filius dilectio est: Spiritus S. amor Patris & Filii est: haec caritas & haec dilectio aliquid simile in nobis requirit, scil. caritatem, qua velut quadam affinitate consanguinitatis ei fociemur & coniungamur. sociemur & coniungamur. sociemur & coniungamur.

Te, fons divinitatis et conditor orbis, Pater aeterne; te, nec posterior, nec minor Patre, servator generis humani et sospitator, aeterne Fili; te, qui ab utroque procedis, neutri maiestate inferior, sanctificator animarum fidelium, Spiritus Sancte, quam devotissime fieri potest, oro, veneror et obtestor, ut qua gratia nos miseros peccatores praevenisti, eadem comiteris perpetuo et prosequaris, quo in lumine revelationis tuae, lumen et solem nostrum, clare videamus, fincere amemus, constanter colamus.

Condones, o Pater! liberis tuis resipiscentibus peccata: ornes, o Deus Fili! ipses veste iustitiae tuae; incolas eosdem et impleas, o Spiritus Sancte! donis tuis, quo sobrie, iuste et pie vivant in praesenti saeculo, exspectantes vitam beatam in regno gloriae.


## 6 On Divine Actions in General, and on Creation


### Question IV. How are divine actions ad extra distinguished?

Question I.

What are divine actions?

They are second acts of the infinite power of God.

Question II.

How are divine actions distinguished?

Divine actions are distinguished into those which are within God, and those which are outside of God.

Divine actions ad intra are those which tend toward an object which is God himself: Actions ad extra are those whose object is created things.

Proof Every action involves a transcendental relation to a certain object.

Therefore, the object of divine actions is either God himself or creatures.

Question III.

How are divine actions ad intra distinguished?

Divine actions ad intra are either essential or personal.

The former are those which regard God as an object, and whose acting principle is the divine essence considered indeterminately, as it is common to all three persons of the divinity (a): The latter is that which terminates at a divine person, and whose acting principle is the divine essence viewed determinately, as it is marked by a certain hypostatic character (b).

Proof a. Certain divine actions flow from the essence of God considered indeterminately, e.g., the acts of the divine intellect and will.

For God knows himself, loves himself, and rests in his own goodness; these are essential actions ad intra.

Proof b. The generation of the Son of God and the spiration of the Holy Spirit are personal divine actions ad intra: for it terminates in producing a divine person, and their acting principle is the divine essence, marked by a certain hypostatic character. Regarding these, that well-worn saying holds true: Divine works ad intra are divided, i.e., not common to all three persons of the divinity.

Question IV.

How are divine actions ad extra distinguished?

Divine actions ad extra are distinguished into immanent and transient.

The former are those which indeed terminate at creatures, but are perfected within the essence of God.

These are called [actions] which are both performed outside the divine essence, and regard an object distinct from God (b).

Prob. a. God knows, loves, and destines creatures to certain ends: which actions are indeed performed within God, but are terminated upon creatures.

The divine decrees of creation, conservation, predestination, and reprobation pertain to this.

Prob. b. Transitive actions are distinguished into personal and essential.

The former are those which are performed outside the end of the deity, and belong to one certain person by economic appropriation.

The latter are those which are performed outside the divine essence, and are common to all three persons of the divinity, the order of them being nevertheless preserved.

Concerning this distinction it must be carefully observed: (1) That actions toward the outside [ad extra] that are personal are considered in two ways: (a) inchoatively, or by reason of the principle; for thus they are common to all three persons of the divinity: (b) terminatively, or by reason of the term; thus they belong to one divine person, and are terminated in the same.

E.g. The Incarnation is a divine work toward the outside that is personal, which is inchoatively common to all three persons of the divinity, viz. regarding the production of the flesh of Christ, and also regarding the coupling or union of the two natures in Christ; but if it is viewed terminatively, it belongs to the Word alone, or the Son of God, into whose hypostasis the flesh of Christ was assumed.

Similarly, the appearance of the Holy Spirit in the visible form of a dove, Matt. III, 16, is common to all three divine persons inchoatively, viz. regarding the production of the dove-like form, and the exhibition of the produced form; but terminatively, by reason of the intuition, external appearance, and descent, it belongs to the Holy Spirit alone.

(2) Essential actions toward the outside are undivided, i.e., common to all three persons of the divinity, the order of them being nevertheless preserved.

E.g. The creation of the world is an external essential work, common to God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the order of the divine persons being nevertheless preserved.

For just as the Father is from himself, but the Son of God is from the Father, and the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son: so God the Father is said to have created the world through the Son in the Holy Spirit.

Quest. V. What is creation?

Creation is a divine action toward the outside, by which God the Father through his Son in the Holy Spirit omnipotently founded both immaterial substances and simple bodies from nothing, and mixed bodies from unsuitable and indisposed matter within six days by the sole command of his will, for the glory of his wisdom, power, and goodness, and for the utility of men.

Latin:

Quaestio I.

Quid sunt actiones divinae?

Sunt actus secundi infinitae Dei potentiae.

Quaestio II.

Quomodo distinguuntur actiones divinae?

Actiones divinae distinguuntur in eas, quae sunt intra Deum, et quae sunt extra Deum.

Actiones divinae ad intra sunt, quae tendunt ad obiectum, quod est ipse Deus: Actiones ad extra sunt, quarum obiectum sunt res creatae.

Prob. Omnis actio relationem involvit transcendentalem ad certum obiectum.

Est itaque obiectum actionum divinarum vel ipse Deus, vel creaturae.

Quaestio III.

Quomodo distinguuntur actiones divinae ad intra?

Actiones divinae ad intra vel sunt essentiales, vel personales.

Illae sunt, quae respiciunt Deum, velut obiectum, et quarum principium agens est essentia divina indeterminate considerata, prout communis est omnibus tribus divinitatis personis (a): Haec est, quae terminatur ad personam divinam, et cuius principium agens est essentia divina determinate spectata, prout certo charactere hypostatico insignita est (b).

Prob. a. Quaedam actiones divinae fluunt ex essentia Dei indeterminate considerata, v. gr. actus intellectus et voluntatis divinae.

Deus enim seipsum cognoscit, seipsum amat, in bonitate sua acquiescit; sunt hae actiones ad intra essentiales.

Prob. b. Generatio Filii Dei et spiratio Spiritus S. sunt actiones divinae ad intra personales: terminatur enim ad producendam personam divinam, earumque principium agens est essentia divina, certo charactere hypostatico notata, De his valet tritum illud: Opera divina ad intra personalia sunt divisa, i. e. non communia omnibus tribus divinitatis personis.

Quaestio IV.

Quomodo distinguuntur actiones divinae ad extra?

Actiones divinae ad extra distinguuntur in immanentes et transeuntes.

Illae sunt, quae ad creaturas quidem terminantur, intra essentiam vero Dei perficiuntur

Hae dicuntur, quae & extra essentiam divinam perficiuntur, & obiectum a Deo distinctum respiciunt (b).

Prob. a. Deus creaturas cognoscit, amat, ad certos fines destinat: quae actiones intra Deum quidem perficiuntur, ad creaturas autem terminantur.

Pertinent huc decreta divina creationis, conservationis, praedestinationis, reprobationis.

Prob. b. Actiones transeuntes distinguuntur in personales, & essentiales.

Illae sunt, quae extra deitatis finem perficiuntur, & uni certae personae per appropriationem οἰκονομικὴν competunt.

Hae sunt, quae extra essentiam divinam perficiuntur, & omnibus tribus divinitatis personis communes sunt, servato tamen earum ordine.

Circa hanc distinctionem probe observandum est: (1) Quod actiones ad extra personales bifariam considerentur: (a) inchoative, seu ratione principii; sic enim communes sunt omnibus tribus divinitatis personis: (b) terminative, seu ratione termini; ita uni personae divinae competunt, & in eadem terminantur.

V. gr. Incarnatio est opus divinum ad extra personale, quod inchoative commune est omnibus tribus divinitatis personis, sc. quoad carnis Christi productionem, nec non quoad copulationem aut vnitionem duarum naturarum in Christo; at si terminative spectetur, soli λόγῳ, sive Filio Dei, competit, in cuius hypostasin caro Christi assumpta est.

Similiter apparitio Spiritus sancti in visibili specie columbae, Matth. III, 16. communis est omnibus tribus personis divinis inchoative, sc. qua speciei columbinae productionem, & productae speciei exhibitionem; terminative vero, ratione intuitionis, externae apparitionis & descensionis soli competit Spiritui sancto.

(2) Actiones ad extra essentiales sunt indivisae, i. e. communes omnibus tribus divinitatis personis, servato tamen earum ordine.

V. gr. Creatio mundi est opus externum essentiale, commune Deo Patri, Filio & Spiritui sancto, servato tamen personarum divinarum ordine.

Sicut enim Pater est a seipso, Filius autem Dei a Patre, & Spiritus S. a Patre & Filio: ita Deus Pater per Filium in Spiritu S. mundum creasse dicitur.

Quaest. V. Quid est creatio?

Creatio est actio divina ad extra, qua Deus Pater per Filium suum in Spiritu sancto tum substantias immateriales & corpora simplicia ex nihilo, tum corpora mixta ex materia inhabili & indisposita intra sextiduum solo voluntatis imperio omnipotenter condidit, ad sapientiae, potentiae & bonitatis suae gloriam, atque hominum utilitatem.


### Question IV. How are divine actions ad extra distinguished?: Obs

Obs.

Creation is taken either properly or improperly.

Properly it signifies, both in a stricter sense, the production of a subsistent thing either from nothing, or from unsuitable matter; and in a broader sense, the production of a being dependent on the creator in its coming-to-be: in which broader sense being is distinguished by metaphysicians into created and uncreated, and God is said to create through generating parents.

Improperly it signifies (a) renewal Ps.

LI, 12. (b) the sending of the most just judgments of God, Is.

XLV, 7. (c) the effecting of wondrous things, Num.

XVI, 20. Quest. VI.

Who created the world?

God alone (a) Father (b), Son (c), and Holy Spirit (d).

Prob. a. (1) Because Moses in the historical description of creation clearly testifies that Jehovah created the heaven and the earth.

Gen.

II, 4.

(2) By the exclusive particle, everyone who is not God is removed from the work of creation. For God alone is said to have stretched out the heavens, Job 9:8, Isa. 44:24.

(3) Creation is a mark (γνώρισμα) of the true God, by which He is distinguished from false gods, Ps. 96:5, Isa. 45:5, 6, 7. Prob. b. 1 Cor. 8:6. To us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things. The work of creation is attributed in the Holy Scriptures and the Apostles' Creed peculiarly to God the Father on account of the order of operating; in that the Father has from Himself that He acts and creates, the Son of God and the Holy Spirit from the Father. Because God the Father manifested His omnipotence by the most efficacious word of command in the work of creation, Gen. 1:3. Creation is the first divine work ad extra, and therefore is said of the first person of the divinity by a certain appropriation.

Prob. c. John 1:3. All things were made through Him (the Word, or Son of God). Note that by "all things" are understood not only those things which pertain to the business of salvation and religion under the New Testament, as the Socinians wish; but all things which are contained within the compass of heaven and earth. For thus St. Paul explains "all things" (τὰ πάντα), made through the Son of God, Col. 1:16: By the Son of God all things were founded, which are in the heavens, and which are on earth, visible and invisible.

Prob. d. Ps. 33:6. By the word of Jehovah the heavens were made, and by the spirit of His mouth all their host. By the spirit of the divine mouth is hinted the Holy Spirit, of whom Moses speaks in Gen. 1:2, 3. But then the Spirit of God was moving Himself over the faces of the waters; and God said: Let there be light! And there was light. Which words D. Seb. Schmid explains concisely in his annotations on Genesis, p. 4. Then in this His spirit, moving Himself over the waters, God the Father said through His internal word, the Son, this spoken (προφορικόν) dictum: Let there be light!

Antithesis of the Socinians, who maintain that God the Father alone is the primary cause of creation; whose arguments are: I. God the Father is called creator in the Apostles' Creed. Therefore creation is not a work common to all three persons of the divinity. Resp. God the Father is indeed called creator in the Apostles' Creed appropriatively, but not exclusively, since the Son of God and the Holy Spirit are also the same creator.

II. Whoever can do nothing of Himself, he is not the creator of the world. But the Son of God, etc. Therefore. The major is certain: because the creator is independent, as in being, so in operating. The minor is evident from John 5:19. The Son can do nothing of Himself. Resp. The Son can do nothing of Himself not because of a defect of power, but because of the identity of nature, which He has from the Father not through dependence, but through eternal birth, and therefore the sense of the cited words is: The Son, as He is from the Father through eternal generation, and receives from the Father the same power of operating which the Father has; so He can do nothing from Himself, and apart from the Father, but whatever He does, He does together with the Father.

III. Through whom all things were made, He is not the principal cause, but the instrumental cause of creation. But through the Son of God, etc. John 1:2. Therefore. The major is certain; because the particle, διά, "through," denotes an instrument. Resp. (1) The particle, "through," is not always an index of an instrumental cause; for it is used of God the Father in 1 Cor. 1:9, Eph. 1:1, Rom. 6:4, Heb. 2:10. (2) God the Father created all things through the Son, not as through an instrument, but as through His wisdom, and hypostatic (ὑποστατικήν) virtue, Prov. 8:30, 1 Cor. 1:24.

IV. Whatever spirit, having been produced as prime matter, began to operate, he is not the creator of the world. But the Spirit of God, etc. Therefore. The major is proven; because Elohim in the beginning created the heaven and the earth. The minor is evident from Gen. 1:2, where Moses testifies concerning the Spirit of God that, when the heaven and the earth had been created, the Spirit of God moved Himself over the waters. Resp. The motion of the Holy Spirit over the faces of the waters is not to be understood with exclusion of a prior operation, but with inclusion and relation to the following works; otherwise anyone might perhaps argue by the same reasoning: God the Father on the sixth day created man from the slime of the earth. Therefore, He is not the creator of heaven and earth.

VII. Are the three persons of the divinity three associate causes of creation? The three persons of the divinity are not three associate causes, not three authors of creation, but one cause, one author of creation, one creator. Proof: For associate causes, there is required (1) a diversity of essence, (2) a diversity of power, (3) a partial influence. But indeed, the three persons of the divinity have the same essence and the same power of creating; and it is alien to the divine majesty to establish that the persons of the Holy Trinity influence partially. For the Father created all things, the Son all things, the Holy Spirit all things. Just as the divine essence is one and indivisible, so the act of creating is one and indivisible.

You say: If God the Father, as such, the Son of God, as such, the Holy Spirit, as such, created the world, it follows that there are three associate causes of creation. The antecedent is true. Therefore, the consequent as well. The consequence of the major is proven; because, if the Father in contradistinction to the Son is the creator, he will certainly be the principle and cause of creation formally, and thus the same must be judged concerning the Son of God and the Holy Spirit. But the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as they are taken formally, are not one thing, but are three, namely three causes of creation not subordinated; because thus God the Son and the Holy Spirit would be instrumental causes: Therefore, they are coordinated, or associate.

Resp. I deny the consequence of the major. For although they are three distinct persons, they nevertheless influence the work of creation with one power. If they influenced with a diverse power of operating, they would be associate causes.

Quaest. VIII. Can the power of creating also be communicated to a creature? The power of creating, to a creature subsisting in itself and ultimately, is incommunicable. Proof: For creation, an infinite power is required, proper to God alone. Hence Jehovah said, thy redeemer and thy former from the womb: I (am) Jehovah, making all things, stretching forth the heavens alone, spreading abroad the earth by myself, Conf. Job IX, 8.

The antithesis is that of the old and recent Scholastics, who maintain that the power of creating could have been communicated to a creature, if not as a principal cause, then as an instrumental cause; their arguments are: I. Whatever can regenerate, the same can create. But a certain creature can regenerate. Therefore. The major is proven because to regenerate is of as great a virtue as to create. Indeed, Scripture itself has designated regeneration and renovation by the name of creation, Ps. LI, 12. 2 Cor. V, 12.

Minor is proven because water in baptism and the minister of the church baptizing concur instrumentally to regeneration. Resp. Creation is of substances; regeneration and renovation are of accidents.

Although, therefore, an intermediate cause is employed by the first cause to produce an accident; dens; since the effect is not absolutely nobler than the intermediate cause: yet an instrument cannot be employed in creation by the force of that proportion; because that effect exceeds the power of the intermediate cause by a very great distance. II. Whatever can be an instrument of a miraculous operation, that also can be an instrument of creation. But a creature &c. Therefore. The major is evident; because an equally infinite power is required to produce a miraculous effect, as to complete a creation. Resp. The reason for creation and miraculous production is different. The former presupposes either no subject, or certainly an unsuitable one. The latter does not occur except in an already established order, and consequently presupposes a subject, concerning which the miraculous operation happens. Therefore, creation exceeds miraculous operation, so that it is not permitted to infer from the latter that a creature can be elevated to such a degree that it is an instrument of creation. III. He who can annihilate, can also create. Nature can annihilate. Therefore. The major is evident; because creation proceeds from non-being to being, annihilation from being to non-being. In both cases, the distance is infinite. The minor is proven; because by nature not only the bodies of animals and plants, but also the forms or souls of the same are eventually annihilated. Resp. 1) To the major: It is easier to destroy what is perfect than to construct that which is not yet perfect. 2) To the minor: By nature, the bodies of animals are not annihilated, but are resolved into atoms, or particles, of which they consist: However, how their forms perish, or are annihilated, is hardly demonstrable or explainable. IV. A creative power was communicated to the human nature of Christ, Matt. XXVIII, 18. Therefore, a creative power is communicable to a creature. Resp. Dist. between a mere creature, ultimately subsisting by itself, and a creature that is indeed true, but assumed into the hypostasis of the λόγος. To this one, every power, and thus also the power of creating, κατὰ συνδίασιν, by the grace of the personal union, is communicated; but to a mere creature, κατὰ μετέκβασιν, according to external procession, it is incommunicable.

Latin:

Obs.

Creatio sumitur vel proprie, vel improprie.

Proprie significat, tum sensu strictiori, productionem rei subsistentis vel ex nihilo, vel ex materia inhabili; tum sensu latiori productionem entis dependentis a creatore in fieri: quo latiori sensu a metaphysicis ens in creatum, & increatum distinguitur, & Deus, parentibus generantibus, creare dicitur.

Improprie significat (a) renouationem Ps.

LI, 12. (b) immissionem iustissimorum Dei iudiciorum, Es.

XLV, 7. (c) rerum mirabilium effectionem, Num.

XVI, 20. Quaest. VI.

Quis creavit mundum?

Solus Deus (a) Pater (b), Filius (c), & Spiritus sanctus (d).

Prob. a. (1) Quia Iehouam creasse coelum & terram, Moses in historica descriptione creationis luculenter testatur.

Gen.

II, 4.

(2) Per particulam exclusiuam, omnis, qui non est Deus, ab opere creationis remouetur. Nam solus Deus cælos expandisse dicitur, Iob. IX, 8. Es. XLIV, 24.

(3) Creatio est γνώρισμα veri Dei, quo is a falsis diis discernitur, Ps. XCVI, 5. Es. XLV, 5. 6. 7. Prob. b. 1 Cor. IIX, 6. Nobis unus est Deus, Pater, ex quo omnia. Opus creationis Deo Patri in sacris litteris & symbolo apostolico peculiariter tribuitur propter ordinem operandi; eo, quod Pater a se habet, quod agat & creet, Filius Dei & Spiritus S. a Patre. Quia Deus Pater omnipotentiam suam efficacissimo verbo mandati in opere creationis manifestauit, Gen. I, 3. Creatio est opus diuinum ad extra primum, adeoque de prima diuinitatis persona per quandam appropriationem dicitur.

Prob. c. Jo. I, 3. Omnia per ipsum (λόγον, seu Filium Dei) facta sunt. Obs. quod per omnia intelligantur non tantum ea, quæ ad salutis & religionis negotium sub N. T. pertinent, vt volunt Sociniani; sed omnia, quæ ambitu cæli & terræ continentur. Nam sic τὰ πάντα, omnia, per Filium Dei facta, exponit S. Paullus, Col. I, 16: Per Filium Dei condita sunt omnia, quæ in cælis, & quæ in terra, visibilia & inuisibilia.

Prob. d. Ps. XXXIII, 6. Verbo Iehouæ cæli facti sunt, & spiritu oris eius omnis exercitus eorum. Per spiritum oris diuini innuitur Spiritus sanctus, de quo Moses Gen. I, 2. 3. Tum vero Spiritus Dei mouebat se super faciebus aquarum; & dixit Deus: Fiat lux! & facta est lux. Quæ verba concinne explicat D. SEB. SCHMID. in annotat. in Gen. p. 4. Tum in hoc spiritu suo, se super aquis mouente, dixit Deus Pater per verbum suum internum, Filium, dictum hoc προφορικόν: Fiat lux!

Antithesis Socinianorum, statuentium, solum Deum Patrem esse caussam primam creationis; quorum argumenta sunt: I. Deus Pater dicitur creator in symbolo apostolico. Ergo creatio non est opus commune omnibus tribus personis diuinitatis. Resp. Deus Pater in symbolo apostolico dicitur quidem creator appropriatiue, sed non exclusiue, cum etiam Filius Dei & Spiritus S. sint idem creator.

II. Quicunque nihil potest a seipso facere, is non est creator mundi. Atqui Filius Dei &c. Ergo. Maior constat: quia creator est independens, vt in essendo, ita in operando. Minor patet ex Jo. V, 19. Filius nihil potest a seipso facere. Resp. Filius nihil potest a seipso facere non ob defectum virtutis, sed ob identitatem naturæ, quam habet a Patre non per dependentiam, sed per æternam natiuitatem, adeoque sensus verborum citatorum est: Filius, vt per æternam generationem e Patre est, & eandem operandi potentiam, quam Pater habet, a Patre accipit; ita nihil potest facere a se, & seorsum a Patre, sed quidquid facit, simul cum Patre facit.

III. Per quem omnia facta sunt, ille non est caussa principalis, sed instrumentalis creationis. Atqui per Filium Dei &c. Jo. I, 2. E. Maior constat; quia particula, διά, per, notat instrumentum. Resp. (1) Particula, per, non semper est index caussæ instrumentalis; vsurpatur enim de Deo Patre 1 Cor. I, 9. Eph. I, 1. Rom. VI, 4. Hebr. II, 10. (2) Deus Pater creauit omnia per Filium, non tanquam per instrumentum, sed vt per suam sapientiam, & virtutem ὑποστατικήν, Prou. VIII, 30. 1 Cor. I, 24.

IV. Quicunque spiritus, materia prima producta, cœpit operari, is non est creator mundi. Atqui Spiritus Dei &c. E. Maior probatur; quia Elohim in principio creauit cælum & terram. Minor liquet e Gen. I, 2. vbi de Spiritu Dei testatur Moses, quod, cum cælum & terra essent creata, Spiritus Dei se mouerit super aquis. Resp. Motio Spiritus sancti super faciebus aquarum non est intelligenda cum exclusione præuiæ operationis, sed cum inclusione & relatione ad opera sequentia; ceteroqui eadem ratione quispiam forte argumentataretur: Deus Pater sexto die condidit hominem e limo terrae. Ergo non est creator caeli & terrae.

VII. Suntne tres personae divinitatis tres causae sociae creationis? Tres divinitatis personae non sunt tres causae sociae, non tres auctores creationis, sed una causa, unus auctor creationis, unus creator. Prob. Ad causas socias requiritur (1) diversitas essentiae, (2) diversitas potentiae, (3) partialis influxus. At vero tres divinitatis personae eandem habent essentiam, eandemque creandi potentiam; & alienum est a maiestate divina statuere, quod personae S. Trinitatis partialiter influant. Nam Pater condidit omnia, Filius omnia, Spiritus sanctus omnia. Sicut una & indivisibilis est essentia divina: ita unus & indivisibilis actus creandi est.

Dicis: Si Deus Pater, ut talis, Filius Dei; ut talis, Spiritus S. ut talis, mundum creavit, sequitur, tres esse causas socias creationis. Antecedens est verum. Ergo & consequens. Consequentia maioris probatur; quia, si Pater in contradistinctione ad Filium est creator, utique erit principium & causa formaliter creationis, & sic etiam de Filio Dei & Spiritu sancto iudicandum. Sed Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus ut formaliter accipiuntur, non sunt unum quid, sed sunt tres, nempe tres causae creationis non subordinatae; quia sic Deus Filius & Spiritus sanctus forent causae instrumentales: Ergo coordinatae, sive sociae.

Resp. Neg. consequentiam maioris. Nam licet tres distinctae sint personae, una tamen virtute influunt in opus creationis. Si diversa operandi virtute influerent, forent causae sociae.

Quaest. VIII. Potestne vis creandi etiam creaturae communicari? Vis creandi, creaturae, per se & ultimate subsistenti, est incommunicabilis. Prob. Ad creationem requiritur vis infinita, soli Deo propria. Proinde dixit Iehouah redemtor tuus & formator tuus ab utero: Ego (sum) Iehouah, faciens omnia, expandens caelos solus, extendens terram a me ipso, Conf. Job. IX, 8.

Antithesis est Scholasticorum veterum & recentiorum, statuentium, vim creandi potuisse creaturae communicari, si non causae principali, tamen ut causae instrumentali; quorum argumenta sunt: I. Quidquid potest regenerare, idem potest creare. Atqui quaedam creatura potest regenerare. Ergo. Maior prob. quia tantae virtutis est, regenerare, quanta est, creare. Quinimmo ipsa scriptura regenerationem & renovationem creationis nomine insigniuit, Ps. LI, 12. 2 Cor. V, 12.

Minor prob. quia ad regenerationem instrumentaliter concurrit aqua in baptismo, & minister ecclesiae baptizans. Resp. Creatio est substantiarum; regeneratio & renovatio accidentium.

Licet itaque a causa prima adhibeatur causa intermedia ad producendum accidens; dens; cum effectus non sit absolute nobilior caussa intermedia: non tamen in creatione adhiberi potest instrumentum vi illius proportionis; quia effectus ille vim caussæ intermediæ longissime excedit. II. Quidquid potest esse instrumentum miraculosæ operationis, illud quoque potest esse instrumentum creationis. Atqui creatura &c. E. Maior constat; quia pariter infinita requiritur vis ad producendum effectum miraculosum, atque ad creationem perficiendam. Resp. Dispar est ratio creationis, & miraculosæ productionis. Illa aut nullum, aut certe inhabile, supponit subiectum. Hæc non fit, nisi ordine iam constituto, & consequenter præsupponit subiectum, circa quod contingit miraculosa operatio. Excedit igitur creatio miraculosam operationem, vt ab hac colligere non liceat, creaturam eo vsque eleuari posse, vt sit instrumentum creationis. III. Qui potest annihilare, potest etiam creare. Natura potest annihilare. Ergo. Maior constat; quia creatio progreditur a non esse ad esse, annihilatio ab esse ad non esse. Vtrobique infinita est distantia. Minor probatur; quia per naturam non tantum corpora animalium & plantarum, sed etiam formæ seu animæ eorundem tandem annihilantur. Resp. 1) Ad maiorem: Facilius est, perfectum destruere, quam id, quod nondum perfectum est, exstruere. 2) Ad minorem: Per naturam corpora animalium non annihilantur, sed in atomos, siue particulas resoluuntur, e quibus constant: Quomodo autem formæ eorum pereant, aut annihilentur, vix demonstrabile, aut explicabile est. IV. Communicata est vis creatrix humanæ Christi naturæ, Matth. XXVIII, 18. Ergo creaturæ vis creatrix est communicabilis. Resp. Dist. inter creaturam meram, ultimate per se subsistentem, & inter creaturam veram quidem, sed assumtam in hypostasin τοῦ λόγου. Huic omnis potentia, adeoque etiam potentia creandi, κατὰ συνδίασιν, propter vnionis personalis gratiam, est communicata; creaturæ autem meræ, κατὰ μετέκβασιν, secundum externam egressionem, est incommunicabilis.


### Question IV. How are divine actions ad extra distinguished?: Quæst. IX. Whether the world, and all things that are in it, were founded out of nothing, or out of pre-existing matter?

Quæst. IX. Whether the world, and all things that are in it, were founded out of nothing, or out of pre-existing matter?

The world, and all things that are in it, were founded partly out of nothing, partly out of unsuitable matter. The angels, the soul of Adam, the heaven and the elements were created out of nothing a). The remaining bodies were produced out of unsuitable and indisposed matter, from which the work to be produced would not have emerged without the action of omnipotent power b). Obs. Dist. Between primary, or immediate creation, which is out of nothing absolutely, and this has no pre-existing matter; and secondary, or mediate creation, which is indeed out of pre-existing matter, but unsuitable and unfit, in which there is only an obediential potency in order to the first cause, acting with infinite virtue. The works of the first day were created out of purely negative nothing: the works of the remaining days (except the human soul) were produced out of the works of the first day, but indisposed and undigested. These also can in a certain respect be said to be founded out of nothing, partly mediately, because they owe their origin to matter produced out of …nothing; partly because matter that is indisposed with respect to the works that emerged from it is considered as nothing. Prob. a. 1) Because Moses in the historical description of creation makes no mention of matter, but simply says: In the beginning God created heaven and earth. Gen. I, 1. 2) God, about to create, called (or commanded to be present) all τὰ μὴ ὄντα, which in no way were, as ὄντα, and as if they truly existed, (so that, namely, they truly existed through creation). Rom. IV, 17. 3) By faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear, Hebr. XI, 3. Where by τὰ μὴ φαινόμενα, things not appearing, the apostle indicates τὰ μὴ ὄντα, things that are not, just as in 2 Maccab. VII, 4, God is said to have made heaven and earth ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων, out of things not existing.

4) In the interval of six days God created heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them, Exod. XX, v. 11. From which we gather: Whatever matter truly exists, it was created within the first six days. Whatever matter is said to be pre-existent to creation, it was not created within the first six days. Therefore, matter pre-existent to creation does not truly exist.

Proof b. The raw and indigestible mass created on the first day is called תהו ובהו, waste, void, and so ill-disposed that by the power of no secondary causes could plants and animals have proceeded from it. Therefore, with respect to these, it is considered as nothing.

The antithesis is that of the Materialists (who are also called Hermogenians), who posited matter as co-eternal with God, to whom some also add the Socinians, whose arguments are:

I. Out of nothing, nothing is made. Therefore, out of nothing, nothing is created. Resp. Out of nothing, nothing is generated by the powers of nature: But by the infinite power of God, the world, and all that is in it, were created out of nothing, or immediately.

II. Whatever action is most noble, that is not the production of a thing out of nothing. Creation is the most noble action. Therefore. The major is proved because that action which tends from good to good, from being to being, is far nobler than that which tends from non-being to being. Resp. I deny the consequence of the major. To the proof we say that the nobility of an action is to be estimated not from the term from which, but from the term to which. Creation is therefore far nobler than the other kinds of production, for the very reason that it is a production from non-being to this infinitely distant term of being.

III. If creation is production out of nothing, then it will either be something intermediate between the creator and the creature, or it will be either the creator himself or the creature. If it is something intermediate; a medium will be given between immediately opposed terms. If it is the creator, it will be eternal. If it is a creature; it is produced by another creation; because every creature is such through creation. Concerning that creation I ask again: Whether it is a created being, or uncreated: And thus the process goes on to infinity. Resp. This argument presupposes that creation is a being strictly so called; when yet it is only a movement of the infinite being, or the creator. Being, strictly so called, is divided into creator and creature; but the modes of beings are not divided by the same reason. IV. The production of a thing, which is done out of nothing, is creation. The production of intelligible species is done out of nothing. Therefore the production of intelligible species is creation. The minor is evident; because intelligible species are immaterial, and thus their production is not done from matter, but from nothing. Resp. Creation is done out of nothing, i.e., without matter, both ingredient and pre-existing. Intelligible species are indeed produced without ingredient matter, yet they have a natural dependence on pre-existing matter.

V. Every creature is made out of nothing. Man is not, etc. Therefore. Resp. Every creature is made out of nothing either mediately or immediately. Man was mediately created out of nothing; because he derives his origin from matter created out of nothing.

Latin:

Quæst. IX. Vtrum mundus, & omnia, quæ in eo sunt, ex nihilo, an ex præexistente materia sunt condita?

Mundus, & omnia, quæ in illo sunt, partim ex nihilo, partim ex materia inhabili condita sunt. Ex nihilo creati sunt angeli, anima Adami, cælum & elementa a). Reliqua corpora producta sunt ex materia inhabili & indisposita, ex qua opus producendum, citra actionem virtutis omnipotentis, non emersisset b). Obs. Dist. Inter creationem primam, siue immediatam, quæ est ex nihilo absolute, & hæc nullam habet præiacentem materiam; & creationem secundam, siue mediatam, quæ est ex materia præiacente quidem, sed inidonea & inhabili, in qua tantum datur potentia obedientialis in ordine ad caussam primam, infinita virtute agentem. Opera primi diei ex nihilo pure negatiuo creata sunt: opera reliquorum dierum (excepta anima humana) ex operibus primi diei, sed indispositis & indigestis producta sunt. Possunt & hæc certo respectu dici condita ex nihilo, partim mediate, quia originem debent materiæ ex nihilo productæ; partim ideo, quod materia indisposita respectu operum, quæ ex ea emerserunt, pro nihilo habetur. Prob. a. 1) Quia Moses in historica creationis descriptione nullam facit mentionem materiæ, sed simpliciter dicit: In principio creauit Deus cœlum & terram. Gen. I, 1. 2) Deus creaturus vocauit (seu adesse iussit) omnia τὰ μὴ ὄντα, quæ nullo modo erant, ὡς ὄντα, ac si reuera essent, (vt scil. per creationem reuera exsisterent). Rom. IV, 17. 3) Fide intelligimus, coagmentata esse secula verbo Dei, ita vt ex non apparentibus ea, quae videntur, facta sint, Hebr. XI, 3. Vbi per τὰ μὴ φαινόμενα, non apparentia, apostolus τὰ μὴ ὄντα indicat, sicut 2 Maccab. VII, 4. ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων, e non exsistentibus, Deus coelum & terram fecisse dicitur.

4) Sex dierum intervallo condidit Deus coelum & terram, mare & omnia, quae in illis sunt, Exod. XX, v. 11. E quibus colligimus: Quaecunque materia vere exsistit, illa est creata intra primum festiduum. Quae materia dicitur praeexistens creationi, non est creata intra primum festiduum. Ergo materia praeexistens creationi vere non exsistit.

Prob. b. Rudis & indigesta moles primo condita die dicitur תהו ובהו, vasta, inanis, adcoque indifposita, vt nullarum secundarum causarum vi plantae & animalia ex ea prodire potuerint. Ergo respectu horum habetur pro nihilo.

Antithesis est Materiariorum (qui etiam Hermogeniani dicuntur) qui coaeternam Deo materiam statuerunt, quibus nonnulli & Socinianis accedunt, quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Ex nihilo nihil fit. Ergo ex nihilo nihil creatur. Resp. Ex nihilo nihil per vires naturae generatur: At per vim Dei infinitam mundus, & omnia, quae in illo sunt, creata sunt ex nihilo, vel immediate.

II. Quaecunque actio est nobilissima, illa non est productio rei ex nihilo. Creatio est actio nobilissima. Ergo. Maior prob. quia illa actio, quae tendit a bono ad bonum, ab ente ad ens, longe nobilior est ea, quae a non ente ad ens tendit. Resp. Neg. consequ. maioris. Ad probationem dicimus, quod nobilitas actionis aestimanda sit non a termino a quo, fed a termino ad quem. Longe ergo nobilior est creatio reliquis productionum speciebus, eo ipso, quod est productio a non ente ad istum infinite distantem terminum entis.

III. Si creatio est productio ex nihilo, tunc aut medium quid erit inter creatorem & creaturam, aut erit vel ipse creator, vel creatura. Si est medium quid; dabitur medium inter terminos immediate oppositos. Si est creator, erit aeterna. Si creatura est; per aliam creationem producta est; quia omnis creatura talis est per creationem. De illa creatione iterum quaero: Vtrum fit ens creatum, an increatum: Et sic processus fit in infinitum. Resp. Hoc argumentum praesupponit, creationem esse ens proprie dictum; cum tamen sit motus tantum entis infiniti, siue creatoris. Ens, stricte dictum, diuiditur in creatorem & creaturam; non autem eadem ratione diuiduntur modi entium. IV. Productio rei, quae fit ex nihilo, est creatio. Productio specierum intelligibilium fit ex nihilo. Ergo productio specierum intelligibilium est creatio. Minor patet; quia species intelligibiles sunt immateriales, adeoque earum productio non fit ex materia, fed ex nihilo. Resp. Creatio fit ex nihilo, i. e. fine materia, tum ingrediente, tum praeiacente. Species intelligibiles producuntur quidem fine materia ingrediente, habent tamen dependentiam naturalem ad materiam praeiacentem.

V. Omnis creatura facta ex nihilo est. Homo non &c. E. Resp. Omnis creatura facta est ex nihilo vel mediate, vel immediate. Homo mediate creatus est ex nihilo; quia originem ducit a materia ex nihilo condita.


### Question IV. How are divine actions ad extra distinguished?: Question X. Is creation out of nothing knowable from the light of nature?

Question X. Is creation out of nothing knowable from the light of nature?

Creation out of nothing, taken generally and abstractly, becomes known not only from the light of revelation, but also from the light of nature a).

But specifically, according to order and manner considered, is known only from the light of revelation .

Prob. a. 1) Reason gathers: The created world is either from nothing, or from pre-existing matter. If from nothing; I have my intent. If from pre-existing matter...; that pre-existing matter is either created, or uncreated. If it is created; the same question returns: if uncreated; it will be the same as eternal, and therefore either God himself, or co-eternal with God. But two eternal, infinite, and independent principles cannot exist at the same time.

2) Clear sayings of scripture testify that the creation of the world is knowable by nature. Rom. I, 20. Acts XIV, 17. Job XII, 7. Isa. XL, 26.

Prob. b. From Heb. XI, 3. Πίστει νοῦμεν κατηρτίσθαι τοὺς αἰῶνας ῥήματι Θεοῦ. By faith we understand that the ages were framed by the word of God.

Observe two things here: 1) that the word κατηρτίσθαι signifies to fit, to frame, to adjust, so that by the same the orderly arrangement of creation is indicated. 2) That ῥῆμα Θεοῦ denotes the word of command; by which itself the λόγος ὑποστατικός (hypostatic Word) is not excluded, because God said: Let there be light. He said that by commanding not without a word, but through the hypostatic Word, through whom all things were made. John I, 3. We argue: Whoever knows the order of creation, made by the word of divine command, only by faith, he does not know the same by natural knowledge. But man is enlightened, etc. Therefore.

There is an antithesis of certain Scholastics, maintaining that creation is a pure article of faith; whose arguments are:

I. The doctrine of creation is contained in the apostolic symbol. Therefore it is a pure article of faith. Resp. The doctrine of creation is a mixed article of faith, which in so far as it is known from the light of revelation, is believed: in so far as it becomes known from the light of reason, it is evidently known.

II. Paul testifies, Heb. XI, 3. that by faith we understand that the ages were framed. Resp. The Apostle speaks of creation not generally, but specifically considered according to manner and order. That the world is founded from nothing, reason knows; how, it does

not. III. Reason dictates, out of nothing nothing is made. Therefore it is ignorant of creation. Resp. Reason dictates, by the powers of nature nothing is made from nothing; yet it acknowledges the omnipotence of God, in whose power it is to found this universe from nothing.

Latin:

Quaest. X. Estne creatio ex nihilo cognoscibilis e lumine naturae?

Creatio ex nihilo, generatim & abstractiue sumta, non solum ex lumine reuelationis, sed & ex lumine naturae innotescit a).

At speciatim, secundum ordinem et modum considerata, non nisi ex lumine revelationis cognoscitur .

Prob. a. 1) Ratio colligit: Mundus creatus est vel ex nihilo, vel ex praeiacente materia. Si ex nihilo; habeo intentum. Si ex praeiacente materia; illa praeexistens materia vel est creata, vel increata. Si est creata; eadem redit quaestio: si increata; eadem erit aeterna, adeoque vel Deus ipse, vel Deo coaeterna. Atqui duo aeterna, infinita et independentia principia simul exsistere nequeunt.

2) Testantur luculenta scripturae dicta creationem mundi natura esse cognoscibilem. Rom. I, 20. Act. XIV, 17. Job. XII, 7. Es. XL, 26.

Prob. b. Ex Hebr. XI, 3. Πίστει νοῦμεν κατηρτίσθαι τοὺς αἰῶνας ῥήματι Θεοῦ. Fide intelligimus, coagmentata esse saecula verbo Dei.

Duo hic obferues: 1) quod verbum κατηρτίσθαι significet aptare, coagmentare, concinnare, vt eodem concinnus creationis ordo indicetur. 2) Quod ῥῆμα Θεοῦ notet verbum mandati; quo ipso non excluditur λόγος ὑποστατικός, quia Deus dixit: Fiat lux. Dixit id iubendo non sine verbo, sed per verbum hypostaticum, per quod facta sunt omnia. Io. I, 3. Argumentamur: Quicunque ordinem creationis, factum verbo mandati diuini, tantum cognoscit fide, ille non cognoscit eundem notitia naturali. Atqui homo illuminatus et c. Ergo.

Antithesis est quorundam Scholasticorum, statuentium, creationem esse articulum fidei purum; quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Doctrina de creatione comprehenditur symbolo apostolico. E. est articulus fidei purus. Resp. Doctrina de creatione est articulus fidei mixtus, qui in quantum cognoscitur ex lumine revelationis, creditur: in quantum innotescit ex lumine rationis, euidenter scitur.

II. Paullus testatur, Hebr. XI, 3. quod fide intelligimus, coagmentata esse saecula. Resp. Apostolus loquitur de creatione non generatim, sed speciatim considerata secundum modum et ordinem. Quod, non quomodo, conditus fit mundus ex nihilo, ratio cognoscit.

III. Ratio dictitat, ex nihilo nihil fieri. Ergo ignorat creationem. Resp. Ratio dictitat, viribus naturae ex nihilo nihil fieri; agnoscit tamen omnipotentiam Dei, penes quem est potestas condendi hoc vniuersum ex nihilo.


### Quaest. XI. Did God create this visible world from his own essence?

God did not create this visible world from his own essence, nor did he as it were diffuse this into parts, so that any creature could be called a particle of the deity.

Prob. I. Because creation formally denotes not a production from the substance of God, but from nothing, Gen. I, 1. Rom. IV, 17. II. God is Spirit, John IV, 24. Hence the essence of God cannot be diffused into parts. III. Creatures daily change and perish: but God is immutable, Mal. III, 6. IV. It is blasphemous to say that the devil and sinful men are parts of the divine essence.

Latin:

Deus mundum hunc aspectabilem non creauit ex essentia sua, neque hanc in partes quasi diffudit, vt quaelibet creatura deitatis particula dici possit.

Prob. I. Quia creatio formaliter non productionem ex substantia Dei, sed ex nihilo notat, Gen. I, 1. Rom. IV, 17. II. Deus est Spiritus, Io. IV, 24. Proinde essentia Dei in partes diffundi nequit. III. Creaturae indies mutantur et intereunt: Deus autem immutabilis est, Mal. III, 6. IV. Blasphemum dictu est, diabolum et homines peccatores esse partes diuinae essentiae.


### Quaest. XII. What is the form of creation?

Form of creation The form of creation, considered generally, consists in this, that creation is an action not inward, but outward: not necessary, but free: not successive, but instantaneous by reason of individual created beings. Considered specifically, it is completed in three degrees. I. By the production of the undigested mass from nothing purely negative.

II. On the distinction and arrangement of those things which were created from no pre-existing matter. III. On the adornment and completion of this universe. Prob. a. Creation is a divine action directed outward; therefore, it terminates not in God, but in creatures, which did not emanate from the very essence of God, but were made by speaking, or commanding, while God applied His effective power for creating by the command of His will, directed by the practical knowledge of His intellect. Furthermore, creation is a free divine action; because God founded this universe not led by necessity, entirely as if He were in need of the service of creatures, since He is αὐταρκέστατος [self-sufficient]; but freely, so that He could create and not create, sooner or later, in this or another way, to found it. Finally, creation, in respect to individual created beings, is an instantaneous divine action; for God did not create individual things by motion or laborious effort, but when He said: let there be light; it was made suddenly. The same judgment should be formed regarding the production of the remaining works.

Although, if created beings are viewed collectively, creation is completed through six νυχθήμερα [days and nights]; not that God spent all those six days on creation, but that He created something in the moments of each individual day. *Prob. b. On the first day of creation, God founded the O. M. [Orbis Mundi - World/Universe], a rude and indistinct mass of heaven, earth, and water, and on that same first day, He divided the light from the darkness; on the second, the lower waters from the upper, with the firmament interposed; on the third, He furnished the earth, separated from the waters, with grass, herbs, and trees; on the fourth day, He adorned and filled the heaven with luminaries, on the fifth the water with fish and the air with birds, and on the sixth the earth with animals, and finally with man. The order observed by the most wise Creator is most accurate. For He first created inanimate and simple bodies, then mixed and living ones, then sensitive ones, and finally the intelligent animal, man.

The antithesis is that of Philo, Procopius, Cajetan, and others, who think that God created all things simultaneously and in one moment, and not by an interval of six days; they rely on the following arguments: I.

Moses writes in Gen. II, 4: These are the generations of the heaven and the earth, when they were created in the day that God made the heaven and the earth and every plant of the field. If the heaven, and the earth, and the plant of the field were founded on the same day, surely they were not made within a six-day period.

Resp. The word "day" in a general sense not rarely signifies time; that time, however, comprises many days.

*II.

Sirach ch. XVIII, 1 says: He who lives forever created all things together. Resp. 1) God created all things together in the same common time, without an interrupted series of creation, although not at the same singular moment of time: just as a whole fleet is said to have set sail from port together, although one ship sets sail before and another after, provided no long interval intervenes.

2) In the Greek text there is the adverb, κοινῇ, which signifies commonly, and thus denotes not precisely συγχρονίαν [synchronicity], a community of time, but συλλογήν [collection], or a community of origin and dependence; because this is common to all creatures, that they depend on God in their becoming and being, and nothing exists outside of God that was not created by God. III. God is omnipotent, not producing anything by slow effort. Therefore, one cannot invent any reason why the progress in creating was made at such a slow pace.

Resp. Because God is omnipotent, He could have produced this universe in an instant, and He could also have produced it by an interval of six days. That He did not produce it in one instant is to be attributed to His free will.

Nevertheless, the reasons for the creation being protracted through the six days are given by authors as follows: 1) It pleased the divine wisdom, both so that it might be more evidently established that the world is not from eternity, and so that we might meditate more distinctly and attentively on the individual works of God: indeed, that we might also ponder with ourselves the triple state of the founded world, namely the state of creation from nothing, of distinction, and of adornment. 2) He willed the Creator warns us by this example, what the beginnings of divine works are usually like, that He first places some slight rudiment, then gradually bestows increments, until He brings the matter to perfection. 3) In the opinion of Ambrose, God willed us to be His imitators, that we might first do some things, and afterwards adorn them, lest, while we attempt both at once, we be able to fulfill neither. 4) God willed to teach that six days were assigned for labors, but the seventh was to be spent on divine praises, and the memory of divine benefits, and especially of creation. 5) Finally, there are some who think that the world was founded by God in the space of six days for the reason that it is to endure for six thousand years; which matter, however, is uncertain .

Latin:

Forma creationis Forma creationis, generatim spectata, consistit in hoc, quod creatio actio est non ad intra, sed ad extra: non necessaria, sed libera: non successiua, sed ratione singulorum entium creatorum instantanea . Speciatim considerata tribus absoluitur gradibus. I. Productione indigeftae molis ex nihilo pure negativo.

II. Distinctione ac dispositione earum rerum, quæ ex nulla præexistente materia conditæ sunt. III. Exornatione & consummationatione huius vniversi . Prob. a. Creatio est actio diuina ad extra; ideo, quod terminatur non in Deo, sed in creaturis, quæ non ex ipsa essentia Dei emanarunt, sed factæ sunt dicendo, seu iubendo, dum Deus imperio voluntatis suæ, intellectus scientia practica directæ, potentiam suam effectiuam ad creandum applicauit. Deinde creatio est actio diuina libera; propterea, quod Deus hoc vniversum condidit, non adductus necessitate, prorsus ac si famulitio creaturarum indigeret, cum sit αὐταρκέστατος; sed libere, vt potuerit creare & non creare, citius, aut ferius, hoc, vel alio modo, condere. Est denique creatio, ratione singulorum entium creatorum, actio diuina instantanea; neque enim motu, aut operosa molitione, Deus singula condidit, sed cum dixit: fiat lux; subito facta est. Idem formetur iudicium de reliquorum operum effectione.

Quamuis, si collectim spectentur entia creata, per sex νυχθήμερα absoluta fit creatio; non quod totos illos sex dies Deus creationi impenderit, sed quod singulorum dierum momentis aliquid creauerit. *Prob. b. Primo creationis die condidit Deus O.* M. rudem & indistinctam massam cœli, terræ & aquæ, eodemque die primo lucem a tenebris, altero aquas inferiores a superioribus, interposito firmamento, diuisit; tertio terram, ab aquis separatam, gramine, herbis, arboribusque instruxit; quarto die cœlum luminaribus, quinto aquam piscibus, aërem volatilibus, sexto terram animalibus, tandemque homine, ornauit & impleuit. Ordo obseruatus est a sapientissimo creatore accuratissimus. Creauit enim primum corpora inanimata & simplicia, tum mixta, viuentia, post sensitiva, postremo animal intelligens, hominem.

Antithesis est Philonis, Procopii, Caietani & aliorum, arbitrantium, Deum omnia simul & vno momento creasse, non vero sex dierum interuallo; qui sequentibus innituntur argumentis: I.

Scribit Moses Gen. II, 4. Istæ sunt generationes cœli & terræ, quando creatæ sunt in die, quo fecit Deus cœlum, & terram & omne virgultum agri. Si cœlum, & terra, & virgultum agri, eodem die condita sunt, vtique non facta sunt intra sextiduum.

Resp. Dies sensu generali haud raro significat tempus; illud vero tempus plures dies complectitur.

*II.

Siracides cap.* XVIII, 1. inquit: Qui viuit in æternum, creauit omnia simul. Resp. 1) Deus creauit omnia simul eodem tempore communi, non interrupta creationis ferie, licet non eodem singulari temporis momento: sicut tota classis dicitur simul soluta e portu, licet vna prius, & altera posterius fit soluta nauis, modo non longum intercedat interuallum.

2) In græco textu est aduerbium, κοινῇ, quod significat communiter, adeoque non præcise συγχρονίαν, communitatem temporis, sed συλλογήν, siue communitatem originis & dependentiæ notat; quia hoc commune est omnibus creaturis, quod a Deo in fieri & esse dependent, & nihil extra Deum exsistit, quod a Deo non sit creatum. III. Deus est omnipotens, non tardo molimine aliquid efficiens. Nullam igitur causam comminisci licet, cur tam lento gradu in creando fit progressus.

Resp. Quia Deus est omnipotens, potuit hoc vniversum in instanti, potuit etiam sex dierum interuallo producere. Quod autem non in vno instanti produxerit, liberæ eius voluntati tribuendum est.

Causæ tamen protractæ per sextiduum creationis ab auctoribus redduntur sequentes. 1) Placuit ita sapientiæ diuinæ, tum vt euidentius mundum non esse ab æterno constaret, tum vt distinctius & attentius singula opera Dei meditemur: quin & subinde pensitemus nobiscum statum triplicem mundi conditi, nempe statum creationis ex nihilo, distinctionis & exornationis. 2) Voluit creator hoc exemplo nos admonere, qualia sint plerumque initia operum diuinorum, quod primum tenue aliquod rudimentum ponat, deinde incrementa sensim largiatur, donec ad perfectionem rem perducat, 3) Censente Ambrosio, Deus voluit nos sui esse imitatores, vt primo faciamus aliqua, postea venustemus, ne, dum simul vtrumque adorimur, neutrum possimus implere, 4) Docere voluit Deus, sex dies ad labores esse assignatos, septimum vero impendendum esse diuinis laudibus, & memoriae beneficiorum diuinorum, inprimis vero creationis. 5) Sunt denique nonnulli, qui existimant, ideo mundum sex dierum spatio a Deo conditum esse, quod sex annorum millibus duraturus sit; quae tamen res incerta est .


### Q. XIII. Could the world have been created from eternity?

The world could not have been created from eternity.

Prob. I. Whatever cannot come to be without a beginning of existing, that cannot be created from eternity. But the world, etc. Therefore. The major is evident: because whatever has a beginning of existing is not eternal. The minor is proved; because, when a creature is made, it begins to be: for it has being after non-being, and thus a beginning of existing.

II. Eternity is an attribute of God alone: from which God is called the God of eternity, Gen. 21: 33. The eternal God, Rom. 16:26. The King of ages incorruptible, 1 Tim. 1:17.

III. Everything eternal is infinite and interminable. But the world is not infinite or interminable. Therefore the world is not eternal. The major is clear: because eternity is an infinite and interminable duration. The minor is manifest: because the world is a structure of many bodies. But no body, since it has a determinate quantity, can be infinite.

IV. Just as something cannot be reduced to nothing and remain eternal: so something cannot be created from nothing and be from eternity. For the reason is equal on both sides.

There is an antithesis of certain Scholastics and Pontificians, maintaining that the world could have been created from eternity; whose arguments are:

I. Whatever does not involve a contradiction, that can be done by God. But the eternal creation of the world, etc. Therefore. The minor is proved; because creation from eternity, neither on the part of the creator, nor on the part of the creature, involves a contradiction. Not on the part of the creator; because He is omnipotent powerful and eternal, and therefore could create from eternity. Not on the part of the creature; because just as we rightly conclude: God could have made the world from eternity; so also we rightly conclude: God could have willed from eternity that the world be made, and consequently the world could have been made from eternity.

Resp. 1) A manifest contradiction is involved on the part of the creature; since it is as little capable of infinity as it is capable of eternity; since eternity is an infinite duration.

ATHANAS. says wisely in orat. II. against the Arians I. Objection:

Neither on the part of God creating, nor on the part of the thing which is produced, does a contradiction seem to be involved, if the creation of the world is posited as eternal. Not on the part of God creating; because the power of God to create is no less than the power of the sun to illuminate; but if the latter were eternal, it could illuminate from eternity. Therefore God, who is truly eternal, can create the world from eternity.

Nor on the part of the thing which is produced; for the Son is generated from the Father from eternity, and exists coeternal with Him. Resp. The examples adduced are irrelevant.

For 1) the creation of the world was made out of nothing: the Son of God emanates from the essence of the Father, rays from the essence of the sun. 2) Creation is a free and voluntary action: the generation of the Son of God, and the illumination of the sun, are necessary acts. For ὁ λόγος, or the hypostatic word of God, is the Son of God τῇ φύσει, by nature, not τῇ βουλήσει, by will, says BASIL THE GREAT L. IV. against Eunom. cited by D. CALOV. tom. III p. 595.

And the sun pours forth rays from itself by necessity of nature.

II. If the world is not eternal, God, by creating the world, became mutable. But God, by creating the world, did not become mutable. Therefore the world is eternal.

The consequence of the major is clear; for God became creating from non-creating. Resp. Distinguish between divine actions ad intra, and ad extra.

Creation is a divine action ad extra. But divine actions ad extra terminate in creatures, not in the creator. Hence it happens that creation denominates God not intrinsically, but extrinsically; which extrinsic denomination does not effect a change.

III. If the motion of the sun is eternal, the sun itself together with the heaven in which it is moved is eternal. But the antecedent is true. Therefore also the consequent. The consequence of the major is evident; because the motion of the sun is its affection: and such as the affections of some being are, such is the being itself.

The antecedent is clear; because the motion of the sun is in perpetual flux, nor can a first motion be given; for even that would be from a prior motion, and thus not the first. Resp. A first motion can be from an action which occurs without motion.

God created the world, yet He Himself was not moved. IV. Every being that is good from eternity is communicative from eternity. But God &c. Therefore.

Resp. Distinguish between necessary and free communication. God communicates His goodness to creatures freely, when and where He wills.

V. God could have created the world a hundred thousand years ago, and again a hundred times a hundred thousand years ago. Therefore from eternity. Resp.

The question is not whether God could create the world earlier, but whether He could have created it infinitely earlier.

We deny the latter. VI. Whatever is not created in time, that is created from eternity.

But the world &c. Therefore. The minor is evident; because no time was present when the world was created. Resp.

The world was created in time not pre-existing, but coexisting.

(). () The world existed not in time, but with time, or rather, if we wish to speak accurately, time existed with the world. For what is time? Nothing surely other than the determination of finite things, by reason of duration, through a continuous succession of moments. Therefore time is a property. Quest. XIV. What is the end of creation? The ultimate end of creation is the glory of divine goodness, power, and wisdom, to be acknowledged and proclaimed by creatures. a). The intermediate end is the utility of men b).

The intermediate end is the utility of men.

Prob. a.

From Ps. XIX, 2. The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament showeth his handiwork.

Obs.

1. Although the royal psalmist deals primarily with the heaven of grace and the preaching of the Gospel, as Paul testifies in Rom. X, 18; he nevertheless took the whole manner of speaking from the book of nature, so that the preaching of the Gospel and the preaching of nature might each illustrate the other.

King David therefore underlies and presupposes in this psalm the truth of natural knowledge, just as every trope presupposes a proper meaning and the truth of the thing from which the translation is made.

The heavens therefore declare the glory of God, not effectively, or by the proclamation of an articulate voice, but objectively, or by exhibiting the matter and argument for acknowledging and proclaiming the majesty of God; for this reason, that they so present and object themselves to human minds, that they perpetually inculcate in them that they are a theater of divine glory, or a most lucid mirror, from which the glory of divine goodness, which He communicated to creatures, of power, which He exerted by producing all things from nothing, and of wisdom, by which He disposed all things in this universe most artfully, shines forth most clearly.

Moreover, the heavens do not declare the glory of God exclusively, as if the remaining creatures were excluded; but the sacred psalmist implies that all creatures praise their creator.

For whatever is the reason why the heavens ought to praise God, that is also the reason why the remaining creatures celebrate divine praises.

Prob. b.

Since God granted man dominion over sublunary creatures in Gen. I, 26, did He not indicate that they were created for the utility of man?

For dominion, granted by the creator to man over creatures, cannot be conceived by way of simple power, but under the aspect of use, for which the creature, by virtue of its subjection, is bound to serve man.

You say: I.

I. Man does not have dominion over the heaven and the stars. Therefore, not all things were created for the sake of man.

Resp.

Resp. Man does not have direct dominion over the heaven and the stars; he obtains, however, indirect dominion over them, insofar as he converts their influence to his own utility.

You say: II.

But dominion over creatures was lost through the fall. Resp.

Dominion full, and its own, and easy, was lost through the fall: yet there remained after the fall remnants and traces of that dominion, not to be exercised without trouble and difficulty.

Quest. XV. What is the effect of creation? The effect of creation is substance, both visible and invisible.

Prob.

I. Because accidents, which are beings of a being, are said not so much to be created as to be concreated.

II. Just as generation is terminated in the production of substance: so also creation, as the most noble action, ought to have a most noble term.

That substance is more noble than an accident escapes no one: but an accident was concreated with substance. [It is] a certain state of finite things, and thus of the whole world, as something added, or an accident, and indeed an inseparable one, since a determined succession cannot be separated from the very nature of finite things, insofar as they are finite.

But every accident, or adjunct, cannot be without a subject, nor be prior to it.

Therefore, there is a manifest contradiction if anyone says that time existed before the world existed.

That is just as absurd as if anyone should dare to say that an adjunct existed either without a subject or before it.

Latin:

Mundus ab aeterno creari non potuit.

Prob, I. Quidquid non potest fieri fine initio essendi, illud non potest creari ab aeterno. Atqui mundus &c. Ergo. Maior constat: quia quidquid habet initium essendi, non est aeternum. Minor probatur; quia, quando creatura fit, esse incipit: habet enim esse post non esse, adeoque initium essendi.

II. Aeternitas est attributum solius Dei: ex quo vocatur Deus aeternitatis, Gen. XXI, 33. Aeternus Deus, Rom. XVI, 26. Rex saeculorum incorruptibilis, 1 Tim. 1, 17.

III. Omne aeternum est infinitum & interminabile. Atqui mundus non est infinitus, aut interminabilis. Ergo mundus non est aeternus. Maior patet: quia aeternitas est infinita & interminabilis duratio. Minor liquet: quia mundus est compages multorum corporum. At nullum corpus, cum determinatam habeat quantitatem, potest esse infinitum.

IV. Sicut non potest aliquid redigi in nihilum, & permanere aeternum: ita non potest aliquid creari ex nihilo, & esse ab aeterno. Par enim vtrobique est ratio.

Antithesis est quorundam Scholasticorum & Pontificiorum, statuentium, mundum potuisse creari ab aeterno; quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Quidquid non inuoluit contradictionem, illud a Deo potest fieri. Atqui creatio mundi aeterna &c. Ergo. Minor probatur; quia creatio ab aeterno, neque ex parte creatoris, neque ex parte creaturae, inuoluit contradictionem. Non ex parte creatoris; quia ille est omnipotens atque æternus, adeoque ab æterno potuit creare. Non ex parte creaturæ; quia sicut recte concludimus: Deus potuit ab æterno mundum facere; ita quoque recte concludimus: Deus potuit ab æterno velle mundum fieri, & consequenter mundus ab æterno fieri potuit.

Resp. 1) Manifesta involvitur contradictio ex parte creaturæ; quippe quæ, vt minime capax est infinitatis, ita non est capax æternitatis; cum æternitas sit duratio infinita.

Scite inquit ATHANAS. orat II. contra Arianos I.

Instantia Neque ex parte Dei creantis, neque ex parte rei, quæ producitur, contradictio involvi videtur, si creatio mundi æterna statuatur. Non ex parte Dei creantis; quia non minor est virtus Dei ad creandum, quam virtus solis ad illuminandum; at hic si æternus esset, ab æterno posset illuminare. Ergo Deus, qui reuera æternus est, ab æterno mundum potest creare.

Neque ex parte rei, quæ producitur; nam Filius ab æterno a Patre generatur, ipsique existit coæternus. Resp. Exempla adducta sunt aliena.

Nam 1) creatio mundi facta est ex nihilo: Filius Dei ex essentia Patris, radii ex essentia solis emanant. 2) Creatio est actio libera & voluntaria: Generatio Filii Dei, & illuminatio solis, sunt actus necessarii. Etenim ὁ λόγος, siue verbum Dei hypostaticum, τῇ φύσει, natura, non τῇ βουλήσει, voluntate, Filius Dei est, inquit BASILIVS M.

L. IV. contra Eunom. citante D. CALOV. tom. III p. 595. Et sol necessitate naturæ radios ex se fundit.

II. Si mundus non est æternus, Deus creando mundum, factus est mutabilis. Sed Deus, creando mundum, non factus est mutabilis. Ergo mundus est æternus.

Conseq. mai. est clara; nam Deus ex non creante factus est creans. R. Dist. inter actiones diuinas ad intra, & ad extra.

Creatio est actio diuina ad extra. Actiones autem diuinæ ad extra terminantur in creaturis, non in creatore. Inde fit, vt creatio Deum non intrinsece, sed extrinsece denominet; quæ extrinseca denominatio non efficit mutationem.

III. Si motus solis æternus est, ipse sol vna cum cœlo, in quo mouetur, æternus est. Sed antecedens est verum. Ergo & consequens. Consequentia maioris patet; quia motus solis est eius affectio: quales autem sunt affectiones alicuius entis, tale est ipsum.

Antecedens liquet; quia motus solis est in perpetuo fluxu, neque potest dari primus motus; nam & ille a priori esset motu, adeoque non primus. Resp. Primus motus potest esse ab actione, quæ fit sine motu.

Creauit Deus mundum, neque tamen ipse inotus est. IV. Omne ens, ab æterno bonum, est ab æterno fuit communicatiuum. Atqui Deus &c. Ergo.

Resp. Dist. inter communicationem necessariam, & liberam. Deus communicat suam bonitatem creaturis libere, quando & vbi vult.

V. Deus potuit mundum creare ante centena millia annorum, & rursus ante centies centena millia. Ergo ab æterno.

Resp. Non quæritur, an Deus mundum prius creare, sed an infinities prius eundem creare potuerit.

Posterius negamus. VI. Quidquid non est creatum in tempore, illud est creatum ab æterno. Atqui mundus &c.

E. Minor patet; quia nullum aderat tempus, cum mundus crearetur.

Resp. Mundus creatus est in tempore non præexistente, sed coëxistente.

(*). Quaest. XIV. Quis est finis creationis? Finis creationis ultimus est gloria bonitatis, potentiae & sapientiae divinae, a creaturis agnoscenda & depraedicanda. a). Finis intermedius est hominum utilitas b).

Finis intermedius est hominum utilitas.

Prob. a.

E Ps. XIX, 2. Caeli enumerant gloriam Dei, & opus manuum eius annuntiat firmamentum.

Obs.

1. Quod psaltes regius praecipue de caelo gratiae & praedicatione evangelii, teste Paulo Rom. X, 18. agat; totam tamen loquendi rationem sumpserit ex libro naturae, ut praedicatio evangelii, & praedicatio naturae, & una alteram illustret.

Substernit & supponit itaque rex David hoc psalmo veritatem notitiae naturalis, quemadmodum omnis tropus supponit propriam significationem, & rei, a qua fit translatio, veritatem.

Enumerant itaque caeli gloriam Dei, non effective, sive articulatae vocis praeconio, sed obiective, sive exhibendo materiam & argumentum agnoscendi & depraedicandi maiestatem Dei; ideo, quod ita se sistunt & obiiciunt animis humanis, ut iis perpetuo inculcent, se esse theatrum gloriae divinae, aut lucidissimum speculum, ex quo gloria divinae bonitatis, quam creaturis communicavit, potentiae, quam producendo omnia ex nihilo exseruit, sapientiae, qua omnia in hoc universo artificiosissime disposuit, clarissime effulgecit.

Ceterum enumerant caeli gloriam Dei non exclusive, ac si reliquae creaturae excludantur; sed innuit hieropfaltes, omnes creaturas creatorem suum dilaudare.

Nam quae est ratio, cur caeli laudare debeant Deum, ea quoque est ratio, cur reliquae creaturae encomia divina concelebrent.

Prob. b.

Cum Deus homini dominium in creaturas sublunares Gen. I, 26. concessit, easdem in hominis utilitatem conditas esse indicauit?

Neque enim concipi potest dominium, a creatore in creaturas homini concessum, per modum simplicis potestatis, sed sub ratione usus, in quem creatura homini, vi subiectionis suae, inferuire tenetur.

Dicis: I.

I. Homo non habet dominium in caelum & astra. E. non omnia propter hominem condita sunt.

Resp.

Resp. Non habet homo dominium directum in caelum & astra; obtinet tamen in eadem dominium indirectum; quatenus eorum influxum in suam utilitatem convertit.

Dicis: II.

Sed dominium in creaturas per lapsum amissum est. Resp.

Dominium plenum, suaque, & facile, per lapsum amissum est: manserunt tamen post lapsum reliquiae & vestigia illius dominii, non sine molestia & difficultate exercendi.

Quaest. XV. Quis est effectus creationis? Effectus creationis est substantia tam visibilis, quam invisibilis.

Prob.

I. Quia accidentia, quae sunt entia entis, non tam creari, quam concreari dicuntur.

II. Sicut generatio terminatur ad producendam substantiam: ita & creatio, tanquam actio nobilissima, debet habere terminum nobilissimum.

Nobiliorem esse substantiam accidente, neminem fugit: accidens autem cum substantia concreatum est. tas quaedam rerum finitarum, adeoque mundi vniverfi, vtpote adiunctum aliquid, fiue accidens, & quidem inseparabile, quoniam determinata successio non potest ab ipsa natura rerum finitarum, quatenus sunt finitae, separari.

Omne autem accidens, sive adiunctum, non potest esse sine subiecto, nec eo prius esse.

E. manifesta est repugnantia, si quis dicat, tempus ante fuisse, quam mundus exstiterit.

Id est aeque absurdum, ac si quis ausit dicere, adiunctum aut sine subiecto, aut ante illud fuisse.


### Question XVI

XVI. What are the works of the first day? The works of the first day of creation are: (a) the substance of the heaven, the earth, and the water, undigested and formless: (b) the πρωτόκτισος (protoktistos), or primordial, light.

(c) The angels are probably reckoned among the works of the first day. Proof a. Moses writes explicitly in Gen. I, 1: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. Obs. There are those who persuade themselves that the sum of the entire history of creation is comprehended epitomically in the first verse. There are others, on the contrary, who maintain that Moses, by the name of heaven and earth, indicates the raw matter of the future work. The latter opinion is approved by us.

1) Because when the heaven and earth were being founded, there was no distinction of day and night, no distinction of darkness and light, which finally arrived, v. 3.

2) Because when the first light was created, there was not yet a distinction of earth and waters, for that was made on the second day of creation, v. 6.

3) Nor was there a distinction of earth and waters, which finally followed on the third day, v. 9.

4) Because before the brooding of the Holy Spirit over the faces of the waters, the earth was waste and void; by which words a horrible vastness and confusion is signified. Therefore, by the LXX interpreters, the Hebrew words תהו ובהו (tohu va-bohu) are rendered in Greek: Ἡ γῆ ἦν ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύασος, the earth was indeed invisible (because covered by waters) and undisposed.

Conf. Deut. XXXII, 10. Job XII, 24. Is. XXXIV, 11. Jer. IV, 23. 5) The author of the Book of Wisdom addresses God with the following words, c. XI, 17: Thy hand created the world out of formless matter.

Indeed, that book is not in the canon, yet it testifies that the Israelites once believed that God first created a certain undigested mass, lacking complete form, from which the other bodies were created by the infinite power of God. Proof b. Gen. I, 3: And God said: Let there be light! And there was. By light we understand a most bright and fiery substance, mobile around the undigested mass, which by its approach brought about day, and by its withdrawal night, within the space of 24 hours.

That the primordial light was a substance is gathered 1) from the fact that it was created by a specific action; now the terminus of creation is substance.
