Because the mobility which belongs to it is an affection of corporeal substances. That, however, that πρωτόκτισος (protoktistos) light was a fiery substance is clear from the fact that all the properties of fire belonged to it; for it performed the functions of the sun, and by the will of God it migrated into the substance of the sun. But that the sun is fiery and formally hot, we shall prove below.

Proof c. From a comparison of Gen. I, 1, where it is said that God in the beginning created the heaven and the earth, with Job XXXVIII, 4, 7: Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? --- When the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy? Job is speaking about the stars, which are the sons of God. Therefore he does not understand the stars of heaven; since these are never called the sons of God in Scripture, nor does any excellent inanimate creature bear this name.

Rather, Job indicates the angels, whom he distinguished by the same name in c. I, 6. We observe here 1) that the angels were created before men. For Jehovah says: Where wast thou, when the morning stars sang together, etc.? Job could have replied: Although I did not yet exist then, my first father, Adam, did. God meets this objection: Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? when the morning stars sang together? But when the earth was being founded, Adam had not yet been created.

We note 2) that the angels were created on the first day of creation; for the reason that they are not only called morning stars, but are also said to have sung the praises of God when the earth was founded by Him. Now the earth was founded on the first day of creation.

Most worthy of note are the words of D. CALOVIUS, tom. III. system. p. 905.

it is established that the angels were not created before the beginning of creation, but in the very beginning; yet, ὡς ἐν πλάτει & with a certain latitude, so that, although in that first beginning the invisible and immaterial creatures were the first to be founded, the heaven and the earth are nevertheless rightly said to have been created in that beginning; because God created the heaven and the earth also in that very beginning.

For if these were said to have been founded even at the second moment of that beginning, the creation of the angels would nevertheless be prior.

The antithesis is 1) of the Papists, who deny that God first created an undigested mass of heaven, earth, and water. 2) Of the Socinians and Arminians, who assert that the angels existed many centuries before the origin of corporeal things.

Against the undigested mass of heaven and earth, they argue:

I. Whoever historically commemorates that in the beginning heaven and earth were created, he does not understand a rude and undigested mass, but heaven and earth properly so called. But Moses historically commemorates, etc. Therefore. The major is certain; because in history one must not depart from the clear letter. The minor is evident from Gen. I, 1.

Resp. I deny the major. For the undigested mass of heaven and earth is the true heaven and earth, by reason of substance, although a certain accidental difference occurs by reason of distinct state and completion. Nor do we understand heaven or earth metaphorically.

Instance I. The Hebrew emphatic he indicates that this heaven, this earth, such as it now is, which is trodden by feet, is understood.

Resp. 1) The demonstrative he is sometimes taken infinitely, Deut. VIII, 3. Levit. XVIII, 5. 2) That earth which is called הָאָרֶץ has the He prefixed, and yet it is not understood as a fully distinct or adorned earth.

Instance II. An inform heaven and earth is not true heaven or true earth, because it lacks the form through which heaven and earth is what it is.

Resp. Distinguish between substantial and accidental form. Heaven and earth, originally founded, did not lack substantial and internal form; they did, however, lack accidental and external form: since the distinction and adornment of heaven, earth, and water followed in subsequent days.

II. Whoever created all things most orderly, he did not create a confused chaos. But God, etc. Therefore. The minor is proven; because God is the author not of confusion, but of order, and the first and most noble action of God O. M. ad extra is undoubtedly most orderly. Whence the author of Wisdom, chap. XI, 22, says: God created all things in number, weight, and measure.

Resp. 1) Whatever poets have dreamed about a confused chaos, we do not make our own, but with B. LUTHER we assert that God in the beginning of his works founded a rude and undigested mass of heaven, earth, and water, in which we recognize the true substance of heaven, earth, and water, but unadorned and unarranged.

I deny the major. Because this order is most fitting, when the progress is made from non-being to being, from the imperfect to the perfect, from the unpolished to the polished and adorned. Therefore, creation is not to be called confused, even if some work at the beginning of creation was undigested, to be more and more digested and distinguished in the following days. 3) All things are said to be created in number, weight, and measure, insofar as they are in a complete state of being, not insofar as they were created indistinctly on the first day without adornment.

III. If chaos was created on the first day, nowhere in the history of creation is there mention of created heaven and earth. The consequent is absurd. Therefore also the antecedent. Resp. I deny the consequence of the major. For there is mention of created heaven and earth, insofar as heaven and earth are commemorated as created indistinctly on the first day, but heaven was made and adorned distinctly on the second day, and earth on the third.

Against the igneous substance of the first light, they argue:

I. Whatever penetrates a body, that is not a corporeal substance. But the primordial light, etc. Therefore. The minor is proven, because all light, and thus also the primordial, has the power of penetrating glass, crystal, etc.

Resp. Distinguish between true and apparent penetration. The luminous substance insinuates itself into the pores of the glass as the air yields, and thus, speaking accurately, it does not penetrates.

Nor is that penetration to be denied, even if it appears in fire, although it is a corporeal substance.

II. No substance is immediately sensible.

The primordial light was immediately sensible.

Therefore, the primordial light was not a substance.

The major premise is evident...; because the immediate object of the senses are sensible species, which are qualities.

Resp. In the major premise, light is taken abstractively; in the minor, concretively.

For by primordial light, in philosophical precision, one is not to understand an intentional species, or an accident, which cannot be the terminus of creation, but a luminous substance, which is sensed by means of light.

III. That light in Gen.

1:2 is understood as that which coincides with the day.

But fire does not coincide with the day.

Therefore, that light was not fire.

The major premise is certain; because God called that light day, and the darkness night, Gen. 1:

5. The minor is proved: because no one has ever said that day is fire or a substance, since it is a mere quantity.

Resp.

1) Primordial light is called day causally, because by its motion it distinguished day and night, not formally.

2) Day, since it is a quantity, cannot formally be light.

IV. If the primordial light was fire, it was either elemental or culinary fire.

But it was not elemental fire, because that does not shine: nor culinary, because that does not suffice to illuminate the whole world.

Therefore, it was clearly not fire.

Resp.

The primordial light was an igneous substance collected like a flame, and thus luminous.

But whether it was similar to elemental or culinary fire, it is of no concern to inquire anxiously.

For there is given a fire which is neither culinary nor merely elemental, namely, celestial fire, such as is in the sun.

Instance: Not all light is igneous.

Resp.

All light participates in something of fire, although the more rare and dispersed it is, the less it heats.

Just as vapor is rarefied water, which moistens nothing, or little, on account of its rarity: so light is sometimes like a rarefied flame, which heats little on account of its rarity; but it heats all the more, the more collected it becomes.

Conf.

D.

10. ADAMI OSIANDRI in colleg. system. part.

II. p.

88. Question.

Latin:

XVI. Quænam sunt opera primæ diei? Opera primæ diei creationis sunt: (a) substantia cœli, terræ & aquæ indigesta & informis: (b) lux πρωτόκτισος, sive primæva.

(c) Probabiliter operibus primæ diei accensentur angeli. Prob. a. Diserte scribit Moses Gen. I, 1. In principio creauit Deus cœlum & terram. Obs. Sunt, qui versu primo ἐπιτομικῶς totius historiæ creationis summam comprehendi, sibi persuadent. Sunt contra, qui statuunt, Mosen nomine cœli & terræ rudem materiam futuri operis indigitare. Posterior sententia nobis probatur.

1) Quia cum conderetur cœlum & terra, nulla erat distinctio diei & noctis, nulla tenebrarum & lucis, quæ demum accedebat, v. 3.

2) Quia creata prima luce nondum erat distinctio terræ & aquarum, quippe quæ facta est secundo creationis die, v. 6.

3) Nec fuit distinctio terræ & aquarum, quæ demum tertio die insecuta est, v. 9.

4) Quia ante incubationem Spiritus S. super faciebus aquarum, terra erat vasta & inanis; quibus verbis horribilis vastitas & confusio significatur. Idcirco a LXX. interpret. verba hebræa: תהו ובהו græce redduntur: Ἡ γῆ ἦν ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύασος, terra vero erat invisibilis (quia aquis tecta) & indisposita.

Conf. Deut. XXXII, 10. Iob. XII, 24. Es. XXXIV, 11. Ier. IV, 23. 5) Auctor libri sapientiæ alloquitur Deum sequentibus verbis, c. XI, 17. Manus tua creauit mundum ex informi materia.

Non equidem liber iste in canone, testatur tamen olim Israëlitas credidisse, Deum primum creasse molem quandam indigestam & forma completa carentem, e qua cetera corpora infinita Dei virtute creata sunt. Prob. b. Gen. I, 3. Et dixit Deus: Fiat lux! & facta est. Per lucem intelligimus candidissimam, eamque igneam substantiam, mobilem circa indigestam molem, quæ accessu suo diem, recessu vero noctem, intra 24. horarum, spatium induxerit.

Quod lux primæva fuerit substantia, colligitur 1) ex eo, quod peculiari actione fuit creata; creationis autem terminus est substantia. Quia mobilitas, quæ ipsi competit, est affectio substantiarum corporearum. Quod autem lux illa πρωτόκτισος ignea fuerit substantia, liquet ex hoc, quod omnes proprietates ignis ipsi conuenerint; objuit enim munja solis, & volente Deo in ipsius substantiam migrauit. At vero solem esse igneum, formaliterque calidum, infra probabimus.

Prob. c. E collatione Gen. I, 1. vbi dicitur Deus in principio creasse cœlum & terram, cum Iob. XXXVIII, 4. 7. Vbi fuisti, cum fundarem terram? --- Quum canerent simul stellæ matutinæ, & clangerent omnes filii Dei? Serino est Iob de stellis, quæ sunt filii Dei. Non igitur intelligit sidera cœli; cum hæc nunquam in scriptura dicantur filii Dei, neque vlla creatura inanimata excellens hoc nomen gerat.

Quin potius angelos indigitat Iobus, quos eodem nomine infigniuit c. I, 6. Nos heic obseruamus 1) angelos creatos esse ante homines. Dicit enim Iehouah: Vbi fuisti, cum canerent simul stellæ matutinæ &c. Potuisset Iobus excipere: Etsi ego tum nondum fuerim, fuit tamen primus meus pater, Adamus. Huic obiectioni occurrit Deus: Vbi fuisti, cum terram fundarem? cum canerent simul stellæ matutinæ? At cum terra fundaretur, nondum creatus erat Adamus.

Notamus 2) angelos conditos esse primo creationis die; propterea, quod non solum stellæ matutinæ vocantur, sed etiam cecinisse dicuntur laudes Dei, cum terra ab ipso fundaretur. Fundata autem est terra primo creationis die.

Notatu dignissima sunt verba D. CALOVII tom. III. system. p. 905.

ti statuuntur angeli non ante principium creationis, sed in ipso principio, tamen, ὡς ἐν πλάτει & cum latitudine aliqua, ut, quamuis primo illo principio conditae primum sint creaturae invisibiles & immateriales, recte tamen in principio illo caelum & terra condita dicantur; quia actum in illo ipso principio creauit Deus quoque caelum & terram.

Nam si vel altero saltim momento istius principii haec condita dicantur, angelorum tamen creatio prior erit.

Antithesis est 1) Pontificiorum, negantium, Deum primum indigestam caeli, terrae & aquae molem creasse. 2) Socinianorum & Arminianorum, asserentium, angelos multis saeculis ante rerum corporalium originem fuisse.

Contra indigestam caeli & terrae molem argumentantur:

I. Quicunque historice commemorat, in principio caelum & terram esse creata, is non intelligit rudem & indigestam molem, sed caelum & terram proprie dictam. Atqui Moses historice commemorat &c. Ergo. Maior constat; quia in historia a clara littera non est recedendum. Minor patet ex Gen. I, 1.

Resp. Neg. maior. Nam indigesta caeli terraeque massa est caelum & terra vera, ratione substantiae, licet differentia quaedam accidentalis obtingat ratione status distincti & complementi. Neque nos caelum, aut terram metaphoricam intelligimus.

Instantia I. He emphaticum hebraeum indicat, hoc caelum, hanc terram, qualis nunc est, quae pedibus teritur, intelligi.

Resp. 1) He demonstrativum quandoque infinite sumitur, Deut. VIII, 3. Levit. XVIII, 5. 2) Terra illa, quae dicitur הָאָרֶץ habet He praefixum, neque tamen terra plene distincta, aut exornata intelligitur.

Instantia II. Caelum & terra informis non est verum caelum, aut vera terra, quia caret forma, per quam caelum & terra est id, quod est.

Resp. Dist. inter formam substantialem, & accidentalem. Caelum & terra, primitus condita, non caruerunt forma substantiali & interna; caruerunt tamen forma accidentali & externa: siquidem distinctio & exornatio caeli, terrae & aquae sequentibus diebus accessit.

II. Quicunque ordinatissime omnia creauit, is non creauit confusum chaos. Atqui Deus &c. Ergo. Minor probatur; quia Deus est auctor non confusionis, sed ordinis, & creatio prima & nobilissima Dei O. M. actio ad extra haud dubie ordinatissima est. Ex quo auctor sapientiae cap. XI, 22. inquit: Deus omnia creauit in numero, pondere & mensura.

Resp. 1) Quidquid de confuso chao poetae somniarunt, nostrum non facimus, sed cum B. LVTHERO asserimus, Deum in principio operum suorum condidisse rudem & indigestam caeli, terrae & aquae molem, in qua veram substantiam caeli, terrae & aquae, sed inornatam & impositam agnoscimus.

Negat. mai. Quia hic ordo est maxime concinnus, quando progressus fit a non esse ad esse, ab imperfecto ad perfectum, ab impolito ad politum & exornatum. Non itaque creatio dicenda est confusa, licet aliquod opus in principio creationis fuerit indigestum, sequentibus diebus magis magisque digerendum & distinguendum. 3) Dicuntur omnia creata in numero, pondere & mensura, quatenus sunt in esse completo, non quatenus citra exornationem die primo indistincte creata sunt.

III. Si die primo chaos creatum est, nusquam in historia creationis fit mentio creati caeli & terrae. Consequens est abfurdum. Ergo & antecedens. Resp. Negat. consequ. maior. Nam fit mentio creati caeli & terrae, quatenus caelum & terra commemorantur primo die indistincte creata, distincte autem caelum altero, terra tertio die facta & exornata.

Contra igneam lucis primae substantiam argumentantur:

I. Quidquid penetrat corpus, illud non est corporea substantia. Atqui lux primigenia &c. E. Minor prob. quia omnis lux, adeoque etiam primigenia, habet vim penetrandi vitrum, crystallum &c.

Resp. dist. inter penetrationem veram & apparentem. Luminosa substantia se insinuat in poros vitri cedente aere, adeoque vitrum accurate loquendo non penetrat.

Neque igni apparens illa penetratio deneganda est, licet corporea sit substantia.

II. Nulla substantia est immediate sensibilis.

Lux primigenia fuit immediate sensibilis.

Ergo lux primigenia non fuit substantia.

Maior est evidens...; quia sensuum obiectum immediatum sunt species sensibiles, quae sunt qualitates.

Resp. in maiori lux sumitur abstractive, in minori concretive.

Neque enim per lucem primaevam in praecisione philosophica intelligenda est species intentionalis, aut accidens, quod non potest esse terminus creationis, sed substantia luminosa, quae mediante lumine sentitur.

III. Illa lux Gen.

I, 2. intelligitur, quae coincidit cum die.

At ignis non coincidit cum die.

Ergo lux illa non fuit ignis.

Maior constat; quia Deus lucem illam vocavit diem, & tenebras noctem, Gen.

I, 5. Minor prob. quia nemo unquam dixit, diem esse ignem vel substantiam, cum sit mera quantitas.

Resp.

1) Lux primaeva dicitur dies causaliter, quia motu suo diem & noctem interflinxit, non formaliter.

2) Dies, cum sit quantitas, formaliter lux esse nequit.

IV. Si lux primaeva fuit ignis, aut elementaris, aut culinaris ignis fuit.

At non fuit ignis elementaris, quia ille non lucet: neque culinaris, quia ille toti mundo illuminando non sufficit.

Ergo plane non fuit ignis.

Resp.

Lux primaeva fuit substantia ignea instar flammae collecta, atque adeo lucida.

Vtrum autem elementari, an culinari igni similis fuerit, anxie rimari nil attinet.

Datur enim ignis, qui neque culinaris, neque mere elementaris fit, nimirum ignis coelestis, qualis est in sole.

Instantia: Non omnis lux est ignea.

Resp.

Omnis lux de igne aliquid participat, licet, quo rarior & magis dispersa est, eo minus calefaciat.

Sicut vapor est aqua rarefacta, quae nihil, aut parum, propter raritatem, humectat: ita lux interdum est sicut flamma rarefacta, quae parum calefacit propter raritatem; tanto plus autem calefacit, quanto facta fuerit collectior.

Conf.

D.

10. ADAMI OSIANDRI in colleg. system. part.

II. p.

88. Quæst.


### Q. XVII

Was the empyrean heaven created by God on the first day? It cannot be clearly demonstrated from the Scriptures that, under the auspices of the creation of the world, any heaven was established by God above the firmament for the purpose of being the palace of God, the dwelling of the angels, and of the blessed souls, which is to be called the empyrean or empyraeum.

Prob.

I.

Because it was Moses' purpose to set forth the origin and seat of visible creatures.

If it had been his intention to describe the dwelling of invisible creatures, or angels, he would certainly have made mention of the angels in the history of creation.

But he did not expressly commemorate them: Therefore, neither did he express their dwelling .

II. The heaven of God cannot have been created, because it is eternal.

Rather, by the majestic heaven of God must be understood the eternal and infinite majesty or glory, which God has had in Himself from eternity, and will have for eternity, as well as the divine, celestial, omnipresent, and omnipotent dominion over all things, Ps. II, 4. CII, 20. TERTULLIAN aptly says against Prax.: Before all things God was alone, He was to Himself both world and place.

III. The heaven of God and the heaven of the angels cannot be one and the same "where."

For that of the angels is definitive, and that of God is repletive.

That prodigal son in Luke XV, 18 says: Father, I have sinned against heaven, i.e., against the divine majesty; no one sins against the heaven of the angels.

IV. The heaven of the angels cannot be a determined place, established above the starry heaven; because otherwise the angels, while guarding little children on earth, could not be in the heavens and see the face of God the Father διὰ παντὸς, or continuously, Matth.

XVIII, 10. V. The heaven described by Moses will conflagrate and perish on the last day.

2 Pet. III, 7. Luke XXI, 33. But the angelic heaven will not perish.

Therefore, it is not commemorated by Moses in Gen. I, 1.

VI. It is barbarous to call heaven "empyreum" or "empyraeum"; because that which is fiery is not called in Greek ἐμπύρεον or ἐμπύραιον, but ἔμπυρον.

This is the antithesis of most Scholastics and Papists, who establish that under the auspices of the creation of the world, the empyrean heaven was created by God, most vast, most lucid, and established above this visible world.

Their arguments are: I. The aerial and starry heaven, founded on the second day, is in the midst of the sub- and supra-celestial waters.

The heaven created on the first day is not in the midst of the sub- and supra-celestial waters. Therefore, the heaven created on the first day is neither aerial nor starry, but far more sublime.

Resp. The heaven of the first day differs from the heaven of the second day, not in substance, but in state, distinction, and external form, which is more complete and polished.

II. Angels are either everywhere, or nowhere, or somewhere. They are not everywhere, because ubiquity belongs to God alone.

Nor are they nowhere, because they truly exist. Therefore, they are somewhere.

If angels are somewhere, their "where" is either created or uncreated. Not uncreated; which belongs only to God: Therefore it is created, namely on the first day of creation, when the angels themselves were created: But the angelic "where," created on the first day, is the empyrean heaven.

Resp.

A real being, properly speaking, is divided into created and uncreated. "Where" is not so much a being as a mode of being.

But if it is said that a definitive "where" was co-created with the angels, it cannot be clearly demonstrated that it is expressed by Moses in Gen.

I, 1. For just as Moses does not explicitly mention the angels, so neither does he mention the angelic heaven.

III. There is a third heaven, 2 Cor.

XII, 2. Therefore, there is an empyrean heaven. The reason for the consequence is: because just as the aerial heaven is the lowest, and the ethereal is the middle, so the empyrean heaven is the third and most sublime.

Resp. Under the guidance of Scripture, heaven is divided into the heaven of nature, of grace, and of glory, not by reason of position or place, but by reason of state.

Hence it happens that angels on earth are in heaven, because they carry their heaven, or their beatitude, with them everywhere: but a local heaven does not belong to them, because they are not in a place, but in a definitive "where."

We add no more; because it is not for our fragility to discuss the secrets of the heavens, as judged by AUGUSTINE in *De fide et symbolo*, chapter 17.

Since he then commemorated the angels, it is much less to be thought that a dwelling prepared for them was indicated by the sacred writer. And this sacred locution, "to be in the heavens," denotes not so much a place as a state, namely, supreme dignity and perfect beatitude.

Quest. XVIII. What are the works of the second day? The works of the second day of creation are both the רקיע (raqia), and the separation of the upper and lower waters (a). רקיע is more correctly rendered in Latin as "expanse" than as "firmament" (b), and in the historical description of creation, it denotes that continuous tract which consists of air and ether, and extends from the terrestrial globe up to the supra-celestial waters (c).

Proof a. Gen. I, 6. 7. 8. Afterward God said: Let there be an expanse in the midst of the waters: and let it divide between the waters and the waters. And God made the expanse, and distinguished between the waters which were under the expanse and the waters which were above the expanse: and it was so. And God called the expanse heaven.

Proof b. רקיע is from the root רקע, which signifies "to expand" or "to stretch out," and in the scriptures it is used regarding the earth firmly expanded, Is. XLI, 5, and regarding a plate of gold, silver, or copper stretched out by a hammer. We expand something (1) by dilation; just as a mass of gold is expanded when stretched into very thin plates: (2) by rarefaction; just as water, boiling when fire is applied, is extended into a larger mass: (3) by unfolding, when that which was rolled up and complicated is unrolled and unfolded, which is accustomed to be done with tapestries and curtains. These things can be accommodated analogically to the creation of heaven; since God stretches out the heaven like a curtain, Ps. CIV, 2. He stretches out the heavens like a thin thing, and expands them like a tent to dwell in, Is. XL, 22. For this reason, the heaven was created on the first day in a confused state like a folded tapestry, which on the second day was unfolded and expanded; whence it is called the expanse. See D. GERHARD in disput. isagog. p. 451. Although the name "expanse" prevails over "firmament," heaven can nevertheless also be designated by this name, both because of its incorruptibility, by which, as a most simple body, it is subject to no corruption; and because of its immobility, by which the whole is never moved in a circle (for the circular motion of the heavens does not follow from the motion of the stars); and because of its maximum capacity, and in that fluidity, a stable and firm roundness; and because of the stupendous quantity of the stars as solid bodies which move in the heaven. Conf. D. VAREN. in Gen. p. 48.

Proof c. (1) The word רקיע is either placed nakedly for the aerial heaven, or for the ethereal alone, or for both. Not for the aerial alone; because thus (a) that to which the meaning of רקיע eminently belongs, viz., the ethereal expanse, would be excluded; (b) that to which the denomination "Schamaim" excellently belongs would be excluded; (c) there would be no relation of this second day and v. 6. 7. 8. to the work of the fourth day and v. 15. 16. 17., when yet that sidereal רקיע must be included entirely, and indeed principally in that which was created on the second day. (2) Not for the ethereal alone; because thus the creation of the air, which is also a created expanse and is more often expressed in the scriptures by the name "Schamaim," would be omitted, and only the ethereal heaven would distinguish between the waters and the waters, and would begin lower down from the element of water, which is absurd. Therefore, it is placed for both, and thus whatever comes in the scriptures by the name of created Rakia and Schamaim comes here by that name, namely, that entire expanse of air and ether, from the element of water and earth, up to the final surface of the heaven, touching the supra-celestial waters. Confer D. VAREN. in Gen. p. 45. (3) Ether and air are of the same substance, and differ only in qualities, since both ether and air are a body not solid or thick, but thin, permeable, and fluid, of which the motion of the stars testifies. For planets sometimes ascend, sometimes descend. That which could not happen if the heaven were of a thick and hard substance. Conveniently, therefore, they can be comprehended by the one word רקיע. See SPERLINGIUS, institut. phys. p. 424.

There is an antithesis between the Scholastics and the Pontificians, who maintain that the ether is not homogeneous with the air in terms of matter, but is solid and hard like crystal, and therefore does not constitute the Rakia with the ether. Their arguments are:

I. The creation of the heaven is described on the first day of creation. Therefore, the expanse created on the second day is not the ether, but the air. Resp. The heaven, folded and indistinct like a curtain, was created on the first day: but it was unfolded and distinguished, and established on the second day, whence it is called the expanse. Just as the heaven of the first day denotes the crude substance of ether and air, so the expanse of the second day is both ethereal and aerial.

II. The air is nowhere in the Holy Scripture called רקיע. Therefore, the expanse of the second day is not ethereal-aerial. Resp. (1) Grant that by the expanse in other places of Scripture the air is not denoted, it does not follow from this that in this place the air cannot be understood by the expanse; since the circumstances of the text openly prove this meaning by the very fact that it denotes heaven, and connotes the ether as air, because the ether and air do not differ except by certain qualities, and that expanse is designated which distinguishes the upper waters from the lower. And yet not only the ether, but also the air, distinguishes the same waters. For just as the ether makes the same distinction on the side of the upper waters, so the air does on the side of the lower waters. (2) Gen. 1:20 is explicitly stated, that birds fly above the faces of the expanse of the heavens. But birds do not fly above the ethereal heaven. Therefore, in the cited passage, the aerial heaven is understood.

You say: the particle על signifies at, towards, over against, so that the sense may be: Die Vögel fliegen gegen die Veste des Himmels. Resp. That exposition is not solid. For the text is whole; and the bird flies above the earth, and above the faces of the expanse of the heavens. But just as a bird truly flies above the earth, not necessarily towards the earth; so it truly flies above certain parts of the air. Add that in v. 2 the same phrase is used concerning the Spirit of God, when it is said that it moved above the faces of the abyss, where על-פני implies superiority, or presence above the faces of the abyss: so also the presence, or flight of birds, above the faces, not of the ethereal expanse (which is impossible), but of the aerial.

III. The air did not yet exist on the second day, but emerged only when the waters were separated from the dry land on the third day. Resp. On the day that the expanse was produced, the air was made, which according to the rudiments already existed on the first day, signified by the name of heaven, and placed between the upper and lower waters, together with the ether, by one undivided action.

IV. That in which the host of the stars is placed is the ether. In the expanse of the second day, etc. Therefore. The major is clear; because the stars are not in the air, but in the ether. The minor is evident from Gen. 1:14, 15. Resp. I limit the major. That in which the host of the stars is placed is the ethereal heaven, namely with respect to that part in which the host of the stars is, but another part remains, namely the aerial, not occupied by the host of the stars. Otherwise, one could argue by the same reasoning: That is true Germany, in which the French have placed their army. But the French have not placed their army in lower Germany. Therefore, lower Germany is not true Germany.

Latin:

E scripturis liquido demonstrari nequit, sub auspicium creationis mundi conditum esse cœlum aliquod supra firmamentum divinitus constitutum eo fine, vt fit palatium Dei, domicilium angelorum, animarumque beatarum, quod vocandum fit empyreum vel empyræum.

Prob.

I.

Quia Mosi propositum erat, creaturarum visibilium originem & sedem exponere.

Si ipsi deliberatum fuisset, creaturarum invisibilium, sive angelorum domicilium describere, vtique angelorum mentionem in historia creationis iniecisset.

At hos diserte non commemoravit: Ergo nec eorum domicilium expressit .

II. Cœlum Dei non potest esse creatum, quia est æternum.

Quin potius per cœlum Dei maiestaticum intelligenda est æterna & infinita maiestas siue gloria, quam Deus in fe habuit ab æterno, & in æternum habiturus est, atque diuinum, cœleste, omni præfens ac omni potens dominium fuper omnia, Pf. II, 4. CII, 20. Apposite ait TERTULLIANVS contra Prax. Ante omnia Deus erat solus, ipse sibi & mundus, & locus.

III. Cœlum Dei & angelorum vnum esse nequit vbi.

Nam angelorum est definitiuum, & Dei est repletivum.

Filius ille prodigus Luc. XV, 18. inquit: Pater peccaui in cœlum, i. e. in diuinam maiestatem, in cœlum angelorum nemo peccat.

IV. Cœlum angelorum non potest esse determinatus locus, supra cœlum fidereum con stitutus; quia cæteroqui in terris angeli, custodientes paruulos, in cœlis esse, & faciem Dei Patris videre nequirent διὰ παντὸς, siue continuo, Matth.

XVIII, 10. V. Cœlum descriptum a Mofe in die nouissimo conflagrabit & peribit.

2 Petr. III, 7. Luc. XXI, 33. At cœlum angelicum non peribit.

E. illud a Mofe Gen. I, 1. non est commemoratum.

VI. Barbare cœlum dicitur empyreum, vel empyraum; quia id, quod igneum est, non dicitur græce ἐμπύρεον vel ἐμπύραιον, sed ἔμπυρον.

Antithefis est plecorumque Scholasticorum & Pontificiorum, statuentium, fub auspicium creationis mundi a Deo creatum esse cœlum empyreum, amplissimum, lucidissimum, supra hunc mundum adspectabilem constitutum.

Quorum argumenta sunt: I. Cœlum aëreum & fidereum, conditum fecundo die, est in medio aquarum fub- & fu pracœlestium.

Cœlum, creatam primo die, non est in medio aquarum fub- & supracœle stium. E. cœlum creatum primo die neque aëreum, neque fidereum est, sed longe subli mius.

Resp. Cœlum primi diei a cœlo fecundi diei differt, non qua fubstantiam, sed qua statum distinctionem, & formam externam magis completam & perpolitam.

II. Angeli aut sunt vbique, aut nullibi, aut alicubi. Non sunt vbique, quia vbiquitas est folius Dei.

Neque sunt nullibi, quia vere existunt. Ergo sunt alicubi.

Si angeli sunt alicubi, vbi illorum vel est creatum, vel increatum. Non increatum; quod soli competit Deo: Ergo creatum, nimirum primo creationis die, quo ipsi angeli creati sunt: Vbi autem angelicum, primo die creatum, est cœlum empyreum.

Resp.

Ens reale, proprie loquendo, diuiditur in creatum, & increatum. Vbi non tam ens, quam modus entis est.

Quod fi dicatur vbi definitiuum angelis concreatum, non tamen liquido demonstrari potest, illod a Mofe Gen.

I, 1. esse expreffum. Sicut enim Mofes diferte non meminit angelorum, ita nec cœli angelici.

III. Datur cœlum tertium 2 Cor.

XII, 2. Ergo datur cœlum empyreum. Ratio confequentia est; quia sicut cœlum aëreum est infimum, æthereum medium, ita cœlum empy reum est tertium & sublimissimum.

Resp. Ductu scripturæ diuiditur cœlum in cœlum naturæ, gratiæ, & gloriæ, non ratione fitus aut loci sed ratione status.

Inde fit; vt angeli in terris sint in cœlo, quia cœlum suum, siue beatitudinem suam secum paffim circumferunt: cœlum autem locale ipfis non competit, quia non sunt in loco, sed in vbi definitiuo.

Plura non addimus; quia nostræ fragilitatis non est cœlorum secreta discutere, iudice AVGVSTINO de fid. & symbol. cap. 17.

Quæst. dein angelos commemorauit, multo minus cogitandum est, domicilium, eis paratum, a scriptore sacro indicatum fuisse. Et sacra hæc loquutio, in cœlis esse, non tam locum, quam statum denotat, nimirum summam dignitatem, perfectamque beatitatem.

Quaest. XVIII. Quænam sunt opera secundæ diei? Opera secundæ creationis diei sunt tum רקיע, tum distinctio aquarum superiorum & inferiorum (a), רקיע rectius latine redditur per expansum, quam per firmamentum (b), & in historica creationis descriptione notat continuum illum tractum, qui ex aere & aethere constat, & a globe terraqueo vsque ad aquas supra-cœlestes extenditur (c).

Prob. a. Gen. I, 6. 7. 8. Postea dixit Deus: Fiat expansum in medio aquarum: & fit diuidens inter aquas & aquas. Et fecit Deus expansum, & distinxit inter aquas, quæ essent supra expansum: factumque est ita. Vocauit autem Deus expansum cœlum.

Prob. b. רקיע est a radice רקע, quæ significat, expandit, vel diduxit, & in scripturis de terra firmiter expansa, Es. XLI, 5. de lamina auri, argenti, aeris, malleo diducta, vsurpatur. Expandimus autem aliquid (1) per dilatationem; sicut auri massa in tenuissimas laminas diducta expanditur: (2) per rarefactionem; quemadmodum aqua, subiecto igne feruescens, in ampliorem molem extenditur: (2) Per explicationem, cum, quod erat conuolutum & complicatum, euoluitur atque explicatur, quod in aulæis & cortinis fieri consueuit. Quæ ἀναλογικῶς ad creationem cœli accommodari possunt; siquidem Deus extendit cœlum, sicut cortinam Ps. CIV, 2. Extendit, sicut tenue, cœlos, & expandit eos sicut tentorium ad habitandum, Es. XL, 22. Quam ob rem cœlum primo die in statu confuso creatum erat instar aulæi complicati, quod altero die explicabatur & expandebatur; vnde expansum vocatur. Vid. D. GERHARD. in disput. isagog. pag. 451. Quamuis autem nomen expansi, præualeat firmamento; hoc nomine tamen etiam insigniri potest cœlum, tum propter incorruptibilitatem; qua, vt corpus simplicissimum, nulli corruptioni est obnoxium; tum propter immobilitatem, qua totum in orbem nunquam mouetur (neque enim ex motu stellarum sequitur motus circularis cœli); tum propter maximam capacitatem, & in illa fluiditate stabilem firmamque rotunditatem; tum propter stellarum velut corporum solidorum, quæ in cœlo mouentur, stupendam quantitatem. Conf. D. VAREN. in Gen. p. 48.

Prob. c. (1) Vox רקיע aut nude ponitur pro cœlo aereo, aut pro solo athereo, aut pro vtroque. Non pro solo aereo; quia sic (a) excluderetur id, cui significatio רקיע eminenter competit, scil. expansum ethereum; (b) excluderetur id, cui excellenter competit denominatio, Schamaim; (c) nulla esset huius diei secundi & v. 6. 7. 8. ad opus diei quarti & v. 15. 16. 17. relatio, cum tamen id רקיע sidereum omnino fit includendum, & quidem principaliter in illo, quod est secundo die creatum. (2) Non pro solo athereo; quia sic omissa esset aeris, qui etiam expansum creatum est, & nomine Schamaim fæpius in scripturis exprimitur, creatio, & solum cœlum ethereum distingueret inter aquas & aquas, inciperetque inferius ab elemento aquæ, quod est absurdum. Ergo ponitur pro vtroque, atque adeo quidquid in scripturis venit nomine Rakia & Schamaim creati, hic illo nomine venit, totum scilicet illud expansum aeris & atheris, ab elemento aquæ & terræ, ad vltimam vsque cœli superficiem, attingentem aquas supracœlestes. Confer D. VAREN. in Gen. p. 45. (3) Ether & aer eiusdem sunt substantiæ, & differunt tantum qualitatibus, cum tam æther, quam aër, fit corpus non solidum, aut crassum, sed tenue, peruium & fluidum, de quo testatur motus stellarum. Planetæ enim modo ascendunt, modo descendunt. Id quod fieri haud posset, si cœlum crassæ ac duræ substantiæ foret. Commode igitur vna voce רקיע comprehendi possunt. Vid. SPERLINGII institut. phys. p. 424. instit. phys. p. 424.

Antithesis est Scholasticorum & Pontificiorum, statuentium, ætherem non esse aëri, qua materiam, homogeneum, sed instar crystalli solidum & durum, adeoque cum æthere non idem constituere Rakia. Quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Creatio cæli descripta est primo die creationis. Ergo expansum secundo die creatum non est æther, sed aër. Resp. Cœlum, instar aulæi complicatum & indistinctum, creatum est primo die: Sed explicatum & distinctum, conditum est die secundo, vnde expansum dicitur. Quemadmodum autem cælum primi diei rudem substantiam ætheris & aëris notat: ita expansum secundi diei tam æthereum, quam aëreum est.

II. Aër nullibi in S. scriptura dicitur רקיע. Ergo expansum secundi diei non est æthereo-aëreum. Resp. (1) Fac, per expansum in aliis scripturæ locis non notari aërem, non tamen ex eo sequitur, hoc loco per expansum non posse intelligi aërem; cum circumstantiæ textus hanc significationem aperte probent eo ipso, quod cælum notat, ætherem connotare aërem, propterea, quod æther & aër non differunt, nisi quibusdam qualitatibus, & illud expansum designatur, quod distinguit aquas superiores ab inferioribus. Atqui non solum æther, sed & aër, easdem aquas distinguit. Sicut enim æther ex parte aquarum superiorum, ita aër ex parte aquarum inferiorum eandem distinctionem facit. (2) Gen. I, 20. diserte dicitur, quod aues volitent super faciebus expansi cælorum. Sed non volitant aues super cælum aëreum. Ergo loco citato intelligitur cælum aëreum.

Dicis: particula על significat ad, versus, e regione, vt sensus sit: Die Vögel fliegen gegen die Veste des Himmels. Resp. Illa expositio non est solida. Textus enim integer est; & auis volitet super terram, & super faciebus expansi cælorum. Sicut autem auis vere volitat super terram, non necessario versus terram; ita vere volitat super quasdam aëris partes. Adde, quod v. 2. de Spiritu Dei eadem adhibeatur phrasis, dum dicitur, quod se moverit super faciebus abyssi, vbi על-פני infert superioritatem, siue præsentiam super faciebus abyssi: ita etiam præsentiam, siue volatum auium, super faciebus, non expansi ætherei (quod impossibile), sed aërei.

III. Aër secundo die nondum fuit, sed emersit demum, quum aquæ ab arida segregatæ sunt tertio die. Resp. Quo die productum est expansum, eodem factus est aër, qui secundum rudimenta iam exstitit primo die, significatus nomine cæli, & locatus inter aquas superiores & inferiores, vna cum æthere, vna indiuisa actione.

IV. In quo astrorum positus est exercitus, illud est æther. In expanso secundi diei &c. Ergo. Maior liquet; quia astra non sunt in aëre, sed æthere. Minor patet ex Gen. I, 14. 15. Resp. Limit. maior. In quo astrorum positus est exercitus, illud est cælum æthereum, scil. respectu illius partis, in qua est exercitus astrorum, sed superest alia pars, nempe aërea, ab exercitu astrorum non occupata. Ceteroqui eadem ratione argumentari liceret: Illa est vera Germania, in qua Galli exercitum suum locarunt. Atqui in Germania inferiori Galli exercitum suum non locarunt. Ergo Germania inferior non est vera Germania.


### Quest. XIX. What do you understand by the upper waters?

By the upper waters are not understood clouds (a), but the supercelestial waters, homogeneous to the lower waters (b).

Prob. a. (1) Clouds and rainwater did not yet exist on the second day: This is evident from Gen. 2:5, 6, where it is said that it had not yet rained, when the herb germinated on the third day, and only then did a vapor ascend from the earth. But since the vapor did not ascend into the middle region of the air, there is not yet a cloud. (2) Clouds or rainwater are not above the Rakia, nor is the ethereal [region], which is conceded, nor the aerial, because they are in the aerial expanse, and therefore not above it: just as a man immersed in the sea is not said to be above it: nor can clouds be called the superior waters, because they are not in the highest region of the air.

(3) The expanse placed between the waters ought to set a boundary for both, and thus be a certain medium, or a separator, so that they would not be confounded again, v. 6. But the air alone does not constantly mediate between the inferior waters and the rainwater; since not only is the air very often full of clouds and rainwater, but also the vapors ascending by the force of the sun, resolved into droplets, descend and are mixed with them.

(4) The supercelestial waters are fixed and perpetual, homogeneous to the subcelestial waters: Clouds, however, are not fixed, nor perpetual in place.

Hence it happens that clouds in the nominative case are never called waters in the sacred code, as HOTTINGER observes in h. stor. creat. p. 85.

Prob. b. From Gen. I, 7. God made the expanse, and distinguished between the waters which were under the expanse, and between the waters which were above the expanse. Whence we argue: Whatever in the first creation was placed higher, with respect to the intervening Rakia, that is placed above the starry heaven. Water properly so called &c. Therefore. The major is clear; because Rakia denotes the whole tract consisting of air and ether.

You say I.

In the text there is not על [above], but מעל [from above], so that it may be indicated that in the upper part of the expanse there are waters from above; es seyn Wasser von oben her [there are waters from above], which can conveniently be explained as clouds resolving themselves into rains and dripping from above.

Resp. The word מעל was translated by PAGNINUS, ARIAS MONTANUS, and SEBAST. SCHMIDT as "above," and by the LXX as ἐπάνω. If, therefore, it meant "from above," why would the error not have been detected by Arias Montanus in Pagninus's version? Or why would Schmid not have corrected the error of Arias Montanus? Moreover, that the prefix מ with the following על does not inflect the meaning of the word is evidenced by the fact that it also occurs in the other word מתחת without an inflection of meaning. How truly, therefore, those waters are under the expanse, notwithstanding the prefix מ: just as truly, notwithstanding that, the superiority of the waters is noted by the Mosaic phrase.

Imagine that מעל signifies "from above the clouds"; yet by reason of the whole expanse they cannot be said to be above, since they do not rise beyond three Batavian miles.

You say II.

Just as birds are said to fly above the faces of the expanse of the heavens, i.e., above the air: so the waters are above the expanse, i.e., the air. Resp. Birds are said to fly above the faces, i.e., parts of the air; but the waters are said to be above the expanse, with respect to the waters below the expanse; whence those are above the whole expanse, because these are under the ethereal-aerial expanse. Indeed, if by Rakia, above which the superior waters are, the air were understood, the Rakia would be in its smallest part in the midst of the waters, and in its greatest part not in the midst of the waters; namely, the whole ethereal expanse and the highest region of the air; and thus it would not be dividing between the waters and the waters.

(2) From the parallel passage Ps.

CXLVIII, 4. Praise him, ye heavens of heavens, and the waters that (are) above the heavens. Where by the heavens of heavens is understood the highest heaven, above which are said to be the waters, which are indeed supercelestial. They are in vain who wish these waters to be understood as clouds; since meteors, of which number clouds are, are enumerated by the royal psalmist in v. 8.

III. From the testimony of the primitive Jewish church, which is evident from the song of the children Dan. III, 60. Bless God, all ye waters that are above the heaven. Although that song is apocryphal, it nevertheless testifies to the faith of the Jews, that the ancient Jews believed with us in supercelestial waters.

The antithesis is of certain Theologians and Philosophers, denying supercelestial waters, and maintaining that by the waters placed above the expanse, clouds are understood by Moses: whose arguments are:

I. Moses did not describe to a rude people invisible things, such as the supracelestial waters. E. By waters placed above the expanse he understands the clouds. Resp. 1) The ether itself is invisible, and yet it is described by Moses. 2) The supracelestial waters, by reason of the property of their nature, are visible, although they are not actually seen because of the distance.

II. Above the heaven there cannot be a natural place for waters: Therefore there are no supracelestial waters. The antecedent is clear: because water is a heavy element, tending naturally to the center of the world's middle: it must be established, therefore, if those waters are admitted, that they are there either violently, or supernaturally and miraculously; both of which are absurd. For God assigned to every creature a place in which it is naturally. Resp. BONAVENTVRA says aptly: That is a natural space, which God assigned to each in the first creation. Therefore, the gravity of the waters is not to be considered; but the will and dominion of the creator. In a natural place, elements neither gravitate nor levitate.

III. If supracelestial waters had been created, they would be corruptible; since they would be diminished and corrupted by solar rays. Resp. Solar rays are not projected above the firmament. Granting that they reach there, they do not, however, corrupt the supracelestial waters, just as they do not exhaust the subcelestial waters. The most wise creator preserves them from corruption.

IV. If supracelestial waters were to be established, there would not be two, but three kinds of waters: 1. supracelestial waters; 2. rain waters in the clouds; 3. subcelestial waters flowing through the passages of the earth. Resp. 1) Rain waters in the clouds are to be reckoned among the inferior, or subcelestial waters; because they are not raised beyond the highest mountains, and in comparison to the whole expanse they are like vapor, rising from a boiling pot, which is deservedly reckoned as subsistent water. 2) If clouds were the superior waters, then there would be three kinds of waters; because often a thicker cloud in the lowest region of the air is below a thinner one in the middle region of the air.

V. There is no use for supracelestial waters. E. They do not exist. Resp. They contribute to the glory of God, and to the completion and ornament of this universe.

Latin:

Per aquas superiores non intelliguntur nubes (a), sed aquæ supræcœlestes, aquis inferioribus homogeneæ (b).

Prob. a. (1) Nubes & aquæ pluuiæ die secundo nondum exstiterunt: Id quod patet e Gen. II, 5. 6. vbi dicitur nondum pluisse, cum die tertio germinaret herba, & tum demum e terra ascendisse vaporem. Sed cum non ascendit vapor in mediam aëris regionem, nondum est nubes. (2) Nubes vel aquæ pluuiales non sunt supra Rakia, neque æthereum, quod conceditur, neque aëreum, quia sunt in expanso aëreo, adeoque non supra illud: sicut homo immersus mari non dicitur super illud esse: neque nubes vocari possunt aquæ superiores, quia non sunt in suprema aëris regione.

(3) Expansum aquis interiectum debet vtriusque terminum ponere, adeoque esse medium quoddam, seu diuersorium, ne rursus confunderentur, v. 6. At solus aër inter aquas inferiores, & aquas pluuiales, non constanter mediat; quoniam non tantum aër fæpissime nubibus & aquis pluuialibus plenus est, sed & vapores ascendentes vi solis in guttulas resoluti descendunt, iisque permiscentur.

(4) Aquæ supracœlestes sunt fixæ & perpetuæ, aquis subcœlestibus homogeneæ: Nubes autem non sunt fixæ, nec loco perpetuæ.

Inde fit, vt nubes in casu recto nunquam vocentur aquæ in sacro codice, obferuante HOTTINGER. in h. stor. creat. p. 85.

Prob. b. Ex Gen. I, 7. Fecit Deus expansum, & distinxit inter aquas, quæ essent sub expanso, & inter aquas, quæ essent supra expansum. Vnde argumentamur: Quidquid in prima creatione locatum est superius, respectu interiecti Rakia, id positum est supra cœlum fidereum. Aqua proprie dicta &c. Ergo. Maior patet; quia Rakia totum tractum constantem ex aëre & æthere notat.

Dicis I.

In textu non est על supra, sed מעל desuper, vt indicetur, in superiori parte expansi esse aquas desuper; es seyn Wasser von oben her, quod commode de nubibus sese in pluuias resoluentibus, & desuper stillantibus exponi potest.

Resp. Vocabulum מעל versum est a PAGNINO, ARIA MONTANO & SEBAST. SCHMIDIO supra, a LXX. ἐπάνω. Si itaque significaret, desuper, qui non deprehensus esset error ab Aria Montano in versione Pagnini? Aut quare errorem Aria Montani non correxisset Schmidius? Præfixum autem מ sequente על non inflectere vocis significationem, indicio est, quia illud etiam occurrit in altera voce מתחת fine inflexione significationis. Quam vere igitur aquæ istæ sunt subter expansum, non obstante præfixo מ: tam vere, non obstante illo, superioritas aquarum, phrasi Mosaica notatur.

Finge, מעל significare desuper nubes; tamen ratione expansi totius non possunt dici desuper esse, quoniam vltra tria milliaria Batauica non eleuantur.

Dicis II.

Sicut aues dicuntur volitare super faciebus expansi cœlorum, i. e. super aërem: ita aquæ sunt supra expansum i. e. aërem. Resp. Aues dicuntur volitare super faciebus, i. e. partibus aëris; sed aquæ dicuntur esse supra expansum, respectu aquarum infra expansum; vnde illæ supra totum expansum sunt, quia hæ sub expanso æthereo-aëreo sunt. Sane si per Rakia, supra quod aquæ superiores sunt, intelligeretur aër, Rakia minutissima fui parte foret in medio aquarum, & maxima fui parte non in medio aquarum; nempe totum æthereum expansum, & suprema aëris regio; atque adeo non esset diuidens inter aquas & aquas.

(2) Ex loco parallelo Ps.

CXLVIII, 4. Laudate eum cœli cœlorum, & aquæ, quæ (sunt) supra cœlos. Vbi per cœlos cœlorum intelligitur cœlum summum, super quod dicuntur esse aquæ, quæ sane supracœlestes sunt. Frustra sunt, qui has aquas de nubibus intellectas volunt; siquidem meteora, e quorum numero sunt nubes, v. 8. a psalte regio recensentur.

III. E testimonio ecclesiæ pristinæ Iudaicæ, quod patet e cantico puerorum Dan. III, 60. Benedicite Deo aquæ omnes, quæ super cœlum. Quanquam canticum illud ἀπόκρυφον fit, de fide tamen Iudæorum testatur, quod antiqui Iudæi crediderint nobiscum aquas supracœlestes.

Antithesis est quorundam Theologorum & Philosophorum, aquas supracœlestes negantium, & statuentium, per aquas supra expansum locatas a Mose intelligi nubes: quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Moses non descripsit populo rudi res invisibiles, quales sunt aquae supracoelestes. E. per aquas locatas supra expansum intelligit nubes. Resp. 1) Ipse aether invisibilis est, & tamen a Mose describitur. 2) Aquae supracoelestes, ratione proprietatis naturae, sunt visibiles, licet ob distantiam actu non videantur.

II. Supra coelum non potest esse naturalis locus aquarum: Ergo non dantur aquae supracoelestes. Antecedens patet: quia aqua est elementum grave, tendens naturaliter ad medium mundi centrum: statuendum igitur, admissis illis aquis, aut easdem esse ibi violenter, aut supernaturaliter & miraculose; quod utrumque absurdum. Nam Deus cuilibet creaturae assignavit locum, in quo illa est naturaliter. Resp. Concinne inquit BONAVENTVRA: Illud spatium naturale est, quod cuique assignavit Deus in prima creatione. Non itaque respicienda est gravitas aquarum; sed creatoris voluntas & dominium. In loco naturali elementa nec gravant, nec leuitant.

III. Si creatae fuissent aquae supracoelestes, forent corruptibiles; siquidem a radiis solaribus imminuerentur & corrumperentur. Resp. Radii solares non proiiciuntur supra firmamentum. Esto, quod eo pertingant, non tamen corrumpunt aquas supracoelestes, sicut non exhauriunt aquas subcoelestes. Praeservat eas a corruptione creator sapientissimus.

IV. Si statuerentur aquae supracoelestes, non duplices, sed triplices forent aquae: 1. aquae supracoelestes; 2. aquae pluuiales in nubibus; 3. aquae subcoelestes fluentes per terrae meatus. Resp. 1) Aquae pluuiae in nubibus accensendae sunt aquis inferioribus, siue subcoelestibus; quia vltra montes altissimos non eleuantur, & in comparatione ad totum expansum sunt sicut vapor, ex olla feruente ascendens, qui aquae subsistenti merito accensetur. 2) Si nubes essent aquae superiores, vtique triplices forent aquae; quia saepe nubes crassior in infima aeris regione est infra subtiliorem in media aeris regione.

V. Nullus est vsus aquarum supracoelestium. E. Non dantur. Resp. Faciunt ad gloriam Dei, & huius vniuersi complementum atque ornamentum.


### Quaest. XX. What are the works of the third day?

Opera tertiae diei a) the gathering of the waters into a certain place. b) The separation and drying of the earth. c) The procreation of plants. Prob. a. Gen.

Prob. a. Gen. I, 9. Afterward God said: Let the waters under the heaven be gathered together unto one place. Obs. 1) The gathering of the waters was made by the omnipotent word of God, by which even now the waters are held, lest they overwhelm the earth. Job XXVIII, 8. 2) The waters were gathered into their own place, so that, even if there are many collections, all water nevertheless consists in a certain and predefined place.

Prob. b. Gen. I, 9. God said: Let the dry land appear. The earth was indeed founded on the first day of creation, but covered with waters. But when at the thunder of the divine voice: Let the waters be gathered together, these fled in a precipitous fall into the predefined place, the dried earth appeared, about to provide an origin for vegetables, and a dwelling for living creatures.

Prob. c. Gen. I, 11. Then God said: Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, after his kind; and the tree yielding fruit after his kind, whose seed is in itself upon the earth; and it was so. The earth produced plants, not as an active principle, or effect, but as material and passive, in as much as it supplied the matter, from which, at God's command, the herbs sprouted. Furthermore, that stones and metals, and the garden of Eden itself were produced on this third day of creation, is not rashly believed. The same seems to be said of minerals.

Latin:

Opera tertiae diei a) congregatio aquarum in certum locum. b) Segregatio & exsiccatio terrae. c) Procreatio plantarum.

Prob. a. Gen. I, 9. Postea dixit Deus: Congregentur aquae sub caelo ad locum vnum. Obs. 1) Facta est congregatio aquarum omnipotente Dei verbo, quo etiamnum aquae tenentur, ne terram obruant. Iob. XXVIII, 8. 2) Congregatae sunt aquae in locum quaeque suum, vt, etsi plures sint collectiones, aqua tamen omnis certo & praefinito loco consistat.

Prob. b. Gen. I, 9. Dixit Deus: appareat arida. Terra primo quidem creationis die condita est, sed aquis cooperta. At cum ad tonitru vocis diuinae: Congregentur aquae, hae lapsu praecipiti in praefinitum confugerent locum, exsiccata apparuit terra, vegetabilibus originem, animantibus hospitium praebitura.

Prob. c. Gen. I, 11. Tum dixit Deus: progerminet terra gramen, herbam feminificantem semen, secundum speciem suam; & lignum faciens fructum secundum speciem suam, cuius semen fit in eo super terra; & factum est sic. Terra produxit plantas, non vt principium actiuum, aut effectum, sed vt materiale & passiuum, in quantum suppeditauit materiam, e qua iubente Deo herbae progerminarunt. Caeterum lapides & metalla, ipsumque hortum Eden hoc tertio creationis die productum esse, non temere creditur. Idem de mineralibus dicendum videtur.


### Question XXI. Is the created earth mobile, so that it moves in a circle, and defines the seasons by its own motion?

The most wise creator founded the earth so that it does not move ordinarily and universally, but rests. To the celestial luminaries, however, he gave this duty, that they define the seasons by their own motion.

Prob. a. Prob. a. 1) Because Holy Scripture denies motion to the earth. Ps. 104:5. He founded the earth upon its bases, it shall not be moved forever and ever. Just as an architect builds a building upon a solid foundation, so that it persists unmoved against storms: so the celestial craftsman founded this machine of the earth most solidly, and at no time whatsoever, even until the last day, can the whole of it be moved from its place.

2) Because stability, or rest, is attributed to the earth. Eccl. 1:4. The earth stands forever. Ps. 119:90. You have established the earth and it stands.

Prob. b. 1) Because motion is attributed to the celestial luminaries. Eccl. 1:5-6. The sun rises and the sun sets: and it pants toward its place; rising again, it is there. It goes to the south, and circles to the north.

2) Christ is compared with the running sun. Ps. 19:6. The sun is like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber: he rejoices, like a hero, to run his course. From the end of the heavens is his going forth, and his circuit is to their ends. These words of Ps. 19 are indeed to be understood of the mystical sun, Christ, which is evident from the citation of Paul, Rom. 10:18. But they are taken from the realm of nature, and Christ is compared with the physical sun, namely that Christ shows himself no less eager to complete his course than the natural sun; which comparison would certainly be nothing if the sun stood unmoved, and the earth, like a planet, were moved around the sun.

3) The station of the sun, which happened while Joshua was warring, is held to be an astonishing miracle, Josh. 10:12-14. If the sun is not moved, but ordinarily stands immobile; why did Joshua command: Sun, do not move over Gibeon, and moon against the valley of Ajalon?

There is an antithesis of some astronomers, among whom NICOLAUS COPERNICUS stands out, who maintain that the sun rests and the earth is moved, who rely on the following arguments:

I. Every natural body is moved. Therefore also the earth. Resp. I deny the antecedent, because motion and rest is a disjunctive affection of natural bodies, of which some are moved, some rest. See SPERLING'S Instit. physic., p. 370.

II. The earth is most apt for motion. Therefore it is probable that it is moved. The antecedent is proved, because 1) it is round, 2) it has air poured around it, 3) it is in a place. Therefore it has local motion. Resp. 1) If something is moved for that reason, because it is round, then certainly the sun is moved. 2) Motion of any body is to be judged not by the surrounding air, but by divine ordination. Because God commanded the earth to stand in the air, it remains immobile. 3) A stone is in a place, and yet it is not moved. Both inherent gravity and the state of the center impede the motion of the earth.

III. The earth abounds in magnetic fibers. Therefore it is moved around the poles, to which the magnet turns itself. Resp. 1) We are doubtful about the abundance of magnetic fibers. 2) We doubt whether the power of the magnetic fibers is so great that they can turn the heavy and thick body of the earth toward the poles. Whatever is asserted about magnetic fibers is uncertain.

…IV. Whatever is moved from place to place with trembling pillars, that is truly and really moved. But the earth, etc. Therefore. The minor is proved from Job 9:6. Resp. I distinguish between natural ral, ordinary, and universal: and between violent, extraordinary, and particular motion. Job speaks of violent and extraordinary motion, which is stirred up by the fury of God.

V. If only the heaven with the stars is moved, it follows that the stars around the equator run through 876 German miles every second of an hour or in a single pulse of an artery, according to the world-distances of TYCHO; which is improbable. But if the earth rotates from west to east, and meets the motion of the heaven in part, it will proceed only 225 German miles in the space of an hour, and 250 paces in a pulse of an artery; which is far more probable. Resp. Since Scripture clearly testifies that the sun is moved, an argument for divine power and wisdom is to be sought from the most rapid motion of the sun. How suddenly solar light diffuses its rays! How suddenly lightning and wind are moved! Who can measure such sudden motion? (*)

Latin:

Condidit creator sapientissimus terram, vt ordinarie & vniuersaliter non moueatur, sed quiescat. Luminaribus autem coelestibus id muneris dedit, vt motu suo tempora definiant.

Prob. a. 1) Quia S. scriptura terrae motum denegat. Ps. CIV, 5. Fundauit terram super bases suas, non mouebitur aeternum vnquam. Sicut architectus aedificium solidae basi substruit, vt aduersus tempestates immotum persistat: ita hanc terrae machinam coelestis opifex solidissime fundauit, et nullo vnquam tempore vsque ad diem nouissimum tota loco suo moueri queat.

2) Quia terrae tribuitur status, siue quies. Eccl. I, 4. Terra stat in aeternum. Ps. CIX, 90. Firmasti terram & stat.

Prob. b. 1) Quia luminaribus coelestibus motus tribuitur. Eccl. I, 5. 6. Oritur sol & occidit sol: & ad locum suum dum anhelans est; iterum oriens ille est ibi. Abit ad meridiem, & circuit ad septentrionem.

2) Christus cum sole currente comparatur. Ps. XIX, 6. Sol est sicut sponsus exiens e conclaui suo: gaudet, sicut heros, ad currendum viam suam. A fine coelorum est exitus eius, & circuitio eius ad fines eorum. Sunt quidem verba Ps. XIX. intelligenda de sole mystico, Christo, quod patet e citatione Pauli, Rom. X, 18. At sumta sunt e regno naturae, & comparatur Christus cum sole physico, quod nempe Christus non secus alacrem ad cursum suum absoluendum se praebeat, ac sol naturalis; quae certe comparatio nulla foret, si fol immotus staret, & terra, planetae instar, circa solem moueretur.

3) Statio solis, quae contigit belligerante Iosua, stupendum habetur miraculum, Ios. X, 12. 13. 14. Si sol non mouetur, sed ordinarie stat immobilis; ecquid Iosua praecepit: Sol extra Gabaon ne mouearis, & luna contra vallem Aialon?

Antithesis est nonnullorum Astronomorum, quos inter eminet NICOLAVS COPERNICVS, statuentium, solem quiescere, & terram moueri, qui sequentibus innituntur argumentis:

I. Omne corpus naturale mouetur. Ergo & terra. Resp. Neg. antecedens, quia motus & quies est affectio disiuncta corporum naturalium, quorum quaedam mouentur, quaedam quiescunt. Vid. SPERLINGII instit. physic. p. 370.

II. Terra ad motum maxime apta est. Ergo probabile est, eam moueri. Antecedens probatur, quia 1) est rotunda, 2) habet aerem circumfusum, 3) est in loco. Ergo habet motum localem. Resp. 1) Si ideo aliquid mouetur, quod rotundum est, vtique sol mouetur. 2) Non a circumfuso aere, sed ab ordinatione diuina motus alicuius corporis diiudicandus est. Quia Deus iussit terram stare in aere, consistit immobilis. 3) Lapis est in loco, neque mouetur. Motum terrae impedit tum insita grauitas, tum status centri.

III. Terra abundat fibris magneticis. E. mouetur circa polos, ad quos magnes se conuertit. Resp. 1) De abundantia fibrarum magneticarum ambigimus. 2) Dubitamus, an tanta sit vis fibrarum magneticarum, vt graue & crassum terrae corpus possint ad polos conuertere. Quidquid de fibris magneticis asseritur, incertum est.

IV. Quidquid mouetur de loco in locum cum columnis trementibus, illud vere & realiter mouetur. Atqui terra &c. E. Min. prob. e Iob. IX, 6. Resp. Dist. inter motum naturalem, ralem, ordinarium & vniuersalem: & inter motum violentum, extra rdinarium & particularem. Loquitur Iobus de motu violento & extraordinario, qui concitatur a furore Dei.

V. Si solum cœlum cum astris mouetur, sequitur, stellas circa æquatorem singulis horæ scrupulis secundis vel vnico arteriæ pulsu, secundum TYCHONIS diastemata mundi, 876. milliaria germanica decurrere; quod est improbabile. At si terra ab occasu in ortum se rotat, motuique cœli ex parte occurrit, horæ spatio tantum. 225. milliaria germanica, pulsu arteriæ 250. passus procedet; quod longe probabilius. Resp. Cum scriptura clare testetur, solem moueri, argumentum potentiæ & sapientiæ diuinæ petendum est e motu solis rapidissimo. Quam subito lux solaris suos diffundit radios! Quam repente fulmen & ventus mouentur! Ecquis eiusmodi subitum motum dimetiri potest? (*)


### Quest. XXII. What are the works of the fourth day?

The works of the fourth day are the sun, the moon, and the other stars.

Proof. Gen. 1:14, 15. After God said: let there be lights in the expanse of the heaven to distinguish between day and night: and let them be for signs, and for set times, and for days and for years. And let them be lights in the expanse of the heaven to give light upon the earth. By which words Moses teaches that God, on the fourth day of creation, founded the sun, the moon, and the other stars, for a triple end: (1) for an illuminating end; that they may shine upon the earth; (2) a distinguishing end, that they may be for times, days, and years, i.e., that they may measure years and their parts; (3) a signifying end, that they may be signs of natural events, of rain, of drought, of winds, of sowing, of harvest.

Latin:

Opera quartæ diei sunt sol, luna & ceteræ stellæ.

Prob. Gen. I, 14. 15. Post dixit Deus: fiant luminaria in expanso cœli ad distinguendum inter diem & inter noctem: & sint in signa, & in stata tempora, & in dies & in annos. Et sint luminaria in expanso cœli ad dandum lucem super terram. Quibus verbis Moses docet, Deum quarto creationis die condidisse solem, lunam & ceteras stellas, ob triplicem finem: (1) ob finem illuminatiuum; vt luceant super terra; (2) distinctiuum, vt sint in tempora, dies & annos i. e. vt annos, eorumque partes mensurent; (3) significatiuum, vt sint signa euentuum naturalium, pluviæ, siccitatis, ventorum, sementis, messis.


### Quest. XXIII

That the matter of the sun, moon, and stars is the primordial light is not gathered in vain.

Proof. (1) From the identity of office. For just as the πρωτόκτισος (first-created) light distinguished day and night, Gen. 1:5: so subsequently the sun and moon, Gen. 1:14.

(2) From the evident absurdity of the contrary opinion. If the primordial light was not made the matter of the stars, it would follow that it was destroyed or annihilated. But that anything was destroyed or annihilated at the beginning of the world, which God saw to be good, is extremely absurd.

Latin:

Solis, lunæ & stellarum materiam esse lucem primigeniam, haud ex vano colligitur.

Prob. (1) Ex officii identitate. Nam sicut lux πρωτόκτισος distinxit diem & noctem, Gen. I, 5: ita deinceps sol & luna. Gen. I, 14.

(2) Ex euidenti contrariæ sententiæ absurditate. Si lux primigenia non facta est materia stellarum, sequeretur illam esse destructam, aut annihilatam. At in exordio mundi quidquam destructum, aut annihilatum esse, quod Deus vidit esse bonum, perquam absurdum est.


### Question XXIII. What is the matter from which the sun, moon, and stars were made?

The sun is entirely igneous, and therefore formally hot.

Prob. (1) The sun appears as a most luminous flame, it shines, illuminates, and heats. Therefore, the sun, like a burning torch, is formally hot. The antecedent is clear; because the sun appears to our sight no otherwise than a burning flame, and the learned eye observes through telescopes that the sun is a fiery globe. That the sun heats, however, is evident both from sense and from burning glasses, in which the rays solar rays collected exert a burning force. (2) Sirach describes the sun as a globe of fire, endowed with the power of burning, ch. XLIII, 3. 4. The sun in its meridian dries up the region, and who shall stand against its heat? It blows the furnace in the works of heat; the sun burns the mountains threefold, (namely) by breathing out fiery vapors; and by illuminating, it dims the eyes with its ray…s.

There is an antithesis of certain philosophers, asserting that the sun is not formally hot, whose arguments are:

I. A burning torch is extinguished. The sun is not extinguished. Therefore, the sun is not a burning torch. Resp: Limit the major. A burning torch is extinguished when the fuel fails. But the fuel of the sun is perennial, and never failing.

II. If the sun is igneous: the sublunary world would be burned up by its heat, and the middle region of the air would be hotter than the lowest region of the air; the consequent is false: Therefore, the antecedent is also. The consequence of the major is proved, because the sun is larger than the earth. If, therefore, the sun were igneous, it would burn the whole earth, and the middle region of the air would be filled with more intense heat than the lowest region. Resp. Deny the consequence. To the proof we say that a huge part of the ethereal and aerial expanse separates the sun from the sublunary world; since this is rare, it cannot be burned. The lowest region of the air, however, is hotter than the middle, both because of the reflection of the solar rays, and because of the congregation of igneous atoms erupting from the pores of the earth, which, joining with the heat of the solar rays, make it greater.

III. A burning flame can be looked at with a direct gaze: But the sun cannot be looked at with a direct gaze: Therefore. Resp. A small flame, and one not intensely bright, can be looked at with a direct gaze; I concede. — But the sun is a globe of fire, by far the largest, and most intensely bright, injuring the sight, as an excellent sensible object is accustomed to inflict a certain force upon the sense.

Latin:

Sol totus igneus, adeoque formaliter calidus est.

Prob. (1) Sol vt lucidissima flamma apparet, lucet, illuminat & calefacit. Ergo sol instar facis ardentis formaliter calidus est. Antecedens patet; quia sol visui nostro haud aliter apparet, ac flamma ardens, & oculus eruditus per telescopia animaduertit, solem esse globum igneum. Solem autem calefacere, constat tum ex sensu, tum ex pyroptris, in quibus radii folares collecti vim combustiuam exserunt. (2) Siracides solem vt globum igneum, vrendi vi præditum, describit c. XLIII, 3. 4. Sol in meridie suo exsiccat regionem, & contra ardorem eius quis consistet? Caminum inflat in operibus æstus; tripliciter fol exurit montes, (scil.) vapores ignitos inspirans; & illuminans radiis hebetat oculos.

Antithesis est quorundam Philosophorum, asserentium, solem non esse formaliter calidum, quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Fax ardens exstinguitur. Sol non exstinguitur. E. Sol non est fax ardens, Resp: Limit. maior. Fax ardens deficiente pabulo exstinguitur. At pabulum solis est perenne, nec vnquam deficiens.

II. Si fol igneus est: mundus sublunaris eius ardore comburetur, & media aëris regio calidior erit infima aëris regione; Consequens est falsum: Ergo & antecedens. Consequentia maioris probatur, quia fol est maior terra. Si igitur fol esset igneus; totam terram combureret, & media aëris regio intensiori repleta esset calore, quam infima regio. Resp. Neg. consequ. Ad probationem dicimus, quod solem a mundo sublunari separet ingens pars expansi ætherei & aërei; hoc cum sit rarum, comburi nequit. Infima autem aëris regio calidior est media, tum ob repercussionem radiorum solarium, tum ob congregationem atomorum igneorum, ex poris terræ erumpentium, qui, cum calore radiorum solarium coëuntes, maiorem efficiunt.

III. Flamma ardens directo vultu potest conspici: Sed fol non potest directo vultu conspici: Ergo. Resp. Flamma exigua, & non intensiue lucida, directo vultu potest aspici; concedo. - At fol est globus igneus longe maximus, & intensissime lucidus, lædens visum, vt excellens sensile confueuit sensui quandam vim inferre.


### Quest. XXV

What use of signifying do the stars have? The stars have a natural and civil use of signifying a): yet they do not pre-signify the voluntary actions of men b). Prob. a. The Savior himself confirms by his own calculation the natural use of signifying which the stars have, Matt. XVI, 3. For they signify storms, rains, droughts, the fruitfulness of the fields. They also have a civil use of signifying, insofar as they signify the times which are more apt than others for doing things, namely, when to sail, to fish, to sow, to cut wood.

Prob. b. 1) The voluntary actions of men proceed from the will, which is a distinguished faculty of the rational soul: But this is far superior and nobler than the stars. 2) Voluntary actions are free, which are not determined by the stars.

There is an antithesis of the Astrologers, who, from the position of the stars, or the genethliacal theme, strive to precognize and predict every man’s nature, will, affection, condition, fortune, and finally the very kind of his death. Their arguments are: I. The stars are for signs, with respect to all sublunary things, Gen. I, 14. Therefore also with respect to man, who is under the moon. Resp. SENECA says excellently: The mind of the wise man is above the moon, always serene there.

For although the mind of man is under the moon, if you look at the local condition; yet it is not under the moon, by reason of government. II. Victory and slaughter depend on the stars, Judg. V, 20. Therefore voluntary actions are directed by the stars to a happy or unhappy outcome. Resp. The stars fought against Sisera and his associates, not ordinarily and naturally, but by an extraordinary and miraculous divine direction; and not immediately, through an influx into the wills, but immediately, through an influx into the air, by stirring up meteors, lightnings, thunders, hailstones, and a great storm, as witnessed by Josephus, book V, Jewish Antiquities, ch.

Latin:

Qualem signandi vsum habent astra? Astra habent vsum signandi naturalem & ciuilem a): non tamen præsignificant actiones hominum voluntarias b). Prob. a. Vsum signandi naturalem, quem habent astra, calculo suo comprobat ipse Saluator, Matth, XVI, 3. Signant enim tempestates, pluuias, ficcitates, fœcunditates agrorum. Habent vsum signandi etiam ciuilem, quatenus significant tempora, quæ rebus gerendis præ reliquis apta sunt, nimirum, quando nauigandum, piscandum, seminandum, ligna cædenda.

Prob. b. 1) Actiones hominum voluntariæ proficiscuntur a voluntate, quæ est insignis facultas animæ rationalis: At hæc astris est longe superior & nobilior. 2) Actiones voluntariæ sunt liberæ, quæ ab astris non determinantur.

Antithesis est Astrologorum, qui ex astrorum positu, siue themate genethliaco, cuiusque hominis naturam, voluntatem, affectionem, conditionem, fortunam, ipsum denique mortis genus, præcognoscere & prædicere nituntur. Quorum argumenta sunt: I. Astra funt in signa, respectu omnium rerum sublunarium, Gen. I, 14. Ergo etiam respectu hominis, qui sub luna est. Resp. Præclare inquit SENECA: Sapientis animus supra lunam est, semper ibi serenum.

Quamuis enim animus hominis fit sub luna, si spectes localem conditionem; non tamen est sub luna, ratione gubernationis. II. Victoria & clades pendent ab astris, Iudic. V, 20. E. actiones voluntariæ ab astris ad felicem, aut infelicem exitum diriguntur.... Resp. Stellæ pugnarunt contra Sisseram & socios, non ordinarie & naturaliter, fed extraordinarie & miraculosa directione diuina; neque immediate, per influxum in voluntates, fed imediate, per influxum in aërem, concitando meteora, fulmina, tonitrua, grandines, & tempestatem ingentem, teste Iosepho libr. V. Iudaic. antiqu. c.


### Question XXVII. What are the works of the sixth day?

The works of the fifth day are aquatic creatures, which were... produced from the water , and flying creatures, which were produced from the earth .

Proof a. Gen. 1:20. Furthermore God said: Let the waters bring forth the reptile, the living soul. Objection 1) By 'reptile' here the fish is indicated, according to the following verse, 21. 2) Water was the material and passive principle from which, at God's command, the fish emerged: moreover, it is a place of habitation accommodated to fish.

Proof b. Gen. 2:19. When Jehovah, God, had formed from the earth every beast of the field and every bird of the sky. Here it is said quite clearly that birds were created from the earth. Whence it is not to be thought, as others do, that they were formed from the water as if they were fish.

There is an antithesis of certain Fathers and interpreters, asserting that both birds and fish proceeded from the waters. Their arguments are:

I. The production of fish and birds is joined together, inasmuch as it was done on the fifth day. Gen. 1:20. But just as the former emerged from the water, so also did the latter. Response. The production of fish and birds is joined together, not because of the identity of the material principle, but because of the common day of production. For when Moses had said: Let the waters bring forth the reptile, the living soul; he makes a great sensible segment through the Atnach, and adds: And let the bird fly above the earth; where the flow is changed, so that שרץ is not the object of the preceding verb שרץ but the subject of the following predicate עוף, and therefore it is to be expounded in the nominative, not in the accusative, so that you may rightly translate: Das Wasser rege sich mit webenden und lebendigen Thieren; und das Gevögel fliege auf der Erden. From which it is clear that birds and fish in that place did not proceed from the same matter.

Instance. But if these words are expounded thus: And let the volatile fly above the earth, it will not be taught by the same that birds were created, but only that they were ordered to fly above the earth. Response. Certainly the creation of birds is indicated. For a bird cannot fly unless it is created. Moreover, the matter of the creation is implicitly hinted at, while the bird is ordered to fly above the earth, which designates not only the natural place of dwelling, but also the matter of production.

II. There is a great analogy between fish and birds; for there are flying fish and aquatic birds. Therefore, they proceeded from one matter. Response. From that analogy the matter of production is not validly proven. A greater analogy is given between birds and terrestrial animals.
