For they live in the same element, they agree in gradation, in dry flesh, in the structure of the parts of the body, and when decaying they are resolved into the earth. Therefore, birds were produced from the earth.

III. Fish and birds are mixed bodies: Therefore, they have a material origin from all four elements. Response. The production of mixed bodies is to be estimated according to the predominant element. Thus, in the substance of fish, the element of water predominates; but birds were created principally from the earth, and less principally from the other elements.

Question XXVII.

What are the works of the sixth day? The works of the sixth day are living creatures, terrestrial brutes , and man, the principal inhabitant of this visible world .

Proof a. Gen. 1:24. Afterward God said: Let the earth bring forth the living soul, according to its (each) kind, and the beast according to its (each) kind, and every reptile of the earth, according to.

its (own) kind. Obs. 1. The production of living creatures is attributed to the earth, as the matter from which, and the passive subject, from which God caused them to come forth by creating brute animals. 2) Living soul denotes an animal, and indeed here a terrestrial one, the species of which are enumerated: 1) בהמה, a tame and domestic beast: 2) רמש, a reptile, comprising various kinds of serpents and worms: 3) חיתו ארץ, a wild beast, which is either never or with difficulty tamed.

Prob. b. Man occupies the last place among the works of the hexaëmeron: Concerning whom AMBROSE, Epist. XXXII, discourses excellently: Man was rightly created last, as if the sum total of the work, as if the cause of the world, for whose sake all things were made, as if the inhabitant of all elements; he lives among wild beasts, swims with fish, flies above birds, converses with angels, inhabits the earth, and serves in the heavens, furrows the sea, is nourished by the air, a cultivator of the soil, a traveler of the deep, a fisherman in the waves, a fowler in the air, an heir in heaven, a co-heir of Christ. But we shall consider the origin and production of man thoroughly below.

Quest. XXVIII. What practical uses will you extract from the doctrine concerning the creation of the universe?

Accurate and serious meditation on the creation of this universe excites in us a) trust, to be placed in God, who is most powerful, best, and most wise, b) sincere love of God, c) filial fear of God, d) prompt obedience to be rendered to God, e) invocation, and f) celebration of the divine name.

Prob. a. We fix all our trust not in creatures, but in the creator. For the omnipotent creator can rescue us from a thousand dangers: And the same best father will deny us no help, comfort, or advantage; since he deigned to create all things out of nothing for our sake. And he who abundantly testified to his wisdom in the first creation will most wisely direct the course of our life for the glory of his name and our benefit.

Prob. b. We love creatures because they are good; how much more is the creator to be loved, from whom, as from a fountain, the rivulets of goodness flowed into the creatures.

Prob. c. God himself took an argument from creation when he exhorts us to reverence and fear of him, Jer. 5:22. Will you not fear me? says Jehovah. Will you not tremble before me, who have placed the sand as a boundary for the sea?

Prob. d. Creation is the primary foundation and bond obliging the creature, who is a participant in reason, to worship the creator. Rom. 1:18 seqq.

Prob. e. Come, let us bow down, and humble ourselves, and bend our knees before Jehovah, our maker; because he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture, and the flock of his hand, says the king prophet, Ps. 95:6, 7.

Prob. f. If the article concerning creation is exercised daily, impressed upon the mind, and properly recalled to memory, the heart will certainly grow warm, and will be wondrously inflamed to perform acts of thanksgiving promptly, so that we may use all things for the glory and praise of God, says the blessed LUTHER in the larger catechism, p. 492.

SIGH.

I cannot but silently admire and gratefully venerate your power and wisdom, O nourishing Parent and Maker of this universe. What king or prince is to be compared with you! For you, having preceded by innumerable ages, at the point of time that pleased you, architected this world, and all things contained within its circuit, without any tools, without any iron implements, without any matter, out of nothing. You also created me, Creator Best and Greatest, the least of your servants. There is nothing good in me that has not been bestowed by you. And you gave me this fragile little body, and the spirit that rules these limbs. Do not forsake me, the work of your hands. For I hang entirely upon you, as a branch from the vine, a ray from the sun. You, the author of my life, are always in my heart, always on my lips, to be esteemed with a pious heart, to be praised with a full mouth.

Latin:

Opera quintae diei sunt aquatilia, quae ex aqua , & volatilia, quae e terra ...producta sunt .

Prob. a. Gen. I, 20. Porro dixit Deus: Repere faciant aquae reptile, animam viuentem. Obs. 1) per reptile indigitatur hic piscis, iuxta vers. sequentem 21. 2) Aqua fuit principium materiale & passiuum, e quo, iubente Deo, pisces emerferunt: Est praeterea piscibus accommodatus locus habitationis.

Prob. b. Gen. II, 19. Quum formasset Iehouah, Deus, e terra omnem bestiam agri & omnem auem caeli. Hic satis clare dicuntur aues conditae esse e terra. Vnde non putandum est cum aliis, quasi cum piscibus ex aqua formatae fuerint.

Antithesis est quorundam Patrum & interpretum, asserentium, tam aues, quam pisces ex aquis prodiisse. Quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Productio piscium & auium coniungitur, quippe quae facta est quinto die. Gen. I, 20. Sed sicut illi ex aqua, ita & hae ex aqua emerferunt. Resp. Coniungitur productio piscium & auium, non ob identitatem principii materialis, sed ob communem diem productionis. Cum enim Moses dixisset: Repere faciant aquae reptile, animam viuentem; facit magnum segmentum sensuale per Atnach, & addit: Et auis volitet super terram; vbi flus mutatur, vt שרץ non sit obiectum verbi praecedentis שרץ sed subiectum praedicati sequentis עוף, adeoque exponendum in nominatiuo, non in accusatiuo, vt recte vertas: Das Wasser rege sich mit webenden und lebendigen Thieren; und das Gevögel fliege auf der Erden. E quibus liquet, quod aues & pisces l. c. non ex eadem materia prodierint.

Instantia. Quod si haec verba ita exponantur: Et volatile volet super terram, non docebitur iisdem, aues esse creatas, sed tantum volare iussas super terram. Resp. Vtique creatio indicatur auium. Neque enim auis volitare potest, nisi sit creata. Materia autem creationis implicite innuitur, dum iubetur auis volitare super terram, quae non tantum naturalem commorandi locum, sed productionis, etiam materiam designat.

II. Magna est analogia inter pisces & aues; dantur enim pisces volatiles & aues aquatiles. E. ex vna prodierunt materia. Resp. Ex analogia illa materia productionis non valide probatur. Maior datur analogia inter aues & animalia terrestria. Viuunt enim in eodem elemento, conueniunt gradatione, carne sicca, structura partium corporis, & putrescentes in terram resoluuntur. E. aues e terra productae sunt.

III. Pisces & aues sunt corpora mixta: E. ex omnibus quatuor elementis materialem habent originem. Resp. Productio corporum mixtorum aestimanda est secundum elementum praedominans. Sic in piscium substantia praedominatur elementum aquae; at aues principaliter ex terra, minus principaliter ex ceteris elementis conditae sunt.

Quaest. XXVII. Quaenam sunt opera sextae diei?

Opera sextae diei sunt animantia, bruta terrestria , & homo, praecipuus huius mundi aspectabilis incola .

Prob. a. Gen. I, 24. Post dixit Deus: Producat terra animam viuentem, secundum speciem (quamque) suam, & bestiam secundum speciem (quamque) suam, & omne reptile terrae, secundum.

speciem (quodque) suam. Obs. 1. Terrae tribuitur productio animantium, tanquam materiae ex qua, & subiecto patienti, e quo Deus bruta creando prodire fecit. 2) Anima viuens notat animal, & quidem hic terrestre, cuius recensentur species: 1) בהמה, bestia mansueta & domestica: 2) רמש, reptile, complectens serpentum & vermium varia genera: 3) חיתו ארץ, bestia fera, quae vel nunquam, vel difficulter mansuefecit.

Prob. b. Postremum inter opera hexaëineri locum obtinet homo: De quo AMBROSIVS epist. XXXII. praeclare disserit: Recte nouissime conditus est homo, quasi totius summae operis, quasi causa mundi, propter quam facta sunt omnia, quasi omnium habitator elementorum, inter feras viuit, cum piscibus natat, super aves volat, conuersatur cum angelis, terram inhabitat, & caelo militat, sulcat mare, aere pascitur, cultor soli, viator profundi, piscator in fluctibus, in aere auceps, in caelo haeres, cohaeres Christi. Sed originem & productionem hominis infra penitus consideraturi sumus.

Quaest. XXVIII. Quos usus practicos e doctrina de creatione vniversi excerpes?

Accurata & seria meditatio creationis huius vniuersi in nobis excitat a) fidum , in Deo potentissimo, optimo & sapientissimo collocandam, b) sincerum amorem Dei, c) filialem timorem Dei, d) promptam obedientiam Deo praestandam, e) inuocationem, & f) celebrationem nominis diuini.

Prob. a. Non in creaturis, sed in creatore omnem nostram fiduciam defigimus. Omnipotens enim creator e mille periculis nos potest eripere: Idemque pater optimus nil auxilii, solatii aut commodi nobis denegabit; quippe qui nostri gratia omnia e nihilo creare dignatus est. Et qui sapientiam suam in prima creatione abunde testatus est, cursum vitae nostrae in nominis sui gloriam, & nostrum emolumentum sapientissime diriget.

Prob. b. Amamus creaturas, eo, quod sunt bonae; quanto magis diligendus est creator, ex quo velut fonte riuuli bonitatis in creaturas emanarunt.

Prob. c. Ipse Deus ex creatione argumentum desumsit, cum ad reuerentiam & timorem sui nos adhortatur, Ier. V, 22. Num me non timebitis? dictum Iehouae. Num coram me non trepidabitis, qui posui arenam terminum maris?

Prob. d. Creatio est primum fundamentum & vinculum obligans creaturam, rationis participem, ad colendum creatorem. Rom. I, 18. seqq.

Prob. e. Venite, incuruabimus nos, & humiliabimus nos, & genua flectemus coram Iehouah, factore nostro; quia ille est Deus noster, & nos populus pascui eius, & grex manus eius, inquit rex propheta, Ps. XCV, 6. 7.

Prob. f. Si articulus de creatione quotidie exerceatur, menti infigatur, & in memoriam probe reuocetur, incalescet certe pectus, & ad gratiarum actionem promte agendam mirifice inflammabitur, vt omnibus rebus ad Dei gloriam & laudem vtamur, ait b. LVTHER. in catechism. maior. p. 492.

SVSPIRIVM.

Non possum, quin tuam, o alme Parens & Opifex huius vniuersi, potentiam & sapientiam mirer tacitus, gratusque venerer. Ecquis regum aut principum tecum conferendus est! Etenim tu, cum innumerabilibus saeculis antecessisses, quo temporis puncto tibi placuit, hunc mundum, & omnia, quae ipsius ambitu continentur, sine vllis vestibus, sine vllis ferramentis, sine vlla materia ex nihilo architectatus es. Condidisti & me Creator Optime, Maxime, seruorum tuorum minimum. Nihil boni est in me, quod non a te collatuni. Et fragile hoc corpusculum, & spiritum, qui hos regit artus, mihi dedisti. Ne desere me, opus manuum tuarum. Totus enim pendeo a te, vt palmes a vite, radius a sole. Tu auctor vitae meae, semper mihi es in corde, semper in ore, corde pio aestimandus, ore pleno laudandus.


## 7 Concerning Angels

Quest. I. What are angels? Angels are finite, complete spirits, created by God, intelligent, free in will, and ordained to perform ministries pleasing to God.

Obs. I. The name, angel, if you look at the force of the word, denotes a messenger; for it descends from ἀγγέλλειν, to announce. Among the Hebrews, מלאך signifies one sent, a legate, a messenger. For although the root מלאך has become obsolete among the Hebrews, it is nevertheless found today in the related language of the Ethiopians, and it has the meaning of sending. And by usage and the style of Scripture, it is often used as a name of nature, and it does not occur except in reference to persons.

Obs. II. The word, angel, is used 1) of the uncreated angel, the Son of God, the creator and lord of all finite angels. The Son of God is called an angel, both before the incarnation, but with respect to the same, and after the incarnation. Before the incarnation, he is called the Angel of the face of God, Is. LXIII, 7. The Angel of the covenant, Mal. III, 2. The redeeming Angel, Gen. XLVIII, 16. &c. After the incarnation, Apoc. VII, 30. 35. c. VIII, 2. c. X, 1. c. XIX, 1. 2) The word, angel, is used of visible creatures, and indeed of teachers of the church in general, Mal. II, 7. Apoc. I, 20. and of John the Baptist in particular, Mal. III, 1. Mark I, 2. Matt. XI, 10. Luke VII, 27. 3) Of invisible and incorporeal creatures, or finite and complete spirits, Heb. I, 14. Ps. CIV, 4. &c.

Quest. II. Whence is the existence of angels known? The existence of angels is known with certainty from Holy Scripture, and is believed by divine faith ): it is gathered from the principles of reason topically and probably ), not apodictically and irrefragably ).

Prob. a. The existence of angels is taught both by the assertions of Holy Scripture, concerning which [we speak] below, and by many and various apparitions of angels, among which stands out that which was made to Abraham, Gen. XVIII, 2, where the Son of God, and with him two angels in the form of three men, appeared to the believing patriarch; as well as the angelic apparition which happened to Lot, Gen. XIX, 1, whom two angels went to deliver from the Sodomite conflagration.

Prob. b. Reason gathers: 1) Where one of opposites is given, there it is necessary that the other also be given, so that one may be most clearly distinguished from the other; for opposites, placed next to each other, shine forth more brightly: But corporeal substances are given: Therefore also spiritual ones. 2) If it is necessary for knowledge that this universe be in some way assimilated to its creator; it must also be known that there are creatures similar to the creator by reason of spirituality, intellect, and will: The antecedent is true: Therefore also the consequent [*].

3) Possessed and demoniac men have often performed wondrous things, men have often performed wondrous things, men.

far beyond the kinds, powers, and knowledge of men. For they have spoken in foreign languages which they never learned; they have spoken blasphemous words which could not have proceeded from a separated soul, nor from God; they have displayed strength firmer than the strength of many men; they have carried immense burdens; they have broken through chains and fetters; all of which must necessarily arise from some extrinsic principle, a being more powerful than man . 4) The Gentile philosophers acknowledged angels, or δαιμόνια, kinds. We are always led by our thought from the lesser to the greater. Thus, for example, the perfection of an herb is greater than that of grass; that of a flower greater than that of an herb; that of metals greater than that of stones, and among the metals themselves, one excels another. The construction of the body is more perfect in a certain genus of living beings than in others. Powers, too, naturally inherent in diverse things, differ much among themselves in various perfections. In some there is the power of growing, namely in plants, in grass, in herbs: in others, besides that, the power also of bearing fruit, namely in crops and trees: again in others, along with that doubled power, the power of sensing, as in brute animals and even minute creatures: finally, in one genus of things there is not only that triple power, but also the most excellent power of thinking and enjoying the use of reason; namely in man; who, however, needs external senses, which provide many objects to the mind. But since many imperfect perceptions and thoughts arise from these, it follows that the most perfect of all created things is that which is intelligent, which needs no ministry of bodily senses.

II. In the whole of nature there is no leap, but there are degrees distinguished gradually and little by little. We do not even observe two genera separated by such an interval, nor even two species of one and the same genus, without some third intermediate genus, or some species intervening, consisting of both genera or both species, and in some way participating in both natures. E.g., between an animate and an inanimate body, there is some medium, a ζωόφυτον, the sea nettle, see PLINY in Hist. Anim. c. 9, and DAMASCENUS in Dial. c. 47. Shellfish constitute another certain genus, the conch, the pinna, the slug, the tortoise. Between terrestrial and aquatic animals there is a certain medium, namely the ἀμφίβιον, and this too has more than one species. Between terrestrial animals and flying ones there are intermediate animals, as the goose and the duck. Between a spirit endowed with reason and a body there would be nothing intermediate, unless man were it, who has a nature composed of both. But he could not be intermediate unless there were spirits endowed indeed with reason, but entirely devoid of body.

III. Among all created things there is none which approaches so nearly to the highest perfections of the best Creator as that whose nature is spiritual, endowed with intellect and free will. Such indeed is man; but not the whole of man's nature, only his other part. Nor is there any doubt that far greater perfections can belong to spirits more excellent than man. Now from the various degrees of perfections in created things it becomes highly probable that God not only could, but also willed, to create spirits of such a kind that He would bestow upon them such perfection as a certain thing, most excellent of all created things, was capable of. It is altogether most likely that between the Creator and man there exist certain substances whose perfections are superior to human ones and nearer to divine ones, and whose nature accordingly agrees closely with the human, insofar as in it is spirit, endowed with reason; but also with the divine, insofar as God is assuredly a complete and most simple spirit, in which nothing is mixed and concreted, nothing joined with Him that is corporeal and born of earth. This is indeed most true: since God is an immense, infinite, necessary, independent spirit, certainly the distance between God and created spirits, none excepted, is always infinite, nor can it fail to be. But yet, since God is a complete spirit, and likewise infinite; while man is a spirit not only finite but also incomplete, inasmuch as he is joined to his body as by the closest bond: hence created things, intermediate between the Creator and man, are complete spirits indeed and devoid of all body, insofar as they are the most perfect of all created things; yet finite and circumscribed by their own limits, insofar as they are created things, in no way to be compared with the immense and infinite Creator.

Prob. c. The reasons adduced do indeed flatter us with a certain probability; but they are not beyond exception. For it can be answered to I. It was within the most free will of God to join spirits to bodies. For it is not necessary that a species should always be joined to an opposite species. To II. This universe is assimilated to God generally, insofar as the effect testifies to the power, wisdom, and goodness of the architect, not specially, so that the creatures themselves are participants of spirituality, intellect, and will. To III. The effects of the possessed are indeed to be wondered at: but yet some separated soul, or some superior power, whatever that may be, of a subtle body, or a spirit, can produce those effects. This argument, therefore, consists within the sphere of probability; but it does not convince the mind. To IV. If the Gentiles had any knowledge concerning genii

ἐνεργέυτος ἐν αὐτοῖς [working in them], whence it is called spiritual possession, if we listen to nature and experience as witnesses, two arguments of probability offer themselves to us. One is provided to us by thoughts that are entirely unexpected, which enter the mind, and of which not even the slightest coherence with the preceding ones is perceived. Let us assume these two axioms, which are certainly most true: 1) There is a certain natural connection of ideas and thoughts, by which it happens that antecedent thoughts contain within themselves the reason for the subsequent ones, unless something intervenes from elsewhere by which the mind is suddenly called away to think of other things. 2) It is a certain property of the human mind, insofar as it enjoys the use of reason, to be conscious of itself. Therefore, every man, being conscious of his own thoughts, will easily be able, by investigating, to know how subsequent thoughts cohere with prior ones, and how the operation of the mind has followed one from another. But indeed, one dwelling within himself sometimes notices in his own mind something entirely unexpected and not at all coherent, so that he is plainly ignorant of the very reason by which it came into his mind. What of the fact that those unexpected and very swift thoughts are sometimes entirely contrary to the preceding ones? It happens sometimes that a good man, always an enemy to sins, and now even so entirely occupied and involved in some most holy business that all his thoughts remain fixed on this one thing, is, beyond all expectation, snatched away to the worst thoughts, even most unwillingly and not without horror. Whence, I ask, do those come? Is it not more probable that they have arisen from the instinct of some other spirit, preparing snares for him, than from his own motion and the agitation of his own mind? The other argument is supplied to us by thoughts that are entirely inhuman and deeply repugnant to nature; to nature, I say, 1) proper to this man, since it is accustomed to happen that a very gentle man, both by nature and discipline, most mild and most meek—which is the character of a sanguine temperament—is troubled by truculent and most fierce and vehement movements of the mind, so that he rages against his own vitals; 2) common to all men. There are certain sins so monstrous, detestable, and not to be thought of without trembling, and thus so deeply contrary to universal human nature, that he who has applied his mind to such crimes seems to have stripped off all humanity and to have extinguished and extirpated all σοφὴν [wisdom], such as is, such as is, killing one's own offspring, or committing voluntary death upon oneself. Is that a proof of a malice by which a man is driven that is far greater than human? The traitor Judas is an example, whose most wicked perfidy, if one considers it accurately and weighs all the surrounding circumstances, one will find nothing in it that was consistent with human nature, even if most depraved. This crime, therefore, was more than human; consequently, diabolical, John XIII, 2. Thus, experience and reason persuade us that this is highly probable, which the Holy Scripture teaches us is most true. Those who go off to the contrary side have nothing with which to defend themselves except this one thing: that it cannot be conceived by the mind how a spirit is able to exercise a certain action upon another spirit. But let them first define the nature of a spirit, intimately known and perceived! Let them further explain by what bond the spirit of a man is so tightly coupled with his own body, which certainly can and is accustomed to communicate its thoughts daily with another spirit, likewise dwelling in a body! Let them finally arrogantly claim for themselves infinite knowledge of all things, and reveal any mysteries to us! Or let them ingenuously confess that this consequence is most false: that cannot happen which, provided it does happen, they themselves do not understand.

genii or demons, they drew this from Jewish tradition, and indeed from knowledge at least confused. Add that they wrote about genii not as spirits, but as more subtle and robust bodies. For they also numbered the strongest heroes among the genii.

Latin:

Quæst. I. Quid sunt angeli? Angeli sunt spiritus finiti, completi, conditi a Deo, intelligentes, voluntate liberi, & ordinati ad obeundum grata Deo ministeria.

Obs. I. Nomen, angelus, si vim vocis spectes, notat nuntium; descendit enim ab ἀγγέλλειν annuntiare. Apud Hebræos מלאך significat missum, legatum, nuntium. Quamvis enim radix מלאך apud Hebræos obsoleuerit, invenitur tamen hodienum in cognata Aethiopum lingua, & mittendi significationem habet, Et vsu, & stilo scripturæ sæpe vt nomen naturæ adhibetur, nec nisi de personis occurrit.

Obs. II. Adhibetur vox, angelus, 1) de angelo increato, Filio Dei, omnium angelorum finitorum creatore & domino. Vocatur autem Filius Dei angelus, tum ante incarnationem quidem, sed cum respectu ad eandem, tum post incarnationem, Ante incarnationem dicitur Angelus faciei Dei, Es. LXIII, 7. Angelus fœderis, Mal. III, 2. Angelus redemtor, Gen. XLVIII, 16. &c. Post incarnationem, Apoc. VII, 30. 35. c. VIII, 2. c. X, 1. c. XIX, 1. 2) Vsurpatur vox, angelus, de creaturis visibilibus, & quidem de doctoribus ecclesiæ in genere, Mal, II, 7. Apoc. I, 20. tum de Ioanne baptista in specie, Mal. III, 1. Marc. I, 2. Matth. XI, 10. Luc. VII, 27. 3) De creaturis invisibilibus & incorporeis, sive spiritibus finitis & completis, Hebr. I, 14. Psal. CIV, 4. &c,

Quæst. II. Vnde innotescit existentia angelorum? Existentia angelorum certo innotescit e scriptura sacra, & creditur fide divina ): ex principiis rationis topice & probabiliter ), non apodictice & irrefragabiliter ) colligitur.

Prob. a. Existentiam angelorum docent tum assertiones S. scripturæ, de quibus infra, tum multæ & variæ angelorum apparitiones, quas inter eminet illa, quæ Abrahamo facta est, Gen. XVIII, 2. vbi Filius Dei, & cum eo duo angeli in forma trium virorum patri credentium apparuerunt; nec non apparitio angelica, quæ contigit Lothi, Gen. XIX, 1. quem duo angeli ab incendio Sodomitico vindicatum iuerunt.

Prob. b. Colligit ratio: 1) Vbi datur vnum oppositorum, ibi & alterum detur, necesse est, vt vnum ab altero luculentissime discernatur; nam opposita, iuxta se posita, magis elucescunt: At dantur substantiæ corporeæ: Ergo & spirituales. 2) Si cognitu necessarium est, hoc vniversum quodammodo creatori suo assimilari; cognoscendum & hoc est, quod dentur creaturæ, ratione spiritualitatis, intellectus & voluntatis similes creatori: Antecedens est verum: Ergo & consequens [*].

3) Homines energumeni & arreptitii sæpe patrarunt admiranda, virifæpe patrarunt admiranda, viri.

generibus, viribus & notitia hominum longe sublimiora. Locuti enim sunt linguis peregrinis, quas nunquam didicerunt, locuti sunt verba blasphema, quæ nec ab anima separata, nec a Deo prouenire potuerunt, ostentarunt robur multorum hominum robore firmius, portarunt onera immania, perfregerunt feras & catenas; quæ a principio quodam extrinseco, homine valentiore, oriantur, necesse est . 4) Philosophi gentiles agnouerunt angelos, siue δαιμόνια, generibus. Semper a minori ad maius cogitatione nostra perducimur. Ita v. g. maior est perfectio herbæ, quam graminis; maior floris, quam herbæ; maior metallorum, quam lapidum, & in ipsis quoque metallis vnum præstat altero. Constructio corporis est perfectior in quodam genere animantium, quam in aliis. Vires etiam, diuersis rebus naturaliter insitæ, variis perfectionibus multum inter se differunt. In quibusdam inest vis crescendi, nempe in plantis, in gramine, in herba: in aliis, præter illam, vis quoque fructum ferendi, nimirum in frugibus atque arboribus: rursus in aliis, vna cum illa vi duplicata, vis etiam sentiendi, quippe in brutis animalibus, ac vel minutis bestiolis: In vno denique rerum genere non solum triplex illa vis inest, sed & excellentissima vis cogitandi, ac rationis vsu gaudendi; videlicet in homine; qui tamen sensibus indiget externis, menti multas res obiectas ministrantibus. Quum vero ex iis multæ perceptiones cogitationesque exoriantur imperfectæ: efficitur, vt perfectissima omnium rerum creatarum sit ea intelligens; quæ nullius egeat ministerii sensuum corporeorum.

II. In vniuersa rerum natura nullus saltus est, sed gradus sunt sensim paulatimque distincti. Ne duo quidem genera intuemur, tanto interuallo seiuncta, ac ne duas quidem species vnius eiusdemque generis, quin tertium genus aliquod medium, aut species quædam intercedat, ex vtroque genere, aut ex vtraque specie constans, & vtriusque naturæ quodam saltem modo particeps. E. g. Inter corpus animatum, atque inanimatum, est medium quidpiam, ζωόφυτον, vrtica marina vid. PLINIVS in hist. anim. c. 9. & DAMASCENVS in dial. c. 47. Aliud quoddam genus constituunt animalia testacea, concha, pinna, limax, testudo. Inter animalia terrena, & aquatilia, est medium quoddam, nimirum ἀμφίβιον, atque etiam huius non vna est species. Inter terrena, & volatilia, sunt media animalia, vt anser & anas. Inter spiritum rationis compotem, & corpus, nihil esset medium, nisi homo esset, qui habet naturam ex vtroque compositam. Is vero non posset esse medius, nisi spiritus quidam esset, ratione quidem præditi, corpore autem prorsus vacui.

III. Inter omnes res creatas nulla est, quæ ad summas perfectiones Creatoris optimi tam prope accedit, quam ea, cuius natura est spiritualis, intellectu ac libero arbitrio prædita. Talis est quidem homo; sed non tota hominis natura, pars dumtaxat eius altera. Nec vero est dubitum, quin multo maiores possint esse perfectiones spirituum, homine præstantiorum. Atqui ex variis gradibus perfectionum in rebus creatis admodum probabile efficitur: Deum non modo potuisse, verum etiam voluisse, spiritus creare eiusmodi, quibus tantam ipse perfectionem tribueret, quantæ quidem capax esset res quædam, creatarum omnium excellentissima. E. veri fit simillimum, inter creatorem, & hominem, interesse substantias quasdam, quarum perfectiones sint humanis superiores, ac diuinis propiores, quarum adeo natura proxime conueniat cum humana quidem, quatenus in ea est spiritus, ratione præditus; sed etiam cum diuina, quatenus nimirum Deus est spiritus completus ac simplicissimus, in quo nihil est admixtum & concretum, nihil cum eo copulatum, quod corporeum atque ex terra natum fit. Est quidem hoc profecto verissimum: Quum Deus sit spiritus immensus, infinitus, necessarius, independens, certe infinita semper est, nec potest non esse, distantia inter Deum, ac spiritus creatos, nullo demto. At enim, quum Deus sit spiritus completus, idemque infinitus; homo autem sit spiritus non solum finitus, sed etiam incompletus, vtpote cum corpore arctissimo velut vinculo coniunctus: hinc res creatæ, inter Creatorem & hominem mediæ, sunt spiritus completi quidem omnisque corporis expertes, quatenus sunt rerum creatarum omnium perfectissima: at finiti tamen suisque terminis circumscripti, quatenus sunt res creatæ, cum infinito immensoque Creatore neutiquam comparandæ.

Prob. c. Rationes adductæ probabilitate quadam nobis abblandiuntur quidem; at non funt exceptione maiores. Nam refponderi poteft ad I. Penes liberrimum Dei arbitrium fuit, corporibus adiungere fpiritus. Neque enim neceffe eft, vt vni fpeciei femper iungatur fpecies oppofita. Ad II. Hoc vniuerfum affimilatur Deo generaliter, prout effectus teftatur de potentia, fapientia & bonitate architecti, non fpecialiter, vt ipfæ creaturæ fint participes fpiritualitatis, intellectus & voluntatis. Ad III. Effecta obfefforum funt quidem admiranda: At vero anima quædam feparata, aut vis aliqua fuperior, qualiscunque illa fit, corporis fubtilis, aut fpiritus, illos effectus producere poteft. Confiftit ergo hoc argumentum intra fphæram probabilitatis; at animum non conuincit. Ad IV. Si quid cognitum habuerunt gentiles de geniis

ἐνεργέυτος ἐν αὐτοῖς, vnde dicitur fpiritualis obfeffio, fi naturam atque experientiam teftem audiamus, duo fe nobis offerunt probabilitatis argumenta. Vnum nobis præbent cogitationes omnino inopinata, quæ mentem fubeunt, & quarum ne minima quidem cum præcedentibus cohærentia percipitur. Adfumamus hæc duo axiomata, fane certiffima: 1) Eft naturalis quadam connexio idearum & cogitationum, qua fit, vt cogitationes antecedentes rationem fubfequentium in fe contineant, nifi aliunde interueniat quidpiam, quo animus ad alias res cogitandas fubito auocetur. 2) Eft proprietas quædam mentis humanæ, quoad ea rationis vfu gaudet, fui confcium effe. Ergo homo quisque, fuarum cogitationum ipfe confcius, facile poterit indagando cognofcere, quo modo cogitationes pofteriores cum prioribus cohæreant, ac mentis operatio alia ex alia fequuta fit. At enim vero fecum habitans animaduertit non nunquam in fua mente aliquid, omnino infperatum, minimeque cohærens, vt plane nefciat, qua demum ratione id fibi in mentem venerit. Quid? quod inopinatæ illæ celerrimæque cogitationes funt aliquando antecedentibus prorfus contrariæ. Accidit interdum, vt homo probus, femper peccatis inimicus, nunc etiam fanctiffimo quodam negotio ita totus occupatus atque implicitus, vt cogitationes ipfius omnes in hoc vno defixæ hæreant, præter omnem opinionem ad cogitationes peffimas, vel maxime inuitus, non fine horrore abripiatur. Vnde, quæfo, illæ? Nonne magis eft probabile, ex instinctu alius cuiusdam fpiritus, infidias ipfi parantis, quam ex fuo motu fuæque mentis agitatione, exortas effe? Alterum nobis argumentum fuppeditant cogitationes omnino inhumanæ, ac penitus naturæ repugnantes; naturæ, inquam, 1) propriæ huius hominis, quandoquidem fieri folet, vt homo leniffimus, & natura, & difciplina, mittiffimus, mansuetiffimus, quæ eft temperamenti fanguinei indoles, truculentis maximeque ferocibus ac vehementiffimis animi motibus turbetur, vt in fua fæuiat vifcera; 2) communi omnium hominum. Sunt peccata quædam, tam immania, deteftabilia, nec fine tremore cogitanda, atque adeo vnluerfæ naturæ humanæ ita penitus aduerfaria, vt, qui ad eiufmodi facinora animum adplicuerit, is omnem humanitatem exuiffe, omnemque σοφὴν exftinxiffe atque extirpaffe videatur, cuiusmodi eft, cuiusmodi eft, fuam prolem interficere, mortem fibi voluntariam confcifcere. Illudne documentum eft malitiæ, qua homo impellitur, longe maioris, quam humanæ? Exemplo eft Iudas proditor, cuius fceleratiffimam perfidiam fi quis adcurate contempletur, omnesque res circumftantes perpendat, nihil in ea deprehendet, quod naturæ humanæ, tametfi maxime deprauatæ, fuerit confentaneum. Hoc igitur fcelus erat plus, quam humanum; proinde diabolicum, Ioann. XIII, 2. Itaque experientia ac ratio id nobis valde probabile effe perfuadent, quod fcriptura facra veriffimum effe, nos edocet. Qui in contrariam partem abeunt, nihil habent, quo fe tueantur, præter hoc vnum: mente concipi non poffe, quo pacto fpiritus in alio fpiritu actionem quandam exercere valeat. Sed, definiant primum naturam fpiritus, intime cognitam ac perfpectam! Explicent porro, quo vinculo fpiritus hominis cum ipfius corpore adeo arcte copulatus fit, qui certe cum alio fpiritu, item in corpore habitante, cogitationes fuas communicare quotidie & poteft, & folet! Arrogent tandem temere fibi ipfi infinitam rerum omnium fcientiam, & quæuis arcana nobis patefaciant! aut fateantur ingenue, falliffimam effe hanc confequutionem: id fieri non poffe, quod, modo fiat, ipfi non intelligunt.

geniis aut daemoniis, hauserunt id ex traditione Iudaica, & quidem cognitione saltem confusa. Adiice, quod scripserint de geniis non ut spiritibus, sed ut corporibus subtilioribus, & robustioribus. Nam & fortissimos heroas geniis annumerarunt. Quaest.


### Q. 3. Are angels spirits, devoid of all corporeal mass?

Angels are spirits, devoid of all matter, both of the coarser and the more subtle kind.

Prob. 1) Paul describes angels as πνεύματα λειτουργικὰ, ministering spirits, Heb. 1:7. 2) The sacred psalmist supports this, singing Ps. 104:4: Who makes his angels spirits.

For thus Luther translates it in German: Du machst deine Engel zu Winden. Resp. 1) There is no sign of comparison present. For it is not said: Who makes his angels רוחות, like winds. 2) In a more significant sense רוח denotes spirit, which more significant sense ought to hold the first place, wherever it can.

Instance. But it is added: His ministers a flaming fire. That angels are of a fiery nature, no one would assert. Wherefore, just as angels are metaphorically called flames, so also are winds. Resp. 1) The noun אש, fire, is found not only regarding corporeal fire; but we also have incorporeal fire in the scriptures, so much so that God is called a burning fire, not indeed because of the attribute of justice alone, by which he punishes most severely, but also because of a most subtle, most pure, incorporeal substance; because otherwise there would be no need to add the epithet, burning. 2) Be it so, that in the latter member of the cited verse angels are metaphorically called burning flames; yet in the former member they are properly called spirits. For the apostle had this passage in view when he called angels πνεύματα λειτουργικὰ, ministering spirits, Heb. 1:7. Cf. D. SEB. SCHMIDT, Collegium Biblicum, part 2, p. 195. 3) Evil angels are called spirits, Matt. 8:16, Eph. 2:2, ch. 6:12. 4) Angels are able to penetrate stones, doors, and other solid bodies, Acts 12:7; entire legions can inhabit one man, Mark 5:9, Luke 8:30. 5) Angels are by nature invisible, Col. 1:16; they appeared having assumed bodies, and again disappeared at will.

There is an antithesis held by certain Fathers, Scholastics, Socinians, and Arminians, to whom add HUGO GROTIUS and ERNEST SOHNER, formerly Professor at Altdorf, who attribute most subtle bodies to angels, and rely on the following arguments: I. Angels can be seen, Gen. 18:2: Therefore they are not spirits.

Resp. Angels were seen, not in themselves, but in assumed bodies, not in their essence, but in the economy and office of the apparition which they performed.

II. Angels ate, Gen. 18:8: Therefore they are not spirits. Resp. Angels ate, by taking food into the mouth, not by digesting it through the vital operation of a body, but by consuming it through a superior power. Just as dry earth consumes water in one way, and the sun consumes the same in another. The former through need, the latter through virtue and power.

III. Angels were moved from place to place, Is. 6:2: Therefore they have bodies. For local motion is an affection of a natural body. Resp. Angels were moved from place to place, not in themselves, but in assumed bodies, which they did not assume περιχορητικῶς, or by essential union, but παρὰστατικῶς, or by accidental union. For an angel is not a form informing the assumed body, but a form assisting it: just as a charioteer assists and presides over a chariot, a pilot over a ship, a leader of war over an army.

IV. Whatever is mutable, that has matter: But angels are mutable: Therefore. The major is proved because the root of mutability is matter. By reason of matter, something is generated and corrupted, altered, and moved from place to place. The minor is evident: because angels not only change their ubi (where), but also certain angels were corrupted through the fall. R. 1) I distinguish between substantial and accidental change. The root of substantial change is matter; but accidental change falls even upon Spirits devoid of matter . 2) Angels indeed vary their ubi, but properly speaking they do not change place; since they are in a definitive ubi, not a circumscriptive or occupative one. The fallen angels were corrupted accidentally, not substantially.

V. Those of which a certain number is given, they have matter. A certain number of angels is given. Therefore. The major is evident; because number is a discrete quantity. But given quantity, matter is posited. Resp. Given quantity of mass, matter is posited, I concede. But discrete quantity belongs also to immaterial things, since it is called quantity improperly.

VI. Whoever sing and praise God, they are not pure Spirits, devoid of all matter. But angels, etc. Therefore: The major is clear; because without a mouth, tongue, and lungs, no one can form a voice, sing, and praise. The minor is proved from Is. VI, 3. Resp. Whoever sing and praise God with bodily organs, they are not pure Spirits, I concede. But Angels praise God in a spiritual manner, which is in this life uninvestigable and inexplicable to us.

VII. ORIGEN, De Principiis ch. II. TERTULLIAN, in the book On the Flesh of Christ, and other fathers of the early church, attributed subtle bodies to angels. Resp. 1) The writings of the fathers are not the norm of theology. 2) Some, but not all, fathers judged angels to be corporeal. 3) The fathers either understood σώματα (bodies) as persons, or they opposed body to phantom and nothingness, or they took matter for the subject of accidents, and indeed in comparison with God, who is so pure a Spirit and act, that not even an accident can fall upon Him.

VIII. Objection: The fathers of the early church did not without reason attribute bodies to angels: But 1) because the Sons of God, by whom they understood angels, took the daughters of men as their wives, Gen. VI, 2. 2) Because fire is said to be prepared for the devil and his angels, Matt. XXV, 41. Resp. to I. By the Sons of God in the cited place are understood the sons born of the pious patriarchs and educated in the church: these saw the daughters of men with an inordinate gaze, because they were beautiful, and took wives from all whom they chose according to their own pleasure, against the will and word of God. It is absurd, however, to think here of angelic spirits, for whom marriage was not instituted; and they neither beget nor are begotten. To II. The infernal fire is not elemental, which burns only bodies, but a singular one, prepared singularly by God together with hell, Matt. XXV, 41, so that it may burn spirits and damned men eternally. For who would doubt that God can create such a fire, which may also torment evil angels with vengeance?

Latin:

Angeli sunt spiritus, omnis materiae, tam crassioris, quam subtilioris expertes.

Prob. 1) Paullus angelos describit per πνεύματα λειτουργικὰ, spiritus ministratorios, Hebr. I, 7. 2) Suffragatur hieropsaltes canens Ps. CIV, 4. Qui facit angelos suos spiritus.

Dicis: Per רוחות intelliguntur venti. Nam ita germanice vertit Lutherus: Du machst deine Engel zu Winden. Resp. 1) Non adest ulla comparationis nota. Non enim dicitur: Qui facit angelos suos רוחות, sicut ventos. 2) Potiori significatione רוח notat spiritum, quae significatio potior obtinere locum primum debet, ubicunque potest.

Instantia. Sed additur: Ministros suos ignem flammantem. Angelos ignea esse naturae, nemo asseruerit. Quare sicut angeli metaphorice dicuntur flaminae, ita & venti. Resp. 1) Nomen אש, ignis, non tantum de igne corporeo invenitur; sed etiam ignem incorporeum in scripturis habemus, adeo, ut Deus ignis ardens appelletur, non sane propter solum attributum iustitiae, quo punit severissime, sed & propter substantiam subtilissimam, purissimam, incorpoream; quia alias non opus foret, addere epitheton, ardens. 2) Esto, quod in membro posteriori versus citati angeli metaphorice dicuntur flaminae ardentes; in membro tamen priori proprie appellantur spiritus. Nam apostolus hunc spectavit locum, cum angelos vocavit πνεύματα λειτουργικὰ, spiritus ministratorios, Hebr. I, v. 7. Conf. D. SEB. SCHMIDII colleg. bibl. poster. p. 195. 3) Angeli mali nuncupantur spiritus, Matth. VIII, 16. Eph. II, 2. c. VI, 12. 4) Angeli lapides, ianuas, aliaque corpora solida penetrare queunt, Act. XII, 7. integrae legiones unum incolere possunt hominem, Marc. V, 9. Luc. VIII, 30. 5) Angeli sunt natura invisibiles. Col. I, 16. qui assuntis corporibus apparuerunt, & rursus pro lubitu disparuerunt.

Antithesis est quorundam Patrum, Scholasticorum, Socinianorum & Arminianorum, quibus adde HVGONEM GROTIVM & ERNESTVM SOHNERVM, olim Profess. Altdorfinum qui angelis subtilissima tribuunt corpora, & sequentibus innituntur argumentis:

I. Angeli possunt videri, Gen. XVIII, 2: Ergo non sunt spiritus. Resp. Visi sunt angeli, non in se, sed in assuntis corporibus, non in essentia sua, sed in apparitionis οἰκονομίᾳ & officio, quod obierunt.

II. Angeli comederunt, Gen. XVIII, 8: Ergo non sunt spiritus. Resp. Angeli comederunt, cibum in os sumendo, non vitali corporis operatione digerendo, sed vi superiori consumendo. Sicut terra arida aliter consumit aquam, aliter sol eandem absumit. Illa per indigentiam, hic per virtutem & potentiam.

III. Angeli moti sunt de loco in locum, Es. VI, 2: Ergo habent corpora. Nam motus localis est affectio corporis naturalis. Resp. Angeli moti sunt de loco in locum, non in se, sed in corporibus assuntis, quae non assumerunt περιχορητικῶς, sive per vnionem essentialem, sed παρὰστατικῶς, sive per vnionem accidentalem. Neque enim angelus est forma informans corporis assunti, sed forma assistens: Sicut auriga assistit & praeest currui, gubernator naui, dux belli exercitui.

IV. Quidquid est mutabile, illud habet materiam: Atqui angeli sunt mutabiles: Ergo. Maior prob. quia mutabilitatis radix est materia. Ratione materiae aliquid generatur & corrumpitur, alteratur, de loco in locum mutatur. Minor constat: quia angeli non tantum mutant ubi suum, sed & quidam angeli per lapsum corrupti sunt. R. 1) Distinguo, inter mutationem substantialem, & accidentalem. Mutationis substantialis radix est materia; at mutatio accidentalis cadit etiam in Spiritus materiae expertes . 2) Angeli variant quidem suum ubi, sed proprie loquendo non mutant locum; cum sint in ubi definitiuo, non circumscriptiuo, aut occupatiuo. Angeli lapsi corrupti sunt accidentaliter, non substantialiter.

V. Quorum datur certus numerus, illi habent materiam. Angelorum datur certus numerus. Ergo. Maior constat; quia numerus est quantitas discreta. At posita quantitate ponitur materia. Resp. Posita quantitate molis, ponitur materia, concedo. At quantitas discreta est etiam rerum immaterialium, cum improprie dicatur quantitas.

VI. Quicunque canunt & laudant Deum, illi non sunt Spiritus puri, omnis materiae expertes. Atqui angeli &c. Ergo: Maior patet; quia fine ore, lingua & pulmonibus nemo formare vocem, canere & laudare potest. Minor probatur ex Es. VI, 3. Resp. Quicunque canunt & laudant Deum organis corporeis, illi non sunt Spiritus puri, concedo. At Angeli laudant Deum modo spirituali, nobis in hac vita imperuestigabili & inexplicabili.

VII. ORIGENES, περὶ ἀρχῶν cap. II. TERTULLIANUS, libro de carne Christi, & alii patres primitiae ecclesiae, subtilia angelis tribuerunt corpora. Resp. 1) Scripta patrum non sunt norma theologiae. 2) Quidam, sed non omnes patres censuerunt angelos esse corporeos. 3) Patres vel intellexerunt σώματα personas, vel corpus opposuerunt phantasmati, & nihilo, vel sumserunt materiam pro subiecto accidentium, & quidem in comparatione cum Deo, qui adeo purus est Spiritus & actus, vt ne accidens quidem in illum cadat.

VIII. Instantia: Patres primitiae ecclesiae non sine ratione angelis tribuerunt corpora: Sed 1) quia Filii Dei, per quos intellexerunt angelos, filias hominum sibi duxerunt uxores, Gen. VI, 2. 2) Quia ignis paratus dicitur diabolo, & angelis eius, Matth. XXV, 41. Resp. ad I. Per Filios Dei l. c. intelliguntur filii a piis patriarchis nati, & in ecclesia educati: hi viderunt filias hominum adspectu inordinato, quod essent pulchrae, & duxerunt uxores ex omnibus, quas elegerunt pro lubitu suo, contra voluntatem & verbum Dei. Ineptum autem est, cogitare hic de spiritibus angelicis, quibus matrimonium institutum non est; & ipsi nec generant, nec generantur. Ad II. Ignis infernalis non est elementaris, qui tantum corpora vrit, sed singularis, a Deo singulariter vna cum inferno paratus, Matth. XXV, 41. vt in aeternum spiritus & homines damnatos vrat. Quis enim dubitet, Deum posse eiusmodi ignem, qui angelos malos vltione quoque cruciet, condere?


### Q. 3. Are angels spirits, devoid of all corporeal mass?: IX. The difference of angels

IX. The difference of angels.

Angels differ from God in that their spiritual essence is dependent and finite a), from the separated soul in that their substance is complete b), from the remaining creatures in that they rejoice in intellect and free will c). Prob. a. God is an independent and infinite spirit; angels, since they have their being not from themselves, but from God, are dependent and finite spirits. Prob. b. The human soul is an incomplete spirit, ordered by itself and by its nature to the composition of the whole man. Hence also the separated soul has a natural propensity and inclination it has no relation to a body, with which it constitutes a complete human being as a component part; but angels are not naturally ordered to constitute a single thing, in themselves, with some component part, but have an essence terminated in themselves. Therefore, the soul is an incomplete spirit, while angels are complete spirits.

Hence the soul is an incomplete Spirit, angels are complete Spirits.

Prob. c.

Visible creatures, if you depart from man, lack intellect and will.

But angels are endowed with intellect and free will.

For the angels of God are wise, 2 Sam.

XIV, 20. Evil angels know Jesus the Son of God, Marc.

V, 7. Therefore angels, both good and evil, are participants of intellect.

The will of the angels is proven by a) the obedience of good angels, which they render to God, Psalm.

CIII, 20. and the apostasy of the evil ones, 2 Petr.

II, 4. b) The pious desire of good angels to look into the mystery concerning Christ, 1 Petr.

I, 12. The impious desire of evil angels to devour men, 1 Petr.

V, 8. c) Rewards bestowed upon good angels, and punishments inflicted upon the impious. Furthermore, the intellect and will of angels are indeed conceived by us, like the soul, as distinct from one another: but on the part of the thing, they differ neither from the angelic essence, nor from each other.

This is proven: 1) because angels live a spiritual life, which formally consists in intellect and will.

But just as life is of the essence of an angel, so too are intellect and will. 2) Intellect is of the essence of man.

Therefore, much more so of the essence of an angel. The antecedent is clear; because intellect, or reason, is the constitutive difference of man.

The consequence is proven: because angels understand more promptly and perfectly than men; since they are not so much averted from understanding by sensitive appetite as men are.

From which they are called intelligences and demons, because their being consists in the faculty of understanding.

3) If intellect and will do not enter into the essence and constitution of angels, they could be separated from them by the absolute power of God.

But the latter is absurd (ἄτοπον).

Therefore the former is as well. The consequence is proven: because proper accidents are separable from their subjects by divine power.

The latter is a manifest absurdity; for if intellect and will were separated from angels, there could be given an angel devoid of intellect, or irrational, and destitute of all liberty of acting, and thus plainly idle.

4) An angel approaches God most closely of all creatures.

Therefore it pertains to his perfection to know immediately, without a really distinct power, (though sometimes with an impressed species).

And indeed it cannot be denied that moral actions proceed immediately from an angel; otherwise they could not be imputed to them.

But since the principle of moral actions must be formally free, and only the will is free: it follows that the angelic will is the angelic essence itself.

There is an antithesis of certain Scholastics, who deny that intellect and will are of the essence of angels.

Their arguments are: I.

No creature can operate immediately without superadded accidents.

Therefore neither can an angel. The antecedent is proven: because to operate immediately belongs to God alone.

Resp.

I deny the antecedent; because created substances produce their natural properties immediately through emanative action, e.g., fire produces heat, water humidity, etc.

Instantia: God alone acts through his essence.

Therefore God alone acts without superadded qualities.

Resp.

To act through essence either signifies to act independently, or to act according to one's own nature, without the intervention of a superadded quality.

God understands independently: the intellect of angels depends on God.

Yet an angel is said to understand through his essence, insofar as the intellect is not a quality superadded to the angelic essence, but enters into the essential constitution of the angel.

II. If an angel understood through his essence, he would not need intelligible species to know: The consequent is false: Therefore the antecedent is also.

Resp.

1) An angel knows himself [The angel] knows through its own essence, because it is sufficiently proportioned to its intellect, and does not differ from itself: Therefore, for the knowledge of itself, it does not need an intelligible species. 2) Angels do indeed know external objects through intelligible species, because of distance; but it does not follow from this that the intellect is really distinct from the angelic essence, since the intelligible species may have been co-created with the angelic essence itself, as some wish, or they may be formed by the same and derived from the objects. III. An angel does not perpetually understand and will: Therefore it does not understand and will immediately. The antecedent is clear, because the angelic intellect and will can be hindered. The consequence is clear; because that which operates immediately (e.g., God) operates perpetually. Resp. 1) Distinguish between an uncreated immediate efficient cause, which is most pure act: and a created one, which is act pure only in a certain respect. That is God alone, who acts through his essence far differently than an angel, who is created, and is only in a certain respect pure act. God knows all things by one simple and eternal act of understanding: But angels know neither all things, nor simultaneously, but distinctly and through diverse concepts, yet not by simply apprehending, but also by composing and reasoning. 2) It is not absurd that an angel always knows itself, since intellection is the most vital action of angels, from which they seem never to cease. IV. If the intellect and will do not really differ from the angelic essence, the angelic intellect will be the angelic will: The consequent is absurd: Therefore the antecedent is also. The consequence of the major is evident from the most trite axiom: Those things which agree in a third thing, agree among themselves. Resp. Distinguish between the identical sense and the formal sense. If the intellect and will of angels are considered in the identical sense, as they are one and the same in the angelic nature; that proposition is true: the intellect of the angel is the will of the angel. But if they are viewed in the formal sense, as they are in our concepts; that proposition: the angelic intellect is the angelic will, is false; for the intellect and will of angels, because of the distinct acts they exercise, are represented by distinct inadequate concepts, and are said to differ virtually. Conf. D. BECHMANNI institut. theolog. p. 248. & D. BAYERI comp. theol. p. 285.

Latin:

IX. Angelorum differentia.

Differunt angeli a Deo, quod eorum essentia spiritualis dependens & finita est a), ab anima separata, quod eorum substantia completa est, b) a reliquis creaturis, quod intellectu & voluntate libera gaudent c). Prob. a. Deus est spiritus independens & infinitus; angeli, cum esse suum non a se, sed a Deo habeant, sunt spiritus dependentes & finiti. Prob. b. Anima humana est spiritus incompletus, per se & natura sua ordinatus ad totius hominis compositionem. Hinc etiam anima separata naturalem propensionem & inclinationem nein habet ad corpus, cum quo velut parte componente completum constituit hominem: at angeli naturaliter ordinati non sunt ad constituendum vnum, per se, cum parte quadam componente, sed habent essentiam in se terminatam. Proinde anima est Spiritus incompletus, angeli sunt Spiritus completi.

Proinde anima est Spiritus incompletus, angeli sunt Spiritus completi.

Prob. c.

Creaturæ visibiles, ab homine si discesseris, carent intellectu & voluntate.

At angeli intellectu & voluntate libera sunt præditi.

Etenim angeli Dei sunt sapientes, 2 Sam.

XIV, 20. Angeli mali cognoscunt Iesum Filium Dei, Marc.

V, 7. Ergo angeli tam boni, quam mali, sunt participes intellectus.

Voluntatem angelorum probant a) Angelorum bonorum obedientia, quam Deo præstant, Psalm.

CIII, 20. & malorum apostasia, 2 Petr.

II, 4. b) Angelorum bonorum pium desiderium introficiendi mysterium de Christo, 1 Petr.

I, 12. Angelorum malorum impium desiderium abforbendi homines, 1 Petr.

V, 8. c) Præmia in bonos angelos collata, & supplicia impiis irrogata. Ceterum intellectus & voluntas angelorum concipiuntur quidem a nobis, vt anima, & inter se distinctæ: at ex parte rei neque ab essentia angelica, neque inter se differunt.

Id quod probatur: 1) quia angeli viuunt vitam spiritualem, quæ formaliter consistit in intellectu & voluntate.

Sicut autem vita est de essentia angeli, ita & intellectus atque voluntas. 2) Intellectus est de essentia hominis.

Ergo multo magis de essentia angeli. Antecedens patet; quia intellectus, vel ratio, est differentia constitutiva hominis.

Consequentia probatur: quia angeli promtius & perfectius intelligunt, quam homines; quum appetitu sensitivo ab intelligendo non adeo auertantur vt homines.

Ex quo intelligentiæ & dæmones vocantur, propterea quod eorum esse in facultate intelligendi consistit.

3) Si intellectus & voluntas non ingreditur essentiam constitutionem angelorum, per absolutam Dei potentiam ab iis potest separari.

At posterius est ἄτοπον.

Ergo & prius. Consequentia probatur: quia accidentia propria per divinam potentiam separabilia sunt a subiectis suis.

Posterius est absurditas manifesta; nam si intellectus & voluntas separaretur ab angelis, posset dari angelus intellectus expers, vel irrationalis, omnique agendi libertate destitutus, atque adeo plane otiosus.

4) Angelus omnium creaturarum proxime accedit ad Deum.

Ergo ad perfectionem eius pertinet, immediate, citra potentiam realiter distinctam, (licet aliquando cum specie impressa) cognoscere.

Et sane negari non potest, actiones morales immediate ab angelo proficisci; ceteroqui ipsis imputari non possent.

Cum autem principium actionum moralium debeat esse formaliter liberum, sola vero voluntas fit libera: sequitur, voluntatem angelicam esse ipsam essentiam angelicam.

Antithesis est quorundam Scholasticorum, negantium, intellectum & voluntatem esse de essentia angelorum.

Quorum argumenta sunt: I.

Nulla creatura sine superadditis accidentibus immediate operari potest.

Ergo nec angelus. Antecedens probatur: quia immediate operari solius est Dei.

Resp.

Neg. antecedens; quia substantiæ creatæ immediate producunt suas naturales proprietates per actionem emanatiuam, v. gr. ignis calorem, aqua humiditatem &c.

Instantia: Solus Deus agit per essentiam.

Ergo solus Deus agit sine superadditis qualitatibus.

Resp.

Per essentiam agere, vel significat independerter agere, vel propriam agere naturam, sine interuentu superadditæ qualitatis.

Deus intelligit independerter: Angelorum intellectus a Deo dependet.

Dicitur tamen angelus per essentiam intelligere, quatenus intellectus non est superaddita essentiæ angelicæ qualitas, sed essentialem angeli constitutionem ingreditur.

II. Si angelus per essentiam intelligeret, non indigeret ad cognoscendum speciebus intelligibilibus: Consequens est falsum: Ergo & antecedens.

Resp.

1) Angelus seipsum cognoscit gnoscit per essentiam suam eo, quod intellectui suo satis proportionatus est, neque a seipso distat: Ergo ad sui ipsius cognitionem non indiget specie intelligibili. 2) Objecta externa cognoscunt quidem angeli per species intelligibiles, propter distantiam; at inde non sequitur, intellectum realiter ab essentia angelica esse distinctum, cum vel ipsi essentiae angelicae concreatae sint species intelligibiles, quod volunt nonnulli, vel ab eadem formentur & ab obiectis desumantur. III. Angelus non perpetuo intelligit & vult: Ergo non intelligit & vult immediate. Antecedens patet, quia intellectus & voluntas angelica impediri potest. Consequentia est clara; quia operans immediate (v. gr. Deus) perpetuo operatur. Resp. 1) Dist. inter caussam efficientem immediatam increatam, quae est actus purissimus: & creatam, quae est actus secundum quid purus. Illa est solus Deus, qui agit per essentiam longe aliter, quam angelus, qui creatus, & tantum secundum quid actus purus est. Deus vno simplici & aeterno intelligendi actu omnia cognoscit: At angeli neque omnia, neque simul cognoscunt, sed distincte & per diuersos conceptus, non tamen simpliciter apprehendendo, sed etiam componendo & discurrendo. 2) Non absurdum est, angelum seipsum semper cognoscere, cum intellectio sit actio angelorum maxime vitalis, a qua nunquam cessare videntur. IV. Si intellectus & voluntas realiter non differunt ab essentia angelica, intellectus angelicus erit voluntas angelica: Consequens est absurdum: Ergo & antecedens. Consequentia maioris liquet e tritissimo axiomate: Quae conueniunt in vno tertio, illa inter se conueniunt. Resp. Dist. inter sensum identicum, & formalem. Si intellectus & voluntas angelorum considerentur in sensu identico, prout in angelica natura sunt vnum & idem; propositio illa vera est: intellectus angeli est voluntas angeli. At si spectentur in sensu formali, prout in nostris sunt conceptibus; propositio illa: intellectus angelicus est voluntas angelica, est falsa; nam intellectus & voluntas angelorum ob distinctos, quos exercent actus, distinctis conceptibus inadaequatis repraesentantur, & virtualiter differre dicuntur. Conf. D. BECHMANNI institut. theolog. p. 248. & D. BAYERI comp. theol. p. 285.


### Quaest. V. Who created the angels?

God the Father a), the Son of God b), and the Holy Spirit c) created the angels. Prob. a. God the Father made his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire. Heb. 1:7. Conf. Ps. 104:4. Prob. b. By the Son of God were created all things that are in heaven, and that are on earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers, Col. 1:16. Invisible thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers are angels, so named because of the signal excellence and power conferred upon them by the Creator. Prob. c. By the Spirit of the mouth of God the heavens were made, and all the host of them. Ps. 33:6. That angels are also included under all the host of the heavens, we learn from 1 Kings 22:19. I saw Jehovah sitting upon his throne, and all the host of heaven standing by him, on his right hand and on his left. Conf. Neh. 9:6.

Latin:

Angelos creauit Deus Pater a), Filius Dei b), & Spiritus sanctus c). Prob. a. Deus Pater fecit angelos suos spiritus, & ministros suos ignis flammam. Hebr. I, 7. Conf. Ps. CIV, 4. Prob. b. Per Filium Dei creata sunt omnia, quae in coelis, & quae super terra visibilia & inuisibilia, siue throni, siue dominationes, siue principatus, siue potestates, Col. I, 16. Invisibiles throni, dominationes, principatus & potestates sunt angeli, ob insignem excellentiam & potentiam, ipsis a creatore collatam, ita denominati. Prob. c. Per Spiritum oris Dei caeli facti sunt, & omnis exercitus eorum. Ps. XXXIII, 6. Comprehendi autem sub omni exercitu coelorum etiam angelos, discimus ex 1 Reg. XXII, 19. Vidi Iehouam sedentem super throno suo, & vniuersum exercitum cœlorum stantem iuxta eum, a dextra eius & a sinistra eius. Conf. Nehem. IX, 6.


### Quaest. VI. Were the angels created before the fabrication of the world?

The angels were not created long before the fabrication of the world, but within the hexaemeron of creation described by Moses. Prob. I. Because Moses presents the beginning of all created things. Gen. 1:1. II. He openly testifies the same, that God finished all creation in the space of six days; and rested on the seventh day. Gen. 2:1, 2. III. Before the hexaemeron of creation there was nothing, except the Creator God, as John testifies: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. John 1:1, 2.

IV. By the style of Scripture, everything antemundane is eternal, Ps. XC, 2. Isa. XLVIII, 13. Prov. VIII, 22. V. Angels are reckoned among the works of the hexaemeron, Ps. CIV, 3. seqq. There is an antithesis of certain Fathers, Socinians, Arminians, Conrad Vorstius, Genebrard, and others, who are of the opinion that angels existed many centuries before this world was created. Who confirm their opinion with the following arguments: I. Moses, when he describes the creation of this universe, does not mention the angels. Therefore, the angels were not created with this universe. Resp. 1) It is not permitted to argue negatively from Holy Scripture in historical accounts. Moses was silent in the history of creation about the production of metals and minerals, which nevertheless, by the confession of all, were produced within the six days of creation. 2) Moses clearly described the origin of things that fall into the senses, but he insinuated the origin of the angels in Gen. II, 1, when he says: thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them. That angels belong to the host of the heavens, we have shown above from 1 Kings XXII, 19. Neh. IX, 6. II. Whoever, when the earth was founded, praised God, they were before the foundation of the earth: But the angels &c. Job XXXVIII, 8. Therefore. Resp. I deny the major. For those who praised God at the foundation of the earth could have existed simultaneously with the earth, even if they did not exist before it. Therefore, there is a distinction between antecedent existence and simultaneous existence. III. Whoever always see the face of God, they are from eternity: But the angels &c. Matt. XVIII, 10. Therefore. Resp. The angels always see the face of God, after they are created and translated into a glorious state. That διὰ παντὸς in Matt. XVIII, 10 denotes a duration, perennial without end, but not without a beginning. IV. To whom the blessed hope was promised before the times of the ages, they existed from eternity: But to the angels &c. Therefore. The minor is evident from Tit. I, 2. where the Apostle says: which blessed hope God promised before the times of the ages. But God did not promise the blessed hope from eternity to men, because it is manifest that they were created on the sixth day of creation: Therefore to the angels. Resp. In the cited passage, the Apostle is speaking not of angels, but of elect men, v. 1, to whom the hope of blessedness was promised before the times of the ages, by reason of the divine decree, and revealed through the Gospel at a divinely appointed time. But the divine promise, conceived by an eternal decree, does not require creatures existing from eternity. Men were chosen before the foundations of the world were laid, Eph. I, 4, yet they did not exist from eternity. V. That opinion from which a sudden fall of the angels from the beginning of creation is inferred, that is not probable: From that opinion, by which it is established that angels were created within the hexaemeron, it is inferred &c. Therefore. The major is proved; because it is improbable that creatures, divinely endowed with exceptional holiness, would have immediately fallen away from their concreated holiness. The minor is evident; because it is gathered that the angels who were the seducers of the protoplasts of men fell within the six days in which they are thought to have been created. Resp. I deny the minor. For we do not assert that the angels fell within the hexaemeron of creation; since God, having looked upon the works of the hexaemeron, judged them to be very good, Gen. I, 31. Nor can those who dissent teach by a valid argument that the devil stood in the truth for a long time.

Latin:

Angeli non longe ante fabricationem mundi, sed intra hexaemeron creationis a Mose descriptum sunt conditi. Prob. I. Quia Moses principium omnium rerum creatarum sistit. Gen. I, 1. II. Idem aperte testatur, Deum omnem creationem sex dierum spatio absoluisse; & die septimo quieuisse Gen. II, 1. 2. III. Ante hexaëmeron creationis nil fuit, nisi creator Deus, teste Ioanne: In principio erat verbum, & verbum erat apud Deum, & Deus erat verbum. Ioann. I, 1. 2.

IV. Stilo scripturæ omne antemundanum æternum est, Ps. XC, 2. Es. XLVIII, 13. Prou. IIX, 22. V. Angeli operibus hexaëmeri accensentur, Ps. CIV, 3. seqq. Antithesis est quorundam Patrum, Socinianorum, Arminianorum, Conradi Vorstii, Genebrardi & aliorum, opinantium, angelos multis sæculis ante hunc mundum conditum exstitisse. Qui suam opinionem sequentibus firmant argumentis: I. Moses, cum describit creationem huius vniuersi, non meminit angelorum. Ergo angeli cum hoc vniuerso non sunt conditi. Resp. 1) Ex sacra scriptura in historicis relationibus negatiue argumentari haud licet. Reticuit Moses in historia creationis productionem metallorum & mineralium, quæ tamen omnium confessione intra sextiduum creationis producta sunt. 2) Moses originem rerum in sensus incurrentium luculenter quidem descripsit, originem autem angelorum insinuauit Gen. II, 1. cum inquit: absoluti itaque sunt cœli & terra, & omnis exercitus eorum. Ad exercitum cœlorum pertinere angelos, supra ostendimus ex 1 Reg. XII, 19. Nehem. IX, 6. II. Quicunque, cum fundaretur terra, Deum laudarunt, illi fuerunt ante fundationem terræ: Atqui angeli &c. Iob. XXXVIII, 8. Ergo. Resp. Neg. maior. Nam qui laudarunt Deum in fundatione terræ, cum terra simul esse potuerunt, licet non ante eam exstiterint. Dist. itaque est inter exsistentiam antecedaneam, & simultaneam. III. Qui semper vident faciem Dei, illi sunt ab æterno: Atqui angeli &c.Matth. XVIII, 10. Ergo. Resp. Angeli semper vident faciem Dei, postquam sunt creati & in statum gloriosum translati. Illud διὰ παντὸς Matth. VIII, 10. notat durationem, fine fine perennem, at non initii expertem. IV. Quibus beata spes ante tempora sæcularia est promissa, illi ab æterno exstiterunt: Atqui angelis &c. Ergo. Minor patet ex Tit. I, 2. vbi Apostolus inquit: quam beatam spem promisit Deus ante tempora sæcularia. Non promisit autem Deus beatam spem ab æterno hominibus, quia palam est, illos sexto creationis die conditos esse: E. angelis. Resp. Loco citato apostolo sermo est non de angelis, sed de hominibus electis, v. 1. quibus promissa est beatitudo speranda, ante tempora sæcularia, ratione decreti diuini, & reuelata per euangelium diuinitus statuto tempore. At promissio diuina, concepta æterno decreto, non requirit creaturas ab æterno exsistentes. Homines ante iacta mundi fundamenta sunt electi, Eph. I, 4. neque tamen ab æterno exstiterunt. V. Ex qua sententia infertur subitus angelorum a primordio creationis lapsus, illa non est probabilis: Ex sententia illa, qua statuuntur angeli conditi intra hexaëmeron, infertur &c. Ergo. Maior probatur; quia iinprobabile est, creaturas, eximia sanctitate diuinitus præditas, confestim a concreata sanctitate desciuissē. Minor patet; quia angelos seductores protoplastorum hominum intra sextiduum, in quo putantur esse conditi, defecisse colligitur. Resp. Neg. minor. Neque enim afferimus, angelos esse lapsos intra creationis hexaëmeron; quoniañ Deus intuitus opera hexaëmeri, ea valde bona esse, ex vero æstimauit. Gen. I, 31. Neque valido argumento docere queunt dissidentes, diabolum diu in veritate stetisse.


### Question VII. What attributes are common to all angels?

Attributes common to good and evil angels are partly affirmative, partly negative. The negative are: indivisibility a), invisibility b), immutability c), immortality d), illocality e).

Prob. a. Angels are indivisible into quantitative parts; for the reason that they are devoid of matter: for the root of quantity and divisibility is matter.

Prob. b. Angels are invisible, because they are spirits. They are invisible by nature, they have been seen by economy, or by a peculiar divine dispensation. They are invisible in themselves and their nature, they have been seen in assumed bodies: which they adopted, and united to themselves, by a union not essential, or personal, but merely accidental.

Prob. c. Angels are immutable not absolutely and simply, but comparatively and respectively. God alone is simply immutable, angels are immutable in a certain respect; because they are not subject to physical mutations, which are proper to natural bodies. For angels neither beget, nor are begotten; nor do they grow, nor are they diminished: nor do they age, nor are they corrupted: nor do they proceed on feet (which indeed they do not have) from place to place. Nor are they, however, superior to every mutation; for they vary their 'where', they rejoice, they are saddened, they love, they are averse: which are moral mutations.

Prob. d. Angels are immortal and incorruptible not independently, originally, and by eternal essence; for thus God alone is immortal, 1 Tim. VI, 6. but they are immortal dependently, participatively, and by the grace of God creating and preserving. By equal reason they are said to be incorruptible physically from within, and from without. From within they are incorruptible: because they do not have an internal principle of mutation or corruption in themselves, which is matter. Nor is any physical body of such power that it is able to corrupt a spirit or an angel from without. But if it be said metaphysically that what can be reduced to nothing by absolute divine power is corruptible, angels are not incorruptible; because at God's command they can fall back into that nothingness from which they emerged. In which sense D. SCHERZER, system. theol. p. 102, prefers to call angels annihilable, rather than corruptible.

Prob. e. Angels are illocal; because they are not material, nor do they have parts outside of parts. For locality is an affection of a natural body, which occupies a certain space commensurate to itself.

Latin:

Attributa, angelis bonis & malis communia, alia sunt affirmatiua, alia negatiua. Negatiua sunt indiuisibilitas a), inuisibilitas b), immutabilitas c), immortalitas d), illocalitas e).

Prob. a. Indiuifibiles sunt angeli in partes quantitatiuas; eo, quod materiæ sunt expertes: quantitatis enim & diuifibilitatis radix est materia.

Prob. b. Inuifibiles sunt angeli, quia sunt spiritus. Sunt inuisibiles per naturam, visi sunt per œconomiam, siue per peculiarem dispensationem diuinam. Inuifibiles sunt in se & natura sua, visi sunt in assumtis corporibus: quæ adsciuerunt, sibique vniuerunt, vnione non essentiali, aut personali, sed mere accidentali.

Prob. c. Immutabiles sunt angeli non absolute & simpliciter, sed comparate & respectiue. Solus Deus simpliciter immutabilis est, angeli sunt immutabiles secundum quid; quia non subiacent mutationibus physicis, quæ corporibus naturalibus sunt propriæ. Neque enim angeli generant, nec generantur; nec crescunt, nec minuuntur: nec senescunt, nec corrumpuntur: nec progrediuntur pedibus (quippe quos non habent) de loco in locum. Neque tamen omni mutatione superiores sunt; variant enim suum vbi, lætantur, tristantur, amant, auersantur: quæ sunt mutationes morales.

Prob. d. Immortales & incorruptibiles sunt angeli non independenter, originaliter, & per essentiam æternam; nam sic solus Deus est immortalis, 1 Tim. VI, 6. sed sunt immortales dependenter, participatiue, & per Dei creantis atque conseruantis gratiam. Pari ratione dicuntur incorruptibiles physice ab intra, & ab extra. Ab intra sunt incorruptibiles: quia non habent internum in seipsis mutationis, aut corruptionis principium, quod est materia. Neque vllum corpus physicum tantæ est virtutis, vt spiritum, aut angelum ab extra corrumpere valeat. At si metaphysice dicatur corruptibile, quod in nihilum redigi potest a potentia diuina absoluta, angeli non sunt incorruptibiles; quia iubente Deo in illud recidere queunt nihilum, e quo emerferunt. Quo sensu D. SCHERZER. system. theol. p. 102. angelos mauult appellare annihilabiles, quam corruptibiles.

Prob. e. Illocales sunt angeli; quia non sunt materiales, neque habent partes extra partes. Localitas enim est affectio corporis naturalis, quod occupat certum spatium sibi commensuratum.


### Quæst. VIII. What are the affirmative attributes common to all angels?

The affirmative attributes common to good and evil angels are a) knowledge, b) freedom of will, c) power, d) eternal duration, e) definitive 'ubietas' (being-in-a-place), f) agility.

Prob. a. Since not only good angels, but also evil ones possess intellect, knowledge of many things is not to be denied to them. But what, and of what kind, the cognition of good and evil angels is, becomes known more certainly and clearly from the original state of both, and that which followed it, whether of glory or of misery.

Prob. b. Will accompanies intellect, and freedom accompanies will. Angelic will is free, both by reason of immanent acts, the volition or nolition of this or that object, and by reason of various external effects, while it does now this, now that, freely.

Prob. c. The power of angels is great, but finite. It is great; for they are indeed called mighty in strength, Ps. CII, 20, armed strong ones, Luke XI, 21. For they can a) move bodies by transferring them from place to place, Matt. IV, 5, 8, Acts VIII, 39. b) Prostrate bodies, 2 Kings XIX, 35. c) Assume bodies, and unite them to themselves not indeed essentially or personally, but accidentally, and assist them, as a pilot assists a ship, d) speak with God, angels, and men. They speak with God by directing their thoughts to God, while they adore and praise Him: they speak with angels, while they freely imprint intelligible species upon themselves: they speak with men, with a sensible & distinct voice, formed in the air in imitation of the human voice.

Angelic power is finite, not infinite; for since infinite power is proper to the Creator, it is incommunicable to a mere creature.

Hence it follows that angels cannot create; since creation is a work of infinite virtue, which angels lack: to generate.

For if an angel generates, it generates either as a spirit, or as clothed in a body. Not as a spirit; because generation is a vegetative act, i.e., a vegetative principle, which an angel is not, presupposing: Not as clothed in a body; for the assumed body is either living or dead. If it is living, the generation does not proceed from the angel, but from the body, endowed with a living soul: If it is devoid of life, it is not a principle of vital action. Therefore, angels cannot generate.

You say: There are changelings (lycanthropes) who are so monstrous that they have no father other than the devil.

Resp. Monstrous births are from nature erring or failing in generating.

Some changelings are not true humans, but diabolical specters. Some changelings are born from possessed or deranged humans, whose imagination the devil has disturbed, so that it might fail in generating, whose fetuses the devil can substitute in place of legitimate children.

Nor can angels change substances.

For no one can turn the course of nature, except God, the author of nature.

Therefore, the changing of creatures is held to be the criterion, or most certain indication, of the most glorious divine power, Jo.
