II, 9. Some object in vain: 1) that the Egyptian magicians, by the help of the devil, changed rods into serpents; 2) that experience testifies that there are lycanthropes, i.e., men who have been turned into wolves by the devil.

Resp. to 1. The rods of the Egyptian magicians were changed into serpents not truly or really, but apparently, through the illusions of the evil spirit, who cast a film over the eyes of the onlookers, and very quickly threw the serpents into the midst from nearby pools.

To 2. Those who seem to be lycanthropes are in reality men. To perform true miracles.

For miracles are varied and unusual effects, beyond the order of all created nature, produced by God.

Hence only Jehovah is said to perform miracles. Ps. LXXII, 18.

Nevertheless, angels can perform certain wondrous things by dazzling the eyes and disturbing the medium, or by applying active things to passive things very quickly; which speed snatches the minds of the onlookers into admiration. To drive away all diseases.

For diseases are divinely sent either as punishment (τιμωρία), the penalties of sins, or as discipline (παιδεία), fatherly chastisements, Amos III, 6, which no creature, no angel can avert.

But those diseases which the devil inflicts, he has the power to remove; although no help should be sought from him.

For the evil spirit heals the body so that it may destroy the soul. To resurrect the dead; for no one can restore life to these, except the arbiter of life.

Abraham acknowledged that, who believed in God, who gives life to the dead, Rom.

IV, 17. You say: The devil raised the prophet Samuel from the dead, 1 Sam.

XXVIII, 7. Resp.

Distinguish between the true Samuel and the personated or masked one.

He who was represented to Saul under the guise of Samuel through the illusions of the devil was not the true Samuel, but had merely put on the external appearance of Samuel, but in actual fact was a diabolical specter.

Proof of the same.

The duration of angels indeed has a beginning, but lacks an end, and therefore is commonly called an aeon; for this recognizes a beginning, but knows no end.

That an aeon is rightly ascribed to angels is clear from the fact that angels have no principle of corruption from within, and thus cannot be naturally destroyed, but always continue their duration of living without danger of corruption.

Proof of the same. Angels are in a definitive place; since they define for themselves at will a certain space, in which they are whole in the whole, and whole in any part of the space; because their essence is indivisible.

Obs.

God is said to be in a repletive place; since He fills all things in all things.

Physical bodies are in a circumscriptive place; therefore, because it is commensurate with itself, or occupying; therefore, because it is commensurate with itself.

Latin:

Attributa affirmatiua angelis bonis & malis communia sunt a) scientia, b) voluntatis libertas, c) potentia, d) duratio æuiterna, e) vbietas definitiua, f) agilitas.

Prob. a. Cum angeli boni haud tantum, sed & mali intellectu polleant, multarum rerum scientia illis non est deneganda. At quæ, & qualis sit bonorum & malorum angelorum cognitio, ex vtrorumque statu originali, & hunc insecuto vel gloriæ, vel miseriæ certius & liquidius innotescit.

Prob. b. Intellectum voluntas, voluntatem libertas comitatur. Libera autem est voluntas angelica, tum ratione actuum immanentium, volitionis aut nolitionis huius vel illius obiecti, tum ratione diuersorum effectuum externorum, dum modo hoc, modo aliud facit libere.

Prob. c. Potentia angelorum magna, sed finita est. Magna est; dicuntur quippe fortes robore, Ps. CII, 20. fortes armati, Luc. XI, 21. Possunt enim a) corpora mouere de loco in locum transferendo, Matth. IV, 5. 8. Act. VIII, 39. b) Corpora prosternere, 2 Reg. XIX, 35. c) Corpora assumere, eaque non quidem essentialiter aut personaliter, sed accidentaliter sibi vnire, iisque assistere, vti assistit gubernator naui, d) loqui cum Deo, angelis & hominibus. Cum Deo loquuntur, cogitationes suas ad Deum dirigendo, dum ipsum adorant & laudant: cum angelis loquuntur, dum species intelligibiles sibi libere imprimunt: cum hominibus loquuntur, voce sensibili & distincta, ad vocis humanæ imitationem efformata in aëre.

Finita, non autem infinita est potentia angelica; infinita enim potentia cum creatori sit propria, creaturæ meræ est incommunicabilis.

Inde fit, vt angeli nequeant creare; cum creatio sit opus infinitæ virtutis, qua carent angeli: generare.

Nam si angelus generat, generat vel vt spiritus, vel vt corpore vestitus. Non vt spiritus; quia generatio est actus vegetativus, i. e. principium vegetativum, quale non est angelus, supponens: Non vt corpore vestitus; nam corpus assumtum vel est viuum, vel mortuum. Si viuum est, generatio non prouenit ab angelo, sed a corpore, anima viuente prædito: Si est expers vitæ, non est principium actionis vitalis. Ergo angeli non possunt generare.

Dicis: Dantur campsores (λυκάνθρωποι) qui adeo monstrosi sunt, vt nullum alium nisi diabolum, patrem habeant.

Resp. Partus monstrosi sunt a natura in generando aberrante, vel deficiente.

Quidam campsores non sunt veri homines, sed spectra diabolica. Quidam campsores geniti sunt ab hominibus obsessis, vel correptitiis, quorum phantasiam diabolus turbauit, vt deficeret in generando, quorum fœtus loco legitimorum liberorum diabolus potest substituere.

Nec possunt angeli substantias immutare.

Naturæ quippe cursum nemo conuertere potest, nisi naturæ auctor Deus.

Idcirco immutatio creaturarum gloriosissimæ potentiæ diuinæ habetur κριτήριον, seu certissimum indicium, Io.

II, 9. Frustra obiiciunt nonnulli: 1) quod magi Aegyptiaci ope diaboli mutauerint baculos in serpentes; 2) quod experientia testetur, dari λυκάνθρωπος, i. e. homines, qui in lupos per diabolum sint conuersi.

Resp. ad 1. Baculi magorum Aegyptiacorum sunt mutati in serpentes non vere aut realiter, sed apparenter, per præstigias cacodæmonis, qui glaucoma aspectantium oculis offudit, serpentesque celerrime lacubus vicinis in medium proiecit.

Ad 2. qui videntur esse λυκάνθρωποι, reuera sunt homines. Vera miracula facere.

Miracula enim sunt effectus vari & insoliti, præter ordinem totius naturæ creatæ, a Deo producti.

Hinc solus Iehouah miracula facere dicitur. Ps. LXXII, 18.

Facere tamen possunt angeli mirabilia quædam, oculos præstringendo, & medium turbando, vel actiua passiuis celerrime applicando; quæ celeritas animos spectantium in admirationem rapit. Morbos omnes depellere.

Sunt enim morbi diuinitus immissi vel τιμωρία, pœnæ peccatorum, vel παιδεία, paternæ castigationes, Amos. III, 6. quas nulla creatura, nullus angelus auertere potest.

At quos morbos diabolus infligit, hos amoliri valet; quamuis nullum ab eo expetendum sit auxilium.

Sanat quippe cacodæmon corpus, vt perdat animam. Mortuos resuscitare; his enim reddere vitam nemo, nisi arbiter vitæ, potest.

Agnouit id Abraham, qui credidit Deo, viuificanti mortuos, Rom.

IV, 17. Dicis: Diabolus prophetam Samuelem ex mortuis excitauit, 1 Sam.

XXVIII, 7. Resp.

Dist. inter Samuelem verum, & personatum, seu laruatum.

Qui per præstigias diaboli sub habitu Samuelis Sauli repræsentabatur, non erat verus Samuel, sed externam tantum speciem Samuelis induerat, re autem vera spectrum diabolicum erat.

Prob. d.

Duratio angelorum habet quidem initium, sed caret fine, ideoque communiter vocatur æuum; hoc enim agnoscit initium, sed nescit finem.

Recte autem angelis æuum adscribi, liquet ex eo, quod angeli nullum ab intra principium corruptionis habent, adeoque naturaliter destrui nequeunt, sed suam viuendi durationem sine periculo corruptionis semper continuant.

Prob. e. Sunt angeli in vbi definitiuo; quoniam pro lubitu certum sibi definiunt spatium, in quo toto sunt toti, & toti in qualibet spatii parte; propterea quod essentia illorum est indiuisibilis.

Obs.

Deus dicitur esse in vbi repletiuo; quoniam omnia in omnibus implet.

Corpora physica sunt in vbi circumscriptiuo; ideo, quod commensuratum sibi circumscriptiuo, seu occupatiuo; ideo, quod commensuratum sibi.


### Question X. How many states of angels are there?

occupy space, and are circumscribed by the surrounding air.

But angels are not in a repletive place; because they are not everywhere, like God: nor in an occupative place; since, according to the nature of their spiritual essence, they do not occupy a commensurate space.

For measure follows quantity, of which the angel is devoid.

Prob. f. The agility and velocity of angels is wondrous, so that without local motion, such as that of bodies, and thus without the succession of parts, which they do not possess, they can vary their place most swiftly.

Nor, however, does it seem that all motion should be denied to angels, since they are present now here, now elsewhere.

And although the motion of angels is most rapid, it is nevertheless not instantaneous, for the reason that the space in which they move is extended and continuous, which no creature can traverse in an instant.

Quest. IX. How great is the number of angels?

Prob. The Holy Scriptures teach that the number of both good and evil angels is immense.

For it is said that a thousand thousands minister to God, and a myriad of myriads stand before him, Dan.

VII, 10. Moreover, Christ himself asserts that, were he to ask, more than twelve legions of angels would easily be sent to him by the Father.

Furthermore, an entire legion of impure spirits is said to have inhabited one man, Mark.

V, 8. A legion among the Romans was commonly a multitude of six thousand soldiers.

Quest. X. How manifold is the state of angels?

Obs. In the state of grace, angels were wayfarers.

See GERHARD'S disput. isagog. p.

557. In the state of glory are the good, in the state of misery the evil.

Prob. a. 1) All things that God made were in the beginning very good, Gen.

I, 31. Therefore, also the angels.

You say: The cited passage refers to natural goodness, such as that of simple and mixed bodies.

Resp. It refers to the goodness adapted to the nature of each created thing: but for free agents, of whose rank angels are, the adapted and fitting goodness is moral: for when this is lacking, they are evil.

2) The devil did not stand in the truth, John.

VIII, 44. Therefore, before the fall, he was instructed in true wisdom and justice. The reason for the consequence is: because privation presupposes a habit; nor can anyone rightly be said not to persist in a thing, unless the concession of the thing in which he ought to have persevered is presupposed.

Prob. b. The good angels διὰ παντὸς, always see the face of God, Matt.

XVIII, 10. Those who have been admitted to the everlasting intuition of God cannot but perpetually enjoy and be most fully satisfied by the goodness of God; since before the face of God is the fullness of joys, and pleasures at his right hand.

Ps. XVI, 11. The number of angels is indeed very great, but to us humans it is innumerable.

The state of angels is either original, or that which followed the original.

The original state is the state of grace, which in the first creation through the grace of the creator O.

M. all angels obtained, and were created equally wise and holy in the same, and were placed on the way to eternal beatitude a).

The state which followed the original is either of glory or of misery.

The state of glory is that in which the angels, who persisted in the concrete wisdom and holiness, admitted to the clear intuition of God, perpetually enjoy his most exuberant goodness b).

The state of misery is the most sorrowful condition of those angels who of their own accord fell away from God c).

Prob. c. That the condition of the fallen angels is most miserable, St. Peter teaches in 2 Epist. c. II, 4. God did not spare the angels who sinned, but casting them down into chains of darkness, delivered them to be reserved for judgment.

The antithesis was formerly (1) of the Manichaeans, who maintained that not all angels were created good in the first creation, but that some were created evil; (2) of certain Papists, denying that the angels were created in justice and holiness, but in a state of pure naturals, i.e., neither just nor unjust. Their arguments are: I. Whoever was a murderer immediately from the beginning, he was not created good. But the devil &c. Therefore. The minor is proved from John VIII, 44. Resp. The place cited is not understood as the beginning of creation, but of the defection, so that the sense may be: As soon as the devil departed from the rule of right, he intended the death of men. He enticed the first-formed men into sin with a great gap of promises, which death followed. For which reason the author of Wisdom says in chapter II, 24. By the envy of the devil death entered into the world. Instance: The devil is said to have sinned from the beginning, 1 John III, 8. Therefore from the beginning of creation. Resp. (1) John teaches that the devil is the author of sin. (2) John does not say: The devil sinned from the beginning, but he sins from the beginning, as if to say: From the time when the devil first sinned, he has not ceased to sin: It is proper and perpetual to him to do evil. II. If all things were created good by God, God will not be the creator of the devil; for he is the enemy of all goodness: But God is the creator of the devil: Therefore. Resp. The devil is considered either as a creature, or as the devil, the slanderer of the highest good. He was created by God as a creature, not as a slanderer.

Latin:

spatium occupant, & ab ambiente aere circumscribuntur.

At angeli non sunt in ubi repletivo; quia non sunt ubique, sicut Deus: neque in ubi occupativo; quoniam iuxta indolem spiritualis suae naturae commensuratum non occupant spatium.

Mensura enim sequitur quantitatem, cuius expers est angelus.

Prob. f. Mira est angelorum agilitas & velocitas, ut sine motu locali, quale est corporum, atque adeo sine successione partium, quas non habent, ubi suum celerrime variare queant.

Neque tamen omnis motus angelis denegandus videtur, cum modo hic, modo alibi adsint.

Et quamuis angelorum motus sit rapidissimus, non tamen est instantaneus, propterea, quod spatium, in quo mouentur, extensum atque continuum est, quod nulla creatura in instanti transire potest.

Quaest. IX. Quantus est numerus angelorum?

Prob. Ingentem tam bonorum, quam malorum angelorum esse numerum, docent sacrae litterae.

Etenim dicuntur mille millia ministrare Deo, & myrias myriadum coram eo stare, Dan.

VII, 10. Quin & Christus ipse asserit, sibi roganti facile plures, quam duodecim legiones angelorum a patre missum iri.

Impurorum autem spirituum integra legio vnum incoluisse hominem dicitur, Marc.

V, 8. Legio apud Romanos communiter sex millium militum multitudo erat.

Quaest. X. Quotuplex est angelorum status?

Obs. In statu gratiae angeli fuerunt viatores.

Vid. GERHARDI disput. isagog. p.

557. In statu gloriae sunt boni, in statu miseriae mali.

Prob. a. 1) Omnia, quae Deus fecit, fuerunt initio valde bona, Gen.

I, 31. E. & angeli.

Dicis; Intelligitur loco citato bonitas naturalis, qualis est corporum simplicium & mixtorum.

Resp. Intelligitur bonitas, cuique naturae rerum creatarum attemperata: at agentibus liberis, e quorum censu sunt angeli, attemperata & conueniens bonitas est moralis: hac enim deficiente sunt mali.

2) Diabolus in veritate non stetit, Io.

VIII, 44. E. ante lapsum vera sapientia & iustitia fuit instructus. Ratio consequentiae est; quia priuatio praesupponit habitum: nec potest recte quispiam dici non persistere in re, nisi praesupponatur concessio rei, in qua perseuerare debuit.

Prob. b. Angeli boni διὰ παντὸς, semper vident faciem Dei, Matth.

XVIII, 10. Qui ad sempiternum Dei intuitum sunt admissi, non possunt non bonitate Dei perpetuo frui & plenissime satiari; siquidem coram facie Dei est satietas gaudiorum, & amoenitates ad dextram eius.

Ps. XVI, 11. Numerus angelorum est quidem admodum magnus, sed nobis hominibus innumerabilis.

Status angelorum est vel originalis, vel originalem secutus.

Status originalis est status gratiae, quem in prima creatione per gratiam creatoris O.

M. omnes angeli sunt nacti, & in eodem aequaliter sapientes sanctique conditi, atque in via ad aeternam beatitudinem collocati sunt a).

Status, originalem secutus, est vel gloriae, vel miseriae.

Status gloriae est, in quo angeli, qui in concreta sapientia & sanctitate perstiterunt, admissi ad clarum intuitum Dei, huius exuberantissima bonitate perpetuo fruuntur b).

Status miseriae est conditio tristissima illorum angelorum, qui sponte sua a Deo defecerunt c).

Prob. c. Tristissimam esse conditionem angelorum lapsorum, docet S. Petrus 2 Epist. c. II, 4. Deus angelis, qui peccarunt, non pepercit, sed catenis tenebrarum detrudens tradidit in iudicium asse uatos.

Antithesis fuit olim (1) Manichæorum, qui statuerunt, non omnes angelos in prima creatione bonos, sed quosdam malos esse conditos; (2) quorundam Pontificiorum, negantium, angelos fuisse creatos in iustitia & sanctitate, sed in statu purorum naturalium, i. e. nec iustus, nec iniustos. Quorum argumenta sunt: I. Quicunque statim ab initio fuit homicida, is non est bonus creatus. Atqui diabolus &c. E. Minor prob. ex Io. VIII, 4. Resp. Loc. cit. non intelligitur primordium creationis, sed defectionis, vt sensus sit: Simulatque diabolus a regula recti desciuit, hominum mortem intendit. Illexit magno promissorum hiatu homines protoplastos in peccatum, quod mors secuta est. Qua de caussa inquit auctor Sapientiæ cap. II, 24. Inuidia diaboli mors in mundum intrauit. Instantia: Diabolus ab initio peccasse dicitur, 1 Io. III, 8. Ergo ab initio creationis. Resp. (1) Docet Ioannes, diabolum esse auctorem peccati. (2) Non dicit Ioannes: Diabolus ab initio peccauit, sed ab initio peccat, q. d. Ex quo primum diabolus peccauit, peccare non desiit: Est ipsi proprium & perpetuum, male agere. II. Si omnia bona a Deo creata sunt, Deus non erit creator diaboli; nam hic omnis bonitatis hostis est: At Deus est creator diaboli: E. Resp. Diabolus consideratur vel vt creatura, vel vt diabolus, calumniator summi boni. Conditus est a Deo, vt creatura, non vt calumniator.


### Question XI. With what gifts and powers did God instruct the angels in the state of grace?

The angels in the state of grace were adorned by God with exceptional wisdom and perfect holiness.

Prob. (1) Because all angels were created for eternal blessedness; for they were created equal in condition and of the same nature. That some, outside the intuition of the fall, were created for eternal damnation, is repugnant to divine justice. Therefore, it is necessary that all were created for eternal blessedness. Wherefore they were also instructed with sufficient powers and necessary grace, by which they could attain the end for which they were created. That grace implied (1) on the part of the intellect a certain habitual light of the intellect, or concreated knowledge, for knowing God and His will, (2) habitual holiness of the will, by which the angels in the state of the way could institute and perfect all actions conformably to the eternal law of God. (2) The devil did not stand in the truth, John VIII, 44. i.e. he did not retain the concreated wisdom of the intellect and the true holiness of the will, with which, as a divine image, the angels were adorned in the first creation. Compare D. DANNMAV. hodof. phænom. III. p. 28. You say: If the angels were originally created in exceptional wisdom and perfect justice, they could not depart from God. Resp. Perfect justice was concreated to the angels, but not immutable or unlosable. For the will of the angels in the state of grace was not determined to perpetually love and choose the good, but God had granted the angels freedom of will with a concreated propensity toward the good, so that there was in them not a proximate, but a most remote power to sin, consisting in the negation of the impossibility of sinning, and the unlosability of the concreated gifts. But the angels, having abused their freedom of will, of their own accord departed from God, the highest good.

Latin:

Angeli in statu gratiæ a Deo eximia sapientia & sanctitate perfecta exornati erant.

Prob. (1) Quia angeli omnes creati sunt ad æternam beatitudinem; æquales enim conditione & eadem natura creati sunt. Nonnullos, extra intuitum lapsus, creatos esse ad æternam damnationem, iustitiæ diuinæ repugnat. Omnes ergo ad æternam beatitudinem conditos esse oportet. Quapropter etiam sufficientibus viribus & gratia necessaria instructi fuerunt, qua finem, ad quem conditi sunt, consequi potuerunt. Gratia illa importabat (1) ex parte intellectus lucem quandam habitualem intellectus, seu concreatam scientiam, ad cognoscendum Deum, eiusque voluntatem, (2) sanctitatem habitualem voluntatis, qua poterant angeli in statu viæ actiones omnes æternæ Dei legi conformiter instituere & perficere. (2) Diabolus non stetit in veritate, Io. VIII, 44. h. e. concreatam intellectus sapientiam, & sanctitatem voluntatis veram non retinuit, qua velut imagine diuina angeli in prima creatione ornati fuerunt. Confer. D. DANNMAV. hodof. phænom. III. p. 28 . Dicis: Si angeli in sapientia eximia & iustitia perfecta primitus conditi fuerunt, a Deo desciscere nequiuerunt. Resp. Concreata erat angelis iustitia perfecta, sed non immutabilis aut inamissibilis. Neque enim voluntas angelorum in statu gratiæ determinata erat ad perpetuo amandum & eligendum bonum, sed concesserat Deus angelis libertatem arbitrii cum concreata propensione ad bonum, vt non proxima, sed remotissima in ipsis esset potentia ad peccandum, consistens in negatione impossibilitatis ad peccandum, & inamissibilitatis donorum concreatorum. At angeli libertate arbitrii abusi sponte sua a Deo summo bono desciuerunt.


### Question XII

XII. Who are the good angels?

Good angels are those who have persisted in the true wisdom and holiness with which they were created, and, having been illuminated by God with the light of glory, and thus confirmed in good, are so immune from the danger of sinning that they clearly behold God and perpetually enjoy His goodness. Obs. I. The good angels were confirmed in good at the time when the light of glory was infused into them by God, so that their confirmation in good, as regards the thing itself, is nothing other than the infusion of the light of glory, by which they know God intuitively.

Obs. II.

In the state of pilgrimage, the angels were able not to sin, i.e., there was not in them a proximate power or propensity to sin, yet there was in them a remote power to transgress: in the state of glory, the angels cannot sin, i.e., there is in them neither a proximate nor a remote power to transgress, but their ἀναμαρτησία, or impeccability, is immutable, and their holiness is unloseable. Proof.

1) From the election of the angels. The good angels are called elect, 1 Tim. V, 21, because they were destined by the eternal decree of God to blessedness everlasting without end. For God foresaw the persevering obedience of certain angels, not indeed as a meritorious cause; since the obedience of the angels, being due and temporary, has no power of merit before God, nor the power of impelling His will to decree or give the good of eternal blessedness; but as a certain condition annexed to His decree, which He benevolently regarded, and moved by most liberal goodness, He granted the reward of confirmation to the angels.

They were not indeed elected by God as sinful men are said to be elected on account of the merit of Christ apprehended by persevering faith: yet they were separated from the fallen angels and transferred to eternal glory. 2) From the beatific vision of God, to which the good angels have been admitted; because they always behold the face of God, Matth. XVIII, 10. But he who clearly beholds God, the supreme good, cannot but burn with perpetual love for Him, since nothing but what is good and lovable is discerned in Him: but he who perpetually loves God cannot sin.

3) From the exemplary holiness of the angels. That angelic holiness is the norm and example of our holiness, Christ teaches in Matth. VI, 10. Therefore, the will of God which we ought to do constantly in imitation of the angels, that the angels execute unceasingly.

For which reason they are said to celebrate God without end, Is. VI, 3, to minister to Him perpetually, Dan. VII, 10, and to be occupied with none but holy actions, Ps. CIII, 20. 4) From the eternal blessedness of men, who in eternal life are said to be ἰσάγγελοι (equal to the angels), Luke XX, 36. But the holiness of blessed men will be unloseable: Therefore, so too is that of the angels.

Antithesis 1) Of the Arminians, who deny that the confirmation of the good angels can be proven by a solid argument; 2) Of the Jews, who maintain that it has happened more often that good angels become evil. Their arguments are: I. Job says: Behold, He puts no trust in His servants, and He charges His angels with folly. Job IV, 18 [IV, 19]. & XV, 15. Behold, He puts no trust in His saints, and the heavens are not pure in His eyes.

Resp. The words of Job are to be understood comparatively, that the holiness of the angels, when compared with the divine, is many degrees more imperfect.

That is independent and original, inasmuch as God has it from Himself from eternity: this is dependent and participated, inasmuch as the angels have it from grace, by no merits.

provoked: which imperfection of the angels is a comparative impurity before the purest eyes of God.

II. Every reward is rejectable: the gift of confirmation is a reward: Therefore. Resp. Every reward in the state of the way is rejectable; but rewards bestowed in the state of glory are eternal & unrejectable.

III. If the elect angels are so confirmed in good that they cannot sin, they will not have perfect freedom of will: The latter is absurd: Therefore the former. Resp. Freedom of will toward good and evil does not imply such a perfection simply. For the most perfect freedom is not to be able to sin, with which perfection God excels in the highest degree, being most free in acting.

Latin:

XII. Quinam sunt angeli boni?

Angeli boni sunt, qui in concreata vera sapientia & sanctitate perstiterunt, & a Deo lumine gloriae illustrati, atque adeo in bono confirmati sunt, ut a periculo peccandi immunes Deum clare intueantur, eiusque bonitate perpetuo fruantur. Obs. I. Angeli boni tum in bono confirmati sunt, quando lumen gloriae ipsis a Deo infusum est, ut confirmatio eorum in bono, quoad rem, nihil aliud sit, quam infusio luminis gloriae, quo Deum intuitive cognoscunt.

Obs. II.

In statu viae angeli poterant non peccare, i. e. non erat in ipsis potentia proxima, aut propensio ad peccandum, erat tamen in illis potentia remota ad delinquendum: in statu gloriae angeli non possunt peccare, i. e. in ipsis nec proxima, nec remota ad delinquendum est potentia, sed ἀναμαρτησία, seu impeccabilitas eorumdem est immutabilis, sanctitasque inamissibilis. Prob.

1) Ex electione angelorum. Angeli boni dicuntur electi, 1 Tim. V, 21. quia aeterno Dei decreto ad beatitudinem sine fine perennem destinati sunt. Praeuidit enim Deus quorundam angelorum perseverantem obedientiam, non quidem ut caussam meritoriam; siquidem obedientia angelorum debita & temporaria vim meriti apud Deum, aut vim impellendi voluntatem eius ad decernendum aut dandum beatitudinis aeternae bonum non habet; sed ut conditionem quandam decreto suo annexam, quam beneuole respexit, & praemium confirmationis liberalissima motus bonitate angelis indulfit.

Non electi quidem sunt a Deo, vt homines peccatores, ob meritum Christi perseuerante fide apprehensum, electi dicuntur: Segregati tamen sunt ab angelis lapsis, & ad aeternam gloriam translati. 2) Ex visione Dei beatifica, ad quam angeli boni sunt admissi; quia διὰ παντὸς semper vident faciem Dei, Matth. XVIII, 10. At qui Deum summum bonum clare intuetur, non potest non perpetuo ipsius amore flagrare, cum nihil nisi bonum & amabile in eo cernatur: qui autem perpetuo Deum amat, non potest peccare.

3) Ex sanctitate angelorum exemplari. Sanctitatem angelicam nostrae sanctitatis esse normam & exemplar, docet Christus Matth. VI, 10. E. quam voluntatem Dei nos facere constanter debemus ad imitationem angelorum, illam angeli indefinenter exsequuntur.

Qua de caussa Deum sine fine celebrare, Es. VI, 3. perpetuo ipsi ministrare, Dan. VII, 10. nec aliis, nisi sanctis actionibus vacare, Ps. CIII, 20. dicuntur. 4) Ex aeterna beatitate hominum, qui in vita aeterna dicuntur futuri ἰσάγγελοι, Luc. XX, 36. At hominum beatorum sanctitas erit inamissibilis: Ergo & angelorum.

Antithesis 1) Arminianorum, negantium, confirmationem bonorum angelorum solido argumento probari posse; 2) Iudaeorum, statuentium, saepius accidisse, vt ex angelis bonis fiant mali. Quorum argumenta sunt: I. Iobus inquit: Ecce in feruis suis non fidit, & in angelis suis ponet stultitiam. Iob. IV, 19. & XV, 15. Ecce in sanctis suis non fidit, & caeli non sunt puri in oculis eius.

Resp. Verba Iobi intelligenda sunt comparate, quod sanctitas angelorum, cum diuina comparata, multis gradibus imperfectior sit.

Illa est independens & originalis, quippe quam Deus habet ex se ab aeterno: haec est dependens & participata, vtpote quam angeli habent ex gratia, nullis meritis

prouocata: quæ imperfectio angelorum comparatiua coram purissimis Dei oculis quædam impuritas est.

II. Omne præmium est reiicibile: donum confirmationis est præmium: Ergo. Resp. Omne præmium in statu viæ est reiicibile; at præmia collata in statu gloriæ sunt æterna & irreiicibilia.

III. Si angeli electi ita confirmati sunt in bono, vt peccare nequeant, non habebunt perfectam libertatem arbitrii: Posterius est absurdum: E. & prius. Resp. Libertas arbitrii ad bonum & malum non infert perfectionem simpliciter talem. Nam perfectissima libertas est, non posse peccare, qua perfectione in gradu summo eminet Deus in agendo liberrimus.


### Q. XIII. Is

the glory of the angels confirmed in good is to be attributed to an absolute divine decree, or to the proper merit of the angels? The glory of the angels confirmed in good is to be attributed neither to an absolute divine decree, nor to the merit of Christ, nor to angelic merit, but to the most bountiful goodness of God, who rewards the persevering obedience of the angels beyond what is condign.

Prob. a. An absolute decree of God excludes every foreseen condition to be fulfilled in the subject being chosen: But the decree of God choosing the angels does not exclude every condition to be fulfilled in them: Therefore. The minor is proved 1) From the harmony of decree and execution. For just as God in time bestowed beatitude only upon those angels who persevered in good: so the eternal decree concerning the angels to be saved at some time rested upon the foreknowledge of that condition to be fulfilled in time. 2) From the opposite. Just as the devils were not reprobated by an absolute decree of God, but because they did not stand in the truth, John 8:44: So the good angels were elected and raised to glory because they stood in the truth and did not abandon their principality, Jude 6, 2 Pet. 2:4.

Prob. b. 1) Christ is called the mediator of God and men, 1 Tim. 2:5, not of angels; whose nature He never assumed into His own hypostasis, Heb. 2:16. But for a mediator, a union of both natures is required, to which as mediator He ought to intercede. Wherefore, since Christ consists not of an angelic, but of a human and divine nature, He is not the mediator of angels, but only of men and God. 2) The Son of man came to save that which was lost, Matt. 18:11. But the angels had never perished, i.e., they had never been in a state of corruption. Therefore Christ did not come to save the angels.

Prob. c. Because merit is the performance of an undue work, directed to the benefit of another, to obtain a reward proportioned to the work. But truly, whatever good work the pilgrim angels performed, that was entirely due; for they were obligated to perform it by the right of creation, preservation, and governance: nor did it result in the benefit of the Creator; since He, being most blessed, cannot be increased by any benefit: nor is there any proportion between temporal angelic service and the eternal glory with which the angels are crowned.

There is an antithesis from the Papists, some of whom attribute the crown of angelic confirmation to the merit of Christ, others to angelic merit. They fortify their opinion with the following arguments: I. Whoever are called elect, they are raised to their glory on account of the merit of Christ: Certain angels are called elect, 1 Tim. 5:21: Therefore. The major is clear from the parallel example of men, who are said to be elected in Christ, Eph. 1:4. Resp. I deny the major. To the proof we say that the exam the example of men and angels becomes clearly disparate. For men were chosen out of perdition, Matth. XVIII, 11. They were sick, miserable, and in need of medicine, namely the blood of Christ: and therefore for their sake the savior came into the world. Matth. IX, 12. But indeed the good angels were never in a state of perdition, misery, or sickness; but they are called elect, since by the grace of the creator, who rewards their praiseworthy constancy in the truth beyond what is deserved, they were separated from the fallen angels, peculiarly beloved by God, confirmed in good, and translated to heavenly glory.

II. Christ is called the head of the angels, Eph. I, 22. And the angels were redeemed by Christ as mediator, and chosen in him. Resp. Christ is called the head of the angels, not because of an internal influx of mediatorial grace into the angels as members, but because of the excellence, power, direction, and external dominion which belongs to Christ over the angels.

III. God proposed to restore (to reduce to one head, as interpreted by CHRYSOSTOM) all things in Christ, which are in heaven and on earth, Eph. I, 10. Resp. By that ἀνακεφαλαιώσιν (recapitulation) the angels were not reconciled to God, inasmuch as they had never offended him; but harmony was restored between the angels and men; for the angels had shunned these as enemies, being exasperated by their disobedience toward the creator: but with men reconciled to God through Christ, the angels associated themselves as friends.

Instance: Therefore a certain fruit redounds to the angels from the merit of Christ. Resp. From the restoration of angelic and human harmony, no advantage, no perfection returns to the angels; otherwise they would progress for the better as often as a sinner returns to the way.

IV. The angels were chosen either by an absolute decree of God, or because of foreseen merits of works: But they were not chosen by an absolute decree of God. Therefore. Resp. A third option is given: The angels were chosen neither by an absolute decree of God, nor because of the merits of works, but in view of persevering obedience; which indeed does not rise to the dignity or value of merit; nevertheless, it was a condition to be fulfilled in the choosing of the angels. That constancy in the truth was the way of the kingdom, not the cause of reigning. Therefore the angels were chosen by a respective decree.

Latin:

gloria angelorum in bono confirmatorum absoluto diuino decreto, aut merito angelorum proprio accepta referenda? Gloria angelorum, in bono confirmatorum, neque absoluto diuino decreto , neque merito Christi , neque merito angelico , sed liberalissima bonitati Dei, perseuerantem angelorum obedientiam vltra condignum remunerantis, tribuenda est.

Prob. a. Decretum Dei absolutum omnem præuisam conditionem in subiecto eligendo implendam excludit: At decretum Dei eligentis angelos non omnem conditionem in ipsis implendam excludit: Ergo. Minor prob. 1) Ex harmonia decreti & executionis. Sicut enim Deus in tempore beatitudinem non nisi illis contulit angelis, qui in bono perseuerarunt: ita decretum æternum de angelis aliquando saluandis nitebatur præuisione illius conditionis in tempore implendæ. 2) Ex opposito. Sicut diaboli non ex absoluto Dei decreto reprobati sunt, sed quia non steterunt in veritate, Io. VIII, 44: Ita angeli boni ad gloriam electi & euecti sunt, quia steterunt in veritate & principatum suum non defuerunt, Iud. V, 6. 2 Petr. II, 4.

Prob. b. 1) Christus dicitur mediator Dei & hominum, 1 Tim. II, 5. non angelorum; quorum naturam nunquam intra hypostasin suam assumpsit, Hebr. II, 16. Requiritur autem ad mediatorem vnio naturæ vtriusque, cui tanquam mediator intercedere debet. Quare cum non ex angelica, sed ex humana & diuina natura constet Christus, non angelorum, sed hominum & Dei tantum mediator est. 2) Venit Filius hominis saluare, quod perierat, Matth. XVIII, 11. Sed angeli nunquam perierant, i. e. nunquam in statu corruptionis fuerant. Non venit igitur Christus ad saluandum angelos.

Prob. c. Quia meritum est præstatio operis indebiti, in alterius commodum directi, ad obtinendam mercedem operi proportionatam. At vero quidquid boni operis angeli viatores expedierunt, id fuit omnino debitum; eo, quod ad illud præstandum iure creationis, conseruationis & gubernationis fuerunt obligati: neque cessit in commodum creatoris; quippe qui beatissimus nullo commodo augeri potest: neque datur proportio vlla inter obsequium angelicum temporale, & æternam gloriam, qua angeli sunt coronati.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, quorum quidam coronam angelicæ confirmationis merito Christi, quidam merito angelico acceptam referunt. Qui suam opinionem sequentibus muniunt argumentis: I. Quicunque dicuntur electi, illi ob meritum Christi ad gloriam suam sunt euecti: Quidam angeli dicuntur electi, 1 Tim. V, 21: Ergo. Maior liquet ex pari hominum exemplo, qui electi dicuntur in Christo, Eph. I, 4. Resp. Neg. maior. Ad probationem dicimus, quod exemplum hominum et angelorum plane dispar fit. Nam homines electi sunt ex perditione, Matth. XVIII, 11. Fuerunt aegroti, miseri, indigi medicinae, scilicet sanguinis Christi: ideoque illorum causa salvator in mundum venit. Matth. IX, 12. At vero angeli boni nunquam fuerunt in statu perditionis, miseriae aut aegritudinis; sed dicuntur electi, quoniam ex gratia creatoris laudabilem eorum in veritate constantiam ultra condignum remunerantis ab angelis lapsis sunt segregati, Deo peculiariter dilecti, in bono confirmati, et ad gloriam caelestem translati.

II. Christus dicitur caput angelorum, Eph. I, 22. Et angeli a Christo tanquam mediatore sunt redempti, et in illo electi. Resp. Christus dicitur angelorum caput, non ob internum gratiae mediatoriae influxum in angelos velut membra, sed ob excellentiam, potestatem, directionem et dominium externum, quod Christo in angelos competit.

III. Deus proposuit instaurare (ad vnum caput reducere, interprete CHRYSOSTOMO) omnia in Christo, quae sunt in caelo et in terra, Eph. I, 10. Resp. Per ἀνακεφαλαιώσιν illam non reconciliati sunt angeli Deo, utpote quem nunquam offenderant; sed redintegrata est concordia inter angelos et homines; hos enim velut inimicos defuerant angeli, ipso rum inobedientia in creatorem exacerbati: at hominibus per Christum cum Deo reconciliatis angeli, velut amici, se affociarunt.

Instantia: Redundat igitur fructus quidam in angelos ex merito Christi. Resp. Ex instauratione concordiae angelicae et humanae nihil commodi, nihil perfectionis in angelos redit, ceteroqui toties proficerent in melius, quoties peccator in viam redit.

IV. Angeli electi sunt aut absoluto Dei decreto, aut ob praeuisa operum merita: At non electi sunt absoluto Dei decreto. Ergo. Resp. Datur tertium: Angeli electi sunt neque absoluto Dei decreto, neque ob merita operum, sed intuitu perseuerantis obedientiae; quae quidem ad meriti dignitatem aut valorem non assurgit; attamen conditio fuit in angelis eligendis implenda. Illa in veritate constantia fuit via regni, non causa regnandi. Ergo electi sunt angeli decreto respectiuo.


### Q. XIII. Is: Quest. XIV. Have the attributes of the angels been rendered more eminent by the benefit of confirmation?

Quest. XIV. Have the attributes of the angels been rendered more eminent by the benefit of confirmation?

By the benefit of confirmation, the angels have obtained more excellent knowledge a), more perfect holiness b), more outstanding liberty c), greater power d), and closer harmony e).

Proof. a. The good angels are eminent in most excellent knowledge, and indeed 1) natural, which is implanted in the angelic intellect by creation. They did not lose this, because they persisted in the truth. Jo. VIII, 44. 2) Experimental, drawn from the observation of many years. The manifold wisdom of God is made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places through the church, Eph. III, 10. 3) Revealed, which they obtain both from the ordinary revelation of the divine word and from peculiar and extraordinary revelation, 1 Petr. I, 12. 4) Intuitive, since they always see the face of God, Matth. XVIII, 10. Seeing the face of God does not precisely denote the expectation of a divine command, as Arminius wrongly explains (although it connotes the same), but the beatific vision of God. For which reason the good angels know a) God intuitively and immediately. For the light of glory, with which they are divinely suffused, exhibits the divine essence intimately present to the angels, illuminates their intellect most splendidly, and elevates them to see God clearly. From which the good angels are called angels of light, 2 Cor. XI, 14. b) The angels also know themselves intuitively. For an angel does not differ from his own intellect, as if by an intelligible species. needs, but rather the angelic intellect enters into the essential constitution of the angels. c) Angels know other angels and material things abstractively, or through intelligible species, as if they were images. For although an angel knowing has a proportion with another angel, by reason of a spiritual nature; yet the angel who is known is not sufficiently present to the intellect of the knowing angel, so that he can behold his essence immediately. There is need, therefore, for the angels to have intelligible species representing others.

Concerning material things, this is proved more easily, since they have neither proportion with the angelic intellect, nor are they sufficiently present, or intimately conjoined to it; which they certainly know through intelligible species, which, in the opinion of many authors, are concreated with them, or impressed upon them in their first production by God. For which reason, since angels do not know created things immediately and intuitively, but abstractively through intelligible species; we conclude that angelic cognition does not occur only through simple apprehension, but also through composition, as well as through demonstrative or probable discourse, both a priori and a posteriori.

Furthermore, although angels are multiscient, they are not, however, omniscient, because their knowledge is not infinite.

For they do not know 1) apart from divine revelation, future contingents, with certain and infallible knowledge.

The reason is at hand; because no created, or finite, intellect can know any future thing, unless from its own causes. But indeed, from causes acting freely, it cannot be inferred that an effect is necessarily to be future, since such causes, by the very fact that they act freely, can produce an effect, and can not produce it. Hence it happens that God alone designates Himself by the character of the knowledge of future contingents, Is.

XLI, 12. Nevertheless, a conjectural knowledge of future contingents, arising from certain external signs, is not to be denied to the angels.

For if a prudent man augurs future things, why not angels, whose whole life is intellectual? 2) Angels do not know with certainty and infallibly the secret thoughts of human hearts.

For καρδιογνωσία [kardiognosia], or the scrutiny of hearts, is an axiom of the omniscient God alone. Thou, Jehovah, alone knowest the heart of the sons of man, says King Solomon, 1 Reg. VIII, 39. We readily grant, meanwhile, that from external signs angels can acquire for themselves a probable knowledge of human thoughts.

Latin:

Quaest. XIV. An attributa angelorum beneficio confirmationis reddita sunt eminentiora?

Nacti sunt angeli beneficio confirmationis scientiam excellentiorem a), sanctitatem perfectiorem b), libertatem praestantiorem c), potentiam maiorem d), concordiam arctiorem e).

Prob. a. Eminent angeli boni scientia excellentissima, et quidem 1) naturali, quae per creationem angelico intellectui est insita. Hanc non amiserunt, quia in veritate perstiterunt. Jo. VIII, 44. 2) Experimentali, hausta ex multorum annorum obseruatione. Innotescit principatibus et potestatibus in supracaelestibus per ecclesiam multiuaria sapientia Dei, Eph. III, 10. 3) Revelata, quam consequuntur tum ex ordinaria verbi diuini reuelatione, tum ex reuelatione peculiari et extraordinaria, 1 Petr. I, 12. 4) Intuitiua, quoniam semper vident faciem Dei, Matth. XVIII, 10. Videre faciem Dei non praecise notat expectationem mandati diuini, ut perperam exponit Arminius (quamuis eandem connotet), sed beatificam Dei visionem. Quam ob rem cognoscunt angeli boni a) Deum intuitive et immediate. Nam lumen gloriae, quo diuinitus perfunduntur, essentiam diuinam angelis intime praesentem exhibet, intellectum ipsorum splendidissime illuminat, et ad Deum clare videndum eleuat. Ex quo angeli boni vocantur angeli lucis, 2 Cor. XI, 14. b) Seipsos cognoscunt angeli etiam intuitive. Angelus quippe ab intellectu suo non distat, ut specie intelligibili. suo non distat, vt specie intelligibili indigeat, sed potius intellectus angelicus essentialem constitutionem angelorum ingreditur. c) Cognoscunt angeli alios angelos & res materiales abstractive, seu per species intelligibiles, tanquam imagines. Nam quamuis angelus cognoscens cum alio angelo proportionem habeat, ratione spiritualis naturæ; non tamen angelus, qui cognoscitur, angeli cognoscentis intellectui fatis præsens est, vt essentiam eius immediate intueri queat. Opus igitur est angelis speciebus intelligibilibus, alios repræsentantibus.

De rebus materialibus id facilius probatur, quoniam illæ neque proportionem habent cum intellectu angelico, neque eidem satis præsentes, siue intime coniunctæ sunt; quas vtique cognoscunt per species intelligibiles, quæ, multorum auctorum sententia, illis sunt concreatæ, siue in prima productione a Deo ipsis impressæ. Quam ob rem, cum angeli res creatas non immediate & intuitive, sed abstractive per species intelligibiles cognoscant; colligimus, angelicam cognitionem non fieri tantum per apprehensionem simplicem, sed & per compositionem, iuxta atque discursum demonstrativum aut probabilem tum a priori, tum a posteriori.

Ceterum quamuis angeli sint multisci, non tamen sunt omnisci, quia eorum scientia non est infinita.

Neque enim cognoscunt 1) citra reuelationem diuinam futura contingentia, notitia certa & infallibili.

Ratio est in promptu; quia nullus intellectus creatus, seu finitus, potest aliquod futurum cognoscere, nisi ex eiusdem causis. At vero ex caussis libere agentibus non potest inferri, effectum necessario esse futurum, cum eiusmodi caussæ eo ipso, quod libere agunt, possint effectum producere, & non producere. Exinde fit, vt solus Deus charactere scientiæ futurorum contingentium seipsum designet, Es.

XLI, 12. Coniecturalis tamen notitia futurorum contingentium, e quibusdam exterioribus signis subnascens, angelis non est deneganda.

Quod si enim vir prudens auguratur futura: quidni angeli; quorum tota vita est intellectualis? 2) Angeli non cognoscunt certo & infallibiliter secretas cordium humanarum cogitationes.

Nam καρδιογνωσία, siue scrutinium cordium, est axioma solius Dei omniscii. Tu Iehouah solus nosci cor filiorum hominis, inquit rex Salomo, 1 Reg. VIII, 39. Facile largimur interim, quod ex signis exterioribus angeli sibi comparare queant probabilem cogitationum humanarum notitiam.


### Q. XIII. Is: Dicis: I

Dicis: I.

Angels always see the face of God: Matth. XVIII, 10. Therefore they see all things that are in God, and consequently also all objects of the divine intellect and will; and thus they see all things that God knows and wills.

Resp. Angels see all things that are formally in God; but they do not know all things that are virtually from God, or that can be freely effected by God; otherwise they would know God not intuitively, but comprehensively.

Dicis: II.

Whoever are intelligent spirits can place themselves proximately present to a human soul, they can perceive human thoughts: But angels, etc. Therefore.

The major is proved; because where there is an intelligent spirit, a proportioned object, and proximate presence, there is intellection. The minor is evident: because angels can enter a human body; for the density of the body does not obstruct a spirit: and thus they can place themselves present to a human soul, and perceive its thoughts.

Resp. That approximation to the soul does not bring about the knowledge of human thoughts, for the reason that these are free, not necessary.

The blessed in heaven stand proximately to God, yet they do not know his free decrees: Thus, although angels may be proximately present to a soul, they do not penetrate its free concepts.

Prob. b. In the state of grace, angels were placed outside the power, at least the remote power, of sinning: But in the state of glory, the holiness of the angels is so stable and rooted, that it excludes even the most remote power to sin. For the beatific vision introduces impeccability, Matth. ...

XVIII, 10.

Prob. c. There belongs to the blessed angels 1) freedom from coaction.

For they do not worship God coactively, but freely. 2) Freedom from internal necessity; because their will is free and indifferent is in order to created goods, so that whatever of them it wills, it can also not will (which is called liberty of contradiction, or of exercise,) or for one thing willed, another (which is liberty of contrariety, or of specification,) unless one thing must necessarily be sought on account of God's command. To the command and nod of God the good angels are perpetually intent. (3) Liberty from misery, and from the root of misery, sin, and indeed most remote from the power of sinning. Which liberty is surely most excellent: for by this the good angels approach in some measure to the likeness of God, who in acting is most free and cannot deflect from the rule of rectitude.

Prob. d. The good angels obtained great power through creation, and greater through glorification. That good angel gave a specimen of stupendous power, who in the Assyrian army struck down 185,000 soldiers, 2 Kings XIX, 25. Nor is there any doubt that the good angels surpass the evil in strength; since they are at hand to faithful men against demons, Ps. XXXIV, 8. Apoc. XII, 7. Yet the power of the angels is finite, not infinite; inasmuch as it is not in their power to convert a sinful man, to regenerate, to justify, to recall from the dead into life, or to make eternally blessed.

Prob. e. In the state of the way, at that point in time when the fall of the angels occurred, the entire chorus of angels was divided into different pursuits: some retained their origin, others abandoned their own dwelling. But indeed, angels in the state of beatitude cannot be at odds with themselves. For full beatitude does not flourish there, where discord and adversity creep in.

Latin:

Dicis: I.

Angeli semper vident faciem Dei: Matth. XVIII, 10. Ergo vident omnia, quæ sunt in Deo, consequenter etiam omnia obiecta intellectus & voluntatis diuinæ; adeoque omnia vident, quæ Deus scit & vult.

Resp. Angeli vident omnia, quæ sunt formaliter in Deo; sed non cognoscunt omnia, quæ sunt a Deo virtualiter, seu quæ a Deo libere effici queunt; ceteroqui non intuitive, sed comprehensue Deum cognoscerent.

Dicis: II.

Quicunque spiritus intelligentes possunt se proxime præsentes sistere animæ humanæ, illi possunt cogitationes humanas perspicere: Atqui angeli &c. Ergo.

Maior probatur; quia, vbi est spiritus intelligens, obiectum proportionatum, & propinqua præsentia, ibi est intellectio. Minor patet: quia angeli possunt ingredi corpus humanum; neque enim crassities corporis obstat spiritui: atque adeo animæ humanæ se præsentes sistere, eiusque cogitationes perspicere.

Resp. Illa approximatio ad animam non infert cognitionem cogitationum humanarum, eo, quod hæ sunt liberæ, non necessariæ.

Beati in cœlo Deo proxime adstant, neque tamen libera eius decreta cognoscunt: Ita licet angeli proxime adsint animæ, liberos tamen eius conceptus non penetrant.

Prob. b. In statu gratiæ angeli erant extra potentiam saltem remotam peccandi positi: At in statu gloriæ angelorum sanctitas adeo stabilis & radicata est, vt vel remotissimam ad peccandum potentiam excludat. Visio quippe beatifica impeccabilitatem... introducit, Matth.

XVIII, 10. Prob. c.

Competit angelis beatis 1) libertas a coactione. Neque enim coacte, sed libere colunt Deum.

2) Libertas a necessitate interna; quia voluntas eorum libera atque indifferens est in ordine ad bona creata, ita, ut quodlibet eorum, quod vult, possit etiam non velle (quae dicitur libertas contradictionis, seu exercitii,) vel pro uno velle alterum (quae est libertas contrarietatis, seu specificationis,) nisi unum ill...lud propter mandatum Dei sit necessario expetendum. Ad mandatum & nutum Dei angeli boni perpetuo sunt intenti. (3) Libertas a miseria, miseriaeque radice, peccato, quin & peccandi potentia remotissima. Quae sane libertas praestantissima est: Hac enim angeli boni accedunt quadantenus ad similitudinem Dei, qui in agendo liberrimus a regula rectitudinis deflectere nequit.

Prob. d. Potentiam angeli boni per creationem adepti sunt magnam, maiorem per glorificationem. Specimen stupendae potentiae edidit angelus ille bonus, qui in exercitu Assyriaco percussit 185. militum millia, 2 Reg. XIX, 25. Neque ullum est dubium, quin angeli boni malos superent viribus; siquidem hominibus fidelibus aduersus cacodaemones praesto sunt, Ps. XXXIV, 8. Apoc. XII, 7. Est tamen potentia angelorum finita, non infinita; vtpote quos penes haud est, hominem peccatorem convertere, regenerare, iustificare, ex mortuis in vitam reuocare, aeternum beare.

Prob. e. In statu viae eo temporis puncto, quo angelorum contingebat lapsus, vniuersus angelorum chorus in diuersa studia scindebatur: alii retinebant originem suam, alii domicilium proprium deferebant. At vero angeli in statu beatitudinis sibi nequeunt aduersari. Neque enim plena ibi viget beatitas, vbi discordia gliscit, & aduersitas. Quaest.


### Q. XV. By what works and offices do the good angels perform their duties?

The blessed angels perform their works and offices by standing before God a), by assisting pious men b), and by resisting devils and evil men c).

Prob. a. The blessed angels stand before God, so that 1) with most joyful psalmody (ψαλμῳδίᾳ) they may sing the praises of Jehovah, Ps. CXLVIII, 2. Is. VI, 2. 2) with most humble worship (λατρείᾳ) they may venerate and adore God, Ps. XCVII, 7. Heb. I, 7. 3) with most prompt service (λειτουργίᾳ) they may execute the will of God. Ps. CIII, 20. Dan. VII, 10.

Prob. b. The good angels assist pious men, partly as individuals, partly in society, or in a certain hierarchy. They are present to individual men at the beginning, progress, and end of life. At the beginning of life they look after the interests of infants, Matt. XVIII, 10. In the progress of life they guard adults, Ps. XXXIV, 8. XCI, 11. 12. At the end of life they accompany the souls of the dying, Luke XVI, 22.

Prob. c. They assist the ecclesiastical state by promoting the ministry of the divine word. For they were present, as ministers, at the promulgation of the Mosaic law, Deut. XXXIII, 2. Gal. III, 19. they announced the advent of Christ in the flesh, Luke I, 26. ch. II, 9. they drive away idolatry when it creeps into the church, Jude v. 9. they are present at sacred assemblies even today, 1 Cor. XI, 10. 1 Tim. V, 21. They bring aid to the political state by watching over religion and justice, Dan. X, 13. and by defending the magistrate, Dan. VI, 22. They are at hand to the economic state by promoting the marriages of the pious, Gen. XXIV, 7. by guarding family property, Job I, 10. by protecting children from dangers, Matt. XVIII, 10.

Latin:

Angeli beati opera & officia sua expediunt coram Deo consistendo a), hominibus piis assistendo b), atque diabolis & hominibus malis resistendo c).

Prob. a. Consistunt angeli beati coram Deo, vt 1) ψαλμῳδίᾳ laetissima laudes Iehouae decantent, Ps. CXLVIII, 2. Es. VI, 2. 2) λατρείᾳ humillima Deum venerentur & adorent, Ps. XCVII, 7. Hebr. I, 7. 3) λειτουργίᾳ promptissima voluntatem Dei exfequantur. Ps. CIII, 20. Dan. VII, 10.

Prob. b. Assistunt angeli boni piis hominibus, partim singulis, partim in societate, siue hierarchia quadam conflutitis. Singulis hominibus adsunt in vitae ingressu, progressu & egressu. In vitae ingressu infantum rationibus prospiciunt, Matth. XVIII, 10. In vitae progressu adultiores custodiunt, Ps. XXXIV, 8. XCI, 11. 12. In vitae egressu animas morientium comitantur, Luc. XVI, 22.

Prob. c. Statui ecclesiastico assistunt, ministerium verbi diuini promouendo. Nam affuerunt, velut ministri, promulgationi legis Mosaicae, Deut. XXXIII, 2. Gal. III, 19. aduentum Christi in carnem annuntiarunt, Luc. I, 26. c. II, 9. idolatriam, quando ferpit in ecclesiam, profligant, Iud. ep. v. 9. coetibus sacris hodienum intersunt, 1 Cor. XI, 10. 1 Tim. V, 21. Statui politico ferunt suppetias, pro religione & iustitia vigilando, Dan. X, 13. & magistratum defendendo, Dan. VI, 22. Statui oeconomico praesto sunt, coniugia piorum promouendo, Gen. XXIV, 7. rem familiarem custodiendo, Job. I, 10. liberos a periculis vindicando, Matth. XVIII, 10.


### Q. XVI. Is a peculiar guardian angel assigned to every man?

That a peculiar guardian angel, who ordinarily accompanies him in all places and at whatever time, has been assigned by God to every man, it is not permitted to affirm for certain.

Proof 1) Because, as Holy Scripture testifies, the guardianship of one faithful man is entrusted to several angels, Ps. XCI, 11. 2) That several angels have surrounded a man with their company, the examples of Jacob, Gen. XXXII, 2; Elisha, 2 Kings VI, 16; Joshua, Zech. III, 7; Lazarus, Luke XVI, 22, teach. 3) Several angels rejoice over the repentance of one sinner, Luke XV, 20.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, who assert that a special guardian angel is divinely deputed to every man, and who strive to fortify their opinion with the following arguments:

I. Jacob makes mention of one angel, by whose help he was redeemed from all evil, Gen. XLVIII, 16. Resp. The redeeming angel is not a created angel, but an uncreated one, namely the Son of God, whose office it is to redeem from all evil.

II. One angel, who is called Raphael, led Tobias, Tob. II, 27. Resp. One angel led Tobias in visible form; yet several could have been present in invisible presence. Nor can it be proven from this example that in every case only one angel accompanies us. Two angels lead Lot out of Sodom, Gen. XIX, 12. Two Seraphic hosts surrounded Jacob with their protection, Gen. XXXII, 2.

III. The assembled Christians said: It is his angel, Acts XII, 15. Resp. These words were not of the Holy Spirit, but of certain Christians speaking from the opinion of the common people, or Jewish persuasion. For the Jews thought that a man's angel appeared in visible form shortly before or shortly after the man's death.

Quest. XVII. Is a special guardian angel appointed for every region?

That a special guardian angel is appointed for every province, we cannot define for certain.

Proof 1) Entire hosts of angels surrounded the city of Dothan, 2 Kings VI, 17; why, therefore, should several angels not be present for entire kingdoms? 2) Entire camps surround and encompass one man, Gen. XXXII, 2; why not an entire province?

The antithesis is that of the Papists, in whose mind a special guardian angel is appointed for every region; their chief argument is that in Dan. X, 12, mention is made of the prince of the kingdom of Persia, who resisted Gabriel. R. By the prince of the kingdom of Persia, loc. cit., is not understood a good angel appointed over the kingdom of Persia, but rather a certain courtly evil spirit, who strove to incite the king of Persia and his counselors against the people of the Lord, so that they would not be released from captivity. See D. CALOV. bibl. illustr. in h. l. fol. 674.

Latin:

Vnicuique homini peculiarem angelum tutelarem, qui eum ordinarie viuis locorum & quocunque tempore comitetur, a Deo esse assignatum, pro certo affirmare haud licet.

Prob. 1) Quia teste scriptura S. pluribus angelis vnius hominis fidelis custodia commendata est, Ps. XCI, 11. 2) Plures angelos comitatu suo vinum stipasse hominem, docent exempla Iacobi, Gen. XXXII, 2. Elisaei, 2 Reg. VI, 16. Iosuae, Zach. III, 7. Lazari, Luc. XVI, 22. 3) Plures angeli de vnius peccatoris poenitentia gaudent, Luc. XV, 20.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, asserentium, vnicuique homini peculiarem angelum tutelarem diuinitus esse deputatum, qui suam opinionem munire nituntur sequentibus argumentis:

I. Iacobus vnius angeli mentionem iniicit, cuius ope redemptus sit ab omni malo, Gen. XLVIII, 16. Resp. Angelus redemptor non est angelus creatus, sed increatus, nempe Filius Dei, cuius est ab omni malo redimere.

II. Angelus vnus, qui vocatur Raphael, Tobiam deduxit, Tob. II, 27. Resp. Vnus angelus forma visibili deduxit Tobiam; potuerunt tamen plures adesse praesentia inuisibili. Neque ex hoc exemplo conuinci potest, in omni casu vnum tantum nos comitari angelum. Lothum duo angeli Sodoma educunt, Gen. XIX, 12. Iacobum duo exercitus Seraphici praesidio suo cinxerunt, Gen. XXXII, 2.

III. Dixerunt congregati christiani: Angelus ipsius est, Act. XII, 15. Resp. Haec verba fuerunt non Spiritus S. sed quorundam christianorum loquentium ex opinione vulgi, siue Iudaica persuasione. Iudaei enim opinabantur angelum hominis breui ante, vel paulo post decessum hominis visibili specie comparere.

Quaest. XVII. Num cuique regioni peculiaris praefectus est angelus tutelaris?

Vnicuique prouinciae peculiarem praepositum esse angelum tutelarem, pro certo definire nequimus.

Prob. 1) Ciuitatem Dothan cingebant integri exercitus angelorum, 2 Reg. VI, 17. quidni ergo regnis integris plures adsint angeli? 2) Vnum hominem stipant & circumuallant castra integra, Gen. XXXII, 2. quidni integram prouinciam?

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, ex quorum mente vnicuique regioni peculiaris praepositus est angelus custos; quorum argumentum praecipuum est, quod Dan. X, 12. mentio fit principis regni Persarum, qui Gabrieli restitit. R. Per principem regni Persarum loc. cit. non intelligitur angelus bonus regno Persarum praefectus, sed potius cacodaemon quidam aulicus, qui regem Persarum, eiusque consiliarios aduersus populum Domini, ne dimitteretur ex captiuitate, instigare nitebatur. Vid. D. CALOV. bibl. illustr. in h. l. fol. 674.


### Q. XVIII

Is a certain order given among the angels? That there is a certain order among the good angels, there is no doubt , but what this angelic order may be, we judge that no one knows .

Prob. a. From the general rule, by which God in the militant church wills all things to be done decently & according to order, 1 Cor. XIV, 40. There is therefore no doubt that a certain order exists in the triumphant church among the blessed angels, and it is so much the more perfect, as the triumphant church is more splendid than the militant. 2) From the diverse denominations of the heavenly spirits. St. Paul says, Eph. I, 21: He set (God the Father, Christ) above every principality, and power, and virtue, and dominion. Likewise Col. I, 16: In him were created things visible and invisible, whether thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers, 1 Thess. IV, 16. & Jude Ep. v. 9. mention is made of archangels. (*) Diverse names imply a distinction of angels. 3) From a parity. There is an order among the evil angels. Therefore also among the good. The antecedent is clear from Luke XI, 15, where Beelzebub is called the prince of demons: & Matt. XXV, 41. mention is made of the devil, & his angels.

Prob. b. From the diverse denominations of the angels it can neither be validly gathered, nor certainly defined, in what the distinction of angels consists, and how widely it extends. There is an antithesis of the Papists from PSEUDO-DIONYSIUS, lib. I. de caelesti hierarchia cap. 6, who distinguishes the angels into nine orders, and these again into three hierarchies, so that in the highest are Seraphim, Cherubim & thrones; in the middle, dominions, virtues & powers; in the lowest, principalities, archangels. They strive to confirm their opinion I, from Dan. VII, 10: Thousand thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him: where angels are distinguished into ministering and assisting. R. That ministering angels differ from assisting ones cannot be solidly proven. For all angels are ministering spirits, Hebr. I, 14. Angels minister by assisting, and assist by ministering: just as a minister stands before a prince, to execute his commands. II, Diverse names of angels indicate diverse orders. Resp. From the mere diversity of names, without other distinctive marks, to enumerate determined orders of angels is rash.

Q. XIX.

Are angels to be pursued with a religious cult of adoration?

Angels are not to be religiously adored, nor invoked.

Prob. 1) God alone is to be religiously adored, Deut. VI, 13. Matt. IV, 10. Therefore not angels. Exception. God alone is to be adored, as the first being, & the principal giver of every good. Angels are to be adored as friends of God. Resp. Religious adoration flows from true faith, & pertains to the first table of the decalogue, to which it is not permitted to insert the friends of God. Therefore Paul reckons θρησκείαν τῶν ἀγγέλων, the worship of angels, Col. II, 18. 23. among ταῖς ἐθελοθρησκείαις, voluntary and superstitious cults.

2) Whoever is not omnipotent, omniscient, all-merciful, omnipresent, he is not to be invoked. But angels are not omnipotent, omniscient, all-merciful & omnipresent. Therefore. The major is evident, because with undoubted trust of heart we implore the help of him who is omnipotent, that he may be able to help us; omniscient, that he may have our intimate desires perceived; all-merciful, that he may be benevolently inclined toward all men; omnipresent, that he may be present everywhere to us who labor.

3) Whoever are ministers of God, they are not to be religiously venerated. But angels are, etc., Hebr. I, 14. Therefore. 4) Whatever is refused by the angels, that is not to be rendered to them. But religious adoration, etc. [is refused]. Therefore.

The minor premise is established from Rev. 19:10; 22:8.

You say: I. John thought that the one whom he was about to worship was not a created angel, but Christ.

Resp. Grant that John did not know whether the angel was created or uncreated; he heard, however, that the created angel repudiated religious worship.

You say: II. The angel repudiated latreia, the highest religious worship, owed to God alone: he did not refuse douleia, religious worship inferior to the highest, or subordinate.

Resp. The distinction between latreia and douleia is fabricated; since Holy Scripture uses these words indiscriminately.

Certainly, we are bound to douleuein even the eternal God. Matt. 6:24; 1 Thess. 1:9; Rom. 16:18.

You say: III. The angel refused religious worship out of modesty; although he knew that the same belonged to him by a most just right.

Resp. He refused not out of modesty, but with serious affect, having brought forward the most weighty reasons for the non-admissibility of the worship, a) because he is a fellow-servant, b) a brother, c) not God, who alone is to be worshipped [*].

Latin:

Dari inter angelos bonos certum ordinem, nullum est dubium , sed qualis sit iste ordo angelicus, in hac vita arbitramur, scire neminem .

Prob. a. Ex regula generali, qua Deus in ecclesia militante omnia vult fieri decore & secundum ordinem, 1 Cor. XIV, 40. Nullum igitur est dubium, quin certus ordo sit in ecclesia triumphante inter angelos beatos, isque tanto perfectior, quanto splendidior est ecclesia triumphans militante. 2) A diversis spirituum coelestium denominationibus. S. Paullus Eph. I, 21. inquit: Collocauit (Deus Pater Christum) super omnem principatum, & potestatem, & virtutem, & dominationem. Item Col. I, 16. In ipso condita sunt visibilia & invisibilia, siue throni, siue dominationes, siue principatus, siue potestates, 1 Thess. IV, 16. & Iudae Ep. v. 9. fit mentio archangelorum. (*) Diversa nomina discrimen angelorum inferunt. 3) A pari. Datur ordo inter angelos malos. E. & inter bonos. Anteced. liquet ex Luc. XI, 15. vbi Beelzebul princeps daemoniorum dicitur: & Matth. XXV, 41. mentio fit diaboli, & angelorum eius.

Prob. b. Ex diversis angelorum denominationibus neque valide colligi, neque certo definiri potest, in quo consistat angelorum discrimen, & quam late sese extendat. Antithesis est Pontificiorum ex PSEVDO-DIONYSIO lib. I. de caelesti hierarchia cap. 6. angelos in nouem ordines, & hos iterum in tres hierarchias distinguentium, ita, vt in suprema sint Seraphim, Cherubim & throni; in media dominationes, virtutes & potestates; in infima principatus, archangeli. Opinionem suam firmare nituntur I, ex Dan. VII, 10. Mille millia ministrabant ei, & myrias myriadum coram eo stabant: vbi angeli in ministrantes & assistentes distinguuntur. R. Angelos ministrantes ab assistentibus differre, solide probari nequit. Nam omnes angeli sunt spiritus administratorii, Hebr. I, 14. Ministrant angeli assistendo, & assistunt ministrando: sicut minister stat coram principe, huius iussa exsecuturus. II, Diversa angelorum nomina diversos ordines indicant. Resp. Ex sola nominum diversitate, sine aliis notis distinctiuis, angelorum determinatos enumerare ordines, temerarium est.

Quaest. XIX.

Suntne angeli religioso adorationis cultu prosequendi?

Angeli religiose non adorandi, neque inuocandi sunt.

Prob. 1) Solus Deus religiose adorandus est, Deut. VI, 13. Matth. IV, 10. Ergo non angeli. Except. Solus Deus adorandus est, vt ens primum, & largitor principalis omnis boni. Angeli adorandi sunt, vt amici Dei. Resp. Adoratio religiosa fluit ex vera fide, & pertinet ad primam tabulam decalogi, cui amicos Dei inferere haud licet. Idcirco Paullus θρησκείαν τῶν ἀγγέλων, cultum angelorum, Col. II, 18. 23. ταῖς ἐθελοθρησκείαις cultibus voluntariis & superstitiosis accenset.

2) Quicunque non est omnipotens, omnisciens, omnimisericors, omnipraesens, is non est inuocandus. Atqui angeli non sunt omnipotentes, omniscii, omnimisericordes & omnipraesentes. Ergo. Maior constat, quia indubitata cordis fiducia illius imploramus opem, qui est omnipotens, vt nos iuvare queat; omnisciens, vt intima nostra desideria perspecta habeat: omnimisericors, vt in cunctos homines beneuole propendeat; omnipraesens, vt nobis laborantibus vbique praesto sit.

3) Quicunque sunt ministri Dei, illi non sunt religiose venerandi. Atqui angeli &c, Hebr. I, 14. Ergo. 4) Quidquid ab angelis recusatur, id ipsis non est deferendum. Atqui adoratio religiosa &c. Ergo.

Minor constat ex Apoc. XIX, 10. c. XXII, 8.

Dicis: I. Ioannes existimauit, illum, quem adoraturus erat, non esse angelum creatum, sed Christum.

Resp. Fac, Ioannem ignorasse, creatus, an increatus fuerit angelus; audiuit tamen, angelum creatum cultum religiosum repudiare.

Dicis: II. Repudiauit angelus τὴν λατρείαν, cultum religiosum summum, soli Deo debitum: non recusauit τὴν δουλείαν, cultum religiosum summo inferiorem, vel subordinatum.

Resp. Distinctio inter λατρείαν, & δουλείαν conficta est; siquidem scriptura S. has voces promiscue usurpat.

Certe tenemur δουλεύειν etiam aeterno Deo. Matth. VI, 24. 1 Thess. I, 9. Rom. XVI, 18.

Dicis: III. Angelus recusauit cultum religiosum ex modestia; quamuis sciueret, eundem sibi aequissimo iure competere.

Resp. Recusauit non ex modestia, sed serio affectu, adductis grauissimis non admissi cultus caussis, a) quia sit conseruus, b) frater, c) non Deus, qui solus adorandus [*].


### Q. XVIII: The Antithesis is of the Papists

The Antithesis is of the Papists

The Antithesis is of the Papists, who persuade themselves that angels can be worshipped religiously, not indeed with the worship of latreia, which they attribute to God alone, but of douleia, which holds a middle seat between the worship of God and of men.

They adduce I. The examples of Abraham, Gen. 18; Lot, Gen. 19; Jacob, Gen. 48; Joshua, ch. 5, who worshipped angels.

Resp. Distinguish between the created and the uncreated angel: The latter they worshipped; the former they treated with civil worship.

II. Angels, because of their excellence, are to be worshipped either with civil or religious worship. Not with civil worship; because they are not citizens or men, but greater and more eminent than men placed in civil dignity: Therefore with religious worship.

Resp. By civil worship is understood either strictly the worship befitting men, or broadly every non-religious worship, or moral reverence. However, there are degrees of non-religious worship according to the greater or lesser excellence of creatures.

But a degree does not vary the species; nor is religious worship founded upon the finite excellence of God.

III. Angelic worship is commanded to us, Job 5:1. Call, come, is there anyone answering? and to which of the saints will you turn?

Resp. By saints in the cited place are not understood angels, but holy men.

Eliphaz indicates that no one is found among the saints whom God has overwhelmed with miseries as grave as those of Job.

Therefore he says: Call, or name, I pray, does anyone attest that he is like you?

To which of the saints will you turn?

Whose example of a pious man will you be able to produce? [] IV.

Angels [*] Contemplation

IV. Angels carry our prayers to God, Apoc. VIII, 3. Tob. XII, 12. Therefore, our prayers can be commended to angels, so that they may be carried to God by them. Response: The angel whom John mentions, Apoc. VIII, 3, is uncreated, or the Son of God; inasmuch as the priestly act, which created angels do not perform, is attributed to him. However, the angel of Tobias in the apocryphal book does not deserve faith, for he committed a lie, Tob. V, 12, and suggested to Tobias a superstitious and profane counsel, ch. VI, 4. Christ alone is our advocate carrying our prayers to God, 1 John II, 2, and the unique priest, obtaining for us a hearing through his intercession, Heb. VII, 25. Furthermore, granting but not conceding that angels offer our prayers to God, they are not for that reason to be religiously venerated.

V. Angels are our intercessors. Therefore, they can be invoked. The antecedent is proven from Job XXXIII, 23: "If there be an angel with him, an interpreter, one among a thousand; to announce to man his uprightness." Response: (1) Not all intercessors are to be religiously invoked. (2) Nothing is held in the text regarding the intercession of an angel; but the office of an angel is described, that he should announce to man his uprightness, or justice, through which he ought to be liberated or saved. That angel is Christ. See D. Seb. Schmid in his commentary on Job at this place, p. 162 seq. VI. The Apostle John prays for grace and peace from the seven spirits who are before the throne of God, Apoc. I, 4. Those seven spirits are seven angels according to the mind of the Papists, who will argue by the following reasoning: Those from whom the Apostle John prays for grace and peace, it is lawful and fitting to invoke. But from the angels, etc. Therefore. Response: By the seven apocalyptic spirits, angels are not understood. For it is repugnant (1) to the analogy of faith to seek spiritual grace and peace from created angels, the source and bestower of which is God alone, Rom. XI, 36, James I, 17. (2) The seven apocalyptic spirits are placed between two divine and uncreated persons. Therefore, created spirits are not designated by them. Indeed, in the order of holy blessing, no creature is to be placed between two divine persons. (3) The seven spirits are honored with the same worship as God the Father and the Son: which worship is *latria* owed solely to the eternal God. For this reason, by the seven spirits we understand the Holy Spirit, who is indeed one by reason of essence and person, yet is described metonymically by John through the septenary number, on account of the multitude and perfection of the charisms which the Holy Spirit exercised largely and abundantly in those seven Asiatic churches mentioned in the Apocalypse, just as if there were as many spirits, each working perfectly in its own church. All the pious, who pray for grace and peace from the Triune God, invoke this Holy Spirit, one in nature and sevenfold in function, with God the Father and the Son. Cf. 2 Cor. XIII, 13.

VI. It is lawful to call upon men so that they may intercede for us before God: Therefore, also the angels. Response: The sacred scriptures do not teach us to ask for the intercession of deceased men. We do indeed seek the prayers of the living for us, but it is wrong to conclude from that: Therefore, angels can be invoked so that they may intercede for us. For (1) we have a divine command regarding seeking the mutual suffrages of the living, James V, 14. Regarding imploring the patronage of angels, no command exists. (2) The imploring of the suffrages of the faithful in the church is an officious invitation and a work of charity: but the invocation of angels, according to the mind of the dissenters, is religious *dulia*. (3) The mutual intercession of the faithful is not *hilastike*, satisfactory, or expiatory; but *synagonistike* [struggling together]... [to the] members, or are they to be supplicated? Not at all; but for investigating and knowing whether any of the saints is conspicuous for such perfect holiness that he has something of which he himself can boast before God? See the entire context, but especially the antecedent chapter IV. 4) The error of the Vulgate interpreter is to be noted. In the sources, the meaning of the words is entirely contrary: מַה הַקְדּוֹשִׁים, to which of the saints will you turn? That is, to none at all. For it is a most well-known hermeneutical rule: An affirming interrogation strongly denies. S. V. Deylingius has explained this argument more fully, Obs. S. T. l. 28.

of the members of the militant church, as it were struggling for one another in prayers. This intercession, as it were a fellow-soldiering, Paul teaches in Rom. XV, 30. I beseech you, Brethren, for our Lord Jesus Christ's sake, and for the love of the Spirit, that ye strive together with me in your prayers to God for me. But angels do not struggle with us in prayers, since they are not members of the militant church; nor are they conflicted with the same enemies and miseries by which Christians are harassed.

Latin:

Antithesis est Pontificiorum

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, qui sibi persuadent, angelos posse religiose coli, non quidem cultu λατρείας, quem soli tribuunt Deo, sed δουλείας, quae mediam obtineat sedem inter cultum Dei & hominum.

Adducunt I. Exempla Abrahami, Gen. XVIII. Lothi, Gen. XIX. Iacobi, Gen. XLVIII. Iosuae, c. V. qui angelos adorarunt.

Resp. Dist. inter angelum creatum, & increatum: Hunc adorarunt; angelos assistentes cultui ciuili prosecuti sunt.
