II. Angeli ob excellentiam suam colendi sunt aut cultu ciuili, aut religioso. Non cultu ciuili; quia non sunt ciues aut homines, sed maiores & eminentiores hominibus in dignitate ciuili positis: Ergo cultu religioso.

Resp. Per cultum ciuilem aut stricte intelligitur cultus hominibus competens, aut late omnis cultus non religiosus, vel moralis reuerentia. Dantur autem gradus cultus non-religiosi secundum excellentiam maiorem, vel minorem creaturarum.

At gradus non variat speciem; neque cultus religiosus in excellentia finita Dei fundatur.

III. Cultus angelicus nobis praecipitur, Iob. V, 1. Voca, age, num est respondens? & ad quem sanctorum respicies?

Resp. Per sanctos l. c. non intelliguntur angeli, sed homines sancti.

Indicat Eliphaz, neminem inter sanctos reperiri, quem Deus tam grauibus, quam Iobum miseriis obruerit.

Propterea dicit: Voca, feu nomina, quaeso, num attestatur quipiam, quod fit tui similis.

Ad quem sanctorum respicies?

Cuius viri pii exemplum producere poteris? [] IV.

Angeli [*] Contemplatione

IV. Angeli preces nostras Deo deferunt, Apoc. VIII, 3. Tob. XII, 12. E. angelis preces nostræ commendari possunt, vt ab ipsis Deo deferantur. R. Angelus, cuius meminit Ioannes, Apoc. VIII, 3. est increatus, siue Filius Dei; vtpote cui actus sacerdotalis, quo non perfunguntur angeli creati, tribuitur. Angelus autem Tobiæ in libro apocrypho non meretur fidem, commisit enim mendacium, Tob. V, 12. & suggeffit Tobiæ consilium superstitiosum ac profanum. c. VI, 4. Solus Christus est aduocatus noster preces nostras Deo deferens, 1 Io. II, 2. & facerdos vnicus, intercessione sua exauditionem nobis impetrans, Heb. VII, 25. Ceterum posito, sed non concesso, angelos preces nostras Deo offerre, non tamen ea de caussa religiose venerandi sunt.

V. Angeli sunt nostri intercessores. Ergo inuocari possunt. Antecedens probatur ex Iob. XXXIII, 23. Si fuerit apud illum angelus interpres, vnus ille ex millibus; ad annuntiandum homini rectitudinem suam. Resp. (1) Non omnes intercessores religiose inuocandi sunt. (2) De intercessione angeli nihil habetur in textu; fed describitur officium angeli, quod annuntiet homini rectitudinem, siue iustitiam, per quam liberari, vel saluari debet. Angelus ille Christus est. Vid. D. SEB SCHMID. in commentar. in Iob. ad h. l. p. 162. sequ. VI. Apostolus Ioannes gratiam & pacem precatur a septem spiritibus, qui sunt coram throno Dei. Apocal. I, 4. Septem illi Spiritus sunt septem angeli ex mente Pontificiorum, qui sequenti rationi arguent: A quibus apostolus Ioannes gratiam & pacem precatur, illos inuocare licet & decet. Atqui ab angelis &c. Erg. Resp. Per septem Spiritus apocalypticos non intelliguntur angeli. Repugnat enim (1) Analogiæ fidei, ab angelis creatis expetere gratiam & pacem spiritualem, cuius fons & largitor solus Deus est, Rom. XI, 36. Iacob. I, 17. (2) Septem spiritus apocalypticos ponuntur inter duas personas diuinas & increatas. Proinde per illos non designantur spiritus creati. In ordine quippe fanctæ benedictionis nulla creatura inter duas personas diuinas collocanda est. (3) Septem spiritus eodem cultu, quo Deus Pater & Filius honorantur: qui cultus est λατρεία foli æterno Deo debita. Quam ob rem per septem spiritus intelligimus Spiritum S. qui ratione essentiæ & personæ quidem vnus est, per numerum tamen septenarium a Ioanne metonymice describitur, propter multitudinem & perfectionem charismatum, quæ Spiritus S. in septem illas ecclesias Asiaticas, quarum in apocalypsi fit mentio, large cumulateque exercebat, perinde, ac si totidem essent Spiritus, in sua quisque ecclesia perfecte operantes. Hunc Spiritum S. vnum natura, & septiformem munere, cum Deo Patre & Filio inuocant omnes pii, qui gratiam & pacem a Deo trinuno precantur. Conf. 2 Cor. XIII, 13.

VI. Compellare licet homines, vt apud Deum pro nobis intercedant: Ergo & angelos. Resp. Defunctorum hominum poscere intercessionem, non docent nos sacræ litteræ. Viuorum quidem preces pro nobis expetimus, fed inde concludere nefas est: Ergo angeli possunt inuocari, vt pro nobis intercedant. Nam (1) de mutuis viuentium suffragiis expetendis diuinum habemus mandatum, Iacob. V, 14. De angelorum patrocinio implorando nullum exstat mandatum. (2) Imploratio suffragiorum fidelium in ecclesia est officiosa inuitatio & opus caritatis: at angelorum inuocatio ex mente dissidentium est δλεία religiosa. (3) Mutua fidelium intercessio non est ἱλασική, fatisfactoria aut expiatoria; fed συναγωνιστική membroeos, aut eis supplicandum? minime gentium; fed ad peruestigandum & cognoscendum, num quis sanctorum adeo perfecta sanctitate fit conspicuus, vt habeat, de quo ipse coram Deo gloriari queat? vid. contextus integer, præfertim vero antec. cap. IV, 4) Notandus est error vulgati interpretis. In fontibus prorsus contraria est verborum fententia: מַה הַקְדּוֹשִׁים, ad quemnam sanctorum conuerteris? Hoc est, omnino ad nullum. Est enim notissima regula hermeneutica: Interrogatio adfirmans maxime negat. Vberius de hoc argumento exposuit S. V. DEYLINGIVS, obs. S. T. l. 28.

membrorum ecclesiae militantis, pro se invicem precibus quasi concertantium. Hanc intercessionem quasi commilitantem docet Paulus Rom. XV, 30. Adhortor vos, Fratres, per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, & per dilectionem Spiritus, συναγωνίσασθαί μοι, ut concertetis mecum in precibus pro me ad Deum. At angeli in precibus nobiscum non concertant, cum non sint membra ecclesiae militantis; neque cum iisdem hostibus ac miseriis, a quibus christiani lacessuntur, conflictantur.


### Q. XX. Whether the angel seen by the eyes of the fathers in the O. T., and described everywhere as God, was a created or an uncreated being?

The angel seen by the fathers in the O. T. under a visible form, called Jehovah, described by attributes and works proper to God alone, and honored with divine worship, was an uncreated angel, namely the Son of God, prefiguring his future incarnation.

It is proved by a general syllogism: To whatever angel are attributed the names proper to God, the essential attributes of God, works truly divine, and the worship of religious adoration and invocation, he was not a created angel, but an uncreated one, namely the Son of God. But to the angel in the O. T. seen by the fathers are attributed the names, etc. Therefore. The minor is evident, because the Angel who was the monitor of the fugitive Hagar, Gen. XVI, 7. The principal guest of Abraham, attended by two ministering angels, Gen. XVIII, 1. The host of Lot, Gen. XIX, 18. The comforter of Hagar, Gen. XXI, 7. The wrestler with Jacob, Gen. XXXII, 24. The redeemer of Jacob, Gen. XLVIII, 16. The inhabitant of the Bush, Exod. III, 2. The leader of Israel through the desert into the land of Canaan, Exod. XIII, 21. c. XXIII, 20. The moderator of Balaam, Num. XXII, 28. The Prince of the host of the Lord and commander of Joshua, Josh. V, 11. The informer of Manoah, Jud. XIII, 18. is distinguished by divine names, is described by the essential attributes of God, is said to have performed works truly divine, and is honored with religious worship. Look into the biblical context in any of these places, and compare D. CALOV. syst. t. IV. from p. 211 to p. 283, and with him D. QUENSTED. p. I. theol. did. pol. from f. 494 to f. 509.

The antithesis is that of the Papists and Socinians, who deny that the Son of God appeared in the O. T. in such a visible form as angels were accustomed to be seen in.

I. Whoever has spoken with men in these last times, he has not spoken to the fathers in the O. T. But Christ, etc. Heb. I, 2. Therefore. Resp. Distinguish between an ordinary visible prophet and an extraordinary one. Christ in the N. T., as an ordinary prophet, in flesh hypostatically [ὑποστατικῶς] flowing, was seen and spoke. In the O. T., the Son of God, by an economy, spoke to the fathers extraordinarily for a certain time, and presented himself to be seen by few.

II. If the Son of God appeared according to his own person, as an angel in the O. T., he appeared either in angelic or human form. Not in angelic form; since that cannot be seen: nor in human form; for from this he cannot be called an angel. Therefore, he clearly did not appear according to his own person, as an angel, in the O. T. R. The Son of God in the O. T. appeared in the visible form of some man, such as angels were accustomed to be seen in elsewhere: and he is called an angel, on account of his mission from the Father for an extraordinary prophetic act.

III. Whoever is called an angel for the reason that he was sent by God, he is not the supreme God: But by the evangelical doctors the Word [ὁ λόγος] is called an angel for the reason that he was sent by God: Therefore the Word [ὁ λόγος] is not the supreme God. R. Distinguish between a mission made by command and one made by voluntary consent. Whoever is called an angel because of a mission made by God by command, he is not the supreme God, I concede. But the Son of God was sent by the Father with most free consent. It is agreed among all, however, that an equal can send an equal who consents.

IV. If the Son of God appeared in angelic form, God the Father also appeared in the same: The consequent is absurd: Therefore the antecedent is also. The consequence of the major is proved; because an apparition in visible form is a work of God ad extra. But divine works ad extra are indivisible, i. e.

common to all three persons of the divinity. Resp. That apparition was indeed a divine work ad extra, but not essential, rather personal. However, works ad extra that are personal, by reason of the principle, are common, but by reason of the term are appropriated to one person of the divinity. The example of the Holy Spirit, who appeared under the visible form of a dove, is similar.

V. Jehovah in the O. T. in our opinion, appeared as an angel: God the Father is Jehovah: Therefore God the Father, in our opinion, appeared as an angel. Resp. Jehovah in the major premise is taken relatively, and denotes the Son of God. Hence in the minor premise it is wrongly subsumed under God the Father.

VI. The Son of God appeared in the O. T. either in his own hypostasis, or through a legate, or angel: Not in his own hypostasis, because that is invisible: Therefore through an angel. Resp. Christ appeared in his own hypostasis, but clothed in a visible form, which we call angelic; since in such a visible symbol angels are accustomed to appear.

VII. Whoever teaches that the Son of God, by assuming an angelic form, appeared in his own person, they must teach that the angelic form was the proper hypostasis of the Son of God. But orthodox doctors need not teach that; because the Son of God did not assume angels into his hypostasis, but the seed of Abraham, Hebr. II, 16. The major is proven, because the Son of God terminates that angelic form, as personally united to himself. Resp. The major is denied. To the proof we say that the Word (ὁ λόγος) terminates the angelic form, not as personally united, but as accidentally and extrinsically assumed, insofar as he clothed himself in it, and economically (οἰκονομικῶς) presented himself to be seen in it: just as the Holy Spirit joined the form of a dove to himself not hypostatically (ὑποστατικῶς), but representatively (παραστατικῶς).

VIII. An angel is a messenger and legate, and is subject to him by whom he is sent: Therefore Christ, being without flesh (ἄσαρκος), and outside the business of the incarnation and redemption, is not to be called an angel, unless we wish to concede to the Arians that Christ is inferior to God the Father. Resp. (1) The word angel designates a mission, but does not necessarily include ministry and an inferior state. (2) The name of angel is indeed attributed to the Son of God outside the business of the incarnation and redemption; but not outside the respect to the same.

IX. An angel, created, sustaining the person of God, can assume his name, be adorned with the same attributes, and be honored with the same worship as God: E. From the proper name of God, the divine attributes, and the most humble worship in the apparitions, it cannot validly be concluded that the angel seen by the fathers in the O. T. was the Son of God. Resp. Angels do not assume the proper name of God, nor do they suffer divine worship to be paid to themselves. That arrogance is far from the modesty of angels, far from the λειτουργία by which they minister to God. Conf. Apoc. XIX, 10.

Latin:

Angelus sub visibili forma in V. T. a patribus conspectus, vocatus Iehouah, descriptus ab attributis & operibus soli Deo propriis, cultuque diuino honoratus, fuit angelus increatus, nimirum Filius Dei, futurae suae incarnationi praeludens.

Probatur syllogismo generali: Cui angelo tribuuntur nomina Deo propria, attributa Dei essentialia, opera vere diuina, & cultus religiosae adorationis atque inuocationis, is non fuit angelus creatus, sed increatus, nimirum Filius Dei. Atqui angelo in V. T. a patribus conspecto tribuuntur nomina &c. E. Min. patet, quia Angelus fugitiuae Hagaris monitor, Gen. XVI, 7. Abrahami hospes principalis, duobus angelis ministris stipatus Gen. XVIII, 1. Lothi hospitator, Gen. XIX, 18. Hagaris consolator, Gen. XXI, 7. Jacobi colluctator Gen. XXXII, 24. Jacobi redemtor, Gen. XLVIII, 16. Rubi habitator, Exod. III, 2. Ductor Israëlis Aegypto per desertum in terram Canaan, Exod. XIII, 21. c. XXIII, 20. Bileami moderator, Num. XXII, 28. Princeps exercitus domini & Iosuae imperator, Ios. V, 11. Manoaei informator, Iud. XIII, 18. nominibus diuinis insignitur, ab attributis Dei essentialibus describitur, opera vere diuina patrasse dicitur, cultu religioso honoratur. Inspice vbiuis locorum contextum biblicum, & conf. d. CALOV. syst. t. IV. a p. 211. vsque ad p. 283. & cum eo D. QVENSTED. p. I. theol. did. pol. a f. 494. vsque ad f. 509.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum & Socinianorum, negantium, Filium Dei in forma visibili tali, in quali conspici consueuere angeli, in V. T. apparuisse. Quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Quicunque vltimis temporibus locutus est cum hominibus, ille non locutus est ad patres in V. T. Atqui Christus &c. Hebr. I, 2. E. Resp. Dist. inter prophetam visibilem ordinarium, & extraordinarium. Christus in N. T. vt ordinarius propheta, in carne ὑποστατικῶς affluenta, visus & locutus est. In V. T. Filius Dei per oeconomiam ad certum tempus locutus est patribus extraordinarie, paucisque se conspiciendum praebuit.

II. Si Filius Dei apparuit secundum personam propriam, vt angelus in V. T. vel apparuit in forma angelica, vel humana. Non in forma angelica; quippe quae videri nequit: neque in forma humana; ab hac enim non potest dici angelus. Ergo plane non apparuit secundum propriam personam, vt angelus, in V. T. R. Filius Dei in V. T. apparuit in forma alicuius viri visibili tali, in quali alias conspici consueuerunt angeli: & dicitur angelus, ob missionem a patre ad actum propheticum extraordinarium.

III. Quicunque ideo dicitur angelus, quia a Deo missus est, is non est summus Deus: Atqui per doctores euangelicos ὁ λόγος ideo dicitur angelus, quia a Deo missus est: Ergo ὁ λόγος non est summus Deus. R. Dist. inter missionem factam per imperium: & factam consensu voluntario. Quicunque ob missionem a Deo factam per imperium dicitur angelus, is non est summus Deus, concedo. At Filius Dei missus est a Patre cum consensu liberrimo. Constat autem inter omnes, quod aequalis possit mittere aequalem consentientem.

IV. Si Filius Dei apparuit in forma angelica, etiam Deus Pater in eadem apparuit: Consequens est absurdum: E. & antecedens. Consequentia maioris probatur; quia apparitio in forma visibili est opus Dei ad extra. Sed opera diuina ad extra sunt indiuisu, i. e.

IV. communia omnibus tribus divinitatis personis. Resp. Apparitio illa fuit quidem opus divinum ad extra, verum non essentiale, sed personale. Opera autem ad extra personalia, ratione principii, sunt communia, ratione termini vero uni divinitatis personæ appropriantur. Par est exemplum Spiritus S. qui sub forma visibili columbæ apparuit.

V. Iehouah in V. T. nostra quidem sententia, apparuit, ut angelus: Deus Pater est Iehouah: E. Deus Pater, nostra sententia, apparuit, ut angelus. Resp. Iehouah in maiori sumitur relate, & notat Filium Dei. Proinde in minori male subsumitur de Deo Patre.

VI. Apparuit Filius Dei in V. T. vel in hypostasi propria, vel per legatum, sive angelum: Non in hypostasi propria, quia illa est invisibilis: E. Per angelum. Resp. Apparuit Christus in hypostasi propria, sed vestita forma visibili, quam angelicam appellamus; quoniam in tali symbolo visibili angeli consueverunt comparere.

VII. Quicunque docent, Filium Dei assumendo formam angelicam in propria persona apparuisse, illos oportet docere, formam angelicam fuisse propriam hypostasin Filii Dei. At doctores orthodoxos non oportet id docere; quia Filius Dei in hypostasin suam non assumsit angelos, sed semen Abrahæ, Hebr. II, 16. Maior probatur, quia Filius Dei illam formam angelicam terminat, ut sibi personaliter unitam. Resp. Negatur maior. Ad probationem dicimus, quod ὁ λόγος terminet angelicam formam, non ut personaliter unitam, sed ut accidentaliter & extrinsecus adscitam, quatenus eadem se vestivit, & οἰκονομικῶς in illa se conspiciendum præbuit: sicut Spiritus S. formam columbæ copulabat non ὑποστατικῶς, sed παραστατικῶς.

VIII. Angelus est nuntius & legatus, ac subiicitur ei, a quo legatur: Christus ergo ἄσαρκος, & extra incarnationis ac redemptionis negotium, non est dicendus angelus, nisi velimus concedere Arianis, Christum esse inferiorem Deo Patre. Resp. (1) Vox angelus missionem designat, sed non includit necessario ministerium & inferiorem statum. (2) Nomen angeli tribuitur Filio Dei quidem extra negotium incarnationis & redemptionis; at non extra respectum ad eandem.

IX. Angelus creatus, sustinens personam Dei, nomen illius assumere, iisdem attributis ornari, eodemque, quo Deus, cultu honorari potest: E. Ex nomine Dei proprio, attributis divinis, cultuque humillimo in apparitionibus valide colligi nequit, angelum conspectum patribus in V. T. fuisse Filium Dei. Resp. Nomen Dei proprium non assumunt angeli, neque cultum divinum sibi tribui patiuntur. Illa arrogantia procul est a modestia angelorum, procul a λειτουργίᾳ, qua Deo ministrant. Conf. Apoc. XIX, 10.


### Of Evil Angels


### Q. XXI. Who are the evil angels?

Evil angels are those who did not persevere in the wisdom and justice created with them, but having turned of their own accord from God and the rule of the right, they became perpetual enemies of God and men, to be tormented with eternal punishments.

Latin:

Angeli mali sunt, qui in concreata sapientia & iustitia non perseverarunt, sed sponte sua a Deo & regula recti aversi, perpetui facti sunt Dei hominumque hostes, æternis cruciatibus torquendi.


### Q. XXII. Why are certain angels called evil?

Certain angels are called evil not on account of their essence, which they have from God; but on account of their spontaneous apostasy, or free aversion of the will from God the highest good, and the rule of the right, which nevertheless they could have kept by the grace of creation.

Latin:

Quidam angeli mali dicuntur non ob essentiam, quam habent a Deo; sed ob spontaneam apostasin, sive liberam voluntatis aversione a Deo summo bono, & regula recti, quam tamen ex creationis gratia servare poterant.


### Question XXIV

(1) The devil did not stand in the truth, says the Savior, John VIII, 44. By truth in this place is understood the concreated perfection of wisdom and justice, with which, as with a divine image, the angels were adorned in their first creation: He did not stand, i.e., he did not persevere.

Therefore, before he fell, he had the truth actually impressed and concreated, for rendering and obtaining faith in God (not, indeed, meritoriously) the crown of confirmation, and for declining the fall, the powers, weapons, and aids.

Cf. DANNHAV. in hodosoph phæn. III. p. 284.

(2) The apostle Jude describes the apostasy of certain angels in words most worthy of remembrance, ep. v. 6. Those angels who did not keep their origin, but left their own dwelling, he has reserved in everlasting chains under darkness for the judgment of the great day.

Obs. (a) By ἀρχὴν (beginning/principality) we understand the original state of the angels, which embraces both the internal perfection of the angelic intellect and will, and the external dignity of the angels. From which some interpreters have rendered ἀρχὴν, in Latin as principatum (principality), D. LUTHER, ihr Fürstenthum (their principality).

(b) Ὀικητήριον (dwelling) designates the happy and in its own way blessed mansion of the angels, yet not yet perfectly glorious, which the beatific vision and the gift of confirmation make serene. Cf. DANNHAV. l.c.p 285.

The angels were able to retain their principality and their dwelling: But they deprived themselves of both by their own will.

(3) The apostle Peter makes mention of the angelic fall, 2 Ep. II, 4, saying: God did not spare the angels who sinned. Ἁμαρτάνειν (to sin) properly signifies to wander from the rule.

Hence ἁμαρτία (sin) is called ἀνομία (lawlessness), 1 John III, 4.

St. Peter therefore hints that certain angels transgressed against the divine will, the rule of all justice.

Quest. XXIII. How could the angels, created wise and holy, fall? The fall of the angels, adorned with the concreated perfection of intellect and will, was not impossible; because the holiness inherent in them in the state of grace was not immutable.

Proof. Although God created all angels good and holy: He had not, however, determined the will of the angels in their first creation to choose the good always and everywhere; but had granted them freedom of choice toward good and evil, so that there was in them, by the power of the concreated divine image, a propensity toward the good, and a most remote potentiality toward evil. Hence it happened that not a few of the angels, having turned away from the good by a voluntary abuse of free will, turned themselves toward evil.

Quest. XXIV. What was the first sin of the fallen angels? The Holy Scriptures teach generally that the angels sinned; but they do not explicitly express what the special first sin of the angels was, from which, as from a fountain, the other sins of the angels flowed.

We conclude probably that pride was the first sin of the angels b).

Proof. a. The apostle Peter, 2 ep. II, 4, describes the fallen angels generally as sinners unworthy of pardon; but he does not determine the species of the first sin into which they fell.

Proof. b. It is probably concluded that a certain angel of the highest order aspired to a more excellent deiformity or a perfection and dignity greater than that which was concreated, and seduced other angels either by example or by some persuasion.

1) From the temptation by which Satan approached and overcame our first parents, Gen. III, 5. Namely, because he instilled in them a desire for a perfection more eminent than the concreated divine image. To commit which sin the devil seems to have instigated the first humans, having committed the same himself.

2) From the avoided machinations of Satan, by which he goes about arrogating to himself the glory of God, Matth. IV, 9. 3) Because the beginning of sin is called pride.

You say: Envy seems to have been the first... sin of the devil. For he is called the father of lies and a murderer from the beginning, John VIII, 44. But he who was a liar and a murderer from the beginning, he was envious from the beginning.

From which it can be gathered that envy toward the human race, [because of] heavenly glory

Latin:

(1) Diabolus in veritate non stetit, inquit Saluator Io. VIII, 44. Per veritatem h. l. intelligitur concreata perfectio sapientiae ac iustitiae, qua, vt diuina imagine, angeli in prima creatione ornati fuerunt: Non stetit, i. e. non perseuerauit.

Igitur antequam laberetur, habuit veritatem actu impressam & concreatam, ad fidem Deo praestandam & consequendam (non id quidem meritorie) confirmationis coronam, & declinandum lapsum, vires, arma, auxilia.

Conf. DANNHAV. in hodosoph phæn. III. p. 284.

(2) Apostasiam angelorum quorundam verbis memoratu dignissimis describit apostolus Iudas ep. v. 6. Angelos eos, qui non retinuerunt suam originem, sed reliquerunt proprium domicilium in iudicium magni diei, vinculis perpetuis sub tenebris reseruauit.

Obf. (a) Per ἀρχὴν intelligimus statum originalem angelorum, qui tum internam perfectionem intellectus & voluntatis angelicae, tum externam angelorum dignitatem complectitur. Ex quo nonnulli interpretes ἀρχὴν reddiderunt, latine per principatum, D. LVTHERVS, ihr Fürstenthum.

(b) Ὀικητήριον designat mansionem angelorum felicem & suo modo beatam, nondum tamen perfecte gloriosam, quam visio beatifica, & confirmationis donum ferenat. Conf. DANNHAV. l.c.p 285.

Poterant angeli retinere principatum & domicilium suum: At illi sponte sua vtroque se priuarunt.

(3) Apostolus Petrus lapsus angelici mentionem facit, 2 Ep. II, 4. inquiens: Deus angelis, qui peccarunt, non pepercit. Ἁμαρτάνειν proprie significat a regula aberrare.

Exinde ἁμαρτία dicitur ἀνομία, 1 Io. III, 4.

Innuit igitur S. Petrus, quosdam angelos aduersus voluntatem diuinam, omnis iustitiae regulam, praeuaricatos esse.

Quaest. XXIII. Quomodo labi potuerunt angeli, creati sapientes & sancti? Non impossibilis fuit lapsus angelorum, concreata intellectus & voluntatis perfectione exornatorum; quia insita ipsis sanctitas in statu gratiae non fuit immutabilis.

Prob. Quamuis Deus angelos omnes condiderit bonos & sanctos: Non tamen voluntatem angelorum in prima creatione ad bonum semper & vbique eligendum determinauerat; sed concesserat ipsis libertatem arbitrii ad bonum & malum, ita vt ipsis inesset vi concreatae imaginis diuinae propensio ad bonum, & potentia remotissima ad malum. Inde factum, vt haud pauci angelorum, voluntario liberi arbitrii abusu a bono auersi, ad malum se conuerterint.

Quaest. XXIV. Quodnam primum fuit peccatum angelorum lapsorum? Angelos peccasse, generatim docent sacrae litterae; sed eadem non diserte exprimunt, quodnam speciale fuerit angelorum peccatum primum, e quo velut fonte cetera angelorum peccata manauerint .

Probabiliter colligimus, superbiam fuisse primum angelorum peccatum b).

Prob. a. Apostolus Petrus 2 ep. II, 4. generatim describit angelos lapsos, vt peccatores venia indignos; at non determinat speciem peccati primi, in quod prolapsi sint.

Prob. b. Angelum quendam supremi ordinis excellentiorem deiformitatem aut concreata eminentiorem perfectionem ac dignitatem affectasse, aliosque angelos aut exemplo, aut suasione quadam seduxisse, probabiliter colligitur.

1) Ex tentatione, qua fatan protoplastos nostros adgressus debellauit, Gen. III, 5. Quippe quibus cupidinem eminentioris concreatae imagine diuina perfectionis instillauit. Ad quod peccatum perpetrandum diabolus primos homines instigauit, idem commisisse videtur.

2) Ex vitatis Satanae machinamentis, quibus gloriam Dei sibi arrogatum it, Matth. IV, 9. 3) Quia initium peccati dicitur superbia.

Dicis: Inuidia videtur primum... fuisse diaboli peccatum. Dicitur enim pater mendacii & homicida ab initio, Io. VIII, 44. Sed qui ab initio fuit mendax & homicida, is ab initio fuit inuidus.

Ex quo colligere licet, inuidiam erga genus humanum coelesti gloria


### Quaest. XXV. Was the sin of the angels very grave?

to be the first sin of the devil. Resp. The devil was not simply and absolutely a liar or a murderer from the beginning, but relatively, from the time when his correlate, or the object of his envy, namely man, existed: Now envy is the offspring of pride. It is therefore consistent with truth that the first sin of the angels was pride (*); which was accompanied by many sins, contempt of the eternal Divinity, refusal of obedience, lying, envy, and other things of that kind.

Quaest. XXV.

Was the sin of the angels very grave? The sin of the angels was by far the most grave and most atrocious.

Prob. The atrocity of the angelic sin is estimated 1) from the injured object, which is God, the best and greatest creator of the angels: 2) From the safeguards, by which they could have avoided evil. For the intellect of the angels shone with an extraordinary light of wisdom. Their will excelled in perfect holiness: 3) From the manner of sinning. For the angels did not sin out of infirmity or inadvertence, but out of full intellect, deliberate counsel, and voluntary abuse of free will, with no one inciting them,

Latin:

beandum fuisse primum diaboli peccatum. Resp. Diabolus non simpliciter & absolute ab initio mendax, aut homicida fuit, sed relate, ex quo correlatum, sive obiectum invidiae, nempe homo, exstitit: Est autem invidia superbiae proles. Vero igitur consentaneum est, primum angelorum peccatum fuisse superbiam (*); quam comitata sunt plura peccata, contemptus aeterni Numinis, obsequii detractatio, mendacium, invidia, & id genus alia.

Quaest. XXV. Fuitne peccatum angelorum admodum grave?

Peccatum angelorum fuit longe gravissimum & atrocissimum.

Prob. Atrocitas peccati angelici aestimatur 1) ex obiecto laeso, quod est Deus, angelorum creator optimus, maximus: 2) Ex praesidiis, quibus malum declinare poterant. Angelorum quippe intellectus eximia sapientiae luce resplendebat. Voluntas sanctitate perfecta eminebat: 3) Ex modo peccandi. Peccarunt enim angeli non ex infirmitate, aut inadvertentia, sed ex pleno intellectu, deliberato consilio & voluntario liberi arbitrii abusu, nemine instigante,


### XXVI. Are the fallen angels under a certain leader?

and it is probable that the evil angels fell under a certain leader or prince, whom Holy Scripture calls Satan and the devil . Who, either by persuasion or by example, lured many angels into the fellowship of the same sin .

Prob. a. 1) Because in the singular the devil is said not to have stood in the truth, John VIII, 44. 2) Because the same ἄρχων τῶν δαιμονίων, prince of the demons, is called so, Luke XI, 15.

Prob. b. Apoc. XII, 4, mention is made of the angels of Satan: Where Satan denotes him who most opposes God, the rest are only called angels of Satan; because they followed the persuasion and example of this adversary of God in sinning. Conf. Matth. XXV, 41.

Latin:

Probabile est, angelos malos lapsos esse sub certo quodam duce aut principe, quem Satanam & diabolum sacra scriptura appellat . Qui vel suasione, vel exemplo, plures angelos ad societatem eiusdem peccati pellexit .

Prob. a. 1) Quia in singulari diabolus dicitur non stetisse in veritate, Io. VIII, 44. 2) Quia idem ἄρχων τῶν δαιμονίων princeps daemoniorum appellatur, Luc. XI, 15.

Prob. b. Apoc. XII, 4. mentio fit angelorum Satanae: Vbi Satanas notat eum, qui Deo maxime aduersatur, reliqui tantum dicuntur angeli Satanae; quia huius aduersarii Dei suasionem & exemplum in peccando secuti sunt. Conf. Matth. XXV, 41.


### Q. XXVII. At what time did the angels fall?

The angels did not fall within the six days of creation, but after it was completed . Before the fall of the first men, in the second week of the created world, it is uncertain on what day .

Prob. a. When the works were finished within the six days, the most wise creator added a eulogy of goodness: For God saw everything that he had made, and it was very good, Gen. I, 31. But if all creatures made within the six days, by the judgment of God, were good, how are the fallen angels to be judged to have abandoned their original goodness within that six-day period?

Prob. b. The fall of the angel undoubtedly preceded the fall of man: otherwise, if he had persisted in the truth, he would not have tempted man to sin. Yet the fall of the angel did not extend beyond the second week of the time of the created world. For the devil is a murderer from the beginning, John VIII, 44, and so he did not retain his origin for long.

Latin:

Angeli lapsi sunt non intra hexaëmeron creationis, sed eo absoluto . Ante Tempus lapsum primorum hominum, secunda orbis conditi hebdomade, incertum, qua die .

Prob. a. Consummatis intra sextiduum operibus, creator sapientissimus bonitatis elogium adiecit: Nam vidit Deus omne, quod fecit, & erat bonum valde, Gen. I, 31. Quod si omnes intra hexaëmeron factae creaturae, arbitro Deo, bonae fuerunt, quomodo intra illud sextiduum angeli lapsi originalem bonitatem reliquisse censendi sunt?

Prob. b. Lapsum hominis haud dubie antecessit lapsus angeli: ceteroqui, si perstitisset in veritate, hominem ad peccandum non follicitasset Neque tamen vltra alteram septimanam, orbis conditi tempus lapsus angelici se extendit. Est enim diabolus homicida ab initio, Io. VIII, 44. adeoque non diu originem suam retinuit.


### Q. XXVIII. Do evil angels in the state of misery have a certain knowledge, freedom of action, and power?

Fallen angels have a certain knowledge, but it is surrounded by the darkness of doubts and errors. Their will, cast toward evil, does not enjoy that freedom which brings indifference toward good and evil, or toward several goods; but their freedom is concerned with particular evils. Their power is indeed superior to human power, yet it is bound by divine virtue, so that they can accomplish nothing without the permission of God.

Prob. a. Evil angels know God, themselves, the state of this universe, and certain future things. They know God indeed, but they shudder entirely at this θεογνωσία (knowledge of God). You believe that God is one: you do well. But even the demons believe, and (yet) tremble, James II, 19. Evil angels know themselves. For if the spirit of man, which is in man, knows what is in man, 1 Cor. II, 11: Why should the same not be established concerning evil angels? Evil angels know the state of this universe. This we learn from Job I, 6, where Satan says that he has traversed the earth. Conf. 1 Pet. V, 8. Evil angels know certain future things. Indeed, they know with certainty and evidence future things which proceed from determined causes and according to the order of nature always behaving in the same way, e.g., they know eclipses of the sun and moon with certainty from their causes. But contingent future things, which depend on free will, demons either know with certainty from divine revelation, Job I, 12, 1 Kings XXII, 22, or they foreknow with probability by natural sagacity from the characters of men, temperaments, customs, and present things, diligently observed, yet in such a way that that foreknowledge is uncertain and fallacious. Hence it happens that the event does not always correspond to diabolical predictions.…

Proof b. Regarding particular evils, demons have a certain freedom of will, insofar as they can choose this from among several evils, and not choose it (which is the freedom of exercise or contradiction); likewise, they can choose one over another (which is the freedom of contrariety, or specification).

Proof c. That the power of evil angels is great is evident from the fact that the devil is called by Christ ἰσχυρὸς, a strong man armed, Luke 11:22, and by Paul the malignant spirits are called ἐξουσίαι καὶ κοσμοκράτορες, powers and world-rulers, Eph. 6:12. But that the power of demons is circumscribed by God within certain limits is clear from the fact that they can do only as much as is permitted to them by the secret command of the Almighty, as AUGUSTINE says, lib. 2 de C. D. c. 23. Cf. Exod. 8:18, Job 1:12, Matt. 8:13.

Latin:

Est angelis lapsis scientia quaedam, sed dubitationum & errorum tenebris circumfusa. Voluntas eorum ad malum proiecta non gaudet libertate ea, quae infert indifferentiam ad bonum & malum, vel ad plura bona; sed versatur libertas eorum circa mala particularia. Potentia illorum est quidem humana superior, attamen virtute diuina ligata, vt absque permissione Dei nihil efficere valeant.

Prob. a. Cognoscunt angeli mali Deum, seipsos, statum huius vniuersi, & quaedam futura. Deum cognoscunt quidem, sed vt ad hanc θεογνωσίαν toti cohorrescant. Tu credis, quod Deus vnus sit: bene facis. Atqui etiam daemonia credunt, & (tamen) contremiscunt, Iac. II, 19. Cognoscunt angeli mali seipsos. Nam si spiritus hominis, qui est in homine, nouit, quae sunt in homine, 1 Cor. II, 11: Quidni idem de angelis malis statuendum erit? Cognoscunt angeli mali statum huius vniuersi. Id quod discimus ex Iob. I, 6. vbi Satan dicit, se terram peragrasse. Conf. 1 Petr. V, 8. Cognoscunt angeli mali quaedam futura. Nimirum certo & euidenter cognoscunt futura, quae a causis determinatis & secundum ordinem naturae semper eodem modo se habentibus proficiscuntur, v. gr. eclipses solis & lunae certo cognoscunt ex suis causis. Futura autem contingentia, quae a voluntate libera dependent, daemonia vel certo cognoscunt ex reuelatione diuina, Iob. I, 12. 1 Reg. XXII, 22. vel sagacitate naturali probabiliter praecognoscunt ex ingeniis hominum, temperamentis, moribus & rebus praesentibus, diligenter spectatis, ita tamen, vt illa præcognitio sit incerta & fallax. Inde fit, vt prædictionibus diabolicis non semper respondeat euentus.

Prob. b. Circa mala particularia dæmonia habent quandam libertatem arbitrii, quatenus ex pluribus malis hoc eligere, & non eligere (quæ est libertas exercitii vel contradicfionis); item vnum præ alio eligere, (quæ est libertas contrarietatis, vel specificationis) possint.

Prob. c. Potentiam angelorum malorum esse magnam, patet ex eo, quod diabolus a Christo vocatur ἰσχυρὸς, fortis armatus, Luc. XI, 22. & a Paullo spiritus maligni appellantur ἐξουσίαι καὶ κοσμοκράτορες, potestates & mundi potentes, Eph. VI, 12. At certis limitibus a Deo circumscriptam esse dæmoniorum potentiam, liquet ex eo, quod tantum possunt, quantum secreto omnipotentis imperio illis permittitur, dicente AVGVSTINO lib. II. de C. D. c. 23. Conf. Exod. VIII, 18. Iob. I, 12. Matth. VIII, 13.


### Q. XXX. How manifold is diabolical obsession?

The operations of evil angels are indeed various; but all are directed toward the undermining of divine glory a), and toward the ruin, no less temporal than eternal, both of individual men and of hierarchical states b).

Proof a. The great dragon instructed and armed his angels against Michael, i.e., Christ, intending to destroy his kingdom, Rev. 12:7.

Proof b. Evil angels burn with the desire to harm both individual men and the three hierarchies. For they often inflict diseases upon the bodies of men, Luke 12:11. They lay snares for the wealth of men and inflict violence, Job 1:12; they beset souls as well as bodies, and they delude the senses of men with specters, and pour forth terror.

Question 30. How many kinds of diabolical obsession are there?

Diabolical obsession is twofold, spiritual and corporal. The former is that by which the devil blinds the minds of impious men, instructs them with the worst counsels, incites them to nefarious sins, and leads them, as if caught in snares, to his own will a). The latter is that by which the impure spirit, with God permitting and punishing preceding sins, enters the bodies of men, dwells within them according to its own substance, and operates in them b).

Proof a. (1) The god of this world has blinded the senses of the unbelievers, lest the light of the gospel should shine upon them, Eph. 2:2. (2) He put this counsel into the heart of Judas, that he should betray Jesus, John 13:2. (3) He incited David to number the people, 1 Chron. 21:1. (4) He takes many ζωγρεῖ, i.e., ensnares them like beasts, and leads them to his own will, 2 Tim. 2:16.

Proof b. That obsessed men, who are also called demoniacs, energumens, and possessed, are occupied by demons substantially present and are tormented in a horrible manner, is taught both by the sacred scriptures, Matt. 6:24, ch. 8:28, ch. 9:32, ch. 12:22, Luke 4:33, Acts 8:7, ch. 19:12, and is testified to by experience (*).

Question.

Quest. XXXI. What are the causes of bodily obsession?

The efficient cause of obsession is the devil a); the meritorious cause is sin b); the cause, vindicating or punishing sin through the bodily obsession of the devil, is God c); the intermediate end is punishment or chastisement d); the ultimate end is the manifestation of divine justice, wisdom, & power e).

Proof a. The devil is in the obsessed κατ' ὀσίαν ϰὴ ἐνέργειαν, that is, by substantial and operative presence. For he dwells in them according to substance, see Luke IV, 33, and takes to himself many companions, unclean spirits, Luke XI, 26, Mark IV, 6, and performs stupendous and most foul operations in them, Matthew VIII, 28, cf. XV, 22, on account of which horrendous ἐνεργείας, or operations, they are called ἐνεργόμενοι.

Proof b. Sin is either original or actual, and the latter is either involuntary or voluntary, that is, proæretic. For the most part, the causes of bodily obsession are proæretic sins, persistently continued; such as contempt of the divine word, carnal security, curses and blasphemies, fornication and adultery, drunkenness, avarice, pride, and a desired pact with evil spirits. St. Paul delivered the incestuous man to Satan, for the destruction of the flesh, 1 Cor. V, 5. Nevertheless, God sometimes permits the devil to bodily obsess a man who is polluted by original and involuntary, but not proæretic, sin. Let the lunatic in Mark IX, 21 be an example to us, whom a mute and deaf devil had occupied from childhood.

Proof c. God, by the bodily obsession of an evil demon, either as a most just judge, vindicates the great sins of the impious; or as a most good father, afflicts the pious with this plague, so that they may be chastised and tested: Just as, with God permitting, Satan struck Job with a foul ulcer, and his angel buffeted Paul, Job II, 7, 2 Cor. XII, 7. (*) Although it must be carefully observed that Job and Paul were afflicted not by an internal indwelling of Satan, but by an external assistance. For bodily diabolical obsession, it is required that the demon occupy the body of a man ἀυτοπροσώπως, and torment it.

…Proof d. & e. From what has been said, it is clear that the intermediate end of diabolical obsession, on the part of God, is partly τιμωρίαν, a punishment inflicted by an angry God; partly παιδείαν, a chastisement arising from God propitiated. The end, on the part of God, is the ultimate manifestation of divine justice, by which sins are avenged; of wisdom, by which a certain limit is set to diabolical fury: of power, by which Satan is expelled. On the part of the devil, indeed, the end of corporal obsession is the destruction of man; which, however, God, for His immense goodness, often turns to the salvation of the obsessed, so that they may repent and be saved. Conf. Matth. XV, 28. 1 Cor. V, 5.

Question XXXII. What are the signs of corporal obsession?

The signs of corporal obsession are enumerated as various, some of which are proper to the obsessed; some are common to the melancholic, the ecstatic, and the phrenetic, and therefore they are not to be taken and considered separately, but conjunctively, lest we take those afflicted with serious diseases for the obsessed.

Proof. The indications of corporal obsession are: 1) Knowledge of foreign languages and disciplines, acquired without any study: 2) Knowledge and manifestation of hidden and future things: 3) Speech, made with an open mouth, without the due disposition of the organs: 4) Representation of birds, sheep, oxen, pigs, bears, etc.: 5) Strength more than human in carrying immense burdens: 6) Horrendous blasphemies belched forth against the most holy deity: 7) Very agile stretching of bodies without the dissolution of the structure of the body, Luc. IV, 35. 8) Impure, savage, terrible gestures and acts, e.g., they sometimes foam at the mouth, gnash their teeth, throw themselves into water, into fire, and strive to commit suicide: 9) Grave vexation within the bowels and parts of the body, and swelling of the belly: 10) Cessation of the senses, both internal and external, and of the locomotive faculty, Matth. XV, 22. c. XVII, 16. Luc. VIII, 25-35. Marc. I, 24.

Latin:

Operationes angelorum malorum sunt variæ quidem; at omnes directæ ad labefactationem gloriæ diuinæ a), & ad perniciem non temporalem minus, quam æternam tum hominum singulorum, tum statuum hierarchicorum b).

Prob. a. Draco magnus instruxit & obarmat angelos suos aduersus Michaëlem, i. e. Christuin, regnum ipsius destructurus, Apoc. XII, 7.

Prob. b. Angeli mali flagrant cupiditate nocendi tum hominibus singulis, tum tribus hierarchiis. Etenim hominum corporibus sæpe immittunt morbos, Luc. XII, 11. Opibus hominum struunt insidias & vim inferunt, Iob. I, 12. animas pariter atque corpora obsident, & spectris hominum sensibus illudunt, atque formidinem offundunt.

Quæst. XXX. Quotuplex est obsessio diabolica?

Obsessio diabolica est duplex, spiritualis & corporalis. Illa est, qua diabolus animos hominum impiorum excæcat, pessimis consiliis instruit, ad nefanda peccata instigat, eosque, velut laqueis captos, ad voluntatem suam ducit a). Hæc est, qua spiritus impurus, permittente, & peccata antegressa vindicante Deo, corpora hominum ingreditur, intra eadem secundum substantiam suam habitat, & in illis operatur b).

Prob. a. (1) Deus huius sæculi excæcauit sensus incredulorum, ne illucesceret illis lumen euangelii, Eph. II, 2. (2) In cor Iudæ hoc immisit consilium, vt proderet Iesum. Io. XIII, 2. (3) Instigauit Dauidem, vt numeraret populum, 1 Chron. XXI, 1. (4) Multos ζωγρεῖ, i. e. velut bestias illaqueat, & ducit ad voluntatem suam, 2 Tim. II, 16.

Prob. b. Homines obsessos, qui etiam dæmoniaci, energumeni & arreptitii vocantur, a dæmonibus substantialiter præsentibus occupari, & horrendum in modum diuexari, tum sacræ litteræ docent, Matth. VI, 24. c. VIII, 28. c. IX, 32. c. XII, 22. Luc. IV, 33. Act. VIII, 7. c. XIX, 12. tum experientia testatur (*).

Quæst.

Quæst. XXXI. Quæ sunt caussæ obseffionis corporalis?

Caussa efficiens obseffionis est diabolus a); caussa promerens est peccatum b); caussa, corporali diaboli obseffione peccatum vindicans, aut castigans est Deus c); finis intermedius est pœna vel castigatio d); ultimus est iustitiæ, sapientiæ & potentiæ diuinæ manifestatio e).

Prob. a. Diabolus est in obseffis κατ' ὀσίαν ϰὴ ἐνέργειαν, qua substantialem & operosam præsentiam. Habitat enim in iisdem secundum substantiam, vid. Luc. IV, 33. & adsciscit socios plures spiritus immundos, Luc. XI, 26. Marc. IV, 6. & stupendas, turpissimasque in ipsis operationes perficit, Matth. VIII, 28. c. XV, 22. ob quas horrendas ἐνεργείας, siue operationes, ἐνεργόμενοι vocantur.

Prob. b. Peccatum est vel originale, vel actuale, & hoc vel inuoluntarium, vel voluntarium siue proæreticum. Plerumque caussæ obseffionis corporalis sunt peccata proæretica, perseueranter continuata; qualia sunt contemtus verbi diuini, securitas carnalis, diræ & blasphemiæ, stuprum & adulterium, ebrietas, auaritia, superbia, desideratum cum spiritibus malis pactum. S. Paullus hominem incestuosum tradidit Satanæ, in perniciem carnis, 1 Cor. V, 5. Permittit tamen Deus interdum diabolo, vt corporaliter obsideat hominem, originali & inuoluntario quidem, sed non proæretico peccato pollutum. Exemplum nobis esto lunaticus ille, Marc. IX, 21. quem diabolus mutus & surdus inde a puero occupauerat.

Prob. c. Deus obseffione cacodæmonis corporali, vel vt iustissimus iudex, vindicat grandia impiorum peccata; vel vt pater optimus affligit plaga ista pios, vt castigentur & probentur: Sicut permittente Deo Satanas vlcere malo percussit Iobum, eiusque angelus colaphos impegit Paullo, Iob: II, 7. 2 Cor. XII, 7. (*) Quamuis probe obseruandum sit, afflictos esse Iobum & Paullum non per internam Satanæ inhabitationem, sed externam assistentiam. Ad obseffionem diabolicam corporalem requiritur, vt dæmon ἀυτοπροσώπως corpus hominis occupet, idque cruciet.

Prob. d. & e. E iam dictis liquet, finem intermedium obseffionis diabolicæ, ex parte Dei, esse partim τιμωρίαν, pœnam inflictam a Deo irato; partim παιδείαν, castigationem ortam a Deo propitiato. Finis, ex parte Dei, ultimus est manifestatio diuinae iustitiae, qua peccata vindicantur; sapientiae, qua furori diabolico certa praefigitur meta: potentiae, qua Satan expellitur. Ex parte diaboli quidem, corporalis obsessionis finis est pernicies hominis; quam tamen Deus, pro immensa sua bonitate, saepe in obsessorum salutem conuertit, vt resipiscant & saluentur. Conf. Matth. XV, 28. 1 Cor. V, 5.

Quaest. XXXII. Quanam sunt signa obsessionis corporalis?

Signa obsessionis corporalis recensentur varia, quorum quaedam obsessis sunt propria; quaedam melancholicis, ecstaticis, & phreneticis communia, ideoque non disiunctim, sed coniunctim sumenda & consideranda sunt, ne grauibus morbis afflictos pro obsessis habeamus.

Prob. Indicia corporalis obsessionis sunt: 1) Linguarum peregrinarum atque disciplinarum notitia, nullo studio comparata: 2) Occultorum & futurorum scientia atque manifestatio: 3) Loquela, aperto ore, absque debita organorum dispositione facta: 4) Auicularum, ouium, boum, porcorum, vrforum &c. repraesentatio: 5) Robur plus quam humanum in portandis oneribus immanibus: 6) Blasphemiae horrendae in sanctissimum numen eructatae: 7) Agillima corporum diductio sine dissolutione compagis corporis, Luc. IV, 35. 8) Gestus & actus impuri, faeui, terribiles, v. gr. spumant interdum ore, frendent dentibus, abiiciunt se in aquam, in ignem, & mortem sibi consciscere nituntur: 9) Grauis vexatio intus in visceribus & partibus corporis, ventrisque intumescentia: 10) Cessatio sensuum, tam internorum, quam externorum, & facultatis locomotiuae, Matth. XV, 22. c. XVII, 16. Luc. VIII, 25-35. Marc. I, 24.


### Q. XXXIII. What are the antidotes against bodily obsession?

The most present antidotes against corporal obsession are prayers and fasting.

Proof from Matth. XVII, 21. But this kind (of demons) does not go out, except by prayer and fasting. From which it was solemn for the primitive church to proclaim days of fasting, to institute public assemblies, to introduce the demoniac into the church, and to send pious prayers to heaven over him. AUGUSTIN. lib. XXII. de C. D. c. 8.

Question XXXIV. Do demons also mock men with specters?

That evil demons mock men with specters, the sacred scriptures teach.

Proof. 1) שְׂעִירִים, commonly called satyrs, appearing in the form of goats, Es. XIII, 21. &c. XXXIV, 14. were specters. 2) The author of Wisdom says concerning specters: c. XVII, 3. 4. They were troubled by images --- and phantoms appeared with mournful countenances. 3) In the N. T. mention is made of specters, Matth. XIV, 26. Luc. XXIV, 37.

Question XXXV. Are specters the souls of the deceased?

Specters are not the souls of the deceased.

Prob. The souls of the impious dead do not return to this life, Luke XVI, 26. But the souls of the pious rest in the hand of God, Wis. III, 1.

Latin:

Antidota praesentissima aduersus obsessionem corporalem sunt preces & ieiunium.

Prob. ex Matth. XVII, 21. Hoc autem genus (daemoniorum) non exit, nisi per preces & ieiunium. Ex quo solenne fuit primitiuae ecclesiae, indicere dies ieiuniorum, instituere conventus publicos, introducere in ecclesiam daemoniacum, & super eo pias in coelum mittere preces. AVGVSTIN. lib. XXII. de C. D. c. 8.

Quaest. XXXIV. Num etiam spectris illudunt hominibus daemones?

Cacodaemones hominibus illudere spectris, sacrae docent litterae.

Prob. 1) שְׂעִירִים satyri vulgo dicti, hircorum specie apparentes Es. XIII, 21. &c. XXXIV, 14. fuerunt spectra. 2) Auctor sapientiae de spectris inquit: c. XVII, 3. 4. Simulacris perturbati sunt --- & phantasmata flebilibus speciebus apparebant. 3) In N. T. fit mentio spectrorum, Matth. XIV, 26. Luc. XXIV, 37.

Quaest. XXXV. Suntne spectra animae defunctorum?

Spectra non sunt animae defunctorum.

Prob. Animae defunctorum impiorum non redeunt in hanc vitam, Luc. XVI, 26. Piorum vero animae requiescunt in manu Dei, Sap. III, 1.


### Q. XXXVI. By what means are specters driven away?

Specters are driven away by a) invincible faith, b) ardent prayers, c) serious amendment of life, d) constant patience.

Prob. a. We resist the devil, steadfast in faith, 1 Pet. V, 9. This is the shield by which we receive the fiery darts of the devil. Eph. VI, 16.

Prob. b. Demons are put to flight by prayer and fasting. Matt. XVII, 21.

Prob. c. Let those infested by specters amend their vices with virtues. For Christ teaches in Luke XI, 24-26 that the devil takes the greatest delight in these dwellings, which have been contaminated by various filth.

Prob. d. Behold! We call those blessed who have endured. You have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; for the Lord is very merciful and compassionate. Jas. V, 11. He who endures the incursions of demons with a calm mind, reflects from time to time that for those who love God, all things work together for good, Rom. VIII, 28.

Latin:

Profligantur spectra a) fide inuicta, b) precibus ardentibus, c) seria vitae emendatione, d) patientia constanti.

Prob. a. Resistimus diabolo stabiles fide, 1 Petr. V, 9. Haec est scutum, quo tela ignita diaboli excipimus. Eph. VI, 16.

Prob. b. Daemones fugantur precatione & ieiunio. Matth. XVII, 21.

Prob. c. Infestati spectris vitia virtutibus emendent. Docet namque Christus Luc. XI, 24. 25. 26. diabolum istis habitaculis vt plurimum delectari, quae varia spurcitie contaminata sunt.

Prob. d. Ecce! beatos praedicamus, qui perpessi sunt. Patientiam Iobi audiuistis, & finem domini vidistis; nam valde misericors est dominus, & miserator. Iac. V, 11. Qui incursiones daemonum placido animo sustinet, subinde recogitat, quod iis, qui diligunt Deum, omnia cooperentur in bonum, Rom. VIII, 28.


### Q. XXXVII. By what operations are demons occupied regarding the hierarchical states?

Evil spirits diligently meditate on how to disturb, pull down, and utterly overturn the ecclesiastical a), political b), and economic c) states.

Prob. a. The devil and his angels vehemently oppose the ecclesiastical state, 1) by sowing heresies: for the devil, that most crafty enemy, sows tares in the field of the church, while men are buried in the sleep of security. Matt. XIII, 27. 2) By hindering the efforts of the pious ministers of the church. Satan hindered Paul from going to the Thessalonians, 1 Thess. II, 18. 3) By calling away the minds of the hearers from the meditation and practice of the divine word: for the devil takes away the seed of the word from the heart of the hearers, Luke VIII, 12. 4) By exciting persecutions against the kingdom of Christ; for the infernal dragon fights against Michael. Rev. XII, 7.

Prob. b. The devil disturbs the political state, 1) by pulling down the harmony of the republic either through internal dissensions or external wars. Thus, an evil spirit incited Ahab to undertake war against the Syrians. 1 Kings XXII, 21. 2) By suggesting wicked and destructive counsels to those in command; such was the counsel regarding the numbering of the people, which he supplied to David. 1 Chron. XXII, 1.

Prob. c. The devil afflicts the economic state, 1) by distracting the minds of spouses: for he is a murderer from the beginning, who delights in causing strife, John VIII, 44. 2) By lying in wait for the children and goods of spouses. The devil deprived the most pious Job of both his wealth and his children. Job I, 13.

Latin:

Cacodaemones statum ecclesiasticum a), politicum b), & oeconomicum c), turbare, conuellere, penitusque euertere assidue meditantur.

Prob. a. Statui ecclesiastico diabolus & ipsius angeli vehementer aduersantur, 1) haereses spargendo: ferit enim diabolus, hostis vafetrimus, zizania in agrum ecclesiae, hominibus somno securitatis sepultis. Matth. XIII, 27. 2) Conatus piorum ecclesiae ministrorum impediendo. Paullum profecturum ad Thessalonicenses Satanas impedivit 1 Thess. II, 18. 3) Auditorum mentes a meditatione & praxi verbi diuini auocando: tollit enim diabolus semen verbi e corde audientium, Luc. VIII, 12. 4) Persecutiones aduersus regnum Christi excitando; dimicat quippe draco infernalis aduersus Michaëlem. Apoc. XII, 7.

Prob. b. Statum politicum turbat diabolus, 1) harmoniam reipublicae aut intestinis dissidiis, aut externis bellis conuellendo. Sic spiritus malignus concitauit Achabum ad bellum suscipiendum aduersus Syros. 1 Reg. XXII, 21. 2) Iniqua & exitiosa consilia imperantibus suggerendo; quale consilium fuit de numerando populo, quod Dauidi suppeditauit. 1 Chron. XXII, 1.

Prob. c. Statum oeconomicum affligit diabolus, 1) mentes coniugum distrahendo: est enim homicida ab initio, qui litibus ferendis delectatur, Io. VIII, 44. 2) Coniugum liberis, bonisque infidiando. Iobum piissimum diabolus & opibus, & liberis orbauit. Iob. I, 13.


### Q. XXXVIII. How manifold is the punishment of the evil angels?

The punishment of the fallen angels is twofold: the punishment of loss and of sense. The punishment of loss, is the most sorrowful loss of grace and glory a). The punishment of sense, or positive, is the torments which demons have felt to be very great since their fall b), and they will undergo greater ones on the day of the final judgment c).

Prob. a. The fallen angels, by their most grievous sin, deprived themselves of the state of grace and glory, and thus they lost both their concreated wisdom and justice, and fell from the hope of the beatific vision of God. Cf. John VIII, 44; ep. Jude v. 6.

Prob. b. We are taught that fire is prepared for the devil and his angels, Matt. XXV, 41, where the Savior undoubtedly understands a singular fire acting upon spirits and inflicting the most exquisite pains. Prob. c.

Prob. c. St. Peter, 2 ep. ch. II, 4, asserts that God did not spare the angels who sinned, but cast them down into hell in chains of darkness, and delivered them to be kept for judgment, cf. Jude v. 6. By chains of darkness is denoted the obligation of the angels to punishment and state. horrible and sad in the squalor of misery. With these chains God has so bound the fallen angels that they are nowhere and never able to shake them off or escape. For although God permits them to dwell in this air and tempt men until the day of the final judgment, they nevertheless carry their punishment and misery everywhere with them, like captive slaves carrying their chain. Moreover, the apostle says that the fallen angels are kept for judgment, so that on the day of the universal judgment they may be openly declared by Christ the judge to be violators of the most holy divine will, and may obtain an increase or completion of their punishments.

Q. XXXIX. Will the punishments of the angels be eternal? The punishments of the evil angels will be eternal and everlasting without end.

Prob. 1) Matt. XXV, 41. Eternal fire is said to be prepared for the devil and his angels; into which also wicked men will be sent, of whom Christ says in v. 46: The unjust will go into eternal punishment; but the righteous into eternal life. From which opposition it is clear that an eternity devoid of an end is designated.

For just as the life into which the elect are about to enter is eternal, so is the punishment which the demons and wicked men will suffer eternal. 2) The apostle Jude in ep. v. 6 asserts that the angels who did not keep their origin, but deserted their own dwelling, are kept in eternal bonds under darkness. But those who are held in eternal bonds, i. e., never to be loosened, under darkness, i. e., in tartarus, cf. 2 Pet.

II, 4. from which there is no redemption, for them no hope of pardon remains. 3) St. John in Rev. XX, 10 says: The devil, who was seducing them, was cast into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophet are, and they will be tormented day and night forever and ever. 4) Evil angels have nothing of their own with which to satisfy an angry God: nor is a mediator, reconciler, or intercessor destined for them: nor are any aids of conversion, justification, or renewal granted to them.

Therefore, they cannot return into favor with God. The antithesis is commonly attributed to Origen, the Adamantine doctor; whom some, however, go to excuse, because he did not seriously assert the restitution of the angels to their integrity, but only disputed about it problematically, for the sake of investigating the truth more accurately.

See D. CALOV. in syst. th. tom. IV. p. 374.

The Anabaptists, however, in the 16th

century boldly affirmed that the demons would eventually be saved, once an end had been put to their torments. But the Socinians dream that the demons are not to be tormented by hellfire eternally, but are to be utterly abolished, and they support their opinion with the following arguments: I.

Whatever sin was finite, that cannot, while maintaining equity, be affected by eternal punishments.

But the sin of the angels &c. Therefore.

The major premise is certain; because between offenses and their punishments, a certain proportion must intervene, otherwise justice would be violated.

Now, indeed, there is no proportion between a finite sin and an infinite punishment.

Resp. The angelic sin is not indeed infinite by reason of the transitory act, but it is considered infinite by reason of the guilt, because of the infinite majesty of God, which was injured by the angelic sin.

Finitude and infinitude in faults are to be estimated not by duration, but by moral obligation. A physical or mathematical proportion between the finite and the infinite is not given, but a moral one is. Thus a king can, with justice unimpaired, banish forever and erase the memory of a citizen by whom his majesty was injured in one act, committed in one hour.

II. The mercy of God endures forever, Lam.

III, 22. 31. Therefore, He does not cast out the fallen angels eternally.

Resp.

Resp. The justice of God also endures forever.

Just as God is merciful, so also is He just. God justly punishes averted sinners, and mercifully receives those who are converted.

Instance: But if men can be converted: why not also the devils? Resp. For fallen men, a restorer of lost integrity, Jesus Christ, was divinely ordained and sent; but not for the angels, who are turned away from God. For Christ did not take hold of them.

Heb. II, 16.

Therefore, God did not spare the angels who sinned, 2 Pet. II, 4. The cause of the perpetually denied to demons

of grace, while Holy Scripture is silent, we cannot render with certainty and infallibility: However, the holy fathers, cited by D. CALOV, tom. IV. syst. p. 319, have brought forward the following reasons: IRENAEUS L. IV. 28: The devil sinned out of full malice, man out of negligence. GREGORY THE GREAT l. IX. moral. c. 36: Man was seduced by the devil, the devil fell of his own accord. CHRYSOSTOM homil. I. on Adam & Eve: In the fall of the angels, not the whole angelic nature perished, as the whole human nature would have perished had the first man sinned. For the rest, we venerate the most just judgment of God, in whose power lies the decision of receiving a sinner into grace, and of deferring it perpetually.

III. Christ on the day of the final judgment will destroy every principality and every power and virtue, 1 Cor. XV, 24: I.e., He will bring to nothing the principalities, powers, and the world-rulers of the darkness of this age, Eph. VI, 11, i.e., the malignant spirits. Resp. The word καταργεῖν, which is found in the source, does not signify simply to annihilate, but to withdraw or take away from anyone their force, efficacy, and operation. Conf. Luke XIII, 7. Rom. III, 31. 1 Cor. XIII, 8. 10. Gal. III, 17. chap. V, 4. 11. Eph. II, 14. Therefore, Christ will destroy the force, power, and empire of the demons, but will not reduce them to nothing.

Latin:

Poena angelorum lapsorum est duplex, poena damni, & sensus. Poena damni, est tristissima iactura gratiae & gloriae a). Poena sensus, seu positiva, sunt cruciatus, quos persentiscunt daemones inde a lapsu permagnos b), maiores subibunt in die extremi iudicii c).

Prob. a. Angeli lapsi peccato suo grauissimo seipsos statu gratiae & gloriae priuarunt, atque adeo tum concreatam sapientiam & iustitiam amiserunt, tum spe visionis Dei beatificae exciderunt. Conf. Io. VIII, 44. ep. Iud. v. 6.

Prob. b. Diabolo & angelis ipsius paratum esse ignem, docemur, Matth. XXV, 41. vbi haud dubie intelligit Saluator ignem singularem in spiritus agentem & dolores exquisitissimos inferentem.

Prob. c. S. Petrus 2 ep. c. II, 4. affert, Deum angelis, qui peccarunt, non pepercitse, sed catenis tenebrarum in tartarum eos detrusisse, atque tradidisse in iudicium asseruatos, conf. Iudae v. 6. Per catenas tenebrarum notatur obligatio angelorum ad poenam & statum. squalore miseriae horridum ac tristem. His catenis Deus angelos lapsos ita alligauit, vt eas nusquam & nunquam excutere, aut euadere valeant. Quamuis enim Deus vsque ad diem extremi iudicii, ipsis in hoc aere versari, hominesque tentare permittat: suam tamen poenam miseriamque, velut captiua mancipia catenam suam, vbique circumferunt. Ceterum dicit apostolus, angelos lapsos asseruari in iudicium, vt in die vniuersalis iudicii palam a Christo iudice declarentur, vt violatores sanctissimae voluntatis diuinae, & augmentum, vel complementum suppliciorum nanciscantur.

Quæst. XXXIX. Eruntne pænæ angelorum æternæ? Angelorum malorum poenæ aeternae & sine fine perennes erunt.

Prob. 1) Matth. XXV, 41. Diabolo & angelis eius paratus dicitur ignis aeternus ; in quem etiam mittentur homines reprobi, de quibus Christus v. 46. inquit: Ibunt iniusti in supplicium aeternum; pii vero in vitam aeternam. Ex qua oppositione dispalescit, aeternitatem finis expertem designari.

Nam vti aeterna est vita, quam ingressuri sunt electi: ita aeternum est supplicium, quod luent daemones & homines reprobi. 2) Apostolus Iudas ep. v. 6. asserit, angelos, qui non retinuerunt originem suam, sed deseruerunt proprium domicilium, aeternis vinculis sub caligine asseruari. At qui vinculis aeternis, i. e. nunquam laxandis, sub caligine, h. e. in tartaro, conf. 2 Petr.

II, 4 . e quo nulla redemtio, detinentur, illis nulla spes veniae superest. 3) S. Io. in Apoc. XX, 10. ait: Diabolus, qui seducebat eos, coniectus est in stagnum ignis & sulphuris, vbi bestia & pseudopropheta, & cruciabuntur dies & noctes in saecula saeculorum. 4) Angeli mali nec de suo habent, vnde irato Deo satisfaciant: nec ipsis destinatus est mediator, reconciliator, intercessor: nec vlla iisdem concessa sunt conuersionis, iustificationis, renouationis subsidia.

Ergo cum Deo in gratiam redire nequeunt. Antithesis tribuitur communiter Origeni, doctori Adamantio; quem tamen nonnulli excusatum eunt, quod angelorum restitutionem in integrum non serio asseruerit, sed de eadem tantum problematice disputauerit, veritatis accuratius indagandae caussa.

Vid. D. CALOV. in syst. th. tom. IV. p. 374 .

Anabaptistae tamen Sec.

XVI. audacter affirmarunt, daemones tandem, imposito cruciatibus ipsorum fine, saluatum iri. At Sociniani somniant, daemones non aeternum igne infernali torquendos, sed penitus abolendos esse, qui suam opinionem sequentibus argumentis firmant: I.

Quodcunque peccatum fuit finitum, illud salua aequitate aeternis poenis non potest affici.

Atqui peccatum angelorum &c. Ergo.

Maior constat; quia inter delicta, & eorum poenas, intercedere debet proportio quaedam, ceteroqui violaretur iustitia.

Iam vero peccati finiti ad poenam infinitam nulla datur proportio.

Resp. Peccatum angelicum non quidem ratione actus transitorii, attamen ratione reatus, infinitum censetur propter infinitam Dei maiestatem, quae peccato angelico laesa est.

Finitas & infinitas in culpis non ex duratione, sed obligatione morali aestimanda est. Finiti ad infinitum non quidem physica aut mathematica, attamen moralis proportio datur. Sic rex ciuem, a quo ipsius maiestas vno actu, vna hora commisso, laesa est, in perpetuum relegare, eiusque memoriam delere potest, illaesa iustitia.

II. Misericordia Dei durat in perpetuum, Thren.

III, 22. 31 . E. angelos lapsos in aeternum non proiicit.

Resp.

Resp. Iustitia Dei etiam durat in perpetuum.

Sicut Deus misericors, ita etiam iustus est. Iuste Deus vindicat peccatores auerfos, clementer recipit conuersos.

Instantia: Sed si homines possunt conuerti: quidni & diaboli? Resp. Hominibus lapsis diuinitus ordinatus & missus est reparator integritatis amissae, Iesus Christus; non autem angelis, a Deo auersis. Hos enim Christus non assumsit.

Hebr. II, 16 .

Proinde etiam angelis, qui peccarunt, Deus non pepercit, 2 Petr. II, 4 . Causlam perpetuo denegatae daemoni-bus 4. Caussam perpetuo denegatæ dæmonibus

gratiae, tacente scriptura S. certo infallibiliter reddere nequimus: Sequentes autem rationes sancti patres, citante D. CALOV. tom. IV. syst. p. 319. adduxerunt, IRENAEVS L. IV. 28: Diabolus ex malitia plena peccauit, homo ex negligentia. GREGORIVS M. l. IX. moral. c. 36: Homo a diabolo seductus, diabolus sua sponte defecit. CHRYSOST. homil. I. de Adamo & Eva: In angelorum lapsu non tota angelica natura, ut homine primo peccante tota natura humana periisset. Ceterum nos veneramur iudicium Dei iustissimum, quem penes est arbitrium, peccatorem in gratiam recipiendi, ac perpetuo deferendi.

III. Christus in die extremi iudicii destruet omnem principatum & omnem potestatem ac virtutem, 1 Cor. XV, 24: E. in nihilum rediget principatus, potestates, & mundi potentes tenebrarum huius saeculi, Eph. VI, 11. i. e. spiritus malignos. Resp. Verbum καταργεῖν, quod habetur in fonte, non significat simpliciter annihilare, sed vim, efficaciam & operationem alicui subtrahere, aut adimere. Conf. Luc. XIII, 7. Rom. III, 31. 1 Cor. XIII, 8. 10. Gal. III, 17. cap. V, 4. 11. Eph. II, 14. Destruet igitur Christus vim, potestatem & imperium daemonum, non illos in nihilum rediget.


### Quest. XL. What practical uses will you extract from the doctrine concerning angels?

The doctrine concerning angels affords us a) a distinguished paraenetic use, for fleeing sins, performing repentance, and cultivating virtue; b) a paracletic use, so that, being certain of the guardianship of angels in all dangers and adverse cases, we may lift up our soul.

Prob. a. 1) Let us solicitously take care that we do nothing unbecoming while angels are looking on. To this points that admonition of St. Paul, 1 Cor. XI, 10: A woman ought to have power (a veil, a sign of subjection toward her husband) upon her head, because of the angels. BERNARD inculcates the same, serm. XII. on Ps. XCI: In every corner have reverence for your angel; and do not do in his presence what you would blush to do in mine. 2) Let us perform repentance maturely, both so that we may continue to enjoy the guardianship of angels, and so that we may excite a certain joy in them. There will be joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents. Luke XV, 10. 3) Let us imitate the virtues of the angels. Angels revere God, sing His praises, and do what is commanded not unwillingly. Therefore, let us fear God. The angel of Jehovah encamps around those who fear Him, Ps. XXXIV, 8. Let us give thanks to God, both for all benefits and especially for angelic protection. Finally, let us most promptly obey divine precepts; since obedience is a sacrifice most pleasing to God.

Prob. b. For if we walk in the ways of our calling, the angels will accompany us, protect us, and render us safe from dangers. For God has commanded His angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways; they shall bear you up on their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone, says the sacred psalmist, Ps. XCI, 11. 12.

SIGH.

With what words, O most merciful God, shall I proclaim your prone benevolence toward me? You created me, and having created me, you protected me. I refer both my life and the security of my life to you. For those most pure spirits who stand before your majesty as most prompt ministers, at your command, stand by me as most faithful guardians. Let the devil rage: I do not succumb, surrounded by heavenly athletes. Let the world insult: I am not overwhelmed, supported by angelic protection. I acknowledge with a grateful heart, O most benign Deity, your most propense grace toward me, and I pray most ardently that you may perpetually rule me, going and returning, by your Spirit, so that I may run the way of my calling, the way of piety, with an unoffending foot. For I believe it will come to pass that the holy angels will encamp around me, render me safe from the insults of enemies, and finally transfer my soul, wearied with human affairs, into the bosom of Christ, where is a secure and most delightful abode.

Latin:

Confert doctrina de angelis nobis a) insignein usum paraeneticum, ad fugienda peccata, agendam poenitentiam & colendam virtutem b); usum paracleticum, vt, de custodia angelorum in omnibus periculis & casibus aduersis certi, animum erigamus.

Prob. a. Sollicite 1) caueamus, ne aspectantibus angelis quidquam praeter decorum faciamus. Quo spectat illud monitum S. Paulli 1 Cor. XI, 10. Mulier debet habere potestatem (velamen, subiectionis erga maritum signum) super capite, propter angelos. Idem inculcat BERNARDVS serm. XII. in Ps. XCI. In quouis angulo angelo tuo reuerentiam habe; nec illo praesente facias, quod me praesente erubesceres. 2) Mature poenitentiam agamus, tum vt porro angelorum custodia fruamur, tum vt gaudium quoddam iisdem excitemus. Gaudium erit coram angelis Dei, super uno peccatore, poenitentiam agente. Luc. XV, 10. 3) Virtutes angelorum imitemur. Angeli Deum reuerentur, ipsius laudes decantant, & imperata haud inuiti faciunt. Quare nos Deum timeamus. Castra metatur angelus Iehouae circa timentes ipsum, Ps. XXXIV, 8. Gratias agamus Deo, cum pro omnibus beneficiis, tum inprimis pro praesidio angelico. Praeceptis denique diuinis promptissime obtemperemus; cum obsequium sit sacrificium Deo gratissimum.

Prob. b. Quod si in viis vocationis nostrae ambulemus, angeli nos comitabuntur, protegent, a periculis tutos praestabunt. Nam Deus angelis suis praecepit de te, ad custodiendum te in omnibus viis tuis; qui super manibus portabunt te, ne forte impingas in lapidem pedem tuum, inquit hieropsaltes, Ps. XCI, 11. 12.

SVSPIRIVM.

Quibus verbis, o Deus misericordissime, pronam tuam in me beneuolentiam depraedicem? Tu me condidisti, conditum protexisti. Et vitam, & vitae securitatem, tibi acceptam refero. Etenim qui genii purissimi coram tua maiestate stant, vt ministri promptissimi, te iubente, mihi adstant, vt custodes fidelissimi. Frendeat diabolus: Non succumbo stipatus athletis coelestibus. Infultet orbis: Non perfundor, angelico praesidio fultus. Agnosco grato pectore, o benignissimum Numen, tuam in me gratiam propensissimam, & ardentissime precor, vt me euntem & redeuntem spiritu tuo perpetuo regas, quo viam vocationis meae, viam pietatis inoffenso pede decurram. Sic enim futurum esse credo, vt sancti angeli circa me castra metentur, ab insultibus hostium me tutum praestent, & tandem animam meam, rebus humanis fessam, in gremium Christi, vbi secura & iucundissima mansio, transferant.


## 8 Concerning Man


### Q. I. What is man?

Man is an animal, consisting of a rational soul and an organic body, created by God, and adorned in his first creation with His own image, for the purpose of sincerely worshipping the Creator, living a pious life, and attaining eternal blessedness. Obs. I. We are dealing here with man, not insofar as he is a sinner; for in that state he is the subject of theological operation, the consideration of which pertains to the second part of theology: But insofar as man is one of the most noble creatures, the center of creation, the principal inhabitant of the visible world, into whom the most abundant streams of divine goodness overflow.

Obs. II. Philosophers succinctly define man as a rational animal: but it is the theologian’s task to describe man through his four causes.

Latin:

Homo est animal, constans anima rationali & corpore organico, a Deo conditum, ipsiusque imagine in prima creatione condecoratum, ad creatorem sincere colendum, vitam pie traducendam, & aeternam beatitatem consequendam. Obseru. I. Agimus hic de homine, non quatenus est peccator; sic enim est subiectum operationis theologicae, cuius consideratio pertinet ad secundam partem theologiae: Sed quatenus homo est creaturarum nobilissimarum altera, creationis centrum, praecipuus mundi aspectabilis incola, in quem vberrimi bonitatis diuinae riuuli redundant.

Obs. II. Philosophi succincte definiunt hominem per animal rationale: at theologi est, hominem per quatuor describere causas.


### Q. II. Who was the first man?

The first of all men was Adam, the parent of the entire human race.

Proof 1) Because Adam is called the first man in express words. There is no reason for you to object that Adam is called the first man relatively, having regard to the last Adam, who is Christ. For he is called the first man absolutely; since Adam would have been the first man even if Christ had never come. Adam is compared with Christ not by reason of priority; but insofar as the former is the author of sin and death, and the latter of righteousness and life. 2) Gen. II, 5. Moses openly writes that there was no man (before Adam) to till the ground. If there was no man before Adam to till the ground: with what appearance of truth can it be asserted that Gentiles were produced before Adam? 3) Because, when Adam was created, no helper, or female assistant, was found, Gen. I, 19. But truly, if Gentiles had been created long before Adam, a helper would certainly have been found for Adam. 4) Because Eve is called the mother of all living, Gen. III, 20. If women had lived before Eve, she would not have been adorned with that title. 5) The Apostle testifies, Acts XVII, 26, that God made of one blood every human race. But truly, if Gentiles were created before Adam, it could not be said that God made every race of men of one blood.

The antithesis is that of Isaac Peyrère, who in the year 1655 spread a monstrous opinion concerning Pre-Adamites, whose stronger arguments are:

I. A double creation of men is described in the Holy Scriptures. The former in Gen. I, where male and female are said to be created in one act, not in an interrupted series.

Later, Gen. II, where the series of creation is interrupted, and the creation of Adam and Eve is delineated according to distinct acts, Gen. I. the origin of the Gentiles, Gen. II. the creation of the Jews seems to be described in Adam. Resp. 1) The creation of man described in chapters I and II of Genesis is one, the circumstances of which are recounted more clearly in chapter II, and although in Gen. I the creation of Adam and Eve is joined together, that conjunction does not indicate one act, but it is proposed there only in a general way, and in ch. II it is explained specifically through distinct acts. 2) If the creation of man described in ch. II of Gen. is different from that which is contained in Gen. I, it must be said that when it is said in Gen. II, 4: These are the generations of the heaven and the earth, another heaven and another earth are also to be understood than in Gen. I, 1; likewise when it is said in Gen. II, 5 that plants and herbs were produced, other herbs and plants are to be understood than those which are said to be produced in Gen. I, which is absurd. Indeed, it is clear from the text itself that the works which are mentioned as created in Gen. I are repeated in Gen. II with certain circumstances added.

II. Whoever, being a murderer, is about to set out into foreign lands and fears the punishments of men, presupposes that more men live there. But Cain, etc. Therefore, the major premise is evident: If a murderer were to go into a foreign land, empty of men, he would fear no man there. The minor premise is evident from Gen.
