IV, where Cain addresses God thus: Behold, you have cast me out from (the place) upon the face of this earth, so that I am forced to hide myself from your face: Whence I shall be a wanderer and a fugitive in the (remaining) earth, so that whoever finds me may kill me. But if no men had lived besides Adam and Eve, no fear would have been cast upon Cain, who was about to seek foreign lands. Response: 1) A murderer fears even the safest places, with his conscience tormenting him within. 2) Cain feared his father Adam as an avenger, he feared the descendants of Abel as avengers, he feared that one of his own children would be an Absalom.

III. There are men who have not sinned in the likeness of Adam's transgression. Rom. V, 14. Therefore, not all men were created from the blood of Adam. Response: The transgression of Adam was an actual prohaeretic sin, the consequence of which was death, reigning not only over those who sinned after the likeness of Adam ἐκ τῆς προαιρέσεως (from choice), but also over embryos, which are extinguished, and over newborn infants, who are not contaminated by prohaeretic sins, but are infected by original sin, which flowed from Adam to his descendants.

IV. That not all men descend from Adam is taught by the example of Melchizedek, who, if he had been an Adamite, would not be called ἀπάτωρ (without father) Heb. VII, 3. Response: Melchizedek is called ἀπάτωρ with respect to our knowledge; since it has not been divinely revealed to us who his parent was .

V. If no men had been created before Adam, in the course of many centuries no one would have enjoyed the fruits of trees born in Germany, Poland, Gaul, etc., which fruits would have hung in vain on the trees, and tame and wild animals would have run in vain in the fields, mountains, forests, etc. But God and nature do nothing in vain. Response: Distinguish between the act and the power of enjoying. By God's command and operation, trees bring forth fruit so that man may enjoy them; although man does not always actually enjoy them. Many herbs and many fruits perish which no one turns to his own use, which nevertheless were born for the use of men.

Latin:

Primus omnium hominum fuit Adam, parens vniuersi humani generis.

Prob. 1) Quia Adam disertis verbis appellatur primus homo. Non est, quod excipias, Adamum dici primum hominem respective, habito respectu ad vltimum Adamum, qui est Christus. Vocatur enim primus homo absolute; siquidem Adamus primus fuisset homo, licet Christus nunquam venisset. Comparatur Adamus cum Christo non ratione prioritatis; sed quatenus ille auctor peccati & mortis, hic iustitiae & vitae est. 2) Gen. II, 5. Moses aperte scribit, nullum fuisse (ante Adamum) hominem ad colendam terram. Si nullus fuit ante Adamum homo, qui terram coleret: qua specie veri asseri potest, quod ante Adamum producti sint gentiles? 3) Quia, cum conderetur Adamus, non inuentum est adiutorium, siue foemina adiutrix, Gen. I, 19. At vero, si gentiles diu ante Adamum fuissent conditi, vtique inuentum fuisset pro Adamo adiutorium. 4) Quia Eua dicitur mater omnis viuentis, Gen. III, 20. Si ante Euam vixissent foeminae, illo titulo non fuisset ornata. 5) Apostolus testatur, Act. XVII, 26. Deum fecisse ex vno sanguine omne genus humanum. At vero si ante Adamum gentiles fuerunt creati, dici non posset, Deum omne genus hominum fecisse ex vno sanguine.

Antithesis est Isaaci Peyrerii, qui anno 1655. sparsit opinionem monstrosam de Praeadamitis, cuius potiora sunt argumenta:

I. Duplex hominum creatio describitur in sacris litteris. Prior Gen. I. vbi masculus & foemina vno actu, non abrupta serie, dicuntur conditi.

Posterior Gen. II. vbi series creationis abrumpitur, & creatio Adami atque Euae secundum actus distinctos delineatur, Gen. I. Gentilium origo, Gen. II. Iudaeorum creatio in Adamo descripta videtur. Resp. 1) Creatio hominis descripta cap. I. & II. Geneseos vna est, cuius circumstantiae cap. II. luculentius recensentur, & quamuis Gen. I. creatio Adami & Euae coniungatur, non tamen illa coniunctione vnus actus indicatur, sed generatim tantum ibi proponitur, & c. II. speciatim per distinctos actus explanatur. 2) Si alia est creatio hominis cap. II. Gen. descripta ab ea, quae Gen. I. continetur, dicendum erit, quod cum Gen. II, 4. dicitur: Hæ sunt generationes cæli & terræ, etiam aliud cælum & alia terra intelligatur, quam Gen. I, 1.; item cum Gen. II, 5. dicitur, quod plantæ & herbæ fuerint productæ, aliæ intelligendæ sint herbæ & plantæ, quam quæ Gen. I. dicuntur productæ, quod absurdum. Sane ex ipso textu patet, quod quæ opera Gen. I. creata commemorantur, Gen. II. adiectis quibusdam circumstantiis repetantur.

II. Quicunque homicida profecturus in terras peregrinas, extimescit hominum pœnas, ille plures ibi homines viuere præfupponit. At Cainus &c. E. Maior constat: Si homicida abiret in terram peregrinam, hominibus vacuam, nullum ibi hominem extimesceret. Minor patet e Gen. IV. vbi Cainus Deum ita alloquitur: Ecce eiecisti me de (loco) fuper faciebus terræ huius, ita vt a faciebus tuis me abscondere cogar: Vnde vagus & agitatus ero in terra (reliqua), vt quisquis offenderit me, occidat me. At si præter Adamum & Euam non vixissent homines, Caino peregrinas petituro terras, nulla formido fuisset offusa. R. 1) Homicida etiam tutissima loca timet, torquente intus conscientia. 2) Timuit Cainus patrem Adamum vindicem, timuit vltores Habelis posteros, timuit e liberis suis quendam fore Absolonem.

III. Dantur homines, qui non peccarunt in similitudine præuaricationis Adami. Rom. V, 14. E. non omnes homines sanguine Adami creti sunt. R. Præuaricatio Adami erat peccatum actuale proæreticum, cuius consequens erat mors dominans non tantum in eos, qui ad instar Adami ἐκ τῆς προαιρέσεως peccarunt, sed & in embryones, qui exstinguuntur, & in infantes recens natos, non peccatis proæreticis contaminatos, sed peccato originali, quod ex Adamo in posteros dimanauit, infectos.

IV. Non omnes homines descendere ab Adamo, docet exemplum Melchisedeci, qui si fuisset Adamigena, non diceretur ἀπάτωρ Hebr. VII, 3. Resp. Melchisedecus dicitur ἀπάτωρ, respectu nostræ notitiæ; quoniam nobis diuinitus reuelatum non est, quis ipsius fuerit parens .

V. Si ante Adamum nulli conditi fuissent homines, multorum fæculorum decursu nemo fruitus esset fructibus arborum natarum in Germania, Polonia, Gallia &c. qui fructus millecufli frustra pependissent in arboribus, frustra cucurrissent animalia cicura & fera in campis, montibus, fyluis &c. At Deus & natura nihil faciunt frustra. Resp. Dist. inter actum, & potentiam fruendi. Iubente & operante Deo arbores proferunt fructus, vt homo iis possit frui; quamuis homo non semper actu iisdem fruatur. Intereunt multæ herbæ, multique fructus, quos nemo vertit in vfum suum, qui tamen in vfum hominum sunt nati.


### Quæst. III. Who created man

The efficient cause of man.

Proof from Gen. I, 26. God אֱלֹהִים said; נַעֲשֶׂה let us make (we shall make) man in our image, according to our likeness.

Obs. 1) By this heavenly oracle, a plurality of divine persons is hinted at. For there is used a) the name Elohim, which not only by its termination,

Latin:

Caussa efficiens hominis.

Prob. e Gen. I, 26. Dixit אֱלֹהִים Deus; נַעֲשֶׂה faciamus (faciemus) hominem in imagine nostra, secundum similitudinem nostram.

Obs. 1) Oraculo hoc cœlesti pluralitas perfonarum diuinarum innuitur. Adhibetur enim a) nomen Elohim, quod non tantum terminatione,


### Of what matter was man created?

and that it is plural in meaning, we have proven above. b) To the plural verb, we shall make, c) are annexed suffixes of the plural number: In our image, according to our likeness.

2) In the opinion of most theologians, God is introduced by Moses consulting about creating man in His own image. He judges that it is not so much a consultation as the intention and decree of God that is designated, and he renders the Hebrew verb נעשה into Latin: we shall make; because a) the most proper meaning of the future is simply expressed; b) the harmony of the decree and the execution itself, which is immediately added in v. 27, is shown more clearly; c) with this exposition standing, there is no need to invent an anthropopathy in consulting, nor is it permitted for Jews and Photinians to concoct a consultation with angels.

I add the annotation: And God said within Himself (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit with supreme consensus).

The reason is: Because the words; Let us make man, etc., are not the words of one inviting to consult, but of one decreeing; the execution of which decree immediately follows in v.

27. And so God created man, etc.

But the decrees of God concerning things ad extra, just as the execution of the decrees, are common to all three persons of the deity.

You say: God speaks of Himself in the number of a multitude after the manner of great men; and thus the plurality of the divine persons is not indicated in the cited place.

Resp. We have satisfied this objection above.

Quest.

IV. From what matter was man created?

Prob. a. Gen. II, 7. And the Lord God formed man, dust from the ground. Obs.

1) The material principle of man is called אדמה, properly red earth, since in the Babylonian land the earth is red in many places; although the same word taken generally signifies any earth whatsoever, and beasts were formed from the same matter, Gen. II, 19, so that earth becomes the common principle of origin for man and beasts, and the common dwelling place of both. 2) Moses indicates that the predominant element from which the body of Adam was produced is earth; yet he does not simply exclude the remaining elements, water, air, and fire.

For from whatever matter the human body consists, from that same matter it was originally produced: Now it consists of four elements. 3) Man is said to be formed dust from the earth, so that it may be signified that he is not only from the dust of the earth, but also that he is nothing but the dust of the earth, if he is estimated without the soul and the co-created image of God from the principles of his origin. Whence, this having been lost, he heard this voice: dust you are, and to dust you shall return!

Gen. III, 12. Prob. b.

Gen. II, 21. 22. Then (finally) Jehovah God caused a deep sleep to fall upon the man, so that he slept, and He took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh in its place, and Jehovah God built the rib, which He had taken from the man, into a woman.

Obs.

1) Since the body of Eve was to be built from Adam, he lay immersed in sleep, so that he would not be a spectator of the divine architecture, but an admirer of the woman who had been built. For just as physicians use narcotics in more serious treatments, so that the patient does not feel what is being done: so God sent Adam into a very deep sleep, so that the fabrication of Eve from the rib of Adam would create no pain for him. 2) That sleep was not without illustrious divine revelations, but the mind of the sleeping Adam was so elevated and divinely illuminated that he understood the rib was being taken from his body.

From which תרדמה is rendered by the LXX Interpreters as ecstasy: although it was not a perfect ecstasy, but a prophetic sleep analogous to ecstasy.

Conf. d.

Conf. d. VAREN. dec. VII. Mos. p. 183. 3) The rib, from which the body of Eve was constructed, was not superfluous, but natural, and owed to the integrating of Adam's body.

For the rib which God had taken away, He compensated with flesh, Gen. II, 23. But restitution cannot happen unless the removal of the owed part is presupposed. Nor does it stand in the way that it is not explicitly said that the rib was restored, but only the flesh.

For as God, by extracting the rib from the body of Adam, at the same time extracted flesh; which, had it not happened, Adam could not have said of Eve,

The body of Adam was formed from the earth a), the body of Eve from the rib of Adam b). would have been, that she is bone of his bones, and flesh of his flesh: thus by rendering flesh, it is understood that the rib was also rendered; even if Moses does not say it explicitly.

(4) It was the rib of Adam, from which Eve was made, not lifeless, but animated. For (a) it is not said that Eve's soul was inspired, as Adam's was. (b) It was a part of a living and animated body. (c) 1 Cor. XI, 8. The woman is said to have been taken from the man. But woman is the name of a supposit, which consists not only of body, but also of soul. Indeed, in that way the woman is said to be from the man, in which the man is not from the woman. But the man is not from the woman as much by reason of the body as by reason of the soul, because God immediately inspired the latter. Therefore, according to soul and body, the woman is from the man.

Q. V.

How did God create the first human beings?

The mode which God employed in creating the first humans consists a) in the artful fashioning of Adam's body; b) in the inspiration of the soul; c) in the singular construction of Eve's body. Prob. a. The mode of production is expressed by the Hebrew words יצר and ברא. יצר signifies to make something ornately and decently; יצר properly denotes to fashion, and is used of potters, who induce an elegant figure upon the clay which they knead. Thus God formed man ornately and decently, and induced a harmony fitting to the human body and due to all its members.

Prob. b. Gen. II, 7. God breathed into the nostrils of man the soul of lives, and man became a living soul.

Obj. 1) To the body fashioned indeed, but lying like a trunk, devoid of motion, sense, and reason, the soul was inspired and united, as an entelechy, or form, by which it was to be actuated, moved, and perfected. 2) As for the fashioned body, or formation; so for the soul, an inspiration. But God is said to have breathed anthropopathically, in a human manner, which is to be understood theoprepically, in a manner befitting God. For it does not denote the emission of a bodily breath; since God is incorporeal: but (a) the mode of action by which the soul was communicated to Adam's body; which communication was made in an easy and spiritual manner, since the soul is said to be produced and inspired by the same inspiration: (b) the effect of the action, because the effect produced is a spirit distinct from the body and all matter.

(3) The soul is said to be inspired by God, but not from God. For God did not inspire the soul into man from His own substance, as the Stoics, Epictetus, Seneca, and Cicero said the soul was a particle of the divine aura, and as the Manichaeans and Priscillianists asserted that human souls existed from the substance of God, for which they were condemned in the Council of Braga, can. V, because the substance of God is both indivisible and incommunicable to a mere creature.

4) God inspired the soul into man into the nostrils; because in these the most wise creator willed that the soul should manifest itself through respiration and vital actions. 5) Moses calls the soul the breath of lives, i.e., not only living immortally by itself, and vivifying the body, and breathing through the nostrils. 6) Through this breath of lives man was made into a living soul, i.e., into a perfect living animal. You say: From our opinion clearly set forth it follows that first the body, then the soul was created; which could not happen, because 1) creation is an instantaneous action, and therefore man was created in an instant without succession or delay of time.

2) The body of Adam as soon as it was created, was a living body, endowed with a soul, otherwise it would have been a corpse. 3) It was organic, and therefore animated. Resp. to 1) Creation, as such, is instantaneous; but as it is plastic, formative, and as it were that of a potter, it admits of delay, so that one part is created after another. Yet the creation of man can be called an instantaneous creation of a supposit, because in a moment the soul was inspired into the body, so that it was a living animal. To 2) For the truth of the body, from which man is to be composed, a soul is not required: for the body of Christ was a true body during the three days of death, although physically it was not living. To 3) I distinguish between the order of nature to be established, and that which is established. In the latter way, no body is called organic unless it is animated: But in the former way, an organic body is that which is fashioned as if by the hands of the creator himself, and made suitable for receiving a soul. Prob. c. The body of Eve is said to be built, by an architectonic term, i. e. decorously joined together, so that it may be indicated that the woman would not only be a seat of virtues, but also that her womb would be a future house, in which the human race is to be built up and propagated through generation. Quaest.

Latin:

sed & significatione plurale esse, supra evicimus. b) Verbo plurali, faciemus, c) annectuntur suffixa pluralis numeri: In imagine nostra, secundum similitudinem nostram.

2) Ex mente plurimorum theologorum Deus a Mose introducitur consultans de creando homine ad imaginem suam. censet, non tam consultationem, quam intentionem & decretum Dei designari, & verbum hebraeum נעשה latine reddit: faciemus; quia a) propriissima significatio futuri simpliciter exprimitur; b) harmonia decreti, & ipsius executionis, quae confestim additur v. 27. luculentius ostenditur; c) stante isthac expositione, nec ανθρωποπάθειαν in consultando fingere opus est, nec consultationem cum angelis comminisci Iudaeis & Photinianis licet.

Addo annotationem Et dixit apud se Deus (Pater, Filius, & Spiritus S. summo consensu).

Ratio est: Quia verba; Faciamus hominem &c. non sunt verba ad consultandum inuitantis, sed decernentis; cuius decreti executio immediate v.

27. sequitur: Creauit itaque Deus hominem &c.

Decreta vero Dei de rebus ad extra, sicut & executio decretorum, omnibus tribus personis deitatis sunt communia.

Dicis: Deus more magnatum de se in numero multitudinis loquitur; adeoque pluralitas personarum diuinarum l. c. non indicatur.

Resp. Huic obiectioni supra satisfecimus.

Quæst.

IV. Ex qua materia conditus est homo?

Prob. a. Gen. II, 7. Formauitque Deus hominem, puluerem de terra. Obs.

1) Principium materiale hominis dicitur אדמה, proprie terra rubra, siquidem in terra Babylonica terra passim rubeat; quamuis eadem vox generatim sumta quamcunque terram significet, & ex eadem materia formatae sint bestiae, Gen. II, 19. vt terra commune ortus principium fit homini atque bestiis, & commune vtriusque habitaculum. 2) Indicat Moses, elementum praedominans, e quo productum est corpus Adami, esse terram; reliqua tamen elementa, aquam, aerem, & ignem, non simpliciter excludit.

Ex qua namque materia corpus humanum constat, ea eadem productum est primitus: Constat autem ex quatuor elementis. 3) Formatus dicitur homo puluis de terra, vt significetur, eum non solum de puluere terrae, sed etiam nil, nisi terrae puluerem esse, si absque anima & concreata imagine Dei ex ortus fui principiis aestimetur. Vnde, hac amissa, audiebat hanc vocem; puluis es, & in puluerem reuerteris!

Gen. III, 12. Prob. b.

Gen. II, 21. 22. Tum (denique) cadere fecit Iehouah Deus somnum grauem super hominem, vt obdormiret, sumfitque vnam de costis eius, & inclusit carnem pro ea, aedificauit que Iehouah Deus costam, quam sumserat de homine in mulierem.

Obs.

1) Cum corpus Evae ex Adamo extruendum esset, iacuit hic sopore mersus, vt diuinae architectonicae non spectator, sed admirator foeminae aedificatae esset. Vt enim medici narcotica adhibent in grauioribus curationibus, vt aegrotus, quid agatur, non sentiat: ita Deus Adamum demisit in soporem altissimum, vt fabrica Evae ex costa Adami nullum ipsi crearet dolorem. 2) Non fuit ille somnus sine illustribus reuelationibus diuinis, sed mens dormientis Adami sic eleuata & diuinitus illustrata fuit, vt costam e corpore sibi eximi intellegeret.

Ex quo תרדמה a LXX. Interpr. redditur per έκστασιν: quamuis non perfecta έκστασις, sed sopor propheticus ectasi analogus fuerit.

Conf. d.

Conf. d. VAREN. dec. VII. Mos. p. 183. 3) Costa, e qua exstructum est corpus Evae, non fuit superflua, sed naturalis, & integrando corpori Adami debita.

Quam enim costam Deus abstulerat, carne compenfauit, Gen. II, 23. Non autem potest fieri restitutio, nisi praesupponatur debitae partis ablatio. Nec obstat, quod non diserte costa dicatur restituta, sed tantum caro.

Nam vt Deus extrahendo ex corpore Adami costam vna extraxit carnem; quod nisi contigisset, Adamus de Eua dicere non potuisset,

Corpus Adami ex terra a), corpus Evae ex costa Adami formatum est b). tuisset, illam esse os de ossibus suis, & carnem de carne sua: ita reddendo carnem, subintelligitur, redditain etiam esse costam; etsi Moses id diserte non dicat.

(4) Fuit costa Adami, e qua facta est Eua, non exanimis, sed animata. Nam (a) non dicitur inspirata anima Euae, vt Adamo. (b) Fuit pars corporis uiui & animati. (c) 1 Cor. XI, 8. mulier dicitur sumta esse ex viro. At mulier est nomen suppositi, quod ex corpore non tantum, sed & anima constat. Sane eo modo mulier dicitur esse ex viro, quo vir non est ex muliere. Atqui vir non est ex muliere tam ratione corporis, quam ratione animae, quia illam immediate inspirauit Deus. Ergo secundum animam & corpus mulier est ex viro.

Quaest. V.

Quomodo condidit Deus homines protoplastos?

Modus, quem Deus in condendis primis hominibus adhibuit, consistit a) in artificiosa effigiatione corporis Adami; b) in inspiratione animae; c) in singulari corporis Euae aedificatione. Prob. a. Modus productionis vocibus hebraeis יצר & ברא exprimitur. יצר significat ornate & decenter aliquid facere; יצר proprie notat fingere, & vsurpatur de figulis, qui argillae, quam subigunt, elegantem inducunt figuram. Ita Deus hominem ornate & decenter formauit, concinnamque corpori hominis, atque debitam membris vniuersis harmoniam induxit.

Prob. b. Gen. II, 7. Inspirauit Deus in nares hominis animam vitarum, & factus est homo in animam viuentem.

Obs. 1) Corpori effigiato quidem, at iacenti instar trunci, experti motus, sensus, rationis, inspirata & vnita est anima, velut ἐντελέχεια, siue forma, qua actuandum, mouendumque & perficiendum erat. 2) Vti corpori effigiato, siue formatio; ita animae ἐμπνευσις, seu inspiratio. Inspirasse autem Deus dicitur ἀνθρωποπαθῶς, more humano, quod intelligendum est θεοπρεπῶς, modo Deo conuenienti. Neque enim notat halitus corporei emissionem; cum Deus fit incorporeus: sed (a) modum actionis, quo anima corpori Adami est communicata; quod communicatio illa facta sit modo facili atque spirituali, siquidem eadem inspiratione anima fit producta, simul atque inspirata dicitur: (b) effectum actionis, quod effectus productus sit spiritus corpore atque materia omni distinctus.

(3) Anima inspirata dicitur a Deo, sed non ex Deo. Neque enim de substantia sua Deus animam homini inspirauit, vti Stoici, Epictetus, Seneca, Cicero animam diuinae particulam aurae, dixere, & Manichaei ac Priscillianistae animas humanas ex Dei substantia extitisse asseruere, in concilio Bracarensi can. V. ideo damnati, quia substantia Dei & indiuisibilis, & merae creaturae incommunicabilis est.

4) Deum animam homini inspirauit in nares; quia in his maxime animam per respirationem & vitales actiones sese prodere voluit sapientissimus creator. 5) Animam vocat Moses spiraculum vitarum, h. e. non tantum per se immortaliter viuentem, & corpus viuificantem, & per nares spirantem. 6) Per hoc spiraculum vitarum homo factus est in animam viuentem, h. e. in perfectum animal viuens. Dicis: Ex sententia nostra luculente exposita sequitur, primum corpus, deinde animam creatam esse; quod fieri non potuit, quia 1) creatio est actio instantanea, adeoque homo in instanti est creatus citra successionem, aut moram temporis.

2) Corpus Adami simul atque creatum fuit, corpus fuit viuum, anima praeditum, ceteroqui fuisset cadauer. 3) Fuit organicum, adeoque animatum. Resp. ad 1) Creatio, vt sic, est instantanea; at prout est plastica, formativa & quasi figulina, admittit moram, ita, ut vna pars post alteram creetur. Dici tamen potest creatio hominis instantanea suppositi, quia in momento anima corpori est inspirata, vt esset animal viuum. Ad 2) Ad veritatem corporis, e quo homo componendus est, non requiritur anima: nam corpus Christi verum erat corpus in triduo mortis, licet physice non esset vivum. Ad 3) distingu. inter ordinem naturae constituendum, & constitutum. Posteriori modo nullum dicitur corpus organicum, nisi fit animatum: At priori modo corpus organicum est, quod ipsius creatoris quasi manibus effigiatum, & ad recipiendam animam idoneum factum est. Prob. c. Corpus Evae, voce architectonica, aedificatum, i. e. decore coagmentatum, dicitur, vt indicetur, mulierem non tantum fore sedem virtutum, sed & uterum eius futuram esse domum, in qua per generationem aedificandum atque propagandum fit genus humanum. Quaest.


### VI. Of how many parts does man consist?

Parts of man.

Man consists of two parts, a rational soul, and an organic body.

Prob. I. From the creation of man. For, as Moses testifies, Gen. II, 7. The body was formed from the earth, into which the breath of life, the soul, was breathed. The holy historiographer does not add a third part.

You say: Three parts are expressly posited by Moses, the earthly body, the breath of life, and the living soul. Resp. Mention is indeed made of three by Moses, but of two as essential parts, and of the third as a composite resulting from that union of parts: which composite is called a living soul, the denomination being made from the former.

4) From the assertion of Christ: Matth. X. 28. Fear not them which can kill the body: but are not able to kill the soul. Where the savior himself enumerates two parts of man, to wit, the soul and the body.

3) From the death of man. When he dies, he is resolved into nothing but two parts, Eccles. XII, 7. E. and is composed of nothing but two parts.

4) From the state after death. For there are no essential parts constituting man besides those which will either triumph in heaven, or be tormented in hell.

But those are only the soul and the body, Matth.

There is an antithesis of Paracelsus, Comenius, Weigelius, and others, in whose opinion there are three parts of man, spirit, soul, and body, whose chief argument is taken from 1 Thess. V, 23. And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly; and your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

St. Paul in this vow of his seems to assign three parts to man, to be preserved whole and blameless. Resp. What is understood by spirit in that place is not explained in one way. There are those who, with Chrysostom, understand by spirit the gifts and effects of the Holy Spirit in the regenerate man, so that the spirit is opposed to the flesh, Rom. VI. Gal. V. In which sense the spirit is not a peculiar part of man, but a spiritual gift, by which primarily the soul, and secondarily the body, is instructed for the exercises of piety. There are others who, with Augustine and our Luther, wish to designate by spirit the higher faculty of the soul, by which we understand and reason, by soul the lower faculty of the soul, by which we feel and desire, and by body they understand the domicile of the soul, whose members serve as organs for the soul's practice of piety.

But here spirit, soul, and body are considered not physically, but theologically, according to the state of regeneration and renewal. Which latter opinion seems more agreeable to the vow of Paul. I give, therefore, this paraphrase of Paul's vow: I sincerely vow and pray that the God of peace may illuminate your spirit (intellect) and keep it immune from errors, your senses and affections pure from inordinate acts, and your body intact from filth, so that you may think on what is true and salutary; desire what is holy; and that you may devote all the limbs of your body to the living practice of what is pure and chaste, lest before God and men in the day of universal judgment you incur a tremendous reproach.

By the same reasoning, the words of St. Mary, Luc. I, 46. 47. My soul doth magnify the Lord: And my spirit hath rejoiced, seem to be expounded as if to say: That joy which I have conceived concerning the savior of the human race, of the torrent of —

has flooded all my affections, all my senses, so that my mind, suffused with celestial light, may piously esteem the most exalted glory of God, and be wholly fixed upon celebrating it.

Latin:

Partes hominis.

Homo constat ex duabus partibus, anima rationali, & corpore organico.

Prob. I. E creatione hominis. Nam, teste Mose, Gen. II, 7. Corpus formatum est e terra, cui spiraculum vitae, anima, est inspiratum. Tertiam partem S. historiographus non addit.

Dicis: Tres partes expresse a Mose ponuntur, terrenum corpus, spiraculum vitae, anima viuens. Resp. Trium quidem mentio fit a Mose, sed duorum, vt partium essentialium, tertii vero vt compositi ex ista partium vnione resultantis: quod compositum dicitur anima viuens, denominatione facta a priori.

4) Ex assertione Christi: Matth. X. 28. Ne timete vobis ab iis, qui occidere corpus possunt: animam vero occidere nequeunt. Vbi ipse saluator duas hominis partes recenset, animam scil. & corpus.

3) Ex morte hominis. Quando hic moritur, nonnisi in duas partes resolvitur, Eccles. XII, 7. E. non nisi ex duabus partibus componitur.

4) Ex statu post mortem. Nullae enim sunt partes essentiales constituentes hominem praeter eas, quae vel in caelo triumphant, vel in inferno cruciabuntur.

At illae sunt tantum anima & corpus, Matth. XX, 28. Luc. XVI, 22. 1 Cor. V, 5. 2 Cor. V, 8. 10.

Antithesis est Paracelsi, Comenii, Weigelii & aliorum, ex quorum mente tres sunt partes hominis, spiritus, anima & corpus, quorum praecipuum argumentum petitur ex 1 Thess. V, 23. Ipse vero Deus pacis sanctificet vos integros, & integer vester spiritus, & anima & corpus irreprehenfibiliter in aduentum domini nostri Iesu Christi feruetur.

S. Paullus hoc suo voto tres videtur homini assignare partes, integras & irreprehensibiles feruandas. Resp Quid per spiritum l, c. intelligatur, non vno modo explicatur. Sunt, qui cum Chrysostomo per spiritum intelligunt dona & effecta Spiritus S. in homine renato, ita, vt spiritus opponatur carni, Rom. VI. Gal. V. Quo sensu spiritus non est peculiaris pars hominis, sed donum spirituale, quo primario anima, secundario corpus ad exercitia pietatis instruitur. Sunt alii, qui cum Avgvstino & Lvthero nostro, per spiritum designari volunt superiorem animae facultatem, qua intelligimus & ratiocinamur, per animam inferiorem facultatem animae, qua sentimus & appetimus, per corpus intelligunt domicilium animae, cuius membra velut organa ad praxin pietatis animae inferuiunt.

Considerantur autem hic spiritus, anima & corpus non physice, sed theologice, secundum statum regenerationis & renouationis. Quae posterior sententia voto Paullini conuenientior videtur. Do igitur, hanc paraphrasin voti Paullini: Id voueo fincere & precor, vt Deus pacis spiritum (intellectum) vestrum illustret, & immunem ab erroribus, sensus & affectus puros ab inordinatis actibus, corpus intactum a sordibus praestet, vt quae vera & salutaria sunt, cogitetis; quae sancta, appetatis; quae pura & casta sunt, iisdem viua praxi exercendis omnes corporis artus deuoueatis, ne coram Deo & hominibus in die vniuersalis iudicii tremendam incurratis reprehensionem.

Eadem ratione verba S. Mariae, Luc. I, 46. 47. Magnificat anima mea dominum: Et exultauit spiritus meus, exponenda videntur, q. d. Quod de seruatore generis humani cepi gaudium, torrentis in-

star omnes meos affectus, omnes sensus inundauit, vt mens mea luce caelesti perfusa celsissimam Dei gloriam pie aestimet, & in ea concelebranda tota defixa sit.


### VI. Of how many parts does man consist?: II. 1 Cor. XIV, 14. Paul says: For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful

II. 1 Cor. XIV, 14. Paul says: For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful.

In this place Paul distinguishes the spirit from the mind. Resp. In this place, by "spirit" is understood that inspiration of God by which the apostle was endowed with the gift of tongues; or also the motion of the spirit, excited by that inspiration, which manifests itself through foreign tongues. By "mind" is denoted the sense or meaning of the prayer, which is called ἄκαρπος, unfruitful, not with respect to the speaker, but to the hearer, so that the sense of Paul’s words is: If I, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, pour out prayers from my soul in a sacred assembly in an exotic tongue, the meaning of those prayers will escape the hearers who are ignorant of the foreign tongue, so that they derive no utility from my prayer.

Quest. VII. Is the body a true part of man, or only his instrument?

The body is a true part of man, without which there is not a true and whole man.

Prob. 1) Because the essence of man is completed by two parts, the soul and the organic body; as we demonstrated in the preceding question. 2) If the soul alone completed the essence of man, man would never die, but when the soul was separated from the body, man would merely be laying aside his instrument. 3) If the entire essential perfection of man consists in the soul, there is no need for a resurrection; because with the flesh removed, the whole human being would persist.

The antithesis is that of the Platonists, Socinians, and Arminians: some of whom openly deny that the body is a part of man; some doubt whether it is a part or an instrument of man. Their arguments are the following:

I. The body is compared to a garment and a tent, 2 Cor. V, 3, 4, 5. Resp. That similitude is not to be extended beyond the third point. For the soul is said to be clothed with the body on account of their natural union. Therefore, it is wrongly inferred from this metaphorical way of speaking that the body is not a part of man. Certainly, the flesh of Christ is also compared to a garment and a tabernacle τῷ λόγῳ (to the Word), yet it is nonetheless a part of the theanthropic Christ.

II. A part of a living man remains the same in number perpetually: The body does not remain the same in number perpetually: Therefore, the body is not a part of a living man. The major premise is certain; because when a true part is removed, the whole does not remain. The minor is clear; since from infancy each of us has worn away many bodies. Resp. I deny the minor. For although the ὄγκος, or external bulk of the body, grows and decreases, increases and diminishes: yet the body remains the same in number, as to its οἰκείαν ὕλην, its proper and radical matter.

III. Paul says 2 Cor. XII, 2: I know a man in Christ fourteen years ago (whether in the body, I do not know; or whether out of the body, I do not know; God knows), caught up even to the third heaven. The apostle indicates that although he was out of the body in his rapture, he nevertheless remained a man. Therefore he says: I know a man. Whence the argument arises: Whoever, constituted out of the body, remains a true and whole man, the body does not belong to his essential integrity: But a certain man (Paul) caught up into the third heaven, constituted out of the body, remained a true and whole man. Therefore. Resp. The apostle does not doubt whether in the ecstasy the soul informed the body, or was separated from it; for if the soul had been separated, the apostle would have been dead. But he doubts whether the soul, united to the body, was elevated to hear τὰ ῥήματα ἄρρητα τοῦ θεοῦ (the unspeakable words of God) without the body cooperating, or with the body admitted and concurring; or, to speak more clearly: The apostle doubts whether he perceived the ineffable words of God only with his internal mind, or whether he also heard them with his body, through his ears. Therefore, the apostle was not constituted out of his body in his rapture.

IV. The true part gives being to man: But the body does not &c. Therefore.

Minor is evident from the philosophical axiom: Form gives being to a thing. The body is not the form: Therefore it does not give being to the thing. Response.

Form gives being to a thing not adequately & completely, but inadequately and incompletely. Form gives ultimate, determined, and specific being: Matter gives inchoate, indeterminate, and generic being: Both joined together give total being.

V. The human body is called organic by philosophers, because it is an instrument, not a part of man. Response.

The body is called organic not with respect to man, but with respect to the soul; of which it is indeed a co-part, by reason of the natural union, by which man becomes one per se: But it is an instrument of the same soul, by reason of the operation, which occurs through bodily members, as if they were organs. You should carefully observe, however, that bodily members are called organs of the soul in an excellent sense; since they are not separate, but joined, not ineffective, but effective instruments.

Quest. VIII. Has the human soul been thrust by God into the body as if into an impure prison? The human soul has not been cast by God into the body, as if into a squalid prison, by which it is hindered from being able to raise itself more promptly, and fly up to know, love, and venerate God.

Antithesis is 1) of Pythagoras, Plato, and their disciples, who taught προϋπαρξιν, or the pre-existence of souls, which, when they had begun to love terrestrial things with a loathing for celestial goods, were thrust into the body as if into a muddy prison. From which Plato explicitly calls the body the prison of the soul, in Cratyl. page 264. Sap. Aegypt. L.

II. c. 5. For which reason these philosophers taught καθάρσιν, or purgation from the feculent filth of the body, concerning which see

SCHEFFER. in philosoph. Ital. cap. VI. I. p. 73. who cites Porphyry writing thus: Purgation is a divorce from the body, and from the irrational motion of the passions. Wherefore IO.

SCHEFFERUS , about to explain the mind of the Pythagoreans, says: It is sufficiently clear from these definitions what Pythagoras and his followers understood by purgation. They said the body is a material, thick, feculent thing, by which the soul is pressed and drawn to these inferior things, which are mortal and full of vices and evils: and therefore it is defiled and polluted, just as in a squalid and muddy prison.

Therefore, before it can arrive at true wisdom, it has need of καθάρσει, that is, a certain purgation, by which its filth may be washed away. 2) Of Hermes Trismegistus, who, about to teach his son the mode of regeneration, says: Abrogate the senses of the body, then there will be the birth of divinity: purge yourself from the bonds of matter, destitute of reason. 3) Of mystical authors, who think more abjectly than is just of the human body.

ORIGEN leads them on , who, as testified by PRATEOLUS, in elencho haeres. l. 13. num. 5. asserted that this punishment was divinely inflicted upon human souls, because they sinned, that they should be detained in bodies as if in prisons.

Abrahamus a Franckenberg calls the body the external man, but the soul the internal man, and philosophizes with the following reasoning in the book which is inscribed: Know thyself: part II. p. 89. The inner man originates from the single Center of the life-light, from the holy Power-Being of the Trinity of GOD: on the other hand, the outer man, or the perishable fleeting body, is the earthly dark Sack of sorrow, the outer earthly shell, and base worthless inn, the assumed Adam's-fur, the housing of transience.

Latin:

II. 1 Cor. XIV, 14. Paullus inquit: Si namque orauero lingua, Spiritus meus orat, mens vero infrugifera est.

Hoc loco Paullus spiritum a mente distinguit, Resp. Hoc loco per spiritum intelligitur afflatus ille Dei, per quem dono linguarum ornatus fuit apostolus; vel etiam motus spiritus, ab illo flatu excitatus, qui per peregrinas linguas se exserit. Per mentem denotatur sensus vel sententia precationis, quae dicitur ἄκαρπος, infrugifera, non respectu loquentis, sed audientis, vt verborum Paullinorum sensus sit: Si ego duce Spiritu S. ex animo fundam preces in coetu facro lingua exotica, precum illarum sensus fugiet audientes linguae peregrinae ignaros, vt nihil vtilitatis ex oratione mea capiant.

Quaest. VII. Estne corpus vera pars hominis, an tantum eius instrumentum?

Corpus est vera pars hominis, fine quo non est verus & integer homo.

Prob. 1) Quia essentia hominis duabus absoluitur partibus, anima & corpore organico; vti in praecedenti quaestione demonstrauimus. 2) Si sola anima essentiam hominis absolueret; homo nunquam moreretur, sed quando anima separaretur a corpore, homo tantum instrumentum suum deponeret. 3) Si tota essentialis hominis perfectio consistit in anima, non opus est resurrectione; quia carne sublata totum esse humanum persisteret.

Antithesis est Platonicorum, Socinianorum & Arminianorum: quorum quidam aperte negant, corpus esse partem hominis; quidam dubitant, sitne pars, an instrumentum hominis. Quorum argumenta sunt sequentia:

I. Corpus comparatur cum veste & cum tentorio, 2 Cor. V, 3. 4. 5. Resp. Similitudo illa non est extra tertium extendenda. Nam dicitur anima corpore vestita, propter vnionem naturalem. Male igitur ex hac loquendi ratione metaphorica infertur, quod corpus non fit pars hominis. Certe caro Christi etiam comparatur vesti & tabernaculo τῷ λόγῳ, nihilo tamen minus pars Christi θεανδρώπης est.

II. Pars hominis viuentis eadem numero perpetuo manet: Corpus non perpetuo idem numero manet: E. Corpus non est pars hominis viuentis. Maior constat; quia vera parte sublata non manet totum. Minor liquet; quoniam ab infantia quilibet nostrum multa corpora detriuit. Resp. Neg. min. Quamuis enim ὄγκος, seu moles externa corporis crescat, & decrescat, augeatur & minuatur: manet tamen idem numero corpus, qua οἰκείαν ὕλην, materiam propriam & radicalem.

III. Paullus inquit 2 Cor. XII, 2. Noui hominem in Christo ante annos quatuordecim (siue in corpore, non scio; siue extra corpus fuerit, non scio; Deus scit), raptum talem vsque in tertium caelum. Indicat apostolus, quod licet in suo raptu extra corpus fuerit, verustamen homo manserit. Ideo dicit: Noui hominem. Vnde nascitur argumentum: Quicunque, extra corpus constitutus, manet verus ac integer homo, ad illius integritatem essentialem corpus non pertinet: Atqui quidam homo (Paullus) raptus in tertium caelum, extra corpus constitutus, verus ac integer permansit homo. Ergo. Resp. Non dubitat apostolus, vtrum in ecstasi anima corpus informauerit, an ab eo separata fuerit; nam si anima separata fuisset, apostolus fuisset mortuus. Sed dubitat, vtrum anima vnita corpori, fine cooperante corpore, an cum coadmisso & concurrente corpore, eleuata fuerit ad audiendum τὰ ῥήματα ἄρρητα τοῦ θεοῦ, siue, vt clarius loquar: Dubitat apostolus, vtrum tantum interna mente ineffabilia verba Dei perceperit, an corpore etiam auribus eadem audiuerit. Non ergo in raptu suo apostolus constitutus fuit extra corpus.

IV. Vera pars dat esse homini: Atqui corpus non &c. E.

Minor patet ex axiomate philosophico: Forma dat esse rei. Corpus non est forma: Ergo non dat esse rei. Resp.

Forma dat esse rei non adaequatum & completum, sed inadaequatum & incompletum. Forma dat esse ultimatum, determinatum & specificum: Materia dat esse inchoatum, indeterminatum & genericum: Vtraque iuncta dat esse totale.

V. Corpus humanum appellatur organicum a philosophis, quia est instrumentum, non pars hominis. Resp.

Corpus vocatur organicum non respectu hominis, sed respectu animae; cuius quidem compars est, ratione unionis naturalis, qua homo fit unum per se: At eiusdem animae instrumentum est, ratione operationis, quae fit per membra corporea, velut organa. Probe autem observes, quod membra corporea excellenti ratione dicuntur organa animae; siquidem non separata, sed coniuncta, non inefficacia, sed efficacia sunt instrumenta.

Quaest. VIII. An anima humana a Deo in corpus tanquam in carcerem impurum detrusae est? Anima humana non est a Deo coniecta in corpus, tanquam in carcerem squalidum, quo impediatur, quo minus prompte se eleuare, & subuolare possit ad Deum cognoscendum, amandum & venerandum.

Antithesis est 1) Pythagorae, Platonis & eorum discipulorum, qui docuerunt προϋπαρξιν, siue praeexistentiam animarum, quae, cum fastidio bonorum coelestium coepissent amare res terrestres, in corpus velut carcerem lutulentum sint detrusae. Ex quo Plato diserte corpus vocat, animae carcerem, in Cratyl. pag. 264. Sap. Aegypt. L.

II. c. 5. Qua de caussa hi philosophi docebant καθάρσιν, siue purgationem a feculentis corporis sordibus, de qua vid.

SCHEFFER. in philosoph. Ital. cap. VI. I. p. 73. qui adducit Porphyrium ita scribentem: Purgatio est diuortium a corpore, & ab irrationali passionum motu. Quamobrem IO.

SCHEFFERUS explicaturus mentem Pythagoraeorum inquit: Liquet satis ex his definitionibus, quid intellexerint Pythagoras, & eius sectatores per purgationem. Corpus est materiale quid, crassum, feculentum esse dicebant, quo prematur anima, & trahatur ad haec inferiora, mortalia & vitiis malisque plena: & idcirco faedetur atque inquinetur, haud secus ac in squalido & lutulento carcere.

Igitur priusquam peruenire valeat ad veram sapientiam, opus habere καθάρσει, hoc est purgatione quadam, qua ei sordes abluantur. 2) Hermetis Trismegisti, qui, filium suum modum regenerationis edocturus, ait: Corporis sensus abroga, tum erit deitatis genitura: purga te a materiae vinculis, ratione destitutis. 3) Mysticorum auctorum, iusto abiectius de corpore humano sentientium.

Praiuit ipsis ORIGENES, qui, teste PRATEOLO, in elencho haeres. l. 13. num. 5. asseruit, animabus humanis, quia peccarunt, hanc diuinitus irrogatam esse poenam, vt in corporibus velut carceribus detineantur.

Abrahamus a Franckenberg corpus vocat externum hominem, animam autem internum hominem, atque sequenti ratione philosophatur in libro, qui inscribitur: Nosce teipsum: part. II. p. 89. Der innere Mensch urständet aus dem einigen Centro des lebens-lichtes, aus dem heiligen Kraft-Wesen der Dreyheit GOttes: hergegen der äusserliche Mensch, oder der vergängliche flüchtige Leib ist der irdische finstere Trauer-Sack, die äussere irdische Schale, und schnöde nichtige Herberge, der angenommene Adams-Pelz, das Gehäuse der Vergänglichkeit.


### VI. Of how many parts does man consist?: Exposition

EXPOSITION

Obs.

Both the soul and the human body can be viewed in two ways: 1) κατ' ουσίαν, according to themselves, or their essence: 2) καθ' ἁμαρτίαν, according to the state of corruption, or according to sin, adhering by accident. If they are considered according to themselves, they are good creanature, created for the glory of God. Glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's, says Paul 1 Cor. VI, 20. Obs. II. The primary seat of sin is the human soul with its faculties. For they deflect from the divine law: the intellect through ignorance, opinion, and error; the will through the choice of a good that is not true, but apparent; the sensitive appetite through a blind impulse toward a good that is pleasing to the senses, but forbidden by divine law. The secondary seat of sin is the organic body of man, insofar as it serves the sinful soul in committing offenses.

CONFIRMATION

Proof.

1) Whatever body is created by God, and skillfully fashioned so that it might be a pleasing dwelling for the soul, and together with it, as a natural part, would constitute the whole man, that is wrongly considered a troublesome prison for the soul: But the human body is such, etc. Therefore.

The minor premise is proved from Gen. I, 27. II, 7. Job inculcates the most beautiful fashioning of the body, ch. X, 10. and King David, Ps. CXXXIX, 15.

2) The physical, proximate, and special cause of the formed body is the soul communicated or transmitted in and with the seed by the generator. Therefore, the body cannot be its prison. The reason for the consequence is: because no architect builds for himself a prison in which he might dwell.

The antecedent is clear to any sensible person. For α) the work of the formation of the body is wondrously varied, and restricted according to the nature of each species. Otherwise, for example, the body of a lion, otherwise of a bear, otherwise of a man, is formed according to size, shape, color, and the position of parts. Therefore, it is necessary that a specific cause, determined by its own nature to this such work, be present everywhere: but what is that, if not the soul of each body itself? β) The formation of the body is a work natural to the seed; indeed, most natural. Therefore, by the definition which all assign to nature, it is from an intrinsic cause and principle: but what is that other than the soul?

It is γ) a vital work, therefore from the soul. Cf. D. SENNERT, Physical Hypomnema IV, ch. IX, p. 251.

3) No squalid prison is a temple of the Holy Spirit. For who would dare to affirm that a temple is a prison, and that the Holy Spirit is held in chains? But the body of a reborn man is a temple of the Holy Spirit 1 Cor. VI, 15. Therefore.

4) The body will be reunited with the soul in the resurrection of the just. Therefore, it is not the soul's prison. The reason for the consequence is: because the resurrection of the just is a huge benefit, obtained by the merit of Christ. But it would be a huge punishment if the soul, which had been separated from the body, were thrust again through the resurrection into the body, as if into a perpetual prison. Certainly, the sisters of Lazarus would have given Christ no thanks if He had recalled the soul of their deceased brother into a prison.

5) Two absurdities follow the opposing opinion: a) That God did not act justly when He preserved Noah in the flood and Lot in the conflagration of Sodom, and destroyed innumerable wicked men. What would this have been other than to release wicked men from prisons, but to confine good men for longer? b) That that blessing: increase and multiply, was a curse; for it would pertain to the long-term detention of the soul in the dungeon of the body. 6) The opinion of the dissenters was condemned in the Council of Braga, canon VI. If anyone says that human souls sinned previously in a heavenly habitation, and for this were cast down into human bodies on earth, as Priscillian said, let him be anathema.

Latin:

ΕΚΘΕΣΙΣ

Obs.

Tam anima, quam corpus humanum bifariam spectari possunt: 1) κατ' ουσίαν, secundum se, vel essentiam suam: 2) καθ' ἁμαρτίαν, secundum statum corruptionis, siue secundum peccatum, per accidens adhaerens, Si considerentur secundum se, sunt bonae creaturæ, ad gloriam Dei conditæ. Glorificate Deum corpore vestro, & spiritu vestro, quæ sunt Dei, ait Paullus 1 Cor. VI, 20. Obs. II. Primaria sedes peccati est anima humana cum suis facultatibus. Deflectunt enim a lege divina intellectus per ignorantiam, opinionem, errorem; voluntas per electionem boni non veri, sed apparentis; appetitus sensitivus per cæcum impetum in bonum sensibus gratum, sed lege divina vetitum. Secundaria sedes peccati est corpus hominis organicum, quatenus animæ peccatrici in delinquendo inferuit.

ΒΕΒΑΙΩΣΙΣ

Prob.

1) Quodcunque corpus a Deo est creatum, & affabre effigiatum, ut gratum esset animæ domicilium, & cum hac, velut pars naturalis, totum hominem constitueret, illud male censetur molestus animæ carcer: Atqui corpus humanum &c. E.

Minor probatur ex Gen. I, 27. II, 7. Pulcherrimam corporis effigiationem inculcat Jobus, c. X, 10. & rex Dauid, Ps. CXXXIX, 15.

2) Causa physica, proxima & specialis corporis formati est anima in & cum semine a generante communicata, seu traducta. E. Corpus non potest eius esse carcer. Ratio consequentiæ est; quia nullus architectus sibi ipsi fabricat carcerem, quem incolat.

Antecedens cuiuis cordato patet. Nam α) opus formationis corporis est mire varium, & pro ratione cuiusque speciei restrictum. Aliter v. gr. leonis, aliter ursi, aliter hominis corpus, secundum magnitudinem, figuram, colorem, situm partium formatur. Vbiuis ergo causa specifica natura sua ad hoc tale opus determinata adsit, necesse est: quæ vero illa, nisi ipsa cuiusuis corporis anima? β) Formatio corporis est opus semini naturale; imino naturalissimum. Ergo vi definitionis, quam naturæ omnes assignant, a causa & principio intrinseco: quod vero illud aliud, nisi anima?

Est γ) opus vitale, ergo ab anima. Conf. D. SENNERTI hypomnema physicum IV. c. IX. p. 251.

3) Nullus carcer squalidus est templum Spiritus sancti. Ecquis enim ausit affirmare, templum esse carcerem, & Spiritum S. in vinculis detineri? Atqui corpus hominis renati est templum Spiritus S. 1 Cor. VI, 15. Ergo.

4) Corpus in resurrectione iustorum redunietur cum anima. E. non est animæ carcer. Ratio consequentiæ est: quia resurrectio iustorum ingens est beneficium, merito Christi partum. At foret ingens supplicium, si anima, quæ fuit a corpore separata, per resurrectionem denuo in corpus, velut perpetuum carcerem, detruderetur. Sane sorores Lazari Christo nullas egissent gratias, si animam defuncti fratris in carcerem reuocasset.

5) Aduersam sententiam sequuntur duo absurda: a) Deum non egisse iuste, cum in diluuio Noachum, in conflagratione Sodomæ Lothum conseruauit, & innumerabiles homines improbos peremit. Ecquid hoc fuisset aliud, quam viros improbos e carceribus dimittere, viros probos autem longius coërcere? b) Benedictionem illam: crescite & multiplicamini, fuisse maledictionem; pertineret enim ad diuturnam detentionem animæ in corporis ergastulo. 6) Condemnata est sententia diffidentium in concilio Bracarensi, canone VI. Si quis animas humanas dicit prius in cœlesti habitatione peccasse, & pro hoc in corpora humana in terram deiectas, sicut Priscillianus dixit, anathema fit.


### VI. Of how many parts does man consist?: Dissolution

DISSOLUTION

The opponents object I. from Ps.

CXLII, 8. Bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise thy name. Where by prison they understand the mortal body. R.

By prison the sacred psalmist understands the cave of Adullam, of which mention is made in 1 Sam. XXIV, 3, in which David felt such great distress as a man who is a criminal experiences when detained in prison. II.

From Ps. CXVI, 7. Return unto thy rest, O my soul!

The human soul is said to return to its rests, i. e., to the most tranquil heavenly mansions, in which it enjoyed the sweetest rest is prior to being thrust into the body, which is subject to many dangers and afflictions, as if into a squalid prison. R. By the cited words, the king-prophet stirred himself up, while he was dwelling in distress (according to Rabbi Kimchi), so that the soul, variously vexed by anxieties, might betake itself to God, as the author of all tranquility, and expect consolation from Him. Furthermore, it is to be noted that the soul is said to return to its rest, not because it existed in rest at some time before the body was formed, but because it fell through sin from that rest which it could have had in Adam.

III. Whatever body the rational soul is pressed and burdened by, that is aptly called its prison; But the corruptible body, etc. E. The major is established; because every prison is a troublesome place, where the soul is oppressed by sorrow. The minor is proved from Wisd. ch. IX, 15. The corruptible body presseth down the soul, and the earthy tabernacle weigheth down the mind that museth upon many things. Resp. 1) The Book of Wisdom is not canonical, but, in the judgment of LUDOVICUS VIVES, it is believed to be by Philo the Alexandrian Jew, who lived in the times of the apostles, to whom he was also a friend. There is such eloquence in the Greek speech that the Greeks said of him: ἢ Φίλων πλατονίζει, ἢ Πλάτων Φιλονίζει (either Philo Platonizes, or Plato Philonizes). 2) Whatever body, considered in itself, the soul is burdened by, that can be called its prison. But, if the soul and body were integral, the body would not burden the soul. But since both parts of man have become vitiated through the fall, it happens accidentally that the soul is distracted by excessive and inordinate care for the body, so that it is not at leisure to contemplate divine things.

IV. The body from which a reborn man desires to be delivered is his squalid prison. But from the mortal body, etc. E. The minor is proved from Rom. VII, 24, where the apostle groans: O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death? Resp. By the body of death is not understood a physically mortal body, but the depraved and corrupt concupiscence of the flesh, which, like some body, embraces the entire structure of vices or members, and thus brings about death, Col. III, 5. From this corruption of the flesh the apostle desires to be delivered. Grant that a mortal body is denoted by the apostle; it is not, however, understood κατ' οὐσίαν (according to essence), in itself, but καθ' ἁμαρτίαν (according to sin) inherent in it, from which Paul desires to be delivered.

V. It cannot be denied that there are many impurities in the human body. Resp. The soul is not defiled by the physical impurities of the body, because it is a spirit: But the primary seat of moral impurities is the sinful soul, to which the body serves by sinning.

Latin:

ΔΙΑΛΥΣΙΣ

Obiiciunt οἱ ἐξ ἐναντίας I. e Ps.

CXLII, 8. Educ e carcere animam meam ad confitendum nomini tuo. Vbi per carcerem intelligunt corpus mortale. R.

Per carcerem hieropsaltes intelligit speluncam Adullam, cuius fit mentio 1 Sam. XXIV, 3. in qua Dauid sensit angustias tantas, quantas experitur homo maleficus in carcere detentus. II.

E Ps. CXVI, 7. Reuertere in requies tuas, anima mea!

Dicitur anima humana reuerti in requies suas, i. e. in mansiones cœlestes tranquillissimas, in quibus dulcissima quiete gauisa est prius, quam in corpus, plurimis periculis & afflictionibus obnoxium, velut in squalidum carcerem detrusa est. R. Verbis citatis rex propheta semet ipsum excitauit, cum in ærumnis versaretur, (secundum Rabbi Kimchi) vt anima, angustiis varie diuexata, se reciperet ad Deum, tanquam tranquillitatis omnis auctorem, atque ab eo solatium exspectaret. Porro notandum, quod anima dicatur reuerti in requiem, non quod aliquando ante formatum corpus in requie exstiterit, sed quia illa requie, quam habere poterat in Adamo, per peccatum excidit.

III. Quocunque corpore anima rationalis premitur & grauatur, illud concinne appellatur eius carcer; Atqui corpore corruptibili &c. E. Maior constat; quia omnis carcer est locus molestus, vbi anima moerore opprimitur. Minor probatur e Sap. c. IX, 15. Corruptibile corpus aggrauat animam, etiam deprimit terrenum tentorium mentem multa intelligentem. Resp. 1) Liber sapientiæ non est canonicus, sed, iudice LUDOVICO VIVES, creditur Philonis Iudæi Alexandrini, qui vixit temporibus apostolorum, quibus & amicus fuit. Tanta in sermone græco est facundia, vt de illo Græci dixerint: ἢ Φίλων πλατονίζει, ἢ Πλάτων Φιλονίζει. 2) Quocunque corpore, per se considerato, anima grauatur, illud potest eius dici carcer. At, si anima & corpus forent integra, corpus animam non grauaret. At cum vtraque pars hominis per lapsum fit vitiata, per accidens fit, vt anima nimia & inordinata corporis cura distrahatur, vt ne rebus diuinis contemplandis vacet.

IV. A quo corpore homo renatus liberari cupit, illud est squalidus eius carcer. Sed a corpore mortali &c. E. Minor prob. e Rom. VII, 24. vbi apostolus ingemiscit: Miser ego homo! quis me eripiet e corpore mortis huius. Resp. Per corpus mortis non intelligitur corpus physice mortale, sed concupiscentia carnis praua & corrupta, quæ instar alicuius corporis vniuersam vitiorum vel membrorum compagem complectitur, atque adeo mortem infert, Col. III, 5. Ab hac carnis corruptione apostolus liberari exoptat. Fac, ab apostolo denotari corpus mortale, non tamen illud intelligitur κατ' οὐσίαν, secundùm se, sed καθ' ἁμαρτίαν, secundum peccatum inhærens, a quo Paullus liberari cupit.

V. Negari non potest, multas sordes esse in corpore humano. Resp. Sordibus corporis physicis non inquinatur anima, quia est spiritus: Sordium autem moralium primaria sedes est anima peccatrix, cui corpus delinquendo inferuit.


### Q. IX. Whether the human soul is created today, or propagated by traducianism?

The human soul is not created immediately today, but is generated by parents by means of fruitful seed, and is transmitted into the children.

Obs. I. A distinction must be made between the word creation taken in a general, special, and most special sense. In a general sense, creation denotes the act by which God produces something in any way, whether immediately out of nothing, or from some pre-existing matter, or with a second cause intervening, or in its absence. In a special sense, creation signifies the act by which God, with no second cause intervening, produces something, whether it be made out of pure nothing, or from unfit matter. In the most special sense, creation designates the act by which God immediately, without the concurrence of second causes, out of nothing, with no pre-existing matter, produces something.

Obs. II. A distinction must be made between tradux (traducianism) taken concretely and abstractly. Concretely, it is taken either in a general or a special sense. Specifically, it denotes a suitable cutting of some tree, vine, or plant (in Greek ἀπόσπασμα), that is, an avulsed part of the plant apt for propagation; in German, ein abgeschnittener Zweig, ein Sprößling, ein Pfropfreißlein, whereby the tree or the plant can be propagated. In a general sense, it designates any fruitful seed of plants and animals, and is commonly called prolific sperma. Abstractly, tradux denotes the very act of transmission (traduction).

Obs. III. Distinction between traductio κατὰ μετέκβασιν [by transference], or mere conveyance, and κατ' ἀλλοποίησιν [by alteration], or productive communication. Traductio here does not signify mere conveyance; for to that extent traductio would naturally apply even to a moral cause (e.g., to a vintner or a grafter); but it is understood as productive, communicative, and multiplicative traductio, by which parents multiply their own soul and, as it were, diffuse it into their children.

Obs. IV. The soul is not generated from the tradux, or fecund seed, as a material principle, but is propagated through the tradux, or by means of the prolific seed, as a vehicle.

The assertion is proved 1) from the divine blessing, Gen. 1:28, 9:1. Every soul by the power of the divine blessing is multiplicative of itself: Therefore, also the human soul.

2) From the definition of generation. Generation is the communication of essence through fecund seed to the image of the generator. From which definition we conclude: Whoever communicates essence to a generated human, communicates a soul to him. But the generating father, etc. Therefore.

3) From the effect. Whoever generates a human, he generates not only the body, but the soul. But the parent, etc. Therefore.

The major is evident; because the generator is a univocal cause, and according to the celebrated physical axiom: Every generator generates its like. 4) From the nature or property of the soul, which is the power of vivifying.

From whom we have life, from them we have the soul. But from parents, etc.

The major is clear; because life, taken in the first act, is the soul itself; or, if it be taken for the second act, it is something emanating from the soul.

5) From the term of generation, which is the image of the parent. Whoever generates a son in his own image, he generates the son's soul. The parent generates, etc. Gen. 5:3. Certainly, the image of the father cannot be propagated without his soul, since this is the πρῶτον δεκτικόν [primary recipient], the primary subject of the image.

6) From the divine rest. From whatever work of creating God rested, that God does not create once the nature of things has been established. But God rested from creating all the works of nature, Gen. 2:2.

You say: God rested from creating new species, but not from creating individuals.

Resp. 1) God indeed concurs with secondary causes for the production of individuals, but He does not create them immediately and by Himself alone. 2) Extraordinarily and miraculously God sometimes immediately creates new individuals (e.g., new stars): But generation is an ordinary and most natural work.

7) From the nature of the fecund seed. Whoever emits living seed, they propagate a soul. But parents, etc. Therefore. The major is proved; because without a soul nothing corporeal lives. The minor is clear; because from non-living seed a living human cannot proceed.

8) From the propagation of original sin. From whom original sin is propagated into children, from them the soul is propagated. But from parents, etc. Therefore. The major is evident; because the πρῶτον δεκτικόν [primary recipient] of original sin is the human soul. Once that which is in the soul is propagated, it is necessary that the soul itself be propagated.

9) From various absurdities which press upon the opinion of the adversaries.

For a) those who posit that souls are immediately created by God must either deny original sin, or God must be accused of injustice. For God created the soul either impure or pure. If impure, He will be the cause of sin: If pure, He is not just, because He subjected a pure soul to an impure matter. b) It will follow that parents no longer generate humans; because a human cannot be said to be generated by parents whose soul is not generated by them. c) The father will not be the physical cause of his son, but only a moral cause; because he only applied the passive subject, namely the matter, to the active principle, namely the soul created by God. d) It will follow that the soul of Christ was not generated, and consequently our soul was not redeemed. For τὸ ἀπρόσληπτον ἀθεράπευτον [what is not assumed is not healed].

Antithesis The antithesis is that of most Scholastics and Pontificians, who defend the creation or infusion of souls which occurs immediately by God, to which some philosophers assent.

They wish to fortify their opinion with the following arguments:

I. Everything generable is corruptible: According to the evangelical doctors, the human soul is generable; Therefore. The major is evident from induction: Sheep, oxen, donkeys, etc., are generated and die. Resp. 1) The major is not universal; because if man had remained in the state of integrity, he would indeed have been generable, but not corruptible. 2) Every induction ought to be made from like things. But the adversaries form an induction from unlike things, namely from bodies, and they apply it wrongly to the human soul, which is a spirit.

II. Whatever soul is not divisible, from that soul the offspring cannot proceed: But the soul of parents, etc. Therefore. The major is proven; because whatever is essential to parents, and yet proceeds from them, is as it were detached from them. Resp. Distinguish between detachment and derivation. The soul of children is indeed derived from the soul of parents, but it is not detached.

III. If the soul of children is made from the soul of parents, it is made from the same either decisively, or subjectively, or constitutively. But it is not made decisively; because it is indivisible: Not subjectively; for thus the soul of the son would exist subjectively in the father: Not constitutively; for thus the soul of the parent would be an essential and constituent part of the son. Resp. One member of the division is omitted, namely multiplicatively and propagatively. For every soul, by virtue of the divine blessing, is multiplicative of itself.

IV. The soul of the son is generated either solely from the soul of the father, or solely from the soul of the mother, or from both. Not solely from the soul of the father; because thus the mother would not generate a human; nor solely from the soul of the mother; because thus the father would not generate a son; nor from both; because thus a composition or confusion of souls would occur; Therefore the soul of the son clearly does not proceed from the soul of the parents. Resp. In generation, the father and mother stand as one cause. For they are associate causes, from which one effect flows. Therefore the soul of the son proceeds from both. Nor yet is a composition or confusion of souls to be feared; because the soul is a simple act, not composing or confusing.

V. If the soul of the son is drawn from the soul of the parent, either the whole soul passes into the son, or a part of it. But not the whole soul, because thus the parent would not retain the soul: Not a part, because the soul is indivisible. Resp. This argument 1) rests upon a false hypothesis; as if the soul were some whole divisible into parts. The soul is neither a whole, nor does it have parts. By the Scholastics, indeed, the spirit is said to be whole potentially; because it contains many powers, in a certain way united. But powers, or faculties of a thing, strictly speaking are not its parts. 2) When a flame ignites a flame, neither does the whole igniting flame pass into the ignited one, nor does a part of it descend into it. Thus the soul of the parents generates the soul of the son, so that nothing is lost to it.

VI. The human soul is either made from nothing, or from matter. But it is not made from matter. Therefore, from nothing, and consequently it is created. The consequence of the major is proven; because nothing has ever been made which has not been made either from matter or from nothing. Resp. a) A disjunctive syllogism is not made from immediate members. For a third is given; from a pre-existing form. You object in vain that the particle "from" denotes matter; for taken more broadly, it also designates form; for physicists teach with great consensus that a natural body consists of matter and form. b) We respond to the proof: Whatever is material or corporeal is made either from matter or from nothing; But the soul is not material or corporeal.

VII. Whoever is called the Father of spirits, from Him the soul has its origin. But God, etc. Heb. 12: 9. Therefore. Resp. 1) Limit the major. Whoever is called the Father of spirits, from Him the soul has its origin either immediately or mediately. The soul of Adam has its origin from God immediately; our soul mediately. 2) God l. c. is called the Father of Spirits not on account of the creation of souls, but on account of spiritual regeneration.

VIII. God gives the human soul, Eccl. 12: 7, and forms the human spirit, Zech. 12: 1. Therefore He creates the human soul. The reason of the consequence is; because whatever God gives, or fashions it, He gives and fashions it through creation. Resp. Eccl. XII. the first origin of the soul is regarded. For just as, when it is said that dust returns to the earth, whence it was, the first creation is regarded: So when it is said that the spirit returns to God, who gave it, the same is regarded, in which the spirit was immediately created by God. Today God gives the spirit mediately, through the intervention of secondary causes; just as He also gives the body, 1 Cor. XV, 38. Zechariah likewise considers the first origin of the soul; just as also the creation of heaven and earth made in the beginning is indicated.

Latin:

Anima humana hodie non immediate creatur, sed mediante semine fœcundo a parentibus generatur, & in liberos traducitur.

Obs. I. Distinguendum est inter creationis vocem sumtam sensu generali, speciali & specialissimo. Sensu generali creatio notat actum, quo Deus aliquid producit quocunque modo, siue immediate ex nihilo, siue ex præexistente quadam materia, siue interueniente caussa secunda, siue ea absente. Sensu speciali creatio significat actum, quo Deus, nulla interueniente caussa secunda, aliquid producit, siue fiat ex nihilo puro, siue ex materia inhabili. Sensu specialissimo creatio designat actum, quo Deus immediate, sine concursu caussarum secundarum ex nihilo, nulla præiacente materia, aliquid producit.

Obs. II. Distinguendum est inter traducem dictam concretiue, & abstractiue. Concretiue sumitur vel sensu generali, vel speciali. Speciatim notat idoneam alicuius arboris, vitis aut plantæ decisum (græce ἀπόσπασμα) siue auulsam plantæ particulam ad propagationem aptam; Germanice, ein abgeschnittener Zweig, ein Sprößling, ein Pfropfreißlein, dadurch der Baum, oder die Pflanze, kan fortgezielet werden. Generatim designat quoduis semen fœcundum plantarum & animalium, & dicitur vulgo sperma prolificum. Abstractiue tradux notat ipsam traductionem.

Obs. III. Dist. inter traductionem κατὰ μετέκβασιν, sive nudam transvectionem, & κατ' ἀλλοποίησιν, sive productivam communicationem. Traductio heic non significat nudam transvectionem; nam eatenus etiam causae morali (v. gr. vinitori, vel infitori) traductio naturalis competeret; sed intelligitur traductio productiva, communicativa & multiplicativa, qua parentes animam suam multiplicant & in liberos quasi diffundunt.

Obs. IV. Non generatur anima ex traduce, sive semine foecundo, tanquam principio materiali, sed per traducem, seu mediante semine prolifico, tanquam vehiculo, propagatur.

Probatur assertum 1) ex benedictione divina, Gen. I, 18. c. IX, 1. Omnis anima vi benedictionis divinae est sui multiplicativa: Ergo & anima humana.

2) Ex definitione generationis. Generatio est communicatio essentiae per semen foecundum ad imaginem generantis. Ex qua definitione colligimus: Quicunque homini genito communicat essentiam, communicat illi animam. Atqui pater generans &c. Ergo.

3) Ab effectu. Quicunque generat hominem, ille non tantum corpus, sed animam generat. Atqui parens &c. Ergo.

Maior constat; quia generans est causa univoca, & iuxta decantatum axioma physicum: Omne generans generat sibi simile. 4) Ab indole vel proprietate animae, quae est vis vivificandi.

A quibus habemus vitam, ab illis habemus animam. At a parentibus &c.

E. Maior patet; quia vita, sumta in actu primo, est ipsa anima; vel, si pro actu secundo accipiatur, est aliquid ab anima emanans.

5) A termino generationis, qui est imago parentis. Quicunque generat filium ad imaginem suam, ille generat animam filii. Parens generat &c. Gen. V. 3. Certe imago patris fine eius propagata anima esse nequit, cum haec sit πρῶτον δεκτικόν, subiectum primum imaginis.

6) A quiete divina. A quocunque opere faciendo Deus quievit, illud rerum natura constituta Deus non creat. Atqui ab omnibus naturae operibus condendis Deus quievit, Gen. II, 2.

E. Dicis: Acquievit Deus a condendis novis speciebus, sed non a creandis individuis.

Resp. 1) Concurrit quidem Deus cum causis secundis ad productionem individuorum, sed ea immediate & per se solus non creat. 2) Extraordinarie & miraculose Deus interdum nova individua (v. gr. novas stellas) immediate creat: At generatio est opus ordinarium & naturalissimum.

7) A natura feminis foecundi. Quicunque semen vivum emittunt, illi propagant animam. Atqui parentes &c. Ergo. Maior probatur; quia sine anima nullum corporeum vivit. Minor liquet; quia e semine non-vivo non potest provenire homo vivus.

8) A propagatione peccati originalis. A quibus propagatur peccatum originis in liberos, ab illis propagatur anima. Atqui a parentibus &c. Ergo. Maior constat; quia πρῶτον δεκτικόν peccati originis est anima humana. Propagato eo, quod est in anima, necesse est ipsam animam propagari.

9) A variis absurdis, quae sententiam adversariorum premunt.

Nam a) qui statuunt, animas immediate a Deo creari, illis vel negandum est peccatum originis, vel Deus iniustitiae insimulandus est. Creavit enim Deus animam vel impuram, vel puram. Si impuram; erit causa peccati: Si puram; iustus non est, quia animam puram impure materiae inferuit. b) Sequetur, parentes non amplius generare homines; quia homo non potest dici a parentibus generari, cuius anima ab illis non generatur. c) Pater non erit causa physica filii sui, sed tantum causa moralis; quia subiectum passivum, puta materiam tantum applicavit principio activo, nempe animae a Deo creatae. d) Sequetur, animam Christi non esse generatam & consequenter animam nostram non esse redemtam. Nam τὸ ἀπρόσληπτον ἀθεράπευτον.

Antithesis est plerorumque Scholasticorum & Pontificiorum, creationem, vel infusionem animarum quæ immediate a Deo fiat, defendentium, quibus nonnulli philosophi adstipulantur.

Munitam volunt opinionem suam sequentibus argumentis: Antithesis Antithesis est plerorumque Scholasticorum & Pontificiorum, creationem, vel infusionem animarum quae immediate a Deo fiat, defendentium, quibus nonnulli philosophi adstipulantur. Munitam volunt opinionem suam sequentibus argumentis:

I. Omne generabile est corruptibile: Per doctores euangelicos anima humana est generabilis; Ergo. Maior patet ex inductione: Oues, boues, asini &c. generantur & moriuntur. Resp. 1) Maior non est vniuersalis; quia si homo in statu integritatis mansisset, generabilis quidem fuisset, at non corruptibilis. 2) Omnis inductio debet fieri ex paribus. At aduersarii formant inductionem ex imparibus, nempe ex corporibus, & illam male applicant ad humanam animam, quæ est spiritus.

II. Quæcunque anima non est diuisibilis, ab illa anima liberorum prouenire nequit: At anima parentum &c. Ergo. Maior probatur; quia quidquid essentiale est parentibus, & tamen ab illis prouenit, ab iisdem quasi deciditur. Resp. Dist. inter decisionem, & deductionem, Anima liberorum ab anima parentum deducitur quidem, sed non deciditur.

III. Si anima liberorum fit ab anima parentum, ab eadem fit vel decisive; vel subiectiue, vel constitutive. At non fit decisive; quia est indiuisibilis: Non subiectiue; sic enim anima filii subiectiue existeret in patre: Non constitutive; sic enim anima parentis esset pars essentialis & constituens filii. Resp. Omittitur vnum membrum diuisionis, nempe multiplicatiue & propagatiue. Nam omnis anima, vi benedictionis diuinæ, est fui multiplicatiua.

IV. Anima filii vel vnice generatur ab anima patris; vel vnice ab anima matris, vel ab vtraque. Non vnice ab anima patris; quia sic mater non generaret hominem; neque vnice ab anima matris; quia sic pater non generaret filium; neque ab vtraque; quia sic fieret compositio aut confusio animarum; Ergo anima filii plane non prouenit ab anima parentum. Resp. In generatione pater & mater stant pro causa vna. Sunt enim causæ sociæ, a quibus vnus fluit effectus. Ergo ab vtroque prouenit anima filii. Neque tamen metuenda est animarum compositio, aut confusio; quia anima est actus simplex non componens, aut confundens.

V. Si anima filii trahitur ex anima parentis; aut tota anima transit in filium, aut eius pars. At non tota anima, quia sic parens animam non retineret: Non pars, quia anima est indiuisibilis. Resp. Hoc argumentum 1) nititur hypothesi falsa; quasi anima sit aliquod totum diuisibile in partes. Anima nec est tota, nec habet partes. A Scholasticis quidem spiritus dicitur totus potestatiue; quia continet plures potentias, certo modo vnitas. Sed potentiæ, seu facultates rei, proprie loquendo non sunt eius partes. 2) Cum flamma accendit flammam, neque tota flamma accendens transit in accensam, neque pars eius in eam descendit. Ita anima parentum generat animam filii, vt ei nihil decedat.

VI. Anima humana vel fit ex nihilo, vel ex materia. Sed non fit ex materia. E. ex nihilo, & consequenter creatur. Consequentia maioris probatur; quia nihil vnquam factum est, quod non vel ex materia, vel ex nihilo factum sit. Resp. a) Syllogismus disiunctiuus non fit ex membris immediatis. Nam datur tertium; ex præexistente forma.
