Frustra excipis, quod particula ex materiam notet; nam latius sumta etiam formam designat; docent enim physici magno consensu, corpus naturale constare ex materia. & forma. b) Respondemus ad probationem: Quodcunque materiatum, aut corporeum fit, illud fit vel ex materia, vel ex nihilo; At anima non est materiata, aut corporea.

VII. Quicunque dicitur pater spirituum, ab illo anima habet originem. Atqui Deus &c. Hebr. XII, 9. Ergo. Resp. 1) Limit. maior. Quicunque dicitur pater spirituum, ab illo anima habet originem vel immediatam, vel mediatam. Anima Adami immediatam, nostra anima mediatam a Deo originem habet. 2) Deus l. c. dicitur, Pater Spirituum, non ob animarum creationem, sed spiritualem regenerationem.

VIII. Deus animam humanam dat, Eccl. XII, 7. spiritumque humanum fingit, Zach. XII, 1. Ergo animam humanam creat. Ratio consequentiae est; quia quidquid Deus dat, aut fingit, illud dat & fingit per creationem. Resp. Eccl. XII. respicitur prima animæ origo. Nam quemadmodum, quando dicitur pulvis reuerti in terram, vnde erat, respicitur ad primam creationem: Sic quando dicitur spiritus redire ad Deum, qui dedit illum, ad eandem respicitur, in qua spiritus immediate a Deo fuit creatus. Hodie Deus spiritum dat mediate, interuenientibus causis secundis; sicut etiam dat corpus, 1 Cor. XV, 38. Zacharias itidem primam originem animæ considerat; quemadmodum etiam creatio cœli & terræ in principio facta indigitatur.


### Q. IX. Whether the human soul is created today, or propagated by traducianism?: Q

Q.

The human soul neither flowed out from the divine essence, nor does it return or flow back into the divine essence through spiritual regeneration and mystical union with the triune God.

The antithesis is 1) of Plato, who maintains that God is the center of all things, from whom human souls have proceeded, or emanated, and into whom they return. The opinion of Plato is more clearly explained by his follower, MARSILIO FICINO, in Timaeus c. 6. All things are from God in such a way that not even the smallest things are ever separated from God. For indeed the divine unity flourishes, through which all things consist: and they are wonderfully revolved in a certain perpetual, nay, circular motion toward God Himself, from whom and in whom they are, otherwise they would suddenly fall into nothingness. From the divine unity all things proceed, and proceeding they retain a certain unity impressed upon them, an image of the divine unity, by which they are called into it, and being recalled they are perfected. This very thing draws souls to the desires by which union with God is fully fulfilled in us. But if nature, flowing from God, has implanted in certain things properties suitable to the celestial beings, through which they turn themselves in a certain way toward the celestial beings, as sunflowers toward the sun, and lunar things toward the moon: much more has the Father of souls impressed upon them powers drawing them to Himself; which indeed are seen to be situated primarily in a certain divine unity, a superior intellect, and not least in actual reflection itself. But our own restitution into God, arising from this, is absolutely consummated by suppliant adoration.

2) Of Hermes Trismegistus, thus addressing his son Tatius, in the Pymander, cap. XII. Mind, O Tatius, is from the proper essence of God. For there is some essence of God, whatever that may be; this alone knows Him absolutely. Mind indeed is not cut off from the essence of God; because it is also like the splendor of the diffused sun. But this mind in men is indeed God: for that reason some men are gods, and their humanity is akin to divinity.

For thus writes J. TAULER in the treatise on the following of the poverty of Christ §. 3.: Some say that this is the highest poverty, and the nearest detachment, that man should be as he was, when he was not yet.

Then he understood nothing, then he wanted nothing, then he was God with God. Let us also hear H. HARPHIUS in theol. myst. l. 5. collat. 2. p. 683. inquiring: Thus our spirit, turning itself into its origin, i.e., the apex of the mind, and beyond, reclining itself into the uncreated spirit, happily merits to be renewed. For while it immerses itself wholly in the uncreated spirit, that it may melt; and flows back again into that infinite abyss, its image is always renewed, that it may happily merit to hear: Thou art my son, today I have begotten thee, p. 684. O my soul, whence did thy flow take its beginning? Is it not from that abyss of divinity, as essence from essence, life from life, intelligence from intelligence, light from light? but creaturely, not essentially: not God from God, but deified by God. So also GOTTFR. ARNOLD. in theol. myst. c. 6. p. 149. I say that out of a Christian man a god becomes. He adds the reason for this assertion p. 152. Because this doctrine has God Himself as the final end of all its secret knowledge and working; so it expresses His beauty according to its ability, while it contemplates it, and whoever becomes partaker of it, it makes him, as it were, a holy and bright mirror, that it catches the ray of the highest Godhead and of the primordial light, and shoots it back again into God Himself, from whom it flowed.

Upon this hypothesis rests that Weigelian formula of speaking in the Dialogue on Christianity, p. 13: "We must be new creatures in him, with him, and through him, born of God himself, essential children of God, and not imputatively."

Latin:

Quæst. X. An anima humana ex essentia diuina emanauit, & in eandem per regenerationem atque vnionem mysticam redit, & quasi refluit?

Anima humana neque ex essentia diuina effluxit, neque per spiritualem regenerationem, atque mysticam cum Deo triuno vnionem, in essentiam diuinam redit, aut refluit.

Antithesis est 1) Platonis, statuentis, Deum esse centrum omnium rerum, e quo animæ humanæ prodierint, siue emanauerint, & in illud redeant. Sententiam Platonis clarius exponit ipsius assecla, MARSILIVS FICINVS, in Timaum c. 6. Omnia ex Deo ita sunt, vt nusquam vel minima quæque deferantur a Deo. Vtique enim diuina viget vnitas, per quam res quæque consistunt: ac perpetuo quodam, immoque circulo ad Deum ipsum, a quo & in quo sunt, mirabiliter reuoluuntur, alioquin in nihilum repente proruerent. Ab vnitate diuina omnia prodeunt, prodeuntiaque vnitatem quandam ipsis impressam retinent diuinæ vnitatis imaginem, quæ euocantur in illam, & reuocata perficiuntur. Hæc ipsa animas rapit ad vota, quibus vnio cum Deo nobis penitus impleatur. Quod si natura ex Deo manans quasdam rebus quibusdam conuenientes cum superis proprietates inferuit, per quas quodammodo ad superos sese vertant, ceu ad solem solaria, ad lunam vero lunaria: multo magis animarum pater rapientes ad se vires eis impressit; quæ quidem in primis in diuina quadam vnitate, intellectu superiore, nec non in ipsa actuali reflexione fitæ videntur. Ipsam vero nostram in Deum restitutionem adoratio supplex hinc orta absolute consummat.

2) Hermetis Trismegisti, filium suum Tatium ita alloquentis, in Pymandro, cap. XII. Mens, o Tati, ex propria essentia Dei est. Aliqua siquidem est essentia Dei, qualiscunque tamen illa fit; hæc ipsum sola absolute nouit. Mens vtique ab essentia Dei non est præcisa; quia etiam velut diffusi solis splendor instar. Hæc autem mens in hominibus quidem Deus est: ea de causa homines aliqui dii sunt, ac ipsorum humanitas diuinitati est confinis.

3) Mysticorum. Sic enim scribit 10. TAVLERVS in tr. von der Nachfolgung der Armuth Christi §. 3.: Etliche sprachen, daß das die höchste Armuth, und die nechste Abgeschiedenheit sey, daß der Mensch also sey, als er war, da er noch nicht war.

Da verstunde er nichts, da wollte er nichts, da war er Gott mit Gott. Audiamus etiam H. HARPHIVM in theol. myst. l. 5. collat. 2. p. 683. inquirientem: Sic spiritus noster in suam originem i. e. mentis apicem se conuertens, & vltra, in spiritum increatum se reclinans, feliciter meretur renouari. Quia dum increato spiritu se totum immergit, ut liquefcat; & in illam abyssum infinitam defluat denuo, semper illius imago renouatur, ut audire feliciter mereatur: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie te genui, p. 684. O anima mea, vnde profluxus tuus sumsit exordium? Nonne ex illa abysso diuinitatis, velut essentia de essentia, vita de vita, intelligentia de intelligentia, lumen de lumine? sed creaturaliter, non essentialiter: non Dea de Deo, sed deificata a Deo. Ita etiam GOTTFR. ARNOLD. in theol. myst. c. 6. p. 149. Ich sage, daß aus einem christlichen Menschen ein Gott werde. Rationem assertionis addit p. 152. Weil diese lehre zum Endzweck aller ihrer geheimen Erkänntniß und Wirkung GOtt selbst hat; so drücket sie dessen Schönheit nach Vermögen aus, indem sie solche beschauet, und wer ihrer theilhaftig wird, den machet sie gleichsam zu einem heiligen und hellen Spiegel, daß er den Strahl der höchsten Gottheit, und des uhranfänglichen Lichtes fasset, und wiederum in GOtt selbst, daraus er geflossen, zurücke schiesset.

Huic hypothesi innititur illa formula loquendi Weigeliana in dialogo de christianismo p. 13.: Wir müssen in ihm, mit ihm, und durch ihn neue Creaturen seyn, aus Gott selber geboren, wesentliche Kinder Gottes, und nicht imputiatuisch.


### Q. IX. Whether the human soul is created today, or propagated by traducianism?: E K T H E S I S [Exposition]

E K T H E S I S [Exposition]

Objection I. Holy Scripture testifies that God gave the soul and breathed it into man, Eccl. 12:7, Gen. 2:7. But it nowhere says that the human soul emanated from the divine essence itself.

It is therefore from God energētikōs [effectively], as from an efficient cause, but not ousiōdōs [essentially], as from a constituent principle.

Objection II. By the benefit of regeneration, a new and spiritual life of faith is conferred, through which, with sins remitted, we are rendered adoptive sons of God, John 1:12, not natural or essential sons of God.

B E B A I Ō S I S [Confirmation]

Our assertion is proved: 1) Whoever has emanated from the divine essence is essentially God.

But the human soul is not essentially God: Therefore.

The major is clear; because no one can emanate from the essence of God without being God. The Logos, or Son of God, is therefore essentially God because he emanates from the essence of God the Father through eternal generation.

The minor is evident; because if the human soul were essentially God, it would be omnipotent, omnipresent, omniscient, and to be worshipped: which is impious to think and blasphemous to say.

2) The divine essence is unique, invisible, and most simple: Therefore, it cannot be dispersed or diffused into nearly innumerable souls; otherwise, there would be as many gods as there are human souls.

M. T. Cicero felt the force of this argument, writing not in vain in Book I of De Natura Deorum:

"Pythagoras, who thought that God was a soul intent upon and passing through the nature of all things, from which our souls were taken, did not see that by the distraction of human souls God would be torn apart and lacerated; and since human souls were miserable, which happens to most, then a part of God would be miserable, which cannot happen."

3) Whatever has emanated from the divine essence is immutable: for the divine essence is invariable, Ps. 102:28, Mal.

102, 28.

3:6. But the human soul is not immutable: for it becomes evil through sin, and again from evil, good through grace. Therefore.

Therefore.

4) The mystical doctors, by their nefarious dogma concerning the origin of the human soul from the divine essence, detract greatly from the divine majesty by making: a) The human soul equal to the Son of God and the Holy Spirit. For the former emanated from the essence of God the Father through eternal generation, the latter through eternal procession; to whom the soul, through the dogma of the outflow from the abyss of divinity, is equated. b) By constituting the essence of God as the subject of sin and misery.

For after the fall, the soul is corrupted and subject to divine punishments and afflictions.

If, therefore, the soul were a particle of the divine essence, sin would inhere in it no less than affliction would befall it; which is atopon [absurd].

5) The opinion of the adversaries has long since been condemned by the ancient church in the Council of Braga, canon V:

"If anyone believes that human souls existed from the substance of God, as Manichaeus and Priscillian said, let him be anathema."

Leo I, Epistle 93 to Turbius, Jerome in his epistle to Marcellinus, and Augustine in Epistle 28 to Jerome rejected the same opinion as impious, heretical, and blasphemous.

6) Through regeneration, the human soul does not become a natural Son of God; otherwise, Christ would not be the only-begotten Son of God, John 1:14. Therefore, through the same, it does not return into the divine nature as its constitutive principle. 7) Through the mystical union, God dwells in the reborn soul as in His temple, 1 Cor. 3:16. Therefore, the reborn soul is not transformed or melted into the essence of God. Who has ever heard it said that a dwelling has been changed into an inhabitant, or an inhabitant into a dwelling? RESOLUTION.

The dissenters object: I. Whatever soul was first breathed into man by God, that emanated from the substance of God. But the intelligent soul, etc. Therefore.

The major is proved: because God produced the other creatures by speaking, or by the word of His command, but He breathed in the soul, a clear indication that it proceeded from the divine essence in the same way that breath proceeds from the mouth. Resp. To breathe in signifies to produce and communicate a spirit; which God produces either from His essence or from nothing. From the substance of God is breathed and proceeds the Holy Spirit, the third person of the divinity: from nothing were produced finite spirits, namely, angels and the human soul. For this was indeed breathed in by God ἐνεργητικῶς (energetically), as from an external efficient cause, but not οὐσιωδῶς (essentially), as if from an internal constitutive cause. God created the soul as a finite spirit and sent this into the formed body, but He did not infuse the soul into the body as a particle of His own essence. You object: But no reason can be given why the human soul was not founded by the omnipotent word, like other creatures, but communicated to man by inspiration, unless it be this one: that it is derived or drawn from the substance of God. Ἐμπνευσις (Inspiration) denotes 1) the origin of the soul, that it, having been created from without by God, was infused into the body; 2) the mode of inspiration, that this divine action was performed in a singular and excellent way, yet as easily as it is for a man to emit breath from his mouth; 3) the effect of inspiration, that it is not a body, but a spirit not only distinct from the body and all matter, but also capable of spiritual things. But just as the breath of the mouth is not a particle of the soul, so neither is the soul a particle of the divine essence.

II: We are called the offspring of God, Acts 17:28. But the foundation of offspring consists in the communication of essence. Whence arises the argument: Whoever are the offspring of God, to them God has communicated His essence: But men, etc. Therefore. Resp. We are called the offspring of God not because of a participation in the divine essence, but because of a production similar to Him as an exemplary cause. Thus Adam is called the Son of God, Luke 3:38, because he was created in the image of God.

III. Whatever soul is a partaker of the divine nature, that emanated from the essence of God. But the faithful soul is a partaker of the divine nature, as Peter testifies, 2 Ep. ch. 1:4. Therefore. Resp. I deny the major. Because not every human soul, but only the reborn and justified, is said to be a partaker of the divine nature, not because of an emanation from the essence of God, but because of the gracious indwelling of God in the faithful soul, which brings about a participation in the divine nature that is not essential, but accidental. If the human soul had flowed from the substance of God, not only the reborn but also the unregenerate soul would be from God, which is ἄγραφον (unwritten) and ἀντίγραφον (contrary to scripture); for he who sins is of the devil. 1 John 3:8.

Latin:

Ε Κ Θ Ε Σ Ι Σ

Obs. I. Deum animam dedisse, & homini inspirasse, testatur S. scriptura, Eccl. XII, 7. Gen. II, 7. At nusquam dicit, hominis animam ex ipsa essentia diuina emanasse.

Est igitur a Deo ἐνεργητικῶς, tanquam a causa efficiente, non autem οὐσιωδῶς, tanquam a principio constituente.

Obs. II. Beneficio regenerationis confertur noua & spiritualis vita fidei, per quam reddimur, remissis peccatis, filii Dei adoptiui, Io. I, 12. non filii Dei naturales aut essentiales.

Β Ε Β Α Ι Ω Σ Ι Σ

Probatur assertio nostra: 1) Quicunque ex essentia diuina emanauit, is essentialiter Deus est.

At animus humanus non est essentialiter Deus: E.

Maior liquet; quia nemo ex essentia Dei emanare potest, quin sit Deus. Ὁ λόγος, siue filius Dei ideo essentialiter Deus est; quia ex essentia Dei patris per æternam generationem emanat.

Minor patet; quia si animus humanus essentialiter Deus esset, foret omnipotens, omnipræsens, omnisciens & adorandus: quod cogitatu impium, & dictu blasphemum est.

2) Essentia diuina vnica, inuisibilis & simplicissima est: E. in animas prope innumerabiles dispergi, aut diffundi nequit; alioqui tot forent dii, quot sunt animæ humanæ.

Vim huius argumenti sensit M.

T. CICERO, haud vane scribens, libr. I. de natura deorum: Pythagoras, qui censuit, Deum animum esse per naturam rerum omnium intentum & commeantem, ex quo animi nostri caperentur, non vidit, distractione humanorum animorum discerpi & dilacerari Deum; & cum miseri humani animi essent, quod plerisque contingeret, tum Dei partem esse miseram, quod fieri non potest.

3) Quicquid ex essentia diuina emanauit, illud est immutabile: nam essentia diuina est inuariabilis, Ps.

CII, 28.

Mal. III, 6. At anima humana non est immutabilis: fit enim mala, per peccatum, & rursus ex mala bona, per gratiam.

Ergo.

4) Doctores mystici, nefando suo dogmate de origine animæ humanæ ex essentia diuina, plurimum derogant maiestati diuinæ, facendo a) animam humanam æqualem Filio Dei, & Spiritui S. Nam ille ex essentia Dei Patris per æternam generationem, hic per æternam spirationem emanauit; cui anima, per dogma de profluxu ex abysso diuinitatis, æquiparatur. b) Constituendo essentiam Dei subiectum peccati & miseriæ.

Nam post lapsum corrupta, atque pœnis diuinis & afflictionibus subiecta est anima.

Quod si itaque anima particula foret essentiæ diuinæ, huic non minus peccatum inhæreret, quam afflictio obtingeret; quod est ἄτοπον.

5) Sententia aduersariorum iam dudum condemnata est ab antiqua ecclesia in concilio Bracarensi, canone V.

Si quis animos humanos ex Dei credit substantia extitisse, sicut Manichæus & Priscillianus dixerunt, anathema sit.

Reiecerunt eandem opinionem, tanquam impiam, hæreticam & blasphemam LEO I. epist. 93. ad Turbium, HIERONYMVS epist. ad Marcellinum, AVGVSTINVS epist. 28. ad Hieronymum.

6) Per regenerationem animus humanus non fit Filius Dei naturalis; ceteroqui Christus non foret Filius Dei vnigenitus, Io. I, 14. E. per eandem non redit in naturam diuinam, tanquam principium suum constitutiuum. 7) Per vnionem mysticam Deus in anima renata habitat, tanquam in templo suo 1 Cor. III, 16. E. anima renata non transformatur, aut liquescit in essentiam Dei. Ecquis fando audiuit, domicilium in incolam, aut incolam in domicilium fuisse commutatum? ΔΙΑΛΥΣΙΣ.

Obiiciunt diffidentes: I. Quaecunque anima homini primo a Deo est inspirata, illa ex substantia Dei emanauit. Atqui anima intelligens &c. Ergo.

Maior probatur: quia Deus reliquas creaturas dicendo, siue verbo mandati sui, produxit, animam autem inspirauit, luculento indicio, eandem ex essentia diuina sic processisse, quemadmodum halitus ex ore prouenit. Resp. Inspirare, significat spiritum producere & communicare; quem Deus producit vel ex essentia sua, vel ex nihilo. Ex substantia Dei spiratur & procedit Spiritus S. tertia diuinitatis persona: ex nihilo producti sunt spiritus finiti, scil. angeli, & anima humana. Hae quippe a Deo quidem ἐνεργητικῶς, tanquam a causa externa efficiente, non autem οὐσιωδῶς, velut ex interna causa constituente, inspirata est. Creauit Deus animam, vt spiritum finitum, & hunc immisit corpori formato, non autem animam, vt particulam essentiae suae, corpori infudit. Excipis: Sed ratio nulla dari potest, cur anima humana verbo omnipotenti non sit condita, vt ceterae creaturae, sed per inspirationem homini communicata, nisi haec vnica, quod ex substantia Dei deriuata, aut delibata fit. Ἐμπνευσις, siue inspiratio notat originem animae, quod illa, ab extra condita a Deo, corpori fit infusa; 2) modum inspirationis, quod haec actio diuina facta fit modo quidem singulari & eximio, tam facili tamen, quam procliuine homini est, halitum oris emittere; 3) effectum inspirationis, quod is non fit corpus, sed spiritus a corpore & materia omni non tantum distinctus, sed & spiritualium mutuum capax. At sicut halitus oris non est particula animae, ita nec anima particula essentiae diuinae.

II: Dicimur genus Dei, Act. XVII, 28. At fundatio generis in communicatione essentiae consistit. Vnde nascitur argumentum: Quicunque sunt genus Dei, illis Deus summet essentiam communicauit: Atqui homines &c. Ergo. Resp. Dicimur genus Dei, non propter essentiae diuinae participationem, sed propter similem ad illam, tanquam caussam exemplarem, productionem. Sic Adamus dicitur Filius Dei, Luc. III, 38. quia in imagine Dei creatus est.

III. Quae anima particeps est naturae diuinae, illa ex essentia Dei emanauit. Atqui anima fidelis est particeps naturae diuinae, teste Petro 2. ep. c. I, 4. E. Resp. Neg. maior. Quia non omnis anima humana, sed tantum renata & iustificata dicitur particeps naturae diuinae, non ob emanationem ex essentia Dei, sed ob gratiosam Dei inhabitationem in anima fideli, quae infert participationem naturae diuinae non essentialem, sed accidentalem. Si anima humana fluxisset e substantia Dei, non tantum renata, sed & irregenita anima ex Deo esset, quod est ἄγραφον & ἀντίγραφον; nam qui peccat, ex diabolo est. 1 Jo. III, 8.


### Quest. XI. For what end did God create man?

God created man a) for the glory of His name; b) for the eternal salvation of man.

Prob. a) Rom. 11:36. For of Him, and through Him, and to Him are all things: To Him be glory forever! Amen!

b) That man was created for eternal life, the law prescribed in paradise teaches, Gen. II, 19. Just as the penalty of eternal death was proposed to him who transgressed it: so, conversely, it is gathered that for man, who keeps that law holily, the reward of eternal life is established.

Q. XII. How manifold is the state of man?

The state of man is fivefold: The first is the state of innocence, which was concreated with the first humans. The second is the state of misery, into which, by the fault of the protoplasts, the human race has fallen. The third is the state of grace, which the faithful obtain through Christ. The fourth is the state of glory, into which the elect will be transferred on the day of the universal judgment. The fifth state is that of ignominy, by which the reprobate will be afflicted by the just judgment of God.

Obj. States are accidental conditions of men, according to which they can and ought to be considered in various ways. These diverse states of all men will be weighed more accurately below.

Q. XIII. What practical uses does

anthropology provide? Anthropology,

or the doctrine of man, when sent more deeply into the soul, rightly and deservedly produces in us a) a becoming submission of the soul; b) love of God and neighbor; c) a desire for eternal life.

Prob. a) God created man, dust from the earth, Gen. II, 7, so that man, mindful of his first origin, might conduct himself submissively before God. What is viler or more abject than dust, which we trample under our feet? Abraham ingenuously acknowledged this, who, having begun to pray, said: Behold, I pray, I have dared to speak to the Lord, though I am but dust and ashes! Gen. XVIII, 27.

b) God breathed into man the breath of life, Gen. II, 7. So that the soul might live perpetually for the author of life, might cling to Him inseparably, and might rest in Him, as in a harbor. O Lord, You have made us for Yourself, and our heart is restless, unless it rests in You. God created Eve from the rib of Adam, so that He might make of one blood every nation of men to dwell upon the whole face of the earth, Acts XVII, 26. Since, therefore, all men who live under heaven were created from the one blood of Adam: by the right of blood they are obligated to mutual love.

c) Since man is created for eternal life, let him be held by the love of eternal goods, let him burn with desire, let him be delighted by memory. Thither the spirit must be directed (I speak with BERNARD) whither it is to go. Thither we must hasten, where we may live forever, and where we may no longer fear to die.

SIGH

But if I did not especially worship and assiduously venerate You, O most benign Sower of the human race, I would be ungratefully impious and impiously ungrateful. For when I was nothing, You made me, so that I might be not a beast devoid of mind, not a poisonous worm, but a man illuminated by the torch of reason and speech. You made me from dust, so that I might not blush to cast myself into the dust before Your face. You gave me a soul, the breath of life, so that I might acknowledge that all reasons for breathing and hoping are suspended from You. I hang from You, O best Creator, as a bee from a flower, a shadow from a body. I love You above all, I esteem You most highly. Be to me a most indulgent father, I am and remain the most humble of Your children.

Latin:

Deus condidit hominem a) in nominis sui gloriam; b) ad aeternam hominis salutem.

Prob. a) Rom. XI, 36. Ex ipso Deo, & per ipsum, & in ipso sunt omnia: Ipsi gloria in saecula! Amen!

Prob. b) Hominem conditum esse ad vitam aeternam, docet lex praescripta in paradiso, Gen. II, 19. Quemadmodum illam transgredienti proposita erat poena aeternae mortis: ita e contrario colligitur, quod homini, legem illam sancte observanti, constitutum sit praemium aeternae vitae.

Quaest. XII. Quotuplex est status hominis?

Status hominis est quintuplex: Primus est status innocentiae, quae fuit primis hominibus concreata. Secundus est status miseriae, in quam, culpa protoplastorum, prolapsum est genus humanum. Tertius est status gratiae, quam fideles per Christum consequuntur. Quartus est status gloriae, in quam electi in die vniversalis iudicii transferentur. Quintus status est ignominiae, qua reprobi iusto Dei iudicio afficientur.

Obs. Status sunt accidentales hominum conditiones, secundum quas illi diversimode considerari possunt ac debent. Hi status diversi omnium hominum infra accuratius expendentur.

Quaest. XIII. Quos usus practicos suppeditat ἀνθρωπολογία?

Ἀνθρωπολογία,

sive doctrina de homine, in animum penitius demissa, iure meritoque in nobis pariat a) decentem animi submissionem; b) amorem Dei & proximi; c) vitae aeternae desiderium.

Prob. a) Creavit Deus hominem, pulverem de terra, Gen. II, 7. vt homo, primae vain recordatus originem, coram Deo se submisse gerat. Quid pulvere, quem pedibus proculcamus, vilius aut abiectius est? Ingenue hoc agnovit Abrahamus, qui, precari orsus, dixit: Ecce, quaeso, ausus sum loqui ad dominum, cum ego tamen pulvis & cinis sim! Gen. XVIII, 27.

b) Inspirauit Deus homini spiraculum vitae, Gen. II, 7. Vt anima auctori vitae viuat perpetuo, ipsi indiuulse adhaerescat, & in eo, velut portu, conquiescat. Domine, fecisti nos ad te, & irrequietum est cor nostrum, nisi quiescat in te. Vt anima auctori vitae viuat perpetuo, ipsi indiuulse adhaerescat, & in eo, velut portu, conquiescat. Domine, fecisti nos ad te, & irrequietum est cor nostrum, nisi quiescat in te. Euam condidit Deus de costa Adami, vt faceret ex vno sanguine quoduis genus hominum habitare super totam faciem terrae, Act. XVII, 26. Cum igitur vno Adami sanguine omnes, qui sub caelo viuunt homines, sint creati: iure sanguinis ad mutuum amorem obligantur.

c) Cum homo ad aeternam vitam creatus fit, aeternorum bonorum amore teneatur, desiderio flagret, memoria delectetur. Illuc spiritus est dirigendus (cum BERNHARDO loquor) quo est iturus. Illuc festinare debemus, vbi semper viuamus, & vbi mori amplius non timeamus.

SUSPIRIVM

Quod si non praecipue te, o Sator generis humani benignissime, colerem, & assidue venerarem, ingrate impius, & impie ingratus forem. Etenim cum nihil essem, fecisti me, vt essem non bestia mentis inops, non vermis venenatus, sed homo rationis & orationis face collustratus. Fecisti me ex pulvere, vt coram facie tua in puluerem me abiicere non erubescam. Animam, vitae spiraculum, mihi dedisti, vt omnes spirandi sperandique rationes a te suspensae esse, agnoscam. Pendeo a te, creator optime, vt apis a flore, vmbra a corpore. Te potissimum amo, te maxime aestimo. Sis mihi pater indulgentissimus, ego sum maneoque filiorum tuorum humillimus.


## 9 On Divine Providence


### Q. XIII. What practical uses does

I. What is divine providence? Divine providence is the external action of the Triune God, by which He, according to the infallible foreknowledge of His intellect and the benevolent decree of His will, most powerfully preserves all creatures, most effectively cooperates with those that act, and most wisely governs all things for the glory of His name and the benefit of men, especially the pious.

Quest. II. From where is the word providence derived? Providence is derived from providendo (providing); pro, in composition, signifies the same as prae (before), or in front.

Proof. The author of Book II to Herennius says: Providence is that by which something future is seen before it happens.

Yet, from the usage of speech, providere (to provide) implies more than praevidere (to foresee). An astrologer foresees an adverse storm, without having any care for those whom it will strike; but providere, along with the foresight of the mind, denotes the solicitous care of the will. Thus, the Greek word πρόνοια is also from προνοέω, which signifies: I anticipate in my mind, I foresee, I take care of.

Quest. III. Is the word πρόνοια read in the canonical books?

The word πρόνοια is indeed read in the apocryphal book of Wisdom a), but not in the canonical books, in which divine providence is called the vision of God b). Proof. a) The author of Wisdom, chap. XIV, 3, says: Your providence, O Father, governs all things. The word, διακυβερνῶν, is nautical. For just as a shipmaster steers a ship so that it is not carried headlong into the rocks, so God rules men with His provident care, so that they are not broken by adverse things or completely overturned.

Proof. b) Abraham, committing the whole matter to divine providence, says: יהוה יראה, The Lord will see, Gen. XXII, 8.

The providence of God is called vision, not without emphasis, because God sees all things in one intuition. Foresight and foreknowledge are attributed to God only anthropopathos (in a human manner). Speaking properly, God foresees nothing, He foreknows nothing, since for Him nothing is future, but all things are most present, and thus He sees and beholds all things most presently from eternity: He is said to foresee only in respect to us, who are engaged in time, and measure things that happen in time according to before and after.

Quest. IV. In how many ways is the word providence taken? The word providence is taken in two ways: a) broadly, b) strictly.

Proof. a. Providence taken broadly comprises 1) πρόγνωσιν (prognosis), or foreknowledge, which is an act of the intellect by which God foreknows what is conducive to creatures. 2) Πρόθεσιν (prothesis), purpose, or decree, which is an act of the will by which God wills to order and dispose of what He has foreseen as conducive to creatures. 3) Διοίκησιν (dioikesis), the divine conservation and governance itself.

The providence of God, as πρόγνωσιν and πρόθεσιν, is an internal act of the divine intellect and will, as διοίκησιν it is an external action. *Prob. b. Strictly speaking, the providence of God is a divine action ad extra: for it is concerned with creatures, and is terminated outside the bosom of the deity.

In this stricter sense, the actual providence of God is the very preservation, cooperation, and governance of creatures; however, foreknowledge and the decree concerning things to be preserved and governed are presupposed as acts of the divine intellect directing and the will commanding.

Quest. V. From what principle is the providence of God known? The providence of God is known partly from the light of nature a), partly from the light of scripture b).

Prob. a. 1) From the creation of things, because once creation is posited, divine providence must necessarily be posited; without which created things cannot subsist.

Why would God create all things if He did not wish to take care of them? says THEODORET, lib. II. de prouid. Who would not feel that this world, perfected with such wonderful reason, is governed by some providence?

Since there is nothing that can subsist without any moderator.

If a house deserted by its inhabitant falls into ruin, a ship without a helmsman goes to destruction, and a body abandoned by the soul decays; much less should we think that such a great mass could either be constructed without an architect or stand for so long without a ruler, LACTANTIUS aptly says, lib. III. instit. cap. 19.

2) From the constant order of created things, which is observed in the fixed and perennial motion of the celestial spheres, in the certain vicissitude of seasons and weather, in the fertility of the earth, the perpetuity of rivers, the generation of diverse species: which order is preserved not by chance and fortune, but by God Himself, [*].

3) From [*] This illustrious document of divine providence is most worthy of accurate contemplation.

All the properties of the world, which both reason and experience teach us, must be considered.

Latin:

I. Quid est providentia divina? Providentia divina est actio Dei unitrini externa, qua is iuxta praescientiam intellectus sui infallibilem, & benignum voluntatis decretum, creaturas omnes potentissime conservat, cum operantibus efficacissime cooperatur, & omnia sapientissime gubernat ad nominis sui gloriam, & hominum, in primis piorum, utilitatem.

Quaest. II. Unde vox providentia deducitur? Providentia deducitur a providendo; pro, in compositione idem valet, quod prae, vel ante.

Prob. Auctor Lib. II. ad Herennium inquit: Providentia est, per quam futurum aliquod videtur, antequam fit.

Plus tamen ex usu loquendi infert providere, quam praevidere. Astrologus praevidet tempestatem adversam, nulla habita cura eorum, quos illa feriet; at providere, cum praevisione mentis sollicitam voluntatis curam notat. Sic & graeca vox πρόνοια est a προνοέω, quod significat, mente praecipio, praevideo, procuro.

Quaest. III. Num vox, πρόνοια, in libris canonicis legitur?

Vox πρόνοια legitur quidem in libro apocrypho sapientiae a), at non in libris canonicis, in quibus providentia divina vocatur visio Dei b). Prob. a) Auctor sapientiae, cap. XIV, 3. inquit: Tua, pater, providentia omnia gubernat. Verbum, διακυβερνῶν, nauticum est. Vt enim nauclerus gubernat navem, ne in scopulos praeceps feratur: ita Deus regit prouida sua cura homines, ne rebus aduersis frangantur, aut penitus euertantur.

Prob. b) Abrahamus, providentiae diuinae rem omnem committens, inquit: יהוה יראה, Dominus videbit, Gen. XXII, 8.

Providentia Dei dicitur visio, non sine emphasi, quia Deus vno intuitu omnia videt. Praevisio & praescientia Deo tantum tribuitur ἀνθρωποπαθῶς. Proprie loquendo Deus nil praevidet, nil praescit, cum ipsi nil sit futurum, sed omnia praesentissima, adeoque ab aeterno omnia praesentissime videat & intueatur: Praevidere solum dicitur respectu nostri, qui in tempore versamur, & res, quae in tempore fiunt, secundum prius & posterius mensuramus.

Quaest. IV. Quot modis sumitur vox providentia? Vox providentia duobus sumitur modis: a) late, b) stricte.

Prob. a. Late sumta providentia complectitur 1) πρόγνωσιν, seu praescientiam, quae est actus intellectus, quo Deus praecognoscit, quid creaturis fit conducibile. 2) Πρόθεσιν, propositum, sive decretum, quod est actus voluntatis, quo Deus, quae conducibilia creaturis praevidit, ordinare & disponere vult. 3) Διοίκησιν, ipsam conservationem & gubernationem diuinam.

Providentia Dei, qua πρόγνωσιν καὶ πρόθεσιν, est actus intellectus & voluntatis diuinae internus, qua διοίκησιν actio externa. *Prob. b. Stricte loquendo prouidentia Dei est actio diuina ad extra:.* versatur enim circa creaturas, & extra sinum deitatis terminatur.

Quo sensu strictiori actualis Dei prouidentia est ipsa conseruatio, cooperatio & gubernatio creaturarum; praescientia autem, & decretum de rebus conseruandis & gubernandis praesupponuntur, vt actus intellectus diuini dirigentis, & voluntatis imperantis.

Quaest. V. Ex quo principio innotescit prouidentia Dei? Prouidentia Dei cognoscitur partim ex lumine naturae a), partim ex lumine scripturae b).

Prob. a. 1) E rerum creatione, quia posita creatione, necessario ponenda est prouidentia diuina; sine qua res creatae consistere nequeunt.

Cur Deus res omnes procrearet, si curam earum nolit gerere? inquit THEODORET. lib. II. de prouid. Quis non sentiat hunc mundum, tam mirabili ratione perfectum, aliqua prouidentia gubernari?

Quandoquidem nihil est, quod possit sine ullo moderatore consistere.

Si domus ab habitatore deserta, delabitur, nauis sine gubernatore abit pessum, & corpus relictum ab anima defluit; nedum putemus, tantam illam molem aut construi sine artifice, aut stare tamdiu sine rectore potuisse, scite ait LACTANT. lib.

III. instit. cap. 19. 2) E rerum creatarum costante ordine, qui conspicitur in fixo & perenni motu orbium coelestium, in certa vicissitudine temporum & tempestatum, in foecunditate terrae, perennitate fluminum, generatione diuersarum specierum: qui ordo non casu & fortuna, sed ab ipso Deo conseruatur, [*].

3) Ex [*] Illustre hoc prouidentiae diuinae documentum accurata contemplatione dignissimum est.

Considerandae sunt omnes, quas & ratio, & experientia nos edocet, mundi proprietates.


### Q. XIII. What practical uses does: 1, The contingency of this universe

1, The contingency of this universe.

That is called contingent which can be, and not be, or be otherwise than it is.

It is not through itself, but through the will of its author and maker.

Its entire continuation also depends on the will of the maker.

As is the existence, as philosophers speak, so also is the whole nature of the thing, or essence.

The continuation of existence is called duration; we call the continuation of essence preservation.

By whose will a thing exists, by the same will it also endures and is preserved.

Also, whatever things pertain to the existence and essence of a thing in such a way that they cannot be separated from it, depend entirely on the will of that author, by whose most free will that thing both endures and is preserved.

To the essence of an animate body, endowed with reason, insofar as it is animate, belongs the power of moving itself; insofar as it is a participant in reason, the power of acting toward some certain end proposed to itself.

The power of moving itself, insofar as it depends on the will of another, is said to be sustained, and not without the most wise determination.

The power of acting, insofar as it depends on the will of another, is said to be governed.

The whole world, and whatever is animate in it, and whatever also possesses the use of reason, each and every one is always preserved in its essence by that author by whose most free will it first exists, always sustained and determined in its motion, and always governed in its action, to be directed toward a certain end.

These three, however—preservation, sustenance with arbitrary and wise determination, and governance—are what we comprehend under the one name of providence.

II. The harmony and agreement of all parts of the world, always the same and perpetual among so many and such great vicissitudes, at the same time the continuous coupling and succession of the most apt ends and means in individual things, even the smallest.

Which indeed openly indicates the most profound wisdom of the one and common author and moderator of all things.

III. The multitude and variety of things, especially human affairs, which all and each wonderfully agree toward one general end, namely, the utility and society of the whole human race.

Specifically, however, there are six indications of divine providence, to be weighed with the greatest attention of mind: 1) The diverse inclinations of minds toward various kinds of life and duties, partly the most lowly, which almost all men, though unjustly, hold in contempt, partly the most sordid, which all others loathe, partly the most dangerous, which all the rest fear,

3) From the omniscience, omnipotence, goodness, and omnipresence of the creator. If God, the founder of the world, did not provide for the reasons of created things, it would be either because he did not know them; or because he could not provide for them; or because he did not wish to; or because he was very far removed from them. The first detracts from divine omniscience, the second from omnipotence, the third from goodness, the fourth from omnipresence. Wherefore it is most validly concluded that the creator of this universe, being omniscient, omnipotent, most good, and omnipresent, provides most excellently and most wisely for the salvation of the things founded by him.

4) they fear, yet all things necessary for social life and the benefit of the commonwealth, to the choosing of which certain men are carried by a certain natural instinct, nay even by an impulse, and with this difference, that in no state or kind of life does there occur a lack of necessary things for men, or an abundance of superfluous ones. That that propensity, and most valid inclination of the will, naturally implanted and innate in man, is not to be attributed to parents alone as the cause, is apparent from this: that (α) it often happens that offspring is both most prompt and most apt for that duty and kind of life from which its parents were far removed, and from which they even greatly abhorred: that (β) the admirable proportion of so many and so varied propensities, and the order of them all, and their conjunction with the common salvation of the whole human race, demonstrates one and a common cause. And not even that must be passed over in silence, that with men multiplied, the arts also have been multiplied and increased by things discovered by us.

2) The distinction of forms and faces. How great a benefit this is, and with how wise a counsel it was bestowed upon us, the ancient NEMESIUS taught excellently, whose excerpted words were given by the blessed BUDDEUS, in his instit. theol. dogm. L. II. c. 2. §. 43. not. * 3) The entirely unexpected uncovering of clandestine crimes, and those hidden by the utmost study of cunning and astuteness, and not without a wonderful conjunction of surrounding circumstances. Which argument the aforementioned NEMESIUS also pursued. But the most weighty importance and strength is added to this argumentation by the fact that from that uncovering of crimes the punishment of retaliation shines forth. Which thing is a manifest document that a most just as well as most wise Divinity presides over human affairs. Men are to be reproved, whose lightness of mind is so shameful and insane that they do not wish to turn their own mind to knowing the divine judgments, Ps. XXVIII, 5.

4) The closest coherence of those things which happen to man as auspicious and fortunate, since indeed all things are connected and fitted among themselves, so that experience perpetually illustrates this most true adage: πάντα συνεργεῖ εἰς ἀγαθόν. Rom. VIII, 28. 5) The direction of most bitter calamities toward a salutary outcome. Genes. L, 20. 6) New events, and not only the rarest, such as plague and famine, but also those entirely singular, which, if they proceeded from natural causes alone, without a provident ruler and moderator, could not but happen more often and return in a cycle. They provide us with a clear example in the conversions and subversions of commonwealths, which grew from a thin beginning in a wonderful manner, but the greater increments they took, the more they were inclined, and the closer they were to destruction. But the destruction of the Jewish land and nation is entirely singular. An unheard-of fate, to which there has never been any like, nor will there be in the future, which can be compared and likened to it, Matth. XXIV, 21. From which it is simultaneously known with how close a bond the things done in the kingdom of nature are connected with those things which pertain to the kingdom of grace; for since the promises and benefits, entirely singular and preeminent, by which the Jewish nation was distinguished from all others, pertained to Christ who was to come, and was rejected by that nation, and since the Jews were contaminated with a certain singular sin: therefore they also endured a singular calamity themselves.

These indeed are the most evident documents, from which it is concluded that the providence of God not only exists, but also is never absent from all created things, nor was occupied only in the first constitution. 'God works ἕως ἄρτι, Ioann. V, 17. Christ pronounced this with that intent, that he might teach his hearers that σάββατον, the quiet of God, pertains not to all external works, but only to the works of the first creation. God has indeed ceased to create, that is, to bring forth new genera of things and new species: but he will never cease to preserve, sustain, and govern created and propagated things, διδὸς adhuc πᾶσι ζωήν, καὶ πνοήν, καὶ τὰ πάντα. Act. XVII, 25.

4) From the dictate of conscience, which presents God as a severe judge, and thus exhibits the providence of God in respect to those things which are done by men. Hence it is that, after crimes have been committed, even those feel terrors in their conscience who have no man privy to their misdeeds, or who do not acknowledge any superior on earth whom they might fear. Therefore, those struck by the lashes of conscience testify that there is a superior God in heaven who takes care of those things which are done by them.

Prob. b. The whole of Holy Scripture is nothing other than a clear mirror, from which, wherever you turn, that ever-watchful eye of providential direction shines forth; since the keeper of Israel never sleeps, Ps. CXXI.

4. Concerning the preserving providence of God, the sacred psalmist testifies in Ps. XXXVI, 7: You save man and beast, O Jehovah!

By these words he teaches that divine providence is occupied not only with creatures endowed with intellect, angels and men, but also with those devoid of reason, namely beasts, which God preserves by averting harmful things from them and bestowing all the most useful things. St. Paul asserts the co-operating providence of God in Acts XVII, 27, 28: God is not far from each one of us: for in Him we live, and move, and have our being. God, filling all things in all, is present to all creatures by the presence of His power, to faithful men by the presence of His grace, to angels and blessed men by the presence of His glory; but there is no presence of God that is not efficacious or active. Therefore the apostle says: in Him we live, as an embryo in its mother's womb; in Him we move, as ships in the sea; in Him we are, as birds in the air, fish in the river.

But in Him in whom we live, move, and have our being, He co-operates with us as we work. (3) Jeremiah teaches the governing providence of God, ch. X, 23: I know, O Jehovah, that the way of man is not (in himself), nor is it in man to walk, or to establish his own step. The prophet implies that the counsels and actions of men are indeed advanced by the freedom of human will, but they are subject to divine providence, by reason of government and direction toward a certain end.

Latin:

1, Contingentia huius vniuersi.

Contingens vocatur id, quod potest esse, & non esse, aut aliter esse, quam est.

E, non per se est, sed per voluntatem auctoris sui atque effectoris.

E, etiam continuatio eius tota ex effectoris pendet arbitrio.

Qualis existentia est, vt philosophi loquuntur, talis quoque est tota natura rei, siue essentia.

Continuatio existentiae nominatur duratio, continuationem essentiae adpellamus conseruationem.

E, cuius voluntate res aliqua existit, eiusdem voluntate eadem & durat, & conseruatur.

E, etiam ea, quaecunque tum ad existentiam rei, tum ad essentiam ita pertinent, vt ab ea separari nequeant, omnino pendent ex arbitrio eius auctoris, cuius liberrima voluntate res illa & durat, & conseruatur.

Ad essentiam corporis animati, simul ratione prediti, quatenus id quidem animatum est, pertinet vis se ipsum mouendi; quatenus vero rationis est particeps, vis agendi, ad certum aliquem finem, sibi propositum.

Vis semet mouendi, quoad ea quidem ex alterius arbitrio pendet, dicitur sustentari, nec sine sapientissima determinatione.

Vis agendi, quoad ea ex alterius arbitrio pendet, dicitur gubernari.

E, mundus vniuersus, & quidquid in eo animatum est, quidquid etiam rationis vsu pollet, id, vnumquodque ab eo auctore, cuius liberrima voluntate primum existit, semper conseruatur in sua essentia, semper sustentatur ac determinatur in sua motione, semper etiam gubernatur in sua actione, ad certum quendam finem dirigenda.

Haec autem tria, conseruatio, sustentatio, cum arbitraria ac sapiente determinatione, & gubernatio, sunt, quae vno nomine prouidentia comprehendimus.

II. Harmonia & conuenientia omnium mundi partium, inter tot ac tantas vicissitudines semper eadem ac perpetua, simul finium ac mediorum aptissimorum in rebus singulis, ac vel minimis, continua copulatio & successio.

Quae profecto sapientiam vnius & communis omnium auctoris ac moderatoris profundissimam aperte indicat.

III. Multitudo ac varietas rerum, praesertim vero humanarum, quae vniuersae ac singulae ad vnum finem generalem, nimirum ad vtilitatem societatemque vniuersi hominum generis, mire consentiunt.

Speciatim vero sex sunt indicia prouidentiae diuinae, maxima animi attentione perpendenda: 1) Diuersae animorum propensiones ad varia vitae genera atque munera, partim vilissima, quae homines plerique omnes, tametsi iniuria, despicatui ducunt, partim sordidissima, quae omnes alii fastidiunt, partim periculosissima, quae omnes reliqui reformidant,

3) Ex omniscientia, omnipotentia, bonitate & omnipraesentia creatoris. Si Deus, conditor orbis, rerum creatarum rationibus non prospiceret, vel ideo non prospiceret, quod eas non cognosceret; vel quod iis prospicere non posset; vel quod non vellet; vel quod ab iisdem longissime abesset. Primum detrahit omniscientiae divinae, secundum omnipotentiae, tertium bonitati, quartum omnipraesentiae. Quare validissime colligitur, quod creator huius vniversi omnisciens, omnipotens, optimus, & omnipraesens, rerum a se conditarum saluti optime & sapientissime consulat.

4) E formidant, omnia tamen ad vitam socialem reique publicae commodum necessaria, ad quae eligenda quidam homines naturali quodam instinctu, immo & impetu feruntur, & cum ea quidem differentia, vt nullo in statu, aut vitae genere, vel defectus necessariorum hominum fit, vel abundantia superuacaneorum. Illam vero propensionem, ac validissimam voluntatis inclinationem, naturaliter homini insitam atque innatam, non solis parentibus, tamquam causae, adferendam esse, adparet ex eo: quod (α) saepe numero accidit, vt progenies & promptissima sit, & aptissima ad illud munus ac vitae genus, a quo longe alienissimi fuerunt parentes eius, a quo etiam illi maxime abhorruerunt: quod (β) admirabilis proportio tot, tamque variarum propensionum, earúmque omnium & ordo, & coniunctio cum salute communi vniversi hominum generis, vnam & communem caussam demonstrat. Ac ne illud quidem silentio transeundum est, quod multiplicatis hominibus multiplicatae quoque fuerint artes, ac nobis repertis auctae.

2) Formarum ac facierum distinctio. Quae quantum sit beneficium, & quam sapiente consilio nobis tributum, egregie docuit inter veteres NEMESIVS, cuius verba excerpta dedit b. BVDDEVS, in suis instit. theol. dogm. L. II. c. 2. §. 43. not. * 3) Facinorum clandestinorum, & summo calliditatis astutiaeque studio occultatorum patefactio prorsus inopinata, nec fine mira rerum circumstantium coniunctione. Quod argumentum itidem laudatus NEMESIVS persequutus est. Grauissimum autem huic argumentationi pondus ac robur additur eo, quod ex illa delictorum patefactione poena talionis elucet. Quae res manifesto documento est, inflissimum aeque, ac sapientissimum Numen rebus humanis praeesse. Arguendi sunt homines, quorum tam turpis ac vesana est leuitas animi, vt mentem ipsi aduertere nolint ad iudicia divina cognoscenda, Ps. XXVIII, 5.

4) Eorum, quae homini fausta ac fortunata accidunt, artissima cohaerentia, quando quidem omnia inter se connexa atque apta sunt, vt experientia perpetuo illustret verissimum hoc effatum: πάντα συνεργεῖ εἰς ἀγαθόν. Rom. VIII, 28. 5) Calamitatum acerbissimarum, ad euentum salutare directio. Genes. L, 20. 6) Casus noui, nec solum rarissimi, vt pestis & annona, verum etiam plane singulares, qui, si a caussis tantum naturalibus, fine prouido rectore ac moderatore, proficiscerentur, non possent non saepius euenire atque in orbem redire. Luculentum nobis exemplum praebent conuersiones atque euersiones rerum publicarum, quae a tenui initio mirandum in modum creuerunt, sed quo maiora ceperunt incrementa, eo magis fuerunt inclinatae, eoque propius ab interitu abfuerunt. Prorsus autem singulare est exitium terrae gentisque Iudaicae. Fatum inauditum, cui nullum vnquam fuit simile, nec erit in posterum, quod cum illo conferri & comparari queat, Matth. XXIV, 21. Ex quo simul cognoscitur, quam arcto vinculo res gestae in regno naturae connexae sint cum iis rebus, quae ad regnum gratiae spectant; quoniam enim promissiones ac beneficia, prorsus singularia, atque eximia, quibus Iudaica gens ab omnibus aliis discernebatur, ad Christum pertinebant venturum, atque ab ea gente repudiatum, & quoniam singulari quodam peccato Iudaei contaminati sunt: idcirco etiam singularem ipsi calamitatem sunt perpessi.

Haec profecto sunt euidentissima documenta, ex quibus efficitur, prouidentiam Dei non modo esse, verum etiam rebus creatis omnibus nunquam non adesse, nec solum in prima constitutione occupatam fuisse. 'Deus operatur ἕως ἄρτι, Ioann. V, 17. Id Christus pronuntiavit ea mente, vt doceret auditores, σάββατον, quietem Dei non ad omnia opera externa, sed dumtaxat ad opera primae creationis pertinere. Desiit quidem Deus creare, hoc est, noua rerum genera nouasque species efficere: at nunquam definet, res creatas & propagatas conseruare, sustentare, gubernare, διδὸς adhuc πᾶσι ζωήν, καὶ πνοήν, καὶ τὰ πάντα. Act. XVII, 25.

4) E dictamine conscientiae, quae Deum sistit ut severum iudicem, adeoque providentiam Dei exhibet respectu eorum, quae ab hominibus fiunt. Vnde est, quod post commissa flagitia etiam illi in conscientia terrores sentiant, qui vel hominem conscium suorum facinorum habent nullum, vel superiorem in terris, quem metuant, non agnoscunt. Testantur igitur verberibus conscientiae caesi, superiorem esse in coelis Deum, qui curam gerat eorum, quae ab ipsis fiunt.

Prob. b. Tota sacra scriptura nihil aliud est, quam pellucidum speculum, e quo, quocunque te vertas, promicat peruigil ille oculus prouidae directionis; siquidem custos Israel nunquam dormit, Ps. CXXI.

4. De prouidentia Dei conferuatrice testatur hieropsaltes Ps. XXXVI, 7. Hominem & bestiam seruas, o Iehouah!

Quibus verbis docet, pro-noeam diuinam occupari non tantum circa creaturas intellectu praeditas, angelos & homines, sed & rationes expertes, nempe bestias, quas Deus seruat, noxia ab iis auertendo, & vtilissima quaeque conferendo. Prouidentiam Dei cooperatricem asserit S. Paullus Act. XVII, 27. 28. Non procul abest Deus ab vnoquoque nostrum: In ipso enim viuimus, mouemur & sumus. Deus, omnia in omnibus implens, cunctis adest creaturis praesentia potentiae, hominibus fidelibus praesentia gratiae, angelis & hominibus beatis praesentia gloriae; sed nulla praesentia Dei non est efficax, aut operosa. Idcirco inquit apostolus: in ipso viuimus, vt embryo in vtero matris, in ipso mouemur, vt naues in mari, in ipso sumus, vt aues in aere, pisces in flumine.

At in quo viuimus, mouemur & sumus, ille nobiscum operantibus cooperatur. (3) Prouidentiam Dei gubernatricem docet Ieremias, c. X, 23. Noui Iehouah, quod non (fit) homini via eius, nec viro ambulare, aut firmare gressum suum. Innuit propheta, quod consilia & actiones hominum proficiantur quidem a libertate voluntatis humanae, subiaceant autem pronae diuinae, ratione gubernationis & directionis ad certum finem.


### Q. XIII. What practical uses does: The antithesis is that of the Atheists, who deny the providence of God, whose arguments are: I

The antithesis is that of the Atheists, who deny the providence of God, whose arguments are: I.

God does not care for oxen, 1 Cor. IX, 9. Therefore divine providence does not provide for the salvation of all. Resp. The words of Paul are not to be taken absolutely, as if he entirely withdrew oxen from the care of divine government. Scripture asserts the contrary, Ps. XXXVI, 7; CXLVII, 9. But comparatively, that primary care is not taken by God for oxen, but for men. The apostle brings forward the divine precept about not muzzling oxen, because of the general reason of the law, which is: The means of life are not to be denied to those who labor. From which he teaches us to conclude: If the mouth of the threshing ox is not to be bound, much less are the foods of life to be withheld from the ministers of the divine word who are performing their duty. For God does not take care of oxen only, or chiefly, but He takes the greatest account of faithful men, among whom the ministers of the church are not the least.

II. If the providence of God were occupied with all created things, there would be no defect in natural things: The consequent is false: Therefore, the antecedent is also. The consequence of the major is evident; because God, being most perfect, acts in the most perfect way. Therefore, if God co-operates with working creatures, no imperfect thing can be produced. The falsity of the consequent is manifest: For every day monstrous, blind, deaf, lame, etc., men are generated. Resp. The defects of created things are not to be ascribed to God, but to particular causes; for these, either destitute of sufficient strength, or hindered by an object as if by a brake, did not produce a perfect work. Yet such effects, produced with a defect, are not entirely withdrawn from divine providence, since they do not happen without the general concurrence of God.

III. God rested from His works, Gen. II, 2. Therefore no care of God watches over them. Resp. Rest is said of God not simply, but in a certain sense and in a certain respect. God rested from founding the world, from creating new species; He did not rest from preservation and government. of created things, He did not cease from propagating the individuals of the species. Nay, rather, rest is spoken of differently regarding God, and differently regarding man. Man rests either weary from laboring, or sleeping from sloth. God rests by acting, and acts by resting.

IV. If all men were the care of God, He would surely grant more prosperous successes to the pious than to the impious: But experience speaks the contrary. Resp. (1) One must judge concerning the prosperous successes of things not from the dictate of blind reason, but from the Word of God. What seems to many to be the chief part of happiness is not rarely a path made ready for them to hell. On the contrary, the calamity of this age is for many a mother of prayers, a training ground for patience, fortitude, and constancy, and an expeller of vices. He who suffers in the flesh ceases from sin. (2) Distinguish between the beginning, the middle, and the end of successes. Let us not estimate the beginnings or the courses of successes, but let us look to their end and outcome. The evil man is reserved for the day of destruction: he is led forth to the day of wrath.

V. If the providence of God governed all things, no place would be left for chance or fortune. But that much place is left to chance and fortune, Solomon ingenuously confesses. Time and chance happen to them all. Resp. (1) Providence excludes chance in the order of universal cause; for to its directing foreknowledge and commanding will, all things are subject: But not in the order of particular cause; inasmuch as it can disturb or deflect something in acting, so that the desired event does not respond to the undertakings, e.g., a killing is called fortuitous with respect to the woodcutter, from whom the iron fell, but not with respect to God, who caused the man to meet the one killed into the hand of the slayer. (2) In the Hebrew there is the word פגע, which properly denotes an occasion or an encounter, and thus the sense is: The occasion for a thing to be done according to one's wish does not always give itself to us at hand, but it is provided for us by God, in whose hand is both the occasion and the outcome of the occasion.

VI. It is absurd to reduce the majesty of God to this, that He should know by individual moments how many gnats are born, or how many die, or what the multitude of fleas and flies is, or how many fish swim in the waters, says HIERONYM. in Habakkuk ch. I. Resp. (1) Let Jerome, a most learned father, be excused, because he speaks of successive and discursive knowledge, by which what was previously unknown is known successively through individual moments, whereas God knows and penetrates all things in one act infallibly. (2) But if Jerome has absolutely denied that the providence of God extends to the vilest things, we do not stand on his side. Indeed, not only the hairs of our head, but also lice are subject to divine care.

Latin:

Antithesis est Atheorum, prouidentiam Dei negantium, quorum argumenta sunt:. I.

Deo boues non sunt curae, 1 Cor. IX, 9. Ergo prouidentia diuina non omnium saluti consulit. Resp. Verba Paulli non sunt accipienda absolute, quasi prorsus subtrahat boues a cura gubernationis diuinae. Contrarium asserit scriptura, Ps. XXXVI, 7. CXLVII, 9. Sed comparate, quod cura primaria Deo non fit de bobus, sed de hominibus. Adducit apostolus praeceptum diuinum de non capistrandis bobus, ob generalem legis rationem, quae est: Laborandi vitae subsidia non sunt deneganda. Ex qua concludere nos docet: Si boui triturani os obdurandum non est: multo minus verbi diuini ministris, officium suum facientibus, alimenta vitae subtrahenda sunt. Neque enim boum curam Deus gerit tantum, aut praecipue, sed potissimam ducit rationem hominum fidelium, quos inter haud postremi sunt antistites ecclesiae.

II. Si prouidentia Dei circa res omnes creatas occupata esset, non daretur defectus vllus in rebus naturalibus: Consequens est falsum: E. & antecedens. Consequentia maioris patet; quia Deus perfectissimus modo perfectissimo agit. Proinde si Deus cum operantibus creaturis cooperatur, nullum imperfectum produci potest. Falsitas consequentis manifesta est: Quotidie enim generantur homines monstrosi, coeci, surdi, claudi &c. Resp. Defectus rerum creatarum non Deo, sed causis particularibus sunt adscribendi; quippe quae vel viribus sufficientibus destitutae, vel obiecto quasi sufflamine impeditae, opus perfectum non produxerunt. Neque tamen eiusmodi effectus, cum defectu producti, plane subducuntur prouidentiae diuinae, cum non fiant sine concursu Dei generali.

III. Deus quieuit ab operibus suis, Gen. II, 2. Ergo pro ipsis cura Dei nulla excubat. Resp. Quies dicitur de Deo non simpliciter, sed secundum quid, & certo respectu. Quieuit Deus a condendo mundo, a creandis nouis speciebus, non quieuit a conseruatione & gubernatione rerum creatarum, non cessavit a propagandis specierum individuis. Quin immo quies aliter de Deo, aliter de homine dicitur. Quiescit homo vel fessus laborando, vel desidia indormiens. Deus agendo quiescit, quiescendo agit.

IV. Si Deo curae essent omnes homines, utique prosperiores successus largiretur piis, quam impiis: At contrarium loquitur experientia. Resp. (1) De prosperis rerum successibus non ex caecae rationis dictamine, sed verbo Dei iudicandum est. Quae multis videtur esse praecipua pars felicitatis, haud raro ipsis expedita ad orcum est via. Contra calamitas huius saeculi multis est mater precum, patientiae, fortitudinis, constantiae palaestra, vitiorum expultrix. Qui patitur carne, abstinet a peccato. (2) Dist. inter successus initium, medium, & finem. Non initia, non decursus successuum aestimemus, sed eorum finem & exitum respiciamus. In diem interitus reservatur malus: in diem irarum ducitur.

V. Si providentia Dei omnia regeret, nihil loci relictum foret casui, aut fortunae. Sed plurimum loci casui & fortunae relictum esse, ingenue fatetur Salomo. Tempus & casus contingit omnibus. Resp. (1) Providentia excludit casum in ordine causae universalis; quippe cuius praescientiae dirigenti, & voluntati imperanti, omnia sunt subiecta: Sed non in ordine causae particularis; vtpote quam in agendo aliquid turbare aut inflectere potest, vt coeptis optatus non respondeat euentus, v. g. Caedes dicitur fortuita, respectu lignifissoris, cui ferrum excidit, non autem respectu Dei, qui occurrere fecit virum occisum in manum occidentis. (2) In hebraeo est vocabulum, פגע quod proprie notat occasionem, vel occursum, adeoque sensus est: Non semper ad manum se nobis dat occasio rei ex voto gerendae, sed illa nobis praebetur a Deo, in cuius manu & occasio, & occasionis euentus est.

VI. Absurdum est, ad hoc deducere Dei maiestatem, vt sciat per momenta singula, quot culices nascantur, quotue moriantur, quota pulicum & muscarum fit multitudo, quotue pisces natent in aquis, ait HIERONYM. in Habacuci cap. I. Resp. (1) Excusetur Hieronymus, pater doctissimus, quod loquatur de successiva & discursiva notitia, qua per singula momenta successiue cognoscatur id, quod erat antea ignotum, cum Deus vno actu omnia infallibiliter cognoscat & penetret. (2) Quod si Hieronymus absolute negauerit, providentiam Dei ad vilissima quaeque extendi, ab eius partibus non stamus. Subsunt sane curae diuinae non tantum capilli capitis nostri, sed & pediculi.


### Quest. VI. Who is the Lord looking out for all created things?

The Lord, preserving and governing all created things by His providential care, is God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Prob. a. The inspector, preserver, and governor of this world is the Creator. For just as creation is a work of infinite power: so to preserve and govern the created world is of infinite virtue, goodness, and wisdom. Appositely says ANSELM, in Monolog.: Just as nothing was made except through the creative essence of God: so nothing thrives except through His preserving power, citing D. GERHARD, in disput. isagog. p. 647.

Prob. b. John V, 17. My Father is working until now, and I also am working. The Savior implies that God the Father, from the first creation down to this very day, works effectively and continuously, by sustaining creatures, by supplying them with suitable powers, and by influencing their actions. Therefore, since the divine essence is the same, and the power of the Father and the Son is the same, the Son of God is also assiduously occupied in promoting the advantages of creatures, especially of men.

Prob. c. The Son of God upholds all things by the word of his power, Hebr. 1: 3. The Son of God is the divine person upholding, as he who was previously called the brightness of glory and the character of the Father's person; to whom, in the words immediately following, the cleansing of sins is attributed. The context therefore teaches that the Son of God upholds all things. Φέρειν among the Greeks signifies as much to uphold as to act, or to move. Wherefore by this emphatic word, both the sustaining and the governing of all created things is indicated. The apostle adds that the Son of God upholds, acts, and moves all things by the word of his power, i.e., by his nod, command, and authority, by which all things are nourished and live, Matth. 4: 4. Prob. d. Concerning the Holy Spirit, 1 Cor. 12:11, it is said that he distributes spiritual gifts for the preservation and government of the church; which is special providence. Concerning general providence, that saying of David is to be understood: Ps. 104: 30. Thou shalt send forth thy spirit and they shall be created. The creator Spirit, who at the beginning of creation moved himself over the face of the waters, Gen. 1:2, continually creates, i.e., preserves creatures; since preservation is a certain continuous creation.

Latin:

Dominus, prouida sua cura omnia creata conservans & gubernans, est Deus , Pater , Filius , & Spiritus S. .

Prob. a. Creator mundi huius inspector, conservator & gubernator est. Vt enim creatio est opus infinitae potentiae: ita mundum creatum conservare & gubernare, infinitae virtutis, bonitatis & sapientiae est. Apposite inquit ANSHELMVS, in monolog. Sicut nihil factum est, nisi per essentiam Dei creatricem: ita nihil viget, nisi per potentiam ipsius servatricem, citante D. GERHARDO, in disput. isagog. p. 647.

Prob. b. Io. V, 17. Pater meus vsque nunc operatur; ideo etiam ego operor. Innuit Saluator, Deum Patrem inde a prima creatione in hunc vsque diem efficaciter & continuo operari, creaturas sustentando, congruas ipsis vires sufficiendo, & in ipsarum actiones influendo. Ideo cum sit eadem essentia diuina, eadem vis Patris & Filii, etiam Filius Dei circa creaturarum, inprimis hominum commoda promovenda assidue occupatur. promouenda affidue occupatur. promouenda affidue occupatur.

Prob. c. Filius Dei omnia portat verbo virtutis suae, Hebr. I, 3. Persona divina portans est Filius Dei, vt qui antea dicebatur splendor gloriae & character personae Patris; cui verbis proxime sequentibus tribuitur mundatio peccatorum. Docet igitur contextus, Filium Dei omnia portare. Φέρειν apud Graecos tam portare, quam agere, seu mouere significat. Quare hoc verbo emphatico tum sustentatio, tum gubernatio rerum omnium creatarum indicatur. Addit apostolus, quod Filius Dei omnia portet, agat ac moueat, verbo virtutis suae. i. e. nutu, iussu ac imperio suo, quo aluntur & viuunt omnia, Matth. IV, 4. Prob. d. De Spiritu S. 1 Cor. XII, 11. dicitur, quod distribuat dona spiritualia ad conseruationem & gubernationem ecclesiae; quae est prouidentia specialis. De prouidentia generali intelligendum est illud effatum Dauidis: Ps. CIV, 30. Emittes spiritum tuum & creabuntur. Spiritus creator, qui sub primordium creationis sese mouit super faciem aquarum, Gen. I, 2. continuo creat, i. e. conseruat creaturas; cum conseruatio sit continua quaedam creatio.


### Quaest. VII. To what things does God provide?

God provides for all creatures , the greatest , and the least .

Obs. 1. God himself does not pertain to the object of divine providence. For the providence of God is an action ad extra, which is performed outside the bounds of the deity, and is terminated upon creatures. Add that the object of divine providence is everything that can be preserved and governed. But God is not preservable; because he can neither perish, nor depend upon a superior preserving cause: nor is he governable; for the governing cause is superior and wiser, such as God does not acknowledge.

Obs. 2. The object of divine providence can be distinguished into general and special. The general object of divine providence is the whole system of the world, and all creatures contained therein, which are heaped with the temporal benefits of God. The special object is the church of God, both militant, or the assembly of faithful men, and triumphant, or the assembly of angels and blessed men, enjoying the spiritual and eternal benefits of God.

Conf. D. GERHARD, disput. isagog. p. 653. Prob. a. From Gen. 1: 31. Then God saw everything that he had made, and behold it was very good. As widely as the divine eye extends itself, seeing the goodness of creatures; so widely does divine providence extend itself. But it extends itself to all and singular creatures: Therefore this also. The reason for the consequence is that to see the goodness of creatures is an act of divine providence.

Prob. b. The most noble and greatest of creatures are angels and men, created originally after the image of divine wisdom and holiness. God commands the good angels, Ps. 91:11, and sends them forth for his ministries, Hebr. 1:14, who themselves shall also minister in the resurrection of the dead, and the citation to judgment, 1 Thess. 4:16. Therefore God governs them by his providence. God puts bridles upon evil angels, Job 1:12, and loosens them, Matth. 8:31. Therefore evil angels also are subject to the divine government. The most benign God takes account of men, both good and evil. For he makes his sun to rise upon the evil and the good, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust, Matth. 5:45. Yet he consults primarily for the salvation of faithful men. For he is the savior of all, especially of the faithful, 1 Tim. 4:10. The church, therefore, or the assembly of the faithful, is ruled, preserved, and adorned with spiritual gifts by God in a special manner.

Prob. c. The most wise care of God, the thrice-best, does not neglect even the least creatures. For he provides for ravens, Ps. 147:9, for sparrows, Matth. 10:29, for lice, Exod. 8:13, for lilies and grass, Matth. 6:28, 30, he moderates the waters, rains, winds, and lightnings, Job 28:25, 26.

produces grain, must, and oil from the earth, Hos. 2:32. He has the stars in number, Ps. 147:4. the hairs, Matt. 10:30. and our tears, Ps. 56:9.

Latin:

Prospicit Deus omnibus creaturis , maximis , & minimis .

Obs. 1. Ad obiectum prouidentiae diuinae non pertinet Deus ipse. Etenim prouidentia Dei est actio ad extra, quae extra sinum deitatis peragitur, & ad creaturas terminatur. Adiice, quod obiectum prouidentiae diuinae sit omne conseruabile & gubernabile. At Deus non est conseruabilis; quia nec interire, nec a causa superiori conseruante dependere potest: nec est gubernabilis; causa enim gubernans est superior & sapientior, qualem Deus non agnoscit.

Obs. 2. Obiectum prouidentiae diuinae distingui potest in generale, & speciale. Obiectum generale prouidentiae diuinae est totum mundi systema, & omnes in eo contentae creaturae, quae temporalibus Dei beneficiis cumulantur. Obiectum speciale est ecclesia Dei tam militans, siue coetus hominum fidelium, quam triumphans, siue coetus angelorum, & beatorum hominum, spiritualibus & aeternis Dei beneficiis perfruens.

Conf. D. GERHARDI disput. isagog. p. 653. Prob. a. E Gen. I. 31. Tum vidit Deus omne, quod fecit, & ecce bonum erat valde. Quam late se extendit oculus diuinus, videns bonitatem creaturarum; tam late se porrigit prouidentia diuina. At ille se extendit ad vniuersas & singulas creaturas: Ergo & haec. Ratio consequentiae est, quia videre bonitatem creaturarum est actus prouidentiae diuinae.

Prob. b. Creaturarum nobilissimae & maximae sunt angeli & homines, primitus ad exemplar sapientiae & sanctitatis diuinae conditi. Angelis bonis Deus mandat, Ps. XCI, 11. eosque ad ministeria sua emittit, Hebr. I, 14. qui ipsi etiam ministrabunt in resuscitatione mortuorum, & citatione ad iudicium, 1 Thess. IV, 16. Ergo Deus illos prouidentia sua gubernat. Angelis malis Deus fraena iniicit, Iob. I, 12. & laxat, Matth. VIII, 31. Ergo & angeli mali regimini diuino subiacent. Hominum tam bonorum, quam malorum rationem habet Deus benignissimus. Nam solem suum exoriri facit super malos & bonos, & pluuiam mittit super iustos & iniustos, Matth. V, 45. Hominum tamen fidelium saluti inprimis consulit. Est enim seruator omnium, maxime fidelium, 1 Tim. IV, 10. Ecclesia igitur, seu coetus fidelium, speciali ratione a Deo regitur, conseruatur, & spiritualibus donis ornatur.

Prob. c. Sapientissima Dei ter optimi cura ne minimas quidem creaturas negligit. Prospicit enim coruis, Ps. CXLVII, 9. passeribus, Matth. X, 29. pediculis, Exod. VIII, 13. liliis & gramini, Matth. VI, 28. 30. moderatur aquas, pluuias, ventos & fulgura, Iob. XXVIII, 25. 26.

producit e terra frumentum, mustum & oleum, Hos. II, 32. in numerato habet stellas, Ps. CXLVII, 4. capillos,


### Question VIII. How does the providence of God moderate the life of men?

The providence of God moderates the ingress , progress , and egress of human life. Prob.

a. Prob. a. The ingress of human life embraces both formation and preservation in the mother's womb, and extraction from the womb. The most pious Job ascribes the formation of the embryo and its preservation in the womb to God, ch. X, 8. 9. 10. 11. 12. Your hands have formed me and made me; and indeed at once all around, and yet you consume me. Remember, I pray, that like clay you have made me, and you will bring me back into dust. Did you not pour me out like milk, and curdle me like cheese into shape? And you clothed me with flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews. You have granted me life and kindness: and your watchfulness has kept my spirit. Obs. (1) God is said to form man in the mother's womb not exclusively, as though the womb itself were excluded, or the plastic power of the soul, or the menstrual blood, or other causes; but since all natural causes lie subject to God, and he acts through these, he is rightly said to form and preserve us in the womb, (2) Job skillfully delineates the ingress of his own life. For he credits it to the hands of God, by which he understands the creative power of God; for God creates through parents generating. He compares his formation in the womb now with the shaping of clay, now with the curdling of milk, now with the putting on of a garment, intending to express his humble origin indeed, but the sublime action of God. That he lives his life and draws breath, he holds to depend entirely on the constant vision of God, with paternal care and guardianship, cf. Ps. CXXXIX, 14. 15. 16. Concerning extraction from the mother's womb the royal prophet testifies, Ps. XXXI, 6: Out of the bowels of my mother you are my deliverer, that is, You acted as it were in the place of a midwife, and loosed me from my maternal bonds. Or: You yourself so guided the midwife's hands, lest anything be harmed in my tender infancy, but that I might come forth unharmed into these airs.

Prob. b. God moderates the progress of life by bestowing the nourishment of life, Ps. 145:6. by directing our steps, i.e., by advancing counsels, undertakings, and deeds to desired outcomes, Ps. 37:23. by repelling the snares of enemies, or open force from us, Ps. 3:8, 9. by fitting and calling us to a certain kind of life, Jer. 1:5, 6, 7.

Prob. c. God infallibly foreknows the term, or egress, of life. (1) This is what the Psalmist indicates, Ps. 139:16. "Your eyes saw my embryo; and in your book all the days were written, which were destined, when not one of them yet existed." God infallibly knows our embryo, i.e., the formless mass from which we were formed in our mother's womb. He also foreknew all the future days of our life, destined for us by divine appointment for the enjoyment of this light.
