But him whom all the days of our life do not escape, neither does the last hour of living deceive. (2) God preordained and established the term of life. This Job teaches, ch. XIV, 5. "If his days are defined; the number of his months is with you: You have made his appointments, and he shall not transgress them." By which words it is signified that certain days of living have been defined for man by God, and that the number of months has been established by reason of prescience and the divine decree, which man cannot transgress. The term of life has been prefixed, however, by a decree not absolute, preceding or excluding all secondary causes, but by a hypothetical and ordered decree, founded in secondary causes, and formed according to their condition. Namely, by common and ordinary law God establishes for man a physical, or natural, term of life, according to the nature and temperament of each man. We prove our assertion (a) because God, just as he foreknows from eternity what nature each one is going to receive from his parents by the natural force of generation, and how far he will prolong life according to the order of nature with his general concurrence, so also from eternity he established that secondary causes should yield only such influx as is indeed owed to them by the law of nature, until they reach the term set by nature reach the determined point, and natural powers fail.

For this is the principle of divine providence, that it does not overturn the common course of nature and the order of secondary causes and their powers of acting, but preserves them, and provides its own influx to them, congruent and proportionate to the powers and nature of each. As often as Holy Scripture promises the prolongation of life to the followers of piety, but threatens the abbreviation of the same to the impious: it indicates that God has established a term of life for man according to his nature and temperament.

For to prolong life is to extend it beyond the established term, and to abbreviate the same is to anticipate the established term.

Where by established term nothing else can be understood than that which nature itself, with the general concurrence of God, established by common law. The example of King Hezekiah proves the same, whose term of life, when he was sick, the prophet Isaiah, by God's command, announced to be at hand: Set in order, he said, thy house, for thou shalt die, and not live, Is.

38:2. Where without doubt death was predicted to be imminent for him in view of the term which secondary causes, by common law, with the general concurrence of the primary cause, had prefixed: which God afterwards, at the prayers of Hezekiah, prolonged beyond the accustomed course of nature by adding fifteen years. If the term of life were absolutely fatal, the divine promises concerning the prolongation of life for the pious would be in vain, Exod.

23:25-26, Prov. 3:2; the threats concerning the cutting off and abbreviating of life for the impious would be in vain, Ps. 55:24; the prayers for a longer life, or for a peaceful kind of death, would be in vain, Is. 38:2, Phil. 2:27; the use of medicines ordained by God would be in vain, Sir. 38:1; the avoidance of dangers would be in vain. Moreover, divine providence is not absolutely and simply bound to secondary causes: but as it operates otherwise than the order of nature and the course of secondary causes according to the reason of divine wisdom: so it sometimes establishes for human life a term other than that which secondary causes with their natural concurrence prefix, and establishes it as either longer or shorter, for certain reasons; which term they commonly call hyperphysical, supernatural, or preternatural.

Cf. D. Feverborn, fasc. 5, disp. 6, p. 844. This preternatural term of life God establishes either positively, by decreeing it and ordaining the means by which it is reached; or permissively, by not hindering it, by withdrawing His grace, and thus by just judgment permitting that man be snatched away by premature death sooner than should have happened through the course of nature.

Positively, God establishes a hyperphysical term, by virtue of His promises, adduced above, as a gratuitous reward for piety, by prolonging life beyond and outside the course of nature, as happened to King Hezekiah, Is.

38; or even to avert evils and dangers, He calls someone from this mortality sooner than should have happened by nature, as it is said in Wis. 4:14: His soul was pleasing to the Lord: therefore He hastened from the midst of wickedness. Which hyperphysical term of life, whether shorter or longer, since it depends particularly on the benign decree of the divine will and the means ordained by Him, is specifically called the term of grace. Permissively, God constitutes a preternatural term of life as often as man, either by his own intemperance, drunkenness, lust, and other sins, brings diseases upon himself and accelerates death, or through imprudence or rashness exposes his head to dangers and perishes by shipwreck, or war, or by the hand of robbers, or falls into the power of a judge on account of crimes and is put to death, or in despair inflicts violent hands upon himself and cuts short the life which he could otherwise have prolonged for many years.

For just as God by His providence does not impose necessity upon man's will: so He finally leaves the despisers of His grace, who sin by free will or expose themselves to dangers, to their own just judgment, and so that by the aforementioned and other ways by premature death they perish prematurely, He permits. This hyperphysical term, established permissively, is commonly called the term of wrath.

But if it be asked now: is the term of life, prefixed by the eternal decree of God in such diverse ways, necessary and immovable? or contingent and movable? we answer that it is the same, necessary not by necessity of the consequent, or absolute, but by necessity of the consequence, or hypothetical: in equal measure, the term of life is immovable hypothetically, in the composite and complex sense; but it is movable, in the divided sense, through the apocope of the pre-defined condition.

For the physical term can be anticipated by diseases accelerated through an inordinate life, and by other means: therefore, it is not absolutely necessary that anyone reach that term of life to which he could have reached by the powers of nature and the course of secondary causes, with the general concurrence of God. However, positing that God has foreseen from eternity that a man will arrive at that term through secondary causes and His general concurrence, and has decreed from eternity that he should depart from this life when natural powers fail according to the customary course of nature, it is necessary to die when that term arrives.

In equal measure, the natural term is immovable hypothetically, in the composite sense, e.g., Let us suppose that God has formed the following decree: King David, if he takes careful account of the temperament which he has obtained well-disposed through the natural generation of his parents, by abstaining from gluttony, lust, anger, and enormous sins, shall complete 70 years of life. This term of life, in the composite sense, is immovable, but movable in the divided sense, through the apocope of the annexed condition.

For if David does otherwise, he will not reach that longer term, but another, shorter one. As regards the hyperphysical term, it is always hypothetical, including the condition of piety, or impiety, or the contempt of means.

Antithesis The Antithesis is (1) of Gisbertus Voetius, and others who follow him, asserting that for every man the term of life is fatal, that is, certain and immovable, prefixed by the secret and absolute decree of God, so that it is absolutely and simply impossible for anyone to succumb at another time, in another manner, or by another kind of death than that which has been decreed by God. (2) Of Simon Episcopius, and others adhering to him, in whose mind every term of life is immovable. Who rely on the following arguments:

I. Whoever’s term of life is constituted by divine decree so that it cannot be passed over, that is absolutely fatal. But the natural term of life &c. John XIV, 5. Therefore.

Resp. Whoever’s term of life is constituted by an absolute divine decree, that is simply fatal; I concede. But the divine decree, by which the physical term of life is constituted, is ordered and respective; inasmuch as it respects the order of secondary causes, natural temperament, the use of medicines, the cautious avoidance of impediments, in view of which God can recede from the course of nature, and positively or permissively constitute a term other than that which nature itself determines.

II. God is not bound to physical causes: Therefore He does not respect their powers in constituting the term of life.

Resp. God, acting by absolute power, is not bound to secondary causes: But acting by ordered power, He adapts Himself to the order established by Himself in the very kingdom of nature, and according to the temperament of each, constitutes the natural term of life.

III. All our times are in the hand of God, Ps. XXXI, 16. Therefore also the days of life and death.

Resp. We concede that all our times, and the very day of death, depend upon the divine hand; but we deny that this day of death is so simply fatal that it cannot be anticipated by intemperance, rashness, and suicide (ἀυτοχειρίᾳ).

IV. God absolutely prefixed the term of life to the whole first world at the time of the flood, and to all living in it. If to these, why not to others?

Resp. The term of life was not prefixed to them absolutely, without regard to any impulsive cause: but God was looking at the unamendable malice of the most ferocious men.

V. If the term of life is fixed by an ordained divine decree, will obedient children lead a longer life than the disobedient? But experience teaches that the consequent is false: Therefore, the antecedent is also. Resp. The term of grace is twofold, longer and shorter. The common rule indeed is that longevity is to be expected by obedient children, Exod. XX, 12. But this rule suffers an exception, if, namely, God foresees that in the passage of time their malice is going to pervert their intellect, and that most harsh accidents are about to overwhelm them, Sap. IV, 8. 9. Hence, by a premature death, they are sometimes snatched away by God from the theater of malice.

VI. Some evangelical doctors themselves, among whom is DANNHAVERVS, concede that the term of life is fatal. Resp. Dannhauer teaches that the term of life is fatal (i.e., defined by a certain decree of God): (1) by physical fatality, which is generally defined as 70 years, Ps. XC, 10, and is accustomed to be estimated individually from the temperament of one's nature. Yet this fatality, taken separately, is mutable, and is either dilatable by a temperate diet, medical care, piety toward parents, and the extraordinary grace of God, such as happened to Hezekiah; or abbreviatable by intemperance, neglect of medicine, Absolonic impiety, self-murder (αὐτοχειρίᾳ), or the just wrath of God the judge, etc. (2) By complex fatality, if you look at the whole dance of causes—natural, voluntary, fortuitous, and those extended beyond the order of heaven. But not (3) by absolute fatality, preceding all respects, conditions, and causes, but by conditional fatality, looking to the course of natural, supernatural, and voluntary causes. v. Hodom. S. C. p. 865. (*)

Latin:

Providentia Dei moderatur vitae humanae ingressum , progressum , & egressum .

Prob. a. Vitae humanae ingressus complectitur tum formationem & conservationem in utero matris, tum extractionem ex utero. Formationem embryonis & conservationem in utero piissimus Iobus Deo vindicat, c. X, 8. 9. 10. 11. 12. Manus tuae formaverunt me & fecerunt me; & quidem simul circumquaque, & tamen abforbes me. Memento, quaeso, quod sicut lutum feceris me, & in pulverem me sis redacturus. Nonne sicut lac fudisti me, & sicut caseum in formam infudisti me? Et carne induisti me, & ossibus atque nervis compegisti me. Vitam & benignitatem fecisti mecum: Et visio tua custodivit spiritum meum. Obs. (1) Deus dicitur formare hominem in utero matris non exclusive, quasi excludantur vel uterus ipse, vel vis plastica animae, vel sanguis menstruus, vel aliae causae; sed cum Deo omnes causae naturales subiaceant, & ipse per has agat, recte nos in utero formare & conservare dicitur, (2) Scite delineat Iobus vitae suae ingressum. Hunc quippe acceptum refert Dei manibus, per quas intelligit potentiam Dei creatricem; nam parentibus generantibus creat Deus. Suam in utero formationem comparat iam cum effigiatione luti, iam cum coagulatione lactis, iam cum induitione vestimenti, originem quidem suam humilem; at actionem Dei sublimem expressurus. Quod vitam agit, spiritumque ducit, id totum a visione Dei assidua, paternaque cura & tutela suspensum habet, Conf. Ps. CXXXIX, 14. 15. 16. De extractione ex utero matris testatur rex propheta, Ps. XXXI, 6: E visceribus matris meae tu eductor meus, q. d. Tu obstetricis quasi vices gessisti, maternisque me vinculis exsoluisti. Vel: Tu ipsemet obstetricis manus ita gubernasti, ne tenello mihi infantulo quidquam laederetur, sed incolumis ego in has prodirem auras.

Prob. b. Vitae progressum moderatur Deus alimenta vitae largiendo, Ps. CXLV, 6. gressus nostros dirigendo, i. e. consilia, coepta, factaque ad optatos exitus prouehendo, Ps. XXXVII, 23. hostium insidias, aut apertam vim a nobis propulsando, Ps. III, 8. 9. ad certum vitae genus nos aptando & vocando, Ierem. I, 5. 6. 7.

Prob. c. Terminum, vel egressum vitae Deus (1) infallibiliter praescit. Id quod indicat Psaltes, Ps. CXXXIX, 16. Glomus meum viderunt oculi tui; & super libro tuo omnes scripti sunt dies, qui destinati sunt, cum nec unus esset de illis. Deus infallibiliter cognoscit glomus nostrum, i. e. informem massam, e qua in utero materno formati sumus. Praenovit etiam omnes vitae nostrae futuros, ad huius lucus vfuram divinitus nobis destinatos. At quem non praetereunt omnes vitae nostrae dies, illum nec vltima viuendi hora fallit. (2) Deus terminum vitae praeordinauit & constituit. Id quod docet Iobus, c. XIV, 5. Si definiti sunt dies eius; numerus mensium eius est apud te: Statuta eius fecisti, & non transgredietur. Quibus verbis significatur, definitos esse homini a Deo certos viuendi dies, numerumque mensium ratione praescientiae & decreti diuini constitutum, quem homo transgredi nequeat. Praefixus autem est vitae terminus decreto non absoluto, omnes causas secundas antecedente, aut excludente, sed decreto hypothetico & ordinato, in causis secundis fundato, & pro illarum conditione formato. Nimirum lege communi & ordinaria Deus constituit homini terminum vitae physicum, siue naturalem, pro natura cuiusque hominis & temperamento. Probamus assertionem nostram (a) quia Deus, vt ab aeterno praescit, quam naturam quisque a parentibus suis vi naturalis generationis accepturus, & quousque iuxta naturae ordinem cum ipsius generali concursu vitam protracturus fit: ita ab aeterno etiam constituit, causis secundis tantum praebere influxum, quantus quidem de lege naturae ipsis debetur, vsque dum ad terminum a natura determinatum pertingant, & vires naturales deficiant.

Hæc enim providentiæ divinæ ratio est, vt communem naturæ cursum & causarum secundarum ordinem viresque agendi non evertat, sed conservet, & suum ipsis influxum præbeat, viribus & naturæ cuiusque congruum & proportionatum. Quotiescunque S. scriptura pietatis sectatoribus prolongationem vitæ pollicetur, impiis vero eiusdem abbreviationem comminatur: toties indicat, Deum homini pro natura & temperamento ipsius terminum vitæ præstituisse.

Nam prolongare vitam, est, eam vltra terminum præstitutum extendere, & eandem abbreviare, est, terminum præstitutum antevertere.

Vbi per terminum præstitutum alius intelligi non potest, quam is, quem ipsa natura cum Dei concursu generali lege communi præstituit. Idem evincit exemplum regis Hiskiæ, cuius terminum vitæ tum, cum ægrotaret, adesse, Dei iussu denuntiabat propheta Iesaias: Dispone, inquiens, domum tuam, quia morieris tu, & non viues, Es.

XXXVIII, 2. Vbi citra dubium mortem ei imminere prædicebatur intuitu termini, quem lege communi causæ secundæ, cum generali causæ primæ concursu, præfixerant: quem postea Deus ad preces Hiskiæ, præter consuetum naturæ cursum, adiectis annis quindecim prolongauit. Si terminus vitæ absolute fatalis esset, frustraneæ promissiones divinæ de vita piis proroganda, Exod.

XXIII, 25. 26. Prou. III, 2. frustraneæ comminationes de vita impiis abrumpenda & abbrevianda, Ps. LV, 24. frustraneæ preces pro vita longiori, aut placido mortis genere, Es. XXXVIII, 2. Phil. II, 27. frustraneus vsus medicamentorum a Deo ordinatorum, Sir. XXXVIII, 1. frustranea declinatio periculorum. Ceterum providentia divina non absolute & simpliciter alligata est ad causas secundas: sed vt alias præter naturæ ordinem & causarum secundarum cursum pro ratione divinæ sapientiæ operatur: ita vitæ humanæ quandoque terminum alium, quam quem causæ secundæ cum ipsius concursu naturali præfigunt, eumque vel longiorem, vel breviorem, certis de causis præstituit; quem terminum hyperphysicum, supernaturalem vel præternaturalem communiter appellant.

Conf. D. FEVERBORN fasc. V. disp. Vi. p. 844. Hunc terminum vitæ præternaturalem præstituit Deus vel positive, decernendo eum, & media, quibus attingatur, ordinando; vel permissive, non impediendo, gratiam suam subtrahendo, atque sic iusto iudicio permittendo, vt citius, quam per cursum naturæ fieri debebat, homo morte præmatura abripiatur.

Positive Deus præstituit terminum hyperphysicum, vi promissionum suarum, supra adductarum, in gratuitam pietatis remunerationem, vitam vltra & præter naturæ cursum prolongando, vt regi Hiskiæ contigit,

Es. XXXVIII. vel etiam ad auertenda mala & pericula imminentia citius, quam per naturam fieri debuisset, ex hac mortalitate quempiam euocat, sicut Sap. IV, 14. dicitur: Grata erat domino anima ipsius: propterea festinauit e medio malitiæ. Qui terminus vitæ hyperphysicus breuior & longior, cum a benigno voluntatis divinæ decreto, mediisque ab ipso ordinatis peculiariter dependeat, speciatim terminus gratiæ vocatur. Permissive Deus terminum vitæ præternaturalem constituit, quotiescunque homo vel sua intemperantia, ebrietate, libidine, aliisque peccatis morbos sibi accersit, & mortem accelerat vel per imprudentiam, aut temeritatem periculis caput obiicit, & naufragio, vel bello, vel latronum manu perit, vel ob delicta in iudicis incidit potestatem, & capite plectitur, vel desperabundus violentas sibi ipsi manus infert, vitamque, quam alias in annos multos protrahere potuisset, abrumpit.

Quem ad modum enim Deus providentia sua hominis voluntati necessitatem non imponit: ita gratiæ suæ contemptores, qui voluntate libera peccant, aut periculis se exponunt, iusto iudicio sibi tandem relinquit, & vt prædictis aliisque modis morte præmatura pereant, permittit. Hic terminus hyperphysicus, permissive constitutus, vulgo nominatur terminus iræ.

Quod si iam quæratur: sitne terminus vitæ, modis tam diversis æterno Dei decreto præfixus, necessarius & immobilis? an contingens & mobilis? respondemus, eundem esse necessarium, non necessitate consequentis, aut absoluta, sed necessitate consequentiæ, vel hypothetica: pari ratione esse terminum vitæ immobilem hypothetice, in sensu composito & complexo; esse vero eundem mobilem, in sensu diviso, per apocopen præfinitæ conditionis.

Terminus enim physicus anteverti potest acceleratis per vitam inordinatam morbis, aliisque modis: proinde absolute necessarium non est, quemquam ad eum pertingere vitæ terminum, ad quem per naturæ vires, & causarum secundarum cursum, cum concursu Dei generali pertingere poterat. Posito autem, Deum prævidisse ab æterno, hominem ad eum terminum per causas secundas & suum concursum generalem perventurum esse, & ab æterno constituisse, ut tum ex hac vita decedat, cum vires naturales iuxta consuetum naturæ cursum deficiunt, necessarium est, cum termino illo adveniente mori.

Pari ratione terminus naturalis est immobilis hypothetice, in sensu composito, v. gr. Ponamus, Deum sequens formasse decretum: Rex Dauid, si temperamenti, quod bene dispositum per naturalem parentum generationem nactus est, rationem habeat sollicitam, abstinendo a crapula, libidine, ira, & enormibus delictis, 70. annos vivendo expleat. Hic terminus vitæ, in sensu composito, est immobilis, mobilis autem in sensu diviso, per apocopen annexæ conditionis.

Nam si Dauid secus fecerit, non terminum illum longiorem, sed alium breviorem attinget. Quod attinet ad terminum hyperphysicum, is semper est hypotheticus, includens conditionem pietatis, vel impietatis, vel contemptum mediorum. Antithesis

Antithesis est (1) Gisberti Voëtii, & aliorum, qui ipsum sequuntur, afferentium, homini cuique terminum vitæ esse fatalem, hoc est, certum & immobilem, Dei occulto & absoluto decreto præfixum, vt alio tempore, alio modo, alioue mortis genere, quam quo a Deo decretum est, quemquam occumbere, absolute & simpliciter impossibile fit. (2) Simonis Episcopii, & aliorum, ipsi adhærentium, ex quorum mente omnis vitæ terminus immobilis est. Qui sequentibus innituntur argumentis: I.

Quicunque vitæ terminus decreto divino constitutus est, vt præteriri nequeat, ille est absolute fatalis. Atqui naturalis vitæ terminus &c. Io. XIV, 5. Ergo.

Resp. Quicunque vitæ terminus decreto divino absoluto constitutus est, ille simpliciter fatalis est; concedo. At decretum divinum, quo constituitur vitæ terminus physicus, est ordinatum & respectivum. quippe quo respicitur ordo causarum secundarum, temperamentum naturale, usus medicamentorum, cauta declinatio impedimentorum, quorum intuitu Deus a cursu naturæ recedere, & alium, quam ipsa natura determinat, terminum positive, aut permissive constituere potest.

II. Deus non alligatus est ad causas physicas: Ergo illarum vires in constituendo vitæ termino non respicit.

Resp. Deus, potestate absoluta agens, non alligatus est ad causas secundas: At agens potentia ordinata, ordini, a se in ipso regno naturæ constituto, se attemperat, & secundum cuiusque temperamentum, terminum vitæ naturalem constituit.

III. Omnia nostra tempora sunt in manu Dei, Ps. XXXI, 16. Ergo & dies vitæ atque mortis.

Resp. Concedimus, omnia nostra tempora, ipsumque diem mortis a manu divina pendere; sed negamus, hunc diem mortis adeo simpliciter fatalem esse, vt intemperantia, temeritate & ἀυτοχειρίᾳ anteverti nequeat.

IV. Deus toti primo mundo tempore diluvii, & omnibus in eo viventibus terminum vitæ absolute præfixit. Si his, cur non & aliis?

Resp. Terminus vitæ illis non absolute, citra intuitum vllius causæ impulsivæ, præfixus erat: sed respiciebat Deus inemendabilem hominum ferocissimorum malitiam. absolute, citra intuitum vllius cauffæ impulfluæ, præfixus erat: sed respiciebat Deus inemendabilem hominum ferociffimorum malitiam.

V. Si terminus vitae decreto divino ordinato praefixus est, longiorem vitam agent filii morigeri, quam immorigeri: At consequens falsum esse, docet experientia: Ergo et antecedens. Resp. Terminus gratiae duplex est, longior, et brevior. Communis quidem regula est, filiis morigeris exspectandam esse longevitatem, Exod. XX, 12. At patitur haec regula exceptionem, si nimirum Deus praevideat, quod successu temporis malitia illorum intellectum fit perversura, et casus asperrimi eosdem sint obruturi, Sap. IV, 8. 9. Hinc praematura quandoque morte e medio malitiae theatro divinitus rapiuntur.

VI. Ipsi doctores evangelici nonnulli, quos inter DANNHAVERVS, concedunt, terminum vitae esse fatalem. Resp. Dannhauerus docet, terminum vitae esse fatalem, (i. e. certo Dei decreto definitum): (1) fatalitate physica, quae universim LXX. annis definitur, Ps. XC, 10. ac sigillatim ex temperamenti indole aestimari solet. Quae tamen fatalitas seorsum accepta mobilis est, atque vel dilatabilis est temperanti dieta, cura medica, pietate in parentes, gratia Dei extraordinaria, qualis Hiskiae contigit; vel abbreviabilis, intemperantia, medicinae neglectu, impietate Absolonica, αὐτοχειρίᾳ, iusta Dei iudicis ira, etc. (2) Fatalitate complexa, si totam choream causarum naturalium, voluntariarum, fortuitarum, et caelo extra ordinem porrectarum, intueare. Non autem (3) fatalitate absoluta, omnes respectus, conditiones et causas antecedente, sed conditionata, respiciente ad causarum naturalium, supernaturalium ac voluntariarum cursum. v. Hodom. S. C. p. 865. (*)


### Quest. IX. What acts does divine providence embrace?

Divine providence, taken broadly, in its general complex comprehends a) πρόγνωσιν, fore-vision, or foreknowledge, b) πρόθεσιν, purpose, or decree of God, c) διοίκησιν, the actual conservation and government of created things.

Prob. a. (1) The word, providence, derived from providing, by its native force denotes the cognition or vision of future things before they happen. Therefore, foreknowledge cannot be excluded from the acts of divine providence.

(2) The Hebrews designate the whole complex of providence by the name of vision, Gen. XXII, 8.

(3) If foreknowledge is denied, the exact providence of God is taken away. For how can you wisely rule things unknown to you? How can you avoid things not foreseen?

(4) HUGO DE S. VICTORE warns that in divine providence three things are to be considered: the directing knowledge, the commanding will, and the executing power. Paul seems to embrace these three, Eph. I, 11: God works all things according to the counsel of his will. Where counsel elegantly denotes the directing knowledge, will the commanding will, and the word works the executing power. Βουλή, or divine counsel, cannot exist without foreknowledge.

…Antithesis of Socinus, who excludes foreknowledge from the acts of providence, whose argument is: Foreknowledge of contingent things undermines providence and renders God idle. for what does it profit to contemplate God perpetually, what is done by men, if He already knows it from eternity? Resp. Foreknowledge does not undermine providence, but stabilizes it. For nothing happens in the present time without God being aware, because God is prescient of future things. Hence, what necessity divine knowledge has for present and past things, the same it has for future things.…

Obs. The word πρόγνωσις, taken in a special sense, denotes the forevision of the persevering faith of the elect, according to which election was made, Rom. VIII, 29. Here, however, it is taken in a general sense, for the universal knowledge of all those things which are, have been, and will be; by which the omniscient God exactly knows not only good things, but also evil things, which depend on human will; since He knows all things from eternity, Act. XV, 18.

Prob. b. 1) Our God is in the heavens; He does all that He wills, Ps. CXV, 3. The Psalmist teaches that all divine works depend on the will of God, as the immediately moving principle. This same principle exerts itself in a twofold way: by willing something, either absolutely, without regard to any condition to be fulfilled by creatures; or orderly, with some condition presupposed, upon the fulfillment or non-fulfillment of which, God wills to do or not to do something.

2) God works all things according to the counsel of His will, Eph. I, 11. Obs. Βυλὴ, or counsel, taken strictly, is the eternal act of the divine intellect concerning those things which God wills to be done for the glory of His name: sometimes, however, in the scriptures it is used for the most wise decree of God. Conf. Act. II, 23. cap. IV, 28. In which sense ESTIUS in his notes to this passage judges the counsel in the l. c. to be accepted, because of the certainty of divine cognition, which the decree presupposes.

3) There is no God besides You, who has care for all things, says the author of Wisdom, c. XII, 13. While God in time takes care of all things created by Him, we gather that He decreed from eternity that He would provide for them: for the reason that He does nothing in time that He did not decree from eternity that He would do, because of the immutability of the divine will. Wisely says AUGUSTINE, and from him PROSPER, sentent. LVIII: The will of God is the highest and first cause of all bodily and spiritual motions. For nothing happens visibly and sensibly that is not either commanded or permitted from the invisible and intelligible court of the supreme commander according to the ineffable justice of rewards and punishments, graces and retributions in that very vast and immense republic of the whole creation.

Obs. The divine decree is an act of the divine will, by which God, with most wise counsel and free authority, wills to effect whatever is good for creatures, but sometimes to permit evil; and thus 1) it is distinguished into effective and permissive. By the effective decree, God determines to effect good things; by the permissive, to permit evil things. 2. Into absolute and non-absolute. Absolute is that which God conceived without regard to any condition, means ordained to produce the effect, or external impulsive causes. Non-absolute, according to a different way of considering it, is called conditional, ordered, and respective. A non-absolute decree is called conditional because of the condition in view of which it was made. e.g. If that nation, against which I have spoken, turns from its evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do to it. Jer. XVIII, 7. 8. The most just God had decreed to cut off an evil people, if they persistently indulge in wicked sins: this condition being removed, He had determined to spare them. The same non-absolute decree is called ordered because of the τάξιν, or order of means divinely constituted, in view of which it was sanctioned by God, e.g. He who believes and is baptized shall be saved, Mark XVI, 16. God decreed to save men through the ordinary means of grace and salvation, namely baptism and faith. Finally, a non-absolute decree is called respective, because of the respect to external impulsive causes, in view of which it was formed by God, e.g. God chose us in Christ before the foundations of the world were laid, Ephes. I, 4. The decree of election was made in respect to the merit of Christ, as an external impulsive cause. There are some theowho do not admit a conditional decree, (since he is properly said to decree, who, having considered all circumstances, wills something simply and without condition); but they inculcate a decree respective of external impulsive causes: whom D. Mvsaevs addresses in his dissertation on the eternal decree of election, p. 273, distinguishing thus: The decree of election, although we say it was made in view of foreseen faith, we by no means say it was made conditional, or under the condition of faith; but if τὸ absolute is said in opposition to τὸ conditional, we fearlessly maintain that the decree of election is absolute, or unconditional, nor do we deny that it is absolute in any other sense than that in which it is called absolute to exclude the respect of an impulsive cause outside of God, or external. However, a decree is not immediately conditional because it is made in view of some impulsive cause, but if it is made in view of an impulsive cause already constituted in act, or distinctly foreknown as future, then it is absolute, or unconditional. Cf. D. Breithavpt. Instit. theol. p. 356.

Prob. c. Διοίκησις denotes administration, dispensation, government. Concerning this, the author of Wisdom says c. XII, 18, μετὰ πολλῆς Φειδοῦς διοικεῖς ἡμᾶς, with great sparingness (indulgence) you administer us. Which words B. Lvther rendered in German: You govern us with much sparing. Διοίκησις draws its origin ἀπὸ τοῦ οἴκου, from the house. For just as a householder provides for the accounts of his household: so God administers the vast house of the world, and takes account of all creatures. This διοίκησις properly constitutes the absolute actual providence of God; for it is an action of God ad extra, and the execution of the divine will, and thus presupposes an internal act of the divine mind and will, and in the customary usage of speaking, approved by the church, it embraces preservation, cooperation or concurrence, and government; although we would not deny that διοίκησις in a stricter sense designates only direction, or government.

Latin:

Prouidentia diuina, late sumta, generali suo complexu comprehendit a) πρόγνωσιν, prauisionem, vel praescientiam, b) πρόθεσιν, propositum, aut decretum Dei, c) διοίκησιν, actualem rerum creatarum conseruationem et gubernationem.

Prob. a. (1) Vox, prouidentia, a prouidendo deriuata, vi natiua denotat futurorum, antequam fiant, cognitionem, seu visionem. Ergo praescientia ab actibus prouidentiae diuinae excludi nequit.

(2) Hebraei totum prouidentiae complexum nomine visionis designant, Gen. XXII, 8.

(3) Negata praescientia, tollitur exacta Dei prouidentia. Qui enim sapienter regas cuiusque ignota? Qui declines non prouisa?

(4) HVGO DE S. VICTORE monet, in prouidentia diuina tria esse consideranda, scientiam dirigentem, voluntatem imperantem, et potentiam exsequentem. Tria haec complecti videtur Paullus, Eph. I, 11: Deus omnia secundum consilium voluntatis suae operatur. Vbi consilium scientiam dirigentem, voluntas voluntatem imperantem, vox operatur potentiam exsequentem eleganter notat. Βουλή, siue consilium diuinum, fine praescientia esse nequit.

Antithesis est Socini, praescientiam ab actibus prouidentiae excludentis, cuius argumentum est: Praescientia contingentium labefactat prouidentiam, et Deum reddit otiosum. Quid enim attinet, Deum perpetuo contemplari, quæ ab hominibus fiunt, si ea iam ab æterno novit? Resp. Præscientia prouidentiam non labefactat, sed stabilit. Nihil enim tempore præsenti sit Deo non conscio, quia Deus futurorum est præscius. Hinc quæ necessitas scientiæ divinæ est ad præsentia & præterita, eadem est ad futura.

Obs. vox πρόγνωσις, sumta sensu speciali, notat præuisionem fidei perseuerantis electorum, iuxta quam est facta electio, Rom. VIII, 29. Hic autem sumitur sensu generali, pro scientia vniuersali omnium eorum, quæ sunt, fuerunt, & erunt; qua non tantum bona, sed & mala, quæ ex voluntate humana dependent, exacte cognoscit Deus omniscius; siquidem omnia ab æterno nouit, Act. XV, 18.

Prob. b. 1) Deus noster in cælis; omnia, quæ vult, facit, Ps. CXV, 3. Docet psaltes, omnia opera diuina a voluntate Dei, vt principio proxime mouente, dependere. Quod ipsum principium duplici modo se exserit: volendo aliquid, vel absolute, citra respectum vllius conditionis, a creaturis implendæ; vel ordinate, præsupposita aliqua conditione, qua impleta, vel non impleta, Deus aliquid facere, vel non facere vult.

2) Deus omnia operatur iuxta consilium voluntatis suæ, Eph. I, 11. Obs. Βυλὴ, siue consilium, stricte sumtum, est actus intellectus diuini æternus de his, quæ Deus fieri vult ad gloriam nominis sui: aliquando tamen in scripturis vsurpatur de decreto Dei sapientissimo. Conf. Act. II, 23. cap. IV, 28. Quo sensu l. c. accipi consilium censet ESTIVS in notis ad h. l. ob certitudinem cognitionis diuinæ, quam decretum præsupponit.

3) Non est Deus præter te, cui cura est de omnibus, inquit auctor sapientiæ, c. XII, 13. Dum Deus in tempore curam gerit rerum omnium a se conditarum, colligimus, quod ab æterno se iisdem prospecturum esse decreuerit: propterea, quod nihil in tempore agit, quod non ab æterno se acturum esse decreuit, propter voluntatis diuinæ immutabilitatem. Scite ait AVGVSTINVS, & ex eo PROSPER, sentent. LVIII: Voluntas Dei est summa & prima caussa omnium corporalium, spiritualiumque motuum. Nihil enim sit visibiliter & sensibiliter, quod non de inuisibili & intelligibili summi imperatoris aula aut iubeatur aut permittatur secundum ineffabilem iustitiam præmiorum atque pænarum, gratiarum & retributionum in ipsa totius creaturæ amplissima quadam immensaque republica.

Obs. Decretum diuinum est actus voluntatis diuinæ, quo Deus, quidquid creaturis bonum est, efficere, malum vero interdum permittere, sapientissimo consilio, liberaque auctoritate vult; atque adeo 1) distinguitur in effectiuum, & permissiuum. Decr.to effectiuo Deus bona efficere, permissiuo mala permittere constituit. 2. In absolutum, & non absolutum. Absolutum est, quod Deus concepit citra intuitum vllius conditionis, mediorum ad effectum producendum ordinatorum, aut caussarum impulsivarum externarum. Non absolutum pro diuersa considerandi ratione, vocatur conditionatum, ordinatum & respectiuum. Decretum non absolutum dicitur conditionatum ob conditionem, cuius intuitu factum est. v. gr. Si conuersa fuerit gens ista a malitia sua, propter quam locutus sum contra eam: pœnitebit me mali, quod cogitaui facere super illa. Ier. XVIII, 7. 8. Decreuerat Deus iustissimus exscindere populum malum, si peccatis nefandis pertinaciter indulgeat: sublata hac conditione, eidem parcere constituerat. Idem decretum non absolutum adpellatur ordinatum ob τάξιν, seu ordinem mediorum diuinitus constitutorum, quorum intuitu a Deo sancitum est, v. gr. Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, saluabitur, Marc. XVI, 16. Decreuit Deus per ordinaria gratiæ salutisque media, nimirum baptismum & fidem, homines saluare. Decretum denique non absolutum dicitur respectivum, ob respectum caussarum impulsiuarum externarum, quarum intuitu a Deo formatum est, v. gr. Deus elegit nos in Christo ante iacta mundi fundamenta, Ephes. I, 4. Decretum electionis factum est respectu meriti Christi, tanquam caussæ impulsivæ externæ. Sunt nonnulli theoqui non admittunt decretum conditionatum, (cum decernere proprie dicatur, qui consideratis omnibus circumstantiis aliquid simpliciter & fine conditione vult); inculcant autem decretum causarum impulsivarum externarum respectivum: quos interest D. Mvsaevs in dissertatione de æterno electionis decreto p. 273. ita differens: Electionis decretum, licet intuitu fidei prævisæ factum dicamus, conditionatum tamen, aut sub conditione fidei factum minime dicimus, sed si τὸ absolutum dicatur in oppositione ad τὸ conditionatum, decretum electionis absolutum, sive inconditionatum esse, intrepide statuimus, nec alio sensu id absolutum esse negamus, quam quo absolutum dicitur ad excludendum respectum causæ impulsivæ extra Deum, sive externæ. Non autem statim conditionatum est decretum, quod intuitu alicuius causæ impulsivæ fit, sed si fiat intuitu causæ impulsivæ, iam in actu constitutæ, vel distincte præcognitæ, ut futuræ, tum absolutum, sive inconditionatum est. Conf. D. Breithavpt. Insit. theol. p. 356.

Prob. c. Διοίκησις, administrationem, dispensationem, gubernationem notat. De hac inquit auctor Sapientiæ c. XII, 18. μετὰ πολλῆς Φειδοῦς διοικεῖς ἡμᾶς, cum magna parcitate (indulgentia) administras nos. Quæ verba B. Lvther. germanice reddidit: Du regierest uns mit viel Verschonen. Διοίκησις ἀπὸ τοῦ οἴκου, a domo trahit originem. Sicut enim paterfamilias domesticorum suorum rationibus consulit: ita Deus ingentem mundi domum administrat, & omnium creaturarum rationem ducit. Hæc διοίκησις proprie constituit & absolutum actualem Dei prouidentiam; quippe quæ est actio Dei ad extra, & voluntatis diuinæ exsecutio, adeoque internum mentis & voluntatis diuinæ actum supponens, atque consueto loquendi usu, ecclesiæ approbato, complectens conservationem, cooperationem sive concursum, & gubernationem; quamquam nolimus negare, διοίκησιν sensu strictiori designare tantum directionem, vel gubernationem.


### Quest. IX. What acts does divine providence embrace?: Quest. X. Does divine foreknowledge rest upon a prior decree?

Quest. X. Does divine foreknowledge rest upon a prior decree?

The foreknowledge and the decree of God concerning future things are eternal and simultaneous on the part of God; but in our mode of conceiving, the foreknowledge of God precedes the divine decree.

Prob. 1) Although in truth in God being, understanding, and willing are the same: yet by effect the divine will is distinguished from the intellect. For the will decrees concerning that which the intellect has recognized as good. No wise person forms a decree concerning unknown things; for this would be blind, vain, and void. There is nothing in the will that was not first in the intellect, and there is no desire for the unknown.

2) Such is the perfection of the divine intellect that it perceives and infallibly knows the present, past, and future by itself and immediately, without any prior decree of the will. For all things are naked and laid bare to the divine eyes, Hebr. IV, 13, all things are present to Him, by reason of infallible intuition.

3) The Apostle Paul places πρόγνωσιν, or foreknowledge, before the eternal decree of election, Rom. VIII, 29. Whom He foreknew, He also predestined. And St. Peter writes in 1 Epist. I, 2 to the elect according to the foreknowledge of God.

4) God knows all possibilities through His infinite knowledge, even those which are never to exist, concerning which He makes no decree. Therefore, He also foresees future contingencies through His essential omniscience without a prior decree. For there is no reason why God should know possibilities in one way and future contingencies in another: for He sees all things by the light of His infinite intellect.

You say: Mere possibles, which will never exist, God indeed knows without a prior decree; but there are no futures, nor can there be, which God has not decreed to effect or to permit, and which He may eventually effect or permit. For things are not foreseen as future otherwise than as they are future; otherwise they would be falsely foreseen. Resp. Although there is no future that God has not decreed to effect or to permit, yet God does not therefore foresee the future because He has decreed it, but because He is omniscient. For before God decrees a future, He foresees its possibility and the transition from possibility into existence, while He foresees the free inclination of the human will, which it is about to produce as an effect, if He is to impart His necessary concurrence. Thereafter, He decrees to impart His concurrence, and He knows how the human will is to use His concurrence to produce the effect.

5) God knows future sins, which He has not decreed to effect. Therefore, His foreknowledge does not rest upon a prior determining decree.

You say: God has not indeed decreed to effect future sins, but He has decreed to permit them. Resp. The divine decree concerning the permitting of evils presupposes the foreknowledge of evils, that, unless they are divinely hindered, they will certainly be future; therefore, the permissive decree does not, according to our mode of conceiving, precede the divine foreknowledge, but follows it.

6) God foreknew conditionally future things, concerning which He made no decree; e.g., Christ foreknew the repentance of the Tyrians and Sidonians, if the miracles which occurred in the towns of Chorazin and Bethsaida had been performed among them, Matt. XI, 22.

Antithesis of certain Scholastics, Scotists, and Dominicans, whom others follow. According to their opinion, the infallible reason for divine foreknowledge is founded upon the predefinition of God, or the decree of doing and permitting future things. They strive to strengthen their opinion with the following arguments:

I. If possibles cannot pass into the condition of futures unless they are determined by a decree of the divine will, then futures cannot be known by God without a prior decree: The antecedent is true: Therefore, the consequent is also. The consequence of the major is evident; because what is in no way future, God does not know as future, since true knowledge is conformable to its object. The antecedent is proved; because possibles are by their nature indifferent to future existence and non-future existence; and thus some cause is required which may determine that indifference, and cause them to pass from purely possible things into the condition of futures. A cause of this kind is not to be sought outside of God, for the reason that this transition from the condition of possibles into the condition of futures was made from eternity; for whatever things are future are future from eternity, otherwise they could not have been known even by God as future, and that from eternity. Wherefore, because from eternity there was nothing that could be the cause of that transition outside of God, it is validly concluded that the decree of the divine will determines the condition of possibles, so that they migrate into the condition of futures.

Resp. 1) God knows conditionally future things, which are never absolutely future; e.g., the repentance of the Tyrians and Sidonians, which was conditionally future: nor is His foreknowledge therefore false. For this proposition is true in the composite sense: The Tyrians and Sidonians would have performed true repentance, if the same miracles which were performed among the Chorazinites had been performed among them. 2) The transition of all possibles into the state of future existence is not from the predetermining will of God: but from the free cause itself, determining itself to act, whose inclination and powers God foresaw and foreknew, that it was about to produce an effect, if He were to impart His concurrence; thereafter He decrees to impart sufficient concurrence. Therefore foreknowledge precedes the decree. 3) Nor has the transition from the condition of possibles into the condition of futures been made from eternity, although it has been foreseen from eternity. For such is the power and perfection of the divine intellect, that things which are future in time He makes present to Himself from eternity.

Future things cannot be present from eternity. Resp. Future things cannot be present from eternity, as regards real and actual being, although, as regards ideal objective being, they stand present to the divine intellect for knowing.

II. If a thing is future, and not decreed by God, it will be independent: The consequent is absurd: Therefore the antecedent. Resp. We concede that future entities are decreed by God, and depend upon Him; but we urge this, that a certain divine foreknowledge, at least conditional, with respect to the object, precedes the divine decree, as we have clearly shown.

III. Whoever knows an object without a prior decree, his knowledge depends upon the object: But divine knowledge depends upon no object; because it is independent: Therefore God does not know an object without a prior decree. The major is evident; because according to the common axiom: Knowledge depends upon things, not things upon knowledge. Resp. Divine knowledge indeed regards the object, but properly does not depend upon it. Objective dependence is said to be so not ἀκριβῶς (precisely) and accurately, but ἀτύπως (vaguely) and improperly.

IV. Whoever knows something, which he did not previously decree, his intellect is changed: But the divine intellect is not changed. Therefore God knows nothing which He did not previously decree. The major is established; because by this reasoning the intellect is led into act and potency. For it could know free acts, before they were done; after they were done, it began to know them in act. But this is a change from potency to act. Resp. Distinguish between a finite intellect, and an infinite one. The former is led from potency into act; the latter in eternity and infinite clarity knows all things most perfectly.

Latin:

Quæst. X. An præscientia diuina præuio innititur decreto?

Præscientia, & decretum Dei conceptum de rebus futuris, æterna & simul sunt ex parte Dei; nostro autem concipiendi modo præscientia Dei decretum diuinum antecedit.

Prob. 1) Licet re vera in Deo idem sit, esse, intelligere, velle: effectu tamen discernitur voluntas diuina ab intellectu. Nam quod bonum intellectus cognouit, de illo voluntas decernit. Nemo sapiens de rebus ignoratis format decretum; foret quippe hoc cæcum, vanum & irritum. Nihil est in voluntate, quin prius fuerit in intellectu, & ignoti nulla est cupido.

2) Ea est intellectus diuini perfectio, ut per se & immediate, absque vllo præuio decreto voluntatis, præsentia, præterita & futura perspiciat, & infallibiliter cognoscat. Omnia namque oculis diuinis sunt nuda & circumcirca denudata, Hebr. IV, 13. omnia ipsi præsentia, ratione intuitus infallibilis.

3) Apostolus Paulus æterno electionis decreto præmittit πρόγνωσιν, sive præscientiam, Rom. VIII, 29. Quos præcognouit, etiam prædestinauit. Et S. Petrus 1 Epist. I, 2. scribit electis secundum præcognitionem Dei.

4) Deus cognoscit omnia possibilia, per infinitam suam scientiam, etiam ea, quæ nunquam sunt exstitura, de quibus nullum facit decretum. Ergo etiam per omniscientiam suam essentialem futura contingentia præuidet absque præuio decreto. Nulla enim ratio est, cur Deus aliter possibilia, aliter futura contingentia cognoscat: omnia quippe lumine intellectus sui infiniti videt.

Dicis: Mere possibilia, nunquam exstitura, Deus quidem cognoscit sine praeuio decreto; at futura nulla sunt, nec esse possunt, quae Deus non decreuit efficere, aut permittere, & tandem efficiat, aut permittat. Nec enim res aliter praescientur futurae, quam sunt futurae; alias falso praescirentur. Resp. Licet nullum futurum fit, quod Deus non decreuit efficere, aut permittere, non tamen ideo Deus praescit futurum, quia decreuit, sed quia omnisciens est. Antequam enim Deus futurum decernat, praeuidet illius possibilitatem, & transitum ex possibilitate in existentiam, dum liberam praescit voluntatis humanae inclinationem, quod effectum sit productura, si concursum suum necessarium sit impertiturus. Deinceps decernit concursum suum impertiri, & cognoscit, quomodo voluntas humana suo concursu ad effectum producendum sit vsura.

5) Deus cognoscit peccata futura; quae efficere non decreuit. Ergo praescientia eius praeuio decreto determinante non nititur.

Dicis: Deus peccata futura non quidem efficere, attamen permittere decreuit. Resp. Decretum diuinum de permittendis malis supponit praescientiam malorum, quod, nisi diuinitus impediantur, certo futura sint, E. decretum permissiuum praescientiam diuinam, secundum nostrum concipiendi modum, non antecedit, sed sequitur.

6) Deus praenouit conditionate futura, de quibus nullum fecit decretum, v. gr. praenouit Christus poenitentiam Tyriorum & Sidoniorum, si ea, quae in oppidis Chorazin & Bethsaida contigerunt miracula, apud eos patrata fuissent, Matth. XI, 22.

Antithesis quorundam Scholasticorum, Scotistarum & Dominicanorum, quos alii sequuntur. Horum de sententia infallibilis ratio praescientiae diuinae fundatur in praedefinitione Dei, seu decreto faciendi & permittendi futura. Firmare nituntur suam opinionem sequentibus argumentis:

I. Si possibilia non possunt transire in conditionem futurorum, nisi decreto voluntatis diuinae determinentur, sine praeuio decreto futura a Deo cognosci nequeunt: Antecedens est verum: Ergo & consequens. Consequentia maioris patet; quia quod nulla ratione futurum est, Deus vt futurum non cognoscit, cum vera scientia obiecto sit conformis. Antecedens probatur; quia possibilia natura sua indifferentia sunt ad futuram existentiam, & non futuram existentiam; adeoque causa aliqua requiritur, quae determinet indifferentiam istam, eaque ex pure possibilibus transire faciat in conditionem futurorum. Huiusmodi causa non est quaerenda extra Deum, propterea, quod transitus iste e conditione possibilium in conditionem futurorum factus est ab aeterno; nam ab aeterno futura sunt, quaecunque futura sunt, alioqui, ne a Deo quidem, vt futura cognosci potuissent, idque ab aeterno. Quam ob rem, quia ab aeterno nihil fuit, quod transitus illius causa esse potuit extra Deum, valide colligitur, decretum voluntatis diuinae determinare conditionem possibilium, vt migrent in conditionem futurorum.

Resp. 1) Deus cognoscit conditionate futura, quae nunquam absolute sunt futura; v. gr. Tyriorum & Sidoniorum resipiscentiam conditionate futuram: neque tamen eius praescientia falsa est. Nam haec propositio in sensu composito vera est: Tyrii & Sidonii veram egissent poenitentiam, si eadem miracula, quae apud Chorazinos facta sunt, apud eosdem patrata fuissent. 2) Non omnium possibilium transitus in statum futurae existentiae est a voluntate Dei praedeterminante: sed ab ipsa causa libera, ad agendum seipsam determinante, cuius inclinationem viresque Deus praeuidit & praescit, quod effectum sit productura, si concursum suum impertiretur; postea decernit sufficientem praebere concursum. Praecedit igitur praescientia decretum. 3) Neque transitus e conditione possibilium in conditionem futurorum factus est ab aeterno, licet ab aeterno sit praeuisus. Nam ea est vis & perfectio intellectus diuini, vt quae in tempore futura sunt, sibi ab aeterno praesentia fiat. quæ in tempore futura sunt, sibi ab æterno præfentia sistat.

Futura non possunt esse praesentia ab aeterno. Resp. Futura ab aeterno non possunt esse praesentia, quoad esse reale et actuale, licet, quoad esse ideale obiectivum, intellectui divino ad cognoscendum praesentia sistant.

II. Si res futura est, et non decreta a Deo, erit independens: Consequens est absurdum: Ergo et antecedens. Resp. Concedimus, entia futura a Deo esse decreta, et ab ipso pendere; at hoc urgemus, quod praescientia quaedam divina, saltem conditionata, respectu obiecti, decretum divinum praecedat, prout luculenter ostendimus.

III. Quicunque cognoscit obiectum sine praevio decreto, illius scientia dependet ab obiecto: Atqui scientia divina a nullo dependet obiecto; quia est independens: E. Deus non cognoscit obiectum sine praevio decreto. Maior patet; quia iuxta commune axioma: Scientia a rebus, non res a scientia pendent. Resp. Scientia divina obiectum quidem respicit, sed proprie ab eo non dependet. Obiectiva dependentia non ἀκριβῶς et accurate, sed ἀτύπως et improprie ita dicitur.

IV. Quicunque aliquid cognoscit, quod prius non decrevit, illius intellectus mutatur: At intellectus divinus non mutatur. E. Deus nihil cognoscit, quod prius non decrevit. Maior constat; quia hac ratione intellectus traducitur in actum et potentia. Poterat enim actus liberos scire, antequam fierent; postquam facti sunt, coepit illos scire actu. Sed haec est mutatio a potentia ad actum. Resp. Dist. inter intellectum finitum, et infinitum. Ille traducitur a potentia in actum; hic in aeternitate et infinita claritate omnia perfectissime cognoscit.


### Quaest. XI. Does divine providence impose necessity upon created things, especially upon the human will?

Although all things, which God has foreseen, happen necessarily, by hypothetical necessity; yet divine providence does not impose upon all things, especially upon the human will, absolute necessity.

Obs. I. The proposed question can be understood concerning the providence of God, as it is both an immanent act of God, and a transient one. When the providence of God is considered as an immanent act of God, it comprises with foreknowledge the decree of the divine intellect: viewed as a transient act, it is the preservation and governance of creatures. We shall look in this question primarily at the foreknowledge of God joined with the divine decree, whether that imposes necessity upon all created things.

Obs. II. Necessity is one thing absolute, or of the consequent, which some authors also call antecedent and causal; another is hypothetical, and of the consequence, which is also called subsequent and non-causal. The former arises from the indissoluble cohesion of the cause with the effect, e.g. By absolute necessity, according to the ordinary course of nature, the sun illuminates, water moistens, rhubarb purges, everything light is carried upward, everything heavy downward. The latter is, when something happens to a thing contingently if its nature be viewed in itself, yet given some hypothesis it cannot but happen to it, e.g. It happens that a man walks; yet given that he runs, it is necessary that he walks.

Prob. 1) If all things happen necessarily, by the necessity of an antecedent cause, or of providence, necessitating secondary causes to their operations, contingency is removed in human affairs. For that is properly contingent, which can be and not be. But those things which are necessarily from an antecedent necessary and immutable cause, namely from the immutable decree of God and the divine influx proceeding thence, determining secondary causes immutably to the effect, those cannot are not. Therefore contingencies are not. But to remove contingency from human affairs is absurd. 2) If divine providence imposes necessity upon all created things, so that they cannot act otherwise than God has decreed, the liberty of the human will is removed in all things, even in external and civil matters. For liberty implies indifference toward either side, and the will is and is called free by this, that all things requisite for acting being posited, it can act and not act, act this and act that. But assuming that by divine providence the will of man is determined to do this which it does, so that it can neither not do it nor do its opposite, it will not be indifferent toward either side, and consequently not free. But to remove the liberty of the human will is absurd.

You say: Indifference toward both opposites is not of the nature of free will; because even those who do not act under compulsion act freely, although they cannot act otherwise. Thus the holy angels most freely praise and worship God, whom nevertheless they cannot but praise and worship. The wicked, however, freely hate God: even if they cannot but hate. Resp. Certainly, indifference toward both opposites is of the nature of free will. If it were sufficient for the liberty of the will to act without compulsion, then even brutes would be free agents, which in many things do not act under compulsion. Nor do the examples alleged to the contrary hinder us. For the holy angels, in so far as they freely praise and worship God, are to that extent indifferent toward either of the opposites. They do indeed praise and worship God freely, not with a liberty of contrariety or specification: for they are determined to praise and worship God by their own intrinsic holiness; but with a liberty of contradiction or exercise, so that the act of praise or worship which they now exercise, they could for this instant not exercise. The same must be thought of the wicked angels, who are determined to evil, and by this lack the liberty of contrariety toward good and evil; whom nevertheless, since they exercise these evil acts freely, they exercise them in such a way that they could not exercise them, and thus they still possess the liberty of contradiction or exercise.

Antithesis The antithesis is that of Scotus, and those who follow him. Their arguments are: I. Whatever God has foreseen, that happens necessarily: God has foreseen every created thing: Therefore, every created thing happens necessarily. The major is proved; because, if those things which God foresaw as future did not happen necessarily, God would be deceived in his foreknowledge. Resp. Whatever God has foreseen, that happens necessarily either by absolute necessity, or or hypothetical.

Absolute necessity arises from the indissoluble cohesion of cause with effect. But divine foreknowledge is not the cause of things. Therefore, not everything that God foresees happens necessarily by absolute and causal necessity. Cf. what was deduced above, p. 273.

II. God is not an idle spectator of future events, but a powerful and wise director, who has all secondary causes in His hand, and directs them no less wisely than powerfully, where, when, and how He wills. Thus, therefore, future events do not depend on simple foreknowledge, but on will and power, and consequently they are not foreknown unless in an order where the will precedes, from which they are to have their existence through effectuation or permission.

Resp. 1) God remains not an idle spectator, but a wise and powerful director, although by an absolute decree He does not predetermine them in such a way that they cannot happen otherwise.

For, as AUGUSTINE testifies, lib. VII. de civit. Dei c. 30, God administers all things which He has created in such a way that He allows them to exercise their own movements.

2) That the decree of the divine will does not follow, but precedes, foreknowledge, we have proven in the superior question.

Instance: If the decree of the divine will does not predetermine future events, the divine intellect does not know them determinately; for they can be and not be, happen and not happen, if they are considered outside the decree of God.

Resp. Future contingencies are not predetermined by the divine decree: for thus they would not even be contingencies; because they would not proceed from secondary causes contingently, but necessarily.

For this reason, it is to be well noted that future contingencies can be viewed in two ways: (1) insofar as they can be produced or not produced by a particular cause, to be or not to be; in which respect they are called contingencies: (2) insofar as they are produced by their cause, which has freely determined itself to production; in which sense they are called future events.

Future contingencies are presented to the eternal, infinite knowledge of God to be known, just as they are to exist or not exist determinately through their free causes: for nothing that is to be certainly escapes the infinite knowledge of God.

III. Whatever cannot be hindered, that happens necessarily by absolute necessity: Whatever God foresees and has decreed, cannot be hindered: Therefore.

The minor is proved from Ps. CXV, 3. Our God is in the heavens; He does all that He wills, Is. XLVI, 10. My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my will. Resp.

Whatever God wills by an absolute will, and decrees to do by irresistible power (of which the cited passages seem to be understood), that cannot be hindered.

But besides the absolute will of God, there is also a conditional one, by which God wills something under a condition which is not fulfilled by all, e.g., Jn. XIV, 14. If you ask anything in my name, I will do it, Rom. VIII, 13. If by the Spirit you mortify the deeds of the body, you will live.

Besides the irresistible power of God, there is also a resistible one, e.g., God can convert and save all men through the Word and sacraments.

But many resist this power of God.

Cf. Luke VII, 30. Matt. XXIII, 37. You say: There is no conditional will of God and resistible power: For if a conditional will of God were given, it would depend on a condition: But the will of God is independent: And if a creature could resist the divine power, it would be more perfect and powerful than the Creator Himself, which is absurd. Resp.

The conditional will of God does not depend on a condition, but respects it in distributing benefits and punishments.

And a creature, by resisting the ordained power of God, is not more perfect or powerful than the Creator; because it resists not through some perfection and power, but through a shameful imperfection, e.g., through the blindness of the intellect, the perversity of the will, and the ἀταξίαν (disorder) of the desires; which are imperfections. Because even then, when God is hindered in the acts which He wills to effect by His ordained power, He could act in such a way that He would not be hindered, if indeed He willed to act by irresistible power.

IV. Every wise and powerful master necessarily attains the desired end by his provident care: God is a most wise and most powerful master: Therefore, by His provident care, He necessarily attains the end. Furthermore: He who necessarily attains his own end, his acts cannot be hindered: But God, etc. Therefore. The major is proved, because a wise and powerful lord does not direct his actions toward an end which he foreknows he will not attain: Men are frustrated of their end for lack of wisdom. Resp. There is a twofold end of divine providence: One common, namely, the manifestation of the glory of God: The other particular, which is the good of creatures. God always and everywhere attains the common end by his provident care: He does not always obtain the particular end, because he had decreed to attain the same under a certain condition, by a resistible power. Nor does this conflict with the wisdom and power of God. For a wise and powerful prince intends the safety of all citizens by prescribed laws, even though he foresees that many will not obey the laws, but will bring destruction upon themselves by their own fault.

V. This consequence is firm: God according to his eternal decree wills this to be done: Therefore it will immutably come to pass in the way in which he wills it to be done. The reason for the consequence is; because the will of God is immutable. I am Jehovah, I change not, Mal. III, 6. Resp. By distinguishing the consequent: Therefore it will immutably come to pass in the way in which God wills it to be done, with an immutability either causal or hypothetical, according as God willed that thing to be done either absolutely or under a certain condition.

VI. If necessity is not imposed upon creatures by the providence of God, especially upon the human will, this will be the queen and absolute mistress of divine concurrences, and of all free acts: The omnipotent dominion of God over the free acts of angels and men will be evacuated, and all things will be subjected to the dominion of fortune. But all these things are absurd: Therefore, by the providence of God, necessity is imposed upon created things, especially upon the human will, so that they act in this and not in another way. Resp. The human will is not the queen of divine concurrences, nor the absolute mistress of free acts, but is subordinated to divine providence, by which it is ruled, with a governance not captivating the liberty of the will, but sweetly disposing and ordinarily attempering it to created things. The omnipotent dominion of God is not evacuated or diminished, even if God does not always exercise it by absolute and irresistible power, but sometimes by ordered and resistible power. Nothing is committed to the dominion of fortune, because divine providence holds a middle ground between the chance and fortune of the Epicureans, and the fate of the Stoics, most wisely directing all things indeed, but not by any means taking away all liberty and all contingency.

Latin:

Quamuis omnia, quae Deus praeuidit, fiant necessario, necessitate hypothetica; non tamen prouidentia diuina imponit rebus omnibus, inprimis voluntati humanae, necessitatem absolutam.

Obs. I. Quaestio proposita intelligi potest de prouidentia Dei, prout tum actus Dei immanens, tum transiens est. Quando prouidentia Dei consideratur vt actus Dei immanens, complectitur cum praescientia intellectus decretum diuinae: spectata vt actus transiens, est conseruatio et gubernatio creaturarum. Respiciemus in hac quaestione potissimum praescientiam Dei cum decreto diuino coniunctam, an illa rebus creatis omnibus imponat necessitatem.

Obs. II. Necessitas alia est absoluta, siue consequentis, quam nonnulli auctores etiam antecedentem et causalem vocant; alia hypothetica, et consequentiae, quae etiam sequens et non causalis dicitur. Prior oritur ex indissolubili cohaesione causae cum effectu, v. gr. Absoluta necessitate, secundum ordinarium naturae cursum, sol illuminat, aqua humectat, rhabarbarum purgat, omne leue sursum, omne graue deorsum fertur. Posterior est, cum aliquid conuenit rei contingenter si eius natura in se spectetur, facta tamen aliqua hypothesi non potest ipsi non conuenire, v. gr. Hominem progredi contingit; posito tamen quod currat, necesse est ipsum progredi.

Prob. 1) Si omnia fiunt necessario, necessitate causae antecedentis, siue prouidentiae, causas secundas ad operationes suas necessitantis, tollitur contingentia in rebus humanis. Contingens enim proprie est, quod potest esse, et non esse. Sed quae sunt necessario ex antecedente causa necessaria, et immutabili, nempe ex immutabili Dei decreto et hinc proueniente influxu diuino, causas secundas ad effectum immutabiliter determinante, illa non possunt sunt non esse. Ergo contingentia non sunt. Sed contingentiam tollere ex rebus humanis, absurdum est. 2) Si prouidentia diuina omnibus rebus creatis imponit necessitatem, vt non aliter possint agere, quam Deus decreuit, tollitur libertas voluntatis humanæ in omnibus etiam externis & ciuilibus. Nam libertas inportat indifferentiam ad vtrumlibet, & voluntas per hoc est & dicitur libera, quod positis omnibus ad agendum requisitis potest agere, & non agere, agere hoc, & agere illud. Sed stante, quod per prouidentiam diuinam voluntas hominis determinetur ad agendum hoc, quod agit, vt neque id non agere, neque eius oppositum agere possit, non indifferens ad vtrumlibet, adeoque nec libera erit. Tollere autem libertatem voluntatis humanæ, absurdum est.

Dicis: De ratione liberi arbitrii non est indifferentia ad vtrumque oppositorum; quia libere agunt etiam ii, qui non agunt coacte, licet aliter agere nequeant. Ita sancti angeli liberrime Deum laudant & colunt, quem tamen non possunt non laudare & colere. Mali vero libere Deum oderunt: etiam si non possunt non odisse. Resp. Vtique indifferentia ad vtrumque oppositorum est de ratione liberi arbitrii. Si ad libertatem arbitrii sufficeret non coacte agere, bruta etiam essent libere agentia, quæ in multis non agunt coacte. Neque exempla in contrarium allegata nobis obsunt. Angeli sancti enim, in quantum libere laudant & colunt Deum, in tantum sunt indifferentes ad vtrumlibet oppositorum. Laudant vero & colunt Deum libere, non libertate contrarietatis, siue specificationis: Sunt enim ad laudandum & colendum Deum sua intrinseca sanctitate determinati; sed libertate contradictionis, siue exercitii, ita vt quem laudationis, vel cultus actum nunc exercent, possint pro hoc instanti non exercere. Idem sentiendum est de angelis malis, qui sunt determinati ad malum, & per hoc carent libertate contrarietatis ad bonum & malum; quos tamen actus malos libere exercent, eos ita exercent, vt possint non exercere, & sic pollent adhuc libertate contradictionis, siue exercitii .

Antithesis Antithesis est Scoti, & qui eum sequuntur. Quorum argumenta sunt: I. Quidquid Deus præuidit, id fit necessario: Omne creatum Deus præuidit: E. omne creatum fit necessario. Maior probatur; quia, si non necessario fierent, quæ Deus futura præuidit, Deus in sua præscientia falleretur. Resp. Quidquid Deus præuidit, id fit necessario vel necessitate absoluta, vel hypothetica.

Absoluta necessitas oritur ex indissolubili cohaesione causae cum effectu. At praescientia diuina non est causa rerum. E. non omne, quod Deus praevidet, fit necessario necessitate absoluta & causali. Conf. supra deducta, p. 273.

II. Deus non est otiosus spectator futurorum, sed potens & sapiens director, qui omnes causas secundas in sua habet manu, & non minus sapienter, quam potenter dirigit, quo, quando & quomodo vult. Sic ergo futura non a simplici pendent praescientia, sed a voluntate & potentia, adeoque non praescientur, nisi ordine praeunte voluntate, a qua existentiam suam sunt habitura per effectionem, aut permissionem.

Resp. 1) Manet Deus non otiosus spectator, sed sapiens & potens director, licet decreto absoluto ea sic non praedeterminet, vt aliter euenire nequeant.

Nam teste AVGVSTINO lib. VII. de ciuit. Dei c. 30. Deus omnia, quae creauit, ita administrat, vt ipsa proprios exercere motus sinat.

2) Praescientiam decretum voluntatis diuinae non sequi, sed praecedere superiori quaestione euicimus.

Instantia: Si decretum voluntatis diuinae futura non praedeterminat, intellectus diuinus ea determinate non cognoscit; possunt enim esse, & non esse, euenire & non euenire, si extra decretum Dei considerentur.

Resp. Futura contingentia a decreto diuino non praedeterminantur: sic enim ne essent quidem contingentia; quia a causis secundis non contingenter procederent, sed necessario.

Quam ob rem probe notandum, quod contingentia futura bifariam spectari possint: (1) quatenus a causa particulari possunt produci, & non produci, esse, & non esse; quo respectu vocantur contingentia: (2) quatenus a causa sua ad productionem libere se determinata producuntur; quo sensu dicuntur futura.

Futura contingentia ab aeterno infinitae Dei scientiae cognoscenda obiiciuntur, prout illa per suas causas liberas determinate exstitura, aut non exstitura sunt: infinitam quippe scientiam Dei nihil certo futurum fugit.

III. Quidquid non potest impediri, illud fit necessario necessitate absoluta: Quidquid Deus praeuidet & decreuit, non potest impediri: Ergo.

Minor probatur e Pf. CXV, 3. Deus noster in caelis est; omnia, quae vult, facit, Es. XLVI, 10. Consilium meum stabit, & omnem voluntatem meam faciam.

Resp. Quidquid Deus vult voluntate absoluta, & decernit facere potentia irresistibili (de qua loca citata intelligenda esse videntur), illud non potest impediri.

At praeter voluntatem Dei absolutam datur etiam conditionata, qua Deus aliquid vult sub conditione, quae non ab omnibus impletur, v. gr. Io. XIV, 14. Si quid petieritis in nomine meo, ego faciam, Rom. IIX, 13. Si spiritu actiones corporis mortificatis, viuetis.

Praeter potentiam Dei irresistibilem datur etiam resistibilis, v. gr.

Deus potest per verbum & sacramenta omnes homines conuertere & saluare. At multi huic potentiae Dei resistunt. Conf.

Luc. VII, 30. Matth. XXIII, 37. Dicis: Non datur voluntas Dei conditionata & potentia resistibilis: Nam si daretur voluntas Dei conditionata, illa a conditione dependeret: At voluntas Dei est independens: Et si creatura potentiae diuinae posset resistere, perfectior & potentior esset ipso creatore, quod est absurdum.

Resp. Voluntas Dei conditionata a conditione non dependet, sed eandem in distribuendis beneficiis & suppliciis respicit.

Et creatura resistendo potentiae Dei ordinatae non est perfectior, aut potentior creatore; quia non per quandam perfectionem & potentiam, sed per turpem quandam imperfectionem resistit, v. gr. per caecitatem intellectus, peruersitatem voluntatis, & ἀταξίαν cupiditatum; quae sunt imperfectiones. Quin etiam tum, cum Deus in actibus, quos potentia ordinata vult efficere, impeditur, ita posset agere, vt non impediretur, si nimirum agere vellet potentia irresistibili.

IV. Omnis dominus sapiens & potens necessario assequitur prouida sua cura desideratum finem: Deus est dominus sapientissimus & potentissimus: Ergo prouida sua cura necessario assequitur finem. Porro: Qui suum finem necessario assequitur, illius actus non possunt impediri: Atqui Deus &c. Ergo. Maior probatur, quia dominus sapiens & potens suas actiones non in eum dirigit finem, quem se non affecuturum esse prænouit: Frustrantur homines fine ob defectum sapientiæ. Resp. Duplex est finis prouidentiæ diuinæ: Vnus communis, nempe manifestatio gloriæ Dei: Alter particularis, qui est bonum creaturarum. Finem communem Deus prouida sua cura semper & vbique assequitur: Finem particularem non semper obtinet, propterea, quod eundem sub certa conditione, potentia resistibili assequi decreuerat. Neque hoc pugnat cum sapientia & potentia Dei. Nam princeps sapiens & potens præscriptis legibus omnium ciuium intendit salutem, licet plurimos legibus non obtemperaturos, sed propria culpa perniciem sibi attracturos esse, prospiciat.

V. Firma est hæc consequentia: Deus secundum æternum suum decretum hoc vult fieri: Ergo immutabiliter fiet eo modo, quo vult fieri. Ratio confequentiæ est; quia voluntas Dei est immutabilis. Ego Iehouah, nec mutor, Mal. III, 6. Resp. Distinguendo consequens: Ergo immutabiliter fiet eo modo, quo Deus vult fieri, immutabilitate siue causali, siue hypothetica, prout Deus id voluit fieri vel absolute, vel sub certa conditione.

VI. Si per prouidentiam Dei non imponitur necessitas creaturis, inprimis voluntati humanæ, hæc erit regina & absoluta domina concursuum diuinorum, & omnium actuum liberorum: Dominium omnipotens Dei in actus liberos angelorum & hominum euacuabitur, fortunæ autem dominatui omnia subiicientur. At hæc omnia sunt absurda: E. per prouidentiam Dei imponitur necessitas rebus creatis, inprimis voluntati humanæ, vt hoc & non alio modo agant. Resp. Voluntas humana non est regina concursuum diuinorum, neque absoluta domina actuum liberorum, sed subordinatur prouidentiæ diuinæ, a qua regitur, regimine non captiuante libertatem arbitrii, sed fuauiter disponente & rebus creatis ordinarie attemperato. Omnipotens Dei dominium non euacuatur, aut imminuitur, licet Deus illud non semper exerceat potentia absoluta & irreſiſtibili, sed interdum potentia ordinata & refiſtibili. Fortunæ dominatui nihil committitur, quia prouidentia diuina inter Epicureorum casum fortunamque, & Stoicorum fatum medium tenet, sapientissime quidem omnia dirigendo, non vero omnem libertatem omnemque contingentiam prorsus tollendo.


### Quest. XII. Is fate to be admitted in the government of created things?

The Stoic fate is not to be asserted, by which all things happen by absolute and inevitable necessity; nor the more rigid astrological fate, by which even the free acts of the human will depend upon and are determined by the influx of the stars: but the Christian fate is to be acknowledged, which is the necessary connection of causes and effects, by an extrinsic necessity, insofar as it is infallibly foreknown by God, constituted by an absolute or conditioned decree, and governed by a divine governance that sweetly disposes.

Obs. 1. The name fatum (fate) has its origin from fando (speaking), just as scitum (decree) from sciendo (knowing). Fate, therefore, is that which one has fatus (spoken), i.e., destined, decreed: just as a pactum (covenant) is that which one has pactus (agreed).

Obs. 2. Fate is either mental, or active, or real, or subjective. The former is the command and decree of God, which he himself has from eternity fatus, i.e., decreed, that it should come to pass. The latter is the order of secondary causes executing divine providence. It is called fate by extrinsic denomination: just as a desired apple is said to be loved by me, because my love terminates in the apple. See DANNHAUER, Hodosophia Christiana, Phænomenon III, p. 321.

Obs. 3. Fate is divided into physical, astrological or mathematical, Stoic, and Christian. Physical fate is the order of natural causes, necessary and infallible effects physical, astrological or mathematical, Stoic, and Christian. Physical fate is the order of natural causes, necessary and infallible effects

bringing them forth, subject to God the author of nature; e.g., If rain falls from the clouds, it irrigates the earth, the sun absorbs the rain.

Astrological fate is the influx of the stars into inferior bodies, variously disposing and directing these, and it is either more rigid or more soft, in the view of the astrologers, who explain it in diverse ways. It is more rigid, in that all human acts, even voluntary ones, are said to depend upon and be determined by the influx of the stars.

It is more soft, in that it proceeds with human liberty unharmed.

Stoic fate is defined by Gellius, L. VI. N. A. c. 2, as being a certain eternal, unchangeable series of things, and a chain rolling itself, and implicating itself through eternal orders of consequence, from which it is fitted and connected.

The property of this Stoic fate is absolute and inevitable necessity.

Seneca teaches this in lib. II. Qu. natural. Q. 36. What do you understand by fate? I think it is the necessity of all things and actions, which no force may break.

Obs. 4. Christian fate is defined by the connection of causes and effects, which the memorable utterance of God teaches us in Hos. II, 21.
