I will hear the heavens, and they shall hear the earth, and the earth shall hear the corn, and the wine, and the oil, and these shall hear Israel. Contained in these divine words is the concatenated series of creatures depending upon the governance of the first cause. Christian fate is called the necessary connection of causes and effects: because if necessity of fate is not its form, it is certainly its inseparable property.

For it is called something fatal for this reason; because it is necessary, immutable, and certain. Lipsius, lib. I. physiol. stoic. cap. 12, calls the necessity of fate a sister, as it were, a twin. But one must accurately distinguish between intrinsic, absolute, consequent, or causal necessity, and extrinsic, hypothetical, consequential, or non-causal necessity.

Fate is called a connection of causes and effects, necessary not by intrinsic, absolute, and causal necessity, or by a species of foreknowledge, or divine decree.

For foreknowledge is extrinsically concerned with its knowable object, and is not the cause of it. The antistites of the primitive church taught this excellently. Origen in Rom. IIX. says: Something will not be because God knows it will be future; but because it is future, therefore it is known by God before it happens. Chrysost. homil. LX. in Matth. Not because the Savior foretold that scandals were to come, do they therefore happen; but because they were altogether going to be, therefore He foretold them.

Augustin. libr. III. de lib. arbitr. c. IV. supports this. Just as by your memory you do not force things to have happened which have passed: So by His foreknowledge God does not force things to be done which are to be future.

And just as you have done some things which you did, and yet not all things which you remembered: So God foreknows all things of which He Himself is the author; yet He is not the author of all things which He foreknows. See D. Calov. in system. tom. II. p. 546. Nor by reason of the divine decree, to which the order and connection of causes and effects is subject, is divine fate necessary by absolute causal necessity; because the divine decree does not predetermine future things, but disposes them sweetly and easily according to the nature and capacity of creatures, so that the contingency of things and the liberty of human will may not be taken away. The divine decree, directing the connection of causes and effects, is in one respect absolute, in another conditioned, or hypothetical.

The former is done divinely without regard to a condition to be fulfilled by creatures; the latter includes a condition to be fulfilled by creatures. Obs. 5. By like reason, Christian fate is divided into absolute and conditioned. The former is when the order of causes and effects is governed by an absolute decree of the divine will, and is simply immovable and invincible: The latter is when the connection of causes and effects flows under a hypothetical divine decree, and thus is immutable only with the supplement of the hypothesis. Into ordinary and extraordinary.

The former is tempered to the nature and ordinary course of creatures: The latter transcends the order of nature.

Prob. 1 Absolute Christian fate from those sayings of Scripture in which the will of God and His irresistible power are treated. The royal psalmist says gravely, Ps. CXV, 4. Our God is in heaven; he does all that he wills. The prophet Isaiah asserts the same, c. XIV, 27. Jehovah Zebaoth has decreed; who then shall make it void? And his hand is stretched out; and who shall restrain it? And c. XLIV, 10. My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure. By most clear examples. Absolutely fatal is the creation and preservation of the world, Ps. CIV, 5. the duration of the catholic church (not particular, Jerusalemite, or Roman) to the end of the world, Matth. XVI, 8. the necessity of dying incumbent upon all men, and the final judgment, Hebr. IX, 27. Absolutely fatal was the hour of Christ's passion, Io. VII, 30. absolutely fatal the hour in which Christ turned water into wine, Io. II, 4. it is absolutely fatal that I was born in this province, at this hour and day. D. DANNHAVER calls every divine hour absolutely fatal, in Hodoph. III. p. 325. Absolutely fatal are those things which happen against the effort, motion, and counsels of creatures, e.g. Esau, meeting Jacob, had conceived a plan to oppress him; but God moderated all other things: for he addressed Jacob in a friendly manner, embraced him blandly, and kissed him sweetly, Gen. 33.

Prob. 2 Christian fate is hypothetical, or conditional. Conditionately fatal is the temporal prosperity and dignity of men. This we learn from Deut. XXVIII, 1. ff. If by obeying you shall obey the voice of Jehovah your God, keeping to do all his commandments, which I am commanding you today: Jehovah your God will set you high above all the nations of the earth. For all these blessings shall come upon you, and overtake you; if you obey the voice of Jehovah your God. Blessed shall you be in the city, blessed in the field. It is illustrated by an example. According to the decree of God, Joseph shall cast light in the Egyptian kingdom, and be a sun among his brothers; if he shall perform obedience to his father Jacob, walk piously, prudently, and chastely in the house of Potiphar, interpret all things both for his fellow-captives in prison and for King Pharaoh, and offer useful counsel to him. But if he shall do otherwise, either by struggling against his father, or by following lust, or by despising his fellow-captives, he shall perish ingloriously. Conditionately fatal are marriages. For house and wealth are the inheritance of fathers: but from Jehovah is an intelligent wife. Prov. XIX, 14. Fatal, I say, are marriages, not by reason of an inflexible decree, as if it were simply impossible for a man to marry another wife than he does, or for a woman to marry another man than she does; but by reason of a hypothetical decree, which regards the piety of the man or the woman, Ps. CXXVIII, ff. Sir. XXVI, 3. Hypothetically fatal is the end of life. See above qu. VIII. Conditionately fatal are the occasions of doing things opportunely, shown by the divine finger; he who seizes them is master of fatal happiness. The spoil left by the fleeing Syrian army was offered to the Samaritans by the divine hand, which, when they embraced it, they held by fate. 2 Reg. VII, 16.

You say: I. The doctrine of fate has long since been eliminated from the church. For AUGUSTINE says shrewdly, tr. 37. in Io. O! if your heart were not fatuous, you would not believe in fate. Therefore, the doctrine of fate is not to be introduced into the church by postliminy. R. Stoic and astrological fate, more rigid, has long since been eliminated from the church. For thus AUGUSTINE, L. V. de C. D. c. I. If anyone therefore attributes human affairs to fate, because he calls the very will or power of God by the name of fate, let him hold his opinion, but correct his language. For why does he not say this first, which he is about to say later, when someone has asked him what he meant by fate? For when men hear that, they do not understand it, except as the force of the position of the stars. But concerning Christian fate the presbyter of Hippo judges far otherwise, L. V. de C. D. c. 7. But those who call by the name of fate the connection and series of all causes, whereby everything that happens comes to pass, are not to be contended with much nor labored with over a dispute about a word; seeing that they ascribe the very order of causes, and a certain connection, to the supreme will of God. Nor is the doctrine of fate useless; for through it, when rightly taught, there remains a hope inclined toward the divine, not indeed wandering and idle.

standing, the glory of foreknowledge and decree, and to man liberty, whether native in the lower sphere, or given in the higher, as judged by Dannhav. in hodof. phanom. III. p. 328.

You say: II. Whatever removes the contingency of things and the liberty of human will, that is not to be asserted; but by fate it is removed, etc. Therefore. Response: If we were to teach that fate is a chain of causes and effects, necessary in human life by intrinsic necessity, determined from heaven and absolutely decreed, we could rightly and deservedly be accused of destroying by the doctrine of fate the contingency of things and the liberty of human will; but we teach and confess that fate is a connection of causes and effects, necessary in human life by extrinsic necessity, insofar as it is infallibly foreknown by God, and established by an absolute or conditional decree, and is governed by the divine regime sweetly disposing all things.

From which we distinguish between absolute fate and conditional fate.

You say: III. Every fate, properly so called, is immobile, or immutable. Hypothetical fate is not immutable. Therefore hypothetical fate is not fate properly so called. The major premise is evident; because we commonly call that fatal which is immutable.

Response: Absolute fate is simply and immutably so; but hypothetical fate is immutable in a composite and complete sense, if it is taken together with the fulfillment of the hypothesis, e.g.,

If Noah will constantly worship God, and at His command will build an ark, he will enter the built ark, he will not perish in the flood, but will be saved, the fate is immutable: yet it can be changed by the cutting off of the hypothesis, or the non-fulfillment of the annexed condition.

Latin:

Non afferendum est fatum Stoicum, quo omnia absoluta & ineuitabili necessitate eueniant; neque fatum astrologicum rigidius, a quo etiam actus liberi voluntatis humanæ ab influxu astrorum dependeant ac determinentur: sed agnoscendum est fatum christianum, quod est connexio caussarum & effectuum necessaria, necessitate extrinseca, quatenus a Deo infallibiliter præscita, decreto absoluto vel conditionato constituta, & regimine diuino fuauiter disponente gubernata est.

Obs. 1. Fatum nomen habet a fando, sicut, scitum a sciendo. Fatum igitur est, quod quis fatus est, i. e. destinauit, decreuit: sicut pactum est, quod quis pactus est.

Obs. 2. Fatum aliud mentale, siue actiuum, aliud reale, siue subiectiuum est. Illud est iussum & decretum Dei, quod ipse ab æterno fatus est, i. e. decreuit, vt fiat. Hoc est ordo caussarum secundarum prouidentiam diuinam exsequentium. Vocatur fatum denominatione extrinseca: fient pomum dicitur a me anatum, quia amor meus ad pomum terminatur. Vid. DANNHA V. hodof. phæn. III. p. 321.

Obs. 3. Diuiditur fatum in physicum, astrologicum, siue mathematicum, Stoicum, & christianum. Fatum physicum est caussarum naturalium ordo, effectus necessarios & infallibiles physicum, astrologicum, siue mathematicum, Stoicum, & christianum. Fatum physicum est causarum naturalium ordo, effectus necessarios & infallibiles

biles inferens, Deo naturae auctori subiectus; v.gr.

Si e nubibus pluuia decidit, haec irrigat terram, sol pluuiam resorbet. Fatum astrologicum est astrorum in corpora inferiora influxus, varie ista disponens ac dirigens, estque vel rigidius, vel mollius, respectu astrologorum, illud diuersimode explicantium. Rigidius est, quo omnes actus humani, etiam voluntarii, ab astrorum influxu dependere & determinari dicuntur.

Mollius est, quod illaesa libertate humana procedit.

Fatum Stoicum definitur a Gellio L. VI. N. A. c. 2. quod sit sempiterna quaedam indeclinabilis series rerum, & catena voluens semetipsam, sese & implicans per aeternos consequentiae ordines, ex quibus apta, connexaque est.

Huius fati Stoici proprietas est absoluta & ineuitabilis necessitas.

Docet hanc Seneca lib. II. Qu. natural. Q. 36. Quid intelligis per fatum? Existimo necessitatem rerum omnium actionumque, quam nulla vis rumpat.

Obs. 4. Fatum christianum definitur per connexionem causarum & effectuum, quam memorabile effatum Dei nos docet Hos. II, 21. Exaudiam caelos, & hi exaudient terram, & terra exaudiet frumentum, mustum & oleum, & haec exaudient Israelem. Continentur in his verbis diuinis concatenata series creaturarum a gubernatione causae primae dependentium. Fatum Christianum dicitur connexio causarum & effectuum necessaria: quia necessitas fati si non forma, certe inseparabilis proprietas est.

Nam ideo aliquid fatale dicitur; quia necessarium, immutabile & certum est. Lipsius lib. I. physiol. stoic. cap. 12. vocat necessitatem fati sororem quasi gemellam. Accurate autem distinguendum est inter necessitatem intrinsecam, absolutam, consequentis, siue caussalem: & inter necessitatem extrinsecam, hypotheticam, consequentiae, siue non caussalem.

Fatum dicitur connexio causarum & effectuum, necessaria non necessitate intrinseca, absoluta & caussali, siue species praescientiam, siue decretum diuinum.

Nam praescientia extrinsece versatur circa suum scibile, neque huius caussa est. Praeclare hoc docuerunt antifites primitiuae ecclesiae. Origenes in Rom. IIX. inquit: Non propterea aliquid erit, quia id scit Deus futurum; sed quia futurum est, ideo scitur a Deo, antequam fiat. Chrysost. homil. LX. in Matth. Non quia scandala futura praedixit faluator, idcirco eueniunt; sed quoniam omnino futura erant, idcirco praedixit.

His suffragatur Augustin. libr. III. de libr. arbitr. c. IV. Sicut memoria tua non cogis facta esse, quae praeterierunt: Sic praescientia sua Deus non cogit facienda, quae futura sunt.

Et sicut tu quaedam, quae fecisti, nec tamen omnia, quae meministi, fecisti: Ita Deus omnia, quorum ipse auctor est, praescit; non tamen omnium, quae praescit, auctor est. Vid. D. Calov. in system. tom. II. p. 546. Neque ratione decreti diuini, cui subiacet ordo & connexio causarum atque effectuum, necessarium est fatum diuinum necessitate absoluta caussali; propterea quod decretum diuinum res futuras non praedeterminat, sed suauiter & facile secundum indolem & capacitatem creaturarum disponit, vt ne contingentia rerum, arbitriique humani libertas tollatur. Decretum diuinum, connexionem causarum & effectuum dirigens, aliud est absolutum, aliud conditionatum, siue hypotheticum.

Illud diuinitus factum est citra intuitum conditionis a creaturis implendae, hoc conditionem, a creaturis implendam, includit. Obs. 5. Pari ratione diuiditur fatum christianum in absolutum, & conditionatum, Illud est, quando ordo causarum & effectuum regitur a decreto voluntatis diuinae absoluto, atque simpliciter immobile ac inuincibile est: Hoc est, quando connexio causarum & effectuum fluit sub decreto diuino hypothetico, adeoque non nisi cum supplemento hypotheseos sumtum immutabile est. In ordinarium, & extraordinarium.

Illud indoli & currui ordinario creaturarum est attemperatum: Hoc ordinem naturae transcendit.

Prob. 1 Fatum christianum absolutum ex iis dictis scripturae, in quibus de voluntate Dei, potentiaque ipsius irresistibili agitur. Grauiter ait psaltes regius, Ps. CXV, 4. Deus noster in caelis est; omnia, quae vult, facit. Idem asserit propheta Iesaias, c. XIV, 27. Iehovah Zebaoth decrevit; quis ergo irritum reddet? Et manus eius extensa est; & quis reprimet eam? Et c. XLIV, 10. Consilium meum stabit, & omnem meam voluntatem faciam. Exemplis clarissimis. Absolute fatalis est mundi creatio & conservatio, Ps. CIV, 5. ecclesiae catholicae (non particularis, Solymitanae, vel Romanae) duratio ad finem mundi, Matth. XVI, 8. omnibus hominibus incumbens moriendi necessitas, & extremum iudicium, Hebr. IX, 27. Absolute fatalis erat hora passionis Christi, Io. VII, 30. absolute fatalis hora, qua Christus aquam convertebat in vinum, Io. II, 4. absolute fatale est, me in hac provincia, hac hora & die natum esse. D. DANNHAVERVS omnem horam divinam vocat absolute fatalem, in hodoph. III. p. 325. Absolute fatalia sunt, quae eveniunt contra nixum, motum & consilia creaturarum, v. gr. Esauus Iacobo occurrens hunc opprimendi consilium ceperat; omnia vero alia moderante Deo faciebat: nam Iacobum amice compellabat, blande amplexabatur, & suaviter osculabatur, Gen. 33. *

Prob. 2 Fatum christianum hypotheticum, sive conditionatum.* Conditionate fatale est hominum temporalis prosperitas & dignitas. Id quod discimus ex Deut. XXVIII, 1. sqq. Si obediendo obedueris voci Iehovah Dei tui, custodiendo ad faciendum omnia praecepta eius, quae ego sum praecipiens tibi hodie: dabit te Iehovah Deus tuus excelsum super omnes gentes terrae. Venient enim super te omnes benedictiones hae, & assequentur te; si obedueris voci Iehovah Dei tui. Benedictus tu eris in urbe, benedictus in agro. Illustratur exemplo. Iuxta decretum Dei Iosephus ingesserit lumen in regno Aegyptiaco, & sol inter fratres; si patri Iacobo praestabit obsequium, in domo Potipharis pie, prudenter & caste ambulabit, omnia tum concaptivis in carcere, tum regi Pharaoni interpretabitur, atque utile huic consilium suggeret. Sin secus fecerit, vel patri obluctando, vel libidinem sectando, vel concaptivos despiciendo, inglorius peribit. Conditionate fatalia sunt connubia. Nam domus & opes sunt hereditas patrum: sed a Iehovah est uxor intelligens. Prou. XIX, 14. Fatalia sunt, inquam, coniugia, non ratione decreti inflexibilis, quasi simpliciter impossibile sit, virum aliam ducere uxorem, quam ducit, vel mulierem alii nubere viro, quam cui nubit; sed ratione decreti hypothetici, quo respicitur pietas viri, vel mulieris, Ps. CXXIIX, sqq. Sir. XXVI, 3. Hypothetice fatalis est terminus vitae. Vid. supra qu. VIII. Conditionate fatales sunt occasiones rerum opportune gerendarum, digito divino monstratae; quas qui arripit, fatalis compos est felicitatis. Praeda a Syriaco exercitu fugitivo relicta Samaritanis divina manu est oblata, quam cum sunt amplexi, fato tenuerunt. 2 Reg. VII, 16.

Dicis: I. Doctrina de fato iamdudum ex ecclesia eliminata est. Argute enim inquit AVGVSTIN. tr. 37. in Io. O! si cor tuum non esset fatuum, non crederes fatum. Ergo doctrina de fato postliminio in ecclesiam non est introducenda. R. Fatum Stoicum & astrologicum rigidius iamdudum ex ecclesia eliminatum est. Sic enim AVGVSTIN. L. V. de C. D. c. I. Si propterea quisquam res humanas fato tribuit, quod ipsam Dei voluntatem, vel potestatem fati nomine appellet, sententiam teneat, linguam corrigat. Cur enim hoc primum non dicit, quod postea dicturus est, cum ab illo quisquam quaesiverit, quid dixerit fatum? Nam id homines quando audiunt, non intelligunt, nisi vim positionis fiderum. De fato autem christiano longe aliter iudicat praesul Hipp. L. V. de C. D. c. 7. At qui omnium connexionem seriemque causarum, qua fit omne, quod fit, fati nomine appellant, non multum cum eis de verbi controversia certandum atque laborandum est; quandoquidem ipsum causarum ordinem, & quandam connexionem summae Dei tribuunt voluntati. Neque inutilis est doctrina de fato; liquidem per eam, recte traditam, manet divinae pronae, non sane peregrinanti ac otiose spe.

stanti, gloria praescientiae decretique, & homini libertas, seu nativa in sphaera inferiori, seu dativa in superiori, iudice Dannhav. in hodof. phanom. III. p. 328.

Dicis: II. Quocunque tollitur contingentia rerum & libertas arbitrii humani, illud non est afferendum; Atqui fato tollitur &c. Ergo. Resp. Si doceremus, fatum esse catenam causarum & effectuum, in vita humana necessariam necessitate intrinseca, coelitus determinatam ac absolute decretam, iure meritoque accusari possemus, quod doctrina de fato sublatum iremus contingentiam rerum & libertatem arbitrii humani; sed docemus & confitemur, fatum esse connexionem causarum & effectuum, in vita humana necessariam necessitate extrinseca, quatenus infallibiliter a Deo praescita, & decreto absoluto, vel conditionato constituta, regimine divino suaviter disponente gubernatur.

Ex quo distinguimus inter fatum absolutum, & conditionatum.

Dicis: III. Omne fatum, proprie dictum, est immobile, seu immutabile. Fatum hypotheticum non est immutabile. Ergo fatum hypotheticum non est fatum proprie dictum. Maior constat; quia id communiter appellamus fatale, quod est immutabile.

Resp. Fatum absolutum est simpliciter & immobile; fatum autem hypotheticum est immutabile in sensu composito atque completo, si una cum suppletio hypothesios sumatur, v.gr.

Si Noachus Deum constanter colet, & ad iussum ipsius arcam exstruet, exstructam intrabit, non peribit in diluvio, sed feruabitur, fatum est immutabile: mutari tamen potest per apocopen hypothesios, sive non-impletionem annexae conditionis.


### Q. XIII. Is there such a thing as fortune?

Fortune, which is an event by accident, accompanying an effect intended in itself by a freely acting cause, does not exist by reason of the omniscient and most wise God ; but with respect to the ignorant man .

Proof a. With respect to God, there is nothing fortuitous or unforeseen; because the providence (πρόνοια) of God governs all things, Wis. XIV, 3.

There is therefore no place for fortune in the kingdom of divine providence, but what we call a fortuitous good is offered by the hand of the most wise God. Gen. XXII, 8.

Proof b. A farmer plowing his field with a plowshare finds a treasure unexpectedly. He calls the finding of the treasure fortune, or a fortuitous effect. He did not intend to find the treasure; since he was ignorant that it lay hidden in the field.

For which reason folly, and error, and ignorance of things and causes, introduced the name of fortune, as Lactantius judges in lib. III. instit. c. 29.

Latin:

Fortuna, quae est euentus per accidens, effectum per se intentum causae libere agentis concomitans, non datur ratione Dei omniscii, & sapientissimi ; sed respectu hominis ignorantis .

Prob. a. Respectu Dei non datur aliquid fortuitum aut improuisum; quia πρόνοια Dei cuncta gubernat, Sap. XIV, 3.

Nullus igitur fortunae in regno prouidentiae divinae locus, sed quod nos vocamus bonum fortuitum, offertur a manu Dei sapientissimi. Gen. XXII, 8.

Prob. b. Agricola vomere proscindens agrum suum, ex improuiso inuenit thesaurum. Inuentionem thesauri vocat fortunam, seu effectum fortuitum. Thesaurum inuenire non intendebat; quippe quem in agro delitescere ignorabat.

Quam ob rem stultitia, & error, & ignoratio rerum & causarum, nomen fortunae induxit, censente Lactantio lib. III. instit. c. 29.


### Q. XIV. By what acts is the administration (διοίκησις), or providence of God strictly so called, completed?

Administration (διοίκησις),

or the actual providence of God, is completed by three acts: conservation, cooperation, and government.

Obs. I. These are the general or common acts of divine providence, concerning all creatures; but there are also more special acts, which, since they spread through the whole of theology, cannot be considered here, but must be explained in their own peculiar places or seats.

Obs. II. In the opinion of some theologians, the acts to which divine providence, exercised concerning creatures, is limited, are two, conservation and government, which are said to import both a universal concurrence with secondary causes and a special direction of created agents.

Cf. D. Baier, compend. theol. p. 356.

Latin:

Διοίκησις,

siue actualis Dei prouidentia, absoluitur tribus actibus, conseruatione, cooperatione, & gubernatione.

Obs. I. Sunt hi actus prouidentiae diuinae generales, siue communes, omnes creaturas concernentes; Dantur autem actus etiam specialiores, qui cum per totam theologiam se diffundant, hic considerari nequeunt, sed in peculiaribus locis aut sedibus suis explicandi sunt.

Obs. II. Ex mente nonnullorum theologorum actus, ad quos, circa creaturas exercendos, terminatur prouidentia diuina, sunt duo, conseruatio & gubernatio, quae tum vniuersalem cum causis secundis concursum, tum specialem agentium creatorum directionem importare dicitur.

Conf. D. Baieri compend. theol. p. 356.


### XV. What is conservation?

Conservation is an act of divine providence, by which God sustains all things created by Him, so that they may persist in their own nature, innate properties, and powers received in creation.

Obj. I. Creation and conservation are divine acts distinct not in themselves, on the part of the thing, but by our intellect, from a diverse connotation; for conservation is indeed continued creation. Nor is God said to conserve a creature for any other reason than insofar as He positively continues the action by which He had produced the creature. This is evident most of all from the fact that, just as duration, on the part of the thing, is nothing other than continued existence; so conservation is nothing other than continued creation. It is illustrated by a simile: By the same emanative action by which the sun first poured forth rays from itself, it continues the perennial efflux of rays: So God, by the same action by which He first conferred being upon creatures, continues to confer being upon them. They are distinguished, however, by diverse connotations. For creation connotes that the thing did not exist before; conservation presupposes that the thing existed before: creation gives the beginning of being; conservation, the continuation of being.

Obj. II. Divine conservation is not a merely negative or indirect act; for it does not consist in this, that God does not wish to destroy or annihilate created things, but leaves them to their own vigor, as far as they can be vigorous and endure, by the force implanted in them through creation; but it is a positive and direct act, by which God, in general, flows into the efficient causes of things to be conserved by a true and real influx, so that they may persist and remain in their nature, properties, and powers.

Obj. III. God conserves species and individuals. He conserves species by vindicating the essences of things from destruction, and by imparting perseverance to them. He conserves individuals by substituting new ones in the place of those that perish, so that the essence of the species may persevere.

Obj. IV. Annihilation is opposed to conservation, which is the destruction of creatures through the subtraction of divine influx. God can, however, if He wills, annihilate all creatures, both spiritual and corporeal. For just as all creatures depend on God in being and acting: so they can be annihilated by the same, through the subtraction of His conserving hand.

Obj. V. God conserves some creatures by Himself alone, such as angels, the heavens, and simple bodies: others He conserves with creatures concurring, such as men, plants, etc. The divine conservation of creatures is proved both from the light of Scripture and from the light of nature. The whole of Holy Scripture abundantly testifies to the conservation of created things through divine influx. It suffices for us to have adduced the following.

In the O.T., the hierophant proclaims the providence of God, the conservatrix of this universe, Ps. 119:89, 90, 91. Thou art forever, Jehovah. Thy word stands in the heavens. Thy faithfulness is unto generation and generation: Thou hast established the earth and it stands. But Thy judgments stand even today: because all things are Thy servants. The sense is: Heaven, earth, and whatever is in them, by the word of Thy command and the truth of Thy governance, O Lord, persist and remain, both by reason of substance and by reason of powers of acting: for all creatures are truly Thy servants, so that whatever they are, they are Thine, and whatever they do, they do under Thy command and governance; since, like servants, they obey all Thy commands most promptly. In the N.T., Heb. 1:3, the conservation and sustentation of all things is ascribed to the Son of God (though not excluding God the Father and the Holy Spirit). For it is said φέρων τὰ πάντα τῷ ῥήματι τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ, bearing all things by the word of His power. Obj. Others translate τὸ φέρειν as to carry, to bear, to sustain. Others render it, to act, to move, to govern. In the judgment of SEB. SCHMIDT in Comm. in loc. p. 45, the word φέρειν can here be taken so broadly as to embrace both. For God does not merely carry things at rest, but also moves things in motion. By ῥῆμα we understand act of God, most free and most easy, through his power, the divine omnipotence itself. Πάντα (All things) comprehend everything, except the one who carries them. But God alone, Father and Holy Spirit, with the Son of God, carry all things; and thus τὰ πάντα (all things) are all created things, whether they be things, or persons, or actions. Wherefore this is the meaning of the apostle's words: The Son of God, together with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, sustains, cherishes, and moderates all created things by the act of his infinite power, most freely and most easily.

From the light of nature we learn (1) That preservation is continued creation. He who created the world, and whatever is in it, the same preserves it. For just as the light of the sun does not exist, does not shine, does not remain constantly, unless it emanates from the sun: So no creature exists, endures, or acts, unless it is preserved by God. (2) That God is most present to creatures. Wherefore the supreme inspector and ruler of the world, to which creatures he is most present, can preserve them according to his omnipotence, knows them according to his infinite wisdom, and wills to preserve them according to his most exuberant goodness. (3) That if created things could consist without the influx of God, something could remain while God resisted, or withdrew his influx. But if God withdraws his influx, all things collapse, and fall back into nothingness.

Qvæst. XVI. What is cooperation, or the concurrence of God?

Concurrence, or the cooperation of God, is an act of divine providence, by which God gently flows into the actions and effects of secondary causes with a general and immediate influx, according to the requirement and nature of each creature.

Objection. God not only gives creatures the powers of acting, and commands those given to endure, but also flows immediately into the action and effect of creatures, so that that effect is produced not by God alone, nor by the creature alone, but by one and the same total efficiency simultaneously from God and the creature; from God, namely, as the first and universal cause, and from the creature, as the second and particular cause.

The divine concurrence is proved both from the light of revelation and from the light of reason. The light of revelation testifies (1) that not only our powers of moving and acting, but the motion itself, or action, depends on God. Most well-known are the words of Paul, Acts 17:27-28. God is not far from each one of us; for in him we live, move, and have our being. (2) All our works are attributed to God, as the first and universal cause, 1 Cor. 12:6. And there are divisions of operations: But it is the same God who works all things in all. Whoever effects all things in all, he cooperates with the acting creatures: But God does so, etc.: Therefore. (3) The sacred scriptures teach that God, while parents generate, creates man, Job 10:8. Your hands have fashioned me, and made me, and indeed altogether round about. Whoever, while parents generate, makes and forms the infant in the mother's womb with his own hands, he concurs immediately to the work of generation: But God does so, etc.: Therefore. (4) The cooperation of God is gathered from the divine presence, which in biblical style and complex sense implies both substantial presence and efficacious operation. See above, ch. 1, quest. 49, p. 275 ff.

The light of reason shows us 1) that all creatures are essentially subordinated to God, so that they depend on him in becoming, being, and acting. 2) Whatever positively exists and happens outside of God is a being dependent on the creator. The actions of secondary causes, and their effects, positively exist and happen outside of God E. 3) If the essence of any creature were from God, but not its acts and effects; it would follow that the action of the creature would be nobler than its own essence, and the effect nobler than its own cause, nay, that the action would be an independent being, and therefore God himself, which is most absurd. 4) The divine cooperation shines forth from preservation itself. For the first cause preserves and sustains the second in its being and vigor, in which it was originally created. But the being of the creatu-

of creatures and vigor is not an idle thing, but everywhere operative. E. both the powers of creatures, and the exercises of these are from God. For if God sustains every being, certainly He also preserves the action through an efficacious production, since preservation is nothing other than the continuous production of a thing.

5) When God suspends His cooperation, the creature does not act according to its inherent powers, as it is accustomed to act, e.g., the Sun is not moved, Job X; fire in the Babylonian furnace does not burn, Dan. III. And from these reason gathers that secondary causes cannot operate according to their ordinary course, unless the first cause cooperates.

Latin:

Conservatio est actus providentiae divinae, quo Deus res omnes, a se creatas, sustentat, ut in natura sua, proprietatibus innatis, & viribus in creatione acceptis, persistere possint.

Obs. I. Creatio, & conservatio, sunt actus divini distincti non per se, ex parte rei, sed per intellectum nostrum, ex diverso connotato; conservatio quippe est continuata creatio. Neque enim alia ratione Deus creaturam conservare dicitur, nisi quatenus actionem, qua creaturam produxerat, porro positive continuat. Patet hoc vel maxime ex eo, quod sicut duratio, ex parte rei, nihil aliud est, quam continuata existentia; ita conservatio nihil aliud est, quam continuata creatio. Illustratur simili: Qua actione emanativa sol radios primum ex se fudit, eadem perennem radiorum effluxum continuat: Ita Deus, qua actione primum creaturis contulit esse, eadem confert porro esse. Distinguuntur autem diversis connotatis. Nam creatio connotat, rem ante non fuisse; conservatio rem ante fuisse, supponit: creatio dat essendi initium; conservatio essendi continuationem.

Obs. II. Conservatio divina non est actus mere negativus, aut indirectus; neque enim in eo consistit, quod Deus res conditas non velit destruere aut annihilare, sed eas vigori suo relinquere, quoad vigere possunt ac durare, ex vi per creationem ipsis indita; sed est actus positivus & directus, quo Deus in genere in causas efficientes rerum conservandas influxu vero & reali influit, ut in natura, proprietatibus & viribus suis persistant ac permaneant.

Obs. III. Conservat Deus species & individua. Species conservat, essentias rerum ab interitu vindicando, & perseverantiam iis impertiendo. Individua conservat, in locum intereuntium noua substituendo, ut essentia specierum perseveret.

Obs. IV. Conservationi opponitur annihilatio, quae est creaturarum per influxum divini subtractionem destructio. Potest autem Deus, si velit, omnes creaturas tam spirituales, quam corporales annihilare. Vt enim omnes creaturae a Deo in esse & operari dependent: ita ab eodem, per subtractionem manus conservatricis, annihilari possunt.

Obs. V. Alias creaturas Deus per se tantum conservat, ut angelos, coelum & corpora simplicia: alias conservat concurrentibus creaturis, ut homines, plantas &c. Probatur divina creaturarum conservatio tum e lumine scripturae, tum e lumine naturae. Tota scriptura sacra de conservatione rerum creatarum per influxum divinum abunde testatur. Nobis sufficiat, sequentia adduxisse.

In V. T. hierofaltes providentiam Dei, huius vniversi conservatricem, depraedicat Ps. CXIX, 89. 90. 91. In aeternum es, Iehouah. Verbum tuum consistit in caelis. In generationem & generationem est fidelitas tua: Firmasti terram & stat. At iudicia tua stant hodieque: quia omnia sunt servi tui. Sensus est; Coelum, terra, & quaecunque in iis sunt, verbo mandati & veritate gubernationis tuae, o Domine, persistant & permanent, tum ratione substantiae, tum ratione virium agendi: nam omnes creaturae reuera sunt servi tui, vt quidquid sunt, tuum sint, & quidquid agunt, sub tuo imperio & gubernatione agant; cum feruorum instar ad omnia iussa tua promptissime obediant. In N. T. Hebr. I, 3. adscribitur Filio Dei (non tamen excluso Deo Patre & Spir. S.) conservatio & sustentatio omnium. Dicitur namque φέρων τὰ πάντα τῷ ῥήματι τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ, portans omnia verbo potentiae suae. Obs. τὸ φέρειν alii transferunt, portare, ferre, sustinere. Alii reddunt, agere, mouere, moderari. Iudice SEB. SCHMIDIO in Comm. in loc. p. 45. tam late verbum φέρειν hic accipi potest, vt utrumque complectatur. Neque enim Deus tantum portat res quiescentes, sed etiam mobiles mouet. Per ῥῆμα intelligimus actum Dei liberrimum & facillimum, per potentiam ipsam omnipotentiam diuinam. Πάντα comprehendunt omnia, præter portantem. Solus autem Deus, Pater & Spirit. S. cum Filio Dei omnia portant; adeoque τὰ πάντα sunt omnia creata, siue sint res, siue personæ, siue actiones. Quare hæc est verborum apostoli sententia: Filius Dei vna cum Deo Patre & Spiritu S. omnia creata actu suæ infinitæ potentiæ liberrimo facillimoque sustentat, fouet & moderatur.

E lumine naturæ discimus (1) Conseruationem esse continuatam creationem. E. qui mundum, & quidquid in illo est, creauit, idem conseruat. Sicut enim lumen solis non est, non lucet, non constanter manet, nisi emanet a sole: Ita nulla creatura est, durat, aut agit, nisi conferuetur a Deo. (2) Deum creaturis esse præsentissimum. Quocirca supremus inspector & rector orbis, quibus creaturis præsentissime adest, easdem pro sua omnipotentia potest, pro infinita sapientia nouit, pro bonitate exuberantissima vult conferuare. (3) Quod si res creatæ absque influxu Dei consisterent, manere aliquid posset Deo repugnante, vel influxum suum subtrahente. At subtrahente Deo influxum suum, omnia collabascunt, & in nihilum recidunt.

Qvæst. XVI. Quid est cooperatio, siue concursus Dei?

Concursus, siue cooperatio Dei est actus prouidentiæ diuinæ, quo Deus cum causis secundis in ipsarum actiones & effectus influxu generali & immediato, iuxta cuiuslibet creaturæ exigentiam & indolem, suauiter coinfluit.

Obs. Deus creaturis non solum dat vires agendi, datasque perennare iubet, sed & immediate in actionem & effectum creaturarum influit, ita, vt ille effectus nec a solo Deo, nec a sola creatura, sed vna eademque efficientia totali simul a Deo & creatura producatur; a Deo videlicet, tanquam causa prima & vniuersali, creatura, vt causa secunda & particulari.

Probatur concursus diuinus tum e lumine reuelationis, tum e lumine rationis. Lumen reuelationis testatur (1) quod non tantum nostræ vires mouendi agendique, sed motus ipse, siue actio a Deo dependeat. Notissima sunt verba Paulli, Act. XVII, 27. 28. Deus non procul ab vnoquoque nostrum exsistit; in ipso enim viuimus, mouemur, & sumus. (2) Deo omnia opera nostra, vt causæ primæ & vniuersali, tribuuntur, 1 Cor. XII, 6. Et diuisiones operationum sunt: Vnus tamen est Deus, qui operatur omnia in omnibus. Quicunque efficit omnia in omnibus, ille cum creaturis operantibus cooperatur: Atqui Deus &c: E. (3) Docent sacræ litteræ, Deum, generantibus parentibus, hominem creare, Iob. X, 8. Manus tuæ fauerunt me, & fecerunt me, & quidem simul circumquaque. Quicunque, generantibus parentibus, inanibus suis facit & format infantem in vtero matris, ille ad opus generationis immediate concurrit: Atqui Deus &c. E. (4) Colligitur cooperatio Dei ex præsentia diuina, quæ stylo biblico & sensu complexo tum substantialem adessentiam, tum efficacem operationem infert. Vid. supra cap. I. quæst. 49. p. 275. sqq.

Lumen rationis nobis ostendit 1) quod omnes creaturæ Deo essentialiter subordinentur, vt in fieri, esse & operari ab ipso dependeant. 2) Quidquid positiue extra Deum est & fit, est ens a creatore dependens. Actiones causarum secundarum, earumque effecta, positiue extra Deum sunt & fiunt E. 3) Si essentia cuiuslibet creaturæ esset a Deo, non autem eiusdem actus & effectus; sequeretur, actionem creaturæ eiusdem essentia, & effectum causa sua esse nobiliorem, immo actionem esse ens independens, atque adeo ipsum Deum, quod est absurdissimum. 4) Ex ipsa conseruatione elucescit cooperatio diuina. Nam conseruat & sustentat causa prima secundam in esse & vigore suo, in quo primitus fuit condita.

creaturarum et vigor non est otiosum quid, sed vbivis operosum. E. et creaturarum vires, et harum exercitia sunt a Deo. Si enim Deus omne ens sustentat, vtique etiam actionem conferuat per efficacem productionem, cum conseruatio nihil aliud fit, quam continua rei productio.

5) Deo cooperationem suam suspendente, creatura iuxta vires insitas non agit, quod agere consueuit, v. gr. Sol non mouetur, Ios, X. ignis in fornace Babylonica non vrit, Dan. III. Et quibus ratio colligit, causas secundas non posse secundum ordinarium suum cursum operari, nisi cooperetur causa prima.


### Quest. XVII. What kind of concurrence of God is understood here?

Since we are presently dealing with the general providence of God, we understand here a concurrence of God that is general and indeterminate a), immediate b), and accommodated to the requirement and nature of each cause c).

Prob. a. Here is considered the influx of divine cooperation into the actions of all creatures; which is undoubtedly general and indeterminate. But if we look at human actions, they are in a twofold difference. Some can be elicited by man by natural powers, some transcend the natural powers of man. Those which can be elicited by man by natural powers are either indifferent, or morally good, or morally evil. If the actions are indifferent, such as the action of eating, drinking, God concurs to them with a general and indeterminate concurrence, the human will freely determining itself to act according to the reason of the object and circumstances. If the actions are morally good, God concurs to them by His providence (1) physically, (2) morally. Physically, He provides a general concurrence to moral actions by sustaining the powers of mind and body suitable for acting. Morally, He concurs by commanding and promising. To the formal of morally evil actions, namely the anomia or ataxia, God does not concur by positive influx; because malice is a defect and privation, not proceeding from the most perfect God, into whom no defect can fall, but from the human will failing in acting. However, God concurs to the remote material of morally evil actions, not the proximate. The former is an indeterminate act; the latter is an act determined and applied to a forbidden thing. E.g., When Eve extended her hand to the forbidden fruit, two acts were present (1) the extension of the hand, (2) the extension applied to the forbidden fruit. The former act is called the remote material, the latter the proximate material. To this God does not concur; because His concurrence is general and indeterminate, and therefore the determination to this or that object is not from God, as from a first and universal cause, but from a secondary and particular cause. Supernatural actions, however, are considered either as to their generic being, or as to their specific being. As to their generic being, they are motions of the intellect and will, to which God concurs by a general concurrence; as to their specific being, those motions are excited by the Holy Spirit by a special concurrence. But supernatural acts are not yet being treated here. To natural acts, God indeed concurs by a general concurrence, but not exclusively; for extraordinarily, under that general influx, there is also contained a peculiar influx, conferring more intense powers of acting and a stronger motion to one creature than to another.

Prob. b. God concurs to the actions of creatures by an immediation of power and of subject. He concurs by an immediation of subject; since God is present to operating creatures by His substance; inasmuch as He fills all in all, Jer. XXIII, 24. He also concurs by an immediation of power, by an efficacious influx reaching the action of the creature, and its effect, immediately and proximately; in that He works all in all, 1 Cor. XII, 6.

You say: God works through creatures: Therefore not immediately. Resp. One is said to act immediately, either exclusively, or inclusively. Exclusively; when one acts alone: Inclusively; when one one together with other cooperating things reaches the action and effect immediately. God flows into the actions of creatures immediately, not exclusively; as if creatures were excluded from action, or were idle; but every creature does what is its own; but God, together with the creatures operating, reaches the action and effect by His own influx immediately and proximately.

This is what the author of Wisdom ch. 8, 1 seems to suggest. He reaches from end to end mightily, and disposes all things sweetly.

Prob. c. God concurs with the actions of secondary causes by a gentle, easy, and accommodated concurrence to the requirement and nature of the creatures. For while God concurs uniformly with things acting necessarily, e.g., with fire, that it may burn, with the sun, that it may shine: He concurs multiformly with things acting freely, leaving to them free will, and the free power of choosing this or that; for the order which God has once established, He does not easily change. Ps. 119, 9. Wisely says AUGUSTINE, book 7 of the City of God, ch. 30. God administers all things which He created, so that He even allows them to exercise and perform their own proper motions.

Antithesis is that of Pelagius, Durandus, and the Arminians, who either deny divine cooperation entirely, or at least call it into doubt. They are prompted by frequent arguments:

I. If God by cooperating produced the same action as the creature, God would have to be said to eat while a man is eating: The consequent is false: Therefore the antecedent. The consequence of the major is clear; because those who do the same things receive the same denomination from the same action. Resp. The consequence of the major is denied. To the proof we say that that acting cause from which the effect is terminated, or from which it is received, obtains the denomination from the action. When God concurs with the natural eating of a man, the food is received by the man, and therefore not God, but the man is said to eat.

II. Whoever concur in the same action are associate causes. But God and nature are not associate causes. E. The major is clear in itself. The minor is proved: because associate causes flow into an action by a partial influx, which brings in imperfection. Resp. Whatever causes are coordinate, or of the same order, concur in the same action, those are associate causes. But God and nature are not of the same order. For God is the first cause, independent and universal, the creature is a subordinate, secondary, dependent, and particular cause.

III. One action cannot proceed from most diverse agents. God and the creature are most diverse agents. Therefore. The major is evident; because there is a certain harmony among cooperating causes. Resp. One action cannot proceed from most diverse agents, unless the lower agent is subordinated to the higher. But the creature is essentially subordinated to God, and is subject to His government.

IV. Whoever concurs in all the actions of men, he concurs also in sins: But God concurs, etc. Therefore. Resp. Distinguish between human actions and their disorder (ἀταξίαν), also between effects and defects. Because the divine concurrence is general, indifferent, and indeterminate, therefore God does indeed concur to the remote material of an evil action, which is a certain physical mode of the will, intellect, eyes, hand, etc. Not to the proximate material of the same, which is the motion or action applied and determined to a prohibited object; which determination is from a particular cause, not a universal one. To the disorder (ἀταξίαν) and defect God does not concur; because the defect is to be imputed to the erring secondary cause, just as, e.g., the soul flows into the progressive motion of a limping man; but the limping is not to be imputed to the soul, but to the broken leg.

V. A creature either has sufficient strength to perform its own work, or it does not have it: If the former, it does not need the concurrence of God: If the latter; the creature will be nothing else than an instrument of God. Resp. The creature has sufficient strength to act in its own kind (in the kind of dependent beings) and therefore nothing prevents it from acting as a principal cause, or being able to act, with the eff that its powers may not exceed; yet those powers are not absolutely sufficient, but the divine concurrence and dependence on the first cause is always included.

VI. The action of divine concurrence is either mediate or immediate: If it is mediate; God acts through secondary causes, not with them: If it is immediate; the action is miraculous: But miracles are not performed daily, nor should they be feigned beyond cause. Resp. Divine concurrence is called an immediate action not in an exclusive sense, Gen. 2, 2. but in an inclusive sense, since it thus concurs with secondary causes, so that it reaches the action and its effect immediately together with them.

VII. Whoever holds that concurrence is laborious, troublesome, and unworthy of the divine majesty, is not to be attributed to God: But the daily and continuous concurrence for all the actions of all and singular creatures is laborious, etc. Therefore. The major is evident, 1) because God, having finished creation, rested from his works, Gen. 2, 2. a most perfect deity, of whom nothing indecorous is to be asserted. The minor is clear; because in one day many myriads of actions are performed, among which many are by far the most sordid.

Resp. The concurrence of God is not troublesome or laborious: for the reason that God moderates all things by the word of his power, i.e., by the act of his most free and easy omnipotence, Hebr. 1, 3. God also knows how to act while resting, and to rest while acting, as AUGUSTINE says in De C.D. Book XII, ch. 17. God, the most pure Spirit, is not contaminated by physical filth, but God does not concur with moral filth, i.e., sins.

VIII. If divine concurrence is general and indifferent, these absurdities will follow: 1) That in one year there is not a greater abundance of grain than in another: 2) That God contributes no more to the formation of a man than to the formation of a beast: 3) That the creature determines the indeterminate concurrence of God: 4) That the concurrence for natural and supernatural acts is the same. Resp. a) generally: The general concurrence of God does not entirely exclude peculiar and extraordinary modes or degrees of concurring: Since God is not bound to the common law or order of creatures. The heavenly Father, bestowing food on his children by a general distribution, is able to grant a more abundant meal to one son than to another.

Indeed, God granted greater fertility to the sheep of Jacob than to the sheep of Laban. b) Specifically: to 1) Although God concurs with creatures every year, he has not so bound his hands that he does not have the power to bestow more gifts in one year than in another. For God acts ordinarily with nature, and extraordinarily above the accustomed course of nature. To 2) God concurs with an influx accommodated to the requirement, nature, and capacity of the creatures.

Hence it happens that the formation of man is nobler than that of a beast. 3) Speaking accurately, the creature does not determine the general concurrence of God, but God, looking forward with the light of omniscience into which direction free agents will determine themselves, tempers his concurrence to them. To 4) Supernatural acts, viewed as a generic being, as they are acts of the mind and will, are accompanied by the general concurrence of God; but viewed as a specific being, as they are spiritual, they are directed by the special concurrence of God. Q.

XVIII. Must a previous or predetermining concurrence of God be established? God concurs in the actions and effects of creatures not by a previous concurrence, but by a simultaneous one, not by predetermining, but by sweetly disposing. Prob. 1) Those who teach a previous concurrence commit a contradiction in terms. For if God concurs, he does not precede; if he cooperates, he does not pre-operate. Premotion is an antecedent act: but concurrence does not precede, but happens when the action itself is produced.

2) Premotion, or predetermination, is terminated only at the cause, not at the action or the effect of it.

causes. Therefore, the action itself and its effect do not depend on God after that premotion, but only the cause, which is impelled and moved; although divine cooperation is required for this reason, because the action and effect of secondary causes depend on God. 3) Natural agents are already predetermined in creation, so that they act uniformly in the ordinary course, e.g., so that water moistens, fire heats, the sun shines; and thus they do not need a predetermining divine concurrence. 4) If divine concurrence were to predetermine free agents to action, they would act necessarily, not freely. But divine concurrence does not take away the freedom of the will. For God concurs with secondary causes according to their own nature, with free ones freely, with necessary ones necessarily, with weak ones weakly, with strong ones strongly, by operating according to his most sweet universal disposition, says TOLETUS lib. II, phys. c. 3, q. 8. 5) Predetermining concurrence has no place in human actions, whether good or evil. If God were to predetermine good actions by his concurrence, they could not resist the divine predetermination. But men often resist God, Acts 7:51. God indeed permits the evil actions of men, by not placing an unavoidable obstacle; but he determines no one to commit this or that sin; otherwise God would be the cause of sin.

There is an antithesis of the Scotists and Dominicans, who assert that secondary causes, primarily the will of man, are predetermined to act by a prior divine motion.

Their arguments are:

Whence, when God is said to incline human wills, it is done by moral bending through arguments, promises, and threats: Just as a farmer directs streams, yet does not necessitate their motion, by which they flow of their own accord. Thus, the heart of Samson was inclined to love the Timnite by the persuasion of arguments by which his intellect was convinced; to which Samson easily assented, already burning with vengeance against the Philistines; otherwise he would have loved as necessarily as one who, having been given a love potion, cannot not love; in which case, indeed, Samson, while he pined for the Philistine woman, would have been miserable. Thus, when God glides into the minds of men, and softens, bends, turns, and moves them, whatever pleases him; he does this not certainly and forcefully, but sweetly and easily, by leaving to minds free will and free choice, he does it, as D. DANNHAV. judges in his Hodogeticus , p. 317. Add that civil actions are ordinarily done by free will; the success of which is entirely from God; for man proposes, God disposes.

II. God concurs in the crucifixion of Christ with a predetermining concurrence: Therefore, this is not to be denied. The antecedent is proven: 1) because the crucifixion of Christ was a physical action, and thus dependent on divine influx: 2) The Jews received him, delivered by the definite counsel and foreknowledge of God, through the hands of the wicked, and they crucified and killed him, Acts

And thus they did whatever the hand of God and his counsel had predetermined to be done, Acts 4: 28.

Resp. The crucifixion of Christ was a monstrous sin, concerning which three things are to be observed: 1) The remote material, which was a physical action, considered indeterminately, to which God concurs by an active and direct influx, because of the dependence of the secondary cause on the first: 2) The proximate material, which is an action determined and applied to the most innocent Jesus; which is not to be attributed to divine concurrence, since that is general and indeterminate, but to the hands of the wicked, Acts 2:23: 3) Anomia or ataxia [lawlessness or disorder], by which is not to be imputed to the most holy and most perfect God, but to the erring Jews, and to those deviating from the rule of right. Meanwhile, the most wise counsel of God permitted this atrocious sin, set limits to it, and directed it to a good end, which is the redemption of the human race. Whence Peter says, that the hand and counsel of God foreordained, not that they might do it, but that it might be done: Which word looks to the end, for the sake of which God permitted the crucifixion of Christ.

III. A secondary cause does not act, unless it is moved by the first: Therefore it cannot act, unless it is pre-determined by God to act. The consequence is proven: because pre-determination is nothing other than a prior, or antecedent, motion. Resp. 1) Between a principal and an instrumental cause there is indeed this order, that one moves the other: But between the first and secondary cause this order does not intervene, that one moves the other: since a secondary cause is not properly an instrument; but one is prior in perfection, illimitation, and necessity. Thus the human will, in that it is free, has power in itself, by which, once an object is shown, it can move itself. 2) Although we do not deny that God sometimes moves agents specifically, both natural and free, both efficiently, by impressing a quality or by introducing a good thought, and objectively, by pre-showing an object convenient to the nature of the agent, or congruent to the present disposition of the divine will; yet that prior motion is not pre-determining, or imposing necessity, but sweetly disposing and easily bending, by which the liberty of acting is not taken away.

IV. The evangelical doctors themselves teach that God determines the actions of creatures. See KOENIGII th. posit. p. 59. Resp. The evangelical doctors understand a determination that is not necessitating, but limiting. The former imposes necessity, so that the agent cannot not act: The latter sets limits by reason of time and degree, within which the agent contains itself.

Latin:

Cum in praesenti de prouidentia Dei generali agamus, intelligitur hic a nobis concursus Dei generalis atque indeterminatus a), immediatus b), et ad exigentiam atque indolem cuiuscumque causae accommodatus c).

Prob. a. Consideratur hic cooperationis diuinae influxus in omnium creaturarum actiones; qui haud dubie generalis et indeterminatus est. Si autem spectemus actiones humanas, illae in duplici sunt differentia. Quaedam elici possunt ab homine viribus naturalibus, quaedam vires naturales hominis transcendunt. Quae naturalibus viribus ab homine possunt elici, sunt vel indifferentes, vel moraliter bonae, vel moraliter malae. Si actiones sunt indifferentes, qualis est actio edendi, bibendi, Deus ad easdem concursu generali et indeterminato concurrit, voluntate humana pro obiecti et circumstantiarum ratione ad agendum se libere determinante. Si actiones sunt moraliter bonae, Deus ad illas concurrit sua prouidentia (1) physice, (2) moraliter. Physice generalem concursum ad actiones morales praebet, vires animi et corporis ad agendum idoneas sustentando. Moraliter concurrit praecipiendo, et promittendo. Ad actionem moraliter malarum formale, nimirum anomian vel ataxian, Deus positiuo influxu non concurrit; quia malitia est defectus et priuatio, non proueniens a Deo perfectissimo, in quem nullus potest cadere defectus, sed a voluntate humana in agendo deficiente. Concurrit autem Deus ad actionum moraliter malarum materiale remotum, non proximum. Illud est actus indeterminatus; hoc est actus determinatus et ad rem prohibitam applicatus V. gr. Quando Eua extendebat manum ad fructum vetitum, duo aderant actus (1) extensio manus, (2) extensio applicata ad fructum vetitum. Prior actus dicitur materiale remotum, posterior materiale proximum. Ad hoc Deus non concurrit; quia eius concursus est generalis et indeterminatus, adeoque determinatio ad hoc vel illud obiectum non est a Deo, tanquam a causa prima et vniuersali, sed a causa secunda et particulari. Actiones autem supernaturales considerantur vel qua esse genericum, vel qua esse specificum. Qua esse genericum sunt motus intellectus et voluntatis, ad quos Deus concurrit concursu generali; qua esse specificum illi motus excitati sunt a Spiritu S. concursu speciali. Sed de actibus supernaturalibus hic nondum agitur. Ad actus naturales concurrit Deus quidem concursu generali, sed non exclusive; nam extraordinarie sub illo influxu generali continetur etiam influxus peculiaris, intensiores agendi vires, validioremque motum vni creaturae, quam alteri conferens.

Prob. b. Concurrit Deus ad actiones creaturarum immediatione virtutis et suppositi. Immediatione suppositi concurrit; quoniam Deus substantia sua proxime adest creaturis operantibus; siquidem omnia in omnibus implet, Jer. XXIII, 24. Concurrit etiam immediatione virtutis, efficaci influxu actionem creaturae, eiusque effectum immediate et proxime attingendo; eo, quod omnia in omnibus operatur, 1 Cor. XII, 6.

Dicis: Deus operatur per creaturas: Ergo non immediate. Resp. Immediate agere quis dicitur, vel exclusive, vel inclusive. Exclusive; cum quis solus agit: Inclusive; cum quis piam vna cum aliis cooperantibus actionem & effectum proxime attingit. Immediate Deus influit in actiones creaturarum, non exclusive; quasi creaturae ab actione excludantur, aut otiosae sint; sed quaelibet creatura agit, quod suum est; Deus autem vna cum creaturis operantibus actionem & effectum influxu suo immediate & proxime attingit.

Id quod innuere videtur auctor Sap. c. VIII, 1. Attingit a fine ad finem fortiter, & disponit omnia suaviter.

Prob. c. Concurrit Deus ad actiones causarum secundarum concursu suavi, facili & accommodato exigentiae atque indoli creaturarum. Nam cum necessario agentibus Deus concurrit uniformiter, v. gr. cum igne, vt vrat, cum sole, vt luceat: Cum libere agentibus concurrit multiformiter, liberum ipsis arbitrium, liberamque hoc vel illud eligendi potestatem relinquens; quem enim Deus ordinem semel constituit, non facile mutat. Ps. CXIX, 9. Scite inquit AVGVSTIN. libr. VII. de C. D. c. 30. Deus administrat omnia, quae creavit, vt etiam ipsa proprios exercere atque agere motus sinat.

Antithesis est Pelagii, Durandi & Arminianorum, qui cooperationem diuinam vel negant penitus, vel saltim in dubium vocant. Innuituntur frequentibus argumentis:

I. Si Deus cooperando eandem actionem produceret, quam creatura, Deus edente homine, dicendus esset edere: Consequens est falsum: E. & antecedens. Consequentia maioris est clara; quia qui idem agunt, ab eadem actione eandem denominationem accipiunt. Resp. Consequ. mai. neg. Ad probationem dicimus, quod denominationem ab actione nanciscatur illa causa agens, in qua effectus terminatur, seu a qua recipitur. Quando Deus ad manducationem hominis naturalem concurrit, cibus ab homine recipitur, adeoque non Deus, sed homo edere dicitur.

II. Quicunque ad eandem actionem concurrunt, sunt causae sociae. At Deus & natura non sunt causae sociae. E. Maior per se clara est. Minor probatur: quia causae sociae influunt in actionem influxu partiali, qui imperfectionem infert. Resp. Quaecunque causae co-ordinate, siue eiusdem ordinis ad eandem actionem concurrunt, illae sunt causae sociae. At Deus & natura non sunt eiusdem ordinis. Nam Deus est causa prima, independens & vniuersalis, creatura est causa subordinata, secunda, dependens & particularis.

III. A diuersissimis agentibus vna actio proficisci nequit. Deus & creatura sunt agentia diuersissima. Ergo. Maior patet; quia inter causas cooperantes quaedam est harmonia. Resp. A diuersissimis agentibus vna proficisci nequit actio, nisi agens inferius superiori subordinetur. At creatura Deo essentialiter subordinatur, eiusque gubernationi subest.

IV. Quicunque concurrit ad omnes hominum actiones, is concurrit etiam ad peccata: Atqui Deus concurrit &c. Ergo. Resp. Dist. inter actiones humanas, & earum ἀταξίαν, item inter effectus & defectus. Quia concursus diuinus generalis, indifferens & indeterminatus est, ideo concurrit quidem Deus ad actionis malae materiale remotum, quod est modus quidam physicus voluntatis, intellectus, oculorum, manus &c. Non ad eiusdem materiale proximum, quod est motus vel actio applicata & determinata ad obiectum prohibitum; quae determinatio est a causa particulari, non vniuersali. Ad ἀταξίαν & defectum Deus non concurrit; quia defectus iimputandus est causae secundae aberranti, sicut v. gr. anima influit in motum progressiuum hominis claudicantis; at claudicatio non animae, sed tibiae fractae imputanda est.

V. Creatura aut sufficientes habet vires ad opus suum patrandum, aut non habet: Si illud, non indiget concursu Dei: Si hoc; creatura nil aliud erit, quam instrumentum Dei. Resp. Habet creatura ad agendum vires sufficientes in suo genere (in genere entium dependentium) adeoque nil impedit, quo minus vt causa principalis agat, aut agere possit, cum esse etus illius vires non excedat; non tamen illae vires absolute sufficientes sunt, sed semper includitur concursus divinus & dependentia a causa prima.

VI. Actio concursus divini aut est mediata, aut immediata: Si est mediata; Deus agit per causas secundas, non cum illis: Si est immediata; actio miraculosa est: Sed miracula non fiunt quotidie, neque praeter causam fingenda sunt. Resp. Concursus divinus dicitur actio immediata non in sensu exclusivo, Gen. II, 2. sed in sensu inclusivo, cum sic concurrat cum causis secundis, vt una cum illis actionem & eius effectum immediate attingat.

VII. Quicunque concursus est laboriosus, molestus & maiestate divina indignus, is Deo non est tribuendus: Atqui concursus quotidianus & continuus ad omnes actiones omnium & singularum creaturarum est laboriosus &c. Ergo. Maior patet, 1) quia Deus consummata creatione, quievit ab operibus suis, Gen. II, 2. numen perfectissimum, de quo nihil indecore est afferendum. Minor liquet; quia vno die multae myriades actionum expediuntur, quas inter multae sunt longe sordidissimae.

Resp. Concursus Dei non est molestus aut laboriosus: propterea, quod Deus omnia moderatur verbo potentiae suae, i. e. actu omnipotentiae suae liberrimo & facillimo, Hebr. I, 3. Nouit etiam Deus quiescent agere, & agens quiescere, dicente AVGVSTINO de C.D. L. XII. c. 17. Sordibus physicis Deus Spiritus purissimus non contaminatur, ad sordes autem morales, i. e. peccata Deus non concurrit.

VIII. Si concursus divinus est generalis & indifferens, sequentur haec absurda: 1) Quod vno anno non fit maior annonae copia, quam altero: 2) Quod Deus ad formationem hominis non plus conferat, quam ad formationem bestiae: 3) Quod creatura concursum Dei indeterminatum determinet: 4) Quod concursus ad actus naturales & supernaturales idem sit. Resp. a) generatim: Concursus Dei generalis non penitus excludit peculiares & extraordinarios concurrendi modos, aut gradus: Siquidem Deus non alligatus est ad communem creaturarum legem, aut ordinem. Pater coelestis generali distributione largiens filiis suis cibum, copiosiorem escam vni, quam alteri filio impertiri valet.

Sane Iacobi ouibus Deus maiorem indulsit foecunditatem, quam ouibus Labani. b) Speciatim: ad 1) Quamvis singulis annis Deus concurrat cum creaturis, non tamen ita sibi ligavit manus, vt eadem non vno anno plura dona, quam altero dilargiendi facultatem habeat. Agit quippe Deus ordinarie cum natura, & extraordinarie supra consuetum naturae cursum. Ad 2) Concurrit Deus influxu accommodato ad exigentiam, indolem & capacitatem creaturarum.

Inde fit, vt nobilior fit formatio hominis, quam bestiae. 3) Accurate loquendo creatura concursum Dei generalem non determinat, sed Deus, lumine omniscientiae prospiciens, in quam partem libere agentia se determinatura sint, iisdem concursum suum attemperat. Ad 4) Actus supernaturales, qua esse genericum spectatos, prout sunt actus mentis, & voluntatis, comitatur concursus Dei generalis; sed spectati qua esse specificum, vt sunt spirituales, diriguntur concursu Dei speciali.

Quaest. XVIII. Estne statuendus concursus Dei praeuius, aut praedeterminatus? Concurrit Deus ad actiones & effecta creaturarum non concursu praeuio, sed simultaneo, non praedeterminante, sed suaviter disponente. Prob. 1) Qui docent concursum praeuium, committunt contradictionem in adiecto. Nam si Deus concurrit, non praecurrit, si cooperatur, non praeoperatur. Praemotio est actus antecedens: concursus vero non antecedit, sed fit, cum actio ipsa producitur.

2) Praemotio, vel praedeterminatio, terminatur tantum ad causam, non ad actionem, vel effectum illius.

causae. Non igitur ipsa actio, eiusque effectus dependet a Deo post istam praemotionem, sed tantum causa, quae impellitur & movetur; cum tamen cooperatio divina ideo requiratur, quia causae secundae actio & effectus a Deo dependet. 3) Agentia naturalia iam in creatione sunt praedeterminata, vt ordinarie agant vniformiter, v. gr. vt aqua humectet, ignis calefaciat, sol luceat; adeoque non indigent concursu divino praedeterminante. 4) Si concursus divinus praedeterminaret agentia libera ad actionem, necessario agerent, non libere. At concursus divinus non tollit libertatem voluntatis. Concurrit enim Deus cum causis secundis iuxta ipsarum naturam, cum liberis libere, cum necessariis necessariis, cum debilibus debiliter, cum fortibus fortiter, pro sua suavissima dispositione vniversali operando, ait TOLETVs l. II. phys. c. 3. q. 8. 5) Concursus praedeterminans non habet locum in actionibus hominum bonis, neque malis. Si Deus concursu suo praedeterminaret actiones bonas; non possent praedeterminationi divinae resistere. At homines Deo saepe resistunt, Act. VII, 51. Actiones hominum malas Deus quidem permittit, ineluctabile impedimentum non obiiciendo; at neminem determinat ad hoc illudue peccatum committendum; ceteroqui Deus causa peccati foret.

Antithesis est Scotistarum & Dominicanorum, causas secundas, in primis voluntatem hominis, praevio motu divino ad agendum praedeterminari asserentium.

Quorum argumenta sunt: I. Quicunque cor hominis habet in manu sua, vt illud flectat pro arbitratu suo, ille hominem ad agendum praedeterminat: Atqui Deus &c. Ergo. Maior probatur; quia flectere cor hominis ad agendum, idem est, quod praedeterminare. Minor patet ex Prou. XVI, 9. c. XXI, 1. Ier. X, 23. Resp. dist. inter praedeterminationem ad agendum necessitantem, & inter flexionem suaviter disponentem, atque vtiliter ad finem dirigentem. Non praedeterminat Deus necessitatem imponendo causis secundis, aut libertatem arbitrii humani captiuando, sed suaviter disponit ordinarie, rerum creatarum insitis proprietatibus se accommodando.

Vnde cum Deus inclinare dicitur voluntates humanas, morali id fit flexione per argumenta, promissa, minas: Sicut agricola dirigit riuos, non tamen necessitatem eorum motum, quo sponte fluunt. Sic Simsonis cor inclinatum est ad diligendam Timnathitem ex argumentorum, quibus eius intellectus persuasus est, suada; cui facile annuit Simson, iam dum nemesi in Philistaeos ardens; alioqui tam necessario amasset, quam qui philtro propinato non potest non amare; quo quidem in casu Simson, dum deperiit Philistaeam, miserabilis fuisset. Ita Deus cum mentibus hominum illabitur, easque mollit, flectit, gyrat, agit, quodcunque ei placuerit; id non certo & fortiter, sed suaviter & facile, relinquendo mentibus liberum arbitrium, liberamque electionem, facit, cenfente D. DANNHAV. in hodof. p. 317. Adiice, quod actiones civiles ordinarie fiunt a libero arbitrio; quorum successus totus est a Deo; nam homo proponit, Deus disponit.

II. Concurrit Deus ad crucifixionem Christi concursu praedeterminante: Ergo hic non est negandus. Antecedens probatur: 1) quia crucifixio Christi fuit actio physica, adeoque ab influxu divino dependens: 2) Iudaei definito consilio & praescientia Dei deditum acceperunt per manus iniquorum, crucifixerunt & interfecerunt, Act.

II, 23. atque adeo fecerunt, quaecunque manus Dei & consilium ipsius praefinuerat fieri, Act. IV, 28.

Resp. Crucifixio Christi fuit immane peccatum, circa quod tria obseruanda sunt: 1) Materiale remotum, quod fuit actio physica, indeterminate considerata, ad quam Deus concurrit actiuo & directo influxu, ob dependentiam causae secundae a prima: 2) Materiale proximum, quod est actio determinata & applicata ad innocentissimum Iesum; quae non est tribuenda concursu divino, quippe qui generalis & indeterminatus est, sed manibus iniquorum, Act. II, 23: 3) Ἀνομία vel ἀταξία, qua quae non Deo sanctissimo & perfectissimo, sed Judaeis errantibus, & a regula recti deflectentibus imputanda est. Interim consilium Dei sapientissimum atrox hoc peccatum permisit, limites ei praefixit, & ad finem bonum, qui est redemtio generis humani, direxit. Vnde Petrus ait, quod manus & consilium Dei praedefinuerint, non ut facerent, sed ut fierent: Quod verbum respicit finem, ob quem Deus crucifixionem Christi permisit.

III. Non agit causa secunda, nisi moueatur a prima: Ergo non potest agere, nisi a Deo ad agendum praedeterminetur. Consequentia probatur: quia praedeterminatio nil aliud est, quam motus praeuius, seu antecedaneus. Resp. 1) Inter caussam principalem & instrumentalem quidem est hic ordo, vt vna alteram moueat: At inter caussam primam & secundam non intercedit hic ordo, vt vna alteram moueat: cum caussa secunda proprie non sit instrumentum; sed vna alta sit prior perfectione, illimitatione & necessitate. Sic voluntas humana, eo, quod libera est, virtutem habet in se, qua, monstrato obiecto, semetipsam mouere queat. 2) Quamuis non negemus, Deum quandoque mouere specialiter agentia, tam naturalia, quam libera, tum efficienter, qualitatem imprimendo, aut bonam cogitationem inferendo, tum obiective, praemonstrando obiectum conueniens naturae agentis, aut congruum praesenti dispositioni voluntatis diuinae; non tamen ille motus praeuius est praedeterminians, aut necessitatem imponens, sed suauiter disponens & facile flectens, quo non tollitur agendi libertas.

IV. Ipsi doctores euangelici docent, Deum actiones creaturarum determinare. Vid. KOENIGII th. posit. p. 59. Resp. Doctores euangelici intelligunt determinationem non necessitantem, sed limitantem. Illa imponit necessitatem, vt agens non possit non agere: Haec limites ratione temporis & gradus ponit, quos intra agens se continet.


### Q. XIX. What is the government of God?

The government of God is an act of divine providence, by which God, according to the counsel of His will, most freely orders, moderates, and directs all created things, and their powers, actions, and passions to the proposed ends, the glory of the Creator, the good of this universe, and the salvation of men, especially the pious.

Prob. God governs us with supreme indulgence, Wis. XII, 18. For He is the king of the whole world, because He is its creator, whose providence (πρόνοια) governs all things, Wis. XIV, 3. He is the king of kings, Dan. II, 47. 1 Tim. VI, 15. the lord of all things, Deut. X, 17. 1 Chron. XXIX, 11. 12.

Latin:

Gubernatio Dei est actus prouidentiae diuinae, quo Deus secundum consilium voluntatis suae omnes res creatas, earumque vires, actiones & passiones liberrime ordinat, moderatur & dirigit ad propositos fines, gloriam creatoris, huius vniuersi bonum, & hominum, in primis piorum, salutem.

Prob. Deus summa indulgentia nos gubernat, Sap. XII, 18. Est enim rex totius orbis, quia ipsius conditor, cuius πρόνοια cuncta gubernat, Sap. XIV, 3. Est rex regum, Dan. II, 47. 1 Tim. VI, 15. vniuerforum dominus, Deut. X, 17. 1 Par. XXIX, 11. 12.


### Q. XX. What is the end of divine providence?

The ultimate end of divine providence is the glory of God a): The intermediate general end is the good of this universe b), the special end is the temporal and eternal salvation of pious men c).

Prob. a. God works all things according to the counsel of His will, that we might be to the praise of His glory. Eph. I, 11. 12. From the preserving, cooperating, and governing providence of God, the glory of divine power, goodness, and wisdom flourishes. For God preserves the macrocosm and the microcosm (man) most powerfully, cooperates with acting creatures most excellently and most sweetly, and governs all actions and passions most wisely.

Prob. b. Just as God originally created all things good, Gen. I, 31. so He procures the good of all. For He loves all beings, and abominates nothing of those which He has made, Wis. XI, 24.

Because God loves all things which He has made, He desires the good of all to be promoted and established.

Prob. c. The ever-watchful care of the eternal divinity directs all things for the benefit of pious men; concerning which the most pious king sang excellently, Ps. XXXIII, 18. Behold, the eye of Jehovah is upon those who fear Him, upon those who wait for His mercy, to deliver their soul from death, and to keep them alive in famine. Hence it comes to pass that for those who love God, all things work together for good, Rom. VIII, 28.

Latin:

Finis prouidentiae diuinae vltimus est gloria Dei a): Finis intermedius generalis est huius vniuersi bonum b), specialis est hominum piorum temporalis & aeterna salus c).

Prob. a. Deus omnia operatur iuxta consilium voluntatis suae, vt simus nos in laudem gloriae ipsius. Eph. I, 11. 12. Ex prouidentia Dei conseruatrice, cooperatrice, & gubernatrice, gloria potentiae, bonitatis, & sapientiae diuinae efflorescit. Conseruat enim Deus macrocosmum & microcosmum (hominem) potentissime, cooperatur cum creaturis agentibus optime & suauissime, gubernat omnes actiones & passiones sapientissime.

Prob. b. Sicut Deus omnia bona primitus condidit, Gen. I, 31. ita omnium bonum procurat. Amat enim entia omnia, & nihil abominatur eorum, quae fecit, Sap. XI, 24.

Quia Deus omnia, quae fecit, amat, omnium bonum promotum & stabilitum cupit.

Prob. c. Peruigil aeterni numinis cura omnia dirigit in piorum hominum commodum; de quo egregie cecinit rex piissimus, Ps. XXXIII, 18. Ecce oculus Iehovae (est) super timentibus ipsum, exspectantibus misericordiam eius, ad eripiendum a morte animam eorum, et ad viuificandum eos in fame. Inde fit, vt Deum diligentibus omnia cooperentur in bonum, Rom. VIII, 28.


### Quest. XXI. How is the providence of God distinguished?

The providence of God is distinguished a) into general and special. The former is that by which God preserves and governs the whole world and whatever is contained within its compass: The latter is that by which God most benignly looks upon, most mercifully cherishes, and most sweetly rules the church, both the militant, or the assembly of faithful men, and the triumphant, or the choir of angels and elect men. b) Into ordinary and extraordinary. The former is that by which God acts according to the predefined law of nature: The latter is that by which God works above the established order of nature. c) Into that which is concerned with good, and that which is concerned with moral evil. The former is that by which He protects the good of creatures by preserving it, promotes it by cooperating, and directs it by governing it to the praise of divine glory: The latter is that by which God is occupied with moral evil, not as an idle spectator, but as a most just judge, and thus exerts justice, tempered by His grace, in acts preceding, accompanying, and following the sin.

Prob. a) Christ Himself teaches the distinction between general and special divine providence in Matt. VI, 26. Look at the birds of the air: for they neither sow, nor reap, nor gather into barns: yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they? i.e., God exercises a general care for birds, but a special and excellent care for pious men, as His own children.
