b) Although God for the most part adapts the acts of His providence to the nature and properties of creatures: He has not, however, so bound Himself to the powers of creatures that He cannot act above them. Thus, at the nod of God, the sun stands still, an ass speaks, water turns into wine. All miracles are effects of the extraordinary providence of God.

c) That God is not an idle spectator of sins—just as men come to watch stage plays while on holiday—but a most just, yet placable judge of the same, will be clearly revealed from the acts of divine providence which either precede, accompany, or follow the consummation of sin.

Quest. XXII. What acts of divine providence precede sin?

Preceding the consummation of sin are a) divine foreknowledge or prescience, b) the aversion of the foreseen sin, c) the hindrance.

Prob. a) That God foresaw the perfidy and disobedience of the people of Israel, we perceive from Isa. XLVIII, 8. I knew that you would deal very treacherously, and were called a transgressor from the womb. This divine foreknowledge is indeed infallible, but it is not an absolute necessity. Hence the following sophism fails: Whatever God foresees, that happens necessarily: But sin, etc. Therefore. Resp. Distinguish between the necessity of the consequent and of the consequence. Although sins happen necessarily, as they are foreseen by God, that necessity is one of consequence, not absolute; it is hypothetical, not absolute.

For sins will not happen because they were foreseen; but they were foreseen because they will certainly happen. b) You are not a God who approves of impiety; the wicked shall not dwell with you. Ps. 5:5. God not only does not take pleasure in impiety, but He detests it most of all, and He does not deem the architects of crimes worthy of His special grace. You say: I. Nothing happens without God simply willing it, or in no way willing it: for who shall resist the will of God? Rom. 9:19. Resp. Sins happen not because God simply does not will it, or is unwilling; for no one can resist the will and absolute power of God: nor because He simply wills it; because God neither approves of sins nor takes pleasure in them: but because He does not will it, that is, He permits it. Between 'not willing' [nolle] and 'not willing' [non velle] there is this difference, that the former denotes a privation of will with repugnance and contrary action; the latter, however, denotes a privation of will, without violent reluctance. God does not will evil, but only the permission of evil. You say: II. God does not indeed will sin formally and in itself, as it is ἀνομία [lawlessness]: yet He wills it as a means of exercising vindictive justice. Resp. God does not will sin as a means of exercising vindictive justice, but with the act of sin foreseen and supposed, God cannot not exercise His vindictive justice. Proof. c. God hinders both the will and the faculty of the sinner. He hinders the will 1) by the word of the law prohibiting it, Exod. 20. 2) by distracting it through men, Gen. 37:28. 3) internally by the Holy Spirit struggling against the flesh, which is prone to illicit pleasures. Gal. 5:17. 4) extraordinarily by deterring through dreams, Gen. 20:3. He hinders the faculty 1) by the removal of life, e.g., by the suffocation of Pharaoh, 2) by the removal of the object, e.g., of Ahithophel, through Hushai, 3) by the opposition of greater power, thus angelic powers resist human ones, 1 Kings 6:16. 4) by the perturbation of the mind, 2 Kings 7:6. 5) by the diminution of strength, 1 Kings 13:4.

Question 23. What acts of divine providence accompany sin? The acts of divine providence accompanying sin are: the sustaining of the nature acting evilly a), the concurrence to the remote material of the vicious action b), the permission of the ἀταξία [disorder] adhering to the sinful action c), the determination limiting the sin d), the direction toward a good end e). Proof. a. God declares His μακροθυμίαν [long-suffering], or His patience, because He sustains the members of the sinner, which are weapons of unrighteousness, and does not always destroy the wicked man in the act of sin: Which goodness of God leads the sinner to repentance. Rom. 2:4. Proof. b. The remote material of sin is the physical action, to which God contributes: But He does not concur to the action applied or determined to a prohibited object (which is the proximate material of sin), for the reason that the determination is from secondary causes acting freely, not from the general, indifferent, and indeterminate concurrence of God. Proof. c. Divine permission is not 1) a mild indulgence, as if God does not care at all when men commit crimes: Nor is it 2) a relaxation of the law, as if He permits license to sin to men: Nor 3) is it impotence in God, or a lack of knowledge, as if He wills or approves of evil; or a lack of power, as if He could not restrain sin: Nor 4) does it make God an idle spectator of sins, who neither forbids sins, nor sets a limit to malice, nor punishes crimes: But it is 5) a negative act, consisting in the negation or suspension of an inescapable impediment. God could indeed restrain or coerce the sinner by placing a violent or insurmountable impediment; but there are most just causes for the most holy Deity to permit sin. Meanwhile, He restrains the will of the sinning man with a legal impediment and invites the sinner to repentance by proposing punishments and rewards.

You say: Sins follow divine permission: Therefore God, permitting sins, is the indirect and accidental cause of them.

Resp. The indirect cause of a sin is that which can and ought to prevent it. But God is bound by no law to restrain sin by violent impediment.

Sins indeed follow divine permission eventually, but not causally. Prob. d.

Prob. d. God determines sin by setting limits both to the duration and to the atrocity of the crime. The Israelite church venerates this determining providence of God.

If Jehovah had not been for us, when man rose up against us; then they would have swallowed us up alive, when their wrath was kindled against us. God permits the enemies of celestial truth to rage against the church, but He sets limits to their rage, lest they vomit forth the whole poison of their bitterness.

The tyrant Pharaoh had devoured the Israelites in his hope; but the supreme Arbiter of things halted his monstrous attack.

Prob. e. Joseph praises the direction of the divine purpose toward the intended end.

You indeed thought evil against me: but God thought it for good, to do as it is this day, to save much people alive. The brothers had sold Joseph, thinking he would be a most miserable slave.

But God converted misery into glory, the burden of servitude into honor next to the royal summit, the adverse fortune of the son into the favorable fortune of the father and brothers.

Quest. XXIV. What acts of divine providence follow sin?

The infliction of divine punishments a) and the remission of sins b) follow sin. Prob. a. The most just God avenges crimes with spiritual and corporal punishment. Spiritual punishments are desertion, or the withdrawal of grace, consternation, delivery into the power of Satan, blinding, and hardening. Corporal punishment is either temporal or eternal.

Temporal punishment is either individual, or hereditary, or epidemic.

For God does not absolve the guilty, but visits the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, and upon the children's children, unto the third and fourth generation. Prob. b.

To repenting sinners, God remits guilt and punishment. Repent and convert yourselves, that your sins may be blotted out.

Quest. XXV. How will you transfer the doctrine of the providence of God into practice? Prob. a. Let us adhere with firm trust to God, who dispenses all things, and let us roll the whole weight of our cares upon Him. This is what the most pious king teaches us. Cast thy burden upon Jehovah, and he shall sustain thee.

To which St. Peter gives his support.

Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.

AUGUSTINE says aptly in Ps. XXXIX: He who had care of you before you existed, how will He not have care of you, now that you are what He willed you to be?

Prob. b.

Prob. b. God, the inspector and ruler of our life, is most worthy of ardent and burning love. For just as no moment passes in which we do not enjoy the goodness of God: so let no moment flow by in which our heart does not grow warm with the love of God, and surrender itself completely to Him.

Practical use. A deeper consideration of divine providence should excite in our souls undoubted trust a), ardent love b), filial fear c), and submissive veneration of God the best and greatest d).

Prob. c. In whatever place we stand, let us fear the eyes of God, lest we offend this omnipotent governor and all-seeing judge with sins, and break the thread of our life; for men of blood and deceit shall not halve their days, Ps. 55:24.

Prob. d. No hour should be passed by without revering God with pious prayers and acts of thanksgiving. By prayers we become partakers of the benefits which the providence of God dispenses. For Jehovah is near to all who call upon him; to all who call upon him in truth. He will fulfill the desire of those who fear him, and will hear their cry, and will save them, Ps. 145:18, 19. Prayers are as it were channels, through which the streams of divine charisms descend into us: Through the act of thanksgiving those streams are led back to their fountainhead, which is the most exuberant goodness of God. Wherefore bless God, all you who do all things magnificently, who exalts our days from the womb, and deals with us according to his mercy. Sir. 50:21.

Latin:

Prouidentia Dei distinguitur a) in generalem, et specialem. Illa est, qua Deus totum terrarum orbem, et quidquid eius ambitu continetur, conseruat et gubernat: Haec est, qua Deus ecclesiam, tam militantem, siue coetum hominum fidelium, quam triumphantem, siue chorum angelorum et hominum electorum benignissime intuetur, clementissime fouet, et suauissime regit. b) In ordinariam, et extraordinariam. Illa est, qua Deus iuxta praefinitam naturae legem agit: Haec est, qua Deus supra constitutum naturae ordinem operatur. c) In eam, quae circa bonum, et quae circa malum morale occupatur. Illa est, qua bonum creaturarum conseruando tuetur, cooperando promouet, et gubernando ad laudem gloriae diuinae dirigit: Haec est, qua Deus circa malum morale versatur non vt otiosus spectator, sed vt iustissimus iudex, atque adeo iustitiam, gratia sua temperatam, actibus peccatum antecedentibus, concomitantibus et consequentibus exserit.

Prob. a) Discrimen prouidentiae diuinae generalis, et specialis docet et ipse Christus Matth. VI, 26. Inspicite volatilia caeli: Nam non serunt, neque metunt, neque conuehunt in horrea: tamen pater vester caelestis alit illa. Nonne vos magis praecellitis illa? q.d. Gerit Deus curam auium generalem, hominum piorum, tanquam filiorum suorum, specialem et eximiam.

b) Quamuis Deus prouidentiae suae actus naturae et proprietatibus creaturarum vt plurimum accommodet: Non ita tamen ad vires creaturarum se alligauit, quin supra eas agere queat. Sic ad nutum Dei sol stat, asina loquitur, aqua in vinum abit. Omnia miracula sunt effecta prouidentiae Dei extraordinariae.

c) Deum non esse otiosum peccatorum spectatorem; sicut homines feriantes spectatum veniunt ludos scenicos, sed iustissimum quidem, placabilem tamen iudicem eorundem, ex actibus prouidentiae diuinae, qui peccati consummationem vel antecedunt, vel comitantur, vel consequuntur, liquido patefiet.

Quaest. XXII. Quinam actus prouidentiae diuinae peccatum antecedunt?

Antecedunt peccati consummationem a) praeuisio, siue praescientia diuina, b) peccati praeuisi auersio, c) impeditio.

Prob. a) Praeuise Deum populi Israelitici perfidiam et inobedientiam, perspicimus ex Ies. XLVIII, 8. Noui, quod perfide agendo perfide acturus esses; et praeuaricatoris ab vtero vocatum est nomen tibi. Quae diuina praeuisio infallibilis quidem, non absolute autem necessitas est. Vnde fallit sequens sophisma: Quidquid Deus praeuidet, illud fit necessario: Atqui peccatum etc. Ergo. Resp. Dist. inter necessitatem consequentis, et consequentiae. Quanquam peccata necessario eueniunt, vti a Deo sunt praeuisa, ea tamen necessitas est consequentiae, non absoluta, est hypothetica, non absoluta. Nesunt præuifa, ea tamen necessitas est confequentiæ, non consequentis, est hypothetica, non absoluta.

Neque enim ideo peccata euenient, quia præuisa sunt; sed ideo sunt præuisa, quia certo euenient. b) Non Deus approbans impietatem tu es; non manebit apud te malus. Pf. V, 5. Deus non tantum impietate non delectatur, sed eandem maxime detestatur, scelerumque architectos speciali gratia sua haud dignatur. Dicis: I. Deo simpliciter nolente, vel nullo modo volente, nihil fit: nam Dei voluntati quis resistet? Rom. IX, 19. Resp. Peccata fiunt Deo non simpliciter nolente, seu inuito; nemo enim voluntati & potentiæ Dei absolutæ potest repugnare: nec simpliciter volente; quia Deus peccata nec approbat, nec iis delectatur: sed non volente, hoc est, permittente. Inter nolle, & non velle hæc est differentia, quod illud notet priuationem voluntatis cum repugnantia & actione contraria; hoc autem notet priuationem voluntatis, sine violenta reluctatione. Deus non vult malum, sed tantum permissionem mali. Dicis: II. Deus non quidem vult peccatum formaliter & per se, vt est ἀνομία: vult tamen illud, vt medium iustitiæ vindicatiuæ exercendæ. Resp. Deus non vult peccatum, vt medium exercendæ iustitiæ vindicatiuæ, sed præuiso & supposito peccati actu non potest non Deus suam iustitiam vindicatiuam exercere. Prob. c. Impedit Deus tum voluntatem; tum facultatem peccatoris. Voluntatem impedit 1) verbo legis illud prohibendo, Exod. XX. 2) per homines id distrahendo, Gen. XXXVII, 28. 3) interne per Spiritum S. carni, ad illicitas voluptates procliui, obluctando. Gal. V, 17. 4) extraordinarie per somnia deterrendo, Gen. XX, 3. Facultatem impedit 1) vitæ ablatione, v. gr. Pharaonis suffocatione, 2) obiecti remotione, v. gr. Achitophelis, per Chusehaium, 3) maioris potentiæ oppositione, sic viribus humanis obstant angelicæ, 1 Reg. VI, 16. 4) animi perturbatione, 2 Reg. VII, 6. 5) virium imminutione, 1 Reg. XIII, 4.

Quæst. XXIII. Quinam actus prouidentiæ diuinæ peccatum comitantur? Actus prouidentiæ diuinæ peccatum comitantes sunt: sustentatio naturæ male agentis a), concursus ad actionis vitiosæ materiale remotum b), ἀταξίας actioni peccaminosæ adhærentis permissio c), determinatio peccati limitans d), directio ad bonum finem e). Prob. a. Declarat Deus μακροθυμίαν, siue longanimitatem suam, quod membra peccatoris, quæ sunt arma iniustitiæ, sustentat, neque semper hominem maleficum in flagranti peccato perimit: Quæ bonitas Dei peccatorem ad pœnitentiam ducit. Rom. II, 4. Prob. b. Peccati materiale remotum est actio physica, ad quam Deus coinfluit: Non autem concurrit ad actionem, ad obiectum prohibitum applicatam, vel determinatam (quæ est peccati materiale proximum), propterea, quod determinatio est a caussis secundis libere agentibus, non a concursu Dei generali, indifferenti & indeterminato. Prob. c. Permissio diuina non est 1) blanda indulgentia, quasi Deus plane non curet, quando homines scelera committunt: Nec est 2) relaxatio legis, quasi peccandi licentiam hominibus permittat: Neque 3) est impotentia in Deo, vel defectus scientiæ, quasi malum velit, aut probet; vel defectus potentiæ, quasi peccatum cohibere nequeat: Neque 4) Deum facit otiosum peccatorum spectatorem, qui nec vetet peccata, nec metam malitiæ ponat, neque flagitia pœnis coërceat: Sed est 5) actus negatiuus, consistens in negatione, vel suspensione impedimenti ineluctabilis. Posset quidem Deus, obiecto impedimento violento, aut imperuincibili, peccatorem refrænare aut coërcere; at sunt numini sanctissimo caussæ permittendi peccatum iustissimæ. Cohibet interim hominis peccantis voluntatem impedimento legali & subinde peccatorem propositis pœnis & præmiis ad pœnitentiam inuitat.

Dicis: Permissionem divinam sequuntur peccata: Ergo Deus, peccata permittens, eorundem est causa indirecta & per accidens.

Resp. Indirecta causa peccati est, quae illud impedire potest & debet. Deus autem ad cohibendum impedimento violento peccatum nulla lege obligatur.

Sequuntur quidem peccata permissionem divinam eventualiter, non autem causaliter. Prob. d.

Prob. d. Determinat Deus peccatum, tum durationi, tum atrocitati sceleris limites praefigendo. Quam providentiam Dei determinatricem veneratur ecclesia Israelitica

Nisi Iehouah fuisset pro nobis, quum insurrexit contra nos homo; tunc viuos deglutiissent nos, cum arderet ira eorum contra nos. Permittit Deus, vt hostes veritatis coelestis in ecclesiam saeuiant, sed saeuitiae praefinit metas, ne omne acerbitatis virus euomat.

Tyrannus Pharao Israelitas spe deuorauerat; at eius immanem impetum stitit summus rerum arbiter.

Prob. e. Pronae divinae directionem ad propositum finem collaudat Iosephus, .

Vos quidem cogitastis super me malum: Deus autem cogitauit illud in bonum, vt faceret iuxta diem hunc ad viuificandum populum magnum. Iosephum vendiderant fratres, rati, illum fore mancipium longe miserrimum.

At miseriam Deus conuertit in gloriam, seruitutis onus in honorem regio culmini proximum, fortunam aduersam filii in fortunam secundam patris & fratrum.

Quaest. XXIV. Quinam actus providentiae divinae peccatum consequuntur?

Peccatum consequuntur poenarum divinarum irrogatio a), peccatorum remissio b). Prob. a. Vindicat Deus iustissimus scelera poena spirituali & corporali. Poenae spirituales sunt desertio, siue subtractio gratiae, consternatio, traditio in potestatem Satanae, excoecatio, induratio. Poena corporalis alia temporalis, alia aeterna est.

Temporalis est vel singularis. vel hereditaria, vel epidemica.

Neque enim nocentem Deus absoluit, sed visitat iniquitatem patrum super filios, & super filios filiorum, super tertianos & quatanos . Prob. b.

Peccatoribus resipiscentibus Deus culpam & poenam remittit. Agite paenitentiam & conuertite vos, vt deleantur vobis peccata vestra, .

Quaest. XXV. Quomodo doctrinam de providentia Dei ad praxin transferes? Prob. a. Firma fiducia Deo cuncta dispensanti adhaereamus, & totam curarum nostrarum molem in ipsum deuoluamus. Id quod nos docet rex piissimus, . Proiice super Iehouam onus tuum, ille sustentabit te.

Cui suffragatur S. Petrus, .

Omnem curam vestram iniicite in ipsum; quia ipsi cura est pro vobis.

Apposite inquit AVGSTIN. in Ps. XXXIX. Qui curam habuit tui antequam esses, quomodo non habebit cu am, cum iam hoc es, quod voluit, ut esses?

Prob. b.

Prob. b. Deus, inspector & rector vitae nostrae, ardenti conflantique amore longe dignissimus est. Sicut enim nullum transit momentum, quo bonitate Dei non fruamur: Sic nullum effluat momentum, quo amore Dei cor nostrum non incalescat, eique se penitus confecet.

Usus praxis. Penitior providentiae divinae consideratio excitet in animis nostris indubitatam fiduciam a), ardentem amorem b), filialem timorem c), submissamque venerationem Dei optimi, maximi d).

Prob. c. Quocunque consistimus loco, vereamur oculos Dei, ne hunc gubernatorem omnipotentem, & iudicem omnituentem peccatis offendamus, vitæque nostræ filum abrumpamus; etenim viri sanguinum & doli non dimidiabunt dies suos, Ps. LV, 24.

Prob. d. Nulla prætermissa hora venerandus est Deus piis precibus & gratiarum actionibus. Precibus beneficiorum, quæ providentia Dei dispensat, compotes evadimus. Propinquus enim est Iehouah omnibus invocantibus ipsum; omnibus, qui invocant ipsum in veritate. Voluntatem timentium ipsum faciet, & clamorem ipsorum audiet, & seruabit eos, Ps. CXLV, 18. 19. Preces sunt quasi canales, per quos fluenta diuinarum charismatum in nos descendunt: Per gratiarum actionem fluenta illa in scaturiginem suam, quæ est bonitas Dei exuberantissima, reducuntur. Quam ob rem benedicite Deo omnes; qui magnifice facit omnia, exaltantem dies nostros ex utero, & facientem nobiscum iuxta misericordiam suam. Sir. L, 21.


### Quest. XXI. How is the providence of God distinguished?: S I G H T

S I G H T.

Your provident care, supreme Arbiter, which embraces, sustains, fosters, and moderates all created things, and especially faithful men, I silently admire, gratefully acknowledge, and joyfully proclaim. All the hope of the pious is placed in your providence: all prosperity depends upon your most wise governance. You, Lord, will provide, nay, you have provided from eternity. You have gifted me with light and life: at the very threshold of life you led me in a wondrous manner by your most high counsel; you advanced the harsh labors of youth to desired outcomes. In my manly age you assigned me a sacred station, and that I might subsequently defend it, you inspired me with strength. I have followed your nod without murmuring, and I shall follow it henceforth, unwearied throughout the whole course of my life. This I most humbly pray of you above all, that you fill my breast with your most holy Spirit, show me the ways and methods of walking rightly, call my mind away from the windings of errors and sins, and at last, having exercised me with various labors, command me to enter the tranquil port of eternal beatitude.

Latin:

S V S P I R I V M.

Providam tuam curam, supreme Arbiter, cum omnes res creatas, tum in primis homines fideles complecti, sustentare, fouere, moderari, & tacitus admiror, & gratus cognosco, & lætus prædico. Omnis piorum spes in prouidentia tua est collata: omnis prosperitas a sapientissimo tuo moderamine suspensa. Tu, Domine, prouidebis, quin & ab æterno prouidisti. Tu me luce & vita donasti: in primo vitæ limine altissimo tuo consilio mirum in modum me duxisti; asperos iuuentæ labores ad optatos exitus prouexisti. In ætate virili sacram mihi stationem assignasti, & vt eam deinde tuerer, vires adspirasti. Nutum tuum sine murmure sum secutus, & sequar deinceps impiger in toto vitæ meæ cursu. Hoc potissimum humillime a te precor, vt Spiritu tuo sanctissimo pectus meum impleas, vias rationesque recte eundi mihi commonstres, ab anfractibus errorum & peccatorum mentem meam auoces, ac tandem, variis me exercitum laboribus, tranquillum æternæ beatitatis portum ingredi iubeas.


## 10 On the Formal End of Theology, the Vision and Enjoyment of God


### Quest. I. What do you call the formal end of theology?

The formal end of theology is the attainment of the highest good ), and it is a certain operation of the rational soul concerning God, and that a perfect one, by which it is rendered a participant of His very goodness, so that it is most fully satisfied by the same ). It is otherwise called beatitude ), and eternal life ).

Prob. a. The formal end in practical disciplines is the acquisition and possession of that good, for the sake of which the science exists. Whence THOMAS in book II, q. 1, a. 8, says: Beatitude denotes the attainment of the ultimate end []). []

Prob. b. The very concept of beatitude indicates that the attainment of the ultimate end and the highest good consists in a certain operation of the rational soul. For the common people and the wise alike accept beatitude, a blessed life, to be blessed, and to live blessedly, indiscriminately. But since vital operations in man are threefold—vegetative, sensitive, and rational—the attainment of the ultimate end and the highest good can be constituted in none other than the rational soul. For the highest good is the proper good of man, which belongs to him as he is man. Therefore, it is obtained only through the operation proper to man, and which belongs to him as man. Moreover, the operations of the sensitive soul are common to man with the brutes, and those of the vegetative soul are common even with plants. It remains, therefore, that the beatitude of man formally consists in the operation of the rational soul alone.

Prob. c. Beatitude is attributed to one who sees God, Matt. 5:8. Therefore, the operation of the intelligent soul, knowing God intuitively, is rightly called Beatitude.

Prob. d. Beatitude is called eternal life, John 3:15. By this word it is implied that the operation of the intellect and will, by which man possesses and enjoys God as his ultimate end and highest good, is vital, and that it is most happy and most constant. For life is not considered here merely in itself, as it is the bare existence of living things; since that also belongs to the damned in hell, whose state, however, is called eternal death in the sacred scriptures, never eternal life: but it is considered here according to the most happy condition and operation of the living.

Obf. Eternal life is here presupposed as the formal end of theology, to which the means of grace and salvation are to be directed. In the third part of theology, where the acts of applying divine grace are examined, it is considered as the effect of glorifying grace. For which reason, although eternal beatitude, taken in its full breadth, embraces all internal and external goods by which the elect are perfected and adorned in heaven: yet in the present, considered according to its intrinsic and formal notion, it denotes the vital operation of the intellectual soul by which man, being elect and having departed from this life, possesses and enjoys God, his highest good, in the heavenly fatherland.

Quaest. II. From what principle is the eternal beatitude of man known? Solid and clear knowledge of eternal beatitude is drawn from the scripture of the old and new testament . But from the principles of reason we know to a certain extent that God is the highest good of man , that the human soul is immortal , and that after this life there is another life in which it will go well for the good and ill for the wicked . But reason, left to itself, is ignorant of the formal notion of eternal beatitude .

Prob. filled with numbers and parts. Thus CICERO, Tusc. Disp. Bk. V, ch. 8: "I do not understand what he who is blessed could require to become more blessed." Ch. 10: "They are called blessed who are in good things, with no evil attached." In the sacred scriptures, this word sometimes has a wider scope, and generally denotes a good condition by which one excels another, Acts 20:35. And even he who is indeed unhappy, but yet happier than others whom more grievous troubles press, is called blessed, Luke 23:29. But for the most part, it is used in a stricter sense 1) of supreme and infinite perfection, when God, and He indeed the only one, is called blessed, 1 Tim. 1:11, 6:15. 2) Of the perfect enjoyment of the highest good, as much as falls into a finite nature, and the attainment, possession, and use of the ultimate end, so perfect that nothing more can be desired, and indeed so certain that no evil is ever to be feared; which is the blessedness of men, and indeed consummated blessedness, Matt. 5:8.

Prob. a. That eternal beatitude is given, we know clearly from the prophetic writings of the Old Testament. For 1) God threatens: In whatever day you eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall die the death. Gen. II, 17. Therefore it signifies that he would live eternally if he did not eat. For God, most just, to those men who were about to transgress his law, threatened death, but to those who were about to observe the law (since the reason for contraries is contrary) he promised life. But to the first-formed, and in them to all, he threatened death. E. 2) After the fall, God promised the seed of the woman, the meritorious cause of eternal salvation. The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent, Gen. III, 15. i.e., he shall destroy the kingdom of Satan, take away death, and restore perfect justice and eternal life. 3) To those keeping the prescribed law, God promised eternal life: Keep my laws; for the man who does them shall live in them, Lev. XVIII, 5. i.e., he shall obtain eternal life. For Christ, to the question: How shall I attain eternal life? replied only this: You know the commandments. Luke XVIII, 20. alluding to the passage in Lev. XVIII, 5. which the apostle also expounds concerning eternal life in Rom. X, 5. Gal. III, 11. 4) That men finally believing by the grace of God are to obtain eternal life, the prophets teach, Hab. II, 4. The just shall live by his faith. That eternal life is noted here, the apostle teaches, Rom. I, 17. Gal. III, 13. Heb. X, 38. & Dan. XII, 2. Many shall awake to eternal life. 5) The reborn men of the Old Testament raised and refreshed their spirit with the hope of eternal life. Jacob, near to death, says in Gen. XLIX, 18. I await your salvation, O Jehovah. The patriarch was looking toward a salvation that was not temporary and transitory; for he said in Gen. XLVIII, 1. Behold I die: but toward an eternal one, which he most firmly believed and expected would be given to him on account of the Messiah. 6) God translated the candidates for eternity, Enoch and Elijah, alive into heaven, so that we might rely on the most certain hope of future beatitude. Job relied on this, ch. XIX, 26. I shall see my God in my flesh.

Prob. b. The Scripture of the New Testament most clearly and indeed everywhere inculcates that men perseveringly believing in Jesus obtain eternal life, John III, 16. an incorruptible inheritance, 1 Pet. I, 4. eternal salvation, Heb. V, 9.

Prob. c. Human reason conceives God as the first being, which is from itself and the cause of other things; and which preserves and governs all things. This being, indeed, as it is the first, so also is it the last, and a good desirable for its own sake. Wherefore true beatitude can neither be sought nor found, except in the attainment and possession of this highest good.

Prob. d. The light of nature teaches that every single thing tends toward an end proportioned to itself, and upon obtaining it, is blessed. It teaches further that the soul is not perishable, but immortal. Therefore it tends toward an eternal end, which is its beatitude. The human soul is immortal; because it is a spirit. Its invisibility, its power of penetrating bodies, and its perichoristic information of them, as well as operations independent of matter, testify to the spiritual nature of the soul, which demonstrate that the form itself is independent of matter, i.e., immaterial, and therefore immortal; since a cause is not inferior or more ignoble than its effect. Indeed, the acts of the rational soul, e.g., to contemplate God, eternal things, intelligible species, to abstract universals from particulars, subsequently to reflect upon itself, to gather the future from the past, to deliberate prudently about future things, and to choose freely what things are good, are independent of matter, and producible without any cooperation of the body, and therefore spiritual. It must be, therefore, that the soul itself is a spirit.

Prob. e. By the guidance of the light of nature we know that divine providence governs all things and directs them toward ends congruous to each thing. Since, therefore, we experience in fact that in this life joyful things not rarely accompany the wicked, and sorrowful things the good, we gather by no vain inference that, by the force of providence of [divine] justice, that another life remains, where conversely it will go well for the good and ill for the wicked, concerning which the domestic tribunal of conscience passes judgment for everyone.

Latin:

Finis formalis theologiæ est adeptio summi boni ), estque operatio quædam animæ rationalis circa Deum, eaque perfecta, qua bonitatis ipsius ita redditur particeps, vt eadem plenissime satietur ). Vocatur alias beatitudo ), & vita æterna ).

Prob. a. Finis formalis in disciplinis practicis est acquisitio & possessio illius boni, cuius caussa scientia est. Ex quo THOMAS in l. II. q. 1. a. 8. inquit: Beatitudo notat adeptionem ultimi finis [*]). [*]

Prob. b. Adeptionem finis ultimi & boni summi in operatione quadam animae rationalis consistere, ipse beatitudinis conceptus indicat. Beatitudinem enim & vitam beatam, beatum esse, beate vivere, vulgus pariter & sapientes promiscue accipiunt. Cum vero operationes vitales in homine triplices sint, vegetativa, sensitiva, & rationalis, adeptio finis ultimi & boni summi in nulla, quam in anima rationali constitui potest. Bonum summum enim est bonum hominis proprium, quod ei, qua homo est, convenit. Ergo non nisi per operationem hominis propriam, & quae ei ut homini convenit, obtinetur. Operationes autem animae sensitivae homini cum brutis, vegetativae etiam cum plantis communes sunt. Relinquitur ergo, quod beatitudo hominis formaliter consistat in sola animae rationalis operatione.

Prob. c. Beatitudo tribuitur videnti Deum, Matth. V, 8. Ergo operatio animae intelligentis, Deumque intuitiva cognoscentis, recte dicitur Beatitudo.

Prob. d. Beatitudo vocatur vita aeterna, Io. III, 15. Qua voce innuitur, operationem intellectus & voluntatis, qua homo Deo, tanquam ultimo suo fine, summoque bono potitur, & fruitur, vitalem, eamque felicissimam & constantissimam esse. Neque enim vita hic tantum secundum se spectatur, prout est nuda viventium existentia; quippe quae etiam damnatis competit in inferno, quorum status tamen in sacris litteris mors aeterna, nunquam vita aeterna appellatur: sed consideratur in praesenti secundum felicissimam viventium conditionem & operationem.

Obs. Praecognoscitur hic vita aeterna, ut finis formalis theologiae, ad quem media gratiae salutisque dirigenda sunt. In parte tertia theologiae, ubi actus gratiae divinae applicatricis expenduntur, consideratur ut effectus gratiae glorificantis. Quam ob rem, licet aeterna beatitudo, sumta in tota sua latitudine, complectatur omnia bona interna & externa, quibus electi in caelo perficiuntur & exornantur: in praesenti tamen, secundum intrinsecam & formalem suam rationem considerata, notat animae intellectualis operationem vitalem, qua homo electus, & ex hac vita egressus, Deo, summo bono suo, in patria caelesti potitur & perfruitur.

Quaest. II. Ex quo principio aeterna hominis beatitudo innotescit? Solida & liquida aeternae beatitudinis notitia hauritur ex scriptura veteris , et noui testamenti . Ex principiis autem rationis quadantenus cognoscimus, Deum hominis esse summum bonum , animam humanam esse immortalem , post hanc vitam dari aliam vitam, in qua bonis bene, malis male futurum fit . Rationem autem formalem aeternae beatitudinis ratio sibi relicta ignorat .

Prob. bus numeris ac partibus expletam. Ita CICERO, quaest. Tusc. L. V. c 8 Qui beatus est, non intelligo, quid requirat, ut fit beatior. c. 10: Beati dicuntur, qui sunt in bonis, nullo adiuncto malo. In sacris litteris interdum quidem haec vox latius patet, & generatim denotat bonam conditionem, qua alter altero praestat, Act. XX, 35. atque etiam is, qui infelix quidem est, at felicior tamen aliis, quos grauiora premunt incommoda, nominatur beatus, Luc. XXIII, 29. Plerumque vero strictiori significatione adhibetur 1) de summa atque infinita perfectione, cum Deus, & is quidem unus, beatus dicitur, I Tim. I, 11. VI, 15. 2) De perfecto summi boni fructu, quantum quidem in naturam finitam cadit, & summi finis consecutione, possessione atque usurpatione, tam perfecta, nihil ut desiderari possit amplius, immo etiam tam certa, ut nihil unquam metuendum sit mali; quae est hominum beatitas, & consummata quidem beatitas, Matth. V, 8.

Prob. a. Dari aeternam beatitudinem, e scriptis propheticis V. T. liquido cognoscimus. Nam 1) comminatur Deus: Quacunque die comedes de arbore scientiae boni & mali, morte morieris. Gen. II, 17. Ergo significat, aeternum victurum, si non comederit. Nam Deus iustissimus, quibus hominibus, legem suam transgressuris, minatus est mortem, illis legem observaturis (quia contrariorum contraria est ratio) pollicitus est vitam. At protoplastis, & in illis omnibus, minatus est mortem. E. 2) Post lapsum promisit Deus semen mulieris, caussam aeternae salutis meritariam. Semen mulieris conteret caput serpentis, Gen. III, 15. i. e. destruet regnum Satanae, auferet mortem, reducet perfectam iustitiam & vitam aeternam. 3) Custodientibus legem praescriptam Deus pollicitus est vitam aeternam: Custodite leges meas; faciens enim homo vivet in eis, Leu. XIIX, 5. i. e. obtinebit vitam aeternam. Christus namque ad quaestionem: Quomodo consequar vitam aeternam? id vnum regessit: Nosti praecepta. Luc. XIIX, 20. alludens ad locum Leu. XIIX, 5. quem etiam apostolus Rom. X, 5. Gal. III, 11. de vita aeterna exponit. 4) Homines finaliter credentes ex gratia Dei consecuturos esse vitam aeternam, docent prophetae, Habac. II, 4. Iustus in fide sua vivet. Notari hic vitam aeternam, docet apostolus, Rom. I, 17. Gal. III, 13. Hebr. X, 38. & Dan. XII, 2. Multi evigilabunt ad vitam aeternam. 5) Homines renati V. T. spe vitae aeternae animum erexerunt & recrearunt. Iacobus morti vicinus dicit Gen. XLIX, 18. Salutem tuam exspecto, Iehouah. Respiciebat patriarcha salutem non temporariam & transitoriam; aiebat enim Gen. XLIIX, 1. En ego moriar: sed aeternam, quam propter Messiam sibi dandam firmissime credebat & exspectabat. 6) Deus candidatos aeternitatis, Enochum & Eliam, vivos in coelum transtulit, vt certissima futurae beatitatis spe niteremur. Nixus ea est Iobus, c. XIX, 26. Videbo Deum meum in carne mea.

Prob. b. Scriptura noui testamenti luculentissime & quidem passim locorum inculcat, homines perseveranter credentes in Iesum, consequi vitam aeternam, Io. III, 16. hereditatem incorruptibilem, 1 Petr. I, 4. salutem aeternam, Hebr. V, 9.

Prob. c. Ratio humana concipit Deum vt ens primum, quod a se & ceterorum caussa est; quodque omnia conferuat & gubernat. Hoc sane ens, vt primum, ita & vltimum, & propter se expetibile bonum est. Quare nec quaeri, nec inueniri vera beatitudo potest, nisi in adeptione & possessione huius summi boni.

Prob. d. Lumen naturae docet, vnamquamque rem tendere ad finem sibi proportionatum, eoque obtento beatam esse. Docet porro, animam non esse caducam, sed immortalem. Ergo tendit ad finem aeternum, qui eius est beatitudo. Immortalis est anima humana; quia est spiritus. De spirituali animae natura testantur eius inuisibilitas, vis penetratrix corporum, & horum informatio perichoristica, nec non operationes a materia independentes, quae formam ipsam a materia independentem, i. e. immateriabilem, adeoque immortalem esse demonstrant; cum caussa non fit deterior aut ignobilior effectu suo. Sane actus animae rationalis, v. gr. contemplari Deum, res aeternas, species intelligibiles, a singularibus vniuersalia abstrahere, subinde in seipsam reflectere, ex praeteritis colligere futura, de futuris prudenter deliberare, & quae bona sunt, libere eligere, sunt a materia independentes, & sine vlla corporis cooperatione producibiles, adeoque spirituales. Animam ergo ipsam spiritum esse oportet.

Prob. e. Ductu luminis naturae cognoscimus, prouidentiam diuinam omnia gubernare & ad congruos cuilibet rei fines dirigere. Cum ergo reapse experiamur, in hac vita non raro laeta omnia malos, tristia omnia bonos comitari; haud ex vano colligimus, vi prouidentiae tiæ & iustitiæ divinæ aliam superesse vitam, vbi vice versa bonis bene, malis male futurum fit, de quo vnicuique tribunal domesticum conscientiæ sententiam dicit .


### Quest. I. What do you call the formal end of theology?: I argue II

I argue II.

II. from the excellence of man, by which he alone stands out among all animals.

The first principle of all is: That which is repugnant to itself cannot possibly exist, and two things at the same time, of which one is repugnant to the other, cannot be true.

But there would be a manifest repugnance in these things: that man excels all brute animals whatsoever; yet nevertheless, in that part by which he alone far excels all others, he is of a far worse condition.

I do not reason thus: If man is more excellent than other animals; therefore he is not worse.

This consequence does not hold.

Why could both not be true, in a different respect, in one way and another?

It escapes no one what most learned men, both ancient and modern, have disputed concerning this: in what brute animals excel humans.

But indeed this is the argument on which I rely: If man, in that very part and by the same reason by which he excels all animals without exception, is to be judged altogether inferior to all, it follows that two things must be affirmed which are openly in conflict with each other.

The consequent is absurd: therefore the antecedent is also absurd.

I shall complete the argument: If there is no salvation for man, no perfection of his state to be expected after death: it follows that man, in the same part and by the same reason by which he alone is more excellent than all brute animals, is far inferior to them all.

The latter is false and absurd: Therefore

Let it be permitted to me to bring forward certain things for these arguments, to be declared a little more fully.

I argue I. from the nature of man and his properties.

Man consists of two parts, soul and body.

The soul is the nobler part of human nature.

The soul is an immortal spirit, the clearest proofs of which we receive from thought, free will, and preparation for future events, and from the desire for perpetual and never-ending happiness, with which men are inflamed by a certain natural instinct.

That indeed which all feel, by which all are incited, and which bids them aspire not to evil, but to good and to the perfection of their state, that, I say, is to be attributed not to custom, nor to whim, but to the nature common to all, and not to natural corruption, but to natural constitution.

The corruption of nature arose entirely from the fact that the soul turned away from the highest good and inclined itself toward goods that were either false and specious, or unsuitable and insufficient for it.

The soul, since it is an immortal spirit, finds indeed nothing suitable for itself and sufficient for its satisfaction, except that which is spiritual and perpetual.

But such is now the perversity of the depraved soul that, although it is desirous of perpetual happiness, it nevertheless seeks and pursues no good except that which is earthly, perishable, and destined to perish suddenly, from which an insatiable desire cannot but always arise.

But what is no less worthy of observation: The soul of man is endowed with such a faculty that it can perceive the future through thought.

This faculty remains constant and always exercises its power, even then, when it is time for it to depart from the body.

Now let us assume this principle: Everything that exists, certainly exists for a certain end, and no other than one suitable to itself and its own nature.

Let us proceed by concluding from the lesser to the greater: If not even the smallest thing is destined for no end; it is absolutely not credible that the soul, the most noble of all things, or something in the soul—least of all that which is its own proper and chief attribute, namely providence and thought about the future, closely coupled with the highest desire for perpetual life and perfect beatitude—has no end proposed for itself.

But that end can be none other than the attainment of that toward which that thought and desire is uniquely directed.

Therefore, there is to be a future state of the soul, perfectly blessed, to be expected after the final fates.

In order that this may be more illustrated, let us ask in general: For what purpose was the faculty of providing and thinking about the future given to man?

Certainly for this reason, that he may take good counsel for himself, and, through this providence, arrive at obtaining the future security of his life, whether for the attainment of the future, if it be judged good, or for the avoidance of it, if it be judged to be evil.

Since this is most true in a general sense and placed beyond all doubt: what then, specifically, shall be considered the end for which that power of the mind to foresee and desire the future does not cease to be, but remains even now, nay rather is more confirmed, at that last moment when one must depart from this life?

Indeed this, so that the dying person, having overcome mortality, may attain eternal life.

Prob. f. Although the light of nature teaches that God is the highest and eternal good, and the ultimate end, to the attainment of which the immortal soul ought to aspire, and another after this Therefore also prior. But the excellence and prerogative of man, and that indeed the chief one, is undoubtedly reason. Here two things offer themselves to us to be weighed: The use of reason, and the cultivation of the same.

1) The more rightly a man exercises the use of reason, the greater thought and care he himself bestows upon whatever things are at hand, and in whatever business is to be undertaken. But the more cumulatively occupation is increased, the more and graver difficulties of labors he himself experiences, the greater becomes the anxiety about finding means and overcoming obstacles, the more dangers, and not always to be avoided, does man see, and burdens of evils to be endured, the more uncertain are his desires and vows, indeed most just ones, but for the most part vain, and destitute of the desired outcome: yet he is nowhere able in this mortality to arrive at that, to which he ought most especially to strive, namely, to the consummated tranquility of the soul.

He must always think to himself: more beyond. One must always be incumbent upon this, always laboring at it, so that his condition may receive increments daily: E. the highest end, always proposed to himself, he never attains.

I will explain a little more distinctly what has been said so generally.

The use of reason is seen most especially in three ways: The recollection of things past: The contemplation and consideration of present things, as much as concerns individual surrounding things, to be investigated by judgment: The providence of future things.

As regards the first: Recollection is either of pleasant things, or of sad ones.

In both ways perturbations and motions of the soul are renewed, according to this moral axiom: with the return of ideas, joined with a certain affection, the same affection returns. If the image of pleasant times enters the mind, pleasure and desire are excited anew, which can never be satisfied. But if of sad ones; the wounds of the soul, over which a scar had scarcely been drawn, will break out again.

I will speak of the second: Contemplation of those things which are now being done, wisely weighs all surrounding things.

Of what use are these, I ask? To gather the goods of fortune? What will those profit us, unless we use them well, as means to be applied to a nobler end? Nor is it to be denied that a huge heap of faculties and honors brings with it very many and very great inconveniences, it does not lighten, but increases the most grave adversities, by which this wretched life is pressed, care, labor, envy, snares, dangers, fear, loss, and finally the difficulty of rendering an account.

It stimulates desire more than it satisfies it, for its thirst is never quenched, the more waters are drunk, the more they are thirsted for. Finally, the more joy a man perceives while alive from the abundance of all things, the more bitter pains he will feel when dying, when he will labor under the lack of all things.

Nothing is so miserable as to be miserable from being happy. To what end then?

But to live well and happily? Rightly indeed, nay most rightly.

But in what way?

Why do we give effort to virtue? With what counsel do we strain all our nerves in successfully performing things?

Do we not labor for the sake of attaining the rewards proposed for virtues? It is so indeed.

But where are those? What and how great?

How rare and thin is the remuneration of the greatest virtue wont to be among men, of whom scarcely the fewest are the most just appraisers and judges of merits!

With good men it generally goes badly in this age, with bad men well. What I mentioned third: It is the part of a wise man to foresee what is to be.

From which fear and hope are born.

Fear is the dread of an approaching evil, distress about that future thing, and often a vain opinion of impending danger.

Hope is indeed the pleasant expectation of a future good, but that is for the most part uncertain, fallacious, and joined with the fear of the opposite.

From which it is understood how truly SIRACIDES, c.

40, 2, has numbered hope among the various parts of the calamity of mortals to be endured through this life. 2) The more study learned men, who are wise beyond the common herd, have bestowed upon the cultivation of the intellect, the more each of them perceives the vanity of the age, and in a certain way also the vanity of all sciences, as far as we perceive their fruit only in this mortality, and especially the perversity of men, with whom it behooves him to deal prudently, nay even the manifold defect of his own state, as well as its mutability and inconstancy.

Youths likewise, and men of the lowest plebs, feel much smaller troubles and pains than learned and wise men, most highly cultivated in disciplines, studies, and doctrine.

The more a man has experienced, so that he has left almost nothing untried, and the more keenly he has acquired judgment, the more certainly he will understand the calamitous condition of the world, and the more it will take hold of him with a weariness of such a wretched life.

He who knows well the sentiment of the divine book Coheleth, and holds it sacredly, surely he is methat this life is given; yet it does not clearly demonstrate in what the formal reason of eternal beatitude consists. For since the vision of God is a supernatural act, it transcends the sphere of natural light. Whence Paul says, 1 Cor. II, 9: Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him.

You say: I. Eternal beatitude is naturally desirable: Therefore it is naturally knowable. The antecedent is clear; because naturally all men wish to be happy. The consequence is evident: because natural appetite presupposes natural knowledge. There is no desire for the unknown. Resp. Eternal and supreme beatitude is not naturally desirable by an efficacious appetite, since it transcends the capacity of man, left to himself; although we do not deny that men naturally desire, by an inefficacious appetite, under the condition of possibility, a certain perennial beatitude; but whether that consists in the clear vision of God, the animal man does not know.

You say: II. It is certain from natural light that our beatitude consists in the most perfect operation. But the most perfect operation of our intellect is the vision of God. It is certain, therefore, from natural light, that our beatitude consists in the vision of God. Resp. Although it is certain from the light of nature that our beatitude consists in the most perfect operation; it is not, however, known from the same that the vision of God is possible. Nay rather, reason left to itself will judge that our beatitude consists in the abstractive knowledge and contemplation of the first being.

Quest. III. In what does our eternal beatitude formally consist? Our eternal and supreme beatitude consists in the perfect vision and fruition of God. The former is an act of the intellect; the latter of the will: By the former we possess God, the supreme good; by the latter we enjoy Him and find rest in Him.

Note. We have used "fruition" here in the stricter sense with AUGUSTINE, who writes in Book X of the Trinity, ch. X: We enjoy things known, in which the will finds rest, being delighted in them for their own sake.

Latin:

Argumentor II.

II. ex præstantia hominis, qua inter omnia animalia ipse vnus eminet.

Principium omnium primum est: Quod sibi repugnat, id omnino non potest fieri, & duo simul, quorum alterum alteri repugnat, non possunt esse vera.

Esset autem manifesta repugnantia harum rerum: hominem præstare brutis animantibus quibusque; at nihilo tamen minus ea parte, qua ipse vnus longe omnibus præstat, longe deterioris esse conditionis.

Non ita ratiocinor: Si homo est præstantior ceteris animalibus; ergo non est deterior.

Hæc non valet consequentia.

Quidni vtrumque possit esse verum, diuersa ratione, alio atque alio modo?

Neminem præterit, quid viri doctissimi, cum veteres, tum recentiores, disputarint de eo: in quo bruta animalia hominibus antecellunt.

At enim vero hæc est, qua nitor, argumentatio: Si homo ea ipsa parte, eademque ratione, qua ipse præstat animalibus ad vnum omnibus, omnino inferior omnibus est estimandus; sequitur, vt adfirmanda sint duo, aperte inter se pugnantia.

Consequens est absurdum: absurdum igitur & antecedens.

Perficiam argumentationem: Si nulla est hominis salus, nulla perfectio status sui post mortem exspectanda: efficitur, vt homo eadem parte, eademque ratione, qua ipse vnus excellentior est brutis animalibus omnibus, longe illis omnibus sit inferior.

Posterius est falsum atque absurdum: Ergo

Adferre quædam mihi liceat ad hæc argumenta, paullo vberius declaranda.

Argumentor I. ex natura hominis, eiusque proprietatibus.

Homo constat ex duabus partibus, animo, & corpore.

Animus est nobilior pars humanæ naturæ.

Animus est spiritus immortalis, cuius clarissima documenta capimus ex cogitatione, libera voluntate, ac præparatione ad futuros euentus, ex desiderio perpetuæ & nunquam terminandæ felicitatis, quo flagrant homines naturali quodam instinctu.

Id vero, quod omnes sentiunt, quo omnes incitantur, & quod eos non ad malum, sed ad bonum, & ad perfectionem status sui adspirare iubet, id, inquam, non consuetudini, nec arbitrio, sed naturæ omnium communi, nec naturali corruptioni, sed naturali constitutioni, vtique tribuendum est.

Corruptio naturæ tota exorta est ex eo, quod animus a summo bono deflexit, & se ad bona tum falsa ac speciosa, tum sibi non conuenientia, nec sufficientia, inclinauit.

Animus, quum sit spiritus immortalis, reperit sane sibi conueniens, ac satiando sufficiens, nullum aliud, nisi spirituale ac perpetuum.

Sed ea nunc est peruersitas deprauati animi, vt, quamuis perpetuæ felicitatis cupidus sit, tamen nullum bonum, nisi terrestre, caducum ac subito interiturum, anquirat & consectetur, ex quo non potest non exsistere semper insatiabilis cupiditas.

Quod vero non minus obseruatione dignum est: Ea facultate instructus est hominis animus, vt possit cogitatione præcipere futura.

Hæc facultas permanet constans, suamque vim exercet semper, etiam tum, cum e corpore emigrare cum oportet.

Nunc adsumamus hoc principium: Omne, quidquid est, certe est propter certum quendam finem, neque alium, quam sibi suæque naturæ conuenientem.

Concludendo progrediamur a minori ad maius: Si ne minima quidem res ad nullum finem destinata est; prorsus non est credibile, animum, rerum omnium nobilissimam, aut aliquid in animo, omnium minime id, quod ipsius proprium ac præcipuum est, nempe prouidentiam & cogitationem de futuro, cum summo desiderio perpetuæ vitæ ac perfectæ beatitatis, arcte copulatam, nullum habere finem sibi propositum.

Alius autem non potest esse finis ille, nisi consecutio eius, ad quod vnice dirigitur ista cogitatio ac desideratio.

E. est futurus quidam status animi, perfecte beatus, post suprema fata exspectandus.

Id vt magis illustretur, quæramus in vniuersum: Quo consilio homini data sit facultas prouidendi & cogitandi futuræ?

Propter ea certe, vt bene sibi consulat ipse, &, per hancce prouidentiam, ad futuram vitæ suæ securitatem obtendendam perueniat, fiue ad consecutionem futuri, si bonum sit cognitum, siue ad deuitationem, si malum fore iudicetur.

Quod quum ita generatim verissimum sit, & extra omnem dubitationem positum: quid igitur speciatim pro fine habendum erit, quam ob rem illa mentis potestas, futura præfentiendi atque adpetendi non desinat esse, sed permaneat adhuc, immo magis confirmetur, vltimo illo momento, quo discedendum est ex hac vita?

Quippe hoc, vt moriens, superata mortalitate, vitam sempiternam consequatur.

Prob. f. Quamuis lumen naturæ doceat, Deum esse summum æternumque bonum, & vltimum finem, ad cuius adeptionem adspirare debet anima immortalis, aliamque post hanc Ergo & prius. Atqui excellentia ac prærogatiua hominis, & ea quidem præcipua, haud dubie est ratio. Hic duo se nobis offerunt perpendenda: Vsus rationis, & cultura eiusdem.

1) Quo rectius homo vsum rationis exercet, eo maiorem ipse confert cogitationem curamque in quasuis res, sibi obuias, in quæuis negotia obeunda. Tanto autem cumulatius augetur occupatio, tanto plures & grauiores experitur ipse difficultates laborum, tanto maior fit solicitudo de mediis reperiendis atque impedimentis vincendis, tanto plura, nec semper declinanda, videt homo pericula, & malorum onera perferenda, tanto magis incertum desideria, & vota, iustissima quidem illa, sed plerumque irrita, atque euentu exoptato destituta: neque vsquam tamen in hac mortalitate peruenire valet eo, quo potissimum studere debet, nimirum ad consummatam animi tranquillitatem.

Semper cogitandum ipsi est: plus vltra. Semper in id incumbendum est, semper in eo elaborandum, vt incrementa in dies capiat ipsius conditio: E. summum finem, semper sibi propositum, nunquam adsequitur.

Explicabo paullo distinctius, quod ita generaliter dictum est.

Rationis vsus triplex potissimum cernitur: Recordatio præteritorum: Contemplatio consideratioque præsentium, quantum ad singulas res circumstantes, iudicio inuestigandas: Prouidentia futurorum.

Quod ad primum attinet: Recordatio est vel iucundarum rerum, vel tristium.

Vtroque modo renouantur perturbationes ac motus animi, secundum hoc axioma morale: redeuntibus ideis, cum adfectu quodam coniunctis, redit idem adfectus. Si iucundorum temporum imago mentem subit, denuo excitatur voluptas & cupiditas, cui satis fieri nunquam potest. Sin tristium; recrudescent vulnera animi, quibus vix obducta fuerat cicatrix.

Dicam de altero: Contemplatio eorum, quæ nunc aguntur, res circumstantes vniuersas sapienter ponderat.

Quorum ista, quæso? Ad bona fortunæ colligenda? Ecquid nobis proderunt illa, nisi bene illis vtamur, tanquam mediis, ad finem nobiliorem adhibendis? Nec est negandum, quod ingens facultatum atque honorum cumulus plurima ad maxima secum fert incommoda, non leuat, sed auget grauissimas aduersitates, quibus premitur hæc ærumnosa vita, curam, laborem, inuidiam, insidias, pericula, metum, iacturam, rationis denique reddendæ difficultatem.

Cupiditatem magis stimulat, quam satiat, eius enim sitis nunquam expletur, quo plus sunt potæ, plus sitiuntur aquæ. Tandem homo, quo maiorem lætitiam percipit viuus ex omnium rerum adfluentia, eo acerbiores dolores sentiet moriens ipse, cum omnium rerum inopia laborabit.

Nihil tam miserum, quam ex beato miser.

Quorsum igitur?

At bene beateque viuendum? Recte quidem, immo rectissime.

Ecquo autem modo?

Cur virtuti damus operam? Quonam consilio neruos omnes in rebus feliciter peragendis contendimus?

Nonne propter ea laboramus, vt præmia virtutibus proposita consequamur? Ita est sane.

Sed vbi sunt illa? quæ & quanta? quæin rara ac tenuis esse solet virtutis maximæ remuneratio inter homines, quorum vix paucissimi sunt meritorum æquissimi æstimatores ac iudices!

Cum bonis viris male plerumque agitur in hoc sæculo, cum malis bene.

Quod tertium commemoraui: Sapiens est, prouidere, quid futurum sit.

Ex quo timor ac spes gignuntur. Timor est metus mali adpropinquantis, ægritudo de eo futuro, & fæpe inanis opinio impendentis periculi.

Spes est iucunda quidem boni futuri exspectatio, ea vero plerumque incerta, fallax, & cum formudine oppositi coniuncta.

Ex quo intelligitur, quam vere SIRACIDES, c XL.

2. spem mortalium inter varias partes calamitatis, per hanc vitam sustinendæ, nunnerauerit.

2) Quo plus studii cultura intellectus tribuerunt eruditi homines, qui vltra vulgus sapiunt, eo magis perspicit eorum quisque vanitatem sæculi, quodam etiam modo vanitatem omnium scientiarum, quoad quidem earum fructum non, nisi in hac mortalitate, percipimus, in primisque peruersitatem hominum, quibuscum prudenter versari ipsum decet, immo etiam status sui tam defectum multiplicem, quam mutabilitatem atque inconstantiam.

Iuuenes pariter, ac de infima plebe homines, multo minores ærumnas ac dolores sentiunt, quam docti ac sapientes viri, disciplinis, studiis, doctrina maxime exculti. Quanto plus homo expertus est, vt nihil fere intentatum reliquerit, & quanto acrius ipse nactus est iudicium, tanto certius intelliget calamitosam mundi conditionem, tantoque magis ipsum capiet tædium tam ærumnosæ vitæ.

Qui sententiam diuini libri Coheleth probe scit, sancteque tenet, næ is mehanc dari vitam; non tamen liquido demonstrat, in quo ratio formalis aeternae beatitudinis consistat. Cum enim visio Dei sit actus supernaturalis, sphaeram luminis naturalis transcendit. Ex quo Paulus inquit, 1 Cor. II, 9: Oculus non vidit, auris non audivit, & super cor hominis non ascenderunt, quae praeparavit Deus iis, qui diligunt ipsum.

Dicis: I. Aeterna beatitudo est naturaliter appetibilis: Ergo est naturaliter cognoscibilis. Antecedens patet; quia naturaliter omnes homines beati esse volunt. Consequentia est evidens: quia appetitus naturalis praesupponit notitiam naturalem. Ignoti nulla cupido. Resp. Aeterna & summa beatitudo naturaliter non est appetibilis appetitu efficaci, cum captum hominis, sibi relicti, transcendat; quamuis non negemus, homines naturaliter appetere appetitu inefficaci, sub conditione possibilitatis, perennem quandam beatitudinem; an autem illa consistat in clara Dei visione, homo animalis ignorat.

Dicis: II. Constat ex lumine naturali, nostram beatitudinem consistere in operatione perfectissima. At perfectissima operatio intellectus nostri est visio Dei. Constat ergo ex lumine naturali, beatitudinem nostram consistere in visione Dei. Resp. Quamuis ex lumine naturae constet, beatitudinem nostram consistere in operatione perfectissima; non tamen ex eodem innotescit, visionem Dei esse possibilem. Quin potius ratio sibi relicta iudicabit, beatitudinem nostram consistere in abstractiva entis primi cognitione & contemplatione.

Quaest. III. In quo formaliter consistat nostra aeterna beatitudo? Aeterna & summa nostra beatitudo consistat in perfecta Dei visione & fruitione. Illa est operatio intellectus; haec voluntatis: Illa Deo summo bono potimur; hac eodem perfruimur & acquiescimus.

Obf. Fruitionem sensu strictiori hic fuimus cum AVGVSTINO, qui L. X. de Tr. c. X. scribit: Fruimur cognitis, in quibus voluntas ipsis propter seipsa delectata conquiescit.


### Quest. I. What do you call the formal end of theology?: Hence we indeed use the world, but we enjoy God

Hence we indeed use the world, but we enjoy God.

Quest. IV. What is the beatific vision of God?

Vision of God is the beatific act of the intellect, illuminated by the light of glory, by which it knows God clearly and immediately, as He is in Himself. Note I. Intuitive knowledge of God is called beatific vision: Vision indeed by a metaphorical expression, because we shall know God as distinctly and clearly as we know a thing that we see with our eyes: Beatific, however, because it becomes the formal reason by which we are constituted happy. Note II. The knowledge of any thing is twofold: one abstractive, the other intuitive. Abstractive is that by which a thing is known mediately, in another, through the species of another thing, e.g., when you know an emperor from an image or from the report of others, or fire from smoke; intuitive, when you know an object immediately and through itself, e.g., when you look at a man face to face, and know him by his own countenance.

Abstractive knowledge of God, therefore, is when we know Him from reflection upon creatures under the light of nature, or from reflection upon the revealed word under the light of grace. When he perceives that that book was written with the intention that this very argument might be placed in the light. But the reason why we can receive from the light of reason not certain knowledge of a better life, but only probable information, is this: that 1) the truths known from nature, through the corruption of the mind innate in us, are greatly obscured, 2) the true reason for eternal beatitude, the origin of evil and of the common falling away of men from God, and most especially the reconciliation of man with God, and the way to recover lost salvation, not nature, but Scripture alone can teach us.

Intuitive knowledge of God is when we know Him through His own essence, as He is in Himself, without the intervention of another object, under the light of glory; and this is reserved for the other life, and is far more perfect than abstractive [knowledge]. Obf.

Objection III. Although the intuitive knowledge of God is perfect, it is not, however, comprehensive, taking the term in a strict sense for an adequate knowledge of a thing, in the way that God alone is the comprehensor of Himself. The blessed will know the whole essence of God, but not totally, and in an infinite manner, but in a way befitting their finite nature. The blessed are indeed commonly called "comprehensors," not because they know God adequately; for that cannot happen due to the infinity of the divine essence and the narrowness of human minds, since there is no proportion between the finite and the infinite: but they are called "comprehensors" of the divine essence because nothing of those things which are formally in God escapes them, but they know all those things in the highest degree of perfection of which a finite intellect, elevated by the light of glory, is capable.

Obs. IV. Three things are required for the beatific vision of God: 1) The intellect, as the principle and cause of intellection, with God concurring as the primary cause. 2) The light of glory, which is a heavenly and supernatural gift, which will show the divine essence present in time, and will most perfectly illuminate, corroborate, and elevate the intellect of the blessed to see God clearly.

This light of glory is proved (a) from Ps. 36:10: "In thy light we shall see light." From which words we argue: Whoever shall see in the light of God the objective light itself, God, they will be instructed by the light of glory illuminating and elevating the intellect. But the blessed in the other life, etc. You say: The discourse of the royal Psalmist is about the light of grace, not the light of glory; namely, in the light of grace we shall see light, i.e., God. Resp. V. 9. The sacred psalmist recounts positive spiritual benefits, the beginning of which is given in this life, the completion in the future life. V. 10. He describes the fountain of those benefits, and rises by a certain gradation to the ultimate of spiritual benefits, which is the vision of eternal light in eternal light. (b) Just as in this life no knowledge of God can be had except by the benefit of the light of nature or the light of grace: so in the other life there cannot be a clear and immediate knowledge of God except by the benefit of the light of glory.

(3) The essence of God is required as the object to which the beatific vision will tend and in which it will terminate. Obf.

Obs. V. The object of intuitive knowledge is God, and all things which are in Him actually and formally, such as the essence, attributes, divine persons, and their properties. But those things which are in God only eminently or virtually are not known by the power of intuitive knowledge; because they are not in God actually and as regards their entity. Hence the blessed, by the power of the beatific vision, will not know all creatures, or things done in this life after their departure. For neither these nor those are in God formally, but only virtually and eminently. They will indeed know the will of God clearly enough, insofar as it is identified with His essence, but since it determines itself toward creatures freely, by decreeing this or that, they do not see or know those free decrees in God. Hence it is that the angels, although blessed from the clear vision of God, are ignorant of the day of the final judgment, which is freely determined by God. Matt. 24: 26. We do not deny, however, that the blessed, either by a special revelation of God or by the report of angels and souls who have migrated from this mortal to that immortal life, can know many things that are done on earth: But they do not have those things explored by the power of intuitive cognition.

In intuitive knowledge of God the formal reason of eternal beatitude is proved to consist: (1) From Matt. 5:8. "Blessed are the clean of heart; for they themselves shall see God." In which words the Saviour describes eternal beatitude through the vision of God.

(2) From 1 John III, 1. Beloved, now we are the children of God, and it does not yet appear what we shall be. But we know that, if he shall appear, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is. The Apostle means to say: We are in this life the children of God; and we have some likeness to the heavenly Father in the kingdom of grace; but it has not yet appeared what we shall be: we know, however, that when that glory shall appear, we shall be perfectly like God, and shall possess that image and likeness of God which we lost in Adam; the foundation and cause of the divine image, fully restored, will be the vision of God, by which we shall see him as he is, i.e., in his essence, without an impressed species representing the divine essence. We argue: Whatever is the apex of our future glory, and the radical cause of the fully restored divine image, in that our eternal beatitude formally consists. But the beatific vision of God, etc. Therefore.

(3) From 1 Cor. XIII, 12. We see now through a glass in a riddle; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then I shall know, even as also I am known. The human intellect, suffused with the light of grace, sees God in this life through a glass in a riddle, i.e., less clearly: But it will see him far more clearly in the eternal life, illuminated by the light of glory. The Θεογνωσία of this age is imperfect: the θεογνωσία of the future age will be most perfect, as much as can indeed fall to a rational creature. But that eternal life consists in theognosia, Christ teaches in John XVII, 3.

Latin:

Hinc mundo quidem utimur, Deo autem fruimur.

Quaest. IV. Quid est visio Dei beatifica?

Visio Dei beatifica est actus intellectus, lumine gloriae collustrati, quo is Deum clare & immediate, vt in se est, cognoscit. Obf. I. Cognitio Dei intuitiva dicitur visio beatifica: Visio quidem locutione metaphorica, quod ea tam distincte & clare Deum cognituri sumus, quam distincte & clare cognoscimus rem, quam oculis videmus: Beatifica autem, quod fit formalis ratio, qua constituimur beati. Obf. II. Cognitio alicuius rei duplex est: abstractiva alia, alia intuitiva. Abstractiva est, qua res cognoscitur mediate, in alio, per speciem alterius rei, v. g. cum imperatorem ex imagine vel ex relatione aliorum, ignem ex fumo cognoscis; intuitiva, cum obiectum immediate & per seipsum cognoscis, v. gr. cum hominem coram intueris, & ex facie propria cognoscis.

Abstractiva igitur Dei cognitio est, cum eum ex reflexione ad creaturas sub lumine naturae, vel ex reflexione ad verbum revelatum sub lumine gratiae cognoscimus. cum sentiet, illum librum eo consilio scriptum esse, vt hoc ipsum argumentum in luce poneretur. Quare autem ex lumine rationis non certam melioris vitae cognitionem, sed probabilem dumtaxat notitiam accipere queamus, causa haec subest: quod 1) veritates, ex natura cognitae, per corruptionem animi, nobis innatae, valde obscuratae sunt, 2) veram rationem aeternae beatitatis, originem mali & communis hominum ...a Deo defectionis, maxime vero hominis cum Deo reconciliationem, ac viam ad recuperandam salutem deperditam, non natura, fed scriptura sola nos edocere potest.

Intuitiva cognitio Dei est, cum eum per suam essentiam, vti in se ipso est, sine interventu alius obiecti sub lumine gloriae cognoscimus; & haec alteri vitae reseruatur, estque longe perfectior, quam abstractiva.

Obs. III. Quamuis intuitiva Dei cognitio sit perfecta, non tamen est comprehensiva, termino stricte sumpto, pro adaequata rei cognitione, quomodo solus Deus sui comprehensor est. Cognoscent beati totam Dei essentiam, verum non totaliter, & modo infinito, sed finitae naturae suae conuenienti. Comprehensores quidem vulgo dicuntur beati, non quod Deum adaequate cognoscant; id enim per essentiae diuinae infinitatem & humanarum mentium angustiam fieri nequit, cum finiti ad infinitum nulla sit proportio: sed ideo essentia diuinae comprehensores dicuntur, quod nihil eorum, quae formaliter sunt in Deo, eos lateat, sed illa omnia in summo perfectionis gradu, quantum intellectus finitus, a lumine gloriae eleuatus, capax est, cognoscant.

Obs. IV. Tria requiruntur ad visionem Dei beatificam: 1) Intellectus, tanquam principium & causa intellectionis, Deo tanquam causa prima concurrente. 2) Lumen gloriae, quod est donum coeleste & supernaturale, quod essentiam diuinam in time praesentem monstrabit, intellectum beatorum perfectissime illuminabit, corroborabit, & ad Deum clare videndum eleuabit.

Probatur hoc lumen gloriae (a) e Ps. XXXVI, 10. In lumine tuo videmus lumen. E quibus verbis argumentamur: Quicunque visuri sunt in lumine Dei ipsum lumen obiectiuum Deum, illi lumine gloriae intellectum illustrante & eleuante erunt instructi. Atqui beati in altera vita &c. E. Dicis: Sermo est psalterii regio de lumine gratiae, non de lumine gloriae; nempe in lumine gratiae videbimus lumen, h. e. Deum. Resp. V, 9. Hieropsaltes recenset beneficia positiua spiritualia, quorum inchoamentum in hac vita, complementum in futura vita datur. V. 10. fontem istorum beneficiorum describit, assurgitque gradatione quadam ad vltimum beneficiorum spiritualium, quod est visio luminis aeterni in lumine aeterno. (b) Sicut in hac vita nulla potest haberi cognitio Dei, nisi vel luminis naturae, vel luminis gratiae beneficio: ita in altera vita non potest esse clara & immediata Dei cognitio, nisi beneficio luminis gloriae.

(3) Requiritur essentia Dei tanquam obiectum, ad quod beatifica visio tendet, ac se terminabit.

Obs. V. Obiectum intuitivae cognitionis est Deus, & omnia, quae in ipso actu & formaliter sunt, vt essentia, attributa, personae diuinae, earumque proprietates. Quae vero in Deo sunt tantum eminenter aut virtualiter, vi intuitivae cognitionis non cognoscuntur; quia actu, & quoad entitatem, non sunt in Deo. Hinc beati, vi beatificae visionis, non cognoscent creaturas omnes, vel res post discessum suum in hac vita gestas. Nam nec hae, nec illae formaliter, sed virtualiter & eminenter tantum sunt in Deo. Voluntatem quidem Dei, quatenus cum essentia eius identificatur, satis clare cognoscent, sed cum illa ad creaturas libere, hoc vel illud docernendo, se determinet, libera illa decreta in Deo non vident, aut norunt. Hinc est, quod angeli, quamuis ex clara Dei visione beati, diem extremi iudicii a Deo libere determinatum ignorent. Matth. XXIV, 26. Non imus tamen inficias, beatos vel ex peculiari Dei reuelatione, vel ex relatione angelorum & animarum, quae ex hac mortali ad illam immortalem vitam commigrarunt, multa, quae in terris geruntur, cognoscere posse: At illa non explorata habent vi intuitivae cognitionis.

In intuitiva Dei cognitione formalem rationem aeternae beatitudinis consistere probatur: (1) Ex Matth. V, 8. Beati mundi corde; quia hi ipsi Deum videbunt. Quibus verbis Saluator aeternam beatitudinem per visionem Dei describit.

(2) Ex 1 Ioh. III, 1. Dilecti, iam Filii Dei sumus, sed nondum manifestatum est, quid futuri simus. Scimus tamen, quod, si manifestabitur, similes ipsi futuri simus, quia videbimus ipsum, sicut est. Apostolus vult dicere: Sumus in hac vita Filii Dei; & habemus aliquam similitudinem cum Patre cœlesti in regno gratiæ; sed nondum apparuit, quid futuri erimus: scimus autem, quod, cum apparuerit ista gloria, nos perfecte Deo similes, imaginem & similitudinem istam Dei habituri simus, quam in Adamo decoximus; fundamentum autem & caussa imaginis diuinæ, plene restitutæ, erit visio Dei, qua ipsum videbimus, sicut est, i. e. in essentia sua, citra speciem impressam, essentiam diuinam repræsentantem. Argumentamur: Quidquid est apex futuræ nostræ gloriæ, & caussa radicalis plene restauratæ imaginis diuinæ, in eo formaliter consistit æterna nostra beatitudo. Atqui visio Dei beatifica &c. Ergo.

(3) Ex 1 Cor. XIII, 12. Videmus nunc per speculum in ænigmate; tunc vero a facie ad faciem: nunc cognosco ex parte; tunc vero cogniturus sum, sicut etiam cognitus sum. Intellectus humanus lumine gratiæ perfusus videt Deum in hac vita per speculum verbi diuini in ænigmate, i. e. minus claré: Videbit autem ipsum longe clarius in vita æterna lumine gloriæ collustratus. Θεογνωσία huius sæculi est imperfecta: θεογνωσία futuri sæculi erit perfectissima, quanta quidem in creaturam rationalem cadere potest. At in theognosia consistere vitam æternam, docet Christus Io. XVII, 3.


### Question V. Are the blessed in heaven also to see God with bodily eyes?

That the blessed in heaven will see God with bodily eyes is not indeed apodictically certain a), yet it is probable b).

Prob. a. 1) Because to see, according to the usage of the holy language, sometimes signifies the same as to know something by the intellect, 1 Cor. XIII, 12, and thus it can be explained as mental vision.

2) Angels are said in heaven to see the face of God the Father, who are destitute of bodily eyes, Matt. XVIII, 10. As therefore the vision of the angels is intellectual: so for the blessed in the future life an intellectual vision of God is to be hoped for.

Prob. b. 1) Job, in a most afflicted state, sustaining himself with effective consolation, says: From my flesh I shall see God: Whom I shall see for myself, and my eyes shall see, and not another. ch. XIX, 27. Job confesses that he will see Christ, not only as man, but also as God, and indeed with bodily eyes. Certainly no necessity compels us to depart from the propriety of the word and understand the eyes of the mind tropically.

2) The bodily eyes of the blessed in the future life will be spiritual (not by reason of substance but of qualities), 1 Cor. XV, 22. Therefore it is probable that the spiritual eye will see God.

3) The finite intellect can be elevated by the light of glory to such a degree that it may immediately, without an intelligible species, see the essence of God: Therefore, by equal reasoning, bodily eyes, equipped with spiritual powers, can be raised to such a degree of perfection that they may clearly behold God. The consequence is evident, because it is equally possible and easy for God to elevate the eyes of the body to see him, as it is possible for the same to elevate the finite intellect to intuitively know the infinite essence.

The antithesis is that of most Papists, who deny that God can be seen with bodily eyes, whose stronger arguments are:

I. No spirit can be seen with bodily eyes. But God is a spirit, and that most pure and subtle, John IV, 24. Therefore. R. No spirit can be seen with animal bodily eyes, I concede. But it is consistent with truth that the same can be seen with spiritual bodily eyes.

II. God is invisible, whom no one can see. Resp. God is called invisible, in respect of physical vision: not hyperphysical; and so no one can see God in this life with unglorified eyes. God himself limits it thus, My face (Jehovah speaks to Moses) you cannot see (with the eyes of the body): Why? Because man (with his eyes) cannot see me, and live (this life).
