III. In the same sense that angels are said to see the face of God, in the same sense also blessed men are said to behold God. But angels are said to see God with the eyes of the mind. Therefore, also blessed men. The major premise is certain; because the blessed will be like the angels, In a certain respect we shall be like the angels in the future life, but not simply or absolutely. It suffices that the blessed, both with the eyes of the mind and with the eyes of the body, by reason of spiritual qualities, will see God, just as the angels behold God in a spiritual manner.

IV. Whatever vision by which a bodily eye would transcend the sphere of its object, that is not to be asserted. But by the vision of the divine essence the bodily eye &c. Therefore. The major premise is clear; because every sense contains itself within the limits of its object. The minor is evident; because the object of the eyes is a colored and luminous body. Resp. Distinguish between an animal eye, or one not glorified, and a spiritual one. Whatever vision by which a bodily eye, instructed by spiritual gifts, would exceed the sphere of its object, that is not to be asserted; I concede. But the spiritual eye, seeing God who is spirit, does not exceed the sphere of the object, which is peculiarly established by God. God can elevate the eyes of the blessed beyond their nature, so that they may see the deity itself. He is shameless who dares to measure or limit the infinite power of God by physical reasons taken from the common and ordinary course of nature.

Latin:

Beatos in cœlo Deum oculis corporeis visuros esse, non quidem apodictice certum a), probabile tamen est b).

Prob. a. 1) Quia videre ex usu linguæ sanctæ interdum idem significat, quod intellectu aliquid cognoscere, 1 Cor. XIII, 12. adeoque de visione mentali exponi potest.

2) Angeli dicuntur in cœlo videre faciem Dei Patris, qui oculis corporeis destituti sunt, Matth. XIIX, 10. Sicut igitur visio angelorum est intellectualis: Ita beatis in futura vita speranda est visio Dei intellectualis.

Prob. b. 1) Iobus in statu afflictissimo efficaci se solamine sustentans inquit: Ex carne mea videbo Deum: Quem ego videbo mihi, & oculi mei videbunt, & non alius. c. XIX, 27. Confitetur Iobus, se visurum esse Christum, non tantum vt hominem, sed etiam vt Deum, & quidem oculis corporeis. Certe nulla necessitas nos cogit, vt a proprietate vocis discedamus, & oculos mentis tropicos intelligamus.

2) Oculi beatorum corporei in futura vita erunt spirituales (non ratione substantiæ sed qualitatum), 1 Cor. XV, 22. E. probabile est, oculum spiritualem visurum esse Deum.

3) Intellectus finitus lumine gloriæ eo vsque eleuari potest, vt immediate sine specie intelligibili essentiam Dei videat: Ergo pari ratione oculi corporei spiritualibus viribus instructi eo perfectionis euehi possunt, vt Deum clare intueantur. Consequentia est evidens, quia Deo peræque possibile & facile est, oculos corporis eleuare ad videndum ipsum, quam possibile eidem est, intellectum finitum eleuare ad intuitiue cognoscendam infinitam essentiam.

Antithesis est plerorumque Pontificiorum, Deum oculis corporeis videri posse, negantium, quorum potiora sunt argumenta:

I. Nullus spiritus oculis corporeis videri potest. Atqui Deus est spiritus, isque purissimus & subtilissimus, Io. IV, 24. Ergo. R. Nullus spiritus oculis corporeis animalibus videri potest, concedo. Vero tamen consentaneum est, videri eundem posse oculis corporeis spiritualibus.

II. Deus est invisibilis, quem nemo videre potest. Resp. Deus dicitur invisibilis, respectu visionis physicae: non hyperphysicae; adeoque nemo Deum videre potest in hac vita oculis non glorificatis. Ipse Deus ita limitat, Faciem meam (Mosen alloquitur Iehouah) videre non potes (oculis corporis): Cur? Quia homo (oculis suis) me videre non potest, & viuere (hanc vitam).

III. Quo sensu angeli dicuntur faciem Dei videre, eodem sensu & homines beati dicuntur Deum intueri. Atqui angeli dicuntur Deum videre oculis mentis. E. & homines beati. Maior constat; quia beati angelis erunt similes, Certo respectu erimus in futura vita angelis similes, sed non ἁπλῶς aut simpliciter. Sufficit, quod beati tum oculis mentis, tum oculis corporis, ratione qualitatum spiritualibus, Deum visuri sint, sicut angeli spirituali modo Deum contuentur.

IV. Quacunque visione oculus corporeus sphaeram obiecti sui transcenderet, illa non est afferenda. Atqui visione essentiae diuinae oculus corporeus &c. E. Maior patet; quia omnis sensus intra limites obiecti sui se continet. Minor liquet; quia oculorum obiectum est corpus coloratum & lucidum. Resp. Dist. inter oculum animalem, siue non glorificatum, & spiritualem. Quacunque visione oculus corporeus, spiritualibus dotibus instructus, excederet sphaeram obiecti sui, illa non est afferenda; concedo. At oculus spiritualis, Deum spiritum videns, non excedit sphaeram obiecti, a Deo peculiariter statutam. Potest Deus beatorum oculos vltra naturam ipsorum eleuare, vt ipsam deitatem videant. Effrons fit, qui infinitam Dei potentiam rationibus physicis ex communi & ordinario naturae cursu petitis dimetiri, aut limitare ausit.


### Quaest. VI. What is the enjoyment of God?

The enjoyment of God is an act of the will, by which the blessed in the heavenly fatherland most avidly embrace God, the highest good, most sweetly perceive him, and are most fully satisfied by him.

Prob. from I shall see your face in righteousness: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with your image. David opposes his hope, placed in the future vision and enjoyment of God, to the machinations and boasting of his enemies, whose belly God had filled with bodily goods. For he says two things: 1) that he will see God, 2) that he will be satisfied with the image of God, i.e., that he will perceive solid joys from the intuition of the divine majesty. By the image of God in the cited place, some theologians understand the majesty of God, which, showing itself gloriously, alone can satisfy the appetite.

You say: If eternal beatitude, as sacred scripture testifies, consists in the vision of God, which is an act of the intellect, it does not consist in the enjoyment of God, which is an act of the will. For it would be in two subjects, when yet one and the same thing should be in one subject only. Resp. Eternal beatitude (God) being terminated, and having a certain order both among themselves and toward the same beatific object: Whence it is no wonder that it is in different subjects, or rather in the powers of one subject, namely man. For each power reaches the beatific object immediately, the intellect by vision, the will by enjoyment. The root of beatitude is indeed in the intellect, namely the intuitive knowledge of God; but the enjoyment of God in the will completes and perfects beatitude. Take away from the clear vision of God its enjoyment in the will, just as these two can be conceived separately in the mind, certainly the beatitude of the human soul will be very mutilated and lacking, according to that saying: What does the aspect (vision of God) help, if the use (enjoyment of God in the will) is not granted?

Holy Scripture indeed describes eternal beatitude through the intuitive cognition of the intellect, yet it does not exclude the fruition of the will. For it is customary for the Hebrews to connote affection with words of knowledge.

Q. VII.

will inseparably accompany the beatific vision and fruition of God? The beatific vision and fruition of God will be inseparably accompanied by the most ardent love of God, the most abundant joy, the everlasting celebration of the divine name, ἀναμαρτησία, or immunity from the danger of sinning, and most constant holiness.

Prob. a. Such is the power of the good, when perfectly known by the intellect and most greedily accepted by the will, that it moves and entices the latter to the love of itself; since nothing is found in it except what is lovable. Wherefore, since God is supremely good, clearly known by the intellect, and most sweetly perceived by the will, He cannot but be most ardently loved by the blessed in the heavenly fatherland. From which Augustine describes the fruition of God through the love of God (a posteriori), lib. I. de doctrina Christ. c. III. To enjoy the good is nothing else than to adhere to it by love for its own sake.

Prob. b. Connected with the love of God in the heavenly fatherland is the most abundant and purest joy; for because the gift is clearly known, sweetly tasted, and intensely loved, it produces solid joy. Therefore, the faithful servants shall enter into the joy of the Lord, Matt. XXV, 23. And there shall be fullness of joys before the face of God, Ps. XVI, 11.

Prob. c. He who enjoys God, the supreme good, cannot but sing His praises. Wherefore the blessed, admitted to the intimate intuition and embrace of God, will sing day and night without ceasing with the holy angels: Holy, holy, holy Lord God Almighty, who was, who is, and who is to come, Apoc. IV, 8.

Prob. d. Such holiness will adorn the blessed souls as can fall upon a creature (namely, finite and dependent). For since they behold God perpetually and love Him most ardently, so that they cannot cease from His love, they are immune from sin and the danger of sinning, concerning which St. Paul asserts that the triumphant church shall not have spot or wrinkle, Eph. V, 27, where he speaks of the spot of sin. And St. John describes the blessed as being clothed in fine linen, white and clean, Apoc. XIX, 14, by which the righteousness of the saints is noted, v. 8.

Latin:

Fruitio Dei est actus voluntatis, quo beati in patria coelesti Deum, summum bonum, auidissime complectuntur, suauissime percipiunt, & eodem plenissime satiantur.

Prob. e Ego in iustitia videbo facies tuas: Saturabor, cum euigilauero, imagine tua. Dauid machinis & iactantiae hostium, quorum ventrem Deus bonis corporalibus faturauerat, opponit spem suam positam in futura Dei visione & fruitione. Duo enim dicit: 1) se Deum visurum, 2) se satiatum iri imagine Dei, i. e. se solida gaudia ex intuitu maiestatis diuinae percepturum esse. Per imaginem Dei l. c. nonnulli theologi intelligunt maiestatem Dei, quae, gloriose se ostendens, sola appetitum satiare potest. Conf. ADAM. OSIANDRI coll. system. Part. VI. p. 205.

Dicis: Si aeterna beatitudo, teste scriptura sacra, consistit in visione Dei, quae est actus intellectus, non consistit in fruitione Dei, quae est actus voluntatis. Foret enim in duobus subiectis, cum tamen vna eademque res in vno tantum fit subiecto. Resp. Aeterna beatitudo (Deum) terminatis, & ordinem quendam tam inter se, quam ad idem obiectum beatificum habentibus: Vnde nil mirum est, quod in diuersis fit subiectis, siue potius potentiis vnius subiecti, nempe hominis. Vtraque enim potentia obiectum beatificum immediate attingit, intellectus visione, voluntas fruitione. Radix beatitudinis est quidem in intellectu, nempe intuitiua Dei cognitio; sed fruitio Dei in voluntate beatitudinem complet & perficit. Tolle a clara Dei visione fruitionem eius in voluntate, quemadmodum haec duo mente seorsim concipi possunt, certe animae humanae beatitudo valde mutila erit, & manca, iuxta illud: Quid iuvat aspectus (visio Dei), si non conceditur usus (fruitio Dei in voluntate)?

S. scriptura quidem describit aeternam beatitudinem per intuitivam intellectus cognitionem, voluntatis autem fruitionem non excludit. Solemne quippe est Hebraeis, verbis notitiae affectum connotare.

Quaest. VII. Quae perfectiones animae humanae

visionem & fruitionem Dei beatificam indiuulse comitabuntur? Visionem & fruitionem Dei beatificam indiuulse comitabuntur, amor Dei ardentissimus , gaudium cumulatissimum , sempiterna nominis diuini celebratio , ἀναμαρτησία, siue immunitas a peccandi periculo, & sanctitas constantissima .

Prob. a. Ea vis est boni, perfecte cogniti ab intellectu, & auidissime acceptati a voluntate, vt hanc ad amorem sui moueat & pelliciat; cum nihil, nisi amabile, in eo deprehendatur. Quare cum Deus sit summe bonus, ab intellectu clare cognitus, & a voluntate suauissime perceptus, in patria coelesti non potest non a beatis ardentissime amari. Ex quo AVGVSTINVS fruitionem Dei per amorem Dei (a posteriori) describit, libr. I. de doctrina Christ. c. III. Frui bono, nihil est aliud, quam amore ei inhaerere propter ipsum.

Prob. b. Cum amore Dei in patria coelesti connexum est gaudium cumulatissimum & purissimum; quippe quod donum clare cognoscitur, suauiter gustatur, & impense amatur, id solidum parit gaudium. Intrabunt igitur serui fideles in gaudium domini, Matth. XXV, 23. & erit satietas gaudiorum coram facie Dei, Ps. XVI, 11.

Prob. c. Qui Deo summo bono perfruitur, non potest non eius laudes decantare. Quare homines beati, ad intuitum & complexum Dei intimum admissi, diu noctuque sine intermissione cum sanctis angelis concinent: Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus Dominus Deus omnipotens, qui erat, qui est, & qui venturus est, Apoc. IV, 8.

Prob. d. Sanctitas tanta ornabit animas beatas, quanta in creaturam cadere potest (scil. finita & dependens). Cum enim Deum perpetuo intueantur, ardentissimeque ament, vt ab amore eius cessare nequeant, a peccato, peccantique periculo immunes sunt, de quo S. Paullus asserit, ecclesiam triumphantem non habituram esse maculam aut rugam, Eph. V, 27. vbi de macula peccati loquitur. Et S. Ioannes describit beatos, quod induti sint byssino albo & mundo, Apoc. XIX, 14. quo notatur iustitia sanctorum v. 8.


### Q. VIII. Will God impart His essential beatitude, holiness, and glory to the blessed in heaven?

God does not make the blessed in the heavenly fatherland participants of His essential beatitude, holiness, and glory.

Prob. 1) God is essentially blessed; because He is blessed from Himself, through Himself, and in Himself. But the elect are blessed by the grace of God that glorifies. God is holy independently and by essence: the elect are holy dependently and through superadded qualities. Therefore the most pious Hannah says, 1 Sam. II, 2: There is no one holy as Jehovah. The glory of the blessed is finite; but the glory of God is infinite and incommunicable to creatures (except for that one to whom God personally united Himself). My glory I will not give to another, says Jehovah, Is. XLII, 8.

2) If the blessed in heaven were participants of the essential divine glory, they would be Gods and adorable: the consequent is false: therefore, the antecedent is also. The falsity of the consequent is most clearly evident from the fact that the blessed cast their crowns before the throne of God, saying: Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory ...ry, etc. Rev. 4:11. And the angels, to whom the blessed are like, do not wish the cult of adoration to be attributed to themselves, Rev. 19:10.

The antithesis is that of the Quakers, who assert that the blessed are participants in the essential divine beatitude, whose chief arguments are:

I. God will be all in all to the blessed, 1 Cor. 15:28. Therefore, the divine beatitude, holiness, and glory will be the beatitude of the elect. Response: Distinguish between objective and moral beatitude. The former is God, the highest good of the elect: the latter is the fruition of God. It is not of the former, but of the latter that we are speaking, which is certainly dependent and finite.

II. The blessed in heaven are Gods: Therefore, they are participants in the essential divine glory. The antecedent is proven; because they are children of God, John 1:12, born of God, i.e., born of the divine essence, John 3:6, participants of the divine nature, 2 Pet. 1:4. Response: They are children of God, not natural, but adoptive; born not of the essence, but of the gracious operation of God. They are participants of the divine nature on account of the spiritual union and communion of God with the elect, not an essential nor a personal one.

A SIGH.

You have made us, most holy God, for Yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in You. You are all in all to it: You are light to the mind, food to the will, the center to the affections. You are delightful to behold, pleasant to possess, sweet to enjoy. It is always pleasing to look upon You, always to love You, always to be delighted by You, and to enjoy You. Therefore, give Yourself to me, and restore me to Yourself, so that in the heavenly fatherland I may see You most clearly, love You most perfectly, and rejoice in You, the highest good, most perfectly. To You be praise and glory forever and ever!

PART II OF THEOLOGY

CHAPTER I.

Latin:

Deus beatos in patria coelesti essentialis suae beatitudinis, sanctitatis & gloriae non facit participes.

Prob. 1) Deus essentialiter beatus est; quia a seipso, per seipsum, & in seipso beatus est. At electi sunt beati, ex gratia Dei glorificante. Deus est sanctus independenter, & per essentiam: Electi sunt sancti dependenter & per superadditas qualitates. Idcirco piissima Hanna inquit, 1 Sam. II, 2. Non est sanctus, sicut Iehouah. Gloria beatorum est finita; gloria autem Dei infinita & creaturis (praeter eam, cui Deus se personaliter vniuit) incommunicabilis. Gloriam meam alteri non dabo, ait Ichouah, Es. XLII, 8.

2) Si beati in caelo participes essent essentialis gloriae diuinae, essent Dii, & adorabiles: consequens est falsum: E. & antecedens. Consequentis falsitas vel clarissime ex eo liquet, quod beati coronas suas ante thronum Dei proiiciunt, dicentes: Dignus es, Domine, qui accipias gloriam riam &c. Apoc. IV, 11. & angeli, quibus beati sunt similes, adorationis cultum sibi tribui nolunt, Apoc. XIX, 10.

Antithesis est Quakerorum, asserentium, beatos essentialis beatitudinis diuinae esse participes, quorum palmaria argumenta sunt:

I. Deus beatis erit omnia in omnibus, 1 Cor. XV, 28. E. diuina beatitudo, sanctitas & gloria erit beatitudo electorum. Resp. Dist. inter beatitudinem obiectiuam, & moralem. Illa est Deus, summum electorum bonum: Haec est fruitio Dei. Non de illa, sed de hac nobis sermo est, quae vtique dependens & finita est.

II. Beati in coelo sunt Dii: E. essentialis gloriae diuinae participes. Antecedens probatur; quia sunt filii Dei, Io. I, 12. ex Deo, i.e. essentia diuina nati, Io. III, 6. naturae diuinae participes, 2 Petr. I, 4. Resp. Sunt filii Dei, non naturales, sed adoptiui; non ex essentia, sed gratiosa operatione Dei nati. Sunt participes naturae diuinae, ob vnionem & communionem Dei cum electis spiritualem, non essentialem, nec personalem.

S V S P I R I V M.

Fecisti nos, Deus sanctissime, ad te, & irrequietum est cor nostrum, nisi quiescat in te. Tu illi omnia es in omnibus: Tu lumen menti, cibus voluntati, centrum es affectibus. Tu delectabilis es ad videndum, suauis ad habendum, dulcis ad perfruendum. Semper libet te aspicere, semper amare, semper delectari te, & perfrui. Quare da te mihi, & redde me tibi, vt in patria coelesti videam te clarissime, amem te perfectissime, laeter de te, summo bono, perfectissime. Tibi sit laus & gloria in sempiterna saecula!

PARTIS II. THEOLOGIAE

CAPVT I.


## 11 On the Subject of Theology, Fallen Man, and the Image of God

THE SUBJECT OF THEOLOGY,

NAMELY, CONCERNING FALLEN MAN, OR THE SINNER, TO BE BROUGHT BACK TO GOD.

Latin:

SVBIECTO THEOLOGIAE,

NEMPE DE HOMINE LAPSO, SEV PECCATORE, AD DEVM REDVCENDO.


### Question I. What things are to be considered concerning the fall of man?

Concerning the fall of man, both the term from which and the term to which must be considered. The term from which is the state of innocence, or integrity.

Proof. The misery of fallen man cannot be accurately weighed unless the happiness that preceded it, of which man deprived himself by turning away from God, is exactly pondered. For privation is known from the opposite habit, and the gravity of an evil is worthily estimated from the good that has been lost.

Latin:

Circa lapsum hominis considerandus est tum terminus a quo, tum terminus ad quem. Terminus a quo, est status innocentiae, siue integritatis.

Prob. Miseria hominis lapsi accurate expendi nequit, nisi exacte ponderetur eam antegressa felicitas, qua homo a Deo auersus seipsum priuauit. Priuatio namque cognoscitur ex opposito habitu, & grauitas mali digne aestimatur ex amisso bono.


### Question II. What was the state of integrity?

The state of integrity was the first, and most happy, condition of man, who was created in the image of God.

Latin:

Status integritatis fuit prima, eaque felicissima, hominis, ad imaginem Dei creati, conditio.


### Q. III. What is the image of God?

The image of God is a natural perfection, consisting in an excellent conformity with the prototype of God, in wisdom, justice, purity, immortality, and majesty, created together with the first humans, so that they might truly recognize the creator, worship him piously, lead a holy life, and attain glorious blessedness. Obs. I. The formal requirements of an image, when generation is considered, are: 1) Similarity, or agreement with the exemplar or prototype; because it is of the nature of an image to represent the thing of which it is an image. This, however, cannot happen without similarity: 2) Origin, or the procession of the image from the exemplar, because an image is expressed for the imitation of the prototype, and therefore for representation . Obs.

II. A trace is distinguished from an image. An image represents clearly that of which it is an image: A trace refers obscurely to that of which it is a trace. In all creatures, traces of divine power, wisdom, and goodness are detected; but in the whole human being, the image of God shone forth in full radiance. Cf. CALOV, Metaphysica divina, p. 641.

Latin:

Imago Dei est perfectio naturalis, in excellente conformitate cum Dei prototypo, sapientia, justitia, puritate, immortalitate, & majestate consistens, primis hominibus concreata, ut creatorem vere agnoscerent, pieque colerent, vitam sanctam transigerent, & beatitatem gloriosam consequerentur. Obs. I. Formalia requisita imaginis, generationi consideratæ, sunt: 1) Similitudo, sive convenientia cum exemplari, vel prototypo; quia imaginis est, repræsentare rem, cujus est imago. Hoc autem sine similitudine fieri nequit: 2) Origo, vel processio imaginis ab exemplari, quia imago ad imitationem prototypi, repræsentationis ergo, expressa est . Obs.

II. Distinguitur vestigium ab imagine. Imago repræsentat manifeste id, cujus est imago: Vestigium obscure refert id, cujus est vestigium. In omnibus creaturis deprehenduntur vestigia potentiæ, sapientiæ & bonitatis divinæ; at in homine integro pleno jubare effulgebat imago Dei. Conf. CALOVII metaphys. divin. p. 641. Quæst.


### Question III. What is the image of God?

The image of God is in one way substantial, in another accidental. The former is the eternal Son of God; because he expresses the whole essence of the Father in himself, distinct from him in the mode of subsistence a). The latter is that whose accidental perfections are conformable to the infinite perfections of God, according to the measure of human capacity b). Prob. a. Christ is called the image of God by the apostle Paul, 2 Cor. IV, 4. The image of God, invisible, Col. I, 15. The character of the Father's person, Heb. I, 3. because he represents the person of the Father, taken concretely, insofar as it consists of essence and subsistence. Cf. SEB. SCHMID, Commentary on the Ep. to the Hebrews, c. I, 3. Prob. b.

Because of accidental perfections, responding in some measure to the infinite perfections of God, man is said to have been created in the primeval state in the image of God, Gen. I, 26, 27; c. V, 1. And man, when converted, is renewed into the image of God, Col. III, 10. Indeed, even the man, with respect to the dominion which he has not only over the brutes but also over the woman, is called in the nominative case the image and glory of God, 1 Cor. XI, 7 .

Latin:

Imago Dei alia est substantialis, alia accidentalis. Illa est æternus Dei Filius; quia totam essentiam Patris in se exprimit, modo subsistendi ab eo distinctus a). Hæc est, cujus accidentales perfectiones infinitis Dei perfectionibus, secundum modum capacitatis humanæ, conformes sunt b). Prob. a. Christus ab apostolo Paulo vocatur imago Dei, 2 Cor. IV, 4. Imago Dei, invisibilis, Col. I, 15. Character personæ patris, Hebr. I, 3. quia personam patris, concretive sumtam, quatenus essentia & subsistentia constat, repræsentat. Conf. SEB. SCHMID. commentar. in Ep. ad Hebr. c. I, 3. Prob. b.

Ob accidentales perfectiones, infinitis Dei perfectionibus quadantenus respondentes, homo in statu primævo ad imaginem Dei conditus esse dicitur, Gen. I, 26. 27. c. V, 1. Et homo conversus renovatur ad imaginem Dei, Col. III, 10. Quin & vir, respectu ad dominium, quod non tantum in bruta, sed & in fœminam habet, in casu recto imago & gloria Dei vocatur, 1 Cor. XI, 7. .


### Quæst. V. In how many ways is the accidental image of God spoken of?

The accidental image of God is taken in two ways b): Generally, ἀκυρως & abusively, for a certain general analogy, or agreement with God a): Specifically, κυρίως & properly, for an excellent and most similar conformity with God the archetype b).

Prob. a. The very substance of the human soul expresses a certain θεῖα, or divine [nature], and reflects the exemplar of divinity. For God is an immaterial spirit, intelligent, acting by free will, invisible, indivisible, illocal, immortal. Which predicates can be affirmed of the human soul in a certain way. But that general agreement is indeed placed subjectively under the divine image, properly so called, but it does not formally constitute it.

The divine image is taken specifically & properly when God says, Gen. I, 26: Let us make man in our image, after our likeness. In the source, two words are employed, צֶלֶם image & דְּמוּת likeness, not to the end that they might be symbols of distinct things, and that image might denote the very substance of the human soul, and likeness its accidental perfections (as some Papists wish); but that the latter might be exegetical of the former, and that a most similar, or very similar, image might be designated.

We confirm our assertion. 1) Because it is solemn for the Hebrews to join two substantives, either synonyms or of disparate signification, of which one sustains the role of an adjective, and has its meaning with emphasis. Which formula of speaking is called ἓν διὰ δυοῖν. See GLASSIUS, Philol. S. lib. III. tr. I. can VI. p. 392. 2) The same is evident from the comparison of the divine decree and its execution. In the decree v. 26 both words, image & likeness, are joined: But in the execution v. 27 only the word צֶלֶם, image, is read. From which we gather that by image the same is signified in the execution as was signified by image & likeness in the decree, on account of the harmony of the execution and the decree. 3) Under likeness the image of God is comprehended, Gen. V, 3. Jas. III, 9. 4) Those two words are joined in the oblique case, Wis. II, 23. God created man in incorruption, to the image of his own likeness (SEB. SCHMIDT: propriety) he made him. 5) As Adam is said to have begotten Seth in his own image & likeness, Gen. V, 3: So God created Adam in his own image & likeness; Gen. I, 26. But there, different things are not signified by those two words צֶלֶם & דְּמוּת. 6) What the image of God denotes in renewal, the same it signifies in creation. But in renewal [there is] not a strictly expressed image of the Father, χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ, Heb. I, 3. inasmuch as all the perfections and properties of God, not even one excepted, are in the Son, in the same way, namely naturally and necessarily, just as in the Father, and also in an equal degree, i.e., the highest and infinite, so that the Son is ἴσος to the Father, Jo. V, 18. To the created man, divine perfections were indeed attributed, but only certain ones, and in a different way; for in God they are natural, or, to speak customarily, essential and necessary; in man they were not so, but accidental & contingent: nor indeed in a far lesser degree; for they could not but be finite perfections, & contingent: divinely imparted to man, just as the very nature of man.

There was, therefore, and at some time will have to be restored, ὁμοιότης, by no means ἰσότης, Jas. III, 9. John III, 2. But a certain image is called perfect or imperfect, by reason not of the ἐκτύπου, but of the ἀρχετύπου, namely, according to whether those things which are in the ἀρχετύπῳ appear expressed in the ἐκτύπῳ either all equally, or not all equally, although the ἔκτυπον has those properties and perfections in their entirety which agree with its own nature and ends, so that nothing is lacking. This ambiguity, which lies hidden in the word, must be accurately observed and removed when it is asked: Whether the image of God in man was perfect or not? Namely, the sense of the question is either this: Whether all the properties and perfections which are in God were communicated to man in exactly the same way and in an equal degree? This we deny. Or this: whether all those perfections of which man is capable, and which agree with his nature and ends, were divinely fittingly attributed to him? This is what we affirm. divinely fittingly attributed to him? This is what we affirm.

it designates not the substance, but the qualities, Col. III, 10. Eph. IV, 24. Therefore. Meanwhile, D. VARENIUS accurately observed in decad. I. Mosaic. p 120. that צלם & דמות agree materially, but not formally. For צלם is an image expressed according to an exemplar, God: דמות is a likeness, or a correspondence between the archetype and the image. דמות is the foundation of the relation: צלם is the term of the relation (*).

Latin:

Imago Dei accidentalis b fariam sumitur: generaliter, ἀκυρως & abusiue, pro generali quadam analogia, aut conuenientia cum Deo a): Specialiter, κυρίως & proprie, pro excellenti & simillima conformitate cum Deo archetypo b).

Prob. a. Ipsa substantia animæ humanæ quandam θεῖα, seu diuina exprimit, & exemplar diuinitatis refert. Nam Deus est spiritus immaterialis, intelligens, voluntate libera agens, inuisibilis, indiuisibilis, illocalis, immortalis. Quæ prædicata de anima humana certo modo affirmari possunt. At illa conuenientia generalis imagini diuinæ, proprie dictæ, subiectiue quidem substernitur, sed formaliter eam non constituit.

Prob. b. Specialiter & prorie accipitur imago diuina, cum Deus inquit, Gen. I, 26. Faciamus hominem in imagine nostra, secundum similitudinem nostram. In fonte duæ adhibentur voces צֶלֶם imago & דְּמוּת similitudo, non eo fine, vt distinctarum rerum symbola sint, & imago ipsam animæ humanæ substantiam, similitudo ipsius perfectiones accidentales denotet (vt volunt nonnulli Pontificii); sed vt posterior prioris fit exegetica, & imago simillima, aut valde similis designetur.

Firmamus assertionem nostram. 1) Quia solemne est Hebræis duo substantia, vel synonyma, vel disparatæ significationis coniungere, quorum alterum adiectiui vicem sustinet, eiusque habet significationem cum emphasi. Quæ loquendi formula vocatur ἓν διὰ δυοῖν. Vid. GLASSII philol. S. libr. III. tr. I. can VI. p. 392. 2) Idem patet e decreti diuini, eiusque exsecutionis comparatione. In decreto v. 26 vtraque vox, imago & similitudo, coniungitur: At in exsecutione v. 27 tantum vox צֶלֶם, imago, legitur. Ex quo colligimus, per imaginem idem significari in exsecutione, quod per imaginem & similitudinem in decreto significabatur, ob harmoniam exsecutionis & decreti. 3) Sub similitudine imago Dei comprehenditur, Gen. V, 3. Iac. III, 9. 4) Duæ illæ voces in casu obliquo coniunguntur, Sap. II, 23. Deus creauit hominem in incorruptione, ad imaginem propriæ similitudinis (SEB. SCHMIDIVS proprietatis) fecit illum. 5) Vt Adam Sethum ad imaginem & similitudinem suam genuisse dicitur, Gen. V, 3: Ita Deus Adamum ad imaginem & similitudinem suam creauit; Gen. I, 26. At ibi non significant res diuersæ per duas illas voces צֶלֶם, & דְּמוּת. 6) Quod notat imago Dei in renouatione, idem significat in creatione. At in renouatione non secte expressa Patris effigies, χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ, Hebr. I, 3. quando quidem perfectiones ac proprietates Dei omnes, ne vna quidem excepta, in Filio insunt, eodem modo, nimirum naturaliter ac necessario, sicut in Patre, pari etiam gradu, h. e. summo atque infinito, vt Filius fit ἴσος Patri, Io. V, 18. Creato homini tributæ quidem fuerunt perfectiones diuinæ, sed quædam dumtaxat, diuerso etiam modo, in Deo enim sunt naturales, seu, vt vsitate loquar, essentiales, ac necessariæ; in homine non item fuerunt, sed accidentales & contingentes: nec non longe minori gradu; finitæ enim non poterant non esse perfectiones, nec non longe minori gradu; finitæ enim non poterant non esse perfectiones, & contingentes: diuinitus homini impertitæ, quem ad modum ipsa hominis natura.

Fuit igitur, & quandoque instauranda erit, ὁμοιότης, nequaquam ἰσότης, Iac. III, 9. Ioan. III, 2. Dicitur autem perfecta imago quædam, aut imperfecta, ratione non ἐκτύπου, sed ἀρχετύπου, nempe quoad ea, quæ in ἀρχετύπῳ insunt, aut omnia pariter, aut non omnia peræque, in ἐκτύπῳ expressa adpareant, quamuis ἔκτυπον habeat eas proprietates perfectionesque vniuersas, quæ cum ipsius natura ac finibus congruunt, vt nihil desit. Hæc, quæ in voce latet, ambiguitas adcurate obseruanda est, ac tollenda, cum quæritur: Vtrum imago Dei in homine fuerit perfecta, nec ne? Scilicet sententia quæstionis aut illa est: Num omnes, quæ in Deo insunt, proprietates perfectionesque, eodem prorsus modo, & pari gradu, cum homine fuerint communicatæ? Id negamus. Aut hæc: an omnes, quarum homo capax est, & quæ cum eius natura ac finibus congruunt, perfectiones, diuinitus conuenienter ipsi tributæ fuerint? Hoc est, quod affirmamus. diuinis conuenienter ipsi tributæ fuerint? Hoc est, quod affirmamus.

non substantiam, sed qualitates designat, Col. III, 10. Eph. IV, 24. Ergo. Accurate interim obseruauit D. VARENIVS decad. I. Mosaic. p 120. צלם & דמות conuenire materialiter, sed non formaliter. Nam צלם est imago expressa ad exemplar, Deum: דמות est similitudo, siue conuenientia inter archetypum, & imaginem. דמות est relationis fundamentum: צלם relationis terminus (*).


### Q. VI. In how many ways is the accidental image of God, properly so called, taken?

The accidental image of God is taken either μερικῶς, i.e., inadequately, or ὁλικῶς, i.e., adequately. Μερικῶς denotes knowledge and original justice a): Ὁλικῶς embraces all things which complete the image of God, whether they pertain to the image of God principally or less principally b).

Proof a. The image of God is described by the apostle Paul through the knowledge of God, Col. III, 10. and the justice and holiness of truth, Eph. IV, 24. Because the more powerful part of the divine image is original justice, through which, by theological usage, a complex of virtues, both intellectual and moral, concreated in the first man, is indicated. It is called original, both so that it may be distinguished from acquired justice; and because the protoplasts possessed the same from the very beginning, by way of a concreated habit; and finally, because it was to be transmitted to descendants through generation, so that they too might attain this natural perfection with their origin in the state of innocence, just as now, in the state of sin, original sin is propagated, and is called original from that propagation. Conf. D. CALOV. in system. theol. tom. IV. p. 598.

Proof b. The image of God taken ὁλικῶς & adequately denotes not only knowledge and original justice, but also the faculty of ruling over sublunary creatures. Therefore, when man is said to have been made in the image of God, it is immediately added that dominion was granted to him, Gen. I, 27. Conf. Sir. XVII, 3. 4. Indeed, it also embraces ἀφθαρσίαν, or the immortality of the body, Sap. II, 23.

Latin:

Imago Dei accidentalis sumitur vel μερικῶς, s. inædæquate, vel ὁλικῶς, s. adæquate. Μερικῶς notat cognitionem & iustitiam originalem a): Ὁλικῶς omnia complectitur, quæ imaginem Dei absoluunt, siue principaliter, siue minus principaliter ad imaginem Dei pertineant b).

Prob. a. Describitur imago Dei ab apostolo Paullo per cognitionem Dei, Col. III, 10. atque iustitiam & sanctitatem veritatis, Eph. IV, 24. Quia potior imaginis diuinæ pars est iustitia originalis, per quam ex vsu theologico complexus virtutum, tam intellectualium, quam moralium, homini primo concreatarum indigitatur. Dicitur originalis, tum, vt discernatur a iustitia acquisita; tum, quia homines protoplasti eandem ab ortu ipso, per modum habitus concreati, possidebant; tum denique, quia per generationem in posteros transmitti debebat, vt & illi cum origine sua naturalem hanc perfectionem consequerentur in statu innocentiæ, quem ad modum nunc, in statu peccati, originale peccatum propagatur, & ab illa propagatione originale vocatur. Conf. D. CALOV. in system. theol. tom. IV. p. 598.

Prob. b. Ὁλικῶς & adæquate sumta imago Dei non tantum cognitionem & iustitiam originalem, sed & facultatem dominandi creaturis sublunaribus notat. Ideo, cum ad imaginem Dei factus dicitur homo, statim additur, quod concessum ei fuerit dominium, Gen. I, 27. Conf. Sir. XVII, 3. 4. Quin & ἀφθαρσίαν, seu immortalitatem corporis complectitur, Sap. II, 23.


### Question VII. Is the image of God the very substance of the human soul, or a faculty of the rational soul, the intellect or the will?

The image and likeness of God, in which the first man is said to have been created, was neither the essence of the human soul itself, nor the intellect, nor the will, but an accidental perfection, and that an intimate and most eminent one.

Proof 1) Because only the Son of God is the essential image of God, Hebr. I, 3. What is proper to the Son of God alone belongs to no creature.

2) The image of God was lost through the fall of the first men, Rom. III, 23. But neither the substance of the human soul itself, nor the intellect, nor the will was lost.

3) The image

3) The image of God belongs to good men, Gen. I, 31. and to the upright, Eccl. VII, 29. But the soul, the intellect, and the will are common to the pious and the impious.

4) According to Paul, the image of God consists in the knowledge of God, Col. III, 10. and in the justice and holiness of truth, Eph. IV, 24. Therefore, it is not the soul itself, but the perfection of the soul; not the intellect and will themselves, but the light of the intellect and the rectitude of the will.

5) If the image of God had been the very essence of the whole man, then he would have been essentially holy and absolutely impeccable: The consequent is false: Therefore, so is the antecedent.

6) Original sin, which succeeded the image of God, is not the substance of man itself: Therefore, the image of God was not the substance of man either. For the reason for opposites is the same.

Antithesis is 1) of most Papists, in whose opinion the image of God consists primarily in the very substance of the human soul, and secondarily in accidental perfections. 2) Of Flacius and the Flacians, who contend that the image of God was the very substance of the rational soul (although some explain MATTHIAS FLACIUS, a theologian of profound erudition, more kindly, saying that he did not look to the essence of man as he is man, but as he was whole. See D. CALOVIUS, System, vol. IV, p. 576).

Their chief arguments are: I. That which is in man of God is that which is in him most noble and most excellent: But the human soul, etc. Therefore. The major premise stands; because by the image of God the most eminent perfection is designated. The minor is evident: because the substance of the soul excels its qualities. Response: I limit the major: Whatever in man, as a subject of inherence, is most noble and most excellent, that is the image of God. But the soul is not in man as a subject of inherence, since it is an essential part of man. Rather, the soul of the whole man was the subject, or seat, in which the image of God shone forth eminently.

II. Whatever was the source of every right motion and every good action in the protoplasts, that itself was the image of God. But the human soul itself, etc. Therefore. The major premise is clear; because the image of God in the first man was the cause of good actions. The minor is evident; because the soul enables one to act well or badly: Well, in the state of innocence; badly, in the state of misery. Response: Whatever was the source or the proximate and immediate cause of good actions in the protoplasts, that was the image of God in them; I concede this. But the human soul is a remote and mediate cause, which, through the image of God, renders man prompt to good actions.

III. Whatever gave being to the whole man, that was his form, and thus his substance: But the image of God, etc. E. The minor is clear: because by and through the image of God, man was whole and free from fault. Response: I distinguish between man's absolute being and his relative being. Man received absolute being from his substantial form; relative being, from his accidental form. The image of God was not of the essence of man, considered absolutely, but of the essence of the whole man: Just as learning is of the essence of the learned man, not absolutely of the essence of man.

IV. Right nature was the substance of man: The image of God was the right nature of man. E. Response: I deny the minor. For the image of God was not right nature, but the rectitude of nature.

V. That to which the formal requirements of the divine image belong, that is the image of God. But the substance of man, etc. Therefore. The minor is certain: because the substance of man 1) has its origin from God, 2) has a likeness and agreement with God, so that it represents Him. Response: I distinguish between a general likeness or agreement, and a special one. A general agreement makes a footprint of God; but a special agreement constitutes an image most like to God.

VI. Whatever is restored in a man reborn through the renewal of the Holy Spirit, that is the image of God; for we are renewed unto the image of God: but the mind itself, etc.: Therefore. The minor premise is proved from Eph. 4:23: "Be renewed in the spirit of your mind." Response: Paul is speaking about the subject of the image of God, not about its constitutive part.

VII. The image of God was either an extrinsic accident, or a substance: But it was not an extrinsic accident, like iron or a bridle, which lies adjacent extrinsically (as the Papists maintain), since it was natural, and that an intimate perfection: Therefore it was a substance. I respond: The major premise is not established by immediate members. For between a substance & an extrinsic accident there is a third thing, namely an internal quality, or an intrinsic perfection.

IIX. If we say that the image of God consists in original justice alone: the reason which God brings forward, Gen. IX, v. 6, why no man is to be killed with impunity, because he was created in the image of God, and Iacob. III, v. 9, why we ought not to curse our neighbor, because he was made in the likeness of God, this reason, I say, would be null, where it concerns men who are not participants of regeneration. For if anyone were to respond that these things are to be understood of the first origin of man, there would seem to be no consequence: The blood of man, which is shed, shall be avenged, even of him in whom the image of God is not; because Adam was created in the image of God in the beginning. Certainly, we cannot revere the image of God in him in whom it has been deleted in every part. D. DANNHAU. responds to this objection in hodom. spirit. calu. p. 1086. The consequence does not hold; because ἀσυλία (immunity from violence being brought upon one) can be attributed to someone, and reverence [can be shown] out of respect for a past habit, not a present one, out of respect for the right to have the thing restored, out of respect for the holy things themselves, such as the light of truth and the seed of good that are still remaining: Thus the apostle reveres the Jews according to the flesh, even though they have already boiled away the grace of God, Rom. IX, 5. And we permit ἀσυλία to modern Apelles, out of respect for their most ancient family. Likewise, man was made to restore the image. 2) To Gen. IX, 6, D. SEB. SCHMID. responds in Commentar. in Gen. p. 101. In the image of God, immortality is intended, while he was created for eternal life; which divine intention remains, notwithstanding temporal death, from which all shall be resurrected to judgment, and shall die no more. 3) To Iacob. III, 9, D. CALOV. responds in bibl. illustr. in H. l. fol. 1443. Man is said to have been made in the image of God, not as he is now, but as he was before the fall; to which, however, he is here restored through Christ, Eph. IV, 24. Col. III, 10. 2 Cor. V, 17.

Latin:

Imago & similitudo Dei, in qua primus homo conditus esse dicitur, nec ipsa essentia animæ humanæ, nec intellectus, nec voluntas fuit, sed perfectio accidentalis, eaque intima & eminentissima.

Prob. 1) Quia solus Filius Dei est essentialis Dei imago, Hebr. I, 3. Quod soli Filio Dei proprium est, nulli competit creaturæ.

2) Imago Dei per lapsum primorum hominum est amissa, Rom. III, 23. At nec ipsa substantia animæ humanæ, nec intellectus, nec voluntas est deperdita.

3) Imago

3) Imago Dei competit hominibus bonis, Gen. I, 31. & rectis, Eccl. VII, 29. At anima, intellectus & voluntas, piis impiisque est communis.

4) Teste Paulo, consistit imago Dei in cognitione Dei, Col. III, 10. atque iustitia & sanctitate veritatis, Eph. IV, 24. Ergo non est ipsa anima, sed animae perfectio, non ipse intellectus, atque voluntas, sed lux intellectus, & voluntatis rectitudo.

5) Si imago Dei fuisset ipsa essentia hominis integri, vtique is fuisset essentialiter sanctus & absolute impeccabilis: Consequens est falsum: Ergo & antecedens.

6) Peccatum originale, quod imagini Dei successit, non est ipsa substantia hominis: Ergo nec imago Dei substantia hominis fuit. Oppositorum quippe eadem est ratio.

Antithesis est 1) plerorumque Pontificiorum, quorum de sententia imago Dei primario in ipsa substantia animae humanae, secundario in perfectionibus accidentalibus consistit. 2) Flacii & Flacianorum, contendentium, imaginem Dei fuisse ipsam substantiam animae rationalis (quamuis MATTHIAM FLACIVM, theologum profundae eruditionis, nonnulli benignius explicent, quod non essentiam hominis, qua homo est, sed qua integer fuit, respexerit. Vid. D. CALOVIVS system. tom. IV. p. 576.). Quorum praecipua sunt argumenta:

I. Illud est in homine Dei, quod in ipso nobilissimum & praestantissimum est: Atqui anima humana, &c. E. Maior constat; quia imagine Dei perfectio eminentissima designatur. Minor patet: quia substantia animae praestat qualitatibus. Resp. Limit. maior: Quidquid in homine, tanquam subiecto inhaesionis, nobilissimum & praestantissimum est, illud est imago Dei. At anima non est in homine, tanquam subiecto inhaesionis, cum hominis pars essentialis sit. Quin potius anima hominis integri fuit subiectum, aut sedes, in qua imago Dei eminuit.

II. Quidquid protoplastis fuit fons omnis motus recti, omnisque actionis bonae, id ipsum fuit imago Dei. Sed ipsa anima humana &c. E. Maior liquet; quia imago Dei in primo homine fuit causa bonarum actionum. Minor patet; quia anima dat operari bene, vel male: Bene, in statu innocentiae; male, in statu miseriae. Resp. Quidquid in protoplastis fuit fons, vel causa proxima & immediata bonarum actionum, illud fuit in ipsis imago Dei; concedo. At anima humana est causa remota & mediata, quae, per imaginem Dei, hominem ad actiones bonas promptum reddit.

III. Quidquid homini integro dedit esse, id fuit ipsius forma, atque adeo substantia: Atqui imago Dei &c. E. Minor liquet: quia per & propter imaginem Dei homo fuit integer & labis expers. Resp. Dist. inter hominis esse absolutum, & respectiuum. Esse absolutum, accepit homo a forma substantiali; respectiuum, a forma accidentali. Fuit imago Dei non de essentia hominis, absolute considerati, sed de essentia hominis integri: Sicut doctrina est de essentia hominis docti, non absolute de essentia hominis.

IV. Natura recta fuit substantia hominis: Imago Dei fuit natura recta hominis. E. Resp. Neg. minor. Nam imago Dei non fuit natura recta, sed naturae rectitudo.

V. Cui conueniunt requisita formalia imaginis diuinae, illud est imago Dei. At substantiae hominis &c. E. Minor constat: quia substantia hominis 1) habet originem a Deo, 2) similitudinem & conuenientiam cum Deo, vt eundem repraesentet. Resp. Dist. inter similitudinem, seu conuenientiam generalem, & specialem. Conuenientia generalis facit vestigium Dei; sed conuenientia specialis imaginem Deo simillimam constituit.

VI. Quidquid in homine renato per renouationem Spiritus sancti instauratur, illud est imago Dei; nam ad imaginem Dei renouamur: at mens ipsa &c.: Ergo. Minor probatur ex Eph. IV, 22. Renouamini spiritu mentis vestrae. Resp. Paullus loquitur de subiecto imaginis Dei, non de parte eius constitutiua.

VII. Imago Dei aut fuit extrinsecum accidens, aut substantia: At non fuit extrinsecum accidens, instar ferti aut freni, quod extrinsece adiacet (vt volunt Pontificii) quoniam fuit naturalis, eaque intima perfectio: Ergo fuit substantia. Resp. Maior non constat membris immediatis. Nam inter substantiam & accidens extrinsecum datur tertium, nempe interna qualitas, vel intrinseca perfectio.

IIX. Si dicamus, in sola iustitia originali consistere Dei imaginem: ratio, quam affert Deus, Genes. IX, v. 6. cur homo nullus sit impune occidendus, quia ad imaginem Dei creatus est, & Iacob. III, v. 9. cur proximo non debeamus maledicere, quia ad similitudinem Dei factus est, haec ratio, inquam, nulla esset, vbi ageretur de hominibus, qui regenerationis non sunt participes. Si quis enim responderet, haec intelligenda esse de prima hominis origine, nulla videretur esse consequentia: Vindicabitur sanguis hominis, qui effunditur, etiam eius, in quo imago Dei non est; quia Adam ad imaginem Dei initio creatus est. Certe reuereri non possumus imaginem Dei eo, in quo omni ex parte deleta est. Respondet ad hanc obiectionem D. DANNHAU. in hodom. spirit. calu. p. 1086. Consequentia non militat; quia potest ἀσυλία (immunitas ab inferenda violentia) alicui tribui, ac reuerentia ex respectu non praesentis habitus, sed praeteriti, ex respectu iuris ad rem reparandam, ex respectu sanctorum ipsorum, qualia sunt lumen veri & semen boni adhuc residua: Ita veneratur apostolus Iudaeos secundum carnem, etsi iam dum gratiam Dei decoxerint, Rom. IX, 5. Et nos hodiernis Apellis ἀσυλίαν permittimus, ex respectu antiquissimae familiae. Item homo factus est ad imaginem restaurandam. 2) Ad Gen. IX, 6. respondet D. SEB. SCHMID. in Commentar. in Gen. p. 101. In imagine Dei intenditur immortalitas, dum ad vitam aeternam creatus est; quae intentio diuina manet, non obstante morte temporali, ex qua omnes resuscitabuntur ad iudicium, nec morientur amplius. 3) Ad Iacob. III, 9. respondet D. CALOV. in bibl. illustr. in H. l. fol. 1443. Ad imaginem Dei homo factus dicitur, non qualis nunc est, sed qualis ante lapsum erat; ad quam tamen hic reparatur per Christum, Eph. IV, 24. Col. III, 10. 2 Cor. V, 17.


### Question VIII. What is the efficient cause of the image of God?

The triune God, Father, Son & Holy Spirit, is both the efficient and the exemplary cause of the image of God. Proof from Gen. I, 26. Finally God said: Let us make man in our image, according to our likeness. v. 27. And so God created man in his image. Indicated by these words are 1) the plurality of persons a) by the noun אֱלֹהִים, which is plural both in termination and signification; b) by the verb נַעֲשֶׂה, which is expounded by some interpreters as: let us make; by others: we shall make. In the latter way, this would be an expression of intention; in the former, of consultation.

D. VAREN. prefers the latter in decad. I. Mosaica. p. 15. For what God the Father decreed in all eternity through the Son in the Holy Spirit, that he now said was to be fulfilled: We shall make man. c) By the twin plural pronoun בְּצַלְמֵנוּ & כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ affixed. From which it is manifest that several divine persons are designated by Moses.

2) The unity of the divine essence. This is hinted at a) by the singular verb בָּרָא, which is constructed with a plural noun, so that we may revere unity in trinity and trinity in unity; b) by the verb וַיִּבְרָא, so that the unity of action may be indicated; c) by the identity of the image. For God said (Father, Son & Holy Spirit with highest consent): we shall make (or let us make) man in our image, according to our likeness, so that the unity of both the archetype and the image may be insinuated. From which it is validly gathered that the triune God is not only the efficient, but also the exemplary cause of the image of God. Far be it, therefore, that we should posit that the image of God in man was expressed according to the model of the angelic [nature]! For He who made man is the model of the image in man. who is He, who made man, is uniquely Elohim the creator. Therefore, uniquely Elohim the creator is the exemplar of the image in man.

Latin:

Deus trinus, Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. est tum efficiens, tum exemplaris causa imaginis Dei. Prob. e Gen. I, 26. Tandem dixit Deus: Faciamus hominem in imagine nostra, secundum similitudinem nostram. v. 27. Creauit itaque Deus hominem in imagine sua. Indigitatur his verbis 1) pluralitas personarum a) nomine אֱלֹהִים, quod & terminatione & significatione plurale est; b) Verbo נַעֲשֶׂה, quod ab aliis interpretibus: faciamus; ab aliis: faciemus, exponitur.

Posteriori modo hic esset expressio intentionis; priori, consultationis. Posterius mauult D. VAREN. decad. I. Mosaica. p. 15. Quod enim in omni aeternitate Deus Pater per Filium in Spiritu S. decreuit, id nunc adimplendum dixit: Faciemus hominem. c) Gemino pronomine plurali בְּצַלְמֵנוּ & כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ affixo.

E quibus manifestum est, plures personas diuinas a Mose designari. 2) Essentiae diuinae vnitas. Haec innuitur a) verbo singulari בָּרָא, quod construitur cum nomine plurali, vt vnitatem in trinitate & trinitatem in vnitate veneremur; b) verbo וַיִּבְרָא, vt indicetur vnitas actionis; c) Identitate imaginis. Nam dixit Deus (Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. summo consensu): faciemus (vel faciamus) hominem in imagine nostra, secundum similitudinem nostram, vt vnitas tam archetypi, quam imaginis insinuetur. E quibus valide colligitur, Deum trinum non tantum efficientem, sed & exemplarem causam esse imaginis Dei. Absit igitur, vt statuamus imaginem Dei in homine expressum esse ad exemplar angelicae! Nam ille, qui fecit hominem, est exemplar imaginis in homine. qui ille, qui fecit hominem, unice est Elohim creator. Ergo unice Elohim creator est exemplar imaginis in homine.


### Question IX. Was the first man created according to the model of the human nature of Christ?

The first man was not created after the likeness of the human nature of Christ, preconceived in the divine mind.

Proof 1) Because God said to Himself (Father, Son & Holy Spirit): let us make man in our image, according to our likeness, Gen. I, 26. Therefore the first man was created after the exemplar of God, Father, Son & Holy Spirit. AUGUSTINE presses the force of this consequence, ad lit. op. imperf., citing D. CALOV., tom. IV. system. p. 583: God the Father, speaking to the Son, does not say: Let us make man after your image, or after my image, but He says in the plural, after our image & likeness; from which plurality who would dare to separate the Holy Spirit?

2) The decree concerning the forming of man in the image of God was in the divine intellect prior to the decree concerning the sending of the Son of God into the flesh, for the repairing of the lost image; because the divine decree concerning the incarnation of the Son of God was not formed except with respect to the fall, and redemption from the fall, Matt. IX, 11. Luke XIX, 10. 1 Tim. I, 16. Gal. IV, 4. Therefore, the Son of God, to be incarnated in a posterior decree, cannot be the exemplar of the divine image, to be created in man in a prior decree.

3) The image of God consists in the knowledge of God, righteousness, and holiness, Col. III, 10. Eph. IV, 24: Therefore, it does not consist in the members or stature of the body.

The antithesis is that of Andreas Osiander, who, in a booklet published at Königsberg in the year 1550 concerning the image of God, contends that the image of God, after which man was created, is the face, the stature, and thus the whole substance of the glorified human nature of Christ, as it was in the transfiguration, Matt. XVII, but perfectly now, when He sits at the right hand of God the Father. But because this image did not really exist in the nature of things before the incarnation, he imagines that the Son of God presented Himself to be seen by the fathers of the O.T. in the idea of His future human nature, which becomes the most express likeness of the Son, and that Adam was created according to this likeness. His principal arguments are:

I. Whoever is the substantial image of God, according to whose likeness Adam was created: But the incarnate Son of God is the substantial image of God: Therefore, Adam was created according to the likeness of the incarnate Son of God. The major is proved: because God did not say: let us make man after the exemplar of us, but said: let us make man in our image, i.e., who has the same image that we have. But the image of God is Christ, true God & true man, Col. I, 15. Heb. I, 3. Who, since He did not yet exist in the beginning, God said that He would make man according to the likeness of the face and stature in which Christ presented Himself to be seen by the fathers before the incarnation.

Resp. This argument labors under an enormous misinterpretation. For 1) that image and likeness of God signify the same thing materially, has been shown above. 2) The text itself teaches that Adam was created in the image of God and according to the likeness of God triumus. But the Son of God neither is, nor is anywhere said in the scriptures to be, the image of the SS. Trinity: for thus He would be the image of Himself and of the Holy Spirit, which is ἄτοπον; but He is the image of the person of the Father, Heb. I, 3. on account of His eternal generation from the Father. Therefore Moses does not understand precisely the Son of God by the image of God. 3) Although the Son of God, both as God and as man, on account of the unity of person, is the image of God (as God, the substantial image of God the Father; as man, the personal image, as GERHARD says in disput. isagog. p. 787.): nevertheless, when Adam was created, ὁ λόγος was not yet incarnate, nor had the decree concerning the incarnation τοῦ λόγου preceded the divine decree concerning the creation of Adam: since the decree concerning the incarnation τοῦ λόγου presupposes the fall.

Latin:

Ad similitudinem humanae Christi naturae, in mente divina praeconceptae, primus homo conditus non est.

Prob. 1) Quia dixit apud se Deus (Pater, Filius & Spiritus S.): faciamus hominem in imagine nostra, secundum similitudinem nostram, Gen. I, 26. Ergo primus homo ad exemplar Dei, Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. conditus est. Vim huius consequentiae urget AVGUSTIN. ad lit. op. imperf. citante D. CALOV. tom. IV. system. p. 583. Non ait Deus Pater Filio loquens: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem tuam, aut ad imaginem meam, sed pluraliter ait, ad imaginem & similitudinem nostram, a qua pluralitate Spiritum S. separare quis audeat?

2) Decretum de formando homine ad imaginem Dei in intellectu divino prius fuit decreto de mittendo Filio Dei in carnem, ad reparandam imaginem amissam; quia decretum divinum de incarnatione Filii Dei non, nisi respectu lapsus, & redemptionis a lapsu, formatum est, Matth. IX, 11. Luc. XIX, 10. 1 Tim. I, 16. Gal. IV, 4. Ergo Filius Dei, incarnandus in decreto posteriori, non potest esse exemplar imaginis divinae, homini concreandae in decreto priori.

3) Imago Dei in cognitione Dei, iustitia & sanctitate consistit, Col. III, 10. Eph. IV, 24: Ergo non consistit in membris aut statura corporis.

Antithesis est Andreae Osiandri, qui libello edito Regiomonti Anno 1550. de imagine Dei, contendit, imaginem Dei, ad quam conditus est homo, esse faciem, staturam, adeoque totam substantiam humanae Christi naturae glorificatam, utcunque in transfiguratione, Matth. XVII. perfecte autem nunc, cum sedet ad dextram Dei Patris. Quia vero haec imago ante incarnationem realiter non fuit in rerum natura, ideo autumnat filium Dei e tribus V. T. conspiciendum praebuisse in futurae suae humanae naturae idea, quae fit expressissima similitudo Filii, atque secundum hanc similitudinem creatum esse Adamum. Cuius praecipua sunt argumenta:

I. Quicunque est substantialis imago Dei, secundum illius similitudinem conditus est Adamus: Atqui Filius Dei incarnatus est substantialis Dei imago: Ergo secundum similitudinem Filii Dei incarnati conditus est Adamus. Maior probatur: quia Deus non dixit: faciamus hominem ad exemplar nostri, sed dixit: faciamus hominem in imagine nostra, i. e. qui eandem habeat imaginem, quam nos habemus. Imago autem Dei est Christus, verus Deus & verus homo, Col. I, 15. Hebr. I, 3. Qui cum in principio nondum esset, dixit Deus, sese hominem facturum esse secundum similitudinem faciei & staturae, in qua Christus sese patribus ante incarnationem conspiciendum praebuit.

Resp. Hoc argumentum enormi laborat ψευδερμηνεία. Nam 1) imaginem & similitudinem Dei materialiter idem significare, supra ostensum est. 2) Ipse textus docet, Adamum conditum esse in imagine Dei & secundum similitudinem Dei triunius. At Filius Dei nec est, nec vllibi in scripturis dicitur imago SS. Trinitatis: sic enim foret imago sui ipsius & Spiritus S. quod est ἄτοπον; sed est imago personae Patris, Hebr. I, 3. ob aeternam a Patre generationem. Proinde Moses per imaginem Dei non praecise intelligit Filium Dei. 3) Quamuis Filius Dei, & qua Deus, & qua homo, ob vnitatem personae sit imago Dei (qua Deus, imago Dei Patris substantialis; qua homo, imago personalis, dicente GERHARD. in disput. isagog. p. 787.): attamen cum Adamus crearetur, ὁ λόγος nondum incarnatus erat, nec decretum de incarnatione τοῦ λόγου decretum divinum de creatione Adami praecesserat: siquidem decretum de incarnatione τοῦ λόγου praesupponit lapsum.


### Quaest. X. What impelled God to decorate the protoplast humans with his image?

of man and his liberation from the fall.

It is agreed, however, among all, that the exemplar is prior to the image.

4) Concerning the similarity of the face and stature of Christ, according to which Adam was created, not even a γεῦ (hint) is had in the text.

5) Whether by the image and likeness of God the ἔκτυπον, the image properly so-called, otherwise a simulacrum, an exemplatum, or the ἀρχέτυπον, or exemplar, is understood, is called into doubt: D.

CALOV. answers most simply in his system. tom. IV. p. 631. The matter certainly comes to the same thing, if the words are explained, as 'to our image,' or 'to our exemplar,' or as it becomes 'the image of us'; for the sense remains the same.

D.

VARENIVS however teaches, decad.

1. Mosaic. p. 146. that similarity and image in the phrase of scripture always denotes the ἔκτυπον: and thus in Gen.

I, 25. 27. the exemplar is not designated, except by the plural suffix. He proves the assertion: 1) because every biblical צֶלֶם is contrasted with the exemplar, and its expression is in the ἔκτυπον, nor is צֶלֶם (the same reason applies to τῆς εἰκόνος) ever attributed to the πρωτοτύπῳ, as such.

2) Otherwise there would not be an image in man, but in God, and thus man would not be created to the image, or in the image of God, nor could he be called the image of God.

3) In God, besides the essence, there would be a צֶלֶם, or the same thing would be for the same reason the exemplar and image of itself.

Christ indeed is the image of the Father, nay, most perfectly and intimately expressing the character of the Father: but he is not the same as the image of the Trinity; nor did he create man as a naked image, but as an exemplar and principle: And that very thing indeed, which was the image in the first man, was also in the divinity; but it was not there in the same way as in the first man, nor by the same relation, but as substance and exemplar.

To these we add the not inelegant exposition of D.

SEB. SCHMIDII in annot. in Gen. p. 14. God said: let us make man in our image according to our likeness, i.e., in our perfect image, according to the concept and idea of our most perfect intellect.

The Apostle calls it ἀλήθειαν, i.e., truth, when in Eph.

IV, 24 he says: ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ καὶ ὁσιότητι τῆς ἀληθείας, as if said in Hebrew: in the image of our true likeness. II.

Paul says explicitly, Rom.

VIII, 30 . Whom he foreknew, he also predestined, (to become) conformed to the image of his son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers.

Resp.

In the cited place the image of Christ is considered accidentally.

For Paul speaks of conformity with Christ by reason of humiliation and exaltation, which is varying and successive.

Humiliation and exaltation, however, do not intrinsically constitute the image of God, but only extrinsically, and they regard it in respect of a certain status.

III. If man by reason of his body was also conformed to God the prototype; it follows that not only the divine essence, but also the human nature of Christ is the exemplar, to which Adam was created: Theologians assert the former: Ergo, and the latter.

The consequence of the major is evident; because God is Spirit, Io.

IV, 24 . But Spirit and body have no proportion, or similarity.

Resp.

Theologians indeed assert that the secondary subject of the image of God was the body of the whole man; but not by reason of substance, or corporeal mass, but by reason of qualities, impassibility and immortality.

Quaest. X. What impelled God to decorate the protoplast humans with his image?

Causa impulsiva That God might perfect man with his image, the most liberal goodness moved him.

Prob. Every good is communicative of itself, and as it were diffusive.

Therefore, whatever is better, the further and more widely it spreads the rays of its goodness.

Thus the sun shines for all, the air encompasses and refreshes all, fountains, rivers, and seas are open to all.

God, the fountain and origin of every good, diffuses the goodness of his divinity into man, as soon as he created him, by conferring upon him his image, an incomparable endowment.

For just as a prince [confers upon] a minister

Latin:

hominis & liberationem a lapsu.

Constat autem inter omnes, exemplar prius esse imagine.

4) De similitudine faciei & staturae Christi, secundum quam Adamus conditus sit, ne γεῦ quidem habetur in textu.

5) Utrum per imaginem & similitudinem Dei τὸ ἔκτυπον, imago proprie dicta, alias simulacrum, exemplatum, an τὸ ἀρχέτυπον, sive exemplar intelligatur, indubium vocatur: simplicissime respondet D.

CALOV. in system. tom. IV. p. 631. Res utique eodem redit, si explicentur verba, ad imaginem nostram, vel ad nostri exemplar, vel vt fit imago nostri; sensus enim idem manet.

D.

VARENIVS autem docet, decad.

1. Mosaic. p. 146. quod similitudo & imago phrasi scripturae semper notet ἔκτυπον: atque adeo Gen.

I, 25. 27. exemplar non designetur, nisi per affixum plurale. Probat assertum: 1) quia omne צֶלֶם biblicum est exemplari contradistinctum, & eius expressio in ἐκτύπῳ, nec vnquam צֶלֶם (eadem ratio est τῆς εἰκόνος) tribuitur πρωτοτύπῳ, vt sic.

2) Ceteroqui non esset in homine, sed Deo imago, atque adeo nec homo ad imaginem, vel in magine Dei conditus, nec imago Dei dici posset.

3) In Deo praeter essentiam צֶלֶם esset, vel idem eadem ratione sui ipsius exemplar & imago esset.

Christus quidem imago patris, imo perfectissime & intime exprimens character patris est: at nec idem est imago Trinitatis; nec creauit hominem vt nuda imago, sed vt exemplar & principium: Et illud ipsum quidem, quod fuit imago in primo homine, fuit & in diuinitate; sed nec ibi fuit eo modo, quo in primo homine, nec eadem relatione, sed vt substantia & exemplar.

His adiungimus haud inconcinnam expositionem D.

SEB. SCHMIDII in annot. in Gen. p. 14. Dixit Deus: faciamus hominem in imagine nostra secundum similitudinem nostram, h. e. in imagine nostra perfecta, iuxta nostri intellectus perfectissimi conceptum & ideam.

Apostolus vocat ἀλήθειαν, f. veritatem, cum Eph.

IV, 24. inquit: ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ καὶ ὁσιότητι τῆς ἀληθείας, quasi hebraice dictum: in imagine verae similitudinis nostrae. II.

Paullus diserte ait, Rom.

VIII, 30. Quos praecognouit, etiam praedestinauit, conformes (fieri) imaginis filii sui, ut hic fit primogenitus inter multos fratres.

Resp.

Loco citato imago Christi consideratur accidentaliter.

Loquitur enim Paullus de conformitate cum Christo ratione humiliationis & exaltationis variante & successiua.

Humiliatio autem & exaltatio non constituunt intrinsece imaginem Dei, sed extrinsece solum & respectu certi status illam respiciunt.

III. Si homo ratione corporis etiam conformis fuit Deo prototypo; sequitur, quod non tantum diuina essentia, sed & humana Christi natura fit exemplar, ad quod conditus est Adamus: Prius afferunt theologi: E. & posterius.

Consequentia maioris patet; quia Deus est Spiritus, Io.

IV, 24. Spiritus autem & corpus nullam habent proportionem, aut similitudinem.

Resp.

Afferunt quidem theologi, subiectum secundarium imaginis Dei fuisse corpus hominis integri; at non ratione substantiae, aut corporeae molis, sed ratione qualitatum, impassibilitatis & immortalitatis.

Quaest. X. Quid impulit Deum, homines protoplastos imagine sua condecorare?

Causa impulsiva Vt Deus hominem imagine sua perficeret, ipsum pernouit bonitas liberalissima.

Prob. Omne bonum est sui communicatiuum, & quasi diffusiuum.

Proinde, quocquid est melius, eo longius latiusque bonitatis suae radios dispergit.

Sic sol lucet omnibus, aer ambit & recreat omnes, fontes, flumina & maria patent omnibus.

Deus, omnis boni fons & origo, bonitates suae diuinitatis diffundit in hominem, simul atque ipsum condidit, imaginem suam, dotem incomparabilem, in eundem conferendo.

Quem ad modum enim princeps ministrum


### Quaest. XI. Did God adorn man of both sexes with his own image?

to himself in a few things dear, as a sign of unusual grace, he gives his own likeness: so God, moved by a singular affection of love and favor, impressed his own image upon the first man, not by appending it externally, but by implanting it internally.

Question XI.

Did God adorn man of both sexes with his own image? God polished man of both sexes, male and female, with his own image.

Proof 1) from Gen. I, 27. So God created man in his own image; in the image (I say) of God he created him, male and female he created them. Moses here expressly says that the man, whom God created in the image of himself, was not an individual of one masculine sex, but male and female. Cf. Gen. V, 2. 2) He who is to be renewed in the image of God was first created in the same. But not only men, but also women must be renewed in the image of God, Eph. IV, 24. Col. III, 10. Gal. III, 28. Therefore. 3) Just as not only the male, but also the female enjoys the right of inheriting the life of heaven: so the image of God belongs to both. For he who is devoid of true holiness and righteousness, which is the chief part of the image of God, is excluded from the heavenly inheritance, 1 Petr. III, 7. Hebr. XII, 14. The antithesis was once that of the Encratites, who judged the female sex to be a creature impure in itself; whom some haters of the female sex followed, thinking that Eve was not created in the image of God.

They object: I. Dominion over brutes, which is a significant part of the divine character, was not granted to the female, as is evident from 1 Cor. XI, 7. Resp. The apostle does not deny dominion to the female sex over brutes simply, but dominion over the husband. Rather, he asserts that in the marital state the prerogative belongs to the husband, because of marital dominion over the female; which indeed, placed in the state of innocence, he could exercise most temperately toward his wife.

II. Moses testifies that God breathed into Adam the soul of lives, Gen. II, 7. From which inspiration he obtained the image of God: The same is not said of the female. Resp. The soul of Eve was either created immediately by God, or derived from Adam, by means of the rib. If it was created, Eve obtained the divine image immediately from God: If it was derived, which not a few judge to be more probable, the divine character, which was in the soul, was derived at the same time. By which reasoning there was in Eve the image of God, not indeed primitive, yet arisen and derived from Adam. From which D. DANNHAV. in hodof. phaenom. V. p. 428. argues: The image of Adam is the image of God. The image of Eve is the image of Adam. Therefore, the image of Eve is the image of God. See 1 Cor. XI, 7. Thus, a copy of an effigy is no less a true image of the prototype, although not immediate.

Question XII.

Were angels also created in the image of God?

The sacred scriptures neither expressly affirm nor deny that angels shine with the image of God; yet from them it is not invalidly gathered that they were divinely endowed with the image of God. Proof 1) Angels are called Sons of God, Job XXXVIII, 7. Therefore they bear the image of God. The reason for the consequence is manifest; because every son reflects the father from whom he draws his origin. You say: Angels are called sons of God; because God pursues them with singular love. Resp. If sonship were based precisely on love, even a brother could be called the son of a brother; but more is required for sonship, namely either generation, or adoption, or creation in the image. Now, however, angels are neither begotten of the substance of God, nor adopted by the same; since the foundation of divine adoption is the merit of Christ, Eph. I, 5, the fruit of which does not return to the angels. Therefore, they were created in the image of God. 2) To

2) For the image in the order of creatures, a likeness and dependence upon the prototype is required. Angels enjoy both. For they are wise and holy spirits created in the beginning of things, and they depend upon God the archetype. 3) In the perfect restoration of the image of God, blessed men will be ἰσάγγελοι, like unto the angels, Therefore, if not by greater, certainly by no lesser rays than blessed men, do the angels shine with the divine image.

There is an antithesis of some Fathers and Theologians, who deny that angels were created in the image of God. The palm-bearing argument of these is that angels are said to be sent not for dominion, but for ministry, Resp. 1) Angels are not so much our ministers as God's: They minister to God, but for our sake: They are not our servants, but fellow-servants are they. But a guardian is not always a minister of him whom he has guarded. Any captain can guard even the lowest of rustics. 2) The faculty of ruling over brutes is an accessory to the divine image: in the primary part, namely holiness and justice, the angels are not destitute. What? That not every power of commanding beasts seems to be denied to the angels. We read that they stopped the mouths of lions,

Latin:

sibi in paucis carum, in signum inusitatae gratiae, effigie sua donat: ita Deus, adductus singulari amoris & favoris affectu, homini primo imaginem suam impressit, non exterius appendendo, sed interius inferendo.

Quaest. XI.

An Deus hominem utriusque sexus imagine sua exornavit? Deus hominem utriusque sexus, marem & foeminam, imagine sua perpolivit.

Prob. 1) e Gen. I, 27. Creauit itaque Deus hominem in imagine sua; in imagine (inquam) Dei creauit eum, masculum & foeminam creauit eos. Moses hic expresse dicit, hominem, quem Deus ad imaginem sui condidit, non fuisse vnius sexus masculini indiuiduum, sed marem & foeminam. Conf. Gen. V, 2. 2) Qui ad imaginem Dei renouandus est, is primum ad eandem conditus fuit. At non viri tantum, sed etiam mulieres ad imaginem Dei renouari debent, Eph. IV, 24. Col. III, 10. Gal. III, 28. Ergo. 3) Vti non tantum mas, sed etiam foemina in iure cernendi hereditatem vitae gaudet: Ita vtrique imago Dei competit. Nam expers verae sanctitatis & iustitiae, quae praecipua pars est imaginis Dei, exsors est hereditatis coelestis, 1 Petr. III, 7. Hebr. XII, 14. Antithesis fuit olim Encratitarum, qui sexum muliebrem creaturam per se impuram esse iudicarunt; quos secuti sunt nonnulli osores sexus foeminei, arbitrati, Euam non esse creatam ad imaginem Dei.

Obiiciunt: I. Dominium in bruta, quod est insignis pars characteris diuini, non fuit concessum foeminae, vt patet ex 1 Cor. XI, 7. Resp. Non denegat apostolus dominium foemineo sexui in bruta simpliciter, sed dominium in maritum. Contra asserit, competere in statu coniugali marito praerogatiuam, ob dominium maritale in foeminam; quod quidem temperattissimum in vxorem exercere poterat, in statu innocentiae collocatus.

II. Testatur Moses, Deum Adamo inspirasse animam vitarum, Gen. II, 7. Ex qua inspiratione imaginem Dei nactus est: Idem de foemina non dicitur. Resp. Anima Euae aut immediate a Deo est creata, aut ab Adamo, mediante costa, traducta. Si creata est; Eua immediate a Deo imaginem diuinam adepta est: Si traducta est, quod haud pauci censent probabilius, simul character diuinus, qui fuit in anima, traductus est. Qua ratione in Eua fuit imago Dei non quidem primitiua, orta tamen & deriuata ab Adamo. Ex quo D. DANNHAV. in hodof. phaenom. V. p. 428. arguit: Imago Adami est imago Dei. Imago Euae est imago Adami. E. imago Euae est imago Dei. Vid. 1 Cor. XI, 7. Sic effigies apographa non minus est vera imago prototypi, licet non immediata.

Quaest. XII.

An etiam angeli ad imaginem Dei creati sunt?

Angelos imagine Dei refulgere, diserte nec affirmant, nec negant sacrae litterae; ex iisdem tamen haud inualide colligitur, illos diuinitus donatos esse imagine Dei. Prob. 1) Angeli vocantur Filii Dei, Iob. XXXVIII, 7. Ergo imaginem Dei gerunt. Ratio consequentiae est manifesta; quia omnis filius refert patrem, a quo ducit originem. Dicis: Angeli dicuntur filii Dei; quia Deus illos singulari amore prosequitur. Resp. Si filiatio praecise fundaretur in amore, etiam frater filius fratris dici posset; at plus requiritur ad filiationem, nempe vel generatio, vel adoptio, vel creatio ad imaginem. Iam vero angeli neque sunt de substantia Dei geniti, neque ab eodem adoptati; cum adoptionis diuinae fundamentum sit meritum Christi, Eph. I, 5. cuius fructus in angelos non redit. E. ad imaginem Dei sunt creati. 2) Ad

2) Ad imaginem in ordine creaturarum requiritur similitudo & dependentia a prototypo. Vtraque gaudent angeli. Sunt enim spiritus sapientes & sancti in primordio rerum conditi, pendentque a Deo archetypo. 3) In perfecta restauratione imaginis Dei homines beati ἰσάγγελοι, similes angelis erunt, Ergo angeli, si non maioribus, certe non minoribus, quam homines beati, imaginis divinae radiis corruscant.

Antithesis est nonnullorum Patrum & Theologorum, qui negant, angelos ad imaginem Dei esse creatos. Palmarium istorum argumentum est; quia angeli non ad dominium, sed ad ministerium dicuntur missi, Resp. 1) Angeli non tam nostri, quam Dei ministri sunt: Ministrant Deo, sed pro nobis: Non nostri servi, sed conferui sunt. At custos non semper minister est illius, quem custodivit. Capitaneus quispiam potest custodire vel ultimum rusticorum. 2) Facultas dominandi brutis faltum adiunctum est imaginis divinae: parte primaria, nempe sanctitate & iustitia, angeli non destituuntur.
