Quid? quod non omnis vis imperandi bestiis deneganda angelis videtur. Compescuisse illos ora leonum legimus,


### Q. XIII

What was the principal seat of the image of God? What was the less principal? The principal seat, and as it were the most splendid citadel, in which the image of God shone forth, was the soul of the whole man, and in it the intellect and appetite, both rational (which is called the will), and sensitive. The less principal seat was the body of the first-formed man, the most convenient dwelling of the soul, and its living organ.

Obs. In philosophical terms this doctrine is proposed thus: The matter in which, or the subject of the image of God, is either that which, or total, or that by which, or partial. The total subject is the whole man, by reason of both sexes. The partial is either primary or secondary. The primary is the rational soul of man, with its faculties, namely the intellect, the will, and the sensitive appetite. The secondary is the body, informed by the rational soul.

Latin:

Quae fuit sedes imaginis Dei principalis? Quae minus principalis? Sedes princeps, & quasi arx splendidissima, in qua imago Dei eminuit, fuit anima hominis integri, & ea intellectus atque appetitus, tam rationalis (quae vocatur voluntas), quam sensitivus. Sedes minus principalis fuit corpus hominis protoplasti, commodissimum animae domicilium, vivumque organum.

Obs. Terminis philosophicis haec doctrina ita proponitur: Materia in qua, sive subiectum imaginis Dei est vel quod, sive totale, vel quo, sive partiale. Subiectum totale, est totus homo, ratione utriusque sexus. Partiale est vel primarium, vel secundarium. Primarium est hominis anima rationalis, cum suis facultatibus, intellectu scilicet, voluntate & appetitu sensitivo. Secundarium est corpus, anima rationali informatum.


### Q. XIV

In what did the image of God formally consist? The image of God consisted in the excellent conformity of the first man with the wisdom, justice, purity, immortality, and majesty of God, the archetype a), according to the measure of capacity which is given in an intelligent creature b).

Prob. a. The most benign divinity bestowed upon the first-formed men those perfections which were necessarily required for obtaining the end for the sake of which they were created: Namely, that they might duly worship God, pass their life justly and temperately, and finally at some time attain to glorious blessedness. Prob. b.

Prob. b. Conformity of the copy with the archetype is not always required to be all-encompassing and absolute, but sometimes an accommodating and respective one suffices, according to the capacity of him who sustains the image of the prototype. Hence there is a huge difference between the perfections of God and of the first-formed man. For the wisdom and justice of God is essential, infinite, eternal, and immutable: The wisdom and justice of the first man was accidental, finite, temporal, and mutable.

Q. XV.

What were the principal perfections with which God endowed the first-formed men? The principal perfections, constituting the image of God, were: excellent knowledge of the intellect, perfect holiness and liberty of the will, sincere purity of the sensitive appetite, and a most sweet, as it were, harmony of the affections, with the dictate of the intellect and in the governance of the will, to the wisdom, holiness, and purity of God, according to the capacity of the first man, conformable.

Latin:

In quo formaliter consistebat imago Dei? Consistebat imago Dei in excellenti conformitate primi hominis cum sapientia, iustitia, puritate, immortalitate & maiestate Dei, archetypi a), secundum modum capacitatis, quae datur in creatura intelligenti b).

Prob. a. Impertivit benignissimum numen homines protoplastos iis perfectionibus, quae necessario requirebantur ad obtinendum finem, cuius gratia creati erant: Nimirum, vt Deo rite colerent, vitam iuste moderateque transducerent, & beatitatem gloriosam tandem aliquando consequerentur.

Prob. b. Non semper requiritur conformitas ectypi cum archetypo omnimoda & absoluta, sed sufficit interdum accommoda & respectiva, secundum capacitatem eius, qui prototypi sustinet imaginem. Proinde ingens est discrimen inter perfectiones Dei, & hominis protoplasti. Nam sapientia & iustitia Dei est essentialis, infinita, aeterna & immutabilis: Sapientia & iustitia primi hominis fuit accidentalis, finita, temporalis & mutabilis.

Quaest. XV.

Quae fuerunt perfectiones principales, quibus Deus homines protoplastos impertivit? Perfectiones principales, imaginem Dei constituentes, fuerunt: excellens scientia intellectus, perfecta sanctitas & libertas voluntatis, sincera puritas appetitus sensitivi, & suavissimus quasi concentus affectuum, cum dictamine intellectus & regimine voluntatis, sapientiae, sanctitati & puritati Dei, pro captu hominis primi, conformes.


### Q. XVI. What was the knowledge of the first man?

The knowledge of the first man was a light and habitual perfection of the intellect, concreated in the integral man, for the knowing of God, himself, and the creatures.

Obs. 1. This perfection of the intellect, or wisdom, which shone forth in the first man, was as great as no one after the fall in these lands, whether from the principles of nature or from written revelation, can acquire for himself, so that Adam left Solomon, whose wisdom is especially celebrated, a long interval behind him. For in this life, after the fall, even the regenerate know only in part, and thus imperfectly, 1 Cor. XIII, 12, because they have only the firstfruits of the Spirit, Rom. VIII, 23. It was nevertheless finite; because Adam did not know the free and secret decrees of God, not the thoughts of angels and men, not all the individuals of every species. From which it also follows that the knowledge of the protoplasts was to be further perfected, both by supernatural revelation and by experience and personal observation; and therefore it does not exclude an ignorance of pure negation, although it was immune from an ignorance of depraved disposition.

Obs. 2. The knowledge of Adam was indeed excellent and sufficient for the primordial state: but it was not an intuitive knowledge of God. For a clear vision of God is not given in these lands, but is promised to be given in the heavens, 1 Cor. XIII, 12; 1 John III, 2. Certainly, he who knows God intuitively is not turned away from the Supreme Deity by his will, as Adam was turned away.

Proof of our assertion: 1) From the end of the image, which is the glory of God. If man in the state of innocence had neither known nor worshipped God, he would have been an atheist: which statement is impious.

2) From the renewal of justified men. For we are renewed unto knowledge according to the image of him who created us, Col. III, 10. That knowledge according to the image of the Creator unto which we are renewed, Adam possessed; since renewal is the new repair, or restitution, of the old which was lost.

3) From the remarkable specimens of connatural wisdom produced by Adam: such as are a) ὀνομαϑεσία, or the nomenclature of animals, not merely grammatical, devised at will, but also logical, congruent to the nature of the living creatures and the affections of the beasts, approved by the consent of God, Gen. II, 19. 20. From which it is concluded that the first man, by an innate perspicacity of intellect, penetrated and perceived the properties of living creatures. b) The recognition of Eve as fashioned from the rib of the sleeping Adam, Gen. II, 23. c) The prophetic prediction of the future solidity of the conjugal bond, Gen. II, 24. (*).

4) From the granted dominion over the brutes, which the protoplast man could not have exercised without significant prudence.

5) From the notions innate in the minds of men today; which are the remnants of the lost divine image, and testify to the pristine wisdom, just as ruins testify to a splendid house collapsed ().

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, who deny that the first man was endowed with exceptional wisdom; which is supported by the following arguments.

, of those who deny that the first man was endowed with extraordinary wisdom; which are supported by the following arguments.

I. Whoever were ignorant of their nakedness, they were not remarkably wise. But the protoplasts, etc. The minor premise is proved from Gen. III, 7. Response: They were ignorant of nakedness not of nature, but of ignominy. If they had been ignorant of physical nakedness, they would have lacked eyes. But they were ignorant of nakedness considered ethically, as it is shameful and disgraceful: whence, after the fall, the genital members, in which the lust of the flesh is felt, must be covered. Since the uncorrupted man did not feel this, he needed no covering.

Instance: But the eyes were opened only after the forbidden fruit was eaten, to recognize nakedness. Response: The eyes of the mind were opened to recognize the shameful nakedness experimentally.

II. The protoplasts were ignorant that God is more truthful than the devil; otherwise they would not have given assent to him. Response: Distinguish between ignorance that is concreated, and that which arises from negligence. Ignorance was not concreated in our first parents, but they owe their fall to negligence, or to the omission of a more accurate scrutiny.

III. The first men were ignorant of the power of the tree of life; otherwise they would have eaten, and preserved themselves from death. Response: They were not ignorant of the power of the tree of life: they would have eaten of it longer, had they not been prohibited by angelic protection.

IV. The protoplasts were ignorant that they were mortal. Response: They were ignorant practically that they were mortal; because they discovered no cause of mortality in themselves: just as a healthy physician does not know a disease in himself practically.

V. The same were ignorant of the mystery of the Trinity and the Incarnation; since that is not known except from the light of revelation. Response: Certainly Adam also had knowledge of the mystery of the Trinity, not only through revelation, but also through the creation of the image itself; because he knew his creator. But this God is one in essence, and three in persons. The mystery of the incarnation, however, presupposes the fall, which it was not for the uncorrupted man to know determinately.

Latin:

Scientia primi hominis fuit lux & perfectio habitualis intellectus, homini integro concreata, ad cognoscendum Deum, seipsum & creaturas.

Obs. 1. Perfectio haec intellectus, sive sapientia, quae in primo homine eluxit, tanta fuit, quantam post lapsum nemo in his terris, sive ex principiis naturae, sive ex revelatione scripta sibi comparare potest, vt Adamus Salomonem, cuius sapientia praecipue celebratur, longo post se intervallo reliquerit. In hac enim vita, post lapsum, etiam renati ex parte, adeoque imperfecte cognoscunt, 1 Cor. XIII, 12. quia tantum primitias spiritus habent, Rom. VIII, 23. Fuit tamen finita; quia Adamus non cognovit libera & arcana Dei decreta, non cogitationes angelorum & hominum, non omnia cuiuslibet speciei individua. Ex quo etiam scientia protoplastorum ulterius perficienda fuit, tum per supernaturalem revelationem, tum per experientiam & propriam observationem; ac proinde non excludit ignorantiam pure negationis, quamvis immunis fuerit ab ignorantia pravae dispositionis.

Obs. 2. Eximia quidem & sufficiens pro statu primaeuo fuit scientia Adami: At non fuit cognitio Dei intuitiva. Nam clara Dei visio non datur in his terris, sed promittitur danda in coelis, 1 Cor. XIII, 12. 1 Io. III, 2. Sane, qui Deum intuitive cognoscit, per voluntatem a summo numine non auertitur, vt auersus est Adamus.

Prob. assertio nostra 1) ex fine imaginis, qui est gloria Dei. Si homo in statu innocentiae Deum neque agnouisset, neque coluisset, fuisset atheus: Quod dictum impium est.

2) Ex renovatione hominum iustificatorum. Renouamur enim ad cognitionem secundum imaginem eius, qui creauit nos, Col. III, 10. Ad quam cognitionem secundum imaginem creatoris nos renouamur, illam habuit Adamus; siquidem renouatio est noua veteris, quod amissum est, reparatio, aut restitutio.

3) Ex egregiis speciminibus connaturalis sapientiae ab Adamo editis: qualia sunt a) ὀνομαϑεσία, siue nomenclatura animalium, non tantum grammatica, pro arbitratu excogitata, sed etiam logica, indoli animantium & affectibus bestiarum congrua, consensu Dei comprobata, Gen. II, 19. 20. Ex quo conficitur, quod primus homo animantium proprietates, insita intellectus perspicacia, penetrauerit ac peruiderit. b) Agnitio Euae ex costa Adami dormientis fabricatae, Gen. II, 23. c) Praedictio prophetica futurae soliditatis vinculi coniugalis, Gen. II, 24. (*).

4) Ex concesso dominio in bruta, quo perfungi homo protoplastus sine insigni prudentia nequiuit.

5) Ex notitiis hominum mentibus hodiernum innatis; quae sunt amissae imaginis divinae reliquiae, & testantur de pristina sapientia, haud secus, ac rudera de splendida domo collapsa ().

Antithesis est Socinianorum

, negantium, hominem primum eximia fuisse præditum sapientia; quæ sequentibus innituntur argumentis.

I. Quicunque ignorarunt nuditatem suam, illi non fuerunt insigniter sapientes. Atqui protoplasti &c. Minor prob. e Gen. III, 7. Resp. Ignorarunt nuditatem non naturæ, sed ignominiæ. Si nuditatem physicam ignorassent, oculis caruissent. At ignorarunt nuditatem ethice consideratam, prout est turpis & probrosa: Vnde velanda sunt post lapsum membra genitalia, in quibus lascivia carnis sentitur. Quam cum non senserit homo integer, nullo indiguit velamine.

Instantia: At oculi comesto fructu vetito demum aperti sunt ad cognoscendam nuditatem. Resp. Oculi mentis aperti sunt ad experimentaliter cognoscendam nuditatem ignominiosam.

II. Ignorarunt protoplasti, Deum esse magis veracem, quam diabolum; ceteroqui huic assensum non præbuissent. Resp. Dist. inter ignorantiam concreatam, & ex negligentia ortam. Ignorantia primis parentibus non erat concreata, sed debent illi lapsum suum negligentiæ, vel omissioni accuratioris scrutinii.

III. Ignorarunt primi homines vim arboris vitæ; ceteroqui comedissent, & a morte se præferuassent. Resp. Vim arboris vitæ non ignorarunt: Comedissent etiam diutius de eadem, nisi angelico præsidio prohibiti fuissent.

IV. Ignorarunt protoplasti, se esse mortales. Resp. Ignorarunt practice, se esse mortales; quia nullam mortalitatis caussam in se deprehenderunt: sicut medicus sanus in se nescit morbum practice.

V. Ignorarunt iidem mysterium trinitatis & incarnationis; quippe quod non, nisi e lumine reuelationis, innotescit. Resp. Vtique etiam Adamus habuit cognitionem mysterii Trinitatis non tantum per reuelationem, sed & ipsius imaginis creationem; quia nouerat creatorem suum. Hic autem est vnus in essentia, & trinus in personis Deus. Mysterium autem incarnationis præsupponit lapsum, quem determinate scire non erat hominis integri.


### Q. XVII. What was the holiness of the uncorrupted man?

The holiness of the uncorrupted man was the perfection of the will, by which he loved God above all things, and his neighbor as himself, and all works consonant with the divine will, which the intellect, illuminated by innate light, dictated should be done, he performed promptly and freely.

Obs. I. The perfection of the will, with which the first man was divinely endowed, embraces both the propensity toward the good, and the free execution of the good, so that it might represent the holy liberty of God, and the free holiness of God.

Obs. II. The good, toward which the uncorrupted man inclined, is to be estimated from the norm of the innate law, the sum of which is the love of God and neighbor: which law, as a mirror of the divine will, the intellect of the first man, illuminated by the light of the divine image, never ceased to contemplate. Thence, what he knew to be pleasing and approved to the divine will, he dictated should be done here and now.

Prob. 1) from Gen. I, 31. God saw everything that he had made: and behold, it was very good. The most wise architect of this universe, having contemplated all the works of the six days, saw them in a goodness appropriate to each. The remaining creatures rejoiced in natural goodness, man moreover excelled in moral goodness; for this is due and proper to him. Imagine in the first man a languor of nature, and an inclination toward evil: would it not follow that God had made something which was not very good, and therefore that He Himself is the cause of evil? But if the remaining creatures were very good; why not man, for whose sake they were created?

2) From Eccl. VII, 30. God made man upright. He is morally upright who is just and holy. The Hebrew word יָשָׁר is used of God Himself, Deut. XXXII, 4, and thus implies a rectitude of will conformable to divine justice and holiness.

3) From the renewal of justified men. For the converted, reborn, and justified sinner, through powers bestowed from above, puts on the new man, who is created according to God, in righteousness and holiness of truth, Eph. IV, 24. To put on the new man, who is created according to God, in righteousness and holiness of truth, is to be renewed to the ancient holiness and righteousness, once possessed by man, who was created according to God, or in His image.

4) From the absurd. If the protoplasts did not reflect the most holy and most just God with concreated holiness and righteousness, they were not created in an image most similar to God; for they were not conformable to God, but difform.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, who deny that perfect holiness was concreated in the first man. Their stronger arguments are: I. Whoever is originally just and holy, he is impeccable. Our first parents were not impeccable. Therefore, they were not originally just and holy.

Resp. 1) Distinguish between absolute and limited impeccability. The former is that by which one can in no way sin. The latter is that by which the first man, from concreated powers, was able not to sin, or to decline sin, and thus is more accurately called non-peccable than impeccable.

2) Distinguish between immutable and mutable holiness. Immutable holiness belongs by essence to God, and by grace to angels confirmed in good and to blessed men in heaven. But the first man's justice was mutable.

Whence I limit the major: Whoever is immutably just and holy, he is impeccable absolutely and simply; I grant it. But thus the minor is denied.

Instance I. Given the distinction, the image of God is overturned, and is withdrawn from the first man. For to every image, conformity of the ectype with the archetype is required. But the holiness of God the archetype is immutable. Therefore, the holiness of the first man also ought to have been immutable, if it was expressed according to the exemplar of divine holiness.

Resp. To an image, conformity of the ectype with the archetype is required not absolutely and in every way, but relatively and accommodately, according to the mode of capacity which is given in him who bears the image.

Instance II. If the first man could decline sin from concreated powers, he was absolutely impeccable: Theologians assert the former: Therefore also the latter. The consequence of the major is evident; because in him there is no power of sinning, who can decline sin from concreated powers.

Resp. Distinguish between remote and proximate power of sinning. There was not in the protoplasts a proximate power of sinning, or a proclivity to evil: But there was not lacking to them a remote power of sinning, or repugnance.

Instance III. If God created the first man with a remote power of sinning, He created him labile, and thus is the cause of the Adamic fall.

Resp. The consequence is denied. For he is called labile who is prone to falling, and thus receives the denomination from a physical, or proximate, power.

From a power of non-repugnance, or remote, a denomination is not made. e.g. God created the sun, which could be worshipped by the Gentiles. But you conclude wrongly: Therefore God made the sun adorable to the Gentiles.

II. If the image of God consisted in concreated holiness, man after the fall cannot be said to be created in the image of God: But man after the fall is said to be created in the image of God: Therefore.

Resp. We shall satisfy this argument below. Resp. We shall satisfy this argument below.

Latin:

Sanctitas hominis integri erat perfectio voluntatis, qua Deum super omnia, proximumque sicut seipsum diligebat, omniaque opera, voluntati diuinæ consona, quæ intellectus, insita luce illustratus, facienda dictabat promte libereque expediebat.

Obs. I. Perfectio voluntatis, qua primus homo diuinitus præditus erat, complectitur tum propensionem ad bonum, tum liberam boni exsecutionem, vt sanctam Dei libertatem, liberamque Dei sanctitatem repræsentaret.

Obs. II. Bonum, ad quod homo integer propendebat, æstimandum est ex norma legis insitæ, cuius summa est amor Dei & proximi: quam legem, velut speculum voluntatis diuinæ nunquam non intuebatur intellectus primi hominis, lumine imaginis diuinæ collustratus. Exinde quæ voluntati diuinæ grata probataque esse nouerat, hic & nunc facienda dictabat.

Prob. 1) e Gen. I, 31. Vidit Deus omne, quod fecit: & ecce, bonum erat valde. Contemplatus sapientissimus huius vniuersi architectus omnia opera hexaëmeri, vidit ea in bonitate singulis conueniente. Reliquæ creaturæ gaudebant bonitate naturali, homo insuper bonitate eminebat morali; hæc enim illi est debita & propria. Finge in homine primo languorem naturæ, ac inclinationem ad malum: Nonne sequetur, Deum aliquid fecisse, quod non fuerit valde bonum, adeoque ipsum esse caussam mali? Quod si reliquæ creaturæ fuerunt valde bonæ; eur non homo, propter quem illæ sunt conditæ?

2) Ex Eccl. VII, 30. Deus fecit hominem rectum. Moraliter rectus est, qui est iustus & sanctus. Vox hebraea יָשָׁר usurpatur de ipso Deo, Deut. XXXII, 4. adeoque infert rectitudinem voluntatis conformem iustitiae & sanctitati divinae.

3) Ex renouatione hominum iustificatorum. Nam peccator conuersus, renatus, & iustificatus, per vires superne collatas induit nouum hominem, qui secundum Deum creatus est, in iustitia & sanctitate veritatis, Eph. IV, 24. Induere nouum hominem, qui secundum Deum creatus est, in iustitia & sanctitate veritatis, est, renouari ad antiquam sanctitatem & iustitiam, olim aliquando possessam ab homine, qui secundum Deum, siue ad eius imaginem fuit conditus.

4) Ex absurdo. Si protoplasti non retulerunt concreata sanctitate & iustitia Deum sanctissimum & iustissimum, ad imaginem Deo simillimam non sunt conditi; neque enim Deo conformes, sed difformes fuerunt.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, infitiantium concreatam primo homini sanctitatem perfectam. Quorum potiora sunt argumenta: I. Quicunque originaliter iustus & sanctus est, ille est impeccabilis. Primi nostri parentes non fuerunt impeccabiles. Ergo non fuerunt originaliter iusti & sancti.

Resp. 1) Dist. inter impeccabilitatem absolutam, & limitatam. Illa est, qua quis nullo modo potest peccare. Haec est, qua homo primus ex viribus concreatis poterat non peccare, seu peccatum declinare, adeoque accuratius non-peccabilis, quam impeccabilis dicitur.

2) Dist. inter sanctitatem immutabilem, & mutabilem. Sanctitas immutabilis per essentiam Deo, per gratiam angelis in bono confirmatis & hominibus beatis in coelo competit. Sed primi hominis iustitia mutabilis erat.

Vnde limito maiorem: Quicunque immutabiliter iustus & sanctus est, ille est impeccabilis absolute & simpliciter; concedo. At sic negatur minor.

Instantia I. Data distinctione, euertitur imago Dei, primoque homini subtrahitur. Nam ad omnem imaginem requiritur conformitas ectypi cum archetypo. At sanctitas Dei archetypi est immutabilis. Ergo & sanctitas primi hominis debuit esse immutabilis, si ad exemplar sanctitatis diuinae fuerit expressa.

Resp. Ad imaginem requiritur conformitas ectypi cum archetypo non absoluta & omnimoda, sed respectiua & accommoda, secundum modum capacitatis, quae datur in eo, qui gerit imaginem.

Instantia II. Si homo primus ex viribus concreatis peccatum declinare potuit, fuit absolute impeccabilis: Prius afferunt theologi: Ergo & posterius. Consequ. maioris patet; quia in illo nulla est potentia peccandi, qui ex concreatis viribus peccatum declinare potest.

Resp. Dist. inter potentiam peccandi remotam, & proximam. Non fuit in protoplastis potentia peccandi proxima, siue procliuitas ad malum: At non defuit illis potentia peccandi remota, siue repugnantia.

Instantia III. Si Deus primum hominem cum potentia peccandi remota condidit, eundem creauit labilem, atque adeo lapsus Adamitici caussa est.

Resp. Negatur consequ. Nam labilis dicitur, qui pronus ad labendum est, adeoque a potentia physica, seu proxima denominationem accipit.

A potentia non repugnantiae, siue remota, non fit denominatio. v. gr. Deus creauit solem, qui a gentilibus potuit adorari. Sed male concluseris: Ergo Deus fecit solem adorabilem gentilibus.

II. Si imago Dei constitit in concreata sanctitate, homo post lapsum non potest dici creatus ad imaginem Dei: At homo post lapsum dicitur creatus ad imaginem Dei: Ergo.

Resp. Huic argumento infra satisfaciemus. Resp. Huic argumento infra fatisfaciemus.


### Q. XVIII. What was the purity of the sensitive appetite in the first man?

The purity of the sensitive appetite was a perfection concreated in the first man, by which his appetite readily, and without struggle, subjected itself to the right judgment of the intellect and the holy command of the will, and gave no place to inordinate affections.

Obs. In the first man there was the most exact harmony and a wondrous consensus of the higher and lower powers. For reason obeyed the divine law, the will obeyed reason, the sensitive appetite obeyed the will, the affections obeyed the appetite, and the members of the body most readily obeyed the affections.

Proof. 1) From the dictation of the intellect and the governance of the will. Whoever possesses eminent wisdom and holiness governs his appetite in such a way that all affections conspire amicably with the dictation of the intellect and the governance of the will: But the integral man possessed eminent wisdom and holiness: Therefore. The major premise is self-evident and is corroborated from Wisd. 7:30 "Malice does not prevail against wisdom.

2) From the removal of the cause of shame. In an adult, wise, and holy man who covers his genital members with no clothing, there is no appetite rebellious to reason and will: But the first humans, etc. Therefore. AUGUSTINE confirms the major premise, lib. II. de Gen. ad lit. c. 1. "Why should they be ashamed, when they felt no law in their members repugnant to the law of their mind?

There was no movement in the body to which shame is due. They thought nothing needed to be covered, who felt nothing needed to be restrained." The minor premise is evident from Gen. 2:25 . 3) From the absurd. If the protoplast humans did not reflect the most pure and chaste God by the purity of their affections, they did not bear the image of God: they were not in a state of integrity, nor were they good creatures: nay, even God Himself would be the cause of sin. The latter are ἄλογα καὶ ἄτοπα (irrational and absurd). Therefore, the former. The consequence of the major is manifest: because man, subject to impure affections, is not conformable to the most pure and chaste God; but is difform: he does not live in a state of innocence, but of misery and corruption; for the struggle of appetite and reason is from original sin, Rom. 7:23 . Nor would God be most holy if He had sown in the first man a proneness to evil.

The antithesis is that of the Papists and Socinians, who attribute to the protoplast humans a concreated rebellion of the sensitive appetite against the judgment of right reason. Their principal arguments are: I. In whomever the sensitive appetite dominates reason, in him there is a rebellion of the flesh against reason: But the sensitive appetite dominated the reason of the protoplasts: Therefore, in them there was a rebellion of the flesh against reason. The major is certain; because it is the role of reason to command, and of appetite to obey; otherwise, the rebellion of the latter against the former arises. The minor is evident; because not only Eve, but also Adam succumbed to the depraved desire of eating of the fruit of the forbidden tree.

Resp. Distinguish between an appetite ἔσωθεν (from within), or one intrinsically inclining itself to sin, and one stimulated ἔξωθεν (from without), or extrinsically. There was no internal inclination to evil in the sensitive appetite of the protoplasts; however, they were stimulated extrinsically by the devil, to whom, having omitted a more accurate investigation, they succumbed [*].

II. Whoever has flesh subject to reason cannot sin: but the first parents sinned: Therefore. Resp. Whoever has flesh immutably subject to reason cannot sin; I concede. But Adam did not have flesh immutably subject to reason. Wherefore he was not absolutely impeccable, but was non-peccable. He sinned, however, because he abused his free will.

Instance I. If Adam sinned from a voluntary abuse of free will, the origin of sin can be imputed to God. R. God had indeed granted to the integral man the liberty of will for good and e- [*]

& evil, but He had equipped him with sufficiently strong powers to decline evil & to pursue good. Nor was the supernatural aid of the Holy Spirit lacking to him.

Objection II. Why did God not confer such a perfection, that he might be carried toward the good indeed freely, but immutably; just as the angels, confirmed in the good, serve God indeed freely, yet cling to Him inseparably, so that they cannot fall away from Him? Resp. It pleased the most wise God thus, that liberty in either direction might be available to man: in whose will and wisdom one must simply acquiesce. Probable reasons are brought forward: (a) that the spontaneous obedience of man might be established, (b) that God might confer rewards upon man, who obeys freely. Conf. D. CALOV. system. tom. IV. p. 707.

III. There was in the uncorrupted man a sensitive appetite, and a rational one: But the sensitive appetite desires a sensible good, i.e., one pleasing to the senses: The rational appetite desires an honest good: But sensible and honest good are often contrarily opposed. R. Sensible and honest good are not formally contrary, but disparate; which, that they may be decently reconciled, the reason of a wise man (such as Adam was in an excellent degree) dictates and commands. Indeed, there was in Adam a sensitive appetite, but not an appetite of ἀταξία. There was in him an appetite whole, not vitiated, not rebellious, not deformed, but subjected and conformed to reason, suffused with the light of concreated wisdom.

Latin:

Puritas appetitus sensitivi erat concreata primo homini perfectio, qua ipsius appetitus promte, & sine lucta, recto intellectus iudicio & sancto voluntatis imperio se subiiciebat, neque affectibus inordinatis locum dabat.

Obs. In primo homine erat exactissima harmonia, mirusque consensus virium superiorum & inferiorum. Nam legi divinae ratio, rationi voluntas, voluntati appetitus sensitivus, appetitui affectus, affectibus membra corporis promptissime obsequebantur.

Prob. 1) Ex dictamine intellectus & regimine voluntatis. Qui pollet eximia sapientia & sanctitate, is appetitum suum ita regit, ut affectus omnes cum dictamine intellectus & regimine voluntatis amice conspirent: At homo integer pollebat eximia sapientia & sanctitate: E Maior per se patet, & corroboratur ex Sap. 30. Sapientiae non praevalet malitia.

2) Ab remotione causae pudoris. Qui homo adultus, sapiens & sanctus, membra genitalia nullis indumentis velat, in illo non datur appetitus, rationi & voluntati rebellis: At primi homines &c. Ergo. Maiorem comprobat AVGVSTINVS lib. II. de Gen. ad lit. c. 1. Quid puderet illos, quando nullam legem senserunt in membris suis repugnantem legi mentis suae?

Nullus erat motus in corpore, cui verecundia debetur. Nihil putabant velandum, qui nihil senserunt refranandum. Minor patet e Gen. 5. 3) Ab absurdo. Si homines protoplasti non retulerunt puritate affectuum Deum purissimum & castissimum, non gesserunt imaginem Dei: non fuerunt in statu integritatis, nec bonae creaturae: quin ipse etiam Deus causa erit peccati. Posteriora sunt ἄλογα καὶ ἄτοπα. E & prius. Consequentia maioris est manifesta: quia homo, obnoxius impuris affectibus, Deo purissimo & castissimo non conformis; sed difformis est: non vivit in statu innocentiae, sed miseriae & corruptionis; nam lucta appetitus & rationis est a peccato originali, Rom. 23. Neque Deus sanctissimus foret, si primo homini pronitatem ad malum insevisset.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum & Socinianorum, tribuentium hominibus protoplastis concreatam rebellionem appetitus sensitivi aduersus rectae rationis iudicium. Quorum praecipua sunt argumenta: I. Cuiuscunque rationi dominatur appetitus sensitivus, in illo datur rebellio carnis adversus rationem: Atqui protoplastorum rationi dominabatur appetitus sensitivus: E. in illis dabatur rebellio carnis aduersus rationem. Maior constat; quia rationis est, imperare; appetitus, parere; ceteroqui rebellio huius aduersus illam exoritur. Minor patet; quia non Eua tantum, sed & Adamus succubuit prauae cupiditati comedendi de fructu arboris vetitae.

Resp. Dist. inter appetitum ἔσωθεν, seu intrinsece se inclinantem ad peccatum, & stimulatum ἔξωθεν, seu extrinsece. Nulla erat in appetitu sensitivo protoplastorum interna inclinatio ad malum, extrinsece autem stimulabantur a diabolo, cui, omissa accuratiori indagine, succumbebant [*].

II. Qui carnem rationi subiectam habet, is non potest peccare: at primi parentes peccarunt: Ergo. Resp. Quicunque carnem rationi immutabiliter subiectam habet, non potest peccare; concedo. Sed Adamus carnem rationi non immutabiliter subiectam habuit. Quare non absolute impeccabilis, sed non-peccabilis fuit. Peccauit autem, quia libero arbitrio abusus est.

Instantia I. Si Adamus peccauit ex voluntario liberi arbitrii abusu, origo peccati Deo imputari potest. R. Concesserat quidem Deus homini integro libertatem arbitrii ad bonum &

& malum, sed viribus satis validis eundem instruxerat ad declinandum malum & sectandum bonum. Neque supernaturale Spiritus S. auxilium ipsi deerat.

Instant. II. Cur Deus non contulit eiusmodi perfectionem, vt libere quidem, sed immutabiliter in bonum ferretur; vti angeli, in bono confirmati, libere quidem Deo seruiunt, indiuulse tamen ei adhærescunt, vt ab ipso deficere nequeant? Resp. Placuit ita Deo sapientissimo, vt homini suppeteret libertas in vtramque partem: cuius in voluntate & sapientia simpliciter acquiescendum est. Probabiles adducuntur rationes: (a) vt constaret spontaneum hominis obsequium, (b) vt Deus conferret præmia homini, libere obsequenti. Conf. D. CALOV. system. tom. IV. p. 707.

III. Fuit in homine integro appetitus sensitiuus, & rationalis: At appetitus sensitiuus appetit bonum sensibile, s. sensibus gratum: Appetitus rationalis appetit bonum honestum: At bonum sensibile, & honestum, sæpe contrarie opposita sunt. R. Bonum sensibile, & honestum, non sunt formaliter contraria, sed disparata; quæ, vt decenter concilientur, ratio hominis sapientis (qualis erat Adamus in gradu excellenti) dictat & imperat. Nimirum erat in Adamo appetitus sensitiuus, sed non appetitus ἀταξία. Erat in illo appetitus integer, non vitiatus, non rebellis, non difformis, sed subiectus & conformis rationi, luce concreatæ sapientiæ perfusæ.


### Question XIX. What were the less principal perfections, which God granted to the protoplast humans?

The less principal perfections, by which the image of God is completed, are the immunity of the body, uninfected by any stain of sin, from corruptive passions a), the immortality of the same b), and the full power of commanding sublunary creatures, especially beasts c). In which power of dominating, however, the image of God did not consist principally, much less solely d).

Proof a. Painful and destructive passions (such as the trouble of labors, pain in childbirth, diseases, exile, etc.) are punishments of sin, Gen. III, 16. sqq. Sir. XXXIIX, 15. For which reason the first man, immune from sin, was also devoid of bitter passion.

Proof b. 1) God threatened man with death under this condition, if he should sin, Gen. II, 17. Thence through sin death came into the world, Rom. V, 18. And death is the wages of sin, Rom. VI, 2. Therefore, with sin absent from the uncorrupted man, there was no danger from death. 2) The first man was created ἐπ᾽ ἀφθαρσίᾳ, in incorruptibility, Sap. I, 13. 3) The most efficacious preservative means of perennial life was the tree of life, Gen. II, 9. c. III, 22.

Proof c. 1) From the formal reason of the divine image, which consists in conformity with the majesty of God, the supreme lord.

2) From the assertion of holy scripture, Gen. I, 26. God said: Let us make man in our image, according to our likeness: and let him have dominion over the fish of the sea, and the bird of the sky, and the beast, and all the earth, and every reptile that creeps upon the earth. Obs. a) God granted to the first man dominion over sublunary things, extended through seas and lands, but not over the stars of the sky, except insofar as he converts their influence to his own utility. b) That dominion was not absolute and direct, but respective and useful, which denotes the inhabitation of the world, with the usufruct. 2) Dominion is taken either radically, for the right and power of dominating, or formally, for actual dominion. In the former sense, it is called a less principal part of the divine image; in the latter sense, it was an extrinsic accident, or an appendix of the image of God.

3) From the act of God, who brought all the animals of the earth to Adam, so that he might impose names upon them: by which very act Adam was inducted into the possession of that dominion which God had granted to him. Prob. d. The image of God is not solely, nor principally, completed by dominion. Not solely; because man does not please God by dominion alone, 1 Cor. I, 26. If the constitution of the essential divine image were completed by dominion alone, not only would poor Christians who have been renewed, but also Christ, in the state of humiliation, have been destitute of the divine image: on the contrary, the children of this world and the masters of things would be endowed with the divine image. Nor principally; because those perfections principally constitute the image of God, to which a justified man is renewed in this life, and with which he shone in eternal glory. But he is renewed to the knowledge of God, Col. III, 10, and true holiness and righteousness, Eph. IV, 24. And in eternal life the image of God will consist in the intuitive knowledge of God, 1 Io. III, 2, and in consummated righteousness, Ps. XVII, 15. Therefore these are the principal parts of the image of God.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, according to whose opinion the body of the whole man was immune neither from painful passions nor from the condition of mortality; on the contrary, the image of God consisted solely and principally in dominion. Who fortify their opinion with the following arguments: I. The body of Adam, in the state of integrity, was fleshy and soft, and therefore vulnerable and exposed to bitter passions. Resp. Although the body of Adam was not simply invulnerable; nevertheless, if he had persisted in the state of innocence, he would never have been wounded: for both the providence of God and the excellent wisdom of the whole man would have averted wounds. What? That in the state of integrity man would have been placed outside the danger of being wounded. For the beasts were subject to his full dominion, and man did not harm man even with a look. II. Adam labored, because he tilled the field, Gen. II, 15. Resp. The labor of Adam was sweet and pleasant, not harsh and troublesome. III. Whoever was dust from the first origin of creation, he was mortal: But Adam &c. Therefore. The major is evident; because God himself gives this cause of mortality, Gen. III, 19. Dust you are, and to dust you shall return. The minor is clear from Gen. II, 7. Resp. a) The cited words are to be understood concerning the state of nature destitute, not instituted. b) There was in the whole man a remote, not proximate, power of dying. The proximate power of dying in the fallen Adam arose from the obedience rendered to Eve. See Gen. III, 17. IV. Every earthly and animal body is corruptible: The body of the whole Adam was earthly: Therefore. The major is evident from 1 Cor. XV, 47. Resp. a) In the cited place the image of the fallen Adam is understood, not the whole one. b) An earthly body in the loc. cit. is opposed not to a mortal one, but to a heavenly one, just as an animal one is opposed to a spiritual one, and therefore in the mind of Paul it is earthly and animal, which, being affected by earthly qualities, is in need of food and drink: on the contrary, a heavenly and spiritual body is that which, adorned with heavenly and spiritual qualities, has no need of food and drink, digestion, refreshment, &c. See CALOV. in bibl. illustr. in h. l. fol. 408. V. The immortal cannot procreate: Man before the fall could procreate. Therefore. The major is clear from Luc. XX, 35. Resp. The immortal cannot procreate in a spiritual or glorified body: but the body of Adam was natural. VI. Christ took away all the punishments of sin: He did not take away death: Therefore death is not a punishment of sin. Resp. distinguish between eternal and temporal punishments. Christ took away eternal punishments: he changed temporal ones into paternal chastisements, and especially death into sleep and a way to eternal life. Concerning dominion over creatures, the Socinians object I. God himself described the divine image through dominion over creatures, Gen. I, 26. Therefore the image of God consisted solely and principally in dominion.

Resp. We distinguish between the inclusive and exclusive sense. God does not say that the divine image consisted only in dominion over creatures. Certainly, dominion presupposes wisdom. For it is the way of fools to serve, not to command.

II. Nothing is more excellent in God than the dominion over all things: Therefore, the image of God consisted principally in that. Resp. We deny the antecedent; because God's actual dominion began with the creatures, whereas His wisdom and justice are eternal.

III. In the other world, our principal glory will be dominion over the devil and hell: Therefore, in this world, before the fall, the principal part of the divine image was dominion. Resp. The image of God before the fall did not consist in dominion over the devil, but over the beasts. Moreover, the principal glory of the blessed man in the other world will be the beatific vision and enjoyment of God.

Latin:

Perfectiones minus principales, quibus imago Dei absoluitur, sunt corporis, nulla peccati labe infecti, immunitas a passionibus corruptiuis a), eiusdem immortalitas b), & plena imperandi creaturis sublunarious, in primis bestiis, potestas c). In qua tamen potestate dominandi non principaliter, nedum vnice, imago Dei constitit d).

Prob. a. Passiones dolorificæ & destructiuæ (quales sunt molestia laborum, dolor in partu, morbi, exsilium &c.) sunt pœnæ peccati, Gen. III, 16. sqq. Sir. XXXIIX, 15. Quam ob rem homo primus, peccati immunis, etiam passionis acerbæ expers fuit.

Prob. b. 1) Deus homini sub hac conditione, si peccaret, mortem interminatus est, Gen. II, 17. Exinde per peccatum mors venit in mundum, Rom. V, 18. Estque mors stipendium peccati, Rom. VI, 2. Ergo, absente peccato ab homine integro, nullum a morte fuit periculum. 2) Primus homo conditus erat ἐπ᾽ ἀφθαρσίᾳ, in incorruptibilitate, Sap. I, 13. 3) Efficacissimum perennis vitæ medium conseruatiuum erat arbor vitæ, Gen. II, 9. c. III, 22.

Prob. c. 1) Ex formali ratione imaginis diuinæ, quæ consistit in conformitate cum maiestate Dei, summi domini.

2) Ex assertione sacræ scripturæ, Gen. I, 26. Dixit Deus: Faciamus hominem in imagine nostra, secundum similitudinem nostram: & dominetur in piscem maris, & in auiem cæli, & in bestiam, & in omnem terram, & in omne reptile, quod repit super terram. Obs. a) Concessit Deus homini primo dominium in res sublunares, extensum per maria & terras, non autem per sidera cæli, nisi quatenus horum influxum in suam vtilitatem conuertit. b) Dominium illud non fuit absolutum & directum, sed respectiuum & vtile, quod denotat incolatum orbis, cum vsu fructu. 2) Dominium accipitur vel radicaliter, pro iure & potestate dominandi, vel formaliter, pro actuali dominio. Priori sensu, pars minus principalis imaginis diuinæ dicitur; posteriori sensu, accidens extrinsecum, aut appendix imaginis Dei fuit.

3) Ex facto Dei, qui vniuersa terræ animalia ad Adamum adduxit, vt illis nomina imponeret: quo ipso Adamus in possessionem illius dominii, quod ipsi Deus concesserat, immissus est. Prob. d. Imago Dei nec vnice, nec præcipue absoluitur dominio. Non vnice; quia solo dominio homo Deo non placet, 1 Cor. I, 26. Si solo dominio essentialis imaginis diuinæ constitutio absolueretur, non solum pauperes christiani renouati, sed & Christus, in statu exinanitionis, imagine diuina destitutus fuisset: contra, filii huius sæculi & rerum domini, imagine diuina præditi essent. Nec præcipue; quia illæ perfectiones principaliter imaginem Dei constituunt, ad quas homo iustificatus renouatur in hac vita, & quibus refulgebat in æterna gloria. At renouatur ad cognitionem Dei, Col. III, 10. & veram sanctitatem & iustitiam. Eph. IV, 24. Et in vita æterna imago Dei consistet in intuitiua Dei cognitione, 1 Io. III, 2. & in consummata iustitia, Ps. XVII, 15. Ergo hæ sunt partes principales imaginis Dei.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, quorum de sententia corpus hominis integri nec a passionibus dolorofis, nec a mortalitatis conditione immune fuit; contra, imago Dei in dominio vnice præcipue constitit. Qui suam opinionem sequentibus muniunt argumentis: I. Corpus Adami, in statu integritatis, fuit carneum & molle, adeoque vulnerabile & acerbis passionibus expositum. Resp. Quamuis corpus Adami non simpliciter fuerit inuulnerabile; attamen, si in statu innocentiæ perstitisset, nunquam fuisset vulneratum: quippe vulnera tum prouidentia Dei, tum excellens sapientia hominis integri auertisset. Quid? quod in statu integritatis homo extra periculum vulnerationis positus fuisset. Nam bestiæ pleno ipsius dominio subiacebant, & homo hominem ne vultu quidem lædebat. II. Adam laborauit, quia coluit agrum, Gen. II, 15. Resp. Labor Adami suauis & iucundus, non asper & molestus fuit. III. Quicunque fuit puluis a prima creationis origine, is fuit mortalis: Atqui Adamus &c. Ergo. Maior constat; quia Deus ipse hanc mortalitatis caussam reddit, Gen. III, 19. Puluis es, & in puluerem reuerteris. Minor patet e Gen. II, 7. Resp. a) Verba citata intelligenda sunt de statu naturæ destitutæ, non institutæ. b) Erat in homine integro potentia moriendi remota, non proxima. Proxima moriendi potentia in Adamo lapso oriebatur ex obsequio Euæ præstito. Vid. Gen. III, 17. IV. Omne corpus terrenum & animale est corruptibile: Corpus Adami integri fuit terrenum: Ergo. Maior constat ex 1 Cor. XV, 47. Resp. a) Loco citato intelligitur imago Adami lapsi, non integri. b) Corpus terrenum l. c. non mortali, sed cælesti, sicut animale spirituali opponitur, adeoque ex mente Paulli terrenum & animale est, quod terrenis qualitatibus affectum, cibo & potu indiget: contra, corpus cæleste & spirituale est, quod qualitatibus cælestibus & spiritualibus exornatum cibo & potu, concoctione, refectione, &c. opus non habet. Vid. CALOV. in bibl. illustr. in h. l. fol. 408. V. Immortales non possunt generare: Homo ante lapsum poterat generare. Ergo. Maior liquet ex Luc. XX, 35. Resp. Immortales non possunt generare in corpore spirituali seu glorificato: at corpus Adami erat naturale. VI. Omnes pœnas peccati Christus sustulit: Mortem non sustulit: Ergo mors non est pœna peccati. Resp. dist. inter pœnas æternas & temporales. Pœnas æternas Christus sustulit: temporales in castigationes paternas, & inprimis mortem in somnum & viam ad vitam æternam mutauit. De dominio in creaturas obiiciunt Sociniani I. Deus ipse imaginem diuinam per dominium in creaturas descripsit, Gen. I, 26. Ergo imago Dei vnice & præcipue in dominio constitit.

Resp. dist. inter sensum inclusivum & exclusivum. Deus non dicit, quod imago divina tantum constiterit in dominio in creaturas. Certe dominium sapientiam præsupponit. Stultorum enim est, servire, non imperare.

II. Nihil præstantius est in Deo, dominatu cunctarum rerum: E. Imago Dei in illo principaliter constitit. Resp. Neg. antecedens; quia actuale Dei dominium cœpit cum creaturis, sapientia autem & iustitia eius est æterna.

III. In altero sæculo principalis nostra erit gloria, dominium in diabolum & infernum: Ergo in hoc sæculo, ante lapsum, principalis imaginis divinæ pars dominium. Resp. Consistebat imago Dei ante lapsum non in dominio in diabolum, sed in bestias. Principalis autem hominis beati gloria in altero sæculo erit visio & fruitio Dei beatifica.


### Quæst. XX

Was the image of God a natural perfection of the first man, or a supernatural gift? The image of God did not indeed constitute the nature of the first man by way of an essential part, nor did it emanate from his nature per se and necessarily, as an inseparable property ; nevertheless, it was natural to the first man, because it began to exist with the very nature of man through creation; and thus it was both due to him and most deeply implanted in him, just as it intimately perfected the nature of the whole man for the attainment of his end, and could be propagated to descendants through natural generation .

Obj. Something is called natural 1) constitutively, which constitutes the nature of a thing as a part. Thus, the essential parts, body and soul, are called natural to man. 2) Consecutively, which flows essentially from the form, like the faculties of the soul. 3) Principatively, which begins to exist simultaneously with the nature itself through creation or the institution of nature. 4) Subjectively, which is most deeply implanted in nature as in a subject. 5) Perfectively, which intimately perfects and adorns nature. 6) Transitively, which is propagated to descendants with the nature itself through natural generation.

Prob. a. The image of God was not natural to the first man constitutively, nor consecutively; because it was neither a part of man, nor a proper faculty of the human soul: for it would follow that man after the fall was destitute of some essential part, or some faculty of the soul, which is absurd.

Prob. b. 1) Whatever was concreated with the first man was natural to him: But the image of God, etc. Therefore. The major is evident: because the natural attributes of the first man must be judged from the first creation of the human creature; just as we call that natural to other animals which is concreated with them. The minor is clear from the divine intention and decree, Gen. I, 26. "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness." To which the execution corresponds in v. 27. "So God created man in his own image." Therefore, the whole man was endowed with the image of God at the first moment of his existence.

2) From the goodness and moral rectitude befitting human nature. For God created man very good, Gen. I, 31. And made him upright, Eccl. VII, 29. Whoever is created by God as very good and upright, to his nature belongs a befitting or due goodness and moral rectitude. But the first man, etc. Therefore. The major is evident; because that perfection is called connatural, or due to nature, which has the same origin as man: on the contrary, that is supernatural which does not reside in nature from its first origin, but is superadded by God, out of special grace, to supply for its imperfection.

3) From the natural end of man. Man was created for the sake of God, that he might acknowledge Him, celebrate Him once acknowledged, and become a participant in eternal blessedness. BONAVENT. 2. dist. 19. art. 1. quæst. 1 teaches this. It is so true and certain that man was made to participate in supreme blessedness, that no one doubts it, unless his reason is entirely subverted. We argue: To whom eternal blessedness was natural, to him also the image of God was natural: But to the first man &c. Therefore. The major shines with its own light; because to him who is destined for an end proportionate to his nature, natural means, or natural powers for obtaining that end, are conferred by God: otherwise man would have been worse off than the brutes, which are equipped with the necessary means for attaining their end.

4) From natural propagation. Whatever can be propagated to descendants through generation is natural: But the image of God &c. Therefore. The major is evident; because not supernatural gifts, but natural perfections are propagated to descendants through generation. The minor is proven: Just as Adam after the fall is said to have begotten a son in his own image and likeness, Gen. V, 3, whence all his descendants are said to be children of wrath by nature, Eph. II, 3: So, if Adam had persisted in the state of integrity, he would certainly have begotten a son according to the image of God, and all his descendants would by nature have been beloved children of God.

5) From a parity. The truth of wisdom and justice was connatural to the angels, Jo. VIII, 44. Therefore also to the first man. For no suitable reason can be given why holiness should be natural to angels, but supernatural to the first man.

6) From the contrary. If original sin is natural to man after the fall, the image of God was natural to man before the fall: The antecedent is true: see Eph. II, 3. Therefore also the consequent. The reason for the consequence is: because contraries do not differ in their entire genus.

7) From the relics of the divine image. The relics of the divine image are natural. Therefore also the image of God in the first man was a natural perfection. The consequence is proven; because, when the whole and the part are homogeneous, then the nature of the whole and the part is the same. The antecedent is clear: because the relics of the divine image are the light of truth and the seed of goodness, or innate notions and stimuli of virtues, which are natural to man. For the apostle brings forward that the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature the things that are of the law. Rom. II, 14.

8) That immortality was natural to the first man is proven a), because man was created for incorruption, Wis. II, 23. Everything co-created is natural. b) By the envy of the devil death entered the world, Wis. II, 24. Therefore it is not a condition of the nature created by God. c) Death is the punishment of sin and destroys nature. Therefore immortality, which is opposed to death, was connatural to integral man, or suitable to his very nature. d) To him who is not to be killed, immortality is due to his nature. But no man &c. Therefore. The minor is established from Gen. IX, 6. Whoever shall shed the blood of man (whether it be beast or man) by man (the legitimate avenger) let his blood be shed: because in the image of God He (God) made man. The nerve of the argument consists in this: To whose nature immortality, a significant part of the image of God, is due, to him death is not to be inflicted: But to man's nature immortality, a significant part of the image of God, is due: Therefore death is not to be inflicted upon man. e) The immortality of the first man could be preserved through a natural medium, namely the eating of the tree of life, Gen. II, 9. c. III, 22. Therefore immortality was natural to the first man. f) The soul naturally desires to be united to the body. Therefore the conjunction of the soul with the body is natural to man: but death, which is the dissolution of soul and body, is preternatural to man.

The Antithesis is that of most Papists, who assert that the image of God was a supernatural gift, added to man to supply his connatural imperfection: just as iron or a garment outwardly adorns man, and a bridle curbs the horse. But just as, subla- The Antithesis is that of most Papists, who assert that the image of God was a supernatural gift, added to man to supply his connatural imperfection: just as iron or a garment outwardly adorns man, and a bridle curbs the horse. But just as, With the garment and bridle removed, the nature of man and horse remains uncorrupted: thus, the same people opine that, through the fall, the image of God having been removed, the nature of man was not corrupted, but remained intact.

Latin:

Fuitne imago Dei perfectio primi hominis naturalis, an donum supernaturale? Imago Dei, non quidem naturam primi hominis per modum partis essentialis constituit, neque ex natura eiusdem per se & necessario, velut proprium inseparabile, emanauit a); attamen primo homini naturalis fuit, quia per creationem cum ipsa hominis natura esse cœpit; adeoque ipsi tum debita, tum penitissime infixa fuit, iuxta atque naturam hominis integri ad obtinendum finem ipsius, intime perfecit, & per naturalem generationem ad posteros propagari potuit b).

Obs. Naturale aliquid dicitur 1) constitutive, quod tanquam pars naturam rei constituit. Ita naturales homini dicuntur partes essentiales corpus & anima. 2) Consecutive, quod a forma, instar animæ facultatum, essentialiter fluit. 3) Principative, quod simul cum ipsa natura per creationem sive naturæ institutionem, esse incipit. 4) Subiective, quod naturæ, tanquam subiecto, penitissime est infixum. 5) Perfective, quod naturam intime perficit & exornat. 6) Transitive, quod per naturalem generationem cum ipsa natura ad posteros propagatur.

Prob. a. Non fuit imago Dei primo homini naturalis constitutive, neque consecutive; quia neque pars hominis, neque facultas animæ humanæ propria fuit: sequeretur enim, hominem post lapsum destitui aliqua parte essentiali, aut facultate quadam animæ, quod est absurdum.

Prob. b. 1) Quidquid homini primo est concreatum, illud ipsi fuit naturale: Atqui imago Dei &c. Ergo. Maior constat: quia naturalia primi hominis diiudicanda sunt ex prima creatione humanæ creaturæ; sicut reliquis animalibus id naturale dicimus, quod ipsis concreatum est. Minor patet ex intentione & decreto divino, Gen. I, 26. Faciamus hominem in imagine nostra secundum similitudinem nostram. Cui respondet exsecutio v. 27. Creauit itaque Deus hominem in imagine sua. Ergo homo integer in primo exsistentiæ momento imagine Dei præditus fuit.

2) A bonitate & rectitudine morali naturæ humanæ conveniente. Creauit enim Deus hominem valde bonum, Gen. I, 31. Et fecit eum rectum, Eccl. VII, 29. Quicunque a Deo valde bonus & rectus est conditus, illius naturæ conveniens vel debita est bonitas & rectitudo moralis. Atqui homo primus &c. Ergo. Maior constat; quia illa perfectio dicitur connaturalis, vel debita naturæ, quæ eundem cum homine habet ortum: contra, supernaturale est, quod non inest naturæ a prima ipsius origine, sed ad imperfectionem eius supplendam a Deo, ex speciali gratia, superadditur.

3) A fine naturali hominis. Conditus est homo propter Deum, vt illum agnosceret, agnitum celebraret, & æternæ beatitudinis particeps fieret. Docet hoc BONAVENT. 2. dist. 19. art. 1. quæst. 1. Adeo verum & certum est, hominem esse factum ad participandam summam beatitudinem, vt nullus de eo dubitet, nisi cuius ratio omnino est subuersa. Argumentamur: Cui æterna beatitudo fuit naturalis, illi etiam imago Dei fuit naturalis: Atqui primo homini &c. Ergo. Maior sua radiat luce; quia qui destinatur ad finem naturæ proportionatum, illi media naturalia, seu vires naturales ad finem illum obtinendum a Deo conferuntur: alias deterior fuisset homo brutis, quæ necessariis ad finem suum adipiscendum mediis sunt instructa.

4) A naturali propagatione. Quidquid per generationem ad posteros propagari potest, illud est naturale: Atqui imago Dei &c. Ergo. Maior patet; quia non dona supernaturalia, sed perfectiones naturales per generationem ad posteros propagantur. Minor probatur: Sicut Adamus post lapsum dicitur genuisse filium ad imaginem & similitudinem suam, Gen. V, 3. vnde omnes eius posteri dicuntur filii iræ natura, Eph. II, 3: Ita, si Adamus in flatu integritatis perstitisset, vtique genuisset filium secundum imaginem Dei, & omnes eius posteri natura fuissent filii Dei dilecti.

5) A pari. Angelis connaturalis fuit veritas sapientiæ & iustitiæ, Jo. VIII, 44. Ergo & primo homini. Neque enim idonea dari potest ratio, cur sanctitas angelis naturalis, homini primo supernaturalis sit.

6) A contrario. Si peccatum originale post lapsum homini est naturale, ante lapsum imago Dei homini fuit naturalis: Antecedens est verum: vid. Eph. II, 3. Ergo & consequens. Ratio consequentiæ est: quia contraria toto genere non differunt.

7) A reliquiis imaginis diuinæ. Reliquiæ imaginis diuinæ sunt naturales. Ergo & imago Dei in primo homine perfectio naturalis fuit. Consequentia probatur; quia, quando totum & pars sunt homogenea, tunc eadem est natura totius & partis. Antecedens patet: quia reliquiæ imaginis diuinæ sunt lumen veri & semen boni, seu notitiæ innatæ & stimuli virtutum, qui homini sunt naturales. Affert enim apostolus, gentes, quæ legem non habent, natura ea, quæ legis sunt, facere. Rom. II, 14.

8) Immortalitatem primo homini fuisse naturalem, probatur a), quia homo ἐπ' ἀφθαρσίᾳ conditus est, Sap. II, 23. Omne concreatum naturale est. b) Inuidia diaboli mors inuressa est mundum, Sap. II, 24. Ergo non est naturæ a Deo creatæ conditio. c) Mors est pœna peccati & naturam destruit. Ergo morti opposita immortalitas homini integro fuit connaturalis, seu ipsius naturæ conueniens. d) Qui non occidendus est, illius naturæ debita est immortalitas. Atqui nullus homo &c. Ergo. Minor constat e Gen. IX, 6. Quisquis effuderit sanguinem hominis (siue bestia, siue homo fuerit) per hominem (vindicem legitimum) sanguis eius effundatur: quia in imagine Dei fecit hominem (Deus). Neruus collectionis in hoc consistit: Cuius naturæ immortalitas insignis pars imaginis Dei est debita, illi mors non est inferenda: Atqui hominis naturæ immortalitas insignis pars imaginis Dei est debita: Ergo homini mors non est inferenda. e) Immortalitas primi hominis per medium naturale, nempe esum arboris vitæ, potuit conseruari, Gen. II, 9. c. III, 22. Ergo immortalitas primo homini fuit naturalis. f) Anima naturaliter appetit corpori vniri. Ergo coniunctio animæ cum corpore homini est naturalis: mors autem, quæ est dissolutio animæ & corporis, homini præternaturalis est.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum plerorumque, statuentium, imaginem Dei fuisse donum supernaturale, ad supplendam connaturalem imperfectionem homini superadditum: sicut ferrum aut vestimentum extrinsece ornat hominem, frenum compescit equum. Sicut autem, sublaest. Antithesis est Pontificiorum plerorumque, statuentium, imaginem Dei fuisse donum supernaturale, ad supplendam connaturalem imperfectionem homini superadditum: sicut ferrum aut vestimentum extrinsecè ornat hominem, frenum compescit equum. Sicut autem, sublato vestimento & freno, natura hominis & equi manet incorrupta: ita iidem opinantur, per lapsum summota imagine Dei naturam hominis non esse corruptam, sed mansisse integram.


### Quæst. XX: Their stronger arguments are: I

Their stronger arguments are: I.

Whatever is natural to man is inseparable from him: The justice of the first man was not inseparable from him: Therefore. The major premise is evident: because, with the natural removed, nature itself is overturned. Resp. Whatever is a constitutive natural to man is inseparable from him: I concede. But the image of God neither constituted the nature of the first man, nor did it necessarily flow from his essence: it was, however, natural, on account of natural convenience, adhesion, perfection, and propagation.

Instance I. A natural constitutive and consecutive exhausts the whole breadth of the natural. Resp. Not everything that is natural is a constitutive part or an inseparable property.

For there are given idiosyncrasies, or singular temperaments, and those are natural: e.g., there are those who can neither bear a cat nor eat cheese. There is given a natural impulse of parents toward children, a natural impulse or stimulus toward virtue, and that is greater in one, smaller in another.

From which some men are said to be strong by nature, just by nature, as witnessed by ARISTOTLE, Book 6 of the Nicomachean Ethics, chapter 13. There is given the natural sagacity of certain dogs.

Instance II. Natural things remain intact, to which the image of God as a supernatural gift was superadded.

Resp. Natural things do indeed remain, but not intact, not pure. Certainly, an intellect blind and filled with errors is not intact; a perverse will is not intact; an inordinate appetite is not intact or pure.

II. Such as the image is now restored, such it was lost. But a supernatural image of God is now being restored. Therefore. The consequence of the major is manifest; because one must judge the nature of the concreated image from the nature of the divine image being restored.

Resp. I deny the major. For the image of God which was connatural to an intact nature is rightly called supernatural when restored in a corrupt nature. Indeed, the image of God was concreated with an intact nature, but it is superadded to a corrupt nature by special grace, obtained by the merit of Christ. In the intact man, the image of God was perfect: in the reborn man, it is repaired imperfectly, with the original stain remaining.

The image of God was propagable to descendants along with an intact nature: but after the fall, it is not derived to descendants through generation.

Instance: The evangelical doctors themselves argue from the restored image of God to the concreated one. For Dr. GERHARD writes clearly in his isagogic disputation, p. 791. The formal aspect of the divine image shines forth from the renewal, through which we are reformed to the image of God. The reason is: because through renewal that which was lost in the first man is restored. Therefore, from the nature of that which is restored to us through renewal, one can judge the nature of that which we received and lost in Adam.

Resp. The evangelical doctors, judging the nature of the concreated image from the nature of the restored image, look to the formal perfections flowing into the essence of the divine image: But the distinction between the natural image in the state of innocence and the supernatural one in the state of misery is accidental, arising remotely from sin, and proximately from the merit of Christ.

For, since the image of God has the same origin as an intact nature; but original sin is born with a corrupt nature, to which, for the sake of restraining it by the power of Christ's merit, the image of God is superadded by the benefit of regeneration and renewal. III. Whatever was conferred upon the first man to restrain the sensitive appetite was an extrinsic and supernatural gift: But the image of God, etc.

Therefore. The major is clear; because supernatural gifts are conferred to amend natural things, which incline toward evil. The minor is evident; because the sensitive appetite of the first man needed no bridle, for the reason that it was not ferocious, stubborn, incontinent, [but subject] to right reason. un-minor-born; but he was upright, well-composed, refined, and most promptly obedient to reason without any struggle: such an appetite as has a place in the human nature of Christ.

Instantia I. The sensitive appetite in the state of integrity tended toward the sensible good, which often differs from the spiritual good by an immense amount. Resp. The sensible and spiritual good, with respect to the first man, were indeed disparate, but not contrary, but subordinated.

Instantia II. No cause of the first man's fall can be given other than the removal of the supernatural gift, which restrained the appetite of man as a bridle. Resp. The cause of the fall was both the seduction of the devil and the abuse of the co-created free will.

IV. Whatever adorned man by way of a crown, which can easily be taken off, that is not natural to man: But the image of God, etc. E. The major is evident: because a crown does not pertain to the nature of man; for when it is removed, nature remains safe. The minor is proved, and Ps. VIII, 6. Thou hast crowned him with glory and honor. Resp. Ps. VIII treats of Christ, which the citation of the apostle, Heb. II, 9, teaches beyond the context.

V. Whatever is compared to a garment, that was something supernatural and extrinsic: But the image of God, etc. E. The major is clear: because a garment is not of the nature of man. The minor is proved from Sir. c. XVII, 1. 3. The Lord created man from the earth according to himself, he clothed them with strength, and made them according to his own image: Resp. 1) The word to clothe is metaphorical, and often denotes that which is connatural. Thus Job says that he was clothed by God with flesh and skin, c. X, 11. God is said to clothe the lilies of the field, whose beauty is natural, Matt. V, 30. 2) In the source we read ἐνέδυσεν αὐτὲς ἰσχὺν he clothed them with strength, i.e., God instructed men with valid powers of intellect and body for accomplishing tasks.

VI. Whatever man receives immediately from God by grace, that was not natural to him: But the first man received the image of God immediately by grace. Therefore. Resp. Distinguish between the general grace of creation and the special grace of regeneration. The first man received the image of God through the general grace of creation, just as he obtained his soul, body, and natural members from God: through the special grace of regeneration and renewal, the image is repaired after the fall.

VII. The origin of justice is not from the principles of nature, but from God: Therefore justice was not natural to the first man. The reason for the consequence is; because whatever does not flow from the principles of nature, but is received immediately from God, is a supernatural gift. Resp. 1) The first man received his rational soul not from the principles of nature, but immediately from God: which nevertheless was a natural part of the first man. 2) If you look at the origin of justice, it was indeed a gift of God; but in its inner natural convenience and inhesion, it was a perfection due to integral nature, and most deeply impressed upon it for obtaining the end proportioned to nature.

VIII. By actual sin, natural gifts are not lost, but supernatural and spiritual ones: But the sin of Adam was actual: Therefore. The major is evident; because by sin the gracious indwelling of God is indeed lost, but no natural gift. Resp. 1) Even by actual sin, natural gifts can be lost or destroyed. Thus the vigor of the body and the happiness of memory are lost through drunkenness and fornication. Through homicide, the natural union of body and soul is dissolved. 2) The transgression of Adam is not to be estimated from the actual sins of other men; for it is far graver and more atrocious than those. For it is not only personal or individual, but also in a certain respect common and universal, a) by reason of imputation; because the sin of Adam, who was the stock and head of the whole human race, is imputed to all men: b) by reason of transgression; because in the sin of Adam all the precepts of the decalogue were violated: c) by reason of propagation; because original sin, which from the transgression

Adam initially flowed, and was derived to all the descendants of Adam. To this is added, that Adam was fortified with such safeguards, that he could easily decline sin, since he was not provoked by any internal incentive of sin.

IX. The natural image of God is the natural Son of God: Man in his integrity was not the natural Son of God. Therefore. Resp. 1) We do not assert that the first man was the natural image of God, but that the divine image was concreated in him, owed to, or suitable for, his integral nature. 2) He is called the natural Son of God for two reasons: a) because he was begotten from eternity from the essence of the Father; in which sense only Christ is the natural Son of God: b) because he reflects the most wise and most holy God by his connatural wisdom and holiness; in which sense the first man can be called a natural son of God. D. DANNHAVER says shrewdly, hodom. I. phant. V. pag. 1004. The first man was not the son of God naturally, i.e., substantially (which axiom belongs only to the λόγος); just as he was not the substantial image of God: yet he was a son of God by nature and with nature, to whom this dignity was concreated.

X. Whatever body consists of four elements and qualities contrary among themselves, that is by nature mortal: But the body of Adam consisted of such, etc. Therefore. The major premise is evident: because a body, mixed from elements, naturally tends toward destruction on account of the qualities contrary among themselves. Resp. 1) Gold is a body mixed from four elements, and yet it is in a certain way incorruptible (ἄφθαρτον). The moon is not devoid of mixture, yet it is superior to corruption. The body of Christ consists of four elements, and yet it is not by nature mortal. 2) One must judge the nature of a composite not only from the condition of the matter, but also a) from the connection, or union of the form with the matter. Namely, the holy soul of Adam, always adhering to God, the fountain of life, in the state of integrity, was joined to the body by a bond not dissoluble, except through sin. BONAVENTURE says not badly, Lib. II. Dist. XIX. artic. III. qu. 1. Death could not be in man, unless nature were disordered. If the disordering of human nature introduced death, the immortality of human nature is owed in the ordinary course. b) One must look to the goodness of the temperament, which Adam had obtained most perfectly; the harmony of qualities conspiring in a friendly way, and not tending toward destruction; and the absence, or lack of the causes of death, such as hunger, thirst, old age, fatigue of the body, diseases; to which the first man was not at all subject, and therefore his nature was not mortal.

XI. He for whom the tree of life was destined, to repair fallen powers, he was not by nature immortal: But for the first man, etc. Therefore. The major premise is evident: because fallen powers incline toward destruction; which if it is divinely averted by some external means; the immortality divinely conferred is not natural, but supernatural. Resp. a) Adam needed the tree of life, not to repair fallen powers, but to preserve them whole. b) The powers of Adam were to be preserved by the fruit of the tree of life, because the immortality of Adam was not absolute, but ordained. c) We invert the argument: He whose immortality depends on food and a natural means, he is naturally immortal.

XII. Whoever is by nature immortal, he cannot die: The first man could die. Therefore. Resp. Absolute immortality belongs to God: That which flows from the simplicity of nature belongs to angels, and human souls: That which depends on the grace of glorification belongs to the blessed: but it was concreated in the first man as ordained, because it was to be continued by certain means, and it was a hypothetical immortality; because the body of the first man was to remain not mortal as long as he did not sin. Moreover, when we say that man in his integrity was immortal, we do not deny the remote potentiality of dying; for if he had been immune from this, he would not have died after the fall; but we deny the proximate potentiality, arising from internal causes of death, namely diseases, the consumption of innate heat and radical moisture, etc. From which some theologians prefer to call the first man not mor

mortal, than immortal. See D. SCHERZER in colleg. Anti-Socinian. p. 278. For in the state of innocence man could not die, in the state of glory he cannot die, in the state of misery he cannot but die.

XIII. Everything generable is corruptible: The body of Adam was generable: Therefore. Resp. I deny the major. For the soul also is generable, and yet it is not corruptible.

XIV. An immortal does not use food, 1 Cor. 13. Adam used food. Resp. An immortal in the state of glory, with the belly and food destroyed, does not use food. The first man was not in the state of glory, but in the state of innocence, whose ordained immortality was sustained by food.

Latin:

Quorum potiora argumenta sunt: I.

Quidquid homini est naturale, ab eo est inseparabile: Justitia primi hominis ab ipso non fuit inseparabilis: Ergo. Maior est evidens: quia, sublato naturali, ipsa evertitur natura. Resp. Quidquid homini constitutiva naturale est, ab ipso inseparabile est: concedo. At imago Dei neque naturam primi hominis constituit, neque ex essentia eiusdem necessario fluxit: fuit tamen naturalis, ob naturalem convenientiam, inhaesionem, perfectionem, & propagationem.

Instantia I. Naturale constitutivum, & consecutivum exhaurit totam naturalis latitudinem. Resp. Non omne, quod naturale est, pars constitutiva, aut proprietas inseparabilis est.

Dantur enim ἰδιοσυγκρασίαι, sive temperamenta singularia, eaque naturalia: v. gr. sunt, qui neque felem ferre, neque caseum comedere possunt. Datur naturalis ὁρμὴ parentum in liberos, naturalis ὁρμὴ, sive stimulus ad virtutem, isque in uno maior, in altero minor.

Ex quo nonnulli homines natura fortes, natura iusti dicuntur, teste ARISTOTELE L. 6. Nicomach. cap. 13. Datur naturalis quorundam canum sagacitas.

Instantia II. Manferunt naturalia integra, quibus imago Dei vt donum supernaturale fuit superadditum.

Resp. Manferunt quidem naturalia, sed non integra, non pura. Sane intellectus caecus, & erroribus oppletus, non est integer, voluntas perversa non est integra, appetitus inordinatus non est integer, aut purus.

II. Qualis imago nunc restauratur, talis est deperdita. Sed supernaturalis imago Dei nunc instauratur. E. Consequentia maioris est manifesta; quia ex natura imaginis divinae instaurandae iudicandum est de natura imaginis concreatae.

Resp. Neg. maior. Nam, quae imago Dei naturae integrae fuit connaturalis, eadem instaurata in natura corrupta recte dicitur supernaturalis. Naturae quippe integrae imago Dei fuit concreata, naturae autem corruptae ex speciali gratia, merito Christi parta, superadditur. In homine integro imago Dei fuit perfecte: in homine renato reparatur imperfecte, remanente lue originali.

Imago Dei cum natura integra ad posteros fuit propagabilis: at post lapsum per generationem in posteros non derivatur.

Instantia: Ipsi doctores evangelici ab instaurata imagine Dei ad concreatam argumentantur. Diferte enim scribit D. GERHARD. in disp. isagog. p. 791. Formale divinae imaginis ex renovatione, per quam ad imaginem Dei reformamur, elucefcit. Ratio est: quia per renovationem restituitur id, quod in primo homine fuit amissum. Proinde ex natura illius, quod per renovationem nobis restituitur, iudicari potest de natura eius, quod in Adamo accepimus & amisimus.

Resp. Doctores evangelici, de natura imaginis concreatae iudicantes ex natura imaginis instauratae, respiciunt perfectiones formales, essentiam imaginis divinae confluentes: At discrimen inter imaginem naturalem in statu innocentiae & supernaturalem in statu miseriae est accidentale, ortum remote ex peccato, proxime ex merito Christi.
