Nam, cum natura integra imago Dei eundem habet ortum; naturae autem corruptae connascitur peccatum originale, ad quod refrenandum vi meriti Christi imago Dei beneficio regenerationis & renovationis superadditur. III. Quidquid primo homini collatum est ad refrenandum appetitum sensitivum, id fuit donum extrinsecum & supernaturale: Atqui imago Dei &c.

E. Maior patet; quia dona supernaturalia conferuntur ad emendandum naturalia, quae in malum propendent. Minor liquet; quia appetitus sensitivus primi hominis nullo freno indigebat, eo, quod non ferox, continuax, incontinens, rectae rationi unimminorigenus erat; sed erat rectus, bene compositus, defaecatus, & rationi sine ulla lucta promptissime obediens: qualis appetitus in humana Christi natura locum habet.

Instantia I. Appetitus sensitivus in statu integritatis propendebat ad bonum sensibile, quod a bono spirituali saepe immane quantum dislidet. Resp. Bonum sensibile & spirituale, respectu primi hominis, disparata quidem, at non contraria, sed subordinata fuerunt.

Instantia II. Nulla potest dari causa defectionis primi hominis, quam remotio doni supernaturalis, quod freni appetitum hominis coercuit. Resp. Causa defectionis fuit tum diaboli seductio, tum concreati liberi arbitrii abusus.

IV. Quidquid per modum coronae, quae facile detrahi potest, hominem exornavit, illud homini non est naturale: Atqui imago Dei &c. E. Maior constat: quia corona non pertinet ad naturam hominis; quippe qua sublata, salua manet natura. Minor probatur, et Ps. VIII, 6. Gloria & honore coronasti eum. Resp. Ps. VIII. agit de Christo, quod praeter contextum docet citatio apostoli, Hebr. II, 9.

V. Quidquid cum vestimento comparatur, id fuit aliquid supernaturale & extrinsecum: Atqui imago Dei &c. E. Maior est clara: quia vestimentum non est de natura hominis. Minor probatur ex Sir. c. XVII, 1. 3. Dominus creavit hominem de terra secundum seipsos, vestivit eos virtute, & iuxta imaginem suam fecit ipsos: Resp. 1) Verbum vestire metaphoricum est, & saepe notat id, quod connaturale est. Sic Iobus dicit, se a Deo carne & cute vestitum esse, c. X, 11. Deus dicitur agri lilia vestire, quorum pulcritudo naturalis est, Matth. V, 30. 2) In fonte legimus ἐνέδυσεν αὐτὲς ἰσχὺν induit eos robore, i. e. instruxit Deus homines validis, ad expedienda negotia, viribus ingenii & corporis.

VI. Quidquid homo ex gratia immediate a Deo accipit, id non fuit ei naturale: Atqui imaginem Dei primus homo ex gratia immediate accepit. Ergo. Resp. Dist. inter gratiam generalem creationis, & specialem regenerationis. Primus homo accepit imaginem Dei per gratiam generalem creationis, sicut animam, corpus & membra naturalia a Deo adeptus est: per specialem regenerationis & renouationis imago post lapsum reparatur.

VII. Origo iustitiae non est a principiis naturae, sed a Deo: Ergo iustitia primo homini non fuit naturalis. Ratio consequentiae est; quia quidquid non fluit e principiis naturae, sed immediate accipitur a Deo, supernaturale donum est. Resp. 1) Primus homo animam rationalem non e principiis naturae, sed immediate a Deo accepit: qua tamen pars naturalis primi hominis fuit. 2) Si spectes originem iustitiae, vtique donum Dei fuit; fin penites naturalem convenientiam & inhaesionem intimam, fuit perfectio debita naturae integrae, & huic penitissime impressa ad obtinendum finem naturae proportionatum.

VIII. Per peccatum actuale non amittuntur dona naturalia, sed supernaturalia & spiritualia: Atqui peccatum Adami fuit actuale: Ergo. Maior patet; quia per peccatum amittitur quidem gratiosa Dei inhabitatio, sed nullum donum naturale. Resp. 1) Etiam per peccatum actuale dona naturalia amitti aut destrui possunt. Sic vigor corporis & felicitas memoriae per ebrietatem & scortationem amittitur. Per homicidium vnio naturalis corporis & animae diffluitur. 2) Delictum Adami non ex aliorum hominum peccatis actualibus aestimandum est; ideo quod illis longe gravius est & atrocius. Neque enim tantum personale, aut individuale est, sed etiam certo respectu commune & vniuersale, a) ratione imputationis; quia peccatum Adami, qui stirps & caput erat totius generis humani, omnibus hominibus est imputatum: b) ratione transgressionis; quia peccato Adami omnia praecepta decalogi sunt violata: c) ratione propagationis; quia peccatum originale, quod ex delicto

Adaminitico fluxit, in omnes Adami posteros derivatum est. His accedit, quod Adamus iis munitus fuerit praesidiis, ut peccatum facile declinare potuerit, cum nullo interno peccati fomite lacesseretur.

IX. Imago Dei naturalis est Filius Dei... naturalis: Homo integer non fuit Filius Dei naturalis. Ergo. Resp. 1) Non asserimus, primum hominem fuisse imaginem Dei naturalem, sed ipsi concreatam esse imaginem divinam, naturae integrae debitam, seu convenientem. 2) Filius Dei naturalis duabus de causis dicitur: a) quia ab aeterno ex essentia patris genitus est; quo sensu solus Christus est Filius Dei naturalis: b) quia connaturali sapientia & sanctitate Deum sapientissimum & sanctissimum refert; quo sensu primus homo filius Dei naturalis dici potest. Argute inquit D. DANNHAVER. hodom. I. phant. V. pag. 1004. Non fuit primus homo filius Dei naturaliter, h. e. substantialiter (quod axioma solius est λόγος); sicat nec substantialis fuit imago Dei: fuit tamen filius Dei a natura & cum natura, cui haec dignitas fuit concreata.

X. Quodcunque corpus constat ex quatuor elementis & contrariantibus inter sese qualitatibus, illud natura mortale est: Atqui corpus Adami constitit &c. Ergo. Maior constat: quia corpus, ex elementis mixtum, naturaliter vergit ad interitum ob qualitates inter sese contrariantes. Resp. 1) Aurum est corpus mixtum ex quatuor elementis, & tamen est quadantenus ἄφθαρτον. Luna non est expers mixtionis, corruptione tamen superior. Corpus Christi constat ex quatuor elementis, & tamen non est natura mortale. 2) Iudicandum est de natura compositi non tantum ex conditione materiae, sed & a) ex connexione, sive unione formae cum materia. Nempe sancta Adami anima Deo, vitae fonti, semper adhaerens in statu integritatis, iuncta erat corpori, vinculo non solubili, nisi per peccatum. Haud male inquit BONAVENTVRA, Lib. II. Dist. XIX. artic. III. qu. 1. Mors non poterat inesse homini, nisi deordinaretur natura. Si mortem introduxit deordinatio naturae humanae, immortalitas naturae humanae est debita ordinarie. b) Respicienda est bonitas temperamenti, quod perfectissimum Adamus nactus erat; harmonia qualitatum amice conspirantium, & ad interitum non vergentium; & absentia, seu defectus causarum mortis, quales sunt fames, sitis, senium, defatigatio corporis, morbi; quibus minime obnoxius erat primus homo, adeoque natura non mortalis.

XI. Cui destinata fuit arbor vitae, ad vires prolapsas reparandas, ille natura non fuit immortalis: Atqui homini primo &c. Ergo. Maior constat: quia vires prolapsae inclinant ad interitum; qui si divinitus auertatur externo quodam medio; immortalitas divinitus collata non est naturalis, sed supernaturalis. Resp. a) Indiguit Adamus arbore vitae, non ad reparandas vires prolapsas, sed ad integras conferuandas. b) Conferuandae erant vires Adami fructu arboris vitae, quia immortalitas Adami non erat absoluta, sed ordinata. c) Inuertimus argumentum: Cuius immortalitas a cibo & medio naturali dependet, ille naturaliter immortalis est.

XII. Quicunque natura immortalis est, is non potest mori: Primus homo potuit mori. E. Resp. Immortalitas absoluta competit Deo: Fluens ex simplicitate naturae est angelorum, & animarum humanarum: Pendens a gratia glorificationis est beatorum: concreata autem est primo homini ordinata, quia certis mediis erat continuanda, & hypothetica immortalitas; quia tamdiu non mortale mansurum erat corpus hominis primi, quamdiu non peccaret. Ceterum cum dicimus hominem integrum fuisse immortalem, non negamus potentiam moriendi remotam; si enim ab hac immunis fuisset, post lapsum non fuisset mortuus; sed proximam, ortam ex internis causis mortis, nempe morbis, absumtione calidi innati & humidi radicalis &c. Ex quo nonnulli theologi malunt hominem primum appellare non

morin colleg. Anti-Socinian. p. 278. Nam in statu innocentiae homo poterat non mori, in statu gloriae non potest mori, in statu miseriae non potest non mori.

XIII. Omne generabile est corruptibile: Corpus Adami erat generabile: E. Resp. Neg. maior. Nam anima etiam est generabilis, neque tamen corruptibili.

XIV. Immortalis non utitur cibis, 1 Cor. 13. Adamus usus est cibis. E. Resp. Immortalis in statu gloriae, ventre & esca destructis, non utitur cibis. Primus homo non erat in statu gloriae, sed in statu innocentiae, cuius immortalitas ordinata cibis continuabatur.


### XXI. Was man created in a state of pure naturals?

The state of pure naturals, in which man is made ἀδιάφορος (indifferent), indifferent to moral good and evil, without the knowledge of the Triune God, without the desire for eternal life, with the rebellion of the flesh against the spirit, exposed to various calamities, diseases, and death, is a most vain fiction.

Proof. The state of pure naturals, which the adversaries invent, is repugnant 1) as much to the intention of God regarding the creation of the first man as to the execution of the divine intention. For both the purpose and the execution of God in creating man tended to this, that man should be created with the divine image, consisting in the knowledge of God and the holiness of the will. But this does not coexist, nor is it compossible, with the state of pure naturals.

2) It is repugnant to divine holiness. For if God had created an appetite repugnant to the spirit, He would be the cause of sin. Or if that rebellion in the state of pure naturals had not been sin, neither would it be sin today.

3) It is repugnant to divine justice. For the most just God does not subject an innocent man, who has never sinned, to calamities, diseases, and death.

4) It is repugnant to the excellent goodness and uprightness of the first man; for he was created very good, Gen. 1:31, and upright, Eccles. 7:30. But if he had been created indifferent to good and evil, without the knowledge of the Triune God, without the desire for eternal life, with the rebellion of the flesh against the spirit, he would not have been very good and upright.

5) It is repugnant to the state of integrity. For original sin is a state without the fear of God, without trust toward God, with concupiscence. See Augsburg Confession, Art. II. But the state of pure naturals is a state without the fear of God, without trust toward God, and with concupiscence. Therefore, the state of pure naturals is a state of sin, and thus Adam would have been created upright with original sin, which is blasphemous against the Creator.

6) It is repugnant to the nature of man. For no creature that is a participant of reason is, or can be, ἀδιάφορος, or indifferent to moral good and evil, but is either morally good or morally bad; either pleasing to God or hateful to Him.

7) It is repugnant to the end for the sake of which man exists. Namely, he was created to know and worship the Creator, to pass his life holily, and to attain eternal blessedness. But if he had been created in a state of pure naturals, he would never have attained this end.

The antithesis is that of the Scholastics and most Papists, who assert the state of pure naturals, most of whose arguments have been examined.

I. Whatever state has a foundation in reality is not fictitious: But the state of pure naturals, etc. Therefore. The minor is proved: because 1) it is not repugnant to divine power, the power of God, the power of God, the power of God, the power of God,

to create man without exceptional wisdom & righteousness. 2) Because even today after the fall certain natural things are pure & integral, e.g., the light of truth & the seed of good. Resp. 1) In a divided sense I concede that God could have created man without exceptional wisdom & righteousness, if He did not intend to create man in His image according to His likeness: but given that intention, God neither willed nor could He have fashioned man without excellent wisdom & holiness; for otherwise man would not have borne an image most similar to God. 2) The light of truth & the seed of good, remaining today in the intellect & will of man, are thin relics of the divine image.

Since these are natural, the image of God must have been natural to the first man. 3) Man could not have been created by God with the struggle of flesh & spirit; because that struggle is in itself evil & sinful, and thus could not have God, who is most holy, as its author.

You say: The rebellion of appetite & reason would not have proceeded from the intention of the author of nature, but would have existed in man beyond His intention, if man had been created in pure naturals: just as a smith fashioning a sword from iron is not the cause of the rust on the sword, which arises later from the condition of the material. Resp. Thus God would be accused of either imprudence or impotence. Of the former; because He did not foresee the same stain, ἀταξίαν (disorder): of the latter; because He could not remove the same stain. Both are blasphemous against the Creator. The analogy brought forward is dissimilar. For the smith does not make the material itself, as God does; nor does he possess such powers that he can preserve the sword from rust; nor does rust necessarily follow the material.

II. There were in integral man natural faculties & supernatural gifts, which can be represented by distinct concepts. For there were in man intellect, will, sensitive appetite, as natural faculties; there were exceptional wisdom & original righteousness, as supernatural gifts. Resp. a) Concerning the precision of the mind there is no question: for we concede that natural faculties could be abstracted from supernatural gifts by the benefit of the intellect, and considered distinctly. But the question remains: was the first man created in a state of pure naturals without ignorance of the true God, & with the rebellion of flesh & spirit? The sacred scriptures teach otherwise, namely that the state of the first man was a state of integrity, conspicuous with the splendor of the divine image. b) The wisdom & righteousness of the first man was not supernatural, but concreated and, for the obtaining of the end, namely eternal blessedness, owed to integral nature, and most deeply impressed upon it.

III. Whatever mystery transcends the grasp of human reason, that does not become known to man without supernatural revelation: But the mystery of the Trinity etc. Therefore. Resp. Distinguish between the reason of the sinner after the fall, and the reason of integral man before the fall. The mystery of the Trinity is above the reason of fallen man: but indeed before the fall there was created an infinite light and perfection of the first man in his intellect, by which, being illuminated, he knew his Creator, who is one God, Father, Son & Holy Spirit. That man was created in this knowledge of the Creator, Paul teaches Col. III, 10.

IV. He to whom freedom of will in both directions is concreated, is created αὐτέρετος (self-determining), or indifferent to good & evil: But the first man etc. Therefore. The major is evident; because indifference to good & evil is nothing other than freedom of will in both directions. Resp. He to whom freedom of will in both directions is concreated, so that he inclines equally to evil as to good, he is created αὐτέρετος; I concede. But although freedom of will was concreated in the first man, there was nevertheless in him no natural propensity, or proximate power to desire evil, but only a remote power, or non-repugnance. For there was concreated in him for this end wisdom of intellect, righteousness of will, & rectitude of sensitive appetite, so that he might be borne prone to good freely chosen and promptly done. There was also at hand for him supernatural aid of the Holy Spirit, concreated perfections with the light of supernatural grace supernatural grace supernatural grace ral, illuminating, preserving, enriching. There was lacking to him only confirmation, or determination toward the good, which brings about the immutability of concrete justice: which increase God would have most liberally added in the heavenly fatherland; if the first-formed humans had run the course of the life of holiness with unoffending foot.

V. If human nature could not be created by God without original justice, it follows that a dead man cannot be recalled by God into life, unless endowed with justice, without which, however, many have been resurrected. See 1 Kings XVII, 22. 2 Kings IV, 33. Matt. IX, 25. Luke VII, 15. John XI, 43. Response: 1) The reason for nature first instituted is one thing, that of nature destitute is another. The former could not be created infected with evil, saving the goodness and justice of God: the latter, because it had of its own accord enslaved itself to sin, could not be resurrected from the same while not immune to evil. For God, by resurrecting nature contaminated by sin, does not do evil, but finds it. 2) Those examples are extraordinary, from which nothing certain can be defined. For it is not certainly established whether those who were recalled into this life were subject to sin, and died again, or whether they had lived for some time devoid of sin, as the first-formed before the fall, and without the intervention of death had been translated alive into heaven after the manner of Enoch and Elijah. Cf. D. Meisner in Anthropologia, decade I, p. 52, and D. Calov, vol. IV, System, p. 683.

Latin:

Status purorum naturalium, in quo homo conditus fit ἀδιάφορος, in differens ad bonum & malum morale, sine cognitione Dei triunius, sine desiderio vitae aeternae, cum rebellione carnis adversus spiritum, variis calamitatibus, morbis, & morti expositus, vanissimum commentum est.

Prob. Status purorum naturalium, quem adversarii comminiscuntur, repugnat 1) tam intentioni Dei de creando primo homine, quam intentionis divinae executioni. Nam tum propositum, tum executio Dei in condendo homine eo tendebat, ut homo crearetur cum imagine divina, consistente in agnitione Dei & sanctitate voluntatis. Haec autem non coëxistit, nec compossibilis est cum statu purorum naturalium.

2) Repugnat sanctitati divinae. Si enim Deus condidisset appetitum spiritui repugnantem, esset causa peccati. Aut si rebellio illa in statu purorum naturalium non fuisset peccatum, neque hodie peccatum foret.

3) Repugnat iustitiae divinae. Neque enim Deus iustissimus hominem innocentem, qui nunquam peccavit, calamitatibus, morbis & morti subiicit.

4) Repugnat eximiae bonitati & rectitudini primi hominis; quippe qui conditus erat valde bonus, Gen. 1, 31. & rectus, Eccles. VII, 30. At si creatus fuisset indifferens ad bonum & malum, sine cognitione Dei triunius, sine desiderio vitae aeternae, cum rebellione carnis adversus spiritum, non fuisset valde bonus & rectus.

5) Repugnat statui integritatis. Nam peccatum originis est status sine metu Dei, sine fiducia erga Deum, cum concupiscentia. Vid. August. Confess. artic. II. At status purorum naturalium est status sine metu Dei, sine fiducia erga Deum, & cum concupiscentia. Ergo status purorum naturalium est status peccati, adeoque Adamus integer conditus fuisset cum peccato originis, quod est blasphemum in creatorem.

6) Repugnat naturae hominis. Nam nulla creatura rationis particeps est, aut esse potest ἀδιάφορος, sine indifferens ad bonum & malum morale, sed vel moraliter bona, vel moraliter mala; vel grata Deo, vel ipsi exosa est.

7) Repugnat fini, cuius gratia homo existit. Nimirum conditus est ad creatorem cognoscendum & colendum, vitam sancte transigendam, & aeternam beatitudinem consequendam. At si conditus esset in statu purorum naturalium, hunc finem nunquam assecutus esset.

Antithesis est Scholasticorum & Pontificiorum plerorumque, statum purorum naturalium afferentium, quorum pleraque argumenta examinata sunt. Praeterea tamen argumentantur:

I. Qui status habet fundamentum in re, is non est commentitious: Atqui status purorum naturalium &c. Ergo. Minor probatur: quia 1) non repugnat potentiae divinae, fabripotentiæ diuinæ, fabripotentiæ diuinæ, fabri-

care hominem fine eximia sapientia & iustitia. 2) Quia hodienum post lapsum quaedam naturalia sunt pura & integra, v. gr. lumen veri & semen boni. Resp. 1) In sensu diviso concedo, Deum potuisse hominem condere fine eximia sapientia & iustitia, si non intenderet hominem creare in imagine sua secundum similitudinem suam: at supposita illa intentione, Deus hominem fine excellenti sapientia & sanctitate fabricare nec voluit, nec potuit; ideo, quod ceteroquin homo non gessisset imaginem Deo simillimam. 2) Lumen veri & semen boni, hodienum in intellectu & voluntate hominis residua, sunt tenues reliquiae imaginis divinae.

Quae cum sint naturales, imaginem Dei primo homini naturalem fuisse oportuit. 3) Cum lucta carnis & spiritus homo primus a Deo creari nequiuit; quia lucta illa per se mala & peccaminosa est, adeoque Deum sanctissimum auctorem habere non potuit.

Dicis: Rebellio appetitus & rationis non prouenisset ex intentione auctoris naturae, sed praeter eius intentionem in homine exstitisset, si in puris naturalibus homo creatus fuisset: sicut faber ex ferro gladium fabricans, non est causa rubiginis in gladio, quae ex materiae conditione postea oritur. Resp. Sic accusaretur Deus vel imprudentia, vel impotentia. Illius; quia eandem labem ἀταξίαν non prauiderit: huius; quia eandem labem summovere non potuerit. Vtrumque est blasphemum in creatorem. Allatum simile est dissimile. Nam faber non ipsam materiam efficit, vt Deus; neque illis pollet viribus, vt gladium a rubigine praeservare queat; nec rubigo necessario materiam insequitur.

II. Erant in homine integro facultates naturales & dona supernaturalia, quae distinctis conceptibus repraesentari possunt. Nam erant in homine intellectus, voluntas, appetitus sensitivus, tanquam facultates naturales; erant eximia sapientia & iustitia originalis, tanquam dona supernaturalia. Resp. a) De praecisione mentis nulla est quaestio: concedimus enim, quod facultates naturales a donis supernaturalibus beneficio intellectus praescindi, distincteque considerari potuerint. At manet quaestio: an primus homo in statu purorum naturalium sine ignoratione veri Dei, & cum rebellione carnis & spiritus creatus sit? Aliud docent sacrae litterae, nimirum statum primi hominis fuisse statum integritatis, splendore imaginis divinae conspicuum. b) Sapientia & iustitia primi hominis non erat supernaturalis, sed concreata & ad obtinendum finem, nempe aeternam beatitudinem, naturae integrae debita, eique penitissime impressa.

III. Quodcunque mysterium rationis humanae captum transcendit, illud homini citra revelationem supernaturalem non innotescit: Atqui mysterium Trinitatis &c. Ergo. Resp. Dist. inter rationem peccatoris post lapsum, & rationem hominis integri ante lapsum. Mysterium Trinitatis est supra rationem hominis lapsi: at vero ante lapsum creata erat infinita lux & perfectio hominis primi in intellectu, qua illustratus creatorem suum, qui est vnus Deus, Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. cognoscebat. In hac cognitione creatoris hominem esse conditum, docet Paullus Col. III, 10.

IV. Cui concreata est libertas arbitrii in vtramque partem, is conditus est αὐτέρετος, siue indifferens ad bonum & malum: Atqui primo homini &c. Ergo. Maior est euidens; quia indifferentia ad bonum & malum nihil aliud est, quam libertas arbitrii in vtramque partem. Resp. Cui concreata est libertas arbitrii in vtramque partem, vt aeque propendeat ad malum, atque ad bonum, ille conditus est αὐτέρετος; concedo. At licet primo homini concreata sit libertas arbitrii, nulla tamen in ipso erat propensio naturalis, aut potentia proxima ad concupiscendum malum, sed tantum potentia remota, siue non repugnantia. Eum namque in finem ipsi concreata erat sapientia intellectus, iustitia voluntatis, & rectitudo appetitus sensitivi, vt pronus ferretur ad bonum libere eligendum, promteque faciendum. Praesto ipsi etiam erat supernaturale auxilium Spiritus S., concreatas perfectiones luce gratiae supernaturalis gratiæ supernaturalis gratiæ supernaturalis illustrans, conferuans, locupletans. Deerat tantum ei confirmatio, aut determinatio ad bonum, quæ immutabilitatem concretæ iustitiæ infert: quod augmentum Deus in patria cœlesti liberalissime adiecisset; si homines protoplasti vitam sanctitatis inoffenso pede decurrissent.

V. Si natura humana non potuit a Deo creari sine iustitia originali, sequitur, non posse hominem mortuum a Deo in vitam reuocari, nisi iustitia præditum, sine qua tamen multi resuscitati sunt. Vid. 1 Reg. XVII, 22. 2 Reg. IV, 33. Matth. IX, 25. Luc. VII, 15. Io. XI, 43. Resp. 1) Alia est ratio naturæ primum institutæ, alia destitutæ. Illa malo infecta condi non potuit salua Dei bonitate ac iustitia: hæc, quia sponte sua se mancipauerat peccato, ab eodem non immunis malo resuscitari potuit. Neque enim Deus resuscitando naturam, peccato contaminatam, malum facit, sed inuenit. 2) Extraordinaria sunt illa exempla, e quibus nihil certi definire licet. Neque enim certo constat, vtrum illi, qui in hanc vitam reuocati sunt, peccato fuerint obnoxii, & rursus mortui, an peccati expertes aliquandiu vixissent, vt protoplasti ante lapsum, ac sine mortis interuentu ad instar Enochi & Eliæ in cœlum viui translati fuerint. Conf. D. MEISN. in anthropol. decad. I. p. 52. & D. CALOV. tom. IV. syst. p. 683.


### XXI. Was man created in a state of pure naturals?: Question XXII

Question XXII.

What supernatural gifts accompanied the image of God? Although divine grace and the indwelling of the Most Holy Trinity in the first man was not supernatural, but natural a): yet one must not deny that other gifts were given to the first man, placed above nature, especially extraordinary revelation and those things which were connected to it b).

Proof a. There are indeed some theologians of great name who think that the grace of God and the indwelling of the Most Holy Trinity was supernatural to the first man. See D. Gerhard, Disputatio isagogica, p. 803. However, if we consider 1) that the nature of the first man neither ever was, nor could have been, whole without the divine Spirit indwelling and sanctifying, 2) that original sin, which succeeded in the place of the divine image after the fall of Adam, brought upon fallen man not only bodily, but also spiritual death (which is the privation of the mystical union of the soul with God); we accede to those authors who maintain that the divine grace and the indwelling of the Most Holy Trinity was not supernatural, but natural to the first man. Confer D. J. A. Osiander, Collegium theologicum, part II, p. 283. D. Fecht, in Syllogismi controversi, disp. XIV. D. Breithaupt, in Theses credendorum, p. 28.

Proof b. Adam had obtained the positive law concerning abstinence from the fruits of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil from the supernatural revelation of God, Gen. II, 16, 17. Nor is there any doubt that powers and supernatural gifts were bestowed upon the first man by the indwelling Holy Spirit for fulfilling the positive law, and for persisting in the state of integrity. For the indwelling of the Holy Spirit carries with it a heap of many spiritual gifts, Eph. III, 19.

Question XXIII.

What bodily and temporal goods accompanied the image of God? External bodily and temporal goods in the state of integrity concern most especially human society, and the seat divinely granted. The former was full of love a), the latter of sweetness b).

Proof a. If man had remained in the state of integrity, and the human race had been multiplied in the same, a most honorable and most pleasant friendship would have flourished among men, born from the mutual consent of souls, and the communion of goods. For if the faithful in the primitive church were one heart and one soul, Acts 4:32: how much closer a bond would have joined together men whole and pure of life and crime? Since all good things were common to them, there were no causes for bringing lawsuits: because all were established as lords of the earth and of living creatures in Adam. You say: Man would have been lord of man even in the state of integrity, and thus not all would have been lords; since God is the author of order, not of confusion. 1 Cor. 14:33. Resp. In the state of integrity, man would have indeed obtained over man a πατρικὸν or paternal lordship, such as that of a father over his children, but not a δεσποτικὸν or masterly one, such as that of a master over slaves. One would have been subject to the other by a spontaneous and free subjection, not a coerced and servile one; since in that state, to obey would have been no less a liberty than to command. Prob. b. The seat and place of man's habitation in the state of integrity was paradise, or a garden situated in Eden between the Tigris and the Euphrates, where the most fertile fields of Babylonia, Mesopotamia, and Armenia are, Gen. 2:14. Paradise, moreover, was filled with the most excellent trees, among which stood out the tree of life and of the knowledge of good and evil. The former approached the likeness of a pharmacy, from which fruits were plucked to preserve the strength of the body; the latter was like a certain altar, at the sight of which man learned to reverence God, the supreme lord and legislator of all things, continually.

Latin:

Quæst. XXII. Quænam dona supernaturalia comitata sunt imaginem Dei?

Quamuis gratia diuina & inhabitatio SS. Trinitatis in primo homine non supernaturalis, sed naturalis fuerit a): non neganda tamen sunt primo homini data dona alia, supra naturam posita, reuelatio inprimis extraordinaria & quæ ei erant connexa b).

Prob. a. Sunt quidem nonnulli theologi magni nominis, qui censent gratiam Dei & inhabitationem SS. Trinitatis primo homini fuisse supernaturalem. Vid. D. GERHARD. disput. isagog. p. 803. Attamen, si consideramus 1) naturam hominis primi nec vnquam fuisse, nec esse potuisse integram, sine Spiritu diuino inhabitante & sanctificante, 2) peccatum originale, quod in locum imaginis diuinæ post lapsum Adami successit, non tantum corporalem, sed & spiritualem mortem (quæ est priuatio mysticæ vnionis animæ cum Deo) homini lapso intulisse; iis accedimus auctoribus, qui gratiam diuinam & inhabitationem SS. Trinitatis primo homini non supernaturalem, sed naturalem fuisse statuunt. Confer. D. I. A. OSIANDR. colleg. theol. part. II. pag. 283. D. FECHT. in fyllogism. controu. disp. XIV. D. BREITHAVPT. in thes. cred. p. 28.

Prob. b. Legem positiuam de abstinentia a fructibus arboris scientiæ boni & mali Adamus e reuelatione Dei supernaturali nactus erat, Gen. II, 16. 17. Neque dubium est, quin a Spiritu S. inhabitante vires & dona supernaturalia homini primo collata sint ad legem positiuam implendam, & ad persistendum in statu integritatis. Nam inhabitatio Spiritus S. secum fert cumulum multorum donorum spiritualium, Eph. III, 19.

Quæst. XXIII. Quænam bona corporalia & temporalia imaginem Dei comitabantur?

Externa bona corporalia & temporalia in statu integritatis concernunt potissimum societatem humanam, & sedem diuinitus concessam. Illa plena amoris (a), hæc suauitatis erat (b).

Prob. a. Si homo mansisset in statu integritatis, & genus humanum in eodem multiplicatum fuisset, honestissima & iucundissima inter homines viguisset amicitia, nata e mutuo animorum consensu, & bonorum communione. Si enim fideles in primitiua ecclesia fuere vnum cor & una anima, Act. IV, 32: quanto arctius vinculum coniunxiffet homines integros vitæ, scelerisque puros? Quibus cum omnia bona effent communia, nullæ ferendarum litium erant caussæ: quia omnes terræ ac animantium in Adamo erant constituti domini. Dicis: Homo hominis fuiffet dominus etiam in statu integritatis, adeoque non omnes fuiffent domini; cum Deus auctor sit ordinis, non confusionis. 1 Cor. XIV, 33. Resp. In statu integritatis homo in hominem obtinuiffet quidem dominium πατρικὸν seu paternum, quale est patris in liberos, non autem δεσποτικὸν vel herile, quale est heri in servos. Alter alteri fuiffet subiectus subiectione spontanea & libera, non coacta & servili; siquidem in illo statu non minus parere, quam imperare, libertas fuiffet. Prob. b. Sedes & locus habitationis hominis in statu integritatis erat paradisus, vel hortus in Eden situs inter Tigrim & Euphratem, vbi sunt pinguiffimi campi Babyloniæ, Mesopotamiæ & Armeniæ, Gen. II, 14. Paradisus autem refertus erat arboribus longe præstantiffimis, quas inter eminebant arbor vitæ, & scientiæ boni & mali. Illa accedebat ad similitudinem pharmacothecæ, e qua fructus decerpebantur ad vires corporis conservandas; hæc erat veluti ara quædam, ad cuius conspectum homo Deum, summum rerum omnium dominum & legislatorem, reuereri iugiter condiscebat.


### Q. XXIV. What was the end of the image of God?

The absolutely ultimate end of the image of God bestowed upon the first man is the glory of divine wisdom, goodness, and power a). The end ultimate in a certain respect is eternal beatitude b). The intermediate end is a holy life, pleasing to God c).

Prob. a. Since every soul created by God praises its author, Ps. 150:6, then especially the soul, endowed with the image of God, was a most beautiful temple of the Holy Trinity. A son bearing the image of his father owes him piety; a minister endowed with the likeness of his master owes him the most prompt obedience; a city, adorned with a gilded statue of the king, owes it singular loyalty: so man, created in the image of God, is bound to acknowledge, love, and venerate God, thrice best, thrice greatest. Prob. b. Every creature, participant in reason, tends toward its goal, which is perennial beatitude: and the immortal soul desires to enjoy blessed immortality. Prob. c. Just as the image of God comprised those powers, or perfections of intellect, will, and sensitive appetite, which were sufficient for living holily, according to the will of the creator: Thus a holy life was an intermediate end, looking toward the ultimate end, which was eternal beatitude, which man, if he had remained in the state of integrity, would not indeed have earned by living holily, since the holy life of an integral man was not an unowed thing, yet he would have obtained it from the grace of God, who compensates the pursuit of holiness most liberally and beyond merit.

Latin:

Finis absolute vltimus collatæ homini primo imaginis Dei est gloria sapientiæ, bonitatis & potentiæ diuinæ a). Finis secundum quid vltimus est æterna beatitudo b). Finis intermedius est vita sancta, Deoque placens c).

Prob. a. Cum omnis anima a Deo creata, auctorem suum laudet, Ps. CL, 6. tum in primis anima, imagine Dei prædita, pulcerrimum S. S. Trinitatis templum erat. Filius gerens imaginem patris, huic pietatem; minister donatus effigie domini, promtiffimum huic obsequium; vrbs, condecorata inaurata regis statua, huic singularem fidem debet: ita homo ad imaginem Dei creatus, obstrictus est ad agnoscendum, diligendum, venerandum Deum ter optimum, ter maximum. Prob. b. Omnis creatura, rationis particeps, tendit ad scopum suum, qui est perennis beatitudo: & anima immortalis beata frui immortalitate desiderat. Prob. c. Quemadmodum imago Dei eas complectebatur vires, aut perfectiones intellectus, voluntatis & appetitus sensitivi, quæ ad sancte viuendum, iuxta voluntatem creatoris, sufficientes erant: Ita vita sancta erat finis intermedius, respiciens finem vltimum, qui erat æterna beatitudo, quam homo, si in statu integritatis mansiffet, sancte viuendo non quidem promeruiffet, cum vita sancta hominis integri non fuerit indebita, obtinuiffet tamen ex gratia Dei, studium sanctitatis liberalissime & vltra meritum compensantis.


### Q. XXV. Is the image of God lost through the fall of the first-formed humans?

The image of God was lost through the sin of Adam both meritoriously and naturally.

Obs. We say that the image of God was lost 1) meritoriously; because the first man by a single sinful act merited that the image of God should be removed from him. For God decreed from eternity to confirm man, if he did not fall, in original justice with his posterity, in such a way that he could not thereafter fall at all, just as He confirmed the angels who did not fall. But the fall having occurred, He decreed to deprive him of original justice, and to leave him in that state with all his posterity, in which otherwise, outside of the remedy found by Himself, he would have had to perish. And not only meritoriously, but also 2) naturally, insofar as by the force of that sin the integrity and harmony of the concreated powers, convenient to human nature is destroyed in man, and all justice is driven out, not otherwise than as poison destroys and expels the health of the body.…

Which two modes can well consist together: for they do not conflict, that it is moral, and that it concurs naturally, just as a self-slayer [αὐτόχειρ] naturally and morally loses his life: morally indeed as meritoriously, so that God may abandon him; naturally truly, by moving the knife.

Prob. 1) The image of God is to be renewed. Therefore it is lost. For of that which is not lost, there can be no place for its restitution.

2) Those who are destitute of the glory of God, the image of God is lacking to them: The descendants of Adam etc. Therefore.

The major is evident, because the image of God was the notable glory of God, partly because it draws its origin from God the most glorious, partly because it was communicated to man, created in the image of God, as the glorious resplendence of God; from which man is called the image and glory of God, The minor is clear from

3) Adam, after the fall, begat children in his own image, not in the image of God, so that, as Paul explains, now in Adam all die. Therefore Adam lost the image of God.

4) Adam had received the image of God under this law, that he should persist in it; but the same, if he should violate God's interdict, he would lose again, Therefore meritoriously on account of the transgression and in exchange for the penalty he lost the image of God.

5) Just as the apostate angels lost their integrity meritoriously, through the non-preservation, or abandonment of their principality and happy state, so also Adam, by not preserving his integrity, which he had, merited that it should be taken away from him. Which process God observes even today in the economy of grace, so that to him who has it is given, and from him who has not (or is unwilling to have more) by the just judgment of God even that which he has is taken away,

6) We are now by nature [φύσει], or through natural generation, children of wrath, having a mind darkened by shadows, altogether alienated from the life of God, Therefore the very nature of Adam was corrupted by the fall, and thus the image of God was naturally lost. For a) nothing, which is not natural, can be propagated by natural generation. b) As shadows naturally expel light: so the sin of Adam shook off the light of the image of God.

7) That which is born of sinful flesh (by natural generation), that is now naturally sinful flesh,

There is an antithesis of some Papists, who refer the image of God to the very nature of man, but judge that the likeness of God denotes accidental perfections. Hence they teach that the likeness of God, but not the divine image, has been lost. 2) Of the Socinians, asserting that the image of God consists in dominion over the remaining creatures; which, since it was not lost through the fall, they conclude that the image of God was not destroyed. 3) Of the Arminians, denying that the image of God was physically destroyed by the sinful act of Adam (as health is destroyed by poison), but teaching that it was lost only meritoriously, because God by a judicial act deprived man of original justice. Whose chief arguments are:

I. Man after the fall is said to be created in the image of God, Where God forbids the shedding of human blood, because man was made in the image of God. Therefore the image of God was not lost through the fall of Adam. Resp. 1) generally: Man after the fall is said to be made in the image of God, a) on account of the first creation of man, who was created in the image of God. Therefore all men received the image of God in Adam as the head and stock of the human race, b) on account of the remaining vestiges of the divine image, which are the light of truth and the seed of good, or the principles of reason born with us, both theoretical, as well as practical. c) Because man after the fall itself is capable of the divine image, to which this also, by virtue of the divine intention, is owed, although in fact it does not reside in him. d) Because, by virtue of the catholic merit of Christ, the image of God is to be restored in all men, both in this and in the other life, and thus man has a right to the recovery of the image of God.

2) Resp. Specifically: Gen. IX, 6, by the image of God is understood immortality, because man was created for eternal life; which divine intention remains, notwithstanding temporal death, from which all will be resurrected to judgment, and will die no more.

II. Man after the fall is called the image & glory of God, 1 Cor. XI, 7, which is the reason why the woman ought to obey the man. Resp. The man is called the image & glory of God, i.e., the glorious image of God, because of the dominion which God possesses over all creatures, of which a certain image shines forth in the man, since to him belongs dominion not only over the beasts, but also over the wife herself.

III. Whoever possesses dominion over the beasts after the fall, he is not deprived of the image of God on account of the fall of the first men. But after the fall, dominion belongs to man, etc. Therefore. The major is evident; because dominion over the beasts is a significant part of the divine image. The minor is proved from Gen. IX, 2. Resp. 1) Distinguish between full dominion and broken or diminished dominion. Full dominion over the beasts does not belong to man after the fall. For before the fall he could play with lions and leopards as if with Maltese lapdogs, the sight of whom he flees and dreads after the fall. How often does it happen that man is overcome, torn to pieces, and devoured by beasts? 2) Actual dominion was an adjunct and appendix of the image of God: but the power of ruling is only a less principal part of the same.

IV. The fall of Adam was a single act. Therefore, it did not have the power which could deprave the very nature of Adam. Resp. Deny the consequence. The apostate angels overturned their state and corrupted their nature by a single sinful act. The serpent infects the whole nature of man with poison in one strike. Sight is snatched away by one wound inflicted on the eye.

V. Whatever God as a just judge took away, that was not lost naturally, but only meritoriously. But God [took away] the primeval image, etc. Therefore. The major is certain; because a judicial privation is moral, not physical. Resp. Deny the major. For through gluttony a man physically snatches health away from himself. Meanwhile, however, God as a just judge punishes the drunkard through the abbreviation of life.

VI. That whose cause was not physical cannot be called physical and natural. But the cause of the loss of the primeval image was not physical. Therefore. The major is self-evident; because, such as the cause, such is the effect. The minor is clear; because the cause of the lost image was the fall of Adam, which was a morally evil act. Resp. The cause of the loss of the divine image was both physical and moral: moral, while the protoplasts by sinning incurred the punishment of God, who by a judicial act deprived them of original righteousness; physical, while they themselves by a sinful act expelled the created habit; just as he who takes poison both acts morally against himself and physically expels health.

Latin:

Imago Dei per peccatum Adami & meritorie & naturaliter deperdita est.

Obs. Dicimus, imaginem Dei amissam esse 1) meritorie; quia primus homo actu vnico peccaminoso meruit, vt imago Dei ipsi summoueretur. Deus enim ab æterno constituit, hominem, si non laberetur, in iustitia originali cum posteris ipsius confirmare, ita, vt postea plane labi non posset, prout angelos non lapsos confirmauit. Posito autem lapsu, decreuit priuare eundem iustitia originali, & in eo statu relinquere cum tota posteritate, in quo alias extra medelam, a se inuentam, ei esset pereundum. Nec tantum meritorie, sed & 2) naturaliter, quatenus vi ipsius peccati integritas & harmonia virium concreatarum, naturæ humanæ conuedestructa est in homine, omnisque iustitia exturbata, non aliter, ac venenum sanitatem corporis destruit atque expellit.

Qui duo modo probe consistere possunt: neque enim repugnant, morale esse, & naturaliter concurrere, sicut αὐτόχειρ naturaliter & moraliter amittit vitam: moraliter quidem ceu meritorie, vt Deus ipsum deferat; naturaliter vero, admouendo cultrum.

Prob. 1) Imago Dei est renouanda. Ergo est amissa. Quod enim amissum non est, eiusdem restitutioni nullus esse potest locus.

2) Qui destituuntur gloria Dei, illos deficit imago Dei: Posteri Adami &c. Ergo.

Maior patet, quia imago Dei fuit insignis gloria Dei, partim quod a Deo gloriosissimo originem ducit, partim quod homini, in imagine Dei creato, ceu gloriosa resplendentia Dei fuit communicata; ex quo vir imago & gloria Dei dicitur, Minor liquet ex

3) Adamus, post lapsum, ad imaginem suam, non ad imaginem Dei liberos genuit, vt, sicut Paullus exponit, iam in Adamo omnes moriantur. Ergo Adamus imaginem Dei amisit.

4) Adamus imaginem Dei hac lege acceperat, vt in ea persisteret; eandem vero, si Dei interdictum violaret, rursus amitteret, Ergo meritorie propter transgressionem & in vicem poenae imaginem Dei amisit.

5) Quemadmodum angeli apostatae amiserunt integritatem suam demeritorie, per nonseruationem, seu derelictionem sui principatus ac status felicis, ita etiam Adamus integer non seruando, quod habebat, meruit, vt ei auferretur. Quem processum Deus in oeconomia gratiae hodienum obseruat, vt habenti detur, non habenti (siue amplius habere nolenti) iusto Dei iudicio auferatur etiam id, quod habet,

6) Sumus iam φύσει, natura, siue per naturalem generationem, filii irae, tenebris obscuratam mentem habentes, prorsus a vita Dei alienati, Ergo ipsa natura Adami per lapsum corrupta, adeoque imago Dei naturaliter perdita fuit. Nam a) nihil, quod naturale non est, naturali generatione propagari potest. b) Vt tenebrae naturaliter expellunt lucem: ita peccatum Adami lumen imaginis Dei excussit.

7) Quod ex carne peccaminosa (naturali generatione) nascitur, id iam naturaliter peccaminosa caro est,

Antithesis est Pontificiorum nonnullorum, qui imaginem Dei ad naturam ipsam hominis referunt, similitudinem autem Dei accidentales perfectiones notare censent. Hinc docent, similitudinem Dei, non autem imaginem diuinam esse amissam. 2) Socinianorum, asserentium, imaginem Dei consistere in dominio in reliquas creaturas; quod cum per lapsum non sit amissum, nec imaginem Dei esse deperditam statuunt. 3) Arminianorum, negantium, imaginem Dei actu peccaminoso Adami physice (vt sanitas veneno destruitur) esse deperditam, sed docentium eam amissam esse meritorie tantum, quia Deus actu iudiciali hominem iustitiae originali priuauit. Quorum argumenta praecipua sunt:

I. Homo post lapsum ad imaginem Dei conditus esse dicitur, Vbi Deus prohibet effundere sanguinem humanum, quia homo in imagine Dei factus est. Ergo imago Dei per lapsum Adami non est amissa. Resp. 1) generatim: Homo post lapsum in imagine Dei factus esse dicitur, a) ob primam creationem hominis, qui in imagine Dei creabatur. Acceperunt igitur omnes homines imaginem Dei in Adamo tanquam capite & stirpe generis humani, b) ob residua imaginis diuinae rudera, quae sunt lumen veri & semen boni, seu principia rationis nobiscum nata, tam theoretica, quam practica. c) Quia homo post lapsum ipsum capax est imaginis divinae, cui haec etiam, vi intentionis divinae, est debita, licet de facto ei non insit. d) Quia, vi catholici meriti Christi, imago Dei in omnibus hominibus instauranda est, tum in hac, tam in altera vita, adeoque homo ius ad recuperandam imaginem Dei habet.

2) Resp. Speciatim: Gen. IX, 6. per imaginem Dei intelligitur immortalitas, quia homo ad vitam aeternam creatus est; quae intentio divina manet, non obstante morte temporali, ex qua omnes resuscitabuntur ad iudicium, nec morientur amplius.

II. Vir post lapsum dicitur imago & gloria Dei, 1 Cor. XI, 7. quae est ratio, cur mulier obtemperare debeat viro. Resp. Vir imago & gloria Dei, i. e. gloriosa imago Dei dicitur propter dominium, quod Deus in omnes creaturas obtinet, cuius imago quaedam in viro relucet, quippe cui dominium competit non tantum in bestias, sed & ipsam uxorem.

III. Cui competit post lapsum dominium in bestias, ille propter lapsum primorum hominum imagine Dei non est privatus. Atqui post lapsum homini competit &c. Ergo. Maior patet; quia dominium in bestias est insignis pars imaginis divinae. Minor probatur ex Gen. IX, 2. Resp. 1) Dist. inter dominium plenum & fractum seu imminutum. Homini post lapsum non competit dominium plenum in bestias. Etenim ante lapsum cum leonibus & pardis veluti cum catellis melitaeis lufitare poterat, quorum conspectum post lapsum fugit & horret. Quoties contingit, vt homo a bestiis superetur, dilanietur & deuoretur? 2) Dominium actuale erat adiunctum & appendix imaginis Dei: potestas autem dominandi eiusdem pars tantum minus principalis est.

IV. Lapsus Adami vnus actus fuit. Ergo vim eam, quae deprauare ipsam naturam Adami poterat, non habebat. Resp. Neg. consequ. Angeli apostatae per vnum actum peccaminosum statum suum euerterunt, naturamque corruperunt. Serpens vno ictu totam hominis naturam veneno inficit. Vno vulnere oculo inflicto visus eripitur.

V. Quodcunque Deus vt iustus iudex abstulit, illud non naturaliter, sed meritorie tantum fuit amissum. Atqui imaginem primaeam Deus &c. Ergo. Maior constat; quia priuatio iudicialis moralis, non physica est. Resp. Neg. maior. Nam per crapulam homo physice sibi eripit sanitatem. Interim tamen Deus vt iustus iudex punit ebriosum per vitae abbreviationem.

VI. Cuius caussa non fuit physica, illud non physicum & naturale potest dici. Atqui caussa amissionis imaginis primaeae non fuit physica, Ergo. Maior per se patet; quia, qualis caussa, talis effectus. Minor liquet; quia caussa imaginis amittae fuit lapsus Adami, qui erat actus moraliter malus. Resp. Caussa amissionis imaginis divinae & physica & moralis fuit: moralis; dum protoplasti peccando poenam Dei, qui actu iudiciali ipsos iustitia originali priuauit, incurrerunt: physica; dum iidem actu peccaminoso habitum creatum expulerunt; sicut, qui venenum sumit, & moraliter in se agit, & sanitatem physice expellit.


### Quest. XXVI. What practical use does the doctrine of the image of God confer?

The doctrine of the image of God, drawn from the fountain of Holy Scripture, pours forth from itself a significant use into all parts of theology.

Prob. For from that, once solidly perceived, we 1) call to memory the goodness of the Creator, who out of most free grace communicated Himself to man originally created, and wondrously adorned the same, as if a holy temple which He was about to fill with His gracious presence, with perfections very similar to His own wisdom, holiness, purity, immortality, and power. 2) We acknow-holy temple, which He was about to fill with His gracious presence, with perfections very similar to His own wisdom, holiness, purity, immortality, and power.

2) We acknowledge from this doctrine the abyss of misery into which man, having lost the image of God through the abuse of free will, has fallen. For in the place of the lost image succeeded a horrible corruption of human nature, through which we have become guilty of divine wrath and eternal damnation. There migrated, alas! into the intellect darkness instead of light, into the will iniquity instead of holiness, into the appetite depravity instead of rectitude, into the body frailty instead of immortality, and into the whole of life a heap of various calamities instead of pristine happiness.

Remember, O man, from whence you have fallen, and repent, Apoc. II, 5.

3) Struck with amazement, we admire the abyss of divine mercy provoked by the merit of Christ. For Jesus, the author of our salvation, has merited for us the restoration of the divine image, both by the most full fulfillment of the divine law and by His bloody passion and satisfactory death; from which He begins to reform the divine likeness in us through the Holy Spirit in this life, intending to consummate that work of grace in eternal life, in which we shall be rendered like unto Him. Io. III, 2.

S I G H T.

The memory very often comes upon us, O eternal God, best and greatest Creator of this universe, that You fashioned our first parents after the pattern of Your wisdom, and impressed upon them the most brilliant image of Your holiness. Nothing more splendid than this light of souls, nothing more beautiful than this adornment, nothing more excellent than such an open pledge of divine goodness can be said or imagined. We bitterly mourn that the loss of so excellent a gift, of such incomparable perfection, was brought about by the instigation of the devil and the consent of man, and we abhor with our whole heart that the mask of the devil has been induced upon human minds. But to You, sweetest Jesus, we give abundant thanks that by the shedding of Your blood You have opened for us a way to recover Your likeness. Send, I beseech You, Your Spirit into our hearts, who may draw and paint therein the lines of Your image, so that by chaste manners of life we may, O good Jesus, never cease to reflect You!

PART II.

Latin:

Hausta e fonte S. scripturae doctrina de imagine Dei insignem in omnes theologiae partes ex se fundit vsum.

Prob. Nam ex illa solide percepta nobis 1) in memoriam reuocamus bonitatem creatoris, qui ex gratia liberrima homini primitus condito seipsum communicauit, & eundem velut sanctum templum, quod gratiosa praesentia sua impleturus erat, perfectionibus, sua sapientiae, sanctitati, puritati, immortalitati & potestati perquam fumilibus, mirifice exornauit. 2) Agnosanctum templum, quod gratiosa præfentia sua impleturus erat, perfectionibus, fuæ fapientiæ, fanctitati, puritati, immortalitati & potestati perquam similibus, mirifice exornauit.

2) Agnoscimus ex hac doctrina abyſſum miſeriæ, in quam homo, amiſſa per abuſum liberi arbitrii imagine Dei, prolapſus eſt. Nam in locum amiſſæ imaginis ſucceſſit horribilis naturæ humanæ corruptio, per quam iræ diuinæ & æternæ damnationis rei facti ſumus. Immigrauit, proh dolor! in intellectum pro luce caligo, in voluntatem pro ſanctitate iniquitas, in appetitum pro rectitudine prauitas, in corpus pro immortalitate fragilitas, in totam vitam pro priſtina felicitate variarum calamitatum cumulus.

Recordare, o homo, vnde excideris, & age pœnitentiam, Apoc. II, 5.

3) Stupore defixi miramur abyſſum diuinæ miſericordiæ merito Chriſti prouocata. Salutis enim noſtræ auctor Ieſus tum pleniſſima legis diuinæ impletione, tum cruenta paſſione & morte ſatisfactoria inſtaurationem imaginis diuinæ nobis promeruit; ex quo effigiem diuinam per Spiritum S. in nobis reformare incipit in hac vita, conſummaturus iſtud opus gratiæ in vita æterna, in qua ſimiles ipſi reddemur. Io. III, 2.

S V S P I R I V M.

Memoriam noſtram fæpiſſime ſubit, Deus æterne, conditor huius vniuerſi optime, Maxime, te primos noſtros parentes ad exemplar tuæ ſapientiæ effinxiſſe, iisdemque ſanctitatis tuæ imaginem impreſſiſſe luculentiſſimam. Nihil iſthac animarum luce ſplendidius, nihil iſto decore pulcrius, nihil tam aperto bonitatis diuinæ pignore præſtabilius dici fingique poteſt. Iacturam tam eximii doni, tam incomparabilis perfectionis, inſtigante diabolo & conſentiente homine, factam eſſe, acerbe lugemus, laruamque diaboli mentibus humanis inductam eſſe, toto pectore exhorreſcimus. At tibi, dulciſſime Ieſu, prolixas agimus gratias, quod fuſo ſanguine tuo ad recuperandam effigiem tuam viam nobis aperueris. Imitte, obſecro, vel cordibus noſtris Spiritum tuum, qui in iis lineas tuæ imaginis ducat & pingat, quo caſtis vitæ moribus te, bone Ieſu, nunquam non referamus!

PARTIS II.


## 12 Of Sin in General


### Of Sin in General

Quest. I. What is sin? Sin is an aberration from the divine law.

It is defined more fully: Definition of sin. Sin is an aberration from the divine law, binding rational creatures, culpable, and bringing upon itself temporal and eternal punishment.

This definition is proved from Io. III, 4, where sin is briefly described by St. John: Ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐστὶν ἡ ἀνομία, sin is lawlessness.

Obj. 1) The word, ἀνομία, is not translated in only one way. That it is derived from ἄνομος is certain. But that this adjective, ἄνομος, denotes one who is without law, or who has no law, is evident from Rom. II, 12; 1 Cor. IX, 21; yet for the most part it denotes a wicked person and one who is contrary to the laws.

Whence ἀνομία could indeed be a state outside the law, or without law: In Scripture, however, as Mr. ERASMUS SCHMID also well notes on this passage, it is never found used in that way; but it is always found in such a way that the alpha is privative, or adversative, by which a certain contrariety is indicated.

The Vulgate translates τὴν ἀνομίαν as iniquity.

But iniquity seems to imply more than sin considered in general. For every man freely confesses himself a sinner, but to call himself an iniquitous person sometimes [is] to blush—

blushes. There are those who translate it with one word, illegality; but that is neither accepted by the Latins, nor is it sufficiently clear. Indeed, the name illex, which PLAUTUS uses, is the same for VALLA as exlex; in which way it agrees with the former meaning of ἀνομία, but not with the latter, which belongs to this place. Therefore, by BEZA, ERASMUS, SCHMIDIUS, and others, it is rendered as transgression of the law. But this translation also does not satisfy, and restricts it rather to actual sin, than including original sin as well. All these things considered, by D. SEB. SCHMIDIUS in colleg. bibl. poster. p. 135, it is rendered as dislegality and contralegality, so that it may note a disagreement with the law. Moreover, ἀνομία is indeed one word, yet it virtually contains two or more. To most theologians, the α in ἀνομία seems to be στερητικόν, or privative, from whose opinion it notes a privation, as an analogical genus of sin; but the difference is taken from the norm of justice, namely from the law, from which sin deflects. But D. IO. ADAM OSIANDER observes in theol. posit. p. 262, that the form of sin consists not in mere privation, but also in a contrariety opposed to the law. Therefore he defines sin by prevarication against the law, given and laid down by God. l. c. p. 260. We have described sin by an aberration from the law, through which a privation is indeed indicated, but not a mere one, since a certain aberration from the law resists the law in a hostile and stubborn manner. Objection 2) To the former definition, which consists of an analogical genus and a difference, we have added a more prolix one, so that the subject of inhesion may also be expressed, which are rational creatures, that is, intelligent ones, angels and men, to whom the divine law is both inscribed and prescribed, so that their will may be contained within the limits of moral goodness; and also the consequence, the state of guilt and punishment. For sin is not only base and unbecoming to a rational creature, in which sense it is called culpable; but it also renders sinning creatures liable to temporal punishments no less than to eternal ones.

Latin:

Quæſt. I. Quid eſt peccatum? Peccatum eſt aberratio a lege diuinæ.

Vberius definitur: Definitio peccati. Peccatum eſt aberratio a lege diuinæ, creaturas rationales obligante, culpabilis, & pœnam temporalem atque æternam inferens.

Probatur hæc definitio ex Io. III, 4. vbi a S. Ioanne peccatum breuiter deſcribitur: Ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐστὶν ἡ ἀνομία, peccatum eſt dislegalitas.

Obs. 1) Vox, ἀνομία, non vno modo vertitur. Deductum eſſe ab ἄνομος, certum eſt. Hoc vero adiectiuum, ἄνομος modo notare eum, qui fine lege eſt, ſeu qui nullam legem habet, conſtat ex Rom. II, 12. 1 Cor. IX, 21. plerumque tamen ſceleratum & legibus contrariantem denotat.

Vnde ἀνομία poſſet quidem eſſe ſtatus extra legem, vel fine lege: In ſcriptura tamen, quod bene etiam annotat Dn. ERASM. SCHMIDIVS in h. l. nunquam iſto modo vſurpatum inuenitur; ſed ſemper ita, vt alpha ſit ἐνατιτικὸν, ſeu aduerſatiuum, quo contrarietas quædam indicatur, reperitur.

Vulgatus τὴν ἀνομίαν iniquitatem vertit.

At plus inferre videtur iniquitas, quam peccatum in genere conſideratum. Nam omnis homo ſe libere peccatorem fatetur, iniquum vero dicere nonnunquam eruverò dicere nonnunquam verò dicere nonnunquam verò dicere nonnunquam

erubescit. Sunt, qui una voce, illegalitas, interpretantur; sed ea nec recepta a Latinis, nec satis clara est. Quin immo nomen illex, quo PLAVTVS utitur, VALLAE idem est, quod exlex; quomodo cum priori significatione ἀνομίας convenit, non autem cum posteriori, quae huius loci est. Idcirco a BEZA, ERASM. SCHMIDIO, & aliis redditur, legis transgressio. Verum haec quoque versio non satisfacit, & ad peccatum actuale potius restringit, quam peccatum originale quoque includit. Quibus omnibus consideratis, a D. SEB. SCHMIDIO in colleg. bibl. poster. p. 135. dislegalitas, & contralegalitas redditur, ut notet disconvenientiam cum lege. Ceterum ἀνομία una quidem vox est, virtualiter tamen duas vel plures continet. Plerisque theologis τὸ α, in ἀνομίᾳ, videtur esse στερητικόν, seu privativum, quorum de sententia notat privationem, tanquam genus analogicum peccati; differentia autem sumitur a norma iustitiae, nempe a lege, a qua peccatum deflectit. At vero observat D. IO. ADAM OSIANDER in theol. posit p. 262. quod forma peccati consistat non in mera privatione, sed & contrarietate opposita legi. Ideo peccatum definit, per praevaricationem contra legem, a Deo datam & latam. l. c. p. 260. Nos descripsimus peccatum per aberrationem a lege, per quam indicitatur quidem privatio, sed non mera, cum quaedam aberratio a lege hostiliter & praefracte legi repugnet. Obs. 2) Definitioni priori, quae genere analogo & differentia constat, prolixiorem adiunximus, ut exprimatur etiam subiectum inhaesionis, quod sunt creaturae rationales, sive intelligentes, angeli & homines, quibus lex diuina tum inscripta, tum praescripta est, ut voluntas earum intra bonitatis moralis limites contineatur; nec non consequens, reatus culpae & poenae. Nam peccatum non tantum est turpe & indecorum creaturae rationali, quo sensu dicitur culpabile; sed & creaturas peccantes poenis temporalibus non minus, quam aeternis obnoxias reddit.


### Quæst. II. From where is sin derived?

From where is sin derived? Sin (peccatum) is said to come from pecco (to sin), and this from the Latin noun pecus (cattle).

Proof. For to sin is to act without reason after the manner of cattle. Compare IVL. CAESAR SCALIGER, c. 31. Cauff. lat. lingu. and BECMANN, orig. lat. lingu. p. 818.

Latin:

Peccatum dicitur a pecco, & hoc a latino nomine pecus.

Prob. Nam peccare, est more pecudum sine ratione agere. Conf. IVL. CAESAR SCALIGER, c. 31. Cauff. lat. lingu. & BECMANN. orig. lat. lingu. p. 818.


### Quæst. III. In how many ways is the word 'sin' taken?

Sin generally denotes any deflection from a rule; specifically it designates a deflection from the rule of divine law.

Proof. Sin, taken in a general sense, varies according to the variety of the rule from which it deflects. Thus, one thing is natural sin, e.g., a monster; another is artificial, e.g., a statue incongruously crafted; another is moral, which is defined either in an ethical and political sense, or in a theological sense. To politicians, occupied in the civil forum, sin is an action committed by one who knows and wills, against natural, international, and civil law. Original sin, and the internal motions of the appetite, which precede reason, the same people either ignore or hold in little regard. Theologically, however, any ἀνομία, or dislegality, is called sin, whether that ἀνομία be original or actual, whether it be committed ἄνευ προαιρέσεως (without deliberate choice), out of ignorance and infirmity, or whether it proceeds ἐκ τῆς προαιρέσεως (from deliberate choice), out of a deliberate counsel of the mind.

Latin:

Peccatum generatim notat quamlibet deflexionem a regula; speciatim designat deflexionem a regula legis diuinae.

Prob. Peccatum, sumtum sensu generali, pro varietate regulae, a qua deflectit, variat. Sic aliud est peccatum naturale, v. gr. monstrum; aliud artificiale, v. gr. statua incongrue elaborata; aliud morale, quod funitur vel in sensu ethico & politico, vel in sensu theologico. Politicis, in foro civili versantibus, peccatum est actio, a sciente & volente, contra legem naturalem, gentium & civilem commissa. Peccatum originis, motusque appetitus internos, rationem anteuertentes, iidem vel ignorant, vel parum pensi habent. Theologice autem quaelibet ἀνομία, siue dislegalitas, dicitur peccatum, siue illa ἀνομία fit originalis, siue actualis, siue committatur ἄνευ προαιρέσεως, ex ignorantia & infirmitate, siue proficiscatur ἐκ τῆς προαιρέσεως, ex deliberato animi consilio.


### Quæst. IV. In how many ways is sin taken theologically?

Theologically, sin is considered in two ways: 1) abstractly, insofar as it notes the dislegality itself, or discrepancy from divine law; 2) concretely, insofar as both the dislegality, and the act, or habit, to which the dislegality adheres, it signifies.

Prob. Theft comprises two things: a) ἀνομίαν i.e., discrepancy from the law, b) the extension of the hand, by which against the law, the owner being unwilling, something is taken away.

Latin:

Theologice peccatum bifariam consideratur 1) abstractive, quatenus ipsam dislegalitatem, seu discrepantiam a lege diuina notat; 2) concretive, quatenus tum dislegalitatem, tum actum, vel habitum, cui dislegalitas adhæret, significat.

Prob. Furtum duo complectitur: a) ἀνομίαν f. discrepantiam a lege, b) extensionem manus, qua contra legem invito domino aliquid aufertur.


### Q. V. What is the cause of sin?

Of sin, considered abstractively, there is no efficient physical cause . But, if it be considered concretively, it altogether has an efficient physical cause .

Prob. a. An efficient physical cause is that which through a positive action produces a real and positive effect. But sin is a defect, not an effect: it is a privation, not a positive being, and therefore it proceeds from no cause, physically efficient, of ἀνομία.

Prob. b. Sin, considered concretively, is an act, or habit, to which ἀνομία adheres; which act, or habit, since it is something positive, certainly depends on a physical cause, e.g., of that striking by which Abel was killed, the physical cause was Cain.

Latin:

Peccati, abstractive spectati, non datur causa efficiens physica . At, si consideretur concretive, omnino causam efficientem physicam habet .

Prob. a. Causa efficiens physica est, quæ per actionem positivam producit effectum realem & positivum. At peccatum est defectus, non effectus: est privatio, non ens positivum, adeoque a nulla causa, physice efficiente, ἀνομία proficiscitur.

Prob. b. Peccatum, concretive spectatum, est actus, vel habitus, cui ἀνομία adhæret; qui actus, vel habitus, cum sit aliquid positivum, utique a causa physica dependet, v. gr. percussionis illius, qua Habel est occisus, causa physica fuit Cain.


### Q. VI. What is

moral cause of sin considered abstractively? The moral cause of sin, considered abstractively, is an intelligent creature, determined to the good, whose free and mutable will deflects from the divine law, and thus in acting fails of its own accord.

Prob. In the genus of morals, the efficient cause is that which, although it does not produce τὴν ἀνομίαν, or dislegality, by a real and positive influx, since it is a defect, nevertheless intends it directly or indirectly, so that in view of that intention the ἀνομία is imputed to it, just as if it had produced it by a real influx: e.g., If anyone performs an action, with which he knows ἀνομίαν to be conjoined, in the genus of morals he is called the cause of that dislegality itself, or sin, taken abstractively.

Others prefer to call it a deficient cause, with AUGUSTINE lib. XII. de Civit. D. c. VI., namely, that if the agent is considered precisely in relation to ἀνομία, not by reason of any influx, but by reason of some defect in causing, or because it does not act conformably, it is called its cause. Indeed the apostle John says clearly, 1 Epist. c. III, 4. He who does τὴν ἁμαρτίαν, i.e., sin, at the same time does τὴν ἀνομίαν, or contrariety to law, namely by this very fact, that he does τὸ ἄνομον, which differs from the law. Now indeed intelligent creatures, angels and men, deflecting from the rule of the divine law, do τὸ ἄνομον, which they know to be difform to the divine law. Therefore to them ἡ ἀνομία is imputed, just as if they had provided a real influx into the dislegality itself; therefore they are the moral causes of sin, considered abstractively. Yet the same rational creatures can be called deficient causes of sin, because when they are considered precisely in relation to τὴν ἀνομίαν, they are denominated causes τῆς ἀνομίας not on account of a positive influx provided into this, but on account of a certain defect in acting, or aberration from the rule. This is inculcated in the Augustan Confession, art. XIX. They teach concerning the cause of sin, that although God creates and preserves nature, yet the cause of sin is the will of the wicked, namely of the devil and the impious, which, God not assisting, turns itself away from God, as Christ says, Jo. VIII, 44. When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own self.

Latin:

causa moralis peccati abstractive spectati? Causa moralis peccati, abstractive spectati, est creatura intelligens, ad bonum determinata, cuius voluntas libera & mutabilis a lege diuina deflectit, atque adeo in agendo sponte sua deficit.

Prob. In genere morum causa efficiens est, quæ τὴν ἀνομίαν, siue dislegalitatem, cum sit defectus, reali & positivo influxu non producit, eam tamen directe, vel indirecte, intendit vt illius intentionis intuitu ἀνομία ipsi imputetur, ac secus, ac si reali influxu eam produxisset: v. gr. Si quis patrat actionem, cum qua ἀνομίαν coniunctam esse nouit, in genere morum dicitur causa ipsius dislegalitatis, siue peccati, abstractive sumti. Alii causam deficientem appellare malunt, cum AVGVSTINO lib. XII. de Ciuit. D. c. VI. scilicet, quod, si præcise in ordine ad ἀνομίαν agens consideretur, non ratione alicuius influxus, sed ratione alicuius in causando defectus, seu quod non conformiter agit, eius causa dicatur.

Sane apostolus Ioannes diserte inquit, 1 Epist. c. III, 4. Qui facit τὴν ἁμαρτίαν, f. peccatum, simul facit τὴν ἀνομίαν, siue contralegalitatem, scilicet hoc ipso, quod facit τὸ ἄνομον, quod a lege discrepat. Iam vero creaturæ intelligentes, angeli & homines, a regula legis diuinæ deflectentes, faciunt τὸ ἄνομον, quod legi diuinæ difforme esse nouerunt. Ergo ipsis ἡ ἀνομία imputatur, perinde, ac si in ipsam dislegalitatem realem influxum præbuissent; ideo peccati, abstractive spectati, sunt causæ morales. Possunt tamen eadem creaturæ rationales vocari peccati causæ deficientes, quia cum præcise in ordine ad τὴν ἀνομίαν considerantur, non ob præstitum in hanc positivum influxum, sed ob quendam in agendo defectum, aut aberrationem a regula, causæ τῆς ἀνομίας denominantur. Inculcatur hoc in Augustan. confessione, art. XIX. De causa peccati docent, quod tametsi Deus creat & conferuat naturam, tamen causa peccati est voluntas malorum, videlicet diaboli & impiorum, quæ, non adiuuante Deo, auertit se a Deo, sicut Christus ait, Io. VIII, 44. Cum loquitur mendacium, ex se ipso loquitur.


### Q. VII. Is God the cause of sin?

God is neither the moral a), nor the physical cause of sin b). Prob. a. The moral cause of sin is that which intends it, so that by reason of an efficacious intention it can be imputed to it: But God in no way intends sin: Therefore. The minor is proved: 1) God is most holy and by essence good, Matt. XIX, 17. Therefore, his holiness and goodness being saved, he cannot intend evil.

2) God does not will sin: Therefore he does not intend that it be committed. The antecedent is evident from Ps. V, 5, 6, 7. For God, not approving impiety, you (are), the evil man shall not dwell with you: the boastful shall not stand before your eyes: You hate all workers of iniquity. God so greatly detests sin that he by no means approves it, but excludes sinners from the communion of his grace, and pursues them with hatred. But he who so greatly disapproves of sin, that he excludes delinquents from the communion of his grace, and burns with hatred against them, he neither directly nor indirectly intends that sin be perpetrated by any creature.

3) God instigates, entices, or solicits no one to sin. This is what St. James teaches most openly c. I, 13. Let no one, when he is tempted, say; because I am tempted by God. For God is un-temptable by evils, for God cannot be tempted by evils; whence he himself (also) tempts no one. The Apostle uses an argument of great weight: Whoever excels in such constant and immutable holiness that he permits himself to be instigated to evil by no temptation, he solicits no one to evil: But God does so, etc. Therefore. The major is manifest; because every temptation directed to evil, as much active as passive, is repugnant to essential and immutable holiness. To whom every instigation to evil is hateful, he neither receives in himself a temptation to evil, nor solicits another to evil.

4) In particular, indeed, that God is not the author or cause of the Adamic fall is proven: a) because God had adorned the first man with an image most similar to himself, and had intimately perfected him, Gen. I, 26, 27, and therefore had not created him prone to sin. b) The causes of the Adamic fall, as Moses relates, were the devil seducing and man freely consenting, Gen. III, 1, etc. c) God had forbidden sin to the protoplast humans under the threat of most grievous punishment, Gen. II, 17. d) God punished the committed sin with the greatest penalty. But, of whom God is the avenger, of him he is not the author.

5) Of sins that have arisen, or are derived from the first sin to posterity, the cause is not God, but a) the devil, who did not stand in the truth and is the father of lies, John VIII, 44, to whom nothing is earlier or more ancient than to blind the minds of men, 2 Cor. IV, 4, to work in the children of disobedience, Eph. II, 2, and to hold them captive, 2 Tim. II, 29; b) the world lying in the evil one, 1 John V, 19, whom whoever loves, in him is not the love of the father, 1 John II, 15; c) the inclination of the will to evil, Rom. III, 12; the concupiscence of the flesh, by which men are drawn away from the good and are baited to evil, James I, 14. Proof b.

That God is not the physical cause of sin, taken concretely, or of the sinful act and habit, is clearly evident; since God, as the universal cause, concurs with all actions of creatures, and therefore also with those actions of men which are evil, but not insofar as they are evil: he concurs, I say, with actions, insofar as they are physical motions, unlimited and indifferent, not insofar as they are determined to a certain object. From this it follows that God, on account of his general and indeterminate concurrence with the evil actions of men, is not called their physical cause. The reason is: because the determination and specification of acts, and the denomination which depends on these, is not from the universal cause, but from the particular. Therefore the latter, not the former, is called the cause of the inordinate or irregular motion. Thus the gait of one limping, insofar as it is motion, depends on the locomotive faculty of the soul, but not insofar as it is a deformed and inordinate motion: for this proceeds from another cause coming from without, a fall, a contusion, or a collision of the foot. Therefore not the soul or its locomotive faculty, but the luxated or bruised foot is called the physical cause of the limping. By the same reasoning, when a thief extends his hand to steal the goods of another, that extension of the hand is both from God, as the universal cause, and from the thief, as the cause particular action, depends: on God; as it is an indifferent and indeterminate action: on the thief; insofar as it is an action determined to steal the goods of another against the will of the owner. Wherefore, not God, but the thief is denominated the physical cause of that sinful action; for it is not the former, but the latter who fails in acting.

Antithesis is 1) of the ancient heretics, Simon Magus, the Valentinians, the Manichaeans, the Marcionites, the Priscillianists, who had no religion, to call God the cause of sins: 2) of the Socinians, who likewise constitute God as the cause of sin.

Whose stronger arguments are:

I. God hardens and blinds men: Therefore God is the cause of sin.

The consequence is evident; because hardening and blinding is a great sin.

The antecedent is proved from Exod.

VII, 3.

Rom.

IX, 18.

Is.

VI, 6.

Resp. God does not harden men causally or effectively, by injecting hardness into the hearts of men, but judicially, permissively, and by desertion.

For hardening is a judicial act, by which, on account of preceding voluntary and avoidable malice, God justly permits a habitually evil man to rush into graver crimes, and withdraws His grace from him, and finally delivers him to the power of Satan, by whom he is subsequently driven into greater sins, until he finally falls away from the right of the heavenly inheritance.

See

KOENIG. theol. positiu. p.

98. Furthermore, it can be said that Pharaoh was hardened by God first ἐκβατικῶς, or eventually and occasionally: not as if God by His own intention offered Pharaoh the occasion of hardening, but because Pharaoh, while neither his strength was immediately and entirely confused, out of the kindness and long-suffering of God, which he foully abused, seized the occasion to harden his own mind.

See

FRANZ. de interpr.

S. scripturae qu.

24. & 26.

Afterwards God hardened Pharaoh διασημῶς or judicially.

Instance. God is said to have excited Pharaoh to demonstrate His power to him.

Rom.

IX, 17.

Therefore God effectively hardened him through an internal impulse.

Resp. 1) Not excitement to hardening, but the preservation of life, is hinted at in the Hebrew manner in the cited place.

For Exod.

IX, 16.

(from which place the words of Paul are taken) the verb העמדתי is used, I made you stand, i.e., I did not suddenly strike you and cut you off from the earth, but I made you subsist, so that you might most humbly acknowledge my power, and perform true repentance for sins, and so that all nations might be invited to the veneration of my name.

(*).

Latin:

Deus neque est moralis a), neque physica causa peccati b). Prob. a. Causa moralis peccati est, quæ illud intendit, vt ratione intentionis efficacis ipsi imputari queat: At Deus nullo modo peccatum intendit: Ergo. Minor probatur: 1) Deus est sanctissimus & per essentiam bonus, Matth. XIX, 17. Ergo, salua sanctitate & bonitate sua malum intendere nequit.

2) Deus peccatum non vult: Ergo non intendit, vt illud committatur. Antecedens patet e Ps. V, 5. 6. 7.
