Non enim Deus approbans impietatem tu (es), non manebit apud te malus: non consistent gloriabundi coram oculis tuis: Odisti omnes operatores iniquitatis. Deus tantopere peccatum detestatur, vt illud nequaquam approbet, sed peccantes a communione gratiae suae excludat, eosque odio prosequatur. Sed qui peccatum tantopere improbat, vt delinquentes a communione gratiae suae excludat, in eosque odio ardeat, ille neque directe, neque indirecte intendit, vt peccatum ab vlla creatura perpetretur.

3) Deus neminem ad peccatum instigat, allicit, aut sollicitat. Id quod apertissime docet S. Iacobus c. I, 13. Nemo, quum tentatur, dicito; quia a Deo tentor. Ο γὰρ θεὸς ἀπείραστός ἐσι κακῶν, Deus enim non tentari potest a malis; vnde ipse (etiam) neminem tentat. Apostolus vtitur argumento magni ponderis: Quicunque adeo constanti & immutabili eninet sanctitate, vt nulla tentatione ad malum se instigari permittat, is neminem ad malum sollicitat: Atqui Deus &c. Ergo. Maior est manifesta; quia sanctitati essentiali & immutabili omnis ad malum directa tentatio tam actiua, quam passiva repugnat. Cui exosa est omnis ad malum instigatio, is neque tentationem ad malum in se recipit, neque alium ad malum sollicitat.

4) In specie vero Deum non esse auctorem, aut caussam lapsus Adamitici, probatur: a) quia Deus hominem primum imagine sibi simillima exornauerat, intimeque perfecerat, Gen. I, 26. 27. adeoque ad peccatum procliuem non creauerat. b) Caussae lapsus Adamitici, referente Mose, fuerunt diabolus seducens & homo libere consentiens, Gen. III, 1. sq. c) Peccatum Deus hominibus protoplastis sub comminatione poenae grauissimae interdixerat. Gen. II, 17. d) Commissum peccatum Deus maximo supplicio vindicauit. At, cuius Deus est vltor, illius non est auctor.

5) Peccatorum ortorum, siue e peccato primo ad posteros deriuatorum, caussa non est Deus, sed a) diabolus, qui in veritate non stetit & pater est mendacii, Io. VIII, 44. cui nihil prius aut antiquius est, quam mentes hominum excaecare, 2 Cor. IV, 4. in filiis incredulitatis operari, Eph. II, 2. eosque captiuos tenere, 2 Tim. II, 29; b) mundus iacens in maligno, 1 Io. V, 19. quem qui diligit, in illo non est dilectio patris, 1 Io. II, 15; c) voluntatis inclinatio ad malum, Rom. III, 12; concupiscentia carnis, a qua homines a bono abstrahuntur & ad malum inescantur, Iac. I, 14. Prob. b.

Deum non esse caussam physicam peccati, concretive sumti, siue actus & habitus peccaminosi, liquido constat; siquidem Deus, vt caussa vniuersalis, ad omnes actiones creaturarum, adeoque etiam ad illas hominum actiones, quae sunt malae, non autem quatenus sunt malae, concurrit: concurrit, inquam, ad actiones, prout sunt motus physici illimitati & indifferentes, non prout ad certum obiectum sunt determinati. Exinde fit, vt Deus, ob concursum generalem & indeterminatum ad actiones hominum malas, harum caussa physica non dicatur. Ratio est: quia determinatio & specificatio actuum, & quae ab his dependet denominatio, non est a caussa vniuersali, sed particulari. Proinde haec, non illa, motus inordinati vel irregularis caussa appellatur. Sic claudicantis incessus, in quantum est motus, dependet ab animae facultate locomotiua, non autem quatenus est deformis & inordinatus motus: hic enim ab alia caussa forinsecus superueniente, lapsu, contritione aut collisione pedis proficiscitur. Idcirco non anima aut eius facultas locomotiua, sed pes luxatus, aut contusus, caussa physica claudicationis appellatur. Pari ratione, cum fur extendit manum ad furripiendum bona aliena, illa extensio manus tum a Deo, vt caussa vniuersali, tum a fure, vt caussa fa particulari, dependet: a Deo; vt est actio indifferens & indeterminata: a fure; quatenus est actio determinata ad furripiendum bona aliena inuito domino. Quapropter actionis illius peccaminosae non Deus, sed fur causa physica denominatur; neque enim ille, sed hic in agendo deficit.

Antithesis est 1) veterum haereticorum, Simonis Magi, Valentinianorum, Manichaeorum, Marcionitarum, Priscillianistarum, quibus nulla fuit religio, Deum appellare causam peccatorum: 2) Socinianorum, qui itidem Deum causam peccati constituunt.

Quorum potiora sunt argumenta:

I. Deus homines indurat & excaecat: Ergo Deus est causa peccati.

Consequentia patet; quia induratio & excaecatio est grande peccatum.

Antecedens probatur ex Exod.

VII, 3.

Rom.

IX, 18.

Es.

VI, 6.

Resp. Deus non indurat homines causaliter aut effective, cordibus hominum duritiem immittendo, sed iudicialiter, permissive & desertive.

Est enim induratio actus iudicialis, quo ob antegressam voluntariam & euitabilem malitiam Deus hominem habitualiter malum iuste permittit ruere in scelera grauiora, eidemque gratiam suam subtrahit, & denique Satanae potestati eum tradit, a quo in maiora subinde peccata propellitur, donec excidat finaliter iure haereditatis coelestis.

Vid.

KOENIG. theol. positiu. p.

98. Praeterea dici potest, quod Pharao a Deo induratus sit primum ἐκβατικῶς, seu euentualiter & occasionaliter: non perinde, ac si Deus propria intentione Pharaoni occasionem indurationis obiecerit, sed quia Pharao, dum neque statim & nequa omnis eius vis penitus confusa fuit, ex benignitate & longanimitate Dei, qua foede abusus est, arripuit occasionem obdurandi animum suum.

Vid.

FRANZ. de interpr.

S. scripturae qu.

24. & 26.

Postea Deus Pharaonem iudurauit διασημῶς seu iudicialiter.

Instantia. Deus dicitur excitasse Pharaonem ad demonstrandam ipsi potentiam suam.

Rom.

IX, 17.

Ergo Deus eundem effective indurauit per internum impulsum.

Resp. 1) Non excitatio ad indurationem, sed conservatio vitae, more hebraico l. c. innuitur.

Nam Exod.

IX, 16.

(e quo loco verba Pauli desumta sunt) usurpatur verbum העמדתי, stare feci te, i. e. non subito te percussi & e terra excidi, sed te subsistere feci, vt meam potentiam humilliune agnosceres, feriamque peccatorum poenitentiam ageres, atque adeo omnes gentes ad venerationem nominis mei inuitarentur.

(*).


### Q. VII. Is God the cause of sin?: 2) Pharaoh effectively hardened himself

2) Pharaoh effectively hardened himself,

Exod. VIII, 32.

II.

Whoever sends to men the efficacy of error, he is the cause of sin: for error in matters of faith is no light sin.

But God &c.

2 Thess.

II, 11.

Therefore.

Resp. by limiting: Whoever causally and by positive influx sends to men the efficacy of error, he is the cause of sin; I concede.

But the most holy God, on account of the preceding sins of men, sends the efficacy of error, partly permissively, by permitting effective errors, partly negatively, by withdrawing perfecting grace and that which illuminates with full effect.

III. Whoever commands a man to sin, he is the cause of sin: But God, etc. Therefore. The minor is proven, 1) by the example of Abraham, whom God commanded to kill his own son, Gen. 22:2; 2) by the example of Shimei, whom God commanded to curse his king, 2 Sam. 16:10, which it is established is a very great sin from Exod. 22:28.

Resp. I deny the minor.

To the former example we say that God is the author and Lord of life; by whose command, he who takes life from another does not sin.

To the latter, we respond that that sin was at the same time a punishment, and thus an action with respect to Shimei, a passion with respect to David.

The sinful action proceeded from the malevolent mind of Shimei and the instigation of the devil; which, when God foresaw, He said (it is not in the Hebrew source: He commanded) to Shimei, i.e., He granted the power, so that by the curse, which he himself had conceived in his mind by the instigation of the devil, he might afflict David the exile, by which he might be the more brought to the recognition and detestation of his own sin.

Hence was born the most common verse: The action displeased; the passion was pleasing.

IV. Whoever leads us into temptation, he is the cause of sin. But God, etc. Therefore. The minor is clear from Matt. 6:10, where we pray against divine temptations.

Resp. Distinguish a) between the temptation of probation and of seduction.

Into the former, not the latter, God effectively leads us. b) God indeed permits men to be led into the temptation of seduction, but He does not impel the enemies of the soul to it.

V. Whoever makes vessels of wrath, he is the cause of sin. But God, etc. Rom. 9:

22. Therefore. Resp.

A pseudermēneia (false interpretation) is committed.

For vessels of wrath are prepared for destruction not by God (since the context does not teach this); but by themselves.

For God is said to tolerate the vessels of wrath.

Whatever someone tolerates, he neither does himself, nor intends that it be done by others.

VI. Whoever incites a man to pride, he is the cause of sin. But God, etc. Therefore. The minor is evident from 2 Sam.

24:1, where God is said to have incited David to number the people. Resp.

God is said to have moved David to number the people not by an efficacious suggestion, but by a judicial permission, in that He granted power to Satan, on account of preceding sins, by punishing David through the instigation to sin.

For a) 1 Chron.

21:1, Satan is said to have instigated David.

Namely, God permissively; Satan effectively, and of himself, instigates. b) The word סות in Hiphil conveniently admits a permissive meaning, which the parallel passage requires. c) If God had effectively instigated, David would have deserved not punishment, but praise and rewards, by obeying God.

VII. God commanded the Israelites to despoil the Egyptians, Exod. 11:2.

Therefore He is the cause of sin.

Resp. The Israelites, the goods which they took from the Egyptians, did not steal, but the supreme Lord of things had assigned them as wages for labors exhausted over many years.

Nor did they find the former masters unwilling, but compliant, God reconciling them and transferring the ownership to them.

You say: A borrower, stealing a thing borrowed for a certain use, steals.

Resp. Unless it is assigned to the possessor by the authority of either the supreme owner or the supreme judge.

VIII. God is said to have delivered the nations into impurity, Rom. 1:24.

Therefore He intended that the nations should live impurely.

Resp. God delivered the nations into impurity, not by impelling their minds to impurity, but by His just judgment by permitting them to their own desires and delivering them into the power of Satan, who, as a most impure spirit, instilled into them an ever more shameful impurity.

IX. Whoever by His decree delivered the Lord Jesus to Pilate, Herod, the Jews, and the crucifiers, so that He might be mocked and killed by them, he is the cause of sin. But God, etc.

Acts 2:23, Acts 4:28.

Resp. 1) Distinguish between the passion of Christ and the sinful action of the Jews; 2) between permission and approbation.

God had indeed decreed that the Lord Jesus should redeem the human race through a most bitter passion and reconcile it to God, but He did not impel the Jews to the most cruel action, or crucifixion.

For the passion could have occurred in other ways. Nevertheless, He permitted the foreseen crucifixion, and directed the permitted [act] toward a good end.

Wherefore the crucifixion, insofar as it was a most immense action of the Jews, is to be attributed neither to divine impulse nor to an approving decree, but only to divine permission and direction.

But insofar as the crucifixion of Christ is taken passively, as it was a notable part of the passion of Christ, it was certainly pleasing and approved by God.

X. God delivered the wives of David into the hands of Absalom, that he might lie with them, 2 Sam.

XII, 11. 12. Therefore He is the author of illicit intercourse.

Resp.

The incest of Absalom comprises two things: 1) moral evil, or sin; 2) troublesome evil, or punishment.

God permitted the moral evil, so that Absalom, delivered to the devil, might commit it: but God directed that evil deed into a most grave punishment for David, which he had deserved by his adultery with Bathsheba.

Which punishment excited the greater repentance in David's soul, the harsher it was.

XI. God is said to do evil.

For He made the evil for the day of evil, Prov. XVI, 4. There is no evil in the city that the Lord has not done.

Amos III, 6. Resp.

Distinguish between the evil of punishment and of fault.

God brings it about by His governance that an unhappy day befalls an impious man: and that the punishment inflicted upon a city immersed in sins is sent by the most just God.

Quest. VII. Is God piously and rightly called the cause of sin per accidens (accidentally)?

God is called the cause of sin per accidens neither piously nor truly.

Prob.

1) Because the origin of sin is not to be reduced to God at all, but to a particular cause deficient in acting, or straying from the rule of the law.

For sin formally is a defect, not an effect. Therefore it proceeds neither per se nor per accidens from God, who is most perfect in acting.

2) God is the cause of sin per accidens neither in its first instance nor in its arising.

For if the first sin were to be imputed to God, it would be imputed to Him either because He created free will for the first man; or because He foresaw the fall of man, yet did not prevent it. But in neither way is God piously and truly called the cause of sin per accidens: not in the former way; because a cause per accidens receives its denomination from actual influence, not from the most remote granted power of sinning: not in the latter way; because by the foreknowledge of sin no one is called its cause per se or per accidens.

However, God went about restraining sin by a sufficient moral impediment, by prescribing a law to the protoplast, and by attaching a most severe threat. But no law binds [Him] to place a physical and violent impediment against sin.

Nor is God the cause of sin per accidens in its arising.

For that is both original and actual. But God is not the cause of original sin per accidens; because that is propagated through the generation of parents: nor of actual sin; because its cause is the devil and the perverse will of man.

3) 3) That phrase: God is the accidental cause of sin, contradicts a) divine sanctity. For if God were the accidental cause of injustice, He would accidentally do unjust things. b) It contradicts divine wisdom, for an accidental cause is said to be that which produces an effect beyond intention, whether this happens through ignorance or thoughtlessness.

But whatever God does, He does with the wisest decree and provident intention. 4) That phrase is not necessary. For the ancient doctors of the church solidly explained those scriptural sayings that are objected to us, and yet they did not call God an accidental cause.

*The antithesis is of certain Theologians, to whom that phrase: God is the accidental cause of sin, does not seem reprehensible (*). We will consider their arguments: 1. Whoever permits sin (), which he could have prevented, is the accidental cause of sin: But God, etc. Therefore.

The major premise is proven; because permission makes the cause moral. Resp. I deny the major; because the bare permission of any act carries with it no denomination of cause, unless one is bound to prevent it. But he who does not prevent an act, but permits it, when he was both bound and able to prevent it, is the cause of that committed act per se (in the genus of morals), not per accidens. But what law can bind God to prevent sin? Surely the most holy divinity had fortified the first man with sufficiently valid safeguards to decline the fall. What then? He had opposed a legal impediment to sin. He was not obligated to provide a violent check, since man had lost the original powers, which the image of God embraced, by the voluntary abuse of free will.

Latin:

2) Pharao seipsum effective indurauit,

Exod. VIII, 32.

II.

Quicunque mittit hominibus efficaciam erroris, ille est causa peccati: nam error in rebus fidei haud leue peccatum est.

Atqui Deus &c.

2 Thess.

II, 11.

Ergo.

Resp. limitando: Quicunque causaliter & positivo influxu mittit hominibus efficaciam erroris, ille est causa peccati; concedo.

At Deus sanctissimus, ob peccata hominum antegressa, mittit efficaciam erroris, partim permissive, efficaces errores permittendo, partim negative, gratiam perficientem & cum pleno effectu illuminantem subtrahendo.

III. Quicunque hominem peccare iubet, is est causa peccati: Atqui Deus &c. Ergo. Minor probatur, 1) exemplo Abrahami, cui Deus praecepit proprium occidere filium, Gen. XXII, 2; 2) exemplo Simei, quem Deus iussit maledicere regi suo, 2 Sam. XVI, 10. quod permagnum esse peccatum constat ex Exod. XXII, 28.

Resp. Neg. min.

Ad prius exemplum dicimus, quod Deus fit auctor & dominus vitae; cuius iussu, qui alteri vitam adimit, non peccat.

Ad posterius resp. quod peccatum illud simul fuerit poena, atque adeo actio respectu Simei, passio respectu Danidis.

Actio peccaminosa profecta est a maleuolo Simei animo, & instigante diabolo; quam cum Deus prauideret, dixit (non est in fonte hebraeo: iussit,) Simei, i. e. potestatem concessit, vt maledictione, quam ipse instinctu diaboli animo conceperat, Dauidem exulem affligeret, quo is eo magis ad peccati fui agnitionem & detestationem redigeretur.

Inde natus est versus tritissimus: Actio displicuit; passio grata fuit.

IV. Quicunque nos inducit in tentationem, ille est causa peccati. Atqui Deus &c. E. Minor patet ex Matth. VI, 10. vbi tentationes diuinas deprecamur.

Resp. Dist. a) inter tentationem probationis, & seductionis.

In illam, non in hanc Deus effectiue nos inducit. b) In tentationem seductionis Deus homines quidem induci permittit, fed ad eam hostes animae non impellit.

V. Quicunque vasa irae efficit, ille est causa peccati. Atqui Deus &c. Rom. IX, 22.

E.

Resp. Committitur ψευδερμηνεία.

Nam vasa irae apparata sunt ad interitum non a Deo (cum hoc contextus non doceat); sed a se ipsis.

Deus enim dicitur tolerare vasa irae.

Quidquid aliquis tolerat, nec ipse facit, nec, vt ab aliis fiat, intendit.

VI. Quicunque hominem incitat ad superbiam, ille est causa peccati. Atqui Deus &c. E. Minor liquet ex 2 Sam.

XXIV, 1. vbi Deus dicitur incitasse Dauidem ad numerandum populum.

Resp. Deus dicitur mouisse Dauidem ad numerandum populum non efficaci suggestionis, sed iudiciali permissione, in quantum potestatem concessit Satanae, ob peccata antegressa, Dauidem instigatione ad peccatum puniendo.

Nam a) 1 Par.

XXI, 1. Satan dicitur instigasse Dauidem.

Nimirum Deus permissiue; Satan efficaciter, & per se instigat. b) Verbum סות in Hiphil significationem permissiuam, quam locus parallelus exigit, commode admittit. c) Si Deus efficaciter instigauit, non poenam, sed laudem & praemia meruit Dauid, Deo obtemperando.

VII. Deus iussit Israëlitas spoliare Aegyptios, Exod. XI, 2.

E. est causa peccati.

Resp. Israëlitae, quae bona ab Aegyptiis abstulerunt, non furati sunt, fed eadem supremus rerum Dominus pro mercede laborum, plurimis annis exhaustorum, assignauerat.

Neque pristinos dominos experti sunt inuitos, sed faciles, conciliante Deo, & dominium in ipsos transferente.

Dicis: Commodatarius, rem ad certum vsum commodatam furripiens, furatur.

Resp. Nisi vel summi proprietarii, vel summi iudicis auctoritate assignetur possidenti.

VIII. Deus dicitur tradidisse gentes in impuritatem, Rom. I, 24.

Ergo vt gentes viuerent impure, intendit.

Resp. Deus tradidit gentes in impuritatem, non mentes earum ad impuritatem impellendo, sed ex iusto iudicio illas propriis earum cupiditatibus permittendo & in potestatem Satanae tradendo, qui spiritus impurissimus impuritatem subinde turpiorem ipsis instillauit.

IX. Quicunque decreto suo tradidit Dominum Iesum Pilato, Herodi, Iudaeis & crucifixoribus, vt ab ipsis illuderetur & occideretur, is est causa peccati. Atqui Deus &c. Act.

II, 23. Act.

IV, 28. Resp. 1) Dist. inter passionem Christi & actionem peccaminosam Iudaeorum; 2) inter permissionem & approbationem.

Decreuerat quidem Deus, vt Dominus Iesus per passionem acerbissimam genus humanum redimeret, Deoque reconciliaret, sed ad actionem crudelissimam, siue crucifixionem Iudæos non impellebat.

Poterat enim ...passio aliis fieri modis. Præuisam tamen crucifixionem permittebat, permissam ad bonum finem dirigebat.

Quare crucifixio, quatenus actio Iudæorum immanissima fuit, neque impulsuiv diuino, neque decreto approbatiuo, sed tantum permissioni & directioni diuinæ tribuenda est.

At quatenus crucifixio Christi passiue sumitur, prout insignis pars passionis Christi fuit, vtique Deo grata fuit & probata.

X. Deus tradidit vxores Dauidis in manus Absolonis, vt cum iisdem concumberet, 2 Sam.

XII, 11. 12. Ergo est auctor illiciti concubitus.

Resp.

Incestus Absolonis duo complectitur: 1) malum morale, siue peccatum; 2) malum molestum, siue pœnam.

Malum morale Deus permisit, vt Absolon diabolo traditus, illud patraret: at direxit Deus illud malefactum in pœnam Dauidis grauissimam, quam adulterio cum Bathseba erat promeritus.

Quæ pœna eo maiorem in animo Dauidis excitauit pœnitentiam, quo asperior fuit.

XI. Dicitur Deus malum facere.

Nam fecit malum in diem mali, Prou. XVI, 4. Non est malum in ciuitate, quod non fecerit Dominus.

Amos III, 6. Resp.

Dist. inter malum pœnæ & culpæ.

Deus facit gubernatione sua, vt homini impio dies infelix contingat: & quod supplicium ciuitati peccatis immersæ irrogatur, a Deo iustissimo immititur.

Quæst. VII. Num Deus pie & recte dicitur causa peccati per accidens?

Deus neque pie, neque vere dicitur causa peccati per accidens.

Prob.

1) Quia origo peccati plane non est reducenda in Deum, sed in caussam particularem in agendo deficientem, siue a regula legis aberrantem.

Peccatum enim formaliter est defectus, non effectus. Ergo neque per se, neque per accidens proficiscitur a Deo, in agendo perfectissimo.

2) Deus neque peccati primi, neque orti causa per accidens est.

Nam si peccatum primum Deo imputandum foret, vel ideo ipsi imputaretur, quia homini primo liberum arbitrium concreauit; vel ideo, quod lapsum hominis præuidit, neque tamen impediuit. Atqui neutro modo Deus pie & vere dicitur causa peccati per accidens: non modo priori; quia causa per accidens ab influxu actuali, non a concessa peccandi potentia remotissima denominationem accipit: non modo posteriori; quia præuisione peccati nemo ipsius causa per se, aut per accidens dicitur.

Impedimento autem morali sufficienti Deus peccatum cohibitum iuit, legem protoplastis præscribendo, & comminationem feuerissimam annectendo. At impedimentum physicum & violentum peccato obiiciendum nulla lege adstringitur .

Neque peccati orti causa per accidens Deus est.

Nam illud est tum originale, tum attuale. At Deus non est causa per accidens peccati originalis; quia istud propagatur per generationem parentum: neque peccati actualis; quia illius causa est diabolus & peruersa hominis voluntas. caussa est diabolus & peruersa hominis voluntas.

3) 3) Phrafis illa: Deus est caussa peccati per accidens, repugnat a) sanctitati diuinæ. Nam fi Deus esset caussa per accidens iniustitiæ, per accidens iniusta faceret. b) Repugnat sapientiæ diuinæ, caussa quippe per accidens dicitur, quæ præter intentionem effectum producit, siue id fiat per ignorantiam, siue per incogitantiam.

At quidquid Deus facit, sapientissimo decreto & prouida intentione facit. 4) Phrafis illa non est necessaria. Nam veteres doctores ecclesiæ folide illa scripturæ dicta explicarunt, quæ nobis obiiciuntur, neque tamen Deum vocarunt caussam per accidens.

*Antithefis est quorundam Theologorum, quibus phrafis illa: Deus est caussa per accidens peccati, non videtur improbanda (*). Quorum considerabimus argumenta: 1. Quicunque permittit peccatum (), quod impedire poterat, is est caussa peccati per accidens: Atqui Deus &c. Ergo.

Maior probatur; quia permissio facit caussam mopermissio moralem. Resp. Neg. maior.; quia nuda permissio alicuius facti nullam causae denominationem infert, nisi quis teneatur id impedire. At, qui factum non impedit, sed permittit, quod impedire et tenebatur et poterat, is facti illius commissi causa per se (in genere morum), non per accidens est. Quae autem lex adstringere potest Deum ad impediendum peccatum? Sane numen sanctissimum satis validis praesidiis muniuerat primum hominem ad declinandum lapsum. Quid? quod impedimentum legale peccato opposuerat. Ad sufflamen violentum obiiciendum non obligabatur, ex quo homo pristinas vires, quas imago Dei complectebatur, voluntario liberi arbitrii abusu perdiderat.


### Q. VII. Is God the cause of sin?: II. Whoever withdraws from sinners the grace by which sin could be averted, he is the cause of sin per accidens: But God, etc.: Therefore

II. Whoever withdraws from sinners the grace by which sin could be averted, he is the cause of sin per accidens: But God, etc.: Therefore.

The major is evident: because a removing and prohibiting cause is a cause per accidens. Resp. 1) I deny the major. For he who withdraws his grace, which someone abuses, is not the cause of subsequent sins, neither per se nor per accidens. God, as a most just judge, withdraws from the delinquent that grace which they have basely abused. 2) God does not withdraw all converting grace from the sinner. For there remains for the sinner a converting, prevenient, and knocking grace, through the law implanted and written. Indeed, the approach to the gospel and the sacraments also lies open. 3) If God were to withdraw his grace from the sinner in such a way that sin would necessarily follow from that subtraction, just as the fall of a stone incumbent on a column necessarily follows from the subtraction of the column; he would be the cause of sin per se, not per accidens.

III. Whoever delays the punishment due to sins, he is the cause of sin per accidens: But God, etc. Therefore.

The major is established by the example of a magistrate, who, while he lets sins run rampant with impunity, nourishes and strengthens them. Resp. Whoever delays the punishment due to sins out of negligence and connivance, he is the cause of sin. But God delays punishment with the intention that man may be invited by long-suffering to perform repentance, Rom. II, 4 .

IV. Whoever nourishes and sustains the sinner, he is the cause of sin per accidens: But God, etc. Therefore.

Resp. Whoever nourishes and sustains the sinner, insofar as he sins, he is the cause of moral sin. But God nourishes and preserves man, insofar as he is a creature, to whom sin adheres, the origin of which must be attributed to the particular and proximate cause, deficient in acting, not to the first and universal cause acting most wisely and perfectly.

V. Whoever ordains and directs sins to a good end, he is the cause of sins per accidens: But God, etc. Therefore.

The major is evident; because we elicit good from evil per accidens. The minor is established by the example of Joseph, whose perfection God directed to a good end, Gen. L, 20. Resp. 1) Whoever directs sins, as means destined by himself, to a good end, he is the cause of sins per accidens; I concede. But God did not destine sins as means leading to an end per se, but because he foresaw that they would certainly come to pass, he advances them to a good end. 2) Divine ordination to an end does not make sins, but presupposes them already committed. VI. Since

permission is a certain action of free will. Resp. He certainly wills; but what does he truly will, and insofar as what? Namely, that which he himself permits, and insofar as he permits it; that is, he does not will that sin be committed, but to tolerate it, until the day appointed for judgment, unless man has repented, nor to apply force to prevent it. Therefore, certain theologians have wisely distinguished these two: It is one thing for God, willing, to permit; another for him, permitting, to will sin. The latter is not to be thought of, as if God, permitting, willed the sin itself, insofar as it is sin; but the former, since God not unwillingly, nor impotently, but by his most free will and power, permits and allows man to sin, insofar as this permission is an outstanding proof of admirable divine forbearance and gentleness. When another effect, not intended, is joined to the effect of something that is intended in itself, that is the cause per accidens of this effect, which is not intended. But with the effect of God, it is intended &c. Therefore. The major is clear from the definition of a cause per accidens.

The minor is evident; because all human actions depend on God, as the primary cause, with which sins, not intended by God, cohere. Resp. The cause per accidens must be rightly explained. An unintended effect is said to be that which happens beyond intention due to ignorance, inadvertence, or the impotence of the agent. But God is omniscient, all-wise, and omnipotent, who foresees that sin adheres to the action of the creature, which He sustains, and He intends to prevent it, both by forbidding it and by threatening punishments; yet He does not prevent the foreseen sin by a violent means, because He is neither going to make an irrational creature out of a rational one, nor is He going to employ extraordinary remedies, since the sinner petulantly rejects ordinary remedies.

VII. The cause of a cause is also the cause of the caused: But God is the cause of free will, as the cause of sins: Therefore He is also the cause of the sins themselves. Resp. The major holds for causes essentially subordinated.

But free will and sin do not cohere essentially, but the latter is from the abuse of the former. Certainly, the angels, confirmed in good, had free will from the first moment of creation, and yet they did not sin.

VIII. If the word of God is a cause of sin per accidens, then God Himself can be a cause of sin per accidens. The antecedent is true. Therefore the consequent. The consequence of the major is clear: because the word of God is a concept of the mind of God.

But whatever happens to the divine mind, happens to God Himself. The antecedent is proven, because the word of God is per accidens a savor of death unto death, 2 Cor. 2: 15. Resp. The word of God is an intermediate cause, God is the primary cause.

Not everything that is said of an intermediate cause can be affirmed of the primary cause.

Nor is the word of God accurately called a cause of sin per accidens, even if to the impious it becomes a savor of death unto death; because the gospel does not destroy anyone, but rather the contempt of it does.

IX. Christ is a stone of stumbling per accidens, Rom. 9:32.

Therefore He is a cause of sin per accidens. Resp. Christ does not actively offend men per accidens, but the Jews took scandal from the preaching and the cross of Christ. Quaest. VIII. Who is a sinner?

A sinner is a rational creature, endowed with free will, and subject to the divine law, straying from it in doing and omitting ). And he is either a fallen angel ), or a man who is a wayfarer ). Prob. a. Only a rational creature is capable of divine law. Therefore only that is capable of sin. The antecedent is evident from the fact that the divine law was given and enacted for those creatures who know the divine law, and whose freedom of will, lest it wander beyond what is proper, must be restrained by the reins of laws.

Prob. b. Fallen angels are called sinners, 2 Pet. 2:4. God did not spare the angels who sinned.

But it is not relevant to treat the angelic sin more fully here, since in this part of the second theology, man the sinner is considered as one to be brought back to God. Prob. c.

There is no man who does not sin, 1 Kings 8:46. Indeed, all men who are wayfarers are sinners, as much the protoplasts as their descendants, descending from them by carnal generation, so that Christ alone is excepted, Heb. 7:26. Quaest.

IX. Does sin also fall upon brutes? Upon brutes, due to a lack of intellect and free will, sin properly so-called does not fall.

Prob. Beasts, as they are not capable of divine law, nor of holiness; so they are devoid of sin. There are in them images of virtues and vices, not true virtues or vices: for they act necessarily with all things required for acting, without choice (προαίρεσιν). You say: Beasts are capable of punishment: Therefore also of sins. Resp. Punishment is taken either materially and physically, for any painful passion whatsoever, or morally and formally, for a painful passion, presupposing guilt. In the former, not the latter sense, beasts are said to be affected by punishments, e.g. Gen. IX, 5. For properly speaking, punishments are inflicted upon those creatures, in whose power it stood, that they might not sin.

Latin:

II. Qui peccatoribus subtrahit gratiam, qua peccatum auerti poterat, is est causa peccati per accidens: Atqui Deus et c.: Ergo.

Maior patet: quia causa remouens et prohibens est causa per accidens. Resp. 1) Neg. mai. Nam qui gratiam suam, qua quis abutitur, subtrahit, is sequentium peccatorum causa neque per se, neque per accidens est. Deus, vt iudex iustissimus, delinquentibus eam subtrahit gratiam, qua turpiter sunt abusi. 2) Deus non omnem gratiam conuertentem subtrahit peccatori. Nam relinquitur peccatori gratia conuersiua, praeueniens, et pulsans, per legem insitam et scriptam. Quin patet etiam aditus ad euangelium et sacramenta. 3) Si Deus ita subtraheret gratiam suam peccatori, vt eam subtractionem necessario consequeretur peccatum, quemadmodum subtractione columnae necessario sequitur casus lapidis, columnae incumbentis; causa peccati per se foret, non per accidens.

III. Quicunque poenam differt, peccatis debitam, is est causa peccati per accidens: Atqui Deus et c. Ergo.

Maior constat exemplo magistratus, qui, dum peccata impune grassari finit, ea alit et roborat. Resp. Quicunque poenam peccatis debitam differt ex negligentia et conniuentia, ille est causa peccati. At Deus poenam differt ea intentione, vt longanimitate homo ad poenitentiam agendam inuitetur, Rom. II, 4 .

IV. Qui alit et sustentat peccatorem, is est causa peccati per accidens: Atqui Deus et c. Ergo.

Resp. Qui alit et sustentat peccatorem, quatenus peccat, is est causa peccati moralis. At Deus alit et conferuat hominem, quatenus est creatura, cui adhaeret peccatum, cuius origo vindicanda est causae particulari et proximae in agendo deficienti, non causae primae et vniuersali sapientissime et perfectissime agenti.

V. Quicunque ordinat et dirigit peccata ad bonum finem, is est causa peccatorum per accidens: Atqui Deus et c. Ergo.

Maior patet; quia ex malo bonum per accidens elicimus. Minor constat exemplo Iosephi, cuius perfectionem Deus direxit in bonum finem, Gen. L, 20 . Resp. 1) Quicunque peccata, tanquam media, ab ipso destinata, ad bonum finem dirigit, ille peccatorum causa per accidens est; concedo. At Deus peccata, non vt media ad finem per se ducentia, destinauit, sed quia praeuidit, ea certo euentura esse, ad finem bonum eadem prouehit. 2) Ordinatio diuina ad finem, peccata non facit, sed iam facta supponit. VI. Cum

permissio est actio quaedam liberae voluntatis. Resp. Vult certe; quid vero vult, et quatenus? Id nimirum, quod ipse permittit, et quatenus id permittit; hoc est, non peccatum committi vult, sed illud tolerare, vsque ad diem iudicio dictum, nisi homo resipuerit, nec vim ad illud impediendum adhibere. Idcirco Theologi quidam sapienter distinxerunt haec duo: Aliud est, Deus volens permittit; aliud permittens vult peccatum. Non hoc posterius est existimandum, tamquam Deus permittens vellet ipsum peccatum, quatenus est peccatum; sed prius illud, quandoquidem Deus non inuitus, neque impotens, sed pro liberrima voluntate sua, ac potestate, permittit ac finit hominem peccare, quatenus hoc permissium est insigne documentum admirabilis tolerationis ac lenitudinis diuinae. VI. Cum cuius effectu, per se intento, coniungitur effectus alius, non intentus, ille est causa per accidens istius effectus, non intenti. Atqui cum effectu Dei intento &c. Ergo. Maior patet ex definitione causae per accidens.

Minor liquet; quia omnes actiones humanae dependent a Deo, tanquam causa prima, cum quibus peccata, a Deo non intenta, cohaerent. Resp. Causa per accidens rite explicanda est. Effectus non intentus dicitur, qui praeter intentionem euenit ob ignorantiam, inaduertentiam aut impotentiam agentis. At Deus est omnisciens, omnisapiens, & omnipotens, qui peccatum actioni creaturae, quam sustentat, adhaerere praevidet, idque tum prohibendo, tum poenas interminando, impedire intendit; praevisum tamen peccatum violento medio non inhibet, quia neque ex creatura rationali irrationalem facturus, neque remedia extraordinaria adhibiturus est, cum remedia ordinaria peccator petulanter reiiciat.

VII. Causa causae est etiam causa causati: Atqui Deus est causa liberi arbitrii, ceu causae peccatorum: E. & ipsorum peccatorum causa est. Resp. Maior valet de causis essentialiter subordinatis.

Sed liberum arbitrium & peccatum non cohaerent essentialiter, sed hoc ab illius est abusu. Certe angeli, in bono confirmati, habuerunt a primo creationis momento liberum arbitrium, neque tamen peccarunt.

VIII. Si verbum Dei est causa peccati per accidens, utique ipse Deus potest esse causa peccati per accidens. Antecedens est verum. E. & consequens. Consequentia maioris est clara: quia verbum Dei est conceptus mentis Dei.

At quidquid menti diuinae accidit, ipsi Deo accidit. Antecedens probatur, quia verbum Dei per accidens est odor mortis ad mortem, 2 Cor. II, 15. Resp. Verbum Dei est causa intermedia, Deus causa principalis. Non omne, quod de causa intermedia dicitur, de causa principali affirmari potest.

Neque verbum Dei accurate dicitur causa peccati per accidens, licet impiis fit odor mortis ad mortem; quia non euangelium quenquam perimit, sed ipsius contemptus.

IX. Christus est lapis offensionis per accidens, Rom. IX, 32. E. est causa peccati per accidens.

Resp. Christus homines non actiue per accidens offendit, sed sumserunt Iudaei scandalum ex praedicatione & cruce Christi. Quaest. VIII. Quis est peccator? Peccator est creatura rationalis, voluntate libera praedita, & legi diuinae subiecta, ab hac in faciendo & omittendo aberrans ).

Estque vel angelus lapsus ), vel homo viator ). Prob. a. Sola creatura rationalis est capax legis diuinae.

Ergo illa sola est capax peccati. Antecedens constat ex eo, quod lex diuina data & lata est illis creaturis, quae legem diuinam cognoscunt, & quarum libertas arbitrii, ne euagetur vltra decorum, legum frenis cohibenda est. Prob. b.

Angeli lapsi vocantur peccatores, 2 Petr. II, 4. Deus angelis, qui peccarunt, non pepercit. Sed de peccato angelico hic vberius agere nil attinet, cum in hac parte II theol. consideretur homo peccator ad Deum reducendus.

Prob. c. Non est homo, qui non peccet, 1 Reg.

VIII, 46. Nempe peccatores sunt omnes homines viatores tam protoplasti, quam eorum posteri, carnali generatione ab ipsis descendentes, vt solus excipiatur Christus, Hebr. VII, 26. Quaest.

IX. Num etiam in bruta cadit peccatum? In bruta, ob defectum intellectus & liberae voluntatis, non cadit peccatum proprie dictum.

Prob. Bestiae, ut nec legis divinae, nec sanctitatis sunt capaces; ita peccati sunt expertes. Dantur in iisdem simulacra virtutum & vitiorum, non verae virtutes aut vitia: nam omnibus ad agendum requisitis necessario agunt citra προαίρεσιν. Dicis: Bestiae sunt capaces poenae: Ergo & peccatorum. Resp. Poena sumitur vel materialiter & physice, pro qualicunque passione dolorifica, vel moraliter & formaliter, pro passione dolorifica, praesupponente culpam. Priori, non posteriori sensu, bestiae dicuntur poenis affici, v. g. Genes. IX, 5. Proprie enim loquendo poenae irrogantur iis creaturis, quas penes stetit, quo minus peccarent.


### Q. X. Is both the soul and the body the seat of sin?

The primary seat of sin is the soul, with its faculties, acts, and habits a). The secondary seat is the body b).

Prob. a. Just as the image of God primarily perfected the soul of the whole man with wisdom and justice: so sin, which succeeded into the place of the divine image, first infected the soul with folly and injustice. The faculties of the soul are the intellect and the appetite, both rational (the will) and sensitive. But these faculties deflect most of all from the divine law: the intellect through ignorance, opinion, and error; the will through the choice of a good that is not true, but apparent; the sensitive appetite through a blind impulse toward a good, pleasant indeed to the senses, but forbidden by divine law.

Prob. b. The organic body of man serves the sinful soul in committing sin. From which Paul distinguishes moral uncleanness into the defilement of the flesh and of the spirit, 2 Cor. VII, 1. The fornicator sins against his own body, 1 Cor. VI, 18. The members of the wicked are instruments of injustice, Rom. VI, 13. Obf.

I. In philosophical terms this doctrine is proposed in the following manner. The matter in which, or the subject of sin, are both fallen angels and men. With respect to man, the subject of sin is either total or partial. Total is the whole man, ultimately receiving the denomination from sin. Partial is either primary or secondary. Primary, or the first recipient (πρῶτον δεκτικόν), is the soul, with its powers or faculties: secondary is the body. Obf.

II. By the material of sin, taken abstractly, theologians generally understand not man, or the soul, but that which is joined with lawlessness (ἀνομίᾳ), whether it be a connate quality, or an acquired habit, or an act deviating from the law. e.g. In original sin the subject of lawlessness (ἀνομίας) is concupiscence, in theft it is the extension of the hand toward another's goods. Obf.

III. The material of sin is either remote or proximate. Remote is the action considered generally, as an indeterminate physical motion: proximate is the action applied or determined to an object forbidden by divine law, e.g. When a thief extends his hand, the extension of the hand is an indeterminate physical motion: But the extension of the hand toward a stolen thing is the proximate material of sin. God concurs with the remote material of sin; because He grants only motion in general, and sustains the creature in acting: but He does not determine the motion itself to this species of vice.

Latin:

Primaria sedes peccati est anima, cum suis facultatibus, actibus & habitibus a). Secundaria sedes est corpus b).

Prob. a. Sicut imago Dei principaliter animam hominis integri sapientia & iustitia perfecit: ita peccatum, quod in locum imaginis divinae successit, primum animam stultitia & iniustitia infecit. Facultates animae sunt intellectus & appetitus, tam rationalis (voluntas), quam sensitivus. At hae facultates potissimum a lege divina deflectunt: intellectus per ignorantiam, opinionem & errorem; voluntas per electionem boni non veri, sed apparentis; appetitus sensitivus per caecum impetum in bonum, sensibus iucundum quidem, sed lege divina vetitum.

Prob. b. Corpus hominis organicum animae peccatrici in delinquendo inservit. Ex quo Paullus moralem immunditiem distinguit in inquinationem carnis, & spiritus, 2 Cor. VII, 1. Scortator in proprium corpus peccat, 1 Cor. VI, 18. membra impiorum sunt instrumenta iniustitiae, Rom. VI, 13.

Obs. I. Terminis philosophicis haec doctrina sequenti ratione proponitur. Materia in qua, seu subiectum peccati, sunt tum angeli lapsi, tum homines. Respectu hominis, subiectum peccati est vel totale, vel partiale. Totale est totus homo, a peccato denominationem ultimato accipiens. Partiale est vel primarium, vel secundarium. Primarium, seu πρῶτον δεκτικόν, est anima, cum suis potentiis seu facultatibus: secundarium est corpus.

Obs. II. Per materiale peccati, abstractive sumti, a theologis plerumque non homo, aut anima, sed id, quod cum ἀνομίᾳ coniunctum est, intelligitur, sive fit connata qualitas, sive habitus acquisitus, sive actus a lege aberrans. v. gr. In peccato originali subiectum ἀνομίας est concupiscentia, in furto est extensio manus ad bona aliena.

Obs. III. Materiale peccati est vel remotum, vel proximum. Remotum est actio considerata generatim, vt motus physicus indeterminatus: proximum est actio ad obiectum lege divina prohibitum applicata, vel determinata, v. gr. Cum fur extendit manum, extensio manus est motus physicus indeterminatus: At extensio manus ad rem furtivam, est materiale proximum peccati. Ad materiale peccati remotum concurrit Deus; quia largitur tantum motum in genere, & sustentat creaturam in agendo: motum ipsum autem non determinat ad hanc vitii speciem.


### Q. XI. What is the rule, or norm, from which sin deflects?

The primary and adequate norm, from which sin deflects, is the divine law, and that natural, or moral, inscribed upon the minds of the first-formed humans a), but so obliterated by their fall, that meager remnants of it remained after the fall b). And therefore it was repeated from time to time by God through special revelations made to the patriarchs, and finally solemnly promulgated on Mount Sinai, the sum of which is contained in the decalogue, and is explained more clearly here and there in the sacred scriptures c).

Prob. a. The natural law commands those things which are honorable in themselves, and prohibits those things which are base in themselves. Base in themselves are sins, which are unbecoming to a rational creature. This natural law obligates all men to obedience, or, if this be absent, to punishment, both because it has as its author God, most wise, most good, and most powerful, the creator and lord of all men: and because it commands those things which are suitable to a rational creature, insofar as it is such, and prohibits those things which are unsuitable to it. The same is called the moral law, because it directs the morals of men, and composes them to the nod of the divine will (although the moral law, sometimes taken specially, denotes only the law promulgated extrinsically). Moreover, the law of nature, inscribed with the image of God upon the protoplasts, could not but be most known to them. For there was bestowed upon them an excellent knowledge of principles, and the same faculty for applying them to individual actions and the circumstances of actions.

Prob. b. Through the fall of the first parents, that innate part of the law of nature was lost which prohibits and convicts interior sins, namely the sin of origin, first movements, and depraved thoughts. Hence it is that today the inscribed law of nature is not an adequate norm for knowing individual sins. Indeed, Paul himself could not, except from the written law (which says in express words: Thou shalt not covet, Deut. V, 11.), know that concupiscence is a sin, Rom. VII, 7. Wherefore one must properly distinguish between a certain and confused knowledge of sins, which is had even after the fall, from the innate law of nature (for the Gentiles, who do not have the (written) law of Moses, do by nature the things that are of the law: these, though they do not have the law, are a law unto themselves: for they demonstrate the work of the law written in their hearts); and between a full and distinct knowledge of sins, which is to be sought from the law prescribed divinely. Moreover, the inscribed natural law and the prescribed moral law are the same materially, although they differ from it formally. For the former is congenital, the latter is superadded to the congenital law of nature to supply its defect, and to show the guilt of eternal death, which inseparably accompanies sin.

Prob. c. That God, from the beginning of the world up to the flood, and then from Noah up to Moses, declared the natural law to the patriarchs, CHEMNITIUS accurately teaches in L. de leg. Dei p. 20. The Decalogue, however, solemnly promulgated on Mount Sinai, exhibits the sum of the natural law with singular brevity, Exod. XX., succinctly comprising whatever pertains to the love of God and neighbor. Wherefore the Sinaitic law, contained in the Decalogue as an epitome of the natural law, and explained more clearly here and there in Holy Scripture, is for the present time an adequate rule and standard for us to discern and judge good and evil works. Paul looked to this, Rom. III, 20., saying: By the law is the knowledge of sin (as much theoretical as practical). For he speaks of that law which is joined with the law of the prophets, v. 21., and is contradistinguished from the law of faith, v. 27.

Latin:

Norma primaria & adaequata, a qua peccatum deflectit, est lex divina, eaque naturalis, seu moralis, mentibus hominum protoplastorum inscripta a), sed per lapsum ipsorum ita oblitterata, vt exiguae eiusdem post lapsum manserint reliquiae b). Ideoque a Deo per speciales reuelationes, patriarchis factas, subinde repetita, & tandem in monte Sinai solemniter promulgata est, cuius summa continetur in decalogo, & passim in sacris litteris clarius explicatur c).

Prob. a. Lex naturalis præcipit ea, quæ per se honesta, & prohibet ea, quæ per se turpia sunt. Per se turpia sunt peccata, creaturæ rationali indecora. Obligat hæc lex naturalis omnes homines ad obedientiam, aut, si hæc absit, ad pœnam, tum quia auctorem habet Deum sapientissimum, optimum & potentissimum, omnium hominum creatorem & dominum: tum quia præcipit ea, quæ creaturæ rationali, quatenus tali, conueniunt, prohibetque ea, quæ illi disconueniunt. Vocatur eadem lex moralis, quia mores hominum dirigit, & ad nutum voluntatis diuinæ componit (quamuis lex moralis, interdum specialiter sumta, tantum notet legem extrinsece promulgatam). Ceterum lex naturæ, cum imagine Dei inscripta protoplastis, non potuit non iisdem esse notissima. Collata quippe ipsis erat eximia scientia principiorum, & facultas eadem ad singulas actiones & actionum circumstantias applicandi.

Prob. b. Per lapsum primorum parentum amissa est illa legis naturæ insita pars, quæ prohibet & arguit peccata interiora, nempe peccatum originis, primos motus & prauas cogitationes. Inde sit, vt hodie lex naturæ inscripta non sit norma adæquata singula peccata cognoscendi. Sane ipse Paullus non, nisi ex lege scripta (quæ disertis verbis dicit: Non concupisces Deut. V, 11.), cognoscere potuit, quod concupiscentia sit peccatum Rom. VII, 7. Quare probe distinguendum est inter cognitionem peccatorum aliqualem & confusam, quæ habetur post lapsum etiam, ex lege naturæ insita (nam gentes, quæ legem (Mosis scriptam) non habent, natura ea, quæ legis sunt, faciunt: hi licet legem non habeant, sibi ipsis lex sunt: quippe qui demonstrant opus legis scriptum in cordibus suis); & inter cognitionem peccatorum plenam & distinctam, quæ ex lege diuinitus præscripta petenda est. Ceterum lex naturalis inscripta, & moralis præscripta, eadem est materialiter, quamuis ab ea formaliter differat. Nam illa congenita, hæc legi naturæ congenitæ superaddita est ad illius defectum supplendum, & ad ostendendum æternæ mortis reatum, qui peccatum indiuulse comitatur.

Prob. c. Deum inde ab exordio mundi vsque ad diluuium, deinde a Noacho vsque ad Mosen, legem naturalem patriarchis declarasse, accurate docet CHEMNITIVS L. de leg. Dei p. 20. Decalogus autem, in monte Sinai solemniter promulgatus, summam legis naturæ singulari breuitate exhibet, Exod. XX., succincte complectens, quidquid ad dilectionem Dei & proximi pertinet. Quare lex Sinaitica in decalogo velut epitome legis naturalis comprehensa, & in sacra scriptura passim clarius explicata pro præsenti tempore nobis adæquata regula & amussis est, bona & mala opera dignoscendi & diiudicandi. Hanc respexit Paullus, Rom. III, 20. inquiens: Ex lege est agnitio peccati (tam theoretica, quam practica). Loquitur enim de illa lege, quæ coniuncta est cum lege prophetarum, v. 21. & legi fidei contradistinguitur, v. 27.


### Quest. XII. Is the divine positive law, and human law, also a norm of sin?

A secondary and particular norm for knowing sins is the divine positive law a) and human law, enacted by the magistrate b), unless this is contrary to the divine law c).

…Prob. a. The divine positive law is concerned with those things which would be neither morally good nor evil works, unless God had commanded or prohibited them by his most free will. Therefore, the divine positive law does not obligate all men, nor perpetually (*), but only those to whom it is prescribed, and as long as it remained in force by the will of God: of which kind was the paradisiacal law concerning not eating the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; as also the ceremonial and forensic law of the O. T. The obligation of this positive law is founded in the law of nature, which commands that God is to be obeyed in all things; he who does otherwise, sins.

Prob. b. Human law, issued by a magistrate, obliges mediately, in that it is founded in divine law, which commands that the magistrate is to be obeyed.

Prob. c. If human law is contrary to divine law, that apostolic saying holds, Acts V, 29. We must obey God rather than men.

Latin:

Norma secundaria & particularis cognoscendi peccata est lex diuina positiua a) & lex humana, lata a magistratu b), nisi hæc contrarietur legi diuinæ c).

Prob. a. Lex diuina positiua versatur circa ea, quæ neque moraliter bona, neque mala forent opera, nisi liberrima Deus voluntate ea præcepisset, aut prohibuisset. Proinde lex diuina positiua obligat non omnes homines, neque perpetuo (*), sed illos tantum, quiest praescripta, et quamdiu ex voluntate Dei illa viguit: cuiusmodi erat lex paradisiaca de non comedendo fructu arboris scientiae boni et mali; ut et lex caerimonialis et forensis V. T. Cuius legis positivae obligatio fundatur in lege naturae, quae praecipit Deo in omnibus obtemperandum esse; qui secus facit, peccat.

Prob. b. Lex humana, lata a magistratu, obligat mediate, eo, quod fundatur in lege divina, quae praecipit, magistratui morem esse gerendum.

Prob. c. Si lex humana contrarietur legi divinae, valet illud apostolicum, Act. V, 29. Obedire oportet Deo magis, quam hominibus.


### Q. XIII. Whether human actions, by which the moral law of God is violated, are evil in themselves?

or only for the reason that God by his free will prohibited them by his law?

Human actions, by which the moral law of God is violated, are evil in themselves; and even if no written law of God existed concerning avoiding them, they would be base by nature, and by no means indifferent.

Prob. 1) The natural law inscribed, and morally prescribed, is materially the same. But the natural law prohibits that which is base in itself.

2) Hatred of God, blasphemy, perjury, impiety toward parents, adultery, etc., are not sins because they are forbidden by written law; but they are prohibited by law because they are contrary to the eternal law, which is in God, namely to the wisdom, holiness, and essential justice of God .

The antithesis is that of Durandus and other Scholastics, who maintain that no human acts are evil in themselves, but are considered sinful only because they are forbidden by divine law. They object: I. If the adequate norm of sins is the moral law of God; no human action is evil in itself, but only because God by his free will prohibited it by his law: But the former is most certain: Therefore the latter is also.

The consequence of the major is proved; because God, compelled by no necessity, bound by no obligation, brought forth his law, but promulgated it by the same free will, both by voice and by writing, so that it might be clear to men what was morally good, what was evil. Take away this law, and you immediately posit indifference: for if there is no law, there is no transgression, Rom. IV, 15. Resp. 1) It was indeed free for God to prescribe his law to men; but, granted that he willed to bring it forth, or did bring it forth, he could not but bring forth a law that was holy and conformable to his justice. But sin is contrary to divine justice. 2) If even the written law of God did not exist at all, the law implanted in nature would nevertheless dictate that at least external sins are base in themselves, because they are inconsistent with a rational creature, as such.

II. Sin is ἀνομία (lawlessness). Therefore it is opposed not to divine justice, but to the law, issued by the free will of God. Resp. Sin is opposed immediately to the law, mediately to divine justice, of which the law is as it were an express image. The law is the principle manifesting sin; but the holiness of God is the radical principle of good, to which sin is repugnant.

III. If sins were evil in themselves; God could have commanded neither the immolation of Isaac to Abraham, nor the despoiling of the Egyptians to the Israelites: But he commanded both this and that: Therefore. Resp. Human life, and the goods of fortune (as they are commonly called) depend on divine dominion. When therefore the supreme lord of life and faculties commands one to take away life or wealth from another, for grave reasons, neither homicide nor theft is committed.

Latin:

an ideo tantum, quod Deus libera voluntate eas lege sua prohibuit?

Actiones humanae, quibus lex Dei moralis violatur, per se sunt malae; et licet de iis fugiendis nulla lex Dei scripta exstaret, natura turpes, minime autem indifferentes forent.

Prob. 1) Lex naturalis inscripta, et moraliter praescripta, materialiter eadem est. At lex naturalis prohibet id, quod per se turpe est.

2) Odium Dei, blasphemia, periurium, impietas in parentes, adulterium et c. non ideo peccata sunt, quia lege scripta vetantur; sed ideo lege prohibentur, quia aeternae legi, quae est in Deo, nimirum sapientiae, sanctitati, et iustitiae Dei essentiali aduersantur .

Antithesis est Durandi et aliorum Scholasticorum, statuentium, nullos actus humanos per se esse malos, sed tantum ideo censeri peccaminosos, quod lege divina vetiti sunt. Obiiciunt: I. Si peccatorum norma adsequata est lex Dei moralis; nulla actio humana per se mala est, sed ideo tantum, quod Deus libera voluntate eam lege sua prohibuit: Atqui prius est certissimum: Ergo et posterius.

Consequentia maioris probatur; quia Deus nulla necessitate coactus, nulla obligatione devinctus, legem suam tulit, sed eandem libera voluntate, qua voce, qua scripto promulgavit, ut hominibus constaret, quid moraliter bonum, quid malum esset. Tolle hanc legem, et statim pones indifferentiam: si enim non est lex, non est transgressio, Rom. IV, 15. Resp. 1) Liberum quidem Deo fuit, legem suam hominibus praescribere; at posito, quod illam ferre voluerit, aut talerit, non potuit non sanctam, iustitiaeque suae conformem legem ferre. At peccatum iustitiae divinae aduersatur. 2) Si vel maxime non exstaret lex Dei scripta, insita tamen naturae lex dictaret, peccata saltim exteriora per se esse turpia, propterea quod creaturae rationali, quatenus tali, disconveniunt.

II. Peccatum est ἀνομία. Ergo non iustitiae divinae, sed legi, libera Dei voluntate latae, opponitur. Resp. Peccatum opponitur immediate legi, mediate iustitiae divinae, cuius expressa quasi imago lex est. Lex est principium peccati manifestativum; sed sanctitas Dei principium boni radicale, cui peccatum repugnat.

III. Si peccata per se mala forent; Deus nec Abrahamo immolationem Isaaci, nec Israelitis spoliationem Aegyptiorum praecipere potuisset: At et hanc, et illam praecepit: E. Resp. Vita humana, et bona fortunae (uti vulgo vocantur) pendent a dominio divino. Quando ergo summus vitae et facultatum dominus iubet alteri vitam, aut opes, gravibus de caussis adimere, neque homicidium, neque furtum committitur.


### XIV. In what does sin formally consist?

Sin formally consists in the privation of conformity with the divine law, to the keeping of which man is obligated.

Proof. Moses describes sin through the non-continuance in all things which are prescribed in the law, Deut. XXVII, 26. And John through ἀνομίαν (anomian), lawlessness. Both imply that sin is the privation of conformity with the divine law, to the perfect obedience of which man is obligated through his dependence on the Creator. Therefore, sin is a defect of moral rectitude due to be present in man, or the absence of the image of God, with which man, by virtue of the divine intention, ought to be adorned. Furthermore, sin is indeed a true privation, but not a mere one; because it not only turns man away from the will of God, declared by law, but also opposes it. Nor is the due rectitude only taken away by sin, but there is also posited an undue determination toward acts prohibited by law, and an inordinate disposition of the soul, which is certainly something morally positive.

You say: Not every sin is ἀνομία (anomia), or an aberration from the law; but there is also given a sin which is an aberration from the gospel, namely ἀπισία (apistia), or unbelief in Christ, which the law does not prohibit, because it knows nothing of Christ. Resp. 1) Distinguish between the law alone, or considered separately, and [the law] illuminated by the light of the gospel. The law alone knows nothing of faith or ἀπισία (apistia) in Christ; yet, illuminated by the light of the gospel, it prohibits and condemns the same. 2) Unbelief is considered either by reason of its genus, or by reason of a certain object. In the former way, it can and must be referred only to the law: in the latter way, in place of an object, it regards either God as legislator, or, according to the gospel, it has Christ the mediator in place of an object. This respect does not change the genus of unbelief, but only varies the object, so that unbelief, although it is directed immediately toward Christ, nevertheless strikes against the first commandment of the Decalogue, which commands one to believe in God, in whatever way He is considered, whether as Creator and Preserver, or as Legislator, or as Redeemer.

Question XV. Does τὸ ἑκούσιον (to hekousion), or the voluntary, enter into the very definition of sin? The voluntary does not enter into the definition of sin, considered generally.

Obs. I. Sin is called voluntary either subjectively, insofar as it inheres in the will, or efficiently, as it proceeds from a deliberate will. In the latter way, not every sin is voluntary.

Obs. II. Sin is called voluntary either formally, which is committed by one's own will; or virtually, which was voluntary in the root and stock of the human race, from which it was propagated to descendants; whose will would have been the same as Adam's, if they had lived at the same time with him.

Proof. 1) Because John simply defines sin by ἀνομία (anomia), not by voluntary ἀνομία (anomia). 2) Because besides voluntary sins, there are also given involuntary ones, namely those of infirmity and ignorance, of which [we shall speak] below. 3) Original sin in the descendants of Adam is not voluntary, but connatural to them.

Antithesis is 1) of the Papists, 2) of the Socinians, who define sin by the voluntary transgression of the law. They are hinted at by the saying of James, ch. I, 15. "Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death." Where the conception of sin denotes the consent of the will. They add the authority of AUGUSTINE, who [wrote in] L. de v. relig. relig. cap. 14. writes: Sin is so far voluntary, that it is in no way sin, unless it is voluntary. Resp. Both speak of actual sins, and not all of them, but those that are proæretic and actually deadly (*).

Quæst. XVI. What is the end of sin?

The end of sin, properly speaking, is not given a): meanwhile, however, the devil, by inciting man to sin, intends the offense of the Creator, the misery and ignominy of man, and the increase of his own kingdom b): but man, sinning, looks to some apparent good c).

Prob. a. The end and the good are materially the same. But it is so far from the case that the end of sin is truly good, that it rather calls man away from the end due to him, which is the enjoyment of the highest good.

Prob. b. Just as by the envy of the devil death (the wages of sin) entered into the world, Wis. II, 24.: so the devil, burning with envy against God and man, strives both to displease God, and to destroy man, and to increase his own kingdom, while he solicits man to sin.

Prob. c. The sinner would not fall away from God, the highest good, and His law, unless the appearance of an apparent good were to entice him. For the appetite is not carried toward evil, as such, but toward a true or apparent good.

Quæst. XVII. What is the consequence of sin?

The consequence of sin is the guilt of fault and of punishment.

Quæst. XVIII. What is fault, and the guilt of fault?

Fault is the foulness or moral deformity resulting from an act discordant with the law and indecorous to a rational creature, and adhering to the sinner by way of a base stain. The guilt of fault is the obligation by which a man, on account of an act discordant with the moral law, is held as if bound under sin and a stain, so that because of that act the sinner is judged and denominated detestable.

Obs. I. An act discordant with the law, which is called sin, passes away; but the fault remains and adheres to the sinner, e.g. On account of the act of adultery, once committed, a man is held so bound under the stain of adultery that because of that act he is held and called an abominable adulterer.

Obs. II. Fault differs from punishment. For the former precedes, the latter follows; fault merits punishment, punishment is owed to fault, and is as it were its wages, Rom. VI, 23.; fault proceeds from the will, the will of the sinner abhors punishment; the sinner contracts fault by acting, he sustains punishment by suffering.

Th the foulness of sin is proved: How foul a stain sin is, is clear to anyone considering how indecorous it is for a rational creature to deflect from the law, inscribed in nature and prescribed in divine scripture. For that is nothing other than, in the manner of beasts, to act without reason, to disturb the divine order, and to rush with blind impulse into the offense of the supreme judge and avenger incur. See Ps. XIV, 1. 3. Rom. III, 11. sqq. But since there is no man who does not sin, 1 Kings VIII, 46, the whole world is guilty before God. Rom. III, 19.

Latin:

Peccatum formaliter consistit in privatione conformitatis cum lege divina, ad quam servandam homo obligatur.

Prob. Moses describit peccatum per non permanentiam in omnibus, quae praescripta sunt in lege, Deut. XXVII, 26. Et Ioannes per ἀνομίαν, dislegalitatem. Uterque innuit, peccatum esse privationem conformitatis cum lege divina, ad cuius perfectam obedientiam homo per dependentiam a creatore obligatur. Est itaque peccatum defectus rectitudinis moralis, homini adesse debitae, vel absentia imaginis Dei, qua homo, vi intentionis divinae, exornatus esse debet. Ceterum peccatum est privatio quidem vera, sed non mera; quia non tantum hominem a voluntate Dei, lege declarata, avertit; sed et eidem aduersatur. Neque tollitur tantum peccato rectitudo debita, sed ponitur etiam determinatio ad actus, lege prohibitos, indebita, et inordinata animae dispositio, quae sane aliquid positivum morale est.

Dicis: Non omne peccatum est ἀνομία, sive aberratio a lege; sed datur etiam peccatum, quod est aberratio ab evangelio, nimirum ἀπισία, sive incredulitas in Christum, quam lex non prohibet, quia nihil de Christo novit. Resp. 1) Dist. inter legem solam, sive seorsum consideratam, et lumine evangelii collustratam. Lex sola nihil novit de fide, aut ἀπισία in Christum, collustrata tamen luce evangelii eandem prohibet et damnat. 2) Incredulitas consideratur vel ratione sui generis, vel ratione certi obiecti. Priori modo non, nisi ad legem, referri potest ac debet: posteriori modo, obiecti loco, respicit vel Deum, tanquam legislatorem, vel, iuxta evangelium, obiecti loco habet Christum mediatorem. Hic respectus non mutat genus incredulitatis, sed tantum obiectum variat, ita, ut incredulitas, licet directe in Christum feratur, tamen impingat in primum decalogi praeceptum, quod iubet Deo credere, quocunque modo, sive ut creator et conservator, sive ut legislator, sive ut redemptor consideretur.

Quaest. XV. Num τὸ ἑκούσιον, sive voluntarium, ipsam peccati definitionem ingreditur? Peccati, generatim considerati, definitionem non ingreditur τὸ ἑκούσιον, sive voluntarium.

Obs. I. Voluntarium dicitur peccatum vel subiective, quatenus voluntati inhaeret, vel efficienter, prout a voluntate deliberata proficiscitur. Posteriori modo non omne peccatum est voluntarium.

Obs. II. Voluntarium dicitur peccatum vel formaliter, quod propria voluntate committitur; vel virtualiter, quod voluntarium fuit in generis humani radice et stirpe, a qua propagatum est in posteros; quorum eadem fuisset voluntas, quae Adami, si cum hoc eodem tempore vixissent.

Prob. 1) Quia Ioannes simpliciter definit peccatum per ἀνομίαν, non per ἀνομίαν voluntariam. 2) Quia praeter peccata voluntaria dantur etiam involuntaria, nempe infirmitatis et ignorantiae de quibus infra. 3) Peccatum originis in posteris Adami non est voluntarium, sed iis connatum.

Antithesis est 1) Pontificiorum, 2) Socinianorum, qui peccatum definiunt per voluntariam legis transgressionem. Innuituntur iidem dicto Iacobi, c. I, 15. Concupiscentia postquam concipit, parit peccatum; peccatum vero, quando consummatum est, parturit mortem. Ubi conceptio peccati notat consensum voluntatis. Addunt auctoritatem AVGVSTINI, qui L. de v. relig. relig. cap. 14. scribit: Vsque adeo peccatum est voluntarium, vt nullo modo sit peccatum, nisi fit voluntarium. Resp. Vterque loquitur de peccatis actualibus, iisque non omnibus, sed proæreticis & actu mortiferis (*).

Quæst. XVI. Quis est finis peccati?

Finis peccati, proprie loquendo, non datur a): interim tamen diabolus, instigando hominem ad peccatum, creatoris offensionem, hominis miseriam & ignominiam, regnique sui incrementum intendit b): homo autem peccans respicit aliquod bonum apparens c).

Prob. a. Finis, & bonum, idem sunt materialiter. Tantum autem abest, vt finis peccati vere bonus sit, vt potius hominem a fine ipsi debito, qui est fruitio summi boni, auocet.

Prob. b. Sicut inuidia diaboli mors (stipendium peccati) ingressa est in mundum, Sap. II, 24.: ita diabolus, inuidia in Deum & hominem æstuans, & Deo ægre facere, & hominem perdere, & regnum suum augere connititur, dum hominem ad peccandum sollicitat.

Prob. c. Non deficeret peccator a Deo summo bono, eiusque lege, nisi species boni apparentis ipsi abblandiretur. Neque enim appetitus fertur in malum, quatenus tale, sed in bonum verum, aut apparens.

Quæst. XVII. Quodnam est consequens peccati?

Consequens peccati est reatus culpæ & pœnæ.

Quæst. XVIII. Quid est culpa, & reatus culpæ?

Culpa est fœditas, vel deformitas moralis ex actu legi difformi & creaturæ rationali indecoro resultans, atque per modum turpis maculæ peccatori adhærens. Reatus culpæ est obligatio, qua homo, propter actum, legi morali difformem, sub peccato & macula quasi constrictus tenetur, vt ab illo actu peccator detestabilis censeatur & denominetur.

Obs. I. Actus legi difformis, qui peccatum dicitur, transit; at culpa manet & peccatori adhæret, v. gr. Propter actum adulterii, semel commissum, homo sub macula adulterii ita constrictus tenetur, vt ab actu isto adulter abominabilis habeatur & dicatur.

Obs. II. Culpa differt a pœna. Nam illa præcedit, hæc sequitur; culpa meretur pœnam, pœna culpæ debetur, eiusque quasi stipendium est, Rom. VI, 23.; culpa a voluntate proficiscitur, a pœna voluntas peccatoris abhorret; culpam peccator contrahit agendo, pœnam sustinet patiendo.

Probatur fœditas peccati: Quam fœda macula sit peccatum, cuilibet liquet consideranti, quam indecorum sit creaturæ rationali, a lege, naturæ inscripta, & in scriptura diuina præscripta, deflectere. Id quippe nil aliud est, quam, pecudum more, sine ratione agere, ordinem diuinum conturbare, & in offensam summi iudicis ac vindicis cæco impetu incurrere. Vid. Ps. XIV, 1. 3. Rom. III, 11. sqq. Cum autem non fit homo, qui non peccet, 1 Reg. VIII, 46. totus mundus reus est Deo. Rom. III, 19.


### Q. XIX. What is punishment and the liability to punishment?

Divine punishment is a troublesome evil by which God, the offended judge, vindicates a preceding and not yet remitted fault, so that He may demonstrate His justice and assert His majesty and the authority of the law against contempt . Liability to punishment is the obligation by which a sinner is held bound by God, the angry judge, to sustain the vindication of a fault not remitted .

Proof a: God is the avenger of sinners, 1 Thess. IV, 6, who does not absolve the guilty without satisfaction having been rendered, Exod. XXXIV, 7, for the reason that those who do evil are worthy of death, Rom. I, 32.

Proof b: The infliction of punishments is ascribed to the ἀνταποδοτικῇ, retributive, justice of God, 2 Thess. I, 6. It is just before God to repay affliction. And it is attributed to τῇ δικαιοκρισίᾳ, the just judgment of God, to render to each according to his works affliction and distress of soul to the one working evil, Rom. II, 5. 6. 9. For this reason, the condemnation of the impious is called just, Rom. III, 8.

Proof c. The sinner denies to God the worship owed; he denies obedience to the divine law. By this atrocious injury, he provokes God to inflict punishments, so that He may assert His majesty against contempt and keep the authority of His law safe and sound. The prophet Samuel indicates this, speaking gravely to King Saul: You have rejected the word of Jehovah, and Jehovah has rejected you. 1 Sam. XV, 26.

Proof d: Liability to punishment is founded proximately upon the threatening annexed to the divine law, Gen. II, 17. Deut. XXVII, 26. Therefore, God cannot, with His truth and justice saved, remit sin unpunished without satisfaction having been rendered.

Obs. I: Punishment is described as a troublesome evil, so that it may be distinguished from moral evil. The will of the sinning man is directed rather toward the latter; the sinner undergoes the former against the inclination of his will. A troublesome evil is also called an evil of passion. Hence, punishment is succinctly defined as that which is an evil of passion, inflicted on account of an evil of action. Cf. SAMUEL PUFFENDORF, de I. N. & G. book VIII, ch. III, p. 1046.

Obs. II: Punishment (in Greek τιμωρία) must be accurately distinguished from chastisement or the paternal affliction of God (*), which in the Holy Scriptures comes under the name of the cross. Punishment is a troublesome evil vindicative of a fault not yet remitted, inflicted by God as an angry judge. But the affliction of the faithful, although at first glance it may appear to be a troublesome and bitter evil, is nevertheless not an evil vindicative of a fault, nor is it inflicted by God as an angry judge, but is a medicinal evil, sent by God as a propitious father, by which either faith is tested or life is amended. This paternal chastisement is 1) δοκιμασία, or probation, by which the progress of an innocent man (innocence of cause, not of person, which is in Christ alone)

Latin:

Poena diuina est malum molestum, quo Deus iudex offensus culpam antegressam, & nondum remissam vindicat , vt iustitiam suam demonstret & suam maiestatem, legisque auctoritatem a contemptu asserat . Reatus poenae est obligatio, qua peccator a Deo, iudice irato, obstrictus tenetur, ad sustinendam vindictam culpae, non remissae .

Prob. a Deus est peccatorum vindex, 1 Thess. IV, 6. qui nocentem, circa praestitam satisfactionem, non absoluit, Exod. XXXIV, 7. propterea, quod mala facientes digni sunt morte, Rom. I, 32.

Prob. b. Irrogatio poenarum iustitiae diuinae ἀνταποδοτικῇ, retributiuae, adscribitur 2 Thess. I, 6. Iustum est apud Deum retribuere afflictionem. Et τῇ δικαιοκρισίᾳ, iusto Dei iudicio, tribuitur, reddere vnicuique secundum opera ipsius afflictionem & angustiam animae, malum operanti, Rom. II, 5. 6. 9. Id propter impiorum condemnatio iusta dicitur, Rom. III, 8.

Prob. c. Peccator denegat Deo cultum debitum; denegat obsequium legi diuinae. Qua atroci iniuria lacessit Deum ad irrogandum supplicia, vt maiestatem suam a contemptu asserat, & auctoritatem legis suae sartam tectam praestet. Id indicat propheta Samuel, regem Saulem grauiter alloquens: Repudiafti verbum Iehouae, & repudiauit te Iehouah. 1 Sam. XV, 26.

Prob. d. Reatus poenae proxime fundatur in comminatione, legi diuinae annexa, Gen. II, 17. Deut. XXVII, 26. Non potest igitur Deus, salua veritate & iustitia sua, citra praestitam satisfactionem, peccatum impunitum dimittere.

Obs. I. Describitur poena per malum molestum, vt distinguatur a malo morali. Ad hoc potius est voluntas hominis peccantis, illud peccator subit contra voluntatis inclinationem. Malum molestum vocatur etiam malum passionis. Hinc poena succincte definitur, quod fit malum passionis, inflictum propter malum actionis. Conf. SAMVEL. PVFFENDORFE. de I. N. & G. libr. VIII. c. III. p. 1046.

Obs. II. Accurate distinguenda est poena (graece τιμωρία) a castigatione, vel afflictione Dei paterna (*), quae in sacris litteris crucis nomine venit. Poena est malum molestum culpae nondum remissae vindicatiuum, inflictum a Deo irato iudice. At afflictio fidelium, licet prima fronte videatur malum molestum & acerbum, non tamen est malum vindicatiuum culpae, neque infligitur a Deo, iudice irato, sed est malum medicinale, immissum a Deo patre propitio, quo vel fides probatur, vel vita emendatur. Quae castigatio paterna est 1) δοκιμασία, siue probatio, qua hominis innocentis (innocentia causae, non personae, quae in solo Christo est) profectus


### Quest. XX

of faith, love, hope, and patience are examined and tested in the school of God, Wis. III, 5. 6. Such a cross was the temptation of Abraham, the prison of Joseph, the calamity of Job. To this also pertains 2) τὸ μαρτύριον, or the painful passion, which is inflicted upon the faithful by the enemies of celestial truth, on account of the testimony borne to the orthodox religion: 3) παιδεία, a somewhat harsher discipline, by which God, having been reconciled, chastises the converted sinner, so that He may amend him and deter him from relapse. Thus David, king of the Israelites, having obtained forgiveness for adultery, was pressed by more than one calamity sent divinely, so that in the future he would live enslaved not to the flesh, but to God.

Q. XX. How manifold is the punishment of sin?

A manifold punishment is inflicted upon man by the most just God on account of sin. The punishment of sin can be distinguished 1) into temporal and eternal a): the former is the vindication by God of guilt in this life; the latter is inflicted in hell without end: 2) into positive, or of sense, by which the impious man is afflicted with many and great pains, and privative, or of loss, by which, by the just judgment of God, the goods of soul, body, and fortune are taken away from the sinner b): 3) into personal, or private, by which one sinner is restrained, and common, or public, which many, associates of the same crime, pay c).

Proof a. Miriam, infected with leprosy, Manasseh cast into prison, the thief nailed to the cross, and many others, for whom the temporal punishment was a stimulus to perform penance, underwent temporal punishment. But those who neither acknowledge God nor obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, they will pay the punishment, eternal destruction, 2 Thess. I, 8. 9.

Proof b. Death, the wages of sin, leads the procession of privative punishments, Rom. VI, 23. Now death is either spiritual, which is the separation of the soul from the gracious fellowship of God, bringing about the defect of all spiritual powers, or corporal, which is the separation of the soul departing from the body; or eternal, which is the separation from the beatific vision and fruition of God (*).
