Spiritual death is followed by corporal and eternal death. For as soon as the soul is separated from the gracious fellowship and influx of God, the body is subject to death on account of sin, Rom. VIII, 10, and the soul is made guilty of eternal death. Furthermore, a privative punishment is never not joined with a positive punishment. Cf. D. HULSEMANN in breu. enucl. p. 1101.

Proof c. Some punishments are common, some are personal. Common punishments, on account of atrocious crimes, are sent upon many, associates of the same crime, and are either universal, which are common to the whole human nature, namely the defect of the divine image, mortality, sweat-inducing labor; or national, which befall a whole nation, such are those grave punishments, λιμὸς, λοιμὸς καὶ πόλεμος, famine, pestilence, war, by which an entire nation is frequently infested: or particular, which are struck upon a gathering of the impious, in cities or fields, such as were divinely sent upon Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboim. Personal, or singular, punishments are either of the mind, or of the body, or of fortune, which God, all hater and avenger of evil, inflicts upon individual sinners in proportion to their crimes; examples of these are daily obvious to human senses.

Latin:

fectus fidei, dilectionis, spei & patientiæ, in schola Dei examinantur & probantur, Sap. III, 5. 6. Hujusmodi crux fuit tentatio Abrahami, carcer Josephi, calamitas Iobi. Huc etiam pertinet 2) τὸ μαρτύριον, siue passio dolorifica, quæ infertur fidelibus ab hostibus veritatis cœlestis, ob perhibitum religioni orthodoxæ testimonium: 3) παιδεία, disciplina aliquanto asperior, qua Deus reconciliatus peccatorem conuersum castigat, vt ipsum emendet, & a relapsu deterreat. Sic Dauid, rex Israëlitarum, adulterii veniam consecutus, haud vna calamitate diuinitus immissa premebatur, vt in posterum non carni, sed Deo mancipatus viueret.

Quæst. XX. Quotuplex est pœna peccati?

Pœna multiplex ob peccatum homini a Deo iustissimo irrogatur. Distingui potest pœna peccati 1) in temporalem, & æternam a): illa vindicatur a Deo culpa in hac vita; hæc in inferno sine fine infligitur: 2) in positiuam, siue sensus, qua homo impius multis magnisqve doloribus adficitur, & priuatiuam, siue damni, qua iusto Dei iudicio peccatori bona animæ, corporis & fortunæ auferuntur b): 3) in personalem, siue priuatam, qua vnus coërcetur peccator, & communem, siue publicam, quam plures, eiusdem criminis socii, luunt c).

Prob. a. Subiuerunt pœnam temporalem Miriam, lepra infecta, Manasses in carcerem coniectus, latro in crucem actus, multique alii, quibus pœna temporalis fuit stimulus ad agendum pœnitentiam. At qui nec agnoscunt Deum, nec obediunt euangelio Domini nostri Iesu Christi, illi pœnam luent, interitum æternum, 2 Thess. I, 8. 9.

Prob. b. Pœnarum priuatiuarum agmen ducit mors, stipendium peccati, Rom. VI, 23. Est autem mors vel spiritualis, quæ est separatio animæ a gratioso Dei consortio, defectum omnium virium spiritualium inferens, vel corporalis, quæ est separatio animæ a corpore abeuntis; vel æterna, quæ est separatio a visione & fruitione Dei beatifica (*). Mortem spiritualem sequitur mors corporalis & æterna. Nam simulatque anima a gratioso Dei consortio & influxu separata est, corpus morti subiectum est propter peccatum, Rom. VIII, 10. & anima rea facta est æternæ mortis. Ceterum pœna priuatiua nunquam non est coniuncta cum pœna positiua. Conf. D. HVLSEMANN. in breu. enucl. p. 1101.

Prob. c. Pœnæ quædam sunt communes, quædam personales. Pœnæ communes, ob delicta atrocia, pluribus, eiusdem criminis sociis, immittuntur, suntque vel vniuersales, quæ toti naturæ humanæ communes sunt, nempe defectus imaginis diuinæ, mortalitas, labor sudorificus; vel nationales, quæ toti nationi obtingunt, eiusmodi sunt graues illæ pœnæ, λιμὸς, λοιμὸς καὶ πόλεμος, fames, pestis, bellum, quibus integra sæpenumero natio infestatur: vel particulares, quæ impiorum cœtui, in vrbibus, aut agris congregato, incutiuntur, quales Sodomæ, Gomorræ, Adamæ & Zeboim diuinitus immittebantur. Pœnæ personales, siue singulares, sunt vel animi, vel corporis, vel fortunæ, quas Deus, omnis mali osor & vltor, pro ratione delictorum singulis peccatoribus infligit; harum exempla quotidie sensibus humanis sunt obuia. Quaest.


### Question XXI

Although for certain sins, because of preceding transgressions, an external punitive respect from God, the offended judge, may be added: nevertheless, the manner of speaking of those who assert that God punishes sins with sins is improper and never to be imitated.

Proof. 1) The cause of punishments is the vindicatory justice of God, Rom. II, 5. 6. 2 Thess. I, 6. But it is so far from the case that divine justice is the cause of sins, that these are clearly adverse and hateful to divine justice.

2) If God punished sins with sins, He would send sins into the hearts of men: for God is truly said to send punishments: But the former is false: Therefore the latter is also.

You say: I. God punished the adultery of David with the rebellion of his son Absalom: Therefore He punished sin with sin. Resp. The rebellion of Absalom against his father David comprises two things: 1) a moral evil, or an act deformed by the law, committed by Absalom; 2) a troublesome evil, or a painful passion, which, under God's direction, resulted for David as a vindicatory punishment for the adultery committed. God does not concur causally or efficiently in the rebellion of Absalom, which was a morally evil act, but merely permitted that sinful act.

The passion, however, which David endured, was not a sin, because it was only a troublesome evil, not a moral one. Indeed, the action displeased God, the passion was pleasing, as Prosper once sang.

You say: II. God punished the stubborn disobedience of Pharaoh with hardening, which was a great sin: Therefore God punishes sin with sin. Resp. God hardened Pharaoh not by a positive influx of sending hardness into Pharaoh's mind: since Pharaoh himself is said to have hardened his heart, Exod. VIII, 15. but merely by permitting the hardening, and by a just judgment withdrawing the softening grace, which had been stubbornly rejected. Wherefore, not the hardening, but the permission of the hardening and the withdrawal of grace, properly speaking, was the punishment inflicted upon Pharaoh by God. But neither the permission nor the withdrawal of grace is a sin. Therefore God did not punish sin with sin.

XXII. Can the guilt of fault and of punishment be removed?

The guilt of fault and of punishment is inseparable from sin. However, it is separated from the sinning person, not insofar as he indulges in sins, but insofar as he performs true repentance, and by sincere faith apprehends the satisfaction of Christ, provided for the human race, and is thus justified by God, the propitious judge.

Proof a. Sin in itself is foul and abominable, Ps. XIV, 3, and subject to divine curse, Deut. XXVII, 26. Wherefore, just as committed sin cannot be rendered undone, so it can never be free from guilt.

Proof b. God relaxes the bond of guilt by remitting sin to the repenting sinner, that is, by not imputing it to punishment. To David, confessing his sin, his iniquity was remitted, i.e., he was reckoned righteous and free from fault, Ps. XXXII, 5. The heavenly King had mercy on the servant who was repenting and praying, and remitted to him the fault and the punishment, Matt. XVIII, 26, 27.

Proof c. God does not remit sin absolutely, without any satisfaction; since the vindicatory justice of God demands the punishment merited by sins, either from the sinner or from the sinner's sponsor, Christ, whose satisfactory passion, he who applies to himself by true faith, is justified, i.e., is absolved from the guilt of fault and of punishment. Paul teaches this in Rom. III, 23, 24, 25. All have sinned, and are destitute of the glory of God: But they are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God has set forth as a propitiation through faith in His blood, for the demonstration of His justice. From which there is οὐδὲν κατάκριμα, no condemnation in those who are in Christ Jesus, Rom. VIII, 1.

S I G H.

To lift my eyes to heaven, and to spread out my hands before Thy majesty, O most holy God, I can scarcely endure. For as often as I recall to memory my sins, both most numerous in count and most grave in weight, as often as I measure the contracted fault against the standard of Thy law, as often as I ponder the punishments merited by my sins; so often does my soul tremble, my mind grow numb, my limbs shake. I have injured the supreme authority of Thy name, which I ought to have revered most holily: I have violated the law which Thou didst prescribe: I have spurned the commands which Thou didst give. Hence shame, hence sorrow and tears. Whither shall I turn, oppressed by grief? To what asylum shall I flee? Whom shall I seek, or find as a fountain of solace? O heavenly mercy, look upon me, a wretch! O piety, spare a great debtor! O clemency, admit one who detests his sins! Do not turn away from me, while I turn to Thee. I confess that I am guilty of death. But as much as I fear death because of my sins, so much do I hope for life because of Thy merit, O Jesus, life of my life! Blot out, I beseech Thee, my debts with Thy blood! Absolve me from temporal and eternal punishments! Instruct me with spiritual strengths, so that in the future, enslaved not to the flesh, not to the devil, but to Thee, I may live eternally!

Latin:

Quamuis quibusdam peccatis, ob antegressa delicta, externus respectus punitivus a Deo, offenso iudice, accedat: impropria tamen, nec vnquam imitanda est eorum lucutio, qui afferunt, Deum peccata peccatis punire .

Prob. 1) Poenarum causa est iustitia Dei vindicatiua, Rom. II, 5. 6. 2 Thess. I, 6. At tantum abest, vt iustitia diuina sit causa peccatorum, vt haec iustitiae diuinae plane sint aduersa & exosa.

2) Si Deus peccata peccatis puniret, peccata cordibus hominum immitteret: nam poenas immittere Deus vere dicitur: At prius est falsum: Ergo & posterius.

Dicis: I. Deus puniuit adulterium Dauidis rebellione filii Absolonis: Ergo puniuit peccatum peccato. Resp. Rebellio Absolonis aduersus patrem Dauidem duo complectitur: 1) malum morale, siue actum legi difformem, patratum ab Absolone; 2) malum molestum, siue passionem dolorificam, quae, dirigente Deo, cessit Dauidi in poenam adulterii commissi vindicatiuam. Ad rebellionem Absolonis, quae fuit actus moraliter malus, Deus causaliter aut efficienter non concurrit, sed actum illum peccaminosum tantum permisit.

Passio autem, quam Dauid sustinuit, non fuit peccatum, quia tantum malum molestum, non autem morale fuit. Nimirum actio Deo displicuit, passio grata fuit, vti Prosper olim cecinit.

Dicis: II. Deus contumacem Pharaonis inobedientiam puniuit induratione, quae grande fuit peccatum: E. Deus peccatum peccato punit. Resp. Deus indurauit Pharaonem non potitiuo influxu duritiem animo Pharaonis immittendo: siquidem Pharao ipse cor suum indurasse dicitur, Exod. VIII, 15. sed tantum indurationem permittendo, & iusto iudicio gratiam emollientem, pertinaciter reiectam, subtrahendo. Quapropter non induratio, sed permissio indurationis & subtractio gratiae, proprie loquendo, poena Pharaoni a Deo inflicta fuit. At neque permissio, neque subtractio gratiae peccatum est. E. Deus peccatum peccato non puniuit.

XXII. Potestne reatus culpae & poenae tolli?

Reatus culpae & poenae a peccato est inseparabilis ). Separatur autem a persona peccante, non prout peccatis indulget, sed quatenus veram poenitentiam agit ), & sincera fide satisfactionem Christi, pro genere humano praestitam, apprehendit, atque adeo a Deo, iudice propitio, iustificatur ).

Prob. a. Peccatum per se est foedum & abominabile, Ps. XIV, 3. & maledictioni divinae subiectum, Deut. XXVII, 26. Quare, sicut peccatum commissum reddi nequit infectum: ita nunquam immune a reatu esse potest.

Prob. b. Relaxat Deus vinculum reatus, peccatum peccatori resipiscenti remittendo, hoc est, ad poenam non imputando. Dauidi, confitenti peccatum, huius iniquitas remittebatur, i. e. iustus & culpa vacans ille reputabatur, Ps. XXXII, 5. Serui poenitentis & deprecantis misertus est rex coelestis, remisitque illi culpam & poenam, Matth. XVIII, 26. 27.

Prob. c. Remittit Deus peccatum non absolute, citra ullam satisfactionem; siquidem iustitia Dei vindicativa poenam peccatis promeritam exigit, vel a peccante, vel a peccantis sponsore, Christo, cuius passionem satisfactoriam, qui vera sibi fide applicat, iustificatur, i. e. a reatu culpae & poenae absolvitur. Docet hoc Paulus Rom. III, 23. 24. 25. Omnes peccauerunt, & destituuntur gloria Dei: Iustificantur autem gratis gratia ipsius per redemptionem, quae est in Christo Iesu, quem proposuit Deus propitiatorium per fidem in ipsius sanguine in demonstrationem iustitiae suae. Ex quo οὐδὲν κατάκριμα, nihil condemnationis est in iis, qui sunt in Christo Iesu, Rom. VIII, 1.

S V S P I R I V M.

Erigere oculos in coelum, & expandere manus meas coram maiestate tua, o Deus sanctissime, vix sustineo. Quoties enim peccata mea, & numero plurima, & gravitate maxima, memoria recolo, quoties culpam contractam ad normam legis tuae exigo, quoties poenas, peccatis promeritas, penito; toties pauescit animus, stupefcit mens, contremiscunt artus. Summam auctoritatem nominis tui, quam sanctissime reuereri debebam, laesi: legem, quam praescripsisti, violaui: mandata quae dedisti, spreui. Hinc pudor, hinc dolor & lacrymae. Quo me vertam, moerore oppressus? Ad quod confugiam asylum? Quem inquiram, aut inveniam fontem solatii? O misericordia coelestis, respice me miserum! O pietas, parce debitori maximo! O clementia, admitte detestantem peccata sua! Noli auerti a me, dum ego conuertor ad te. Fateor, me esse reum mortis. At quanto timeo mortem propter peccata mea, tantum spero vitam propter meritum tuum, o Iesu, vita vitae meae! Expunge, obsecro, debita mea sanguine tuo! Exsolue me poenis temporalibus & aeternis! Instrue me viribus spiritualibus, vt in posterum non carni, non diabolo, sed tibi mancipatus, aeternum viuam!


## 13 On the First and Original Sin of Men


### On the First and Original Sin of Men

Quest. I. How is sin divided?

Sin is divided into the first, and that which arose from the first. The first sin is either absolutely first, or first in the human race. The absolutely first is the ἀποστασία (apostasy) of the angels, who did not retain their origin: the first in the human race is the fall of the first-formed humans in paradise.

Latin:

Quaest. I. Quomodo diuiditur peccatum?

Peccatum diuiditur in primum, & a primo ortum. Peccatum primum est vel absolute primum, vel primum in genere humano. Absolute primum est ἀποστασία angelorum, qui originem suam non retinuerunt: primum in genere humano est lapsus hominum protoplastorum in paradiso.


### Q. III

II. What is the first sin of men? The first sin of men is the transgression of the paradisiacal law, by which the first-formed humans, persuaded by the devil and abusing the freedom of their will, violated the divine prohibition against eating the fruit of the knowledge of good and evil, and derived upon themselves and their descendants, who were to be propagated from them by the order of nature, having lost the divine image, a great guilt and the liability to temporal and eternal punishment. Obs.

I. In the Holy Scriptures, the first sin is called the transgression of Adam, Rom. V, 14. And the disobedience of one man, by which many were made sinners, Rom. V, 19. Obs. II. By the Scholastics, this first sin is called the originating sin, and the corruption of human nature that flowed from it is called the originated original sin. But it must be diligently noted that the primordial sin is truly actual and individual, which becomes ours morally and imputatively: But the sin that flowed from it, and is commonly called original, is habitual, hereditary, and universal, and becomes ours through natural generation.

Quest. III. What is the cause of the first sin? The cause of the first sin is not God a), but the devil as the persuader b), and man, the transgressor of the divine law, overcome by the persuasion of the devil and having abused the freedom of his will c). Prob. a.

1) God created man upright, Eccl. VII, 29. very good, Gen. I, 31. shining with the image of God, Gen. I, 27. 2) He severely forbade the first sin to man, under the threat of heavy punishment, Gen. XVII. 3) He punished fallen man with the harshest torments, Gen. III, 26. sqq. Therefore, God was in no way the cause of the first sin.

You say: I. If God had measured out to the first man such a measure of grace by which he could have avoided every sin and overcome any temptation whatsoever, he would never have fallen. Therefore, God, by not conferring such aid, seems to have willed the fall of man, which He had foreseen. Resp. The image of God, in which man was created, contained sufficient strength to decline sin and to overcome any temptation whatsoever.

To provide greater aid, God was bound by no law, by no covenant. The most wise creator of nature could have addressed the first man with the most just right: My grace is sufficient for thee. You say: II. If the first man had received sufficient strength from God to overcome any temptation whatsoever, he would not have succumbed to the diabolical temptation. Resp. God had conferred upon man sufficient strength to overcome any temptation whatsoever; but He had not determined his will toward the good, so that he would immutably adhere to it, but had granted him the freedom of the will toward good and evil; yet in such a way that, by the power of the divine image with which he was endowed, his will was inclined toward the good, and he had only a remote power toward evil, or a power of resistance.

Moreover, God had granted freedom of the will, both so that man's obedience might be spontaneous, and so that the creator might bestow rewards upon the freely obeying man. Prob. b.

The devil is called a murderer from the beginning and the father of lies, John VIII, 44. He could not, however, be the cause of slaughter or human death unless he were the cause of the first sin; since men were immortal before sin, and death entered the world through sin. Rom. V, 11. He is called the father of lies because, by lying, he drew men away from the faith and obedience owed to God.

For he neither compelled the first-formed humans to sin by violent means, nor did he infuse error into their minds as a physical cause; for both are repugnant to the state of integrity and exceed the powers of the devil, since he could not slip into the mind and will of Eve and bend or determine her by physical action: but he attacked Eve with fraudulent persuasions enticed the sow to sin. That most crafty enemy acted in the serpent more as a slanderer or impostor than as an orator. 1) The devil attempted to persuade the woman as if the nakedness of herself and her husband were a thing too shameful. But since he could not persuade those who were devoid of sin of any shame, he feigned that they did not perceive it due to a lack of knowledge: that there was a tree in the middle of the garden which, to those who ate, would give such great knowledge of good and evil. 2) Because God had forbidden men the eating of that tree, he dared to insinuate that the most holy God was envious, just as if He envied the tasting of a most pleasant tree, most suitable for producing knowledge. For he said to the woman: Even this (it is out of envy), that God said, you shall not eat of every tree of the garden, Gen. III, 1. By which slander he laid snares for Eve, so that she would not place firm trust in the benevolence of God. 3) He dared to accuse God of lying, by openly contradicting His word: You shall not surely die, Gen. III, 4. 4) He ensnared the woman with a flattering promise of a more eminent conformity with God, and of a more excellent knowledge than they had received with the image of God of the first-formed man. 5) He overcame the wavering Eve with the blandishments of the most delicate fruit offered to her.

Prob. c. Eve sinned first, not being simpler in intellect than Adam, but more yielding in will. Since she was not omniscient, she did not know by simple ignorance whether the interlocutor was a good angel or an evil one lurking under the serpent: for she knew that a natural serpent lacked the faculty of speech. Perhaps she believed that a good angel was speaking from the serpent, and that he was either softening or entirely abrogating the law previously promulgated, which seemed exceedingly rigid. For when the demon contradicted the divine word, saying: you shall not surely die; he immediately pretended that he was a friend of God, privy to the secrets of God. He therefore added a reason to his assertion: For God knows that in the day you eat of it (the fruit), your eyes will be opened: and then you will be like God, knowing good and evil; just as if he were arguing: The enjoyment of which tree will be followed by a more excellent degree of knowledge, and assimilation with Elohim, its effect will not be death. But the tree of knowledge &c. Therefore. Moved by this argument, Eve did not believe that the execution of the divine threat or the obligation to death would certainly happen: but rather, there hovered in her mind partly the good appearing to be promised by the demon, namely, a closer and fuller assimilation with God to be obtained through the eating of the forbidden fruit, and a notable increase of wisdom, and partly the pleasantness of the tree, which she had looked upon with a feeling of delight, and was persuaded that it had not been created by God in vain. And thus, overcome by the persuasion of the devil, she sinned by eating, and drew her husband Adam into the fellowship of sin.

Latin:

II. Quid est peccatum hominum primum? Peccatum hominum primum est transgressio legis paradisiacae, qua homines protoplasti interdictum divinum de non comedendo fructus scientiae boni & mali, a diabolo persuasi, & libertate voluntatis abusi, violarunt, inque se & posteros suos, ordine naturae ex se propagandos, amissa imagine divina, grandem culpam, & reatum poenae temporalis atque aeternae derivarunt. Obs.

I. In sacris litteris peccatum primum vocatur transgressio Adami, Rom. V, 14. Et inobedientia unius hominis, per quam peccatores constituti sunt multi, Rom. V, 19. Obs. II. A Scholasticis peccatum hoc primum appellatur peccatum originans, & quae intima naturae humanae corruptio ex eodem fluxit, dicitur peccatum originis originatum. At sedulo notandum est; quod primordiale peccatum reuera sit attuale & individuale, quod nostrum fit moraliter & imputative: At peccatum, quod ex illo manauit, & communiter originale dicitur, est habituale, haereditarium & universale, fitque nostrum per naturalem generationem.

Quaest. III. Quae est causa peccati primi? Causa peccati primi non est Deus a), sed diabolus suasor b), & homo, transgressor legis divinae, persuasione diaboli victus, & libertate arbitrii abusus c). Prob. a.

1) Deus condidit hominem rectum, Eccl. VII, 29. valde bonum, Gen. I, 31. imagine Dei coruscantem, Gen. I, 27. 2) Peccatum primum homini feuere interdixit, sub comminatione grauis poenae, Gen. XVII. 3) Hominem lapsum asperrimis suppliciis mactauit, Gen. III, 26. sqq. E. Deus nullo modo causa primi peccati fuit.

Dicis: I. Si Deus primo homini eam admensus fuisset gratiam mensuram, qua omne peccatum vitare, & quancunque tentationem superare potuisset, nunquam fuisset lapsus. E. Deus, non conferendo tantum auxilium, lapsum hominis, quem praeuiderat, voluisse videtur. Resp. Imago Dei, in qua conditus erat homo, sufficientes vires complectebatur ad declinandum peccatum, & vincendam quamlibet tentationem.

Ad maius suppeditandum auxilium Deus nulla lege, nullo pacto obligabatur. Poterat sapientissimus naturae opifex primum hominem aequissimo iure compellare: Sufficiat tibi gratia mea. Dicis: II. Si primus homo sufficientes a Deo vires accepisset, ad superandam quamlibet tentationem, non succubuisset tentationi diabolicae. Resp. Sufficientes vires ad superandam tentationem quancunque Deus homini contulerat; at voluntatem ipsius ad bonum, vt huic immutabiliter adhaereret, non determinauerat, sed concesserat ipsi libertatem arbitrii ad bonum & malum; ita tamen, vt, vi imaginis diuinae, qua praeditus erat, voluntas eius prona ferretur in bonum, & ad malum tantum ipsi esset potentia remota, siue potentia repugnantia.

Libertatem autem arbitrii indulserat Deus, tum vt hominis constaret spontaneum obsequium, tum vt praemia creator conferret in hominem libere obsequentem. Prob. b.

Diabolus appellatur homicida ab initio & pater mendacii, Io. VIII, 44. Non posset autem esse caedis, aut mortis humanae causa, nisi esset causa primi peccati; cum homines ante peccatum fuerint immortales, mors autem per peccatum intrauerit in mundum. Rom. V, 11. Idem dicitur pater mendacii, quia mentiendo homines a fide & obsequio, Deo debito, abstraxit.

Neque enim coegit protoplastos ad peccandum medio violento, neque vt causa physica errorem mentibus ipsorum infudit; vtrumque enim tum statui integritatis repugnat, tum vires diaboli excedit, quippe qui non potuit illabi in mentem & voluntatem Euae, illamque actione physica flectere aut determinare: sed fraudulentis suasionibus Euam aggressus sus ad peccandum pellexit. Egit autem ille hostis vaferrimus in serpente magis calumniatorem, aut impostorem, quam oratorem. 1) Conatus est diabolus mulieri persuadere, quasi nuditas ipsius & mariti res nimis turpis esset. Cum autem persuadere non posset turpitudinem hominibus, peccati expertibus, finxit, ex defectu scientiæ id illos non deprehendere: esse autem arborem in medio horto, quæ comedentibus tantam scientiam boni & mali datura esset. 2) Quia Deus hominibus esum illius arboris interdixerat, ausus est Deum sanctissimum insinuare invidiæ, perinde, ac si gustum arboris amœnissimæ, ad pariendam scientiam accommodatissimæ, invideret. Dixit enim ad mulierem : Etiam hoc (ex invidia est), quod dixit Deus, non comedetis de omni arbore horti, Gen. III, 1. Qua calumnia insidias struxit Evæ, ne firmam in benevolentia Dei fiduciam collocaret. 3) Ausus est Deum accusare mendacii, aperte ipsius verbo contradicendo: Non moriendo moriemini, Gen. III, 4. 4) Inescavit mulierem blanda promissione eminentioris conformitatis cum Deo, & excellentioris scientiæ, quam cum imagine Dei protoplasti acceperant. 5) Vacillantem Evam vicit blanditiis porrecti fructus delicatissimi.

Prob. c. Primum peccavit Eua, non intellectu simplicior Adamo, sed voluntate facilior. Quæ cum non esset omniscia, ignorantia simplici nesciebat, vtrum collocutor angelus bonus, an malus sub serpente delitesceret: nam serpentem naturalem loquendi facultate carere, sciebat. Forte credidit, angelum bonum loqui e serpente, eumque legem, antea promulgatam, quæ perquam rigida videbatur, aut emollire, aut penitus abrogare. Etenim cum dæmon verbo diuino contradiceret, inquiens: non moriendo moriemini; confestim simulabat, se esse amicum Dei, conscium arcanorum Dei. Addebat igitur suæ affertioni rationem: Quin nouit Deus, quod, quo die comederitis de eo (fructu), aperientur oculi vestri: tumque eritis sicut Deus, scientes bonum & malum; perinde, ac si argumentaretur: Cuius arboris fruitionem sequetur excellentior scientiæ gradus, & assimilatio cum Elohim, illius effectus non erit mors. Atqui arboris scientiæ &c. Ergo. Mota hoc argumento Eua non credidit, certo futuram comminationis diuinæ exsecutionem, aut obligationem ad mortem: quin potius obuersabatur animo partim promissum a dæmone bonum apparens, videlicet obtinenda per esum fructus vetiti propior & plenior assimilatio cum Deo, atque insignis sapientiæ accessio, partim iucunditas arboris, quam cum affectu oblectationis aspexerat, neque frustra eandem a Deo conditam esse persuasa erat. Atque adeo, victa suasu diaboli, comedendo peccauit, & maritum Adamum in societatem peccati traxit.


### Quest. IV. By what instrument did the devil use in seducing the first man?

The devil, in seducing the first man, used a real and natural serpent a), corporally possessed by him b), as an instrument.

Prob. a. Regarding the serpent, Moses writes Gen. III, 1. But indeed the serpent was made crafty (through the entry of the Devil) above all the beasts of the field which Jehovah God had made. That this was a real and natural serpent is gathered 1) from its natural craftiness, since when compared with the beasts of the field, it is said to have been craftier than them. Which serpentine craftiness Christ himself does not pass over, Matt. X, 16. 2) From the inflicted punishment, which is to be endured by the serpent through crawling upon the ground and the eating of dust, Gen. III, 14. (*) Prob. b. That it was not a mere serpent, but ἐνεργούμενον [energoumenon], or possessed by the devil, is gathered 1) from the fact that a mere serpent cannot speak. But the paradisiacal serpent used articulate speech. 2) From the seduction of man. The serpent is a good creature of God. But the paradisiacal serpent was the seducer of the first man. 3) From the bruising of the heel; which is referred not to a natural, but to an infernal serpent. From which it is concluded that the devil was united with the serpent παρασατικῶς [parasatikōs], or accidentally.

V. What law did the protoplasts violate by their fall?

The first parents by their fall immediately violated the positive law promulgated in paradise, concerning not eating the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil a); mediately and virtually by their disobedience they broke down the barriers of the entire moral law b).

Prob. a. To eat of the fruits of the tree is morally neither evil nor so in itself: however, with the divine interdict intervening, it becomes evil on account of the authority of the supreme Lord and legislator. Now, however, God by positive law had specifically and expressly interdicted the protoplasts from eating of the fruits of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, Gen. II, 17. Wherefore the first men, by eating of the same tree, immediately violated the positive law of God.

Prob. b. The reason for the positive law was δοκιμασία [dokimasia], or the testing of obedience, which the entire moral law requires as owed to God. But he who does not fear to transgress one precept does not blush to violate the remaining precepts, since they have the same author and the same power of obligating.

Wherefore TERTULLIAN well says L. II. cont. Marc. II. The primordial law given to Adam and Eve in paradise is as it were the matrix of all the precepts of God. Indeed, the protoplasts by their disobedience virtually and by consequence violated all and each of the precepts of the decalogue: I. the precept by distrust and apostasy; II. by the perverse interpretation of the divine mandate and the translation of guilt onto God: III. by contempt of the divine word: IV. by disobedience and ingratitude which lay hidden in that.

2) Eve possessed such knowledge that she could not be ignorant that the serpent was a brute animal, void of all reason, and incapable of speech; from which she could not but immediately notice the fraud and abhor that conversation. That the masked serpent, by Eve’s false knowledge and wisdom, did not seem so suspicious to her, is brought about by these surrounding circumstances: (α) The woman knew well that there were many spirits created by God, and that all were good and devoid of vice: (β) It did not escape her that they were adorned with greater perfections than men: (γ) She also knew the office commanded to the angels, by which they perpetually sang the praises of God and performed what was commanded, and were also always present as companions to man, so that no danger was to be feared from them by him.

(Which, however, is in no way apt for excusing Eve’s sin. She ought to have been content with the word of God, which is altogether immutable and never to be revoked, and to adhere to it constantly with her whole being): (δ) Nor did she doubt that it could happen that those spirits might assume some form of body: Finally (ε) it is quite probable that the defection of the perfidious angels had not occurred before this very action, by which they began to envy the virtue and happiness of men; see the notes on page 198. Therefore she thought it was a good spirit, from whom she expected nothing but what was good and salutary to come. 3) The serpent, the author and instigator of the first sin of men, is called the devil, Apoc.

XII, 9. 4) The n prefixed to the noun is an indication that this serpent was clearly singular, whose property was craftiness. He is compared with all kinds of animals, and even with venomous serpents themselves.

But a comparison sometimes has the force of a negation, as John III, 19 & 20, 2 Tim. III, 4. Therefore this is the meaning: This serpent was cunning and sharp for fraud, of the kind of which there is no animal, even though he bore the appearance of a certain animal.

5) He brought forth speech, and that insidious and mendacious, also wrapped in many ambiguities. 6) Punishment, properly so called, cannot be inflicted upon any brute animal. 7) This punishment, if the words are understood properly, is a condition of such a kind that it is appropriate for serpents, and indeed for all animals creeping on the ground: for they tell a fable who say that serpents previously with an erect body creeping previously with an erect creeping previously with an erect titude toward God, the heavenly Father and supreme Lord, by whom they had been heaped with so many benefits; V. by homicide, since it was the moral cause of the spiritual, bodily, and eternal death of their descendants; VI. by intemperance and the lust of gluttony, the perfidy of Eve toward her husband, and the inordinate love of Adam for his wife; VII. by theft, while they handled another's property (a fruit not their own) against the owner's will; VIII. by false testimony and the approbation of false testimony; IX. & X. by the concupiscence of a depraved divine likeness, of a certain supernatural knowledge, and of the forbidden fruit.

VI. In what does the first sin formally consist? The first sin of men formally consists in the turning away from the positive law of God promulgated in paradise, concerning not eating the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Which lawlessness (ἀνομία) involved sinful acts: on the part of the intellect, unbelief (ἀπισία) ; on the part of the will, self-love (φιλαυτία) and pride ; on the part of the sensitive appetite, the inordinate concupiscence of the forbidden fruit ; from which emerged the external act, prohibited by the paradisiacal law .

Prob. a. When Eve hesitated, hanging between the word of God: In the day that you eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall die the death, Gen. II, 17, and the word of the devil: You shall not die the death, Gen. III, 4. She turned her mind away from the divine word, by denying faith to it, and turned her spirit toward the diabolical word, by granting assent to it; which is truly a wicked unbelief (ἀπισία), the root of the first sin.

For as faith is the principle of access to God, Hebr. XI, 1, so infidelity is the principle of aversion from God, Io. XVI, 19. Certainly the devil first solicited man to doubt the truth of the divine word; then he openly contradicted the divine word, intending to show it to be false; finally, he bent the will of Eve toward pride.

Prob. b. The devil incited the will of Eve to affect a more eminent assimilation with God, and to covet a greater pinnacle of knowledge than that which she had obtained with the divine image from the Creator. having moved with a body, and having been furnished with feet.

8) This punishment, denounced to this masked serpent, is in other places attributed to the evil demon, in translated words, or clearly the same, or those of the same value; specifically (α) you shall go upon your belly, which manner of speaking denotes the most humble state, see Ps. XLIV, 26, add. Apoc. XII, 9. (β) you shall eat dust, that which designates the most sorrowful state, without any recreation, Ps. LXXII, 9. CII, 10. add. Is. LXV, 25, in which place the prophet foretells certain things concerning the chief adversary of the sacred assembly in the New Testament (who is indeed without doubt the devil); and the continuous and perpetual duration of this condition of misery is predicted by this addition: all the days of your life. (γ) That statement: The seed of the woman shall crush the serpent's head, that it is nothing other than the first prophecy concerning Christ, who was to destroy the works of the devil, is agreed upon among all who are truly addicted to Christ.

Against these such clear arguments, there is nothing ready for the most learned men who deny it, except this one objection: that our interpretation does not agree with the properties of the historical style.

But the answer will be easy: 1) Even all those who understand a natural serpent, although not only (for that he was only that is the absurd opinion of recent Jews, and likewise of the Socinians), cannot but admit certain figurative locutions, both metonymical and metaphorical, namely, the seed of the woman, for the man who was generated from the woman; in the sweat of your face, that is, in difficult, troublesome labor, full of miseries; you shall eat dust, that cannot be thought to be spoken otherwise than figuratively (for it is not the way of a serpent to eat dust, but to lick it, as it is of any animal that creeps on the ground, Mich. VII, 17). Indeed, whatever they think was inflicted as a punishment on the natural serpent, they cannot but interpret it improperly.

2) The historical manner of speaking also demands that diverse subjects be named distinctly and clearly, such a difference as is seen nowhere in this place. 3) The style in this narrative is not only historical, but also dogmatic; it is at the same time prophetic, as much regarding the punishment to be undergone by the serpent, as the medicine prepared for the whole human race. And yet, by the custom of sacred speech, and most especially Hebrew, future events are often predicted by translated words.

nacted. For the deceiver was saying: Indeed, God knows that on the day you eat of it (the fruit), your eyes will be opened, and then you will be like God, knowing good and evil, Gen. III, 5. The devil did not persuade man with these words of equality with the true and supreme God, but of a certain perfection more sublime in the image of God, so that he would come to know good and evil as certainly and solidly as God knows it, if he were to eat of the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. For we do not think that men, created in perfect wisdom, were so imprudent as to believe that a creature could become equal to the supreme God. Conf. annot. D. SEB. SCHMID. in Gen. p. 40.

Prob. c. Therefore the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes and desirable to give understanding, Gen. III, 6. The woman looked at the tree of the knowledge of good and evil with the eyes of both body and mind, and considered that its fruit was delicate, beautiful, and useful for producing solid and perfect knowledge of good and evil; by which very thing the appetite of the woman was stimulated to taste that fruit, against the law prescribed by the Creator.

Prob. d. Therefore she (the woman) took of its fruit, and ate: and she also gave to her husband with her, who (also) ate. Gen. III, 6. By which words the sin finished (ἡ ἁμαρτία ἀποτελεσθεῖσα), the sin of the first man, which brings forth death (Iac. I, 15.), is described by Moses, which deed openly opposes the positive divine law, laid down by God in paradise, Gen. II, 17.

Latin:

Diabolus in seducendo primo homine serpente vero & naturali a), a se corporaliter obsesso b), velut instrumento vsus est.

Prob. a. De serpente scribit Moses Gen. III, 1. Verum enim vero serpens factus est astutus (per Diaboli ingressum) præ omnibus feris agri, quas fecerat Iehouah Deus. Serpentem hunc verum & naturalem fuisse colligitur 1) ex naturali calliditate, cum comparatus cum bestiis agri, his dicitur fuisse astutior. Quam calliditatem serpentinam Christus ipse non reticet, Matth. X, 16. 2) Ex inflicta pœna, quæ serpenti per reptioneın super terram, & comestionem pulueris sustinenda est, Gen. III, 14. (*) Prob. b. Non fuisse serpentem merum, sed ἐνεργούμενον, sive a diabolo obsessum, colligitur 1) ex eo, quod serpens merus non potest loqui. At serpens paradisiacus articulato utebatur sermone. 2) Ex hominis seductione. Serpens est bona Dei creatura. At serpens paradisiacus fuit primi hominis seductor. 3) Ex calcanei contritione; quæ non ad naturalem, sed infernalem serpentem refertur. Ex quo conficitur, diabolum cum serpente παρασατικῶς, seu accidentaliter fuisse vnitum.

V. Quam legem protoplasti lapsu violarunt?

Primi parentes lapsu suo immediate violarunt legem positivam in paradiso promulgatam, de non comedendo fructu arboris scientiæ boni & mali a); mediate & virtualiter inobedientia sua totius legis moralis repagula perfregerunt b).

Prob. a. Comedere de fructibus arboris moraliter neque malum est neque per se: accedente autem interdicto diuino fit malum ob auctoritatem summi domini, & legislatoris. Iam autem Deus lege positiva esum de fructibus arboris scientiæ boni & mali speciatim & diserte protoplastis interdixerat, Gen. II, 17. Quare primi homines comedendo de eadem arbore immediate violarunt legem Dei positivam.

Prob. b. Ratio legis positivæ erat δοκιμασία, sive probatio obedientiæ, quam, Deo debitam, tota lex moralis requirit. Qui autem non veretur vnum præceptum transgredi, is non erubescit reliqua violare præcepta, cum eundem auctorem, eandemque vim obligandi habeant.

Quocirca præclare ait TERTVLLIANVS L. II. cont. Marc. II. Primordialis lex data Adæ & Euæ in paradiso, est quasi matrix omnium præceptorum Dei. Nimirum protoplasti inobedientia sua omnia & singula præcepta decalogi virtualiter & per consequentiam violarunt: I. præceptum diffidentia & apostasia; II. mandati diuini peruersa interpretatione & culpæ in Deum translatione: III. verbi diuini contemptu: IV. inobedientia atque ingratitudine qui in illo latuerit.

2) Tanta scientia pollebat Heua, vt ignorare non posset, serpentem esse brutum animal, omni ratione vacuum, neque orationis capax; ex quo ea non poterat non fraudem protinus animaduertere, atque ab ista colloquutione abhorrere. Personatum autem serpentem, falsa Heuæ scientia ac sapientia, non ita suspectum ipsi finisse, efficitur ex his rebus circumstantibus: (α) Probe sciebat mulier, spiritus a Deo creatos multos esse, omnesque bonos ac vitii expertes: (β) Non eam præteribat, eos maioribus, quam homines, perfectionibus exornatos esse: (γ) Nouerat etiam officium, angelis mandatum, quo Dei laudes perpetuo canerent, atque imperata facerent, nec non semper homini adessent comites, vt nullum ipsi periculum ab eis esset metuendum.

(Id quod tamen minime aptum est excusando Heuæ delicto. Contenta esse debebat verbo Dei, prorsus immutabili, nec vnquam reuocando, eique tota constanter adhærescere): (δ) Nec dubitabat, quin fieri possit, vt spiritus illi formam corporis aliquam adsumerent: Denique (ε) admodum est probabile, defectionem angelorum perfidorum non prius factam fuisse, quam hac ipsa actione, qua hominum virtuti ac felicitati inuidere cœperunt; vid. adnotata ad pag. 198. Bonum igitur putabat esse spiritum, a quo nihil, nisi bonum ac salutare, exspectabat futurum.

3) Serpens, primi peccati hominum auctor furaforque, dicitur diabolus, Apoc. XII, 9. 4) Nomini vna præfixum n indicio est, serpentem hunc fuisse plane singularem, cuius proprietas fuerit astutia.

Comparatur ille cum omnibus animalium generibus, ipsisque adeo serpentibus venenatis. Comparatio autem interdum habet vim negationis, vt Ioan. III, 19 & 20, 2 Tim. III, 4. Est igitur hæc sententia: Hic serpens fuit callidus & ad fraudem acutus, cuiusmodi nullum est animal, tametsi ille animalis cuiusdam speciem præ se tulerit.

5) Sermonem protulit, eumque insidiosum ac mendacem, multis etiam ambiguitatibus implicitum. 6) Pœna, proprie sic dicta, nulli animali bruto irrogari potest. 7) Hæc pœna, si proprie verba intelligantur, est conditio eiusmodi, quæ serpentibus, immo & omnibus animalibus, humi repentibus, conuenit: fabulam enim narrant, qui dicunt, serpentes antea erecto corpore serpentes antea erecto serpentes antea erecto titudine erga Deum, cœlestem patrem & dominum summum, a quo tot beneficiis erant cumulati; V. homicidio, dum caussa moralis sunt mortis spiritualis, corporalis & æternæ posterorum; VI. intemperantia & gulæ libidine, perfidia Evæ in maritum, inordinato Adami amore in uxorem; VII. furto, dum contrectarunt rem alienam (fructum non suum) invito domino; VIII. falso testimonio & falsi testimonii approbatione; IX. & X. pravæ divinæ similitudinis, supernaturalis cuiusdam scientiæ, & fructus prohibiti concupiscentia.

VI. In quo formaliter consistit peccatum primum? Peccatum hominum primum formaliter consistit in deflexione a lege Dei positiva in paradiso promulgata, de non comedendo fructu arboris scientiæ boni & mali. Quæ ἀνομία involuit actus peccaminosos, ex parte intellectus ἀπισίαν sive incredulitatem , ex parte voluntatis φιλαυτίαν & superbiam , ex parte appetitus sensitivi inordinatam fructus vetiti concupiscentiam ; e quibus emersit actus externus, lege paradisiaca prohibitus .

Prob. a. Cum Heua anceps hæreret inter verbum Dei: Quo die comedes de arbore scientiæ boni & mali, moriendo morieris, Gen. II, 17. & verbum diaboli: Non moriendo moriemini, Gen. III, 4. Illa a verbo divino mentem avertit, fidem illi derogando, & ad verbum diabolicum animum convertit, assensum illi præbendo; quæ sane nefanda est ἀπισία, radix primi peccati.

Vt enim fides principium accessus ad Deum est, Hebr. XI, 1. ita infidelitas est principium aversionis a Deo, Io. XVI, 19. Certe diabolus primum follicitauit hominem ad dubitationem de veritate verbi diuini; deinde palam verbo diuino contradixit, indicaturus id falsum esse; postremo voluntatem Heuæ ad superbiam flexit.

Prob. b. Irritauit diabolus voluntatem Heuæ ad affectandam eminentiorem cum Deo assimilationem, & ambiendum maius scientiæ fastigium, quam cum imagine diuina a creatore nacta corpore incessisse, ac pedibus fuisse instructos.

8) Hæc pœna, huic serpenti personato denunciata, aliis in locis malo dæmoni tribuitur, verbis translatis, aut plane eisdem, aut idem valentibus; sigillatim (α) ventre incedes, quæ dicendi ratio denotat statum humillimum, vid. Ps. XLIV, 26. add. Apoc. XII, 9. (β) puluerem comedes, id quod designat statum tristissimum, sine vlla recreatione, Ps. LXXII, 9. CII, 10. add. Ies. LXV, 25. quo in loco vates prænuntiat quædam de præcipuo aduersario sacri cœtus in N. F. (is vero haud dubie est diabolus); & miseriæ huius conditionis duratio continua ac perpetua prædicitur hoc additamento: ad dies vitæ tuæ. (γ) Istud effatum: Semen mulieris conteret serpentis caput, nihil aliud esse, quam primam vaticinationem de Christo, opera diaboli destructuro, constat inter omnes, Christo vere addictos.

Aduersus hæc adeo luculenta argumenta nihil in promptu est diffitentibus viris doctissimis, præter hanc vnam oppositionem: quod nostra interpretatio non conueniat proprietatibus styli historici.

At facilis erit responsio: 1) Omnes etiam illi, qui serpentem naturalem, quamuis non solum (solum enim eum fuisse, est absurda Iudæorum recentiorum, itemque Socinianorum opinio) intelligunt, non possunt non admittere figuratas quasdam loquutiones, tum metonymicas, tum metaphoricas, nimirum semen mulieris, pro homine, qui ex semine generatus est; in sudore faciei tuæ, hoc est, labore difficili, molesto, ærumnarum pleno; puluerem comedes, id not potest aliter, quam figurate dictum putari (rion enim edere puluerem, sed eum lambere, serpentis est, vt & animalis cuiusque, quod humi repit Mich. VII, 17.). Immo quidquid pænæ serpentis naturali inflictum esse arbitrantur, id non possunt non improprie interpretari.

2) Historica dicendi ratio etiam illud postulat, vt subiecta diuersa distincte ac perspicue nominentur, qualis differentia hoc in loco nulla cernitur. 3) Stylus in hac narratione non solum historicus est, sed etiam dogmaticus; est simul propheticus, quantum ad pœnam, serpenti subeundam, & medicinam vniuerso hominum generi paratam. Atqui sermonis sacri, ac potissimum hebraici, consuetudine euentus futuri sæpe numero verbis translatis prænuntiantur.

nacta erat. Dicebat enim veterator: Quin novit Deus, quod quo die comeditis de eo (fructu), aperientur oculi vestri, tumque eritis sicut Deus, scientes bonum & malum, Gen. III, 5. Non persuasit diabolus verbis istis homini æqualitatem cum Deo vero & summo, sed perfectionem quandam imagine Dei sublimiorem, vt tam certo & solide bonum & malum cogniturus fit, quam id scit Deus, si comedat de fructu arboris scientiæ boni & mali. Neque enim putamus homines, in perfecta sapientia creatos, tam imprudentes fuisse, vt crederent, creaturam Deo summo æqualem fieri posse. Conf. annot. D. SEB. SCHMID. in Gen. p. 40.

Prob. c. Vidit itaque mulier, quod bona esset arbor in cibum, & quod appetibilis oculis & desiderabilis ad dandum intellectum, Gen. III, 6. Aspexit mulier arborem scientiæ boni & mali tam corporis, quam animi oculis, & consideravit, quod fructus eius delicatus, pulcer & vtilis ad gignendum solidam perfectamque scientiam boni & mali esset; quo ipso stimulatus est appetitus mulieris ad degustandum istum fructum, contra legem a creatore præscriptam.

Prob. d. Ideo sumsit (mulier) de fructu eius, & comedit: deditque etiam viro suo secum, qui (etiam) comedit. Gen. III, 6. Quibus verbis ἡ ἁμαρτία ἀποτελεσθεῖσα, peccatum primi hominis consummatum, quod parturit mortem (Iac. I, 15.) a Mose describitur, quod factum legi divinæ positivæ, in paradiso a Deo latæ, Gen. II, 17. aperte repugnat.


### VII. Was Adam not less seduced by the devil than Eve?

Adam was not immediately seduced by the devil, as the woman was a). Yet he was mediately and by the persuasion of the woman drawn into the same sin, and thus the fall of Adam also returns to the devil, as the primary author of sin b). Prob. a. That the devil first attacked the woman, the history recounting the fall of the first humans teaches, Gen. III, 1. ff. and Paul confirms 2 Tim. II, 14. Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived in the transgression. The apostle speaks of the order and manner of the seduction. Indeed, not Adam first, but Eve was deceived. Eve was immediately seduced by the devil, Adam mediately by the same through the woman. Eve, having been seduced, was the cause of the transgression for Adam, but Adam, having been seduced, was not the author of Eve's prevarication.

Prob. b. Adam obeyed Eve, deceived by the serpent, and persuading him to the eating of the forbidden fruit, Gen. III, 6. Therefore Adam was deceived by the serpent through the woman. The consequence is proved 1) from the intention of the devil, who had destined to deceive and to cast down from the breath of original happiness not only the woman, but also the man. From which he is called the father of lies and a murderer from the beginning, Io. VIII, 44. 2) Because without doubt Eve overcame Adam with the same arguments of persuasion with which she had been overcome by the serpent; although there was added the most tender affection for his wife and the experience which testified that his wife had not died from the eating of the forbidden fruit.

There is an antithesis of Bellarmine and others, who maintain that Adam was not properly seduced. Their stronger arguments are: I. Paul expressly denies that Adam was deceived or seduced, 1 Tim. III, 14. Resp. Paul does not deny ἁπλῶς, or simply, that Adam was seduced, but he denies that he was the first to be deceived by the serpent, so that he was the cause of Eve's transgression.

II. The cause of Adam's error was excessive love toward his spouse; not the persuasion of the serpent or of the woman. For he did not wish to sadden his companion, and his only one. Resp. I. It is false that Adam was not deceived by the persuasion of Eve, but was blinded by love for her. The judgment of God pronounced against Adam teaches otherwise: Because you have obeyed the voice of your wife, Eve, &c. Gen. To this is added that the love of a woman, as long as it is subordinated to trust in God, cannot be the cause of a fall.

III. Adam was not properly deceived or seduced, because Eve did not have the intention of deceiving, but of increasing the excellence or happiness of her husband.

Resp. 1) Seduction is not judged by the intention of the seducer or the seduced, but by the thing itself.

Whence, wherever anyone is led away from the path of true doctrine and eternal salvation, whether an explicit intention to deceive exists in the seducer or not; there is seduction, 1 John

II, 26. 2) Someone can be a seducer of himself, 2 Tim.

III, 13. although there is hardly found a man who has the intention of deceiving himself. 3) The seduction of Adam, with respect to the seducing cause, does not terminate in Eve, but in the serpent, to whom it primarily belongs.

Although, therefore, there was no intention in Eve to deceive her husband, there was, however, in the serpent the intention, through Eve—already corrupted by sin—as through a convenient instrument, to seduce Adam.

Question VIII. What end does the devil the tempter, and man, the transgressor of the Paradisiacal law, intend?

Prob. a. God reserved the angels, who did not keep their origin but left their own dwelling, for the judgment of the great day, in perpetual chains under darkness.

See ep. Jude v. 6. From which the prince of darkness burns with an insatiable desire for vengeance, which, because it is impossible (ἐκ τῶν ἀδυνάτων ἐστί) to exact it from God Himself, he strives to exact it from man, by corrupting him and tearing him away from God, so as to spite the father and lord of man.

Prob. b.

In creation, God had adorned man, the prince of visible creatures, with His own image, encompassing the distinguished perfections of soul and body; but, when the serpent said: God knows that on the day you eat of that fruit, your eyes will be opened; then you will be as God, knowing good and evil, a desire seized man to aspire to a more perfect assimilation with God, and a degree of wisdom more excellent than that which had been granted to them by the Creator.

Question IX. What are the consequences of the Adamic fall?

Prob. a.

Guilt, or moral foulness, which resulted from the eating of the forbidden fruit, is to be estimated 1) from the majesty of the legislator, injured by the illicit act.

The first sinner injured God, the best creator, the most wise legislator, the most just judge. 2) From the amplitude or extension of the guilt.

For the stain contracted from the act, which was non-conforming to the Paradisiacal law, not only adhered to Adam and Eve, but was also sprinkled upon all their descendants, except Christ, 3) From the ease of the prescribed law.

The Paradisiacal law consisted of a single interdict regarding one thing, easy to observe, about not eating the fruit of one tree. But since paradise abounded with many and most wholesome fruits, it was extremely easy to abstain from one tree.

Truly, how shameful it is not to holily cherish and observe even a single precept of God.

4) From the safeguards with which man was fortified against the fall. He was adorned with the divine image, by virtue of which he possessed extraordinary wisdom, by which he most exactly discerned good from evil; he was eminent in perfect holiness, by which he inclined toward the good; but he turned away from evil.

5) From the consideration of the circumstances.

For where did Adam sin? In paradise, in which there were no incitements to sin, and very many incitements to worship God.

When did he transgress?

Not long after.

The devil, in inciting man to the first sin, intended vengeance against God, the judge and avenger of his apostasy (ἀποστασίας). The consequence of the Adamic fall is the liability of guilt and punishment.

long after creation, when man was as if still warm from the hands of God. 6) From the indignity of the deed. What is more unworthy of man than to refuse assent to the most truthful word of Jehovah, and to assent to the most fallacious word of the devil? What is more indecorous than not to live content with a most happy condition, divinely dispensed? What is more detestable than to wish to seize deiformity, just as Absalom, a son of most profligate impiety, deemed royal dignity to be a prize, into which he strove to fly. 7) From the virtual violation of all the precepts of the entire decalogue, concerning which above, quest. V. Prob. b. Punishment pressed upon guilt as an individual companion. The most holy God had threatened man with death if he should transgress the prescribed law; Gen. II, 17. By death was denoted spiritual, corporal, and eternal death. Spiritual death, the root of every evil, is the immediate consequence of τῆς ἀποστασίας or the first sin. For at the moment man turned his mind away from the divine law, he deprived himself of spiritual union with God, who is the life of the soul, and thus, deserted by God, he was spiritually dead. This spiritual death drew with it the loss of the divine image, the most profound corruption of the entire human nature, and the defect of free will in spiritual matters. Spiritual death, or that of the soul, is followed by the death of the body, encompassing all diseases and miseries externally surrounding man. To this pertains the harsh and troublesome labor, to be constantly endured by man, Gen. III, 17, and the painful childbirth of the wife, v. 16. Although, however, the protoplasts did not suffer the death of the body at the first moment of the fall, they nevertheless immediately became debtors to death, since this is the wages of sin, Rom. VI, 23. Eternal death is the perpetual exclusion from the beatific fruition of God, joined with perennial torments, and those by far the most bitter; which, by the force of the threat annexed to the divine law, would have had to be undergone by Adam and his entire posterity, had not Jesus Christ, the redeemer of the human race and the restorer of the lost divine image, intervened.

Latin:

Adamus non fuit immediate seductus a diabolo, vt mulier a). Mediate tamen & suasu mulieris in idem peccatum pertractus, adeoque lapsus Adami etiam in diabolum, vt primum peccati auctorem, redit b). Prob. a. Diabolum primum aggressum esse fœminam, docet historia recensens lapsum primorum hominum, Gen. III, 1. sqq. & confirmat Paullus 2 Tim. II, 14. Adam non fuit deceptus, sed mulier decepta in trasgressione fuit. Loquitur apostolus de ordine & modo seductionis. Nimirum non prior Adam, sed Eua decepta est. Eua immediate a diabolo, Adam ab eodem mediate per mulierem seductus est. Eua seducta causa transgressionis fuit Adamo, sed Adamus seductus non fuit auctor præuaricationis Euæ.

Prob. b. Adam obedivit Euæ, a serpente deceptæ, & manducationem fructus vetiti suadenti, Gen. III, 6. Ergo Adam a serpente per mulierem deceptus est. Probatur consequentia 1) ab intentione diaboli, qui destinauerat decipere & de flatu primæ felicitatis deturbare non tantum fœminam, sed & virum. Ex quo pater mendacii & homicida ab initio audit, Io. VIII, 44. 2) Quia haud dubie Eua iisdem persuadendi argumentis Adamum vicit, quibus victa erat a serpente; quamuis accederet tenerrimus in vxorem adfectus & experientia, quæ testabatur, vxorem ab esu fructus vetiti non esse mortuam.

Antithesis est Bellarmini & aliorum, statuentium, Adamum proprie non esse seductum. Quorum potiora sunt argumenta: I. Paullus diserte negat, Adamum esse deceptum aut seductum, 1 Tim. III, 14. Resp. Paullus non ἁπλῶς, aut simpliciter negat, Adamum esse seductum, sed negat, eundem primum esse deceptum a serpente, vt causa fuerit transgressionis Euæ.

II. Causa erroris Adami fuit amor nimius erga coniugem; non serpentis, vel mulieris persuasio. Noluit enim sociam, eamque vnicam contristare. Resp. I. Falsum est, Adamum non Euæ persuasione deceptum, sed amore eius fuisse excæcatum. Aliud docet iudicium Dei pronuntiatum aduersus Adamum: Quia obtemperasti voci vxoris, Euæ, &c. Gen. Huc accedit, quod amor mulieris, quamdiu fiduciae Dei subordinatur, non possit esse causa lapsus.

III. Adam non est proprie deceptus, aut seductus, quia Eva non habuit intentionem fallendi, sed augendi excellentiam, aut felicitatem mariti.

Resp. 1) Seductio non aestimatur ex intentione seducentis, aut seducti, sed ex re ipsa.

Unde ubicunque a via verae doctrinae & salutis aeternae quispiam abducitur, sive explicita fit intentio fallendi in seducente, sive non; ibi seductio est, 1 Io.

II, 26. 2) Potest aliquis esse seductor sui ipsius, 2 Tim.

III, 13. cum tamen vix inveniatur homo, qui intentionem habeat se ipsum fallendi. 3) Seductio Adami, respectu causae seducentis, non terminatur in Eva, sed in serpente, cui illa principaliter convenit.

Licet ergo in Eva non fuerit intentio fallendi maritum, fuit tamen in serpente intentio per Evam, iam corruptam peccato, vt per instrumentum commodum, seducendi Adamum.

Quaest. VIII. Quem finem intendit diabolus tentator, & homo, legis Paradisiacae transgressor?

Prob. a. Deus angelos, qui non retinuerunt suam originem, sed reliquerunt proprium domicilium, in iudicium magni diei, vinculis perpetuis sub tenebris reseruauit.

Vid. ep. Iud. v. 6. Ex quo princeps tenebrarum ardet inexplebili vindictae cupiditate, quam quia ab ipso Deo exigere ἐκ τῶν ἀδυνάτων ἐστί, connititur eam repetere ab homine, hunc corrumpendo & a Deo auellendo, vt hominis patri & domino aegre faciat.

Prob. b.

Deus in creatione hominem, principem creaturarum visibilium, condecorauerat imagine sua, complectente insignes perfectiones animae corporisque; at, cum diceret serpens: Nouit Deus, quod, quo die comederitis de eo fructu, aperientur oculi vestri; tum eritis sicut Deus, scientes bonum & malum, incessit hominem cupido aspirandi ad perfectiorem cum Deo assimilationem, & gradum sapientiae excellentiorem, quam qui a creatore ipsis concessus erat.

Quaest. IX. Quenam sunt lapsus Adamitici consequentia?

Prob. a.

Culpa, vel foeditas moralis, quae e manducatione fructus vetiti resultauit, aestimanda est 1) ex maiestate legislatoris, actu illicito laesi.

Laesit primus peccator Deum, creatorem optimum, legislatorem sapientissimum, iudicem iustissimum. 2) E culpae amplitudine, vel extensione.

Macula enim contracta ex actu, legi paradisiacae difformi, non tantum adhaesit Adamo & Evae, sed aspersa etiam est omnibus eorum posteris, excepto Christo, 3) Ex legis praescripta facilitate.

Lex paradisiaca vnico constabat interdicto de re vna, servatu facili, de non comedendo fructu vnius arboris. At cum paradisus & plurimis, & faluberrimis abundauerit fructibus, perquam facile fuit, ab vna arbore abstinere.

Sane quam turpissimum est, ne vnicum quidem praeceptum Dei sancte colere & obseruare.

4) Ex praesidiis, quibus homo contra lapsum munitus erat. Condecoratus erat imagine diuina, vi cuius pollebat eximia sapientia, qua bonum a malo exactissime discernebat; eminebat perfecta sanctitate, qua ad bonum propendebat; malum autem auersabatur.

5) Ex circumstantiarum consideratione.

Vbi enim peccabat Adamus? In paradiso, in quo ad peccandum irritamenta nulla, ad colendum Deum incitamenta plurima.

Quando delinquebat?

Haud diu

Diabolus, concitando hominem ad peccatum primum, intendit vindictam in Deum, suae ἀποστασίας iudicem & vindicem Consequentia lapsus Adamitici reatus culpae & poenae.

diu post creationem, cum homo a manibus Dei recens quasi caleret. 6) Ex facti indignitate. Quid homine indignius est, quam assensum verbo Iehouæ verissimo abnuere, & verbo diaboli fallacissimo annuere? Quid indecorum magis, quám conditione felicissima, diuinitus dispensata, non viuere contentum? Quid detestabilius, quam velle deiformitatem rapere, haud secus ac Absolon, filius profligatissimæ impietatis, regiam dignitatem rapinam esse censebat, in quam inuolare nitebatur. 7) Ex violatione virtuali omnium præceptorum totius decalogi, de qua supra, quæst. V. Prob. b. Culpam pœna pressit indiuidua comes. Interminatus erat Deus sanctissimus homini, si legem præscriptam transgrederetur, mortem; Gen. II, 17. Per mortem denotabatur mors spiritualis, corporalis & æterna. Mors spiritualis, radix omnis mali, τῆς ἀποστασίας siue peccati primi immediatum est consequens. Nam quo momento homo animum a lege diuina auertit, se ipsum priuauit vnione spirituali cum Deo, qui est vita animæ, adeoque a Deo desertus spiritualiter mortuus est. Quæ mors spiritualis secum traxit amissionem imaginis diuinæ, profundissimam totius humanæ naturæ corruptionem, & defectum liberi arbitrii in rebus spiritualibus. Mortem spiritualem, siue animæ, sequitur mors corporis, complectens omnes morbos & miserias extrinsece hominem circumstantes. Quo pertinet labor asper & molestus, viro iugiter exantlandus, Gen. III, 17. & partus vxoris dolorificus, v. 16. Quamvis autem primo lapsus momento protoplasti mortem corporis non oppetierint, illico tamen debitores mortis facti sunt, cum isthæc peccati sit stipendium, Rom. VI, 23. Mors æterna est perpetua a beatifica Dei fruitione exclusio, cum cruciatibus perennibus, iisque longe acerbissimis coniuncta; quæ vi comminationis, legi diuinæ annexæ, subeunda fuisset Adamo, & vniuersæ ipsius posteritati, nisi Iesus Christus, redemtor generis humani, & reparator amissæ imaginis diuinæ, interuenisset.


### VII. Was Adam not less seduced by the devil than Eve?: Quest. X. Is the first sin of Adam truly and justly imputed to his posterity?

Quest. X. Is the first sin of Adam truly and justly imputed to his posterity?

The first sin of Adam, insofar as he is viewed as the common parent, head, stock, and representative of the entire human race, is truly (a) and by the just judgment of God (b) imputed to all his posterity for guilt and punishment.

Prob. a. from Rom. V, 12. Just as through one man sin entered into the world, and death through sin; and so death passed through to all men, in whom all have sinned. 1) By one man can be understood in the loc. cit. Adam and Eve, who are called one man, both by reason of economic communion, because through marriage spouses become one flesh, Gen. II, 24; and by reason of communion in sinning, because they were one heart by consent of sin, which they ought to have been by consent of obedience; yet the apostle especially regards Adam, the root, source, seed-plot, and representative of the entire human race, the type of the second Adam, v. 14, and the head of Eve, 1 Cor. XI, 3. 2) By sin is first understood the fall of Adam, consequently original sin, or habitual and hereditary depravity. 3) Sin entered into the world, i.e., into man, who is a μικροκόσμος, or little world: it entered not by God effecting, compelling, or impelling, but through the voluntary abuse of free will; it entered, not by imitation, since it is also attributed to infants, who did not sin in the likeness of Adam's transgression, v. 14, i.e., who could not imitate Adam by sinning: but partly through the imputation of the Adamic fall; partly through carnal propagation, if you look at the habitual depravity which redounded from the fall of Adam. 4) Through sin entered spiritual, corporal, and eternal death. But death passed through to all men (scil. through one man) in whom all have sinned. Some interpreters of the Greek words of Paul: ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον, with ERASMUS, to whom the Socinians and Arminians accede, have rendered it reduplicatively or causally: insofar as, because, for the reason that all have sinned; most of whom reject the imputation of the Adamic fall, and from it arisen original sin. LUTHER, indeed, also rendered it causally: "In that all have sinned," but not without respect to Adam, as head or root; because it cannot be conceived by the mind how we have sinned in Adam, as in a subject, unless it be said that sin has passed from him into us causally. The Latin and Greek Fathers, except THEODORET, explain it in a relative or subjective sense, since the Vulgate… interpreter also expresses a relative sense.

FELBINGER, a Socinian, in his version of the New Testament, combines the causal and subjective sense, and renders the words of Paul in German: "Therefore, as through one man sin has entered into the world, and through sin death, even so death has entered into all men, in that (or in whom) all have sinned.

The relative or subjective sense, by which ἐφ᾽ ᾧ is rendered in Latin, "in whom," seems analogous to the text, and is proved: 1) because ἐφ᾽ ᾧ in the New Testament is most frequently taken relatively, and not reduplicatively or causally. See Mark II, 4; Luke V, 25; XI, 22; Rom. VI, 2; Phil. IV, 10; 1 Thess. III, 7. Compare ERASMUS SCHMID on the New Testament in this place. Only one biblical passage seems to favor those who dissent, Phil. III, 12, ἐφ᾽ ᾧ καὶ κατελήφθην, which words ERASMUS SCHMID explains as, "insofar as I have been apprehended by Christ Jesus"; but SEB. SCHMID translates, "in whom I have also been apprehended." With these things considered, it is clear that ἐφ᾽ ᾧ in the New Testament never signifies "because" or "for the reason that." 2) The coherence of the text teaches a relative sense. For the apostle connects in verse 12 the propagation of sin, the origin of death, and the magnitude of the first sin, to wit: Through Adam sin entered into the world: Through Adam's sin death passed into all: In Adam all have sinned. 3) The antithesis proves this sense, by which Christ is opposed to Adam, which likewise has three opposites: Through Christ the grace of God: through grace the gift came into the world, v. 15. Through Christ's obedience grace passed into all, v. 18. In Christ they are constituted righteous, as many as are justified, v. 19. 4) The apostle uses a not dissimilar phrase, 1 Cor. XV, 22: In Adam all die. These things being set forth, we argue: To those who have sinned in Adam, the sin of Adam is also imputed: But all have sinned in Adam, etc. Therefore. The major is proved: because no evil men existed when Adam transgressed the commandment of God, so that they could become participants of the Adamic sin in their own person, actually and formally: Therefore they became participants of the same fact morally, by imputation, according to the estimation or judgment of God.

2) From Rom. V, 19. As by the disobedience of one man many were constituted sinners: so also by the obedience of one righteous man many are constituted righteous. Objection 1) By the disobedience of one man is understood the transgression of Adam, v. 14, which is opposed to the obedience of Christ. 2) As the obedience of Christ, so the disobedience of Adam is a singular or personal act. But no singular or personal act, morally good or evil, can be common to several persons who are essentially distinct, except by imputation. For it implies a contradiction for an act to be singular and formally common to many. 3) By many men are understood all, because all men are in reality many. Compare Dan. XII, 2; John V, 28. We gather from these: 1) Whosoever men differ essentially from Adam, and nevertheless are constituted sinners before the divine tribunal through his disobedience, to them the disobedience of Adam is imputed for guilt: But all men, etc. Therefore. 2) Whosoever are constituted sinners in the same way through the disobedience of Adam, as they are constituted righteous through the obedience of Christ, they are sinners through the disobedience of Adam imputatively: But all men born according to the series of nature, etc. Therefore. 3) The punishment of Adam is imputed to his posterity: Therefore also his guilt. The consequence is manifest: because guilt and punishment are relative; and therefore the latter has the former as its companion or presupposes it. Indeed he cannot be a sharer in another's punishment who is without share in that guilt itself. The antecedent stands: because in Adam we were stripped of the image of God, cast out of paradise, subjected to labors, pains, diseases, death.

Prob. b. The justice and equity of the imputation of the Adamic fall into the guilt and punishment of his descendants is evident from this, that Adam is the common parent of all men, inasmuch as they existed in him virtually or seminally; and also the moral head of the whole human race. It is certain, moreover, that the enormous and very grave crime of a father is by most just right imputed to his descendants for guilt and punishment; for example, a vassal of some king, committing the crime of high treason, is deprived of the fiefs granted by the king, not only the father himself, but also his descendants lose them. Since, therefore, all men were in Adam, as in a father and stock, not indeed as regards individual reason, but as regards specific existence, or representation, by most just right the sin of the common father is imputed to all men who existed in him. Add that Adam was also the moral, or federal, head of the human race; for this reason, that he was not only created morally good, but God, the thrice best, had also entered into a covenant with him, by the force of which He had promised him the perennial perfection and happiness of paradise for soul and body, but under the condition of constant obedience; but He had decreed the punishment of spiritual, corporal, and eternal death for disobedience. Gen. II, 17. Obedience, δοκιμασία, according to the divine intention, was abstinence from the fruits of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Wherefore, when Adam refused obedience and sinned, his entire posterity was judged by the most just estimation of God to have sinned, and thus the concreated perfection and the promised happiness of paradise was lost: on the contrary, from the transgression of Adam, guilt and punishment redounded to the descendants of Adam.

2) The image of God and the happiness connected with it was not a personal good, but one common to the whole human species, Gen. V, 1, 2. Therefore, when Adam, the representative of the human species, was deprived of that common good, which he had received no more for himself than for his descendants, by the most just judgment of God on account of disobedience, all men were at once deprived of the same. For it is most just that he should feel the disadvantage to whom the advantage would have come.

3) The will of the sinning Adam was interpretatively the will of all men, inasmuch as Adam revealed and declared it by the abuse of free will.

For all and singular men who are, have been, or shall be, except Christ, if they had lived at the same time as Adam, would have consented to his sin. Which is evident a) from this, that Adam, the parent and head of the human race, easily consented to the transgression of Eve: b) As is the earthly one (as the natural stock of the whole human species), such are all the earthly ones (in will and intellect), 1 Cor. XV, 48. But he who consents to a most atrocious sin, by which the supreme majesty is injured, is not unjustly considered guilty of guilt and punishment: Since, therefore, God foresaw the virtual consent of all men to the first sin, He imputed to all, by a most just judgment, the guilt and punishment which accompanies the fall of Adam.

Antithesis is 1) of the Socinians, who deny that the crime of Adam is imputed to his descendants; 2) of the Arminians, some of whom deny the imputation of the first sin; some assert that the cause of the imputation is not the just judgment of God, but His own free will.

I. The imputation of the Adamic transgression cannot be solidly proven from sacred scripture. For 1) Rom.

V, 12. the little words, ἐφ' ᾧ, cannot be rendered subjectively, "in whom," but must be explained causally, "in that." If they were rendered "in whom," they would refer to one man, which the interjected words do not allow. Furthermore, that the apostle is speaking of actual sin, and that which is proper to each man, the following v. 13 teaches. 2) Rom. V, 19, by the disobedience of Adam men are constituted such that sin inheres in them. Therefore the apostle l. c. does not treat of the imputation of sin. 3) Men die not because the guilt of sin attaches to all, but because they draw their origin from Adam. Reply to 1): That a relative pronoun is not always joined proximately to the subject to which it refers, the Pauline passage teaches, 2 Thess. II, 9. Sometimes more regard must be had is the series of things, as the order of words: τὸ ἐφ᾽ ᾧ (that in which) is aptly referred to τὸν ἄνθρωπον (the man), of whom there was previous discourse. Moreover, the apostle speaks in v. 12 of sin not as personal, but as common and universal, because he says that in one man all have sinned, namely morally, on account of the imputation of the Adamic fall; v. 13 treats of actual sins, insofar as they manifest the first sin a posteriori.

To 2): Through the disobedience of Adam we are constituted sinners before the divine tribunal imputatively, because the guilt resulting from the transgression of Adam is imputed to us; and this is the reason why original sin, which flowed from the first sin, inheres in us.

For just as the obedience of Christ is imputed to us for righteousness: so the disobedience of Adam is imputed to us for guilt.

To 3): The liability to punishment precedes the liability to guilt.

God imposes the punishment of death on no one, unless he is guilty of a fault.

God can and is accustomed to succor those who do not deserve it with the praise of his clemency; but he cannot punish those who do not sin, without the subversion of justice, says AUGUSTINE, book II, Op. imperfecti.

II. Whoever, when Adam sinned, did not exist, in them the sin of Adam could not descend: But the descendants etc. Therefore. Whoever, when Adam sinned, did not exist either actually in their own life, or virtually or seminally in the stock, in them the sin of Adam could not descend; I concede. But the descendants of Adam were in him, as in the root, stock, and fountain of the human race, virtually or seminally, when he violated the paradisiacal law. Moreover, that the sins of parents can be imputed to children and descendants, although they do not exist actually with them, is clear from the divine threat, Exod. XX, 5. The avarice of Gehazi was imputed to his seed, i.e., to his descendants, existing seminally in him, 2 Reg. V, 27. in perpetuity.

III. To those who did not consent to the sin of Adam, the sin cannot be imputed morally: But the descendants of Adam etc. The major is evident; because the sin of another can never be imputed to anyone, unless he has a moral connection with him, which consists in command, counsel, consent, etc. The minor is clear; because while Adam was living and sinning, his descendants did not live, and thus they could not have consented to his sin.

Resp. Distinguish between formal and virtual consent. Whoever did not consent to the sin of Adam either formally or virtually, to them the sin of Adam cannot be imputed; I concede. But the descendants consented to the sin of Adam virtually, who, if they had coexisted with the sinning Adam, would have abused the liberty of their will for the same reason as he did. For the will of Adam is interpretatively the will of his descendants.

Instantia I. But infants did not sin in the likeness of the transgression of Adam, Rom. V, 14. Therefore, the will of Adam is not interpretatively the will of infants. Resp.
