Infants are said by Paul to have sinned not in the likeness of the transgression of Adam; because they did not sin in their own person proæretically; yet they sinned in Adam as their stock and father.

Instantia II. Where sin can be imputed, there knowledge of the law has preceded. But in infants there is no knowledge of the law: Therefore, neither can sin be imputed to them. Resp. 1) There are also sins of ignorance, Ps. XIX, 13. 2) Infants die: Therefore, the sin of Adam, whose punishment is death, Gen. II, 17. is imputed to them.

IV. If the sin of Adam is imputed by divine judgment to all who existed in the loins of Adam, then it is certainly imputed to Christ himself: But it is not to Christ etc. Therefore. The consequence of the major is evident: because Christ also was in the loins of Adam; for he is called the son of Adam, Luc. III, 38. Resp. Distinguish between Adam whole and Adam sinning. Christ is called the son of Adam whole, not sinning or fallen: for he was not in the loins of Adam insofar as he fell, because he did not descend from Adam according to the order of corrupted nature through carnal generation, but in a supernatural manner, through the miraculous advent of the Holy Spirit, with whose immense gifts he was anointed, so that he might be holy, harmless, undefiled, separated from sinners, Hebr. VII, 26. Therefore he is opposed to Adam the sinner from the side [of the contrast], Rom. V, 14. sqq.

V. If the sin of Adam is imputed to his descendants for the reason that he is their head, then the sins of Esau are also imputed to the Edomites for the same reason: The latter is false: Therefore the former is also. The consequence is proved by parity: Just as Adam is the head of the Adamites; so Esau is the head of the Edomites. Resp. 1) The reason is different: for Adam was not only the natural head of his descendants, but also their moral head, on account of the covenant which God established with Adam, that if he observed the prescribed law, he would propagate his original justice and happiness to his descendants; but if he sinned, he would corrupt both himself and his descendants: such a covenant God did not establish with Esau. 2) Adam also has a different status as a natural head, when compared with other heads of families. From him human nature, specifically considered, is derived: from them descend certain individuals. He received from God goods common to all men: they received personal goods, which terminate in the lineage.

VI. If the propagation of guilt is to be derived from the specific reason of the existence of the human race in Adam; then by the same force, the repentance of Adam and the remission of sins will redound to his descendants: The latter is false: Therefore the antecedent is also. The reason for the consequence is; because Adam, by repenting, represented the human race just as much as by sinning. Resp. I deny the consequence of the major. For Adam, by repenting, did not represent the human race equally as he did by sinning. By sinning he lost the natural goods to be propagated to his descendants; by repenting he received the supernatural grace of God, which is not transferred to his descendants.

VII. Another's sin cannot be our sin: The sin of Adam is another's: Therefore. The major is evident; because the sin of any man proceeds from his own will. Resp. 1) Another's sin cannot be ours formally, yet it can be ours imputatively. 2) There are also involuntary sins. 3) The will of Adam sinning was interpretatively our will.

Latin:

Quæst. X. An peccatum primum Adami ipsius posteris vere & iuste imputatur?

Primum peccatum Adami, quatenus is vt communis parens, caput, stirps & repræsentator totius generis humani spectatur, omnibus ipsius posteris vere (a) & iusto Dei iudicio (b) ad culpam & pœnam imputatur.

Prob. a. ex Rom. V, 12. Sicut per vnum hominem peccatum in mundum intrauit, & per peccatum mors; & sic in omnes homines mors pertransiit, in quo omnes peccauerunt. 1) Per vnum hominem intelligi possunt l. c. Adamus & Eua, qui dicuntur vnus homo, tum ratione communionis æconomicæ, quia per matrimonium coniuges fiunt vna caro, Gen. II, 24.; tum ratione communionis in peccando, quia erant vnum cor, consensu peccati, quod esse debebant consensu obsequii; præcipue tamen respicitur ab apostolo Adamus, totius generis humani radix, sons, seminarium & repræsentator, secundi Adami typus, v. 14. & caput Euæ, 1 Cor. XI, 3. 2) Per peccatum primo intelligitur lapsus Adami, consequenter peccatum originale, siue habitualis & hereditaria prauitas. 3) Peccatum intrauit in mundum, i. e. in hominem, qui est μικροκόσμος, siue paruus mundus: intrauit non efficiente, cogente aut impellente Deo, sed per voluntarium liberi arbitrii abusum; intrauit, non per imitationem, siquidem etiam tribuitur infantibus, qui non peccarunt in similitudine transgressionis Adami, v. 14. h. e. qui Adamum peccando imitari nequiuerunt: sed partim per imputationem lapsus Adamitici; partim per carnalem propagationem, si spectes habitualem prauitatem, quæ e lapsu Adami redundauit. 4) Per peccatum intrauit mors spiritualis, corporalis & æterna. Pertransiit autem mors in omnes homines (scil. per vnum hominem) in quo omnes peccarunt. Nonnulli interpretes græca verba Paulli: ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον, cum ERASMO, cui accedunt Sociniani & Arminiani, reddiderunt reduplicatiue vel caussaliter: quatenus, quoniam, eo quod omnes peccarunt; quorum plerique imputationem lapsus Adamitici, & ex eo ortum peccatum originale infitiantur. LUTHERVS quidem etiam reddidit causaliter: Dieweil sie alle gesündiget haben, sed non citra respectum ad Adamum, vt caput, vel stirpem; quia mente concipi nequit, quomodo in Adamo, tanquam subiecto, peccauerimus, nisi causaliter ex illo in nos peccatum transiisse dicatur. Sensu relatiuo, vel subiectiuo exponunt Patres latini & græci, præter THEODORETVM, cum & vulgatus interpres sensum relatiuum exprimat.

FELBINGERVS, Socinianus, in versione N. T. sensum causalem & subiectiuum coniungit, & germanice verba Paulli reddit: Derhalben wie durch einen einigen Menschen die Sünde ist in die Welt eingegangen, und durch die Sünde der Tod, eben also ist der Tod zu allen Menschen eingegangen, dieweil (oder in welchem) sie alle gesündiget haben.

Sensus relatiuus, vel subiectiuus, quo ἐφ᾽ ᾧ redditur latine, in quo, textui analogus videtur, & prob. 1) quia ἐφ᾽ ᾧ in N. T. frequentissime relatiue, non autem reduplicatiue, vel causaliter accipitur. Vid. Marc. II, 4. Luc. V, 25. XI, 22. Rom. VI, 2. Phil. IV, 10. 1 Thess. III, 7. Confer. ERASM. SCHMID. in N. T. h. l. Dissentientibus vnus tantum locus biblicus fauere videtur, Phil. III, 12. ἐφ᾽ ᾧ καὶ κατελήφθην, quæ verba exponit ERAS. SCHMIDIVS, quatenus & apprehensus sum a Christo Iesu; at SEB. SCHMID. vertit, in quo etiam apprehensus sum. Quibus consideratis patet, ἐφ᾽ ᾧ in N. T. nunquam significare, quia, vel eo quod. 2) Cohælio textus sensum relatiuum docet. Connectit enim apostolus versu 12. peccati propagationem, mortis originem & primi peccati amplitudinem, h. m. Per Adamum peccatum intrauit in mundum: Per Adami peccatum mors pertransiit in omnes: In Adamo omnes peccauerunt. 3) Comprobat hunc sensum antithesis, qua Christus Adamo opponitur, quæ itidem tria opposita habet: Per Christum gratia Dei: per gratiam donum in mundum venit, v. 15. Per Christi obedientiam gratia pertransiit in omnes, v. 18. In Christo iusti constituuntur, quotquot iustificantur v. 19. 4) Haud absimili phrasi vtitur apostolus, 1 Cor. XV, 22. In Adamo omnes moriuntur. His præstitutis, argumentamur: Qui peccarunt in Adamo, illis etiam peccatum Adami imputatur: Atqui omnes peccarunt in Adamo &c. Ergo. Maior probatur: quia nulli homines mali existebant, cum Adamus mandatum Dei transgrederetur, vt in propria persona actu & formaliter peccati Adamitici participes fierent: Ergo participes eiusdem facti sunt moraliter, per imputationem, secundum æstimationem aut iudicium Dei.

2) Ex Rom. V, 19. Sicut per inobedientiam vnius hominis peccatores constituti sunt multi: ita etiam per obedientiam vnius iusti constituuntur multi. Obs. 1) Per inobedientiam vnius hominis intelligitur transgressio Adami v. 14. quæ opponitur obedientiæ Christi. 2) Sicut obedientia Christi; ita inobedientia Adami est actus singularis, vel personalis. At nullus actus singularis, aut personalis, moraliter bonus, vel malus, pluribus personis, essentialiter distinctis, potest esse communis, nisi per imputationem. Nam esse actum singularem, & pluribus formaliter communem, contradictionem implicat. 3) Per multos homines intelliguntur omnes, quia omnes homines reuera multi sunt. conf. Dan. XII, 2. Io. V, 28. Colligimus ex his: 1) Quicunque homines ab Adamo essentialiter differunt, & nihilominus per illius inobedientiam coram tribunali diuino peccatores constituuntur, illis inobedientia Adami imputatur ad culpam: Atqui omnes homines &c. Ergo. 2) Quicunque eodem modo peccatores constituuntur per inobedientiam Adami, quomodo iusti constituuntur per obedientiam Christi, illi per inobedientiam Adami peccatores sunt imputatiue: Atqui omnes homines secundum seriem naturæ prognati &c. Ergo. 3) Posteris Adami imputatur ipsius pœna: Ergo & culpa. Consequentia est manifesta: quia culpa & pœna sunt relatæ; ideoque hæc illam comitem habet aut præsupponit. Sane non potest esse consors alterius pœnæ, qui exsors est ipsius culpæ. Antecedens constat: quia in Adamo exuti sumus imagine Dei, eiecti e paradiso, laboribus, doloribus, morbis, morti subiecti.

Prob. b. Iustitia atque aequitas imputationis lapsus Adamitici in culpam & poenam posterorum liquet ex eo, quod Adamus est communis parens omnium hominum, quippe qui in ipso virtualiter aut seminaliter exstiterunt; nec non caput morale totius generis humani. Constat autem, enorme & perquam grave delictum patris aequissimo iure imputari posteris in culpam & poenam; v.gr. Vassallus regis alicuius, committens crimen laesae maiestatis, feudis, a rege concessis, orbatur, non tantum ipse pater, sed & posteri iisdem excidunt. Cum igitur homines omnes in Adamo, tanquam patre & stirpe, fuerint, non quidem quoad individualem rationem, attamen quoad specificam existentiam, sive repraesentationem, iure aequissimo peccatum communis patris omnibus hominibus, qui in ipso exstiterunt, imputatur. Adiice, quod Adamus quoque fuerit caput morale, aut foederale generis humani; ideo, quod non tantum moraliter bonus conditus erat, sed etiam Deus ter optimus cum ipso inuerat pactum, vi cuius ipsi promiserat perennem animae corporisque perfectionem atque felicitatem paradisi, sed sub conditione constantis obedientiae; inobedientiae autem poenam mortis spiritualis, corporalis & aeternae indixerat. Gen. II, 17. Obedientia δοκιμασία ex intentione diuina erat abstinentia a fructibus arboris scientiae boni & mali. Quare, obsequium detrectante & peccante Adamo, vniuersa ipsius posteritas iustissima Dei aestimatione peccasse iudicata, atque adeo desperdita est concreata perfectio & felicitas paradisi promissa: contra, ex transgressione Adami culpa & poena in posteros Adami redundauit.

2) Imago Dei & connexa cum ea felicitas non erat bonum personale, sed commune toti speciei humanae, Gen. V, 1. 2. Proinde cum Adamus, repraesentator speciei humanae, illo bono communi, quod pro se non magis, quam pro posteris acceperat, propter inobedientiam iustissimo Dei iudicio priuaretur, vna omnes homines eodem orbati sunt. Aequissimum enim est, eum sentire incommodum, ad quem commodum peruenturum fuisset.

3) Voluntas Adami peccantis interpretatiue erat voluntas omnium hominum, quippe quam Adamus abusu liberi arbitrii prodidit & declarauit.

Vniuersi enim & singuli homines, qui sunt, fuerunt, erunt, excepto Christo, si eodem, quo Adamus tempore vixissent, in ipsius peccatum consensissent. Quod patet a) ex eo, quod Adamus parens & caput generis humani facile in transgressionem Euae consensit: b) Qualis terrenus (tanquam stirps naturalis totius speciei humanae) tales omnes terreni (voluntate & intellectu), 1 Cor. XV, 48. At qui consentit in atrocissimum peccatum, quo summa maiestas laeditur, haud iniuria reus culpae & poenae censetur: Cum itaque Deus omnium hominum virtualem consensum in peccatum primum prauideret, omnibus culpam & poenam, quae lapsum Adami comitatur, iustissimo iudicio imputauit.

Antithesis est 1) Socinianorum, qui negant delictum Adami posteris imputari; 2) Arminianorum, quorum quidam imputationem primi peccati negant; quidam afferunt, caussam imputationis non esse iustum Dei iudicium, sed liberum ipsius arbitrium. Quorum potiora sunt argumenta:

I. Imputatio transgressionis Adamiticae non potest solide & sacra scriptura probari. Nam 1) Rom.

V, 12. voculae, ἐφ' ᾧ, non possunt subiectiue reddi, in quo, sed debent caussaliter exponi, eo quod. Si redderentur, in quo, referrentur ad vnum hominem, quod verba interiecta non patiuntur. Praeterea de peccato actuali, & cuilibet homini proprio, apostolo sermonem esse, docet sequens v. 13. 2) Rom. V, 19. per inobedientiam Adami homines constituuntur, vt peccatum ipsis inhaereat. Ergo apostolus l. c. de imputatione peccati non agit. 3) Moriuntur homines non, quod reatus peccati omnes attineat, sed quod ex Adamo ortum trahant. Resp. ad 1): Pronomen relatiuum non semper subiecto, ad quod refertur, proxime iungi, docet locus Paullinus, 2 Thess. II, 9. Interdum magis respicienda est series rerum, quam ordo vocum: τὸ ἐφ᾽ ᾧ apposite refertur ad τὸν ἄνθρωπον, de quo prius sermo erat institutus. Ceterum loquitur apostolus v. 12. de peccato non personali, sed communi & vniversali, quia dicit, quod in vno homine omnes peccauerint, scilicet moraliter, ob imputationem lapsus Adamitici; v. 13. agit de peccatis actualibus, quatenus a posteriori peccatum primum manifestant.

Ad 2): Per inobedientiam Adami coram tribunali diuino constituimur peccatores imputatiue, quia culpa ex trasgressione Adami resultans nobis imputatur; & ratio est, cur peccatum originale quod e peccato primo fluxit, nobis inhæreat.

Sicut enim obedientia Christi nobis imputatur ad iustitiam: ita inobedientia Adami nobis imputatur ad culpam.

Ad 3): Reatum pœnæ præcedit reatus culpæ.

Deus nemini irrogat pœnam mortis, nisi reus sit culpæ.

Subvenire non merentibus potest & solet Deus cum laude clementiæ; punire autem non peccantes non potest, sine euersione iustitiæ, ait AVGVSTINVS libr. II. Op. imperfecti.

II. Quicunque, Adamo peccante, non exstiterunt, in illos peccatum Adami non potuit descendere: Atqui posteri &c. E. R. Quicunque, Adamo peccante, neque actu in vita propria, neque in stirpe virtualiter, aut seminaliter exstiterunt, in illos peccatum Adami non potuit descendere; concedo. At posteri Adami in hoc, tanquam radice, stirpe & fonte generis humani virtualiter, aut seminaliter fuerunt, cum is legem paradisiacam violauit. Ceterum peccata parentum liberis & posteris imputari posse, quamuis cum iisdem actu non existant, liquet comminatione diuina, Exod. XX, 5. Auaritia Gehasi imputabatur semini ipsius, i. e. posteris, seminaliter in ipso exstistentibus, 2 Reg. V, 27. in perpetuum.

III. Qui non consenserunt in peccatum Adami, illis peccatum moraliter imputari nequit: Atqui posteri Adami &c. Maior patet; quia nunquam potest alicui alterius peccatum imputari, nisi moralem cum eo connexionem habeat, quæ consistit in iussione, consilio, consensu &c. Minor liquet; quia viuente & peccante Adamo non vixerunt ipsius posteri, adeoque in illius peccatum consentire nequiuerunt.

Resp. Dist. inter consensum formalem, & virtualem. Quicunque in peccatum Adami neque formaliter, neque virtualiter consenserunt, illis peccatum Adami non potest imputari; concedo. At posteri consenserunt in peccatum Adami virtualiter, qui, si Adamo peccanti coexstitissent, eadem ratione, qua ille, libertate voluntatis fuissent abusi. Nam voluntas Adami interpretatiue est voluntas posterorum.

Instantia I. Sed infantes non peccarunt in similitudine transgressionis Adami, Rom. V, 14. E. voluntas Adami non est interpretatiue voluntas infantum. Resp. Infantes dicuntur a Paulo peccasse non in similitudine transgressionis Adami; quia non peccarunt in propria persona proæretice; peccarunt tamen in Adamo tanquam stirpe & patre.

Instantia II. Ibi peccatum imputari potest, vbi præcessit scientia legis. Atqui in infantibus non datur scientia legis: Ergo nec peccatum illis imputari potest. Resp. 1) Dantur etiam peccata ignorantiæ, Ps. XIX, 13. 2) Infantes moriuntur: Ergo peccatum Adami, cuius pœna mors est, Gen. II, 17. illis imputatur.

IV. Si omnibus, qui in lumbis Adami exstiterunt, peccatum Adami diuino iudicio imputatur, vtique ipsi Christo imputatur: Sed Christo non &c. E. Consequentia maioris patet: quia etiam Christus fuit in lumbis Adami; dicitur enim filius Adami, Luc. III, 38. Resp. Dist. inter Adamum integrum, & peccantem. Christus dicitur filius Adami integri, non peccantis, aut lapsi: neque enim in lumbis Adami fuit, quatenus ille lapsus est, propterea, quod non secundum ordinem naturæ corruptæ per carnalem generationem, sed modo supernaturali ab Adamo descendit per miraculosum superuentum Spiritus sancti, cuius donis immensis vnctus fuit, vt fuerit sanctus, innoxius, impollutus, separatus a peccatoribus, Hebr. VII, 26. Idcirco Adamo peccatori e latere opponitur, Rom. V, 14. sqq.

V. Si posteris Adami eo imputatur illius peccatum, quod illorum caput est, etiam Esaui peccata Edomitis eadem de causa imputantur: Posterius est falsum: Ergo et prius. Consequentia probatur a pari: Sicut Adamus est caput Adamigenarum; ita Esauus est caput Edomitarum. Resp. 1) Dispar est ratio: nam Adamus posterorum suorum non tantum fuit caput naturale, sed etiam morale, propter pactum, quod sanxit Deus cum Adamo, ut, si legem praescriptam observaret, suam iustitiam originalem et felicitatem ad posteros propagaret; fin peccaret, et se et posteros corrumperet: cuiusmodi foedus Deus cum Esauo non constituit. 2) Etiam ut caput naturale disparem habet rationem Adamus, comparatus cum ceteris familiarum capitibus. Ab illo natura humana, specifice considerata, derivatur: ab his descendunt certa individua. Ille accepit a Deo bona communia omnibus hominibus: hi acceperunt bona personalia, quae in stirpe terminantur.

VI. Si ex ratione specifica existentiae generis humani in Adamo derivanda est propagatio reatus; eiusdem quoque vi, poenitentia Adami et remissio peccatorum in posteros redundabunt: Posterius est falsum: Ergo et antecedens. Ratio consequentiae est; quia Adamus poenitendo aeque repraesentavit genus humanum, ac peccando. Resp. Neg. conseq. maior. Nam Adamus poenitendo non peraeque, ac peccando repraesentavit genus humanum. Peccando amisit bona naturalia ad posteros propaganda; poenitendo recepit gratiam Dei supernaturalem, quae ad posteros non transfertur.

VII. Peccatum alienum non potest esse peccatum nostrum: Peccatum Adami est alienum: E. Maior constat; quia cuiuslibet hominis peccatum a propria voluntate proficiscitur. Resp. 1) Peccatum alienum non potest esse nostrum formaliter, potest tamen nostrum esse imputative. 2) Dantur etiam peccata involuntaria. 3) Voluntas Adami peccantis interpretative fuit voluntas nostra.


### XI. Was the fall of Adam necessary for the manifestation of divine justice and mercy?

The fall of Adam was not necessary for the manifestation of divine justice and mercy.

Prob. 1) Because God has no need of a sinful man, Sir. XV, 12. But sinners would be necessary to Him, if the fall of Adam had been necessary to declare divine justice and mercy.

2) The glory of divine goodness and grace was most sufficiently declared by the creation of the world and the formation of man in the image of God: But divine justice shone forth from the punishment denounced against the transgressor of the law, and from the casting down of the fallen angels to eternal torments.

3) It is a malevolent benevolence, if one wishes someone to be miserable, so that he may be able to pity him, AUGUSTINE, lib. III. Conf. c. 2. And, conversely, justice will not be just, if one had not found a guilty person to punish, but is said to have made one.

You say: If the fall of Adam had not been necessary to manifest divine justice and mercy, God would never have permitted him to fall. But He permitted him to fall. Therefore.

Resp. God did not simply permit the fall of Adam, but He set before him a moral impediment, namely the law fortified by a most grave threat; He is not obligated to oppose a physical and violent impediment. The declaration of divine justice and mercy indeed followed the permission of the Adamitic fall eventually, but not causally. For God does not permit evils to the end that goods may come; but when evils occur, He directs them to a good end.

Latin:

Lapsus Adami non fuit necessarius propter manifestationem iustitiae et misericordiae divinae.

Prob. 1) Quia Deus non opus habet homine peccatore, Sir. XV, 12. Necessarii autem ei essent peccatores, si lapsus Adami ad declarandam iustitiam et misericordiam divinam fuisset necessarius.

2) Gloria divinae bonitatis et gratiae sufficientissime declarata est creatione mundi et formatione hominis ad imaginem Dei: Iustitia autem divina eluxit e poena transgressori legis denuntiata, et ex abiectione angelorum lapsorum ad perpetuos cruciatus.

3) Maleuola est beneuolentia, si quis aliquem velit esse miserum, ut eius possit misereri, AVGUSTIN. lib. III. Conf. c. 2. Et, vice versa, iustitia iusta non erit, si quis puniendum reum non invenisset, sed fecisse dicatur.

Dicis: Si lapsus Adami non fuisset necessarius ad manifestandam iustitiam et misericordiam divinam, nunquam Deus permisisset, ut laberetur. Sed permisit eum labi. E.

Resp. Deus non simpliciter permisit lapsum Adami, sed eidem impedimentum morale, scilicet legem comminatione gravissima munitam obiecit; ad opponendum impedimentum physicum et violentum non obligatur. Secuta quidem est permissionem lapsus Adamitici declaratio iustitiae et misericordiae divinae eventualiter, sed non causaliter. Neque enim Deus permittit mala eum in finem, ut eueniant bona; sed cum eueniunt mala, ea ad bonum finem dirigit.


### Q. XII. What is original sin?

Original sin is the intimate corruption of human nature, deprived of original justice by the fall of our first parents, and prone to every evil.

It is defined more fully. Original sin is the privation of original justice, joined with a depraved inclination, intimately corrupting the whole of human nature, derived from the fall of our first parents, and propagated through carnal generation into all men, rendering them inept for spiritual goods, but prone to evils, and making them guilty of divine wrath and eternal condemnation.

Obs. I. By an ecclesiastical, not biblical, phrase, this sin, having arisen from the fall of Adam, is called original, and indeed not by reason of the origin of the world or of man, but 1) because it is derived from Adam, the root and principle of the human race; 2) because it is joined with the origin of the generations of Adam; 3) because it is the origin and source of actual sins.

Obs. II. In the sacred writings this innate depravity is called: 1) Indwelling sin, Rom. VII, 17, for the reason that after the fall it fixed a firm seat in man, nor does it depart unless the domicile of soul and body is dissolved: 2) Ἁμαρτία εὐπερίστατος, the sin which surrounds; because it girds us on every side, like a long garment, hindering the runner, Hebr. XII, 2. 3) The law in the members, Rom. VIII, 23. For as a law rules and moderates the agent; so original sin directs the members of the body to perform depraved works: 4) Τὸ κακὸν παρακείμενον, the evil lying near, Rom. XII, 21, for the reason that it lies near to man, about to do good, like a brake.

Latin:

Peccatum originale est intima corruptio naturae humanae, per lapsum primorum parentum iustitia originali priuatae, & ad omne malum pronae.

Plenius definitur. Peccatum originale est priuatio iustitiae originalis, cum praua inclinatione coniuncta, totam naturam humanam intime corrumpens, ex lapsu primorum parentum deriuata, & per carnalem generationem in omnes homines propagata, ipsos ineptos ad bona spiritualia, ad mala uero propensos reddens, reosque faciens irae diuinae & aeternae condemnationis.

Obs. I. Phrasi ecclesiastica, non biblica, hoc peccatum, e lapsu Adami ortum, dicitur originale, & quidem non ratione originis mundi aut hominis, sed 1) quia ab Adamo, radice & principio generis humani, deriuatum; 2) quia cum origine Adami generum coniunctum; 3) quia origo & fons est peccatorum actualium.

Obs. II. In sacris litteris connata haec prauitas uocatur: 1) Peccatum inhabitans, Rom. VII, 17. eo, quod post lapsum in homine firmam sedem fixit, nec discedit, nisi domicilio animae & corporis dissoluto: 2) Ἁμαρτία εὐπερίστατος, peccatum circumstans; quia nos undique cingit, instar uestis prolixae, curforem remorantis, Hebr. XII, 2. 3) Lex in membris, Rom. VIII, 23. Nam ut lex regit & moderatur agentem; ita peccatum originale membra corporis ad patrandum opera praua dirigit: 4) Τὸ κακὸν παρακείμενον, malum adiacens, Rom. XII, 21. ideo, quod homini, bonum facturo, sufflaminis instar adiacet.


### Q. XIII. Is original depravity sin properly so called, propagated by carnal generation into all the descendants of Adam?

Original depravity is sin in the true sense of the word, propagated through carnal generation into all men born in the natural way from the blood of Adam.

Proof 1) From Ps. LI, 7. Behold! I was formed in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me. Obs. a) The sacred singer does not speak of the sin of his parents, committed in the active generation; since they were pious and had brought forth this son in a legitimate marriage bed; but of his own sin: a fact which is evident from the preceding and following verses. For v. 5 & 6 he says: I acknowledge my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me. Against thee only have I sinned, and done evil in thy sight. v. 9. Thou shalt purge me with hyssop, that I may become clean. From which it is gathered that he also in v. 7 complains of his own sin. b) David speaks without hyperbole (which the Socinians invent here), since the agonies of conscience which David felt admitted of the hyperbolic flowers of rhetoricians, nor is any necessity imposed upon us to depart from the literal sense; since the sacred singer said nothing more about his iniquity than what ought to have been said. c) David is not speaking of actual sin, but of original and hereditary sin. For he complains of iniquity inherent in him from conception, and of sin transmitted into him from his parents. d) From David, by force of parity, we rightly conclude to the whole human race. For such as was the conception and formation of David in the maternal womb, such is the conception and formation of all men.

With these things presupposed we argue: Whoever from the first conception and formation in the maternal womb was polluted by sin, to him sin is congenital. But David and all men naturally born &c. Therefore. 2) Concerning original sin, the first movements, or figments of the human heart, bear witness; concerning which Moses, Gen. VI, 5. When therefore Jehovah saw that the malice of man was multiplied in the world; and moreover every figment of the thoughts of his heart was only evil (was) every day. Conf. Gen. IIX, 21. The figment of the heart is evil from childhood. Obs. a) יצר מחשבת denotes not only a formed thought, but also the very formation of the thought, Is. XXIX, 5. b) Not only voluntary, but also innate formations of thoughts are designated. For it is said every figment of the thoughts is evil, every day, מנעוריו from childhood, or infancy, and the exclusive particle רק, only, is added. If every figment of the heart is only evil; neither concupiscence nor proneness to sin will be excepted. From these an argument is born: Whoever every day, from his infancy, thinks only evil, to him sin is innate: But every man &c. Therefore. 3) From Gen. V, 3. Adam begat (a son) in his likeness, according to his image. Obs. 1) Adam begat a son not as whole, but as fallen and corrupted by sin. 2) It is notably said: Adam begat in his image, not God's. From these we form an enthymeme: The son of Adam, and consequently all sons naturally descending from him, are born in the image of a corrupted man: Therefore they themselves are most deeply corrupted. The consequence is proven. Such as the begetter, such is the begotten. A leper begets a leper, a gouty man a gouty man. Thus Adam, deprived of the image of God, procreated a son, lacking original justice, and infected with the plague of sin. 4) From John III, 6. Whatever is born of the flesh, is flesh. By these words the universality of innate corruption is indicated. For flesh is not taken here physically, but morally, since it is opposed to spirit, and concretely denotes a corrupted nature, abstractly the corruption of nature. Hence an argument is born: Whoever are born from parents corrupted by sin, to them moral corruption is congenital: But all men &c. Therefore. 5) From Eph. II, 3. We were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest. The apostle joins Jews and Gentiles in general, and asserts that all are children of wrath, i.e., guilty of fault and punishment, φύσει, by nature, i.e., from birth. For the word φύσει is here properly accepted, and is opposed to τῇ χάριτι, i.e., to grace. For just as in this v. 3 it is said children of wrath by nature: so afterwards in v. 8 it is said to be saved by grace. Therefore τῇ φύσει here is the same as from birth, from the womb we are liable to divine wrath and punishment, because of the sin in which we are born, just as in Gal. II, 15 it is written: We are Jews φύσει, gebohrne Jüden: which word is opposed to proselytes, who are called Jews not φύσει, but ἔθει. For thus Gentiles are said to do τῇ φύσει, by nature, the things which are of the law, Rom. II, 14. From which we conclude: Whoever from birth are children of wrath because of sin, to them sin is congenital: But all, as well Gentiles as Jews &c. Therefore. You say: The apostle writes: we were. Which past imperfect denotes that which has passed, or has ceased to be present: But original sin never ceases to be present, but always remains, as much in the regenerate as in the unregenerate: Therefore the apostle does not speak of original sin. Resp. To the Ephesians already made alive with Christ, the guilt of wrath was not present, yet sin was present, which by itself is worthy of wrath and punishment. For the guilt of wrath is separated from the person sinning and repenting in justification, but not from the sin itself (*).

The antithesis was once that of the Pelagians; today it is that of the Socinians, Arminians, Anabaptists, and Weigelians, who either plainly deny original sin, or certainly assert that it has been entirely abolished in the N. T. [New Testament].

Latin:

Prauitas originalis est ueri nominis peccatum, per carnalem generationem in omnes homines, modo naturali ex sanguine Adami ortos, propagatum.

Prob. 1) E Ps. LI, 7. Ecce! in iniquitate formatus sum, & in peccato calefecit me mater mea. Obs. a) Non loquitur hieropfaltes de peccato parentum, commisso in generatione actiua; quippe qui pii & in legitimo thoro hunc filium enixi erant; sed de peccato suo: id quod patescit ex antecedentibus & consequentibus. Nam v. 5. & 6. inquit: Prauaricationes meas ego agnosco, & peccatum meum coram me (est) ingiter. Tibi soli peccaui, & malum in oculis tuis feci. v. 9. Expiabis me hyssopo, ut mundus fiam. Ex quo colligitur, eundem & v. 7. de suo conqueri peccato. b) Loquitur Dauid sine hyperbole (quam hic comminiscuntur Sociniani), quianque angores conscientiae, quos Dauid sentiebat, hyperbolicos rhetorum flosculos admiserunt, neque nobis a sensu litterali recedendi ulla imponitur necessitas; siquidem hieropfaltes de sua iniquitate nihil dixit amplius, quam dici oportuit. c) Non est sermo Dauidi de peccato actuali, sed originali & hereditario. Nam conqueritur de iniquitate, sibi a conceptione inhaerente, & de peccato, a parentibus suis in se traducto. d) A Dauide, vi paritatis, ad uniuersum genus humanum recte concludimus. Nam qualis fuit conceptio & formatio Dauidis in utero materno, talis est omnium hominum conceptio & formatio.

Quibus praesuppositis arguimus: Quicunque a prima conceptione & formatione matione in vtero materno peccato fuit pollutus, illi peccatum est congenitum. Atqui Dauid & omnes homines naturaliter geniti &c. Ergo. 2) De peccato originali testantur motus primi, siue figmenta cordis humani; de quibus Moses, Gen. VI, 5. Cum itaque videret Iehouah, quod multiplicaretur malitia hominis in mundo; insuper omne figmentum cogitationum cordis eius tantum malum (esset) omni die. Conf. Gen. IIX, 21. Figmentum cordis malum a pueritia. Obs. a) יצר מחשבת non tantum cogitationem formatam, sed & ipsam formationem cogitationis notat, Es. XXIX, 5. b) Non tantum voluntariæ, sed & connatæ efformationes cogitationum designantur. Dicitur enim omne figmentum cogitationum malum, omni die, מנעוריו a pueritia, siue infantia, & additur particula exclusiua רק, tantum. Si tantum malum est omne figmentum cordis; nec concupiscentia aut pronitas ad peccatum excepta erit. Nascitur ex his argumentum: Quicunque omni die, ab infantia sua, tantum malum cogitat, illi peccatum est connatum: Atqui omnis homo &c. Ergo. 3) E. Gen. V, 3. Adamus genuit (filium) in similitudine sua, secundum imaginem suam. Obs. 1) Genuit Adamus filium non qua integer, sed qua lapsus & peccato corruptus. 2) Notanter dicitur: Adamus genuit ad imaginem suam, non Dei. Ex his formamus enthymema: Filius Adami, & consequenter omnes filii ex ipso naturaliter descendentes, geniti sunt ad imaginem hominis corrupti: Ergo ipsi profundissime sunt corrupti. Consequ. prob. Qualis generans, talis genitus. Leprosus leprosum, podagricus podagricum gignit. Ita Adamus, priuatus imagine Dei, filium progenerauit, iustitia originali carentem, & lue peccati infectum. 4) E Io. III, 6. Quidquid ex carne natum est, caro est. Indicatur his verbis vniuersalitas connatæ corruptionis. Neque enim physice, sed moraliter caro hic sumitur, quoniam spiritui opponitur, & concretiue naturam corruptam, abstractiue corruptionem naturæ denotat. Nascitur hinc argumentum: Quicunque sunt a parentibus, peccato corruptis, nati, illis moralis corruptio est congenita: Atqui omnes homines &c. Ergo. 5) Ex Eph. II, 3. Eramus filii iræ natura, sicut & reliqui. Coniungit apostolus in vniuersum Iudæos & gentiles, & asserit, omnes esse filios iræ, i. e. reos culpæ & pœnæ, φύσει, natura, i. e. a natiuitate. Vox φύσει enim hic proprie accipitur, & opponitur τῇ χάριτι, s. gratiæ. Nam quemadmodum hoc v. 3. dicitur filii iræ natura: ita postea v. 8. dicitur gratia saluari. Proinde idem est hic τῇ φύσει, ac a natiuitate, ab vtero sumus iræ pœnæque diuinæ obnoxii, propter peccatum, in quo nascimur, quemadmodum Gal. II, 15. scribitur: Nos φύσει Iudæi sumus, gebohrne Jüden: quæ vox opponitur proselytis, qui Iudæi dicuntur non φύσει, sed ἔθει. Sic enim gentiles τῇ φύσει, natura, dicuntur facere, quæ sunt legis, Rom. II, 14. E quibus concludimus: Quicunque a natiuitate ob peccatum sunt filii iræ, illis peccatum est congenitum: Atqui omnes, tam gentiles, quam Iudæi &c. Ergo. Dicis: Apostolus scribit: eramus. Quod præteritum imperfectum notat id, quod præteriit, aut inesse desiit: Atqui peccatum originale nunquam inesse definit, sed semper manet, tam in regenitis, quam irregenitis: Ergo apostolus non loquitur de peccato originali. Resp. Ephesiis cum Christo iam viuificatis non inerat reatus iræ, inerat tamen peccatum, quod per se ira pœnaque dignum est. Separatur enim reatus iræ a persona peccante & resipiscente in iustificatione, non autem ab ipso peccato (*).

Antithesis olim erat Pelagianorum, hodie est Socinianorum, Arminianorum, Anabaptistarum, et Weigelianorum, peccatum originale vel plane negantium, vel certe afferentium, illud in N. T. penitus sublatum esse.


### Q. XIII. Is original depravity sin properly so called, propagated by carnal generation into all the descendants of Adam?: They contend against us with the following arguments

They contend against us with the following arguments.

I. Ezek. XVIII, 20. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father. From which words they conclude: Whoever are sons of Adam ought not to bear his iniquity: But all descendants of Adam are his sons: Therefore.

Resp. 1) Distinguish between the father of certain individuals and the father of the entire human race. It is not permitted to argue from the former to the latter. For the latter had received gifts and privileges to be either preserved or lost for the entire human race: since he lost them with the fall, the loss redounded to the entire human race. Wherefore the sin of Adam is common, or universal; the sins of other fathers are personal, or singular. The prophet is speaking of these, and thus his meaning is: An innocent son shall not bear the personal sin of his immediate parent, i.e., he shall not sustain the punishment for the singular sin of an impious parent, if he himself cultivates piety. For the prophet is acting not regarding the guilt to be derived to descendants, but regarding the punishment to be inflicted upon them.

2) Even if original sin is granted, we suffer the punishment not so much of Adam’s sin as of our own; because original sin, propagated into us, inheres in us, and thus properly pertains to us.

II. A single act cannot produce a habit; the disobedience of the first parents was a single act: Therefore, it could not produce a sinful habit.

Major is certain; because an acquired habit is obtained by frequent actions. Resp. Distinguish between perfective habits and vicious or corruptive ones. A vicious habit can be obtained by a single act and transmitted to descendants,

ONE: That there is a certain hereditary sin

; is certain from the clearest indications: These are primarily to be learned from natural principles: I.

That human nature is thoroughly corrupted. For there is in every man a certain natural repugnance against nature, which indeed clearly declares a huge corruption of nature, adverse to its first constitution. This, as it is illustrated by the consensus of philosophers, not the weakest among the pagan nations (whose testimonies are exhibited collected by H. GROTIUS, on Luke II, 22; HUETIUS in demonstr. evang. and in quaest. Alnet.; PFANNERUS in syst. Theol. gent. pur.; and many others), is thus demonstrated by evident experience; nor did CLERICUS dare to go into denials, otherwise thinking falsely about this matter.

Argument from the definition to be premised: Corruption is a change contrary to its nature, ends, and perfections. But to perfections belong primarily the excellence and all the prerogatives by which that thing is distinguished from other things inferior to it. But man discovers in himself all such things which are entirely contrary to the nature of man, and not only to his own, but also to common nature and its excellence.

Man is an animal endowed with reason, and also created for society. Therefore, the nature of man, and indeed that common one, is entirely threefold: one is animal, and that indeed most noble, insofar as man is an animal, and indeed the chief one (but there are two properties of animal nature, which man indeed has in common with other living creatures; but at a degree nevertheless far more eminent; that we live, that we feel); the second is moral, insofar as man is considered as an animal participating in reason; the third is social, insofar as man is a member of human society, obligated to preserve it, and not sufficient by himself to sustain himself outside of it, so that he may live well and happily. But if we wish to observe, we suddenly understand that there are many things in man contrary to animal nature, and that indeed most noble, especially these two, which are perceived by sense: Vehement motions of the mind, which, unless they are restrained, carry man so far that immoderate desire, nay, ferocity more unbridled than that of beasts, makes him worse than all living creatures, so that he wallows in luxury, so that he wallows in that lust which is called Sodomitic, so that he pollutes himself entirely with sins παρὰ φύσιν [contrary to nature], Rom.

I, 26. so that he plainly becomes ἄσοφος [foolish], ibid. v. 31. 2 Tim. III, 3. The misery of life, by which man has been made much inferior to any brute animals, a huge heap of troubles, diseases both innumerable and most grave, the chief cause of which are usually παθήματα [passions], vehement motions of the mind; yet the structure of the human body is entirely admirable, incomparable, and much excelling the body

to be sent, e.g., phthisis can arise from one immoderate draught of wine, or beer, leprosy from one contact with a leper; which plague is not rarely transmitted to posterity. Fallen angels fell into a vicious habit by one inordinate act. 2) There are also perfective habits acquired by one act, e.g., In the demonstration of the why (τῷ διότι), if the cause of the conclusion has been known certainly and evidently by one act of demonstration, the habit of science is acquired without this conclusion.

III. Whatever evil act is not ours, its effect does not redound upon us: But the fall of Adam is not, nor was it, our act: Therefore the effect, which is original sin, does not redound upon us. Resp. Whatever evil act is not ours, neither physically nor morally, its effect could not have redounded upon us; I concede. To the point: the sinful act of Adam is ours, morally and by imputation, because we all were in Adam, the stock, root, and principle as much natural as moral of the whole human race.

IV. Infants are innocent, Ps. 106, 38. The infants of the pious are called holy, 1 Cor. 7, 14. Therefore they are not contaminated by original sin. Resp. 1) Infants are innocent by a comparative, not absolute, innocence. They are comparatively innocent, because they have committed no prohaeretic sins; but they are not absolutely holy, because they are conceived in sins, Ps. 51, 7. and are by nature children of wrath, Eph. 2, 3. 2) The infants of the pious are called holy, by the holiness of the church, or external; since they are born in the church, and to them the nearest access to the benefits of the church lies open: but they are not holy before baptism by the holiness of faith, or internal.

In the body of every lover. These things surely are all contrary to the excellence and preeminence of man, provided we deem his animal nature most worthy of contemplation. 2) Things contrary to the moral nature of man, namely: (α) A perpetual repugnance against the law, as it is in the proverb: We always strive for what is forbidden, and desire what is denied. But indeed, God has not sanctioned laws other than good and salutary ones, most agreeable to reason, nay even necessary for man's life and happiness, as are all natural ones. First, one must note the vehement intention of the mind to cast out from the soul the truth of all things, which is primary and clearer than light itself: which is God. (β)

The appetite for many things, which right reason commands us to oppose. Man sees the better things, and approves them, but follows the worse. (γ) Pleasure contrary to the honesty of nature, by which man, being beguiled, accommodates himself only to that which is present, omitting providence and the consideration of future events, which he himself could have foreseen by thought, and ought to have; whence at last, long after the deed, comes a change of mind, which is called repentance. 3) Things contrary to the social nature of man; of such a kind are: great and persistent dissension among men, even those most closely joined by kinship, enmities and continuous vexations, feuds, slaughters, spoils. There is no plague, as CICERO says, so detestable that it does not arise for man from man. Thus indeed the bond is openly broken, by which nature associated men, and than which there can be none tighter. Concerning which injury CICERO, de offic. L. III. c. 5, complained, having conveniently employed a similitude, taken from the conjunction of members, of which the whole body consists, which PAUL, illuminated by divine light, usurped, 1 Cor. 12, 14-26.

II. That this great corruption of man is a native evil, not an acquired one, it will suffice to have brought forward three proofs. First: Infants, and all of them to a man, from the beginning of their age, and indeed before they can take an example from others, betray their viciousness, always strive for what is forbidden, always desire what is denied. Second: They could not so easily acquire the ability and habit of sinning unless there were implanted in them naturally, or rather innate, a certain propensity of the soul inclined toward sin. What anyone attempts against his will, as it were with Minerva, that is, with nature opposing and resisting, will be most difficult for him; on the contrary, nothing will be accomplished more easily than that toward which nature itself is prone and inclined. Third: All immediately and gladly follow examples of vices; but scarcely a few, and with difficulty, suffer themselves to be enticed and governed by examples of virtues and most salutary precepts. E. by imitation not uniquely nor principally, but by a certain natural instinct, nay rather impulse, men sin.

Infancy: In baptism sin is taken away: Therefore sin does not inhere in baptized infants. Resp. Sin is taken away in baptism, not so that it does not exist, but so that it is not imputed. The guilt and dominion of sin are taken away in baptism, not the root of sin.

V. Whoever are ignorant of the law do not sin: Infants are ignorant of the law: Therefore. The major premise is constructed: since for sin, the presupposed knowledge of the law is required. Resp. Whoever are ignorant of the law, and cannot know it; they do not commit actual and voluntary sins. But original sin is a hectic and naturally congenital depravity, and is an aberration from the inscribed law, even if infants are ignorant of the prescribed law.

VI. Whatever is natural to man is not sin properly so called: Original sin is natural to man: Therefore. The major premise shines with its own light; because natural things are not morally base. Resp. 1) Whatever is natural to man in the state of instituted nature, that is not sin properly so called: I concede. But original sin is natural to man in the state of destitute nature. 2) Constitutive and consequential natural things are not base: but those which are subjective, transitive, and corruptive can be base, either morally or physically. A hereditary disease is natural, and yet physically base.

VII. If original sin is propagated through generation, marriages are to be condemned: But these are not to be condemned: Therefore original sin is not propagated through generation. The consequence of the major premise is proven; because marriages would be impure if original sin were propagated into children born of a legitimate bed. Resp. Distinguish between marriages considered in themselves, insofar as they are divinely ordained; and considered accidentally, insofar as vice adheres to natural generation. The vices of nature do not take away the benefits of God.

Question . ARISTOTLE called evil οὐγγενὲς (congenital), although he was not able to explain its true reason and causes.

III. That it is necessary that the origin of this corruption, innate to humans, was ἀναρχον (without beginning) and common. For the corruption itself is common, without any exception, either of man, or of vice, or of human trouble and misery. But the effect testifies to the cause. Therefore, we conclude by necessary reason that the common and same effect proceeds from some common and same first cause.

IV. That God cannot be the cause of this evil. He, indeed, the effector of human nature, to whom not only its creation but also its preservation must be attributed; if he had corrupted the same, and placed it in this state of repugnance, he would dissent from himself; which is openly repugnant to both the goodness and the wisdom that is most perfect and immutable in God.

ANOTHER: However, what kind of sin this is, what its origin was, how great its guilt is, and finally what remedy must be applied to it, is established from nowhere else than from divine revelation. Artic. Smalcald. p. 317. Declar. Form. Conc. page 639. This argument, derived a posteriori, I indeed think has the greatest force: If anyone could demonstrate the mode and origin of this depravity from the principles of reason, or attain it by any conjecture; it could certainly not have happened that among so many and such discrepant sects of philosophers, one or another most wise man would not have been correctly and happily engaged in investigating this matter. But all philosophers have been much deceived, lacking the light of revelation and indulging their own genius. Some of them imagined an ἀναιμάρτητον (sinless) state of souls, as if all souls had sinned together, long before each was joined with its own body. For whence that common corruption of human nature, in so many and such diverse generations? (Prop. I. & III.) Others established a μετεμψύχωσιν (transmigration of souls), or rather μετενσωμάτωσιν (reincarnation), which opinion is no less absurd, nor less inept, for rendering a reason: why this most miserable condition is common. (Prop. III.) Most have fallen into such rashness that they have thought there are two eternal principles, neither of which depends on the will of the other, but they are indeed contrary, one good, one evil. Which opinion, indeed, although most ancient, is certainly the most absurd of all, and if it is accurately weighed, it contains a manifest repugnance in itself. All the most excellent philosophers profess that nothing in the whole of philosophy is more difficult than this discussion: concerning the origin of evil. Therefore, there is no doubt about the necessity of revelation.

Quest. XIV. What is the efficient cause of original sin? The remote efficient cause of original sin are the protoplasts [first-formed humans]; whose fall, when it was imputed to the whole human race, could not but result in moral filth being derived to all descendants through carnal generation.

The proximate cause, however, of this connate stain are our parents, from whose impure blood the original spot has flowed into our soul.

Proof a. Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death, and thus death passed through to all men, in whom all have sinned, Rom. V, 12. We have examined these words of the apostle above. Here we only observe that the fall of Adam, by which he deprived himself no less than his descendants of original righteousness, becomes the foundation of the propagation of original sin through carnal generation.

For the apostle, intending to teach that through Adam sin entered into the world, i.e., all men, or was propagated, gives this reason for sin being most widely propagated: because in Adam all have sinned.

But all did not sin in Adam physically; since they did not yet exist when Adam sinned: therefore morally, or by imputation.

Naturally, the fall of Adam was adjudged to the whole human race by the most just estimation of God, so that on account of the first sin, Adam and his descendants were reckoned sinners before the divine tribunal, i.e., devoid of original righteousness, and inclined to every evil.

Hence it happens that the defect of concreated righteousness and the inclination to evil accompanies the generation of all men who descend from Adam by the natural way.

Nor does God extraordinarily, and by miracle, impede the propagation of this stain, and its accompaniment with the generation of a rational creature, which, by first transgressing the divine law, abused the freedom of the will.

Cf. Hvlsem. breuiar. enucleat. p. 286.

Proof b. Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?

Job XIV, 4.

Job is speaking not of the external uncleanness of the body, but of the internal uncleanness of the soul, on account of which we are rendered liable to the judgment of God, v. 3: nor is his discourse about actual uncleanness, but habitual and universal, inasmuch as it proceeds from an impure birth and adheres intimately to the soul.

Thus everyone follows the nature of his own.

Neither does a black raven produce a white dove, nor a fierce lion a gentle lamb, nor does man, polluted by congenital sin, produce a holy son.

Latin:

Dimicant adversus nos sequentibus argumentis.

I. Ezech. XVIII, 20. Filius non portabit iniquitatem patris. E quibus verbis colligunt: Quicunque sunt filii Adami, non debent eius portare iniquitatem: Atqui omnes posteri Adami sunt eius filii: Ergo.

Resp. 1) Dist. inter patrem certorum individuorum, et patrem totius generis humani. Ab illo ad hunc argumentari non licet. Nam ille acceperat dona et privilegia toti generi humano aut conferuanda, aut amittenda: quae cum lapsu amiserit, in totum genus humanum iactura redundauit. Quare peccatum Adami est commune, sive universale; reliquorum patrum peccata sunt personalia, sive singularia. De his sermo est prophetae, adeoque eius mens est: Non portabit parentis proximi peccatum personale filius innocens, i. e. non sustinebit poenam ob peccatum singulare parentis impii, si ipse pietatem colet. Agit enim propheta non de culpa in posteros deriuanda, sed de poena iis irroganda.

2) Concesso peccato originis, non tam Adamitici, quam proprii peccati poenam luimus; quia peccatum originis in nos propagatum nobis inhaeret, atque adeo nobis proprie competit.

II. Unus actus non potest producere habitum; Parentum primorum inobedientia fuit unus actus: E. non potuit producere habitum peccaminosum.

Maior constat; quia habitus acquisitus crebris comparatur actionibus Resp. Dist. inter habitus perfectivos, et vitiosos, sive corruptivos. Habitus vitiosus uno actu potest comparari, et in posteros transmitti,

VNVM: Esse peccatum quoddam hereditarium

; ex clarissimis constat indiciis: Sunt haec potissimum, ex principiis naturalibus discenda: I.

Quod humana natura penitus corrupta sit. Est enim in quouis homine naturalis quaedam adversus naturam repugnantia, quae profecto ingentem naturae corruptionem, primae eius constitutioni adversariam, manifesto declarat. Id, ut illustratur consensu philosophorum, inter gentes profanas haud infirmorum (quorum testimonia collecta exhibent H. GROTIVS, ad Luc. II, 22. HVETIVS in demonstr. evang. et in quaest. Alnet. PFANNERV S in syst. Theol. gent. pur. plures alii), sic demonstratur experientia fat evidente; neque infitias ire ausus est CLERICVS, ceteroquin falso de hac re sentiens.

Argumentum ex definitione praemittenda: Corruptio est mutatio, eius natura, finibus ac perfectionibus contraria. Ad perfectiones autem pertinent in primis excellentia omnesque praerogativae, quibus res illa ab aliis rebus, illa inferioribus, discernitur. Atqui homo in se deprehendit omnia eiusmodi, quae prorsus contraria sunt naturae hominis, nec propria solum, sed communi etiam naturae, atque eius praestantiae.

Homo est animal, ratione praeditum, idemque ad societatem conditum. E. natura hominis, et communis quidem illa, omnino triplex est: una animalis, et ea tamen nobilissima, quatenus homo est animal, et quidem praecipuum (animalis autem naturae proprietates duae sunt, quas homo cum reliquis animantibus communes quidem habet; at gradu tamen dispari longeque eminentiores; quod vivimus, quod sentimus); altera moralis, quoad homo consideratur ut animal rationis particeps; tertia socialis, quatenus homo est membrum societatis humanae, ad eam servandam obligatus, atque extra eam sustentando sibi ipse non sufficiens, ut bene beateque vivere queat. Quod si autem animaduertere velimus, subito intelligimus multa in homine inesse contraria naturae animali, et illi quidem nobilissima, praesertim vero hae duo, quae sensu percipiuntur: Vehementes animi motus, qui, nisi coerceantur, hominem usque eo rapiunt, ut immoderata cupiditas, immo effrenata ferocia magis, quam beluina, ipsum animantibus omnibus deteriorem efficiat, vt in luxuriam, vt in eam libidinem, quae dicitur Sodomitica, se ingurgitet, vt flagitiis παρὰ φύσιν totum se polluat, Rom.

I, 26. vt plane fiat ἄσοφος, ibid. v. 31. 2 Tim. III, 3. Miseria vitae, quo homo brutis animalibus quibusque multo inferior factus est, ingens aerumnarum cumulus, morbi et innumerabiles, et gravissimi, quorum plerorumque causa praecipua esse solent παθήματα, vehementes animi motus; at structura tamen humani corporis prorsus est admirabilis, incomparabilis, multumque praestans corpore

mitti, v. gr. phthisis ex uno immoderato haustu vini, aut cerevisiae, lepra ex uno contactu leprosi suboriri potest; quae lues haud raro in posteros transmittitur. Angeli lapsi uno actu inordinato inciderunt in habitum vitiosum. 2) Dantur etiam habitus perfectivi uno actu comparati, v. gr. In demonstratione τῷ διότι, si uno demonstrationis actu certo & evidenter cognita fuerit causa conclusionis, habitus scientiae citra hanc conclusionem comparatus est.

III. Quicunque actus malus non est noster, illius effectus in nos non redundat: Atqui lapsus Adami non est, aut fuit noster actus: Ergo effectus, qui est peccatum originale, in nos non redundat. Resp. Quicunque actus malus non est noster, neque physice, neque moraliter, illius effectus in nos non potuit redundare; concedo. Ad actus peccaminosus Adami est noster, moraliter & per imputationem, propterea, quod omnes fuimus in Adamo, stirpe, radice & principio tam naturali, quam morali totius generis humani.

IV. Infantes sunt innocentes, Ps. CVI, 38. Piorum infantes dicuntur sancti, 1 Cor. VI, 34. Ergo peccato originali non sunt contaminati. Resp. 1) Infantes sunt innocentes innocentia comparata, non absoluta. Comparate innocentes sunt, quia nulla peccata proaretica commiserunt; at absolute non sunt sancti, quia in peccatis concepti, Ps. LI, 7. & natura filii irae sunt, Eph. II, 3. 2) Infantes piorum dicuntur sancti, sanctitate ecclesiae, sive externa; quoniam in ecclesia sunt nati, iisque proximus aditus ad beneficia ecclesiae patet: non autem ante baptismum sunt sancti, sanctitate fidei, seu interna.

In corpore amantis cuiusque. Haec sane omnia adversantur praestantiae excellentiaeque hominis, dum modo animalem eius naturam contemplatione digniffimam censemus. 2) Contraria naturae hominis morali, videlicet: (α) Perpetua adversus legem repugnantia, vt est in prouerbio: Nitimur in vetitum semper, cupimusque negata. At enim, leges non alias Deus sanxit, quam bonas ac salutares, rationi maxime consentaneas, immo etiam necessarias ad hominis vitam ac felicitatem, vt sunt naturales omnes. In primis notanda est vehemens animi intentio ad eiiciendam ex animo veritatem omnium primam, eamdemque luce clariorem: quod fit Deus. (β)

Adpetitio multarum rerum, quas recta ratio auersari nos iubet. Videt homo meliora, probatque, deteriora sequitur. (γ) Voluptas naturae honestati contraria, qua delinitus homo ad id solum, quod praesens est, se accommodat, omissa providentia & consideratione futurorum eventuum, quos ipse quidem cogitatione praecipere poterat, ac debebat; vnde sera tandem aliquando post factum mutatio animi, quae vocatur poenitentia. 3) Contraria naturae hominis sociali; cuiusmodi sunt: hominum, ac vel maxime propinqua cognatione coniunctorum, magna ac pertinax inter se dissensio, inimicitiae ac vexationes continuae, simultates, caedes, spolia. Nulla, vt ait CICERO, tam detestabilis pestis est, quae non homini ab homine nascatur. Ita vero aperte disrumpitur vinculum, quo natura homines consociavit, & quo nullum esse potest arctius. De qua iniuria conquestus CICERO, de offic. L. III. c. 5. commode adhibuit similitudinem, a coniunctione membrorum, ex quibus totum constat corpus, arcessitam, quam, diuina luce illuminatam, PAVLLVS usurpauit, 1 Cor. XII, 14-26.

II. Quod haec tanta hominis corruptio natinum malum sit, non adscitum, tria documenta protulisse, satis erit. Primum: Infantes, & illi quidem omnes ad unum, ab ineunte aetate, atque adeo prius, quam exemplum ab aliis fumere queant, vitiositatem suam produnt, semper nituntur in vetitum, semper cupiunt negata. Secundum: Habilitatem & consuetudinem peccandi tam facile adquirere non possent, nisi naturaliter ipsis insita, sive potius innata esset propensio quaedam animi, ad peccatum proclivis. Quod quis molitur invita quasi Minerua, hoc est, adversante ac repugnante natura, id illi difficillimum erit; contra vero, nihil confectabitur facilius eo, ad quod natura ipse pronus atque inclinatus est. Tertium: Vitiorum exempla protinus libenterque omnes sequuntur; contra ea vero exemplis virtutum, & saluberrimis praeceptis se allici ac gubernari vix pauci aegre patiuntur. E. imitatione nec vnice, nec praecipue, sed naturali quodam instinctu, immo impetu, peccant homines.

Infantia: In baptismo tollitur peccatum: Ergo peccatum infantibus baptizatis non inhæret. Resp. Tollitur in baptismo peccatum, non vt non fit, sed vt non imputetur. Tollitur in baptismo reatus & dominium, non radix peccati.

V. Quicunque ignorant legem, non peccant: Infantes ignorant legem: Ergo. Maior conflat: quoniam ad peccatum requiritur præsupposita legis notitia. Resp. Quicunque legem ignorant, nec poffunt eam cognoscere; illi non committunt peccata actualia & voluntaria. At peccatum originale est prauitas hectica & naturaliter congenita, essque aberratio a lege inscripta, licet infantes legem præscriptam ignorent.

VI. Quidquid homini naturale est, non est peccatum proprie dictum: Peccatum originale est homini naturale: Ergo. Maior sua luce radiat; quia naturalia non sunt moraliter turpia. Resp. 1) Quidquid in statu naturæ institutæ homini est naturale, illud non est peccatum proprie dictum: concedo. At peccatum originis est, homini naturale in statu naturæ destitutæ. 2) Naturalia constitutiua, & confecutiua talia, non sunt turpia: at quæ sunt naturalia subiectiua, transitiua, & corruptiua, poffunt esse turpia moraliter, aut phyfice. Morbus hereditarius est naturalis, & tamen phyfice turpis.

VII. Si peccatum originale per generationem propagatur, damnanda sunt coniugia: At hæc non sunt damnanda: E. peccatum originale per generationem non propagatur. Confequentia maioris probatur; quia coniugia erunt impura, fi in liberos, legitimo toro natos, peccatum originis propagatur. Resp. Dist. inter coniugia confiderata fecundum fe, quatenus diuinitus sunt ordinata; & confiderata per accidens, quatenus vitium naturali generationi adhæret. Vitia naturæ non tollunt beneficia Dei.

Quæst . ARISTOTELES adpellauit malum οὐγγενὲς, quamquam veram eius rationem caussasque explicare non valuit.

III. Quod necesse fit, originem huius corruptionis, hominibus innatæ, ἀναρχον & communem fuisse. Ipsa enim corruptio est communis, fine vlla exceptione, aut hominis, aut vitii, aut molestiæ miferiæque humanæ. Effectus autem testatur de re caussa. Communem igitur, eumdemque effectum ab aliqua caussa prima, communi eademque proficisci, necessaria ratione concludimus.

IV. Quod Deus non possit esse caussa huius mali. Is nimirum, humanæ naturæ effector, cui eius non solum creatio, sed etiam conferuatio adferenda est; fi eamdem corrupisset, atque in hoc statu repugnantiæ collocasset, secum ipse dissentiret; id quod & bonitati, & sapientiæ, quæ in Deo inest perfectiffima atque immutabilis, aperte repugnat.

ALTERVM: Quale autem fit hoc peccatum, quæ eius origo fuerit, quanta fit culpa eius, quod denique remedium illi adhibendum, non aliunde constat, quam ex patefactione diuina. Artic. Smalcald. p. 317. Declar. Form. Conc. pag. 639. Argumentum hoc, a posteriori ductum, equidem puto vim maximam habere: Si quis posset ex principiis rationis modum ortumque huius deprauationis demonstrare, vel vlla coniectura adsequi; fieri profecto non potuiffet, quin inter tot tamque discrepantes, philofophorum fectas vnus atque alter sapientissimus in hac re inuestiganda recte feliciterque esset verfatus. At omnes multum allucinati sunt philofophi, reuelationis lumine carentes, & suo indulgentes ingenio. Quidam eorum finxerunt ἀναιμάρτητον animorum, quasi omnes vna peccaffent animi, diu ante, quam cum suo quisque corpore coniungeretur. Vnde enim communis illa naturæ humanæ corruptio, in tot tamque diuerfis generationibus? (Propof. I. & III.) Alii statuerunt μετεμψύχωσιν, siue potius μετενσωμάτωσιν, quæ sententia non minus absurda est, nec minus inepta, ad reddendam rationem: quare communis fit miserrima hæc conditio. (Prop. III.) Plerique eo temeritatis delapsi sunt, vt putarint, duo esse principia æterna, quorum quidem neutrum ex alterius arbitrio pendeat, ea vero contraria, alterum bonum, alterum malum. Quæ certe pro opinio, tametfi antiquissima, sane omnium absurdissima est, & fi adcurate ponderetur, manifestam in fe continet repugnantiam. Philofophi præstantissimi quique profitentur, nihil in tota philofophia difficilius esse hac disputatione: de origine mali. Itaque non est dubitandum de necessitate reuelationis.

Quaest. XIV. Quae est causa efficiens peccati originalis? Peccati originalis causa efficiens remota sunt homines protoplasti; quorum lapsus cum toti generi humano imputatus fit, non potuit non foeditas moralis per carnalem generationem ad omnes posteros derivari .

Proxima autem connatae huius labis causa sunt parentes nostri, quorum impuro sanguine macula originalis ad animam nostram permanavit .

Prob. a. Per unum hominem peccatum in mundum intravit, et per peccatum mors, et sic in omnes homines mors pertransiit, in quo omnes peccaverunt, Rom. V, 12. Haec apostoli verba supra expendimus. Hic tantum observamus, quod lapsus Adami, quo hic se non minus, quam posteros iustitia originali privauit, imputatio fundamentum fit propagationis peccati originalis per carnalem generationem.

Nam apostolus docturus, per Adamum peccatum in mundum, i. e. omnes homines, intrasse, sive propagatum esse, hanc peccati latissime propagati rationem reddit: quia in Adamo omnes peccaverunt.

Peccaverunt autem omnes in Adamo non physice; quippe qui peccante Adamo nondum erant: ergo moraliter, sive per imputationem.

Nimirum lapsus Adami toti generi humano iustissima Dei aestimatione adiudicatus est, ut propter peccatum primum Adamus et posteri ipsius coram tribunali divino reputati sint peccatores, i. e. iustitiae originalis expertes, et ad omne malum proclives.

Inde fit, ut defectus concreatae iustitiae et proclivitas ad malum omnium hominum, qui via naturali ab Adamo descendunt, generationem comitetur.

Neque Deus impedit extraordinarie, ac per miraculum, huius labis propagationem, eiusque comitantia cum generatione creaturae rationalis, quae, legem divinam primum transgrediendo, libertate arbitrii abusa est.

Conf. Hvlsem. breuiar. enucleat. p. 286.

Prob. b. Quis dabit mundum ex immundo?

Iob. XIV, 4.

Loquitur Iobus non de immunditie externa corporis, sed interna animae, propter quam obnoxii reddimur iudicio Dei, v. 3: neque sermo ipsi est de immunditie actuali, sed habituali et universali, vtpote quae ex natiuitate impura profecta, animae intime inhaeret.

Adeo naturae sequitur femina quisque suae.

Nec niger coruus albam columbam, nec ferox leo mitem agnum, nec homo, peccato congenito pollutus, sanctum producit filium.


### Q. XIII. Is original depravity sin properly so called, propagated by carnal generation into all the descendants of Adam?: Quest. XV. Who is infected with original sin?

Quest. XV. Who is infected with original sin?

All men descending from Adam by natural generation are infected with original sin.

Obs.

The original stain is sprinkled upon all and singular men to whom a natural origin from Adam has happened.

Therefore Christ was contaminated by neither original nor actual stain; for the reason that he was not begotten by the ordinary way of nature, but conceived through the ἐπέλευσιν or supernatural and miraculous coming upon of the Holy Spirit, and thus he is holy, harmless, undefiled, and separate from sinners. Hebr. VII, 26.

Proof 1) From John

III, 5. 6. Unless one is born of water and the spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God: that which is born of the flesh is flesh. The Savior urges the universal necessity of regeneration on account of the universal corruption of the human race, and confirms that all men who are to enter the kingdom of God are unworthy of regeneration, in that all men are flesh born of flesh, i.e., begotten from parents polluted by sin, and stained by the contagion of corrupt flesh.

2) All men have sinned, and are destitute of the glory of God, Rom. III, 23. By which words the apostle describes original sin through the privation of the divine image. For the defect of that glory, which man had received in creation, is designated by the same, just as if he were concluding from the consequent: Whoever sins, they are destitute of concreated justice: But all men sin. Therefore, all men are destitute of concreated justice.

You say: Enoch and Elijah were devoid of original sin, otherwise they would not have been taken up alive into heaven, into which nothing unclean enters, Apocal. XXI, 27. Resp. Enoch and Elijah were by nature children of wrath and thus subject to original sin, Eph. II, 3. but by grace they were regenerated and reputed righteous.

Latin:

Quaest. XV. Quis peccato originis infectus est?

Peccato originis infecti sunt homines omnes, naturali generatione ab Adamo descendentes .

Obs.

Labes originalis aspersa est universis et singulis hominibus, quibus naturalis ex Adamo ortus contigit.

Proinde Christus nec originali, nec actuali macula contaminatus est; propterea, quod non ordinaria naturae via genitus, sed per ἐπέλευσιν sive superventum supernaturalem et miraculosum Spiritus S. conceptus, adeoque sanctus, innoxius, impollutus et a peccatoribus segregatus est. Hebr. VII, 26.

Prob. 1) E Io.

III, 5. 6. Nisi quis genitus fuerit ex aqua et spiritu, non potest ingredi in regnum Dei: quod natum est e carne, caro est. Vrget Salvator universale regenerationis necessitatem ob universale generis humani corruptionem, et confirmat, omnes homines, ingressuros regnum Dei, regeneratione esse indignos, eo, quod omnes homines caro de carne nati, i. e. ex parentibus peccato pollutis geniti, et contagio corruptae carnis coinquinati sunt.

2) Omnes homines peccauerunt, & destituuntur gloria Dei, Rom. III, 23. Quibus verbis apostolus peccatum originale per priuationem imaginis diuinæ describit. Nam designatur ab eodem defectus illius gloriæ, quam homo in creatione acceperat, perinde, ac si a posteriori concluderet: Quicunque peccant, illi concreata iustitia sunt destituti: Atqui omnes homines peccant. E. omnes concreata iustitia sunt destituti.

Dicis: Enochus & Elias expertes fuerunt peccati originalis, ceteroqui viui non sublati fuissent in cœlum, in quod nullum immundum ingreditur, Apocal. XXI, 27. Resp. Enochus & Elias natura fuerunt filii iræ atque adeo peccato originali obnoxii, Eph. II, 3. ex gratia autem regeniti & iusti reputati sunt.


### Quaest. XVI. Was the Blessed Mary, Mother of God, conceived without original sin?

The Blessed Virgin Mary was not conceived without original sin.

Proof 1) Because original sin has been diffused into all men born of Adam in the natural way of blood. See the preceding question.

2) A conception immune from sin belongs to Christ alone, Luke I, 35. If the Blessed Mary had been devoid of sin, why was the blood mass, from which the body of Christ was to be built, sanctified by the miraculous intervention of the Holy Spirit? But since this was done by the most profound counsel of God, we conclude that Christ alone among men enjoyed the privilege of τῆς ἀναμαρτησίας (sinlessness). He alone is said to be separated from sinners, Hebr. VII, 26.

3) The actual sins (although venial) of St. Mary are recounted in the sacred code: Carelessness in guarding Jesus, so that he might not be lost, Luke II, 43. Πολυπραγμοσύνη (meddlesomeness) at the wedding in Cana, truly rebuked by Christ, John II, 3, 4. Untimely interruption of Jesus while preaching, Matt. XII, 46; Mark III, 31. But actual sins bear witness to the sin of origin, just as fruit does to the root, offspring to the mother, and streams to the fountain.

The antithesis is that of the Franciscans, Scotists, and Jesuits among the Papists, who opine that St. Mary was conceived without the contagion of Adam, and have bound themselves by the faith of an oath to defend this opinion. On the contrary, the Thomists and Dominicans maintain that Mary was indeed conceived in original stain, but was afterwards so sanctified that she was immune from sins. Most of the arguments of the Franciscans are futile; the following seem worthy of being recounted:

I. Mary is called full of grace and blessed among women, Luke I, 28. From which words they conclude: Whatever woman is full of grace and blessed among women, she is devoid of sin: But Mary is, etc. Therefore. Resp. 1) Mary is called passively κεχαριτωμένη, i.e., having obtained grace. But the faithful also are κεχαριτωμένοι, i.e., having obtained grace, Eph. I, 6. Jael is called Ἐυλογημένη or blessed among women, Jud. V, 24. Therefore, the sinlessness of Mary cannot be concluded from the words of the angel. 2) By the grace which Mary obtained, the singular and most eminent privilege of motherhood is denoted, that by divine favor she was to be the mother of the Messiah.

II. Mary is all fair without spot, Cant. IV, 7. Therefore, her conception is immaculate. Resp. The bride who is all fair, without spot, is the triumphant church, which has no spot or wrinkle, as Paul testifies, Eph. V, 27.

III. Mary is called the closed gate, Ezech. XLIV, 2. Therefore, access to the soul of Mary was not open to the Devil inciting to sin. Resp. Ezekiel speaks of the gate of the temple: yet the ancient doctors judged that the perpetual virginity of Mary, not absolute impeccability, was typically shadowed forth by the prophet. See Dr. Scherzer's Anti-Bellarmine, p. 675.

IV. Eve was a type of Mary: But Eve was formed without original sin: Therefore, Mary was also conceived without original sin. Resp. 1) Holy Scripture nowhere asserts that Eve is a type

of Mary. 2) Not all things which are in the type are predicated of the antitype. For Eve was formed in a state of integrity, Mary in a state of corruption. 3) By the same reasoning we conclude: David was a type of Christ: David was born of a sinful mother: Therefore, so was Christ.

V. If Christ was begotten of a sinful mother, he himself was contaminated by original stain: The latter is false: Therefore, so is the former. The consequence of the major is proven; because a sinful mother begets a sinful son. For who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? Job XIV, 4. Resp. I deny the consequence. For a sinful mother begets a sinful son, unless an extraordinary and miraculous grace of the Holy Spirit intervenes, preventing the concomitance of original sin with the generation of the mother and the production of the offspring.

Instance: But the little drops of Mary's blood, from which the body of Christ was formed, were infected with the poison of sin: Therefore Christ was conceived and born from impure blood. Resp. The little drops of Mary's blood, from which the body of Christ was formed, considered according to their respective being, insofar as they were divinely appointed for the conception of τοῦ λόγου, were separated from the poison of sin by the miraculous intervention of the Holy Spirit. From which Christ is said to be separated from sinners, Heb. VII, 26.

Latin:

B. Maria virgo non est sine peccato originali concepta.

Prob. 1) Quia peccatum originale in omnes homines, modo naturali sanguine Adami satos, diffusum est. Vid. quæst. præced.

2) Soli Christo immunis a peccato conceptio competit, Luc. I, 35. Si B. Maria expers fuisset peccati, cur massa sanguinea, e qua exstruendum erat corpus Christi miraculoso superuentu Spiritus S. sanctificabatur? At cum hoc profundissimo Dei consilio factum sit, colligimus, solum Christum inter homines priuilegio τῆς ἀναμαρτησίας gauisum fuisse. Ille solus a peccatoribus segregatus dicitur, Hebr. VII, 26.

3) Peccata actualia (quamuis venialia) S. Mariæ in sacro codice recensentur: Incuria in custodiendo Iesu, ne amitteretur, Luc. II, 43. Πολυπραγμοσύνη, in nuptiis Cananæis vere a Christo reprehensa, Io. II, 3. 4. Intempestiua interpellatio concionantis Iesu, Matth. XII, 46. Marc. III, 31. At peccata actualia testantur de peccato originis, haud secus, ac fructus de radice, proles de matre, riuuli de fonte.

Antithesis est Franciscanorum, Scotistarum & Iesuitarum inter Pontificios, qui S. Mariam absque contagio Adami conceptam esse opinantur, & opinioni huic defendendæ iurisiurandi fide se obstrinxerunt. Contra, Thomistæ & Dominicani statuunt, Mariam in originali labe quidem conceptam, sed postea ita sanctificatam esse, vt immunis a peccatis fuerit. Pleraque argumenta Franciscanorum sunt futilia, recensitu digna videntur sequentia:

I. Maria dicitur gratiæ plena & beata in mulieribus, Luc. I, 28. E quibus verbis colligunt: Quæcunque mulier est gratiæ plena & beata in mulieribus, illa est expers peccati: Atqui Maria &c. E. Resp. 1) Maria dicitur passiue κεχαριτωμένη, i. e. gratiam consecuta. Sed & fideles sunt κεχαριτωμένοι, i. e. gratiam consecuti, Eph. I, 6. Ἐυλογημένη siue benedicta præ mulieribus dicitur Iaël, Iud. V, 24. Ergo e verbis angeli ἀναμαρτησία Mariæ concludi nequit. 2) Per gratiam, quam consecuta est Maria, denotatur singulare & eminentissimum priuilegium maternitatis, quod ex dignatione diuina mater futura sit Messiæ.

II. Maria est tota pulcra sine macula, Cant. IV, 7. E. illius conceptio est immaculata. Resp. Sponsa tota pulcra, sine macula, est ecclesia triumphans, quæ non maculum aut rugam habet, teste Paullo, Ephes. V, 27.

III. Maria dicitur porta clausa, Ezech. XLIV, 2. E. Diabolo ad peccatum instiganti non patuit aditus in animam Mariæ. Resp. Ezechiel loquitur de porta templi: antiqui tamen doctores perpetuam Mariæ virginitatem, non absolutam impeccabilitatem a propheta typice adumbratam esse, censuerunt. Vid. D. SCHERZERI Anti-Bellarm. p. 675.

IV. Eua fuit typus Mariæ: Sed Eua sine peccato originali est formata: Ergo & Maria sine peccato originis est concepta. Resp. 1) S. scriptura nullibi asserit, Euam esse typum

Mariæ. 2) Non omnia, quæ sunt in typo, prædicantur de antitypo. Nam Eua formata est in statu integritatis, Maria in statu corruptionis. 3) Eadem ratione concludimus: Dauid fuit typus Christi: Dauid natus est e matre peccatrice: Ergo & Christus.

V. Si Christus genitus est e matre peccatrice, ipse originali labe contaminatus est: Posterius est falsum: Ergo & prius. Consequentia maioris probatur; quia mater peccatrix gignit filium peccatorem. Quis enim dabit mundum de immundo? Iob. XIV, 4. Resp. Neg. consequ. Nam mater peccatrix gignit filium peccatorem, nisi interueniat extraordinaria & miraculosa gratia Spiritus S. impediens concomitantiam peccati originalis cum generatione matris & productione sobolis.

Instantia: Sed guttulæ sanguinis Mariæ, e quibus corpus Christi formatum est, fuerunt veneno peccati infectæ: Ergo Christus ex impuro sanguine conceptus & natus est. Resp. Guttulæ sanguinis Mariæ, e quibus formatum est corpus Christi, consideratæ quoad esse respectiuum, quatenus scilicet diuinitus deputatæ fuerunt ad conceptionem τοῦ λόγου, miraculoso superuentu Spiritus S. segregatæ fuerunt a veneno peccati. Ex quo Christus dicitur a peccatoribus segregatus, Hebr. VII, 26.


### Q. XVII. Does original sin reside in the soul of man, or in the body?

The primary seat of original sin is the soul with its faculties a): the secondary seat is the body with its members b).

Proof a.
