Just as the soul was the πρῶτον δεκτικὸν, or the primary seat of concreated wisdom and holiness; so original sin, which succeeded into its place, proximately and immediately infected the soul and its faculties, so that the intellect is darkened in knowing spiritual goods, the will inclines toward evils, and the sensitive appetite, having shaken off the command of reason, is carried headlong into the desires of the flesh.

Proof b. The body indeed seems in itself a brute thing, incapable of sin; but insofar as it is subject to the command of the soul, which is contaminated by sin, it is called the secondary subject of original sin; because the faculties of the soul in sin use the bodily members as instruments. For this reason, St. Paul gravely exhorts, Rom. VI, 12: Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, that you should obey it in the lusts thereof, neither yield ye your members as instruments of unrighteousness unto sin.

Latin:

Sedes primaria peccati originalis est anima cum facultatibus suis a): sedes secundaria est corpus cum suis membris b).

Prob. a. Sicut anima fuit πρῶτον δεκτικὸν, siue sedes primaria concreatæ sapientiæ & sanctitatis; ita peccatum originis, quod in eius locum successit, proxime & immediate infecit animam, eiusque facultates, vt intellectus ad cognoscendum bona spiritualia caliget, voluntas ad mala propendeat, appetitus sensitiuus, excusso rationis imperio, in cupiditates carnis præceps feratur.

Prob. b. Corpus quidem per se videtur res bruta, peccati haud capax; at in quantum subest imperio animæ, peccato contaminatæ, dicitur subiectum peccati originalis secundarium; eo, quod facultates animæ in peccato membris corporeis, velut organis, vtuntur. Qua de caussa grauiter cohortatur S. Paullus, Rom. VI, 12. Ne igitur regnato peccatum in mortuo vestro corpore, vt obediatis illi in concupiscentiis eius, neque sistite membra vestra instrumenta iniustitiæ peccato.


### Q. XVIII. In what does original sin formally consist?

Original sin formally consists in the privation of original justice, which was due to be in man a), and in carnal concupiscence, or an inclination toward evil b).

Obs. I. Privation is divided into simple and composite. Simple privation is the absence of a thing, which by nature ought to be present, in a capable subject, e.g., blindness in a man. Composite privation is that which is joined with an act or a depraved habit. Certainly, blindness and depraved vision differ, deafness and perverse hearing, the lack of sound in a lyre and a harsh sound, the ignorance of simple negation and of a depraved disposition. We maintain that original sin is indeed a privation, but not a mere or simple one, but one joined with a depraved habit.

Obs. II. The positive is taken either in a metaphysical sense, or in an ethical, or moral, sense. In the metaphysical sense, the so-called positive is distinguished into entitative and modificative. The entitative positive is being itself, and that either uncreated or created, or substance or accident. The modificative positive is given in the modes of being, e.g., in transcendental goodness, truth, duration, presence of being. In the ethical, or moral, sense, the positive is an inclination or determination inducing, instigating, and effectively disposing toward evil. It is called by Theologians depraved concupiscence, inordinate disposition, corrupt habit, habit turned toward evil.

Obs. III. Dr. Chemnitz, in his Loci Theologici on original sin, fol. m. 225, shows that Augustine defined original sin by concupiscence; Anselm, by the lack of original justice, which ought to be present; Hugo, however, taught that original sin is ignorance in the mind and concupiscence in the flesh: that the Sententiaries later contended among themselves regarding those definitions, as to which is truer and better: that Scotus with his followers embraced Anselm's definition; that others fought for Augustine's definition in such a way that they rejected Anselm's; but that Bonaventure prudently judged that both definitions are true, and that one of them is included in the other. The Augsburg Confession, Art. II, does not depart from this latter opinion. The churches among us teach that after the fall of Adam, all men, propagated according to nature, are born with sin, that is, without the fear of God, without trust toward God, and with concupiscence. This doctrine of the Augsburg Confession is explained and confirmed in the Apology, p. 55: 'We have rightly expressed both in the description of original sin, namely those defects: not being able to believe in God; not being able to fear and love God: Likewise, having concupiscence, which seeks carnal things against the word of God, that is, it seeks not only the pleasures of the body, but also carnal wisdom and justice, and trusts in these goods, despising God.' And not only the ancients, but also the more recent ones, if there are any more sensible ones, teach that these things together are truly original sin, namely the defects listed and concupiscence. For thus says Thomas: 'Original sin has the privation of original justice, and with this, an inordinate disposition of the parts of the soul, whence it is not a pure privation, but a certain corrupted habit.' And Bonaventure: When it is asked what original sin is, 'it is rightly answered that it is immoderate concupiscence; it is also rightly answered that it is the lack of due justice; and in one of these answers the other is included.' Hugo felt the same when he said: that original sin is ignorance in the mind and concupiscence in the flesh.

Obs. IV. The word concupiscence, when it is contrasted with an act, is ambiguous: for it denotes either the natural power of desiring, or a superadded depraved inclination. Between the former and the latter, a huge distinction is given. For the natural appetite of man, or the appetitive power of the soul, which is conceived as the subject or material of original sin, is one thing; and the original evil concupiscence, which corrupts that power and formally constitutes original sin, is another. For the former is from God, the latter is not; the former is a positive being, strictly taken and created, the latter is not; the former is indifferent, the latter is determinate; the former is a natural and concreated power, the latter is a superadded and introduced quality; the former perfects human nature, the latter destroys and contaminates it.

Prob. a. 1) Every sin is ἀνομία, 1 John III, 4, i.e., a defect of moral rectitude, which we are obligated by the law to possess. Therefore, original sin is as well.

2) Paul defines original sin by the lack of the glory of God, Rom. III, 23, designating the defect of that glory with which man was adorned by God in creation; whence we conclude that the privation of the divine image, which we all lack after the fall, is noted. For the image of God was the glory granted to man by God in creation, and we are all destitute of it, after we suffered the loss of original justice in Adam.

Prob. b. 1) Because original sin in the intellect is not only ignorance of simple negation, but also of depraved disposition, or a horrendous error; since unregenerate Gentiles not only were ignorant of the true God, but also changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, and four-footed beasts, and creeping things, Rom. III, 23. Indeed, there is also detected in the intellect of unregenerate man, besides ignorance of spiritual things, a certain connate proneness to pass rash and false judgments about them. For spiritual things are foolishness to the unregenerate man, 1 Cor. II, 14, i.e., he judges that the mysteries of faith are clearly absurd and impossible. But that propensity toward rash judgments regarding matters of faith signifies more than a deprivation of knowledge.

2) Original sin in the human will is not merely a lack of original justice, but also an inclination and determination toward evil. For this reason, man, established outside the state of grace, is called a slave of sin, Rom. VI, 13, and sin is said to reign in his mortal body, to obey it through its desires, v. 12; which is to say, since he cannot of himself do those things which are holy, he is carried conversely into those things which are evil, just as if it were necessary for him to act so, or as if his will were bent by the command of a superior. Hence, besides the lack of divine love, there is given in the human will hatred and enmity against God, security and contempt for spiritual things, Φιλαυτία, care for the world, and trust fixed upon created things.

2) Original sin in the sensitive appetite is not merely a deprivation of the obedience owed to the superior faculties, but also a rebellion of the flesh against the spirit, Gal. V, 17, a beastly inclination, asinine stupidity, peacock-like pride, wolfish avarice, fox-like cunning, leonine ferocity.

4) Original sin, as the Holy Scripture testifies, approaches the analogy of an active and difficult-to-move habit. For it is called ἐυπερίςατον, most deeply inherent, surrounding on all sides, and pressing in from everywhere, Heb. XII, 1. It is said to inhabit and work, Rom. VII, 17. Certainly, no deprivation works positively, as original sin does. For innate concupiscence, which we call the formal positive of original sin, produces actual sin through an abstractive act, as ἐξέλκυσα; an alluring one, as δελεάζυσα; a hardening one, as συλλαβῦσα. James I, 14. Therefore, it is a positive habit, and not a mere deprivation; for the latter cannot positively draw a man away, entice him, conceive actual sin, and bring it forth, or lead it into act.

The antithesis is 1) of some Scholastics and for the most part of the Papists, 2) of the Arminians, who posit that original sin is a mere deprivation of original justice, which is owed. Their principal arguments are:

I. Everything positive is good, and is either uncreated or created. But original sin is neither good, nor uncreated, nor created. Therefore, original sin is not something positive. The major premise is evident; because everything positive is a being, and therefore good, and either uncreated, like God; or created, like a creature, whose efficient cause is God. Response: Distinguish between positive in a metaphysical sense and in a moral sense. A metaphysical positive, and that which is entitative, is a good being, and is either the creator or a creature. But a moral positive is neither the creator nor always a creature; for example, an inclination toward evil is something positive, yet it was not created by God; because God created man upright and very good, without any depraved inclination. Temptation toward evil is something positive, yet it does not derive its origin from God, but from original concupiscence, James I, 14. Determination toward evil is something positive, yet it does not proceed from God; because God is the universal cause, determining no one toward evil.

II. If there is given some positive thing in creatures that does not depend on God, there will be given a being that was not made by God. The consequent is false; therefore, the antecedent is also. The falsity of the consequence appears from John I, 3: All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made. Response: 1) Not every positive thing is a being, since there is also given a modifying positive, for example, in presence, duration, etc. If you call the determination toward evil a modifying positive, you will not have strayed from the truth. 2) It is not absurd that there be given some positive thing not produced by God, if it is morally evil. Who would dare to assert that depraved concupiscence, and its fruitfulness and impregnation, James I, 14, evil thoughts, the inordinate disposition of the soul, the rebellion of the sensitive appetite against right reason, the determination of physical motion toward evil, and its conjunction with viciousness, proceed from

God? Would not God be constituted the cause of sin by such an assertion? 3) John 1:3. Properly, the discourse is about natural beings, produced in the first hexaëmeron, and not truly about moral good or evil. Compare D. HULSEMANN, brev. enucl. p. 273 et seqq.

III. Every ἀνομία is a privation: Original sin is ἀνομία: Therefore. Resp. Distinguish between simple and composite privation. The sin of origin is indeed a privation, but not a mere or simple one; rather, it is composite, and joined with a depraved habit, or perverse concupiscence, inclination, and determination toward evil.

IV. Depraved concupiscence, or inclination and determination toward evil, pertains to the material, not the formal, part of original sin. Indeed, original sin, taken concretely, denominatively, and materially, includes concupiscence, proclivity, and determination toward evil; but if it is taken abstractly and formally, it is only the privation of original justice, which is due to be present. Resp. This is just as if you wished to describe a harsh sound by the absence of a pleasant sound, error by the defect of true knowledge, rebellion by the privation of obedience: which descriptions would be by no means sufficient. For a harsh sound is more than the absence of a pleasant sound; error is more than the defect of true knowledge; rebellion is more than the privation of obedience; namely, they import the position of a contrary act or habit. For a like reason, the sin of origin is less adequately defined by the lack of original justice, which is due to be present, because in the place of the lost divine image there succeeded a habitual inclination toward internal and external acts prohibited by divine law, which we commonly call original concupiscence. This pertains to the formal part of original sin: because it enters into its definition and is predicated of the same in the nominative case: For original sin, as HUGO defines it, is ignorance in the mind and concupiscence in the flesh.

V. Whoever asserts that original sin is an accident, a quality, and a habit, they must confess that the sin of origin is an entity produced by God: But the evangelical doctors, etc. Therefore. The consequence of the major premise is proven; because a habit is a quality, a quality is an accident, and an accident is an entity produced by God. Resp. The evangelical doctors assert that original sin is a habit, a quality, and an accident, not in a metaphysical ἀκριβείᾳ (precision), but in a moral and therefore broader sense. For original sin is called an accident, quality, and habit analogically; because it inheres in the vitiated soul by way of an accident. By way of a quality, it is a principle of evil action: by way of a habit, it renders man prompt and ready to sin.

Latin:

Peccatum originale formaliter consistit in priuatione iustitiæ originalis, homini inesse debitæ a) & carnali concupiscentia, siue inclinatione ad malum b).

Obs. I. Priuatio diuiditur in simplicem, & compositam. Priuatio simplex est absentia rei, per naturam inesse debitæ, in subiecto capaci, v. gr. cæcitas in homine. Priuatio composita est, quæ cum actu, vel habitu prauo coniuncta est. Sane differunt cæcitas & prava visio, surditas & peruersus auditus, carentia soni in chely, & sonus asper, ignorantia simplicis negationis & prauæ dispositionis. Statuimus, peccatum originis esse quidem privationem, at non meram, aut simplicem, sed cum prauo habitu coniunctam.

Obs. II. Positiuum sumitur vel in sensu metaphysico, vel in sensu ethico, seu morali. Sensu metaphysico dictum positiuum distinguitur in entitatiuum & modificatiuum. Positivum entitatiuum est ipsum ens, idque vel increatum, vel creatum, vel substantia, vel accidens. Positiuum modificatiuum datur in modis entis, v. gr. in transcendentali bonitate, veritate, duratione, præsentia entis. Sensu ethico, vel morali, positiuum est inclinatio vel determinatio ad malum inducens, instigans & efficaciter disponens. Vocatur a Theologis praua concupiscentia, inordinata dispositio, habitus corruptus, habitus conuersiuus ad malum.

Obs. III. D. CHEMNITIVS in locis theol. de peccato originali fol. m. 225. ostendit, AVGVSTINVM definisse peccatum originis, per concupiscentiam; ANSELMVM, per carentiam iustitiae originalis, inesse debitae; HVGONEM vero docuisse, peccatum originis esse ignorantiam in mente, concupiscentiam in carne: Sententiarios postea inter se dimicasse, de illis definitionibus, vtra verior & melior sit: SCOTVM cum suis amplexum esse Anselmi definitionem; alios pro Augustini definitione ita pugnasse, vt Anselmi reiicerent; BONAVENTVRAM vero prudenter iudicasse, vtramque definitionem veram esse, & in vna illarum includi alteram. A postrema sententia non abit Augustana Confessio art. II. Ecclesiae apud nos docent, quod post lapsum Adae omnes homines, secundum naturam propagati, nascantur cum peccato, hoc est, sine metu Dei, sine fiducia erga Deum & cum concupiscentia. Quae doctrina Augustanae Confessionis explicatur & confirmatur in apologia, p. 55. Nos recte expressimus vtrumque in descriptione peccati originalis, videlicet defectus illos, non posse Deo credere; non posse Deum timere ac diligere: Item habere concupiscentiam, quae carnalia quaerit contra verbum Dei, hoc est, quaerit non solum voluptates corporis; sed etiam sapientiam & iustitiam carnalem, & confidit his bonis, contemnens Deum. Neque solum veteres, sed etiam recentiores, si qui sunt cordatiores, docent simul ista vere peccatum originis esse, defectus videlicet recensitos, & concupiscentiam. Sic enim inquit THOMAS: Peccatum originis habet priuationem originalis iustitiae, & cum hac inordinatam dispositionem partium animae, vnde non est priuatio pura, sed quidam habitus corruptus. Et BONAVENTVRA: Cum quaeritur, quid sit originale peccatum, „recte respondetur, quod sit concupiscentia immoderata; recte etiam respondetur, quod sit „debitae iustitiae carentia; & in vna istarum responsionum includitur altera.“ Idem sensit HVGO cum ait: originale peccatum esse ignorantiam in mente & concupiscentiam in carne.

Obs. IV. Vox concupiscentia, quando actui contradistinguitur, ambigua est: vel enim notat potentiam naturalem concupiscendi, vel superadditam inclinationem prauam. Inter illam, & hanc ingens datur discrimen. Aliud enim est naturalis appetitus hominis, vel potentia animae appetitiua, quae vt subiectum vel materiale peccati originis concipitur; & aliud est originalis concupiscentia mala, quae illam potentiam corrumpit, & formaliter peccatum originis constituit. Nam illa est a Deo, haec non est; illa est ens positiuum stricte sumtum & creatum, haec non est; illa indifferenter se habet, haec determinate; illa est potentia naturalis & concreata, haec est qualitas superaddita & introducta; illa naturam humanam perficit, haec destruit & contaminat.

Prob. a. 1) Omne peccatum est ἀνομία, 1 Io. III, 4. i. e. defectus rectitudinis moralis, ad quam habendam per legem obligamur. Ergo & peccatum originis.

2) Paullus definit peccatum originale per carentiam gloriae Dei, Rom. III, 23. designans defectum illius gloriae, quo homo in creatione a Deo condecoratus erat; vnde priuationem imaginis diuinae, qua omnes caremus post lapsum, notari colligimus. Etenim imago Dei erat gloria, homini a Deo concessa in creatione, & ea destituimur omnes, postquam in Adamo iustitiae originalis iacturam fecimus.

Prob. b. 1) Quia peccatum originale in intellectu non tantum est ignorantia simplicis negationis, sed etiam prauae dispositionis, siue horrendus error; siquidem gentiles irregeniti verum Deum ignorarunt haud tantum, sed mutarunt etiam gloriam incorruptibilis Dei in similitudinem corruptibilis hominis, & volatilium, & quadrupedum, & reptilium, Rom. III, 23. Quin deprehenditur etiam in intellectu hominis irregeniti, praeter ignorantiam rerum spiritualium, pronitas quaedam connata ad ferendum de iis iudicia temeraria & falsa. Nam spiritualia homini irregenito sunt stultitia, 1 Cor. II, 14. i. e. iudicat, mysteria fidei esse absurda plane, & impossibilia. At illa propensio ad iudicia temeraria de rebus fidei plus importat, quam priuationem notitiæ.

2) Peccatum originale in voluntate hominis non est tantum carentia iustitiæ originalis, sed etiam inclinatio & determinatio ad malum. Id propter homo, extra statum gratiæ constitutus, dicitur seruus peccati, Rom. VI, 13. & peccatum regnare in eius corpore mortali, ad obediendum illi per cupiditates eius, v. 12. quod videlicet, quum ea, quæ sancta sunt, agere ex se non possit, in ea, quæ mala sunt, ex aduerso feratur, perinde, ac si ita agere eum oporteret, aut superioris imperio voluntas flecteretur. Hinc, præter carentiam amoris diuini, datur in voluntate hominis odium & inimicitia aduersus Deum, securitas & contemtus rerum spiritualium, Φιλαυτία, cura sæculi & fiducia in creaturis defixa.

2) P. O. in appetitu sensitiuo non est tantum priuatio obsequii, superioribus facultatibus debiti, sed & rebellio carnis aduersus spiritum, Gal. V, 17. bestialis inclinatio, asininus stupor, pauonina superbia, lupina auaritia, vulpina calliditas, leonina ferocia.

4) P. O. teste S. scriptura accedit ad analogiam habitus operosi & difficulter mobilis. Dicitur enim ἐυπερίςατον, penitissime inhærens, circumcirca cingens, & vndiquaque insistens, Hebr. XII, 1. Dicitur inhabitare & operari, Rom. VII, 17. Sane nulla priuatio positiue operatur, sicut P. O. Nam concupiscentia connata, quam nos P. O. formale positiuum appellamus, producit peccatum actuale per actum abstractiuum, vt ἐξέλκυσα; illectivum, vt δελεάζυσα; obfirmatiuum, vt συλλαβῦσα. Iacob. I, 14. Ergo est habitus positivus, & non mera priuatio; quippe quæ non potest hominem positiue abstrahere, inescare, peccatum actuale concipere & parere, siue in actum deducere.

Antithesis est 1) nonnullorum Scholasticorum & plerumque Pontificiorum, 2) Arminianorum, statuentium, peccatum originis esse meram priuationem iustitiæ originalis, inesse debitæ. Quorum præcipua sunt argumenta:

I. Omne positiuum est bonum, & vel increatum, vel creatum. At P. O. neque bonum est, neque increatum, neque creatum. Ergo P. O. non est aliquid positiuum. Maior constat; quia omne positiuum est ens, adeoque bonum, & vel increatum, vt Deus; vel creatum, vt creatura, cuius caussa efficiens est Deus. Resp. Dist. inter positiuum metaphyficum, & morale. Positiuum metaphysicum, idque entitatiuum est ens bonum, & vel creator, vel creatura. At positiuum morale neque creator, neque semper creatura est, v. gr. inclinatio ad malum est aliquid positiuum, neque tamen ipsa a Deo creata est; quia Deus condidit hominem rectum & valde bonum, sine vlla praua inclinatione. Tentatio ad malum est aliquid positiuum, neque tamen originem ducit a Deo, sed a concupiscentia originali, Iac. I, 14. Determinatio ad malum est aliquid positiuum, neque tamen prouenit a Deo; quia Deus est caussa vniuersalis ad malum neminem determinans.

II. Si datur aliquod positiuum in creaturis, quod non pendet a Deo: dabitur ens, quod non factum est a Deo: Consequens est falsum: Ergo & antecedens. Falsitas consequentiæ apparet e Io. I, 3. Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, & sine ipso factum est nihil, quod factum est. Resp. 1) Non omne positiuum est ens, cum detur positiuum etiam modificativum, v. gr. in præsentia, duratione &c. Quod si determinationem ad malum appellaueris positiuum modificatiuum, a vero non deflexeris. 2) Non est absurdum, dari aliquod positiuum a Deo non productum, si sit moraliter malum. Ecquis ausit asserere, concupiscentiam prauam, eiusque fœcunditatem & imprægnationem, Iacob. I, 14. cogitationes malas, inordinatam animæ dispositionem, rebellionem appetitus sensitiui aduersus rectam rationem, motus physici determinationem ad malum, eiusque coniunctionem cum vitiositate proficisci a

Deo? Nonne eiusmodi assertione Deus caussa peccati constituetur? 3) Io. I, 3. proprie sermo est de entibus naturalibus, primo hexaëmero productis, non vero de bono aut malo morali. Confer. D. HVLSEMANN. breu. enucl. p. 273. seqq.

III. Omnis ἀνομία est priuatio: Peccatum originale est ἀνομία: Ergo Resp. Dist. inter priuationem simplicem, & compositam. Peccatum originis est quidem priuatio, sed non mera, aut simplex, verum composita, & cum prauo habitu, siue peruersa concupiscentia, inclinatione & determinatione ad malum coniuncta.

IV. Praua concupiscentia, siue inclinatio & determinatio ad malum, pertinet ad materiale, non ad formale peccati originalis. Nimirum peccatum originale, concretiue, denominatiue & materialiter sumtum, includit concupiscentiam, procliuitatem & determinationem ad malum; at si sumatur abstractiue & formaliter, est tantum priuatio iustitiæ originalis, inesse debitæ. Resp. Hoc perinde est, ac si velles sonum asperum describere per absentiam soni iucundi, errorem per defectum veræ scientiæ, rebellionem per priuationem obsequii: quæ descriptiones inadæquatæ minime sufficientes forent. Nam plus sonus asper, quam absentia soni iucundi; error, quam defectus veræ scientiæ, rebellio, quam priuatio obsequii, positionem scil. contrarii actus aut habitus important. Pari ratione minus adæquate definitur peccatum originis per carentiam iustitiæ originalis, inesse debitæ, eo, quod in locum amissæ imaginis diuinæ successit habitualis inclinatio ad internos & externos actus, lege diuina prohibitos, quam communiter concupiscentiam originalem vocamus. Hæc pertinet ad formale peccati originalis: quia huius definitionem ingreditur, & in casu recto de eodem prædicatur: Nam peccatum originale, definiente HVGONE, est ignorantia in mente & concupiscentia in carne.

V. Quicunque afferunt, peccatum originale esse accidens, qualitatem & habitum, illos oportet fateri, peccatum originis esse ens a Deo productum: Atqui doctores euangelici &c. Ergo. Consequentia maioris probatur; quia habitus est qualitas, qualitas est accidens, accidens est ens a Deo productum. Resp. Doctores euangelici afferunt, peccatum originale esse habitum, qualitatem & accidens, non in ἀκριβείᾳ metaphysica, sed sensu morali, eoque latiori. Dicitur enim peccatum originale accidens, qualitas & habitus analogice; propterea, quod per modum accidentis animæ vitiatæ inhæret. Per modum qualitatis, est principium actionis malæ: per modum habitus, hominem promtum & expeditum reddit ad peccandum.


### Quaest. XIX. Is original sin the substance of man?

Original sin is not the substance of man itself, but is a depravity devoid of due good, and prone to undue evil, like an hereditary and abominable disease, most deeply inhering in the substance of man.

Proof. 1) The Holy Scriptures openly distinguish the original stain from the substance of man itself. Paul, Rom. 7:21, calls original sin the evil that lies near. V. 17 he says: It is no longer I who perform it, but the sin dwelling in me. Heb. 12:1, it is called the sin that surrounds. But whatever lies near to man, dwells in him, and surrounds him, that is not the substance of man itself.

2) Every sin is ἀνομία, John 3:4. Therefore also original sin. But ἀνομία is an aberration from the law, and thus a privation. Who of sound mind would dare to call the substance of man a privation?

3) The contrary opinion is repugnant to many articles of faith, and indeed a) to the article of creation. For God not only created human nature before the fall; but even after the fall, the same is the work and creature of God. Your hands have formed me, and made me; says Job, chap. X, 8. Conf. Ps. CXXXIX, 13. Eccl. XII, 7. But God is not the creator or author of original sin; since that is the work of the devil. b) Article of the incarnation. For the Son of God in a personal union assumed human nature, but without sin, Hebr. IV, 15. c. VII, 26. c) Article of renewal. For God washes and sanctifies man from sin, 1 Cor. VI, 11. But that which is sanctified is one thing, and that which is removed by sanctification is another. d) Article of the resurrection. For Christ will raise up this same nature of ours from the dead, and will adorn it with great glory; but God will not raise up original sin in the elect, nor will he ever adorn it with heavenly glory, or save it, but in that blessed resurrection it will be plainly abolished. See the solid declaration of the Form of Concord, p. 647 ff.

The antithesis is 1) of the Manichaeans, who maintained that there are two coeternal principles, good and evil: that evil substance is produced from the evil principle, and good from the good, and that man consists of these substances, and that on the last day the evil substance is to be separated from the good. 2) Of Matthias Flacius Illyricus, first a Professor at Wittenberg, then at Jena, little versed in philosophy, but otherwise a most learned theologian, who in the heat of the dispute with Victorinus Strigelius in the year 1561, held at Weimar, imprudently asserted that original sin is the substance of man. But he distinguished between formal and material substance: by the former he understood the image of God in our first parents, by the latter man himself consisting of soul and body. Therefore he said that the formal substance was corrupted, and that original sin had succeeded in its place; but that the material substance remained, although greatly vitiated. Furthermore, he distinguished between man considered physically and theologically. If man is considered in philosophy, his substance is body and soul; but in theology it is taught that original sin is of the essence of corrupted man. From which it is evident that Flacius did not teach so absolutely that original sin is the very substance of man, but that theologically it is called the essence of corrupted man. His ruder disciples, having gone further, did not hesitate to affirm that O. S. [Original Sin] is the very substance of man. Conf. D. Johann Musaeus, lectures on the Form of Concord, p. 45. The chief arguments of the Flacians are the following:

I. Whatever sin is of the essence of corrupted man is not wrongly called his substance: But original sin is &c. Therefore. Resp. I deny the major and distinguish between absolute and respective essence. Whatever is of the essence of man, insofar as he is corrupted, cannot be called the substance of man absolutely. The reason is: because whatever is asserted of a certain state of man is not affirmed of him simply, e.g., learning is of the essence of a learned man, insofar as he is a learned man; yet this is not his substance.

II. If O. S. were not a substance, it could not corrupt the whole substance of man: But O. S. has corrupted the whole substance of man: Therefore. I prove the major of the consequence, because an accident has no power to corrupt the whole substance. Resp. 1) Distinguish between the physical and theological corruption of man. By physical corruption, the natural body is resolved into the parts of which it consists: but in the theological sense, the nature of man is said to be corrupted by O. S. not absolutely and simply, but in relation to spiritual objects, pious motions, and acts concerning spiritual things; for the reason that by the sin of men the human intellect is first blinded, so that it does not understand those things which are of the Spirit: the will is rendered inept for choosing spiritual good, and prone to evil; the sensitive appetite has become rebellious to the superior faculties, and inclined to seize upon the good that appears pleasing to the senses. a) Corruption, theologically so called, is subjective, not terminative. It is subjective; because it is a horrendous depravation of the subject, remaining in its own substance: but it is not terminative; because it has not so destroyed human nature as to make it cease to be what it was before. Therefore we easily answer the objection taken from the ecclesiastical refrain:

III. ecclesiastical: Through Adam's fall, human nature is entirely corrupted, corrupta est substantiae, non terminativae . See IOANN. MVSAEVS l.c. pag. 62 .

III. Whatever is described in the sacred scriptures by words denoting human substance, that is the substance of man. But original sin, etc. Therefore. The minor premise is proven because it is called flesh, John III, 6 ; *old man, Romans VI, 6. Colossians III, 9* ; body of sin, Romans VI . Response: Distinguish between the description of original sin taken abstractively and concretively. When original sin is taken formally and abstractively, it is defined by ἀνομίαν , 1 John III, 4 . But when it is taken concretively, it connotes that subject to which it most intimately adheres. Thus it is called flesh; which word denotes both the substance of man and the vice adhering to it. It is called old man, not physically by reason of substance, but ethically and theologically, by reason of qualities. *For the old man concretively designates the nature of man corrupted by original sin; abstractively it denotes the corruption inherent in human nature*. Body of sin signifies not the corporeal substance of man, but the accumulation of sin. For just as a flock, a people, a legion are called bodies, so original sin is called a body, because it spreads into various actual sins and manifests itself through various operations, just as if there existed a certain body, consisting of and composed of diverse members, Colossians III, 4 .

IV. Whatever is an accident, that can be present and absent without the destruction of the subject: But original sin cannot be present without the destruction of the subject. Therefore. The major premise is clear from the definition of an accident. The minor premise is clear because 1) by original sin, the spiritual powers of the soul, once created, are corrupted: 2) because original sin is not absent until man himself perishes. Response: Distinguish between a predicable accident and a predicamental accident. The former is said of its subject contingently, and is opposed to essence: the latter is in another as in a subject, and is opposed to substance. Original sin is called by some theologians not a predicable accident, but a predicamental accident, because it is not an external, easily movable accident, but an internal and difficultly movable one. Furthermore, original sin is called an accident not univocally, but analogically, because it inheres in fallen man in the manner of a vicious habit, and renders him ready and prone to sin.

V. Whatever fights against the law of God, that is sin, 1 John III, 4 . But the whole unregenerate man, etc. Therefore. Response: Whatever formally and per se fights against the law of God, that is sin: I grant. But the whole man does not formally and per se, insofar as he is man, fight against the law of God, but insofar as he is corrupted by sin, and thus per accidens fights against the law of God. *Namely, man is the subject of τῆς ἀνομίας , not ἀνομία itself*.

VI. If original sin is not the substance of man, Christ cannot be called sin: But Christ is called sin: Therefore. The consequence of the major premise is proven: because Christ, by putting on human nature, put on sin, 2 Corinthians V, 21 . Response: I deny the consequence of the major premise; because Christ put on human nature through personal union, without inherent sin; but he transferred our sins to himself imputatively.

VII. P. LVTHERVS called original sin sin of nature, sin of person, substantial sin, or essential sin. Therefore, in the judgment of this eminent doctor of the church, original sin pertains to the very essence of man. Response: Luther's expressions are to be understood not ἁπλῶς , or absolutely, but συγκριτικῶς , or comparatively, with respect to actual sins. Namely, Blessed Luther used those forms of speech to show the distinction between original and actual sin, and called original sin sin of nature, of person, essential, not as if it were essentially constitutive, or consecutive of human nature, but because 1) *it has the same origin as the nature, essence, and person of man, and is therefore σύμφυτον , or connatural to him*; just as to one who is blind from birth, blindness is called natural: 2) because nature it adheres intimately to human nature, has infected the whole of it, and is thus subjectively natural: 3) because it is transitively natural, for the reason that it is propagated from man to his descendants through natural generation.

Latin:

Peccatum originis non est ipsa substantia hominis, sed est prauitas boni debiti expers, & ad malum indebitum propensa, morbi instar hereditarii & abominabilis, substantiæ hominis penitissime inhærens.

Prob. 1) Sacræ litteræ aperte distinguunt maculam originalem ab ipsa substantia hominis. Paullus Rom. VII, 21. peccatum originale vocat malum adiacens. V. 17. inquit: Non iam ego perpetro illud, sed habitans in me malum. Hebr. XII, 1. appellatur peccatum circumstans. At, quidquid homini adiacet, in ipso habitat, eundemque circumstat, id non est ipsa substantia hominis.

2) Omne peccatum est ἀνομία, Io. III, 4. Ergo & peccatum originale. At ἀνομία est aberratio a lege, adeoque priuatio. Ecquis compos mentis substantiam hominis priuationem appellare ausit?

3) Sententia aduersa repugnat multis articulis fidei, & quidem a) articulo creationis. Deus enim non modo ante lapsum humanam naturam creauit; verum etiam eadem post lapsum est Dei opus & creatura. Manus tuæ formauerunt me, & fecerunt me; inquit Iobus, cap. X, 8. Conf. Ps. CXXXIX, 13. Eccl. XII, 7. At peccati originis Deus non est creator, vel auctor; cum istud fit opus diaboli. b) Articulo incarnationis. Nam filius Dei in vnionali personali assumpsit humanam naturam, sed sine peccato, Hebr. IV, 15. c. VII, 26. c) Articulo renouationis. Deus enim hominem a peccato abluit & sanctificat, 1 Cor. VI, 11. Aliud autem est id, quod sanctificatur, aliud, quod per sanctificationem tollitur. d) Articulo resurrectionis. Nam eandem nostram naturam Christus e mortuis resuscitabit, & ingenti gloria ornabit; sed peccatum originis Deus non resuscitabit in electis, neque vnquam gloria coelesti ornabit, aut saluabit, sed in beata illa resurrectione plane illud erit abolitum. Vid. solid. declarat. Form. concord. pag. 647. seqq.

Antithesis est 1) Manichaeorum, qui statuerunt, duo esse principia coeterna, bonum & malum: a malo principio esse productam substantiam malam, a bono bonam, & ex his substantiis constare hominem, inque die extremo substantiam malam a bona esse separandam. 2) Matthaei Flacii Illyrici, Professoris primum Wittebergensis, deinde Ienensis, in philosophia parum versati, cetera doctissimi theologi, qui in feruore disputationis, cum Victorino Strigelio Anno 1561. Vinariae habitae, imprudenter asseruit, peccatum originis esse substantiam hominis. At distinguebat inter substantiam formalem, & materialem: per illam imaginem Dei in primis parentibus, per hanc hominem ipsum ex anima & corpore constantem intelligebat. Proinde dicebat substantiam formalem esse corruptam, & in eius locum successisse peccatum originis; materialem autem remansisse, licet valde vitiatam. Porro distinguebat inter hominem physice, & theologice consideratum. Si homo consideretur in philosophia, substantiam eius esse corpus & animam; at in theologia doceri, peccatum orginale esse de hominis corrupti essentia. E quibus euidens est, Flacium non ita absolute docuisse, quod peccatum originis fit ipsa hominis substantia, sed quod theologice vocetur hominis corrupti essentia. Discipuli eius rudiores, longius progressi, non dubitarunt affirmare, P. O. esse ipsam hominis substantiam. Conf. D. Ioann. Mvsaei praelet. in Form. Concord. p. 45. Praecipua Flacianorum argumenta sunt sequentia:

I. Quodcunque peccatum est de essentia hominis corrupti, haud male dicitur eius substantia: Atqui peccatum originis &c. Ergo. Resp. neg. maiorem & disting. inter essentiale absolutum & respectiuum. Quidquid est de essentia hominis, quatenus corruptus est, non absolute dici potest hominis substantia. Ratio est: quia quidquid de certo hominis statu asseritur, non simpliciter de eodem affirmatur, v. gr. doctrina est de essentia hominis docti, quatenus doctus est homo; neque tamen haec eiusdem est substantia.

II. Si P. O. non esset substantia, non posset totam substantiam hominis corrumpere: Atqui P. O. totam corrupit substantiam hominis: Ergo. Consequ. mai. prob. quia accidenti non est vis, totam substantiam corrumpendi. Resp. 1) Dist. inter corruptionem hominis physicam & theologicam. Physica corruptione corpus naturale resoluitur in partes, & quibus constat: sensu theologico autem natura hominis P. O. dicitur corrupta non absolute & simpliciter, sed in ordine ad obiecta spiritualia, pios motus & actus circa res spirituales; eo, quod peccato hominum primo intellectus humanus est occaecatus, vt non intelligat ea, quae sunt Spiritus: voluntas ad eligendum bonum spirituale reddita est inepta, & ad malum propensa; appetitus sensitiuus superioribus facultatibus factus est rebellis, & proclinis ad bonum apparens sensibus gratum arripiendum. a) Corruptio theologice dicta est subiectiua, non terminatiua. Subiectiua est; quia est subiecti, in substantia sua permanentis, horrenda deprauatio: sed non est terminatiua; quia naturam humanam non sic destruxit, vt desierit esse id, quod antea fuit. Facile ergo respondemus ad obiectionem sumtam ex cantilena ecclesiastica:

III. fiaftiaca: Durch Adams Fall ist ganz verderbt menschlich Natur corrupta est substantiae, non terminativae. Vid. IOANN. MVSAEVS *l.c. pag. 62*.

III. Quidquid in sacris litteris describitur verbis, ipsam substantiam humanam denotantibus, illud est substantia hominis. Atqui peccatum orig. &c. Ergo. Minor probatur, quia dicitur caro, *Io. III, 6. homo vetus, Rom. VI, 6. Col. III, 9. corpus peccati, Rom. VI*. Resf. Dist. inter descriptionem peccati originalis sumti abstra&tive, & concretive. Quando P. O. sumitur formaliter & abstra&tive, definitur per ἀνομίαν, *1Io. III, 4*. Cum autem sumitur concretive, connotat subiectum illud, cui penitissime inhæret. Sic dicitur caro; quæ vox tum substantiam hominis, tum ei adhærens vitium notat. Dicitur vetus homo, non physice ratione substantiae, sed ethice ac theologicae, ratione qualitatum. *Vetus enim homo concretive designat naturam hominis, P. O. corruptam; abstra&tive notat insitam natura humana corruptionem*. Corpus peccati non substantiam hominis corpoream, sed colluviem peccati significat. Sicut enim grex, populus, legio dicuntur corpora, ita peccatum originis dicitur corpus, quia in varia peccata actualia se diffundit, variisque se operationibus exerit, perinde, ac si existeret corpus quoddam, ex diuersis membris constans & compositum, *Col. III, 4*.

IV. Quidquid est accidens, illud adesse & abesse potest sine subiecti interitu: Atqui peccatum originis non potest adesse fine subiecti interitu. Ergo. Maior patet ex definitione accidentis. Minor est clara, quia 1) peccato originis vires animæ spirituales olim concreatæ sunt corruptæ: 2) quia P. O. non prius abest, quam ipse homo intereat. Resf. Dist. inter accidens prædicabile, & prædicamentale. Illud dicitur de subiecto suo contingenter, & opponitur essentiæ: hoc est in alio tanquam in subiecto, & opponitur substantiæ. Dicitur P. O. nonnullis theologis accidens non prædicabile, sed prædicamentale, ideo, quod non est accidens externum facile mobile, sed internum & difficulter mobile. Ceterum dicitur P. O. accidens non vniuocæ, sed analogicæ, eo quod per modum habitus vitiosi homini lapso inest, atque eundem ad peccandum expeditum & pronum reddit.

V. Quidquid pugnat cum lege Dei, illud est peccatum, 1Io. III, 4. Sed totus homo irregenitus &c. Ergo. Resf. Quidquid formaliter & per se pugnat cum lege Dei, illud est peccatum: concedo. At totus homo non formaliter & per se, quatenus est homo, pugnat cum lege Dei, sed quatenus peccato corruptus est, adeoque per accidens pugnat cum lege Dei. Nimirum homo est subiectum τῆς ἀνομίας, non ipsa ἀνομία.

VI. Si peccatum originale non est substantia hominis, Christus non potest dici peccatum: At Christus dicitur peccatum: Ergo. Consequ. maior, probatur: quia Christus induendo humanam naturam, induit peccatum, *2 Cor. V, 21*. Resf. neg. consequ. maioris; quia Christus humanam naturam induit per vnionem personalem, sine inhærente peccato; at nostra peccata in se transtulit imputative.

VII. P. LVTHERVS peccatum originale vocauit peccatum naturæ, peccatum personæ, peccatum substantiale, aut essentiale. Ergo, censente hoc ecclesiæ doctore eximio, peccatum originale ad ipsam essentiam hominis pertinet. Resf. Locutiones Lutheri non ἁπλῶς, siue absolute, sed συγκριτικῶς, siue comparate, habito respectu ad peccata actualia, intelligendæ sunt. Nimirum B. Lutherus illis loquendi formulis vsus est, vt ostenderet discrimen inter peccatum originale & actuale, & peccatum originale vocauit peccatum naturæ, personæ, essentiale, non quasi sit essentiale constitutivum, aut consecutivum naturæ humanæ, sed quia 1) eandem cum natura, essentia, & persona hominis habet originem, adeoque ipsi σύμφυτον, aut connatum est; sicut illi, qui ex natiuitate cæcus est, cæcitas dicitur naturalis: 2) quia naturae humanae intime inhaeret, eandem totam infecit, atque adeo subiective naturale est: 3) quia transitiue naturale est, propterea, quod ab homine per naturalem generationem ad posteros propagatur.


### Quaest. XIX. Is original sin the substance of man?: Q. XX

Q. XX.

What are the effects of original sin? The effects, or consequences, of original sin are: internal and external actual sins, the defect of free will in spiritual matters, and its infirmity in natural matters , the privation of grace and the wrath of God opposed to this , temporal death and the diseases preceding it, and the various miseries of this life , and finally eternal condemnation .

Proof a. The royal prophet, imploring from the most merciful God the remission of the sins he had committed, indicates that the source of these is original sin by lamenting, Ps. 51:7: Behold! I was formed in iniquity: and in sin did my mother conceive me. The apostle supports this, complaining, Rom. 7:17: Now then it is no more I that do it (evil), but sin that dwelleth in me. Therefore, all the first and involuntary motions of depraved concupiscence, as well as all external sins, are the evil fruits of original sin as the root.

Proof b. 1 Cor. 2:14: The natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him, neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned. The apostle teaches that such darkness has been induced upon the human intellect by original sin that it can neither apprehend things that are merely spiritual, unless it be divinely illuminated, nor rightly represent them to the will, which in itself is a blind power. Hence it happens that the intellect passes rash and false judgments concerning the mysteries of faith, while the will turns away from spiritual goods and is converted to temporal, perishable, and carnal goods.

Proof c. From Eph. 2:3: We were by nature the children of wrath, even as others. An unconverted and unregenerate man exists in a state of wrath, from birth. Therefore, because of congenital sin, he is both devoid of grace and liable to the wrath of God.

Proof d. Whatever comes under the name of death, God threatened to man for sin. Gen. 2:17. Therefore, the reatus (guilt) of spiritual, bodily, and eternal death followed original sin. The precursors of temporal death are diseases, and the companions are the various miseries of this life, which God, the hater and avenger of sin, denounced to Eve, seduced by the serpent, and to the fallen Adam, Gen. 3:16, 17. Proof e.

By the sin of one, (the result) proceeds unto all men to κατακριμα, to condemnation, Rom. 5:18. Adam’s first sin, from which original sin was derived, is the meritorious cause of the universal condemnation of men, which, however, the regenerate decline, embracing the satisfaction of the sponsor Christ by true faith.

Latin:

Quaest. XX. Quinam sunt effectus peccati originalis?

Effectus, siue consequentia peccati originalis sunt; peccata actualia interna, et externa , defectus liberi arbitrii in spiritualibus, et infirmitas eius in naturalibus , priuatio gratiae et huic opposita ira Dei , mors temporalis et hanc antecedentes morbi, variaeque huius vitae aerumnae , aeternaque tandem condemnatio .

Prob. a. Propheta regius efflagitans a Deo misericordissimo remissionem peccatorum, quae commiserat, horum fontem esse peccatum originis indicat ingemiscendo, Ps. LI, 7. Ecce! in iniquitate formatus sum: et in peccato calefecit me mater mea. Suffragatur apostolus conquerens. Rom. VII, 17. Iam vero non amplius ego operor illud (malum), sed habitans in me peccatum. Omnes itaque motus primi atque inuoluntarii concupiscentiae prauae, nec non omnia peccata externa sunt mali fructus peccati originalis velut radicis.

Prob. b. 1 Cor. II, 14. Animalis homo non suscipit ea, quae sunt Spiritus Dei: stultitia enim illi sunt, et non potest scire, quia spiritualiter diiudicantur. Docet apostolus, peccato originali intellectui humano eam inductam esse caliginem, ut neque res mere spirituales, nisi diuinitus illuminetur, apprehendere, neque easdem voluntati, quae in se potentia caeca est, recte repraesentare queat. Inde fit, ut intellectus temeraria et falsa de mysteriis fidei ferat iudicia, voluntas autem a bonis spiritualibus auertatur, et ad bona temporalia caduca et carnalia conuertatur.

Prob. c. Ex Eph. II, 3. Eramus filii irae natura, sicut et reliqui. Homo inconuersus et irregenitus versatur in statu irae, inde a natiuitate. Ergo ob congenitum peccatum et gratiae expers, et irae Dei obnoxius est.

Prob. d. Quidquid nomine mortis venit, Deus homini peccati interminatus est. Gen. II, 17. Secutus ergo est peccatum originis reatus mortis spiritualis, corporalis et aeternae. Prodromi mortis temporalis sunt morbi, comitesque huius vitae variae aerumnae, quas Deus peccati osor et vltor Euae, a serpente seductae, ac Adamo lapso denuntiauit, Gen. III, 16. 17.

Prob. e. Per unius peccatum in omnes homines eis κατακριμα, in condemnationem, (res procedit), Rom. V, 18. Adami peccatum primum, ex quo peccatum originale derivatum est, causa meritoria est vniuersalis hominum condemnationis, quam tamen declinant renati, satisfactionem sponsoris Christi vera fide amplectentes.


### Q. XXI

What are the affections, or properties, of original sin? The affections of original sin are: propagability , and persistent adhesion extended until the end of life .

Proof a. That which is born of the flesh is flesh. He who is born of parents infected with original contagion is a participant in the same plague, and thus in need of regeneration if he is to enter into the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven.

Proof b. Regenerate parents do not propagate original sin; because they have been washed of it. 1 Cor. 6:11. Resp. As a learned father (begets) an unlearned son: so the regenerate generates the unregenerate, which still draws its oldness among the children of the world, not from that which he has promoted into newness among the children of God, as AUGUSTINE says, De peccat. merit. et remiss., Book II, ch. 9. Proof c.

Original sin is αμαρτια ευπεριστατος, the sin which doth so easily beset us, Heb. 12:1. It is called besetting; because it adheres to us most tenaciously, it surrounds us on all sides and embraces like a garment, which delays the runner; which the reborn never completely put off or cast away, although, aided by the Holy Spirit, they resist its motions, and diminish the powers of the same through the exercises of piety, and thus far are said to put it off.

Latin:

Affectiones peccati originalis sunt: propagabilitas , et inhaesio pertinax vsque ad finem vitae protensa .

Prob. a. Quod natum est e carne, caro est. Qui ex parentibus, contagio originali infectis, nascitur, eiusdem luis est particeps, adeoque indigus regenerationis, si hereditatem regni caelestis aditurus fit.

Prob. b. Parentes renati non propagant peccatum originis; quia eodem abluti sunt. 1 Cor. VI, 11. Resp. Vt pater doctus filium indoctum: ita regenitus irregenitum generat quod adhuc vetustatem trahit inter filios saeculi, non ex hoc, quod in nouitatem promouit inter filios Dei, dicente AVGVSTINO I. II. de peccat. merit. et remiss. cap. 9. Prob. c.

Peccatum originale est αμαρτια ευπεριστατος, peccatum circumstans, Hebr. XII, 1. Dicitur circumstans; quia tenacissime nobis adhaeret, nos vndique circumcingit et complectitur instar vestis, quae curforem remoratur; quod nunquam renati penitus deponunt aut exuunt, licet adiuti a Spiritu S. illius motibus obsistant, viresque eiusdem per exercitia pietatis imminuant, & hactenus illud deponere dicantur.


### Q. XXII. Is depraved concupiscence in justified and renewed men a sin in the true sense of the word?

Depraved original concupiscence, together with the first inordinate motions by which it exerts itself, is truly and properly called sin.

Obj. The question is not about natural and indifferent concupiscence; such as is the appetite for food, drink, sleep: nor about spiritual concupiscence, desiring a supernatural good, which is proper to the reborn, who with David desire to see God Ps. XLII, 1. but about depraved concupiscence, which is either original or actual. Actual concupiscence is either mortal, which is joined with consent, delight, and the prosecution of that thing to which the flesh stimulates us; or venial, which denotes the first motions of the soul soliciting us to sins, which we repress through the Holy Spirit, lest they break forth into an external act . Original concupiscence is a habitual inclination to evil, exerting itself in inordinate motions. The question is, whether original concupiscence, depraving the intellect, the will, and the sensitive appetite, together with the first inordinate motions in justified and renewed men, is truly and properly considered and called sin? To which question we answer in the affirmative.

Prob. 1) All ἀνομία, or lawlessness, is sin properly so called: But all depraved concupiscence is ἀνομία: Therefore. The minor is proved from the assertion of the apostle, Rom. VII, 7. I had not known sin, except through the law. For I had not even known concupiscence (to be sin), unless the law had said: thou shalt not covet, Exod. XX, 17. By which divine prohibition all depraved concupiscence, as much original as actual, is forbidden.

You say: By the divine precept, not involuntary, but deliberate and voluntary concupiscence is forbidden; which is evident 1) from the Hebrew word חמד, which word does not signify to have concupiscence, which is a vice of our nature, but simply to covet and desire. 2) This precept is not given to brutes, not to children, but to an intelligent creature, using reason and free will, who alone is capable of the law, and alone can fulfill or transgress the law. But involuntary motions are no more human acts, or in the power of man, than they are in the power of a lion, a dog, or a horse. Just as, therefore, it cannot be commanded to a lion that he not be angry; to a dog, that he not snarl; to a horse, that he not neigh: so neither to a man, that he not feel the first motions of concupiscence; and he who would punish them would be a tyrant.

Resp. 1) By the divine precept all illicit concupiscence is forbidden, since it is limited by no restriction. But when Paul says that he had not known concupiscence to be sin, unless the law had said: thou shalt not covet; he refers especially to indeliberate and involuntary concupiscence; since he could not have known it to be sin, except from the decalogue law; but that voluntary desires are sins, the sounder gentiles acknowledged from the unwritten natural law. 2) Although it cannot be proven from the word חמד that involuntary concupiscence is prohibited, it can nevertheless be shown from the words לֹא תַחְמֹד, that you should not cause yourself to covet. 3) There is a huge difference between a man, to whom a law is prescribed, and a beast, to whom no law is set; although after the fall man cannot perfectly perform the law. What? That even in a beast, savage ferocity is restrained without tyranny; whereby it happens that, mindful of blows, it unlearns its ferocity.

2) Paul calls concupiscence, remaining in the reborn, sin more than once explicitly, Rom. VII, 7. 8. 9. 11. 12. 13. 17. 20. 23. 25. Compare Rom. VI, 6. 12. 13. 14. Rom. VIII, 5. 10.

You say: Concupiscence is called sin by metonymy; because it is the cause of sin, if it is obeyed. I respond: Concupiscence is properly and formally called sin, since no necessity compels us to depart from the proper meaning of the word, especially because chapter VII of Romans is the proper seat of this doctrine. Indeed, Holy Scripture does not speak tropically about articles of faith in their proper seat, or at least it indicates and declares the trope. Furthermore, if concupiscence is the cause of sin, it is certainly sin itself. Therefore, Paul calls concupiscence something not good, but evil, Rom. VII, 19. But everything morally evil is sin.

3) The effects of depraved concupiscence are: to render the reborn man partly carnal, to sell him under sin, to work evil, to fight against the law of the mind, and to make man a captive under the law of sin, and thus before the face of God most miserable, Rom. VII, 14. 20. 23. 24. to lust against the spirit, Gal. V, 17. to merit eternal damnation, Rom. II, 13.

You say: Paul in Rom. VII does not speak of himself as a reborn man, but puts on and sustains the person of an unregenerate man constituted under the law, not yet endowed with the Spirit of Christ; which is proven from this, because to the carnal man described in Rom. VII, 14, those predicates are vindicated which can be attributed to no reborn person, let alone to the most enlightened Paul. For he is said a) to be sold under sin, v. 14. But the reborn is freed from sin, Rom. VI, 18. b) Captivated by the law of sin, from which the reborn is likewise freed, Rom. VIII, 2. c) Serving the law of sin with the flesh, v. 25. But the reborn is a servant of righteousness, Rom. VI, 18. d) He is said to do what he does not want, and not to do what he wants, v. 20. But the reborn has the Holy Spirit and with Him the freedom of acting, 1 Cor. III, 17. I respond: א) Generally. In the seventh chapter to the Romans from verse 14 to the end, Paul is immediately understood, and consequently any reborn man; which is proven 1) because the apostle likewise speaks of himself in the present tense: I want, I hate, I do, I consent, I give thanks: He expresses the state under Pharisaism and the law using words designating the past tense in v. 9. I was living without the law formerly, i.e., without a true understanding of the law. 2) The man described in the aforementioned place wants the good, v. 18, and does not work the evil, v. 15. But the unregenerate does not want the spiritual good; because he is dead in sins, Eph. II, 1, and is a rotten tree producing bad fruits, Matt. VII, 17. 3) The man designated there consents to and serves the divine law, v. 23. 25. The unregenerate cannot be subject to the law, Rom. VIII, 7. 4) The man delineated by the apostle consents to the law according to the inner man, v. 22. The inner man is renewed. Compare 2 Cor. IV, 10. Eph. IV, 24. Col. III, 9. 5) There is given in the man described here a struggle of the flesh and the spirit, v. 23. 25. But the struggle of the flesh and the spirit is given in the renewed man, in whom the Holy Spirit dwells, Gal. V, 17. 6) The man who is introduced in this place gives thanks to God through our Lord Jesus Christ for the begun liberation from sin; although this liberation has not yet attained its completion in this life, v. 25. But the man freed from sin, and by that name giving thanks to God through Christ, is truly reborn, not constituted under the law, but under the grace of Christ. I respond: ב) Specifically to a): Paul says he is carnal not entirely, but from part: not simply & absolutely, but in a certain respect & comparatively; insofar as he had the oldness of the flesh, and was hindered by this, so that he could not fulfill the law, which is spiritual, and requires spiritual and perfect obedience, according to the plumb-line. Likewise, he also says that he is sold under sin, not as if he were sold to the full obedience of a predominating sin, like King Ahab, 1 Kings XXI, 20, but because of the force, endeavor, and sense of original concupiscence; because he felt the impulses and goads of concupiscence, which, against his will, snatched him away from the good and endeavored to enslave him to sin, although they could not bring it to effect; because, aided by the Holy Spirit, he repressed these impulses and goads of concupiscence, which were seeking dominion, and shook off the yoke. To b) Distinguish between voluntary and involuntary captivity. The unregenerate deliver themselves of their own accord to be bound by the chains of sin; but the regenerate groans and complains that, being bound by the chains of innate depraved concupiscence, he is carried away, like Samson’s captivity, to do that which he does not will with a joyful spirit. To c) The Apostle serves the law of God with an enlightened mind; but he serves the law of sin with the flesh, i.e., insofar as he is infected by the stain of indwelling sin, not by spontaneous but by involuntary servitude. To d) Distinguish between freedom from the dominion and from the sense of sin. Although the renewed man has been freed from the dominion of sin, he is not yet immune from the sense and root of sin. Hence it happens that, although the regenerate wish to do good eagerly and readily, yet, when concupiscence grows strong, they cannot perform it.

4) There is in the regenerate not only concupiscence συλλαβοῦσα, conceiving, i.e., joined with the deliberate consent of the will, but also ἐξέλκουσα καὶ δελεάζουσα, drawing away and enticing, even if consent does not follow, James I, 14. Wherefore even the first inordinate motions are sins, since they are the external causes of sin. But the cause of sin is either the sinning person, or sin, bringing forth other transgressions from itself.

5) That concupiscence, which remains in the regenerate after baptism, is truly sin, AUGUSTINE demonstrates in tract. XLI on John, from Rom. VI, 12. The apostle says: Let not sin reign in your mortal body to obey its desires, neither present your members as weapons of iniquity to sin. He does not say: let it not be; but: let it not reign. As long as you live, sin must necessarily be in your members, at least let its kingdom be taken away, so that what it commands may not be done.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, who deny that concupiscence remaining in the regenerate after baptism, with first-first motions without the involuntary, is sin in the true sense; their stronger arguments are: I. Concupiscence is distinguished from sin, as cause from effect, as St. James testifies, Ep. ch. I, 15. E. Concupiscence is not sin properly so called. Resp. Distinguish between sin begetting and begotten. Concupiscence is indeed not begotten sin, i.e., consummated in act and work, yet it is begetting sin, i.e., original. Just as it is not permitted to conclude: The father begets a man: Therefore the father is not a man; so it is wicked to infer: Concupiscence begets sin: Therefore concupiscence is not sin, since the contrary is true, namely, that the mother and the offspring are of the same nature.

II. Whatever is not in our power, God does not bind us to by His precept: To avoid the first motions of concupiscence is not in our power: E. God does not bind us to avoid the first motions of concupiscence. The major premise is evident; because everyone who commands impossibilities is unjust. The minor is clear; because after the fall of the first man, inordinate motions do not depend on the deliberation of man, but flow spontaneously from original concupiscence. Resp. We deny the major. To the proof we say that everyone who commands impossibilities that are simply & in every state impossible becomes unjust. But one who commands impossibilities whose performance has been made impossible by the fault of the offender is not unjust. Thus that king, Matth. XVIII, 24, having demanded from his debtor servant ten thousand talents, which he was not able to pay. God most justly which he was not able to pay.

demands from drunkards, who by their own fault have lost their memory, the light of faith, and the ability to pray devoutly, vigilance, faith, and the ardor of prayer. If only that which is in our power is forbidden by divine law, original sin will be prohibited by no precept, and thus will not be sin properly so-called.

Latin:

Concupiscentia originalis prava, una cum primis motibus inordinatis, quibus se exserit, vere & proprie dictum peccatum est. Obs.

Non quaeritur de concupiscentia naturali & indifferente; qualis est appetitus cibi, potus, somni: neque de concupiscentia spirituali, bonum supernaturale appetente, quae est propria renatorum, qui cum Dauide Deum videre desiderant Ps. XLII, 1. sed de concupiscentia prava, quae vel originalis, vel actualis est. Concupiscentia actualis est vel mortalis, quae coniuncta est cum consensu, delectatione, & prosecutione eius rei, ad quam caro nos exstimulat; vel venialis, quae notat primos animae motus ad peccata nos sollicitantes, quos per Spiritum S. reprimimus, ne in externum proruinpant actum . Concupiscentia originalis est habitualis inclinatio ad malum, inordinatis motibus se exserens. Quaestio est, an concupiscentia originalis intellectum, voluntatem & appetitum sensitivum deprauans, una cum primis motibus inordinatis in hominibus iustificatis & renovatis, vere & proprie censeatur dicatur peccatum? Ad quam quaestionem nos affirmative respondemus.

Prob. 1) Omnis ἀνομία, sive dislegalitas, est peccatum proprie dictum: Atqui omnis concupiscentia prava est ἀνομία: E. Minor prob. ab affeueratione apostoli, Rom. VII, 7. Peccatum non nouissem, nisi per legem. Nam etiam concupiscentiae (peccatum esse) non noueram, nisi lex dixisset: non concupisces, Exod. XX, 17. Quo interdicto diuino omnis concupiscentia praua tam originalis, quam actualis prohibetur.

Dicis: Praecepto diuino prohibetur non concupiscentia inuoluntaria, sed deliberata & voluntaria; quod patet 1) ex verbo Hebr. חמד, quae vox non significat habere concupiscentiam, quae naturae nostrae vitium est, sed nude appetere & desiderare. 2) Hoc praeceptum non datur brutis, non pueris, sed creaturae intelligenti, ratione & libera voluntate utenti, quae sola legis est capax, solaque potest legem implere vel transgredi. At motus inuoluntarii non magis sunt humani actus, aut in potestate hominis, quam sunt in potestate leonis, canis, equi. Sicut ergo leoni imperari nequit, ne irascatur; cani, ne ringatur; equo ne adhinniat: sic nec homini, ne primos concupiscentiae motus sentiat; & qui eos puniret, tyrannus esset.

Resp. 1) Praecepto diuino omnis concupiscentia illicita vetatur, cum nulla restrictione limitetur. Quando autem Paullus dicit, se, concupiscentiam esse peccatum, non nouisse, nisi lex dixisset: non concupisces; respicit potissimum concupiscentiam indeliberatam & inuoluntariam; quippe quam peccatum esse, non poterat, nisi ex lege decalogica, cognoscere; at cupiditates voluntarias esse peccata, ex lege naturali non scripta saniores ores agnouerunt gentiles. 2) Etsi ex verbo חמד, probari nequeat, prohibitam esse concupiscentiam inuoluntariam, ostendi tamen potest ex verbis לֹא תַחְמֹד, ne facias te concupiscere. 3) Ingens discrimen est inter hominem, cui lex est præscripta & inter bestiam, cui nulla lex est posita; quamuis post lapsum homo legem perfecte præstare nequeat. Quid? quod etiam in bestia sine tyrannide coërceatur ferocia immanis; quo fit, vt verberum memor ferociam desuescat.

2) Paullus concupiscentiam, in renatis residuam, plus vice simplici diserte peccatum appellat Rom. VII, 7. 8. 9. 11. 12. 13. 17. 20. 23. 25. Conf. Rom. VI, 6. 12. 13. 14. Rom. VIII, 5. 10.

Dicis: Concupiscentia dicitur peccatum per metonymiam; quia est caussa peccati, si ei obediatur. Resp. Concupiscentia proprie & formaliter vocatur peccatum, siquidem nulla necessitas nos cogit, vt a propria vocabuli significatione recedamus, in primis quia c. VII. Rom. propria sedes est huius doctrinæ. Sane scriptura S. de articulis fidei in sede propria non loquitur tropice, aut certe tropum innuit & declarat. Ceterum si concupiscentia est caussa peccati, vtique ipsa peccatum est. Propterea Paullus concupiscentiam vocat aliquid non bonum, sed malum, Rom. VII, 19. At omne moraliter malum est peccatum.

3) Effecta concupiscentiæ prauæ sunt: reddere hominem renatum ex parte carnalem, venundare ipsum sub peccatum, operari malum, repugnare legi mentis, & facere hominem captiuum sub lege peccati, adeoque coram facie Dei longe miserrimum, Rom. VII, 14. 20. 23. 24. concupiscere aduersus spiritum, Gal. V, 17. mereri damnationem æternam, Rom. II, 13.

Dicis: Paullus Rom. VII, non loquitur de se vt homine renato, sed induit ac sustinet personam hominis irregeniti sub lege constituti, necdum spiritu Christi præditi; quod probatur exinde, quia homini carnali Rom. VII, 14. descripto ea vindicantur prædicata, quæ nulli renato, nedum Paullo illuminatissimo, attribui possunt. Dicitur enim a) venundatus sub peccatum, v. 14. Sed renatus liberatus est a peccato, Rom. VI, 18. b) Captivatus lege peccati, qua renatus itidem liberatus est, Rom. VIII, 2. c) Carne feruiens legi peccati, v. 25. Sed renatus est seruus iustitiæ, Rom. VI, 18. d) Dicitur facere, quæ non vult, & non facere, quæ vult, v. 20. Sed renatus habet Spiritum S. & cum eo libertatem agendi, 1 Cor. III, 17. Resp. א) Generatim. Capite septimo ad Romanos a versu 14. vsque ad finem immediate Paullus, consequenter quilibet homo renatus intelligitur; quod probatur 1) quia itidem apostolus loquitur de se in tempore præsenti: Ego volo, odi, facio, consentio, gratias ago: Statum sub Pharisaismo & lege verbis tempus præteritum designantibus exprimit v. 9. Ego viuebam sine lege olim, i. e. sine vero legis intellectu. 2) Homo l. c. descriptus vult bonum, v. 18. & non operatur malum, v. 15. At irregenitus non vult bonum spirituale; quia in peccatis est mortuus, Eph. II, 1. & est putris arbor fructus malos faciens, Matth. VII, 17. 3) Homo, isthic designatus, legi diuinæ consentit & seruit v. 23. 25. Irregenitus legi subdi non potest, Rom. VIII, 7. 4) Consentit homo, ab apostolo delineatus, legi secundum hominem internum, v. 22. Internus homo est renouatus. Conf. 2 Cor. IV, 10. Eph. IV, 24. Col. III, 9. 5) Datur in homine, hic descripto, lucta carnis & spiritus v. 23. 25. Sed lucta carnis & spiritus datur in homine renouato, in quo Spiritus S. habitat, Gal. V, 17. 6) Homo, qui hoc loco introducitur, Deo gratias agit per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum pro inchoata liberatione a peccato; quamuis hæc liberatio complementum suum in hac vita nondum consecuta sit, v. 25. At homo a peccato liberatus, & eo nomine Deo per Christum gratias agens, vere renatus est, non sub lege, sed sub gratia Christi constitutus. Resp. ב) Speciatim ad a): Paullus dicit, se esse carnalem non ex toto, sed ex parte: non simpliciter & absolute, sed certo respectu & comparate; quatenus habebat vetustatem carnis, & hac impediebatur, quo minus legem, quæ spiritualis est, spiritualemque & perfectam obedientiam requirit, ex amussi impleret. Pariter quoque dicit, se esse venundatum sub peccatum, non quasi venditus sit ad plenum obsequium peccati prædominantis, instar Regis Achabi, 1 Reg. XXI, 20. sed ob vim, conatum & sensum concupiscentiæ originalis; propterea, quod impetus stimulosque concupiscentiæ sentiebat, qui ipsum invitum, a bono abreptum, peccato mancipare conabantur, licet id effectum dare non possent; quia adiutus a Spiritu S. hos impetus stimulosque concupiscentiæ, dominium affectantis, reprimebat & iugum excutiebat. Ad b) Dist. inter captivitatem voluntariam & involuntariam. Irregeniti sponte sua vinculis peccati se constringendos tradunt; at renatus ingemiscit & conqueritur, quod vinculis innatæ concupiscentiæ pravæ constrictus, Samsonis captivitati instar, rapiatur ad faciendum id, quod læto animo non vult. Ad c) Apostolus servit mente illuminata legi Dei; servit autem carne, i. e. quatenus labe inhærentis peccati infectus est, legi peccati non servitute spontanea sed involuntaria. Ad d) Dist. inter libertatem a dominio, & a sensu peccati. Quamvis homo renovatus liberatus sit a dominio peccati, non tamen a sensu & radice peccati immunis est. Inde fit, ut, licet renati bonum alacriter & expedite facere velint, inualescente tamen concupiscentiæ, perficere nequeant.

4) Datur in renatis non tantum concupiscentia συλλαβοῦσα, concipiens, i. e. cum deliberato voluntatis consensu conjuncta, sed etiam ἐξέλκουσα καὶ δελεάζουσα, abstrahens & inescans, licet consensus non accedat, Iac. I, 14. Quare & primi inordinati motus peccata sunt, cum sint peccati externi causæ. At causa peccati aut est persona peccans, aut peccatum, alia ex se delicta pariens.

5) Concupiscentiam, quæ post baptismum in renatis superest, vere peccatum esse, demonstrat AVGVSTIN. tract. XLI. in Ioan. ex Rom. VI, 12. Ait apostolus: Non regnet peccatum in vestro mortali corpore ad obediendum desideriis eius, neque exhibeatis membra vestra arma iniquitatis peccato. Non ait: non fit; sed: non regnet. Quamdiu viuis, peccate necesse est esse in membris tuis, saltem illi regnum auferatur, ne fiat, quod iubet.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, negantium, concupiscentiam in renatis, post baptismum residuam, cum motibus primo primis, sine involuntariis esse veri nominis peccatum; quorum potiora sunt argumenta: I. Concupiscentia distinguitur a peccato, vt causa ab effectu, teste S. Iacobo, Ep. c. I, 15. E. Concupiscentia non est peccatum proprie dictum. Resp. Dist. inter peccatum gignens, & genitum. Concupiscentia non est quidem peccatum genitum, i. e. actu & opere consummatum, est tamen peccatum gignens, i. e. originale. Sicut concludere non licet: Pater generat hominem: Ergo Pater non est homo; ita colligere nefas est: Concupiscentia gignit peccatum: Ergo concupiscentia non est peccatum, cum contrarium verum sit, nempe matrem & prolem esse eiusdem naturæ.

II. Quidquid non est in nostra potestate, ad illud Deus nos præcepto suo non obligat: Euitare primos concupiscentiæ motus, non est in nostra potestate: E. ad euitandos primos concupiscentiæ motus Deus nos non obligat. Maior constat; quia omnis imperans impossibilia, iniustus est. Minor liquet; quia post lapsum primi hominis motus inordinati non pendent a deliberatione hominis, sed sponte fluunt a concupiscentia originali. Resp. Neg. maior. Ad probationem dicimus, quod omnis imperans impossibilia, quæ simpliciter & in omni statu sunt impossibilia, iniustus fit. At imperans impossibilia, quorum præstatio ex culpa delinquentis facta est impossibilis, non est iniustus. Sic rex ille Matth. XVIII, 24. postulato a seruo debitore decem millia talentorum, quibus ille soluendis non erat. Deus iustissime folvendis non erat.

postulat ab ebriosis, qui propria culpa memoriam, lumen fidei, facultatem deuote precandi perdiderunt, vigilantiam, fidem, precum ardorem. Si id tantum lege diuina interdicitur, quod in nostra est potestate, peccatum originis nullo prohibebitur praecepto, adeoque non erit peccatum proprie dictum.


### Q. XXII. Is depraved concupiscence in justified and renewed men a sin in the true sense of the word?: III. Sin is taken away by baptism E. In the baptized and regenerate there is no remaining sin

III. Sin is taken away by baptism E. In the baptized and regenerate there is no remaining sin.

The antecedent is evident from Eph. V, 26, where we are said to be sanctified and cleansed by the washing of water in the word.

Resp. Sin is taken away in baptism, not so that it does not exist, but so that it does not harm, or is not imputed. The guilt is taken away in baptism, as is the dominion of concupiscence, not concupiscence itself. Instance If inordinate concupiscence, remaining after baptism, is sin in the true sense, it certainly induces guilt, because guilt is inseparable from sin.

Resp. Guilt is taken away not from the sin, but from the person sinning and repenting, through justifying grace.

IV. God either hates remaining sin, or He does not. If the latter; it is not sin: If the former; it has not been remitted.

Resp. God hates sin, because it is ἀνομία (lawlessness); but He does not always hate the person sinning, on account of the merit of Christ, apprehended by true faith: Just as a father hates the vices in his son, but does not hate the son himself.

V. If in a justified man there were remaining concupiscence which is truly considered and called sin, it would certainly be something damnable in him: but there is nothing damnable in a justified man: E.

The consequence of the major is evident; because every sin, by itself and by its own nature, is mortal and damnable. The antecedent is clear from Rom. VIII, 1. There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.

Resp. Condemnation is one thing, that which is damnable is another. The former is the act of the condemning judge.

Conf. Rom. V, 16. 1 Tim. V, 12. The latter is the fault of a man transgressing the law, which by itself deserves condemnation. The apostle does not say there is nothing damnable, but that there is no condemnation in the regenerate. Although there is concupiscence in them, damnable by its nature; yet they undergo no condemnation, Christ delivering His regenerate and elect from the guilt of sin, so that it loses the power to condemn them, and by His Spirit blunting and restraining sin so that it may not rule.

Sin, after regeneration, is therefore like wasps, which, having lost their sting, cannot sting, even if they buzz loudly.

VI. Christ so sanctifies and cleanses the church That He might make it glorious to Himself, not having spot or wrinkle, Eph.

V, 26. If the church is so sanctified and cleansed through baptism that it becomes glorious and splendid, without spot or wrinkle, it is devoid of all sin after baptism.

Resp. Christ sanctifies and cleanses the church in this age through baptism, partly by justifying it, partly by renewing it. Through justifying grace, the church receives the perfect remission of sins. Renewal is not completed in this life, but is begun, and continued from day to day. However, the exhibition or presentation of the church without spot or wrinkle will take place not in this, but in the future life; namely, at the marriage of the future age, Rev. XIX, 7. 8. which interpretation AUGUSTINE confirms in book I. retract. c. 7. Since the whole church says: Forgive us our debts, it is certainly not here without spot or wrinkle, or anything of the kind: yet from that which it receives here, it is led to that glory, which is not here, and to perfection. Confer D. CALOVIUS, bibl. illustr. in h. l. fol. 724.

Latin:

III. Peccatum tollitur per baptismum E. in baptizatis & renatis nullum residuum est peccatum.

Antecedens patet ex Eph. V, 26. vbi dicimur sanctificati & mundati lauacro aquae in verbo.

Resp. Tollitur peccatum in baptismo, non vt non sit, sed vt non obsit, aut non imputetur. Tollitur in baptismo reatus, vt & dominium concupiscentiae, non concupiscentia ipsa. Instantia Si concupiscentia inordinata, post baptismum residua, veri nominis peccatum est, vtique reatum inducit, propterea, quod reatus a peccato inseparabilis est.

Resp. Tollitur reatus non a peccato, sed a persona peccante & resipiscente, per gratiam iustificantem.

IV. Deus peccatum residuum vel odit, vel non odit Si hoc; peccatum non est: Si illud; remissum non est.

Resp. Odit Deus peccatum, quia est ἀνομία; at non semper odit personam peccantem, ob meritum Christi, vera fide apprehensum: Sicut pater odit vitia in filio, sed non odit ipsum filium.
