V. Si in homine iustificato residua esset concupiscentia Quae vere censetur & dicitur peccatum, vtique aliquid damnabile esset in eodem: sed nihil damnabile est in homine iustificato: E.

Consequentia maioris patet; quia omne peccatum, per se & natura sua, est mortale atque damnabile. Antecedens liquet e Rom. VIII, 1. Nihil nunc condemnationis est in iis, qui sunt in Christo Iesu.

Resp. Aliud est condemnatio, aliud condemnabile. Illa est actus iudicis condemnantis.

Conf. Rom. V, 16. 1 Tim. V, 12. Hoc est culpa hominis legem transgredientis, quae condemnationem per se meretur. Non dicit apostolus, nihil condemnabile, sed nihil condemnationis esse in renatis. Quamuis in his fit concupiscentia, natura sua damnabilis; nullam tamen condemnationem subeunt, liberante Christo renatos & electos suos a reatu peccati, vt vim eosdem condemnandi amittat, & per Spiritum suum peccatum, ne dominetur, retundente atque cohibente.

Est itaque peccatum, post regenerationem, instar vesparum, quae amisso aculeo pungere nequeunt, etiamsi multum obstrepant.

VI. Christus ita sanctificat & mundat ecclesiam Vt fiat eam sibi gloriosam, non habentem maculam aut rugam, Eph.

V, 26. Si ecclesia per baptismum ita sanctificatur & mundatur, vt fit gloriosa ac splendida, fine macula ac ruga, illa post baptismum omnis peccati expers est.

Resp. Christus ecclesiam sanctificat & mundat in hoc saeculo per baptismum, eam partim iustificando, partim renouando. Per gratiam iustificantem accipit ecclesia perfectam remissionem peccatorum. Renouatio in hac vita non perficitur, sed inchoatur, & de die in diem continuatur. Exhibitio autem siue praesentatio ecclesiae sine macula & ruga fiet non in hac, sed futura vita; nempe in futuri saeculi nuptiis, Apoc. XIX, 7. 8. quam interpretationem confirmat AVGVSTINVS libr. I. retract. c. 7. Cum tota dicat ecclesia: Dimitte nobis debita nostra, non vtique hic est fine macula & ruga, aut aliquo eiusmodi: ex eo tamen quod hic accipit, ad illam gloriam, quae hic non est, perfectionemque perducitur. Confer. D. CALOVII bibl. illustr. in h. l. fol. 724.


### Quest. XXIII. What happens to original sin?

It happens to original sin that in some men it reigns, in others it does not reign . It reigns in those who promptly obey its irritations: it does not reign in those who place an obstacle to its depraved habits and suggestions .

a. Let not sin reign in your mortal body, that you should obey it in its lusts, Rom. VI, 12. The apostle does not say: let it not be: because during this life it cannot be extirpated: but let it not reign, i.e., resist sin, dwelling in your mortal body, lest it exercise its power and obtain supreme dominion. Wherefore do not comply with its inordinate motions, soliciting you to great sins, but repress and restrain them.

Prob. b. Sin shall not have dominion over you; for you are not under the law, but under grace. Rom. VI, 14. Whoever are reborn, justified, and renewed by the grace of the Holy Spirit, they are neither under the coercion of the law, in that they obey the divine will with a joyful and free spirit: nor do they perform the things commanded by original sin; for they overcome its incitements by faith, so that it cannot reign, although it may occasionally affect dominion.

Obf. Otherwise, reigning sins are also called actual sins repeated by frequent actions, which are not diminished by the unregenerate, but are committed more often, grow strong, flourish, and stimulate to other sins: those are called non-reigning, whose principles the regenerate oppose, lest they break forth and be consummated by external work.

Latin:

Peccato originali accidit, quod in aliis hominibus regnat, in aliis non regnat . Regnat in illis, qui eius irritationibus prompte obsequuntur: non regnat in illis, qui ipsius prauis moribus & suggestionibus, obicem ponunt . obsequuntur: non regnat in P. O. illis, qui ipsius prauis moribus & suggestionibus, obicem ponunt b).

a. Ne regnato peccatum in mortali vestro corpore, ut obediatis illi in concupiscentiis eius, Rom. VI, 12. Non dicit apostolus: ne esto: quia durante hac vita exstirpari nequit: sed ne regnato, q. d. obsistite peccato, habitanti in mortali vestro corpore, ne vim suam exerceat, summumque dominium obtineat. Quare nolite obtemperare ipsius inordinatis motibus, ad grandia vos peccata sollicitantibus, sed hos reprimite & cohibete.

Prob. b. Peccatum vobis non dominabitur; non enim sub lege estis, sed sub gratia. Rom. VI, 14. Quicunque gratia Spiritus S. sunt renati, iustificati & renouati, illi neque sunt sub coactione legis, eo quod læto liberoque spiritu voluntati diuinæ morem gerunt: neque imperata faciunt peccati originalis; quippe cuius irritamenta fide vincunt, vt regnare nequeat, quamuis dominium subinde affectet.

Obf. Solent ceteroqui peccata regnantia, etiam vocari peccata actualia crebris actionibus repetita, quæ ab irregenitis non imminuuntur, sed fæpius committuntur, inualescunt, vigent, & ad alia peccata estimulant: non regnantia dicuntur, quorum principiis renati obstant, ne foras erumpant, & externo opere consummentur.


### Q. XXIV. What practical use does the doctrine of original sin provide?

Prob. a. LUTHER says gravely, part III, Smalcald articles, art. 1. We must confess, as Paul affirms in Rom. V, that sin originated from one man, Adam, and entered into the world, by whose disobedience all men were made sinners, subject to death and the devil. This is named original, hereditary, principal, and capital sin.

Prob. b. But when the kindness and love of God our Savior toward man appeared, not by works which (were done) in righteousness, which we have done, but according to His mercy He saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Spirit, Tit. III, 4. Through original sin we were made children of wrath: through baptism we are rendered children of grace. By the former we were deformed; by the latter we are renewed. By the former the approach to death; by the latter the door to life is opened.

Prob. c. Let us solicitously beware, lest we loosen the reins to the desires of the flesh. For if we live according to the flesh, we shall die; but if by the spirit we mortify the deeds of the body, we shall live, Rom. XII, 13.

S I G H T.

I humbly acknowledge, O most merciful God! the plague innate to me, the hereditary evil, the most foul leprosy of the soul. I deplore the misery contracted by the fall of our first parents, and I seek Thy mercy, O sweetest Jesus. Thou art the chief physician of my soul, Thou art the avenger and protector of my salvation. Thou didst prepare the medicine for my lethal disease in baptism, and didst confer it upon me once prepared. Thou didst wash away congenital sin, by taking away its power to condemn, and by blunting its impulses and stings, lest they should prostrate me. I give Thee immortal thanks for so great a benefit, and I most ardently pray that Thou wouldst instruct me, languid and infirm, with spiritual strength, whereby I may restrain, repress, and crush the incitements of the flesh, which solicit my mind to sin.

Latin:

Prob. a. Grauiter ait LVTHERVS part. III. artic. Smalcaldic. artic. 1. Confitendum nobis, vt Paulus Rom. V. affirmat, peccatum ab uno homine Adamo ortum esse, & introiisse in mundum, per cuius inobedientiam omnes homines facti sunt peccatores, morti & diabolo obnoxii. Hoc nominatur originale, hereditarium, principale & capitale peccatum.

Prob. b. Quando vero apparuit benignitas & amor hominum seruatoris nostri Dei non ex operibus, quæ (facta) in iustitia, quæ fecimus nos, sed iuxta suam misericordiam saluauit nos per lauacrum regenerationis & renouationis Spiritus sancti, Tit. III, 4. Per peccatum originis facti sumus filii iræ: per baptismum reddimur filii gratiæ. Per illud deformati sumus; per hunc renouamur. Illo aditus ad mortem; hoc ianua ad vitam aperitur.

Prob. c. Sollicite caueamus, ne frena laxemus cupiditatibus carnis. Nam si secundum carnem viuimus, moriemur; si vero spiritu actiones corporis mortificamus, viuemus Rom. XII, 13.

S V S P I R I V M.

Submisse agnosco, o Deus misericordissime! connatam mihi luem, malum hereditarium, lepram animæ fœdissimam. Contractam lapsu primorum parentum deploro miseriam, & tuam, Iesu dulcissime, quæro misericordiam. Tu archiater es animæ meæ, tu affertor es vindex salutis meæ. Tu medicinam lethali meo morbo in baptismo parafti, paratam mihi contulisti. Eluisti peccatum congenitum, vim condemnandi ei adimendo, & impetus stimulosque ipsius, ne me prosternerent, retundendo. Gratias pro tanto beneficio ago tibi immortales, & ardentissime precor, vt me languentem atque infirmum viribus spiritualibus instruas, quo irritamenta carnis, quæ ad peccandum animum meum sollicitant, cohibeam, reprimam, elidam.


## 14 On Actual Sin


### I. What is actual sin?

Actual sin is the deflection of a human act from the rule of divine law.

It is defined more fully: Actual sin is the deflection of a human act committed, or omitted, from the rule of divine law, bringing with it the guilt of fault and punishment.

Proof. Sin is defined generally by ἀνομία [lawlessness], or deflection from the law, 1 John 3:4. Which ἀνομία is either original or actual. Therefore, actual sin differs from original in this very point, that the former is a second act, the latter is a habit inclining and soliciting toward evil.

Yet actual sin can also be defined as that which is done as an action, or an omission of an action, fighting against the eternal law of God; just as AUGUSTINE, book 22 against Faustus, ch. 22, described sin: that which is done as a deed, or word, or desire against the law of God. For thus the material of sin, which is the action committed or omitted, is placed in the position of the genus, and the formal constituent, which is ἀνομία, or contrariety to law, is placed in the position of the difference. Moreover, the formal consequence of actual sin is the guilt of fault and punishment.

Latin:

Peccatum attuale est deflexio actus humani a regula legis divinae.

Vberius definitur: Peccatum attuale est deflexio actus humani commissi, vel omissi, a regula legis divinae, reatum culpae & poenae inferens.

Prob. Peccatum generatim definitur per ἀνομίαν, sive deflexionem a lege, 1 Io. III, 4. Quae ἀνομία vel originalis, vel actualis est.

Differt itaque peccatum attuale ab originali eo ipso, quod illud est actus secundus, hoc est habitus ad malum inclinans & sollicitans. Potest tamen etiam peccatum attuale definiri, quod fit actio, aut actionis omissio, pugnans cum lege Dei aeterna; sicut AVGVSTINVS l. 22. contra Faustum c. 22. descripsit peccatum: quod fit factum, vel dictum, vel concupitum contra legem Dei. Nam sic materiale peccati, quod est actio commissa, vel omissa, loco generis, & formale constituens, quod est ἀνομία, sive contralegalitas, loco differentiae ponitur. Formale autem consequens peccati actualis est reatus culpae & poenae. Quaest.


### Q. II. Whence is it called actual sin?

Actual sin is called [so] from an act, prohibited by divine law, and by that [act] being committed or omitted.

Proof. Actual sin obtained its name from a sinful act; for the reason that actual sin in the descendants of Adam proceeds from original sin, as a second act proceeds from a habit, a stream flows from a fountain; fruit is born from a tree. For original sin is the evil tree, bearing evil fruits, Matthew 7:17. Although, however, actual sin, by the force of the word, is that sin which is perfected by a certain act, or by doing: yet by the usage of the word, those things are also called actual sins which are done by not doing. For just as some laws are issued concerning things to be done, others concerning things to be omitted: so sins, opposed to the laws, are committed, some indeed by doing what is prohibited by law, others by not doing, or by omitting an act commanded by law.

Latin:

Peccatum attuale dicitur ab actu, lege divina prohibito, eoque commisso, vel omisso.

Prob. Peccatum attuale ab actu peccaminoso obtinuit nomen; eo, quod peccatum attuale in posteris Adami proficiscitur a peccato originali, vt actus secundus prouenit ex habitu, riuulus manat ex fonte; fructus nascitur ex arbore. Est enim peccatum originis mala arbor, ferens fructus malos, Matth. VII, 17. Quamuis autem peccatum attuale, vi vocis, sit illud peccatum, quod actu quodam, seu agendo perficitur: ex vsu tamen vocis, etiam peccata actualia dicuntur, quae non agendo fiunt. Sicut enim leges aliae de faciendis, aliae de omittendis feruntur: ita peccata, legibus opposita, alia quidem agendo, quod lege prohibitum est, alia non agendo, seu omittendo actum, lege praeceptum, patrantur. Quaest.


### Q. III. In how many ways is actual sin taken?

Actual sin is taken either more loosely and generally, for all inordinate motions or acts proceeding from original sin, whether they are joined with prior deliberation, or, without consultation of the intellect and choice of the will, creep upon men against their will: a) or more strictly and specially, for actions performed with deliberate counsel of the mind and destined malice of the will b).

Proof a. Original sin behaves like a cause, established in perpetual motion, whose effects are actual sins. For it is not idle, but laborious, and of the greatest activity, which like a poisoned fountain pours forth its own similar waters, emptying itself into actual sins of every kind, which are either internal indeliberate vicious motions, or consulted and pre-elected acts. Indeliberate acts, or first motions, fall even upon infants. For every figment of the human heart is only evil every day, from infancy. Gen. 6:13; ch. 8:21.

Proof b. When it is said of the reborn that they do not commit sin, 1 John 3:9; likewise, that infants not yet born are said to have done nothing, neither good nor evil; Rom. 9:11; actual sins, strictly so called, are understood, which are done from choice and deliberate counsel.

It provides a pedagogical use, for lamenting the most profound corruption of men after the fall and their extreme misery, and for seeking with the most ardent desire the physician of souls, Christ, a); a paracletic use for recognizing the ineffable mercy of God, who prepared for us a salutary remedy for this lethal evil in baptism and regeneration b); a corrective use, for suppressing the desires of the flesh remaining after baptism c).

IV. How are actual sins called in the Holy Scriptures?

Actual sins are called in the Holy Scriptures iniquitous works, dead works, unfruitful works of darkness, works of the flesh, actions of the old man, actions of the flesh, works of impiety.

Proof. St. Peter calls actual sins ἔργα ἄνομα, iniquitous works, 2 Ep. ch. II, 8, because they deviate from the norm of divine law. St. Paul calls the same dead works, Hebr. VI, 1. Naturally, because they are the effects of men who are spiritually dead, they turn man away from God, the author of life, and finally produce eternal death. He also calls them unfruitful works of darkness, Eph. V, 11. They are unfruitful works because they bring no benefit, but much detriment, to those who sin. They are works of darkness because they are for the most part perpetrated in hidden and dark places, at the persuasion of the prince of darkness, by those whose mind is filled with the darkness of ignorance and malice, whom they finally drive headlong into eternal darkness. He calls them works of the flesh, Gal. V, 19, because the flesh, or carnal concupiscence, tempts and ensnares man to them, James I, 14. He calls them actions of the old man, Col. III, 9, because they proceed from the corrupt nature derived from Adam to his descendants. He calls them actions of the flesh, Rom. VIII, 13, or of nature, depraved by original sin; because they are both inflamed by the senses of the flesh, and carried out through the ministry of the bodily members, and finally directed toward that which is pleasing and agreeable to the body. St. Jude names them ἔργα ἀσεβείας, works of impiety, ep. v. 15, for the reason that by them the majesty of God, the Lord, the legislator, and the supreme judge, is violated.

Q. V. What is the efficient cause of actual sins?

The efficient cause of actual sins is the sinning man. Proof. Because the sinning man is the physical cause of that act to which ἀνομία, i.e., illegality, adheres; in that he produces it by a real influence, ἀνομία itself, or the deflection from the law, does not indeed have an efficient cause, but a deficient one: yet it is reduced to a particular cause, straying from the divine law, which is its moral cause. For when he produces an effect with which he knows ἀνομία to be conjoined, he intends the ἀνομία itself, if not directly, at least indirectly, so that the ἀνομία is imputed to him as an effect, just as if he were influencing it really. For example, Cain is the efficient cause of fratricide; the material of which is the act of striking, but the ἀταξία or disorder adjacent to it is the formal element of the sin. The act of striking is from Cain, as a physical cause, really influencing; and the illegality, or disorder, adjacent to the striking, is from Cain as a moral cause, to whom it is imputed with the most just right.

Q. VI.

What are the causes impelling man to actual sin, or inducing him in any way? Internally, depraved concupiscence, dwelling in the flesh, solicits man to a sinful act a): externally, the devil b), and the world, or men c), and things existing in the world d), impel or incite him.

Proof. a. St. James, ch. I, 14, 15, shows us the Ἀμαρτιγένεσιαν, or origin of actual sin. Every man is tempted by his own concupiscence, while he is drawn away and ensnared. Then concupiscence, when it has conceived, brings forth sin: but sin, when it is finished, brings forth death. According to the interpretation of Dr. CHEMNITIUS, part III, Book on the distinction of mortal and venial [sins], p. 109, the following degrees are indicated by St. James, through which one ascends to a deliberate sin finished by an external act. 1) It is named by the apostle ἰδία ἐπιθυμία, which is original concupiscence: 2) τὸ πειράζειν of that concupiscence, when it begins to solicit us to evil, 3) τὸ δελεάζειν (to entice), which are the inviting allurements. For just as little birds and fish are caught by allurements: so it invites by the allurements of original concupiscence: 4) τὸ ἐξέλκειν (to draw away), when the will is dragged sideways by the fires of evil affections toward obedience.

And even the reborn can reach this far, for Paul, Rom. VII, 23, grieves and complains that he is sometimes thus taken captive; yet because he remains in Christ, and resists, there is no condemnation in him, Rom. IIX, 1: 5) τὸ συλλαμβάνειν (to conceive), which is the evil proposal or machination toward evil. And when malice progresses this far, repentance and faith are already cast off: 6) τὸ τίκτειν (to bring forth), when the work itself is completed, by the perpetration of which sin generates death.

D. GERHARD explains this origin of actual sins and their gradual progress concisely in disp. isag. p. 927.

The Apostle James commemorates five degrees of interior sins. The first is ἐπιθυμία (concupiscence), a depraved concupiscence, habitually inherent, which is original sin itself, the fuel of which remains in the reborn even after baptism. The second is τὸ πειράζειν (to tempt) of that concupiscence, when, namely, the flesh casts depraved thoughts before us: when the fuel emits, as it were, certain sparks. The third is τὸ δελεάζειν (to entice), when various allurements are cast before us, by which we are solicited to choose evil against the judgment of the mind renewed by the Spirit, and thus that τὸ δελεάζειν is like a fan, by which the sparks of the fuel are excited. The fourth is τὸ ἐξέλκειν (to draw away), when the will is, as it were, taken captive and reduced to servitude, so that it begins to consent to depraved allurements. The fifth is τὸ συλλαμβάνειν (to conceive), when a deliberate proposal is added, and means are sought to lead that into act. All these pertain to interior sins, from which arises τὸ τίκτειν (to bring forth), the external work itself, by the perpetration of which sin generates death.

Furthermore, there is no doubt that actual sins, more often repeated, are not rarely the causes of subsequent sins, partly insofar as they incline toward similar sinful acts, partly insofar as they cast out grace, which being taken away, men rush into graver sins .

Prob. b. The devil is the cause of human sin; for the reason that he works effectively in the children of disobedience, Eph. II, 2. He blinds the minds of the unbelievers, lest the light of the gospel should shine upon them, 2 Cor. IV, 4. He disturbs the imagination of Saul, 1 Sam. XVI, 25. He incites David to number the people, 1 Paral. XXI, 1. He fills the heart of Ananias to tell a lie, Acts V, 3. He persuades Judas with arguments, taken from utility, to betray Christ, John XIII, 2.

From which the devil is called ὁ πειράζων (the tempter), Matt. IV, 3. The devil tempts by calling away from the good, and by instigating to evil.

Yet he does not necessitate, nor determine the human will to an illicit act, but he counsels and suggests depraved thoughts; which impostor the reborn can resist, so that he may flee from them, James IV, 17.

Prob. c. Men, who come under the name of the world, provide incentives to other men to act wickedly, by persuading and by inviting them with their own example. Wives enticed Solomon to idolatry, 1 Kings 11:4. Jeroboam made Israel to sin by his example, 1 Kings 15:26. Prob. d.

The things of the world, running into the senses, objectify the will and the sensitive appetite and move them to sin. Precious plunder moved Achan to theft, Josh. 7:21. The uncovered feet of Bathsheba moved David, 2 Sam. 11:26.

Latin:

Peccatum attuale sumitur vel laxius & generalius, pro omnibus motibus vel actibus inordinatis, ex peccato originis procedentibus, siue cum praeuia deliberatione sint coniuncti, siue, citra consultationem intellectus, & proaeresin voluntatis, hominibus inuitis obrepant: a) vel pressius & specialius, pro actionibus, deliberato mentis consilio, & destinata voluntatis malitia patratis b).

Prob. a. Peccatum originis habet se instar causae, in perpetuo motu constitutae, cuius effectus sunt peccata actualia. Neque enim otiosum, sed operosum, maximaque activitatis est, quod tanquam fons venenatus suas scaturit consimiles aquas, in omnis generis peccata actualia se effundens, quae vel sunt motus vitiosi interni indeliberati, vel actus consulti & praeelectiui. Actus indeliberati, vel motus primi cadunt etiam in infantes. Omne enim figmentum cordis humani tantummodo malum est omni die, ab infantia. Gen. VI, 13. c. VIII, 21.

Prob. b. Quando de renatis dicitur, quod non faciant peccatum, 1 Io. III, 9. item, quod infantes nondum nati nihil, neque boni, neque mali fecisse dicuntur; Rom. IX, 11. intelliguntur peccata actualia, stricte dicta, quae ex proaeresi & deliberato consilio fiunt.

Suppeditat vsum pædeuticum, ad profundissimam hominum post lapsum corruptionem extremamque miseriam deplorandam, & medicum animarum, Christum, flagrantissimo desiderio quærendum, a); paracleticum ad agnoscendam ineffabilem misericordiam Dei, qui lethali huic malo salutare remedium in baptismo & regeneratione nobis parauit b); epanorthoticum, ad supprimendum desideria carnis post baptismum residua c).

IV. Quomodo appellantur peccata actualia in sacris litteris?

Peccata actualia in sacris litteris vocantur opera iniqua, opera mortua, opera infructuosa tenebrarum, opera carnis, actiones veteris hominis, actiones carnis, opera impietatis.

Prob. S. Petrus peccata actualia vocat ἔργα ἄνομα, opera iniqua, 2 ep. c. II, 8. quia a norma legis divinae discrepant. S. Paullus eadem appellat opera mortua, Hebr. VI, 1. Nimirum propterea, quod sunt effecta hominum, spiritualiter mortuorum, a Deo, auctore vitae, hominem avertunt, mortem denique aeternam pariunt. Appellat etiam opera infructuosa tenebrarum. Eph. V, 11. Sunt opera infructuosa; quod nihil emolumenti, multum autem detrimenti peccantibus afferunt. Sunt opera tenebrarum; quoniam plerumque in locis occultis & tenebrosis, suasore principe tenebrarum, perpetrantur ab iis, quorum animus ignorantiae & malitiae tenebris est oppletus, quos tandem in aeternas tenebras praecipites agunt. Appellat opera carnis, Gal. V, 19. quia caro, sive concupiscentia carnalis, ad ea hominem tentat & inescat, Iacob. I, 14. Appellat actiones veteris hominis, Col. III, 9. eo; quod a natura corrupta ab Adamo in posteros derivata proficiscuntur. Appellat actiones carnis; Rom. VIII, 13. sive naturae, peccato originali depravatae; quia tum sensibus carnis inflammantur, tum ministerio membrorum corporeorum peraguntur, tum denique ad id, quod corpori gratum & iucundum est, diriguntur. S. Iudas ea nominat ἔργα ἀσεβείας, opera impietatis, ep. v. 15. ideo, quod iisdem maiestas Dei domini, legislatoris & iudicis summi, violatur.

Quaest. V. Quae est causa efficiens peccatorum actualium?

Causa efficiens peccatorum actualium est homo peccans. Prob. Quia homo peccans est causa physica illius actus, cui ἀνομία, f. dislegalitas adhaeret; eo, quod illum reali influxu producit, ἀνομία ipsa, sive deflexio a lege non habet quidem causam efficientem, sed deficientem: reducitur tamen in causam particularem, a lege divina aberrantem, quae illius causa moralis est. Cum enim producit effectum, cum quo novit ἀνομίαν esse coniunctam; ipsam ἀνομίαν, si non directe, saltim indirecte intendit, vt ipsi ἀνομία imputetur, tanquam effectus, haud secus, ac si realiter influeret. V. gr. Cain est causa efficiens fratricidii; cuius materiale est actus percussionis, sed ἀταξία sive inordinatio illi adiacens, est formale peccati. Actus percussionis est a Caino, ceu causa physica, realiter influente; ac illegalitas, sive inordinatio, percussioni adiacens, est a Caino tanquam causa morali, cui illa iure iustissimo imputatur.

Quaest. VI.

Quae sunt causae, hominem ad peccatum actuale impellentes, aut quacunque ratione inducentes? Interne hominem ad actum peccaminosum sollicitat concupiscentia praua, in carne habitans a): externe impellunt, aut incitant diabolus b), & mundus, seu homines c), & res in mundo existentes d).

Prob. a. Ἀμαρτιγένεσιαν, feu originem peccati actualis nobis commonstrat S. Iacobus c. I, 14. 15. Quilibet tentatur a propria concupiscentia, dum abstrahitur & inescatur. Deinde concupiscentia, postquam concepit, parit peccatum: peccatum vero, quando consummatum est, parit mortem. Interprete D. CHEMNITIO part. III. L. de discrim. p. mortal. & venial. p. 109. sequentes a S. Iacobo indicantur gradus, per quos ad peccatum proaereticum opere externo consummatum ascenditur. Nominatur 1) ab apostolo ἰδία ἐπιθυμία, quae est concupiscentia originalis: 2) τὸ πειράζειν illius concupiscentiae, quando incipit nos sollicitare ad malum, cogitationes: 3) τὸ δελεάζειν, quod sunt illecebrae inuitantes. Sicut enim auiculae & pisces illecebris inescantur: ita concupiscentiae originalis illecebris inuitat: 4) τὸ ἐξέλκειν, quando voluntas per incendia malorum affectuum rapitur transuersum ad obsequium.

Et hucusque etiam renatus peruenire potest, Nam Paullus Rom. VII, 23. dolet & conqueritur, se interdum sic captiuari; quia tamen manet in Christo, & repugnat, nihil in ipso est damnationis, Rom. IIX, 1: 5) τὸ συλλαμβάνειν, concipere, quod est malum propositum, seu machinatio ad malum. Et quando hucusque progreditur malitia, iam excussa est poenitentia & fides: 6) τὸ τίκτειν, quando ipsum opus confecitur, quo perpetrato peccatum generat mortem.

Quam originem peccatorum actualium & gradualem progressum concinne explicat D. GERHARDVS in disp. isag. p. 927.

Apostolus Iacobus quinque gradus peccatorum interiorum commemorat. Primus est ἐπιθυμία, praua concupiscentia, habitualiter inhaerens, quae est ipsum originale peccatum, cuius fomes etiam post baptismum in renatis adhuc manet. Secundus est τὸ πειράζειν illius concupiscentiae, quando scil. prauas cogitationes caro nobis obiicit: quando fomes quasi scintillas quasdam emittit. Tertius est τὸ δελεάζειν, quando variae obiiciuntur illecebrae, quibus sollicitamur, vt malum eligamus contra iudicium mentis per spiritum renouatae, sicque illud δελεάζειν est velut flabellum, quo fomites scintillae excitantur. Quartus est ἐξέλκειν, quando voluntas quasi captiuatur, & in seruitutem redigitur, vt consentire incipiat prauis illecebris. Quintus est τὸ συλλαμβάνειν, quando accedit deliberatum propositum, & quaeruntur media in actum illud deducendi. Haec omnia pertinent ad peccata interiora, ex quibus oritur τὸ τίκτειν, ipsum opus externum, quo perpetrato peccatum generat mortem.

De cetero nullum est dubium, quin etiam peccata actualia, saepius iterata, sequentium peccatorum haud raro caussae sint, partim quatenus inclinant ad actus similes peccaminosos, partim quatenus excutiunt gratiam, qua ablata, homines in peccata grauiora ruunt .

Prob. b. Diabolus est caussa peccati humani; propterea, quod efficaciter operatur in filiis incredulitatis, Eph. II, 2. excoecat sensus incredulorum, ne illucescat illis lumen euangelii, 2 Cor. IV, 4. turbat phantasiam Saulis, 1 Sam. XVI, 25. incitat Dauidem ad numerandum populum, 1 Paral. XXI, 1. implet cor Ananiae ad dicendum mendacium, Actor. V, 3. persuadet Iudae argumentis, ab vtili sumtis, ad prodendum Christum, Io. XIII, 2. ex quo diabolus audit ὁ πειράζων, tentator, Matth. IV, 3. Tentat autem diabolus a bono auocando, & ad malum instigando.

Neque tamen idem necessitat, aut determinat voluntatem humanam ad actum illicitum, sed consulit, prauasque cogitationes suggerit; cui impostori renati possunt resistere, vt ab ipsis fugiat, Iac.

IV, 17.

Prob. c. Homines, qui mundi nomine veniunt, stimulos subdunt aliis hominibus ad male agendum, suadendo, suoque exemplo inuitando. Salomonem ad idololatriam pellexerunt vxores, 1 Reg. XI, 4. Ieroboamus exemplo suo peccare fecit Israelem, 1 Reg. XV, 26.

Prob. d. Res mundi, in sensus incurrentes, voluntatem & appetitum sensitivum obiiciunt mouent ad peccandum. Achanem mouit ad furtum pretiosa præda, Ios. VII, 21. Davidem denudati pedes Bathsebæ, 2 Sam. XI, 26.


### Question VII. Upon whom does actual sin fall?

Actual sin falls upon all men), even the regenerate), and infants).

Prob. a. From the testimony of Solomon, 1 Kings 8:46: There is no man who does not sin.

Prob. b. 1) From the proclivity to sin, from which the regenerate are not immune. For, as St. James testifies, we all stumble often, James 3:2. The apostle addresses his spiritual brothers, v. 1, and dissuades them from untimely censure of others. In place of a reason, he brings forward the infirmity and proclivity of all to sin. The man of God does not except himself; because the mortal condition does not allow a man to be pure from every stain, as Lactantius says, Inst. Div., book 6, ch. 13. 2) From the daily deprecation of sins. The regenerate must pray daily: Forgive us our debts, Matt. 6:12. 3) From the example of the most holy Paul, who complains of himself, Rom. 7:19: The good that I will, I do not; but the evil that I will not, that I do. He who does not do the good that he wills, but does the evil that he does not will, commits actual sin, but involuntary.

Prob. c. 1) From the nature of original sin, which is never idle, but always active, like an evil root, bringing forth its own rotten fruits. Therefore, although actual proæretic (deliberate) sins do not always germinate from original sin; nevertheless, first inordinate motions, preceding reason, sprout up without proæresis (deliberate choice), inasmuch as they are inseparable from original sin. Whence we conclude: Infants are capable of original sin, which is always active: Therefore they are capable of actual sins. 2) From divine testimony, Gen. 8:21: The imagination of man’s heart is evil from his youth. By the imagination of the heart are designated inordinate motions, both first and second, carrying themselves out from the heart, Matt. 15:19, through which innate malice exerts itself, from the first breath of life to the last moment of life. 3) That sin congenital to infants erupts into actual sins, the midday of truth testifies. For by experience we learn that year-old infants strike their mothers, bite, and envy their twin brother for the abundance of milk: it is evident that a boy is by nature carried toward evil, apprehending good with the greatest difficulty, evil with the greatest ease; holding onto good with the greatest difficulty, evil with the greatest firmness; thinking, speaking, and doing good with the greatest weariness and drowsiness, evil with the greatest sweetness and joy; finally, that man left to himself never becomes virtuous, but always most wicked; that he is educated to piety with immense labor, the inculcation of precepts, the detestation of vices and sins, most frequent exhortations, and finally promises and blows; and finally, that if you wish him to be vicious, given to sins, and wicked, there is no need for any labor or instruction, he becomes such spontaneously. Add that even uncomposed gestures are sins. See Dannhauer in Hodof. phænom. IV, p. 357.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians and Anabaptists, who assert that a regenerate man can rise to such a degree of perfection that he is without any sin: the same, together with the Papists, maintain that infants are not capable of actual sins. Their stronger arguments are:

I. Whoever neither sins, nor can sin, upon them actual sin does not fall: But the reborn, etc.

Therefore. The minor is proved from 1 John III, 9: "Whosoever is born of God doth not commit sin; for his seed remaineth in him: and he cannot sin, because he is born of God.

Resp. John speaks of the reborn man considered in a reduplicative sense, insofar as he is reborn, or exists in the state of regeneration.

2) Of the seed of the divine word, insofar as it is preserved alive in the mind and is translated into living practice; for it is that which guards and draws man back from sins by commanding, forbidding, promising, and threatening. 3) Of proæretic [deliberate], moral sins that devastate the conscience, not of involuntary, venial sins, and those that creep in through ignorance or the infirmity of nature, contrary to the will.

John therefore wishes to teach, as the blessed HVNNIVS interprets, that rebirth and the purpose of sinning are so opposed that they necessarily remove and destroy one another, and can by no means consist in the same man at the same time.

Therefore, he who is born of God, insofar as he is reborn, and as long as he remains reborn, certainly does not commit sin; namely, sin against the conscience, and that which proceeds from a deliberate purpose and counsel of the mind. Indeed, he cannot sin, in the way explained, so that he would simultaneously sin against the conscience and nevertheless remain reborn.

Rather, as soon as he sins knowingly and willingly by purpose, he immediately ceases to be reborn, that is: he loses the gift of rebirth, faith, and the grace of God, the seed of the word being suffocated and the Holy Spirit being shaken off.

For that the reborn can again fall away from the grace of God through mortal, or reigning, sins is evident from the XVIII chapter of Ezekiel, 1 Cor. IX, Rom. XI, and many other places.

II. A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, Matth. VII, 18. But a reborn man is a good tree, Ps. I, 3: Therefore. Resp. 1) A perfectly good tree cannot bear bad fruit: But the reborn are imperfectly good: and therefore they can sin venially.

2) A good tree cannot bear bad fruit: but it can become sterile, rotten, and finally vicious, and when it has become such, it can be cut down. It cannot bring forth bad fruit, says HIERONYMVS on that place of Matthew, as long as it perseveres in the pursuit of goodness; and conversely, a bad tree can become good, TERTVLLIANVS in the book De Anima: A bad tree will not give good fruit if it is not cultivated, and a good one will give bad if it is not tended.

Cf.

CALOVIVS in Bibl. Illustrat. on 1 Io. III, 9, fol. 1632. III. God can preserve the reborn immune from falling, and set them irreprehensible in the sight of his glory with joy, ep. Jude v. 24. Therefore the reborn, aided by the power of God, can lead their lives so circumspectly that they never slip or sin.

Resp. God can, if He wills, by His absolute omnipotence preserve the reborn immune from voluntary and involuntary, mortal and venial falling; but by His ordained power He can and wills to render them immune from malicious and deadly falling, if, following the guidance of the divine word and supported by the grace of the Holy Spirit, they place an obstacle to inordinate motions and mortify the actions of the flesh, Rom. VIII, 13, and crucify them, Gal. V, 24.

IV. Whoever does neither good nor evil, upon them actual sin does not fall: But infants, etc.

Rom. IX, 11. E. Resp. Whoever do evil neither from proæresis [deliberate choice] nor from the infirmity of nature prone to evil, upon them actual sin does not fall; I grant it. But although infants do not sin from a deliberate purpose of mind, they nevertheless sin from the infirmity of nature on account of the indwelling original sin, from which vicious first motions are not absent. Instance: Infants do not even know evil, Deut. I, 39. E. they do no evil at all. Resp. The conclusion should have been inferred thus: Therefore they do no evil knowingly and willingly: which we grant.

V. Into whom the knowledge of the law does not fall, upon them no actual sin falls: But upon infants it does not fall, etc.

Therefore. The major is evident: because sin is a deviation from a known law.

Resp. Distinguish between the law prescribed and the law inscribed. Although infants are ignorant of the prescribed law, they nevertheless deflect from the inscribed, and naturally known, law.

VI. Infants are innocent: E. actual sins do not fall upon them.

The antecedent is established from Ps. 106:38. Resp. Infants are innocent not absolutely, but comparatively. 1) They are innocent before the forum of the earth, not of heaven. 2) They are innocent: because they are immune from proairetic sins, which are joined with the full use of reason and the pre-election of the will; but they are not devoid of involuntary sins.

Latin:

Peccatum actuale cadit in omnes homines ), etiam renatos ), & infantes ).

Prob. a. E testimonio Salomonis, 1 Reg. IIX, 46. Non est homo, qui non peccet.

Prob. b. 1) E procliuitate ad peccandum, a qua renati non sunt immunes. Etenim, teste S. Iacobo, fæpe labimur omnes, Iac. III, 2. Compellat apostolus fratres spirituales, v. 1. eosque dehortatur ab intempestiua in alios censura. Rationis loco adducit infirmitatem & procliuitatem omnium ad peccandum. Seipsum non excipit vir Dei; quia mortalis conditio non patitur esse hominem ab omni macula purum, dicente Lactantio, libr. VI. instit. c. 13. 2) E quotidiana peccatorum deprecatione. Renatis quotidie orandum est: Dimitte nobis debita nostra, Matth. VI, 12. 3) Exemplo Pauli sanctissimi, qui de seipso conqueritur, Rom. VII, 19: Non, quod volo, facio bonum, sed, quod non volo, malum, hoc facio. Qui non facit bonum, quod vult, sed facit malum, quod non vult, is committit actuale peccatum, sed inuoluntarium.

Prob. c. 1) Ex natura peccati originalis, quod nunquam est otiosum, sed semper operosum, instar malæ radicis, putres suos proferens fructus. Licet itaque e peccato originis non semper progerminent peccata actualia proæretica; suppullulant tamen absque proæresi motus primi inordinati, rationem præuenientes, vtpote qui a peccato originis sunt inseparabiles. Vnde colligimus: Infantes sunt capaces peccati originalis semper actuosi: Ergo sunt capaces peccatorum actualium. 2) E testimonio diuino, Gen. IIX, 21. Figmentum cordis hominis malum est a pueritia sua. Per figmentum cordis designantur motus inordinati tam primi, quam secundi, e corde se efferentes, Matth. XV, 19. per quos malitia innata se exserit, a primo vitæ haustu, ad vltimum vitæ momentum. 3) Peccatum infantibus congenitum erumpere in peccata actualia, testatur veritatis meridies. Experimento enim discimus, paruulos anniculos matres suas ferire, mordere, ac fratri gemello inuidere lactis copiam: constat, puerum natura ferri ad malum, bona apprehendere difficillime, mala facillime, bona tenere ægerrime, mala firmissime, bona cogitare, loqui & facere cum summo tædio & somnolentia, mala cum summa suauitate & gaudio; denique sibi relictum hominem nunquam fieri virtuosum, semper autem nequissimum; ad pietatem educari ingenti cum labore, præceptorum inculcatione, vitiorem & peccatorum detestatione, frequentissimis hortatibus, promissis denique ac plagis, eundem denique, si vitiosum, peccatis deditum ac sceleratum habere velis, nullo labore, nulla informatione esse opus, sponte talem euenire. Adde, & gestus incompositos peccata esse. Vid. Dannhav. in hodof. phænom. IV. p. 357.

Antithesis est Socinianorum & Anabaptistarum, qui asserunt, hominem renatum eo perfectionis assurgere posse, vt sine omni sit peccato: iidem vna cum Pontificiis statuunt, infantes peccatorum actualium non esse capaces. Quorum potiora sunt argumenta:

I. Quicunque nec peccant, nec peccare possunt, in illos non cadit peccatum actuale: Atqui renati &c.

Ergo. Minor probatur ex 1 Io. III, 9. Omnis, qui natus est ex Deo, peccatum non facit; quia semen ipsius in ipso manet: immo non potest peccare, eo, quod ex Deo natus est.

Resp. Loquitur Ioannes de homine renato considerato in sensu reduplicativo, quatenus renatus est, sive in statu regenerationis existit.

2) De semine verbi divini, in quantum illud in animo vegetum conservatur, & ad vivam praxin traducitur; quippe quod hominem a peccatis arcet & retrahit iubendo, vetando, pollicendo, comminando. 3) De peccatis proæreticis, moralibus, & conscientiam vastantibus, non de peccatis involuntariis, venialibus, & per ignorantiam aut infirmitatem naturæ, præter voluntatem, obrepentibus.

Docere itaque vult Ioannes, interprete b. HVNNIO, renascentiam & peccandi propositum sic esse opposita, ut se mutuo ex necessitate tollant & destruant, & consistere in eodem homine simul eodemque tempore minime queant.

Proinde qui ex Deo natus est, quatenus is est renatus, & quamdiu renatus permanet, peccatum certe non committit; peccatum scil. contra conscientiam, & ex deliberato animi proposito consilioque profectum. Immo non potest peccare, modo explicato, ut scilicet simul contra conscientiam peccet, ac nihilominus renatus maneat.

Quin potius quam primum ex proposito sciens volensque peccat, confestim renatus esse definit, hoc est; amittit donum renascentiæ, fidem & gratiam Dei, suffocato semine verbi, excussoque Spiritu S.

Posse enim renatos gratia Dei rursus excidere per peccata mortalia, seu regnantia, ex XVIII. cap. Ezech. 1 Cor: IX. Rom. XI. aliisque pluribus locis evidens est.

II. Bona arbor non potest ferre malos fructus, Matth. VII, 18. Atqui homo renatus est bona arbor, Ps. I, 3: Ergo. Resp. 1) Arbor perfecte bona non potest ferre malos fructus: At renati imperfecte boni sunt: ideoque peccare possunt venialiter.

2) Arbor bona non potest ferre malos fructus: at fieri sterilis, putris, vitiosa denique, & ubi talis facta est, excindi potest. Non potest proferre fructus malos, ait ad eum locum Matthæi HIERONYMVS, quamdiu in bonitatis studio perseverat; & contra, arbor mala fieri bona potest, TERTVLLIANVS in libro, de anima: Non dabit arbor mala fructus bonos, si non inferatur, & bona malos dabit, si non colatur.

Conf.

CALOVIVS in bibl. illustrat. Io. III, 9. fol. 1632. III. Potest Deus renatos conservare a lapsu immunes, & statuere in conspectu gloriæ suæ irreprehensibiles cum gaudio, ep. Iudæ v. 24. Ergo renati, virtute Dei adiuti, adeo circumspecte traducere possunt vitam suam, ut nunquam labantur, aut peccent.

Resp. Potest Deus, si velit, omnipotentia sua absoluta renatos conservare a lapsu voluntario & involuntario, mortali & veniali immunes; at potentia ordinata eosdem potest & vult immunes præstare a lapsu malitioso & mortifero, si ductum verbi divini sequentes, gratia Spiritus S. suffulti, motibus inordinatis obicem ponant, actionesque carnis mortificent, Rom. VIII, 13. & crucifigant. Gal. V, 24.

IV. Quicunque nec bonum, nec malum faciunt, in illos non cadit peccatum actuale: Atqui infantes &c.

Rom. IX, 11. E. Resp. Quicunque neque ex proæresi, neque ex infirmitate naturæ, ad malum pronæ, malum faciunt, in illos non cadit peccatum actuale; concedo. At licet infantes non peccent ex deliberato animi proposito peccant tamen ex infirmitate naturæ ob inhabitantes peccatum originale, a quo non absunt motus primi vitiosi. Instantia: Infantes ne malum quidem sciunt, Deut. I, 39. E. nullum malum faciunt. Resp. Conclusio sic erat inferenda: Ergo nullum malum faciunt scientes & volentes: id quod concedimus.

V. In quos non cadit notitia legis, in illos nullum cadit peccatum actuale: Atqui in infantes non cadit &c.

Ergo. Maior patet: quia peccatum est aberratio a lege cognita.

Resp. Dist. inter legem præscriptam, & inscriptam. Quamvis infantes ignorent legem præscriptam, deflectunt tamen a lege inscripta, & naturaliter nota. inscripta, & naturaliter nota.

VI. Infantes sunt innocentes: E. in illos non cadunt peccata actualia.

Antecedens constat ex Ps. CVI, 38. Resp. Infantes sunt innocentes non absolute, sed comparate. 1) Innocentes sunt coram foro soli, non poli. 2) Innocentes sunt: quia sunt immunes a peccatis proareticis, quae cum pleno usu rationis & praeelectione voluntatis sunt coniuncta; non autem expertes sunt peccatorum involuntariorum.


### Q. VIII. How are actual sins divided?

Actual sins are divided: 1) by reason of the cause, into voluntary and involuntary: 2) by reason of the total subject, or the person sinning, into mortal and venial: 3) by reason of the partial subject, into sins of the heart, of the mouth, and of the deed: 4) by reason of the act, into sins of commission and omission: 5) by reason of the object, into sins against God, against one's neighbor, and against the sinner himself: 6) by reason of the effect, into crying and non-crying: 7) by reason of the adjuncts, into graver and lighter, hidden and manifest, dead and living, remaining and remitted, joined with hardening and separated from it, remissible and irremissible.

Latin:

Peccata actualia diuiduntur: 1) ratione causae, in voluntaria, & inuoluntaria: 2) ratione subiecti totalis, siue personae peccantis, in mortalia, & venialia: 3) ratione subiecti partialis, in peccata cordis, oris & operis: 4) ratione actus, in peccata commissionis, & omissionis: 5) ratione obiecti, in peccata in Deum, in proximum, & ipsum peccantem: 6) ratione effectus, in clamantia, & non clamantia: 7) ratione adiunctorum, in grauiora, & leuiora, occulta & manifesta, mortua & viuentia, manentia & remissa, coniuncta cum induratione, & ab ea seiuncta, remissibilia, & irremissibilia.


### Q. IX. What is a voluntary sin?

A voluntary sin is an act discordant with divine law, committed or omitted by a man knowing and willing.

More fully it is defined: A voluntary sin is an act by which a man transgresses divine law against the dictate of conscience with a deliberate purpose of the will.

Obs. I. A voluntary sin is not called so here subjectively, because it inheres in the will; but effectively, because it proceeds from a deliberate will, determining itself spontaneously to a sinful act.

Obs. II. A voluntary sin is committed 1) by a man knowing that the act which he commits is discordant with divine law. Knowledge, however, dictating that an act is conformable or discordant with divine law, is commonly called conscience. 2) By a man willing, so that the cause of it is a full and deliberate will, which, through the prior deliberation of the intellect, intends to perform an act prohibited by divine law. Intention in moral matters is divided into full and semi-full. The former is that by which the will, having first sufficiently weighed the matter and not being carried away by the vehemence of the affections, is borne toward a certain act and strives effectively to perform it, e.g., when Judas intends the betrayal of Christ. The latter is where sufficient deliberation was not present, or reason was shaken by a whirlwind of affections, e.g., when David, offended by Nabal, thinks of inflicting death upon him and his household, 1 Sam. 25:13. The full intention of the will, which the Greeks call προαίρεσιν, we call a deliberate purpose of the will.

Obs. III. A voluntary sin is also called proairetic, or pre-elective; a sin against conscience; a sin committed with a high hand, Num. 15:30. King David calls voluntary sins presumptuous, Ps. 19:13.

Latin:

Peccatum voluntarium est actus legi diuinae difformis ab homine sciente & volente commissus vel omissus.

Vberius definitur: Peccatum voluntarium est actus, quo homo legem diuinam contra dictamen conscientiae deliberato voluntatis proposito transgreditur.

Obs. I. Peccatum voluntarium hic non dicitur subiectiue, quod voluntati inhaeret; sed effectiue, quod a voluntate deliberata, ad actum peccaminosum se sponte determinante, proficiscitur.

Obs. II. Committitur peccatum voluntarium 1) ab homine sciente, actum, quem committit, legi diuinae esse difformem. Scientia autem, dictans actum legi diuinae esse conformem, vel difformem, communiter vocatur conscientia. 2) Ab homine volente, ita, ut ipsius causa fit voluntas plena & deliberata, quae praeia intellectus deliberatione effectum lege diuina prohibitum perficere intendit. Diuiditur autem intentio in moralibus in plenam, & semiplenam. Illa est, qua voluntas, re prius sufficienter expensa, & per affectuum vehementiam non abrepta, in actum quendam fertur, eumque perficere efficaciter nititur, v. gr. cum Iudas intendit proditionem Christi. Haec est, vbi sufficiens non adfuit deliberatio, aut ratio affectuum turbine est concussa, v. gr. quando Dauid a Nabale offensus, de morte ipsi & domesticis inferenda cogitat, 1 Sam. XXV, 13. Plenam voluntatis intentionem, quam Graeci vocant προαίρεσιν, nos appellamus deliberatum voluntatis propositum.

Obs. III. Peccatum voluntarium dicitur etiam proareticum, siue praeelectiuum; peccatum contra conscientiam; peccatum elata manu commissum, Num. XV, 30. Rex Dauid peccata voluntaria vocat superba, Ps. XIX, 14.


### Q. X. In how many ways is voluntary sin considered?

A voluntary sin is considered both in relation to conscience and in relation to the purpose of the will.

Latin:

Consideratur peccatum voluntarium tum in ordine ad conscientiam, tum in ordine ad voluntatis propositum.


### Question IX. What is voluntary sin?

A sin against conscience is fourfold. For it is committed either against a right conscience, when a man in acting or omitting [follows] the dictate of conscience, of knowledge, while agreeing with the divine law, does not follow, but despises a); or against an erroneous conscience, when a man in acting or omitting deviates from the dictate of a conscience imbued with error b); or against a probable conscience, when someone sins against the dictate of the intellect, which for probable reasons persuades that something is to be done or omitted here and now c); or against a doubtful conscience, when someone does or omits that about which he doubts whether it should be done or omitted d).

Prob. a. He who sins against the dictate of a right conscience sins most gravely; for it is as it were an internal herald, proposing to man the divine law and that of nature, and showing what is certainly and undoubtedly agreeable to it, and what is disagreeable. From which sin, perpetrated against a right conscience, follows remorse, anguish, despair. This bite of conscience was felt by Cain, Ahithophel, Judas the traitor, and very many others.

Prob. b. He who follows an erroneous conscience in a matter base in itself and prohibited by laws, whether he acts according to or against his conscience, sins, v. gr. If a Persian had once been persuaded that the sun was a God to be worshipped; he, by worshipping the sun, sinned; because he venerated with religious worship him who is not the true God: by not worshipping he also sinned; because he acted against the dictate of conscience, and thus, as far as in him lay, wished to act against the law of God, who gave us conscience as a guide for acting: hence the darkness of error must be dispelled either by the natural light of right reason, or by the supernatural light of the divinely revealed word. But in an indifferent matter, neither commanded nor prohibited by laws, he sins who acts against it; he does not sin who acts according to it. V. gr. At the beginning of the N. T. some Christians thought it not lawful to eat idolothyta, or meats sacrificed to an idol, when yet an idol is nothing in the world (by reason of divinity and divine virtue, which the heathens attributed to them). Here they would have sinned by eating against their conscience, even though erroneous; by not eating, they would not have sinned, because they would have followed their conscience as a cynosure. See 1 Cor. VIII, 7. So today, he who maintains that it is illicit for a Christian to be a soldier, he sins by serving as a soldier; he does not sin when he abstains from serving as a soldier.

Prob. c. He sins against a probable conscience who neglects the safer way. V. gr. A physician sins by applying a desperate medicine to drive away a desperate disease. For although it may happen that by applying the same the patient may recover; it is not, however, safe. For it may happen that by that violent medicine the life of the patient may be extinguished.

Prob. d. He sins against a doubtful conscience who embraces either part of a contradiction, whichever it may be. V. gr. If a man, addicted to the Augsburg Confession, were a servant of a popish prince, and remained in doubt whether it were lawful for him to accompany the prince to the popish mass, or illicit? He would sin as much by accompanying as by not accompanying. Because 1) whatsoever is not of faith (i.e., whatsoever is undertaken with a wavering mind) is sin, Rom. XIV, 23. 2) Because he wills some evil. For since he perceives some malice in either object, whichever he undertakes, he will have inclined toward evil. Therefore, the matter must always be settled either by one's own prudence or by the counsel of wiser men, lest he remain in doubt any longer, and his mind hang in suspense.

Latin:

Peccatum contra conscientiam est quadruplex. Committitur enim, vel contra conscientiam rectam, cum homo in agendo vel omittendo dictamen conscientiae, scientiae, cum lege divina consentiens, non sequitur, sed contemnit a); vel contra conscientiam erroneam, quando homo in agendo, vel omittendo, a dictamine conscientiae errore imbutae deflectit b); vel contra conscientiam probabilem, cum quis delinquit contra dictamen intellectus, probabiles ob causas aliquid hic & nunc agendum vel omittendum suadentis c); vel contra conscientiam dubiam, quando quis id agit, vel omittit, de quo dubitat, sitne agendum, vel omittendum d).

Prob. a. Qui contra conscientiae rectae dictamen delinquit, gravissime peccat; est enim illa quasi praeco internus, homini legem divinam & naturae proponens, atque ostendens, quid illi certo & indubitato consentaneum, quid dissentaneum fit. Ex quo peccatum, contra conscientiam rectam perpetratum; sequitur morsus, angor, desperatio. Quem conscientiae morsum senserunt Cainus, Achitophel, Iudas proditor, & plurimi alii.

Prob. b. Qui sequitur conscientiam erroneam in re per se turpi, ac legibus prohibita, is, sive secundum, sive contra conscientiam agat, peccat, v. gr. Si Persa olim fuisset persuasus, solem esse Deum adorandum; is, adorando solem, peccauit; quia cultu religioso veneratus est eum, qui verus Deus non est: non adorando etiam peccaut; quia egit contra dictamen conscientiae, atque adeo, quantum in ipso, agere voluit contra legem Dei, qui conscientiam nobis, vt agendi ducem, dedit: hinc discutienda est caligo erroris aut lumine naturali rectae rationis, aut lumine supernaturali verbi divinitus reuelati. At in re adiaphora, legibus nec praecepta, nec prohibita, is delinquit, qui agit contra eam; non peccat, qui secundum eam agit. V. gr. Sub initium N. T. nonnulli christiani arbitrabantur, non licere idolothytis, seu carnibus idolo immolatis, vesci, cum tamen idolum nihil fit in mundo (ratione diuinitatis & virtutis diuinae, quam ethnici illi affingebant). Hic peccassent comedendo contra conscientiam, licet erroneam; non edendo, non peccassent, quia conscientiam suam, tanquam cynosuram secuti fuissent. Vid. 1 Cor. VIII, 7. Sic hodie, qui statuit, illicitum esse christiano militare, is peccat militando; non peccat, cum a militando abstinet.

Prob. c. Contra conscientiam probabilem peccat, qui viam tutiorem negligit. V. gr. Peccat medicus, morbo desperato depellendo adhibens medicinam desperatam. Quamuis enim fieri possit, vt eadem adhibita aegrotus conualescat; non tamen tutum est. Nam fieri potest, vt violento illo medicamine vita aegroti exstinguatur.

Prob. d. Contra conscientiam dubiam peccat, qui alterutram contradictionis partem, quaecunque ea sit, amplectitur. V. gr. Si homo, Augustanae confessioni addictus, fatelles foret principis pontificii, & in dubio haereret, vtrum sibi licitum sit comitari principem ad missam pontificiam, an illicitum? Is peccaret tam comitando, quam non comitando. Quia 1) quidquid ex fide non est (i. e. quidquid animo fluctuante suscipitur) peccatum est, Rom. XIV, 23. 2) Quia vult aliquod malum. Cum enim in vtroque obiecto sentiat aliquam malitiam, quodcunque susceperit, in malum inclinauerit. Semper igitur vel propria prudentia, vel aliorum sapientiorum consilio res transigenda est, ne diutius anceps haereat, animique pendeat.


### Quaest. XII

…How manifold is voluntary sin by reason of the purpose of sinning? Voluntary sin, viewed in relation to the purpose of the will, is twofold. For one is that which is from mere malice and a plainly free will a) another, which is committed out of a will inclined by force or fear and surrounding dangers (b).…

Prob. a. Just as every moral action is either involuntary, which is either extorted by force or undertaken out of ignorance; or spontaneous, which is performed out of certain knowledge and an internal inclination of the appetite; or mixed, which is done out of fear of an imminent greater evil, but would never be done if it were permitted to escape that graver evil by another way (e.g., an action is mixed if someone, with the danger of shipwreck imminent, throws his goods into the sea so that he himself may escape safe, having avoided the shipwreck; or, if someone, meeting robbers on the road, for the sake of redeeming his own life, gives or promises a sum of money not without his own loss: which mixed action is neither simply spontaneous, because a man would not prepare himself for it unless the danger of a greater evil were imminent; nor also simply involuntary, because it is joined with the knowledge of all circumstances, and could also have been interrupted, if it had been pleasing to undergo the greater evil. Yet a mixed action is more spontaneous than involuntary 1) by reason of the principle, which is the knowledge of circumstances and the pre-election of the will, 2) by reason of the end, which is the avoidance of a graver evil and the preservation of a greater good, whether true or apparent): Thus in theological matters, one sin is simply involuntary, another is voluntary respectively, which is perpetrated out of fear of an instant graver evil, outside of which case it would never be committed. This distinction is illustrated by examples. The betrayal of Judas, by which the Lord Jesus was handed over into the hands of enemies, was a sin simply voluntary, committed out of mere malice and a will plainly free. For he was not compelled to that nefarious crime by any fear of dangers, but was enticed by prior consultation and an internal inclination of the will, by which he was carried toward profit.

Prob. b. Peter sinned by denying Jesus three times. Which sin was not simply voluntary, in that Peter did not deny Jesus out of mere malice and a will plainly free; nor was it simply involuntary, because it was not committed by Peter unknowingly and unwillingly: but it was voluntary in a certain respect, and in a certain regard; because Peter, with danger imminent, wished to consult for his own life by the denial of Christ. Yet the sin of Peter is not to be extenuated, as it is by certain Romanists, among whom are MALDONATUS and CORNELIUS A LAPIDE. For 1) Peter could have avoided this danger by another way, by not entering the praetorium of the high priest. 2) Impiously, Peter preferred the preservation of his own life to the confession of Christ, thinking the loss of life to be a greater evil, and the denial of Christ to be a lesser evil. 3) He accumulated sins by lying, by swearing falsely, by imprecating anathema upon himself. Let us hear the judgment concerning the fall of Peter by S. HIERONYMUS, which is to be read in DANNHAWER, in hodof. p. 859. I know that some who are piously affected toward the apostle Peter have interpreted this passage in such a way as to say that Peter did not deny God, but a man, and that the sense is: I do not know the man, because I know God. How frivolous this is, the prudent reader understands. They defend the apostle in such a way that they make God guilty of a lie. For if this man did not deny, then the Lord lied, who had said: because this night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times, not a man. There remains, therefore, the enormous sin of Peter, that is, of him who was a lion before the battle, a stag in the battle, of that most firm pillar, trembling at the impulse of a single breeze. It was an incredible lie to have said that he did not know the Lord, when there was hardly anyone who did not know Jesus by sight, famous for so many miracles. Why did he come into the palace if he did not know Jesus? More enormous was the confirmation by oath. The highest crime was the execration of himself, by which, having prayed ill for himself, he bound himself with curses, perhaps using an ancient formula: May God do these things to me, and add these things!

Latin:

Peccatum voluntarium, in ordine ad propositum voluntatis spectatum, duplex est. Aliud enim est, quod ex mera malitia & voluntate plane libera a); aliud, quod ex voluntate, vi metuue & circumstantibus periculis inclinata (b), committitur.

Prob. a. Sicut omnis actio moralis vel est inuita, quæ vel per vim extorquetur, vel ex ignorantia suscipitur; vel spontanea, quæ ex certa scientia & interna appetitus inclinatione perficitur, vel mixta, quæ fit ex metu imminentis maioris mali, nunquam autem fieret, si grauius illud malum alia via liceret effugere (v. gr. actio mixta est, si quis imminente naufragii periculo merces suas in mare abiiciat, vt ipse saluus euadat, declinato naufragio; vel, si quis latronibus in via occurrentibus, vitæ suæ redimendæ caussa, pecuniæ summam non sine damno suo det vel promittat: quæ actio mixta neque simpliciter spontanea est, quia ad eam homo se non accingeret, nisi maioris mali periculum immineret; neque etiam simpliciter inuita, quia coniuncta est cum notitia omnium circumstantiarum, & intermitti quoque potuisset, si maius subire malum libuisset. Est tamen actio mixta magis spontanea, quam inuita 1) ratione principii, quod est cognitio circumstantiarum, & præelectio voluntatis, 2) ratione finis, qui est declinatio grauioris mali & conseruatio maioris boni, vel veri, vel apparentis): Ita in theologicis peccatum aliud est simpliciter inuoluntarium, aliud voluntarium respectiue, quod perpetratur ex metu instantis grauioris mali, extra quem casum nunquam committeretur. Illustratur hoc discrimen exemplis. Proditio Iudæ, qua Dominus Iesus in manus hostium traditus est, fuit peccatum simpliciter voluntarium, ex mera malitia & voluntate plane libera commissum. Neque enim vlla periculorum formidine ad nefandum illud facinus est compulsus, sed præuia consultatione & interna voluntatis inclinatione, qua in lucrum ferebatur, illectus est.

Prob. b. Peccauit Petrus, ter Iesum abnegando. Quod peccatum non fuit simpliciter voluntarium, eo, quod Petrus non ex mera malitia & voluntate plane libera Iesum abnegauit; neque fuit simpliciter inuoluntarium, quia non a Petro inscio & nolente commissum est: sed fuit voluntarium secundum quid, & certo respectu; quia Petrus, imminente periculo, consulere voluit vitæ suæ, abnegatione Christi. Neque tamen extenuandum est peccatum Petri cum quibusdam Romanensibus, quos inter sunt MALDONATVS & CORNELIVS A LAPIDE. Nam 1) Petrus hoc periculum alia via declinare poterat, prætorium pontificis non ingrediendo. 2) Impie prætulit Petrus conseruationem vitæ suæ confessioni Christi, ratus, iacturam vitæ maius malum, & abnegationem Christi esse minus malum. 3) Peccata cumulauit mentiendo, peierando, anathema sibi ipsi imprecando. Audiamus iudicium de lapsu Petrino S. HIERONYMI, quod legere est apud DANNHAWER. in hodof. p. 859. Scio quosdam pie affectos erga apostolum Petrum locum hunc ita interpretatos, vt dicerent, Petrum non Deum negasse, sed hominem, & esse sensum: nescio hominem, quia scio Deum. Hoc quam friuolum sit, prudens lector intelligit. Sic defendunt apostolum, vt Deum reum mendacii faciant. Si enim iste non negauit, ergo mentitus est dominus, qui dixerat: quia hac nocte, antequam gallus cantet, ter me negabis, non hominem. Manet ergo enorme peccatum Petri, illius scilicet ante prælium leonis, in prælio cerui, illius firmissimæ columnæ, ad vnius auræ impulsum contremiscentis. Incredibile mendacium fuit, dixisse, non nosse dominum, cum vix quisquam esset, qui Iesum de vultu non nosset, tot miraculis celebrem. Eccur venit in palatium, si Iesum non nouit? Enormior fuit confirmatio per iusiurandum. Summum scelus fuit sui ipsius exsecratio, qua sibi male precatus, semet diris obligauit, fortassis veteri vsus formula: Hæc mihi Deus faciat, & hæc addat!


### XIII. Does voluntary sin also fall upon the reborn?

Voluntary sin does not indeed fall upon the reborn, insofar as they are and remain reborn a); yet it does fall upon them, insofar as, overcome by depraved concupiscence, they slip from the state of grace b).

Proof a. 1 John III, 9. Everyone who has been born of God does not commit sin; because His seed remains in him; indeed, he cannot sin, insofar as he has been born of God. Proof b. There exist examples of the reborn who have slipped into deliberate sins: David, Judas, Peter, and others. Therefore, the king-prophet prays most humbly: Do not take Your Holy Spirit from me, Ps. LI, 13. He who asks that the Holy Spirit not be taken from him, he without doubt acknowledges that it has been taken away, or fears that it is losable.

Quest. XIV. What is involuntary sin?

Involuntary sin is an act, difform to divine law, not proceeding from certain knowledge, nor from a deliberate purpose of the will.

Latin:

Non cadit quidem peccatum voluntarium in renatos, quatenus sunt & manent renati a); cadit tamen in eos, quatenus a praua concupiscentia victi, e statu gratiæ prolabuntur b).

Prob. a. 1 Io. III, 9. Omnis, qui natus est ex Deo, peccatum non facit; quia semen ipsius in eo manet; immo non potest peccare, quatenus ex Deo natus est. Prob. b. Exstant exempla renatorum in peccata proæretica prolapsorum, Dauidis, Iudæ, Petri & aliorum. Idcirco humillime precatur rex propheta: Spiritum sanctitatis tuæ ne aufer a me, Ps. LI, 13. Qui Spiritum S. a se non auferri rogat, is sine dubio ablatum agnoscit, aut amissibilem metuit.

Quæst. XIV. Quid est peccatum inuoluntarium?

Peccatum inuoluntarium est actus, legi diuinæ difformis, non profectus ex certa scientia, nec ex deliberato voluntatis proposito.


### Q. XV. How is involuntary sin divided?

Involuntary sin is divided into the sin of ignorance and of infirmity.

Latin:

Peccatum inuoluntarium diuiditur in peccatum ignorantiæ, & infirmitatis.


### Question XIV. What is involuntary sin?

The sin of ignorance is an act, difform to divine law, the cause of which is ignorance not affected or supine, but invincible in itself and in its cause, joined with serious repentance.

Obs. I. It is one thing when someone sins while ignorant, and another when he sins through ignorance. He sins while ignorant who, at the very moment he sins, is ignorant of what he is doing, such as a drunkard or an angry person; yet that very ignorance is not the cause of the sinful act; but something else is, which induced that ignorance, namely drunkenness or anger. But he sins through ignorance when the cause of the evil action is ignorance, insofar as it excludes knowledge which otherwise would have prevented the act of sinning. For ignorance is a removing, hindering cause.

Obs. II. The cause of involuntary sin is invincible ignorance, which cannot be dispelled or overcome even when due diligence is applied, e.g., if someone were splitting wood with an axe in a forest and were to strike and kill a man hiding among the shady thickets, he would not be a voluntary murderer. But vincible ignorance, which can be overcome and removed when diligence is applied, does not make an involuntary sin; for it argues for a man's negligence or malice, and is therefore supine or affected. Furthermore, sometimes ignorance seems to be invincible which, however, if you look at the cause, is vincible, e.g., if someone has willingly loaded himself with wine or beer and were to kill a man while drunk, his ignorance seems to be invincible, but in reality it is vincible, for he could have abstained from the drink, which was consumed intemperately.

Obs. III. Some ignorance precedes the act of the will, some accompanies it, some follows it. Antecedent ignorance is the cause that a man wills something which he would not have willed if he had known. Such ignorance is when someone is ignorant of those things which he could not know in this or that matter, nor was he bound to know, and it coincides with invincible ignorance; e.g., when someone, about to kill an enemy in battle, kills his brother, whom he neither knew nor could have known to be present at that battle. Concomitant ignorance is said to be when someone does something while ignorant which, however, if he knew the same thing, he would have wanted to do; e.g., if someone, about to hunt a beast, kills an enemy whom he would have wanted to kill anyway if he had known. Consequent ignorance is that of which someone is the cause for himself through his will, and it is either affected or supine. Affected ignorance is when a man on purpose does not

Latin:

Peccatum ignorantiæ est actus, legi diuinæ difformis, cuius caussa est ignorantia non affectata aut supina, sed inuincibilis in se & caussa sua, cum seria pœnitentia coniuncta.

Obs. I. Aliud est, cum quis ignorans peccat, & aliud, quando per ignorantiam peccat. Ignorans peccat, qui eo ipso dum peccat, ignorat, quid agat, vt ebrius, iracundus; illa ipsa tamen ignorantia non est caussa actus peccaminosi; sed aliud quidpiam, quod ignorantiam illam induxit, videlicet ebrietas aut iracundia. Per ignorantiam vero peccat, quando actionis malæ caussa est ignorantia, quatenus excludit scientiam, quæ alias actum peccandi fuisset impeditura. Est enim ignorantia caussa remouens, impediens.

Obs. II. Caussa peccati inuoluntarii est ignorantia inuincibilis, quæ debita diligentia adhibita depelli aut superari nequit, v. gr. Si quis in silua securi finderet ligna, & feriret occideretque hominem, inter vinbrosa virgulta latentem, non esset voluntarius homicida. At non facit peccatum inuoluntarium ignorantia vincibilis, quæ adhibita diligentia superari ac tolli potest; quippe quæ arguit hominis negligentiam aut malitiam, adeoque supina, vel affectata est. Ceterum videtur interdum ignorantia inuincibilis esse, quæ tamen, si caussam respicias, vincibilis est, v. gr. Si quis lubens vino vel ceretisia se onerauerit, & hominem occideret ebrius, illius ignorantia videtur esse inuincibilis, sed reuera vincibilis est, potuisset enim a potu, intemperantius hausto, abstinere.

Obs. III. Ignorantia alia actum voluntatis antecedit, alia concomitatur, alia consequitur. Antecedens ignorantia est caussa, vt homo aliquid velit, quod non vellet, si sciuisset. Talis ignorantia est, cum ea quis ignorat, quæ nescire poterat in hac aut illa re, nec scire tenebatur, & coincidit cum ignorantia inuincibili; v. gr. cum quis in prælio hostem interfecturus, interficit fratrem, quem nec sciuit, nec scire potuit, prælio isti interesse. Concomitans ignorantia dicitur, cum quis ignorans aliquid facit, quod tamen, si sciret idem, facere vellet; v. gr. si quis, bestiam petiturus, occidit hostem, quem alias, si sciuisset interficere voluisset. Consequens ignorantia est, cuius aliquis sibi per voluntatem caussa est, estque vel affectata, vel supina. Affectata ignorantia est, quando homo data opera aliquid scire non


### Question XVII

want to know something, so that he may be able to sin more freely; e.g., when the impious man wants to be ignorant that God is the most just avenger of crimes. Supine ignorance is when someone, through negligence, is ignorant of that which he could have known. Thus, the Jews are said to have killed the author of life, Christ, through ignorance, Acts 3:17, which ignorance was contracted through negligence, and was therefore supine. Concomitant ignorance does not make a sin involuntary; supine. Concomitant ignorance does not make a sin involuntary; for those things which are followed by no sorrow are held to be voluntary. 2) Affected ignorance, just as it is absolutely voluntary, so it does not make a sin involuntary. 3) Supine ignorance, contracted through negligence, diminishes the τὸ voluntarium in a certain way, although it does not make the action entirely involuntary. Wherefore, a sin of ignorance is properly that whose cause is antecedent ignorance, and that which is invincible in itself and in its cause.

XVII. What is a sin of infirmity?

A sin of infirmity is an act, conflicting with the divine law, both arising from depraved concupiscence that is always active, suddenly creeping in around the full consent of the will, and committed from the vehemence of the affections and precipitation.

Obs. I. To sins of infirmity belong 1) sudden inordinate motions, which proceed from a connate concupiscence that is always operative, as if by a necessity of nature, without the full consent of the will; and therefore by some authors they are referred to original sin itself. See CHEMNIT. loc. p. 257. Rightly, however, they are also called actual sins, because they are second acts opposing the divine law. As D. KROMAYER observes in his theologia positivo-polem., some distinguish between the first and second motions of concupiscence, and subdivide those again into first-first and second-first, undoubtedly following JEROME, who calls the first motions προπάθειαν; e.g., the suggestion, sense, and motion was first-first, when this perverse thought crept into Achan: what? if I were to make this golden tongue my own? To which was added delight, or semi-full consent, from which is the second-first motion: It would be useful to me for this golden tongue to become mine. Finally, full consent supervenes, the second motion: I will make this tongue my own. Full consent makes a sin. 2) It is also called a sin of infirmity when the judgment of reason is disturbed by the vehemence of the affections, and a man is carried away to do something, without the consent of the intellect and will, by the sole impulse of the sensitive appetite, as when someone does something out of vehement anger, excessive love, and fear, e.g., when the apostle Peter, inflamed by vehement anger, cuts off the right ear of Malchus, John 18:10; the disciples, struck by fear, abandon Jesus and flee, Matthew 26:56. (*).

Latin:

vult, vt eo liberius peccare possit; v. gr. cum impius nescire vult, Deum esse iustissimum scelerum vindicem. Supina ignorantia est, quando quis per negligentiam id ignorat, quod scire poterat. Sic Iudæi ducem vitæ, Christum, per ignorantiam interfecisse dicuntur, Act. III, 17. quæ ignorantia per negligentiam contracta, adeoque supina erat. Non facit peccatum inuoluntarium 1) ignorantia concomitans; quippe ea, quæ nullus subsequitur dolor, pro voluntariis habentur. 2) Ignorantia affectata, sicut absolute voluntaria est, ita non facit peccatum inuoluntarium. 3) Ignorantia supina, per negligentiam contracta, minuit τὸ voluntarium quodammodo, licet non faciat actionem prorsus inuoluntariam. Quare proprie peccatum ignorantiæ est, cuius caussa est ignorantia antecedens, eaque inuincibilis in se, & in caussa sua.

XVII. Quid est peccatum infirmitatis?

Peccatum infirmitatis est actus, cum lege diuina pugnans, tum ex praua concupiscentia semper actuosa, subito circa plenum voluntatis consensum surrepens, tum ex vehementia affectuum & præcipitantia commissus.

Obs. I. Ad peccata infirmitatis pertinent 1) motus inordinati subitanei, qui a connata concupiscentia semper operosa velut ex naturæ necessitate citra plenum voluntatis consensum proficiscuntur; ideoque a quibusdam auctoribus ad ipsum peccatum originis referuntur. Vid. CHEMNIT. loc. p. 257. Recte tamen etiam peccata actualia vocantur, quia sunt actus secundi legi diuinæ aduersantes. Obseruante D. KROMAYERO in theologia positiuo-polem. quidam inter motus concupiscentiæ primos & secundos distinguunt, & illos rursus in primo-primos & secundo-primos subdiuidunt, dubio procul secuti HIERONYMVM, qui motus primos προπάθειαν vocat; v. gr. suggestio, sensus & motus primo primus fuit, cum Achani subrepsit hæc peruersa cogitatio: quid? si hanc linguam auream meam facerem? Cui accessit delectatio, siue consensus semiplenus, ex quo est motus secundo-primus: Vtile mihi esset, hanc linguam auream fieri meam. Tandem superuenit consensus plenus, motus-secundus: Hanc linguam faciam meam. Consensus plenus facit peccatum. 2) Peccatum infirmitatis vocatur etiam, quando per affectus vehementiam iudicium rationis turbatur, & homo abripitur ad aliquid agendum, citra consensum intellectus & voluntatis, solo impetu appetitus sensitiui, vt, cum quis ex vehementi ira, nimio amore & metu aliquid facit, v. gr. Cum apostolus Petrus, vehementi accensus ira, Malcho dextram aurem amputat, Io. XVIII, 10. discipuli, metu perculsi, Iesum derelinquunt & fugiunt, Matth. 26, 56. (*).


### Q. XVIII. What is a mortal sin?

A mortal sin, or deadly sin, is that which is imputed to the sinner in the second act unto death.

Latin:

Peccatum mortale, seu mortiferum est, quod peccanti actu secundo ad mortem imputatur. Quaest.


### Q. XIX. How will you define mortal sin more specifically, with respect to the reborn who succumb to the flesh?

a mortal sin is that by which the reborn, overcome by the flesh and thus failing to remain in the state of regeneration, transgress the divine law against the dictate of conscience with a deliberate purpose of the will, and by that very act lose saving faith, cast off the grace of the Holy Spirit, and plunge themselves into a state of wrath, death, and condemnation.

Latin:

Peccatum mortale est, quo renati a carne victi, atque adeo in statu regenerationis non permanentes, contra dictamen conscientiae, deliberato voluntatis proposito, legem divinam transgrediuntur, & eo ipso fidem salvificam amittunt, gratiam Spiritus sancti excutiunt, seque ipsos in statum irae, mortis & condemnationis coniiciunt. Quaest.


### Q. XX. What is a venial sin?

A venial sin is that which, although it may be worthy of death, is not however imputed to the sinner unto death.
