It is defined more fully: A venial sin is every involuntary sin in the reborn, which neither casts off the indwelling grace of the Holy Spirit, nor extinguishes faith, but at the same moment in which it is committed, has forgiveness joined to it by an inseparable bond. Obs.

Obs. I. The distinction of sin into mortal and venial is not taken from the merit of sin; for every sin of itself, and by its own nature, in the legal forum is damnable by merit: but from a certain malicious ignorance (α), 2 Pet. III, 5. Luc. XII, 48. to which must be referred a malicious interpretation of law and right, and a false opinion of a just cause, Luc. XXIII, 34. Io. XVI, 2. Act. III, 17. 1 Tim. I, 13. seqq. (β) A right and integral deliberation can never exist in any transgression; for it would be such, if one had weighed all the reasons not only from one side but from both sides before he sinned: in which way it could never happen that the reasons on both sides would be seen as if placed in equilibrium; the reasons for the good side could not but have much more weight and moment, through the power of truth, being far greater than any error. (γ) Also, all deliberation is sometimes absent from a man in the most serious of all sins, if one has acquired a habit and custom of doing evil, to the extent that he is not even conscious of his own action. Nor does the impious man always have space for deliberation, yet he is perpetually prone, ready, and headlong to do evil. Although a singular and, as it is said, actual purpose is not present, at least regarding this action, with the occasion offered more quickly than thought: yet there is always in the mind a general, or, as it is said, habitual purpose: What I will, that I will do. The principle of acting in an impious man is always his own will, an adversary to the divine. Suppose, therefore, that he was constrained by the straits of time and destitute of counsel in this action, and thus undertook it hastily; it is asked: whether he would have done his business better, or much worse, if it had been permitted to him to meditate long before; and not to institute the matter without counsel and deliberation? Ierem. IX, 5. It will not be difficult to explain the sins of both kinds by an accurate definition. Namely, infirmity is a certain defect of strength. For whatever is infirm, it certainly has some strength, even if attenuated and diminished, certainly not yet perfect. Therefore, in a moral sense, infirmity is a certain defect of the strength to do good, since the effect does not always correspond to the will and endeavor, Rom. VII, 18. But where there is strength to do good, there is spiritual life. For a man, even if he is most infirm, yet he is alive, it must be. That life, however, is salutary and is a trust placed in Christ, Gal. II, 20. In a man born again and renewed, but not yet perfect, there is 1) a continuous sorrow for innate depravity, and its motions, which he himself feeling, but not consenting to, experiences daily, 2) a continuous study

1) From the diverse condition of the subject, or the person sinning. For venial sin is in the reborn; mortal sin is in those who either were never reborn, or, overcome by the predominating flesh, have fallen from the state of grace. 2) From the estimation of God according to the Gospel; because God, as a reconciled and gracious Father, does not impute the sins of infirmity and ignorance to the reborn for guilt and punishment. 3) From the event. Mortal sin casts the sinner headlong into a state of wrath, death, and condemnation, so that if he should die in that state without repentance, he would be entirely condemned: but venial sin, because it has forgiveness as an inseparable companion, can consist with the grace of God and saving faith.

Obs. II. The distinction between mortal and venial sin does not coincide in all respects with the distinction of sin into voluntary and involuntary. For sins are called voluntary and involuntary by reason of the cause; mortal and venial by reason of the subject, the divine estimation, and the event. In the unregenerate, every sin, whether it be voluntary or involuntary, is mortal, or actually deadly; for he who does not believe in the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him, John 3:36. But in the reborn, who succumb to the flesh, those sins are deadly which are committed with the full intention of the will; but those which are committed either out of ignorance or out of the infirmity of the flesh, those God, being propitious, deems worthy of forgiveness.

Obs. III. The distinction of sin into mortal and venial is most firmly founded in the Holy Scriptures and has long been received in the Church. For as St. Paul testifies: There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit, Rom. 8:1. Also v. 13: If you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you mortify the deeds of the body, you will live. The sense of these apostolic pronouncements is: As long as the reborn, by the power of the Holy Spirit, suppress and mortify the disordered motions of the flesh, those vicious motions will not actually condemn them, but will be venial sins. But if the reborn yield to the irritations of the flesh, so that it predominates, they will be cast into a state of death and condemnation, and their sins will be actually deadly (*) TERTULLIAN in his book De Pudicitia uses the same diction, saying: Some sins are capital or mortal, others of daily incursion. AUGUSTINE, book XI. of De Civitate Dei calls mortal sins crimes that devastate the conscience.

Question.

of amendment and growth to be taken daily, with the providence and care to avoid every occasion for sinning. Corollary: In an impious man, not yet renewed, since he is indeed devoid of all spiritual life, Eph. 2:1, nor is he able to do anything well, nothing but evil, רע רק, Gen. 6:5, in him therefore there is absolutely no sin of infirmity, nor can there even be any. Malice (which name is indeed that of a certain specific vice, if we wish to speak Latin, but by usage, which we follow, it extends more broadly) is a perversity of the mind, alienated from God and not yet reconciled to God, recalling everything to its own will. Hence 1) there is no sorrow in him for sins, no detestation of them, except by reason of certain temporal and earthly effects, which Φιλαυτία, to which alone he yields, warns him that he has harmed himself: 2) no zeal for repenting and acting more cautiously in his own affairs for the future, except for civil reasons, Jer. 8:6. He is always wax to be bent into vice, harsh to those who admonish him. Corollary: In recognizing the sins of malice, not only this or that action ought to be considered, but also the whole disposition and viciousness of the mind. Whatever, therefore, an ἄπισος man, not reconciled to God, does, whether knowingly or unknowingly, whether thoughtfully, so that the crime was meditated long before, or hastily and agitated by vehement motions of the mind, all that is of malice.

Latin:

Peccatum veniale est, quod licet morte dignum sit, non tamen ad mortem peccanti imputatur.

Uberius definitur: Peccatum veniale est omne peccatum involuntarium in renatis, quod neque gratiam inhabitantem Spiritus sancti excutit, neque fidem exstinguit, sed eodem momento, quo committitur, veniam indivulso nexu coniunctam habet.

Obs. I. Distinctio peccati in mortale, & veniale non est petita a merito peccati; omne namque peccatum ex se, & natura sua, in foro legali est damnabile merito: sed a dimim (α) est quaedam ignorantia malitiosa, 2 Pet. III, 5. Luc. XII, 48. ad quam referri debet malitiosa iuris legisque interpretatio, & falsa iustae causae opinio, Luc. XXIII, 34. Io. XVI, 2. Act. III, 17. 1 Tim. I, 13. seqq. (β) Deliberatio recta, eademque integra nunquam potest esse in ullo delicto; esset autem ea, si quis ante, quam deliquerit, rationes non solum ab una parte sed in utramque partem omnes ponderasset: quo pacto fieri non posset unquam, ut rationes utrimque, tamquam in equilibrio positae cernerentur; rationes in bonam partem non possent non multo plus habere ponderis ac momenti, per vim veritatis, errore omni longe maioris. (γ) Deliberatio etiam omnis interdum ab homine abest in peccatis omnium gravissimis, si quis habitum adquisivit, & consuetudinem male agendi, usque eo, ut ne conscius quidem ipse sit actionis suae. Nec semper habet impius homo spatium deliberationis, perpetuo tamen pronus, promtus ac praeceps, ad male agendum. Quamuis non adsit propositum singulare, & ut dici solet, attuale, quantum quidem ad hancce actionem, opinione citius oblata occasione: semper tamen in animo inest propositum generale, seu, ut dicitur, habituale: Quod volam, id agam. Principium agendi in homine improbo semper est sua voluntas, divinae aduerfaria. Fac igitur, eum in hac actione angustiis temporis cohibitum & consilii inopem fuisse, atque adeo festinanter illam suscepisse; quaeritur: utrum melius rem suam egisset, anne multo peius, si licuisset ipsi, diu ante meditari; nec fine consilio ac deliberatione rem instituere? Ierem. IX, 5. Non erit difficile, adcurata definitione peccata utriusque generis explicare. Scilicet infirmitas est defectio quaedam virium. Quidquid enim infirmum est, id profecto habet vires aliquas, tametsi attenuatas atque imminutas, certe nondum perfectas. Morali igitur ratione infirmitas est defectus quidam virium bene agendi, quando quidem voluntati & conatui non semper effectus respondet, Rom. VII, 18. Vbi autem vires sunt bene agendi, ibi est vita spiritualis. Homo enim, etiam si maxime infirmus fit, tamen vivus fit, necesse est. Illa vero vita est salutaris & in Christo collocata fiducia, Gal. II, 20. In homine denuo nato ac renouato, sed nondum perfecto, est 1) continuus dolor de innata vitiositate, eiusque motibus, quos ipse sentiens, at non consentiens, quotidie experitur, 2) continuum studium

1) a diuersa conditione subiecti, siue personæ peccantis. Nam peccatum veniale est in renatis; peccatum mortale in iis, qui vel nunquam fuerunt regeniti, vel a prædominante carne victi, e statu gratiæ exciderunt. 2) Ab æstimatione Dei secundum euangelium; quia Deus reconciliatus & gratiosus pater renatis peccata infirmitatis & ignorantiæ ad culpam & pœnam non imputat. 3) Ab euentu. Peccatum mortale peccantem in statum iræ, mortis & condemnationis præcipitem agit, vt, si in illo statu absque pœnitentia moriatur, omnino condemnetur: peccatum autem veniale, quia veniam indiuiduam comitem habet, cum gratia Dei & fide saluifica consistere potest.

Obs. II. Distinctio peccati mortalis, & venialis, non per omnia coincidit cum distinctione peccati in voluntarium, & inuoluntarium. Nam voluntaria, & inuoluntaria dicuntur peccata ratione caussæ; mortalia, & venialia ratione subiecti, æstimii diuini, & euentus. In irregenitis omne peccatum, voluntarium, an inuoluntarium fuerit, est mortale, siue actu mortiferum; qui enim non credit filio, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super illo, Io. III, 3. 6. Renatis autem, carni succumbedtibus, mortifera sunt peccata, quæ fiunt plena voluntatis intentione; at quæ vel ex ignorantia, vel ex infirmitate carnis patrantur, illa Deus propitius venia dignatur.

Obs. III. Est distinctio peccati in mortale, & veniale in sacris litteris fundatissima, & in ecclesia dudum recepta. Teste namque S. Paullo: Nihil condemnationis est in iis, qui in Christo Iesu non secundum carnem ambulant, sed secundum Spiritum, Rom. VIII, 1. it. v. 13. Si secundum carnem viuitis, moriemini; si vero Spiritu actiones corporis mortificatis, viuetis. Quorum effatorum apostolicorum sensus est: Quamdiu renati virtute Spiritus S. inordinatos carnis motus supprimemt & mortificabunt; tamdiu motus illi vitiosi actu non damnabunt, sed erunt peccata venialia. At si renati obsequentur irritationibus carnis, vt hæc prædominetur; in statum mortis & condemnationis coniicientur, eruntque peccata eorum actu mortifera (*) TERTVLLIANVS libr. de pudicit. eadem vtitur dictione inquiens: Quædam peccata sunt capitalia seu mortalia, quædam quotidianæ incursationis. AVGVSTIN. libr. XI. de C. D. mortalia peccata vocat crimina conscientiam vastantia.

Quæst.

emendationis atque incrementi quotidie capiendi, cum prouidentia & cura euitandi omnem ad peccandum occasionem. Consectarium: In homine impio, nondumque renouato, quoniam is quidem omni caret vita spirituali, Eph. II, 1. nec valet quidpiam bene agere, nil, nisi male, רע רק, Gen. VI, 5. in eo igitur omnino nullum est, ac ne potest quidem vllum esse, infirmitatis peccatum. Malitia (quod quidem nomen certi cuiusdam vitii est, si latine loqui velimus, sed vsu, quem sequimur, latius patet) est peruersitas animi, a Deo abalienati, nondumque Deo reconciliati, omnia ad suum arbitrium reuocantis. Hinc 1) nullus in eo dolor est de peccatis, nulla eorum detestatio, nisi ratione effectuum quorumdam temporalium, ac terrestrium, quod Φιλαυτία, cui vni obsequitur, ipsum admonet, se sibi nocuisse: 2) nullum studium resipiscendi, remque suam in posterum cautius agendi, nisi ob ciuiles rationes, Ierem. VIII, 6. Semper ipse est cereus in vitium flecti, monitoribus asper. Consectarium: In cognoscendis peccatis malitiæ non solum hæc, vel illa actio debet considerari, sed & tota animi indoles ac vitiositas. Quidquid igitur homo ἄπισος, nec Deo reconciliatus, agit, siue sciens, siue insciis, siue cogitate, vt multo ante meditatum sit scelus, siue festinanter, ac vehementibus animi motibus agitatus, id omne est malitiæ.


### Q. XXI. Are certain sins venial by their own nature?

No sins are so light that they are worthy of pardon by their own nature; but all sins by their own nature in the legal forum are mortal, or worthy of death and eternal damnation.

Proof 1) Because every sin by itself and by its own nature is ἀνομία (lawlessness), 1 John 3:4. Therefore, every sin by itself and by its own nature is joined with the offense of God and the guilt of eternal damnation. The consequence is proven: because, as the divine law binds to perfect obedience under the threat of eternal damnation; so its transgression, even in the smallest matters, offends God, and brings upon the transgressor the wrath of God and eternal damnation.

2) Deut. 27:26; Gal. 3:10 it is expressly said: Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all things which are written in the book of the law: But he who commits a venial sin does not remain in all things which are written in the book of the law: Therefore he is cursed by the law on account of that sin.

3) The wages of every sin is death, Rom. 6:23. Therefore death is the wages even of venial sin.

4) Whoever shall have kept the whole law, but has stumbled in one (point), has become guilty of all, James 2:10. Therefore he who commits a sin of infirmity is guilty of all divine precepts. But if sin draws the guilt of wrath and damnation on account of the violated whole divine law, it is certainly not venial by itself, but is mortal.

5) Whoever shall have broken one of these least commandments shall be called least in the kingdom of God, Matt. 5:19. He who commits a venial sin breaks one of the least of God's commandments.

pardon we may now obtain; or whose pardon we may be able to obtain. The second interpretation is true; the first is entirely false; the third is not of this place. For as regards the second, venial sins are infirmities, namely those which fall upon men born again, because they are and remain such. But as to the first, no sin is venial; and as to the third, all are venial, as long as a man is among the living and a participant of the calling grace, if you depart from one, the sin against the Holy Spirit; of which it will be necessary to speak hereafter. But that is called sin not unto death which is not so imputed to the sinner as to truly make him guilty of damnation, although it could make him so by merit, if it were not for the intercession and it is most clearly evident to the man who has trusted wholly in Christ, that it is granted. Thus also the opposition is most rightly and most clearly evident. For pardon is not so openly opposed to death. But to die, and not to die, these are finally the opposites. But this is what is debated: What is sin unto death? I do not think that one sin is signified by that name, in the way indeed it pleases those to interpret it, to whom JOHN seems to speak of nothing else than the sin against the Holy Spirit, and in whose number the blessed Author also professes his own name below, at Q. 47. What then? Indeed it is one genus, in which many and various sins are contained. The arguments are clear to me, derived 1) from the distinction and opposition; for sin unto death is distinguished from all that which is not unto death, which, although it is likewise designated by the number of unity, no one will deny that it is not to be understood of some singular sin, but that it is spoken generally. The blessed LUTHER first indeed in v. 16 translates it into German thus: eine Sünde; then truly in the following verse in this way: etliche Sünde: 2) From the general definition, v. 17. πᾶσα ἀδικία ἁμαρτία ἐσί (all unrighteousness is sin), to which the division joined must be adequate, so that not a certain transgression is distinguished from the whole genus, but one genus from another: 3) From the diverse condition of the subjects. For impious and wicked men are not opposed to other impious men; but two genera of men are distinguished, in one of which are all those born again, in the other all who are contrary to them, v. 18. 19. Therefore it is necessary that two genera of sins also be distinguished, in both of which are numbered all the sins which are contained in the whole genus. I.e., sin not unto death is the universal genus of sins of infirmity, which are committed by men born again. On the contrary, that which is said to be unto death is the universal genus of sins of malice, which are perpetrated by men not born of God.

Therefore he shall be the least, i.e., nothing in the kingdom of heaven. For in heaven, as AUGUSTINE judges, there shall be nothing except what is great. 6) An account shall be required for every idle word even on the day of judgment. Matth. XII, 36. 37. Therefore, even a venial sin, to which the Papists refer the idle word, offends the heavenly judge. The antithesis is 1) of the Papists, asserting that certain sins are so light that they deserve pardon by their own nature. 2) Of the Socinians and Arminians, who extenuate sins of infirmity, just as if no account were taken of them in the kingdom of Christ. Their principal arguments are: I. A sin is called venial because it is worthy of pardon. Resp. A sin is called venial, not because it is worthy of pardon by its own nature; but because God, out of mercy, on account of the satisfaction and intercession of Christ, deems it worthy of pardon. Wherefore it is called venial not by itself, but by something extrinsic, and from an accidental outcome. II. There are given some sins which neither bring death to the soul, nor are they worthy of eternal punishment by their own nature: Therefore there are given some sins that are venial by their own nature. Resp. The antecedent, which is two-membered, is ambiguous regarding the first member, and false regarding the latter. For in the first member, the death of the soul can be taken either for eternal damnation, or for the loss, or lack, of grace. If the death of the soul is taken in the former way, the antecedent is false: since he is called cursed, whoever has not remained in all things which are written in the book of the law; but the curse of the law imports eternal death. But if in the latter way; it is indeed true that there are given sins which do not actually bring death to the soul; but it is denied that there are given sins which are not by their own nature such that they deserve the death of the soul and can bring it about. For that God does not withdraw His grace from the sinner for all sins is not from the nature and condition of the sins, but from the mercy of God and the merit of Christ. III. Consummated sin brings forth death, but not concupiscence, tempting, drawing away, and enticing, Iac. I, 15. Therefore, tempting concupiscence is a sin venial by its own nature. Resp. Sin, consummated by an external act and committed with deliberate malice, brings forth death actually: but concupiscence deserves death, and can bring it forth, unless it is remitted by the grace of God on account of the satisfaction and intercession of Christ. IV. Christ, Matth. V, 22, adjudges the punishment of hell not to anger against a brother, nor to uncomposed gestures, but only to manifest reviling: Therefore, anger and uncomposed gestures are sins venial by their own nature. Resp. Rash anger toward a brother is not a venial sin, but because it is a work of the flesh, it is mortiferous in act, as Paul teaches, Gal. V, 10. Wherefore by the names of judgment, council, and hell, eternal damnation is noted, and at the same time certain degrees of damnation are designated, which are recounted according to the custom of the Jewish polity. V. If all sins were mortal by their own nature, all sins would be equal: But the consequent is false: Therefore the antecedent is also. The falsity of the consequent is evident from the fact that some sins are like a gnat, some like a camel, Matth. XXIII, 24, some like a mote, some like beams, Luc. XXIV. Therefore some are venial by their own nature. Resp. Sins are unequal because of gradual guilt and greater or lesser malice, not because of an inherent dignity by which they might deserve pardon by their own nature. VI. Sins are venial either by themselves and by their own nature, or by accident and eventually: Not by accident and eventually; because thus even sins that are actually mortiferous would be venial; for the reason that it happens that even those are eventually forgiven to those who repent: Therefore, by themselves and by their own nature they are venial. Resp. A third option is given. Sins of infirmity are venial not by themselves; for thus they would be venial even in the unregenerate: nor only eventually: but because of the gracious estimation of God, who does not impute them to those who believe in Christ, but forgives them.

Latin:

Nulla peccata adeo leuia sunt, vt per se venia digna sint; sed omnia peccata ex natura sua in foro legali sunt mortalia, siue morte ac damnatione aeterna digna.

Prob. 1) Quia omne peccatum per se & natura sua est ἀνομία, I Io. III, 4. E. omne peccatum per se & natura sua coniunctum est cum offensa Dei, & reatu aeternae damnationis. Consequentia probatur: quia, vt lex diuina ad perfectam obedientiam sub comminatione aeternae damnationis obligat; ita eius transgressio etiam in minimis offendit Deum, accersitque transgressori iram Dei & damnationem aeternam.

2) Deut. XXVII, 26. Gal. III, 10. expresse dicitur: Maledictus omnis, qui non permanet in omnibus, quae scripta sunt in libro legis: At qui peccatum veniale committit, non permanet in omnibus, quae scripta sunt in libro legis: Ergo maledictus est per legem ob illud peccatum.

3) Omnis peccati stipendium mors est, Rom. VI, 23. E. mors stipendium est etiam peccati venialis.

4) Quisquis totam legem seruauerit, lapsus vero fuerit in vno (aliquo), factus est omnium reus, Iacob. II, 10. Ergo qui peccatum infirmitatis committit, omnium praeceptorum diuinorum reus est. At si peccatum attrahit reatum irae & damnationis, ob violatam totam legem diuinam, vtique per se non veniale, sed mortale est.

5) Quisquis soluerit vnum ex hisce mandatis minimis, minimus vocabitur in regno Dei, Matth. V, 19. Qui committit peccatum veniale, soluit vnum ex mandatis Dei minimis. Ergo

veniam iam impetremus; aut cuius veniam impetrare possimus. Secunda interpretatio vera est; prima prorsus falsa; tertia non huius loci. Nam quod ad secundam attinet, venialia peccata sunt infirmitates, nimirum ea, quae cadunt in denuo natos homines, quod sunt permanentque tales. Quantum vero ad primam, nullum peccatum est veniale; & quantam ad tertiam, omnia sunt venialia, quod homo in viuis est, & gratiae vocantis particeps, si ab vno discesseris, peccato in Spiritum Sanctum; de quo deinceps differendum erit. Peccatum vero non ad mortem nominatur illud, quod peccanti non ita imputatur, vt eum damnationis reum vere efficiat, tametsi posset ex merito efficere, nisi intercederet apertissimeque constat homini, qui totus Christo confisus est, tributa. Ita etiam rectissime apertissimeque constat oppositio. Non enim venia adeo aperte opponitur morti. Sed mori, & non mori, haec demum sunt opposita. Hoc autem in disceptatione versatur; Quid sit peccatum ad mortem? Non vnum peccatum eo nomine significari existimo, quem ad modum quidem interpretari illis placet, quibus IOANNES videtur loqui de non alio, quam peccato in Spiritum Sanctum, & quorum in numero b. Auctor suum quoque nomen profitetur infra, ad quaest. 47. Quid igitur? Quippe vnum genus, in quo multa ac varia peccata continentur. Luculentia mihi sunt argumenta depromta 1) ex distinctione atque oppositione; discernitur enim peccatum ad mortem ab omni eo, quod non est ad mortem, quod, quamuis itidem numero vnitatis designetur, nemo tamen ibit infitias, non de singulari aliquo peccato intelligendum, sed generaliter dictum esse. B. LVTHERVS primum quidem v. 16. germanice ita conuertit: eine Sünde; deinde vero v. seq. hoc modo: etliche Sünde: 2) Ex generali definitione, v. 17. πᾶσα ἀδικία ἁμαρτία ἐσί, cui adiunctam diuisionem oportet ad adaequatam esse, vt non delictum quoddam ab vniuerso genere, sed genus alterum ab altero distinguatur: 3) Ex diuersa subiectorum conditione. Non enim impii ac scelerati homines aliis impiis opponuntur; sed discernuntur duo hominum genera, quorum in vno sunt omnes denuo nati, in altero omnes illis contrarii, v. 18. 19. Necesse est igitur, peccatorum etiam duo genera distingui, quorum in vtroque numerentur omnia peccata, quae in toto genere continentur. E. peccatum non ad mortem est vniuersum genus peccatorum infirmitatis, quae ab hominibus denuo natis committuntur. Contra, quod ad mortem dicitur, est vniuersum genus peccatorum malitia, quae ab hominibus non ex Deo natis perpetrantur.

Ergo erit minimus, i. e. nullus in regno cœlorum. In cœlo enim, censente AVGVSTINO, nihil, nisi magnum, erit. 6) De quocunque verbo otioso etiam in die iudicii exigetur ratio. Matth. XII, 36. 37. Ergo & peccatum veniale, ad quod a Pontificiis refertur verbum otiosum, iudicem cœlestem offendit. Antithesis est 1) Pontificiorum, asserentium, quædam peccata adeo leuia esse, vt per se veniam mereantur. 2) Socinianorum & Arminianorum, peccata infirmitatis extenuantium, perinde, ac si eorum in regno Christi nulla habeatur ratio. Quorum præcipua sunt argumenta: I. Peccatum dicitur veniale; quia venia dignum est. Resp. Peccatum dicitur veniale, non quia per se venia dignum est; sed quia Deus ex misericordia, propter satisfactionem & intercessionem Christi, illud venia dignatur. Quare veniale dicitur non per se, sed per aliquod extrinsecum, & ab accidentali euentu. II. Dantur aliqua peccata, quæ nec mortem animæ afferunt, nec æterna pœna per se digna sunt: Ergo dantur quædam peccata per se venialia. Resp. Antecedens, quod bimembre est, quoad prius membrum, ambiguum, quoad posterius, falsum est. Nam in priori membro mors animæ accipi potest, vel pro damnatione æterna, vel pro amissione, siue carentia gratiæ. Si priori modo mors animæ accipiatur, falsum est antecedens: cum maledictus dicatur, quisquis non manserit in omnibus, quæ scripta sunt in libro legis; maledictio legis autem mortem æternam importat. Sin posteriori modo; verum quidem est, quod dentur peccata, quæ actu non afferant mortem animæ; negatur autem, dari peccata, quæ non suapte natura talia sint, vt mortem animæ mereantur, & afferre possint. Quod enim non ob peccata omnia gratiam suam Deus subtrahat peccatori, non est ex natura & conditione peccatorum, sed ex Dei misericordia & merito Christi. III. Peccatum consummatum parit mortem, non autem concupiscentia, tentans, abstrahens & inescans, Iac. I, 15. Ergo concupiscentia tentans, est peccatum per se veniale. Resp. Peccatum, opere externo consummatum, & destinata malitia commissum, parit mortem actu: at concupiscentia mortem meretur, eamque parere potest, nisi ex gratia Dei propter satisfactionem & intercessionem Christi remittatur. IV. Christus Matth. V, 22. non iræ in fratrem, neque incompositis gestibus, sed manifesto duntaxat conuitio pœnam gehennæ adiudicat: E. ira & incompositi gestus sunt peccata per se venialia. Resp. Ira temeraria erga fratrem non est peccatum veniale, sed quia opus carnis, mortiferum actu, docente Paullo, Gal. V, 10. Quare nominibus iudicii, concilii, & gehennæ, æterna notatur damnatio, & simul designantur certi damnationis gradus, qui secundum consuetudinem politiæ Iudaicæ recensentur. V. Si omnia peccata per se mortalia essent, omnia peccata forent paria: At consequens est falsum: Ergo & antecedens. Consequentis falsitas ex eo patet, quod quædam peccata sunt similia culici, quædam camelo, Matth. XXIII, 24. quædam festucæ, quædam trabibus, Luc. XXIV. Ergo quædam per se venialia sunt. Resp. Peccata sunt inæqualia ob culpam gradualem, & malitiam maiorem, vel minorem, non ob propriam dignitatem, ex qua per se veniam mereantur. VI. Peccata sunt venialia vel per se & natura sua, vel per accidens & euentualiter: Non per accidens & euentualiter; quia sic etiam peccata actu mortifera forent venialia; eo quod accidit, vt etiam illa resipiscentibus euentualiter condonentur: E. per se & natura sua sunt venialia. Resp. Datur tertium. Peccata infirmitatis sunt venialia non per se; nam sic etiam in irregenitis forent venialia: neque tantum euentualiter: sed propter gratiosam Dei æstimationem, qui eadem in Christum credentibus non imputat, sed condonat.


### Q. XXI. Are certain sins venial by their own nature?: Q

Q.

The causes of remission, or non-imputation, are: the mercy of God , the satisfaction and intercession of Christ , the efficacious operation of the Holy Spirit , and the daily repentance of the regenerate .

Proof a. As a father has compassion on his children, so Jehovah has compassion on those who fear Him. Ps. 103:13. But as a father forgives blemishes to his children, so God grants pardon to His regenerate children who sin out of ignorance or the infirmity of the flesh.

Proof b. My little children, I write these things to you, so that you may not sin: but if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. And He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world. 1 Jn. 2:1, 2. Thus John attributes the forgiveness of sins to the propitiation and intercession of Christ. There is therefore no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh, but according to the spirit, Rom. 8:1.

Proof c. The Holy Spirit, dwelling in the regenerate, represses the machinations of the flesh, lest it obtain dominion, and suggests good thoughts and pious desires. Hence it comes about that the law does not have the power to accuse and condemn the regenerate. Paul teaches this in Gal. 5:16, 17, 18. Walk in the Spirit, and you shall by no means fulfill the lust of the flesh. For the flesh does not merely lust against the spirit: but the spirit also against the flesh. And these are contrary to one another, so that you do not do the things that you wish. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.

Proof d. Therefore those sins in the regenerate are venial, which in the unregenerate are actually mortal; because the regenerate acknowledge the filth of sins adhering to them, grieve seriously over them, seek to have them covered by the merit of Christ, as by a shield of grace, and through the Spirit resist the lusts of the flesh. If by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live, Rom. 8:13.

Latin:

Quaest. XXII. Quae sunt causae, propter quas peccatum involuntarium renatis ad culpam & poenam actu secundo non imputatur?

Causae remissionis, sive non imputationis, sunt: misericordia Dei , satisfactio & intercessio Christi , efficax operatio Spiritus sancti , quotidiana poenitentia renatorum .

Prob. a. Sicut miseretur pater filiorum suorum: ita miseretur Iehouah timentium ipsum. Ps. CIII, 13. At sicut pater naevos condonat filiis: ita Deus veniam indulget renatis suis filiis ex ignorantia, aut infirmitate carnis peccantibus. Proinde benevole respicit miserum, afflictum spiritu, & timentem sibi super verbo Dei, Es. LXVI, 2.

Prob. b. Filii mei, haec scribo vobis, ut non peccetis: quod si quis peccauerit, paracletum habemus apud patrem, Iesum Christum iustum. Et ille est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, immo pro nostris non tantum, sed etiam pro totius mundi. 1 Io. II, 1. 2. Sic Ioannes veniam peccatorum tribuit propitiationi & intercessioni Christi. Nihil ergo condemnationis est in iis, qui in Christo Iesu non secundum carnem ambulant, sed secundum spiritum, Rom. VIII, 1.

Prob. c. Spiritus S. in renatis habitans, reprimit molitiones carnis, ne haec dominium obtineat, & suggerit bonas cogitationes, atque pia desideria. Inde fit, ut lex non habeat vim accusandi & damnandi renatos. Docet id Paullus Gal. V, 16, 17. 18. Spiritu ambulate, tum concupiscentiam carnis neutiquam perficietis. Non caro quidem concupiscit contra spiritum: sed & spiritus contra carnem. Haec autem aduersantur inuicem, ut non, quae vultis, ea faciatis. Quod si spiritu agimini, non estis sub lege.

Prob. d. Ideo peccata illa in renatis sunt venialia, quae in non renatis actu sunt mortalia; quia renati sordes peccatorum, sibi adhaerentes, agnoscunt, serio de illis dolent, merito Christi, velut gratiae vinbraculo, eas tegi petunt, & per Spiritum concupiscentiis carnis resistunt. Si spiritu actiones corporis mortificatis, viuetis, Rom. VIII, 13.


### Q. XXIII. What are

The effects of voluntary and mortal sin are: the loss of divine grace and the indwelling Spirit , the shipwreck of faith and the sting of conscience , and eternal death, unless earnest repentance is performed .

Proof a. Most worthy of note are the words of the Blessed LUTHER in the Smalcald Articles, p. 328. It must be known that if the saints, who still feel that they have original sin and daily repent of it and struggle with it, furthermore fall into manifest sins, such as David into adultery, murder, and blasphemy, these cast away faith and the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit does not allow sin to rule, to grow strong, and to obtain the victory and be consummated, but represses and restrains it, so that it cannot do what it wishes. But if it does what it wishes, certainly the Holy Spirit and faith are lost, nor do they exist together. For thus says John, 1 Ep. 3:9: Whoever has been born of God does not sin, and cannot sin.

Proof b. Hold faith and a good conscience, which some have rejected, and concerning the faith have suffered shipwreck, 1 Tim. 1:19. Faith and a good conscience are joined together by the apostle. For when this anchor is lost, the ship of faith is broken. That faith, which receives the remission of sins in a terrified heart that flees from sin, does not remain in those who obey their desires, nor does it exist with mortal sin, as the Apology of the A.C. teaches, p. 96.

Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, [drunkards, nor revilers, drunkards, nor revilers,]

nor shall extortioners inherit the kingdom of God, 1 Cor. VI, 9. 10. Those who indulge in mortal sins preclude for themselves access to the kingdom of glory.

Latin:

Effectus peccati voluntarii & mortalis sunt: gratiae diuinae & Spiritus inhabitantis amissio , naufragium fidei & morsus conscientiae , mors aeterna, nisi feria agatur poenitentia .

Prob. a. Memoratu dignissima sunt verba B. LUTHERI in articulis Smalcaldicis p. 328. Sciendum est, quod si sancti, qui originale peccatum adhuc habere sentiunt, & quotidie de eo poenitent, & cum eo luctantur, insuper ruant in manifesta peccata, ut Dauid in adulterium, homicidium, & blasphemiam, eos excutere fidem & spiritum S. Spiritus enim S. non finit peccatum dominari, inualescere & victoriam obtinere, ac consummari, sed reprimit & coercet, ne facere possit, quod vult. Si vero facit, quod vult, certe Spiritus S. & fides amittuntur, nec simul adsunt. Sic enim inquit Ioannes, 1 Ep. III, 9: Qui ex Deo natus est, non peccat, & peccare non potest.

Prob. b. Habeas fidem & bonam conscientiam, quam quidam repulerunt, & circa fidem naufragium fecerunt, 1 Tim. I, 19. Fides & bona conscientia ab apostolo coniunguntur. Nam amissa hac ancora, nauis fidei frangitur. Fides illa, quae accipit remissionem peccatorum in corde perterrefacto & fugiente peccatum, non manet in his, qui obtemperant cupiditatibus, nec existit cum mortali peccato, docente Apologia A. C. p. 96.

Prob. c. Ne errate: neque scortatores, neque idololatrae, neque moechi, neque molles, neque concumbentes cum maribus, neque fures, neque auari, neque ebriosi, neque calumniatores, ebriosi, neque calumniatores, ebriosi, neque calumniatores,

neque raptores, regnum Dei in hereditatem possidebunt, 1 Cor. VI, 9. 10. Qui peccatis mortalibus indulgent, aditum ad regnum gloriae sibi praecludunt.


### Q. XXIV. What is our own sin?

what is another's?

Our own sin is a vicious act, produced by our real influence a); another's sin, imputed to us, is an illicit act, to the production of which we contribute not indeed by real influence, but by effective intention, so that it may rightly be imputed to us b).

Proof a. Sin, formally our own, is perpetrated not only by our persuasion or exhortation, but also by our own powers, and thus by our real influence.

Proof b. He contributes to another's sin by effective intention who commands, counsels, consents, connives, does not oppose, does not manifest, and is thus the moral cause of another's sin.

The verses concerning moral cause are well known: Commanding, counseling, consenting, flattering, recurring, participating, being silent, not opposing, not manifesting. Paul gravely warns: Do not participate in the sins of others.

1 Tim. V, 22. The apostle implies that the sins of others can become our own, participatively and imputatively.

Question XXV. What are the sins of heart, mouth, &amp; deed?

Sins of the heart are depraved thoughts &amp; desires, which are cherished within the bosom of the human soul a); sins of the mouth are evil words &amp; gestures, which are expressed by the mouth b); sins of deed are acts, which are committed against the law of God by the external exertion of the limbs.

Proof. Christ joins the sins of deed, mouth, &amp; heart, Matth. V, 21. 22. You have heard that it was said to those of old: You shall not kill; but whoever kills shall be liable to judgment. But I say to you, that whoever is angry with his brother rashly; shall be liable to judgment: and whoever says: Raca; shall be liable to the council: but whoever says: You fool; shall be liable to the fire of hell. The Pharisees considered only those sins deadly which are consummated by external deed: but Jesus, the avenger of salvation, teaches that even sins of the heart (e.g., hatred toward one's neighbor) &amp; of the mouth (if one says: Raca, or: You fool,) attract the guilt of fault &amp; punishment.

Question XXVI. What are the sins of commission &amp; omission?

Sins of commission are positive acts, by which the negative precepts of God are violated.

Sins of omission are the suspensions of acts prescribed by the affirmative precepts of God.

Proof. The apostle James inculcates this distinction, ep. c. IV, 16. 17. But now you boast in your arrogance. All such boasting is evil. Therefore, to him who knows to do good, but does not do it, it is sin. Evil boasting is a sin of commission; not doing good is a sin of omission.

Obs. Although there is usually in a sin of omission some illicit positive act, either interior of the will; such as: willing to omit what is commanded: or exterior, such as: an operation by which one is hindered from that which one is bound to do: yet such a positive act is not always or necessarily required, but the very not doing of what is commanded is a sin.

Question XXVII.

What sins are committed against God, the neighbor, and the sinner himself? Sins against God are those which immediately and directly injure God Himself a). Sins against the neighbor are those which immediately regard and offend the neighbor b). Sins against the sinner himself are those which are directed straight toward the person of the sinner himself c).

Proof a. Sins which are committed against the first table of the Decalogue immediately injure God, e.g., idolatry, blasphemy, perjury, magic, contempt of the divine word. The priest Eli proposes to his sons the distinction between sins against God and the neighbor, 1 Sam. II, 25: If a man sins against a man, God will judge him; but if a man sins against Jehovah, who shall intercede for him?

Proof b. He who strikes against the precepts of the second table of the Decalogue sins partly against himself, partly against his neighbor, by beating, killing, defrauding, slandering, etc., the same. Proof c. Through fornication, drunkenness, αὐτοχειρίαν [self-murder], etc., a man sins against himself. In a peculiar way, the fornicator is said to sin against his own body, 1 Cor. VI, 13, because he abuses his own body and converts it into the matter of illicit pleasure. That which the drunkard abuses is outside of his own body, but the αὐτόχειρ [self-murderer] destroys his own body.

Latin:

quod alienum?

Peccatum nostrum est actus vitiosus, reali nostro influxu productus a); peccatum alienum, nobis imputatum, est actus illicitus, ad cuius productionem nos non reali quidem influxu, efficaci tamen intentione concurrimus, vt iure nobis imputari queat b).

Prob. a. Peccatum, formaliter nostrum, non nostro tantum suasu, aut hortatu, sed & viribus propriis, adeoque reali nostro influxu perpetratur.

Prob. b. Efficaci intentione concurrit ad peccatum alienum, qui praecipit, consulit, consentit, conniuet, non obstat, non manifestat, atque adeo causa moralis est peccati alieni.

Noti sunt versus de causa morali: Iussio, consilium, consensus, palpo, recursus, Participians, mutus, non obstans, non manifestans. Graviter monet Paullus: Ne participa de peccatis alienis.

1 Tim. V, 22. Innuit apostolus peccata aliena posse fieri nostra, participatiue, atque imputatiue.

Quaest. XXV. Quae sunt peccata cordis, oris & operis?

Peccata cordis sunt prauae cogitationes & cupiditates, quae intra sinum animi humani fouentur a); peccata oris sunt mala verba & gestus, quae ore exprimuntur b); peccata operis sunt facta, quae externo membrorum nisu contra legem Dei patrantur.

Prob. Christus peccata operis, oris, & cordis coniungit, Matth. V, 21. 22. Audiistis, quod veteribus dictum sit: Non occides; quisquis autem occiderit, obnoxius erit iudicio. Ego vero dico vobis, quod quisquis irascitur fratri suo temere; obnoxius erit iudicio: quicunque vero dixerit: Racha; obnoxius erit synedrio: quicunque autem dixerit: stulte; obnoxius erit gehennae ignis. Pharisaei illa peccata tantum censebant mortifera, quae externo opere consummantur: at salutis vindex Iesus docet, etiam peccata cordis (v. gr. odium in proximum) & oris (si quis dicat: Racha, aut: stulte,) reatum culpae & poenae attrahere.

Quaest. XXVI. Quae sunt peccata commissionis & omissionis?

Peccata commissionis sunt actus positivi, quibus praecepta Dei negatiua violantur.

Peccata omissionis sunt suspensiones actuum, praeceptis Dei affirmatiuis praescriptorum.

Prob. Apostolus Iacobus hoc discrimen inculcat, ep. c. IV, 16. 17. Nunc vero gloriamini in arrogantiis vestris. Omnis gloriatio talis mala est. Ei ergo, qui scit bonum facere, sed non facit, peccatum est. Gloriatio mala est peccatum commissionis; non facere bonum, est peccatum omissionis.

Obs. Quamuis plerumque in peccato omissionis sit aliquis actus positiuus illicitus, vel interior voluntatis; vt: velle omittere, quod praeceptum est: vel exterior, vt: operatio, qua impeditur quis ab eo, quod facere tenetur: non tamen semper aut necessario requiritur talis actus positiuus, sed ipsum non facere, quod praeceptum est, peccatum est.

Quaestio XXVII.

Quae peccata committuntur in Deum, proximum & ipsum peccantem? Peccata in Deum sunt, quae immediate & directe ipsum Deum laedunt a). Peccata in proximum sunt, quae immediate proximum respiciunt & offendunt b). Peccata in ipsum peccantem sunt, quae in ipsam peccantis personam directe feruntur c).

Prob. a. Quae peccata committuntur aduersus primam decalogi tabulam, immediate laedunt Deum, v. gr. idolatria, blasphemia, periurium, magia, contemptus verbi diuini. Discrimen peccatorum in Deum, & proximum sacerdos Eli filiis suis considerandum proponit, 1 Sam. II, 25. Si peccauerit vir viro, iudicabit eum Deus, si ergo Iehouae peccauerit vir, quis deprecabitur pro illo?

Prob. b. Impingens in praecepta secundae tabulae decalogi partim in se, partim in proximum peccat, eundem verberando, occidendo, defraudando, calumniando &c. Prob. c. Per scortationem, ebrietatem, αὐτοχειρίαν &c. homo in se ipsum peccat. Peculiari ratione scortator in proprium corpus peccare dicitur, 1 Cor. VI, 13. quia suo corpore abutitur, idque in materiam illicitae voluptatis conuertit. Id, quo ebrius abutitur, extra ipsius corpus est, αὐτόχειρ autem corpus suum destruit.


### Question XXVIII

Which sins are crying, and which are non-crying, or of toleration? Crying sins are vicious acts which, even while men are silent or conniving, provoke God to vengeance a). Non-crying sins are called those which God tolerates by His long-suffering, and either defers the punishment or, if they have been committed by the reborn, remits it b).

Proof a. Crying sins, as the Scripture testifies, were: 1) Fratricide, committed by Cain, Gen. IV, 10: The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me. 2) Sodomitic sins, Gen. XVIII, 20: The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is multiplied, and their sin has become very grave. 3) The oppression of the Israelites in Egypt, Exod. III, 9: Hear their cry. Add the oppression of widows and orphans, Exod. XXII, 22. 4) The denial of wages to be paid to laborers, James V, 4. Whence the verses were born: The voice of blood, and of Sodom, cries to heaven, The voice of the oppressed, and the withheld wage of labors. These four sins are called crying, not exclusively, as if there were not more, but because they are individually recounted in the sacred letters. Otherwise, there is no doubt that enormous sins, by which the same measure of iniquity is filled, cry to heaven and demand vengeance, e.g., blasphemy, parricide, adultery, rapine, etc.

Proof b. God is said to have overlooked the ignorance of the Gentiles until the coming of the Messiah, Acts XVII, 30. God tolerated the polygamy of the fathers under the Old Covenant, and remitted it to those who continued in daily repentance.

Latin:

Quenam peccata sunt clamantia, quae non-clamantia, seu tolerationis? Peccata clamantia sunt actus vitiosi, qui, hominibus etiam tacentibus, vel conniuentibus, ad vindictam Deum prouocant a). Peccata non-clamantia dicuntur, quae Deus longanimitate sua tolerat, & poenam vel differt, vel, si a renatis sint commissa, remittit b).

Prob. a. Peccatum clamans, teste scriptura, erant: 1) Fratricidium, a Caino commissum, Gen. IV, 10. Vox sanguinum fratris tui ad me clamat. 2) Peccata Sodomitica, Gen. XVIII, 20. Clamor Sodomae & Gomorrae multiplicatus est, & eorum peccatum valde graue factum. 3) Oppressio Israëltarum in Aegypto, Exod. III, 9. Clamorem eorum exaudi. Adde oppressionem viduarum & orphanorum, Exod. XXII, 22. 4) Denegatio mercedis operariis soluendae, Iac. V, 4. Vnde nati versus: Clamitat ad caelum vox sanguinis, & Sodomorum, Vox oppressorum, merces detenta laborum. Haec quatuor peccata dicuntur clamantia, non exclusive, quasi non dentur plura, sed quia sigillatim in sacris litteris recensentur. Nullum ceteroqui est dubium, quin peccata enormia, quibus eadem iniquitatis mensura impletur, clament in caelum, & vindictam poscant, v. gr. blasphemia, parricidium, adulterium, rapinae, &c.

Prob. b. Ignorantiam gentilium Deus vsque ad Messiae aduentum dissimulasse dicitur, Act. XVII, 30. Polygamiam patrum sub veteri foedere Deus tolerauit, iisdemque quotidiana poenitentiam continuantibus remisit.


### Question XXIX

Which sin is considered graver? Which lighter? Sins are called graver and lighter on account of greater and lesser guilt, or the foulness adhering to them. Proof. The sins of Jerusalem are reckoned graver than the offenses of Samaria and Sodom, Ez. XVI, 47, which God Himself calls to mind, saying: You have corrupted yourself more than all of them in your ways. The citizens of Jerusalem had walked in more perverse ways than the Samaritans or the Sodomites, those famous architects of crimes.

Sodomites, famous architects of crimes.

Obs. One sin is graver than another: 1) By reason of the efficient cause, or the person sinning. A Christian sins more gravely than a Gentile, binding himself by the same crime; 2) By reason of the impelling cause. He sins more gravely who commits adultery with his neighbor's wife for the sake of satisfying lust, than he who steals, compelled by hunger. 3) By reason of the object. He offends more gravely who kills his father than he who kills an enemy. 4) By reason of the norm. He sins more gravely who violates the first table of the Decalogue than he who violates the second. 5) By reason of the effect. The more damage a sin brings, the graver it is considered.

Latin:

Quodnam peccatum censetur grauius? quod leuius? Grauiora, & leuiora dicuntur peccata ob maiorem & minorem culpam, siue foeditatem adhaerentem. Prob. Peccata Hierosolymae reputantur grauiora delictis Samariae & Sodomae, Ez. XVI, 47. quae ipsi Deus in mentem reuocat, inquiens: Corrupisti te prae omnibus illis in viis tuis. Ciues Hierosolymae peruersiores iuerant vias, quam Samaritani, aut Sodomitae famosi scelerum architecti.

Sodomitæ famosi scelerum architecti.

Obs. Peccatum unum altero gravius est: 1) Ratione causae efficientis, seu personae peccantis. Gravius peccat christianus, quam gentilis, eodem se obstringens crimine; 2) Ratione causae impellentis. Gravius delinquit, qui explendae libidinis causa stuprum infert uxori proximi, quam qui, fame coactus, furatur. 3) Ratione obiecti. Gravius impingit, qui patrem, quam qui hostem interficit. 4) Ratione normae. Gravius peccat, qui primam, quam qui secundam tabulam decalogi violat. 5) Ratione effectus. Quo plura damna affert peccatum, eo gravius censetur.


### Q. XXX. What sin is occult?

what manifest?

An occult sin is that which is unknown even to the sinner himself, or which is known only to the sinner and a few others who wish it to be suppressed .

A manifest sin is that which has become known to many, and if it is joined with the stumbling-block of others, it is called scandal .

Who can understand his errors? Cleanse thou me from secret faults (which were either not known to the intellect, or buried in oblivion)? Ps. 19:3.

Prob. b. 1 Tim. V, 24. The sins of some men are manifest. Prob. b. 1 Tim. V, 24. The sins of some men are manifest.

Latin:

quod manifestum?

Peccatum occultum est, quod vel ipsi peccanti ignotum est, vel quod soli peccanti & paucis aliis, qui id suppressum volunt, notum est .

Peccatum manifestum est, quod multis innotuit, & si cum aliorum offendiculo coniunctum fit, vocatur scandalum .

Prob. a. Delicta quis intelligit? ab occultis meis (quae vel intellectui non fuerunt cognita, vel oblivione sepulta) munda me? Ps. XIX, 3.

Prob. b. 1 Tim. V, 24. Quorundam hominum peccata manifesta sunt.


### Q. XXXI. What is scandal?

Scandal is a manifest sin which offers an occasion of sinning to those to whom it has become known. It is commonly distinguished into scandal given, or active, and accepted, or passive. The former is a manifest sin which offers an occasion of sinning to others

Latin:

Scandalum est peccatum manifestum, quod, quibus innotuit, occasionem peccandi praebet. Distinguitur vulgo in scandalum datum, sive activum, & acceptum, sive passivum. Illud est peccatum manifestum, quod aliis peccandi occasionem offert


### XXXII. What is a dead sin?

What is a living one?

A dead sin is that whose gravity is neither recognized by the man to whom it adheres, nor is its power to irritate and torment felt. A living sin is that which exerts its own powers and rages in the sinning man, so that it both irritates desire to strive for a thing forbidden by law, and terrifies and torments the conscience.

Proof from Rom. VII, 8. 9. Without the law sin is dead. For I was alive without the law once: but when the commandment came, sin revived. That is to say: Without the law, when accurately considered, sin is dead, not as to the thing itself, but as to the sense, i. e., its foulness is not recognized, nor is the goad felt, by which it incites desire to strive for what is forbidden and pricks the conscience. But, upon the arrival of the meditation of the law, sin, like a dog awakened from sleep, revives and exercises greater powers, both by kindling a more vehement desire to do that which is prohibited by law, and by biting and tormenting the conscience.

Latin:

quod viuens?

Peccatum mortuum est, cuius neque gravitas ab homine, cui inhæret, agnoscitur, neque vis irritandi & cruciandi sentitur. Peccatum viuens est, quod vires suas exserit, & in homine peccante furit, vt tum cupiditatem ad nitendum in rem, lege vetitam, irritet, tum conscientiam terreat & cruciet.

Prob. ex Rom. VII, 8. 9. Sine lege peccatum mortuum est. Ego vero viuebam sine lege olim: veniente vero præcepto peccatum revixit. q. d. Absque lege, accurate considerate, peccatum est mortuum, non quoad rem, sed quoad sensum, i. e. non agnoscitur eius fœditas, neque stimulus, quo cupiditatem ad nitendum in vetitum incitat, & conscientiam pungit, sentitur. At, accedente meditatione legis, peccatum, instar canis e somno excitati, reviviscit maiores vires exercet, tum vehementiorem cupiditatem ad faciendum id, quod lege prohibitum est, accendendo, tum conscientiam mordendo & cruciando. Quaest.


### Q. XXXIII. What sin is remaining?

What is remitted?

A remaining sin is that which presses upon the sinner by its own weight, guilt, sense, and dominion. A remitted sin is that from whose guilt and dominion a man reborn has been liberated through the justifying and renewing grace of God.

Proof from John IX, 41. Jesus said to them: If you were blind, you should not have sin. But now you say: We see: therefore your sin remains. The sense is: If you recognized that you were blind, you would receive the light of my gospel for the illumination of your souls, so that by believing you might obtain the remission of sins. But because you say: We see, i. e., we abound in the knowledge of heavenly things; you spurn my doctrine. Wherefore your sin persists, adheres, accuses, and dominates.

Latin:

quod remissum?

Peccatum manens est, quod pondere suo, reatu, sensu & dominio peccatorem premit. Peccatum remissum est, cuius reatu & dominio homo renatus per gratiam Dei iustificantem & renouantem liberatus est.

Prob. ex Io. IX, 41. Dixit illis Iesus: si cæci essetis, non haberetis peccatum. Iam vero dicitis: quia videmus: ideo vestrum peccatum manet. Sensus est: Si agnosceretis, vos esse cæcos, lucem euangelii mei ad illuminationem animarum vestrarum reciperetis, vt credentes peccatorum remissionem consequeremini. At quia dicitis: videmus, i. e. scientia rerum cœlestium abundamus; meam doctrinam spernitis. Quare peccatum vestrum perstat, inhæret, accusat, dominatur. Quaest.


### Q. XXXIV. What sin is conjoined with hardness of heart?

What is separated from it?

A sin conjoined with hardness of heart is a most atrocious sin, by which the polluted mind of man remains turned away from the word of God and blind, the will, hardened in evil, resists the Holy Spirit, the appetite indulges in beastly pleasures, and thus the sinner, with difficulty or not at all corrigible, brings upon himself temporal and eternal punishments. A sin without hardness of heart is the sin of a man who is corrigible and curable.

Latin:

quod ab hac seiunctum?

Peccatum cum induratione coniunctum est peccatum atrocissimum, quo polluta mens hominis a verbo Dei auersa & cæca manet, voluntas in malo obfirmata Spiritui S. resistit, appetitus belluinis voluptatibus indulget, atque adeo peccator, difficulter, aut plane non corrigibilis, temporales & æternas pœnas sibi accersit. Peccatum absque induratione est peccatum hominis corrigibilis & sanabilis. Quaest.


### Q. XXXV. What is the cause of hardness of heart?

The cause of hardness of heart is not God a); but partly the devil, bringing evils from evils, blinding the mind and filling the heart with malice b); partly man, repelling the ordinary means of salvation, and continually enslaving himself to the study and practice of sinning c).

Proof a. God is the hater and avenger of sin, Ps. V, 5. who uses now the hammer of the law, now the rain of the gospel to soften the mind of the sinner; but this man, spurning the voice of God, complies with the suggestions of the devil and the allurements of the world.

You say: God himself says: I will harden the heart of Pharaoh. Ex. VII, 3. Resp. God hardens the sinner, not positively; or effectively, by putting hardness into the heart; but 1) occasionally and eventually, while, like a most benign father, he tolerates the sinner with his long-suffering, defers punishment, and heaps benefits upon him, so that the man might return to a better way of life.

But he, noticing that he is not punished in flagrant sin, abuses the long-suffering, and from the benefits conferred, he seizes the opportunity of sliding into security and the habit of sinning.

2) Judicially, when on account of prior voluntary and avoidable malice, God, the most just judge, permits man, a contemner of all means of salvation, to rush into graver crimes, and withdraws His grace from him, and finally delivers him to the power of Satan, by whom he is subsequently driven into greater sins, until he finally falls from the right of the heavenly inheritance.

Prob. b. The devil blinds the minds of the unbelievers, 2 Cor. IV, 4. fills the heart with malice, Acts V, 3. works in the children of unbelief. Eph. II, 2. Prob. c. Matth. XIII, 15. Christ says: The heart of this people has grown dull, and they have heard heavily with their ears, and have closed their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn themselves, and I heal them. He who closes the eyes of the mind to the light of the Gospel, and hardens his ears to hearing the voice of God, he hardens himself.

Latin:

Causa indurationis non est Deus a); sed partim diabolus, mala ex malis ferens, mentem excæcans & cor malitia implens b); partim homo, ordinaria salutis media repellens, & continuo peccandi studio atque exercitio se mancipans c).

Prob. a. Deus est osor & vltor peccati, Ps. V, 5. qui ad emolliendum animum peccatoris iam malleo legis, iam pluuia euangelii vtitur; at hic, vocem Dei aspernans, obsequitur diaboli suggestionibus & mundi lenociniis.

Dicis: Deus ipse inquit: Ego indurabo cor Pharaonis. Ex. VII, 3. Resp. Indurat Deus peccatorem, non positiue; aut effectiue, duritiem cordi immittendo; sed 1) occasionaliter euentualiter, dum, instar patris benignissimi, longanimitate sua peccatorem tolerat, pœnam differt, & beneficiis ipsum cumulat, vt homo ad meliorem frugem se recipiat.

Contra ille animaduertens, se in flagranti peccato non puniri, longanimitate abutitur, & ex beneficiis neficiis collatis occasionem arripit prolabendi in securitatem et consuetudinem peccandi.

2) Iudicialiter, cum ob antegressam voluntariam, evitabilemque malitiam Deus, iustissimus iudex, permittit hominem, omnium mediorum salutis contemptorem, ruere in scelera grauiora, eidemque gratiam suam subtrahit, et denique Satanae potestati tradit, a quo in maiora subinde peccata propellitur, donec excidat finaliter iure hereditatis caelestis.

Prob. b. Diabolus excaecat mentes infidelium, 2 Cor. IV, 4. cor implet malitia, Act. V, 3. operatur in filiis incredulitatis. Eph. II, 2. Prob. c. Matth. XIII, 15. inquit Christus: Incrassatum est cor populi huius, et auribus grauiter audierunt, et oculos suos occluserunt, ne forte videant oculis, et auribus audiant, et corde intelligant, et conuertant se, et sanem illos. Qui oculos mentis ad lucem euangelii occludit, et aures ad audiendam vocem Dei obdurat, is seipsum indurat.


### Q. XXXVI. How manifold is the hardness of heart?

The hardness of heart is twofold, original and actual. The former is drawn from parents, infected by sin, from birth a): the latter is acquired by a continued habit of sinning b).

Prob. a. Concerning the original hardness of heart, God says, Ez. XXXVI, 26. I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh. There lies in the marrow of our flesh a heart of stone, naturally inept for receiving every spiritual good.

Prob. b. Pharaoh continued to sin, and hardened his heart, Ex. IX, 34. i.e., by an assiduous habit of sinning he contracted hardness for himself.

Latin:

Durities cordis duplex est, originalis, et actualis. Illa a parentibus, peccato infectis, ex natiuitate trahitur a): haec continuato peccandi studio comparatur b).

Prob. a. De originali cordis duritie inquit Deus, Ez. XXXVI, 26. Remouebo cor lapideis et carne vestra. Latet in medullio carnis nostrae cor lapideum, ad omne bonum spirituale recipiendum naturaliter ineptum.

Prob. b. Pharao perrexit peccare, et aggrauauit cor suum, Ex. IX, 34. i. e. assiduo peccandi studio indurationem sibi contraxit.


### Q. XXXVII. What sin is remissible?

What is irremissible?

A remissible sin is that which, just as it does not exclude repentance by its nature, so also can be and is wont to be remitted. An irremissible sin is that which, by itself and insofar as it is such, is joined with final impenitence, and thus is never remitted. It is commonly called the sin against the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

quod irremissibile?

Peccatum remissibile est, quod, sicut poenitentiam natura sua non excludit: ita quoque remitti potest ac solet. Peccatum irremissibile est, quod per se, et quatenus tale, cum impoenitentia finali coniungitur, atque adeo nunquam remittitur. Vocatur communiter peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum.


### Q. XXXVIII. What is the sin against the Holy Spirit?

The sin against the Holy Spirit is the malicious denial, hostile impugnation, horrendous blasphemy, and the obstinate and finally persevering rejection of all means of salvation of divine truth clearly acknowledged and approved in the conscience *).

The sin against the Holy Spirit is not taken here in the general sense, in which every sin is against the Holy Spirit; but in a special sense, for that most grievous sin, which is committed not so much against the person of the Holy Spirit, as against his office, which he exercises through the ministry of the word in converting the souls of men. The Holy Spirit is therefore considered not ουσιωδῶς, essentially, nor ὑποστατικῶς, personally; but ἐνεργητικῶς, effectively, by reason of his office and spiritual operation, insofar as the Holy Spirit reveals the will of God through the doctrine of the gospel, illuminates minds, converts hearts, convinces consciences, and testifies of the truth of the divine word. Those who maliciously and perseveringly resist this operation of the Holy Spirit are said to sin against the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

Peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum est veritatis diuinae euidenter agnitae, et in conscientia approbatae malitiosa abnegatio, hostilis impugnatio, horrenda blasphematio, et omnium mediorum salutis obstinata et finaliter perseuerans reiectio *).

Peccatum in Spiritum S. h. l. non sumitur sensu generali, quo omne peccatum contra Spiritum S. est; sed sensu speciali, pro gravissimo illo peccato, quod committitur non tam in personam Spiritus Sancti, quam eius officium, quod per ministerium verbi in convertendis hominum animis exercet. Consideratur itaque Spiritus S. non ουσιωδῶς, essentialiter, neque ὑποστατικῶς, personaliter; sed ἐνεργητικῶς, effective, ratione officii & operationis spiritualis, quatenus Spiritus S. per doctrinam evangelii voluntatem Dei patefacit, mentes illuminat, corda convertit, conscientias convincit, de verbi divini veritate testatur. Cui operationi Spiritus S. malitiose & perseveranter obluctantes, in Spiritum S. peccare dicuntur.


### Question XXXIX. What is denoted by the divine truth, which is denied and impugned by this sin?

By divine truth, which is said to be denied, is understood here the divine doctrine, which is by far the most true, and indeed secondarily the legal doctrine , primarily the evangelical doctrine .

Prob. a. If anyone were to petulantly proclaim, impugn, and blaspheme the very doctrine of the divine law, clearly acknowledged and approved in his own conscience, as false and diabolical, he would certainly sin against the Holy Spirit; because the law is also an instrument of the Holy Spirit by which he leads us to repentance, Rom. VII, 7.

You say: I. The law is objectively distinguished from the sin against the Holy Spirit, Hebr. X, 28.

Resp. The law, in that place, is not considered as it is divine truth, which apostates deny, but as it is a norm of morals, from which sinners deviate in acting. 4.

Not only those who were previously illuminated and renewed, but now are perfidious and falling away, are accused of this sin, Hebr. VI, 4. 6. X, 29. but also the impious, and those not yet illuminated in a saving way, Mark III, 22. & 30. cf. with 1 Cor. II, 8.

5. Where this sin is discussed, mention is also made of the gifts and effects of saving grace, and indeed of the means of grace, not only of the ordinary ones, Hebr. VI, 5. but also of the extraordinary and abundant ones, in the same verse, coll. with ch. II, 4. Mark III, 22-30. XVI, 20. (see princ.

3). 6. This is one sin, and no other, which cannot be forgiven, Matt.

XII, 31. & in parallel passages. 7. The reason for the denied forgiveness is clearly placed in this: that it can never happen that one who is guilty of this sin truly repents, Hebr. VI, 4. 6.

8. The Holy Spirit has a divine nature common to and the same as the Father and the Son, and as far as his person is concerned, he is indeed distinct from both of them, yet in such a way that he is equal and equivalent to both. E. Therefore, neither in the nature of the Holy Spirit nor in his person is there anything singular and exceptional, for which reason the sin against the Holy Spirit should be thought of as something singular, distinct from all others, or clearly more grievous than that which is committed against the Father or the Son.

9. The gifts and means of grace that illuminate, renew, bless, and whatever pertains to the application of salvation, are assigned in a certain singular way to the Holy Spirit, 1 John V, 6. 8.

1 Cor. XII, 3. 4. just as the acquisition of our salvation is attributed specifically and properly to Christ, and the eternal decrees concerning salvation, to be imparted to us, are ascribed to the Father.

10. The grace of God calling to salvation, always earnest and effective, as is the acquisition of salvation, obtained by the merits of Christ, pertains to all men equally and to each one individually, and there is no sin for which Christ has not made satisfaction.

11. Grace is never not greater and more powerful than any sin, even the most grievous and the greatest of all.

12. The acquisition of recovered salvation profits no one without its right application.

You say: II. Sin against the Holy Spirit is commonly defined as an abnegation not of legal truth, but of evangelical truth. Resp. Sin against the Holy Spirit is defined through the abnegation of evangelical truth not exclusively, but comparatively and by way of excellence, so that a nobler and more sublime object may be expressed, while the law is not entirely excluded. Furthermore, observe that the Mosaic law can be considered in a twofold manner: 1) insofar as it is a norm of moral actions: 2) insofar as it is the word of God, or divine doctrine and heavenly truth. In the former way, he sins against the law who transgresses and violates it: in the latter way, he sins who denies that the Mosaic law is the word of God, or heavenly truth. On account of vicious morals or a perverse life, no one is called a sinner against the Holy Spirit, although a perverse life and the turpitude of morals may accompany sin against the Holy Spirit: but those who petulantly proclaim, oppose, blaspheme, and pertinaciously reject the very doctrine of divine law, once evidently recognized and approved in their own conscience, sin against the Holy Spirit, because they maliciously resist the Holy Spirit working through the ministry of the law.

Prob. b.

That those sinning against the Holy Spirit strike principally and most powerfully at the doctrine of the Gospel, prob.

1) from Matth. XII, 24. 31. and Mark III, 22 - 29. where sin against the Holy Spirit is considered professedly. Namely, the Pharisees sinned against the Holy Spirit by blaspheming the redeemer of the world, and by asserting that he cast out demons and performed miracles by the help of the devil; when nevertheless they had been more correctly taught concerning the divine power of Christ, and were convicted in their conscience.

They therefore committed the sin against the Holy Spirit by rejecting the marrow or core of the Gospel.

Wherefore the apostle also teaches that sinners against the Holy Spirit trample underfoot the Son of God, and the blood of the covenant 13.

The order of salvation demands that, in this application and perception of salvation, μετάνοια (repentance), a salutary change of mind, precedes the remission of sins. 14. This change cannot be effected otherwise than by the means of grace being applied, and indeed rightly used.

These being thus rejected and repudiated, so that a man with the greatest obstinacy of mind does not even wish to hear, let alone meditate and know, it cannot happen that a man ever repents with a salutary change of mind. Therefore, that which makes μετάνοια impossible, the same likewise makes the remission of sin impossible.

(princ. 13.) 15. Continuation and remaining is not a certain moral action, but is a duration joined to an action, and therefore by itself it is neither a vice nor to be considered a virtue.

But it becomes either evil or good, from the nature of the action to which it is joined.

Therefore, perseverance in good is good, remaining in evil is always evil.

Consequences to be drawn from these principles:

1. Sin against the Holy Spirit, insofar as it is such, cannot but be something entirely singular, different from all others (by princ. 2. & 6.).

2. It is committed neither against the divine nature of the Holy Spirit, nor against his person (by princ. 8.): but against his gifts and effects, or the means of grace (by princ. 3.

5. 9.).

3. It is therefore nothing other than a malicious and contumacious repugnance against all means of grace, both ordinary and extraordinary and abundant (by princ. 5.): whether they have ever been known and perceived, or never (by princ.

4.): especially, however, if that repugnance is joined with contumely, by which the mind is entirely turned away from the truth, and is an adversary to it (by princ.

1.).

4. The reason why this sin can never be remitted is not situated in the gravity of this offense, even though it is the gravest of all (by princ. 11.): nor in the fact that the grace of God and the merit of Christ do not pertain to this sin (by princ. 10.): but it is entirely placed in the very nature of this sin, which is entirely singular and proper, since in this one thing μετάνοια cannot occur, nor the right application of salvation, recovered through Christ (by princ. 7. 12.

13. 14.).

5. Obstinacy of mind perpetual until the end of life, or, as is the custom to speak, final impenitence, is not the very nature of this sin, but a consequence and something joined to it (by princ. 15.), since this sin is of such a kind that all means of grace are repudiated, whether ordinary or extraordinary and abundant (by definit. in consequence 3.): but without these means, no μετάνοια can ever occur (by princ. 14.): Therefore, a perpetual obstinacy of mind will then be necessary.

to esteem the common [blood] of the covenant, Heb. 10:29.

2) Sinners against the Holy Spirit are said to have tasted the good word of God, Heb. 6:5. But the good word of God is the gospel, sweeter than honey. For it is a joyful message, Luke 2:10, the word of peace, Eph. 2:17, the word of our reconciliation with God; 2 Cor. 5:19. The divine law, although good in itself, as a good rule of life, having proceeded from the best author: yet eventually it is not good to the sinful man, in that it denounces to him the wrath of God and the curse, Rom. 4:15, Deut. 27:26. 3) The sin against the Holy Spirit is described by παράπτωσιν, apostasy, or falling away from the faith, by which men, having been enlightened, have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, but falling away, they have crucified the Son of God anew and put him to open shame, Heb. 6:5, 6. But faith looks to the gospel, and apostasy from the faith in Christ is known distinctly from the gospel.

You say: Every sin is prohibited by divine law. Therefore, also the sin against the Holy Spirit. I answer: The sin against the Holy Spirit is considered in two ways: 1) generally, insofar as it is a sin, and thus it is prohibited by law: 2) specifically, insofar as it is a sin against the Holy Spirit, and thus it is a voluntary and stubborn denial of the evangelical truth.

Latin:

Per veritatem divinam, quæ abnegari dicitur, hic intelligitur doctrina divina, quæ longe verissima est, & quidem secundario doctrina legalis , primario doctrina evangelica .

Prob. a. Si quis ipsam legis divinæ doctrinam evidenter agnitam, & in conscientia sua approbatam, tamquam falsam & diabolicam petulanter proclamaret, oppugnaret & blasphemaret, utique in Spiritum S. peccaret; quia & lex est instrumentum Spiritus S. quo nos ad pœnitentiam ducit, Rom. VII, 7.

Dicis: I. Lex peccato in Spiritum S. obiective contradistinguitur, Hebr. X, 28.

Resp. Lex l, c. non consideratur, vt est veritas divina, quam apostatæ abnegant, sed vt est norma morum, a qua in agendo peccatores deflectunt.

4. Arguuntur huius peccati non solum ante hac illuminati ac renovati homines, nunc perfidi ac deficientes, Hebr. VI, 4. 6. X, 29. sed etiam impii, ac nondum salutari modo illuminati, Marc. III, 22. & 30. conf. cum 1 Cor. II, 8.

5. Vbi de hoc peccato disseritur, ibi mentio fit etiam de donis atque effectibus gratiæ salutaris, & quidem de mediis gratiæ, non solum de ordinariis, Hebr. VI, 5. verum etiam de extraordinariis, atque abundantibus, in eodem versu, coll. cum cap. II, 4. Marc. III, 22-30. XVI, 20. (vid. princ.

3). 6. Vnum hoc peccatum est, neque vllum aliud, quod remitti non potest, Matth. XII, 31. & in locis parall. 7.

Ratio denegatæ remissionis diserte ponitur in eo: quod fieri non possit vnquam, vt quis, huius peccati reus, vere resipiscat, Hebr. VI, 4. 6. Id quod in primis arcte tenendum est.

8. Spiritus S. naturam divinam cum Patre & Filio communem atque eandem habet, & quod ad personam ipsius attinet, diuersus est quidem ab vtroque illo, verum tamen ita, vt vtrique par atque æqualis sit. E. neque in natura Spiritus S. neque in eiusdem persona est aliquid singulare atque eximium, quam ob rem peccatum in Spiritum S. aut singulare quoddam putandum fit, ab omnibus aliis distinctum, aut plane grauius eo, quod vel in Patrem, vel in Filium committitur.

9. Donæ ac media gratiæ illuminantis, renovantis, beantis, & quæcunque ad salutis adplicationem pertinent, singulari quoddam modo adsignantur Spiritui S. 1 Io.

V, 6. 8. 1 Cor. XII, 3. 4. sicut adquisitio salutis nostræ sigillatim ac proprie Christo tribuitur, ac decreta æternæ de salute, nobis impertienda, Patri adferuntur.

10. Gratia Dei ad salutem vocans, semper feria atque efficax, vt & adquisitio salutis, pro meritis Christi parta, pertinet ad homines peræque omnes ac singulos, neque vllum est peccatum, pro quo Christus satis non fecerit.

11. Gratia nunquam non est maior ac validior quouis peccato, etiam grauissimo omniumque maximo.

12. Adquisitio salutis recuperatæ nemini prodest, fine recta eius adplicatione.

Dicis: II. Definitur communiter peccatum in Spiritum S., quod fit abnegatio veritatis non legalis, sed evangelicae. Resp. Definitur peccatum in Spiritum S. per abnegationem veritatis evangelicae non exclusive, sed comparative & exochice, vt exprimatur obiectum nobilius & sublimius, lex vero non penitus excludatur. Ceterum obserues, quod lex Mosaica duplici ratione considerari possit: 1) quatenus est norma actionum moralium: 2) quatenus est verbum Dei, aut doctrina divina & veritatis coelestis. Priori modo peccat in legem, qui eam transgreditur & violat: posteriori modo peccat, qui negat, legem Mosaicam esse verbum Dei, aut veritatem coelestem. Ob vitiosos mores, aut vitam peruersam, nemo dicitur peccator in Spiritum S., licet vita peruersa & morum turpitudo peccatum in Spiritum S. comitetur: at qui ipsam legis divinae doctrinam evidenter agnitam, & in conscientia sua approbatam, falsam petulanter proclamant, oppugnant, blasphemant & pertinaciter reiiciunt, in Spiritum S. peccant, quia iidem Spiritui S. per ministerium legis operanti malitiosae obsistunt.

Prob. b.

Peccantes in Spiritum S. principaliter & potissimum impingere in doctrinam evangelii, prob.

1) ex Matth. XII, 24. 31. ac Marc. III, 22 - 29. vbi peccatum in Spiritum S. ex professo consideratur. Nimirum Pharisaei peccarunt in Spiritum S., redemptorem mundi blasphemando, & asserendo, ipsum ope diaboli eiicere daemones, & miracula patrare; cum tamen de divina Christi potentia rectius edocti, & in conscientia convicti essent.

Comiserunt ergo peccatum in Spiritum S., evangelii medullam, aut nucleum reiiciendo.

Quare etiam apostolus docet, peccatores in Spiritum S. conculcare filium Dei, & sanguinem foederis 13.

Ordo salutis ita postulat, vt, in hac salutis adplicatione ac perceptione, peccatorum remissionem praecedat μετάνοια, mentis mutatio salutaris. 14. Hac mutatio non potest aliter effici, quam mediis gratiae adhibitis, & recte quidem usurpatis.

His ita reiectis ac repudiatis, vt homo maxima animi obstinatione ne audire quidem velit, nedum meditari & cognoscere, fieri non potest, vt homo unquam salutari mentis mutatione resipiscat. E. quod impossibilem facit μετάνοιαν, idem pariter impossibilem facit remissionem peccati.

(princ. 13.) 15. Continuatio ac permansio non est actio quaedam moralis, sed est actioni adiuncta duratio, ideoque per se nec in vitio est, nec laudi ducenda.

Fit autem vel mala, vel bona, ex natura actionis, cui ea est adiuncta.

Itaque perseuerantia in bono bona est, permansio in malo semper mala.

Consectaria ab his principiis ducenda:

1. Peccatum in Spiritum S. quatenus est tale, non potest non esse aliquid prorsus singulare, ab omnibus aliis diversum (per princ. 2. & 6.).

2. Neque in divina Spiritus S. naturam, neque in personam (per princ. 8.): sed in eius dona atque effectus, siue media gratiae committitur (per princ. 3.

5. 9.).
