Libertas contradictionis est, quae circa vnum idemque obiectum versatur inter terminos contradictorios, velle, & non velle, agere, & non agere, v. gr. Studiosi philosophiae liberum est philosophiam amare, & non amare, exercere, & non exercere. Appellatur etiam libertas exercitii; quia postquam voluntas ad alterutram contradictionis partem se determinauit, in exercitio tamen libera manet.

4) Notat libertatem a peccati reatu, dominio, sensu & radice. Libertas a peccati reatu est, qua homini poenitenti peccata ad culpam & poenam non imputantur: hanc peccatores conuersi nanciscuntur per gratiam iustificationis. Libertas a dominio peccati est, quando caro spiritui subiecta est, & seruitus peccati soluta: hanc iustificati obtinent beneficio renouationis. Libertas a sensu & radice peccati est, qua hominibus renouatis aufertur stimulus & fomes peccati per dissolutionem animae & corporis.

5) Designat libertatem a miseria, qua beati in caelo triumphantes non tantum a peccati sensu & radice, sed & a castigationibus, peccatum sequentibus, prorsus liberati sunt. Neque enim illi morbis, morti, aut vlli calamitati obnoxii sunt.

Obs. III. Diuiditur libertas hominis in libertatem naturae, gratiae, & gloriae. Libertas naturae est immunitas a coactione & necessitate interna, respectu rerum naturalium & ciuilium, rationi subiectarum. Quo spectant verba Pauli, 1 Cor. VII, 37. Qui stat firmus in corde, nec habet necessitatem, potestatem vero habet circa propriam voluntatem, & hoc indicauit in corde suo, quod retinere velit virginem suam, bene facit. Libertas gratiae est, per quam renati liberati sunt a reatu & dominio peccati, de qua apostolus inquit, Rom. VI, 18. Liberati a peccato, serui facti estis iustitiae. Libertas gloriae est immunitas a sensu & radice peccati, & omni miseria; de qua sermo fit, Rom. VIII, 21. Ipsa creatura liberabitur a seruitute corruptionis in libertatem gloriae filiorum Dei.

Obs. IV. Libertati opponitur necessitas & seruitus. Repugnat enim libertati 1) necessitas absoluta & consequentis, qua aliquid ob indissolubilem connexionem causae cum effectu, aliter esse non potest: quomodo aqua necessario humectat. Stare autem cum libertate potest necessitas hypothetica, & consequentiae, qua aliquid propter actum existendi, vel conditionem extrinsecam aliter esse nequit. Sic necesse est hominem esse doctum, si agere nitatur philosophiae professorem. 2) Pugnat libertas cum necessitate externa coactionis, quae est determinatio naturae ad vnum, praeter, vel contra eius voluntatem, facta a principio violento externo. Distinguere solent auctores inter actus voluntatis elicitos, & imperatos. Voluntas, quoad actus elicitos, cogi nequit. Sunt autem actus eliciti, qui immediate a voluntate exercentur, v. gr. velle, amare, eligere. Quibus opponuntur actus imperati, qui veniente.

Mala: si quis, intellectu obcaecato, falsam ac temerariam rationem sequutus, non potest non ita male velle, quem ad modum falso atque imprudenter opinatur & iudicat. Hac libertati contraria est; illa non item, sed cum vera libertate, quae multum sane differt a vaga libidine atque indomita licentia, arcte copulata est; sicut in Deo est summa quidem necessitas moralis, nihil vnquam, nisi bene, immo optime, decernendi atque agendi; at nihilo tamen minus summa libertas, nullis terminis circumscripta, nullis vnquam impedimentis cohibenda. Vid. not. ad pag. 435.

qui voluntatis quidem imperio, sed mediante alia facultate, perficiuntur, v. gr. loqui, ambulare, scribere. Ad actus elicitos voluntatis ideo homo cogi nequit, quod coactio fit a principio externo, volitio autem ex principio interno. Quamobrem coacte aliquid velle, contradictionem in adiecto infert. Ad actus imperatos homo cogi potest, sed tum non agit secundum liberum arbitrium, sed præter, vel contra voluntatem. Sic homo per vim abripi aliquo potest, vt autem raptus ille violentus sit ex voluntate eius, qui abripitur, fieri nequit. Si enim voluntarius est; violentus esse definit. 3) Repugnat libertati necessitas interna immutabilitatis, quæ est determinatio subiecti agentis ad vnum, proficiscens a principio interno, immutabiliter ad effectum se habente. Quidquid autem ad vnum est determinatum, liberum non est. Sic libera dicitur actio, quæ ita ab agente procedit, vt in potestate agentis fuerit agere, & non agere, agere hoc, & agere illud. Consistere autem potest cum libertate necessitas obligationis, quæ est determinatio directiva voluntatis ad bonum amplectendum, & malum fugiendum, ad normam mandati superioris. Sic angeli & homines determinati sunt ad normam legis divinæ, subditi ad leges principis, qui tamen libero pollent arbitrio. Moralis quippe, sive legalis determinatio non captiuat libertatem arbitrii, neque irresistibiliter necessitat. Determinat quidem lex divina creaturas intelligentes suadendo ac iubendo ea, quæ sunt secundum voluntatem Numinis, prohibendo ac diffuadendo, quæ contra; ordinarie tamen non cogendo ac vim quasi inferendo. Nihil quidem fit contra voluntatem Numinis absolutam ac potentissimam, multa tamen, ac multo plura, præter, quam secundum Numinis nutum, ait DANNHAV. in hodof. phænom. III. p. 312.

4) Repugnat libertati servitus turpis & probrosa, non decora & honesta. Servitus honesta consistit tum in debito pie vivendi, tum in ministerio Deo præstando. Sic homines renati dicuntur servi iustitiæ, Rom. VI, 18. ideo, quod ad præscriptum legis divinæ iustitiam libenter colunt. Iidem dicuntur servire Deo, Rom. VI, 22. quia se totos cultui divino consecrant. Contra servitus probrosa est captiuitas voluntatis, qua per peccatum voluntas hominis ita ligata & captiuata est, vt serviat tantum peccato, Io. VIII, 34. Hæc servitus opponitur libertati a necessitate immutabilitatis.


### Quæst. III. In how many ways is free will understood?

Free will is here understood chiefly in two ways: materially for the subject of liberty, which is the will a): formally for the powers of the will, by which it is equipped to act and not to act, to do this and to do that b).

Prob. a. The will is the proximate and immediate subject of liberty; because this is its attribute, power and perfection. Hence it comes about that will and liberty are distinguished even by their names, nor is it said that liberty is the will; or conversely: but that liberty is of the will, or in the will, and the will has liberty, or is endowed with liberty. Wherefore ἡ οὐσία, or the essence of the will, cannot be called free choice on any other account than in the material and subjective sense. In this sense indeed free choice is said to be inseparable from man: for this reason, that the will enters into the essence of man.

Prob. b. 1) Ἐνέργεια, or the powers of acting, are the reason which constitutes the will as potent to act and not to act, to do this and to do that. Therefore the powers of acting and not acting are liberty formally considered. This, however, must be understood of the powers insofar as they inhere in the will. Hence the matter comes back to the same thing, whether I conclude concerning the powers or concerning the essence of the will, taken together with the powers connoted by it. For the will has itself after the manner of a principle which acts; but the powers of acting have themselves after the manner of a principle by means of which the will acts.

2) The question is: Is the human will, after spiritual powers have been lost through the fall, still indifferent to good and evil? Or has it indeed lost this indifference?

The former cannot be said, since Scripture teaches everywhere that after the fall humans are slaves of sin, and that the natural man understands nothing of the things that are of the Spirit, but is himself dead to all good things. The latter is therefore left, from which it further follows that, with the powers of acting and not acting lost, the indifference to good and evil, which is the formal nature of free will, is taken away. Obs.

Besides the two principal meanings of free will set forth, there are also two less principal meanings among the Fathers of the primitive church; inasmuch as they 1) sometimes understand by freedom of will the freedom from coercion, which is also called interior freedom and spontaneity; which, however, does not complete the formal nature of free will, unless we wish to concede that even brutes are free agents, since they do many things of their own accord and with no one compelling them. 2) Sometimes the same Fathers designate by the name of free will ἱκανότητα, or the capacity and passive power of admitting and receiving the grace of the Holy Spirit; since man is not, like a stone, a trunk, a beast, or the devil, entirely incapable of converting grace.

But here one must carefully distinguish between natural passive power and obediential [passive power].

The former can be actuated by the powers of nature, the latter only by the special and gracious concurrence of God. Paul speaks of natural passive power, Rom.

VIII, 7. The mind of the flesh is enmity against God. For it does not submit itself to the law of God; nor indeed can it. Furthermore, that passive power does not constitute the form of free will; since this is formally the active power of the will, because it is occupied in acting, and effectively produces its own acts.

Quest. IV. Is the term "free will" found in Scripture?

Prob. Among the Hebrews, the verb בָּחַר is used, which means "he chose," and thus according to them free will is the faculty of choosing one thing over another, according to the dictate of reason. In the N.

T. it is called ἑκούσιον, spontaneous, or voluntary, Philem. v. 14, which is opposed to the external necessity of coercion; ἐξουσία περὶ τοῦ ἰδίου θελήματος, power of one's own will, 1 Cor. VII, 37, by which is understood the faculty of choosing, free both from the necessity of immutability and from law and obligation; προαίρεσις, election, which is free will viewed in its second act, 2 Cor. IX, 7; ἐλευθερία, liberty, 2 Cor. III, 17, where the liberty of grace is understood. Outside of Holy Scripture, by Greek authors, it is called αὐτεξούσιον and αὐτεξούτης, which term, in this infirmity of nature, is too arrogant, in the judgment of D.

CHEMNITIUS; for it belongs more to God than to humans or angels. For that is properly called αὐτεξούσιον, τὸ αὐτοδέσποτον, and αὐτοκρατορικόν, which is subject to no one's command, but is of its own right and power, and which can be prohibited or hindered by no one.

IRENAEUS, book IV, c. 71, calls free will the power of election. JUSTIN uses three terms: the first is αὐτεξούσιον, which is of its own right and power; the second, ἐλευθέρα προαίρεσις, free election; the third, τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, which is in our power. I gather from these denominations that free will is formally not the will itself, but its active power.

The term "free will" does not indeed exist in Holy Scripture expressly, in so many letters and syllables; yet there is in it that which is the thing and terms that are equivalent.

Latin:

Liberum arbitrium hic potissimum duobus modis accipitur: materialiter pro subiecto libertatis, quod est voluntas a): formaliter pro viribus voluntatis, quibus hæc instructa agere & non agere, agere hoc, & agere illud potest b).

Prob. a. Voluntas est subiectum proximum & immediatum libertatis; eo, quod hæc illius attributum, vis & perfectio est. Inde fit, vt voluntas & libertas etiam vocabulis distinguantur, nec dicatur, libertas est voluntas; vel contra: sed libertas est voluntatis, vel in voluntate, & voluntas habet libertatem, vel libertate prædita est. Quare ἡ οὐσία, sive essentia voluntatis alia ratione liberum arbitrium dici non potest, quam in sensu materiali & subiectivo. Quo quidem sensu dictum liberum arbitrium ab homine est inseparabile: propterea, quod voluntas essentiam hominis ingreditur.

Prob. b. 1) H' ἐνέργεια, sive vires agendi, sunt ratio, quæ constituit voluntatem potentem operandi, & non operandi, operandi hoc, & operandi illud. Ergo vires agendi, & non agendi, sunt libertas formaliter spectata. Intelligendum autem hoc est de viribus, quatenus insunt voluntati. Proinde eodem res recidit, sive concludam de viribus, sive de essentia voluntatis, sumta cum connotatis viribus. Nam voluntas habet se per modum principii, quod operatur; vires autem agendi habent se per modum principii, quo mediante voluntas operatur.

2) Quæritur: An hominis voluntas, postquam vires spirituales per lapsum sunt deperditae, adhuc fit indifferens ad bonum & malum? an vero indifferentiam hanc amiserit?

Prius dici nequit, cum scriptura passim doceat, post lapsum homines esse servos peccati, & hominem animalem nihil quidquam de iis intelligere, quæ sunt Spiritus, sed ipsum esse ad omnia bona mortuum. Posterius ergo relinquitur, ex quo porro fluit, deperditis viribus agendi, & non agendi, tolli indifferentiam ad bonum & malum, quæ est formalis ratio liberi arbitrii. Obs.

Præter expositas duas significationes liberi arbitrii principales, dantur etiam duæ significationes minus principales apud Patres primitiuæ ecclesiæ; vtpote qui 1) interdum per libertatem arbitrii intelligunt libertatem a coactione, quæ etiam vocatur libertas interior & spontaneitas; quæ tamen formalem rationem liberi arbitrii non absoluit, nisi concedere velimus, etiam bruta esse libera agentia, quippe quæ sua sponte, & nemine cogente, multa agunt. 2) Interdum iidem Patres nomine liberi arbitrii designant ἱκανότητα, siue capacitatem & potentiam passiuam, admittendi & recipiendi gratiam Spiritus Sancti; cum homo non instar lapidis, trunci, bestiæ aut diaboli, gratiæ conuertentis fit prorsus incapax.

Probe autem hic distinguendum est inter potentiam passiuam naturalem, & obedientialem.

Illa viribus naturæ, hæc solo speciali & gratioso Dei concursu actuari potest. De potentia passiva naturali sermo est Paulo, Rom.

VIII, 7. Sensus carnis inimicitia est contra Deum. Legi enim Dei non subiicit se; neque enim potest. Ceterum illa potentia passiva non constituit formam liberi arbitrii; cum hoc formaliter fit vis actiua voluntatis, quoniam in agendo est occupata, & suos ipsa actus effectiue producit.

Quæst. IV. Num terminus liberi arbitrii in scriptura habetur?

Prob. Apud Hebræos vsitatum est verbum בָּחַר, quod significat, elegit, adeoque iuxta eosdem liberum arbitrium est facultas eligendi vnam rem præ alia, secundum dictamen rationis. In N.

T. vocatur ἑκούσιον, spontaneum, siue voluntarium, Philem. v. 14. quod opponitur externæ necessitati coactionis; ἐξουσία περὶ τοῦ ἰδίου θελήματος, potestas propriæ voluntatis, 1 Cor. VII, 37. per quam intelligitur facultas eligendi libera, tum a necessitate immutabilitatis, tum a iure & obligatione; προαίρεσις, electio, quæ est liberum arbitrium in actu secundo spectatum, 2 Cor. IX, 7; ἐλευθερία, libertas, 2 Cor. III, 17. vbi intelligitur libertas gratiæ. Extra S. scripturam a Græcis auctoribus αὐτεξούσιον, καὶ αὐτεξούτης, quod vocabulum in hac infirmitate naturæ arrogantius est, iudice D.

CHEMNITIO; quippe quod Deo potius, quam hominibus aut angelis competit. Dicitur enim proprie αὐτεξούσιον, τὸ αὐτοδέσποτον, καὶ αὐτοκρατορικόν, quod nullius imperio subest, sed sui iuris ac potestatis est, quodque a nemine prohiberi, vel impediri potest.

IRENÆUS libr. IV. c. 71. liberum arbitrium appellat potestatem electionis. IVSTINUS tribus vtitur vocabulis: primum est, αὐτεξούσιον, quod sui iuris ac potestatis est; secundum, ἐλευθέρα προαίρεσις, libera electio; tertium, τὸ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, quod penes nos est. Colligo ex his denominationibus, liberum arbitrium formaliter non esse ipsam voluntatem, sed eiusdem vim actiuam.

Terminus liberi arbitrii non quidem διαρρήδην explicite, totidem litteris atque syllabis in sacra scriptura exstat; habetur tamen in eadem, quod rem & quod terminos equipollentes.


### Quæst. III. In how many ways is free will understood?: Quest. V. What nature possesses free will?

Quest. V. What nature possesses free will?

An intelligent nature possesses free will, and indeed an infinite or divine one, in a most excellent and perfect manner; a finite one, whether angelic or human, in a more imperfect manner. However, a nature destitute of intellect is devoid of free will.

Prob. a. Although God wills and loves Himself necessarily, because He is the first, highest, and most perfect good; yet He wills creatures freely, so that He is also able not to will them. For He does not need the companionship of creatures, because He is αὐταρκέστατος (self-sufficient). Hence God is said to do all things that He wills, Ps. CXV, 3; to work all things according to the counsel of His will, Eph. I, 11; and to distribute His gifts as He wills, 1 Cor. XII, 11. Moreover, God is free not only from all misery and sin, but also from the law and obligation of any other being whatsoever. God is also not subject or submissible to any coercion, even in the smallest part; and since He does not acknowledge a superior cause by which He could be determined, He works indeterminately, so that He is able to act and not to act, to produce now this, now that effect.

Prob. b. The will of the elect angels is indeed no longer indifferent to good and evil; yet it is indifferent in relation to created goods, such that any one of them, which it wills, it can also not will, or will one instead of another, unless the created good must necessarily be desired on account of the will of God. The apex of angelic liberty is that whatever God commands, the holy angels perform with the greatest delight, and whatever God has permitted to be free, they will, will not, and exercise without necessity and coercion. We shall now consider the liberty of human will according to its diverse objects and distinct degrees.

Prob. c. A nature lacking intellect does not possess freedom of will, since it is determined to one thing. This is evident from the fact that: 1) beasts act in the same way, e.g., bees always make honey in the same way, all sheep flee from a wolf in the same manner, all spiders weave their webs in the same fashion. 2) With all things required for acting present, they cannot but act. A hungry dog, with all impediments removed, cannot but devour the food present. However, just as a certain shadow of reason, so also of liberty, is observed in brutes, while they stand, lie down, or proceed in the fields as they please, and pluck now this, now that herb; yet these acts of beasts are more correctly called spontaneous than free.

Quest. VI. What is the proper and adequate seat of free will?

The proper and adequate seat of free will is the will. However, the intellect concurs antecedently and παρασκευαστικῶς (preparatorily) to the exercise of free will.

Obs. Certain authors establish that free will has its seat in the intellect as well as in the will. Hence, citing CHEMNITIUS l. c. fol. 181, ORIGEN in book III of περὶ ἀρχῶν (On First Principles) says it is a faculty of reason for discerning good or evil; of the will, for choosing either. AUGUSTINE says it is a faculty of reason and will. THOMAS says it is an elective power, which is indeed mixed from intelligence and appetite; yet it inclines more to the appetite. Part. II. c. 38.

art. 3. Prob. a. Because 1) free will is called by St. Paul the power of one's own will, 1 Cor. VII, 37. 2) The Fathers, in the Council of Orange, Canon XIII, call it the free will of the will, to show that liberty formally pertains to the will. 3) Free will, in the judgment of IRENAEUS, is the power of election, or the faculty of choosing; but election is an action of the will. is an action of the will. is an action of the will.

4) The intellect is free neither regarding the species of its act nor regarding the exercise of its act. It is not free regarding the exercise of its act; because a) in order for a power to determine itself to act, it is necessary that this be done either by the impetus of nature or by a free appetition of the act. But free powers, as such, do not act from the impetus of nature: Therefore, [they act] by free inclination and voluntarily. Now, something is called voluntary in two ways: elicited and commanded. In the former way, the acts of the intellect are not voluntary, for instance, in such a way that it itself wills them; for the intellect is not an appetitive faculty, nor one that elicits any willing from itself. In the latter way, indeed, they are voluntary, not because of the freedom of the intellect, but [because] of the will, by which the intellect is moved and excited to act. b) Given the object and the presence of the requisites, the intellect can no more not know a thing than an open eye in the midst of light can fail to see its object. Nor is the intellect free regarding the species of its act, or [in the sense of] whether it assents to a thing or dissents when it considers or knows it. For that thing is either perspicuous and evident (but then the intellect necessarily assents, if it is true; or necessarily dissents, if it is false); or it is obscure (and then it elicits neither act; because the object is not presented to the intellect, just as we do not see when light is lacking); or finally, the thing is probable on both sides (and then again it neither assents nor dissents, unless perhaps the will moves it to embrace one side or the other). From which it is clear that the intellect per se and immediately is not free.

Prob. b. The intellect concurs with the act of free will antecedently and παρασκευασικῶς [preparatorily], as a condition without which the will cannot exercise its freedom. For the will is a blind power, which was not given for knowing. Wherefore it is necessary that, if it wishes to choose a certain object, that object be shown to it by the intellect, as the knowing and pre-illuminating faculty. But if the will truly acts by blind impetus, without the intellect, then it is not properly called free will. Therefore, certain antecedent acts are required for free will: 1) Knowledge of the object, and if several objects are present, a prudent comparison and judgment of them. For the will is not borne toward an unknown thing, since there is no desire for the unknown. 2) The proposition, or presentation, of the known object; by which, when the intellect has known the object, it then proposes it to the will either to be chosen or to be neglected. 3) The commendation or dissuasion of the proposed object. For if the human intellect judges a certain thing to be convenient for man, then it urges and commends the same to the will; but if it judges it to be inconvenient, it dissuades. These three acts of the intellect are followed at last by election, which is the act proper to free will, when the human will chooses that which was judged by the intellect to be convenient for man, and is borne and tends toward uniting itself to it with every effort. There are those who establish that the root of liberty is in the intellect. If by "root" they understand the antecedent condition without which there is no free election, they agree with us. But if by "root of liberty" they mean that the intellect is the cause of free election, they err. For when the will chooses a good proposed and commended by the intellect, it does this from its own freedom, not from the determination of the intellect. For it happens not rarely in practice that the intellect proposes and urges better things, [but] the will follows worse ones (*).

You say: the intellect is indifferent in its acts and in the objects it proposes. Whence the indifference of the will is commonly said to be from the indifference of the intellect. Resp. Distinguish between indiffeobjective and formal difference. The intellect is said to be indifferent not formally, but objectively, insofar as it shows to the will that a thing is indifferent, or that this object as well as that can be freely chosen.

Latin:

Quæst. V. Quæ natura habet liberum arbitrium?

Liberum arbitrium habet natura intelligens, & quidem infinita, sive divina, modo excellentissimo & perfectissimo ; finita, sive angelica & humana, modo imperfectiori . Natura autem intellectu destituta, liberi arbitrii expers est .

Prob. a. Quamvis Deus seipsum velit & amet necessario, quia est primum, summum & perfectissimum bonum; creaturas tamen vult libere, vt etiam possit eas non velle. Neque enim indiget consortio creaturarum, quia est αὐταρκέστατος. Proinde dicitur Deus omnia, quæ vult, facere. Ps. CXV, 3. omnia operari secundum consilium voluntatis suæ, Eph. I, 11. & dona sua, prout vult, distribuere, 1 Cor. XII, 11. Liber autem est Deus non tantum ab omni miseria & peccato, sed & a iure atque obligatione alterius cuiuscunque. Nulli quoque Deus coactioni, vel minima ex parte, subiectus aut subiicibilis est; & cum causam superiorem non agnoscat, a qua determinari queat, indeterminate operatur, vt possit agere, & non agere, iam hunc, iam illum effectum producere.

Prob. b. Voluntas angelorum electorum non est quidem amplius indifferens ad bonum & malum; indifferens tamen est ordine ad bona creata, ita, vt quodlibet eorum, quod vult, possit etiam non velle, aut pro uno velle alterum, nisi propter voluntatem Dei bonum creatum necessario fit appetendum. Apex libertatis angelicæ est, quod, quidquid Deus imperat, sancti angeli summa cum delectatione peragant, & quidquid Deus permisit liberum, sine necessitate & coactione velint; nolintque, & exerceant. Libertatem arbitrii humani secundum diversa obiecta, distinctosque gradus iamiam pensitabimus.

Prob. c. Natura intellectu carens, non pollet libertate arbitrii, cum determinata sit ad unum. Quod patet ex eo: quia 1) bestiæ eodem modo agunt, v. gr. Apes semper eodem modo mellificant, oues omnes pari ratione lupum fugiunt, aranex omnes eodem pacto suas texunt telas. 2) Omnibus ab agendum requisitis præsentibus, non possunt non agere. Canis famelicus præsentem cibum, remoto omni impedimento; non potest non devorare. Quemadmodum vero vmbra quædam rationis, ita & libertatis, in brutis animadvertitur, dum in campis pro lubitu stant, iacent, progrediuntur, iam hanc, iam illam herbam decerpunt; qui tamen bestiarum actus rectius spontanei, quam liberi dicuntur.

Quæst. VI. Quæ est propria & adæquata sedes liberi arbitrii?

Propria & adæquata sedes liberi arbitrii est voluntas . Ad exercitium autem libertatis arbitrii intellectus antecedenter & παρασκευαστικῶς concurrit .

Obs. Quidam auctores statuunt liberum arbitrium tam in intellectu, quam in voluntate sedem suam habere. Hinc, citante CHEMNITIO l. c. fol. 181. ORIGENES libr. III. περὶ ἀρχῶν dicit, esse facultatem rationis, ad bonum malumve discernendum; voluntatis, ad utrumque eligendum. AVGVSTINVS dicit, esse facultatem rationis & voluntatis. THOMAS dicit, esse vim electiuam, quæ mixta quidem fit ex intelligentia & appetitu; magis tamen ad appetitum inelinet. Port. II. c. 38.

art. 3. Prob. a. Quia 1) liberum arbitrium a S. Paullo vocatur potestas propriæ voluntatis 1 Cor. VII, 37. 2) Patres, in concilio Arausicano, Canone XIII, liberum voluntatis arbitrium appellant, vt ostendant, voluntati formaliter libertatem competere. 3) Liberum arbitrium, iudice IRENÆO, est potestas electionis, vel facultas eligendi; electio autem est actio voluntatis. est actio voluntatis. est actio voluntatis.

4) Intellectus, neque quoad speciem actus, neque quoad exercitium actus, liber est. Non est liber, quoad exercitium actus; quia a) vt potentia se determinet ad agendum, necesse est, id fieri vel impetu naturæ, vel libera appetitione actus. At potentiæ liberæ, qua tales, non agunt ex impetu naturæ: Ergo libera inclinatione & voluntariæ. Voluntarium autem aliquid duobus modis dicitur, elicitum, & imperatum. Priori modo actus intellectus non sunt voluntarii, puta, vt ipse eos velit; neque enim intellectus est facultas appetitiua, aut quæ ex se eliciat vllum velle. Posterioriquidem modo voluntarii sunt, non ob libertatem intellectus, sed voluntatis, a qua intellectus ad agendum mouetur & excitatur. b) Posito obiecto, & requisitis præsentibus, non magis potest intellectus rem non cognoscere, ac oculus apertus in media luce obiectum suum videre. Neque liber est intellectus, quoad speciem actus, seu vt assentiatur rei, aut dissentiat, cum eam considerat aut cognoscit. Nam res ea vel est perspicua & euidens (at tum necessario intellectus assentitur, si est vera; vel necessario dissentit, si est falsa); vel est obscura, (& tum neutrum actum elicit; quia obiectum intellectui non præsentatur, plane vt non videmus, cum lumen deest); vel denique res in vtramque partem est probabilis (& tum iterum nec assentitur, nec dissentit, nisi forsan voluntas ad alterutram partem amplectendam ipsum moueat). E quibus patet, intellectum per se & immediate non esse liberum.

Prob. b. Concurrit intellectus ad actum secundum liberi arbitrii antecedenter & παρασκευασικῶς, tanquam conditio, sine qua non voluntas suam libertatem exercere & exercere potest. Voluntas quippe potentia cæca est, quæ ad cognoscendum non est data. Quare necesse est, vt, si illa obiectum quoddam velit eligere, id ei ostendatur ab intellectu, tanquam facultate cognoscente & prælucente. Quod si vero voluntas aliquid agit cæco impetu, absque intellectu, tunc proprie liberum arbitrium non dicitur. Præquiruntur igitur ad liberum arbitrium quidam actus antecedanei: 1) Obiecti cognitio, & si plura adsint obiecta, prudens eorum collatio & diiudicatio. Neque enim voluntas fertur in rem incognitam,quoniam ignoti nulla cupido. 2) Obiecti cognitio propositio, siue præsentatio; qua, cum intellectus obiectum cognouit, tunc illud voluntati vel ad eligendum, vel ad negligendum proponit. 3) Obiecti propositi commendatio, vel dissuasio. Si enim intellectus humanus rem quandam homini conuenientem esse iudicet, tum eandem voluntati suadet & commendat; sin inconuenientem esse censeat, dissuadet. Hos tres actus intellectus sequitur tandem electio, quæ est actus liberi arbitrii proprius, cum voluntas humana illud, quod homini conueniens iudicatum fuit ab intellectu, eligit, omnique nisu si id vnire sertur & tendit. Sunt, qui statuunt, radicem libertatis esse in intellectu. Qui, si per radicem intelligant conditionem antecedentem, sine qua non sit libera electio, nobiscum faciunt. Sin per radicem libertatis intellectum velint causam liberæ electionis, errant. Nam cum voluntas bonum ab intellectu propositum & commendatum eligit, tum facit hoc ex libertate sua, non ex determinatione intellectus. Haud raro quippe vsu venit, vt intellectus meliora proponat & suadeat, voluntas deteriora sequatur (*).

Dicis: intellectus est indifferens in suis actibus & proponendis obiectis. Vnde communiter indifferentia voluntatis dicitur esse ab indifferentia intellectus. Resps. Dist. inter indiffeAPP: (*) praecedentem differentiam obiectivam, & formalem. Intellectus dicitur indifferens non formaliter, sed obiective, quatenus voluntati ostendit rem esse indifferentem, seu tam hoc, quam illud obiectum libere eligi posse.


### Q. VII. In what does free will formally consist?

The form of free will, viewed in its primary act, is the indifference of the will toward either of the opposites, insofar as it is opposed to determination toward one, and by the power of choosing, and of not choosing, or of choosing one rather than the other, and of determining itself toward either one.

Proof. According to the opinion of some authors, the formal notion of free will consists in liberty from coercion, or spontaneity, by which a man desires and performs something of his own accord, without any coercion. But indeed, although immunity from coercion, which is also called interior liberty, always and in every state accompanies the will, and is thus natural to it; it does not, however, exhaust the form of free will; because it is common to man with brutes, which perform many things of their own accord without any coercion, and are not therefore considered to possess free will. But the indifference of the will toward either of the opposites accurately expresses the liberty of the will, provided it is explained dexterously. For by it is not designated a) indifference toward good and evil in general; because in this special way of signifying, neither God, nor angels, nor blessed men enjoy free will; but indifference toward diverse objects, and distinct acts, or the election and rejection of one object. Nor b) by the indifference of the will toward either of the opposites is understood a mathematical indifference, and equal on both sides, which would involve the powers to perform either with equal ease. For such powers and such indifference toward either act, or toward the exercise of an act and its suspension, either never, or rarely, fall to man. In the state of innocence, the first-formed man had free will toward good and evil, yet so that he had a propensity toward good, or a proximate power, and toward evil only a remote power. Reborn men have free will, and through the grace of the Holy Spirit they can act well in spiritual matters; they can also do the opposite through the infirmity of the flesh still inherent; but they perform evil more easily than good, Rom. VII, 15. Wherefore, indifference must be taken in opposition to the determination of the faculty toward one, so that it is called a faculty indifferent toward either, which is not determined toward one, but can do either, although it may perform one more easily than the other. c) Indifference, or indetermination, is understood, both regarding the species and regarding the exercise of the act, so that the will can choose one object and repudiate another, which is the liberty of specification; or can choose and repudiate one object, which is the liberty of exercise. d) Indifference of the will is understood as joined with the power of determining itself toward either part, otherwise the will would always fluctuate [things] yielding and long since past.

You say: 2) It is most true, what is current in the proverb: I see better things, and I approve, I follow worse things. Therefore the will decides and acts not only without reason, but even against it. I affirm indeed, but I also limit: against some reason, not all: When the intellect judges, it always weighs, compares, and confers reasons among themselves on both sides, although in this comparison and estimation it may not be rightly directed. Therefore, several reasons are joined, of which some indeed are true, others false, which nevertheless commend themselves to man by a certain appearance of truth, so that he thinks the specious good is to be preferred to the true good, and what seems greater to the lesser, which he himself falsely opines to be less. The last of so many and so diverse reasons is that which determines the will to act. Therefore, no decree of the will can be made without some error and prejudiced opinion. This is a certain false reason. Therefore, the will decides against true reason indeed, but it follows a false and specious reason, as if it were true.

luntas [is] indifference, without application to a certain act and determined object. But there is supplied to it a power, co-created by God, of applying itself to either part.

Latin:

Forma liberi arbitrii, in actu primo spectati, est indifferentia voluntatis, ad utrumque oppositorum, quatenus illa opponitur determinationi ad unum, & vi facultatem eligendi, & non eligendi, vel eligendi unum præ altero, atque se ipsam ad alterutrum determinandi.

Prob. Nonnullorum auctorum de sententia formalis ratio liberi arbitrii consistit in libertate a coactione, sive spontaneitate, qua homo aliquid sponte sua, citra ullam coactionem appetit & peragit. At vero, quamvis immunitas a coactione, quæ etiam libertas interior vocatur, voluntatem semper & in omni statu comitetur, atque adeo ipsi naturalis sit; non tamen formam liberi arbitrii absoluit; quia communis est homini cum brutis, quæ multa vltro citra ullam agunt coactionem, neque ideo libero pollere arbitrio censentur. Indifferentia autem voluntatis ad utrumque oppositorum libertatem arbitrii accurate exprimit, modo dexte explicetur. Neque enim per illam vniversum designatur a) indifferentia ad bonum & malum; quia hoc speciali significandi modo neque Deus, neque angeli, neque beati homines libero gaudent arbitrio; sed indifferentia ad diversa obiecta, distinctosque actus vel unius obiecti electionem & reiectionem. Neque b) per indifferentiam voluntatis ad utrumque oppositorum intelligitur indifferentia mathematica, & vtrimque æqualis, quæ involuat vires ad utrumque æque facile peragendum. Etenim tales vires & talis indifferentia ad utrumque actum, vel ad exercitium actus & eius suspensionem, aut nunquam, aut raro in hominem cadunt. In statu innocentiæ habebat homo protoplastus arbitrium ad bonum & malum, ita tamen, ut haberet ad bonum propensionem, sive potentiam proximam, ad malum tantum potentiam remotam. Homines renati habent arbitrium liberum, & per gratiam Spiritus S. possunt bene operari in spiritualibus; possunt etiam oppositum facere per carnis infirmitatem adhuc inhærentem; facilius autem perpetrant malum, quam bonum, Rom. VII, 15. Quare sumenda est indifferentia in oppositione ad determinationem facultatis ad unum, vt dicatur facultas indifferens ad utrumque, quæ non est determinata ad unum, sed utrumque potest, licet unum facilius, quam alterum agat. c) Intelligitur indifferentia, sive indeterminatio, tum quoad speciem, tum quoad exercitium actus, vt voluntas unum obiectum eligere, alterum repudiare queat, quæ est libertas specificationis; vel unum obiectum eligere & repudiare possit, quæ est libertas exercitii. d) Intelligitur indifferentia voluntatis coniuncta cum vi, seipsam ad alterutram partem determinandi, alioqui semper fluctuaret voluntas cedentes & iam diu præteritas.

Dicis: 2) Verissimum est, quod in prouerbio versatur: video meliora, proboque, deteriora sequor. Itaque voluntas decernit agitque non modo sine ratione, sed etiam contra eam. Adfirmo equidem, sed & limito: contra aliquam rationem, non omnem: Cum intellectus iudicat, semper ille ponderat, comparat atque inter se confert rationes in vtramque partem, quamuis in hac comparatione atque æstimatione haud recte versetur. Coniunctæ igitur sunt plures rationes, quarum aliæ quidem veræ sunt, aliæ falsæ, quæ tamen specie quadam veritatis se homini ita commendant, vt speciosum bonum vere bono, & quod maius videatur, minori, quod falso quidem opinatur ipse minus, esse anteferendum putet. Tot, tamque diuersarum, rationum postrema est, quæ voluntatem ad agendum determinat. E. nullum fieri potest voluntatis decretum, sine errore quodam, & præiudicata opinione. Hæc est falsa quadam ratio. E. voluntas decernit contra veram quidem rationem, at falsam tamen, ac speciosam rationem, ac si esset vera, sequitur.

CAP. V. luntas indifferentia, sine applicatione ad certum actum & determinatum obiectum. Suppetit autem illi vis, a Deo concreata, ad alterutram partem se applicandi.


### Q. VIII. What is free will considered in the second act?

Free will considered in the second act is the free choice of the will, by which it desires one proposed thing, or rejects it, or embraces one from among several things, and repudiates the rest, according to the judgment of reason.

Proof. The proper act of free will is ἐλευθέρα προαίρεσις (free choice), as Justin Martyr speaks; a free choice, by which it is described or declared in the Holy Scriptures, Deut. XXX, 19. Josh. XXIV, 15. 2 Cor. IX, 7.

Latin:

Liberum arbitrium in actu secundo spectatum est libera electio voluntatis, qua haec unam rem propositam appetit, vel reiicit, aut e pluribus rebus unam amplectitur, & reliquas repudiat, secundum iudicium rationis.

Prob. Actus proprius liberi arbitrii est ἐλευθέρα προαίρεσις, vt loquitur Iustinus Martyr; libera electio, per quam in sacris litteris describitur aut declaratur, Deut. XXX, 19. Ios. XXIV, 15. 2 Cor. IX, 7.


### Q. IX. Is the will determined in choosing by the last practical judgment of reason?

The last practical judgment of reason indeed represents and commends a certain object to the will; but it does not so command the will that it must necessarily embrace it, and therefore it is not determined by it to choose a certain object.

Observation. The practical intellect, or practical reason, is said to be that which is concerned about τὰ πρακτά (things to be done), things to be acted upon, and deliberates whether something is to be done, or otherwise. Its last judgment is the conclusion judging what is to be undertaken. It is usually expressed in these words: This now, all things considered, is to be chosen, or done.

Proof. 1) Because the will, as a free power, all prerequisites being posited, can act and not act, choose and not choose. But the judgment of practical reason pertains to the prerequisites of choice. Therefore, that being posited, the will can choose and not choose, and therefore it is not determined by it to choose [*].

2) When the intellect shows two goods to be equal, the will freely chooses this or that, not predetermined by any command of the intellect.

3) The will in choosing one object over another often does not follow the last judgment of practical reason; but neglects it, especially if it be carried away sideways by the affections. Which is evident a) from the Holy Scriptures. For the Gentiles, with conscience (the last judgment of practical reason) protesting, nevertheless acted evilly, Rom. I, 32. Sinners against the Holy Spirit, after sufficient recognition and approbation of the truth, and therefore against conscience, ἑκουσίως (voluntarily), freely sin, Heb. VI, 4. c. X, 26. []. b) From experience, by which, having been taught, the Ovidian Medea in book VII of the Metamorphoses confesses of herself: But [*] It is necessary, however, that there always be some reason why the will chooses one from among many.

For the will is entirely concerned with the desire for good and the aversion to evil, whether that which truly is so, or that which appears to be. Therefore, man wills or does not will, because he thinks this to be good or evil, greater or lesser; nor can he not will as he thinks it to be. To think is a judgment of the intellect. Therefore, some operation of the intellect always determines the will.

But liberty is not opposed to reason and the internal determination of the mind, but to an impediment, by which a man is less able to act in accordance with reason, and indeed with reason rightly known and sufficiently weighed. See what we noted at p. 435. [] Even a practical judgment is either true or false.

Conscience, if it be right, indeed commands what is to be done or omitted, in accordance with divine law. But there intervenes a prejudiced opinion, one after another, which patronizes unjust desire, and serves to excuse or plainly defend sin. And yet, not only truths which a right conscience teaches a man must be referred to the practical judgment; but also errors contrary to them, false judgments, counsels of the flesh, of which if any becomes the last, this determines the will to act evilly, against a right conscience indeed, but not against the last judgment of the practical intellect.

But a new force drags me, unwilling, and desire suggests one thing, the mind another: I see the better things and approve them, I follow the worse.

You say: The will cannot will anything without the judgment of the reason: Therefore, if the judgment is determined, it too will be determined: But the final practical judgment is altogether determined. Resp. A persuasive judgment belongs to the intellect, but not a command. The intellect judges what is eligible, yet it remains in the discretion of the will to obey the judging intellect or to resist it. Reason, as BERNARD says, is given to the will to instruct it, not to destroy it. But it would destroy it if it imposed any necessity, such that it could not move itself according to its own discretion. And DAMASCENE comments in his book De O. F., ch. 26, writing: The intellect is at least the directive principle of our actions, but the will is the imperative and primarily effective one.

Latin:

Ultimum rationis iudicium practicum voluntati quidem certum obiectum repraesentat & commendat; non autem sic imperat voluntati, vt illud necessario amplectatur, adeoque ab eodem ad eligendum certum obiectum non determinatur.

Obs. Intellectus practicus, vel ratio practica dicitur, quae versatur circa τὰ πρακτά, agibilia, & sitne aliquid faciendum, vel secus, deliberat. Ultimum vero eius iudicium est conclusio iudicans, quid suscipiendum fit. Exprimi solet his verbis: Hoc nunc, omnibus consideratis, eligendum, aut faciendum est.

Prob. 1) Quia voluntas, tanquam potentia libera, omnibus praerequisitis positis potest agere, & non agere, eligere, & non eligere. At iudicium rationis practicae pertinet ad praerequisita electionis. E. illo posito, potest voluntas eligere & non eligere, adeoque ab illo ad eligendum non determinatur [*].

2) Quando intellectus ostendit, duo bona esse aequalia, voluntas libere hoc, aut illud eligit, nullo imperio intellectus praedeterminata.

3) Voluntas in eligendo vno obiecto prae alio, saepe non sequitur ultimum rationis practicae iudicium; sed illud negligit, inprimis si affectibus in transuersum abripiatur. Quod patet a) e sacris litteris. Nam gentiles, reclamante conscientia (ultimo iudicio rationis practicae) nihilominus egerunt male, Rom. I, 32. Peccatores in Spiritum S. post sufficientem agnitionem & approbationem veritatis, adeoque contra conscientiam, ἑκουσίως, libere peccant, Hebr. VI, 4. c. X, 26. []. b) Ex experientia, qua edocta Medea Ouidiana libro VII. metamorph. de se fatetur: Sed [*] Necesse est tamen, vt semper aliqua sit ratio, quare voluntas vnum ex pluribus eligat.

Voluntas enim tota versatur in adpetitione boni, atque auersatione mali, siue quod vere ita fit, siue quod videatur esse. E. vult homo, aut non vult, quoniam hoc putat esse bonum, aut malum, maius, aut minus; nec potest non ita velle, vt putat esse. Putare, est iudicium intellectus. E. semper operatio quaedam intellectus voluntatem determinat.

Libertas autem non rationi atque internae mentis determinationi opponitur, sed impedimento, quo minus possit homo agere, rationi conuenienter, & quidem recte cognitae ac satis ponderatae. Vid. quae notauimus ad p. 435. [] Etiam practicum iudicium vel verum est, vel falsum.

Conscientia, si recta fit, imperat quidem, quid agendum sit, omittendumue, legi diuinae congruenter. Sed intercedit praeiudicata opinio alia ex alia, quae cupiditati iniustae patrocinatur, & peccato excusando, aut plane defendendo inferuit. Atqui ad practicum iudicium referri debent non solum veritates, quas recta conscientia hominem docet; sed etiam errores illis contrarii, falsa iudicia, consilia carnis, quorum si quid vltimum fit, hoc determinat voluntatem ad male agendum, contra rectam quidem conscientiam, nec vero contra vltimum intellectus practici iudicium.

Sed trahit invitam nova vis, aliudque cupido, Mens aliud suadet: video meliora proboque, Deteriora sequor.

Dicis: Voluntas non potest aliquid velle, sine iudicio rationis: Ergo si iudicium determinatum fit, & ipsa determinata erit: At iudicium ultimum practicum omnino est determinatum. Resp. Competit intellectui persuadens iudicium, sed non imperium. Iudicat intellectus, quid sit eligibile, in voluntatis tamen arbitrio manet, iudicanti intellectui obedire, vel reluctari. Est ratio, dicente BERNHARDO, data voluntati, ut instruat illam, non ut destruat. Destrueret autem, si necessitatem ullam imponeret, quo minus pro arbitrio suo sese volueret. Et cominentatur DAMASCENI in libro de O. F. c. 26. scribit: Nostrarum actionum intellectus principium saltem directivum est, voluntas vero imperativum atque primario effectivum.


### Q. X. Concerning what does free will revolve?

Free will revolves around every agible object proposed to the will by the intellect, whether it be present or future, which the will desires under the aspect of good, even though it may not always be a true good, but only an apparent one. Prob. Because free will is an active power of the will, its object must be agible, i.e., that which can be obtained through the natural or supernatural active power of the will. Whatever is simply impossible is not πρακτὸν, or agible. But concerning impossibles we neither deliberate nor form a decree of election. Furthermore, every agible thing is either present or future. Free will is of both present and future things. It is of future things: because we consult about them. But those things of which there is consultation, of those there is free election. It is of present things: because those things about which we have previously deliberated, we choose in the present. However, nothing is chosen by the will except under the aspect of good, whether it be a true good or an apparent one. But since an apparent good is in itself evil, a certain object of free will, considered materially, is evil. In which sense not only goods, but also evils, fall under free election.

Latin:

Liberum arbitrium versatur circa omne obiectum agibile, ab intellectu voluntati propositum, sive sit præsens, sive futurum, quod voluntas sub ratione boni appetit, tametsi non semper sit bonum verum, sed tantum apparens. Prob. Quia liberum arbitrium est vis activa voluntatis, obiectum eius oportet esse agibile, i. e. quod per activam voluntatis vim naturalem, aut supernaturalem obtineri potest. Quidquid simpliciter impossibile est, illud non est πρακτὸν, seu agibile. De impossibilibus autem neque deliberamus, neque decretum electionis formamus. Ceterum omne agibile vel est præsens, vel futurum. Liberum arbitrium est tam præsentium, quam futurorum. Est futurorum: quia de illis consultamus. At quorum est consultatio, illorum est libera electio. Est præsentium: quia illa, de quibus antea deliberavimus, in præsenti eligimus. Nihil autem eligitur a voluntate, nisi sub ratione boni, sive sit bonum verum, sive apparens. At cum bonum apparens in se sit malum, quoddam obiectum liberi arbitrii materialiter consideratum malum est. Quo sensu sub liberam electionem cadunt non tantum bona, sed & mala.


### Q. XI. How are the objects of free will distinguished?

The objects of free will are distinguished according to two hemispheres, of which one is lower, the other higher. The lower embraces physical, ethical, political, economic, artificial, pedagogical, and divine things and actions, insofar as they can be known from the light of reason and produced by the powers of nature, aided by the general concurrence of God a). The higher, in its ambit, encompasses merely spiritual things and actions, which, placed above the grasp of reason left to itself, are known from the light of supernatural revelation and are performed by the special grace of the Holy Spirit b). Prob. a. The objects of the human will are known either from the light of reason or from the light of supernatural revelation. From the light of reason are known things and actions 1) physical, which concern the natural body as such, e.g., to eat, to drink, to walk; 2) ethical, which pertain to the governing of human morals, e.g., to cultivate temperance, modesty, etc.; 3) political, which pertain to the state of the city, e.g., to pay tribute, to sustain the office of magistrate; 4) economic, which are occupied in governing a family, e.g., to take a wife, to educate children honestly; 5) artificial, which depend on art, e.g., to paint, to sew shoes; 6) pedagogical, or external sacred, which indeed are external and revolve around a sacred object, yet are in themselves indifferent, and by reason of the outcome are now good, now evil, e.g., to frequent with the feet the tem- e.g., to frequent with the feet e.g., to frequent with the feet e.g., to frequent with the feet

temple, to receive the word with external ears.

They are called pedagogical, because they ought to lead man as if by the hand to a further inquiry into sacred things.

7) Divine, in so far as they are knowable from nature, e.g., from the contemplation of creatures to infer the existence, goodness, and omnipotence of God.

Prob. b. Things and actions that are merely spiritual are known from supernatural illumination, and are performed by the gracious influx of the Holy Spirit, e.g., conversion, regeneration, renewal, etc. These merely spiritual actions are proposed in the law and the gospel.

Latin:

Obiecta liberi arbitrii distinguuntur secundum duo hemisphæria, quorum unum inferius, alterum superius est. Inferius complectitur res & actiones physicas, ethicas, politicas, œconomicas, artificiales, pædagogicas & diuinas, quatenus e lumine rationis cognosci, viribusque naturæ, concursu Dei generali adiutis, produci possunt a). Superius ambitu suo comprehendit res & actiones mere spirituales, quæ, supra rationis, sibi relictæ, captum positæ, e lumine supernaturalis revelationis cognoscuntur, & speciali Spiritus S. gratia præstantur b). Prob. a. Obiecta voluntatis humanæ cognoscuntur vel e lumine rationis, vel e lumine supernaturalis revelationis. E lumine rationis cognoscuntur res & actiones 1) physicæ, quæ corpus naturale, quatenus tale, concernunt, v. gr. edere, bibere, ambulare; 2) ethicæ, quæ ad mores hominum regendos pertinent, v. gr. colere temperantiam, modestiam, &c. 3) politicæ, quæ ad statum civitatis pertinent, v. gr. tributum soluere, sustinere officium magistratus; 4) œconomicæ, quæ in familia regenda occupantur, v. gr. ducere uxorem, honeste educare liberos; 5) artificiales, quæ ab arte pendent, v. gr. pingere, consuere calceos; 6) pædagogicæ, sive sacræ externæ, quæ quidem externæ circa obiectum sacrum versantur, per se tamen indifferentes, ratione euentus, iam bonæ, iam malæ sunt, v. gr. pedibus frequentare temv.gr. pedibus frequentare v.gr. pedibus frequentare v.gr. pedibus frequentare

templum, auribus externis accipere verbum.

Dicuntur paedagogicae, quia hominem veluti manu ducere debent ad inquisitionem ulteriorem rerum sacrarum.

7) Divinae, in quantum ex natura cognoscibiles sunt, v. gr. ex intuitu creaturarum colligere existentiam, bonitatem, omnipotentiam Dei.

Prob. b. Res & actiones mere spirituales ex illuminatione supernaturali cognoscuntur, & gratioso Spiritus S. influxu praestantur, v. gr. conversio, regeneratio, renovatio &c. Proponuntur hae actiones mere spirituales in lege & euangelio.


### Q. XII. According to how many states is free will to be considered?

Free will is to be considered according to a fourfold state: a) of innocence before the fall; b) of misery after the fall; c) of grace after conversion; d) of glory in eternal beatitude.

Prob. a. In the state of innocence, before the fall, the protoplasts were free not from law or obligation toward God, since every creature is obligated to worship the creator: but 1) from coaction, or external necessity; 2) from the internal necessity of immutability, because they were not yet determined toward good, but their will was indifferent to good and evil, yet so that they had a proximate power for good, and a most remote power for evil. 3) They possessed the liberty of rectitude. For they were immune from the guilt, dominion, and sense of sin, and from every misery of body and soul. Therefore, they freely and readily chose the good, for the embracing of which and the avoiding of evil they were instructed with sufficient powers through the image of God.

Prob. b. In the state of misery, after the fall, the corrupt sinner has freedom of will, in so far as it materially denotes τὴν ἑκουσίον [the voluntary], or the essence of the will. For just as he did not lose his rational soul through the fall, so neither did he suffer the loss of the faculties of the soul considered essentially. 2) There remains to him after the fall a passive obedientiary power to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit. For he is neither a log nor a devil, who is in no way capable of grace. 3) He is free from coaction, because this interior liberty always and in every state accompanies the will. 4) He has external liberty for the good that is naturally knowable; but he is destitute of free will for choosing the good that is merely spiritual.

Prob. c. In the state of grace, after conversion, the reborn man is free 1) from coaction, 2) from the necessity of immutability, because after conversion his will is no longer determined toward evil, as it was before conversion: but he can freely choose the spiritual good through the grace of the Holy Spirit indwelling and assisting, and he can also choose evil through the remnants of the flesh still clinging to him. He enjoys, therefore, the liberty of rectitude; in that he has obtained freedom from the guilt of sin in justification, and from the dominion of sin in renewal.

Prob. d. In the state of glory, the blessed man is free not only from coaction, and not only from guilt and dominion, but also from every sense of sin, just as from every misery of body and soul. This liberty will be far more perfect than that of man before the fall. For here he was able not to sin, but the blessed truly cannot sin. XIII. Does the unregenerate man, before conversion, possess freedom of will to choose the merely spiritual good, or at least some natural power to prepare himself for his own conversion? Before the conversion of the unregenerate man, the intellect is filled with such thick darkness that it does not truly know and approve the supernatural good a). His will, subjected to the servitude of sin, is impotent to choose the spiritual good b). Therefore, the unconverted man is destitute of every natural power παρασκευασικῇ, or preparatory, for his own conversion c).

Obj. Free will is not taken here materially, for τῇ οὐσίᾳ, or the essence of the human will, which, together with the intellect, pertains to the essence of man, and undoubtedly resides in man even after the fall, before he is regenerated: but formally, for τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ, for the powers of the will, by which he is able to act and not to act, to do this and to do that.

The Solid Declaration of the Formula of Concord, p. 655, teaches this. This is the true and only state of the controversy: What the intellect and will of a man not yet reborn can perform, in the very act of conversion and regeneration, out of his own powers remaining after the fall; namely, when the Word of God is preached and the grace of God is offered to us. Here it is asked: whether man can apply himself to apprehend this grace, embrace it, and assent to the Word of God.

Proof a. 1) From the blindness of the human intellect in merely spiritual matters, from 1 Cor. II, 14: "The natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness unto him, neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned."

From which we argue: He who does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, nor can know them, his intellect is utterly blind in merely spiritual matters. The major premise is evident; because where there is some spiritual light, there is also the faculty of knowing the things of the Spirit of God; indeed, the faculty of knowing the things of the Spirit of God consists in spiritual light, and thus it implies a contradiction to have some powers of perceiving the things of the Spirit of God, and yet not be able to know spiritual things. The minor is clear from the cited passage of Paul; for the things of the Spirit of God must be discerned spiritually, i.e., from the light of grace, which the Holy Spirit kindles through the Word.

But he is a natural man, because he is not illuminated by the Holy Spirit. This exposition is clear from verse 10, where the apostle says: "The Holy Spirit has revealed them unto us."

2) From the nature and condition of spiritual things, which far exceed the natural light of reason, so that they are called mysteries hidden from the ages, Eph. III, 9; Col. I, 26; and kept secret since the world began, Rom. XVI, 25. We conclude: Whatever by its nature far exceeds the grasp of human reason, regarding those things the intellect of the unregenerate man has no spiritual powers whatsoever: But the things of the Spirit of God by their nature far exceed the grasp of human reason:

Therefore.

3) From the origin of saving knowledge, which is entirely attributed to divine grace, John VI, 65: "No man can come unto me, except it were given unto him of my Father," i.e., No man can believe in me, unless it were given to him by the Father.

Let the argument be such: That which happens to no one, unless it is given to him by God, does not fall under the powers of the natural man: But the saving knowledge of spiritual things, etc.: Therefore. The major is clear: For that which falls under the powers of natural human reason can naturally happen to man, nor is there need that it be given to him supernaturally by God.

Proof b. 1) From the spiritual death of the unregenerate man. For the unregenerate man is said to be dead in sins, Eph. II, 1; Col. II, 13. The argument in form will be such: He who is spiritually dead, his will is destitute of spiritual powers to exercise pious acts regarding spiritual goods; APP: a) 1 Cor. 2:14. b) Rom. 7:14, 18, 19. c) Rom. 8:7. spiritual things: But the unregenerate man, etc.: Therefore. The major is confirmed by the Formula of Concord, p. 658. Just as a man who is corporally dead cannot prepare or accommodate himself by his own powers to receive eternal life: so a man, spiritually dead in sins, cannot prepare, apply, or turn himself by his own powers to attain spiritual and heavenly righteousness and life, unless he be liberated from the death of sin and vivified by the Son of God. 2) From the base and shameful servitude of the unregenerate man. Concerning which Christ says in John VIII, 34: Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. Paul supports this in Rom. V, 16, 17, 18. Do you not know that to whom you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves to whom you obey? Whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness. But thanks be to God, that you were slaves of sin, but you obeyed from the heart that form of doctrine to which you were delivered. Being therefore liberated from sin, you became slaves of righteousness. Cf. 2 Pet. II, 19. We argue: The will of whatever man is subject to the servitude of sin, for him there is no freedom of will to produce spiritual acts: But the will of the unregenerate man, etc. Therefore. The major is evident: because the servitude of sin is opposed by Paul to the freedom of grace, and in the Petrine style, he is a slave who has been conquered and captivated by another. But he who has been conquered and captivated by sin does not freely pursue spiritual and heavenly righteousness. 3) The impotence of the will of the unregenerate is evident from the oracle of the Savior in John XV, 5: Without me you can do nothing. Those who without Christ, the heavenly vine, can bear no spiritual fruit, they are made inept for every good spiritual work. But all men existing outside the state of regeneration, etc. Therefore.

You say: Without Christ assisting, the unregenerate man does not bear spiritual fruit, which however he produces of himself, assisted by the grace of Christ. Resp. The words of Christ are to be expounded not privatively, but negatively; not conjunctively, but exclusively, so that it may detract from human powers the beginning, progress, and completion of spiritual operation, and claim it entirely for the grace of Christ.

Prob. c. That a man can in no way prepare himself by his own powers for his own conversion is easily gathered from the blindness of the intellect and the impotence of the will in the unregenerate, and this has already been proven by the preceding arguments. We add only two arguments, which clearly prove the natural ineptitude for beginning and promoting conversion. 1) Paul denies to men the aptitude for thinking of spiritual good, 2 Cor. III, 5: We are not sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God. Whoever can think nothing good of themselves, but owe all and every good thought to divine grace, they can neither begin nor promote their own conversion by their own powers.

You say: The cited words are not to be understood concerning the powers of the will regarding spiritual things, but concerning the evangelical ministry. Resp. Although the apostle speaks principally concerning the ministry of the word: yet from the greater to the less, one may gather from the apostle's statement: If the reborn ministers of God are not of themselves sufficient to do, or to say, or even to think anything, and hence are in need of an aptitude to be received from God; much less will men not yet reborn be of themselves sufficient in the work of conversion for spiritual good, either to think, or to say, or to do.

2) The same Apostle says in Rom. VIII, 7: φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς ἔχθρα εἰς θεόν. The mind of the flesh is enmity against God: for it does not submit itself to the law of God, nor indeed can it. φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς is not only the prudence and meditation of the blinded intellect, but also the care and desire of the perverted will. Flesh denotes the corruption congenital to man after the fall, opposed to the spirit. Of this mind of the flesh it is said that it becomes enmity against God, by which is designated rebellion, contrariety, resistance, because corrupt flesh neither submits itself to the law of God, nor can by natural powers submit itself. From which we argue: That man whose intellect and will in its thoughts and desires opposes God about to begin conversion in him, resists His law, and cannot obey Him by natural powers, that man cannot prepare himself for his own conversion: But the intellect and will of the unregenerate man, etc. Therefore.

The antithesis was formerly that of the Pelagians, who did not fear to affirm that man, without the Holy Spirit , could convert himself to God by his own powers. That of the Semipelagians, or Massilians (so called from Cassian, a presbyter of Massilia), who attributed the beginning of conversion sometimes to free will, sometimes to the Holy Spirit, according to the diverse condition of the different subjects. To these are added most Scholastics and Papists, according to whose opinion free will was indeed weakened by the fall, but not lost. The Socinians maintain that by the fall of the protoplasts neither was original sin introduced, nor was free will in spiritual matters lost, whom the Arminians follow.

Latin:

Liberum arbitrium considerandum est secundum quadruplicem statum: a) innocentiae ante lapsum; b) miseriae post lapsum; c) gratiae post conversionem; d) gloriae in aeterna beatitudine.

Prob. a. In statu innocentiae, ante lapsum homines protoplasti liberi erant non a lege, aut obligatione erga Deum, cum omnis creatura sit obligata ad colendum creatorem: sed 1) a coactione, sive necessitate externa; 2) a necessitate interna immutabilitatis, propterea, quod ad bonum nondum erant determinati, sed voluntas eorum erat indifferens ad bonum & malum, ita tamen, vt ad bonum potentiam proximam, ad malum potentiam remotissimam haberent. 3) Polebant libertate rectitudinis. Erant quippe immunes a reatu, dominio & sensu peccati, omnique miseria corporis & animae. Proinde libere & expedite bonum eligebant, ad quod amplectendum, & malum evitandum sufficientibus viribus per imaginem Dei instructi erant.

Prob. b. In statu miseriae, post lapsum habet homo peccator corruptus libertatem arbitrii, quatenus materialiter notat τὴν ἑκουσίον, sive essentiam voluntatis. Nam sicut per lapsum non deperdidit animam rationalem, ita nec iacturam fecit facultatum animae essentialiter consideratarum. 2) Suppetit illi post lapsum potentia passiva obedientialis, ad recipiendam gratiam Spiritus S. Neque enim truncus aut diabolus est, qui gratiae minime est capax. 3) Liber est a coactione, quia haec libertas interior voluntatem semper & in omni statu comitatur. 4) Habet libertatem exteriorem ad bonum naturaliter cognoscibile; sed destituitur libero arbitrio ad bonum mere spirituale eligendum.

Prob. c. In statu gratiae, post conversionem liber est homo renatus 1) a coactione, 2) a necessitate immutabilitatis, quia post conversionem voluntas ipsius non amplius determinata est ad malum, sicut ante conversionem: sed potest libere eligere bonum spirituale per gratiam Spiritus S. inhabitantem & adiuuantem, potest etiam eligere malum per carnis reliquias adhuc in ipso haerentes. Gaudet ergo libertate rectitudinis; eo, quod nactus est libertatem a reatu peccati in iustificatione, & a dominio peccati in renouatione .

Prob. d. In statu gloriae, homo beatus liber est non tantum a coactione, nec solum a reatu ac dominio, sed etiam ab omni sensu peccati, iuxta atque ab omni miseria corporis & animae. Haec libertas longe perfectior erit, quam hominis ante lapsum. Hic enim poterat non peccare, beati vero non possunt peccare. XIII. Estne homini irregenito ante conuersionem libertas arbitrii ad eligendum bonum mere spirituale, aut saltem vis quædam naturalis præparandi se ad sui conuersionem? Ante conuersionem hominis irregeniti intellectus tam spissis oppletus est tenebris, vt bonum supernaturale vere non cognoscat & approbet a). Voluntas ipsius, peccati seruituti subiecta, impotens est ad eligendum bonum spirituale b). Idcirco homo inconuersus omni vi naturali παρασκευασικῇ, seu præparatiua ad conuersionem sui destituitur c).

Obf. Liberum arbitrium heic non sumitur materialiter, pro τῇ οὐσίᾳ, seu essentia voluntatis humanæ, quæ vna cum intellectu ad essentiam hominis pertinet, & haud dubie homini inest etiam post lapsum, antequam regeneretur: sed formaliter, pro τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ, pro viribus voluntatis, quibus infructa agere & non agere, agere hoc, & agere illud potest.

Docet hoc fol. declar. Form. Concordiæ p. 655. Hic est verus & vnicus controuersiæ status: Quid hominis nondum renati intellectus & voluntas, in ipsa conuersione & regeneratione, ex propriis suis & post lapsum reliquis viribus præstare possit; quando scilicet verbum Dei prædicatur & Dei gratia nobis offertur. Hic quæritur: an homo ad hanc gratiam apprehendendam sese applicare, eam amplecti, & verbo Dei assentiri possit.

Prob. a. 1) A cæcitate intellectus humani in rebus mere spiritualibus, ex 1 Cor. II, 14. Animalis homo non suscipit ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei; stultitia enim illi funt, & non potest scire, quia spiritualiter diiudicantur.

Ex quo argumentamur: Qui non suscipit ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, nec potest ea cognoscere, illius intellectus prorsus cæcus est in rebus mere spiritualibus. Maior est euidens; quia vbi est lux aliqua spiritualis, ibi etiam est facultas cognoscendi ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei; immo facultas cognoscendi ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei consistit in luce spirituali, adeoque implicat contradictionem, habere aliquas vires percipiendi ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, & tamen non posse cognoscere spiritualia. Minor patet ex loco citato Paulli; nam ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, spiritualiter, i. e. ex lumine gratiæ, quod Spiritus S. per verbum accendit, sunt diiudicanda.

Animalis autem homo est, quia Spiritu S. non est illuminatus. Quæ expositio patet ex versu 10. vbi apostolus inquit: nobis reuelauit Spiritus S.

2) Ex natura & conditione rerum spiritualium, quæ naturale rationis lumen longissime excedunt, ita vt dicantur mysteria a sæculis abscondita, Eph. III, 9. Coloss. I, 26. & a temporibus sæcularibus tacita, Rom. XVI, 25. Colligimus: Quæcunque natura sua rationis humanæ captum longissime excedunt, circa illa intellectus hominis non renati nihil quidquam habet virium spiritualium: Atqui ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, natura sua captum rationis humanæ longissime excedunt:

Ergo.

3) Ab origine cognitionis salutaris, quippe quæ in solidum gratiæ diuinæ accepta fertur, Io. VI, 65. Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi fuerit ei datum a Patre meo, i. e. Nemo potest credere in me, nisi fuerit datum ei a Patre.

Argumentum esto tale: Quod nemini obtingit, nisi cui a Deo datur, id sub naturalis hominis vires non cadit: Atqui salutaris rerum spiritualium cognitio &c: Ergo. Maior patet: Quod enim sub naturales humanæ rationis vires cadit, id naturaliter potest obtingere homini, nec opus est, vt supernaturaliter ei a Deo detur.

Prob. b. 1) A morte spirituali hominis irregeniti. Dicitur enim homo non renatus mortuus in peccatis, Eph. II, 1. Col. II, 13. Argumentum in forma tale erit: Qui spiritualiter mortuus est, illius voluntas destituitur viribus spiritualibus ad exercendos pios actus circa bona spiritualia: Atqui homo irregenitus &c: Ergo. Maiorem confirmat Formula Concordia p. 658. Sicut homo, qui corporaliter mortuus est, seipsum propriis viribus praeparare, aut accommodare non potest, ut vitam aeternam recipiat: ita homo, spiritualiter in peccatis mortuus, seipsum propriis viribus ad consequendam spiritualem & caelestem iustitiam & vitam praeparare, applicare, aut vertere non potest, nisi per Filium Dei a morte peccati liberetur & vivificetur. 2) a servitute turpi & probrosa hominis irregeniti. De qua Christus Io. VIII, 34. inquit: Omnis faciens peccatum, servus est peccati. Suffragatur Paullus Rom. V, 16. 17. 18. Nonne scitis, quod, cui sistitis vos ipsos servos in obedientiam, servi sitis, cui obeditis? Sive peccati in mortem, sive obedientiae in iustitiam. Gratia vero Deo, quod eratis servi peccati, obedivistis vero ex animo, in quem traditi estis typum doctrinae. Liberati itaque a peccato, servi facti estis iustitiae. Conf. 2 Petr. II, 19. Argumentamur: Cuiuscunque hominis voluntas servituti peccati subiecta est, illi non suppetit libertas arbitrii edendi actus spirituales: Atqui voluntas hominis irregeniti &c. Ergo. Maior constat: quia feruitus peccati libertati gratiae a Paullo opponitur, & stilo Petrino servus est, qui ab altero est victus & captiuatus. At qui a peccato victus & captiuatus est, is libere non sectatur iustitiam spiritualem & caelestem. 3) Impotentia voluntatis inregeniti constat ex oraculo Salvatoris Io. XV, 5. Sine me nihil potestis facere. Qui fine Christo, vite caelesti, nulluin spiritualem possunt ferre fructum, illi ad omne bonum opus spirituale fiunt inepti. At omnes homines extra statum regenerationis existentes &c. Ergo.

Dicis: Sine Christo adiuuante homo irregenitus non fert fructum spiritualem, quem tamen ex se profert, gratia Christi adiutus. Resp. Verba Christi non priuatiue, sed negatiue; non coniunctiue, sed exclusive exponenda sunt, vt initium, progressus & complementum spiritualis operationis viribus humanis deroget, & gratiae Christi in solidum vindicet.

Prob. c. Hominem propriis viribus ad conuersionem sui se praeparare minime posse, ex caecitate intellectus & impotentia voluntatis in irregenito facile colligitur, idque iam antecedentibus argumentis euictum est. Addimus tantum duo argumenta, quae naturalem ineptitudinem ad inchoandam & promouendam conuersionem luculente probant. 1) Paullus aptitudinem ad cogitandum bonum spirituale hominibus derogat, 2 Cor. III, 5. Non idonei sumus a nobis ipsis cogitare aliquid, tanquam ex nobis ipsis, sed quod idonei sumus, ex Deo est. Quicunque ex seipsis nihil boni cogitare possunt, sed omnes & singulas bonas cogitationes gratiae diuinae debent, illi propriis viribus conuersionem suam nec inchoare, nec promouere possunt.

Dicis: Verba citata non intelligenda sunt de viribus voluntatis circa spiritualia, sed de ministerio euangelico. Resp. Quamuis apostolus principaliter loquatur de ministerio verbi: a maiori tamen ad minus ex effato apostoli colligere licet: Si renati Dei ministri ex se non sunt idonei ad aliquid non modo efficiendum, vel dicendum, sed & cogitandum, & hinc indigi sunt aptitudinis a Deo accipiendae; multo minus homines nondum renati ex se idonei erunt in opere conuersionis ad bonum spirituale, vel cogitandum, vel dicendum, vel faciendum.

2) Idem Apostolus Rom. VIII, 7. inquit: φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς ἔχθρα εἰς θεόν. Sensus carnis inimicitia est contra Deum: Legi enim Dei non subiicit se, neque enim potest. φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς non est tantum prudentia & meditatio intellectus occaecati, sed & cura & desiderium voluntatis peruerfae. Caro notat congenitam homini post lapsum corruptionem, spiritui oppositam. De hoc sensu carnis dicitur, quod fit inimicitia erga Deum, qua designatur rebellio, contrarietas, resistentia, eo, quod caro corrupta neque legi Dei se subiicit, neque peruires naturales se subiicere potest. E quibus argumentamur: Cuius hominis intellectus & voluntas in cogitationibus & desideriis suis Deo conuersionem inchoaturo obsistit, legi eius obnititur, eique per vires naturales obedire nequit, ille homo ad conuersionem sui non potest se praeparare: Atqui hominis irregeniti intellectus & voluntas &c. Ergo.

Antithesis fuit olim Pelagianorum, qui non veriti sunt affirmare, quod homo sine Spiritu Sancto propriis viribus ad Deum se convertere possit. Semipelagianorum, sive Massiliensium (ita dicebantur a Cassiano, Massiliensium Presbytero), qui conversionis initium modo libero arbitrio, modo Spiritui S. tribuebant, pro subiectorum diversorum diversa conditione. His accedunt plerique Scholastici & Pontificii, quorum de sententia liberum arbitrium per lapsum quidem est debilitatum, sed non amissum. Sociniani statuunt, per lapsum protoplastorum neque introductum esse peccatum originis, neque liberum arbitrium in spiritualibus esse deperditum, quos sequuntur Arminiani.


### Q. XII. According to how many states is free will to be considered?: Their arguments are

Their arguments are:

I. Whoever by their doctrine transforms man into a brute, or plainly into a log, their doctrine does not deserve approval.

But the Protestant doctors, etc. do this.

Therefore.

The minor is clear: since Protestants teach, 1) that free will was lost by the fall, when yet by that very thing man is distinguished from beasts, because these act uniformly, but man behaves indifferently toward diverse objects and their acts: 2) the same teach that man does not even bring a passive potency to his own conversion; by which very thing he is assimilated to a log, which has neither active nor passive potency to bend itself.

Resp.

This argument is easily refuted, provided the doctrine of the Protestants is correctly explained.

For 1) they do not deny that there is freedom of will in man after the fall, if this is taken materially, so that it denotes τὴν οὐσίαν, the essence of the human will; but the same take free will formally for τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ, or the powers of choosing or acting (to avoid which equivocation some authors call them the powers of free will).

Nor do they simply and universally deny to the will all powers of choosing spiritual things.

2) They do not deny that there is in the unregenerate a remote and obediential passive potency of receiving the grace of conversion, but they only teach that the unregenerate man lacks a natural and proximate passive potency for receiving the supernatural influx of the Holy Spirit: by which very thing he is distinguished both from a brute and from a log.

II. God commands and enjoins that we convert ourselves, Zech.

I, 4. Joel II, 13.

Jer.

III, 1.

Which precepts will be vain and void if man does not have the powers to convert himself.

Resp.

1) From a precept to a fact, from "ought" to "can" does not follow.

Christ commanded the dead daughter of Jairus: Arise!

Mark V, 41, who could not arise by her own powers.

So also the unregenerate man is dead in sins, Eph. II, 1.

2) Divine precepts are not given in vain; but considered legally, they do not indeed show the measure of our powers; yet they a) indicate the right of God, demanding those powers which He had conferred upon the first man; b) prescribe the norm of our duty; c) require from us passive obedience, i. e., non-resistance; d) convict us of our infirmity; e) pedagogically lead us to Christ, Gal. III, 24.
