Considered evangelically, insofar as they have divine grace conjoined, they are effective and persuasive, as efficacious means by which the powers of converting are offered and conferred upon those who do not morosely and pertinaciously resist.

III. He who commands those things which exceed the powers of the will is a tyrant: God is not a tyrant: Therefore.

Resp.

He who commands those things which simply and always exceed the powers of men is a tyrant.

But God does not do that; but 1) He had indulged the protoplasts with the powers of perfectly worshipping God.

By His right God demands that which man lost by his own malice.

2) God prevents the impotent by nature with His grace, so that he may become potent through grace. 3) Man, prevented by divine grace, can by contumacious malice not resist, can not place a malicious obstacle to the Holy Spirit, can admit the means divinely ordained, so that the Holy Spirit may kindle saving faith in him through the divine word.

IV. Whoever are commanded to awake from sleep, they rise by their own powers: But unregenerate men &c. Eph. V, 14: Therefore. The major is evident: because a sleeper, when awakened, rises by his own powers. Resp. Unregenerate men are awakened and rise from dead works not by their own virtue, but by the virtue of this powerful and efficacious word, Hebr. IV, 12. For this precept, considered legally, does not express the measure of our powers, but the norm of our debt: considered evangelically, it is an efficacious medium for awakening one dead in sins, and for illuminating the blind, provided he does not stubbornly resist, but allows himself to be illuminated.

V. The divine command of conversion is not above us, Deut. XXX, 11. Therefore it can be performed by the powers of our free will. Resp. The cited words according to the Hebrew source are as follows: This precept, which I am commanding you today, is not wonderful before you, nor is it far off. Paul repeats this precept, Rom. X, 6. 7. 8. and adds: This is the word of faith, which we preach. Wherefore by the divine precept, given by Moses to the Israelite people, is not understood precisely the word of the law, but also the word of the gospel, as Paul teaches. This word is fulfilled not by our own powers, but by the efficacy of the divine promise, by which saving faith is kindled.

VI. Whoever does not have free will of the will, for him neither punishments nor rewards are to be established: The opinion of the Protestants, the unregenerate man &c: Therefore. The major is proven: because he is afflicted with punishments in whose power it was to decline that which he committed; he is honored with rewards who willingly performed that which he ought. Resp. Distinguish between things of the superior and inferior hemisphere. In matters of the inferior hemisphere, concerning this life, man after the fall has free will, and so by reason of these, punishment and temporal reward are established for man. In matters of the superior hemisphere, man is indeed destitute of the powers of free will; yet it is in his power not to resist the means of conversion divinely offered. He is punished if he maliciously resists; he is not punished if he does not struggle against the offered means.

VII. If man can receive the offered means by the powers of nature, then he certainly has free will in spiritual matters: The antecedent is true: Therefore also the consequent. The major is proven, because the offered means are spiritual goods. But if man can receive those by natural powers, it is validly concluded that free will remains after the fall in spiritual matters. Resp. The offering of means pertains to the preventing grace of God, by which the natural passive incapacity connate to all is taken away, so that man becomes capable of the passive reception of the means; from which it is wrongly concluded in favor of free will; for that, by common opinion, is the active power of the will. To this is added, that man, prevented by grace, may indeed use the means of conversion externally, but does not effect the internal conversion by his own powers; just as a sick man indeed receives the medicine administered by the doctor, yet does not have the powers of healing himself.

VIII. Siracides c. XV, 14. 15. attributes to man the freedom of will, saying: God made man from the beginning, and left him in the hand of his own counsel: If you will, you shall keep the commandments. Resp. 1) The book of Siracides is outside the canon, and thus dogmas of faith cannot be proven from it. 2) Siracides speaks of man before the fall in his instituted nature; after the fall, the unregenerate man is a slave of sin.

IX. Moses, Deut. XXX, 19. and Joshua, c. XXIV, 15. grant to the Israelites the option, or free choice. Therefore they attribute free will to them. Resp. Moses and Joshua speak with the Israelites as with reborn men. But the question is about the unregenerate man: can he choose a merely spiritual object by natural powers, and act concerning it?

X. God did not deny to Cain the fratricide dominion over sin, but rather commanded it, Gen. IV, 7. Therefore He grants to every most grievous sinner free will in spiritual matters. Resp. 1) From a precept it is badly concluded to a power. 2) Distinguish between internal sins, or subtile-

ora, and external, or coarser. Fratricide is an external and coarse sin, from which even heathens can abstain.

XI. Whatever will is the cause of the knowledge of the doctrine of Christ, that is the cause of faith: The human will &c: Therefore. The major is proved: because the knowledge of the doctrine of Christ is a part of faith. The minor is evident from John 7:16-17. If any man will do the will of the Father, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God, or whether I speak of myself. Resp. Christ speaks not generally of the evangelical or legal will of the Father, but specifically of the divine will, which urges the scrutiny and meditation of the scriptures, so that the sense is: If any man wills to do the will of the Father, i.e., according to His precept to scrutinize with attention the scriptures of the Old Testament, he shall know of that doctrine which I have brought forth with my own mouth, whether it be from God or not. But this does nothing to establish the free will of an unregenerate man in spiritual matters.

XII. Sin is either necessary or voluntary. If it is necessary, it is inevitable, and therefore not a sin. If it is voluntary, it can be avoided, and hence man has free will in moral matters; since he can sin, and not sin. Resp. The opposition between necessary and voluntary sin is not accurate, but sin is distinguished into voluntary and involuntary. From voluntary to the negation of necessary, no inference can be made; since in a different respect one and the same action can be both voluntary and necessary. Voluntary, by reason of the internal motion and delight, as to its species; necessary, by reason of the external object and determination, as to its genus. Quæst.

Latin:

Quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Quicunque doctrina sua hominem in brutum, aut plane in truncum transformant, illorum doctrina non meretur approbationem.

Atqui doctores protestantes &c.

Ergo.

Minor liquet: quoniam Protestantes docent, 1) liberum arbitrium per lapsum esse amissum, cum tamen eo ipso homo a bestiis discernatur, quod hæ uniformiter agant, homo autem ad diversa obiecta, eorumque actus se indifferenter habeat: 2) iidem docent, hominem ad conversionem sui ne potentiam quidem passivam afferre; quo ipso trunco assimilatur, qui neque activam, neque passivam potentiam habet ad se flectendum.

Resp.

Hoc argumentum facile refellitur, modo doctrina Protestantium recte explicetur.

Etenim 1) illi non negant, dari post lapsum in homine libertatem arbitrii, si hoc sumatur materialiter, vt notet τὴν οὐσίαν, essentiam voluntatis humanæ; sed sumunt iidem liberum arbitrium formaliter pro τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ, sive viribus eligendi, aut agendi (ad quam æquivocationem evitandam nonnulli auctores vocant vires liberi arbitrii).

Neque simpliciter & vniversum derogant voluntati omnes vires eligendi res spirituales.

2) Non negant dari in irregenito potentiam passivam remotam & obedientialem recipiendi gratiam conversionis, sed docent tantum, homini irregenito potentiam passivam naturalem, & proximam, ad recipiendum influxum supernaturalem Spiritus S. deesse: quo ipso & a bruto, & a trunco discernitur.

II. Deus iubet & præcipit, vt nos convertamus, Zach.

I, 4. Ioel. II, 13.

Ier.

III, 1.

Quæ præcepta vana & irrita erunt, si homo non habet vires seipsum convertendi.

Resp.

1) A præcepto ad factum, a debere ad posse n. v. c.

Christus filiæ Iairi mortuæ præcipiebat: Surge!

Marc. V, 41. quæ viribus propriis surgere non poterat.

Ita & homo irregenitus in peccatis mortuus est, Eph. II, 1.

2) Præcepta diuina non frustra data sunt; sed legaliter considerata, non ostendunt quidem mensuram virium nostrarum; attamen a) indicant ius Dei, repetentis illas vires, quas primo homini contulerat; b) præscribunt normam officii nostri; c) requirunt a nobis obsequium passivum, i. e. non repugnantiam; d) nos coarguunt nostræ infirmitatis; e) pædagogice nos ad Christum perducunt, Gal. III, 24.

Evangelice considerata, quatenus gratiam diuinam coniunctam habent, sunt effectiva & persuasiva, tanquam efficacia media, quibus vires convertendi offeruntur & conferuntur illis, qui morose & pertinaciter non resistunt.

III. Qui præcipit ea, quæ vires voluntatis superant, ille est tyrannus: Deus non est tyrannus: E.

Resp.

Qui præcipit ea, quæ simpliciter & semper vires hominum superant, ille est tyrannus.

At Deus id non facit; sed 1) protoplastis indulserat vires Deum perfecte colendi.

Iure suo Deus id exigit, quod homo malitia sua perdidit.

2) Prævenit Deus gratia sua impotentem per naturam, vt per gratiam potens fiat. 3) Homo gratia diuina præventus potest contunaci malitia non resistere, potest malitiosum obicem Spiritui S. non ponere, potest media diuinitus ordinata admittere, vt Spiritus S. per diuinum verbum salvificam fidem in ipso accendat. faluificam fidem in ipso accendat.

IV. Quicumque iubentur evigilare e somno, illi propriis viribus surgunt: Atqui homines irregeniti &c. Eph. V, 14: Ergo. Maior constat: quia dormiens excitatus propriis viribus surgit. Resp. Irregeniti excitantur & surgunt ab operibus mortuis non virtute propria, sed virtute huius verbi potentis & efficacis, Hebr. IV, 12. Neque enim praeceptum hoc, legaliter consideratum, exprimit mensuram virium nostrarum, sed normam debiti nostri: evangelice spectatum, est efficax medium in peccatis mortuum excitandi, & caecum illuminandi, modo non obsistat morose, sed se illuminari patiatur.

V. Mandatum divinum conversionis non est supra nos, Deut. XXX, 11. E. viribus arbitrii nostri praestari potest. Resp. Verba citata secundum fontem hebraeum ita se habent: Praeceptum hoc, quod ego sum praecipiens tibi hodie, non est mirabile prae te, neque longinquum illud. Repetit Paulus hoc praeceptum, Rom. X, 6. 7. 8. & addit: Hoc est verbum fidei, quod praedicamus. Quare per praeceptum divinum, a Mose populo Israelitico datum, non intelligitur praecise verbum legis, sed & verbum evangelii, docente Paulo. Hoc verbum impletur non viribus propriis, sed efficacia promissionis divinae, qua fides salvifica accenditur.

VI. Quicumque non habet liberum voluntatis arbitrium, illi nec poenae, nec praemia sunt constituenda: Sententia Protestantium, homo irregenitus &c: Ergo. Maior probatur: quia poenis is affligitur, in cuius viribus erat, declinare id, quod commisit; praemiis honoratur, qui lubens praestitit id, quod debuit. Resp. Dist. inter res superioris, & inferioris hemisphaerii. In rebus hemisphaerii inferioris, vitam hanc concernentibus, homo post lapsum habet liberum arbitrium, adeoque ratione illarum homini constituitur poena & praemium temporale. In rebus hemisphaerii superioris, destituitur quidem homo viribus liberi arbitrii; penes tamen eundem est, non resistere mediis conversionis divinitus oblatis. Punitur, si malitiose obsistat; non punitur, si oblatis mediis non obnitatur.

VII. Si homo oblata media potest viribus naturae recipere, utique in spiritualibus liberum arbitrium habet: Antecedens est verum: Ergo & consequens. Maior probatur, quia oblata media sunt bona spiritualia. Quod si homo illa viribus naturalibus recipere potest, valide concluditur, liberum arbitrium post lapsum in spiritualibus superesse. Resp. Oblatio mediorum pertinet ad gratiam Dei praevenientem, qua aufertur incapacitas naturalis passiva omnibus connata, vt homo capax fit passivae mediorum receptionis; ex qua male concluditur pro libero arbitrio; quippe quod, communi de sententia, est vis activa voluntatis. Huc accedit, quod homo, gratia praeuentus, media conversionis externe quidem adhibeat, interiorem autem conversionem suis viribus non efficiat; sicut aegrotus propinatum a medico pharmacum quidem recipit, neque tamen proprias habet se sanandi vires.

VIII. Siracides c. XV, 14. 15. homini tribuit libertatem arbitrii, inquiens: Deus initio fecit hominem, reliquit eum in manu arbitrii sui: Si volueris, conferuabis mandata. Resp. 1) liber Siracides est extra canonem, atque adeo dogmata fidei ex eodem probari nequeunt. 2) Loquitur Siracides de homine ante lapsum in natura inflituta; post lapsum homo irregenitus est servus peccati.

IX. Moses, Deut. XXX, 19. & Iosua, c. XXIV, 15. Israelitis concedunt optinem, sive liberam electionem. Ergo ipsis tribuunt liberum arbitrium. Resp. Loquuntur Moses & Iosua cum Israelitis, tanquam hominibus renatis. Sed quaestio est de homine irregenito: an ille obiectum mere spirituale viribus naturalibus eligere, & circa illud agere queat?

X. Deus Caino fratricidae non denegauit, sed potius mandauit dominium in peccata, Gen. IV, 7. Ergo gravissimo cuique peccatori liberum arbitrium in spiritualibus concedit. Resp. 1) A praecepto ad posse male concluditur. 2) Dist. inter peccata interna, sive subtili-

ora, & externa, sive crassiora. Fratricidium est peccatum externum & crassum, a quo etiam ethnici abstinere queunt.

XI. Quaecunque voluntas est causa cognitionis doctrinae Christi, illa est causa fidei: Voluntas humana &c: Ergo. Maior probatur: quia cognitio doctrinae Christi est pars fidei. Minor patet ex Io. VII, 16. 17. Si quis voluerit voluntatem Patris facere, cognoscet de doctrina, utrum a Deo fit, an a me ipso loquar. Resp. Loquitur Christus non generatim de voluntate Patris evangelica, aut legali, sed in specie de voluntate divina, quae vrget scrutinium & meditationem scripturarum, vt sensus fit: Si quis vult voluntatem Patris facere, h. e. iuxta eius praeceptum scrutari cum attentione scripturas veteris testamenti, is cognoscet de doctrina illa, quam ego ore meo prodidi, vtrum sit a Deo, nec ne. Sed hoc nihil facit ad stabiliendum liberum arbitrium hominis irregeniti in spiritualibus.

XII. Peccatum aut est necessarium, aut voluntarium. Si est necessarium, est inevitabile, adeoque non peccatum. Si est voluntarium, vitari potest, & proinde homo est liberi arbitrii in moralibus; quippe qui potest peccare, & non peccare. Resp. Non est accurata oppositio peccati necessarii, & voluntarii, sed peccatum distinguitur in voluntarium, & involuntarium. A voluntario ad negationem necessarii non potest fieri illatio; cum diverso respectu vna eademque actio & voluntaria esse possit, & necessaria. Voluntaria, ratione interioris motus & delectationis, quoad speciem; necessaria, ratione externi obiecti & determinationis, quoad genus. Quæst.


### Quæst. XIV. Do men, after the fall, have free will to choose things of the lower sphere?

The will of men, regenerate and unregenerate, after the fall, possesses the power to choose diverse things subject to reason, or to embrace one over another a), although those powers are languid and weak b).

Prob. a. 1) But by apostolic testimony, Rom. 2:13. The Gentiles, which have not the law, do by nature the things contained in the law. The Gentiles, who were ignorant of the law prescribed by Moses, led by nature, performed acts in some measure conformable to the moral law. Therefore, according to the Augsburg Confession, article XVIII, our churches teach concerning free will, that the human will has some liberty to perform civil justice, and to choose things subject to reason.

2) Sound reason demonstrates this liberty of will in natural, civil, and artificial actions. For if man does not have liberty of will in natural things, he will not be the principal cause of his own actions; he will deliberate in vain with himself or with others; for his actions he will neither be praised, nor blamed, nor punished. To punish a sinner who could not have acted otherwise is not consistent with equity.

3) It is proved by examples. It was entirely open to Lot to go from Abraham to the right or to the left, Gen. 13:9. Paul could have taken a sister with him, and could have abstained from it, 1 Cor. 9:15. It stood with Solomon to ask of God riches, or wisdom, 1 Kings 3:13.

Prob. b. By internal and external impediments, free will in things subject to reason is broken and weakened.

Internal impediments are 1) blindness of the intellect, erring in deliberations. 2) Languor of the will to pursue the good, and a proclivity to embrace the evil. 3) The vehemence of the affections is often so great that, like a torrent, it carries the will away with it and disturbs the judgment of reason.

External impediments are: 1) the craftiness of the devil, leading man away from the love of the good; 2) of the world 2) the blandishments and terrors of the world; 3) the direction of God limiting, overturning counsels, and diminishing or cutting off the ability to act.

Latin:

Voluntas hominum renatorum & irregenitorum, post lapsum, pollet viribus, diuersas res, rationi subiectas, eligendi, vel vnam prae altera amplectendi a), quamuis illae vires sint languidae & infirmae b).

Prob. a. 1) At testimonio apostolico, Rom. II, 13. Gentes, quae legem non habent, natura, quae legis sunt, faciunt. Gentiles, qui praescriptam Mosis legem ignorarunt, ducente natura, patrarunt actus, legi morali quadantenus conformes. Idcirco, teste Augustana confessione, artic. XVIII. nostra ecclesiae de libero arbitrio docent, quod humana voluntas habeat aliquam libertatem ad efficiendam civilem iustitiam, & deligendas res, rationi subiectas.

2) Sana ratio hanc libertatem arbitrii in actionibus naturalibus, ciuilibus & artificialibus commonstrat. Nam si homo non habet libertatem arbitrii in naturalibus, non erit causa principalis actionum suarum; frustra deliberabit secum, aut cum aliis; ob actiones suas nec laudabitur, nec reprehendetur, nec punietur. Punire peccatorem, qui secus agere nequivit, aequitati non est consentaneum.

3) Probatur exemplis. Loth o integrum erat abire ab Abrahamo versus dextram & sinistram, Gen. XIII, 9. Paullus poterat sororem secum ducere, & ab ea abstinere, 1 Corinth. IX, 15. Stabat penes Salomonem expetere a Deo diuitias, aut sapientiam, 1 Reg. III, 13.

Prob. b. Obiectis impedimentis internis & externis liberum arbitrium in rebus rationi subiectis frangitur & infirmatur.

Impedimenta interna sunt 1) caecitas intellectus, in deliberationibus errantis. 2) Languor voluntatis ad sectandum bonum, & procliuitas ad amplexandum malum. 3) Vehementia affectuum saepe tanta, vt torrentis instar voluntatem secum abripiat & iudicium rationis turbet.

Externa impedimenta sunt: 1) diaboli versutia, hominem ab amore boni abducentis; 2) mundi blanditiae & terriculamenta; 3) directio Dei limitans, consilia subuertens, & facultatem agendi imminuens, aut praecidens.


### Q. XV. What use does the doctrine concerning the defect of free will in spiritual matters confer upon us?

Prob. a. We labor under ἀδυναμίᾳ, or infirmity of powers, regarding spiritual things, so that without Christ we can do nothing and bear no fruit; just as a branch cut off from the vine does not even have the power to bear fruit. Therefore, we must glory in nothing, because nothing is our own. Let us meanwhile diligently use the means of salvation, and with assiduous prayers let us implore the aid of the Holy Spirit.

Prob. b. Who could express by speaking the magnitude of divine grace? For God, most merciful, goes before the unwilling, that he may will; he follows the willing, that he may not will in vain: he goes before, that we may be healed; he follows, that we may be called; he follows, that we may be glorified: he goes before, that we may live piously; he follows, that we may always remain with him: just as AUGUSTINE speaks in his book On Nature and Grace, ch. 32.

SIGH. Without thee, sweetest JESUS, I avail nothing, I know nothing.

Without thee I think nothing good, I desire nothing salutary, I undertake nothing pious, I accomplish nothing fruitful. Strengthen, I beseech thee, me who am languishing, correct me who am erring, support me who am wavering, lead me as I go from this valley of tears into the heavenly paradise.

It confers upon us a) a hortatory use, that with a submissive mind we may acknowledge the infirmity of our own powers, may fittingly use the means of grace, and may pray assiduously; b) a consolatory use, that by considering the magnitude of divine grace with us, we may lift up our soul with the hope of salvation.

Latin:

Prob. a. Laboramus ἀδυναμίᾳ, siue infirmitate virium, circa res spirituales, vt sine Christo nihil facere, nullumque fructum ferre queamus; sicut palmes a vite praecisus ne potentiam quidem fructificam habet. In nullo igitur gloriandum, quia nihil nostrum est. Vtamur interim sedulo mediis salutis, & assiduis precibus opem Spiritus S. imploremus.

Prob. b. Magnitudine gratiae diuinae quis fando exprimeret? Deus enim misericordissimus praeuenit nolentem, vt velit; subsequitur volentem, ne frustra velit: praeuenit, vt sanemur; subsequitur, vt vocemur; subsequitur, vt glorificemur: praeuenit, vt pie viuamus; subsequitur, vt semper cum illo maneamus: Quemadmodum AVGVSTINVS loquitur libr. de nat. & grat. c. 32.

SVSPIRIVM.

Sine te, dulcissime IESV, nil valeo, nil sapio, Sine te nil bonum cogito, nil salutare desidero, nil pium suscipio, nil frugiferum perficio. Corrobora, quaeso, me languentem, corrige me errantem, suffulci me vacillantem, duc me euntem ex hac lacrymarum valle in paradisum coelestem.

Confert nobis a) vsum paraeneticum, vt animo submisso infirmitatem virium nostrarum agnoscamus, mediis gratiae decenter vtamur, & assidue precemur; b) vsum paracleticum, vt magnitudine gratiae diuinae reputantes nobiscum, spe salutis animum erigamus.


## 16 On the Principles of Salvation, and the Universal Benevolence of God

Question I. What are the principles of salvation?

The principles of salvation are acts of divine grace, upon which the external salvation of men depends.

Proof. Just as divine grace is the internal impulsive cause which impelled God to bless the sinner; so the same is the fountain and spring from which the beginning, progress, and completion of our salvation flows. The Apostle hints at this, Eph. II, 8, saying: By grace you have been saved through faith. Wherefore every act of divine grace, occupied with the procurement of our salvation, is called a principle of salvation.

Question II. How many are the principles of salvation?

The principles of salvation are three. The first is the benevolence of God the Father toward fallen man to be raised up and blessed. The second is the fraternal redemption of Christ from sin and its punishments. The third is the gracious and, through certain means, effective operation of the Holy Spirit, by which the salvation obtained by Christ is offered and conferred.

Proof. The Savior himself points out these three principles of salvation in John III, 16. For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. God the Father, by loving the world and giving the Son as mediator, shows himself benevolent. The Son was given so that he might rescue the world, i.e., the entire human race inhabiting this globe of the earth, from destruction, and thus be its redeemer. The means of enjoying the redemption of Christ is true faith, fixed upon the merit of Christ, which the Holy Spirit kindles by a gracious operation effective through the word and sacraments; indeed, he is called the Spirit of faith, 2 Cor. IV, 13.

Latin:

Quaestio I. Quid sunt salutis principia?

PRincipia salutis sunt actus gratiae diuinae, a quibus externa hominum salus dependet.

Prob. Quemadmodum gratia diuina est caussa impulsiua interna, quae Deum ad peccatorem beandum impulit; ita eadem fons & scaturigo est, e qua nostrae salutis initium, progressus & complementum fluit. Innuit hoc Apostolus, Eph. II, 8. inquiens: Gratia saluati estis per fidem. Quamobrem omnis actus gratiae diuinae, circa procurationem salutis nostrae occupatus, vocatur principium salutis.

Quaest. II. Quot sunt principia salutis?

Principia salutis sunt tria. Primum est beneuolentia Dei Patris erga hominem lapsum erigendum & beandum. Secundum est fraterna Christi redemtio a peccato & eius poenis. Tertium est gratiosa & per certa media efficax operatio Spiritus Sancti, qua salus a Christo parta offertur, & confertur.

Prob. Tria haec salutis principia indigitat ipse Saluator Io. III, 16. Adeo Deus dilexit mundum, vt filium suum vnigenitum daret, vt omnis, qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed vitam aeternam habeat. Deus Pater diligendo mundum, & dando Filium mediatorem, se ostendit beneuolum. Datus est Filius, vt mundum, i. e. vniuersum genus humanum, hunc terrarum orbem incolens, ab interitu vindicaret, adeoque eiusdem esset redemtor. Medium fruendi redemtione Christi est vera fides, in merito Christi defixa, quam gratiosa & per verbum ac sacramenta efficaci operatione accendit Spiritus Sanctus; quippe qui dicitur Spiritus fidei, 2 Cor. IV, 13.


### Question III. How manifold is the benevolence of God toward fallen men?

The benevolence of God toward fallen men is twofold, general or universal, and special. The former embraces all men constituted in misery, and to the same ordains and offers valid means of salvation: He has determined to bestow eternal salvation upon those sinners who embrace these offered means of salvation.

Q. IV.

What is the universal benevolence of God? The universal benevolence of God is an act of divine grace by which God, having regarded the common misery of fallen men, was moved not only to seriously will the salvation of them all, but also to give Christ as Mediator to procure this, and likewise to destine efficacious means, with the intention that all men might use the same, conceive from them true faith in Christ, and through Him obtain and enjoy the salvation wrought for them, to the praise of the divine goodness.

Obs. I. The benevolence of God is not viewed here in the first act, insofar as it is an essential attribute of God; but in the second act, as it denotes a full and efficacious intention of succoring miserable sinners, and the destination of means for raising up and saving men who have fallen into sin.

Obs. II. The benevolence of God is expressed in the Holy Scriptures by equivalent terms; which, however, are distinguished by peculiar connotations. For it is called a) the grace of God, insofar as it is opposed to all debt and all merit of works. And thus the grace of God here denotes the gratuitous favor of God, or the benevolence of the eternal Deity, provoked by no merits; concerning which the Apostle says in Eph. 2:8: "By grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not of yourselves, it is the gift of God; not of works, lest anyone should boast." b) The mercy of God, insofar as God regards the common misery of men, corrupted by sins, and wills to avert it. c) Χρηστότης καὶ Φιλανθρωπία, kindness and love for mankind. Paul uses these words in Tit. 3:4: "The kindness and love for mankind of our Savior, God, appeared." He is called χρηστὸς who is useful to another. Χρηστότης therefore, or kindness, is the benevolent propensity of God to promote the advantages of men. Φιλανθρωπία, however, or love for mankind, embraces the act of benevolence together with its object, which is men. It is of love to impart good to another. And Φιλανθρωπία is the will of God, prone to communicate good to miserable men. By theologians it is commonly called the antecedent will of God.

Q. V.

How manifold is the will of God occupied about the business of salvation? The will of God is one and simple in itself; but insofar as it is terminated upon external objects, primarily fallen men, and, according to their diverse condition and consideration, exerts itself in distinct acts, it is distinguished in our mode of understanding into antecedent and consequent. The antecedent will is that by which God wills the salvation of all fallen and miserable men, and for the attainment of this has given Christ as Mediator, and has ordained those means by which the salvation wrought through Christ, and the powers of believing, are offered to all men, with a serious intention of conferring them. The consequent will is that by which God, out of the fallen human race, has elected those to eternal life whom He foresaw would use the ordinary means and would persevere unto the end of life in faith in Christ: conversely, He has reprobated from the human race those whom He foresaw would pertinaciously reject the ordinary means and would remain in infidelity until the last breath of life.

Obs. The will of God is called antecedent and consequent: Not 1) by reason of time, as if the antecedent will precedes the consequent in time: for as God is devoid of time; so He does not have any will which precedes another in time. 2) Nor on the part of the divine will itself; as if there were in God two wills distinct in reality. For the divine will is the very essence of God, with the object connoted, conceived by way of an act of willing. 3) But the will of God is called antecedent and consequent, from the order of our reason, distinguishing the diverse acts of willing in God according to the diverse consideration of objects, and considering one act before another; so that it may at least be noted that the antecedent will precedes the consequent in the sign of divine reason. For it is prior, in our mode of understanding, for God to will to procure salvation and the means of salvation for men, than for Him to will to finally confer eternal salvation upon those who will believe in Christ, or to finally adjudge eternal damnation to the impenitent.

This distinction is proven, 1) because it is underpinned by a certain foundation. For (a) the antecedent will of God is borne toward the miserable man, insofar as he is miserable, without any regard for his obedience and faith, or disobedience and infidelity: but the consequent will is concerned with the miserable man, insofar as he is either obedient and faithful, or disobedient and incredulous, and thus follows the consideration of obedience and disobedience. (b) By the antecedent will, God destines and offers the means of salvation to all men: by the consequent will, He chooses those for eternal life who accept the destined and offered means, but rejects those who stubbornly repudiate the ordained means. (c) The antecedent will of God is universal; because it consists in a simple respect, by which the beneficent will of God holds itself equally toward all: the consequent will is particular, because it consists in a determined respect, according as the same will holds itself toward men, either following or neglecting that order of means by the act itself.

2) This distinction is necessary, on account of the wonderful temperament of divine mercy and justice, to be reconciled with one another. For there exist in the sacred scriptures utterances which show the mercy of God to be prone toward all sinners, 1 Tim. II, 6. 2 Petr. III, 9. There exist others which note the justice of God, and exclude from the inheritance of salvation those who resist the divine order, Io. III, 18. Marc. XVI, 16. Finally, there exist biblical sayings in which both mercy and divine justice are proclaimed, Matth. XXIII, 37. Christ, by His antecedent will, as much as was in Him, wished to gather the children of Israel, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings; but by His consequent will, because they would not be gathered, He wished their house to be left desolate. Confer Act. XIII, 46.

3) This distinction is insinuated in the parables of Christ. For the heavenly king invited many men to the wedding of his son by his antecedent will; those few appearing, and duly dressed, he received sumptuously at the royal table, but those refusing to come and those destitute of the wedding garment he rejected and destroyed by his consequent will. Matth. XXII, 1. Confer Luc. XIV, 16.

4) This distinction is approved by venerable antiquity. For CHRYSOSTOM distinguishes between the first and second will of God, homil. I. in epist. ad Eph. I. ANSELM in cap. VI. Matth. distinguishes between the will of mercy and of justice. DAMASCENE, Book II. de O. F. cap. XXIX. teaches that God antecedently (προηγουμένως) wills all to be saved, and to attain His kingdom; for He did not fashion us to punish us, but that He might make us partakers of His goodness, as He is good: but He wills that sinners be punished, as He is just. Therefore, the first is called the preceding will, and good pleasure, existing from Himself (God): but the second is called the consequent will, and permission, existing on account of our cause. To this tend the words of TERTULLIAN, in the book de resurret. carn.: God, from His own [nature], is best; from ours, just.

The antithesis is of Maccovius and other Reformed [theologians], who impugn the distinction of the antecedent and consequent will of God with the following arguments:

I. Whatever will is eternal cannot be distinguished into antecedent and consequent. But the will of God is eternal. Therefore. The major is evident; because in eternity there is no prior or posterior. Resp. The will of God is distinguished into antecedent and consequent, not on the part of the divine will, but on the part of the willed objects, considered in diverse ways. For the will of God is not a produced act, but the very essence of God, conceived with a connatural object by way of an act of willing: which, as it is terminated toward some prior or posterior reason in the object of willing, so it is conceived by us as a prior or posterior, antecedent or consequent will, not by reason of time, but by reason of order according to our mode of conceiving.

II. Two contradictory wills are not given in God: The antecedent and consequent will, etc. Therefore. The major is clear; because in God a) all things are ταυτὸ, one and the same. b) If there were two contradictory wills in God, one would overturn or expunge the other. The minor is proven; because God is said by an antecedent will to have mercy on all, and by a consequent will not to have mercy on all, which bring about a contradiction. Resp. I deny the minor. For contradictory things are said of the same thing, insofar as it is the same, or insofar as it is considered in the same respect. But the antecedent and consequent will of God are concerned with man, considered in diverse ways. For the antecedent will of God is concerned with man, insofar as he is man, with no regard had for the circumstances in this object; but the consequent will of God is concerned with man considered with certain circumstances, according as he is either a believer or an unbeliever. Wherefore the antecedent and consequent will of God are not opposed to each other contrarily or contradictorily, but are subordinated. The former is contained materially in the latter, and passes into the latter, the condition being posited. Which I show thus: By an antecedent will God wills that all men be saved, if they finally believe. But those who rightly use the ordinary means of salvation are those who finally believe. Therefore the antecedent will of God is not overturned, rescinded, or expunged by the consequent will, but rather, the condition being fulfilled, it passes into the same.

III. Whatever will is inefficacious is not to be attributed to God: But the antecedent will is inefficacious: Therefore. The major is clear; because it is a matter of religion for us not to attribute weak wishes and inefficacious desire to God. The minor is evident: because the will of God does not attain the intended end. Resp. I deny the minor. For a will is called inefficacious, either in order to the attainment of the end, or in order to the intention through certain means. Although the antecedent will of God is not always efficacious in the former way; since it does not obtain the intended effect in all men; it is nevertheless efficacious, by way of a full and serious intention and the destination of most efficacious means. Indeed, medicine is not rarely most efficacious, which, being rejected or trampled upon, is frustrated of the desired outcome. Wherefore it is one thing to be ἀνεπίβατικὸν, devoid of outcome; another to be ἀνενέργητον, destitute of efficacy.

IV. No one can resist the divine will, Rom. IX, 19. Many resist the antecedent will. Therefore the antecedent will is not the divine will. Resp. No one can resist the divine will acting absolutely through absolute power. But the will of God in the economy, or dispensation of salvation, is not absolute, but ordered, and thus to be fulfilled according to the τάξιν, or order of means, divinely destined. Not a few men despise this order against themselves, Luke VII, 30, and by this reason they resist the divine will, not by a greater power, but by impotence, or defect, namely through the blindness of the intellect and the perversity of their own will.

V. Whoever is wise does not suspend the end of his will upon a condition which he foreknows will not be fulfilled: But God is most wise: Therefore. The major is evident: because a wise man does nothing in vain, but for a certain end, which he can attain through valid means. Resp. 1) By denying the major. For a good prince is not to be defrauded of the glory of patience, even though, in establishing just laws, he foresees in his mind that they will not be kept by all citizens. 2) The condition which God predetermined: if they finally believe, is not impossible; because it is fulfilled by many: it can also be fulfilled by the rest, provided they admit, and do not morosely reject, the means destined for obtaining the end. 3) Although in not a few cases God does not attain the proper, or special, end; yet he always attains the common, or general, end, which is the glory of the divine goodness. Of the proper end, or eternal salvation, sinners who are stubbornly contumacious deprive themselves by their own fault ).

Latin:

Beneuolentia Dei erga homines lapsos duplex est, generalis, siue vniuersalis, & specialis. Illa complectitur omnes homines in miseria constitutos, iisdemque valida salutis media ordinat & offert: haec peccatores oblata salutis media amplectentes aeterna salute donare constituit.

Quæst. IV.

Quid est beneuolentia Dei vniuersalis? Beneuolentia Dei vniuersalis est actus gratiae diuinae, qua Deus, spectata communi hominum lapsorum miseria, permotus est, vt non tantum eorum omnium serio velit salutem, sed etiam ad hanc procurandam Christum dederit mediatorem, iuxta atque efficacia media destinauerit, ea intentione, vt omnes homines iisdem vtantur, veram ex illis concipiant fidem in Christum, & per hunc parta salute aeterna potiantur atque fruantur in laudem bonitatis diuinae.

Obs. I. Beneuolentia Dei heic non spectatur in actu primo, quatenus est attributum Dei essentiale; sed in actu secundo, prout notat plenam & efficacem intentionem succurrendi peccatoribus miseris, & destinationem mediorum ad erigendum & saluandum homines in peccatum prolapsos.

Obs. II. Beneuolentia Dei in sacris litteris exprimitur aequipollentibus vocibus; quae tamen peculiaribus connotatis distinguuntur. Dicitur enim a) gratia Dei, quatenus opponitur omni debito, omnique operum merito. Adeoque gratia Dei hic denotat fauorem Dei gratuitum, seu beneuolentiam aeterni Numinis, nullis meritis prouocatam; de qua Apostolus Eph. II, 8. inquit: Gratia saluati estis per fidem; & hoc non ex vobis, donum Dei est; non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur. b) Misericordia Dei, quatenus Deus communem hominum, peccatis corruptorum, miseriam respicit, eamque vult auertere. c) Χρηστότης καὶ Φιλανθρωπία, benignitas & amor hominum. His vocibus vtitur Paullus Tit. III, 3. Benignitas & amor hominum apparuit Seruatoris nostri, Dei. Χρηστὸς dicitur, qui alteri est vtilis. Χρηστότης igitur, siue benignitas, est beneuola Dei propensio, commoda hominum prouehendi. Φιλανθρωπία autem, seu amor hominum, actum beneuolentiae simul cum ipsius obiecto, quod sunt homines, complectitur. Amoris est, bonum alteri impertiri. Et Φιλανθρωπία est voluntas Dei, prona ad communicandum hominibus miseris bonum. A theologis communiter vocatur voluntas Dei antecedens.

Quæst. V.

Quotuplex est voluntas Dei circa negotium salutis occupata? Voluntas Dei in se vna & simplex est; quatenus autem terminatur ad obiecta externa, in primis homines lapsos, &, pro diuersa eorum habitudine atque consideratione, distinctis se exserit actibus, nostro intelligendi modo distinguitur in antecedentem, & consequentem. Voluntas antecedens est, qua Deus omnium hominum lapsorum & miserorum vult salutem, & ad hanc consequendam dedit mediatorem Christum, eaque ordinauit media, quibus parta per Christum salus, viresque credendi, omnibus hominibus offeruntur, feria cum intentione conferendi. Voluntas consequens est, qua Deus ex humano genere lapso eos ad vitam aeternam elegit, quos praeuidit ordinariis mediis vfuros, & ad finem vitae in fide in Christum perseueraturos esse: contra reprobauit ex genere humano eos, quos praeuidit ordinaria media pertinaciter reiecturos, & ad nouissimum vitae halitum in infidelitate permansuros esse.

Obs. Voluntas Dei dicitur antecedens & consequens: Non 1) ratione temporis, quasi voluntas antecedens consequentem tempore praecedat: vti enim Deus temporis est expers; ita non habet voluntatem aliquam, quae alteram tempore anteuertat. 2) Nec ex parte ipsius voluntatis diuinae; quasi dentur in Deo duae reapse distinctae voluntates. Est enim voluntas diuina ipsa essentia Dei, cum connotato obiecto, per modum actus volendi concepta. 3) Sed dicitur voluntas Dei antecedens & consequens, ab ordine rationis nostrae, diuersos volendi actus in Deo pro diuersa obiectorum consideratione distinguentis, & vnum actum prae altero considerantis; vt saltem notetur, voluntatem antecedentem praecedere consequentem in signo rationis diuinae. Prius quippe est, nostro intelligendi modo, Deum velle hominibus salutem & media salutis procurare, quam eundem velle finaliter in Christum credituris aeternam salutem actu conferre, vel finaliter impoenitentibus aeternam damnationem adiudicare.

Probatur haec distinctio, 1) quia certo fundamento subnixa est. Nam (a) voluntas Dei antecedens fertur in hominem miserum, quatenus miser est, nullam habita ratione illius obedientiae & fidei, vel inobedientiae & infidelitatis: voluntas autem consequens versatur circa hominem miserum, quatenus vel obediens & fidelis, vel inobediens & incredulus est, adeoque considerationem obedientiae & inobedientiae subsequitur. (b) Voluntate antecedente Deus omnibus hominibus salutis media destinat & offert: voluntate consequente eligit eos ad vitam aeternam, qui destinata & oblata media acceptant, reprobat autem eos, qui ordinata media pertinaciter repudiant. (c) Voluntas Dei antecedens est vniuersalis; quia constat respectu simplici, quo benefica Dei voluntas aequaliter se habet erga omnes: voluntas consequens est particularis, quia constat respectu determinato, prout eadem voluntas se habet ad homines, τάξιν illam mediorum ipso actu vel sequentes, vel negligentes.

2) Necessaria est haec distinctio, ob mirabile misericordiae & iustitiae diuinae, inter se conciliandae, temperamentum. Exstant enim in sacris litteris effata, quae misericordiam Dei in omnes peccatores pronam ostendunt, 1 Tim. II, 6. 2 Petr. III, 9. Exstant alia, quae notant iustitiam Dei, & ab hereditate salutis excludunt eos, qui ordini diuino refragantur, Io. III, 18. Marc. XVI, 16. Exstant denique dicta biblica, in quibus tam misericordia, quam iustitia diuina depraedicantur, Matth. XXIII, 37. Christus voluntate antecedente, quantum in se erat, volebat congregare filios Israël, vt gallina pullos suos sub alis congregat; sed voluntate consequente, quia nolebant congregari, volebat domum eorum desertam relinqui. Confer Act. XIII, 46.

3) Insinuata est haec distinctio parabolis Christi. Inuitauit enim rex coelestis multos homines ad nuptias filii sui voluntate antecedente; paucos comparentes, & rite vestitos, regali mensa laute excepit, renuentes venire & nuptiali veste destitutos reiecit ac perdidit voluntate consequente. Matth. XXII, 1. Confer Luc. XIV, 16.

4) Approbata est haec distinctio a venerabili antiquitate. Distinguit enim CHRYSOSTOMVS inter voluntatem Dei primam, & secundam, homil. I. in epist. ad Eph. I. ANSHELMVS in cap. VI. Matth. distinguit inter voluntatem misericordiae, & iustitiae. DAMASCENVS Libr. II. de O. F. cap. XXIX. docet, Deum antecedenter (προηγουμένως) velle omnes saluari, & regnum eius consequi; non enim ad puniendum nos plasmauit, sed vt efficiat nos bonitatis suae participes, vt bonus: peccantes autem puniri vult, vt iustus. Dicitur igitur prima, praecedens voluntas, & beneplacitum, ex ipso (Deo) existens: Secunda vero voluntas, consequens, & permissio ex nostra causa existens. Quo spectant verba TERTULLIANI, in libro de resurret. carn. Deus de suo optimus, de nostro iustus est.

Antithesis est Maccovii & aliorum Reformatorum, qui distinctionem voluntatis Dei antecedentis & consequentis impugnant sequentibus argumentis:

I. Quaecunque voluntas est aeterna, in antecedentem & consequentem non potest distingui. Atqui voluntas Dei est aeterna. E. Maior constat; quia in aeternitate non datur prius aut posterius. Resp. Voluntas Dei distinguitur in antecedentem & consequentem, non ex parte voluntatis diuinae, sed ex parte obiectorum volitorum, diuersimode consideratorum. Voluntas enim Dei non est actus productus, sed ipsa essentia Dei, cum connato obiecto, per modum actus volendi concepta: quae vt terminatur ad aliquam priorem, aut posteriorem in obiecto volendi rationem; ita concipitur a nobis vt prior, aut posterior, antecedens, aut consequens voluntas, non ratione temporis, sed ratione ordinis secundum nostrum concipiendi modum.

II. Duae contradictoriae voluntates non dantur in Deo: Voluntas antecedens & consequens &c. Ergo. Maior patet; quia in Deo a) omnia sunt ταυτὸ, vnum & idem. b) Si in Deo essent duae contradictoriae voluntates, vna alteram euerteret, aut expungeret. Minor probatur; quia Deus dicitur voluntate antecedente omnium misereri, voluntate consequente non omnium misereri, quae contradictionem inferunt. Resp. Neg. minorem. Nam contradictoria dicuntur de eodem, quatenus idem est, seu quatenus eodem respectu consideratur. At voluntas Dei antecedens & consequens versantur circa hominem, diuersimode consideratum. Nam voluntas Dei antecedens versatur circa hominem, quatenus homo est, nulla habita ratione circumstantiarum in hoc obiecto; voluntas autem Dei consequens versatur circa hominem cum certis circumstantiis consideratum, prout vel fidelis, vel incredulus est. Quare voluntas Dei antecedens & consequens sibi non contrarie, aut contradictorie opponuntur, sed subordinantur. Haec in illa materialiter continetur, & in illam, posita conditione, transit. Quod sic ostendo: Voluntate antecedente Deus vult, vt omnes homines saluentur, si finaliter credant. Atqui ordinariis salutis mediis rite vtentes, sunt illi, qui finaliter credunt. Ergo voluntas Dei antecedens voluntate consequente non euertitur, rescinditur, aut expungitur, sed potius conditione impleta in eandem transit.

III. Quaecunque voluntas est inefficax, Deo non tribuenda: Atqui voluntas antecedens est inefficax: Ergo. Maior liquet; quia imbecillia vota & inefficax desiderium Deo tribuere, nobis sit religio. Minor patet: quia voluntas Dei intentum finem non assequitur. Resp. Neg. minorem. Nam inefficax dicitur voluntas, vel in ordine ad consecutionem finis, vel in ordine ad intentionem per certa media. Licet voluntas Dei antecedens non semper sit efficax priori modo; quoniam in omnibus hominibus intentum non sortitur effectum; est tamen efficax, qua plenam seriamque intentionem & destinationem efficacissimorum mediorum. Sane medicina haud raro est efficacissima, quae repulsa aut conculcata exoptato frustratur euentu. Quare aliud est ἀνεπίβατικὸν, euentus expers; aliud ἀνενέργητον, efficacia destitutum.

IV. Voluntati diuinae nemo potest resistere, Rom. IX, 19. Voluntati antecedenti multi resistunt. Ergo voluntas antecedens non est voluntas diuina. Resp. Voluntati diuinae absolutae per potentiam absolutam agenti nemo potest resistere. Voluntas autem Dei in oeconomia, siue dispensatione salutis, non est absoluta, sed ordinata, atque adeo implenda secundum τάξιν, siue ordinem mediorum, diuinitus destinatorum. Hunc ordinem haud pauci homines aduersus seipsos spernunt, Luc. VII, 30. & hac ratione voluntati diuinae obsistunt, non per potentiam maiorem, sed per impotentiam, siue defectum, nimirum per caecitatem intellectus & peruersitatem propriae voluntatis.

V. Quicunque est sapiens, non suspendit finem voluntatis suae a conditione, quam non impletum iri praescit: At Deus sapientissimus: Ergo. Maior constat: quia vir sapiens nihil agit frustra, sed ob certum finem, quem per valida media attingere potest. Resp. 1) Negando maiorem. Nam bonus princeps gloria patientiae non est defraudandus, quamvis iustas ponendo leges mente prospiciat, eas non ab omnibus civibus servatum iri. 2) Quam conditionem Deus praefiniuit: si finaliter credant, non est impossibilis; eo quod a multis impletur: impleri etiam potest a reliquis, modo admittant, & morose non repudient media ad finem obtinendum destinata. 3) Quamvis in haud paucis Deus non assequatur finem proprium, sive specialem; semper tamen attingit finem communem, sive generalem, qui est gloria bonitatis divinae. Fine proprio, sive aeterna salute, peccatores praefracte contumaces sua se culpa priuant ).


### Quest. VI. By what inadequate acts is the universal benevolence of God completed?

The universal benevolence of God is completed by four inadequate acts; the first of which is the commiseration of the entire human race, circumvented by the fraud of the devil and corrupted by will ): The second act is the divine intention of procuring salvation for all men fallen into sin ): The third is the liberal donation of Christ the mediator, by which satisfaction may be made to injured divine justice ): The fourth is the destination of means, by which both eternal salvation, obtained through the satisfaction of Christ, and the powers of believing are offered to all men, that they may be able to accept and apply to themselves the satisfaction of Christ unto salvation ).

Prob. a. God concluded all under incredulity, that he might have mercy on all, Rom. XI, 32. God convicted all men of congenital ἀπιστίας, or incredulity, and demonstrated by invincible arguments that all men without exception, created from the blood of Adam and begotten in the natural way, are guilty of eternal death, and worthy of everlasting punishments, if he were to deal with them according to the rigor of justice. But God is placable, using a tempering of right toward the miserable fallen, and has had mercy on all by granting pardon of crimes to all, so that divine mercy might be diffused as widely as human misery extends itself. Divine mercy is desirous of the salvation of all mortals: for the most merciful God wills that all men be saved, and come to the knowledge of the truth, 1 Tim. II, 4. He wills that the impious turn from his way and live, Ezech. XVIII, 23. c. XXXIII, 11. Prob. c. Because in God there is not only grace and mercy, but also justice, grace moves God to decree salvation for men not in any way whatsoever, but insofar as that could be done while His justice remained immutable. Vindictive justice, however, moves God to demand satisfaction for sins, or, that being lacking, to punish sins with eternal death. Wherefore, since the sinner was unequal to providing the satisfaction due for himself and for others (For a brother shall not redeem, shall a man redeem? He shall not give to God his expiation. For the redemption of their soul is more precious, and he shall cease forever, Ps. XLIX, 8.): mercy moved God, so that for men, to whom He wished to offer the remission of sins and eternal life, He might provide for an alien satisfaction, which Christ, the eternal Son of God, willingly performed, who gave Himself as a ransom (ἀντίλυτρον), the price of redemption for all, 1 Tim. II, 6. Therefore, it is to be attributed to the universal benevolence of God that God gave to the whole fallen human race a mediator, Christ, who might fulfill the law for sinners and pay the vicarious penalties of transgressions.

Which divine philanthropy (φιλανθρωπίαν) the Savior Himself proclaims, John III, 16. For God so loved the world that He gave His only-begotten Son. And Paul, Rom. V, 8. God commends His love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.

St. John commends the same, 1 ep. IV, 9. 10. In this was the love of God manifested toward us, that God sent His only-begotten Son into the world, that we might live through Him. In this is love, not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as a propitiation for our sins.

Prob. d. The satisfaction of the mediator Christ would not profit us, unless the means were divinely provided to us, by which we might make it our own, or apply it to ourselves. Those means are both the word and the sacraments, by which, the satisfaction of Christ having been accomplished, salvation is offered to all; and also true faith, by which the satisfaction of Christ is accepted and applied to salvation. These means God denies to no man absolutely and simply.

For God, the lover of mankind (φιλανθρωπος), commanded the gospel to be preached to every creature, Mark XVI, 15. And Christ, about to be taken up into heaven, instructed His disciples thus: Going therefore, make disciples (for me) of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

Nay, God even offers faith to all, Acts XVII, 31. Quæst. VII. Whose salvation does God will?

Prob. a. 1) Because God did not spare the angels who sinned, 2 Pet. II, 4. God, the most just judge, punishes the horrendous apostasy of the angels with the subtraction of all grace eternally.

Which St. Jude clearly teaches, ep. v. 6. God has reserved those angels who did not keep their origin, but left their own habitation, in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day.

2) Since no mediator was divinely given to the fallen angels, they cannot be freed from punishments while divine justice remains intact. Therefore the Apostle, Heb. II, 16, says, nowhere did the Son of God take hold of angels, but the seed of Abraham. 3) The cause why the devil is reputed to be beyond mercy by divine judgment, Holy Scripture does not express; yet the ancient fathers [proposed] certain probable God does not will to have mercy on the fallen angels, but He does will to have mercy on all and each of the men corrupted by sins; whom, by divine judgment, God shows that He seriously wills to rescue from the abyss of misery and to lead to eternal beatitude by certain means . and have rendered reasons analogous to the faith for the rigor of the divine judgment upon the fallen angels, which D. GERHARD collected in Comment. in 2 Petr. II. p. 205. Indeed, all divine grace was denied to the devil, because a) he fell away from God of his own accord, with no one instigating him, and was the seducer of the seduced man, with direct hatred toward the Creator. b) Although the remaining fallen angels were also seduced by their leader and ringleader the devil, yet all sinned by a most free προαιρέσει [choice]; but the descendants of Adam fell into the guilt of sin by the necessity of being born. c) Unless God had pitied us, the entire human race would have perished by the sin of one man; whereas, by the sin of one angel, not all perished, but each one of them contracted misery by his own sin.

Prob. b. The mercy of God embraces all sinful men, not insofar as or because they are sinners: for God, not willing iniquity, hates those who work iniquity, Ps. V, 5. But insofar as they are miserable, corrupted by sins and dead in them, destitute of their own powers to restore themselves to a state of grace. Wherefore, the common misery of men being present to the divine intellect, He has pitied all, and seriously intends to procure the liberation and salvation of all through certain means.

For 1) the very assertor and vindicator of salvation, Jesus, proclaims the universal cosmophilia [love of the world] of God, John III, 16. God so loved the world, that He gave His only begotten Son, that whoever believes in Him should not perish, but have eternal life.

In this golden compendium of the Gospel, the lover, the object of love, the mode, and the end are proposed for our consideration.

The lover is God the Father (not, however, excluding the second and third person of the Godhead: for Christ also loved us, Eph. V, 25. Gal. II, 20. and the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, Rom. V, 5). Love is attributed in a peculiar way to God the Father; for just as He is the fountain of the Godhead, so also is He the fountain of τῆς φιλανθρωπίας [the love of mankind] toward men. The object of love is the world, by which are understood all sinful men, not insofar as they are sinners, but insofar as they are in need of commiseration.

This exposition is confirmed a) from v. 18, where the world, or men signified by the world, are divided into two classes, believers and non-believers; and it is added: that those who believe from the world may have eternal life: but others from the world, who do not believe, may be condemned. b) The word, world, taken in a special sense, denotes impious men, e.g., the world cannot receive the Spirit of truth, John XIV, 17. the whole world lies in the wicked one, 1 John V, 19. Taken in a general sense, it designates both pious and impious men, as in this place, but never and nowhere in the whole of Holy Scripture does it signify the elect alone. c) That world is understood to which the Gospel concerning Christ is to be preached, Matt.

XXVIII, 19. But that world is the entire human race, Mark XVI, 15. The mode of love is hinted at by the particle, ὅτως, so , that a most ardent and intense love may be designated, of which the most illustrious argument and incomparable pledge is the only begotten Son of God, given to the world as mediator and satisfier.

The end of love is that all men, applying to themselves the satisfaction of Christ by true faith, may be immune from eternal condemnation, and possessors of eternal life. We argue: Whatever love embraces all men inhabiting this world, that is universal by reason of its object. But the most ardent love of God the Father, by which He was moved to give His only begotten Son to the world as mediator, so that all men applying to themselves His satisfaction by true faith might have eternal life, embraces all men inhabiting this world. Therefore (*). 2) The Aposto.

2) The Apostle Paul says explicitly in 1 Tim. II, 4: God desires all men to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth. We observe in this classic saying (a) the antecedent will of God concerning miserable men to be saved, (b) the object of this will: all men, by whom are understood not all kinds of men, but individual men constituted in a state of misery, and thus in need of salvation and salvable (not yet actually damned). Which exposition becomes manifest from the συναφεία (connection) of the text; because (α) the word, all, primarily signifies individuals of the kinds: secondarily kinds of individuals. Now, the analogy stands for the more principal meaning as long as the cohesion of the text does not force us to depart from the same. (β)

This exposition is confirmed from the antecedents and consequents. For those men, for whom God commands that prayer be made, He desires to be saved. But God commands that prayer be made for all and individual men, even those who are later damned. Therefore, He desires all and individual men, even those who are later damned, to be saved. The truth of the major and minor premises is evident from the antecedents. From the consequents, however, we gather thus: For which men Christ gave Himself as an ἀντίλυτρον, or price of redemption, those God desires to be saved. But Christ gave Himself as an ἀντίλυτρον for all men. Therefore (*).

Therefore (*). 3) The universality of divine grace is proved from Rom. XI, 32: God concludes all men in unbelief, that He might have mercy on all. Obs. a) God concludes all men in unbelief not αἰτιωδῶς, causally, or effectively, by injecting or infusing unbelief into the minds of men; but δικαστικῶς, judicially, and declaratively, by convicting all men of innate unbelief, and declaring that all unconverted and unregenerate men are devoid of saving faith, and thus guilty of eternal death. b) Since all were destitute of natural powers to emerge from unbelief, from that impotence and misery God took the occasion to have mercy on all. Whence the argument: Those whom God has convicted of innate unbelief, and declared to be guilty of eternal death, of them He has had mercy: But all men etc.

Therefore. 4) Paul commends the universality of divine grace in Acts XVII, 30, 31: The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now commands all men everywhere to repent: because He has appointed a day, in which He is about to judge the world in righteousness by the man whom He has destined, offering faith to all, after He raised Him from the dead. Obs. a) The times of ignorance are called the times of the O.T. compared to the light of the Gospel, most widely diffused by the ministry of the apostles in the N.T. b) Ὑπεριδὼν denotes the long-suffering of God, who, although He might have had abundant causes for destroying sinners, yet did not do this, but awaited the times of the N.T., under which the Gospel was to be preached to all, if even then they might repent of their ignorance. c) Universal grace of God is most openly commended by this Pauline saying; since, as the Apostle testifies, God invites all men, dwelling at all intervals of places, to repentance, and is ready to give faith to all through ordained means. From which an argument can be woven: To which men God commands to repent, and offers faith; their salvation He desires. But to all men living everywhere etc.

5) Concerning the universality of the saving grace of God the same Apostle testifies clearly, Tit. II, 11: The grace of God that brings salvation has appeared to all men. The apostle teaches by these words that the saving grace of God is accessible to all, exposed to all equally. For just as the natural sun shines upon all men: so the grace of God has appeared to all, and desires to illuminate all, provided they do not maliciously close the eyes of the mind. 6) Universality maliciously close.

6) The universality of divine grace is also evident from the clear statement of the Apostle Peter, 2 Epist. III, 9. God is long-suffering towards us, not willing that some should perish, but that all should come to repentance.

In these words of St. Peter, divine long-suffering is represented, which also extends to the reprobate. Rom. II, 4. The Apostle declares the reason for τῆς μακροθυμίας, or divine long-suffering, both negatively and affirmatively. The negative statement is: God does not will that any should perish; which admits of no exception or exclusion. The affirmative is: God wills that all should come to repentance. This proposition is universal in respect of its object, and therefore not to be restricted to individuals of a kind, or to the predestined alone. For God calls and exhorts all men to repentance, Luke XXIV, 47. Acts XVII, 30. just as He demonstrates His μακροθυμίαν towards all, by still deferring the day of judgment, concerning which v. 10. which also extends to the very mockers who say: Where is the promise of His coming? the context teaches. From these we gather: Towards whom God is long-suffering, and whom He does not will to perish, but to be converted to repentance, those are embraced by God's saving grace: But God is long-suffering towards all men, and wills that none should perish, but that all should be converted to repentance: Therefore, God's saving grace embraces all men.

You say: St. Peter speaks only of the elect; because he says: God is long-suffering towards us. Reply: By those words the apostle does not refer to the differing condition of men based on faith or unbelief, but to the condition of misery after the fall, common to all men. To whom Peter numbers himself, according to that of Paul, Rom. III, 23. For all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God.

7) God confirms His universal benevolence with an oath, Ezek. XXXIII, 11. As I live, saith Adonai Jehovah, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live. Observe: a) The most benevolent God declares by this oath His affection, most inclined towards all men, at all times. For no convertible wicked person should be excepted here, whom God does not except: and as long as the wicked, being in the way, is capable of salvation, God does not will his death, but life. b) The discourse is about eternal death, which the penitent can avoid through God's grace; but temporal death is not avoidable even for the penitent. By the same token, the discourse is about life not temporal; for He often prolongs it for many years for him who does not convert: but about eternal life, inasmuch as it is the end of conversion Acts XI, 18. c) Τὸ velle here does not denote only εὐαρεσίαν, or delight, but also εὐδοκίαν, or serious and efficacious good pleasure; by which God wills the end, or the life of the sinner, through a powerful means, namely repentance. These things being established, we gather: Whoever seriously intends the conversion and eternal life of all the wicked, his benevolence towards fallen mankind is universal: But God &c. Therefore (). () miserable.

Latin:

Benevolentia Dei vniversalis quatuor inadaequatis absoluitur actibus; quorum primus est commiseratio vniversi generis humani fraude diaboli circumuenti & volentiae corrupti ): Secundus actus est intentio diuina omnibus hominibus in peccatum prolapsis salutem procurandi ): Tertius est liberalis donatio mediatoris Christi, quo laesa iustitiae diuinae fiat satis ): Quartus est destinatio mediorum, quibus tum aeterna salus satisfactione Christi parta, tum vires credendi omnibus hominibus offeruntur, vt satisfactionem Christi ad salutem acceptare, & sibi applicare queant ).

Prob. a. Concludit Deus omnes sub incredulitatem, vt omnium misereatur, Rom. XI, 32. Conuicit Deus omnes homines congenita ἀπιστίας, siue incredulitatis, atque argumentis inuictis demonstrauit, omnes omnino homines, sanguine Adami cretos & via naturali genitos, aeternae mortis reos, atque perennibus suppliciis dignos esse, si ex rigore iustitiae cum illis acturus esset. At Deus placabilis, vsus temperamento iuris in lapsos miserabiles, omnium misertus est veniam criminum omnibus concedendo, vt tam late diffunderetur misericordia diuina, quam late se extendit miseria humana. Misericordia divina est cupida salutis omnium mortalium: vult enim Deus misericordissimus omnes homines salvari, & ad agnitionem veritatis venire, 1 Tim. II, 4. vult, ut impius convertatur a via sua & vivat, Ezech. XVIII, 23. c. XXXIII, 11. Prob. c. Quia in Deo non tantum est gratia & misericordia, sed etiam iustitia, movet gratia Deum ad decernendam hominibus salutem non quocunque modo, sed quoad illud salua eius iustitia immutabili fieri poterat. Iustitia vero vindicativa movet Deum ad exigendam pro peccatis satisfactionem, aut, ea deficiente, ad vindicandum peccata morte aeterna. Quamobrem, cum peccator propriae praestandae satisfactioni pro se & pro aliis esset impar (Frater quippe non redimendo redimet virum; non dabit Deo expiationem eius. Pretiosior namque est redemtio animae eorum, ut omittat in aeternum, Ps. XLIX, 8.): misericordia Deum movit, ut hominibus, quibus volebat remissionem peccatorum & vitam aeternam offerre, prospiceret de aliena satisfactione, quam lubens praestitit Christus, aeternus Dei filius, qui dedit seipsum ἀντίλυτρον, pretium redemptionis pro omnibus, 1 Tim. II, 6. Idcirco benevolentiae Dei universali tribuendum est, quod Deus universo generi humano lapso dederit mediatorem Christum, qui pro peccatoribus legem impleret, & poenas transgressionum vicarias folueret.

Quam diuinam φιλανθρωπίαν deprædicat ipse Salvator, Io. III, 16. Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum unigenitum dederit. Et Paullus Rom. V, 8. Commendat suam dilectionem erga nos Deus, quod, adhuc peccatoribus existentibus nobis, Christus pro nobis mortuus est.

Collaudat eandem S. Ioannes 1. ep. IV, 9. 10. In hoc manifestata est dilectio Dei erga nos, quod Filium suum unigenitum misit Deus in mundum, ut vivamus per illum. In hoc est dilectio, non quod nos dilexerimus Deum, sed quod ille dilexerit nos & miserit Filium suum propitiationem pro peccatis nostris.

Prob. d. Non prodesset nobis satisfactio mediatoris Christi, nisi divinitus suppeditata nobis essent media, quibus eam nostram faceremus, aut nobis applicaremus. Media illa sunt tum verbum & sacramenta, quibus parta satisfactione Christi salus omnibus offertur; tum vera fides, qua satisfactio Christi acceptatur, & ad salutem applicatur. Haec media Deus nulli homini absolute & simpliciter denegat.

Iussit enim Deus φιλανθρωπος euangelium praedicari omni creaturae, Marc. XVI, 15. Et Christus in caelum subuecturus discipulos suos sic instruebat: Euntes ergo discipulos facite (mihi) omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomine Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus Sancti. Quin fidem etiam Deus omnibus offert, Act.

XVII, 31. Quæst. VII. Quorum vult Deus misereri? Obiectum benevolentia. Deus non vult misereri angelorum lapsorum a), vult autem misereri omnium & singulorum hominum peccatis corruptorum; quos iudicio divino miserabiles Deus ex abysso miseriae eruere, & per certa media ad aeternam beatitudinem deducere se serio velle ostendit b).

Prob. a. 1) Quia Deus angelis, qui peccarunt, non pepercit, 2 Petr. II, 4. Horrendam angelorum apostasiam Deus iudex iustissimus subtractione omnis gratiae aeternum punit.

Id quod perspicue docet S. Iudas ep. v. 6. Deus angelos eos, qui non retinuerunt suam originem, sed reliquerunt proprium domicilium, in iudicium magni diei vinculis perpetuis sub tenebris reservauit.

2) Cum angelis lapsis nullus divinitus datus fit mediator, salua iustitia divina a suppliciis liberari nequeunt. Ideo Apostolus Hebr. II, 16. nuspiam, ait, Filius Dei angelos assumsit, sed semen Abrahae. 3) Caussam, cur diabolus iudicio divino immiserabilis sit reputatus, non exprissit S. scriptura; prisci tamen patres probabiles quasdam fideique analogas reddiderunt rationes rigorosi iudicii diuini in angelos lapsos, quas collegit D. GERHARD. in Comment. in 2 Petr. II. p. 205. Nimirum omnis gratia diuina denegata est diabolo, quia a) sponte sua, nemine instigante, a Deo defecit, & seductor fuit hominis seducti, directo in creatorem odio. b) Quamuis etiam reliqui angeli lapsi a duce & antesignano diabolo sint seducti: omnes tamen liberrima προαιρέσει peccarunt; at posteri Adami necessitate nascendi in peccati reatum inciderunt. c) Nisi Deus nostri misertus esset, periisset vnius hominis peccato vniuersum genus humanum; cum tamen vnius angeli peccato non omnes perierint, sed vnusquisque eorum peccato proprio miseriam contraxerit.

Prob. b. Misericordia Dei complectitur omnes homines peccatores, non quatenus, aut quia peccatores sunt: Deus enim iniquitatem nolens odit operantes iniquitatem, Ps. V, 5. Sed quatenus sunt miserabiles, corrupti peccatis & in his inortui, propriis viribus destituti, ad restituendum seipsos in statum gratiae. Quare obuersante intellectui diuino communi hominum miseria, omnium est misertus, omniumque liberationem & salutem per certa media procurare serio intendit.

Etenim 1) ipse salutis assertor & vindex, Iesus, cosmophiliam Dei vniuersalem praedicat, Io. III, 16. Adeo Deus dilexit mundum, vt Filium suum vnigenitum daret, vt omnis, qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed vitam aeternam habeat.

Quo aureo euangelii compendio considerandus nobis proponitur dilector, dilectionis obiectum, modus & finis.

Dilector est Deus Pater (non tamen exclusa secunda & tertia diuinitatis persona: Nam & Christus nos dilexit, Eph. V, 25. Gal. II, 20. & per Spiritum Sanctum dilectio Dei effusa est in cordibus nostris, Rom. V, 5). Tribuitur autem dilectio peculiari ratione Deo Patri; sicut enim is est fons diuinitatis: ita etiam est fons τῆς φιλανθρωπίας erga homines. Obiectum dilectionis est mundus, per quem intelliguntur omnes homines peccatores, non quatenus peccatores, sed quatenus indigi sunt commiserationis.

Confirmatur haec expositio a) ex v. 18. vbi mundas, siue homines, per mundum significati, in duas classes dispescuntur, credentes & non credentes; & additur: vt, qui ex mundo credunt, vitam aeternam habeant: alii vero ex mundo, qui non credunt, damnentur. b) Vox, mundus, sumta sensu speciali, notat homines impios, v. gr. mundus non potest recipere Spiritum veritatis, Io. XIV, 17. mundus totus in maligno iacet, 1 Io. V, 19. Sensu generali accepta tam pios, quam impios homines designat, vt hoc loco, nunquam autem & nusquam in vniuersa scriptura S. significat solos electos. c) Mundus ille intelligitur, cui euangelium de Christo est praedicandum, Matth.

XXIIX, 19. Sed mundus ille est vniuersum genus humanum, Marc. XVI, 15. Modus dilectionis innuitur particula, ὅτως, adeo, vt designetur dilectio ardentissima & intensissima, cuius illustrissimum argumentum & incomparabile pignus est Filius Dei vnigenitus, datus mundo mediator & satisfactor.

Finis dilectionis est, vt omnes homines, satisfactionem Christi vera fide sibi applicantes, immunes sint ab aeterna condemnatione, compotes autem aeternae vitae. Argumentamur: Quaecunque dilectio complectitur omnes homines mundum hunc incolentes, illa ratione obiecti est vniuersalis. Atqui ardentissima Dei Patris dilectio, qua permotus est ad dandum mundo Filium suum vnigenitum mediatorem, vt omnes homines vera fide satisfactionem ipsius sibi applicantes aeternam vitam habeant, complectitur omnes homines mundum hunc incolentes. Ergo (*).

2) Apostolus Paullus diserte dicit 1 Tim. II, 4. Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri, & ad agnitionem veritatis venire. Obferuamus in hoc dicto classico (a) voluntatem Dei antecedentem de hominibus miseris saluandis, (b) voluntatis huius obiectum: omnes homines, per quos non intelliguntur omnis generis homines, sed homines singuli in statu miseriæ constituti, adeoque salutis indigi & saluabiles (nondum actu damnati). Quæ expositio ex συναφεία textus dispalefcit; quia (α) vox, omnis, primario significat singulos generum: secundario genera singulorum. Tamdiu autem stat analogum pro significatu principaliori; quamdiu cohæsio textus ab eodem nos recedere non cogit. (β)

Firmatur hæc expositio ex antecedentibus & consequentibus. Nam eos homines, pro quibus orandum esse præcepit Deus, vult saluos fieri. Sed pro omnibus & singulis hominibus, etiam illis, qui postea damnantur, orandum esse, præcepit Deus. Ergo omnes & singulos homines, etiam illos, qui postea damnantur, vult saluos fieri. Maioris & minoris veritas patet ex antecedentibus. E consequentibus autem sic colligimus: Pro quibus hominibus Christus seipsum dedit ἀντίλυτρον, siue pretium redemptionis, illos vult Deus saluos fieri. Sed pro hominibus omnibus Christus seipsum dedit ἀντίλυτρον. Ergo (*).

3) Vniuersalitas gratiæ diuinæ probatur ex Rom. XI, 32. Concludit Deus omnes homines in incredulitatem, vt omnium misereatur. Obs. a) Concludit Deus omnes homines in incredulitatem non αἰτιωδῶς, caussaliter, aut effectiue, hominum mentibus incredulitatem immittendo, aut infundendo; sed δικαστικῶς, iudicialiter, & declaratiue, omnes homines connatæ incredulitatis conuincendo, & declarando, omnes homines inconuerfos & irregenitos, saluificæ fidei esse expertes, adeoque æternæ mortis reos. b) Cum omnes destituerentur naturalibus viribus emergendi ex incredulitate, ex illa impotentia & miseria Deus occasionem sumsit omnium miserendi. Vnde argumentum: Quos Deus connatæ incredulitatis conuicit, & declarauit, æternæ mortis esse reos, illorum misertus est: Atqui homines omnes &c. Ergo.

4) Vniuersalitatem gratiæ diuinæ commendat Paullus Act. XVII, 30. 31. Tempora ignorantiæ videre transmisit Deus, in præsens præcipit hominibus omnibus vbique, vt pœnitentiam agant: propterea quod constituit diem, in quo iudicaturus est orbem in iustitia per virum, quem destinauit, fidem offerens omnibus, postquam suscitauit illum ex mortuis. Obs. a) Tempora ignorantiæ vocantur tempora V. T. comparata ad lucem euangelii, ministerio apostolorum in N. T. latissime diffusam. b) Ὑπεριδὼν notat longanimitatem Dei, cui licet abunde caussarum fuerit delendi peccatores, hoc tamen non fecit, sed tempora N. T. sub quo euangelium omnibus prædicandum erat, exspectauit, si vel tum de ignorantia sua pœnitentiam agerent. c) Apertissime commendatur hoc dicto Paullino gratia Dei vniuersalis; quoniam teste Apostolo Deus omnes homines, omnibus locorum interuallis degentes ad pœnitentiam inuitat, & promtus est ad dandum fidem omnibus per ordinata media. E quibus necti potest argumentum: Quibus hominibus Deus præcipit pœnitentiam agere, fidemque offert; illorum vult salutem. Atqui omnibus hominibus vbique viuentibus &c. Ergo.

5) De vniuersalitate gratiæ Dei salutiferæ perspicue testatur idem Apostolus, Tit. II, 11. Apparuit gratia Dei salutaris omnibus hominibus. Docet apostolus his verbis, gratiam Dei salutiferam omnibus esse obuiam, omnibus ex æquo expositam. Vt enim sol naturalis omnibus hominibus illucescit: ita gratia Dei omnibus apparuit, omnesque vult illuminare, modo oculos mentis malitiose non claudant. 6) Vniuersalitas malitiofe non claudant.

6) Vniversalitas gratiae divinae patet etiam e luculento effato Apostoli Petri, 2 Epist. III, 9. Deus longanimus est erga nos, non volens quosdam perire, sed omnes ad poenitentiam reuerti.

Repraesentatur his verbis S. Petri longanimitas divina, quae etiam ad reprobos extenditur. Rom. II, 4. Rationem τῆς μακροθυμίας, siue longanimitatis divinae, Apostolus tum negative, tum affirmative enuntiat. Enuntiatio negativa est: Deus non vult aliquos perire; quae nullam exceptionem aut exclusionem admittit. Affirmativa est: Deus vult, ut omnes ad poenitentiam reuertantur. Quae propositio ratione obiecti vniversalis est, adeoque non restringenda ad genera singulorum, aut solos praedestinatos. Omnes quippe homines Deus ad poenitentiam vocat & hortatur, Luc. XXIV, 47. Act. XVII, 30. sicut erga omnes μακροθυμίαν suam demonstrat, differendo adhuc diem iudicii, de quo v. 10. quam etiam ad ipsos empaectas, qui aiunt: Vbi est promissio aduentus ipsius? sese extendere, συνάφεια textus docet.
