Ex his colligimus: Erga quos homines Deus est longanimus, quosque non vult perire, sed ad poenitentiam conuerti, illos complectitur gratia Dei salutifera: Sed Deus est longanimus erga homines omnes, neque vllum vult perire, sed omnes ad poenitentiam conuerti: Ergo gratia Dei salutifera complectitur omnes homines.

Dicis: S. Petrus loquitur de solis electis; quia dicit: Deus longanimus est erga nos. Resp. Verbis illis apostolus non respicit conditionem hominum ex fide vel incredulitate diuersam, sed conditionem miseriae post lapsum, omnibus hominibus communem. Quibus se annumerat Petrus, iuxta illud Paulli, Rom. III, 23. Omnes enim peccauerunt, & destituuntur gloria Dei.

7) Deus vniversalem suam beneuolentiam iuramento confirmat, Ezech. XXXIII, 11. Vivus ego, dictum Adonai Iehouah, si velim mortem impii, sed vt conuertatur impius a via sua & viuat. Obs. a) Declarat Deus benignissimus hoc iuramento affectum suum in omnes, homines, omni tempore propensissimum. Neque enim vllus impius conuertibilis hic excipi debet, quem Deus non excipit: & quamdiu impius, in via constitutus, salutis capax est, Deus non vult eius mortem, sed vitam. b) Sermo est de morte aeterna, quam poenitens per gratiam Dei euitare potest; at mors temporalis ne poenitenti quidem est declinabilis. Pari ratione sermo est de vita non temporali; quippe quam in multos saepe annos producit, qui non conuertitur: sed de vita aeterna, vtpote quae est finis conuersionis Act. XI, 18. c) Τὸ velle hic non notat tantum εὐαρεσίαν, siue delectationem, sed etiam εὐδοκίαν, siue serium & efficax beneplacitum; quo Deus vult finem, siue vitam peccatoris, per validum medium, nimirum poenitentiam. Quibus praestitutis colligimus: Quicunque omnium impiorum conuersionem & aeternam vitam serio intendit, illius beneuolentia in genus humanum lapsum est vniversalis: Atqui Deus &c. Ergo (*). (*) miserabilia.


### Quest. VI. By what inadequate acts is the universal benevolence of God completed?: Doubts against the universality of divine grace can be formed as follows

Doubts against the universality of divine grace can be formed as follows.

I. Those whom God wills to be saved by the will of his good pleasure, they are saved: But not all are saved: Therefore, God does not will by the will of his good pleasure that all be saved. The major is proved; ...because man, being impotent, cannot resist the will of the omnipotent God, Rom. IX, 19. Resp. Those whom God wills to be saved absolutely by His absolute power, they necessarily become saved. Reason: because man, being impotent, cannot impede the absolute will and power of God: But God wills that man, having fallen into sin, be saved under a certain τάξει, or order of means, through His ordained power; which man resists by neglecting the constituted order. Therefore, one ought not to judge the efficacy of the divine will from the event. Indeed, God wills the perfect observance of the decalogue, which nevertheless is not rendered to Him by men.

II. Whoever has mercy on whom He wills to have mercy, and hardens whom He wills to harden, His mercy is not universal, but particular, not conditional or ordered, but absolute: But God, etc. Therefore. The major is clear in itself.

The minor is proved from Rom. IX, 18.

Resp. a) The Apostle does not speak in the cited place of the general or universal mercy of God, but of the special mercy by which He justifies those who believe in Christ, as can be seen from v. 30, and thus he does not treat of the antecedent will of God, but of the consequent. b) The mercy of God is indeed free, but not absolute.

It is free from the necessity of obligation, both because no law obligates God to have compassion on the fallen human race; and because the economy of salvation, to be obtained through faith in Christ, depends on the most free will of God; which, however, is perfectly conformed to equity and justice. c) God hardens whom He wills, not led by mercy, [He] willed to provide for the salvation of men to be recovered.

Mercy looks to nothing except misery. The misery of men of the natural condition is indeed the same and equal for all and each, without any difference, Rom. III, 23. Therefore, divine mercy looks equally to all and each of men.

Of this kind are especially four sayings: Matt. XVIII, 11. Luke XIX, 10. Rom. XI, 32. and most plainly and openly, Rom. V, 18, 19, 20, where we see a most clear testimony that the benevolence of God, by which He has had mercy on men, in respect to the men who have sinned, extends just as widely as their calamity; but as for sins, much more widely, v. 15, 16.

In the FIFTH [class] are contained those sayings which do not allow one to doubt that the merits of Christ pertain to all mortals, 1 Tim. II, 5, 6, and indeed in such a way that among all, those who have trusted in Christ are named specifically and especially, whose salvation is indeed most greatly [theirs], obtained at such a price (namely, in respect to the reception and the fruit), 1 Tim. IV, 10. The legate of Christ does not speak of the providence of God and the preservation of temporal life, as the adversaries wrongly persuade themselves, thinking that divine providence, both general and special, is signified by these words: Falsely.

We indeed affirm that God the Father is sometimes called σωτήρ, e.g., 1 Tim. II, 3, 4, Tit. III, 4, coll. with v. 6. But we deny that He is so named by reason of providence and preservation.

For 1) This name, σωτήρ, does not denote a preserver, but a deliverer, who snatches someone from misery. 2) Everywhere this word is referred to that grace which has been eminently declared in Christ, which has provided for the recovery of lost salvation, not only temporal but also eternal, which is excellently called χάρις ἡ σωτήριος, at Tit. II, 11, III, 4, 7. Therefore, wherever the Father is called σωτήρ, His decree concerning eternal salvation is indicated by that name, along with all things necessary for both acquiring and applying it, as is clearly apparent from the cited places, 1 Tim.

II, 3, 4, Tit. III, 4, 6. 3) In this very place, which we are engaged in explaining, there are three arguments, clearer than light.

(α) Paul spoke before of eternal life, v. 8. (β) He employs this affirmation: πιστὸς ὁ λόγος, καὶ πάσης ἀποδοχῆς ἄξιος, v. 9, which way of speaking is not accustomed to be used of other matters than those pertaining to eternal salvation, restored by the benefit of Christ, see c. I, 15, III, 1, coll. with the preceding II, 15, 2 Tim. II, 11, 12, add. v. 10, Tit. III, 7, 8. (γ) He discourses on that matter for which he himself had endured the most grievous vexations, v. 10. That thing, however, which brought such great inconveniences to him, which also sustained his …soul with the greatest consolation, was nothing else than the saving trust placed in Christ the sponsor and God reconciled, relying on which he himself awaited eternal blessedness, 2 Tim. I, 12. The SIXTH class is constituted by the words of Scripture, the meaning of which is this; that it is possible that those, whose hardness is not produced effectively, but judicially, because God, in punishment for preceding sins, permits the impious to be hardened, withdraws the grace so often repudiated, deserts the refractory sinner, and delivers the same to Satan and his own desires. III. Whoever loved Jacob and pursued Esau with hatred before they had done anything good or evil, he does not will the salvation of all men:… But God, etc. Therefore. The major premise is certain; because whom God hates without regard to sin, him He absolutely reprobates from eternal salvation. The minor is evident from Rom. IX, 11. 12. 13. When they (the boys) were not yet born, nor had done anything good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might remain; not of works, but of Him who calls, it was said to her: because the greater shall serve the lesser. As it is written: Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated. Resp. Both the literal sense and the typical accommodation of this apostolic oracle must be weighed. (1) For correctly understanding the literal sense, a comparison of the sayings of the O.T. which the Apostle regards will do much. When in v. 12 he says; The greater shall serve the lesser, he regards Gen. XXV, 23. Jehovah said: Two nations are in thy womb, and two peoples shall be separated from thy bowels: but one people shall prevail over the other; and the greater shall serve the lesser. From which words it is clear that the Apostle speaks 1) not of the individual persons of Esau and Jacob, but of the entire nations that would arise from them, which, insofar as they were then considered to have been in their loins, are said to be in the womb of Rebecca; and that to the lesser people, or those who were to derive their origin from Jacob, the son of Rebecca born the lesser, dominion is promised over the greater people to be procreated from the blood of Esau, the son of Rebecca born the greater and firstborn. Which the event itself also proved: since Christ died for the cause, they undergo eternal destruction. Rom. XIV, 15. 1 Cor. VIII, 11. In the SEVENTH are those things which make us certain that even damned men are Christ's own, and that they perfidiously deny Him, their Lord and Liberator. Matth. XXIII, 37. Jo. I, 11. 2 Petr. II, 1. The reason for the dominion, which must be asserted for Christ alone, is contained in the price which He alone paid for all, and thus by the right of purchase He made us bound and obligated to Himself, 2 Cor. V, 15. 2 Petr. II, 1. Sayings of this kind are to be observed the more holily, the more confidently the adversaries attack us with this opposition: that Christ never called the worst of mortals, adjudged to damnation, His sheep. It suffices that He confessed them to be His. The reason, however, why He held them unworthy of the name of His sheep, lies in this: that the simile, which is drawn from sheep, designates mutual love, both of Christ toward men, and of men in turn toward Christ, to whose word they are obedient, Jo. X, 4. 5. 12. 14. 26. 27. The EIGHTH kind offers for our consideration sayings of this sort, which clearly teach us that the means of grace applying to men are offered even to those who are stubborn to the very end, and to these no less than to those who obey the will of God. Act. XVII, 31. (πᾶσιν, i.e., to individuals, which is evident from the coherence of the words: whomever God is at some time to judge, to them He is also prepared to give saving faith), Rom. X, 16. add. 18. 19. Hebr. IV, 2. (καθάπερ, just as, to them. Therefore, the distinction of calling grace, which is one thing effective, another not so, which the Reformed and those who stand on the side of JANSENIUS have devised, is of no value). We add this argumentation: God in the business of our salvation deals with us in no other way than through certain means (a thing which the Reformed, and the Jansenists and Predestinarians, themselves profess). These means of salvation, in respect to men, are either the same for all or different. But no other medium is commended to us except the word and the Sacraments, and the word is nothing other than the written word, announced in accordance with the scriptures, and perceived by the ears. Rom. X, 14. 17. Therefore, the same means are employed. The word, which the elect hear, is likewise proposed to be heard by the damned. This word has its efficacy in itself, namely the power of divine truth, always one and the same, Jerem. XXIII, 29. 1 Pet. I, 23. & 25. Hebr. IV, 12. (that he who would dare to deny this, it would be necessary that he be imbued with fanatical opinions). Let us complete the argumentation: If the means of salvation are the same, if they are always effective in themselves, if the power of truth is always the same, always one and the same: it is a consequence that grace itself is also always the same, and effective in the same way, and nothing more is required than the attention of the mind and the right use of the means, as far as men are concerned. Of the NINTH kind are those which indicate the severity of the judgment, on account of the neglect of the contempt indeed Esau never served Jacob, but rather Jacob with singular submission venerated Esau, see Gen. XXXIII, 3 ; but the Idumeans, tracing their origin to Esau, served the Jews, the descendants of Jacob: for David had sent them into servitude, 2 Sam. VIII, 14 .

Wherefore God in conferring temporal benefits preferred the descendants of Jacob to the descendants of Esau. Which the Apostle further confirms from Mal. I, 2. 3. I have loved Jacob, and I have hated Esau.

Where 2) the discourse is not about positive hatred, by which someone is despised, rejected, and attacked, but comparative, by which someone is loved less. For the word, hatred, in the familiar style of scripture sometimes denotes postponement or lesser love, as Gen. XXIX, 30. 31. Deut. XXI, 15 . Luke XIV, 16. compared with Matt. X, 37. John XII, 35. Certainly Esau was not rejected by God by simple positive hatred, since it is established that he was not left devoid of every blessing.

For by faith concerning things to come Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau, as the Apostle says, Heb. XI, 20 . Concerning which see Gen. XXVII, 39. 40. 41 . 3) The love of God is one thing as saving, by which eternal salvation is conferred: another is generally called beneficial, by which temporal benefits are conferred. When God says: I have loved Jacob, and I have hated Esau, the discourse is not about the saving love of God, as if all the descendants of Jacob were elected to eternal life, and conversely, all the descendants of Esau were eternally reprobated; but about beneficial love, so that the sense is: I have loved Jacob more, by conferring upon him and his descendants greater benefits, and by granting to him the possession of the land of Canaan, flowing with milk and honey, according to the prerogative of dominion; but I have loved Esau and his descendants less, inasmuch as to them only the desert and the offer of grace, offered to the ungrateful.

Which is done in five ways: 1) by admonishing every one of mortals to avoid this supreme injury, 2 Cor. VI, 1. Heb. IV, 15

the deserts of Seir shall yield to habitation; which also in the appointed time shall serve the posterity of Jacob. Moreover, the Lord even adds, Mal. I, 3. I have laid his mountains waste, and his heritage for the dragons of the wilderness, i.e., the mountainous region of the Idumeans, Nebuchadnezzar leading the inhabitants into captivity, shall remain laid waste; but the posterity of Jacob shall be given the benefit of returning to the land of Canaan, and enjoying the utmost fertility of the region.

Latin:

Dubia adversus universalitatem gratiae divinae sequentia formari possunt.

I. Quos Deus vult salvari voluntate beneplaciti, illi salvantur: At non omnes salvantur: E. non vult Deus feria voluntate beneplaciti omnes salvari. Maior probatur; ...quia homo impotens voluntati Dei omnipotentis non potest resistere, Rom. IX, 19. Resp. Quos Deus vult salvari absolute per absolutam suam potentiam, illi necessario fiunt salvi. Ratio: quia homo impotens voluntatem & potentiam Dei absolutam non potest impedire: At Deus vult hominem, in peccatum prolapsum, salvari sub certa τάξει, seu ordine mediorum per potentiam ordinatam; cui homo resistit, ordinem constitutum negligendo. Proinde ex eventu de efficacia voluntatis divinae iudicare haud licet. Sane Deus vult perfectam decalogi observantiam, quae tamen eidem ab hominibus non praestatur.

II. Quicunque miseretur, quorum vult misereri, & indurat, quos vult indurare, illius misericordia non est universalis, sed particularis, non conditionata aut ordinata, sed absoluta: Atqui Deus &c. Ergo. Maior per se est liquida.

Minor probatur ex Rom. IX, 18.

Resp. a) Non loquitur Apostolus l. c. de misericordia Dei generali, aut universali, sed speciali, qua credentes in Christum iustificat, vt videre est e v. 30. adeoque non agit de voluntate Dei antecedente, sed consequente. b) Misericordia Dei libera quidem, sed non absoluta est.

Libera est a necessitate obligationis, tum quia nullum ius Deum obligat ad commiserationem generis humani lapsi; tum quia oeconomia salutis, per fidem in Christum impetrandae, a liberrima Dei voluntate pendet; quae tamen aequitati & iustitiae apprime conformis est. c) Indurat Deus quem vult, non miseratione ductus, procurare voluit hominum salutem recuperandam.

Miseratio respicit nil, nisi miseriam. Miseria hominum conditionis naturalis est profecto omnium ac singulorum eadem & aequalis, sine ulla differentia, Rom. III, 23. E. divina misericordia pariter ad omnes ac singulos spectat homines.

Huius generis dicta sunt potissimum quatuor: Matth. XVIII, 11. Luc. XIX, 10. Rom. XI, 32. & planissime apertissimeque, Rom. V, 18. 19. 20. vbi clarissimum cernimus testimonium, quod benevolentia Dei, qua is hominum misertus est, ratione quidem hominum, qui peccarunt, aeque late pateat, ac eorum calamitas; quantum vero ad peccata, multo latius, v. 15. 16. In QVINTO continentur ea dicta, quae non dubitare non sinunt, quin Christi promerita ad omnes pertineant mortales, 1 Tim.

II, 5. 6. & ita quidem, vt inter omnes speciatim ac praecipue nominentur Christo confisi, quorum quidem maxime sit salus, tanto pretio parta (nimirum ratione acceptionis fructusque) 1 Tim. IV, 10. Non de providentia Dei & conservatione vitae temporalis loquitur Legatus Christi, vt perperam sibi persuadent aduersarii, divinam prouidentiam, rati, tum generalem, tum specialem, his verbis significatam esse: Falso.

Adfirmamus quidem, Deum Patrem interdum appellari σωτήρ, v. g. 1 Tim. II, 3. 4. Tit. III, 4. coll. cum v. 6. Negamus autem, eum ita nominari ratione providentiae & conservationis.

Etenim 1) Nomen hoc, σωτήρ, non conservatorem denotat, sed liberatorem, qui aliquem ex miseria eripit. 2) Vbique haec vox refertur ad eam gratiam, quae in Christo eximie declarata est, quae recuperandae saluti deperditae, non temporali solum, sed & sempiternae consuluit, quae excellenter dicitur χάρις ἡ σωτήριος, ad Tit. II, 11. III, 4. 7. Itaque, sicubi Pater vocatur σωτήρ, indicatur eo nomine decretum ipsius de aeterna salute, omnibusque rebus, ad eam tum adquirendam, tum adplicandam, necessariis, vt plane adparet ex locis citatis, 1 Tim.

II, 3. 4. Tit. III, 4. 6. 3) In hoc ipso loco, in quo explanando versamur, tria argumenta sunt, luce clariora.

(α) Paullus ante dixit de vita aeterna, v. 8. (β) Adhibet hanc adfeuerationem: πιστὸς ὁ λόγος, καὶ πάσης ἀποδοχῆς ἄξιος, v. 9. quae dicendi ratio non de aliis rebus usurpari solet, quam de causis ad salutem aeternam, Christi beneficio restitutam, spectantibus, vid. c. I, 15. III, 1. coll. cum antec. II, 15. 2 Tim. II, 11. 12. add. v. 10. Tit. III, 7. 8. (γ) De ea re disserit, propter quam ipse grauissimas vexationes erat perpessus, v. 10. Id vero, quod tanta ipsi incommoda adtulit, quod etiam consolatione maxima animum sustentauit, nihil fuit aliud, quam fiducia salutaris, in Christo sponsore Deo-que reconciliato posita, qua fretus ipse aeternam beatitatem exspectauit, 2 Tim. I, 12. SEXTVM genus constituunt verba scripturae, quorum haec est sententia; fieri posse, vt illi, quorum non effectiue duritiem immittendo, sed iudicialiter, propterea, quod Deus in pœnam peccatorum præcedentium impios permittit indurari, gratiam toties repudiatam subtrahit, peccatorem refractarium deserit, eundemque Satanæ & propriis cupiditatibus tradit. III. Quicunque Iacobum dilexit, & Esauum odio prosecutus est, priusquam quidquam boni, aut mali fecerunt, is non omnium hominum vult salutem: Atqui Deus &c. Ergo. Maior constat; quia quem Deus citra intuitum peccati odit, illum absolute ab æterna salute reprobat. Minor patet ex Rom. IX, 11. 12. 13. Cum nondum nati essent (pueri), neque fecissent quidquam boni aut mali, vt, quod secundum electionem Dei (est) propositum maneret; non ex operibus; sed ex vocante dictum illi est: quia maior seruiet minori. Sicut scriptum est: Iacobum amaui, Esauum vero odio habui. Resp. Oraculi huius apostolici tum sensus litteralis, tum accommodatio typica pensitanda est. (1) Ad recte intelligendum sensum litteralem multum faciet collatio dictorum V. T. quæ Apostolus respicit. Cum v. 12. inquit; Maior seruiet minori, respicit Gen. XXV, 23. Dixit Iehouah: Duæ gentes sunt in vtero tuo, & duo populi ex visceribus tuis separabuntur: sed populus præ populo præualebit; maiorque seruiet minori. E quibus verbis patet, Apostolum loqui 1) non de personis singularibus Esaui & Iacobi, sed de integris gentibus orituris ex ipsis, quæ quatenus in eorum lumbis tum fuisse censebantur, dicuntur esse in vtero Rebeccæ; atque populo minori, seu qui ex Iacobo, filio Rebeccæ natu minori, ortum ducturus esset, dominium promitti in populum maiorem ex Esaui, filii Rebeccæ natu maioris & primogeniti, sanguine procreandum. Quod ipsum etiam euentus comprobauit: quandoquidem caussa Christus mortem oppetiit, æternam subeant perniciem. Rom. XIV, 15. 1 Cor. VIII, 11. In SEPTIMO sunt ea, quæ certiores nos faciunt, damnatos etiam homines Christi proprios esse, eumque, Dominum suum ac Liberatorem, perfide negare. Matth. XXIII, 37. Io. I, 11. 2 Petr. II, 1. Ratio autem dominii, quod Christo vni adserendum est, continetur in pretio, quod pro omnibus soluit ipse vnus, atque adeo iure emtionis nos sibi obstrictos deuinctosque fecit, 2 Cor. V, 15. 2 Petr. II, 1. Huius generis effata tanto sanctius obseruanda sunt, quanto maiori confidentia aduersarii nos impugnant hac oppositione: quod. Christus pessimos mortalium, damnationi adiudicatos nunquam oues suas vocauerit. Sufficit, quod suos esse, fassus est. Ratio autem, quam ob rem ouium suarum nomine indignos eos habuerit, sita est in eo: quod similitudo, quæ ab ouibus ducitur, amorem designat mutuum, & Christi erga homines, & hominum vicissim in Christum, cui dicto audientes sunt illi, Io. X, 4. 5. 12. 14. 26. 27. OCTAVVM genus nobis consideranda præbet dicta huiusmodi, quæ clare nos edocent, media gratiæ adplicantis hominibus ad extremum vsque contumacibus offerri, & his quidem non minus, quam illis, qui voluntati Dei obsequuntur. Act. XVII, 31. (πᾶσιν, i. e. singulis, quod patet ex cohærentia verborum: quoscunque Deus aliquando iudicaturus est, eisdem & fidem salutarem dare paratus est), Rom. X, 16. add. 18. 19. Hebr. IV, 2. (καθάπερ, pariter, ac illis. E. nequidquam valet, quam reformati, & qui a IANSENII stant partibus, excogitarunt, distinctio gratiæ vocantis, quæ alia sit efficax; alia non item). Adiungimus hanc argumentationem: Deus in negotio salutis nostræ nobiscum agit haud aliter, quam per certa quædam media (id quod Reformati, & Iansenistæ ac Prædeterminantes, ipsi profitentur). Hæc salutis media, ratione hominum ad vnum omnium, aut eadem sunt aut diuersa. At nullum nobis medium commendatur aliud, præter verbum & Sacramenta, verbum autem non aliud, quam scriptum, scripturæ congruenter nuntiatum, auribusque perceptum. Rom. X, 14. 17. E. eadem adhibentur media. Verbum, quod electi audiunt, itidem audiendum damnatis proponitur. Hoc verbum suam in se habet efficacitatem, nimirum vim veritatis diuinæ, semper vnam eamdemque, Ierem. XXIII, 29. 1 Pet. I, 23. & 25. Hebr. IV, 12. (quod qui infitiari ausit, ne eum oporteret fanaticis opinionibus imbutum esse). Perficiamus argumentationem: Si eadem sunt media salutis, si ea semper sunt per se efficacia, si eadem perpetuo est vis veritatis, semper vnius eiusdemque: consequens est, vt gratia quoque ipsa sit eadem semper, eodemque modo efficax, & nihil requiratur amplius, quam animi attentio, rectusque vsus mediorum, quod ad homines attinet. Ex NONO genere sunt ea, quæ seueritatem animaduersionis indicant, ob neglectionem contemdoquidem Esauus nunquam seruivit Iacobo, sed potius Iacobus singulari submissione veneratus est Esauum, vid. Gen. XXXIII, 3 ; Idumaei autem, originem suam referentes ad Esauum, feruierunt Iudaeis, posteris Iacobi: Dauid enim in seruitutem eos miserat, 2 Sam. VIII, 14 .

Quamobrem Deus in conferendis beneficiis temporalibus posteros Iacobi posteris Esau praetulit. Id quod Apostolus porro confirmat ex Malach. I, 2. 3. Dilexi Iacobum, Esauum autem odio habui.

Vbi 2) sermo est non de odio positivo, quo quis contemnitur, reiicitur & oppugnatur, sed comparatiuo, quo quis minus amatur. Vocabulum enim, odium, stilo scripturae familiari aliquando notat postpositionem aut dilectionem minorem, vt Gen. XXIX, 30. 31. Deut. XXI, 15 . Luc. XIV, 16. collato Matth. X, 37. Ioann. XII, 35. Certe Esauus a Deo non simpliciter odio positivo reiiectus est, cum constet, illum non omnis benedictionis expertem relictum esse.

Nam per fidem de futuris benedixit Isaacus Iacobo & Esauo, vt ait Apostolus, Hebr. XI, 20 . De quo vide Gen. XXVII, 39. 40. 41 . 3) Dilectio Dei alia est saluifica, qua aeterna confertur salus: alia generatim dicta benefica, quae beneficia temporalia conferuntur. Quando Deus dicit: Dilexi Iacobum, Esauum autem odio habui, non est sermo de dilectione Dei saluifica, perinde, ac si omnes posteri Iacobi ad vitam aeternam electi, contra, omnes posteri Esau aeternum reprobati sint; sed de dilectione benefica, vt sensus fit: magis amaui Iacobum, conferendo in ipsum & posteros eius maiora beneficia, atque concedendo ipsi possessionem terrae Canaan, melle & lacte fluentis, iuxta atque praerogatiuam dominii; minus autem amaui Esauum & posteros eius, quippe quibus tantum deserta tionemque gratiae, ingratis oblatae.

Id quod quinque fit modis: 1) vnum mortalium quemque de euitanda hac summa iniuria admonendo, 2 Cor. VI, 1. Hebr. IV, 15

deserta Seir cedent in habitationem; qui etiam statuto tempore posteris Iacobi feruient. Quin addit etiam Dominus, Mal. I, 3. posui montes eius vastitatem, & hereditatem eius draconibus deserti, h. e. Montosa Idumæorum regio a Nebuchodonosare, incolas in captiuitatem abducente, vastata manebit; posteri autem Iacobi in terram Canaan redire, summaque regionitate frui meo dabitur beneficio.


### Quest. VI. By what inadequate acts is the universal benevolence of God completed?: (II.) Now follows the typical accommodation

(II.) Now follows the typical accommodation.

Just as God preferred the posterity of Jacob to the posterity of Esau in temporal benefits, by giving the posterity of Jacob dominion over the posterity of Esau, and that neither in consideration of the condition of birth, nor in consideration of good works done by them, so that the purpose of God, which is according to election (the Apostle understands election to the prerogative of empire), might remain firm not from works, but from him who calls (he who calls is God, who was calling Jacob to the prerogative of dominion by his decree and promise): So in spiritual benefits God, according to his good pleasure, prefers the Gentiles to the Jews, by granting to the Gentiles, who have embraced Christ by faith, and not to the Jews, who are most averse to the faith of Christ, the righteousness of Christ, with no regard had for birth and carnal origin, or the works of the law.

For the Apostle intends this uniquely in the whole of chapter IX to the Romans, that he might protect and defend this doctrine against those who contradict it, that the Gentiles have attained righteousness, not having pursued righteousness from works; but the Jews have not attained righteousness, having pursued it from the works of the law.

See v. 30, 31. Whence it follows that the Gentiles have been adopted into the peculiar people of God, whom he justifies by grace on account of Christ, apprehended by true faith: but that the Jews have been rejected from the fellowship of the church and the prerogatives which they previously enjoyed.

See v. 4, 5. You say: Esau, Hebr. XII, 17, is called profane and rejected, who found no place for repentance, though he sought it with tears. Therefore God pursued Esau not only with comparative hatred, but also with positive hatred, or the hatred of enmity.

Resp. 1) Esau is called profane on account of the contempt and sale of his birthright. 2) He is called rejected not from eternal salvation, but from the privileges and temporal benefits which accompany the right of birthright; such as the priesthood and the kingdom, and also the promise concerning Christ, who was to be born from the seed of him who was to have the right of birthright among the patriarchs.

3) The Apostle is not speaking of the repentance of Esau, but of his father Isaac. For Esau hoped that he could move his father Isaac with his tears, so that he might repent of the blessing conferred upon Jacob, but he could by no means obtain this from his father. The blessed LUTHER in his Commentary on chapters 25 and 33 of Genesis conjectures that Esau did repent, and was saved through faith in the Messiah. For he returned into favor with his brother Jacob, upon his return from Mesopotamia, Gen. XXXIII, by whom without doubt he was admonished to cultivate piety in a brotherly manner, especially concerning the burial of their parent, Gen. XXXV. 4) Grant that Esau was eternally rejected, yet he was not rejected by an absolute hatred without regard to his incredulity.

Latin:

(II.) Sequitur iam accommodatio typica.

Sicut Deus temporalibus beneficiis posteros Iacobi posteris Esaui prætulit, dando posteris Iacobi dominium in posteros Esaui, idque nec intuitu conditionis nascendi, nec intuitu factorum ab ipsis bonorum operum, ut propositum Dei, quod est secundum electionem (intelligit Apostolus electionem ad prærogatiuam imperii), firmum maneret non ex operibus, sed ex vocante (vocans est Deus, qui ad prærogatiuam dominii Iacobum per suum decretum & promissum vocabat): Ita in spiritualibus beneficiis Deus, pro suo beneplacito, gentiles præfert Iudæis, donando gentilibus, fide Christum amplexis, non Iudæis, a fide Christi auersissimis, iustitiam Christi, nulla habita ratione natiuitatis & ortus carnalis, vel operum legis.

Id enim vnice intendit Apostolus toto capite IX. ad Romanos, vt tueatur atque aduersus contradicentes defendat hanc doctrinam, quod iustitiam consecutæ sint gentes, non sectatæ iustitiam ex operibus; Iudæi vero non consecuti sint iustitiam, sectati eam ex operibus legis.

Vid. v. 30. 31. Vnde consequitur, gentiles esse adscitos in populum Dei peculiarem, quem ex gratia propter Christum, vera fide apprehensum, iustificat: reiectos autem esse Iudæas a consortio ecclesiæ & prærogatiuis, quibus antea gaudebant.

Vid. v. 4. 5. Dicis: Esauus Hebr. XII, 17; dicitur profanus, & reprobatus, qui pœnitentiæ locum non inuenit, licet cum lacrymis eam quæsierit. Ergo Deus Esauum non tantum odio comparatiuo, sed etiam positiuo, siue odio inimicitiæ prosecutus est.

Resp. 1) Esauus vocatur profanus, ob contemptum & venditionem primogenituræ. 2) Dicitur idem reprobatus non ab æterna salute, sed a priuilegiis & beneficiis temporalibus, quæ ius primogenituræ comitantur; qualia sunt sacerdotium & regnum, nec non promissio de Christo, ex illius, qui ius primogenituræ inter patriarchas habiturus esset, semine nascituro.

3) Non est Apostolo sermo de pœnitentia Esaui, sed patris Isaaci. Sperabat quippe Esauus, f: lacrymis suis patrem Isaacum permouere posse, vt benedictionis in Iacobum collatæ ipsum pœniteret, sed hoc a patre impetrare minime potuit. Coniicit b. LVTHERVS in Comment. in cap. 25. & 33. Genes. Esauum pœnitentiam egisse, & per fidem in Messiam saluatum fuisse. Rediit enim in gratiam cum fratre Iacobo, reuerfo ex Mesopotamia, Gen. XXXIII. a quo fine dubio de colenda pietate fraterne monitus est, in primis circa sepulturam parentis, Gen. XXXV. 4) Fac, æternum reprobatum esse Esauum, non tamen odio absoluto citra intuitum incredulitatis reiectus est.


### Quest. VI. By what inadequate acts is the universal benevolence of God completed?: IV. In those men in whom God willed to show his wrath, he does not will to have mercy

IV. In those men in whom God willed to show his wrath, he does not will to have mercy.

Yet in certain men God willed to show his wrath, Rom. IX, 21. Resp. God willed to show his wrath and make known his power in certain men, by a consequent will and secondary intention, on account of the malicious rejection of the means of grace offered; which vessels of wrath, however, prepared for destruction by their own malice, God bore for a long time with much lenity by his primary intention, that he might invite them to repentance, Rom. II, 4.

IX, 22. Therefore he does not will the salvation of all.

Resp. The words of the Apostle are: What if God, willing to show his wrath, and to make his power known, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction, and that he might make known the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy, which he had prepared unto glory. From which words it is clear that God indeed prepared the vessels of mercy unto glory; but the vessels of wrath are not said to be prepared by God, but to be tolerated by God with much longsuffering.

men hardened not by God, but by themselves, and by their own malice and voluntary perversity, have been made vessels of wrath, prepared for destruction; because they spurn the counsel of God against themselves, Luc. VII, 30.

Instance: God is compared to a potter, who has absolute power, that from the same lump he may make vessels, one indeed for honor, another truly for ignominy, Rom. IX, 12. Therefore God by absolute power created some men for eternal glory, some for eternal ignominy. Resp. 1) A simile is not to be extended beyond the scope of the author. The Apostle had said v. 18. God, whom he wills, he has mercy on; and whom he wills, he hardens. A certain antagonist could object: Why does he still blame? For who has resisted his will? Although the Apostle could have dissolved this objection with a direct response and said, that God in the business of justification does not act by absolute power, which no one can resist, but by ordained power, by converting and justifying men through certain means, which ordinary means many repel: yet it pleased Paul to answer a) indirectly, by rebuke, restraining the audacity of men speaking against God: But yet, O man, who are you, who answer back to God? Shall the thing formed say to him who formed it: why have you made me so? i.e. Is it right for the creature to expostulate with the creator, and to demand reasons for the deed from him? β) He answers directly, partly by showing that God has the free power of hardening some men, partly by teaching that God has a cause for justly accusing the hardened. He shows the power of God, by comparing him in v. 12 to a potter. For if the potter has power over the clay, that from the same lump he may make vessels, one indeed for honor, another truly for ignominy; why should God not have the most free power, from the fallen human race, of justifying, or pronouncing, those who submit themselves to the divine will and order and believe in Christ, to be vessels prepared for the glory of divine grace; but of hardening, and declaring, those who stubbornly resist the divine will and order and do not believe, to be vessels prepared for ignominy by their own malice? Observe, that the potter is compared with God by reason of free power; he differs from him, in that a) the potter uses absolute power, God in the business of salvation uses ordained power; b) that the potter effectively and by positive influx fashions a vessel for ignominy, but God hardens judicially, by permitting hardening, by abandoning the stubborn, and by declaring those who are hardened to be vessels of wrath, made for ignominy by their own fault. Furthermore, the Apostle teaches that God has a cause for justly accusing the hardened, v. 22, in that he tolerates with much long-suffering the vessels of wrath, prepared for destruction; this benign tolerance is intended to invite hardened sinners to repentance, Rom. II, 4. 2 Petr. III, 9. Wherefore God accuses hardened sinners of persevering disobedience, by which they have earned eternal punishments, with the most just right.

VI. Whoever wills the salvation of all and singular men, he also wills the salvation of men actually damned: God does not will the salvation of men actually damned: Therefore he does not will the salvation of all and singular men. The major is evident; because under all and singular men even the damned are included. Resp. God wills the salvation of all men, namely those capable of salvation, who being established in the way can be converted. Those actually damned have already received the final sentence, and therefore are not capable of salvation.

VII. If God wills to save all men, he wills the salvation of all men either absolutely, or conditionally. If he wills the salvation of all men absolutely, all are saved; because the absolute effect depends on the absolute will of God. If conditionally; God either only demands that condition, or he wills to effect it. If he only demands that condition; it will be impossible for man, on account of free will laboring under defect in spiritual things. If he wills to effect it; he effects it either absolutely, or conditionally. If absolutely; all will believe and be saved. If conditionally ditioned; the question will return, and either there will be a process to infinity in the conditions of conditions, or finally He willed the ultimate condition absolutely, which being posited, it will be necessary that all preceding ones also be posited, because they all depend upon one another. Resp. God wills to save all conditionally, under the condition of faith; which condition God not only demands, but also wills to effect the same, not absolutely, but under another condition: if they do not voluntarily resist the Holy Spirit (it is called voluntary, or free, resistance, in opposition to natural). Furthermore, God also wills this other condition, namely: that they do not voluntarily resist the Holy Spirit; truly not in the same conditional way as the former, but absolutely and without condition; and thus one must stop here, nor is there a process to infinity in the conditions of conditions. Nor is there a simply necessary nexus between those conditions, such that one being posited, it is necessary that the other be posited. For when the means of grace for effecting repentance or faith are posited, it is not simply necessary that repentance and faith be posited, since the Word of God is often preached even to those who do not repent and believe.

Latin:

IV. In quibus hominibus Deus iram voluit ostendere, illorum non vult misereri.

Atqui in quibusdam hominibus Deus suam ostendere voluit iram, Rom. IX, 21. Resp. Deus in quibusdam hominibus ostendere iram & notificare potentiam suam voluit, voluntate consequente & intentione secundaria, ob malitiosam oblatorum gratiæ mediorum reiectionem; quæ tamen vasa iræ propria malitia apparata ad interitum Deus longo tempore multa lenitate pertulit intentione primaria, vt ea ad pœnitentiam inuitet, Rom. II, 4.

V. Deus ex nonnullis hominibus facit vasa iræ, Rom. IX, 22. Ergo non vult omnium salutem.

Resp. Verba Apostoli sunt: Quod si, cum vult Deus demonstrare iram, & notam facere potentiam suam, tulit cum multa longanimitate vasa iræ, apparata ad interitum, & vt notas faceret diuitias gloriæ suæ super vasa misericordiæ, quæ præparauit ad gloriam. E quibus verbis liquet, quod Deus quidem præparauerit vasa misericordiæ ad gloriam; at vasa iræ non dicuntur a Deo apparata, sed a Deo cum multa longanimitate tolerata.

THEOL. PART. III. SECT. I. CAP. I. 598 homines indurati non a Deo, sed a se ipsis, & a propria malitia ac voluntaria perversitate, facti sunt vasa irae, apparata ad interitum; propterea, quod consilium Dei adversus seipsos spernunt, Luc. VII, 30.

Instantia: Deus comparatur cum figulo, qui habet absolutam potestatem, vt ex eadem massa faciat vasa, vnum quidem in honorem, alterum vero in ignominiam, Rom. IX, 12. Ergo Deus absoluta potestate quosdam homines ad aeternam gloriam, quosdam ad aeternam ignominiam creauit. Resp. 1) Simile non est extendendum vltra scopum auctoris. Dixerat Apostolus v. 18. Deus, cuius vult, miseretur; & quem vult, indurat. Poterat antagonista quidam obiicere: Quid adhuc incusat? Voluntati enim eius quis restiterit? Hanc obiectionem licet Apostolus potuisset responsione directa diluere & dicere, Deum in negotio iustificationis non agere potentia absoluta, cui nemo resistere possit, sed ordinata, per certa media homines conuertendo & iustificando, quae ordinaria media multi repellunt: placuit tamen Paulo respondere a) indirecte, per obiurgationem, hominum Deo obloquentium audaciam compescendo: Veruntamen, o homo, tu quis es, qui contra respondes Deo? Num dicet figmentum factori: quare me fecisti sic? q. d. Num fas est, creaturam expostulare cum creatore, factique rationes ab eodem exigere? β) Respondet directe, partim ostendendo, Deum habere liberam potestatem quosdam homines indurandi, partim docendo, suppetere Deo caussam, induratos iuste accusandi. Potestatem Dei ostendit, ipsum v. 12. comparando cum figulo. Quodsi enim figulus potestatem habet luti, vt ex eadem massa faciat vasa, vnum quidem in honorem, alterum vero in ignominiam; quidni Deus liberrimam habeat potestatem ex genere humano lapso alios quidem, qui voluntati & ordini diuino se submittentes in Christum credunt, iustificandi, siue pronuntiandi, eos esse vasa, ad decus gratia diuina praeparata; alios vero, qui voluntati & ordini diuino pertinaciter resistentes non credunt, indurandi, & declarandi, eos esse vasa, ad dedecus propria malitia apparata? Obserues, quod figulus comparetur cum Deo ratione potestatis liberae; differat ab eodem, quod a) figulus potestate absoluta, Deus in negotio salutis potestate ordinata vtatur; b) quod figulus effectiue & potitiuo influxu vas ad dedecus coagmentet, Deus autem induret iudicialiter, indurationem permittendo, prefracte contumaces deferendo, iuxta atque induratos vasa irae, ad ignominiam propria culpa factos, declarando. Porro docet Apostolus, Deo suppetere caussam induratos iuste accusandi, v. 22. eo quod vasa irae, apparata ad interitum, multa cum longanimitate toleret; benigna haec tolerantia induratos peccatores ad poenitentiam inuitaturus, Rom. II, 4. 2 Petr. III, 9. Quamobrem Deus induratos peccatores perseuerantis inobedientiae, qua aeternas commuere poenas, aequissimo iure accusat.

VI. Quicunque vult omnium & singulorum hominum salutem, ille vult etiam salutem hominum, actu damnatorum: Deus non vult salutem hominum actu damnatorum: Ergo non vult omnium & singulorum hominum salutem. Maior patet; quia sub omnibus & singulis hominibus etiam damnati comprehenduntur. Resp. Deus vult omnium hominum, scilicet capacium salutis, qui in via constituti conuerti possunt, salutem. Actu damnati sententiam finalem iam acceperunt, ideoque non sunt salutis capaces.

VII. Si Deus homines omnes vult saluare, vult omnium hominum salutem vel absolute, vel conditionate. Si omnium hominum salutem vult absolute, omnes sunt salui; quia a voluntate Dei absoluta absolutus pendet effectus. Si conditionate; Deus aut exigit tantum istam conditionem, aut vult eam efficere. Si tantum exigit illam conditionem; erit impossibilis homini, defectu liberi arbitrii in spiritualibus laboranti. Si eam vult efficere; efficit eam vel absolute, vel conditionate. Si absolute; omnes credent & saluabuntur. Si conditionate ditionate; redibit quaestio, &, vel processus dabitur in infinitum, in conditionum conditionibus, vel tandem ultimam conditionem absolute voluit, qua posita omnes etiam antecedentes poni necesse erit, quia omnes a se invicem pendent. Resp. Deus vult omnes salvare conditionate, sub conditione fidei; quam conditionem Deus non tantum exigit, sed & eandem efficere vult non absolute, sed sub alia conditione: si non resistant voluntarie Spiritui S. (dicitur resistentia voluntaria, seu libera, in oppositione ad naturalem). Praeterea vult Deus & alteram hanc conditionem, nempe; ut non resistant voluntarie Spiritui Sancto; verum non itidem conditionaliter, ut priorem, sed absolute & fine conditione; adeoque hic subsistendum est, nec datur processus in infinitum in conditionum conditionibus. Neque datur simpliciter necessarius nexus inter conditiones illas, ut una posita, alteram poni necesse sit. Neque enim mediis gratiae ad resipiscentiam, vel fidem efficiendam, positis, simpliciter necessarium est, ut resipiscentia & fides ponatur, cum verbum Dei etiam iis saepe praedicetur, qui non resipiscunt & credunt.


### Quest. VI. By what inadequate acts is the universal benevolence of God completed?: Q. VIII What is the nature of the mercy and benevolence of God toward sinners?

Q. VIII.

What is the nature of the mercy and benevolence of God toward sinners?

The mercy of God toward miserable sinners is a) gratuitous and liberal, b) sincere and earnest, c) efficacious, d) equal, e) not absolute, but tempered by justice, f) ordered, g) and conditioned. Prob. a. Those whom God has concluded under sin and unbelief, He has mercy upon, Gal. III, 22. Rom. XI, 32. Therefore His mercy is provoked by no merits. The misery of the sinner does not move God causally, but only provides an occasion, and presents to God a miserable object, toward which He ought not, but can, exercise φιλανθρωπίαν (philanthropy). For in man there is clearly no impelling cause. See, if you please, D. Hülsemann’s Breviar. enucl. p. 351. Therefore, just as the mercy of God toward miserable men is gratuitous, so it is also liberal; since with Christ He gives us all things that are necessary for salvation. Which liberty of divine mercy Paul brings forward, Rom. VIII, 32. He who did not spare His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all, how shall He not also with Him freely give us all things? Prob. b.

The benevolence of God toward the human race, fallen into sin, is not feigned or masked, but earnest and sincere; for the reason that in the procurement of human salvation, the will of sign with the will of divine good pleasure; the precept and the promise with the divine intention, most amicably conspire. He acts the hypocrite who utters one thing with his mouth and hides another in his heart; to think this of God is a crime. Indeed, a clear testimony of the most sincere divine will concerning the having of mercy on miserable sinners is the oath of God, Ezek. XXXIII, 11. As I live, says Adonai Jehovah, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live. Therefore God swears, so that if we do not believe God promising, we might at least believe Him swearing for our salvation, says Jerome, tom. II. epist. XLVI. Prob. c.

The universal benevolence of God is not an empty wish, not a sterile velleity, not an idle complacency, by which someone does not desire to effect or attain a thing which pleases him and which he loves in itself, and therefore does not wish to use the means leading to this end; but it is an efficacious will, by which God most ardently loves the salvation of men, and seriously intends to effect it and attain it through sufficient and efficacious means. Which efficacious grace of God Paul commends, Rom. II, 4. Or do you despise the riches of the goodness of God? Not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance? Thence arises the argument: Whatever kindness is so copious that it leads a sinner turned away from God to repentance, that is not an idle complacency, but an efficacious intention of bringing the sinner back into the way of salvation: But divine kindness &c. Therefore.

Prob. d.

Just as all were created in Adam in the image of God, and in him all sinned: so also the condition and misery of all men in the eternal foreknowledge of God was altogether equal; and therefore He has embraced all sinful men, as His equally miserable creatures, with equal benevolence and equal mercy. Paul teaches this in Rom. III, 22, 23. There is no distinction, for all have sinned, and are destitute of the glory of God, and are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. We grant easily, however, that the accidental degrees of manifesting this grace are unequal; concerning which, see below.

Prob. e.

Prob. g. The divine will to confer salvation upon sinners is also called conditional; because it is of the antecedent will, if they believe: of the consequent, who believe. The will is called conditional from the condition, which follows the antecedent will; it precedes the consequent, as DANNHAUER judges, in Hodof. phænom. VIII, p. 539. It is called conditional, not as if God only willed the end and did not will the means; or willed the end under a condition which He Himself, out of mere good pleasure, does not will to be fulfilled by many: but insofar as God, willing men to be saved, does not will them to be made saved without satisfaction or the fulfillment of any condition, but to be led to salvation under the condition of certain means.

Latin:

Quaest. VIII. Qualis est misericordia & benevolentia Dei erga peccatores?

Misericordia Dei erga peccatores miseros est a) gratuita & liberalis, b) sincera & feria, c) efficax, d) aequalis, e) non absoluta, sed iustitia temperata, f) ordinata, g) & conditionata,

Prob. a. Quos Deus sub peccatum & incredulitatem conclusit, eorum miseretur, Gal. III, 22. Rom. XI, 32. Ergo illius misericordia nullis meritis est provocata. Miseria peccatoris non movet Deum causaliter, sed praebet tantum occasionem, & obiicit Deo obiectum miserum, erga quod φιλανθρωπίαν exercere non debeat, sed queat. In homine enim nulla plane est causa impellens. Vide, si lubet, D. Hvlsemanni breviar. enucl. p. 351. Sicut igitur misericordia Dei erga homines miseros est gratuita: ita eadem est liberalis; quoniam cum Christo omnia, quae ad salutem sunt necessaria, nobis donat. Quam divinae misericordiae libertatem affert Paulus, Rom. VIII, 32. Qui proprio filio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum, quomodo non etiam cum ipso omnia nobis gratificabitur?

Prob. b. Non funulata aut fucata, sed feria & sincera est benevolentia Dei erga genus humanum, in peccatum prolapsum; propterea, quod in procuratione salutis humanae voluntas signi cum voluntate beneplaciti divini; praeceptum, & promissio cum intentione divina, quam amicissime conspirant. Hypocritam agit, qui aliud ore promit, aliud corde praemit; id quod de Deo cogitare, nefas est. Sane luculentum voluntatis divinae sincerissimae de abendis peccatoribus miseris testimonium est iuramentum Dei, Ezech. XXXIII, 31. Vivus ego, dictum Adonai Iehouah, si velim mortem impii, sed ut convertatur impius a via sua & viuat. Idcirco iurat Deus, vt si non credimus promittenti Deo, credamus saltem pro salute iuranti, ait HIERONYMVS tom. II. epist. XLVI.

Prob. c. Benevolentia Dei vniversalis non est inane votum, non sterilis velleitas, non otiosa complacentia, qua quis rem, quae libi placet, & quam in se amat, non cupit efficere, aut consequi, adeoque mediis ad hunc finem ducentibus non vult vti; sed est voluntas efficax, qua Deus salutem hominum, ardentissime amatam, etiam efficere atque per media sufficientia ac efficacia consequi ferio intendit. Quam efficacem gratiam Dei commendat Paulus, Rom. I, 4. An diuitias bonitatis Dei contemnis? Ignorans, quod bonitas Dei te ad paenitentiam ducit? Inde nascitur argumentum: Quaecunque benignitas adeo copiosa est, vt peccatorem a Deo auerfum ad paenitentiam ducat, illa non est otiosa complacentia, sed efficax intentio peccatorem in viam salutis reducendi: Atqui benignitas diuina &c, Ergo.

Prob. d. Sicut in Adamo omnes erant ad imaginem Dei conditi, & in eodem omnes peccarunt: ita etiam omnium hominum in æterna Dei præscientia par omnino erat conditio & miseria; ideoque etiam omnes homines peccatores, vt creaturas suas æque miseras pari beneuolentia & æquali misericordia complexus est. Docet hoc Paullus Rom. III, 22, 23. Non est discrimen, omnes enim peccauerunt, & destituuntur gloria Dei, atque iustificantur gratis gratia ipsius per redemptionem, quæ est in Christo Iesu. Gradus tamen accidentales manifestandi hanc gratiam, dispares esse, damus faciles; de quibus infra.

Prob. e. Quamuis prima Dei commiseratio, qua misertus est generis humani in peccatum prolapsi, nec non ordinatio mediatoris, mediorumque salutis procuratio sit absoluta, misericors tamen Dei voluntas conferendi hominibus remissionem peccatorum & æternam salutem, non est absoluta, sed respectiua, & iustitia temperata. Respicit quippe satisfactionem Christi, qua iustitiæ diuinæ satisfactum est. Vid. supra quæst. 6. prob. c.

Prob. f. Beneuolentia Dei falutifera est ordinata, ideo quod Deus altissimo consilio certam mediorum τάξιν aut ordinem constituit, quem in beandis peccatoribus respicit. Sunt illa media verbum Dei & sacramenta, quibus Deus peccatores ad regnum gratiæ vocare, conuertere, regenerare, iustificare, saluare serio intendit. Hac voluntate ordinata Deus vult, vt omnes homines non tantum saluentur, sed etiam vt omnes homines ad agnitionem veritatis perueniant. 1 Tim. II, 4.

Prob. g. Voluntas diuina conferendi peccatoribus salutem appellantur etiam conditionata; quia voluntatis antecedentis est, si credant: consequentis, qui credunt. Dicitur voluntas conditionata a conditione, quæ voluntatem antecedentem sequitur; consequentem præcedit, iudice DANNHAVERO, in hodof. phænom. VIII. p. 539. Conditionata dicitur, non quasi Deus tantum velit finem, non velit media; aut velit finem sub conditione, quam ipse ex mero beneplacito penes multos nolit impleri: sed quatenus Deus volens homines saluari, non vult eos citra satisfactionem, vllamue conditionem implendam saluos fieri, sed sub conditione certorum mediorum ad salutem deduci.


### Quæst. IX. Does God will to give saving faith to all men?

God wills to confer saving faith upon all men through ordinary means.

Prob. 1) From the explicit assertion of St. Paul, Acts XVII, 31. God has appointed a day in which He is about to judge the world in justice by the man whom He has destined, offering faith to all. Τὸ παρέχειν πίστιν denotes both the offering of the powers of believing and the collation of faith itself, provided that the means of regeneration are not maliciously rejected. For τὸ παρέχειν generally signifies not only some external offering, but also a real collation. Thus God is said παρέχειν πάντα πλουσίως, to give all things abundantly, 1 Tim. VI, 17. Cf. Luke XVIII, 5. Acts XXII, 2. We argue: Whoever offers faith to all men who are to be presented before the tribunal of Christ, he wills to confer faith upon all men: But God does so, etc. Therefore.

2) From the individual connection of obtaining the end and the means through which the end is attained. Thus Paul connects the divine will of saving all men and conferring upon all saving faith. God wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, 1 Tim. II, 4. He who wills all men to come to the knowledge of the truth, so that they may be saved, he wills to endow all men with saving faith: But God does so, etc. Therefore. The major is proved: because the knowledge of the truth is faith, and this is the gift of God, Eph. II, 8.

3) From the intention of God to convert all sinners. For God does not will that some should perish, but that all should be converted to repentance, 2 Pet. III, 9. He who wills all to return to repentance, he wills to bestow upon all faith, which is the chief part of repentance.

4) Concerning the satisfaction of Christ applicable to all. To whatever men God has destined Christ as mediator, to them He wills to impart faith: But to all men &c.

The major premise is evident: because God, by destining a mediator, willed that men, having fallen into sin, should apprehend His satisfaction and merit by true faith, and apply it to themselves for salvation. But since sinners are destitute of the natural powers of believing, without doubt God will out of grace give faith to those to whom He has given a mediator, so that they may be able to apply His merit to themselves.

Paul teaches this in Rom.

VIII, 32. God did not spare His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all: how shall He not also with Him freely give us all things, i.e., grant them out of grace? By which words the apostle implies that Christ was both delivered into death for us all, and given to us all. From which he further concludes that God, just as He will give all things necessary for salvation, so He will give saving faith, for the apprehending of Christ, the greatest gift, to all men.

5) To whomsoever the gospel is to be preached by divine will, and the sacraments are to be dispensed, to them God seriously intends to confer saving faith: But to all men &c.

Therefore. The major premise is clear: because the word of God is ῥῆμα τῆς πίστεως, the word of faith, Rom.

X, 8. and the seed of regeneration, 1 Petr. I, 23. Likewise also baptism is the washing of regeneration and renewing, Tit. III, 5. The minor premise is evident from Mark

XVI, 15. Matth. XXVIII, 19. I.

Latin:

Deus omnibus hominibus per ordinaria media saluificam vult conferre fidem.

Prob. 1) Ex diserta assertione S. Paulli Act. XVII, 31. Deus constituit diem, in quo iudicaturus est orbem in iustitia per virum, quem destinauit, fidem offerens omnibus. Τὸ παρέχειν πίστιν notat tum oblationem virium credendi, tum collationem ipsius fidei, modo ne media regenerationis malitiose respuantur. Nam τὸ παρέχειν generatim significat non tantum externam aliquam oblationem, sed etiam realem collationem. Sic Deus dicitur παρέχειν πάντα πλουσίως dare omnia abundanter, 1 Tim. VI, 17. Conf. Luc. XVIII, 5. Act. XXII, 2. Argumentamur: Quicunque omnibus hominibus fistendis coram tribunali Christi fidem offert, is hominibus omnibus fidem vult conferre: Atqui Deus &c. Ergo.

2) Ab indiuidua connexione obtinendi finis & medii, per quod finis attingitur. Sic Paullus connectit voluntatem diuinam, omnes homines saluandi, fideque saluifica omnibus conferendi. Deus vult omnes homines saluari, & ad agnitionem veritatis venire, 1 Tim. II, 4. Qui vult omnes homines venire ad agnitionem veritatis, vt saluentur, ille omnes homines saluifica vult donare fide: Atqui Deus &c. E. Maior probatur: quia agnitio veritatis est fides, & hæc est donum Dei, Eph. II, 8.

3) Ab intentione Dei omnes peccatores conuertendi. Deus quippe non vult quosdam perire, sed omnes ad pœnitentiam conuerti, 2 Petr. III, 9. Qui vult omnes redire ad pœnitentiam, is omnibus vult largiri fidem, quæ pars pœnitentiæ præcipua est.

4) A satisfactione Christi omnibus applicabili. Quibuscunque hominibus Deus destinauit mediatorem Christum, illis vult impertiri fidem: Atqui omnibus hominibus &c.

Maior patet: quia Deus destinando mediatorem, voluit, vt homines in peccatum prolapsi ipsius satisfactionem & meritum vera fide apprehenderent, sibique ad salutem applicarent. Cum autem peccatores naturalibus credendi viribus destituantur, dubio procul Deus ex gratia fidem dabit iis, quibus dedit mediatorem, vt ipsius meritum sibi applicare queant.

Docet hoc Paullus Rom.

VIII, 32. Deus proprio filio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum: quomodo non etiam cum ipso omnia nobis χαρίσεται, i.e. ex gratia donabit? Quibus verbis apostolus innuit, Christum tum pro nobis omnibus in mortem esse traditum, tum nobis omnibus donatum. Ex quibus porro colligit, Deum, vt omnia ad salutem necessaria, ita fidem saluificam, ad apprehendendum Christum, donum maximum, omnibus hominibus daturum esse.

5) Quibus ex voluntate diuina prædicandum est euangelium, & dispensanda sunt sacramenta, illis fidem saluificam conferre Deus serio intendit: Atqui omnibus hominibus &c.

Ergo. Maior liquet: quia verbum Dei est ῥῆμα τῆς πίστεως, verbum fidei, Rom.

X, 8. & semen regenerationis, 1 Petr. I, 23. Sic & baptismus est lauacrum regenerationis & renouationis, Tit. III, 5. Minor patet ex Marc.

XIV, 15. Matth. XXVIII, 19. I.


### Quæst. IX. Does God will to give saving faith to all men?: The following doubts seem to stand against our assertion

The following doubts seem to stand against our assertion.

I. To whomsoever God wills to give faith by an efficacious will, they believe: But not all men believe: Therefore God does not will to give faith to all by an efficacious will.

Resp. To those to whom God wills to give faith by an absolute will, through absolute and irresistible power, they necessarily believe; I concede this.

But God wills to endow men with faith through ordained power and the ordinary means of grace, instituted by Himself, which many reject, or to which they stubbornly resist.

II. II. If many men do not believe for the reason that they reject the means of grace, or resist them, faith will depend on the free will of man: The consequent is false; because faith is a gift of God: Therefore.

The consequence of the major premise is manifest: because men can reject the means of grace at their own discretion.

Resp. The defect or lack of faith is one thing, faith itself is another.

The defect of faith is remotely from the defect of the powers of free will in spiritual matters, and proximately from the malicious repugnance of man, which, besides daily experience, the Holy Scripture teaches, Acts VII, 51. Matth.

XXIII, 37. and elsewhere throughout.

Faith itself, however, is a gift of God, and efficiently depends entirely on God, but in no way on the natural powers of man: yet the production of faith requires the external use of the means of grace, which pertains to pedagogical actions, concerning which man after the fall has some powers of free will, albeit languid.

III. III. Whoever believes for the reason that they externally use the ordinary means of kindling faith, they efficiently cooperate by their own powers toward the production of their faith: But unregenerate man does not efficiently cooperate toward the production of his faith: Therefore unregenerate men do not believe for the reason that they externally use the ordinary means of kindling faith. The major premise is proven; because by this reasoning the external use of means, which is in the power of man, is held to be the cause of generating faith.

Resp. The external use of the means of grace is not the efficient cause of faith, but only a condition, prerequisite on the part of the subject to be converted, which does not influence the production of faith itself efficiently, just as he who places water on the fire so that it may be heated, or he who removes the shutters so that a room may be illuminated, does not influence the heating or the illumination efficiently.

Nor is that external use a condition by reason of an always salutary outcome, since even reprobate men hear the word of God, when nevertheless they impede its power and efficacy with the thorns of the pleasures and cares of this age, or, offended by persecutions, they fall away, and the glory of this they prefer to the heavenly things of the world. See Christ's parable of the four parts of the field, Matth. XIII, 4. ff. & confer. D. HVLSEMANN's brief enucl. p.335.

IV. If therefore men do not believe because they resist the Holy Spirit who is about to kindle faith, no unregenerate men can be given faith: The consequent is false: Therefore, the antecedent is also false. The consequence of the major is proven from Rom. VIII, 7. The carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God; neither indeed can it be. But in all unregenerate men there is the carnal mind. Response. Distinguish between natural and malicious resistance. The Holy Spirit breaks and restrains the former through prevenient grace: the latter is less in some men, greater and more fierce in others, which often prevents true faith from being kindled in the heart of an unregenerate man.

Instance I. All resistance that opposes the means of grace is malicious. Response. Malicious resistance is here called, in a special sense, that which arises from malice voluntarily contracted, while natural resistance flows from the innate corruption of nature itself.

Instance II. Although malicious resistance is within the power of man: nevertheless, non-malicious resistance is due to divine grace. Response. Just as malicious resistance either opposes the external use of means or internal converting grace: so also non-malicious resistance denotes either the negation of resistance opposed to the external use of means, or the negation of the same opposed to internal converting grace. The former is subject to the powers of free will, the latter is due to divine grace, which takes away the stony heart. Conf. D. MVSEVS in dissertat. de aeterno elect. decreto §. CCLXXXI.

Instance III. God can, by His omnipotence, remove all malicious resistance: and when He does not do this, He Himself is the cause that many persevere in unbelief and do not cease to resist the Holy Spirit. Response. If God wished to kindle faith by absolute and irresistible power, He could certainly remove all stubbornness. But since it has pleased Him to deal with us as with men, not as with brutes or stones: therefore He ordains means by which He wills to work faith in the hearts of men: and he who neglects these is not converted, nor is he imbued with true faith. Yet, the blame is not therefore to be attributed to the most holy God, that men remain without faith, because He does not remove malicious resistance, which is an impediment to the generation of faith: for it is not immediately true that he who can remove an impediment, and does not remove it, is the cause of the impeded effect; but he is only then to be considered the cause if he is also bound to prevent or remove the impediment. But by what right is God obligated to remove malicious resistance from those who obstinately resist the means of grace, or to infuse faith into those who stubbornly resist?

V. True faith in Christ seems to be so peculiar to the elect alone, that God is unwilling to bestow faith on the reprobate out of mere good pleasure. As many as were ordained to eternal life believed. Act. XIII, 48. Response. Those who believed in the passage cited are not called πεπροωμένοι, predestined, nor προτεταγμένοι, preordained, but τεταγμένοι, ordained. This word indicates divine order; because God does not act by absolute grace in the matter of salvation: but has prescribed a certain τάξιν of means, which those who do not exclude, but admit, namely by hearing the word, not stopping their ears and hearts to it, not resisting the Holy Spirit who wills to work through it, these are τεταγμένοι. Nor indeed do we affirm that they are τεταγμένοι by themselves, but rather this belongs to divine grace working through the word, by which alone we are made τεταγμένοι καὶ εὐθετοι εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῦ Θεῦ, as Luke says in c. IX, 62.; while we leave room for it, and do not repudiate the τάξιν of divine means, but observe it, which pertains to pedagogical acts, nor is it denied to be so far within our powers. And thus the τεταγμένοι are distinguished from the ἀτάκτοις, or refractory, who repel the word of God, and judge themselves unworthy of eternal life. Act. XIII, 46.

Objection: Christ says explicitly: You do not believe, because you are not of my sheep, John 10:26. Therefore, election, or reprobation, is the cause of unbelief, not the latter of the former. Resp. The particle, ὅτι, here is not αἰτιολογικὴ, causal, but συλλογιστικὴ, or ratiocinative, by which the antecedent is gathered from the consequent, through a demonstration a posteriori. For in the order of nature, it is prior that we conceive faith from hearing the voice of Christ the shepherd, than that we are spiritual sheep; since we, by nature wolves, are finally tamed by hearing the voice of the shepherd, and are as it were transformed into the sheep of Christ.

VI. He who willed to hide the mysteries of faith and salvation from the wise of this world, he does not will to grant faith efficaciously to each one to whom the word is preached: But God, etc. Therefore. The major is evident: because in those the light of faith cannot be kindled, to whom the mysteries of faith and salvation remain hidden. The minor is proved from Matt. 11:25. I confess to thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that thou hast hidden these things from the wise and understanding: Certainly, Father, because so it was well-pleasing before thee. Resp. The discourse in the cited place by Christ is concerning the ministerial gifts, conferred by the heavenly Father upon his disciples, but denied to the scribes and Pharisees: and not concerning the occultation of the mysteries of faith, which are necessary to be known for salvation. For that, concerning which Christ gives thanks to the heavenly Father, and which he referred to the Father’s εὐδοκίαν, or good pleasure, was not that he did not will to work faith in all through his grace; but that he employed νηπίοις, infants, i.e., rude, unlearned, and vile men for the arduous duty of teaching, and revealed to them those things which were necessary for them to fulfill the duty of teaching; and on the contrary hid them from the wise and understanding, i.e., from the scribes and Pharisees, who, puffed up with wisdom, wished to be teachers of others. For Christ had first sent twelve disciples, rude and unlearned fishermen, to whom he had added seventy other disciples, likewise ignorant of letters, who, when they had returned, saying with joy: Lord, even the demons are subject to us through thy name, Luke 10:21. Christ in that very hour rejoiced in spirit, and said: I confess to thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that thou hast hidden such things from the wise and understanding, and hast revealed them to infants. Yea Father: because so it was well-pleasing before thee. Which good pleasure of God the Father is not absolute, but respective: for the heavenly Father regarded the pride of the Pharisees, who rejected the counsel of God against themselves, Luke 7:30.

Latin:

Assertioni nostræ sequentia obstare videntur dubia.

I. Quibuscunque Deus voluntate efficaci vult dare fidem, illi credunt: At non omnes homines credunt: Ergo Deus voluntate efficaci non vult omnibus dare fidem.

Resp. Quibus Deus vult dare fidem voluntate absoluta, per potentiam absolutam & irresistibilem, illi necessario credunt; concedo.

At Deus vult homines donare fide per potentiam ordinatam & ordinaria media gratiæ, a se instituta, quæ multi reiiciunt, aut iisdem pertinaciter resistunt.

II. II. Si ideo multi homines non credunt, quia media gratiæ reiiciunt, aut iis resistunt, fides pendebit a libero hominis arbitrio: Consequens est falsum; quia fides est donum Dei: Ergo.

Consequentia maioris est manifesta: quia homines pro arbitratu suo media gratiæ reiicere possunt.

Resp. Aliud est defectus vel carentia fidei, aliud ipsa fides.

Defectus fidei remote est a defectu virium liberi arbitrii in spiritualibus, proxime a malitiosa hominis repugnantia, quod præter quotidianam experientiam, docet sacra scriptura, Act. VII, 51. Matth.

XXIII, 37. & alibi passim.

Fides ipsa autem est donum Dei, & efficienter tota dependet a Deo, nullatenus autem a naturalibus hominis viribus: prærequirit tamen productio fidei externum mediorum gratiæ vsum, qui ad actiones pertinet pædagogicas, circa quas homo post lapsum aliquas vires liberi arbitrii, quamuis languidas, habet.

III. III. Quicunque ideo credunt, quod ordinariis accendendæ fidei mediis externe vntuntur, illi propriis viribus efficienter cooperantur ad fidei suæ productionem: At homo irregenitus ad fidei suæ productionem efficienter non cooperatur: Ergo homines irregeniti non ideo credunt, quod ordinariis accendendæ fidei mediis externe vntuntur. Maior probatur; quia hac ratione externus mediorum vsus, qui in hominis potestate est, habetur caussa fidei generandæ.

Resp. Externus mediorum gratiæ vsus non est caussa efficiens fidei, sed tantum conditio, ex parte subiecti conuertendi prærequisita, quæ tam in ipsam fidei productionem non efficienter influit, quam non efficienter influit ad calefactionem, qui aquam igni, vt calefiat, apponit, aut in illuminationem conclauis, qui valuas, vt illuminari queat, remouet.

Neque externus ille vsus, est conditio ratione euentus semper salutaris, cum etiam homines reprobi audiant verbum Dei, cum tamen spinis voluptatum & curarum huius sæculi eius vim & efficaciam impediunt, vel persecutionibus offensi deficiunt, & gloriam huius mundi cœlestibus anteponunt. Vide parabolam Christi de quadruplici parte agri, Matth. XIII, 4. feqq. & confer. D. HVLSEMANNI breu. enucl. p.335.

IV. Si ideo homines non credunt, quia Spiritui S. fidem accenfuro restitunt, nulli homines irregeniti fide donari poffunt: Confequens est falfum: E. & antecedens. Confequentia maioris probatur ex Rom. IIX, 7. Senfus carnis est inimicitia aduerfus Deum: legi enim Dei non fubijcit fe; neque enim potest. At in omnibus irregenitis est sensus carnis. Resp. Dist. inter resistentiam naturalem, & malitiosam. Illam Spiritus S. per gratiam prævenientem frangit & refrenat: hæc in aliis hominibus minor, in aliis maior & ferocior est, quæ sæpe impedit, quo minus vera fides in corde hominis irregeniti accendatur.

Instantia I. Omnis resistentia, mediis gratiæ fe opponens, est malitiosa. Resp. Malitiosa resistentia speciali sensu hic dicitur, quæ provenit ex malitia sponte contracta, naturalis autem resistentia fluit ex ipsa naturæ corruptione connata.

Instant. II. Quamuis resistentia malitiosa fit in potestate hominis: non-resistentia tamen malitiosa debetur gratiæ diuinæ. Resp. Sicut resistentia malitiosa vel opponitur externo mediorum vfui, vel gratiæ conuersionis internæ: ita & non-resistentia malitiosa denotat vel negationem resistentiæ, externo mediorum vfui oppofitæ, vel negationem eiusdem, gratiæ conversionis internæ oppofitæ. Illa viribus arbitrii subest, hæc gratiæ diuinæ, cor lapideum auferenti, debetur. Conf. D. MVSEVS in differtat. de æterno elect. decreto §. CCLXXXI.

Instant. III. Deus omnipotentia sua omnem malitiosam resistentiam tollere potest: quod dum non facit, ipse in caussa est, quod multi in incredulitate perfeuerent, nec Spiritui S. repugnare definant. Resp. Si Deus per potentiam abfolutam & irrefistibilem, fidem accendere vellet, vtique omnem contumaciam tollere posset. At cum ipsi placuerit nobiscum agere, tanquam cum hominibus, non tanquam cum brutis aut lapidibus: ideo ordinat media, per quæ fidem in cordibus hominum vult operari: quæ qui negligit, non conuertitur, neque vera fide imbuitur. Neque tamen ideo tribuenda est culpa Deo sanctissimo, quod homines fidei expertes manent, quia malitiosam repugnantiam, quæ est impedimentum generandæ fidei, non tollit: propterea, quod non statim, qui potest impedimentum tollere, nec tollit, caussa est impediti effectus; sed tunc demum pro caussa is habendus est, fi etiam teneatur impedire, vel impedimentum tollere. Deus autem quo iure obligatus tenetur, vt iis, qui mediis gratiæ obstinate resistunt, malitiosam repugnantiam adimat, vel fidem morose reluctantibus infundat?

V. Vera in Christum fides videtur folis electis adeo propria esse, vt Deus reprobis ex mero beneplacito fidem conferre nolit. Crediderunt, quotquot erant ordinati ad vitam æternam. Act. XIII, 48. Resp. Credentes l. c. non dicuntur πεπροωμένοι, prædestinati, neque προτεταγμένοι, præordinati, sed τεταγμένοι, ordinati. Quæ vox indigitat ordinem diuinum; quia Deus non abfoluta agit gratia in negotio salutis: sed certam τάξιν mediorum præscriptit, quam qui non excludunt, sed admittunt, verbum nempe audiendo, ad illud aures & corda non obturando, Spiritui S. per illud operari volenti non resistendo, illi reταγμένοι sunt. Neque vero aff:rimus, quod a fe ipfis sint τεταγμένοι, quin potius diuinæ gratiæ per verbum operanti hoc conuenit, qua sola nos reddimur τεταγμένοι καὶ εὐθετοι εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῦ Θεῦ, vt Lucas loquitur c. IX, 62.; dum ei locum relinquimus, & τάξιν mediorum diuinorum non repudiamos, sed obferuamus, quod ad actus padagogicos pertinet, & in nostris adeo viribus esse non negatur. Et distinguuntur ita τεταγμένοι ab ἀτάκτοις, siue refractariis, qui verbum Dei repellunt, & feipfos indignos iudicant vita æterna. Act. XIII, 46.

Instantia: Christus diserte dicit: Vos non creditis, quia non estis ex ovibus meis, Io. X, 26. Ergo non electio, sive reprobatio, est causa incredulitatis, non hæc illius. Resp. Particula, ὅτι, hic non est αἰτιολογικὴ, causalis, sed συλλογιστικὴ, sive ratiocinativa, qua ex consequente colligitur antecedens, per demonstrationem a posteriori. Ordine naturæ quippe prius est, ex auditu vocis pastoris Christi nos fidem concipere, quam oves esse spirituales; cum nos, natura lupi, audiendo vocem pastoris demum mansuefcamus, & in oves Christi quasi transformemur.

VI. Qui sapientibus huius mundi mysteria fidei & salutis abscondere voluit, is non vult singulis, quibus verbum prædicatur, fidem efficaciter donare: At Deus &c. Ergo. Maior patet: quia in illis lux fidei accendi nequit, quibus mysteria fidei & salutis abscondita manent. Minor probatur ex Matth. XI, 25. Confiteor tibi, Pater, domine cœli & terræ, quod abscondisti hæc sapientibus & intelligentibus: Certo, Pater, quia sic beneplacitum factum est coram te. Resp. Sermo est l. c. Christo de donis ministrantibus, discipulis suis a patre cœlesti collatis, scribis autem & pharisæis denegatis: non vero de occultatione mysteriorum fidei, ad salutem cognitu necessariorum. Id enim, de quo Patri cœlesti Christus agit gratias, quodque in Patris εὐδοκίαν, sive beneplacitum retulit, non erat, quod non in omnibus fidem per gratiam suam operari velit; sed quod νηπίοις, infantes, h. e. rudes, indoctos & viles homines adhibuerit ad arduum docendi munus, iisque revelauerit, quæ ad munus docendi obeundum ipsis necessaria erant; & contra a sapientibus & intelligentibus, h. e. a scribis & pharisæis, qui sapientia inflati aliorum doctores esse volebant, ea absconderit. Miserat enim Christus primum duodecim discipulos, piscatores rudes & idiotas, quibus addiderat alios septuaginta discipulos, itidem litterarum ignaros, qui, ubi reversi fuerant, cum gaudio dicentes: Domine, etiam dæmonia subiiciuntur nobis per nomen tuum, Luc. X, 21. Christus ea ipsa hora exultauit spiritu, dixitque: Confiteor tibi, Pater, domine cœli & terræ, quod occultasti talia a sapientibus & intelligentibus, revelasti autem ea infantibus. Næ Pater: quia ita fuit beneplacitum coram te. Quod beneplacitum Dei patris non est absolutum, sed respectiuum: respexit enim pater cœlestis superbiam pharisæorum, qui consilium Dei aduersus seipsos spreuerunt, Luc. VII, 30.


### Q. X. What salutary use does the doctrine of the universal grace of God confer upon us?

The doctrine of the universal benevolence of God most efficaciously raises up and comforts the sinner, tempted concerning his own election and salvation , and moves us to render immortal thanks to God who is propitious, because he has deigned to embrace us most miserable sinners with his mercy .

Prob. a. A sinner terrified by the magnitude of his crimes can salutarily apply to himself the promise of universal divine grace, and raise up his mind struggling with despair, by concluding with the following reasoning: God wills to embrace all sinners with his grace, he wills all to be saved. Therefore he deigns to embrace even me, a miserable one, with his mercy, he wills even me to be saved. Hence he further concludes: If God wills me to be saved out of unmerited grace; I will not despond, but will place firm confidence in his mercy. If grace were particular, the sinner could not conclude thus, since it does not follow: God wills some to be saved: Therefore he wills me also to be saved.

Prob. b. We celebrate the universal grace of God with the Psalmist, from Ps. 57:10, 11. I will confess to thee among the nations, Adonai, I will sing to thee among the peoples: Because thy mercy is great even to the heaven, and thy truth even to the ether.
