The heaven is extended most widely, and in its circuit it is extended most wide and surrounds all men with its own: the mercy of God extends more widely and comprehends all sinners.

This is what the same [men] rightly and deservedly acknowledge with a grateful mind, and fully praise with their mouth God, who forgives all iniquity, Ps. 103:3. Q. XI. How are those to be treated who abuse the amplitude of divine grace for carnal security? It must be seriously impressed upon them that the universal grace of God invites us not to the lasciviousness or security of the flesh, but to repentance ): Neither is God only a merciful father, but also a just avenger of crimes ).

Prob. a. St. Paul says gravely: Do you despise the riches of the goodness and patience and long-suffering of God? Do you not know that the goodness of God leads you to repentance? But thus, according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are treasuring up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath and of the just judgment of God?

Rom. 2:4-5. And Tit. 2:11, The grace of God that brings salvation has appeared to all men, teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly in the present age.

Prob. b. Do not say: the compassion of God is great, it will reconcile the multitude of my sins; for mercy and wrath are with him, and his fury rests upon sinners, as Sirach says, ch.

5:6. SIGH. This one thing supports and comforts my sick soul, struggling with various temptations concerning my election and salvation, that your grace, O most merciful Father, extends itself even to the greatest and most foul sinners, for whom your Son, the catholic redeemer of the human race, did not hesitate to shed his most precious blood and to undergo a most bitter death.

I do not draw a veil over my crimes: I do not deny that they are very many in number and most heavy in weight. But if you should wish to deal with me according to the rigor of justice, my salvation is at an end. But as a suppliant I implore your clemency, O my God, and I seek forgiveness for my crimes, on account of the wounds of Christ. Do not withdraw, O most mild Father, your grace from me: let the bowels of your mercy be open, I pray, to me, who detest my sins. With the cords of your kindness and love, draw me to repentance, [which I am] lacking: make me a possessor and holder of true and living faith. As long as breath remains in me here, I shall be an estimator of the inexhaustible riches of your goodness, and I shall most joyfully proclaim them.

Latin:

Doctrina de vniversali Dei beneuolentia peccatorem, tentatum de sui electione & salute, efficacissime erigit & solatur , & mouet nos ad agendum immortales Deo propitio gratias, quod nos miserrimos peccatores misericordia sua complecti dignatus est .

Prob. a. Peccator magnitudine criminum suorum perterritus promissionem gratiæ diuinæ vniversalis sibi salutariter applicare, & animum cum desperatione luctantem erigere potest, sequenti ratione colligendo: Deus omnes peccatores gratia sua vult complecti, vult omnes saluos fieri. Ergo etiam me miserum sua dignatur misericordia, vult etiam me saluum fieri. Hinc porro colligit: Si Deus me vult saluum fieri ex gratia indebita; non despondebo animum, sed validam in misericordia eius fiduciam collocabo. Si particularis esset gratia, non posset peccator ita concludere, cum non sequatur: Deus aliquos vult saluos fieri: Ergo me etiam vult saluum fieri.

Prob. b. Gratiam Dei vniversalem concelebramus cum hieropfalte, ex Ps. LVII, 10. 11. Confitebor tibi inter gentes, Adonai, psallam tibi inter populos: Quia magna est vsque ad cœlum misericordia tua, & vsque ad ætherem veritas tua. Cœlum latissime extenditur, ambituque latiffime extenditur, ambituque latiffime extenditur, ambituque suo omnes circumdat homines: latius extenditur misericordia Dei omnesque comprehendit peccatores.

Id quod iidem iure meritoque grato agnoscunt animo, pleneque collaudant ore Deum, omnem iniquitatem condonantem, Ps. CIII, 3. Quæst. XI. Quomodo tractandi sunt illi, qui gratiæ divinæ amplitudine ad carnalem securitatem abutuntur? Iisdem serio inculcandum est, gratiam Dei universalem non ad carnis lasciviam aut securitatem, sed ad pœnitentiam nos invitare ): Neque Deum tantum esse misericordem patrem, sed & iustum scelerum vindicem ).

Prob. a. Graviter inquit S. Paullus: An divitias bonitatis & patientiæ & longanimitatis Dei contemnis? Ignoras, quod bonitas Dei ad pœnitentiam te ducit? Atqui sic iuxta duritiem tuam & impœnitens cor thesaurizas tibi ipsi iram in die iræ & iusti iudicii Dei?

Rom. II, 4. 5. & Tit. II, 11, Apparuit gratia Dei salutaris omnibus hominibus, erudiens nos, ut abnegemus impietatem & mundanas concupiscentias, ac sobrie, & iuste, & pie vivamus in præsenti sæculo.

Prob. b. Ne dicas: miseratio Dei est multa, multitudinem peccatorum meorum reconciliabit; misericordia enim & ira apud ipsum est, & super peccatoribus requiescit furor eius, dicente Siracide c.

V, 6. SVSPIRIVM. Hoc unum animum meum ægrum, variisque cum tentationibus de mea electione & salute conflictantem fulcit & solatur, quod gratia tua, o Pater misericordissime, etiam ad maximos fœdissimosque se extendat peccatores, pro quibus filius tuus, redemptor generis humani catholicus, sanguinem suum pretiosissimum fundere, mortemque acerbissimam subire haud dubitavit.

Non obduco velum criminibus meis: non diffiteor, ea & numero esse plurima, & pondere gravissima. Quodsi ex rigore iustitiæ mecum agere velis, actum est de salute mea. At supplex imploro tuam, o Deus mi, clementiam, petoque criminum veniam, propter vulnera Christi. Ne subtrahas, o Pater mitissime, mihi gratiam tuam: pateant, quæso, viscera misericordiæ tuæ mihi, peccata mea detestanti. Benignitatis & amoris tui funiculis trahe me ad pœnitentiam tuci expertem: veræ vitæque fidei me fac compotem atque tenacem. Quamdiu hic mihi supererit spiritus, inexhaustas divitias bonitatis tuæ & maximi sum æstimaturus, & lætissime prædicaturus.


## 17 On the Special Benevolence of God, and Predestination


### Concerning the Special Benevolence of God and the Predestination of Those Finally Believing Unto Eternal Life

Q. I. What is predestination? Definition of predestination. Predestination is the eternal decree of God concerning the conferring of eternal salvation upon all and singular men, whom God foresaw would finally believe in Christ.

It is defined more fully: Predestination is an act of the consequent divine will, by which God, moved by gratuitous mercy, on account of the merit of Christ, to be apprehended by persevering faith, from the fallen human race, [chooses] those only and singular men, whom in Christ he foresaw would finally believe, he segregated, and ordained to obtain eternal salvation, to the praise of his glorious grace. Obf.

I. The decree of God is defined generally as being an act of the divine will, by which, with most wise counsel and most free authority, he determines concerning those things which happen or ought to happen for his glory . Therefore it is the same whether predestination is described by the decree of God or by the act of the divine will. Moreover, this is an act of the divine consequent will; for this reason, because it follows faith in man foreseen, or prior in order, in our mode of conceiving. From which it follows that predestination, just as the consequent will itself, is not universal in respect of the object, but particular. Obf.

II. Predestination, derived from the verb praedestino, is called as it were a certain prior destination; because it is a destination that is eternal and precedes all time. In Greek it is called προορισμός, from προορίζειν, which signifies both the end and the means leading to the end, to ordain and to constitute; for ὅρος denotes an end and a limit. Ὁρίζειν, however, is more often the same as to decree, to determine in mind, and to ordain. Therefore, predestination is an act by which something is predetermined or preordained. The particle prae in the word praedestinatio denotes the priority of time which intervenes between the decree of predestination and the men who are called predestined; and thus προορισμός, or divine predestination, is the destination of men, before they themselves existed, to obtain eternal salvation through means ordained by God. Quaest.

Latin:

Quæst. I. Quid est prædestinatio? Definitio prædestinationis. Prædestinatio est æternum Dei decretum de conferenda salute æterna omnibus & singulis hominibus, quos Deus in Christum finaliter credituros esse prævidit.

Vberius definitur: Prædestinatio est actus voluntatis divinæ consequentis, quo Deus, gratuita motus misericordia, propter meritum Christi, perseveranti fide apprehendendum, ex genere humano lapso solos & singulos illos homines, quos in Christum finaliter credituros esse praevidit, segregauit, & ordinauit ad salutem aeternam consequendam, in laudem gloriosae suae gratiae.

Obs. I. Decretum Dei generatim definitur, quod sit actus diuinae voluntatis, quo sapientissimo consilio, liberrimaque auctoritate constituit de iis, quae fiunt, aut fieri debent ad gloriam suam . Idcirco perinde est, siue per decretum Dei, siue per actum voluntatis diuinae describatur praedestinatio. Caeterum haec est actus voluntatis diuinae consequentis; propterea, quod fidem in homine prauisam, seu ordine priorem, nostro concipiendi modo subsequitur. Ex quo consequitur, praedestinationem, perinde, ac ipsam voluntatem consequentem, ratione obiecti non esse vniuersalem, sed particularem.

Obs. II. Praedestinatio, a verbo, praedestino, deducta, dicitur quasi praeuia quaedam destinatio; quia est aeterna & omne tempus antecedens destinatio. Graecis vocatur προορισμός, ἀπὸ τοῦ προορίζειν, quod significat & finem, & media, ad finem ducentia, ordinare & constituere; ὅρος enim finem ac terminum notat. Ὁρίζειν autem saepius idem est, quod decernere, animo constituere & ordinare. Ergo praedestinatio est actus, quo aliquid praedecernitur, vel praeordinatur. Particula, prae, in voce, praedestinatio, notat prioritatem temporis, quae intercedit inter decretum praedestinationis, & inter homines, qui dicuntur praedestinati; adeoque προορισμός, siue praedestinatio diuina, est destinatio hominum, antequam ipsi exstiterent, ad aeternam salutem per diuinitus ordinata media obtinendam.


### II. How is predestination otherwise called?

Predestination is also called election ; which two words agree materially and by reason of the subject a), but differ in the mode of signifying, or in respect of formal signification b). It is also called an inscription in the book of life, which is said of God ἀνθρωποπαθῶς, in a human manner, but is to be understood θεοπρεπῶς, in a more eminent manner, befitting the omniscient God c).

Prob. a. Predestination and election agree by reason of the subject; in that no one is predestined to eternal salvation who is not made elected to it, nor is any one elected who is not made predestined.

Prob. b. Predestination and election differ in respect of formal signification. Election in its formal concept looks to the objects to be chosen, but predestination looks to the end and the order of the means which lead to the end of election or eternal life. For the particle prae in the word praedestinatio connotes the priority and eternity of the divine ordination; but the particle e in the word electio connotes the common assembly of men and that by which the segregation of certain men is made, and thus divine election is the segregation of certain men from the common mass of corruption, and an adoption to the inheritance of eternal salvation *). Observe furthermore, that προορισμὸς, or predestination, strictly so called, 1) presupposes προγνωσιν, the foreknowledge of certain persons, finally believing, Rom.

VIII, 29. Whom he foreknew, he also predestinated; 2) formally denotes the ordination of those men, who admit the means of grace according to divine foreknowledge and constantly observe them, unto eternal life, Act.

XIII, 48. Election however 1) presupposes the love of God, Eph.

I, 6. 2) formally denotes the segregation of those men, whom he foresaw would persevere in believing in Christ, from the common mass of perdition.

You are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hates you, Io.

XV, 19. Prob. c.

Paul makes mention of the book of life, Phil.

IV, 3. Whose names are in the book of life, & Ioann.

Apoc. III, 5. He that overcomes, shall be clothed in white garments, and I will not blot his name out of the book of life.

It is also called the book of life of the lamb, Apoc.

XIII, 8. The inscription into the book of life is commemorated in Apoc.

XVII, 8. c. XXII, 19. Elsewhere it is simply called the writing in the book, Dan.

XII, 1. Exod. XXXII, 32. Truly by a certain ἀνθρωποπάθειαν & συγκατάβασιν, according to the likeness of a human act, by which the names of certain persons are inscribed in a catalogue of citizens, families, or soldiers: so God has inserted into the catalogue of the saved those whom he chose out of mere grace on account of the merit of Christ to be apprehended by persevering faith, and thus foreseen, before the foundations of the world were laid.

For as a book, attributed to God in a general sense, denotes God's foreknowledge and providence, by which he knows, disposes, and governs the origin, life, actions, and end of life of all men; so the book of life in particular is nothing else than the singular knowledge of the saved and, according to προγνωσιν, the election of the same, 2 Tim.

II, 19. This book of life is compared by D.

DANNHAV. in hodof phanom. VII. p. 542. with a testamentary book, and is explained by the same as being a certain, accurate, & living knowledge of God concerning his own; knowledge, namely, a) προγνωστικὴ, the science of vision, by which God from all eternity saw as in a mirror who from the corrupt mass would be his own, and who the devil's; and it is 1) eternal Eph.

I, 4. 2) intimate & καρδιογνωσικὴ; for those who are true & living members of the church, their judgment cannot be other than from the internal renewal of the heart.

Now indeed this knowledge belongs to God alone.

3) Most singular, knowledge namely κατ’ ὄνομα, Io.

X, 3. Exod. XXXIII, 17. Es. XLIII, 2. 4) Infallible and immutable.

And because words of knowledge connote affection, therefore 5) dilective.

He who loves God is known by him, and thus rejoices in his reciprocal love, 1 Cor.

VIII, 3. This love indeed manifests itself in six hundred other ways, but especially in friendly remembrance, paternal commiseration, and gracious approbation, and finally salvation.

For as he will one day say to the reprobate: I do not know you; so to the elect: I know you; and at the same time he will lead them triumphing into glory.

(b) προοριστικὴ, elective.

For election and a certain segregation flow from accurate foreknowledge, love, and peculiar care; which is most especially regarded by the Apostle in 2 Tim. II, 19, is clear from all the circumstances, and thus it is called the book of life, because those who are to live forever by a certain divine lot stand inscribed in it, as if in a catalog of the living, whose names are written in heaven, Luke X, 20.

Furthermore, since this does not refer to natural life, but to spiritual life, and that is twofold, of grace and of glory: therefore some authors distinguish the book of life into the book of grace and of glory. In the book of grace all the faithful are inscribed, in the book of glory all those persevering in faith, and thus certainly to be saved.

Regarding which distinction, the judgment of D. Bayer in compend. theol. p. 673 is worth noting.

The inscription into the book of life is twofold, insofar as men are inscribed by God either precisely into the number of the faithful, or into the number of those certainly to be saved: The former coincides with the decree concerning men to be regenerated, and to be justified, and to be adopted as sons: the latter coincides with the act of election or predestination. Although it must be admitted that, with the term "inscription into the book of life" taken absolutely, it is not so much the former as the latter act that is understood.

Question III. In how many ways is the word election taken? The word election is taken a) generally for temporal election to the church, and to some office to be performed in it; b) specifically for eternal election to glory and eternal life: in which latter signification it is taken here.

Proof a. Moses speaks of temporal election, which occurs through the calling to the church, in Deut. VII, 6: The Lord your God has chosen you, that you might be a peculiar people to him.

The peculiar people of God is a gathering of men, called by God and segregated from infidels, to whom He has communicated the means of grace and salvation for the attainment of righteousness and eternal life: which people of God is commonly called the church.

Hence it happens that those who perform a public office in the church are called elect in a peculiar sense.

Thus Christ addresses his disciples: Have I not chosen you twelve? John VI, 70, where the Savior is speaking of election to the apostolate.

Proof b. The Apostle treats of eternal election in Eph. I, 4: He chose us in Christ before the foundations of the world were laid, i.e., from eternity.

From which we gather that the Apostle here points to the eternal decree of God concerning bestowing eternal salvation upon those who will finally believe: of which eternal decree of election St. Paul also treats in 2 Thess. II, 13: But we ought to give thanks to God always for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, because God chose you from the beginning for salvation in the sanctification of the Spirit and faith of the truth.

That the Apostle is speaking here of election to eternal salvation is clear from this: 1) that he asserts that God chose us from the beginning, i.e., from eternity, as this formula of speaking is used in 1 John II, 13; Micah V, 1. 2) Because election made from the beginning is distinguished from calling in time, v. 14. 3) God is said to have chosen us for salvation: which word, taken absolutely, denotes eternal blessedness.

Question IV. In how many ways is the word predestination taken? The word predestination is taken differently in the ecclesiastical sense, and differently in the biblical sense.

Some fathers and doctors of the church have taken the word predestination ἀκυρως (improperly) and more loosely than is just, for the divine decree concerning both the saving of believing men and the condemning of infidels a).

In the biblical sense, however, the word predestination is always taken in a good sense, to denote the divine decree concerning the saving of fallen men b).

Prob. a. AUGUSTINE lib. XV. de civ. D. c. I. divides the human race into two societies, of which one is destined to reign eternally with God, the other to undergo eternal punishment with the devil. Cf. PROSPER in Resp. XIV. ad capitula Gallorum; FULGENTIUS lib. II. ad Monim. c. XIV. But that locution is improper and not conformable to Holy Scripture, in which προορισμὸς, in Latin predestination, is always taken in a good sense. 2) It is unbecoming to the most holy God. For predestination, besides the end which it regards, also includes the order of means. But the most holy God has destined no one to the means of reprobation, which are the rejection of the divine word and final incredulity. 3) It is absurd. For predestination regards the end of man, and the means of obtaining it effectively. But eternal death, speaking accurately, is not the end of man; although it may be called the extremity of impenitent men. For an end by its nature is good and desirable; but who, being of sound mind, would judge eternal death to be good and desirable? Wisely says AUGUSTINE L. VI. hypognost. God only permits evils, He does not predestine them: but He both foreknows and predestines good things.

You say: Προορισμὸς, or predestination, seems to be taken in a bad sense, Acts IV, 17. 18. They gathered in this city against thy holy Son Jesus, whom thou hast anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the people of Israel, to do whatsoever thy hand and thy counsel προώρισε, predestined to be done. Resp. The reprobation of the impious is not described in that place, but the decree of the passion and death of Christ, which is the external impulsive cause of our election to eternal life. With an evil counsel, indeed, and a wicked attempt, the Jews and Gentiles killed Christ; but God, although He permitted that to be done, nevertheless directed it to a good and salutary end for the whole human race.

Prob. b. That προορισμὸν, or predestination, is always taken in the better sense in the sacred writings and denotes the divine decree concerning the saving of men who have fallen into sin, is clear from the apostolic statement, Rom. VIII, 30. Whom God predestined, them He also called: and whom He called, them He also justified; and whom He justified, them He also glorified. The same is evident from Eph. I, 5. God προώρισε, predestined us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ.

Latin:

Praedestinatio etiam vocatur electio ; qua duae voces conueniunt materialiter & ratione subiecti a), differunt autem modo significandi, siue respectu formalis significationis b). Appellatur quoque inscriptio in librum vitae, quae de Deo dicitur ἀνθρωποπαθῶς, more humano, intelligenda vero est θεοπρεπῶς, modo eminentiori, Deo omniscio conuenienti c).

Prob. a. Praedestinatio & electio conueniunt ratione subiecti; eo, quod nullus est praedestinatus ad aeternam salutem, qui ad eam non fit electus, nec vllus electus, qui non fit praedestinatus.

Prob. b. Praedestinatio, & electio respectu formalis significationis differunt. Electio in suo formali conceptu ad obiecta eligenda, praedestinatio vero ad finem & ordinem mediorum, quae ad electionis finem seu vitam aeternam ducunt, respicit. Etenim particula, prae, in voce, praedestinatio, ordinationis diuinae prioritatem & aeternitatem; particula, e, autem in voce electionis communem hominum coetum, & quo fit segregatio quorundam hominum, connotat, adeoque electio diuina est quorundam hominum e communi corruptionis massa segregatio, & ad hereditatem aeternae salutis adoptatio *). Observes praeterea, quod προορισμὸς, sive praedestinatio, strictissime dicta, 1) praesupponat προγνωσιν, praenotionem certarum personarum, finaliter credentium, Rom.

VIII, 29. Quos praecognovit, etiam praedestinavit; 2) formaliter notet ordinationem eorum hominum, qui media gratiae secundum praenotionem divinam admittunt & constanter observant, ad aeternam vitam, Act.

XIII, 48. Electio autem 1) praesupponit dilectionem Dei, Eph.

I, 6. 2) formaliter notat segregationem eorum hominum, quos in Christum perseveranter credituros esse praevidit, e communi perditionis massa.

Ex mundo non estis, sed ego elegi vos ex mundo, propter hoc vos odit mundus, Io.

XV, 19. Prob. c.

Libri vitae mentionem inicit Paullus, Phil.

IV, 3. Quorum nomina sunt in libro vitae, & Ioann.

Apoc. III, 5. Qui vicerit, hic induetur vestimentis albis, & non delebo nomen eius e libro vitae.

Dicitur etiam liber vitae agni, Apoc.

XIII, 8. Inscriptio in librum vitae Apoc.

XVII, 8. c. XXII, 19. commemoratur. Alias simpliciter scriptio in libro vocatur, Dan.

XII, 1. Exod. XXXII, 32. Nimirum per ἀνθρωποπάθειαν & συγκατάβασιν quandam, secundum similitudinem actus humani, quo certarum personarum nomina catalogo civium, familiarum aut militum adscribuntur: ita Deus catalogo salvandorum inseruit eos, quos ex mera gratia propter meritum Christi fide perseverante apprehendendum, & ita praevisum, ante iacta mundi fundamenta elegit.

Vt enim liber, in genere Deo attributus, notat Dei praescientiam, & providentiam, qua omnium hominum ortum, vitam, actiones, vitaeque exitum novit, disponit & gubernat; sic liber vitae in specie nihil aliud est, quam singularis salvandorum cognitio & iuxta προγνωσιν eorundem electio, 2 Tim.

II, 19. Comparatur hic liber vitae a D.

DANNHAV. in hodof phanom. VII. p. 542. cum libro testamentario, & ab eodem explicatur, quod fit certa, accurata & viva Dei cognitio suorum; cognitio scilicet a) προγνωστικὴ, scientia visionis, qua Deus ab omni aeternitate tanquam in speculo vidit, qui e massa corrupta fui futuri sint, qui diaboli; eaque 1) aeterna Eph.

I, 4. 2) intima & καρδιογνωσικὴ; qui namque vera & viva sunt ecclesiae membra, eorum iudicium non potest esse aliud, quam ex interna cordis renovatione.

Iam vero soli Deo haec notitia convenit.

3) Singularissima, notitia scilicet κατ’ ὄνομα, Io.

X, 3. Exod. XXXIII, 17. Es. XLIII, 2. 4) Infallibilis ac immutabilis.

Et quia verba notitiae affectum connotant, ideo 5) dilectiva.

Qui diligit Deum, is cognitus est ab illo, adeoque reciproco eius amore gaudet, 1 Cor.

VIII, 3. Exserit vero se ista dilectio cum sexcentis modis aliis, tum maxime amica recordatione, paterna commiseratione, & gratiosa approbatione, denique salvatione.

Vt enim olim reprobis dicturus est: Non novi vos; ita electis: novi vos; & simul triumphantes in gloriam inducet.

(b) προοριστικὴ, electiva.

Fluit namque ex praenotione accurata, dilectione & cura peculiari electio & segregatio quaedam; quam potissimum ab Apostolo 2 Tim. II, 19. spectari, ex omnibus circumstantiis liquet, adeoque dicitur liber vitae, quia in aeternum victuri ex forte quadam divina, in eo, tanquam catalogo viventium, consignati exstant, quorum nomina in caelo scripta, Luc. X, 20.

Ceterum cum hic non intelligatur vita naturalis, sed spiritualis, eaque duplex fit gratiae & gloriae: ideo nonnulli auctores librum vitae distinguunt in librum gratiae, & gloriae. Libro gratiae omnes fideles, libro gloriae omnes perseverantes in fide, atque adeo certo saluandi, inscripti sunt.

De qua distinctione notari meretur iudicium D. Bayeri in compend. theol. p. 673.

Inscriptio in librum vitae duplex est, quatenus homines a Deo vel in numerum fidelium praecise, vel in numerum certo saluandorum inscribuntur: Prior cum decreto de hominibus regenerandis, & iustificandis, & in filios adoptandis: posterior cum electionis, aut praedestinationis actu coincidit. Quamuis fatendum sit, termino inscriptionis in librum vitae absolute posito, non tam priorem, quam posteriorem actum intelligi.

Quaest. III. Quot modis sumitur vox electionis? Vox electionis sumitur a) generatim pro electione temporali ad ecclesiam, & ad officium aliquod in ea obeundum; b) speciatim pro electione aeterna ad gloriam, & vitam aeternam: qua posteriore significatione hic accipitur.

Prob. a. De electione temporali, quae fit per vocationem ad ecclesiam, loquitur Moses Deut. VII, 6. Te elegit Dominus, Deus tuus, ut fis ei populus peculiaris.

Populus Dei peculiaris est coetus hominum, a Deo vocatus & segregatus ab infidelibus, cui media gratiae & salutis ad consequendam iustitiam, vitamque aeternam communicavit: qui populus Dei peculiaris communiter vocatur ecclesia.

Inde fit, ut peculiari ratione electi vocentur ii, qui publico in ecclesia munere perfunguntur.

Sic Christus suos affatur discipulos: Nonne ego vos duodecim elegi? Io. VI, 70. vbi sermo est saluatori de electione ad apostolatum.

Prob. b. De electione aeterna agit Apostolus, Eph. I, 4. Elegit nos in Christo ante iacta mundi fundamenta, i. e. ab aeterno.

Ex quo colligimus, Apostolum hic indigitare aeternum Dei decretum de impertienda finaliter credituris aeterna salute: de quo aeterno electionis decreto S. Paullus etiam agit 2 Thess. II, 13. Nos vero debemus gratias agere Deo semper pro vobis, fratres dilecti a Domino, quod elegit vos Deus ab initio ad salutem in sanctificatione Spiritus, & fide veritatis.

Loqui h. l. Apostolum de electione ad salutem aeternam, liquet ex eo 1) quod asserit, Deum nos elegisse ab initio, i. e. ab aeterno, vti haec loquendi formula funnitur 1 Io. II, 13. Mich. V, 1. 2) Quia electio facta ab initio, distinguitur a vocatione in tempore, v. 14. 3) Deus nos elegisse dicitur ad salutem: quae vox, absolute posita, notat aeternam beatitudinem.

Quaest. IV. Quot modis sumitur vox praedestinationis? Vox praedestinationis aliter sumitur in sensu ecclesiastico, aliter in sensu biblico.

Nonnulli patres & doctores ecclesiae ἀκυρως abusiue & iusto laxius vocem praedestinationis sumserunt pro decreto diuino, tum de saluandis hominibus credentibus, tum de condemnandis infidelibus a).

In sensu autem biblico vox praedestinationis semper in bonam partem accipitur, vt denotet decretum diuinum de hominibus lapsis saluandis b).

Prob. a. AVGVSTINVS lib. XV. de civ. D. c. I. genus humanum in duas dispescit societates, quarum fit vna, quæ prædestinata sit in æternum regnare cum Deo, altera, æternum subire supplicium cum diabolo. Conf. PROSPER in Resp. XIV. ad capitula Gallorum; FVL-GENTIVS lib. II. ad Monim. c. XIV. At locutio illa impropria non est S. scripturæ conformis, in qua προορισμὸς, latine prædestinatio, semper in bonam accipitur partem. 2) Est indecora Deo sanctissimo. Prædestinatio enim præter finem, quem respicit, etiam mediorum ordinem includit. Deus autem sanctissimus ad media reprobationis, quæ sunt reiectio verbi diuini & incredulitas finalis, neminem destinauit. 3) Est absurda. Prædestinatio enim respicit finem hominis, media efficacia obtinendum. At mors æterna accurate loquendo non est finis hominis; licet hominum impoenitentium extremum vocari queat. Finis quippe natura sua est bonus & appetibilis; quis autem, sanæ mentis compos, æternam mortem iudicaret esse bonam & appetibilem? Scite inquit AVGVSTIN. L. VI. hypognost. Mala Deus tantum præsit, non prædestinat: bona vero & præscit & prædestinat.

Dicis: Προορισμὸς, siue prædestinatio, videtur in malam partem accipi, Act. IV, 17. 18. Conuenerunt in ciuitate ista contra sanctum Filium tuum Iesum, quem vnxisti, tam Herodes, quam Pontius Pilatus, cum gentibus & populis Israëlis, ad faciendum, quæcunque manus tua & consilium προώρισε, prædestinauit fieri. Resp. Non describitur l. c. impiorum reprobatio, sed decretum passionis & mortis Christi, quæ est electionis nostræ ad vitam æternam caussa impulsiua externa. Malo quidem consilio, auſuque nefario, Iudæi & gentiles Christum occiderunt; at Deus, quamuis illud permiserit fieri, direxit tamen ad bonum, totique generi humano salutarem finem.

Prob. b. Προορισμὸν, siue prædestinationem, in sacris litteris semper fumi in meliorem partem & notare decretum diuinum de saluandis hominibus, in peccatum prolapsis, liquet ex effato apostolico, Rom. VIII, 30. Quos Deus prædestinauit, eos etiam vocauit: & quos vocauit, eos etiam iustificauit; quos vero iustificauit, eos etiam glorificauit. Patet idem ex Eph. I, 5. Deus προώρισε, prædestinauit nos in adoptionem filiorum per Iesum Christum.


### Quæst. V. In how many senses is predestination, taken in a good sense, expounded by orthodox theologians?

Predestination, with Holy Scripture shining as a light, when taken in a good sense, insofar as it is the decree of God concerning the saving of sinful men, is expounded by orthodox theologians in a triple sense: a) general, or broader, insofar as it embraces the universal economy of salvation, or the whole apparatus of the means of salvation: b) In a special, or stricter sense, as it signifies the ordination of the faithful to salvation, complicated with προθέσει and προγνώσει: c) In a most special and strictest sense, by which προορισμὸς, or predestination, is distinguished from προθέσει and προγνώσει, and denotes the eternal decree of God, determined, or applied to certain individuals of men, whom God chose from the common mass of corruption to eternal life, because He distinctly foresaw that they would finally believe in Christ.

To recognize the decree of predestination, insofar as, taken in a broader sense, it denotes the universal economy of salvation, or the whole ordination of those to be saved unto salvation, including all causes and all means of salvation, the order of the divine acts must be diligently observed, as they follow one another in the sign of reason, according to divine revelation: tur: what order of divine decrees is presented for our consideration in the Declaratio solida of the Formula of Concord, p. 802. God in His counsel and purpose has decreed:

I. That the human race should be truly redeemed, and reconciled with God through Christ; who merited for us innocence and most perfect obedience, by His most bitter passion and death, the righteousness which avails before Him, and eternal life.

II. That the merit of Christ, and His benefits, should be offered, exhibited, and distributed to us through the Word and Sacraments.

III. He also decreed that He wills to be efficacious in us by His Holy Spirit, through the Word announced, perceived by hearing, and commended to memory, and to incline hearts to perform true repentance, and to preserve them in true faith.

IV. It is His eternal purpose that He wills to justify, receive into favor, and adopt as sons and heirs of eternal life, all who truly perform repentance and embrace Christ with true faith.

V. And that He wills to sanctify those justified by faith in true charity; as the Apostle testifies, Eph.

1:4.

VI. The same He proposed in His eternal counsel, that He would defend those justified, even in their manifold and various infirmity, against the devil, the world, and the flesh, and would lead and govern them in His ways; and, if they should have fallen, would put forth His hand, so that in the cross and temptations they might perceive solid consolation, and be preserved unto life.

VII. It is His eternal decree that He wills to promote, confirm, and preserve unto the end that good work begun by Him in them: provided only that they constantly lean upon His Word, as upon a staff, implore His aid with ardent prayers, persevere in the grace of God, and faithfully and well employ the gifts received.

VIII. He also decreed in His eternal counsel that He wills to save, and adorn with eternal glory, in the other eternal life, those whom He has chosen, called, and justified.

And indeed, God in that counsel, purpose, and ordination of His, did not only procure the salvation of His own in a general way: but He also graciously foreknew all and singular the persons of the elect (who are to be saved through Christ), chose them unto salvation, and decreed that in that way (which we have now recited) He wills to make them partakers of eternal salvation, to help them, to promote their salvation, and to confirm and preserve them, through His grace, gifts, and efficacy.

All these things, according to Scripture, are comprehended in the article of predestination and the eternal divine election unto adoption as sons and unto eternal salvation.

With these things from the Formula of Concord adduced and set forth, predestination taken in a wider sense can be defined as: the eternal divine decree by which God, out of His immense mercy, determined to give His Son as mediator to all men whom He foresaw from eternity would fall into sin, and to offer Him to be embraced through universal preaching, to confer faith through the Word and Sacraments upon all who would not resist, to justify all believers, and to renew those continuing to use the means of grace, to preserve faith in them until the end of life, and finally to save the believers themselves.

Obs. Some Fathers and Theologians have not hesitated to assert that faith in Christ is the effect of election, and that predestination constitutes the end and ordains the means, and that we would have believed because we were elect. They take the term predestination and election in this looser sense, for the entire ordination of those to be saved unto salvation; which, as it embraces all the principles and means of salvation, so it takes the eternal purpose of God concerning faith in Christ, through the Word and Sacraments, as predestination and election they take in this looser sense, for the entire ordination of those to be saved unto salvation; which, as it embraces all the principles and means of salvation, so it takes the eternal purpose of God concerning faith in Christ, through the Word and Sacra-

in all who do not obstinately and stubbornly resist, it includes the bringing about. See D. MUSAEUS, dissertation on the eternal decree of predestination, p. 206. Prob. b. Predestination taken in a stricter sense comprises both the πρόθεσιν, i.e., the general and indeterminate divine decree concerning the imparting of eternal salvation to all sinful men who will finally believe in Christ, and the πρόγνωσιν, i.e., the foreknowledge of certain persons, or human individuals, who will retain true faith in Christ until the very last breath of life.

In this stricter sense, taken as predestination, persevering faith in Christ enters not as a meritorious cause, on account of which God elects us, but as an instrumental one, because it apprehends the grace of the electing God and the merit of Christ, as AEGID. HUNNIUS says in his treatise on providence and predestination, fol. 826. From which some theologians also call faith in Christ a part of the order of predestination. Conf. D. GERHARD, isagogic disputations, p. 723, and D. MEISNER, anthropology, decade II, p. 153. D. DANNHAV. hodof. phenom. VII, p. 578. Prob. c. Predestination taken in the strictest sense, as it is the eternal decree of God applied to certain human individuals (Abraham, Peter, etc.), presupposes the πρόθεσιν, or the indeterminate decree concerning the saving of men who will finally believe, and the πρόγνωσιν, or the foreknowledge of faith in Christ, as prior in order; and thus faith is neither a part of that, but a less principal impulsive reason, which God the elector regarded most graciously.

Election indeed precedes faith in terms of actual existence, but according to known being, faith precedes election in the sign of reason. See D. MUSAEUS, dissertation on the eternal decree of predestination, p. 209.

Latin:

Prædestinatio, prælucente sacra scriptura, in bonam partem accepta, quatenus est decretum Dei de hominibus peccatoribus saluandis, a theologis orthodoxis triplici exponitur sensu: a) generali, seu latiori, quatenus vniuersam salutis oeconomiam, feu totum mediorum salutis apparatum complectitur: b) Sensu speciali, siue strictiori, prout significat ordinationem fidelium ad salutem, cum προθέσει & προγνώσει complicatam: c) Sensu specialissimo & strictissimo, quo προορισμὸς, siue prædestinatio, a προθέσει & προγνώσει distinguitur, & notat æternum Dei decretum, determinatum, siue applicatum ad quosdam secundum individua homines, quos Deus ex communi corruptionis massa ad vitam æternam elegit, propterea, quod illos in Christum finaliter credituros esse, distincte præuidit.

Prob. a. Ad agnoscendum decretum prædestinationis, quatenus, sensu latiori sumtum, vniuersam salutis oeconomiam, siue totam saluandorum ordinationem ad salutem, omnes caussas, omniaque media salutis includentein, denotat, diligenter obseruandus est ordo actuum diuinorum, prout in signe rationis, iuxta reuelationem diuinam, alii alios sequuntur: tur: qui ordo decretorum divinorum nobis considerandus exhibetur in Declarat. solid. Form. Concord. p. 802. Deus in consilio et proposito suo decrevit:

I. Vt humanum genus vere redimeretur, atque cum Deo per Christum reconciliaretur; qui nobis innocentiam atque perfectissimam obedientiam, passione ac morte acerbissima, justitiam, quae coram ipso valet, et vitam aeternam promeruit.

II. Vt Christi meritum, eiusque beneficia per verbum et sacramenta nobis offerrentur, exhiberentur et distribuerentur.

III. Decrevit etiam, se Spiritu S. suo, per verbum annuntiatum, auditione perceptum, et memoriae commendatum, velle in nobis efficacem esse, et corda ad veram poenitentiam agendam inflectere, et vera fide conferuare.

IV. Illius aeternum propositum est, quod omnes, qui poenitentiam vere agunt, et Christum vera fide amplectuntur, iustificare, in gratiam recipere, et in filios atque heredes vitae aeternae adoptare velit.

V. Et quod fide iustificatos in vera caritate sanctificare velit; ut Apostolus testatur Eph.

1, 4.

VI. Idem in aeterno suo consilio proposuit, se iustificatos etiam in multiplici et varia ipsorum infirmitate adversus diabolum, mundum et carnem defensurum, et in viis suis deducturum atque gubernaturum; et, si lapsi fuerint, manum suppositurum, ut in cruce atque tentationibus solidam consolationem percipiant, atque ad vitam conferuentur.

VII. Illius aeternum decretum est, quod opus illud bonum a se in illis inceptum promovere, atque confirmare, et ad finem usque seruare velit: si modo verbo ipsius, tanquam scipioni, constanter innitantur, ipsius opem ardentibus precibus implorent, in gratia Dei perfeuerent, et dona accepta fideliter et bene collocent.

VIII. Ille etiam aeterno suo consilio decrevit, quod eos, quos elegit, vocauit, iustificauit, in altera aeterna vita saluos facere, et aeterna gloria ornare velit.

Et quidem Deus in illo suo consilio, proposito et ordinatione, non tantum in genere salutem suorum procurauit: verum etiam omnes et singulas personas electorum (qui per Christum saluandi sunt) clementer praescivit, ad salutem elegit, et decreuit, quod eo modo (quem iam recitauimus) ipsos per suam gratiam, dona atque efficaciam salutis aeternae participes facere, iuvare, eorum salutem promovere, ipsos confirmare et conferuare velit.

Haec omnia secundum scripturam in articulo praedestinationis et aeternae electionis diuinae ad adoptionem in filios et aeternam salutem comprehenduntur.

Quibus e Form. Concord. adductis et praestitutis, praedestinatio sensu latiore accepta definiri potest, quod sit aeternum decretum diuinum, quo Deus ex immensa sua misericordia hominibus omnibus, quos in peccatum prolapsuros ab aeterno praeuidit, Filium suum mediatorem dare, et per praedicationem vniuersalem amplectendum offerre, omnibus etiam, qui non repugnaturi essent, fidem per verbum et sacramenta conferre, credentes omnes iustificare, ac mediis gratiae porro utentes renouare, fidem usque ad finem vitae in illis conferuare, ipsos denique credentes salutare constituit.

Obs. Nonnulli Patres atque Theologi haud dubitarunt asserere, fidem in Christum esse electionis effectum, et praedestinationem constituere finem et ordinare media, nosque fuisse credituros, quia electi eramus. Illi vocem praedestinationis atque electionis sumunt in hoc sensu laxiori, pro tota saluandorum ordinatione ad salutem; quae, ut omnia salutis principia et media complectitur, ita propositum Dei aeternum de fide in Christum, per verbum et sacramenta prædeftinationis atque electionis sumunt in hoc sensu laxiori, pro tota faluandorum ordinatione ad salutem; quæ, vt omnia salutis principia & media complectitur, ita propositum Dei æternum de fide in Christum, per verbum & sacra-

in omnibus, qui obstinate & præfracte non restiterint, efficienda, includit. Vid. D. MVSAEI dissert. de æterno prædestinat. decreto p. 206. Prob. b. Sensu strictiori sumta prædestinatio tum πρόθεσιν, i. e. decretum divinum generale & indeterminatum de æterna salute impertienda omnibus hominibus peccatoribus, in Christum finaliter credituris, tum πρόγνωσιν, h. e. prænotionem certarum personarum, sive individuorum humanorum, quæ veram in Christum fidem usque ad novissimum vitæ halitum retentura sunt, complectitur.

Quo sensu strictiori acceptam prædestinationem perseverans in Christum fides ingreditur non ut causa meritoria, propter quam Deus nos eligat, sed ut instrumentalis, quod gratiam eligentis Dei, meritumque Christi apprehendat, dicente AEGID. HVNNIO in tractat. de proud. & præd. fol. 826. Ex quo etiam nonnulli Theologi fidem in Christum partem ordinis prædestinatori appellant. Conf. D. GERHARDI disputat. isagog. p. 723. & D. MEISNERI anthropol. decad. II. p. 153. D. DANNHAV. hodof phænom. VII. p. 578.

Prob. c. Prædestinatio sensu strictissimo sumta, prout est æternum Dei decretum ad certa individua humana (Abrahamum, Petrum &c.) applicatum, πρόθεσιν, sive decretum indeterminatum de saluandis hominibus finaliter credituris, & πρόγνωσιν, seu præcognitionem fidei in Christum, vt ordine priorem præsupponit, adeoque fides neque pars illius, sed ratio impulsiva minus principalis est, quam Deus elector gratiosissime respexit. Antecedit quidem electio fidem, ratione actualis existentia, sed secundum esse cognitum fides electionem antecedit in signo rationis.


### Question VI. What is the cause of election, taken in the most special sense?

The efficient cause of election, taken in the strictest sense, is the triune God a), Father b), Son c), and Holy Spirit d).

Obs. The efficient cause is twofold: 1) In being formally, which produces a real effect, really distinct from itself. Such a cause is, for example, the human intellect, when it produces an act of understanding, which is not only real, but also really produced by its cause, namely, the intellect. 2) In being virtually, which does not indeed produce an effect really distinct from itself, yet is conceived by us as a cause; and if that of which it is called the cause had a true cause, this cause, virtually such, would be sufficient. It is otherwise called the reason of being a priori. Now, when we assert that God is the efficient cause of predestination, it is not to be understood as an efficient cause in being formally; because God does not produce the decree of predestination as something really distinct from Himself (for every decree of God is ταὐτὸ, one and the same, with the most simple divine essence): but it is to be understood as a cause in being virtually; because God is conceived as an efficient cause, and if the decree of predestination had, or could have, a true cause, God would be its efficient cause. Conf. D. MUSAEUS in the disp. on the eternal decree of predestination, § 22, and D. BECHMANN in Institut. theol. p. 443. D. BAYER in compend. theol. p. 647.

Prob. a. Since election is not a personal action, such as to beget, to be begotten, and to proceed, but essential and undivided, it therefore belongs to all and each of the three persons of the Godhead. Namely, to the Father, Son, and H. S.; just as justification and glorification, which are given to execution through the decree of election, belong to all three persons. Furthermore, election is indeed an immanent act of the divine will, yet regarding an object placed outside of God; and therefore, as is done in other divine acts ad extra, so also in the act of election an order must be maintained, in the distinction of the divine persons, so that God the Father is said to have elected us through the Son, in the Holy Spirit. Nor, however, are the three persons of the Godhead associate causes of predestination, nor is Christ the instrumental cause of election, for if we were to assert this, the ὁμοουσία of the divine persons would be undermined.

Prob. b. St. Paul proclaims the kindness of God the Father in choosing us for eternal life, Eph. I, 3. 4. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ: just as He chose us in Him before the foundation of the world. To God the Father, the fountain of every blessing, is attributed the election, but the remaining divine persons are not excluded, whose essence is one, and thus the acts of the will belong equally to all. However, in the place cited, there is a peculiar regard of the one choosing for him in whom He chooses.

Prob. c. Christ compels His disciples, John XV, 19. If you were of the world, the world would love its own: but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, for this reason the world hates you. Christ is speaking of the election of the apostles, not simply to the apostleship, but insofar as this is joined with the election to eternal life. For all Christians perseveringly believing in Christ are chosen out of the world, which lies entirely in the evil one, 1 John V, 19. Now the world is that multitude of men who, enslaved to the flesh and the vanities of the world, burn with internecine hatred against the worshippers of piety, and harass them. But Christ says that He chose the apostles, and their imitators, out of the world, i. e., that He separated them from the dregs of impious men, and destined them for the possession of the heavenly inheritance.

Prob. d. From 2 Thess. II, 13. But we ought to give thanks to God always for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, because God chose you from the beginning for salvation in the sanctification of the Spirit, and faith of the truth. The Apostle testifies that God the Father chose them ἐν ἁγιασμῷ πνεύματος, in the sanctification of the Spirit; by which is not understood the holiness inherent in the reborn, since that, being lacking and mutilated, cannot withstand the censorial judgment of God, but the actual sanctification of the divine Spirit, by which miserable sinners are called to the heavenly kingdom, are illuminated, converted, and regenerated; so that they are gifted with faith in Christ, in which, persisting, they are chosen by the divine and eternal immutable decree for heavenly glory.

Dicis I. Glorification, or the salvation of faithful men, which corresponds to predestination, has a true cause: Therefore, the decree of predestination also has a true and, in being, formal cause, since it is the same cause of the execution and of the decree. Resp. I deny the consequence. For glorification, or the salvation of the faithful, happens outside of God, where a true and, in being, formal cause has a place. But the decree of predestination is in God Himself, not differing in reality from the divine essence. Furthermore, the impulsive cause of the execution and of the decree is the same, although the efficient cause, not really distinct from the decree, produces in the execution an effect really distinct from itself.

Dicis II. Predestination is an action ad intra (inward). But actions ad intra are divided, or not common to all three persons of the divinity. This is evident from the eternal generation of τοῦ λόγου (the Word). Resp. Predestination is indeed a divine internal and immanent action; but it is not an action ad intra, but ad extra (outward), in that it tends toward an object placed outside of God, namely, the miserable sinner believing in Christ. Add that while actions ad intra may indeed be personal, actions ad intra are not essential. See KOENIG, Theol. Positiv., pp. 41, 42.

Dicis III. The Son of God is the meritorious and impulsive cause of predestination; hence we are said to be chosen in Christ, i. e., on account of Christ, Eph. I, 4. Therefore, He is not the efficient cause of predestination, since these causes are mutually contradistinguished from one another. Resp. The Son of God can be viewed in two ways: 1) As He is one with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God: 2) Insofar as in time He assumed human nature, and in it made satisfaction for men. In this latter way the Son of God is the meritorious and external impulsive cause of eternal salvation, and of election to salvation. In the former way He is one with the Father and the Holy Spirit, the efficient cause of predestination, and indeed one cause. For the will of the three persons is one, and by one act of will the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit chose to eternal salvation as many as are saved in time.

Latin:

Causa efficiens electionis, sensu strictissimo acceptæ, est Deus triunus a), Pater b), Filius c), & Spiritus Sanctus d).

Obs. Causa efficiens est duplex: 1) In essendo formaliter, quæ producit effectum realem, realiter a se distinctum. Talis causa est v. gr. intellectus humanus, cum producit actum intelligendi, qui non solum realis est, sed & realiter a causa sua, nempe intellectu, productus. 2) In essendo virtualiter, quæ non quidem producit effectum, a se realiter distinctum, a nobis tamen concipitur vt causa; & si id, cuius causa dicitur, haberet veram causam, hæc causa, virtualiter talis, sufficiens esset. Vocatur alias ratio essendi a priori. Iam cum afferimus, Deum esse causam efficientem prædestinationis, non intelligenda est causa efficiens in essendo formaliter; quia Deus non producit prædestinationis decretum, vt a se realiter distinctum (omne quippe decretum Dei cum essentia divina simplicissima est ταὐτὸ, vnum & idem): sed intelligenda est causa in essendo virtualiter; quia Deus concipitur vt causa efficiens, & si decretum prædestinationis haberet, vel habere posset veram causam, Deus illius efficiens causa esset. Conf. D. MVSAEVS in disp. de æt. prædest. decr. § 22. & D. BECHMANN. in Institut. theol. pag. 443. D. BAYER. in compend. theol. p. 647.

Prob. a. Cum electio non sit actio personalis, quales sunt gignere, gigni, & procedere, sed essentialis & indivisa, ideo omnibus & singulis tribus deitatis personis competit. Patri scil. Filio & Spiritui S.; perinde ac iustificatio & glorificatio, quæ per decretum electionis executioni dantur, omnibus tribus personis competunt. Ceterum electio est quidem actus voluntatis divinæ immanens, respiciens tamen obiectum extra Deum positum; ideoque fient in reliquis diuinis ad extra, ita quoque in actu electionis feruandus est ordo, in discrimen personarum diuinarum, vt Deus Pater per Filium, in Spiritu S. nos elegisse dicatur. Neque tamen tres deitatis personæ sunt causæ prædestinationis sociæ, neque Christus est causa electionis instrumentalis, quod si assereremus, labefactaretur personarum diuinarum ὁμοουσία. perfonæ sunt cauffæ prædeftinationis fociæ, neque Christus est caussa electionis instrumentalis, quod si afferereinus, labefactaretur perfonarum diuinarum ὁμοουσία.

Prob. b. Dei Patris benignitatem ad vitam aeternam nos eligentis praedicat S. Paulus Eph. I, 3. 4. Benedictus Deus & Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui benedixit nobis omni benedictione spirituali in supracaelestibus in Christo: quemadmodum elegit nos in ipso ante fundamentum mundi. Deo Patri, fonti omnis benedictionis, tribuitur electio, sed non excluduntur reliquae personae divinae, quarum una est essentia, ita & actus voluntatis omnibus aeque competunt. Habetur autem l. c. peculiaris respectus eligentis ad eum, in quo elegit.

Prob. c. Christus suos discipulos compellat, Io. XV, 19. Si ex mundo essetis, mundus proprium diligeret: quia vero ex mundo non estis, sed ego elegi vos ex mundo, propter hoc odit vos mundus. Sermo est Christo de electione apostolorum non simpliciter ad apostolatum, sed quatenus haec coniuncta est cum electione ad vitam aeternam. Omnes quippe christiani perseveranter in Christum credentes, electi sunt de mundo, qui totus in maligno iacet, 1 Io. V, 19. Est autem mundus multitudo illorum hominum, qui, carni & vanitatibus mundi mancipati, in cultores pietatis odio internecino flagrant, eosque diuexant. At Christus dicit, se apostolos, eorumque imitatores elegisse de mundo, i. e. a colluvie impiorum hominum secreuisse, & ad possessionem hereditatis caelestis destinasse.

Prob. d. Ex 2 Thess. II, 13. Nos vero debemus gratias agere Deo semper pro vobis, fratres dilecti a Domino, quod elegit vos Deus ab initio ad salutem in sanctificatione Spiritus, & fide veritatis. Testatur Apostolus, Deum Patrem eos elegisse ἐν ἁγιασμῷ πνεύματος, in sanctificatione Spiritus; per quam non intelligitur sanctitas renatis inhaerens, quippe quae manca & mutila censorium Dei iudicium sustinere nequit, sed actua Spiritus diuini sanctificatio, qua miseri peccatores ad regnum caeleste vocantur, illuminantur, conuertuntur & regenerantur; vt fide in Christum donentur, in qua persistentes decreto diuino aeternaque immutabili ad gloriam caelestem electi sunt.

Dicis I. Glorificatio, vel saluatio hominum fidelium, quae praedestinationi respondet, habet veram caussam: E. decretum praedestinationis quoque veram & in essendo formalem caussam habet, cum eadem sit caussa executionis & decreti. Resp. Neg. consequentiam. Nam glorificatio, siue saluatio fidelium fit extra Deum, vbi caussa vera & in essendo formalis locum habet. At vero decretum praedestinationis est in ipso Deo, ab essentia diuina secundum rem non differens. Ceterum eadem est caussa impulsiva executionis & decreti, licet caussa efficiens, a decreto realiter non distincta, in executione effectum a se realiter distinctum producat.

Dicis II. Praedestinatio est actio ad intra. Actiones autem ad intra sunt diuisae siue non communes omnibus tribus personis diuinitatis. Id quod patet ex generatione τοῦ λόγου aeterna. Resp. Praedestinatio est quidem actio diuina interna & immanens; at non est actio ad intra, sed ad extra, eo quod tendit ad obiectum, extra Deum positum, nempe peccatorem miserum, in Christum credentem. Adiice, quod actiones ad intra personales quidem sint diuisae, non autem actiones ad intra essentiales. Vid. KOENIGII theol. pofitiu. p. 41. 42.

Dicis III. Filius Dei est caussa meritoria & impulsiva praedestinationis; hinc dicimur eligi in Christo, h. e. propter Christum, Eph. I, 4. E. non est caussa efficiens praedestinationis, cum hae caussae sibi inuicem contradistinguantur. Resp. Filius Dei dupliciter spectari potest: 1) Vt est vnus cum Patre & Spiritu S. Deus: 2) Quatenus in tempore humanam naturam assumsit, & in ea pro hominibus satisfecit. Hoc posteriori modo Filius Dei est caussa meritoria atque impulsiva externa aeternae salutis, atque electionis ad salutem. Priori modo est vna cum Patre & Spiritu S. praedestinationis caussa efficiens, & quidem vna caussa. Vna enim trium personarum voluntas est, & vno voluntatis actu Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. ad salutem aeternam elegerunt, quotquot in tempore saluantur.


### Question VII. What is the impulsive cause of election?

The impulsive cause of the election of fallen men, and those reconciled to God, unto eternal life is partly internal, partly external. The internal impulsive cause of election is εὐδοκία, benevolence, or the grace of God; provoked by no merits of men.

Proof. That God was moved unto our predestination by εὐδοκία, or benevolence inclined toward men, Paul teaches in Eph. 1:5-6. God predestined us unto the adoption of sons through Jesus Christ unto himself according to the good pleasure of his will, to the praise of his grace, in which he made us acceptable to himself in the beloved. By which words the Apostle teaches, 1) that we were predestined by God unto eternal glory, κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ, according to the good pleasure, or benevolent affection of his will; which εὐδοκία is the benevolence of God, or his gratuitous and most free favor. Divine εὐδοκία can be considered in two ways: a) generally, b) specifically. Considered generally, the good pleasure of God pertains to the antecedent will of God, and is the fountain and origin of all saving means, through which the merciful God willed from eternity that an approach to eternal life should lie open to men who are fallen and, because of sin, liable to eternal death, under this condition: that they rightly use the means ordained for obtaining salvation, namely the Word and sacraments, and persevere in believing in Christ by his grace, by which he wills to work and preserve faith in them through those means. In which general sense εὐδοκία, or the benevolence of God, is the impulsive cause of forming the eternal decree concerning the saving of sinful men who will finally believe in Christ. Taken specifically, εὐδοκία, or the divine good pleasure, as it pertains to the consequent will of God, is not so much the cause of predestination as it is predestination itself; since there is no difference between the internal predestination of those to be saved unto eternal life, and the good pleasure of God, by which he willed from eternity to certainly endow with heavenly life those who are to persevere in believing in Christ.

The Apostle asserts 2) that we were predestined by God unto the adoption of sons through Jesus Christ, understanding the consummated and glorious adoption, which brings with it κληρονομίαν, or the inheritance of eternal life, which we obtain not through the pursuit of good works, but through faith in Christ, John 1:12. St. Paul shows 3) that God predestined us to the praise of the glory of his grace, which praise of the glorious grace of God is the ultimate end of election. But if the election of us was made solely to the praise of the glorious grace of God, then certainly it was not made on account of the merits of our works: otherwise even men studious of good works would have something to boast about. The same [Apostle] teaches 4) that God made us acceptable to himself in the beloved, i.e., in Christ. So far are we from being acceptable to God by the condition of our nature, that we are children of wrath, and even hated, Eph. 2:3. Wherefore, that we are beloved by God and elected unto eternal life is to be referred entirely not to our works, but to the grace of God founded in the merit of Christ.

The Apostle inculcates 5) that God chose us that we should be holy and blameless, v. 4. Therefore we were not elected because we were holy.

The choosing grace 6) the doctor of the Gentiles opposes diametrically to the merits of works, Rom. 11:6. So therefore also at the present time a remnant has been made according to the election of grace. But if by grace, it is no longer of works; since grace is no longer grace. But if of works, it is no longer grace; since a work is no longer a work.

From which we learn that God was moved to choose certain men from the common mass of perdition, not by their foreseen works, but by his own unmerited and gratuitous grace. It is not grace in any way, if it is not gratuitous in every way, as Augustine elegantly says somewhere.

The antithesis is of the Socinians, and of certain Papists, asserting that our election was made in view of good works; whose stronger arguments are:

I. Whoever is therefore called a vessel unto honor of God, because he cleanses himself from sins, he is elected on account of the pursuit of good works. But the reborn man, etc. The major is evident; because a vessel unto honor of God is an elected man, who, when he becomes a vessel unto honor through cleansing from sins, is certainly elected on account of the pursuit of good works. The minor is proved from 2 Tim. II, 21. Resp. The words of the Apostle are: If any man shall have purged himself from these, he shall be a vessel unto honor: He does not say: he shall become; just as if cleansing from sins were the cause of election: but the Apostle only indicates by what external sign the elect is known.

II. He who reprobates unbelieving men on account of evil works, predestinates reborn men to salvation on account of good works: But God, etc. Therefore. The major is evident; because the reason for opposites is opposite, if they are equally perfect on both sides. But good works are imperfectly good; evil works are perfectly evil. Whence it is not permitted to conclude from these to those.

III. Those for whom the kingdom of heaven is prepared because they fed the hungry, gave drink to the thirsty, etc., they are elected on account of the pursuit of good works: But for reborn men, etc. Therefore. The minor is proved from Matt. XXV, 34, 35. The kingdom of heaven is prepared for you from the foundation of the world: For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; where the reason for election to the kingdom of glory is rendered as beneficence through the causal particle, γὰρ, for, namely. Resp. The particle γὰρ in the cited place is not αἰτιολογικὴ, or causal, but συλλογιστικὴ, ratiocinative, by which is gathered not the effect from the cause, but the cause from the effect, or the consequent, through demonstration a posteriori, just as if I were to gather: It is necessary that there be fire in this house; for smoke ascends from it. Furthermore, that the kingdom is not prepared on account of good works is clear, because in the cited place it is called κληρονομία, which falls to someone without merits.

IV. Whoever studies to make their calling and election sure through good works, their election depends on good works: But men to be saved, etc. 2 Pet. I, 10. The major is evident: because by that which something is confirmed, it depends on it, if not in becoming, or in being, at least in being preserved. Resp. 1) The words of the text are: study to make your calling and election sure. The Προσδιορισμός, or that addition, through good works, is not held in the authentic text. 2) Although good works can be understood, yet the Apostle does not assert that men to be saved are elected on account of good works, but only that election is confirmed through works, namely, that it may be known a posteriori. For works are truly τεκμήρια, and firm signs, by which the elect are validly distinguished from the reprobate.

V. God chose us, that we should be holy and blameless before him in love, Eph. I, 4. Therefore. God in making the decree of election looked at the pursuit of true piety. Resp. The Apostle does not say: God chose us, when we were holy and blameless, but he chose us, that we should be holy and blameless. Therefore we were not chosen by God on account of inherent holiness, as an impulsive cause, but the holy obedience to be rendered to God, and the pursuit of sincere piety, is with respect to the intention of the divine end, and with respect to the execution, the effect of election; by which faithful men declare and testify to the memory of a grateful mind toward God the elector.

Latin:

Causa impulsiva electionis hominum lapsorum, & Deo reconciliatorum, ad vitam aeternam alia est interna, alia externa. Causa impulsiva electionis interna est εὐδοκία, benevolentia, vel gratia Dei; nullis hominum meritis provocata.

Prob. Ad praedestinationem nostri motum esse Deum εὐδοκίᾳ, siue benevolentia in homines propensa, docet Paulus Eph. I, 5. 6. Deus praedestinavit nos in adoptionem filiorum per Iesum Christum in seipsum iuxta beneplacitum voluntatis suae, in laudem gratiae ipsius, in qua gratos nos sibi fecit in dilecto. Quibus verbis Apostolus docet, 1) nos esse a Deo praedestinatos ad aeternam gloriam, κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ, secundum beneplacitum, siue benevolum affectum voluntatis suae; quae εὐδοκία est benevolentia Dei, vel favor ipsius gratuitus & liberrimus. Considerari potest εὐδοκία diuina dupliciter, a) generatim, b) speciatim. Generatim spectatum beneplacitum Dei pertinet ad voluntatem Dei antecedentem, estque fons & origo omnium salutarium mediorum, per quae misericors Deus lapsis, & ob peccatum aeternae morti obnoxiis hominibus aditum ad vitam aeternam patere ab aeterno voluit, sub hac conditione, si mediis ad salutem obtinendam ordinatis, verbo scilicet & sacramentis, recte utantur, & in Christum ipsius gratia, qua fidem per illa media operari & conferuare in ipsis vult, perseueranter credant. Quo sensu generali accepta εὐδοκία, siue benevolentia Dei causa impulsiva est formandi decretum aeternum de saluandis hominibus peccatoribus, finaliter in Christum credituris. Speciatim sumta εὐδοκία, siue beneplacitum diuinum, prout ad voluntatem Dei consequentem pertinet, non tam praedestinationis causa, quam ipsa praedestinatio est; cum nihil inter se differant interna praedestinatio saluandorum ad vitam aeternam, & Dei beneplacitum, quo illos, qui perseueranter in Christum sunt credituri, vita coelesti certo donare ab aeterno voluit.

Asserit 2) Apostolus, nos esse a Deo praedestinatos in adoptionem filiorum per Iesum Christum, intelligens adoptionem consummatam & gloriosam, quae infert κληρονομίαν, siue hereditatem aeternae vitae, quam non per studium bonorum operum, sed per fidem in Christum adipisciimur, Io. I, 12. Ostendit 3) S. Paullus, Deum nos praedestinasse in laudem gloriosae gratiae ipsius, quae laus gloriosae gratiae Dei est finis electionis vltimus. Quod si autem electio nostri vnice facta est in laudem gloriosae gratiae Dei, vtique facta non est ob merita operum nostrorum: ceteroqui etiam homines bonorum operum studiosi haberent, de quo gloriarentur. Docet idem 4), Deum nos sibi gratos fecisse in dilecto, e. Christo. Tantum abest, vt naturae nostrae conditione Deo simus grati, vt simus filii irae, adeoque exosi, Eph. II, 3. Quare quod a Deo dilecti & ad vitam aeternam electi sumus, id non nostris operibus, sed gratiae Dei in merito Christi fundatae in solidum acceptum referendum est.

Inculcat 5) Apostolus, Deum nos elegisse, vt simus sancti & irreprehensibiles, v. 4. Ergo non sumus ideo electi, quia sancti fuimus.

Gratiam eligentem 6) doctor gentium e diametro operum meritis opponit, Rom. XI, 6. Sic ergo etiam in praesenti tempore reliqui secundum electionem gratiae facti sunt. Si vero gratia, non amplius ex operibus; quoniam gratia non amplius est gratia. Si vero ex operibus, non amplius est gratia; quoniam opus non amplius est opus.

E quibus discimus, Deum ad eligendum quosdam homines e communi perditionis massa, non praeuisis eorum operibus, sed sua gratia indebita & gratuita permotum esse. Non est gratia vllo modo, si non est gratuita omni modo, eleganter alicubi ait AVGVSTINVS.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, & quorundam Pontificiorum, afferentium, electionem nostri factam esse intuitu bonorum operum; quorum potiora sunt argumenta:

I. Quicunque ideo dicitur vas in honorem Dei, quia se emundat a peccatis, ille propter studium bonorum operum est electus, Atqui homo renatus &c. Maior constat; quia vas in honorem Dei est homo electus, qui cum fiat vas in honorem per emundationem a peccatis, vtique propter studium bonorum operum electus est. Minor prob. ex 2 Tim. II, 21. Resp. Verba Apostoli sunt: Si quis se purgauerit ab his, erit vas in honorem: Non dicit: fiet; perinde ac si emundatio a peccatis sit causa electionis: sed indicat tantum Apostolus, quo signo externo electus innotescat.

II. Qui propter mala opera homines incredulos reprobat, propter bona opera homines renatos ad salutem praedestinat: Atqui Deus &c. E. Maior est evidens; quia oppositorum opposita est ratio, si vtrinque sint pariter perfecta. At bona opera imperfecte bona; mala opera perfecte mala sunt. Vnde ab his ad illa concludere non licet.

III. Quibus paratum est regnum coelorum ideo, quod esurientes cibarunt, sitientes potarunt &c. illi ob studium bonorum operum sunt electi: Atqui hominibus renatis &c. E. Minor prob. ex Matth. XXV, 34. 35. Paratum est vobis regnum coelorum a fundatione mundi: Nam esuriui, & dedistis mihi, quod ederem; vbi electionis ad regnum gloriae ratio redditur beneficentia per particulam causalem, γὰρ, enim, nam. Resp. Particula γὰρ loco citato non est αἰτιολογικὴ, siue causalis, sed συλλογισικὴ, ratiocinatiua, qua colligitur non effectus e causa, sed causa ex effectu, siue consequente, per demonstrationem a posteriori, perinde ac si colligerem: Oportet in his aedibus esse ignem; nam ex iisdem adscendit sumus. Ceterum quod non propter bona opera paratum sit regnum, patet, quia loco citato vocatur κληρονομία, quae citra merita alicui obtingit.

IV. Quicunque student per bona opera firmam facere suam vocationem & electionem, illorum electio pendet a bonis operibus: Atqui homines saluandi &c. 2 Petr. I, 10. Maior constat: quia per quod aliquid firmatur, ab illo dependet, si non in fieri, aut esse, saltim in conseruari. Resp. 1) Verba textus sunt: studete firmam facere vestram vocationem & electionem. Προσδιορισμός, siue additamentum illud, per bona opera, non habetur in textu authentico. 2) Quamuis bona opera subintelligi queant, non tamen asserit Apostolus, homines saluandos propter bona opera eligi, sed tantum, electionem per opera firmari, scilicet quod cognosci a posteriori. Sunt enim opera vere τεκμήρια, & notae firmae, quibus electi a reprobis valide dignoscuntur.

V. Deus elegit nos, vt fimus sancti & irreprehensibiles coram ipso in dilectione, Eph. I, 4. E. Deus in faciendo decreto electionis respexit verae pietatis studium. Resp. Non ait Apostolus: Deus elegit nos, cum essemus sancti & irreprehensibiles, sed elegit nos, vt essemus sancti & inculpati. Non ergo a Deo electi sumus ob inhaesuam sanctitatem, vt causam impulsivam, sed sanctum Deo praestandum obsequium, sinceraeque pietatis studium respectu intentionis diuinae finis, respectu executionis effectus electionis est; quo homines fideles erga Deum electorem grati animi memoriam declarant & testantur.


### Quaest. VIII. What is the external impulsive cause of election?

The external impulsive cause of election is the merit of Christ, to be apprehended by true and persevering faith, foreseen from eternity by God, who is omnisci

Observ. The sense of our assertion is: God elected certain men from the common throng of lost men to eternal life not on account of their own merits, nor from absolute grace, excluding all regard for an impulsive reason outside of God: but in the eternal decree of election He looked solely to the most full and sufficient merit of His Son, by which He was also moved to choose certain sinners—namely, those alone and individually—for eternal life, whom He foresaw from eternity in the light of His omniscience as those who would embrace the merit of Christ by true faith and would persevere in that faith until the very last breath of life: and thus the merit of Christ is the external impulsive cause of election, not insofar as it is viewed merely by reason of acquisition (for thus it pertains to all men); but also by reason of final application, which occurs through persevering faith; in which respect the merit of Christ profits only the reborn.

The assertion is proved 1) from Eph. 1:3, 4, 5, 6, 7. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ: just as He chose us in Him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before Him in love: having predestined us to the adoption of sons by Jesus Christ to Himself, according to the good pleasure of His will. In whom we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of sins according to the riches of His grace. This is a classic dictum of Scripture, or the proper seat of the doctrine concerning the election of men to eternal life. Wherefore we draw the following arguments from this oracle.

We argue a): Whoever are elected by God to eternal glory on account of Christ the mediator, God is moved and impelled to their election by the merit of Christ. But the reborn, etc. Therefore. The major is evident; because on account of whose merit some decree is formed, he must be the impulsive cause by virtue of that merit. For the meritorious cause is that which, under the aspect of merit or demerit, moves and impels the efficient cause to give a reward or inflict a punishment. The minor is clear; because Paul says we are elected by God in Christ, that is, on account of Christ. For the Greek particle ἐν frequently in the sacred writings has the same value as "on account of," as in Matt. 6:7, where the discourse is about the Gentiles: they think they will be heard ἐν πολυλογίᾳ αὐτῶν, on account of their much speaking; Acts 7:29. Moses fled ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τούτῳ, on account of this word, when, namely, of the quarreling Israelites, among whom he had gone to reconcile peace, one said: Do you wish to kill me, as you did the Egyptian yesterday? Eph. 3:13. I ask that you do not lose heart ἐν θλίψεσι μου, on account of my afflictions. Indeed, the particle ἐν is rendered by the Apostle himself as διὰ, v. 5.

You say: I. Paul's words can be explained: We are elected in Christ as in a head. Resp. The word "head" denotes both an order toward the members and causality. If "head" is taken causally, we are truly said to be elected in Christ as in a head, foundation, and impulsive cause of election. But if it is taken only ordinally, namely, that Christ was elected first in the sign of the divine reason, and we were predestined afterward; that explanation is inconvenient for the reason that Christ was never in the common mass of perdition; and thus He was never segregated and elected.

You say: II. The Apostle's words can be explained: We are elected that we might be in Christ, so that the final cause is noted, not the impulsive. Resp. If the Apostle had said: We are elected εἰς τὸν Χριστὸν (unto Christ), that explanation would be congruent with the text. But he says: We are elected in Christ, as in a mediator, whose merit impelled God to choose certain men.

You say: III. The Greek particle ἐν is indeed put for διὰ, but it denotes the efficient cause of election, and the sense becomes: God the Father elected us through Christ, His coeternal Son, and thus Christ is considered not as mediator, but as God. Resp. God who elects is openly distinguished from Christ, in whom, as in a foundation, the election was made; and in the whole context the Apostle speaks of Christ not merely qua God, but qua θεάνθρωπος and mediator, in whom we have redemption through His blood, v. 7. You say: IV. The sense of the Apostle is: God chose us to be holy and blameless in Him. Resp. This interpretation does violence to the text, by taking away something from it which is necessary to complete the sense.

For in the Pauline text the pronoun ἡμᾶς is read, placed twice, and the mark of distinction inserted is constructed once with the verb ἐξελέξατο, and again with the verb εἶναι, in this way: ἐξελέξατο ἡμᾶς ἐν αὐτῷ πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, εἶναι ἡμᾶς ἁγίους. But according to the interpretation just reviewed, the mark of distinction would have to be removed, just as if the pronoun ἡμᾶς had been placed only once, and with the words transposed it would have to be read thus: ἐξελέξατο ἡμᾶς εἶναι ἐν αὐτῷ ἁγίους i. e. He chose us to be holy in Him.

You say: V. God chose us in Christ, namely to be adopted. Resp. This exposition adds something to the text beyond necessity.

When these things are accurately weighed, it is manifest that our explanation alone, which we gave above, is conformable to the context and expresses the genuine mind of the Apostle.

What more? Our interpretation is confirmed by the vote of the Helvetic Confession, cap. X, the Anhalt Confession, cap. XI, and not a few doctors of the Reformed Church, whom Mr. D. HOLZEVSIVS mentions and praises in his dissertation on predestination, p. 133 et seqq.

We argue b): Whoever is the meritorious cause of spiritual blessing, he is the meritorious cause of eternal election: But Christ is, etc. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, in Christ; καθὼς, just as He chose us in Him. The emphatic particle καθὼς, just as, says the Apostle, God blesses us in Christ in the same way in which He chose us in Him.

But God blesses us in Christ, as the fountain and meritorious cause of blessing, Gen. XII, 3, c. XVIII, 18, c. XXII, 18, Acts IV, 12, Gal. III, 13, 14. Therefore He chose us in Christ, as the fountain and meritorious cause of election to eternal salvation.

You say: Christ is indeed the meritorious cause of election, but not the impulsive cause. Resp. The meritorious cause is comprehended under the impulsive, as a species under a genus: for every meritorious cause is impulsive, although not every impulsive cause is meritorious.

This is defined as that which is a cause, which under the aspect of merit impels the efficient cause to give a reward. Therefore every meritorious cause is essentially impulsive.

We argue c): Whomever God predestined to the adoption of sons through Jesus Christ in Himself, those He chose in view of the merit of Christ: But He predestined reborn men, etc. Therefore. The major is proven, because predestination to the consummated υἱοθεσία (adoption), which is given in heaven, is election to eternal life, since that consummated and glorious υἱοθεσία includes or brings with it the heavenly inheritance.
