We argue d): Whoever is the impulsive cause for which God loves us, he is the impulsive cause for which God chose us to eternal life: But Christ is, etc. The major is proven: because love internally impelled God to choose certain men, so that no one is elect who is not loved.

But God did not love certain men absolutely without view of Christ. The minor is evident from verse 6, to the praise of the glory of His grace, in which He made us acceptable in the Beloved.

Sinners would have perished, had they not been rendered acceptable to God.

No creature could make them acceptable to God; because no creature could blot out sin, from which all enmity results. Wherefore, lest the miserable sinners should perish, God in His glorious benevolence made them from enemies into friends, and acceptable to Himself, by sending His most beloved Son into the flesh, in whom, through whom, and for whose sake sinners are loved.

We argue e): In whom we have the remission of sins, he is the fundamental cause of our election: But in Christ, etc. Therefore. The major is clear; because God chose sinners, not insofar as they are hated, but insofar as they are reconciled and restored to the grace of God.

Therefore, the decree of election presupposes, in the order of reason, the divine decree concerning the justification of man.

The minor premise is evident from v. 7:

"In whom (Christ) we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace."

Proved 2) from the conformity of the decree and its execution.

Whatever is the impulsive cause on account of which God in time confers salvation upon certain men, that is the impulsive cause on account of which God from eternity elected certain men to salvation: But the merit of Christ is the impulsive cause on account of which God in time confers salvation upon certain men.

Therefore, the merit of Christ is the impulsive cause on account of which God elected certain men to eternal life. The major premise rests upon a universal canon: The impulsive causes of the decree are the same as the impulsive causes of the execution of the decree; the truth of which is evident 1) from an induction of examples.

When a magistrate rewards his citizens, a master his servants, a parent his children, a teacher his students, or a commander his soldiers—some for diligence in their duty, and others for offenses he punishes—it is easily gathered that, just as diligence and offenses were the causes impelling the distribution of rewards and punishments, so they were also the causes impelling the decreeing of rewards and punishments. Because the crying sins of Sodom were the cause why God destroyed it, Gen.

XIX, 20, we conclude not in vain that God, on account of those sins, decreed to destroy it. 2) That the impulsive causes of the decree and its execution are the same is proved a priori, both from the nature of the impulsive cause itself and from the nature of voluntary actions.

From the nature of the impulsive cause: for this is the nature and character of an impulsive cause, by which one is moved to the exercise of some external act, that it moves the will or appetite of the efficient cause to will or desire that which the efficient cause executes through the external act.

The same is also perceived from the nature of voluntary actions. For just as he who acts also wills to act, and it is at least prior in nature to will to act than to act; so also, by whatever cause one is moved to act, by the same one is moved to will to act, and it is at least prior in nature to will to act, moved by some cause, than to act, moved by some cause.

The minor premise is confirmed by the Holy Scriptures, which teach that there is salvation in no other than in Christ, Acts IV, 12. "If, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son: much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved in his life," Rom. V, 10.

"God hath not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation by our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us, that, whether we wake or sleep, we should live together with him," 1 Thess. V, 9, 10.

Latin:

Causa impulsiva externa electionis est meritum Christi, vera & perseuerante fide apprehendendum, ab aeterno prauisum a Deo omniscio & placabili.

Obseru. Sensus assertionis nostrae est: Deus quosdam homines e communi perditorum hominum coetu ad vitam aeternam elegit non ob merita propria, neque ex gratia absoluta, omnem respectum rationis impulsivae extra Deum excludente: sed in aeterno electionis decreto unice ad Filii sui plenissimum et sufficientissimum meritum respexit, quo etiam permotus est, ut quosdam peccatores, illos scilicet solos et singulos ad vitam aeternam eligeret, quos in luce omniscientiae suae ab aeterno praevidit, meritum Christi vera fide amplexuros, et in fide illa usque ad novissimum vitae halitum perseveraturos esse: adeoque meritum Christi est causa impulsiva externa electionis, non quatenus illud spectatur tantum ratione acquisitionis (sic enim ad omnes pertinet homines); sed etiam ratione finalis applicationis, quae fit per fidem perseverantem; quo respectu meritum Christi solis renatis prodest.

Probatur assertum 1) ex Ephes. I, 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. Benedictus Deus et Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui benedixit nobis omni benedictione spirituali in supercaelestibus in Christo: quemadmodum elegit nos in ipso ante fundationem mundi, ut simus sancti et irreprehensibiles coram ipso in dilectione: dum praefinivit nos in adoptionem filiorum per Iesum Christum in seipsum, iuxta beneplacitum voluntatis suae. In quo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ipsius, remissionem peccatorum iuxta divitias gratiae ipsius. Est hoc dictum scripturae classicum, sive propria sedes doctrinae de electione hominum ad vitam aeternam. Quamobrem ex hoc oraculo sequentia ducimus argumenta.

Argumentamur a): Quicunque a Deo ad aeternam gloriam electi sunt propter Christum mediatorem, ad illorum electionem Deus merito Christi motus et impulsus est. Atqui renati et cetera. Ergo. Maior patet; quia propter cuius meritum decretum aliquod formatur, illum oportet esse vi illius meriti causam impulsivam. Nam causa meritoria est, quae sub ratione meriti, vel demeriti, causam efficientem ad dandum praemium, vel irrogandam poenam movet et impellit. Minor liquet; quia Paullus dicit, nos esse a Deo electos in Christo, hoc est propter Christum. Nam graeca particula ἐν frequenter in sacris litteris idem valet, quod propter, ut Matth. VI, 7. ubi sermo est de ethnicis: putant, se ἐν πολυλογίᾳ αὐτῶν, propter multiloquium suum, exauditum iri; Act. VII, 29. Fugit Moses ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τούτῳ, propter sermonem hunc, cum nimirum altercantium Israëlitarum, inter quos pacem conciliatum iuerat, alter diceret: Num tu me vis interimere, quemadmodum heri Aegyptium illum. Eph. III, 13. Peto, ne segnefcatis ἐν θλίψεσι μου, propter afflictiones meas. Quin etiam ab ipso Apostolo particula ἐν per διὰ redditur, v. 5.

Dicis: I. Verba Paulli exponi possunt: Electi sumus in Christo tanquam capite. Resp. Vox, caput, tum ordinem ad membra, tum causalitatem notat. Si sumatur caput causaliter; vere dicimur electi in Christo tanquam capite, fundamento et causa impulsiva electionis. Sin sumatur tantum ordinaliter, quod scil. Christus in signo rationis divinae prius electus, et nos posterius praedestinati fimus; illa expositio est incommoda ideo, quod Christus in communi perditionis massa nunquam fuit; adeoque eadem nunquam segregatus et electus est.

Dicis: II. Verba Apostoli exponi possunt: Electi sumus, ut simus in Christo, ut notetur causa finalis, non impulsiva. Resp. Si Apostolus dixisset: Electi sumus, εἰς τὸν Χριστὸν, illa expositio textui congrua foret. At dicit: Electi sumus in Christo, tanquam mediatore, cuius meritum Deum ad eligendum quosdam homines impulit.

Dicis: III. Graeca particula ἐν, pro διὰ quidem est posita, sed notat causam electionis efficientem, et sensus fit: Deus Pater elegit nos per Christum, Filium suum coaeternum, adeoque Christus non ut mediator, sed ut Deus consideratur. Resp. Deus eligens a Christo, in quo, ut fundamento, electio facta est, aperte distinguitur, et in toto contextu Apostolus de Christo non qua Deo tantum, sed qua θεανθρώπῳ et mediatore loquitur, in quo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ipsius, v. 7. sanguinem ipsius, v. 7. Dicis: IV. Sensus Apostoli est: Deus elegit nos esse in ipso sanctos & irreprehensibiles. Resp. Hoc interpretamentum vim facit textui, eidem aliquid detrahendo, quod ad complendum sensum necessarium est.

Nam in textu Paullino legitur pronomen ἡμᾶς, bis positum, & interiecta distinctionis nota construitur semel cum verbo ἐξελέξατο, iterum: cum verbo εἶναι, hoc modo, ἐξελέξατο ἡμᾶς ἐν αὐτῷ πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, εἶναι ἡμᾶς ἁγίους. At secundum iam recensitum interpretamentum nota distinctionis esset tollenda, perinde ac si pronomen ἡμᾶς semel tantum esset positum, verbisque traiectis sic esset legendum: ἐξελέξατο ἡμᾶς εἶναι ἐν αὐτῷ ἁγίους i. e. elegit nos esse in ipso sanctos.

Dicis: V. Elegit nos Deus in Christo, scilicet adoptandos. Resp. Hæc expositio textui, præter necessitatem, aliquid superaddit.

Quibus accurate pensitatis manifestum est, solam nostram explicationem, quam supra dedimus, contextui esse conformem, & genuinam Apostoli mentem exprimere.

Quid? quod nostram interpretationem calculo suo comprobent confessio Helvetica, cap. X. confessio Anhaltina, cap. XI. & haud pauci doctores ecclesiæ reformatæ, quos commemorat & laudat Dn. D. HOLZEVSIVS dissertat. de prædestinat. p. 133. seqq.

Argumentamur b): Quicunque est causa meritoria benedictionis spiritualis, ille est causa meritoria æternæ electionis: Atqui Christus &c. Benedictus Deus & Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui benedixit nobis omni benedictione spirituali in supracælestibus, in Christo; καθὼς, sicut nos elegit in ipso. Particula emphatica καθὼς, quemadmodum, inquit Apostolus, Deum in Christo nobis benedicere eodem modo, quo nos in eodem elegit.

At benedicit nobis Deus in Christo, vt fonte & causa meritoria benedictionis, Gen. XII, 3. c. XVIII, 18. c. XXII, 18. Act. IV, 12. Gal. III, 13. 14. Ergo nos in Christo, vt fonte & causa meritoria electionis ad salutem æternam elegit.

Dicis: Christus est quidem causa meritoria electionis, sed non causa impulsiva. Resp. Causa meritoria sub impulsiva, vt species sub genere comprehenditur: omnis namque causa meritoria est impulsiva, licet non omnis causa impulsiva sit meritoria.

Hæc definitur, quod fit causa, quæ sub ratione meriti causam efficientem ad dandum præmium impellit. Itaque omnis causa meritoria essentialiter est impulsiva.

Argumentamur c): Quoscunque Deus prædestinavit in adoptionem filiorum per Iesum Christum in seipsum, illos intuitu meriti Christi elegit: Atqui homines renatos &c. Ergo. Maior probatur, quia prædestinatio ad υἱοθεσίαν consummatam, quæ datur in cœlo, est electio ad vitam æternam, quippe illa consummata & gloriosa υἱοθεσία hereditatem cœlestem includit, aut infert.

Argumentamur d): Quicunque est causa impulsiva, ob quam Deus nos diligit, ille est causa impulsiva, ob quam Deus nos ad vitam æternam elegit: Atqui Christus &c. Maior probatur: quia dilectio interne Deum ad eligendum quosdam homines impulit ita, vt nullus sit electus, qui non dilectus.

At non dilexit Deus quosdam homines absolute citra intuitum Christi. Minor patet e versu 6. in laudem gloriosæ gratiæ suæ, in qua gratos nos fecit in dilecto.

Periissent peccatores, nisi Deo grati redditi fuissent.

Nulla creatura poterat illos Deo gratos efficere; quia nulla creatura poterat delere peccatum, ex quo omnis resultat inimicitia. Quare ne miseri perirent peccatores, Deus gloriosa sua benevolentia eosdem ex inimicis fecit amicos, sibique gratos, misso in carnem Filio suo dilectissimo, in quo, per quem, & propter quem peccatores diliguntur.

Argumentamur e): In quo habemus remissionem peccatorum, ille est causa fundamentalis nostræ electionis: Atqui in Christo &c. Ergo. Maior liquet; quia Deus elegit peccatores catores non quatenus sunt exosi, sed quatenus reconciliati, gratiae Deo redditi.

Praesupponit ergo decretum electionis, in signo rationis, decretum divinum de homine justificando.

Minor patet, e v.

7. In quo (Christo) habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ipsius, remissionem peccatorum juxta divitias gratiae ipsius.

Prob.

2) ex conformitate decreti & executionis. Quidquid est causa impulsiva, propter quam Deus in tempore quibusdam hominibus salutem confert, illud est causa impulsiva, propter quam Deus ab aeterno quosdam homines ad salutem elegit: Atqui meritum Christi est causa impulsiva, propter quam Deus in tempore quibusdam hominibus salutem confert.

Ergo meritum Christi est causa impulsiva, ob quam Deus quosdam homines ad vitam aeternam elegit. Maior nititur canone universali: Eadem sunt causae impulsivae decreti, quae sunt causae impulsivae executionis decreti; cujus veritas 1) ex inductione exemplorum patet.

Quando magistratus cives suos, dominus servos, parens liberos, magister discipulos, imperator milites, alios quidem ob praestitam in officio diligentiam praemiis ornat, alios vero ob delicta poenis afficit; facile colligitur, diligentiam & delicta, vti causae fuerint impellentes ad distribuenda praemia & poenas, ita etiam fuisse causas impellentes ad praemia & poenas decernendas. Quia Sodomae peccata clamantia causa fuerunt, cur Deus eam male exciderit, Gen.

XIX, 20. concludimus haud ex vano, Deum propter illa peccata decrevisse eam perdere. 2) Easdem esse causas impulsivas decreti & executionis eius, probatur a priori, cum ex ipsius causae impulsivae, tum etiam ex actionum voluntariarum natura.

Ex natura causae impulsivae: nam haec est natura & indoles causae impulsivae, qua quis ad exercitium alicujus actus externi movetur, vt voluntatem vel appetitum causae efficientis moueat ad volendum vel appetendum id, quod causa efficiens per actum externum exsequitur. Idem quoque ex natura actionum voluntariarum perspicitur.

Nam has quemadmodum qui agit, etiam vult agere, & prius saltem natura est velle agere, quam agere; ita etiam qua causa permotus quis agit, eadem permotus vult agere, & prius saltem natura est, aliqua causa permotum velle agere, quam aliqua causa permotum agere. Minorem confirmant sacrae litterae, quae docent, quod non sit in alio salus, quam in Christo, Actor.

IV, 12. Si, cum essemus hostes, reconciliati fuimus Deo per mortem Filii ipsius: multo magis reconciliati salvabimur in vita eius, Rom.

V, 10. Non ponit Deus nos in iram, sed in possessionem salutis, per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, qui mortuus est pro nobis, vt, sive vigilemus, sive dormiamus, una cum ipso vivamus, 1 Thess.


### Quaest. VIII. What is the external impulsive cause of election?: V, 9

V, 9.

"Christ, though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered: and being made perfect, he became the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him," Heb. V, 8, 9.

Proved 3) from the foreknowledge of God. Election was made κατά πρόγνωσιν, according to foreknowledge, Rom.

VIII, 29; c. XI, 2;

1 Pet.

I, 2. But the object of that foreknowledge, according to which election was made, is Christ with his most holy merit, whence 1 Pet.

But the object of that foreknowledge, according to which the election was made, is Christ, with his most holy merit, whence 1 Peter.

I, 19, we are said to be redeemed with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot, who was foreknown (προγνωσμένοι) indeed before the foundation of the world.

From these arises the argument: Whatever election was made κατά πρόγνωσιν, or according to the foreknowledge of Christ, to be apprehended by true faith, that was not made from an absolute good pleasure without regard to Christ: But the election of fallen men to eternal glory, etc. Therefore. The major premise is evident; because that decree is called absolute which is conceived without respect to an external impulsive cause.

Proof.

Proved 4) From the condition of election.

Election is a work of immense love and mercy.

But God is not only merciful, but also just, and as his mercy [moves him] to will grace for us, so his justice, offended by our sins, [moves him] to will punishment for sinners, his justice, offended by our sins, to will for sinners pun

for it was moving. It was necessary, therefore, that the merit of Christ should intervene, by which satisfaction might be made to the injured justice, which, joined to the divine mercy, together with it constitutes the complete rationale of willing, by which God is moved in our mode of understanding, so that, while immutable justice is preserved, He wills sinners to be saved. For we have been reconciled to God by the death of His Son. Rom. V, 10.

There is an antithesis of 1) the Socinians, who plainly deny the satisfaction of Christ; 2) of certain Papists and Reformed, who posit an absolute decree of election. For that not all doctors of the Reformed church exclude the merit of Christ from the eternal decree of predestination, the Lord D. Holzevs, Professor at Frankfurt, shows at length in his dissertation on predestination, p. 133 and following . Arguments are objected to us:

I. Whoever are elected out of mere grace, they are not elected on account of the merit of Christ: But the faithful are, etc. Therefore. The major is evident; because mere grace is opposed to all merit. The minor is proved from Eph. I, 5. God predestined us, according to the good pleasure of His will. Response. Mere grace is opposed to our own merits of works, not to the merit of Christ. For the Apostle says, v. 6. ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ, He made us acceptable to Himself in the Beloved, Christ. The Apostle therefore understands an ordered good pleasure, not an absolute one.

Instance: But the Apostle asserts that the grace of God choosing is simply absolute and free, saying, Rom. IX, 18. God has mercy on whom He wills: and whom He wills, He hardens. Response. Chapter IX of the epistle to the Romans primarily and first deals with the justification of the sinner through faith in Christ; yet subsequently and by a ready consequence the words of the Apostle can be applied to the eternal decree of election. For in the same way that God justifies sinners in time, in the same way He decreed to justify them. These things being posited, we say that the grace of God justifying and choosing is indeed free, but not simply absolute. It is free from the necessity of obligation, both because no law obligated God to the commiseration of the fallen human race (for it was in God's power to receive fallen man into grace, or to punish him without hope of pardon); and because the economy of salvation, to be obtained through faith in Christ, depends on the most free will of God. It is not simply absolute; because it is founded in the merit of Christ, and restricted to a certain order (τάξιν) of means, to which God Himself most freely bound Himself. Grace was given to us in Christ before the ages of time, says the Apostle, 2 Tim. I, 9.

II. If we are elected on account of the merit of Christ, election will be universal: The consequent is false: Therefore the antecedent is also. Response. Distinguish between the merit of Christ viewed in terms of acquisition, and considered in terms of application, or insofar as it is apprehended by faith. In the former way, the merit of Christ is indeed universal, but the application is not made by all.

…III. Whatever is performed in time, that cannot be the meritorious or impulsive cause of an eternal decree: But the merit of Christ is, etc. Therefore. The major is proved; because nothing can exercise the function of a cause, unless it exists: & every cause is prior to its effect. But the merit of Christ did not exist from eternity: therefore it could not be the cause of the eternal decree. Resp. Distinguish between the merit of Christ foreseen, and actually performed, or fulfilled by the work itself. Viewed in the former way, it is the cause of eternal election; considered in the latter… way, it is the meritorious cause of salvation being exhibited and conferred upon us. Moreover, that not every cause is prior to its caused [effect] in terms of real existence, is evident from the final cause. Hence the end is said to be first not by reason of existence, but only by reason of intention; by reason of existence, however, and in execution, it is the last. The impulsive cause exercises the function of a cause, not according to its real being, like a physical efficient cause, but according to its objective being, and as known by the intellect of the principal agent. From this it follows that the merit of Christ profited the fathers of the O.T. for salvation; because it was foreknown by God from eternity, although at that time it had not been actually performed. Indeed, even the sins of the unfaithful are, by the consensus of all, the cause of the eternal decree of reprobation, in that they are the object of divine omniscience, and through it are objectively presented to the divine will from eternity under the aspect of evil, although they were committed in time.

IV. Whoever is himself predestined, he is not the impulsive cause of our election. But Christ &c. Therefore. The major is evident; because he who is predestined is indeed the object of eternal election, but not the impulsive cause. The minor is evident from 1 Pet. I, 20. Resp. In the cited passage Christ is called προεγνωσμένος, foreknown, not προωρισμένος, predestined. He is called foreknown, because our election was made κατὰ πρόγνωσιν, according to the foreknowledge of the mediator Christ, who strictly speaking is not elected; because election is of man, who is subject to eternal death on account of sin, destined out of mere mercy to eternal life. But Christ was never subject to eternal damnation on account of sin.

V. Whatever is a medium of execution, or of actual salvation, that is not the impulsive cause of the eternal decree of predestination. But the merit of Christ &c. Therefore. The major is proved; because the media of salvation are distinguished from the causes and principles of salvation. And whatever is only a medium of execution cannot be the cause of an eternal decree, since it is an immediate act of the divine will. The minor is clear; because the merit of Christ is commonly called the medium by which divine justice was satisfied, so that eternal salvation might be conferred upon us. Resp. A medium of salvation, taken strictly, is an instrument offering or receiving salvation. The offering media are the word of God and the sacraments: the receiving medium is faith in Christ. The merit of Christ cannot be added to these, because it is the principal impulsive cause of salvation. But if medium is taken loosely, so that it also includes the meritorious cause within its scope, the major proposition of the argument is false, for the reason that the meritorious cause of salvation is an impulsive cause, which moved God both to decree and to give salvation, on account of the perpetual harmony of the decree and its execution itself.

VI. Whatever is an independent, immobile, and immutable principle, of that there is no impulsive cause: The divine will is an independent, immobile, and immutable principle: Therefore. The major is evident; because whatever has a cause, that depends upon it; whatever is impelled, is moved and changed. The minor is evident; because the will of God is in reality the very essence of God, independent, immobile, and immutable. Resp. Distinguish between a cause formally, and virtually causing. The former is a true and real cause actually influencing the effect: the latter is a certain reason a priori, having itself in the manner of a cause in our mode of conceiving. We do not assert that the merit of Christ is the impulsive cause of the eternal decree of predestination properly so …called and formally causing, which would move and impel the will of God to elicit the act of the decree of election. (For it is agreed among all that the decrees of God are not acts really distinct from the divine will, and elicited by it; but are the very will of God conceived in the manner of an act with the connoted objects, about which it is concerned, and consequently no cause of them properly so called can be given). But we say that the merit of Christ is the cause of election, less properly so called, and virtually causing, which is only a reason a priori, and in our mode of conceiving behaves like an impulsive cause, by whose intuition the divine will, without true and real motion of itself, and without an elicited act, wills and decrees our salvation, not otherwise than if it were its properly called impulsive cause: just as it would also be a properly called impulsive cause if the divine decree acknowledged or admitted such a cause. See D. MVSAEVS, dissertation on the eternal decree of predestination, §. 7. p. 3.

Latin:

V, 9.

10. Christus, licet et filius, didicit tamen ex iis, quae passus est, obedientiam: & consummatus, factus obedientibus ipsi omnibus auctor salutis aeternae, Hebr. V, 8. 9. Prob.

3) ex praevisione Dei. Electio facta est κατά πρόγνωσιν, secundum praenotionem, Rom.

VIII, 29. c. XI, 2.

1 Petr.

I, 2.

At praevisionis illius, iuxta quam electio facta est, obiectum est Christus, cum sanctissimo suo merito, vnde 1 Petr.

I, 19. dicimur redempti pretioso sanguine Christi, tanquam agni immaculati & incontaminati, praecogniti (προγνωσμένοι) quidem ante fundationem mundi. Nascitur ex his argumentum: Quaecunque electio facta est κατά πρόγνωσιν, seu secundum praevisionem Christi, vera fide apprehendendi, illa non est facta ex absoluto beneplacito citra intuitum Christi: Atqui electio hominum lapsorum ad aeternam gloriam &c.

Ergo. Maior est evidens; quia illud decretum dicitur absolutum, quod conceptum est citra respectum causae externae impulsivae.

Prob.

4) Ab electionis conditione.

Electio est opus immensae dilectionis & misericordiae.

At Deus non solum misericors, sed & iustus est, & vt misericordia ipsius ad volendum nobis gratiam, ita iustitia ipsius, peccatis nostris laesa, ad volendum peccatoribus poenam iustitia ipsius, peccatis noftris læfa, ad volendum peccatoribus pœ-

nam mouebat. Oportuit igitur interuenire meritum Christi, quo laxae iustitiae fieret satis, quod, misericordiae diuinae iunctum, vna cum illa constituit completam volendi rationem, qua Deus nostro intelligendi modo mouetur, vt salua iustitia immutabili peccatores velit saluos fieri. Reconciliati enim sumus Deo morte Filii ipsius. Rom. V, 10.

Antithesis est 1) Socinianorum, satisfactionem Christi plane infitiantium; 2) quorundam Pontificiorum & Reformatorum, decretum electionis absolutum statuentium. Nam non omnes doctores ecclesiae reformatae respectu meriti Christi ex aeterno praedestinationis decreto excludere, prolixe ostendit Dn. D. Holzevs. Professor Francof. in dissertat. de praedesti. nat. p. 133. & seqq. . Obiiciuntur nobis argumenta:

I. Quicunque electi sunt ex mera gratia, illi non sunt electi propter meritum Christi: Atqui fideles &c. Ergo. Maior est euidens; quia mera gratia opponitur omni merito. Minor prob. ex Eph. I, 5. Deus praedestinauit nos, secundum beneplacitum voluntatis suae. Resp. Mera gratia opponitur nostro uni operum meritis, non merito Christi. Dicit enim Apostolus, v. 6. ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ, gratos nos sibi fecit in dilecto, Christo. Intelligit ergo Apostolus beneplacitum ordinatum, non absolutum.

Instantia: Sed Apostolus asserit, gratiam Dei eligentis esse simpliciter absolutam & liberam, inquiens, Rom. IX, 18. Deus, cuius vult, miseretur: & quem vult, indurat. Resp. Cap. IX. epist. ad Romanos πρώτως & primo agit de iustificatione peccatoris per fidem in Christum; ἐπομένως tamen & per pronam consequentiam verba Apostoli ad aeternum electionis decretum applicari possunt. Etenim quo modo Deus in tempore peccatores iustificat, eodem modo ipsos iustificare decreuit. Quibus praestitutis, dicimus, gratiam Dei iustificantis & eligentis esse quidem liberam, sed non simpliciter absolutam. Libera est a necessitate obligationis, tum quia nullum ius Deum obligauit ad commiserationem generis humani lapsi (erat enim penes Deum, hominem lapsum in gratiam recipere, aut sine spe veniae punire); tum quia oeconomia salutis, per fidem in Christum impetranda, a voluntate Dei liberrima pendet. Simpliciter absoluta non est; quia est in merito Christi fundata, & ad certam mediorum τάξιν adstricta, ad quam Deus ipse se liberrime adstrinxit. Data est nobis gratia in Christo ante tempora saecularia, inquit Apostolus, 2 Tim. I, 9.

II. Si propter meritum Christi sumus electi, electio erit vniuersalis: Consequens est falsum: Ergo & antecedens. Resp. Dist. inter meritum Christi spectatum ratione acquisitionis, & consideratum ratione applicationis, siue quatenus fide perferendatur apprehenditur. Priori modo quidem vniuersale est meritum Christi, sed applicatio non fit ab omnibus.

III. Quidquid est praestitum in tempore, illud non potest esse causa meritoria, aut impulsiua aeterni decreti: Atqui meritum Christi &c. Ergo. Maior probatur; quia nihil potest exercere munus caussæ, nisi exsistat: & omnis caussa prior est effectu. At meritum Christi ab æterno non exstitit: ergo non potuit esse caussa æterni decreti. Resp. Dist. inter meritum Christi prævisum, & actu præstitum, sive opere ipso impletum. Priori modo spectatum, est caussa electionis æternæ; posteriori modo consideratum, est caussa meritoria salutis nobis exhibendæ & conferendæ. Ceterum non omnem caussam caussato priorem esse, qua exsistentiam realem, patet e caussa finali. Hinc finis dicitur primum non ratione exsistentiæ, sed tantum ratione intentionis; ratione exsistentiæ autem & in exsecutione ultimum est. Caussa impulsiva exercet munus caussæ, non secundum esse suum reale, sicut caussa efficiens physica, sed secundum esse objectivum, & intellectu agentis principalis cognitum. Inde fit, vt meritum Christi patribus V. T. profuerit ad salutem; quia ab æterno a Deo fuit præcognitum, licet id temporis non fuerit reapse præstitum. Quin peccata etiam infidelium sunt omnium consensu caussa æterni decreti reprobationis, eo quod obiectum sunt omniscientiæ diuinæ, & per eam voluntati diuinæ ab æterno sub ratione mali obiectiue exhibita, licet in tempore sint commissa.

IV. Quicunque ipse prædestinatus est, is non est caussa impulsiva nostræ electionis. Atqui Christus &c. Ergo. Maior constat; quia qui prædestinatus est, æternæ quidem electionis obiectum, non autem caussa impulsiva est. Minor patet ex 1 Petr. I, 20. Resp. Loco citato Christus dicitur προεγνωσμένος, præcognitus, non προωρισμένος, prædestinatus. Præcognitus dicitur, quia electio nostri facta est κατὰ πρόγνωσιν, secundum prænotionem mediatoris Christi, qui stricte loquendo non est electus; quia electio est hominis, propter peccatum æternæ morti obnoxii, ex mera misericordia destinati ad æternam vitam. At Christus propter peccatum æternæ damnationi nunquam obnoxius fuit.

V. Quidquid est medium exsecutionis, seu actualis saluationis, illud non est caussa impulsiva æterni prædestinationis decreti. Atqui meritum Christi &c. Ergo. Maior prob. quia media salutis caussis & principiis salutis contradistinguuntur. Et quidquid tantum est medium exsecutionis, non potest esse caussa æterni decreti, quippe quod est actus voluntatis diuinæ immediatus. Minor liquet; quia meritum Christi communiter vocatur medium, quo iustitiæ diuinæ satisfactum est, vt æterna salus nobis conferri queat. Resp. Medium salutis, stricte sumtum, est organon salutem offerens, vel recipiens. Media offerentia sunt verbum Dei & sacramenta: medium recipiens est fides in Christum. His accenseri nequit meritum Christi, quia est caussa salutis impulsiva principalis. At si medium laxe sumatur, vt ambitu suo etiam caussam meritoriam complectatur, maior argumenti propositio falsa est, eo, quod caussa salutis meritoria est caussa impulsiva, quæ Deum tum ad decernendam, tum ad dandam salutem mouit, ob perpetuam harmoniam decreti & ipsius exsecutionis.

VI. Quidquid est principium independens, immobile & immutabile, illius nulla datur caussa impulsiva: Voluntas diuina est principium independens, immobile & immutabile: Ergo. Maior constat; quia quidquid habet caussam, id ab ea dependet; quidquid impellitur, mouetur & mutatur. Minor patet; quia voluntas Dei reapse est ipsa essentia Dei independens, immobilis & immutabilis. Resp. Dist. inter caussam formaliter, & virtualiter caussantem. Illa est vera & realis caussa actu influens in effectum: hæc est ratio quædam a priori, nostro concipiendi modo se per modum caussæ habens. Non asserimus, meritum Christi esse caussam impulsivam æterni prædestinationis decreti proprie dictam & formaliter caussantem, quæ voluntatem Dei ad actum decreti electionis eliciendum moueat & impellat. (Constat enim inter omnes, decreta Dei non esse actus a voluntate diuina realiter distinctos, & ab ea elicitos; sed esse ipsam Dei voluntatem per modum actus cum connotatis obiectis, circa quæ versatur, conceptam, & consequenter nullam eorum caussam proprie dictam dari posse). Sed dicimus, meritum Christi esse electionis caussam minus proprie sic dictam, & virtualiter caussantem, quæ tantum sit ratio a priori, & nostro concipiendi modo se instar caussæ impulsiuæ habeat, cuius intuitu voluntas diuina, citra veram & realem sui motionem, citraque actum elicitum, salutem nostram velit & decernat, non secus, ac si proprie dicta eius caussa impulsiua esset: sicuti etiam proprie dicta caussa impulsiua futura esset, si decretum diuinum huiusmodi caussam agnosceret, vel admitteret. Vid. D. MVSAEVS dißertat. de æt. præd. decr. §. 7. p. 3.


### Question IX. Is the election of fallen men to eternal life made in consideration of faith?

The election of men, corrupted by sin, to eternal life was made by the most merciful God in view of faith in Christ a), persevering to the very end of life b).

Obs. Our theologians, in explaining the eternal decree of predestination, agree most amicably regarding the thing itself, teaching with great consensus that God, to whom even future things are objectively present, by the infinite light of his intellect foresaw from eternity the faith of certain men who had fallen into sin, and in view of faith in Christ foreseen, chose them for eternal salvation. They differ only in the manner of speaking and the use of technical terms.

Our theologians agree 1) that faith, foreseen from eternity, is in our mode of conceiving prior to the decree of election, and thus behaves toward it as a reason, by whose intuition we are chosen. For so teaches the Book of Concord on eternal predestination, declaration, p. 812. In this there is no doubt, that God most certainly and exactly foresaw before the times of the world and even today knows who from the number of those who are called would believe or would not believe: likewise who among the converted would persevere; and who after the fall would return, and who indeed, hardened, would perish. And in the epitome p. 619. In Christ the eternal election of God the Father is to be sought: For He in his eternal and divine counsel decreed that, besides those who acknowledge his Son Jesus Christ and truly believe in him, he wills to save no one.

They agree 2) that foreseen faith enters into the decree of election, not as a quality or act, nor by reason of any proper goodness, dignity, or perfection, but solely and entirely by reason of the object into which it is carried, and which it apprehends and applies to us, namely the merit of Christ. Excellently says D. AEGID. HVNNIVS, in the treatise on providence and predestination, vol. I. of works, fol. 826. Faith enters the mystery of election, not insofar as it is weighed in its own dignity, merit, or condition, as a certain quality, habit, or virtue, but only as it behaves relatively toward Christ, as the unique rock and foundation of eternal election.

They agree 3) that we are not chosen because of faith, but through faith. Skillfully, no less than truly, says D. BALTH. MEISN. in anthropology, decade II. disputation XIV. p. 159. We are chosen not to faith, as a term, not because of faith, as a merit, but through faith, as a medium, or in faith, as a part of the predestinatory order.

Our theologians differ in the manner of speaking and the use of terms of art. Some have not feared to call faith in Christ the cause of the decree of election. For so spoke the Wurttemberg theologians in the Mompelgart colloquy, p. 518. Faith in Christ is not of nature or our human powers, but the work of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, when faith is said to be the cause of election, it by no means tastes of the dogma of the Pelagians, who attributed to the powers of nature what only the Holy Spirit can perform. At first glance, the Formula of Concord, declaration p. 821, seems to contradict the Mompelgart colloquy. It is false, and fights with the word of God, when it is taught that not only the mercy of God and the unique most holy merit of Christ, but also something in us is a cause of divine election; because of which God predestines us to eternal life stinauerit.

But the mind of the Formula of Concord is: regarding election, apart from the mercy of God and the merit of Christ, which is to be apprehended by faith, there is given no cause on the part of man, which by its own merit, dignity, or value could have moved God, so that from eternity He chose us to eternal life. These things having been duly considered, D. Aegidius Hunnius in his tractate on providence and predestination, fol. 826, says: Faith enters into the mystery of election, not as a meritorious cause, on account of which God might choose us, but as an instrumental one. But indeed, since no one could object to this most consummate Theologian; the eternal decree of election is an immanent, immediate, and inorganic act of the divine will, proceeding from the will of God, without the intervention of any instrument: D. Aegid. Hunnius replied in the same place, fol. 676: Faith is not an instrument by which election itself is apprehended; but by which the grace of the choosing God is apprehended, and the merit of Christ, in which the election of salvation is founded; just as in justification faith is not said to apprehend justification itself, but the grace of the justifying God, obtained by the merit of Christ.

Others, therefore, to cut off every handle for caviling, preferred to call faith a condition of election, or a condition required on the part of the object to be chosen, or a part of the predestinarian order; among whom is D. Meisner in his Anthropologia, decad. II, disput. XIV, p. 153. When faith is called a cause of election, do not understand it as the principal, impelling, and meritorious cause, but only as the instrumental, and indeed not of the whole decree, but rather of a part, namely the merit of Christ, which faith apprehends.

For when it is made a cause of a part of the decree, hence in a popular mode of speaking it is called a cause of the decree itself. It is more convenient, however, to name faith either a condition of election, lest it be imagined to be absolute, or a part of the predestinarian order, which God from eternity beheld no less than the death of Christ.

Nay, D. Dannhauer in his Hodologia, phaenom. VII, p. 576, calls faith a testamentary condition, to which the testator and elector, God, looks. But indeed D. Musaeus observed in his dissertation on the eternal decree of predestination, § 65 ff., p. 47, that by these modes of speaking the respect or habit of faith toward the decree of election itself is not clearly expressed. The term of condition is indeed general, and insinuates the necessity of faith on the part of the man to be chosen; but whether faith in itself, as it is a habit or an act, or whether it becomes necessary by reason of the object which it apprehends, and how it stands toward the decree of election itself; by that it is not signified. Likewise, to be a part of the predestinarian order is something common to faith with other things included in the predestinarian order, nor can it be understood by the force of the words whether faith is included in it only as a medium of execution, or also as a cause or reason of the decree, and that a principal or less principal one.

Those who said that faith in Christ is the instrumental cause of the decree of election did not look so much to the habit of faith, as it precisely imports the decree of election, as to the habit which it imports for apprehending the merit of Christ, by whose intuition we are chosen. All these things having been weighed, D. Musaeus determined that faith, considered in order to the decree of predestination itself, is to be called the less principal impulsive cause or reason of the decree of election: The words of D. Musaeus are § 70, p. 50. Therefore, only the term of the less principal impulsive cause or reason expresses the habit of faith toward the decree of election fittingly, exactly, and without impropriety, and declares that 1) faith stands toward the decree of election as a reason for decreeing, or as a reason by whose intuition the will of God determined itself to choose these before those; yet 2) not by any of its own dignity, goodness, price, or value of another principal cause or impulsive reason; which is none other than the merit of Christ, which it apprehends and applies to us.

For in this consists the nature and concept of the less principal impulsive cause or reason, that it stands toward the will of the agent as a reason for willing, not by its own goodness, dignity, price, or value (which belongs only to the principal impulsive cause), but by the goodness, dignity, price, or value of another principal cause or impulsive reason.

D. Musaeus is followed closely by D. Scherzer in his Systema theologiae, loc. XVIII, p. 488 ff. D. FRIDER. BECHMANN in Instit. Theol. p. 953. D. CHRISTOPH. FRANCKIVS in Exercit. Anti-WENDEL. exerc. II. p. 85. D. BAYER in Compend. Theol. p. 153. Nor does D. BALTHAS. MEISNERVS differ regarding the matter in Anthropol. decad. II. disput. XIV. p. 153, saying: "It seems most convenient that faith not be considered separately, as a cause of election peculiar and distinct from the merit of Christ, but conjointly together with the merit itself apprehended; so that both, coupled together, constitute one impelling cause of election. For neither the merit without application, nor faith by itself, moved God to elect, but both combined in foreknowledge, that is, the merit of Christ apprehended by faith, or faith apprehending the merit of Christ." D.

MEISNER thus judging, the relation of faith to election is such as that which a cause or impulsive reason has to that of which it is said to be the cause; yet not insofar as it is by itself, or in itself absolutely, but insofar as it is considered on the part of the merit of Christ; so that the merit of Christ and faith do not stand toward the decree of election as two allied or partial causes, but as subordinate causes, and by way of a principal and instrumental cause (which, just as in the genus of efficient cause they produce an effect by one influx, although they are otherwise distinguished among themselves; so in the genus of impulsive cause they do not move the will of the agent to decree as if by an impulse).

See D. BAYER’S Compend. Theol. p. 958. Furthermore, it must not be passed over in silence that D. CALOVIVS has lawfully observed that faith in Christ confers nothing of its own dignity or activity to the decree of election, but here it behaves only passively, in System. Theol. tom. X. p. 632.

Yet the same author concedes that faith moves God not κυρίως (properly), ἀλλ’ ὀργανικῶς (but instrumentally), since even misery itself is commonly said to have moved God, the Father of mercies, to the reception of us into grace, justification, and election, which is a προκαταρκτική (procatarctic/preliminary) cause. Why, then, should not the same be said more appropriately of faith and the merit of Christ apprehended through faith, which in a more eminent way are προκαταρκτικαὶ (procatarctic) causes in this most holy matter? l. c. p. 655.

That faith behaves passively in the mystery of election is also taught by D. WILHELM. LYSERVS in System. Theol. p. 761, saying: "Faith here is not considered as a quality, but as a medium for receiving the sufferings of Christ."

D. FECHTIVS supports this, who in Syllog. Controu. Recent. disput. XIX says: "It is an instrument of apprehending the sufferings of the electing grace, analogous to a physical cause."

Nor does D. DANNHAVERVS seem to differ in Hodof. Phaenom. VII. p. 576:

"Faith here is not a work or merit, but a foreseen begging hand. Whence no glory, not even the least, is left to faith, which receives, does not give or acquire. Whence also God saw no active dignity in man, nothing good that was not from Him. Faith, although it is not the cause of the decree, is nevertheless the receptive instrument of salvation, foreseen in the decree."

He does not meanwhile deny that faith is a reason for the predestinatory decree; for it is not because God decreed to elect Paul that he believed; but because Paul constantly believed, and did not resist the means of salvation, he was elected by God to eternal life.

Let us also listen to D. HOLTZPVS, a Frankfurt theologian addicted to the Reformed religion, in Dissert. de Praedeft. p. 142, discoursing in the following manner: "Evangelicals agree 1) that faith enters into the decree of election and constitutes a part of the divine τάξεως (order); for as God in time saves no one without faith: so also He decreed to save no one without faith.

2) That faith is a necessary medium or condition for obtaining salvation. 4) That this faith, however, is not from us, but the principle of it is the grace of God. 5) That this faith is not an act of mercenaries, but an act of beggars."

It is evident from these that the authors speak in diverse ways about faith in Christ insofar as it enters into the mystery of election, but that they agree on the matter itself.

Wherefore, finally, we add the judgment of D. MVSAEVS, which is held in Praelect. in Form. Concord. p. 372.

"Whatever happens, and by whatever name faith may be designated, it will matter little to the subject.

For we shall move a dispute with no one regarding this matter; provided this remains for us:

That God from eternity chose only those whom He foresaw would finally believe in Christ; or that He chose them not absolutely, but in view of the merit of Christ to be apprehended by faith, or in view of faith in Christ, which they would have in time by His grace: ... or furthermore, whether faith be called a cause, or a condition, or an instrument, it will be the same to us. 1) From 2 Thess.

1) From 2 Thess. II, 13. God chose you from the beginning for salvation in sanctification of the Spirit & faith of the truth. Obs. a) God chose us ἀπ' ἀρχῆς, i. e. from eternity Eph. I, 4. b) In sanctification of the Spirit, i. e. through the regenerating grace of the Holy Spirit, by which faith is kindled and conferred. c) In faith of the truth, which is that which is held toward the evangelical truth, and relies upon it, and thus is true, solid, and saving faith. From these we argue: Whoever are chosen from the beginning for salvation in sanctification of the Spirit and faith of the truth, those very ones are not chosen absolutely, but with respect to faith that is to exist in time: But sinners, not spurning the means of grace, are chosen from the beginning &c. Therefore.

2) From James II, 5. Did not God choose the poor of this world, rich in faith?

The holy Apostle teaches that those chosen for eternal life are not all men, not the wealthy of this age, trusting in earthly riches, not certain men absolutely, viewed apart from the application of the merit of Christ, but the rich in faith, who indeed apprehend the riches of divine grace and the merit of Christ by faith. From which it is gathered that even languid faith is objectively opulent, in that it embraces Christ the highest good, just as the tender hand of an infant holds a most precious pearl.

3) Whoever are chosen in Christ, they are predestined to eternal life through faith relying on the merit of Christ: But sinners, anticipated by divine mercy, are chosen in Christ, Eph. I, 4. The major is evident; because where Christ is viewed in the business of conferring salvation upon us, there it is necessary that our faith be present, which embraces Christ; since without faith Christ does not actually profit a sinful man.

4) We are chosen according to the foreknowledge of God 1 Pet. 1, 2. Rom. VIII, 29. Therefore we are chosen according to the foreknowledge of faith, which is to embrace Christ. The consequence is proven: because the object of foreknowledge could not be other than faith in Christ, as the medium ordained for righteousness and salvation. For God in the eternal decree of election did not look upon our works, our dignity, our use of free will, but only the merit of Christ.

But because that is applied to no one, nor does it profit without faith; hence the eyes of the Lord are said to look upon faith, Jer. V, 3. For these phrases do not differ in the matter: we are chosen through the merit of Christ, to be apprehended by faith; and: we are chosen through faith, apprehending the merit of Christ.

For when we are said to be chosen in view of the merit of Christ, to be apprehended by faith, the merit of Christ behaves by way of that which is signified in the nominative case, faith is signified in the oblique case. But when I say that we are chosen in view of faith in Christ, then faith is signified in the nominative case, the merit of Christ is connoted in the oblique case, by way of an object. If, therefore, you look at the thing itself, no difference intervenes: For both are a cause of election.

The merit of Christ is the meritorious cause, and thus the principal impulsive cause. Faith in Christ is the instrumental cause of election, and thus the less principal impulsive cause. The former by the power of its own dignity and value; the latter by the power of the apprehended merit of Christ, moves God to choose miserable sinners.

5) Whoever do not please God without faith, they are not chosen without a view of faith: But men fallen into sin &c: Therefore.

The major is proven; because election is an outstanding argument of special grace, love, and divine good pleasure. Cf. Rom. XI, 5. Eph. I, 5. 6.

Minor proven from Heb. XI, 6. Without faith it is impossible to please God. 1 Cor. I, 21. It pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe. the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe. You say: We do not please God without the pursuit of good works, Luke 6:46, 1 Thess. 1:3, and yet we are not elected through works. Therefore, although we may not please God without faith, it does not follow that we are elected through faith.

I respond: We please God through faith, as the medium apprehending Christ, who is the most singularly beloved Son of God, in whom, through whom, and on account of whom, God loves us and elects us to eternal life.

The pursuit of good works, however, is not the medium of apprehending Christ, but is the fruit of the Spirit in the believing man.

We are therefore elected so that we may be holy and blameless, but we are not elected so that we may be in Christ through faith; but because, according to divine foreknowledge, we are in Christ through faith, kindled by the Holy Spirit through the Gospel: therefore God loved us in Christ our mediator and redeemer, and thus elected those loved to eternal life.

6) The elect are described in the scriptures: a) that they are μέλλοντες πιστεύειν, about to believe, or destined to believe in Christ, 1

Tim. 1:16, John 17:20. Therefore God elected from the assembly of sinners only those whom He foresaw would believe in Christ.

b) That they are children of God predestined to υἱοθεσίαν (adoption, consummate and glorious). Eph.

1: 5. But without faith no one is a child of God, John 1: 12. Therefore, without the intuition of faith, no one is predestined to υἱοθεσίαν.

Latin:

Electio hominum, peccato corruptorum, ad vitam æternam a Deo misericordissimo facta est intuitu fidei in Christum a), ad finem vsque vitæ perseuerantis b).

Obs. Theologi nostrates in explicando æterno prædestinationis decreto, qua rem ipsam, amicissime conspirant, magno consensu docentes, Deum, cui etiam futura obiectiue præsentia sunt, infinito luminę intellectus quorundam hominum, in peccatum prolapsorum, fidem ab æterno præuidisse, & intuitu fidei in Christum præcognitæ eosdem ad æternam salutem elegisse. Discrepant modo loquendi & vsurpatione terminorum technicorum.

Conueniunt nostrates Theologi 1) quod fides, ab æterno præuisa, nostro modo concipiendi prior sit decreto electionis, atque adeo ad illud se habeat vt ratio, cuius intuitu simus electi. Sic enim docet liber Concordiæ de æterna prædest. declarat. p. 812. In eo dubium nullum est, quin Deus certissimus & exactissimus ante tempora mundi præuiderit & hodie etiam norit, quinam ex numero eorum, qui vocantur, credituri, aut non credituri: item qui ex conuersis perseueraturi; & qui post lapsum reuersuri, qui vero indurati perituri essent. Et in epitome p. 619. In Christo æterna Dei Patris electio quærenda est: Is enim in æterno ac diuino suo consilio decreuit, quod præter hos, qui Filium eius Iesum Christum agnoscunt, & in eum vere credunt, neminem saluum facere velit.

Consentiunt 2) quod fides præuisa decretum electionis ingrediatur, non vt qualitas, aut actus est, nec ratione alicuius propriæ bonitatis, dignitatis, vel perfectionis, sed vnice & in solidum ratione obiecti, in quod fertur, quodque apprehendit & nobis applicat, scilicet meriti Christi. Præclare inquit D. AEGID. HVNNIVS, in tract. de prouid. & prædest. tom. I. oper. fol. 826. Fides ingreditur mysterium electionis, non quatenus in sua dignitate, merito aut conditione pensitatur, vt qualitas quædam, habitus, aut virtus, sed tantummodo, vt illa se habet relatiue ad Christum, tanquam vnicam æternæ electionis petram & fundamentum.

Consentiunt 3) quod non electi simus propter fidem, sed per fidem. Scite non minus, quam vere ait D. BALTH. MEISN. in anthropol. decad. II. disput. XIV. p. 159. Eligimur non ad fidem, vt terminum, non propter fidem, vt meritum, sed per fidem, tanquam medium, vel in fide, tanquam parte ordinis prædestinatorii.

Discrepant Theologi nostrates modo loquendi, & vsu terminorum artis. Nonnulli fidem in Christum decreti electionis caussam dicere, nihil veriti sunt. Ita enim locuti sunt Theologi Wurtenbergici in colloquio Mompelgartens. p. 518. Fides in Christum non est naturæ, aut nostrarum humanarum virium, sed Spiritus S. opus. Cum ergo fides caussa electionis esse dicitur; nequaquam Pelagianorum dogma sapit, qui naturæ viribus tribuerunt, quod solus Spiritus S. præstare potest. Colloquio Mompelgartensi prima fronte contradicere videtur Form. Concord. declarat. p. 821. Falsum est, & cum verbo Dei pugnat, cum docetur, quod non sola Dei misericordia, & vnicum sanctißimum Christi meritum, verum etiam aliquid in nobis caussa sit electionis diuinæ; propter quod nos Deus ad vitam æternam prædestinauerit.

At mens Form. Concord. est: electionis praeter Dei misericordiam & meritum Christi, fide apprehendendum, ex hominis parte nulla datur causa, quae merito suo, dignitate aut valore Deum mouerit, vt ab aeterno nos ad vitam aeternam elegerit. Quibus probe consideratis, D. AEGIDIVS HVNNIVS in tract. de prou. & praedest. fol. 826. ait: Fides ingreditur mysterium electionis, non vt causa meritoria, propter quam nos Deus eligat, sed vt instrumentalis. At vero cum nemo huic Theologo consummatissimo obiiceret; aeternum electionis decretum est actus voluntatis diuinae immanens, immediatus & inorganicus, proficiscens a voluntate Dei, sine vllius instrumenti interuentu: respondebat D. AEGID. HVNN. d. l. fol. 676. Fides non est instrumentum, quo ipsa apprehendatur electio; sed quo apprehenditur gratia eligentis Dei, & meritum Christi, in quo fundatur electio salutis; sicut in iustificatione fides non dicitur apprehendere ipsam iustificationem, sed gratiam iustificantis Dei, merito Christi partam.

Alii igitur, ad praecidendam omnem cauillandi ansam, maluerunt fidem appellare conditionem electionis, vel conditionem ex parte obiecti eligendi requisitam, vel partem ordinis praedestinatorii; quos inter est D. MEISNERVS in anthropol. decad, II. disput. XIV. p. 153. Cum fides electionis causa dicitur, non intelligas principalem, impellentem ac meritoriam, sed tantum instrumentalem, & quidem non totius decreti, sed potius partis, nempe meriti Christi, quod fides apprehendit.

Quum enim fit causa partis decreti, hinc populari loquendi modo causa dicitur ipsius decreti. Conuenientius tamen est, fidem nuncupare vel conditionem electionis, ne fingatur esse absoluta, vel partem ordinis praedestinatorii, quam Deus ab aeterno non minus, ac Christi mortem aspexerit.

Quin & D. DANNHAVERVS in hodof. phaenom. VII. p. 576. vocat fidem conditionem testamentariam, ad quam respicit testator ac elector Deus. At vero obseruauit D. MVSAEVS in dissertat. de aeterno praedest. decret. §. 65. sqq. p. 47. quod istis loquendi modis non luculenter exprimatur respectus, vel habitudo fidei ad ipsum decretum electionis. Nimirum terminus conditionis generalis est, & insinuat quidem necessitatem fidei ex parte hominis eligendi; an autem fides in se, vt habitus, vel actus est, an vero ratione obiecti, quod apprehendit, necessaria fit, & quomodo ad ipsum electionis decretum se habeat; eo non significatur. Perinde, esse partem ordinis praedestinatorii, commune quid est fidei cum aliis in ordine praedestinatorio inclusis rebus, neque an fides, vt medium exsecutionis tantum, an vero etiam vt causa, vel ratio decreti, eaque principalis, vel minus principalis, in eo includatur, ex vi vocum intelligi potest.

Causam decreti electionis instrumentalem qui fidem in Christum dixerunt, non tam respexerunt ad habitudinem fidei, quam praecise ad electionis decretum importat, quam ad habitudinem, quam importat ad apprehendendum meritum Christi, cuius intuitu sumus electi. Quibus omnibus expensis, D. MVSAEVS fidem, consideratam in ordine ad ipsum praedestinationis decretum, appellandam esse causam, vel rationem impulsiuam minus principalem decreti electionis, statuit: Verba D. MVSAEI sunt §. 70. p. 50. Solus igitur causae, siue rationis impulsivae minus principalis terminus exprimit habitudinem fidei ad electionis decretum congrue, exacte & absque improprietate, declaratque, quod 1) ad decretum electionis fides se habeat, vt ratio decernendi, siue vt ratio, cuius intuitu voluntas Dei se determinauerit, ad hos prae illis eligendos; nec tamen 2) vlla sua propria dignitate, bonitate, pretio aut valore alterius principalis causae, vel rationis impulsivae; quae non est alia, quam Christi meritum, quod apprehendit, nobisque applicat.

In hoc enim consistit causa, siue rationis impulsivae minus principalis natura & conceptus, quod se habeat ad voluntatem agentis ratio volendi, non sua propria bonitate, dignitate, pretio aut valore (quod solius causae impulsivae principalis est), sed bonitate, dignitate, pretio aut valore alterius principalis causae, seu rationis impulsivae.

D. MVSAEVM κατά πόδα sequuntur D. SCHERZER. in systen. theol. loc. XVIII. p. 488. sqq. D. FRIDER. BECHMANN. in instit. theol. p. 953. D. CHRISTOPH. FRANCKIVS in exercit. Anti-WENDEL. exerc. II. p. 85. D. BAYER. in compend. theol. p. 153. Neque quoad rem diffentit D. BALTHAS. MEISNERVS in anthropol. decad. II. disput. XIV. p. 153. inquiens: Conuenientissimum videtur, fidem non considerari seorsum, vt caussam electionis peculiarem a merito Christi distinctam, sed coniunctim vna cum ipso merito apprehenso; vt sic vtrumque copulatum vnam electionis caussam impellentem constituat. Neque enim meritum fine applicatione, neque fides per se mouit Deum ad eligendum, sed vtrumque in praescientia coniunctum, hoc est meritum Christi, fide apprehensum, vel fides meritum Christi apprehendens.

Censente itaque D. MEISNERO, fidei habitudo ad electionem talis est, qualem habet caussa, vel ratio impulsiva ad id, cuius caussa esse dicitur; nec tamen quatenus ipsa seorsum, aut in se absolute, sed quatenus ex parte meriti Christi consideratur; ita vt non velut duae caussae sociae, aut partiales, sed tanquam caussae subordinatae, & per modum caussae principalis & instrumentalis (quae sicut in genere caussae efficientis vno influxu producunt effectum, licet inter se alias distinguantur; ita in genere caussae impulsivae non velut impulsu moueant voluntatem agentis ad decernendum) sese habeant meritum Christi, & fides ad decretum electionis.

Vid. D. BAYERI compend. theol. p. 958. Ceterum silentio praetereundum non est, D. CALOVIVM fol. licite obseruasse, quod fides in Christum ad decretum electionis nil propriae dignitatis, aut activitatis conferat, sed hic tantum passiue se habeat, in system. theol. tom. X. p. 632.

Concedit tamen idem, quod fides Deum moueat non κυρίως, ἀλλ’ ὀργανικῶς, cum & ipsa miseria Deum, patrem misericordiae, mouisse ad nostri in gratiam receptionem, iustificationem & electionem, communiter dicatur, quae est caussa προκαταρκτική. Quidni ergo potius id de fide & merito Christi per fidem apprehenso dicendum, quae eminentiori modo sunt caussae προκαταρκτικαὶ in sanctissima hac caussa? l. c. p. 655.

Fidem in mysterio electionis se habere passiue, docet etiam D. WILHELM. LYSERVS in system. theol. p. 761. inquiens: Fides here non consideratur vt qualitas, sed vt passuum Christi recipiendi medium.

Suffragatur D. FECHTIVS, qui in syllog. controu. recent. disput. XIX. ait, est instrumentum apprehendendi gratiae eligentis passuum, caussa physica analogum.

Neque diffentire videtur D. DANNHAVERVS in hodof. phaenom. VII. p. 576.

Fides hic non est opus, aut meritum, sed manus mendica praeuisa. Vnde nihil gloriae vel minimae relinquitur fidei, quae accipit, non donat, aut acquirit. Vnde etiam nihil dignitatis actiuae Deus in homine vidit, nihil boni, quod non esset ex ipso. Fides, tametsi non sit caussa decreti, tamen est instrumentum salutis receptiuum, in decreto praevisum.

Non diffitetur interim, quod fides sit ratio decreti praedestinatorii; non enim quia Deus decrevit Paullum eligere, creditit; sed quia Paullus constanter credidit, ac mediis salutis non restitit, a Deo ad vitam aeternam electus est.

Aufcultemus etiam D. HOLTZPVS. Theologum Francofurtensem, reformatae addictum religioni, in dissert. de praedeft. p. 142. sequenti ratione discurrentem: Consentiunt Euangelici 1) fidem decretum electionis ingredi, & partem τάξεως diuinae constituere; vt enim Deus in tempore neminem sine fide saluat: ita quoque neminem sine fide seruare decreuit.

2) Fidem esse necessarium medium, siue conditionem ad obtinendam salutem. 4) Fidem hanc tamen non ex nobis esse, sed principium eius esse gratiam Dei. 5) Fidem hanc non esse actum mercenariorum, sed actum mendicorum.

Dispalescit ex his, auctores de fide in Christum, quatenus mysterium electionis ingreditur, diuersimode loqui, qua rem ipsam autem consentire.

Quamobrem denique iudicium D. MVSAEI, quod habetur in praelect. in Ferm. Concord. p. 372. addimus.

Quidquid fit, & quocunque nomine fides indigitetur, parum ad rem faciet.

Nos enim nemini hac de re litem mouebimus; modo hoc nobis remaneat.

Deum ab aeterno elegisse eos tantum, quos praevidit in Christum finaliter credituros; sive elegisse eos non absolute, sed intuitu meriti Christi fide apprehendendi, vel intuitu fidei in Christum, quam in tempore eius gratia essent habituri:... sive praeterea fides dicatur causa, sive conditio, sive instrumentum, nobis perinde erit.

1) Ex 2. Thess. II, 13. Elegit vos Deus ab initio ad salutem in sanctificatione Spiritus & fide veritatis. Obs. a) Deus nos elegit ἀπ' ἀρχῆς, i. e. ab aeterno Eph. I, 4. b) In sanctificatione Spiritus, h. c. per gratiam Spiritus S. regenerantem, qua fides accenditur & confertur. c) In fide veritatis, quae scilicet veritati evangelicae habetur, eique innititur, adeoque vera, solida & salvifica fides est. Ex his argumentamur: Quicunque electi sunt ab initio ad salutem in sanctificatione Spiritus & fide veritatis, illi ipsi non sunt electi absolute, sed cum respectu fidei in tempore exstiturae: Atqui peccatores, media gratiae non spernentes, electi sunt ab initio &c. Ergo.

2) Ex Iac. II, 5. Nonne Deus elegit pauperes huius mundi divites in fide?

Docet S. Apostolus, ad vitam aeternam electos esse non homines omnes, non opulentes huius saeculi, terrenis divitiis confidentes, non quosdam homines absolute, citra applicationem meriti Christi spectatos, sed divites in fide, qui nimirum divitias gratiae divinae & meriti Christi fide apprehendunt. E quibus colligitur, etiam fidem languidam obiective esse opulentam, eo quod Christum summum bonum amplectitur, perinde, ac tenella manus infantis vel pretiosissimam margaritam tenet.

3) Quicunque electi sunt in Christo, illi ad vitam aeternam praedestinati sunt per fidem merito Christi innixam: Atqui peccatores, misericordia divina praeuenti, electi sunt in Christo, Eph. I, 4. E, Maior constat; quia vbi in negotio salutis nobis conferendae conspicitur Christus, ibi nostra adsit fides, quae Christum complectitur, necesse est; quoniam sine fide Christus homini peccatori actu non prodest.

4) Electi sumus secundum praescientiam Dei 1 Petr. 1, 2. Rom. VIII, 29. Ergo electi sumus secundum praenotionem fidei, Christum amplexurae. Consequentia probatur: quia praecognitionis obiectum aliud esse non potuit, quam fides in Christum, tanquam medium ad iustitiam & salutem ordinatum. Neque enim Deus in aeterno electionis decreto respexit nostra opera, nostram dignitatem, nostram liberi arbitrii usum, sed solum Christi meritum.

Quia vero illud nemini applicatur, nec prodest absque fide; hinc oculi domini respicere dicuntur fidem, Ier. V, 3. Neque enim quod rem differunt hae phrases: electi sumus per meritum Christi, fide apprehendendum; &: electi sumus per fidem, meritum Christi apprehendentem.

Nam quando dicimur electi intuitu meriti Christi, fide apprehendendi, meritum Christi habet se per modum eius, quod significatur in casu recto, fides significatur in casu obliquo. Quando autem dico, nos esse electos intuitu fidei in Christum, tunc fides significatur in casu recto, meritum Christi in casu obliquo connotatur, per modum obiecti. Rem ipsam ergo si spectes, nihil intercedit discriminis: Vtrumque enim est causa electionis.

Meritum Christi est causa meritoria, adeoque causa impulsiva principalis. Fides in Christum est causa electionis instrumentalis, atque adeo causa impulsiva minus principalis. Illud vi propriae dignitatis & valoris; haec vi meriti Christi apprehensi, Deum ad eligendum peccatores miseros permouet.

5) Quicunque Deo sine fide non placent, illi sine intuitu fidei non sunt electi: Atqui homines in peccatum prolapsi &c: Ergo.

Maior probatur; quia electio est eximium specialis gratiae, dilectionis & beneplaciti diuini argumentum. Conf. Rom. XI, 5. Eph. I, 5. 6.

Minor prob. ex Hebr. XI, 6. Sine fide impossibile est placere Deo. 1 Cor. I, 21. Complacuit Deo per stultitiam praeconii saluare credentes. stultitiam præconii faluare credentes. Dicis: Deo non placemus absque studio bonorum operum, Luc. VI, 46. 1 Thess. I, 3. & tamen per opera non sumus electi. Ergo licet non placeamus Deo fine fide: non tamen sequitur, nos esse electos per fidem.

Resp. Placemus Deo per fidem, tanquam medium apprehendens Christum, qui est Dei Filius singularissime dilectus, in quo, per quem, & propter quem, Deus nos diligit, & ad vitam aeternam eligit.

Studium autem bonorum operum non est medium Christum apprehendendi, sed est fructus Spiritus in homine credente.

Sumus igitur electi, vt simus sancti & irreprehensibiles, non autem sumus electi, vt simus in Christo per fidem; sed quia iuxta praescientiam diuinam sumus per fidem, a Spiritu S. per euangelium accensam, in Christo: ideo Deus nos in Christo mediatore & redemptore nostro dilexit, & sic delectos elegit ad vitam aeternam.

Eph. I, 4. 5. 6. 7. 6) Electi in scripturis describuntur:

a) quod sint μέλλοντες πιστεύειν, credituri in Christum, 1 Tim. I, 16. Io. XVII, 20. Ergo Deus e coetu peccatorum solos illos elegit, quos in Christum credituros praeuidit.

b) Quod sint filii Dei praedestinati eis υἱοθεσίαν (consummatam & gloriosam).

Eph. I, 5. Sed sine fide nemo est filius Dei, Io. I, 12. Ergo fine intuitu fidei nemo est υἱοθεσίαν praedestinatus.


### Question IX. Is the election of fallen men to eternal life made in consideration of faith?: 7) Our assertion is proven from the harmony, or conformity, of the eternal decree of election and the execution of the same

7) Our assertion is proven from the harmony, or conformity, of the eternal decree of election and the execution of the same.

Of which, as a cause or impulsive reason of less importance, God saves us in time, by the intuition of that same cause or reason of less importance, He decreed from eternity to confer salvation upon us in time: But faith in Christ is that, by the intuition of which, as a cause or impulsive reason of less importance, God saves us in time: Therefore.

The major premise is evident; because the execution of salvation in time is the mirror of the eternal decree.

For the temporal mode of saving cannot be other than that which is defined in the eternal decree of God; otherwise, divine constancy, immutability, and wisdom would waver. The minor premise is proven from those places of scripture where it is said that one is justified by faith, from faith, through faith.

Rom. 3:28, Hab. 2:4, Eph. 2:8, Heb. 10: 38. Where a certain causality of faith is ascribed in order to our salvation, and that not of an efficient or principal impulsive cause; but instrumental, and of a less important impulsive cause, or, that God, who saves, is moved to that end, that He might will to save, through faith, not indeed considered by reason of its own dignity (for we are not said to be saved on account of faith); but insofar as it apprehends the merit of Christ, so that by its intuition God might will to save and does save.

Proof b. By the name of faith, which we call the motive reason of election, is not understood faith πρόσκαιρος, or temporary, which fails in the time of temptation, or is extinguished by sins against conscience, but persevering faith, which the Apostle calls μέχρι τέλους βεβαίαν, firm unto the end, Heb. 3:6. Moreover, persevering faith is called not only that which never fails, but also that which is rekindled in the heart of man before the end of life, and lasts until the end, even if a man has fallen away from it for a time.

That God, in the eternal decree of election, looked not to temporary faith, but to persevering faith, is clear 1) from the apostolic chain, Rom. 8:29-30. Those whom God predestined, He also glorified.

But God does not glorify those believing for a time, and afterwards casting off faith: Therefore He did not predestine them to eternal life.

2) A crown of righteousness is decreed for those keeping the faith, 2 Tim. 4:8. 3) He who perseveres unto the end shall be saved, Matt.

10:22, 24:13. And to the faithful man unto death will be given the crown of life.

Rev. 2:10. There is an antithesis 1) of certain Scholastics and Papists; 2) of certain Reformed doctors, who deny that we are elected by the intuition of faith persevering in Christ.

Their stronger arguments are:

I. Whatever action of God is immanent, immediate, and inorganic, that does not occur through faith as a medium or instrument: But election is an action of God that is immanent, immediate, and inorganic: Therefore. The major is evident: because an immanent and inorganic action does not occur through an instrument, nor does it admit an instrumental cause. The minor is clear in itself; because election is carried out within the very bosom of the deity, without the intervention of any instrument.

Resp. Evangelical theologians do not teach that faith is an instrument of the decree of election itself, by which election is carried out or apprehended; but they assert that God, in choosing certain men, had regard for their persevering faith, as an ὄργανον ληπτικόν, or receptive instrument, by which both the merit of Christ, on account of which we are chosen, and the grace of God choosing unto eternal life is received or apprehended: just as faith is commonly called the instrumental cause of justification, not as if it were an instrument by which the act of justification itself is apprehended, but because it acts by way of an instrument by which that for which we are justified, namely the merit of Christ, is apprehended and applied to us. In relation to the decree of election itself, however, faith in Christ acts by way of a cause, or a less principal impulsive reason.

Instance: A receptive instrument cannot be an impulsive cause, since it does not have such power that it could move an acting cause; but an acting cause is moved by the intuition of a meritorious cause.

Resp. One must distinguish between a principal impulsive cause and a less principal one. A meritorious cause is a principal impulsive cause, which moves the agent by its own goodness, dignity, and value; but a receptive organ can be a less principal impulsive cause.

E.g., A casket, which indeed consists of the vilest material, but contains a most precious diamond, can move a man to esteem and love it, not by itself or its own dignity, but on account of the most noble gem which it contains. Thus, faith in Christ moves God to choose, not by itself, not by its own power or value, but by the power of the merit of Christ, which it embraces.

II. The effect of election cannot be the reason moving God to make the decree of election: Faith in Christ is an effect of election. Therefore. The major is clear: because the reason moving God to choose is prior to election itself in the order of nature: but an effect is posterior.

The minor is proved: 1) from Acts XIII, 48. And as many as were ordained to eternal life believed. By which words it is indicated that ordination to eternal life, or election, is the cause of faith.

2) From John X, 26. You do not believe; because you are not my sheep. Resp. a) generally: Faith, existing actually in the heart of man, is an effect of regeneration, not of election, although it is a consequence of it.

For election was made from eternity, actual faith is given in time.

Resp. b) Specifically to 1): The passage Acts XIII, 48 does not treat of eternal predestination, but of the disposition in time. See above ch. I. Qu. IX. obs. V. Yet, suppose the cited passage is to be understood of the eternal decree of predestination: by what consequence of law will it be deduced from the same that election is the cause of faith? The causal particle "because" or "that" is not found in the text. For it is not said: certain ones believed, because they were ordained to eternal life; but: as many as were ordained to eternal life believed. Therefore, the proposition of Luke is not reduplicative, or designative of a cause, but specificative of the subject, so that the sense is: those men believed whom God had foreseen would observe the order of salvation, and by the intuition of that had destined for eternal salvation.

To 2): The particle "because," John X, 26, does not express a cause, but notes the reason of the consequence a posteriori, just as it is taken in Luke VII, 47. Her many sins are remitted, because she loved much.

Instance: LUTHER himself, in the preface prefixed to the epistle to the Romans in our German bibles, asserts that faith in Christ flows from election: Therefore faith in Christ, by the testimony of LUTHER, is an effect of election, and hence not its impulsive reason. Resp. LUTHER l. c. on impulsive. Resp. LUTHER l. c. speaks of election in a broader sense, by which it denotes the entire economy of salvation, or the whole ordination of those to be saved unto salvation, comprising all the causes and means of salvation: in which sense it is also accepted in the Formula of Concord, Declaration, p. 82. If it is accepted in this broader sense, there is no doubt that faith is rightly called its effect.

We, however, use the name of election in the strictest sense, by which it denotes the divine decree concerning the eternal salvation to be imparted to men who will finally believe, in view of the merit of Christ and foreseen faith in Christ.

III. Whatever is a gift of God depending efficiently upon God alone, and in no way accruing to us from our own powers, that cannot be to the divine will a cause or impulsive reason for decreeing eternal salvation to us: But faith in Christ, etc. Therefore. The major is clear; since the acting cause is moved to the love and election of one over another, not by that gift which is from the acting cause itself, but by a gift or quality proceeding from the person loved, or existing in them. Resp.

1) It is not repugnant for something to be a gift of the lover and at the same time a motive of love. Cant. IV,

9. Christ, the heavenly bridegroom, professes concerning the necklace and eyes of his bride (namely, his own gifts) that his soul was captured by those eyes and that necklace. Christ himself is the gift of the Father, who loves us, Jo.

III, 16. by whom, nevertheless, the Father is moved to embrace us with love. Eph. I,

6. 2) Faith in Christ, notwithstanding the fact that it is a gift of God, is the cause why God justifies and saves us in time: why could it not also be the cause, from eternity, why He chose us unto salvation?

IV. Those in whom God finds nothing that could move Him to the love and election of the same, those God predestined to eternal salvation by an absolute decree, without regard to any motive existing in them; But in men fallen into sin God finds nothing, etc. Therefore.

The minor is proved; because He chose men dead in sins, inept for every good work, guilty of eternal death.

But in such men God finds nothing that could move Him to love and election.

Resp. 1) To the major: In those in whom there was nothing, neither by nature nor by supernatural grace, that could move God to love and election, their election was made by an absolute decree; I concede.

But although in those whom God chose there was nothing by nature, there was nevertheless something by grace (not indeed in act, but in potency, as that which would actually and in fact exist in them at some time, just as sin also was in them only in potency), namely, faith in Christ, which, by the power of the merit of Christ apprehended, moved God to love and election.

For God made us pleasing to Himself in the Beloved, Eph.

I, 6. 2) To the minor: God chose men dead in sins, inept for every good work, and guilty of eternal death: not insofar as they were still such in the divine prescience when they were chosen (for men dead in sins are hateful to God), but insofar as they are in the divine foreknowledge redeemed by Christ, regenerated by the virtue of the Holy Spirit, gifted with faith in Christ, and thus, with all offenses forgiven, rendered acceptable to God in His beloved Son.

V. Whatever did not exist from eternity, in view of that the eternal decree of God concerning choosing certain men is not formed: But faith in Christ, etc. Therefore.

Resp. Whatever did not exist from eternity, neither according to real being nor according to known being, or as an object in the divine mind, in view of that the eternal decree of election was not formed by God; I concede.
