But although faith in Christ did not exist from eternity according to its real being, it was nevertheless from eternity according to its known or objective being in the divine mind, to which even future things are most present.

For faith, as a less principal impulsive reason for election, exercises its function, not according to real being, but according to objective being and as known by the divine intellect: for it moves the will of God not of itself, but by the power of the merit of Christ apprehended. to decree salvation for us, under the aspect of a good, known by the divine intellect, and objectively exhibited to the divine will through the cognition of the intellect. Briefly, others distinguish between actual faith and foreseen faith. Actual faith is conferred in time through the grace of the Holy Spirit, but faith foreseen is from eternity, in the infinite light of the divine intellect.

VI. Faith is an instrumental cause, as much of salvation, which occurs in time, as of election to salvation, which was made from eternity. We are said to be saved not because of faith, but through faith. Therefore, faith is not an impulsive cause of election. Resp. Faith is called an instrumental and impulsive cause of election, just as it is of salvation, in a different respect. It is an instrumental cause insofar as it apprehends the merit of Christ, on account of which we are saved in time and were elected from eternity, and applies it to us. It is, however, a moving reason, or impulsive cause, if it is considered in order to the decree of election itself, or that very act of the divine will by which He decreed to save us. But we were not elected because of faith, as a meritorious or principal impulsive cause, but through faith, as a less principal impulsive cause, or by intuition of faith, or from foreseen faith.

You say: Certain theologians have refused to call faith an impulsive cause of election. For thus says D. B. MEISNERUS in antropol. decad. II. disp. XIV. p. 153. When faith is called a cause of election, do not understand it as a principal, impelling, or meritorious cause. Confer D. HUTTER. in *F.

C.* p. 1103. D. AEGID. HUNN. in tract. de prouid. & praedeft. p. 678. Resp.

Those authors understand by impulsive cause a meritorious or principal impulsive cause. And indeed, the term impulsive cause, taken so nakedly and without addition, stands by usage of speech for the more famous meaning, and denotes that which, by its own merit, or by some goodness, dignity, and perfection of its own, moves the efficient cause to act; since this does not befit faith, it is a matter of conscience for us also to call it so absolutely and simply an impulsive cause of election. Where, however, by applying the distinction of impulsive cause into principal and less principal, it is established that for a less principal cause there is not required, as there is for a meritorious one, some merit of its own, nor some proper goodness or dignity, but it suffices if, by virtue of another’s merit, goodness, or dignity, it behaves as a reason, by whose intuition the will of the agent—e.g., the will of God—determines itself to act, or determined itself from eternity; so far are our own from denying, or intending to deny, that faith is a less principal impulsive cause of the decree of election, that they all attribute the thing itself, denoted by the term "less principal cause," to faith in Christ, however they may express it in other words.

For they teach with great consensus that faith, besides being the instrument that apprehends the merit of Christ, also enters into the decree of election itself, so that God looks upon it and has regard for it in decreeing salvation for us, not on account of any dignity or merit of its own, but on account of the merit of Christ apprehended. Confer D. MUSAEUS in differtat. de praedeft. §.

62. 63. VII. If God elected sinners to eternal life by intuition of faith, then surely He also elected them by intuition of inherent holiness or good works. But God did not elect sinners by intuition of inherent holiness, but that they might be holy. Therefore, He also did not elect them by intuition of foreseen faith, but that they might believe.

The consequence of the major is proven: because faith and the holiness of life cohere in an inseparable bond: therefore, in whatever way faith enters the decree of election, in the same way does the holiness of life relate to it. The consequent is evident; since we were elected, not because we are holy, but that we might be holy and blameless, Eph. I, 4. Resp.

Things that are conjoined do not always act conjointly, or in the same way. Justifying faith, the pursuit of good works, and the peace of conscience are conjoined; yet faith alone is the medium by which grace [is received, and] conscience [is pacified]; yet faith alone is the medium by which the justifying grace of God, founded in the merit of Christ, is accepted. Whence it is impious to argue: As God justifies us, that we may walk in newness of life: so He justifies us, that we may believe.

Instance: But faith is a part of inherent holiness. Rightly therefore it is gathered: God chose us, that we might be holy: Therefore He chose us, that we might believe.

Resp. Faith is considered in two ways. In one way, as it is a quality inherent in us and a Christian virtue, and the mother of other virtues: in the other, insofar as it is an instrument of apprehending the merit of Christ, and as it is viewed on the part of Him who is apprehended, or to be apprehended.

But can it not be that faith, which is a part of holiness, besides that it exerts itself in us for the holiness of life, is also an instrument of apprehending the merit of Christ, and in this view an impulsive reason for election? Does not something similar happen in justification, that is to say, that faith, which is a part of holiness, is also an instrument of apprehending the merit of Christ, and on the part of Him who is apprehended, an impulsive reason for justification?

Conf. D.

MVSAEVS l. c. §. 320.

VIII. If faith in Christ foreseen impelled God to our election made from eternity, the same likewise impelled God to our vocation made in time: But the consequent is false; Therefore the antecedent is also.

The consequence of the major is proved: because as God chose us from eternity: so He called us in time, as the Apostle testifies, 2 Tim. I, 9. The falsity of the consequent is manifest; because we have been called, that we may believe, not because we believe.

Resp. I deny the consequence, because vocation is universal and common as much to the reprobate as to the elect: but election is particular. The former pertains to the antecedent will of God, which the condition of faith follows; the latter pertains to the consequent will of God, which presupposes the condition of faith.

IX. If election depends on foreseen faith, it follows that we chose God first:

But the consequent is false: Therefore the antecedent is also. The consequence of the major is evident: because if God before He [chose] us

Latin:

7) Probatur assertio nostra ex harmonia, siue conformitate aeterni electionis decreti, & exsecutionis eiusdem.

Cuius, tanquam causae, aut rationis impulsiuae minus principalis, intuitu Deus nos in tempore saluat, eius tanquam causae aut rationis minus principalis intuitu ab aeterno decreuit nobis in tempore salutem conferre: Atqui fides in Christum est illud, cuius, tanquam causae, aut rationis impulsiuae minus principalis intuitu, Deus nos in tempore saluat: Ergo.

Maior constat; quia exsecutio salutis in tempore est speculum aeterni decreti.

Modus quippe saluandi temporalis non potest esse alius, quam qui in aeterno Dei decreto est definitus; ceteroqui vacillaret constantia, immutabilitas & sapientia diuina. Minor probatur ex illis scripturae locis, quibus dicitur iustificari fide, ex fide, per fidem.

Rom. III, 28. Habac. II, 4. Eph. II, 8. Hebr. X, 38. Vbi fidei causalitas quaedam in ordine ad salutem nostram adscribitur, eaque non causae efficientis, aut impulsiuae principalis; sed instrumentalis, atque impulsiuae minus principalis, seu, quod Deus, qui saluat, ad id, vt saluare velit, moueatur per fidem, non quidem ratione suae dignitatis spectatam (non enim dicimur saluari propter fidem); sed quatenus apprehendit meritum Christi, vt sic eius intuitu Deus saluare velit & saluet.

Prob. b. Nomine fidei, quam rationem motiuam electionis dicimus, non intelligitur fides πρόσκαιρος, siue temporaria, quae tempore tentationis deficit, vel peccatis contra conscientiam exstinguitur, sed perseuerans, quam Apostolus appellat μέχρι τέλους βεβαίαν, vsque ad finem firmam, Hebr. III, 6. Ceterum perseuerans fides vocatur non solum ea, quae nunquam deficit, sed etiam ea, quae in corde hominis ante finem vitae iterum accenditur, & ad finem vsque durat, etiam si homo ea ad tempus exciderit.

Respexisse autem Deum in aeterno electionis decreto non ad fidem temporariam, sed ad perseuerantem, liquet 1) e catena apostolica, Rom. VIII, 29. 30. Quos Deus praedestinauit, illos etiam glorificauit.

At credentes ad tempus, & postea fidem excutientes Deus non glorificat: Ergo eosdem ad vitam aeternam non praedestinauit.

2) Decreta est corona iustitiae fidem seruantibus, 2 Tim. IV, 8. 3) Qui perseuerauerit vsque ad finem, saluus erit, Matth.

X, 22. c. XXIV, 13. Et homini fideli vsque ad mortem dabitur corona vitae.

Apoc. II, 10. Antithesis est 1) quorundam Scholasticorum & Pontificiorum; 2) quorundam doctorum Reformatorum, negantium, nos intuitu perseuerantis in Christum fidei electos esse.

Quorum potiora sunt argumenta:

I. Quaecunque actio Dei est immanens, immediata & inorganica, illa non fit per fidem tanquam medium, aut instrumentum: Atqui electio est actio Dei immanens, immediata & inorganica: Ergo. Maior constat: quia actio immanens & inorganica non fit per instrumentum, neque admittit causam instrumentalem. Minor per se clara est; quia electio peragitur intra ipsum deitatis sinum, citra interventum alicuius instrumenti.

Resp. Non docent Theologi evangelici, fidem esse instrumentum ipsius decreti electionis, quo electio peragatur, aut apprehendatur; sed afferunt, Deum in eligendis quibusdam hominibus respexisse illorum perseverantem fidem, tanquam ὄργανον ληπτικόν, sive instrumentum receptivum, quo tum meritum Christi, propter quod eligimur, tum gratia Dei eligentis ad vitam aeternam recipitur, vel apprehenditur: sicut fides communiter vocatur causa instrumentalis iustificationis, non quasi fit instrumentum, quo ipse actus iustificationis apprehendatur, sed quia se habet per modum instrumenti, quo id, propter quod iustificamur, meritum Christi scilicet, apprehenditur, nobisque applicatur. In ordine vero ad ipsum decretum electionis, fides in Christum se habet per modum causae, vel rationis impulsivae minus principalis.

Instantia: Instrumentum receptivum non potest esse causa impulsiva, cum tanta eius vis non sit, vt causam agentem mouere queat; sed causa agens mouetur intuitu causae meritoriae.

Respond. Distinguendum inter causam impulsivam principalem, & minus principalem. Causa meritoria est causa impulsiva principalis, quae propria sua bonitate, dignitate & valore agentem mouet; organum vero receptivum potest esse causa impulsiva minus principalis.

V. gr. Scrinium, quod constat quidem ex vilissima materia, sed complectitur adamantem pretiosissimum, mouere potest hominem ad aestimium & amorem sui, non per se, aut propria dignitate, sed propter geminam nobilissimam, quam conprehendit. Ita fides in Christum mouet Deum ad eligendum, non per se, non vi aut valore proprio, sed vi meriti Christi, quod illa amplectitur.

II. Effectus electionis non potest esse ratio, mouens Deum ad faciendum decretum electionis: Fides in Christum est effectus electionis. Ergo. Maior liquet: quia ratio mouens Deum ad eligendum ipsa electione ordine naturae prior est: effectus autem est posterior.

Minor probatur: 1) ex Act. XIII, 48. Et crediderunt, quotquot ad vitam aeternam ordinati sunt. Quibus verbis indicatur, ordinationem ad vitam aeternam, sive electionem, esse causam fidei.

2) Ex Io. X, 26. Vos non creditis; quia non estis oues meae. Resp. a) generatim: Fides, actu existens in corde hominis, est effectus regenerationis, non electionis, licet huius sit consequens.

Nam electio facta est ab aeterno, fides actualis datur in tempore.

Resp. b) Speciatim ad 1): Locus Act. XIII, 48. non agit de praedestinatione aeterna, sed dispositione in tempore. Vid. supra cap. I. Qu. IX. obs. V. Fac tamen, locum citatum intelligendum esse de aeterno praedestinationis decreto: qua consequentia lege ex eodem deducetur, electionem esse causam fidei? Vocula causalis quia, vel quod non habetur in textu. Neque enim dicitur: crediderunt quidam, quia erant ordinati ad vitam aeternam; sed: crediderunt, quotquot erant ordinati ad vitam aeternam. Est itaque propositio Lucae non reduplicativa, aut designativa causae, sed specificativa subiecti, vt sensus sit, crediderunt homines illi, quos Deus ordinem salutis obseruaturos esse prauiderat, & illius intuitu ad salutem aeternam destinarat.

Ad 2): Particula quia, Io. X, 26. non exprimit causam, sed notat rationem consequentiae a posteriori, sicut sumitur Luc. VII, 47. Remissa illi sunt peccata multa, quia amauit multum.

Instantia: LVTHERVS ipse, in praefatione, epistolae ad Romanos in bibliis nostris germanicis praefixa, asserit, fidem in Christum fluere ex electione: Ergo fides in Christum, teste LVTHERO, est effectus electionis, adeoque non eius ratio impulsiva. Resp. LVTHERVS l. c. de impulsiua. Resp. LVTHERVS l. c. de electione loquitur in latiori significatu, quo vniversam salutis oeconomiam, siue totam saluandorum ad salutem ordinationem, causas & media salutis omnia complectentem, denotat: quo sensu etiam accipitur in Form. Concord. declar. p.

82. Quo significatu latiori si accipiatur, nullum dubium est, quin fides eius effectus recte dicatur. Nos autem electionis nomine vtimur in significatione strictissima, qua notat decretum diuinum de salute aeterna, hominibus finaliter credituris impertienda, intuitu meriti Christi, & praeuisa fidei in Christum.

III. Quidquid est donum Dei a solo Deo efficienter dependens, & nullatenus ex viribus nostris nobis obtingens, illud non potest voluntati diuinae esse causa, vel ratio impulsiva, ad salutem aeternam nobis decernendam: Atqui fides in Christum &c. Ergo. Maior liquet; quoniam mouetur causa agens ad dilectionem & electionem vnius prae alio, non illo dono, quod ex ipsa causa agente est, sed dono, aut qualitate proficiente a persona dilecta, aut in illa exsistente.

Resp. 1) Non repugnat, esse aliquid donum amantis, & simul motiuum amoris. Cant. IV,

9. Christus, sponsus coelestis, de sponsae suae torque & oculis (suis scilicet donis) profitetur, istis oculis & torque isto animum suum captum esse.

Christus ipse est donum Patris, nos amantis, Io. III, 16. quo tamen Pater mouetur, vt nos amore complectatur. Eph. I,

6. 2) Fides in Christum, non obstante, quod Dei donum fit, causa est, cur in tempore Deus nos iustificet & saluet: quidni etiam ab aeterno, cur ad salutem nos elegerit, causa esse potuerit?

IV. In quibus Deus nihil inuenit, quod ipsum ad amorem & electionem eorundem permovere potuit, illos Deus ad aeternam salutem praedestinauit absoluto decreto, citra intuitum vllius motiui, in ipsis exsistentis; Atqui in hominibus in peccatum prolapsis Deus nihil inuenit &c.

Ergo. Minor probatur; quia elegit homines in peccatis mortuos, ad omne bonum opus ineptos, aeternae mortis reos.

At in eiusmodi hominibus Deus nihil inuenit, quod ipsum ad amorem & electionem permovere potuit. Resp.

1) ad maiorem: In quibus nihil fuit, neque per naturam, neque per supernaturalem gratiam, quod Deum ad amorem & electionem permovere potuit, illorum electio facta est absoluto decreto; concedo.

At quamuis in iis, quos Deus elegit, nihil fuerit per naturam, fuit tamen aliquid per gratiam (non quidem actu, sed potentia, vt quod reapse & actu aliquando in ipsis exstiturum esset, sicut & peccatum in ipsis tantum fuit potentia), nempe fides in Christum, quae vi meriti Christi apprehensi ad amorem & electionem Deum permouit.

Deus enim nos sibi gratos fecit in dilecto, Eph. I, 6. 2) Ad minorem:

Elegit Deus homines in peccatis mortuos, ad omne bonum opus ineptos, & aeternae mortis reos: non quatenus tales adhuc fuerunt in praescientia diuina, cum eligerentur (homines enim in peccatis mortui Deo sunt exosi), sed quatenus in precognitione diuina sunt a Christo redemti, virtute Spiritus S. regenerati, fide in Christum donati, atque adeo, condonatis omnibus offensis, accepti Deo redditi in dilecto suo Filio.

V. Quidquid ab aeterno non exstitit, illius intuitu aeternum Dei decretum de eligendis quibusdam hominibus non est formatum: At fides in Christum &c.

Ergo. Resp.

Quidquid ab aeterno non exstitit, neque quoad esse reale, neque quoad esse cognitum, siue obiectum in mente diuina, illius intuitu aeternum electionis decretum a Deo non est formatum; concedo. At licet fides in Christum non exstiterit ab aeterno, secundum esse suum reale, fuit tamen ab aeterno secundum esse cognitum, siue obiectiuum in mente diuina, cui etiam futura sunt praesentissima.

Exercet enim fides, tanquam ratio electionis impulsiva minus principalis, munus suum, non secundum esse reale, sed secundum esse obiectiuum & ab intellectu diuino cognitum: mouet namque voluntatem Dei non per se, sed vi meriti Christi apprehensi. ad decernendam nobis salutem, sub ratione boni, ab intellectu divino cogniti, & voluntati divinae per cognitionem intellectus obiective exhibiti. Breuiter alii distinguunt inter fidem actualem, & prauisam. Fides actualis per gratiam Spiritus S. confertur in tempore, sed fides prauisa est ab aeterno, in infinito intellectus diuini lumine.

VI. Fides est causa instrumentalis, vt saluationis, quae fit in tempore, ita & electionis ad salutem, quae facta est ab aeterno. Non propter fidem, sed per fidem saluari dicimur. Ergo fides non est causa impulsiva electionis. Resp. Fides diuerso respectu, vt saluationis, ita electionis causa instrumentalis, & impulsiva vocatur. Est causa instrumentalis, quatenus meritum Christi, propter quod saluamur in tempore, & electi sumus ab aeterno, apprehendit, nobisque applicat. Est autem ratio mouens, siue causa impulsiva, si consideretur in ordine ad ipsum decretum electionis, siue ipsum voluntatis diuinae actum, quo nos saluare decreuit. Non autem electi sumus propter fidem, tanquam causam meritariam, aut impulsivam principalem, sed per fidem, tanquam causam impulsivam minus principalem, vel intuitu fidei, aut ex prauisa fide.

Dicis: Quidam Theologi fidem electionis causam impulsivam dicere recufarunt. Sic enim inquit D. B. MEISNERVS in antropol. decad. II. disp. XIV. p. 153. Cum fides electionis causa dicitur, non intelligas causam principalem, impellentem, aut meritariam.

Confer. D. HVTTER. in F. C. p. 1103. D. AEGID. HVNN. in tract. de prouid. & praedest. p. 678. Resp.

Auctores illi per causam impulsivam intelligunt meritariam, aut causam impulsivam principalem. Et sane causae impulsivae terminus, ita nude & fine additamento acceptus, ex vsu loquendi stat pro significatu famosiori, notatque id, quod suo merito, vel sua quadam bonitate, dignitate & perfectione, causam efficientem ad agendum mouet; quod cum fidei non conueniat, nobis etiam religio fit, eam ita absolute & simpliciter electionis causam impulsivam dicere. Vbi autem, adhibita distinctione causae impulsivae in principalem, & minus principalem, constiterit, ad minus principalem causam non perinde, vt ad meritariam, requiri eius quoddam meritum proprium, non propriam quandam bonitatem, aut dignitatem, sed sufficere, si vi alieni meriti, bonitatis aut dignitatis, se habeat vt ratio, cuius intuitu voluntas agentis ad agendum, v. gr. voluntas Dei ad decernendam nobis salutem, se determinet, aut ab aeterno determinarit; tantum abest, vt fidem decreti electionis causam impulsivam minus principalem nostrates negaturi sint, aut negent, vt ipsam rem, termino causa minus principalis denotatam, fidei in Christum omnes adferant, vtut aliis atque aliis verbis eam enuntient.

Magno quippe consensu docent, fidem, praeterquam quod apprehendit meriti Christi instrumentum est, ingredi etiam ipsum electionis decretum, vt Deus eam aspiciat & in decernenda nobis salute illius rationem habeat, non ob vllam suam dignitatem, aut meritum, sed ob meritum Christi apprehensum. Confer. D. MVSAEVS in dissertat. de praedest. §. 62. 63.

VII. Si Deus peccatores intuitu fidei elegit ad vitam aeternam, vtique etiam intuitu sanctitatis inhaerentis, aut bonorum operum eos elegit. Sed non elegit Deus peccatores intuitu sanctitatis inhaerentis, sed vt sint sancti. E. etiam eosdem elegit non intuitu prauisae fidei, sed vt credant. Consequentia maioris probatur: quia fides & vitae sanctitas indiuulso nexu cohaerent: Quocunque igitur modo fides ingreditur decretum electionis; eodem modo ad illud se habet vitae sanctitas.

Consequens patet; quoniam electi sumus, non quia sumus sancti, sed vt sumus sancti & irreprehensibiles, Eph. I, 4. Resp.

Non quae coniuncta sunt, semper coniunctim, seu eodem modo agunt. Fides iustifica, studium bonorum operum & pax conscientiae coniunguntur; sola tamen fides est medium, quo gratia confcientiæ coniunguntur; sola tamen fides est medium, quo gratia Dei iustificans, in merito Christi fundata, acceptatur. Vnde argumentari nefas est: Sicut Deus nos iustificat, vt in nouitate vitæ ambulemus: ita nos iustificat, vt credamus.

Instantia: Sed fides est pars sanctitatis inhærentis. Recte igitur colligitur: Deus nos elegit, vt simus sancti: Ergo nos elegit, vt credamus.

Resp. Fides consideratur bifariam. Vno modo, ut est qualitas nobis inhærens & virtus christiana, ceterarumque virtutum genitrix: altero, in quantum organon est apprehendendi meriti Christi, & prout ex parte eius apprehensi, vel apprehendendi spectatur.

Annon autem fieri potest, vt fides, quæ sanctitatis pars est, præterquam quod ad sanctimoniam vitæ in nobis se exserit, etiam sit organon apprehendendi meriti Christi, & hoc intuitu ratio electionis impulsiva? Annon in iustificatione simile quid contingit, vt scilicet fides, quæ sanctitatis pars est, etiam sit organon apprehendendi meriti Christi, & ex parte eius apprehensi ratio iustificationis impulsiva?

Conf. D.

MVSAEVS l. c. §. 320.

VIII. Si fides in Christum præuisa impulit Deum ad nostri electionem factam ab æterno, eadem pariter Deum impulit ad vocationem nostri factam in tempore: Atqui consequens est falsum; E. & antecedens.

Consequentia maioris probatur: quia sicut Deus nos elegit ab æterno: ita nos vocauit in tempore, teste Apostolo, 2 Tim. I, 9. Consequentis falsitas est manifesta; quia vocati sumus, vt credamus, non quia credimus.

Resp. Neg. consequ. quia vocatio est vniuersalis & communis tam reprobis, quam electis: electio autem est particularis. Illa pertinet ad voluntatem Dei antecedentem, quam conditio fidei sequitur; hæc pertinet ad voluntatem Dei consequentem, quæ conditionem fidei præsupponit.

IX. Si electio pendet ex fide præuisa, sequitur, nos priores Deum elegisse: At consequens est falsum: E. & antecedens.

Consequentia maioris patet: quia si Deus antequam


### Quæst. X. The directing, or norming, principle, according to which election was divinely instituted, is either first and mediate or…

he had chosen us, he had foreseen that we would believe, and therefore he had chosen us; he would certainly have chosen us, because in his provision we were adhering to him, and we had already chosen him beforehand: for whoever adheres to God, having neglected Satan, chooses him. Resp. 1) We do not establish the dependence of election upon any cause; because dependence requires a cause formally causing. 2) I deny the consequence of the major. For it does not follow that we chose God because we were adhering to him in his provision. For the sense is: God foresaw that we ourselves would adhere. But from this it does not follow that we chose God first, but only this, that God saw, before he chose us, that we were about to choose him, that is, that we were about to adhere to him rather than to Satan, or to believe in him, and that not from our own powers, but through divine grace. For he did not choose us by reason of faith actually existing, but as still future and at least foreseen.

X. If faith in Christ foreseen is the cause of election, the object of election will be a justified man: But the consequent is false: Therefore the antecedent. The consequence of the major is proven: because he who believes in Christ is justified. The falsity of the consequence is evident, because justification happens in time. Resp. I deny the consequence of the major. For just as faith foreseen denotes faith that will at some time exist; so it implies justification that is future, not actually present. From which it follows that the object of eternal election was man not actually believing, but about to believe, and thus through grace not yet restored and justified, but at some time to be restored and justified.

XI. Whatever election is gratuitous, that is not made according to the foreknowledge of our faith: But the election of us to eternal life, etc. Therefore. The major is proven: because gratuitous [acts] of God's benefit exclude every condition that comes from us. The minor is evident from Rom. XI, 5. 6. Resp. The gratuitous [nature] excludes our merits, not the τάξιν [order], or the order divinely established. Faith here is not a work or merit, but the receptive instrument of the merit of Christ and as it were a begging hand foreseen, which does not give, does not acquire by laboring, but receives from the mercy of God who gives. Nor is faith itself from man, but from the grace of the Holy Spirit regenerating.

XII. If God intends the salvation of men before he decreed to endow the same with faith; the decree of election concerning the saving of certain men is absolute with respect to faith: But the antecedent is true: Therefore the consequent. The consequence of the major is proven: because, given that the decree of election is respective, faith must be prior to the decree of election in the sign of divine reason. The antecedent is clear: because faith is the means, eternal life is its end, 1 Petr. I, 9. But no wise man decides to give the means before deciding to give the end: Thought concerning the end is always prior to thought concerning the means. The end is first in intention, although it is last in execution. Resp. Distinguish between the antecedent and consequent will of God. By his antecedent will, God indeed intends the salvation of men before he thought of the means of salvation (in our mode of conceiving). Which will of God, since it is universal and conditional, by it God willed to save all men under the condition of persevering faith. But by his consequent will, God willed to confer eternal salvation upon certain singular persons, whose constant faith in Christ he foreknew from eternity, determinately, categorically, and simply. By this consequent will, by which God chose us to eternal life, faith foreseen in Christ is prior in our mode of understanding.

Quæst. X.

The directing, or norming, principle, according to which election was divinely instituted, is either first and mediate or proximate and immediate. The primary normative principle is πρόθεσις (prothesis), or the divine purpose, by which God from eternity willed all fallen men to be made saved, whoever would persevere in believing in Christ ): The proximate normative principle is πρόγνωσις (prognosis), or divine foreknowledge, by which God from eternity foresaw which men individually would in time finally believe in Christ ).

Prob. a. St. Paul teaches in Eph. I, 11 that we are προορισθέντες κατὰ πρόθεσιν (prooristhentes kata prothesin), predestined according to the purpose of God. He says the same in 2 Tim. I, 9: God saved us, and called us with a holy calling; not according to our works, but according to His own purpose and grace given to us in Christ Jesus before the ages of time. And Rom. VIII, 28: We know that to those who love God, all things work together for good, (namely to those) who are called according to the purpose of God: for whom He foreknew, He also predestined.

Obf. 1. That πρόθεσις, or the purpose of God, is taken by some theologians in a stricter sense, and referred to the consequent will of God. Thus says D. Koenig in theol. posit. p. 115: The primary normative principle is πρόθεσις, which is not taken here for the purpose of primary mercy; nor for the purpose of universal mercy, which pertains to the antecedent will of God, indeed it is the very antecedent will of God itself; but most strictly and most specially concerning the purpose of saving those who are to persevere in Jesus Christ until the end of life, John III, 16, which itself is nothing but an act of the consequent will. D. Quensted uses the same words in system. theol. part. III. cap. II. fol. 17. Yet the same author, l. c. fol. 42, takes the purpose of God in a broader sense, saying: ἡ πρόθεσις (he prothesis), or the purpose of God, regards and ordains the means of salvation 1) to be acquired, Christ the redeemer, 2) to be offered and dispensed, the word and sacraments, 3) to be received, faith in Christ, the end of which is the salvation of souls, 1 Petr. III, 9. According to this purpose of God, predestination is made, which approves the foreseen faith and applies the promised salvation to believers. The same is asserted by D. Hulsemann in breu. enucl. p. 975. Πρόθεσις is the εὐδοκία (eudokia) of God, by which He, having foreseen the fall first of all, by an antecedent will decreed to save all men whatsoever, 1 Tim. II, 4, and indeed if they finally believe in Christ. And this was the first of all decrees in the matter of predestination, which includes α) the foreseen and permitted sin of created man, β) the redeemer from this sin, Christ, γ) the calling, and δ) the offered grace of believing. This purpose of saving is universal, and of the antecedent will, whereas predestination is particular and of the consequent will. Cf. D. Dannhau. hodof. phænom. VII. p. 574. and D. Sebast. Schmid, in aphorismis theol. p. 292. Obf.

2. Πρόθεσις, or the purpose of God, is not predestination itself, but as it were a rule and normative principle. For we are said to be predestined κατὰ πρόθεσιν (kata prothesin), Eph. I, 11.

Obf. 3. Πρόθεσις is the primary directing principle of election, not immediate, but mediate: because it concurs to election by means of πρόγνωσις (prognosis), or the foreknowledge of the individuals who will finally believe.

Prob. b. That πρόγνωσις (prognosis), or divine foreknowledge, is the proximate and immediate normative principle of election is clear from Rom. VIII, 29: ὅς προέγνω, καὶ προώρισε (hos proegno, kai proorise), whom He foreknew (as being about to be in Christ Jesus through faith, according to v. 1) He also predestined. The same is evident from 1 Petr. I, 3, where we are said to be elect κατὰ πρόγνωσιν (kata prognosis), by the foreknowledge of God the Father. The reason is: because, if you were to pluck out the eye of foreknowledge, election would be blind. However, by πρόγνωσις is understood not a general and indefinite foreknowledge, which extends itself as much to evils as to goods, but a most singular one, and determined to certain objects, which is knowledge κατ' ὄνομα (kat' onoma), John X, 3.

For Christ calls his sheep κατ' ὄνομα, by name, i.e., individually; he knows distinctly the names of the individual persons who are finally to believe in Christ. Rejoice, says Christ, that your names are written in heaven. Luc. X, 20. And Paul says, 2 Tim. II, 10. The firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: the Lord knows who are his, and let everyone who names the name of Christ depart from iniquity. By the firm foundation the Apostle denotes the irrevocable purpose of God, or the counsel concerning the saving of men through faith in Christ, whose seal, which is for us, indeed, concerning the gracious will of God toward us, by which each of the faithful is sealed by the Holy Spirit, is πρόγνωσις (foreknowledge), by which he knows specifically, and embraces with his grace his own, i.e., the individuals believing in Christ.

There is an antithesis of the Socinians, who deny that the decree concerning the choosing of men made before the ages concerns certain individuals by name, against those who assert that election is a general decree, and regards in general all those who believe and obey God calling them to salvation. They urge most strongly that the sayings of Holy Scripture, which treat of election, are general, not conceived concerning certain individuals. Thus Paul says in general that God chose Us. Eph. I, 4. It is said that the kingdom was prepared from eternity for all in general who would feed Christ, Matth. XXV, 34. I respond: because God chose certain individuals by name; therefore the Apostle could truly say that God chose Us; for in this pronoun the Apostle includes himself as an individual. Nor could the kingdom be destined by the omniscient God to all in general who would feed Christ, in such a way that he would not determinately know who by name they were. For God knows (even from eternity Act. XV, 18.) who are his, 2 Tim. II, 19. whose names he wrote in the book of life of the lamb, Apoc. XIII, 8. We gather from these that predestination, by reason of the object, is individual, Conf. D. W. LYSERVS in system. theol. p. 758.

Latin:

nos elegisset, prævidisset, nos credituros, & ideo nos elegisset; vtique elegisset, quia in prouisione eius ipsi adhærebamus, & iam ipsum ante elegeramus: qui enim adhæret Deo, neglecto Satana, ipsum elegit. Resp. 1) Non statuimus dependentiam electionis ab vlla causa; quia dependentia requirit causam formaliter causantem. 2) Neg. consequ. maioris. Neque enim sequitur, nos Deum elegisse, quia in eius prouisione ipsi adhærebamus. Sensus namque est: Deus præuidit, nos ipsi adhæsuros esse. At ex hoc non sequitur, quod nos priores Deum elegerimus, sed hoc tantum, Deum prius, quam nos elegerit, vidisse, quod ipsum essemus electuri, h. e. ipsi præ Satana adhæfuri, seu in ipsum credituri, idque non ex nostris viribus, sed per diuinam gratiam. Non enim ratione fidei actu existentis, sed adhuc futuræ & saltem præuisæ, nos elegit.

X. Si fides in Christum præuisa est electionis causa, obiectum electionis erit homo iustificatus: At consequens est falsum: E. & antecedens. Consequentia maioris probatur: quia qui credit in Christum, iustificatus est. Consequentia falsitas patet, quia iustificatio fit in tempore. Resp. Neg. consequent. maior. Sicut enim fides præuisa notat fidem aliquando exstituram; ita infert iustificationem futuram, non realiter præsentem. Ex quo sequitur, obiectum æternæ electionis fuisse hominem non actu credentem, sed crediturum, & sic per gratiam non iam instauratum & iustificatum, sed aliquando instaurandum & iustificandum.

XI. Quæcunque electio est gratuita, illa non est facta secundum præuisionem nostræ fidei: Atqui electio nostri ad vitam æternam &c. E. Maior prob. quia gratuitæ Dei beneficii omnem conditionem, quæ fit ex nobis, excludunt. Minor constat ex Rom. XI, 5. 6. Resp. Tò gratuitum excludit merita nostra, non τάξιν, siue ordinem diuinitus constitutum. Fides hic non est opus aut meritum, sed meriti Christi receptiuum instrumentum & quasi manus mendica præuisa, quæ non donat, non laborando acquirit, sed ex misericordia donantis Dei accipit. Neque fides ipsa est ex homine, sed ex gratia Spiritus S. regenerante.

XII. Si Deus prius intendit salutem hominum, quam eosdem fide donare decreuit; decretum electionis de saluandis quibusdam hominibus respectu fidei est absolutum: Sed verum est antecedens: E. & consequens. Consequentia maioris probatur: quia posito, quod decretum electionis sit respectiuum, fidem decreto electionis priorem esse oportet in signo rationis diuinæ. Antecedens patet: quia fides est medium, vita æterna finis eius, 1 Petr. I, 9. At nemo sapiens prius decernit dare medium, deinde dare finem: Cogitatio de fine semper prior est cogitatione de mediis. Finis est primus in intentione, licet sit vltimus in exsecutione. Resp. Dist. inter voluntatem Dei antecedentem, & consequentem. Voluntate antecedente Deus quidem prius intendit hominum salutem, quam de mediis salutis cogitauit (nostro concipiendi modo). Quæ voluntas Dei cum sit vniuersalis & conditionata, eadem Deus omnes homines saluare voluit sub conditione perseuerantis fidei. At voluntate consequente Deus quibusdam personis singularibus, quarum constantem in Christum fidem ab æterno prænouit, æternam salutem conferre, determinate, categorice & simpliciter voluit. Hac voluntate consequente, qua Deus ad æternam salutem nos elegit, præuisa in Christum fide prior est nostro intelligendi modo.

Quæst. X. Quodnam est principium dirigens, siue normans, secundum quod facta est electio?

Principium dirigens, seu normans, secundum quod diuinitus instituta est electio, est vel primum & mediatum vel proximum & immediatum. pium normans primum est πρόθεσις, siue propositum diuinum, quo Deus ab æterno voluit omnes homines lapsos fieri saluos, quicunque in Christum perseueranter essent credituri ): Principium normans proximum est πρόγνωσις, seu præscientia diuina, qua Deus ab æterno præuidit, quinam homines in indiuiduo essent in tempore finaliter in Christum credituri ).

Prob. a. Docet S. Paullus Eph. I, 11. quod simus προορισθέντες κατὰ πρόθεσιν, prædestinati secundum propositum Dei. Idem inquit 2 Tim. I, 9. Deus saluos fecit nos, & vocauit nos vocatione sancta; non secundum opera nostra, sed iuxta proprium propositum & gratiam datam nobis in Christo Iesu ante tempora antesecularia. Et Rom. VIII, 28. Scimus, quod iis, qui diligunt Deum, omnia cooperentur in bonum, (iis nempe) qui iuxta propositum Dei vocati sunt: siquidem quos præcognouit, etiam prædestinauit.

Obs. 1. Quod πρόθεσις, siue propositum Dei a nonnullis Theologis strictiori sumatur significatione, & ad voluntatem Dei consequentem referatur. Sic ait D. KOENIGIVS in theol. posit. p. 115. Principium normans primum est πρόθεσις, quæ hic non accipitur pro proposito miserationis primæ; neque pro proposito misericordiæ vniuersalis, quæ ad voluntatem Dei antecedentem pertinet, imo est ipsissima voluntas Dei antecedens; sed strictissime ac specialissime de proposito saluandi eos, qui in Iesum Christum vsque ad finem vitæ perseueraturi sunt, Ioann. III, 16. quod ipsum non nisi consequentis voluntatis actus est. Iisdem vtitur verbis D. QVENSTED. in system. theol. part. III. cap. II. fol. 17. Idem tamen l. c. fol. 42, propositum Dei latiori significatu accipit, inquiens: ἡ πρόθεσις, siue propositum Dei respicit & ordinat media salutis 1) acquirendæ, Christum redemtorem, 2) offerendæ & dispensandæ, verbum & sacramenta, 3) recipiendæ, fidem in Christum, cuius finis est salus animarum, 1 Petr. III, 9. Secundum hoc Dei propositum facta est prædestinatio, quæ fidem præuisam approbat, credentibus promissam salutem applicat. Idem asserit D. HVLSEMANNVS in breu. enucl. p. 975. Πρόθεσις est εὐδοκία Dei, qua is, præuiso lapsu primo omnium, voluntate antecedente decreuit omnes omnino homines saluare, 1 Tim. II, 4. & quidem si in Christum finaliter credant. Et hoc fuit omnium decretorum in negotio prædestinationis primum, quod α) creati hominis præuisum ac permissum peccatum, β) redemtorem ab hoc peccatum, Christum, γ) vocationem, & oblatam δ) gratiam credendi includit. Hoc propositum saluandi est vniuerfale, & voluntatis antecedentis, cum prædestinatio sit particularis & voluntatis consequentis. Conf. D. DANNHAV. hodof. phænom. VII. p. 574. & D. SEBAST. SCHMID, in aphorismis theol. p. 292.

Obs. 2. Πρόθεσις, siue propositum Dei non est ipsa prædestinatio, sed quasi regula & principium normatiuum. Dicimur quippe prædestinati κατὰ πρόθεσιν, Eph. I, 11.

Obs. 3. Πρόθεσις est electionis principium dirigens primum, non immediatum, sed mediatum: Propterea, quod mediante προγνώσει, seu præuisione indiuiduorum, finaliter crediturorum, ad electionem concurrit.

Prob. b. Πρόγνωσιν, seu præscientiam diuinam, esse electionis principium normans proximum & immediatum, liquet e Rom. VIII, 29. ὅς προέγνω, καὶ προώρισε, quos præcognouit (futuros esse in Christo Iesu per fidem, iuxta v. 1.) etiam prædestinauit. Constat idem ex 1 Petr. I, 3. vbi dicimur electi κατὰ πρόγνωσιν, υἱα præcognitionem Dei Patris. Ratio est: quia, si erueres præscientiæ oculum, cæca foret electio. Intelligitur autem per πρόγνωσιν non præscientia generalis & indefinita, quæ tam ad bona, quam ad mala se extendit, sed singularissima, & ad certa obiecta determinata, quæ est notitia κατ' ὄνομα, Ioann. X, 3.

Christus enim vocat oues suas κατ' ὄνομα, nominatim, i. e. sigillatim; cognoscit distincte nomina singularium personarum, quæ in Christum finaliter sunt credituræ. Gaudete, inquit Christus, quod nomina vestra scripta sunt in cælo. Luc. X, 20. Et Paullus ait, 2 Tim. II, 10. Firmum Dei fundamentum subsistit, habens sigillum hoc: nouit dominus, qui sui sunt, & desistat ab iniustitia omnis, qui nominat nomen Christi. Per firmum fundamentum notat Apostolus irreuocabile Dei propositum, siue consilium de saluandis hominibus per fidem in Christum, cuius sigillum, quod nos nimirum, de gratiosa Dei erga nos voluntate, qua quisque fidelium per Spiritum S. obsignatur, est πρόγνωσις, qua speciatim nouit, & gratia sua complectitur suos, i. e. singulos in Christum credentes.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, negantium, decretum de eligendis hominibus ante sæcula factum, certa individua nominatim concernere, contra afferentium, electionem esse decretum generale, & respicere in genere omnes eos, quicunque vocanti ad salutem Deo credunt & obtemperant. Vrgent potissimum, quod dicta S. scripturæ, quæ de electione agunt, sint generalia, non concepta de certis individuis. Sic Paullus in genere dicit, quod Deus Nos elegerit. Eph. I, 4. Generatim omnibus, qui Christum cibarant, ab æterno regnum præparatum dicitur, Matth. XXV, 34. Resp. quia Deus certa nominatim individua elegit; ideo potuit Apostolus vere dicere, quod Deus Nos elegerit; huic enim pronomini Apostolus se ipsum individuo includit. Neque generatim omnibus, Christum cibaturis, regnum potuit destinari a Deo omniscio, ita vt determinate nesciret, quinam nominatim illi essent. Nouit enim Deus (etiam ab æterno Act. XV, 18.), qui sint sui, 2 Tim. II, 19. quorum nomina scripsit in libro vitæ agni, Apoc. XIII, 8. Colligimus ex his, prædestinationem, ratione obiecti, esse individualem, Conf. D. W. LYSERVS in system. theol. p. 758.


### Question XI. In what does election formally consist?

Election formally consists a) in the eternal segregation of certain individuals, according to the foreknowledge of final faith in Christ, from the common mass of lost men; and b) in their ordination to eternal salvation according to the purpose of God.

Obs. The form of the eternal decree concerning the saving of certain men, as D. SCHERZER holds in system. theol. loc. XVIII. p. 518, consists in συνδρομῇ προθέσεως, προγνώσεως & προορισμοῦ, in the concurrence or confluence of divine purpose, foreknowledge, and predestination. For thus the Apostle: To those who love God all things work together for good; to those, I say, who are called according to his πρόθεσιν (purpose); for whom he προέγνωσε (foreknew), them he also προώρισε (predestined), that they might be conformed to the image of his son. Rom. VIII, 28. ff. Whence emerges such a

Rom. VIII, 28. ff. Whence emerges such a Predestinatory Syllogism: Every one who is to believe in Christ perseveringly until the end of life will certainly be saved, and therefore is chosen and inscribed in the book of life.

But this one, that one, the other one, Abraham, Peter, Paul, etc., are to believe in Christ perseveringly until the end of life.

Therefore this one, that one, the other one, Abraham, Peter, Paul, etc., will certainly be saved, and therefore are chosen, and inscribed in the book of life.

The major proposition is πρόθεσις, or the divine purpose concerning the saving of sinful men who are finally to believe in Christ.

The minor is formed by foreknowledge, by which God from eternity foresaw who as individuals were to believe finally in time. Whence follows conclusion, which contains προορισμὸν [predestination], or the election itself formally, by which God from eternity decreed to save this one, that one, and the other one at a certainly and infallibly appointed time. There are not, indeed, in reality, dianoetic acts succeeding one another in order in God, because of the supreme simplicity and immutability of God: but that we conceive of signs of the divine reason, providing a certain order according to divine revelation, is the infirmity of our concepts.

Prob. a. That the segregation of certain individuals of men from the common assembly of sinners is the formal act of election is evident from the words of Christ, John 15:19. I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hateth you. By the world is designated the entire human race not reborn, and thus contaminated by sin, indulging in the pleasures of the flesh, and obnoxious to divine wrath and eternal damnation. Rom. 3:19. Christ therefore says: I have chosen you out of the world, i.e., I have separated you from the world, which lies entirely in the evil one, as in leaven, 1 John 5:19. I have separated you from the common mass of perdition, and have set you apart for myself as a peculiar treasure. Observe that the segregation of those who will finally believe from the common mass, made by the eternal decree of election, is not external and real, such as will happen in time, Matt. 25:32, but internal and mental, and that honorable, by which God in his decree preferred those who will believe to the unbelievers. For in every election, through an act of mind and will, the better is preferred to the worse.

Prob. b. Since election, which is made through determination to an end, exists between the term from which and the term to which, the other formal act of election is the eternal ordination or destination of men who, by constant faith, will embrace Christ unto eternal life. For God chose us from the beginning unto salvation. 2 Thess. 2:13. This ordination unto eternal salvation is made κατὰ πρόθεσιν, according to the divine purpose, which is expounded by Christ in clear words. John 6:40. This is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the son, and believes in him, may have eternal life. From which also believers are called τεταγμένοι εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον, ordained, i.e., destined by a certain order unto eternal life, Acts 13:48.

Latin:

Electio formaliter consistit a) in æterna certorum individuorum, iuxta præuisionem finalis in Christum fidei, segregatione a communi perditorum hominum massa; & b) eorum ordinatione ad æternam salutem iuxta propositum Dei.

Obs. Forma æterni decreti de saluandis quibusdam hominibus, censente D. SCHERZERO in system. theol. loc. XVIII. p. 518. consistit in συνδρομῇ προθέσεως, προγνώσεως & προορισμοῦ, in concursu vel confluxu diuini propositi, præscientiæ & prædestinationis. Ita enim Apostolus: Diligentibus Deum omnia cooperantur in bonum; his, inquam, qui iuxta πρόθεσιν (propositum) sunt vocati; quos enim προέγνωσε (præsciuit), hos etiam προώρισε (prædestinauit), vt sint conformes imagini filii eius. Rom. VIII, 28. seqq. Vnde emergit talis

Syllogismus prædestinatorius: Omnis perseueranter vsque ad finem vitæ crediturus in Christum, certo saluabitur, atque adeo electus esto & inscriptus in librum vitæ.

Atqui hic, ille, iste, Abrahamus, Petrus, Paullus &c. perseueranter vsque ad finem vitæ in Christum credituri sunt.

Ergo hic, ille, iste, Abrahamus, Petrus, Paullus &c. certo saluabuntur, atque adeo electi sunto, & inscripti in librum vitæ.

Maior propositio est πρόθεσις, seu propositum diuinum de saluandis hominibus peccatoribus in Christum finaliter credituris.

Minorem format προγνωσις, qua Deus ab æterno præuidit, quinam secundum individua sint in tempore finaliter credituri. Vnde sequitur conclusio, quæ continet προορισμὸν, seu ipsam electionem formaliter, qua Deus ab æterno decrevit, hunc, illum, istum certo & infallibiliter statuto tempore salvare. Non dantur quidem, quoad rem, actus dianoëtici ordine sibi succedentes in Deo, propter summam simplicitatem & immutabilitatem Dei: quod autem signa rationis divinæ, ordinem, quendam iuxta revelationem divinam præbentia, concipiamus, nostri conceptus infirmitas est.

Prob. a. Segregationem quorundam in individuo hominum a communi peccatorum cœtu esse actum formalem electionis, patet e verbis Christi, Ioann. XV, 19. Ego elegi vos ex mundo, propter hoc odit vos mundus. Per mundum designatur universum genus humanum non renatum, atque adeo peccato contaminatum, voluptatibus carnis indulgens, iræque divinæ & æternæ damnationi obnoxium. Rom. III, 19. Dicit itaque Christus: Elegi vos ex mundo, h. e. separavi vos a mundo, qui totus in maligno, velut in fermento, iacet, 1 Ioann. V, 19. fecrevi vos a communi perditionis massa, mihique vos in peculium seposui. Observes, quod æterno electionis decreto facta fit segregatio finaliter crediturorum a communi massa non externa, & realis, qualis continget in tempore, Matth. XXV, 32. sed interna & mentalis, eaque honorifica, qua Deus in decreto suo credituros incredulis prætulit. Nam in omni electione, per actum mentis & voluntatis, melius deteriori præfertur.

Prob. b. Cum electio, quæ per determinationem ad finem fit, versetur inter terminum a quo & ad quem, alter electionis actus formalis est æterna ordinatio vel destinatio hominum constante fide Christum amplexurorum ad vitam æternam. Elegit enim Deus nos ab initio ad salutem. 2 Thess. II, 13. Fit hæc ordinatio ad salutem æternam κατὰ πρόθεσιν, iuxta propositum divinum, quod a Christo luculentis verbis exponitur. Ioann. VI, 40. Hæc est voluntas eius, qui misit me, ut omnis, qui vidit filium, & credit in eum, habeat vitam æternam. Ex quo etiam credentes dicuntur τεταγμένοι εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον, ordinati, h. e. certo ordine destinati ad vitam æternam, Act. XIII, 48.


### Question XII. Must the eternal decree of election therefore be established as absolute or conditional?

The eternal decree of election is not absolute, but ordained a) and respective b); nor is it conditional, but categorical and simple c).

Prob. a. That the decree of election is not absolute, but ordained, or determined by a certain order of means, is clear from the fact that we are called elect according to the purpose of God, by which he ordained the means of acquiring, offering, and receiving salvation. Concerning which Paul says 1 Cor. 1:21: It pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe.

Prob. b. That the decree of predestination is respective is evident; because God, when he predestined some from fallen men, and indeed these rather than those, unto eternal life, looked to something outside himself, as to an external impulsive cause, namely the merit of Christ, to be apprehended by persevering faith. Which we have demonstrated above in Q. 8 and 9.

The decree of predestination, insofar as it is taken precisely and most strictly, denotes the eternal decree concerning the imparting of eternal salvation to those who will finally believe in view of the merit of Christ, and of faith foreseen in certain individuals, is not conditional, with a condition concerning the future, but categorical and simple, as D. SEBAST. SCHMID says in colleg. bibl. posteriori p. 235. For God simply and categorically decreed to save this man, that man, and the other man, because he certainly foresaw his persevering faith in Christ. D. MVSAEVS shows this clearly in dissert. de decreto elect. p. 273. The decree of election, although we say it is made in view of foreseen faith, we by no means say it is made conditional, or under the condition of faith, but if the absolute be said in opposition to τὸ conditionatum [the conditioned], that the decree of election is absolute, or unconditioned, we fearlessly maintain; nor do we deny that it is absolute in any other sense than that in which it is called absolute to exclude the consideration of an impulsive cause outside of God, or external. However, a decree is not immediately conditioned because it is made in view of some impulsive cause; but if it be made in view of an impulsive cause, already constituted in act, or distinctly foreknown as future, then it is absolute or unconditioned. God, out of His immense goodness, willed to grant salvation to all under the condition of faith in Christ, which was a conditioned will, but not a conditioned decree of election. But because God from eternity had known and perceived that not all would believe in Christ by His grace, but [only] some, and those who were about to believe He knew distinctly, He willed to bestow salvation upon these, whom He foresaw would believe, in view indeed of faith in Christ, or in view of the merit of Christ, to be apprehended by faith, yet absolutely, i.e., without condition: and this will of His is finally the decree of election, and that is unconditioned, or absolute, if absolute be said in opposition to a conditioned decree; yet not absolute, if absolute be said to exclude the consideration of an external impulsive cause, which Dr. BREITHAUPT supports in Instit. p. 315. When the decree of predestination is not called absolute, it is not by that very fact to be established as conditioned. For the opinion is not that God chose this or that person for salvation from eternity, if he were about to believe in Christ and depart from this life in true faith; but because he was about to believe and persevere: so that faith, viewed before the act of predestination in the will of God, becomes indeed a condition under which He Himself desires the salvation of all; but in the decree itself it does not act as a condition under which the election was made; but rather as the reason by which God was moved to elect. Therefore, it is not to be denied that the decree is absolute, in order to the conditioned, but [it is denied] so that the consideration of the reason a priori, outside of God, as a part in the predestinatory order, namely, faith in Christ foreseen from eternity, or what amounts to the same thing, the merit of Christ apprehended by faith, may not be excluded. Nor is the decree to be confused with the antecedent will of God, which, that it does not exclude a condition, but rather ordains it, we affirm from the Word of God (conf. Rom. XI, 23.)

Latin:

Aeternum electionis decretum non est absolutum, sed ordinatum a) & respectivum b); neque est conditionatum, sed categoricum & simplex c).

Prob. a. Decretum electionis non esse absolutum, sed ordinatum, sive certo mediorum ordine determinatum, liquet ex eo, quod electi dicimur secundum propositum Dei, quo is media salutis acquirendæ, offerendæ & recipiendæ ordinavit. De quo Paullus 1 Cor. I, 21: Complacuit Deo per stultitiam præconii salvare credentes.

Prob. b. Decretum prædestinationis esse respectivum patet; quia Deus, cum e lapsis hominibus aliquos, & quidem hos potius, quam illos, ad vitam æternam prædestinaret, respexit ad aliquid extra se, tanquam ad caussam impulsivam externam, scilicet meritum Christi, perfeueranti fide apprehendendum. Id quod demonstratum dedimus supra Q. 8. & 9.

Prob. c. Decretum prædestinationis, quatenus, præcise & strictissime sumtum, notat decretum æternum de impertienda finaliter credituris æterna salute intuitu meriti Christi, & præcognitæ in certis individuis fidei, non est conditionatum, conditione de futuro, sed categoricum & simplex, dicente D. SEBAST. SCHMID. in colleg. bibl. posteriori p. 235. Simpliciter quippe & categorice decrevit Deus hunc, illum, istum hominem salvare, quia perseverantem ipsius in Christum fidem certo præuidit. Perspicue hoc ostendit D. MVSAEVS in dissert. de decreto elect. p. 273. Electionis decretum, licet intuitu fidei prævisæ factum dicamus, conditionatum tamen, aut sub conditione fidei factum minime dicimus, sed si τὸ absolutum dicatur in oppositione ad τὸ conditionatum, decretum electionis absolutum, sive inconditionatum esse, intrepide statuimus; nec alio id sensu absolutum esse negamus, quam quo absolutum dicitur ad excludendum respectum causae impulsivae extra Deum, sive externae. Non autem statim conditionatum est decretum, quod intuitu alicuius causae impulsivae fit; sed si fiat intuitu causae impulsivae, iam in actu constitutae, vel distincte praecognitae, ut futurae, tum absolutum vel inconditionatum est. Voluit Deus pro immensa sua bonitate omnibus salutem donare sub conditione fidei in Christum, quae erat voluntas conditionata, non autem decretum electionis conditionatum. Quia autem Deus ab aeterno cognitum & perspectum habuit, non omnes gratia sua credituros in Christum, sed aliquos & eos, qui credituri erant, distincte nouerat, voluit salutem his largiri, quos credituros praevidit, intuitu quidem fidei in Christum, vel intuitu meriti Christi, fide apprehendendi, absolute tamen, h. e. sine conditione: & haec eius voluntas demum est decretum electionis, idque inconditionatum, sive absolutum, si absolutum dicatur in oppositione ad decretum conditionatum; at tamen non absolutum, si absolutum dicatur ad excludendum respectum causae impulsivae externae, cui suffragatur D. BREITHAVPT in instit. p. 315. Quando decretum praedestinationis haud dicitur absolutum, eo ipso non statuendum est conditionatum. Neque enim sententia est, quod hunc vel illum ad salutem ab aeterno elegerit Deus, si is in Christum crediturus esset, inque fide vera hinc discessurus; sed quia crediturus & perseveraturus erat: ut fides, ante actum praedestinationis spectata, in voluntate Dei, conditio fit quidem, sub qua ipse omnium salutem cupit; in decreto autem ipso non ut conditio se habeat, sub qua electio facta; verum ut ratio, qua Deus permotus ad eligendum. Non igitur negandum est, decretum absolutum esse, in ordine ad conditionatum, sed ne excludatur respectus rationis a priori, extra Deum, tanquam partis in ordine praedestinatorio, fidei nimirum in Christum ab aeterno praevisae, vel quod eodem recidit, meriti Christi, fide apprehensi. Neque confundendum est decretum cum voluntate Dei antecedente, quae quod conditionem non excludat, verum ordinet, ex verbo Dei (conf. Rom. XI, 23.) affirmamus.


### Q. XIII. Who are the elect in Christ unto eternal life?

The elect are miserable sinful men, chosen by God in Christ the Redeemer, not indiscriminately all, however they may conduct themselves a), but those whom God from eternity distinctly foresaw would finally believe in Christ b). Obs.

I. The material object of election is sinful men, considered in the sign of the divine reason, or the foreknowledge of God, as miserable and curable, and thus in need of a redeemer: The formal object, or the reason under which they are predestined, is final faith in Christ, foreseen from eternity by the omniscient God; and thus the adequate object of predestination is sinful men, but not indiscriminately, or indifferently all, but those whom God from eternity foresaw would finally believe in Christ. Obs.

II. Some authors distinguish between the specific and the adequate object of predestination. The specific object of election is not Christ Himself, not angels, not man to be created, nor created and constituted in the state of integrity before the fall, but considered in the state of misery after the fall. The ἐκνὸν [proper] and adequate object, according to the whole reason of the divine intuition, is the sinner redeemed by Christ, called, illuminated, converted, reborn and gifted with faith, justified and sanctified, whom God from eternity viewed as one who would not reject the first or common grace offered to all, as also the subsequently succeeding greater degrees of grace, but would believe through the offered grace, and would persevere in that grace. Conf. D. HULSEM. breu. cap. XV. p. m. 1020. 1024. And IOANN. ADAM. OSIANDRI colleg. theol. system. part VI. p. 107, 108. seq.

Prob. a I) By way of negation: a) Christ was not elected to glory from the common mass of corruption, since He was never a particle of it, on account of His miraculous conception by the Holy Spirit, Luke 1:35.

We are dealing here with the election of sinful men. But Christ was never in a state of sin, on account of the all-encompassing holiness of His whole life, Heb. 7:26.

We are dealing with the election of sinners in Christ, Eph. 1:4. But to say that Christ was elected in Christ, you would speak absurdly. b) Neither good nor evil angels enter into the circle of the elect in Christ.

The evil ones, by divine judgment, have been deemed miserable, and thus incurable. God did not spare the angels who sinned, says St. Peter, 2 Pet. 2:4. But the good angels were never in a state of misery and sin, which is the terminus from which election is made. But where the terminus of predestination from which, namely misery, has no place, there predestination itself has no place. Election strictly so-called was made in Christ, who is the redeemer and mediator of men, 1 Tim. 2:5, not of angels, Heb.

2:16. c) The object of election is not man to be created, or creatable, since election presupposes the existence of the object in the sign of divine reason, concerning which God is about to dispose something.

Whom God willed to save and glorify, Him He first willed to be. No father thinks of raising his children to dignity before begetting them. d) Man created, and established in a state of integrity before the fall, is not the object of election. For the elect are vessels of mercy, Rom. 9:23. Mercy presupposes misery. But man in his integrity was not miserable. Man was elected in Christ, Eph. 1: 4. But Christ came to save and seek that which was lost, Luke 19: 10. Man in his integrity was not lost. Therefore Christ did not come to seek and save man in his integrity, but man corrupted by sins.

Prob. a II). By way of affirmation, or positively: a) From the same existing clay, or mass of corruption, common to the elect and the reprobate (the assembly of fallen men), God prepared vessels of mercy for eternal glory, Rom. 9: 21. Therefore, He elected fallen men. β) God made those dead in sins to trust in the heavenly places, Eph. 2:6. γ) We are elected in Christ. But Christ is the redeemer of sinners, 1 John 2:21. δ) Election includes the remission of sins. For we are said to be elected, that the glory of God's grace might be praised, in which He made us acceptable (to Himself) in the beloved, in whom we have redemption through His blood, the remission of sins, Eph. 1:7. Therefore, the elect are sinful men. Prob. b.

The objects of election are indeed fallen men; but not insofar as they are and remain fallen, or sinners, for thus no one is elected or beloved, but all are hateful; but rather insofar as they are redeemed by Christ, regenerated by the power of the Holy Spirit, gifted with faith in Christ, and are to persevere in this faith to the end of life. Whence the elect are called μέλλοντες πιστεύειν, those about to believe in Christ unto eternal life, 1 Tim. 1:16, John 17:20. God chose the poor of this world, rich in faith, James 2:5. And whoever are elected in Christ, Eph. 1:4, they, as members, are grafted into Christ through faith, on account of the perpetual and indissoluble bond of Christ and faith in the business of salvation. Therefore THEOPHYLACTUS in Eph. 1: He chose us through Him, that is, through faith in Him.

But that God did not choose all who would believe, but only those who are to persevere in faith even to the last breath of life, for heavenly glory, we have proven.

Qu. 9, prob. b.

Latin:

Electi sunt a Deo in Christo redemptore homines peccatores miserabiles, non promiscue omnes, quomodocunque se habentes a), sed quos Deus finaliter in Christum credituros esse ab aeterno distincte praevidit b).

Obs. I. Obiectum materiale electionis sunt homines peccatores, in signo rationis divinae, seu praenotione Dei, considerati ut miserabiles & sanabiles, adeoque redemptoris indigii: Obiectum formale, seu ratio, sub qua praedestinati sunt, est fides finalis in Christum, ab aeterno praevisa a Deo omniscio; adeoque adaequatum obiectum praedestinationis sunt homines peccatores, at non promiscue, aut indifferenter omnes, sed, quos Deus finaliter in Christum credituros esse ab aeterno praevidit.

Obs. II. Distinguunt nonnulli auctores inter obiectum praedestinationis specificum & adaequatum. Electionis obiectum specificum non est Christus ipse, non angeli, non homo creandus, neque creatus & in statu integritatis ante lapsum constitutus, sed in statu miseriae post lapsum consideratus. Obiectum ἴδιον & adaequatum, secundum universam intuitus divini rationem, est peccator a Christo redemptus, vocatus, illuminatus, conversus, renatus ac fide donatus, iustificatus & sanctificatus, quem ab aeterno Deus intuitus est, tanquam non reiecturum primam seu communem omnibus vocatis gratiam, vt & deinceps succedentes maiores gratiae gradus, sed crediturum per oblatam gratiam, & in illa gratia pe Conf. D. HVLSEM. breu. perfeueraturum. Conf. D. HVLSEM. cap. XV. p. m. 1020. 1024. Et IOANN. ADAM. OSIANDRI colleg. theol. system. parte VI. p. 107, 108. seq.

Prob. a I) Κατ' ἄρσιν: a) Christus non electus est ad gloriam ex communi corruptionis massa, quippe cuius particula nunquam fuit, ob miraculosam conceptionem a Spiritu S.

Luc. I, 35. Agimus hic de electione hominum peccatorum. At Christus in statu peccati nunquam fuit, ob omnimodam totius vitæ sanctitatem, Hebr. VII,

26. Agimus de electione peccatorum in Christo, Eph. I, 4. Christum autem in Christo electum esse, absurde diceres. b) Circulum electorum in Christo non ingrediuntur angeli neque boni, neque mali.

Mali iudicio diuino reputati sunt immiserabiles, adeoque insanabiles. Angelis, qui peccarunt, Deus non pepercit, inquit S. Petrus 2 Ep. II, 4. Angeli boni autem nunquam fuerunt in statu miseriæ & peccati, qui est terminus, a quo facta est electio. At vbi terminus praedestinationis a quo, scil. miseria, locum non habet; ibi nec ipsa praedestinatio. Electio stricte dicta facta est in Christo, qui est redemptor & mediator hominum, 1 Tim. II, 5. non angelorum, Hebr.

II, 16. c) Obiectum electionis non est homo creandus, aut creabilis, cum electio existentiam obiecti in signo rationis diuinae, de quo aliquid dispositurus est Deus, praesupponat.

Quem Deus voluit saluare & glorificare, illum prius voluit esse. Nullus pater cogitat de liberis ad dignitatem euchendis prius, quam generandis. d) Homo creatus, & in statu integritatis ante lapsum constitutus, non est obiectum electionis. Nam electi sunt vasa misericordiae, Rom. IX, 23. Misericordia praesupponit miseriam. At homo integer non fuit miser. Electus est homo in Christo, Eph. I, 4. Venit autem Christus ad saluandum & quaerendum, quod perierat, Luc. XIX, 10. Homo integer non perierat. Ergo Christus non venit ad quaerendum & saluandum hominem integrum, sed peccatis corruptum.

Prob. a II). Κατὰ θέσιν, seu positiue: a) Ex luto eodem exsistente, seu massa corruptionis, electis & reprobis communi (hominum lapsorum coetu), praeparauit Deus vasa misericordiae ad aeternam gloriam. Rom. IX, 21. E. elegit homines lapsos. β) Deus mortuos in peccatis confidere fecit in caelestibus. Eph. II, 6. γ) Electi sumus in Christo. Sed Christus peccatorum est redemptor. 1 Ioann. II, 21. δ) Electio includit remissionem peccatorum. Dicimur enim electi, vt laudetur gloria gratiae Dei, in qua gratos nos fecit (sibi) in dilecto, in quo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ipsius, remissionem peccatorum. Eph. I, 7. E. electi sunt homines peccatores. Prob. b.

Obiectum electionis sunt quidem homines lapsi; non autem quatenus sunt & manent lapsi, vel peccatores, sic enim nemo electus dilectusue, sed omnes sunt exosi; verum quatenus a Christo redempti, virtute Spiritus S. regenerati, fide in Christum donati, & in hac fide ad finem vitae perseueraturi sunt. Vnde electi vocantur μέλλοντες πιστεύειν, credituri in Christum ad vitam aeternam. 1 Tim. I, 16. Ioann. XVII, 20. Deus elegit pauperes huius mundi, diuites in fide. Iacob. II, 5. Et quicunque electi sunt in Christo, Eph. I, 4. illi, velut membra Christo per fidem sunt insiti, ob perpetuum & indissolubilem nexum Christi & fidei in negotio salutis. Idcirco THEOPHYLACTUS in Eph. I. Elegit nos per ipsum, hoc est, per fidem in ipsum.

Quod autem Deus non omnes credituros, sed illos tantum, qui in fide vsque ad nouissimum vitae halitum perseueraturi sunt, ad gloriam caelestem elegerit, euicimus.

Qu. IX, prob. b.


### Quæst. XIV. Did God choose all men whatsoever unto eternal life?

The antithesis is of certain Papists, Scholastics, and other Doctors, in whose opinion the object of election is also Christ, the angels, and man constituted in the state of integrity. There are also those who contend that the decree of creation is in the sign of divine reason posterior to election, i.e., that God conceived man as eligible before he conceived him as creatable. Their stronger arguments are:

I. Christ himself is called predestined. Rom. 1, 4. Resp. Christ is not called in that place προορισθεὶς, predestined, but ὁρισθεὶς, declared, manifested, so that the sense is: Christ is declared and manifested as the true and natural Son of God by the most divine resurrection from the dead: inasmuch as he himself raised up his own flesh. John 10, 17. II. Christ is called προεγνωσμένος, foreknown, i.e., predestined. 1 Pet. 1, 20. Therefore he is not the cause of predestination. Resp. 1) Christ is not called predestined, but foreknown, namely for the acquiring of salvation, whereas we are predestined for the receiving of salvation. 2) The argument can be inverted: Christ with his merit is foreknown before the foundation of the world, v. 20. And election was made κατὰ πρόγνωσιν, v. 2. Therefore the consideration of the merit of Christ is not to be excluded from the decree of election. III. Christ is called a stone chosen by God, 1 Pet. 2, 4. Therefore he is not the cause of our election. Resp. 1) By the Hebrew phrase, 'chosen' means preeminent and excellent: 2) Christ is called a stone chosen by God, who is divinely ordained and constituted as the foundation of the church, of faith, of salvation, and of our election unto salvation. IV. Paul makes mention of τῶν ἐκλεκτῶν ἀγγέλων, the elect angels, 1 Tim. 5, 21. Therefore angels also are elect, not by consideration of the merit of Christ, for the reason that he is not the redeemer of angels; therefore it is by an absolute decree. Resp. 1) The election of angels is not called ἀτριαιori in the sense in which the election of men, who have fallen into sin and misery, is accepted; inasmuch as that has respect to the merit of Christ and the faith to be fixed in him: 2) The election of angels was not absolute, excluding every foreseen condition, to be freely but certainly fulfilled on the part of the angels. For just as God in time conferred blessedness upon those angels who rendered constant obedience to him: so God in his eternal decree concerning the choosing of certain angels unto glory benevolently regarded that persevering obedience, not as a meritorious cause; for that obedience was due to the Creator and temporary, and therefore had no force of merit before God: but as a non-meritorious condition, which God most liberally compensated beyond its worth.

Quæst. XIV.

Did God choose all men whatsoever unto eternal life? God did not choose all men indiscriminately, without any respect to faith in Christ, unto eternal life.

Prob. 1) The word 'election' itself implies particularity.* For to choose, when it is used of persons, signifies to segregate some from a common and indiscriminate group. Hence Christ says: I have chosen you out of the world, John 15, 19.

For nowhere in the sacred code do we read that few indeed are ἐκλεκτοὶ, but all are ἐκλελεγμένοι. For between those two there is no difference. Because of ἐκλεκτὲς (nominally) and ἐξελέξατο (verbally), and thus only ἐκλελεγμένους (participially), God has shortened the days, Mark 13, 20. For whoever is chosen verbally, he is also elect participially. But every one elect nominally is chosen verbally: Therefore.

3) St. Paul testifies clearly that God has chosen not many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble, but the foolish things of the world, 1 Cor. 1:27, 28. 4) Men are chosen to salvation in sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth, 2 Thess. 2:13. But faith is not of all, 2 Thess. 3:2. Therefore, not all men are chosen, but only a few, namely those who, according to the foreknowledge of God, have been regenerated by the Holy Spirit and gifted with true faith in Christ.

The antithesis was that of Sam. Huber, a Bernese from the Swiss, a Wittenberg theologian, who, after the Formula of Concord was written, in the year 1593, attempted to defend a universal election (in the most absolute sense), or one of all men whatsoever; his chief arguments were: I. That which has universal causes is itself universal. But all the causes of election are universal; namely, the benevolence of God the Father, the merit of the Son, and the calling of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, election is universal. Resp. I concede that that which has all its causes, both principal and instrumental, or less principal, as universal, is itself universal. But the instrumental or less principal cause, namely faith in Christ, is not of all, 2 Thess. 3:2.

Objection: Faith is posterior to election. Therefore, it is not a cause. Resp. Faith is posterior to predestination regarding existence, yet it is prior regarding divine foreknowledge. For God first knew that these or those would finally believe, then in view of this final faith, He predestined them to salvation.

II. Whoever are chosen in Christ, their election is universal: But miserable sinners, etc. Therefore. The major is evident: because Christ is a catholic redeemer. The minor is clear from Eph. 1:4. Resp. Christ enters into the decree of election not absolutely without the application of men, but in respect of the final application, which is made by man, apprehending the merit of Christ.

III. Whomever God willed to be holy and blameless, He chose them, Eph. 1:4. But He willed all men to be holy and blameless. Therefore. Resp. I deny the major, because the election of men was not made according to the antecedent will of God, by which He wills all men to be holy; but according to the consequent will of God, which follows πρóγνωσιν, or the foreknowledge of the obedience of men, and thus concerns man insofar as he is foreseen as faithful or obedient. But not all men obey God, who demands the pursuit of holiness from all. Therefore, not all are chosen. Furthermore, we argue by a not dissimilar reasoning: Whomever men God willed to be holy and blameless, He justified them: But He willed all men, etc. Therefore.

IV. If God did not choose all men to eternal salvation, He passed over some by an absolute decree: But God passed over no men absolutely. Therefore, He chose all men to eternal salvation. The consequence of the major is evident; because whom God does not choose to salvation, He passes over in the decree of election. Resp. I distinguish between an absolute decree and an ordered one. God established this order, that all men should conceive faith in Christ through the means of grace, and retain it until the end of life; those who do not submit themselves to this order, God passes over not absolutely, but on account of their petulant rejection of the means of grace and final incredulity .

Latin:

Antithesis est quorundam Pontificiorum, Scholasticorum, aliorumque Doctorum, quorum de sententia obiectum electionis etiam est Christus, angeli, & homo in statu integritatis constitutus. Sunt etiam, qui contendunt, decretum creationis in signo rationis diuinae esse posterius electione, h. e. Deum prius concepisse hominem eligibilem, quam creabilem. Quorum potiora argumenta sunt:

I. Christus ipse dicitur praedestinatus. Rom. I, 4. Resp. Christus non dicitur l. c. προορισθεὶς, praedestinatus, sed ὁρισθεὶς, declaratus, manifestatus, vt sensus sit: Christus declaratus & manifestatus est Filius Dei verus & naturalis ex diuinissima resurrectione ex mortuis: quippe qui carnem suam ipse resuscitauit. Ioann. X, 17. II. Christus dicitur προεγνωσμένος, praecognitus, i. e. praedestinatus. 1 Petr. I, 20. Ergo non est praedestinationis causa. Resp. 1) Christus non dicitur praedestinatus, sed praecognitus, nimirum ad salutem acquirendam, nos praedestinati sumus ad salutem accipiendam. 2) Inverti potest argumentum: Christus cum suo merito est praecognitus ante mundi constitutionem, v. 20. Et electio facta est κατὰ πρόγνωσιν, v. 2. Ergo intuitus meriti Christi a decreto electionis non est excludendus. III. Christus dicitur lapis a Deo electus, 1 Petr. II, 4. E. non est nostrae electionis causa. Resp. 1) Phrasi hebraea electus est praestans & excellens: 2) Christus dicitur a Deo electus lapis, qui diuinitus ordinatus & constitutus est fundamentum ecclesiae, fidei, salutis & electionis nostrae ad salutem. IV. Paullus mentionem facit τῶν ἐκλεκτῶν ἀγγέλων, electorum angelorum, 1 Tim. V, 21. Ergo etiam electi sunt angeli non intuitu meriti Christi, propterea, quod is non est redemtor angelorum; ergo absoluto decreto. Resp. 1) Electio angelorum non dicitur ἀτριαιori eo sensu, quo accipitur electio hominum, in peccatum & miseriam prolapsorum; vtpote quae respectum habet ad meritum Christi, & fidem in illo defigendam: 2) Electio angelorum non fuit absoluta, omnem praeuisam conditionem, ex parte angelorum libere, sed certo implendam, excludens. Sicut enim Deus in tempore beatitudinem illis contulit angelis, qui constantem ipsi praestiterunt obedientiam: ita Deus in decreto aeterno de quibusdam angelis ad gloriam eligendis perseuerantem illam obedientiam beneuole respexit, non vt caussam meritioriam; fuit enim illa obedientia creatori debita ac temporaria, adeoque vim meriti apud Deum non habuit: sed vt conditionem non meritoriam, quam Deus vltra condignum liberalissime compensauit.

Quæst. XIV. Num Deus omnes omnino homines ad vitam aeternam elegit?

Deus non omnes homines promiscue, citra vllum fidei in Christum respectum, ad vitam aeternam elegit. *

Prob. 1) Ipsa vox, electio, particularitatem infert.* Nam eligere, quando de personis vsurpatur, significat aliquos a communi & promiscuo coetu segregare. Hinc Christus dicit: Elegi vos ex mundo, Ioann. XV, 19.

2) Dicta Christi vox est: Multi sunt vocati, sed pauci electi, Matth. XX, 16. c. XXII, 14. Frustra hic distinguitur inter ἐκλεκτὲς (nominaliter), & ἐκλελεγμένους (participialiter). Nullibi enim in sacro codice legimus, quod pauci quidem sint ἐκλεκτοὶ, omnes vero sint ἐκλελεγμένοι. Inter duo enim illa non est discrimen. Propter ἐκλεκτὲς (nominaliter), & ἐξελέξατο (verbaliter), adeoque tantum ἐκλελεγμένους (participialiter), Deus abbreuiauit dies, Marc. XIII, 20. Quicunque enim eligitur verbaliter, ille etiam electus est participialiter. Sed omnis electus nominaliter eligitur verbaliter: Ergo.

3) Perspicue testatur S. Paullus, quod Deus non multos sapientes secundum carnem, non multos potentes, non multos nobiles, sed quae stulta sunt mundi, elegerit, 1 Cor. 1:27, 28. 4) Electi sunt homines ad salutem in sanctificatione Spiritus et fide veritatis, 2 Thess. 2:13. At fides non est omnium, 2 Thess. 3:2. Ergo non omnes homines sunt electi, sed pauci tantum, nimirum qui secundum praescientiam Dei a Spiritu S. renati, et vera in Christum fide donati sunt.

Antithesis fuit Sam. Huberi, Bernatis ex Helvetiis, Theologi Wittenbergensis, qui post conscriptam F.
