C. anno 1593. electionem (in sensu praecidissimo) vniversalem, seu omnium omnino hominum defendere conatus est; cuius praecipua fuerunt argumenta: I. Cuius causae omnes sunt vniversales, illud est vniversale. Atqui electionis causae omnes sunt vniversales; nempe benevolentia Dei Patris, meritum Filii, et vocatio Spiritus S. Ergo electio est vniversalis. Resp. Cuius omnes causae, tum principales, tum instrumentales, seu minus principales, sunt vniversales, id ipsum est vniversale, concedo. At causa instrumentalis, seu minus principalis, nimirum fides in Christum non est omnium, 2 Thess. 3:2.

Instantia: Fides est posterior electione. E. non est causa. Resp. Fides est posterior praedestinatione, quoad existentiam, prior tamen est, quoad praevisionem diuinam. Prius enim Deus cognouit hos vel illos finaliter credituros esse, deinde intuitu huius fidei finalis praedestinauit eos ad salutem.

II. Quicunque electi sunt in Christo, illorum electio est vniversalis: Atqui peccatores miseri etc. E. Maior constat: quia Christus est redemtor catholicus. Minor liquet ex Eph. 1:4. Resp. Christus ingreditur decretum electionis non absolute citra hominum applicationem, sed respectu finalis applicationis, quae fit ab homine, meritum Christi apprehendente.

III. Quoscunque Deus voluit esse sanctos et irreprehensibiles, illos elegit, Eph. 1:4. Atqui voluit omnes homines esse sanctos et irreprehensibiles. E. Resp. Neg. maior, quia electio hominum non est facta secundum voluntatem Dei antecedentem, qua omnes homines vult esse sanctos; sed secundum voluntatem Dei consequentem, quae πρóγνωσιν, seu praecognitionem obedientiae hominum subsequitur, adeoque versatur circa hominem, quatenus praevisus est fidelis, vel obediens. At non omnes homines Deo sanctitatis studium a cunctis exigenti obediunt. Ergo non omnes sunt electi. Ceterum haud dispari ratione argumentamur: Quoscunque homines Deus voluit esse sanctos et inculpatos, illos iustificauit: Atqui voluit omnes homines etc. Ergo.

IV. Si Deus non omnes homines ad aeternam salutem elegit, quosdam absoluto decreto praeteriit: Atqui Deus nullos homines absolute praeteriit. E. omnes homines ad aeternam salutem elegit. Consequentia maioris est euidens; quia quem Deus ad salutem non eligit, illum praeterit in decreto electionis. Resp. Dist. inter decretum absolutum, et ordinatum. Deus hunc sanciuit ordinem, vt omnes homines per media gratiae fidem in Christum concipiant, eamque vsque ad finem vitae retineant; qui ordini huic se non submittunt, illos Deus praeterit non absolute, sed ob petulantem reiectionem mediorum gratiae, finalemque incredulitatem . gratiæ, finalemque incredulitatem *).


### Q. XV. Can the elect fall into mortal sins, cast off the grace of the Holy Spirit, and utterly lose faith in Christ?

The elect, following the desires of the flesh, can fall into proæretic [deliberate] and mortal sins, and can cast off the grace of the Holy Spirit and totally lose saving faith, not indeed until the end of life, but for a time.

Obj. I. The question is not about the fall of the reborn, whom we showed above to fall into mortal sins, but about the fall of the elect. For there is a certain distinction between the reborn and the elect . The reborn are properly those who have been gifted with true faith in Christ through the grace of the Holy Spirit; yet not a few of them believe only for a time, extinguishing the faith they received through final impenitence. The elect are those who, also reborn through the Holy Spirit, fall for a time from faith into voluntary sins, and fail, but they do not persist in these finally; rather, having fallen, they rise again and truly repent. Therefore, the reborn are judged by their present faith: the elect by their final faith. And so, not all the reborn are elect: nor are all the elect always and at every time reborn. For there are reborn who are reprobated on account of final impenitence: there are also elect who, on account of proæretic sins to which they indulge, are sometimes not in a state of regeneration.

Obj. II. Distinguish between the total and the final loss of faith. The former is that by which saving faith is totally lost, so that from a son of grace one becomes a son of wrath: the latter is that by which a man, succumbing to the flesh, deprives himself of true faith and never recovers it, but departs from this life in infidelity.

We prove the assertion indirectly from the lesser to the greater, taking the argument from the fall of the first-formed humans, who shone with created justice, and nonetheless fell into a most grave sin, contracted for themselves the offense of God, and broke the bond of gracious union with God. For God had gravely threatened death to the disobedient, Gen. II, 17. Where by the name of death is understood not only bodily death, but also spiritual, which consists in the dissolution of union with God. You say:

I. Original justice could be lost, but evangelical justice, which has the promise of stability, is not losable. Resp. Man established in the state of integrity was firmer for retaining justice, and fortified with greater safeguards against sin, than man reborn and elect after the fall. In him there was excellent wisdom of intellect, perfect holiness of will, and signal purity of sensitive appetite: but this man is in part carnal, sold under sin, who does not acknowledge what he does; for he does not do what he wants, but he does what he hates, Rom. VII, 15. 16. You say:

II. The example of the first-formed is foreign to the purpose, because they never lost faith in Christ, about which the question here is, in the state of integrity: for man in his integrity did not need a mediator. Resp. The question here is ventilated not only about the loss of justifying faith, but also about the casting off of divine grace, which the first-formed poured out by their disobedience just as the reborn and elect after the fall cast off the same by proæretic sins.

Prob. 2) Directly, and indeed by examples of both the Old and New Testaments. From the Old Testament we shall bring forward only two examples: a) Aaron, whom the Psalter (Ps. 106:19) calls the saint of the Lord. By the casting of the golden calf, he committed two evils: One, that the Israelites might perpetrate in reality and deed the crime of idolatry, which they had conceived only in mind and thought: The other, that what they seemed about to do by private error, they might do by public authority, when they received the idol from the high priest, around which they might revel.

Objection: The sin of Aaron was not prohaereticum [deliberate/premeditated], in that he yielded to the clamors of the tumultuous people against his own will, and was forced by the insane mob to form the calf. Response: Let it be a matter of conscience for us not to extenuate the great sin of Aaron. For thus Moses says of him in Deut. 9:20: "And Jehovah was very angry with Aaron to have destroyed him; and I prayed for Aaron also the same time.

It was the duty of the high priest to undergo a thousand deaths rather than to assent to the impious desire of the tumultuous people, and to approve profane worship by his authority. b) King David, whose adultery and homicide are established from 2

Sam. 11:15. But adulterers and murderers contract for themselves the guilt of eternal death, as Paul teaches (Gal. 5:19; 1 Cor. 6:9).

You say: King David did not sin with full will, but out of the weakness of the flesh. He committed adultery out of burning concupiscence, which clouded his mind: but homicide out of fear of the infamy that would redound to him. That he did not utterly lose the grace of God is gathered from the fact that God, moved by mercy, sends to him the prophet Nathan, by whose brief admonition he is recalled to perform repentance. Add that in Ps. 51:13 he does not pray: "Restore to me your Holy Spirit taken away"; but: "Take not the spirit of your holiness from me," which is an indication that the Holy Spirit had not been expelled from his heart.

Response: If such excuses were of any avail, it would be easy for any enormous sinner to cloak his villainies. For who is so ferociously depraved as to wish to sin with the fullest election of mind and liberty of will? For man is tempted by his own concupiscence, while he is drawn away and enticed.

Then concupiscence, when it has conceived, brings forth sin; but sin, when it is finished, brings forth death (James 1:14-15). David polluted himself with an adulteress; God will judge every adulterer (Heb. 13:4). To adultery he added homicide; every murderer does not have eternal life abiding in him (1 John 3:15).

He sinned securely, performing no repentance for ten whole months, and hence was held as a son of death in the judgment of God (2 Sam. 12:7). Therefore, he utterly cast off the indwelling grace of God, although he did not lose the grace of God externally assisting, knocking, and exciting, by which he was recalled to the way through the prophet Nathan.

David prayed against the removal of the Holy Spirit in Ps. 51 not while he still remained impenitent in his sins, but when he repented at the hearing of the prophetic sermon.

From the New Testament, we likewise bring forward two examples: a) One is the Apostle Peter, who by denying Christ made a total loss of faith (Matt.

26:70). For whoever truly believes in Christ, he confesses Him (2 Cor. 4:13).

Peter not only did not confess Christ, but furthermore even denied Him. Therefore, he did not have true faith then.

True faith receives Christ (John 1:12); denial repudiates Christ. Therefore, true faith does not consist with denial in one heart.

True faith overcomes the world (1 John 5:4). But Peter was overcome by a little maid. Therefore, Peter did not truly believe then.

No one who devotes himself to curses and swears falsely has justifying faith in any way; Peter, by denying Christ, devoted himself to curses and swore falsely. Therefore, where conversion is needed, there aversion has preceded.

Peter needed conversion, as Christ testifies: "When you are converted, strengthen your brethren" (Luke 22:32). Therefore.

You object I: Peter did not sin ἑκουσίως [voluntarily]... with destined malice, but struck by the fear of imminent danger, he denied Christ, so that he might save his life. Wherefore his sin was not prohaereticum [deliberate], or deadly, but involuntary, by which faith is not extinguished.

Response: Although Peter at first he did not sin with deliberate malice, his breast being shaken by the horror of death itself, and the struggle between the Spirit and the flesh still enduring; yet when this ceased, and the flesh carried off the victory, he sinned ἑκουσίως, or voluntarily.

For he suffered himself to be overcome by the flesh, and denied Christ three times; which Petrine progression and perseverance in denying Christ argues his election. Which is also evident from this, that he thought the lesser of two evils should be chosen, namely, he preferred to deny Christ rather than to expose himself to the dangers of life: by which very act he sinned gravely.

For Christ said to his disciples: Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and (thus) follow me.

For whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it, Mark VIII, 34. 35. Objection II.

Christ prayed for Peter, that his faith might not fail, Luke XXII, 32. Resp. Distinguish between a final and a total failure of faith.

Peter was preserved by the prayers of Christ from a final failure of faith, so that after his denial he would not fall into despair, but that he might repent, recover saving faith, and retain it until the end of his life, and thus become a partaker of eternal salvation.

Objection III. Peter denied Christ with his mouth, but not with his heart. Resp.

If this is posited, Peter becomes guilty of a most foul lie. b) Another example is that of the incestuous Corinthian, mention of whom is made in 1 Cor.

V, 1 sqq. His enormous crime could not consist with true faith.

For it was nefarious, detestable in the judgment of the more sensible Gentiles, and notorious, because not secretly, but openly, and with the knowledge of the church, he abused his stepmother for most shameful lust. St. Paul, by the power conferred by Christ, delivered him to Satan, not that he might be reprobated or damned, but that his spirit might be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus. He was not, therefore, of the number of the reprobate or the damned, but of the elect and those to be saved.

For he did not remain impenitent or an unbeliever until the end of his life, but repented and recovered his faith. From which the Apostle, as he returned to the way, forgave the abominable crime in the sight of Christ. 1

1 Corinthians

Latin:

Electi desideriis carnis obsequentes in peccata proæretica atque mortifera prolabi, gratiam Spiritus S. excutere fidemque salvificam non quidem usque ad finem vitæ, ad tempus tamen totaliter amittere possunt.

Obs. I. Quæritur non de lapsu renatorum, quos in peccata mortifera ruere, supra ostendimus, sed de lapsu electorum. Datur quippe discrimen quoddam inter renatos, & electos . Renati proprie sunt, qui per gratiam Spiritus S. vera in Christum fide donati sunt; quorum tamen haud pauci ad tempus tantum credunt, finali impoenitentia acceptam fidem exstinguentes. Electi sunt, qui & ipsi per Spiritum S. regeniti, ad tempus fide, in peccata voluntaria prolapsi, deficiunt, in istis vero finaliter non persistunt, sed lapsi resurgunt, vereque resipiscunt. Renati igitur æstimantur ex fide præsenti: Electi ex fide finali. Ideoque non omnes renati sunt electi: nec omnes electi semper & omni tempore sunt renati. Dantur enim renati, qui ob finalem impoenitentiam reprobantur: dantur etiam electi, qui, ob peccata proæretica, quibus indulgent, aliquando non sunt in statu regenerationis.

Obs. II. Dist. inter amissionem fidei totalem, & finalem. Illa est, qua fides salvifica tota perditur, vt ex filio gratiæ fiat filius iræ: Hæc est, qua homo, carni succumbens, seipsum vera fide privat, eamque nunquam recuperat, sed in infidelitate ex hac vita discedit.

Probamus assertum indirecte a minori ad maius, sumto argumento e lapsu hominum protoplastorum, qui creata refulserunt iustitia, & nihilo minus in gravissimum prolapsi peccatum, offensam Dei sibi contraxerunt, & vinculum gratiosae unionis cum Deo ruperunt. Graviter quippe comminatus erat Deus mortem immorigeris, Gen. II, 17. Vbi nomine mortis non tantum mors corporalis, sed & spiritualis, quæ in dissolutione unionis cum Deo consistit, intelligitur.

Dicis: I. Iustitia primæva potuit amitti, non autem amissibilis est iustitia evangelica, quæ promissionem stabilitatis habet. Resp. Homo constitutus in statu integritatis firmior erat ad retinendam iustitiam, maioribusque munitus præsidiis aduersus peccatum, quam homo renatus & electus post lapsum. In illo erat eximia sapientia intellectus, perfecta sanctitas voluntatis, & insignis puritas appetitus sensitivi: at hic ex parte carnalis est, venundatus sub peccatum, qui, quod operatur, non agnoscit; non enim quod vult, hoc facit, sed quod odit, id facit, Rom. VII, 15. 16.

Dicis: II. Exemplum protoplastorum alienum est a proposito, quia illi fidem in Christum, de qua hic quæstio est, in statu integritatis nunquam amiserunt: homo namque integer mediatore non indigebat. Resp. Quæstio hic ventilatur non tantum de amissione fidei iustificæ, sed etiam de excussione gratiæ divinæ, quam protoplasti inobedientia suæ peræque effuderunt, ac renati & electi post lapsum eandem peccatis proæreticis excutiunt.

Prob. 2) Directe, & quidem exemplis tam veteris, quam novi testamenti. Ex vet. test. duo tantum proferemus exempla: a) Aaronis, quem sanctum Domini Psalterium CVI, 19. appellat. Qui conflatione vituli aurei duo mala commisit: Unum, ut Israelitae idololatriae scelus, quod animo & cogitatione tantum conceperant, reipsa & facto perpetrarent: Alterum, ut quod privato errore facturi videbantur, id publica auctoritate facerent, dum a summo sacerdote idolum acceperunt, circa quod debacharentur.

Except. Peccatum Aaronis non fuit prohaereticum, eo, quod tumultuantis populi clamoribus contra voluntatem suam cessit, & formare vitulum ab insana plebe coactus est. Resp. Grande Aaronis peccatum extenuare, nobis sit religio. Sic enim Moses de illo inquit Deut. IX, 20. Contra Aaronem ira motus est Iehovah valde ad perdendum eum; oravi vero etiam pro Aarone tempore isto.

Summi sacerdotis erat, mille potius subire mortes, quam impio tumultuantis populi desiderio annuere, & cultum profanum auctoritate sua approbare. b) Regis Davidis, cuius adulterium & homicidium constat e 2

Sam. XI, 15. Adulteros autem & homicidas aeternae mortis reatum sibi contrahere, docet Paullus Gal. V, 19. 1 Cor. VI, 9.

Dicis: Non peccauit rex Dauid plena voluntate, sed ex carnis imbecillitate. Commisit adulterium ex aestuante concupiscentia, quae mentem eius obnubilauit: homicidium autem ex metu infamiae ad se redundaturae. Quod autem gratiam Dei non penitus amiserit, colligitur ex eo, quod Deus motus misericordia ad eum mittit prophetam Nathanem, cuius brevi admonitione ad agendam poenitentiam revocatur. Adiice, quod Ps. LI, 13. non precatur: Spiritum S. tuum ablatum redde mihi; sed: Spiritum sanctitatis tuae ne aufer a me, quod indicio est, Spiritum S. ex corde eius non expulsum fuisse.

Resp. Si eiusmodi excusationes quidquam proficerent, cuilibet enormi peccatori promptum foret, flagitia sua palliare. Ecquis enim adeo efferate proteruit, ut cum plenissima mentis electione & voluntatis libertate peccare velit? Tentatur quippe homo a propria concupiscentia, dum abstrahitur & inescatur.

Deinde concupiscentia, postquam concipit, parit peccatum; peccatum vero, quando consummatum est, parturit mortem, Iac. I, 14. 15. Polluit se Dauid adultero; adulterium omnem Deus iudicabit, Hebr. XIII, 4. Adulterio adiecit homicidium; omnis homicida non habet vitam aeternam in se manentem, 1 Io. III, 15.

Peccauit secure, nullam agens per menses integros decem poenitentiam, & inde Filius mortis in iudicio Dei habitus est, 2 Sam. XII, 7. Proinde penitus excussit gratiam Dei inhabitantem, quamuis non amiserit gratiam Dei externe assistentem, pulsantem & excitantem, qua per prophetam Nathanem in viam revocatus est.

Ablationem Spiritus S. deprecatus est Dauid Ps. LI. non cum adhuc impoenitens haereret in peccatis, sed cum ad auditum concionis propheticae resipuit.

Ex nouo testamento itidem duo adducimus exempla: a) Unum est Apostoli Petri, qui abnegando Christum totam fidei fecit iacturam, Matth.

XXVI, 70. Qui namque vere in Christum credit, is illum confitetur, 2 Cor. I, 13.

Petrus Christum non tantum non est confessus, sed insuper etiam negauit. E. tunc veram fidem non habuit.

Vera fides Christum recipit, Io. I, 12.; abnegatio Christum repudiat. Ergo vera fides cum abnegatione in vno corde non consistit.

Vera fides vincit mundum, 1 Io. V, 4. At Petrus victus est a muliercula. Ergo Petrus tunc vere non credit.

Nullas, qui seipsum diris deuouet & peierat, habet fidem iustificantem vllo modo, Petrus Christum abnegando seipsum diris deuouit & peierauit. E. Vbi conuersione opus est, ibi auersio praecessit.

Petrus conuersione opus habuit, teste Christo: Tu conuersus, confirma fratres tuos, Luc. XXII, 32. E.

Excipis I. Petrus non peccauit ἐκουσίως,... destinata malitia, sed metu imminentis periculi perculsus abnegauit Christum, vt vitam seruaret. Quare peccatum eius non fuit prohaereticum, aut mortiferum, sed involuntarium, quo fides non exstinguitur.

Resp. Quamuis Petrus primum non peccauerit destinata malitia, horrore mortis ipsius pectus conquassante, & durante adhuc Spiritus & carnis lucta; hac tamen cessante, & carne victoriam reportante, peccauit ἑκουσίως, siue voluntarie.

Passus enim est, se a carne vinci, & ter Christum abnegauit; quæ Petrina Christum abnegandi progressio & perseuerantia arguit ipsius præelectionem. Quæ hinc etiam elucet, quod e duobus malis minus eligendum putauit, nempe maluit Christum abnegare, quam periculis vitæ se obiicere: quo ipso grauiter peccauit.

Dixit enim Christus discipulis suis: Quisquis voluerit post me venire, abnegato seipsum, tollatque crucem suam, ac (ita) sequatur me. Qui enim voluerit animam seruare, perdet eam, Marc.

VIII, 34. 35. Excipis II.

Christus rogauit pro Petro, ne fides ipsius deficiat, Luc. XXII, 32. Resp.

Dist. inter defectionem fidei finalem, & totalem. A finali fidei defectione Petrus precibus Christi præseruatus est, ne post abnegationem incideret in desperationem, sed vt resipisceret, fidemque saluificam reciperet, & vsque ad finem vitæ retineret, atque adeo æternæ salutis particeps fieret.

Excipis III. Petrus abnegauit Christum ore, sed non corde.

Resp. Posito hoc, Petrus fœdissimi reus fit mendacii. b) Alterum exemplum est incestuosi Corinthiaci, cuius mentio fit 1

Cor. V, 1 sqq. Huius scelus enorme cum vera fide consistere nequiuit.

Fuit enim nefandum, iudicio saniorum gentilium detestabile, & notorium, quia non clam, sed palam, & conscia ecclesia, nouerca sua ad turpissimam libidinem abusus est. S. Paullus ex potestate, a Christo collata, eundem tradidit Satanæ, non vt reprobaretur, aut damnaretur, sed vt Spiritus ipsus saluaretur in die Domini Iesu. Non igitur fuit e numero reproborum, aut damnatorum, sed electorum & saluandorum.

Neque enim vsque ad finem vitæ impoenitens aut incredulus permanfit, sed resipuit, fidemque recuperauit. Ex quo Apostolus ipsi in viam redeunti facinus abominandum in conspectu Christi condonauit.

1 Cor.


### Q. XV. Can the elect fall into mortal sins, cast off the grace of the Holy Spirit, and utterly lose faith in Christ?: Cor. II, 10

Cor. II, 10

Proof 3

3) By the most famous sayings of Scripture, of which, for the sake of brevity, we shall cite only two.

The first we take from 1 Tim.

I, 17. 18. This charge I commit to you, son Timothy, according to the prophecies previously made concerning you, that you may wage the good warfare in them; having faith and a good conscience, which some have rejected, and concerning the faith have made shipwreck.

We doubt not that Timothy was predestined from eternity to celestial glory. For he was, by prophecy, or a special revelation of the Holy Spirit, set over the office of teaching, a genuine son of Paul in the faith, and a possessor of sincere faith.

Cf. 1

Tim. I, 2.

2 Tim.

I, 5. Paul exhorted him to wage the good warfare, by manfully struggling against the devil, the world, and the flesh, so that he might carry off a glorious victory. The Apostle shows, however, that this spiritual warfare cannot be legitimately performed unless faith in Christ is kept holily and chastely, as it is the shield, divinely ordained, for extinguishing the fiery darts of the devil.

Eph. VI, 16. Furthermore, he teaches that faith cannot be guarded unless a good conscience is kept, and one abstains from voluntary sins, by which the serenity of the conscience is clouded, which doctrine he confirms by proposing the examples of those who made shipwreck concerning the faith, having cast away a good conscience through proæretic [deliberate] sins.

From which this argument flows: Whoever is solicitously admonished of his duty, with the fear of an opposing defection, he can fail totally: A certain elect person (Timothy) is solicitously admonished, etc. Therefore.

The latter we take from the Johannine Apocalypse, ch. III, 11. where the Son of God addresses the Bishop of Philadelphia: hold what you have, that no one may take away your crown.

The meaning is: continue to keep the faith entire, and a good conscience, lest the crown of glory, destined for you, be taken away. We gather from these that the elect can lose faith.

For why would Christ admonish: hold what you have, if no loss of faith were to be feared? Why would he place before their eyes the danger of the crown being taken away, if this were absolutely destined without regard to persevering faith?

Prob. 4 From the daily prayers of the pious: And lead us not into temptation? Matt. VI, 13. By which all the faithful, and thus even the elect, testify both to the atrocity of the enemies with whom they must struggle, and to the infirmity of their own strength, because, abandoned by God and left to themselves, they could succumb to enemies soliciting them to the gravest of sins, and be swept headlong into infidelity and despair. To these daily prayers must be added the prayer of David: Take not thy holy spirit from me! Ps. LI, 13. A prayer for the Spirit not to be taken away argues for the possibility of its removal. There is an antithesis of the Anabaptists, in whom the Augsburg Confession in article XII condemned grace as being totally unloseable, in these words: They condemn (our churches) the Anabaptists, who deny that those once justified can lose the Holy Spirit.

The stronger of their arguments are: I. Whoever are elected to heavenly glory, in view of faith persevering in Christ, their faith does not fail: But reborn men, as the Evangelicals themselves teach, are elected in view of persevering faith: Therefore. Resp. Distinguish between perseverance that is continuous, or incessant, and that which is not continuous, or interrupted. The former belongs to men who never sin out of deliberate malice, but only out of infirmity, which, because of the imperfection of renewal and the remnants of the old man, happens to travelers in this mortality with difficulty, or rarely. The latter is broken for a time by deliberate sins, but is restored through serious repentance, and lasts until the end of life. In the article of election, perseverance of faith is understood as lasting to the end of life, whether it be continuous or not continuous.

II. No one can snatch Christ's sheep from his hand: Truly the faithful are Christ's sheep: Therefore. The major is clear from John X, 28. Resp. Christ's sheep, as long as they hear the voice of Christ the shepherd and follow him, no one can snatch from Christ's hand. But if the sheep cease to hear the voice of Christ the shepherd and to follow him, Christ himself casts them from his hand, and ceases to exercise the protection of them that he previously exercised. And thence, unless they allow themselves to be recalled from error, they finally fall as prey to the infernal wolf: which certainly is not to be snatched from the hand of Christ .

III. The elect never totally lose or cast away justifying faith; because they are like trees that are planted by the rivers of water, which always bear fruit, and never wither, Ps. I, 3. If, therefore, the elect always bear the fruits of righteousness, the tree of faith never withers. Resp. Trees planted by the rivers of water retain fertility and leaves as long as they draw moisture and nourishment from the rivers by which they are planted; but when they have suffered vice or force, they are hindered from doing so, and gradually wither and die. Thus the faithful bear timely fruits and retain the beauty of righteousness as long as they draw sap from the flowing grace of the word and sacraments. But indeed, if, indulging in vices, they despise the word and sacraments, they lose the life of grace and die spiritually. The psalmist himself insinuates this limitation, Ps. I, 3: Blessed is the man who meditates in the law of the Lord day and night: for he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water.

IV. Who-

Under the evangelical covenant, God imparts to them the gift of perseverance, so that they may never depart from Him: But the elect, etc.: Therefore. The major is proved from Jer. 32:40. "I will make an everlasting covenant with them; that I will not turn away from them, to do them good; but I will put my fear in their hearts, that they shall not depart from me." Resp. The covenant of God with men is not absolute, but ordered, or conditional. The divine promise in the cited place, "I will put my fear in their hearts, that they shall not depart from me," includes the tacit condition of the operation of grace not being hindered by the voluntary and free resistance of men. For in putting the fear of Himself into our hearts, God does not act irresistibly, but resistibly, and with the liberty of resisting left behind. Hence it happens that none are excluded from the participation of the goods promised in the covenant, unless those who voluntarily resist God, who deprive themselves of these same goods by their own fault. Conf. Ezek. 11:20, 21.

V. Whosoever falling God does not cast away, but supports with His hand, their fall is not total, shaking off the grace of God: But the just falling, etc. Ps. 37:24. Therefore. Resp. Distinguish between an external fall, or of fortune, and an internal one, or of the soul. The whole of Psalm 37 speaks of the external falls of the pious and the impious, of the prosperity of the former and the unhappiness of the latter, and therefore the cited place does not strike the mark.

VI. Whoever is apprehended by the divine hand is always with God, he cannot fall from the grace of God: But the elect, etc. Therefore. The major is evident: because to be always with God and to fall from divine grace are opposites, which cannot consist together. The minor is clear from Ps. 73:23. Resp. The apprehension and sustentation, which is done by the divine hand, is neither irresistible nor indeclinable; for the reason that God permits him who maliciously departs to fall.

VII. Whoever cannot be seduced, they cannot lose faith: But the elect cannot be seduced. Therefore. The major is evident; because the loss of faith is from the seduction of the devil, the world, and the flesh. The minor is proved from Matt. 24:24. "There shall arise false Christs and false prophets, and shall show great signs and wonders, so as to lead into error, if possible, even the elect." Resp. Distinguish between impossibility absolute and hypothetical. It is impossible for the elect to be seduced, not by an absolute or causal impossibility proceeding from an irresistible operation of grace, but by a hypothetical impossibility, resting upon the hypothesis of election, made according to the prevision of persevering faith. But since perseverance is in one way continuous, and in another not continuous, the elect can be seduced for a time totally, but not finally, on account of the infallibility of divine foreknowledge.

VIII. Nothing can separate the faithful from the love of God. Rom. 8:38. Resp. 1) No external creature can separate the faithful from the love of God: but indwelling sin, which is not a creature, if dominion is permitted to it, tears them away from God. 2) Nothing is so powerful that it can by itself and by its own strength separate the faithful from the charity of God. For in all things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us, Rom. 8:37; provided we are willing to use the strengths granted by Him and the prepared help of the Holy Spirit. But the faithful can separate themselves from the love of God, which are in themselves invalid for separating them, if they are wanting to themselves; and throwing away their weapons, they surrender themselves voluntarily to the enemy: just as Samson, making light of the vow of Naziriteship, was captured by his own fault and his own betrayal, when he could not be captured by the strength and power of the enemies, Judg. 15 and

IX. Those who believe in Christ have in themselves food which remains unto eternal life. John 6:27. Resp. Spiritual food of itself and by its own nature remains unto eternal life, even if by the fault of the eater it happens that, just as it was eaten by him through faith, so through infidelity, as if by some vomiting, it is cast out again.

X. The gifts of God are ἀμεταμέλητα, i.e., immutable, Rom. 11:29. Faith is a gift of God: Therefore, faith is immutable, and thus cannot perish. Resp. Some gifts God gives absolute will, which are simply immutable: some He gives by ordained will, by which a certain order of means is regarded, which is to be duly observed. God gives faith by ordained will and wills that it be preserved through ordinary means s; he who neglects these, by his own fault suffers the loss of faith.

XI. Believers are sealed by the Holy Spirit, Eph. 1:13. Therefore they remain constant in faith. Resp. Believers are sealed and remain by the Holy Spirit as long as they follow His guidance. But if they struggle against the governance of the Holy Spirit, they are deprived of the sealing of the Holy Spirit and lose their faith.

Latin:

II, 10

Prob.

3) Clarissimis scripturæ dictis, quorum breuitatis caussa duo tantum citabimus.

Prius petimus e 1 Tim.

I, 17. 18. Hoc mandatum depono tibi, fili Timothee, iuxta prægrefas de te prophetias, vt milites in illis bonam militiam; habens fidem & bonam conscientiam, quam quidam repulerunt, & circa fidem naufragium fecerunt.

Timotheum ad cœlestem gloriam ab æterno prædestinatum fuisse, nulli dubitamus. Erat quippe ex prophetia, siue peculiari Spiritus S. reuelatione, muneri docendi præfectus, germanus Paulli filius in fide, sinceræque fidei possessor.

Conf. 1

Tim. I, 2.

2 Tim.

I, 5. Hunc Paullus monebat, vt bonam militaret militiam, aduersus diabolum, mundum & carnem mascule decertando, quo gloriosam reportaret victoriam. Ostendit autem Apostolus hanc spiritualem militiam legitime perfici non posse, nisi fide in Christum sancte casteque seruata, vtpote quæ est scutum, ad exstinguendum ignita diaboli tela, diuinitus ordinatum.

Ephes. VI, 16. Porro docet, non posse custodiri fidem, nisi seruetur bona conscientia, & abstineatur a peccatis voluntariis, quibus ferenitas conscientiæ obnubilatur, quam doctrinam confirmat, propositis exemplis eorum, qui circa fidem fecerunt naufragium, abiecta per peccata proæretica bona conscientia.

E quibus hoc fluit argumentum: Quicunque sollicite admonetur sui officii, cum formidine oppositæ defectionis, ille deficere potest totaliter: Quidam electus (Timotheus) sollicite admonetur &c. Ergo.

Posterius depromimus ex Apocalypsi Ioannæa, c. III, 11. vbi Filius Dei Episcopum Philadelphiensem compellat: tene, quod habes, vt nemo auferat coronam tuam.

Sensus est: perge seruare integram fidem, bonamque conscientiam, ne coronam glorix, tibi destinata, adimatur. Colligimus ex his, electos amittere posse fidem.

Cur enim moneret Christus: tene, quod habes, si nulla timenda esset fidei iactura? Cur ob oculos poneret periculum auferendæ coronæ, si hæc citra respectum perseuerantis fidei absolute destinata esset?

*Prob. 4 A piorum precibus quotidianis:.* Nec nos inducas in tentationem? Matth. VI, 13. Quibus omnes fideles, adeoque etiam electi, tum hostium atrocitatem, quibuscum confligendum ipsis est, tum propriarum virium infirmitatem testantur, quod a Deo derelicti, sibique permissi, hostibus, ad gravissima quaeque peccata sollicitantibus, succumbere, & in infidelitatem atque desperationem praecipites rapi queant. His precibus quotidianis addenda est oratio Dauidis: Spiritum sanctitatis tuae ne aufer a me! Ps. LI, 13. Precatio pro non auferendo Spiritu, ablationis possibilitatem arguit. Antithesis est Anabaptistarum, in quibus gratiam totaliter inamissibilem damnauit Augustana confessio articulo XII. his verbis: Damnant (nostrae ecclesiae) Anabaptistas, qui negant, semel iustificatos posse amittere Spiritum Sanctum. Quorum potiora sunt argumenta:

I. Quicunque electi sunt ad gloriam coelestem, intuitu fidei in Christum perseuerantis, illorum fides non deficit: Atqui homines renati, docentibus ipsis Euangelicis, electi sunt intuitu fidei perseuerantis: Ergo. Resp. Dist. inter perseuerantiam continuam, siue incessabilem, & non continuam, siue interruptam. Illa competit hominibus, nunquam ex destinata malitia, sed tantum ex infirmitate peccantibus, quae ob imperfectionem renouationis & reliquias veteris hominis in hac mortalitate viatoribus vix, vel raro contingit. Haec peccatis proareticis ad tempus rumpitur, per seriam autem poenitentiam instauratur, & ad finem vitae durat. In articulo electionis intelligitur perseuerantia fidei ad finem vitae durans, siue illa continua, siue non continua sit.

II. Oues Christi nemo e manu eius rapere potest: Vere fideles sunt oues Christi: Ergo. Maior liquet ex Io. X, 28. Resp. Oues Christi, quamdiu vocem pastoris Christi audiunt, eumque sequuntur, nemo e manu Christi rapere potest. At si oues desinant vocem pastoris Christi audire, eundemque sequi, Christus ipse proiicit eas de manu sua, & quam antea gessit tutelam earum, gerere definit. Indeque, nisi ab errore se reuocari patiantur, infernali lupo tandem in praedam cedunt: quod sane non est rapi e manu Christi [*].

III. Electi fidem iustificantem nunquam amittunt, vel abiiciunt totaliter; quia sunt instar arborum, quae ad riuos aquarum sunt plantatae, quae fructus semper ferunt, & nunquam arescunt, Ps. I, 3. Quod si itaque electi iustitiae fructus semper ferunt, arbor fidei nunquam arescit. Resp. Seruant arbores, plantatae ad riuos aquarum, fertilitatem & folia, quamdiu e riuis, ad quos plantatae sunt, humiditatem & nutrimentum attrahunt; at ubi vitium uel vim passae, id facere impediuntur, paullatim exarescunt & emoriuntur. Ita fideles tamdiu tempestiuos edunt fructus, iustitiaeque retinent decus, quamdiu succum trahunt e fluentis gratiae verbo & sacramentis. At vero, si vitiis indulgentes verbum & sacramenta contemnant, vitam gratiae amittunt, & spiritualiter moriuntur. Hanc limitationem insinuat ipse hieropsaltes, Ps. I, 3: Beatus vir, qui in lege Dei meditatur diu noctuque: erit enim sicut arbor plantata ad riuos aquarum.

IV. Qui-

sub foedere evangelico, illis Deus impertitur donum perseverantiae, ut ab ipso nunquam recedant: Atqui electi &c.: Ergo. Maior probatur ex Ier. XXXII, 40. Feriam cum ipsis foedus foeculi; quod non auersurus me fim ab eis, ut benefaciam iis, timorem autem meum dabo in cor eorum, ut non recedant a me. Resp. Foedus Dei cum hominibus non est absolutum, sed ordinatum, vel conditionatum. Promissio divina l.c. Timorem meum dabo in cor eorum, ut non recedant a me, includit tacitam conditionem non impeditae operationis gratiae per voluntariam & liberam hominum resistentiam. Inditurus enim cordibus nostris timorem fui Deus non agit irresistibiliter, sed resistibiliter, & relicta repugnandi libertate. Inde fit, ut a bonorum, foedere promissorum, participatione nulli excludantur, nisi Deo voluntarie resistentes, qui iisdem bonis propria culpa se privant. Conf. Ezech. XI, 20. 21.

V. Quoscunque cadentes Deus non abiicit, sed manu sua suffulcit, illorum lapsus non est totalis, gratiam Dei excutiens: Atqui iustos cadentes &c. Ps. XXXVII, 24. Ergo. Resp. Dist. inter casum externum, seu fortunae, & internum, seu animae. Totus Psalmus XXXVII. loquitur de externis piorum & impiorum casibus, de illorum prosperitate, & horum infelicitate, adeoque locus citatus non ferit scopum.

VI. Quicunque apprehensus manu divina semper est cum Deo, is non potest gratia Dei excidere: Atqui electus &c. E. Maior constat: quia semper esse cum Deo, & gratia divina excidere sunt opposita, quae simul consistere nequeunt. Minor patet Ps. LXXIII, 23. Resp. Apprehensio & sustentatio, quae fit manu divina, nec irresistibilis, nec indeclinabilis est; propterea, quod Deus malitiosae deferentem permittit labi.

VII. Quicunque non possunt seduci, illi non possunt fidem amittere: Atqui electi non possunt seduci. E. Maior constat; quia amissio fidei est a seductione diaboli, mundi & carnis. Minor probatur e Matth. XXIV, 24. Surgent falsi Christi & falsi prophetae, & dabunt signa magna & prodigia, ut in errorem inducant, si possibile, etiam electos. Resp. Dist. inter impossibilitatem absolutam, & hypotheticam. Electos seduci impossibile est impossibilitate non absoluta, aut cauffali, ex irresistibili operatione gratiae profecta, sed impossibilitate hypothetica, nixa hypothesi electionis, factae secundum praevisionem fidei perseverantis. Cum autem perseverantia alia sit continua, alia non continua, electi ad tempus seduci possunt totaliter, non autem finaliter, ob infallibilitatem praescientiae divinae.

VIII. Nihil fideles separare potest a dilectione Dei. Rom. VIII, 38. Resp. 1) Nulla creatura externa fideles separare potest a dilectione Dei: at inhabitans peccatum, quod non est creatura, si ei permittatur dominatus, eosdem a Deo divellit. 2) Nihil tam potens est, vt ex fe & vi sua valeat separare fideles a caritate Dei. In omnibus enim plusquam vincimus per eum, qui dilexit nos, Rom. VIII, 37; dum modo viribus ab ipso concessis, & parato Spiritus S. auxilio vti velimus. Possunt autem fideles separare a dilectione Dei, quae ex fe inualida sunt ad separandum eos, si illi sibi ipsis desint; & arma proiicientes se vltro dedant hosti: quemadmodum Simfon flocce ifaciens Nazireatus votum, propria culpa, fuique ipsius proditione captus est, cum vi & robore hostium capi non posset, Iudic. XV. &

XVI. IX. Qui credunt in Christum, in se cibum habent, qui permanet in vitam aeternam. Ioann. VI, 27. Resp. Cibus spiritualis ex se & natura sua permanet in vitam aeternam, etsi vitio comedentis fiat, vt, quemadmodum per fidem ab ipso comefus est, ita per infidelitatem, quasi vomitu quodam, iterum eiiciatur.

X. Dona Dei sunt ἀμεταμέλητα, i. e. immutabilia, Rom. XI, 29. Fides est donum Dei: E. Fides est immutabilis, adeoque interire nequit. Resp. Dona quaedam Deus dat voluntate absoluta, quae simpliciter sunt immutabilia: quaedam dat voluntate ordinata, qua respicitur certus mediorum ordo, rite observandus. Fidem Deus dat voluntate ordinata & vult, ut per ordinaria media conservetur; quae qui negligit, propria culpa iacturam fidei facit.

XI. Credentes obsignati sunt per Spiritum S. Eph. I, 13. E. in fide constantes manent. Resp. Credentes tamdiu obsignati sunt & manent Spiritu S. quamdiu eius ductum sequuntur. At si regimini Spiritus S. obluctentur, obsignatione Spiritus S. destituuntur, fidemque amittunt.


### Q. XV. Can the elect fall into mortal sins, cast off the grace of the Holy Spirit, and utterly lose faith in Christ?: Quaest. XV

Quaest. XV.

Is the election of those who finally believe in Christ immutable? The divine election of men, finally believing in Christ, is immutable and irrevocable, so that from an elect person one cannot become a reprobate. Obf. I. We use here the name of election in the strictest sense, as it denotes the divine decree concerning the saving of those sinners whose faith in Christ, persevering, was foreseen by God from eternity: Huberus uses the name of election in a general sense, in which it coincides with the calling to the church.

Some Tübingen theologians use the word 'election' not in the general sense, nor even in the strictest, but in a stricter and intermediate sense, so that it denotes the ordination of all believers, whether they believe until the end of life or only for a time, to eternal salvation; in which sense every believer is elect, and with faith extinguished by mortal sins, one becomes a reprobate from being elect. Confer D. 10, Adami Osiandri, Colleg. Theol. System., part VI, p. 110. Obf.

II. Election is called immutable not by an absolute, intrinsic, and causal immutability, but by a hypothetical, extrinsic, and non-causal one. For we do not assert that election is immutable because of an absolute decree by which God chose certain sinners to eternal life, however they might behave, only because it so pleased God; nor because of any predetermining decree by which the will of elect men is so determined to the perseverance of faith that they can never lose it through deliberate sins, nor ever recede from the state of grace: but we maintain that election is immutable because of the supposition of the ordained decree and the infallibility of divine foreknowledge.

Prob. I. 1) All the elect obtain the inheritance to which they are predestined. Matt. 25:34; James 2:5. Therefore, no elect persons become reprobates. Matt. 25:34; James 2:5. Therefore, no elect persons become reprobates.

2) Whoever cannot be deceived (finally), they cannot perish. But the elect, etc. Matt. 24:24. Therefore.

3) For those who perish, no inheritance is reserved in heaven. But for all those who are elect according to the foreknowledge of God, an inheritance is reserved in heaven. 1 Pet. 1:2. 4. Therefore, none of them perishes.

4) Those who cannot be snatched (finally) from the hands of Christ, they cannot perish eternally. But the elect, etc. John 10:28. Therefore.

5) All inscribed in the book of life are to be delivered, Dan. 12:1. Therefore, none of them can perish.

6) All whom God predestined, He glorifies, Rom. 8:29-30. Therefore, no predestined person is reprobated.

7) If the elect could perish, the foreknowledge of God, according to which He chose, Rom. 8:29, would be deceived, which is an impious statement. The antithesis is that of the Socinians and Arminians, according to whose opinion one can become a reprobate from being elect. Their principal arguments are: I. Whoever can be expunged from the book of life, their election is not immutable: But those who finally believe in Christ, etc. Therefore. The major is proved because the book of life is a catalog of the elect; he who is expunged from the same, is a reprobate. The minor premise is clear from the example of Moses, who in Exod. XXXII, 32, asked of God that He blot him out of the book of life, if He were unwilling to spare the Israelites otherwise. Resp. Moses did not simply wish to be expunged from the book of life, nor did he think that one once inscribed could be expunged, but rather, by a reason taken from the impossible, he attempted to obtain pardon for his brothers the Israelites. Indeed, Moses, out of a certain immense security of divine familiarity, after he had brought forward one and another pressing reason, not to excuse his own, but to obtain pardon for them, v. 11 seq., now, having discovered the foulness of the matter, thinking he must use a final and by far the strongest reason in the second intercession, wishes to say: Lord, either forgive them this sin, or blot me out of your book! I demand one or the other with my prayers, intending to bring a friendly force upon you! The latter you will never do, because it is impossible that one once inscribed and held as elect be expunged: therefore you should do the former, as far as it is possible for you and easy to do. You say: God answers categorically: I will blot out of my book him who has sinned. Resp. Distinguish between negative deletion and privative deletion. Negative deletion from the book of life is the same as non-inscription in the book of life: which exegesis is held in Ps. LXIX, 29. Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous. Wherefore the sense is: I will not inscribe the one sinning stubbornly and finally in the catalog of the elect; conf. D. PFEIFFER in dub. vex. p. 385. The same can be answered to Apoc. III, 5. c. XXII, 19. Some authors distinguish between inscription in the book of grace, which refers to the antecedent will of God, and inscription in the book of glory, which pertains to the consequent will of God. The former is deletable, the latter is indelebilis. II. Whoever can become reprobate, under the condition of neglected spiritual crucifixion, their election is not immutable: But the elect, etc. Therefore. The minor premise is established by the example of Paul, who in 1 Cor. IX, 27, says of himself: I subdue my body and make it a slave, lest perhaps preaching to others, I myself should become a reprobate. Resp. Whoever can become reprobate, under the condition of neglected spiritual crucifixion, their election is not immutable absolutely; I concede: yet it is immutable from the hypothesis of election made according to the foreknowledge of persevering faith (*). But faith does not persevere in a man in whom the flesh predominates. Wherefore the Apostle puts this under the yoke, lest faith, extinguished by the dominion of the flesh, fall into the judgment of eternal reprobation. You say: Therefore from the elect, reprobates can be made. I answer with the words of D. B. MEISNER; The elect are either considered by reason of themselves, and thus they can finally fall: or by reason of the foreseen and decreed divine preservation, and thus they cannot be seduced. See anthropol. decad. II. disp. XIV. p. 230. Conf. Disp. DANN HAVER. de hypopiasmo Paullino §. 33. The Apostle could not indeed become a reprobate in the composite sense, if he was elect; he could, however, in the divided sense, if he is considered separately in his conditions, because if he had known himself to be absolutely elect, he would have avoided reprobation in vain.

Latin:

Quaest. XV.

Estne electio finaliter in Christum credentium immutabilis? Electio diuina hominum, finaliter in Christum credentium, est immutabilis & irreuocabilis, vt ex electo non possit fieri reprobus. Obs. I. Vtimur hic nomine electionis in sensu strictissimo, prout notat decretum diuinum de saluandis illis peccatoribus, quorum fides in Christum perseuerans ab aeterno praeuisa est a Deo: HVBERVS nomen electionis usurpat in sensu generali, quo cum vocatione ad ecclesiam coincidit.

Nonnulli Theologi Tubingenses vocem, electio, adhibent non in sensu generali, neque etiam strictissimo, sed in sensu strictiori & medio, vt notet ordinationem omnium credentium, siue usque ad finem vitae, siue ad tempus credant, ad aeternam salutem; quo sensu omnis credens est electus, & extincta per peccata mortifera fide, ex electo fit reprobus. Confer. D. 10. ADAMI OSIANDRI colleg. theol. system. parte VI. p. 110.

Obs. II. Immutabilis dicitur electio non immutabilitate absoluta, intrinseca & caussali, sed hypothetica, extrinseca & non caussali. Neque enim asserimus, immutabilem esse electionem propter decretum absolutum, quo Deus quosdam peccatores ad vitam aeternam elegerit, quomodocunque se habeant, ideo tantum, quia Deo sic placuit; neque ob decretum aliquod praedeterminans, quo voluntas hominum electorum sic determinata fit ad perseuerantiam fidei, vt hanc per peccata proaeretica nunquam amittere, neque vnquam a statu gratiae recedere queant: sed statuimus electionem esse immutabilem propter suppositionem decreti ordinati, & infallibilitatem praescientiae diuinae.

Prob. I. 1) Omnes electi haereditatem, ad quam praedestinati sunt, consequuntur. Matth. XXV, 34. Iac. II, 5. Ergo nulli electi fiunt reprobi.

2) Quicunque non possunt seduci (finaliter), illi non possunt perire. Atqui electi &c. Matth. XXIV, 24. Ergo.

3) Illis, qui pereunt, nulla reseruatur in coelis haereditas. Atqui omnibus illis, qui secundum praeuisionem Dei sunt electi, reseruatur in coelis haereditas. 1 Petr. I, 2. 4. Ergo nullus eorum perit.

4) Qui e manibus Christi (finaliter) eripi nequeunt, illi aeternum perire non possunt. Atqui electi &c. Io. X, 28. Ergo.

5) Omnes libro vitae inscripti sunt liberandi, Dan. XII, 1. E. nemo illorum perire potest.

6) Omnes, quos Deus praedestinauit, glorificat, Rom. VIII, 29. 30. E. nullus praedestinatus reprobatur.

7) Si electi perire possent, praeuisio Dei, secundum quam elegit, Rom. VIII, 29. falleretur, quod dictum impium est. Antithesis est Socinianorum & Arminianorum, quorum de sententia ex electis possunt fieri reprobi. Quorum praecipua sunt argumenta: I. Quicunque expungi possunt e libro vitae, illorum electio non est immutabilis: At qui finaliter in Christum credentes &c. Ergo. Maior prob. quia liber vitae est catalogus electorum; qui ex eodem expungitur, sit reprobus. Minor liquet exemplo Mosis, qui Exod. XXXII, 32. a Deo petiit, vt se deleret e libro vitæ, si aliter Israëlitis parcere nollet. Resp. Moses non simpliciter se e libro vitæ expungi optauit, neque putauit, semel inscriptum expungi posse, verum ratione ab impossibili petita conatus est Israëlitis fratribus suis veniam impetrare. Nimirum Moses, ex ingenti quadam diuinæ familiaritatis securitate, postquam vnam alteramque stringentem rationem adduxerat, non ad excusandos suos, sed ad impetrandum iis veniam, v. 11. seq. iam, rei fœditate comperta, vltima, eaque longe fortissima ratione in altera intercessione sibi vtendum ratus, vult dicere: Domine, aut dimitte illis hanc noxam, aut dele me e libro tuo! Alterutrum posco precibus meis, amicam tibi vim illaturus! Posterius nunquam facies, quia impossibile est, semel inscriptum & pro electo habitum expungi: ergo prius facias, quoad tibi possibile & factu facile est. Dicis: Deus categorice respondet: Delebo e libro meo eum, qui peccarit. Resp. Dist. inter deletionem negatiuam, ac priuatiuam. Deletio negatiua e libro vitæ idem est, ac non scriptio in libro vitæ: quæ exegesis habetur Ps. LXIX, 29. Deleantur e libro vitarum, & cum iustis non scribantur. Quare sensus est: præfracte & finaliter peccantem catalogo electorum non inscribam; conf. D. PFEIFFER in dub. vex. p. 385. Idem responderi potest ad Apoc. III, 5. c. XXII, 19. Dist. nonnulli auctores inter inscriptionem in librum gratiæ, quæ ad voluntatem Dei antecedentem refertur, & inter inscriptionem in librum gloriæ, quæ ad voluntatem Dei consequentem pertinet. Prior delebilis, posterior indelebilis est. II. Quicunque possunt fieri reprobi, sub conditione neglectæ crucifixionis spiritualis, illorum electio non est immutabilis: Atqui electi &c. Ergo. Minor constat exemplo Paulli, qui 1 Cor. IX, 27. de se ipso inquit: subigo corpus meum & seruum facio, ne forte aliis prædicans, ipse reprobus fiam. Resp. Quicunque possunt fieri reprobi, sub conditione neglectæ crucifixionis spiritualis, illorum electio non est immutabilis absolute; concedo: est tamen immutabilis ex hypothesi electionis factæ secundum præuisionem fidei perseuerantis (*). Non autem perseuerat in homine fides, in quo caro prædominatur. Quare hanc sub iugum mittit Apostolus, ne exstincta per dominium carnis fide in æternæ reprobationis iudicium incidat. Dicis: Ergo ex electis possunt fieri reprobi. Respondeo verbis D. B. MEISNERI; Electi vel considerantur ratione sui, atque sic finaliter labi possunt: vel ratione præuisæ & decretæ conseruationis diuinæ, atque sic seduci non possunt. Vid. anthropol. decad. II. disp. XIV. p. 230. Conf. Disp. DANN HAVER. de hypopiasmo Paullino §. 33. Non potuit quidem Apostolus reprobus fieri in sensu composito, si electus fuit; potuit tamen in sensu diuiso, si seorsim in suis conditionibus consideretur, quia si se absolute electum sciuisset, frustra reprobationem cauisset.


### Quest. XVI. Is a regenerate man certain of his election to eternal life?

A reborn man in the middle of the course of life is certain of his election conditionally a); but at the end of life he enjoys the same with the certainty of his predestination absolutely b). Prob. a. The reborn are certain of present faith: a) Test yourselves, whether you are in the faith? prove yourselves: Or (do) you not know yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you? unless you are reprobates, 2 Cor. XIII, 5. They are certain b) that God the Father will grant the perseverance of faith.

I am persuaded that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ. Phil. I, 6. They are certain c) of the intercession of Christ.

I have prayed for you, that your faith might not fail, says the Savior, Luke XXII, 23. He prayed not for Peter only, or the remaining disciples of Christ, but also for those who will believe through their word, John XVII, 20. They are certain d) of the sealing of the Holy Spirit.

Believing, you were sealed with the holy Spirit of promise. Eph. I, 13. This bears witness, with our spirit, that we are children of God, Rom. VIII, 17. Thence the reborn man validly concludes: I am certain of present faith, of the preserving grace of God the Father, of the intercession of Christ, of the sealing and internal testimony of the Holy Spirit: Therefore I am most persuaded that my name is written in heaven.

Luke X, 20. Which certainty of election in the middle of the course of life is not absolute, but ordered & conditional.

For if Paul therefore chastised his body, lest he be made a reprobate, 1 Cor. IX, 29, he was not absolutely certain of his own election. Why does Christ so gravely admonish the Bishop of Philadelphia: Hold what you have, that no one may take away your crown? Apoc. III, 11. And Paul: The firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: the Lord knows those who are his, and let everyone who names the name of Christ depart from iniquity!

2 Tim. II, 19. These admonitions indicate that the certainty of election in this course of life is conditional.

Prob. b. At the end of life, with the condition placed in act, the reborn man is as absolutely certain of his election as he is of his present faith, so that he may dare to say intrepidly with Paul: I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; as for the rest, a crown of righteousness is laid up for me.

2 Tim IV, 7. Q. XVII. What is the end of election?

The proximate end of election is eternal salvation, to be conferred upon the elect in time a): The end of election.

The ultimate end is the glory of the divine goodness b). Prob. a. From Matt. XXV, 34, where the faithful are said to be about to enter the inheritance of the kingdom, prepared for them from the beginning of the world.

Prob. b. From Eph. I, 5, 6, where we are said to be elected by God, that the glory of his grace might be praised. OF REPROBATION.

Q. I. What is opposed to election to eternal salvation?

Reprobation is immediately opposed to election. Prob. Just as between believers & unbelievers, between sheep & goats, between the children of God & of the devil, between the elect & the reprobate no middle or third is given; so election & reprobation are immediately opposed.

Q. II. What is reprobation? Reprobation is the eternal decree of God concerning the condemning of all and individual sinners, whose final rejection of the merit of Christ was foreseen from eternity.

Definition of reprobation. It is defined more fully: Reprobation is an act of the consequent divine will, by which God, out of his vindicatory justice, [condemns] all and individual contumacious sinners, whom he foresaw would finally reject the offered grace of vocation & justification, & [would die] without faith in Christ He foresaw those who were about to depart from this life, [and] adjudged [them] to eternal condemnation for the everlasting glory of His justice.

Obs. I. Reprobation is called in Greek ἀποδοκιμασία, which word is ἄγραφος, or is not found in the same syllables in the sacred writings. The word ἀδόκιμος, reprobate, is used, 1 Cor. IX, 27; 2 Cor. XIII, 5; Hebr. VI, 8. To reprobate signifies to reject that which is judged unworthy and wicked.

Obs. II. ’Αποδοκιμασία, or reprobation, is taken: a) most generally for the rejection of any useless thing, Jer. VI, 8; b) specially for rejection from grace, Rom. XI, 1; c) most specially for rejection from eternal glory, in which sense it is taken here.

Obs. III. Reprobation in the Epistle of Jude v. 4 is called προγραφὴ εἰς τὸ κρῖμα, a prescript, or a writing beforehand (done from eternity) unto judgment. "There have crept in certain men (who were of old prescribed unto this judgment), ungodly men, who turn the grace of our God into lasciviousness and deny the only Lord God and our Lord, Jesus Christ." The Apostle implies that false teachers, asserting that the grace of God can well consist with the foulest lust, and denying the divinity of Christ, have been inscribed in the book of death or the catalog of those to be damned. You should observe that some authors doubt whether the book of death is rightly attributed to God. But indeed, just as when the book of life is attributed to God, nothing else is implied than that God has the most exact knowledge of all the elect, to whom He will certainly grant eternal life, as if He had them registered in a book; so in the same sense the book of death can be attributed to God, for by it nothing else is signified than the most exact knowledge which God has of all those whom He has determined to adjudge to eternal death in view of their final incredulity. Among the ancients, GREGORY NAZIANZEN calls it βίβλον τῶν ζωῶν καὶ βίβλον νεκρῶν, the book of the living and the book of the perishing. Cf. D. DANNHAV. hodof. phænom. VII. p. 583.

Latin:

Homo renatus in medio vitæ cursu suæ electionis certus est conditionate a); at in termino vitæ idem gaudet certitudine prædestinationis suæ absoluta b). Prob. a. Certi sunt renati fidei præsentis: a) Vos ipsos tentate, num sitis in fide? vos ipsos probate: Aut (num) non cognoscitis vos ipsos, quod Iesus Christus sit in vobis? nisi reprobi estis, 2 Cor. XIII, 5. Certi sunt b) quod Deus Pater fidei perseverantiam largiturus fit.

Persuasus sum, quod qui incepit in vobis bonum opus, absoluturus fit usque in diem Iesu Christi. Phil. I, 6. Certi sunt c) intercessionis Christi.

Ego oraui pro te, ne fides tua deficeret, ait Saluator, Luc. XXII, 23. Non pro Petro tantum, aut reliquis discipulis Christi orauit, sed etiam pro his, qui credent per verbum illorum, Io. XVII, 20. Certi sunt d) obsignationis Spiritus Sancti.

Credentes obsignati estis Spiritu promissionis sancto. Eph. I, 13. Hic testatur, cum spiritu nostro, quod sumus filii Dei, Rom. VIII, 17. Inde valide concludit renatus: Ego certus sum fidei praesentis, gratiae Dei Patris conferuatricis, intercessionis Christi, obsignationis internique testimonii Spiritus S.: Ergo persuafissimus sum, nomen meum scriptum esse in coelis.

Luc. X, 20. Quae certitudo electionis in medio vitae cursu non est absoluta, sed ordinata & conditionata.

Si enim ideo Paullus corpus suum castigauit, ne reprobus efficiatur, 1 Cor. IX, 29. suae sibi electionis absolute certus non fuit. Eccur Christus Episcopum Philadelphiensem tam grauiter admonet: Tene, quod habes, ut nemo auferat coronam tuam? Apoc. III, 11. Et Paullus: Firmum fundamentum Dei subsistit, habens hoc sigillum: nouit Dominus, qui sunt sui, & desistat ab iniustitia omnis, qui nominat nomen Christi!

2 Tim. II, 19. Haec monita indicant, certitudinem electionis in hoc vitae curriculo esse conditionatam.

Prob. b. In fine vitae, conditione in actu posita, homo renatus ut praesentis fidei, ita electionis suae absolute certus est, ut intrepidus cum Paullo dicere ausit: Certamen bonum certaui, cursum abfolui, fidem seruaui; quod reliquum, reposita est mihi corona iustitiae.

2 Tim IV, 7. Quæst. XVII. Quis est finis electionis?

Finis electionis proximus est aeterna salus, electis in tempore conferenda a): Finis electionis.

Finis ultimus est gloria bonitatis diuinae b). Prob. a. Ex Matth XXV, 34. vbi fideles haereditatem regni, sibi parati ab exordio mundi, adituri dicuntur.

Prob. b. Ex Eph. I, 5. 6. vbi dicimur electi a Deo, vt laudetur gloria gratiae suae. DE REPROBATIONE.

Quæst. I. Quid opponitur electioni ad aeternam salutem?

Electioni immediate opponitur reprobatio. Prob. Sicut inter credentes & incredulos, inter oues & haedos, inter filios Dei & diaboli, inter electos & reprobos nullum datur medium siue tertium; ita electio, & reprobatio immediate sunt opposita.

Quæst. II. Quid est reprobatio? Reprobatio est aeternum Dei decretum de condemnandis omnibus & singulis peccatoribus, quorum finalis meriti Christi reiectio ab aeterno praeuisa est.

Definitio reprobationis. Uberius definitur: Reprobatio est actus voluntatis diuinae consequentis, quo Deus ex iustitia sua vindicatiua omnes & singulos peccatores contumaces, quos oblatam vocationis & iustificationis gratiam finaliter excuffuros, & sine fide in Christum ex hac vita deceffuros præuidit, æternæ condemnationi adiudicauit in perennem iuftitiæ fuæ gloriam.

Obf. I. Reprobatio græce dicitur ἀποδοκιμασία, quæ vox eft ἄγραφος, feu non inuenitur totidem fyllabis in facris litteris. Vox ἀδόκιμος, reprobus, vfurpatur, 1 Cor. IX, 27. 2 Cor. XIII, 5. Hebr. VI, 8. Reprobare fignificat, id, quod indignum & improbum cenfetur, reiicere.

Obf. II. ’Αποδοκιμασία, fiue reprobatio, fumitur, a) generaliffime pro cuiusuis rei inutilis reiectione, Ier. VI, 8.; b) fpecialiter pro reiectione a gratia, Rom. XI, 1.; c) fpecialiffime pro reiectione ab æterna gloria, quo fenfu hic accipitur.

Obf. III. Reprobatio in epiftola Iudæ v. 4. προγραφὴ εἰς τὸ κρῖμα præfcriptio, fiue fcriptio ante (ab æterno facta) in iudicium dicitur. Subingreffi funt quidam homines, (qui olim præfcripti fuerunt in hoc iudicium) impii, qui Dei noftri gratiam transmutant in lafciuiam & folum dominatorem Deum & Dominum noftrum, Iefum Chriftum abnegant. Innuit Apoftolus, falfos doctores, gratiam Dei cum fpurciffima libidine bene confiftere poffe, afferentes, atque diuinitatem Chrifti abnegantes, libro mortis vel catalogo damnandorum infcriptos effe. Obferues, quod nonnulli auctores dubitent, an liber mortis Deo recte tribuatur. At vero ficut, quando Deo tribuitur liber vitæ, nihil aliud innuitur, quam quod Deus exactiffimam habeat cognitionem omnium electorum, quibus vitam æternam certo collaturus eft, quafi eos in libro confignatos habeat; ita eodem fenfu Deo liber mortis poteft tribui, quippe quo nihil aliud fignificatur, quam exactiffima notitia, quam Deus habet omnium eorum, quos morti æternæ intuitu finalis incredulitatis addicere conftituit. Ex veteribus GREGORIVS NAZIANZENVS nominat βίβλον τῶν ζωῶν καὶ βίβλον νεκρῶν, librum viuentium, & librum pereuntium. Conf. D. DANNHAV. hodof. phænom. VII. p. 583.


### Quest. XVI. Is a regenerate man certain of his election to eternal life?: Q. III. Who reprobates men?

Q. III. Who reprobates men?

The Triune God, the most just judge of men, and the avenger of crimes and of grace despised.

Proof. God indeed, by His antecedent will, willed the salvation of all, under the condition of faith persevering in Christ; but since He foresaw that this condition would not be fulfilled by all, He decreed to reprobate eternally those who are contumacious toward divine grace, which was procured by the merit of Christ and offered in the Gospel, and who are despisers of it. To this point tend the words of Christ, Jo. III, 17, 18: "God did not send (by His antecedent will) His Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through Him. He who believes in Him is not judged; but he who does not believe is already judged (by the eternal decree of His consequent will), because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God."

Q. IV. What is the internal impulsive cause of reprobation, or [that which is] within God?

The internal impulsive cause is the vindicatory justice of God, by which God, being most just, not only did not elect sinners—who are stubbornly impious and finally impenitent—or inscribe them with the just in the book of life, but also decreed to adjudge them to eternal torments.

Proof. For just as the damnation of men doing evil, which occurs in time, is called just, Rom. II, 8, so it must be acknowledged that, when God from eternity decreed to damn very many sinners, the reason for decreeing was punitive justice, because of the necessary agreement between the decree and the execution.

Q. V. What is the external impulsive cause of reprobation?

The external impulsive cause is all the sins of men a), insofar as they are joined with persevering incredulity, or the final repudiation of the merit of Christ b).

Prob. a. The external impulsive cause of reprobation is all sins: 1) original sin. For the wages of every sin is death. Rom. VI, 23. But the vice of origin is truly sin, condemning and bringing even now eternal death to those who are not reborn through baptism and the Holy Spirit, as Augustine testifies, Confess. artic. II. Original sin is a cause of reprobation. 2) Actual sins, especially deliberate sins, by which the grace of the Holy Spirit is shaken off, and true faith is extinguished. That man falls into the judgment of reprobation on account of such sins, Paul teaches Gal. V, 19, 20, 21. The works of the flesh are manifest, which are: adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness, idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variances, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies, envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like; of the which I tell you before, as I have also told you in time past, that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God. Whatever excludes man from the inheritance of eternal life, that is the impulsive cause of eternal reprobation: But deliberate sins, or the works of the flesh, etc.: Therefore.

Prob. b. Although any sin is an external impulsive, or meritorious, cause of reprobation; yet it is only remote and mediate: but the proximate and immediate cause of the same is the final repudiation of the merit of Christ, or impenitence and unbelief lasting until the end of life. For the remaining sins, if faith in Christ has intervened, can be abolished, as regards guilt, so that men are not condemned on account of them, since there is οὐδὲν κατάκριμα, no condemnation in those who are in Christ Jesus, Rom. VIII, 1. Acts X, 43. But given ἀπιστία, or final unbelief, condemnation follows by inevitable necessity, as Christ teaches, Mark XVI, 16. He that believeth not shall be damned, and John III, 36. He that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him.

Obs. D. Menzervs distinguishes in defens II. part. conuers. Pruten. p. 80. between the meritorious cause and the organic cause, which does not apply, but rejects, the grace of God. That sins merit damnation is settled, and so also unbelief, as a sin against the first commandment, merits death; and in this sense it is true that not only unbelief, but also other sins are a cause of damnation, namely, the meritorious one. But when unbelief is directly opposed to faith, as an organic cause, or an applying instrument, then, as man is justified only by faith, and by no other organ, apprehending the remission of sins in the promise of the gospel; so he is condemned only by unbelief, not applying, or repelling, the promise of the gospel, Mark XVI, 16. D. Dannhav. delivers things akin to these in hodof. Man himself is the maker of his own fortune, and his final ἀπιστία, foreseen, in a sound sense alone (not excluding meanwhile other sins from the merit of damnation) condemns; just as a sick man dies not immediately by the vice of a lethal disease, but by the rejection of the medicine.

Latin:

Quæft. III. Quis homines reprobat?

Deus trinunus, iuftiffimus hominum iudex, fcelerumque & fpretæ gratiæ vindex.

Prob. Deus quidem voluntate antecedente omnium voluit falutem, fub conditione perfeuerantis in Chriftum fidei; cum autem præuiderit, hanc conditionem non ab omnibus impletum iri, contumaces gratiæ diuinæ, merito Chrifti partæ, & in euangelio oblatæ, contentores æternum reprobare decreuit. Quo fpectant verba Chrifti, Io. III, 17. 18. Non mifit Deus (voluntate antecedente) Filium fuum in mundum, vt iuditet mundum, fed vt faluetur mundus per ipfum. Qui credit in ipfum, non iudicatur; qui autem non credit, iam (æterno decreto voluntatis confequentis) iudicatus eft, quia non credit in nomen vnigeniti Filii Dei.

Quæft. IV. Quæ eft cauffa impulfiua reprobationis interna, fiue intra Deum?

Cauffa impulfiua interna eft iuftitia Dei vindicatiua, qua Deus iuftiffimus peccatores, præfracte impios & finaliter impoenitentes, non tantum non elegit, aut cum iuftis libro vitæ non infcripfit; fed etiam æternis cruciatibus addicere decreuit.

Prob. Sicut enim hominum male agentium damnatio, quæ fit in tempore, dicitur iufta, Rom. II, 8. ita agnofcendum eft, quod, cum Deus ab æterno decreuit plurimos peccatores damnare, ratio decernendi fuerit iuftitia punitiua ob neceffariam conuenientiam decreti & exfe cutionis.

Quæft. V. Quæ eft cauffa impulfiua reprobationis externa?

Cauffa impulfiua externa funt omnia hominum peccata a), quatenus cum perfeuerante incredulitate, fiue finali meriti Chrifti repudio, funt coniuncta b).

Prob. a. Reprobationis causa impulsiva externa sunt omnia peccata: 1) peccatum originale. Nam omnis peccati stipendium mors est. Rom. VI, 23. At vitium originis vere est peccatum, damnans & afferens nunc quoque aeternam mortem his, qui non renascuntur per baptismum & Spiritum sanctum, teste August. Confess. artic. II. E. Peccatum originis est causa reprobationis. 2) Peccata actualia, imprimis peccata proaeretica, quibus gratia Spiritus S. excutitur, veraque fides exstinguitur. Quod propter eiusmodi peccata homo in iudicium reprobationis incidat, docet Paullus Gal. V, 19. 20, 21. Manifesta sunt opera carnis, quae sunt: adulterium, scortatio, immunditia, proteruia, idololatria, magia, inimicitiae, contentiones, zeli, irae, rixae, dissensiones, haereses, inuidia, caedes, ebrietates, commessationes, & similia his; de quibus praedico vobis, sicut etiam pradixi, quod, quia talia faciunt, regnum Dei non sint in hereditatem accepturi. Quidquid hominem ab hereditate vitae aeternae excludit, illud est causa impulsiva aeternae reprobationis: Atqui peccata proaeretica, siue opera carnis &c: Ergo.

Prob. b. Quamuis quodlibet peccatum sit causa reprobationis impulsiva externa, seu meritoria; remota tamen & mediata tantum est: at proxima & immediata eiusdem causa est finale repudium meriti Christi, seu impoenitentia & incredulitas vsque ad finem vitae durans. Reliqua namque peccata, si interuenerit fides in Christum, aboleri possunt, quoad reatum, ne propterea homines damnentur, siquidem οὐδὲν κατάκριμα, nulla condemnatio est in iis, qui sunt in Christo Iesu, Rom. VIII, 1. Actor. X, 43. Posita autem ἀπιστία, siue incredulitate finali, ineuitabili necessitate sequitur damnatio, docente Christo, Marc. XVI, 16. Qui non crediderit, condemnabitur, & Ioann. III, 36. Qui non credit Filio, non videbit vitam; sed ira Dei manet super illo.

Obs. Distinguit D. Menzervs in defens II. part. conuers. Pruten. p. 80. inter caussam meritoriam & organicam, gratiam Dei non applicantem, sed reiectantem. Peccata mereri damnationem, ratum est, & sic etiam incredulitas, tanquam peccatum contra primum praeceptum meretur mortem; & in hoc sensu verum est, non solum incredulitatem, sed etiam cetera peccata damnationis esse caussam, nempe meritoriam. Quando autem incredulitas directe opponitur fidei, tanquam caussae organicae, seu instrumento applicanti, tunc, vt tantum homo iustificatur fide, & nullo alio organo, remissionem peccatorum in euangelii promissione apprehendente; sic tantum incredulitate, euangelii promissionem non applicante, vel repellente, damnatur, Marc. XVI, 16. His gemina tradit D. Dannhav. in hodof. Ipse homo fortunae suae faber, ac praeuisa eiusdem finalis ἀπιστία sano sensu sola (non exclusis interim aliis peccatis a merito damnationis) damnat; sicut aegrotus moritur non immediate morbi lethalis vitio, sed medicinae repulsa.


### Quaest. VI. What is the directing, or norming, principle of reprobation?

The norming principle of reprobation, first and mediate, is πρόθεσις, or the general divine purpose concerning the condemning of sinners who are finally impenitent and unbelieving a). The proximate directing principle is πρόγνωσις, or the foreknowledge of final unbelief in certain individuals b).

Prob. a. The purpose, or general decree of God, shines forth from the words of Christ: He that believeth not shall be damned, Mark XVI, 16.

I, 2: so the unregenerate are reprobate according to the foreknowledge of persevering unbelief, by which the satisfaction of Christ is pertinaciously rejected.

Quest. VII. In what does reprobation formally consist?

Reprobation formally consists in the exclusion from the inheritance of eternal salvation, and the adjudication of eternal punishment, according to the purpose and foreknowledge of God. Our assertion is proved a posteriori, and indeed from the process of the final judgment. For Christ, the heavenly judge, says to those on the left (the reprobate): Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire, prepared for the devil and his angels! Matt. XXV, 41. Those who depart eternally from Christ are excluded from the kingdom of glory, and those who will go into eternal fire will be addicted to eternal punishment. For this reason, just as Christ will execute the judgment of condemnation on the last day; so he decreed from eternity to judge contumacious sinners, on account of the συμφωνίαν of the decree and the execution. Obs. For the sake of easier doctrine and knowledge, our weak intellect conceives and forms the following reprobatory syllogism: Whoever are sinners who will reject the merit of Christ by final incredulity, let them be excluded from the inheritance of eternal salvation and addicted to eternal punishment. But this one, that one, that one, Cain, Judas, etc., are going to reject the merit of Christ by final incredulity. Therefore, this one, that one, that one, Cain, Judas, etc., are excluded from the inheritance of eternal salvation, and let them be addicted to eternal punishment. The major proposition is the πρόθεσις itself, or the divine purpose concerning the condemning of impenitent sinners, rejecting the merit of Christ until the end of life. The minor is formed by the πρόγνωσις, or divine foreknowledge, by which God from eternity foresaw which men in particular would pertinaciously repudiate the satisfaction of Christ. The conclusion exhibits τὴν ἀποδοκιμασίαν, or the eternal decree of reprobation.

Quest. VIII. Who are the men eternally reprobated?

Men, rejected from eternal glory to eternal ignominy, are contumacious, impenitent sinners, and those who repudiate the merit of Christ until the last breath of life. Prob. For in impenitent sinners there is the impulsive reason for eternal reprobation, namely, the final repudiation of the merit of Christ, by which very thing they summon the wrath of God upon themselves, John III, 36. And they are called in Rom. IX, 22, vessels of wrath, i.e., men who have accumulated and as it were gathered for themselves the wrath of God against the day of judgment, not by light or any kind of sins, but by their atrocious sins and crimes, and thus by the abuse of the riches of divine goodness and patience. These vessels of wrath are said to be fitted for destruction. In Greek κατηρτισμένα, prepared, perfected and consummated, and thus ripe for destruction, because by their own fault, obstinacy, and voluntary hardening in sins, and by perseverance and final impenitence in the same, they have made themselves worthy of eternal ruin. In what sense the word καταρτίζειν & καταρτίζεσθαι & κατηρτισμένος is taken in Luke VI, 40. I Cor. I, 10. Eph. IV, 12. 2 Tim. III, 7. See D. HOLTZFVSSEN dissertat. prædest. p. 155.

Quest. IX. What is the end of reprobation?

The end of reprobation is the punishment of sinners a), and the glory of divine vindicatory justice b).

a. For to this end the impious were destined by the decree of reprobation to punishment on account of foreseen final impenitence, that this might be inflicted upon them in time. The reprobate shall go away into eternal punishment, says Christ, Matt. XXV, 46.

Prob. b. Paul teaches in Rom. IX, 22: That God, willing to show his wrath, and to make his power known, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction. Doubtless God foresaw that impious men would prepare themselves for destruction by their own fault; therefore He decreed to reject the same, having abused the divine longsuffering, that He might show His wrath, i.e., vindicatory justice.

Latin:

Principium normans reprobationis primum & mediatum est πρόθεσις, seu propositum diuinum generale de condemnandis peccatoribus finaliter impoenitentibus & incredulis a). Principium dirigens proximum est πρόγνωσις, seu praeuisio incredulitatis finalis in certis indiuiduis b).

Prob. a. Propositum, seu decretum Dei generale elucescit e verbis Christi: Qui non crediderit, condemnabitur, Marc. XVI, 16.
