Prob. b. Sicut renati electi sunt κατά πρόγνωσιν, secundum praenotionem finalis in Christum fidei, 1 Petr. I, 2: ita irregeniti reprobati sunt secundum praescientiam incredulitatis peruerantis, qua satisfactio Christi pertinaciter reiicitur.

Quæst. VII. In quo formaliter consistit reprobatio?

Reprobatio formaliter consistit in exclusione ab hæreditate æternæ salutis, & adiudicatione æternæ pœnæ, secundum propositum & præscientiam Dei. Probatur assertio nostra a posteriori, & quidem a processu iudicii extremi. Dicit enim Christus iudex cælestis iis, qui a sinistris (reprobis): Discedite a me, maledicti, in ignem æternum, paratum diabolo, & angelis eius! Matth. XXV, 41. Qui a Christo æternum discedunt, exclusi sunt regno gloriæ, & qui ibunt in ignem æternum, addicti erunt æternæ pœnæ. Quam ob rem sicut Christus iudicium condemnationis in die nouissimo exsequetur; ita peccatores contumaces iudicare ab æterno decreuit, ob συμφωνίαν decreti & exsecutionis. Obs. Facilioris doctrinæ & cognitionis caussa, infirmus noster intellectus sequentem concipit & format syllogismum reprobatorium: Quicunque peccatores finali incredulitate meritum Christi reiecturi sunt, illi ab hereditate æternæ salutis exclusi & æternæ pœnæ addicti sunto. Atqui hic, ille, iste, Cain, Iudas &c. finali incredulitate meritum Christi sunt reiecturi. Ergo hic, ille, iste, Cain, Iudas &c. ab hereditate æternæ salutis exclusi, & æternæ pœnæ addicti sunto. MAior propositio est ipsa πρόθεσις, seu propositum diuinum de condemnandis peccatoribus impœnitentibus, meritum Christi vsque ad finem vitæ reiicientibus. Minorem format πρόγνωσις, seu præscientia diuina, qua Deus ab æterno præuidit, quinam homines in indiuiduo satisfactionem Christi pertinaciter sint repudiaturi. Conclusio exhibet τὴν ἀποδοκιμασίαν, siue æternum reprobationis decretum.

Quæst. VIII. Quinam sunt homines æternum reprobati?

Homines, ab æterna gloria ad æternam ignominiam reiecti, sunt peccatores contumaces, impœnitentes, & vsque ad nouissimum vitæ halitum meritum Christi repudiantes. Prob. In peccatoribus enim impœnitentibus locum habet ratio impulsiua æternæ reprobationis, scil. finale repudium meriti Christi, quo ipso iram Dei sibi accersunt, Ioann. III, 36. atque dicuntur Rom. IX, 22. vasa iræ, i e. homines, qui iram Dei non leuibus, & qualibuscunque, sed atrocibus peccatis & sceleribus suis, atque adeo abusu diuitiarum bonitatis & patientiæ diuinæ, sibi ipsis in diem iudicii cumularunt, & quasi collegerunt. Dicuntur hæc vasa iræ aptata esse in interitum. Græce κατηρτισμένα, apparata, perfecta & consummata, adeoque matura ad interitum, quia sua culpa, obstinatione & voluntaria induratione in peccatis, & perseuerantia atque impœnitentia finali in iisdem, seipsos dignos effecerunt exitio æterno. Quo sensu verbum καταρτίζειν & καταρτίζεσθαι & κατηρτισμένος accipitur Luc. VI, 40. I Cor. I, 10. Eph. IV, 12. 2 Tim. III, 7. Vid. D. HOLTZFVSSEN dissertat. prædest. p. 155.

Quæst. IX. Quis est finis reprobationis?

Finis reprobationis est peccatorum pœna a), & iustitiæ diuinæ vindicatiuæ gloria b).

Prob. a. Eo fine enim impii ob praevisam finalem impoenitentiam decreto reprobationis destinati sunt ad poenam, ut haec in tempore illis infligatur. Abibunt reprobi in poenam aeternam, inquit Christus, Matth. XXV, 46.

Prob. b. Docet Paullus Rom. IX, 22. Quod Deus, cum voluit demonstrare iram, et notam facere potentiam suam, tulerit cum multa longanimitate vasa irae apparata ad interitum. Nimirum praevidit Deus, quod homines impii propria culpa se sint paraturi ad interitum; ideo decrevit, eosdem, longanimitate divina abusos, reiicere, ut ostenderet iram suam, i. e. iustitiam vindicativam.


### Q. X. Is the decree of reprobation immutable?

The decree of reprobation is irrevocable and immutable, with an immutability not absolute, but hypothetical.

Prob. Those who have been rejected from the participation of eternal salvation, in view of foreseen final infidelity, just as they could have believed finally in Christ through the grace of vocation and regeneration, so they could have not been reprobated, but saved. However, when they were foreseen as finally impenitent, and thus reprobated; just as they cannot be at the same time finally infidel and not-finally-infidel: so when they are reprobated, by hypothetical necessity they cannot be non-reprobated.

Latin:

Decretum reprobationis est irreuocabile, et immutabile, immutabilitate non absoluta, sed hypothetica.

Prob. Qui reiiecti sunt a participatione aeternae salutis, intuitu infidelitatis finalis praevisae, illi sicut per gratiam vocationis et regenerationis poterant credere finaliter in Christum; ita poterant non reprobari, sed saluari. Quando autem tanquam finaliter impoenitentes praeuisi, et sic reprobati sunt; sicut non possunt esse simul infideles finaliter, et non-infideles finaliter: ita cum reprobati sunt, necessitate hypothetica non possunt esse non-reprobati.


### Q. XI. Can the reprobate be in a state of regeneration?

The reprobate can for a time be in the state of the truly regenerate.

Prob. from Luke VIII, 13: They on the rock are they, which, when they hear, receive the word with joy; and these have no root, which (as it were) for a while believe, and in time of temptation fall away. Those who believe for a time are for a time in the state of regeneration. Perseverance does not enter into the essence of faith, but accompanies it.

Latin:

Reprobi ad tempus possunt esse in statu vere renatorum.

Prob. ex Luc. VIII, 13. Qui super petra sunt, qui, quando audierint, cum gaudio suscipiunt verbum; sed radicem non habent, (tanquam) qui ad tempus credunt, verum in tempore tentationis deficiunt. Qui ad tempus credunt, ad tempus sunt in statu regenerationis. Perseverantia fidei essentiam non ingreditur, sed comitatur.


### Q. XII. Has God adjudged certain men to eternal damnation by an absolute decree, without respect to sins and incredulity?

God excludes no man from the inheritance of eternal life, nor has He decreed to consign him to eternal destruction, out of an absolute and most freely preconceived hatred, without any respect to an impulsive cause; but the sins of men, joined with final incredulity, moved God to reprobate from eternal glory those who are stubbornly impious. Obf.

Bellarmine, a patron of the absolute decree, lib. II. de gratia et libero arbitrio, cap. XVI, distinguishes between the negative act of reprobation and the affirmative or positive. The former is that by which God, out of His most free good pleasure, does not will to have mercy on some, nor to save them: it is otherwise called the decree of preterition. The latter is that by which God has determined to afflict with eternal punishments contumacious sinners, whom He foresaw would perseveringly spurn the offered grace of vocation, regeneration, and justification: it is also called the decree of predamnation. Bellarmine, therefore, and all who side with him, maintain that the decree of predamnation altogether presupposes sin in man, since in the most just God there cannot be a will to punish except sinners, nor can the destination or infliction of punishment be just without fault. See Gen. XVIII, 25. We must therefore prove against Bellarmine and his followers that God, by an eternal decree of preterition, has excluded no man from grace and glory absolutely and without respect to fault foreseen in man.

1) Because, speaking accurately, the negative and positive act of reprobation is in truth one act, and they do not differ, except in name alone.

Which is evident a) from examples.

Pharaoh and Judas, by that very act by which they were passed over and not elected, were predestined to damnation. b) It is clear from the opposite.

Just as election is predestination to salvation; so preterition is predestination to damnation.

Since, therefore, the decree of preterition and predestination is one and the same: different causes cannot be assigned to it.

2) It is the same, whether God destines a man to damnation, or does that from which damnation necessarily follows.

Whomever God has not elected, whether he is called passed over or reprobated, he is always excluded from the grace of God.

This exclusion is followed by certain damnation, because without the grace of God there is no salvation.

From which we conclude that there is one cause of preterition and predestination.

3) God does not pass over or desert a man, unless He is first deserted by him: Therefore, God deserts no man by an absolute decree.

The consequence is evident; because he who passes someone over, does so because he has been deserted by him, not out of an absolute will or mere good pleasure does he pass him over, but moved by a grave cause, he excludes the same from his favor.

The antecedent is confirmed by many sayings of Scripture, 1 Sam.

XV, 23. Because you have rejected the word of Jehovah, therefore he has rejected you.

Ps.

LXXXI, 12. 13. The people did not obey my voice, and Israel did not acquiesce to me.

Therefore I dismissed him in the hardness of their heart, that they might walk in their own counsels.

1 Chron.

XXIX, 19. If you desert him, he will abandon you forever.

Hos.

IV, 6. Because you have rejected knowledge, I will also reject you.

4) The decree of preterition, which is imagined, is repugnant to the grace of God, the merit of Christ, and universal calling.

He who has mercy on all, excludes no one from his mercy absolutely: But God, etc.

Rom.

XI, 32. E.

For whom Christ died out of incomparable love, those he did not pass over in electing without a most grave cause: But for all, etc.

2 Cor.

V, 14. E.

To whom the gospel is to be preached, him God did not pass over by an absolute decree.

But to every rational creature, etc.

Marc.

XVI, 15. Therefore.

The stronger arguments of BELLARMINE are

I. Whoever loved Jacob and hated Esau, before they had done any good or evil; he passed over Esau by an absolute decree: But God, etc.

Rom. IX, 11. 12. 13.

Therefore.

Resp.

We have satisfied this argument in the preceding chapter, qu. VII. obj. III.

II. Whoever has mercy on whom he wills to have mercy, and hardens whom he wills to harden, he excludes the man whom he hardens from his grace by an absolute will: But God, etc.

Rom. IX, 18.

Resp.

See l. c. obj. II. III.

God is compared with a potter, who has absolute power; to make from the same lump vessels, one indeed for honor, but another for dishonor, Rom.

IX, 21.

Therefore God by absolute power created some men for eternal glory, some for eternal dishonor.

Resp.

See l. c. obj. V.

God raised up Pharaoh, a hardened man, that he might demonstrate his power in him.

Rom. XI, 7.

Therefore God by an absolute decree created him for hardening and perdition.

Resp.

The words of Paul are taken from Exod.

IX, 15. 16. where God addresses Pharaoh through Moses thus.

For this הֶעֱמַדְתִּיךָ I have made you stand, that I may show you my virtue, and that my name may be announced in all the earth.

Obs. a) God does not say: I created you; but: I have made you stand I made you, that is, I preserved you, and having placed you as if under a blow, while you were already tottering, ἤγειρα, I raised you up.

Thus the word ἤγειρα, in the sense of raising up from sickness, is read in James 5:15: The prayer of faith shall save the sick, καὶ ἐγερεῖ αὐτὸν ὁ κύριος, & the Lord shall raise him up. b) God does not say: I have raised you up, or I have made you stand, in order to harden you, but in order to demonstrate my power in you, and that my name might be declared in all the earth, i.e., that all men together with you might acknowledge my power, humble themselves before it, and repent of their sins, and thus celebrate my name.

If God had reprobated Pharaoh to eternal destruction by an absolute decree, he certainly would not have shown him his power to the end that he might humble himself before it and repent.

Cf. D. Seb. Schmid’s Colleg. Bibl. prius p. 350. V. If God were to reprobate men because of sins, he would certainly reprobate all men: The consequent is false; therefore, the antecedent is also.

The consequence of the major is proved; because all men are sinners. Rom. 3:23. Resp.

God reprobates impious men because of sins, insofar as they are joined with final ἀπιστίᾳ (unbelief). But not all men are infidels until the end of life. Therefore, God does not reprobate all. Instance: But all men fallen by nature are unbelieving.

For God has concluded all in unbelief. Rom. 11:32. Therefore, all men are reprobated. Resp. Distinguish between innate and acquired unbelief.

Not because of the former, but because of the latter, God has rejected certain men from eternal salvation. VI. The Lord has made the impious for the day of evil.

Prov. 16:4. Therefore, by an absolute will, he has reprobated the same. Resp. In the Hebrew source, the cited words flow thus: Jehovah has made all things to answer to himself: yea, even the wicked for the day of evil.

Indeed, God has made all things so that they might answer to one another and observe a harmonic order, and thus, in proportion to the most just decree, the permission of the evil of fault might be answered by the evil of punishment inflicted. From which it is gathered that the decree is not absolute, but respective. Quest.

XIII. What use does the doctrine of predestination and reprobation confer upon us? The doctrine of predestination and reprobation, consonant with Holy Scripture, entices us to the love of God, the divine word, and the sacraments a), but calls us away from the lusts of the flesh b); it also consoles the elect in all adversities c).

Prob. a. From the decree of predestination we recognize the immense goodness of God toward us, who was occupied with our salvation when we did not yet exist, and ordained those means from which it has been given to us to conceive a constant faith in Christ through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Let our soul, therefore, burn with the love of God, let it assiduously meditate on the divine word, and let it strengthen and sustain itself by the use of the sacraments. Prob. b. The elect, with Paul, subdue their body and make it a servant, so that they may make it manifest that they are not of the number of the reprobate.

1 Cor. 9:27. Prob. c. The elect are the care and concern of Christ, the shepherd and bishop of faithful souls.

Not even the infernal wolf shall snatch these sheep from the hands of that great shepherd. S I G H. As often as, O sweetest Jesus, I do not so much probe as marvel at the sublime mystery of predestination, so often do I fix the eyes of my mind upon your wounds, from which predestination shines forth.

By the shedding of your blood, you reconciled to me God, who was offended by my sins, so that he might embrace me with fatherly love. I therefore embrace you, the rock and foundation of election. To you I cling and lean with true and sincere faith, never to be torn away from you. For I, a miserable man, having fallen into many sins, have been raised up through you, chosen through you, saved through you. This is what I pray for as a suppliant, my Jesus, that you may strengthen my faith, fixed in your merit, sustain it while struggling, and crown it while triumphant, so that I may be yours in the kingdom of grace, yours in the kingdom of glory!

Latin:

Deus nullum hominem ex absoluto liberrimeque praeconcepto odio, citra omnem causae impulsiuae respectum, ab hereditate vitae aeternae excludit, aeternoque addicere exitio decrevit, sed ad reprobandum ab aeterna gloria homines, praefracte impios, Deum mouerunt peccata ipsorum, cum finali incredulitate coniuncta.

Obs. Bellarminus, absoluti decreti patronus, lib. II. de gratia et libero arbitrio, cap. XVI. distinguit inter actum reprobationis negatiuum, et affirmatiuum, seu positiuum. Ille est, quo Deus pro liberrimo beneplacito quorundam non vult misereri, neque eos saluare: vocatur alias decretum praeteritionis: hic est, quo Deus peccatores contumaces, quos oblatam vocationis, regenerationis, et iustificationis gratiam perseueranter aspernaturos esse praevidit, aeternis poenis afficere constituit: dicitur etiam decretum praedamnationis. Statuit igitur Bellarminus, et omnes, qui cum ipso faciunt, decretum praedamnationis omnino supponere peccatum in homine, cum in Deo iustissimo non possit dari voluntas puniendi, nisi peccatores, nec poenae destinatio, vel inflictio, iusta esse queat sine culpa. Vid. Gen. XIIX, 25. Probandum igitur nobis est contra Bellarminum, eiusque asseclas, quod Deus aeterno praeteritionis decreto nullum hominem absolute et citra respectum culpae, in homine praevisae, a gratia et gloria excluserit.

1) Quia accurate loquendo actus negativus & positivus reprobationis est reuera unus actus, nec differunt, nisi solo nomine.

Quod patet a) exemplis.

Pharao & Iudas eo ipso actu, quo praeteriti & non electi sunt, praedamnati sunt. b) Liquet ex opposito.

Sicut electio est praedestinatio ad salutem; ita praeteritio, est praedamnatio.

Cum igitur decretum praeteritionis, & praedamnationis sit vnum idemque: diuersae causae eidem assignari nequeunt.

2) Perinde est, siue Deus destinet hominem ad damnationem, siue id faciat, ex quo damnatio necessario sequatur.

Quemcunque Deus non elegit, siue omissus dicatur, siue reprobatus, semper est exclusus a gratia Dei.

Hanc exclusionem certa damnatio sequitur, quia sine gratia Dei non est salus.

Ex quo colligimus, vnam esse causam praeteritionis & praedamnationis.

3) Deus non praeterit, aut deserit hominem, nisi prius ab eo deferatur: Ergo Deus absoluto decreto nullum hominem deserit.

Consequentia est euidens; quia, qui aliquem praeterit, ideo, quod ab illo desertus est, non ex absoluta voluntate, aut mero beneplacito ipsum praeterit, sed graui motus causa eundem fauore suo excludit.

Antecedens confirmatur ex plurimis scripturae dictis, 1 Sam.

XV, 23. Propterea, quod repudiafti verbum Iehouae, ideo repudiauit te.

Ps.

LXXXI, 12. 13. Non obediuit populus voci meae, & Israël non acquieuit mihi.

Ideo dimisi eum in duritie cordis eorum, vt irent in consiliis suis.

1 Chron.

XXIX, 19. Si deferueris illum, derelinquet te perpetuum.

Hos.

IV, 6. Quia tu scientiam repudiafti & repudiabo te.

4) Decretum praeteritionis, quod fingitur, repugnat gratiae Dei, merito Christi, & vocationi vniuersali.

Qui omnium miseretur, nullum misericordia sua absolute excludit: Atqui Deus &c.

Rom.

XI, 32. E.

Pro quibus Christus ex amore incomparabili mortuus est, illos sine grauissima causa in eligendo non praeteriuit: Atqui pro omnibus &c.

2 Cor.

V, 14. E.

Cui euangelium praedicandum est, illum Deus absoluto decreto non praeteriuit.

Atqui omni creaturae rationali &c.

Marc.

XVI, 15. Ergo.

Argumenta BELLARMINI potiora sunt

I. Quicunque Iacobum dilexit, & Esauum odio prosecutus est, priusquam quicquam boni, aut mali fecerunt; is Esauum decreto absoluto praeteriuit: Atqui Deus &c.

Rom. IX, 11. 12. 13.

Ergo.

Resp.

Huic argumento satisfecimus cap. praeced, qu. VII. obi. III.

II. Quicunque miseretur, quorum vult misereri, & indurat, quos vult indurare, ille hominem, quem indurat, voluntate absoluta excludit gratia sua: Atqui Deus &c.

Rom. IX, 18.

Resp.

Vid. l. c. obi. II. III.

Deus comparatur cum figulo, qui habet absolutam potestatem; vt ex eadem massa faciat vasa, vnum quidem in honorem, alterum vero in ignominiam, Rom.

IX, 21.

Ergo Deus absoluta potestate quosdam homines ad aeternam gloriam, quosdam ad aeternam ignominiam creauit.

Resp.

Vid. l. c. obi. V.

Deus Pharaonem hominem induratum excitauit, vt in ipso demonstraret potentiam suam.

Rom. XI, 7.

Ergo Deus absoluto decreto eum creauit ad indurationem & perditionem.

Resp.

Verba Pauli sumta sunt ex Exod.

IX, 15. 16. vbi Deus Pharaonem per Mosen ita compellat.

Propter hoc הֶעֱמַדְתִּיךָ stare feci te, vt ostendam tibi virtutem meam, & vt annuntietur nomen meum in omni terra.

Obs. a) Non dicit Deus: creaui te; sed: stare feci te, i. e. conservavi te, ac quasi sub ictu positum te, iam labantem, ἤγειρα, erexi.

Sic verbum ἤγειρα, in significatione erigendi ex morbo, legitur Iac. V, 15. Oratio fidei servabit laborantem, καὶ ἐγερεῖ αὐτὸν ὁ κύριος, & eriget ipsum dominus. b) Non dicit Deus: Erexi te, vel stare te feci, ut te indurarem, sed ut in te demonstrarem potentiam meam, & ut annuntietur nomen meum in omni terra, q. d. vt omnes homines vna tecum potentiam meam agnoscant, coram ea se humilient, & peccatorum suorum poenitentiam agant, atque adeo nomen meum celebrent.

Si Deus absoluto decreto Pharaonem reprobasset ad aeternum exitium, vtique non ostendisset illi potentiam suam cum in finem, vt coram illa humiliaretur & poenitentiam ageret.

Conf. D. seb. schmidii colleg. bibl. prius p. 350. V. Si Deus propter peccata homines reprobaret, vtique omnes homines reprobaret: Consequens est falsum; E. & antecedens.

Consequentia maioris probatur; quia omnes homines sunt peccatores. Rom. III, 23. Resp. Deus homines impios reprobat propter peccata, quatenus cum finali ἀπιστίᾳ sunt coniuncta, At non omnes homines vsque ad finem vitae sunt infideles.

E. Deus non omnes reprobat. Inflantia: Sed omnes homines lapsi natura sunt increduli.

Concludit enim Deus omnes in incredulitatem. Rom. IX, 32. E. omnes homines sunt reprobati. Resp. Dist. inter incredulitatem connatam & adscititiam.

Non propter illam, sed propter hanc Deus quosdam homines ab aeterna salute reiecit. VI. Deus impium fecit ad diem malum propter seipsum.

Prou. XVI, 4. Ergo absoluta voluntate eundem reprobauit. Resp. In fonte hebraeo verba citata sic fluunt: Omnia fecit Iehouah, vt sibi respondeant: quin etiam malum, in diem mali.

Nimirum fecit Deus omnia, vt sibi inuicem respondeant, & ordinem harmonicum obseruent, atque adeo, pro ratione decreti iustissimi, malo culpae permissio respondeat malum poenae immissum. Ex quo colligitur non decretum absolutum, sed respectiuum. Quaest.

XIII. Quem vsum nobis confert doctrina de praedestinatione & reprobatione? Doctrina de praedestinatione & reprobatione, S. scripturae consona, ad amorem Dei, verbi diuini & sacramentorum nos allicit a), a cupiditatibus autem carnis nos auocat b); solatur etiam electos in omnibus aduersitatibus c).

Prob. a. E decreto praedestinationis cognoscimus immensam erga nos bonitatem Dei, qui circa nostram salutem, cum nondum essemus, occupatus fuit, eaque ordinauit media, e quibus constantem in Christum fidem per gratiam Spiritus S. concipere nobis datum est.

Ardeat igitur anima nostra amore Dei, assidue meditetur verbum diuinum, sacramentorum vsu se corroboret & sustentet. Prob. b. Electi cum Paulo subigunt corpus suum, & seruum faciunt, vt testatum faciant, se non esse e numero reproborum.

1 Cor. IX, 27. Prob. c. Electi Christo, pastori & episcopo animarum fidelium, sunt curae cordique.

Ne infernalis quidem lupus has oues e manibus magni illius pastoris rapiet. S V S P I R I V M. Quotiescunque, o dulcissime Iesu, sublime praedestinationis mysterium non tam rimor, quam miror, toties oculos mentis meae defigo in vulnera tua, e quibus praedestinatio effulget.

Tu fuso sanguine tuo conciliasti mihi Deum, peccatis meis offensum, vt paterno me amore complecteretur. Complector igitur te, electionis petram & fundamentum. Tibi adhaereo & innitor vera finceraque fide, nunquam a te auellendus. Nam miser ego, in peccata plurima prolapsus, per te sum erectus, per te electus, per te saluatus. Hoc est, quod supplex precor, mi Iesu, vt fidem meam, in merito tuo defixam, firmes, luctantem sustentes, triumphantem corones, vt sim tuus in regno gratiae, tuus in regno gloriae!


## 18 On the Redemption of Christ, His Person and Office


### Concerning the Fraternal Redemption of Christ, as the Second Principle of Salvation


### Member I. Concerning the Names, Natures, and Person of Christ

Q. I. Who is the redeemer of the human race?

The redeemer of the human race is Jesus Christ. Q. II. Who is Jesus Christ? Jesus Christ is true God, begotten of the substance of the Father from eternity, and true man, born of the Virgin Mary in the fullness of time, the only redeemer of the whole human race, which had fallen into sin.

Q. III. Why is our redeemer called Jesus ? Jesus, i.e., Savior, was so named by the angel: because he himself was to save his people from their sins.

Obs. The names of Christ, if you look at the grammatical usage of the words, were aptly divided by the blessed GERHARD, in *loc. Theol.* T. I. loc. IV. c. 8. §. 25. sqq., into proper and figurative, to which typical ones closely approach.

But if you consider the thing itself, they must be distributed into three kinds. For since a name is a sign by which a certain thing is distinguished from others, and there is no doubt that there are altogether three things proper to our Liberator, by which he alone can be distinguished from all others, namely 1) one person, which consists of two natures, 2) a twofold state, 3) a threefold office: it follows that the division of the names which are attributed to Christ cannot but be tripartite. I will enumerate them one by one, and since the narrowness of space prevents me from explaining them according to the dignity of the subject, I will briefly run through them in the order that is fitting.

I. Some names of the PERSON are general, which express both natures: 1) Immanuel, by which we understand the same thing as θεάνθρωπος (God-man).

For this name was given to Christ alone, not to the Father, nor to the Holy Spirit. It is necessary, therefore, that there be some reason that is entirely singular and proper to Christ: The signification of this name indicates a certain most intimate conjunction of God with men alone, and with no other of created things, not even with the angels themselves. Therefore, it is also necessary that a certain singular excellence of the human race be signified. But no mode can be conceived by which Christ, and he alone, could be called God associated with men, and with them alone, unless it be a divine conjunction with a human nature, and indeed such a conjunction as befits neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit, but Christ alone, and also pertains to men alone.

Hence, Immanuel denotes that divine person who assumed a human nature, by which reason Christ is not ashamed to call us his brothers, but not the angels, Heb. II, 11, 14, 16. Therefore, this name obtains the same force as θεάνθρωπος.

Therefore, that name, θεάνθρωπος, is not merely ecclesiastical, nor invented by the ingenuity of men. 2) Mediator, 1 Tim.

II, 5, which, although it denotes the office of Christ, at the same time indicates the subject, since the μεσίτης (mediator) himself performed the parts according to both natures, the human indeed, by acting and enduring; the divine, however, by attributing an infinite price to his actions and his sufferings of evils, Acts XX, 28; Heb. IX, 12. 3) The fairest of men, Ps.

XLV, 3, where in the sources there exists a form mixed and composed of Kal, and there exists a form mixed and composed of Kal, and Püal,

Objection I. The name Ἰησοῦς [Jesus] is expressed by ישוע [Yeshua], both in the Syriac paraphrase and in the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew; which Hebrew word is also read in Nehemiah 12:10, and descends from the root Pual, by which reasoning a twofold nature is designated: one, by which he is beautiful; the other, by which he has been made beautiful.

But there are other special names which denote one or the other nature. α) Names of the divine nature. Some of these are appropriate to Christ as God, by which he is indeed distinguished from all created things, which, however, he has in common with the Father and the Holy Spirit; others are of such a kind that they are so proper to Christ, insofar as he is the eternal Son of God, begotten of the Father, that by them he is distinguished not only from the whole universe of created things, but also from the Father and the Holy Spirit. A).

Latin:

Quæst. I. Quis est redemtor generis humani?

Redemtor generis humani est Iesus Christus. Quæst. II. Quis est Iesus Christus? Iesus Christus est verus Deus, ex substantia patris ab æterno genitus, & verus homo, ex Maria virgine in plenitudine temporis natus, vnicus totius generis humani, in peccato prolapsi, redemtor.

Quæst. III. Quare redemtor noster vocatur Iesus ? Iesus, h. e. Saluator, dictus est ab angelo: quia ipse populum suum saluaturus erat a peccatis eorum.

Obs. Nomina Christi, si grammaticam verborum vsurpationem spectes, apte diuisit b. GERHARDUS, in loc. Theol. T. I. loc. IV. c. 8. §. 25. seqq. in propria, & figurata, ad quæ proxime accedunt typica.

Quod si autem rem ipsam consideres, distribuenda sunt in tria genera. Quum enim nomen fit signum, quo res quædam ab aliis discernitur, nec fit dubium, quin omnino sint tria Liberatoris nostri propria, quibus ipse vnus ab aliis omnibus distingui queat, nimirum 1) persona vna, quæ ex duabus naturis constat, 2) duplex status, 3) triplex officium: efficitur, vt tripartita non possit non esse diuisio nominum, quæ Christo sunt tributa. Numerando percenfebo singula, & quum spatii angustia me prohibeat, quo minus ea, pro rei dignitate, explicem, breuiter percurram eo, quo decet, ordine.

I. Nomina PERSONAE alia quidem sunt generalia, quæ vtramque naturam exprimunt: 1) Immanuel, id quod intelligimus idem esse, ac θεάνθρωπος.

Etenim hoc nomen Christo soli datum est, nec Patri, nec Spiritui S. Necesse est igitur, rationem aliquam esse plane singularem, & Christi propriam: Significatio huiusce nominis indicat arctissimam quamdam Dei coniunctionem cum hominibus solis, & cum nulla alia rerum creatarum, ac ne ipsis quidem angelis. Ergo etiam necesse est, vt singularis quædam humani generis excellentia significetur. Atqui nullus cogitari potest modus, quo Christus, & is quidem solus, adpellari possit Deus cum hominibus, & solis quidem illis, consociatus, nisi coniunctio diuina cum humana natura, & talis quidem coniunctio, qualis nec Patri, nec Spiritui S. sed vni Christo conuenit, atque etiam ad homines solos pertinet.

Proinde Immanuel denotat personam illam diuinam, quæ naturam adsumsit humanam, qua ratione Christum non pudet, nos adpellare fratres suos, non item angelos, Hebr. II, 11. 14. 16. E. hoc nomen eamdem obtinet vim, ac θεάνθρωπος.

E. nomen istud, θεάνθρωπος, non est dumtaxat ecclesiasticum, neque hominum ingenio fictum. 2) Mediator, 1 Tim.

II, 5. quod, quamquam officium Christi denotat, simul tamen indicat subiectum, quando quidem μεσίτης partibus ipse functus est secundum vtramque naturam, humanam quidem, peragendo ac perferendo; diuinam autem, actionibus suis ac malorum perpessionibus infinitum pretium tribuendo, Act. XX, 28. Hebr. IX, 12. 3) Pulcherrimus hominum, Ps.

XLV, 3. vbi in fontibus exstat forma mixta & composita ex Kal, & exstat forma mixta & composita ex Kal, & Püal,

*Obiectio I Nomen Ἰησοῦς tum in paraphrasi syriaca, tum in euangelio Matthæi hebraico exprimitur per ישוע, quæ vox hebræa etiam legitur Nehem.* XII, 10. & descendit a rad. Püal, qua ratione designatur duplex natura, vna, qua pulcher est, altera, qua pulcher factus est.

Alia vero sunt specialia, quæ alterutram notant naturam. א) Nomina diuinæ naturæ. Horum alia Christo conueniunt, vt Deo, quibus ipse quidem ab omnibus rebus creatis discernitur, quæ tamen ipse communia habet cum Patre & Spiritu Sancto; alia sunt eiusmodi, quæ Christi, quatenus est æternus Dei Filius, ex Patre generatus, ita sunt propria, vt illis ipse non solum a tota rerum creatarum vniuersitate, verum etiam a Patre & Spiritu S. distinguatur.


### Member I. Concerning the Names, Natures, and Person of Christ: A)

A).

These are the proper names of God: 1) יהוה [YHWH], and indeed in the nominative case (as the Theologians speak), Ex. 3:7, where יהוה is said to be the same one who, a little before, v. 2, had been called מלאך יהוה [Angel of YHWH]; Ps. 102:13, concerning which saying, that it is to be understood of Christ, the Legate of Christ makes us certain, Heb. 1:10-12, add. v. 8; Isa. 45:24, 25, coll. with Rom. 14:10, 11. Thus, indeed, the Apostle explicitly interprets that utterance concerning Christ.

With that also agrees this, Apoc. 1:8, ὁ ὢν, καὶ ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος [who is, and who was, and who is to come], which is the very name יהוה, rendered in Greek. For יהוה is a mark of the future; ἐρχόμενος is an indication of the participle, which denotes presence; ὁ ὢν, ἦν is the past, ἦν.

Therefore, יהוה signifies an immutable nature, because God is always the same.

2) יהוה צבאות [YHWH of Hosts], Isa. 6:3, add. v. 8, 9, 16, and John 12:41.

3) אלהי אברהם אלהי יצחק אלהי יעקב [God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob], Exod. 3:2, 6. 4) אלהי ישראל [God of Israel], ibid. coll. Luke 1:16, 17; for he is called thus who was using John as a forerunner, and he is undoubtedly Christ, add. v. 43, 76. 5) יהוה צדקנו [YHWH our righteousness], Jer. 23:6.

6) Various names, which truly befit the one God, we see accumulated and closely joined, Isa.

9:6. 7) Θεός [God], also ὁ Θεός [the God], which is valid as an argument κατ’ ἄνθρωπον [according to man], because of the rule, albeit false, which SOCINUS devised.

Heb. 1:2, where the doubled particle, γὰ [for], is an indication that this name, ὁ Θεός, pertains equally to both, as much to Christ as to the Father, John 1:1, 20:28, Acts 20:28. But most notable is the fivefold addition, for each one demonstrates the highest divinity.

Thus, indeed, Christ is called: α) Θεός ὁ ἀληθινός [the true God], 1 John 5:20. β) Ὁ μέγας Θεός [the great God], Tit. 2:13. γ) Ὁ ὢν ἐπὶ πάντων, ἐυλογητὸς εἰς τὰς αἰῶνας [who is over all, blessed forever], Rom. 9:5. Whatever the Arians or Photinians may dare to say against this, with whom the school of SOCINUS agrees, this is certainly clearer than light, that that very description and praise is attributed to Christ.

He is called ὁ ὢν ἐπὶ πάντων [who is over all], even in the most humble state, nay, even before he had been clothed in flesh, John 3:31. The same is proclaimed ὁ ἐυλογητὸς εἰς τὰς αἰῶνας [the blessed forever], and indeed no less than the Father, also with accumulated words, to designate the highest degree of veneration, Apoc. 5:13. δ) Ὁ Θεός τῶν ἁγίων προφητῶν [the God of the holy prophets], Apoc. 22:6; that this pertains to Christ clearly appears from v. 16. ε) Ὁ Θεός τῦ Ἰσραήλ [the God of Israel], Luke 1:16, 17. 8) Κύριος [Lord], which Greek name, insofar as it signifies the highest divinity, undoubtedly corresponds to the Hebrew יהוה and אדני [Adonai]; but in a certain way it must be referred to the glorious state of the human nature, as clearly appears from those things which I shall presently bring forward.

Latin:

A).

Dei propria nomina hæc sunt: 1) יהוה, & quidem in casu recto (vt Theologi loquuntur,) Ex. III, 7. vbi יהוה dicitur is idem, qui paullo ante, v. 2. appellatus fuerat מלאך יהוה, Ps. CII, 13, quod dictum de Christo esse intelligendum, de eo certiores nos facit Legatus Christi, Hebr. I, 10-12. add. v. 8. Ief. XLV, 24. 25. coll. cum Rom. XIV, 10. 11. Ita nimirum Apostolus effatum illud diserte de Christo interpretatur.

Cum illo congruit etiam hoc, Apoc. I, 8. ὁ ὢν, καὶ ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος, id quod est ipsum nomen יהוה, græce redditum. Nam יהוה est nota futuri, ἐρχόμενος, est indicium participii, quod præsentiam denotat, ὁ ὢν, ἦν est præteritum, ἦν.

Itaque יהוה significat immutabilem naturam, quod Deus fit semper idem.

2) צבאות יהוה, Ief. VI, 3. add. v. 8. 9. 16. & Ioann. XII, 41. 3) אלהי אברהם אלהי יצחק אלהי יעקב, Exod.

III, 2. 6. 4) אלהי ישראל, ibid. coll. Luc. I, 16. 17, is enim ita vocatur, qui prænuntio vtebatur Ioanne, is vero haud dubie est Christus add. v. 43. 76. 5) יהוה צדקנו, Ierem.

XXIII, 6. 6) Varia nomina, quæ Deum profecto vnum decent, cumulatius aucta arcteq; copulata cernimus Ief.

IX, 6. 7) Θεός, etiam ὁ Θεός, quod valet tanquam argumentum κατ’ ἄνθρωπον, propter regulam, tametsi falsam, quam SOCINVS excogitauit.

Hebr. I, 2. vbi geminata vocula, γὰ, indicio est, nomen hoc ὁ Θεός, ad vtrumque pariter, tam ad Christum, quam ad Patrem pertinere, Ioann. I, 1. XX, 28. Actor. XX, 28. Maxime autem notabile est quintuplex additamentum, vnum enim quodque summam demonstrat diuinitatem.

Ita nimirum Christus appellatur. α) Θεός ὁ ἀληθινός, 1 Ioann. V, 20. β) Ὁ μέγας Θεός, Tit. II, 13. γ) Ὁ ὢν ἐπὶ πάντων, ἐυλογητὸς εἰς τὰς αἰῶνας, Rom. IX, 5. Quidquid contra audeant dicere, siue Ariani, siue Photiniani, quibus cum consentit SOCINI schola, hoc certe luce clarius est, quod ea ipsa descriptio ac laudatio Christo tribuatur.

Dicitur ipse, ὁ ὢν ἐπὶ πάντων, etiam in statu humillimo, quin immo ante, quam carne indutus esset, Ioann. III, 31. Prædicatur idem, ὁ ἐυλογητὸς εἰς τὰς αἰῶνας, & quidem non minus, quam Pater, cumulatis quoque verbis, ad designandum summum venerationis gradum, Apoc V, 13. δ) Ὁ Θεός τῶν ἁγίων προφητῶν, Apoc XXII, 6. id vero ad Christum pertinere, luculenter adparet ex v. 16. ε) Ὁ Θεός τῦ Ἰσραήλ, Luc. I, 16. 17. 8) Κύριος, quod græcum nomen, quoad diuinitatem summam significat, haud dubie respondet hebraicis, יהוה & אדני, quodam autem modo referri debet ad statum gloriosum humanæ naturæ, vt plane adparet ex iis, quæ deinceps proferam.


### Member I. Concerning the Names, Natures, and Person of Christ: B)

B).

These are the principal names of the Son of God:

1) בן [Son], Ps. 2:7, Isa. 9:5, in which place the diverse natures in Christ are pronounced by distinct words and phrases, by the interpretation of PAUL, Gal. 4:4, ἐξαπέσαλεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν υἱὸν αὐτῦ [God sent forth his Son], that is, בן-לש, γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικὸς [born of a woman], that is, ילד-ילד.

2) צמח יהוה [Branch of YHWH], Isa. 4:2, Zech. 3:8, 12. We rely on this argumentation: In the sense that Christ is called צמח יהוה [Branch of YHWH] as it pertains to his human nature, namely the Son of David, in the same sense he is called צמח יהוה, as far as the divine nature is concerned, indeed as the Son of God.

3) υἱὸς τῦ Θεῦ [Son of God], and indeed ὁ μονογενής [the only-begotten]. (see the notes on page 308.) 4) λόγος [Word], who was πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν [with God] and indeed before he σὰρξ ἐγένετο [became flesh], John 1:2 and 14. β) Names of the human nature; of which some look generally to the thing itself, but others pertain specifically to various circumstances.

A).

The general ones are:

1) זרע האשה [Seed of the woman], Gen. 3:15. For that this illustrious prophecy is nothing other than the πρωτευαγγέλιον [first gospel] concerning Christ, is abundantly evident both from this very passage and from the whole series of words, and indeed from parallel passages.

2) ἄνθρωπος [man], 1 Tim. 2:5, and also 3) which is much more usual and more significant, the Hebrew ישע [Yesha], which is indeed less used in Kal, but in Hiphil הושיע [Hoshia], he saved, is used most frequently; whence originates ישוע [Yeshua], salvation; and thus Ἰησοῦς [Jesus] is Savior. This word more significantly said, ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου [the Son of man]. It must now be inquired into the true and sufficient reason for this name. I do not indeed deny, if you say that by it is designated α) the truth of the human nature in Christ, β) his origin from the seed of the mother, γ) his most ardent love toward the human race, δ) the preeminence and excellence, for which reason he alone above others is called ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου [the Son of man], Ps. 45: 3. But you will also grant me this: that all those reasons do not suffice, unless you add ε) the state of misery, because, namely, Christ, as long as he lived on earth, experienced all the infirmities of human nature, and indeed in the place of all men. That this is the principal reason for this name, I will confirm with clear arguments: a) By the use of this name; it is indeed used very often before the glorious transformation of Christ, from that time never (if you except a few places, Acts 7:56, where this cause underlies it, because Christ showed himself to be seen by Stephen in human form, and likewise Apocal. 1:13, 14:14). Therefore, after Christ himself sat down at the right hand of the Father, he is nowhere called the Son of man; he is everywhere adorned with splendid titles, which befit his highest dignity, such as: Lord, King of Kings. But what then? Did he cease to be true man, born of a virgin? Was his love for men diminished, or entirely extinguished? Was anything detracted from the preeminence of the human nature, which he enjoys? Nothing at all. You see, therefore, that all those reasons are not sufficiently adequate, but that this is the principal one: that that name was most rightly accommodated to the state of humility, in which, namely, Christ bore not only the human nature, but also the entire calamity, and vicariously. For every name, the more it is befitting to the state of someone, the more apt it is. b) By the conjunction of this name with various descriptions, which are documents of the most humble condition, e.g., Matt. 8:20, Luke 18:31, 32, 33. c) By another name, very similar to this, since not the humanity of Christ itself, but his humility is indicated by the name of the days of his flesh, Heb. 5:7. d) By prophecies, and indeed of both kinds, partly literal (among which stands out the most clear prophecy, Ps. 8, in which both states of Christ are predicted, and indeed in such a way that distinct names are also used; Son of man, as far as the most miserable condition, v. 5, then Lord, as far as the most glorious state pertains, v. 7 and 10, add. Phil. 2:9, 11); partly typical (for there are certain typical names, just as Ezekiel is called בן אדם [son of man] almost as often as Christ is called by the same name in the sacred monuments. That, indeed, for that very reason, because that divine prophet, much more than any other, passed a life full of troubles and miseries; and all those learned in Hebrew know that the custom of the holy language is such that miserable men, and those of the lowest census, are named בני אדם [sons of man], to whom are opposed בני איש [sons of men/nobles], noble and fortunate men, as Ps. 49:3). Corollary: Therefore, this name, Son of man, pertains not so much to the human nature of Christ, as rather to the calamitous state. B.) The special ones are 1) Of the nation: σπέρμα τοῦ Ἀβραάμ [seed of Abraham], Gal. 3:16. 2) Of the tribe: ὁ λέων ὁ ὢν ἐκ τῆς φυλῆς Ἰούδα [the lion who is from the tribe of Judah], which name is partly of the glorious state, insofar as he is called a lion, who brought back victory, partly of the nation, since he is said to have arisen from the tribe of Judah. 3) Of the family: צמח דוד [Branch of David], Jer. 23:5, ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ Δαβίδ [the Son of David], Matt. 15:22, 22:42, ἡ ῥίζα Δαβίδ [the root of David], Apoc. 5:5, conf. with Isa. 11:1. 4) Of the place of education: Ναζωραῖος [Nazarene], Matt. 2: 23. II. Names of STATE. α) The general one, which pertains to both conditions, is ἀμνὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ [Lamb of God], John 1: 29. And so more often. The principal reason why Christ is compared with a lamb is situated in this: that he offered himself to God as a victim. For the origin of this name must be sought from the type of lambs, which in the age of the O.T. were destined for sacrifice, and especially for the burnt offering, and which it was necessary to be whole, without any blemish and spot; but especially from the type of the paschal lamb, 1 Cor. 5:7. That John also looked to this lamb appears from this: that this word came out of his mouth not, as very learned men think, near the day of the feast of atonement, but with the Passover impending. Compare, I pray, John 1:29 with v. 35, 43, and 2:11, 12, 13. But let us perceive the sense of this name, and its use, and more deeply, two principles and as many corollaries will effect it. Princ. 1. The sacrifice, performed by Christ, looks indeed this Latin seems to some to have been introduced into Latium from the times of Tertullian; but BORRICHIUS observed that the same already flourished in the century of Trajan. See CELLARIUS, latinit. restit. p. 89. to his calamitous state, as far as the action itself pertains, yet at the same time to the office, commanded to Christ, as far as the power and dignity. Corollary: Therefore, ἀμνὸς τῷ Θεῷ [Lamb of God] is a name of both state and office. Therefore he is called a lamb, because he was slaughtered and sacrificed (this pertains to the state of misery). But he is so called with this significant addition: Lamb of God, insofar as he was destined by God for sacrifice, and approved by God (that which must be attributed to both offices of Christ). Princ. 2. The host, which Christ immolated, if you consider the sacrifice-action itself, was consummated at the time when Christ breathed out his soul, Heb. 7:27, 9:28, John 19:30; but the salutary effect is always continued, and remains perpetual into all eternity, Heb. 9:12, 10:14. Corollary: Therefore, this name, ἀμνὸς τῷ Θεῷ, must be referred in a diverse way to both states of Christ; formally indeed, so to speak, to the humble state, but in truth effectively to the eminent state. Apoc. 5:6, 9, 12, 13. 2) The special ones are partly of the calamitous state, as υἱὸς τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ [Son of man], about which it was said a little before; partly of the glorious state: 1) δεσπότης [Master], by right of purchase, 2 Pet. 2:1. 2) λέων ὁ νικῶν [the lion who conquers], Apoc. 5:5. 3) κύριος [Lord]. But this name, to be considered in a diverse way, sometimes pertains to the divine nature of Christ, sometimes to the state of highest dignity, to which he himself ascended according to human nature. I shall ask for certain hermeneutical laws. Then it is a name of the divine nature in Christ, when α) it is attributed to Christ before his human nature was adorned with heavenly glory, e.g., Luke 2:11, Matt. 16:22, with which must be compared that confession, v. 16, δ. υἱὸς τῷ Θεῷ ζῶντος [the Son of the living God], nay, before, having assumed human nature, he himself ἐκένωσεν [emptied himself], 1 Cor. 15:47. β) when it is joined with certain most certain indications of the divine nature, as Matt. 21:3, Mark 2:28, 9:24, Luke 5:8, 17:5, 6. But then it is a sign of the glorious state, in which his human nature has been placed, α) when it is so brought to Christ alone, that he is thereby distinguished from the Father, 1 Cor. 8:6. β) when Christ is said to have been made κύριος [Lord], Acts 2:36. γ) when it is numbered among the effects of death and recovered life, Rom. 14:9. δ) when mention is made of exaltation, as is commonly said, Ps. 110:1, Phil. 2:9, 11. III. Names of OFFICE. They are likewise a) General, which contain in their scope the entire threefold office which Christ performed, as are: 1) מָשִׁיחַ [Messiah], in Greek χρισός [Christ], John 1:42. 2) מַלְאַךְ יְהוָה [Angel of YHWH], & מַלְאַךְ בְּרִית [Angel of the Covenant], to which is adjacent that, ἀπόστολος [Apostle], Heb. 3:1, add. John 10:36. 3) שִׁילֹה [Shiloh], Gen. 49:10, Job 19:25. 4) Ἰησοῦς [Jesus], which name by reason of usage indeed denotes the subject, as in this statement, 1 John 5:1: ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἐστὶν ὁ Χριστός [that Jesus is the Christ], i.e., that Jesus of Nazareth, and no one else, is that true Christ; but by reason of signification it pertains to the office, and all its parts, as there is none of them which contributes nothing to the imparting of salvation to us. 5) Σωτήρ [Savior], that which in the thing itself is the same as Ἰησοῦς, by the interpretation of the heavenly messenger, Matt. 1:21. 6) Ποιμήν [Shepherd], This is apt for all three offices of Christ: α) to the Priestly, if indeed he met death for the sheep, to be bought back with his own blood, John 10:11. β) to the Prophetic, since the sheep hear his voice, ibid. v. 3, 5, and for that reason Christ is called ὁ ἀρχιποιμήν [the chief Shepherd], 1 Pet. 5:4, for the pastors of the N.T. church are teachers, not Priests, properly so called, and much less commanders, ibid. v. 3. γ) to the Kingly, insofar as he defends his own sheep from every danger, and commands them to aspire to eternal salvation, John 10:28, add. Ps. 78:72. 2) Special, which are of the office a) Priestly: 1) ἱερεύς [priest], Heb. 5:6, 7:17, 25. 2) ἀρχιερεύς [high priest], and indeed with a fourfold addition most especially: α) μέγας [great], namely in view of the high Priest of the O.T. who, although he was high, and excelled other Priests in dignity, was nevertheless far inferior to Christ. Heb. 4:14. β) κατὰ τὴν τάξιν τῷ Μελχισεδέκ [according to the order of Melchizedek], Heb. 5:10. γ) ἐς τὸν αἰῶνα [forever], Heb. 7:21, add. 23 & 25. δ) ὃς ἐκάθισεν ἐν δεξιᾷ τῷ Θεῷ [who sat down at the right hand of God], Heb. 8:1. 3) שָׁרָה צִדְקוּ [The Lord our righteousness], Jer. 33:16, conf. with Rom. 4:6, 2 Cor. 5:21. 4) ἱλασία [propitiation], and likewise πάσχα [passover], as far as the first part of the Priestly office pertains, 1 Cor. 5:7. 5) παράκλητος [advocate], as far as the second, 1 John 2:2. b) Prophetic: 1) ὁ προφήτης [the prophet], as also, προφήτης μέγας [a great prophet], Luke 7:16, John 6:14. 2) διδάσκαλος [teacher], John 3:2, Mark 14:14. 3) ἐπίσκοπος [overseer/bishop], 1 Pet. 2:25. c) Kingly: מֶלֶךְ [King], or מֹושֵׁל [ruler] & βασιλεύς [king], and indeed with a fourfold excellence: α) Eternal King, Mic. 5:1. β) King of righteousness, & γ) King of peace, Heb. 7:2, add. Isa. 9:6, and I like the opinion of those who interpret the name שִׁילֹה [Shiloh], Gen. 49:10, in such a way that he is the reconciler of peace, δ) King of Kings, Apoc. 17:14, 19:16. more significantly the Hebrew, ישע, which indeed is less used in Kal, but in Hiphil, however, הושיע, he saved, is used most frequently; from which originates ישוע, salvation; and thus Ἰησοῦς is Savior.

This word more significantly stated, ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου [the Son of man]. It will now be necessary to inquire into the true and sufficient reason for this name.

I do not indeed deny, if you should say that by it is designated a) the truth of the human nature in Christ, β) the origin of the same from the seed of the mother, γ) his most ardent love toward the human race, δ) the preeminence and excellence, for which reason he alone above others is called ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, Ps. XLV, 3. But you will also grant me this: that all those reasons do not suffice, unless you add ε) the state of misery, because, namely, Christ, as long as he lived on earth, experienced all the infirmities of human nature, and indeed in the place of all men.

That this is the principal reason for this name, I will confirm with clear arguments: a) By the use of this name; it is indeed used frequently before the glorious transformation of Christ, from that time never (if you except a few places, Acts VII, 56, where this cause underlies it, since Christ presented himself to be seen by Stephen in human form, and likewise Apocal. I, 13, XIV, 14). And so Christ, after he himself sat down at the right hand of the Father, is nowhere called the Son of man, but is everywhere adorned with splendid titles, which befit his highest dignity, such as: Lord, King of Kings.

But what then? Did he cease to be true man, born of a virgin? Was his love for men diminished, or entirely extinguished? Was anything taken away from the preeminence of the human nature, which he enjoys? Nothing at all. You see, therefore, that all those reasons are not sufficiently adequate, but that this is the principal one: that that name would be most correctly accommodated to the state of humiliation, in which, namely, Christ bore not only human nature, but also universal and vicarious calamity.

For every name, the more it is fitting to the state of someone, the more apt it is. b) By the conjunction of this name with various descriptions, which are proofs of a most humble condition, e.g., Matth. VIII, 20, Luke XVIII, 31, 32, 33. c) By another name, very similar to this, when indeed not the humanity of Christ itself, but his humiliation is indicated by the name of the days of his flesh, Hebr. V, 7. d) By prophecies, and indeed of both kinds, partly literal (among which stands out the most clear prophecy, Ps. VIII, in which both states of Christ are predicted, and indeed in such a way that distinct names are also used; Son of man, as regards the most miserable condition, v. 5, then Lord, as regards the most glorious state, v. 7 and 10, add Phil. II, 9, 11); partly typical (for there are certain typical names, just as Ezekiel is called בן אדם [son of man] almost as often as Christ is called by the same name in the sacred records. That, however, is for that very reason, because that divine prophet passed a life much more sorrowful and full of miseries than any other; and all those learned in Hebrew know that the custom of the holy language is such that miserable men, and those of the lowest census, are named בני אדם [sons of man], to whom are opposed בני איש [sons of man/nobles], noble and fortunate men, as Ps. XLIX, 3). Corollary: Therefore, this name, Son of man, pertains not so much to the human nature of Christ, as rather to his calamitous state.

B.) Special ones are 1) Of the nation: σπέρμα τοῦ Ἀβραάμ [seed of Abraham],

II. Names of STATE. α) The general one, which pertains to both conditions, is ἀμνὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ [Lamb of God], John I, 29. And so more frequently. The principal reason why Christ is compared with a lamb lies in this: that he offered himself as a victim to God. For the origin of this name must be drawn from the type of the lambs, which in the age of the O. T. were destined for sacrifice, and especially for the burnt offering, and which had to be whole, without any blemish or spot; but most of all from the type of the paschal lamb, 1 Cor. V, 7. That John also looked to this lamb is apparent from this: that this word went forth from his own mouth not, as most learned men judge, near the day of expiation, but with the Passover at hand. Compare, I pray, John I, 29 with v. 35. 43. & II, 11. 12. 13. But two principles, and as many corollaries, will make us perceive the sense of this name fully and more thoroughly.

Princip. 1. The Sacrifice, accomplished by Christ, regards who-

This Latin seems to some to have been introduced into Latium from the times of Tertullian; but BORRICHIUS observed that it flourished even then in the century of Trajan. See CELLARIUS, latinit. resit. p. 89.

to his calamitous state, as far as the action itself is concerned, but at the same time to the office, commanded to Christ, as far as power and dignity are concerned. Conclusion E.

ἀμνὸς τῷ Θεῷ (the Lamb of God) is a name both of state and of office. Therefore he is called the Lamb, because he was slaughtered and sacrificed (this pertains to the state of misery). But he is truly called so with this distinguished addition: the Lamb of God, in so far as he was destined by God for sacrifice, and approved by God (which must be attributed to both of Christ's offices). Principle

2. The Host, which Christ immolated, if you consider the sacrificial action itself, was completed at the time when Christ breathed out his soul, Hebr. VII, 27. IX, 28. John XIX, 30.; but the salutary effect is continued always, and remains perpetual for all eternity, Hebr. IX, 12. X, 14. Conclusion E.

This name, ἀμνὸς τῷ Θεῷ, must be referred in a diverse manner to both of Christ's states; formally, so to speak, to the humble state, but effectively to the eminent state. Apoc. V, 6, 9. 12. 13. 2) Special names are partly of the calamitous state, as υἱὸς τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ (Son of Man), of which it was spoken a little before; partly of the glorious state: 1) δεσπότης (Master), by right of purchase, 2 Pet. I, 2. 2) λέων ὁ νικῶν (the Lion who conquers), Apoc. V, 5. 3) κύριος (Lord). But this name, to be considered in a diverse manner, pertains sometimes to the divine nature of Christ, sometimes to the state of highest dignity, to which he himself ascended according to his human nature. I shall examine certain hermeneutical laws. Then it is a name of the divine nature in Christ, when α) it is attributed to Christ before his human nature was adorned with heavenly glory, e.g. Luke II, 11. Matt. XVI, 22. with which this confession must be compared, v. 16. δ. υἱὸς τῷ Θεῷ ζῶντος (the Son of the living God), indeed before he himself ἐκένωσεν (emptied himself), having assumed human nature, 1 Cor. XV, 47. β) when it is joined with certain most certain proofs of the divine nature, as Matt. XXI, 3. Mark II, 28. IX, 24. Luke V, 8. XVII, 5, 6. But then it is a sign of the glorious state, in which his human nature has been placed, α) when it is applied to Christ alone in such a way that he is thereby distinguished from the Father, 1 Cor. VIII, 6. β) when Christ is said to have been made κύριος (Lord), Acts II, 36. γ) when it is numbered among the effects of death and recovered life, Rom. XIV, 9. δ) when mention is made of exaltation, as is commonly said, Ps. CX, 1. Phil. II, 9, 11. CX, 1. Phil. II, 9. 11.

Latin:

B).

Filii Dei nomina hæc sunt præcipua: 1) בן,

Ps. II, 7. Ief. IX, 5. quo in loco distinctis vocibus ac locutionibus diuersæ in Christo naturæ pronuntiantur, PAVLLO interprete, Gal. IV, 4. ἐξαπέσαλεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν υἱὸν αὐτῦ, hoc est, בן-לש, γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικὸς, hoc est, ילד-ילד.

2) צמח יהוה, Ief. IV, 2. Zach. III, 8. 12. Nitimur hac argumentatione: Quo sensu Christus dicitur צמח יהוה, quod ad humanam eius naturam attinet, scilicet Filius Dauidis, eadem sententia vocatur, צמח יהוה, quantum ad diuinam naturam, quippe Filius Dei.

3) υἱὸς τῦ Θεῦ, & quidem ὁ μονογενής. (vid. annotata ad pag. 308.) 4) λόγος, qui fuit πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν & quidem ante, quam σὰρξ ἐγένετο, Ioann. I, 2. & 14. ב) Nomina humana naturæ; quorum alia quidem generatim ad rem ipsam spectant, alia vero speciatim ad varias circumstantes pertinent.

A).

Generalia sunt: 1) זרע האשה,

Gen. III, 15. Hanc enim illustrem vaticinationem nihil esse aliud, quam πρωτευαγγέλιον de Christo, tum ex hoc ipso atque ex vniuersa verborum serie, tum vero ex locis parallelis abunde constat.

2) ἄνθρωπος, 1 Tim. II, 5. atque etiam 3) quod multo & vsitatius est, & significantius hebræa, ישע, quæ quidem in Kal minus vsitata est, in Hiphil autem הושיע, saluauit, frequentissime adhibetur; vnde originem ducit ישוע, salus; adeoque Ἰησοῦς est Saluator.

Vox hæc significantius dictum, ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου. Inquirendum nunc... erit in veram ac sufficientem huius nominis rationem.

Haud equidem abnuo, si dixeris eo designari a) veritatem humanæ in Christo naturæ, β) originem eiusdem ex matris semine, γ) amorem ipsius ardentissimum erga hominum genus, δ) præstantiam excellentiamque, quam ob rem ipse vnus præ cæteris nuncupatur ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, Ps. XLV, 3. Sed dabis mihi etiam hoc: vniuersas illas rationes non sufficere, nisi adiunxeris ε) statum miseriæ, quod nimirum Christus, donec in terra versabatur, humanæ naturæ infirmitates omnes fuerit expertus, & vice quidem omnium hominum.

Hanc esse præcipuam huius nominis rationem, perspicuis confirmabo argumentis: a) Vsu huius nominis; id nimirum vsurpatur fæpe numero ante gloriosam Christi mutationem, ab eo tempore nunquam (pauca si exceperis loca, Act. VII, 56. vbi causa hæc subest, quoniam Christus forma humana se Stephano conspiciendum præbuit, itemque Apocal. I, 13. XIV, 14.). Itaque Christus post, quam ipse ad dextram Patris consedit, nusquam adpellatur Filius hominis, vbique splendidis ornatur titulis, qui summæ ipsius dignitati conueniunt, cuiusmodi sunt: Dominus, Rex Regum.

Ecquid vero? An desijt esse verus homo, ex virgine ortus? Num amor ipsius in homines imminutus fuit, aut plane extinctus? Detractum ne fuit quidquam de præstantia humanæ, quæ gaudet, naturæ? Nihil profecto minus. Vides igitur, omnes illas rationes non esse fat idoneas, sed hanc esse principalem: quod nomen illud rectissime accommodatum esset ad statum humilitatis, in quo nimirum Christus humanam non solum naturam, sed & calamitatem vniuersam, ac vicariam pertulit.

Omne enim nomen, quo magis illud statui alicuius conueniens est, co est aptius. b) Coniunctione huiusce nominis cum variis descriptionibus, quæ sunt humillimæ conditionis documenta, v. gr. Matth. VIII, 20. Luc. XVIII, 31. 32. 33. c) Alio nomine, huic simillimo, quando quidem non ipsa Christi humanitas, sed eius humilitas indicatur nomine dierum carnis, Hebr. V, 7. d) Vaticinationibus, & vtriusque quidem generis, partim literalibus (inter quas eminet luculentissimum vaticinium, Ps. VIII. in quo status Christi vterque prædicitur, & ita quidem, vt distincta etiam nomina adhibeantur; filius hominis, quantum ad conditionem miserrimam, v. 5. deinde Dominus, quod ad statum gloriosissimum attinet, v. 7. & 10. add. Phil. II, 9. 11.); partim typicis (sunt enim nomina quædam typica, quem ad modum Ezechiel fere toties adpellatur בן אדם, quoties Christus in monumentis sacris eodem nomine nuncupatur. Id vero ob eam ipsam causam, quod ille vates diuinus multo magis, quam alius quispiam, ærumnosam vitam ac miseriarum plenam transegit; & norunt omnes hebraice docti, consuetudinem sanctæ linguæ ita ferre, vt homines miseri, atque infimi census nominentur בני אדם, quibus opponuntur בני איש, viri nobiles ac fortunati, vt Ps. XLIX, 3.). Consectarium: E. nomen hoc, filius hominis, non tam ad naturam Christi humanam, quam potius ad statum calamitosum pertinet.

B.) Specialia sunt 1) Gentis: σπέρμα τοῦ Ἀβραάμ, Gal. III, 16. 2) Tribus: ὁ λέων ὁ ὢν ἐκ τῆς φυλῆς Ἰούδα, quod quidem nomen partim status gloriosi est, quatenus dicitur leo, qui victoriam reportauit, partim nationis, quando quidem dicitur ex tribu Iudu exortus. 3) Familiæ: צמח דוד, Ierem. XXIII, 5. ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ Δαβίδ, Matth. XV, 22. XXII, 42. ἡ ῥίζα Δαβίδ, Apoc. V, 5. conf. cum Ies. XI, 1. 4) Loci educationis: Ναζωραῖος, Matth. II, 23.

II. Nomina STATVS. α) Generale, quod ad vtramque pertinet conditionem, est ἀμνὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ, Ioann. I, 29. Et ita fæpius. Ratio præcipua, quare Christus cum agno comparatur, sita est in eo: quod semet Deo victimam obtulit. Origo enim huius nominis arcessenda est a typo agnorum, qui ætate V. T. ad sacrificium, in primisque ad holocaustum, erant destinati, & quos oportebat integros esse, fine vlla labe & macula; præfertim vero a typo agni paschalis, 1 Cor. V, 7. Ad hunc agnum etiam Ioannem respexisse, adparet ex eo: quod verbum hoc ex ore ipsius exiit non, vt viri quidem doctissimi arbitrantur, prope diem festum expiationis, sed instante pascha. Compara, quæso, Ioann. I, 29. cum v. 35. 43. & II, 11. 12. 13. Sensum vero huiusce nominis, vlumque, et penitins perspiciamus, efficient duo principia, totidemque consectaria.

Princip. 1. Sacrificium, a Christo peractum, spectat qui-

hæc latina quibusdam videtur a temporibus Tertulliani in Latium introducta; at observauit BORRICHIVS eandem iam tum sæculo Traiani viguisse. Vide CELLARII latinit. resit. p. 89.

dem ad statum ipsius calamitosum, quod ad ipsam actionem attinet, simul tamen ad officium, Christo mandatum, quantum ad vim ac dignitatem. Confect. E.

ἀμνὸς τῷ Θεῷ est nomen tum status, tum officii. Idcirco dicitur agnus, quoniam mactatus fuit, ac sacrificatus (hoc ad statum miseriæ pertinet). Ita vero dicitur cum insigni hoc additamento: agnus Dei, quatenus fuit a Deo ad sacrificium destinatus, Deoque probatus (id quod officio Christi vtrique tribuendum est). Princip.

2. Hostia, quam Christus immolauit, si ipsam sacrificat-actionem consideres, consummata fuit eo tempore, quo Christus animam efflauit, Hebr. VII, 27. IX, 28. Io. XIX, 30.; effectus autem salutaris continuatur semper, & permanet perpetuus in omnem æternitatem, Hebr. IX, 12. X, 14. Confect. E.

nomen hoc, ἀμνὸς τῷ Θεῷ, diuersa ratione ad vtrumque Christi statum debet referri; formaliter quidem, vt ita dicam, ad statum humilem, at enim vero effectiue ad statum eminentem. Apocal. V, 6, 9. 12. 13. 2) Specialia sunt partim status calamitosi, vt υἱὸς τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ, de quo dictum est paullo ante; partim status gloriosi: 1) δεσπότης, iure emtionis, 2 Pet. I, 2. 2) λέων ὁ νικῶν, Appc. V, 5. 3) κύριος. Hoc autem nomen, diuersa ratione considerandum, modo ad diuinam Christi naturam pertinet, modo ad statum summæ dignitatis, ad quam ipse secundum humanam naturam adscendit. Sciscam leges quasdam hermeneuticas. Tunc illud est nomen naturæ in Christo diuinæ, cum α) Christo tribuitur ante, quam gloria cœlesti exornata fuit humana eius natura, e. g. Luc. II, 11. Matth. XVI, 22. quicum conferenda est ista confessio, v. 16. δ. υἱὸς τῷ Θεῷ ζῶντος, immo ante, quam, humana natura adsumta, se ipse ἐκένωσεν, 1 Cor. XV, 47. β) cum coniungitur cum certissimis quibusdam diuinæ naturæ indiciis, vt Matth. XXI, 3. Marc. II, 28. IX, 24. Luc. V, 8. XVII, 5 6. Tum vero est signum status gloriosi, in quo humana ipsius natura collocata est, α) cum Christo soli ita adferitur, vt is eo ipso a Patre discernatur, 1 Cor. VIII, 6. β) cum Christus dicitur factus κύριος, Act. II, 36. γ) cum illud in effectibus mortis ac recuperatæ vitæ numeratur, Rom. XIV, 9. δ) cum mentio fit exaltationis, vt vulgo dicitur, Ps. CX, 1. Phil. II, 9. 11.


### Member I. Concerning the Names, Natures, and Person of Christ: III. Names of Office

III. Names of OFFICE.

These likewise are a) General, which contain in their scope the entire triple office which Christ performed, as are: 1) מָשִׁיחַ (Messiah), in Greek χρισός (Christ), John I, 42. מַלְאַךְ יְהוָה (Angel of the Lord), & מַלְאַךְ בְּרִית (Angel of the Covenant), to which that is akin, ἀπόστολος (Apostle), Hebr. III, 1. add. John X, 36. 3) שִׁילֹה (Shiloh), Gen. XLVIII, 16. Job XIX,

25. 4) Ἰησοῦς (Jesus), which name, by reason of usurpation indeed, denotes the subject, as in this statement, 1 John V, 1: ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἐστὶν ὁ Χριστός (that Jesus is the Christ), i.e. that Jesus of Nazareth, and no one else, is that true Christ; but by reason of signification it pertains to the office, and all its parts, since there is none of them which does not contribute to imparting salvation to us. 5) Σωτήρ (Savior), which is the same thing in reality as Ἰησοῦς, according to the heavenly messenger, Matt. I, 21. 6) Ποιμήν (Shepherd), This is apt for all three of Christ's offices: α) to the Sacerdotal, if indeed he himself suffered death for the sheep, to be bought back by his own blood, John X, 11. β) to the Prophetic, since the sheep hear his voice, ibid. v. 3, 5. and for that reason Christ is called ὁ ἀρχιποιμήν (the Chief Shepherd), 1 Petr. V, 4, for the pastors of the N. T. church are teachers, not presbyters, properly so called, and much less rulers, ibid. v. 3. γ) to the Regal, in so far as he himself defends his own sheep from all danger, and commands them to aspire to eternal salvation, John X, 28. add. Ps. LXXVIII, 72. 2) Special names, which are of the office a) Sacerdotal: 1) ἱερεύς (presbyter), Hebr. V, 6. VII, 17. 25. 2) ἀρχιερεύς (high presbyter), and indeed especially with a fourfold addition: α) μέγας (great), namely with respect to the supreme Pontiff of the O. T., who, although he was supreme and excelled the other presbyters in dignity, yet was far inferior to Christ. Hebr. IV, 14. β) κατὰ τὴν τάξιν τῷ Μελχισεδέκ (according to the order of Melchizedek), Hebr. V, 10. γ) ἐς τὸν αἰῶνα (forever), Hebr. VII, 21. add. 23. & 25. δ) ὃς ἐκάθισεν ἐν δεξιᾷ τῷ Θεῷ (who sat down at the right hand of God), Hebr. VIII. 1. 3) שָׁרָה צִדְקוּ (the Lord our righteousness), Jerem. XXXIII, 16. conf. with Rom. IV, 6. 2 Cor. V, 21. 4) ἱλασία (propitiation), likewise πάσχα (Passover), which pertains to the first part of the Sacerdotal office, 1 Cor. V, 7. 5) παράκλητος (Advocate), in so far as the second part is concerned, 1 Io. II, 2. b) Of the Prophetic office: 1) ὁ προφήτης (the Prophet), as also προφήτης μέγας (a great prophet), Luc. VII, 16. John VI, 14. 2) διδάσκαλος (Teacher), John III, 2. Mark XIV, 14. 3) ἐπίσκοπος (Overseer), 1 Petr. II, 25. c) Of the Regal office: מֶלֶךְ (King), or מֹושֵׁל (Ruler) & βασιλεύς (King), and indeed with a fourfold excellence: α) an eternal King, Mich. V, 1. β) a King of righteousness, & γ) a King of peace, Hebr. VII, 2. add. Ies. IX, 6. and the opinion pleases me of those who interpret the name שִׁילֹה (Shiloh), Gen. XLIX, 10. in such a way that he becomes the reconciler of peace, δ) King of Kings, Apoc. XVII, 14. XIX, 16.

In Greek he is called σωτήρ, which word is rendered by some authors in Latin as seruator (preserver); but less fully. For he who preserves is one who provides so that salvation is not lost; he who saves is one who gives salvation. GROTIUS explains it by sospitator (savior/deliverer), because Jesus is the author of all prosperity. The angel provides the reason for the denomination, Matt. 1:21: "He shall save his people from their sins." The angel expressed the term of salvation from which, which is sin, the origin of every evil. Therefore, Christ saves us from the wrath of God, from the accusation and curse of the law, from the judgment of condemnation, from temporal and eternal punishment. For all these things descend from sin, as from their head. The term to which is the grace of God, righteousness, life, and eternal salvation. Dan. 9:24. Obj. II. The name of Savior can also be attributed to God the Father and the Holy Spirit, if you look at the efficacy and the act of saving.

For God the Father saves us, insofar as He sends the Son and, on account of His merit, forgives sins, and eventually bestows salvation in reality: the Holy Spirit is said to save us by regenerating us, by kindling in us the saving faith by which the merit of Christ is applied to us. And in this way, the Son of God Himself is also said to save us; because salvation, as an act ad extra, is common to all three persons of the Godhead. But indeed, when Christ is called Savior, it is done in a peculiar way, namely by reason of merit, because Christ alone is the meritorious cause of our salvation. Whence the name Jesus does not in any way import a respect to the act of saving, but to the merit of Christ, through which we obtain salvation, and Christ is Savior insofar as He saves His people through His merit and satisfaction.

Obj. III. Jesus is not a typical, bodily, and imperfect savior, such as Joshua and Hosea were (to whom the name was related); but a proper, spiritual, and perfect one, because He saves from sin, the fountainhead of every evil. He saves by merit and efficacy; He saves inchoatively in this life, and consummatively in the life to come. Therefore, Jesus is the fountain of salvation, Isa. 12:3; the horn of salvation, Luke 1:69; the author of eternal salvation, Heb. 5:9, in whom alone our salvation is sought and found, Acts 4:12, since He alone is our Goël, or our redeemer by right of blood.

Obj. IV. Christ is the Savior of all men, by reason of merit and acquisition; because He merited salvation for all by His passion and death: but He is the Savior only of believers by reason of fruit and application; because they alone are made partakers of salvation through faith.

You say: Christ is called ישוע, saved, Zech. 9: 9. Therefore, He is not the author of salvation. Resp. Christ is called "Saved" not meritoriously, but efficiently, for the reason that by His own divine power He was delivered from the injuries with which He was afflicted, and the troubles with which He was pressed in His bloody passion.

Latin:

III. Nomina OFFICII.

Ea itidem sunt a) Generalia, quæ vniuersum, quo Christus functus est, munus triplex suo ambitu continent, vt sunt: 1) מָשִׁיחַ, græce χρισός, Ioann. I, 42. מַלְאַךְ יְהוָה, & מַלְאַךְ בְּרִית, cui finitimum est illud, ἀπόστολος, Hebr. III, 1. add. Io. X, 36. 3) שִׁילֹה, Gen. XLVIII, 16. Iob. XIX,

25. 4) Ἰησοῦς, quod nomen ratione usurpationis quidem subiectum denotat, vt in hoc enuntiato, 1 Io. V, 1: ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἐστὶν ὁ Χριστός, h. e. quod Iesus Nazarenus, & nemo alius, sit verus ille Christus; sed ratione significationis pertinet ad officium, eiusque partes vniuersas, vtpote quarum nulla est, quæ nihil conferat ad salutem nobis impertiendam. 5) Σωτήρ, id quod re ipsa idem est, ac Ἰησοῦς, interprete cœlesti nuntio, Matth. I, 21. 6) Ποιμήν, Hoc aptum est ad omnia tria Christi munera: α) ad Sacerdotale, si quidem mortem ipse oppetiit pro ouibus, suo sanguine coemendis, Io. X, 11. β) ad Prophetieum, quoniam vocem eius audiunt oues, ibid. v. 3. 5. ob eamque caussam Christus vocatur ὁ ἀρχιποιμήν, 1 Petr. V, 4, ecclesiæ enim N. T. pastores sunt doctores, non Sacerdotes, proprie ita dicti, multoque minus imperantes, ibid. v. 3. γ) ad Regium, quatenus suas ipse oues ab omni periculo defendit, atque ad æternam salutem adspirare iubet, Ioann. X, 28. add. Ps. LXXVIII, 72. 2) Specialia, quæ sunt officii a) Sacerdotalis, 1) ἱερεύς, Hebr. V, 6. VII, 17. 25. 2) ἀρχιερεύς, & quidem cum adiectione potissimum quadruplici: α) μέγας, nimirum intuitu summi Pontificis V. T. qui, tametsi summus esset, cæterisque Sacerdotibus dignitate antecelleret, Christo tamen longe erat inferior. Hebr. IV, 14. β) κατὰ τὴν τάξιν τῷ Μελχισεδέκ, Hebr. V, 10. γ) ἐς τὸν αἰῶνα, Hebr. VII, 21. add. 23. & 25. δ) ὃς ἐκάθισεν ἐν δεξιᾷ τῷ Θεῷ, Hebr. VIII. 1. 3) שָׁרָה צִדְקוּ, Ierem. XXXIII, 16. conf. cum Rom. IV, 6. 2 Cor. V, 21. 4) ἱλασία, itemque πάσχα, quod ad primam muneris Sacerdotalis partem attinet, 1 Cor. V, 7. 5) παράκλητος, quantum ad alteram, 1 Io. II, 2. b) Prophetici: 1) ὁ προφήτης, vt &, προφήτης μέγας, Luc. VII, 16. Io. VI, 14. 2) διδάσκαλος, Io. III, 2. Marc. XIV, 14. 3) ἐπίσκοπος, 1 Petr. II, 25. c) Regii: מֶלֶךְ, vel מֹושֵׁל & βασιλεύς, & quidem cum quadruplici excellentia: α) Rex æternus, Mich. V, 1. β) Rex iustitiæ, & γ) Rex pacis, Hebr. VII, 2. add. Ies. IX, 6. mihique placet eorum sententia, qui nomen שִׁילֹה, Gen. XLIX, 10. ita interpretantur, vt fit pacis reconciliator, δ) Rex Regum, Apoc. XVII, 14. XIX, 16.

Græcis dicitur σωτήρ, quæ vox a nonnullis auctoribus latine redditur seruator; at minus plene. Seruat enim, qui, ne salus amittatur, præstat; saluat, qui salutem dat. GROTIVS exponit per sospitatorem, propterea, quod Iesus omnis prosperitatis auctor est. Rationem denominationis reddit angelus, Matth. I, 21. Ille saluabit populum suum a peccatis eorum. Expreffit angelus terminum saluationis a quo, qui est peccatum, omnis mali origo. Saluat igitur Christus nos ab ira Dei, ab accusatione & maledictione legis, a iudicio condemnationis, a pœna temporali & æterna. Hæc quippe cuncta e peccato, velut capite, descendunt. Terminus ad quem est gratia Dei, iustitia, vita & salus æterna. Dan. IX, 24.

Obf. II. Nomen Saluatoris etiam Deo Patri & Spiritui S. tribui potest, si spectes efficaciam & actum saluandi. Deus enim Pater nos saluat, quatenus mittit Filium & propter meritum eius peccata remittit, atque salutem aliquando reapse largitur: Spiritus S. saluare nos dicitur per regenerationem, fidem saluificam, qua meritum Christi nobis applicatur, in nobis accendendo. Et hoc modo etiam ipse Filius Dei nos saluare dicitur; quia saluatio, vt actus ad extra, communis est omnibus tribus personis deitatis. At vero cum Christus dicitur Saluator, id fit peculiari modo, nimirum ratione meriti, quia solus Christus est salutis nostræ causa meritoria. Vnde nomen Iesus non quocunque modo respectum importat ad actum saluandi, sed ad meritum Christi, per quod salutem consequimur, & Christus est saluator, quatenus populum suum saluat per meritum & satisfactionem suam.

Obf. III. Iesus est saluator non typicus, corporalis & imperfectus, quales fuere Iosua & Hoseas (quibus cognatum fuit nomen); sed proprius, spiritualis & perfectus, quia saluat a peccato, omnis mali fcaturigine. Saluat merito & efficacia; saluat inchoatiue in hac vita, & consummatiue in vita futura. Est igitur Iesus fons salutis, Ef. XII, 3. cornu salutis, Luc. I, 69. auctor salutis æternæ, Hebr. V, 9. in quo solo nostra salus quæritur & inuenitur, Act. IV, 12. cum solus sit noster Goël, siue ex iure sanguinis noster redemtor.

Obf. IV. Christus est Saluator omnium hominum, ratione meriti & acquisitionis; propterea, quod omnibus sua passione & morte salutem promeruit: est autem duntaxat credentium Saluator ratione fructus & applicationis; quia illi soli per fidem participes salutis redduntur.

Dicis: Christus dicitur ישוע, saluatus, Zach. IX, 9. E. non est salutis auctor. Resp. Christus dicitur Saluatus non meritorie, sed efficienter, ideo, quod fuamet virtute diuina ab iniuriis, quibus afficiebatur, & molestiis, quibus in cruenta passione premebatur, liberatus est.


### Q. IV. How much should the name of Jesus be esteemed?

The name of Jesus should be most sweet to us a), most holy b), and most eminent c).

Prob. a. The name of Jesus is compared by the Holy Spirit to oil poured out, Cant. 1:3. Because it breathes forth wondrous sweetnesses.

Prob. b. The name of Jesus is most holy; because it was imposed by divine decree by the angel before conception, Luke 1:31; before birth, Matt. 1:21; before circumcision, Luke 2:2. Prob. c.

The name of Jesus is most eminent; since angels have adored this name, demons have trembled, and men take it up for salvation, as HILARY says in Ps. 51. Therefore, at the pronunciation of the name of Jesus, we bend our knees, mindful of the apostolic precept, Phil. 2:10: "At the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth." Furthermore, at the mention of the name of Jesus, we uncover our heads; which uncovering of the head is a ceremony freely assumed by the church, which genuine sons of the church ought to observe. It was placed in the Christian liberty of the church to show outward worship of adoration at the mention of one, or of many, of this or that, nay, of all divine names, they might exhibit.

But the name Jesus was chosen, either as an epitome of the revelations and benefits of the whole Most Holy Trinity, by the pronouncing and honoring of which, devotion is not directed precisely to Christ, but to... the universal fountain of our salvation; or as a character of profession, by which they might go separated both from the Jews, who confessed some Christ but were unwilling that Jesus of Nazareth should be the Christ, and from the Arians, who acknowledged the Father as God, but denied that Jesus was God. It may be objected: Whatever law prohibits the worship of images, that prohibits the worship of the name of Jesus.

But the divine law, etc., Exod. XX, 4. Therefore. The major is proved: because names are images of concepts, and concepts are images of things.

Resp. I deny the major, because the name of Jesus in this place is not considered as an object of determined worship, which is God alone; nor as an object of relative worship, in the manner in which the Papists worship images; but only as a memorial sign, by the pronouncing or hearing of which, we are carried into the acknowledgment and worship of the person himself.

Quest. V. Why is our Redeemer called Christ? Our Redeemer is called Christ, i.e., anointed; because he was anointed by the Holy Spirit as our King, Priest, and Prophet.

Prob. Χριστὸς is said from χρίω, to anoint, and thus denotes the anointed, and corresponds to the Hebrew name מָשִׁיחַ. We have found the Messiah, which is, if you interpret it, Christ, says Andrew, John I, 41. Now our Redeemer is called Christ, on account of the office which he performs, royal, sacerdotal, and prophetic.

Just as in the Old Testament, kings and priests, Exod. XXIX, 7; 1 Sam. XVI, 13, and Elisha among the prophets, 1 Kings XIX, 16, were sprinkled with sacred oil at the inauguration of their office: so our Redeemer was anointed with the Holy Spirit and power, Acts X, 38, that he might be our King, Priest, and Prophet.

Yet, that there is a huge difference between the anointing of the kings, priests, and prophets of the Old Testament and the anointing of our Savior, the royal prophet teaches, Ps. XLV, 8: God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows.
