The fellows, or partners of Christ, are said in a general sense to be all the faithful who are participants in both the spiritual anointing and the Christian name; in a special sense, his fellows are the priests, kings, and prophets, both on account of the typical prefiguration of the threefold office of Christ, and on account of the internal bestowal of gifts for their offices: Christ is far superior and more eminent than all these.

The kings, priests, and prophets of the Old Testament were anointed by men, as Saul and David by Samuel: but our Savior was anointed by God himself, Ps. XLV, 8. The kings, priests, and prophets were anointed with external oil: Christ with internal, namely the Holy Spirit. Whence Isa.

LXI, 1, the Messiah himself says: The Spirit is upon me, wherefore God hath anointed me. The kings, priests, and prophets were anointed at an adult age; Christ in the maternal womb. The anointing of the kings, priests, and prophets externally signified finite administrative gifts, which the Holy Spirit conferred internally: but Christ receives infinite and immense gifts immediately from God, since to him God gave not the Spirit by measure, John III, 34. The prerogative of the anointing of our Redeemer is excellently taught by AUGUSTINE, tract. in Io.

III, 24: Christ is singularly anointed, preeminently anointed, whence all Christians are anointed; for all the saints are his participants, but he is singularly the holy of holies, singularly Christ, singularly anointed.

Obf. When our Savior is called Christ, or anointed, the anointing agent is the Divinity, the anointed is the humanity, the oil is the Holy Spirit; whence the profession of Christ is a confession of the whole Trinity, as BASIL the Great says. The profession of Christ is a confession of the whole Trinity, as BASIL the Great says.

Latin:

Nomen Iesu sit nobis suauissimum a), sanctissimum b), & eminentissimum c).

Prob. a. Nomen Iesu a Spiritu S. comparatur oleo effuso, Cant. I, 3. Eo, quod mirificas aspirat suauitates.

Prob. b. Sanctissimum est nomen Iesu; quia decreto diuino ab angelo impositum est ante conceptionem, Luc. I, 31. ante partum, Matth. I, 21. ante circumcisionem, Luc. II, 21.

Prob. c. Eminentissimum est nomen Iesu; quoniam hoc nomen adorarunt angeli, tremuerunt dæmones, homines ad salutem assumunt, dicente HILARIO in Pf. LI. Idcirco pronuntiato nomine Iesu genua flectimus, memores præcepti apostolici, Phil. II, 10. In nomine Iesu omne genu se flectat, supracœlestium, terrestrium & subterraneorum. Quin etiam ad mentionem nominis Iesu capita nostra detegimus; quæ denudatio capitis est cærimonia, libere ab ecclesia assumta, quam obseruare decet genuinos ecclesiæ filios. In libertate christiana ecclesiæ positum fuit, vt extrinsecum adorationis cultum ad mentionem vnius, vel plurium, huius vel illius, immo omnium nominum diuinorum exhiberent.

Electum autem est nomen Iesu, vel vt epitome reuelationum & beneficiorum totius SS. Trinitatis, quo pronuntiato, & honorato non ad Christum præcise fertur deuotio, sed ad ...vniuersum salutis nostræ fontem; vel vt character professionis, quo se cum a Iudæis, qui Christum aliquem fatebantur, Iesum Nazarenum nolebant esse Christum, tum ab Arianis, qui Patrem Deum agnonerunt, Iesum Deum esse negarunt, seiunctum irent. Obiici potest: Quæcunque lex prohibet cultum imaginum, illa prohibet cultum nominis Iesu.

Atqui lex diuina &c. Exod. XX, 4. E. Maior probatur: quia nomina sunt imagines conceptuum, conceptus imagines rerum.

Resp. Neg. maior, quia nomen Iesu h. l. non consideratur, vt obiectum cultus determinati, quod est solus Deus; neque vt obiectum cultus respectiui, ad eum modum, quo Pontificii imagines colunt; sed tantum vt signum memoriale, quo pronuntiato, vel audito, ferimur in agnitionem & cultum ipsius personæ.

Quæst. V. Quare redemtor noster vocatur Christus? Redemtor noster vocatur Christus, h. e. vnctus; quia a Spiritu S. in regem, sacerdotem & prophetam nostrum vnctus est.

Prob. Χριστὸς dicitur a χρίω vngo, adeoque notat vnctum, & respondet nomini hebraico מָשִׁיחַ. Inuenimus Messiam, quod est, si interpreteris, Christus, inquit Andreas, Io. I, 41. Dicitur autem redemtor noster Christus, ob officium, quo fungitur, regium, sacerdotale & propheticum.

Quemadmodum in vet. testam. reges & sacerdotes, Exod. XXIX, 7. 1 Sam. XVI, 13. atque Elifæus inter prophetas, 1 Reg. XIX, 16. in inauguratione officii sacro perfusi sunt oleo: ita redemtor noster vnctus est Spiritu S. & virtute, Act. X, 38. vt esset rex, sacerdos & propheta noster.

Ingens tamen esse discrimen inter vnctionem regum, sacerdotum & prophetarum vet. testam. & inter vnctionem nostri Saluatoris, docet propheta regius, Ps. XLV, 8. Vnxit te, o Deus, Deus tuus oleo lætitiæ præ sociis tuis. Socii, vel consortes Christi, sensu generali dicti sunt omnes fideles tam vnctionis spiritualis, quam nominis Christiani participes; sensu speciali ipsius socii sunt sacerdotes, reges & prophetæ, tum propter typicam tergemini officii Christi præfigurationem, tum propter internam donorum ad officia collationem: his omnibus longissime superior & eminentior est Christus.

Reges, sacerdotes & prophetæ vet. testam. vngebantur per homines, vt Saul & Dauid per Samuelem: Saluator autem noster vnctus est ab ipso Deo, Ps. XLV, 8. Reges, sacerdotes & prophetæ vncti sunt oleo externo: Christus interno, scilicet Spiritu S. Vnde Es. LXI, 1. ipse Messias dicit: Spiritus est super me, quare vnxit me Deus. Reges, sacerdotes & prophetæ vncti sunt in ætate adulta; Christus in vtero materno.

Vnctio regum, sacerdotum & prophetarum externe significauit dona administrantia finita, quæ interne contulit Spiritus S.: at Christus immediate a Deo accipit dona infinita & immensa, quippe cui Deus non ex mensura dedit Spiritum, Io. III, 34. Prærogatiuam vnctionis nostri redemtoris præclare docet AVGVSTINVS tract. in Io.

III, 24. Christus singulariter vnctus est, præcipue vnctus, vnde omnes christiani vnguntur; participes enim eius omnes sancti, sed ille singulariter sanctus sanctorum, singulariter Christus, singulariter vnctus. Obs.

Quando Saluator noster dicitur Christus, vel vnctus, vngens est diuinitas, vncta humanitas, oleum Spiritus S.; vnde Christi professio totius trinitatis est confessio, dicente BASILIO M. Christi professio totius trinitatis est confessio, dicente BASILIO M.


### Q. X. By what arguments is the truth of Christ’s human nature demonstrated?

Question VI. In what respect is the person of our redeemer considered here? The person of our redeemer is considered here not as ἄσαρκος [without flesh], or as he was from eternity before the incarnation; but as ἔνσαρκος [in the flesh], or as he began to be in the fullness of time, through the assumption of our human nature into his own divine hypostasis.

Proof. We have recognized the person of the Son of God as ἄσαρκος, or as he was from eternity before flesh was assumed, above in Part I of theology, p. 305 et seqq.: but here, where we are occupied with the economy of divine grace, the person of our redeemer must be considered as he is ἔνσαρκος, or insofar as God is manifested in the flesh, 1 Tim. III, 16. For this reason, that Christ is our redeemer according to both natures, divine and human: for God acquired the church through his own blood, Acts XX, 28.

Question VII. What and how many are the natures of our redeemer? There are two, divine and human. He has the divine communicated from the Father by eternal generation, according to which he is true God: he assumed the human in time, produced from the blood of the Virgin Mary, through the miraculous ἐπέλευσιν [overshadowing], or operation, of the Holy Spirit, according to which he is true man (*).

Proof. Because Christ is man from the fathers indeed according to the flesh, but at the same time God blessed over all forever, Rom. IX, 5. He is God manifested in the flesh, 1 Tim. III, 16. He is that man who is the Lord God, 2 Sam. VII, 19. Therefore the same one, who is made from the seed of David, is said to be the Son of God, Rom. I, 3. That same one, who is born of Mary, is said to be the Son of the Most High, Luke [I], 35. The same one, who is the Word of God, and God, is said to have been made flesh, John I, 14. Consequently, Christ is a σύνθετος [composite], or compound person, in whom the divine nature is joined with the human.

Question VIII. In how many ways are the two natures in the one person of Christ considered? The two natures of Christ are considered 1) absolutely and in themselves, 2) relatively and in union.

Question IX. By what arguments is the true and eternal divinity of our redeemer proved? The true and eternal divinity of our redeemer is proved by most solid arguments taken from divine names, from attributes proper to the true God alone, from personal and essential acts of God, from religious worship owed to God alone, and from an accurate collation of the sayings of the Old and New Testament Scripture.

Observation. We examined the arguments by which the divinity of Christ is proved in Part I of theology, from p. 305 et seqq.

Question X. By what arguments is the truth of Christ's human nature demonstrated? That Christ is true man is demonstrated a) from human names, b) from the essential parts of man, c) from attributes proper to a true man, d) from human operations, e) from the genealogy of Christ the man.

Prob. a. Christ calls himself a man; You seek to kill me, a man, who have told you the truth, John 8:40. There is one mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus, says Paul, 1 Tim. 2:5. Christ is called the son of man eighty-two times in the sacred code. Prob. b. A true man consists of an organic body and an intelligent soul. But Christ consists of a body, John 2:21, flesh, blood, and bones, Heb. 2:14, Luke 24:39. He has a soul, which he laid down for whom he chose, John 10:15, and which was sorrowful even unto death, Matt. 26:38. He has an intelligent soul, according to which he increased in wisdom, Luke 2:52, and endowed with a will, John 5:21, Matt. 26:39.

Prob. c. He who hungers, thirsts, sleeps, is sorrowful, weeps, is troubled, he is a true man. But Christ hungered, Matt. 4:2, thirsted, John 19:28, slept, Matt. 8:24, was sorrowful, Matt. 25:37, wept, Luke 19:41, was troubled, John 11:33. Therefore Christ is a true man. You should observe that the affections already mentioned were pure and refined in Christ. For just as clear water is moved in a crystal glass, and yet is not dirtied; so the affections of Christ were moved without the stain of sin.

Prob. d. A true man speaks and asks, disputes from Holy Scripture, teaches, etc. But Christ spoke and asked, Luke 2:46, 48, disputed with Satan from Holy Scripture, Matt. 4:1 ff., taught in the temple, Matt. 26:55.

Prob. e. The genealogy of Christ, regarding the ascending line, Luke 3:23, and regarding the descending line, Matt. 1:1, clearly shows that Christ is a true man.

Latin:

Quæst. VI. Quo respectu persona redemtoris nostri hic consideratur? Persona redemtoris nostri hic consideratur non vt ἄσαρκος, siue qualis ante incarnationem ab æterno fuit; sed qua ἔνσαρκος, siue qualis esse cœpit in plenitudine temporis, per assumtionem naturæ nostræ humanæ in hypostasin suam diuinam.

Prob. Personam Filii Dei ἄσαρκον, siue qualis ante assumtam carnem ab æterno fuit, supra part. I. theol. p. 305. seqq. cognouimus: hic vero, vbi in œconomia gratiæ diuinæ versamur; consideranda est persona redemtoris nostri, prout est ἔνσαρκος, siue quatenus Deus in carne est manifestatus, 1 Tim. III, 16. propterea, quod Christus redemtor noster est secundum vtramque naturam, diuinam & humanam: Deus enim ecclesiam acquisiuit per proprium sanguinem, Act. XX, 28.

Quæst. VII. Quæ & quot sunt redemtoris nostri naturæ? Sunt duæ, diuina & humana. Diuinam æterna generatione a Patre communicatam habet, secundum quam est verus Deus: humanam ex sanguine Mariæ virginis, per miraculosam Spiritus S. ἐπέλευσιν, seu operationem, productam, in tempore assumsit, secundum quam est verus homo (*).

Prob. Quia Christus est homo ex patribus quidem secundum carnem, sed simul Deus super omnia benedictus in sæcula, Rom. IX, 5. Est Deus in carne manifestatus, 1 Tim. III, 16. Est homo ille, qui Dominus Deus est, 2 Sam. VII, 19. Idcirco idem, qui est factus e semine Dauidis, dicitur esse Filius Dei, Rom. I, 3. Idem ille, qui ex Maria nascitur, dicitur esse Filius altissimi, Luc. XXXV. Idem, qui est Verbum Dei, & Deus, dicitur caro factus esse, Io. I, 14. Proinde Christus est persona σύνθετος, siue composita, in qua natura diuina cum humana est coniuncta.

Quæst. VIII. Quot modis considerantur duæ naturæ in vna persona Christi? Considerantur duæ Christi naturæ 1) absolute & in se, 2) relate & in vnione.

Quæst. IX. Quibus argumentis vera & æterna diuinitas redemtoris nostri probatur? Vera & æterna diuinitas redemtoris nostri probatur argumentis solidissimis sumtis a nominibus diuinis, ab attributis soli vero Deo propriis, ab actibus Dei personalibus & essentialibus, a cultu religioso soli Deo debito, ab accurata collatione dictorum scripturæ V. & N. T.

Obs. Argumenta, quibus diuinitas Christi probatur, expendimus P. I. theolog. a p. 305. seqq.

Quæst. X. Quibus argumentis veritas humanæ Christi naturæ demonstratur? Christum esse verum hominem, demonstratur a) ex nominibus humanis, b) ex partibus hominis essentialibus, c) ex attributis vero homini propriis, d) ex operationibus humanis, e) e genealogia Christi hominis.

Prob. a. Christus seipsum hominem appellat; Quæritis me interficere, hominem, qui vobis veritatem dixi, Io. VIII, 40. Vnus est mediator Dei & hominum, homo Iesus Christus, inquit Paullus, 1 Tim. II, 5. Christus filius hominis octogies bis in sacro codice vocatur. Prob. b. Verus homo constat e corpore organico & anima intelligente. At Christus constat e corpore, Io. II, 21. carne, sanguine & ossibus, Hebr. II, 14. Luc. XXIV, 39. Habet animam, quam pro quibus posuit, Io. X, 15. quæque tristis fuit vsque ad mortem, Matth. XXVI, 38. Habet animam intelligentem, secundum quam profecit sapientia, Luc. II, 52. & voluntate præditam, Io. V, 21. Matth. XXVI, 39.

Prob. c. Qui esurit, sitit, dormit, tristatur, lacrymatur, turbatur, ille est verus homo. At Christus esuriuit, Matth. IV, 2. sitiuit, Io. XIX, 28. dormiuit, Matth. VIII, 24. tristatus est, Matth. XXV, 37. lacrymauit, Luc. XIX, 41. turbatus est, Io. XI, 33. Ergo Christus est verus homo. Obserues, quod affectus iam memorati in Christo fuerint puri & defecati. Vt enim aqua limpida in crystallino vitro commouetur, nec tamen fordidatur; ita affectus Christi commoti sunt sine labe peccaminosa.

Prob. d. Verus homo loquitur & interrogat, disputat e S. scriptura, docet &c. Atqui Christus locutus est & interrogauit, Luc. II, 46. 48. disputauit cum Satana e S. scriptura, Matth. IV, 1. sqq. docuit in templo, Matth. XXVI, 55.

Prob. e. Genealogia Christi, quoad lineam ascendentem, Luc. III, 23. & quoad lineam descendentem Matth. I, 1. luculenter ostendit, Christum esse verum hominem. Quæst.


### Q. XI. Did Christ also assume human infirmities?

Christ assumed natural infirmities, common to all men constituted in a natural state a): but not personal ones, arising from particular causes, much less did he take on morally vicious defects b).

Prob. a. Natural infirmities of men are common, which are in all men after the fall, e.g., to hunger, to thirst, to be fatigued, to be cold, to be hot, to suffer pain, to be indignant, to be troubled, to weep; which, since they are blameless, Christ, as Holy Scripture testifies, assumed, not by compulsion, but freely, not for his own sake, but for our sake, not forever, but for a time, namely in the state of emptying, but he did not retain the same in the state of exaltation.

Prob. b. Personal infirmities are those which proceed from particular causes, and either from a defect of the δυνάμεως πλασικῆς, or formative power in the begetter, such as phthisis, arthritis, etc., or from a particular fault, namely from excessive gluttony, lust, or other excesses, such as fever, gout, dropsy, etc., or from a peculiar nemesis or divine judgment, such as the diseases of the family of Joab, 2 Sam. 3:20, etc., draw their origin. These are very far removed from the most holy humanity of Christ, since it was neither expedient for the human race that they be assumed, and it would have detracted from the dignity of his nature, as LOMBARD judges, lib. 3 sent. dist. 10. Moreover, Christ as man could not be convicted of morally vicious infirmities even by his enemies, John 8:46.

Latin:

Christus assumsit infirmitates naturales, omnibus hominibus in statu naturali constitutis communes a): non autem personales, e causis particularibus prouenientes, multo minus moraliter vitiosos defectus adsciuit b).

Prob. a. Infirmitates hominum naturales communes sunt, quæ omnibus hominibus post lapsum insunt, v. gr. esurire, sitire, defatigari, algere, æstuare, dolere, indignari, turbari, lacrymari; quas, cum sint inculpabiles, Christus, teste S. scriptura, assumsit, non coacte, sed libere, non propter se, sed propter nos, non in perpetuum, sed ad tempus, scilicet in statu exanitionis, non autem retinuit easdem in statu exaltationis.

Prob. b. Infirmitates personales sunt, quæ a causis particularibus proficiscuntur, & vel a vitio δυνάμεως πλασικῆς, siue virtutis efformatiuæ in generante, vt phthisis; arthritis &c. vel a culpa particulari, nimirum ab ingurgitatione nimia, venere, aut aliis excessibus, vt febris, podagra, hydrops, &c. vel a peculiari nemesi aut iudicio diuino, vt morbi familiæ Ioabi, 2 Sam. III, 20, &c. ortum trahunt. Hæc a sanctissima Christi humanitate longissime absunt, quippe quas assumi, nec generi humano expediebat, & dignitati naturæ derogasset, censente LOMBARDO libr. III. sentent. dist. X. Ceterum infirmitatum moraliter vitiosarum Christus homo ne ab hostibus quidem conuinci poterat, Io. VIII, 46. Quæst.


### Q. XII. By what individual properties, as if by certain prerogatives, does the human nature of Christ excel?

Certain individual properties belong to the human nature of Christ: by which it excels other men as if by certain ὑπεροχαῖς or prerogatives: such prerogatives are a) ἀνυποστασία, the lack of proper subsistence, compensated by the divine hypostasis of the Son of God, as being far more eminent; b) ἀναμαρτησία, by which Christ is devoid of all personal sin, both original and actual; c) the singular excellence of soul and body.

Prob. a. If the human nature of Christ had retained its own subsistence, there would be two persons in Christ, and thus two mediators, contrary to 1 Tim. 2:5. The reason is: because a person is formally constituted in its being by a subsistence, which is ultimately complete, and thus the unity of the person is to be estimated from the unity of the subsistence. It is necessary, therefore, that one or the other of the natures which coalesce into one person should lack its own proper subsistence; and since the divine nature, which is really the same as its own subsistence, cannot lack the same, it is evident that the lack of a proper subsistence must be attributed to the human nature.

Dicis: I. Every substance subsists by itself: The human nature of Christ is a substance: Therefore. Resp. Subsistence is taken either generally, and is explained by independence from a subject of inhesion; or specially, and is expounded by the notion of subsisting incommunicably, or being ultimately complete. In the former sense, subsistence denotes the formal notion of substance; in the latter sense, it denotes suppositality.

Dicis: II. If the human nature of Christ lacks its own proper subsistence, the same will be more imperfect than our nature, which is ἀνυπόστατος (anupostatos), or subsisting by itself: Resp. The perfection of a thing is to be estimated from its essence, not from its subsistence. Add that the lack of proper personality in the human nature of Christ is supplied by the subsistence of the Word (τοῦ λόγου). The human nature of Christ is therefore ἀνυπόστατος (anupostatos), if it is considered precisely and in itself, in that it does not actually have its own proper subsistence: but when the same is considered in union with the divine nature, it is rightly called ἐνυπόστατος (enupostatos), that is to say, subsisting in the Word (ἐν τῷ λόγῳ).

Prob. b. Christ was never defiled by any sin, neither original nor actual. For He knew no sin, 2 Cor. 5:21. He is ἄκακος (akakos), ἀμίαντος (amiantos), κεχωρισμένος ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν (kechorismenos apo ton hamartolon), innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, Heb. 7:26. Dicis: Christ was made sin, 2 Cor. 5:21. Therefore He is not devoid of all sin. Resp. Christ was made sin, not as if sin properly inhered in Him, but because whatever sin there is, it was imputed to Him in the divine judgment by reason of guilt equally as of punishment. For all sin was cast upon Him.

Es. LIII, 6. Prob. c. It was fitting for Christ ἐν πᾶσι πρωτεύειν, to hold the first place in all things. Col. I, 18. The soul of Christ holds the first place in wisdom, by which it so shines forth that in the twelfth year of His age He taught in the midst of the temple and the assembly of the chief doctors of the church, Luke II, 46, and no man ever spoke as this greatest prophet, Io. VII, 46. The soul of Christ holds the first place in holiness; for it deemed the vanities of the world as nothing, rejected the allurements of the flesh, abstained from laughter, cultivated gravity, endured immense tortures for the fallen human race, and conquered the most bitter death.

The body of Christ holds the first place in beauty; since He is called the most beautiful among the sons of men, Ps. 45:3. The beauty of the body of Christ is conjectured from the excellence of the indwelling soul, which undoubtedly fashioned for itself a most elegant dwelling, and from the immediate operation of the Holy Spirit, by whose overshadowing (ἐπελεύσεως) the most splendid temple of the body of Christ was constructed. Those things which God does by Himself are certainly more perfect than those He does using secondary causes as ministers.

To this is added that the body of Christ is distinguished by ἀθανασίᾳ (athanasia), or immortality, which belongs to Him both because of the integrity of His impeccable nature, Rom. 6:23, and because of the indissoluble bond of personal union.

Dicis: How could the immortal die? Resp. Christ is immortal by reason of an intrinsic principle, but that He died, this is from an extrinsic principle, and according to the voluntary economy (οἰκονομίαν), John 10:17-

18. Nevertheless, the body of Christ remained in the death freely accepted ἄφθαρτον (aphtharton), or immune from corruption. Ps. 16:10; Acts 2:31.

XIII. Is the flesh of Christ ὁμοούσιος, or consubstantial, to us? The flesh of Christ has the same essence in species as we do, and therefore it is ὁμοούσιος, or consubstantial, to us.

Proof. 1) From Heb. II, 14. Since the children have become partakers of flesh and blood, he himself likewise took part in the same.

Observe here: a) that Christ calls us his brothers, v. 11, his children and little ones, v. 9, 12: b) that Christ is our brother not only because of brotherly affection, but also because of the communion of the same flesh and blood: which the Apostle teaches in v. 14. From which we argue: Whoever is our brother because of the communion of the same flesh and blood, he is ὁμοούσιος or consubstantial to us: But Christ is, etc.

Therefore.

2) From the testimony of the Council of Chalcedon: We confess true God and true man, the same from a rational soul and body: coessential with the Father according to his divinity, and coessential with us according to his humanity, in all things like us, sin excepted.

The antithesis is both that of the ancient heretics, the Marcionites, Cerdonians, and Manichaeans, who denied the truth of Christ's human nature; and that of the Anabaptists, Socinians, Schwenckfeldians, and Weigelians, [*] who impugn the ὁμοούσιος nature of Christ's flesh with the following arguments:

I. Whoever is sent in the likeness of human flesh, his flesh is not consubstantial with our flesh (likeness is an index of quality, not of substance): But Christ is, etc. Rom. VIII, 3. Resp.

Christ is not simply said to be sent in the likeness of flesh; but only in the likeness of sinful flesh: and thus the truth of the human nature of Christ being consubstantial with us is not denied, but the filth of sin is removed from Christ.

II. Christ was found ἐν σχήματι (in fashion), as a man, Phil. II, 8. Therefore he is not a true man. The reason for the consequence is; because σχῆμα denotes an external figure, or phantom, and is opposed to substance.

Resp. σχῆμα in the cited place does not designate an empty figure or phantom, but external gestures and habits, from which the true humanity of Christ became known.

III. Whoever is opposed to the first man formed from the earth, as the Lord from heaven, his body is not earthly, but heavenly and sidereal, and therefore not consubstantial with us: But Christ is, etc. 1 Cor. XV, 47. Therefore.

Resp.

The second man is called the Lord from heaven, not because he is not a true man, but because he is not a mere man, because he is at the same time true and eternal God, who is said to have come from the highest, John

I, 14. because his origin is supernatural (**). IV. Whoever descends from heaven, he brought a body from heaven: for such as the descent is, such is the origin. But Christ &c. John III, 13. Therefore. Resp. The Son of God descended from heaven, not by bringing a body from heaven, but by assuming flesh in the womb of the virgin, and by manifesting himself to men in the assumed flesh.

V. Christ denies that Mary is his mother. Matt. XII, 48. Therefore he did not assume from her a nature consubstantial to us. Resp. Christ, in the cited place, inquired about his mother, not by denying the origin of his human nature from his mother, but by comparing paternal ministries with maternal affections, and preferring the former to the latter. And therefore Christ did not suffer himself, upon the arrival of his mother, to be drawn back or called away from the administration of the office committed to him by the Father. Add that the Savior indicated that the bonds of minds are more religious than those of bodies, as AMBROSE teaches and CALOVIUS cites in bibl. illustrat. on this passage, fol. 295.

VI. If the flesh of Christ is consubstantial to us, Christ according to his human nature will be a creature; a way of speaking from which the ancients recoiled. It is answered: The Arians contended that the λόγος in himself, even without the human nature assumed, was a creature made from nothing. Therefore the ancients, because of the snares of the Arians, rejected this proposition: Christ is a creature. But because of Schwenckfeld, who denied that Christ according to his human nature is a creature, in the Smalcald assembly of 1537 this phrase concerning Christ according to his human nature was used. We disapprove, they say, of the delirium of Schwenckfeld, and we say that the human nature in Christ both is and remains a creature, as John says: The Word was made flesh. Compare D. GERHARD, exeg. locus IV, p. 428.

VII. Whoever is not conceived from male seed, but by the ἐπελεύσει, or the coming upon of the Holy Spirit, his flesh is not consubstantial to us: But Christ &c. Luke I, 35. Therefore. Resp. I deny the major. For the origin of the flesh of Christ is indeed dissimilar, but the nature is similar. If you seek the truth of the human nature, recognize the matter. If you examine the reason of the origin, confess the divine power; says LEO, sermon II on the nativity.

VIII. The human nature of Christ is destitute of its own subsistence: Therefore it is not consubstantial to us. Resp. Subsistence does not pertain to the essence of man, for the reason that it does not make man, but terminates him.

IX. Christ does not have the same essence in number as we do: Therefore he is not ὁμοούσιος to us. The consequence is proved from the fact that the λόγος is called ὁμοούσιος to God the Father, because he has the same essence in number with God the Father. Resp. Ὁμοουσία is twofold: specific and numerical. Christ as man is ὁμοούσιος to us, not according to number, but according to species; because he is of the same genus and species as our nature.

Latin:

Competunt humanæ Christi naturæ quædam proprietates indiuiduales: quibus eadem velut ὑπεροχαῖς siue prærogatiuis nonnullis ceteros homines antecellit: cuiusmodi prærogatiuæ sunt a) ἀνυποστασία, carentia propriæ subsistentiæ, diuina filii Dei hypostasi, tanquam longe eminentiori, compensata; b) ἀναμαρτησία, qua Christus omnis peccati proprii tam originalis, quam actualis expers est; c) singularis animæ & corporis excellentia.

Prob. a. Si humana Christi natura propriam retinuisset subsistentiam, duae in Christo forent personae, adeoque duo mediatores, contra 1 Tim. II, 5. Ratio est: quia persona per subsistentiam, ultimo completam, in esse suo formaliter constituitur, adeoque ex vnitate subsistentiae vnitas personae aestimanda est. Oportet igitur naturam alterutram ex his, quae in vnam personam coalescunt, carere propria sua subsistentia; cumque diuina natura, quae cum subsistentia sua realiter eadem est, carere eadem non possit; patet humanae naturae tribuendam esse carentiam propriae subsistentiae.

Dicis: I. Omnis substantia per se subsistit: Humana Christi natura est substantia: Ergo. Resp. Subsistentia sumitur vel generaliter, & explicatur per independentiam a subiecto inhaesionis; vel specialiter, & exponitur per rationem subsistendi incommunicabilem, seu ultimo completam. Priori sensu subsistentia formalem substantiae rationem, posteriori sensu suppositalitatem notat.

Dicis: II. Si humana Christi natura caret subsistentia propria, eadem imperfectior erit natura nostra ἀνυπόστατος, siue per se subsistente: Resp. Perfectio rei ex essentia, non ex subsistentia aestimanda est. Adiice, quod personalitatis propriae carentia in humana Christi natura suppleta fit subsistentia τοῦ λόγου. Est igitur humana Christi natura ἀνυπόστατος, si consideretur praecise & secundum se, eo, quod propriam subsistentiam actu non habet: at quando eadem consideratur in vnione cum natura diuina, eadem recte dicitur ἐνυπόστατος, h. e. subsistens ἐν τῷ λόγῳ. Prob. b.

Christus nullo peccato neque originali, neque actuali vnquam foedatus fuit. Neque enim nouit peccatum, 2 Cor. V, 21. Est ἄκακος, ἀμίαντος, κεχωρισμένος ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν, innocens, impollutus, a peccatoribus segregatus, Hebr. VII, 26. Dicis: Christus factus est peccatum, 2 Cor. V, 21. E. non est omnis peccati expers. Resp. Christus factus est peccatum, non quasi peccatum proprium ipsi inhaereret, sed quia, quidquid peccati est, ipsi imputatum est in iudicio diuino ratione culpae pariter, ac poenae. Omne quippe peccatum in ipsum coniectum est.

Es. LIII, 6. Prob. c. Decuit Christum ἐν πᾶσι πρωτεύειν, in omnibus primas tenere. Col. I, 18. Anima Christi primas tenet sapientiae, qua sic resplendescit, vt duodecimo aetatis anno in medio templo atque concessu praecipuorum ecclesiae doctorum doceret, Luc. II, 46. & nullus vnquam homo ita loqueretur, vt hic propheta maximus, Io. VII, 46. Primas tenet anima Christi sanctitatis; quippe quae vanitates mundi flocci fecit, illecebras carnis reiecit, a risu abstinuit, grauitatem coluit, immanes pro lapso genere humano cruciatus sustinuit, mortem acerbissimam vicit.

Corpus Christi primas tenet pulcritudinis; siquidem pulcerrimus inter filios hominum audit, Ps. XLV, 3. Coniicitur pulcritudo corporis Christi ex animae inhabitantis excellentia, quae haud dubie elegantissimum sibi domicilium fabricauit, atque ex operatione immediata Spiritus S., cuius ἐπελεύσεως templum corporis Christi splendidissimum exstructum est. Perfectiora vtique sunt, quae Deus facit per se, quam cum causis secundis administris vtitur. Asserimus autem pulcritudinem corporis Christi non foemineam, sed virilem, h. e. quae grauem, honestuinque decet virum.

Huc accedit, quod Christi corpus emineat ἀθανασίᾳ, siue immortalitate, quae ipsi competit tum ob integritatem naturae impeccabilis, Rom. VI, 23., tum ob vinculum vnionis personalis indissolubile.

Dicis: Quomodo immortalis potuit mori? Resp. Christus ratione principii intrinseci est immortalis, quod autem mortuus est, hoc est a principio extrinseco, & secundum voluntariam οἰκονομίαν Io. X, 17.

18. Mansit tamen corpus Christi in morte libere suscepta ἄφθαρτον, siue immune a corruptione. Ps. XVI, 10. Act. II, 31.

XIII. Estne caro Christi nobis ὁμοούσιος, sive consubstantialis? Caro Christi essentiam specie eandem nobiscum habet, adeoque nobis ὁμοούσιος, seu consubstantialis est.

Prob. 1) Ex Hebr. II, 14. Quoniam pueri participes facti sunt carnis & sanguinis, & ipse similiter participem se fecit ipsorum.

Observes hic: a) quod Christus nos vocet fratres suos, v. 11. filios & pueros suos, v. 9. 12: b) quod Christus frater noster sit non tantum ob affectum fraternum, sed etiam ob eiusdem carnis & sanguinis communionem: id quod docet Apostolus v. 14. E quibus argumentamur: Quicunque est frater noster ob eiusdem carnis & sanguinis communionem, ille est nobis ὁμοούσιος sive consubstantialis: Atqui Christus &c.

Ergo.

2) E testimonio concilii Chalcedonensis: Confitemur verum Deum & verum hominem, eundem ex rationali anima & corpore: coëssentialem Patri secundum diuinitatem, & coëssentialem nobis secundum humanitatem, per omnia nobis similem, demto peccato.

Antithesis est tum veterum hæreticorum, Marcionitarum, Cerdonianorum & Manichæorum, qui veritatem humanæ Christi naturæ negarunt; tum Anabaptistarum, Socinianorum, Schwenckfeldianorum & Weigelianorum, [*] qui ὁμοούσιαν carnis Christi impugnant sequentibus argumentis:

I. Quicunque in similitudine carnis humanæ missus est, illius caro nostræ carni non est consubstantialis (similitudo est index qualitatis, non substantiæ): Atqui Christus &c. Rom. VIII, 3. Resp.

Christus non simpliciter dicitur missus in similitudine carnis; sed duntaxat in similitudine carnis peccatricis: atque adeo non negatur humanæ Christi naturæ nobis consubstantialis veritas, sed remouetur a Christo peccati fœditas.

II. Christus inuentus est ἐν σχήματι, vt homo, Phil. II, 8. E. non est verus homo. Ratio consequentiæ est; quia σχῆμα notat externam figuram, aut phantasma, & opponitur substantiæ.

Resp. σχῆμα l. c. non designat inanem figuram aut phantasma, sed gestus habitusque externos, e quibus vera Christi humanitas innotuit.

III. Quicunque primo homini de terra formato opponitur, vt dominus de cœlo, illius corpus non est terrestre, sed cœleste & sidereum, adeoque nobis non consubstantiale: Atqui Christus &c. 1 Cor. XV, 47. Ergo.

Resp.

Secundus homo dicitur dominus de cœlo, non, quod non sit verus homo, sed, quod non sit merus homo, quia simul verus & æternus Deus est, qui e supremis venisse dicitur, Io.

I, 14. quia ipsius origo est supernaturalis (**). IV. Quicunque descendit de cœlo, ille ex cœlo corpus attulit: nam qualis descensus, talis origo. Atqui Christus &c. Io. III, 13. Ergo. Resp. Filius Dei de cœlo descendit, non corpus e cœlo afferendo, sed carnem in vtero virginis assumendo, & in assumta carne se hominibus manifestando.

V. Christus negat, Mariam esse suam matrem. Matth. XII, 48. Ergo ex illa naturam nobis consubstantialem non assumsit. Resp. Christus l. c. quæsiuit de matre sua, non originem humanæ naturæ ex matre negando, sed ministeria paterna cum affectibus maternis comparando, & illa his præferendo. Ideoque non passus est Christus, aduentu matris se ab administratione officii, a Patre commissi, retrahi, aut auocari. Adjice, quod Saluator indigitatum iuerit, religiosiores esse copulas mentium, quam corporum, docente AMBROSIO' & citante CALOVIO in bibl. illustrat. in h. l. fol. 295.

VI. Si caro Christi nobis est consubstantialis, Christus secundum humanam naturam erit creatura; a qua loquendi ratione veteres abhorruerunt. Respondetur: Ariani contendebant, λόγον secundum se, etiam non assumta natura humana, esse creaturam factam ex nihilo. Ideo veteres, propter Arianorum insidias, reiecerunt hanc propositionem: Christus est creatura. Sed propter Schwenckfeldium, qui negauit, Christum quoad humanam naturam esse creaturam, in conuentu Smalcaldico 1537. hæc phrasis de Christo secundum humanam naturam fuit vsurpata. Improbanus, inquiunt, Schwenckfeldii delirium, & dicimus, humanam naturam in Christo & esse & manere creaturam, vt Ioannes inquit: Verbum caro factum est. Confer. D GERHARDI exeg. loco IV. p. 428.

VII. Quicunque non conceptus est e semine virili, sed ἐπελεύσει, seu superuentu Spiritus S., illius caro nobis non est consubstantialis: Atqui Christus &c. Luc. I, 35. Ergo. Resp. Neg. maior. Nam origo carnis Christi est quidem dissimilis, sed natura consimilis. Si veritatem quæris humanæ naturæ, cognosce materiam. Si rationem scrutaris originis, virtutem confitere diuinam; inquit LEO sermon. II. de natiuit.

VIII. Humana Christi natura destituitur propria subsistentia: Ergo non est nobis consubstantialis. Resp. Subsistentia non pertinet ad essentiam hominis, propterea, quod hominem non facit, sed terminat.

IX. Christus non eandem numero essentiam nobiscum habet: E. non est nobis ὁμοούσιος. Consequentia probatur ex eo, quod ὁ λόγος Deo Patri dicitur ὁμοούσιος, ideo quod eandem numero essentiam cum Deo Patre habet. Resp. Ὁμοουσία est duplex: specifica, & numerica. Christus homo est nobis ὁμοούσιος, non secundum numerum, sed secundum speciem; quia eiusdem generis ac speciei est cum natura nostra.


### Quæst. XIV. From whom does the human nature of Christ have its origin?

The human nature of Christ has its origin from the triune God a), from God the Father b), from the Son of God c), from the Holy Spirit, to whom the production of the flesh of Christ is appropriated in the sacred scriptures d).

Prob. a. The production of the flesh of Christ, and its application to the hypostasis of the Son of God, is a work ad extra and undivided, or common to the three divine persons. The ancients declared this mystery by a simile taken from three virgins, one of whom is clothed or crowned, but each one contributes something to the ornament.

Prob. b. God the Father in the fullness of time sent the Son born of a woman, Gal. IV, 4. He sent him in the likeness of sinful flesh, and to pay for sin, Rom. VIII, 3.

Prob. c. The Son of God, the hypostatic power of the Most High, overshadowed the virgin Mary: whence also, that which is born of her, being holy, is called the Son of God, Luke I, 35. Obf. a) The power of the Most High here is not the Holy Spirit, since it is distinguished from Him, who was mentioned previously. To the Holy Spirit is attributed ἐπέλευσις, the coming upon; to the power of the Most High, ἐπισκιασμὸς, the overshadowing. Who would believe that the angel was ταυτόλογον (tautological), and in a vigorous description of a most sublime mystery said the same, or nearly the same, twice? Nor is the essential omnipotence of God understood by the power of the Most High, for the reason that the overshadowing of the virgin Mary is attributed to the power (namely, of God the Father) as a personal action. Since, therefore, actions belong to supposita, we judge that by the power of the Most High is indicated the hypostatic power, or the Son of God, who comes under this name in 1 Cor. I, 24. Just as also among humans the son is called the power of the father, Gen. XLIX, 3. Ἐπισκιασμὸς, or overshadowing, denotes the mysterious and admirable filling of the temple of the body, constructed by the Holy Spirit. Namely, the Son of God overshadowed the virgin Mary, while in an unsearchable manner He descended into the womb of the virgin, and filled the virginal mass of blood, excited by the Holy Spirit, with a peculiar approximation, and united it to Himself, so that He might dwell in her σωματικῶς, corporally, as in His own temple, Col. II, 9. Of which there was once some figure in the tabernacle of the covenant, as also in the temple of Solomon, which, when both were constructed, the divine majesty filled with an ἐπισκιασμῷ, or overshadowing intervening, Exod. XL, 35; 1 Kings VIII, 10, where likewise the word ἐπισκιάζειν is used by the LXX interpreters.

Obser. b) The consequence of this overshadowing is the birth of the Son of God, now made the son of man from Mary, which is expressed by the words of the angel: Διὸ καὶ τὸ γεννώμενον ἐκ σοῦ ἅγιον, κληθήσεται υἱὸς Θεοῦ. Therefore also, that which is born of you, being holy, shall be called the Son of God. From which words we gather anew that by the power of the Most High here, not the Holy Spirit, but the Son of God is to be understood. For the proximate cause why the son of Mary is the Son of God is not the singular conception by the Holy Spirit (which, if the angel had intended to indicate, he would have said: therefore also the holy thing which is born of you shall be called the son of the Holy Spirit); but the incarnation τῷ λόγῳ (by the Word). For the heavenly messenger wishes to say: Διὸ, therefore that holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called and truly shall be the Son of God, because the substantial power of God will assume flesh in you and from you.

Prob. d. The angel says: Πνεῦμα ἅγιον ἐπελεύσεται ἐπί σε, The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, Luke I, 35. Obf. a. The ἐπέλευσις (coming upon) of the Holy Spirit was not idle, but industrious and most efficacious. For a special, and clearly singular, divine presence, such as happened here, is never without efficacious operation. Yet it was not an ἐπέλευσις σπερματικὴ, a communicative of seed (because the Holy Spirit is not the father of Christ; since He, as to His human nature, is ἀπάτωρ, without father, Heb. VII, 3.); but 1) δημιουργικὴ (as DAMASCENE speaks, book III, de O. F. c. III), or the excitative of the mass of blood in the womb of the virgin, from which the human nature of Christ was produced; 2) ἐπέλευσις sanctificativa, by which the adhering sin was wiped away, so that whatever was born of Mary would be holy, which the ancients explained by a simile taken from a bee, sucking honey without poison from a rose; 3) ἐπέλευσις conjunctiva, or unitive, by which ὁ λόγος, the eternal Word, was joined to the virginal mass of blood, as a bridegroom to a bride, with an indissoluble bond.

Obs. b. The conception of the God-man is appropriated to the Holy Spirit: 1) Because the universal work of fecundation is ascribed to Him, Gen. I, 2: 2) That the purity of the mass of blood, from which the flesh of Christ grew, might be more evident: 3) That thus the same cause might be the generation of Christ the man, and of our regeneration, namely the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

Humana Christi natura originem habet a Deo triuno a), a Deo Patre b), a Filio Dei c), a Spiritu Sancto, cui productio carnis Christi in sacris litteris appropriatur d).

Prob. a. Productio carnis Christi, eiusque applicatio ad hypostasin Filii Dei, est opus ad extra & indiuisum, seu commune tribus personis diuinis. Veteres hoc mysterium declararunt simili sumto a tribus virginibus, quarum vna vestitur aut coronatur, quælibet autem ad ornamentum aliquid confert.

Prob. b. Deus Pater in plenitudine temporis misit Filium natum ex muliere, Gal. IV, 4. Misit ipsum in similitudine carnis peccati, & ad luendum pro peccato, Rom. VIII, 3.

Prob. c. Filius Dei, virtus hypostatica altissimi, virginem Mariam obumbravit: unde etiam, quod natum est ex illa sanctum, vocatum est Filius Dei, Luc. I, 35. Obs. a) Virtus altissimi heic non est Spiritus S. quippe a quo prius memorato, distinguitur. Spiritui S. ἐπέλευσις, superventus; virtuti altissimi ἐπισκιασμὸς, obumbratio, tribuitur. Ecquis credat, angelum fuisse ταυτόλογον, & in nervosa sublimissimi mysterii descriptione idem, vel pene idem bis dixisse? Neque per virtutem altissimi intelligitur omnipotentia Dei essentialis, propterea, quod virtuti, (scilicet Dei Patris) obumbratio virginis Mariae tamquam actio personalis tribuitur. Cum itaque actiones sint suppositorum, per virtutem altissimi indigitari censemus virtutem hypostaticam, seu Filium Dei, qui hoc nomine venit 1 Cor. I, 24. Sicut etiam in humanis filius nominatur virtus patris, Gen. XLIX, 3. Ἐπισκιασμὸς, seu obumbratio notat arcanam & admirabilem impletionem templi corporis, a Spiritu S. exstructi. Nempe Filius Dei obumbravit virginem Mariam, dum modo impervestigabili in uterum virginis descendit, & massam sanguinis virgineam, a Spiritu S. excitatam, peculiari approximatione implevit, sibique vnivit, vt σωματικῶς, corporaliter, velut in proprio templo in ea habitaret, Col. II, 9. cuius aliqua figura olim fuit in tabernaculo foederis, vt & in templo Salomonis, quod vtrumque cum exstructum esset, maiestas diuina ἐπισκιασμῷ, seu obumbratione interueniente implevit, Exod. XL, 35. 1 Reg. VII, 10. vbi pariter a LXX. interpretibus verbum ἐπισκιάζεσv adhibetur.

Obseru. b) Consequens huius obumbrationis est natiuitas Filii Dei, ex Maria nunc facti filii hominis, quae exprimitur verbis angeli: Διὸ καὶ τὸ γεννώμενον ἐκ σοῦ ἅγιον, κληθήσεται υἱὸς Θεοῦ. Ideo etiam, quod nascitur ex te Sanctum, vocabitur Filius Dei. Ex quibus verbis denuo colligimus, per virtutem altissimi heic non Spiritum S. sed Filium Dei intelligendum. Etenim causa proxima, cur filius Mariae sit Filius Dei, non est conceptio singularis de Spiritu S. (quam si indigitaturus fuisset angelus, dixisset: ideo etiam sanctum, quod ex te nascitur, vocabitur filius Spiritus S.); sed incarnatio τῷ λόγῳ. Nam dicere vult legatus coelestis: Διὸ, propterea sanctum illud, quod ex te nascetur, vocabitur & vere erit Filius Dei, quia substantialis Dei virtus in te, & ex te carnem assumet.

Prob. d. Angelus dicit: Πνεῦμα ἅγιον ἐπελεύσεται ἐπί σε, Spiritus S. veniet super te, Luc. I, 35. Obs. a. Ἐπέλευσις Spiritus S. non fuit otiosa, sed operosa & efficacissima. Praesentia enim diuina specialis, & plane singularis, qualis hic contigit, nunquam est sine efficaci operatione. Neque tamen fuit ἐπέλευσις σπερματικὴ, communicativa feminis (quia Spiritus S. non est pater Christi; quippe qui, qua humanam naturam, est ἀπάτωρ Hebr. VII, 3.); sed 1) δημιουργικὴ (vt loquitur DAMASCEN. libr. III. de O. F. c. III.), seu excitativa massae sanguineae in vtero virginis, e qua humana Christi natura producta est; 2) ἐπέλευσις sanctificatiua, qua adhaerens peccatum absterfum est, vt quidquid natum esset ex Maria, esset sanctum, quod veteres simili, sumto ab ape, ex rofeto mel fine veneno exsugente, explanarunt; 3) ἐπέλευσις coniunctiua, seu vnitiva, qua ὁ λόγος aeternus massae sanguineae virgineae, velut sponsus sponsae, vinculo indissolubili coniunctus est.

Obs. b. Appropriatur conceptio θεανθρώπης Spiritui Sancto: 1) Quia opus vniuersum foecundationis ipsi adscribitur, Gen. I, 2: 2) Vt puritas massae sanguineae, e qua creuit caro Christi, esset euidentior: 3) Vt sic eadem esset causa generationis Christi hominis, & regenerationis nostrae, scilicet Spiritus S. Christi, esset euidentior: 3) Vt sic eadem esset caussa generationis Christi hominis, & regenerationis noftræ, scilicet Spiritus S.


### Quæst. XIV. From whom does the human nature of Christ have its origin?: Question XV What is the material, or passive, principle of the conception and production of the human nature of Christ?

Question XV.

What is the material, or passive, principle of the conception and production of the human nature of Christ? The material, and indeed total, principle of the conception and production of the man Christ is Mary, the undefiled virgin a), and of the lineage of David, and thus sprung from the tribe of Judah b); the partial and proximate material principle is the animated seed of the virgin Mary c).

Prob. a. 1) Because Christ is said to be born not only in Mary (locally) Matt. 1:20, but from Mary (materially) Luke 1:35. 2) Because Christ is called the fruit of Mary’s womb, Luke 1:42. 3) Because Christ is γενόμενος, made from a woman, Gal. 4: 4. Prob. b. Because the genealogy of Mary delineated by the evangelist Luke, ch. 3, shows that Mary was procreated from the blood of David. For Luke traced the genealogy of Jesus from Eli, who was the natural father of Mary, as the very ancient writer Africanus commemorates, up to David, through the line of Nathan, who was as much the Son of David by Bathsheba as was Solomon, 1 Chron. 3: 5. For this reason, Christ is called everywhere in Holy Scripture the son of David, the fruit of the loins of David, Acts 2: 30. From which it is evident that Christ as man draws his origin from the tribe of Judah, to which King David owes his birth. Furthermore, the undefiled virginity of Mary is proved 1) from Isaiah 7:14, where Jehovah, about to give Ahaz a sign of miraculous liberation from enemies, says: Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.

Obj. (1) עלמה in the sacred code always denotes an undefiled virgin. This Hebrew word occurs seven times: Gen. 24:43, Exod. 2:8, Ps. 68:16, Cant. 1:3, ch. 6:7, Is. 7:14, Prov. 30:19. The words of the last passage are: These three things are wonderful above me, and four I do not know. The way (namely) of an eagle in the heavens, the way of a serpent upon a rock, and the way of a man with a maid (virgin). From this passage, modern Jews strive to gather that not every עלמה is a pure and undefiled virgin; but most ineptly. Certainly, the way to a pure and secluded virgin is far more abstruse than to a harlot, or a brothel, which either offers itself voluntarily or does not make its availability difficult to one seeking it. (2) If עלמה did not always denote a virgin, the sign given to Ahaz would not be so valid.

You say: The son of the virgin was to be named Immanuel, not Jesus. Resp. Jesus and Immanuel are the same name, not in sound, but in sense, as TERTULLIAN says in book 3 against Marcion. 2) Mary, to whom the angel announced the conception, is explicitly called a virgin, Luke 1:27, who had not known a man v. 34, who was made fruitful by the wonderful overshadowing of the Holy Spirit v. 35. Mary was therefore a virgin before conception, in conception, and in birth; but whether she was ἀειπάρθενος, ever-virgin, even after birth, cannot be demonstrated apodictically from the sacred letters.

Nevertheless, some conjecture the perpetual virginity of Mary from the fact that Christ, affixed to the cross, committed his mother to the care of John, intending to commend her to surviving sons, if she had borne any, having known a man. Prob. c. 1) Christ assumed the Abrahamic seed, Heb. 2:16, which he joined to himself from no one except Mary. 2) As children are partakers of flesh and blood, he himself likewise became a partaker, Heb.

2:14. But children are made partakers of blood through animated seed. Therefore, so is Christ. 3) If Christ had not assumed a soul from the soul of Mary, he would not have redeemed the human soul. For τὸ ἀπρόσληπτον ἀθεράπευτον, what Christ did not assume, he did not heal, says GREGORY NAZIANZEN, epistle 2 to Cledonius. But indeed it was the intention of the Son of God to heal the whole human nature infected by the stain of sin, of which the πρῶτον δεκτικόν, the first seat, is the soul, to heal. T. He assumed the whole human nature, consisting of body and soul. The antithesis is that of the Anabaptists and Socinians, some of whom deny that Mary was descended from the stock of Judah, while others deny that Christ was born from the... seed of Mary. They contend against us with the following arguments: I.

Elizabeth was of the daughters of Aaron, and thus of the tribe of Levi, Luke 1:5, who is called συγγενὴς (kinswoman) of Mary, Luke 1:36. From which it is gathered that Mary also was of the tribe of Levi. Resp.

Elizabeth was indeed from a priestly father, but from a mother who was born of the tribe of Judah and the house of David. II.

Whoever was not in the loins of Adam, he does not derive his origin from the tribe of Judah and the royal lineage of David: But Christ was not in the loins of Adam: Therefore. The minor is proved because he who is sprung from the loins of Adam is a sinner: since in Adam all have sinned, Rom. 5:12. Resp. Christ was not in the loins of Adam when he sinned, because the power of generating and procreating offspring, implanted in man, preceded the fall, Gen. 1:28, but by the power of the promise made only after the fall, Gen. 3:15, he was indeed derived from the blood of Adam, but sanctified. III.

Women lack seed: T. Christ was not born from the seed of Mary. Resp. Physicists demonstrate with firm reasons that women have seed.

In the sacred code, the seed of the woman is commemorated, Gen. 3:15, c. 12:3. Sarah is said to have received, being made fruitful, δύναμιν εἰς καταβολὴν σπέρματος (power to conceive seed), Heb. 11:11. IV. Whatever is a sinner, from its seed the holy flesh of Christ does not derive its origin: But Mary is a sinner: T.

Resp. Whatever is a sinner, from its seed, not purified by the Holy Spirit, the flesh of Christ does not derive its origin. But the seed of Mary was purified by the ἐπελεύσει (overshadowing) of the Holy Spirit, by whom indeed the poison of sin was wiped away.

Latin:

Quaestio XV.

Quodnam est principium materiale, seu passivum, conceptionis et productionis humanae Christi naturae? Principium materiale, idque totale conceptionis et productionis Christi hominis est Maria, virgo illibata a), et regio Dauidis stemmate, atque adeo e tribu Iuda prognata b); Principium materiale partiale et proximum est semen virginis Mariae animatum c).

Prob. a. 1) Quia Christus natus dicitur non tantum in Maria (localiter) Matth. I, 20. sed ex Maria (materialiter) Luc. I, 35. 2) Quia Christus appellatur fructus ventris Mariae, Luc. I, 42. 3) Quia Christus est γενόμενος, factus ex muliere, Gal. IV, 4. Prob. b. Quia genealogia Mariae delineata ab euangelista Luca c. III. ostendit, Mariam regio Dauidis sanguine procreatam esse. Pertexit enim Lucas genealogiam Iesu ab Eli, qui fuit pater naturalis Mariae, commemorante Africano scriptore vetustissimo, vsque ad Dauidem, per lineam Nathanis, qui aeque Filius Dauidis e Bathseba fuit, ac Salomo, 1 Paral. III, 5. Quam ob rem Christus passim in S. scriptura vocatur filius Dauidis, fructus lumborum Dauidis, Act. II, 30. E quibus patefcit, Christum hominem trahere ortum ex tribu Iuda, cui natales suos rex Dauid debet. Ceterum illibata Mariae virginitas probatur 1) ex Esaiae VII, 14. vbi daturus Iehouah Achafo signum miraculosae liberationis ab hostibus inquit: Ecce virgo concipiet et pariet filium, et vocabit nomen eius Immanuel.

Obf. (1) עלמה in sacro codice semper notat virginem illibatam. Septies haec vox hebraea occurrit, Gen. XXIV, 43. Exod. II, 8. Ps. LXVIII, 16. Cant. I, 3. c. VI, 7. Es. VII, 14. Prou. XXX, 19. Verba loci vltimi sunt: tria haec mirabilia sunt supra me, et quatuor non cognoui. Viam (scilicet) aquilae in caelis, viam serpentis super petra, et viam in virgine. Ex hoc loco colligere nituntur Iudaei hodierni non omnem עלמה esse puram et intaminatam virginem; sed perinepte. Certe via ad virginem puram et reconditam longe abstrusior est, quam ad meretricem, siue prostibulum, quod vel vltro se offert, vel haud difficulter amabienti facit sui copiam. (2) Si עלמה non semper notaret virginem, signum Achafo datum non adeo validum foret.

Dicis: Filius virginis nuncupandus erat Immanuel, non Iesus. Resp. Iesus et Immanuel idem nomen est non sono, sed sensu, dicente TERTULLIANO libr. III. contra Marcion. 2) Maria, cui angelus conceptionem denuntiauit, diserte dicitur virgo, Luc I, 27. quae virum non cognouerat v. 34. quae admirando superuentu Spiritus S. foecundata est v. 35. Fuit itaque Maria virgo ante conceptionem, in conceptione et in partu; an vero fuerit ἀειπάρθενος, semper-virgo, etiam post partum, e sacris litteris apodictice ostendi nequit.

Perennem tamen Mariae virginitatem coniciunt nonnulli ex eo, quod Christus affixus cruci matrem commiserit curae Ioannis, commendaturus eam superstitibus filiis, si quos, a viro cognita, peperisset. Prob. c. 1) Christus assumsit semen Abrahamicum, Hebr. II, 16. quod ex nemine, nisi Maria, sibi copulauit. 2) Sicut pueri participes fiunt carnis et sanguinis; et ipse Christus fimiliter particeps factus est, Hebr.

II, 14. At pueri participes redduntur sanguinis per semen animatum. E. et Christus. 3) Si Christus non assumsisset animam ab anima Mariae, animam humanam non redemisset. Nam τὸ ἀπρόσληπτον ἀθεράπευτον, quod Christus non assumsit, non sanauit, inquit GREGOR. NAZIANZENUS epist. 2. ad Cledonium. At vero mens erat Filio Dei, totam humanam naturam infectam labe peccati, cuius πρῶτον δεκτικόν, prima sedes, est anima, sanare. E. totam humanam naturam, constantem ex corpore & anima, assumsit. Antithesis est Anabaptistarum & Socinianorum, quorum quidam negant, Mariam ortam esse e stirpe Iuda, quidam infitiantur, Christum natum esse e ...semine Mariae. Dimicant iidem aduersus nos sequentibus argumentis:

I. Elisabetha fuit e filiabus Aaron, adeoque ex tribu Leui, Luc. I, 5. quae dicitur συγγενὴς cognata Mariae, Luc. I, 35. Ex quo colligitur, etiam Mariam fuisse e tribu Leui.

Resp. Elisabeth quidem fuit ex patre sacerdote, sed ex matre, quae nata erat e tribu Iuda, atque domo Dauidis.

II. Quicunque non fuit in lumbis Adami, ille non trahit originem ex tribu Iuda, & stemmate regio Dauidis: Atqui Christus non fuit in lumbis Adami: Ergo. Minor prob. quia qui e lumbis Adami ortus est, ille est peccator: siquidem in Adamo omnes peccauerunt, Rom. V, 12. Resp. Christus non fuit in lumbis Adami cum peccauit, quia vis generandi ac procreandi sobolem, homini insita, lapsum antecessit, Gen. I, 28. sed vi promissionis demum post lapsum factae, Gen. III, 15. deriuatus quidem est e sanguine Adami, sed sanctificato.

III. Mulieres carent semine: E. Christus e semine Mariae non est natus. Resp. Mulieres habere semen, Physici firmis rationibus demonstrant.

In sacro codice commemoratur semen mulieris, Gen. III, 15. c. XII, 3. Sara foecundata dicitur accepisse δύναμιν εἰς καταβολὴν σπέρματος, vim ad deiectionem feminis, Hebr. XI, 11. IV. Quaecunque est peccatrix, ex illius semine sancta caro Christi non ducit originem: Atqui Maria est peccatrix: E.

Resp. Quaecunque est peccatrix, ex illius semine, per Spiritum S. non purificato, caro Christi non ducit originem. At semen Mariae ἐπελεύσει Spiritus S. purificatum fuit, quippe a quo venenum peccati est abstersum.


### On the Act of Personal Union

Q. XVI. Are there two persons in Christ, just as there are two natures in him? The person of Christ is one a), and that σύνθετος (composite), or compound, in which the divine nature of the Son of God is most closely and inseparably joined with the assumed human nature by a personal union b). Proof a.

If there were two persons of our redeemer, there would be two Christs, two mediators, two saviors. But there is one Lord, Jesus Christ, 1 Cor. 8:6, one mediator 1 Tim. 2:5, one Savior, outside of whom there is no salvation, Acts 4:12. Therefore, the person of our redeemer Jesus Christ is one. Proof b.

Christ is called a σύνθετος (composite) person, not because he consists of two natures as parts, but because in Christ the divine nature is so composed or joined with the human, that the two natures, intimately united, have coalesced into one person.

The reason is that, the union having been effected, the human nature, stripped of its own hypostasis, subsists by the subsistence of the λόγος (Word) communicated to it. Hence it happens that the same one who is born of Mary is said to be the Son of the Highest, Luke 1:35.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, who maintain that it is impossible by any reason for Christ to be a σύνθετος (composite) or compound person; their arguments are: I.

Every composite is constituted of parts: Christ is not constituted of the divine and human nature as parts: Therefore Christ is not a composite person. The major is self-evident: because every composite is formed from parts into which it can be resolved. The minor is clear: because the divine nature of the λόγος (Word) cannot be a part of Christ; since it is such in subsisting, [it cannot be a part of Christ; since it is such in subsisting,] as

which is complete in being. Resp. a) Every essential and integral composite is indeed constituted of parts; but not a personal composite, inasmuch as it consists of two natures complete in being; of which one, within its union, divests itself of ultimate subsistence, and is terminated by the personality of the other nature. b) Distinguish between a composite *from* these, and *with* these. Not every composite is constructed from parts, but often one is composed with another, which is not a part of the composite, e.g., when an angel appears in an assumed body, the angelic nature does not put on the character of a part. Wherefore we do not say that Christ is composed of two natures, but that in Christ the divine nature is joined with the human.

Instance: Christ consists of two natures: Therefore, he is composed of two natures. Resp. Christ consists of two natures, not as of two parts, but as of two substances, personally united. Therefore, THOMAS, part III, quest. II, notably teaches that Christ is not a composite person by reason of parts, as if he consisted of two essential parts, but by reason of number, because he is one person in two natures.

II. Whatever is incommunicable cannot be communicated to another: But the hypostasis of the Word is incommunicable: Therefore, the hypostasis of the Word cannot be communicated to a human nature. The minor is clear: since the hypostasis is an incommunicable mode of subsisting. Resp. Distinguish between the communication which is of a person, and the communication which is of a nature. The hypostasis of one person cannot be communicated to another person, for the reason that every person is complete and terminated in ultimate subsisting; but it is not repugnant for the hypostasis of one person to be communicated to some other united nature; because this communication does not cause that which is communicated to be terminated by another.

Question XVII. What is the principle by which the composite person of Christ obtains its unity?

The principle by which the composite person of Christ received and retains its unity is the personal union of the two natures in Christ.

Proof. A personal union is called that by which two complete natures are united to constitute one person: For it is called a personal union from the term to which, because such a union is terminated at the God-man person, or because through such a union one person is constituted in two natures, who is at once true God and true man.

Question XVIII. In how many ways is the personal union considered?

The personal union is considered in two ways: a) as to the act: b) as to the state.

The act of union is also called unification, the state of union is properly and specifically the personal union, called in Greek *henosis hypostatike*.

Proof. Unification and union, strictly so called, differ. 1) Unification is the act by which two diverse natures, divine and human, are joined: union is the state of the natures joined through unification. 2) Unification is the cause by which natures divided in themselves obtain a certain indivision in the unity of the person: but union is the proximate effect of unification, and the very personal indivision of the two natures. 3) Unification is transient and momentary: union is permanent and perpetual. 4) Union is reciprocal; for the Son of God is united to the assumed flesh, and the flesh is united to the Son of God: but unification is not reciprocal. We rightly say: The Son of God united the flesh to himself; you would less rightly say: the flesh united the Son of God to itself. 5) Other propositions flow from unification, others from union. The subject of the former is the non-composite person, or the Word without flesh: the subject of the latter is the composite person, or the Word incarnate.

Latin:

Quaest. XVI. Suntne duae in Christo personae, sicut duae in ipso sunt naturae? Persona Christi est una a), eaque σύνθετος, siue composita, in qua natura diuina Filii Dei cum assumta natura humana per vnionem personalem arctissime & indiuulse coniuncta est b).

Prob. a. Si duae redemptoris nostri personae essent, duo Christi, duo mediatores, duo saluatores forent. At vnus est Dominus, Iesus Christus, 1 Cor. VIII, 6. vnus mediator 1 Tim. II, 5. vnus Saluator, extra quem non est salus, Act. IV, 12. Ergo vna est persona redemptoris nostri Iesu Christi. Prob. b. Christus dicitur persona σύνθετος, non quod e duabus naturis velut partibus constet, sed quia in Christo natura diuina cum humana ita composita vel coniuncta est, vt duae naturae intime vnitae in vnam coaluerint personam.

Ratio est, quia facta vnione, natura humana propria hypostasi exuta, subsistentia τοῦ λόγου, sibi communicata, subsistit.

Inde fit, vt idem ille, qui ex Maria nascitur, dicatur esse filius altissimi, Luc. I,

35. Antithesis est Socinianorum, statuentium, nulla ratione fieri posse, vt Christus sit persona σύνθετος, siue composita; quorum argumenta sunt: I.

Omne compositum constituitur ex partibus: Christus ex natura diuina & humana tanquam partibus non constituitur: Ergo Christus non est persona composita. Maior per se est euidens: quia omne compositum conflatur ex partibus, in quas resolui potest. Minor patet: quia natura diuina τοῦ λόγου non potest esse pars Christi; quippe quae tam in subsistendo, τῶ λόγῳ non potest esse pars Christi; quippe quæ tam in subsistendo,

quam in essendo completa est. Resp. a) Omne compositum essentiale & integrale quidem e partibus constituitur; at non compositum personale, vtpote quod duabus naturis in essendo completis constat; quarum vna intra vnionem suam exuit subsistentiam vltimam, & alterius naturæ personalitate terminatur. b) Dist. inter compositum ex his, & cum his. Non omne compositum conflatur ex partibus, fed fæpe vnum cum altero componitur, quod compositi pars non est, v. gr. Quando angelus apparet in corpore assumto, natura angelica non induit indolem partis. Quamobrem non dicimus, Christum e duabus naturis effe compositum, fed in Christo naturain diuina:n cum humana effe coniunctam.

Instantia: Christus constat ex duabus naturis: E. e duabus naturis est compositus. Resp. Christus constat e duabus naturis, non vt e duabus partibus, fed vt e duabus substantiis, personaliter vnitis. Ideo notanter THOMAS part. III. quæst. II. docet, Christum non effe personam compositam ratione partium, quasi e duabus partibus essentialibus constet, fed ratione numeri, quia est vna persona in duabus naturis.

II. Quidquid est incommunicabile, alteri communicari nequit: Atqui hypostasis τῶ λόγῳ est incommunicabilis: E. hypostasis τῶ λόγῳ humanæ naturæ communicari nequit. Minor est liquida: quoniam hypostasis est incommunicabilis subsistendi ratio. Resp. Dist. inter communicationem, quæ fit perfonæ, & inter communicationem, quæ fit naturæ. Hypostasis vnius perfonæ alteri perfonæ communicari nequit, eo, quod vnaquæque persona in subsistendo vltimo completa & terminata est; at non repugnat hypostasin vnius perfonæ alteri cuidam naturæ vnitæ communicari; quia hæc communicatio non efficit, vt id, quod communicatur, ab alio terminetur.

Quæst. XVII. Quodnam est principium, per quod persona Christi σύνθετος suam obtinet vnitatem?

Principium, per quod persona Christi σύνθετος suam accepit retinetque vnitatem, est vnio personalis duarum in Christo naturarum.

Prob. Vnio personalis dicitur, qua duæ naturæ completæ ad constituendam vnam personam vniuntur: Vocatur enim vnio personalis a termino ad quem, quia talis vnio terminatur ad personam θεάνθρωπον, fiue quia per talem vnionem constituitur vna persona in duabus naturis, quæ simul verus Deus & verus homo est.

Quæst. XVIII. Quot modis consideratur vnio personalis?

Vnio personalis consideratur bifariam: a) quoad actum: b) quoad statum.

Actus vnionis dicitur etiam vnitio, status vnionis proprie & specifice vnio personalis, græce ἕνωσις ὑποσατικὴ appellatur.

Prob. Vnitio, & vnio stricte dicta, differunt. 1) l'nitio est actus, quo duæ diuerfæ naturæ, diuina & humana, coniunguntur: vnio est status naturarum, per vnitionem coniundtarum. 2) Vnitio est caussa, per quam naturæ in fe diuisæ quandam in vnitate perfonæ nanciscuntur indiuisionem: vnio vero est effectus proximus vnitionis, & ipsa duarum naturarum personalis indiuisio. 3) Vnitio est transiens & momentanea: vnio permanens & perpetua. 4) Vnio est reciproca; nam Filius Dei est vnitus carni assumtæ, & caro est vnita Filio Dei: at vnitio non est reciproca. Recte dicimus: Filius Dei sibi vniuit carnem; minus recte dixeris: caro sibi vniuit Filium Dei. 5) Aliæ propositiones fluunt ex vnitione, aliæ ex vnione. Illarum subiectum persona ἀσύνθετος, fiue λόγος ἄσαρκος: haruin subiectum est persona σύνθετος, fiue λόγος ἔνσαρκος.


### Quest. XIX. By what equivalent term is the union of the two natures in Christ called?

The union, or the actual coalition of the divine and human nature into one person, is commonly called by the θεανδρώπω [God-man] incarnation. Obs. As Chemnitz teaches in his book De duabus naturis Christi, chap. IX, p. 108 seqq., Irenaeus was the first to call the personal union, taken effectively, σάρκωσιν καὶ ἐνσάρκωσιν, incarnation; Ignatius, ἐνανθρώπησιν καὶ ἐνσωμάτωσιν, inhumanation and incorporation; Athanasius, πρόσληψιν, the assumption of humanity into the divinity of the Son of God; most Greeks called it οἰκονομίαν, dispensation. They used the word οἰκονομία: 1) Because the supreme divine majesty, without any diminution of itself, submitted to union with the wretched mass of our nature: 2) Because it so exalted that which was assumed that it now pertains to the very person of the Son of God: 3) Because now in the economy, or administration of the kingdom and office of Christ, neither nature acts without the other, but both act with the communication of the other.

Latin:

Vnitio, siue actualis coalitio diuinae & humanae naturae in vnam personam θεανδρώπω communiter vocatur incarnatio. Obs. Docente Chemnitio in libro de duab. nat. Christi, cap. IX. p. 108. seqq. primus Irenaeus vnionem personalem, effectiue sumtam, vocauit σάρκωσιν καὶ ἐνσάρκωσιν, incarnationem; Ignatius ἐνανθρώπησιν καὶ ἐνσωμάτωσιν, inhumanationem & incorporationem, Athanasius πρόσληψιν, assumtionem humanitatis in diuinitatem Filii Dei, plerique Graeci οἰκονομίαν, dispensationem, appellarunt. Οἰκονομίας voce vsi sunt: 1) Quia summa maiestas diuina, sine sui diminutione, submisit se ad vnionem cum massa misera naturae nostrae: 2) Quia illam assumtam ita exaltauit, vt iam ad ipsius Filii Dei personam pertineat: 3) Quia iam in oeconomia, seu administratione regni & officii Christi, neutra natura sine altera, sed vtraque agit cum communicatione alterius.


### Quest. XX. What is the incarnation?

The incarnation is a divine action, by which the Son of God assumed human nature in the womb of the virgin Mary into the unity, or person. It is defined more fully: The incarnation is a divine action, by which the Son of God assumed human nature, consubstantial with us, yet devoid of sin and lacking its own subsistence, in the womb of his mother the virgin Mary into the unity of his person, and communicated to it both his hypostasis and his divine nature, so that Christ the θεάνθρωπος [God-man] now subsists perpetually in two natures, divine and human, most closely united.

Obs. I. The incarnation, taken broadly, embraces both the production of the flesh in the womb of Mary and the assumption of the flesh produced: taken strictly, it denotes only the assumption of the flesh into the person of the λόγος [Word]. The production of the flesh is common to all three persons of the deity: The act of assumption proceeds from the divine power common to the three persons: The terminus of the assumption is the hypostasis of the λόγος. Therefore, the incarnation is the work of the three divine persons efficiently and inchoatively, but of the Son of God alone formally and terminatively.

Obs. II. The assumption of the flesh and the incarnation are indeed synonymous in a certain respect: but this difference intervenes, that the λόγος is said to be actively incarnate, and the human nature passively incarnate.

The incarnation of the Son of God is proved 1) from John 1:14, ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο, The Word became flesh. By λόγος is understood God from God, or the Son of God: For John says: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. See above part I, p. 309. But it is manifest that God is subject to no change or conversion. By flesh is understood man consisting of body and soul, by a phrase familiar to Scripture, e.g., Gen. 6:12, All flesh, i.e., all men, had corrupted his way. Isa. 40:6, All flesh, i.e., all men, is grass. John uses the word flesh rather than man to indicate a) the ἀνυποστασίαν [anhypostasia] of human nature viewed in itself, that the λόγος assumed not a person, but the nature of man, i.e., true and integral humanity, lacking its own ὑποστάσει [hypostasis]; b) on account of the συγγένειαν, or consanguinity of our nature; c) on account of the φιλανθρωπίαν, by which, moved to our most miserable and abject condition, from the majesty of his own fo-

the Son of God descended. The Socinians wish to understand "flesh" as fragility; but they err and are led into error, for the reason that 1) that meaning is unusual in Scripture: 2) Fragility, which is an accident, cannot exist without a subject: 3) The glory of this flesh was seen. Having established these points, he argues: Whoever is the eternal and immutable God, and becomes flesh, he is not changed into flesh, but assumes the same, and unites it intimately to himself: But the hypostatic Word of God [is such] &c. Therefore.

2) From Heb. II, 14. Since the children have become partakers of flesh and blood, he himself likewise made himself a partaker of them. Whoever is God, and becomes a partaker of flesh and blood, just as our children, he assumes flesh and blood into the unity of his person: But the Son of God [is such] &c: Therefore.

3) From Heb. II, 16. He does not at any time take hold of angels: but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham. Whoever is a partaker of flesh and blood in such a way that he takes hold of the seed of Abraham, he has personally united the human nature to himself: But the Son of God [is such] &c: Therefore.

You say: The word ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι signifies to receive, and the seed of Abraham is taken collectively, to designate the posterity of Abraham, so that the sense becomes: Christ receives the posterity of Abraham into favor.

Resp. Be it so, that ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι in general signifies to receive, here, however, according to the underlying subject matter, it signifies to assume the seed of Abraham, so that the one assuming, the Son of God, becomes a partaker of flesh and blood, v. 14, and like his brethren, v. 17. That "seed" is not always taken collectively, Paul teaches, Gal. III, 16.

4) From Rom. IX, 5. Of whom (the fathers) is Christ κατὰ σάρκα, as far as the flesh is concerned, who is over all God blessed forever, amen. Whoever is the supreme God, and has flesh propagated from the fathers of the Israelites, he has personally united flesh to himself: But Christ [is such] &c: Therefore. The major is proved; because God cannot be predicated of man in the nominative case, unless God and man are united; for personal union is the foundation of such a predication.

5) From Gal. IV, 4. The Son of God was made of a woman: Therefore the immutable Son of God was made man, not by a substantial change, but by a personal union.

6) From 1 Tim. III, 16. Confessedly great is the mystery of godliness (this): God was manifested in the flesh. By God in this place is understood the Son of God, who is also called God, John I, 2. Acts XX, 28. 1 John V, 21. and is said to have been made flesh, John I, 14. He rendered and demonstrated his glory conspicuous in the flesh and through his flesh, that he is the true God. John teaches this c. I, 14. The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, and chap. II, 11. Christ manifested his glory. But he could not have manifested his glory in the flesh, unless he had assumed flesh. Antithesis

The Antithesis is that of the Socinians, who fervently impugn the mystery of the incarnation; they rely upon the most futile inventions of reason:

I. The incarnation of the Son of God is repugnant to sound reason, which dictates that it is impossible for two substantial forms, and those perfect ones, to fall into one and the same suppositum: since thus not one, but two diverse supposita would exist.

Resp. a) Reason, left to itself, knows nothing of the incarnation of the Son of God, since it is ὁμολογουμένως μέγα μυστήριον, 1 Tim. III, 16. Therefore it must be believed on account of divine revelation. Reason, taking upon itself judgment concerning the mysteries of faith, is not sound, but unsound, corrupted, and raging. b) Who has ever called the divinity of Christ a form? c) That the forms of the elements remain in one suppositum, philosophy teaches.

II. If the divine nature of the Son of God is incarnate, then the divine nature of the Father and the Holy Spirit is also incarnate: The latter is heretical; for by it the heresy of the Sabellians and

of the Patripassians. Resp. We assert that the Son of God, or the second person of the deity, who is not the Father and the Holy Spirit, was incarnate; not, indeed, with the divine nature of the Logos excluded. But we distinguish between the nature considered absolutely, as it is common to all three persons, and viewed relatively, as it is distinguished by the hypostatic character of the Son of God.

III. He whose human nature is a true person cannot be a divine person: But Christ’s human nature is a true person: Therefore. The major premise is established: because two persons cannot coalesce into one person. The minor is proved a) from the description of a person. For every primary and intelligent substance is a person, But Christ’s human nature is a primary and intelligent substance. b) The human nature is man and the son of man, which cannot but be a person. c) Actions and passions belong to supposita. Christ’s human nature acts and suffers. d) The prophetic, priestly, and kingly office belongs to Christ’s human nature, which office no one performs unless he is a person.

Resp. To a): Every primary and intelligent substance that is anypostatos is a person. But Christ’s human nature is not anypostatos, i.e., enjoying its own subsistence, but enypostatos, i.e., destitute of its own subsistence: it is terminated by the subsistence of the Logos communicated to it, and therefore it is not a person, but "personated," as they commonly speak. To b): The human nature of Christ, viewed in itself, apart from the hypostasis of the Logos, is not man, nor the son of man; but taken with the hypostasis of the Logos, it is man and the son of man. For "man" and "son of man" signify by way of supposita, and connote a hypostasis. We also concede that the son of man subsisting in the Son of God is a syntheton, or composite person, who is called the God-man (theanthropos). To c): Not only supposita act. For a separated soul also acts, which nevertheless is not a person. But what they commonly bring forward, that actions are of supposita, does not have this meaning—that a thing has from its own suppositality the fact that it acts, or can act—but that by the law of nature a thing, before subsistence, is not constituted in a complete state accommodated for operating.
