But if some thing, destitute of its own subsistence, is constituted from elsewhere and through a subsistence communicated by another in a complete state accommodated for operating, then nothing prevents the nature itself from properly acting and suffering. And such is the case with Christ’s human nature. To d): The threefold office belongs to Christ the God-man, not to the human nature alone, viewed in itself, apart from the connoted divine hypostasis.

IV. One and the same subject cannot simultaneously be two disparates, nor can one of the disparates be the other, nor can two disparates be predicated of the same subject: But the supreme God and man are disparates: Therefore, Christ cannot simultaneously be God and man. God cannot be man: nor can God and man be predicated of Christ. Resp. Disparates, viewed in themselves, apart from their union, cannot be predicated of one another, nor can one subject be two disparates, nor can one of the disparates be the other. But if it happens that two disparates are united with one another, then it is not repugnant for one to be predicated of the other, not indeed in the abstract, but in the concrete, and with the union connoted; and one and the same subject can simultaneously be two disparates, and one of the disparates can be the other, not indeed according to the same respect, but in one respect and another. E.g.,

E.g., I rightly say: a certain white thing is sweet (milk): a certain soldier is a musician (King David): a certain philosopher is a theologian (Justin Martyr).

Instance: Two complete substantial disparates cannot be predicated of one another: e.g., sheep and wolf are not affirmed of one another. Resp. Two complete substantial disparates are not united by the law of nature to constitute one suppositum, but by divine power it is not repugnant for them to be united.

repugnant. Which when it happens (as was done in the incarnation of Christ); then in the concrete they can be predicated of one another, not indeed by a customary predication, but by an unusual one. For philosophers formed their canons by the induction of natural examples, by which it is not permitted to impugn the mysteries of the faith. We believe the scripture saying: The Word was made flesh, John 1, 14. The Branch of David is Jehovah. Jer. 33, 5. V. No complete intelligent substance can lack its own personality, and subsist by an alien one: But human nature &c: Therefore. Resp. I deny the major. For personality is not of the formal notion of a complete substance, but is the ultimate mode, or degree of subsisting, posterior to nature, and in creatures really differing from the subsistence itself. But truly everything prior can exist without the posterior, and things which are really distinct in a finite essence can be separated from one another by infinite power. Let us piously and submissively acknowledge that it is a perfection of the Word (τοῦ λόγου), that it can terminate by its own hypostasis (ὑπόστασει) a singular humanity, indeterminate of itself in subsisting, yet intimately united to itself, since no contradiction is involved with that very thing. And since to perform that is in the power of the Son of God, humanity also could receive it; for to the active power of God corresponds in creatures an obediential power.

Latin:

Incarnatio est actio diuina, qua Filius Dei naturam humanam in vtero virginis Mariae in vnitatem siue personae assumsit. Vberius definitur: Incarnatio est actio diuina, qua Filius Dei naturam humanam, nobis consubstantialem, peccati vero expertem, propriaque subsistentia destitutam, in vtero matris virginis Mariae in vnitatem personae suae assumsit, eidemque tum hypostasin, tum naturam suam diuinam communicauit, vt iam perpetuo in duabus naturis diuina & humana, arctissime vnitis, subsistat Christus θεάνθρωπος.

Obs. I. Incarnatio, late sumta, tam productionem carnis in vtero Mariae, quam carnis productae assumtionem complectitur: stricte accepta, tantum notat assumtionem carnis in personam τοῦ λόγου. Productio carnis omnibus tribus deitatis personis est communis: Actus assumtionis procedit ex virtute diuina tribus personis communi: Terminus assumtionis est hypostasis τοῦ λόγου. Est itaque incarnatio opus trium personarum diuinarum efficienter & inchoatiue, solius autem Filii Dei formaliter & terminatiue.

Obs. II. Assumtio carnis, & incarnatio sunt quidem certo respectu synonyma: id discriminis vero intercedit, quod ὁ λόγος actiue incarnatus, natura humana passiue incarnata dicatur.

Incarnatio Filii Dei probatur 1) ex Ioann. I, 14. ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο, Verbum caro factum est. Per λόγον intelligitur Deus de Deo, siue Filius Dei: Nam Ioannes inquit: In principio erat Verbum, & Verbum erat apud Deum, & Deus erat Verbum. Vid. supra part. I. p. 309. Deum autem nulli mutationi aut conuersioni obnoxium esse, manifestum est. Per carnem intelligitur homo constans ex corpore & anima, phrasi scripturae familiari, v. gr. Gen. VI, 12. Corrupit omnis caro, i. e. omnis homo, viam suam. Es. XL, 6. Omnis caro, i. e. omnis homo, est foenum. Voce autem carnis potius, quam hominis, Ioannes vtitur ad indicandam a) naturae humanae in se spectatae ἀνυποστασίαν, quod non personam, sed naturam hominis, i. e. veram & integram humanitatem, propria ὑποστάσει destitutam ὁ λόγος assumserit; b) ob συγγένειαν, siue consanguinitatem naturae nostrae; c) ob φιλανθρωπίαν, qua motus ad miserrimam & abiectissimam nostram conditionem de maiestatis suae fo. ὑπεστάσει destitutam ὁ λόγος assumserit; b) ob συγγένειαν, fiue consanguinitatem naturæ noftræ; c) ob φιλανθρωπίαν, qua motus ad miserrimam & abiectissimam nostram conditionem de maiestatis fuæ

folio Filius Dei descendit. Sociniani per carnem intellectam volunt fragilitatem; sed fallunt & falluntur, ideo, quod 1) illa significatio scripturae est inusitata: 2) Fragilitas, quae est accidens, sine subiecto esse nequit: 3) Carnis huius visa est gloria. Quibus praestitutis argumentatur: Quicunque est aeternus immutabilisque Deus, & fit caro, is non in carnem mutatur, sed eandem assumit, intimeque sibi vnit: Atqui Verbum Dei hypostaticum &c. Ergo.

2) Ex Hebr. II, 14. Quoniam pueri participes facti sunt carnis & sanguinis, & ipse similiter participem se fecit ipsorum. Quicunque est Deus, & fit particeps carnis & sanguinis, aeque, ac nostri pueri, ille carnem & sanguinem assumit in vnitatem personae: Atqui Filius Dei &c: Ergo. Minor prob. ex cap. I. ep. ad Hebr. (in quo capite diuinitas Christi demonstratur) collat. cum cap. II, 14.

3) Ex Hebr. II, 16. Non vnquam angelos assumit: sed semen Abrahae assumit. Quicunque ita est particeps carnis & sanguinis, vt semen Abrahami assumat, ille humanam naturam sibi personaliter vniuit: Atqui Filius Dei &c: Ergo.

Dicis: Verbum ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι significat recipere, & semen Abrahae collective sumitur, vt designet posteritatem Abrahami, vt sensus fit: Christus posteritatem Abrahami recipit in gratiam.

Resp. Esto, quod ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι in genere significet recipere, hic tamen, pro substrata materia, significat assumere semen Abrahami, vt assumens, Filius Dei, fiat particeps carnis & sanguinis, v. 14. fratribusque suis similis. v. 17. Semen non semper collective sumi, docet Paullus, Gal. III, 16.

4) Ex Rom. IX, 5. Ex quibus (patribus) est Christus κατὰ σάρκα, quantum ad carnem, qui est super omnia Deus benedictus in saecula, amen. Quicunque est summus Deus, & habet carnem propagatam ab Ifraelitarum patribus, ille carnem sibi personaliter vniuit: Atqui Christus &c: Ergo. Maior probatur; quia Deus de homine in casu recto praedicari nequit, nisi Deus & homo vniantur; unio quippe personalis est fundamentum eiusmodi praedicationis.

5) Ex Gal. IV, 4. Filius Dei factus est ex muliere: Ergo immutabilis Dei Filius factus est homo, non per mutationem substantialem, sed per vnionem personalem.

6) Ex 1 Tim. III, 16. In confesso magnum est pietatis mysterium (hoc): Deus manifestatus est in carne. Per Deum h.l. intelligitur Filius Dei, qui & Deus appellatur, Ioann. I, 2. Actor. XX, 28. 1 Ioann. V, 21. & caro factus dicitur, Ioann. I, 14. Hic in carne ac per carnem suam gloriam conspicuam reddidit ac demonstravit, se verum esse Deum. Docet hoc Ioannes c. I, 14. Verbum caro factum est, & habitauit in nobis, & vidimas gloriam ipsius, gloriam sicut vnigeniti a Patre, & cap. II, 11. Christus manifestauit gloriam suam. At non potuisset gloriam suam in carne manifestare, nisi carnem assumisset. Antithesis

Antithesis est Socinianorum, mysterium incarnationis feruide impugnantium; qui futilissimis rationis commentis innituntur:

I. Incarnatio Filii Dei repugnat sanae rationi, quae dictat, fieri non posse, vt duae formae substantiales, exque perfectae, in vnum idemque suppositum cadant: cum sic non vnum, sed duo diuersa exsisterent supposita.

Resp. a) Ratio, sibi relicta, de incarnatione Filii Dei nihil nouit, cum sit ὁμολογουμένως μέγα μυστήριον, 1 Tim. III, 16. Ergo credendum est propter diuinam reuelationem. Ratio, sibi iudicium sumens de mysteriis fidei, non est sana, sed male sana, corrupta & ferociens. b) Quis vnquam diuinitatem Christi vocauit formam: c) Formas elementorum manere in vno supposito, docet philosophia.

II. Si natura diuina Filii Dei est incarnata, etiam natura diuina Patris & Spiritus S. est incarnata: Posterius est haereticum; quippe quo reducitur haeresis Sabellianorum &

Patripassianorum. Resp. Asserimus, Filium Dei, seu secundam personam deitatis, quae non est Pater & Spiritus S., incarnatam esse; non quidem exclusa natura divina τοῦ λόγου. Sed distinguimus inter naturam consideratam absolute, prout omnibus ...tribus personis est communis, & spectatam relate, prout charactere hypostatico Filii Dei est insignita.

III. Cuius natura humana est vera persona, ille non potest esse persona divina: Atqui Christi humana natura est vera persona: Ergo. Maior constat: quia duae personae non possunt coalescere in unam personam. Minor probatur a) e descriptione personae. Nam omnis substantia prima & intelligens est persona, Atqui humana Christi natura est substantia prima & intelligens. b) Natura humana est homo & filius hominis, qui non potest non esse persona. c) Actiones & passiones sunt suppositorum. Humana Christi natura agit & patitur. d) Competit humanae Christi naturae officium propheticum, sacerdotale & regium, quo officio nemo fungitur, nisi sit persona.

Resp. Ad a): Omnis substantia prima & intelligens ἀνυπόστατος est persona. At humana Christi natura non est ἀνυπόστατος, h. e. propria gaudens subsistentia, sed ἐνυπόστατος, i. e. propria subsistentia destituta: terminatur subsistentia τοῦ λόγου sibi communicata, adeoque non est persona, sed personata, ut communiter loquuntur. Ad b): Natura humana Christi, in se, citra ὑπόστασιν τοῦ λόγου, spectata, non est homo, nec filius hominis; sumta autem cum ὑπόστασει λόγου, homo & filius hominis est. Homo enim & filius hominis significant per modum suppositorum, & connotant ὑπόστασιν. Concedimus etiam, filium hominis in filio Dei subsistentem esse personam σύνθετον, sive compositam, quae vocatur θεάνθρωπος. Ad c): Non sola supposita agunt. Nam & anima separata agit, quae tamen non est persona. Quod autem vulgo afferunt, actiones esse suppositorum, non hunc habet sensum, quod ab ipsa suppositalitate res habeat, quod agat, aut agere possit, sed quod de lege naturae res, ante subsistentiam, non sit in statu completo & ad operandum accommodato constituta. Quod si res aliqua, propria subsistentia destituta, aliunde & per subsistentiam, ab alio communicatam, in statu completo & ad operandum accommodato constituatur, tunc nihil impedit, naturam etiam proprie agere & pati. Ita autem comparatum est cum humana Christi natura. Ad d): Officium triplex competit Christo θεανθρώπῳ, non soli humanae naturae, in se, citra connotatam ὑπόστασιν divinam, spectatae.

IV. Vnum & idem subiectum duo disparata simul esse non potest, nec unum disparatorum potest esse alterum, neque duo disparata de eodem subiecto praedicari queunt: At Deus summus, & homo, sunt disparata: Ergo Christus non potest esse simul Deus & homo. Deus non potest esse homo: neque Deus & homo de Christo praedicari queunt. Resp. Disparata, in se, citra unionem sui spectata; non possunt de se praedicari, nec unum subiectum potest esse duo disparata, nec unum disparatorum potest esse alterum. Si autem contingat, ut duo disparata inter se uniantur, tunc non repugnat, unum praedicari de altero non quidem in abstracto, sed in concreto, & cum connotata unione; & unum idemque subiectum simul potest esse duo disparata, atque unum disparatorum potest esse alterum, non quidem secundum idem; sed alio atque alio respectu. v. gr.

Recte dico: quoddam album est dulce (lac): quidam miles est musicus (rex Dauid): quidam philosophus est theologus (Iustinus Martyr).

Instantia Duo disparata completa substantialia de se invicem praedicari nequeunt: v. gr. ouis & lupus de se non affirmantur. Resp. Duo disparata substantialia completa de lege naturae non uniuntur ad constituendum unum suppositum, divina autem potentia ea uniri, non

Quod quando fit (vt in Christi incarnatione factum est); tunc in concreto de se inuicem praedicari queunt, non quidem praedicatione vsitata, sed inusitata. Philosophi quippe inductione exemplorum naturalium suos formarunt canones, quibus mysteria fidei impugnare haud licet. Nos credimus scripturae dicenti: Verbum caro factum est, Ioann. I, 14. Germen Dauidis est Iehouah. Ier. XXXIII, 5. V. Nulla substantia completa intelligens propria personalitate carere, & aliena subsistere potest: Atqui natura humana &c: Ergo. Resp. Neg. mai. Nam personalitas non est de formali substantiae completae, sed vltimus modus, vel gradus subsistendi natura posterior, & in creaturis realiter ab ipsa subsistentia differens. At vero omne prius potest esse sine posteriore, & quae distincta sunt realiter in essentia finita, ab inuicem separari queunt potentia infinita. Pie & submisse agnoscamus, eam esse perfectionem τοῦ λόγου, vt queat terminare ὑπόστασει sua humanitatem singularem de se in subsistendo indeterminatam, intime tamen sibi vnitam, cum eo ipso nulla inuoluatur contradictio. Et cum id praestare sit penes Filium Dei, etiam humanitas id potuit accipere; potentiae enim Dei actiuae respondet in creaturis potentia obedientialis.


### Q. XXI. In what does the incarnation formally consist?

Form of the incarnation The incarnation formally consists in the assumption of flesh into the unity of a person a), and the communion of the divine nature b).

Prob. a. The incarnation is the personal union of two natures, the term to which is one person, for the reason that through the personal union of the assumed human nature, which of itself does not subsist, the subsistence of the Word (τοῦ λόγου) was communicated, so that those two natures, the divine of Christ, and the human, are one person. Prob. b. The incarnation of the Word (τοῦ λόγου) is not completed by the communication of subsistence alone, but also embraces the assumption of flesh into the communication of the divine nature of the Word (τοῦ λόγου). From which ATHANASIUS described it in his symbol *), by the assumption of humanity into deity (πρόσληψιν ἀνθρωπότητος εἰς θεότητα). The reason is: because the subsistence of the Son of God cannot be communicated to the assumed flesh without his own divine nature; therefore, that which is a hypostasis is a mode, outside, or apart from the nature, from which it does not really differ, it cannot by any reason exist. Wherefore, the divine subsistence being communicated to the flesh, the divine nature and essence of the Son of God itself cannot but be communicated.

Latin:

Forma incarnationis Incarnatio formaliter consistit in assumtione carnis in vnitatem personae a), & communionem naturae diuinae b).

Prob. a. Incarnatio est vnitio duarum naturarum personalis, cuius terminus ad quem est vna persona, propterea, quod per vnitionem personalem naturae assumtae humanae, ex se non subsistenti, communicata est subsistentia τοῦ λόγου, vt duae illae naturae, diuina Christi, & humana, sint vna persona. Prob. b. Incarnatio τοῦ λόγου non absoluitur sola communicatione subsistentiae, sed complectitur etiam assumtionem carnis in communicationem naturae diuinae τοῦ λόγου. Ex quo ATHANASIVS eam descripsit in symbolo suo *), per πρόσληψιν ἀνθρωπότητος εἰς θεότητα, assumtionem humanitatis in deitate. Ratio est: quia subsistentia Filii Dei non potest assumtae carni communicari sine ipsius natura diuina; ideo, quod hypostasis est modus, extra, vel citra naturam, a qua realiter non differt, nulla ratione esse potest. Quare, communicata carni subsistentia diuina, non potest non comunicari ipsa diuina natura & essentia Filii Dei.


### Q. XXII. What is the communication of the hypostasis, or subsistence?

Communication of the hypostasis is that by which the Son of God truly and really conferred his own divine hypostasis (ὑπόστασιν) upon the assumed human nature, destitute of its own personality, for communion and participation, so that the same might be terminated, completed in subsisting, and constituted in the ultimate hypostatic being.

Obf. I. The divine and human natures, existing in the one composite (συνθέτῳ) person of the Son of God, have one and the same hypostasis, yet in a diverse mode of having. For the divine nature has it primarily (πρώτως, καὶ κατ' αὐτὸ), by itself and independently; but the human nature has it secondarily (δευτέρως καὶ κατ' ἄλλο), on account of the personal union, and therefore participatively.

Obs. II. The flesh of Christ has been made a participant of the divine subsistence for possession, usurpation, and denomination.

For possession; because the Son of God so assumed the human nature into his own hypostasis, that the hypostasis of the Son of God became the hypostasis of the human nature, or of the assumed flesh, which was conferred upon it not by transfusion, but by communication. For usurpation; so that, by virtue of this communication, the human nature actually and personally enjoys, possesses, and subsists by the very hypostasis of the Son of God. For denomination; so that from thence it is not indeed called ὑπόστασις (hypostasis), or ὑφιστάμενον (subsistent thing), but ἐνυπόστατος (enhypostatic), or ὑποστᾶσα ἐν τῷ λόγῳ (subsisting in the Word), as DAMASCENUS speaks, L. III. de O. F. c. 11., subsisting in the Son of God, and therefore not a person, but personated, which term the commentator of Damascenus uses.

The communication of the hypostasis is proved: 1) from John 1:14, "The Word was made flesh," which is to be understood thus, as DAMASCENUS notes, L. III. de O. F. c. 11., that the hypostasis of the Word, without conversion, became the hypostasis of the flesh. Whence we conclude: Whatever hypostasis, proper to the Son of God from eternity, was made in time the hypostasis of the assumed flesh, that has been communicated to the flesh: But the divine and infinite hypostasis, etc. Therefore. The major is evident: because it cannot be that what is proper to one should be possessed by another, except through a real communication of itself with that other. 2) Christ, consisting of the divine and human nature, is one person: Therefore he has one hypostasis, or personality. For where there is a double personality, there are two persons. Hence we further conclude: Whoever, consisting of the divine and human nature, has one hypostasis, in the same either the divine nature communicated its hypostasis to the human nature; or the human nature communicated its hypostasis to the divine nature; or finally, from the hypostasis of the divine nature and the hypostasis of the human nature, one was conflated. But neither did the human nature communicate its subsistence to the divine nature, because ὁ λόγος (the Word) subsists from eternity in the most perfect way, while the flesh began to exist and to subsist ἐν λόγῳ (in the Word) only in time: nor did one hypostasis arise from the hypostasis τῷ λόγῳ (of the Word) and the hypostasis of the flesh, because this denotes a mode of subsisting that is incommunicable and ultimately complete. But it is simply impossible for a third incommunicable and ultimately complete [hypostasis] to be conflated from two incommunicable and ultimately complete ones. Therefore, the divine nature communicated its hypostasis to the human. 3) If ὁ λόγος (the Word) had not communicated his hypostasis to the assumed flesh, the son of the Virgin Mary would not be called the son of the Most High. But he is rightly so called, Luke 1:35. Therefore. The consequence is proved: because for the truth of that proposition it is required that the son of Mary be personally the same who is the Son of God, or have the very hypostasis of the Son of God: which how would the human nature of Christ have, unless it had received it communicated from the divine? (*).

Latin:

Communicatio hypostaseos est, qua Filius Dei assumtae naturae humanae, propria personalitate destitutae, diuinam suam ὑπόστασιν ad communionem & participationem vere & realiter contulit, vt eadem terminetur, in subsistendo compleatur, atque in esse vltimo hypostatico constituatur.

Obs. I. Diuina & humana naturae, in vna persona συνθέτῳ Filii Dei existentes, vnam eandemque habent hypostasin, modo tamen habendi diuerso. Natura enim diuina eam habet πρώτως, καὶ κατ' αὐτὸ, primario, per se & independenter; natura autem humana δευτέρως καὶ κατ' ἄλλο, secundario, propter vnionem personalem, adeoque participatiue.

Obs. II. Particeps facta est caro Christi divinae subsistentiae ad possessionem, usurpationem & denominationem.

Ad possessionem; quia Filius Dei ita assumsit naturam humanam in hypostasim suam, ut hypostasis Filii Dei facta sit hypostasis humanae naturae, seu, carnis assumtae, quae collata ipsi est non per transfusionem, sed per communicationem. Ad usurpationem; vt, vi huius communicationis, natura humana actu personali Filii Dei reapse gaudeat, fruatur, eademque subsistat. Ad denominationem; vt inde non dicatur quidem ὑπόστασις, vel ὑφιστάμενον, sed ἐνυπόστατος, vel ὑποσᾶσα ἐν τῷ λόγῳ, vt loquitur DAMASCENVS L. III. de O. F. c. 11., subsistens in Filio Dei, adeoque non persona, sed personata, qua voce vtitur commentator Damasceni.

Probatur communicatio hypostaseos: 1) e Io. I, 14. Verbum caro factum est, quod ita intelligendum est, notante DAMASCENO L. III. de O. F. c. 11. vt Verbi hypostasis, sine conuersione, facta sit carnis hypostasis. Vnde colligimus: Quaecunque hypostasis, Filii Dei ab aeterno propria, facta est in tempore assumtae carnis hypostasis, illa carni est communicata: Atqui hypostasis divina & infinita &c. Ergo. Maior constat: quia fieri nequit, vt, quod vnius est proprium, ab altero possideatur, nisi per realem sui cum altero illo communicationem. 2) Christus constans e natura divina & humana est vna persona: Ergo vnam habet hypostasin, siue personalitatem. Nam vbi gemina est personalitas, ibi duae sunt personae. Hinc vlterius colligimus: Quicumque constans ex natura divina & humana vnam habet hypostasin, in eodem vel natura divina suam hypostasin communicavit naturae humanae; vel natura humana suam hypostasin communicavit naturae divinae, vel denique ex hypostasi naturae divinae & hypostasi naturae humanae vna est conflata. At neque natura humana naturae divinae suam subsistentiam communicavit, eo, quod ὁ λόγος ab aeterno modo perfectissimo subsistit, caro demum in tempore exsistere, atque ἐν λόγῳ subsistere coepit: neque ex hypostasi τῷ λόγῳ & hypostasi carnis vna orta est hypostasis, quia haec notat modum subsistendi incommunicabilem & vltimo completum. At e duobus incommunicabilibus, & vltimo completis, tertium incommunicabile & vltimo completum conflari, simpliciter impossibile est. Ergo natura divina humanae suam communicavit hypostasin. 3) Si ὁ λόγος assumtae carni suam hypostasin non communicasset, filius Mariae virginis non diceretur filius altissimi. At ita recte dicitur, Luc. I, 35. Ergo. Consequentia probatur: quia ad veritatem illius propositionis requiritur, vt filius Mariae personaliter idem sit, qui est Filius Dei, vel ipsam hypostasin Filii Dei habeat: quam quomodo haberet humana Christi natura, nisi a divina communicatam accepisset? (*).


### Q. XXII. What is the communication of the hypostasis, or subsistence?: Dicis: I

Dicis: I. Hypostasis is a mode of subsisting that is incommunicable:

Therefore the hypostasis of the Word (τοῦ λόγου) could not be communicated to the assumed flesh. Resp. Hypostasis is incommunicable to another person ultimately subsisting; it is not incommunicable to another nature, which is destitute of its own subsistence.

Dicis: II.

If the Word (ὁ λόγος) communicated its own subsistence to the human nature, the human nature will be a person; and thus there will be two persons in Christ, which is Nestorian. The consequence is evident; because whatever ultimately subsists is a person.

Resp. I deny the consequence.

For human nature is not a person for this reason, because it has a communicated subsistence; to the end, or, to speak more in Latin, for what counsel and purpose did the divine nature of Christ receive human nature into its own hypostasis (ὑπόστασιν)?

For it was an altogether singular and incomparable end, not fitting to any created things; neither to a mortal, nor to an angel. It was, indeed, a vicarious satisfaction to be rendered to God for all men and for each individual, the reconciliation of God and men. To accomplish so great a task, two things were altogether necessary: of which one was a most perfect obedience, to be rendered both by doing and by suffering; the other, indeed, was the infinite price of it, equal to placating the infinite God and sufficient for the task. Both are contained in this one saying, Heb. 12 .

But the former was proper to human nature, while this latter was of the divinity. I shall complete the argument: If two things are required for one end, one to be attributed to the divine nature, the other to the human, and in such a way that each must be joined as if by a most tight bond for the consummation of one effect and work, to be performed by one and the same subject: it is necessary that the two natures be joined in one subject.

Therefore, the one Reconciler of God and men cannot but be one person, in whom there are two natures. Right reason and an illuminated mind detect nothing here that is absurd, nothing that is repugnant to itself.

But he thinks absurdly who, proceeding from human affairs, indeed even from common and perpetual ones, to a divine matter, and one that is altogether singular, concludes.

There is no man who can co-opt another nature into his own hypostasis (ὑπόστασιν): Therefore, could not God do this?

Is there, then, no difference between God and men, let alone an infinite one?

The finite is not capable of the infinite.

I concede this, as far as comprehension goes.

Human nature does not grasp and comprehend the divine nature in Christ: Rightly so.

Who denies it?

Therefore, also as it pertains to the conjunction to be received and perpetually retained?

Will the infinite also not be capable of the finite, so that it can join this whole to itself and assume it into its own hypostasis (ὑπόστασιν)?

Either you will rashly deny every union by which God can be present to created things; or you will easily grant me this: If God can join himself, as he wills, with all his effects, but especially with men, παραστατικῶς (in a way that stands by/supports), so that in him we live, and move, and have our being, Acts 17, 28 .

Why could he not himself join human nature to himself in a singular way, by a most tight bond, ὑποστατικῶς (hypostatically)?

Nor is there the danger, which PETRUS BAYLIUS fears in vain, that our opinion leads to skepticism.

He argued in a wondrous way: If the conjunction of soul with body is not sufficient for the person of a man (a thing which, as he says, the example of Christ taught us): it follows that no one can know for certain that he is a person.

Who does not see that the consequence is of no validity, which is led from the altogether singular condition of one man, and not φιλανθρώπης (philanthropic/loving mankind), born for the salvation of all, to the common lot of all men?

We also deny, and utterly deny, the antecedent.

Who ever said, or what Theology of ours taught, that the coupling of soul and body is not sufficient to constitute the person of a man, insofar as he is a man?

Who among our people attributed to Christ a person, philosophically so called, that is human?

We all with one mouth and mind profess his divine person, and in it his human nature, and are most certainly persuaded that the conjunction of soul with body was not sufficient for the person of Christ and God-man (θεανθρώπης), not insofar as he is a man, but insofar as he is Christ and God-man (θεανθρώπης), the one mediator (μεσίτης), interceding between God and men.

That the divine nature of Christ should assume human nature into its own hypostasis (ὑπόστασιν), that was necessary not for the truth and integrity of the human nature, which he himself assumed, so that Christ might be a man, but for that altogether singular end, that he might be the mediator (ὁ μεσίτης) and God-man (θεανθρώπης), for whom this was the purpose, that he might perfectly perform the parts of a Reconciler of peace between God and men.

catam; but by that very fact it is not a person, but is personated, namely participatively, having personality, not independently, and αὐθυποστάτως (self-subsistently). Not everything that subsists in any way is a person, but that which is αὐθυπόστατον (self-subsistent), i.e., that which subsists by itself and incommunicably, and does not depend on another in subsisting.

You say: III. To whom the hypostatic character of the Word (τοῦ λόγου) is not communicated, to him also the hypostasis of the same is not communicated: But it is not communicated to the human nature &c. Therefore. The major is clear: since the hypostatic character of the Son of God does not really differ from the hypostasis itself, but is constituted in the being of the son through it. The minor is proved: because the hypostatic character of the Son of God is eternal passive generation; which is not communicated to the human nature. I respond: the hypostatic character of the Son of God, properly speaking, is not generation, but filiation, although its foundation is generation. Into the communion of filiation, indeed, the human nature has been received, because Christ the God-man (θεάνθρωπος) is one proper and natural Son of God, subsisting in two natures, divine and human.

Instance: The Son of God is the proper & natural [Son], begotten from eternity: The human nature of Christ is not begotten from eternity: E. The human nature of Christ is not the natural & proper Son of God. I concede the whole argument. For Son of God is a name of a person. Therefore just as we do not say: the human nature is a hypostasis, or person, but ἐνυπόστατος (ensubsistent) & personated; so also we do not say: the human nature is the Son of God begotten from eternity, but it has been assumed into the filiation of the Son of God, begotten from eternity. Whence in concreto: the Son of the virgin Mary, the Son of God, begotten from eternity, is rightly said. Cf. John 1:14.

Latin:

Dicis: I. Hypostasis est modus subsistendi incommunicabilis:

Ergo hypostasis τοῦ λόγου non potuit assumtae carni communicari. Resp. Hypostasis est incommunicabilis alteri personae ultimate subsistenti; non est incommunicabilis alteri naturae, propria subsistentia destitutae.

Dicis: II.

Si ὁ λόγος suam subsistentiam humanae naturae communicauit, humana natura erit persona; adeoque duae erunt in Christo personae, quod est Nestorianum. Consequentia est euidens; quia, quidquid ultimate subsistit, persona est.

Resp. Neg. consequentiam.

Nam humana natura ideo non est persona, quia subsistentiam habet communicatam;

in finem, siue, vt magis latine dicam, quo consilio ac proposito diuina Christi natura in suam ὑπόστασιν receperit humanam naturam? Quippe omnino singularis atque incomparabilis finis erat, nulli rerum creatarum; neque mortali, neque angelo conueniens. Erat nimirum satisfactio vicaria pro hominibus vniuersis ac singulis Deo praestanda, Dei hominumque reconciliatio. Ad tantum negotium conficiendum, omnino duo erant necessaria: quorum quidem unum erat obedientia perfectissima, cum peragendo, tum perferendo praestanda; alterum uero infinitum eius pretium, infinito Deo placando par satisque idoneum. Vtrumque continetur vno hocce dicto, Hebr.

12 . Atqui prius illud erat humanae naturae proprium, hoc autem alterum diuinitatis erat.

Perficiam argumentationem: Si duo sunt ad unum finem requisita, alterum diuinae naturae, alterum humanae tribuendum, & ita quidem, vt utrumque arctissimo uelut uinculo coniunctum esse debeat ad consummationem unius effectus atque operis, ab uno eodemque subiecto perficiendi: necesse est, duas naturas esse in uno subiecto coniunctas. E. unus Dei hominumque Reconciliator non potest non una persona esse, in qua duae sunt naturae.

Nihil hic deprehendit recta ratio & mens illuminata, quod absurdum sit, nihil, quod sibi repugnet.

Is uero absurde cogitat, qui a rebus humanis, immo etiam communibus ac perpetuis, ad rem diuinam, eamdemque prorsus singularem, procedendo concludit.

Nullus homo est, qui possit aliam quamdam naturam in suam ὑπόστασιν cooptare: Ergo nec Deus id ualeat?

Nullane igitur inter Deum ac homines interest differentia, nedum infinita?

Finitum non est capax infiniti.

Concedo, quantum ad comprehensionem.

Humana natura non capit & comprehendit diuinam in Christo naturam: Recte.

Quis negat?

Ergo etiam quod attinet ad coniunctionem accipiendam perpetuoque retinendam?

Itane etiam infinitum non erit capax finiti, vt illud possit hoc totum secum coniungere atque in suam ὑπόστασιν adsumere?

Aut temere negabis omnem vnionem, qua Deus possit rebus creatis adesse; aut facile mihi hoc dabis: Si Deus cum effectibus suis quibusque, praesertim uero cum hominibus, se potest, ut uolet, coniungere παραστατικῶς, ut in ipso uiuamus, moueamur, & simus, Act.

17, 28 . quidni possit ipse humanam naturam secum coniungere singulari quodam modo, arctissimo uinculo, ὑποστατικῶς; Nec est periculum, quod frustra metuit PETRVS BAYLIVS, ne scepticismo nostra sententia.

Argumentatus est ille mirum in modum: Si ad personam hominis non sufficit coniunctio animi cum corpore (id quod, ut ait, exemplum Christi nos docuit): sequitur, ut nemo possit certo scire, se esse personam.

Quis non uidet, minime ualere consequentiam, quae a conditione prorsus singulari unius hominis, nec φιλανθρώπης, in salutem omnium nati, ad communem hominum omnium sortem ducitur?

Negamus etiam, ac pernegamus antecedens.

Quis unquam dixit, aut quae nostra Theologia docuit, copulationem animi corporisque non esse sufficientem ad constituendam personam hominis, quatenus est homo?

Quis Nostratium Christo adseruit personam, philosophice sic dictam, humanam?

Diuinam eius personam, in eaque humanam naturam omnes uno ore atque animo profitemur, certissimeque persuasi sumus, coniunctionem animi cum corpore non suffecisse ad personam Christi ac θεανθρώπης, non quoad est homo, sed quatenus est Christus ac θεανθρώπης, unus uel μεσίτης, inter Deum ac homines intercedens.

Vt diuina Christi natura humanam in suam adsumeret ὑπόστασιν, id erat necessarium non ad ueritatem integritatemque humanae, quam ipse adsumsit, naturae, ut Christus esset homo, sed ad finem illum omnino singularem, ut esset ὁ μεσίτης ac θεανθρώπης, cui hoc erat propositum, ut Conciliatoris pacis inter Deum atque homines partibus perfecte fungeretur.

catam; quin eo ipso non persona, sed personata est, participative scil., habens personalitatem, non independenter, & αὐθυποστάτως. Non quidquid quomodocumque subsistit, est persona, sed quod est αὐθυπόστατον, i. e. quod per se & incommunicabiliter subsistit, nec in subsistendo ab alio dependet.

Dicis: III. Cui non est communicatus character hypostaticus τοῦ λόγου, illi etiam non est communicata eiusdem hypostasis: Atqui humanae naturae non est &c. Ergo. Maior est liquida: quoniam character hypostaticus Filii Dei ab ipsa hypostasi realiter non differt, sed per eundem in esse filii constituitur. Minor probatur: quia character hypostaticus Filii Dei est aeterna generatio passiva; quae humanae naturae non est communicata. Resp. character hypostaticus Filii Dei proprie loquendo non est generatio, sed filiatio, quamuis eius fundamentum sit generatio. In communionem filiationis vtique recepta est humana natura, quia Christus θεάνθρωπος est vnus Filius Dei proprius & naturalis, in duabus naturis, divina & humana subsistens.

Instantia: Filius Dei proprius & naturalis est ab aeterno genitus: Humana Christi natura non est ab aeterno genita: E. Humana Christi natura non est Filius Dei naturalis & proprius. Concedo totum argumentum. Nam Filius Dei est nomen personae. Sicut igitur non dicimus: humana natura est hypostasis, aut persona, sed ἐνυπόστατος & personata; ita etiam non dicimus: humana natura est Filius Dei ab aeterno genitus, sed est assumta in filiationem Filii Dei, ab aeterno geniti. Vnde in concreto: Filius Mariae virginis Filius Dei, ab aeterno genitus, recte dicitur. Conf. Io. I, 14.


### Q. XXII. What is the communication of the hypostasis, or subsistence?: Q. XXII. What is the end of the incarnation?

Q. XXII. What is the end of the incarnation?

The proximate end of the incarnation is the redemption of the human race corrupted by sins a): the ultimate end is the glory of God b). Proof a. From the words of Matt. 20:28. The Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom (λύτρον) for many.

Proof b. When the Son of God was exhibited in the flesh, the angels sang, Luke 2:14: Glory to God in the highest. For from the mystery of the incarnation shines forth the glory of divine goodness, justice, wisdom, and omnipotence.

Latin:

Quaest. XXII. Quis est finis incarnationis?

Finis incarnationis proximus est redemtio generis humani peccatis corrupti a): finis vltimus est gloria Dei b). Prob. a. E verbis Matth. XX, 28. Filius hominis non venit, vt ipsi ministretur, sed vt ipse ministret, & det animam suam (λύτρον) redemtionem pro multis.

Prob. b. Filio Dei in carne exhibito cecinerunt angeli, Luc. II, 14.: Gloria Deo in altissimis. Elucescit quippe ex mysterio incarnationis gloria bonitatis, iustitiae, sapientiae & omnipotentiae diuinae.


### Q. XXIV. Would Christ have come in the flesh, if man had not sinned?

The Son of God would not have assumed flesh, if man had not sinned.

Proof 1) Because, as Holy Scripture teaches, the end of the incarnation is the redemption of the human race. But redemption presupposes sin, and the misery contracted from sin. To avert this, the Son of God put on our flesh. For since the children were made partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise made himself a partaker of them, that through death he might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver them, who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage. Heb. 2:14.

2) The Son of God was to come in the flesh not on the basis of some absolute decree, but he was promised after man had been seduced by the devil, that he might crush the head of the serpent, Gen. 3:15, and might procure blessing in place of the curse, Gen. 12:3. What therefore was done from the evangelical covenant after the fall; that had no place before the fall. Moreover, the promise concerning the sending and coming of the Son of God in the flesh was made by virtue of the evangelical covenant.

The antithesis is that of certain Scholastics (to whom ANDREAS OSIANDER, professor at Königsberg, gave his approval) and the Socinians, who posit that Christ would have come in the flesh even if man had not sinned. Their principal arguments are:

I. Whoever ordained the hypostatic wisdom to undertake the priestly, kingly, and prophetic office before all His works, he decreed to send the eternal Son into the flesh before he decreed to create men or to raise up the fallen: But God the Father, etc. Therefore. The major premise is evident; because the hypostatic wisdom, ordained to an office, is the Son of God. The minor is proved from Prov. VIII, 23, where the Son of God, or heavenly wisdom, says: Jehovah possessed me, the beginning of his way; before his works, from which (it is) from eternity, נסכתי, I was ordained, anointed, inaugurated, viz., to the kingly, priestly, and prophetic office. Resp. 1) The word נסכתי is rendered: I was poured out, and thus the eternal generation of the λόγος is described by this word metaphorically. Not in vain does D. CALOVIUS say in Bibl. illustr. on this passage, fol. 450: Some also trace that personal property in the word נסכתי v. 22, I was anointed, because, by the divine essence being communicated to the Son through eternal generation, divine majesty and dominion over all created things is also communicated. 2) The same author concedes that the anointing here is properly the destination of the eternally begotten Son to the office—not only kingly, but also priestly and prophetic—made from eternity, just as kings, priests, and prophets were accustomed to be inaugurated into their office by anointing. But although that destination of the Son of God to the office preceded the creation and works of the world in the order of divine reason, it did not, however, precede the divine decree concerning the creation of the world; and although that decree concerning sending the Son to the office is eternal and immutable, it is not absolute, but respective, made κατὰ πρόγνωσιν (according to the foreknowledge) of sin.

II. No most glorious act of God depends upon sin: The incarnation of the Son of God is a most glorious act of God: Therefore. Resp. We do not say that the incarnation of the Son of God depends upon sin as a cause; but we assert that sin, foreseen, offered to God the occasion for forming the decree concerning sending his Son into the flesh and delivering the human race from the misery of sin.

III. The Son of God is called the firstborn of creatures, Col. I, 15, because God the Father made the decree concerning sending his Son before [the decree] concerning creating any things or raising up the fallen. Resp. Christ is called the firstborn of every creature, not because he was begotten in creation or among creatures; but because he was begotten before every creature. Which predicate belongs to him by reason of his divine nature, not in respect of the incarnation.

IV. Whatever contributes much both to the manifestation of divine goodness and to the sublimity of the human race, that God would have procured, even if man had not sinned: But the incarnation of the Son of God, etc. Therefore. The major is evident; because God wills his goodness to be declared and man's excellence to be promoted, even with no sin existing. The minor is proved because 1) the incarnation of the λόγος is a signal document of divine goodness: for while the λόγος assumes flesh, the divine and human nature are most sweetly united, so that man may not doubt the love of God. 2) Through the incarnation, human nature is exalted into the person of the λόγος, which sublimity of human nature is incomparable. Resp. 1) Before the fall, God manifested his goodness most clearly through the bestowal of his image upon man; he would have declared it more clearly in the blessed life, if man had never sinned. 2) Nothing would have been lacking to the essential perfection or excellence of man, even if human nature had never been raised into the hypostasis of the λόγος; just as the nature of the angels confirmed in good remains excellent, although it is constituted outside the hypostasis of the λόγος.

Quest. XXV. Was the incarnation of the Son of God necessary?

The incarnation of the Son of God was not necessary absolutely a); but given this hypothesis, that God wished to receive fallen man into grace and save him eternally while preserving His justice b).

Proof a. The incarnation of the Son of God would not have been necessary if man had persisted in a state of integrity. Nor was it simply necessary in the state of misery after the fall; for the reason that God could have most justly punished man, who had fallen into sin, with eternal torments.

Proof b. The incarnation of the Word (τοῦ λόγου), as far as is evident from the scriptures, was necessary from the hypothesis: if God decreed to raise up fallen man and endow him with heavenly beatitude. 1) There is salvation in no one else (than Jesus). For neither is there any other name under heaven, which is given among men, in which it behooves us to be saved, says Peter, Acts IV, 12. 2) No one can lay another foundation of salvation besides that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ, 1 Cor. III, 11. 3) If another remedy had existed against sin, God would have spared His own Son. But He did not spare Him, but delivered Him up for us unto most bitter death, so that with Him He might freely give us all things necessary for salvation. Rom. VIII, 32. Therefore, an insoluble damnation would have remained without the incarnate Word, says AUGUSTINE in sermon V on the nativity.

You say: I. In fact, indeed, there is salvation in no one else than in Jesus: from this, however, it cannot be gathered that God had no other means of restoring the salvation of men than the incarnation of His Son.

Resp. The Apostle Peter, in the place cited, does not only say that there is salvation in no one else than in Jesus; but he also adds that no other name under heaven has been given in which it behooves us to be saved, so as to indicate that the salvation of the human race depended upon the satisfaction of the Son of God as a person, which the incarnation of the Word (τοῦ λόγου) necessarily preceded.

You say: II. God, the absolute Lord of all creatures, could have absolutely justified the sinful man by His power and received him into grace, without the intervention of satisfaction: Therefore, the incarnation was not necessary.

Resp. What God can do by absolute power is not clearly evident to us, as scripture is silent, for He can do more abundantly than we understand, Eph. III, 20. Our discussion is about the ordained power of God, by which God, while preserving His justice, could not receive the sinner into grace without satisfaction. For every earthly judge who justifies the wicked is an abomination to God, Prov. XVII, 15. Therefore, it is repugnant to the essential justice of God to justify the wicked without the intervention of satisfaction, for the performance of which the incarnation of the Son of God was necessary.

Latin:

Filius Dei non assumsisset carnem, si homo non peccasset.

Prob. 1) Quia, docente sacra scriptura, finis incarnationis est redemtio generis humani. Redemtio autem praesupponit peccatum, & miseriam e peccato contractam. Hanc vt auerteret Filius Dei, nostram induit carnem. Nam quoniam pueri participes facti sunt carnis & sanguinis, & ipse similiter participem se fecit ipsorum, vt per mortem aboleret eum, qui virtutem habebat mortis, hoc est diabolum, & dimitteret eos, quotquot timore mortis per omnem vitam obnoxii erant servituti. Hebr. II, 14.

2) Filius Dei in carnem venturus erat non ex absoluto aliquo decreto, sed promissus est, postquam homo a diabolo seductus erat, vt caput serpentis contereret, Gen. III, 15. & pro maledictione benedictionem conciliaret, Gen. XII, 3. Quod ergo ex foederis euangelici post lapsum factum est; id ante lapsum locum non habuit. Promissio autem de mittendo & venturo Filio Dei in carnem facta est vi foederis euangelici.

Antithesis est quorundam Scholasticorum (quibus album calculum adjecit ANDREAS OSIANDER, professor Regiomontanus) & Socinianorum, statuentium, Christum in carnem venturum fuisse, licet homo non peccasset. Quorum praecipua sunt argumenta:

I. Quicunque sapientiam hypostaticam ordinavit ad obeundum officium sacerdotale, regium & propheticum, ante omnia opera sua, is decrevit aeternum filium mittere in carnem prius, quam decrevit homines creare, aut lapsos erigere: Atqui Deus Pater &c. Ergo. Maior constat; quia sapientia hypostatica, ad officium ordinata, est Filius Dei. Minor prob. e Prou. VII, 23. vbi Filius Dei, siue sapientia coelestis, inquit: Iehovah possedit me, principium viae suae; ante opera eius, ex quo (est) ab aeterno, נסכתי, ordinata, inuncta, inaugurata sum, scil. ad officium regium, sacerdotale & propheticum. Resp. 1) verbum נסכתי redditur: effusa sum, adeoque aeterna τῆς λόγος generatio hac voce μεταφορικῶς describitur. Haud ex vano inquit D. CALOVIVS in bibl. illustr. in h. l. fol. 450.: Nonnulli eam proprietatem personalem etiam indagant in voce נסכתי v. 22., inuncta sum, quod, communicata Filio per aeternam generationem diuina essentia, communicata etiam fit diuina maiestas & imperium super omnes res creandas. 2) Concedit idem, quod vnctio hic proprie fit Filii ab aeterno geniti ad officium non regium tantum, sed etiam sacerdotale ac propheticum destinatio ab aeterno facta, quemadmodum reges, sacerdotes & prophetae ad officium suum per vnctionem inaugurari solebant. At licet destinatio illa Filii Dei ad officium in signo rationis diuinae antecesserit creationem & opera mundi, non tamen antecessit decretum diuinum de mundo creando; & quamuis decretum illud de mittendo filio ad officium sit aeternum & immutabile, non tamen est absolutum, sed respectiuum, factum κατὰ πρόγνωσιν peccati.

II. Nullus actus Dei gloriosissimus dependet a peccato: Incarnatio Filii Dei est actus Dei gloriosissimus: Ergo. Resp. Non dicimus, incarnationem Filii Dei dependere a peccato, velut causa; sed asserimus, peccatum praeuisum obtulisse Deo occasionem ad formandum decretum de mittendo filio suo in carnem & liberandum genus humanum a miseria peccati.

III. Filius Dei dicitur primogenitus creaturarum, Col. I, 15. quia Deus Pater de mittendo filio suo decretum fecit prius, quam de vllis rebus creandis, aut lapsis erigendis. Resp. Christus dicitur primogenitus omnis creaturae, non quia genitus est in creatione, aut inter creaturas; sed quia genitus est ante omnem creaturam. Quod praedicatum ipsi competit ratione naturae diuinae, non respectu incarnationis.

IV. Quidquid multum facit tum ad manifestationem bonitatis diuinae, tum ad sublimitatem generis humani, illud Deus procurasset, licet homo non peccasset: Atqui incarnatio Filii Dei &c. E. Maior est euidens; quia Deus suam bonitatem declaratam, & hominis excellentiam vult promotam, nullo exsistente peccato. Minor prob. quia 1) incarnatio τοῦ λόγος est insigne documentum diuinae bonitatis: dum enim ὁ λόγος carnem assumit, diuina & humana natura suauissime vniuntur, vt homo de amore Dei nullus dubitet. 2) Per incarnationem natura humana in personam τοῦ λόγος est exaltata, quae sublimitas humanae naturae est incomparabilis. Resp. 1) Deus ante lapsum collatione imaginis suae erga hominem suam bonitatem manifestauit clarissime; clarius eam in vita beata declaraturus, si homo nunquam peccasset. 2) Essentiali hominis perfectioni aut excellentiae nil decessisset, licet humana natura in hypostasin τοῦ λόγος nunquam fuisset euecta; sicut natura angelorum in bono confirmatorum manet excellens, tametsi extra hypostasin τοῦ λόγος sit constituta.

Quaest. XXV. Fuitne incarnatio Filii Dei necessaria?

Necessaria fuit incarnatio Filii Dei non absolute a); sed posita hac hypothesi, quod Deus hominem lapsum salva iustitia sua in gratiam recipere, & aeternum salvare voluerit b).

Prob. a. Non necessaria fuisset incarnatio Filii Dei, si homo in statu integritatis perstitisset. Neque simpliciter necessaria fuit in statu miseriae post lapsum; propterea, quod Deus hominem in peccata prolapsum iure iustissimo aeternis mactare poenis poterat.

Prob. b. Incarnatio τοῦ λόγου, quantum e scripturis patet, necessaria fuit ex hypothesi: si Deus decrevit hominem lapsum erigere, & caelesti donare beatitate. 1) non est in alio ullo (quam Iesu) salus. Neque enim nomen est aliud sub caelo, quod datum inter homines, in quo oporteat salvari nos, ait Petrus, Act. IV, 12. 2) Fundamentum salutis aliud nemo potest ponere, praeter positum, quod est Iesus Christus, 1 Cor. III, 11. 3) Si aliud remedium exstitisset aduersus peccatum, Deus proprio pepercisset filio . At huic non pepercit, sed illum pro nobis tradidit in mortem acerbissimam, vt cum illo nobis omnia ad salutem necessaria gratis donaret. Rom. VIII, 32. Ergo insolubilis damnatio mansisset fine verbo incarnato, inquit AVGVSTIN. sermone V. de nati.

Dicis: I. De facto quidem in nullo alio est salus, quam in Iesu: exinde tamen colligere haud licet, quod Deo nulla alia media reparandae salutis hominum fuerint, quam incarnatio filii fui.

Resp. Apostolus Petrus l. c. non tantum dicit, quod in nullo alio, quam in Iesu sit salus; sed addit etiam, quod nullum aliud nomen sub caelo datum sit, in quo nos salvari oporteat, vt indicet, salutem generis humani dependisse a Filii Dei, tanquam personae satisfactione, quam necessario antecessit incarnatio τοῦ λόγου.

Dicis: II. Deus, absolutus omnium creaturarum dominus, poterat hominem peccatorem potentia sua absolute iustificare & in gratiam recipere, citra interuentum satisfactionis: E. incarnatio non fuit necessaria.

Resp. Quid Deus absoluta potestate facere queat, nobis, tacente scriptura, liquido non constat, potest enim abundantius facere, quam nos intelligimus, Eph. III, 20. Sermo nobis est de potentia Dei ordinata, qua Deus, salua iustitia sua, citra satisfactionem, peccatorem in gratiam recipere nequiuit. Nam omnis iudex terrestris, iustificans impium, Deo est abominabilis, Prou. XVII, 15. Ergo repugnat iustitiae Dei essentiali, iustificare impium citra interuentum satisfactionis, quae vt praestaretur, necessaria fuit incarnatio Filii Dei.


### Quest. XXVI. Has the Son of God, the redeemer of the human race, already been incarnated?

The Son of God, who is the promised Messiah and redeemer of the human race, has already come into the flesh long ago.

Proof. 1) Because the scepter has already been taken away from the tribe of Judah long ago. But the scepter ought not to have been completely removed from the tribe of Judah until Shiloh should come, that singular peacemaker, namely the Messiah. For thus holds the swan song of the aged prophet Jacob, Gen. XLIX, 10. The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver (born) from between his feet, until Shiloh comes, and to him shall be the gathering of the peoples.

Obs. 1) Shiloh is most conveniently derived from שָׁלוֹם (he was tranquil), and thus denotes the tranquilizer, or the author of eternal peace and tranquility, so that the sense is: Judah will indeed be conflicted by various evils, yet the scepter will not depart entirely until let the peacemaker come, who may bring true peace to it. עַד כִּי, until, does not imply, at that moment in which Shiloh shall come, that the Jewish government and Sanhedrin must be cast down suddenly and as if by one blow; rather, it admits a certain latitude in this way: Around that time in which Shiloh shall come, it may indeed happen that the Jewish polity may incline and gradually begin to collapse, yet it will not be utterly abolished before he comes. Indeed, the Jews were indeed sent under the yoke of servitude by the Romans before the advent of Christ, yet they were permitted to live by their own laws, and thus they enjoyed a certain αὐτονομία [autonomy], especially when Herod lived by Jewish customs. The scepter of Judah was therefore shaken by Pompey and Herod, but it was broken finally not long after the advent of the Messiah, and clearly removed by Vespasian, who leveled the city of Jerusalem to the ground. Wherefore, the Jewish republic being utterly overturned, we conclude most validly: The scepter has long since been taken away from the tribe of Judah: Therefore, the Messiah has long since come. 2) The Jerusalem temple has long since been destroyed, and has remained destroyed for many centuries from then; although the Messiah ought to have come before the destruction of the second temple, to be destroyed indeed a little later with a notable commotion of the whole Jewish people and of the religion itself. See Hag. II, 7, compared with Heb. XII, 26, Mal. III, 1. 3) The family of David has so perished that it cannot be demonstrated by any suitable argument who, or which man or woman, is descended from that family, yet the promised Messiah ought to have come while the family of David was still surviving; since he was to be born from it, and was then known, so that he could be recognized as the son of David from it. See Ps. LXXXIX, 30, 37, 2 Sam. VII, 16, Jer. XXIII, 5, ch. XXXIII, 15, Mic. V, 2, Isa. VII, 14. 4) The seventy weeks of Daniel have without doubt long since elapsed; which not even the Jews can deny, even if you were to grant them the calculation which they wish to be observed in counting the kings of Persia and the years of their empire. But the Messiah ought to have come before the completion of the course of those weeks, as witnessed by Dan. IX, 24. That the term from which the seventy annual weeks of Daniel are to be reckoned is the seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus (in which Ezra came to Jerusalem at the special command and decree of King Artaxerxes, to restore the city that had been torn down, and to restore the polity, both ecclesiastical and civil: See Ezra VII, 8, seqq.) and that the term to which it is to be ordered so that the passion of the Savior falls in the middle of the last week, has been demonstrated by firm arguments by D. CALOVIUS in bibl. illustr. in h. l. p. 653, seqq., with whom compare D. PFEIFFER'S dubia vexata p. 911. 5) Not only have the gentile oracles failed; but also the Levitical ceremonies have been abrogated, and the sacrificial fire itself has been extinguished. Now indeed, the gentile oracles ought to have failed gradually under the advent of the Messiah, and the Levitical ceremonies with the sacrificial fire ought to have been extinguished, Zech. XIII, 2, 4, Jer. III, 16, Dan. IX, 26, 27. 6) Whatever has been predicted in the Old Testament concerning the Messiah, or the redeemer of the human race, and which looks toward demonstrating and recognizing him, is so constituted that all things flow together into some certain person who was born long ago, and can be explained most fittingly concerning him; which person we are now about to solidly demonstrate to be Jesus of Nazareth.

Latin:

Filius Dei, qui est promissus Messias & redemtor generis humani, iam pridem in carnem venit.

Prob. 1) Quia sceptrum a tribu Iuda iam pridem sublatum est. At non debuit sceptrum a tribu Iuda penitus auferri, donec veniret Schiloh, pacificator ille singularis, scilicet Messias. Ita enim habet cygnaeum annofi vatis Iacobi carmen, Gen. XLIX, 10. Non recedet sceptrum de Iuda, nec legislator (natus) a pedibus eius, vsque dum veniat Schiloh, & huic fit adhaesio populorum.

Obs. 1) Schiloh commodissime deducitur a שָׁלוֹם tranquillum fuit, adeoque notat tranquillatorem, seu aeternae pacis & tranquillitatis auctorem, vt sensus fit: Variis malis quidem conflictabitur Iuda, non tamen prorsus recedet sceptrum, donec pacificator veniat, qui illi veram pacem afferat. עַד כִּי, donec, non infert, eo momento, quo Schiloh veniet, repente & quasi vno ictu deiiciendum regimen & synedrium Iudaicum; verum admittit quandam latitudinem hoc modo: Circa illud tempus, quo Schiloh veniet, poterit quidem fieri, vt inclinet, & paullatim incipiat ruere politia Iudaica, non tamen penitus abolebitur, antequam veniat. Nimirum Iudæi erant quidem sub iugum seruitutis missi a Romanis, ante Christi aduentum, permittebantur tamen suis viuere legibus, adeoque qualicunque gaudebant αὐτονομίᾳ, præsertim cum Herodes Iudaicis viueret moribus. Conquassatum itaque est sceptrum Iudæ a Pompeio & Herode, fractum vero tandem non diu post Messiæ aduentum, & plane sublatum a Vespasiano, qui vrbem Hierosolymam solo æquauit. Quapropter, funditus euerfa republica iudaica, validissime concludimus: Sceptrum a tribu Iudæ iam dudum est ablatum: E. Messias iam pridem venit. 2) Templum Hierosolymitanum iam dudum destructum est, & plurimis abhinc sæculis destructum mansit; cum tamen Messias venire debuerit ante destructionem templi secundi, destruendi quidem paullo post cum insigni totius populi Iudaici commotione & ipsius religionis. Vid. Hag. II, 7. collat. Hebr. XII, 26. Mal. III, 1. 3) Familia Dauidis adeo interiit, vt nullo idoneo argumento demonstrari possit, quis, vel quæ ex familia ista vir, mulierue oriundi sint, iam vero promissus Messias venire debuit familia Dauidis, tum superstite; quoniam, ex illa nascendus erat, tum nota, vt ex ea tanquam filius Dauidis cognosci posset. Vid. Ps. LXXXIX, 30. 37. 2 Sam. VII, 16. Ier. XXIII, 5. c. XXXIII, 15. Mich. V, 2. Ef. VII, 14. 4) Septuaginta septimanæ Danielis sine dubio pridem elapsæ sunt; quod nec Iudæi infitias ire possunt, etiamsi ipsis concesseris, quem in numerandis Persiæ regibus, annisque imperii eorum obseruari velint calculum. At Messias ante completum septimanarum istarum decursum venire debuit, teste Dan. IX, 24. Terminum a quo septuaginta hebdomadum annuarum Danielis esse annum septimum Artaxerxis Longimani (quo Esra ad peculiare mandatum & diploma regis Artaxerxis venit Hierosolymam, vrbem dirutam instauraturus, & politiam tum ecclesiasticam, tum ciuilem restituturus: Vid. Esræ VII, 8. seqq.) & terminum ad quem ita ordinandum esse, vt in vltimæ septimanæ medium incidat passio Saluatoris, firmis argumentis demonstrauit D. CALOVIVS in bibl. illustr. in h. l. p. 653. seqq. cum quo conf. D. PFEIEFFERI dubia vexata p. 911. 5) Non tantum oracula gentilia defecerunt; sed & cærimoniæ Leuiticæ abrogatæ sunt, ipseque ignis sacrificialis exstinctus est. Iam vero oracula gentilia sub Messiæ aduentum paullatim deficere, & cærimoniæ Leuiticæ cum igne sacrificiali exstingui debuerunt, Zach. XIII, 2. 4. Ierm. III, 16. Dan. IX, 26. 27. 6) Quæcunque in veteri testamento de Messia, siue redemtore generis humani, prædicta sunt, & ad eum demonstrandum atque agnoscendum spectant, ita se habent, vt in certam aliquam personam, quæ pridem nata est, omnia confluant, & de ea conuenientissime explicari queant; quam personam esse Iesum Nazarenum iam solide demonstraturi sumus.


### Quest. XXVI. Has the Son of God, the redeemer of the human race, already been incarnated?: Question XXVII. Is Jesus of Nazareth the true Messiah promised in the O.t.?

Question XXVII. Is Jesus of Nazareth the true Messiah promised in the O.T.?

Jesus of Nazareth, in whom, as the author of eternal salvation, we Christians sincerely believe, is the true Messiah, in whom all the prophecies of the O.T. published concerning the Messiah square exactly (*).

Proof.

Prob. 1) Whoever is God and man, he is the true Messiah: But Jesus of Nazareth, etc. Therefore. The major is evident from 2 Sam. VII, 12. 13. Ps. CX, 1. Mic. V, 1. Jer. XXIII, 5. The minor is established: the first of these propositions, which the Jews profess with us, is supported by the prophecies of the O.T. by which all the signs of Christ were foretold and determined. The second is confirmed by this, both because the time spoken of for the future Christ has long since passed, and because those things from which certain signs of the coming Christ were to be known have long ceased to exist, e.g., where is the temple today? Where is the family of David? Where is the distinction of the tribes into which the Jewish nation was divided? Where are the genealogies? Finally, the third is effected by this, that all the signs, not even one excepted, agree in Jesus of Nazareth, and thus we see all the predictions fulfilled in him alone. No one else ever showed himself to be such as the Messiah had to show himself, which is so manifest that the Jews themselves, although after our Jesus was brought into the light (for before that no ψευδόχριστος [false Christ] existed), they were deceived by many, yet they could never consistently place faith in any. From which it appears clearer than light that the Jews did not doubt that the time had been completed when the ψευδόχριστοι [false Christs] induced them to follow them credulously. Therefore, the whole proof is to be completed in such a way that we diligently collect the signs of the Messiah foretold by the divine Prophets, and compare them, with none omitted, to those things which have been committed to records concerning the properties and deeds of Jesus of Nazareth. Those signs are indeed

I. The Person, which pertains either generally to both natures, divine and human: that he would be Immanuel, Isa. VII, 14. add. Matt. I, 23. the son of David, and the same David’s Lord, Ps. CX, 1. add. Matt. XXII, 42. 43. (see note to quest. 3.); or specifically to one or the other nature, to the divine indeed, which is that he becomes the second person of the H. Trinity, the Son of God, through eternal generation, Ps. II, 7. Isa. IX, 6. Mic. V, 1. add. Luke I, 32. 35. Gal. IV, 4. Heb. I, 3. 5. but to the human, and its 1) origin, 2) holiness, Ps. XLV, 8. Dan. IX, 24. Isa. LIII, 9. add. Heb. I, 9. Luke I, 35. John VIII, 46. 1 Pet. II, 22. 3) perpetuity, that the human nature of Christ is never to be separated from the divine, and much less to be destroyed, nay rather, the body of Christ would be entirely devoid of corruption, even though lifeless, Ps. XVI, 10. add. Acts II, 27. seqq. As far as the origin pertains, various surrounding circumstances are determined: α) Whence?

We have four indications, of which the first indeed signifies from which nation the Messiah was to be born, Gen. XXII, 18. add. Gal. III, 16. Rom. IX, 4. John IV, 22; the second, from which tribe, Gen. XLIX, 10. add. Heb. VII, 14. Acts XIII, 22. 23. Rev. V, 5; the third, from which family, namely David’s, Jer. XXIII, 5. XXXIII, 15. conf. with Matt. XXII, 42. but yet one greatly attenuated and diminished, Isa. XI, 1. conf. with Rev. V, 5. and add the genealogy of our Jesus, recorded in writing by Matthew and Luke, the difficulties of which are solved, besides many and supreme men, by the Blessed GOTTFR. OLEARIVS in the excellent book which he entitled: Iesus der wahre Messias; finally, the fourth, from which mother, namely from a virgin, Isa. VII, 14. for thus Christ had to be the seed of the woman, not of the man, in accordance with the πρωτευαγγελίῳ [protoevangelium], Gen. III, 15. add. Luke I, 34. 35. Matt. I, 23. β) Where on earth?

Namely in the land of Canaan, and specifically in the town of Bethlehem, Mic. V, 1. add. Matt. II, 4. 5. Luke II, 4. γ) When? There were three marks.

It behooved Christ to be born, a) while the government still lasted in the tribe of Judah, but with affairs inclined almost to ruin, Gen. XLIX, 10. add. Luke II, 1.: b) while the second temple was not yet destroyed, Mal. III, 1. Hag. II, 9. for the word הנה [behold] points out with a finger, as it were, that very temple which was then built, whatever ABARBANEL, with some of his own, may argue to the contrary: c) near the end of the LXX weeks of years, the limit of which is indeed established at the exile of the Jewish land, Dan. IX, 24. end. add.

Matt. XXIV, 15. II. The State, that it would be entirely 1) twofold, and the former indeed of misery and lowest humility, but the latter of highest glory and dignity, 2) both in one and the same Christ, Ps. XXII. whole, CX. v. last, Isa. LIII. whole, conf. with Acts VIII, 34. From which it appears lucidly how absurd is the fable of recent rabbis concerning a double Messiah. III. The Office, whence the name משיח [Messiah], or χριστός [Christ], adhered to him. α) Generally and in universal there are three signs: 1) How manifold; and what kind of office should be entrusted to Christ?

Namely, it is altogether threefold, and indeed of such a kind: the Sacerdotal, Prophetic, and Regal. The saying in which these three offices are jointly foretold, most indeed consider this to be, Isa. XXXIII, 22. These three offices are jointly foretold, most indeed consider this to be, Isa. XXXIII, 22.

it is certain: because the Jews do not deny that Jesus of Nazareth is a true man; but they prove the divinity of Jesus of Nazareth with very many arguments, and especially with miracles performed αὐτοκρατορικῶς (by his own authority) and for his own glory, to which Jesus himself appeals, Matt. XI, 5. John X, 25. 2) Which-

But yet in this place nothing more is signified than the royal office, מַלְכוּת, and its two principal parts, namely the legislative power (although even when clothed in flesh Christ never brought forth new laws, yet he confirmed the old and perfect ones anew by his own authority, using this manner of speaking: ἐγὼ λέγω ὑμῖν [I say to you]), מְחֹקֵק, and the judicial, שָׁפָט. There are indeed other most illustrious utterances of the Prophets, especially two: One, Isa. XI, where there is predicted a) the Priestly office, expressed by the word יְהוָה, v. 3. add. Gen. VIII, 21. and more often in Leviticus, Eph. V, 2: b) the Prophetic office, v. 4. in the latter part, add. 2 Thess. II, 8: c) the Royal office, in the former part of the same verse. The other exists in Ps. XXII. in which is foretold the Priestly office, v. 1-22. then the Prophetic, v. 23. 26. finally also the Royal, v. 28. to the end.

And this also was to be something peculiar to Christ, that he alone would perform these three offices at once, as God willed and brought it about that they were never joined in one man.

It was never permitted to anyone to administer the province of priest, teacher, and King at the same time. We see the fulfillment in Heb. IV, 14. John III, 2. XVIII, 36. 37. 2) In what manner he himself was to be anointed and inaugurated: namely with oil, not properly so called, Ps. XLV, 8. Isa. XI, 2. LXI, 1. add. John III, 34. Acts X, 38. but especially John I, 33. by this locution, τὸ πνεῦμα μένον ἐπ' αὐτὸν [the Spirit remaining upon him], he manifestly responds to that prediction, as it is in Isaiah XI, 2: נָחָה עָלָיו רוּחַ יְהוָה [the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him]. 3) What forerunner he would use, Mal. III, 1. IV, 5. which the Jews have wrongly interpreted, as is the custom among them even today, concerning Elijah himself, who was to return from heaven to earth, Mark IX, 11. Matt. XI, 14. XVII, 10. ff. Luke I, 17. Mark I, 2. 3. a) It was especially necessary that there should be certain properties and prerogatives of the individual offices, by which this one Priest, Prophet, and supreme Ruler would be distinguished from all others.

There were therefore individually a) Of the Priestly office: 1) That he himself would be a priest after the order of Melchizedek, not of Aaron, Ps. CX, 4. add. Heb. VII. throughout. 2) that he would offer no other victim than himself, Isa. LIII, 10. add. Eph. V, 2. Heb. IX, 25. 26.: 3) that he would be a piacular sacrifice not for his own sins, which were absolutely none, but entirely for ours, himself. Isa. LIII, 5. 6. 7. add. Heb. VII, 26. 27.: 4) that once this victim was slaughtered, and offered to God and accepted, the typical sacrifices of the O.T. would be entirely abolished, and there would be no use for them in the future, no force, no efficacy, Dan. IX, 27. Jer. III, 16. XXX, 31. ff. Ps. XL, 7. 8. add. Heb. VIII, 5. 7. ff.

b) Of the Prophetic office: That this Prophet would be the one greatest of all: 1) like Moses, Deut. XVIII, 15. ff. coll. with XXXIV, 10. 11. 12. add. Acts III, 22. 26.: 2) the common teacher of all nations, Isa. II, 2. 3. 4. IX, 1. ff. add. Matt. IV, 16. Isa. XLII, 6. XLIX, 6. add. Luke II, 32. Acts XIII, 47.: 3) the herald of salvation and justice, to be found in no one else, except in him, Isa. XLV, 22. 24. add. Matt. XI, 28. Acts IV, 12.: 4) most meek, and conspicuous for a truly singular gentleness, Isa. XLII, 2. 3. add. Matt. XI, 5. and that indeed clearly singular and extraordinary, such as no other Prophet ever did, John IX, 32. XV, 24. γ) by prophesying, and also by knowing any secret things whatsoever, Isa. XI, 3. which words ABARBANEL himself interpreted thus: So great will be his prophecy that he will come to know even the secrets of the human heart, although they are declared by no external signs; add. John II, 24. 25. IV, 29. Matt. XXVI, 68.: 6) using also a certain singular manner or method of teaching, namely the parabolic, Ps. LXXVIII, 2. add. Matt. XIII, 35.

c) Of the Royal office: That his kingdom would be 1) spiritual, namely of justice, Isa. XLV, 23. seqq. & of peace, Isa. II, 4. XI, 9. IX, 6. 7. and above all Zach. IX, 9. 10. add. Matt. XXI, 5. vid. Heff. Hebopfer Vol. I. p. 433. 2) universal, so that not only the Jews, but also the profane nations should owe obedience to the empire of Christ alone, and indeed in all regions of the earth, Ps. II, 8. 10, LXXII, 8. 11. add. Rom. XV, 8. 9. Isa. XLV, 23. add. Rom. XIV, 11. even to the supreme Rulers themselves, not excepted. Ps. II, 11, 12: 3) continuous and perpetual, without any either intermission or termination, Ps. XLV, 7. LXXII, 17. Isa. IX, 7. Dan. VII, 13, 14. add. Luke I, 33. Heb. I, 8.

2) Whoever is born of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Judah, of the royal lineage of David, and of an inviolate virgin, he is the true Messiah: But Jesus of Nazareth, etc. Therefore. The major is evident from Gen. XXII, 18; ch. XLIX, 10; 2 Sam. VII, 12; Is. VII, 14. The minor is manifest: because Jesus of Nazareth was born of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Judah, of the royal lineage of David, as witnessed by the genealogy which Luke ch. III, 23 sqq. recounts according to the ascending line, and Matthew ch. I, sqq. according to the descending line; he was also born of a most chaste and inviolate virgin, inasmuch as she had not known a man, Luke II, 34.

3) Whoever is the ruler of Israel, as God, begotten from eternity, as man in the fullness of time, born in Bethlehem, to be magnified unto the ends of the earth, he is the true Messiah: But Jesus of Nazareth, etc. Therefore. The major is clear in the prophecy of Micah ch. V, 1. The minor is confirmed by Matthew ch. II, 6.

4) Whoever had a divinely destined forerunner prepare the way for his coming, he is the true Messiah. But for Jesus of Nazareth, etc. Therefore. The major is evident from Is. LX, 3; Mal. III, 1. The minor is manifest from Mark I, 2, 3.

5) Whoever is the king of Zion who entered Jerusalem poor and humble, riding upon an ass, he is the true Messiah, Zech. IX, 9. But Jesus of Nazareth, etc. Matt. XXI, 5. Therefore.

6) Whoever is the Goel, or redeemer by right of consanguinity, Job XIX, 25; a prophet like Moses, Deut. XVIII, 15; a universal king, Zech. IX, 9; Ps. LXXII, 8; a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, Ps. CX, 4; a priest interceding for sinners, Is. LIII, 12; one about to suffer extreme things, Ps. XXII; Is. LIII; about to die, Dan. IX, 26; to be buried, Is. LIII, 9; to be immune from corruption, to descend into hell and to rise again, Ps. XVI, 10; to ascend into heaven, Ps. LXVIII, 18; to sit at the right hand of God the Father, Ps. CX, 1; he is the promised Messiah. All of which the New Testament proclaims concerning Jesus of Nazareth.

The antithesis is that of the Jews, who maintain that the Messiah has not yet come, and deny that Jesus of Nazareth is the true Messiah. Their principal arguments are:

I. The Messiah is to be called Immanuel, not Jesus, Is. VII, 14. Resp. The name Immanuel is the same as the name Jesus, not as to the sound of the word, but as to the truth of the thing signified. For the name Immanuel implies that God will be with us, not by mere παράστασιν (presence) and gracious assistance, but by the communion of our nature, and thus it is a name of person and office. For just as the name Jesus primarily designates the office, but nevertheless presupposes and connotes the θεάνθρωπον (God-man) person, to whom alone the office of saving belongs; so the name Immanuel primarily designates the θεάνθρωπον person, but at the same time implies the end of the personal union of the divine and human nature, the reconciliation of God and man, and the reduction of man to God, and thus the salvation of the human race. Whence, by the very fact that Christ is Jesus, i.e., Savior, he is also Immanuel, by reason of his person; because no one can save a sinful man from sins, unless he is Immanuel, God and man.

II. The Messiah ought to have come with the scepter removed from Judah: But Jesus came while the scepter was not yet removed: Therefore, Jesus of Nazareth is not the Messiah. The major is evident from the prophecy of the patriarch Jacob, Gen. XLIX, 10. The minor is clear: because, when Jesus was born, Herod was king of the Jews, Matt. II, 3. Resp. The patriarch Jacob did not predict that the scepter was to be removed from Judah before the coming of Shiloh, but that the scepter was not to be removed from Judah before the coming of the Messiah, although he was to live in a restless state and one troubled by various wars . For this reason he predicted that Shiloh, or the peaceful one, would come. *). For this reason he predicted that Shiloh, or

peacemaker, so that pious Israelites, pressed by calamities, might think that the Messiah, the tranquillizer, was to come, by whose benefit they would have peace with God, far nobler than any temporal peace. Furthermore, Herod, an Idumean by nation and a Jew by religion, was indeed not a foreign ruler, yet he was a vassal of the Roman Emperor, and thus the Jewish scepter, upon the arrival of Shiloh, was not indeed completely broken, but it was shaken; which is shown by 1) the census taken by the Emperor Augustus, Luke 2:1. 2) The exaction of tributes through publicans and solemn registrations, Matt. 22:17. 3) The imposition of garrisons and the quartering of Roman soldiers, Matt. 8:9. 4) The lack of capital jurisdiction, John 18:31.

III. The promised Messiah will be the ruler of Israel, Mic. 5:1, who raised up the collapsed kingdom of David, Isa. 9:7, Jer. 33:15: But Jesus of Nazareth never ruled over the Israelites, nor did he raise up the collapsed kingdom of David: Therefore. Resp. The dominion of Jesus of Nazareth, the true Messiah, is spiritual, and that universal, according to the antecedent will of God: although not a few Jews, no less than Gentiles, reject his empire, he nevertheless remains the ruler of the true Israel, which is called the Israel of God, Gal. 6:16. And since an eternal throne was promised to David through the prophets, it is easily gathered that it is established not by bodily force, but by spiritual, for the reason that no bodily throne is eternal.

IV. To the repenting Jews, God promises a reduction into the land of Canaan, Lev. 26:44. Resp. God promised that the Jews in the time of the O.T. were to be reduced into their own land if they performed penance; which happened when they were led back from the Babylonian captivity (cf. Neh. 1:8, 9; Isa. 11:11; Jer. 16:15). But in the time of the N.T. (at which time that external constitution of sacrifices and the Mosaic polity was to be abrogated, and the Canaanite land was to be desolated without hope of restitution, Dan. 9:26), God did not completely cast off the Jews, Rom. 11:2, but if they perform true penance, he receives them into grace; which reception into grace is to be understood according to the nature and condition of the N.T., not of a bodily reduction into the long-desolated Canaan, but a spiritual one to the true church, namely, the heavenly Jerusalem.

Latin:

Quæst. XXVII. Estne Iesus Nazarenus verus Messias in V. T. promissus?

Iesus Nazarenus, in quem, vt auctorem æternæ salutis, nos christiani sincere credimus, est verus Messias, in quem omnia vaticinia V. T. de Messia edita, ad amussim quadrant (*).

Prob.
