Prob. 1) Quicunque est Deus & homo, is est verus Messias: Atqui Iesus Nazarenus &c. E. Maior patet e 2 Sam. VII, 12. 13. Ps. CX, 1. Mich. V, 1. Ier. XXIII, 5. Minor constat: rum propositionum prima, quam nobiscum profitentur Iudaei, fulta est vaticinationibus V. T. quibus omnia signa Christi praenuntiata sunt, ac determinata. Secunda confirmatur eo, tum quod tempus futuro Christo dictum, iam diu praeteriit, tum quod illae res, ex quibus signa quaedam venturi Christi cognoscenda erant, dudum desierunt esse, v. g. vbinam est hodieque templum? vbi familia Dauidis? vbi distinctio tribuum, in quas Iudaica gens diuisa fuit? vbi genealogiae? Tertia denique efficitur eo, quod signa vniuersa, ne vno quidem demto, in Iesum Nazarenum conueniunt, atque adeo praedictiones omnes in vno ipso completas cernimus. Nullus vnquam alius talem se praestitit, qualem Messias se praestare debebat, id quod adeo manifestum est, vt Iudaei ipsi, licet post, quam Iesus noster in lucem editus fuit (ante enim nemo exstitit ψευδόχριστος), a multis fuerint decepti, nulli tamen fidem habere constanter potuerunt. Ex quo luce clarius adparet, Iudaeos non dubitasse, tempus consummatum esse tum, cum ψευδόχριστοι ipsos inducerent, vt creduli eos sequerentur. Tota igitur probatio ita erit perficienda, vt signa Messiae, a Vatibus diuinis praedicta, studiose colligamus, & cum singulis illis, nullo praetermisso, conferamus ea, quae de proprietatibus ac rebus gestis Iesu Nazareni monimentis mandata sunt. Sunt nimirum signa illa

I. Persona, quae pertinent vel generatim ad vtramque naturam, diuinam & humanam: quod futurus sit Immanuel, Ies. VII, 14. add. Matth. I, 23. filius Dauidis, idemque Dauidis Dominus, Ps. CX, 1. add. Matth. XXII, 42. 43. (vid. not. ad quaest. 3.); vel sigillatim ad alterutram naturam, ad diuinam quidem, quod fit secunda SS. Trinitatis persona, Filius Dei, per aeternam generationem, Ps. II, 7. Ies. IX, 6. Mich. V, 1. add. Luc. I, 32. 35. Gal. IV, 4. Hebr. I, 3. 5. ad humanam autem, eiusque 1) originem, 2) sanctitatem, Ps. XLV, 8. Dan. IX, 24. Ies. LIII, 9. add. Hebr. I, 9. Luc. I, 35. Io. VIII, 46. 1 Petr. II, 22. 3) perpetuitatem, quod humana Christi natura nunquam fit a diuina, multoque minus destruenda, immo vero corruptionis omnino expers futurum sit Christi corpus, tametsi exanimatum, Ps. XVI, 10. add. Act. II, 27. seqq. Quod ad originem attinet, variae res circumstantes sunt determinatae: α) Vnde?

Quatuor habemus indicia, quorum quidem primum significat, ex qua gente Messias esset oriundus, Gen. XXII, 18. add. Gal. III, 16. Rom. IX, 4. Io. IV, 22; alterum, ex qua tribu, Gen. XLIX, 10. add. Hebr. VII, 14. Act. XIII, 22. 23. Apoc. V, 5; tertium, ex qua familia, nimirum Dauidis, Ierem. XXIII, 5. XXXIII, 15. conf. cum Matth. XXII, 42. at ea tamen valde attenuata atque imminuta, Ies. XI, 1. conf. cum Apoc. V, 5. & adde genealogiam Iesu nostri, a Matthaeo & Luca litteris consignatam, cuius difficultates soluit, praeter plures ac summos viros, B. GOTTFR. OLEARIVS in libro eximio, quem inferipsit: Iesus der wahre Messias; quartum denique, ex qua matre, videlicet ex virgine, Ies. VII, 14. ita enim Christus debebat esse semen mulieris, non viri, πρωτευαγγελίῳ congruenter, Gen. III, 15. add. Luc. I, 34. 35. Matth. I, 23. β) Vbi terrarum?

Quippe terra Canaan, & oppido quidem Bethlehem, Mich. V, 1. add. Matth. II, 4. 5. Luc. II, 4. γ) Quando? Tres erant notae.

Christum oportebat nasci, a) durahte adhuc regimine in tribu Iuda, sed rebus prope modum ad interitum inclinaris, Gen. XLIX, 10. add. Luc. II, 1.: b) nondum diruto templo secundo, Mal. III, 1. Hagg. II, 9. vocabulum enim הנה digito quasi indice demonstrat illud ipsum templum, quod tunc erat exstructum, quidquid in contrariam partem argumentetur ABARBANEL, cum quibusdam suorum: c) prope finem LXX. hebdomadum annorum, quarum quippe terminus constituitur in exilio terrae Iudaicae, Dan. IX, 24. fin. add. Matth. XXIV, 15.

II. Status, quod is omnino futurus esset 1) duplex, & prior quidem miseriae atque humilitatis infimae, posterior autem gloriae ac dignitatis summae, 2) vterque in vno eodemque Christo, Ps. XXII. tot. CX. v. vlt. Ies. LIII. tot. conf. cum Act. VIII, 34. Ex quo dilucide apparet, quam sit absurda verporum recentiorum fabula de duplici Messia. III. Officii, vnde nomen ipsi haesit משיח, siue χριστός. α) Generaliter atque in vniuersum tria sunt signa: 1) Quotuplex; & quale debeat esse munus Christo mandatum?

Scilicet triplex omnino, & tale quidem; Sacerdotale, Propheticum, Regium. Dictum, quo tria haec officia coniuncta praenuntiantur, plerique quidem existimant hoc esse, Ies. XXXIII, 22. Tria hæc officia coniuncta prænuntiantur, plerique quidem existimant hoc esse, Ies. XXXIII, 22.

constat: quia Iesum Nazarenum esse verum hominem non negant Iudaei; divinitatem autem Iesu Nazareni cum argumenta plurima, tum in primis miracula αὐτοκρατορικῶς & in propriam gloriam edita, ad quae ipse Iesus provocat, Matth. XI, 5. Io. X, 25. probant. 2) Qui-

Verum tamen hoc in loco nihil significatur amplius, quam munus regium, מַלְכוּת, eiusque duae partes praecipuae, nempe potestas legislatoria (quamvis etiam carne indutus Christus nunquam novas tulerit leges, antiquas tamen perfectasque sua auctoritate denuo confirmavit, usitata hac dicendi ratione: ἐγὼ λέγω ὑμῖν), מְחֹקֵק, & iudiciaria, שָׁפָט. Sunt vero alia effata Vatum maxime illustria, in primis duo: Vnum, Ies. XI, vbi praedicitur a) munus Sacerdotale, verbo יְהוָה expressum, v. 3. add. Gen. VIII, 21. & in Levitico saepius, Eph. V, 2: b) munus Propheticum, v. 4. parte altera, add. 2 Thess. II, 8: c) munus Regium, in eiusd. v. parte priori. Alterum exstat in Ps. XXII. in quo praenuntiatur officium Sacerdotale, v. 1-22. deinde Propheticum, v. 23. 26. denique & Regium, v. 28. vsque ad finem.

Atque hoc etiam futurum erat aliquid Christi proprium, quod is vnus tria haecce munera simul esset obiturus, vtpote quae nunquam in vno homine consociata esse Deus voluit ac fiuit.

Nemini vnquam licuit, Sacerdotis, doctoris, simul Regis provinciam administrare. Complementum cernimus Hebr. IV, 14. Io. III, 2. XVIII, 36. 37. 2) Quo ipse modo esset vngendus atque inaugurandus: quippe oleo, non proprie ita dicto, Ps. XLV, 8. Ies. XI, 2. LXI, 1. add. Io. III, 34. Act. X, 38. praesertim vero Io. I, 33. hac loquitio, τὸ πνεῦμα μένον ἐπ' αὐτὸν, manifesto respondet illi praedictioni, vt est apud Iesaiam XI, 2: נָחָה עָלָיו רוּחַ יְהוָה. 3) Quo praecursore vteretur, Mal. III, 1. IV, 5. id quod Iudaei perperam interpretati sunt, vt hodieque iis in more positum est, de Elia ipso, ex caelo in terram redituro, Marc. IX, 11. Matth. XI, 14. XVII, 10. seqq. Luc. I, 17. Marc. I, 2. 3. a) Specialiter necesse erat, vt singulorum munerum certae quaedam essent proprietates ac praerogativae, quibus hic vnus Sacerdos, Propheta & summus Imperans, ab omnibus aliis discerneretur.

Erant igitur singulatim a) Officii Sacerdotalis: 1) Ipsum fore sacerdotem ex ordine Melchisedeci, non Aaronis, Ps. CX, 4. add. Hebr. VII. tot. 2) hostiam immolaturum esse haud aliam, quam semet, Ies. LIII, 10. add. Eph. V, 2. Hebr. IX, 25. 26.: 3) nec pro suis peccatis, quae prorsus nulla essent, sed pro nostris omnino, seipsum fore sacrificium piaculare. Ies. LIII, 5. 6. 7. add. Hebr. VII, 26. 27.: 4) hac victima mactata, Deoque oblata & accepta, fore, vt sacrificia typica V. T. prorsus aboleantur, eorumque nullus in posterum vsus sit, nulla vis, nulla efficacitas, Dan. IX, 27. Ier. III, 16. XXX, 31. seqq. Ps. XL, 7. 8. add. Hebr. VIII, 5. 7. seqq.

b) Officii Prophetici: Quod hic Propheta futurus esset vnus omnium maximus: 1) sicut Moses, Deut. XVIII, 15. seqq. coll. cum XXXIV, 10. 11. 12. add. Act. III, 22. 26.: 2) communis gentium omnium praeceptor, Ies. II, 2. 3. 4. IX, 1. seqq. add. Matth. IV, 16. Ies. XLII, 6. XLIX, 6. add. Luc. II, 32. Act. XIII, 47.: 3) praeco salutis & iustitiae, in nemine alio, nisi in ipso, inueniendae, Ies. XLV, 22. 24. add. Matth. XI, 28. Act. IV, 12.: 4) maxime mansuetus, & prorsus singulari lenitudine conspicuus, Ies. XLII, 2. 3. add. Matth. XI, 5. & ea quidem plane fingulario atque eximia, cuiusmodi alius Propheta nullus vnquam fecit, Io. IX, 32. XV, 24. γ) vaticinando, atque etiam res arcanas quasuis cognoscendo, Ies. XI, 3. quae verba ABARBANEL ipse ita interpretatus est: Tanta erit prophetia eius, vt cordis quoque humani arcana cogniturus sit, quamuis ea nullis indiciis externis declarentur; add. Io. II, 24. 25. IV, 29. Matth. XXVI, 68.: 6) singulari etiam quadam docendi ratione, siue methodo, vtens, nimirum parabolica, Ps. LXXVIII, 2. add. Matth. XIII, 35.

c) Officii Regii: Regnum ipsius fore 1) spirituale, nimirum iustitiae, Ies. XLV, 23. seqq. & pacis, Ies. II, 4. XI, 9. IX, 6. 7. in primisque Zach. IX, 9. 10. add. Matth. XXI, 5. vid. Heff. Hebopfer Vol. I. p. 433. 2) vniversale, vt Christi vnius imperio parere debeant non solum Iudaei, sed & profanae gentes & quidem in omnibus terrae regionibus, Ps. II, 8. 10, LXXII, 8. 11. add. Rom. XV, 8. 9. Ies. XLV, 23. add. Rom. XIV, 11. ipsis quoque summis Imperantibus non exceptis. Ps. II, 11, 12: 3) continuum ac perpetuum, sine vlla aut intermissione, aut terminatione, Ps. XLV, 7. LXXII, 17. Ies. IX, 7. Dan. VII, 13, 14. add. Luc. I, 33. Hebr. I, 8.

2) Quicumque e semine Abrahae, tribu Iuda, stirpe regia Dauidis, & ex illibata virgine natus est, is est verus Messias: Atqui Iesus Nazarenus &c. E. Maior liquet e Gen. XXII, 18. c. XLIX, 10. 2 Sam. VII, 12. Es. VII, 14. Minor patet: quia Iesus Nazarenus natus est e semine Abrahae, tribu Iuda, stirpe regia Dauidis, teste genealogia, quam secundum lineam ascendentem Lucas c. III, 23. sqq. iuxta lineam descendentem Matthaeus c. I, sqq. recenset; natus etiam est e castissima, & illasa virgine, quippe quae virum non cognouerat, Luc. II, 34.

3) Quicumque dominator Israelis, vt Deus, ab aeterno genitus, vt homo in plenitudine temporis, natus est Bethlehemi, vsque ad fines terrae magnificandus, is est verus Messias: Atqui Iesus Nazarenus &c. Ergo. Maior claret in vaticinio Michae c. V, 1. Minorem confirmat Matthaeus c. II, 6.

4) Cuicumque aduenienti diuinitus destinatus praecursor viam parauit, is est verus Messias. Atqui Iesu Nazareno &c. E. Maior liquet ex Es. LX, 3. Mal. III, 1. Minor patet e Marc. I, 2. 3.

5) Quicumque rex Sionis pauper & humilis Hierosolymam ingressus est, inequitans asinae, is est verus Messias, Zach. IX, 9. Atqui Iesus Nazarenus, &c. Matth. XXI, 5. Ergo.

6) Quicumque est Goel, siue redemtor iure consanguinitatis, Iob. XIX, 25. propheta similis Mosi, Deut. XVIII, 15. rex catholicus, Zach. IX, 9. Ps. LXXII, 8. sacerdos secundum ordinem Malkizedek, Ps. CX, 4. sacerdos pro peccatoribus intercedens, Es. LIII, 12. extrema passurus, Ps. XXII. Es. LIII. moriturus, Dan. IX, 26. sepeliendus, Es. LIII, 9. immunis futurus a corruptione, descensurus ad inferos & resurrecturus, Ps. XVI, 10. ascensurus ad caelos, Ps. LXVIII, 18. sessurus ad dextram Dei Patris, Ps. CX, 1. is est promissus Messias. Quae omnia de Iesu Nazareno nouum testamentum praedicat.

Antithesis est Iudaeorum, statuentium, Messiam nondum venisse, & negantium, Iesum Nazarenum esse verum Messiam. Quorum praecipua sunt argumenta:

I. Messias vocandus est Immanuel, non Iesus, Es. VII. 14. Resp. Nomen Immanuel idem est, quod nomen Iesus, non qua sonum vocis, sed qua veritatem rei significatae. Etenim nomen Immanuel Deum nobiscum fore infert, non per nudam παράστασιν & gratiosam assistentiam, sed per naturae nostrae consortium, adeoque est nomen personae & officii. Vt enim nomen Iesus primo quidem designat officium, sed supponit ac connotat tamen personam θεάνθρωπον, cui soli officium saluandi competit; sic nomen Immanuel primo designat personam θεάνθρωπον, subinfert autem simul finem vnionis personalis diuinae & humanae naturae, reconciliationem Dei & hominis, ac reductionem hominis ad Deum, adeoque saluationem generis humani. Vnde eo ipso, quo Christus est Iesus, h. e. Saluator, Immanuel quoque est, ratione personae; quia nemo hominem peccatorem a peccatis saluare potest, nisi qui est Immanuel, Deus & homo.

II. Messias venire debuit sceptro a Iuda ablato: At Iesus venit sceptro nondum ablato: E. Iesus Nazarenus non est Messias. Maior patet e vaticinio Iacobi patriarchae, Gen. XLIX, 10. Minor claret: quia, cum nasceretur Iesus, Iudaeorum rex erat Herodes, Matth. II, 3. Resp. non praedixit patriarcha Iacobus, ante aduentum Schiloh sceptrum a Iuda esse auferendum, sed ante aduentum Messiae non esse auferendum sceptrum a Iuda, licet hic victurus fit in statu irrequieto & variis bellis turbato . Ideo enim praedixit venturum Schiloh, siue pacificum. *). Ideo enim prædixit venturum Schiloh, fiue

pacificatorem, vt pii Israelitae, calamitatibus pressi, cogitarent venturum esse tranquillatorem Messiam, cuius beneficio haberent pacem cum Deo, omni pace temporali longe nobiliorem. Ceterum Herodes natione Idumaeus, religione Iudaeus, non fuit quidem dominator peregrinus, fuit tamen vasallus Imperatoris Romani, adeoque sceptrum iudaicum adueniente Schilo non quidem penitus fractum, quassatum tamen fuit; id quod ostendit 1) census ab imperatore Augusto actus, Luc. II, 1. 2) Tributorum per publicanos & solemnes descriptiones exactio, Matth. XXII, 17. 3) Praesidiorum impositio & militum Romanorum hospitatio, Matth. VIII, 9. 4) Iurium capitalium defectus, Ioann. XVIII, 31.

III. Promissus Messias erit dominator Israelis, Mich. V, 1. qui collapsum regnum Dauidis eregit, Es. IX, 7. Ier. XXXIII, 15: At Iesus Nazarenus Israelitis nunquam dominatus est, nec collapsum regnum Dauidis erexit: E. Resp. Dominium Iesu Nazareni, veri Messiae, est spirituale, idque vniuersale, secundum voluntatem Dei antecedentem: quamuis autem haud pauci Iudaei non minus, quam gentiles ipsius imperium detrectent, manet tamen dominator veri Israelis, qui Israel Dei dicitur, Gal. VI, 16. Et cum per prophetas Dauidi promissum sit solium aeternum, facile colligitur, quod illud non vi corporali, sed spirituali stabiliatur eo, quod nullum folium corporale est aeternum.

IV. Iudaeis resipiscentibus Deus promittit reductionem in terram Canaan, Leu. XXVI, 44. Resp. Promisit Deus, Iudaeos tempore V. T. reducendos esse in terram suam, si poenitentiam egerint; quod factum est, cum e captiuitate babylonica reducti sunt (conf. Neh. I, 8. 9. Es. XI, 11. Ier. XVI, 15.). Tempore vero N. T. (quo abroganda erat externa illa sacrificiorum & politiae Mosaicae constitutio, terraque Cananaea sine spe restitutionis desolanda, Dan. IX, 26.) Deus Iudaeos non penitus abiecit, Rom. XI, 2. sed si veram poenitentiam agant, in gratiam recipit; quae quidem receptio in gratiam intelligenda est, pro natura & conditione N. T. non de reductione corporali in Canaan dudum desolatam, sed spirituali ad ecclesiam veram, Hierosolymam scilicet caelestem.


### Quaest. XXVIII. What predications flow from the union?

The predications, or personal propositions, flowing from the union are those in which the act of union with the human nature, considered as in itself ἀνυποστάτῳ (anhypostatic), or lacking subsistence, is predicated of the concrete of the simple person of the λόγος (Word).

Prob. Such propositions are given in the sacred letters, e.g., The Word was made flesh, John 1:14. God was manifested in the flesh, 1 Tim. 3:16. The Son of God assumed the seed of Abraham, ibid. v. 16.

Obf. Predications which flow from the union are not to be confused with propositions which proceed from the union. For in personal propositions, which declare the union, the subject is always the simple person of the Son of God, or the λόγος ἄσαρκος (Word without flesh), but the predicate is the act of his union with the human nature, insofar as this is considered as in itself ἀνυπόστατος (anhypostatic); e.g., The Word (ἄσαρκον) was made flesh: God (the second person of the divinity, ἀσύνθετος [incomposite]) was manifested in the flesh.

But in propositions signifying the state of union, the subject is the person σύνθετος (composite), denominated either from the divine nature, or from the human nature ἐνυποστάτῳ (enhypostatic), or from both natures, the predicate likewise being now the divine nature, now to have come, but it was also necessary that he himself, having been perfected (Heb. 5:9), be revealed, and his advent be announced to all nations, Now let this be the end! by the interpretation of Jesus himself, Matt. 24:14, and also by the witness of experience.

to the human nature in the composite (συνθέτῳ) person, for example: God is man, man is God; likewise: Christ is God, Acts 10:38. In Christ is God, 2 Cor. 5:19.

Latin:

Praedicationes, siue propositiones personales, ex vnitione fluentes sunt, in quibus de concreto personae simplicis τοῦ λόγου praedicatur actus vnionis cum humana natura, considerata vt per se ἀνυποστάτῳ, siue subsistentia experte.

Prob. Dantur eiusmodi propositiones in sacris litteris, v. gr. Verbum caro factum est, Ioann. I, 14. Deus manifestatus est in carne, 1 Tim. III, 16. Filius Dei assumsit semen Abrahae, ibid. v. 16.

Obs. Praedicationes, quae ex vnitione fluunt, non sunt confundendae cum propositionibus, quae ex vnione proueniunt. Nam in propositionibus personalibus, quae vnitionem enuntiant, subiectum semper est persona Filii Dei simplex, siue λόγος ἄσαρκος, praedicatum vero est actus vnionis eiusdem cum humana natura, quatenus haec, vt per se ἀνυπόστατος, consideratur; v. gr. Verbum (ἄσαρκον) caro factum est: Deus (persona secunda diuinitatis ἀσύνθετος) manifestatus est in carne.

In propositionibus vero, statum vnionis significantibus, subiectum est persona σύνθετος, denominata vel a natura diuina, vel a natura humana ἐνυποστάτῳ, vel natura vtraque, praedicatum itidem modo natura diuina, modo venisse, sed & necesse erat, ipsum istum consummatum (Hebr. V, 9.) patefieri, ipsiusque aduentum cunctis gentibus nuntiari, Nunc terminus esto! interprete ipso Iesu, Matth. XXIV, 14. ac teste etiam experientia. teste etiam experientia. teste etiam experientia.

do natura humana in persona συνθέτῳ, seu composita, v. gr. Deus est homo, homo est Deus; item: Christus est Deus, Act. X, 38. In Christo est Deus, 2 Cor. V, 19.


### Q. XXIX. What is personal union?

Personal union is the conjunction of two natures, divine and human, subsisting in one hypostasis of the Son of God, bringing about a mutual and indissoluble communion of each nature.

Obs. In describing personal union, two things must be observed: 1) the conjunction of two natures in one hypostasis of the Word (τοῦ λόγου), 2) the mutual communion (κοινωνία), or communication, of each nature, although it may be doubted whether this enters into the very form of personal union. The Epitome of the Formula of Concord describes the hypostatic union as that which becomes the highest communion, which God truly has with the assumed man, p. 607. The Declaration of the Formula adds 1) that the hypostatic union cannot be conceived or subsist without true communication, and demonstrates that the ancient doctors of the church joined these two words, communion (κοινωνίαν) and union (ἕνωσιν), in the explanation of this mystery, p. 766. Nevertheless, the Formula of Concord says 2) that the highest and ineffable communication of natures follows from the personal union, p. 607, where it is necessary that some distinction be admitted between personal union and the communication of natures. For that which follows from personal union cannot be the personal union itself. Wherefore D. Johann Musaeus, in his lectures on the Epitome of the Formula of Concord, notes that, although in reality personal union and the communication of natures do not differ, they nevertheless differ in our mode of conceiving them. For in the process of understanding, the extremes united to one another are conceived before the communication they have between them is conceived. He admits, meanwhile, that because the communication of natures and personal union do not differ in reality, they cannot be defined by different real definitions.

Latin:

Unio personalis est duarum naturarum, divinae & humanae, in una Filii Dei hypostasi subsistentium, coniunctio, mutuam, eamque indissolubilem, utriusque naturae communionem inferens.

Obs. In describenda unione personali duo observanda sunt: 1) coniunctio duarum naturarum in una hypostasi τοῦ λόγου, 2) mutua utriusque naturae κοινωνία, sive communio, quamvis dubitari queat, an haec ipsam formam unionis personalis ingrediatur. Describit Epitome Form. Concord. unionem hypostaticam, quod fit summa communio, quam Deus cum assumto homine vere habet. p. 607. Addit Declaratio Form. 1) quod unio hypostatica sine vera communicatione nec cogitari, nec subsistere possit, & commonstrat, veteres ecclesiae doctores duo haec vocabula, κοινωνίαν & ἕνωσιν, communicationem & unionem in explicatione huius mysterii coniunxisse, p. 766. Dicit nihilominus F. C. 2) summam ac ineffabilem naturarum communicationem sequi ex personali unione, p. 607. vbi necesse est, vt aliquid discriminis admittatur inter unionem personalem, & communicationem naturarum. Nam quod consequitur ex vnione personali, non potest esse ipsa unio personalis. Quocirca D. IOANN. MVSAEVS in praelect. in epitomen F. C. annotat, quod, licet, quoad rem, nihil differant unio personalis & communicatio naturarum, differant tamen nostro concipiendi modo. Nam in ratione intelligendi concipiuntur prius extrema inter se vnita, quam concipiatur communicatio, quam inter se habent. Fatetur interim, quod, quia communicatio naturarum, & unio personalis, realiter non differunt, diversis definitionibus realibus definiri nequeant.


### Q. XXX. What kind is the union of the two natures in Christ?

The union of the two natures in Christ is not merely verbal, nor notional, nor habitual or respective, but real, and that not accidental, nor essential, but personal and perichoretic.

Proof. The union of the two natures in Christ is not 1) merely verbal, arising either from a title without the reality, as when one is called a prince's counselor who was never of his councils, or from an improper locution, as when Herod is called a fox. For Christ is not merely nominally or improperly, but properly, Immanuel and God-man (θεάνθρωπος). 2) It is not notional, or of reason, by which several concepts distinct by reason are conceived as undivided by the aid of the mind. Such a union exists between genus and difference in a species. For neither is the divine nature of Christ a genus, nor the human nature his difference, or vice versa. 3) It is not relative (σχετική), habitual, or respective, which can consist even if the extremes of this union are in fact separated and distant. For various relative unions exist, namely, moral between friends, whose mind is one even when they are absent; economic between spouses; political between citizens; ecclesiastical between members of the church. For the union of the two natures in Christ is far tighter than a habitual one, which indeed imports a relationship of several things to one another, but without their real conjunction. The Son of God was made a partaker of flesh and blood, like the children, Heb. 2:14. Therefore, the union of the two natures in Christ is real, because it exists between extremes that truly cohere, with the exclusion of any separation or distance. It is not 4) accidental, by which several things, divided among themselves, are joined into some sort of indivision. Such an accidental union exists a) between two or more disparate accidents, coupled in one subject; thus whiteness & sweetness are united in milk: b) Between accident and substance, such as is given in a learned man: c) Between two substances, so united among themselves, that from them results not one thing essentially, but accidentally.

To this pertains physical union κατὰ σύγχυσιν by confusion, or mixture, as in mead; κατὰ παράθεσιν, by apposition of united parts, as in a heap of stones; κατὰ παράστασιν, by assistance, such as is both in contiguous things, present to themselves, as when two embrace with their hands, and in continuous things, as when two boards are joined together.

To accidental union pertains the mystical, which they make threefold: sacramental, gracious, and glorious.

The sacramental is given between a terrestrial and a celestial thing sacramentally united; the gracious between God and believers in the militant church; the glorious between God and the blessed in the triumphant church.

The union of the two natures in Christ is not accidental; for the reason that no species of accidental union can be applied to it.

For this union is neither between two accidents, nor between substance and accident, but between two substances, which are united not by mixture or confusion, because the divine nature, which is spiritual, most simple, and infinite, cannot be mixed with the human; nor by parastasis, assistance, or apposition, since that brings about no κοινωνίαν, or internal communion.

Moreover, this union far surpasses in its eminence the gracious conjunction of believers and the glorious conjunction of the blessed with God.

For no believer in this life, no blessed one in the heavenly life, is one with the Son of God ὑφισάμενον (subsistently).

In no one, as in Christ, does the whole fullness of divinity dwell bodily.

Neither is 5) an essential union, by which two incomplete natures concur to constitute one complete nature, e.g., soul and body constitute one man.

The two natures in Christ are complete in being, and do not concur to one complete nature, but to constitute one σύνθετον (composite) person.

In essentially united things no constituting principle pre-exists by nature; but the divine nature τῷ λόγῳ (in the Word) subsists by itself from eternity.

Therefore the union of the two natures in Christ is μονότροπος καὶ ἐξαίρετος, i.e., wonderfully singular, and singularly wonderful.

For it is a union of natures, but not natural; it is personal, but not of persons, for the reason that it is called personal not by reason of the term from which, as if it were made from two persons, but by reason of the term to which, into one person, because the Word terminated the assumed humanity with His own personal perfection, finally completed it, and constituted it in hypostatic being, and thus the hypostasis of the Word became the hypostasis of the flesh.

This union is called perichoretic, so that it may be indicated that it is not parastatic, exterior, and imperfect, such as is between two boards compacted or glued together, between a man and a garment, between an angel and an assumed body; but intimate and most perfect; which cannot exist without the mutual communication of the united things.

For a perfect ἔνωσις, or union, is defined by SUIDAS and PHAVORINUS as being a συνδρομὴ κοινωνικὴ διεξώτων πραγμάτων, a communicative concurrence of differing things (substances).

See

D.

CALOV. in metaphys. diuin. part. general. p.

315. Since therefore the union of the two natures in Christ is intimate and most perfect, it can neither exist nor be thought of without the communion of both natures.

Latin:

Unio duarum in Christo naturarum non est mere verbalis, neque notionalis, neque habitualis, seu respectiva, sed realis, eaque non accidentalis, nec essentialis, sed personalis & perichoristica.

Prob. Unio duarum in Christo naturarum non est 1) mere verbalis, exsurgens vel ex titulo fine re, vt cum consiliarius principis dicitur, qui nunquam ipsi fuit a consiliis, vel ex locutione impropria, vt cum Herodes vocatur vulpes. Christus enim non nominetenus tantum, aut improprie, sed proprieque Immanuel & θεάνθρωπος est. 2) Non est notionalis, sive rationis, qua plures conceptus per rationem distincti, mentis ope, vt indivisi concipiuntur. Talis unio datur inter genus & differentiam in specie. Neque enim natura divina Christi genus, neque natura humana ipsius differentia est, aut vice versa. 3) Non est σχετική, habitualis, aut respectiva, quae consistere potest, licet extrema huius unionis reapse separata sint & distent. Datur enim varia unio respectiva, nempe moralis inter amicos, quorum etiam absentium unus animus est; oeconomica inter coniuges; politica inter ciues; ecclesiastica inter membra ecclesiae. Longe quippe arctior est unio duarum in Christo naturarum, quam habitualis, quae importat quidem plurium rerum ad invicem habitudinem, sed fine reali earum coniunctione. Filius Dei particeps factus est carnis & sanguinis, sicut pueri, Hebr. II, 14. Est igitur unio duarum naturarum in Christo realis, quia datur inter extrema vere cohaerentia, cum exclusione separationis alicuius, aut distantiae. Non est 4) accidentalis, qua plura, inter se diuisa, ad aliqualem indivisionem coniunguntur. Datur eiusmodi accidentalis unio a) inter duo vel plura accidentia disparata, in vno subiecto copulata; sic albedo & dulcedo vniuntur in lacte: b) Inter accidens & substantiam, qualis datur in homine docto: c) Inter duas substantias, ita inter se vnitas, vt ex illis non vnum per se, sed per accidens resultet.

Huc pertinet vnio physica κατὰ σύγχυσιν per confusionem, vel mixtionem, vt in mulso; κατὰ παράθεσιν, per appositionem partium vnitarum, vt in cumulo lapidum; κατὰ παράστασιν, per assistentiam, qualis est tum in contiguis, sibi præsentibus, vt cum duo se complectuntur manibus, tum in continuis, vt cum duæ afferres compinguntur.

Pertinet ad accidentalem vnionem mystica, quam triplicem faciunt: sacramentalem, gratiosam & gloriosam.

Sacramentalis datur inter rem terrenam & cœlestem sacramentaliter vnitas; gratiosa inter Deum & credentes in ecclesia militante; gloriosa inter Deum & beatos in ecclesia triumphante.

Vnio duarum in Christo naturarum non est accidentalis; propterea, quod nulla species vnionis accidentalis eidem applicari potest.

Neque enim hæc vnio inter duo accidentia, neque inter substantiam & accidens, sed inter duas substantias, quæ vnitæ sunt non per mixtionem aut confusionem, eo, quod natura diuina, quæ spiritualis, simplicissima & infinita est, cum humana commisceri nequit; neque per parastasin, assistentiam, aut appositionem, quippe quæ nullam κοινωνίαν, aut internam communionem infert.

Ceterum hæc vnio gratiosam credentium, & gloriosam beatorum coniunctionem cum Deo, eminentia sua longissime superat.

Nullus enim credens in hac vita, nullus beatus in vita cœlesti, est vnum cum filio Dei ὑφισάμενον.

In nullo peræque, ac in Christo, tota plenitudo diuinitatis habitat corporaliter.

Neque est 5) vnio essentialis, qua duæ naturæ incompletæ ad vnam naturam completam constituendam concurrunt, v. gr. anima & corpus vnum constituunt hominem.

Duæ in Christo naturæ sunt in essendo completæ, neque concurrunt ad vnam naturam completam, sed ad vnam personam σύνθετον constituendam.

In essentialiter vnitis nullum principium constituens per naturam præexistit; at natura diuina τῷ λόγῳ ab æterno per se subsistit.

Est igitur vnio duarum in Christo naturarum μονότροπος καὶ ἐξαίρετος, h. e. mirabiliter singularis, & singulariter mirabilis.

Est enim vnio naturarum, sed non naturalis; est personalis, sed non personarum, propterea, quod personalis dicitur non ratione termini a quo, quasi ex duabus personis esset facta, sed ratione termini ad quem, in vnam personam, quia ὁ λόγος assumtam humanitatem perfectione sua personali terminauit, vltimo compleuit, & in esse hypostatico constituit, adeoque hypostasis τῷ λόγῳ facta est hypostasis carnis.

Vocatur hæc vnio perichoretica, vt indicetur, eandem non esse parastaticam, exteriorem & imperfectam, qualis est inter duas afferes compactos, aut conglutinatos, inter hominem & vestimentum, inter angelum & corpus affiuntam; sed intimam & perfectissimam; quæ sine rerum vnitarum communicatione mutua esse nequit.

Perfecta quippe ἔνωσις, siue vnio definitur a SVIDA & PHAVORINO, quod sit συνδρομὴ κοινωνικὴ διεξώτων πραγμάτων, concursus communicatiuus rerum (substantiarum) differentium.

Vid.

D.

CALOV. in metaphys. diuin. part. general. p.

315. Cum itaque vnio duarum in Christo naturarum fit intima & perfectissima, eadem fine vtriusque naturæ communione nec exsistere, nec cogitari potest.


### Q. XXX. What kind is the union of the two natures in Christ?: Obs

Obs.

The Fathers gathered in the Council of Chalcedon, in the year 448, wishing to express the mode of the hypostatic union, confessed that our Savior exists in two natures ἀσυγχύτως, inconfusedly, ἀτρέπτως, inconvertibly, ἀδιαιρέτως, indivisibly, ἀχωρίστως, inseparably; DAMASCENUS adds the word ἀδιαστάτως, indistantly, because the two natures united in Christ do not stand apart from each other by any space of places or interval, placed separately.

See

CHEMNIT. de d. n. Chr. fol.

64. Quest.

XXXI. What is the communion of the two natures in Christ?

The communion of natures in the person of Christ is the mutual participation of the divine and human nature of Christ, through which the divine nature τῷ λόγῳ (in the Word), having been made a participant of the human nature, permeates it, perfects it; it inhabits it, and appropriates it to itself; but the human [nature], having been made a participant of the divine nature, is permeated, perfected, and inhabited by it. Objection I Κοινωνία (koinōnia) is rendered in Latin by communication and communion: which two terms are sometimes used interchangeably, sometimes distinguished in such a way that the former designates a transient act, the latter a permanent state. It is considered here in the latter way. Objection II

The communion of the two natures in Christ is 1) not merely verbal, as when the wife of a certain Elector, by reason of the marital union, shares the name of Electress, although in reality she is not an Electress, since she does not possess the authority to elect the Emperor. 2) The communion of which we speak is not notional or intellectual, otherwise called communication κατὰ μέθεξιν (by participation), which our intellect conceives between extremes that are the same in reality; by which reasoning a genus communicates its essence to a species, and a species to individuals. But it is 3) a real communion, because the divine nature in the Logos has truly and really been made a participant of, and remains a participant of, the human nature, and the human nature has truly and really been made a participant of, and remains a participant of, the divine nature. Nor 4) is this communion merely a collation of dignity (in Greek κοινωνία κατ’ ἀξίαν), in the way God communicated the dignity of the priesthood to Aaron: for the most eminent communion, of which we are speaking at present, is not between extremes that are diverse in themselves, but its root is the communion of the hypostasis: and therefore 5) it is not a commixtive communion, as when salt is communicated to water through mixing; for the foundation of such a communication is an accidental union; nor 6) is it a natural or essential communication, such as that between form and matter, soul and body, which flows from an essential union; but it is 7) personal, called κατὰ σύνδυσιν (by conjunction), and also κατ’ ἕνωσιν (by union), because it arises from the union of the two natures in the one person of Christ. Objection III

The Greeks call the communion of the two natures in Christ περιχώρησις (perichōrēsis), i.e., inmeation, permeation, circumincession (as the Scholastics rendered τὴν περιχώρησιν). Περιχώρησις is indeed not a biblical term, yet it is ecclesiastical, and it began to be used most especially when Nestorius denied the communion of the natures. However, they did not understand περιχώρησις as local and quantitative, in the way a jar is said χωρεῖν (to contain) water, but as illocal and spoken metaphorically.

The Fathers had occasion to describe the personal περιχώρησις a) from the essential περιχώρησις of the Most Holy Trinity, b) from the natural περιχώρησις of soul and body, c) from the accidental περιχώρησις of fire and iron. For just as one person of the Trinity is in another; the soul permeates the body; fire penetrates all the pores of iron: so the divinity of Christ is in the humanity, which it fills and permeates all around.

And from these it is easy to gather that περιχώρησις denotes: 1) that the personal union is intimate and most perfect. The union is external and imperfect when an angel attends a body, a pilot stands by a ship, a garment adheres to a man; which external union the doctors of the church, wishing to remove, called the personal union and the communion flowing from it περιχώρησις. For just as the soul does not stand by the body externally, nor merely direct its motion, but permeates, enters, and informs it, bestowing its own essence, life, and faculties upon the body: so the Λόγος (Logos) permeates the flesh, and intimately communicates its own divine nature to it.

2) That the communion of the natures is mutual, yet in such a way that the divine nature, as an ἐντελέχεια (entelechy), i.e., the purest act, permeates and perfects the assumed human nature, while the assumed flesh is permeated and perfected. 3) That the union and communion of the natures in Christ is personal, ἀχώριστον, inseparable. The rational soul so insinuates itself into the body that it could by no means be separated from it, unless, through the fall into accident intervening, the violence of death had followed by divine judgment. Indeed the natural union of the soul and body of Christ was dissolved during the three days of death; but the divine nature τῷ λόγῳ was not dissolved from the assumed humanity, but was most present to it. foluebatur natura diuina τῷ λόγῳ ab assumta humanitate, sed huic erat præfentiffima.

4) That the natural union and communion is ἀσύγχυτον, ἄμικτον, καὶ ἄτρεπτον, i.e., that it brings about no confusion, mixture, or transmutation.

The Persons of the Trinity permeate one another without confusion; the soul informs the body without any disturbance, mixture, or mutation of either: so the λόγος permeates his flesh, so that nothing is lost to either in essential matters, nor is one mixed with the other, or confused with the other.

5) That the unity of the natures of Christ is ἀδιαστάτως, or that they are mutually present to one another, the Persons of the Trinity so permeate one another that none is outside or beyond another. The rational soul likewise is in the body in such a way that it is nowhere outside or beyond it: so also the λόγος is in the flesh, in such a way that he is nowhere beyond it, nowhere outside it.

Latin:

Obs.

Patres in concilio Chalcedonensi, Anno CCCCXLIIX, congregati, modum vnionis hypostaticæ expressuri, confessi sunt, Saluatorem nostrum in duabus naturis ἀσυγχύτως, inconfuse, ἀτρέπτως, inconuertibiliter, ἀδιαιρέτως, indiuulse, ἀχωρίστως, inseparabiliter exsistere, DAMASCENUS addit vocabulum ἀδιαστάτως, indistanter, quod duæ in Christo naturæ vnita nullum locorum spatio, aut interuallo a se distent, seorsum positæ.

Vid.

CHEMNIT. de d. n. Chr. fol.

64. Quæst.

XXXI. Quid est communio duarum in Christo naturarum?

Communio naturarum in persona Christi est mutua diuina & humanæ Christi naturæ participatio, pèr quam natura diuina τῷ λόγῳ, particeps facta humanæ naturae, hanc permeat, perficit; inhabitat, sibique appropriat; humana vero, particeps facta divinae naturae, ab hac permeatur, perficitur atque inhabitatur. Obiectio I Κοινωνία latine redditur per communicationem, & communionem: quae duae voces interdum promiscue usurpantur, interdum sic distinguuntur, ut illa actum transeuntem, haec statum permanentem designet. Posteriori modo hic consideratur. Obiectio II

Communio duarum in Christo naturarum non est 1) mere verbalis, ut cum Electoris cuiusdam uxor, propter unionem coniugalem, participat nomen Electricis, licet reipsa non sit electrix, cum non polleat auctoritate eligendi Imperatorem. 2) Non est communio, de qua loquimur, notionalis, vel intellectualis, alias communicatio κατὰ μέθεξιν dicta, quam intellectus noster concipit inter extrema, quae quoad rem idem sunt; qua ratione genus speciei, species individuis suam essentiam communicat. Sed est 3) communio realis, quia divina natura τῷ λόγῳ vere & realiter particeps facta est & manet humanae naturae, & humana natura vere & realiter particeps facta est & manet divinae naturae. Neque 4) haec communio tantum est collativa dignitatis (graece κοινωνία κατ’ ἀξίαν), quomodo Deus Aaroni dignitatem sacerdotii communicavit: eminentissima enim communio, de qua nobis in praesenti sermo est, non est inter extrema per se diversa, sed eius radix est communio hypostaseos: adeoque 5) non est communio commixtiva, ut cum fal per mixtionem communicatur aquae; huiusmodi enim communicationis fundamentum est unio accidentalis; neque 6) est communicatio naturalis, seu essentialis, qualis est inter formam & materiam, animam & corpus, quae fluit ex unione essentiali; sed est 7) personalis, vocata κατὰ σύνδυσιν, item κατ’ ἕνωσιν, quia oritur ex unione duarum naturarum in una persona Christi. Obiectio III

Graeci communionem duarum in Christo naturarum vocant περιχώρησιν, i. e. inmeationem, permeationem, circumincessionem, (uti Scholastici τὴν περιχώρησιν reddiderunt). Non est quidem περιχώρησις terminus biblicus, attamen ecclesiasticus, & tum potissimum usurpari coepit, cum Nestorius communionem naturarum negavit. Non intellexerunt autem περιχώρησιν localem & quantitativam, quemadmodum hydria dicitur χωρεῖν aquam, sed illocalem & metaphorice dictam.

Occasionem περιχωρήσεως personalis describendae fuisserunt Patres a) ex περιχωρήσει SS. Trinitatis essentiali, b) ex περιχωρήσει animae & corporis naturali, c) ex περιχωρήσει ignis & ferri accidentali. Sicut enim una persona trinitatis est in alia; anima permeat corpus; ignis penetrat omnes poros ferri: ita divinitas Christi est in humanitate, quam circumcirca implet & permeat.

Et quibus collectu proclive est, quod περιχώρησις notet, 1) unionem personalem esse intimam & perfectissimam. Externa & imperfecta est unio, cum angelus affluit corpus, gubernator assistit navi, vestimentum adhaeret homini; quam exteriorem unionem remoturi doctores ecclesiae unionem personalem & ex ea fluentem communionem appellarunt περιχώρησιν. Quemadmodum enim anima corpori non externe assistit, neque eius tantum motum dirigit, sed illud ipsum immeat, immigrat, informat, suammet essentiam, vitam, facultates corpori largiendo: ita λόγος immeat carnem, suamque illi divinam naturam intime communicat.

2) Communionem naturarum esse mutuam, ita tamen, ut natura divina, velut ἐντελέχεια, i. e. actus purissimus, assumtam humanam naturam permeat & perficit, assumta caro permeetur atque perficiatur. 3) Unionem & communionem naturarum in Christo personalem esse ἀχώριστον, inseparabilem. Anima rationalis ita se corpori insinuat, ut ab eo separari nullatenus potuisset, nisi, lapsu ex accidente interveniente, divino iudicio, mortis violentia secuta fuisset. Soluebatur quidem unio naturalis animae & corporis Christi in triduo mortis; non autem soluebatur natura divina τῷ λόγῳ ab assumta humanitate, sed huic erat praesentissima. foluebatur natura diuina τῷ λόγῳ ab assumta humanitate, sed huic erat præfentiffima.

4) Vnionem & communionem naturalem esse ἀσύγχυτον, ἄμικτον, καὶ ἄτρεπτον, i.e. nullam inferre confusionem, mixtionem aut transmutationem.

Personæ Trinitatis se mutuo permeant sine confusione; anima corpus informat absque omni vtriusque turbatione, mixtione aut mutatione: ita λόγος permeat suam carnem, vt neutri in essentialibus quidquam decedat, neutrum alteri misceatur, aut cum altero confundatur.

5) Naturas Christi vnitas esse ἀδιαστάτως, siue, esse sibi mutuo præsentes, Personæ Trinitatis ita se inuicem inmeant, vt nulla fit aut extra, aut vltra alteram. Anima itidem rationalis sic est in corpore, vt nuspiam fit extra, aut vltra illud: ita etiam λόγος in carne est, nuspiam vt vltra, nuspiam vt extra illam fit.


### Q. XXX. What kind is the union of the two natures in Christ?: Prob

Prob.

The intimate communion of the two natures in Christ 1) from John I, 14: The Word was made flesh.

Heb. II, 14: Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same. Here Paul teaches in express words that the Son of God was made a partaker of human nature, which is denoted by flesh and blood. But since the Son of God made himself a partaker of human nature, this was indeed assumed into the communication of deity and blessedness, as Eusebius speaks, l. IV. demonstrat. euangel. c. 13. 3) From

Col. II, 9: In him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. In this brief statement the Apostle embraces three things: (1) the indweller, (2) the dwelling-place, (3) the mode of indwelling. The indweller is the whole fulness of the Godhead, by which is denoted the most perfect divinity of the Son of God, and whatever is in it, or pertains to it, with all its properties. The dwelling-place is Christ, considered according to his human nature; for this is indwelt, while the divine nature indwells. The mode of indwelling is expressed by the word σωματικῶς, which Augustine, epist. 457. ad Dardan., explains thus: It is said 'bodily' because in the body of Christ, as in a temple, dwells all the fulness of the Godhead: it dwells indeed also in holy men, but in a singular manner in the body of Christ, as in a temple, personally assumed.

Hence we argue: In that which, as a temple, is personally assumed, the most perfect divinity of the Son of God dwells, there intervenes a certain communion with the divinity of the Son of God: But in the human nature of Christ, etc. Therefore. The major is proved: because just as the soul has communion with its body because it indwells it; so between the indwelling divinity and the indwelt flesh of Christ there is given a communion.

4) If from the mystical union of the faithful with Christ a certain κοινωνία flows, much more from the personal union of the divine and human nature does a certain κοινωνία arise. The antecedent is true: Therefore, the consequent.

The consequence of the major is clear: because a personal union is far closer and more intimate than the gracious union of believers with God. The antecedent is confirmed by the statement of Peter, who affirms that the faithful are κοινωνοὶ τῆς θείας φύσεως, partakers of the divine nature, 2 Pet. I, 4.

5) If the communion of the divine and human nature is denied, the communication of the divine subsistence cannot but be denied; because subsistence is a mode which cannot be outside the nature which it modifies or affects.

6) If the communion of the two natures in Christ is denied, these propositions must be denied: God is man; and man is God. The reason is: because neither can God be said or imagined to be God without the divine nature, nor man without the human nature. 7) If the communion of the natures in the person of Christ is denied, it must be denied that in the works of the office each nature acts with the communion of the other. 8) Samosatenus and Nestorius were condemned by pious antiquity for the reason that they taught that the two natures of Christ were altogether incommunicable with one another.

The antithesis is that of Bellarmine and others, who deny the communion of the two natures in Christ. BELLARMINE, in book III of De Christo, chapter VIII, argues:

I. The personal union was effected through the communication of that which is proper to the Son, not that which is common to the other persons of the Godhead: But only subsistence is proper to the Son, whereas the divine nature is common to the other persons: Therefore, only subsistence was communicated. The major premise is certain: because only the Son of God became flesh. If, however, the divine nature had been communicated to the flesh, the whole Most Holy Trinity would have been incarnate, because the divine nature is common to all three divine persons. Resp. The divine nature is considered either absolutely, and thus it is common to the three divine persons, or relatively, insofar as it is marked by the hypostatic character τῷ λόγῳ [to the Word]: in this mode of consideration, we assert that it has been communicated to the flesh joined to it.

II. If the Godhead is communicated to the human nature, this will be the divine essence itself: The consequent is absurd: Therefore, the antecedent is as well. The consequence of the major premise is evident, because the communication of natures produces a synonymous and essential predication, e.g., an animal communicates its nature to a man: Therefore, man is an animal. Resp. Distinguish between notional communication, or κατὰ μέθεξιν [by participation], and real communication, or κατὰ συνδύασιν [by conjunction]. The former entails synonymous predication, the latter paronymous, e.g., the soul is communicated to the body: Therefore, the body is animated, not the soul itself. Thus, the divine nature is communicated to the human nature: Therefore, the human nature is a participant in the divine nature, not the divine nature itself.

III. A real communion of natures entails their confusion or mixture. Resp. Not every communion of natures is commixtive, but only that which is accidental, not, however, that which is essential or personal. The soul communicates itself entirely to the body, yet it is not mixed with it.

IV. If the divinity is communicated to the flesh of Christ, all divine attributes are also communicated to it: The latter is false: Therefore, the former is as well. The consequence of the major premise is manifest: because the divine attributes and the essence of God are ταὐτό [the same]. Resp. All divine attributes are communicated to the flesh as regards possession; but as far as denomination is concerned, one must distinguish between the ἐνεργητικά [active], or operative, attributes of God, and the ἀνεργητικά [inactive], or quiescent, ones. The former are communicated as regards immediate denomination, the latter as regards mediate denomination. For from that I say: omnipotence, which is independent, infinite, and eternal, is communicated to the flesh of Christ.

V. BECANUS, GREGORY of VALENTIA, and other Jesuits (cited by D. CALOVIUS in System., vol. VII, p. 155) teach that only the subsistence of the Word is communicated proximately, immediately, and formally to the humanity in itself, and through it the humanity subsists proximately, mediately, and formally: and because that subsistence is in reality the same as the divine essence and attributes, therefore consequently and identically the divine essence and attributes are communicated to the humanity. D. CALOVIUS responds: this distinction between immediate and mediate communication is only composed to ensnare and deceive the unskilled. For mediately, consequently, and identically consequently and identically consequently and identically

to be communicated in the Jesuit sense is really not to be communicated; which I show thus: The divine nature and idioms are either communicated really to the human nature according to the mind of the Jesuits (whether immediately, or mediately, or proximately, or consequently, or formally, or identically; thus far it matters little, provided the communication be true and real), or they are not communicated really. If they are communicated really, it must be conceded that the human nature truly becomes a participant of the divine nature, truly a participant of the divine idioms, of omnipotence, of omniscience, of omnipresence; and indeed no less truly a participant of the divine nature and divine idioms than of the divine subsistence, though not equally primarily. But the Jesuits will never admit this. Therefore it is certain that they do not at all believe in a real communication of the divine nature and its attributes. D. JOHANN ADAM OSIANDER supports this in his Colleg. systemat. part. IV. p. 61 , saying: The distinction between mediate and immediate communication is a mere delusion, because they acknowledge no participation of the divine nature in the human; but, if the human does not participate in the divine, strictly speaking it will not be united to the divine nature, it will not be the proper body or dwelling-place of the indwelling deity with all its fullness, nor the divine nature permeating and perfecting it. One thing is 'unible' [capable of union], admitting things really distinct, another is not admitting them, but in which the highest identity reigns. The former indeed admits the distinction of mediate and immediate union, but the latter does not. Let us suppose with certain philosophers that the soul and its faculties differ really, because the soul is spirit and substance, but the intellect and will are faculties and accidents; but these have no place in the union of the λόγος [Word] and the flesh, because the subsistence and nature of the λόγος are indivisibly identified, so that therefore it cannot be said that the subsistence is communicated immediately, but mediately, namely by means of the subsistence itself, the divine nature, for the very reason that the divine nature with its subsistence is indivisibly and really one thing.

Latin:

Prob.

Intima duarum in Christo naturarum communio 1) ex Ioann. I, 14: Verbum caro factum est. Quicunque ab æterno existens immutabilis Deus, factus est caro, non per conuersionem suæ naturæ aut mutationem, sed per eiusdem vnionem cum carne; illius naturæ diuinæ cum vnita carne oportet communionem quandam intercedere: Atqui Filius Dei &c. Ergo. Maior liquet: quia omnis realis, interna & perfecta vnio, definiente SVIDA, est concursus communicatiuus rerum differentium. Minor patet: quia ὁ λόγος non tantum est nomen personæ, sed etiam naturæ diuinæ, caro autem est nomen designans naturam humanam.

2) Ex Hebr. II, 14: Quoniam igitur pueri participes facti sunt carnis & sanguinis, & ipse similiter participem se fecit ipsorum. Hic Paullus conceptis verbis docet, quod Filius Dei particeps factus sit humanæ naturæ, quæ per carnem & sanguinem denotatur. Cum autem Filius Dei se participem fecerit humanæ naturæ, hæc vtique in communicationem deitatis & beatitudinis assumta est, vt loquitur EVSEBIVS l. IV. demonstrat. euangel. c. 13.

3) E Col. II, 9: In ipso habitat omnis plenitudo diuinitatis corporaliter. Breui hoc effato tria Apostolus complectitur: (1) inhabitantem, (2) habitaculum, (3) habitationis modum. Inhabitans est tota plenitudo diuinitatis, per quam notatur perfectissima diuinitas Filii Dei, & quidquid in ea est, siue ad eam pertinet, cum omnibus ipsius proprietatibus. Habitaculum est Christus, consideratus secundum humanam naturam; hæc enim inhabitatur, natura autem diuina inhabitat. Modus inhabitationis exprimitur voce σωματικῶς, quod AVGVSTIN. epist. 457. ad Dardan. sic exponit: Corporaliter dictum est, quia in Christi corpore, tanquam in templo, habitat omnis plenitudo deitatis: habitat hoc quidem etiam in hominibus sanctis, sed singulari ratione in corpore Christi, tanquam in templo, personaliter assumto.

Hinc argumentamur: In quo, velut-templo, personaliter assumto, perfectissima Filii Dei diuinitas habitat, illi intercedit quædam communio cum diuinitate Filii Dei: Atqui in humana Christi natura &c. Ergo. Maior probatur: quia sicut ideo anima communionem habet cum suo corpore, quia hoc inhabitat; ita inter diuinitatem inhabitantem & carnem Christi inhabitatam datur communio.

4) Si ex vnione mystica fidelium cum Christo quædam fluit κοινωνία, multo magis ex vnione personali diuinæ & humanæ naturæ quædam oritur κοινωνία. Antecedens est verum: E. & consequens.

Consequentia maioris patet: quia vnio personalis longe arctior & intimior est, quam vnio gratiosa credentium cum Deo. Antecedens confirmatur ex effato Petri, qui affirmat, quod fideles sint κοινωνοὶ τῆς θείας φύσεως, participes diuinæ naturæ, 2 Petr. I, 4.

5) Negata communione naturæ diuinæ & humanæ, non potest non negari communicatio subsistentiæ diuinæ; quia subsistentia est modus, qui non potest esse extra naturam, quam modificat, aut afficit.

6) Negata communione duarum in Christo naturarum negandae sunt hae propositiones: Deus est homo; & homo est Deus. Ratio est: quia neque sine natura divina Deus, neque sine natura humana homo dici fingiue potest. 7) Negata communione naturarum in persona Christi, negandum est, in operibus officii unamquamque naturam agere cum alterius communione. 8) Samosatenus & Nestorius a pia antiquitate damnati sunt, ideo quod docuerunt, duas Christi naturas inter se esse prorsus incommunicabiles.

Antithesis est Bellarmini & aliorum, communionem duarum in Christo naturarum negantium. BELLARMINVS libr. III. de Christo cap. VIII. argumentatur:

I. Vnio personalis facta est per communicationem eius, quod est proprium filii, non eius, quod est commune aliis deitatis personis: Sed sola subsistentia est propria filio, natura autem divina est communis aliis personis: E. sola subsistentia communicata est. Maior constat: quia solus Filius Dei caro factus est. Si autem natura divina communicata esset carni, tota SS. Trinitas incarnata esset, quia natura divina omnibus tribus personis divinis communis est. Resp. Natura divina consideratur vel absolute, & sic communis est tribus personis divinis, vel relate, prout insignita est charactere hypostatico τῷ λόγῳ: hoc considerandi modo eam carni affluxtae communicatam esse, afferimus.

II. Si deitas communicata est humanae naturae, haec erit ipsa essentia divina: Consequens est absurdum: E. & antecedens. Consequentia maioris est evidens, quia communicatio naturarum gignit praedicationem synonymicam & essentialem, v. gr. Animal suam naturam communicat homini: E. homo est animal. Resp. Dist. inter communicationem notionalem, sive κατὰ μέθεξιν, & realem, sive κατὰ συνδύασιν. Illa infert praedicationem synonymicam, haec paronymicam, v. gr. Anima est communicata corpori: E. corpus est animatum, non anima ipsa. Ita communicata est natura divina humanae naturae: E. humana natura est particeps naturae divinae, non ipsa natura divina.

III. Realis naturarum communio infert earum confusionem, vel mixtionem. Resp. Non omnis communio naturarum est commixtiva, sed ea tantum, quae est accidentalis, non autem ea, quae est essentialis, aut personalis. Anima se totam communicat corpori, neque tamen cum eo miscetur.

IV. Si carni Christi communicata est divinitas, omnia etiam attributa divina ipsi sunt communicata: Posterius est falsum: E. & prius. Consequentia maioris est manifesta: quia attributa divina & essentia Dei sunt ταὐτό. Resp. Omnia attributa divina communicata sunt carni, quoad possessionem; quod autem attinet ad denominationem, distinguendum est inter attributa Dei ἐνεργητικά, sive operantia, & ἀνεργητικά, sive quiescentia. Illa communicata sunt, quoad denominationem immediatam, haec quoad denominationem mediatam. Ex eo enim dico: communicata est carni Christi omnipotentia, quae est independens, infinita & aeterna.

V. BECANVS, GREGORIVS de VALENTIA, & alii Iesuitae (citante D. CALOVIO in system. tom. VII. p. 155.) docent, quod sola subsistentia Verbi proxime, immediate, & formaliter communicata sit humanitati in se, & per illam proxime, mediate & formaliter subsistat humanitas: & quia illa subsistentia re ipsa idem est cum essentia & attributis divinis, ideo consequenter & identice essentia & attributa divina communicata sunt humanitati. Respondet D. CALOVIVS: distinctio haec inter communicationem immediatam, & mediatam tantum composita est ad insecundum & decipiendum imperitos. Nam mediate, consequenter & identice consequenter & identice consequenter & identice

communicari sensu Iesuitico est realiter non communicari; quod sic ostendo: Natura & idiomata diuina vel communicantur realiter humanae naturae ex mente Iesuitarum (siue immediate, siue mediate, siue proxime, siue consequenter, siue formaliter, siue identice; hactenus parum refert, modo vera & realis sit communicatio), vel non communicantur realiter. Si communicantur realiter, concedendum erit, quod humana natura vere particeps fiat diuinae naturae, vere particeps idiomatum diuinorum, omnipotentiae, omniscientiae, omnipraesentiae; & quidem non minus vere diuinae naturae & idiomatum diuinorum particeps, quam diuinae subsistentiae, vt non aeque primario. Sed hoc nunquam admittent Iesuitae. Ergo certum est, quod minime credant communicationem naturae diuinae & attributorum eius realem. Suffragatur D. IOANN. ADAMVS OSIANDER in colleg. systemat. part. IV. p. 61. inquiens: Distinctio inter communicationem mediatam & immediatam merum glaucoma est, quia nullam participationem diuinae naturae in humana agnoscunt; at, si humana non participat de diuina, accurate loquendo non erit unita diuinae naturae, non erit proprium corpus aut habitaculum inhabitantis deitatis cum tota sua plenitudine, non natura diuina permeantis & perficientis. Aliud est vnibile, realiter distincta admittens, aliud non admittens, sed in quo summa regnat identitas. Prius quidem admittit distinctionem vnionis mediatae, & immediatae, at non posterius. Ponamus cum quibusdam philosophis, animam & facultates eius differre realiter, quia anima est spiritus & substantia, intellectus autem & voluntas sunt facultates & accidentia; at haec locum non habent in vnione λόγου & carnis, quia subsistentia, & natura λόγου indiuisibiliter identificantur, vt proin nequeat dici subsistentia immediate communicata, mediate autem, mediante scil. ipsa subsistentia, diuina natura, eo ipso, quod diuina natura cum sua subsistentia indiuisibiliter & realiter vnum quid est.


### Q. XXXII. What is the end of the personal union and communion of the two natures in Christ?

The end of the personal union, and of the intimate communion of the two natures, is the performance of the works of the office. Prob. In the actions of the office, each nature of Christ acts according to what is proper to each, with the communication of the other. But one result cannot flow from diverse principles unless the communion of those principles is presupposed; for example, from a heated sword proceeds a burning cut and a cutting burn; the cause of which is that the sword and fire have a certain communion in the power of cutting and burning: so from the two natures of Christ proceeds the saving effusion of blood, the life-giving death, the victorious passion, the enriching poverty, on account of the mutual περιχώρησις [interpenetration], or the intimate κοινωνία [communion] of the two natures in Christ.

Latin:

Finis personalis vnionis, intimaeque duarum naturarum communionis, est patratio operum officii. Prob. In actionibus officii vtraque Christi natura agit, quod cuiusque proprium est, cum communicatione alterius. Non potest autem e diuersis principiis vnum apotelesma fluere, nisi supponatur illorum principiorum communio, v. gr. a gladio ignito prouenit sectio vrens, & vstio secans; cuius caussa est, quod gladius & ignis quandam communionem habent in virtute secandi & vrendi: ita a duabus Christi naturis proficiscitur effusio sanguinis saluifica, mors viuifica, passio victoriosa, paupertas ditans, ob περιχώρησιν mutuam, siue intimam duarum in Christo naturarum κοινωνίαν.


### Q. XXXIII. What things follow from the personal union and communion?

From the personal union and communion of the two natures of Christ flow personal propositions, just as does the communication of idioms. Prob. The mode of predicating follows the mode of being, and the communication of properties presupposes a perfect and intimate union of the distinct natures and their mutual περιχώρησις [interpenetration].

Latin:

Ex personali vnione & communione duarum Christi naturarum fluunt propositiones personales, iuxta atque communicatio idiomatum. Prob. Modus praedicandi sequitur modum essendi, & communicatio propriorum supponit perfectam & intimam distinctarum naturarum vnionem mutuamque earundem περιχώρησιν.


### Q. XXXIV. What are personal predications?

Personal predications are those in which the concrete of one nature is predicated of the concrete of the other nature in a singular and unusual way, so that the union of the two natures and their communion in the unity of the person may be expressed.

This definition of personal propositions is proven by examples from Scripture and the Church. The examples from Scripture are: The Branch of David is Jehovah our righteousness, Jer. XXIII, 5. XXXIII, 16. The Son of David is the Lord of David, Matt. XXII, 42. Ps. CX, 1. The Son of man is the Son of the living God, Matt. XVI, 13. 16. The Son of Mary is the Son of the Most High, Luke I, 35. The second man is the Lord from heaven, 1 Cor. XV, 47. The examples from the Church are: God is man, man is God .

Objection I These propositions are called personal because they take their origin from the personal union, they express the mystery of the personal union, and their force, truth, and connection must be judged from the personal union. Objection II A concrete of nature is a word by which nature is signified with the connotation of ὑπόστασις, or subsistence; or it is a word which signifies by way of a supposit, as when I say: God, man, Son of God, son of man: for when these words are heard, we immediately conceive in our mind a person, or supposit, which is made and called God, man, son of man, Son of God. A concrete of person is a word which formally signifies the whole person, consisting of both natures, as, Christ Jesus. An abstract of nature is a word which denotes one or the other nature in itself, without the connotation of hypostasis, as, humanity, deity, human nature, divine nature. It is called an abstract because it signifies by way of a form, not by way of a supposit .

Objection III The foundation of this predication: God is man, consists in the personal union and communion of natures. If they are viewed outside the personal union, the divine and human nature, or God and man, are disparate, and one cannot be affirmed of the other. For just as I cannot say: A lion is a horse: so I cannot say: God is man. But if a union intervenes between God and man, and indeed a real union, such as intervenes in Christ between the divine and human nature, they can rightly be predicated of each other in the concrete. The reason is that through the union two natures constitute one person, and any concrete of nature signifies that very person. Since, therefore, the man Christ is that same one who is God, or this person who is God is that same person who is man, it is also rightly said: man is God, and God is man.

But the abstracts of nature, which do not connote hypo hypostasis, or formally they do not signify a person, but a nature in itself, they cannot be predicated of each other . I will illustrate the matter with an example founded on accidental union. Theology and philosophy are accidents: which in the abstract cannot be predicated of each other. But if theology and philosophy are joined in one person, the theologian is rightly called a philosopher. Thus divinity and humanity are not predicated of each other in the abstract: but when both are united in the person of Christ, it is rightly said: God is man, and man is God.

Obs. IV.

Personal propositions are to be resolved in such a way that the unity of the person and the union of the two natures are expressed in them. Therefore, the genuine sense of these propositions: God is man, and man is God, is expressed by the simplest analysis (ἀνάλυσις) as follows: The Son of God is personally the same as the son of man, and the son of man is personally the same as the Son of God.

Conf. D. CALQVII systema tom. VII. p. 149. D. GERHARDVS in exeg. loc. IV. §. 168. explains the same by periphrasis: The Son of God assumes human nature into his own hypostasis, and human nature has been raised into the very hypostasis of the Son of God. B. CHEMNITIVS explains this proposition: God is man, thus: the whole fullness of the deity dwells personally in the assumed flesh by the Word (τῷ λόγῳ). But he explains this proposition: man is God, thus: The human nature of Christ does not subsist in itself, but has the Word (λόγον) as its hypostasis, and has the divine nature personally united to itself.

Latin:

Praedicationes personales sunt, in quibus concretum vnius naturae de concreto alterius naturae modo singulari ac inusitato praedicatur, vt exprimatur duarum naturarum vnio, earumque in vnitate personae communio.

Probatur haec propositionum personalium definitio exemplis scripturae et ecclesiae. Exempla scripturae sunt: Germen Dauidis est Iehouah iustitia nostra, Ier. XXIII, 5. XXXIII, 16. Filius Dauidis est dominus Dauidis, Matth. XXII, 42. Ps. CX, 1. Filius hominis est filius Dei viui, Matth. XVI, 13. 16. Filius Mariae est filius altissimi, Luc. I, 35. Secundus homo est dominus de caelo, 1 Cor. XV, 47. Exempla ecclesiae sunt: Deus est homo, homo est Deus .

Obiectio I Dicuntur hae propositiones personales, quia ex vnione personali originem ducunt, personalis vnionis mysterium exprimunt, & earum vis, veritas atque connexio ex vnione personali diiudicanda est. Obiectio II Concretum naturae est vox, qua significatur natura cum connotatione ὑποστάσεως, siue subsistentiae; vel est vox, quae significat per modum suppositi, vt cum dico: Deus, homo, Filius Dei, filius hominis: hisce enim vocibus auditis statim mente concipimus personam, siue suppositum, quod fit & dicatur Deus, homo, filius hominis, Filius Dei. Concretum personae est vox, quae totam personam, ex vtraque natura constantem, formaliter significat, vt, Christus Iesus. Abstractum naturae est vox, quae denotat alterutram naturam secundum se, non connotata hypostasi, vt, humanitas, deitas, humana natura, diuina natura. Vocatur abstractum, quia significat per modum formae, non per modum suppositi .

Obiectio III Fundamentum huius praedicationis: Deus est homo, in vnione personali & communione naturarum consistit. Si extra vnionem personalem spectentur, diuina & humana natura, vel Deus & homo, disparata sunt, nec vnum de altero affirmari potest. Sicut enim non possum dicere; Leo est equus: ita dicere nequeo: Deus est homo. Si autem vnio intercedat inter Deum & hominem, & quidem realis vnio, qualis intercedit in Christo inter diuinam & humanam naturam, recte de se inuicem praedicari possunt in concreto. Ratio est, quia per vnionem duae naturae constituunt vnam personam, & quodlibet concretum naturae significat illam ipsam personam. Quoniam ergo homo Christus idem ille est, qui Deus est, vel haec persona, quae Deus est, illa ipsa persona est, quae homo est, recte etiam dicitur: homo est Deus, & Deus est homo.

Abstracta autem naturae, quae non connotant hypostasin, sive formaliter non significant personam, sed naturam secundum se, de se invicem praedicari nequeunt . Illustrabo rem exemplo fundato in unione accidentali. Theologia & philosophia sunt accidentia: quae in abstracto de se invicem praedicari nequeunt. At si in una persona coniungantur theologia & philosophia, recte theologus dicitur philosophus. Ita divinitas & humanitas non praedicantur de se invicem in abstracto: at cum utraque unita sit in persona Christi, recte dicitur: Deus est homo, & homo est Deus.

Obs. IV.

Propositiones personales ita resoluendae sunt, vt iisdem vnitas personae, & duarum naturarum vnio exprimatur. Sensus igitur genuinus harum propositionum: Deus est homo, & homo est Deus, ἀνάλυσις simplicissima ita exprimitur: Filius Dei personaliter idem est, qui filius hominis, & filius hominis personaliter idem est, qui Filius Dei.

Conf. D. CALQVII systema tom. VII. p. 149. D. GERHARDVS in exeg. loc. IV. §. 168. easdem per periphrasin explicat: Filius Dei in suam hypostasin assumit humanam naturam, & humana natura in ipsam Filii Dei hypostasin est euecta. B. CHEMNITIVS hanc propositionem: Deus est homo, ita exponit: tota plenitudo deitatis τὸ λόγῳ habitat in assumta carne personaliter. Hanc vero propositionem: homo est Deus, ita explanat: Humana Christi natura non in se subsistit, sed λόγον habet pro hypostasi, & divinam naturam personaliter sibi habet unitam.


### Question XXXV. Are personal propositions merely verbal, improper, identical, or to be judged by other common propositions?

Personal propositions are not merely verbal a), nor improper or tropical b), nor identical c), but they are real, unusual, and without example d).

Prob. a. If the personal propositions, God is man, and man is God, were only verbal, the son of the virgin Mary would be called the son of the Most High only in title, which is Nestorian. For NESTORIVS denied that the virgin Mary had truly given birth to God. Prob. b.

When we say: Man is God, the subject retains its proper meaning no less than the predicate. For by man is understood an intelligent animal, by God an independent spirit. If personal propositions were improper, the son of the virgin Mary would not be God, just as a painted man is not a man.

Prob. c. Personal predications are not identical, because in them the same is not predicated of the same; but the concrete of one nature is predicated of the concrete of another nature with the connotation of hypostasis: and just as personal union is not between the same things, but between the most distinct things; so the predication, flowing from personal union, is not identical. Prob. d.

Personal propositions are real; because they have a true and real foundation, which is the personal union and the communion of the two natures in Christ. However, they are not to be judged by other vulgar propositions; for the reason that they are most singular and unusual in the philosophical circle and in gentile logic. The philosopher does not know from the light of nature, knows that one substantial disparate can be predicated of another disparate in the nominative case. Predications used in philosophy are distinguished into synonymous and paronymous. Personal predications are not synonymous, because in them 1) the predicate is not of the essence of the subject, much less the essence of the subject itself: 2) the foundation of them is not an essential union. For neither is man a part of the divine essence, nor is God a part of the human essence. Man is not God by essence, but by the grace of union, nor is God essentially a rational animal. Personal predications are also not paronymous; since a property and a predicable accident are predicated paronymously. But neither is human nature a property of divinity, nor is divinity an idiom of humanity, nor is man a predicable accident, in relation to τὸν λόγον. For an accident is predicated of its subject, because of an accidental connection with the same; but the foundation of a personal proposition is not an accidental union, but a hypostatic union.

You say: I. That predication, whose predicate does not enter into the essence of the subject, is paronymous. But of this predication: God is man, the predicate does not enter into the essence of the subject. Therefore. Resp. A predication is called paronymous either in a general or a special sense. In a special sense, a predication is called paronymous in which either a property or a predicable accident is predicated of its subject, regarding an accidental union. But in a general sense, a predication is called paronymous whose predicate is not of the essence of the subject: in which general sense it is paronymous, which is attributed to something truly, yet without a preceding essential union, and it is divided into predicamental, transcendent, and mystical. See GVTKII logic p. 125. We do not deny that in this general sense a personal predication can be called paronymous.

You say: II. Personal predications are not unusual, because they frequently occur in Holy Scripture, they are also found in the books of logicians, and many examples are given where two disparates are predicated of each other in the nominative case, e.g., The physician is a consul, the tailor is a senator, etc. Resp. Personal predications are called unusual not with respect to Holy Scripture and theology, but with respect to Aristotelian logic and gentile philosophy, constructed from an induction of natural examples. Christian logicians and philosophers took personal propositions from Holy Scripture or theology. The adduced examples exhibit propositions in which two accidental disparates are predicated of each other. But when I say: God is man, a substantial disparate is predicated of a substantial disparate in its proper signification and in the nominative case: of which a similar example is not given in the whole universe of things. For it is ὁμολογυμένως μέγα μυ- στήριον, God was manifest in the flesh. 1 Tim. III, 16.

Latin:

Propositiones personales non sunt mere verbales a), neque impropriae aut tropicae b), neque identicae c), sed sunt reales, inusitatae & sine exemplo d).

Prob. a. Si propositiones personales, Deus est homo, & homo est Deus, tantum verbales essent, filius virginis Mariae titulotenus vocaretur filius altissimi, quod est Nestorianum. Negauit enim NESTORIVS, virginem Mariam reuera genuisse Deum.

Prob. b. Cum dicimus: Homo est Deus, subiectum non minus, quam praedicatum propriam retinet significationem. Nam per hominem intelligitur animal intelligens, per Deum spiritus independens. Si propositiones personales impropriae essent, filius virginis Mariae esset non Deus, sicut homo pictus est non homo.

Prob. c. Praedicationes personales non sunt identicae, propterea, quod in iisdem non praedicatur idem de eodem; sed concretum vnius naturae praedicatur de concreto alterius naturae cum connotatione hypostaseos: & sicut vnio personalis non est inter eadem, sed inter distinctissima; ita praedicatio, ex vnione personali fluens, non est identica.

Prob. d. Propositiones personales sunt reales; quia habent verum & reale fundamentum, quod est vnio personalis & communio duarum in Christo naturarum. Non tamen diiudicandae sunt ex aliis propositionibus vulgaribus; ideo, quod singularissima & in circulo philosophico atque logica gentili inusitatae sunt. Philosophus ex lumine naturae non cognoscit, scit, quod vnum disparatum substantiale de altero disparato in casu recto prædicari possit. Prædicationes in philosophia usitatæ distinguuntur in synonymicas, & paronymicas. Prædicationes personales non sunt synonymicæ, quia in illis 1) prædicatum non est de essentia subiecti, multo minus ipsa essentia subiecti: 2) fundamentum illarum non est vnio essentialis. Neque enim homo est pars essentiæ diuinæ, neque Deus pars essentiæ humanæ. Homo non est Deus per essentiam, sed per vnionis gratiam, nec Deus essentialiter est animal rationale. Prædicationes personales etiam non sunt paronymicæ; quoniam paronymice prædicantur proprium & accidens prædicabile. At nec humana natura est proprietas diuinitatis, nec diuinitas est idioma humanitatis, neque homo est accidens prædicabile, in ordine ad τὸν λόγον. Accidens enim prædicatur de suo subiecto, ob connexionem cum eodem accidentalem; at fundamentum propositionis personalis non est vnio accidentalis, sed vnio hypostatica.

Dicis: I. Illa prædicatio, cuius prædicatum non ingreditur essentiam subiecti, est paronymica. Sed huius prædicationis: Deus est homo, prædicatum non ingreditur essentiam subiecti. E. Resp. Paronymica dicitur prædicatio vel in sensu generali vel speciali. Sensu speciali paronymica dicitur prædicatio, in qua prædicatur vel proprium, vel accidens prædicabile de suo subiecto, ad vnionem accidentalem. Sensu generali autem paronymica dicitur prædicatio, cuius prædicatum non est de essentia subiecti: quo sensu generali paronymicum est, quod alicui vere, non tamen præcedente vnione essentiali tribuitur, & diuiditur in prædicamentale transscendens, & mysticum. Vid. GVTKII logicam p. 125. Sensu isto generali prædicationem personalem dici posse paronymicam, non diffitemur.

Dicis: II. Prædicationes personales non sunt inusitatæ, quia frequenter occurrunt in S. scriptura, inueniuntur etiam in logicorum libellis, & dantur plura exempla, vbi duo disparata de se inuicem prædicantur in casu recto, v. gr. Medicus est consul, sartor est senator &c. Resp.
