Prædicationes personales dicuntur inusitatæ non respectu S. scripturæ & theologiæ, sed respectu logicæ Aristotelicæ & philosophiæ gentilis, ex inductione exemplorum naturalium exstructæ. Logici & philosophi christiani propositiones personales e S. scriptura, vel theologia depromserunt. Adducta exempla exhibent propositiones, in quibus duo disparata accidentalia de se prædicantur. At cum dico: Deus est homo, disparatum substantiale de disparato substantiali in significatione propria & casu recto prædicatur: cuius exemplum simile in tota rerum vniuersitate non datur. Est enim ὁμολογυμένως μέγα μυστήριον, Deus manifestatus est in carne. 1 Tim. III, 16.


### Q. XXXVI. Is that proposition: Christ, according to his human nature, is the natural Son of God, true?

That proposition: Christ, according to his human nature, is the natural Son of God, is true, in a specificative sense a); false in a reduplicative, or causal sense b).

Obs. I. Limitative particles are sometimes taken αἰτιολογικῶς, or reduplicatively, and signify that that to which they are added is the cause on account of which the predicate belongs to the subject, e.g., Man, insofar as he is a sinner, is mortal, i.e., Sin is the cause on account of which man is mortal. Sometimes they are taken ὁριστικῶς, or …specificatively, and designate the nature, part, or condition according to which the predicate belongs to the subject, e.g., Christ, insofar as he is man, died, i.e., Christ died according to his human nature. With these presuppositions we say that Christ, as man, or according to his human nature, is the natural Son of God, not in a reduplicative or causal sense, but in a specificative or subjective sense, so that the sense may be: Christ, according to his human nature, or Christ as man, is the same supposit, the same person, which is the natural Son of God.…

Obs. II. The subject, of which some idiom or axiom is predicated, is either the dektikon proton (receptive primary), the primary subject to which the predicate belongs per se, immediately, and formally, e.g., Fire is hot: or it is the dektikon deuteron (receptive secondary), the secondary subject to which the predicate belongs on account of something else united to it, and therefore mediately and communicatively, or participatively, e.g., Iron, united to fire, is hot, on account of the fire, and therefore mediately and participatively. Thus Christ as man is called the natural Son of God, not per se, immediately, and formally, but by the grace of the personal union, and therefore mediately and communicatively. The Theologians indicated this very thing when they asserted that Christ, as man, can be called the natural Son of God, not naturally, but personally.

Obs. III. The natural Son is here opposed to the adopted son, and therefore the sense is, Christ as man is not an adopted Son of God, but a natural one, not by eternal generation, but by personal union.

Prob. a. 1) Christ as man is the proper Son of God, whom God the Father did not spare, but whom He delivered up to death, Rom. VIII, 32. Therefore, Christ as man is the natural Son of God. The reason for the consequence is: because the proper Son of God never denotes an adopted son, but a natural one.

2) To gennomenon ek Marias hagion, that holy thing which was born of Mary, is the Son of the Most High, Luke I, 35. Therefore, the Son of the Blessed Virgin Mary is the natural Son of God.

3) The hypostasis of Christ the man is divine, that of the natural Son of God Himself: Therefore, Christ as man is the natural Son of God. The reason for the consequence is: because here the question is not about humanity in the abstract, but in the concrete, insofar as it subsists in the divine hypostasis.

4) The divine nature has been communicated to Christ as man: Therefore, Christ as man is the natural Son of God.

5) Christ, as man, is not a person foreign to God: Therefore, Christ, as man, is not an adopted Son of God. For adoption belongs to a foreign person.

6) The Logos assumed flesh into His own hypostasis, so that He might be the proper Son of God in two natures, just as He was previously the proper Son in one nature. But if, on account of the assumption, He were to be called adopted, then He would be an adopted son of Himself, because only the Son assumed humanity.

Prob. b. The cause on account of which Christ, as man, is the natural Son of God, is not human nature, but personal union.

Antithesis was once that of Felix of Urgell and Elipandus of Toledo, Bishops, who taught that Christ according to His humanity was an adopted Son of God. For this reason, the Council of Frankfurt on the Main was convened in the 8th century, in the year 794, by Charlemagne, in which it was concluded and defined against Felix and Elipandus that Christ, even according to His human nature, is the Son of God. To these are added the Socinians and Arminians, who maintain that Christ the man is an adopted Son of God.

Their stronger arguments are: I. Whoever is the natural Son of God, he is begotten from eternity: Christ as man is not begotten from eternity: Therefore. Resp. Whoever is the natural Son of God per se and naturally, he is begotten from eternity; I concede. But Christ as man is the Son of God not per se and naturally, but personally, on account of the communicated hypostasis and divine nature.

II. According to whatever nature Christ is not begotten from the substance of God the Father, nor is like to God the Father, according to that nature He is not the natural Son of God: But according to human nature, etc.: Therefore. Resp. A third option is given, and therefore the major premise, lest it labor from a defect of parts, ret, it must be formulated thus: According to that nature by which Christ is neither begotten of the substance of God the Father, nor similar to God the Father, nor assumed into the glory of eternal sonship by hypostatic union, according to that nature he is not the natural Son of God: But according to the human nature, etc. Thus the minor premise is false.

III. If Christ is to be called the natural Son of God according to his human nature, then either the human nature is the cause of this denomination, or it is the immediate subject to which eternal sonship pertains per se and formally: But neither is true: Therefore. Resp. A third option is given. The human nature is not the cause of eternal sonship, nor its primary subject; it is, however, a secondary subject, to which eternal sonship does not pertain per se and essentially, but communicatively and by the grace of the personal union.

Instance I. In restrictive propositions, the limiting particle specifies the primary subject to which the predicate pertains per se and immediately, e.g., Man lives according to his soul, because the soul is the primary subject of life. Resp. This is not universal. For I also correctly say: Man lives according to his body, because life is communicated to him by the soul. Thus Christ is the natural Son of God according to his human nature, since it has been assumed into the communion of the supreme sonship.

Instance II. This limiting proposition: Christ is the natural Son of God according to his human nature, must be resolved thus: The human nature of Christ is the natural Son of God, which is false. For the natural Son of God is a person: the human nature of Christ is not a person, but is personated. Resp. The human nature of Christ is not taken here in the abstract, but in the concrete, as it constitutes with the divine nature one σύνδετον (conjoined) person, so that the sense is: Christ as man is not essentially, but personally, the natural Son of God.

IV. Christ according to his human nature is subject to God, and his servant: Therefore, Christ according to his human nature is not the natural Son of God. Resp. The humanity of Christ is considered in three ways: a) by reason of natural condition: b) by reason of spontaneous emptying: c) by reason of personal union. The human nature of Christ in itself is a creature subject to God, and by spontaneous emptying it assumed the form of a servant, which it laid aside in the state of exaltation: but by the personal union it constitutes one person with the divine nature τῷ λόγῳ (with the Word), and thus has been assumed into the communion of the supreme sonship.

XXXVI. Is the Holy Virgin Mary to be called θεοτόκος, or Mother of God?

The Christian Church rightly calls the holy Virgin Mary θεοτόκος, or Mother of God.

Proof 1) That which is born of Mary is the Son of the Most High, as the angel teaches, Luke I, v. 35. 2) Paul, Gal. IV, 4, says: When the fullness of time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman. From these sayings of Scripture we argue: That virgin, of whom God was born, is θεοτόκος. But the Blessed Mary is that virgin, etc. Therefore. The minor is clear: because the Son of the Most High is true God.

Obs. That proposition: Mary is θεοτόκος, or Mother of God, can be understood in two ways. 1) Formally and reduplicatively, in this way: Mary is θεοτόκος, i.e., she begat God, as God, or according to his deity; and thus the proposition is false. For Christ according to his deity was not born in time of the Virgin Mary, but begotten of the substance of his Father from eternity. 2) Materially and specifically, in this way: Mary is θεοτόκος; because she begat God, or him who is true and eternal God; and in this sense that proposition was understood by pious antiquity, and defended against NESTORIUS, in which sense we also understand it. For there is one person of Christ, one suppositum, which is God and man. Wherefore we not only rightly say that Mary PART III. SECT. I. Ss ss begat a man specifically ὁμοούσιον (consubstantial) to us, but also to have generated God himself; since that one and the same [person], who was born of the Virgin Mary, becomes God and man.

DE COMMVNICATIONE IDIOMATVM.

Latin:

Propositio illa: Christus, secundum humanam naturam, est Filius Dei naturalis, est vera, in sensu specificatiuo a); falsa in sensu reduplicatiuo, siue caussali b).

Obs. I. Particulæ limitatiuæ interdum sumuntur αἰτιολογικῶς, siue reduplicatiue, & significant, id, cui adduntur, esse caussam, propter quam prædicatum competit subiecto, v. gr. Homo, quatenus peccator, est mortalis, i. e. Peccatum est caussa, propter quam homo mortalis est. Interdum sumuntur ὁριστικῶς, siue specificatiue, & designant naturam, partem, aut conditionem, secundum quam prædicatum subiecto conuenit, v. gr. Christus, quatenus homo, mortuus est, i. e. Christus secundum humanam naturam mortuus est. Quibus præsuppositis dicimus, quod Christus, vt homo, vel secundum humanam naturam, sit Filius Dei naturalis, non in sensu reduplicatiuo, aut caussali, sed specificatiuo, ve. subiectiuo, vt sensus sit: Christus, secundum humanam naturam, vel Christus homo, est idem suppositum, eadem persona, quae est Filius Dei naturalis.

Obs. II. Subiectum, de quo aliquod idioma, vel axioma praedicatur, vel est δεκτικὸν πρῶτον, subiectum primum, cui per se immediate & formaliter praedicatum competit, v. gr. Ignis est calidus: vel est δεκτικὸν δεύτερον, subiectum secundum, cui praedicatum propter aliud vnitum, adeoque mediate & communicatiue, vel participatiue conuenit, v. gr. Ferrum, igni vnitum, est calidum, propter ignem, adeoque mediate & participatiue. Ita Christus homo dicitur Filius Dei naturalis, non per se, immediate & formaliter, sed per vnionis personalis gratiam, adeoque mediate & communicatiue. Id ipsum indigitatum fuerunt Theologi, cum assuererunt, quod Christus, vt homo, dici possit Filius Dei naturalis, non naturaliter, sed personaliter.

Obs. III. Filius naturalis hic opponitur filio adoptiuo, adeoque sensus est, Christus homo non est Filius Dei adoptiuus, sed naturalis, non per aeternam generationem, sed personalem vnionem.

Prob. a. 1) Christus homo est Filius Dei proprius, cui Deus Pater non pepercit, sed quem in mortem tradidit, Rom. VIII, 32. E. Christus homo est Filius Dei naturalis. Ratio consequentiae est: quia Filius Dei proprius nunquam filium adoptiuum, sed naturalem notat.

2) Τὸ γεννώμενον ἐκ Μαρίας ἅγιον, illud sanctum, quod natum est ex Maria, est filius altissimi, Luc. I, 35. Ergo filius B. virginis Mariae est Filius Dei naturalis.

3) Hypostasis Christi hominis diuina, ipsius Filii Dei naturalis est: Ergo Christus homo est Filius Dei naturalis. Ratio consequentiae est: quia hic de humanitate non in abstracto, sed in concreto, quatenus in hypostasi diuina subsistit, quaeritur.

4) Christo homini communicata est natura diuina: Ergo Christus homo est Filius Dei naturalis.

5) Christus, vt homo, non est persona extranea a Deo: Ergo Christus, vt homo, non est Filius Dei adoptiuus. Adoptio enim est personae extraneae.

6) Carnem in hypostasin suam assumsit ὁ λόγος, vt esset proprius Dei filius in duabus naturis, sicut ante fuit proprius filius in vna natura. Si autem propter assumtionem dicendus esset adoptiuus, tum esset filius adoptiuus sui ipsius, quia solus filius humanitatem assumsit.

Prob. b. Caussa, propter quam Christus, vt homo, est Filius Dei naturalis, non est natura humana, sed personalis vnio.

Antithesis fuit olim Felicis Vrgelitani & Elipandi, Toletani, Episcoporum, qui docuerunt, Christum secundum humanitatem suam esse Filium Dei adoptiuum. Qua de caussa concilium Francofurtanum ad Maen. Sec. VIII. a. DCCXCIV. a Carolo M. coactum est, in quo contra Felicem & Elipandum conclusum ac definitum est, Christum etiam iuxta naturam humanam esse Filium Dei. His accedunt Sociniani & Arminiani, statuentes, Christum hominem esse Filium Dei adoptiuum.

Quorum sunt potiora argumenta: I. Quicunque est Filius Dei naturalis, ille ab aeterno est genitus: Christus homo non est ab aeterno genitus: Ergo. Resp. Quicunque per se & naturaliter est Filius Dei naturalis, is ab aeterno est genitus; concedo. At Christus homo est Filius Dei non per se & naturaliter, sed personaliter, propter communicatam hypostasin & naturam diuinam.

II. Secundum quam naturam Christus non est ex substantia Dei Patris genitus, nec Deo Patri similis, secundum eam naturam non est Filius Dei naturalis: Atqui secundum humanam naturam &c: Ergo. Resp. Datur tertium, adeoque maior, ne defectu partium laboret, ret, ita formanda est: Secundum quam naturam Christus neque ex substantia Dei Patris est genitus, neque Deo Patri similis, neque ex vnione hypostatica in gloriam externæ filiationis assumptus, secundum eam naturam non est Filius Dei naturalis: Atqui secundum naturam &c. Sic minor est falsa.

III. Si Christus secundum humanam naturam dicendus est Filius Dei naturalis, vel humana natura est causa huius denominationis, vel est subiectum immediatum, cui externa filiatio per se & formaliter competit: At neutrum vero est consentaneum: Ergo. Resp. Datur tertium. Natura humana non est causa externæ filiationis, neque eius subiectum primum; est tamen subiectum secundum, cui externa filiatio non competit per se & essentialiter, sed communicativè & per vnionis personalis gratiam.

Instantia I. In propositionibus restrictiuis particula limitatiua specificat subiectum primum, cui prædicatum per se & immediate competit, v. gr. Homo secundum animam viuit, quia anima est vitæ subiectum primum. Resp. Hoc non est perpetuum. Nam & recte dico: Homo secundum corpus viuit, quia vita ipsi ab anima est communicata. Ita Christus secundum humanam naturam est Filius Dei naturalis, quoniam in communionem summæ filiationis assumta est.

Instantia II. Propositio hæc limitatiua: Christus secundum humanam naturam est Filius Dei naturalis, ita resoluenda est: Humana Christi natura est Filius Dei naturalis, quod est falsum. Nam Filius Dei naturalis est persona: humana Christi natura non est persona, sed personata. Resp. Humana Christi natura hic non sumitur in abstracto, sed in concreto, prout cum natura diuina vnam constituit personam σύνδετον, vt sensus sit: Christus homo non est essentialiter, sed personaliter est Filius Dei naturalis.

IV. Christus secundum humanam naturam est Deo subiectus, eiusque seruus: E. Christus secundum humanam naturam non est Filius Dei naturalis. Resp. Humanitas Christi tribus modis consideratur: a) ratione naturalis conditionis: b) ratione spontaneæ exinanitionis: c) ratione personalis vnionis. Humana Christi natura secundum se est creatura Deo subiecta, & spontanea exinanitione seruilem assumsit formam, quam in statu exaltationis deposuit: per vnionem autem personalem vnam cum natura diuina τῷ λόγῳ personam constituit, atque adeo in communionem summæ filiationis assumta est.

Quæst. XXXVI. Esne S. virgo Maria dicenda Θεοτόκος, siue Deipara?

Ecclesia christiana sanctam virginem Mariam recte vocat Θεοτόκον, siue Deiparam.

Prob. 1) Id, quod nascitur ex Maria, est filius altissimi, docente angelo, Luc. I, v. 35. 2) Paullus Gal. IV, 4. inquit: Quando venit plenitudo temporis, misit Deus filium suum natum ex muliere. E quibus dictis scripturæ argumentamur: Illa virgo, e qua natus est Deus, est Θεοτόκος. Atqui B. Maria est illa virgo &c. Ergo. Minor liquet: quia filius altissimi est verus Deus.

Obs. Propositio illa: Maria est Θεοτόκος, siue Deipara, bifariam intelligi potest. 1) Formaliter & reduplicatiue, hoc modo: Maria est Θεοτόκος, i. e. genuit Deum, qua Deum, siue secundum deitatem; & ita propositio falsa est. Christus enim secundum deitatem non est natus in tempore ex Maria virgine, sed de substantia Patris sui genitus ab æterno. 2) Materialiter & specificatiue, hoc modo: Maria est Θεοτόκος, quia genuit Deum, siue illum, qui verus & æternus Deus est; & hoc sensu propositio illa intellecta est a pia antiquitate, & contra NESTORIVM propugnata, quo sensu etiam nos illam intelligimus. Vna enim est persona Christi, vnum supposittum, quod est Deus & homo. Quare non solum recte dicimus, Mariam PARS III. SECT. I. Ss ss genuiffe genuisse hominem nobis specifice ὁμοούσιον, sed ipsam etiam genuisse Deum; cum vnus & idem ille, qui natus est ex Maria virgine, fit Deus & homo.

DE COMMVNICATIONE IDIOMATVM.


### Q. XXXVII

What is the communication of idioms? The communication of idioms is a true and real participation of the properties of the divine and human nature in Christ the θεανδρῴπῳ (God-man), denominated from the one or the other, or both natures, resulting from the personal union. Obs.

I. The personal union and the communication of idioms differ as antecedent and consequent, not in the order of time, but in the order of nature.

Obs. II. Idioma in Latin is called a property. But there are idioms that are ἁπλῶς (simply), or so-called simply, and others that are κατὰ τί (in a certain respect), and such that are respective. Idioms simply and strictly so-called are those which necessarily flow from the essence, affect the same, and distinguish it a posteriori from another thing. Such are the idioms of man: to be risible, capable of wonder, endowed with the faculty of speech, and capable of learning. Idioms κατὰ τί, or respective, are such as distinguish one thing from another in any way, even though they are ἐνεργήματα καὶ ἀποτελέσματα (energies and results), works of office, or even common accidents, e.g., to be born, to die, to shed blood, etc., which are called properties of human nature in a certain respect and relatively, insofar as they belong to human nature outside of its primary concept, and distinguish it to a certain extent from the divine nature.

Obs. III. This phrase, communication of idioms, is not found verbatim in the sacred scriptures; yet the thing itself has most clear foundations in the scriptures. For as often as scripture assigns the actions and works of divine omnipotence to the flesh of Christ, so often by consequence is omnipotence attributed to him, as the first act from which the divine ἐνέργεια (energy), as the second act, flows. What is more? The epistle to the Hebrews clearly shows us the use of this phrase when it uses those two Greek words, and those very emphatic ones, κεκοινώνηκε and μετέσχε, he shared and he partook, and indeed in this very matter concerning the personal union of two natures in Christ, c. II, 14. Although the communication of idioms was first named by the Scholastics, nevertheless, orthodox antiquity in the struggles with NESTORIUS and EUTYCHES employed equivalent formulas of speech, which see in D. HUTTER, in Form. Concord. artic. VIII, de persona Christi, p. 759.

Latin:

Communicatio idiomatum est vera & realis propriorum diuinæ & humanæ naturæ in Christo θεανδρῴπῳ, ab alterutra, vel vtraque natura denominato, participatio, ex vnione personali resultans.

Obs. I. Vnio personalis, & communicatio idiomatum differunt, vt antecedens & consequens non temporis, sed naturæ ordine.

Obs. II. Idioma latine dicitur proprium. Sunt autem idiomata alia ἁπλῶς, siue simpliciter ita dicta, alia κατὰ τί, secundum quid, & respective talia. Idiomata simpliciter & stricte ita dicta sunt, quæ necessario fluunt ex essentia, eandem afficiunt, & a posteriori distinguunt a re alia. Eiusmodi idiomata hominis sunt, esse risiuum, admiratiuum, loquendi facultate præditum, disciplinarum capacem. Idiomata κατὰ τί, seu respective talia sunt, quæ rem vnam ab alia quomodocunque distinguunt, quamuis sint ἐνεργήματα καὶ ἀποτελέσματα, opera officii, vel etiam accidentia communia, v. gr. nasci, mori, fundere sanguinem &c. quæ dicuntur propria humanæ naturæ, secundum quid, & respective, in quantum humanæ naturæ extra primum conceptum conueniunt, eamque a natura diuina quadantenus discernunt.

Obs. III. Phrasis hæc, communicatio idiomatum, sacris in litteris αὐτολεξεὶ non reperitur; res tamen ipsa clarissima habet scripturarum fundamenta. Nam quoties carni Christi actiones & opera diuinæ omnipotentiæ scriptura assignat; toties per consequentiam, omnipotentia ipsi tribuitur, tanquam actus primus, a quo ἐνέργεια diuina, velut actus secundus, manat. Quid? quod epistola ad Hebræos dilucide vsum istius phraseos nobis monstrat, quando vtitur duobus istis verbis græcis, iisque valde emphaticis, κεκοινώνηκε & μετέσχε, communicauit, & participauit, & quidem in hac ipsa materia de vnione personali duarum naturarum in Christo, c. II, 14. Quamuis autem a Scholasticis primum dicta sit communicatio idiomatum: orthodoxa tamen antiquitas in certaminibus cum NESTORIO & EVTYCHE æquipollentes loquendi formulas adhibuit, quas vide apud D. HVTTER. in Form. Concord. artic. VIII. de persona Christi p. 759.


### Q. XXXVIII

What kind is this communication of idioms? The communication of idioms is not merely verbal and titular a), nor intellectual b); but real, between two substances really distinct, but not separated: and therefore it is not equalizing c), nor multiplying d), nor transfusing e); but rather συνδυαστική (combining), between two substances perfectly and intimately united: yet it is not accidental, or commingling f), nor essential or natural g); but personal and supernatural h).

Prob. a. The communication of idioms is not a title without the thing. For Christ the man is truly omnipotent, not just in title, as empirics and quacks not rarely hear themselves called doctors, who are nothing less than such.

Prob. b. Intellectual communication occurs between subjects not really, but only distinct by reason. Thus an animal is said to communicate its properties to a man κατὰ μέθεξιν (by participation), through intellectual communication. But personal communication of properties is between the two natures of Christ, which are really distinct. Prob. c.

The communication of properties does not imply an equalization, neither of the united natures nor of the properties; because such an equalization conflicts with the real difference of the divine and human nature, and of the properties flowing from each nature. Prob. d.

The communication of properties is not multiplicative, such as it is when a man generating, κατ’ ἀλλοποίησιν (by alteration), communicates his soul to his son. For multiplicative communication is between two separate substances; but the communication of properties is between two united substances. Prob. e.

Prob. e. The communication of properties is not transfusive. We believe, however, teach, and confess that no such effusion of the majesty of God and all His properties into the human nature of Christ occurs, by which anything should be lost to the divine nature; or that it should so lavish something of its own to another, that for this reason it does not retain it in itself; or that the human nature in its substance and essence has received an equal majesty, which becomes separated and divided from the divine nature and essence; as when wine, water, or oil is transfused from one vessel into another. For neither the human nature in Christ, nor any other creature in heaven or on earth, is capable of divine omnipotence in such a way that it becomes of itself an omnipotent essence and nature, or has omnipotent properties in itself and by itself. For in this way the human nature in Christ would be denied and would be entirely transmuted into divinity, says F. C. p. 78c.

Prob. f. The communication of properties is not commixtive; because neither the two natures of Christ, nor the properties of either nature, can be mixed. We believe, teach, and confess that the divine and human natures have not been mixed into one substance, nor has one been changed into the other; but that each nature retains its essential properties, so that they cannot become the properties of the other nature, says Form. Concord. p. 606.

The communication of properties is not essential, in the way in which God the Father communicated His essence and all divine properties to His coeternal Son from eternity: whence He is of one essence with the Father, and equal to Him. But in the person of Christ, each nature retains its properties within its own distinct nature and essence; so that the human nature always is and remains inferior to the divinity. Nor is it essential or natural in the way in which the soul communicates its properties to the body; because the foundation of this communication is an essential union, by which two incomplete natures concur to constitute one complete nature: But the two natures of Christ, being complete in their being, are united to constitute one σύνθετον (composite) person. Prob. h.

Therefore, the communication of properties, of which we are speaking at present, is real, συνδυασική (conjunctive), i.e., between united natures, and by that hypostatic union of the two natures in Christ.

The real communication of properties is proved: 1) No union that is perfect and perichoristic can exist without the communication of properties, as the examples of an animate body show. We readily grant that a paraftatic union of two things occurs without the communication of properties, for the reason that that degree of union is the lowest and most imperfect. But indeed, as Scripture defines, the personal union of the two natures in Christ is most absolute, most perfect, and perichoristic: Therefore, it cannot exist without the communication of properties. Furthermore, we conclude: As is the union, so is the communication of properties. But the union of the two natures in Christ is real: Therefore, the communication of properties flowing from it is real.

2) As truly as the humanity of Christ has the hypostasis of the Logos communicated to it, so truly does it also have the divine idioms communicated to it: But the humanity has the hypostasis of the Logos really communicated to it. Therefore, it also has the divine idioms really communicated to it.

The major premise is proved: 1) because divine idioms, on the part of the thing, are the same as the divine hypostasis. And whatever things are really the same, if one is communicated, the other is communicated as well. 2) If the hypostasis is communicated, the idioms will be communicated much more. For these are common to the three divine persons; but the hypostasis is proper to the Logos alone.

3) In that body, as a temple, personally assumed, the whole fullness of divinity dwells; to it the divine idioms are truly and really communicated: But in the body of Christ, etc. Therefore.

4) Whoever, like children, becomes a partaker of human flesh and blood, he becomes a partaker of human idioms: But the Son of God, etc. Therefore. The major premise is evident: because flesh and blood denote human nature, which is never destitute of its own properties.

5) The communication of idioms is necessary for the performance of the works of the office, in which each nature of Christ acts, doing what is proper to each, with the communication of the other.

The antithesis was formerly that of Samosatenus, Sabellius, Nestorius, and Eutyches, who either introduced a confusion of natures or denied the communication of natures and idioms, whom the Papists follow today in many things. Their arguments are:

I. Those whose essence and definition are not common, their properties are not communicable: But the essence and definition of the divine and human natures of Christ are not common. Therefore. The major premise is clear: because communicable predicates pertain to the definition of a thing, e.g., "Animal" communicates its nature to "man," and pertains to the definition of man. Resp. Distinguish between intellectual communication, which is the effect of union katá méthexin, and is between a subject and a predicate that are really the same and distinct only by reason; and real communication, which is the consequence of union katá syndýasin. The argument is valid regarding the former, not the latter communication.

II. Whatever is communicated to another migrates from its own subject: But the properties of the divine and human natures of Christ do not migrate from their own subject: Therefore. Resp. by limiting: Whatever is communicated to another by transfusion: But the communication of idioms in Christ is by no means done by transfusion, but by perichoretic union.

III. Whatever is communicated becomes common: But the properties of the divine and human natures are not common. Therefore. The major premise is evident: because "proper" and "common" are diametrically opposed to each other. The minor premise is certain: because each nature of Christ retains its own properties, as they cannot become the properties of the other.

Resp. 1) Whatever is communicated to another becomes communicable, not common, strictly speaking.

2) Something is called "common" in two ways: a) In a stricter sense, that is called common which belongs to many equally and in the same way; in this special meaning, it is opposed to "proper." b) In a broader sense, that is called common which belongs to many in any way, even a diverse way—to one primarily, immediately, and of itself; to the other secondarily, mediately, and through another. In this broader sense, the properties indeed become common on account of the perichoretic union, and nevertheless remain the properties of that nature to which they belong primarily and of themselves.

IV. Whatever remains distinct in the union itself, their properties are not communicated: The two natures of Christ, etc. Therefore. The major premise is evident: because distinction and communication seem to fight against each other.

Resp. Distraction is repugnant to communication, not distinction.

In a flaming sword, the natures are distinct, yet the power of burning is communicated to the iron, and the power of cutting to the fire.

V. If the properties of the divine nature were communicated to the human nature, they would exist in two subjects: The consequent is false; because one property cannot exist in two subjects: Therefore, the antecedent is also false. Resp. One property cannot exist in two primary and immediate subjects; it can, however, exist in two subjects united by perichoresis, of which one is primary and immediate, the other secondary and mediate.

VI. If the properties of the divine nature had been communicated to the assumed human nature, they would inhere in it: But they do not inhere in the human nature; because they are not accidents, whose nature it is to inhere; Therefore, they are not communicated to the human nature. Resp. The mode of inherence is various.

Divine idioms do not inhere in the human nature by subjective inherence, like accidents, but by intimate union and indwelling.

VII. Whatever dogma introduces an equalization of the divine and human natures is to be rejected: The dogma concerning the communication of idioms, etc. [is such a dogma]. Therefore [it is to be rejected]. The minor is proved: because, according to the doctrine of the communication of idioms, the human nature of Christ is equally omnipotent, omniscient, etc., as His divine nature.

Resp. I deny the minor. For although the omnipotence of the divine and human nature of Christ is the same, the mode of possessing it is nonetheless very different.

For the divine nature is omnipotent formally, immediately, and of itself; the human nature of Christ is omnipotent communicatively, mediately, and through the grace of the personal union.

Quæst. XXXIX. How many kinds of communication of idioms are there? There are three kinds of communication of idioms.

Prob. For there are three general classes to which all the sayings of Scripture that deal with the communication of idioms can be conveniently reduced. Indeed, either the properties of both natures are predicated of the whole person of Christ by one or the other, or by both natures named; whence comes the first kind: or divine perfections are bestowed upon the human nature of Christ; whence comes the second kind: or the works of the office [are performed] according to both natures; whence results the third kind. The first kind is called idiopoia, communication of properties: The second metapoia, communication of majesty: The third koinopoia, communication of apotelesmata, or operations of the office.

Latin:

Qualis est ista communicatio idiomatum? Communicatio idiomatum non est mere verbalis & titularis a), neque intellectualis b); sed realis, inter duas substantias realiter distinctas, sed non separatas: adeoque non est exæquatiua c), neque multiplicatiua d), neque transfusua e); verum συνδυαστική, inter duas substantias perfecte & intime vnitas: neque tamen accidentalis, aut commixtiua f), neque essentialis aut naturalis g); sed personalis & supernaturalis h).

Prob. a. Communicatio idiomatum non est titulus fine re. Etenim Christus homo vere est omnipotens, non titulotenus, sicut empirici & circumforanei haud raro doctores audiunt, qui nihil minus, quam tales sunt.

Prob. b. Communicatio intellectualis intercedit inter subiecta non realiter, sed tantum ratione distincta. Sic animal homini sua idiomata communicare dicitur κατὰ μέθεξιν, per communicationem intellectualem. At personalis communicatio idiomatum est inter duas Christi naturas, realiter distinctas.

Prob. c. Communicatio idiomatum neque naturarum unitarum, neque idiomatum infert exaequationem; quia talis exaequatio pugnat cum reali differentia naturae divinae & humanae, & ex utraque natura fluentium idiomatum.

Prob. d. Communicatio idiomatum non est multiplicativa, qualis est, cum homo generans κατ’ ἀλλοποίησιν animam suam communicat filio. Multiplicativa namque communicatio est inter duas substantias separatas; at communicatio idiomatum est inter duas substantias unitas.

Prob. e. Communicatio idiomatum non est transfusiva. Credimus autem, docemus & confitemur, non fieri talem maiestatis Dei & omnium eius proprietatum effusionem in humanam naturam Christi, qua naturae divinae aliquid decedat; aut ut de suo alii ita largiatur aliquid, quod hac ratione sibi ipsa non in se retineat; aut, quod humana natura in substantia atque essentia sua parem maiestatem acceperit, quae a natura & essentia divina natura fit separata & divisa; quasi cum vinum, aqua aut oleum de uno vase in aliud transfunditur. Neque enim vel humana in Christo natura, vel ulla alia creatura in caelo, aut in terra, eo modo omnipotentia divinae capax est, ut per se omnipotens essentia & natura fiat, aut omnipotentes proprietates in se & per se habeat. Hac enim ratione humana natura in Christo abnegaretur & in divinitatem prorsus transmutaretur, ait F. C. p. 78c.

Prob. f. Communicatio idiomatum non est commixtiva; quia neque duae Christi naturae, neque utriusque naturae idiomata misceri queunt. Credimus, docemus & confitemur, divinam & humanam naturas non in unam substantiam commixtas, nec unam in alteram mutatam esse; sed utramque naturam retinere suas proprietates essentiales, ut quae alterius naturae proprietates fieri nequeunt, inquit Form. Concord. p. 606.

Prob. g. Communicatio idiomatum non est essentialis, eo modo, quo Deus Pater filio suo coeterno essentiam suam & omnes divinas proprietates ab aeterno communicavit: vnde & unius cum Patre essentiae, & ipsi aequalis est. At vero in Christi persona quaelibet natura retinet proprietates suas, intra distinctam naturam & essentiam suam; ita ut humana natura semper fit & maneat inferior divinitate. Neque est essentialis, aut naturalis eo modo, quo anima suas proprietates communicat corpori; propterea, quod huius communicationis fundamentum est unio essentialis, qua duae naturae incompletae concurrunt ad unam naturam completam constituendam: At duae Christi naturae, in essendo completae, unitae sunt ad constituendam unam personam σύνθετον.

Prob. h. Est itaque communicatio idiomatum, de qua nobis in praesenti sermo est, realis, συνδυασική, i. e. inter naturas unitas, eaque unione duarum in Christo naturarum hypostatica.

Communicatio idiomatum realis probatur: 1) Nulla unio perfecta & perichoristica fine communicatione idiomatum esse potest, vti exempla corporis animati ostendunt. Vnionem paraftaticam duorum afferim fieri, fine communicatione idiomatum, faciles largimur, eo, quod ille gradus vnionis est infimus atque imperfectus. At vero, definiente scriptura, unio personalis duarum in Christo naturarum est absolutissima, perfectissima & perichoristica: E. fine communicatione idiomatum esse nequit. Porro colligimus: Qualis unio, talis idiomatum communicatio. Atqui unio duarum in Christo naturarum est realis: E. fluens ex illa communicatio idiomatum est realis.

2) Quam vere humanitas Christi hypostasin τοῦ λόγου habet communicatam, tam vere etiam communicata habet diuina idiomata: Atqui humanitas realiter communicatam habet hypostasin τοῦ λόγου. E. etiam realiter communicata habet idiomata diuina.

Maior prob. 1) quia idiomata diuina, ex parte rei, cum hypostasi diuina sunt idem. At quæcunque realiter idem sunt, eorum vno communicato, communicatur & alterum. 2) Si hypostasis est communicata, multo magis communicata erunt idiomata. Hæc enim tribus personis diuinis sunt communia; hypostasis vero soli λόγῳ est propria.

3) In quo corpore, velut templo, personaliter assuunto, tota plenitudo diuinitatis habitat, illi idiomata diuina vere & realiter sunt communicata: Atqui in corpore Christi &c. Ergo.

4) Quicunque, vt pueri, particeps fit carnis & sanguinis humani, ille fit particeps idiomatum humanorum: Atqui Filius Dei &c. E. Maior constat: quia caro & sanguis humanus notat naturam humanam, quæ suis proprietatibus nunquam destituta est.

5) Necessaria est communicatio idiomatum ad peragenda opera officii, in quibus vtraque Christi natura agit, quod cuiusque proprium est, cum communicatione alterius.

Antithesis fuit olim Samosateni, Sabellii, Nestorii, Eutychis, qui vel confusionem naturarum introduxerunt, vel communicationem naturarum & idiomatum negarunt, quos hodie in multis sequuntur Pontificii. Quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Quorum essentia & definitio non est communis, illorum propria non sunt communicabilia: At diuinæ & humanæ Christi naturarum essentia & definitio non est communis. E. Maior patet: quia prædicata communicabilia pertinent ad definitionem rei, v. gr. Animal communicat naturam suam homini, & pertinet ad definitionem hominis. Resp. Dist. inter communicationem intellectualem, quæ est effectus vnionis κατὰ μέθεξιν, estque inter subiectum & prædicatum realiter idem, & sola ratione distinctum; & inter communicationem realem, quæ est consequens vnionis κατὰ συνδύασιν. Argumentum valet de priori, non de posteriori communicatione.

II. Quidquid communicatur alteri, illud e proprio subiecto emigrat: Sed propria diuinæ & humanæ Christi naturæ non emigrant e subiecto proprio: E. Resp. limitando. Quidquid communicatur alteri, per transfusionem: Atqui communicatio idiomatum in Christo neutiquam per transfusionem fit, sed per vnionem perichoristicam.

III. Quidquid communicatur, fit commune: Sed propria diuinæ & humanæ naturarum non sunt communia. E. Maior est euidens: quia proprium & commune e diametro sibi opponuntur. Minor constat: quia vtraque Christi natura retinet suas proprietates, vt quæ alterius proprietates fieri nequeunt.

Resp. 1) Quidquid alteri communicatur, illud fit communicabile, non commune, stricte loquendo.

2) Commune aliquid bifariam dicitur: a) Sensu strictiori commune dicitur, quod pluribus æque & eodem modo competit; hoc significatu speciali, opponitur proprio. b) Latiori sensu commune dicitur, quod pluribus quocunque ac diuerso etiam modo competit, vni primario, immediate & per se, alteri secundario, mediate & per aliud. Hoc sensu latiori proprietates quidem propter vnionem perichoristicam fiunt communes, & nihilominus manent proprietates illius naturæ, cui primo & per se conueniunt.

IV. Quæcunque in ipsa vnione manent distincta, illorum propria non communicantur: Duæ Christi naturæ &c. E. Maior patet: quia distinctio, & communicatio, inter se pugnare videntur.

Resp. Repugnat communicationi distractio, non distinctio.

In gladio ignito distinctæ sunt naturæ, attamen vis vrendi ferro, & vis incidendi igni communicatur.

V. Si propria divinæ naturæ communicarentur humanæ naturæ, essent in duobus subiectis: Consequens est falsum; quia unum proprium in duobus subiectis esse nequit: E. & antecedens. Resp. unum proprium non potest esse in duobus subiectis primis & immediatis; potest tamen esse in duobus subiectis per περιχώρησιν vnitis, quorum vnum est primum & immediatum, alterum secundum & mediatum.

VI. Si propria divinæ naturæ communicata essent assumtæ humanæ naturæ, eidem inessent: Sed non insunt humanæ naturæ; quia non sunt accidentia, quorum est, inesse; E. non sunt humanæ naturæ communicata. Resp. Modus inessendi varius est.

Idiomata divina non insunt humanæ naturæ per subiectiuam inhæsionem; velut accidentia, sed per intimam vnionem & inhabitationem.

VII. Quodcunque dogma inuehit naturæ divinæ & humanæ exæquationem, illud est reiiciendum: Dogma de communicatione idiomatum &c. E. Minor prob. quia, iuxta doctrinam de communicatione idiomatum, humana Christi natura æque est omnipotens, omniscia, &c. ac divina ipsius natura.

Resp. Neg. min. Quamuis enim eadem omnipotentia divinæ & humanæ Christi naturæ fit, modus tamen habendi est longe diuersissimus.

Nam natura diuina est omnipotens formaliter, immediate & per se; humana Christi natura est omnipotens communicative, mediate & per unionis personalis gratiam.

Quæst. XXXIX. Quot sunt genera communicationis idiomatum? Genera communicationis idiomatum sunt tria.

Prob. Tres enim sunt classes generales, ad quas omnia scripturæ dicta, quæ de communicatione idiomatum agunt, commode reuocari possunt. Prædicantur quippe vel proprietates vtriusque naturæ de tota Christi persona ab alterutra, vel vtraque natura denominata; vnde est primum genus: vel perfectiones divinæ in humanam Christi naturam collatæ; vnde est secundum genus: vel opera officii secundum vtramque naturam; vnde resultat tertium genus. Primum genus vocatur ἰδιοποιία, communicatio proprietatum: Secundum μεταποιία, communicatio maiestatis: Tertium κοινοποιία, communicatio apotelesmatum, seu operationum officii.


### Q. XXXVIII: Obs

Obs.

The order of placing the kinds, or classes, of the communication of idioms is inverted by some theologians; for they distinguish between the order of doctrine and of nature, and because of greater difficulty and prolixity, they postpone metapoia to koinopoia. But since the order should be accommodated to the things, not the things to the order; we, saving the judgment of others, believe that one should treat first of the auchēmasi (glories) communicated to the human nature of Christ, rather than of the apotelesmasi (effects); because the communication of the office necessarily presupposes, as its cause, prior to its effect, the communication of majesty made to the assumed flesh.

Quæst. XL. What is the first kind of communication of idioms? The first kind of communication of idioms is when the properties of the divine or human nature are truly and really attributed to the whole person of Christ, denominated by one or the other or both natures.

Obs. This first kind is called by DAMASCENUS, lib. III. de O. F. c. 4, antidosis, alternation, tropos antidoseōs, mode of alternation, because divine and human [properties] can be predicated alternately of the composite person of Christ, e.g.

Christ is begotten of the Father from eternity:

Christ is in time born of the Virgin Mary.

By THEODORET it is called ἐναλλαγὴ καὶ κοινωνία ὀνομάτων, a permutation and communication of names, not merely verbal, but real, because names are of things. By CYRIL it is called ἰδιοποιία καὶ ἰδιοποίησις, appropriation, because that which is proper to one nature, the whole person, who is God and man, claims for itself and makes its own. It is also called by DAMASCENE ἀλλοίωσις, by which both divine and human idioms are really predicated of one and the same composite person, yet κατ’ ἄλλο καὶ ἄλλο; because the distinctive particles show according to which nature each idiom is predicated of the person. But one must accurately distinguish between a determinative and distinctive ἀλλοίωσις, and a segregative and exclusive ἀλλοίωσις, e.g., God suffered κατ’ ἄλλο, i.e., God truly and really suffered according to the assumed humanity; there the particle, κατ’ ἄλλο, determines the human nature, to which the passion formally belongs, and distinguishes it from the divine nature, but does not segregate it, since the passion is appropriated to it. But if you explain it thus: God suffered κατ’ ἄλλο, i.e., only the human nature suffered, the particle κατ’ ἄλλο is separative, not distinctive, because by that exposition God is excluded from the communication of the passion. Confer GERHARD, exeg. l. IV. §. 188.

Latin:

Obs.

Ordo locandi genera, seu classes communicationis idiomatum a nonnullis Theologis inuertitur; quippe qui distinguunt inter ordinem doctrinæ & naturæ, atque ob difficultatem & prolixitatem maiorem μεταποιίαν τῇ κοινοποιίᾳ postponunt. At cum ordo accomodandus sit rebus, non res ordini; nos, saluo aliorum iudicio, prius agendum censemus de ἀυχήμασι humanæ naturæ Christi communicatis, quam de ἀποτελέσμασι; propterea, quod communicatio officii necessario, tanquam caussam, priorem suo effectu, præsupponit communicationem maiestatis, factam assumtæ carni.

Quæst. XL. Quodnam est primum genus communicationis idiomatum? Primum genus communicationis idiomatum est, quando propria divinæ, vel humanæ naturæ vere & realiter tribuuntur toti personæ Christi, ab alterutra vel vtraque natura dominatæ.

Obs. Vocatur hoc primum genus a DAMASCENO lib. III. de O. F. c. 4. ἀντίδοσις, alternatio, τρόπος ἀντιδόσεως, modus alternationis, quia de persona Christi σύνθετῳ alternatim divina & humana prædicari possunt, v. gr.

Christus est ab æterno genitus a Patre:

Christus est in tempore a Maria virgine genitus.

A THEODORETO appellatur ἐναλλαγὴ καὶ κοινωνία ὀνομάτων, permutatio & communicatio nominum, non nude verbalis, sed realis, quia nomina sunt rerum. A CYRILLO nuncupatur ἰδιοποιία καὶ ἰδιοποίησις, appropriatio, quia illud, quod vni naturæ proprium est, tota persona, quæ Deus & homo est, sibi vindicat & proprium facit. Vocatur etiam a DAMASCENO ἀλλοίωσις, qua de vna eademque persona συνθέτῳ & diuina & humana idiomata realiter prædicantur, κατ’ ἄλλο tamen καὶ ἄλλο; quia particulæ distinctiuæ ostendunt, secundum quam naturam vnumquodque idioma de persona prædicetur. Sed accurate distinguendum est inter ἀλλοίωσιν determinatiuam & distinctiuam, & inter ἀλλοίωσιν segregatiuam & exclusiuam, v. gr. Deus passus est κατ’ ἄλλο, i. e. Deus vere & realiter passus est secundum assumtam humanitatem, ibi particula, κατ’ ἄλλο, determinat humanam naturam, cui passio formaliter competit, eamque a natura diuina distinguit, non autem segregat, quippe cui passio appropriatur. Sed si sic exponas: Deus passus est κατ’ ἄλλο, i. e. sola humana natura est passa, particula κατ’ ἄλλο est separatiua, non distinctiua, quia per illam expositionem Deus a communicatione passionis excluditur. Confer. GERHARD. exeg. l. IV. §. 188.


### Q. XLI. What is

The foundation of the first kind of communication of idioms is both the unity of the person of the God-man (θεανθρώπω), and the true and real difference of the divine and human natures.

Proof. Since in Christ there are two distinct natures, which are neither changed nor confounded in their essences and properties; and yet of both natures there is but one person: those things which are proper to one nature only are attributed not to the other nature separately, as if separated, but to the whole person (who is at once God and man), whether he be named God or man, says the Formula of Concord, p. 770.

Latin:

Fundamentum primi generis communicationis idiomatum est tum vnitas personæ θεανθρώπω, tum diuinæ & humanæ naturarum vera & realis differentia.

Prob. Cum in Christo duæ sint distinctæ naturæ, quæ essentijs & proprietatibus suis neque mutantur, neque confunduntur; vtriusque vero naturæ vna tantum fit persona: ea, quæ vnius tantum naturæ propria sunt, alteri naturæ non seorsim, quasi separatæ, sed toti personæ (quæ simul Deus & homo est) attribuuntur, siue Deus, siue homo nominetur, ait Form. Concord. p. 770.


### Q. XLII. How many species of the first kind of communication of idioms are there?

There are three species of the first kind of communication of idioms. The first species is ἰδιοποίησις, or οἰκείωσις, appropriation, when human idioms are predicated of the concrete of the divine nature ). The second species is κοινωνία τῶν θείων, communication of divine idioms, by which divine idioms are predicated of the person of the incarnate Word, denominated from the human nature, on account of the personal union ). The third species is ἀντίδοσις, or συναμφοτερισμὸς, alternation, or reciprocation, by which both divine and human idioms are predicated of the concrete of the person, or of Christ, denominated from either nature ).

Prob. a. To the first species belong the following idiomatic predications: The Prince of life was killed, Acts 3:15. God purchased the church with his own blood, Acts 20:28. The Lord of glory was crucified, 1 Cor. 2:8. The Son of God loved me, and gave himself for me, Gal. 2:20. God is anointed with the Holy Spirit, Ps. 45:8. Prob. b.

To the second species follow idiomatic propositions: The Son of man shall ascend, where he was before, John 6:62. He was born in the fullness of time, before Abraham was, John 8:58. The second man is the Lord from heaven, 1 Cor. 15:47. Prob. c.

To the third species pertain these idiomatic propositions: Jesus Christ yesterday and today, i.e., from eternity, Heb. 13:8. Christ is from the fathers according to the flesh, Rom. 9:5. Christ was crucified in weakness, 2 Cor. 13:4. Christ was put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit, 1 Pet. 3:18. Obs.

Obs. Idiomatic predications of the first and second species differ from the predications pertaining to the third species. For idiomatic predications, in which of the concrete of the divine nature the human, and conversely, of the concrete of the human nature the divine idiom is predicated denominatively, are so constituted that the predicate belongs to the subject not formally, or according to something that is signified in its formal concept, but κατ’ ἄλλο, or by reason of the other nature, which is personally united to it; for example, when I say: The Son of God has suffered, the predicate does not belong to the subject formally, or according to something that is signified in its formal concept: but κατ’ ἄλλο, or according to another thing, namely, according to the human nature, which is personally united to the Son of God. But when the concrete of the person is placed in the position of the subject, of which a divine or human idiom is predicated, then the predicate belongs to the subject formally, and not κατ’ ἄλλο; for example, when I say: Christ has suffered; this predicate belongs to Christ formally, according to the human nature. Again, when I say: Christ is from eternity, this predicate also belongs to Christ formally, by reason of the divine nature; for since Christ is the concrete of the person, both natures, divine and human, are of the formal definition of Christ. Whence Hutterus says: since the propositions (Christ was tempted by the Jews, 1 Cor. X, 9. of the seed of David, Matth. XXII, 42.) do not declare through any communication the idioms of one nature about the other nature, either in the concrete or in the abstract, but predicate of the whole person that which with respect to one nature is attributed to the whole person; therefore, in these propositions, strictly speaking, there does not seem to be a communication of idioms. Wherefore, in order for a communication to take place, it is necessary that in the place of Christ there be put such a word that has respect to that nature whose idiom is not that which is declared by the predicate.

D. Musaeus D. Baierus notes that, nevertheless, in the propositions just reviewed, a communication of idioms is involved, because of the subject denominated by both natures, and the communicated ὑπόστασις (hypostasis). For unless that were communicated, the subject could neither be denominated by both natures, nor could the divine predicate be attributed to the whole person denominated by the divine and human nature. Indeed, if you consider more deeply the relation of the predicate to both natures comprised in the subject and its signification, it will appear that the predicate is formal only by reason of one nature comprised in the subject, not by reason of the other.

Whence also in those propositions the use of discretive particles has a place, for example: Christ was born from the fathers according to the flesh, Rom. 9:5. Therefore, a distinction must be made between idiomatic propositions, in which the communication of idioms strictly speaking and expressly has a place; and between propositions, in which the communication of idioms is involved in some way. This proposition: God has suffered, most strictly speaking is idiomatic, which Nestorius did not admit; but this proposition: Christ has suffered, is said to be idiomatic in a broader sense, approved by Nestorius.

Latin:

Species primi generis communicationis idiomatum sunt tres. Prima species est ἰδιοποίησις, siue οἰκείωσις, appropriatio, quando humana idiomata de concreto naturæ diuinæ enuntiantur ). Secunda species est κοινωνία τῶν θείων, communicatio diuinorum idiomatum, quam de persona verbi incarnati, ab humana natura denominata, idiomata diuina ob vnionem personalem enuntiantur ). Tertia species est ἀντίδοσις, siue συναμφοτερισμὸς, alternatio, siue reciprocatio, qua tam diuina, quam humana idiomata de concreto personæ, siue de Christo, ab vtraque natura denominato, prædicantur ).

Prob. a. Ad primam speciem pertinent sequentes prædicationes idiomaticæ: Dux vitæ interfectus est, Act. III, 15. Deus acquisivit ecclesiam per proprium sanguinem, Act. XX, 28. Dominus gloriæ crucifixus est, 1 Cor. II, 8. Filius Dei dilexit me, & tradidit seipsum pro me, Gal. II, 20. Deus vultus est Spiritu S. Ps. XLV, 8.

Prob. b. Ad secundam speciem sequentur propositiones idiomaticæ: Filius hominis ascendet, ubi erat prius, Ioann. VI, 62. natus in plenitudine temporis est, antequam Abraham esset, Ioann. VIII, 58. Secundus homo est Dominus de cœlo, 1 Cor. XV, 47.

Prob. c. Ad tertiam speciem spectant hæ propositiones idiomaticæ: Iesus Christus heri & hodie i. e. ab æterno, Hebr. XIII, 8. Christus est ex patribus secundum carnem, Rom. IX, 5. Christus crucifixus est in infirmitate, 2 Cor. XIII, 4. Christus mortificatus est carne, viuificatus autem spiritu, 1 Petr. III, 18.

Obs. Prædicationes idiomaticæ primæ & secundæ speciei differunt a prædicationibus, ad tertiam speciem pertinentibus. Nam prædicationes idiomaticæ, in quibus de concreto naturæ diuinæ humana; & contra, de concreto naturæ humanæ idioma diuinum denominatiue enuntiantur, ita comparatæ sunt, vt prædicatum conueniat subiecto non formaliter, siue secundum aliquid, quod in formali eius conceptu significatur, sed κατ’ ἄλλο, siue ratione alterius naturæ, quæ ei peronaliter vnita est v. gr. cum dico: Filius Dei est passus, prædicatum non conuenit subiecto formaliter, siue secundum aliquid, quod in formali eius conceptu significatur: sed κατ’ ἄλλο, siue secundum aliud, nempe secundum humanam naturam, quæ personaliter vnita est filio Dei. At cum subiecti loco ponitur concretum personæ, de quo prædicatur idioma diuinum, vel humanum, tunc prædicatum subiecto conuenit formaliter, & non κατ’ ἄλλο, v. gr. cum dico: Christus est passus; prædicatum hoc Christo competit formaliter, secundum humanam naturam. Rursus cum dico: Christus est ab æterno, etiam hoc prædicatum Christo conuenit formaliter, ratione diuinæ naturæ; cum enim Christus sit concretum personæ, vtraque natura, diuina & humana, de ratione formali Christi est. Vnde Hvttervs inquit: cum propositiones (Christus est tentatus a Iudæis, 1 Cor. X, 9. ex semine Dauid, Matth. XXII, 42.) non per communicationem aliquam vnius naturæ idiomata de altera natura, vel in concreto, vel in abstracto enuntient, sed de tota persona prædicent id, quod respectu vnius naturæ toti personæ tribuitur; ideoque in his propositionibus proprie loquendo non videtur esse communicatio idiomatum. Quare vt communicatio locum habere possit, necesse est, vt Christi loco ponatur talis vox, quæ respectum habeat ad eam naturam, cuius idioma non est id, quod per prædicatum enuntiatur.

Conf. D. Mvsaevs D. Baievrs monet, quod nihilominus in iam recensitis propositionibus communicatio idiomatum inuoluatur, propter subiectum ab vtraque natura denominatum, & communicatam ὑπόστασιν. Nisi enim illa esset communicata, subiectum nec ab vtraque natura denominari, nec prædicatum diuinum toti personæ a natura diuina & humana denominatæ tribui posset. Quin immo si habitudinem prædicati ad vtramque in subiecto, eiusque significatu comprehensam naturam penitius consideres, apparebit, prædicatum tantum ratione vnius in subiecto comprehensæ naturæ esse formale, non ratione alterius.

Vnde etiam in propositionibus illis vsus particularum discretiuarum locum habet, v. gr. Christus est natus ex patribus secundum carnem, Rom. IX, 5. Distinguendum igitur est inter propositiones idiomaticas, in quibus communicatio idiomatum stricte-loquendo & expresse locum habet; & inter propositiones, in quibus communicatio idiomatum aliquo modo inuoluatur. Hæc propositio: Deus est passus, strictissime loquendo est idiomatica, quam non admisit Nestorius; at isthæc propositio: Christus est passus, latiori sensu dicitur idiomatica, a Nestorio approbata.


### XLIII. What is to be observed concerning idiomatic propositions of the first genus of the communication of idioms?

Concerning predications pertaining to the first genus of the communication of idioms, it is to be observed: a) the subject, which is not an abstract, but a concrete of nature or person; b) the predicate, which designates not the divine or human substance itself, but an idiom of either nature; c) The mode of predication is real and proper, by which divine or human idioms are predicated of the whole God-man person, yet so that by distinguishing particles they are vindicated to the nature to which they formally belong, and appropriated to the other nature to which they belong not formally, but by reason of personal union.

Proof. a. The subject of idiomatic propositions is not an abstract of nature. For 1) Holy Scripture does not use abstractive phrases, but concretive ones. We do not read in the sacred code that deity was crucified, but that the Lord of glory was crucified, 1 Cor. II, 8. That the author of life was killed, Acts III, 15. That the Son of God was delivered to death, Rom. VIII, 32. 2) Deity is ἀπαθής, ἄτρεπτος, καὶ ἀναλλοίωτος, devoid of passion, conversion, and change. 3) Actions and passions belong to supposita. Hence the Apostle Peter does not say: Divinity suffered in the flesh; but: God suffered in the flesh, 1 Pet. IV, 1.

You say: I. God suffered: Deity suffered: Therefore, Deity suffered.

Reply. The major is not universal in the first figure, because it is not permissible to say: Everything that is God suffered. Moreover, God in the major is taken relatively and personally, in the minor absolutely and essentially.

You say: II. Christ suffered: Christ is both natures: Therefore, both natures suffered.

Hence the minor is denied; because both natures per se are not a concrete of person, but both natures are an abstract. Hence four terms arise: for although both natures do not differ really from Christ, they do differ formally. You say:

You say: III. Divinity is incarnate: Therefore, it suffered. Reply. Incarnation is one thing, passion is another. The former is λόγος ἀσάρκος, because it denotes the act of union; the latter is λόγος ἐνσάρκος, and belongs to Him in the state of union. The former implies no change or imperfection per se, the latter implies change and emptying. Therefore, just as it does not follow: Divinity is incarnate: Therefore, it is assumed: So it does not follow: Therefore, it suffered.

You say: IV. The fathers and doctors of the primitive church assert that divinity suffered in the flesh. CYRIL's De incarnat. vnigeniti: cap. XXVIII. is the voice: Divinity suffered impassibly: VIRGIL's lib. II. cap. III. contra Eutych. Divinity was affixed with nails; but it could not be penetrated itself, like the flesh: AUGUSTINE's in meditat. cap. VI. The Deity, which put on my flesh, ascended the gibbet of the cross, and in the assumed flesh bore a grievous punishment. It is also certain that some Theologians of our own use abstractive locutions, namely BRENTIUS, JACOBUS ANDREÆ, SELNECCERUS, and in our age the most learned Theologian, JOHANNES ADAMUS OSIANDER in colleg. theolog. systemat. part. IV. p. 84. Reply. The phrase can be excused is used by the Fathers and theologians: The Divinity suffered in the flesh: since the foundation of this proposition, "God suffered in the flesh," is the unity of the person, which the personal union indeed constitutes, but which is immediately followed (according to our mode of conceiving) by the περιχώρησις, or mutual communication of the natures. Although, therefore, it is said primarily: God suffered in the flesh, yet the aforementioned Fathers and theologians judge that it is not inconveniently said consequently that the divinity suffered in the flesh, for the reason that the divinity truly appropriated to itself that passion which the flesh felt in itself, and rendered the same satisfactory and salutary. But in truth, we say more safely: God suffered in the flesh.

For this proposition is ἔγγραφος, 1 Pet. IV, 1; Acts XX, 28.

2) As actions, so also passions belong to supposita, or persons.

3) The distinction between idiomatic propositions of the first and second kind must be accurately observed. In the latter, the subject can be abstract, not so in the former.

4) It is to be feared that, on account of the use of such abstract propositions, the error of the Theopaschites, who taught that the divinity in Christ grieved and suffered when his flesh was fixed to the cross, might be imputed to our churches.

Cf. D. GERHARD in exeg. l. IV. §. 198; D. BROCHMAND in univers. theol. system. de Christo sect. IV. quaest. unic. p. 784.

Prob. b. The predicate of idiomatic propositions of the first kind does not designate the divine or human substance itself.

For these propositions: God is man, the seed of David is Jehovah, etc., are not idiomatic, but hypostatic, or personal. Wherefore it is right that in idiomatic propositions of the first kind, an idiom of the divine or human nature be placed in the position of the predicate. Idioms, however, are taken here in such a broad signification that they include within their scope also actions, passions, and common accidents.

Furthermore, it must be well observed here that if the predicate includes a use, redundant into the human race, it denotes an ἀποτέλεσμα, or work of office, and pertains to the third kind of communication of idioms; e.g., Christ poured out his blood for us, pertains to the third kind of communication of idioms.

Prob. c. The mode of predicating idiomatic propositions belonging to the first kind of communication of idioms is true, real, and proper, by propriety of signification.

For those things which are proper to humanity κατ' αὐτὸ, or in itself, are truly and properly predicated of the Son of God καθ' ἕνωσιν, or on account of the personal union: and conversely, those things which are proper to the divinity are truly and properly predicated of the Son of Man, on account of the personal union.

But in order that it may be more clearly known which predicates belong to the divine or human nature κατ' αὐτὸ, and which belong to it καθ' ἕνωσιν, certain discretive particles must be strictly noted, by which properties are vindicated for that nature to which they belong in itself and formally: which particles are either ῥητῶς and expressly contained in biblical sayings, or are elicited by the doctors of the church from the context according to the analogy of faith, e.g., The Son of God was born of the seed of David κατὰ σάρκα, according to the flesh, Rom. I, 3. Christ is from the fathers, as far as concerns the flesh, Rom. IX, 5. God acquired the church through his own blood, Acts XX, 28.

Sometimes Holy Scripture, instead of those discretive particles, employs the ablative case, e.g., Christ was put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit, 1 Pet.

III, 18. Familiar to the doctors of the church are the particles: qua, quatenus, in quantum, respectu, tanquam, secundum.

These limiting particles are not χωρισικαὶ, separative of the subject, but a) αἰτιολογικαὶ, demonstrative of the cause and origin on account of which the predicate is enunciated of the subject; b) προσδιορισικαὶ, determinative of the nature to which the predicate belongs κατ' αὐτὸ, in itself, and formally; c) διακριτικαὶ, distinctive from the other nature, to which the properties do not belong formally, but appropriatively or communicatively.

This mode of predicating can be declared by examples: The Son of God was born of the seed of David, according to the flesh, Rom. I, 3. The subject of this idiomatic proposition is the Son of God, by which is denoted the subject of the idiomatic proposition is the Son of God, by which

the whole person of Christ is noted, denominated from the divine nature. The predicate is, to be born from the seed of David, which is a human idiom. This is predicated of the concrete of the divine nature, to which that does not belong κατ' αὐτὸ, by itself, but κατ' ἄλλο, by another, on account of the unity of the person of the God-man. Whence by the limiting particle, κατὰ, according to the flesh, the human idiom is claimed for the human nature, to which temporal birth formally belongs; yet the divine nature is not excluded, or separated from the participation of birth, since to it τὸ to be born from the seed of David belongs appropriatively. We shall take another example from Gen. III, 15. The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent. The subject is the seed of the woman, or the son of the B. virgin Mary, by which the whole composite person is signified, which is God & man. The predicate is the crushing of the serpent's head, which, since it is an act of omnipotence, is a divine idiom, which is enunciated of the concrete of the human nature, to which that indeed does not belong κατ' αὐτὸ, yet καθ' ἕλωσιν, on account of the personal union. The limiting particle ῥητῶς, or expressly, is not in the text, yet according to the analogy of faith it can be added: The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent, insofar as he is true God. The particle, insofar as, is here taken reduplicatively, or causally, & it claims the divine idiom for the divine nature, to which it formally belongs; but it does not exclude the human nature from the crushing of the serpent's head, as that to which that act of omnipotence belongs communicatively.

Latin:

Circa prædicationes, ad primum genus communicationis idiomatum pertinentes, observandum a) subiectum, quod non est abstractum, sed concretum naturæ, vel personæ; b) prædicatum, quod non ipsam substantiam diuinam aut humanam, sed idioma alterutrius naturæ designat: c) Modus prædicandi est realis & proprius, quo de tota persona θεανθρώπῳ diuina vel humana idiomata enuntiantur, ita tamen, vt per particulas discretiuas naturæ, cui formaliter competunt, vindicentur, alteri vero naturæ, cui non formaliter, sed propter vnionem personalem conueniunt, approprientur.

Prob. a. Subiectum propositionum idiomaticarum non est abstractum naturæ. Nam 1) S. scriptura non vtitur phrasibus abstractiuis, sed concretiuis. Non legimus in sacro codice deitatem esse crucifixam, sed Dominum gloriæ esse crucifixum, 1 Cor. II, 8. Auctorem vitæ esse interfectum, Act. III, 15. Filium Dei in mortem esse traditum, Rom. VIII, 32. 2) Deitas est ἀπαθής, ἄτρεπτος, καὶ ἀναλλοίωτος, passionis, conuersionis & mutationis expers. 3) Actiones & passiones sunt suppositorum. Vnde Apostolus Petrus non dicit: Diuinitas est passa in carne; sed: Deus passus est in carne, 1 Petr. IV, 1.

Dicis: I. Deus est passus: Deitas est passa: E. Deitas est passa.

Resp. Maior non est vniuersalis in prima figura, quoniam dicere non licet: Omne id, quod est Deus, est passum. Præterea Deus in maiori sumitur relatiue & personaliter, in minori absolute & essentialiter.

Dicis: II. Christus est passus: Christus est vtraque natura: E. vtraque natura est passa.

Resp. Christus est passus, vt concretum personæ. Hinc negatur minor; quia vtraque natura per se non est concretum personæ, sed vtraque natura est abstractum. Vnde nascuntur quatuor termini: quamuis enim vtraque natura a Christo non differat realiter, differt tamen formaliter.

Dicis: III. Diuinitas est incarnata: E. est passa. Resp. Aliud est incarnatio, aliud est passio. Illa est λόγος ἀσάρκος, quia notat actum vnionis; hæc est λόγος ἐνσάρκος, & competit ipsi in statu vnionis. Illa nullam mutationem ac imperfectionem, hæc mutationem ac exinanitionem per se infert. Quamobrem sicut non sequitur: Diuinitas est incarnata: E. est assumta: Ita non sequitur: Ergo est passa .

Dicis: IV. Diuinitatem in carne passam esse, assuerere patres & doctores primitiuæ ecclesiæ. CYRILLI de incarnat. vnigeniti: cap. XXVIII. vox est: Diuinitas patiebatur impassibiliter: VIRGILII lib. II. cap. III. contra Eutych. Diuinitas clauis confixa est; sed ipsa penetrari non potuit, sicut caro: AVGVSTINI in meditat. cap. VI. Deitas, quæ meam carnem induit, crucis patibulum ascendit, & in carne assumta trifle tulit supplicium. Certum etiam est, quosdam Theologos e nostratibus locutionibus abstractiuis vos esse, nominatim BRENTIVM, IACOBVM ANDREÆ, SELNECCERVM, & nostro æuo doctissimum Theologum, IOANN. ADAMVM OSIANDRVM in colleg. theolog. systemat. part. IV. p. 84. Resp. Excusari potest phrasis tis usurpata a patribus & theologis: Diuinitas passa est in carne: quoniam huius propositionis: Deus passus est in carne, fundamentum est vnitas personæ, quam constituit quidem vnio personalis, proxime autem hanc consequitur (secundum nostrum concipiendi modum) περιχώρησις, seu communicatio mutua naturarum. Quamuis itaque primo dicatur: Deus passus est in carne, consequenter tamen haud incommode dici censent supra memorati Patres & Theologi, diuinitatem passam esse in carne, eo, quod diuinitas illam passionem, quam caro in se sensit, sibi vere appropriauit, eamdemque satisfactoriam & salutiferam reddidit. At vero tutius dicimus: Deus passus est in carne.

Nam hæc propositio est ἔγγραφος, 1 Petr. IV, 1.

Act. XX, 28. 2) Vt actiones, ita & passiones sunt suppositorum, siue personarum.

3) Accurate obseruandum est discrimen inter propositiones idiomaticas primi, & secundi generis. In his subiectum potest esse abstractum, non item in illis.

4) Metuendum est, ne propter vsum eiusmodi propositionum abstractiuarum, Theopaschitarum error, qui docuerunt, diuinitatem in Christo doluisse & passam esse, cum caro eius figeretur in cruce, nostris ecclesiis affricetur.

Conf. D. GERHARD. in exeg. l. IV. §. 198. D. BROCHMAND. in vniuerf. theol. system. de Christo sect. IV. quæst. vnic. p. 784.

Prob. b. Prædicatum propositionum idiomaticarum primi generis non ipsam substantiam diuinam, aut humanam designat. Nam hæ propositiones: Deus est homo, germen Dauidis est Iehouah, &c. non sunt idiomaticæ, sed hypostaticæ, siue personales.

Quamobrem par est, vt in propositionibus idiomaticis primi generis prædicati loco ponatur idioma diuinæ, aut humanæ naturæ. Idiomata autem tam lata significatione hic sumuntur, vt ambitu suo etiam actiones, passiones & accidentia communia complectantur.

Ceterum probe hic obseruandum est, quod, si prædicatum comprehendat vsum, redundantem in genus humanum, illud notet ἀποτέλεσμα, siue opus officii, & pertineat ad tertium genus communicationis idiomatum, v. gr. Christus effudit sanguinem suum pro nobis, pertinet ad tertium genus communicationis idiomatum.

Prob. c. Modus prædicandi propositionum idiomaticarum, ad primum genus communicationis idiomatum pertinentium, est verus, realis, & proprius, proprietate significationis. Nam quæ sunt propria humanitatis κατ' αὐτὸ, siue per se, ea vere & proprie prædicantur de Filio Dei καθ' ἕνωσιν, siue propter vnionem personalem: & vice versa, quæ sunt propria diuinitatis, vere & proprie prædicantur de filio hominis, propter vnionem personalem.

Vt autem luculentius innotescat, quæ prædicata conueniant diuinæ, aut humanæ naturæ κατ' αὐτὸ, & quæ illi competant καθ' ἕνωσιν, oppido notandæ sunt quædam particulæ discretiuæ, quibus vindicantur propria illi naturæ, cui per se & formaliter conueniunt: quæ particulæ vel ῥητῶς & diserte habentur in dictis biblicis, vel a doctoribus ecclesiæ e contextu secundum analogiam fidei eruuntur, v. gr.

Filius Dei natus est e semine Dauidis κατὰ σάρκα, secundum carnem, Rom. I, 3. Christus est ex patribus, quantum ad carnem, Rom. IX, 5. Deus acquisiuit ecclesiam per proprium sanguinem, Act. XX, 28.

Interdum S. scriptura loco illarum particularum discretiuarum adhibet casum ablatiuum, v. gr.

Christus mortificatus est carne, viuificatus autem spiritu, 1 Petr. III, 18. Doctoribus ecclesiæ familiares sunt particulæ, qua, quatenus, in quantum, respectu, tanquam, secundum. Quæ particulæ limitatiuæ non sunt χωρισικαὶ, separatiuæ subiecti, sed a) αἰτιολογικαὶ, ostensiuæ causæ & originis, propter quam prædicatum de subiecto enuntiatur; b) προσδιορισικαὶ, determinatiuæ naturæ, cui prædicatum κατ' αὐτὸ, per se, & formaliter competit; c) διακριτικαὶ, distinctiuæ ab altera natura, cui propria non competunt formaliter, sed appropriatiue, vel communicatiue.

Hic modus prædicandi declarari potest exemplis: Filius Dei natus est e semine Dauidis, secundum carnem, Rom.

I, 3. Subiectum huius propositionis idiomaticæ est Filius Dei, quo notatur propositionis idiomaticæ est Filius Dei, quo

notatur tota persona Christi, denominata a natura divina. Praedicatum est, nasci e semine Dauidis, quod est idioma humanum. Hoc praedicatur de concreto naturae divinae, cui illud non competit κατ' αὐτὸ, per se, sed κατ' ἄλλο, per aliud, ob vnitatem personae θεανθρώπου. Vnde per particulam limitatiuam, κατὰ, secundum carnem, idioma humanum vindicatur naturae humanae, cui natiuitas temporalis formaliter conuenit; non tamen excluditur, aut separatur natura diuina a participatione natiuitatis, quippe cui τὸ nasci e semine Dauidis competit appropriatiue. Alterum exemplum sumemus e Gen. III, 15. Semen mulieris conculcabit caput serpentis. Subiectum est semen mulieris, siue filius B. virginis Mariae, quo significatur tota persona σύνθετος, quae Deus & homo est. Praedicatum est conculcatio capitis serpentini, quae cum sit actus omnipotentiae, est idioma diuinum, quod enuntiatur de concreto naturae humanae, cui illud quidem non competit κατ' αὐτὸ, attamen καθ' ἕλωσιν, propter vnionem personalem. Particula limitatiua ῥητῶς, siue diserte non habetur in textu, secundum analogiam tamen fidei addi potest: Semen mulieris conculcabit caput serpentis, quatenus verus est Deus. Particula, quatenus, heic sumitur reduplicatiue, siue caussaliter, & vindicat idioma diuinum naturae diuinae, cui formaliter conuenit; non autem excludit humanam naturam a conculcatione capitis serpentini, vtpote cui actus ille omnipotentiae competit communicatiue.


### XLIII. What is to be observed concerning idiomatic propositions of the first genus of the communication of idioms?: Q

Q.

The Son of God has truly, really & properly suffered, been crucified & died; since to him is attributed suffering ὑποστατικῶς, personally, ἰδιοποιητικῶς, appropriatively, & ἐνεργητικῶς, effectively.

Prob. a. 1) From the most clear sayings of scripture. For Jehovah is said to be pierced, Zech. XII, 10. cf. John XIX, 37. The Son of God is delivered for us. Rom. VIII, 32. The Author of life killed, Acts III, 15. The Lord of glory crucified, 1 Cor. II, 8. Which sayings of scripture testify, that not only the human nature has suffered, but the Son of God himself, Jehovah himself.

2) From the syllogistic consequence of personal propositions. For we rightly conclude: The Son of man has truly & really been delivered unto death.

3) From the parity of examples. If scripture asserts truly & without trope, that the Son of God was born of the Virgin Mary, Luke I, 35. then it must also be accepted truly & without trope, that the Lord of glory was crucified. 4) If only the human nature has suffered, that of NESTORIUS will be true: Do not glory, O Jew, because you have not crucified God, but a man. See EVAGRIUS b. I, hist. c. 2. hist. tripartit. b. 12. c. 4.

Prob. b. Actions & passions belong to supposits. For which reason when I say: God has suffered; the subject of the passion, as the 'what', is God; the subject, as the 'by which', is the human nature, subsisting in the very hypostasis of the Son of God. Whence I explain this proposition: God has suffered, thus: The Son of God has suffered according to the human nature subsisting in the divine personality. As therefore, when a wound is inflicted on the flesh of Peter, not only the flesh of Peter is said to be wounded, but Peter is truly wounded, or the person of Peter, even though his soul cannot be wounded: so, when the Son of God suffers according to the flesh, not only the flesh, or his human nature, suffers, but the Son of God, or the person of the Son of God, truly suffers, however impassible the divine nature may be.

Prob. c. From the mutual communion of each nature, divine & human, in the one person of Christ. For because a mutual, and that a true & real, communion is given between the two natures in the one person of Christ, and therefore the divine nature truly & really appropriates to itself the idioms of the human nature.

propriat. For two natures come into communion not naked, but clothed with their own properties. Paul refers to this ἰδιοποίησιν, or appropriation, when he says in Acts 20:28: God purchased the church with his own blood.
