From which we gather: Whoever shed his own blood, he truly, really, and properly suffered: But God, etc. Therefore. Truly, God suffered in his flesh as truly and really as Paul and Peter suffered in their own flesh; for just as his flesh is Paul's and Peter's own essentially, so his flesh is the Son of God's own personally. Proof of the minor. God suffered in the flesh ἐνεργητικῶς, or effectively, in that the divine nature of the suffering Christ added weight, strength, efficacy, and value to the passion of the flesh, so that it might be most weighty, most efficacious, most salutary, and plainly satisfactory. The passion of the flesh alone, however righteous, does not satisfy for itself, much less for others, and least of all for the whole world. You say: Whoever suffers really, he feels the passion: But God did not feel the passion: Therefore, God did not really suffer. Response. Whoever suffers really and physically, he feels the passion, I concede. But the Son of God, although he suffered really, yet he did not suffer φυσι- κῶς, but ὑποστατικῶς, or personally, and appropriatively, or as ATHANAS. speaks in book IV de trinit.: The Son of God suffered, not by the nature of the deity, but by the dispensation of the union.

Latin:

Quaest. XLIV. An Filius Dei realiter & proprie passus, crucifixus & mortuus est?

Filius Dei vere, realiter & proprie passus, crucifixus & mortuus est; quippe cui tribuitur passio ὑποσατικῶς personaliter , ἰδιοποιητικῶς appropriatiue , & ἐνεργητικῶς, effective .

Prob. a. 1) E clarissimis scripturae dictis. Dicitur enim Iehouah transfixus, Zach. XII, 10. conf. Ioann. XIX, 37. Filius Dei traditur pro nobis. Rom. VIII, 32. Auctor vitae interfectus, Act. III, 15. Dominus gloriae crucifixus, 1 Cor. II, 8. Quae dicta scripturae testantur, non humanam tantum naturam esse passam, sed ipsummet Filium Dei, ipsummet Iehouam.

2) E syllogistica propositionum personalium consecutione. Recte enim concludimus: Filius hominis vere & realiter traditus est in mortem.

3) Ab exemplorum paritate. Si vere & absque tropo scriptura asserit, Filium Dei esse natum ex Maria virgine, Luc. I, 35. vtique etiam vere & absque tropo accipiendum est, quod Dominus gloriae crucifixus fit. 4) Si sola humana natura passa est, verum erit illud NESTORII: Noli gloriari, Iudae, quia non Deum, sed hominem crucifixisti. Vid EVAGRIVS l. I, histor. c. 2. hist. tripartit. l. 12. c. 4.

Prob. b. Actiones & passiones sunt suppositorum. Quam ob rem quando dico: Deus est passus; subiectum passionis, vt quod, est Deus; subiectum, vt quo, est humana natura, in ipsa hypostasi Filii Dei subsistens. Vnde hanc propositionem: Deus est passus, ita expono: Filius Dei est passus secundum humanam naturam in personalitate diuina subsistentem. Vt ergo, cum vulnus infligitur carni Petri, non sola caro Petri dicitur vulnerata, sed vere vulneratus est Petrus, siue persona Petri, tametsi anima ipsius vulnerari nequeat: ita, cum patitur Filius Dei secundum carnem, non patitur sola caro, vel humana eius natura, sed vere patitur Filius Dei, vel persona Filii Dei, vtut ἀπαθὴς sit natura diuina.

Prob. c. E mutua naturae vtriusque, diuinae & humanae, in vna persona Christi communione. Quia enim mutua, eaque vera & realis datur inter duas naturas in vna persona Christi communio, ideoque natura diuina idiomata humanae naturae sibi vere & realiter appropriat.

propriat. Duæ quippe naturæ in communionem veniunt non nudæ, sed proprietatibus suis vestitæ. Hanc ἰδιοποίησιν, siue appropriationem respicit Paullus, cum Act. XX, 28. inquit: Deus ecclesiam acquisiuit per proprium sanguinem. Ex quo colligimus: Quicunque proprium effudit sanguinem, is vere, realiter & proprie passus est: Atqui Deus &c. E. Nimirum tam vere & realiter Deus passus est in sua carne, quam vere & realiter Paullus & Petrus passi sunt in sua propria carne; quippe quam est Paullo & Petro sua caro propria essentialiter, tam est Filio Dei sua caro propria personaliter. Prob. d. Passus est Deus in carne ἐνεργητικῶς, seu effectiue, eo, quod diuina patientis Christi natura, pondus, robur, efficaciam & valorem passioni carnis addidit, vt esset ponderosissima, efficacissima, saluberrima & plane satisfactoria. Passio solius carnis, quantumuis iustissimæ, pro se non satisfacit, pro aliis minus, pro toto mundo minime. Dicis: Quicunque realiter patitur, is passionem sentit: Atqui Deus passionem non sensit: E. Deus realiter non est passus. Resp. Quicunque realiter & physice patitur, is passionem sentit, concedo. At Filius Dei licet passus sit realiter, non tamen est passus φυσικῶς, sed ὑποστατικῶς, siue, personaliter, & appropriatiue, siue vt ATHANAS. libr. IV. de trinit. loquitur; Passus est Filius Dei, non natura deitatis, sed vnionis dispensatione.


### Question XLV. What is the second kind of communication of idioms?

The second genus of the communication of idioms is that the Son of God communicated his divine majesty to the assumed flesh.

It is defined more fully:

The second genus of the communication of idioms is that by which the Son of God truly and really communicated the idioms of his divine nature to the assumed human nature on account of the personal union, for common possession, usurpation, and denomination.

Latin:

Secundum genus communicationis idiomatum est, quod filius Dei maiestatem suam diuinam assumtæ carni communicauit.

Vberius definitur:

Secundum genus communicationis idiomatum est, quo Filius Dei idiomata divinæ suæ naturæ assumtæ humanæ naturæ propter vnionem personalem vere & realiter communicauit, ad communem possessionem, vsurpationem & denominationem.


### Question XLVI. What must be observed for knowing this second genus of C. I.?

For understanding the second genus of the communication of idioms, the following must be observed: 1) The appellations of this genus, 2) The cause and foundation of the communication, 3) The subject of the communication, 4) The communicated gifts, 5) The end of the communication, 6) The predications resulting from this second genus of C. I.

Latin:

Ad intelligendum secundum genus communicationis idiomatum obseruanda sunt: 1) Appellationes huius generis, 2) Communicationis caussa & fundamentum, 3) Communicationis subiectum, 4) Communicata dona, 5) Communicationis finis, 6) Prædicationes, ex hoc secundo genere C. I. resultantes.


### C. I. Question XLVII. By what names is the second kind of C. I. distinguished?

The Greek prelates of the church distinguished this second genus with emphatic names to express its nature. By Latin doctors it is commonly called the communication of majesty.

Proof. The Greeks call this genus of C. I. 1) βελτίωσιν, an improvement, on account of the infinite gifts bestowed, by which the human nature of Christ is perfected for undertaking a threefold office; 2) προσ- θήκην μεγάλην, a great augmentation, because, given the communicated omnipotence, omniscience, etc., no greater augmentation is given; 3) ὑπερύψωσιν, an exaltation, since through the communicated divine majesty the flesh of Christ is raised to the highest state; 4) μετάδοσιν, a bestowal, namely of infinite majesty; 5) δόξασιν, a glorification; since the flesh of Christ is heaped with that glory which the Son of God has from eternity, John 17:5. 6) μετάληψιν θείας ἀξίας, participation of divine dignity, because from the divine gifts with which the flesh is abundantly adorned, its divine dignity shines forth; 8) μετοχὴν θείας δυνάμεως, participation of divine power, from which results the highest glory; Deification; which DAMASCENUS, lib. III. de O. F. c. 12, explains, noting that the ancients by the term Deification by no means understood a transmutation, confusion, contortion, abolition, or equalization of natures, but that they wished by that term to denote primarily the economy of the hypostatic union: a) because on account of that hypostatic union it is predicated of the man Christ that He becomes God: b) because the ancients by this term indicated the περιχώρησιν [interpenetration] of the natures. Cf. d. CHEMNIT. de d. n. c. 26. The Latins call it the communication of majesty, because the divine and infinite gifts are the very majesty and glory of the eternal God. The occasion for this denomination was taken from the Greeks, who called the divine gifts, given to Christ in time, ἀξιώματα, dignities, and αὐχήματα, excellencies. In the Holy Scriptures, the communication of majesty is called anointing, i.e., the donation of the Holy Spirit without measure, Ps. XLV, 8. John III, 34. Acts X, 38. Quest.

Latin:

Græci ecclesiæ antistites hoc secundum genus nominibus emphaticis ad exprimendam eius indolem insigniuerunt. A latinis doctoribus communiter vocatur communicatio maiestatis.

Prob. Græci hoc genus C. I. vocant 1) βελτίωσιν, meliorationem, ob dona infinita collata, quibus natura Christi humana ad triplex obeundum officium perficitur; 2) προσθήκην μεγάλην, magnum augmentum, ideo, quod communicata omnipotentia, omniscientia &c., nullum datur augmentum maius; 3) ὑπερύψωσιν, exaltationem, quoniam per communicatam maiestatem diuinam caro Christi in celsissimum statum euecta est; 4) μετάδοσιν, collationem, scilicet infinitæ maiestatis; 5) δόξασιν, glorificationem; siquidem caro Christi ea gloria cumulata est, quam habet Filius Dei ab æterno, Ioann. XVII, 5. 6) μετάληψιν θείας ἀξίας, participationem divinae dignitatis, quia ex donis divinis, quibus exornata est caro affluenta, illius dignitas divina relucet; 8) μετοχὴν θείας δυνάμεως, participationem divinae potentiae, e qua resultat gloria summa; Deificationem; quam DAMASCENUS lib. III. de O. F. c. 12. explicat, quod veteres nomine Deificationis nequaquam intellexerint transmutationem, confusionem, contorsionem, abolitionem aut exaequationem naturarum, sed, quod primo oeconomiam hypostaticae unionis eo vocabulo notare voluerint: a) quia propter hypostaticam illam unionem de homine Christo praedicatur, quod fit Deus: b) quia veteres vocabulo hoc, περιχώρησιν naturarum indicarunt. Conf. d. CHEMNIT. de d. n. c. 26. Latini appellant communicationem maiestatis, propterea, quod divina & infinita dona sunt ipsa aeterni Dei maiestas & gloria. Occasio huius denominationis sumta est a Graecis, qui dona divina, Christo in tempore data, vocarunt ἀξιώματα, dignitates, & αὐχήματα, excellentias. In sacris litteris communicatio maiestatis appellatur unctio, i. e. donatio Spiritus S. praeter mensuram, Ps. XLV, 8. Ioann. III, 34. Act. X, 38. Quaest.


### XLVIII. Who communicated the divine idioms to the flesh of Christ?

The Son of God personally communicated the divine αὐχήματα [excellencies] to the assumed flesh a), which, however, God the Father b) and the Holy Spirit c) also gave. Prob. a. For just as the Word assumed human nature into the unity of His person, Heb. II, 16, so the same communicated His divine properties, marked by His hypostatic character, personally to the assumed humanity. The distinction here is between δόσιν [giving] and κοινωνίαν [communication], between donation and communication.

From the Father and the Holy Spirit, the divine αὐχήματα are said to be given to Christ according to His human nature, but not communicated, if we wish to speak strictly and in rigor; because the communication of which we speak here is and is called personal, and therefore presupposes the personal union. Now, however, the personal union is not between the Father and the flesh of Christ, or the Holy Spirit and the flesh of Christ, but between the Word and His assumed flesh.

Prob. b. God the Father gave the Son of Man power, honor, and a kingdom, Dan. VII, 13. Cf. John V, 27. Matt. XI, 27. Prob. c.

The Holy Spirit anointed the Messiah, Is. LXI, 1, and indeed not by measure, John III, 34. Therefore, He endowed the flesh of Christ with immense gifts. Quest.

Latin:

Filius Dei personaliter communicavit assumtae carni αὐχήματα divina a), quae tamen etiam dedit Deus Pater b), & Spiritus S. c). Prob. a. Vt enim ὁ λόγος naturam humanam assumsit in vnitatem suae personae, Hebr. II, 16. ita idem divinas suas proprietates, charactere suo hypostatico insignitas, assumtae humanitati personaliter communicavit. Dist. hic est inter δόσιν καὶ κοινωνίαν, inter dationem, & communicationem.

A Patre & Spiritu S. dicuntur divina αὐχήματα Christo secundum humanam naturam dari, sed non communicari, si stricte & in rigore loqui velimus; quia communicatio, de qua hic loquimur, est & vocatur personalis, adeoque unionem personalem praesupponit. Iam vero vnio personalis non est inter patrem & carnein Christi, vel Spiritum S. & carnem Christi, sed inter λόγον & assumtam eius carnem.

Prob. b. Deus Pater dedit filio hominis potestatem, honorem & regnum, Dan. VII, 13. Conf. Ioann. V, 27. Matth. XI, 27. Prob. c.

Spiritus S. Messiam vnxit, Es. LXI, 1, & quidem non ad mensuram, Ioann. III, 34. Ergo carnem Christi donis immensis donauit. Quaest.


### XLIX. Upon what foundation does the communication of majesty made to the flesh of Christ rest?

The foundation of the majesty communicated to the flesh of Christ is both the personal union, by which the divine hypostasis was communicated to the human nature of Christ a), and the intimate communion of the divine and human natures in the one person of Christ b).

Prob. a. Through the personal union, the ὑπόστασις [hypostasis] of the Word was communicated to the human nature of Christ. Therefore, the properties which are in reality identified with it were also communicated to the same. The reason for the consequence is: because, of those things which are really the same, when one is communicated, the other is communicated also. And again: If the divine idioms cannot be communicated to the human nature, neither could the ὑπόστασις of the Word be communicated; for this is proper to the Son of God, whereas the idioms are common to the remaining divine persons. Certainly, it is much more credible that common attributes were communicated than the proper hypostasis: For the communication of the communicable is less repugnant than that of the incommunicable. The Father communicates the essence to the Son, not the personal property, otherwise the Son would be the Father. In the personal union, both the substance of the Word and His very deity are communicated to the assumed humanity.

Prob. b. No perichoretic union, i. e. one inferring a communication of natures to one another, can exist without a communication of idioms. But the personal union of the two natures in Christ is perichoretic, i. e. inferring a communion of the divine and human natures to one another: Therefore. The major is proved: 1) because that degree of union is the least, which no κοινωνία (communion) follows. 2) A union which occurs by παράστασιν (juxtaposition) or παράθεσιν (apposition) is without a communication of idioms; for example, two metals compacted have no internal communion. Nor does an angel, although it bestows motion upon an assumed body, have union with it by περιχώρησις (perichoresis), because it does not permeate and inform that body as an ἐντελέχεια (entelechy). 3) Where two natures are united κατά σύνδυσιν καὶ κατὰ περιχώρησιν (by conjunction and by perichoresis), of which one is like a δύναμις (power), or potency, and the other like an ἐντελεχείας (entelechy), or act, there the latter communicates its idioms to the former truly and really for common possession, usurpation, and denomination. It is illustrated by examples: The soul, most closely united to the body, truly and really imparts to it vital faculty, just as well as sensitive faculties: fire, having fallen into iron, communicates to it the power of burning and shining. We confirmed the minor above, quest. XXX. Quaest.

Latin:

Fundamentum communicatae cum carne Christi maiestatis est tum vnio personalis, qua humanae Christi naturae communicata est hypostasis divina a), tum intima divinae & humanae naturarum in vna persona Christi communio b).

Prob. a. Per vnionem personalem communicata est humanae Christi naturae ὑπόστασις τοῦ λόγου. Ergo etiam eidem communicatae sunt propria, quae cum ipsa reapse identificantur. Ratio consequentiae est: quia, quae realiter idem sunt, eorum vno communicato, communicatur & alterum. Et rursus: Si idiomata divina non possunt communicari naturae humanae, nec communicari potuit ὑπόστασις τοῦ λόγου; haec quippe propria est filio Dei, idiomata autem sunt communia reliquis personis divinis. Sane multo credibilius est, attributa communia, quam hypostasin propriam communicatam esse: Minus enim repugnat τῷ communicabili communicatio, quam incommunicabili. Pater communicat Filio essentiam, non proprietatem personalem, alioqui Filius esset Pater. In vnione autem personali & substantia τοῦ λόγου, & ipsa eius deitas communicatur assumtae humanitati.

Nulla unio perichoristica, i. e. inferens communicationem naturarum ad se invicem, potest esse sine communicatione idiomatum. At unio personalis duarum in Christo naturarum est perichoristica, i. e. inferens communionem divinae & humanae naturarum ad se invicem: Ergo. Maior prob. 1) quia ille unionis gradus est minimus, quem nulla sequitur κοινωνία. 2) Unio, quae fit per παράστασιν, vel παράθεσιν, sine communicatione idiomatum est, v. gr. duo metalla compacta nullam habent internam communionem. Neque angelus, licet motum largiatur corpori assumto, cum hoc unitus est per περιχώρησιν, quia non permeat & informat illud corpus, ut ἐντελέχεια. 3) Vbi duae naturae κατά σύνδυσιν καὶ κατὰ περιχώρησιν unitae sunt, quorum una est instar δυνάμεως, sive potentiae, altera instar ἐντελεχείας, sive actus, ibi haec communicat illi vere & realiter sua idiomata ad communem possessionem, usurpationem & denominationem. Illustratur exemplis: Anima arctissime unita corpori, huic facultatem vitalem, pariter atque facultates sensitivas vere & realiter impertitur: ignis, illapsus ferrum, huic vim vrendi & lucendi communicat. Minorem confirmavimus supra, quaest. XXX. Quaest.


### L. To whom has divine majesty been given?

The subject to which divine majesty has been given is Christ according to the human nature ), or, which is the same thing, the human nature, assumed into the ὑπόστασιν (hypostasis) of the Word ).

Prob. a. The subject which receives the communication is the person of the Word incarnate. For just as actions and passions belong to persons: so whatever is given, is given to the person, and whatever is received, is received by the person. Whence the Savior says, Matt. XXVIII, 18: All power has been given to me (Christ) in heaven and on earth. And Paul says, Phil. II, 9: God exalted Christ, and gave him a name which is above every name.

Prob. b. The subject by which is the nature, to which the communication of divine majesty has been made. For indeed in the one person of Christ there are two distinct natures, it is asked: according to which nature of the person of Christ has the communication of majesty been made? Where we answer explicitly: according to the human nature. We confirm our assertion: 1) Whatever has been given to the person of Christ not according to the divine nature, that has been given to him according to the human nature: But divine majesty, etc. Therefore. The major is evident: because whatever is predicated of the person of Christ, it pertains either to the divine, or to the human, or to both of his natures; since the person is not something third and really distinct from those two natures, personally united. The minor is proved: because the divine nature is too exalted to be exalted, too opulent to be enriched, too glorious to receive an increase of glory, too perfect for anything to be given or added to it.

2) Holy Scripture designates the subject to which the communication of majesty has been made, John VI, 51, 54, where the flesh of Christ is called life-giving, and the same subject is determined by the specificative particle, John V, 27: The Father gave the Son power to execute judgment; because he is the son of man; where the particle ὅτι (because) is not taken reduplicatively, or causally, because the human nature is not the cause of that giving; otherwise it would follow that all men have ἐξουσίαν κριτικήν (judicial authority), since when the cause is posited and not hindered, the effect follows: but specificatively, so that the nature may be determined according to which divine majesty was given to the person of Christ.

3) There exists a most common rule, approved by the greatest consensus of the entire orthodox church: Whatever Scripture says has been given to Christ in time, that is understood to have been given to him not according to the deity, but according to the assumed humanity. D. Dannhauer limits this rule on account of various instances in hodof. phaenom. VIII. p. 660: Whatever idiom through the grace of union or exaltation, for the perfection of the receiver, is Christ's not only manifestatively but really

was given in time, it was given to him according to his human nature. But that divine gifts (ἀυχήματα) were given to Christ, it is clearly evident; since a) Holy Scripture itself expresses the circumstance of the time in which this donation occurred: Seventy weeks are determined to anoint the holy of holies, says the prophet Daniel, ch. IX, 24. And Christ himself, calling upon the Father, says John XVII, 5: Father, the hour is come: glorify thy Son, that thy Son also may glorify thee! Now therefore glorify thou me, O Father, with thine own self, with the glory which I had with thee before the world was. b) Because exaltation is described as the immediate consequence of emptying. Therefore, exaltation also belongs to Christ according to that nature according to which he was emptied in time, i.e., according to his human nature. The Holy Scriptures teach the connection of emptying and exaltation in many places. Christ ought to enter into his glory through passion, Luke XXIV, 26. He became obedient unto the death of the cross: Wherefore God also hath exalted him, and given him a name, which is above every name, Philipp. II, 8. 9.

Latin:

Subiectum, cui data est maiestas divina, est Christus secundum humanam naturam ), vel, quod idem est, humana natura, in ὑπόστασιν τῷ λόγῳ assumta ).

Prob. a. Subiectum, quod communicatam accipit, est persona τῷ λόγῳ ἐνσάρκῳ. Vt enim actiones & passiones sunt personarum: ita quidquid datur, personae datur, & quidquid recipitur, a persona recipitur. Vnde Salvator inquit, Matth. XXVIII, 18. Data mihi (Christo) ) omnis potestas in caelo & in terra. Et Paullus ait, Phil. II, 9. Deus exaltavit Christum, ac donavit ei nomen, quod est super omne nomen.

Prob. b. Subiectum quo, est natura, ad quam facta est communicatio maiestatis divinae. Etenim in una Christi persona duae distinctae sunt naturae, quaeritur: iuxta quam naturam personae Christi facta sit communicatio maiestatis? Vbi diserte respondemus: secundum humanam naturam. Confirmamus nostram assertionem: 1) Quidquid datum est personae Christi non secundum divinam naturam, illud ipsi donatum est secundum naturam humanam: Atqui maiestas divina &c. Ergo. Maior constat: quia quidquid de persona Christi praedicatur, id vel ad divinam, vel ad humanam, vel ad utramque ipsius naturam pertinet; quoniam persona non est aliquid tertium & realiter distinctum a duabus illis naturis, personaliter unitis. Minor probatur: quia natura divina est excelsior, quam ut exaltari, opulentior, quam ut ditari, gloriosior, quam ut gloriae augmentum capere, perfectior, quam ut ei quidquam dari, vel addi queat.

2) S. scriptura designat subiectum, cui facta est communicatio maiestatis, Io. VI, 51. 54. vbi caro Christi dicitur vivifica, idemque subiectum determinatur per particulam specificativam, Io. V, 27. Pater potestatem dedit Filio iudicium faciendi; quia filius hominis est; vbi particula ὅτι quia, non sumitur reduplicative, aut causaliter, quia natura humana non est causa illius dationis; alioqui sequeretur omnes homines habere ἐξουσίαν κριτικήν, cum posita causa & non impedita, sequatur effectus: sed specificative, vt determinetur natura, secundum quam maiestas divina personae Christi data est.

3) Exstat regula communissima, maximo totius ecclesiae orthodoxae consensu approbata: Quaecunque scriptura dicit, Christo data esse in tempore, illa non secundum deitatem, sed secundum assumtam humanitatem ei data intelliguntur. Quam regulam ob varias instantias limitat D. Dannhav. in hodof. phaenom. VIII. p. 660. Quodcunque idioma per gratiam unionis aut exaltationis, ad perfectionem accipientis, non solum manifestative, sed realiter Christi. solum manifeftatiue, sed realiter

Christo datum est in tempore, id ei iuxta humanam naturam datum est. Data autem esse Christo ἀυχήματα diuina, liquido constat; quoniam a) ipsa S. scriptura circumstantiam temporis, quo hæc donatio contigit, exprimit: Septimanæ septuaginta decisæ sunt ad ungendum sanctum sanctorum, inquit propheta Daniel, cap. IX, 24. Et ipse Christus, compellans Patrem, ait Io. XVII, 5: Pater, venit hora: glorifica filium tuum, ut etiam filius tuus glorificet te! Nunc ergo glorifica me tu, Pater, apud temet ipsum, gloria, quam habui, antequam mundus esset, apud te. b) Quia exaltatio describitur ut immediatum consequens exinanitionis. Ergo etiam secundum eam naturam competit Christo exaltatio, iuxta quam fuit exinanitus in tempore, h. e. iuxta naturam humanam. Connexionem exinanitionis & exaltationis passim locorum docent sacræ litteræ. Oportet Christum per passionem intrare in gloriam, Luc. XXIV, 26. Obediens factus est usque ad mortem crucis: Propterea etiam Deus ipsum exaltauit, & donauit ipsi nomen, quod super omne nomen est, Philipp. II, 8. 9.


### Q. LI. Are truly divine, uncreated, infinite, and immense gifts communicated to Christ according to his human nature?

Through and because of the personal union, truly divine, uncreated, infinite, and immense gifts have been given to Christ according to his human nature.

Obj. Threefold gifts belong to the human nature of Christ. Some belong to it by condition or the character of the nature itself, e.g., health of body, senses, intellect, will, memory, etc. Some belong to it by habitual grace, of which kind are certain peculiar gifts, yet created and finite, which are in him habitually, subjectively, and indeed in the highest degree. Some have been imparted to him through the grace of personal union, which are truly divine, uncreated, and infinite. The question is formed concerning these.

Our assertion is proved 1) from the testimony of Paul saying, Col. II, 9. In Christ dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. Obj. a)

The Greek πλήρωμα denotes all-manner and consummate perfection. Therefore πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος is the full and perfect deity. For the sake of greater emphasis, πᾶν πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος is added, so that it may be indicated that the full and perfect deity, and everything that is really in it, dwells in Christ. Therefore, all the fulness of the Godhead comprises omnipotence, omniscience, omnipresence, and finally all the properties and every energy (ἐνέργειαν) of God. Obj. b) σωματικῶς is rendered by some as 'personally'; by others, 'as in his own body,' as it is expounded by THEODORET; and also by DAMASCENE, τοῦτ' ἔστιν, ἐν σαρκὶ αὐτοῦ, that is, in his flesh, so that it may be hinted that the flesh of Christ is the most sacred temple and dwelling-place of the indwelling Godhead [*].

AUGUSTINE confirms this exposition, epist. VII. to Dardanus. It is said 'bodily' because God dwells in the body of Christ, which he assumed from the Virgin, as in a temple. Where he distinguishes between a common temple and a proper one. The saints are common temples of the indwelling God, but the flesh of Christ is a proper temple assumed personally. c) Indwelling implies habitation or possession.

fession. Hence IGNATIUS called the body of Christ σῶμα ἔχον τὸν Θεὸν ἔνοικον, a body having God inhabiting it; yet it has this not from the condition of human nature, but through supernatural union and communication. These things being premised, we argue: In whose flesh, as in a temple properly and personally assumed, the whole fullness of divinity dwells, he in his flesh has and possesses all divine idioms not of himself, but through union and communication. But in the flesh of Christ, etc. Therefore.

2) From the statement of St. John the forerunner, John III, 34. 35. He whom the Father has sent speaks the words of God, οὐ γὰρ ἐκ μέτρου δίδωσιν ὁ Θεὸς τὸ πνεῦμα, for God does not give the Spirit by measure (to him), the Father loves the Son; and has given all things into his hand. Obf. a) The Giver in this place is God the Father, the fountain of deity, who in the fullness of time sent the Son, born of a woman, Gal. IV, 14. and anointed the same with the Holy Spirit and power; Acts X, 38. and out of most singular love gave all things into his hand. b) The Person to whom the donation was made is Christ according to his human nature: for he is described as sent in time, who also in the course of time had to grow, and into whose hand all things were given. But concerning things given in time, the rule is certain, that they were given to Christ only according to his human nature. c) That which was given is the Holy Spirit, who is understood here not only by reason of his person, but also by reason of his gifts, for his gifts in the communication κατ’ ἔξω are not to be separated from the person. But those gifts are said to be given, if you look at the manner, οὐκ ἐκ μέτρου, i.e., without measure, and thus in an immense manner. Faithful men receive gifts according to the measure of the gift of Christ, Eph. IV, 7. whose gifts are finite: but those things which are given without measure are infinite. Whence we validly conclude: To whomever the gifts of the Holy Spirit are given not by measure, he is endowed with immense and infinite gifts of the Holy Spirit: But the human nature of Christ, etc. Therefore.

You say: The immense gifts of the Holy Spirit were given to the person of Christ, but not to his human nature. Resp. The person is not a third thing, distinct from the natures. Therefore, if the immense gifts of the Holy Spirit were given to the person of Christ; it is asked: according to which nature? whether they were conferred according to the divine or the human nature? But nothing could be given to the divine nature in time: Therefore they were given to the human nature of Christ.

3) From the description of the glory given to Christ, John XVII, 5. Now glorify me, you, Father, with yourself with the glory which I had, before the world was, with you. Obf. a) The glory which Christ had with the Father, before this world was made, is divine, eternal, uncreated & infinite glory. b) Christ had eternal glory with the Father, as God, not by reason of intention or predestination, but in act and in reality itself, as the only-begotten from the Father, John I, 14. The same, as man, he received through personal union, as to possession; but through the ascension into heaven and sitting at the right hand of God, as to use, or plenary exercise. c) The Savior speaks of real glorification, not declarative, or a mere manifestation of glory. For Christ requests that he be glorified with the Father, just as he had glory with him, before the world was founded. But he had the same in act and really, before the foundation of the world. Therefore he also requested the actual and real participation of the same glory in time. These things being premised, we argue: Whatever glory Christ requested, that he might be adorned with it by the Father in time, the same he received as actually communicated according to his human nature: But Christ requested eternal and infinite glory, that he might be adorned with it by the Father in time: Therefore. The major is of manifest truth; for according to that nature did Christ request glory, according to which he could be glorified by the Father. But according to the divine nature he could not be glorified by the Father; because it is immutable, most perfect and most exalted, so that it neither stands in need of glory, nor can be advanced to a greater sublimity. Therefore he requested glorification according to his human nature, according to his human nature, according to his human nature, according to which he had been emptied. Add that the glory which the Savior sought here becomes a gift given to Christ in time. However, whatever gifts were given to Christ in time, they were given to him not according to the divine nature, but the human.

You say: I. The glory in the l. c. [loco citato/cited passage] is not understood as divine glory, but mediatorial, which becomes a glory inferior to the divine, not equal to it, but nearest; yet more sublime than all the glory of creatures.

Resp. That glory is indicated which Christ had with the Father before the world was. But before the world was founded there was nothing except eternity, except infinite majesty. Therefore.

Glory mediatorial is supreme & infinite. You say: II. Christ had glory with the Father before the foundation of the world, by reason of divine predestination.

Resp. There is no indication of predestination in the text. Christ asks to be glorified really in time; and therefore the possession of glory before the world is also real, and not truly consisting only in intention & bare predestination. If Christ had spoken about glorification by reason of a divine decree, he would have said nothing that does not also apply to other elect.

For all the elect receive at the appointed time that glory to which they were predestined before the world was made. You say: III. The words of Christ are to be understood concerning the declaration & manifestation of glory through the resurrection & sitting at the right hand of God.

Resp. Christ here sought to be glorified with the Father, and therefore it cannot be understood as a manifestation of glory before men.

4) From the exaltation of Christ, Phil. II, 9. God exalted Christ, & gave (ἐχαρίσατο, gave out of grace) to him a name which is above every name. A name above every name does not imply a certain finite majesty, but an infinite & truly divine one; for if it were finite, it would not yet be a name above every name, but would have another more infinite & more sublime name above itself.

5) That the majesty of omnipotence, omniscience, omnipresence, & religious adoration has been given to the human nature of Christ, we shall show clearly below.

6) Christ performs the works of his office (redeeming, gathering, illuminating, regenerating, justifying, governing, defending the church &c.) according to both natures. But in order for the human nature of Christ to be able to concur & cooperate in those ἀποτελέσματα [results/effects], it has need not only of created or finite gifts, but of the communion of the very infinite power of the Word; since those works are not of finite virtue, but infinite; concerning which we were to treat in the following questions.

Latin:

Per & propter vnionem personalem Christo secundum humanam naturam dona vere diuina, increata, infinita & immensa data sunt.

Obs. Humanæ Christi naturæ triplicia conueniunt dona. Quædam ei competunt per conditionem, aut indolem ipsius naturæ, v. gr. corporis sanitas, sensus, intellectus, voluntas, memoria &c. Quædam illi conueniunt per gratiam habitualem, cuiusmodi sunt dona quædam peculiaria, creata tamen & finita, quæ ipsi habitualiter, subiectiue, & quidem in summo gradu insunt. Quædam illi impertita sunt per gratiam vnionis personalis, quæ vere diuina, increata & infinita sunt. De his quæstio formata est.

Probatur assertum nostrum 1) e testimonio Pauli inquentis, Col. II, 9. In Christo habitat omnis plenitudo diuinitatis corporaliter.

Obs. a) Græcum πλήρωμα notat omnimodam & consummatam perfectionem. Ergo πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος est plena & perfecta deitas. Maioris emphaseos caussa additur πᾶν πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος, vt indicetur, plenam perfectamque deitatem, & omne, quod in illa realiter est, habitare in Christo. Complectitur igitur omnis plenitudo diuinitatis omnipotentiam, omniscientiam, omnipræsentiam, & denique omnes proprietates & omnem ἐνέργειαν Dei. Obs. b) σωματικῶς a nonnullis redditur, personaliter; a nonnullis, velut in proprio corpore, vt exponitur a THEODORETO; nec non a DAMASCENO, τοῦτ' ἔστιν, ἐν σαρκὶ αὐτοῦ, hoc est, in carne ipsius, vt innuatur, carnem Christi esse inhabitantis diuinitatis templum & domicilium sacratissimum [*].

Comprobat hanc expositionem AVGVSTIN. epist. VII. ad Dardan. Corporaliter dictum est, quia in Christi corpore, quod assumsit ex virgine, tanquam in templo habitat Deus. Vbi dist. inter templum commune, & proprium. Sancti sunt templa inhabitantis Dei communia, caro Christi autem est templum proprium personaliter assumtum. c) Inhabitatio infert habitationem vel possessionem.

fessionem. Hinc IGNATIVS corpus Christi dixit σῶμα ἔχον τὸν Θεὸν ἔνοικον, corpus habens inhabitantem Deum; habet autem non e conditione naturae humanae, sed per supernaturalem vnionem & communicationem. Quibus praestitutis argumentamur: In cuius carne velut templo proprio personaliter assumpto habitat omnis plenitudo diuinitatis, ille in sua carne habet & possidet omnia idiomata diuina non per se, sed per vnionem & communicationem. Atqui in carne Christi &c. Ergo.

2) Ex effato S. Ioannis protobaptistae, Io. III, 34. 35. Quem Pater misit, verba Dei loquitur, οὐ γὰρ ἐκ μέτρου δίδωσιν ὁ Θεὸς τὸ πνεῦμα, non enim ex mensura dedit Deus (illi) Spiritum, Pater amat Filium; & omnia dedit in manum ipsius. Obs. a) Dator h. l. est Deus Pater, fons deitatis, qui in plenitudine temporis misit Filium, natum ex muliere, Gal. IV, 14. eundemque vnxit Spiritu Sancto & virtute; Act. X, 38. & ex amore singularissimo omnia in ipsius manum dedit. b) Persona, cui donatio facta, est Christus secundum humanam naturam: describitur enim, vt missus in tempore, quem etiam successu temporis oportebat crescere, & in cuius manum omnia sunt data. De datis autem in tempore certa est regula, quod Christo non, nisi secundum humanam naturam, data sint. c) Id, quod donatum est, est Spiritus S., qui hic non tantum ratione personae, sed & ratione donorum intelligitur, neque enim dona eius in communicatione κατ’ ἔξω separanda sunt a persona. Dona autem illa dicuntur data, si modum respicias, οὐκ ἐκ μέτρου, h. e. sine mensura, adeoque immensa ratione. Homines fideles accipiunt dona secundum mensuram donationis Christi, Eph. IV, 7. quorum dona sunt finita: at, quae sine mensura data sunt, illa sunt infinita. Vnde valide concludimus: Cuicunque dona Spiritus S. data sunt non ad mensuram, is praeditus est donis Spiritus S. immensis atque infinitis: Atqui humanae Christi naturae &c. Ergo.

Dicis: Immensa Spiritus S. dona data sunt personae Christi, non autem humanae ipsius naturae. Resp. Persona non est tertium quid, distinctum a naturis. Ideo, si personae Christi data sunt immensa dona Spiritus S.; quaeritur: secundum quam naturam? vtrum secundum diuinam, an humanam naturam collata sint? At diuinae naturae in tempore dari nihil potuit: Ergo data sunt humanae Christi naturae.

3) E descriptione gloriae Christo datae, Io. XVII, 5. Nunc glorifica me tu, Pater, apud teipsum gloria, quam habui, antequam mundus esset, apud te. Obs. a) Gloria, quam habuit Christus apud Patrem, priusquam mundus hic fieret, est gloria diuina, aeterna, increata & infinita. b) Habuit Christus, vt Deus, aeternam gloriam apud Patrem, non ratione intentionis, aut praedestinationis, sed actu & re ipsa, vt vnigenitus a Patre, Io. I, 14. Eandem, vt homo, accepit per vnionem personalem, qua χρῆσιν, seu possessionem; per ascensionem vero in caelum & sessionem ad dextram Dei, qua χρῆσιν, siue plenarium vsum. c) Loquitur Saluator de glorificatione reali, non declaratiua, aut nuda manifestatione gloriae. Expetit namque Christus, se glorificari apud Patrem, prout gloriam habuit apud eum, ante mundum conditum. Sed habuit eandem actu & realiter, ante mundi fundationem. Ergo etiam expotauit eiusdem gloriae actualem & realem participationem in tempore. Quibus praemissis argumentamur: Quamcunque gloriam Christus expetiit, vt ea ornaretur a Patre in tempore, eandem reapse communicatam accepit secundum humanam naturam: At Christus aeternam & infinitam gloriam expetiit, vt ea ornaretur a Patre in tempore: Ergo. Maior est manifestae veritatis; nam secundum eam naturam Christus gloriam expetiit, secundum quam glorificari potuit a Patre. At secundum naturam diuinam non potuit glorificari a Patre; quia illa est immutabilis, perfectissima & celsissima, vt neque gloriae fit indiga, neque ad sublimitatem maiorem prouehi queat. Ergo expetiit glorificationem secundum humanam naturam, secundum humanam naturam, secundum humanam naturam, secundum quam exinanitus erat. Adiice, quod gloria, quam hic petiit Salvator, fit donum Christo in tempore datum. Quaecunque dona autem Christo data sunt in tempore, ea non secundum naturam divinam, sed humanam ei data sunt.

Dicis: I. Non intelligitur l. c. gloria divina, sed mediatoria, quae fit inferior gloria divina, non eidem aequalis, sed proxima; sublimior tamen omni gloria creaturarum.

Resp. Ea indigitatur gloria, quam Christus habuit apud Patrem, antequam mundus esset. Sed ante mundum conditum nil fuit, nisi aeternitas, nisi infinita maiestas. E.

Gloria mediatoria est suprema & infinita. Dicis: II. Christus gloriam habuit apud Patrem ante fundationem mundi, ratione praedestinationis divinae.

Resp. Praedestinationis nullum indicium est in textu. Petit Christus in tempore glorificari realiter; ideoque etiam possessio gloriae ante mundum realis est, non vero solum in intentione & praedestinatione nuda consistens. Si Christus locutus fuisset de glorificatione ratione decreti divini, nihil dixisset, quod aliis electis non conveniat.

Nam omnes electi accipiunt statuto tempore eam gloriam, ad quam sunt praedestinati, antequam mundus fieret. Dicis: III. Verba Christi intelligenda sunt de declaratione & manifestatione gloriae per resurrectionem & sessionem ad dextram Dei.

Resp. Christus hic expetiit glorificari apud Patrem, ideoque non potest intelligi manifestatio gloriae coram hominibus.

4) Ab exaltatione Christi, Phil. II, 9. Deus exaltavit Christum, & donavit (ἐχαρίσατο, ex gratia dedit) ei nomen, quod super omne nomen est. Nomen super omne nomen non infert maiestatem quandam finitam, sed infinitam & vere divinam; nam si finita foret, nondum esset nomen supra omne nomen, sed supra se haberet aliud infinitius sublimius nomen.

5) Donatum esse humanae Christi naturae maiestatem omnipotentiae, omniscientiae, omnipraesentiae, & adorationis religiosae, infra dilucide ostensuri sumus.

6) Christus opera officii (ecclesiam redimendo, colligendo, illuminando, regenerando, iustificando, gubernando, defendendo &c.) secundum utramque naturam peragit. Vt autem humana Christi natura ad illa ἀποτελέσματα concurrere & cooperari possit, opus habet non tantum donis creatis aut finitis, sed communione ipsius potentiae infinitae τῆς λόγης; quum opera illa non sint virtutis finitae, sed infinitae; de quibus in sequentibus quaestionibus acturi fuimus.


### Q. LI. Are truly divine, uncreated, infinite, and immense gifts communicated to Christ according to his human nature?: Quest. LII. Whether all divine attributes have been communicated to the flesh of Christ?

Quest. LII. Whether all divine attributes have been communicated to the flesh of Christ?

All divine attributes have been communicated to the flesh of Christ, by way of inhabitation & possession; but to the use and immediate predication, the divine ἐνεργητικά, or operative, idioms have been conferred upon it.

Prob. a. 1) To whom the infinite hypostasis is communicated, to him also are all divine idioms communicated; since they do not really differ from the divine subsistence.

2) The personal union & the perichoristic communion of the divine & human natures necessarily entails the communication of all divine idioms, by way of inhabitation & possession.

For how would all the fullness of the divinity dwell in the flesh of Christ, as in a temple personally assumed, unless all divine attributes dwelt in him?

Prob. b. Divine attributes that are ἀνενέργητα, or quiescent, (e.g., eternity, infinity, immensity &c.) do not admit of a second act, and therefore do not exert themselves through operation toward the outside.

Therefore the same are not [communicated] to the human nature of Christ for χρῆσις, or use, communicated.

For which reason also the quiescent divine idioms are not predicated immediately of the assumed flesh of Christ. But the proper divine ἐνεργητικὰ (energetic/operative ones) exert themselves through operation ad extra, and thus can be communicated for use. Hence it happens that they are predicated immediately of the flesh of Christ, e.g., The human nature of Christ is omnipotent, life-giving, omniscient, a searcher of hearts, etc., since omnipotence, the power of giving life, omniscience, and the searching of hearts exert themselves in and through the flesh of Christ.

The power of the man Christ is infinite, immense, and eternal. The reason is: because infinity, immensity, and eternity do not exert themselves through their own ἐνεργήματα (operations), but through the actions of omnipotence. For the action of omnipotence is of an eternal, immense, and infinite operation. Add that this difference also becomes clear in that the former contribute to the function of the mediatorial, kingly, priestly, and prophetic office, which cannot be carried out without the communicated operative attributes. The Son of God would not perform the priestly, kingly, and prophetic office through the flesh, unless this were instructed with omnipotence, omniscience, omnipresence, majesty, and glory. But the quiescent divine idioms do not concur immediately for the execution of the mediatorial office.

You say: Divine attributes do not differ on the part of God. Therefore, if all are communicated to the flesh of Christ, they can also be predicated of the flesh of Christ. Resp. 1) Divine attributes do not differ κατ' ἔσω (inwardly), or within the most simple complex of the divine essence, but they do differ κατ' ἔξω (outwardly), by reason of external operation. 2) All divine attributes are predicated of the human nature of Christ, the operative attributes immediately, the quiescent attributes mediately. It is illustrated by similars: The soul, united περιχωρητικῶς (perichoretically) to the body, imparts to it life and sensitive faculties, so that the body can be called living and sensing; yet the body is not called spiritual, immortal, and invisible from the spiritual, immortal, and invisible soul. In red-hot iron there is given the power of burning and shining, there is also given lightness and simplicity, since fire is a light and simple body; yet the iron is not therefore called a light and simple body. Thus the flesh of Christ is not immediately denominated from the communicated quiescent divine idioms.

Latin:

Quaest. LII. An omnia attributa diuina carni Christi communicata sunt?

Omnia attributa divina communicata sunt carni Christi, qua inhabitationem & possessionem ; ad usurpationem vero & immediatam praedicationem eidem collata sunt idiomata divina ἐνεργητικά, seu operativa .

Prob. a. 1) Cui communicata est hypostasis infinita, illi etiam communicata sunt omnia idiomata divina; quippe quae a subsistentia divina realiter non differunt.

2) Vnio personalis & communio divinae & humanae naturarum perichoristica necessario infert omnium idiomatum divinorum communicationem, qua inhabitationem & possessionem.

Quomodo enim omnis plenitudo divinitatis in carne Christi, velut templo personaliter assumpto, habitaret, nisi omnia idiomata divina in ipso habitarent?

Prob. b. Attributa divina ἀνενέργητα, sive quiescentia, (v. gr. aeternitas, infinitas, immensitas &c.) non admittunt actum secundum, adeoque per operationem ad extra se non exserunt.

Proinde eadem humanae Christi naturae ad χρῆσιν, seu usurpationem, non sunt communicata. Qua de causa etiam idiomata divina quiescentia de assumpta Christi carne non immediate praedicantur. At propria divina ἐνεργητικὰ per operationem ad extra se exserunt, adeoque ad usurpationem communicari possunt. Inde fit, ut de carne Christi immediate praedicentur, v. gr.

Humana Christi natura est omnipotens, vivifica, omniscia, cordium scrutatrix &c. quum omnipotentia, vis vivificandi, omniscientia, cordium scrutatio exserant se in & per carnem Christi. Attributa autem ἀνενέργητα licet de assumpta Christi carne non praedicentur immediate (neque enim caro Christi dicitur aeterna, infinita &c.; implicat contradictionem esse aeternum & caepisse in tempore, esse infinitum & manere finitum); praedicari tamen de eadem possunt mediate (mediante attributo operativo), v. gr.

Christi hominis potentia est infinita, immensa & aeterna. Ratio est; quia infinitas, immensitas & aeternitas se non exserunt per propria ἐνεργήματα, sed per actiones omnipotentiae. Actio quippe omnipotentiae est aeternae, immensae & infinitae operationis. Adde, quod haec differentia etiam in eo luculenta fit, quod illa faciant ad officii mediatorii, regii, sacerdotalis & prophetici functionem, quae expediri nequit sine communicatis attributis operativis. Non fungeretur Filius Dei officio sacerdotali, regio & prophetico per carnem, nisi haec instructa esset omnipotentia, omniscientia, omnipraesentia, maiestate, & gloria. Idiomata vero divina quiescentia & immediate non concurrunt ad executionem officii mediatorii.

Dicis: Attributa divina ex parte Dei non differunt. E. si omnia carni Christi sunt communicata, etiam de carne Christi praedicari possunt. Resp. 1) Attributa divina non differunt κατ' ἔσω, seu intra simplicissimum essentiae divinae complexum, differunt autem κατ' ἔξω, ratione externae operationis. 2) Omnia attributa divina praedicantur de Christi humana natura, attributa operativa immediate, attributa quiescentia mediate. Illustratur similibus: Anima, περιχωρητικῶς vnita corpori, huic vitam & facultates sensitivas impertiatur, ut dici queat corpus vivum & sentiens; non tamen ab anima spirituali, immortali & invisibili corpus dicitur spirituale, immortale & invisibile. In ferro candente datur vis vrendi & lucendi, datur etiam levitas & simplicitas, siquidem ignis est corpus leve & simplex; neque tamen ideo ferrum dicitur leve & simplex corpus. Ita caro Christi a communicatis idiomatibus divinis quiescentibus immediate non denominatur.


### Quest. LIII. In what mode of communication did the flesh of Christ become a participant of the divine idioms?

The mode of communication by which the flesh of Christ became a participant of the operative divine idioms is not effective, by duplication a), nor transient, or transfusive b), nor adaequative c), nor eversive, or destructive of the human nature d), but entelechial and perichoristic e), not for subjective inhesion f), but for common possession, use, and denomination g).

Prob. a. There is not given a double omnipotence, omniscience, omnipresence, and glory in Christ, but the same glory which the divine nature has by the Word from eternity, the same the assumed flesh receives in time, John XVII, 5. just as the body has the same life as the soul.

Prob. b. The attributes of the Son of God are so communicated to the humanity, that they nevertheless perpetually remain properties of the divine nature, and never become properties of the human nature. For they do not depart from the hypostasis of the Word, and migrate and pass into the human nature as into a subject; but the humanity, assumed into communion of the person by God the Word, at the same time [of] the person assumed by God the Word, at the same time

Latin:

Modus communicandi, quo caro Christi idiomatum divinorum operantium particeps facta est, non est effectivus, per geminationem a), neque transiens, aut transfusivus b), neque adaequativus c) neque eversivus, aut destructivus naturae humanae d), sed entelechialis & perichoristicus e), non ad subiectiuam inhaesionem f), sed ad communem possessionem, usurpationem & denominationem g).

Prob. a. Non datur gemina in Christo omnipotentia, omniscientia, omnipraesentia & gloria, sed quam gloriam divina τῶ λόγῳ natura habet ab aeterno, eandem assumpta caro accipit in tempore, Io. XVII, 5. sicut eandem vitam habet corpus, quam anima.

Prob. b. Attributa Filii Dei ita communicantur humanitati, ut tamen perpetuo maneant proprietates divinae naturae, nec vnquam fiant proprietates humanae naturae. Non enim hypostasin verbi egrediuntur, & in naturam humanam, tanquam in subiectum, immigrant & transeunt; verum humanitas in communionem personae a Deo Verbo assumpta, simul perfonæ a Deo Verbo assumta, simul


### Question LV. To what end were the divine idioms communicated to the flesh of Christ?

also became a participant of the divine nature and its properties. Nor does it receive them into itself as into a subject, so that they become its own properties: but it possesses them in the person of the Word by real communication. Prob. c. For equalization, the communication of the same thing is not sufficient, but furthermore the same mode of having is required; which is one thing regarding God and the Son of God, another regarding the flesh: the former has majesty by eternal generation, the latter by the grace of union. Whence even today Christ, as man, is lesser than the Father, 1 Cor. XV, 28. because the divine idioms which He received, He has by grace, Phil. II, 9. Prob. d. Through the communication of idioms, the human nature is not abolished or destroyed; but it is adorned and perfected for the function of the mediatorial office. For the fullness of the divinity inhabits the body of Christ, as its own temple, not to overturn it, but to illuminate it. Prob. e. & f. The internal and perfect union of two substances, essentially distinct indeed, but intimately conjoined, of which one behaves by way of ἐντελεχείας, i.e., of the perfecting act, the other by way of δυνάμεως, or of the perfectible potency, necessarily entails the communication of idioms, which inhere subjectively in the more virtuous uncreated substance, but are participated in by the other for common possession, usurpation, and denomination. E.g. Life and sensitive faculties inhere in the soul and exert themselves through the members of the body. Fire is in iron, yet it burns and shines through the glowing iron. As pertains specifically to the divine idioms τοῦ λόγου, since they are not qualities or accidents, they inhere in no subject of inhesion: yet the primary and immediate subject of attribution of the same, to which they belong formally and per se, is the divine nature of the Son of God; the secondary and mediate subject of attribution, to which they belong participatively and by the grace of personal union, is the human nature, Prob. g. The divine idioms ἐνεργητικὰ dwell in the flesh of Christ, as in their own temple, operate through the flesh, as an instrument hypostatically united, and are predicated of the flesh, as a secondary or mediate subject of attribution. Obs. We have deduced the mode of communicating more broadly above, quæst. XXXVIII.

Quæst. LIV. At what moment of time was the divine majesty communicated to the flesh of Christ? At the same moment the personal union was made, at that same moment the communication of majesty was made, as regards κτῆσιν, possession, and the first act a). To the exercise, or the full and never-ceasing use of majesty, the flesh of Christ was advanced at the same article of time in which it was exalted to the right hand of God b).

Prob. a. At that point of time the personal union occurred, when the hypostatic virtue of the Most High overshadowed the virgin Mary, i.e., in a mysterious way descended into the womb of Mary, filled the virginal mass of blood, excited by the Holy Spirit, with a peculiar approximation, and united it to Himself, so that the whole fullness of the divinity (to which all divine idioms pertain) might dwell in the body of Christ, as in a most sacred temple, Col. II, 9. Prob. b. Christ exalted received a name above every name, i.e., the highest and truly divine majesty, Phil. II, 9. and was glorified with the glory which He had with the Father, before the world was founded, Io. XVII, 5. namely, as regards the exercise and full use of majesty.

Quæst. LV. To what end were the divine idioms communicated to the flesh of Christ? They were communicated for the salutary function of the priestly, prophetic, and kingly office.

Prob. Christ performs the most exalted duty, priestly, prophetic, and kingly, according to both natures; for the discharging of which salutary office with fruit, the human nature would have been by no means equal, unless it had been endowed with omnipotence, omniscience, omnipresence, and divine glory.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, Socinians, & Arminians, who utterly deny that the divine majesty has been communicated to the flesh of Christ, moved by the following arguments:

I. Whatever nature is finite is not capable of infinite majesty: But the human nature of Christ is &c: Therefore. The major is proved from the most hackneyed axiom: No finite thing is capable of the infinite. Resp. I deny the major. To the proof we say that the finite does not indeed become capable of the infinite by a physical, apprehensive, active, & adequate capacity; yet it becomes capable of the finite infinite by a supernatural, participative, passive, & inadequate capacity. Indeed, it is certain beyond all doubt that no finite thing can actively & adequately grasp or comprehend the infinite; nevertheless, it is also certain that the finite can passively grasp, or inadequately receive, (especially through the supernatural grace of God) the infinite. For all and every creature is capable of its most present creator: as one who, without any division of himself, is whole in all things and everywhere. The same are capable of divine, and thus infinite, preservation and cooperation. The human intellect is capable, in its own way, of knowing God and eternal things. The faithful are capable of the Triune God, who dwells in their hearts by his most benevolent union and communication. The same are capable, as regards both knowledge and fruition, of the infinite satisfaction of Christ, of infinite divine mercy, and also of infinite justifying and saving grace. Finally, the flesh of Christ is capable of the infinitely joined to itself, the infinite λόγος, and his infinite hypostasis: whence Col. 2:9, the whole fullness of the deity is said to dwell in Christ bodily, i.e., in the body of Christ, as in its appropriated temple.

II. To whom divine idioms are communicated, he is God: The human nature of Christ is not God: Therefore. Resp. To whom divine idioms are communicated by essential communication, through eternal generation or procession, so that they are proper to him to whom they are communicated, and thus belong to him of himself, he is God; I grant it. To whom divine idioms are communicated by personal, entelechial, & perichoretic communication, he is God; I deny it. For just as the properties of the soul are communicated to the human body by entelechial & perichoretic communication, yet the body is not therefore called a soul, but animated: so divine idioms are communicated to the human nature of Christ, yet this is not therefore to be called God, but deified, or a participant of divinity, since the divine attributes do not belong to it κατ' αὐτὸ, of itself, but κατ' ἄλλο, by the grace of the personal union.

III. If on account of the personal union & the περιχώρησις of the natures the divine nature communicates its idioms to the human nature, on account of the same the human nature will also communicate its idioms to the divine nature: The consequent is false: Therefore the antecedent. The consequence of the major is proved, because the union is reciprocal, & the περιχώρησις mutual. The falsity of the consequent is evident: because, if the human nature had imparted its idioms to the divine, the deity would have suffered, died, been buried, would be palpable, divisible, &c. Resp. I deny the consequence of the major. The union is indeed reciprocal & the περιχώρησις mutual, but not equally, or in the same way. For the divine nature is not only united, but also uniting; but the human nature is only united. The former is the assuming, the latter the assumed. It is the property of the assuming to give, according to the canon of LEO M., not of the assumed. The advancement is of the assumed, not of the assuming. For it is active on the part of the λόγος, passive on the part of the flesh. The former permeates, the latter is permeated. Hence it happens that the human nature indeed passively receives divine idioms; but it does not actively communicate its own properties to the divinity. To this is added that it is repugnant to the immutable, most perfect, & most simple divine nature to receive any alteration, passion, or finite property into itself.

IV. Whatever doctrine begets a confusion of the divine & human nature, that doctrine is Eutychian: The doctrine of the communication of the divine idioms begets a confusion of the divine & human nature: Therefore. The minor is proved: Of those whose properties are the same, those same are the properties of those, of those the same

...is the nature: But according to the opinion of the Lutherans, the properties of the divine and human nature are the same: Therefore. Resp. I deny the minor of both syllogisms. For the Lutherans do not assert that the divine idioms were communicated to the human nature of Christ by a transient or transfusive communication, so that they become idioms or properties of the human nature, but they teach with the Holy Scripture and the primitive church that, because of the closest union and the intimate communion of the natures, the divine idioms were communicated to the assumed flesh for common possession, usurpation, and denomination, so that the human nature of Christ, although omnipotence does not belong to it formally and as to its primary subject, can nevertheless work through it, and is truly called omnipotent. Therefore, the distinction between the divine and human nature remains unharmed. The former is omnipotent *kath' auto* [in itself], or formally, immediately, *kath' auto*, and per se; the latter is omnipotent *oikonomikos* [economically] or communicatively, mediately (by means of the divine nature), and *kath' allo* [in another], or by the grace of the personal union.

V. If the communication of idioms stands, the arguments that are sought for establishing the divinity of Christ from divine properties perish. For if such an argument is connected: He to whom divine idioms belong is God: But to Christ, etc. Therefore, etc.; the Socinians can object that divine idioms belong to the human nature of Christ; yet this does not make it God. Resp. 1) If the communication of idioms stands, the argument for establishing the divinity of Christ, sought from divine idioms, remains valid, provided it is formed in the following manner: He to whom divine idioms belong per se, formally, and from eternity is the true God: But to Christ, etc. Therefore. 2) Orthodox doctors, through the doctrine of the communication of idioms, do not weaken the demonstration of the divinity of the *Logos*, but rather presuppose it; because divine idioms could not have been communicated to the human nature *apo tou Logou* [from the Logos], unless they had belonged to the *Logos* from eternity.

VI. The divine nature does not have idioms properly so called: Therefore, it does not communicate them to the human nature. The antecedent is evident: because those things which are called idioms of the divine nature are not really distinguished from the divine nature: Therefore, they are not properly called idioms of the divine nature. Resp. For predicamental idioms, it is indeed required that they be really distinguished from the subject of inhesion, but divine idioms are transcendental, which, although they do not differ really from the divine essence, nevertheless differ formally, and are called idioms, or properties, because they are perfections of God which follow the divine essence per se in our mode of conceiving, are predicated of it paronymously, and are reciprocal with it.

Obj. See the remaining arguments which are usually objected to our assertion above, quest. XXXVIII.

Latin:

quoque diuinæ naturæ, & proprietatum eius particeps facta est. Neque eas in se tanquam in subiectum, vt suæ proprietates fiant, recipit: sed in persona Verbi reali communicatione possidet. Prob. c. Ad exæquationem non sufficit rei eiusdem communicatio, sed insuper idem habendi modus requiritur; qui alius est quoad Deum & Filium Dei, alius quoad carnem: ille maiestatem habet per æternam generationem, hæc per gratiam vnionis. Vnde adhuc hodie Christus, vt homo, Patre minor est, 1 Cor. XV, 28. quia, quæ idiomata diuina accepit, ex gratia habet, Phil. II, 9. Prob. d. Per communicationem idiomatum natura humana non aboletur, aut destruitur; sed exornatur & ad functionem officii mediatorii perficitur. Plenitudo namque diuinitatis corpus Christi, velut templum proprium, inhabitat, non vt illud euertat, sed vt illud illustret. Prob. e. & f. Interna & perfecta vnio duarum substantiarum essentialiter quidem distinctarum, sed intime coniunctarum, quarum vna se habet per modum ἐντελεχείας, s. actus perficientis, altera per modum δυνάμεως, siue potentiæ perfectibilis, necessario infert communicationem idiomatum, quæ substantiæ virtuofiori increatæ subiectiue inhærent, ab altera autein ad cominunein possessionem, vsurpationem & denominationem participantur. V. gr. Vita & facultates sensitiuæ inhærent animæ & se exserunt per membra corporis. Ignis inest ferro, vrit tamen & lucet per ferrum candens. Quod speciatim attinet ad idiomata diuina τοῦ λόγου, illa cum non sint qualitates, aut accidentia, nulli subiecto inhæsionis insunt: eorundem tamen subiectum attributionis primum & immediatum, cui formaliter & per se conveniunt, est diuina natura Filii Dei; subiectum attributionis secundum & mediatum, cui competunt participatiue & per vnionis personalis gratiam, est natura humana, Prob. g. Idiomata diuina ἐνεργητικὰ habitant in carne Christi, velut templo proprio, operantur per carnem, vt instrumentum hypostatice vnitum, & prædicantur de carne, vt subiecto attributionis secundo, vel mediato. Obs. Modum communicandi supra latius diduximus, quæst. XXXVIII.

Quæst. LIV. Quo temporis momento carni Christi communicata est maiestas diuina? Quo momento facta est vnio personalis, eodem momento facta est communicatio maiestatis, qua κτῆσιν, possessionem & actum primum a). Ad exercitium, siue vsum plenum & nunquam cessantem maiestatis prouecta est caro Christi eodem temporis articulo, quo exaltata est ad dextram Dei b).

Prob. a. Eo temporis puncto contigit vnitio personalis, quo virtus hypostatica Altissimi virginem Mariam obumbrauit, h. e. arcano modo in vterum Mariæ descendit, massam sanguinis virgineam, a Spiritu S. excitatam, peculiari approximatione impleuit, sibique vniuit, vt tota plenitudo diuinitatis (ad quam pertinent omnia idiomata diuina) in corpore Christi, tanquam sacratissimo templo, habitaret, Col. II, 9. Prob. b. Christus exaltatus accepit nomen super omne nomen, h. e. maiestatem summam & vere diuinam, Phil. II, 9. & glorificatus est gloria, quam habuit apud Patrem, ante orbem conditum, Io. XVII, 5. scilicet qua maiestatis exercitium & plenum vsum.

Quæst. LV. Quem in finem communicata sunt idiomata diuina carni Christi? Communicata sunt ob salutarem functionem officii, sacerdotalis, prophetici, & regii.

Prob. Celsissimo munere, sacerdotali, prophetico, & regio Christus perfungitur secundum vtramque naturam; cui officio salutari cum fructu expediendo minime par fuisset humana natura, nisi omnipotentia, omniscentia, omnipræsentia, & gloria diuina prædita fuisset.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, Socinianorum & Arminianorum, qui maiestatem diuinam carni Christi communicatam esse, penitus infitiantur, moti sequentibus argumentis:

I. Quaecunque natura est finita, infinitae maiestatis non est capax: Atqui natura Christi humana &c: Ergo. Maior probatur ex axiomate decantatissimo: Nullum finitum est capax infiniti. Resp. Neg. maiorem. Ad probationemem dicimus, quod finitum non quidem capax fit infiniti capacitate physica, apprehensiva, activa & adaequata; capax tamen fit finiti infiniti capacitate supernaturali, participativa, passiva & inadequata. Nimirum certo certius est, quod nullum finitum possit active & adaequate capere comprehendere infinitum; nihilo tamen minus & hoc certum est, quod finitum passive capere, siue inadequate recipere, (inprimis per supernaturalem Dei gratiam) queat infinitum. Omnes quippe & singulae creaturae capax sunt praesentissimi sui creatoris: vt qui citra omnem sui diuisionem in omnibus & vbique totus est. Capaces eaedem sunt diuinae, adeoque infinitae conseruationis & cooperationis. Capax est intellectus humanus suo modo cognoscendi Dei, rerumque aeternarum. Capaces sunt fideles Dei triunius, beneuolentissima sui vnione & communicatione in cordibus ipsorum habitantis. Capaces iidem sunt, qua cognitionem aeque ac fruitionem, infinitae satisfactionis Christi, infinitae misericordiae diuinae, infinitae etiam gratiae iustificantis atque faluantis. Caro denique Christi capax est personaliter sibi iunctissimi, infiniti sane λόγος, ipsiusque infinitae hypostaseos: ex quo Col. II, 9. tota deitatis plenitudo in Christo corporaliter, h. e. in corpore Christi, vt appropriato in templo suo, habitare dicitur.

II. Cui communicata sunt idiomata diuina, is est Deus: Humana Christi natura non est Deus: Ergo. Resp. Cui communicata sunt idiomata diuina communicatione essentiali, per generationem aut processionem aeternam, vt illius, cui communicata sunt, sint propria, adeoque ipsi per se conueniant, ille est Deus; concedo. Cui communicata sunt idiomata diuina communicatione personali entelechiali & perichoristica, is est Deus; nego. Sicut enim proprietates animae communicatae sunt corpori humano communicatione entelechiali & perichoristica, neque tamen ideo corpus dicitur anima, sed animatum: ita idiomata diuina communicata sunt humanae Christi naturae, neque tamen haec ideo vocanda est Deus, sed deificata, siue diuinitatis particeps, cum attributa diuina eidem non conueniant κατ' αὐτὸ, per se, sed κατ' ἄλλο, per unionis personalis gratiam.

III. Si propter vnionem personalem & naturarum περιχώρησιν natura diuina communicat naturae humanae sua idiomata, propter eandem etiam natura humana diuinae naturae sua idiomata communicabit: Consequens est falsum: E. & antecedens. Consequentia maioris probatur, quia vnio est reciproca, & περιχώρησις mutua. Falsitas consequentis patet: quia, si humana natura diuinae sua idiomata inpertivisset, deitas esset passa, mortua, sepulta, esset palpabilis, diuisibilis, &c. Resp. Neg. conseq. mai. Est quidem vnio reciproca & περιχώρησις mutua, sed non pariter, vel eodem modo. Nam natura diuina non est tantum vnita, sed & vniens; humana vero natura est tantum vnita. Illa est assumens, haec assumta. Assumentis est, dare, iuxta LEONIS M. canonem, non assumti. Assumti prouectio est, non assumentis. Est enim activa ex parte λόγος, passiva ex parte carnis. Ille permeat, haec permeatur. Inde fit, vt natura humana diuina quidem idiomata passive recipiat; suas autem proprietates diuinitati active non communicet. Huc accedit, quod naturae diuinae immutabili, perfectissimae & simplicissimae repugnet, vllam alterationem, passionem, aut proprietatem finitam in se recipere.

IV. Quodcunque dogma parit confusionem naturae diuinae & humanae, illud est Eutychianum: Dogma de communicatione idiomatum diuinorum parit confusionem naturae diuinae & humanae: Ergo. Minor probatur: Quorum eaedem sunt proprietates, illorum ea eædem sunt proprietates, illorum eadem

dem est natura: Atqui Lutheranorum de sententia eadem sunt proprietates diuinae & humanae naturae: Ergo. Resp. Neg. minorem vtriusque syllogismi. Neque enim afferunt Lutherani, quod idiomata diuina humanae Christi naturae communicata sint communicatione transeunte aut transfusiva, vt fiant idiomata vel proprietates humanae naturae, sed docent cum S. scriptura & primitiva ecclesia, quod propter arctissimam vnionem & intimam naturarum communionem idiomata diuina communicata sint assumtae carni ad communem possessionem, vsurpationem & denominationem, ita vt humana Christi natura, licet ei non formaliter, & vt subiecto suo primo, conueniat omnipotentia, per eam tamen operari possit, ac vere dicatur omnipotens. Permanet ergo illaesum discrimen inter naturam diuinam, & humanam. Illa est omnipotens ϰατ' αὐτὸ, siue formaliter, immediate, ϰατ' αὐτὸ, & per se; haec est omnipotens οἰϰονομιϰῶς siue communicatiue, mediate (mediante natura diuina), & ϰατ' ἄλλο, siue per vnionis personalis gratiam.

V. Stante communicatione idiomatum, facta humanae naturae, pereunt argumenta, quae pro adstruenda diuinitate Christi ex proprietatibus diuinis petuntur. Nam si tale nectitur argumentum: Cui competunt diuina idiomata, is est Deus: Atqui Christo &c. Ergo &c.; excipere possunt Sociniani, quod idiomata diuina competant humanae Christi naturae; vt tamen haec non fit Deus. Resp. 1) Stante communicatione idiomatum, restat validum argumentum pro adstruenda diuinitate Christi, ex idiomatibus diuinis petitum, modo sequenti ratione formetur: Cui idiomata diuina per se, formaliter & ab aeterno conueniunt, is est verus Deus: Atqui Christo &c. Ergo. 2) Doctores orthodoxi per doctrinam de communicatione idiomatum non labefactant demonstrationem diuinitatis τῷ λόγῳ, sed eandem potius supponunt; quia idiomata diuina non potuissent humanae naturae ἀπὸ τοῦ λόγου communicari, nisi eadem ab aeterno τῷ λόγῳ competiissent.

VI. Natura diuina non habet idiomata proprie dicta: E. ea non communicat humanae naturae. Antecedens patet: quia ea, quae dicuntur idiomata diuinae naturae, realiter non distinguuntur a natura diuina: E. non sunt proprie dicta idiomata diuinae naturae. Resp. Ad idiomata praedicamentalia quidem requiritur, vt realiter a subiecto inhaesionis distinguantur, At idiomata diuina sunt transcendentalia, quae licet ab essentia diuina non differant realiter, differunt tamen formaliter, & dicuntur idiomata, vel propria, quia sunt perfectiones Dei, quae essentiam diuinam nostro concipiendi modo per se consequuntur, de eadem paronymice praedicantur, & cum illa reciprocantur.

Obf. Reliqua argumenta, quae assertioni nostrae obiici solent, vide supra quaest. XXXVIII.


### Question LV. To what end were the divine idioms communicated to the flesh of Christ?: Quest. LVI. Has omnipotence been communicated to the flesh of Christ?

Quest. LVI. Has omnipotence been communicated to the flesh of Christ?

There has been communicated by the Son of God to the assumed flesh, through the grace of the personal union, an infinite, uncreated, immense, and thus truly divine power, which we commonly call omnipotence.

Prob. 1) From all power in heaven and on earth given to Christ, Matt. XXVIII, 18. "All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me," Christ was saying, about to ascend into heaven. To whom all power in heaven and on earth is given, to him omnipotence is communicated: But to Christ as man, etc. Therefore.

You say: I. Christ is speaking of his person, not of his human nature. Resp. The person of Christ is *synthetos* [composite], and does not really differ from the two natures. Wherefore, the person being named, it must be examined according to which nature all power is given to Christ. Since, however, it is not given in time to Christ according to the divine nature: inasmuch as it is immutable and most perfect in its own... fui perfection in time receives nothing, it is easy to gather that it was granted to Christ according to his human nature, so that this might be rendered fit for the efficiency of the works of his office, which are here: the institution of the ministry of the word and sacraments, the gathering of the church from all nations, and the protection of the same, until the consummation of the age, v. 19. 20. . II. You say:

II. It is one thing to have ἐξουσία, or right and authority, and another to have δύναμις, power, force, and faculty. Often a prince has the right and power to occupy a province, to whom, however, the force and faculty are lacking. Resp. Human power is sometimes destitute of sufficient strength: but all divine power in heaven and on earth, without divine power, cannot even be conceived.

2) From the power over all flesh given to Christ, John XVII, 2. 3) From the power granted to the son of man to execute judgment, John V, 27. 4) From the proper and supreme power to remit sins, which Christ, as the son of man, exercised even in the state of exinanition, Matt. IX, 6. 5) From the power preponderating over all things, to which all things are subject, Phil. III, 21. which is the conqueror and triumpher over all, Rev. V, 12. 6) From the vivifying virtue, John VI, 51. I am the living bread, which descended from heaven: if anyone shall have eaten of this bread, he shall live forever. But the bread, which I shall give, is my flesh, which I shall give for the life of the world.

There is an antithesis of the Papists, Socinians, and Arminians, who deny that omnipotence has been communicated to the flesh of Christ. The stronger of their arguments are:

I. No dependent being is omnipotent: The flesh of Christ is a dependent being. E. Resp. No dependent being is omnipotent ὠσιωδῶς, formally and of itself; I concede. No dependent being is omnipotent ἐπονομικῶς, participatively and by the grace of union; I deny.

II. Whoever is omnipotent, he is God: The flesh of Christ is not God: E. Resp. 1) In this syllogism there are four terms. For the major is understood of the concrete, or of the person, in this sense: Whatever person is omnipotent, that is God. But in the minor, the abstract subsists, or the human nature, which is designated by the flesh. 2) If the syllogism is formed thus: Whoever is omnipotent, he is God: Christ as man is not God: then the minor is denied; for Christ as man is God personally.

Instance: The argument can be connected thus: Whatever nature is omnipotent, that is God: But the human nature of Christ is omnipotent: Therefore, the human nature of Christ is God. Resp. Whatever nature is omnipotent, in itself and formally, that is God; I concede. The human nature of Christ is omnipotent in itself and formally; I deny. For since the human nature of Christ is omnipotent participatively, and by the grace of the personal union; it is easily gathered that it is not to be called God, but deified, or a participant of deity: for idiomatic predications are not synonymous, but paronymous.

III. Whoever has infinite power, he cannot be overcome by a finite power: Christ as man was overcome by the finite power of the Jews: Therefore, Christ as man is not omnipotent. Resp. Whoever is omnipotent, and fully uses his omnipotence, he cannot be overcome by any finite power; I concede. There was not lacking to Christ as man in the state of exinanition the ktēsis, or possession, of omnipotence, but he suspended the chrēsis, or full use of that omnipotence, so that by his death he might reconcile us to God, Rom. V, 10.

IV. Whatever nature sustains human infirmities and death itself, that is to be called impotent rather than omnipotent: The human nature of Christ sustained human infirmities, and death itself, &c. Therefore. Resp. Whatever nature sustains human infirmities, and death itself by necessity, and not by a most free will, that is not omnipotent. Christ as man assumed human infirmities of his own accord, and by a most free will underwent a most bitter death, so that he might perform his mediatorial office, and become a victim for our sins.
