By which very act he indeed did not exert the second act of omnipotence, but he did not lack infinite power, which is the first act, in the state of exinanition.

V. Whoever is subject to another, his power is not infinite: Christ as man is subject to God the Father, 1 Cor. XV, 28. Therefore. Resp. In whatever respect anyone is subject to another, in that respect his power is not infinite. Christ, with respect to his human nature, considered in itself, is subject to the Father. Therefore, with respect to his human nature, considered in itself, he is not omnipotent; thus we concede the whole argument. Namely, Christ is subject to God the Father according to the act of the human nature, precisely considered, or according to those things which he has from nature, as man; he is not subject to the Father as to the act of the person, or according to those things which he has from the personal union.

Latin:

Quaest. LVI. Estne carni Christi communicata omnipotentia?

Communicata est a Filio Dei assumtae carni, per vnionis personalis gratiam, potentia infinita, increata, immensa, atque adeo vere diuina, quam omnipotentiam communiter appellamus.

Prob. 1) Ex omni potestate in caelo & in terra, Christo data, Matth. XXVIII, 18. Data est mihi omnis potestas in caelo & in terra, dicebat Christus, iamiam in caelum ascensurus. Cui data est omnis potestas in caelo & in terra, illi communicata est omnipotentia: Atqui Christo homini &c. Ergo.

Dicis: I. Loquitur Christus de persona sua, non de natura humana. Resp. Persona Christi σύνθετος, a duabus naturis realiter non differt. Quare, nominata persona, dispiciendum est, secundum quam naturam omnis potestas Christo data fit. Cum autem non data in tempore fit Christo secundum diuinam naturam: quippe quae immutabilis & perfectissima ad fui perfectionem in tempore nihil accipit, collectu proclive est, quod concessa sit Christo secundum humanam naturam, vt hæc idonea redderetur ad efficientiam operum officij, quæ hic sunt: ministerii verbi & sacramentorum institutio, ecclesiæ ex omnibus gentibus collectio, & eiusdem protectio, vsque ad consummationem sæculi, v. 19. 20. . II. Dicis:

II. Aliud est ἐξουσία, siue ius & auctoritas, aliud δύναμις potentia, vis & facultas. Sæpenumero principi est ius & potestas occupandi prouinciam, cui tamen deest potentia & facultas. Resp. Potestas humana interdum destituitur viribus sufficientibus: at omnis potestas diuina in cœlo ac in terra, sine potentia diuina, ne quidem cogitari potest .

2) Ex potestate omnis caro Christo data, Ioann. XVII, 2. 3) Ex concessa filio hominis potestate iudicium faciendi, Ioann. V, 27. 4) Ex potestate propria & summa remittendi peccata, quam Christus, vt filius hominis, etiam in statu exinanitionis exercuit, Matth. IX, 6. 5) Ex potentia omnibus præponderante, cui subiecta sunt omnia, Phil. III, 21. quæ est omnium victrix & triumphatrix, Apoc. V, 12. 6) Ex virtute viuifica, Ioann. VI, 51. Ego sum panis viuens, qui e cœlo descendit: si quis comederit de hoc pane, viuet in sæculum. Panis vero, quem ego dabo, caro mea est, quam ego dabo pro mundi vita.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, Socinianorum & Arminianorum, negantium, carni Christi communicatam esse omnipotentiam. Quorum potiora sunt argumenta:

I. Nullum ens dependens est omnipotens: Caro Christi est ens dependens. E. Resp. Nullum ens dependens est omnipotens ὠσιωδῶς, formaliter & per se; concedo. Nullum ens dependens est omnipotens ἐπονομικῶς, participatiue & per gratiam unionis; nego.

II. Quicunque est omnipotens, ille est Deus: Caro Christi non est Deus: E. Resp. 1) In hoc syllogismo quatuor sunt termini. Nam maior intelligitur de concreto, siue de persona, hoc sensu: Quæcunque persona est omnipotens, illa est Deus. In minori autem subsistit abstractum, siue natura humana, quæ per carnem designatur. 2) Si syllogismus ita formetur: Quicunque est omnipotens, ille est Deus: Christus homo non est Deus: tunc negatur minor; nam Christus homo est Deus personaliter.

Instantia: Argumentum ita necti potest: Quaecunque natura est omnipotens, illa est Deus: Atqui humana Christi natura est omnipotens: E. humana Christi natura est Deus. Resp. Quaecunque natura est omnipotens, per se & formaliter, illa est Deus; concedo. Humana Christi natura est omnipotens per se & formaliter; nego. Cum enim humana Christi natura sit omnipotens participative, & per unionis personalis gratiam; ex facili colligitur, quod illa non sit vocanda Deus, sed deificata, sive deitatis particeps: sunt enim praedicationes idiomaticae non fynonymicae, sed paronymicae.

III. Quicunque infinitam habet potentiam, is a finita potentia non potest superari: Christus homo a finita Iudaeorum potentia superatus est: E. Christus homo non est omnipotens. Resp. Quicunque est omnipotens, & omnipotentia sua plene utitur, is a nulla potentia finita potest superari; concedo. Non deerat Christo homini in statu exinanitionis omnipotentiae κτῆσις, seu possessio, χρῆσιν autem, seu plenum usum illius omnipotentiae suspendebat, ut morte sua nos Deo reconciliaret, Rom. V, 10.

IV. Quaecunque natura infirmitates humanas & ipsam mortem sustinet, illa impotens magis, quam omnipotens dicenda est: Humana Christi natura infirmitates humanas, & mortem ipsam sustinuit, &c. E. Resp. Quaecunque natura infirmitates humanas, & ipsam mortem sustinet ex necessitate, & non ex liberrima voluntate, illa non est omnipotens. Christus homo infirmitates humanas sponte sua assumsit, & liberrima voluntate mortem acerbissimam subiit, ut officio mediatorio perfungeretur, & victima pro peccatis nostris fieret. Quo ipso actum quidem secundum omnipotentiae non exseruit, non autem caruit infinita potentia, qua actum primum, in statu exinanitionis.

V. Quicunque alteri est subiectus, illius potentia non est infinita: Christus homo subiectus est Deo Patri, 1 Cor. XV, 28. Ergo. Resp. Quo respectu quispiam subiectus est alteri, eo respectu potentia eius non est infinita. Christus respectu humanae naturae, secundum se consideratae, Patri est subiectus. Ergo respectu naturae humanae, secundum se consideratae, non est omnipotens; sic concedimus totum argumentum. Nempe Christus subiectus est Deo Patri secundum actum naturae humanae, praecise consideratae, sine secundum ea, quae habet ex natura, ut homo; non est subiectus Patri qua actum personae, sive secundum ea, quae habet ex unione personali.


### Q. LVII. Is omniscience communicated to Christ as man?

To the human nature of Christ, by virtue of the intimate union with the divine nature of the Logos, there was communicated, in the first moment of conception, an infinite and truly divine knowledge of all things, which, however, in the state of exinanition he did not always and everywhere, but freely, when and where he willed, usurp.

Prob. 1). From the testimony of Paul, Col. II, 3. In Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. Obf. 1) All the treasures of wisdom and knowledge designate divine omnisapience and omniscience, which the Apostle calls the depth of the riches and wisdom, and knowledge of God, Rom. XI, 33. 2) These treasures are hidden in Christ, according to his humanity, according to which all the fullness of the divinity dwells in him, as in its own temple, v. 9. They are said, notably, to be hidden, because Christ in the form of a servant did not bring forth or usurp these treasures. Whence arises the argument: If in Christ, as man, all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden; then certainly Christ, as man, is omniscient: The antecedent is true: Therefore, the consequent.

2) From the knowledge of all things ascribed to Christ, John XVI, 30. Now we know that you know all things, and have no need that anyone should question you. Obf.

Obs. 2) To know all things is the same as to be omnisci- a) To know all th

to be omniscient. The Apostles in their assertion regard not only the divine, but also the human nature of Christ, since they say: now we know that you know all things. That Christ, as God, knew all things was not obscure to the Apostles; but now they had learned by experience that the rays of the indwelling omniscience shone forth from the mouth and speech of Christ.

Cf. John 20:17. 3) From the καρδιογνωσία (heart-knowledge), or inspection of hearts, which the Evangelist John attributes to Christ, ch. 2:24-25. Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all, and because he had no need that anyone should testify about man: for he himself knew what was in man. We prove that these words are said of Christ as man by this argument: According to the nature by which Christ, in his earthly and visible conversation, guarded himself from the multitude of weak faith, according to that same nature he also penetrated the recesses of the hearts of those conversing with him by the light of his divine knowledge: But he did so according to his human nature, etc. Therefore. The major premise is evident: because Jesus guarded himself as man from the surrounding multitude of men, because he inspected their hearts, which were prone to perfidy and fraud.

4) From the administration of the future judgment, John 5:27. The Father gave the Son power also to have judgment; because he is the son of man. Here the power of exercising the ecumenical judgment is expressly attributed to Christ as man. From which we gather: According to the nature by which Christ will judge the thoughts, words, and deeds of all men, according to the same he is omniscient: But he does so according to his human nature, etc.

Therefore. Antithesis The antithesis was once that of the Agnoetae, who taught that Christ, according to his human nature, did not know all things in his glory: today it is that of the Papists, Socinians, and Arminians, who deny that infinite and truly divine knowledge was communicated to the soul of Christ. They rely on the following arguments:

I. He who grows in wisdom and knowledge is not omniscient. But Christ as man, etc. Luke 2:53. Resp. Christ grew, as man, in finite, habitual knowledge, which is subjectively inherent in human nature; he did not grow in the omniscience communicated by virtue of the personal union of the soul of Christ, as that admits of no degrees and no increments.

II. Christ as man was ignorant of the day of the final judgment, Mark 13:32, Matt. 24:36. Therefore, the omniscience of the soul of Christ is not communicated. Resp. to both: Some of the ancient Fathers explain the words of Christ concerning ecumenical ignorance, that the son of man did not know the final day not for himself, but for others, i.e., that he did not know the day of the universal judgment so as to reveal it to others. But by the same reasoning, concerning angels and men, to whom Christ compares himself, it could be said that they indeed know the final day for themselves, but not for others, so as not to reveal it. But just as men and angels naturally do not know the supreme day: so Christ, according to the act of his human nature, and thus according to finite and habitual knowledge, truly was ignorant of the day and hour of the universal judgment, which nevertheless he knew according to the act of his person, and thus according to the omniscience communicated by virtue of the personal union. For Christ exactly and infallibly predicted the signs of the final day, Matt. 24:29, Mark 13:24, Luke 21:25. Why would he not have had the final day itself in view? But he did not wish to exercise the knowledge, personally communicated, in the state of exinanition at that time, when he compared himself with angels and other men, intending to restrain the curiosity of the disciples, who were affecting hyper-angelic knowledge (*). He restrained them, says CHRYSOSTOM, sufficing for the apostles what namely, that they ought not to learn or seek what the angels themselves do not know, because they are not superior to the angels and to Christ when considered according to the act of nature, but are far inferior. III.

Christ, according to his human nature, was ignorant of certain things: Therefore, according to his human nature, he is not omniscient: The antecedent is proven: because Christ, as a man, was ignorant of the absence of fruit on the fig tree, which is evident from his approaching it. He would certainly not have approached the tree more closely if he had known that it lacked fruit, Mark

XI, 13. He was also ignorant of the location of Lazarus's tomb, John

XI, 34. Resp.

Christ as man, considered according to the properties of human nature, was truly ignorant of certain things. However, he did not always and everywhere exert the majesty of omniscience, but only when and where it pleased him, in the state of humiliation.

IV. Christ is said to have been tempted, Heb.

II, 18. c. IV, 15. But temptation belongs to one who is ignorant.

Resp. a) Not every temptation belongs to one who is ignorant. How often was the omniscient God tempted by the Israelites in the desert? b) Temptation contributes not a little to experimental knowledge, which, when human nature is precisely viewed as its own condition, formally belongs to it subjectively. But from this, it is not to be denied that omniscience was personally communicated.

Quest. LVIII. Has the majesty of omnipresence been communicated to Christ as man? The Son of God truly and really communicated the majesty of omnipresence to the human nature assumed into his divine hypostasis through personal union, so that from the first moment of conception, together with the divine nature of the Word (τῷ λόγῳ), it was most present to all creatures a), and now indeed in the state of glory, having been raised to the right hand of God the Father, it operates everywhere most presentially, and most powerfully governs all things in heaven and on earth b).

Obs.

I. Distinguish between physical or natural presence, and hyperphysical or supernatural presence.

The former is gross, corporeal, extensive, diffusive, and local: the latter is divine, majestic, spiritual, indivisible, and illocal. Not the former, but the latter was communicated to the flesh of Christ through personal union, namely the same which belongs to the divine nature of the Word (τῷ λόγῳ).

Just as, therefore, the latter is not extended, expanded, or diffused so as to become omnipresent: so neither should or can the assumed flesh be said to be co-extended with the Word (τῷ λόγῳ) so as to become omnipresent. For insofar as human nature is considered in the Word (λόγῳ), in that respect it is certainly as exempt from every place as if there were no place at all: since the hypostasis of the Word (τῷ λόγῳ), within which the humanity subsists, is no less outside all places today than it was formerly, when there was as yet no place in the nature of things. For just as with the hypostasis of the Son of God all times are as a certain atom (ἄτομον), a now, or a moment, Ps.

XC, 4. so before the same hypostasis this universe is like a single speck of dust, or a drop, Is. XL, 15. 17. Therefore, no local extension is required for the divine omnipresence communicated to the flesh of Christ.

Obs.

II. Distinguish between the natural act of the flesh of Christ and the personal act. The flesh of Christ, by the act of nature, while Christ was sojourning on these earths, was in a certain place, in the womb of his mother, on the cross, in the tomb, etc., circumscriptively or occupatively; and now also in the state of glory, according to the property of glorified bodies, it is in some heavenly place (τῷ coelesti), not indeed circumscriptively, but definitively.

But that personal act, by which it is illocally in the Word (λόγῳ), does not stand in the way of this natural act, from which presence all local ideas or concepts must be abstracted.

Latin:

Communicata est humanae Christi naturae, vi unionis intimae cum natura divina τοῦ λόγου, in primo conceptionis momento, infinita vereque divina scientia omnium rerum, quam tamen in statu exinanitionis non semper & ubique, sed libere, quando & ubi voluit, usurpauit.

Prob. 1). E testimonio Paulli, Col. II, 3. In Christo absconditi sunt omnes thesauri sapientiae & scientiae. Obs. 1) Omnes thesauri sapientiae & scientiae designant omnisapientiam & omniscientiam diuinam, quam Apostolus vocat altitudinem diuitiarum & sapientiae, & cognitionis Dei, Rom. XI, 33. 2) Hi thesauri absconditi sunt in Christo, secundum humanitatem, secundum quam omnis plenitudo diuinitatis in ipso, ut proprio templo, habitat, v. 9. Dicuntur, notanter, absconditi, quia Christus in forma seruili hos thesauros non profererat, aut usurpabat. Vnde nascitur argumentum: Si in Christo, ut homine, omnes thesauri sapientiae & scientiae absconditi; vtique Christus, ut homo, est omnisciens: Antecedens est verum: E. consequens.

2) E rerum omnium notitia Christo adscripta, Ioann. XVI, 30. Nunc scimus, quod scias omnia, & non opus habeas, ut quis te interroget.

Obs. 2) Nosse omnia, idem est, quod omniscia) Nosse omnia, idem est, quod

omniscium esse. Respiciunt Apostoli assertione sua non solum divinam, sed & humanam Christi naturam, quoniam dicunt: nunc scimus, quod scias omnia. Christum, vt Deum, omnia nosse, Apostolis non erat obscurum; at nunc experimento didicerant, radios inhabitantis omniscientiae ex ore & sermone Christi effulgere.

Conf. Ioann. XX, 17. 3) E καρδιογνωσία, sive inspectione cordium, quam Evangelista Ioannes Christo tribuit, c. II, 24. 25. Ipse Iesus non credidit se ipsum illis, propterea, quod noscebat omnes, & quia non opus habebat, vt quis testaretur de homine: ipse enim noscebat, quid esset in homine. Verba haec de Christo, vt homine, dici, hoc argumento probamus: Secundum quam naturam Christus, in conversatione sua terrestri & visibili, a sublestae fidei multitudine sibi cavit, secundum eam etiam scientiae suae divinae luce recessus cordium conversantium secum penetravit: Atqui secundum humanam naturam &c. E. Maior est evidens: quia ideo sibi cavit Iesus, qua homo, a circumfusa multitudine hominum, quia corda eorum ad perfidiam & fraudes prona inspiciebat.

4) Ex futuri iudicii administratione, Ioann. V, 27. Pater potestatem dedit filio etiam iudicium habendi; quia filius hominis est. Hic potestas iudicium oecumenicum exercendi diserte Christo, vt homini, attribuitur. Ex quo colligimus: Secundum quam naturam Christus omnium hominum cogitata, dicta & facta diiudicabit, secundum eandem est omnisciens: Atqui secundum humanam naturam &c.

Ergo. Antithesis Antithesis olim fuit Agnoëtarum, qui Christum, secundum humanam naturam, in gloria sua non scire omnia, docuerunt: hodie est Pontificiorum, Socinianorum & Arminianorum, qui scientiam infinitam, vereque divinam, animae Christi communicatam esse, negant. Qui sequentibus innituntur argumentis:

I. Qui crescit sapientia & scientia, ille non est omniscius. At Christus homo &c. Luc. II, 53. Resp. Creuit Christus, qua homo, scientia finita, habituali, & subiective naturae humanae inhaerente, non creuit omniscientia vi unionis personalis animae Christi communicata, vt quae gradus nullos, incrementa nulla admittit.

II. Christus homo ignorauit diem extremi iudicii, Marc. XIII, 32. Matth. XXIV, 36. Ergo omniscientia animae Christi non est communicata. Resp. ad vtrumque: Nonnulli priscorum Patrum verba Christi exponunt de ignorantia oecumenica, quod filius hominis nesciuerit diem extremum non sibi, sed aliis, i. e. quod nefcinerit diem vniuerfalis iudicii, ne aliis reuelet. Sed pari ratione de angelis & hominibus, quibus se Christus confert, dici posset, illos quidem diem extremum scire sibi, sed aliis, nescire, ne reuelent. At vero sicut homines & angeli naturaliter nesciunt diem supremum: ita Christus secundum actum naturae humanae, atque adeo secundum scientiam finitam & habitualem, diem & horam vniuerfalis iudicii vere ignorauit, quam tamen sciuit secundum actum personae, adeoque secundum omniscientiam, vi unionis personalis communicatam. Etenim Christus exacte & infallibiliter praedixit signa extremi diei, Matth. XXIV, 29. Marc. XIII, 24. Luc. XXI, 25. quidni & ipsum extremum diem perspectum habuisset? Noluit autem scientiam, personaliter communicatam, exercere in statu exinanitionis id temporis, quo se cum angelis, aliisque hominibus comparauit, curiositatem discipulorum, hyperangelicam scientiam affectantium, refrenaturus (*). Repressit, inquit CHRYSOSTOMVS, sufficiente apostolos, quod scilicet discere id non debeant aut expetere, quod ipsi angeli nesciunt, quia non superiores angelis et Christo iuxta actum naturae considerato, sed longe inferiores sint. III.

Christus, secundum naturam humanam, quaedam ignorauit: E. secundum humanam naturam non est omnisciens: Antecedens probatur: quia Christus, vt homo, ignorauit absentiam fructuum in ficu, quod patet ex accessu ipsius propiori. Propius vtique non accessisset ad arborem, si eam carere fructibus sciuisset, Marc.

XI, 13. Ignorauit etiam locum sepulchri Lazareani, Ioann.

XI, 34. Resp.

Christus homo, consideratus secundum proprietates humanae naturae, quaedam vere ignorauit. Maiestatem autem omniscientiae, non semper et vbique, sed quando et vbi placuit, in statu exinanitionis exseruit.

IV. Christus dicitur esse tentatus, Hebr.

II, 18. c. IV, 15. Tentatio autem est ignorantis.

Resp. a) Non omnis tentatio est ignorantis. Quoties Deus omnisciens ab Israelitis in deserto tentatus est? b) Tentatio haud parum momenti confert ad notitiam experimentalem, quae humanae naturae praecise spectatae, qua conditionem propriam, formaliter ipsi competentem, subiectiue inest, At exinde neganda non est personaliter communicata omniscientia.

Quaest. LVIII. Estne Christo homini communicata maiestas omnipraesentiae? Filius Dei humanae naturae, in hypostasin suam diuinam assumtae, per vnionem personalem, maiestatem omnipraesentiae vere et realiter communicauit, vt illa a primo conceptionis momento, vna cum diuina natura τῷ λόγῳ, omnibus creaturis praesentissime adfuerit a), iam vero in statu gloriae eadem, ad dextram Dei patris euecta, vbique praesentissime operetur, et omnia in coelo et in terra potentissime gubernet b).

Obs.

I. Distingu. inter praesentiam physicam, seu naturalem, et hyperphysicam, siue supernaturalem.

Illa est crassa, corporea, extensiua, diffusiua et localis: haec est maiestatica diuina, spiritualis, indiuisibilis, et illocalis. Non prior, sed posterior per vnionem personalem communicata est carni Christi, nempe eadem, quae est diuinae τῷ λόγῳ naturae.

Sicut igitur haec non extenditur, expanditur, aut diffunditur, vt fit omnipraesens: ita neque caro assumta dici debet aut potest coextendi τῷ λόγῳ, vt fit omnipraesens. Quatenus enim humana natura consideratur in λόγῳ, eo certe respectu tam exenta est omni loco, quam si locus prorsus nullus sit: siquidem ὑπόστασις τῷ λόγῳ, intra quam subsistit humanitas, non minus hodie est extra loca omnia, quam olim, cum nullus adhuc locus esset in rerum natura. Vt enim apud hypostasin Filii Dei omnia tempora sunt vt quoddam ἄτομον, nunc, siue momentum, Ps.

XC, 4. ita coram eadem hypostasi hoc vniuersum est instar vnius puluisculi, aut guttulae, Es. XL, 15. 17. E. nullo modo ad omnipraesentiam diuinam carni Christi communicatam vlla extensio localis requiritur.

Obs.

II. Dist. inter actum carnis Christi naturalem, et personalem. Caro Christi actu naturae, cum Christus versaretur in his terris, fuit in certo loco, in vtero matris, in cruce, in sepulcro, et c. circumscriptiue, vel occupatiue; et iam quoque in statu gloriae iuxta proprietatem glorificatorum corporum in aliquo τῷ coelesti est, non quidem circumscriptiue, sed definitiue.

Sed huic actui naturali non obstat ille actus personalis, quo illocaliter est in λόγῳ, a qua praesentia omnes locales ideae, aut conceptus abstrahendi sunt.


### Q. LVII. Is omniscience communicated to Christ as man?: Obs. III

Obs. III.

What is the omnipresence of the divine nature of the Word (τοῦ λόγου), the same is the omnipresence of the human nature, though the mode of being is different. For the divine nature is omnipresent by essence; the human nature is omnipresent by the grace of union. The former is omnipresent formally and immediately; the latter is omnipresent participatively and mediately (by means of the hypostasis and the divine nature, of which it has been made a participant through the hypostatic union and the mutual communion of the united natures). In the same sense, the divine nature of the Word (τοῦ λόγου) is said to be omnipresent personally. Cf.

GERHARD. exeg. lib. IV. de Christo

§. 261. But it is strictly to be noted that "personally" (τὸ personaliter) is taken in a double sense: a) It denotes only the subject, namely that the person only, or hypostasis, is present, but not the human nature; which sense is heterodox; or b) it designates the mode and cause, that the human nature itself is present not by the property of its own nature, but through and because of the personal union, because and insofar as it subsists in the person of the Son; which sense is that of our church, and is orthodox.

Obs. IV.

Dist. between the intimate and extimate presence of the divine and human natures.

Intimate presence is that by which the Word (ὁ λόγος) is present to the flesh, and the flesh to the Word, so that neither is the Word outside the flesh, nor the flesh outside the Word. Extimate presence is that by which the Word together with the flesh, and the flesh together with the Word, is most present to creatures, so that nowhere and never is the Word, after the union has been made, where the flesh is not. Extimate presence is a consequence of intimate presence, and is inferred from this by an immovable consequence, as we shall now show.

Obs. V.

Dist. between extimate presence, taken "wholly" (ἑλικῶς), or totally, and taken "partially" (μερικῶς), or partially.

In the phrase of scripture, omnipresence, taken "wholly" (ἑλικῶς), designates a presence that is effectively operating and governing creatures, of which, since there are distinct modes—because one is the presence of power, another of grace, another of glory—it is commonly called modified presence, and also presence of dominion. But omnipresence, taken "partially" (μερικῶς), denotes a bare "non-distancedness" (ἀδιαστασίαν), a substantial proximity, or non-distant existence, to all creatures, and is called simple, absolute presence, and also presence of proximity, or non-distance.

Prob. a. That the flesh of Christ in the state of humiliation was omnipresent is confirmed 1) from the perichoretic and indissoluble union of the two natures in Christ.

Whatever is really and actually, by a total and personal union, united to that which is present to all creatures, the same, by virtue of this union, is also present to all creatures without distance. But the human nature of Christ, constituted in the state of humiliation, is really and actually, by a total and personal union, united to the divine nature, which is present to all creatures. Therefore, the human nature of Christ, constituted in the state of humiliation, by virtue of the personal union also, was present to all creatures without distance.

The major premise is certain: because where one of the united things is, there also is the other; for it is impossible for a real union to exist without the real presence of the united things.

You say:

I. It is not universally true that where one of the united things is, there also is the other. For the human soul is so united to the human head that it is also outside the head in the hands, feet, etc.

Reply: We are speaking of a total and adequate union, the term of which is one subsistent (ὑφισάμενον): the soul and the head are united partially and inadequately.

Venerable antiquity compared the union of the divine and human nature with the communion of soul and body. Just as the rational soul and flesh is one man: so God and man is one Christ, says ATHANASIUS in his creed.

Therefore, just as the soul is not outside the body, nor the body outside the soul, saving the natural union: so neither is the divinity of the Word (τοῦ λόγου) outside the humanity, nor the humanity outside the divinity, saving the personal union. saving the personal union. saving the personal union.

You say: II. Where one of the united things is, there also is the other, as regards intimate presence, but not always as regards extimate presence. Thus the flesh was always present to the Word (λόγῳ): where He exists, yet it does not follow from this that the flesh was present to creatures; to those existing outside the Word (λόγον).

Resp. If extimate presence is removed, the intimate is also removed. For whatever is not present without distance where the Word (λόγος) is present, that is not even present without distance to the Word (λόγῳ) Himself. The reason is manifest: because things that differ somewhere, as distant and non-distant, as present and absent, those two are not present to each other in the same place. If, therefore, the Word (ὁ λόγος) is present to creatures somewhere, where the flesh is distant from them, there the flesh is not present without distance to the present Word (λόγῳ), and thus the Word (λόγος) will be outside the flesh. But if the Word (λόγος) is outside the flesh, there is given a distance (διάστημα) between the divine and human nature of Christ: by which very thing the bond of personal union is dissolved.

2) From the communion of the divine hypostasis. Whatever subsists by a subsistence close to all creatures, that also by virtue of that subsistence is present to all creatures: But the flesh of Christ, etc. Therefore. The major is evident: because, where the hypostasis of the Word (τῦ λόγῳ) is, there also it must be that the flesh is, which is assumed into that hypostasis. For subsistence is not outside the subsisting nature, except as a mode affects and terminates it. It is impossible for a mode to be outside the thing itself of which it is a mode, and for the ultimate act of subsisting to be outside the nature which enjoys that act of subsisting. Indeed, where one subsists, there one exists.

3) From the perichoretic communion of the two natures in Christ. In which nature the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily, or as it dwells in a personally proper temple, to it by this very fact it belongs to be present everywhere in a divine and illocal manner: But in the human nature of Christ, even in the whole state of exinanition, the whole fullness of divinity dwelt bodily, Col. II, 9. Therefore. The major is certain: because, if the divinity is outside the flesh of Christ, it cannot be said that the whole fullness of divinity dwells in the flesh of Christ, or that the whole divinity is incarnate in the Word (τῦ λόγῳ).

4) From the composite (συνθέτῳ) condition of the person. The person, the God-man (θεάνθρωπος), is present everywhere according to both divine and human nature: But Christ in every state, as much of exinanition as of exaltation, is the God-man (θεάνθρωπος). Therefore. The major is clear: Where the divinity of the Word (τῦ λόγῳ) is, where the assumed humanity is not, there Christ is not the God-man (θεάνθρωπος). But Christ, wherever He is, is the God-man (θεάνθρωπος). Therefore, nowhere is the divinity of the Word (λόγῳ) where humanity does not become. Furthermore: If the Word (ὁ λόγος) is somewhere entirely outside the flesh, He will certainly be there without flesh (ἄσαρκος); and again: if He is somewhere entirely in the flesh, He will be there in the flesh (ἔνσαρκος). From which it follows that there are two persons in Christ, one simple, the other composite.

5) From the presence of Christ in heaven and earth. Whoever exists on earth, and at the same time is present in heaven, he is omnipresent: But Christ as man, in his exinanition, existed on earth, and at the same time was present in heaven: Therefore, Christ as man, in his exinanition, existed omnipresent. The minor is proved from John III, 13. No one has ascended into heaven, except He who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who (even now) is in heaven. The discourse is about the Son of Man, who was already visibly conspicuous on earth, and was familiarly using the custom of men, and thus was constituted in the state of exinanition. He, after completing His mediatorial office, was about to ascend into heaven, from which He had descended, by assuming human flesh, and nevertheless He was in heaven, not indeed by natural presence, but by personal presence.

It is proved that to Christ, in the state of exaltation, there belongs according to the human nature a modified omnipresence, or presence of dominion, 1) from the session at the right hand of God. According to which nature Christ sits at the right hand of God, according to the same He rules omnipresently (for the right hand of God fills heaven and earth, Ps. CXXXIX, 7, 8): But according to the human nature, etc. E. The major stands: because to sit at the right hand of God is expounded as to reign.

Cor. XV, 25. Just as, therefore, the right hand of God is everywhere and rules everywhere; for by it is designated in the Holy Scriptures the immense and infinite virtue and power of God, nowhere excluded, nowhere not operative: so to sit at the right hand of God is, by virtue of the exaltation, to rule everywhere with divine power that is truly immense, which cannot even be conceived without omnipresence, since divine dominion is not of one who is absent, but of one who is present.

2) From the kingly office of Christ. According to which nature Christ is king and head of the church, according to the same He is omnipresent: But according to the nature not only divine, but also human, etc. Eph. I, 22. Therefore. The major is clear: because a divine king rules his subjects presently, and a head is not torn away from its members.

3) From the filling of all things, of which Paul speaks in Eph. IV, 10. He who descended is the same also who ascended above all heavens, that He might fill all things. Cf. Eph. I, 22. He (God the Father) gave Him as head over all things to the church: which is His body, the fullness of Him who fills all in all. We conclude: According to which nature Christ ascended above all heavens, that He might fill all things, according to that He is omnipresent, and most presently governs all things in heaven and on earth: But according to the human nature He ascended above all heavens: Therefore. The major is proved: because the presence of God is described as ενεργητικὴ, or operative, through the filling of all things, Jer. XXIII, 13. Wis. I, 7. The minor is evident; because the ascension of Christ is with respect to that nature according to which He could be moved in place, and according to which He suffered and was emptied.

You say: From this passage the governing omnipresence of Christ is not validly concluded. For 1) If Christ was omnipresent even in the state of humiliation, why did He ascend into heaven, that He might fill all things? 2) While it is said that Christ had ascended according to the human nature, it is surely signified that He is absent from us, and not that He is everywhere according to the human nature. 3) The filling of all things does not necessarily denote omnipresence, but either the fulfillment of prophecies, or the outpouring of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, with which He fills the church. Resp. To 1): In the state of humiliation Christ, as man, was omnipresent by a presence of non-distance, or absolute; but the filling of all things denotes a modified omnipresence, or a presence of dominion and incessant operation, to which Christ as man was finally admitted through the exaltation. To 2): The ascension into heaven does not infer an all-encompassing absence from the earth, but only a visible one. The glorified flesh of Christ ascended into heaven visibly, κατ' οἰκονομίαν, according to the character or condition of glorified bodies: although in an invisible manner, by way of the communicated hypostasis, He was most present to every creature, especially the church, by a personal act. Furthermore, it is so far from being the case that the absence of the flesh of Christ is inferred from the ascension of Christ into heaven, that it is rather validly concluded from it. For Christ ascended into heaven for this reason, that He might fill all things with a most omnipresent dominion. To 3): By the phrase of Scripture, the filling of all things, is designated the operative omnipresence of God, by which God works most effectively everywhere, especially in the church; for which reason the church is called the body and the fullness of Him who fills all in all. Eph. I, 22. But when Scripture speaks of the fulfillment of prophecies, it uses this addition: that it might be fulfilled, which was written. The filling of gifts is not treated here, since Christ is said to fill all things, and not only to fill the church. Moreover, when there is talk of gifts, the mention of gifts or grace is added to the verb "to fill," see e.g., Col. I, 9. Phil. I, 11.

Latin:

Obs. III.

Quae est divinae τοῦ λόγου naturae omnipraesentia, eadem est omnipraesentia naturae humanae, modo essendi diverso. Nam divina natura est omnipraesens per essentiam; humana natura est omnipraesens per unionis gratiam. Illa est omnipraesens formaliter & immediate; haec est omnipraesens participative & mediate (mediante hypostasi & natura divina, cuius per unionem hypostaticam & mutuam naturarum unitarum communionem particeps facta est). Eodem sensu divina natura τοῦ λόγου dicitur omnipraesens personaliter. Conf.

GERHARD. exeg. lib. IV. de Christo

§. 261. Sed oppido notandum, quod τὸ personaliter duplici sumatur sensu: a) Notat tantum subiectum, quod nempe persona tantum, seu hypostasis adsit, non vero natura humana; qui sensus est heterodoxus; vel b) designat modum & caussam, quod adsit ipsa humana natura non ex proprietate naturae suae, sed per & propter unionem personalem, quia & quatenus in persona Filii subsistit; qui sensus est ecclesiae nostrae, & orthodoxus.

Obs. IV.

Dist. inter divinae & humanae naturarum praesentiam intimam, & extimam.

Praesentia intima est, qua ὁ λόγος adest carni, & caro λόγῳ, ita vt nec λόγος fit extra carnem, nec caro extra λόγον. Praesentia extima est, qua λόγος una cum carne, & caro una cum λόγῳ, creaturis praesentissime adest, ita, vt nuspiam & nunquam fit λόγος, post factam unionem, vbi non fit caro. Praesentia extima est consequens praesentiae intimae, & ex hac per immotam consequentiam infertur, vti iamiam ostendemus.

Obs. V.

Dist. inter praesentiam extimam, sumtam ἑλικῶς, sive totaliter, & acceptam μερικῶς, sive partialiter.

Phrasi scripturae omnipraesentia, ἑλικῶς sumta, designat praesentiam efficaciter operantem, creaturasque gubernantem, cuius cum distincti sint modi, propterea, quod alia praesentia potentiae, alia gratiae, alia gloriae est, communiter praesentia modificata, item praesentia dominii appellatur. At omnipraesentia, μερικῶς accepta, notat nudam ἀδιαστασίαν, propinquitatem substantialem, vel indistantem existentiam, ad omnes creaturas, & vocatur praesentia simplex, absoluta, item praesentia propinquitatis, vel indistantiae.

Prob. a. Carnem Christi in statu exinanitionis fuisse omnipraesentem, confirmatur 1) ex unione duarum naturarum in Christo perichoristica & indissolubili.

Quidquid realiter & actu, unione totali & personali, illi, quod omnibus creaturis praesens est, vnitur, ipsum vi huius unionis indistanter quoque omnibus creaturis adest. Atqui humana Christi natura, constituta in statu exinanitionis, realiter & actu, unione totali & personali, vnita est naturae divinae, quae omnibus creaturis praesens est. E. humana Christi natura, constituta in statu exinanitionis, vi unionis personalis quoque, indistanter omnibus creaturis adfuit.

Maior constat: quia, vbi est vnum vnitorum, ibi etiam est alterum, Vn. de impossibile est, dari unionem realem, fine vnitorum praesentia reali.

Dicis:

I. Non vniuersaliter verum est, quod, vbi est vnum vnitorum, ibi etiam sit alterum. Nam anima humana sic vnita est capiti humano, vt fit etiam extra caput in manibus, pedibus &c.

Resp. Sermo nobis est de unione totali & adaequata, cuius terminus est vnum ὑφισάμενον: anima & caput vniuntur partialiter & inadæquate.

Veneranda antiquitas vnionem divinae & humanae naturae comparauit cum communione animae & corporis. Sicut anima rationalis & caro vnus est homo: ita Deus & homo vnus est Christus, inquit ATHANASIVS in symbolo suo.

Sicut igitur anima non est extra corpus, nec corpus extra animam, salua vnione naturali: ita nec diuinitas τοῦ λόγου est extra humanitatem, nec humanitas extra diuinitatem, salua vnione personali. salua vnione personali. salua vnione personali.

Dicis: II. Vbi est vnum vnitorum, ibi etiam est alterum, quoad præsentiam intimam, non autem semper quoad præsentiam extimam. Sic caro semper præsens fuit λόγῳ: vbi ille existit, neque tamen ex eo sequitur, quod caro præsens fuerit creaturis; extra λόγον existentibus.

Resp. Sublata præsentia extima tollitur etiam intima. Nam quidquid non indistanter adest ibi, vbi λόγος præsens est, illud ne quidem ipsi λόγῳ indistanter præsens est. Ratio est manifesta: quia, quæ alicubi differunt, vt distans & indistans, vt præsens & absens, illa duo ibidem sibi inuicem non sunt præsentia. Quod si igitur alicubi præsens creaturis est ὁ λόγος, vbi ab iis distat caro, ibi præsenti λόγῳ non indistanter præsens est caro, adeoque λόγος erit extra carnem. Sed si λόγος est extra carnem, datur διάστημα inter naturam diuinam & humanam Christi: quo ipso vinculum vnionis personalis dissoluitur.

2) A communione hypostaseos diuinæ. Quidquid subsistit subsistentia propinqua omnibus creaturis, illud quoque vi illius subsistentiae omnibus creaturis præsens est: Atqui caro Christi &c. Ergo. Maior est euidens: quia, vbi est hypostasis τῦ λόγῳ, ibi etiam oportet esse carnem, quæ est in illam hypostasin assumta. Subsistentia enim non est extra naturam subsistentem, quam vt modus afficit & terminat. Impossibile est, modum esse extra rem ipsam, cuius est modus, actumque subsistendi vltimum extra naturam, quæ isto subsistendi actu gaudet. Sane vbi quis subsistit, ibi exsistit.

3) A perichoristica duarum in Christo naturarum communione. In qua natura tota plenitudo diuinitatis corporaliter habitat, fiue vt in personaliter proprio templo habitat, ei hoc ipso conuenit, diuino & illocali modo vbique adesse: Atqui in humana Christi natura, etiam in toto exinanitionis statu, tota plenitudo diuinitatis corporaliter habitauit, Col. II, 9. Ergo. Maior constat: quia, si diuinitas extra carnem Christi est, dici nequit, totam plenitudinem diuinitatis in carne Christi habitare, aut totam diuinitatem τῦ λόγῳ esse incarnatam.

4) A personæ συνθέτῳ conditione. Persona θεάνθρωπος secundum diuinam & humanam naturam vbique adest: Atqui Christus in omni statu, tam exinanitionis, quam exaltationis, est θεάνθρωπος. Ergo. Maior patet: Sicubi est diuinitas τῦ λόγῳ, vbi non est assumta humanitas, ibidem Christus non est θεάνθρωπος. Sed Christus vbi vbi est, θεάνθρωπος est. E. nullibi est diuinitas λόγῳ, vbi non fit humanitas. Porro: Si ὁ λόγος alicubi est totus extra carnem; erit vtique ibidem ἄσαρκος; & rursus: Sicubi est totus in carne, erit ibidem ἔνσαρκος. Ex quo sequitur, duas in Christo esse personas, vnam simplicem, alteram compositam.

5) A præsentia Christi in cœlo & terra. Quicunque exsistit in terra, & simul præsens est in cœlo, is est omnipræsens: Atqui Christus homo, exinanitus, exstitit in terra, & simul præsens fuit in cœlo: E. Christus homo, exinanitus, exstitit omnipræsens. Minor probatur e Ioann. III, 13. Nemo ascendit in cœlum, nisi qui e cœlo descendit, filius hominis, qui (adhuc) in cælis est. Sermo est de filio hominis, qui iam in terris visibiliter erat conspicuus, atque consuetudine hominum familiariter vtebatur, adeoque in statu exinanitionis constitutus erat. Ille, peracto officio mediatorio, ascensurus erat in cœlum, e quo descenderat, carnem humanam assumendo, & nihilominus in cœlo erat, non quidem præsentia naturali, sed personali.

Prob. b. Christo, in statu exaltationis, secundum humanam naturam competere omnipræsentiam modificatam, siue præsentiam dominii, colligitur 1) e sessione ad dextram Dei. Secundum quam naturam Christus sedet ad dextram Dei, secundum eandem omnipræsenter dominatur (nam dextra Dei implet cœlum & terram Ps. CXXXIX, 7, 8): Atqui secundum humanam naturam &c. E. Maior constat: quia sedere ad dextram Dei per regnare exponitur.

Quemadmodum igitur dextra Dei ubique est & ubique dominatur; quippe qua designatur in sacris litteris virtus & potentia Dei immensa & infinita, nusquam exclusa, nusquam non operosa: ita sedere ad dextram Dei, est, vi exaltationis, divina virtute vere immensa ubique dominari, quod ne cogitari quidem potest sine omnipraesentia, quandoquidem dominium divinum non est absentis, sed praesentis.

2) Ex officio Christi regio. Iuxta quam naturam Christus est rex & caput ecclesiae, secundum eandem est omnipraesens: Atqui iuxta naturam non tantum divinam, sed & humanam &c. Eph. I, 22. Ergo. Maior claret: quia rex divinus suos subditos praesenter regit, & caput a suis membris avulsum non est.

3) Ex impletione omnium, de qua Paullus Eph. IV, 10. Qui descendit, idem est etiam, qui ascendit super omnes caelos, ut omnia impleret. Conf. Eph. I, 22. Dedit illum (Deus Pater) caput super omnia ecclesiae: quae est corpus illius, plenitudo eius, qui omnia in omnibus implet. Colligimus: Secundum quam naturam Christus ascendit super omnes caelos, ut impleret omnia, secundum eam omnipraesens est, omniaque in caelo & in terra praesentissimus gubernat: At secundum humanam naturam ascendit super omnes caelos: Ergo. Maior probatur: quia praesentia Dei ενεργητικὴ, sive operosa per impletionem omnium describitur, Ier. XXIII, 13. Sap. I, 7. Minor patet; quia ascensio Christi est quoad eam naturam, iuxta quam loco moveri poterat, & secundum quam passus & exinanitus est.

Dicis: Ex hoc loco omnipraesentia Christi gubernatrix non valide concluditur. Nam 1) Si Christus in statu exinanitionis etiam omnipraesens fuit, quorsum ascendit in caelum, ut omnia impleret? 2) Dum secundum humanam naturam Christus ascendisset dicitur, vtique a nobis abesse, non autem ubique esse secundum humanam naturam, significatur. 3) Impletio omnium non necessario notat omnipraesentiam, sed vel impletionem vaticiniorum, vel effusionem donorum Spiritus S., quibus ecclesiam implet. Resp. Ad 1): In statu exinanitionis Christus, vt homo, omnipraesens fuit praesentia indistantiae, sive absoluta; at impletio omnium notat omnipraesentiam modificatam, sive praesentiam dominii, & incessantis operationis, ad quam Christus homo admissus demum est per exaltationem. Ad 2): Ascensio in caelum non infert absentiam a terris omnimodam, sed tantum visibilem. Ascendit caro Christi glorificata in caelum visibiliter, κατ' οἰκονομίαν, secundum indolem, aut conditionem corporum glorificatorum: quamuis invisibili ratione, ad modum communicatae hypostaseos, omni creaturae, inprimis ecclesiae, fuerit praesentissimus, qua actum personalem. De cetero tantum abest, vt ex ascensione Christi in caelum inferatur absentia carnis Christi; vt potius ex ea valide colligatur. Nam ideo Christus in caelum ascendit, vt omnia dominio omnipraesentissimo impleret. Ad 3): Phrasi scripturae, impletione omnium, designatur omnipraesentia Dei operatrix, qua Deus ubique, inprimis in ecclesia, efficacissime operatur; qua de caussa ecclesia dicitur corpus & plenitudo eius, qui omnia in omnibus implet. Eph. I, 22. Cum autem scriptura de impletione vaticiniorum loquitur, vtitur hac προθήκην: vt impleretur, quod scriptum est. De impletione donorum hic non agitur, quum Christus dicatur implere omnia, non autem solum, implere ecclesiam. Adhaec, cum de donis sermo est, verbo, implere, adiicitur mentio donorum, vel gratiae, vid. e. gr. Col. I, 9. Phil. I, 11.


### Q. LVII. Is omniscience communicated to Christ as man?: Obs. III (continued)

4) From the universal power and dominion. As it is true and certain that all things have been subjected to Christ, according to the flesh, that all power has been given to Him in heaven and on earth, so also it is just as true and certain that the majesty of omnipresence has been communicated to Him: Yet it is most true and it is most certain, etc. Therefore. The major is proven: because Christ would not have all things subjected to Him, unless all places were also subjected to Him; nor would He exercise full power over all things, subjected to Him in heaven and on earth, unless He were most present to them. The minor is clear from Ps. VIII, 7. 1 Cor. XV, 27. Eph. I, 22. Matth. XXVIII, 18. 5) From Christ's universal operation, which cooperates with sacred preachers everywhere, concerning which Mark XVI, 20. And they went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them, and confirming the word by the signs that followed.

Whoever cooperates with the Apostles, preaching everywhere, is omnipresent: But Christ as man, etc. Therefore. The major is proven: because Christ's cooperation is not that of an absent one, but of a most present one. The minor is clear: because in the cited passage, the discourse is about the Lord, who ascended and was received into heaven.

6) From Christ's promise, which is found in Matth. XVIII, 20. For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them, and chap. XXVIII, 20. Lo! I am with you always, even unto the end of the world. From these we argue: Whoever is in the midst of all the members of the church, wherever they are gathered in the name of Christ, all days until the consummation of the age, is omnipresent: But Christ according to both natures, etc. Therefore. The major is clear: because the members of the church are dispersed throughout the entire globe. He who is present to all of them must be omnipresent.

You say Christ is in the midst of the members of the church, according to His divine nature: because 1) the pronoun "I" indeed denotes a person, but it must be restricted to the divine nature, as in John VIII, 58; 2) because here it is a question of the presence not of the body, but of the spirit and grace; 3) Christ's promise is to be understood of a special, or gracious, presence, not of omnipresence. I respond a) generally.

The Promiser is Christ the θεάνθρωπος, who wherever He is present, there not only His divine, but also His human nature is present, unless the personal union is to be dissolved: just as, where the whole person of Abraham is, there is not only the body, but also the soul of Abraham. The promised presence is a gracious presence in the midst of the faithful, which pertains to Christ's mediatorial and royal office, which Christ exercises according to both natures.

The promise was made to those who are gathered in the name of Christ the θεάνθρωπος, so that we may acknowledge, invoke, and venerate Him not only as God, but also as man, our redeemer.

Therefore, Christ is present in the midst of Christians, not only according to His divine, but also His human nature.

I respond b) Specifically to 1): The passage John VIII, 58 is impertinently adduced. For there, pre-existence before Abraham is predicated of the λόγῳ ἀσάρκῳ: but we assert that Christ ἔνσαρκον is omnipresent according to both natures.

To 2): The presence of grace and spirit does not exclude the body, or the human nature of Christ. This is taught by the συνάφεια of verses 19 and 20.

Whatever two or three shall ask in my name, it shall be done for them by my Father; Reason: because I am in the midst of them. From which we argue: According to which nature Christ makes the prayers of the faithful acceptable and valid to God, according to that He is present to them.

But He makes the prayers of the faithful acceptable and valid to God according to both divine and human nature (because He does this as mediator between God and men according to both natures): Therefore. To 3): From special presence, universal presence is rightly inferred. For the presence of grace presupposes the presence of power, just as well-being presupposes being. Christ could not be present to the faithful with special grace, wherever they are gathered in His name, unless He were omnipresent.

7) From the invocation of Christ. Christ is to be invoked according to both natures (which we are about to demonstrate): Therefore, Christ is omnipresent according to both natures. No one of sound mind invokes an absent person, who neither hears prayers nor is present to help. Hence, Holy Scripture connects religious worship closely with divine presence, Deut. IV, 7. Ps. XCI, 15. Ps. CXLV, 18.

8) From sacramental presence. Whose body and blood is truly and really present in the Holy Eucharist, is present in the whole world: for the Holy Supper can be dispensed in the entire world: But the body and blood of Christ is truly and really present in the Holy Eucharist: Therefore. The antithesis is that of the Papists, Socinians, and Arminians. Their stronger arguments are:

I. Whatever is not immense and infinite, that is not omnipresent. But the flesh of Christ is not immense and infinite: Therefore. The major is evident; because immensity is the root of omnipresence, which the infinite nature enjoys. Resp. Whatever is not immense and infinite, that is not omnipresent by essence; I concede. But the flesh of Christ is said to be omnipresent not by essence, but by the grace of union and communication, in that it subsists in the immense and infinite hypostasis of the Word [τοῦ λόγου].

II. Whose omnipresence is the same, their divine essence is the same (because this does not differ really from that): But according to the mind of the Evangelical doctors, the omnipresence of the divinity of the Word [τοῦ λόγου] and of the assumed humanity is the same. Therefore, according to the mind of the Evangelical doctors, the essence of the divinity and humanity is the same, which to assert is Eutychian. Resp. 1) by instance: Whose infinite hypostasis is the same, their divine essence is the same, because this does not differ really from that. But the infinite hypostasis of the divinity of the Word [τοῦ λόγου] and of the assumed humanity is the same. Therefore, the essence of the divinity of the Word [τοῦ λόγου] and of the assumed humanity is the same. The Papists concede the minor. Whatever, therefore, they will answer to the Socinians, we will reply to them. 2) Whose omnipresence is the same, as an essential property, their divine essence is the same; I concede. But the omnipresence of the divinity of the Word [τοῦ λόγου] and of the assumed flesh is the same, as an essential property of both; I deny. For omnipresence remains an essential property of the divine nature, although through the hypostatic union it has been communicated to the human for common possession, usurpation, and denomination.

III. Every natural body is in one place: The body of Christ is a natural body. Therefore. Resp. a) Generally: The conclusion of this argument is sought from theology, and the major proposition, upon which the syllogism primarily rests, is taken from physics. Therefore, a metabasis eis allo genos [transgression into another genus] is committed. b) Specifically α) to the major, I distinguish: between being locatable, and being in one place. Every body is locatable, i.e., can be in one place; but the infinite power of God can separate actual location from it. β) To the minor, I distinguish: between a natural body by reason of substance, and by reason of qualities or inherent properties. The body of Christ is indeed natural by reason of substance; but it is not natural by reason of singular and hyperphysical affections, but far superior to them, because it is a body most highly and most eminently glorified, assumed into the divine hypostasis, and exalted to the throne of the divine right hand and majesty; whence it is not to be judged according to the rules or laws of physicists.

IV. The opinion of the Lutherans concerning the omnipresence communicated to the flesh of Christ overturns three most serious articles of faith: 1) concerning the truth of the flesh of Christ; 2) concerning the death of Christ; 3) concerning his ascension into heaven. E. The opinion of the Lutherans concerning the omnipresence communicated to the flesh of Christ is not to be tolerated in the church. The antecedent is proved: because a true human nature cannot be extended into infinity, so as to become omnipresent. Then, one who is omnipresent cannot die, because by death the union of body and soul is dissolved. But if Christ is omnipresent, His soul was always there where the body was: Therefore, that union was not dissolved, and consequently Christ did not die. Furthermore, if Christ is omnipresent by virtue of the personal union, surely before the ascension into heaven He was in heaven and on earth. But if He was in heaven before the ascension, how could He ascend into it?

Resp. The opinion of the Lutherans concerning the omnipresence communicated to the flesh of Christ overturns no article of faith. The same is not shaken by 1) the article concerning the truth of the flesh of Christ, since it is not omnipresent by physical and extensive presence, but by hyperphysical, divine, and illocal presence, which belongs to it not formally and of itself, but participatively and by the grace of the personal union. 2) The article concerning the death of Christ is not torn down: For by death the natural union of body and soul was indeed dissolved, yet the hypostatic union of the divine and human natures remained intact; just as when a soldier draws a sword, keeping the sword in one hand and the scabbard in the other, the union of the scabbard and the sword is indeed dissolved, yet nonetheless both this and that remain joined with the soldier. 3) The article concerning the ascension of Christ is not overturned: For before the ascension the flesh of Christ was present in heaven by a presence of non-distance, by which personal act; but κατ' οἰκονομίαν (according to the economy), with His body glorified, He ascended visibly into heaven, so that by the omnipresence of dominion He might fill all things. For Christ, through His divine omnipotence, can present Himself as present in diverse ways.

V. Whoever is true man, and yet omnipresent, must be present in all pots, pans, and filthy places: But Christ as man is not in all, etc. Therefore. Resp. Distinguish between physical and hyperphysical presence: The former entails inclusion in a certain place, the latter does not. The Holy Spirit is omnipresent, yet the pious mind shudders to assert that the Holy Spirit is in all pots, etc.

VI. Christ in the state of humiliation progressed from place to place: Therefore, in the state of humiliation He was not omnipresent. Resp. Distinguish between the natural and the personal act of Christ as man. The former flows from the properties of the human nature, and is common to Christ, as man, with all men, sin excepted: The latter is said of that which befell the human nature of Christ alone from its intimate assumption into the hypostasis of τῷ λόγῳ (the Word). Christ in His humiliation progressed from place to place by His natural act, yet He was omnipresent by His personal act.

VII. If Christ in the state of humiliation was omnipresent, He was conceived in the wombs of all women, crucified on all mountains, buried in all tombs: The consequent is false: Therefore, so is the antecedent. Resp. The same predicates do not belong everywhere to that which is everywhere, since it can exert a particular act in a particular place. Hence you would wrongly conclude: God, who is omnipresent, gave His law on Mount Sinai: Therefore He sanctioned and promulgated it on all mountains. The Holy Spirit, who is omnipresent, appeared in a dove over the baptized Christ: Therefore He showed Himself to be seen in all doves. Furthermore, that Christ was conceived and lay in the womb of one virgin, and was crucified on one mountain, is to be referred to the natural act of Christ as man, but the personal omnipresence of Christ as man is not to be denied.

VIII. Scripture expressly testifies that Christ as man is not everywhere: a) Matt. 26: 11. You will not always have me. b) John 16: 28. I leave the world. c) I am glad that I was not there, John 11: 8. d) The angel says: He is not here, but has risen, Luke 24: 6. Resp. 1) In general. From the negation of a special and modified presence to the negation of a general and absolute presence n. v. c. 2) In particular. Resp. to a): Christ says: you will not always have me, namely in the state of humiliation and servitude, so that you might relieve my need, and anoint me in prefiguration of my death.

To b): Christ leaves the world by withdrawing His visible presence from it, whom, however, having been raised to the right hand of God the Father, in an invisible manner most presentially

most effectively governs. To c): Distinguish between κτῆσιν (possession) and χρῆσιν (use), or between majesty and the exercise of an ἐνεργητικῆς (active), or operative, presence. Christ, according to both natures, had been invisibly present in the house of Mary and Martha, but He had abstained from the exercise of an operative presence by not rendering Lazarus safe and immune from the power of death. To d): Christ was not in the sepulcher locally and visibly; according to the mode of a dead body; for according to that mode the women sought to anoint the body, and did not find it, Luke 24: 3.

Latin:

4) Ex potestate & dominio vniversali. Quam verum certumque est, Christo, secundum carnem, subiecta esse omnia, datam omnem potestatem in caelo & in terra, tam quoque verum & certum est, communicatam eidem esse omnipraesentiae maiestatem: Atqui verissimum & certissimum est &c. Ergo. Maior probatur: quia Christus non haberet sibi subiecta omnia, nisi etiam omnia loca ipsi subiecta essent; neque exerceret plenam potestatem in omnia, in caelo atque terra sibi subiecta, nisi ipsis adesset praesentissimus. Minor patet e Ps. VIII, 7. 1 Cor. XV, 27. Eph. I, 22. Matth. XXVIII, 18.

5) Ex operatione Christi universali, quae praeconibus sacris ubique cooperatur, de qua Marc. XVI, 20. Illi vero exeuntes praedicarunt ubique, Domino cooperante, & verbum confirmante per subsequentia signa. Quicunque Apostolis, ubique praedicantibus cooperatur, is est omnipraesens: Atqui Christus homo &c. Ergo. Maior probatur: quia cooperatio Christi non est absentis, sed praesentissimi. Minor patet: quia loco citato sermo est de Domino, qui ascendit & in caelum receptus est.

6) Ex promissione Christi, quae habetur Matth. XVIII, 20. Vbi sunt duo, aut tres, congregati in nomine meo, ibi sum in medio ipsorum, & cap. XXVIII, 20. Ecce! Ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus, usque ad consummationem saeculi. E quibus argumentamur: Quicunque est in medio omnium ecclesiae membrorum, ubicunque illa in nomine Christi congregata sunt, omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem saeculi, is est omnipraesens: Atqui Christus secundum utramque naturam &c. Ergo. Maior liquet: quoniam membra ecclesiae dispersa sunt per universum terrarum orbem. Qui illis omnibus adest, hunc oportet esse omnipraesentem.

Dicis Christus est in medio membrorum ecclesiae, secundum naturam suam divinam: quia 1) pronomen ego quidem personam notat, sed restringendum est ad naturam divinam, sicut Ioann. VIII, 58; 2) quia hic agitur de praesentia non corporis, sed spiritus & gratiae; 3) promissio Christi intelligenda est de praesentia speciali, sive gratiosa, non de omnipraesentia. Respondeo a) generatim.

Promissor est Christus θεάνθρωπος, qui ubicunque praesto est, ibi non solum adest ipsius divina, sed & humana natura, nisi soluenda sit unio personalis: sicut, vbi tota est persona Abrahami, ibi non solum est corpus, sed & anima Abrahami. Promissa est praesentia gratiosa in medio fidelium, quae pertinet ad officium Christi mediatorium, & regium, quo Christus fungitur secundum utramque naturam.

Promissio facta est illis, qui congregati sunt in nomine Christi θεάνθρωπος, vt illum non tantum vt Deum, sed etiam vt hominem, redemtorem nostrum, agnoscamus, invocemus & veneremur.

Ergo Christus praesens est in medio Christianorum, non tantum secundum divinam, sed & humanam naturam.

Resp. b) Speciatim ad 1): Locus Ioann. VIII, 58. impertinenter adducitur. Ibi enim praeexistentia ante Abrahamum de λόγῳ ἀσάρκῳ praedicatur: nos autem afferimus, Christum ἔνσαρκον secundum utramque naturam esse omnipraesentem.

Ad 2): Praesentia gratiae & spiritus non excludit corpus, vel naturam humanam Christi. Id quod docet συνάφεια vers. 19. & 20.

Quidquid duo, tresue, in meo nomine petierint, fiet illis a meo Patre; Ratio: quia ego sum in medio illorum. Vnde arguimus: Secundum quam naturam Christus fidelium preces Deo acceptas, validasque efficit, secundum illam ipsis praesto est.

At tam secundum divinam, quam humanam naturam fidelium preces Deo acceptas, validasque efficit (quia hoc praestat, vt mediator inter Deum hominesque secundum utramque naturam): Ergo. Ad 3): E praesentia speciali recte infertur universalis. Etenim praesentia gratiae praesupponit praesentiam potentiae, sicut bene esse supponit esse. Non posset Christus fidelibus speciali adesse gratia, ubicunque illi in nomine ipsius congregati sunt, nisi omnipraesens esset.

7) Ex inuocatione Christi. Christus secundum vtramque naturam inuocandus est (quod iamiam demonstraturi sumus): E. Christus secundum vtramque naturam omnipræsens est. Absentem, qui neque preces audiat, neque præsens opitulatur, nemo compos mentis inuocat. Vnde S. scriptura cultum religiosum cum præsentia diuina arcte connectit, Deut. IV, 7. Pf. XCI, 15. Pf. CXLV, 18.

8) Ex præfentia sacramentali. Cuiuscunque corpus & fanguis in S. eucharistia vere & realiter præfens est, in toto terrarum orbe præfens est: potest enim S. cœna in vniuerfo mundo dispensari: Atqui corpus & fanguis Christi in S. eucharistia vere & realiter præfens est: Ergo. Antithefis est Pontificiorum, Socinianorum & Arminianorum. Quorum potiora sunt argumenta:

I. Quidquid non est immenfum & infinitum, illud non est omnipræsens. Atqui caro Christi non est immenfa & infinita: E. Maior est euidens; quia immenfitas est radix omnipræsentiæ, qua gaudet natura infinita. Resp. Quidquid non est immenfum & infinitum, illud non est omnipræsens per effentiam; concedo. At caro Christi dicitur omnipræsens non per effentiam, sed per vnionis & communicationis gratiam, eo, quod fubfistit in hypostasi τῦ λόγυ immenfa & infinita.

II. Quorum eadem est omnipræsentia, eorum eadem est effentia diuina (quia hæc ab illa non differt realiter): Atqui ex mente doctorum euangelicorum eadem est omnipræsentia diuinitatis τῦ λόγυ & assumtæ humanitatis. E. ex mente doctorum euangelicorum eadem est effentia diuinitatis & humanitatis, quod afferere Eutychianum est. Resp. 1) per instantiam: Quorum eadem est hypostafis infinita, eorum eadem est effentia diuina, quia hæc ab illa non differt realiter. Atqui diuinitatis τῦ λόγυ & assumtæ humanitatis eadem est hypostafis infinita. E. diuinitatis τῦ λόγυ & assumtæ humanitatis eadem est effentia. Minorem concedunt Pontificii. Quidquid igitur Socinianis respondebunt, nos illis reponemus. 2) Quorum eadem est omnipræsentia, vt proprietas effentialis, illorum est eadem effentia diuina; concedo. Atqui diuinitatis τῦ λόγυ & assumtæ carnis eadem est omnipræsentia, vt proprietas vtriusque effentialis; nego. Nam omnipræsentia manet diuinæ naturæ proprietas effentialis, quamuis per vnionem hypostaticam humanæ communicata fit ad communem possessionem, vsurpationem & denominationem.

III. Omne corpus naturale est in vno loco: Corpus Christi est corpus naturale. E. Resp. a) Generatim: Conclufio huius argumenti petita est e theologia, & maior propofitio, qua potiffimum fyllogismus nititur, fumta est e phyfica. Committitur ergo μετάβασις εἰς ἄλλο γένος. b) Speciatim a) ad maiorem, dist: inter locabile, & esse vno in loco. Omne corpus locabile, i. e. in vno loco esse potest; actualem autem locationem separare ab ipso potest infinita Dei potentia. β) Ad minorem, dist. inter corpus naturale ratione substantiæ, & ratione qualitatum, siue insitarum proprietatum. Corpus Christi est quidem naturale, ratione substantiæ; non autem est naturale, ratione affectionum singularium, & hyperphyficarum, sed iis longe fuperius, quia est corpus summe eminentiffimeque glorificatum, in diuinam hypostasin assumtum, & in diuinæ dextræ maiestatisque thronum exaltatum; vnde de eodem fecundum regulas aut leges phyficorum non est iudicandum.

IV. Sententia Lutheranorum de omnipræsentia carni Christi communicata tres grauissimi articuli fidei, 1) de veritate carnis Christi; 2) de morte Christi, 3) de ipfius ascensione in cœlum, euertuntur. E. sententia Lutheranorum de omnipræsentia carni Christi communica non est in ecclesia toleranda. Antecedens probatur: quia vera humana natura non potest in infinitum extendi, vt fit omnipræsens. Deinde, qui omnipræsens est, non potest mori, quia per mortem dissolvitur unio corporis & animæ. Sed si Christus omnipræsens est, anima ipsius semper ibi fuit, ubi corpus: E. unio illa non est soluta, & consequenter Christus non est mortuus. Præterea, si Christus omnipræsens est vi unionis personalis, utique ante ascensionem in cœlum fuit in cœlo & in terra. Sed si fuit in cœlo, ante ascensionem, quomodo in illud potuit ascendere?

Resp. Sententia Lutheranorum de communicata carni Christi omnipræsentia nullus articulus fidei evertitur. Non labefactatur eadem 1) articulus de veritate carnis Christi, quippe quæ non est omnipræsens præsentia physica & extensiva, sed hyperphysica, divina & illocali, quæ ipsi non formaliter & per se, sed participative & per unionis personalis gratiam competit. 2) Non convellitur articulus de morte Christi: Nam per mortem soluta quidem est unio naturalis corporis & animæ, salva tamen manente unione hypostatica divinæ & humanæ naturarum; sicut cum miles evaginat gladium, retinens gladium in una, vaginam in altera manu, soluitur quidem uno vaginæ & gladii, nihilo tamen minus & hic, & illa, cum milite coniuncta manet. Non evertitur 3) articulus de ascensione Christi: Nam ante ascensionem caro Christi in cœlo præsens erat præsentia indistantia, qua actum personalem; κατ' οἰκονομίαν autem, corpore glorificato in cœlum visibiliter ascendit, vt omnipræsentia dominii omnia impleret. Christus enim per omnipotentiam suam divinam se diversimode præsentem sistere potest.

V. Quicunque est verus homo, & tamen omnipræsens, illum oportet in omnibus cantharis, patinis & locis sordidis esse præsentem: At Christus homo non est in omnibus &c. E. Resp. Dist. inter præsentiam physicam, & hyperphysicam: Illa infert inclusionem in certo loco, non hæc. Spiritus S. est omnipræsens, horret tamen animus pius asserere, Spiritum S. esse in omnibus cantharis &c.

VI. Christus in statu exinanitionis progressus est de loco in locum: E. & in statu exinanitionis non fuit omnipræsens. Resp. Dist. inter actum Christi hominis naturalem, & personalem. Ille fluit ex proprietatibus humanæ naturæ, & Christo, vt homini, communis est cum omnibus hominibus, excepto peccato: Hic dicitur, qui soli humanæ Christi naturæ obtigit ex intima in hypostasin τῷ λόγῳ assumtione. Progressus est Christus exinanitus de loco in locum, qua actum naturalem, at tamen omnipræsens fuit, qua actum personalem.

VII. Si Christus in statu exinanitionis omnipræsens fuit, in omnium mulierum uteris conceptus, in omnibus montibus crucifixus, in omnibus monumentis sepultus est: Consequens est falsum: E. & antecedens. Resp. Non eadem prædicata competunt ubique illi, quod est ubique, cum in loco peculiari actum peculiarem exserere queat. Hinc perperam colligeres: Deus omnipræsens legem suam tulit in monte Sinai: Ergo eam sancivit & promulgavit in omnibus montibus. Spiritus Sanctus omnipræsens apparuit in columba super Christum baptizatum: Ergo in omnibus columbis se conspiciendum præbuit. Ceterum, quod Christus conceptus iacuit in vnius virginis alvo, crucifixus est in vno monte, id referendum est ad Christi hominis actum naturalem, non vero neganda est Christi hominis omnipræsentia personalis.

VIII. Scriptura diserte testatur, Christum hominem non esse ubique: a) Matth. XXVI, 11. Me non semper habebitis. b) Io. XVI, 28. Relinquo mundum. c) Gaudeo, quod non fuerim ibi, Io. XI, 8. d) Angelus dicit: Non est hic, sed surrexit, Luc. XXIV, 6. Resp. 1) In genere. A negatione præsentiæ specialis & modificatæ, ad negationem præsentiæ generalis & absolutæ n. v. c. 2) In specie. Resp. ad a): Christus dicit: me non semper habebitis, scilicet in statu humili & servili, vt meam indigentiam sublevare, & ad mortem meam præfigurandum me vngere possitis.

Ad b): Christus relinquit mundum, visibilem illi præsentiam subtrahendo, quem tamen, ad dextram Dei Patris evectus, modo invisibili præsentissime euectus, modo inuisibili præsentissime

tissime gubernat. Ad c): Dist. inter κτῆσιν, & χρῆσιν, sive maiestatem & exercitium præsentiæ ἐνεργητικῆς, seu operatricis. Christus, qua utramque naturam, fuerat invisibiliter præsens in ædibus Mariæ & Marthæ, sed præsentiæ operæ exercitio abstinuerat, Lazarum incolumem, & a vi mortis immunem non præstando. Ad d): Christus in sepulcro non erat localiter & visibiliter; secundum modum corporis mortui; nam secundum illum modum mulieres ad corpus ungendum quærebant, & non inveniebant, Luc. XXIV, 3.


### Q. LVII. Is omniscience communicated to Christ as man?: IX. He whom heaven contains is not omnipresent: But Christ, etc

IX. He whom heaven contains is not omnipresent: But Christ, etc.

E. The minor is proved from Acts 3:21, ὃν δεῖ οὐρανὸν μὲν δέξασθαι, whom heaven must receive; and thus, as Peter testifies, heaven contains and comprehends Christ, so that He cannot be everywhere. Resp. The relative pronoun, ὃν (whom), refers to Christ, who is the subject of this sentence, but the remaining words, οὐρανὸν μὲν δέξασθαι (heaven must receive), complete the predicate, so that the majestic occupation, possession, and governance of the heavenly kingdom is designated, and not local containment or inclusion. For Christ has occupied heaven in such a way that, ascending above all heavens, He fills all things in heaven and on earth with a most present dominion, Matt. 28:18; Eph. 1:20. That Christ is not contained by heaven is clear from the fact that after His ascension into heaven He appeared several times in His true body, and was seen by Paul four times: on the road to Damascus, Acts 9:3; in the city of Corinth, Acts 18:9-10; in the Jerusalem barracks, Acts 23:11; in the Roman tribunal, 2 Tim. 4:17; as also by Stephen, Acts 7:55.

X. Christ is not a priest upon earth, Heb. 8:4. Therefore, He is not omnipresent.

Resp. The words of the Apostle are: "For if He were on earth, He would not be a priest." By these words, place is not simply excluded, but the status of an earthly priesthood, so that the sense is: If Christ were on earth, or an earthly and typical priest, He would not be a priest sufficient for our redemption. Christ certainly exercised His priesthood on earth; but He is not an earthly and typical priest, such as those Levitical priests who perform service as figures and shadows of super-celestial things, v. 5.

XI. Christ will come with His body to judgment on the last day, Acts 1:11.

E. before the last day, while we are living on earth, He is not present with His body. Resp. The advent of Christ to judgment will not be a local transit from some higher place to some lower place, but a visible appearance in a certain place, namely, in a cloud, where He will place the throne of His visible judgment. Therefore, the return of Christ to judgment is called ἐπιφάνεια τῆς παρουσίας, the appearing of His presence, 2 Thess. 2:8, so that it may be intimated that Christ, by reason of His human nature, is by no means absent from us, even if His presence does not appear.

If, therefore, the emptied flesh emptied itself of operation, it could not be present to all creatures through divine presence.

Resp. 1) By counter-argument: Operation cannot be separated from divine omnipotence (given the existence of creatures). If, therefore, the emptied flesh emptied itself of operation: Therefore it was not omnipotent in the state of humiliation; which is absurd.

2) Divine presence cannot be separated from operation in Him who is present by nature, or by natural act; but it can indeed be separated in Him who is present only by the grace of union, or by personal act.

Instance: Christ, as an emptied man, abdicated the χρῆσιν (use) of omnipresence and retained its κτῆσιν (possession). Resp. The χρῆσις (use) can be absent from a modified presence, or one of dominion, but not from an absolute presence or one of proximity. For whoever possesses and retains proximity is altogether near. There is no reason for you to understand act by χρῆσιν and power by κτῆσιν. For just as the emptied flesh was united in act, not only in power, τῷ λόγῳ (to the Word): so also in act, not only in power, it was present wherever ὁ λόγος (the Word) was. Most worthy of remembrance are the words of LUTHER, which are recited in the Form. Concord. p. 784. In Christ there are not two separate of persons, but one only is the person.

Wherever it is, there is one only and undivided person. And wherever you may rightly say: here is God; there it must be confessed: Therefore also Christ the man is present. And if you were to point out some place in which God alone, but not man, were present, then immediately the person would be divided. For I could then rightly say: here is that God, who is not man, and who as yet has never been made man.

Latin:

IX. Quem continet cœlum, is non est omnipræsens: Atqui Christus &c.

E. Minor prob. ex Act. III, 21. ὃν δεῖ οὐρανὸν μὲν δέξασθαι, quem oportet cœlum capere; adeoque, teste Petro, cœlum Christum continet & comprehendit, vt non possit esse ubique. Resp. Pronomen relatiuum, ὃν, respicit Christum, qui huius orationis subiectum est, reliqua autem verba, οὐρανὸν μὲν δέξασθαι, absoluunt prædicatum, vt designetur maiestatica regni cœlestis occupatio, possessio & gubernatio, non autem localis continentia, aut inclusio. Nam ita occupauit Christus cœlum, vt super omnes cœlos ascendens omnia impleat in cœlo & in terra, dominio præsentissimo, Matth. XXVIII, 18. Eph. I, 20. Quod Christus cœlo non contineatur, liquet eo, quod post ascensionem in cœlum vero corpore suo aliquoties apparuit, visusque est a Paulo quater, in via Damascena, Act. IX, 3. in vrbe Corintho, Act. XVIII, 9. 10. in castris Hierosolymitanis, Act. XXIII, 11. in dicasterio Romano, 2 Tim. IV, 17. vt & Stephano, Act. VII, 55.

X. Christus non est sacerdos super terra, Hebr. VIII, 4. E. non est omnipræsens.

Resp. Verba Apostoli sunt: si enim esset super terra, neque sacerdos esset. Quibus verbis non simpliciter excluditur locus, sed status terreni sacerdotii, vt sensus sit: Si Christus esset super terra, sive terrenus, typicusque sacerdos, non esset sacerdos, nostræ redemtioni sufficiens. Christus utique in terra functus est sacerdotio; sed non est sacerdos terrenus & typicus, quales sunt illi sacerdotes Leuitici, qui figuræ & vmbræ operam dant supracœlestium, v. 5.

XI. Christus corpore suo venturus est ad iudicium die, extremo, Act. I, 11.

E. ante diem extremum nobis in terra degentibus corpore suo non adest. Resp. Aduentus Christi ad iudicium non erit localis transitus de loco aliquo superiori in locum aliquem inferiorem, sed visibilis apparentia in certo aliquo loco, videlicet in nube, vbi thronum visibilis sui iudicii collocabit. Ideo reditus Christi ad iudicium vocatur ἐπιφάνεια τῆς παρουσίας, apparitio præsentiæ, 2 Thess. II, 8. vt innuatur, & Christum ratione humanæ naturæ minime a nobis abesse, etiamsi non appareat eius præsentia.

Si ergo caro exinanita euacuauit se operatione; omnibus creaturis per præsentiam diuinam adesse non potuit.
