Resp. 1) per instantiam: Ab omnipotentia diuina non potest separari operatio (existentibus creaturis) diuina. Si ergo caro exinanita euacuauit se operatione: Ergo non fuit omnipotens in statu exinanitionis; quod est absurdum.

2) Præsentia diuina non potest separari ab operatione in eo, qui præsens est per naturam, seu actu naturali; bene tamen in eo, qui præsens est tantum per vnionis gratiam, seu actu personali.

Instantia: Christus, qua homo exinanitus, abdicauit se χρῆσει omnipræsentiæ & retinuit eius κτῆσιν. Resp. Χρῆσις abesse potest a præsentia modificata, seu dominii, non autem a præsentia absoluta sive propinquitatis. Quicunque enim possidet & retinet propinquitatem, ille omnino est propinquus. Non est, quod per χρῆσιν actum, per κτῆσιν potentiam intelligas. Sicut enim caro exinanita actu, non solum potentia fuit vnita τῷ λόγῳ: ita etiam actu, non solum potentia, præsens fuit, vbi vbi ὁ λόγος fuit. Memoratu dignissima sunt verba LVTHERI, quæ recensentur in Form. Concord. p. 784. Non sunt in Christo duæ separatæ personae, sed unica tantum est persona.

Ubicunque ea est, ibi est unica tantum & indivisa persona. Et ubicunque recte dixeris: hic est Deus; ibi fateri oportet: Ergo etiam Christus homo adest. Et si locum aliquem monstrares, in quo solus Deus, non autem homo esset, iam statim persona divideretur. Possem enim tum recte dicere: hic est Deus ille, qui non est homo, & qui adhuc nunquam factus est homo.


### Q. LIX. Has the worship of religious adoration been communicated to the human nature of Christ?

To the human nature of Christ, subsisting in the person of the Son of God, there has been communicated through the hypostatic union the worship of religious adoration, so that the flesh of Christ the mediator is to be worshipped and adored with the same adoration as the divine nature of the Word (τοῦ λόγου). Obs.

I. We are not speaking here of civil worship, nor of some worship intermediate between civil and religious, but of religious worship.

Obs. II. We do not assert that the flesh of Christ is to be adored separately, and as a nature apart, but as a nature subsisting (ὑπόστασαν) in the person of the Son of God. For the adequate object of divine adoration, by which Christ is worshipped, is not the human nature alone in Christ, but the whole person, the God-man (θεάνθρωπος), adorable according to both natures, so that the worship of adoration which is exhibited to him may terminate in both natures. The definition of the Council of Ephesus, anathema VIII, must be accurately observed here: If anyone does not worship Emmanuel with one supplication, and pay one glorification, because the Word was made flesh, let him be anathema. We are therefore bound to follow Christ with one glory of adoration, according to his divine and human nature: not to co-adore the man assumed by God the Word. This is likewise explained by the Blessed CYRIL, author of the anathematisms, in his work on the true faith to the queens and in defense of anathematism 8: If anyone says that the flesh of our Lord is unadorable, as that of a man, and not to be adored as the flesh of the Lord and God, the holy and Catholic Church anathematizes him.

Obs. III. The human nature of Christ is not to be adored in itself, on account of some excellence subjectively inherent, nor yet even per accidens, just as those who venerate a king venerate his purple and crown per accidens, but on account of the indwelling of the fullness of the divinity, of which the human nature of Christ is both the proper temple and the organ hypostatically united, and therefore ensouled (ἔμψυχον).

Prob. I. By the words of Christ, John 5:22-23. For neither does the Father judge anyone, but has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honor the Son, even as they honor the Father. Hence we argue: According to the same nature by which God the Father gave to the Son the power of exercising judgment, according to that same nature the Son of God is to be affected with the same worship of honor as the Father, i.e., truly divine: But according to the human nature, etc.

II. By apostolic testimony, Phil. 2:9. God exalted Jesus Christ, and gave him a name which is above every name, that in the name of Jesus every knee should bend of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that the Lord (is) Jesus Christ to the glory of God the Father. From which apostolic testimony we conclude: According to the same nature by which Christ received the name above every name, so that in the name of Jesus the knees of all should bend, according to that nature he is to be religiously adored: But according to the human nature, etc. Therefore.

III. By the mediatorial office. Christ is to be invoked as mediator, Rev. 5:8. But Christ is our mediator, according to both natures. Therefore, according to both natures he is to be invoked.

IV. By the unity of the person. The whole person of Christ is to be adored, John 5:22-23. The whole person of Christ is both his natures: Therefore, both natures of Christ are to be adored. The minor is evident: because the person is not a third something, distinct from the two natures, but the two natures are the person itself. For Christ is not ἐξ ἑτέρων ἕτερόν τι [something else from others], but ἐξ ἀμφοῖν τὰ αὐτά [the same things from both], DAMASC. book 3, ch. 4. You say: The whole Christ is to be adored, but not the whole of Christ. Just as those who venerate a king clothed in purple and crowned do not look to the king’s purple or crown, but to his majesty, although they do not separate the crown and purple from it: so in religious worship one should not look to the humanity, but to the divinity of Christ, although the humanity is not to be segregated from it. Resp. The given analogy does not hold. For a king and his purple are joined by an external, parachoristic, and accidental union; the two natures of Christ are joined by an internal, perichoristic, and personal union. Therefore, just as those who venerate a king honor both the soul and the body of the king: so those who venerate Christ adore his divinity and humanity.

V. By the communication of idioms.* Whatever nature of Christ is a participant in divine omnipotence, omniscience, and omnipresence, that is a participant in divine adorability. But the human nature of Christ is [a participant in these], etc. Therefore.

VI. From the examples of the angels, Ps. XCVII, 7. Heb. I, 6. of the elect in the triumphant church, Rev. V, 12. and of the faithful in the militant church, Matt. II, 11; ch. VIII, 2; ch. V, 22, etc. who adored and invoked Christ as man.

Antithesis of the Papists, Socinians, and Arminians, who attribute to Christ, as man, not the highest and truly divine worship, but one inferior to the divine.

Their arguments are: I. Whoever is not God, he is not to be adored: Christ as man is not God. Therefore. Resp. Whoever is not God, neither essentially nor personally, he is not to be adored: But Christ as man is [God] personally.

II. God will not give His glory to another, Ps. XLII, 8. Therefore, not to the flesh of Christ. Resp. God will not give His glory to another person existing outside of God, whether this be a true or a fictitious person, such as an idol. But the human nature of Christ is neither a person, nor does it exist outside of God, but pertains to the person of the λόγῳ ἐνσάρκῳ [Word incarnate]. For there is not given in Christ ἄλλος καὶ ἄλλος [another and another], a diverse person, but ἄλλο καὶ ἄλλο [one thing and another], a distinct nature.

III. Cursed is he who trusts in man, Jer. XVII, 1. Resp. Cursed is he who trusts in a ψιλανθρώπῳ [mere man]. Christ is a θεάνθρωπος [God-man] deified, or a participant in divinity.

IV. Christ as man is a fellow-servant, Is. LIII, 11. Therefore, he is not to be adored. Resp. l. c. Christ in his state of humiliation is called a servant of the Father because of his voluntary subjection and obedience unto death, but he is nowhere in the Holy Scriptures called our fellow-servant.

V. Whoever adores him who by nature is not God, they are idolaters: Whoever adores Christ as man, adores him who by nature is not God: Therefore. The major is Paul's, Gal. IV, 8. The minor is clear: because Christ as man, although he is said to be God personally, is nevertheless not God by nature. Resp. The Apostle l. c. speaks of the personal and adequate object of adoration, which is not the human nature of Christ; yet this is a part of that adequate object, spoken of analogically, because it makes one σύνθετον [composite] person with the Son of God, to be adored according to both natures.

Instance: It will thus come to pass that Christ is worshipped with a double adoration; because one terminates on the human nature, the other on the divine. Resp. It is not a twofold, but one and indivisible adoration, because in religious worship we do not view the human nature of Christ separately, but conjointly, so that our adoration is terminated upon Christ the θεάνθρωπον [God-man], Immanuel and the giant of twofold substance, in one person.

PART III, SECT. I.

Latin:

Humanae Christi naturae, subsistenti in persona Filii Dei, communicatus est per unionem hypostaticam cultus religiosae adorationis, vt caro Christi mediatoris eadem adoratione cum divina natura τοῦ λόγου fit colenda & adoranda.

Obs. I. Non est nobis hic sermo de cultu civili, neque de cultu quodam medio inter civilem, & religiosum, sed de cultu religioso.

Obs. II. Non asserimus, adorandam esse carnem Christi seorsum, & vt naturam separatam, sed vt naturam ὑπόστασαν, subsistentem in persona Filii Dei. Obiectum enim adaequatum adorationis divinae, qua colitur Christus, non est sola humana natura in Christo, sed tota persona θεάνθρωπος, secundum utramque naturam adorabilis, vt cultus adorationis, qui ei exhibetur, in utraque natura terminetur. Accurate hic observanda est definitio concilii Ephesini, anathemat. VIII. Si quis non una supplicatione veneratur Emanuelem, unamque glorificationem dependit, quod verbum caro factum est, anathema sit. Vna ergo adorationis gloria Christum, secundum divinam & humanam naturam, prosequi tenemur: non coadorare hominem assumtum a Deo Verbo. Quod pariter explicat B. CYRILLVS, anathematisatorum auctor, de recta fid. ad regin. & in defens. anathem. 8. Si quis dicat, inadorabilem Domini nostri carnem, vt hominis, & non adorandam, vt Domini & Dei carnem, hunc anathematizat sancta & Catholica ecclesia.

Obs. III. Non adoranda est humana Christi natura per se, ob aliquam excellentiam subiective inharentem, neque tamen etiam per accidens, sicut venerantes regem per accidens eius purpuram & coronam venerantur, sed propter inhabitationem plenitudinis divinitatis, cuius & templum proprium, & organum hypostatice vnitum, adeoque ἔμψυχον, est humana Christi natura.

Prob. I. Verbis Christi, Io. V, 22. 23. Neque enim Pater iudicat quemquam, sed iudicium omne dedit Filio, vt omnes honorent Filium, quemadmodum honorant Patrem. Hinc argumentamur: Secundum quam naturam Deus Pater Filio dedit potestatem iudicii faciendi, secundum eandem naturam Filius Dei eodem honoris cultu, quo Pater, i. e. vere divino, afficiendus est: Atqui secundum humanam naturam &c. Ergo.

II. Testimonio apostolico, Phil. II, 9. Deus Iesum Christum exaltavit, & dedit ipsi nomen, quod super omne nomen est, vt in nomine Iesu omne genu se flectat supracaelestium, terrestrium, & subterraneorum, & omnis lingua confiteatur, quod Dominus (fit) Iesus Christus in gloriam Dei Patris. E quo testimonio apostolico concludimus; Secundum quam naturam Christus accepit nomen super omne nomen, vt in nomine Iesu flectantur omnium genua, secundum eam naturam religiose est adorandus: Atqui secundum humanam naturam &c. Ergo.

III. Officio mediatorio. Christus invocandus est vt mediator, Apoc. V, 8. At Christus est mediator noster, secundum utramque naturam. E. secundum utramque naturam invocandus est.

IV. Vnitate personae. Tota persona Christi est adoranda, Io. V, 22. 23. Tota persona Christi est utraque ipsius natura: E. utraque natura Christi est adoranda. Minor liquet: quia persona non est tertium quid, a duabus naturis diversum, sed duae naturae sunt ipsa persona. Neque enim Christus est ἐξ ἑτέρων ἕτερόν τι, sed ἐξ ἀμφοῖν τὰ αὐτά, DAMASC. libr. 3. c. 4. Dicis: Totus Christus adorandus est, sed non totum Christi. Sicut venerantes regem purpuratum & coronatum non respiciunt ad regis purpuram aut coronam, sed ad ipsius maiestatem, licet ab hac coronam & purpuram non separent: ita in cultu religioso non est respicienda humanitas, sed divinitas Christi, quamvis ab hac humanitas non sit segreganda. Resp. Datum simile non quadrat. Nam rex & purpura cohaerent unione externa, parachoristica, & accidentali; duae Christi naturae iunctae sunt unione interna, perichoristica, & personali. Sicut igitur venerantes regem, tam animam, quam corpus regis honorant: ita venerantes Christum divinitatem & humanitatem ipsius adorant. *

V. Communicatione idiomatum.* Quaecunque natura Christi est particeps omnipotentiae, omniscientiae & omnipraesentiae divinae, illa est particeps adorabilitatis divinae. Atqui humana Christi natura &c. Ergo.

VI. Ab exemplis angelorum, Ps. XCVII, 7. Hebr. I, 6. electorum in ecclesia triumphante, Apoc. V, 12. & fidelium in ecclesia militante, Matth. II, 11. c. VIII, 2. c. V, 22. &c. qui Christum hominem adorarunt & invocarant. *

Antithesis Pontificiorum, Socinianorum & Arminianorum, tribuentium Christo, ut homini, non cultum summum & vere divinum, sed divino inferiorem. Quorum argumenta sunt:.*

I. Quicunque non est Deus, ille non est adorandus: Christus homo non est Deus. E. Resp. Quicunque non est Deus, neque essentialiter, neque personaliter, ille non est adorandus: At Christus homo est personaliter.

II. Deus gloriam suam alteri non est daturus, Ps. XLII, 8. E. non carni Christi. Resp. Deus non daturus est gloriam suam alteri personae, extra Deum exsistenti, sive haec sit vera, sive ficta persona, ut idolum. At humana Christi natura neque est persona, neque extra Deum exsistit, sed pertinet ad personam λόγῳ ἐνσάρκῳ. Neque enim datur in Christo ἄλλος καὶ ἄλλος, diversa persona, sed ἄλλο καὶ ἄλλο, distincta natura.

III. Maledictus est, qui confidit in homine, Ier. XVII, 1. Resp. Maledictus, qui confidit in ψιλανθρώπῳ, sive mero homine. Christus est θεάνθρωπος deificatus, sive divinitatis particeps.

IV. Christus homo est conservus, Es. LIII, 11. E. non est adorandus. Resp. l. c. Christus exinanitus dicitur servus Patris ob voluntariam subiectionem & obsequium usque ad mortem, sed conservus noster nullibi in sacris litteris dicitur.

V. Quicunque adorant eum, qui natura non est Deus, illi sunt idolatrae: Quicunque adorant Christum hominem, adorant eum, qui natura non est Deus: Ergo. Maior est Pauli, Gal. IV, 8. Minor liquet: quia Christus homo, licet personaliter dicatur Deus, non tamen est natura Deus. Resp. Apostolus l. c. loquitur de obiecto adorationis personali & adæquato, quod non est humana Christi natura; est tamen haec obiecti illius adæquati pars, analogice dicta, eo, quod cum Filio Dei facit unam personam σύνθετον, secundum vtramque naturam adorandam.

Instantia Sic futurum est, vt Christus duplici colatur adoratione; quia vna ad humanam, altera ad diuinam terminatur naturam. Resp. Non est gemina, sed vna eaque indiuisibilis adoratio, eo quod in cultu religioso humanam Christi naturam non seiunctim, sed coniunctim aspicimus, ita vt nostra adoratio terminetur ad Christum θεάνθρωπον, Immanuelem & gigantem geminae substantiae, in vna persona. religioso humanam Christi naturam non feiunctim, sed coniunctim afpicimus, ita vt nostra adoratio terminetur ad Christum θεάνθρωπον, Immanuelem & gigantem geminæ fubftantiæ, in vna persona.

PARS III, SECT. I.


### Q. LX. What things are to be observed concerning idiomatic predications pertaining to the second genus of common idioms?

There must be observed of these predications: a) quality, b) subject, c) predicate, d) foundation, e) difference from other idiomatic propositions.

Obs. a. Predications of this second genus are not synonymous, but paronymous. Hence you would wrongly say: The human nature of Christ is God. The reason is: because a synonymous predication argues and presupposes an essential agreement of the predicate with the subject; and therefore it has no place in a communication which is κατὰ συνδύασιν (by conjunction), but only in a communication κατὰ μέθεξιν (by participation). DAMASCENUS, book III, de O. F. c. 17, calls the flesh of Christ, with CYRIL, GREGORY NAZIANZEN, and other ancients, ἀποθεωθεῖσαν (deified), and adds this exposition: the flesh of Christ is deified, οὐ κατὰ μεταβολὴν Φύσεως, ἢ τροπὴν ἢ ἀλλοίωσιν, ἢ σύγχυσιν (not according to a transmutation of nature, or change, or alteration, or confusion), but according to the οἰκονομίαν (economy), the hypostatic union, and according to the περιχώρησιν (interpenetration) of the natures into one another. BASIL the Great, on the incarnation of the Word, says: The human flesh of the Lord has been made a participant of the deity. Cf. D. CHEMNIT. de d. n. c. 25, fol. m. 152, 165. D. CALOV. de persona Christi p. 168, 170.

Obs. b. The subject of these predications is the person τῷ λόγῳ ἐνσάρκῳ (in the incarnate Word), enunciated sometimes by a concrete term of the person, e.g., All power is given to me (Christ) in heaven and on earth, Matt. XXIX, 18; sometimes by a concrete term of the human nature, e.g., The son of man has power to forgive sins, Mark II, 10; sometimes by an abstract term, e.g., The flesh of Christ is life-giving, John VI, 51. But flesh is the subject of divine attributes (ἀυχημάτων) not primarily, immediately, and formally, since that which is the divine nature belongs to the Word (τῷ λόγῳ); but secondarily, mediately, and participatively. Whence I explain this proposition: The flesh of Christ is omnipotent, thus: The flesh of Christ is omnipotent not formally, but participatively, not immediately, but mediately (by means of the divine nature), not by essence, but by the grace of the personal union.

Obs. c. The predicate of these propositions is not abstract, but concrete, because of the paronymous mode of predicating. The human nature of Christ is not called omnipotence: because this is and remains an essential property of the divinity; but to the human nature it is communicated only as a divine and most sublime gift, by the grace of the union.

Obs. d. The foundation of these predications is the personal union and the intimate communion of the divine and human natures. For since the human flesh of the Lord has been made a participant of the deity, as BASIL says, it is also a participant of all divine idioms, which do not differ really from the deity itself.

Obs. e. Predications of this second genus differ from idiomatic propositions of the first genus of common idioms; because their subject is never abstract, but always concrete, e.g., Holy Scripture does not say that the deity shed its own blood: but the subject of the former can also be abstract . The first genus is reciprocal, and the other

it admits divine and human predicates; but the predicates of the second kind are only divine idioms. When divine idioms in the first kind are predicated of the Son of Man, they are vindicated for the divine nature, to which they formally belong, e.g., the Son of Man is before Abraham, namely, according to the divine nature; but in the second kind, divine idioms are considered as they belong to the human nature communicatively or inhabitatively. The predications of this second kind differ from the idiomatic propositions of the third kind: because the subject of the latter is the person of the Word (τοῦ λόγου) considered according to both natures; but the subject of the former is the person of the Word (τοῦ λόγου) considered according to the human nature: the predicates of the third kind are effects (ἀποτελέσματα), or works of the office; but the predicates of the second kind are divine idioms, by which the endowed human nature becomes an ensouled (ἔμψυχον) instrument for performing the works of the mediatorial office.

Latin:

Observanda est harum prædicationum a) qualitas, b) subiectum, c) prædicatum, d) fundamentum, e) differentia ab aliis propositionibus idiomaticis.

Obs. a. Prædicationes huius generis secundi non sunt synonymicæ, sed paronymicæ. Hinc male diceres: Humana Christi natura est Deus. Ratio est: quia prædicatio synonymica arguit & præsupponit convenientiam essentialem prædicati cum subiecto; ideoque locum non habet in communicatione, quæ est κατὰ συνδύασιν, sed solum in communicatione κατὰ μέθεξιν. DAMASCENUS libr. III. de O. F. c. 17. carnem Christi cum CYRILIO, GREGORIO NAZIANZENO, & aliis veteribus vocat ἀποθεωθεῖσαν, deificatam, & addit hanc expositionem: caro Christi est deificata, οὐ κατὰ μεταβολὴν Φύσεως, ἢ τροπὴν ἢ ἀλλοίωσιν, ἢ σύγχυσιν, non secundum naturæ transmutationem, conversionem, alterationem, aut confusionem, sed secundum οἰκονομίαν, unionem hypostaticam, & secundum περιχώρησιν naturarum in se mutuum. BASILIUS m. de incarnat. verbi inquit: Humana Domini caro particeps facta est deitatis. Conf. D. CHEMNIT. de d. n. c. 25. fol. m. 152. 165. D. CALOV. de persona Christi p. 168. 170.

Obs. b. Subiectum harum prædicationum est persona τῷ λόγῳ ἐνσάρκῳ, enuntiata modo termino concreto personæ, v. gr. Data est mihi (Christo) omnis potestas in cælo & in terra, Matth. XXIX, 18; modo termino concreto naturæ humanæ, v. gr. Potestatem habet filius hominis dimittendi peccata, Marc. II 10; modo termino abstracto, v. gr. Caro Christi est vivifica, Io. VI, 51. Est autem caro subiectum ἀυχημάτων diuinorum non primum, immediatum & formale, quippe quod est natura divina τῷ λόγῳ; sed secundum, mediatum & participativum. Vnde hanc propositionem: Caro Christi est omnipotens, sic expono: Caro Christi est omnipotens non formaliter, sed participative, non immediate, sed mediate (mediante natura divina), non per essentiam, sed per unionis personalis gratiam.

Obs. c. Prædicatum harum propositionum non est abstractum, sed concretum, propter modum prædicandi paronymicum. Natura Christi humana non dicitur omnipotentia: quia hæc est & manet proprietas essentialis divinitatis; naturæ autem humanæ tantum, vt donum divinum & sublimissimum, ex gratia unionis communicatur.

Obs. d. Fundamentum harum prædicationum est personalis unio & intima divinæ & humanæ naturarum communio. Cum enim humana Domini caro particeps facta est deitatis, dicente BASILIO, particeps etiam est omnium idiomatum divinorum, quæ ab ipsa deitate realiter non differunt.

Obs. e. Differunt prædicationes huius secundi generis a propositionibus idiomaticis primi generis comm. idiomat; quia harum subiectum nunquam est abstractum, sed semper concretum, v. gr. non dicit S. scriptura, quod deitas sanguinem proprium effuderit: illarum autem subiectum potest etiam esse abstractum. Primum genus est reciprocum, atque alter-

natim admittit praedicata divina & humana; at secundi generis praedicata sunt tantum idiomata divina. Quando idiomata divina in primo genere praedicantur de filio hominis, vindicantur naturae divinae, cui formaliter conveniunt, v. gr. filius hominis est ante Abrahamum, scil. secundum naturam divinam; at in secundo genere idiomata divina spectantur, prout humanae naturae communicative, aut inhabitative conveniunt. Differunt praedicationes huius secundi generis a propositionibus idiomaticis tertii generis: quia harum subiectum est persona τοῦ λόγου secundum utramque naturam spectata; at illarum subiectum est persona τοῦ λόγου considerata secundum humanam naturam: praedicata tertii generis sunt ἀποτελέσματα, sive opera officii; at praedicata secundi generis sunt idiomata divina, quibus praedita natura humana fit organum ἔμψυχον ad peragendum opera officii mediatorii.


### Q. LXI. What is the third kind of communication of idioms?

The third kind of communication of idioms is when, in the actions of the office, each nature of Christ acts, which is its own, with the communication of the other in acting. Obs.

I. This third kind is called by CYRIL κοινοποιία, also κοινοποίησις, a communion of operations. The reason for this denomination may be sought from the Declar. F. C. p. 773. As far as the reasons of Christ's office are concerned, the person does not act and operate in, or with one, or through one nature only, but rather in, with, according to, and through both natures.

can in itself be considered and ought to be considered. Therefore, it is not permitted to speak thus: the human nature, separated from the subject, is by itself everywhere present, all-powerful, all-knowing (for that would be a real abstract). But this is what we profess: The human nature of Christ, which and insofar as it is in Christ, and it is always and everywhere in Him (which is the logical Abstract). This opinion exists in our Form. Concord. and its declaration, ch. VIII, p. 776, signified by these words: finally, Scripture in this matter does not only make mention of the Son of Man in general, but as it were points its finger at the assumed human nature, when it says: the blood of Christ, the Son of God, cleanses us from all sin. - Thus the flesh of Christ is life-giving, etc. That this Abstract, therefore, is not real, but logical, is declared there quite clearly, both by the addition of this word, assumed, and indeed by the copious exposition, a little before, p. 773 ff., where it is written most plainly that the human nature, so called abstractively, is to be understood as none other than that which is in the person of Christ. To be compared with these is the general preface, prefixed to the symbolical books, §. concerning the phrases, etc. In this way, the disputes stirred up between TILEMANN HESHUSIUS on one side, and JOHANN WIGAND on the other, could be composed without difficulty, concerning which see the Introduction to the Symbolical Books by the magnificent JOHANN GEORG WALCH, p. 836. But it has already been mentioned ibid., p. 834, that even before that time the Würtemberg theologians had disputed against the Crypto-Calvinists concerning the use of the abstract. What was debated on this matter in the Colloquy of Cassel, see in the aforementioned WALCH in the Introduction to the Controversies in the Evangelical Church, Part I, p. 290 seq. We are indeed pleased with the modesty of the theologians, in the blessed HUTTER, in the Concord. conc. ch. XI: p. 680, where these words are read: 1) That they compel no one to use these phrases, provided it remains firm that Christ according to his human nature has been made a participant of the divine majesty, 2) that they do not use those phrases before the unlearned populace, 3) and that they do not wish to use them elsewhere, unless necessity has demanded it. But these last words declare why we ought not entirely abstain from the use of the term, abstract, namely, since one must go to meet the errors of the followers of CALVIN, and especially indeed of the Crypto-Calvinists, seeing that they deny the true and real communication of divine predicates and perfections to the human nature in Christ, and indeed with this intent, that they may draw from it this consequence: The body and blood of Christ are not truly and in very fact present in the most holy feast.

By DAMASCENUS it is called κοινωνία ἀποτελεσμάτων, a communion of effects, a communion of the works of the office; because both natures of Christ in the actions of the office act not separately, but jointly and unitedly to produce one ἀποτέλεσμα (effect), which is referred to both natures. [*] Obs. II. Our definition is taken from the canon of the Council of Chalcedon: Each form (i.e., each nature in the person of Christ) acts with the communication of the other, that which is proper to itself, the Word namely performing what is of the Word; and the flesh executing what is of the flesh. Because this ecumenical council not only expressly names this genus κοινωνίαν, but also adds that each nature in Christ acts μετὰ κοινωνίας, with the communication of the other, that which is ἴδιον, proper, to each nature, therefore this genus is rightly called κοινωνία τῶν ἰδίων, i.e., communication of idioms, the name of idioms being taken in a broader sense.

Quæst. LXII. What must be observed in order to know the third genus of the communication of idioms distinctly? In this third genus of the communication of idioms, one must observe and diligently distinguish the principle of acting, the action itself, the terminus of the action, the communication of both natures, and the foundation of the communication.

Quæst. LXIII. What is the principle of acting? The principle of acting is either the "what" or the "by which." The principle that acts (in Greek ἐνεργῶν) is the whole person, the God-man, God and man a). The principle by which the official action is performed (in Greek ἐνεργητικόν) is both natures of Christ, divine and human b).

Prob. [*] Therefore, this name, ἀποτέλεσμα, is accustomed to be used in a broader signification. For otherwise, when taken more strictly, it does not denote just any action: but the consummation of a work, for the completion of which many combined actions are required. By which reasoning it would only be an ἀποτέλεσμα, strictly so called, when Christ, dying, pronounced: τετέλεσται (it is finished). Most worthy of note is the statement in James 1:15.

This is a great comfort to us. Thus, indeed, by the benefit of Christ, we enjoy such great happiness that, escaping the ἀποτέλεσμα (effect) of sin, we embrace with firm trust the ἀποτέλεσμα of our Liberator, the Best and Greatest.

Between ἐνέργημα (act) and ἀποτέλεσμα (effect), the difference is that an ἐνέργημα is indeed each single action, but an ἀποτέλεσμα is the consummated business, to the completion of which all actions pertain. For Christ to perform the parts of a sponsor, many actions were required, closely connected among themselves, but especially an infinite price, necessary for the reconciliation and eternal salvation of all men, and for it to be recovered and imparted to each. From which it is easily understood what is an ἐνέργημα in the individual offices of Christ, and what is an ἀποτέλεσμα.

In the priestly office (as far as concerns its first part, the sacrifice to be offered to God) each one of those things which Christ performed, both by acting and by suffering, is an ἐνέργημα, but the expiation of sins, consummated through all those actions and likewise the endurance of evils, is an ἀποτέλεσμα, John 17:4. ἐτελέωσα, I have finished the work which you gave me. Add v. 19.

Heb. 10:10. In the prophetic office, each word of Christ, and also each miracle, is an ἐνέργημα, but the entire doctrine and the correction of men, effected through the power of all the words and miracles, is an ἀποτέλεσμα. In the kingly office, individual acts looking toward the governing of the church are ἐνεργήματα, but the entire government itself, and its effects and fruits, namely the preservation and blessedness of the church, is an ἀποτέλεσμα.

But indeed, by common custom, the word ἀποτέλεσμα extends more broadly, so that it contains within its scope any action common to both natures, considered individually. An ἐνέργημα, however, is called in a stricter sense the effect proper to one or the other nature. And indeed, each action of Christ, where neither nature does anything without the communication of the other, is rightly called an ἀποτέλεσμα, for this reason certainly, because each of those actions is in no way deficient, but has that perfection which is required for this act.

Prob. a. Since actions and passions belong to supposits, the actions of the office are attributed to Christ the God-man (theandros), as Holy Scripture shines forth. For thus says Paul, Eph. 5:2: Christ gave himself for us an oblation and a sacrifice to God, for a sweet-smelling savor; and Gal. 3:13: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us.

Prob. b. The principle by which the actions of the priestly, kingly, and prophetic office are carried out is both natures of Christ: and indeed the divine nature is the original principle, to which infinite power of acting formally belongs; but the human nature is the organic principle, with respect to divine operations, e.g., redemption, satisfaction, salvation, etc. For it acts as an instrument personally united with the divine nature, out of divine virtue, communicated to it through the hypostatic union. But the same human nature of Christ is the formal principle with respect to its own actions and passions, e.g., speech, the shedding of blood, etc.

Obf. I. When the human nature of Christ is called the organ or instrument of the actions of the mediatorial office, it is to be understood in a most eminent sense, so that the name of instrument may be cut off from all imperfection. For it is not a separate instrument, as a window is when the sun shines through; not inanimate, like an axe or a smith's hammer; not inactive (anergon), as the rod of Moses: but it is an instrument most perfectly (artismos) and personally united, and a co-worker (synergon). It is a living organ, just as the members of the body are living organs of the soul acting through them. It is not a brute instrument, like Balaam's speaking ass; but an intelligent one: not common, like any minister of the church; but most singular and without equal example.

Obf. II. There is a huge difference between Christ the man and the Prophets and Apostles, who also performed miracles and are called vessels and organs of God. For the Word (Logos) worked in the flesh as in its own temple, with the flesh as personally united, through an instrument most effectively and singularly cooperative, according to the flesh, as a subject partaking of divine majesty. From which it happens that the flesh of Christ in the nominative case is called life-giving, his hand omnipotent, his eye all-seeing, his blood cleansing from sin. Conversely, Christ worked in Paul not as personally united, but as accidentally united; not through Paul as a most singular instrument, but a common one; much less according to Paul as a subject partaking of divine omnipotence. Wherefore the flesh of Paul is not to be called life-giving, nor his hand omnipotent, nor his eye all-seeing.

Latin:

Tertium genus communicationis idiomatum est, quando in actionibus officii utraque natura Christi agit, quod suum est, cum alterius communicatione in agendo.

Obs. I. Tertium hoc genus C. I. dicitur CYRILLO κοινοποιία, it. κοινοποίησις, communio operationum. Rationem huius denominationis petere licet e Declar. F. C. p. 773. Quod ad rationes officii Christi attinet, persona non agit & operatur in, seu, cum una, vel per unam naturam tantum, sed potius in, cum, secundum, atque per utramque naturam. DAMA-

sum in se ipsa considerari queat ac debeat. Itaque non licet ita loqui: humana natura, a subiecto separata, per se est ubique praesens, omnia valens, omnia sciens (id enim esset abstractum reale). Sed hoc est, quod profitemur: Humana Christi natura, quae & quatenus in Christo inest, inest autem semper & ubique (id quod est Abstractum logicum). Haec sententia exstat in nostra Form. Concord. eiusque declar. cap. VIII. p. 776. his verbis significata: postremo, scriptura in hoc negotio non tantum in genere mentionem facit filii hominis, sed quasi digitum in adsumtam humanam naturam intendit, cum inquit: sanguis Christi, Filii Dei, emundat nos ab omni peccato. - Ita caro Christi est vivifica. κ. τ. λ. Hoc igitur Abstractum non reale esse, sed logicum, satis perspicue declaratum ibi est, tum adiecto hocce vocabulo, adsumtam, tum vero copiosa expositione, paullo ante, pag. 773. seqq. vbi planissime scriptum exstat, humanam naturam, abstractine sic vocatam, non aliam intelligendam esse, nisi eam, quae est in persona Christi. Conferenda cum his est praefatio generalis, libris symbol. praemissa, §. quod vero ad phrases &c. Quo pacto haud difficulter componendae erant lites, inter TILEM. HESHVSIVM ab vna parte, & IO. WIGANDVM ab altera, agitatae, de quibus vid. Magnis. IO. GEORG. WALCHII introd. in libr. Symb. p. 836. Sed iam ante illud tempus Theologos Würtembergicos aduersus Crypto-Caluinianos de vsu abstracti disputasse commemoratum est ibid. p. 834. Quid super hac re disceptatum fuerit in Colloquio Caffellano, vid. apud laudatum WALCHIVM in der Einleit. in die Streitigk. in der Ev. Kirche, P. I. p. 290. seq. Placet quidem nobis modestia Theologorum, apud B. HVTTERVM, in Concord. conc. cap. XI: p. 680. vbi haec leguntur verba: 1) Se neminem cogere, vt his phrasibus utatur, modo firmum maneat, Christum secundum humanam naturam factum esse divinae maiestatis participem, 2) coram indocta plebe se phrasibus illis non vti, 3) neque alibi vti velle, nisi vbi necessitas postulauerit. Sed haec postrema verba declarant, quare non prorsus nos abstinere debeamus ab vsu nominis, abstractum, nimirum quum obviam eundum sit erroribus CALVINI sectatorum, praesertim vero Crypto-Caluinianorum, quippe qui diuinarum proprietatum perfectionumque communicationem veram ac realem humanae in Christo naturae denegant, & ea quidem mente, vt hanc ex eo consequutionem efficiant: Corpus sanguinemque Christi in sanctissimo epulo non vere & re ipia adesse.

DAMASCENO vocatur κοινωνία ἀποτελεσμάτων, communio operum officii; quia utraque natura Christi in actionibus officii non diuisim, sed coniunctim & unite agit ad producendum vnum ἀποτέλεσμα, quod ad utramque naturam refertur. [*] Obs. II. Difinitio nostra sumta est ex canone concilii Chalcedonensis: Agit vtraque forma (i. e. vtraque natura in persona Christi) cum communicatione alterius, quod sibi proprium est, Verbo scilicet operante, quod Verbi est; & carne exsequente, quod carnis est. Quia hoc concilium oecumenicum hoc genus non tantum expresse nominat κοινωνίαν, sed etiam addit, vtramque naturam in Christo agere μετὰ κοινωνίας, cum communicatione alterius, quod cuiusque naturæ ἴδιον, proprium, est, ideo hoc genus recte κοινωνία τῶν ἰδίων, h. e. communi-catio idiomatum appellatur, sumto nomine idiomatum sensu latiori.

Quæst. LXII. Quænam obseruanda sunt ad tertium genus communicationis idiomatum distincte cognoscendum? In hoc tertio genere communicationis idiomatum obseruanda & diligenter distinguenda sunt principium agendi, actio ipsa, actionis terminus, vtriusque naturæ communicatio, communicationis fundamentum.

Quæst. LXIII. Quodnam est principium agendi? Principium agendi est vel quod, vel quo. Principium, quod operatur (græce ἐνεργῶν), est tota persona θεάνθρωπος, Deus & homo a). Principium, quo actio officialis peragitur (græce ἐνεργητικόν), est vtraque Christi natura, diuina & humana b).

Prob. [*] Itaque nomen hoc, ἀποτέλεσμα, latiori significatione vsurpari solet. Aliter enim, quippe strictius acceptum, non quamuis actionem denotat: sed consummationem operis, ad quod perficiendum plures actiones coniunctæ requiruntur. Qua ratione id demum esset ἀποτέλεσμα, stricte ita dictum, cum Christus moriens pronuntiauit: τετέλεσται. Notatione dignissimum est effatum Iacobi I, 15.

Id quod magno nobis est solatio. Ita nimirum, Christi beneficio, tanta gaudemus felicitate, vt, effugientes ἀποτέλεσμα peccati, firma nos fiducia ἀποτέλεσμα Liberatoris nostri O. M. amplectamur.

Inter ἐνέργημα, & ἀποτέλεσμα, hoc interest, quod ἐνέργημα quidem est vna quæque actio, ἀποτέλεσμα autem est consummatum negotium, ad cuius absolutionem pertinent vniuersæ actiones. Vt Christus sponsoris partibus fungeretur, multæ requirebantur actiones, arcte inter se connexæ, præfertim vero infinitum pretium, ad hominum omnium reconciliationem æternamque salutem, & recuperandam, & cuique impertiendam, necessarium. Ex quo facile intelligitur, quid in singulis Christi officiis fit ἐνέργημα, quidue ἀποτέλεσμα.

In officio sacerdotali (quantum ad primam eius partem, sacrificium Deo offerendum) vnum quodque eorum, quæ Christus tum agendo, tum sustinendo, præstitit, est ἐνέργημα, sed expiatio peccatorum, per omnes illas actiones, malorum item perpessiones, consummata, est ἀποτέλεσμα, Io. XVII, 4. ἐτελέωσα, perfeci opus, mihi mandatum. Add. v. 19.

Hebr. X, 10. In officio prophetico, vna quæque vox Christi, vnum etiam quodque miraculum, est ἐνέργημα, sed doctrina vniuersa, hominumque correctio, per vim verborum ac miraculorum omnium effecta, est ἀποτέλεσμα. In officio regio, singuli actus, ad gubernandam ecclesiam spectantes, sunt ἐνεργήματα, ipsa vero gubernatio vniuersa, eiusque effectus ac fructus, nimirum ecclesiæ conferuatio ac beatitas, est ἀποτέλεσμα.

At enim, vfitata consuetudine vox, ἀποτέλεσμα, latius patet, vt quamuis actionem naturæ vtriusque communem, singulatim consideratam, suo ambitu contineat. ἐνέργημα autem strictiori significatione adpellatur effectus alterutrius naturæ proprius. Et sane vna quæque Christi actio, vbi neutra natura quidquam sine communicatione alterius, iure suo dicitur ἀποτέλεσμα, hanc certe ob caussam, quia actionum illarum vna quæque nullo modo est deficiens, sed eam habet perfectionem, quæ ad hunc actum requiritur.

Prob. a. Cum actiones & passiones sint suppositorum, Christo θεανδρῴπῳ actiones officii, praelucente sacra scriptura, tribuuntur. Sic enim inquit Paullus, Eph. V. 2. Christus dedit seipsum pro nobis oblationem & sacrificium Deo, in odorem fragrantiae, & Gal. III, 13. Christus nos redemit a maledictione legis, factus pro nobis maledictio.

Prob. b. Principium, quo expediuntur actiones officii sacerdotalis, regii & prophetici, est utraque Christi natura: & quidem natura divina est principium originale, cui infinita vis agendi formaliter competit; natura autem humana est principium organicum, respectu operationum divinarum, v. gr. redemptionis, satisfactionis, salvationis &c. Agit enim, tanquam instrumentum cum natura divina personaliter unitum, ex virtute divina, per unionem hypostaticam sibi communicata. At eadem Christi natura humana est principium formale, respectu propriarum actionum & passionum, v. gr. locutionis, effusionis sanguinis, &c.

Obs. I. Quando humana Christi natura actionum officii mediatorii organum, vel instrumentum dicitur, eminentissima ratione id intelligendum est, vt nomen instrumenti ab omni imperfectione resecetur. Non enim est instrumentum separatum, vti fenestra est, quando sol pellucet; non exanime, sicut securis, aut malleus fabri; non ἄνεργον, vt baculus Mosis: sed est instrumentum ἀρτθισμε & personaliter unitum, atque σύυεργον. Est organum vivum, sicut membra corporis sunt viva organa animae, per ea agentis. Non est instrumentum brutum, vt asina Bileami loquens; sed intelligens: non commune, vt quilibet ecclesiae minister; sed singularissimum & fine pari exemplo.

Obs. II. Ingens est discrimen inter Christum hominem, & Prophetas atque Apostolos, qui etiam ediderunt miracula, & vasa atque organa Dei dicuntur. Nam ὁ λόγος operatus est in carne, vt proprio templo, cum carne, vt personaliter vnita, per instrumentum efficacissime & singularissime cooperativum, secundum carnem, tanquam subiectum divinae particeps maiestatis. Ex quo fit, vt caro Christi in casu recto dicatur vivifica, manus ipsius omnipotens, oculus omnituens, sanguis emundans a peccato. Contra operatus est Christus in Paullo non personaliter, sed accidentaliter vnito; non per Paullum, vt instrumentum singularissimum, sed commune; nedum secundum Paullum, tanquam subiectum omnipotentiae divinae particeps. Quare non dicenda est caro Paulli vivifica, neque manus ipsius omnipotens, neque oculus eiusdem omnituens.


### Question LXIV. Are the energies (energeiai), powers of acting, and operations of the two natures of Christ therefore distinct?

In the mediatorial office, the energies, powers of acting, and operations in Christ are distinct, but not separate. Therefore, each nature in performing the triple office acts according to its own (to idion), which is proper to each.

Prob. 1) Generally: Just as the two natures of Christ are personally united and remain really distinct; so also they act distinctly, but not dividedly. Of those whose nature is distinct, their operation is also distinct, says DAMASCENUS, book III, de O. F. c. 9.

Prob. 2) In the priestly office, the flesh suffers, obeys, intercedes: the divine nature wills the obedience, does not repel the force brought against it, sustains the human nature so that it does not succumb, and adds infinite power, weight, price, and value. In the kingly office, the divine nature rules all things most presently: the human nature understands the same with a conscious mind, wills it, sees it with a human eye, and on the last day will call forth the dead. In the prophetic office, the human nature embraces the divine counsels, wills, executes, speaks, preaches, and offers its mouth, hand, and body for miracles: the divine nature brings forth counsels from the bosom of the Father, performs infinite miracles by its own power, and casts out demons. Conf. DANNH. in hodof. phænom. IX. p. 674. Question

Latin:

In officio mediatorio divinae & humanae naturae in Christo distinctae, sed non separatae sunt ἐνέργειαι, agendi vires, & operationes. Proinde vtraque natura in obeundo triplici officio agit τὸ ἴδιον, quod cuiusque proprium est.

Prob. 1) Generatim: Quemadmodum duae Christi naturae personaliter vnitae sunt, & manent realiter distinctae; ita etiam agunt distincte, at non diuise. Quorum distincta est natura, eorum & distincta est operatio, inquit DAMASCENVS libr. III. de O. F. c. 9.

Prob. 2) In officio sacerdotali caro patitur, obedit, interpellat: diuina natura vult obedientiam, non depellit vim illatam, sustinet naturam humanam, ne fuccumbat, addit vim infinitam, momentum, pretium, valorem. In officio regio diuina natura omnia regit praesentissime: humana conscia mente intelligit, vult eadem, oculo humano videt, in nouissimo die euocabit mortuos. In officio prophetico humana natura diuina consilia amplectitur, vult, exsequitur, loquitur, concionatur, miraculis os, manum, corpus praebet: diuina natura profert consilia e sinu Patris, propria virtute infinita miracula facit & dæmonia eiicit. Conf. DANNH. in hodof. phænom. IX. p. 674.


### Question LXV. What is the end of divine and human energy?

The limit of energeia is the work flowing from it, and it is either an energema [specific effect] or an apotelesma [common result]. Energema is an effect proper to one nature a). Apotelesma is a common effect resulting from the intimate and communicative confluence and effective influx of both natures, divine and human b).

Proof a. The effect of human nature is the shedding of blood: The effect of divine nature is the value and price of the blood.

Proof b. The blood of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, cleansing us from our sins, 1 John 1:7, is an apotelesma, a work common to both natures, divine and human. It is called by DAMASCENUS a theandrikon [divine-human] work, or divine-human. Indeed, even the official actions themselves are commonly called theandrikai [divine-human], because Christ acts in his mediatorial office according to both natures, as Theos [God] and as aner [man].

Latin:

Terminus ἐνεργείας est opus ex illa fluens, estque vel ἐνέργημα, vel ἀποτέλεσμα. 'Ενέργημα est effectus unius naturæ proprius a). 'Αποτέλεσμα est effectus communis ex intimo & communicatiuo vtriusque naturæ, diuinæ & humanæ, confluxu, & efficaci influxu, resultans b).

Prob. a. Effectus naturæ humanæ est sanguis effusus: Effectus naturæ diuinæ est valor & pretium sanguinis.

Prob. b. Sanguis Iesu Christi filii Dei emundans nos a peccatis nostris, 1 Ioann. I, 7. est ἀποτέλεσμα, opus vtriusque naturæ, diuinæ & humanæ commune. Vocatur a DAMASCENO opus Θεανδρικὸν deiuirile, vel diuino-humanum. Quin & ipsæ actiones officiales communiter Θεανδρικαὶ, deiuiriles appellantur, propterea, quod Christus secundum vtramque naturam qua Θεὸς, & qua ἀνὴρ in officio mediatorio agit.


### Question LXVI

In what way do the divine and human natures converge for theandric [divine-human] action? The mode of communication and mutual confluence consists in this: that the divine nature, tō logō [in the Word], not only performs divine works, but also truly and really appropriates to itself the actions of the assumed flesh; while human nature acts in the office of mediator not only according to its natural powers, but also according to that divine power which it has communicated to itself from the personal union.

Proof 1) Generally, from the rule of the Council of Chalcedon: Each nature in Christ acts what is proper to each, with the communication of the other. This is not accomplished koinōs [commonly] by divine concurrence with the action of Christ as man; because God concurs with the actions of all men who act according to their natural powers, yet no theandric work results from this; but a real koinōnia [communion] of natures in acting is also required, from which the divine-human action proceeds, just as from a fiery sword there is a cutting burning and a burning cutting.

Proof 2) Specifically. When S. Paulus in Acts 20:28 asserts that God acquired the church by his own blood, he clearly implies that the divinity, tō logō, appropriated to itself the shedding of blood, which flowed from the flesh of Christ; and when Christ teaches that God the Father gave him authority to execute judgment because he is the Son of Man, John 5:27, he clearly indicates that the assumed human nature concurs in the execution of universal judgment, not only according to natural powers, but also according to the divine power given by the Father to the flesh of Christ. DAMASCENUS illustrates this excellently in Book III. de O. F. c. 17. "Not according to its own operation, but because of the Word united to it, the flesh of the Lord operated divinely, the Word manifesting its own operation through it. For even heated iron burns, not possessing the burning operation by natural reason, but obtaining it from the union of fire and iron. Therefore, the very flesh of the Lord was mortal in itself, and life-giving because of the hypostatic union with the Word."

Latin:

Modus communicationis & mutui confluxus consistit in hoc, quod natura diuina τῷ λόγῳ non tantum diuina patrat opera, sed & actiones assumtæ carnis sibi vere & realiter appropriat; natura autem humana non solum secundum naturales suas vires, sed & secundum eam virtutem diuinam, quam ex vnione personali sibi communicatam habet, in officio mediatoris agit.

Prob. 1) Generatim e regula concilii Chalcedonensis: Vtraque natura in Christo agit, quod cuiusque proprium est, cum communicatione alterius. Quæ κοινῶς non absoluitur concursu diuino cum actione Christi hominis; quia Deus concurrit cum actionibus omnium hominum, qui secundum vires suas naturales agunt, neque tamen exinde resultat opus theandricum; sed requiritur etiam realis κοινωνία naturarum in agendo, a qua est actio diuino-humana, vt a gladio ignito est vftio secans & sectio vrens.

Prob. 2) Speciatim. Cum S. Paulus Act. XX, 28. asserit, Deum ecclesiam acquisiuisse per proprium sanguinem, haud obscure innuit, diuinitatem τῷ λόγῳ effusionem sanguinis, qui e carne Christi fluxit, sibi appropriasse; & quando Christus docet, quod Deus Pater ipsi dederit potestatem iudicium faciendi, quia filius hominis est, Ioann. V, 27. perspicue indicat, assumtam naturam humanam concurrere ad executionem iudicii vniuersalis, non tantum secundum vires naturales, sed & secundum potestatem diuinam a Patre carni Christi donatam. Egregie hoc illustrat DAMASCENVS libr. III. de O. F. c. 17. Non secundum propriam operationem, sed propter vnitum sibi verbum, diuina operabatur (caro Domini), Verbo per eam propriam suam operationem manifestante. Nam & ferrum ignitum vrit, non naturali ratione possidens uftricem operationem, sed obtinens eam ex vnione ignis & ferri. Ipsa igitur caro Domini mortalis erat propter seipsum, & viuifica propter hypostaticam ad Verbum vnionem.


### Question LXVII

The remote foundation of this communication is the unity of person, and the intimate communion of the divine nature in Christ a). The proximate foundation is the communication of idiomata [properties] of the first and second kind b).

Prob. a. From the unity of the person flows the unity and communion of the apotelesmata (results). From the communion of the natures, however, results the confluence and communion of the united operation. We argue: Whatever person is one, consisting of divine and human natures, most closely united, and thus having a mutual communion between them, that person’s each nature has mutual communion in the performing of the works of the office: But the person of Christ, etc. Therefore. The major is evident: because the mode of operating follows the mode of being.

Prob. b. If the divine nature of the Logos incarnate truly appropriates to itself those things which are of the human nature, and communicates its own properties (omnipotence) to this [human nature] for possession and use; it infallibly follows that the divine nature appropriates to itself what the human nature does in the mediatorial office, and that the latter operates not only by natural, but also by communicated divine energeia (energy): The antecedent is true: Therefore, the consequent.

The antithesis is that of Bellarmine, Tanner, Danaeus, and others, who deny the mutual communion of the natures of Christ in acting. Their arguments are:

I. Whatever is an instrument of the operating divine nature, that does not operate by divine virtue: But the human nature of Christ, etc. Therefore. The major is evident; because an instrument does not possess the same virtue as the principal cause, e.g., the staff of Moses was not endowed with the same power as Moses. Resp. Distinguish between a separate instrument and a conjoined one. Not the former, but the latter can be endowed with the same virtue that the principal cause enjoys, e.g., a heated sword burns with the same heat as the fire; the eye sees with the same faculty as the soul. The difference is that the principal cause has the same virtue formally, the instrument participatively. Furthermore, the human nature of Christ is an instrument personally united, living, intelligent, and most effectively cooperative.

II. By whatever doctrine the energeiai (energies) of the divine and human nature are confused, that is not consistent with the truth: But by the doctrine of the Lutherans, etc. Therefore. The major is clear from the rule of the Council of Chalcedon: Each nature in Christ acts what is proper to each. The minor is manifest: because according to the opinion of the Lutherans, the human nature of Christ in theandric actions is said to act not only by virtue proper to itself, but also by divine virtue communicated to it. Resp. 1) To the major: in it the fallacy of division is committed; for the council adds: meta tou heterou koinonias, with the communion of the other. 2) To the minor: Lutherans neither confuse nor separate the energeiai (energies) of the natures, but with orthodox antiquity assert their koinonia (communion). Communion in acting is not confusion. The soul communicates its faculties in operating to the bodily members, without any confusion.

III. If in the works of the office the human nature of Christ were to operate by communicated divine virtue, it would understand by divine omniscience, and would will by the divine will, which is the error of the Monothelites. Resp. The Monothelites, as far as in them lay, took away the proper will from the human nature of Christ: but we teach and believe that the human nature retains its own knowledge and will; but that the intellect of the man Christ is illuminated by the light of divine omniscience, and his human will is perpetually ruled by the divine will.

IV. The works by which the Logos rules the church, by hearing prayers and remitting sins, are performed immediately by the divine nature: Therefore, the human nature of Christ does not accomplish them. The reason for the consequence is: because the divine nature of the Logos uses the human nature, as an organ personally united, in the works of the office. But to hear prayers and to remit sins are inorganic actions, which are accomplished by the mere act of the divine mind and will. Resp. The human nature of Christ indeed not by itself, yet through communicated omniscience truly hears the prayers of the faithful, and remits sins, by virtue of the power communicated to it.

Latin:

Fundamentum huius communicationis remotum est vnitas personæ, & intima communio naturæ diuinæ in Christo a). Fundamentum proximum est communicatio idiomatum primi & secundi generis b).

Prob. a. Ex vnitate personae fluit vnitas & communitas ἀποτελεσμάτων. Ex communione vero naturarum resultat confluxus & communio operationis vnitae. Arguimus: Quaecunque persona est vna, constans ex diuina & humana naturis, arctissime vnitis, adeoque mutuam inter se communionem habentibus, illius personae natura vtraque mutuam habet communionem, in peragendis operibus officij: Atqui persona Christi &c. Ergo. Maior constat: quia modus operandi sequitur modum essendi.

Prob. b. Si diuina natura τοῦ λόγου incarnata vere sibi appropriat ea, quae sunt humanae naturae, & huic suas proprietates (omnipotentiam) ad possessionem & vsurpationem communicat; infallibiliter consequitur, quod natura diuina sibi appropriet, quae in officio mediatorio natura humana agit, & haec non tantum naturali, sed & communicata diuina ἐνεργείᾳ operetur: Antecedens est verum: E. & consequens.

Antithesis est Bellarmini, Tanneri, Danaei & aliorum, negantium mutuam naturarum Christi in agendo communionem. Quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Quidquid est instrumentum naturae diuinae operantis, illud non operatur virtute diuina: Atqui natura Christi humana &c. E. Maior constat; quia instrumentum non eadem pollet virtute, qua causa principalis, v. gr. baculus Mosis non eadem, qua Moses, potentia instructus erat. Resp. Dist. inter instrumentum separatum, & coniunctum. Non illud, sed hoc eadem instructum esse potest virtute, qua gaudet causa principalis, v. gr. gladius ignitus eodem calore vrit, quo ignis, oculus eadem facultate videt, qua anima. Id discriminis est, quod causa principalis eandem virtutem habet formaliter, instrumentum participatiue. Ceterum humana Christi natura est instrumentum personaliter vnitum, viuum, intelligens, efficacissime cooperatiuum.

II. Per quam doctrinam ἐνέργειαι naturae diuinae & humanae confunduntur, illa non est veritati consentanea: Atqui per doctrinam Lutheranorum &c. E. Maior liquet ex regula concilii Chalcedonensis: Vtraque natura in Christo agit, quod cuiusque proprium est. Minor est manifesta: quia ex sententia Lutheranorum natura Christi humana in actionibus theandricis non tantum virtute sibi propria, sed & virtute diuina sibi communicata agere dicitur. Resp. 1) ad maiorem; in illa committi fallaciam diuisionis; addit enim concilium: μετὰ τοῦ ἑτέρου κοινωνίας, cum alterius communione. 2) Ad minorem: Lutherani naturarum ἐνεργείας neque confundunt, neque separant, sed cum orthodoxa antiquitate earum κοινωνίαν afferunt. Communio in agendo, non est confusio. Anima suas facultates in operando membris corporeis communicat, sine vlla confusione.

III. Si in operibus officij humana Christi natura virtute diuina communicata operaretur, intelligeret omniscientia diuina, & vellet voluntate diuina, qui est error Monotheletarum. Resp. Monotheletae naturae Christi humanae propriam voluntatem, quantum in ipsis, adimebant: at nos docemus & credimus, humanam naturam suam retinere scientiam & voluntatem; at intellectum hominis Christi omniscientiae diuinae lumine collustrari, & voluntatem ipsius humanam voluntate diuina perpetuo regi.

IV. Opera, quibus ὁ λόγος regit ecclesiam, exaudiendo preces & remittendo peccata, immediate a natura diuina perficiuntur: E. natura Christi humana ea non expedit. Ratio consequentiae est: quia diuina natura τοῦ λόγου in operibus officij natura humana, vt organo, personaliter vnito, vtitur. At audire preces & remittere peccata sunt actiones inorganicae, quae solo mentis & voluntatis diuinae actu expediuntur. Resp. Humana Christi natura non quidem per se, attamen per communicatam omniscientiam preces fidelium vere exaudit, & peccata, vi communicatae sibi potestatis, remittit. communicatæ sibi potestatis, remittit.


### Q. LXVIII. Of how many orders are the ἀποτελέσματα (effects/results) of Christ?

The effects of Christ are of a double order; some the divinity τῷ λόγῳ (to the Word) cannot produce without the confluence of flesh ); some it does not will to produce without flesh, out of free εὐδοκίᾳ (good pleasure), or benevolence ).

Prob. a. Of the first order are the satisfactory passion, the shedding of blood cleansing from sin, the life-giving death, the enriching poverty. Prob. b. Of the latter order are miracles, which the divinity τῷ λόγῳ (to the Word) could have performed by the mere nod and command of its will, yet by a certain counsel it employed the flesh to perform them, as a most efficacious organ.

Latin:

Apotelesmata Christi sunt duplicis ordinis; quaedam divinitas τῷ λόγῳ citra confluxum carnis producere nequit ); quaedam ex libera εὐδοκίᾳ, sive beneplacito, fine carne producere non vult ).

Prob. a. Prioris ordinis sunt passio satisfactoria, effusio sanguinis emundans a peccato, mors vivifica, paupertas ditans. Prob. b. Posterioris ordinis sunt miracula, quae divinitas τῷ λόγῳ solo voluntatis nutu & imperio perficere potuisset, certo tamen consilio ad ea patranda adhibuit carnem, vt efficacissimum organon.


### Q. LXIX. What things are to be observed concerning the predications of the third kind of communication of idioms?

There are to be observed a) the subject, b) the predicate, c) the mode of predicating.

Obf. a. The subject of propositions of the third kind of communication of idioms is a concrete noun, denominating the person either from both natures, or from one.

1 Cor. 15:3, "Christ died for our sins"; sometimes the concrete of the divine nature, e.g., 1 John 3:8, "The Son of God destroyed the works of the devil"; sometimes the concrete of the human nature, e.g., Luke 9:56, "The Son of man came to save the souls of men.

The predicate is an ἀποτέλεσμα (effect), or operation of the office, as is evident from the biblical propositions adduced. When Paul says, 1 Cor.

15:3, that Christ died for our sins, the predicate "to die for our sins" is a work of the mediatorial office, which comprises partly "to die," which is an idiom of the human nature, and partly the addition of infinite value, so that that death might have the character of a λύτρον (ransom) for our sins, which infinite value is from the divine nature. Obf. c.

The mode of predicating is true and real. For ὁ λόγος (the Word) truly and really appropriates to himself the actions and passions of the human nature, by virtue of the first kind of communication of idioms, and the human nature is truly and really a participant in supernatural powers for acting, by virtue of the second kind of communication of idioms.

Latin:

Observanda sunt a) subiectum, b) praedicatum, c) modus praedicandi.

Obs. a. Subiectum propositionum tertii generis communicationis idiomatum est nomen concretum, sive ab utraque, sive ab una natura personam denominans. Interdum enim adhibetur concretum personae, v. gr.

1 Cor. XV, 3. Christus mortuus est pro peccatis nostris; interdum concretum naturae divinae, v. gr. 1 Ioann. II, 8. Filius Dei dissoluit opera diaboli; interdum concretum naturae humanae, v. gr. Luc. IX, 56. Filius hominis venit salvare animas hominum.

Obs. b. Praedicatum est ἀποτέλεσμα, sive operatio officii, vt patet ex adductis propositionibus biblicis.

Cum Paullus dicit, 1 Cor. XV, 3. quod Christus mortuus fit pro peccatis nostris, praedicatum τὸ mori pro peccatis nostris, est opus officii mediatorii, quod complectitur partim τὸ mori, quod est idioma naturae humanae, partim additionem infiniti valoris, vt illa mors haberet rationem λύτρου pro peccatis nostris, qui infinitus valor est a natura divina.

Obs. c. Modus praedicandi est verus & realis. Nam ὁ λόγος vere & realiter sibi appropriat actiones & passiones humanae naturae, vi primi generis commun. idiomat. & humana natura vere & realiter particeps est virium supernaturalium ad operandum, vi secundi generis communicationis idiomatum.


### Q. LXX. How does the third kind of communication of idioms differ from the first and second kind?

It differs from them by certain κριτηρίοις (criteria).

Prob. In the first kind, properties are claimed for that nature to which they formally belong: in the third kind, the ἀποτελέσματα (effects) are claimed for the person, according to both natures of acting. In the second kind, in place of the subject is placed "Christ as man," in place of the predicate stands a divine idiom: but in the third kind, the subject is the σύνθετος (composite) person, the predicate is a divine-human work.

Latin:

Differt ab iisdem certis κριτηρίοις.

Prob. In primo genere vindicantur propria illi naturae, cui formaliter competunt: in tertio genere ἀποτελέσματα vindicantur personae, secundum utramque naturam operandi. In secundo genere loco subiecti ponitur Christus qua homo, praedicati loco stat idioma divinum: in tertio autem genere subiectum est persona σύνθετος, praedicatum est opus divino-humanum.


### Membrum II. On the Mediatorial Office of Christ


### Q. LXXI

The mediatorial office of Christ is that by which Christ acts as mediator between God who is offended and man who is a sinner, [establishing] the covenant of grace between both by blood and by his death establishing, by his gospel declaring and offering to the sinner, and by his most powerful rule confirming and preserving the thing offered.

Obj. I. The sanction of the covenant of grace pertains to the priestly office of Christ; the declaration and oblation of that covenant pertain to the prophetic office of Christ; the confirmation and preservation of the covenant pertain to the kingly office of Christ.

Obj. II. If the mediatorial office of Christ is taken in a stricter sense, it seems to coincide with his priestly office, according to 1 Tim. II, 5, 6. Yet nothing prevents it from being taken in a broader sense, so as to embrace the prophetic and kingly office. For Moses the prophet is also called a mediator, Gal. III, 18, according to the opinion of some Theologians, and that kings not rarely sustain the persons of mediators, escapes no one.

Latin:

Officium Christi mediatorium est, quo Christus inter Deum offensum, hominemque peccatorem, medias agit partes, foedus gratiae inter utrumque sanguine & morte sua sanciendo, sanctum evangelio suo declarando & peccatori offerendo, oblatum regimine potentissimo confirmando & conservando.

Obs. I. Sanctio foederis gratiae ad officium Christi sacerdotale, declaratio & oblatio illius foederis ad officium Christi propheticum, confirmatio & conservatio foederis ad officium Christi regium pertinet.

Obs. II. Si officium Christi mediatorium strictiori sumatur sensu, cum officio ipsius sacerdotali, videtur coincidere, iuxta 1 Tim. II, 5, 6. Nil tamen prohibet, quo minus illud latiori accipiatur sensu, ut officium propheticum & regium complectatur. Nam & Moses propheta dicitur mediator, Gal. III, 18. ex nonnullorum Theologorum sententia, & reges haud raro mediatorum sustinere personas, neminem fugit .


### Q. LXXII

According to which nature is our Christ a mediator? Christ is our mediator according to both natures ), the divine ) and the human ).

Prob. a. 1) From the name of mediator. ATHANASIUS says wisely in dial. I. de Trinit.: If Christ were only man, or only God, he would not be a mediator between God and man. 2) For the works of the mediatorial office, such as blood blotting out sins, life-giving death, satisfactory passion, etc., the κοινωνία (communion) and confluence of both natures, divine and human, is necessarily required, since, according to the elegant saying of FAUSTUS, neither could God alone feel death, nor could man alone overcome it.

Prob. b. 1) From the Apostolic testimony: God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, 2 Cor. V, 19. From which we argue: According to which nature Christ reconciled us to God, according to that he is our mediator: But he did so according to his divine nature, etc. Therefore . 2) From the end of the incarnation, concerning which Paul says, Gal. IV, 4: When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons of God.

If a mere man could have redeemed sinful men from the curse of the law, and acquired for them divine adoption, the Son of God would never have come in the flesh, would never have subjected himself to the law.

Proof c. 1) From the explicit designation, 1 Tim. II, 5. There is one mediator of God and men, the man Jesus Christ. 2) From the remission of sins, flowing from the blood of the Son of God. 1 John 1, 7. Rom. V, 9. According to the same nature that Christ shed his blood for the remission of sins, and died for our reconciliation with God, according to the same he is our mediator: But according to the human nature &c. Therefore. The antithesis is that of the Osiandrists, who acknowledge Christ as our mediator according to the divine nature alone, and the Stancarists, who, with the Papists, acknowledge him according to the human nature alone.

Whose arguments are: I. According to the same nature that Christ is called our righteousness, according to the same he is our mediator (because the final cause of mediation is righteousness to be repaired): But according to the divine nature &c. Therefore.

The minor premise is evident from Jer. XXIII, 6. Jehovah is our righteousness.

Resp. The words of Jeremiah are: The Branch of David shall be called Jehovah our righteousness. Which is a personal proposition, by which the union of the divine and human natures is expressed, and their communion in the unity of the person, and consequently it is hinted that Christ according to both natures is our righteousness.

II. Whatever nature cannot repair eternal righteousness, according to that Christ is not our righteousness: But according to the human nature he could not &c. Therefore.

The major premise is evident: since the office of the mediator is to repair eternal righteousness, Dan. IX, 24. The minor is clear: since the human nature is not eternal, nor does it have eternal powers.

Resp. Distinguish between human nature subsisting outside the divine hypostasis, and that assumed into the hypostasis of the Word. The former indeed, but not the latter, is destitute of the powers to repair eternal righteousness. And although the human nature of Christ did not exist from eternity, yet the divine power, which is eternal, was communicated to it.

The Papists object I. Our mediator is explicitly called a man, 1 Tim. II, 5. Resp. It is not understood in that place as ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος (a mere man), but as θεάνθρωπος (God-man).

II. If Christ were our mediator according to the divine nature, then God the Father and the Holy Spirit would also be our mediators (because they have the same divine nature as the Son of God): The consequent is false: Therefore the antecedent is also.

Resp. Distinguish between the divine nature viewed absolutely, and viewed relatively, insofar as it is marked by the hypostatic character of the Word. The work of mediation is performed not in the former, but in the latter sense.

III. Every mediator is distant from the party that is offended: The Son of God, according to the divine nature, is not distant from the party that is offended. Therefore.

Resp. Distinguish between a mediator so called because of distance from each disagreeing party; such a one is not required here: and a mediator so called because of union with each party; and such is Christ the God-man. For a mediator is said to be so rather from his union (ἑνώσεως) with both parties, an appropriation, as Irenaeus speaks, lib. III. c. 20, than from distance from both parties.

For the end of the mediator is to [reunite] the separated; we maintain.

Therefore, it is apparent from this that the closest union of the divine and human nature in this one Reconciler was most necessary, to join.

But if the distance is urged precisely, Christ as man is distant from God, as God is distant from man.

IV. If Christ were a priest according to his divinity, according to the same he would be lesser than the Father: The consequent is false: Therefore, the antecedents are also.

The consequence of the major premise is clear: because a priest is lesser than him to whom he sacrifices.

Resp. In a priest there are two things, dignity and subjection. The former is owed to the divinity, the latter to the humanity: just as the Son of God is said to be sent without inequality of his own, and to obey the Father (an obedience not subjective, but voluntary, from the decree of always doing those things which please him, John VIII, 35. Heb.

X, 7.). For the Father is said to παρακαλεῖν (beseech), without diminution of his own majesty. 2 Cor. V, 20.

Quest. LXXIII. What is the priestly office of Christ? The priestly office of Christ is that by which Christ, as mediator and priest of the new testament, by the most exact fulfillment of the law and the sacrifice of his own body, satisfied the divine justice on our behalf, and offers most efficacious prayers to God for our salvation.

Quest. LXXIV. What kind of priest is Christ? Christ is a priest true and properly so called a), supreme b), unique c), eternal d), impeccable e).

Prob. a. Christ is frequently called a priest in the H. Scripture Ps.

CX, 4. Heb.

V. 10. c.

VI, 20. c. VII, 26. c.

IX, 11. c. X, 21. He is not, however, called a priest metaphorically or improperly, but properly and truly: because he performs the duties of priests properly so called.

Now the duties of priests, properly so called, are to offer an expiatory sacrifice for sins, and to intercede for sinners (*). That Christ the priest performs these two things, we shall now show.

Prob. b. Christ is explicitly called ἀρχιερεὺς μέγας, a great high priest (), who has passed through the heavens, Heb.

IV, 14. Which greatness is estimated 1) from the comparison with the priesthood Aaronic, or Levitical priesthood. The dignity of the Aaronic priesthood was supreme, miraculously confirmed by divine authority, Num.

XVI, 35. c. XVII, 8. But as a shadow to the body, so Aaron yielded to Christ in eminence.

For the Levitical priests are said to have served as a copy and shadow (ὑποδείγματι καὶ σκιᾷ) of heavenly things, Hebr.

VIII, 5. But Christ offered himself for us, an oblation and sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savor, Eph.

V, 2. The Levitical priests first offered sacrifices for their own sins, then for the sins of the people: but Christ has no necessity of sacrificing for his own sins, since he is harmless and undefiled (ἄκακος καὶ ἀμίαντος), innocent and unpolluted, Hebr.

VII, 26. 27. 2) From the comparison with the Melchisedechian priesthood.

Melchisedech was greater than Aaron.

Christ is Melchisedech antitypically. Therefore he is also greater than Melchisedech, which argument the Apostle treats at length, Hebr.

VII, 1 ff. (*). Prob. e. to be distinguished from the priests of the New Testament properly so called, namely those who were accustomed to offer a piacular sacrifice to God daily, and especially the high priest, as the vicar of Christ, whose seat is Rome.

The beginning of this error is: that they feign that the Mass is a sacrifice for sins, to be expiated every day.

For that reason they wrongly attribute the title of priest to those who perform sacred rites, and indeed not to all, but only to those to whom the power has been given of consecrating the holy supper, or, as they say, of performing it.

But since that missatic sacrifice is absolutely nothing (Hebr.

X, 14. & 26.): it follows that this definition of the name is to be utterly rejected. Paul certainly, Eph.

IV, 11, when he is engaged in counting the number of sacred orders which Christ established by his own authority, makes no mention of priests, who would have been the first to be named if the opinion of the adversaries had any validity. But we maintain the true opinion, that Christ is so called with respect to all the priests of the Old Testament, and even the high priest himself, for this one high priest (ἀρχιερεὺς) far surpasses him too, wherefore Christ is not so simply called high priest (ἀρχιερεὺς), but with a distinguished addition, great high priest (ἀρχιερεὺς μέγας), and likewise such a high priest (τοῖτος ὁ ἀρχιερεὺς), who sat down at the right hand of the throne, etc.

Hebr. VIII, 1. The dignity of the high priest of the O.

T. was not so great, seeing that he, so far from having sat down on this throne, was not even permitted to perform his duty in the earthly temple while sitting. And it is to be well observed that in all the letters sent to the Hebrews, our Jesus is perpetually opposed to the high priest, whom divine religion commanded all to venerate in the Old Testament.

But of the Roman high Pontiff, both in this epistle and in the whole scripture, there is deep silence.

Latin:

Christus est noster mediator secundum utramque naturam ), divinam ) & humanam ).

Prob. a. 1) Ex nomine mediatoris. Scite inquit ATHANASIVS dial. I. de Trinit. Si Christus esset homo tantum, vel Deus tantum, non esset medius inter Deum & hominem. 2) Ad opera officii mediatorii, qualia sunt sanguis delens peccata, mors vivifica, passio satisfactoria, &c. utriusque naturae divinae & humanae κοινωνία & confluxus necessario requiritur, cum mortem, iuxta elegans dictum FAVSTI, nec solus Deus sentire, nec solus homo superare potuisset.

Prob. b. 1) E testimonio Apostolico: Deus erat in Christo, reconcilians mundum sibi ipsi, 2 Cor. V, 19. Ex quo argumentamur: Secundum quam naturam Christus nos Deo reconciliavit, secundum eam est noster mediator: Atqui secundum naturam divinam &c. Ergo . 2) E fine incarnationis, de quo Paullus, Gal. IV, 4: Quando venit plenitudo temporis, misit Deus Filium suum, natum ex muliere, factum sub lege, vt eos, qui erant sub lege, redimeret, vt adoptionem filiorum Dei acciperemus.

Si homo merus potuisset homines peccatores maledictione legis redimere, & iisdem τήν υἱοθεσίαν diuinam acquirere, Filius Dei nunquam venisset in carnem, nunquam legi se subiecisset.

Prob. c. 1) A diserta denominatione, 1 Tim.II, 5. Vnus est mediator Dei & hominum, homo Iesus Christus. 2) A remissione peccatorum, fluente e sanguine Filii Dei. 1 Ioann. 1, 7. Rom. V, 9. Secundum quam naturam Christus sanguinem suum effudit in remissionem peccatorum, & mortuus est ad reconciliationem nostri cum Deo, secundum eandem est noster mediator: Atqui secundum humanam naturam &c. Ergo. Antithesis est Osiandristarum, qui secundum solam naturam diuinam, & Stancaristarum, qui cum Pontificiis secundum solam naturam humanam Christum pro mediatore nostro agnoscunt.

Quorum argumenta sunt: I. Secundum quam naturam Christus dicitur nostra iustitia, secundum eandem noster est mediator (quia causa finalis mediationis est iustitia reparanda): Sed secundum naturam diuinam &c. Ergo.

Minor constat ex Ierem. XXIII, 6. Iehouah est iustitia nostra.

Resp. Verba Ieremiæ sunt: Germen Dauidis vocabitur Iehouah iustitia nostra. Quæ est propositio personalis, qua exprimitur diuinæ & humanæ naturarum vnio, earumque in vnitare personæ communio, & consequenter eadem innuitur, Christum secundum vtramque naturam esse nostram iustitiam.

II. Quæcunque natura æternam iustitiam non potest reparare, secundum illam Christus non est iustitia nostra: At secundum humanam naturam non potuit &c. Ergo.
