Maior constat: quoniam mediatoris officium est, æternam reparare iustitiam, Dan. IX, 24. Minor liquet: quoniam natura humana non est æterna, neque æternas vires habet.

Resp. Distingu. inter naturam humanam subsistentem extra hypostasin diuinam, & assumtam in hypostasin τῷ λόγῳ. Illa quidem, sed non hæc, destituitur viribus ad reparandam iustitiam æternam. Et quamuis humana Christi natura non exstiterit ab æterno, communicata illi tamen est potentia diuina, quæ æterna est.

Pontificii obiiciunt I. Mediator noster diserte dicitur homo, 1 Tim. II, 5. Resp. non intelligitur l.c. ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος homo merus, sed θεάνθρωπος homo deificatus.

II. Si Christus secundum diuinam naturam noster mediator esset, etiam Deus Pater & Spiritus S. nostri essent mediatores (quia eandem cum Filio Dei habent naturam diuinam): Consequens est falsum: E. & antecedens.

Resp. Dist. inter naturam diuinam absolute, & relate spectatam, quatenus charactere hypostatico τῷ λόγῳ est insignita. Non priori, sed posteriori sensu opus mediationis perticit.

III. Omnis mediator distat ab ea parte, quæ est læsa: Filius Dei, secundum naturam diuinam, non distat ab ea parte, quæ est læsa. Ergo.

Resp. Dist. inter mediatorem, dictum ob distantiam ab vtraque parte diffidente; talis hic non requiritur: & inter mediatorem ita dictum ob coniunctionem cum vtraque parte; & talis est Christus θεάνθρωπος. Mediator enim potius dicitur a sua ad vtramque partem ἑνώσεως, appropriatione, vt loquitur IRENEVS, lib. III. c. 20. quam a distantia ab vtraque parte.

Finis enim mediatoris est, disiunctos cinianos tuemur.

E. vel ex eo adparet, arctissimam coniunctionem diuinæ & humanæ naturæ in uno hoc Reconciliatore maxime necessariam fuisse, tos coniungere.

Quod si autem praecise urgeatur distantia, Christus homo distat a Deo, vt Deus distat ab homine.

IV. Si Christus secundum diuinitatem esset sacerdos, secundum eandem foret patre minor: Consequens est falsum: E. & antecedentes.

Consequentia maioris est liquida: quia sacerdos est minor eo, cui sacrificat.

Resp. In sacerdote duo sunt, dignitas & subiectio. Illa debetur diuinitati, haec humanitati: sicut & Filius Dei absque inaequalitate fui dicitur mitti, & obedire Patri (obedientia non subiectiua, sed voluntaria, ex decreto faciendi semper, quae placent illi, Ioann. VIII, 35. Hebr.

X, 7.). Pater enim dicitur παρακαλεῖν, sine maiestatis suae diminutione. 2 Cor. V, 20.

Quaest. LXXIII. Quodnam est officium Christi sacerdotale? Officium Christi sacerdotale est, quo Christus mediator & sacerdos noui testamenti exactissima legis impletione, & sacrificio corporis sui, nostri caussa laxae iustitiae diuinae satisfecit, & efficacissimas pro salute nostra preces Deo offert.

Quaest. LXXIV. Qualis sacerdos est Christus? Christus est sacerdos verus proprieque dictus a), summus b), vnicus c), aeternus d), impeccabilis e).

Prob. a. Christus frequenter in S. scriptura dicitur sacerdos Ps.

CX, 4. Hebr.

V. 10. c.

VI, 20. c. VII, 26. c.

IX, 11. c. X, 21. Non autem metaphorice aut improprie, sed proprie & vere dicitur sacerdos: quia munia sacerdotum proprie dictorum obit.

Sunt autem munia sacerdotum, proprie dictorum, pro peccatis offerre sacrificium expiatorium, & pro peccatoribus intercedere (*). Haec duo praestare sacerdotem Christum, iamiam ostendemus.

Prob. b. Christus diserte vocatur ἀρχιερεὺς μέγας, sacerdos princeps magnus (), qui caelos penetrauit, Hebr.

IV, 14. Quae magnitudo aestimatur 1) e comparatione cum sacerdotio cerdotio Aaronico, sive Levitico. Summa fuit Aaronici sacerdotii dignitas, divina auctoritate miraculose firmata, Num.

XVI, 35. c. XVII, 8. Sed vt corpori vmbra, ita Aaron Christo in eminentia cessit.

Etenim sacerdotes Levitici ὑποδείγματι καὶ σκιᾷ, figuræ & vmbræ cœlestium feruivisse dicuntur, Hebr.

VIII, 5. At Christus seipsum tradidit pro nobis, oblationem & sacrificium Deo in odorem fragrantiæ, Eph.

V, 2. Sacerdotes Levitici primo pro propriis peccatis sacrificia offerebant, deinde pro populi peccatis: Christus autem non habet necessitatem sacrificandi pro peccatis propriis, cum sit ἄκακος καὶ ἀμίαντος, innocens & impollutus, Hebr.

VII, 26. 27. 2) E comparatione cum sacerdotio Melchisedechiano.

Melchisedech fuit maior Aarone.

Christus est Melchisedech antitypice. E. etiam maior Melchisedeco, quod argumentum prolixe tractat Apostolus, Hebr.

VII, 1 seqq. (*). Prob. e. distingui a sacerdotibus novi Test. proprie ita dictis, nimirum illis, qui sacrificium piaculare Deo quotidie offerre consueverunt, in primisque summo sacerdote, tamquam Christi vicario, cuius sedes est Roma.

Principium erroris hoc est: quod fingunt, Missam esse sacrificium pro delictis, quouis die expiandis.

Ea de caussa titulum sacerdotis perperam tribuunt his, qui sacris operantur, nec vero omnibus, sed iis dumtaxat, quibus facta est potestas consecrandi sacram cœnam, seu, vti loquuntur, conficiendi.

Quum vero sacrificium illud missaticum omnino nullum fit (Hebr.

X, 14. & 26.): efficitur, vt ista nominis ratio prorsus sit repudianda. Paullus certe, Eph.

IV, 11. cum in eo est, vt numerum ineat ordinum sacrorum, quos sua auctoritate Christus constituit, nullam facit mentionem de sacerdotibus, qui vel primo loco fuissent nominandi, si quid valeret aduersariorum opinio. Veram nos sententiam tuemur, Christum ita vocari respectu sacerdotum omnium veteris Testamenti, ipsius etiam summi sacerdotis, nam eum quoque ipsum vnus hiece ἀρχιερεὺς longe superat, quocirca Christus non ita simpliciter appellatur ἀρχιερεὺς, sed cum insigni additamento, ἀρχιερεὺς μέγας, itemque τοῖτος ὁ ἀρχιερεὺς, ὃς ἐκάθισεν ἐν δεξιᾷ τοῦ θρόνου κ. τ. λ.

Hebr. VIII, 1. Tanta non fuit dignitas summi sacerdotis V.

T. quippe qui, tantum abest, vt in hoc throno consederit, vt ne licuerit quidem illi sedenti, in templo terrestri munere suo fungi. Et probe obseruandum est, quod in vniuersis litteris, ad Hebræos missis, Iesus noster perpetuo opponatur summo sacerdoti, quem religio diuina in veteri Test. venerari omnes iussit.

De summo autem Pontifice Romano, tum in hac epistola, tum in tota scriptura, altum est silentium.


### Q. LXXII: (*) Two propositions declare the excellence and preeminence of the priestly office which was entrusted to Christ Propositio Prior: The priesthood of Christ is far more excellent than the Levitical priesthood…

(*) Two propositions declare the excellence and preeminence of the priestly office which was entrusted to Christ.

PROPOSITIO PRIOR: The priesthood of Christ is far more excellent than the Levitical priesthood of the O.

T. For we discern the prerogative of the latter by reason of the subject: Namely 1) Every priest of the O.

T. was a lover of men (φιλάνθρωπος), nothing but a mortal man, c.

VII, 8. and therefore contaminated by sin, c. VII, 28. But Christ, and that one indeed, is God-man (θεάνθρωπος), and the eternal Son of God, l. c. & cap. I, 1. 2. ff. nay even, if you look at his human nature, void of all sin, c.

IV, 15. VII, 26. 2) Every priest of the O.

T. had need to immolate victims, not only for the sins of his own people, but also for his own, c.

V, 2. 3. Much otherwise Christ, c.

VII, 27. 3) Every Priest of the O.

T. derived his origin from the tribe of Levi; but Christ was born from the tribe of Judah, since indeed he alone had to be conspicuous in dignity not only as Priest, but also as King, c.

VII, 14. 4) All Priests of the O.

T., and especially the high priest of all, and even all the functions of so holy an office, were types and images, foreshadowing Christ and his sacred work to be done. But the antitype undoubtedly excels the type, the body excels the shadow in dignity, Hebr.

X, 1 ff. 5) by reason of the legation: 1) Each one of the Priests of the O.

T. was indeed a legate from God, but mediately, through men, and even Aaron himself, by Moses the minister of God, Hebr.

V, 4. coll. with Ex. XXVIII, 1; Christ immediately from his Father, Hebr.

V, 5. and not only so sent, but likewise declared and inaugurated by his Father, Matth.

III, 17: 2) They indeed all to one, without an oath; but Christ received a much more splendid vocation, confirmed by the Father swearingProb. c. 1) The Old Testament differs from the New, in that there were many priests there, but here one: Therefore, in the N.T. there is none but a monadic priest.

The antecedent is evident from Heb.

7:23, 24. And they indeed (the Levitical priests) were made many priests, because they were hindered by death from continuing: but this one, because he remains, has a priesthood that does not pass away.

2) The Old was confirmed, Heb. 7:20, 21.

3) By reason of the object, namely, the sacrifice to be offered to God: 1) The priest of the O.T. was always distinct from the victim; Christ, on the contrary, offered himself as a victim to God, Heb. 9:23-26.

2) The blood by which the priests of the O.T. expiated sins was entirely that of brute animals; but the piacular blood of Christ of the N.C. precedes with infinite value, Heb.

9:12, 13, 14. 3) All the sacrifices of the O.T. had to be repeated many times, and those indeed which foreshadowed the future acquisition of our salvation, once every year, Heb. 9:7, 25; but those which signified the application of the same through faith, to be placed in the merits of Christ, daily, Heb.

9:27; Christ, on the contrary, immolated himself once, as if for always, l.c. & c. 9:26, 28; c. 10:18 & 26.

9, 26. 28. ch. 10, 18. & 26.

4) All the sacrifices of the O.T. had in themselves no power of expiation, Heb. 10:3, 4, 11, but the whole of it depended on the thing signified, and the faith of men in Christ, whom those shadows signified as about to come, Heb. 8:5, 9:22, 10: 1.

In themselves they were worth nothing more than to effect the cleansing of the body, or its Levitical declaration, Heb. 9: 13. But the piacular sacrifice of Christ has all power in itself, ibid., v. 14. 5) It was necessary for the High Priest of the O.T. to enter into the earthly most holy place, and indeed with the blood of another, Heb. 9: 25. But Christ entered into the heavenly sanctuary, and not otherwise than with his own blood, in the same chapter, v. 12 & 24. 7) By reason of the adjunct, namely, duration, all the priests of the O.T. were mortal, and for that reason many, of whom one succeeded into the place of another:

On the contrary, Christ is immortal, and the same is the unique and perpetual Priest of the N.C. Heb.

8:23 & 24. PROPOSITIO POSTERIOR Christ is a priest not of the order of Aaron, but of Melchizedek, Ps. 110:4. Heb. 6:v.v. & 7. tot.

It is not my intention now to fight and conquer: Who was Melchizedek? Christ himself, seen by Abraham in human form? Or someone else, a type and image of Christ? Which latter is indeed more probable. But this dispute pertains more to hermeneutical Theology than to dogmatic.

This one thing pertains here: what was the difference between the Melchizedekian and the Aaronic priesthood?

It is indeed that *) One is true, which the sacred scriptures show us to be fourfold. For it is not credible that in the classic passage, ch. 7 of the epistle to the Hebrews, anything of those things which are true, which are noteworthy, which pertain to the matter, has been omitted.

1) The genealogy of Melchizedek always remained hidden, but the family of Aaron was obscure and unknown to no one. But in this way was this excellence of Christ signified, by which he, God, is ἀμήτωρ (motherless), and the same, man, is ἀπάτωρ (fatherless), Heb. 7:3. 2) Melchizedek was King as well as Priest, v. 1, 2. But it was permitted to no one from the order of Aaron to usurp royal power.

In that, therefore, Melchizedek was an image of Christ the Priest, conspicuous at the same time by royal dignity, and therefore arising from a royal tribe, v. 13, 14.

3) The fruit of the Melchizedekian priesthood pertained to Abraham himself, but the Aaronic pertained only to the descendants of Abraham, v. 5-10.

4) Melchizedek left no successor in office: so also Christ, v. 23, 24. Hence the principal error of the Gichtelians, and proper to this sect, concerning the Melchizedekian priesthood as common to all reborn men, is clearly intolerable.

But, you say, an order is a succession of many, of whom one follows another as is fitting. Resp. α) A certain successor existed, but he was none other than Christ, who succeeded into the place of Melchizedek, not as equal to equal, but as the antitype succeeds the type. β) Order is not always said by reason of succeeding men, but sometimes also in view of things and parts of the office. γ) The Greek name, τάξις, corresponds to the Hebrew, דִּבְרָה, Ps.

110:4, as it denotes not so much an order as an institution, manner, condition, just as the word, τάξις, is sometimes used, e.g., Col. 2:5. *) Another is false, which the Roman Catholics have feigned, the reason for the distinction, thinking it to consist chiefly in this: that the Aaronic priests indeed immolated bloody victims,

Latin:

(*) Excellentiam præstantiamque sacerdotalis, quod Christo demandatum est, officii declarant binæ propositiones.

PROPOSITIO PRIOR: Sacerdotium Christi longe est præstabilius sacerdotio Levitico V.

T. Illius enim prærogativam cernimus ratione subiecti: Scilicet 1) Omnis sacerdos V.

T. fuit φιλάνθρωπος, nil, nisi homo mortalis, c.

VII, 8. ideinque peccato contaminatus, c. VII, 28. Christus autem, & vnus quidem ille, est θεάνθρωπος, atque æternus Dei Filius, l. c. & cap. I, 1. 2. seqq. immo etiam, si humanam ipsius naturam spectes, peccato omni vacuus, c.

IV, 15. VII, 26. 2) Omnis sacerdos V.

T. necesse habebat, non solum pro delictis gentis suæ, sed & pro suis, hostias immolare, c.

V, 2. 3. Multo aliter Christus, c.

VII, 27. 3) Omnis Sacerdos V.

T. originem ducebat a tribu Levi; Christus vero ex tribu Iuda exortus fuit, quoniam quidem is vnus debebat esse dignitate non Sacerdotali solum, verum etiam regia conspicuus, c.

VII, 14. 4) Omnes Sacerdotes V.

T. præfertim vero summus omnium, omnes etiam functiones muneris adeo sancti, erant typi atque imagines, Christum, eiusque rem sacram faciendam adumbrantes. Antitypus autem haud dubie præstat typo, corpus dignitate antecellit vmbræ, Hebr.

X, 1 seqq. 5) ratione legationis: 1) Sacerdotum V.

T. vnus quisque a Deo quidem legatus fuit, sed mediate, per homines, atque adeo Aharon ipse, Mose Dei ministro, Hebr.

V, 4. coll. cum Ex. XXVIII, 1; Christus immediate a Patre suo, Hebr.

V, 5. nec solum ita legatus, sed pariter etiam a suo Patre declaratus atque inauguratus, Matth.

III, 17: 2) Illi quidem ad vnum omnes, fine inter iurando; Christus vero multo splendidiorem accepit vocationem, a Patre iurante confirmac. 1) Vetus Testamentum differt a nouo, quod ibi plures fuerint sacerdotes, hic vnus: Ergo in N. T. non est, nisi monadicus sacerdos.

Antecedens patet ex Hebr. VII, 23.

24. Et illi quidem (Leuitici sacerdotes) plures sunt facti sacerdotes, eo quod morte prohibiti sunt permanere: hic vero propterea, quod manet, non transiens habet sacerdotium.

2) Vetus firmatam, Hebr. VII, 20. 21.

3) Ratione obiecti, nimirum sacrificii Deo offerendi: 1) Sacerdos V. T. semper erat diversus a victima; Christus, contra, semet Deo victimam obtulit, Hebr. IX, 23-26.

2) Sanguis, quo Sacerdotes V. T. delicta expiabant, omnino erat brutorum animantium; infinito autem pretio antecedit Christi sanguis piacularis N. F.

Hebr. IX, 12. 13. 14.

3) Sacrificia V. T. omnia saepe numero erant repetenda, & illa quidem, quae adquisitionem salutis nostrae futuram praenuntiabant, quotannis semel, Hebr. IX, 7. 25. ea vero, quae applicationem eiusdem per fiduciam, in Christi promeritis collocandam, significabant, quotidie, Hebr. IX, 27; Christus, contra, se immolauit semel, tanquam semper, l. c. & c.

IX, 26. 28. c. X, 18. & 26.

4) Sacrificia V. T. omnia nullam per se habebant vim expiandi, Hebr. X, 3. 4. 11, sed ea tota pendebat ex re significata, & fide hominum in Christum, quem illae vmbrae venturum significabant, Hebr. VIII, 5. IX, 22. X, 1.

Per se nihil valebant amplius, quam corporis efficere munditiem, siue declarationem eius Leuiticam, Hebr. IX, 13. Christi vero sacrificium piaculare vim omnem in se habet, ibid, v. 14. 5) Summum Sacerdotem V. T. oportebat in locum sanctissimum terrestrem ingredi, & quidem cum sanguine alieno, Hebr. IX, 25. Christus autem in sanctuarium caeleste introiuit, nec aliter, quam cum suo sanguine in cod. cap. v. 12. & 24.

7) Ratione adiuncti, nimirum durationis, Sacerdotes V. T. omnes fuerunt mortales, ob eamque causam plures, quorum alter in alterius locum successit: Contra, Christus est immortalis, idemque vnicus ac perpetuus N. F. Sacerdos.

Hebr. VIII, 23. & 24. PROPOSITIO POSTERIOR Christus est sacerdos ex ordine non Abaronis, sed Melchisedeci, Ps. CX, 4. Hebr. VI, v. vult. & VII. tot.

Non est mei instituti, iam pugnare ac vincere: Quis fuerit Melchisedech? Christus ipse, humana specie Abrahamo visus? an alius quisquam, Christi typus atque imago? quod alterum quidem magis probabile est, Sed haec disputatio ad hermeneuticam Theologiam propius, quam ad dogmaticam, spectat.

Id vnum huc pertinet: quae fuerit differentia Sacerdotii Melchisedeciani, & Abaronici? Est nimirum ea

*) Alia quidem vera, quam sacrae litterae nobis ostendunt quadruplicem. Non est enim credibile, in loco classico, cap. VII. ep. ad Hebraeos, praetermissum esse aliquid eorum, quae vera sunt, quae notatu digna, quae ad rem pertinent.

1) Melchisedeci genealogia semper manfit abscondita, Aharonis vero familia nemini fuit obscura atque ignorata. Ita vero significata fuit haec Christi excellentia, qua ipse, Deus, ἀμήτωρ est, idemque, homo, ἀπάτωρ, Hebr. VII, 3. 2) Melchizedek tam Rex fuit, quam Sacerdos, v. 1. 2. Nemini autem ex ordine Aharonis licuit, potestatem regiam vsurpare.

In eo igitur Melchisedecus fuit imago Christi Sacerdotis, Regia simul dignitate conspicui, ideoque ex tribu regia oriundi, v. 13. 14.

3) Melchisedeciani Sacerdotii fructus ad ipsum Abrahamum pertinebat, Aharonitici autem ad posteros dumtaxat Abrahami, v. 5.-10.

4) Melchisedecus nullum reliquit in officio successorem: ita & Christus, v. 23. 24. Proinde plane intolerabilis est Gichtelianorum error principalis, & huius sectae proprius, de sacerdotio Melchisedeciano, hominum denuo natorum omnium communi.

At, inquis, ordo est successio plurium, quorum quidem alter alterum sequitur pro eo, ac decet. Resp. u) Exstitit successor quidam, is vero non alius, quam Christus, qui in locum Melchisedeci successit, non vt par pari, sed vt antitypus typo succedit.

B) Ordo non semper dicitur ratione hominum succedentium, sed interdum etiam intuitu rerum & partium officii. γ) Graecum nomen, τάξις, respondet hebraico, דִּבְרָה, Ps CX, 4. vt pote quod non tam ordinem denotat, quam institutum, rationem, conditionem, quem ad modum vox, τάξις, aliquando vsurpatur, v. g. Col. II, 5. *) Alia autem falsa, quam finxerunt Romano-Catholici, discriminis rationem, rati, in eo potissimum sitam esse: quod Abaronici quidem sacerdotes victimas cruentas immolarint,


### Q. LXXII: Melchisedecians

Melchisedecians.

2) The Old Testament differs also from the new by offerings repeated daily and made more than once: Therefore, an offering repeated daily and made more than once cannot have a place in the N. T. The antecedent is clear from Heb. VII, 27. Christ offered himself once; c. X, 14. Christ by one offering has perfected forever those who are sanctified.

3) Christ is not a priest according to the order of Aaron, in which the priesthood was transferred to successors, but according to the order of Melchizedek, who had neither predecessors nor successors in the priesthood. Heb. VIII, 11. 12. 15. Prob. d.

Heb. VII, 3. The Son of God remains a priest forever. The fruit of the priesthood of Christ extends into past and future ages, or the merit of the priest Christ is valid backward and forward.

Prob. e. It was fitting for us to have a high priest holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, made higher than the heavens, Heb. VII, 26. Christ was tempted in all things, according to the likeness (of the common strength of men), except sin, Heb. IV, 15.

The Antithesis is 1) Of the Papists, denying that Christ is the unique, properly so-called priest of the N. T. 2) Of the Arminians, asserting that Christ is a priest not simply impeccable, or immune from all power of sinning (*). 3) Of the Socinians, denying the eternal priesthood of Christ.

The Papists argue with the following reasoning: Christians are called priests, Rev. I, 6. Therefore, Christ is not the unique priest of the N. T. Resp. Christians are called priests metaphorically, on account of the εὐχαριστικὰ (eucharistic) sacrifices of prayers and praise; but Christ is a priest properly so-called, on account of the ἱλαστικὸν (propitiatory) sacrifice, expiatory, which Christ offered once, Heb. VII, 27.

Instance. Christ the high priest indeed offered a bloody sacrifice once: but it belongs to subordinate priests to offer an unbloody sacrifice more often, so that that bloody sacrifice, the acquirer of salvation, may be applied again and again. Resp. The sacrifice of Christ, offered on the altar of the cross, is applied not through another sacrifice, but through the word and sacraments.

But Melchizedek offered an unbloody sacrifice to God, and that a piacular one, namely bread and wine, Gen. XIV, 18. Thus they opine with the express purpose that they may serve their ἱερωσύνης (priesthood) regarding the Mass-sacrifice. Wrongly indeed! For α) that offering of bread and wine was by no means a priestly and sacrificial action, but was only civil, to refresh and restore the strength of Abraham; for Melchizedek did not offer these gifts to God, but to Abraham, and every sacrifice ought to have been consecrated to God alone, and not even so does a sacrifice exist: הַמּוֹצִיא (the one bringing out), or הַבִּיא (the one bringing), but the verb הוֹצִיא (he brought out) is used, which is never accustomed to be used of sacrifices to be offered to God, β) much less is it to be thought that the sacrifice was piacular, of which kind none can exist without the shedding of blood, Heb. IX, 22. γ) Melchizedek is called a priest, not on account of the offered bread and wine, if indeed that action is distinguished from the name of priest by the Athnach accent, but by reason of the blessing, Gen. XIV, 18. Wherefore Paul, certainly the best interpreter, when he is entirely occupied with explaining that type, passes over that action in silence, and mentions nothing except the blessing, Heb. VII, 1. δ) Christ is compared with the Aaronic priests in that he himself performed a bloody sacrifice, Heb. IX, 12. 24. - 26. and indeed in such a way that that, once performed and perfected, is not to be repeated ever, let alone often, nay, even on any day, Heb. X, 10. 12. 17.

The Arminians argue: I. Whoever descends from Adam, he can sin: for Adam, though most holy, was not immune to the power of sinning: But Christ, etc. Therefore. Resp. Whoever descends from Adam by a natural way, he can sin; I concede this. But Christ descended from Adam not by a natural way, of natural propagation, but by a supernatural way, by the power of the supervening promise, Gen. III, 15.

III. Whoever is tempted, comforted in temptation, and has prayed against the cup of temptation, he is not simply impeccable: But Christ, etc. Matth. IV, 1. Luc. XXII, 43. Therefore. Resp. The temptation of Christ does not presuppose his own sinfulness, but the external impudence of the devil, and it yields to Christians a comforting hope of victory, and an example of strenuous battle against the devil. The angelic comfort was not done to prevent some moral instability of Christ, but to support the infirmity of his nature in the highest degree of humiliation. Nor does the prayer against the cup, being conditional and tempered to the will of the Father, argue a power of sinning; but it demonstrates the highest conformity with the will of the Father. For Christ did not resist the draining of the cup absolutely, but with the condition of some other mode of redeeming the human race, through the divine and infinite power of the person.

The Socinians conclude: Whoever did not exist from eternity, he is not an eternal priest: But Christ the man, etc. Therefore. Resp. Christ the man did not indeed exist from eternity naturally, or entity-wise, as to substance; yet he existed from eternity morally, by virtue of the divine decree and foreknowledge, i.e., from eternity Christ was foreseen by God as the impulsive and meritorious cause, moving God to receive sinners into favor.

Latin:

Melchisedeciani.

2) Vetus Testamentum differt etiam a nouo, quotidie repetitis & plus quam semel factis oblationibus: Ergo repetita quotidie, & plus quam semel facta oblatio in N. T. locum habere nequit. Antecedens liquet ex Hebr. VII, 27. Christus semel seipsum obtulit, c. X, 14. Christus vna oblatione consummauit in perpetuum eos, qui sanctificantur.

3) Christus non est sacerdos secundum ordinem Aaronis, in quo sacerdotium transferebatur ad successores, sed secundum ordinem Melchisedech, qui nec antecessores, nec successores in sacerdotio habebat. Hebr. VIII, 11. 12. 15. Prob. d.

Hebr. VII, 3. Filius Dei manet sacerdos in aeternum. Fructus sacerdotii Christi extenditur in retro lapsa, & futura saecula, siue meritum sacerdotis Christi valet retrorsum & antrorsum.

Prob. e. Nos decebat sacerdos princeps sanctus, innoxius, impollutus, separatus a peccatoribus, excelsior caelis factus, Hebr. VII, 26. Christus tentatus est per omnia, secundum similitudinem (communis hominum fortis), excepto peccato, Hebr. IV, 15.

Antithesis est 1) Pontificiorum, negantium, Christum esse sacerdotem N. T. vnicum, proprie dictum. 2) Arminianorum, statuentium, Christum esse sacerdotem non simpliciter impeccabilem, seu ab omni peccandi potentia immunem (*). 3) Socinianorum, aeternum Christi sacerdotium infitiantium.

Pontificii sequenti ratione arguunt: Christiani dicuntur sacerdotes, Apoc. I, 6. E. Christus non est sacerdos vnicus N. T. Resp. Christiani dicuntur sacerdotes metaphorice, ob sacrificia εὐχαριστικὰ, precum & laudis; at Christus est sacerdos proprie dictus, ob sacrificium ἱλαστικὸν, expiatorium, quod Christus semel obtulit, Hebr. VII, 27.

Instantia. Christus summus sacerdos semel quidem obtulit sacrificium cruentum: sed sacerdotum subordinatorum est, saepius offerre sacrificium incruentum, vt cruentum illud sacrificium, salutis acquisitiuum, iterum iterumque applicetur. Resp. Sacrificium Christi, in ara crucis oblatum, applicatur non per aliud sacrificium, sed per verbum & sacramenta.

Melchisedecus autem incruentum Deo obtulerit sacrificium, idque piaculare, quippe panem & vinum, Gen XIV, 18. Ita illi opinantur eo prorsus consilio, vt suae ἱερωσύνης, de sacrificio Missatico seruiant. Perperam sane! Etenim α) oblatio illa panis & vini nequaquam fuit actio sacerdotalis & sacrificialis, sed fuit tantum ciuilis, ad recreandas reficiendasque Abrahami vires; non enim Deo, sed Abrahamo haec dona obtulit Melchisedecus, omne autem sacrificium Deo vni debebat esse consecratum, ac ne ita quidem sacrificium exstat: הַמּוֹצִיא, aut הַבִּיא, sed adhibetur verbum, הוֹצִיא, nunquam de sacrificiis, Deo offerendis, vsurpari solitum, β) multo minus est existimandum, sacrificium fuisse piaculare, cuiusmodi nullum esse potest, sine profuso sanguine, Hebr. IX, 22. γ) Melchisedecus appellatur sacerdos, non propter oblatum panem vinumque, si quidem ista actio per accentum Athnach a nomine sacerdotis distinguitur, sed ratione benedictionis, Gen. XIV, 18. Quo circa Paullus, optimus certe interpres, cum totus in eo versatur, vt typum illum explicet, illam actionem tacendo praeterit, nec, nisi benedictionem, commemorat, Hebr. VII, 1. δ) Christus cum sacerdotibus Abaronicis comparatur eo, quod cruentum ipse sacrificium confecerit, Hebr. IX, 12. 24. - 26. & ita quidem, vt istud, semel peractum perfectumque, non sit vnquam iterandum, nedum saepe, immo quouis etiam die, repetendum, Hebr. X, 10. 12. 17.

Arminiani argumentantur: I. Quicunque descendit ab Adamo, ille potest peccare: nam Adamus sanctissimus non fuit immunis a peccandi potentia: Atqui Christus &c. Ergo. Resp. Quicunque ab Adamo descendit via naturali, is potest peccare; concedo. At Christus descendit ab Adamo non via naturali, propagationis naturalis, sed supernaturali, vi supervenientis promissionis, Gen. III, 15.

III. Quicunque tentatur, in tentatione confortatus, calicemque tentationis deprecatus est, is non simpliciter est impeccabilis: Atqui Christus &c. Matth. IV, 1. Luc. XXII, 43. Ergo. Resp. Tentatio Christi non supponit ipsius peccabilitatem, sed externam diaboli impudentiam, ceditque christianis in solatiferam spem victoriae, & in exemplum pugnae strenuae aduersus diabolum. Confortatio angelica non facta fuit ad praecauendam quandam labilitatem Christi moralem, sed ad infirmitatem naturae ipsius in summo exinanitionis gradu suffulciendam. Neque deprecatio calicis, vpote conditionata, & voluntati Patris attemperata, potentiam peccandi arguit; sed summam conformitatem cum voluntate Patris demonstrat. Nec enim calici exhauriendo Christus repugnauit absolute, sed cum conditione alterius cuiusdam modi redimendi genus humanum, per diuinam & infinitam potentiam suppositi.

Socinianii colligunt: Quicunque ab aeterno non exstitit, is non est sacerdos aeternus: Atqui Christus homo &c. Ergo. Resp. Christus homo non quidem ab aeterno exstitit naturaliter, seu entitatiue, qua substantiam; exstitit tamen ab aeterno moraliter, vi decreti & praescientiae diuinae, i. e. ab aeterno Christus praevisus est a Deo, vt causa impulsiua & meritoria, mouens Deum ad peccatores in gratiam recipiendos.


### Q. LXXII: Q. LXXIV. By what acts is the priesthood of Christ completed?

Q. LXXIV. By what acts is the priesthood of Christ completed?

The priesthood of Christ is completed by two acts, satisfaction and intercession. Prob. The office of the priests of the O. T. consisted 1) in the offering of an expiatory sacrifice; 2) in intercession for the people, that God might forgive them: thus Christ gave himself for us as an offering and a sacrifice, for a sweet-smelling savor, Eph. V, 2. and he intercedes for us. Rom. VIII, 34.

Q. LXXV. What is the satisfaction of Christ?

Satisfaction is an act of the priestly office, by which Christ, by divine decree, through most consummate obedience, active and passive, satisfied divine justice, which had been injured by the sins of men, to the praise of divine justice and mercy, and the acquisition of our righteousness and salvation.

Obs. 1. Satisfaction is not a biblical word, but an ecclesiastical one, of which, however, synonyms exist in the sacred code, namely ἱλασμὸς, propitiation for the sins of the whole world, 1 Jo. II, 2. καταλλαγὴ, reconciliation, Rom. V, 10., ἀπολύτρωσις, redemption, Eph. I, 7., payment of the λύτρον (ransom), Matth. XX, 28. For that redemption denotes the payment of a price, which is sufficient, for a captive, and that reconciliation of God with men is described in the scriptures in such a way that it is evident it was not made without a λύτρον, which divine justice demanded from the mediator. LXXVI. Do the satisfaction and merit of Christ signify the same thing? Satisfaction and the merit of Christ are indeed inseparably joined, yet they differ in diverse respects.

Proof. For 1): Satisfaction precedes, merit follows: for by having performed satisfaction, Christ merited righteousness and eternal life . 2) Satisfaction is made to God, and to His justice: but Christ merited salvation not for God, but for us . 3) Merit, generally speaking, precedes the order toward a reward, satisfaction toward compensating for an injury.

Therefore, Christ compensated by His satisfaction for the injury brought upon God, expiated iniquity, paid the debt, and freed us from eternal punishments: but by His merit He acquired for us righteousness and eternal salvation. 4) The satisfaction of Christ is the payment of our debts, by which we were bound to God: but merit arises from the fulfillment of the law and unmerited suffering. 5) The acts of Christ's humiliation are simultaneously satisfactory and meritorious: the acts of exaltation are only meritorious, if merit is viewed broadly.

Cf. D. FEVRBORN. syntagm. I. p. III, dissert. VIII. Q. LXXVII. To whom did Christ make satisfaction? Christ made satisfaction to God, one and three , infinite , just and wrathful , truthful , wise and merciful .

Proof a. Because God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit had been offended by sin, Ps. 5:5. The triune God had to be expiated.

Observe that Christ in a certain respect made satisfaction to Himself.

For insofar as Christ made satisfaction as mediator, He is regarded as the God-man (θεάνθρωπος): but insofar as He Himself also demands satisfaction, He must be viewed precisely as God, the author and avenger of the law, just by essence. Proof b. The infinite God had been injured, on account of whose offense sin is said to have infinite guilt (not formally, for thus it receives more and less: but objectively).

For the greater the dignity of the person violated, the greater the offense. But here an infinite person was violated. Proof c. The wrath of the most just judge, God, was kindled by the sins of men: For the wrath of God is revealed, provoked from heaven against all impiety and injustice of men, Rom. 1:18.

Wherefore the most just judge could not but avenge evil, either in the sinner himself, or in his sponsor.

Proof d. The most truthful God willed that the threatening decree against Adam and his posterity should stand, Gen. 2:17: You shall die the death. Proof e.

The wisdom and mercy of God shine forth most greatly from the admirable satisfaction of the mediator, by the most precious ransom (τῷ λύτρῳ) most wisely devised, and most mercifully decreed and accepted.

From these divine attributes a most valid argument is born: Whatever judge is of infinite majesty, and hostile to the sins of men, and has threatened to justly avenge the same, to Him satisfaction must be made by an infinite ransom, most wisely devised and most acceptable: But God is such a judge, etc. Therefore [].

Quest.

Latin:

Quæst. LXXIV. Quibus actibus absoluitur sacerdotium Christi?

Sacerdotium Christi absoluitur duobus actibus, satisfactione, & intercessione. Prob. Officium sacerdotum V. T. constabat 1) in oblatione sacrificii expiatorii; 2) in intercessione pro populo, vt Deus ipsi condonaret: ita Christus seipsum tradidit pro nobis oblationem & sacrificium, in odorem fragrantiae, Eph. V, 2. & intercedit pro nobis. Rom. VIII, 34.

Quæst. LXXV. Quid est satisfactio Christi?

Satisfactio est actus officii sacerdotalis, quo Christus, ex decreto diuino, consummatissima obedientia, actiua & passiua, iustitiae diuinae, peccatis hominum laesae, satisfecit, in laudem iustitiae & misericordiae diuinae, & acquisitionem nostrae iustitiae atque salutis.

Obs. 1. Satisfactio non est vox biblica, sed ecclesiastica, cuius tamen synonyma exstant in sacro codice, nempe ἱλασμὸς, propitiatio pro peccatis totius mundi, Io. II, 2. καταλλαγὴ, reconciliatio, Rom. V, 10., ἀπολύτρωσις, redemtio, Eph. I, 7., solutio τοῦ λύτρου, Matth. XX, 28. Nam redemtio ista solutionem pretii, quod satis est, pro captiuo denotat, & reconciliatio illa Dei cum hominibus, ita describitur in scripturis, vt constet eam non sine λύτρῳ, quod diuina iustitia a mediatore poposcerit, factam esse . LXXVI. Num satisfactio & meritum Christi idem uotant? Satisfactio, & meritum Christi sunt quidem inseparabiliter coniuncta, diuersis tamen respectibus differunt. Prob.

Nam 1): Satisfactio antecedit, meritum consequitur: Praestita enim satisfactione, iustitiam & vitam aeternam promeruit Christus . 2) Satisfactio fit Deo, eiusque iustitiae: At non Deo, sed nobis Christus promeruit salutem . 3) Meritum, generatim loquendo, praecedit ordinem ad mercedem, satisfactio ad iniuriam compensandam. Compensauit igitur Christus satisfactione sua iniuriam Deo illatam, iniquitatem expiauit, debitum exsoluit, & a poenis aeternis nos liberauit: merito autem suo nobis iustitiam & salutem aeternam acquisiuit.

4) Satisfactio Christi est exsolutio nostrorum debitorum, quibus Deo eramus obstricti: meritum autem oritur ex impletione legis & passione indebita. 5) Actus exinanitionis Christi sunt simul satisfactorii & meritorii: actus exaltationis sunt tantum meritorii, si meritum late spectetur. Conf.

D. FEVRBORN. syntagm. I. p. III, dissert. VIII. Quaest. LXXVII. Cui Christus satisfecit? Christus satisfecit Deo vnitrino , infinito , iusto & irato , veraci , sapienti & misericordi .

Prob. a. Quia Deus Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. peccato offensus erat Ps. V, 5. E. Deus trinus ex piandus erat.

Obferues, quod Christus certo respectu sibi ipsi satisfecerit.

Quatenus enim Christus satisfecit, vt mediator, respicitur vt θεάνθρωπος: at quatenus ipse etiam satisfactionem postulat, praecise vt Deus, auctor & vindex legis, per essentiam iustus, intuendus est. Prob. b. Laesus erat Deus infinitus, ob cuius offensam peccatum dicitur habere culpam infinitam (non formaliter, sic enim recipit maius & minus: sed obiective).

Quo maior enim est dignitas personae violatae, eo maior offensa. Sed hic violata est persona infinita. Prob. c. Dei iudicis iustissimi ira erat exarfa peccatis hominum: Reuelatur enim ira Dei, prouocata de caelo super omnem impietatem & iniustitiam hominum, Rom. I, 18.

Quare non poterat non iudex iustissimus malum vindicare, vel in ipso peccatore, vel in eius sponsore. Prob. d. Deus veracissimus decretum comminatorium in Adamum, ciusque posteros constare voluit, Gen.

II, 27.: Morte morieris. Prob. e. Sapientia & misericordia Dei maxime ex admiranda mediatoris satisfactione elucet, τῷ λύτρῳ pretiosissimo sapientissime inuento, & misericordissime decreto atque acceptato.

Nascitur ex his attributis diuinis argumentum validissimum: Quicunque iudex est infinitae maiestatis, & infensus peccatis hominum, eademque iuste vindicare comminatus est, illi lytro infinito, sapientissime inuento & maxime acceptabili satisfaciendum est: Atqui Deus est iudex &c.

Ergo [].


### Q. LXXII: By what means did Christ satisfy the Triune God? Christ satisfied by active and passive obedience

By what means did Christ satisfy the Triune God?

Christ satisfied by active and passive obedience. By active obedience, Christ most exactly fulfilled the divine law in our stead, so that penitent sinners, applying this vicarious fulfillment of the law to themselves by true faith, might be reckoned righteous before God the Judge . By passive obedience, Christ transferred the sins of the whole world onto Himself and voluntarily paid the penalties due to them, by shedding His most precious blood and undergoing a most ignominious death for all sinners, so that for those believing in Christ the Redeemer, sins might not be imputed unto eternal punishment .

Proof a. 1) From Gal. IV, 4. 5. When the fullness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons.

Obs. a) The discourse is concerning Christ the θεάνθρωπος (God-man): for He is called the Son of God born of a woman in the fullness of time. b) The law, to which He is subject, is understood as both universal, or moral, and particular, i.e., ceremonial and forensic, to which Christ is subject, not for Himself, out of debt or obligation, but for us out of mere grace, since He is Lord of the law, Mark II, 28. c) The end, or effect, is both our redemption and the reception of spiritual sonship.

We argue:

Whoever is the θεάνθρωπος, and thus the Lord of the law, and fulfilled the law to the end that we might be rendered sons of God, He satisfied divine justice for us: But Christ is such, etc.

Therefore. 2) Rom. X, 4. Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth, cf. Matt. V, 17. Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets:

I am not come to destroy, but to fulfill. We conclude: Whoever is the end of the law, not by destroying it, but by fulfilling it, so that the end of that fulfillment, namely righteousness, might redound unto believers, He satisfied divine justice in our place: But Christ is such, etc.

Therefore. Proof b.

Penal satisfaction is either proper or vicarious. The former is performed by the guilty party himself, the debtor of the penalty; the latter by another, in his stead.

We are not now speaking of proper satisfaction.

If vicarious penal satisfaction is viewed a) formally, there is required 1) substitution, by which another is put in the place of the debtor, and the transfer of guilt, or the imputation of another’s crime; 2) the paying of penalties, in such a way that [the substitute] would not be 1) entirely unfit for knowing and holily observing divine laws, and for feeling the vengeance of an angry Deity; or 2) already obligated to provide obedience to the laws and to undergo penalties (for thus he would not have provided a foreign, or vicarious, satisfaction, but entirely his own, due by himself); or 3) not a participant in human nature, and thus not capable of the duties which are appropriate to human nature, nor of the penalties which are denounced against depraved men; or finally 4) not fit to expiate all sins, and to reconcile the whole multitude of men to God, to appease God, who is infinitely just.

Therefore, four properties are required for this satisfaction: Our Sponsor, if there were to be one, had to be he who 1) enjoyed intellect and free will, 2) was obligated to no laws, and much less already liable to the guilt of sin and penalty, 3) assumed human nature, 4) possessed infinite power.

From these, a necessary conclusion is drawn: The suitable subject could be neither any thing lacking the use of reason (for requirement 1 is missing, along with the others, cf.

Heb. X, 4.

1 Pet. I, 18.); nor any man, as man, and much less one who is guilty of sin (for requirements 2 and 4 are lacking); nor any angel (for requirements 2, 3, and 4 are repugnant); nor any of created things, even if it were the most excellent of all (against requirements 2, 3, and 4);

Therefore, this was valid only for the θεάνθρωπος, the Lord of the law Himself, Mark II, 28, who of His own accord took upon Himself all our obligation, Heb.

X, 7.

luitio, which a surrogate, or sponsor, pays in the place of a debtor: Finally considered, let it be that payment of a penalty for the purpose of obtaining the absolution of the debtor, so that he may be pronounced immune from guilt and punishment. It is easy to demonstrate that these requirements of true satisfaction concur in the satisfaction of Christ.

1) Christ was substituted in the place of all sinners, and transferred their crimes onto himself. Paul teaches this openly, a) 2 Cor. V, 21. Him, who had not known sin (inherently), God made sin (imputatively) ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, for us, so that we might be rendered the righteousness of God in him. Obs. Sin, repeated a second time in this apostolic saying, denotes a sinner imputatively as such, and consequently a sacrifice for sin. b) Gal. III, 13. Christ redeemed us from the curse, having been made ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν κατάρα, a curse for us. E. Christ, substituted for sinners, devolved their guilt upon himself (*).

2) Christ pays the penalties of our sins. a) Christ is said to bear our sins, Is. LIII, 4. He bore our diseases, and carried our pains: 1 Pet. II, 24. He himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree. Conf. Jo. I, 29. To bear, or to carry sin, is to take the penalties of sin upon oneself, and thus to satisfy by the payment of penalties for sin (**). He who bore the sins of men, he pays the penalty owed for sins, and …satisfies divine vindicatory justice: But Christ did so, etc. Therefore. b) Christ transferred the penalties of our sins onto himself: because he was pierced for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities, Is. LIII, 5. delivered unto death, Rom. IV, 25. died for our sins, Gal. I, 4. 1 Cor. XV, 3. 1 Petr. III, 18. Hebr. X, 12. Since therefore death is the wages of sin, Rom. VI, 23. it is easily gathered that Christ derived upon himself the punishments merited by the sins of men. c) The same is proven by the places of Scripture in which Christ is said to have been offered, or to have offered himself for our sins, and to be that unique sacrifice which was foreshadowed by the expiatory sacrifices of the Old Testament. For just as the sacrifices of the Old Testament offered for sins were expiatory on account of the unique sacrifice of Christ: so the thing itself speaks that the sacrifice of Christ is of itself expiatory and satisfactory for sins. Christ was offered once, to bear the sins of many, says the Apostle, Heb. IX, 28. and ch. X, 12. He, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins, sat down forever at the right hand of God.

3) Christ paid the punishments owed for sins, so that the sinner might be absolved from the punishments. For Christ gave his soul (λύτρον) as a price of redemption for many, Matt. XX, 28. Christ gave himself (ἀντίλυτρον) as a price of redemption for all, 1 Tim. II, 6. Therefore we have been reconciled to God through the death of his Son, Rom. V, 10. and we are cleansed from sins by the blood of Christ, 1 John I, 1c. we are washed, Rev. I, 5. so that we might have in his blood the remission of sins, Eph. II, 10. and be justified through the redemption made in Christ Jesus, Rom. III, 24. But he who, with the ransom (λύτρῳ) paid, freed the guilty one from temporal and eternal punishment, from both guilt and penalty, so that he might have remission of sins and be reputed just before the divine tribunal, he truly satisfied divine justice for him: But Christ did so, etc. Therefore.

This antithesis was once that of Photinus, Abelard, and today it is that of the Socinians, Schwenckfeldians, and Weigelians, who deny the satisfaction of Christ for our sins, relying on the following arguments. I. The name of satisfaction is not found in the Holy Scriptures: Therefore, the satisfaction of Christ is not to be believed. Resp. Although the word 'satisfaction' does not exist in the Holy Scriptures, we have already shown that the thing signified is nevertheless contained in them. (*)

II. Whatever a man can perform, God can do much more (otherwise he would be more impotent than man): But man can remit sin without satisfaction: Therefore.

Resp. 1) The question here is not what God could have done absolutely (namely, whether He could have remitted sins without satisfaction), but what He willed, and how He revealed His will concerning the pardoning of sins. If sins could have been pardoned to us without the intervention of satisfaction, it is credible that the most wise God would have spared His only-begotten Son, and would not so easily, and with no urgent necessity, have subjected Him for our sake to such torments and a most ignominious death. 2) Resp. to the major. a) Whatever man can perform, without any note of imperfection, God can do much more; I grant this. But not everything that man does because of some imperfection can God do. Man moves from place to place, eats, drinks; God, the most pure Spirit, cannot do that. Man remits because he himself is a sinner. If he is adorned with any justice, that justice is mutable. But God is most perfectly holy, and His justice is natural. b) Whatever a private man can do, a universal judge can also do; I deny this. For a private man can remit injuries without satisfaction, but saving the right of a superior. But who is superior to God? A judge cannot justify a sinner without satisfaction, saving justice: "He that justifieth the wicked, is an abomination to Jehovah," Prov. 17:15. "Thine eye shall not pity," Deut. 13:8. "The magistrate beareth not the sword in vain, but for vengeance, that justice may be satisfied," Rom. 13:4.

Latin:

Quo medio Christus Deo triuni satisfecit?

Christus satisfecit obedientia activa & passiva. Obedientia activa Christus legem divinam nostri vice exactissime implevit, vt hanc impletionem legis vicariam peccatores poenitentes vera fide sibi applicantes, coram iudice Deo iusti reputentur . Obedientia passiva Christus totius mundi peccata in se transtulit, & poenas iis debitas vltro luit, sanguinem suum pretiosissimum fundendo, & mortem ignominiosissimam pro omnibus peccatoribus obeundo, vt credentibus in redemptorem Christum peccata ad aeternam poenam non imputentur .

Prob. a. 1) Ex Gal. IV, 4. 5. Quando venit plenitudo temporis, misit Deus filium suum natum ex muliere, factum sub lege, vt illos, qui sub lege erant, redimeret, vt adoptionem filiorum acciperemus.

Obs. a) Sermo est de Christo θεάνθρωπος: dicitur enim Filius Dei in plenitudine temporis natus ex muliere. b) Lex, cui subiectus est, intelligitur tum vniversalis, seu moralis, tum particularis, i. e. caerimonialis & forensis, cui Christus subiectus est, non pro se, ex debito aut obligatione, sed pro nobis ex mera gratia, cum fit Dominus legis, Marc.

II, 28. c) Finis, seu effectus est tum redemtio nostra, tum receptio filiationis spiritualis.

Argumentamur: Quicunque est θεάνθρωπος, atque adeo Dominus legis, & eo fine legem implevit, vt filii Dei redderemur, ille pro nobis iustitiae divinae satisfecit: Atqui Christus &c.

Ergo. 2) Rom. X, 4. Finis legis Christus, in iustitiam omni credenti, conf. Matth. V, 17. Ne existimetis, quod venerim soluere legem & prophetas!

Non veni dissoluere, sed implere. Colligimus: Quicunque est finis legis, hanc non soluendo, sed implendo, vt in credentes illius impletionis finis, nempe iustitia, redundet, ille nostri loco iustitiae divinae satisfecit: Atqui Christus &c.

Ergo.

Prob. b. Satisfactio poenalis est vel propria, vel vicaria. Illam praestat reus ipse, poenae debitor: hanc alius, vice illius.

De satisfactione propria nobis iam sermo non est.

Ad satisfactionem poenalem vicariam si a) formaliter spectetur, requiritur 1) surrogatio, qua in debitoris locum alius substituitur, & translatio culpae, siue criminis alieni imputatio; 2) poenarum luitio, modi, quod aut 1) prorsus non aptum esset ad cognoscendum sancteque obseruandum leges diuinas, ac sentiendum vindictam irati Numinis; aut 2) ipsum iam esset obligatum ad praestandam legibus obedientiam, & perferendas poenas (ita enim non alienam, siue vicariam, sed omnino suam, per se debitam, praestitisset satisfactionem); aut 3) non esset humanae naturae particeps, adeoque non capax tum officiorum, quae & quatenus humanae naturae conueniunt, tum poenarum, quae & quatenus hominibus deprauatis sunt denuntiatae; aut denique 4) non esset idoneum ad expianda peccata omnia, & reconciliandum Deo vniuersam hominum multitudinem, ad placandum Deum, infinite iustum.

Ergo quatuor proprietates sunt, ad hanc satisfactionem requisitae: Sponsor noster, si quis esset, debebat is esse, qui 1) intellectu & libera voluntate gauderet, 2) nullis esset legibus obligatus, multo autem minus reatui culpae & poenae iam obnoxius, 3) humanam naturam adfumeret, 4) infinita vi polleret.

Ex his necessaria efficitur consecutio: Subiectum idoneum esse poterat nec vlla res, rationis vsu carens (deest enim requis.

1. vna cum reliquis, conf. Hebr. X, 4.

1 Pet. I, 18.); nec vllus homo, quatenus homo, multo autem minus, quod est peccati reus (deficit enim requis. 2. & 4.); nec vllus angelus (repugnat enim requis. 2. 3. & 4.); nec vlla rerum creatarum; etiam si esset omnium praestantissima (contra requis.

2. 3. & 4.); E. id valebat vnus θεάνθρωπος, ipse legis Dominus, Marc.

II, 28. qui sua sponte omnem nostram obligationem in se suscepit, Hebr. X, 7.

luitio, quas surrogatus vas, aut sponsor, loco debitoris, persoluit: Finaliter considerata, sit illa poenæ persolutio ad impetrandam absolutionem debitoris, vt is a culpa & poena immunis pronuntietur. Hæc requisita veræ satisfactionis concurrere in satisfactione Christi, demonstratu procliue est.

1) Christus in locum omnium peccatorum surrogatus est, eorumque crimina in se transtulit. Aperte id docet Paullus, a) 2 Cor. V, 21. Eum, qui non nouerat peccatum (inhæsiue), Deus ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, pro nobis, peccatum fecit (imputatiue), vt nos redderemur iustitia Dei in ipso. Obs. Peccatum, altera vice repetitum in hoc dicto apostolico, notat peccatorem imputatiue talem, & consequenter hostiam pro peccato. b) Gal. III, 13. Christus nos redemit ab exsecratione, factus ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν κατάρα, pro nobis exsecratio. E. Christus peccatoribus surrogatns culpam eorum in se deuoluit (*).

2) Christus luit pœnas peccatorum nostrorum. a) Christus dicitur portare peccata nostra, Es. LIII, 4. Morbos nostros ille tulit, & dolores nostros portauit: 1 Pet. II, 24. Peccata nostra ipse pertulit in corpore super lignum. Conf. Io. I, 29. Portare, seu ferre peccatum, est, pœnas peccati in se suscipere, atque adeo luitione pœnarum pro peccato satisfacere (**). Qui peccata hominum portauit, is pœnam peccatis debitam luit, & iustitiæ diuinæ vindicatiuæ fatisfecit: Atqui Christus &c. Ergo. b) Pœnas peccatorum nostrorum Christus in se transtulit: quia ille confossus fuit ob præuaricationes nostras, contusus ob iniquitates nostras, Es. LIII, 5. in mortem traditus, Rom. IV, 25. pro peccatis nostris mortuus, Gal. I, 4. 1 Cor. XV, 3. 1 Petr. III, 18. Hebr. X, 12. Cum itaque mors sit stipendium peccati, Rom. VI, 23. ex facili colligitur, quod Christus poenas, peccatis hominum promeritas, in se derivaverit. c) Idem evincunt loca scripturae, in quibus Christus dicitur oblatus, aut se obtulisse pro peccatis nostris, & esse sacrificium illud unicum, quod per sacrificia V. T. expiatoria adumbratum fuit. Vt enim sacrificia V. T. pro peccatis oblata, expiatoria erant, propter Christi sacrificium unicum: ita sacrificium Christi per se expiatorium & satisfactorium esse pro peccatis, res ipsa loquitur. Christus semel oblatus est, ad perferendum multorum peccata, inquit Apostolus, Hebr. IX, 28. & cap. X, 12. Ille postquam unam pro peccatis obtulit hostiam, in perpetuum consedit in dextra Dei.

3) Christus persolvit poenas peccatis debitas, ut peccator a poenis absolveretur. Dedit enim Christus animam suam (λύτρον) pretium redemptionis pro multis, Matth. XX, 28. Christus dedit se ipsum (ἀντίλυτρον) pretium redemptionis pro omnibus, 1 Tim. II, 6. Reconciliati itaque sumus Deo per mortem Filii ipsius, Rom. V, 10. & sanguine Christi a peccatis emundamur, 1 Io. I, 1c. abluimur, Apoc. I, 5. ut habeamus in sanguine ipsius remissionem peccatorum, Eph. II, 10. & iustificemur per redemptionem factam in Christo Iesu, Rom. III, 24. Sed qui, λύτρῳ persoluto, reum temporalis & aeternae poenae a culpa & poena liberavit, ut habeat remissionem peccatorum, & coram tribunali divino iustus reputetur, is pro eo iustitiae divinae vere satisfecit: Atqui Christus &c. Ergo.

Antithesis olim fuit Photini, Abalardi, hodie est Socinianorum, Schwenckfeldianorum & Weigelianorum, qui satisfactionem Christi pro peccatis nostris negant, sequentibus innitentes argumentis. I. Nomen satisfactionis non habetur in sacris litteris: E. satisfactio Christi non est credenda. Resp. Licet vox, satisfactio, non exstet in sacris litteris, rem significatam tamen in illis haberi, iam ostendimus. (*).

II. Quidquid potest homo praestare, id multo magis potest Deus (caeteroqui homine esset impotentior): Sed homo potest sine satisfactione peccatum remittere: E. Resp. (*)

Resp. 1) Non quaeritur hic, quid Deus absolute potuerit (an scilicet potuerit peccata sine satisfactione remittere): sed quid voluerit, & quomodo voluntatem suam de condonandis peccatis revelauerit. Si citra interventum satisfactionis peccata nobis condonari potuissent, credibile est, Deum sapientissimum passurum fuisse Filio suo vnigenito, nec ita facile, nullaque vrgente necessitate, eum nostri causa tantis cruciatibus, mortique ignominiosissimae subiecturum fuisse. 2) Resp. ad maiorem. a) Quidquid homo praestare potest, citra ullam imperfectionis notam, illud multo magis potest Deus; concedo. Sed non quidquid homo ob quandam imperfectionem facit, illud potest facere Deus. Homo de loco in locum mouetur, edit, bibit, illud non potest Deus, Spiritus purissimus. Homo remittit, quia ipse est peccator. Si qua ornatus est iustitia, illa mutabilis est. At Deus est perfectissime sanctus, & iustitia ipsius est naturalis. b) Quidquid potest homo privatus, illud etiam potest facere iudex vniuersalis; nego. Nam homo privatus, iniurias potest remittere sine satisfactione, sed saluo iure superioris. At Deo quis est superior? Iudex sine satisfactione non potest iustificare peccatorem, salua iustitia: Qui iustificat impium, abominatio est Iehouae, Prou. XVII, 15. Non parcet oculus tuus, Deut. XIII, 8. Non frustra magistratus cinctus est gladio, sed ob vindictam, vt iustitia fiat satis, Rom. XIII, 4.


### Q. LXXII: III. Whatever is a debt, that can be remitted without satisfaction: Sins are ὀφειλήματα (debts), or debts: Therefore. The minor is clear…

III. Whatever is a debt, that can be remitted without satisfaction: Sins are ὀφειλήματα (debts), or debts: Therefore. The minor is clear from Matt. 6: 12.

Resp. Distinguish between a pecuniary debt and a blood debt, or offense. The former can be remitted without detriment to the public good out of mere liberality, justice being uninjured; not the latter. Prov. 17: 15.

IV. Whoever is an absolute lord, he can remit offenses without satisfaction; because he does what he wills: But God, etc. Therefore.

Resp. Whoever is an absolute lord, and acts absolutely, without any regard for justice or law, he can remit without satisfaction. But God in the business of justification does not act absolutely, but as a most just judge, who is a law unto Himself, and to whom justice is natural. Hence He set forth His Son as ἱλαστήριον (a propitiation), through faith in His blood, for an ἔνδειξιν δικαιοσύνης (demonstration of His righteousness), Rom. 3: 25.

25. V. Such as our mercy ought to be, such is the mercy of God, Luke 6: 36. But ours ought to be gratuitous, urging no satisfaction, Matt. 18:35: Therefore. Resp. Such as our mercy ought to be, such is the mercy of God, in the thing and in the sincerity of mercy, Matt. 18:35, not in the mode of the thing, or of mercy; otherwise, by the example of God, even a human father could, or ought to, destroy his son, moved by mercy toward the guilty, which would be impious.

VI. God is a king, who remits debts to a servant without satisfaction, Matt. 18:27.

Resp. Even though in that parable there is no mention of the satisfaction of Christ, for the reason that Christ did not wish to declare the whole business of the remission of sins, but only the principal fountain of divine mercy, and to direct it to the confusion of our lack of mercy, on the occasion given by Peter; yet let it suffice that it is proposed in other places of Scripture.

VII. Whatever is impossible with respect to God the Father, that is not to be established: But the satisfaction of the Son of God for sinners is impossible with respect to God the Father: Therefore. The minor is proved. It is impossible for God to lie, Heb. VI, 18. But indeed God has bound himself, that he will not punish one for another; not the father for the son, not the son for the father, Ezek. XVIII, 20. Resp. This passage is cited irrelevantly. For a) the prophet Ezekiel speaks of a son who is a mere man; but Christ is the θεάνθρωπος [God-man]. b) The saying of the prophet is legal, but the passion and death of Christ pertains to the Gospel. The former urges ἀκριβοδίκαιον [strict justice], the highest rigor; the latter shows ἐπιείκειαν [equity], and a tempering of justice and mercy. c) The discourse of the prophet is about personal, or individual sins of the father, not about common ones. For these God is accustomed to visit even upon the children, Exod. XX, 5. Josh. VII, 24. ch. XXI, 20. 2 Sam. XXI, 6.

VIII. Whoever as a judge inflicts capital punishment upon an innocent person for a guilty one, he is neither just nor merciful. According to the mind of the evangelical doctors, God the Father inflicts capital punishment upon the innocent Son for the guilty. Therefore. Resp. The apostle Peter says, 1 Pet. III, 18, Jesus suffered for the unjust. Distinguish therefore a) between God as judge, and man. The latter cannot inflict capital punishment upon an innocent person for a guilty one, since he is not the supreme lord, not the absolute lord of life and death. Indeed, men have power over life delegated only in the case of a capital crime, but God is the supreme arbiter of life. b) Distinguish between an innocent person who is unwilling, and one who is willing; likewise between an innocent person who is simply devoid of all guilt, and one who is a participant in guilt, either by himself or by imputation. Christ, most innocent, was subjected to capital punishment for sinners not unwillingly, but willingly, and he is a participant in human guilt, not indeed by himself, but yet imputatively, not only as a sponsor, but also as a lamb, bearing the sins of the world. Whoever voluntarily bears the sins of another, he transfers that person's punishments onto himself (*).

IX. Whoever loved men before Christ died, his wrath or justice did not need to be satisfied by the death of Christ: But God, etc. John III, 16. Rom. V, 8. Eph. I, 6. Therefore. The major premise is evident: because love and wrath are opposed to each other. One is satisfied by an angry person, not by a friend. Resp. 1) Distinguish between general love and special love. The former is the love of mercy, benevolence, and the ordering of means; the latter is the love of complacency and the conferring of friendship. The former holds a place in God, even when he is somewhat angry at the human race; the latter presupposes God to be appeased. 2) Distinguish between supreme wrath and tempered wrath. The former excludes benevolence, the latter does not. An offended party (e.g., an enemy in war) thinking about reconciling peace can propose conditions of peace, which is a general love of benevolence and placability; but in act he is not appeased, nor does he enter into friendship with the offender, unless satisfaction is made to him.

…X. Whatever cannot become another's, that cannot be handed over to death in place of another: But the life of Christ cannot become the life of a sinner. Therefore. Resp. The life of one cannot become the life of another to happen physically, yet morally and imputatively. Which life, although it is not the same in number, is nevertheless the same in species, and is imputed to another for impunity.…

XI. Whoever has not sustained the same punishment that damnable men were held to sustain, he does not pay their punishment, and thus did not make satisfaction for them: But Christ &c. The Minor is proved: because the punishment of damnable sins is eternal, namely everlasting death: But Christ's death was of three days. Resp. Whoever has not sustained the same punishment that damnable men were held to sustain, nor an equivalent punishment, he could not pay their punishment; I concede. But Christ sustained a punishment equivalent to eternal punishment; for he underwent infernal punishments intensively, as to their force, weight, and substance, although not extensively, as to duration and the accidents of the suffering subjects. He sustained the extremity of torments, not their eternity.

Instance I By understanding we cannot grasp how the three-day death of one man can equal the eternal punishments of many thousands. Resp. The adversaries would understand this, a) if they acknowledged the truly divine and infinite majesty of Christ the God-man, from which the passion and death of the mediator receives infinite force and weight, so that it becomes a λύτρον ἰσάξιον, an equivalent price for the sins of the whole world: b) If they distinguished between the debtor, or the guilty party, upon whom the wrath of God remains, John III, 36, and the sponsor, or surety, who had to taste death in such a way that he would absorb it, 1 Cor. XV, 24. Christ was certainly able, with an infinite price, through the three days of passion, to pay down to the last farthing all that which all men might owe: Therefore he was able to exit after three days. Damned debtors never pay in hell what they owe: Therefore they also never exit.

Instance II The human nature of Christ suffered, which does not have infinite majesty. Resp. God suffered in the human nature of Christ; for he appropriated to himself the passion and death of the flesh, and added to its passion force, value, and weight.

Instance III Christ did not despair: Therefore he did not sustain infernal punishments. Resp. Despair is not a part of infernal torments, but an adjunct of them, and a condition of the damned debtor, who can never pay what he owes.

XII. Whatever obscures the glory of divine grace, that is not to be believed: But satisfaction &c. The Minor is proved because God remits sins to us through the bowels of mercy, Luke I, 77, and we are justified freely, Rom. III, 24. But remission and satisfaction, gratuitous justification and that provoked by some merit, mutually exclude each other. Resp. Gratuitous remission and satisfaction do not mutually exclude each other, but present for consideration a tempering of divine grace and justice. The latter demands punishment either in the guilty party or in his sponsor. Divine grace, however, a) remits sins, without our merit; b) decreed and ordained satisfaction, Rom. V, 8, John III, 16; c) kindly accepted the satisfaction of another; d) derives the same to us, just as if we ourselves had satisfied. Hence it happens that we have remission in the blood of Christ, according to the riches of the grace of God, Eph. I, 7, and are justified freely by the grace of God, through the redemption of Christ, Rom. III, 24.

XIII. Scripture does not say that Christ reconciled God to us, but that we have been reconciled to God by the death of Christ: Therefore God was not angry with us, but we did not love God, but rather pursued him with hatred. Whence it is gathered that God was not reconciled, but that we were converted by the death of Christ, with the hatred of God extinguished, and the love of the same kindled. Resp. Certainly God was angry, which is most evident from the divine threat, Gen. II, 17. But Holy Scripture notably says that we are reconciled to God, because a) God was the offended party, b) man b) sinful man is the offending party, c) the source & origin of reconciliation is found in God, not in the sinner (*).

XIV. If Christ satisfied God the Father for our sins, His mercy towards the human race was greater than the Father's; because He moved the Father to have mercy on us & be reconciled to us: The consequent is absurd: Therefore, the prior is also absurd. Resp. Speculation about the degrees of divine mercy is superfluous. The supreme love of the Father is commended to us in the scriptures, that He did not spare His Son, but delivered Him up for us to death, Rom. VIII, 32. The supreme love of the Son is commended, that He died for enemies, Rom. V, 6. 7. But supreme love admits no degrees.

XV. The passion & death of Christ is an example of patience, Matth. X, 22. charity, Io. XV, 18. most humble obedience, Phil. II, 5. Therefore, it is not a λύτρον, or price of redemption. Resp. Subordinate ends are not to be opposed. The primary end of Christ's passion & death is that it be a λύτρον: the secondary is that it be an example.

XVI. In the O. T. men were justified without a λύτρον, e.g. Abel. Resp. The merit of Christ is valid backward & forward. Abel sacrificing looked with the eye of faith upon τὸν λόγον incarnandum, the lamb slain from the foundation of the world, Apoc. XIII, 8. & Hebr. XI, 4. XVII. The doctrine of satisfaction extinguishes the ardor of piety. Resp. It does not extinguish, but ignites. That which Paul teaches, 2 Cor. V, 15. Christ died for all, so that those who live should not live for themselves, but for Him who died for them & rose again.

IOANN. PISCATOR () denied the satisfaction of Christ through active obedience, rendered to the divine law, whose arguments are: I. Whoever is himself subject to the law cannot satisfy the law in the place of others: But Christ as man &c. Therefore. The Major is evident: because by due obedience we merit nothing. The Minor is proven because Christ as man is a creature; but every creature owes obedience to the creator. (*)

I. Christ, not only as man, but as God-man (θεάνθρωπος), satisfied the divine law; although the human nature of Christ is a creature, it subsists nevertheless in the hypostasis of the Word (τοῦ λόγου), and is a participant of divinity, and thus is not of itself subject to the law.

II. If Christ fulfilled the law in our place, we are not bound to fulfill the same: The latter is false: Therefore the former. Resp. We are not bound to fulfill the law for the sake of satisfaction; we are bound, however, to observe the law to declare faith and to render obedience.

III. Christ by one oblation perfected forever those who are sanctified, Heb. X, 14. Therefore the satisfaction of Christ, by obedience to be rendered to the law, was not necessary.

Resp. The unique oblation of Christ is opposed not to active obedience, but to the repetition of victims, which was commanded in the O.T.

IV. The action of one cannot be the action of another: The fulfillment of the law is the action of Christ: Therefore the fulfillment of the law cannot be our action. Resp. An action is considered either physically, as it is the motion of the agent, or morally, as it is good or evil. Not physically, but morally, the action of one can be the action of another through imputation. Thus the praiseworthy deed of Phinehas, killing the fornicators, was imputed to all the Israelites, that the plague might be averted, Num. XXXV, 8.

V. If Christ satisfied God for us by the holiness of his life, the death of the same will be superfluous: The consequent is false: Therefore the antecedent. The consequence of the major is proven: because, if the fulfillment of the law performed by Christ is imputed to us by God for righteousness, what need will there be for the imputation of the death of Christ? Resp. [The consequence of the major is denied]. For on account of a double end salutary to us, there is need for a twofold satisfaction. We sinners are 1) unjust, on account of contracted guilt, 2) damnable, on account of merited punishment. Christ by suffering and dying, devolved our punishments upon himself, that we might be immune from punishment and damnation; by acting most holily, he fulfilled the law most perfectly in our stead, that he might derive the righteousness redundant from the fulfillment not into himself, but into us.

Latin:

III. Quidquid est debitum, illud sine satisfactione potest remitti: Peccata sunt ὀφειλήματα, seu debita: E. Minor liquet ex Matth. VI, 12.

Resp. Dist. inter debitum pecuniarium, & sanguinarium, seu delictum. Illud citra detrimentum boni publici ex mera liberalitate remitti potest, illaxa iustitia; non hoc. Prou. XVII, 15.

IV. Quicunque est absolutus dominus, ille potest offensas remittere sine satisfactione; quia agit, quod vult: Atqui Deus &c. Ergo.

Resp. Quicunque est absolutus dominus, & absolute agit, nullo habito respectu ad iustitiam, aut legem, ille sine satisfactione potest remittere. At Deus in negotio iustificationis non agit absolute, sed vt iustissimus iudex, qui sibi ipsi lex est, & cui iustitia est naturalis. Hinc Filium suum proposuit ἱλαστήριον, per fidem in sanguine ipsius, eis ἔνδειξιν δικαιοσύνης, Rom. III, 25.

V. Qualis nostra debet esse misericordia, talis est misericordia Dei, Luc. VI, 36. At nostra debet esse gratuita, nullam vrgens satisfactionem, Matth. XVIII, 35: Ergo. Resp. Qualis nostra debet esse misericordia, talis est misericordia Dei, in re & in sinceritate misericordiali, Matth. XVIII, 35. non in modo rei, seu misericordiae; alioqui, exemplo Dei, etiam pater homo filium suum, motus misericordia in reum, posset, aut deberet perimere, quod foret impium.

VI. Deus est rex, qui sine satisfactione seruo debita remittit, Matth. XVIII, 27.

Resp. Etiamsi in parabola illa satisfactionis Christi non fit inentio, eo, quod Christus non totum negotium remissionis peccatorum, sed tantum principalem fontem misericordiae diuinae declarare, & ad confusionem nostrae immisericordiae, occasione a Petro data, dirigere voluit; tamen sufficiat, eam in aliis scripturae locis proponi.

VII. Quidquid respectu Dei Patris est impossibile, illud non est statuendum: At satisfactio Filii Dei pro peccatoribus respectu Dei Patris est impossibilis: E. Minor prob. Impossibile est Deum mentiri, Hebr. VI, 18. At vero obstrinxit se Deus, se non puniturum vnum pro altero; non patrem pro filio, non filium pro patre, Ezech. XVIII, 20. Resp. Locus hic impertinenter citatur. Nam a) propheta Ezechiel loquitur de filio, qui est homo merus; at Christus est θεάνθρωπος. b) Dictum prophetæ est legale, sed passio & mors Christi pertinet ad Euangelium. Illa vrget ἀκριβοδίκαιον, summum rigorem; hoc ostendit ἐπιείκειαν, & temperamentum iustitiæ ac clementiæ. c) Sermo est prophetæ de peccatis personalibus, seu indiuidualibus patris, non de communibus. Nam hæc solet Deus etiam in filiis visitare, Exod. XX, 5. Ios. VII, 24. c. XXI, 20. 2 Sam. XXI, 6.

VIII. Quicunque iudex innoxium capitali afficit supplicio pro nocente, ille neque iustus, neque clemens est. Ex mente doctorum euangelicorum Deus Pater Filium innoxium, pro nocentibus, capitali afficit supplicio. E. Resp. Apostolus Petrus inquit, 1 Petr. III, 18. Iesus passus est pro iniustis. Dist. itaque a) inter iudicem Deum, & hominem. Hic innoxium capitali afficere supplicio non potest, pro nocente, cum non sit summus dominus, non dominus absolutus vitæ & necis. Nimirum homines vitæ potestatem delegatam habent tantum in casu delicti capitalis, Deus vero supremus est arbiter vitæ. b) Dist. inter innoxium nolentem, & volentem; item inter innoxium omnis culpæ simpliciter exsortem, & vel per se, vel per imputationem culpæ participem. Christus innocentiffimus capitali supplicio affectus est pro peccatoribus non inuitus, sed volens, estque culpæ humanæ particeps non quidem per se, attamen imputatiue, non tantum vt sponsor, sed etiam vt agnus, portans peccata mundi. Qui alterius peccata vltro portat, is illius supplicia in se transfert (*).

IX. Quicunque homines dilexit prius, quam Christus moreretur, illius iræ aut iustitiæ morte Christi non fuit satisfaciendum: Atqui Deus &c. Ioann. III, 16. Rom. V, 8. Eph. I, 6. E. Maior constat: quia dilectio & ira sibi opponuntur. Irato, non autem amico, satisfit. Resp. 1) Distingu. inter dilectionem generalem, & specialem. Illa est dilectio misericordiæ, beneuolentiæ & mediorum ordinatiua; hæc est complacentiæ & amicitiæ collatiua. Prior locum obtinet in Deo, etiam subirato generi humano; posterior Deum placatum supponit. 2) Dist. inter iram summam, & temperatam. Illa excludit beneuolentiam, non hæc. Potest offensus (v. gr. hostis in bello) de reconcilianda pace cogitans, proponere conditiones pacis, quod est amor generalis, beneuolentiæ & placabilitatis; actu autem non placatur, aut amicitiam init cum offendente, nisi ipsi fiat satis.

X. Quidquid alterius fieri non potest, illud vice alterius in mortem tradi nequit: At vita Christi non potest peccatoris vita fieri. E. Resp. Vita unius non potest alterius vita fieri fieri physice, attamen moraliter & imputatiue. Quae vita licet non sit eadem numero, est tamen eadem specie, & imputatur alteri ad impunitatem.

XI. Quicunque non eandem sustinuit poenam, quam homines damnabiles sustinere tenebantur, is non luit illorum poenam, adeoque pro ipsis non satisfecit: At Christus &c. E. Minor probatur: quia peccatorum damnabilium poena est aeterna, nempe mors perennis: At Christi mors fuit triduana. Resp. Quicunque non sustinuit poenam eandem, quam homines damnabiles sustinere tenebantur, neque poenam aequipollentem, is non potuit illorum poenam luere; concedo. At Christus sustinuit poenam aequipollentem aeternae poenae; fubiuit quippe poenas infernales intensiue, quoad earum vim, pondus ac substantiam, licet non extensiue, quoad durationem ac subiectorum patientium accidentia. Sustinuit cruciatuum extremitatem, non aeternitatem.

Instantia I Intelligendo consequi non possumus, quomodo mors triduana vnius hominis multorum millium aeternas poenas aequare possit. Resp. intelligerent hoc aduersarii, a) si agnoscerent Christi θεανθρώπου maiestatem vere diuinam & infinitam, a qua vim & pondus infinitum accipit passio & mors mediatoris, vt fit λύτρον ἰσάξιον, pretium aequiualens pro peccatis totius mundi: b) Si distinguerent inter debitorem, siue reum, super quo ira Dei manet, Ioann. III, 36. & sponsorem, vel fideiussorem, qui mortem sic debuit gustare, vt absorberet, 1 Cor. XV, 24. Potuit nimirum Christus infinito pretio, per triduum passionis, ad vltimum quadrantem totum illud exsoluere, quod omnes homines debeant: E. poterat per triduum exire. Debitores damnati nunquam in inferno, quod debent, exsoluunt: E. nunquam etiam exeunt,

Instantia II Humana natura Christi passa est, quae non habet infinitam maiestatem. Resp. Deus in humana Christi natura passus est; quippe qui passionem & mortem carnis sibi appropriauit, eiusque passioni vim, valorem & pondus addidit.

Instantia III Christus non desperauit: Ergo infernales poenas non sustinuit. Resp. Desperatio non est pars cruciatuum infernalium, sed eorum adiunctum, & conditio debitoris damnati, qui nunquam exsoluere potest, quod debet.

XII. Quidquid offuscat gloriam gratiae diuinae, illud non est credendum: At satisfactio &c. E. Minor prob. quia Deus nobis peccata remittit per viscera misericordiae, Luc. I, 77. & iustificamur gratis, Rom. III, 24. At remissio, & satisfactio, iustificatio gratuita, & merito quodam prouocata, se mutuo tollunt. Resp. Gratuita remissio, & satisfactio non se mutuo tollunt, sed considerandum exhibent temperamentum gratiae, & iustitiae diuinae. Haec exposcit poenam aut in reo, aut in eius sponsore. Gratia autem diuina a) remittit peccata, sine nostro merito; b) satisfactionem decreuit & ordinauit, Rom. V, 8. Io. III, 16; c) alienam satisfactionem benigne acceperat, d) eandem, perinde ac si nosmet ipsi satisfecissemus, in nos deriuat. Inde fit, vt habeamus remissionem in sanguine Christi, secundum diuitias gratiae Dei, Eph. I, 7. & iustificemur gratis gratia Dei, per redemptionem Christi, Rom. III, 24.

XIII. Scriptura non dicit Christum reconciliasse nobis Deum, sed nos Deo reconciliatos esse morte Christi: E. Deus nobis non fuit iratus, sed nos Deum non amauimus, verum odio eundem prosecuti sumus. Vnde colligitur, Deum non esse reconciliatum, sed nos morte Christi esse conuersos, exstincto odio Dei, & accenso eiusdem amore. Resp. Vtique Deus iratus erat, quod vel maxime patet ex comminatione diuina, Gen. II, 17. Notanter autem S. scriptura dicit, quod nos sumus Deo reconciliati, quia a) Deus erat pars offensa, b) homo b) homo peccator pars offendens, c) fons & origo reconciliationis reperitur in Deo, non in peccatore (*).

XIV. Si Christus Deo Patri satisfecit pro peccatis nostris, maior eius fuit misericordia in genus humanum, quam Patris; quia hunc permouit, vt nostri misereretur & nobis reconciliaretur: Consequens est absurdum: E. & prius. Resp. Speculatio de gradibus misericordiae diuinae superuacanea est. Commendatur nobis in scripturis summa Patris caritas, quod Filio non pepercerit, sed pro nobis in mortem tradiderit, Rom. VIII, 32. Commendatur summa charitas Filii, quod pro inimicis mortuus fuerit, Rom. V, 6. 7. Summus autem amor gradus non admittit.

XV. Passio & mors Christi est exemplum patientiae, Matth. X, 22. charitatis, Io. XV, 18. humillimi obsequii, Phil. II, 5. E. non est λύτρον, aut pretium redemptionis. Resp.
