Fines subordinati non sunt opponendi. Primarius finis passionis & mortis Christi est, vt fit lytrum: secundarius est, vt fit exemplum.

XVI. In V. T. homines iustificati sunt fine lytro, v. gr. Abel. Resp. Meritum Christi valet retrorsum & antrorsum. Abel sacrificans oculo fidei aspexit τὸν λόγον incarnandum, agnum occisum ab origine mundi, Apoc. XIII, 8. & Hebr. XI, 4. XVII. Doctrina de satisfactione ardorem pietatis exstinguit. Resp. Non exstinguit, sed accendit. Id quod Paullus docet, 2 Cor. V, 15. Christus pro omnibus mortuus est, vt qui viuunt, non sibi viuant, sed ei, qui pro ipsis mortuus est, & resurrexit.

Satisfactionem Christi per obedientiam actuam, legi diuinae praestitam, negauit IOANN. PISCATOR (), cuius argumenta sunt: I. Quicunque ipse obnoxius est legi, aliorum loco legi satisfacere nequit: Atqui Christus homo &c. E. Maior patet: quia debito obsequio nihil promeremur. Minor prob. quia Christus homo est creatura; sed omnis creatura obsequium creatori debet. (*)

I. Christus non tantum ut homo, sed ut θεάνθρωπος, legi divinae satisfecit; quamuis humana Christi natura sit creatura, subsistit tamen in hypostasi τοῦ λόγου, & particeps divinitatis est, adeoque non per se obnoxia est legi .

II. Si Christus nostri loco legem implevit, nos ad eandem implendam non obstringimur: Posterius est falsum: E. & prius. Resp. Nos non tenemur legem implere satisfactionis causa; tenemur tamen legem observare ad declarandam fidem & praestandum obsequium.

III. Christus una oblatione consummauit in perpetuum sanctificandos, Hebr. X, 14. E. satisfactio Christi, per obedientiam legi praestandam, non fuit necessaria.

Resp. Vnica oblatio Christi non obedientiae actuae, sed repetitioni victimarum, quae praecepta erat in V. T., opponitur.

IV. Actio unius non potest esse alterius actio: Impletio legis est actio Christi: E. impletio legis non potest esse nostra actio. Resp. Actio consideratur vel physice, prout est motus agentis, vel moraliter, prout est bona, vel mala. Non physice, sed moraliter actio unius potest esse alterius per imputationem. Sic laudabile factum Phineae, occidentis scortantes, imputabatur omnibus Israëlitibus, ut auerteretur plaga, Num. XXXV, 8.

V. Si Christus sanctimonia vitae suae pro nobis Deo satisfecit, mors eiusdem erit superflua: Consequens est falsum: E. & antecedens. Consequentia maioris probatur: quia, si impletio legis a Christo praestita, nobis imputatur a Deo in iustitiam, quid opus erit imputatione mortis Christi? Resp. Consequ. mai. Nam ob duplicem finem nobis salutarem gemina satisfactione opus est. Nos peccatores sumus 1) iniusti, ob contractam culpam, 2) damnabiles, ob promeritam poenam. Christus patiendo & moriendo, nostras in se devoluit poenas, vt essemus immunes a poena & damnatione; sanctissime agendo, legem nostri vice perfectissime implevit, vt redundantem ex impletione iustitiam non in se, sed in nos derivaret.


### Q. LXXIX. Is the death and oblation of Christ on the cross a true sacrifice, so that on account of it Christ may be properly called a

The death of Christ, which he suffered on the altar of the cross, is a true propitiatory sacrifice, on account of which Christ was on this earth a true, properly so-called, and most perfect priest.

Prob. 1) From the Pauline testimony, Eph. V, 2. Christ loved us, and delivered himself for us, an oblation and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savor. At the time when Christ delivered himself to death, at that same time he offered to God a most acceptable sacrifice: But at the time when Christ was affixed to the cross, he delivered himself to death: Therefore. 2) From the Petrine testimony, 1 Ep.

2) From the Petrine testimony, 1 Ep. II, 24. Christ himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree. At the time when our sins were laid upon Christ to be borne upon the wood of the cross, at that same time he was truly made a sacrifice for our sins: But at the time of the passion, etc. E.

3) From the definition of sacrifices which consists in slaughtering, Lev. I, 3. But Christ was slaughtered and killed on earth.

4) From the cleansing of sins, which preceded the ascension into heaven, of which the Apostle speaks, Heb. 1:3: "When Christ had by himself purged our sins, he sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high." The Apostle speaks of the acquisition of the cleansing of sins, which was completed before Christ's session at the right hand of God; the application of the same, however, by which we are made partakers of the remission of sins, continues as long as this fabric of the world shall stand.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, who maintain that the death of Christ was merely a preparation for his priesthood, and that the sacrifice of Christ was not performed on earth, but is only performed in heaven.

Their primary arguments are:

I. Whoever is not a priest on earth could not offer a sacrifice on earth: But Christ, etc. Therefore. The minor premise is established from Heb. 8:4: "For if he were on earth, he should not be a priest." Resp. The words of the Apostle do not exclude the place, but the status of the earthly priesthood, so that the sense is: If Christ were on earth, that is, an earthly and typical priest, he would not be a priest sufficient for our redemption.

II. Just as all those things which the high priest of the Old Testament did in slaughtering the beast, before he entered into the holy of holies, were merely a preparation for the future sacrifice: so also the very affliction and death of Jesus Christ were merely a certain preparation for his sacrifice, which he truly performed upon entering heaven. Resp. The Socinians wander from the truth by a whole heaven. For the priests of the O.T. sacrificed in the holy place, or the first tabernacle, but not in the holy of holies, for in it there was no altar destined for sacrifices. The high priest entered into the holy of holies once, but sacrifices were not offered only once a year. The high priest was already a priest before he entered the holy of holies; so also was Christ before he entered heaven.

Objection: But Christ entered once into the holy place by his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption, Heb. 9:12. Therefore, the offering of the blood of Christ was made in heaven. Resp. Christ the priest entered into the holy place by his blood, but he did not offer the blood as a sacrifice in the holy place. Offering is one thing, the presentation of blood is another. In the O.T., the presentation of blood and the appearing before God in the holy of holies took place after the sacrifice was completed, not the sacrifice itself. Thus also the sacrificial offering of the blood of Christ was made in his passion, Heb. 9:27; but the presentation of the blood was made in heaven, so that Christ now appears in the presence of God for us, i.e., intercedes for us, Heb. 9:14.

III. We have a high priest who has passed through the heavens, Heb. 4:14. Therefore, Christ is a priest in heaven. Resp. We concede that our priest is in heaven for the sake of interceding for us. But it does not follow from this that Christ was not a priest on earth, nor that he did not sacrifice there: just as it does not follow: The prophet Elijah ascended into heaven; therefore, he was not a prophet on earth, but only became a prophet in heaven. The Apostle describes not the time of the priesthood, but the glorious state of our priest.

Latin:

Mors Christi, quam is in ara crucis oppetiuit, est verum sacrificium propitiatorium, propter quod Christus in his terris fuit verus, proprie dictus & consummatissimus sacerdos.

Prob. 1) E testimonio Paullino, Eph. V, 2. Christus dilexit nos, & tradidit seipsum pro nobis, oblationem & sacrificium Deo in odorem suauitatis. Quo tempore Christus se in mortem tradidit, eodem obtulit Deo gratissimum sacrificium: Atqui eo tempore, quo Christus cruci affixus est, se in mortem tradidit: Ergo.

2) E testimonio Petrino, 1 Ep. II, 24. Christus ipse peccata nostra tulit in corpore suo super lignum. Quo tempore imposita sunt Christo peccata nostra ferenda super lignum crucis, eodem vere pro peccatis nostris factus est sacrificium: Atqui tempore passionis &c. E.

3) Ex sacrificiorum ratione quae consistit in mactatione, Leu. I, 3. Sed Christus mactatus & occisus est in terra.

4) Ex mundatione peccatorum, antegressa ascensionem in cælum, de qua Apostolus, Hebr. I, 3. Christus per seipsum mundationem peccatorum postquam fecisset, consedit in dextra maiestatis in altis. Loquitur Apostolus de acquisitione mundationis peccatorum, quæ ante sessionem Christi ad dextram Dei absoluta est; applicatio vero eiusdem, qua participes reddimur remissionis peccatorum, continuatur, donec hæc mundi machina stabit.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, statuentium, mortem Christi fuisse tantum præparationem ad sacerdotium ipsius, & sacrificium Christi non in terris peractum esse, sed peragi demum in cælis.

Quorum potiora argumenta sunt:

I. Quicunque non est sacerdos in terra, in terra non potuit sacrificium offerre: Atqui Christus &c. Ergo. Minor constat ex Hebr. VIII, 4. Siquidem esset super terra, neque sacerdos esset. Resp. Verbis Apostoli non simpliciter locus, sed status terreni sacerdotii excluditur, ut sensus sit: Si Christus esset super terra, sive terrenus typicusque sacerdos, non esset sacerdos nostræ redemtioni sufficiens.

II. Vt omnia ea, quæ pontifex veteris testamenti faciebat in mactanda pecude, priusquam in sanctum sanctorum ingrederetur, apparatio tantum erant ad futurum sacrificium: sic quoque ipsa Iesu Christi afflictio & mors præparatio tantum quædam ad sacrificium ipsius fuere, quod cælum ingressus reipsa perfecit. Resp. Toto cælo Sociniani aberrant a vero. Nam sacrificabant sacerdotes V. T. in sancto, sive tabernaculo priori, at non in sancto sanctorum, quippe in quo non erat altare, sacrificiis destinatum. Semel in sanctum sanctorum ingressus fuit pontifex, at non semel tantum in anno sacrificatum fuit. Pontifex iam sacerdos fuit, antequam sanctum sanctorum ingrederetur; ita & Christus antequam ingrederetur cælum.

Instantia: Sed Christus per proprium sanguinem ingressus est semel in sancta, ita, ut æternam redemtionem invenerit, Hebr. IX, 12. E. oblatio sanguinis Christi in cælo facta est. Resp. Christus sacerdos ingressus est in sancta per sanguinem, sed in sanctis sanguinem in sacrificium non obtulit. Aliud est oblatio, aliud præsentatio sanguinis. In V. T. sanguinis præsentatio & coram Deo comparitio in sancto sanctorum post peractum sacrificium fiebat, non ipsum sacrificium. Sic quoque oblatio sacrificialis sanguinis Christi facta est in passione, Hebr. IX, 27; præsentatio autem sanguinis facta est in cælo, vt appareat nunc Christus in conspectu Dei pro nobis, i. e. intercedat pro nobis, Hebr. IX, 14.

III. Habemus pontificem, qui cælos penetravit, Hebr. IV, 14. E. Christus sacerdos est in cælo. Resp. Concedimus, sacerdotem nostrum esse in cælo, intercedendi pro nobis caussa. At exinde non sequitur, quod Christus non fuerit sacerdos in terra, neque ibi sacrificauerit: sicut non sequitur: Propheta Elias in cælum ascendit: E. non fuit propheta in terra, sed in cælo demum propheta factus est. Apostolus describit non tempus sacerdotii, sed sacerdotis nostri statum gloriosum.


### Quest. LXXX. For whom did Christ satisfy God?

Christ satisfied the triune God for all the sins a) of all men who have fallen into sin b), and for all the punishments of sins c).

Proof a. 1) From the Johannine testimony, 1 Ep. 2:2: "Christ is the propitiation for our sins: and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world." By this statement, the universality of the merit and satisfaction of Christ is most clearly established. For the Apostle proceeds from the commemoration of the faithful to the entire human race, with a very luminous amplification, saying: not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world. Which amplification was indeed most necessary for the solid force of apostolic consolation, lest anyone despair of sins.

& from the salutary fruit of this intercession of the Paraclete, he excludes himself, swept away by the waves of doubt, and presumes. 2) From the Pauline testimony: Christ gave himself for us, that he might deliver us from all iniquity, Tit.

II, 14. Christ redeemed us from all guilt of sin, because he cleanses us from all sin by his blood, 1 John I, 7; and also from all dominion of sin, that having been made free from sin we might serve righteousness, Rom. VI, 18.

Prob. b. 1) From those sayings of Scripture which are manifestly universal. In the O. T., the oracle of Isaiah is clearer than light, c. LIII, 6. All we like sheep have gone astray, we have turned every one to his own way, and the Lord hath laid on him (the Messiah) the iniquity of us all. In the N. Test., the apostolic utterances diffuse no less light: a) Rom. VIII, 32. God spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all: b) 2 Cor. V, 14. If one died for all, then were all dead: c) Hebr. II, 9. Jesus by the grace of God tasted death for every man: d) 1 Tim. II, 6. One mediator of God and men, who gave himself (ἀντίλυτρον) a ransom for all.

2) From those sayings of Scripture which extend the merit of Christ even to the reprobate, and those perishing by their own fault: a) Rom. XIV, 15. Destroy not him with thy meat, for whom Christ died: b) 1 Cor. VIII, 11. And the weak brother shall perish in thy knowledge, for whom Christ died: c) 2 Petr. II, 1. There shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, and deny the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction: d) Hebr. X, 29. Those sinning against the Holy Spirit are said to be sanctified by the blood of the covenant.

Prob. c. 1) Is. LIII, 5. The chastisement of our peace (was) upon him, and with his wound health is given to us. Obs. מוסר denotes chastisement, or affliction: which has the nature of a penalty, on account of guilt either one's own or imputed. It is called the chastisement of peace, because by the chastisement or affliction of Christ peace and impunity were acquired for us, i.e., therefore Christ sustained penalties for the sins of men, so that men might be immune from penalties.

2) Gal. III, 13. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us. A curse is the execratory and damnatory sentence of the divine law, concerning the undergoing of temporal and eternal penalties owed to sin. But Christ was made a curse for us, i.e., accursed, or execrable, through the divine casting, derivation, and imputation of our sins and punishments upon him, to the end that he might redeem us from the curse of the law, i.e., the temporal and eternal penalty which the law denounces, and deliver us by the payment of a price.

The Antithesis is that of Perkins, Piscator, Jansenius, Weigelius, and others, who deny the universality of the satisfaction and merit of Christ; who rely upon the following arguments: I. Christ gave his soul the price of redemption for many, Matth. XX, 28. Therefore not for all. Resp. There is no accurate opposition between all and many. For all men are many. There is therefore no consequence: Christ redeemed many with his blood, therefore a few elect

II. For whom Christ does not pray, for them He has not died: For both intercession and satisfaction are priestly acts, and therefore of equal breadth: But Christ does not pray for all, John 17:9. Therefore. Resp. Distinguish between the general and the special intercession of Christ. The former prays for all, that they may be converted; the latter intercedes for the faithful, that they may be preserved in the acknowledged truth and concord.

III. For whom Christ died, them God the Father loved, Rom. 5:8. But He did not love the reprobate (for how could God love those whom He reprobates?). Therefore. Resp. Distinguish between the love of benevolence and of friendship. For whom Christ died, them God loved with a love of benevolence; in which sense He also loved the reprobate, not as reprobates, but as creatures and men.

IV. For whom Christ died, them He reconciled to the Father and saves, Rom. 5:10. Conf. 2 Cor. 5:14. But Christ did not reconcile the reprobate, nor does He save them: Therefore. Resp. a) The major is two-fold: 1) that they are reconciled for whom Christ died; 2) that they are saved. Reconciliation is understood either by reason of merit, insofar as it is acquired, or by reason of fruit and event, insofar as it is applied unto salvation. If reconciliation is understood in the former sense, the major is granted, and the minor is denied. For Christ is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world (therefore also of the reprobate). If it is understood in the latter sense, the major is denied. Rom. 5:10 is understood as reconciliation admitted and applied. As regards the latter member, or preservation, the constancy of the reconciled grace is required for it, and thus those who are reconciled with saving effect, and strive to remain in the state of grace, are saved.

V. To whom the satisfaction of Christ is not announced, for them Christ did not satisfy: otherwise the satisfaction and merit of Christ would be entirely useless to them. But it is not announced to all, etc. Therefore. The minor is evident: because there are many Gentiles to whom the gospel concerning the death of Christ has not been announced. Resp. For whom the satisfaction of Christ is not announced by the destined will and counsel of God, for them Christ did not die. But, that the satisfaction of Christ is not announced to many Gentiles, that does not happen by the destined will and counsel of God, who simply denies the grace of vocation, but by the fault of men, who reject the word of the gospel, by which the satisfaction of Christ is announced. Acts 13:46.

Acts 13:46. VI. Whoever died for all men, he also died for the damned: But Christ did not die for the damned. Therefore. The minor is clear: because Christ died for those who are capable of eternal salvation, which the damned are not. Resp. The damned are considered either in a divided sense or in a composite sense. In a divided sense, those are called damned who, in the state of the way, having been offered the means of grace, petulantly rejected them, and thus by their own fault brought condemnation upon themselves: in a composite sense, those are called damned who, having received the final sentence, have been cast into the abyss of hell. Christ satisfied God for all men, even for the damned, insofar as they were in the way, and could have escaped condemnation if they had admitted the means of grace.

VII. For whose sake Christ was not sent, for them He did not die. But Christ was not sent for the sake of all men, Matt. 15:24. Therefore. Resp. Distinguish between the priestly and the prophetic office of Christ. The former is universal; the latter is exercised by the διακονίᾳ (ministry) of Christ either immediately or mediately. Christ performed His immediate prophetic function toward the Israelites; the mediate one through the Apostles... toward the Gentiles. For the children had to be fed before the dogs.

VIII. Christ died for the sheep, John 10:15, for the elect, Rom. 8:34. Therefore, not for the goats, not for the reprobate. Resp. Deny the consequence. Christ indeed died is for all, but not for them alone. By the same reasoning one might perhaps infer: The pious shall rise again: Therefore, not the impious.

IX. Christ never acknowledged the reprobate, Matth. VII, 23. Therefore He did not die for them. Resp. Christ never acknowledged the reprobate by a special knowledge; but by general knowledge He knows no man whom He does not recognize.

X. Those for whom Christ died, they receive the remission of sins. But not all men receive the remission of sins. Therefore, the major premise is established from Eph. I, 7. Col. I, 14. where the redemption made by the death of Christ is explained exegetically (ἐξηγητικῶς) through the remission of sins. Resp. Distinguish between the acquisition of the remission of sins and its application. Those for whom Christ died, they, applying to themselves the death of Christ, receive the remission of sins.

Latin:

Christus satisfecit Deo triuni pro omnibus peccatis a) omnium hominum in peccata prolapsorum b), & pro omnibus peccatorum pænis c).

Prob. a. 1) e testimonio Ioanneo, 1 Ep. II, 2. Christus est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris: immo non pro nostris tantum, sed pro totius mundi (peccatis). Hoc dicto vniversalitas meriti & satisfactionis Christi apertissime stabilitur. Nam Apostolus procedit a fidelium commemoratione ad vniuersum genus humanum, luculenta admodum ampliatione, inquiens: non pro nostris tantum, sed & pro totius mundi peccatis. Quæ quidem ampliatio ad solidam consolationis apostolicæ vim pernecessaria erat, ne quisquam peccatorum desperet.

& ab intercessionis huius paracleti fructu salutari sese exclusum, dubitationum fluctibus abreptus, præfumat.

2) E testimonio Paullino: Christus dedit seipsum pro nobis, ut nos liberaret ab omni iniquitate, Tit. II, 14. Redemit nos Christus ab omni peccati reatu, quia sanguine suo nos ab omni peccato emundat, 1 Ioann. I, 7; nec non ab omni peccati dominio, ut liberi facti a peccato serviamus iustitiæ, Rom. VI, 18.

Prob. b. 1) Ex illis scripturæ dictis, quæ manifesto universalia sunt. In V. T. oraculum Iesaianum luce clarius est, c. LIII, 6. Nos omnes quasi oves erravimus, unusquisque in viam suam declinavit, & posuit Dominus in eo (Messia) iniquitatem omnium nostrum. In N. Test. non minus lumen diffundunt eloquia apostolica: a) Rom. VIII, 32. Deus proprio Filio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum: b) 2 Cor. V, 14. Si unus pro omnibus mortuus est, omnes mortui sunt: c) Hebr. II, 9. Iesus gratia Dei pro omnibus gustavit mortem: d) 1 Tim. II, 6. Unus mediator Dei & hominum, qui dedit seipsum (ἀντίλυτρον) pretium redemptionis pro omnibus.

2) Ex illis scripturæ dictis, quæ meritum Christi etiam ad reprobos, & sua culpa pereuntes extendunt: a) Rom. XIV, 15. Ne cibo tuo illum perdas, pro quo Christus mortuus est: b) 1 Cor. VIII, 11. Et peribit frater infirmus in tua scientia, propter quem Christus mortuus est: c) 2 Petr. II, 1. Inter vos erunt pseudo-doctores, qui subinducent hæreses perditionis, & eum, qui mercatus est illos, Dominum abnegantes, inducentes sibi ipsis celerem interitum: d) Hebr. X, 29. Peccantes in Spiritum S. dicuntur sanctificati sanguine fœderis.

Prob. c. 1) Es. LIII, 5. Castigatio nostræ pacis super eo (fuit) & vulnere eius sanitas data est nobis. Obs. מוסר notat castigationem, seu afflictionem: quæ pœnæ rationem habet, ob culpam vel propriam, vel imputatam. Dicitur castigatio pacis, quia castigatione vel afflictione Christi nobis pax & impunitas acquisita est, q. d. ideo Christus ob peccata hominum sustinuit pœnas, vt homines a pœnis essent immunes.

2) Gal. III, 13. Christus nos redemit a maledictione legis, factus pro nobis maledictio. Maledictio est sententia legis divinæ exsecratoria & damnatoria, de subeundis pœnis temporalibus & æternis peccato debitis. Christus autem factus est pro nobis maledictio, i. e. maledictus, vel exsecrabilis, per divinam nostrorum peccatorum & suppliciorum in ipsum coniectionem, derivationem & imputationem, eo fine, vt nos a maledictione legis, i. e. pœna temporali & æterna, quam lex denuntiat, redimeret, et vel soluto pretio liberaret.

Antithesis est Perkinsti, Piscatoris, Iansenii, Weigelii, & aliorum, universalitatem satisfactionis & meriti Christi negantium; qui sequentibus innituntur argumentis: I. Christus dedit animam suam pretium redemptionis pro multis, Matth. XX, 28. Ergo non pro omnibus. Resp. Non est accurata oppositio omnium, & multorum. Nam & omnes homines inulti sunt. Nulla igitur sequela est: Christus sanguine suo redemit multos, ergo paucos electos

II. Pro quibus Christus non rogat, pro iis non est mortuus: Est enim tam intercessio, quam satisfactio actus sacerdotalis, adeoque aequalis latitudinis: At Christus non rogat pro omnibus, Ioann. XVII, 9. Ergo. Resp. Dist. inter intercessionem Christi generalem, & specialem. Illa orat pro omnibus, vt convertantur; hac pro fidelibus interpellat, vt in agnita veritate & concordia feruentur.

III. Pro quibus Christus mortuus est, illos Deus Pater dilexit, Rom. V, 8. At reprobos non dilexit (quomodo enim diligeret Deus eos, quos reprobat?). Ergo. Resp. Dist. inter amorem beneuolentiae, & amicitiae. Pro quibus Christus mortuus est, illos Deus dilexit amore beneuolentiae; qua ratione & reprobos, non qua reprobos, sed qua creaturas & homines dilexit.

IV. Pro quibus Christus est mortuus, eos Patri reconciliauit & seruat, Rom. V, 10. Conf. 2 Cor. V, 14. Atqui reprobos Christus non reconciliauit, nec seruat: Ergo. Resp. a) Maior est bimembris: 1) quod reconciliati sint, pro quibus Christus mortuus est; 2) quod sint seruati. Reconciliatio intelligitur vel ratione meriti, in quantum est acquisita, vel ratione fructus & euentus, quatenus ad salutem est applicata. Si intelligatur reconciliatio priori sensu, conceditur maior, & negatur minor. Nam Christus est propitiatio pro totius mundi (ergo & reproborum) peccatis. Si intelligatur posteriori sensu, negatur maior. Rom. V, 10. intelligitur reconciliatio admissa & applicata. Quod attinet ad posterius membrum, siue conseruationem, ad eam requiritur constantia gratiae reconciliatae, adeoque qui cum salutari effectu sunt reconciliati, & in statu gratiae permanere connituntur, seruantur.

V. Quibus satisfactio Christi non annuntiatur, pro illis Christus non satisfecit: ceteroqui plane inutilis iisdem foret satisfactio & meritum Christi. Atqui non omnibus &c. Ergo. Minor constat: quia multi dantur gentiles, quibus euangelium de morte Christi non est annuntiatum. Resp. Quibus satisfactio Christi non annuntiatur destinata voluntate & consilio Dei, pro illis Christus non est mortuus. At, quod multis gentilibus satisfactio Christi non annuntiatur, id non fit destinata voluntate & consilio Dei, gratiam vocationis simpliciter negantis, sed culpa hominum, qui verbum euangelii, quo satisfactio Christi annuntiatur, repellunt. Act. XIII, 46.

VI. Quicunque mortuus est pro omnibus hominibus, ille etiam mortuus est pro damnatis: At Christus non est mortuus pro damnatis. E. Minor patet: quia Christus pro iis mortuus est, qui aeternae salutis capaces sunt, quales non sunt damnati. Resp. Damnati considerantur vel in sensu diuiso, vel in sensu composito. In sensu diuiso, damnati dicuntur, qui in statu viae media gratiae, quibus satisfactio Christi offertur, petulanter reiecerunt, adeoque propria culpa condemnationem sibi attraxerunt: in sensu composito, damnati dicuntur, qui, finalem adepti sententiam, in barathrum inferni sunt proiecti. Christus satisfecit Deo pro omnibus hominibus, etiam pro damnatis, quatenus erant in via, & condemnationem, si admisissent media gratiae, effugere poterant.

VII. Quorum caussa Christus non est missus, pro iis non est mortuus. At non omnium hominum caussa Christus est missus, Matth. XV, 24. E. Resp. Dist. inter officium Christi sacerdotale, & propheticum. Illud est vniuersale, hoc exercetur διακονίᾳ Christi vel immediate, vel mediata. Christus immediatam functionem propheticam obiuit ad Israelitas; mediatam per Apostolos ...ad gentes. Satiandi enim erant filii prius, quam canes.

VIII. Christus mortuus est pro ouibus, Ioann. X, 15. pro electis, Rom. VIII, 34. E. non pro haedis, non pro reprobis. Resp. Neg. consequentiam. Christus quidem mortuus est pro omnibus, sed non solis. Eadem ratione forte quis colligeret: Resurgent pii: E. non impii.

IX. Christus reprobos nunquam agnovit, Matth. VII, 23. E. pro illis non est mortuus. Resp. Christus reprobos nunquam agnovit, notitia speciali; notitia vero generali nullum hominem non cognoscit.

X. Pro quibus Christus est mortuus, illi accipiunt remissionem peccatorum. At non omnes homines accipiunt remissionem peccatorum. E. Maior constat ex Eph. I, 7. Col. I, 14. ubi redemtio facta morte Christi per remissionem peccatorum ἐξηγητικῶς declaratur. Resp. Dist. inter remissionis peccatorum acquisitionem, & applicationem. Pro quibus Christus est mortuus, illi, applicantes sibi mortem Christi, accipiunt remissionem peccatorum.


### Quaest. LXXXII. Did Christ, as man, merit anything for Himself by His obedience?

Christ by His death did not reconcile the angels to God, neither the good, nor the evil. Prob. a. 1) Christ is called the mediator of God and men, 1 Tim. II, 5. but not the mediator of God and angels. 2) Christ did not assume the nature of angels, and unite it personally to Himself, Hebr. II, 16. Therefore, He did not redeem the angels.

That which is unassumed is unhealed (Τὸ ἀπρόσληπτον, ἀθεράπευτον), says GREG. NAZIANZ.

Prob. b. The good angels, since they are not only devoid of sin, but also immune from the danger of sinning, do not need a satisfier.

Prob. c. The evil angels are beyond mercy by divine judgment, says DANNHAV. in his Hodof. phænom. VII. p. 532. inasmuch as they are reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day, Jude v. 6. Therefore, no mediator was destined for them, who might loosen those everlasting chains.

You say Paul says expressly in Eph. I, 10. God purposed to gather together in one all things in Christ, both which are in heaven, and which are on earth, cf. Col. I, 19. Resp. The angels in heaven were not reconciled to God through Christ, inasmuch as they were never hateful to Him; but men were reconciled to the angels through Christ. For when God was reconciled, peace was also established with the angels, cf. Luke II, 14. c. XV, 10.

Quaest. LXXXII.

Did Christ, as man, merit anything for Himself by His obedience? Christ, as man, merited nothing for Himself by His obedience.

Prob. 1) Because Christ, through the personal union, was endowed with all the fullness of the Godhead, Col. II, 9. and was anointed with the oil of gladness (the gifts of the Holy Spirit) above His fellows, Ps. XLV, 8. Therefore, it was not necessary that He should merit anything for Himself.

2) Christ obtained a name above every name by grace, Phil. II, 9. and by inheritance (κληρονομίαν), Hebr. I, 4. Therefore, not by merit.

Antithesis is that of the Papists and Socinians, who maintain that Christ merited for Himself the highest and singular grace by His most humble obedience. They urge I. the particle, διὸ, Phil. II, 9: Wherefore God also hath highly exalted Him, and given Him a name which is above every name. Resp. The particle, διὸ, is not taken by the Apostle causally (αἰτιολογικῶς), but syllogistically (συλλογιστικῶς), by way of reasoning, and it indicates not a meritorious cause, but order and consequence.

For the humiliation was the way through which Christ arrived at glory, not the meritorious cause.

II. Hebr. II, 9. We see Jesus crowned with glory on account of the suffering of death. Resp. The particle, διὰ, to be rendered in Latin as 'per' (through), denotes the way to glory and honor, not merit, as if to say.

We see Jesus indeed crowned with glory, yet not except through the passion of death; that is: that he should first suffer death, and by this way enter into glory.

Latin:

Christus morte sua non reconciliavit Deo angelos a), neque bonos b), neque malos c). Prob. a. 1) Christus dicitur mediator Dei & hominum, 1 Tim. II, 5. non autem mediator Dei & angelorum. 2) Christus non angelorum naturam assumsit, & personaliter sibi vnivit, Hebr. II, 16.

E. angelos non redemit. Τὸ ἀπρόσληπτον, ἀθεράπευτον, inquit GREG. NAZIANZ.

Prob. b. Angeli boni, cum non tantum peccati expertes, sed & a peccandi periculo immunes sint, satisfactore non indigent.

Prob. c. Angeli mali iudicio diuino sunt immiserabiles, ait DANNHAV. hodof. phænom. VII. p. 532. quippe qui vinculis perpetuis sub tenebris in iudicium magni diei referuantur, Iud. v. 6. Non ergo illis destinatus est mediator, qui vincula illa perpetua soluat.

Dicis Paullus diserte inquit Eph. I, 10. Deus proposuit instaurare omnia in Christo, & quae in caelis, & quae in terra sunt, Conf. Col. I, 19. Resp. Non angeli in caelo per Christum sunt reconciliati Deo, vtpote cui nunquam fuerunt inuisi; sed homines reconciliati sunt angelis per Christum. Nam Deo reconciliato constituta etiam est pax cum angelis, Conf. Luc. II, 14. c. XV, 10.

Quaest. LXXXII. An

Christus, qua homo, obedientia sua quidquam meruit sibimet ipsi? Christus, qua homo, obedientia sua nihil sibi meruit.

Prob. 1) Quia Christus per vnionem personalem omni plenitudine diuinitatis donatus, Col. II, 9. & oleo lætitiæ (donis Spiritus S.) præ consortibus suis vnctus est, Ps. XLV, 8. Ergo non necesse fuit, vt sibi quidquam mereretur. 2) Christus nomen super omne nomen nactus est ex gratia, Phil. II, 9. & per κληρονομίαν, Hebr. I, 4.

E. non ex merito.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum & Socinianorum, statuentium Christum humillima sua obedientia summam & singularem gratiam sibi meruisse. Qui vrgent I. particulam, διὸ, Phil. II, 9: Quapropter & Deus illum exaltauit, & donauit illi nomen super omne nomen. Resp. Particula, διὸ, ab Apostolo non sumitur αἰτιολογικῶς, caussaliter, sed συλλογιστικῶς, ratiocinatiue, & indicat non caussam meritoriam, sed ordinem & consequentiam.

Humiliatio enim fuit via, per quam Christus ad gloriam peruenit, non caussa meritoria.

II. Hebr. II, 9. Videmus Iesum propter passionem mortis gloria coronatum. Resp. Particula, διὰ, latine reddenda, per, notat viam ad gloriam & honorem, non meritum, q. d.

Videmus Iesum coronatum quidem esse gloria, non tamen nisi per passionem mortis; hoc est: vt prius mortem pateretur, atque hac via in gloriam ingrederetur.


### Q. LXXXIII. What is the intercession of Christ?

The intercession of Christ is the second act of the priestly office, by which Christ the θεάνθρωπος (God-man), by the power of his entire merit, intercedes for all men, but especially for his own elect, truly and properly, yet without any diminution of his majesty, to obtain for the same whatever he knows to be salutary for body and soul.

Latin:

Intercessio Christi est alter actus officii sacerdotalis, quo Christus θεάνθρωπος, vi vniuersi meriti sui, pro omnibus hominibus, inprimis vero electis suis, vere proprieque, at sine vlla maiestatis imminutione interpellat, ad impetrandum iisdem, quæcunque corpori, atque animæ præcipue, salutaria esse nouit.


### Q. LXXXIV. What kind of intercession is that of Christ?

The intercession of Christ is not merely interpretative, through the showing of merits , nor humble, through submission ; but it is ἱλασικὴ, expiatory , and efficacious for obtaining salutary goods for men .

Proof a. Although it is most true that Christ moves God the Father by the virtue of his sacrifice once offered, so that He becomes propitious to sinners; yet the word ἐντυγχάνειν implies more than that real, yet silent, showing of merits; for that seems to pertain to the former act of the priestly office. Therefore, the intercession of Christ is not only real, but also vocal and oral.

Proof b. We are not speaking here of the humble mode of intercession, which pertained to the state of exinanition and the days of his flesh, where he offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears unto him that was able to save him from death, but of that intercession by which Christ, sitting at the right hand of God, intercedes for us. It is called by DANNHAUER (hodof. phænom. VIII) a theandric action, and thus humbly sublime and sublimely humble.

GREGORY NAZIANZEN says excellently (orat. XXXVI): It is not right, when we hear the word of intercession, to conceive in our mind Christ groveling at the feet of the eternal Father for our sake. Far be that servile suspicion, and unworthy of the Spirit! For it is not for the Father to demand these things, or for the Son to suffer them, nor is it pious or right to think so of God. The intercession of Christ is full of majesty, "Father, I will that they also, whom thou hast given me, be with me where I am; that they may behold my glory."

Proof c. The intercession of Christ is ἱλασικὴ, or expiatory, because the foundation of this intercession is the satisfaction of Christ the intercessor, or his entire merit. For by and because of his bloody satisfaction, or by the power of his merit, Christ the priest intercedes for us.

Hence the Apostle says that Christ died for us, and is even risen again, who is at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us; and that the blood of Christ speaketh better things than that of Abel.

Proof d.

The intercession of Christ, the high priest, is efficacious; because whatever he asks of the Father is pleasing and approved by Him. The intercession of Christ is efficacious for obtaining salvation for us, although those who do not believe in Christ do not enjoy the effect. Therefore, it is called efficacious by reason of the salutary intention of Christ, not by reason of the outcome in the incredulous and reprobate.

Latin:

Intercessio Christi non est nude interpretatiua, per ostensa merita , non humilis, per submissionem ; sed est ἱλασικὴ, expiatoria , & efficax ad impetrandum bona hominibus salutaria .

Prob. a. Quamuis verissimum sit, Christum mouere Deum Patrem virtute sacrificii sui semel oblati, vt peccatoribus propitius fit; plus tamen infert verbum ἐντυγχάνειν, quam realem illam quidem, at mutam ostensionem meritorum; quippe quæ ad priorem actum officii sacerdotalis pertinere videtur. Est itaque intercessio Christi non tantum realis, sed & vocalis & oralis.

Prob. b. Non est nobis hic sermo de humili intercessionis modo, qui ad statum exinanitionis & dies carnis pertinuit, vbi preces & supplicationes ad eum, qui poterat seruare ipsum ex morte, cum clamore valido & lacrymis obtulit, sed de intercessione illa, qua Christus sedens ad dextram Dei intercedit pro nobis, Vocatur a DANNHAU. hodof. phænom. VIII. actio theandrica, adeoque humiliter sublimis & sublimiter humilis.

Præclare inquit GREGOR. NAZIANZ. orat. XXXVI. Non fas est, cum interpellationis vocem audimus, animo concipere Christum, nostri caussa ad pedes æterni Patris se aduoluentem. Procul fit ista seruilis suspicio, spirituque indigna! Neque enim Patris est, hæc expostere, aut Filii, pati, nec de Deo cogitare, pium ac æquum est. Maiestate plena est intercessio Christi, Volo, ut vbi ego sum, etiam illi sint mecum, vt videant gloriam meam.

Prob. c. Est intercessio Christi ἱλασικὴ, seu expiatoria, propterea, quod fundamentum huius intercessionis est Christi intercessoris satisfactio, seu vniuersum meritum. Nam per & propter cruentam satisfactionem, siue vi ineriti sui, Christus sacerdos pro nobis interpellat.

Hinc dicit Apostolus, Christum pro nobis mortuum, & iam ad dextram Dei euectum, pro nobis interpellare; & sanguinem Christi meliora loqui, quam sanguinem Habelis.

Prob. d.

Efficax est intercessio Christi, summi sacerdotis; quia quidquid ille petit a Patre, gratum probatumque ipsi est. Efficax est intercessio Christi ad salutem nobis impetrandam, licet effectu non fruantur, qui in Christum non credunt. Proinde dicitur efficax, ratione salutaris Christi intentionis, non ratione euentus in incredulis & reprobis.


### Q. LXXXV. How is the intercession of Christ manifold?

The intercession of Christ is twofold, general and special.

By general intercession, Christ prays to the Father for all men, that the fruits of his salutary death may be to them the fruits of his salutary death may be applied to them a); by special intercession he prays for the reborn & elect, that they may be preserved and grow in faith and holiness b).

Prob. 1) Christ interceded for the transgressors, Is. LIII, 12. Luke XXIII, 34. He prayed for his crucifiers indefinitely, with no one excepted. Yet some of them persisted in their impiety without doubt. Christ, however, praying for them, shows that as far as it depends on him, he does not wish them to be deprived of the fruit of his death, but rather to be converted & saved.

2) Of whatever men Christ is the mediator, of them he is the intercessor: for intercession is the action of a mediator. But Christ is the mediator of all men, 1 Tim II, 5. Therefore he is the intercessor for all.

Prob. b. John XVII, 9. I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me, because they are yours. By the world the Savior understands worldly men, indulging in the lusts of the flesh, & stubbornly impious, for whom he himself does not intercede by special intercession as he does for the Apostles, given by the Father into the school and discipline of Christ.

How he prays for them, we read in John XVII, 11. Holy Father, keep them through your name, whom you have given me, that they may be one, just as we are! & v. 15. I do not pray that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the world.

Furthermore v. 17. Sanctify them in your truth.

From which it is gathered that Christ intercedes for the reborn & elect in such a way that they may be preserved from evil, kept in the unity of faith, & sanctified more and more by the word of truth.

Quest. LXXXVI. Does Christ also intercede for us in heaven? Christ, having been raised to the right hand of God, truly and properly intercedes for all men, primarily for the reborn & elect.

Prob. 1) From the priestly office: Christ in heaven is a priest, Heb. VII, 24. not by the offering of a victim, Heb. X, 12. Therefore by intercession.

2) From the apostolic testimony: Christ is at the right hand of God, & intercedes for us, Rom. VIII, 34. Cf. Heb. VII, 24. 25. ch. IX, 24.

3) From the office of paraclete, or advocate, 1 John

II, 1. My little children, I write these things to you, so that you may not sin, & if anyone has sinned, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, the righteous. There is an antithesis from the Socinians, & some Papists, contending that the intercession of Christ in heaven is not true & proper, but an appearance before God, a glorious presentation of the body of Christ; who fortify their opinion with the following arguments.

I. Whoever has been made Lord of all, possessing absolute power in the business of salvation, he does not properly intercede for us. Reason: because he does not act as lord precariously: But Christ &c.

Matt. XXVIII, 18. Therefore.

Resp. Distinguish between intercession of humility through submission, & of authority through glorious petition. Not the former, but the latter can consist with conferred full power, & supreme lordship.

II. We do not need true intercession; because the Father himself loves us, John

XVI, 26. 27. Resp. When Christ says that he will not pray for the disciples, that is not to be understood ἁπλῶς, simply, because Christ in the chapter immediately following, XVII, prays most earnestly for the disciples, but κατὰ τί, or in a certain respect, so that the sense is: that Christ alone does not wish to pray for the disciples henceforth; not as if the Father, being angry, does not wish to admit the disciples into his sight, but that the Father, being reconciled, loves them in Christ, in whom they believe, & will most benignly accept their prayers, so that by the subtraction of the visible presence of Christ, nothing is lost to the advantage of the disciples.

III. The intercession of Christ in the heavens is described by emphanismos, or the glorious appearing of Christ, and a presentation conformable to the state of glory: [It] is not intercession properly so called.

Resp. Emphanismos, or appearing before the face of God, does not take away enteuxis, or intercession properly so called. The former precedes, the latter follows, Rom. VIII, 34.

Latin:

Intercessio Christi est duplex, generalis & specialis.

Generali intercessione orat Christus Patrem pro omnibus hominibus, vt salutaris mortis suæ fructus illis salutaris mortis fuæ fructus illis applicetur a); speciali intercessione orat pro renatis & electis, vt in fide & sanctitate conseruentur atque crescant b).

Prob. 1) Intercessit Christus pro transgressoribus, Es. LIII, 12. Luc. XXIII, 34. pro crucifixoribus suis indefinite, nullo excepto, orauit. At fine dubio quidam eorum perstiterunt in impietate sua. Christus autem, pro illis orans, ostendit, quod quantum in se est, non velit illos fructu mortis suae priuari, sed potius conuerti & saluari.

2) Quorum hominum Christus est mediator, illorum est deprecator: est enim intercessio actio mediatoris. Sed Christus omnium hominum est mediator, 1 Tim II, 5. E. & omnium deprecator.

Prob. b. Io. XVII, 9. Non pro mundo rogo, sed pro his, quos dedisti mihi, quia tui sunt. Per mundum intelligit Saluator homines mundanos, concupiscentiis carnis indulgentes, & praefracte impios, pro quibus ipse speciali deprecatione non ita interpellat, vt pro Apostolis, a Patre datis in scholam & disciplinam Christi.

Quomodo pro his oret, legimus Io. XVII, 11. Pater sancte, serua eos per nomen tuum, quos dedisti mihi, vt sint vnum, sicut & nos! & v. 15. Non rogo, vt tollas eos e mundo, sed vt serues eos a mundo.

Porro v. 17. Sanctifica eos in veritate tua.

E quibus colligitur, Christum pro renatis & electis sic interpellare, vt a malo praferuentur, in vnitate fidei conseruentur, & verbo veritatis magis magisque sanctificentur.

Quaest. LXXXVI. Num Christus in caelis etiam pro nobis intercedit? Intercedit Christus, euectus ad dextram Dei, vere proprieque pro omnibus hominibus, in primis pro renatis & electis.

Prob. 1) Ex officio sacerdotali: Christus in caelis est sacerdos, Hebr. VII, 24. non per oblationem victimae, Hebr. X, 12. E. per intercessionem.

2) E testimonio apostolico: Christus est in dextra Dei, & intercedit pro nobis, Rom. VIII, 34. Conf. Hebr. VII, 24. 25. c. IX, 24.

3) Ex munere paracleti, seu aduocati, 1 Io.

II, 1. Filioli mei, haec scribo vobis, ne peccetis, & si quis peccauerit, aduocatum habemus apud Patrem Iesum Christum, iustum. Antithesis est Socinianorum, & nonnullorum Pontificiorum, contendentium, interpellationem Christi in caelis non esse veram & propriam, sed apparitionem coram Deo, gloriosam corporis Christi praesentationem; qui suam opinionem sequentibus muniunt argumentis.

I. Quicunque factus est omnium Dominus, absoluta pollens potestate in negotio salutis, ille pro nobis proprie non intercedit. Ratio: quia non precario dominum agit: Atqui Christus &c.

Matth. XXVIII, 18. E.

Resp. Dist. inter interpellationem humilitatis per submissionem, & auctoritatis per gloriosam postulationem. Non illa, sed haec cum collata plena potestate, & dominio summo consistere potest.

II. Non indigemus intercessione vera; quia ipse Pater nos amat, Io.

XVI, 26. 27. Resp. Quando Christus dicit, se non oraturum esse pro discipulis, id non intelligendum est ἁπλῶς, simpliciter, eo, quod Christus capite proxime sequente XVII, quam maxime pro discipulis orat, sed κατὰ τί, siue secundum quid, vt sensus fit: quod Christus solus posthac pro discipulis orare nolit; non quasi Pater iratus in conspectum suum discipulos admittere nolit, sed quod Pater reconciliatus ipsos amet in Christo, in quem credant, corumque preces benignissime accepturus sit, vt visibilis praesentiae Christi subtractione commodo discipulorum nihil decedat.

III. Intercessio Christi in coelis describitur per ἐμφανισμὸν, seu gloriosam apparitionem Christi, & statui gloriae conformem praesentationem: E-non est interpellatio proprie dicta.

Resp. Ἐμφανισμὸς, seu comparitio coram facie Dei, non tollit ἔντευξιν, seu intercessionem proprie dictam. Illa praecedit, haec sequitur, Rom. VIII, 34.


### Q. LXXXVII. What is the end of Christ’s priestly office?

The end of Christ’s priestly office is, on the part of God, the demonstration of a) divine justice; b) divine mercy: on our part, it is redemption c).

Prob. a. From Rom. III, 25. God set forth Christ Jesus as hilasterion, a propitiatory, through faith in his blood, for the demonstration of his justice. Obs. 1) Christ is called hilasterion, a propitiatory; because by his own death and the shedding of his own blood he appeased God, who was hostile to us on account of our sins. 2) Christ is hilasterion through faith in his blood; because our confidence rests upon the blood of Christ, shed for us, without which shedding of Christ's blood there is no propitiation. 3) God set forth Christ as hilasterion eis endeixin dikaiosynes autou, for the demonstration of his justice. By justice we understand the justice that avenges sin; for the reason that Paul is dealing with justice founded in shed blood, or that which demands a bloody death. But where justice is demonstrated in the exaction of a bloody death, there vindicatory justice is declared. It was necessary, therefore, that Christ the priest, being about to expiate the sins of men by divine decree, should undergo a bloody death, so that from this it might most clearly become known to sinners that God, the most just judge, does not leave the crimes of men unpunished, since he has punished them so severely in his Son, the mediator of the human race.

Prob. b. From Rom. V, 8. God commends his love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. The most merciful God gave an illustrious document of incomparable and most highly commendable love by delivering his only-begotten Son into the most bitter death for miserable sinners, so that by this satisfactory death they might be restored to a state of grace. Therefore, the satisfaction of Christ shines forth as a wonderful tempering of divine justice and mercy.

Prob. c. 1) From Gal. IV, 4. For this end the Son of God was made under the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law. 2) From Gal. III, 13. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us.

Latin:

Finis officii Christi sacerdotalis est, ex parte Dei, demonstratio a) divinae iustitiae; b) divinae misericordiae: ex parte nostri, est redemtio c).

Prob. a. Ex Rom. III, 25. Deus proposuit Christum Iesum ἱλαστήριον, propitiatorium, per fidem in ipsius sanguine in demonstrationem iustitiae suae. Obs. 1) Christus dicitur ἱλαστήριον, propitiatorium; quia sua ipsius morte & sanguinis proprii effusione Deum ob peccata nostra nobis infensum placauit. 2) Christus est ἱλαστήριον per fidem in ipsius sanguine; quia fiducia nostra nititur sanguine Christi, pro nobis effuso, fine qua sanguinis Christi effusione nulla est propitiatio. 3) Deus proposuit Christum ἱλαστήριον εἰς ἔνδειξιν δικαιοσύνης αὐτοῦ, in demonstrationem iustitiae suae. Per iustitiam intelligimus iustitiam peccati vindicatricem; propterea, quod Paullus agit de iustitia fundata in sanguine fuso, seu quae exigit mortem cruentam. At vbi demonstratur iustitia in exactione mortis cruentae, ibi declaratur iustitia vindicativa. Oportuit igitur sacerdotem Christum, ex decreto divino expiaturum peccata hominum, cruentam obire mortem, vt ex hac peccatoribus clarissime innotescat, Deum, iustissimum iudicem, crimina hominum non dimittere impunita, cum ea tam feuere in Filio suo, generis humani mediatore, vindicauerit.

Prob. b. Ex Rom. V, 8. Commendat suam dilectionem erga nos Deus, quod adhuc peccatoribus existentibus nobis, Christus pro nobis mortuus est. Illustre dilectionis incomparabilis maximeque commendabilis documentum Deus misericordissimus, tradito Filio vnigenito in mortem acerbissimam pro peccatoribus miseris, dedit, vt hac morte satisfactoria in statum gratiae restituerentur. Elucescit igitur et satisfactio Christi mirabile iustitiae & misericordiae divinae temperamentum.

Prob. c. 1) Ex Gal. IV, 4. Eo fine Filius Dei factus est sub lege, vt eos, qui sub lege erant, redimeret. 2) Ex Gal. III, 13. Christus nos redemit a maledictione legis, factus pro nobis maledictio.


### Q. LXXXVIII. What things must be observed in order to rightly know the redemption of the human race?

For the immense benefit of our redemption to be salutarily known, the following must be weighed with pious estimation of mind: 1) the redemption, 2) the captive, 3) the captive’s chains, 4) the one holding the captive, 5) the redeemer, 6) the end and fruit of the redemption.

Latin:

Ad ingens redemptionis nostrae beneficium, salutariter cognoscendum, pia animi aestimatione pensitanda sunt 1) redemtio, 2) captiuus, 3) captiui vincula, 4) captiuum detinens, 5) redemtor, 6) redemptionis finis & fructus.


### Q. LXXXIX. What kind of redemption is understood?

It is not understood here as a corporal redemption, but a spiritual one a); not extrajudicial, but judicial b); not simple, absolute, and metaphorical, but precious, satisfactory, and proper c).

Prob. a. Corporal redemption is liberation from those evils by which the body is afflicted, e.g., the redemption of the Israelites from Egyptian captivity, in respect to which Moses is called lytrotes, redeemer, Acts VII, 36. Spiritual redemption is liberation from sin, the wrath of God, the execration of the law, and the punishments [arising from the] execration of the law, and from temporal and eternal punishments. Redemption accomplished through Christ is a spiritual liberation from sin, Tit. II, 14; from the wrath of God, 1 Thess. I, 10; from the curse of the law, Gal. III, 13; from the tyranny of the devil, Hebr. II, 14. 15; from hell and eternal death, Hos. XIII, 14. 1 Cor. XV, 54. 55.

Prob. b. Extrajudicial redemption is liberation from a hardship inflicted by one who is not the judge of the afflicted. Thus, often in war, a citizen or soldier captured is redeemed from the power of the enemy; e.g., Lot was redeemed by Abraham from the power of Chedorlaomer, Gen. XIV, 16. Judicial redemption is that by which a subject, having transgressed the law of his lord and judge, and having been sentenced by the same to death, prison, exile, or servitude, is restored to a state of liberty through the intervention of a price of redemption, or through intercession, either his own or another's; e.g., the Jews in Persia, condemned to death, were redeemed from the sentence of King Ahasuerus through the intercession of Esther. Esther VIII, 8.

Prob. c. Judicial redemption is either simple and absolute, or precious and satisfactory. The former is liberation from an imposed punishment without the intervention of a price; e.g., the Prophet Daniel, who was considered to have violated the command of the King of the Persians, was thrown to be torn apart by beasts; but with God moderating and shutting the mouths of the lions, and King Darius likewise pitying and granting a dispensation, he was redeemed, or liberated, from the punishment without any price. The latter is that by which a guilty person is redeemed from guilt and punishment through the payment of a price. Simple liberation is metaphorically called redemption. For, speaking properly, to redeem signifies to buy back, just as the Greek words, λυτρῶν (which is ἀπὸ τοῦ λύτρε, by a price of redemption), ἀγοράζειν, ἐξαγοράζειν, and the Hebrew פדה, גאל, designate a buying or redemption which takes place through the intervention of a price. Wherefore, since in the present argument, where we treat of the redemption of the human race, which had fallen into sin, accomplished by Christ, the same Hebrew and Greek words are used in the sacred code, we accept them in their proper sense, because no necessity appears to us to depart from the proper sense (*).

Latin:

Non intelligitur hic redemtio corporalis, sed spiritualis a); non extraiudicialis, sed iudicialis b); non simplex, absoluta & metaphorica, sed pretiosa, satisfactoria, & propria c).

Prob. a. Corporalis redemtio est liberatio ab iis malis, quibus corpus affligitur, v. gr. Redemtio Israëlitarum e captiuitate Aegyptiaca, cuius respectu Moses dicitur λυτρωτὴς, redemtor, Act. VII, 36. Redemtio spiritualis est liberatio a peccato, ira Dei, exsecratione legis, & poenis exsecratione legis, & pœnis temporalibus atque æternis. Redemtio facta per Christum est spiritualis liberatio a peccato, Tit. II, 14. ab ira Dei, 1 Theff. I, 10. a maledictione legis, Gal. III, 13. a tyrannide diaboli, Hebr. II, 14. 15. ab inferno & morte æterna Hof. XIII, 14. 1 Cor. XV, 54. 55.

Prob. b. Redemtio extraiudicialis est liberatio ab incommodo, illato ab eo, qui non est afflicti iudex. Sic sæpe in bello ciuis, aut miles captus redimitur a potestate hostis, v. gr. Lotus per Abrahamum redemtus est a potestate Kedarlaomeri, Gen. XIV, 16. Redemtio iudicialis est, qua subditus domini & iudicis sui legem transgressus, & ab eodem morti, carceri, exsilio, aut seruituti addictus, interueniente pretio redemtionis, aut deprecatione, vel propria, vel alterius, in statum libertatis restituitur, v. gr. Iudæi, in Persia capitis damnati, intercedente Esthera, a sententia regis Ahasueri redemti sunt. Esther VIII, 8.

Prob. c. Redemtio iudicialis vel est simplex & absoluta, vel pretiosa & satisfactoria. Illa est liberatio ab indicta pœna, fine interueniente pretio, v. gr. Propheta Daniel, qui regis Persarum mandatum violasse censebatur, bestiis dilaniandus proiiciebatur; at moderante Deo & obturante ora leonum, iuxta atque commiserescente atque dispensante rege Dario, citra vllum pretium a pœna redimebatur, siue liberabatur. Hæc est, qua reus a culpa & pœna, persoluto pretio, redimitur. Liberatio simplex metaphorice dicitur redemtio. Nam proprie loquendo redimere, significat, iterum emere, sicut & verba græca, λυτρῶν (quod est ἀπὸ τοῦ λύτρε, pretio redemtionis), ἀγοράζειν, ἐξαγοράζειν, & hebræa פדה, גאל, emtionem, vel redemtionem, quæ fit intercedente pretio, designant. Quamobrem cum in præsenti argumento, vbi de redemtione generis humani, in peccatum prolapsi, præstita per Christum, agimus, exdem voces hebrææ & græcæ in sacro codice vsurpentur, sensu proprio easdem accipimus, eo quod nulla nobis imposita necessitas recedendi a sensu proprio apparet (*).


### Q. XC. What is the redemption of the human race accomplished through Christ?

The redemption of the human race is the spiritual, judicial, and most precious liberation of all men, bound by the chains of sin, from guilt, the offense of God, and temporal and eternal punishment, accomplished by Christ the God-man through his active and passive obedience, which God, the most just judge, benignly accepted as a most perfect λύτρον, so that the human race, vindicated into spiritual liberty, may live eternally with God.

Prob. That the redemption of the human race is not simple or absolute, but most precious and satisfactory, is proven 1) By the testimony of Paul, 1 Cor. VI, 19. 20. Do you not know that your body is the temple of the Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God, and you are not your own? ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς, for you were bought with a price. We argue: Whoever do not have the power to abuse the members of the body for fornication, because they were bought with a price, their redemption is not absolute, but most precious; But all men do not have [the power to abuse their members], etc. Therefore.

2) From the Petrine testimony, 1 Ep. I, 18. Knowing that you were not redeemed with corruptible silver and gold from your vain conversation, delivered by tradition from your fathers; but with the precious blood as of a lamb unspotted and undefiled, Christ.

Obs.

1) St. Peter, by the word λυτροῦν, to redeem, annexes a certain price, by removing gold and silver, by which those things that are profitable and pleasing to the body are bought, and by bringing forward that the price of our spiritual redemption is the blood of the most holy Jesus, far more excellent than all gold and silver.

2) By vain conversation πατροπαράδοτον, the apostle understands a depraved habit of living, delivered from the fathers both by the contagion of original sin and by evil examples.

We conclude: Whoever are redeemed from the corruption of carnal life not by gold and silver, but by precious blood, their redemption is not simple, made without the intervention of a price: But all men, etc. Therefore.

3) From the explicit denomination of λύτρον and ἀντίλυτρον. Christ himself makes mention of λύτρον, Matt. XX, 28. The son of man came to give his life a λύτρον for many, the price of redemption for many. λύτρον, however, by the force of its etymology, denotes a price by which someone is liberated not only from captivity, but also from servitude, exile, death, and other inconveniences. Paul commemorates ἀντίλυτρον, 1 Tim. II, 6. There is one mediator of God and men, the man Jesus Christ, who gave himself an ἀντίλυτρον, a price of redemption, for all. ἀντίλυτρον, as Hugo Grotius explains, is such a λύτρον in which the liberator undergoes a certain evil similar to that which was impending over him who is liberated; the periphrasis of which can be gathered from Gal. III, 13. Christ ἐξηγόρασε, redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us.

We conclude: Whoever redeems sinners with a certain ransom, by undergoing such an evil as was impending over the sinners themselves, his redemption is not simple or absolute, but precious, satisfactory, and meritorious: But Christ, etc. Therefore.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, who maintain that the redemption made by Christ is not satisfactory or meritorious, but simple. Their chief arguments are:

I. Just as we are said to be sold under sin, so we are redeemed from the same by Christ (the reason of opposites is the same): But we were sold under sin without any price. Therefore, we are also redeemed from sin without an intervening price. Resp. I deny the major. The name of sale is more general than that of purchase. A brother can sell a brother, 1) by drawing him into the society of sin; but a brother cannot redeem a brother, Ps. XLIX, 8. 2) He is sold under sin who does it by choice, so that he becomes a servant of sin, John VIII, 34; but we are redeemed not only from servitude, but also from the curse of the law and the punishment of sin, which cannot be done without the intervention of a price.

II. To whom a λύτρον has not been paid, by him we are said to be improperly redeemed: But to the devil, not, etc. Therefore. Resp. 1) I deny the major. For one can be properly redeemed from the punishment of prison by a paid price, and yet no ransom is paid to the prison. 2) Distinguish between the supreme judge and the lictor. God is the supreme judge, to whom alone men principally sin, Ps. LI, 6, who concludes them under sin, Rom. XI, 32, Gal. III, 22. To Him Christ paid the most precious ransom, his own blood, when he offered himself to God as a victim, Eph. V, 2. The devil is the lictor and minister of the prison, to whom the price of redemption is not owed.

III. God redeemed the Israelite people, with no price paid, through Moses, who is also called λυτρωτής, Acts VII, 36, and was a …type of Christ, Deut. XVIII, 15, John VI, 14. Therefore, by the same reason, without a price, Christ redeemed us from the tyranny of the devil. The reason of the consequence is: because whatever is in the type, the same is also in the antitype, and whatever is not in that, is neither in this. Resp. 1) Distinguish between corporeal redemption, which takes place by power, with no intervening ransom and between spiritual redemption, which is done through justice: this must be satisfied by a certain price. 2) The correspondence of the type and antitype is respective and accommodating, not absolute and in every way. IV. God himself made our redemption, Luke I, 68. E. he did not demand a satisfactory redemption. The consequence is proven: In proper redemption, the price is given for the sake of the captive, so that he may be released, but not to him who procures the redemption. God the Father, however, procured the redemption of the Son: E. the price was not given to him. Resp. God himself made the redemption through a decree not absolute, but ordained. For he procured the redemption as a most benevolent Creator; but he demanded satisfaction as a most just Judge, so that his justice might be satisfied. God the Father therefore demonstrated both his justice and his mercy in the work of redemption. Justice; because he most justly punished the penalties of sins to be inflicted on the debtors in their sponsor Christ: mercy; because he decreed the redemption of Christ, accepted his satisfaction: and willed its fruit to be transferred to us. V. Nowhere do we read in the sacred scriptures that we have been redeemed from justice, or divine judgment: E. divine justice did not demand a satisfactory redemption. Resp. We are said to be redeemed from divine wrath, Rom. V, 9. 1 Thess. I, 10. But the wrath of God is the just will of God to punish sins. We are said to be redeemed from the curse of the law, Gal. III, 13; which is the most just sentence of God the judge condemning sinners.

Latin:

Redemtio generis humani est liberatio spiritualis, iudicialis & pretiosissima omnium hominum, vinculis peccati constrictorium, a culpa, offensa Dei, & pœna temporali atque æterna, facta a Christo θεανθρώπῳ per obedientiam ipsius actiuam & passiuam, quam Deus, iudex iustissimus, vt λύτρον perfectissimum benigne acceptauit, vt genus humanum, in spiritualem libertatem vindicatum, æternum cum Deo viuat.

Prob. Redemtionem generis humani non esse simplicem aut absolutam, sed pretiosissimam & satisfactoriam, euincitur 1) E testimonio Paullino, 1 Cor. VI, 19. 20. Annon scitis, quod corpus vestrum templum Spiritus, qui in vobis, sancti sit, quem habetis a Deo, & non sitis vestrum ipsorum, ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς, emti enim estis pretio. Arguimus: Quicunque non habent potestatem abutendi membris corporis ad fornicationem, ideo, quod sunt emti pretio, illorum redemtio non est absoluta, sed pretiosissima; Atqui omnes homines non habent &c. Ergo.

2) E testimonio Petrino, 1 Ep. I, 18. Scientes, quod non corruptibilibus argento & auro liberati sitis ex vana conuersatione, a patribus tradita; sed pretioso sanguine tanquam agni immaculati & incontaminati Christi.

Obs.

1) S. Petrus verbo, λυτροῦν, redimere, annectit certum pretium, remouendo aurum & argentum, quo ea, quæ corpori proficua & grata sunt, emuntur, & afferendo, pretium nostræ spiritualis redemptionis esse sanguinem sanctissimi Iesu, omni auro & argento longe præstabiliorem.

2) Per vanam conuersationem πατροπαράδοτον intelligit apostolus prauam viuendi consuetudinem, a patribus tum per contagium peccati originis, tum per mala exempla traditam.

Colligimus: Quicunque a corruptione carnalis vitæ redemti sunt non auro & argento, sed pretioso sanguine, illorum redemtio non est simplex, facta sine interuentu pretii: Atqui omnes homines &c. Ergo.

3) Ex diserta τοῦ λύτρου καὶ ἀντιλύτρου denominatione. λύτρον mentionem iniicit ipse Christus, Matth. XX, 28. Venit filius hominis dare animam suam λύτρον ἀντὶ πολλῶν, pretium redemptionis pro multis. λύτρον autem, vi etymi, notat pretium, quo aliquis non tantum a captiuitate, sed & seruitute, exilio, morte & aliis incommodis liberatur. ἀντίλυτρον commemorat Paullus, 1 Tim. II, 6. Vnus est mediator Dei & hominum, homo Iesus Christus, qui dedit seipsum ἀντίλυτρον, pretium redemptionis, pro omnibus. ἀντίλυτρον, exponente HVGONE GROTIO, est tale λύτρον, in quo liberator simile quoddam subit ei malo, quod ei imminebat, qui liberatur; cuius περιφράσις colligi potest ex Gal. III, 13. Christus ἐξηγόρασε redemit nos ab exsecratione legis, factus pro nobis exsecratio.

Concludimus: Quicunque certo lytro redemit peccatores, subeundo eiusmodi malum, cuiusmodi ipsis peccatoribus imminebat, illius redemtio non est simplex aut absoluta, sed pretiosa, satisfactoria & meritoria: Atqui Christus &c. Ergo.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, statuentium, redemptionem, factam a Christo, non esse satisfactoriam, aut meritoriam, sed simplicem. Quorum præcipua sunt argumenta:

I. Quemadmodum venditi dicimur sub peccatum, sic ab eodem per Christum sumus redemti (oppositorum eadem est ratio): Atqui venditi sumus sub peccatum sine vllo pretio. E. & redemti sumus a peccato, sine interueniente pretio. Resp. Neg. Mai. Nomen venditionis est generalius, quam emtionis. Vendere potest frater fratrem, 1) in societatem peccati eum pertrahendo; sed frater fratrem non potest redimere, Ps. XLIX, 8. 2) Venditur sub peccatum, qui id facit ex proæresi, vt fiat seruus peccati, Io. VIII, 34.; at nos redemti sumus non tantum a seruitute, sed etiam a maledictione legis & pœna peccati, quod sine interuentu pretii fieri nequit.

II. Cui non est persolutum λύτρον, ab eo dicimur improprie redemti: Atqui diabolo non &c. Ergo. Resp. 1) Neg. Mai. Nam a pœna carceris potest aliquis soluto pretio proprie redimi, neque tamen carceri soluitur lytrum. 2) Dist. inter summum iudicem, & litorem. Deus est summus iudex, cui soli homines principaliter peccant, Ps. LI, 6. qui eos sub peccato concludit, Rom. XI, 32. Gal. III, 22. Huic Christus lytrum pretiosissimum, sanguinem suum, persoluit, cum ille seipsum Deo victimam obtulit, Eph. V, 2. Diabolus est lictor ministerque carceris, cui pretium redemptionis non debetur.

III. Deus redemit populum Israëliticum, nullo soluto pretio, per Mosen, qui etiam dicitur λυτρωτής, Act. VII, 36. & fuit typus Christi, Deut. XVIII, 15. Io. VI, 14. E. eadem ratione, sine pretio, Christus nos a tyrannide diaboli redemit. Ratio consequentiæ est: quia quidquid est in typo, idem etiam est in antitypo, & quidquid non est in illo, id neque in hoc est. Resp. 1) Dist. inter redemptionem corporalem, quæ fit per potentiam, nullo interueniente lytro, tro, & inter redemtionem spiritualem, quæ fit per iustitiam: huic certo pretio est satisfaciendum. 2) Conuenientia typi & antitypi est respectiua & accommoda, non absoluta & omnimoda. IV. Deus ipse fecit redemtionem nostram, Luc. I, 68. E. redemtionem satisfactoriam non poposcit. Consequentia probatur: In redemtione propria pretium datur captiui caussa, vt is soluatur, non autem illi, qui redemtionem procurat. Deus Pater autem procurauit redemtionem Filii: E. illi non est datum pretium. Resp. Deus ipse fecit redemtionem per decretum non absolutum, sed ordinatum. Procurauit enim redemtionem, vt Creator benignissimus; satisfactionem autem poposcit, vt Iudex iustissimus, vt iustitiæ suæ fiat satis. Demonstrauit ergo Deus Pater in opere redemtionis tum iustitiam, tum misericordiam suam. Iustitiam; quia peccatorum pœnas debitoribus infligendas in eorum sponsore Christo iustissime puniuit: misericordiam; quia redemtionem Christi decreuit, eius satisfactionem acceptauit: & eius fructum in nos translatum voluit. V. Nullibi legimus in sacris litteris, quod redemti simus a iustitia, aut iudicio diuino: E. iustitia diuina redemtionem satisfactoriam non postulauit. Resp. Dicimur redemti ab ira diuina, Rom. V, 9. 1 Thess. I, 10. Sed ira Dei est iusta voluntas Dei puniendi peccata. Dicimur redemti ab exsecratione legis, Gal. III, 13; quæ est iustissima iudicis Dei peccatores condemnanti s sententia.


### Quest. XCI. Whom did Christ redeem?

The captive, whom Christ redeemed, is the entire human race.

Prob. Because the whole world is guilty before God, Rom. III, 19. i.e., the entire human race subject to divine law, and liable to guilt and punishment on account of transgressions of the law: therefore Christ gave himself as ἀντίλυτρον for all, 2 Tim. II, 6.

Latin:

Captiuus, quem Christus redemit, est vniuersum genus humanum.

Prob. Quia totus mundus est Deo reus, Rom. III, 19. h. e vniuersum genus humanum legi diuinæ subiectum, & ob transgressiones legis culpæ & pœnæ obnoxium: ideo Christus se dedit ἀντίλυτρον pro omnibus, 2 Tim. II, 6.


### Quest. XCII. What are those bonds from which Christ redeemed the human race?

The bonds from which Christ redeemed the human race are sins a), offenses against God b), and temporal and eternal punishments c).

Prob. a. That sins are snares with which the devil is accustomed to ensnare men, Paul teaches, 2 Tim. II, 25. 26. If perhaps God may give them repentance unto the knowledge of the truth, that they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil, who are taken captive by him at his will. Not only by error of dogmas, but also by vices of life are mortals ensnared by the devil, says THEOPHYLACTUS in this place, citing CALOVIUS in bibl. illustratis fol. 1023. But Christ gave himself for us, that he might deliver us from all iniquity. Tit. II, 14. Prob. b. Jesus delivered us from the wrath to come, says Paul, 1 Thess. I, 10. Obs. Ἰτα ἐρχομένη is that which always threatens, and adheres with silent steps, as it were. The law declares the wrath of God by denouncing a condemnatory sentence: therefore Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having himself become a curse, Gal. III, 13. Prob. c. The punishments of sin are an evil conscience, fear of death, tyranny of the devil, and eternal condemnation; from all these Christ redeemed us, as the Apostle teaches, Hebr. II, 14. Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil; and deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage. The Redeemer himself promised this, Hos. XIII, 14. I will ransom them from the power of the grave; I will redeem them from death.

Latin:

Vincula, a quibus Christus genus humanum redemit, sunt peccata a), offensa Dei b) & pœnæ temporales atque æternæ c).

Prob. a. Peccata esse laqueos, quibus diabolus homines irretire consueuit, docet Paullus, 2 Tim. II, 25. 26. Si forte det ipsis Deus pœnitentiam in cognitionem veritatis, vt sobrii euadant e diaboli laqueo, capti ab eo in ipsius voluntatem. Non solum dogmatum errore, sed etiam vitæ vitiis a diabolo irretiuntur mortales, inquit in h. l. THEOPHYLACTVS, citante CALOVIO in bibl. illustratis fol. 1023. At Christus seipsum dedit pro nobis, vt nos liberaret ab omni iniquitate. Tit. II, 14. Prob. b. Iesus eripuit nos a ventura ira, ait Paullus, 1 Thess. I, 10. Obs. Ἰτα ἐρχομένη est, quæ semper imminet, & tacitis quasi gressibus adhæret. Iram Dei declarat lex, sententiam condemnatoriam denuntiando: ideo Christus nos redemit ab exsecratione legis, factus ipse exsecratio, Gal. III, 13. Prob. c. Pœnæ peccati sunt mala conscientia, timor mortis, tyrannis diaboli, & æterna condemnatio; ab his omnibus Christus nos redemit, docente Apostolo, Hebr. II, 14. Quoniam pueri participes facti sunt carnis & sanguinis, & ipse similiter participem se fecit ipsorum, vt per mortem aboleret eum, qui potestatem habebat mortis, hoc est diabolum, & liberaret eos, quotquot timore mortis per omnem vitam obnoxii erant servituti. Promisit hoc ipse Redemptor, Hos. XIII, 14. E manu inferni redimam eos, e morte liberabo eos.


### Ques. XCIII. Who is the one holding the captive?

The one holding the captive is either the lord... or the minister. The supreme Lord and most just judge is God ): The minister of the prison, and likewise the tyrant, is the devil ).

Proof a. God was offended by the sins of men; inasmuch as He hates all workers of iniquity, Ps. V, 6. Therefore, He judicially concludes all men in unbelief, Rom. XI, 22, and under sin, Gal. III, 22. To Him the ransom had to be paid, not that it might hasten any advantage to Him, but that nothing might be lacking to His justice. Proof b.

Sinners are said to be taken captive by the snare of the devil at his will, 2 Tim. II, 26. Therefore, the devil is the minister of the prison, and the same is the tyrant and hunter [*]), who binds the ungodly with the snares of sins. To him, not a price, but punishment is due. Ques.

Latin:

Captivum detinens est vel dominus,... vel minister. Dominus summus & iudex iustissimus est Deus ): Minister carceris, itemque tyrannus, est diabolus ).

Prob. a. Deus peccatis hominum erat offensus; quippe qui odit omnes operatores iniquitatis, Ps. V, 6. Idcirco iudicialiter concludit omnes homines in incredulitatem, Rom. XI, 22. & sub peccatum, Gal. III, 22. Huic pendendum erat lytrum, non vt illi quidquam commodi acceleret, sed ne ipsius iustitiae quidquam decederet.

Prob. b. Peccatores dicuntur laqueo diaboli capti ad ipsius voluntatem, 2 Tim. II, 26. Est itaque diabolus minister carceris, idemque tyrannus & venator [*]), qui laqueis peccatorum impios constringit. Huic non pretium, sed supplicium debetur.


### XCIV. Who is the redeemer?

The sole ) and catholic [universal] redeemer of the entire human race ) is Christ the God-man (θεάνθρωπος), possessing the right ), the power ), and the will ) to redeem.

Proof a. Christ is the sole redeemer; because He is the one mediator between God and men, who gave Himself a ransom for all, 1 Tim. II, 5, 6. Proof b. Christ is the catholic redeemer; because He is the Savior of the world, 1 John IV, 14. The Savior of all men, especially of those who believe, 1 Tim. IV, 10. Proof c. Christ possesses the right and power to redeem.

He has the right of ownership over us, as God and Lord of all; He also has the right of kinship, as true man, bone of our bones and flesh of our flesh. For which cause He is called by Job גואל (Goel), ch. XIX, 25. Proof d. Christ is furnished with most sufficient powers to redeem, for He is the Almighty (παντοκράτωρ), Rev. I, 8. Proof e. Of the will to redeem, the most ardent love testifies, which Paul proclaims, Eph. V, 25. Christ loved the church, and gave Himself for it. Ques.

Latin:

Redemptor unicus ) & catholicus universi generis humani ) est Christus θεάνθρωπος, iure ), viribus ), & voluntate ) redimendi pollens.

Prob. a. Christus est redemptor unicus; quia est unus mediator Dei & hominum, qui se dedit pretium redemptionis pro omnibus 1 Tim. II, 5, 6. Prob. b. Christus est redemptor catholicus; quia est Salvator mundi, 1 Io. IV, 14. Salvator omnium hominum, maxime fidelium, 1 Tim. IV, 10.

Prob. c. Christus pollet iure & potestate redimendi. Habet in nos ius proprietatis, vt Deus & dominus omnium, habet etiam ius propinquitatis, vt verus homo, os de ossibus nostris & caro de carne nostra. Qua de causa a Iobo vocatur גואל, c. XIX, 25. Prob. d. Viribus sufficientissimis redimendi instructus est Christus, est enim παντοκράτωρ, omnipotens Apoc. I, 8. Prob. e. De voluntate redimendi testatur amor ardentissimus, quem depraedicat Paulus, Eph. V, 25. Christus dilexit ecclesiam, & semet ipsum tradidit pro illa.


### XCV. By what means did Christ redeem us?

The means of redemption is both the most bitter passion of Christ, the shedding of blood, and satisfactory death ), and the most consummate fulfillment of the divine law, performed in our stead ). Proof a. Christ entered once into the holy place, not by the blood of goats and calves, but by His own blood, so that He obtained eternal redemption, Heb. IX, 12.

Christ, having once entered the heaven of divine majesty through his own blood, made satisfaction for the sins of the whole human race, which it has committed and will commit until the end of the world, so that his redemption may avail at any time for all sins.

Prob. b. Just as by the disobedience of one man many were made sinners: so also by the obedience of one just man shall many be made righteous, Rom. V, 18. Therefore Christ performed the most perfect obedience to the divine law in our place, so that, redeemed from sin, we might be accounted righteous before God.

Latin:

Medium redemptionis est tum acerbissima Christi passio, sanguinis effusio & mors satisfactoria ), tum consummatissima legis divinae impletio, nostri vice praestita ). Prob. a. Christus neque per sanguinem hircorum & vitulorum, sed per proprium sanguinem ingressus est semel in sancta, ita, vt aeternam redemptionem invenerit, Hebr. IX, 12.

Christus semel per sanguinem proprium caelum maiestatis divinae ingressus satisfecit pro totius generis humani peccatis, quae commisit, commissurumque est ad finem usque mundi, ita, ut redemtio eius quovis tempore valeat, pro omnibus peccatis.
