Prob. b. Sicut per inobedientiam unius hominis peccatores constituti sunt multi: ita etiam per obedientiam unius iusti constituentur multi, Rom. V, 18. Ideo Christus perfectissimam legi divinae obedientiam praestitit nostri loco, ut a peccato redemti coram Deo iusti reputemur.


### Q. XCVI. What is the end of redemption?

The ultimate end of redemption is the glory of God , the intermediate is freedom from the guilt and dominion of sin .

Prob. a. You were bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God's, 1 Cor. VI, 20.

Prob. b. If the Son shall make you free, you shall be truly free, John VIII, 36. By his satisfactory redemption, Christ acquired for men freedom from the guilt and dominion of sin, of which freedom they are partakers who are in Christ Jesus through faith, Rom. VIII, 1.

Latin:

Finis redemptionis ultimus est gloria Dei , intermedius est libertas a reatu & dominio peccati .

Prob. a. Emti estis pretio: glorificate itaque Deum corpore vestro & spiritu vestro, quae sunt Dei, 1 Cor. VI, 20.

Prob. b. Si filius vos liberos fecerit, vere liberi eritis, Io. VIII, 36. Christus redemtione sua satisfactoria acquisivit hominibus libertatem a reatu & dominio peccati, cuius libertatis participes sunt, qui per fidem sunt in Christo Iesu, Rom. VIII, 1.


### Q. XCVII. What is the prophetic office of Christ?

The prophetic office of Christ is that by which Christ, the God-man (θεάνθρωπος), both expounded the true meaning of the divine law and most clearly revealed the will of God concerning the salvation of men by the word of the Gospel, with such serious intention that the way to attain righteousness and eternal salvation might be evident to all men.

Obf. It was the task of the Prophets of the Old Testament to teach the word of God, to hand down the true worship of God, to know hidden things, and to predict future things [*]. Just as Christ also did these things, so he fulfilled the office of a prophet.

Q.

XCVIII. What kind of prophet is Christ? Christ is the greatest prophet , catholic , most illuminating , most sealed , most efficacious , and exemplary .

Prob. a. A great prophet has been raised up among us, the people said, Luke VII, 16. Christ is that great prophet whom God promised, Deut. XVIII, 18. I will raise up a prophet for them from the midst of their brethren, like you; and I will put my words in his mouth, that he may speak to them all that I shall command him. That Christ is that promised prophet, like Moses, Peter shows in Acts III, 22, and the Jews acknowledged, John I, 45; VI, 14. What more? The Apostle asserts that Christ is far more eminent than Moses. For he was a servant in the house of the heavenly Father; but this one is the only-begotten Son. Heb. III, 5, 6. [].

Christ is the catholic prophet; because he is the true light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world. Jo. I, 9. That the gospel is to be established in such predictions by the Jews themselves, or in their own person, we learn from a similar example, Gal.

III, 16.

As far as the matter is concerned, three things must be accurately observed: I.

Christ is to be compared with Moses, not in all those things which were common to all the Prophets, but by reason of those things which were singular and excellent, proper to Moses, inasmuch as by these he alone stands out among all.

This is surely evident in itself; for otherwise there would be no reason why Christ should have been compared with that one, and not equally with other divine Prophets.

II. Christ not only equaled Moses in words and deeds; but he is also to be held far superior to him, namely by reason of his person, Hebr.

I, 1. 2.

III, 3-6; 2) of office and doctrine, John

I, 17.

Hebr. XII, 18-25.

III. Care must be taken that the third point of comparison, as it is commonly called, is not amplified beyond what is right.

Namely, the reason for comparing that which exists between Christ and Moses, but at the same time preferring the former far above the latter, α) One indeed, true, signified by God himself, of which there are altogether three parts, comprised in one saying, Deut. XXXIV, 10. 11.

12. namely 1) the singular mode of divine revelation, which happened to Moses, and the excellence of his person, since it was permitted to Moses, and to that one alone, to converse familiarly with God, v. 10. add.

Ex. XXXIII, 11.

Num. XII, 6.

8. & conf. with Jo.

I, 18. Matth.

XI, 27: 2) The multitude and magnitude of miracles, v. 11. conf. with John XV, 24: 3) The government of the whole people, over whom that one Prophet, Moses, and the same Leader, presided, v. 12. coll. with Hebr. III, 2. in which place the connection of the words, ὡς καὶ Μωσῆς, is connected not so much with those words, πισὸν ὄντα, (for Moses had that in common with other Prophets, in that therefore there was nothing singular and special) as with these, ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ οἴκῳ αὐτοῦ.

To this third property and excellence of Moses should be referred the function of the office of the mediator (τοῦ μεσίτου) in making the divine covenant, which pertains to the whole nation, Gal.

III, 19. add. Ex. XIX, 3-8.

XX, 19. XXXIV, 27.

Deut. V, 5.

In which not only the comparison of Christ and Moses is seen, but the excellence of Christ is also conspicuous, by reason of α) the covenant, of which Christ is the sponsor and mediator (μεσίτης), both new and better, not of that legal one, but of the evangelical one, Hebr. VIII, 5.

6. XII, 18-25: β) the people, for Christ is the mediator (μεσίτης) not of any one whole nation, as Moses, but of the entire human race, Gal. III, 20. ὁ δὲ μεσίτης (that very one, whom our religion venerates, and who is different from him, of whom mention had been made in v. 19.) ὡς ἕνὸς ἑνός (understand, of a people, and see v. 28. add. Rom.

III, 29. 30.) β) But another false one, which is opposed to the testimonies of Holy Scripture, so far is it from being able to be confirmed by them.

There are indeed four errors to be avoided with all providence: 1) The error of the Jews, α) whom a vain hope deceives, or rather has deceived for so long, that the Messiah, whom they expect in vain, will, just as Moses did for the Jewish nation, having loosened the bonds of captivity and calamity, introduce them into the land of Canaan; as if the salvation to be recovered by the benefit of Christ should not be other than temporal, and as if it pertained to the Jews alone; nor was it Moses, but Joshua as leader, by whom the descendants of Abraham entered into the land granted to them by the benefit of God: β) by whose prejudiced opinion the person of Christ was to be known from a certain heavenly sign, exactly as Moses had shown their ancestors bread sent down from heaven, John VI, 14. coll. with v. 30. 31.

32. 2) The error of the Socinians, who imagine that Christ ascended into heaven under the auspices of openly administering his office, or, as they are accustomed to say, was caught up, with the intention that God might teach him his will, to be announced to men, just as we read reported of Moses in Ex. XXXIV, 27. 28.

This fable of theirs arose from no other cause than extreme desperation, when they could not find how, by denying the divinity of Christ, they could explain the meaning of such sayings, John I, 2. III, 13.

VI, 38. 62.

XVI, 28.

3) The error of certain Roman Catholics, that Moses, just like Christ, performed a triple office, namely priestly, prophetic, and kingly. It is worthy to be read, b.

FRISCHMUTH'S oration against Barthold Nibusius.

4) The common error of the Socinians and Roman Catholics, although proceeding from different principles, who think that Christ was similar to Moses in that he himself brought forth new laws. But yet α) the legislative power does not belong at all to the prophetic office, to which they nevertheless refer it, but entirely to the kingly; and not even to the kingdom of Christ, insofar as he is Christ, do laws properly and strictly so called, and indeed new laws, belong. β) Moses was not a lawgiver, but of the law, which God in that kingdom...

he announced to the Jews, the universal preaching of which among all nations he nevertheless entrusted to the apostles, as he was about to ascend into heaven, Matth.

Prob. c. Christ is a most enlightened prophet; for he is, by virtue of the personal union, endowed with the light of omniscience, and blessed with the most clear vision of God. For he is anointed with the oil of gladness above all his companions, Ps. 45:8, and receives the Holy Spirit οὐ ἐκ μέτρου [not by measure], John 3:34, from whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in him, Col. 2: 3. He rejoiced in the intimate intuition of the heavenly Father. No one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has revealed him to us. John 1: 18.

Prob. d. Christ is a most sealed prophet; inasmuch as God the Father has sealed him, John 6: 27. He sealed and confirmed him both by testimony heard three times from heaven: 1) at the beginning of his office, Matth. 3:17: 2) in the middle of his course, Matth. 17:5: 3) near the end of his course, John 12:28; and by the power of performing miracles, by which, as if by impressed seals, the doctrine of Christ is fortified.

Prob. e. Christ is a most efficacious prophet; as one who taught heavenly truth most clearly, refuted falsehood most solidly, exhorted most gravely, and predicted future things most truly.

Prob. f. Christ is an exemplary prophet, who expressed in deeds what he taught in words. Whence he is called a prophet mighty in deed and word, before God and all the people, Luke 24:19.

Latin:

Officium Christi propheticum est, quo Christus θεάνθρωπος cum veram sententiam legis divinae exposuit, tum voluntatem Dei de salute hominum verbo euangelii clarissime revelauit, ea seria intentione, ut omnibus hominibus constet via ad iustitiam & salutem aeternam consequendam.

Obs. Prophetarum V. T. erat, verbum Dei docere, verum Dei cultum tradere, occulta nosse & praedicere futura [*]. Haec sicut Christus quoque fecit: ita functus est officio prophetae.

Quaest. XCVIII. Qualis propheta est Christus?

Christus est propheta maximus , catholicus , illuminatissimus , obsignatissimus , efficacissimus & exemplaris .

Prob. a. Propheta magnus suscitatus est inter nos, dicebat populus, Luc. VII, 16. Christus est propheta ille magnus, quem promisit Deus, Deut. XVIII, 18. Prophetam excitabo illis e medio fratrum illorum, sicut te; daboque verba mea in os eius, ut loquatur ad eos omne, quod illi praecepero. Christum esse promissum illum prophetam, Mosi similem, ostendit Petrus Act. III, 22. & agnouerunt Iudaei, Io. I, 45. c. VI, 14. Quid? quod Apostolus asserit, Christum Mose esse longe eminentiorem. Nam ille erat seruus in domo Patris coelestis; hic vero vnigenitus filius. Hebr. III, 5, 6. [].

Christus est propheta catholicus; quia est lux vera, quae illuminat omnem hominem venientem in mundum. Io. I, 9. Αυτοπροσώπως quidem, seu in propria persona evangeliiuns Iudaeis in eiusmodi praedictionibus statuendam esse, discimus exemplo simili, Gal.

III, 16.

Quod ad rem attinet, tria sunt accurate observanda: I.

Christus cum Mose comparandus est, non in iis omnibus, quae fuerunt Vatum omnium communia, sed ratione eorum, quae singularia atque eximia fuerunt, Mosis propria, quippe quibus ipse unus inter omnes eminet.

Hoc profecto per se evidens est; aliter enim nulla esset ratio, quam ob rem Christus cum vno illo, nec pariter cum aliis Vatibus diuinis, fuisset conferendus.

II. Christus non solum Mosen dictis factisque aequiparauit; verum etiam longe eo superior est habendus, nimirum ratione persona, Hebr.

I, 1. 2.

III, 3-6; 2) officii ac doctrinae, Ioann.

I, 17.

Hebr. XII, 18-25.

III. Cauendum est, ne tertium, vt vulgo dicitur, comparationis, vltra, ac par est, amplificetur.

Scilicet ea, quae inter Christum ac Mosen intercedit, comparandi, simul vero illum huic longe anteferendi, ratio α) Alia quidem, vera, a Deo ipso significata, cuius omnino tres partes, vno dicto comprehensae, Deut. XXXIV, 10. 11.

12. nimirum 1) singularis modus patefactionis diuinae, quae Mosi contigit, atque excellentia personae, quando quidem Mosi, & vni quidem illi, licuit familiariter cum Deo versari, v. 10. add.

Ex. XXXIII, 11.

Num. XII, 6.

8. & conf. cum Io.

I, 18. Matth.

XI, 27: 2) Miraculorum, & multitudo & magnitudo, v. 11. conf. cum Ioann. XV, 24: 3) Vniversi populi gubernatio, cui vnus ille Propheta, Moses, idemque Dux, praefuit, v. 12. coll. cum Hebr. III, 2. quo quidem in loco vinculum verborum, ὡς καὶ Μωσῆς, connexum non tam cum illis est, πισὸν ὄντα, (id enim Moses cum aliis Vatibus commune habuit, in eo igitur nihil fuit singulare ac praecipuum) quam cum his, ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ οἴκῳ αὐτοῦ.

Ad hanc tertiam Mosis proprietatem ac praestantiam referri debet functio muneris τοῦ μεσίτου in faciendo foedere diuino, quod ad totam gentem attinet, Gal.

III, 19. add. Ex. XIX, 3-8.

XX, 19. XXXIV, 27.

Deut. V, 5.

In quo non solum Christi & Mosis comparatio cernitur, sed conspicua est etiam Christi excellentia, ratione α) foederis, cuius & noui, & melioris sponsor ac μεσίτης est Christus, non legalis illius, sed euangelici, Hebr. VIII, 5.

6. XII, 18-25: β) populi, non enim totius gentis cuiusdam, vt Moses, sed vniuersi hominum generis μεσίτης est Christus, Gal. III, 20. ὁ δὲ μεσίτης (is ipse, quem nostra veneratur religio, & qui diuersus est ab illo, cuius mentio facta erat v. 19.) ὡς ἕνὸς ἑνός (subintellige, λαοῦ, & vid. v. 28. add. Rom.

III, 29. 30.) β) Alia autem falsa, quae testimoniis Scripturae S. aduersatur, tantum abest, vt illis confirmari queat.

Sunt nimirum quatuor errores, omni prouidentia euitandi: 1) Error Iudaeorum, α) quos fallit, immo tam diu iam fefellit, inanis spes, fore, vt Messias, quem frustra exspectant futurum, quem ad modum Moses, gentem Iudaicam, solutis vinculis captiuitatis & calamitatis, introducat in terram Canaan; quasi salus, beneficio Christi recuperanda, non alia esse debeat, quam temporalis, & tanquam ea ad solos Iudaeos pertineat; nec Mose, sed Iosua duce, ingrediebantur Abrahami posteri in terram, Dei beneficio ipsis tributam: β) quorum praeiudicata opinione persona Christi cognoscenda erat ex signo quodam caelesti, plane sic, vti Moses Maioribus ipsorum panem de caelo demissum exhibuerat, Ioann. VI, 14. coll. cum v. 30. 31.

32. 2) Error Socinianorum, qui fingunt, Christum sub auspicium muneris palam administrandi in caelum adscendisse, siue, vt loqui solent, raptum fuisse, eo consilio, vt Deus eum doceret voluntatem suam, hominibus nunciandam, quem ad modum de Mose relatum legimus Ex. XXXIV, 27. 28.

Haec illorum fabula ex causa exstitit non alia, quam extrema desperatione, quum non reperissent, quo pacto, diuinitatem Christi negantes, explicare possent sententiam dictorum huiusmodi, Ioann. I, 2. III, 13.

VI, 38. 62.

XVI, 28.

3) Error Romano-Catholicorum quorumdam, quod Moses perinde, vt Christus, triplici functus sit officio, videlicet sacerdotali, Prophetico, ac Regio. Digna est, quae legatur, b.

FRISCHMVTHEI orat. aduersus Barthold Nibusius.

4) Error communis Socinianorum & Romano-Catholicorum, tametsi a diuersis principiis profectus, qui existimant, Christum Mosi similem fuisse eo, quod nouas leges ipse tulerit. Verum tamen α) potestas legislatoria prorsus non ad propheticum munus pertinet, ad quod tamen illi eam referunt, sed omnino ad regium; ac ne regno quidem Christi, quatenus est Christus, conueniunt leges proprie stricteque ita dictae, & nouae quidem leges. β) Moses non fuit legis lator, sed legis, quam Deus in illa regni nis

Iudaeis annuntiauit, cuius tamen praedicationem vniuersalem inter omnes gentes, iamiam ascensurus in caelum, apostolis demandauit, Matth. XXVIII, 19.

Prob. c. Christus est propheta illuminatissimus; est enim, vi vnionis personalis, lumine omniscientiae donatus, & clarissima Dei visione beatus. Vnctus quippe est oleo laetitiae prae consortibus suis omnibus Ps. XLV, 8. & accipit Spiritum S. οὐ ἐκ μέτρου, Ioann. III, 34. ex quo omnes thesauri sapientiae & scientiae in ipso sunt absconditi, Col. II, 3. Gauisus est intimo patris caelestis intuitu. Deum nemo vidit vnquam, nisi vnigenitus filius, qui est in sinu Patris, ille nobis exposuit. Io. I, 18.

Prob. d. Christus est propheta obsignatissimus; vtpote quem Deus Pater obsignauit Io. VI, 27. Obsignauit & confirmauit eum tum testimonio de caelo ter audito: 1) in officii introitu, Matth. III, 17: 2) in medio cursu, Matth. XVII, 5: 3) prope cursus finem, Io. XII, 28. tum potestate faciendi miracula, quibus velut impressis sigillis doctrina Christi munita est.

Prob. e. Christus est propheta efficacissimus; vt qui veritatem caelestem docuit clarissime, falsitatem confutauit solidissime, adhortatus est grauissime, futura praedixit verissime.

Prob. f. Christus est propheta exemplaris, qui, quod docuit verbis, expressit factis. Ex quo audit propheta potens opere & verbo, coram Deo & omni populo, Luc. XXIV, 19.


### Q. XCVII. What is the prophetic office of Christ?: Q

Q.

99. According to which nature is Christ a catholic prophet? Christ is a catholic and most perfect prophet according to both natures, human a) and divine b).

Prob. a. According to his human nature, Christ taught by living voice for the whole three years and more, indicated that sacraments were to be celebrated, Matth. 26:19, ch. 28:19, and took to himself ministers of the word and sacraments, Matth. 28:19 and John 20:21.

Prob. the form of which is called a theophany, he had sanctioned, as minister and interpreter, wherefore he is called a mediator (μεσίτης), not a lawgiver (νομοθέτης), Gal. 3:19. γ) Christ never brought any new laws. For all those which adversaries bring forward, either are clearly not laws, properly so named (e.g., concerning placing saving faith in Christ, concerning the right use of New Testament sacraments; these, and those which are of this kind, pertain not to the legal will of God, which demands from us duties to be performed, but to the evangelical, which offers us benefits to be received, yet congruently with the order of salvation); or they are not new laws (e.g., the prohibition concerning unjust vengeance, and hatred of enemies, Matth. 5:44, add Exod. 23:4, 5, Lev. 19:17, 18, Rom. 12:19, 20, Deut. 32:35, Prov. 25:21, 22; concerning anxiety of mind and distress, Luke 21:34, Matth. 6:25, add Ps. 37:5, 55:23). But when ancient laws are called new, the reason for the name lies in this, partly, that they have been illuminated and confirmed by new moving arguments, John 13:34: partly because they have been renewed, brought forth as if from darkness into light, and purged of many human corruptions, 1 John 2:7, 8. Therefore, in Matth. 5, Christ did not oppose his doctrine to divine laws, but to the opinion of the Elders, and to a perverse interpretation, as clearly appears from v. 20, 21, 43. Hence this word, πληρῶσαι [to fulfill], v. 17, does not mean to supply, as if there had been some defects in the holy law of God, which was always the most perfect norm of actions; but it means to fulfill, not only by obeying, but also by teaching, namely, to deliver to men the perfect and entire meaning of the law, which had been up to this point miserably depraved and mutilated by the teachers of the Jews; for to this perfection is opposed defect, and indeed in doctrine, v. 19.

Prob. b. According to the divine nature, he joined the power, efficacy, and supreme authority to the word and sacraments. Whence the Lord worked with the Apostles preaching everywhere, Mark XVI, 20 (). Quest. () That we may explain this difference a little more distinctly, the miracles of Christ pertain to his human nature, for a twofold reason: 1) insofar as he himself did them in the name of the Father, John III, 2.

X, 25: 2) insofar as he implored the help of the Father, and professed that he was doing his own work for the glory of the Father, John XI, 41. 42. He himself explicitly added this reason: that they may believe that I have been sent by you: 3) to the divine nature of Christ, in a threefold way: 1) insofar as Christ claims for himself power and authority equal, and altogether the same, as that of the Father, John V, 19: in the latter part, indeed, there is a double nerve of proof: One in the universality of the thing, ὐ γὰρ - - ταῦτα καὶ κ. τ. λ. without any exception (for it would be necessary that something be proper and chief to the Father, unless Christ were the supreme God, equal and like to the Father): The other in the universality of the mode, ὁμοίως ποιά.

But the former words, which our adversaries vehemently object to us, testify nothing more than this: that the son does nothing, nor indeed can he, alone, separated from the Father.

From which very thing shines forth the closest and necessary conjunction of the son with the Father, which, as it becomes mutual, is surely of such value that neither the son without the Father, nor the Father in turn without the son, can effect anything.

See John X, 30. coll. with the preceding v. 28. 29. add. XIV, 10. 2) Insofar as he himself, in his own name, by his own will, and by his own power, effected such great works.

Matt. VIII, 3. 4. Luke VII, 14. Notable above all is this saying, Luke IV, 36. No one sent divinely, nor even an angel, ever dared to act in such a way. All, if they attempted anything, did it under divine auspices, always appealing to the will and authority of the supreme Divinity: כה אמר יהוה The one prophet greatest of all, Moses, never fails to call God the effector of such great things, saying that God did this, but that he himself lent his hands to God Ex.

IV, 22. 23. VII, 16. IX, 14. XIV, 21. 24. At no time did he ever dare to say thus: I will perform this! thus I will, thus I command! which indeed Christ, and that one Christ, did not hesitate to speak.

What? That his Legates performed their miracles in the name of Christ, which would by no means have been permitted to them if the son were inferior to the Father. Certainly they would have had need of this, that they should have appealed simultaneously to the name of the Father, and even have placed that before the name of Jesus.

Acts III, 6. IV, 10. 30. XVI, 18. 3) Insofar as he exhibited his own miracles to men with this mind, that he might reveal his own glory, John II, 11. But all things must be directed to the glory of the one God. As regards the miracles themselves, since Christ had to be not only a Prophet, but also the greatest of all Prophets, and thus greater than Moses: a necessary consequence was that he alone among all should excel in miracles that were clearly singular, John XV, 24.

Let us see, therefore, how excellently our Jesus surpassed all divine [miracles], not even excepting Moses, of the miracles performed by himself I. In multitude, John XX, 30.

XXI, 25. In one hour the number of miracles was huge, Luke VII, 21. The confession of the Jews exists John VII, 31. II. In variety; if indeed there is almost no genus of created things in which many miracles of Christ were not to be seen, namely 1) in heaven, Luke XXIII, 44. 45: 2) in the air, Matt. VIII, 26: 3) on earth, Matt.

XXI, 19: and in fruits, Mark VIII, 6. John VI, 11: 4) in water and sea, Matt. VIII, 26. John VI, 19: 5) in spirits, by expelling malignant demons; 6) in men, as much in the living, but especially in the sick, who were laboring under some incurable disease, as in the dead: 7) in brute animals, especially quadrupeds, Matt. VIII, 32. and in aquatic ones, Mark VIII, 7.

9. John VI, 11. Luke V, 5. 6. John XXI, 3. 6. 11. 2) Nor is there any genus of miracles of which Christ did not give many specimens. That there can be four, and no more, genera of miracles, is apparent from this: that of all things there are not, nor can there be, more than four properties: 1) existence, as philosophers speak, 2) essence, or nature, both common and proper, 3) quantity, and 4) quality.

In all these, therefore, our Jesus manifested a power altogether divine, 1) by first effecting things, and by calling those things which are not yet, just as if they were, John IX, 32. add. Rom. IV, 17: 2) by changing the nature of things, John II, 9:

Latin:

Quæst. XCIX. Secundum quam naturam Christus est propheta catholicus?

Christus est propheta catholicus & perfectissimus secundum vtramque naturam, humanam a) & diuinam b).

Prob. a. Secundum humanam naturam, Christus viua voce toto triennio & vltra docuit, sacramenta celebranda indicauit, Matth. XXVI, 19. c. XXVIII, 19. & ministros verbi ac sacramentorum sibi asciuit, Matth. XXVIII, 19. & Io. XX, 21.

Prob. nis forma, quae dicitur θεοφανία, sanxerat, minister atque interpres, quocirca appellatur μεσίτης, non νομοθέτης, Gal. III, 19. γ) Christus leges nouas nullas nunquam tulit. Omnes enim, quas aduersarii proferunt, aut plane non sunt leges, proprie ita nominatae (v. gr. de fiducia salutari in Christo collocanda, de recte vsurpandis N. F. Sacramentis; haec, & quae sunt huiusmodi, pertinent non ad legalem Dei voluntatem, quae a nobis postulat officia praestanda, sed ad euangelicam, quae nobis offert beneficia accipienda, ordini tamen salutis congruenter); aut non nouae leges (e. gr. interdictum de vindicta iniusta, atque odio inimicorum, Matth. V, 44. add. Exod. XXIII, 4. 5. Leuit. XIX, 17. 18. Roman. XII, 19. 20. Deuter. XXXII, 35. Prou. XXV, 21. 22. de anxietate animi atque aerumna, Luc. XXI, 34. Matth. VI, 25. add. Ps. XXXVII, 5. LV, 23.) Cum autem antiquae leges dicuntur nouae, ratio nominis sita est in eo, partim, quod nouis argumentis mouentibus illuminatae sint, & confirmatae, Ioann. XIII, 34: partim quod fuerint renouatae, ex tenebris velut in lucem prolatae, multisque a corruptelis humanis repurgatae, 1 Ioann. II, 7. 8. Itaque Matth. V. suam Christus doctrinam non legibus diuinis opposuit, sed opinioni Maiorum, ac peruersae interpretationi, vti plane adparet ex v. 20. 21. 43. Proinde verbum hoc, πληρῶσαι, v. 17. non est, supplere, tamquam defectus aliqui fuissent in sancta Dei lege, quae semper perfectissima fuit actionum norma; sed est, implere, non modo obediendo, sed & docendo, nimirum perfectam atque integram legis sententiam, huc vsque a magistris Iudaeorum miserum in modum deprauatam mutilatamque, hominibus tradere; huic enim perfectioni opponitur defectio, & quidem in doctrina, v. 19.

Quaest. (*) Vt hanc differentiam paullo distinctius explicemus, miracula Christi pertinent ad humanam ipsius naturam, duplici ratione: 1) quatenus ea ipse fecit nomine Patris, Ioann. III, 2. X, 25: 2) quoad auxilium Patris implorauit, & se ad Patris gloriam rem suam agere professus est, Ioann.

XI, 41. 42. Diserte hanc ipse rationem adiunxit: vt credant, me abs te missum esse: 3) ad diuinam Christi naturam, triplici modo: 1) quatenus sibi Christus potentiam potestatemque vindicat aequalem, atque omnino eamdem, quae Patris est, Ioann. V, 19: in altera quidem parte duplex inest probationis neruus: Vnus in vniuersitate rei, ὐ γὰρ - - ταῦτα καὶ κ. τ. λ. fine vlla exceptione (oporteret autem aliquid esse Patris proprium ac praecipuum, nisi Christus esset summus Deus, Patri par atque aequalis): Alter in vniuersitate modi, ὁμοίως ποιά.

Priora autem verba, quae nobis vehementer obiiciunt aduersarii, nihil testantur amplius, quam hoc: quod filius nil faciat, ac ne possit quidem, solus, a Patre separatus.

Ex quo ipso elucet arctissima ac necessaria filii cum Patre coniunctio, quae, quam mutua fit, tantum profecto valet, vt nec filius sine Patre, nec Pater vicissim sine filio, efficere quidquam possit.

Vid. Ioann. X, 30. coll. cum antec. v. 28. 29. add. XIV, 10. 2) Quatenus suo ipse nomine, suo arbitrio, suaque potestate tanta opera effecit. Matth. VIII, 3. 4. Luc. VII, 14. Notabile in primis est hoc dictum, Luc. IV, 36. Ita rem agere, nemo diuinitus legatus, ac ne angelus quidem, vnquam ausus est.

Omnes, si quid moliti sunt, fecerunt illud auspiciis diuinis, semper ad summi Numinis arbitrium atque auctoritatem prouocantes: כה אמר יהוה Vates vnus omnium maximus, Moses, nunquam non Deum tantarum rerum effectorem appellat, Deum, ait, hoc fecisse, se autem Deo manus suas commodasse Ex.

IV, 22. 23. VII, 16. IX, 14. XIV, 21. 24. Nullo vnquam tempore ausus est ita dicere: Ego hoc praestabo! sic volo, sic iubeo! quem quidem ad modum Christus, & vnus ille Christus, loqui non dubitauit. Quid? quod eius Legati miracula sua nomine Christi perpetrarunt, quod illis neutiquam fuisset licitum, si filius esset Patre inferior.

Certe hoc habuissent necesse, vt ad Patris nomen simul prouocassent, atque etiam illud nomini Iesu anteposuissent. Act. III, 6. IV, 10. 30. XVI, 18. 3) Quoad sua ipse miracula hominibus exhibuit hac mente, vt suam gloriam patefaceret, Ioann.

II, 11. Omnia autem ad gloriam vnius Dei dirigenda sunt. Quod ad ipsa miracula attinet, quum Christus debuerit esse non Propheta solum, sed maximus etiam omnium Prophetarum, atque adeo Mose maior: necessaria erat consecutio, vt is vnus inter omnes excelleret miraculis plane singularibus, Ioann XV, 24.

Videamus igitur, quam eximie Iesus noster diuinos omnes, ne Mose quidem excepto, vicerit miraculorum, a se factorum I. Multitudine, Ioann. XX, 30. XXI, 25. Vna hora ingens fuit miraculorum numerus, Luc. VII, 21. Iudaeorum confessio exstat Ioann. VII, 31. II. Varietate; si quidem Nullum fere est genus rerum creatarum, in quo non multa Christi miracula fuerint conspicienda, videlicet 1) in caelo, Luc.

XXIII, 44. 45: 2) in aere, Matth. VIII, 26: 3) in terra, Matth. XXI, 19: & frugibus, Marc. VIII, 6. Ioann. VI, 11: 4) in aqua & mari, Matth. VIII, 26. Ioann.

VI, 19: 5) in spiritibus, daemones malignos expellendo; 6) in hominibus, tam viuis, praesertim vero aegrotantibus, qui morbo quodam insanabili laborabant, quam mortuis: 7) in brutis animantibus, speciatim quadrupedibus, Matth. VIII, 32. & aquatilibus, Marc. VIII, 7. 9. Ioann. VI, 11. Luc. V, 5. 6.

Ioann. XXI, 3. 6. 11. 2) Neque vllum est genus miraculorum, cuius specimina multa Christus non dederit. Quatuor, nec plura, esse posse miraculorum genera, adparet eo: quod omnium rerum nec sunt, nec esse possunt, plures, quam quatuor proprietates: 1) existentia, vt philosophi loquuntur, 2) essentia, siue natura, tum communis, tum propria, 3) quantitas, & 4) qualitas.

In his igitur omnibus vim omnino diuinam Iesus noster manifestauit, 1) res, primum efficiendo, & quae nondum sunt, perinde ac si essent, vocando, Ioann. IX, 32. add. Rom. IV, 17: 2) naturam rerum mutando, Ioann. II, 9:


### Quaest. C. What did the prophet Christ teach?

Christ the prophet taught primarily the gospel , secondarily the law .

Proved a. 1) From the testimony of John the Baptist: The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ, John 1:17. Grace and truth are the marrow of the evangelical proclamation, inasmuch as it is the most true doctrine concerning the grace of God.

2) From the utterance of the Messiah, Isa. 61: 1. The Spirit of Adonai Iehouah (is) upon me: Iehouah has anointed me, he has sent me to evangelize the poor; the fulfillment of which prophecy is had in Matt. 11: 5. Let the poor hear the gospel. Understood are the poor in spirit, who hunger and thirst for the righteousness of Christ, Matt. 5:6. 3) The argument of the doctrine which Christ professed in the days of his flesh stands in Mark 1: 14. Jesus came into Galilee, preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and saying: because the time is fulfilled and the kingdom of God has drawn near; Repent and believe in the gospel.

Proved b. Christ neither abrogated, nor mitigated, nor perfected the old moral law, since it is most perfect, Ps. 19:8; yet he vindicated the same from the corruptions of the Pharisees and interpreted it soundly, see Matt. 5:21 sqq. Therefore Christ is not a new legislator, but the interpreter and vindicator of the old law.

Latin:

Christus propheta docuit primario evangelium , secundario legem .

Prob. a. 1) E testimonio Ioannis baptistae: Lex per Mosen data est; gratia & veritas per Iesum Christum facta est, Io. I, 17. Gratia & veritas medulla praeconii evangelici, vtpote quod est verissima de gratia Dei doctrina.

2) Ex effato Messiae, Es. LXI, 1. Spiritus Adonai Iehouah (est) super me: Vnxit Iehouah me, ad euangelizandum pauperibus misit me; cuius vaticinii complementum habetur Matth. XI, 5. Pauperes audiant euangelium. Intelliguntur pauperes spiritu, qui esuriunt & sitiunt iustitiam Christi, Matth. V, 6. 3) Argumentum doctrinae, quam professus est Christus in diebus carnis, exstat Marc. I, 14. Venit Iesus in Galilaeam, praedicans euangelium regni, & dicens: quia impletum est tempus & appropinquauit regnum Dei; Paenitentiam agite & credite euangelio.

Prob. b. Veterem legem moralem Christus neque abrogauit, neque mitigauit, neque perfecit, cum sit perfectissima, Ps. XIX, 8. eandem tamen a corruptelis Pharisaeorum vindicauit & solide interpretatus est, vid. Matth. V, 21. sqq. Proinde Christus non est nouus legislator, sed legis veteris interpres & vindex.


### Quaest. CI. In how many ways does Christ perform the prophetic office?

Christ performs the prophetic office a) immediately, b) mediately.

Proved a. Christ in the days of his flesh with honeyed mouth taught the gospel αὐτοπροσώπως (personally) and immediately, purged the moral law from the Pharisaic leaven, and prepared his disciples for their future ministry.

Proved II, 9: 3) by increasing the quantity, with one word, Mark 8:7-9, John 6:11: 4) by removing the quality, by a wondrous conversion, as in the health of the sick restored, in life returned to the dead, in the fig tree suddenly withering, and what more things are similar to these. All these, without any natural cause, [were] apt and suitable for such great effects. III. By magnitude.

Namely, there are four miracles above all the greatest, and proper to Christ: 1) The opening of the eyes of a man blind from birth, John 9:32: 2) The casting out of demons from bodies, inasmuch as this was a work that befitted no one, except him to whom this had been given, that he alone might destroy the works of the devil: 3) The recalling of the dead to life, and indeed in such a way, however he himself willed, John 5:20, 21: 4) The recalling of his own lifeless body to life, John 2:18, 19; 10:18, of which power and potency the most evident document was the strength of Christ, when he was already about to breathe out his soul, Mark 15:37 and 39.

IV. By utility: For among all the miracles of Christ not even one was ever done to the detriment and ruin of any man, so that all might know that he was born for the salvation of all; Moses on the contrary, Elijah, and other divine Prophets, by their miracles both benefited upright men, and harmed the wicked, Luke 9:54-56. Let us turn our attention also to those things which are singular in the prophecies of Christ, inasmuch as they are indications of divinity, and for that reason fitting to none of the other Prophets, specifically these two: 1) That Christ foretold many things concerning his own affairs, and even those looking toward his own glory, and especially concerning the amplification of his kingdom, Matt. 26:64, 24 and 25 entire, Rev. 1:13 seqq., 2 and 3 entire. 2) That Christ confirmed those things which he himself foretold concerning future events with no other attestation than the authority of himself speaking, and thus swore by himself, for he used for the most part this manner of speaking, which no one else ever usurped: ἀμήν, ἀμήν, λέγω ὑμῖν (Amen, amen, I say to you). Add Matt. 24:34, John 14:29, Rev. 2:1, 8, 12, 18; 3:1, 7, 14. The other Prophets, however, all to a man, never spoke in their own name, [but] always appealed to the authority of God speaking and swearing, by this customary habit of speech, כה אמר יהוה (Thus says the Lord).

Prob. b. Christ, mediately through the Apostles, whom nevertheless He had immediately called, and their successors, the faithful ministers of the church, mediately called by Christ, reveals to men the will of the heavenly Father concerning the means of salvation and salvation itself eternal, and through His doctrine works in the hearts of men. Therefore, there pertain to the prophetic office of Christ 1) the promulgation of the divine counsel concerning the redemption of the human race, effected through the doctrine of the gospel, 2) the institution and preservation of the ecclesiastical ministry, 3) the ordination of the sacraments, 4) the donation of the Holy Spirit, 5) the calling to the church, 6) illumination, conversion, regeneration, renewal, and the confirmation of faith. Quæst.

Latin:

Christus fungitur officio prophetico a) immediate, b) mediate.

Prob. a. Christus in diebus carnis suae ore mellifluo euangelium αὐτοπροσώπως & immediate docuit, legem moralem a fermento pharisaico repurgauit, discipulosque suos ad futurum ministerium praeparauit.

Prob. II, 9: 3) quantitatem augendo, vno verbo, Marc. VIII, 7-9. Ioann. VI, 11: 4) qualitatem tollendo, mira conuersione, vt, in sanitate aegrotorum restituta, in vita mortuis reddita, in ficu subito exarescente, & quae plura sunt his similia. Omnia haec, sine vlla causa naturali, ad tantos effectus apta atque idonea. III. Magnitudine.

Scilicet quatuor potissimum sunt miracula omnium maxima, & Christi propria: 1) Apertio oculorum hominis, a natiuitate caeci, Ioann. IX, 32: 2) Daemonum e corporibus eiectio, quippe quod opus decebat neminem, praeter eum, cui hoc datum erat, vt opera diaboli ipse vnus destrueret: 3) Reuocatio mortuorum ad vitam, & ita quidem, vtcunque ipse voluerit, Ioann. V, 20. 21: 4) Sui corporis exanimati ad vitam reuocatio, Iann. II, 18. 19. X, 18. cuius potestatis ac potentiae euidentissimum documentum erat robur Christi, cum iam in eo esset, vt animam efflaret, Marc. XV, 37. & 39.

IV. Vtilitate: Inter omnia enim Christi miracula ne vnum quidem vnquam factum fuit in hominis cuiusdam detrimentum ac perniciem, vt omnes cognoscerent, ipsum in salutem omnium natum esse; Moses contra, Elias, aliique Vates diuini, suis miraculis & profuerunt probis hominibus, & nocuerunt improbis, Luc. IX, 54-56. Aduertamus animum etiam ad ea, quae in vaticinationibus Christi singularia sunt, vtpote diuinitatis indicia, ob eamque causam nulli aliorum Prophetarum conuenientia, sigillatim haec duo: 1) Quod Christus de suis rebus, atque etiam ad suam gloriam spectantibus, in primisque de amplificatione regni sui, multa praedixit, Matth. XXVI, 64. XXIV. & XXV. tot. Apoc. I, 13. seqq. II. & III. tot. 2) Quod Christus ea, quae ipse de futuris euentibus praenuntiauit, adfeneratione confirmauit haud alia, quam sua dicentis auctoritatis, atque adeo per se iurauit, vfus est enim plerumque hac dicendi ratione, quam nemo alius vnquam vsurpauit: ἀμήν, ἀμήν, λέγω ὑμῖν. Add. Matth. XXIV, 34. Ioann. XIV, 29. Apoc. II, 1. 8. 12. 18. III, 1. 7. 14. Caeteri autem Vates, ad vnum omnes, nunquam suo nomine sunt loquuti, semper ad auctoritatem Dei dicentis, ac iurantis, prouocarunt, vsitata hac sermonis consuetudine, כה אמר יהוה. vfitata hac sermonis confuetudine, & כה אמר יהוה

Prob. b. Christus mediate per Apostolos, quos tamen immediate vocauerat, eorumque successores, fideles ecclesiæ ministros, mediate a Christo vocatos, voluntatem Patris cœlestis de mediis salutis, ipsaque salute æterna hominibus reuelat, & per doctrinam suam in cordibus hominum operatur. Pertinent igitur ad officium Christi propheticum 1) promulgatio consilii diuini de redemtione generis humani, per doctrinam euangelii facta, 2) ministerii ecclesiastici institutio & conseruatio, 3) sacramentorum ordinatio, 4) Spiritus Sancti donatio, 5) vocatio ad ecclesiam, 6) illuminatio, conuersio, regeneratio, renouatio, fidei confirmatio.


### CII. Was Christ caught up into heaven to learn the mysteries of heaven, before He undertook the solemn duty of teaching?

Christ, before the beginning of His prophetic office, was not taken up in His body into heaven to learn the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom.

Prob. 1) Because concerning that rapture of Christ into heaven before the beginning of the prophetic office, there is deep silence in the Holy Scriptures. 2) Christ entered heaven only once, and indeed through His blood, Hebr. IX, 12. He ascended into the heavens once, Act. II, 32. 3) That rapture was not necessary, since Christ possessed all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge of the personal union. Col. II, 3. 4) During the Lenten time, in which the Socinians claim that rapture occurred, He was with wild beasts, not in heaven, tempted for forty whole days, not indeed taught in heaven, Marc. I, 13. He was led by the Holy Spirit into the desert: to that end, that He might be tempted by the devil, not that He might be caught up into heaven, Matth. IV, 1.

There is an antithesis of the Socinians, contending that Christ, before He undertook the public duty of teaching, was carried up into heaven to learn the heavenly mysteries; who persuade us of their most vain opinion with the following arguments:

I. They urge the assertions of Christ: I have descended from heaven, that I may do what He wills, who sent me, Io. VI, 38. I went out from the Father, and came into the world, Io. XVI, 28. Resp. Christ is said to have descended from heaven, and to have gone out from the Father, not in respect of His human nature, but by reason of His divine nature, not by local motion, but by the assumption of human nature and the manifestation made through the same on earth.

Instantia: But the Son of Man is said to have descended from heaven, and to have ascended into heaven, Io. III, 13. Resp. The Son of Man in that place denotes the person, not the nature. That same person, who after the incarnation is the Son of Man, and at the appointed time ascended into heaven, descended before the incarnation, that He might become the Son of Man.

VIII, 28. I do nothing of myself, but as the Father has taught me, I speak. Resp. God the Father taught Christ, not by catching Him up into heaven, but by anointing Him with the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

III. Moses and Paul were caught up into heaven: Therefore, much more must this be established concerning the Lord Jesus. Resp. The argument can be inverted: Moses ascended into Mount Sinai, and Paul was caught up into heaven, that they might learn the will of God, previously unknown to them: Therefore Christ was not caught up into heaven before the beginning of His office, for the reason that from the first moment of His conception He was anointed with the Holy Spirit without measure, Io. III, 15. and He knew all things, Io. XX, 10. Certainly, He does not need a rapture into heaven or heavenly information, who has as an internal teacher the Word, the all-knowing.

Ques. CIII. What is the kingly office of Christ? The kingly office of Christ is that by which Christ, the God-man, being constituted Lord of all things that are in heaven and on earth, and especially King and Head of the Church, governs all things in the kingdom of power, grace, and glory with supreme majesty, so that they may serve the glory of God and the salvation of the elect.

Ques. CIV. What kind of King is Christ? Christ is a most high King a), spiritual b), eternal c), universal d), omnipotent e), omnipresent f), omniscient g), renowned for victory h).

Proof a. Christ is called the prince of the kings of the earth, Rev. I, 5. King of kings, Rev. XIX, 11.

Proof b. Jesus answered: My kingdom is not of this world, John XVIII, 36. Indeed, the kingdom of Christ is in the world and over the world, but it is not of the world; that is: it is not governed after the manner of the princes of this age, not with iron or carnal weapons.

The offered political government Christ refused, John VI, 15. Nor did He wish to perform the duty of a civil judge, Luke XII, 14.

Proof c. Of the kingdom of Christ there is no end, Dan. IV, 31. ch. VII, 14. Luke I, 33.

Proof d. Christ has dominion from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth, Ps. LXXII, 8. Zech. IX, 10.

Proof e. Eph. IV, 10. Christ ascended above all heavens, that He might fill all things.

He fills all things who is omnipresent, Jer. XXIII, 5.

Proof f. Christ is παντοκράτωρ [pantokratōr], Rev. I, 8. i.e., an omnipotent governor, to whom also belongs καρδιαρχία [kardiarchia], dominion over the consciences and hearts of men: a notable example of which He produced in that very contentious transport, of which mention is made, Matt. XXI, 3. where He incited the master of the donkey to lend the animal, and the hearts of the children to sing Hosanna.

Proof g. Christ is an omniscient King, because He knows all things, John XXI, 17. and searches the reins and hearts, Rev. II, 23.

Proof h. The triumph of Christ is threefold: 1) in hell, into which He gloriously descended; 2) on earth, which, having been raised from death, He revisited alive; 3) in heaven, into which He was most magnificently carried up. Thus He triumphed over the world, death, the devil, and hell.

Ques. CV. How manifold is the kingdom of Christ? The kingdom of Christ is threefold: the kingdom of power (*), of grace, and of glory.

Ques. CVI. What is the kingdom of power? The kingdom of power is that by which Christ most powerfully preserves and governs all creatures in this universe, for the praise of the Creator and the prosperity of the creatures.

Obs. The subjects in the kingdom of power are, generally speaking, all creatures, or, in the phrase of Scripture, all the works of the hands of God, Ps. 8:7; 1 Cor. 15:27; Eph. 1:20. Specifically, the subjects of Christ in this kingdom are those whom this King holds under his feet, reigning in their midst, Ps. 110:2; Eph. 1:13. The royal acts in the kingdom of power are: both the preservation and government of all creatures, and indeed the subjection of enemies.

Latin:

Christus ante exordium muneris sui prophetici corpore suo non sublatus est in cœlum, ad discendum mysteria regni cœlestis.

Prob. 1) Quia de illo raptu Christi in cœlum ante exorsum muneris prophetici in sacris litteris altum est silentium. 2) Christus non nisi semel, & quidem per sanguinem ingressus est cœlum, Hebr. IX, 12. semel ascendit in cœlos, Act. II, 32. 3) Non fuit ille raptus necessarius, cum Christus omnes thesauros sapientiæ & scientiæ vnionis personalis possideret. Col. II, 3. 4) Tempore quadragesimali, quo raptum illum contigisse ferunt Sociniani, cum feris, non in cœlo fuit, per integros XL. dies tentatus, non vero in cœlo doctus, Marc. I, 13. Ducebatur a Spiritu S. in desertum: eo fine, vt a diabolo tentaretur, non in cœlum raperetur, Matth. IV, 1.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, contendentium, Christum, antequam publicum docendi munus aggressus est, euectum esse in cœlum, ad discendum mysteria cœlestia; qui suam opinionem vanissimam sequentibus argumentis nobis persuadent:

I. Vrgent assertiones Christi: Descendi de cœlo, vt faciam, quod vult is, qui misit me, Io. VI, 38. Exiui a Patre, & veni in mundum, Io. XVI, 28. Resp. Christus dicitur de cœlo descendisse, & a Patre exiisse, non respectu humanæ naturæ, sed ratione diuinæ naturæ, non motu locali, sed assumtione humanæ naturæ & facta per eandem in terris manifestatione.

Instantia: Sed filius hominis dicitur de cœlo descendisse, & in cœlum ascendisse, Io. III, 13. Resp. Filius hominis l. c. personam, non naturam notat. Eadem illa persona, quæ post incarnationem filius hominis est, & statuto tempore in cœlum ascendit, ante incarnationem, vt filius hominis fieret, descendit.

II. Io. VIII, 28. Ex me ipso facio nihil, sed vt docuit me Pater, loquor. Resp. Deus, Pater Christum docuit, non in cœlum rapiendo, sed donis Spiritus S. vngendo.

III. Moses & Paullus in cœlum rapti sunt: E. multo magis id de domino Iesu statuendum est. Resp. Inuerti potest argumentum: Moses ascendit in montem Sinai, & Paullus raptus est in cœlum, vt discerent voluntatem Dei, sibi ante ignotam: Ergo Christus ante exordium muneris sui non est raptus in cœlum, eo, quod a primo conceptionis momento vnctus est Spiritu S. ἐν ἐκ μέτρῳ, Io. III, 15. & nouit omnia, Io. XX, 10. Sane raptu in cœlum cœlesti, ue informatione non indiget, qui internum habet doctorem τὸν λόγον omniscium.

Quæst. CIII. Quid est officium Christi regium? Officium Christi regium est, quo Christus θεάνθρωπος cum omnium, quæ in cælo & in terra sunt, dominus, tum in primis ecclesiæ rex & caput constitutus, in regno potentiæ, gratiæ & gloriæ omnia maiestate summa gubernat, vt seruiant gloriæ Dei, & electorum saluti.

Quæst. CIV. Qualis Rex est Christus? Christus est Rex celsissimus a), spiritualis b), æternus c), catholicus d), omnipotens e), omnipræsens f), omniscius g), victoria inclytus h).

Prob. a. Christus vocatur princeps regum terræ, Apoc. I, 5. rex regum, Apoc. XIX, 11.

Prob. b. Respondit Iesus: Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo, Io. XVIII, 36. Est quidem regnum Christi in mundo & super mundum, sed non de mundo; hoc est: non more principum huius sæculi, non armis ferreis aut carnalibus gubernatur.

Oblatam gubernationem politicam Christus recusauit, Io. VI, 15. nec munere iudicis ciuilis fungi voluit, Luc. XII, 14.

Prob. c. Regni Christi non est finis, Dan. IV, 31. c. VII, 14. Luc. I, 33.

Prob. d. Dominatur Christus a mari ad mare, & a fluuio vsque ad fines terræ, Ps. LXXII, 8. Zach. IX, 10.

Prob. e. Eph. IV, 10. Ascendit Christus super omnes cælos, vt omnia impleret.

Omnia implet, qui omnipræsens est, Ier. XXIII, 5.

Prob. f. Christus est παντοκράτωρ, Apoc. I, 8. i. e. gubernator omnipotens, cui etiam competit καρδιαρχία, dominium in conscientias & corda hominum: cuius insigne specimen edidit in illa ipsa contentissima vectura, cuius mentio fit, Matth. XXI, 3. vbi dominum asinæ ad commodandum animal, puerorum corda ad decantandum Hosianna instigauit.

Prob. g. Christus est Rex omniscius, quia omnia nouit, Io. XXI, 17. scrutaturque renes & corda, Apoc. II, 23.

Prob. h. Triplex est Christi triumphus 1) in inferno, in quem gloriose descendit; 2) in terra, quam e morte resuscitatus, viuus repetit; 3) in cælo, in quod magnificentissime subuectus est. Triumphauit itaque mundum, mortem, diabolum & infernum.

Quæst. CV. Quotuplex est regnum Christi? Regnum Christi est triplex, regnum potentiæ (*), gratiæ, & gloriæ.

Quæst. CVI. Quodnam est regnum potentiæ? Regnum potentiæ est, quo Christus omnes creaturas in hoc vniuerso potentissime conseruat & gubernat, in Creatoris laudem, & creaturarum prosperitatem.

Obs. Subditi in regno potentiæ generatim sunt omnes creaturæ, seu, phrasi scripturæ, omnia opera manuum Dei, Ps. VIII, 7. 1 Cor. XV, 27. Eph. I, 20. Speciatim in hoc regno subditi Christi sunt, quos hic rex sub pedibus suis tenet, in medio illorum regnans, Ps. CX. 2. Eph. I, 13. Actus regii in regno potentiæ sunt: cum omnium creaturarum conservatio & gubernatio, tum vero hostium subiectio.


### Q. CVII. What is the kingdom of grace?

The kingdom of grace is that by which Christ gathers, governs, adorns with spiritual gifts, preserves, and defends the church militant on earth, for the praise of the divine name, the destruction of the satanic kingdom, and the salvation of the faithful.

Obj. The subjects in this kingdom of grace are all faithful men who constitute the church militant. The royal acts are: the gathering, governing, adorning, preserving, and defending of the church against the enemies of grace, and his dominion in their midst.

Latin:

Regnum gratiæ est, quo Christus ecclesiam in terris militantem colligit, gubernat, spiritualibus donis exornat, conservat & defendit in nominis divini laudem, regni satanici destructionem, & fidelium salutem.

Obs. Subditi in hoc regno gratiæ sunt omnes homines fideles, qui ecclesiam militantem constituunt. Actus regii sunt, ecclesiæ collectio, gubernatio, exornatio, conservatio, defensio adversus hostes gratiæ, & in medio ipsorum dominatio.


### Q. CVIII. What is the kingdom of glory?

The kingdom of glory is that by which Christ most gloriously rules the church triumphant in heaven and fills it with eternal felicity, for the praise of the divine name and the eternal refreshment of the blessed. Obs.

The subjects in this kingdom of glory are both the good angels and the blessed men. The royal acts are: the resurrection of the dead faithful to life; their solemn introduction into eternal life, Matt. 25:34; and a most happy and most glorious government.

You say: There is also a fourth kingdom of Christ, namely, the kingdom of justice over evil angels and damned men. Resp. We refer the kingdom of justice to the kingdom of power.

Latin:

Regnum gloriæ est, quo Christus ecclesiam in cœlis triumphantem gloriosissime regit, & æterna felicitate replet, in nominis divini laudem, & beatorum æternam refectionem.

Obs. Subditi in hoc regno gloriæ sunt tum angeli boni, tum homines beati. Actus regii sunt: resuscitatio fidelium mortuorum ad vitam; horum solemnis introductio in vitam æternam, Matth. XXV, 34. & felicissima atque gloriosissima gubernatio.

Dicis: Datur etiam quartum regnum Christi, scilicet regnum iustitiæ in angelos malos & homines damnatos. Resp. Regnum iustitiæ referimus ad regnum potentiæ.


### Q. CIX. Is the kingdom of Christ to have an end?

The kingdom of grace will indeed be terminated on the last day a), but the kingdom of glory will never cease or be ended b).

Prob. a. For Christ will deliver the kingdom to the Father, 1 Cor. 15:24, both by way of presentation, as if for inspection, and by way of abdication; not as if Christ were to abdicate all kingdom, but because he will no longer administer the kingdom of grace through the Word and sacraments in the midst of enemies. Conf. D. CALOV. in bibl. illustrat. ad h. l. Prob. b.

The sacred writings explicitly testify that there will be no end to the kingdom of Christ, Dan. 7:14; Luke 1:33.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, who posit that the kingdom of Christ will not endure after the end of the world. They object I.

Christ will deliver the kingdom to the Father, 1 Cor. 15:24. Therefore, after the end of the world, he will no longer reign. Resp. Christ will deliver the kingdom of grace to the Father on the last day, so that the kingdom of glory may follow.

II. If Christ were to govern the kingdom of glory, the Apostle would not have said that the Son himself would subject himself to the Father, 1 Cor. 15:28. Resp. ὑποταγή, or passive subjection, is spoken of Christ according to his human nature, and in that place it is not understood simply as such (for even before this, the flesh of Christ was subject to the Father), but as something more illustrious. Indeed, Christ, as man, on the last day, will be subject to the Father both in fact and by confession, because he will openly confess that he refers all [to] refer all power, all dominion to God the Father as received. But for that reason the kingdom of Christ will not cease, for indeed all things, outside of God, will be subjected to him, v. 27. III. It behooves Christ to reign, until he has put all enemies under his feet, ...m1 1 Cor. XV, 25. Therefore, when he has abolished his enemies, the end of the kingdom will be at hand.

Resp. The force of the argument rests on the particle, until, which is sometimes taken finitely, or determinately, so that it denotes a certain limit, and sometimes infinitely and indeterminately, so that it designates perpetuity, even in a most difficult time. It seems here that the word "until" is taken infinitely, so that the sense becomes: It behooves Christ to reign always and forever, even in a most difficult time, when he will have the devil and the impious under his feet.

Conf. D. GEIER in Ps. CX. p. 696. & D. SCHERZER in Colleg. Anti-Socinian. p. 579. D. CALOV. in bibl. illustr. p. 397, however, concedes that the word "until" in this place can be taken determinately, so that a limit is noted not of the kingdom of Christ simply, but of a certain mode of reigning, and thus the sense will be: It behooves Christ to rule the kingdom of grace through the word and sacraments, until all his enemies are fully subjected; and then the kingdom of grace will cease.

But by that very fact the kingdom of glory will not be terminated.

For the Lamb in glory will feed the faithful, Apoc. VII, 17, who will follow him wherever he goes, c. XIV, 4.

IV. If Christ were to rule the kingdom of glory, in the same [kingdom] God the Father would not be all in all. See 1 Cor. XV, 25.

E. Christ will not rule the kingdom of glory. Resp. God the Father will be all in all: because he will govern the kingdom of glory immediately.

He will be himself our teacher, our King, our food, our salvation. But since Christ is ὁμοούσιος (consubstantial) with God the Father, together with God the Father and the Holy Spirit he will be all in all.

Quaest. CX. Was Christ King in the state of humiliation? Christ, at the time when he visibly walked on these earths, was a true King.

Prob. Christ is a born King, Luc. II, 11. A King riding on a donkey, Luc. XIX, 35. A King in the days of his flesh, Marc. XIV, 61. The antithesis is that of the Socinians, who deny that Christ was King in reality before the resurrection; although they do not deny that he was designated King before his death.

The same [people] object: Jesus was only made Christ, i.e., King, after his death, Act. II, 36. Resurrected from the dead, he received a name above every name, Phil. II, 9, and was placed in his kingdom, Luc. XXIV, 26. Therefore, before his death he was not King in reality.

Resp. The adversaries confuse the state of humiliation and [the state of] exaltation, likewise the use (χρῆσιν) and the possession (κτῆσιν) of Christ's rule. For he was anointed to royal dignity immediately at his very conception, and while he lived visibly on these earths he possessed the right of reigning, and occasionally exercised it at his own discretion. But in the state of humiliation he willingly abdicated the most full use of his rule, which never ceases.

MEMBER III. CONCERNING THE TWO-FOLD STATE OF CHRIST. I.

Latin:

Regnum gratiæ quidem terminabitur in extremo die a), at nunquam cessabit aut finietur regnum gloriæ b).

Prob. a. Tradet enim Christus regnum Patri, 1 Cor. XV, 24. tum per modum præsentationis, quasi ad lustrationem, tum per modum abdicationis; non perinde, ac si Christus omne regnum sit abdicaturus, sed quoniam regnum gratiæ per verbum & sacramenta in medio inimicorum non amplius est administraturus. Conf. d. CALOV. in bibl. illustrat. ad h. l.

Prob. b. Diserte testantur sacræ litteræ, regni Christi nullum fore finem, Dan. VII, 14. Luc. I, 33.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, statuentium, regnum Christi post finem mundi non esse duraturum. Obiiciunt

I. Christus regnum tradet Patri, 1 Cor. XV, 24. E. post finem mundi non amplius regnabit. Resp. Christus in extremo die Patri tradet regnum gratiæ, vt subsequatur regnum gloriæ.

II. Si Christus gubernaret regnum gloriæ, non dixisset Apostolus, ipsum Filium se subiecturum esse Patri, 1 Cor. XV, 28. Resp. ὑποταγή, sive subiectio passiva, dicitur de Christo secundum humanam naturam, eaque l. c. non simpliciter talis (nam & antea caro Christi Patri subiecta erat), sed illustrior intelligitur. Nimirum Christus, qua homo, in extremo die, & re, & confessione subiectus erit Patri, quia palam confitebitur, se omne ius, omnem potentiam, omne dominium Deo Patri acceptum referre. At propterea non cessabit regnum Christi, omnia quippe, extra Deum, illi subiecta erunt, v. 27. III. Oportet Christum regnare, donec posuerit inimicos omnes sub pedes suos, 1 Cor. XV, 25. Ergo cum aboleuerit hostes suos, regni finis affuturus est.

Resp. Vis argumenti nititur particula, donec, quae interdum sumitur finite, aut determinate, vt certum notet terminum, interdum infinite & indeterminate, vt designet perpetuitatem, etiam tempore difficillimo. Videtur heic τὸ donec sumi infinite, vt sensus fit: Oportet Christum regnare semper & in perpetuum, etiam tempore difficillimo, quo diabolum & impios sub pedibus suis habebit.

Conf. D. GEIER in Ps. CX. p. 696. & D. SCHERZER in Colleg. Anti-Socinian. p. 579. Concedit tamen D. CALOV. in bibl. illustr. p. 397. τὸ donec h. l. sumi posse determinate, vt notetur terminus non regni Christi simpliciter, sed certi modi regnandi, adeoque sensus erit: Oportet Christum regnum gratiae per verbum & sacramenta regere, donec omnes eius inimici plene subiecti erunt; & tunc regnum gratiae cessabit.

At eo ipso non terminabitur regnum gloriae.

Nam agnus in gloria pascet fideles, Apoc. VII, 17. secuturos eum, quocunque iuerit, c. XIV, 4.

IV. Si Christus regeret regnum gloriae, in eodem Deus Pater non foret omnia in omnibus. Vid. 1 Cor. XV, 25.

E. Christus non reget regnum gloriae. Resp. Deus Pater erit omnia in omnibus: quia immediate gubernabit regnum gloriae.

Erit ipse noster doctor, noster Rex, noster cibus, nostra salus. At cum Christus sit Deo Patri ὁμοούσιος, vna cum Deo Patre & Spiritu S. erit omnia in omnibus.

Quaest. CX. An Christus Rex fuit in statu exinanitionis? Christus eo tempore, quo visibiliter in his terris versatus est, verus Rex fuit.

Prob. Christus est Rex natus, Luc. II, 11. Rex asino vectus, Luc. XIX, 35. Rex in diebus carnis, Marc. XIV, 61. Antithesis est Socinianorum, negantium, Christum ante resurrectionem re ipsa fuisse Regem; quamuis non diffiteantur, eum ante mortem Regem fuisse designatum.

Obiiciunt iidem: Iesus post mortem demum factus est Christus, i. e. Rex, Act. II, 36. A mortuis resuscitatus accepit nomen super omne nomen, Phil. II, 9. & in regno suo collocatus est, Luc. XXIV, 26. E. ante mortem reipsa non fuit Rex.

Resp. Confundunt aduersarii statum exinanitionis, & exaltationis, item χρῆσιν, & κτῆσιν regiminis Christi. Hic enim statim in ipsa conceptione ad regiam dignitatem inunctus est, & consuetus visibiliter in his terris ius regnandi possedit, atque interdum pro arbitratu exercuit. At plenissime & nunquam cessante regiminis vsu in statu exinanitionis volens se abdicauit.

MEMBRVM III. DE DVPLICI STATV CHRISTI. I.


### On the State of Christ's Humiliation

Quaest. CXI. Did Christ always exercise the majesty communicated to his flesh in the same way? Christ did not always exercise the divine majesty communicated to his flesh in the same way, but from his conception until his death and burial, he withdrew and inhibited the full use of it; but having been made alive, resurrected, and raised into heaven, raised into

heaven, and exalted to the right hand of God, He fully assumed the same. From this arises a twofold state of Christ, one of exinanition, the other of exaltation.

Latin:

Quaest. CXI. An Christus communicatam carni suae maiestatem semper eodem modo exseruit? Christus communicatam carni suae maiestatem diuinam non semper eodem modo exseruit, sed a conceptione, vsque ad mortem & sepulcrum, eiusdem plenum vsum retraxit & inhibuit; viuificatus autem, resuscitatus, euectus in coelum resuscitatus, euectus in

cœlum, & exaltatus ad dextram Dei eandem plene vfurpauit. Ex quo oritur duplex Christi status, vnus exinanitionis, alter exaltationis.


### Question CXII. In what does the exinanition of Christ formally consist?

The exinanition of Christ formally consists not in the assumption of human flesh a); nor in the mere κρύψις, or concealment, of divine majesty b); nor in the complete abdication or emptying of divine majesty c); but in the abdication of the full and unceasing use of divine majesty, the assumption of the form of a servant, assimilation with other men, and most humble obedience d).

Proof a. Although in an ecclesiastical and improper sense incarnation is sometimes called exinanition; properly, however, and according to the usage of scripture, incarnation is not to be called exinanition. For 1) exinanition is called κένωσις, emptying, by Paul (*); but incarnation nowhere comes under the name of emptying, nor can it conveniently be so called. 2) Exinanition is said of the Son of God ἀσάρκῳ, or Christ θεανθρώπῳ; incarnation of the Son of God ἀσάρκῳ. 3) That exinanition is understood here which is removed by exaltation; but the state of incarnation remains. 4) That exinanition is designated by the Apostle in Phil. III, 5, which is proposed to us as an example; but incarnation is inimitable.

Proof b. The exinanition of Christ is not a mere κρύψις, or concealment, of divine majesty. For exinanition 1) does not apply to the exalted Christ, to whom, however, the concealment of majesty does apply: For we await the ἐπιφάνειαν καὶ ἀποκάλυψιν, the appearing and revelation of Jesus Christ, 1 Cor. 1, 7. 2) Because Christ was truly emptied before God, angels, and men. But if Christ had only concealed ἀνύπαρκτα, things communicated to Him, He would indeed have been obscure before men, but glorious before God. But He asked to be glorified with God, John XVII, 5. 3) The concealment of gifts is not true exinanition, just as the sun, covered by clouds, is not truly darkened; although we do not deny that Christ concealed the κένωσιν, or possession of communicated majesty, and did not everywhere divest Himself of it.

Proof c. A complete emptying, and as it were effusion, of divine majesty could not 1) have occurred without the dissolution of the personal union; which, since it is a perfect and internal union, cannot exist without the communication of natures and idioms. 2) During the state of exinanition, Christ sometimes (*) Although the Greek κενόω, as well as the Hebrew קקן, commonly and for the most part means the same as "to empty," "not to endure": yet this meaning is not perpetual, nor consistent with the thing signified. For in this way it would follow that we should believe that Christ completely renounced all assumption of divine perfections and properties, which were perpetually communicated with His human nature, and even their possession; which, however, is a confession of falsehood by all of us, and also very far removed from the mind of the blessed Author. But there is another power underlying this word, and one most suited to this matter, namely this: to restrain the effect, and the use of a thing, which indeed always and closely holds its efficacy within itself, but does not always manifest it externally for everyone to accomplish. See Isa. LV, 11. & 1 Cor. 1, 17, 18. Thus Christ ἐκένωσε ἑαυτόν, where, and when, and insofar as He abstained from the use and external effect of divine perfections and properties, which He never ceased to possess in Himself, and whose internal and perpetual efficacy He exercised where, and when, and insofar as it was fitting for the function of His office. Blessed GERHARDUS interpreted this word in the same way, in loc. theol. Exeg. T. I. loc. IV. § 297. Therefore, if the word κένωσις is to be translated into Latin, it is most correctly called abstinentia usurpationis (abstinence from assumption/use).

at times he produced clear specimens of divine majesty dwelling in his flesh, although Christ used that majesty more rarely and as it were extraordinarily.

Prob: d. Four requirements must be connected to describe fully the emptying of Christ: 1) Κένωσις, an evacuation of the full use of the communicated divine majesty, of divine omnipotence, omniscience, modified omnipresence, or that which is effectively operating and governing, and of adorability: 2) Λῆψις μορφῆς δούλου, an assumption of a servile condition. For Christ was treated in the manner of a servant, sold, and affected by servile punishment. 3) Ὁμοίωσις ἀνθρώπων, an assimilation with men of lower and ignoble status, especially the Israelites; in birth, circumcision, weaning, the craft of a carpenter, ἐν σχήματι, in conversation and gesture: 4) Ταπείνωσις ὑποτακτική, a most humble active and passive obedience. All of which are comprehended in that memorable saying of Paul, Phil. II, 5. 6. 7. 8. For let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus: who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: but made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men: and being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.

Obs: a) By this classic saying the submission of Christ is exhibited for us to behold, as an example proposed for imitation. b) The submission is described κατ' ἄρσιν, because he did not claim robbery to be equal to God, i. e. he did not judge that the majesty of the omnipotent and omnipresent Lord was to be publicly displayed like robbery, but he kept it hidden, and only then, when it seemed good to him, did he exert some rays of deiformity. c) By μορφὴν Θεῦ is not understood precisely and immediately the very essence of God, but the glorious status of Christ. For μορφὴ is called, in the judgment of CHEMNITIUS, de duab. nat. p. 352, when a nature or essence is considered in such a way that it is endowed with, and as it were clothed and adorned by, idioms, attributes, and conditions, whether divine or human. Therefore the form of God is divine omnipotence, supreme opulence, omniscience, the dignity of receiving supplication. The Apostle says: ἐν μορφῇ Θεῦ ὑπάρχων, existing in the form of God, i. e. a partaker or possessor of glory, power, and wisdom. d) Εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ signifies that he conducted himself equally to God in glory and majesty. He was not a displayer of the glory owed to him, but a humble abdicator. e) The Apostle describes the submission of Christ κατὰ θέσιν. ἀλλ' ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσε, but he emptied himself, not by pouring out the communicated majesty, but by withdrawing and restraining its full and universal use. . f) Μορφὴ δέλου is not the human nature, which Christ the God-man did not finally assume, but had; which also even through exaltation he did not lay aside: but it is a servile state, and an abject condition. g) Ὁμοίωμα ἀνθρώπων [Likeness of men] is conformity with other men, in natural and artificial actions, in the common way of living, in gesture and conversation, sin alone excepted. h) Ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτὸν γενόμενος ὑπήκοος μέχρι θανάτου [He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death], he humbled himself in a great passion, as much external of the body as internal of the soul, approving to God the Father a most humble active and passive obedience.

Latin:

Exinanitio Christi formaliter confistit non in affumtione carnis humanæ a); neFormale exinanitionis. que in nuda maiestatis diuinæ κρύψει, feu occultatione b); neque in omnimoda maiestatis diuinæ abdicatione, aut euacuatione c); sed in abdicatione pleni atque incessantis vfus diuinæ maiestatis, affumtione formæ feruilis, assimilatione cum aliis hominibus, & humillima obedientia d).

Prob. a. Quamuis in sensu ecclesiastico & improprio interdum incarnatio dicatur exinanitio; proprie tamen & ex vfu scripturæ incarnatio non est vocanda exinanitio. Nam 1) exinanitio à Paullo vocatur κένωσις, euacuatio (*); at incarnatio nullibi euacuationis nomine venit, neque commode ita dici potest. 2) Exinanitio dicitur de Filio Dei ἀσάρκῳ, siue Christo θεανθρώπῳ; incarnatio de Filio Dei ἀσάρκῳ. 3) Illa intelligitur hic exinanitio, quæ per exaltationem est fublata; sed incarnationis status permanet. 4) Ea ab Apostolo Phil. III, 5. defignatur exinanitio, quæ nobis in exemplum proponitur; sed incarnatio est inimitabilis.

Prob. b. Exinanitio Christi non est nuda κρύψις, feu occultatio maiestatis diuinæ. Nam exinanitio 1) non cadit in Christum exaltatum, in quem tamen cadit maiestatis occultatio: Exspectamus enim ἐπιφάνειαν καὶ ἀποκάλυψιν, apparitionem & reuelationem Iefu Christi, 1 Cor. 1, 7. 2) Quia Christus vere exinanitus est coram Deo, angelis & hominibus. Sed fi Christus tantum occultasset ἀνύπαρκτα, sibi communicata, obscurus quidem fuisset coram hominibus, sed gloriofus coram Deo. At petiit glorificari cum Deo, Io. XVII, 5. 3) Occultatio donorum non est vera exinanitio, sicut fol, nubibus tectus, non est vere obtenebratus; quamuis non diffitemur, quod Christus τὴν κένωσιν, feu possessionem communicatæ maiestatis, occultauerit, nec vbique exfueruerit. Prob. c. Omnimoda maiestatis diuinæ euacuatio, & quasi effusio, non potuiffet 1) fieri fine folutione unionis perſonalis; quæ cum fit perfecta & interna vnio, non potest exsistere fine communicatione naturarum & idiomatum. 2) Durante statu exinanitionis Christus interdum (*)

Quamquam græcum, κενόω, pariter ac hebraicum, קקן, vsitate ac plerumque idem valet, ac exinanio, non-fuffero: tamen ista fignificatio perpetua est, nec cum re fignificata congruens. Hoc enim pacto confequens foret, vt existimemus, Christum omni vfurpatione diuinarum, quæ cum humana ipfius natura perpetuo communicatæ sunt, perfectionum ac proprietatum, quin etiam possessione, fefe penitus abdicasse; id quod tamen nostra omnium confessio falfitatis, & atque etiam a mente b. Auctoris longe alienissimum. Sed est alia quædam huic verbo fubiecta potestas, eaque ad hanc rem maxime accommodata, quippe hæc: effectum cohibere, vsumque rei, quæ suam quidem in fe efficacitatem semper arctéque tenet, eam vero non semper extra fe prodere cuique conficiendam. Vid. Ief. LV, 11. & 1 Cor. 1, 17, 18. Ita Christus ἐκένωσε ἑαυτόν, vbi, & quando, & quoad fe ab vfu effectúque externo abstinuit perfectiomum proprietatumque diuinarum, quas quidem in fe poffidere nunquam defiit, quarum etiam internam perpetuamque efficacitatem, vbi, & quando, & quoad muneris functioni erat conueniens, exercuit. Eundem ad modum hanc vocem interpretatus est B. GERHARDVS, in loc. theol. Exeg. T. I. loc. IV. § 297. Itaque, fi latine conuertenda fit vox, κένωσις, rectissime dicitur abstinentia vsurpationis.

terdum luculenta edidit specimina maiestatis divinae in carne sua habitantis, quamvis Christus ea maiestate rarius & quasi extraordinarie usus sit.

Prob: d. Quatuor requisita connectenda sunt, ad plene describendam exinanitionem Christi: 1) Κένωσις, evacuatio pleni usus communicatae divinae maiestatis, divinae omnipotentiae, omniscientiae, omnipraesentiae modificatae, seu efficaciter operantis & gubernantis, adorabilitatis: 2) Λῆψις μορφῆς δούλου, assumtio conditionis servilis. Fuit namque Christus servi in modum tractatus, venditus & servili supplicio affectus. 3) Ὁμοίωσις ἀνθρώπων, assimilatio cum hominibus tenuioribus & ignobilibus, inprimis Israëlitis; in natiuitate, circumcisione, ablactatione, arte fabrili, ἐν σχήματι, in conversatione & gestu: 4) Ταπείνωσις ὑποτακτική, humillima obedientia activa & passiva. Quae omnia comprehenduntur memorabili illo dicto Pauli, Phil. II, 5. 6. 7. 8. Τοῦτο γὰρ Φρονείσθω ἐν ὑμῖν, ὃ καὶ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, ὃς ἐν μορφῇ Θεῦ ὑπάρχων οὐχ ἁρπαγμὸν ἡγήσατο τὸ εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ· ἀλλ' ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσε, μορφὴν δέλου λαβών, ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων γενόμενος καὶ σχήματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτὸν, γενόμενος ὑπήκοος μέχρι θανάτου, θανάτου δὲ σταυροῦ. Hic enim affectus fit in vobis, qui etiam in Iesu Christo: qui licet etiam in forma Dei esset, non rapinam esse existimavit, esse aequalia Deo, sed seipsum exinanivit, formam servi accipiens, ita ut in similitudine hominum esset & habitu inveniretur, ut homo: humiliavit seipsum, ita ut factus sit obediens usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis.

Obs: a) Hoc dicto classico submissio Christi exhibetur nobis intuenda, ut exemplum, ad imitandum propositum. b) Submissio describitur κατ' ἄρσιν, quod non potauerit rapinam, esse aequalia Deo, i. e. non iudicauit, rapinae instar publice ostentandam esse maiestatem omnipotentis & omnipraesentis Domini, sed eandem clam habuit, & tum demum, quando ipsi visum fuit, nonnullos deiformitatis radios exseruit. c) Per μορφὴν Θεῦ non intelligitur praecise & immediate ipsa essentia Dei, sed status Christi gloriosus. Appellatur enim μορφὴ iudice CHEMNITIO, de duab. nat. p. 352. quãndo natura, seu essentia aliqua ita consideratur, sicut idiomatis, attributis & conditionibus, vel divinis, vel humanis praedita, & quasi vestita atque ornata est. Est itaque forma Dei, divina omnipotentia, summa opulentia, omniscientia, dignitas recipiendi supplicationem. Dicit Apostolus: ἐν μορφῇ Θεῦ ὑπάρχων, in forma Dei existens, i. e. gloriae, potentiae, sapientiae particeps, vel possessor. d) Εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ significat, se Deo aequaliter gerere in gloria & maiestate. Non ostentator fuit gloriae sibi debitae, sed humilis abdicator. e) Describit Apostolus submissionem Christi κατὰ θέσιν. ἀλλ' ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσε, sed seipsum evacuauit, non effundendo communicatam maiestatem, sed eius usum plenum & uniuerfalem retrahendo & cohibendo. . f) Μορφὴ δέλου non est natura humana, quam Christus Θεάνθρωπος non demum assumsit, sed habuit; quam etiam per exaltationem non deposuit: sed est status servilis, et conditio abiecta. g) Ὁμοίωμα ἀνθρώπων est conformitas cum aliis hominibus, in naturalibus et artificialibus actionibus, in communi vivendi ratione, in gestu et conversatione, excepto solo peccato. h) Ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτὸν γενόμενος ὑπήκοος μέχρι θανάτου, humiliavit seipsum in passione magna tam externa corporis, quam interna animae, approbando Deo Patri obedientiam activam et passivam humillimam.


### Q. CXIII

What is the emptying [exinanitio] of Christ? Emptying is the state of Christ the God-man [θεάνθρωπος], by which he did not publicly display everywhere the divine majesty communicated to his flesh as if it were a robbery, but for a time having renounced its full and universal use, and having assumed a servile condition, he was not only made like to other men in the common way of living, but also sustained a most bitter passion and death with most humble obedience, so that he might redeem the human race from guilt and punishment, and restore to it the salvation that had been lost.

Latin:

Exinanitio est status Christi θεανθρώπου, quo is communicatam carni suae maiestatem divinam non instar rapinae ubique publice ostentavit, sed ad tempus abdicato eius pleno et universali usu, assumptaque conditione servili, non tantum aliis hominibus in communi vivendi ratione factus est similis, sed et acerbissimam passionem et mortem humillimo obsequio sustinuit, ut a culpa et poena redimeret genus humanum, et amissam ei salutem repararet.


### Q. CXIV

According to which nature was Christ emptied? Christ was emptied a) according to the human nature considered in personal union b).

Proof a. 1) The subject which of the emptying is called Jesus Christ, Phil. II, 5. which names are of a composite [συνθέτου] person, or one composed of both natures. 2) The subject which of obedience is also the subject which of the emptying. But indeed the subject which of obedience is the person of the God-man [θεάνθρωπος], through that of the Apostle: Christ Jesus, being in the form of God, emptied himself, and showed himself humble, becoming obedient even unto the death of the cross.

Phil. II, 5. 7. 8. Proof b. The subject by which is humanity alone, but considered in union; for 1) divinity, since it is immutable and most perfect, cannot be exalted and emptied. 2) The emptying was done even unto the death of the cross, Phil. II, 8. But divinity was neither dead, nor crucified.

You say: I. Christ emptied himself according to his divine nature, by assuming mortal and passible flesh. Response. The assumption of frail flesh is not properly called emptying, although in ecclesiastical style it is called humiliation. For emptying properly denotes an evacuation; but through the incarnation the Word [ὁ λόγος] did not evacuate himself of his majesty.

You say: II. Christ emptied himself by laying aside the God-form [deiformitatem], which belongs to him according to his divine nature. Response. The form of God [Μορφὴ θεοῦ] belongs to the divine nature formally and of itself, but to the human nature participatively and through the grace of personal union. The divine nature of Christ did not lay aside the God-form, inasmuch as it is immutable; but the human nature did, which is capable of emptying.

Latin:

Secundum quam naturam Christus exinanitus est? Exinanitus est Christus a) secundum humanam naturam in unione personali consideratam b).
