Prob. a. 1) Subjectum quod exinanitionis dicitur Iesus Christus, Phil. II, 5. quae nomina sunt personae συνθέτου, seu compositae ex utraque natura. 2) Subjectum quod obedientiae est etiam subjectum quod exinanitionis. At vero subjectum quod obedientiae est persona θεάνθρωπος, per illud Apostoli: Christus Iesus in forma Dei existens semetipsum exinanivit, et humilem praebuit, factus obediens usque ad mortem crucis.

Phil. II, 5. 7. 8. Prob. b. Subjectum quo est sola humanitas, sed in unione considerata; nam 1) divinitas, cum sit immutabilis et perfectissima, exaltari et exinaniri nequit. 2) Exinanitio facta est usque ad mortem crucis, Phil. II, 8. At divinitas nec mortua, nec crucifixa est.

Dicis: I. Christus secundum divinam naturam se exinanivit, assumendo carnem mortalem ac passibilem. Resp. Assumtio carnis fragilis non est proprie dicta exinanitio, licet stylo ecclesiastico humiliatio dicatur. Nam exinanitio proprie notat evacuationem; sed per incarnationem ὁ λόγος sua se maiestate non evacuavit.

Dicis: II. Christus exinanivit se deponendo deiformitatem, quae illi competit secundum divinam naturam. Resp. Μορφὴ θεοῦ competit naturae divinae formaliter et per se, humanae autem naturae participative et per unionis personalis gratiam. Deiformitatem non deposuit divina Christi natura, quippe quae est immutabilis; sed humana natura, quae exinanitionis est capax.


### Q. CXV

Of what use of glory did Christ divest himself in the state of emptying? Generally speaking, Christ in the state of emptying divested himself of the plenary, universal, and indefinite use of eternal glory, by personal union to the flesh assumed com-

having been made man, and at the same time having assumed the human nature into the subsistence [ὑπόστασιν] of the divine, he abstained from the perfect and continuous use of the divine properties and perfections, communicated with the human nature, he took the form of a servant, and undertook all human infirmities to be endured, which was necessary for the consequent humiliation [ταπείνωσιν]. 2) Humiliation [Ταπείνωσις] is a humble way of living, agreeing with the form of a servant, by which Christ rendered perfected obedience to God, even unto an ignominious death.

communicated ). Specifically, He suspended and restrained the use of omnipotence ), omniscience ), most abundant wealth ), omnipresent dominion ), and religious adorability ).

Obs. A distinction must be made between the full, universal, and incessant use of divine majesty, and the partial, particular, and ceasing use of that same majesty. Christ in the state of humiliation did not suspend or intermit every use of the divine majesty communicated to His flesh, but only the full, universal, and incessant one. In certain particular and miraculous actions, Christ in the midst of the state of humiliation truly usurped His divine majesty and vibrated certain rays and sparks of it, e.g., when Christ changed water into wine at the wedding in Cana, He is said to have manifested His glory, John 2:11. But that particular use ceased afterwards for a time.

Prob. a. From John 17:5. And now, O Father, glorify Thou Me with Thine own self with the glory which I had with Thee before the world was. This glorification, of which Christ speaks here, does not designate 1) the donation of the possession of glory; for Christ as man already possessed infinite glory before, John 1:14; nor 2) its particular usurpation, which He had shown in certain miracles; but 3) it denotes the enthronement and introduction of Christ the man into His kingdom to be administered omnipotently, omnipresently, omnisapiently, totally, and universally.

Prob. b. Christ in the assumed form of a servant withdrew the full use of omnipotence; which if He had exercised, the passion of Christ and the satisfactory death for our sins would have been hindered: for He would have repelled all injuries and prostrated all enemies.

Prob. c. Christ suspended the universal use of omniscience: for He truly did not know the day of the final judgment, Matt. 24:36, the barrenness of the fig tree, Matt. 21:19, the burial place of Lazarus, John 11:34.

Prob. d. Christ abstained from the use of wealth; since for our sake He became poor, 2 Cor. 8:9. Cf. Matt. 8:20.

8:20. Prob. e. The same [Christ] restrained the use of omnipresent dominion; of which Martha, the sister of the deceased Lazarus, was not ignorant, saying, John 11:21: Lord, if Thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.

Prob. f. Christ did not always exert the full light of adorable majesty; since He was made lower than the angels, Heb. 2:7.

Latin:

Quo gloriae usu in statu exinanitionis Christus se abdicavit? Generatim loquendo Christus in statu exinanitionis se abdicavit usu plenario, universali et indefinenti aeternae gloriae, per unionem personalem assumtae carni com-

homo factus, simul atque humanam naturam in ὑπόστασιν divinae adsumsit, se ab usu perfecto et continuo divinarum proprietatum perfectionumque, cum humana natura communicatarum, abstinuit, formam sumsit servi, omnesque infirmitates humanas perferendas suscepit, quod necesse fuit ad consequentem ταπείνωσιν. 2) Ταπείνωσις est humilis vivendi ratio, formae servi conveniens, qua Christus consummatam Deo obedientiam praestitit, usque ad mortem ignominiosam.

communicatae ). Speciatim suspendit & cohibuit usum omnipotentiae ), omniscientiae ), abundantissimae opulentiae ), omnipraesentis dominii ) & adorabilitatis religiosae ).

Obs. Distinguendum est inter usum maiestatis divinae plenum, universalem & incessantem, & inter usum eiusdem maiestatis aliqualem, particularem & cessantem. Christus in statu exinanitionis non suspendit aut intermisit omnem communicatae carni suae maiestatis divinae usum, sed tantum plenum, universalem & incessantem. In actionibus quibusdam particularibus & miraculosis Christus in medio exinanitionis statu maiestatem suam divinam vere usurpavit & illius radios & scintillas quasdam vibravit, v. gr. Cum Christus in nuptiis Cananeis aquam in vinum mutavit, suam gloriam manifestasse dicitur, Io. II, 11. Sed ille usus particularis postea ad tempus cessavit.

Prob. a. Ex Io. XVII, 5. Et nunc glorifica me, Pater, apud temet ipsum gloria, quam habui prius, quam hic mundus esset, apud te. Haec glorificatio, de qua Christus hic loquitur, non designat 1) donationem possessionis gloriae; nam Christus ut homo iam ante possedit gloriam infinitam, Io. I, 14.; neque 2) eius particularem usurpationem, quam in miraculis quibusdam ostenderat; sed 3) notat inthronisationem & introductionem Christi hominis in suum regnum omnipotenter, omnipraesenter, omnisapienter, totaliter & universaliter administrandum.

Prob. b. Retraxit Christus in assumta forma servili usum plenum omnipotentiae; quam si exercuisset, passio Christi & mors satisfactoria pro peccatis nostris impeditae fuissent: depulisset enim omnes iniurias, omnesque inimicos prostravisset.

Prob. c. Suspendit Christus usum universalem omniscientiae: vere enim ignorauit diem extremi iudicii, Matth. XXIV, 36. sterilitatem ficus, Matth. XXI, 19. locum sepulcralem Lazari, Io. XI, 34.

Prob. d. Abstinuit Christus ab usu opulentiae; si quidem propter nos egenus factus est, 2 Cor. VIII, 9. Conf. Matth. VIII, 20.

Prob. e. Cohibuit idem usum omnipraesentis dominii; cuius non ignara fuit Martha soror defuncti Lazari, inquiens, Io. XI, 21: Domine, si fuisses hic, frater meus non esset mortuus.

Prob. f. Plenam lucem maiestatis adorabilis Christus non semper exseruit; si quidem minor factus est angelis, Hebr. II, 7.


### Q. CXVI. How long did the state of humiliation last?

The state of humiliation lasted from the first moment of conception until the last moment of rest in the sepulcher. Prob. From Phil.

2:8. Christ humbled Himself, so that He became obedient unto death; even the death of the cross. By death here we understand both the act of the separation of the soul from the body, and the state of Christ the dead man, which also includes the burial and the three days of death.

Latin:

Status exinanitionis duravit a primo momento conceptionis usque ad ultimum momentum quietis in sepulcro.

Prob. Ex Phil. II, 8. Christus humiliavit seipsum, ita ut factus sit obediens usque ad mortem; mortem autem crucis. Per mortem hic intelligimus tum actum separationis animae a corpore, tum statum Christi hominis mortui, qui etiam sepulturam & triduum mortis complectitur.


### Q. CXVII. To what end did Christ humble Himself and abdicate the full use of divine majesty?

Christ humbled Himself not for His own sake, but for us sinners ), so that for the robbery of deiformity, committed by the first parents, He might satisfy divine justice ), and redeem the whole human race from sins ).

Prob. a. From 2 Cor. VIII, 9. Our Lord Jesus Christ for your sake became poor, though he was rich, so that you by his poverty might become rich. We are by nature children of wrath, Eph. II, 3. and thus we lack the riches of grace and righteousness; but for our sake Christ, who is most rich, became poor, so that his indigence might be our opulence.

Prob. b. The Messiah restored what he did not steal, Ps. LXIX, 5. It pleased our first parents indeed, at the suggestion of the devil, to steal deiformity against all right and wrong; but Christ expiated that most foul theft, not by proudly displaying the full use of deiformity communicated to his flesh, but by modestly restraining it.

Prob. c. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us. Gal. III, 13. Christ freed us from the execratory sentence of the law by meeting a detestable death in our place.

Question CXVIII. Which are the principal acts by which the emptying of Christ is completed?

To the emptying of Christ pertain the following acts: 1) conception, 2) birth, 3) circumcision, 4) upbringing, 5) visible conversation among men, 6) great passion, 7) death, 8) burial.

Question CXIX. What is the conception of Christ?

Conception is the supernatural act by which the flesh of Christ, upon the coming of the Holy Spirit, produced from the bloody mass of the virgin Mary, in her womb, received its first being, consubstantial with us.

Obs. We examined above the conception of Christ, questions XIV and XV, where we dealt with the origin of the flesh of Christ; but now we consider it not precisely in itself, but insofar as it pertains to the state of emptying, or insofar as the flesh of Christ, although not from male seed, was nevertheless formed in the womb of a woman; for which reason it is certain that some infirmities concur. Cf. D. Baier's Compendium, p. 607.

Question CXX. What is the birth of Christ?

The birth of Christ is the coming forth of God-the-infant from the maternal womb into these breezes of light.

Proof. That the birth of Christ pertains to the state of humiliation is clear: since Christ was born 1) from a mother who was indeed a virgin, but a poor one; 2) not in a splendid city, but in the small town of Bethlehem; 3) not in a royal citadel, but in a sordid stable; 4) at the time of the Jewish scepter, if not entirely broken, yet not a little shaken, with Octavius Augustus holding power, the tyrant Herod raging, and Quirinius the governor exacting the census.

Observation. By this most poor birth, Christ sanctified our sinful birth, Is. IX, 6, and procured for us spiritual υἱοθεσίαν (adoption) before God, Gal. IV, 4, 5.

Question CXXI. What is the circumcision of Christ?

Circumcision is the bloody amputation of the foreskin of the infant Jesus Christ, performed on the eighth day.

Proof. Circumcision is an act of Christ's most humble obedience, by which Christ not only lay in a deep state of humiliation under the razor of the circumciser, but was also subjected to the divine law; although he is nevertheless the Lord of the law, Matt. XII, 8, Mark II, 28.

Obs. I. By this circumcision Christ obligated Himself to fulfill the whole law, and by the first shedding of drops of blood, He gave a pledge of the future redemption through His blood, see Gal. IV, 4.5. & V, 3.

Obs. II. Other reasons are also usually given for why Christ willed to be circumcised: 1) that He might show that He is true man; 2) that He might be recognized as a Jew, born from the seed of Abraham; 3) that He might put an end to circumcision. Education

Education Q. CXXII. What was the education of Christ?

The education of Christ was His habituation in childhood, both to a way of life worthy of an Israelite, and to the craft of a carpenter.

Proof. The education of Christ is a degree of submission, by which Christ voluntarily subjected Himself to the care of Joseph His father, and to the commands of His mother Mary, Luke II, 51.

Obs. By this obedience, rendered to His parents, Christ produced every kind of prosperity for obedient children.

Conversation Q. CXXIII.

What was the visible conversation of Christ in these lands? The conversation of Christ was His most holy manner of life in the days of His flesh with various, even most contentious men, full of troubles, inconveniences, and dangers.

Proof. Christ conversed familiarly with fishermen, publicans, and sinners, Luke XV, 2. He was surrounded by a company of the blind, the deaf, the lame, and those possessed by demons, Matt. XI, 5. But what calumnies did He not encounter everywhere? What dangers did He not undergo? The Jews had taken counsel to overwhelm Jesus with stones, John VIII, 59, or to destroy Him by some other violent kind of death, Matt. XXI, 46. Nay, even His fellow-countrymen of Nazareth strove to cast Him headlong from the brow of the hill, Luke IV, 29. Furthermore, Christ endured hunger, thirst, and the inconveniences of journeys. All of which testify to the exinanition of Christ.

Obs. By this familiar conversation with sinners and the sick, He both fulfilled the divine law concerning loving one's neighbor, and performed His prophetic office. The Great Passion

The Great Passion Q.

The great passion of Christ is the extreme suffering which our Redeemer exhausted, toward the end of His life, two days before His death, by enduring the greatest and most bitter pains. Therefore, the extreme passion of Christ is partly internal of the soul a), and partly external of the body b).

Obs. The passion of Christ is partly begun and small, partly extreme and great. The former Christ sustained both throughout the whole course of His life, and especially in His prophetic office: the latter befell Him toward the end of His life two days before His death.

Proof. a. How bitter the internal passion of Christ's soul was, is gathered 1) from the names by which its gravity is expressed. For it is called 1) ἀγωνία, agony, by which Christ had to struggle with death, which was still powerful, Luke XXII, 44. 2) λύπη, sorrow, by which the soul of Christ was deprived of all consolation, Matt. XXVI, 37. 3) περίλυπια, an ineffable obsession of pain, even unto death, Matt. l. c. v. 38. 4) ἐκθάμβησις, consternation, such as those who suffer from fever, or are struck by lightning, or have seen a specter are struck with, Mark XIV, 33. 5) ἀδημονία, the anxiety of solitude, due to the lack of present help, both divine and human

l. c. & Marc. l. c. From the external signs, which are: a) the prostration of the body to the ground; b) the deprecation of the cup; c) the bloody sweat of the body, a most clear witness and index of supernatural affliction and of fire burning within; d) the comforting by an angel; e) the most sorrowful complaint of Christ, both on the Mount of Olives, concerning the affliction unto death, and on the cross, concerning the desertion by God, conceived in these words: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? Matth. XXVII, 46. Marc. XV, 34. Objection.

Christ is to be viewed here not in himself, and by himself, but in his mediatorial and priestly office, insofar as he represents the whole human race in the judgment of God, and bears all the sins of all men. In this respect he anxiously complains that he has been forsaken by God. Which desertion formally consists a) not in despair; for these words breathe filial confidence: My God! My God! nor b) in the dissolution of the personal union; for what Christ once assumed, he never laid aside: but c) in the sense of divine wrath, on account of the sins of men imputed to him, and in the privation of all consolation, which otherwise is accustomed to redound from the indwelling Deity.

Proof b. Christ endured a great passion of the body in a triple theater, as it were: earthly, stony, and wooden. The earthly theater of the passion was the Mount of Olives, where Christ, having exhausted his internal passion, was betrayed by the perfidious Judas, and captured and bound by his enemies. The stony theater was both the palace of Caiaphas and the praetorium of Pilate. In both, the hands of Christ suffered bonds, his ears calumnies, his face blows, his lips spittle, and, what is horrible to say, in the praetorian theater, the whole body of Christ was lacerated with scourges, his head crowned with thorns, and his hands dishonored by the insertion of a reed. To these is added the tragic fall of Judas and Peter, the former indeed despairing, the latter, however, revived unto repentance. In the wooden theater of the cross, his hands and feet were pierced with iron nails, and his side was sought and pierced with a lance. To which add so many calumnies, brought upon the Savior by the ignominious company of thieves, by the shameful inscription, and by the stinging words of those standing by or passing by.

Objection. In this great passion, Christ is to be viewed as much in his soul as in his body, as a mirror of wrath, grace, and virtue. Christ felt the wrath of God, on account of the alien sins of men, transferred onto himself: he reconciled the grace of God to sinners by his satisfactory passion; he left to men an incomparable example of virtue, love, meekness, and patience.

Latin:

Christus se exinanivit non propter se, sed propter nos peccatores ), vt pro raptu deiformitatis, a protoplastis commisso, iustitiae divinae satisfaceret ), & universum genus humanum a peccatis redimeret ).

Prob. a. Ex 2 Cor. VIII, 9. Dominus noster Iesus Christus propter vos pauper factus est, cum esset diues, vt vos ipsius paupertate ditesceretis. Nos natura sumus filii iræ, Eph. II, 3. adeoque caremus diuitiis gratiæ & iustitiæ; at propter nos Christus ditissimus factus est pauper, vt illius indigentia nostra esset opulentia.

Prob. b. Soluit Messias, quod non rapuit, Ps. LXIX, 5. Protoplastis quidem nostris collibuit, suggerente diabolo, deiformitatem contra ius & fas omne rapere; at fœdissimum illum raptum expiauit Christus, plenum vsum deiformitatis, carni suæ communicatæ, non superbe ostentando, sed modeste inhibendo.

Prob. c. Christus nos redemit a maledictione legis, factus pro nobis exsecratio. Gal. III, 13. Christus liberauit nos a sententia legis exsecratoria, mortem detestabilem nostri loco oppetendo.

Quæst. CXVIII. Quinam sunt præcipui actus, quibus absoluitur exinanitio Christi?

Ad exanitionem Christi perinent sequentes actus: 1) conceptio, 2) nativitas, 3) circumcisio, 4) educatio, 5) visibilis inter homines conuersatio, 6) passio magna, 7) mors, 8) sepultura.

Quæst. CXIX. Quid est conceptio Christi?

Conceptio est actus supernaturalis, quo caro Christi, superueniente Spiritu S., producta ex massa sanguinea Mariæ virginis, in eiusdem vtero, primum esse, nobis consubstantiale, accepit.

Obs. Expendimus supra conceptionem Christi, quæst. XIV. XV. vbi de origine carnis Christi egimus; jam autem consideramus eam non in se præcise; sed quatenus ad statum exinanitionis pertinet, seu quatenus caro Christi, licet non ex virili semine, tamen in vtero fœminæ formata fuit; qua ratione certum est, nonnullas infirmitates concurrere. Conf. D. BAIERI compend. p. 607.

Quæst. CXX. Quid est natiuitas Christi?

Natiuitas Christi est egressio Dei-infantis ex vtero materno in has lucis auras.

Prob. Natiuitatem Christi pertinere ad statum exinanitionis liquet: quoniam Christus natus est 1) a matre quidem virgine, sed paupercula; 2) non in vrbe splendida, sed in exiguo oppido Bethlehemo: 3) non in arce regia, sed in sordido stabulo; 4) tempore sceptri Iudaici, si non penitus fracti, haud parum tamen quassati, rerum potiunte Octauio Augusto, sæuiente tyranno Herode, censum exigente Quirino præside.

Obs. Hac natiuitate pauperrima Christus peccaminosam nostram natiuitatem sanctificavit, Es. IX, 6. & υἱοθεσίαν spiritualem apud Deum nobis conciliauit, Gal. IV, 4. 5.

Quæst. CXXI. Quid est circumcisio Christi?

Circumcisio est Iesu Christi infantis, octauo die facta, cruenta præputii amputatio.

Prob. Circumcisio est actus humillimæ Christi obedientiæ, qua Christus non tantum in profundo exinanitionis statu iacuit sub nouacula circumcisoris, sed & legi diuinæ subiectus est; cum tamen sit dominus legis, Matth. XII, 8. Marc. II, 28.

Obs. I. Hac circumcisione Christus se obligauit ad totam legem implendam, atque prima sanguinearum guttarum effusione arrham dedit futuræ per sanguinem suum redemptionis, vid. Gal. IV, 4.5. & V, 3.

Obs. II. Solent aliæ etiam causæ reddi, ob quas Christus circumcidi voluerit: 1) vt ostenderet, se esse verum hominem; 2) vt agnosci posset Iudæus, e semine Abrahami prognatus; 3) vt circumcisioni finem imponeret. Educatio

Quæst. CXXII. Quæ fuit educatio Christi?

Educatio Christi fuit assuefactio eiusdem in ætate puerili, tum ad genus viuendi, Israëlita dignum, tum ad artem fabrilem.

Prob. Educatio Christi est gradus submissionis, qua Christus Iosephi patris curæ, & matris Mariæ mandatis se sponte subiecit, Luc. II, 51.

Obs. Hac obedientia, parentibus præstita, Christus liberis morigeris omne prosperitatis genus peperit. Conversatio

Quæst. CXXIII. Quæ fuit conuersatio visibilis Christi in his terris?

Conuersatio Christi fuit sanctissima ipsius consuetudo in diebus carnis suæ cum variis, etiam contentissimis hominibus, plena molestiis, incommodis, periculis.

Prob. Versatus est Christus familiariter cum piscatoribus, publicanis & peccatoribus, Luc. XV, 2. Circumfusus fuit cœtu cœcorum, surdorum, claudorum, a dæmoniis obsessorum, Matth. XI, 5. At, quas non abhorbuit vbique calumnias? quæ non adiuit pericula? Ceperant Iudæi consilium, Iesum lapidibus obruendi, Io. VIII, 59. aut alio violento mortis genere perimendi, Matth. XXI, 46. Quin & sympatriotæ Nazarethani ipsum de supercilio montis præcipitem agere nitebantur, Luc. IV, 29. Præterea Christus famem, sitim, itinerum incommoda tolerauit. Quæ omnia testantur de exinanitione Christi.

Obs. Hac familiari conuersatione cum peccatoribus & ægrotis tum legem diuinam de diligendo proximo impleuit, tum officio prophetico perfunctus est. Passio magna

Quæst. CXXIV. Quæ fuit passio Christi magna?

Passio Christi magna est extrema passio, quam redemptor noster exantlauit, circa finem vitæ, biduo ante mortem, partim in anima, partim in corpore, maximos & acerbissimos dolores perferendo. Est itaque extrema Christi passio alia interna animæ a), alia externa corporis b).

Obs. Passio Christi alia est inchoata & parua, alia extrema & magna. Illam Christus cum in toto vitæ cursu, tum præcipue in officio prophetico sustinuit: hæc illi obtigit circa finem vitæ biduo ante mortem.

Prob. a. Quam acerba fuerit interna animæ Christi passio, colligitur 1) e nominibus, quibus eius grauitas exprimitur. Vocatur enim 1) ἀγωνία, lucta, qua Christo cum morte adhuc valida decertandum fuit, Luc. XXII, 44. 2) λύπη, tristitia, qua anima Christi omni solatio priuata est, Matth. XXVI, 37. 3) περίλυπια, doloris obsessio ineffabilis, vsque ad mortem, Matth. l. c. v.... 38. 4) ἐκθάμβησις, consternatio, quali vel febri laborantes, vel fulmine perculsi, vel spectrum conspicati percutiuntur Marc. XIV, 33. 5) ἀδημονία, anxietas solitudinis, ob defectum præsentis auxilii, tam diuini, quam humani

Matth. l. c. & Marc. l. c. E signis externis, quæ sunt: a) prostratio corporis in terram; b) deprecatio calicis; c) sudor corporis sanguineus, supernaturalis afflictionis ac ignis, intra vrentis, testis & index clarissimus; d) confortatio angeli; e) querela Christi mœstissima, tum in monte oliueti, de afflictione ad mortem, tum in cruce, de desertione Dei, concepta his verbis: Deus mi, Deus mi, propter quid dereliquisti me? Matth. XXVII, 46. Marc. XV, 34.

Obs. Christus spectandus hic non in se, ac per se, sed in officio suo mediatorio ac sacerdotali, quatenus in iudicio Dei totum genus humanum repræsentat, & omnia omnium hominum peccata portat. Hoc respectu anxie conqueritur, se a Deo derelictum esse. Quæ derelictio formaliter consistit a) non in desperatione; filialem quippe confidentiam spirant hæc verba: Deus mi! Deus mi! neque b) in solutione unionis personalis; quod enim Christus semel assumsit, nunquam deposuit: sed c) in sensu iræ divinæ, ob peccata hominum sibi imputata, & in privatione omnis solatii, ex inhabitante Deitate alias redundare soliti.

Prob. b. Magnam corporis passionem Christus sustinuit in triplici quasi theatro, terreno, lapideo & ligneo. Theatrum passionis terrenum fuit mons oliueti, ubi Christus, exantlata passione interna, a perfido Iuda proditus, & ab hostibus captus atque ligatus est. Theatrum lapideum fuit tum palatium Caiphæ, tum prætorium Pilati. In vtroque patiebantur manus Christi vincula, aures calumnias, facies colaphos, otuli sputum, &, quod dictu horrendum est, in theatro prætoriano, totum corpus Christi flagellis laceratum, caput corona spinea redimitum, & manus inferta arundine dehonestatæ sunt. His accedit lapsus tragicus Iudæ & Petri, illius quidem desperantis, huius autem ad pœnitentiam resuscitati. In theatro ligneo crucis, manus pedesque clauis ferreis transfixi sunt, latus autem lancea petitum ac perfoffum est. Quibus adde tot calumnias, a societate latronum ignominiosa, ab inscriptione probrosa, ab aculeatis dictis adstantium aut transeuntium saluatori illatas.

Obs. In magna hac passione tam animæ, quam corporis Christus spectandus est, vt speculum iræ, gratiæ & virtutis. Iram Dei sensit Christus, ob peccata aliena hominum, in se translata: gratiam Dei peccatoribus conciliauit passione satisfactoria; virtutis, amoris, mansuetudinis, patientiæ, incomparabile exemplum hominibus reliquit.


### Question CXXV

Did Christ feel infernal pains? Christ endured infernal pains, as to substance, not as to accidents. He endured pains most grievous intensively, equivalent to the eternal pains of the damned. He endured them not in the place of the damned, but on the Mount of Olives and the wood of the cross.

The assertion is proved: Whosoever pains were so bitter and vehement that they afflicted the soul of Christ even unto death, left him destitute of all aid, excited prayers for the averting of the cup, bathed his whole body prostrate on the ground in a bloody sweat, and expressed a most sorrowful complaint concerning the desertion of God, those pains were intensively infernal: But the internal pains endured by Christ on the Mount of Olives and the wood of the cross were so bitter and vehement: Therefore.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, Socinians, and Arminians, who deny that Christ endured infernal pains. Their chief arguments are:

I. He who suffers infernal pains, he despairs: because infernal pains include despair: But Christ did not despair. Therefore. Response. He who suffers infernal pains, by succumbing to them, he despairs; I concede. Whosoever suffers infernal pains, by overcoming them, he despairs; I deny.

It is far otherwise with the guilty person, upon whom the wrath of God remains; but

ter with a surety, who thus had to taste death, that he might swallow it. Despair coheres with infernal pains not necessarily, but accidentally. For the Lord leads into hell and leads back, 1 Sam. II, 6.

II. Christ did not suffer eternal pains: Therefore he did not suffer infernal pains. Resp. Christ suffered pains, intensively infernal and eternal, by reason of degree: not infernal and eternal extensively, by reason of duration. He suffered pains, if you look at the gravity, equivalent to infernal pains; if you consider the sublimity of the sufferer, surpassing the eternal punishments of the damned.

III. Christ did not feel the wrath of God; because he was always the most holy and most beloved Son of God: Therefore he did not suffer infernal pains. Resp. Christ felt the wrath of God, not on account of his own sins, for thus he was always most holy; but on account of the sins of others, transferred onto himself, on account of which he was made κατάρα, a curse, i.e., subject to the curse, Gal. III, 13.

IV. Christ's soul was always blessed, since it is most closely joined to God: Therefore it did not feel infernal pains. Resp. Christ's soul was always blessed, as to its primary act; his secondary act and the fruition of beatitude were hindered by his passion, which was satisfactory for the sins of the world.

Latin:

Sustinuit Christus infernales dolores, qua substantiam, non qua accidentia. Sustinuit dolores intensiue grauissimos, doloribus æternis damnatorum æquipollentes. Sustinuit eos non in τῷ damnatorum, sed in monte oliueti & ligno crucis.

Probatur assertum: Quicunque dolores adeo acerbi & vehementes fuerunt, vt animam Christi ad mortem vsque afflixerint, omnis auxilii inopem reliquerint, preces pro auertendo calice excitauerint, corpus totum in terram prostratum sudore sanguineo perfuderint, & mœstissimam querelam de desertione Dei expresserint, illi dolores fuerunt intensiue infernales: Atqui dolores interni in monte oliueti, & ligno crucis a Christo tolerati adeo acerbi & vehementes fuerunt: Ergo.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, Socinianorum & Arminianorum, negantium, Christum sustinuisse dolores infernales. Quorum præcipua sunt argumenta:

I. Qui infernales dolores patitur, is desperat: quia dolores infernales desperationem includunt: At Christus non desperauit. E. Resp. Qui dolores infernales patitur, iis succumbendo, ille desperat; concedo. Quicunque dolores infernales patitur, eos superando, ille desperat; nego.

Longe aliter comparatum est cum reo, super quo ira Dei manet; ali Matth. 26, 38. Marc. 14, 34.

ter cum fideiussore, qui mortem sic debuit gustare, vt deglutiret. Cohæret desperatio cum doloribus infernalibus non necessario, sed accidentaliter. Nam Dominus in infernum ducit & reducit, 1 Sam. II, 6.

II. Christus non passus est dolores æternos: Ergo non passus est dolores infernales. Resp. Christus passus est dolores, intensive infernales atque æternos, ratione gradus: non infernales atque æternos extensive, ratione durationis. Passus est dolores, si grauitatem spectes, doloribus infernalibus æquipollentes; si sublimitatem patientis consideres, æternis damnatorum pœnis præpollentes.

III. Christus non sensit iram Dei; quia semper fuit sanctissimus & dilectissimus Dei Filius: E. non passus est dolores infernales. Resp. Christus sensit iram Dei, non ob peccata propria, sic enim semper fuit sanctissimus; sed ob peccata aliena, in se translata, propter quæ factus est κατάρα, maledictio, i. e. maledictioni obnoxius, Gal. III, 13.

IV. Christi anima semper fuit beata, quoniam Deo arctissime est coniuncta: E. non sensit dolores infernales. Resp. Anima Christi semper fuit beata, qua actum primum; actum secundum & fruitionem beatitudinis impedivit satisfactoria pro peccatis mundi passio.


### Quæst. CXXVI. What is the death of Christ?

What is the death of Christ? The death of Christ is the privation of life, on account of the dissolved natural bond of the body and soul of Christ.

Latin:

Quid est mors Christi? Mors Christi est priuatio vitæ, ob dissolutum vinculum naturale corporis & animæ Christi.


### Quæst. CXXVII

What kind is the passion and death of Christ? The passion and death of Christ was true, not putative ; spontaneous, not forced ; undertaken not by chance, but from the certain disposition and counsel of God ; bloody and ignominious ; vicarious, meritorious, and satisfactory .

Prob. a. The Messiah truly bore our infirmities, and carried our pains, Is. LIII, 4. he truly gave up his spirit on the cross, Matt. XXVII, 50.

Prob. b. Christ most promptly approached his passion and death. Therefore he said: Behold I come; in the volume of the book it is written of me: To do thy will, O my God, I have desired, Ps. XL, 8. John V, 46. Prob. c.

Peter says Acts II, 23. This Jesus, delivered up by the definite counsel and foreknowledge of God, you have taken by the hands of the wicked, and by crucifying him have killed him. By counsel the Apostle understands the decree of God concerning delivering his son to death for us, Rom. VIII, 32. which ἔκδοσις, delivery, was directed toward our salvation, although the λῆψις, acceptance, was done with an evil intent.

Prob. d. Christ died on the wood of the cross. But Scripture says: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree, Deut. XXI, 23. Gal. III, 13. The punishment of the cross was, according to Roman customs, most infamous.

Prob. e. The death of Christ is a λύτρον (ransom), Matt. XX, 28, and an ἀντίλυτρον (ransom-price) for our sins, 1 Tim. II, 6. Therefore, it is a vicarious death, i.e., undertaken in our place, satisfactory, by which the divine justice injured by our sins was satisfied, and meritorious, because by that same death the remission of sins was merited for us.

Latin:

Qualis est passio & mors Christi? Passio & mors Christi fuit vera, non putatiua ; spontanea, non coacta ; suscepta non casu, sed ex certa dispositione & consilio Dei ; cruenta & ignominiosa ; vicaria, meritoria & satisfactoria .

Prob. a. Messias vere languores nostros tulit, & dolores nostros portauit, Es. LIII, 4. vere emisit in cruce spiritum, Matth. XXVII, 50.

Prob. b. Christus promptissime adiit passionem & mortem. Propterea dixit: Ecce veni; in volumine libri scriptum est de me: Facere voluntatem tuam, Deus mi, desideraui, Ps. XL, 8. Io. V, 46.

Prob. c. Petrus inquit Act. II, 23. Hunc Iesum, definito consilio & præscientia Dei deditum, accipientes per manus impiorum, crucifigentes interfecistis. Per consilium intelligit Apostolus decretum Dei de tradendo filio suo in mortem pro nobis, Rom. VIII, 32. quæ ἔκδοσις, traditio, directa est in salutem nostram, licet λῆψις, acceptio, malo fit facta animo.

Prob. d. Mortuus est Christus in ligno crucis. At scriptura dicit: Maledictus omnis, qui pependerit in ligno, Deut. XXI, 23. Gal. III, 13. Supplicium crucis Romanis moribus erat maxime infame.

Prob. e. Mors Christi est λύτρον, Matth. XX, 28. & ἀντίλυτρον pro peccatis nostris, 1 Tim. II, 6. E. est mors vicaria, i. e. nostri loco suscepta, satisfactoria, qua læsæ peccatis nostris justitiæ divinæ satisfactum est, & meritoria, quia eadem morte nobis promerita est remissio peccatorum.


### Question CXXVIII

The death of Christ lasted for a triduum (three days), but not a complete or fully consummated one. Cf. Matt. XVII, 23; c. XX, 18; Mark IX, 31; Luke XVIII, 31. You say: Christ in Matthew, c. XII, 40, says: The Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth (dead) for three days and three nights. E. the death of Christ lasted for a complete triduum,

Resp. In the cited passage, three natural days are not understood, but civil ones, or three νυχθήμερα (nights-and-days), according to the received Hebraism, and those not entire, but accepted synecdochically: since Christ suffered on the preparation day of the Passover and the Sabbath, and at the ninth hour, which is our third hour in the afternoon, he gave up his spirit, and at the tenth hour, or our fourth, he was buried; from which two hours still remained from that νυχθήμερον, from which that civil day could be denominated synecdochically, as the whole from the parts; to which succeeded the entire day of the Sabbath spent in the sepulcher, as the second νυχθήμερον, and the third began around the evening of the Sabbath, from which, until the hour of the resurrection on the third day, about ten hours elapsed. Cf. D. CALOV. Chron. S. sect. VIII. qu. 13.

Latin:

Duravit mors Christi triduum, at non completum, aut plene consummatum. Conf. Matth. XVII, 23. c. XX, 18. Marc. IX, 31. Luc. XVIII, 31. Dicis: Christus apud Matthæum, c. XII, 40. inquit: Filius hominis erit in corde terræ (mortuus) tribus diebus & tribus noctibus. E. mors Christi duravit triduum completum,

Resp. Loco citato non intelliguntur tres dies naturales, sed civiles, sive tria νυχθήμερα, hebraismo recepto, eaque non integra, sed synecdochice accepta: siquidem in parasceue paschatis & sabbathi passus est Christus, & hora nona, quæ est tertia nostra pomeridiana, spiritum emisit, hora decima, vel quarta nostra, sepultus; unde duæ adhuc reliquæ erant horæ ex illo νυχθήμερῳ, a quibus dies illa civilis synecdochice, ceu totum a partibus denominari poterat; cui dies integra sabbathi in sepulcro transacta successit, ceu alterum νυχθήμερον, ac tertium cœpit circa vesperam sabbathi, a qua, ad horam resurrectionis in tertio die, horæ circiter decem elapse. Conf. D. CALOV. Chron. S. sect. VIII. qu. 13.


### Question CXXIX. Was Christ a true man during the triduum of his death?

Christ was a true man during the triduum of his death, not physically, from the bond of natural union, which had been disrupted a); but theologically and by the estimation of faith, from the bond of the personal union, which left the triduum of death unharmed b).

Prob. a. A man is said to be physically true who actually lives, while the body and soul are naturally united. But if the natural union of the body and soul of Christ had not been dissolved, Christ would not have been truly dead. If he did not truly die, he did not truly satisfy for our sins, which to assert is ἀθεόλογον (theologically absurd).

Prob. b. The three-day death in no way injured or broke the bond of the hypostatic union, by which the two natures are joined in Christ. For a) Christ in the triduum of death was a σύνθετος (composite) person. Therefore, God and man. b) At the time Christ was a priest, at that time he was a θεάνθρωπος (God-man). But he was a priest during the triduum of death. Therefore. The minor is proved because Christ remains a priest εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς, forever. Heb. VII, 3. c) What ὁ λόγος (the Word) once assumed, he never laid aside: But ὁ λόγος assumed a true human nature: Therefore ὁ λόγος never laid aside the true human nature, and consequently during the triduum of death he was a true θεάνθρωπος.

Latin:

Christus fuit verus homo in triduo mortis, non physice, ex vinculo unionis naturalis, quod disruptum erat a); sed theologice & æstimatione fidei, ex vinculo unionis personalis, quod triduum mortis illæsum reliquit b).

Prob. a. Physice verus dicitur homo, qui actu vivit, dum corpus & anima naturaliter sunt vnita. At si vnio naturalis corporis & animæ Christi soluta non fuisset, Christus haud fuisset vere mortuus. Si non vere mortuus est, non vere satisfecit pro peccatis nostris, quod asserere ἀθεόλογον est.

Prob. b. Mors triduana minime lætit aut rupit vinculum unionis hypostaticæ, qua duæ naturæ in Christo sunt coniunctæ. Nam a) Christus in triduo mortis fuit persona σύνθετος. E. Deus & homo. b) Quo tempore Christus fuit sacerdos, eo tempore fuit θεάνθρωπος. At fuit sacerdos in triduo mortis. Ergo. Minor prob. quia Christus manet sacerdos εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς, in perpetuum. Hebr. VII, 3. c) Quod ὁ λόγος semel assumsit, nunquam deposuit: Sed ὁ λόγος veram humanam naturam assumsit: Ergo ὁ λόγος veram humanam naturam nunquam deposuit, & per consequens in triduo mortis verus θεάνθρωπος fuit.


### Question CXXX

There followed the death of Christ a) miracles, most worthy of eternal memory, b) the conversion of the centurion and the soldiers standing by.

Prob. a. Five miracles followed the death of Christ: 1) the tearing of the veil of the temple, 2) the earthquake, 3) the splitting of the rocks, 4) the opening of the graves, and the coming forth and appearance of the saints, 5) The flowing of blood and water from the side of Christ.

Concerning these miracles, cf.

Matth. XXVII, 51. seqq. &amp; Io.

XIX, 34. Prob. b.

Luc.

XXIII, 47. 48. The centurion, seeing what happened, glorified God, saying: Truly this man was righteous.

Indeed, all the crowds that were present, observing this spectacle, what was happening, and beating their breasts, returned. Quest.

CXXXI. What was the burial of Christ?

The burial of Christ is the placing of the body of our Savior, having expired on the cross, into a new tomb, to declare the truth of Christ's death. Quest.

CXXXII. What is to be observed concerning the burial of Christ?

One must observe a) the antecedents, b) the concomitants, c) the consequences of the burial. Obs. a.

The antecedents are: 1) The time of the burial, which was προσάββατον [the day before the Sabbath], or the day of preparation, and the fourth hour of that day, according to our reckoning.

2) The place, which was a stone cave in a garden, which provided our Savior with a new tomb, which no other body had occupied. 3) The curator of the funeral, namely from the political estate, Joseph of Arimathea, a pious, honorable, and wealthy senator; from the ecclesiastical estate, Nicodemus, once a nocturnal, now a diurnal disciple of Christ, a master of Israel, a defender of Christ's innocence, Io. VII, 50.; from the domestic estate, the women, burning with piety for Christ. Obs. b.

Accompanying the burial of Christ were 1) the removal of the expired body from the cross by the hands of Joseph, and the translation of the same into the garden: 2) the washing of the body, done with warm water; see

R. MAIMONID. de luctu c. IV.; 3) the anointing, or preparation for burial, Io. XIX, 40.; 4) the binding of the feet and hands with burial cloths; 5) the placing of the body in the stone cave; 6) the rolling of the stone to the entrance. Obs. c.

Following the burial of Christ were 1) the mourning of the disciples and female disciples of Christ; 2) the schemes and calumnies of his enemies against the deceased; 3) the sealing of the rolled stone; 4) the guard of soldiers. Quest.

CXXXIII. What kind of burial was Christ's?

The burial of Christ was a) glorious, b) fruitful. Prob. b.

This burial was glorious: 1) Because of the buried body, which is the temple of the deity, a vessel full of the immense anointing of the Holy Spirit, a most effective instrument of many miracles: 2) Because of the honorable curators: 3) Because of the dignity of the tomb.

Prob. b. The fruits of the burial of Christ are: 1) The sealing of our sins, Dan.

IX, 24.; 2) our burial together with him, which happens in renewal, Rom. VI, 4.; 3) the consecration of our graves, Es. LVII, 2. II.

Latin:

Consecuta sunt mortem Christi a) miracula, sempiterna memoria dignissima, b) conuersio centurionis & adstantium militum.

Prob. a. Miracula quinque consecuta sunt mortem Christi: 1) veli templi scissio, 2) terræ motus, 3) diuulsio petrarum, 4) apertio sepulcrorum, & egressio ac apparitio sanctorum, 5) sanguinis & aquae e latere Christi profluxus.

De his miraculis conf.

Matth. XXVII, 51. seqq. & Io.

XIX, 34. Prob. b.

Luc.

XXIII, 47. 48. Videns centurio, quod fiebat, glorificauit Deum dicens: Reuera hic homo iustus erat.

Quin omnes, quae aderant, turbae, super spectaculo hoc spectantes, quae fiebant, pulsantesque pectora sua, reuersae sunt. Quæst.

CXXXI. Quæ fuit sepultura Christi?

Sepultura Christi est impositio corporis Saluatoris nostri, in cruce exanimati, in monumentum recens, ad declarandam mortis Christi veritatem. Quæst.

CXXXII. Quæ obseruanda sunt circa sepulturam Christi?

Obseruanda sunt a) antecedentia, b) concomitantia, c) consequentia sepulturæ. Obs. a.

Antecedentia sunt: 1) Tempus sepulturæ, quod fuit προσάββατον, seu dies parasceues, & eius diei hora quarta, secundum nostrum computum.

2) Locus, qui fuit in horto spelunca saxea, quae praebuit Saluatori nostro recens monumentum, quod nullum aliud corpus occupauerat. 3) Curator funeris, nimirum e statu politico, Iosephus Arimatæus, senator pius, honestus, opulentus; e statu ecclesiastico, Nicodemus, nocturnus olim, nunc diurnus Christi discipulus, magister Israëlis, vindex innocentiæ Christi, Io. VII, 50., e statu oeconomico, mulieres, pietate in Christum ardentes. Obs. b.

Comitabantur sepulturam Christi 1) ablatio corporis exanimati e cruce per manus Iosephi, & eiusdem in hortum translatio: 2) corporis ablutio, facta aqua calida; vid.

R. MAIMONID. de luctu c. IV.; 3) vnctio, siue pollinctura, Io. XIX, 40.; 4) colligatio pedum manuumque fasciis sepulcralibus; 5) repositio corporis in spelunca saxea; 6) lapidis ad ostium aduolutio. Obs. c.

Sepulturam Christi consecuta sunt 1) discipulorum & discipularum Christi luctus; 2) hostium machinae & calumniae in defunctum; 3) obsignatio aduoluti lapidis; 4) custodia militum. Quæst.

CXXXIII. Qualis fuit sepultura Christi?

Sepultura Christi fuit a) gloriosa, b) fructuosa. Prob. b.

Gloriosa haec fuit sepultura: 1) Ob corpus sepultum, quod est deitatis templum, vas plenum vnctione immensa Spiritus S., multorum miraculorum organum efficacissimum: 2) Ob honestos curatores: 3) Ob monimenti dignitatem.

Prob. b. Fructus sepulturæ Christi sunt: 1) Peccatorum nostrorum obsignatio, Dan.

IX, 24.; 2) nostra consepultura, quæ fit in renouatione, Rom. VI, 4.; 3) sepulcrorum nostrorum consecratio, Es. LVII, 2. II.


### On the State of the Exaltation of Christ

Quest.

CXXXIV. What is the state of Christ's exaltation?

The state of Christ's exaltation is that in which Christ, having laid aside the infirmities of the flesh, assumed and exercised the plenary use of divine majesty.

Obs. I. Exaltation is not taken here in the ecclesiastical sense, by which it denotes the exaltation of the incarnation, or the bestowal of divine majesty made to the flesh of Christ by virtue of the personal union; but in the biblical sense, by which it denotes both the exaltation of the cross, John XII, 32, and the exaltation of glorification, John XVII, 5: which, although sometimes taken inadequately, signifies the exaltation of Christ to the right hand of God, yet here it is taken adequately, as it denotes the universal glorification of Christ, freed from death, adequately opposed to the preceding exinanition. Obs.

II. Exaltation sometimes designates the act, or actual glorification; sometimes the eternal glorious state, in which latter sense we have described the same. Taken actively, it is defined: as that which becomes the solemn enthronement & inauguration of the revived Christ to the full and perfect usurpation of the heavenly empire and the government of heaven and earth, especially of the church. See D. GERHARD, Exeg. lib. IV. §. 306. Obs.

III. This exaltation of Christ is also called ὑπερύψωσις, superexaltation, so as to designate the highest exaltation, Phil. II, 9. δόξασις, glorification, John XVII, 5. στεφάνωσις, coronation, Heb. II, 9. ἐνθρονισμός, enthronement, Heb. VIII, 1. Quest.

Latin:

Quæst.

CXXXIV. Quis est status exaltationis Christi?

Status exaltationis Christi est, quo Christus, depositis infirmitatibus carnis, plenarium diuinae maiestatis vsum suscepit & exercuit.

Obs. I. Exaltatio hic non sumitur sensu ecclesiastico, quo notat exaltationem incarnationis, vel collationem maiestatis divinae, vi unionis personalis factam carni Christi; sed biblico, quo tum exaltationem crucis Io. XII, 32. tum exaltationem glorificationis, Io. XVII, 5. denotat: quae, licet interdum, sumta inaedequate significet exaltationem Christi ad dextram Dei, hic tamen adaequate sumitur, prout notat Christi, a morte liberati, universam glorificationem, antegressae exinanitioni adaequate oppositam. Obs.

II. Exaltatio interdum designat actum, sive actualem glorificationem; interdum statum gloriosum aeternum, quo posteriori sensu eandem descripsimus. Active sumta definitur: quod fit solemnis inthronizatio & inauguratio Christi rediuiui ad plenam ac perfectam caelestis imperii usurpationem & gubernationem caeli & terrae, in primis ecclesiae. Vid. D. GERHARDI exeg. lib. IV. §. 306. Obs.

III. Vocatur haec Christi exaltatio etiam ὑπερύψωσις, superexaltatio, vt designet exaltationem summam, Phil. II, 9. δόξασις, glorificatio, Io. XVII, 5. στεφάνωσις, coronatio, Hebr. II, 9. ἐνθρονισμός, inthronizatio. Hebr. VIII, 1.


### CXXXV. According to which nature is Christ exalted?

Christ θεάνθρωπος (God-man) a) is exalted according to his human nature b). Prob. a. The subject which of the exaltation is Christ θεάνθρωπος. For 1) He who as Jesus Christ emptied himself, having taken the form of a servant, having become obedient even unto the death of the cross, αὐτὸν ὑπερύψωσε, the Father superexalted the same, as Paul testifies, Phil. II, 9. 2) Since actions & passions belong to supposita, the whole person of Christ is rightly said to be exalted, just as it was emptied.

Prob. b. The subject by which of the exaltation is the human nature of Christ. For 1) the divine nature τῷ λόγῳ (by the Word) is most high, and therefore cannot be really exalted. 2) Christ, as he was emptied according to his human nature, so he was exalted according to the same. 3) Through exaltation Christ received a name above every name in the fullness of time by grace, which the word ἐχαρίσατο shows, Phil. II, 9. But according to his divine nature he receives nothing in time from the Father by grace, but has all things from the Father through eternal generation. Quest.

Latin:

Christus θεάνθρωπος a) exaltatus est secundum humanam naturam b). Prob. a. Subiectum quod exaltationis est Christus θεάνθρωπος. Nam 1) Qui Iesus Christus seipsum exinanivit, forma servi accepta, obediens factus vsque ad mortem crucis, αὐτὸν ὑπερύψωσε, eundem superexaltavit Pater, teste Paulo, Phil. II, 9. 2) Cum actiones & passiones sint suppositorum, recte tota persona Christi, vt exinanita, ita exaltata dicitur.

Prob. b. Subiectum quo exaltationis est natura Christi humana. Nam 1) natura divina τῷ λόγῳ est altissima, adeoque realiter exaltari nequit. 2) Christus, vt exinanitus erat secundum naturam humanam, ita secundum eandem exaltatus est. 3) Per exaltationem Christus nomen super omne nomen in plenitudine temporis accepit ex gratia, quod ostendit verbum, ἐχαρίσατο, Phil. II, 9. At secundum naturam divinam in tempore a Patre per gratiam nihil accipit, sed omnia habet a Patre per aeternam generationem.


### CXXXVI. In what does the exaltation of Christ formally consist?

The exaltation of Christ formally consists in the deposition of the servile state and of all the infirmities of the flesh, and in the full, universal, and incessant usurpation of the divine majesty communicated through the personal union.

Prob. 1) From Phil. II, 9. 10. Therefore God also exalted him, and gave him a name which is above every name; that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth. Where note a) The particle, διὸ, does not denote a meritorious bestowal, but a consequence of order: b) The bestower of glory is God the Father, to whom, as the source, as of the divine essence, so also of the communicated glory, the bestowal is attributed. Cf. John XVII, 7. Rom. VI, 4. For the rest, there is no doubt that the act of exaltation, being extra-essential, is common to the whole Holy Trinity. For the Son of God himself also raised himself from the dead, John II, 19. c. X, 17. and ascended above all heavens, Eph. IV, 10. and entered into his glory, Luke XXIV, 26.

Latin:

Exaltatio Christi formaliter consistit in status servilis, omniumque infirmitatum carnis depositione, & plena, universali & incessante maiestatis divinae, per unionem personalem communicatae, usurpatione.

Prob. 1) Ex Phil. II, 9. 10. Propterea etiam Deus ipsum exaltavit, & donavit ipsi nomen, quod super omne nomen est; vt in nomine Iesu omne genu se flectat caelestium, terrestrium & subterraneorum. Vbi obs. a) Particula, διὸ, non notat meritoriam collationem, sed consequentiam ordinis: b) Collator gloriae est Deus Pater, cui, tanquam fonti, vt essentiae divinae, ita & communicatae gloriae, collatio tribuitur. Conf. Io. XVII, 7. Rom. VI, 4. De cetero nullum est dubium, quin actus exaltationis, vtpote extraessentialis, toti SS. Trinitati communis sit. Nam & ipse Filius Dei seipsum ex mortuis excitavit, Io. II, 19. c. X, 17. & supra omnes coelos ascendit, Eph. IV, 10. atque in gloriam suam intravit, Luc. XXIV, 26. Et Spiritus S. Christum ex mortuis excitasse dicitur, Rom. VIII, 11 (*): c) Ὑπερύψωσις, sive


### Question CXXXVII

superexaltation, having followed the emptying and humiliation, by force of opposition, brings about, in place of the evacuation of the form of God, the full usurpation of the form of God; in place of the concealment of those things which are equal to God, their public manifestation; in place of the assumption of the form of a servant, the deposition of the same, and the administration of universal dominion. d) The gift of the name above every name designates the bestowal of the highest glory, than which no more sublime can be named, which is through what has been given, as regards the most full possession, or usurpation. e) The consequence of the given glory is the subjection of all creatures, shadowed forth by the knee-bending, or genuflection.

For in the name of Jesus, knees must bend: angels (in a spiritual manner) Ps. 92:7, and the blessed in heaven, Apoc. 5:12, and mortal men upon the earth, Jn. 14:13, and subterranean creatures (by reason of their most squalid state), demons and damned men, with trembling, Jas. 2:19.

2) From Heb. 2:8. But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honor, that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.

The Apostle joins the state of emptying and of exaltation.

He calls the former ἐλάττωσιν, or a condition lower than the angelic. For angels enjoy eternal glory and blessedness: but Christ, in his most bitter passion, was forsaken by God and stripped of all consolation, so that an angel from heaven comforted him.

But passion and death was the most ignominious way to the coronation of Christ.

Moreover, God crowned Christ with royal honor and the glory of omnipotent dominion. This we learn from verses 7 and 8: You made him a little lower than the angels: you crowned him with glory and honor, and set him over all the works of your hands: you have put all things under his feet.

This coronation therefore brings about the actual usurpation of omnipresent dominion and the axiom of adoration.

Quest.

CXXXVII. Are there certain acts, or degrees, of the exaltation of Christ?

Degrees of exaltation.

The acts, or degrees, by which the exalted Christ exercised more and more the divine majesty communicated to his flesh, are: 1) the descent of Christ into hell, 2) the resurrection of the same, 3) the ascension of Christ into heaven, 4) the sitting at the right hand of God.

These degrees of exaltation are preceded by ζωοποίησις, or vivification, as a prerequisite condition, disposing the subject to be exalted.

Proof.

Christ, having returned to life, exercised his divine majesty through certain degrees: 1) By descending into hell, he showed himself alive to evil spirits and damned men as the victor over death: 2) By rising again, he declared to the apostles, and through them to the whole world, that he had satisfied divine justice through his death: 3) By ascending into heaven, he showed to the angels and blessed men that he is the victor not only of death, but also of the demons, and the savior of men: 4) By sitting at the right hand of God, he exercises the most full and universal dominion over all creatures that are in the kingdom of power, grace, and glory.

Obs. Ζωοποίησις, or vivification, is the liberation of Christ from death, and the reunion of soul and body, by which Christ began to revive according to the flesh.

This is not a peculiar degree of exaltation, but a prerequisite condition for disposing the subject, viz.

Christ, for the receiving of the full and universal use of divine majesty.

Quest. [missing text] recalled your Christ to life.

It pleases some to apply this saying to this cause, Rom.

1:4.

But yet others understand by πνεῦμα ἁγιωσύνης the divine nature of Christ, as an opposition: according to the flesh, and according to the spirit. But it suffices, 1) that the Holy Spirit, equally as the Father and the Son, is the true and highest God, 2) that without any exception the general rule holds: Divine works, which are said to be external, are equally common to all three persons in the unity.

Latin:

superexaltatio, exinanitionem & humiliationem confecuta, vi oppositionis, infert loco euacuationis formæ Dei, plenam formæ Dei vsurpationem; loco occultationis eorum, quæ sunt æqualia Deo, publicam eorum manifestationem; loco assumptionis formæ feruilis, eiusdem depofitionem, & dominii vniuerfalis administrationem. d) Donatio nominis fuper omne nomen defignat collationem gloriæ summæ, qua nulla sublimior nominari potest, quæ per donata est, quoad plenissimam χείρωσιν, feu vsurpationem. e) Confequens donatæ gloriæ est subiectio omnium creaturarum, τῇ γονυκαμψία, feu genuflexione adumbrata.

Nam in nomine Iefu flectere debent genua angeli (modo spirituali) Pf.XCII,7. & beati in cœlo, Apoc.V,12. & homines mortales fuper terra, Io.XIV,13. & creaturæ subterraneæ (ratione status squalidiffimi), dæmones & homines damnati, cum tremore, Iac.II,19.

2) Ex Hebr.II,8. Eum vero, qui breue quid intra angelos minor redditus est, videmus Iefum, per paffionem mortis, gloria & honore coronatum, vt gratia Dei pro omni gusta ret mortem.

Coniungit Apostolus statum exinanitionis, & exaltationis.

Illum vocat ἐλάττωσιν, feu conditionem angelica minorem. Angeli enim æterna gloria & beatitudine perfruuntur: Christus autem, in paffione acerbissima, a Deo derelictus & omni folatio orbatus fuit, vt angelus de cœlo eum confortauerit.

At paffio & mors ignominiosissima via fuit ad σεφάνωσιν, feu coronationem Christi.

Coronauit autem Deus Christum honore regio, & gloria omnipotentis dominii. Id quod discimus e verfu 7. & 8. Minorem redditi esti eum e breue quid infra angelos: gloria & honore coronasti eum, & constituisti fuper omnia opera manuum tuarum: omnia subiecisti fub pedes eius.

Infert ergo hæc coronatio actualem vsurpationem omnipræsentis dominii & axiomatís adorationis.

Quæst.

CXXXVII. Suntne certi quidam actus, vel gradus exaltationis Christi?

Gradus exaltationis.

Actus, vel gradus, quibus Christus exaltatus maiestatem diuinam, carni suæ communicatam, magis magisque exercuit, sunt: 1) descensus Christi ad inferos, 2) eiusdem refurrectio, 3) ascensio Christi in cœlum, 4) feffio ad dextram Dei.

Quos gradus exaltationis antecessit ζωοποίησις, f. viuificatio, tanquam conditio prærequisita, disponens fubiectum exaltandum.

Prob.

Christus rediuiuus maiestatem suam diuinam per certos quosdam gradus exercuit: 1) Descendendo ad inferos, spiritibus malis & hominibus damnatis fe viuum exhibuit, vt victorem mortis: 2) Resurgendo, apostolis, & per hos toti mundo declarauit, fe per mortem suam iustitiæ diuinæ fatisfeciffe: 3) Ascendendo in cœlum, angelis & beatis hominibus ostendit, fe esse victorem non tantum mortis, sed & cacodæmonum, hominumque salvatorem: 4) Sedendo ad dextram Dei, plenissimum & vniuerfale dominium in omnes creaturas, quæ sunt in regno potentiæ, gratiæ & gloriæ, exercet.

Obf. Ζωοποίησις, feu viuificatio, est liberatio Christi a morte, & redunitio animæ ac corporis, qua Christus fecundum carnem reuiuiscere cœpit.

Non est hæc peculiaris gradus exaltationis, sed conditio prærequisita ad disponendum fubiectum, scil.

Christum, ad suscipiendum plenum & vniuerfalem maiestatis diuinæ vfum.

Quæst. [missing text] tuum Christum ad vitam reuocauit.

Non nullis placet, ad hanc causam accommodare hoc dictum, Rom.

I, 4.

Verum tamen alii per πνεῦμα ἁγιωσύνης intelligunt diuinam Christi naturam, vt oppositionis: κατὰ σάρκα, & κατὰ πνεῦμα. Sed fufficit, 1) quod Spiritus S. æque, ac Pater & Filius, fit verus ac summus Deus, 2) quod fine vlla exceptione valeat regula generalis: Opera diuina, quæ dicuntur ad extra, sunt omnium trium in vnitate perfonarum peræque communia.


### Q. CXXXVIII

The descent of Christ into hell is a true, real, and supernatural motion, by which Christ, having struggled out of the bonds of death and being revived, betook himself in his whole person to hell, that he might demonstrate himself to the evil spirits and the damned as the victor over death.

Obs. I. The descent into hell is taken a) metaphorically, and designates infernal sorrows, arising from the sense of divine wrath and the deprivation of all consolation. As it is used in 1 Sam. II, 6, where the pious Hannah says: Jehovah brings down to hell, and brings up. And thus Christ, before his death and burial, descended into hell by a metaphorical and sorrowful descent, having suffered immense pains in the garden of Gethsemane, Matt. XXVI, 38, and having complained of the desertion of God on the altar of the cross, Matt. XXVII, 46. b) Taken properly, the descent into hell denotes a true and real departure into the πῦ of the damned, which indeed St. Peter, 1 Ep. ch. III, 19, calls πορείαν, or a journey.

Obs. II. Although the descent of Christ into hell was true and real; it was nevertheless not physical, or local, but was a supernatural motion. For a physical and local motion is proper to natural bodies; but the vivified body of Christ was glorified. Nor was it a successive motion. For it was made ἐν πνεύματι, in the spirit, i.e., by divine power, 1 Pet. III, 19. which knows no slow efforts: this is what Dr. DANNHAV. urges with Dr. AFFELMANN in Christos. p. 306. The descent of Christ was instantaneous, because it was made ἐν πνεύματι, by him who was no longer subject to the weaker necessities and laws of nature. Dr. CALOV. agrees in theol. posit. p. 372. The descent into hell was not successive; because it was accomplished in a single νῦν, nor does the hypostasis of the divine flesh, which is everywhere, need progressive motion, but it teaches that it is present by a demonstration or operation of presence, and to that extent it is also understood to have been present here in hell.

Latin:

Descensus Christi ad inferos est verus, realis & supernaturalis motus, quo Christus, vincula mortis eluctatus & redivivus, tota sua persona ad inferos se contulit, vt spiritibus malis & damnatis hominibus se victorem mortis demonstraret.

Obs. I. Descensus ad inferos sumitur a) metaphorice, & designat dolores infernales, ex sensu iræ divinæ & privatione omnis solatii ortos. Sicut usurpatur, 1 Sam. II, 6. vbi pia inquit Hanna: Iehouah descendere facit in infernum, & ascendere facit. Atque ita Christus, ante mortem & sepulturam, descensu metaphorico & dolorifico descendit ad inferos, in horto Gethsemane dolores immanes perpessus, Matth. XXVI, 38. & in ara crucis de desertione Dei conquestus, Matth. XXVII, 46. b) Proprie sumtus descensus ad inferos notat verum & realem abitum in πῦ damnatorum, quippe quem S. Petrus 1. ep. cap. III, 19. πορείαν, sive profectionem vocat.

Obs. II. Quamvis descensus Christi ad inferos fuerit verus & realis; non tamen physicus fuit, aut localis, sed supernaturalis motus fuit. Nam motus physicus & localis, est proprius corporum naturalium; sed corpus Christi vivificatum erat glorificatum. Neque fuit motus successivus. Factus enim est ἐν πνεύματι, in spiritu, i.e. virtute divina, 1 Petr. III, 19. quæ tarda molimina nescit: id quod cum D. AFFELMANNO vrget D. DANNHAV. in Christos. p. 306. Descensus Christi fuit instantaneus, quia factus est ἐν πνεύματι, ab illo, qui non amplius subiacebat naturæ infirmioribus necessitatibus & legibus. Consentit D. CALOV. in theol. posit. p. 372. Descensus ad inferos non fuit successivus; quia in unico νῦν peractus, neque hypostasis carnis divinæ, quæ vbique est, motu progressivo indiget, sed præsentiæ demonstratione vel operatione se adesse docet, atque eatenus etiam hic in inferno præsto fuisse intelligitur.


### Q. CXXXIX

According to which nature did Christ descend into hell? Christ the God-man a) descended into hell according to his human nature, and that whole, consisting of body and soul b).

Proof a. 1) Christ ζωοποιηθεὶς, or vivified, descended. 1 Pet. III, 18. But ζωοποιηθεὶς is the whole Christ, not the soul alone. Therefore. 2) He who ascended, also descended, Eph. IV, 10. But the whole Christ, not the soul alone, ascended: Therefore also the whole Christ, not the soul alone, descended. 3) Since the descent of Christ is a personal action, it cannot but be ascribed to the whole person of the God-man. Hence, just as it is said of the whole God-man in the Apostolic Creed that he suffered, was crucified, and was buried: so it is also said of the same that he descended into hell. And in the Athanasian Creed: As the rational soul and flesh is one man: So God and man is one Christ, who suffered for our salvation and descended into hell. We believe simply, therefore, that the whole person, God and man, after the burial descended into hell, says Form. Concord. p. 788.

Proof b. 1) The descent into hell is a degree of the exaltation of Christ, and therefore cannot be attributed to the divine nature, which does not receive a further degree of exaltation. 2) Πορεία, or the journey into hell, is postponed by the Apostle Peter to the vivification of Christ, 1 Ep. ch. III, 19. Therefore, the descent of Christ into hell was made after the reunion of soul and body; the soul of Christ did not descend into hell at the time when his body lay in the sepulcher.

You say: I. The descent of Christ precedes the resurrection, by which Christ showed himself alive (as the Apostles' Creed teaches): Therefore, it was not done after the vivification. Resp. Distinguish between the external and internal resurrection. The former is the exit from the sepulcher and the outward manifestation before men, and is designated in the Apostles' Creed: the latter is the vivification itself, of which the Apostle Peter speaks in the cited passage.

You say: II. Every royal and triumphal act belongs to Christ according to both natures (for it is an apotelesma, or official act): But the descent into hell, etc. Therefore. The minor is proved from Col. II, 15. Christ, stripping off principalities and powers, made a show of them openly, triumphing over them by himself. Christ triumphed over the infernal principalities through the descent into hell.

Resp. The descent of Christ into hell is taken either precisely, as it is a real departure from the sepulcher into hell, without connoting the effect of the same: or it is taken complexly, so that it connotes at once the effect and fruit, i.e., the triumph over enemies. In the former sense we accept the descent of Christ into hell: in the latter sense it is accepted as an apotelesma.

Latin:

Christus θεάνθρωπος a) descendit ad inferos secundum humanam naturam, eamque totam, corpore & anima constantem b).

Prob. a. 1) Christus ζωοποιηθεὶς, seu vivificatus, descendit. 1 Petr. III, 18. Atqui ζωοποιηθεὶς, est totus Christus, non sola anima. Ergo. 2) Qui ascendit, etiam descendit, Eph. IV, 10. Atqui totus Christus, non sola anima ascendit: Ergo etiam totus Christus, non sola anima descendit. 3) Descensus Christi cum sit actio personalis, non potest non toti personæ θεανθρώπῳ adscribi. Proinde, sicut de toto θεανθρώπῳ in symbolo apostolico dicitur, quod passus, crucifixus & sepultus sit: ita & de eodem dicitur, quod descenderit in infernum. Et in symbolo Athanasiano: Sicut anima rationalis & caro vnus est homo: Ita Deus & homo vnus est Christus, qui passus est pro nostra salute & descendit ad inferos. Simpliciter igitur credimus, quod tota persona, Deus & homo, post sepulturam ad inferos descenderit, ait Form. Concord. p. 788.

Prob. b. 1) Descensus ad inferos est gradus exaltationis Christi, adeoque naturæ divinæ, quæ non recipit vlteriorem exaltationis gradum, tribui nequit. 2) Πορεία, seu abitus in infernum, postponitur vivificationi Christi ab Apostolo Petro 1 ep. c. III, 19. Factus ergo est descensus Christi ad inferos post redunitionem animæ & corporis; non vero anima Christi ad inferos descendit, eo tempore, quo corpus ipsius in sepulcro iacuit.

Dicis: I. Descensus Christi antecedit resurrectionem, qua Christus se vivum exhibuit (docente symbolo apostolico): E. non est factus post vivificationem. Resp. Dist. inter resurrectionem externam, & internam. Illa est egressio e sepulcro, & exterior coram hominibus manifestatio, & designatur in symbolo apostolico: haec est ipsa vivificatio, de qua sermo est Apostolo Petro, loco citato.

Dicis: II. Omnis actus regius & triumphalis competit Christo secundum utramque naturam (est enim ἀποτέλεσμα, seu actus officialis): Atqui descensus ad inferos &c. Ergo. Minor probatur ex Col. II, 15. Christus exuens principatus & potestates oftentauit palam, triumphans de illis per seipsum. Triumphauit Christus principatus infernales per descensum in infernum.

Resp. Descensus Christi ad inferos sumitur vel praecise, prout est realis abitus e sepulcro in infernum, non connotato eiusdem effectu: vel sumitur complexe, vt simul effectum & fructum, h. e. triumphum de hostibus connotet. Priori sensu nos descensum Christi ad inferos accipimus: posteriori sensu acceptus est apotelesma.


### Quest. CXL. Did Christ therefore descend into the infernal prison itself?

Christ descended into the infernal prison itself, or the τῷ damnatorum [place of the damned].

Prob. That the term to which, the descent of Christ, is the τῷ damnatorum [place of the damned], Peter teaches, 1 Ep. ch. III, 18, 19. Christ was put to death indeed in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit; in which also he went and preached to the spirits who were in prison. (As to those) who were disobedient long ago, when the long-suffering of God once waited in the days of Noah. Where by φυλακὴν [prison] we understand the infernal prison, 1) because in that φυλακῇ are the unbelievers, destroyed by the flood on account of their unbelief, who are surely in the τῷ damnatorum: 2) Because φυλακὴ is also taken for hell in other places of Holy Scripture, Matt. V, 25. Luke XII, 58. Rev. XX, 7.

Latin:

Descendit Christus in ipsum carcerem infernalem, seu τῷ damnatorum.

Prob. Terminum ad quem, descensus Christi, esse τῷ damnatorum, docet Petrus, 1 ep. c. III, 18. 19. Christus mortificatus quidem est carne, viuificatus autem spiritu; in quo etiam iis, qui in custodia erant, spiritibus abiens praedicauit. (Sicut iis) qui increduli fuerunt olim, quum semel expectauit Dei longanimitas, in diebus Noë. Vbi per φυλακὴν intelligimus carcerem infernalem, 1) quia in illa φυλακῇ sunt increduli, per diluuium ob incredulitatem suam extincti, qui sane sunt in τῷ damnatorum: 2) Quia φυλακὴ etiam aliis in locis S. scripturae pro inferno accipitur, Matth. V, 25. Luc. XII, 58. Apoc. XX, 7.


### Quest. CXLI. For what end did Christ descend into hell?

Christ descended into hell not for the purpose that he might suffer any evil from the demons a), but that he might triumph over the demons b), and that he might convict the damned men, justly confined in the infernal prison c).

Prob. a. After death Christ sustained no real passion, because on the cross he exclaimed: It is finished, John XIX, 30. and through death he entered into glory, Luke XXIV, 26.

Prob. b. From Rev. I, 18. I was dead: behold! I live, and I have the keys of hell and of death. Christ, as a victor brought back to life, bears the keys of hell and death, by triumphing over the evil demons and death, Col. II, 15. Wherefore in the infernal prison Christ presented himself alive to the evil spirits, as the victor of death and hell. Conf. Hos. XIII, 14. 1 Cor. XV, 55. Prob. c.

Christ preached in the prison to the spirits, (as to those) who were disobedient long ago, when the long-suffering of God once waited in the days of Noah. 1 Pet. III, 19. The preaching of Christ in hell was not evangelical, which is announced to men only in the kingdom of grace, but legal, elenchtic, terrible, and that both verbal, by which he convicted them that they had merited eternal punishments, and real, by which he struck immense terror into them. Confer DANNH. in hodof. phaenom. VIII. p.

…738. You say: Why is Christ said to have preached in hell only to those who were disobedient in the time of Noah? Why did he not terrify others also with that elenchtic address? Resp. 1) Others are not excluded, but these are proposed as examples of enormous impenitence and singular divine judgment: 2) The Apostle named them particularly, to teach also that even before the antediluvians were bound to believe in Christ, and that therefore they were justly condemned on account of their unbelief: 3) That the Apostle might conveniently pass from the typical flood to the antitypical baptism.…

The antithesis is 1) of the Papists, asserting that Christ descended into hell only according to his soul: (*) 2) of the Socinians, maintaining that the descent of Christ is the state of death in the sepulcher: The stronger arguments of whom are:

I. The descent of Christ to the underworld can be explained by the burial: For the Hebrew word, שאול, for the most part denotes the sepulcher, rarely hell: Therefore, a peculiar article of faith concerning the descent of Christ to the underworld is not to be taught in the church. Resp. 1) This argument proceeds from mere particulars. 2) Ἅδης in the N. T. always denotes the πῦρ of the damned. 3) The apostolic symbol teaches that the church has constantly believed this article.

II. The descent of Christ denotes infernal pains, Ps. XVIII, 6. 1 Sam. II, 6. Therefore, it does not denote a real descent. Resp. The descent of Christ into hell, having been freed from death and revived, is not mournful or painful, but glorious and triumphant, and therefore real.

III. If Christ really descended into hell, he descended either as God or as man. Not as God: because God fills heaven, and earth, and hell with his omnipresence, and therefore he did not really descend into hell. Nor as man: because he descended either in body or in soul. Not in body; because that was in the sepulcher. Not in soul: since this was in paradise. Therefore, Christ clearly did not descend into hell. Resp. A third is given. The whole Christ θεάνθρωπος, having been made alive, 1 Pet. III, 18. i.e., death having been overcome, and the union of soul and body restored, descended into hell, and therefore the body of Christ at that point of time, in which this descent happened, did not lie in the sepulcher.

IV. That descent which Holy Scripture attributes to the soul of Christ, that does not belong to the whole Christ θεάνθρωπος. But the descent to the underworld &c. Therefore. The minor is proved from Ps. XVI, 10. Resp. The Psalmist treats of the descent of Christ to the underworld not in a proper, but in a metaphorical sense. For the phrase itself and the mode of speaking sufficiently indicate that it is not a matter of the glorious descent of the triumphant Christ, but of the painful state of the suffering Christ. He who prays that he may not be left in hell, sufficiently indicates that the state in hell, in which he is not to be left, is by no means joyful or glorious, but full of pains. Furthermore, the Psalmist treats of that state which indeed precedes the burial. For he says: Thou wilt not leave my soul in hell: neither wilt thou suffer thine holy one to see corruption. But a real and proper descent follows the burial. Conf. D. CALOVIUS, bibl. illustrat. in h. l. fol. 966.

Latin:

Descendit Christus in infernum non eo fine, vt a daemonibus quidquam mali pateretur a), sed vt de daemonibus triumphum ageret b), & vt homines damnatos, in carcere infernali iure concludi, conuinceret c).

Prob. a. Post mortem Christus nullam realem sustinuit passionem, eo, quod in cruce exclamauit: consummatum est, Ioann. XIX, 30. & per mortem in gloriam ingressus est, Luc. XXIV, 26.

Prob. b. Ex Apoc. I, 18. Eram mortuus: ecce! viuo, & habeo claues inferorum & mortis. Gerit Christus, vt victor rediuiuus, claues inferni & mortis, de cacodaemonibus & morte triumphum agendo, Coloss. II, 25. Quare in carcere infernali Christus spiritibus malis se viuum stitit, vt victorem mortis & inferni. Conf. Hos. XIII, 14. 1 Cor. XV, 55.

Prob. c. Christus in custodia praedicauit spiritibus, (sicut iis) qui increduli fuerunt olim, quum semel expectauit Dei longanimitas in diebus Noë. 1 Pett. III, 19. Fuit praedicatio Christi in inferno non euangelica, quae hominibus tantum in regno gratiae annuntiatur, sed legalis, elenchtica, terribilis, eaque tum verbalis, qua ipsos aeterna supplicia promeritos esse, conuicit, tum realis, qua immanem terrorem iis incussit. Confer. DANNH. in hodof. phaenom. VIII. p. 738.

Dicis: Cur solis illis, qui tempore Noachi increduli fuerunt, Christus in inferno praedicasse dicitur? Cur non alios etiam ...concione illa elenchtica perterruit? Resp. 1) Non excluduntur alii, sed hi, tanquam enormia impoenitentiae, & singularia iudicii diuini exempla, proponuntur: 2) Peculiariter Apostolus illos nominauit, vt doceret etiam, ante diluuianos debuisse in Christum credere, atque adeo illos propter incredulitatem iure damnatos esse: 3) Vt Apostolus commode transiret a diluuio typico, ad antitypum baptismum.

Antithesis est 1) Pontificiorum, asserentium, Christum tantum secundum animam descendisse in infernum: (*) 2) Socinianorum, statuentium, descensum Christi esse statum mortis in sepulcro: Quorum potiora sunt argumenta:

I. Descensus Christi ad inferos potest explicari per sepulturam: Nam hebræa vox, שאול, plerumque sepulcrum, raro infernum notat: E. non est docendus in ecclesia peculiaris articulus fidei de descensu Christi ad inferos. Resp. 1) Hoc argumentum procedit ex meris particularibus. 2) Ἅδης in N. T. semper denotat πῦρ damnatorum. 3) Ecclesiam hunc articulum constanter credidisse, docet symbolum apostolicum.

II. Descensus Christi notat dolores infernales, Ps. XVIII, 6. 1 Sam. II, 6. E. non notat realem descensum. Resp. Descensus Christi in infernum, a morte liberati & rediuiui, non est luctuosus, aut dolorificus, sed gloriosus & triumphatorius, adeoque realis.

III. Si Christus realiter descendit in infernum, aut vt Deus, aut vt homo descendit. Non vt Deus: quia Deus omnipræsentia sua cœlum, & terram, & infernum implet, adeoque realiter non descendit in infernum. Nec vt homo: quia descendit vel corpore, vel anima. Non corpore; quia illud fuit in sepulcro. Non anima: quoniam hæc fuit in paradiso. E. Christus plane non descendit in infernum. Resp. Datur tertium. Totus Christus θεάνθρωπος viuificatus, 1 Pet. III, 18. i. e. morte superata, & vnione animæ corporisque restaurata, descendit in infernum, adeoque corpus Christi eo temporis puncto, quo hic descensus contigit, non iacuit in sepulcro.

IV. Quem descensum tribuit S. Scriptura animæ Christi, ille non competit toti Christo θεανθρώπῳ. Atqui descensum ad inferos &c. Ergo. Minor probatur e Ps. XVI, 10. Resp. Agit psaltes de descensu Christi ad inferos non proprio, sed metaphorico. Nam phrasis ipsa & modus loquendi satis indicat, non agi de descensu Christi triumphantis glorioso, sed de patientis Christi statu doloroso. Qui precatur, ne in inferno derelinquatur, is satis indicat, statum in inferno, in quo non derelinquendus est, minime esse lætum aut gloriosum, sed doloribus plenum. Præterea de illo statu agit psaltes, qui antecedit quidem in sepulcro. Dicit enim: Non relinques animam meam in inferno: nec dabis sanctum tuum, vt videat corruptionem. At descensus realis & proprius sepulturam sequitur. Conf. D. CALOVII bibl. illustrat. in h. l. fol. 966.


### CXLII. What is the resurrection of Christ?
