…Resurrection is an act of glorious victory, by which Christ the θεάνθρωπος, through the same power as God the Father and the Holy Spirit, brought his body, reunited to his soul and glorified, out of the sepulcher, and presented himself alive to his disciples by various proofs, in confirmation of our peace, fraternity, joy, and hope concerning our future resurrection.

The word, resurrection, is taken in two ways: 1) Broadly; in which sense it embraces in its scope ζωοποίησιν, or vivification, which in the order of nature preceded the descent into hell and the bringing forth of the body from the sepulcher, and is called the interior resurrection: 2) Strictly, as it is distinguished from vivification, and denotes the bringing forth of the body from the sepulcher and its presentation before others. It is taken in the latter sense here.

Latin:

Resurrectio est actus gloriosæ victoriæ, quo Christus θεάνθρωπος, per eandem cum Deo Patre & Spiritu S. potentiam, corpus suum, animæ redunitum & glorificatum, e sepulcro eduxit, variisque indiciis discipulis suis viuum stitit, in confirmationem nostræ pacis, fraternitatis, gaudii & spei de nostra secura resurrectione. Obs.

Vox, resurrectio, duobus modis sumitur: 1) Late; qua ratione ambitu suo complectitur ζωοποίησιν, seu vivificationem, quæ ordine naturæ descensum ad inferos, & corporis e sepulcro eductionem præcessit, & dicitur resurrectio interior: 2) Stricte, prout vivificationi contradistinguitur, & notat corporis e sepulcro eductionem & coram aliis præsentationem . Posteriori sensu hic accipitur.


### Q. CXLIII. By what power did Christ rise again?

Christ rose again by divine power, common to all three persons of the Godhead.

Prob. 1) Generally: The resuscitation of Christ from the dead, the terminus of which is the resurrection, is an action ad extra, common to all three persons of the Godhead. Whence the Savior himself says: Whatever the Father does, the Son also does likewise, John 5:19.

2) Specifically: a) To God the Father, as the fountain of the Godhead, the resuscitation of Christ is attributed for the consolation of our consciences, that we may know that the Father has been abundantly satisfied, and that he has been reconciled to us, otherwise he would not have released our surety from the sepulcher. From which Paul gravely says: Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, Rom. 6:4. Cf. Eph. 1:20, Col. 2:10. b) That Christ raised himself from the dead is evident: α) because Christ has the power of laying down his soul and taking it up again, John 10:17. This power belongs to Christ, as God, by essence; as man, by the grace of union. Certainly the soul of Christ, instructed by divine power, could join its dwelling to itself, and resuscitate it. Therefore β) the Savior asserts that he would raise up the temple of his body, once dissolved, John 2:18. γ) If Christ by divine power, communicated to his flesh through the hypostatic union, raised others, John 5:21; why should he not raise himself by the same? c) The Holy Spirit is said to have raised Christ from the dead, Rom. 8:11.

There is an antithesis of the Socinians, who deny that Christ, being dead, raised himself. They go about to strengthen their opinion with the following arguments:

I. No dead man can raise himself: Therefore, neither can Christ. Resp. No mere man can raise himself from the dead: But Christ is θεάνθρωπος.

II. The resuscitation of Christ is attributed to God the Father: E. therefore he did not raise himself. Resp. The resuscitation of Christ is attributed to God the Father, but not to him alone. For whatever the Father does, the same the Son also does likewise, John 5:19.

Objection: Sabellianism will be introduced if that which belongs to God the Father is attributed to Christ. Resp. Distinguish between personal and essential works. The former are divided, the latter are common to all three divine persons, to which latter actions the resurrection of Christ from the dead is reckoned.

III. If 1. The condition of the witnesses, and indeed their internal state of mind.

There was in them the use of reason and wisdom; for besides women there were men, and not only from the common people, rude in letters and content with ordinary understanding, Acts IV, 13, but also learned and adorned with experience in affairs, especially Paul, Acts XXII, 3, and the same a most bitter adversary, who had long and much opposed this truth, Acts XXVI, 8, 9, 1 Cor. XV, 8, 9: 2) A providence almost excessive; for they were so far from offering themselves as credulous, that their unbelief was rather to be reproved, John XX, 25, Luke XXIV, 25, Mark XVI, 14. 3) Probity, for they were of upright life and pure conduct, never suspected of any fraud, Acts XXIV, 21, 22: 4) Constancy and fortitude of mind, even to the last breath, amidst the most bitter vexations and calamities, Acts IV, 19, 20, although by nature they were most timid, Matt. XXVI, 56; 5) Love for God, overcoming the world, without any desire for temporal gain, with a despising of all honors and pleasures, Phil. III, 7-11.

2) External. One must consider 1) The multitude of witnesses, and also the gathering of many at the time when they were together, John XX, 19, 26, 1 Cor. XV, 6: 2) The contemplation of this matter, more often repeated, and long continued, for forty days, Acts I, 3, also accurate, as far as the individual surrounding circumstances, since they did not only use their eyes to see the face of the revived Christ, but also the signs of the wounds, gestures, actions, and many and various things: they were therefore eyewitnesses, not ear-witnesses, nor negligent, but looking into the matter with a very attentive mind.

3) The agreement of all external senses, John XX, 25, 27, 1 John I, 1. It was not enough that they had seen Christ with their own eyes. The remaining senses sufficed for his most joyful manifestation. They heard him speaking, and felt the power of his words in their inmost heart, Luke XXIV, 32, at the same time the discourses which they had previously perceived were recalled to memory, ibid. v. 44. They touched Christ with their hands, lest there be any suspicion, into which CELSUS rashly led them, that they had been deluded by some specter, Luke XXIV, 37, 39. They tasted bread with their mouths, received from the hands of Christ; and indeed in a certain singular way, by which Christ could be known and distinguished from other men, Luke XXIV, 30, 31, 35, Acts X, 41.

II. The matter attested. This was, to be sure, 1) not absurd, in which there would be something that would openly contradict either itself or other truths, but which could happen through the infinite power of God, Rom. IV, 17, Acts

XXVI, 8: 2) Unexpected, and seemed incredible to all the Apostles of Christ themselves, although it had been predicted by Christ many times; from which it appears clearer than light that they could not even have been deceived by some error, either of a very fallacious imagination or of rash hope: 3) Foretold by prophecies, Luke

XXIV, 25-27, 1 Cor. XV, 4, partly literal, as Ps.

XVI, 10, coll. with Acts II, 25, Ps. XXII, 29-31, LXVIII, 19, Isa. LIII, 10, 11, partly typical, especially two, of Isaac (to whom Christ undoubtedly looked, appealing to the writings of Moses, Luke

XXIV, 27, coll. with Gen. XXII, 12, Rom. VIII, 32, Heb. XI, 19) and of Jonah, Matt. XII, 40: 4) Necessary, because of salutary ends, and especially the declaration of the satisfaction provided and approved by God, and the application of the acquired justice, Rom. IV, 25.

III. The testimony which they gave 1) with unanimous consent, not privately, but publicly, not timidly, but strenuously, against any adversaries whatsoever, Acts

II, 32, IV, 10, 13: 2) most efficacious, for convincing minds, Acts II, 32, 37, 41, IV, 2, 4, VI, 7, 10: 3) confirmed by miracles, Mark

XVI, 20, Acts III, 15, 16, IV, 10, 14, 16, VI, 8, 10.

Conclusion 1. The witnesses of this truth are most worthy of the greatest faith: for not only are all those things which are required for a sufficiently suitable testimony present; but also many more than in any testimony, of whose dignity no one doubts. He who dares to deny this accomplished fact has truly destroyed all historical faith. Conclusion.

2. Faith is to be held in this truth not only human and historical, but also divine: for to all those things which are most valid for historical faith, insofar as it is an accomplished fact, are added absolutely singular documents, given by God, insofar as this matter is divine (by prop.

II 2, 4, & III, 2, & 3.).

III. If Christ raised himself from the dead, he will not be the eternal God: The Evangelicals deny the consequent. Therefore, they ought also to deny the antecedent. The reason for the consequence is: just as the eternal God does not die, so also he cannot raise himself. Resp. The eternal God in his divinity does not die; the ὁ λόγος died in the flesh: but according to the divinity, dwelling in the flesh, he raised himself.

Instance; Therefore he did not raise himself, according to his humanity. Resp. He did not raise himself according to his humanity, as the primary and immediate subject, but as the secondary and mediate subject of the life-giving power. We do not assert that the human nature of Christ acted in the resurrection according to its own powers, but according to communicated ones.

IV. Christ obtained the resurrection of his body from the Father through prayers, Heb. V, 7. Therefore he did not restore life to himself. Resp. Christ prayed in the state of emptying, having assumed the form of a servant, according to which he did not raise himself. For the resurrection is a glorious act of Christ, existing in the form of deity.

Latin:

Resurrexit Christus virtute divina, omnibus tribus personis divinitatis communi.

Prob. 1) Generatim: Resuscitatio Christi ex mortuis, cuius terminus est resurrectio, est actio ad extra, omnibus tribus divinitatis personis communis. Vnde ipse Saluator inquit: Quæcunque Pater facit, similiter & Filius facit, Io. V, 19.

2) Speciatim: a) Deo Patri, vt fonti divinitatis, tribuitur resuscitatio Christi ad consolationem conscientiarum, vt sciamus, Patri abunde satisfactum, eundemque nobis reconciliatum esse, ceteroqui fideiussorem nostrum e sepulcro non dimisisset. Ex quo Paullus grauiter ait: Christus ex mortuis resuscitatus est per gloriam Patris, Rom. VI, 4. Conf. Eph. I, 20. Col. II, 10. b) Christum seipsum e mortuis resuscitasse, patet: α) quia Christus potestatem habet animam suam ponendi, & resumendi, Io. X, 17. Hæc potestas competit Christo, vt Deo, per essentiam; vt homini, per unionis gratiam. Potuit certe anima Christi, divina virtute instructa, suum sibi iungere domicilium, idque resuscitare. Propterea β) asserit Saluator, se templum corporis sui dissolutum erecturum esse, Io. II, 18. γ) Si Christus virtute divina, per vnionem hypostaticam carni suæ communicata, alios excitauit, Io. V, 21; quidni eadem seipsum excitaret? c) Spiritus S. Christum ex mortuis resuscitasse dicitur, Rom. VIII, 11 .

Antithesis est Socinianorum, negantium, Christum mortuum seipsum resuscitasse. Qui suam opinionem firmatum eunt sequentibus argumentis:

I. Nullus homo mortuus seipsum resuscitare potest: E. nec Christus. Resp. Nullus homo merus seipsum mortuum resuscitare potest: At Christus est θεάνθρωπος.

II. Deo Patri resuscitatio Christi tribuitur: E. non seipsum resuscitauit. Resp. Tribuitur resuscitatio Christi Deo Patri, sed non soli. Quæ enim facit Pater, eadem & similiter facit Filius, Io. V, 19.

Instantia: Introducetur Sabellianismus, si Christo tribuatur, quod Dei Patris est. Resp. Dist. inter opera personalia, & essentialia. Illa sunt divisa, haec communia omnibus tribus personis divinis, quibus posterioribus actionibus accensetur resuscitatio Christi ex mortuis.

III. Si 1. Testium conditio, & ea quidem interna animorum.

Erat in illis usus rationis, ac sapientia; etenim praeter mulieres erant viri, nec solum de plebe, litterarum rudes ac vulgari intelligentia contenti, Act. IV, 13. sed etiam eruditi ac rerum peritia ornati, in primis Paulus, Act. XXII, 3. idemque acerrimus adversarius, qui hanc veritatem diu multumque oppugnauerat, Act. XXVI, 8. 9. 1 Cor. XV, 8. 9: 2) Providentia fere nimia; tantum enim abest, ut credulos se vlli praebuerint, vt potius arguenda fuerit ipsorum ἀπιστία, Io. XX, 25. Luc. XXIV, 25. Marc. XVI, 14. 3) Probitas, erant enim integri vitae celerisque puri, fraudis nullius vnquam suspecti, Act. XXIV, 21. 22: 4) Constantia ac fortitudo animi, ad extremum vsque spiritum, inter acerbissimas vexationes & calamitates, Act. IV, 19. 20. quamuis natura fuerint maxime timidi, Matth. XXVI, 56.; 5) Amor in Deum, vincens mundum, sine vlla cupiditate lucri temporalis, cum despicientia omnium & honorum, & voluptatum, Phil. III, 7-11.

2) Externa. Consideranda est 1) Multitudo testium, atque etiam coniunctio plurium eo tempore, quo erant vna, Io. XX, 19. 26. 1 Cor. XV, 6: 2) Contemplatio huius rei, saepius iterata, ac diu continuata, per quadraginta dies, Act. I, 3., etiam adcurata, quantum ad singulas res circumstantes, quando quidem non faciem solum Christi redivivi, sed etiam vulnerum signa, gestus, actiones, & multas, & varias vis usurparunt oculis: oculati igitur erant testes, non auriti, nec negligentes, sed animo valde attento in rem intuentes.

3) Consensio sensuum externorum omnium, Io. XX, 25. 27. 1 Io. I, 1. Non satis erat, suis ipsos oculis Christum vidisse. Reliqui sensus sufficiebant iucundissimae eius patefactione. Audiebant loquentem, & vim verborum in imo pectore sentiebant, Luc. XXIV, 32. simul in memoriam reuocabantur sermones, quos ante perceperant, ibid. v. 44. Manibus tangebant Christum, ne qua esset suspicio, in quam illos temere adduxit CELSVS, spectro quodam ipsos delusos esse, Luc. XXIV, 37. 39. Ore gustabant panem, ex Christi manibus acceptum; & quidem singulari quodam modo, ex quo Christus poterat cognosci, atque ab aliis hominibus distingui, Luc. XXIV, 30. 31. 35. Act. X, 41.

II. Res testata. Haec nimirum erat 1) non absurda, in qua esset aliquid, quod vel sibi, vel aliis veritatibus aperte repugnaret, sed quae fieri poterat per infinitam Dei potentiam, Rom. IV. 17. Act.

XXVI, 8: 2) Insperata, ipsisque Christi Legatis omnibus incredibilis visa, quamvis saepe numero a Christo praedicta fuisset; ex quo luce clarius adparet, ne potuisse quidem eos decipi errore quodam, aut imaginationis admodum fallacis, aut spei temerariae: 3) praenunciata vaticinationibus, Luc.

XXIV, 25-27. 1 Cor. XV, 4., partim literalibus, vt Ps.

XVI, 10. coll. cum Act. II, 25. Ps. XXII, 29-31. LXVIII, 19. Ies. LIII, 10. 11., partim typicis, praesertim duabus, Isaaci (ad quem haud dubie respexit Christus, ad Mosis scripta prouocans, Luc.

XXIV, 27. coll. cum Gen. XXII, 12. Rom. VIII, 32. Hebr. XI, 19) & Ionae, Matth. XII, 40: 4) Necessaria, propter fines salutares, in primisque declarationem satisfactionis praestitae, Deo que probatae, & adplicationem adquisitae iustitiae, Rom. IV, 25.

III. Testimonium, quod illi dederunt 1) unanimi consensione, nec privatim, sed publice, nec timide, sed strenue, contra quosuis aduersarios, Act.

II, 32. IV, 10. 13: 2) efficacissimum, ad conuincendos animos, Act. II, 32. 37. 41. IV, 2. 4. VI, 7. 10: 3) miraculis confirmatum, Marc.

XVI, 20. Act. III, 15. 16. IV, 10. 14. 16. VI, 8. 10.

Confectar. 1. Testes huius veritatis maxima fide dignissimi sunt: nam non solum ea omnia, quae ad testimonium sat idoneum requiruntur, vniversa adsunt; sed multo etiam plura, quam in vllo testimonio, de cuius dignitate nemo dubitat. Qui hanc rem gestam negare audet, nae is omnem sustulit fidem historicam. Confect.

2. Fides huic veritati habenda est non modo humana atque historica, sed etiam diuina: namque ad ea omnia, quae ad fidem historicam validissima sunt, quatenus est res gesta, accedunt prorsus singularia documenta, a Deo data, quatenus haec res est diuina (per propos.

II 2. 4. & III, 2. & 3.).

III. Si Christus seipsum excitauit ex mortuis, non erit æternus Deus: Consequens negant Euangelici. E. negare etiam debent prius. Ratio consequentiæ est; sicut æternus Deus non moritur; ita etiam seipsum resuscitare nequit. Resp. Deus æternus in diuinitate sua non moritur, ὁ λόγος mortuus est in carne: at secundum diuinitatem, in carne habitantem, seipsum resuscitauit.

Instantia; Ergo non resuscitauit seipsum, secundum humanitatem. Resp. Non resuscitauit seipsum secundum humanitatem, tanquam subiectum primum & immediatum, sed subiectum secundum & mediatum potentiæ viuificæ. Non asserimus, quod humana Christi natura egerit in resuscitatione secundum vires proprias, sed communicatas.

IV. Christus resurrectionem corporis sui precibus impetrauit a Patre, Hebr. V, 7. E. sibi ipsi vitam non restituit. Resp. Precatus est Christus in statu exanitionis, assumta forma serui, secundum quam seipsum non excitauit. Etenim resurrectio est actus gloriosus Christi, existentis in forma deitatis.


### Quaest. CXLIV. According to which nature did Christ rise again?

Christ the θεάνθρωπος a) rose again according to his human nature b).

Prob. a. The subject which of the resurrection is the σύνθετος person of Christ. For the angels themselves say that Christ has risen, Luke XXIV, 6. But he did not rise as the daughter of Jairus, or Lazarus, by an alien power; but by a divine one, communicated to himself.

Prob. b. According to the same nature that Christ was crucified and died, according to that same one he rose again. But he died according to his human nature, therefore.

Obs. The subject by which of the resurrection is remotely the human nature, proximately the body, which had fallen.

But what are the adversaries able to oppose to these such great defenses? They have nothing that bears any semblance of truth, except this one thing: If Christ truly lived again, why did he not show himself to be seen by the Jewish Senate, nor by Pilate, nor by any of his enemies, but only to his friends? Thus reasoned SPINOZA, whose warmed-over cabbage the famous EDELMANN recently served up, having brought nothing new. For CELSUS long ago attacked this truth with the same argumentation, against whom ORIGEN disputed. Resp. 1) If this demand were just; could not all ἄπιστοι, and their easy leader, SPINOZA, demand by the same right that Christ show himself alive to them as well? 2) The divine PETER brings forward a most wise reason why Christ, having returned to life, exhibited himself to be seen by the eyes not of everyone, but of those who were judged to be suitable and trustworthy witnesses, Acts X, 40. 41. 3) Not only friends, but also enemies saw Christ, raised from the dead, the guards of the sepulcher, Matt. XXVIII, 11. and Paul, brought to such a point by a most hostile mind that he seemed to be insane and raging, Acts IX, 1. seqq. XXVI, 9-16. Finally 4) such was the obstinacy of their minds that they were unwilling to consider the clearest proofs, but attempted to obscure them all either by force or by fraud, fearing that something might be detracted from their reputation if they were forced to confess openly that they had passed a most unjust sentence against Christ. Matt. XXVIII, 11-14. Acts IV, 14. 16. 17. add. Luke XVI. 30. 31. Would they not have taken Christ for a specter? Just as CELSUS used to invent, when he could find nothing else by which to make the faith of the disciples of Christ suspect. And that indeed the enemies could have suspected much more than the friends from the fact that specters are commonly thought to be mostly occupied around the funerals and sepulchers of wicked men, and the Jews had slandered that Christ had performed his miracles in no other way than with the help of the devil himself, nay, the prince of them.

Quest. CXLV. Did Christ bring out of the sepulcher the same body that had been affixed to the cross and had died?

Christ brought out of the sepulcher the same body in number, as to substance, but clothed with new qualities.

Proof a. The Savior challenges the Jews, John II, 19. Destroy this temple (pointing as it were with his finger to the temple of his body, v. 21.) and in three days I will raise it up (not as another in essence, but the same).

Proof b. The qualities and glorious endowments of the body of Christ are: impalpability, invisibility, illocality, so that, where he wished, he was there in a moment, in a word, spirituality, 1 Cor. XV, 42. Whence also Christ presented himself alive, and disappeared, when it pleased him, Luke XXIV, 13.

On account of which endowments it is called σῶμα τῆς δόξης, by Hebraism, i.e., a glorious body, Phil. III, 21.

Latin:

Christus θεάνθρωπος a) resurrexit secundum humanam naturam b).

Prob. a. Subiectum quod resurrectionis est Christi persona σύνθετος. Nam ipsi angeli dicunt Christum resurrexisse, Luc. XXIV, 6. Non autem resurrexit vt filia Iairi, aut Lazarus, aliena virtute; sed diuina, sibi communicata.

Prob. b. Secundum quam naturam Christus est crucifixus & mortuus, secundum eandem resurrexit. Sed mortuus est secundum humanam naturam, E.

Obs. Subiectum quo resurrectionis remote est humana natura, proxime corpus, quod ceciderat.

Ecquid autem his tantis præsidiis opponere valent aduersarii? Quod veri aliquam similitudinem præ se ferat, nihil habent, præter hoc vnum: Si Christus vere reuixit, cur ipse non Senatui Iudaico, nec Pilato, nec vlli hostium suorum, sed amicis duntaxat, conspiciendum se præbuit? Ita ratiocinatus SPINOSA, cuius crambem recoctam haud ita pridem adposuit famōsus EDELMANNVS, nihil noui attulit. Eadem enim argumentatione hanc veritatem dudum impugnauit CELSVS, aduersus quem ORIGENES disputauit. Resp. 1) Si iustum esset hoc postulatum; possent ne omnes ἄπιστοι, eorumque facile princeps, SPINOSA, eodem iure poscere, vt ipsis quoque Christus se viuum ostenderet? 2) Diuus PETRVS rationem adfert sapientissimam, quam ob rem Christus reuiuiuus oculis cernendum se exhibuerit non quibusque, sed illis, qui iudicarentur testes idonei ac fide digni, Act. X, 40. 41. 3) Non amici solum, sed etiam inimici Christum viderunt, ab inferis excitatum, custodes sepulcri, Matth. XXVIII, 11. & Paullus, animo maxime infenso vsque eo adductus, vt insanire ac furere videretur, Actor. IX, 1. seqq. XXVI, 9-16. Tandem 4) tanta erat animorum obstinatio, vt clarissima documenta nollent considerare, sed ea omnia aut vi, aut fraude, obscurare conarentur, metuentes, ne quid ipsorum existimationi detraheretur, si coacti essent palam fateri, se in Christum iniustissimam dixisse sententiam. Matth. XXVIII, 11-14. Act. IV, 14. 16. 17. add. Luc. XVI. 30. 31. Nonne Christum pro spectro habuissent? quem ad modum comminiscebatur CELSVS, cum nihil reperiret aliud, quo fidem discipulorum Christi suspectam faceret. Et illud quidem inimici multo magis, quam amici, suspicari potuissent ex eo, quod spectra vulgo putantur maxime occupata esse circa funera ac sepulcra improborum hominum, & Iudæi calumniati fuerant, Christum miracula sua non aliter, quam opem ipsi ferente diabolo, immo principe perpetrasse.

Quaest. CXLV. An Christus idem corpus, quod cruci affixum et mortuum erat, e sepulcro eduxit?

Christus eduxit e sepulcro idem numero corpus, qua substantiam , sed novis qualitatibus vestitum .

Prob. a. Compellat Salvator Iudaeos, Io. II, 19. Soluite templum hoc (digito quasi monstrans templum corporis sui, v. 21.) et tribus diebus erigam illud (non qua essentiam aliud, sed idem).

Prob. b. Qualitates dotesque gloriosae corporis Christi sunt: impalpabilitas, invisibilitas, illocalitas, ut, ubi vellet, ibi in momento esset, uno verbo spiritualitas, 1 Cor. XV, 42. Vnde et Christus se vivum stitit, et disparuit, quando placuit, Luc. XXIV, 13.

Ob quas dotes vocatur σῶμα τῆς δόξης, per hebraismum, i.e. corpus gloriosum, Phil. III, 21.


### Q. CXLVI. When did Christ rise again?

Christ rose again on the third day, in the morning time, the sepulcher still closed.

Proof a. That Christ rose on the third day, we learn from Matt. XVII, 23. Mark IX, 31. Luke XVIII, 31. Compare above quest.

CXXVII. Proof b. Luke XXIV, 1. testifies that Christ came forth from the monument at deep dawn, Mark XVI, 1. very early, when the sun had risen (namely above the rational horizon, although not yet above the sensible horizon).

Proof c. Matt. XXVIII, 2. 6. asserts that the angel of the Lord removed the sepulchral stone, not to open an exit for Christ, but to show others the place, abandoned by the resurrected Christ.

You say: Christ brought a true and substantial body out of the sepulcher, which could not penetrate another solid body. Resp. 1) Examples teach that more subtle bodies penetrate thicker ones. Thus solar rays penetrate glass, fire penetrates iron. 2) Distinguish between a physical body and a glorified one. The Apostle is witness, Heb. IV, 14, that our great high priest has penetrated the heavens.

Latin:

Christus resurrexit tertio die , tempore matutino , sepulcro adhuc clauso .

Prob. a. Tertio die Christum surrexisse, discimus ex Matth. XVII, 23. Marc. IX, 31. Luc. XVIII, 31. Confer supra quaest.

CXXVII. Prob. b. Luc. XXIV, 1. testatur, Christum profundo diluculo, Marc. XVI, 1. mane valde, sole orto (scilicet super horizontem rationalem, quanquam nondum super horizontem sensibilem) e monumento prodiisse.

Prob. c. Matth. XXVIII, 2. 6. asserit, angelum domini removisse lapidem sepulcralem, non ad recludendum Christo exitum, sed ad monstrandum aliis locum, a Christo resuscitato derelictum.

Dicis: Verum et substantiale corpus eduxit Christus e sepulcro, quod aliud corpus solidum penetrare nequiuit. Resp. 1) Subtiliora corpora penetrare crassiora docent exempla. Sic radii solares vitrum, ignis ferrum penetrat. 2) Dist. inter corpus physicum, et glorificatum. Testis est Apostolus Hebr. IV, 14. pontificem nostrum magnum caelos penetrasse.


### Q. CXLVII. To what end did Christ rise again?

Christ rose again to manifest his victory obtained over death and the devil, to offer and apply to all men the fruits of his passion and death.

Proof a. Unless Christ had carried off the victory over death and the devil, he could not have come forth from the sepulcher, Acts II, 24. Hos. XIII, 14. He manifested this victory by ten apparitions. I. The apparition refreshed Mary Magdalene. Mark XVI, 9. II. The whole choir of pious women, Matt. XXVIII, 9. III. Peter, Luke XXIV, 34. IV. Cleopas, and his companion traveling to Emmaus, Luke XXIV, 15. V. He delighted the eleven disciples, except Thomas, John XX, 19. VI. Thomas, with the other disciples present, John XX, 28. VII. Seven disciples, at the shore of the sea of Tiberias in Galilee, John XXI, 1. VIII. Five hundred brethren, 1 Cor. XV, 6. IX. James, 1 Cor. XV, 7. X. The assembled disciples on the day of the ascension, Acts I, 9.

The resurrected Christ wished to appear especially to these disciples, so that they might be eyewitnesses of the resurrection of Christ, and divulge it throughout the world, Luke XXIV, 46. 47. 48. He presented himself to them alive ἐν πολλοῖς τεκμηρίοις, in many proofs, Acts I, 3. For he spoke with them about the kingdom of God, and ate with them, Luke XXIV, 41.

Regarding this eating, AUGUSTINE elegantly says, serm. CXLVII. de temp.: "What He ate was a matter of power, not of need. A thirsty earth absorbs water in one way, the touching ray of the sun in another: the former is need, the latter is power." He admitted the disciples to the contact of His body, and showed them His scars, about which AUGUSTINE treats in CXXI, in Ioannem: "To heal the hearts of the doubting, the traces of the nails were retained."

Prob. b. Christ, having been resurrected, commanded His victory to be proclaimed in the world through eyewitnesses, so that the fruits, obtained by His most bitter passion and death, might be offered to the whole human race; such fruits are:

I. Justice.

Christ was resurrected for our justification, Rom. IV, 25. The resurrection of Christ is an evident testimony that Christ, by His death, fully satisfied God who had been offended for our sins, and merited for us the remission of sins and justice: Otherwise, God would not have released our sponsor from the bonds of death.

Therefore also Christ, having been resurrected, willed that the remission of sins be applied to us through the ministry of reconciliation, Io. XX, 23. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them.

II. Spiritual peace, for the sake of which the battle had been fought.

Therefore, having been resurrected, He prays for peace for the disciples, Io. XX, 19.

III. Confirmation of our brotherhood.

For Christ is the firstborn from the dead, Col. I, 17. The faithful, who rise again by His power, are brothers of this firstborn Son of God. Therefore He says: I ascend to my Father, and to your Father, Io. XX, 17.

IV. Living hope of our resurrection.

Christ, having been resurrected from the dead, has been made the ἀπαρχὴ (firstfruits) of those who sleep: For since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead also comes through a man.

For just as in Adam all die: So also through Christ all shall be made alive, 1 Cor. XV, 20. 21. 22.

Of this , those who are in Christ Jesus through faith are partakers.

IV. Renewal, which is a spiritual resurrection from the sepulcher of sin.

Just as Christ was resurrected through the glory of the Father: So let us also walk in newness of life, Rom. VI, 4.

Latin:

Resurrexit Christus, ad manifestandam victoriam suam de morte et diabolo impetratam , ad offerendum et applicandum omnibus hominibus fructus passionis et mortis suae .

Prob. a. Nisi Christus de morte ac diabolo victoriam reportasset, ex sepulcro prodire non potuisset, Act. II, 24. Hos. XIII, 14. Manifestavit hanc victoriam decem apparitionibus. I. Apparitio recreavit Mariam Magdalenam. Marc. XVI, 9. II. Totum piarum mulierum chorum, Matth. XXVIII, 9. III. Petrum, Luc. XXIV, 34. IV. Cleopham, eiusque comitem Emauntem proficifcentes, Luc. XXIV, 15. V. Delectauit undecim discipulos, excepto Thoma, Io. XX, 19. VI. Thomam praesentibus reliquis discipulis, Io. XX, 28. VII. Septem discipulos, ad littus maris Tiberiadis in Galilaea, Io. XXI, 1. VIII. Quingentos fratres, 1 Cor. XV, 6. IX. Iacobum, 1 Cor. XV, 7. X. Congregatos discipulos die ascensionis, Act. I, 9.

His discipulis Christi resuscitatus potissimum apparere voluit, ut essent testes resurrectionis Christi oculati, eamque per terrarum orbem diuulgarent, Luc. XXIV, 46. 47. 48. Stitit se illis viventem ἐν πολλοῖς τεκμηρίοις, in multis indiciis, Act. I, 3. Locutus enim est cum illis de regno Dei, et comedit cum illis, Luc. XXIV, 41.

De qua manducatione eleganter inquit AVGVSTINVS, serm. CXLVII. de temp. Quod manducauit, potestatis fuit, non egestatis. Aliter aborbet terra aquam sitiens, aliter solis radius tangens: Illa indigentia, iste potentia. Admisit discipulos ad contactum corporis sui, iisque ostendit cicatrices suas, de quibus AVGVSTINVS tractat. CXXI, in Ioannem: Ad dubitantium corda sananda, retenta sunt clauorum vestigia.

Prob. b. Christus resuscitatus per testes oculos victoriam suam in orbe diuulgari iussit, vt fructus, acerbissima passione & morte parti, vniuerso humano generi offerrentur; quales fructus sunt:

I. Iustitia.

Christus resuscitatus est propter iustificationem nostram, Rom. IV, 25. Resurrectio Christi est euidens testimonium, quod Christus morte sua peccatis nostris plene satisfecerit Deo offenso, & peccatorum remissionem atque iustitiam nobis promeritus sit: Alioqui Deus sponsorem nostrum e vinculis mortis non dimisisset.

Idcirco etiam Christus resuscitatus per ministerium reconciliationis, remissionem peccatorum nobis applicatam voluit, Io. XX, 23. Si quorum dimiseritis peccata, dimittuntur illis.

II. Pax spiritualis, ob quam militatum erat.

Ideo resuscitatus discipulis precatur pacem, Io. XX, 19.

III. Fraternitatis nostrae confirmatio.

Christus enim est primogenitus ex mortuis, Col. I, 17. Huius primogeniti Filii Dei fratres sunt fideles, qui ipsius virtute resurgunt. Ideo dicit: Ascendo ad Patrem meum, & ad Patrem vestrum, Io. XX, 17.

IV. Spes viua nostrae resurrectionis.

Christus, resuscitatus ex mortuis, est ἀπαρχὴ, primitiae dormientium factus: Quoniam enim per hominem mors; etiam per hominem resurrectio mortuorum est.

Sicut enim in Adamo omnes moriuntur: Sic etiam per Christum omnes viuificabuntur, 1 Cor. XV, 20. 21. 22.

Huius fructus sunt participes, qui per fidem sunt in Christo Iesu.

IV. Renouatio, quae est spiritualis resurrectio e sepulcro peccati.

Sicut Christus resuscitatus est per gloriam Patris: Sic etiam nos in nouitate vitae ambulemus, Rom. VI, 4.


### Q. 148. What is the ascension of Christ?

Ascension is the glorious act of Christ, by which He, having been resurrected, according to His human nature, by a true, real, and local motion through free economy, and in a visible manner up to the clouds, and from there in an invisible manner into the common heaven of the blessed, and to the very throne of God, raised Himself up, so that He might occupy the kingdom of God, having triumphed over His enemies, unlock the closed paradise, and prepare a permanent seat for us in the heavens.

Latin:

Ascensio est actus Christi gloriosus, quo is resuscitatus, secundum humanam naturam, vero, reali, & per liberam oeconomiam locali motu, modoque visibili vsque ad nubes, & inde inuisibili ratione in commune beatorum coelum, & ipsum thronum Dei sese euexit, vt regnum Dei, hostibus triumphatis, occuparet, clausum paradisum referaret, & permanentem in coelis sedem nobis pararet.


### Q. 149. According to which nature does Christ ascend into heaven?

Christ the God-man a) ascended into heaven according to His human nature b).

Prob. a. The subject which of the ascension is the whole God-man. The same one who descended, also ascended, Eph. IV, 10. But the whole God-man descended, who, having been made alive, ascended, 1 Petr. III, 22. Therefore.

Prob. b. The subject by which of the ascension is the human nature, which was lifted up on high, Act. I, 9. which does not fit the divinity, which cannot be carried on high (for this is of bodies alone). For who would say of the divinity: He departed from them, and was carried into heaven? Luc. XXIV, 51.

Latin:

Christus θεάνθρωπος a) ascendit in coelum secundum humanam naturam b).

Prob. a. Subiectum quod ascensionis est totus θεάνθρωπος. Idem, qui descendit, etiam ascendit, Eph. IV, 10. Atqui totus θεάνθρωπος descendit, qui viuificatus ascendit, 1 Petr. III, 22. E.

Prob. b. Subiectum quo ascensionis est natura humana, quae in altum est sublata, Act. I, 9. quod in diuinitatem, quae in altum ferri nequit (hoc enim solorum corporum est), non quadrat. Quis enim de diuinitate dicat: Receffit ab eis, & ferebatur in coelum? Luc. XXIV, 51.


### Q. 150. By what power does Christ ascend into heaven?

Christ ascended into heaven by an infinite power, common to all three persons of the divinity.

Prob. 1) The exaltation of Christ into heaven is an act ad extra, common to all three persons of the deity. 2) Christ is said to be exalted δεξιᾷ τοῦ Θεοῦ, by the right hand of God, Acts 2:3; ch. 5:31, i.e., by the infinite and immense power of God; for the right hand of God is taken here not relatively, but absolutely.

Quest. CLI. What is the terminus from which Christ ascended?

The terminus from which the ascension took place is the Mount of Olives near Bethany. Proof. From Acts 1:12. When Christ was taken up into heaven, the disciples returned to Jerusalem from the mount which is called Olivet.

And Christ, about to ascend, led the disciples out as far as Bethany, Luke 24:50. Quest. CLII. What is the terminus to which Christ’s ascension reached?

The terminus to which Christ arrived in his ascension is both common and proper. The common one is the seat and dwelling-place of the blessed, where Christ presents himself to be beheld face-to-face by the blessed .

The proper and ultimate one is the majestic heaven of God, or the throne of divine majesty . Proof. a. Christ was carried up into paradise, in which the thief was turned with him, Luke 23:43; where Job also is, ch. 19:27; where mansions are prepared for the faithful, John 14:2; where the most glorious Redeemer will exhilarate the souls of the saints with his most joyful sight.

Proof. b. The proper terminus to which is the majestic heaven of God, which is above all the heavens, Eph. 4:10. We have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Heb. 4:14.

He passed through the heavens not by reason of distance, but of most sublime and divine presence. The majestic heaven of God is the very right hand of God, by which Christ was made higher than the heavens, Heb. 7:26, of which the Apostle says, Heb. 8:1: We have such a high priest, who sat down at the right hand of the throne of majesty in the heavens.

Obf. By heaven here is not understood the airy or ethereal heaven of nature, which it is impious to think; nor the heaven of grace, which is the church militant on these earths, from which Christ withdrew his visible presence until the day of the final judgment.

Therefore, the heaven of glory is understood, either finite or infinite. In the finite glory, Christ indeed presents himself to be beheld in the πῇ of the blessed by the angels and the blessed, after the manner of a true glorified body, yet so that infinite glory is also communicated to him through the session at the right hand of God.

Christ was therefore carried up into the majestic heaven of God, that he might fill all things, Eph. 4:10.

Conf. DANNHAV. in hodof. phaenom. VIII. p. 763.

Quest. CLIII. What was the mode of Christ’s ascension? By reason of the mode, the ascension of Christ was not an ἀφανισμός, or disappearance, but a true, real, successively progressive motion , and visible as far as the clouds .

But being lifted up from the cloud, he was exalted to the right hand of God in an invisible manner . Proof. a. From Luke 24:51. He departed from them, and was carried up into heaven.

Departure implies a successive change of place and progressive motion from a place into heaven.

Proof. b. From Acts 1:9. While they were watching, he was taken up, and a cloud received him out of their sight.

Proof. c. Christ passed through the heavens; Heb. 4:14, having become higher than the heavens, Heb.

7:26. Therefore, he was carried up above all the heavens in an invisible manner.

Obf. The visible motion of Christ as far as the clouds was local, not according to the motion of a natural body, which by its nature is carried downward, but of one glorified and endowed with supernatural gifts.

Nor did Christ assume local and visible motion out of the necessity of nature, but by free economy, who, if he had willed, could have been [present] to the disciples in a point of time. to withdraw, and to occupy heaven. But it pleased the Savior to be carried upward gradually, so that the disciples might testify to the true ascension all the more clearly and confidently. From which we gather that Christ indeed ascended as far as the clouds by local motion, but not locally or physically. Conf. D. SCHERZERI system. p. 247.

Question CLIV. For what purpose did he ascend into heaven?

The general purpose of the ascension is that he might gloriously show himself as the victor over death and the devil to the angels and the elect a). The special purposes are that he might occupy the heavenly kingdom b), unlock paradise for us c), and prepare dwellings in heaven d).

Proof a. From Col. II, 15. Having despoiled principalities and powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in himself. Christ showed to evil spirits in hell through his descent into hell, to men on earth through his resurrection, and to angels and blessed souls in heaven, that he had conquered his enemies and was celebrating this triumph over them.

Proof b. From Acts III, 21. Ὃν δεῖ ὀρανὸν μὲν δέξασθαι, ἄχρι χρόνων ἀποκαταστά- σεως πάντων, whom heaven must receive until the time of the restoration of all things. The meaning is: It is necessary for Christ, by the decree of God, to occupy the heavenly kingdom, to be governed by the full and universal use of the communicated divine majesty.

Proof c. From Rev. III, 7. These things says the holy and true one, who has the key of David, who opens, and no one shuts, and shuts, and no one opens. Christ has full power, in the government of the church, of opening heaven and receiving into the church not only the militant, but also the triumphant.

Proof d. From John XIV, 2. In my Father's house are many mansions. If it were not so, I would have told you: I go to prepare a place for you. The Savior teaches that by divine decree a seat and degree of glory is established for everyone. If this were not so, Jesus would have already told the disciples, and would not have fed them with vain hope. But now he says openly that he is about to go to prepare for them, by his merit, a place and a most blessed home, since the divine decree concerning the conferring of a blessed seat is founded upon the merit of Christ.

Question CLV. What is the session of Christ at the right hand of God?

The session at the right hand of God is the highest degree of glory, by which Christ the God-man, according to his human nature, having been raised to the throne of divine majesty, most powerfully and most presently governs all things that are in the kingdom of power, grace, and glory, for the glory of his name and for the comfort and salvation of the afflicted church.

Question CLVI. What do you understand by the right hand of God?

The right hand of God here does not denote a bodily limb a), but infinite power b), and immense glory c).

Prob. a. God is a spirit, John IV, 24. who does not have flesh and bones, Luke XXIV, 39. Prob. b. The right hand of God signifies infinite virtue; because it is called in the Holy Scriptures the right hand of power, Matthew XXVI, 64. the right hand striking, Exodus XV, 6. Prob. c. The right hand of God is also called by the Holy Spirit the right hand of majesty, Hebrews I, 3. ch. VIII, 1. the right hand of the throne of God, Hebrews XII, 2. The right hand of God is above every principality, power, virtue, and dominion, Ephesians I, 21. The right hand of God is omnipresent, Psalm CXXXIX, 10.

Question CLVII. Does the right hand of God designate a place?

The right hand of God does not denote a certain and determined place. Proof. Because the right hand of God is infinite power and immense majesty, as we have already demonstrated, it cannot be a determined place.

You say: It is called the right hand of God in the highest, Heb. 1:3. In the Apostolic Creed we believe that Christ is to come thence from the right hand of God. "Thence" is an adverb of place. Resp. To 1. It is called the right hand in the highest, not by reason of a sublime place, but by reason of a most exalted state. To 2. The adverb, "thence," in the Apostolic Creed is not to be referred to the right hand of God; because Christ, being about to come to judgment, will sit at the right hand of God, Matt. 26:64. And he will not come from thence; but to the heaven of the blessed, or to that blessed [place], in which Christ is according to the mode of his glorified body, as explained by D. AEGIDIUS HUNNIUS, Qu. de maiestate Christi p. 184.

Latin:

Ascendit Christus in coelum virtute infinita, omnibus tribus diuinitatis personis communi.

Prob. 1) Exaltatio Christi in coelum est actio ad extra, omnibus tribus deitatis personis communis. 2) Christus dicitur exaltatus δεξιᾷ τοῦ Θεοῦ, dextra Dei, Act. II, 3. c.

V, 31. i. e. potentia Dei infinita & immensa; dextra enim Dei hic non relate, sed absolute sumitur. Quaest. CLI. Quis est terminus, a quo Christus ascendit?

Terminus a quo ascensionis est mons oliueti prope Bethaniam. Prob. Ex Act. I, 12. Christo in coelum sublato, discipuli reuersi sunt in Hierosolymam a monte, qui dicitur oliueti.

Et Christus ascensurus eduxit discipulos foras vsque in Bethaniam, Luc. XXIV, 50. Quaest. CLII. Quis est terminus ad quem ascensionis Christi?

Terminus, ad quem Christus in ascensione sua peruenit, est tum communis, tum proprius. Communis est sedes & domicilium beatorum, vbi Christus beatis se ad faciem conspiciendum praebet . Proprius & vltimus est coelum Dei maiestaticum, seu thronus maiestatis diuinae .

Prob. a. Euectus est Christus in paradisum, in quo cum ipso est conuersus latro, Luc. XXIII, 43. vbi etiam est Iobus c. XIX, 27. vbi paratae sunt fidelibus mansiones, Io. XIV, 2. vbi redemtor gloriosissimus conspectu suo iucundissimo sanctorum animas exhilarabit.

Prob. b. Terminus ad quem proprius est coelum Dei maiestaticum, quod est super omnes coelos, Eph. IV, 10. Habemus sacerdotem principem magnum, qui penetrauit coelos, Hebr. IV, 14.

Penetrauit coelos non ratione distantiae, sed sublimissima & diuinae praesentiae. Coelum Dei maiestaticum est ipsa dextra Dei, qua coelis excelsior factus est Christus, Hebr. VII, 26. de qua Apostolus, Hebr. VIII, 1. Eiusmodi habemus sacerdotem principem, qui consedit in dextra throni maiestatis in coelis.

Obs. Per coelum hic non intelligitur coelum naturae aereum, vel athereum, quod cogitare impium est: neque coelum gratiae, quod est ecclesia militans in his terris; cui Christus visibilem praesentiam suam vsque ad diem extremi iudicii subtraxit. E. intelligitur coelum gloriae, vel finitae, vel infinitae.

Qua gloriam finitam Christus in πῇ beatorum se vtique conspiciendum praebet angelis & beatis, ad veri corporis glorificati modum, ita tamen, vt ipsi etiam comunicata sit gloria infinita per sessionem ad dextram Dei.

Euectus igitur est Christus in coelum Dei maiestaticum, vt omnia impleret, Eph. IV, 10.

Conf. DANNHAV. in hodof. phaenom. VIII. p. 763.

Quaest. CLIII. Quis fuit modus ascensionis Christi? Ratione modi ascensio Christi non fuit ἀφανισμός, siue disparitio, sed motus verus, realis, successiue progressiuus , & visibilis vsque ad nubes .

At eleuatus a nube modo inuisibili ad dextram Dei exaltatus est . Prob. a. Ex Luc. XXIV, 51. Recessit ab iis, & sublatus est in coelum.

Secessus infert successiuam loci mutationem & motum progressiuum de loco in coelum.

Prob. b. Ex Act. I, 9. Videntibus illis sublatus est, & nubes suscepit ipsum ab oculis ipsorum.

Prob. c. Christus coelos penetrauit; Hebr. IV, 14. factus coelis sublimior, Hebr.

VII, 26. E. inuisibili ratione supra omnes coelos euectus est.

Obs. Visibilis Christi motus vsque ad nubes localis fuit, non secundum motum corporis naturalis, quod natura sua deorsum fertur, sed glorificati & supernaturalibus dotibus instructi.

Neque per indigentiam naturae, sed per liberam oeconomiam Christus assumsit motum localem & visibilem, qui, si voluisset, in puncto temporis discipulis fuisse potuisset. sua deorsum fertur, sed glorificati & supernaturalibus dotibus instructi. Neque per indigentiam naturæ, sed per liberam œconomiam Christus assumsit motum localem & visibilem, qui, si voluisset, in puncto temporis discipulis suis se potuisset subducere, & coelum occupare. At placebat Saluatori sensim ferri sursum, vt discipuli de vera ascensione eo luculentius & confidentius testarentur. Ex quo colligimus, Christum ascendisse quidem vsque ad nubes per motum localem, sed non localiter, aut physice. Conf. D. SCHERZERI system. p. 247.

Quaest. CLIV. Quem in finem ascendit in coelum?

Finis ascensionis generalis est, vt se victorem mortis & diaboli angelis & electis gloriose ostenderet a). Speciales fines sunt, vt regnum coeleste occuparet b), paradisum nobis reseraret c), & habitationes in coelo pararet d).

Prob. a. Ex Col. II, 15. Exuens principatus & potestates, ostentauit palam triumphans de illis per seipsum. Christus in inferno spiritibus malis per descensum ad inferos, in terra hominibus per resurrectionem, in coelo angelis & animabus beatis ostendit, se hostes suos vicisse, & istum de iis agere triumphum.

Prob. b. Ex Act. III, 21. Ὃν δεῖ ὀρανὸν μὲν δέξασθαι, ἄχρι χρόνων ἀποκαταστάσεως πάντων, quem oportet coelum quidem suscipere, vsque ad tempus restitutionis omnium. Sensus est: Oportet Christum vi decreti diuini regnum occupare coeleste, pleno & vniuersali communicatae maiestatis diuinae vsu gubernandum.

Prob. c. Ex Apoc. III, 7. Haec dicit sanctus & verus, qui habet clauem Dauidis, qui aperit, vt nemo claudat, & claudit, vt nemo aperiat. Christus plenam habet potestatem, in ecclesiae regimine, coelum aperiendi, & recipiendi in ecclesiam non militantem solum, sed & triumphantem.

Prob. d. Ex Io. XIV, 2. In domo Patris mei mansiones multae sunt. Si vero non; dixerim vobis: abeo ad parandum locum vobis. Docet Saluator, decreto diuino cuilibet suam esse constitutam sedem, atque gradum gloriae. Quod nisi ita esset, iam ante discipulis, id dixissset Iesus, neque vana ipsos spe lactasset. At nunc aperte dicit, se iamiam abiturum esse ad parandum illis merito suo locum & domicilium beatissimum, cum decretum diuinum, de conferenda sede beata, merito Christi fundatum sit.

Quaest. CLV. Quid est sessio Christi ad dextram Dei?

Sessio ad dextram Dei est gradus gloriae summus, quo Christus θεάνθρωπος, secundum humanam naturam, in thronum maiestatis diuinae euectus, omnia, quae sunt in regno potentiae, gratiae, & gloriae, potentissime praesentissimeque gubernat, in nominis sui gloriam, & ecclesiae afflictae solatium & salutem.

Quaest. CLVI. Quid intelligis per dextram Dei?

Dextra Dei hic non notat membrum corporeum a), sed potentiam infinitam b), & gloriam immensam c).

Prob. a. Deus est spiritus, Io. IV, 24. qui carnem & ossa non habet, Luc. XXIV, 39. Prob. b. Dextra Dei significat virtutem infinitam; quia vocatur in sacris litteris dextra potentiae, Matth. XXVI, 64. dextra percutiens, Exod. XV, 6. Prob. c. Dextra Dei appellatur etiam a Spiritu S. dextra maiestatis, Hebr. I, 3. c. VIII, 1. dextra throni Dei, Hebr. XII, 2. Est dextra Dei supra omnem principatum, potestatem, virtutem & dominationem, Eph. I, 21. Est dextra Dei omnipraesens, Ps. CXXXIX, 10.

Quaest. CLVII. An dextra Dei locum designat?

Dextra Dei non denotat certum & determinatum locum. Prob. Quia dextra Dei est potentia infinita, & maiestas immensa, vti iam demonstravimus, determinatus locus esse nequit.

Dicis: Appellatur dextra Dei in excelsis, Hebr. I, 3. In symbolo apostolico credimus, quod, inde a dextra Dei venturus sit Christus. Inde, est adverbium loci. Resp. Ad 1. Dicitur dextra in excelsis, non ratione loci sublimis, sed ratione status celsissimi. Ad 2. Adverbium, inde, in symbolo apostolico referendum est non ad dextram Dei; quia Christus venturus ad iudicium, in dextra Dei sedebit, Matth. XXVI, 64. E inde non veniet; sed ad caelum beatorum, sive ad illud beatum, in quo Christus est iuxta clarificati sui corporis modum, explicante D. AEGIDIO HVNNIO, Qu. de maiestate Christi p. 184.


### Q. CLVIII

It is called the right hand of God the Father, because the right hand of God, to which Christ has been exalted, is not taken here absolutely, as it is common to all three persons of the divinity, but relatively, insofar as it is the right hand of the first divine person, who is the fountain of deity , and that a notable distinction may be indicated between the right hand of the Father and of Christ .

Prob. a. God the Father said to God the Son: Sit at my right hand, Ps. 110:2. Where the right hand of God cannot be taken absolutely, so as to denote omnipotence and glory, common to all three divine persons. For thus Christ would sit at his own right hand, and at the right hand of the Holy Spirit, which is ἄγραφον (unwritten). Therefore, the right hand of God is taken here relatively, as it denotes divine power and immense majesty, communicated by God the Father to the λόγῳ ἀσάρκῳ (Word without flesh) through eternal generation, and to the λόγῳ ἐνσάρκῳ (Word in the flesh), through the exaltation of the human nature. Conf. D. DANNHAV. in Christol. p. 335.

Prob. b. The right hand of Christ has a contrasted left hand, Matt. 25:33; but to the right hand of the Father no left hand corresponds. "I understand the right hand, lest you should seek a left hand there," says AUGUST. sermon. 119. de temp. The right hand of God the Father is incommunicable to mere men; but the right hand of Christ is communicable. The former denotes infinite glory, the latter finite.

Latin:

Vocatur dextra Dei Patris, quia dextra Dei, ad quam Christus evectus est, hic non sumitur absolute, prout omnibus tribus divinitatis personis est communis, sed relate, quatenus est dextra primae personae divinae, quae est fons deitatis , & vt indicetur notabile discrimen inter dextram Patris, & Christi .

Prob. a. Dixit Deus Pater Deo Filio: Sede ad dextram meam, Ps. CX, 2. Vbi dextra Dei non potest absolute accipi, vt notet omnipotentiam & gloriam, omnibus tribus personis divinis communem. Sic enim Christus ad summet sederet dextram, & ad dextram Spiritus S. quod est ἄγραφον. Sumitur itaque dextra Dei hic relate, prout notat divinam potentiam & immensam maiestatem, communicatam a Deo Patre τῷ λόγῳ ἀσάρκῳ per aeternam generationem, & λόγῳ ἐνσάρκῳ, qua humanam naturam, per exaltationem. Conf. D. DANNHAV. in Christol. p. 335.

Prob. b. Dextra Christi habet contradistinctam sinistram, Matth. XXV, 33; at dextrae Patris non respondet sinistra. Intelligo dextram, ne ibi quaras sinistram, ait AVGUST. sermon. CXIX. de temp. Dextra Dei Patris est incommunicabilis meris hominibus; dextra Christi autem est communicabilis. Illa notat gloriam infinitam, haec finitam.


### Q. CLIX

It is called the right hand of the throne, on account of the royal, spiritual, and most exalted majesty communicated to Christ as man through his exaltation. The right hand of the Father is called the right hand of the throne of God, Heb. 12:2, the right hand of the throne of majesty in the heavens, Heb. 8:1. The throne of God is the divine majesty, glory, opulence, and magnificence, differing from the right hand not in reality, but in reason, in the same manner in which divine majesty differs from divine power. See DANNHAV. in hodof. phaenom. 8. p. 775.

Latin:

Dextra throni vocatur, ob communicatam Christo homini per exaltationem, maiestatem regiam, spiritualem & celsissimam. Dextra Patris appellatur dextra throni Dei, Hebr. XII, 2. dextra throni maiestatis in caelis, Hebr. VIII, 1. Thronus Dei est maiestas, gloria, opulentia ac magnificentia divina, a dextra differens non re, sed ratione, ad eum modum, quo maiestas divina a potentia divina discrepat. Vid. DANNHAV. in hodof. phaenom. VIII. p. 775.


### Q. CLX. What does it mean to sit at the right hand of God?

To sit at the right hand of God signifies: to use fully and ceaselessly the omnipotence and royal majesty communicated by the Father through exaltation, for the universal and most glorious governance in the kingdom of power, grace, and glory: or, which is the same thing, to sit at the right hand of God is, by virtue of the personal union, and the exaltation which followed it, to govern most powerfully, most presently, and most gloriously all the works of the hands of God. Prob. 1) From the Pauline interpretation, 1 Cor. 15:25. "Jesus must reign, until he has put all enemies under his feet." Coll. with Ps. 110:1, 2. "The saying of Jehovah to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet. The scepter of your strength Jehovah will send from Zion (saying): rule in the midst of your enemies.

Prob. 2) Because Christ, crowned with glory and honor, has been constituted over all the works of the divine hands, so that all things are subject under his feet, Heb. 2:7, 8. E. Through exaltation to the right hand of God, universal dominion over all creatures has been conferred upon Christ. universal dominion over all creatures.

Latin:

Sedere ad dextram Dei, significat: communicata a Patre per exaltationem omnipotentia & maiestate regia plene & indefinenter vti, ad regimen universale & gloriosissimum in regno potentiae, gratiae & gloriae: vel, quod idem est, sedere ad dextram Dei, est, vi unionis personalis, & hanc secuta exaltationis, potentissime, praesentissime, & gloriosissime omnia opera manuum Dei gubernare. Prob. 1) Ex interpretatione Paullina, 1 Cor. XV, 25. Oportet Iesum regnare, donec posuerit omnes hostes sub pedes suos. Coll. cum Ps. CX, 1, 2. Dictum Iehovae ad Dominum meum: Sede ad dextram meam, usque dum posuero inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum. Sceptrum roboris tui mittet Iehovah ex Sione (dicens): dominare in medio inimicorum tuorum.

Prob. 2) Quia Christus gloria & honore coronatus, constitutus est super omnia opera manuum divinarum, vt omnia subiecta sint sub pedes eius, Hebr. II, 7, 8. E. per exaltationem ad dextram Dei collatum est Christo dominium universale in omnes creaturas. vniuersale in omnes creaturas.


### Q. CLXI

According to which nature has Christ been exalted to the right hand of God? Christ the God-man has been exalted according to his human nature to the right hand of God .

Prob. a. I have overcome and sat down with my Father in his throne, Apoc. III, 21. Whoever has overcome death and the devil is Christ the God-man: the same is the one sitting on the Father's throne.

Prob. b. 1) From Christ's own assertion: From now on the Son of Man shall be sitting at the right hand of the power of God, Luc. XXII, 69. Christ, placed in the midst of the theater of his humiliation, says that he is ἀπ' ἄρτι, from now on, i.e., that he is about to sit, as the Son of Man, at the right hand of God.

2) From the connection of humiliation and exaltation. According to the same nature that Christ was humiliated, according to the same he is exalted to the right hand of God: but he was humiliated according to his human nature, etc. Therefore. The major premise is evident: because humiliation and exaltation are most tightly connected in the Holy Scriptures and are spoken of regarding the same nature. The minor premise is clear from the Pauline oracle, Rom. VIII, 34. Who is he that condemns? It is Christ who died; yea rather, who is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also makes intercession for us. All these predicates are spoken of Christ according to his human nature.

The antithesis is from the Papists, who assert that exaltation to the right hand belongs to Christ according to both natures; they argue: I. Holy Scripture attributes the session at the right hand of God to the whole person of Christ, Rom. VIII, 34. Eph. I, 20, 21. Resp. Holy Scripture attributes the session at the right hand of God to the whole person of Christ indeed, but according to his human nature. The person is the subject which, the human nature is the subject by which, of the session at the right hand.

II. To sit at the right hand of God is an official royal act: Therefore, it belongs to Christ according to both natures. Resp. To sit at the right hand of God is defined either precisely, as the highest degree of exaltation, or complexly, insofar as it is a royal act, directed for the benefit of the church. Indeed, exaltation to the right hand of the Father belongs to Christ according to his human nature: but the session of Christ, insofar as it denotes the gracious and salutary dominion of Christ, is an ἀποτέλεσμα, or a theandric action.

Latin:

Christus Θεάνθρωπος secundum humanam naturam ad dextram Dei euectus est .

Prob. a. Ego vici & consedi cum Patre meo in throno ipsius, Apoc. III, 21. Quicunque vicit mortem & diabolum, est Christus Θεάνθρωπος: Idem fessor in throno Patris.

Prob. b. 1) Ex ipsius Christi assertione: Ex hoc nunc erit filius hominis sedens ex dextris virtutis Dei, Luc. XXII, 69. Dicit Christus constitutus in medio exinanitionis theatro, se ἀπ' ἄρτι, a modo, i. e. iamiam sessurum esse, vt filium hominis, ad dextram Dei.

2) A connexione exinanitionis, & exaltationis. Secundum quam naturam Christus exinanitus est, secundum eandem est exaltatus ad dextram Dei: Atqui secundum humanam naturam &c. Ergo. Maior constat: quia exinanitio, & exaltatio in sacro codice arctissime connectuntur, & de eadem natura dicuntur. Minor liquet ex oraculo Paullino, Rom. VIII, 34. Quis est, qui condemnat? Christus est, qui mortuus est; magis vero qui resuscitatus est, qui etiam est in dextra Dei, qui & intercedit pro nobis. Prædicata hæc omnia dicuntur de Christo secundum humanam naturam.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, afferentium, exaltationem ad dextram Christo secundum utramque naturam competere; qui argumentantur: I. S. Scriptura toti personæ Christi sessionem ad dextram Dei tribuit, Rom. VIII, 34. Eph. I, 20. 21. Resp. S. scriptura tribuit sessionem ad dextram Dei toti quidem personæ Christi, sed secundum humanam naturam. Persona est subiectum quod, natura humana subiectum quo sessionis ad dextram.

II. Sedere ad dextram Dei est actus officialis regius: E. competit Christo secundum utramque naturam. Resp. Sedere ad dextram Dei, vel funitur præcise, vt summus exaltationis gradus, vel complexe, quatenus est actus regius, in commodum ecclesiæ directus. Nimirum exaltatio ad dextram Patris competit Christo secundum humanam naturam: sed sessio Christi, prout notat dominium Christi gratiosum & salutare, est ἀποτέλεσμα, siue actio theandrica.


### Q. CLXII

By what power has Christ been exalted to the right hand of God? Christ has been exalted by the power common to all three persons of the divinity.

Prob. This exaltation is most frequently attributed in Holy Scripture to God the Father, as the source of divinity, Ps. CX, 1. Eph. I, 29. Phil. II, 9. Nevertheless, since what the Father does, the Son does likewise, Io. V, 19. Therefore, Christ himself is also said to have sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high, Hebr. I, 3. Nor is the Holy Spirit to be excluded from the exaltation of Christ, since it is an undivided external action.

Latin:

Exaltatus est Christus virtute omnibus tribus personis diuinitatis communi.

Prob. Tribuitur frequentissime in S. Scriptura hæc exaltatio Deo Patri, vt fonti diuinitatis, Ps. CX, 1. Eph. I, 29. Phil. II, 9. Attamen, cum, quæ Pater facit, similiter facit Filius, Io. V, 19. Ideo etiam ipse Christus consedisse dicitur in dextra maiestatis in excelsis, Hebr. I, 3. Neque Spiritus S. excludendus est ab exaltatione Christi, cum sit actio ad extra indiuisa.


### Q. CLXIII

Has a truly divine, universal, and omnipresent dominion been granted to Christ through his exaltation to the right hand of God? Through his exaltation to the right hand of God the Father, a truly divine , universal, and omnipresent dominion has been conferred upon Christ.

Prob. a. 1) Such as is the government of God the Father on the throne of his majesty, such is the government of Christ the God-man, sitting at the right hand of God: but the government of God the Father is truly divine. Therefore. The major premise is proven: Just as to subsist by generation and essentially do not differ in the divine; so divine session simply, and session at the right hand essentially, do not differ. See DANNH. in hodof. phænom. VIII. p. 779.

2) From the session of Christ at the right hand of God flow effects of infinite power, which are recounted in Ps. CX, namely 1) the prostration of all enemies to the footstool of his feet, among whom the enemies are most powerful spirits, greatest monarchs and tyrants, 2) the sending forth of the gracious scepter into the whole world, 3) dominion in the midst of enemies, 4) the new generation of an innumerable offspring, 5) the administration of an eternal priesthood, which priesthood is the cause of eternal salvation, Hebr. V, 9. Proof b.

Proof b. 1) Whatever nature has been raised to truly divine rule, that nature reigns substantially present everywhere: But the human nature of Christ &c: Therefore. The minor is clear from what has already been said.

2) Whatever nature has been placed at the omnipresent right hand of God, and sits on an omnipresent throne, that nature governs most omnipresently: But the human nature of Christ &c. Therefore. The major is evident: because every πᾶν [all] of the divine right hand is omnipresent: Therefore, he who sits there, where the right hand of God is, he is omnipresent.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, Socinians, and Arminians, who deny that truly divine and omnipresent dominion has been conferred upon Christ as man; their principal arguments are:

I. If both natures of Christ govern omnipotently and present everywhere, there will be two omnipotent and omnipresent governors: The consequent is absurd: Therefore, the antecedent is as well. Resp. 1) It is a fallacious conclusion from the abstract to the concrete. 2) If both natures of Christ were a person, governing omnipotently and present everywhere, there would be two omnipotent and omnipresent governors: But both natures of Christ make one σύνθετον [composite] person, who is at once God and man.

II. Placement at the right hand of God, and sitting on the divine throne, does not imply omnipresent dominion. For on the last day of judgment, the faithful are to be placed at the right hand of Christ, Matth. XXV, 33, and the elect are said to sit on the throne of Christ, Apoc. III, 21. Resp. Distinguish between the right hand and throne of God the Father; and between the right hand and throne of Christ. The right hand and throne of God the Father denotes infinite power and majesty: The right hand and throne of Christ designates a finite dignity and prerogative, obtained for us by the merit of Christ.

III. The body of Christ is in heaven: Therefore, it does not reign everywhere. Resp. 1) Our Father is in heaven, and yet He reigns everywhere. 2) The body of Christ is in the heaven of the blessed, as an act of the glorified nature: It is, however, in the majestatic heaven of God, as an act of the person so that He might fill all things, Eph. IV, 10. But the glorified body of Christ is not inclusively or circumscriptively in a physical and local heaven.

IV. Christ, as glorified man, was seen by Stephen standing in heaven, Act. VII, 55. Therefore, Christ as man is not omnipresent in the state of glorification. Resp. The vision and revelation of Christ does not weaken omnipresence, but confirms it. For Christ, according to His most free will, can present Himself visibly present in any place, and yet remain personally omnipresent: Just as the patriarch Jacob saw God standing above the ladder in heaven, who nevertheless was also present on earth, Gen. XXVIII, 13.

V. According to whichever nature the Son of God reigns with the same majesty as the Father, according to that nature He is ὁμοούσιος [consubstantial] with God the Father. But according to the human nature, the Son of God is not ὁμοούσιος with the Father. E. The major is clear: because from the session of the Son of God, and His omnipresent government, a valid argument is drawn for establishing the divinity of the Son of God; which argument is weakened if Christ governs with the same majesty as God the Father according to His humanity. Resp. Limit the major: According to whichever nature the Son of God reigns by Himself and essentially with the same majesty iesty with God the Father, according to the same [nature] He is ὁμοούσιος (consubstantial) to God the Father; I concede it. But according to His human nature, Christ does not govern with the same majesty as the Father by Himself or essentially, but by the grace of union and exaltation. Yet it is a good method of arguing from the session at the right hand of God and the divine government to the τὴν ὁμοουσίαν (consubstantiality) with God the Father; because the one sitting at the right hand of God is θεάνθρωπος (God-man), and God does not admit to His right hand a person sitting, unless He be divine.

Latin:

Per exaltationem ad dextram Dei Patris collatum est Christo dominium vere diuinum , vniuersale & omnipræsens .

Prob. a. 1) Qualis est gubernatio Dei Patris in throno fuæ maiestatis, talis est gubernatio Christi Θεάνθρωπος, ad dextram Dei sedentis: at gubernatio Dei Patris est vere diuina. Ergo. Maior probatur: Sicut subsistere γεννητῶς, & essentialiter, in diuinis non differunt; ita sessio diuina simpliciter, & sessio ad dextram essentialiter, non differunt. Vid. DANNH. in hodof. phænom. VIII. p. 779.

2) Ex sessione Christi ad dextram Dei fluunt effectus infinitæ potentiæ, qui recensentur Ps. CX. nempe 1) prostratio omnium hostium ad scabellum pedum, quos inter hostes sunt spiritus potentissimi, monarchae & tyranni maximi, 2) emissio sceptri gratiosi in omnem orbem, 3) dominium in medio inimicorum, 4) noua generatio innumerae prolis, 5) aeterni sacerdotii administratio, quod sacerdotium est causa aeternae salutis, Hebr. V, 9.

Prob. b. 1) Quaecunque natura ad regimen vere diuinum euecta est, illa substantialiter praesens ubique regnat: Atqui humana Christi natura &c: Ergo. Minor, liquet e iam dictis.

2) Quaecunque natura collocata est ad dextram Dei omnipraesentem, & sedet in throno omnipraesente, illa omnipraesentissime gubernat: Atqui humana Christi natura &c. Ergo. Maior constat: quia omne πᾶν dextrae diuinae est omnipraesens: Ergo qui ibi sedet, ubi est dextra Dei, ille est omnipraesens.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, Socinianorum & Arminianorum, negantium Christo homini collatum esse dominium uere diuinum & omnipraesens; quorum praecipua sunt argumenta:

I. Si utraque Christi natura omnipotenter & ubique praesenter gubernat, erunt duo omnipotentes & omnipraesentes gubernatores: Consequens est absurdum: E. & antecedens. Resp. 1) Vitiose concluditur ab abstracto ad concretum. 2) Si utraque Christi natura esset persona, omnipotenter & ubique praesenter gubernans, essent duo omnipotentes & omnipraesentes gubernatores: At utraque natura Christi facit unam personam σύνθετον, quae est simul Deus & homo.

II. Collocatio ad dextram Dei, & sessio in throno diuino non infert omnipraesens dominium. Nam in extremo die iudicii fideles collocandi sunt ad dextram Christi, Matth. XXV, 33. & electi dicuntur sedere in throno Christi, Apoc. III, 21. Resp. Dist. inter dextram & thronum Dei Patris; & inter dextram atque thronum Christi. Dextra thronusque Dei Patris notat potentiam & maiestatem infinitam: Dextra thronusque Christi designat dignitatem & praerogatiuam finitam, merito Christi nobis conciliatam.

III. Corpus Christi est in caelo: E. non regnat ubique. Resp. 1) Pater noster est in caelo, & tamen regnat ubique. 2) Corpus Christi est in caelo beatorum, qua actum naturae glorificatae: Est tamen in caelo Dei maiestatico, qua actum personae ut omnia impleat, Eph. IV, 10. Non autem corpus Christi glorificatum est inclusive, aut circumscriptiue in caelo physico & locali.

IV. Christus, qua homo glorificatus, uisus est a Stephano stans in caelo, Act. VII, 55. E. Christus homo non est omnipraesens in statu glorificationis. Resp. Visio & reuelatio Christi non labefactat omnipraesentiam, sed confirmat. Nam Christus pro liberrima uoluntate se sistere potest uisibiliter praesentem quouis loco, & tamen personaliter omnipraesens manet: Sicut Iacobus patriarcha uidebat Deum stantem supra scalam in caelo, qui tamen etiam in terra praesens erat, Gen. XXVIII, 13.

V. Secundum quam naturam Filius Dei eadem maiestate regnat cum Patre, secundum eam Deo Patri est ὁμοούσιος. At secundum humanam naturam Filius Dei Patri non est ὁμοούσιος. E. Maior patet: quia e sessione Filii Dei, & eiusdem omnipraesenti gubernatione, ualidum depromitur argumentum pro adstruenda diuinitate Filii Dei; quod argumentum eneruatur, si Christus secundum humanitatem eadem maiestate gubernat cum Deo Patre. Resp. Lim. mai, Secundum quam naturam Filius Dei per se & essentialiter eadem regnat maiestate iestate cum Deo Patre, secundum eandem Deo Patri est ὁμοούσιος; concedo. At secundum humanam naturam Christus non per se aut essentialiter, sed per gratiam unionis & exaltationis, eadem cum Patre maiestate gubernat. Bona tamen est ratio argumentandi a sessione ad dextram Dei & gubernatione diuina ad τὴν ὁμοουσίαν cum Deo Patre; quia sessor ad dextram Dei est θεάνθρωπος, & Deus non admittit ad dextram suam personam sedentem, nisi diuinam.


### Q. CLXIV

Christ was exalted to the right hand of God a) for the glory of His name, b) for the salvation of the church.

Prob. a. Because by the exaltation to the right hand of God, Christ was constituted the catholic King to be adored by all creatures in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, Phil. 2:9. Prob. b. Christ sitting at the right hand of God is the head of the church, Eph. 1:22, and therefore He protects the same: He intercedes for us, Rom. 8:34, and renders us partakers of His glory according to the capacity of our nature, Apoc. 3:21; moreover, He will destroy the power of the devil and all enemies, Ps. 110:1.

Latin:

Euectus est Christus ad dextram Dei a) in nominis sui gloriam, b) in ecclesiae salutem.

Prob. a. Quia per euectionem ad dextram Dei Christus constitutus est Rex catholicus ab omnibus creaturis coelestibus, terrestribus & subterraneis adorandus, Phil. II, 9. Prob. b. Christus sedens ad dextram Dei est caput ecclesiae, Eph. I, 22. adeoque eandem tuetur: interpellat pro nobis, Rom. VIII, 34. & nos gloriae suae pro capacitate naturae nostrae participes reddit, Apoc. III, 21.; diaboli autem & omnium hostium potestatem destruet, Ps. CX, 1.


### Q. CLXV

From the knowledge of Christ, both toward all men and especially toward the reborn, there redounds a use that is far most abundant, and that is as much paracletic as it is parenetic.

Prob. a. Let all other sciences be and remain ζημίαν καὶ σκύβαλα (loss and refuse) compared to this χριστογνωσίᾳ (knowledge of Christ). For this one consolation sustains our anxious minds, that our Christ is the most holy and truly divine Priest, by whose death we are reconciled to God, by whose blood we are cleansed from sins; that the same is our Prophet, Leader, and light of the way to heaven; that finally our Jesus Christ is King, possessing such power that He can repel the force of enemies and defend us, the citizens of His kingdom.

Prob. b. May χριστογνωσία (knowledge of Christ) excite in us the study of piety! Christ, the supreme Priest, delivered Himself for us as an oblation and sacrifice to God for an odor of sweetness. Let us offer ourselves, spiritual Priests, omitting no day, our εὐχαριστικὰ (eucharistic) sacrifices to Christ, a contrite heart and prayers burning with piety. Christ, our Prophet, has taught us the way of God in truth. Let us run this way with unoffending feet strenuously, until we reach the goal according to our vow. Christ, in His royal office, is the head of the church, His mystical body. Let us be and remain true and living members of the church, let us adhere to Christ the head, with sincere faith and charity, that He may deem us worthy of His protection and safeguard.

SIGH

In Thee, O Jesus, leader and perfecter of my faith, I look, as often as I refresh the wounds of my soul! Thou wast struck, that I might recover. Thou didst pour out Thy blood, that my filth might be washed away. That I might have the eternal way, Thou didst suffer an ignominious death. That I might not wander in the whole heaven, Thou didst open for me an expedited way to heaven. That I might not be oppressed by enemies, by Thy royal protection Thou didst lift up my head. What shall I render for so many and so great benefits bestowed upon me? I give, I say, I consecrate to Thee, O Jesus, whatever I have. Of a contrite heart, I give Thee a faithful soul, I consecrate a body destined for Thy worship! To Thee be praise, and honor, and glory everlasting!

Latin:

E cognitione Christi cum in omnes homines, tum praecipue in renatos, redundat usus longe vberrimus, isque tam paracleticus , quam paraneticus .

Prob. a. Sint maneantque omnes aliae scientiae ζημίαν καὶ σκύβαλα prae hac χριστογνωσίᾳ. Etenim hoc vnum solatium anxias nostras mentes sustentat, quod Christus noster Sacerdos sanctissimus & vere diuinus est, cuius morte Deo sumus reconciliati, cuius sanguine a peccatis emundamur; quod idem noster est Propheta, Dux & lux viae ad coelum; quod denique Iesus Christus noster rex ea pollet potestate, vt hostium vim repellere, & nos regni sui ciues defendere queat.

Prob. b. Χριστογνωσία excitet in nobis pietatis studium! Christus, Sacerdos summus tradidit seipsum pro nobis oblationem & sacrificium, Deo in odorem fragrantiae. Offeramus nos, spirituales Sacerdotes, nullo praetermisso die, Christo sacrificia nostra εὐχαριστικὰ, cor contritum & preces pietate ardentes. Christus, Propheta noster, viam Dei nos docuit, in veritate. Hanc viam inoffensis pedibus strenue decurramus, donec metam ex voto attingamus. Christus, in officio suo regio est caput ecclesiae, corporis sui mystici. Simus & maneamus nos vera viuaque membra ecclesiae, adhaereamus capiti Christo, sincera fide & charitate, vt sua nos tutela & praesidio dignetur.

SVSPIRIVM

In te, o Iesu, dux & consummator fidei meae, respicio, quoties vulnera animae meae refrico! Tu percussus es, vt ego conualescam. Fudisti sanguinem tuum, vt sordes meae eluantur. Vt aeternum viam, ignominiosam oppetiuisti mortem. Ne toto errem coelo, expeditam ad coelum mihi viam aperuisti. Ne ab hostibus opprimar, regio tuo praesidio caput meum erexisti. Quid retribuam pro tot tantisque in me collatis beneficiis? Do, dico, consecro tibi, o Iesu, quidquid habeo. De cor contritum, dico tibi animam fidelem, consecro corpus tuo cultui destinatum! Tibi fit laus, & honor & gloria sempiterna!


## 19 On the Applying Grace of the Holy Spirit, and the Call


### Concerning the Applying Grace of the Holy Spirit, as the Third Principle of Salvation

AS THE THIRD PRINCIPLE OF SALVATION.

SPECIFICALLY ON THE CALLING GRACE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT. Quest. I. What is the applying grace of the Holy Spirit?

The applying grace of the Holy Spirit is the principle of those divine acts by which the Holy Spirit, through the word of God and the sacraments, dispenses, offers, confers, and seals to us the spiritual and eternal benefits destined for the human race by the most benevolent goodwill of God the Father, and acquired by the brotherly redemption of Jesus Christ.

Obs.

I. Divine grace is opposed 1) to the merit of man, Rom. XI, 6. Eph. II, 8. & 9: 2) to the nature of men, not to its constitution, but to its corruption, Eph. II, 3. & 8: 3) to eternal glory, which differs from grace as the consequent from the antecedent, as the effect from the cause, as the end from the efficacious means, just as the kingdom of grace is distinguished from the kingdom of glory, 1 Corinth. I, 3-8. Tit. III, 7: 4) to wrath and damnation, and that indeed twofold: α) that which follows the first and hereditary sin, and which precedes salvation to be recovered and offered to all, Eph. II, 3. & 7. 8: β) that which follows the obstinacy of souls and salvation offered and rejected, Rom. IX, 22. Hebr. XII, 15. seqq. Jude v. 4. Therefore 1) by virtue of the first opposition, grace is every single benefit of God, whether temporal or eternal, even human nature itself, and not only in the state of defection, but also in the state of integrity, and both its constitution and its preservation, without any merit of man, while he was still integral.

Hence it is called creating and preserving grace, within the scope of which are contained all things that pertain to creation and divine providence, and therefore it is accustomed to be called the grace of the first article (of the Christian faith). 2) By virtue of the second opposition, grace is the restoration of corrupted nature to integrity, and the acquisition as well as the application of lost salvation, and this indeed both begun and consummated, to which pertain all benefits, obtained by the merits of Christ, both temporal and eternal.

This is named saving grace, Tit.
