II, 11. 12. 13. and the same is the grace of the second and third articles. 3) By virtue of the third opposition, grace is the preparation of men for eternal glory, and the bestowing of all those things which pertain to the order of salvation and are necessary for obtaining eternal blessedness.

This is specifically accustomed to be called the grace of the third article. 4) By virtue of the fourth opposition, as far as it pertains to its former part, grace is the compassion of God and the benign will concerning the recovery of the salvation of miserable men through a certain sponsor who would satisfy divine justice fully, and the offering of it equally to all and each; but as far as the latter part is concerned, grace is the benign will of God, which [does not] sometimes [abandon] wicked and contumacious men.

Spiritual benefits are those by which the soul of man, infected by the stain of sin, is divinely liberated from the state of misery, and transferred into the state of grace and glory; such are: the saving knowledge of God, faith in Christ, the remission of sins, righteousness availing before God, liberty from the terror and curse of the law, υἱοθεσία, or adoption as sons of God, our communion with God, peace of conscience, spiritual joy, the gift of perseverance, and eternal life. These spiritual benefits God the Father destined for the human race in His eternal counsel, the Son of God acquired by His active and passive obedience, so that they might redound to sinners with the divine righteousness safe, and the Holy Spirit dispenses the same through ordinary means, and applies them to men, by offering and conferring; but men, instructed by the powers of the Holy Spirit, apply them to themselves by receiving.

Obs. II. This οἰκονομίαν χάριτος (as Paul calls it Eph. III, 2.) i.e. the grace of the Holy Spirit as dispenser and applier, Holy Scripture appropriates to the Holy Spirit, while for this same reason it adorns Him with most sweet names. For He is called the Spirit of grace and of supplications, Zach. XII, 12. when He tolerates, spares them, and exhibits to them means for repentance sufficiently effective, until the time appointed for judgment. Rom. II, 4. 5.

II. Divine grace (we speak, however, of saving grace, which we profess partly in the second, partly in the third article of Christian doctrine) is distinguished in various ways, according to the variety of both things and persons, which are required for the salvation of men, who are to be liberated from their misery, α) By reason of God, whom we venerate as the one author of the salvation of all, grace is divided into that which decrees in the eternal counsel of God, and that which effects in time. Both are preached Eph. I, 4. 6. 7. β) By reason of salvation, grace is 1) of acquisition, through the satisfaction and merit of Christ, and therefore is called the grace of Jesus Christ, Act. XV, 11. 2 Cor. VIII, 9. and in the customary vow of PAUL, Rom. XVI, 24. which JOHN also used, Apoc. XXII, 21: 2) grace of application, through the efficacy of the Holy Spirit, who for that reason is called πνεῦμα τῆς χάριτος, Hebr. X, 29. The same distinction is necessary when we discuss the means of grace and salvation. For these means pertain either to the acquisition of our salvation, or to the application of the same and the reaping of its fruit. The medium of grace, for the acquisition of salvation, is none other than the satisfaction and merit of Christ, Act. IV, 12. For application, these two are necessarily required: oblation, and acceptance. Therefore, the medium of grace, as far as the application of salvation is concerned, is entirely twofold. The one, by which God offers salvation to us, and when we are obedient to the word, confers it upon us; which is the word, especially indeed the gospel (for the law, by the vice and fault of man, effects nothing but wrath, and denounces condemnation to man, Rom. III, 19. 15. VII, 13.) and the sacrament, both of them. The other, by which we receive the salvation offered to us; and this is true faith placed in Christ, which the Holy Spirit kindles and confirms in the mind. γ) By reason of men, and the various divine acts by which they are led to salvation, the grace of application 1) is a certain singular grace given to the ministers of the divine truth, insofar as they are ministers, Eph. III, 8. 1 Corinth. XV, 10. 2 Cor. III, 4. 5. 6. and therefore they are called ministering gifts, of which some indeed are extraordinary and temporary, bestowed upon the first heralds of the Gospel, such as: divine instinct and inspiration, Matth. X, 19. 20. and the power of performing miracles, Marc. XVI, 20. Hebr. II, 4: but others are ordinary and perpetual, to be bestowed upon all until the end of the world, and for the sacred church, either gathered by Christ or to be gathered, Eph. V, 26. 27. Tit. III, 5. 6. 7. The gifts of this grace are called sanctifying. (The general passages, in whose meaning are contained all the gifts of grace, both sanctifying and ministering, and these partly ordinary, partly extraordinary, are these two, Marc. XVI, 15-20. Eph. IV, 11. 12. 13.). As far as the various divine acts are concerned, the grace of application is α) calling, by offering to each one the means of salvation, Rom. X, 16-21. 1 Tim. II, 4. Matth. XXII, 3. 4: β) going before; exciting, preparing, by effecting the first holy motions of the mind, by arousing holy attention of the mind, by removing the impediments which stand in the way of the change of mind, Act. II, 37. XVI, 14. Apoc. III, 19. 20: γ) illuminating, converting and regenerating anew, Tit. III, 5: δ) justifying, Rom. III, 24: ε) renewing, Eph. II, 10. Hebr. XII, 28. XIII, 21: ζ) confirming and preserving, Phil. I, 6. 1 Petr. V, 10: η) perfecting, so that we may arrive at consummate and eternal salvation, 1 Cor. I, 4-8.

XII, 12. Spirit of wisdom and revelation, Eph. I, 17. Spirit of faith, 2 Cor. IV, 13. Spirit of adoption, Rom. VIII, 15. Spirit of glory, 1 Petr. IV, 14. Spirit of promise, by whom believers were sealed, and the earnest of our inheritance, Eph. I, 14. 2) Because the acts of grace (vocation, illumination, etc.) belong appropriately to the Holy Spirit.

Obs. III. The principle of all those divine and supernatural acts, by which the goods obtained by the merit of Christ are dispensed, is the grace of the Holy Spirit, since it is from Him that they proceed.

Latin:

APPLICATRICE, VT TERTIO SALVTIS PRINCIPIO.

IN SPECIE DE GRATIA SPIRITUS SANCTI VOCANTE. Quæst. I. Quid est gratia Spiritus Sancti applicatrix .

Gratia Spiritus Sancti applicatrix est principium illorum actuum diuinorum, quibus Spiritus Sanctus, per verbum Dei & sacramenta beneficia spiritualia & æterna, benignissima Dei Patris beneuolentia humano generi destinata, & fraterna Iesu Christi redemtione acquisita, dispensat, nobisque offert, confert, & obsignat.

Obs.

I. Opponitur gratia diuina 1) merito hominis, Rom. XI, 6. Eph. II, 8. & 9: 2) naturæ hominum, nec eius constitutioni, sed corruptioni, Eph. II, 3. & 8: 3) gloriæ sempiternæ, quæ a gratia differt, vt consequens ab antecedente, vt effectus a causa, vt finis a medio efficaci, quem ad modum regnum gratiæ a regno gloriæ discernitur, 1 Corinth. I, 3-8. Tit. III, 7: 4) iræ ac damnationi, & illi quidem duplici: α) quæ peccatum primum atque hæreditarium sequitur, & quæ salutem recuperandam atque omnibus offerendam antecedit, Eph. II, 3. & 7. 8: β) quæ animorum obstinationem, salutemque oblatam ac repudiatam sequitur, Rom. IX, 22. Hebr. XII, 15. seqq. Iudæ v. 4. Ergo 1) vi oppositionis primæ, gratia est beneficium Dei vnum quodque, siue temporale, siue æternum, ipsa etiam hominis natura, nec solum in statu defectionis, sed & in statu integritatis, eiusque tum constitutio, tum conseruatio, sine vllo hominis, adhuc integri, merito.

Hinc dicitur gratia creans & conseruans, cuius ambitu continentur omnia, quæcunque ad creationem & prouidentiam diuinam pertinent, ideoque vocari solet gratia primi articuli (fidei christianæ). 2) Vi oppositionis secundæ, gratia est naturæ corruptæ in integrum restitutio, & salutis deperditæ tam adquisitio, quam adplicatio, & hæc quidem cum inchoata, tum consummata, ad quam pertinent omnia beneficia, promeritis Christi parta, & temporalia, & æterna.

Hæc nominatur gratia salutaris, Tit. II, 11. 12. 13. eademque gratia secundi ac tertii articuli. 3) Vi oppositionis tertiæ, gratia est præparatio hominum ad gloriam sempiternam, & largitio eorum omnium, quæ ad ordinem salutis spectant, & necessaria sunt ad impetrandam beatitatem æternam.

Hæc speciatim dici solet gratia tertii articuli. 4) Vi oppositionis quartæ, quod quidem ad priorem eius partem attinet, gratia est miseratio Dei ac benigna voluntas, de salute miserorum hominum, per sponsorem quemdam, qui iustitiæ diuinæ satis ex asse faceret, recuperanda, omnibus etiam ac singulis peræque offerenda; quantum vero ad alteram partem, gratia est benigna Dei voluntas, quæ homines improbos & contumaces ali. quando

I. Beneficia spiritualia sunt, per quae anima hominis, labe peccati infecta, a statu miseriae divinitus liberatur, & in statum gratiae atque gloriae transfertur; qualia sunt: salutaris Dei cognitio, fides in Christum, remissio peccatorum, iustitia coram Deo valens, libertas a terrore & maledictione legis, υἱοθεσία, sive adoptio in filios Dei, communio nostri cum Deo, pax conscientiae, gaudium spirituale, donum perseverantiae, & vita aeterna. Haec beneficia spiritualia Deus Pater in aeterno suo consilio generi humano destinavit, Filius Dei obedientia sua actua & passiva acquisivit, ut salua iustitia divina in peccatores redundare queant, Spiritus S. eadem per ordinaria media dispensat, & hominibus applicat, offerendo & conferendo; homines autem, viribus Spiritus S. instructi, ea sibi applicant recipiendo.

Obs. II. Hanc οἰκονομίαν χάριτος (vti Paullus eam appellat Eph. III, 2.) i.e. gratiam Spiritus S. dispensatricem & applicatricem, S. Scriptura Spiritui S. appropriat, dum ob eandem ipsum dulcissimis ornat nominibus. Dicitur enim Spiritus gratiae & precum, Zach. XII, 12. quando tolerat, eisdem parcit, & media ad resipiscendum sat efficacia illis exhibet, vsque ad tempus iudicio dictum. Rom. II, 4. 5.

II. Distinguitur gratia divina (loquimur autem de salutari gratia, quam partim in secundo, partim in tertio doctrinae christianae articulo profitemur) variis modis, pro varietate & rerum, & personarum, quae ad salutem hominum, miseria sua liberandorum, requiruntur, α) Ratione Dei, quem vnum communis omnium salutis auctorem veneramur, gratia diuiditur in decernentem in aeterno Dei consilio, & efficientem in tempore. Vtraque praedicatur Eph. I, 4. 6. 7. β) Ratione salutis, gratia est 1) adquisitionis, per satisfactionem ac meritum Christi, ideoque dicitur gratia Iesu Christi, Act. XV, 11. 2 Cor. VIII, 9. & in voto PAVLLI vfitato, Rom. XVI, 24. quo & IOANNES vfus est, Apoc. XXII, 21: 2) gratia applicationis, per efficacitatem Spiritus S. qui ob eam caussam appellatur πνεῦμα τῆς χάριτος, Hebr. X, 29. Eadem distinctione opus est, cum de mediis gratiae & salutis differimus. Haec enim media pertinet vel ad adquisitionem salutis nostrae, vel ad eiusdem applicationem fructumque percipiendum. Medium gratiae, ad salutis adquisitionem, nullum est aliud, quam satisfactio ac meritum Christi, Act. IV, 12. Ad applicationem necessario requiruntur hae duo: oblatio, & acceptio. E. medium gratiae, quantum ad adplicationem salutis, omnino duplex est. Vnum, quo Deus nobis salutem offert, & cum ipsi dicto audientes sumus, in nos confert; id quod est verbum, praesertim vero euangelium (lex enim, hominis vitio & culpa nil, nisi iram efficit, ac damnationem homini denuntiat, Rom. III, 19. 15. VII, 13.) & sacramentum vtrumque. Alterum, quo nos salutem nobis oblatam accipimus; atque hoc est fiducia vera in Christo collocata, quam Spiritus S. in animo incendit & confirmat. γ) Ratione hominum, & variorum actuum diuinarum, quibus illi ad salutem perducuntur, gratia adplicationis 1) singularis quaedam data est ministris veri diuini, quatenus sunt ministri, Eph. III, 8. 1 Corinth. XV, 10. 2 Cor. III, 4. 5. 6. ideoque dicuntur dona administrantia, quorum alia quidem sunt extraordinaria ac temporaria, primis Euangelii nuntiis tributa, cuiusmodi sunt: instinctus adflatusque diuinus, Matth. X, 19. 20. & potestas miracula faciendi, Marc. XVI, 20. Hebr. II, 4: alia autem ordinaria ac perpetua, omnibus ad finem vsque mundi tribuenda, & ad sacrum ecclesiam, Christo aut collectam, aut colligendam, Eph. V, 26. 27. Tit. III, 5. 6. 7. Huius gratia dona nominantur sanctificantia. (Dicta generalia, quorum in sententia continentur omnia dona gratiae tum sanctificantia, tum administrantia, atque haec partim ordinaria, partim extraordinaria, sunt haec duo, Marc. XVI, 15-20. Eph. IV, 11. 12. 13.). Quod ad diuersos actus diuinos attinet, gratia adplicationis est α) vocans, media salutis cuique offerendo, Rom. X, 16-21. 1 Tim. II, 4. Matth. XXII, 3. 4: β) praeuniens; excitans, praeparans, primos animi motus sanctos efficiendo, sanctam animi attentionem excitando, impedimenta, quae mentis mutationi obstant, remouendo, Act. II, 37. XVI, 14. Apoc. III, 19. 20: γ) illuminans, conuertens ac denuo generans, Tit. III, 5: δ) iustificans, Rom. III, 24: ε) renouans, Eph. II, 10. Hebr. XII, 28. XIII, 21: ζ) confirmans & conseruans, Phil. I, 6. 1 Petr. V, 10: η) perficiens, vt ad consummatam aeternamque salutem perueniamus, 1 Cor. I, 4-8.

XII, 12. Spiritus sapientiae & revelationis, Eph. I, 17. Spiritus fidei, 2 Cor. IV, 13. Spiritus adoptionis, Rom. VIII, 15. Spiritus gloriae, 1 Petr. IV, 14. Spiritus promissionis, quo credentes obsignati sunt, & arrhabo hereditatis nostrae, Eph. I, 14. 2) Quia actus gratiae, (vocatio, illuminatio &c.) Spiritui S. appropriati se competunt.

Obs. III. Omnium illorum actuum divinorum & supernaturalium, quibus bona, merito Christi parta, dispensantur, principium est gratia Spiritus S., quippe a qua proficiscuntur.


### Quaest. II. What kind of grace is that applying grace of the Holy Spirit?

The applying grace of the Holy Spirit is a) active, b) medicinal, c) unowed and gratuitous, d) ordered and mediate, e) universal, f) sufficient and efficacious, but g) resistible.

Prob. a. Applying grace is active, since the Holy Spirit through it actively calls, illuminates, converts, and regenerates men. It is therefore distinguished from passive grace, i. e., from the χαρίσμασι [gifts]; or from divine gifts conferred out of grace, which, by metonymy of the effect for the cause, are called passive grace; concerning which Paul says in Eph. IV, 17: To each one of us grace is given according to the measure of the gift of Christ. Prob. b.

This grace is medicinal; because it is occupied not with preserving a whole man in a happy state, but with healing a sick man, or one corrupted by the leprosy of sin, and transferring him from a state of misery into a state of grace and glory.

Prob. c. Applying grace is unowed on the part of God; because God is bound by no law to confer grace. God is no one's debtor, that He should be bound to give anything to him, Rom. XI, 35. God is not constrained by an obedient creature: and much less by a disobedient one. This grace is entirely gratuitous on our part.

For although it is reconciled to us by the merits of Christ; yet it does not depend on our disposition, dignity, merit, or ἱκανότητι [sufficiency], which itself also is from God, 2 Cor. III, 5. For just as fiefs are not conferred upon those running or fighting bravely, because of the race or because of the battle; so the benefits of divine grace are not dispensed because of our merits. If it is by works, it is no longer grace, says Paul in Rom. XI, 6. Prob. d.

Prob. d. Applying grace is ordered; for the reason that the Holy Spirit works through distinct acts and degrees, succeeding one another in order, so that the second degree of grace follows the first degree lost by sinful man, the third follows this, and so on: conversely, if the first degree of applying grace is neglected or despised, the second degree does not follow, and if the second degree is rejected, the third does not follow; clearly as on a ladder one does not ascend to the highest rung except through the intermediate rungs. Hence, he who does not admit the calling grace does not receive the illuminating grace, and he who despises this does not become a participant in the converting grace; because divine grace does not pour out all its powers or riches at once and simultaneously, nor does it make a holy man out of a most wicked one in a single moment. This grace is mediate; for the reason that the Holy Spirit calls, illuminates, converts, etc., men through the divine word and the sacraments, as the ordinary means of salvation.

Applying grace is universal: Because it is destined by divine intention for all and singular men, not even one excepted, after they have fallen into sin and have been redeemed by Christ. God is, of Himself and by the whole intent of His mind, inclined to call, convert, regenerate, justify, sanctify, and save all and every one. For the saving grace of God has appeared to all men, instructing us, Tit. II, 11. 12. And the Holy Spirit offers faith to all, Act. XVII, 31.

Prob. f. The applying grace is sufficient: Because it is proportionate or adequate to producing its effect, even if it does not achieve the desired outcome. The most benevolent God himself shows this. Is. V. 4. What more was there to be done for my vineyard, that I have not done in it? Why then did I expect it to yield grapes? But it yielded wild grapes. If God did everything he ought to have done so that the Israelite vineyard might be fruitful, and yet it did not bear clusters, but wild grapes; it follows that sufficient grace is given, even with respect to the wicked, however much the desired outcome does not follow. The same sufficient grace is in itself and by its nature efficacious. For Christ said to Paul: My grace is sufficient for you: For my power is made perfect in weakness: Where its power or efficacy is attributed to sufficient grace. Obs. Some theologians admit the distinction of grace into sufficient and efficacious, others reject it. Every grace is efficacious on the part of God offering; the one to whom it is offered introduces the difference, so that while sufficient grace is offered to all, it becomes efficacious in him who embraces it by faith; and thus it is called efficacious by reason of converted men, and sufficient by reason of the unconverted. Confer, D. MEISNER. anthropol. decad. II. p. m. 24. D. BROCHMAND. system. part. I. p. 555. D. DANNHAV. hodof. phænom. IX. p. 856. HULSEMAN rejects this distinction in breuiar. cap. IX. p. 950: Because all divine grace is efficaciously sufficient, and sufficiently efficacious in its order and economy: but from an extrinsic defect of impediment, it is wrongly inferred that there is a defect of intrinsic efficacy (*).

Prob.

(*) So it is: For 1) efficacy must be adequately distinguished from effect, and also from outcome. And one must diligently take care that these three are not confused with one another. Efficacy resides in the very nature of a thing, insofar as it is destined and apt for a certain end, or several. The effect is the attainment of that end, insofar as that thing, always efficacious in itself, has been rightly used. The outcome is something else entirely, alien to the proposed end, indeed altogether contrary to it, through the intervention of other things, or the fault of man, who uses a good thing badly. And so it can happen, and often does, that a certain thing, in itself most fruitful, is accidentally pernicious. See Rom. VII, 10. 2) Great caution must be used, because of the more recent controversies of the Jansenists and others, in whose opinion God exhibits grace to most men only as sufficient, and to a few elect as efficacious. But first, they are mistaken in that they separate sufficient grace from efficacious, assigning one or the other to different men. Then, great ambiguity lies in the words. They interpret sufficient grace either in such a way that it is indeed sufficient for God, for his purpose, but not for men, for salvation; or in such a way that it is indeed sufficient for men, but not in the same way for all, being rejected only as a testimony that such great grace happened to them as God had decreed to give (in this sense they distort sayings of this kind, Matth. X, 18. XXIV, 14. Mark VI, 11.): for the elect alone as a remedy, so that, freed from their misery, they may become participants in salvation. They understand efficacious grace as that which, by some singular power, drives and compels the minds of elect men so that they cannot but obey the divine will. Finally, they do not observe accuracy of speech when they say that efficacious grace is worth more than sufficient. In which they err vehemently. For 1) that which is for salvation is the same as sufficient, 2 Cor. XII, 9: 2) If any difference is to be established, that which is called efficacious will always be less than that which is called sufficient. This I will confirm with three arguments: α) Efficacious is each one of those things which we need to obtain an end: sufficient is the comprehension and coupling of all things necessary for the end, with respect both to the whole end (for thus four acts of grace are required for the eternal salvation of man, of which if one were lacking, the others would not be sufficient, but all together are sufficient, namely new generation, justification, renovation, and finally perfect liberation and freedom from all trouble, 1 Cor. I, 30.) and to the whole man, and all the faculties of the mind, 1 Thessal. V, 23. (thus arguments explaining and proving, which both pertain to the intellect, and moving arguments, which pertain to the will, are indeed each efficacious, but separated they are not sufficient). β) Efficacious is that which is able to begin a thing, or even to continue it: sufficient is that which can complete a thing entirely, so that nothing more can be desired. Prevenient, exciting, preparing, illuminating, converting, justifying, renewing grace is Prob. g. That the applying grace can be resisted, Stephen asserts in most clear words, gravely addressing the Jews: You stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit, Acts 7:51 (*).

Latin:

Gratia Spiritus S. applicatrix est a) activa, b) medicinalis, c) indebita & gratuita, d) ordinata & mediata, e) universalis, f) sufficiens & efficax, sed g) resistibilis.

Prob. a. Gratia applicatrix est activa, cum Spiritus S. per eam homines active vocet, illuminet, convertat, regeneret. Distinguitur itaque a gratia passiva, i. e. a χαρίσμασι; sive a donis divinis ex gratia collatis, quae, per metonymiam effecti pro causa, vocantur gratia passiva; de qua Paullus Eph. IV, 17. Unicuique nostrum data est gratia iuxta mensuram donationis Christi.

Prob. b. Est haec gratia medicinalis; quia occupatur non circa hominem integrum in statu felici conferuandum, sed circa hominem aegrum, vel lepra peccati corruptum, sanandum, & e statu miseriae in statum gratiae & gloriae transferendum.

Prob. c. Gratia applicatrix est indebita ex parte Dei; quia Deus nullo iure ad conferendam gratiam tenetur. Deus nullius est debitor, ut teneatur ipsi aliquid dare, Rom. XI, 35. Non obstrictus est Deus creaturae morigerae: E, multo minus immorigerae.

Est haec gratia plane gratuita, ex parte nostri. Quamuis enim nobis conciliata sit meritis Christi; non tamen dependet e nostra dispositione, dignitate, merito aut ἱκανότητι, quae ipsa quoque ex Deo est, 2 Cor. III, 5. Neque enim vt feuda currentibus, aut fortiter militantibus conferuntur, ob cursum, aut propter pugnam; ita beneficia gratiae divinae ob merita nostra dispensantur. Si ex operibus, non amplius est gratia, ait Paullus Rom. XI, 6.

Prob. d. Gratia applicatrix est ordinata; propterea, quod Spiritus S. per distinctos actus & gradus, sibi ordine succedentes, operatur, ut amissum ab homine peccatore primum gratiae gradum sequatur secundus, hunc tertius, & sic porro: contra, neglecto vel contempto primo gratiae applicatricis gradu non sequatur gradus secundus, reiecto gradu secundo non sequatur tertius; plane vt in scala ad summum gradum non ascenditur, nisi per gradus interiacentes. Hinc qui non admittit gratiam vocantem, non accipit gratiam illuminantem, & qui hanc contemnit, non fit particeps gratiae convertentis; quia simul & semel omnes suas vires aut divitias non profundit gratia divina, nec vno momento ex homine sceleratissimo sanctum efficit. Est haec gratia mediata; ideo, quod Spiritus S. per verbum divinum & sacramenta, tanquam ordinaria salutis media, homines vocat, illuminat, convertit &c.

Prob. e. Gratia applicatrix est universalis: Quia omnibus & singulis hominibus, ne vno quidem excepto, postquam in peccatum prolapsi & a Christo redemti sunt, ex intentione divina destinata est. Deus ex se & tota animi sui sententia propensus est, omnes singulosque vocare, convertere, regenerare, iustificare, sanctificare, saluare. Apparuit enim gratia Dei salutaris omnibus hominibus, erudiens nos, Tit. II, 11. 12. & Spiritus S. omnibus fidem offert, Act. XVII, 31.

Prob. f. Gratia applicatrix est sufficiens: Quia effectui suo producendo proportionata, vel adæquata est, licet optatum euentum non fortiatur. Ostendit id ipsum Deus benignissimus. El. V. 4. Quid faciendum amplius fuit vineæ meæ, quod non fecerim in illa? Quare vero expectavi, ut faceret vuas? Fecit vero illa labruscas. Si Deus omnia fecit, quæ debuit facere, vt ferax esset vinea Israëlítica, nec tamen illa tulit botros, sed labruscas; sequitur, dari gratiam sufficientem, etiam reſpectu improborum, vtut desideratus non sequatur euentus. Eadem gratia sufficiens in se & natura sua est efficax. Dixit enim Christus ad Paulum: Sufficiat tibi gratia mea: Nam virtus mea in infirmitate perficitur: Vbi gratiæ sufficienti sua virtus, vel efficacia tribuitur. Obs. Alii Theologi admittunt distinctionem gratiæ in sufficientem, & efficacem, alii eam reiiciunt. Efficax est omnis gratia, ex parte Dei offerentis; cui offertur, inducit differentiam, vt cum sufficiens omnibus sit oblata, efficax facta sit in eo, qui fide amplectitur; adeoque efficax dicitur ratione hominum conuersorum, sufficiens ratione non conuersorum. Confer, D. MEISNER. anthropol. decad. II. p. m. 24. D. BROCHMAND. sustem. part. I. p. 555. D. DANNHAV. hodof. phænom. IX. p. 856. Reiicit hanc distinctionem HULSEMAN. in breuiar. cap. IX. p. 950: Quia omnis gratia diuina est efficaciter sufficiens, & sufficienter efficax in ordine & œconomia sua: ab impedimento autem defectus extrinseco ad defectum intrinsecæ efficaciæ male colligitur (*).

Prob.

(*) Ita est: Nam 1) efficacitas adæquate distinguenda est ab effectu, atque etiam ab euentu. Et diligenter cauendum est, ne hæc tria inter se confundantur. Efficacitas in ipsa rei natura inest, quatenus ea est ad certum quemdam finem, aut plures, destinata atque apta. Effectus est illius finis consequutio, quatenus ea res, semper per se efficax, recte vfurpata est. Euentus est plane aliud quidquam, a fine proposito alienum, immo prorsus illi contrarium, interuentu aliarum rerum, aut vitio hominis, qui re bona male vtitur. Itaque fieri potest, ac sæpe solet, vt res quædam, per se maxime fructuosa, per accidens sit perniciosa. Vid. Rom. VII, 10. 2) Magna cautio adhibenda est, propter recentiores controuersias Iansenistarum, aliorumque, quorum opinione Deus plerisque hominibus non, nisi sufficientem exhibet gratiam, paucis electis efficacem. Sed primum in eo falluntur, quod gratiam sufficientem ab efficaci disiungunt, alterutram aliis atque aliis hominibus adsignantes. Deinde magna latet in vocibus ambiguitas. Sufficientem gratiam vel ita interpretantur, vt ea sit Deo quidem sufficiens, ad suum propositum, non item hominibus, ad salutem; vel ita, vt hominibus quidem sufficiat, nec vero omnibus eadem ratione, reiectis dumtaxat ad testimonium, quod illis tanta contigerit gratia, quantam Deus dare decreuerit (in hunc sensum detorquent dicta huiusmodi, Matth. X, 18. XXIV, 14. Marc. VI, 11.): electis solis ad remedium, vt sua miseria liberati salutis fiant participes. Efficacem gratiam intelligunt eam, quæ singulari vi quadam adigat & compellat electorum hominum animos, vt voluntati diuinæ non possint non obsequi. Denique adcurationem sermonis non obseruant, cum dicunt, efficacem gratiam plus valere, quam sufficientem. In quo vehementer errant. Etenim 1) quæ ad salutem est, eadem est sufficiens, 2 Cor. XII, 9: 2) Si qua statuenda sit differentia, semper illud, quod efficax vocatur, minus erit, quam id, quod sufficiens dicitur. Id quod tribus confirmabo argumentis: α) Efficax est vnum quodque eorum, quibus ad obtinendum finem indigemus: sufficiens est comprehensio copulatioque omnium, ad finem necessarium, ratione tum totius finis (ita enim ad æternam hominis salutem requiruntur quatuor actus gratiæ, quorum si vnus deesset, reliqui non essent sufficientes, vniuersi autem sufficiunt, scilicet noua generatio, iustificatio, renouatio, tandem perfecta liberatio vacuitasque omnis molestiæ, 1 Cor. I, 30.) tum totius hominis, omniumque animi facultatum, 1 Thessal. V, 23. (sic argumenta explicantia, ac probantia, quæ vtraque ad intellectum spectant, & argumenta mouentia, quæ ad voluntatem pertinent, singula quidem efficacia sunt, separata autem non sunt sufficientia). β) Efficax est, quod valet rem inchoare, siue etiam continuare: sufficiens est, quod potest rem omnino perficere, nihil vt desiderari possit amplius. Gratia præueniens, excitans, præparans, illuminans, conuertens, iustificans, renouans, est Prob. g. Gratiae applicatrici resisti posse, apertissimis verbis asserit Stephanus Iudaeos graviter alloquens: Durae cervicis homines, & incircumcisi corde & auribus, vos perpetuo Spiritui S. resistitis, Act. VII, 51 (*).


### Question III. In what order do the acts of applying grace cohere, and follow one another?

The acts of applying grace are: I. Calling of the sinner to the church: II. Illumination: III. Conversion: IV. Regeneration: V. Justification: VI. Mystical union with the triune God: VII. Renewal: VIII. Preservation of faith and holiness: IX. Glorification.

Prob. We learn this order, and the as it were concatenated series of the acts of applying grace, from Acts 26:17, where Christ addresses Paul: I send you to the Gentiles, behold the grace of vocation! that you may open their eyes, behold illumination! and they may be converted from darkness to light, behold the act of conversion! and from the power of Satan to God, behold regeneration itself, through which we become children of God! that they may receive remission of sins, behold justification! and a lot among those who have been sanctified by faith in me, behold union with Christ through faith, sanctification, preservation of holiness, and glorification!

Latin:

Actus gratiæ applicatricis sunt: I. Vocatio peccatoris ad ecclesiam: II. Illuminatio: III. Conversio: IV. Regeneratio: V. Iustificatio: VI. Unio mystica cum Deo trino: VII. Renovatio: VIII. Conservatio fidei & sanctitatis: IX. Glorificatio.

Prob. Hunc ordinem, & quasi concatenatam seriem actuum gratiæ applicatricis discimus ex Act. XXVI, 17. ubi Christus Paullum compellat: In gentes te mitto, en gratiam vocationis! ut aperias oculos eorum, en illuminationem! & convertantur a tenebris ad lucem, en actum conversionis! & a potestate satanæ ad Deum, en ipsam regenerationem, per quam Filii Dei evadimus! ut accipiant remissionem peccatorum, en iustificationem! & sortem inter eos, qui sanctificati sunt per fidem in me, en unionem cum Christo per fidem, sanctificationem, sanctitatis conservationem & glorificationem!


### Question IV. Is there another distinction of the acts of applying grace?

The applying grace of the Holy Spirit is commonly distinguished into grace that is prevenient, preparing, operating, cooperating, and preserving a). Also into grace that is assisting, and indwelling b).

Prob. a. Prevenient grace is an act of grace by which the Holy Spirit offers to man, dead in sins, the salutary object, the benevolence of God the Father and the merit of Christ through the word of God preached or read, removes natural incapacity, and invites, excites, impels, and knocks for him to perform repentance.

Preparing grace is an act of grace by which the Holy Spirit restrains natural and actual resistance, simple and vincible, imbues the mind with the literal knowledge of the gospel, and crushes the will through the word of the law, so that it may be more and more disposed to receive saving faith. Operating grace, specifically so called, is an act of grace by which the Holy Spirit both confers the powers of believing and kindles justifying faith. To this pertain regeneration, justification, and mystical union. Cooperating grace is an act of grace by which the Holy Spirit [is] indeed effective: but not yet sufficient.

For it is necessary that there be added grace that is corroborating, preserving, and finally delivering us from every evil. γ) Effective is the medium by which, when rightly applied, we attain the end.

Sufficient is the instruction of the mode and order to be observed, by which we ought conveniently to use that medium.

The Gospel is the only effective medium for saving trust, and thus for salvation itself.

But the order of salvation demands a necessary and perpetual conjunction of the law with the gospel. See Declar. Form. Conc. ch. V. p. 713. E. Grace, although most effective, yet would not be sufficient, unless it led us by the use of the law, both elenchtic-pedagogical and didactic, so that we might eagerly embrace the salvation announced to us in the Gospel, and venerate the received grace with a grateful mind. (*)

This must be strictly held against the Reformed and the Jansenists, but also explained, since it seems to be stated ambiguously. Namely, to resist is either to oppose with forces, if not equal, certainly possessing some strength (but who can possess even the least bit against God? although the θεομάχοι [God-fighters] attempt this with rash audacity, yet with vain effort, and in the end with vain anger, Acts 5:39, Rom. 9:19); or to reject a benefit offered, and to be unwilling to obey the prescribed order, just as a perfidious man, although most weak, who does not wish to obey the King and do what is requested, or who repudiates the King's grace, is said to resist him. Which is, ἀντιτάσσεσθαι [to set oneself against], Acts 18:6, ἐχ ὑποτάσσεσθαι τῷ θεῷ [not to be subject to God], Rom. 8:7, 10:3. And that, ἀντιπίπτειν [to fall against/resist], Acts 7:51, what it is, you will be able to know from v. 57: to stop up the ears, to be unwilling to perceive the truth.

For by no arguments, which are moral forces, could they restrain the force of the truth, Acts 6:10.

Sufficient grace they interpret either in such a way that it becomes sufficient indeed for God, for His purpose, but not likewise for men, for salvation; or in such a way that it is sufficient indeed for men, yet not all in the same manner, with the reprobate excepted only for a testimony, that so great grace has befallen them as God decreed to give (they twist sayings of this kind into this sense, Matt. 10:18. 24:14. Mark 6:11); to the elect alone as a remedy, by which, delivered from their misery, they may become partakers of salvation.

Effective grace they understand to be that which drives and compels the souls of the elect with a certain singular force, so that they cannot fail to obey the divine will.

Finally, they do not observe the refinement of speech, when they say that effective grace is stronger than sufficient grace.

In which they greatly err.

For indeed 1) the grace that is effective for salvation is the same as that which is sufficient, 2 Cor. XII, 9: 2) If any difference is to be established, that which is called effective will always be less than that which is said to be sufficient.

That which I will confirm with three arguments: a) Effective is each one of those things by which we have need for obtaining the end: sufficient is the comprehension and conjunction of all things necessary to the end, both on account of the whole of the end (for four acts of grace are required for the eternal salvation of man, and if one were lacking, the rest would not be sufficient, but all together suffice, namely new generation, justification, renewal, finally perfect deliverance and freedom from every trouble, 1 Cor. 1:30), and on account of the whole man, and of all the faculties of the soul, 1 Thess. 5:23, 2 Cor. 7:1 (thus explicating and proving arguments, which both pertain to the intellect, and moving arguments, which pertain to the will, are indeed each effective, but separated they are not sufficient). β) Effective is that which is able to begin a thing, or even to continue it: sufficient is that which can bring the thing entirely to completion, so that nothing more could be desired.

Prevenient, exciting, preparing, illuminating, converting, justifying, renewing grace is with the justified man concurs for his sanctification and the production of good works. To this pertains renewal. Preserving grace is an act of grace, by which faith and the holiness of life are preserved and confirmed; its effect is the perseverance of the faithful.

Concerning this distinction, compare CHEMNITIUS in the locus on free will, fol. 192. D. BREITHAUPT in his Institutio, p. 235, and in his Theses credendorum, p. 129. Prob. b.

Assisting grace is an act of grace, by which the Holy Spirit acts externally around the man to be converted, not only by proposing and showing the salvific object, what ought to be done; but also by touching, knocking, exciting, and disposing the heart of the sinner, so that he may be able to receive faith, and by means of faith, the Holy Spirit may be able to inhabit him. To this assisting grace pertains preventing and preparing grace.

Inhabiting grace (taken in a general sense, by which it embraces regenerating, justifying, and inhabiting grace, taken in a more special sense) is an act of grace, by which the Holy Spirit enters the heart of man, and dwells and works in it, both by conferring the powers of believing, and by kindling, confirming, and increasing salvific faith. Compare D. JOHANN ADAM OSIANDER, Theologia systematica positiva, part III, p. 18, and D. QUENSTEDT, Systema, part III, fol. 494.

The foundation of the distinction into assisting and inhabiting grace is found in Apoc. 3:20, where Christ addresses the bishop of Laodicea: Behold! I stand at the door, and knock: If any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me.

Indicated by these words is a) generally assisting grace; because Christ says that he stands at the door, namely, of the human heart, to convert it: he does not, however, stand idle, but knocks and desires to be let in; he knocks, so that his voice may be heard, which is b) preventing and exciting grace, and indeed he knocks in such a way that the door may be opened, which is c) preparing grace: for, men of unregenerate heart do not open the door by the natural powers of free will, but by new powers conferred through preventing and preparing grace: just as those resurrected from natural death rise again not by their own powers, but by new powers given in the resurrection.

By knocking, therefore, Christ grants the power of opening, which efficacy is proper to the word of the Gospel, Rom. 1:16; but when the door of the heart is opened, Christ enters, which is d) entering and inhabiting grace: for thus Christ enters, that he may sup with us and we with him; Christ enters, by kindling faith through the light of his word and by dwelling in us through faith, Eph. 3:17. Whence arises our most sweet communion with Christ, which is a foretaste of eternal life.

From this saying of the Savior, the grace of the Holy Spirit as the applicator can be distinguished by trichotomy into assisting grace, which works externally around the closed heart of the sinner, and labors to open it: entering grace, which enters the opened domicile of the heart: and inhabiting grace, which dwells in the heart with gracious and efficacious presence. Quaest. V. Are the three ways of the mystics arranged in the right order? The antithesis is that of the mystic authors, who teach with great consensus that a man called to the church can proceed expeditiously to the holy mountain of perfection and deification by THREE WAYS: purgative, illuminative, and unitive.

This is not denied by MAXIMILIANUS SANDEUS, in his Clavis theologiae mysticae, p. 360. Almost all masters of spiritual things are accustomed to circumscribe mystical theology by three ways: purgative, illuminative, and unitive. About to expound this triple way, HUGO DE PALMA, in his Theologia mystica, p. 5, says: The first, the purgative way, is that by which the mind is disposed to learn true wisdom: The second is called the illuminative, by which the mind is kindled to the inflammation of love by thinking: The third, however, is the unitive, by which the mind is directed upward by God alone above all intellect, reason, and intelligence. In these three ways consists the whole of mystical theology.

THOMAS A JESU explains these three ways more clearly, in his book.

The three ways of the mystics are not arranged in a just order a): nor do men, walking in them, certainly reach the end defined by the mystics b). Book 1, Method of Divine Prayer, 1. The purgative way is to purge and perfect the senses; the illuminative, the reason; the unitive, the spirit, or mind, which is the higher part of the soul.

In the purgative, man knows himself; in the illuminative, God; in the unitive, he strives for union and transformation into Him.

Of all , GOTTFRIED unfolds the same ways most clearly and most extensively.

ARNOLDVS in Theol. Myst. ch. VI, p. 103, and following, from which we may be permitted to excerpt a few things pertinent to the matter.

Firstly, God cleanses the senses and the lowest part of the soul, which is as it were its entrance, afterwards the reason, then the understanding and will, and thus God regains dominion over the whole man, as He makes these parts pure and clear.

Finally, He also frees the desires and anger, through deep contrition and humiliation.

And from all this we make such a description: The way of purification is that by which the mind is made fit to learn true wisdom; or it is such an exercise and effort of the mind, by which one arrives at the expulsion of vices, the taming of the affects, or movements of the mind, the renewal of all properties of the soul, the preservation of the heart and the senses, and the avoidance of all debts.

For illumination, the ancients require primarily humility, that one should despair of one's own powers, natural understanding, and self-sought knowledge, and instead hope solely in God and base oneself on His assistance.

Furthermore, that one should withdraw one's mind from external things, and by abandoning all distraction and dissipation, gather it; then, that one should turn oneself toward the divine ray, wish for and ask for illumination from above, and turn oneself with all one's strength toward the contemplation and beholding of God.

Thereupon the Lord of all wisdom will help, and make the heart bright through the gift of His wisdom, and fill it with His radiance.

Therefore, illumination is described as being an occupation of the mind in the contemplation of the wonders of God, especially of the most blessed Trinity, and the most simple, most beautiful Godhead: afterwards in the consideration of the heavenly and supernatural goods of the truth of the Christian faith, and of all spiritual things.

The union is an act which is directed toward the fervor of the purest love, toward the ravishing and flaming falling-in-love with the Godhead, and toward the most fiery, quiet, and secret beholding of the hidden wisdom, likewise that the mind is thereby actually drawn on high by God alone above all understanding and sense, or unites itself with His highest Good through love and contemplation.

And this is precisely the main point and work, the sum and purpose of the secret doctrine of God, for which the previous two stages must serve and promote as preparations, namely, that a Christian man may become a God.

Otherwise it is also called: to be transformed into God, to be deified.

For God shares His essence with a Christian supernaturally, so that he seems to be God himself, and has what God has, himself as well.

And when God shows the soul the highest favor, such a union occurs between them that everything that is God's, and that which is the soul's, is one in a communal union, and the soul then seems to be more God than soul; indeed, it is God through communion, although it is true that it retains its natural essence as distinct from the Divine as before, yet it is transformed into God: just as a glass retains its distinct essence from the ray of the sun by which it has been illuminated, writes IOAN. a CRVCE, Op.

Myst. B. II, ch. V, page 38.

Thus far ARNOLDVS, l. c., p. 150.

Latin:

Distinguitur communiter gratia spiritus S. applicatrix in gratiam prævenientem, præparantem, operantem, cooperantem, & conferuantem a). Item in gratiam assistentem, & inhabitantem b).

Prob. a. Gratia præveniens est actus gratiæ, quo Spiritus S. homini, in peccatis mortuo, obiectum salutificum, benevolentiam Dei Patris & meritum Christi per verbum Dei prædicatum aut lectum offert, incapacitatem naturalem aufert, & eundem ad agendum pœnitentiam invitat, excitat, impellit, pulsat.

Gratia præparans est actus gratiæ, quo Spiritus S. resistentiam naturalem & actualem, simplicem & vincibilem cohibet, mentem notitia evangelii litterali imbuit, & voluntatem per verbum legis conterit, ut ad fidem salutificam suscipiendam magis magisque disponatur. Gratia operans specialiter dicta est actus gratiæ, quo Spiritus S. tum vires credendi confert, tum fidem iustificam accendit. Huc pertinent regeneratio, iustificatio & unio mystica. Gratia cooperans est actus gratiæ, quo Spiritus S. cum profecto efficax: at nondum sufficiens.

Necesse est enim, ut accedat gratia corroborans, conservans, omnique tandem malo nos liberans. γ) Efficax est medium, quo recte adhibito finem consequimur.

Sufficiens est præceptio modi atque ordinis observandi, cui convenienter medio illo uti debeamus.

Evangelium est unicum medium efficax ad fiduciam salutarem, ipsamque adeo salutem.

Sed ordo salutis postulat necessariam perpetuamque legis cum evangelio conjunctionem. Vid. Declar. Form. Conc. cap. V. pag. 713. E. gratia, quamvis maxime efficax, tamen non esset sufficiens, nisi ea per usum legis, & elenchtico-pædagogicum, & didacticum, nos eo duceret, vt salutem, in Evangelio nobis nuntiatam, & avide amplectamur, & acceptam grato animo veneremur. (*)

Id contra Reformatos, & Iansenistas arcte tenendum est, sed & explicandum, quum videatur ambigue dictum esse. Scilicet resistere, est, aut repugnare viribus, si non æquis, certe aliquid valentibus (ecquis autem vel minimum quidquam valeat adversus Deum? quamvis temeraria audacia id moliantur θεομάχοι, irrito tamen conatu, & vana fine viribus ira, Act. V, 39. Rom. IX, 19.); aut reiicere beneficium oblatum, ac præscripto ordini nolle obtemperare, sicut perfidus homo, tametsi maxime imbecillis, qui Regi non vult parere & impetrata facere, vel qui gratiam Regis repudiat, resistere illi dicitur. Id quod est, ἀντιτάσσεσθαι, Act. XVIII, 6. ἐχ ὑποτάσσεσθαι τῷ θεῷ, Rom. VIII, 7. X, 3. Et illud, ἀντιπίπτειν, Act. VII, 51. quid sit, cognoscere poteris ex v. 57: obturare aures, nolle veritatem percipere. Nullis enim argumentis, quæ sunt vires morales, vim veritatis cohibere poterant, Act. VI, 10.

Deinde magna latet in vocibus ambiguitas.

Sufficientem gratiam vel ita interpretantur, vt ea fit Deo quidem sufficiens, ad suum propositum, non item hominibus, ad salutem; vel ita, vt hominibus quidem sufficiat, nec vero omnibus eadem ratione, reiectis dumtaxat ad testimonium, quod illis tanta contigerit gratia, quantam Deus dare decreuerit (in hunc sensum detorquent dicta huiusmodi, Matth. X, 18. XXIV, 14. Marc. VI, 11.); electis solis ad remedium, quo sua miseria liberati salutis fiant participes.

Efficacem gratiam intelligunt eam, quae singulari vi quadam adigat & compellat electorum hominum animos, vt voluntati diuinae non possint non obsequi.

Denique adcurationem sermonis non obseruant, cum dicunt, efficacem gratiam plus valere, quam sufficientem.

In quo vehementer errant.

Etenim 1) quae ad salutem efficax est gratia, eadem est sufficiens, 2 Cor. XII, 9: 2) Si qua statuenda sit differentia, semper illud, quod efficax vocatur, minus erit, quam id, quod sufficiens dicitur.

Id quod tribus confirmabo argumentis: a) Efficax est unum quodque eorum, quibus ad obtinendum finem indigemus: sufficiens est comprehensio copulatioque omnium, ad finem necessariorum, ratione tum-totius finis (ita enim ad aeternam hominis salutem requiruntur quattuor actus gratiae, quorum si vnus deesset, reliqui non essent sufficientes, vniuersi autem sufficiunt, scilicet noua generatio, iustificatio, renuatio, tandem perfecta liberatio vacuitasque omnis molestiae, 1 Cor. I, 30.) tum totius hominis, omniumque animi facultatum, 1 Thessal. V, 23. 2 Cor. VII, 1. (sic argumenta explicantia, ac probantia, quae vtraque ad intellectum spectant, & argumenta mouentia, quae ad voluntatem pertinent, singula quidem efficacia sunt, separata autem non sunt sufficientia). β) Efficax est, quod valet rem inchoare, siue etiam continuare: sufficiens est, quod potest rem omnino perficere, nihil vt desiderari possit amplius.

Gratia praueniens, excitans, praeparans, illuinans, conuertens, iustificans, renouans, est cum homine iustificato concurrit ad ipsius sanctificationem & productionem bonorum operum. Ad hanc pertinet renouatio. Gratia conseruans est actus gratiae, quo fides & vitae sanctitas conseruatur & confirmatur; cuius effectus est perseuerantia fidelium.

De hac distinctione conf. CHEMNITIVM in loc. de lib. arbitr. fol. 192. D. BREITHAVPT. in institut. p. 235. & in thes. cred. p. 129. Prob. b.

Gratia assistens est actus gratiae, quo Spiritus S. externe circa hominem conuertendum agit, non tantum obiectum saluificum proponendo & ostendendo, quid fieri debeat; sed & cor peccatoris tangendo, pulsando, excitando & disponendo, vt fidem suscipere, & mediante fide Spiritus S. ipsum inhabitare queat. Ad hanc gratiam assistentem pertinet gratia praeueniens, & praeparans.

Gratia inhabitans (accepta sensu generali, qua gratiam regenerantem, iustificantem & inhabitantem, sensu specialiorem sumtam, complectitur) est actus gratiae, quo Spiritus S. cor hominis ingreditur, & in illo habitat atque operatur, tum vires credendi conferendo, tum fidem saluificam accendendo, confirmando & augendo. Conf. D. IOANN. ADAMI OSIANDRI theol. system. positiua, part. III. p. 18. & D. QVENSTED. syst. part. III. fol. 494.

Fundamentum distinctionis in gratiam assistentem, & inhabitantem habetur Apoc. III, 20. vbi Christus episcopum Laodicenum alloquitur: Ecce! Sto ad ostium, & pulso: Si quis audiuerit vocem meam, & aperuerit ianuam, ingrediar ad ipsum & coenabo cum ipso, atque ipse mecum. Indicatur his verbis a) generatim gratia assistens; quia Christus dicit, se stare ad ostium, scil. cordis humani, ad illud conuertendum: non autem stat otiosus, sed pulsat & cupit intromitti; pulsat, vt vox eius audiatur, quae est b) gratia praeueniens & excitans, & quidem ita pulsat, vt ianua aperiatur, quae est c) gratia praeparans: nam, homines irregeniti cordis ostium aperiunt non naturalibus liberi arbitrii viribus, sed nouis per gratiam praeuenientem & praeparantem collatis viribus: sicut resuscitati ex morte naturali non suis, sed nouis, in resuscitatione datis, viribus resurgunt.

Pulsando itaque Christus vim largitur aperiendi, quae efficacia verbo euangelii propria est,

Rom. I, 16.; cum vero ianua cordis aperitur, Christus ingreditur, quae est d) gratia ingrediens & inhabitans: sic enim Christus ingreditur, vt nobiscum coenet & nos cum illo; ingreditur Christus, lumine verbi sui fidem accendendo & per fidem in nobis habitando, Eph. III, 17. Vnde oritur dulcissima nostri cum Christo communio, quae est praegustus vitae aeternae.

Potest ex hoc effato Saluatoris gratia Spiritus S. applicatrix per trichotomiam distingui in gratiam assistentem, quae externe circa cor peccatoris clausum operatur, & illud aperire laborat: ingredientem, quae domicilium cordis apertum intrat: Et inhabitantem, quae praesentia gratiosa & efficaci in corde habitat. Quaest. V. An tres viae mysticorum recto ordine sunt dispositae? Antithesis est mysticorum auctorum, magno consensu docentium, hominem ad ecclesiam vocatum, TRIBVS VIIS, purgatiua, illuminatiua & vnitina, ad sanctum montem perfectionis, atque deificationem posse expedite progredi.

Id quod non diffitetur MAXIMILIANVS SANDEVS, in claue theologiae mysticae p. 360. Omnes fere rerum spiritualium magistri tribus solent theologiam mysticam viis circumscribere, purgatiua, illuminatiua, & vnitina. Triplicem hanc viam expositurus HVGO DE PALMA, in theol mystica p. 5. inquit: Prima via purgatiua est, qua mens ad discendum veram sapientiam disponitur: Secunda dicitur illuminatiua, qua mens cogitando ad amoris inflammationem accenditur: Tertia vero vnitina, qua mens supra omnem intellectum, rationem & intelligentiam, a solo Deo sursum actadiriigitur. In his tribus viis tota consistit theologia mystica.

Clarius has tres vias explicat THOMAS A IESV, libr.

Tres mysticorum viae neque iusto ordine sunt dispositae a): neque homines, iis incedentes, ad terminum, a mysticis praefinitum, certo pertingunt b). libr. 1. Meth. diuin. orat. I. Purgatiua via est, purgare & perficere sensus; illuminatiua, rationem; vnitiva, spiritum, seu mentem, quæ est superior animæ pars.

In purgatiua cognoscit homo seipsum; in illuminatiua, Deum: in vnitiva studet vnioni & transformationi in ipsum.

Omnium clarissime & fusissime easdem vias evoluit GOTTFRIED.

ARNOLDVS in theol. myst. c. VI. p. 103. & sqq. e quo pauca, ad rem facientia, excerpere nobis liceat.

Erstlich reiniget Gott die Sinnen, und den untersten Theil der Seele, welche gleichsam ihr Eingang ist, hernach die Vernunst, dann den Verstand und Willen, und also bekommt Gott die Herrschast über den ganzen Menschen wieder, da er diese Theile rein und klar machet.

Endlich befreyet er auch die Begierden und den Zorn, durch tiefe Zernirschung und Demüthigung.

Und aus diesem allen machen wir eine solche Beschreibung: Der Reinigungs-Weg ist, dadurch das Gemüth die wahre Weisheit zu lernen, geschickt gemacht wird; oder es ist eine solche Uebung und Bemühung des Gemüthes, wodurch man zur Austreibung der laster, zur Bezähmung der Affecten, oder Gemüths-Bewegungen, zur Erneuerung aller Eigenschasten der Seelen, zur Bewahrung des Herzens, und der Sinne, und zur Vermeidung aller Schulden gelanget.

Zu der Erleuchtung erfordern die Alten vornehmlich die Demuth, daß man an seinen eigenen Krästen, natürlichen Verstande, und selbst gesuchten Wissen verzage, hingegen allein auf Gott hoffe, und auf dessen Beystand sich gründe.

Ferner, daß man sein Gemüthe von äusserlichen Dingen abziehe, und durch Verlassung aller Zerstreuung und Ausschweifung selbiges sammle, sodann, daß man sich zu dem göttlichen Strahl einwende, die Erleuchtung von oben wünsche und erbitte, und sich zur Betrachtung und Beschauung Gottes aus allen Krästen kehre.

Darauf werde der Herr aller Weisheit helfen, und das Herz durch die Gabe seiner Weisheit hell machen, und mit seinem Glanz erfüllen.

Darum wird die Erleuchtung beschrieben, daß sie sey eine Beschästigung des Gemüthes in Beschauung der Wunder Gottes, sonderlich der höchstseligsten Dreyheit, und der allereinfältigsten allerschönsten Gottheit: hernach in Betrachtung der himmlischen und übernatürlichen Güter der Wahrheit des Christlichen Glaubens, und aller geistlichen Dinge.

Die Vereinigung ist eine Handlung, welche auf die Brünstigkeit der lautersten Liebe, auf die entzückende und flammende Verliebung in die Gottheit, und auf das feurigste, ruhigste und geheimste Anschauen der verborgenen Weisheit gerichtet ist, ingleichen, daß das Gemüthe dadurch über allen Verstand und Sinn von Gott allein wirklich in die Höhe gezogen werde, oder mit seinem höchsten Gut durch die Liebe und Beschauung sich vereinige.

Und dieses ist eben das Hauptstück und Werk, die Summa und Zweck der geheimen Gottes-Lehre, dazu die vorigen zwo Stufen als Vorbereitungen dienen und fördern müssen, nämlich, daß aus einem Christlichen Menschen ein Gott werde.

Sonsten heißt es auch: in Gott verwandelt, vergöttert werden.

Denn Gott theilet einem Christen sein Wesen übernatürlich mit, daß er selbst Gott zu seyn scheinet, und das, was Gott hat, auch selbst hat.

Und wenn Gott der Seelen die höchste Gunst erweiset, wird eine solche Vereinigung unter ihnen, daß alles, was Gottes ist, und das, was der Seelen ist, in einer gemeinschastlichen Vereinigung eins ist, und die Seele alsdenn mehr Gott, als Seele zu seyn scheinet, ja sie ist Gott durch die Gemeinschast, ob es wohl wahr ist, da sie ihr natürliches Wesen von dem Göttlichen so unterschieden behalte, wie zuvor, daß sie doch in Gott verwandelt ist: wie auch ein Glas sein unterschieden Wesen behält von dem Strahl der Sonnen, von welcher es ist erleuchtet worden, schreibt IOAN. a CRVCE Op.

Myst. L. II. c. V. pag. 38.

Huc usque ARNOLDVS l. c. p. 150.


### Question IV. Is there another distinction of the acts of applying grace?: Exposition

EXPOSITION.

Obs. I.

Since all theology shows and opens the way to heaven, or eternal salvation, it is highly to be noted that the way to salvation either denotes the meritorious cause of eternal salvation; tis, by which reason Christ called himself the life, John 14:6; or it may designate the causal medium of salvation, and that either offering and exhibiting, which is the word of God, and therefore is called the way of truth, Ps. 119:30; or apprehending and receiving, which is faith in Christ, through which we have access to grace, Rom. 5:2; or finally it may denote that which is the intermediate between the term from which and to which, in which sense Bernard in his book on grace and free will calls good works the way of the kingdom, not the cause of reigning. How that formula of speaking can be admitted in that sense, D. Quensted teaches in his System of Theology, IV, ch. 9, p. 330.

Obs. II. The mystical authors, in ordering their three ways, followed in the footsteps of the Pythagorean and Platonic philosophers; for they said that before the soul can arrive at true wisdom, it has need of καθάρσεως, i.e., a certain purgation, by which those filthinesses are washed away from it. But they joined further to this purgation a certain conversion, as it were, of the mind into itself, which they wished to be a second, as it were, approach and entrance. For they thought the mind, conscious of its own powers and liberated from the bonds and filth of the body and of matter, should above all be turned into itself, with other things that are outside being as it were consigned to oblivion, and, as not pertaining to itself, cast out of memory.

Moreover, because a mind that is pure and liberated from evils is not yet perfectly blessed, they added a final office of the mind, which they called ἄνοδον, or ascent. Concerning which Iamblichus says in his Protrepticus: From the first purgation of evils, which were born with us, from our rising, there will be immunity. Then there will be present to us the knowledge of a happy and blessed life, how great that is, and what it will be in the future. With this, ascending, we shall contemplate the prince and the divine race of men, and, strengthened in this, we shall attain the end of the most blessed life proposed by the Gods. Cf. Scheffer, Phil. Ital., ch. 9, p. 74 ff.

The end, however, of Pythagorean and Platonic philosophy is ὁμοίωσις θεῷ, assimilation with God, as Hierocles and Stobaeus teach in Scheffer, l.c., ch. 7, p. 42. Hierocles in his preface to the Golden Verses of Pythagoras adds: it is necessary first to become a man, after God. From which we gather that the mystics, in laying out their three ways, had regard for the tenets of Pythagoras and Plato, and accommodated themselves to them. ΒΕΒΑΙΩΣΙΣ

Prob. a. 1) The mystical authors erred in more than one way in arranging their three ways; because they did not clearly set forth the proximate foundation of the division. If by the way to blessedness, both of grace and of glory, the meritorious cause is understood, there is only one way, viz., Christ, whose golden words are: John 14:6, I am the way, the truth, and the life. But Christ is the way, both by reason of merit, because he reconciled us to God by his death, Rom. 5:10; and by reason of example, since he left us an ὑπογραμμόν, an example, that we should follow his footsteps, 1 Pet. 2:21.

2) If by the way to blessedness is understood the causal medium of salvation, by which offered salvation is received or apprehended; again, one way lies open to eternal blessedness, namely, true and sincere faith in Christ. By this, as if by a ready path, we approach to God, Rom. 11:6. By this we have access to the grace of God through Christ, Rom. 5:2. By this we are justified and saved, Rom. 3:22; Mark 16:16.

3) If by the way to blessedness is designated, specifically and determinately, the medium of salvation divinely ordained for men miserable after the fall, offering and exhibiting [it], again there is one way, viz., the way of truth, Ps. 119:30, i.e., the word of the gospel, which is called with peculiar emphasis the word of truth, James 1:18; Eph. 1:13, because it is not only true in itself, equally as the word of the law, but also truly regenerates, and truly bestows that life of grace and glory which it promises.

4) If, however, the causal means of salvation for all men who lived in the state before the fall and after the fall is to be designated by way of beatitude, generally and indeterminately, there will be two ways, namely, the legal way and the evangelical way, which twofold way I shall explain with the words of DANN HAVERI from his hodos. phænom. VI. p. 462, who says: A twofold way, he says, exists revealed in the scriptures, which leads to the heavens and to beatitude: The one is legal, which is of the divine law, as a perfect norm, sealed by a mutual covenant, obliging the conscience to obedience, or to the inevitable punishment of a just judge, most perfect in its observance, beatifying in itself, but thus impossible for us mortals, and accidentally deadly. The other is evangelical, revealed from heaven, which, through the heart of the heavenly Father, and Christ the brother mediator, the supreme gift of the Father having been made manifest, leads most safely, most excellently, and uniquely to the heavens through the life-giving grace of the Holy Spirit.

5) If, however, the mystical writers wish their three ways to be understood as ways of the divine order according to the acts of the grace of the Holy Spirit as the applier, it is certainly plain that they have perverted the order sanctioned by the Divine Spirit. For indeed, as Holy Scripture testifies, the illuminative way precedes the purgative. Intending to demonstrate this, I assume that τὴν γνῶσιν, or the cognition of the mysteries of faith, which cannot be known by the guidance of the light of nature, is the effect of divine illuminating grace. See 2 Cor. IV, 6. Eph. I, 18. Unfolding therefore the sacred book, a) I discover that the Apostles Paul and John place τὴν γνῶσιν, or the cognition of the intellect, before the purgation of the will in express words. The former indeed, Col. I, 9. 10: We do not cease to pray and ask for you, that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding, that you may walk worthily of the Lord unto all pleasing. The latter, however, 1 Ep. III, 2. 3: Beloved, we are now the sons of God, but it has not yet been manifested what we shall be. We know, however, that when he shall be manifested, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. Therefore also everyone who has this hope in him, purifies himself. b) There is nothing in the will that was not first in the intellect. For the will does not operate without an object. But if the intellect does not propose an object to the will, the latter will not have an object around which it may operate. And therefore it is necessary that, since the will is blind in itself, the intellect should illuminate it, and propose and represent the object. For which reason, in order that the will may be purged of the ἀταξίᾳ of the affections, it is necessary first for the intellect to be illuminated by the Holy Spirit, both for recognizing sin from the divine law, Rom. III, 20. c. VII, 7, and for recognizing Christ the mediator, 2 Cor. IV, 4. c) Illumination precedes faith, Jo. I, 7. as it is that from which knowledge flows, which is the first degree, or act of faith. Therefore it also precedes the purgation of the soul, which is done through faith, Acts XV, 9. d) If the will of man can be purged and sanctified without the prior illumination of the intellect, then surely man will be carried with a blind impulse to love God, whom he has never known; to place trust in Christ, of whom he is ignorant; to overcome the world, without faith shining before: which are ἀτοπώτατα. By what appearance of truth, therefore, do the mystical writers place the purgative way before the illuminative? (*). You say: A richer and fuller illumination of the intellect follows the purgation of the will, once the obstacles have been removed. I reply: Although I do not deny that a richer illumination of the intellect follows the sanctification of the will; yet I also affirm this for certain, that a richer illumination precedes a richer sanctification (**).

6) The way

6) The mystical doctors have not explained the purgative way with sufficient clarity. For by purgation, they understand either purgation from the guilt of sin, that is, justification, or purgation from the dominion of sin, that is, renewal, or both. Justification follows illumination and precedes mystical union: but renewal follows both illumination and mystical union in the order of nature. For a) Christ himself says: As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me, John 15:4. b) Paul, Rom. 8:9, says: Ye are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if so be that the Spirit of God dwell in you. The regenerate are not in the flesh, i.e., in the power and dominion of the flesh, but in the kingdom of the Holy Spirit; because the Holy Spirit is not only a guest, but also the master of his own dwelling, which he inhabits, rules, purges, and adorns. Therefore, the ways of the mystics must be arranged in such a series that the first is illuminative, the second unitive, and the third purgative. But if the mystical writers designate both justification and renewal by the term purgation, they are playing with an unseemly equivocation, which is the foul mother of errors; because they embrace with one word two acts of divine grace that applies itself, of which the one precedes mystical union, and the other follows it. But he teaches poorly who does not distinguish well.

7) The mystical authors, in the arrangement of their ways, have neglected and omitted the conversion of the sinner, strictly so called, by which contrition is excited through the divine law; regeneration, by which faith is kindled through the gospel; and justification, by which, on account of the merit of Christ apprehended by true faith, sin is remitted and the righteousness of Christ is imputed. That this gap has long since been reproached to the mystics, I gather from the Theologia Mystica of GOTTFRIED ARNOLD, ch. VIII, p. 208, saying: *Etliche meynen, die Mystici lehren so gar wenig, oder nichts von der Wiedergeburth, welche gleichwohl die Summa, und das einige Nothwendige im Christenthum sey*; and p. 209, again: *besorgen manche, es würden darinnen die gesetzlichen Wege mehr, als das lautere Evangelium vorgetragen, indem die Seele immer auf die angstliche Demuthigung, Reinigung, Abgeschiedenheit, und dergleichen, und dabey wenig auf den Glauben an den Herrn Christum gewiesen würde.* Which scruple, because it is very important and far-reaching, must justly be examined and removed somewhat more accurately. The doctrine concerning regeneration [is] of learning; the other [is] of acting and doing what is commanded.

Both are either general or special. General desire, which pertains to the beginning of correcting one's life, namely the zeal both to learn something and to do well, follows the general cognition of truth, perceived by the intellect: that God has declared his will in Holy Scripture, and what the primary and general dogmas are; but the same precedes the more abundant cognition and illumination of the mind, or special [cognition], namely, what the will of God is, declared by the word consigned to letters, concerning things hitherto known generally, now to be known more clearly, more distinctly, and more certainly. Special desire, which pertains to the increase and progression of a holy life, namely the zeal both to learn more and to do better, or to make progress day by day more and more, follows the cognition of truth and the more abundant and special illumination of the intellect. Phil. 1:9, 10, 11. Col. 1:9, 10, 11. These three principles are indeed most certain: 1) There is no desire for the unknown, and there is greater desire for the better known: 2) Nothing [exists] without a reason, either true or false; either certain or uncertain; either perfectly and altogether, or imperfectly and in some way perceived; 3) The first motion in the will, whether good or evil, exists from the first perception of the intellect, whether of truth or of falsehood. But upon the first perception in the intellect, and the first motion in the will closely joined with it, follow further perceptions in the intellect, and further motions in the will. E.g., there can be no desire in the will unless some cognition has preceded in the intellect. Nor can there be greater cognition in the intellect unless some desire in the will has gone before, following that first and general cognition. E.g., the first and general cognition of divine truth without delay excites the first motions of holy desire, which are followed by the more abundant, clearer, and more certain cognition of each part of divine doctrine, from whose amplification and confirmation more numerous and stronger, constant motions of the holy will arise. motions of the holy will arise. motions of the holy will arise.

tion and faith in Christ is undoubtedly of great moment. For Christ, about to inform Nicodemus, who was lawfully inquiring into the way of salvation, said: Unless one is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God, John 3: 3. When the jailer asked in Acts 16:30: What must I do to be saved? Paul and Silas answered: Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, and your house.

Also of very great weight is the doctrine concerning the justification of the sinner through faith in Christ. For μακαρισμὸς, or beatification, is of the man to whom God imputes righteousness without works, Rom. 4: 6. The article concerning the righteousness of faith is the chief one in the whole Christian doctrine, without which a troubled conscience can have no true and firm consolation, nor rightly recognize the riches of the grace of Christ, as the Formula of Concord judges, p. 683. Prob. b. The end of mystical union is the mount of perfection, which mystics strive to ascend in this life, and deification, or transformation into God.

Cf. D. MOLINOS in Manuduct. lib. 3, c. 4, p. 286. ARNOLD in Theol. Myst. c. 7, p. 163. But indeed no mortal attains this end in this life.

Which we prove: 1) Because the knowledge of God and divine things, and also the holiness of spiritual life, of men who are wayfarers, is imperfect.

Concerning the θεογνωσίᾳ (knowledge of God) of wayfarers, Paul says, 1 Cor. 13:9: ἐκ μέρους γινώσκομεν, we know in part, and we prophesy in part: but when that which is perfect has come, then that which is in part will be done away. Concerning the imperfect holiness of wayfarers, St. James testifies, ep. c. 3:2: In many things we all stumble, and St. John, 1 ep. 1:8: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. But those who have sin, and often stumble, they are not perfectly holy.

But those who have sin, and often fall, they are not perfectly holy.

2) But to aspire to deification is religion for a Christian. For the affected ἀποθέωσις (deification) cast the protoplasts out of paradise. When the king of Babylon said: I will ascend above the heights of the clouds, I will be like the Most High, he was cast down into hell by the most just judgment of God, Isa. 14:14-15. Jehovah addresses the prophet Ezekiel: Son of man, say to the prince of Tyre: Thus says ADONAI JEHOVAH: Because your heart is lifted up, and you say: I am a god, I sit in the seat of God, in the midst of the seas; yet you are a man, and not God. Therefore thus says ADONAI JEHOVAH: because you have given your heart as the heart of God: therefore behold! I will bring against you strangers, the most terrible of the nations: and they shall draw their swords against the beauty of your wisdom, and they shall defile your splendor, Ezek. 28:2, 6-7.

When the priests and Levites of Jerusalem asked John the Baptist: Was he the Christ? he answered: I am not the Christ, John 1: 20. If they had continued to ask: Was he God? John would have answered without a doubt: I am not God, but I am a sinful man, I am dust and ashes before the divine face.

From which it is abundantly clear that mystical authors have erred gravely in determining the end of theology.

All these things having been weighed on the balance of truth, I think that the ways of orthodox theology should be arranged in a fuller and more accurate series, so that THE FIRST WAY IS ILLUMINATIVE, by which a sinful man, called to the church of Christ—for I presuppose the calling to the church—arrives both at the recognition of sin from the law, and at the recognition of Christ the satisfier from the gospel: THE SECOND IS CONVERSIVE, by which the sinful man is led to contrition, or detestation of sins, seriously joined with sorrow: THE THIRD IS REGENERATIVE, by which he is advanced to faith in Christ: THE FOURTH IS JUSTIFICATIVE, which pertains to the remission of sins and the imputed righteousness of Christ: THE FIFTH IS UNITIVE, by which he escapes into a temple consecrated to the triune God, in which He dwells and works by a gracious influx: THE SIXTH IS GLORIFICATIVE, by which he is introduced into the heavenly paradise, in which is the true mount of perfection.

I prove this order and series of mystical ways from Acts 26:17, where Christ addresses Paul: I send you to the Gentiles, to open their eyes, (behold illumination!) and that they may turn from darkness to light (behold conversion!) and from the power

from Satan to God (behold regeneration!) that they may receive remission of sins (behold justification!) and a lot among those who have been sanctified by faith in me (behold union with Christ through faith, sanctification, and glorification!). DISSOLUTION:

6) Viam purgativam doctores mystici non satis perspicue explanarunt. Iustificatio sequitur illuminationem, & praecedit unionem mysticam: renovatio autem tam illuminationem, quam unionem mysticam ordine naturae sequitur. Vos, inquit, non estis in carne, sed in Spiritu, siquidem Spiritus Dei habitat in vobis. Quocirca ea ferie disponendae sunt viae mysticorum, vt prima sit illuminativa, altera unitiva, tertia purgativa. Quod si autem scriptores mystici per purgationem tam iustificationem, quam renovationem designent, indecora aequivocatione, quae errorum foeda est genitrix, ludunt; propterea, quod una voce duos gratiae divinae applicatricis actus complectuntur, quorum alter unionem mysticam antecedit, alter consequitur. Cupiditas specialis, quae ad incrementum ac progressionem vitae sanctae pertinet, videlicet studium & plus discendi, & melius agendi, sive in dies etiam atque etiam proficiendi, sequitur veritatis cognitionem atque intellectus illuminationem uberiorem ac specialem. Phil. I, 9. 10. 11. Col. I, 9. 10. 11. Haec tria principia sane certissima sunt: 1) Ignoti nulla cupido, & magis cogniti maior cupido: 2) Nil fine ratione, aut vera, aut falsa; aut certa, aut incerta; aut perfecte atque omnino, aut imperfecte & quodam modo percepta; 3) Primus in voluntate motus, sive bonus, sive malus, existit ex prima intellectus perceptione, sive veri, sive falsi: Primam autem in intellectu perceptionem, & arcte cum ea copulatum primum in voluntate motum sequuntur plures in intellectu perceptiones, pluresque in voluntate motus. E. nulla potest in voluntate esse cupiditas, nisi praecesserit quadam cognitio in intellectu. Satanæ ad Deum (en regenerationem!) vt accipiant remissionem peccatorum (en iustificationem!) & sortem inter eos, qui sanctificati sunt per fidem in me (en vnionem cum Christo per fidem, sanctificationem & glorificationem!). ΔΙΑΛΥΣΙΣ:


### Question IV. Is there another distinction of the acts of applying grace?: The dissenters object that the three ways of the mystics are not supported by a certain foundation of order I. The author of salvation himself…

The dissenters object that the three ways of the mystics are not supported by a certain foundation of order.

I. The author of salvation himself approves them, John XIV, 21.

He who has my commandments, and does them, he it is who loves me: but he who loves me, will be loved by my Father: and I will love him, and will manifest myself to him, verse 23. he adds: We will come to him, and make our abode with him.

Resp. Verse 20 must also be repeated so that the connection (συνάφεια) of the text may be clearer, where Christ says: In that day you shall know that I am in my Father, and you in me, verse 21. he says: He who has my commandments, and does them, he it is who loves me. From this cohesion of the text it appears that the first illumination, the effect of which is knowledge, precedes sanctification, the effect of which is love for Christ. But when the Savior adds; I will manifest myself to him, he manifests by that a continued illumination, the effect of which is a fuller and richer knowledge of Christ and of divine mysteries. The Lord Jesus, in the cited passage, did not make mention of conversion, regeneration, and justification, because he had not intended at that time to recount each and every act of applying grace.

II. The Holy Spirit approves the three ways of the mystics by addressing the sinner through Paul: Eph. V, 14. Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, that Christ may shine upon you.

Where awakening from the lethargy of security, and resurrection from the dead, is placed before illumination. Resp. From the adduced words of Paul, the mystical writers cannot establish the three ways; for Paul 1) made no mention of the unitive [way]: 2) The Holy Spirit shakes off the lethargy of security through converting grace, so that contrition and detestation of sin may be excited in the will: through regenerating grace man is raised from spiritual death, so that he may receive the life of faith: through justifying grace Christ illuminates man with the light of righteousness (ἐπιφάυει).
