The Apostle therefore recounted the converting, regenerating, and justifying way (*). But if anyone prefers to draw the last words to renewing grace, then it is understood as continued illumination, from which a richer knowledge of Christ (χριστογνωσία) proceeds. But the first and inchoate illumination of the intellect precedes the purgation of the will (). (*)

Latin:

Obiiciunt dissidentes, tres mysticorum vias non destitui certo ordinis fundamento.

I. Ipse salutis auctor eas approbat, Io. XIV, 21.

Qui habet præcepta mea, & facit illa, is est, qui diligit me: qui vero diligit me, diligetur a Patre meo: & ego diligam illum, manifestabo illi me ipsum, versu 23. addit: Veniemus ad illum, & mansionem apud eum faciemus.

Resp. Repetendus etiam est versus 20. vt συνάφεια textus sit luculentior, vbi Christus ait: In illa die cognoscetis vos, quod ego in Patre meo, & vos in me, versu 21. inquit: Qui habet præcepta mea, & facit illa, ille est, qui diligit me. E qua cohæsione textus apparet, quod illuminatio prima, cuius effectus est cognitio, præcedat sanctificationem, cuius effectus est dilectio Christi. Cum autem Salvator addit; manifestabo me illi, manifestat illo illuminationem continuatam, cuius effectus est cognitio Christi & mysteriorum diuinorum plenior & vberior. Conuersionis, regenerationis & iustificationis Dominus Iesus, loco citato, non iniecit mentionem, quia non destinauerat, id temporis omnes & singulos actus gratiæ applicatricis percensere.

II. Comprobat tres mysticorum vias Spiritus S. per Paullum peccatorem alloquens: Eph. V, 14. Expergiscere, qui dormis, & surge ex mortuis, vt tibi Christus illucescat.

Vbi euigilatio e veterno securitatis, & resurrectio a mortuis illuminationi anteponitur. Resp. Ex adductis verbis Paullinis scriptores mystici tres vias stabilire nequeunt; neque enim Paullus 1) vllam mentionem fecit vnitivæ: 2) Spiritus S. veternum securitatis excutit per gratiam conuertentem, vt contritio & detestatio peccati in voluntate excitetur: per gratiam regenerantem homo exsuscitatur e morte spirituali, vt vitam fidei accipiat: per gratiam iustificantem Christus hominem ἐπιφάυει luce iustitiæ collustrat. Recensuit itaque Apostolus viam conuersiuam, regeneratiuam & iustificatiuam (*). Quod si quis malit vltima verba trahere ad gratiam renouantem, tunc intelligitur illuminatio continuata, e qua proficiscitur χριστογνωσία vberior. At prima & inchoata illuminatio intellectus purgationem voluntatis præcedit (). (*)


### Q. I. What is the calling to the kingdom of Christ?

The calling to the kingdom of Christ is an act of grace, by which the Holy Spirit manifests to men, established outside the church, the will of God concerning the saving of sinners through the divine word, and offers to them the benefits from the Redeemer Christ, so that they may be brought to the church, converted, and obtain eternal salvation.

Obj. I. It is called a saving calling to the kingdom and glory, A translation into the kingdom of the Son of God,

Obj. II. We have described the calling to the kingdom of Christ as special, direct, and saving, from which saving conversion takes its beginning, to which is contrasted the calling to the church as general, indirect, and pedagogical, which is a preamble to the saving calling.

Latin:

Vocatio ad regnum Christi est actus gratiæ, quo Spiritus S. hominibus, extra ecclesiam constitutis, voluntatem Dei de saluandis peccatoribus per verbum diuinum manifestat, & ipsis beneficia a redemptore Christo offert, vt ad ecclesiam adducantur, conuertantur, & æternam salutem consequantur. Obs.

I. Appellatur salutaris vocatio ad regnum & gloriam, Translatio in regnum Filii Dei,

Obs. II. Descripsimus vocationem ad regnum Christi specialem, directam & salutarem, a qua salutaris conuersio ducit initium, cui contradistinguitur vocatio ad ecclesiam generalis, indirecta & pædagogica, quæ vocationis salutaris præambula est.


### Q. II. What is the general and pedagogical calling to the church?

The general and pedagogical calling to the church is that by which God invites sinners established outside the church, more obscurely and as if from afar, to seek the true worship of God and the assembly in which it flourishes, and brings them to the door of the church. That general calling occurs: a) objectively, through the proposal of the divine government and beneficence toward creatures; b) effectively, through an efficacious influx and divine impulse, by which, both from innate theoretical and practical notions and from the documents of divine beneficence, practical conclusions are stirred up in the minds of infidels, though in unequal measure, to inquire about the true worship of God; c) cumulatively, through the report about the church, spread throughout the whole world.

From Acts XVII, 25, 26, 27. God gives to all life, and Spirit, and all things, and has made of one blood every nation of men to dwell on all the face of the earth, determining the preordained times and the setting of the boundaries of their habitation: that they should seek the Lord, if altogether so that they might feel after him, and find him. God has proposed his providence to be contemplated concerning the human race in his works, so that in them men might clearly discover the traces of God the best and greatest, and by diligently observing these, and desiring to acquire more than the innate knowledge embraces, they might seek studiously who this great God is, namely Jehovah, and in those very works by natural light might feel after him and confusedly know him, yet not stopping here, might fully find him in the supernatural revelation which God has not denied.

Prob. b. From Rom. II, 4. Or do you despise the riches of his (God's) goodness and patience and longsuffering? Not knowing that the goodness of God invites you to repentance: Obj. 1) The Apostle addresses all men, both Gentiles and Jews, as those judging others for their own guilt, because they are guilty in the judgment of God, and he teaches that they are convicted by their own conscience. 2) By the riches of divine goodness is denoted the most abundant beneficence of God in the kingdom of nature; for in it God did not leave himself ἀμάρτυρον, i. e. without witness, doing good, giving us rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness, Acts XIV, 17. By this beneficence the Gentiles were stimulated to repentance. Therefore the Apostle says: The goodness of God invites (ἄγειν) you to repentance. ἄγειν is in the Greek, which signifies not merely to propose the will of God, and thus verbally to invite to himself, but really to move, and to effect and do something in man. God therefore through nature so copiously, so most amply and intensely dispenses his goodness, that he draws, entices, and moves man to himself in all ways. And indeed to repentance for evil deeds, not only in so far as this is a detestation of a base thing, but also in so far as after a sin committed against God it tends to this, that he might desist from his wrath, and be reconciled to man. For that is to perceive the divine goodness, patience, and likewise longsuffering, so that with man desisting from sins and repenting, God can be good and patient toward him. Although indeed this repentance of man and turning away from sins cannot obtain the effect of divine grace outside the word of the gospel, only from the divine intention to that ἄγειν, he leads and invites through the excitation of practical conclusions, such as are:

I. Because God is the most omnipotent, most wise, best, and most just ruler of the universe, therefore he is to be humbly worshipped, venerated, and feared.

II. God is to be worshipped not in any way whatsoever, but as he himself has prescribed; because every servant, as experience testifies, must worship the Lord not from his own ingenuity, but from the will of the Lord.

III. Therefore it is necessary that there be somewhere in the world a supernatural light, by which God the best has declared his will: it is necessary that there be somewhere a congregation, to which God has prescribed the legitimate mode of worship, which is to be sought most diligently. [*].

Prob. c. A general calling of sinners to the church has also been made through its celebrity. The fame of the sacred rites of the Israelite church has undoubtedly spread throughout the whole world.

What nation has not heard of the circumcision of the Israelites, of sacrifices kindled by heavenly fire, of divine miracles performed in the Israelite church, of prophecies confirmed by infallible outcome, of the celebrity of Jerusalem, the academy of the world, of the splendor of Solomon's temple? The Israelites migrated into Egypt, as through Africa; the same were deported into Chaldea, as through Asia; not a few of them dwelt in Rome, as through Europe, that they might scatter the fragrance of the divine word. The Greek version of the Hebrew bibles under the Egyptian king Ptolemy Philadelphus, as well as the righteousness of proselytes and the multitude of their dwelling, also contributed no small amount to the seeking of the God of Israel.

The celebrity of the church of the New Testament became known everywhere in the world. Concerning the church of Christ, gathered at Rome, the Apostle of the Gentiles testifies, Rom. 1:8: Your faith is announced in the whole world. Rome, while Paul was still alive, was the head of many nations, to which not only subjects but also foreign peoples flocked in crowds. Therefore, what was done in political and sacred matters at Rome could not be hidden, but was divulged in all places. Concerning the church of the Thessalonians, Paul says, 1 Thess. 1:8: From you the word of the Lord has sounded forth not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but also in every place your faith toward God has gone out. Thessalonica was famous for its market, to which merchants from distant places went and returned, who testified to the faith of the church of Thessalonica to remote peoples. Today, the fame of the Christian church, through so many journeys and so many voyages undertaken to the most remote regions and islands, has permeated the entire circuit of the earth.

Latin:

Vocatio generalis & pædagogica ad ecclesiam est, qua Deus peccatores extra ecclesiam constitutos, ad inquirendum verum Dei cultum, & cœtum, in quo ille viget, obscurius & velut e longinquo inuitat, & ad ianuam ecclesiæ adducit. Vocatio illa generalis fit: a) obiectiue, per propositionem regiminis & beneficentiæ diuinæ in creaturas; b) effectiue, per efficacem influxum atque impulsum diuinum, quo tum e notitiis innatis theoreticis & practicis, tum e documentis beneficentiæ diuinæ suscitantur conclusiones practicæ in mentibus infidelium, inæquali tamen mensura ad inquirendum de vero cultu Dei, c) cumulative, per famam de ecclesia, toto orbe diffusam.

Prob. a. Ex Act. XVII, 25. 26. 27. Deus dat omnibus vitam, & Spiritum & omnia, fecitque ex uno sanguine quoduis genus hominum habitare super totam faciem terræ, definiens præordinata tempora & limitum positionem habitationis eorum: vt quærant dominum, si omnino no palpent ipsum, et inveniant. Deus proposuit contemplandam providentiam suam circa humanum genus in operibus suis, ita, vt in illis homines clara deprehendant vestigia Dei optimi, maximi, quo ea sedulo observantes, et plus, quam insita complectitur notitia, acquirere desiderantes, quærant studiose, quis ille tantus Deus sit, Iehovah scilicet, et in ipsis quidem operibus illis lumine naturali eum palpent atque confuse cognoscant, hic tamen non subsistentes in supernaturali revelatione, quam Deus non denegauit, plene inveniant.

Prob. b. Ex Rom. II, 4. An divitias bonitatis illius (Dei) et patientiæ et longanimitatis contemnis? Ignorans, quod bonitas Dei ad pœnitentiam te invitat: Obs. 1) Alloquitur Apostolus homines universos, tam gentiles, quam Iudæos, vtpote alios iudicantes de propria culpa, quod rei sint in iudicio Dei, atque docet eosdem suapte conscientia convinci. 2) Per divitias bonitatis divinæ denotatur beneficentia Dei uberrima in regno naturæ; quippe in quo Deus se non reliquit ἀμάρτυρον, i. e. intestatum benefaciens, cœlitus nobis pluvias dans et tempora frugifera, implens cibo et lætitia corda nostra, Act. XIV, 17. Hac beneficentia gentiles stimulati sunt ad pœnitentiam. Idcirco dicit Apostolus: Bonitas Dei ad pœnitentiam te (ἄγειν) invitat. ἄγειν est in græco, quod significat non proponere tantum voluntatem Dei, adeoque verbaliter ad se invitare, sed realiter commovere, et in homine aliquid efficere et agere. Deus itaque per naturam ita copiose, ita amplissime et intensissime bonitatem suam dispensat, vt omnibus modis hominem ad se trahat, alliciat, commoveat. Et quidem ad pœnitentiam male factorum non tantum, in quantum hæc est detestatio rei turpis, sed et in quantum post peccatum contra Deum commissum eo tendit, vt is ab ira sua desistat, et homini reconcilietur. Id enim est sentire divinam bonitatem, patientiam, item et longanimitatem, vt desistente a peccatis homine et pœnitente, Deus bonus et patiens erga ipsum esse possit. Quanquam vero hæc pœnitentia hominis et aversio a peccatis ipsum effectum divinæ gratiæ extra verbum evangelii obtinere nequeat, tantum ex intentione divina eo ἄγειν, ducit et invitat per excitationem conclusionum practicarum, quales sunt:

I. Quia Deus rector universi omnipotentissimus, sapientissimus, optimus, iustissimus est, ideo submisse colendus, venerandus, et timendus est.

II. Colendus est Deus non quovis modo, sed quem ipse præscripsit; quia omnem ministrum, teste experientia, oportet colere Dominum non ex ingenio suo, sed ex voluntate Domini.

III. Oportet igitur in mundo alicubi esse lumen supernaturale, quo Deus optimus voluntatem suam declaravit: oportet esse alicubi cœtum, cui legitimum colendi modum Deus præscripsit, qui diligentissime inquirendus est. [*].

Prob. c. Facta etiam est vocatio peccatorum generalis ad ecclesiam per huius celebritatem. Fama de sacris ecclesiæ Isræliticæ hau dubie pervagata est totum terrarum orbem.

Quæ gens non audiuit de Israëliturum circumcisione, sacrificiis igne cælesti accensis, de miraculis diuinis in ecclesia Israëlitica factis, de vaticiniis infallibili euentu comprobatis, de celebritate Hierosolymæ, orbis academiæ, de splendore templi Salomonæi? Commigrarunt Israëlitæ in Ægyptum, vt per Africam; deportati sunt iidem in Chaldæam, vt per Asiam; habitarunt haud pauci ex iisdem Romæ, vt per Europam, odorem verbi diuini dispergerent. Haud parum quoque momenti ad quærendum Deum Israëlis attulit cum bibliorum hebræorum sub rege Ægypti Ptolemæo Philadelpho versio græca, tum proselytorum iustitia & domicilii multitudo.

Ecclesiæ noui testamenti celebritas vbique terrarum innotuit. De ecclesia Christi, Romæ colleCta, testatur gentium Apostolus, Rom. I, 8. Fides vestra annuntiatur in toto mundo. Roma erat superstite Paullo caput multarum gentium, ad quam non tantum subiecti, sed & exteri populi agminatim confluebant. Non poterant igitur, quæ in politicis & sacris gerebantur Romæ, latere, sed passim locorum diuulgabantur. De ecclesia Thessalonicensium ait Paullus, 1 Thess. I, 8. A vobis personuit verbum domini non solum in Macedonia & Achaia, sed etiam in omnem locum fides vestra ad Deum exiuit. Thessalonia mercatu erat celebris, quo ibant & redibant inercatores e locis dissitis, qui fidem ecclesiæ Thessalonicensis remotis populis testabantur. Hodie fama de ecclesia christiana tot itineribus, tot nauigationibus in regiones & insulas remotissimas susceptis, vniuersum terrarum ambitum peruasit.


### Q. III. How many-fold is the special calling to the church?

The special calling to the church is either ordinary or extraordinary. The former occurs through the preaching of the divine word, by the work of ministers a). The latter is that which occurs either immediately by God, or through miracles, or through a person not performing the ordinary duty of teaching b).

Proof a. The ordinary and solemn calling occurs through the preaching of the gospel, by the work of the ministers of the church performing the public duty of teaching, through whom men believe, 1 Cor. 3:5.

Proof b. The extraordinary calling is either immediate or mediate. The immediate is that by which God himself calls a sinner to the church without the intervention of means. Of this kind was the calling of Abraham from Ur of the Chaldeans, to whom God himself said, Gen. 12:1: Go from your land, and from your kindred to the land which I will show you. The mediate occurs either through miracles (thus the magi were called to Christ by a miraculous star, Matt. 2:1); or through men extraordinarily sent (thus the Ninevites were called through Jonah): or through persons not admitted to the public office of teaching. Thus Naaman the Syrian was called to the Jewish church through an Israelite girl, 2 Kings 5:7. It not rarely happens that the sacred code is proposed to a Gentile man by a Christian layman to be read, and he is converted: whose calling is indeed less solemn, yet not ineffective.

Obs. A solemn calling occurs through the preached word: a less solemn one through the read, or readable, word.

Latin:

Vocatio specialis ad ecclesiam est vel ordinaria, vel extraordinaria. Illa fit per prædicationem verbi diuini, ministrorum opera a). Hæc est, quæ fit vel immediate a Deo, vel per miracula, vel per hominem, ordinario docendi munere non fungentem b).

Prob. a. Vocatio ordinaria & solemnis fit per prædicationem euangelii, opera ministrorum ecclesiæ, publico docendi munere fungentium, per quos homines credunt, 1 Cor. III, 5.

Prob. b. Extraordinaria vocatio est vel immediata, vel mediata. Immediata est, qua Deus ipse peccatorem ad ecclesiam citra interuentum mediorum vocat. Huiusmodi fuit vocatio Abrahami ex Ur Chaldæorum, ad quem Deus ipse dixit, Gen. XII, 1. Abi e terra tua, & a cognatione tua ad terram, quam ostendam tibi. Mediata fit vel per miracula (sic magi per stellam miraculosam vocati sunt ad Christum, Matth. II, 1.); Vel per homines extraordinarie missos (Sic Niniuitæ vocati sunt per Ionam): Vel per personas, publico docendi officio non admotas. Ita Naaman Syrus per puellam Israëliticam ad ecclesiam Iudaicam vocabatur, 2 Reg. V, 7. Haud raro vsu venit, vt homini gentili a laico christiano legendus proponatur sacer codex, & is conuertatur: cuius vocatio quidem est minus solemnis, non tamen inefficax.

Obs. Vocatio solemnis fit per verbum prædicatum: Minus solemnis per verbum lectum, vel legibile.


### Q. IV. How many-fold is the ordinary calling to the church?

The ordinary calling is either simple or combined. The former is the manifestation of the divine will and the offer of benefits, procured by the merit of Christ, despised and rejected by stubborn sinners a). The latter is an invitation to Christian communion combined with the obedience of those invited b).

Latin:

Vocatio ordinaria est vel simplex, vel coniuncta. Illa est manifestatio voluntatis diuinæ & oblatio beneficiorum, merito Christi partorum, a contumacibus peccatoribus contemta & reiecta a). Hæc est inuitatio ad communionem Christiana cum obsequio inuitatorum coniuncta b).


### Quæst. VI. What moved God to call sinful men to the kingdom of grace?

Prob. a. God has often spread out His hands to a rebellious people, Is. LXV, 2, He invites many to the marriage of His son, who refuse to come, Matt. XXII, 3.

Prob. b. A vocation joined [to election] is called by St. Paul a vocation κατὰ πρόθεσιν, according to the divine purpose, Rom. VIII, 28, to which purpose men most humbly submit and conform themselves.

Quæst. V. Who has called us to the kingdom of Christ? The whole Holy Trinity has called us to the kingdom of Christ, particularly the Holy Spirit, to whom this act of grace is appropriated.

Prob. a. Vocation to the church is a divine action ad extra, common to all three persons of the deity. God the Father is said to have called us, 1 Cor. I, 9: God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of His Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. The word, God, is taken by the Apostle ὑποστατικῶς (hypostatically), and denotes the first person of the divinity, or God the Father; since He is clearly distinguished from the Son of God. Therefore, God the Father called us into the fellowship of His Son, who is the head of the church, which is His body, and His fullness, who fills all in all. Eph. I, 23.

Consequently, he who is not a member of the church does not have fellowship with Christ. Christ Himself, when He was visibly present on these earths, called men into His kingdom. Jesus began to preach and to say: Repent; for the kingdom of heaven is at hand, Matt. IV, 17.

Christ taught that the kingdom of the Messiah, often promised by the prophets, had now drawn near, not because it did not exist in the O.T., but because in the time of the New Testament it had drawn near in a particular way: 1) By reason of the King Messiah exhibited in the flesh: 2) By reason of the acquisition of the benefits in which the kingdom of God consists, Rom. XIV, 17, inasmuch as they were about to be acquired by the death of Christ: 3) By reason of the clearer, more frequent, and more widespread announcement of the kingdom of God: 4) By reason of the translation into the kingdom of God through the word of the gospel and the sacraments of the N.T.

But when Christ was about to be taken up into heaven, He commanded the gospel to be preached to every creature, Mark XVI, 15.

Prob. b. Vocation to the church is appropriated to the Holy Spirit. For the ministry of the word, through which we are called, is called the ministry of the spirit, 2 Cor. III, 6. The Holy Spirit speaks through the ministers of God, Matt. X, 20. The Holy Spirit calls and ordains bishops, who preach the divine word, Acts XX, 28.

Quæst. VI. What moved God to call sinful men to the kingdom of grace? The internal impulsive cause of the gracious vocation is φιλανθρωπία (philanthropy), or the mercy of God toward the human race, which had fallen into sin. The external impulsive cause is Christ the Mediator, who by His active and passive obedience satisfied the offended divine justice, so that, this being satisfied, God might intend our salvation and call us to the kingdom of grace. Human misery, however, did not indeed causally impel God to the gracious vocation, yet it provided Him with the occasion to have mercy.

Prob. a. God has called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to His own purpose and grace given to us in Christ Jesus before the beginning of time, 2 Tim. I, 9.

Obs. a) that our works did not impel God to our vocation, since they are nothing before vocation, regeneration, and faith, Rom. XIV, 23. Wherefore our vocation is entirely gratuitous. b) That πρόθεσις, or the purpose of God, is the divine decree concerning saving those men who are to believe in Christ. c) That we are said to be called according to His purpose and grace.

grace, given to us before the ages of time in Christ; because temporal calling, and leading to salvation, is ordered in the same way as the eternal purpose of God and the eternal predestination to salvation; but this was done according to the good pleasure of the most merciful divine will, Eph. 1:5. Therefore also the former. d) That grace is given to us in Christ; because it is based upon his merit, and indeed was given by reason of the decree before the ages of time, i.e., from eternity, since before the series of times there was nothing, unless it were mere eternity.

Prob. b. Unless Christ the mediator had satisfied God, the most just judge and avenger of sins, by his active and passive obedience performed in our stead, we would have been destined, just like the apostate angels, to the kingdom of darkness without any mercy; because the infinite justice of God, wounded by sins, inflicts eternal punishments: But that God, after the fall, while his justice remains intact, wishes us well, desires our salvation to be promoted, and thus calls us to the kingdom of grace: all this is owed to the satisfaction and merit of Christ. Paul teaches this, 2 Cor. 5:19-20. God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, while he did not impute their sins to them, and he placed in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore, we perform an embassy for Christ, so that God may exhort through us: We beseech you for Christ: be reconciled to God! God, reconciled by the satisfaction of Christ, placed the word of reconciliation in the mouths of sacred heralds, i.e., the gospel, so that, as ambassadors of Christ, they might offer to sinners the reconciliation with God acquired by this mediator, and might entice them by this offered reconciliation to the kingdom of grace. Prob. c.

Our misery, properly speaking, is not an external cause impelling God to our calling, but it only provided an occasion for God, and presented to him the fallen human race as a miserable object, toward which he ought not, but can, exercise philanthropy. For in man the sinner there is absolutely no impelling cause. This is what God himself inculcates, Ezek. 16:5-6. You were cast out upon the face of the field in the loathing of your soul, in the day that you were born. But I passed by you, and saw you trampled in your blood (plainly unclean and impious, so that there was no just cause for exciting any effort to help you, but rather that blood and impurity, voluntarily and maliciously contracted against my severe prohibition, cried out as it were for the vindictive justice of punishing you: Yet moved by mere philanthropy), when you were in your blood, and ought rather to have been punished, (out of mere grace) I said to you: live. Conf. D. HULSEM. in breu. enucl. cap. VII. §. 4. p. 351.

Latin:

Prob. a. Sæpe numero Deus expandit manus suas ad populum rebellem, Es. LXV, 2, Inuitat multos ad nuptias filii sui, venire renuentes, Matth. XXII, 3.

Prob. b. Vocatio coniuncta a S. Paullo dicitur vocatio κατὰ πρόθεσιν, secundum propositum diuinum, Rom. VIII, 28. cui proposito homines se humillime submittunt & conformant.

Quæst. V. Quis nos ad regnum Christi vocauit? Vocauit nos ad regnum Christi tota SS. Trinitas , peculiariter Spiritus S. cui hic actus gratiæ appropriatur .

Prob. a. Vocatio ad ecclesiam est actio diuina ad extra, omnibus tribus personis deitatis communis. Vocasse nos dicitur Deus Pater, 1 Cor. I, 9: Fidelis est Deus, per quem vocati estis ad communionem Filii sui domini nostri Iesu Christi. Vox, Deus, ab Apostolo sumitur ὑποστατικῶς, & notat primam personam diuinitatis, siue Deum Patrem; quippe qui a Filio Dei diserte distinguitur. Vocauit itaque Deus Pater nos ad communionem Filii sui, qui est caput ecclesiæ, quæ est corpus illius, & plenitudo eius, qui omnia in omnibus implet. Eph. I, 23.

Proinde non habet communionem cum Christo, qui non est membrum ecclesiæ. Christus ipse, cum versaretur visibiliter in his terris, homines in regnum suum vocauit. Incepit Iesus prædicare & dicere: Pœniteat vos; appropinquauit enim regnum cælorum, Matth. IV, 17.

Docuit Christus, regnum Messiæ a prophetis sæpe promissum nunc appropinquasse, non quod in V. T. non fuerit, sed quod noui testamenti tempore peculiariter appropinquauerit: 1) Ratione regis Messiæ in carne exhibiti: 2) Ratione acquisitionis beneficiorum, in quibus regnum Dei consistit, Rom. XIV, 17. vtpote quæ erant morte Christi iamiam acquirenda: 3) Ratione annuntiationis clarioris, frequentioris & diffusioris regni Dei: 4) Ratione traductionis in regnum Dei per verbum euangelii & sacramenta N. T.

Cum autem in cælum subvecturus esset Christus, iussit prædicari euangelium omni creaturæ, Marc. XVI, 15.

Prob. b. Vocatio ad ecclesiam Spiritui S. appropriatur. Nam ministerium verbi, per quod vocamur, dicitur ministerium spiritus, 2 Cor. III, 6. Spiritus S. loquitur per ministros Dei, Matth. X, 20. Spiritus S. vocat & ordinat episcopos, verbum diuinum prædicantes, Act. XX, 28.

Quæst. VI. Ecquid permouit Deum, vt homines peccatores ad regnum gratiæ vocaret? Causa impulsiva interna gratiosæ vocationis est φιλανθρωπία, seu misericordia Dei erga genus humanum, in peccatum prolapsum . Causa impulsiva externa est Christus Mediator, qui obedientia sua actiua & passiva satisfecit læsæ iustitiæ diuinæ, vt hac salua Deus nostram salutem intenderet, & ad regnum gratiæ nos vocauerit . Miseria autem humana non quidem causaliter impulit Deum ad vocationem gratiosam, ipsi tamen occasionem commiserescendi præbuit .

Prob. a. Deus vocauit nos vocatione sancta, non secundum opera nostra, sed iuxta proprium propositum, & gratiam datam nobis in Christo Iesu, ante tempora sæcularia, 2 Tim. I, 9.

Obs. a) quod Deum ad vocationem nostri non impulerint opera nostra, quippe quæ nulla sunt ante vocationem, regenerationem & fidem, Rom. XIV, 23. Quare vocatio nostra plane gratuita est. b) Quod πρόθεσις, seu propositum Dei, sit decretum diuinum de saluandis hominibus in Christum credituris. c) Quod vocati dicamur secundum propositum & gratiam.

ante tempora saecularia nobis datam in Christo; quia ita se habet temporalis vocatio, & ad salutem perductio, quemadmodum aeternum Dei propositum & aeterna ad salutem praestinatio; sed haec facta est secundum beneplacitum voluntatis divinae misericordissimae, Eph. I, 5. Ergo & illa. d) Quod gratia nobis data fit in Christo; quia ipsius merito est innixa, & quidem data est ratione decreti ante tempora saecularia, i. e. ab aeterno, cum ante seriem temporum nil, nisi mera fuerit aeternitas.

Prob. b. Nisi Christus mediator Deo, iustissimo peccatorum iudici & vindici, obedientia sua actua & passiva vice nostri praestita fecisset satis, perinde ac angeli apostatae ad regnum tenebrarum, sine ulla commiseratione, destinati fuissemus; propterea, quod infinita iustitia Dei laesa peccatis aeternas irrogat poenas: Quod autem Deus post lapsum, salva sua iustitia; bene nobis cupiat, salutem nostram promotam velit, atque adeo ad regnum gratiae nos vocet: id omne debetur satisfactioni & merito Christi. Docet id Paullus, 2 Cor. V, 19. 20. Deus erat in Christo, mundum reconcilians sibi ipsi, dum non imputabat illis peccata illorum, & posuit in nobis verbum reconciliationis. Pro Christo itaque legatione fungimur, ita, ut Deus adhortetur per nos: Rogamus pro Christo: reconciliamini Deo! Deus, satisfactione Christi reconciliatus, in os praeconum sacrorum posuit verbum reconciliationis, h. e. euangelium, vt, velut legati Christi, ab hoc mediatore acquisitam reconciliationem cum Deo peccatoribus offerant, & eosdem hac oblata reconciliatione ad regnum gratiae alliciant.

Prob. c. Miseria nostra, proprie loquendo, non est causa externa impellens Deum ad vocationem nostri, sed Deo tantum occasionem praebuit, & obiecit ipsi genus humanum lapsum, vt Obiectum miserum, erga quod φιλανθρωπίαν exercere non debeat, sed queat. In homine enim peccatore nulla plane est causa impellens. Id quod inculcat ipse Deus, Ezech. XVI, 5. 6. Proiecta es super facies agri in fastidio animae tuae, in die, quo nata es. Praeteriui vero praeter te, vidique conculcatam te in sanguinibus tuis (plane immundam & impiam, vt nulla iusta causa fuerit, vllum te iuuandi conatum excitandi, quin potius sanguis ille & impuritas, voluntarie ac malitiose contra meum interdictum seuerum contracta, iustitiam vindicatiuam te puniendi quasi inclamauit: Attamen mera φιλανθρωπία motus), cum in sanguine tuo, & punienda potius esses, (ex mera gratia) dixi tibi: viues. Conf. D. HULSEM. in breu. enucl. cap. VII. §. 4. p. 351.


### Quaest. VII. By what means does God call us to the church?

God calls miserable sinners to the church directly and savingly by the word of the gospel a), to which baptism also pertains b). Yet the divine law contributes to the calling of sinners, but not except indirectly, privatively, and accidentally c).

Prob. a. That a saving calling in act proceeds from the gospel, Paul teaches, 2 Thess. 2:14. God called you through our gospel to the possession of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. From which the gospel is called the gospel of the kingdom of God, Mark 1:4; because through it we are introduced into the kingdom of God. It is also called the word of reconciliation, 2 Cor. 5:19; inasmuch as by it the grace of God reconciled through Christ is offered to us. The gospel is the sweetest word, by which we are invited to the spiritual wedding, Matt. 22:4.

Prob. b. Through baptism we enter the kingdom of God, John 3:5. Therefore, through baptism we are called to the church. But since the efficacy of the baptismal water is to be attributed to the divine word, which is in and with the water; since baptism is a washing in the word, Eph. 5:26; therefore we assert. we say, that the saving vocation to the church is made through the evangelical doctrine concerning the grace of God, inclined toward all sinful men, and founded in the merit of Christ, whether it be proposed nakedly and simply, or whether it be accompanied by, and as it were clothed in, the washing of baptism. c. The law is our schoolmaster unto Christ, Gal. III, 24. But the law leads us as a schoolmaster unto Christ not directly, for the reason that it is ignorant of Christ, and since in this weakness of our nature after the fall it cannot be fulfilled, it works wrath, Rom. IV, 15. but indirectly and occasionally, just as sickness leads to a physician.

For the law bestows the spirit of bondage unto servile fear, Rom. IIX, 15. to this end, that we might cease to do evil, just as slaves do through fear of the lash. It terrifies and curses all who do not keep all its commandments, Gal. III, 10. But by this very thing it removes impediments, and thus paves the way for accepting the gospel.

For while the law convicts the conscience of not having kept the law; by this very thing it provides an occasion for seeking and finding another, who has most perfectly fulfilled the law, namely Christ, who is the perfection of the law, Rom. X, 4. Wisely says LUTHER; tom. III. Ien. fol. 29. The law prepares for grace, while it reveals and increases sin, humbling the proud to desire the help of Christ.

And the Apology of the Augsburg Confession says, p. 170. Therefore God terrifies through the law, so that there may be a place for consolation and vivification; because secure hearts, and those not feeling the wrath of God, disdain consolation.

Q. VIII. Through what ministers does God call us to the church?

Prob. a. The sacred heralds are ambassadors of Christ, through whom reconciliation with God is offered to sinners, 2 Cor. V, 20. By whose ministry men are brought to receive the faith, 1 Cor. III, 5. They are those servants through whom the guests are invited to the spiritual marriage of the Son of God, Matth. XXII, 3. Prob. b.

Naaman the Syrian was called to the Jewish church through an Israelite girl, 2 Kings V, 7. Q. IX. What is the term of vocation from which and to which?

Prob. a. Men, acting outside the church, are without hope and atheists, Eph. II, 12. They serve those who by nature are not gods, Gal. IV, 8. They are under the power of darkness, Col. I, 13. And sit in darkness and the shadow of death. Luke I, 79. Prob. b.

The term to which of vocation is the church, the house of the living God, the kingdom of Christ and the workshop of the Holy Spirit, in which the faithful have spiritual communion with Christ the head and the remaining members.

Holy Scripture indicates this term to which of saving vocation in many places. God has called you (says Paul) into his kingdom of grace and glory 1 Thess. II, 12. God has delivered us from the power of darkness and has translated us into the kingdom of his beloved son, Col. I, 13. You were called, that you might be in one body, (the church) Col. III, 15. You were called into the communion of the Son of God Jesus Christ our Lord, 1 Cor. I, 9. In this church we are taught, and by the repeated announcement of the word we are instructed unto salvation, 2 Tim. III, 15. Gal. I, 6. 9.

God ordinarily calls sinful men to the kingdom of Christ through heralds of the divine word, duly admitted to the public office of teaching a).

But out of the ordinary course, that vocation is sometimes carried out through others b). The term from which is the state of sin and most profound misery, in which men live who are constituted outside the kingdom of Christ a).

The term to which is the church b).

Latin:

Deus peccatores miseros ad ecclesiam directe & salutariter vocat verbo euangelii a), ad quod pertinet etiam baptismus b). Facit tamen ad vocationem peccatorum aliquid lex diuina, sed non, nisi indirecte, priuatiue & per accidens c).

Prob. a. Vocationem actu salutarem ab euangelio proficisci, docet Paullus, 2 Thess. II, 14. Deus vocauit vos per euangelium nostrum ad possessionem gloriae domini nostri Iesu Christi. Ex quo euangelium appellatur euangelium regni Dei, Marc. I, 4; quia per illud in regnum Dei introducimur. Vocatur etiam verbum reconciliationis, 2 Cor. V, 9; quippe quo gratia Dei per Christum reconciliati nobis offertur. Euangelium est verbum dulcissimum, quo ad nuptias spirituales inuitamur, Matth. XXII, 4.

Prob. b. Per baptismum ingredimur regnum Dei, Io, III, 5. E. per baptismum ad ecclesiam vocamur. Quoniam autem aquae baptismalis efficacia tribuenda est verbo diuino, quod est in & cum aqua; siquidem baptismus est lauacrum in verbo, Eph, V, 26; ideo afferimus. salutarem vocationem ad ecclesiam fieri per evangelicam de gratia Dei, in omnes homines peccatores propensa, & in merito Christi fundata, doctrina, sive illa nude & simpliciter proponatur, sive lavacro baptismi stipata, & quasi vestita sit. Prob. c. Lex est nobis paedagogus ad Christum, Gal. III, 24. Ducit vero lex instar paedagogi ad Christum non directe, ideo, quod Christum ignorat, & cum in hac imbecillitate naturae nostrae post lapsum impleri nequeat, iram operatur, Rom. IV, 15. sed indirecte & occasionaliter, sicut morbus ad medicum ducit.

Etenim lex largitur spiritum servitutis ad timorem servilem, Rom. IIX, 15. hoc fine, ut definamus male agere, quemadmodum ferui metu flagellorum. Terret & maledicit omnibus, qui non servant omnia eius mandata, Gal. III, 10. At hoc ipso impedimenta removet, atque adeo viam sternit ad acceptandum evangelium.

Dum enim lex conscientiam non servatae legis arguit; hoc ipso alium, qui legem perfectissime implevit, nempe Christum, qui est perfectio legis, Rom. X, 4. quaerendi & inveniendi occasionem praebet. Scite inquit LYTHERVS; tom. III. Ien. fol. 29. Lex ad gratiam praeparat, dum peccatum revelat & auget, humilians superbos ad auxilium Christi desiderandum.

Et Apologia A. C. ait, p. 170. Ideo per legem terret Deus, ut sit locus consolationi & vivificationi; quia secura corda, & non sentientia iram Dei, fastidiunt consolationem.

Quaest. VIII. Per quos ministros Deus nos ad ecclesiam vocat?

Prob. a. Praecones sacri sunt legati Christi, per quos peccatoribus reconciliatio cum Deo offertur, 2 Cor. V, 20. Quorum ministerio homines ad suscipiendam fidem adducuntur, 1 Cor. III, 5. Sunt servi illi, per quos convivae ad spirituales nuptias Filii Dei invitantur, Matth. XXII, 3. Prob. b.

Naaman Syrus per puellam Israeliticam ad ecclesiam Iudaicam vocabatur, 2 Reg. V, 7. Quaest. IX. Quis est terminus vocationis a quo & ad quem?

Prob. a. Homines, extra ecclesiam agentes, sunt expertes spei & athei, Eph. II, 12. Serviunt iis, qui natura dii non sunt, Gal. IV, 8. Sunt sub potestate tenebrarum, Col. I, 13. Et sedent in tenebris atque umbra mortis. Luc. I, 79. Prob. b.

Terminus ad quem vocationis est ecclesia, domus Dei viventis, regnum Christi & officina Spiritus S., in qua fideles cum capite Christo & reliquis membris spiritualem habent communionem.

Hunc salutaris vocationis terminum ad quem S. Scriptura passim locorum indicat. Deus vocavit vos (inquit Paullus) in suum regnum gratiae & gloriam 1 Thess. II, 12. Deus nos eripuit e potestate tenebrarum & transtulit in regnum filii dilectionis suae, Col. I, 13. Vocati estis, ut sitis in uno corpore, (ecclesia) Col. III, 15. Vocati estis in communionem Filii Dei Iesu Christi domini nostri, 1 Cor. I, 9. In hac ecclesia docemur, & iterata verbi annuntiatione erudimur ad salutem, 2 Tim. III, 15. Gal. I, 6.

9. Deus homines peccatores ad regnum Christi ordinarie vocat per praecones verbi divini, publico docendi muneri rite admotos a).

Extra ordinem autem vocatio illa interdum per alios peragitur b). Terminus a quo est status peccati & profundissimae miseriae, in quo vivunt homines extra regnum Christi constituti a).

Terminus ad quem est ecclesia b).


### Question XI. Does God will that the calling to the kingdom of grace should reach all men?

In what does the gracious calling to the church formally consist? A gracious and saving calling formally consists in the manifestation of the universal benevolence of God, and the offering of benefits, procured for us by the merit of Christ, through the preaching of the gospel.

Prob. St. Paul, 1 Tim. II, 4, 5, 6, connects the benevolence of God the Father, the universal redemption of Jesus Christ, and the preaching of the gospel: so that all men, brought to the church, may enjoy the grace of God and the merit of Christ.

The words of the Apostle are: God wills all to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God, and one mediator also of God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for redemption, in the testimony of his own times.

The testimony of his own times is the preaching of the gospel, inasmuch as it is the testimony of the Holy Spirit concerning Christ the mediator, resounding in the church through the ministry of the word, John XV, 25, 27. It is called the testimony of his own times; because the Apostles and their successors in their own times had to testify that Christ had already delivered himself for us as a ransom for redemption, whereas in the Old Testament the Prophets had testified that he was about to deliver himself. For which reason, by the intention of God, all men are to be called through the preaching of the gospel to one kingdom of grace, so that the benevolence of God the Father, concerning the saving of all men through Christ the catholic mediator, may be made known to them.

Question XI.

Does God will that the calling to the kingdom of grace should reach all men? Just as God intends the salvation of all men: so also he wills that all should be called to the church.

But that many peoples are destitute of a saving calling, that happens by their own fault, not by the determined will or counsel of God, who absolutely denies the preaching of the word to them. Objection. When we assert that the calling to the kingdom of God is universal, we do not say this, that the doctrine of the gospel has been announced to all and singular men actually, openly, and immediately, by preachers sent specifically; but that the most merciful God has promulgated the evangelical doctrine concerning obtaining salvation through faith in Christ so clearly, that all men whatsoever can arrive at the knowledge of it, so that God has not, by an absolute decree, denied to any nation, to any man, the opportunity of that doctrine, and the way by which he might be able to arrive at the knowledge of it.

Prob. a. Our assertion from the declaration of universal divine benevolence, concerning which Paul, 1 Tim. II, 4, God wills all men to be saved; and to come to the knowledge of the truth, and Peter, 2 Ep. III, 9, The Lord does not will any to perish, but all to return to repentance, cf. Ezek. XXXIII, 11. From which we gather: Whoever is inflamed with the desire of saving, illuminating, and converting all men, he denies the preaching of the gospel to no man by a determined will: But the most merciful God is such, etc.

Therefore. The major is evident: because he who wills the end, wills also the means necessary for obtaining the end.

But the preaching of the gospel is necessary for illumination, etc. 2) The universal, solemn, and actual calling happens in three distinct turns: a) The first calling was made in Adam, and through Adam, after the fall, who inculcated the gospel concerning the seed of the woman, who would crush the head of the serpent, or the gospel concerning Christ, which he had received from God, without a doubt no less to Cain than to Seth.

But just as Seth propagated the knowledge of this gospel to his posterity, even to Noah: so Cain could have transmitted the same to his own descendants. But that Cain did not transmit the same to his posterity, the cause was the impiety of himself and his descendants, and the contempt of the divine word. b) The second universal calling occurred after the flood in Noah, the second Adam, and through Noah, inasmuch as he was a herald of righteousness, and was made an heir of the righteousness which is by faith. Noah therefore preached to his sons and their descendants righteousness through faith in Christ: who, as long as they remained joined in the use of one language and lip, were imbued with the instruction of Noah, Shem, and others, until the time when, by the divinely sent confusion of languages, they were dispersed, from whom, after the dispersion, the calling could be propagated to all their descendants in various parts of the world. c) The third universal calling happened in the time of the Apostles, who were sent by Christ to teach all nations, going into the whole world and preaching the gospel to every creature, as Paul testifies, The gospel was preached to every creature which is under heaven. From which we gather: Whoever lives under heaven, to them the gospel has been preached: All and individual men live under heaven: Therefore. Nor should the Pauline testimony be passed over in silence, which is held, Their sound went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the habitable world.

Conf. From which we argue: As widely as the line of the heavens extends itself, so widely has the sound of the gospel spread: But the line of the heavens extends itself through the whole world: Therefore, through the whole world the sound of the gospel has spread. AMBROSE says wisely in chapter X of Romans: Everywhere the preaching of the name of Christ has been heard and has reached every place. For where the presence of a man preaching was lacking, the sound and fame nevertheless arrived. Our DANNHAVER also says acutely: Where the foot of the apostles did not come, there at least the apostolic sound or the apostolic epistle penetrated. 3) Although outside the periods of time already recounted, a universal, solemn, and actual preaching of the divine word did not always and everywhere reach all nations; nevertheless, God denied a universal calling to no nation, and envied no man access to the church. For God calls very many peoples a) through a less solemn calling, which occurs through the divine word read, or readable, which is transported into distant regions, or through the Jews, the bearers of the divine law, or through Christians, the guardians and messengers of both law and gospel, dispersed throughout the whole world. b) Through the fame of the church spread far and wide.

For the church is called catholic, not as if the assembly of believers in Christ were illustrious in every place, but because with hands always outstretched it invites all nations to itself, and excludes no people, no man, from its fellowship. c) Through the documents of divine beneficence, everywhere met with in the kingdom of nature. For divine benefits are pedagogical proclamations, and as it were certain trumpets, inviting all men to the court of God, where at last the evangelical mysteries are unfolded. d) Through the efficacious impulse of God, by which practical conclusions are awakened, and consciences are stimulated to inquire after the true worship of God and the assembly in which it flourishes. Prob. b. That nations in the past, and many peoples today, are destitute of the preaching of the word, is their own fault, not by the destined will or counsel of God, who simply denies the light of the gospel.

For 1) those peoples despise and maliciously reject the divine word. This we learn from the words of Paul, It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you: But since you repel it, and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles! And from the threat of the most just God, Behold! the days are coming, says Adonai Jehovah, in which I will send a famine into the land: Not a famine for bread, or a thirst for water; but for hearing the word of Jehovah: And from the parable of Christ, Concerning the man who, having sent out ministers, invited guests to the supper, but with little success, whence Christ concludes the parable thus, I say to you, that none of those men who were called shall taste of my supper. 2) They have neglected the calling and the knowledge concerning Christian dogmas and ceremonies in general, through fame, which today is universal.

For if the fame spread abroad concerning the wisdom of Solomon enticed the queen of Arabia to know Solomon distinctly; why should not the fame spread concerning Christ and his kingdom entice [men] to know Christ? Conf. 1 Kings X, 1. & Matt. XII, 42. They did not translate the pedagogical vocation, presented through the proposition of divine government and beneficence, and the effective [vocation], through the stirring up of practical conclusions and the pricks injected into the conscience, into use, namely, to inquire after the true worship of God and the assembly in which it flourishes.

Wherefore, they deprived themselves by their own fault of the saving vocation which is made through the preaching of the gospel.

This is taught by Paul, Rom. I, 18. 19. The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all impiety and injustice of men, who hold the truth in injustice.

For this reason, that τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ, that which can be known of God, is manifest in them: for God has manifested it to them. For his invisible things are perceived, being understood from the works of the creation of the world, and his eternal power and deity, so that they are without excuse: for this reason, that when they knew God, they did not glorify him as God.

The antithesis is that of Bellarmine, Cornelius Jansen, Beza, and others, who maintain that the gospel has not yet been preached in the whole world, and therefore that the vocation to the church is not universal.

Who rely on the following arguments: I.

Many are called to the church, Matt. XX, 16. ch. XXII, 14. Therefore, not all.

Resp.

Between many and all, there is no formal opposition: Because all are also many, e.g., God created all the stars, and they are very many.

By the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, Rom. V, 18.; who certainly are all.

Conf. Rom. V, 12 (*).

II. In the times of the O.T. the vocation to the kingdom of God was not universal, as the psalmist testifies, Ps.

CXLVII, 19. God revealed his statutes to Israel, he did not do so to the remaining nations.

Resp.

1) We have shown above that in the times of Adam and Noah a universal and actual vocation occurred.

2) The royal psalmist does not absolutely deny to the nations under the O.T. every vocation through the voice of conscience, nature, fame, and reading; but comparatively he denies them the solemn and actual vocation through the preaching of the divine word, which degree of comparison is indicated by the particle "so," as if to say:

God did not reveal his statutes to the nations as clearly and distinctly in the time of the O.T. as to the Israelites.

God invited in the time of the O.

T. also the nations.

Look to me, that you may be saved, all the ends of the earth, Is. XLV, 22.

Ps. XCVI, 3.

Many Gentiles, having cast off idolatry, professed the true God, from whose number are the Edomite, Jethro the Midianite, Uriah the Hittite, Rahab the Canaanite, Ruth the Moabitess, the Queen of Sheba, Naaman the Syrian, the Assyrian Ninevites, Nebuchadnezzar, Darius, Cyrus, and others.

In Jerusalem there were dwelling men εὐλαβεῖς (devout) from every nation that is under heaven, Acts

II, 5.

III. God in past ages allowed the nations to walk in their own ways, Acts XIV, 16.

Therefore, God in past ages did not call the nations to the church.

Resp.

The Apostles speak of the will of God not preceding, but following, because God in just judgment delivered the nations, stubbornly impious, to a reprobate mind, Rom. 1:28, which Gentiles deprived themselves of the saving vocation by their own fault.

Nor, however, was God without every sign, without every testimony of divine beneficence toward the Gentiles; because God never left Himself ἀμάρτυρον, i.e., without witness, Acts 14:17.

IV. The times of the O.T. are called times of ignorance, Acts 17:30.

In the time of the O.

Latin:

In quo formaliter consistit gratiosa vocatio ad ecclesiam? Vocatio gratiosa & salutaris formaliter consistit in manifestatione benevolentiae Dei universalis, & oblatione beneficiorum, merito Christi nobis partorum, per praedicationem evangelii.

Prob. S. Paullus, 1 Tim. II, 4. 5. 6. benevolentiam Dei Patris, redemptionem Iesu Christi universalem & praeconium evangelii connectit: vt homines omnes ad ecclesiam adducti gratia Dei & merito Christi fruantur.

Verba Apostoli sunt: Deus vult omnes salvos fieri, & ad agnitionem veritatis venire. Unus enim Deus est, unus etiam mediator Dei & hominum, homo Christus Iesus, qui dedit seipsum in pretium redemptionis, in testimonium propriorum temporum. Testimonium propriorum temporum est praeconium evangelii, quippe quod est testimonium Spiritus S. de Christo mediatore in ecclesia per ministerium verbi resonans, Io.

XV, 25. 27. Dicitur testimonium propriorum temporum; quia Apostoli & eorum successores suis temporibus testari debuerunt, quod Christus iam se tradiderit pro nobis in pretium redemptionis, quum in V. T. Prophetae testati sint, quod se traditurus sit. Quam ob rem ex intentione Dei omnes homines per praeconium evangelii convocandi sunt ad unum regnum gratiae, vt ipsis innotescat benevolentia Dei Patris, de salvandis omnibus hominibus, per Christum mediatorem catholicum.

Quaestio XI.

An Deus vult, ut vocatio ad regnum gratiae ad omnes homines pertingat? Sicut Deus omnium hominum intendit salutem: ita etiam vult, ut omnes ad ecclesiam vocentur.

Quod autem multi populi salutari vocatione destituantur, illud contingit ipsorum culpa, non destinata voluntate aut consilio Dei, praedicationem verbi ipsis absolute denegantis. Obs. Quando vocationem ad regnum Dei universalem asserimus, non hoc dicimus, quod omnibus & singulis hominibus actu, coram & immediate, per praecones, peculiariter missos, annuntiata sit doctrina evangelii; sed quod Deus misericordissimus doctrinam evangelicam de obtinenda salute per fidem in Christum tam clare promulgaverit, vt omnes omnino homines ad eius notitiam pervenire possint, ita, vt Deus nulli genti, nulli homini copiam illius doctrinae, ac viam, qua in notitiam ipsius pertingere queat, absoluto decreto denegaverit.

Prob. a. Assertionem nostram ex declaratione benevolentiae divinae universalis, de qua Paullus, 1 Tim. II, 4. Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri; & ad agnitionem veritatis venire, & Petrus, 2 ep. III, 9. Non vult Dominus ullos perire, sed omnes ad paenitentiam reverti, conf. Ezech. XXXIII, 11. E quibus colligimus: Quicunque cupidine salvandi, illuminandi, & convertendi omnes homines accensus est, ille nulli homini destinata voluntate praedicationem evangelii denegat: Atqui Deus misericordissimus &c.

E. Maior patet: quia qui vult finem, vult etiam medium ad obtinendum finem necessarium.

Sed praedicatio evangelii est necessaria ad illuminationem &c. 2) Vocatio universalis, solemnis & actualis tribus distinctis contingit vicibus: a) Prima vocatio facta est in Adamo, & per Adamum, post lapsum, qui evangelium de semine mulieris, contrituro caput serpentis, sive evangelium de Christo, quod a Deo acceperat, dubio procul non minus Caino, quam Setho inculcavit.

Sicut autem huius evangelii notitiam Sethus propagavit ad suam posteritatem, usque ad Noachum: ita eandem Cainus ad suos posteros potuisset transmittere. Quod autem Cainus eandem ad posteritatem suam non transfinisit, in caussa fuit ipsius & posterorum eius impietas, verbique diuini contemptus. b) Secunda vocatio vniversalis facta est post diluuium in Noacho, altero Adamo, & per Noachum, quippe qui erat praeco iustitiae, & factus est haeres iustitiae, quae iuxta fidem est, Praedicauit ergo Noachus filiis suis, eorumque posteris, iustitiam per fidem in Christum: Qui quamdiu vnius linguae & labii vsu coniuncti manserunt, Noachi, Semi aliorumque institutione imbuti sunt, vsque ad tempus, quo diuinitus immissa linguarum confusione dispersi sunt, a quibus post dispersionem in varias orbis partes vocatio ad omnes illorum posteros propagari poterat. c) Tertia vocatio vniversalis contigit tempore Apostolorum, qui missi sunt a Christo ad docendum omnes gentes, eundum in mundum vniuersum & praedicandum euangelium omni creaturae, teste Paulo, Euangelium praedicatum est omni creaturae, quae est sub caelo. Ex quo colligimus: Quicunque viuunt sub caelo, illis euangelium est praedicatum: Omnes & singuli homines viuunt sub caelo: E. Neque silentio praetereundum est testimonium Paulinum, quod habetur, In omnem terram exiuit sonus eorum, & in fines terrae habitabilis verba eorum.

Conf. Ex quo argumentamur: Quam late se extendit linea caeli, tam late percrebuit sonus euangelii: Atqui linea caeli per totum mundum se extendit: E. per totum mundum sonus euangelii percrebuit. Scite ait AMBROSIVS in cap. X. Rom.: Vbique audita est, & peruenit in omnem locum praedicatio nominis Christi. Vbi enim praesentia hominis praedicantis defuit, sonus tamen & fama peruenit. Argute etiam noster DANNHAVERVS: Quo non venit pes apostolorum, eo saltem sonus apostolicus, vel epistola apostolica penetrauit. 3) Quamuis extra iam recensitas temporum periodos, vniuersalis, solemnis & actualis verbi diuini praedicatio non semper & vbique omnibus gentibus obtigerit; nulli tamen genti Deus vniuersalem vocationem penitus denegauit, nulli homini aditum ad ecclesiam inuidit. Plurimos enim populos Deus vocat a) per vocationem minus solemnem, quae fit per verbum diuinum lectum, vel legibile, quod transfortatur in regiones dissitas, vel per Iudaeos, legis diuinae baiulos, vel per Christianos, tam legis, quam euangelii custodes & nuntios, toto terrarum orbe dispersos. b) Per famam de ecclesia longe lateque diffusam.

Ecclesia enim dicitur catholica, non quasi vbique locorum fit illustris coetus credentium in Christum, sed quia passis semper manibus omnes gentes ad se inuitat, nullum populum, nullum hominem a suo consortio excludit. c) Per documenta beneficentiae diuinae, in regno naturae vbique obuia. Sunt enim beneficia diuina praeconia pedagogica, & quasi quaedam tubicinia, ad aulam Dei vniuersos homines inuitantia, vbi demum mysteria euangelica panduntur. d) Per efficacem impulsum Dei, quo exsuscitantur conclusiones practicae, & stimulantur conscientiae ad inquirendum verum Dei cultum & coetum, in quo ille viget. Prob. b. Quod gentes olim, & hodie multi populi praedicatione verbi destituuntur, illorum fit culpa, non destinata voluntate, aut consilio Dei, lucem euangelii simpliciter denegantis.

Nam 1) illi populi verbum diuinum contemnunt & malitiose reiiciunt. Id quod discimus e verbis Pauli, Vobis erat necesse primo dici verbum Dei: Quoniam vero repellitis illud, & non dignos iudicatis vos ipsos vita aeterna, ecce vertimus nos ad gentes! Et e comminatione Dei iustissimi, Ecce! dies venturi sunt, dictum Adonai Iehouah, quibus immittam famem in terram: Non famem ad panem, aut sitim ad aquas; sed ad audiendum verbum Iehouae: Atque ex parabola Christi, De homine, emissis ministris, ad coenam conuiuas inuitante, sed successu exiguo, Vnde Christus parabolam ita concludit, Dico vobis, quod nemo virorum istorum, qui vocati fuerunt, gustaturus fit coenam meam. 2) Vocationem & notitiam de Christianorum dogmatibus ac caerimoniis in genere, per famam, quae hodie vniuersalis est, neglexerunt. quæ hodie vniuerfalis est, neglexerunt.

Quod si enim fama diuulgata de sapientia Salomonis allexit reginam Arabiae, ad distincte cognoscendum Salomonem; quidni fama sparsa de Christo & ipsius regno alliceret ad cognoscendum Christum? Conf. 1 Reg. X, 1. & Matth. XII, 42. Vocationem paedagogicam, obiectam per propositionem regiminis & beneficentiae diuinae, & effectiuam, per exuscitationem conclusionum practicarum & iniectos conscientiae stimulos, non traduxerunt ad vsum, scilicet ad inquirendum verum Dei cultum & coetum, in quo ille viget.

Quamobrem vocatione salutari, quae per praedicationem euangelii fit, sua se culpa priuarunt.

Docet hoc Paullus, Rom. I, 18. 19. Reuelatur ira Dei de caelo super omnem impietatem & iniustitiam hominum, qui veritatem in iniustitia detinent.

Propterea, quod τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ, quod cognosci potest de Deo, manifestum est in ipsis: Deus enim ipsis manifestauit. Nam inuisibilia ipsius a creatione mundi operibus intellecta perspiciuntur, aeternaque ipsius potentia & deitas, adeo, vt sint illi inexcusabiles: propterea, quod cum cognoscerent Deum, non, vt Deum, glorificauerunt.

Antithesis est Bellarmini, Cornelii Iansenii, Bezae, & aliorum, statuentium, euangelium nondum in toto mundo esse praedicatum, adeoque vocationem ad ecclesiam non esse vniuersalem.

Qui sequentibus innituntur argumentis: I.

Vocati sunt ad ecclesiam multi, Matth. XX, 16. c. XXII, 14. E. non omnes.

Resp.

Inter multos, & omnes, non est formalis oppositio: Quia omnes etiam sunt multi, v. gr. Deus condidit stellas omnes, easque bene multas.

Per vnius hominis inobedientiam multi sunt facti peccatores, Rom. V, 18.; qui certe sunt omnes.

Conf. Rom. V, 12 (*).

II. Temporibus V. T. vocatio ad regnum Dei non fuit vniuersalis, teste hierosfalte, Ps.

CXLVII, 19. Reuelauit Deus sua statuta Israëli, non sic fecit reliquis nationibus.

Resp.

1) Temporibus Adami & Noachi contigisse vocationem vniuersalem & actualem, supra ostendimus.

2) Psaltes regius non absolute gentibus sub V. T. omnem vocationem per vocem conscientiae, naturae, famae, lectionis, denegat; sed comparate iis denegat vocationem solennem & actualem per praedicationem verbi diuini, qui gradus comparationis particula sic innuitur, q. d.

Deus non tam clare & distincte tempore V. T. statuta sua reuelauit gentibus, quam Israëlitus.

Inuitauit Deus tempore, V.

T. etiam gentes.

Respicite ad me, vt saluemini omnes fines terrae, Es. XLV, 22.

Ps. XCVI, 3.

Multi gentiles, abiecta idololatria, mona sua vero Deo professi sunt, ex quorum numero sunt Idumaeus, Iethro Midianita, Vrias Hethita, Rachab Cananaea, Ruth Moabitis, Regina Sabaea, Naaman Syrus, Niniuitae Assyrii, Nabuchodonosor, Darius, Cyrus & alii.

Hierosolymae erant habitantes viri εὐλαβεῖς ex omni natione, quae sub caelo est, Act.

II, 5.

III. Deus fuit praeteritis aetatibus gentes ire vias suas, Act. XIV, 16.

E. Deus praeteritis aetatibus gentes non vocauit ad ecclesiam.

Resp.

Loquuntur Apostoli de voluntate Dei non antecedente, sed consequente, quia Deus iusto iudicio gentes, praefracte impias, tradidit in sensum reprobum, Rom. I, 28. qui gentiles sua se culpa salutari vocatione priuarunt.

Neque tamen Deus gentiles sine omni face, sine omni testimonio beneficentiae diuinae fuit; quia Deus se nunquam reliquit ἀμάρτυρον, i. e. intestatum, Act. XIV, 17.

IV. Tempora V. T. dicuntur tempora ignorantiae, Act. XVII, 30.

E. tempore V.


### Question XI. Does God will that the calling to the kingdom of grace should reach all men?: T. the universal benevolence of God, and the benefits acquired by Christ, were not known

T. the universal benevolence of God, and the benefits acquired by Christ, were not known.

Resp. The times of the O.T. are called times of ignorance comparatively, and in a certain respect; because the gospel concerning Christ was neither so clearly proposed nor so widely diffused in the times of the O.T. as in the times of the N.T. The gospel is said to have been silent in former ages, i.e., not revealed, Rom. 16:25. Resp.

The words of the apostolic text are: God is able to establish you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery, which was kept secret since the world began, but now is made manifest by the prophetic scriptures. The doctrine concerning Christ is a μυστήριον (mystery), because it is unknown to reason. This doctrine concerning Christ, as to its substance, is proposed in the Old Testament: for it is called a mystery revealed through the prophetic scriptures. But that Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Mary, is the promised Messiah, is a mystery that was silent in former times, in the illustrating of which mystery the whole New Testament is occupied.

The gospel is therefore called a mystery silent for a very long time: a) by reason of fulfillment; because what was promised in the O.T. was fulfilled in the N.T., with Christ exhibited in the flesh: b) by reason of clearer revelation; because it was revealed in the N.T. that Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Mary, is the Christ, which is not evident from the O.T.: c) by reason of more ample promulgation; because the gospel was propagated more widely in the N.T. than in the O.T.

VI. Who has believed our report? and to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed? Is. 53:1. Where the Prophet denies that the arm of the Lord has been revealed to all. But if the arm of the Lord (i.e., the power of Christ in redeeming the human race) has not been revealed to all, a universal vocation is asserted in vain.

Resp. The Prophet does not simply deny the universal revelation of the arm of the Lord; but looking to the times of the N.T., he teaches that few of the Jews were to believe in Christ, and that the greatest part of them would reject the benefit of the Lord through ἀπιστίαν (unbelief), as if it had not been revealed to them, so that the meaning is: Who among you (a few passively obedient ones excepted) draws faith in life from the preaching of the divine word, when most obstinately repel it and remain blind, just as if the gospel concerning Christ had not been revealed to them. The Prophet therefore denies that the revelation attained the effect intended or desired in all.

VII. That men were not called to the kingdom of Christ in the times of the New Testament, they attempt to prove from Matt. 10:5: Go not into the way of the Gentiles.

Resp. Distinguish between a vocation denied and one deferred, or delayed. The vocation of the Gentiles was deferred for a time, because the divine word had first to be inculcated upon the Jews, who, when they rejected the offered word, were set aside, and the transition was made to the Gentiles, Acts 13:46. The Gentiles were meanwhile called objectively, through the proofs of beneficence; effectively, through the stings of conscience; confusedly, through the report concerning the Israelite church, until a distinct and immediately saving vocation followed through the preaching of the gospel concerning Christ at the appointed time.

VIII. Paul and Timothy were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia and Bithynia, Acts 16:7. And the Holy Spirit did not wish... all to be called to the kingdom of Christ.

Resp. Distinguish between different times, or between different hours, and the delays of God. Although at the same moment of time in which the apostolic men wished to travel into Bithynia, they were prohibited by the Holy Spirit; Since He foresaw by the light of omniscience that the word to be preached would bring more utility in Macedonia at that time: yet that the gospel was preached afterwards in Asia and Bithynia, one may gather from 1 Pet. I, 1. Apoc. I, 11.

IX. That not all are called to the church, they strive to prove from 1 Cor. I, 26. Not many wise according to the flesh, not many noble, nor powerful are called. Compare Rom. VIII, 30, where those called are said to be justified. But not all are justified. Therefore, not all are called. Resp. In both places is understood a calling joined with the obedience and saving effect of the hearers, which is called a calling κατὰ πρόθεσιν, v. 28. For they are called according to purpose, who admit the efficacy of the calling passively, and submit themselves to the same with most humble obedience. Which, while the wise according to the flesh, the noble and the powerful do not do, they do not attain the saving effect of the calling.

X. Whatever calling is free, that is not universal: But the calling of sinful men to the church is free: Therefore, it is not universal. The major premise is evident; because a universal calling is said to be that by which all men living at all times and in all places are called. But a free calling is said to be that which, according to the most free disposition of God, can be completed and omitted, can happen now in this, now in another place, now at this, now at another point in time. The minor premise is proved: because the grace of the Holy Spirit calling is compared with the wind, which blows where it wishes, John III, 8. Resp. 1) A universal calling must be understood correctly. We do not maintain that God, through sent heralds of the gospel, has always and everywhere called all men actually, face-to-face and immediately, but that in three periods of time, viz. the time of Adam, Noah, and the Apostles, He notified the doctrine of the gospel to all men so clearly and solemnly that all men, who are obligated to search for the true religion, could have reached a saving knowledge of the same, and that God did not deny the evangelical doctrine to any nation or any man by an absolute decree. 2) The freedom of the calling grace is not repugnant to its universality. For this calling grace is universal by reason of the divine intention, by which God offers faith to all men, Acts XVII, 31; but it is free by reason of its execution. For the actual calling is free regarding the circumstances of manner, place, time, hour, delay, and limit. Conf. D. DANNFAV. H. C. p. 1938. 3) John III, 8 does not deal with the calling to the church, but with the incomprehensible manner of spiritual regeneration.

XI. The Apostles could not penetrate to the extreme provinces of the east, west, south, and north, and to distant islands within the short course of their lives, in such ignorance of nautical matters, and preach the gospel everywhere. Resp. The Apostles had many apostolic men as co-workers, who filled the orb of the earth both by living voice, and by written letters, and by the illustrious fame of the Christian religion. This is taught by histories and annals, the martyrdoms of all nations, and the councils of bishops gathered from Europe, Asia, and Africa. When, therefore, we say that the gospel has been preached in the whole world, we teach and believe that in the time of the Apostles the gospel was preached to all men in such a way that individuals had either the voice of the Apostles or the immediate fame, and that after the times of the Apostles those who previously only had the fame, had then the completed preaching. Conf. D. IOANN. ADAM OSIANDER in colleg. system. loc. X. p. 215.

XII. Experience has taught that many nations in China, Japan, and America had no knowledge of the preached gospel. Therefore, the gospel was not preached to them. Resp. 1) Those nations could have lost the treasure of the gospel received through their own negligence. 2) That traces of the Christian religion have been discovered among the Indians, OSORIUS commemorates; among the Chinese, GONZALES de MENDOZA reports; among the Americans, JEAN DE LÉRY testifies. See IOANN. ADAM OSIANDER l. c. p. 212.

XIII. Many myriads of infants of the gentiles are snatched away by a swift death in the tenderest flower of infancy, who have never been called to the church: therefore, the calling is particular. Resp. The infants of the gentiles were called in their ancestors, to whom the divine word had once been preached and the sacraments granted, so that they might keep these means holily and propagate them to their descendants. For just as they are rightly said to have been created in the image of God in Adam; so also they were called to salvation in their parents. And just as all infants are justly punished by the privation of the image of God, on account of the transgression of Adam: so also by the privation of the means, on account of the ingratitude of their parents . But they are extinguished by an untimely death, before they can inquire into the true worship of God, for the reason that the omniscient One foresaw that they, if they had grown up, would not have accepted the means of salvation, but would have contumaciously rejected them, just as their parents did of old.

Instance: The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, Ezek. XVIII, 20. Why, therefore, is the word denied to posterity, which their ancestors despised? Resp. The son shall not bear the sins of the father, if he has not consented to the sins of the father; of which if he makes himself a participant, he also becomes a participant in the punishment. But God foreknew the future contumacy of the infants of the gentiles, if they had lived longer, equal to the ferocity of their parents.

Latin:

T. beneuolentia Dei vniuersalis, & beneficia a Christo acquisita, non fuerunt cognita.

Resp. Tempora V. T. dicuntur tempora ignorantiae comparate, & certo respectu; quia euangelium de Christo temporibus V. T. neque tam clare propositum, neque tam late diffusum fuit, quam temporibus N. T. V. Euangelium prioribus saeculis dicitur tacitum, i. e. non reuelatum, Rom. XVI, 25. Resp.

Verba textus apostolici sunt: Deus stabilire vos potest secundum euangelium meum & praedicationem Iesu Christi, iuxta reuelationem mysterii, temporibus aeternis taciti, reuelati vero nunc per scripturas propheticas. Doctrina de Christo est μυστήριον, quia rationi est ignota. Haec doctrina de Christo, quantum ad substantiam, est proposita in vet. testamento: dicitur enim mysterium reuelatum per scripturas propheticas. Sed Iesum Nazarenum, Mariae filium, esse Messiam promissum, est mysterium prioribus temporibus tacitum, in quo mysterio illustrando totum occupatur nouum testamentum.

Dicitur itaque euangelium mysterium longissimo tempore tacitum: a) ratione impletionis; quia, quod in V. T. promissum erat, in N. T. impletum est, Christo in carne exhibito: b) ratione clarioris reuelationis; quia in N. T. reuelatum est, Iesum Nazarenum, Mariae filium, esse Christum, quod non constat ex V. T.: c) ratione amplioris promulgationis; quia euangelium in N. T. latius propagatum est, quam in V. T.

VI. Quis credit auditui nostro, & brachium Domini cui reuelatum est? Es. LIII, 1. Vbi Propheta negat, brachium Domini omnibus reuelatum esse. Sed si brachium Domini, (i. e. virtus Christi in redimendo genere humano) non omnibus reuelatum est; frustra asseritur vocatio vniuersalis.

Resp. Non simpliciter negat Propheta reuelationem brachii Domini vniuersalem; sed respiciens tempora N. T. docet, quod pauci ex Iudaeis in Christum sint credituri, & quod maxima ipsorum pars per ἀπιστίαν reiectura fit beneficium Domini, ac si ipsis reuelatum non esset, vt sensus sit: Quis vestrum (paucis passiué obsequiosis exceptis) ex praedicatione verbi diuini vitam fidem haurit, cum plerique illud obstinate repellant, & coeci maneant, perinde, ac si euangelium de Christo ipsis non esset reuelatum. Negat itaque Propheta, reuelationem in omnibus intentum vel optatum fortiri effectum.

VII. Quod temporibus noui testamenti non homines vocati fint ad regnum Christi, probatum eunt ex Matth. X, 5. Nolite abire in vias gentium.

Resp. Dist. inter vocationem denegatam, & dilatam, siue retardatam. Vocatio gentium ad tempus differebatur, propterea, quod verbum diuinum primum inculcandum erat Iudaeis, qui cum reiicerent oblatum verbum, deferebantur, & fiebat transitus ad gentes, Act. XIII, 46. Vocabantur interim gentiles obiectiue, per documenta beneficentiae; effectiue, per stimulos conscientiae; confuse, per famam de ecclesia Israëlitica, donec distincta & proxime salutaris vocatio per praedicationem euangelii de Christo statuto tempore sequebatur.

VIII. Paullus & Timotheus vetiti sunt a Spiritu S. verbum loqui in Asia & Bithynia Act. XVI, 7. E noluit Spiritus S.... omnes ad regnum Christi vocari.

Resp. Dist. inter diuersa tempora, siue inter diuersas horas, & moras Dei. Licet eodem temporis articulo, quo volebant viri apostolici commigrare in Bithyniam, prohiberentur a Spiritu Sancto; quoniam hic lumine omniscientiæ præuidebat, verbum prædicandum id temporis plus vtilitatis in Macedonia allaturum esse: postea tamen in Asia & Bithynia euangelium prædicatum esse, colligere licet ex 1 Petr. I, 1. Apoc. I, 11.

IX. Quod non omnes ad ecclesiam vocati sint, probare nituntur ex 1 Cor. I, 26. Non multi sapientes secundum carnem, non multi nobiles, neque potentes vocati sunt. Confer. Rom. VIII, 30. vbi vocati dicuntur iustificati. Sed non omnes sunt iustificati. E. nec omnes vocati. Resp. Vtrobique intelligitur vocatio coniuncta cum auditorum obsequio & salutari effectu, quæ appellatur vocatio κατὰ πρόθεσιν, v. 28. Sunt autem vocati secundum propositum, qui efficaciam vocationis passiue admittunt, & se eidem humillimo obsequio subiiciunt. Quod dum non faciunt sapientes secundum carnem, nobiles & potentes, salutarem vocationis effectum non consequuntur.

X. Quæcunque vocatio est libera, illa non est vniuersalis: Atqui vocatio hominum peccatorum ad ecclesiam est libera: E. non est vniuersalis. Maior constat; Quia vocatio vniuersalis dicitur, qua omnes homines omni tempore & omnibus locis viuentes vocantur. Sed vocatio libera dicitur, quæ pro liberrima Dei dispositione potest consummari & omitti, potest fieri iam hoc, iam alio loco, iam hoc, iam alio temporis articulo. Minor probatur: quia gratia Spiritus S. vocans comparatur cum vento, qui, vbi vult, spirat, Io. III, 8. Resp. 1) Vocatio vniuersalis dextre intelligenda est. Non statuimus, quod Deus per missos præcones euangelii semper & vbique omnes homines actu, coram & immediate vocauerit, sed quod tribus temporum periodis, scil. tempore Adami, Noachi, & Apostolorum, omnibus hominibus doctrinam euangelii tam clare ac solemniter notificauerit, vt omnes homines, qui ad scrutandam veram religionem obligati sunt, ad salutarem eiusdem notitiam pertingere potuissent, & quod Deus nulli genti, nulli homini doctrinam euangelicam absoluto decreto denegauerit. 2) Vniuersalitati gratiæ vocantis non repugnat eius libertas. Nam vniuersalis est hæc gratia vocans, ratione intentionis diuinæ, qua Deus omnibus hominibus fidem offert, Act. XVII, 31.; libera autem est, ratione exsecutionis. Vocatio enim actualis libera est, quoad circumstantias modi, loci, temporis, horæ, moræ, metæ. Conf. D. DANNFAV. H. C. p. 1938. 3) Io. III, 8. non agitur de vocatione ad ecclesiam, sed de incomprehensibili ratione regenerationis spiritualis.

XI. Apostoli non potuerunt ad extremas orientis, occidentis, meridiei, & septentrionis prouincias, insulasque dissitas intra exiguum vitæ decursum, in tanta rei nauticæ ignorantia penetrare, & vbique euangelium prædicare. Resp. Apostolis fuerunt cooperarii multi viri apostolici, qui & viua voce, & litteris scriptis, & illustri religionis christianæ fama terrarum orbem impleuerunt. Id quod docent historiæ & annales, martyria omnium nationum, concilia episcoporum ex Europa, Asia & Africa conuocatorum. Quando igitur dicimus, euangelium esse prædicatum in vniuerso orbe, docemus & credimus, quod Apostolorum tempore euangelium ita prædicatum sit omnibus hominibus, vt singuli habuerint vel vocem Apostolorum, vel famam proximam, & quod post Apostolorum tempora ii, qui antea tantum habuerunt famam, habuerint deinde prædicationem consummatam. Conf. D. IOANN. ADAM OSIANDER in colleg. system. loc. X. p. 215.
