XII. Experientia docuit, multas gentes in China, Iaponia, America nullam habuisse prædicati euangelii notitiam. E. iisdem euangelium non est prædicatum. Resp. 1) Gentes illæ thesaurum euangelii acceptum incuria sua potuerunt amittere. 2) Deprehensa esse vestigia religionis Christianæ apud Indos, commemorat OSORIVS, apud Chinenses, refert GONZAGES de MENDOZA, apud Americanos, testatur IOANNES LERIVS. Vid. IOANN. ADAM OSIANDER l. c. p. 212.

XIII. Multae myriades infantum gentilium in tenerrimo infantiae flore cita morte rapiuntur, quae nunquam ad ecclesiam vocatae sunt: E. vocatio est particularis. Resp. Infantes gentilium vocati sunt in maioribus, quibus olim verbum divinum praedicatum & sacramenta concessa fuerant, ut haec media sancte custodirent & ad posteros propagarent. Sicut enim recte dicuntur creati ad imaginem Dei in Adamo; ita & vocati sunt ad salutem in parentibus. Et sicut omnes infantes privatione imaginis Dei, ob transgressionem Adae, iuste puniuntur: ita & privatione mediorum, ob ingratitudinem parentum . Immatura autem morte, antequam in verum Dei cultum inquirere possint, exstinguuntur, ideo, quod omnisciens praevidit, ipsos si adolevissent, media salutis non accepturos, sed perinde, ac olim parentes, contumaciter reiecturos fuisse.

Instantia: Filius non portabit iniquitatem patris, Ezech. XVIII, 20. Cur igitur posteris denegatur verbum, quod maiores contemnerunt? Resp. Filius non portabit peccata patris, si non consenserit in peccata patris; quorum si se facit participem, etiam particeps fit poenae. Praesciit autem Deus infantum gentilium futuram contumaciam, si diutius in vivis fuissent, ferociae parentum parem.


### Quaest. XII. Is the calling of God by the word of the gospel sufficient for salvation?

The calling of God, by the word of the gospel preached and read, is sufficient for salvation.

Obf. We are speaking of the special calling through the gospel; whether it be solemn, through the gospel preached, or less solemn, through the gospel read, or readable. Furthermore, the general and pedagogical calling, dispensed through conscience and providence in the kingdom of nature, is sufficient for inquiring into the true worship of God and for seeking out the church; but the confused calling, spread through the report of the church, suffices for obtaining a weak and languid knowledge of the dogmas and ceremonies of the church.

Proof 1) Because through the gospel every counsel of God concerning our salvation is manifested. Acts 20:26. 2) Because those whom God has called, these (admitting the vocation passively) He has justified; those whom He has justified, these He has glorified. Rom. 8:30. Therefore, vocation is sufficient for salvation.

Latin:

Vocatio Dei, per verbum evangelii praedicatum & lectum, ad salutem sufficiens est.

Obs. Sermo nobis est de vocatione speciali per evangelium; sive illa sit solemnis, per evangelium praedicatum, sive minus solemnis, per evangelium lectum, aut legibile. Ceterum vocatio generalis & paedagogica, per conscientiam & providentiam in regno naturae dispensata, sufficiens est ad inquirendum verum Dei cultum & ad indagandam ecclesiam; vocatio autem confusa, per famam de ecclesia diuulgata, sufficit ad comparandam notitiam infirmam & languidam de dogmatibus & caerimoniis ecclesiae.

Prob. 1) Quia per evangelium manifestatur omne consilium Dei de nostra salute. Act. XX, 26. 2) Quia, quos Deus vocavit, hos (vocationem passive admittentes) iustificavit, quos iustificavit, hos glorificavit. Rom. VIII, 30. Ergo vocatio ad salutem sufficit.


### Question XIII. Is the vocation of all men universal, serious, and efficacious?

The universal vocation of all men by God to the kingdom of Christ is so serious that it is manifested not only by sign and precept, but also arises from the intimate divine good pleasure, and seriously intends the salutary illumination and conversion of all men .

The same is efficacious, because He wills all men to be brought to the kingdom of grace and glory through efficacious means .

Proof a. Proof a. The universal vocation of all men to the kingdom of Christ is serious: Because 1) it arises from the will of God, which is desirous of the salvation of men, 1 Tim. 2:4; 2 Pet. 3:9. 2) Because it is founded on the merit of Christ, 2 Cor. 5:19, and is confirmed by divine oath, Ezek. 23:11. 3) Just as a hen with serious affection gathers her chicks under her wings: so God sincerely wills to gather us into one church, Matt. 23:37. 4) God has called us to marvelous light, 1 Pet. 2:9, and commands all men everywhere to repent, Acts 17:30. Therefore, He intends the illumination and conversion of all whom He has called.

5) For which reason God also testifies in express words that the blame for why the impious, though called, are not converted, resides not in Himself, but in them, Prov. 1:24. I have called, and you have refused. Is. 65:2. I have spread out my hands all the day unto a rebellious people.

Proof b. The divine vocation is efficacious: 1) Because God intends the bringing of all men to the kingdom of grace and glory through efficacious means. For men are called by God through the gospel, which is Spirit and life, John 6:63, i.e., animated by the life-giving Spirit: From which it is commonly called the vehicle of the Holy Spirit: 2) Because the divine word has that efficacy of illuminating, converting, and regenerating, which the Holy Spirit has independently and by essence, it has dependently and by participation. Whence it is called the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth, Rom. 1:16. Infants are introduced into the kingdom of Christ through baptism, which is the washing of regeneration and renewing, Tit. 3:5.

You say: I. The internal vocation through the grace of the Holy Spirit, working in the hearts of the elect, is indeed efficacious: but the external vocation, which is done through the ministry of the word, is not always efficacious in the reprobate. I answer: If by external vocation is understood that by which God, through the preached word, as are (for they have hereditary sin in common with those infants who are born of Christian parents), nor would they in any way be partakers of the merit of the common Sponsor of all; or all others also, whom God likewise foresaw would be obstinate and emulators of their wicked ancestors, would have to be extinguished by premature death for the same reason. The latter is false and contrary to experience. The former seems harsh to me. These words are not to be understood simply concerning salutary grace, viewed in the universal, but comparatively and in a certain fixed manner, namely concerning the ordinary mode by which God confers His grace upon men, in our Apology of the Augsburg Confession, p. 156: The promise of salvation pertains also to infants: But it does not pertain to those (infants) who are outside the church of Christ, where there is neither word nor sacraments; because the kingdom of Christ exists only with the word and sacraments. See B. 10. HULSEMANN'S lectures on the Formula of Concord, p. 370, and B. CARPZOV'S Introduction to the Symbolic Books, p. 156 et seqq.

as a sign of his will, commands [men] to repent and believe, without an internal purpose of conferring sufficient strength for conceiving repentance and faith; the distinction of vocation into internal and external is not to be admitted or tolerated. For it is repugnant a) to divine truth. For if God were to call by an external word to the kingdom of grace a man who is reprobate by his own fault, without an internal purpose of drawing him and leading him to that kingdom; he would signify one thing by the external word, and would have decreed another by an internal purpose, which is far removed from the most truthful God. b) It is repugnant to divine goodness. For if God were to command that to a man which He did not will to be done by him, and, lest it be done, were to deny efficacious grace, He would not be good, but would be mocking the man: just as in the judgment of all, a prince would mock him to whom he commanded something under penalty of death, which he did not will to be done by him, and from whom, lest it could be done by him, he withdrew sufficiently valid means. If Christ had said to the paralytic: Take up your bed and walk, Matt. IX, 6, and yet had not willed to bestow upon him the strength to rise, He would have mocked the paralytic. c) It is repugnant to divine wisdom. It is not the part of a wise person to offer means to a man in need of help, which are vain and useless due to a defect of his own assistance. If God at the beginning of creation had said to the creatures: Increase and multiply, and yet had not implanted in them the generative power, that command would have been void, and thus far removed from divine wisdom.

You say: II. By external vocation the reprobate are called: a) that they may be admonished of their duty, b) that they may not be excusable. Resp. to a). The most benign God does not demand duty, without benefit and sufficient means being offered. For how could He demand duty from him to whom neither birth nor gifts supply strength, and from whom God altogether withdraws all grace, without which duty cannot be performed? To b). By external vocation, without an internal purpose of conferring sufficient strength, not every excuse is taken away from the reprobate. For they will be able to say: Lord, we would most willingly have come into your kingdom, we would have believed, and we would have done the duty of a Christian man, provided you had willed to bestow upon us wretches the strength which you could have.

You say: III. Whoever are efficaciously called, they believe. But most men do not believe. Therefore. The major is proved from Heb. IV, 2. The word heard did not profit, not being mixed with faith by those who heard. Resp. 1) Distinguish between vocation efficacious by reason of the cause, and of the effect. Vocation is efficacious on the part of God, as the cause, seriously destining efficacious means through which faith as a salutary effect can be produced; but this effect is hindered by malicious resistance: just as medicine is efficacious in the first act; but in the second act it does not heal, if it is neglected or rejected. 2) The cited words of the Apostle: ἐκ ὠφέλησεν ὁ λόγος τῆς ἀκοῆς ἐκείνους, μὴ συγκεκραμένος τῇ πίστει τοῖς ἀκέσασιν, are to be rendered in Latin: the word heard did not profit them, not being mixed through faith with those who heard. The things to be mixed are not the word of hearing and faith; since the word of hearing produces faith: for how would a cause be mixed with its effect? But the word of hearing, and those who hear the word. These conceive faith from hearing, unless they maliciously resist the operation of the Holy Spirit. Confer SEB. SCHMID. in comment. h. l. p. 418.

Latin:

Vocatio Dei universalis omnium hominum ad regnum Christi adeo seria est, vt non tantum signo & praecepto manifestetur, sed etiam ex intimo beneplacito divino oriatur, omniumque hominum salutarem illuminationem & conversionem serio intendat a).

Eadem est efficax, quia omnes homines per efficacia media ad regnum gratiae & gloriae vult adductos b).

Prob. a. Seria est vocatio universalis omnium hominum ad regnum Christi: Quia 1) oritur ex voluntate Dei, hominum salutis cupida, 1 Tim. II, 4. 2 Petr. III, 9. 2) Quia fundatur in merito Christi, 2 Cor. V, 19. & firmatur iuramento divino, Ezech. XXIII, 11. 3) Quemadmodum gallina serio affectu pullos suos congregat sub alas suas: Ita Deus sincere vult nos congregare in una ecclesia, Matth. XXIII, 37. 4) Deus vocavit nos ad mirabilem lucem, 1 Petr. II, 9. & praecipit omnibus ubique, ut resipiscant, Act. XVII, 30. E. omnium illuminationem & conversionem, quos vocavit, intendit.

5) Quam ob rem Deus etiam culpam, cur impii, licet vocati, non convertantur, non in se, sed in illis residere, disertis verbis testatur, Prou. I, 24. Vocavi, & renuistis. Es. LXV, 2. Expandi manus meas toto die ad populum rebellem.

Prob. b. Efficax est vocatio divina: 1) Quia Deus omnium hominum adductionem ad regnum gratiae & gloriae per efficacia media intendit. Vocantur enim homines a Deo per evangelium, quod est Spiritus & vita, Io. VI, 63. i. e. Spiritu vivificante animatum: Ex quo communiter vocatur vehiculum Spiritus S.: 2) Quia verbum divinum eam efficaciam illuminandi, convertendi, regenerandi, quam Spiritus S. habet independenter & per essentiam, habet dependenter & per participationem. Vnde dicitur potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti, Rom. I, 16. Infantes introducuntur in regnum Christi per baptismum, qui est lavacrum regenerationis & renovationis, Tit. III, 5.

Dicis: I. Vocatio interna per gratiam Spiritus S., operantis in cordibus electorum, est quidem efficax: at vocatio externa, quae fit per ministerium verbi, non est semper efficax in reprobis. Resp. Si per vocationem externam intelligitur ea, qua Deus verbo praedicato, tanquam rentur (peccatum enim hereditarium commune illi habent cum his infantibus, qui christianis parentibus orti sunt), nec meriti Sponsoris omnium communis ullo modo essent participes; aut omnes etiam alii, quos Deus pariter praevidit, obstinatos fore, atque improborum maiorum aemulos, eamdem ob caussam, praematura morte extinguendi essent. Posterius est falsum, atque experientiae contrarium. Prius durum mihi videtur. Non simpliciter de gratia salutari, in universum spectata, sed comparate & certa quadam ratione, nimirum de ordinario modo, quo suam Deus gratiam in homines confert, intelligenda sunt haec verba, in nostra Apolog. Aug. Conf. p. 156: Promissio salutis pertinet etiam ad parvulos: Neque vero pertinet ad illos (parvulos), qui sunt extra ecclesiam Christi, ubi nec verbum, nec sacramenta sunt; quia regnum Christi tantum cum verbo & sacramentis exsistit. Vid. B. 10. HVLSEMANNI praelect. in F. C. p. 370. & B. CARPZOVII Isag. in Libros Symb. p. 156. seqq.

tanquam voluntatis signo, praecipit resipiscere & credere, sine interno proposito conferendi sufficientes ad resipiscentiam & fidem concipiendam vires; distinctio vocationis in internam & externam non admittenda, aut toleranda est. Repugnat enim a) veritati divinae. Nam si Deus verbo externo vocaret ad regnum gratiae hominem, qui sua culpa reprobus est, sine interno proposito, eum trahendi & adducendi ad illud regnum; aliud verbo externo significaret, aliud interno proposito decrevisset, quod a Deo veracissimo longe alienissimum est. b) Repugnat bonitati divinae. Si enim Deus id homini praeciperet, quod fieri ab ipso nollet, & ne fieret, gratiam efficacem denegaret, non fuisse bonus esset, sed illuderet homini: sicut omnium iudicio princeps ei illuderet, cui sub poena mortis praeciperet aliquid, quod ab eo fieri nollet, & cui, ne fieri per eum posset, media satis valida subtraheret. Si Christus dixisset paralytico: Tolle grabbatum tuum & ambula, Matth. IX, 6. neque tamen vires surgendi ei largiri voluisset, paralytico illusisset. c) Repugnat sapientiaedivinae. Non est sapientis, offerre media homini, opis indigo, ex defectu auxilii sui vana & inutilia. Si Deus in principio creationis dixisset creaturis: Crescite & multiplicamini, neque tamen vim generativam ipsis indidisset, illud mandatum fuisset irritum, atque adeo a sapientia divina alienum.

Dicis: II. Vocatione externa reprobi vocantur: a) vt sui officii admoneantur, b) ne sint excusabiles. Resp. ad a). Deus benignissimus nonexigit officium, sine beneficio & sufficientibus atque mediis oblatis. Quomodo enim exigeret officium ab eo, cui natae, neque datiae, suppetunt vires, & cui Deus prorsus omnem subtrahit gratiam, sine qua officium praestari nequit? Ad b). Vocatione externa, sine interno proposito conferendi sufficientes vires, reprobis non omnis adimitur excusatio. Poterunt enim dicere: Domine, libentissime in regnum tuum venissemus, credidissemus, & officium hominis christiani fecissemus, modo nobis miseris vires, quas potuisti, largiri voluisses.

Dicis: III. Quicunque efficaciter vocati sunt, illi credunt. Sed plurimi homines non credunt. Ergo. Maior probatur ex Hebr. IV, 2. Non prodest sermo auditus, non commixtus cum fide ab iis, qui audierunt. Resp. 1) Dist. inter vocationem efficacem ratione causae, & effectus. Vocatio efficax est ex parte Dei, tanquam causae, serio destinantis media efficacia, per quae fides velut salutaris effectus produci potest; sed hic effectus a malitiosa repugnantia impeditur: sicut medicina actu primo est efficax; actu autem secundo non sanat, si negligatur, aut reiiciatur. 2) Verba citata Apostoli: ἐκ ὠφέλησεν ὁ λόγος τῆς ἀκοῆς ἐκείνους, μὴ συγκεκραμένος τῇ πίστει τοῖς ἀκέσασιν, reddenda sunt latine: non profuit illis sermo auditus, non commixtus per fidem cum iis, qui audierunt. Res commiscendae sunt non sermo auditionis & fides; cum sermo auditionis fidem producat: quomodo autem causa cum effectu suo commiscebitur? Sed sermo auditionis, & ii, qui sermonem audiunt. Hi ex auditu fidem concipiunt, nisi operationi Spiritus S. malitiosae resistant. Confer. SEB. SCHMID. in comment. h. l. p. 418.


### Quaest. XIV. Is the vocation to the church equal?

Ordinary vocation is equal in substance, or insofar as it is essentially viewed a): but it is unequal by reason of order, mode and degree, hour and manner b). Prob. a. Ordinary vocation is equal: because 1) we call by grace equally salutary. The grace of God salutary has appeared to all men, as Paul says, Tit. II, 11. Just as the same sun shines upon all: so the same light of saving grace illuminates all men, who do not maliciously close the eyes of the mind. who do not maliciously close. who do not maliciously close. who do not maliciously close.

2) Because the same powers of believing are offered to all, which God also intends to confer upon all, unless they are perversely and stubbornly rejected. Whence God is said to provide (παρέχειν) faith to all, Acts XVII, 31. The reborn also receive ἰσότιμον πίσιν, a faith equally precious (the equally-dear faith), 2 Pet. I, 1. Faith is indeed, by reason of degree, one greater, another smaller: yet it is equal a) by reason of the cause; because it is kindled by the same Holy Spirit: b) by reason of the object; because the faith of all men embraces the same mercy of God, the same Jesus, the same promise: c) by reason of the end; since it looks toward the same crown of righteousness, 2 Tim. IV, 8.

3) Because we are called by the same means, by the same gospel, by the same equally efficacious baptism, if you look at the divine purpose.

Proof b. The inequality of the divine vocation, considered accidentally, is evident: for the reason that 1) by reason of order, the word of the gospel was to be preached first to the Jews, afterwards to the Gentiles, Acts XIII, 46.

2) By reason of mode and degree, a greater light shone upon some, a lesser upon others. Some nations were called through the word solemnly preached; others through the word written and read, supplied by Jews or Christians; others through the report spread about the church, and that either nearer and clearer, or more remote and obscure.

3) By reason of delay and hour, some peoples were called sooner, others later. Upon some, the light of the gospel shone for a longer stretch of time; among others, it was obscured within a few years. Since this accidental inequality cannot be thoroughly investigated in this mortality, let us acquiesce in the divine dispensation of the means of salvation, let us confess, and let us marvel, but let us not anxiously probe the abyss of divine judgments, impenetrable to human minds, Rom. XI, 33.

You say: I. If the vocation to the kingdom of grace were equal; two men, hearing the same divine word, would be converted equally. The consequent is false, as the example of Peter and Judas shows, among others: Therefore, the antecedent is false. I reply: 1) That two, hearing the same divine word, are not converted equally, that is not to be imputed to the principal and organic cause, God and the gospel, but to the subjects, or men, behaving themselves in diverse ways, of whom some embrace the offered grace, some repudiate it. Some men use pedagogical powers, some abuse them. In some, the resistance is simple, in others affected and stubborn. Hence it happens that the gospel does not achieve the same effect in two hearers, just as seed, equally efficacious, scattered into different soil, does not fructify equally. 2) As regards the example of Peter and Judas, the same grace was offered to them, but admitted by Peter, repelled by Judas. Peter sinned, led by the present danger of life; Judas, prompted by mere malice, and from a will clearly free. The former looked upon Christ with a sad eye, desirous of medicinal grace; the latter with a wicked and hypocritical eye. The latter followed the seducing high priests, whom the former fled. The latter forgot the word of Christ; the former remembered it.

You say: II. If the reason for the distinction between faith and infidelity can be detected in the subjects: it follows that the believer can distinguish himself from the unbeliever: The consequent is false. Therefore, the antecedent is also. The falsity of the consequent is evident from 1 Cor. IV, 7. Who distinguishes you? What do you have that you have not received? I reply: The cited passage does not pertain directly to the ascent of faith and the perseverance of infidelity, because the Apostle is speaking of the diversity of charisms already possessed, which the Corinthians were abusing for pride and arrogance. But if it is referred analogically to the distinction between the believer and the unbeliever, one must distinguish between active and passive distinction. The believer from the unbeliever the infidel does not distinguish himself actively, by disposing himself to faith through natural powers, but is distinguished by God, because he passively admits the offered means.

You say: III. Whatever calling occurs by the same means indeed, but operating unequally, that is an unequal calling: Calling to the kingdom of God etc. Therefore. The major is clear: because unequal operation makes an unequal calling. The minor is proved: because the word of God is to some a savor of life unto life, to others a savor of death unto death, 2 Cor. II, 16. I respond:

In itself and from the intention of God, the divine word is to all who are called a savor of life unto life, which is Spirit and life, Io. VI, 63. Accidentally, and by the vice of men who disdain it, it becomes a savor of death unto death: just as Christ is to the pious a rock of salvation, to the impious a rock of offense, 1 Petr. II, 7. Wine is for the use of the healthy, but for the harm of those with a fever.

You say: IV. Whatever grace of calling is sufficient for salvation to some, but insufficient to others, that is an unequal grace of calling to the kingdom of Christ etc. Therefore. The minor is proved from the words of Christ, Matth. XI, 21. Woe to thee Chorazin! Woe to thee Bethsaida! For if the mighty works which were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. From which words it is evident that the grace sufficient for the Tyrians was insufficient for the Chorazinites.

I respond: 1) The grace of calling is called equal, not by reason of the effect or outcome, but by reason of the intention and the means. 2) The cited passage deals with an extraordinary calling, of which the Tyrians and Sidonians were destitute, who nevertheless were called through the fame of the Israelite church, conspicuous for so many miracles, of which they were neighbors. 3) Comparatively, the obstinacy of the Chorazinites was greater than that of the Tyrians. If the divine word, backed by the miracles of Christ, had been preached to them just as it was to the Chorazinites, it would have been a sufficiently valid means for performing repentance.

Latin:

Vocatio ordinaria aequalis est in substantia, sive quatenus essentialiter spectatur a): sed inaequalis est ratione ordinis, modi & gradus, horae & more b). Prob. a. Aequalis est vocatio ordinaria: quia 1) vocamus gratia aeque salutari. Apparuit gratia Dei salutaris omnibus hominibus, dicente Paulo, Tit. II, 11. Quem ad modum idem sol omnibus affulget: ita eadem lux gratiae salutiferae illuminat omnes homines, qui oculos mentis malitiosae non claudunt. malitiose non claudunt. malitiose non claudunt. malitiose non claudunt.

2) Quia eædem vires credendi omnibus offeruntur, quas etiam Deus, nisi proterue & morofe reiiciantur, omnibus conferre intendit. Vnde Deus omnibus fidem præbere (παρέχειν) dicitur, Act. XVII, 31. Accipiunt etiam renati ἰσότιμον πίσιν fidem æque pretiosam, (den gleich-theuren Glauben) 2 Petr. I, 1. Est quidem fides, ratione gradus, alia maior, alia minor: æqualis tamen est a) ratione causæ; quia ab eodem Spiritu S. accenditur: b) ratione obiecti; quia omnium hominum fides eandem misericordiam Dei, eundem Iesum, eandem promissionem amplectitur: c) ratione finis; quoniam eandem respicit coronam iustitiæ, 2 Tim. IV, 8.

3) Quia vocamur iisdem mediis, eodem euangelio, eodem baptismo æque efficaci, si propositum diuinum spectes.

Prob. b. Inæqualitas vocationis diuinæ, accidentaliter consideratæ, constat: propterea, quod 1) ratione ordinis primum Iudæis, postea gentibus verbum euangelii erat prædicandum, Act. XIII, 46.

2) Ratione modi & gradus, quibusdam illuxit lumen maius, quibusdam minus. Aliæ gentes vocatæ sunt per verbum solemniter prædicatum; aliæ per verbum scriptum & lectum, a Iudæis aut Christianis subministratum; aliæ per famam de ecclesia sparfam, eainque vel propiorem & clariorem, vel remotiorem & obscuriorem.

3) Ratione moræ & horæ, quidam populi citius, quidam tardius sunt vocati. Nonnullis longiori temporis tractu lux euangelii fulsit: apud nonnullos intra paucos annos obfuscata est. Quæ accidentalis inæqualitas cum in hac mortalitate nequeat penitus peruestigari, in dispensatione diuina mediorum salutis acquiescamus, fateamur, & miremur, non autem anxie rimeinur abyssum iudiciorum diuinorum, mentibus humanis imperuiam, Rom. XI, 33.

Dicis: I. Si vocatio ad regnum gratiæ æqualis esset; duo homines, idem verbum diuinum audientes, ex æquo conuerterentur. Consequens esse falsum, inter alia ostendit exemplum Petri & Iudæ: E. falsum est antecedens. Refp. 1) Quod duo, idem verbum diuinum audientes, non ex æquo conuertantur, id non imputandum est causæ principali & organicæ, Deo & euangelio, sed subiectis, siue hominibus, diuersimode se habentibus, quorum quidam gratiam oblatam amplectuntur, quidam repudiant. Quidam homines viribus pædagogicis vtuntur, quidam abutuntur. In aliis resistentia actualis est simplex, in aliis affectata & morosa. Inde fit, vt euangelium in duobus auditoribus non eundem fortiatur effectum, sicut femen, æque efficax, in diuersum agrum dispersum, non ex æquo fructificat. 2) Quod attinet ad exemplum Petri & Iudæ, eadem ipsis gratia est oblata, fed admissa a Petro, repulsa a Iuda. Peccabat Petrus, adductus præsenti periculo vitæ, Iudas instinctus mera malitia, & ex voluntate plane libera. Ille adspiciebat Christum oculo tristi, gratiæ medicinalis cupido, hic oculo nequam & hypocritico. Hic fequebatur pontifices seducentes, quos ille fugiebat. Hic verbum Christi oblitus, ille recordatus erat.

Dicis: II. Si ratio discriminis fidei & infidelitatis in subiectis deprehendi potest: sequitur, quod fidelis ab infideli seipsum possit discernere: Consequens est falsum. E. & antecedens. Consequentis falsitas patet ex 1 Cor. IV, 7. Quis te discernit? Quid habes, quod non acceperis? Refp. Locus citatus ad ascensionem fidei & perseuerantiam infidelitatis non pertinet directe, quia loquitur Apostolus de diuersitate charismatum iam habitorum, quibus Corinthii ad fastum & superbiam abutebantur. Sin analogice ad discrimen fidei & infidelis referatur, distinguendum est inter discretionem actiuam, & passiuam. Fidelis ab infideli se non discernit active, per vires naturales se ad fidem disponendo, sed discernitur a Deo, quia oblata media passive admittit.

Dicis: III. Quaecunque vocatio fit medio eodem quidem, sed inaequaliter operante, illa est inaequalis: Vocatio ad regnum Dei &c. Ergo. Maior liquet: quia inaequalis operatio inaequalem facit vocationem. Minor probatur: quia verbum Dei aliis est odor vitae ad vitam, aliis odor mortis ad mortem, 2 Cor. II, 16.

Resp. Per se & ex intentione Dei, verbum divinum omnibus, qui vocantur, est odor vitae ad vitam, quod est Spiritus & vita, Io. VI, 63. Per accidens, & vitio hominum, illud fastidientium, fit odor mortis ad mortem: sicut Christus est piis petra salutis, impiis petra scandali, 1 Petr. II, 7. Vinum sanis est usui, febricitantibus fraudi.

Dicis: IV. Quaecunque gratia vocationis quibusdam ad salutem sufficiens, quibusdam insufficiens est, illa est inaequalis gratia vocationis ad regnum Christi &c. Ergo. Minor probatur e verbis Christi, Matth. XI, 21. Vae tibi Chorazim! Vae tibi Bethsaida! Si enim Tyri & Sidone factae essent virtutes, quae factae sunt in vobis, olim in cilicio & cinere poenitentiam egissent. E quibus verbis constat, gratiam Tyriis sufficientem, Chorazinis fuisse insufficientem.

Resp. 1) Aequalis dicitur gratia vocationis, non ratione effectus, aut eventus; sed ratione intentionis & mediorum. 2) Loco citato agitur de vocatione extraordinaria, qua destituti fuerunt Tyrii & Sidonii, qui tamen per famam de Israëlitica ecclesia, tot miraculis conspicua, cuius contermini fuerunt, vocati sunt. 3) Comparatiue maior erat pertinacia Chorazinorum, quam Tyriorum. His si verbum divinum, miraculis Christi stipatum, aeque ac Chorazinis, praedicatum fuisset, satis validum fuisset medium ad agendam poenitentiam.


### Quaest. XV. What is the end of the calling to the church?

The ultimate end of our calling, on the part of God, is the glory of the divine name , on the part of men the ultimate end is their eternal salvation . Intermediate ends, to be recognized practically and salutarily under the guidance of scripture, according to the diverse respects of salutary conversion, are divided into antecedent, constituent, and consequent .

Prob. a. From 1 Petr. II, 8. You are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a peculiar people; that you may show forth the virtues of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light. To the church, which is a chosen assembly of men, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people ordained for the acquisition of salvation, we have been called to this end, that we may proclaim the virtues (the power, wisdom, grace, and justice, which shine forth most in the business of calling) of God, who called us from the darkness of ignorance to the marvelous light of faith. Prob. b.

The ultimate end, on our part, is eternal salvation. For we have been called to the prize, Phil. III, 14. to the inheritance of blessing, 1 Petr. III, 19. to eternal glory, 1 Petr. V, 10. to eternal life, 1 Tim. VI, 12. Prob. c.

We have been called to repentance, Matth. IX, 13. from darkness to light, 1 Petr. II, 9. to the communion of the Son of God, 1 Cor. I, 9. to sanctification, 1 Thess. IV, 7. to peace, Col. III, 15. to charity, flowing from the one hope of our calling, Eph. IV, 4. to sufferings, of which Christ left us an ὑπογραμμὸν, i.e., an example, or a delineated form, 1 Petr. II, 21. Quaest.

Latin:

Finis vocationis nostrae ultimus, ex parte Dei, est nominis divini gloria , ex parte hominum finis ultimus est aeterna ipsorum salus . Fines intermedii, practice & salutariter agnoscendi ductu scripturae, secundum diversos respectus salutaris conversionis, diuiduntur in antecedentes, constituentes, & consequentes .

Prob. a. Ex 1 Petr. II, 8. Vos estis genus electum, regium sacerdotium, gens sancta, populus in peculium; ut virtutes enumeretis eius, qui e tenebris vos vocauit in admirabilem suam lucem. Ad ecclesiam, quae est coetus hominum electus, regium sacerdotium, gens sancta, populus ad acquisitionem salutis ordinatus, vocati sumus eo fine, ut depraedicemus virtutes (potentiam, sapientiam, gratiam & iustitiam, quae elucent maxime in negotio vocationis) Dei, qui nos vocauit a tenebris ignorantiae ad mirabilem lucem fidei.

Prob. b. Finis ultimus, ex parte nostri, est aeterna salus. Vocati enim sumus ad brabeum, Phil. III, 14. ad hereditatem benedictionis, 1 Petr. III, 19. ad aeternam gloriam, 1 Petr. V, 10. ad vitam aeternam, 1 Tim. VI, 12.

Prob. c. Vocati fuimus ad poenitentiam, Matth. IX, 13. a tenebris ad lucem, 1 Petr. II, 9. ad communionem Filii Dei, 1 Cor. I, 9. ad sanctificationem, 1 Thess. IV, 7. ad pacem, Col. III, 15. ad caritatem, fluentem ex vna spe vocationis, Eph. IV, 4. ad passiones, quarum Christus nobis reliquit ὑπογραμμὸν, i. e. exemplar, aut formam delineatam, 1 Petr. II, 21.


### XVI. What use does the meditation of our calling confer upon us?

The consideration of the calling to the church provides a) a paracletic use, having brought us to the kingdom of Christ, which is not only a kingdom of the cross, but also of light; b) a paraenetic use, for leading a life worthy of our calling.

Prob. a. In the kingdom of Christ, there is an alternation of cross and light. The cross represses the ferocity of the flesh: the light of grace and consolation refreshes the soul. We are therefore certain that the God of all grace, who has called us to his eternal glory in Christ Jesus, after we have suffered a little, will restore, establish, strengthen, and settle us, 1 Pet. V, 10.

Prob. b. Walk worthy of the vocation wherewith you have been called! Eph. IV, 1. For God has not called you to uncleanness, but to holiness, 1 Thess. IV, 7. Therefore, according to him who has called us, who is holy, let us also be holy in all manner of conversation, 1 Pet. I, 15.

S I G H.

To thee, O immortal God! I render immortal thanks, that thou hast brought me, by nature a child of wrath, to the kingdom of grace and the office of thy most holy Spirit. That I was born in the bosom of the church, is thine. That I was sprinkled with the saving water and made a member of the mystical body of Christ, is thine. That the bowels of thy mercy are open to me, and the benefits procured by the blood of the Savior are offered to me, is thine. Recalling all this with a grateful memory, I pray as a suppliant that thou wouldst preserve and protect me in thy kingdom against the insults of the devil, the world, and my own flesh, and supply me with spiritual strength, that I may pass a life worthy of the gospel, worthy of a Christian man!

Latin:

Consideratio vocationis ad ecclesiam praestat a) usum paracleticum nobis adductus ad regnum Christi, quod non tantum regnum crucis, sed & lucis est; b) usum paraeneticum, ad traducendam vitam, vocatione nostra dignam.

Prob. a. In regno Christi crucis, & lucis datur vicissitudo. Crux ferociam carnis reprimit: Lux gratiae & solatii animam reficit. Certi igitur sumus, quod Deus omnis gratiae, qui vocauit nos ad aeternam suam gloriam in Christo Iesu, postquam parum passi fuerimus, nos instauraturus, stabiliturus, confortaturus, fundaturus sit, 1 Pet. V, 10.

Prob. b. Digne ambuletis vocatione, qua vocati estis! Eph. IV, 1. Non autem vocauit vos Deus ad immunditiem, sed ad sanctitatem, 1 Thess. IV, 7. Idcirco iuxta eum, qui vocauit nos, sanctum, ipsi etiam sancti in omni conuersatione simus, 1 Pet. I, 15.

S V S P I R I V M.

Tibi, o Deus immortalis! immortales persoluo gratias, quod me, natura filium irae, ad regnum gratiae & officium Spiritus tui sanctissimi adduxeris. Quod in gremio ecclesiae natus sum, tuum est. Quod aqua salutari perfusus, membrum corporis Christi mystici factus sum, tuum est. Quod viscera misericordiae tuae mihi patent, & parta sanguine Saluatoris beneficia mihi oblata sunt, tuum est. Id omne grata subinde recolens memoria, precor supplex, vt me in regno tuo aduersus insultus diaboli, mundi, carnisque meae, serues protegasque, & spirituales mihi sufficias vires, vt transigam vitam dignam euangelio, dignam homine christiano!


## 20 On Illuminating Grace, and Illumination


### Of Illuminating Grace, or of the Illumination of the Sinner Called to the Church

Quest. I. What is illumination? Illumination is an act of applying grace, by which the Holy Spirit teaches the sinful man, called to the church, through the ministry of the word, and informs him more and more with sincere zeal, so that, having dispelled the darkness of ignorance and errors, He imbues him with the knowledge of the word of God itself, and instills into him from the law the acknowledgment of sin, and from the gospel the knowledge of divine mercy, founded upon the merit of Christ. Obs.

I. Illuminating grace is also called teaching grace; because the Holy Spirit, by illuminating, teaches all things necessary for salvation, John XIV, 26.

Conf. DANNHAV. in hodof. phaenom. IX. p. 938. & lact. catechet. part. VI. p. 195. Likewise anointing grace, from 1 John II, 20. 27.

For it is a chrism not only medicinal and comforting, but also shining forth, the type of which was that chrism which was formerly given to kings and priests and prophets, with instruction for the liturgy of their office, and a change into other men.

Furthermore, illumination is called the opening of the eyes of the mind, Acts XXVI, 18. For just as a blind man obtains the faculty of seeing through the opening of his eyes: so the sinner, filled with the darkness of ignorance, receives through the illumination of the Holy Spirit the faculty of knowing the true God.

Obs. II. Here is not understood objective illumination, by which the light of the divine word is proposed externally, but effective, by which the Holy Spirit kindles the light of knowledge, and subjective, by which the blind sinner, through the operation of the Holy Spirit, suffers himself to be illuminated.

Obj. III. That preparing divine grace consists in illumination is asserted by D. FECHTIVS in his Dissert. de ordine modoque gratiae divinae, aphorism IX, p. 18, although that most celebrated Theologian simultaneously confesses that the term "illumination" is slightly broader than preparing grace. For the latter precedes conversion, whereas some illumination—namely, a more abundant one—also follows conversion. In what manner are Theologians to be reconciled when they refer illumination now to preparing grace, now to indwelling grace?

The primary and principal reason for illumination consists in preparing man for conversion. For it is for this reason that natural darkness, ignorance of the mysteries, and errors opposed to them are expelled from the human intellect through grace, and he is imbued with the knowledge of God and sacred things, and is enlightened as if by a certain light, so that he may be rendered fit to receive justifying grace. Thus, this illuminating grace precedes the completion of conversion.

Latin:

Quaest. I. Quid est illuminatio? Illuminatio est actus gratiae applicatricis, quo Spiritus Sanctus hominem peccatorem, ad ecclesiam vocatum, per ministerium verbi docet, & sincero studio magis magisque informat, vt depulsis ignorantiae & errorum tenebris, ipsum verbi Dei notitia imbuat, atque ex lege agnitionem peccati, ex euangelio misericordiae diuinae, in merito Christi fundatae, cognitionem eidem instillet. Obs.

I. Gratia illuminatrix vocatur etiam gratia docens; quia Spiritus S. illuminando docet omnia ad salutem necessaria, Io. XIV, 26.

Conf. DANNHAV. in hodof. phaenom. IX. p. 938. & lact. catechet. part. VI. p. 195.

Item gratia ungens, ex 1 Io. II, 20. 27. Est enim chrisma non tantum medicum & paracleticum, sed etiam praelucens, cuius typus fuit illud chrisma, quod regibus olim & sacerdotibus atque prophetis datum, cum instructione ad officii liturgiam, & mutatione in alios viros.

Praeterea illuminatio appellatur apertio oculorum mentis, Act. XXVI, 18. Quem ad modum enim caecus per apertionem oculorum nanciscitur videndi facultatem: ita peccator, tenebris ignorantiae oppletus, accipit per illuminationem Spiritus S. facultatem cognoscendi verum Deum.

Obs. II. Non intelligitur hic illuminatio obiectiua, qua lumen verbi diuini externe proponitur, sed effectiua, qua Spiritus S. lucem notitiae accendit, & subiectiua, qua peccator caecus per operationem Spiritus S. se illuminari patitur. se illuminari patitur. se illuminari patitur.

Obs. III. Gratiam divinam praeparantem in illuminatione consistere, asserit D. FECHTIVS in Dissert. de ordine modoque gratiae divinae, aphorismo IX. p. 18. quamvis celeberrimus iste Theologus simul fateatur, vocem, illuminatio, paullo latiorem esse gratia praeparante. Haec enim conversionem antecedit, cum aliqua illuminatio, nempe uberior, etiam conversionem sequatur. Quo pacto conciliandi sunt Theologi, cum illuminationem modo ad gratiam praeparantem, modo ad inhabitantem referunt.

Prima & praecipua illuminationis ratio in praeparando hominem ad conversionem consistit. Ideo enim naturales tenebrae, ignorantia mysteriorum & errores iis oppositi ex intellectu humano per gratiam expelluntur, & ille cognitione Dei & rerum sacrarum imbuitur, & tanquam luce quadam illustratur, vt ad recipiendam iustificantem gratiam aptus reddatur. Antecedit itaque haec illuminans gratia conversionis complementum.


### Q. II. What is

the principal efficient cause of illumination? The principal efficient cause of illumination is the triune God , the Father , the Son of God , and terminatively, or appropriatively, the Holy Spirit .

Proof a. 1) The triune God is light, 1 John 1:5, i.e., the fountain of all light that is in us. From which He is also called the Father of lights, James 1:17.

2) The illumination of a sinner surrounded by darkness is a divine action ad extra, and therefore undivided and common to all three persons of the Godhead.

Proof b. God the Father, who said that light should shine out of darkness, has given light in our hearts, for the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God, which is in the face of Christ, 2 Cor. 4: 6. Proof c.

The Son of God is the true light, illuminating every man coming into this world, John 1: 9. Proof d.

The Holy Spirit illuminates us terminatively, i.e., God the Father illuminates our minds through His Son in the Holy Spirit. For the God of our Lord Jesus Christ gives us the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of Him, Eph. 1: 17. From which also divine information in sacred matters is appropriated to the Holy Spirit. For He teaches us all things, and brings to our remembrance all things that Christ has said, John 14: 26. The Holy Spirit is the anointing which we receive from Christ, remaining in us; therefore we have no need that anyone should teach us: but as the same anointing teaches us concerning all things, and is true, and is not a lie; and just as it has taught us, we shall abide in Him, 1 John 2:27.

Latin:

Causa efficiens principalis illuminationis est Deus triunus , Pater , Filius Dei , & terminative, seu appropriative, Spiritus Sanctus .

Prob. a. 1) Deus triunus lux est, 1 Io. I, 5. i. e. fons omnis lucis, quae in nobis est. Ex quo etiam pater luminum dicitur, Iac. I, 17.

2) Illuminatio peccatoris tenebris circumfusi est actio divina ad extra, adeoque indivisa & communis omnibus tribus personis divinitatis.

Prob. b. Deus Pater, qui dixit, vt ex tenebris lux luceret, lucem dedit in cordibus nostris, ad illuminationem cognitionis gloriae Dei, quae est in facie Christi, 2 Cor. IV, 6.

Prob. c. Filius Dei est vera lux, illuminans omnem hominem, venientem in hunc mundum, Io. I, 9.

Prob. d. Spiritus S. nos terminative illuminat, i, e. Deus Pater per Filium suum in Spiritu S. mentes nostras illustrat. Etenim Deus Domini nostri, Iesu Christi, dat nobis spiritum sapientiae & reuelationis in cognitionem sui, Eph. I, 17. Ex quo etiam informatio diuina in rebus sacris Spiritui S. appropriatur. Ille namque nos docet omnia, & commonefacit nos de omnibus, quae Christus dixit, Io. XIV, 16. Spiritus S. est unctio, quam accipimus a Christo, in nobis manens; proinde non opus habemus, vt quis doceat nos: quemadmodum ipsa unctio docet nos de omnibus, tum verum est, tum non est mendacium; & quem ad modum docuit nos, manebimus in illo, 1 Io. II, 27.


### Q. III

Does the Holy Spirit illuminate us today immediately? The Holy Spirit does not illuminate us immediately, but mediately through the divine word.

Proof 1) From 2 Peter 1:19: We have a more sure prophetic word, to which you do well to pay attention, as to a light shining in a dark place, until the day dawns, and the morning star rises in your hearts. Obj. 1) λόγος προφητικὸς is the word handed down by the Prophets and committed to writing. 2) The prophetic discourse is called more sure than the voice of the Father brought from heaven, not insofar as it is from the Father, but insofar as it was brought forth by the testimony of Peter. Indeed, the prophetic discourse is more sure than the apostolic testimony concerning the heavenly voice, not by reason of itself, but by reason of the readers or hearers; because the authority of the prophetic discourse had been corroborated by long duration of time and the consensus of the elders. The authority of the apostolic testimony, however, was more recent, and therefore was not received with such great veneration. 3) The prophetic word is called a shining light because of its supreme perspicuity and power to illuminate: but the heart of the unregenerate man is called τόπος αὐχμηρὸς, i.e., a squalid and dark place, because of the darkness of ignorance and the filth of sin. 4) The dawning day is the clearer light of saving knowledge: the Morning Star is Christ, the object of saving knowledge, Rev. 22:16. The sense is: Since the divine word is of immovable truth and such great virtue that it can dispel the darkness of the heart, let us turn the eyes of our mind to this light, so that the saving knowledge of Christ may rise in our minds.

Prob. 2) From Ps. XIX, 8. 9. The testimony of Jehovah is sure, making wise the simple. The mandates of Jehovah are right, rejoicing the heart. The precept of Jehovah is pure, enlightening the eyes. Cf. Ps. CXIX, 105. Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.

Quest. IV. Does God today wish to illuminate man immediately through ecstasy, or ecstatic rapture, to confirm his faith, and to confer upon him a foretaste of eternal life?

God does not promise in His word that He wishes to illuminate any man through ecstasy, to confirm his faith, or to impart to him a foretaste of eternal life.

The antithesis is 1) Of the Platonists, whose opinion Iamblichus expounds in De Mysteriis Aegyptiorum, sect. I, ch. 12: "The divine irradiation, which is accustomed to occur during prayer, just as it flashes forth spontaneously, so it operates spontaneously, and is so far removed from any pulling that it manifests itself through divine efficiency and perfection, and anticipates the most free motion in us just as much as the divine volition of the good precedes our choice. Through this volition, the Gods, benevolent and merciful without any parsimony, infuse their light into the priests, call their souls to themselves, procure union with them, and accustom them, while still existing in the body, to allow themselves to be separated from the body and to be turned toward the eternal intellectual principle from which they originated. It is manifest, however, from the very things themselves, that what we are now saying is the very salvation of the soul." 2) Of the Quakers, concerning whom the author of the dissertation on the present state of the church in England, Scotland, and Ireland reports, cited by Colberg in Platonic-Hermetic Christianity, Part I, ch. 7, p. 406: "Quakers frequently fall into such ecstasies that their whole body trembles, because, as they claim, they cannot endure or contain within themselves that magnitude of light and divine splendor with which they are overwhelmed." 3) Of the Mystics, among whom are not the least Christian Hoburg and Gottfried Arnold. The former writes in Theologia Mystica, p. 122: "The soul often falls into ecstasy and rapture; which ecstasy is nothing other than when the soul feels such a power of desire, of taste, of sweetness, that it does not feel the senses." The latter, however, in Theologia Mystica, ch. VI, p. 126, says: "The mind of a perfect person, which ascends to the highest stage, is united with God in a rapturous love that sees outside of itself, and in the resulting movements of the mind, in wondrous peace and tranquility of mind, in the enjoyment of spiritual joys, and in simple contemplation of the Godhead."

Latin:

Spiritus Sanctus nos non immediate, sed mediante verbo diuino illuminat.

Prob. 1) Ex 2 Petr. I, 18. Habemus firmius propheticum verbum, cui recte facitis, quod attenditis, tanquam lumini lucenti in loco tenebricoso, vsque dum dies illucescat, & lucifer oriatur in cordibus vestris. Obs. 1) λόγος προφητικὸς est verbum, a Prophetis traditum, & litteris consignatum. 2) Sermo propheticus dicitur firmior voce Patris, e caelo delata, non quatenus haec a Patre, sed quatenus testimonio Petri prolata erat. Nimirum sermo propheticus est firmior testimonio apostolico de voce caelestis, non ratione sui, sed ratione lectorum, vel auditorum; quia sermonis prophetici auctoritas diuturno tempore & consensu maiorum erat corroborata. Auctoritas vero testimonii apostolici erat recentior, ac proinde tanta cum veneratione non suscipiebatur. 3) Verbum propheticum dicitur lumen lucens, ob summam perspicuitatem & vim illuminandi: Cor autem hominis irregeniti vocatur τόπος αὐχμηρὸς. i. e. locus squalidus & caliginosus, ob tenebras ignorantiae & sordes peccati. 4) Dies illucescens est lux clarior salutaris cognitionis: Phosphorus autem est Christus, salutaris cognitionis obiectum, Apoc. XXII, 16. Sensus est: Quoniam verbum diuinum immotae veritatis, tantaeque virtutis est, vt tenebras cordis discutere possit; ad hanc lucem oculos mentis nostrae conuertamus, vt salutaris agnitio Christi in mentibus nostris oriatur.

Prob. 2) E Ps. XIX, 8. 9. Testimonium Iehovae firmum est, sapientem reddens simplicem. Mandata Iehovae recta sunt, laetificantia cor. Praeceptum Iehovae purum est, illuminans oculos. Conf. Ps. CXIX, 105. Lucerna pedi meo est verbum tuum, et lux semitae meae.

Quaest. IV. Vultne Deus hodienum per ecstasin, vel raptum ecstaticum hominem immediate illuminare, fidem ipsius confirmare, vitaeque aeternae praegustum eidem conferre?

Non promittit Deus in verbo suo, velle se ullum hominem per ecstasin illuminare, fidem illius confirmare, praegustumque vitae aeternae ipsi impertiri.

Antithesis est 1) Platonicorum, quorum sententiam exponit Iamblichus in myster. Aegypt. sect. I. c. 12. Divina irradiatio, quae inter precandum solet fieri, ut sponte emicat, ita sponte operatur, longeque abest a tractione omni, ut quae manifestat seipsam per divinam efficientiam et perfectionem, tantoque anteuertit liberrimam in nobis motionem, quanto divina volitio boni nostram electionem praecurrit. Per hanc volitionem lucem suam Dii, fine omni parsimonia beneuoli et misericordes, sacerdotibus infundunt, eorumque animas ad se vocant, et unionem inuicem procurant, et exsistentes etiamnum in corpore assuefaciunt, ut a corpore se separari, et ad aeternum intellectuale principium, unde ortae sunt, se circumagi patiantur. Manifestum autem est ex ipsis rebus, id, quod nunc dicimus, ipsam esse animae salutem. 2) Quackerorum, de quibus refert auctor dissertat. de hodierno statu ecclesiae in Anglia, Scotia et Hybernia, citante Colbergio in Christianismo Platonico-Hermet. P. I. c. 7. p. 406. Quackeri frequenter in tantas incidunt ecstases, ut toto corpore contremiscant, quia, ut perhibent, magnitudinem illam lucis et splendoris divini, quo obruuntur, perferre nequeunt, vel intra se continere. 3) Mysticorum, quos inter haud postremi sunt Christianus Hobvrgivs, et Gottfrid. Arnoldvs. Quorum ille scribit in theol. myst. p. 122. Die Seele gerath öfters in ecstasin, und Entzückung; welche ecstasis nichts anders ist, als wenn die Seele solche Krast der Begierde, des Geschmacks, der Süssigkeit empfindet, dass sie die Sinne nicht fühlet. Hic autem in theol. myst. c. VI. p. 126. inquit: Das Gemüthe eines Vollkommenen, das zur höchsten Staffel aussteiget, wird mit Gott vereiniget in einer entzückenden, und ausser sich selbst sehenden Liebe, und denen dabey entstehenden Gemüthsbewegungen, in wundersamen Frieden und Gemüthsruhe, in Genuss der geistlichen Freuden, und einsältiger Beschauung der Gottheit.


### Q. III: Exegesis

Exegesis.

Obs. I. Ecstasy, in Latin excessus mentis, in German eine Entzückung, is a rare and extraordinary operation of either God, or a corrupted imagination, or the devil, by which the mind of man is alienated from the senses of the body, so that with the cessation of their use, it becomes more prompt and ready to grasp the images of things presented to it. It differs from rapture; because ecstasy simply denotes the departure of the mind from the senses; rapture, however, adds violence.

Obs. II. Ecstasy is divided into supernatural and preternatural. The former, as Augustine defines it, is an alienation from the senses of the body, so that the spirit of man, inspired by the divine Spirit, may be free to grasp and be infused with images. The latter arises either from a man's corrupted imagination or from the devil. Melancholic and fantastic ecstasy arises from a man's corrupted imagination when, through a vehement affection (love, grief, horror) or even profound speculation, the animal spirits are withdrawn from the external senses, and with the cessation of their use, unusual phantasms are presented to the man's intellect. Diabolical ecstasy, however, is when the evil spirit, having bound the man's senses, represents to his imagination the likenesses of certain things, so that the intellect apprehends and approves them.

DELRIO described diabolical ecstasies graphically in Disquisitiones Magicae, book II, qu. 25, Obs. III.

Mystics distinguish between the ecstasy of the intellect and that of the will. The ecstasy of the intellect is an extraordinary operation of God, by which the human intellect is elevated above natural powers to contemplate divine mysteries, and indeed with a contemplation so sublime that it perceives in them a greater beauty than it could have persuaded itself of, which they also call the ecstasy of admiration. The ecstasy of the will is that by which the soul is inflamed with such ardent love of God that, having abandoned earthly inclinations, it enters into a rapture of celestial fruition and joins itself uniquely and powerfully to the divine goodness.

See FRANCISCUS SALESIUS, De amore Dei, chap. III and following.

B E B A I O S I S (Confirmation).

Thesis We prove our thesis: 1) God in His eternal counsel ordained that the Holy Spirit should call, illuminate, and convert the elect through the Word, and justify all those who embrace Christ with true faith, and confer eternal salvation upon them, as attested by the Formula of Concord, p. 808. For the word of God shines in a dark place (the unregenerate heart) until the day of saving knowledge arises, 2 Pet. 1:19. And faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God, Rom. 10:17. Therefore, the full vigor of the eyes and ears is required so that, by attentively reading and hearing the word of God, we may be illuminated and converted.

But those in ecstasy neither see nor hear what is happening to them. Therefore, through ecstasy, they are neither illuminated nor converted.

2) The means that preserve and confirm faith in Christ and the holiness of life are the word of God and the sacrament of the Supper, Ps. 119:11; Matt. 7:24; Eph. 6:17; John 6:56. How, I ask, will a man deprived of the aid of his senses properly use these confirming means?

3) A foretaste of eternal life is taken from the milk of the Gospel. This is what the Apostle Peter teaches not obscurely, 1 ep. ch.

II, 2. As newborn infants, desire the sincere milk of the word, that you may grow by it; if indeed you have tasted how gracious the Lord is. By these words he implies that God offers Himself to be tasted as far the sweetest in the sweet milk of the Gospel, but the Gospel must be diligently read and heard so that we may be affected by the spiritual taste of God. Therefore, there is no need for ecstasy, by which the senses of the body are bound.

4) Ecstasies are opportune for various illusions of a corrupted imagination and for the devil. MOLINOS does not deny this, who in book III of Manuductio Spiritualis, ch. 19, says: This effective and practical conformity with the divine will in all things, he says, leads the soul to annihilation and transformation with God without the mixture of raptures and exterior ecstasies, or vehement affections; since this way is subject to many illusions, and is joined with the danger of disease or distress of the intellect; those who reach the summit of perfection by this path are rare.

Indeed, it is extremely difficult to distinguish exactly between preternatural, fantastic, and diabolical ecstasies and those that are supernatural and divine.

For PLINY, Natural History, book VII, ch. 83, recorded in writing concerning Hermotimus, and AUGUSTINE, De Civitate Dei, book XIV, concerning Restitutus, that they could abstract their minds from the senses of the body at will, so that they lay on the ground very much like the dead.

There is a witty example of an ecstatic man, which ERASMUS FRANCISCI mentions in Der Gegenstrahl der Morgenröthe: Qu. XVII, p. 753.

Many of them can masterfully feign an ecstasy: like that priest in Rome who, when the words of the Passion history "Consummatum est!" were spoken, used to fall immediately into an ecstasy; until one time Rondeletius, the famous physician, who had conceived a suspicion of fraud from this, demanded a sturdy stick, asserting that he would soon [cure] this ecstatic person. twitching, and to twitch him out of his posture. By which he disturbed the good fellow in his ecstatic devotion, nay, performed such a miracle that he awakened him as it were from the dead, and endowed him with nimble feet.

Contra, horrendous are those things which PRATEOLUS reports in his elenchus hæret. lit. E. n. 12. p. 160, concerning the Anabaptists: "As if they were almost fanatics, inspired by their own Spirit, they would change their countenance, have horrible gestures, and, after the manner of those suffering from the falling sickness, they would fall to the ground and lie as if dead, whence also they would tremble horribly in their bodies.

Rapt into an ecstasy, they would blurt out all sorts of wondrous things, that they had seen Zwingli among the infernal spirits, etc. That the Father had spoken, that the day of the Lord was at hand: the certain time of which they designated. Whence, like madmen, they would run about, crying: 'The day of the Lord, the day of the Lord.'"

Prodigious also are those things which OLAUS MAGNUS recounts in *descript. Regn. Septentr.* L. II. c. 18: "If any stranger desires to know something certain about the condition of his own people, they provide that within the space of 24 hours he may learn what is happening with them, even if they are three hundred miles away, in this manner: The enchanter, after he has called upon his demons with visited ceremonies, suddenly collapses and becomes lifeless, as if, with him extinguished, his soul truly departs from his body.

For neither does any spirit seem to remain in him, nor does any sense or motion remain with life: but it is necessary that some always be present to guard the lifeless body, which if it is not done, the demons carry it off. 24 hours having elapsed, with the spirit returning, the lifeless body awakens with a groan as if from a deep sleep, as if he who considers it were being recalled to life from death. Afterwards, thus restored, he answers the questions asked, and to provide proof to the inquirer, he recounts something by which he may recognize and know for certain that he had been in his house or that of his relatives."

Since, therefore, ecstasy is liable to so many illusions, it will neither kindle faith in Christ, nor confirm it, nor offer a solid taste of eternal life.

Latin:

Exegesis.

Obs. I. Exstasis, latine excessus mentis, germanice eine Entzückung, est rara et extraordinaria operatio vel Dei, vel phantasiae corruptae, vel diaboli, qua mens hominis alienatur a sensibus corporis, ut horum usu cessante, promtior et expeditior fit ad capiendum obiectas rerum imagines. Differt a raptu; quia ecstasis simpliciter notat discessum mentis a sensibus; raptus autem violentiam addit.

Obs. II. Diuiditur ecstasis in supernaturalem, et praeternaturalem. Illa, definiente Avgvstino, est alienatio a sensibus corporis, ut spiritus hominis, a Spiritu diuino affluntus, capiendis atque infundendis imaginibus vacet. Haec oritur vel a corrupta hominis phantasia, vel a diabolo. A corrupta hominis phantasia oritur ecstasis melancholica et phantastica, cum per vehementem affectum (amorem, maerorem, horrorem) vel etiam profundam speculationem, spiritus animales a sensibus externis retrahuntur, et horum usu cessante, insolita phantasinata intellectui hominis obiiciuntur. Diabolica autem ecstasis est, cum cacodaemon, ligatis hominis sensibus, phantasiae ipsius simulacra nonnullarum rerum repraesentat, vt intellectus ea apprehendat & approbet.

Diabolicas ecstases graphice descripsit DELRIO in disquisit. magic. lib. II. qu. 25. Obs. III.

Distinguunt mystici inter ecstasin intellectus, & voluntatis. Ecstasis intellectus est extraordinaria operatio Dei, qua intellectus humanus supra vires naturales elevatur ad contemplandum mysteria divina, & quidem contemplatione adeo sublimi, ut maiorem in illis pulchritudinem deprehendat, quam sibi persuadere potuerat, quam etiam ecstasin admirationis vocant. Ecstasis voluntatis est, per quam anima tam ardenti amore Dei incenditur, vt, derelictis inclinationibus terrenis, in raptum fruitionis coelestis intret, & bonitati divinae se unice & potenter iungat.

Vid. FRANCISC. SALES. de amore Dei cap. III. & seqq.

Β Ε Β Α Ι Ω Σ Ι Σ.

Thesin nostram probamus: 1) Deus in aeterno suo consilio ordinavit, ut Spiritus S. electos per verbum vocet, illuminet atque convertat, atque omnes illos, qui Christum vera fide amplectuntur, iustificet, atque in eos aeternam salutem conferat, teste Form. Concord. p. 808. Etenim verbum Dei lucet in loco tenebroso (corde irregenito), donec dies salutaris cognitionis exoriatur, 2 Pet. I, 19. Et fides est ex auditu: auditus autem per verbum Dei, Rom. X, 17. Quamobrem integer oculorum, auriumque vigor requiritur, vt verbum Dei attente legendo & audiendo illuminemur & convertamur.

Ecstatici autem nec vident, nec audiunt, quid sibi obtingat. Ergo per ecstasin nec illuminantur, nec convertuntur.

2) Media conferuantia & confirmantia fidem in Christum atque sanctimoniam vitae, sunt verbum Dei & sacramentum coenae, Ps. CXIX, 11. Matth. VII, 24. Eph. VI, 17. Io. VI, 56. Quomodo, quaeso, his mediis confirmantibus rite vsurus est homo, sensuum adminiculo destitutus?

3) Praegustus vitae aeternae capitur ex lacte euangelii. Id quod Apostolus Petrus haud obscure docet, 1 ep. c.

II, 2. Tanquam modo geniti infantes, verbale sincerum lac desiderate, ut per illud crescatis; siquidem gustastis, quam benignus sit Dominus. Quibus verbis innuit, Deum vt longe suavissimum in dulci lacte euangelii se gustandum praebere, at euangelium sedulo legendum & audiendum est, vt gustu Dei spirituali afficiamur. Non ergo est opus ecstasi, qua sensus corporis ligantur.

4) Ecstases variis illusionibus corruptae phantasiae & diabolo sunt opportunae. Non diffitetur id MOLINOSVS, qui libr. III. manuduct. spirit. c. 19: Hic, inquit, efficax & practica cum voluntate divina in omnibus rebus conformitas deducit animam ad annihilationem & transformationem cum Deo absque mixtura raptuum & ecstasium exteriorum, aut vehementium affectuum; cum haec via multis obnoxia fit illusionibus, & cum periculo morbi, aut angustiis intellectus fit coniunctus; qua semita, qui ad verticem perfectionis pertingant, rari sunt.

Sane perquam difficile est, ecstases praeternaturales, phantasticas & diabolicas a supernaturalibus & divinis exacte discernere.

Litteris quippe prodidere PLINIVS hist. nat. l. VII. c. 83. de Hermotimo, & AVGVSTINVS de Civ. D. L. XIV. de Restituto, quod pro arbitratu suo mentes suas a sensibus corporis sic abstraxerint, vt mortuis simillimi humi iacuerint.

Lepidum autem est exemplum hominis ecstatici, quod commemorat ERASMVS FRANCISCI in dem Gegenstrahl der Morgenröthe: Qu. XVII. p. 753.

Ihrer viel können eine Verzückung meisterlich erdichten: wie jener Priester zu Rom, welcher, wenn die Worte der Passionshistorie: Consummatum est! gesprochen worden, gleich in eine Entzückung zu fallen pflegte; bis einmal Rondeletius, der berühmte Medicus, welcher einen Argwohn des Betrugs daraus geschöpfet hatte, einen wackern Stock forderte, versichernd, et wollte diesen Verzückten bald zuckend machen, und aus seiner Positur verzucken. Womit er den guten Kerl in seiner verzückten Andacht verstörte, ja ein solches Miracul that, daß er denselben gleichsam von den Todten erweckte, und mit hurtigen Füssen begabte.

Contra, horrenda sunt, quæ PRATEOLVS in elencho hæret. lit. E. n. 12. p. 160. de Anabaptistis refert: Tanquam fere fanatici, suo afflati Spiritu, faciem mutabant, gestus habebant horribiles, ac more morbo comitiali laborantium in terram prolapsi iacebant tanquam mortui, unde & corpore horribiliter tremiscebant.

In ecstasin rapti, mira effutiebant omnia, sese Zwinglium apud inferos vidisse &c. Patrem dixisse, diem domini instare: cuius tempus certum designabaut. Vnde tanquam furiosi cursitabant, clamantes: Dies domini, dies domini.

Prodigiosa etiam sunt, quæ recenset OLAVS MAGNVS, in descript. Regn. Septentr. L. II. c. 18. Si quis peregrinus cupiat de suorum conditione certi quid cognoscere, præstant, ut intra 24. horarum spatium resciscat, quid cum illis agatur, vel si trecentis milliaribus absint, hoc modo: Incantator, postquam visitatis cærimoniis dæmones suos compellauit, subito collabitur, & exanimatur, quasi, exstincto illo, reuera a corpore anima excedat.

Neque enim aut spiritus in eo reliquus esse, aut restare cum vita sensus aliquis motusque videtur: sed vt adsint semper aliqui, oportet, qui exanime corpus custodiant, quod si non fit, dæmones od abripiunt. Horis 24. elapsis, reuertente spiritu, ceu e profundo somno, cum gemitu expergiscitur exanime corpus, quasi reuocetur in vitam ex morte, qui considerat. Postea sic restitutus ad interrogata respondet, & vt fidem faciat percontatori, recenset aliquid, quo agnoscat ille, & certo sciat, in ædibus suis, aut cognatorum fuisse.

Cum itaque ecstasis tot illusionibus sit obnoxia, neque fidem in Christum accendet, neque eam confirmabit, neque solidum vitæ æternæ gustum præbebit.


### Q. III: Dissolution

DISSOLUTION

I. The adversaries appeal to the example of St. Paul, who is said to have come into an ecstasy, Acts 22:17, and to have been caught up into paradise, into the third heaven, 2 Cor. 12:2; where, illuminated by the ὑπερβολῇ ἀποκαλύψεων (abundance of revelations), he heard ῥήματα ἄρρητα (ineffable words).

Which example, although it is extraordinary, shows nevertheless that God can illuminate His beloved children in the same extraordinary way (immediately, without the concurrence of Scripture) and confirm them in faith.

Resp. 1) The question is not about the power, but the will of God. God wills to make us wise unto salvation through faith in Christ Jesus by the intervention of the Holy Scriptures; in which most gracious will of God we acquiesce, 2 Tim. 3:14, 15. 2) The example of Paul is entirely singular and inimitable; for the reason that God was about to confirm Paul in his apostolic office through an ecstatic rapture, so that he could intrepidly appeal to this extraordinary revelation as if to the seal of his apostolic office. But just as not all Christians are Apostles, so neither do all require an ecstatic rapture.

Add that the Apostle, after the ecstasy, felt such a vehement temptation that, by praying against it, he taught curious minds not to affect ecstasy or rapture into the third heaven (*).

II. Not

That not only Paul, but others also had an ecstasy, is evident from 2 Cor. V, 13. "Ειτε γὰρ ἐξέστημεν, θεῷ, εἴτε σωφρονῶμεν, ὑμῖν, whether we are beside ourselves, to God, or whether we are of sound mind, to you. Resp. These words are less appropriately drawn to ecstasy. For it is not likely that the Apostle wished to make mention of an ecstasy of these things abruptly. It is certain that these things are said of madness κατὰ δόξαν (according to opinion), as D. CALOVIUS judges. Therefore OSIANDER paraphrases the words of the Apostle thus: If we act with great zeal among you, and severely correct your errors, so that to some delicate men we seem to be insane, in that matter we serve the Lord, our God, with that pious zeal, whose glory is at stake. But if we treat you humanely and modestly after a sharp correction, we do it for the sake of your own benefit, lest you be alienated from the gospel of Christ, or be oppressed by excessive sadness.

III. Those who taste the powers of the age to come, must have been caught up into the third heaven. For there the heavenly powers are tasted. But reborn men, etc. Hebr. VI, 5. Therefore. Resp. I deny the major premise. For the words of the Apostle are: They have tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the age to come. Therefore they did not taste the powers of the age to come through an ecstatic rapture, but through the good word of God, which contains the promise of future goods, and thus they perceived a certain foretaste of the kingdom of glory from the gospel, while they lived their life in this kingdom of grace. But this argument will be treated more fully in the following question .

Latin:

ΔΙΑΛΥΣΙΣ

I. Prouocant aduersarii ad exemplum S. Pauli, qui in ecstasin venisse, Actor. XXII, 17. & in paradisum, in tertium cælum raptus esse dicitur, 2 Cor. XII, 2.; vbi, ὑπερβολῇ ἀποκαλύψεων illustratus, ῥήματα ἄρρητα, verba inenarrabilia audiuerit.

Quod exemplum, licet sit extraordinarium, ostendit tamen, quod Deus filios suos dilectos eodem extraordinario modo (immediate absque concurrente scriptura,) illuminare, & in fide confirmare possit.

Resp. 1) Non de potestate, sed de voluntate Dei quæritur. Vult Deus nos interuentu sacrarum litterarum sapientes reddere ad salutem per fidem in Christum Iesum; in qua benignissima Dei voluntate acquiescimus, 2 Tim. III, 14. 15. 2) Exemplum Pauli est plane singulare & inimitabile; ideo, quod Deus Paullum per raptum ecstaticum in officio apostolico confirmaturus erat, vt ad extraordinariam hanc reuelationem, velut ad sigillum muneris apostolici, posset intrepidus prouocare. At sicut non omnes Christiani sunt Apostoli; sic nec omnes raptu ecstatico indigent.

Adiice, quod Apostolus post ecstasin tam vehementem senserit tentationem, vt eam deprecatus, doceret animos curiosos, ne ecstasin, vel raptum in cælum tertium affectarent (*).

II. Non

Non Paullum tantum, sed & alios ἔκστασιν habuisse, patet e 2 Cor. V, 13. "Ειτε γὰρ ἐξέστημεν, θεῷ, εἴτε σωφρονῶμεν, ὑμῖν, sive enim mente excedimus, Deo, sive modeste agimus, vobis. Resp. Haec verba minus commode ad ἔκστασιν trahuntur. Nam Apostolum ex abrupto ἔκστασιν harum mentionem facere voluisse, haud verisimile est. De insania κατὰ δόξαν haec dici, certum est, censente D. CALOVIO. Idcirco OSIANDER verba Apostoli ita παραφράζει: Si magno zelo vobiscum agimus, & errata vestra severe corrigimus, ita, ut quibusdam delicatulis hominibus insanire videamur, ea in re pio illo zelo Domino, Deo nostro inferuimus, de cuius gloria agitur. Sin vero humaniter & modeste post acrem correptionem vos tractamus, vestri commodi gratia id facimus, ne ab evangelio Christi abalienemini, aut nimia tristitia opprimamini.

III. Qui virtutes futuri saeculi gustant, hos oportet raptos esse in caelum tertium. Nam ibi virtutes caelestes gustantur. Atqui homines renati &c. Hebr. VI, 5. Ergo. Resp. Neg. maior. Verba namque Apostoli sunt: Gustarunt bonum Dei verbum, virtutesque futuri saeculi. Non itaque gustarunt virtutes futuri saeculi per raptum ecstaticum, sed per bonum Dei verbum, quod promissionem futurorum bonorum continet, adeoque ex evangelio quendam praegustum regni gloriae perceperunt, cum in hoc regno gratiae vitam egerunt. Sed hoc argumentum plenius tractabitur quaestione sequenti .


### Q. V. How manifold is illumination by reason of the illuminating medium?

Illumination, by reason of the illuminating medium, is either legal or evangelical. The former is that which manifests to us sin, the wrath of God, and the temporal and eternal punishments of sin

Prob. b. Paul mentions evangelical illumination in 2 Cor. IV, 4: "The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that the illumination of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, might not shine upon them." The gospel illuminates the hearts of men so that they may recognize the glory of Christ, who was indeed lifted up on the cross, but raised into heaven, and is seated at the right hand of God the Father, of whom he himself is the ἀπαύγασμα [effulgence], Heb. I, 3. Therefore, the gospel declares and manifests the mercy, wisdom, and justice of God the Father in the restored face of Christ, who is His essential image. Col. I, 15. Quest.

Latin:

Illuminatio, ratione medii illuminantis, est vel legalis, vel evangelica. Illa est, quae peccatum, iram Dei, & poenas peccati temporales atque aeternas nobis manifestat

Prob. b. Illuminationis evangelicae mentionem inicit Paulus, 2 Cor. IV, 4. Deus huius saeculi excaecavit sensus infidelium, ut non splendeat illis illuminatio evangelii gloriae Christi, qui est imago Dei. Evangelium illuminat corda hominum, ut agnoscant gloriam Christi, in crucem quidem sublati, in caelum autem evecti, & sedentis ad dextram Dei Patris, cuius ipse est ἀπαύγασμα, Hebr. I, 3. Declarat ergo & manifestat evangelium misericordiam, sapientiam & iustitiam Dei Patris, in refecta facie Christi, qui essentialis eius est imago. Col. I, 15. Quaest.


### VI. What is the difference between legal and evangelical light?

The divine law, like a lightning bolt, possesses a terrifying, killing, and condemning light: the Gospel, however, in the manner of the sun, diffuses an exhilarating and life-giving light a). The law possesses powers of illuminating in a pedagogically salutary way: but from the Gospel arises an illumination that is completely salutary to those men who rightly use the evangelical doctrine according to the intention of God b). Prob. a. From 2 Cor. III, 6. 7. 8. 9. "The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

But if the ministry of death in letters, engraved in stones, was in glory, so that the children of Israel could not look upon the face of Moses, because of the glory of his face, which nevertheless is being abolished: how will the ministry of the Spirit not be more in glory? For if the ministry of condemnation is glory, much more does the ministry of righteousness abound in glory. The Apostle compares the law with the gospel, 1) regarding the nature of both: for the law is the letter; but the gospel is the spirit. The law is called the letter, partly synecdochically, because it was inscribed and engraved by God on stone tablets with many letters; partly in opposition to the gospel, in that it indeed commands the holiness of life, but does not confer the powers to live holily. The gospel, on the contrary, is called the spirit metonymically, because it is the medium by which the Holy Spirit illuminates, regenerates, justifies, and effects union with God. 2) Regarding the diversity of effects: The law declaratively kills and condemns, i.e., it adjudges us to eternal death and condemnation: but the gospel gives life, or regenerates. 3) Regarding the glory, or clarity: The radiance of the law is less, that of the gospel is greater. The brightness of the former is intolerable, symbolically represented in the radiant face of Moses, which had to be covered with a veil: the splendor of the latter is delightful in the face of Christ, flashing with the rays of grace, humanity, and beneficence. The clarity of the former vanishes, diffused by the evangelical clarity, just as a lesser light is overshadowed by a greater one. Prob. b.

The law is our pedagogue unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith, Gal. III, 24. Divine law shows and reveals to us both the innate leprosy of the soul and the diseases voluntarily contracted, and thus provides us with the occasion to seek the physician of souls and the author of saving righteousness, Christ. Evangelical illumination, however, when translated into use, is completely salutaris; for the reason that it gives the knowledge of salvation, which is in the remission of sins, and reveals the bowels of the mercy of our God, in which the sunrise from on high has visited us, Luke I, 77. 78. Cf. D. BREITHAUPT in instit. theol. loc. III. p. 251. seqq. & thes. cred. p. 131. seqq.

VII. But is illumination so bound to the divine word that none of it is given except at the time when it is heard, or read, or considered with intended study?

The power of illuminating, with which the divine word is endowed, is not precisely bound to the acts of hearing, reading, or meditation, but the word of God, once heard, read, transmitted into the mind, and retained therein, always possesses its powers of illuminating.

Proof. Docile auditors and readers receive with meekness [ἐν πραότητι] modestly and courteously the engrafted word [λόγον ἔμφυτον], the implanted word, Jas. 1:21, which is united with the hearts of auditors and readers just as food is with the body, leaven with the dough, seed with the field, a shoot with the tree: which implanted word, as the ordinary medium of the Holy Spirit, can no more save souls than it can illuminate them unto salvation.

Question VIII. Are we truly and properly illuminated by the ministers of the word?

Through the ministers of the word, who duly perform the public office of teaching, the Holy Spirit truly and properly illuminates the souls of men who are in darkness regarding sacred matters.

Objection. The principal cause of illumination is the triune God, and indeed, by appropriation, the Holy Spirit; the ordinary organ or medium of illumination is the word of God; the ministerial cause is the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God, 1 Cor. 4:1.

Proof. 1) From Eph. 3:8-9. "To me, who am less than the least of all saints, was this grace given, that I should preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, and illuminate all." The Apostle ministerially illuminated men who were ignorant of divine things by illustrating the doctrine of the Gospel, and by notifying and inculcating the benefits of Christ to them most abundantly.

2) From 2 Cor. 4:6. "God, who said that light should shine out of darkness, has given light in our hearts, for the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God, which is in the face of Jesus Christ." The Apostles and their successors were brought by the most merciful God to the light of true knowledge for this end, that through them the illumination of true knowledge might reach others.

3) Ministers of the divine word open the eyes of the auditors, that they may turn themselves from darkness to light, Acts 26:18. Therefore, they truly illuminate.

4) Those who teach the word of God are held to be light, e.g., John the Baptist, John 5:35; the Apostles, Matt. 5:14.

Antithesis of the Enthusiasts, Anabaptists, Schwenckfeldians, and Weigelians, who maintain that men are illuminated immediately by the Holy Spirit today. Their stronger arguments are:
