I. Whatever souls are epistles, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God, those are immediately illuminated by the Holy Spirit: But the souls of Christians, etc., 2 Cor. 3:3. Therefore. The minor is clear: since the Apostle excludes the Gospel, written with ink on paper, from the act of illumination. Response. 1) The Apostle does not exclude the ministry of the word from the act of illumination, because he says explicitly: "You are an epistle ministered by us." 2) We do not attribute the efficacy of illuminating to the Gospel considered materially, i.e., insofar as it is written with ink on paper; but viewed formally, by reason of the God-breathed [θεοπνεύστ] sense.

II. St. John, 1 Ep. 2:27, says: "The anointing which you have received from Him abides in you, and you have no need that anyone should teach you." Those who do not need external information, but are fully informed by the anointing abiding within the mind, are immediately illuminated and informed by God: But the regenerate, etc. Therefore. Response. 1) That anointing, commended by St. John, is the Holy Spirit, the principal cause of illumination, who informs us not immediately, but through the medium of the word, 1 John 2:14. Nor do we have need that anyone should teach us things new and different from those which the Prophets and Apostles have taught. 2) St. John refers to those teachers who were offering or obtruding themselves at that time, and were accustomed to seduce the unwary, accusing the doctrine hitherto handed down by the Apostles, whether by living voice or by writing, of insufficiency, and rashly promising a more correct and fuller knowledge of divine things, although they were led by the spirit of Antichrist, according to verses 18, 19, and 26.

III. Whoever are θεοδίδακτοι (taught by God), they are not illuminated by the ministers of the church: But the reborn, etc. Therefore, the minor premise is evident from John 6:45. I respond: Whoever are ἀμέσως θεοδίδακτοι (immediately taught by God), they are not illuminated by the ministers of the church; I concede this. But after the canon of scripture was completed, men are illuminated and taught by God through the ministry of the word, through which God is efficacious, 1 Cor. 3:6. Paul writes concerning the Thessalonians: 'Αυτοὶ ὑμεῖς θεοδίδακτοί ἐσε (You yourselves are taught by God), namely through the ministry of the Apostle Paul, 1 Thess. 4:9, collated with verses 1 and 2. They are therefore θεοδίδακτοι ἐμμέσως (mediately taught by God). Whence in the same place Christ adds: Everyone, therefore, who has heard from the Father and has learned, comes to me. It is not permitted to seek the voice of the Father elsewhere than in the revealed word, with Peter as monitor, 2 Pet. 1:16, 17, 18.

Latin:

Lex divina, fulminis instar, habet lucem terrentem, occidentem & condemnantem: Evangelium autem, benefici ritu solis, diffundit lucem exhilarantem & vivificantem a). Lex pollet viribus illuminandi paedagogice salutaribus: Ex evangelio autem oritur illuminatio complete salutaris iis hominibus, qui doctrina evangelica ex intentione Dei recte utuntur b). Prob. a. Ex 2 Cor. III, 6. 7. 8. 9. Littera occidit, spiritus autem vivificat.

Si vero ministerium mortis in litteris, effigiatum in lapidibus, fuit in gloria, ita ut non potuerint intueri filii Israëlis in faciem Mosis, propter gloriam faciei ipsius, quae tamen abrogatur: Qui non magis ministerium spiritus erit in gloria? Si enim ministerium condemnationis gloria est: multo magis abundat ministerium iustitiae in gloria. Comparat Apostolus legem cum evangelio, 1) quoad utriusque naturam: Lex namque est littera; evangelium vero est spiritus. Dicitur lex littera, partim synecdochice, quia pluribus litteris a Deo tabulis lapideis est inscripta & insculpta; partim in oppositione ad evangelium, eo, quod vitae sanctimoniai quidem praecipit, vires autem sancte vivendi non confert. Evangelium contra dicitur spiritus metonymice, quia est medium, quo Spiritus S. illuminat, regenerat, iustificat, & unionem cum Deo efficit. 2) Quoad diversitatem effectuum: Lex declarative occidit & condemnat, h. e. aeternae morti & condemnationi nos adiudicat: Evangelium vero vivificat, sive regenerat. 3) Quoad gloriam, sive claritatem: Iubar legis minus, evangelii maius est. Illius fulgor est intolerabilis, symbolice repraesentatus in radiante facie Mosis, velamine obtegenda: Huius splendor est delectabilis in facie Christi, radiis gratiae humanitatis, beneficentiae corusca. Illius claritas evanescit, diffusa claritate evangelica, sicut lux minor a maiori obumbratur. Prob. b.

Lex est paedagogus noster ad Christum, ut ex fide iustificemur, Gal. III, 24. Lex divina nobis ostendit & patefacit tum connatam animae lepram, tum morbos voluntarie contractos, adeoque occasionem nobis praebet ad quaerendum animorum medicum & iustitiae salutiferae auctorem, Christum. Illuminatio autem evangelica, ad usum translata, est complete salutaris; ideo, quod dat scientiam salutis, quae est in remissione peccatorum, & revelat viscera misericordiae Dei nostri, in quibus visitavit nos oriens ex alto, Luc. I, 77. 78. Conf. D. BREITHAVPT in instit. theol. loc. III. p. 251. seqq. & thes. cred. p. 131. seqq.

Quaest. VII. Sed num ita alligata est illuminatio verbo divino, ut nihil eius detur, nisi eo tempore, quo auditur illud, vel legitur, vel destinato studio consideratur?

Vis illuminandi, qua praeditum est verbum divinum, non praecise alligata est auditionis, lectionis aut meditationis actibus, sed verbum Dei auditum, lectum, in animum transmissum, eodemque retentum, viribus suis illuminandi semper pollet.

Prob. Auditores & lectores dociles ἐν πραότητι modeste & comiter accipiunt λόγον ἔμφυτον, verbum infitum, Iac. I, 21. quod sic vnitur cum cordibus auditorum & lectorum, sicut cibus cum corpore, fermentum cum massa, semen cum agro, surculus cum arbore: quod verbum infitum, vt ordinarium Spiritus S. medium, animas non saluare magis, quam ad salutem illuminare potest.

Quæst. VIII. An per ministros verbi vere & proprie illuminamur?

Per ministros verbi, publico docendi munere rite perfungentes, Spiritus S. animas hominum, ad res sacras caligantium, vere & proprie illuminat.

Obf. Caussa principalis illuminationis est Deus triunus, & quidem appropriatiue Spiritus Sanctus; ordinarium illuminandi ὄργανον aut medium, est verbum Dei; caussa ministerialis sunt ministri Christi, & œconomi mysteriorum Dei, 1 Cor. IV, 1.

Prob. 1) Ex Eph. III, 8. 9. Mihi, minimo omnium sanctorum, data est gratia hæc, vt inter gentes euangelizarem imperuestigabiles diuitias Christi, & illuminarem omnes. Illuminauit Apostolus ministerialiter homines rerum diuinarum rudes, doctrinam euangelii illustrando, beneficia Christi longe vberrime ipsis notificando atque inculcando.

2) Ex 2 Cor. IV, 6. Deus, qui dixit, vt ex tenebris lux luceret, lucem dedit in cordibus nostris, ad illuminationem cognitionis gloriæ Dei, quæ est in facie Iesu Christi. Apostoli & eorum successores a Deo misericordissimo eo fine ad lucem veræ agnitionis perducti sunt, vt per eosdem aliis illuminatio veræ agnitionis obtingeret.

3) Ministri verbi diuini aperiunt oculos auditorum, vt conuertant se a tenebris ad lucem, Act. XXVI, 18. E. vere illuminant.

4) Docentes verbum Dei perhibentur esse lumen, v. gr. Ioannes baptista, Io. V, 35. Apostoli, Matth. V, 14.

Antithesis Enthusiastarum, Anabaptistarum, Schwenckfeldianorum & Weigelianorum, statuentium, hodienum homines immediate a Spiritu S. illuminari. Quorum argumenta potiora sunt:

I. Quæcunque animæ sunt epistolæ, non atramento, sed Spiritu Dei viuentis scriptæ, illæ immediate a Spiritu S. illuminantur: Atqui animæ christianorum &c. 2 Cor. III, 3. E. Minor liquet: quoniam Apostolus euangelium, atramento inscriptum chartæ, ab actu illuminationis excludit. Resp. 1) Ministerium verbi Apostolus ab actu illuminationis non excludit, quia diferte dicit: Vos estis epistola ministrata a nobis. 2) Efficaciam illuminandi non tribuimus euangelio considerato materialiter, i. e. quatenus atramento chartæ inscriptum est; sed spectato formaliter, ratione sensus θεοπνεύστ.

II. S. Ioannes 1 ep. II, 27. inquit: Vnctio, quam accepistis a Domino, in vobis manet, & non opus habetis, vt quis doceat vos. Qui non indigent externa informatione, sed ab vnctione, intra animum manente, plene informantur, illi immediate a Deo illuminantur & informantur: Atqui renati &c. E. Resp. 1) Vnctio illa, a S. Ioanne commendata, est Spiritus Sanctus, caussa principalis illuminationis, qui nos informat non immediate, sed mediante verbo, 1 Io. II, 14. Neque opus habemus, vt quis nos doceat noua & diuersa ab his, quæ Prophetæ & Apostoli docuerunt. 2) S. Ioannes respicit doctores illos, qui seipsos offerebant, aut obtrudebant tunc temporis, & seducere incautos folebant, doctrinam hactenus ab Apostolis, feu viua voce, feu scripto traditam, insufficientiæ accusantes, & rectiorem ac pleniorem rerum diuinarum cognitionem temere pollicentes, licet spiritu Antichristi ducerentur, iuxta v. 18. 19. & 26.

III. Quicunque sunt θεοδίδακτοι, docti a Deo, illi non sunt illuminati per ministros ecclesiæ: Atqui renati &c. E. Minor patet ex Io. VI, 45. Resp. Quicunque sunt ἀμέσως θεοδίδακτοι, illi non sunt illuminati per ministros ecclesiæ; concedo. At post completum scripturæ canonem homines illuminantur & docentur a Deo per ministerium verbi, per quod Deus efficax est, 1 Cor. III, 6. Paullus de Thessalonicensibus scribit: 'Αυτοὶ ὑμεῖς θεοδίδακτοί ἐσε, vos ipsi a Deo docti estis, scilicet per ministerium Apostoli Paulli, 1 Thess. IV, 9. coll. cum v. 1. & 2. Sunt ergo θεοδίδακτοι ἐμμέσως. Vnde l. c. Christus addit: Omnis ergo, qui audiuit a Patre & didicit, venit ad me. Patris vocem alibi, quam in verbo reuelato quærere non licet, monitore Petro 2 ep. I, 16. 17. 18.


### Quest. IX. What men does God illuminate?

God, most benevolent, indeed intends seriously to illuminate all men ; but in act, those are illuminated who, having been called and brought to the church, admit the grace of the Holy Spirit, and attentively hear, read, and meditate upon the divine word .

Proof a. Christ is the true light, which illuminates every man coming into the world, John 1:9. Christ, the true light, illuminates, as much as is in him, not just one nation, not one man, but all men, coming forth into the darkness of this world. For he came so that the preaching of the gospel might shine into the hearts of all nations, as well as of individual men. Neither the Scythian is excluded, nor the Jew, nor the Spaniard, nor the Goth, nor the Briton, nor king, nor servant, nor male, nor female. Many indeed persevere in the darkness of ignorance and errors: But truly, this is not by the fault of denied light, but by their own fault, just as if someone should stumble at midday because he is unwilling to lift his eyes. Wisely says AUGUSTINE, tract. 27 on John: 'He who resists, how shall he be made alive? He is an adversary to the ray of light by which he is to be penetrated.' He does not turn his sight, but closes his mind.

2) The saving grace of God has appeared to all men, instructing us, Tit. 2:11, 12. The instructing, or illuminating, grace has shone upon all men, according to the gracious intention of God: It shines in the darkness, even if the darkness does not apprehend it, John 1:5.

3) We announce Christ, admonishing every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom, that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus, Col. 1:28. Paul and the apostolic men intended to teach heavenly wisdom to every man, if not by tongue, certainly by pen.

Proof b. A man called to the church, and admitting the divine word, and attentively meditating, is illuminated. For God has called us out of darkness into his marvelous light, 1 Pet. 2:9. Sacred heralds are also sent to open the eyes of the hearers, that they may be converted from darkness to light, Acts 26:18. But the grace of the Holy Spirit is not irresistible; since the sinner, being stubbornly contumacious, can impede supernatural illumination by an interposed veil or an interposed malice. This is what the Apostle hints at, 2 Cor. 4:3, 4. 'If our gospel is hidden, it is hidden in those who are perishing, in whom the god of this age has blinded the senses of the unbelievers, so that the illumination of the gospel of the glory of Christ might not shine upon them.' Indeed, the gospel, in itself lucid, is κεκαλυμμένον (veiled), covered, or hidden by accident, by the fault of men, who labor under blindness not only connate, but also adventitious and voluntarily contracted, and permitted by the judgment of God, when pertinacity, corroborated by Satan, approaches. But the Holy Spirit effectively illuminates through the divine word the sinner who does not morosely struggle against it. The sacred psalmist ingenuously confesses this very thing, Ps. 119:130. The entrance of your words illuminates, makes the simple wise.

As soon as anyone enters into the reading and meditation of Holy Scripture, his intellect is illuminated by heavenly wisdom.

You say: I. Whoever blinds some men, he does not wish to illuminate all: But God, etc. Therefore. The minor is proved from John 12:40. The Jews could not believe, because Esaias said: He hath blinded their eyes. Resp. Distinguish between the antecedent and consequent will of God. By His antecedent will, God wishes to illuminate all men. But by His consequent, or judiciary will, He blinds some, not positively, by infusing blindness into their hearts; but negatively, or privatively, by forsaking them, and by withdrawing the light of grace, which was despised and petulantly repelled by them.

For which reason the inability to believe is not to be attributed to a destined will, or counsel of God, by which He absolutely denied all illuminating grace, but to the malice of the Jews, who perversely rejected the offered light.

But it is not given to all, etc. Matt. 13:11. Therefore. Resp. 1) I deny the major. Because God, by His antecedent will, or mercy, intends to illuminate all men: although in act they are only illuminated to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven who admit the light of the divine word by hearing, reading, and attentively meditating. 2) Those to whom by an absolute divine decree it is not given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, those God does not wish to illuminate; I concede. But the Savior in the cited place speaks of a respective decree, by which He regards the sloth, pride, and contempt of the hearers, and thus by the just judgment of God, and their own vice, a deeper knowledge of the mysteries of God is not given.

The sense, therefore, is: To you, who remain with me hearing, and seeking the interpretation of my parable concerning the seed scattered into different ground , it is given to know savingly the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven: To the rest, who proudly disdain my sermon, and depart from me, the parable was indeed spoken to the letter, but without a deeper understanding of the mystery lying under it, so that they may pay the just penalties for their negligence and pride.

You say: III. God hides the mysteries of faith and salvation from the wise of this world, Matt. 11:25. Therefore, He does not wish to illuminate all. Resp. The discourse in the cited place by Christ is concerning the ministerial gifts conferred by the heavenly Father upon His disciples, but denied to the proud Pharisees by just judgment; not, however, concerning the hiding of the mysteries of faith, which are necessary to be known for salvation.

See above Chapter I, p. 28. Question X.

Latin:

Deus benignissimus omnes homines illuminare quidem serio intendit ; actu autem illuminantur illi, qui ad ecclesiam vocati & adducti gratiam Spiritus Sancti admittunt, verbumque diuinum attente audiunt, legunt & meditantur .

Prob. a. Christus est lux vera, quæ illuminat omnem hominem venientem in mundum, Io. I, 9. Christus vera lux illuminat, quantum in ipso est, non vnam tantum nationem, non vnum hominem, sed omnes homines, prodeuntes in huius mundi tenebras. Venit enim, vt prædicationem euangelii tum omnium nationum, tum singulorum hominum cordibus illucescat. Non excluditur Scytha, non Iudæus, non Hispanus, non Gothus, non Britannus, non rex, non seruus, non mas, non fœmina. Perseuerant quidem multi in tenebris ignorantiæ & errorum: At vero non culpa denegatæ lucis, sed culpa propria, veluti si quis impingat in meridie, quod oculos nolit attollere. Scite inquit AVGVSTIN. tract. XXVII. in Ioann. Qui resistit, quomodo viuificabitur? Aduersarius est radio lucis, quo penetrandus est. Non aduertit aciem, sed claudit mentem.

2) Apparuit gratia Dei salutaris omnibus hominibus, erudiens nos, Tit. II, 11. 12. Gratia erudiens, siue illuminans, omnibus hominibus illuxit, secundum gratiosam Dei intentionem: Lucet in tenebris, etiam si tenebræ eam non apprehendant, Io. I, 5.

3) Nos annuntiamus Christum, admonentes omnem hominem, & docentes omnem hominem in omni sapientia, vt sistamus omnem hominem perfectum in Christo Iesu, Col I, 28. Paullus & apostolici viri omnem hominem, si non lingua, certe calamo docere cœlestem sapientiam intenderunt.

Prob. b. Homo ad ecclesiam vocatus, & verbum diuinum admittens, attenteque meditans illuminatur. Deus quippe e tenebris nos vocauit in admirandam suam lucem, 1 Petr. II, 9. Mittuntur etiam præcones sacri ad aperiendum oculos auditorum, vt conuertantur a tenebris ad lucem, Act. XXVI, 18. Non est autem gratia Spiritus S. irresistibilis; siquidem peccator, præfracte contumax, supernaturalem illuminationem, obiecto velamine, aut obiecto malitioso, impedire potest. Id quod innuit Apostolus, 2 Cor. IV, 3. 4. Si absconditum est euangelium nostrum, in iis, qui pereunt, absconditum est, in quibus Deus sæculi huius excæcauit sensus infidelium, vt non splendeat illis illuminatio euangelii gloriæ Christi. Nimirum euangelium, per se lucidum, κεκαλυμμένον, tectum, vel opertum est per accidens, culpa hominum, laborantium cæcitate non tantum connata, sed etiam adscititia & voluntarie contracta, ac permissa iudicio Dei, cum accedit pertinacia, a Satana corroborata. At peccatorem, morose non obluctantem, Spiritus S. per verbum diuinum efficaciter illuminat. Id ipsum ingenue fatetur hieropsaltes, Ps. CXIX, 130. Aditus verborum tuorum illuminat, intelligentes reddit simplices.

Quamprimum aliquis ingreditur in lectionem & meditationem S. scripturae, intellectus ejus sapientia caelesti collustratur.

Dicis: I. Quicunque nonnullos homines excaecat, is non vult omnes illuminare: Atqui Deus &c. E. Minor prob. ex Io. XX, 40. Iudaei non poterant credere, quia Esaias dixit: Oculos eorum excaecauit. Resp. Dist. inter voluntatem Dei antecedentem, & consequentem. Voluntate antecedente Deus omnes homines vult illuminare. At voluntate consequente, siue iudiciaria, nonnullos excaecat, non positiue, coecitatem cordibus immittendo; sed negatiue, vel priuatiue, eos deferendo, & lucem gratiae, ab ipsis contemptam & petulanter repulsam, subtrahendo.

Quam ob rem impotentia credendi non est tribuenda destinatae voluntati, aut consilio Dei, quo omnem gratiam illuminatricem absolute denegauerit, sed malitiae Iudaeorum, qui oblatum lumen proterue reiecerunt.

Dicis: II. Quibus non est datum, nosse mysteria regni caelorum, illos Deus non vult illuminare: Atqui non omnibus datum est &c. Matth. XIII, 11. E. Resp. 1) Neg. mai. Quia Deus voluntate antecedente, siue misericordia, omnes homines illuminare intendit: licet actu tantum illuminentur ad cognoscendum mysteria regni caelorum, qui lumen verbi diuini audiendo, legendo & attente meditando admittunt. 2) Quibus absoluto decreto diuino non est datum nosse mysteria regni caelorum, illos Deus non vult illuminare; concedo. At Saluator l. c. loquitur de decreto respectiuo, quo respicit auditorum socordiam, superbiam & contemptum, adeoque iusto Dei iudicio, & proprio ipsorum vitio, penitior cognitio mysteriorum Dei non datur.

Sensus itaque est: Vobis, discendi audis, mecum manentibus, & interpretationem parabolae meae de semine in diuersum agrum sparso expetentibus , datum est, salutariter nosse mysteria regni caelorum: Reliqvis, concionem meam superbe fastidientibus, & a me discedentibus, dicta quidem est parabola ad litteram, sed fine penitiori intellectu mysterii sub ea latentis, vt negligentiae suae atque superbiae iustas pendant poenas.

Dicis: III. Deus sapientibus huius mundi mysteria fidei & salutis abscondit, Matth. XI, 25. E, non vult omnes illuminare. Resp. Sermo est l. c. Christo de donis ministrantibus, discipulis suis a Patre caelesti collatis, superbis autem Pharisaeis iusto iudicio denegatis; non vero de occultatione mysteriorum fidei, ad salutem cognitu necessariorum.

Vid. supra Cap. I. p. 28. Quaest. X.


### Quest. IX. What men does God illuminate?: Whether only the intellect, or also the will of the sinner called to the church is illuminated?

Whether only the intellect, or also the will of the sinner called to the church is illuminated?

First, the intellect of the sinner brought to the church is immediately illuminated a): consequently and mediately also his will b). Proof a. 1) Illumination is called Φωτισμὸς τῆς γνώσεως τῆς δόξης τοῦ Θεοῦ, the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God, 2 Cor. 4:6. The intellect is therefore illuminated, that it may know the glory of God. 2) God gives us the enlightened eyes of the mind, that we may know what is the hope of our calling, Eph. 1:18. Proof b. The grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men, teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world, Tit. 2:11, 12. The saving grace of God, which has shone upon all men like the sun, instructs the intellect of the sinner, and suffuses it with the light of knowledge, so that this light may be diffused into the will, for fleeing ungodliness and choosing the holiness of life.

Whence Paul wishes illumination for the Colossians, that they might be able to be sanctified, Col.

1:10. Consider therefore, writes D. FECHTIVS, in diff. de. O. M. gratiae p. 20. The word of illumination in the use of scripture [is] not of the mind only [the text here repeats "scripturæ vfu non mentis" due to a printing error in the original]. not only denotes liberation from ignorance and errors and guidance into all spiritual truth, but also a change of the will into another and better state.

Accurately , however, D. BREITHAVPT observed in thes. credend. that illumination relates more to the intellect, regeneration more to the will. p. 136.

Quest. XI. Can supernatural illumination exist in the human intellect without the sanctification of the will? Since supernatural illumination is a successive act of applying grace a); certainly, imperfect illumination can exist in the human intellect without the sanctification of the will b).

Antithesis is that of all mystical writers, who establish that the purgative way is prior to the illuminative: whose opinion one may perceive from theol. German, whose words these are, c. 12.

Now one should know that no one can be enlightened unless he has first been cleansed, clarified, and emptied, nor can anyone be united with God unless he has first been enlightened.

The same is taught by G. ARNOLD from Hugo de Palma, theol. myst. c. VI. p. 119.

When a disciple of Christ has long walked the way of purification, and now hears the voice of his Bridegroom through an internal prompting speaking to him: Arise, daughter Zion, arise from the dust! (which he will certainly hear if he walks humbly, considers himself a sinful man, and recognizes his nothingness), then he shall arise and proceed to the other way of illumination.

Latin:

Vtrum tantum intellectus, an etiam voluntas peccatoris ad ecclesiam vocati illuminatur?

Primo immediate illuminatur peccatoris, ad ecclesiam adducti, intellectus a): consequenter & mediate etiam illius voluntas b). Prob. a. 1) Illuminatio dicitur Φωτισμὸς τῆς γνώσεως τῆς δόξης τοῦ Θεῦ, illuminatio cognitionis gloriae Dei, 2 Cor. IV, 6. Illuminatur ergo intellectus, vt gloriam Dei cognoscat. 2) Deus dat nobis illuminatos oculos mentis, vt sciamus, quae sit spes vocationis nostrae, Eph. I, 18. Prob. b. Apparuit gratia Dei salutaris omnibus hominibus, erudiens nos, vt abnegemus impietatem, & mundanas concupiscentias, ac sobrie & iuste & pie viuamus in praesenti saeculo Tit. ii, 11. 12. Gratia Dei salutaris, quae omnibus hominibus, benefici instar solis, illuxit, intellectum peccatoris erudit, & perfundit luce cognitionis, vt haec lux diffundatur in voluntatem, ad fugiendum impietatem, & eligendum sanctimoniam vitae.

Vnde Paullus Colossensibus optat illuminationem, vt sanctificari queant, Col.

I, 10. Considerate itaque scribit D. FECHTIVS, in diff. de. O. M. gratiae p. 20. Illuminationis vox scriptura vsu non mentis tantum fcripturæ vfu non mentis tantum ab ignorantia et erroribus liberationem et manuductionem in omnem veritatem spiritualem notat, sed et voluntatis in statum alium et meliorem mutationem.

Accurate tamen observauit D. BREITHAVPT, in thes. credend. quod illuminatio magis intellectum, regeneratio voluntatem magis respiciat. p. 136.

Quaest. XI. Potestne illuminatio supernaturalis in intellectu hominis esse, absque sanctificatione voluntatis? Cum illuminatio supernaturalis sit actus gratiae applicatricis successiuus a); vtique imperfecta illuminatio in intellectu hominis esse potest, sine sanctificatione voluntatis b).

Antithesis est omnium scriptorum mysticorum, qui viam purgatiuam illuminatiua priorem esse statuunt: quorum sententiam perspicere licet e theol. German: cuius haec sunt verba c. 12.

Nun soll man wissen, daß niemand erleuchtet mag werden, er sey denn zuvor gereiniget, erläutert und erlediget, auch mag niemand mit Gott vereiniget werden, sey denn zuvor erleuchtet.

Idem docet G. ARNOLD. ex Hugonis de Palma theol. myst. c. VI. p. 119.

Wenn ein Jünger Christi den Weg der Reinigung lange durchgangen ist, und nun die Stimme seines Bräutigams durch innerliches Eingeben hört zu ihm sprechen: Stehe auf Tochter Zion, stehe auf aus dem Staube! (welches er gewiß hören wird, wenn er demüthig wandelt, sich für einen sündigen Menschen hält, und seine Nichtigkeit erkennet), alsdenn soll er aufstehen, und zu dem andern Wege der Erleuchtung schreiten.


### Quest. IX. What men does God illuminate?: Exposition Obs

EXPOSITION

Obs.

I. Illumination is succinctly described as being an instruction from the Word of God concerning sacred matters, concerning the salvation of men, by the author D. FECHTIVS, in his treatise on the order and mode of divine grace, p. 18.

More fully , however, it can be defined: Illumination is an act of applying grace, by which the Holy Spirit informs a man, called to the church, through the ministry of the Word, concerning God and divine matters, and elevates and strengthens his intellect above natural powers to understand divine mysteries, so that, with the darkness of ignorance and errors dispelled, it imbues him with the knowledge of the true God, and instills in him, from the Law, the recognition of sin, and from the Gospel, the knowledge of Christ and the divine mercy founded in Him.

Obs.

II. The given definition rests on a solid foundation; since a) the end and effect of instruction is certain knowledge.

To teach, or to inform, signifies to make someone knowing or to instill knowledge into someone. Now, the effect of illumination is γνῶσις, or knowledge. For it is called Φωτισμὸς γνώσεως, the illumination of the knowledge of the divine glory, 2 Cor.

IV, 6. The intellect is therefore enlightened, that it may know the glory of God.

God gives us enlightened eyes of the mind, εἰς τὸ εἰδέναι ἡμᾶς, that we may know what is the hope of our calling, Eph. I, 18. b) King David explains "to enlighten" by "to make understanding," Ps. CXIX, 130. The entrance of thy words enlighteneth; it giveth understanding unto the simple.

Which words, intending to explain, D. GEIERS says: The preceding figurative word is explained by the proper word, "enlighteneth." For הֵבִין, taken transitively, signifies "made to understand," "instructed."

Therefore, to enlighten is the same as to instruct, and enlightening grace is teaching, as D. DANNHAV. says in hodof. phanom. IX. p. 938. c) Ministers of the church are said to enlighten their hearers.

Eph. III, 9. 2 Cor. IV, 6. But they cannot enlighten their hearers by any other reason than by informing them. It remains, therefore, firm and fixed that illumination is an instruction from the Word of God concerning sacred matters, concerning the salvation of men.

Obs. III. Theologians distinguish perfect illumination from imperfect, a distinction which D. SEB. SCHMIDT, a theologian of, if any, a refined judgment, also uses in his later biblical college, p. 164. Subjectively, one can be ψυχικὸς, animal, who understands something of those things which are of the Spirit of God; not indeed as such, but as one already imperfectly illuminated by the Spirit of God. That this distinction is solid is agreed upon by all who accurately weigh that illumination is a successive action, which, when it is begun and continued, is imperfect; when it is consummated and brought to an end, it is called perfect.

Obs. IV. Imperfect illumination is also called by theologians literal and pedagogical; perfect is termed spiritual and completely saving. DANNH. in hodof. phænom. XI. p. 1419. begins: Sin against the Holy Spirit is proæretic ἀπιστία, in a man sufficiently illuminated, Hebr. VI, 4. c. X, 26. whether that illumination was pedagogical and of the letter only, or spiritual, joined with a γεύσει of heavenly things. D. QUENSTEDT explains this distinction more clearly in system. Theol. part. II. p. 77. Φωτισμὸς, or illumination, is either παιδαγωγικὴ καὶ γραμματικὴ, pedagogical, merely literal and external, when someone is instructed in the knowledge of divine truth, and convinced of its certainty in his conscience, yet does not have this known truth sealed in his heart by the seal of the Spirit, or confirmed by the gracious indwelling of the Holy Spirit; or πνευματικὴ, spiritual, gracious and internal, when, namely, someone truly regenerate not only has a literal understanding of evangelical doctrine, but is at the same time a temple of the Holy Spirit, which He graciously inhabits, or when he is corroborated, confirmed, and sealed by the internal testimony of the graciously indwelling [Spirit].

Obs. V. Orthodox doctors attribute imperfect and pedagogical illumination to assisting divine grace, not indwelling; which distinction D. IO. ADAM. OSIANDER explains excellently in theol. posit. acroam. P. III. p. 19. Divine grace is distinguished into assisting and indwelling; and indeed that assisting [grace] is that which still operates from the outside, not that it does not touch the heart of man itself, but because, with the Spirit still remaining outside and not indwelling, it exerts its power, to which is assigned preventing grace, which removes the natural incapacity innate in all; preparing [grace], which restrains natural resistance, adverse to spiritual things; finally exciting [grace], which instructs the mind with literal sense, works assent, and crushes the heart: but it is called indwelling when the Holy Spirit himself enters the heart of man, changes it, and inhabits it. From this proceeds perfect illumination, which suffices for exciting faith in Christ, and exerts itself through spiritual and pious motions. The foundation of the distinction into assisting and indwelling grace is found in Apoc. III, 20. where Christ addresses the Laodicean bishop: Behold! I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice, and opens the door, I will enter to him, and will sup with him, and he with me. Indicated by these words are a) assisting grace; because Christ says that he stands at the door, namely, of the human heart, to convert it. He does not, however, stand idle, but knocks, and desires to be let in; he knocks, so that his voice may be heard, and Christ himself, crying and calling, may be recognized from the voice; which is b) preventing and exciting grace. He knocks so that the door may be opened; which is c) preparing grace. For men of unregenerate heart open the door not by the natural powers of free will, but by new powers conferred through preventing and preparing grace: just as those resurrected from natural death rise not by their own powers, but by new powers given in the resurrection. For by knocking, Christ grants the power of opening, which is the efficacy proper to the word of the gospel, Rom. I, 16. When the door of the heart is opened, Christ enters; which is d) entering and indwelling grace. For thus Christ enters, that we may sup with him, and we with him. Christ enters by kindling true and living faith with the light of his word, and by dwelling in us through faith, Eph. III, 17. From which arises our sweetest communion with Christ, which is a foretaste of eternal life. They are mistaken, therefore, who have the effrontery to reject the distinction of grace into assisting and indwelling as if it were a new invention, resting on no firm support. This notable distinction, however, stands unshaken, since the very author of salvation handed it down to us and inculcated it. Obs. VI. Imperfect and pedagogical illumination is not natural, but supernatural; for the reason that it a) proceeds from the light of special revelation; b) is obtained by us through the supernatural operation… of the Holy Spirit; c) is concerned with the mysteries of faith, and d) is divinely ordained to a spiritual end. We cannot but note here carefully that truly orthodox theologians have never distinguished illumination into natural and supernatural. Consider, says the Blessed DORSCHAEVS (citing D. CALOVIVS in bibl. illustr. on Hebr. VI, 4.). There is no illumination of the natural intelligence, as Beza, Piscator, Marloratus, etc., said on the passage of John I, 9. For that is nowhere in the sacred writings called Φωτισμὸς, nor is such a thing understood in John I. For there is pronounced there concerning Christ such a Φωτισμὸς, which properly pertains to the prophetic office of Christ, in respect of which Christ is the Φῶς ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ φαῖνον, in verse 5. concerning which light John the Baptist testified in v. 7. by which illumination the world could have known Christ, had it not loved darkness more than light, John I, 10. c. III, 19. The reason why theologians have deliberately abstained from the distinction of illumination into natural and supernatural is given by our great CHEMNITIVS in his theological loci P. I. on God, p. m. 20. Natural knowledge of God is either none, or imperfect, or languid. None, because all philosophy knows nothing of the gratuitous promise of the remission of sins; for the Son of God revealed that, brought forth from the bosom of the Father, to the Church, John I, 18. Imperfect; because the nations knew only a certain small particle of the law, but reason neither knows nor determines anything certain concerning the interior worships of the first table; languid; because, although it is impressed upon human minds that there is a God, and that He commands obedience, according to the distinction between honorable and base things, yet the assent is not only languid, but is often shaken by horrible doubts (*). Obs. VII. Divine revelation differs from the illumination of the Holy Spirit. For revelation is either natural or supernatural. The former is that by which God manifested Himself both through the light of nature implanted, and through effects to be seen in the kingdom of nature, Rom. I, 19. c. II, 14. 15. The latter is that by which God, partly immediately, partly mediately, through His word, makes Himself and His will known for the salvation of the human race. But the illumination of the Holy Spirit is always a supernatural action, by which the intellect is elevated above the powers of nature to understand divine mysteries, which cannot be known by the guidance of the light of nature. Revelation can take place through the general concurrence of God: illumination always requires a special influx of God. By revelation, saving doctrine is proposed externally: but through illumination, it is received within the mind. Hence it happens that revelation not rarely reaches those who are ignorant of its force and meaning; e.g., Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, the hearers of the Apostles at the Pentecostal feast: but through illumination, the Holy Spirit works and effects knowledge in the intellect of a man who does not maliciously resist. God reveals Himself to the devil, whom, however, the Holy Spirit never deigns to favor with gracious illumination, since that capital enemy of God and men is not capable of illuminating grace, which looks toward eternal salvation. Beware, therefore, of confusing divine revelation with the illumination of the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

ΕΚΘΕΣΙΣ

Obs.

I. Illuminatio succincte describitur, quod sit informatio e verbo Dei de rebus sacris, salutem hominum concernentibus, auctore D. FECHTIO, in tractatu de ordine, modoque gratiae diuinae p. 18.

Vberius autem definiri potest: Illuminatio est actus gratiae applicatricis, quo Spiritus S. hominem, ad ecclesiam vocatum, per ministerium verbi, de Deo, rebusque diuinis informat, atque intellectum eius supra vires naturales eleuat, et corroborat, ad intelligendum mysteria diuina, vt, depulsis ignorantiae errorumque tenebris, ipsum veri Dei notitia imbuat, atque ex lege agnitionem peccati, ex euangelio vero, Christi, et in eo fundatae misericordiae diuinae cognitionem eidem instillet.

Obs.

II. Nititur data definitio solido fundamento; siquidem a) informationis finis et effectus est certa notitia.

Docere, vel informare, significat, aliquem scientem reddere vel notitiam alicui instillare. Iam vero illuminationis effectus est γνῶσις, siue cognitio. Dicitur enim Φωτισμὸς γνώσεως, illuminatio cognitionis gloriae diuinae, 2 Cor.

IV, 6. Illuminatur ergo intellectus, vt gloriam Dei cognoscat.

Deus dat nobis illuminatos oculos mentis, εἰς τὸ εἰδέναι ἡμᾶς, vt sciamus, quae sit spes vocationis nostrae, Eph. I, 18. b) Rex Dauid illuminare exponit, per, facere intelligentem, Ps. CXIX, 130. Aditus verborum tuorum illuminat; intelligentes reddit simplices.

Quae verba explanaturus D. GEIERS, inquit: Voce propria exponitur praecedens figurata, illuminat. Nam הֵבִין, transitiue sumtum, significat, intelligere fecit, instruxit.

Ergo illuminare idem est, quod instruere, et gratia illuminatrix est docens, dicente D. DANNHAV. in hodof. phanom. IX. p. 938. c) Ministri ecclesiae dicuntur auditores suos illuminare.

Eph. III, 9. 2 Cor. IV, 6. Non autem possunt auditores suos alia ratione, quam informando illuminare. Ratum igitur, fixumque manet, quod illuminatio sit informatio e verbo Dei de rebus sacris, salutem hominum concernentibus. sacris, salutem hominum concernentibus.

Obs. III. Distinguunt Theologi illuminationem perfectam ab imperfecta, qua distinctione etiam vtitur D. SEB. SCHMIDIVS, Theologus, si quis alius, exasciati iudicii, in collegio biblico posteriori p. 164. Subiectiue potest esse ψυχικὸς, animalis, qui aliquid intelligit eorum, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei; non quidem qua talis, sed qua iam a Spiritu Dei imperfecte illuminatus. Hanc distinctionem esse solidam, constat inter omnes, accurate pensitantes, illuminationem esse actionem successiuam, quæ, cum inchoatur & continuatur, imperfecta est; cum consummatur & ad finem perducitur, perfecta dicitur.

Obs. IV. Illuminatio imperfecta a Theologis etiam dicitur litteralis & pædagogica, perfecta adpellatur spiritualis & complete salutaris. DANNH. in hodof. phænom. XI. p. 1419. infit: Peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum est ἀπιστία proæretica, in homine satis illuminato, Hebr. VI, 4. c. X, 26. siue pædagogica illa fuerit illuminatio & litteræ tantum, siue spiritualis, cum γεύσει cælestium coniuncta. Quam distinctionem clarius exponit D. QVENSTED. in system. Theol. part. II. p. 77. Φωτισμὸς, siue illuminatio, vel est παιδαγωγικὴ καὶ γραμματικὴ, pædagogica, mere litteralis & externa, quando quis veritatis diuinæ agnitione est instructus, deque eius certitudine in conscientia sua conuictus, nondum tamen cognitam hanc veritatem sigillo Spiritus in corde suo obsignatam, aut per gratiosam Spiritus S. inhabitationem confirmatam habet; vel πνευματικὴ, spiritualis, gratiosa & interna, quando scil. quis vere renatus non tantum habet litteralem doctrinæ euangelicæ intelligentiam, sed simul est templum Spiritus S., quod ipse gratiose inhabitat, siue quando gratiose inhabitantis interno testimonio corroboratur, confirmatur & obsignatur.

Obs. V. Tribuunt doctores orthodoxi illuminationem imperfectam & pædagogicam gratiæ diuinæ assistenti, non inhabitanti; quam distinctionem egregie explicat D. IO. ADAM. OSIANDER in theol. posit. acroam. P. III. p. 19. Distinguitur gratia diuina in assistentem, & inhabitantem; & quidem assistens illa est, quæ extrinsecus adhuc operatur, non quod non ipsum cor hominis tangat, sed quia, adhuc Spiritu exterius versante, nec inhabitante, suam vim exserit, cui assignatur gratia præueniens, quæ incapacitatem naturalem, omnibus connatam, aufert; præparans, quæ naturalem resistentiam, spiritualibus aduersam, cohibet; denique excitans, quæ mentem sensu litterali instruit, assensum operatur, atque cor conterit: inhabitans vero dicitur, cum ipse Spiritus S. cor hominis ingreditur, illud immutat atque inhabitat. Ab hoc proficiscitur illuminatio perfecta, quæ ad excitandam fidem in Christum sufficit, & per spirituales, piosque motus se exserit. Fundamentum distinctionis in gratiam assistentem & inhabitantem habetur Apoc. III, 20. vbi Christus episcopum Laodicenum alloquitur: Ecce! sto ad ostium & pulso. Si quis audiuerit vocem meam, & aperuerit ianuam, ingrediar ad ipsum, & cœnabo cum ipso, atque ipse mecum. Indicatur his verbis a) gratia assistens; quia Christus dicit, se stare ad ostium, scil. cordis humani, ad illud conuertendum. Non autem stat otiosus, sed pulsat, & cupit intromitti; pulsat, vt vox eius audiatur, & ex voce ipse clamans & vocans Christus agnoscatur; quæ est b) gratia præveniens & excitans. Ita pulsat, vt ianua aperiatur; quæ est c) gratia præparans. Nam homines irregeniti cordis ostium aperiunt non naturalibus liberi arbitrii viribus, sed nouis, per gratiam præuenientem & præparantem collatis viribus: sicut resuscitati ex morte naturali non suis, sed nouis, in resuscitatione datis, viribus resurgunt. Pulsando quippe Christus vim largitur aperiendi, quæ efficacia verbo euangelii propria est, Rom. I, 16. Cum ianua cordis aperitur, Christus ingreditur; quæ est d) gratia ingrediens & inhabitans. Sic enim Christus ingreditur, vt nobiscum cœnet, & nos cum illo. Ingreditur Christus, lumine verbi sui veram viuamque fidem accendendo, & per fidem in nobis habitando, Eph. III, 17. Ex quo oritur dulcissima nostri cum Christo communio, quæ est prægustus vitæ æternæ. Falluntur igitur, qui distinctionem gratiæ in assistentem, & inhabitantem, reiicere, frontem fumunt, perinde ac sit nouum commentum, nullo firmo fulcro nixum. Stat autem insignis hæc distinctio inconcussa, cum ipse salutis assertor eam tradiderit nobis, & inculcauerit. Obs. VI. Illuminatio imperfecta & pædagogica non est naturalis, sed supernaturalis; ideo, quod a) a lumine specialis reuelationis proficiscitur; b) per supernaturalem Spiritus S. operationem a nobis obtinetur; c) circa mysteria fidei versatur, & d) ad finem spiritualem diuinitus ordinatur. Non possumus, quin hic sedulo notemus, Theologos, vere orthodoxos, illuminationem nunquam in naturalem, & supernaturalem distinxisse. Considerate inquit B. DORSCHAEVS (citante D. CALOVIO in bibl. illustr. ad Hebr. VI, 4.). Non est illuminatio naturalis intelligentiæ, vti Beza, Piscator, Marloratus &c. ad locum Io. I, 9. dixerunt. Nam illa nuspiam in sacris litteris dicitur Φωτισμὸς, nec Io. I. talis intelligitur. Est enim ibi de Christo pronuntiatus Φωτισμὸς talis, qui proprie ad officium Christi propheticum pertinet, cuius respectu Christus est Φῶς ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ φαῖνον, versu 5. de qua luce testificatus est Ioannes baptista v. 7. qua illuminatione mundus potuisset cognoscere Christum, nisi tenebras plus dilexiffet, quam lucem, Io. I, 10. c. III, 19. Caussam, cur Theologi a distinctione illuminationis in naturalem, & supernaturalem consulto abstinuerint, reddit magnus noster CHEMNITIVS in locis thologicis P. I. de Deo, p. m. 20. Notitia de Deo naturalis aut nulla, aut imperfecta, aut languida est. Nulla, quia de gratuita promissione remissionis peccatorum nihil nouit tota philosophia; illam enim Filius Dei e sinu Patris prolatam reuelauit ecclesiæ, Io. I, 18. Imperfecta; quia gentes aliquam tantum particulam legis nouerunt, de interioribus vero cultibus primæ tabulæ nihil certi vel nouit, vel statuit ratio; languida; quia, etsi impressum est humanis mentibus esse Deum, & præcipere obedientiam, iuxta discrimen honestorum & turpium, tamen assensio non tantum languida est, sed horrendis etiam dubitationibus sæpe excutitur (*). Obs. VII. Differt reuelatio diuina, ab illuminatione Spiritus Sancti. Nam reuelatio est vel naturalis, vel supernaturalis. Illa est, qua Deus se manifestauit tum per lumen naturæ insitum, tum per effecta in regno naturæ conspicienda, Rom. I, 19. c. II, 14. 15. Hæc est, qua Deus partim immediate, partim mediate, per verbum suum, se & voluntatem suam ad salutem generis humani patefacit. Illuminatio autem Spiritus S. semper est supernaturalis actio, qua intellectus eleuatur supra vires naturæ ad intelligendum mysteria diuina, quæ ductu luminis naturæ cognosci nequeunt. Reuelatio fieri potest per concursum Dei generalem: illuminatio semper influxum Dei specialem requirit. Reuelatione doctrina salutaris externe proponitur: at per illuminationem illa intra animum recipitur. Inde sit, vt reuelatio haud raro obtingat ignorantibus eius vim & sensum; v. gr. Pharaoni, Nabuchodonosori, auditoribus Apostolorum in festo pentecostali: per illuminationem autem Spiritus Sanctus cognitionem in intellectu hominis, malitiose non obsistentis, operatur & efficit. Reuelat se Deus diabolo, quem tamen Spiritus S. gratiosa illuminatione nunquam dignatur, cum capitalis ille Dei hominumque hostis gratiæ illuminatricis, æternam salutem respicientis, non sit capax. Caue igitur, reuelationem diuinam cum illuminatione Spiritus Sancti confundas.


### Quest. IX. What men does God illuminate?: Exposition Obs (continued)

Obs. VIII. Illumination differs from regeneration. The former concerns the intellect more; the latter concerns the will more. The former consists formally in information from the divine word concerning sacred things: the latter in the donation of faith. The effect of the former is the knowledge of divine mysteries: the effect of the latter is trust resting on the merit of Christ. The former precedes, the latter follows.

Obs. IX. Illumination differs from sanctification, strictly so called. That sanctification, taken in a broader sense, embraces all acts of applying grace, is agreed upon among all Christians: yet the same, taken in a stricter sense, is distinguished from illumination 1) by reason of the partial subject; because through illumination the intellect is proximately and formally perfected, through sanctification the will: 2) by reason of breadth; because more men are illuminated than are sanctified: 3) by reason of the effect and proper term; because the effect of illumination is γνῶσις, or supernatural knowledge of God and divine things, Eph. I, 18. 2 Cor IV, 6. but the effect of sanctification is ἁγιοσύνη καὶ δικαιοσύνη, holiness and righteousness, Eph. IV, 24.

Β Ε Β Α Ι Ω Σ Ι Σ.

That simple, or imperfect, illumination can exist in the intellect of a man who does not morosely resist, without the sanctification of the will, is proven: 1) Whatever divine illumination precedes saving faith by some interval of time, greater or lesser, that can exist without sanctification: But imperfect divine illumination &c. Therefore. The major is clear: because hearts are purified by faith, Acts XV, 9. Therefore, where there is no faith in the heart, there is no purity or holiness. The minor is proven; because the ordinary illumination of adults is a successive act of grace, which is not completed in one moment, but happens through intervals of time, through degrees, through repeated acts, until they conceive faith fully and savingly, so much so that no act of divine applying grace has more need of delay and duration than illumination, in the judgment of D. FECHT in his most learned treatise on the order and mode of grace, §. 9. p. 19. Which gradual and successive illumination of adult men is taught by a) Practice itself. For a minister of the church, intending to convert a Jew, strives with every effort and study to illuminate him. א. He convinces the Jew that the Messiah, promised in the O.T., has already come long ago, having employed clear testimonies of scripture, and having removed the doubts from the mind of the Jew. Meanwhile, time slips away. ב. He demonstrates that this Messiah is not a mere man, but true God, and the Son of God the Father, begotten from eternity. ג. He shows that this Messiah and θεάν- θρωπον is Jesus of Nazareth, the son of the virgin Mary, having compared prophetic oracles with the birth, doctrine, passion, resurrection, ascension into heaven, and miracles of Christ, where many doubts must be removed for the Jew. Meanwhile, one hour and another flows by. ד. He proves from the Old Testament that in one divine essence there are three persons, God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, where not only must the truth be asserted, but also the scruples injected into the mind of the Jew must be uprooted: which sacred labor requires a certain space of time. ה. He instills in the Jew the doctrine concerning the priestly, prophetic, and kingly office of Christ: which illumination demands a delay of time. ו. He inculcates in the one being converted the δοτικὰ means of salvation, the word of God and the sacraments, through which God deals with man today, that He may convert, regenerate, justify, and save him.

I. He shows that, on our part, true faith, apprehending the merit of Christ, is required for the remission of sins and the attainment of eternal life, and thus that the sinner is justified not by good works but by faith.

The Jew will raise doubts, which must be resolved in due time.

II. He teaches that faith, which has justified, manifests itself through the holiness of life, otherwise it is not living, but dead.

Receiving this information, the Jew is finally sufficiently illuminated, converted, regenerated, and baptized, as he receives it as the seal of regeneration.

From this practice, and the singular examples joined to it, it is clear that illumination is not completed in a moment, but over a longer tract of time.

Let us consider the illumination and conversion of the Jew Gerson, which D. CALIXTUS recounts in his treatise on the authority of Holy Scripture, p. 36, and adduces the very words of Gerson: A certain poor Christian woman, says Gerson, my neighbor, gave me as a pledge a copy of the German New Testament, translated by Luther: to whom I gave in return eight shillings, so that I might earn interest in my own way, and meanwhile peruse the book; not indeed that I doubted the truth of the Jewish religion, or believed any article of the Christian faith to be correct, but that I might know what that error was, so greatly effective, which was seducing so many myriads of souls and casting them headlong into destruction.

Therefore, in the presence of my two kinsmen, Lazarus and Simeon, I read the whole thing, not without blasphemies. Meanwhile, however, my heart was struck, and when I had noticed that the Evangelists and Apostles, and Christ Himself, so often appeal to the Old Testament, and subsequently adduce passages from it one after another: I was enticed to read it again, and indeed secretly, with no one knowing, not even my wife, and to compare the adduced passages with the text of the Old Testament itself. When I did this, such a light shone upon me that for that reason I owe eternal thanks to God.

Who does not see that Gerson's illumination was imperfect for a time, without regeneration and sanctification?

There is an excellent example in AUGUSTINE, who in his books of Confessions explains at length how he was illuminated and converted by God: but he testifies that the Holy Spirit worked in him over a long tract of time, before he was fully illuminated and converted.

In Book V of the Confessions, c. 14, he recounts what happened to him when he had once heard AMBROSE preaching the word of God: namely, that the things proposed entered his mind gradually, and seemed plausible to him, while he had nothing to reply to them: Yet I thought, he says, that more learned men could refute them.

Therefore, he did not yet have faith itself, but remained still doubtful.

Later, in Book VI, he exposes the temptations and doubts with which he was sometimes conflicted.

In Book VIII, c. 2, he recounts what happened when he had approached SIMPLICIANUS, who later succeeded Ambrose in the bishopric of Milan: namely, that Simplicianus had told him about VICTORINUS the Rhetorician, who was converted, that he had been illuminated by the Holy Spirit from the reading of Scripture, and that he had entered the church and publicly professed the Christian faith.

When AUGUSTINE had heard these things narrated by Simplicianus, he says in c. 5, I burned to imitate the example of Victorinus. Yet he could not then strive that far, because of the valid doubts that clung to his mind.

For which thing, he says, I sighed, bound not by another's iron, but by my own iron will.

The enemy held my will, and from it had made a chain for me, and had bound me. Where indeed the intellect of AUGUSTINE was successively illuminated, although his iron will for a time obstructed the converting and regenerating grace. b) If illumination were an ordinary instantaneous action, it would be irresistible; for no impediment can be opposed to an instantaneous divine action.

Creation is an instantaneous action, because it is an irresistible divine action.

When God said: Let there be light! at that same moment light was present, Gen. 1, 3. No one could resist divine creation.

…But if God, by His absolute and irresistible power, wished to illuminate a sinful man, it would certainly be momentary, and always joined with the sanctification of the will. But experience testifies that many mortals struggle against divine grace, which works through ordinary means. AUGUSTINE says wisely in Tract. XXVII on John: 'He who resists, how is he brought to life? He is an adversary to the ray of light by which he is to be penetrated. He does not turn his gaze, but closes his mind.'…

c) In the same way that the Holy Spirit informs us through Holy Scripture by proposing and inculcating the chapters of Christian doctrine to our intellect, so too does He illuminate us as we read or hear Holy Scripture: But the Holy Spirit informs us through Holy Scripture successively, by proposing and inculcating the chapters of Christian doctrine to our intellect one after another: Therefore.

d) A good sower scatters seed in his field, so that it may bear first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain, Mark IV, 28. Thus God, scattering the good seed, His word, into the hearts of men, ordinarily and always intends and wills to confer upon the hearers a more abundant degree of grace, up to completion. From which Christ compels us: 'Take heed how you hear!' For whoever has (receives and retains the first degree of illumination), to him it will be given, Luke VIII, 18.

e) A symbolic example of successive illumination can be seen in the healing of that blind man, of whom Holy Scripture makes mention, Mark VIII, 22 seqq. Christ healed him, having put spittle into his eyes, not by restoring his sight perfectly in a moment; but by opening his eyes slowly and gradually, so that at first he saw faintly, and perceived men walking like trees; then, when Christ laid His hand upon his eyes, with his sight fully restored, he looked upon all things clearly: Thus God opens the eyes of the mind of an unregenerate man more and more through His word, so that his knowledge of God and divine things is at first faint and meager, but with the passage of time it takes on increments, if he continues to meditate on the divine word.

f) The Apostle Paul was illuminated extraordinarily through the immediate revelation and appearance of Christ. Nevertheless, his illumination was not instantaneous. For when he was surrounded by an unusual light shining from heaven, and fell headlong to the ground, he heard a heavenly voice: 'Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?' Saul, ignorant of the author of the heavenly voice, said: 'Who are you, Lord?' But the Lord said: 'I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting; it is hard for you to kick against the goad.' Behold the beginning of supernatural illumination, from which Paul recognized the Lord Jesus and His will, that he should desist from the persecution of Christians. But at that moment in time he was not yet fully converted, although a desire for conversion had been injected into his will. Therefore, trembling and astonished, he said: 'Lord, what do you want me to do?' But the Lord said to him: 'Arise and enter the city; then it will be told to you what you must do.' [6] Therefore, having entered the city of Damascus, he was illuminated more fully by Ananias, and filled with the Holy Spirit, Acts IX.

Prob. 2) If the illumination of the intellect cannot exist without the sanctification of the will, no Jew, no Turk today can be successively illuminated: But Jews, Turks, and Gentiles are today not rarely illuminated successively: Therefore. The consequence is evident; because, where a sinful man is illuminated with the passage of time, there a full conversion of the will is not immediately present.

3) Whatever light shines in an unregenerate heart, as in a dark place, until the day of full knowledge arises, and Christ the morning star shines forth through faith in that same heart, that light irradiates the heart for a time, devoid of holiness: But the prophetic and apostolic light etc. 2 Peter I, 19. Therefore. The words of the Apostle Peter are ἐμφατικώτατα. For thus he says: 'We have the prophetic word made more sure, to which you do well to pay attention, as to a light shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in our hearts.' There is no time, nor is it helpful, to examine each of the Apostle's words at present, but we observe only a) by

τόπον ἀυχμηρὸν, a squalid and dark place, is understood as the human heart, according to the interpretation of B. CALOVIUS, dark without the word of God, which the opposite light, which shines in our hearts, having dispersed the darkness of ignorance and errors, shows, and which is attributed to the prophetic discourse. b) The particle, ἕως, until, up to the time when, indicates a successive illumination. For again and again one must attend, as St. Peter warns, to the prophetic word, as to a light shining in darkness, until the day dawns. For just as at daybreak the shadows of night are gradually dispelled, and the light grows until the full day dawns: so through the light of the prophetic and apostolic word the darkness of ignorance is expelled from the unregenerate heart, until the day of saving knowledge arises and Christ dwells in the heart through faith, and spreads the splendor of his grace more abundantly within it. From this statement of Peter we conclude: a) that the unregenerate heart is illuminated successively through the light of the divine word, and that therefore there is a certain imperfect illumination. b) That illumination precedes regeneration, or the kindling of faith, not only in the order of nature, but also in the order of time. They are therefore in error who dare to assert that there is no true illumination of the intellect which is without the conversion and regeneration of the will; since the first and primary reason for illumination consists in preparing man for conversion. For it is for this reason that natural darkness, ignorance of mysteries, and errors opposed to them, are expelled from the human intellect through grace, and it is imbued with the knowledge of God and of sacred things, and is illuminated as if by a certain light, so that it may be rendered fit to receive justifying grace. The illuminating grace therefore precedes the completion of conversion, in the judgment of D. FECHT, in his treatise on the order and manner of grace, aphorism IX, p. 18.

4) We prove our assertion from the oracle of Christ, Luke 12:47-48. That servant, who knows the will of his master, but neither prepares himself nor does his will, shall be beaten with many stripes. To know the will of the Lord is an effect of illumination; to prepare oneself to do the same is an effect of renewal. But since, as Christ testifies, certain servants of God know the will of the master, yet do not prepare themselves, nor do his will; it follows that a certain illumination of the intellect exists without the conversion and renewal of the will.

5) If no illumination of the mind exists without the sanctification of the will; no one will sin against a conscience illuminated by the word of God, there will be no apostates, no sinners against the Holy Spirit. But many do sin against an illuminated conscience, many are apostates, and sinners against the Holy Spirit. Therefore, the consequence is firm: for he who transgresses against the dictate of an illuminated conscience, at that very moment in which he sins, is still illuminated. Nor does he lose the knowledge of the divine law after the sin committed against conscience. The antecedent is clear: because the first parents, Aaron the priest, King David, and Peter the Apostle, transgressed most gravely against an illuminated conscience. Apostates, however, are graphically delineated by Peter, 2 Ep. 2:20-21. If those who had escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ, are again entangled in them and overcome, the latter state has become worse for them than the first. For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than, after they had known it, to have turned back from the word delivered to them. But the Apostle Paul depicted sinners against the Holy Spirit in vivid colors, Heb. 6:4-6. It is impossible for those who were once illuminated, and have tasted the heavenly gift, and have become partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the age to come, and have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance, since they crucify again for themselves the Son of God, and put him to an open shame. From which it is evident that the intellect of the apostates had been illuminated by such a remarkable light that they knew the way of righteousness and tasted the powers of the future age, whose will, however, departed so far from the holy commandment that they dared to crucify the Son of God again, and to hold him in derision.

6) Whoever through a proæretic [deliberate] sin falls from the state of grace into the state of wrath, and yet retains so much of the light of supernatural knowledge that they can return through it to the state of grace, their illumination is without sanctification: But men sinning with determined malice &c. E. The minor is proved from Apoc. III, 3, where John is commanded to write to the Bishop of Sardis: Remember, how thou hast received and heard, and hold fast, and repent. This Bishop is described as having had a name that he lives, but in very deed being dead, i. e., that he is destitute of regenerating, justifying, and indwelling grace. From which B. DANNHAUER concludes in his Hodof. phænom. p. 878: Some sinners are recalled by that supernatural light which is still in the fallen. And in Lact. catechet. P. IV. conc. XXIII. p. 285: Some who have fallen through grievous sins still have the supernatural light of faith, as far as knowledge is concerned, and a glimmer of it still remains.

Instantia I. Through a proæretic sin the Holy Spirit is cast out, and therefore also the supernatural light of knowledge. Resp. By a proæretic sin the indwelling grace of the Holy Spirit is cast out, but not the assisting [grace], from which illumination comes. A voluntary sin does not immediately expel supernatural light; otherwise no one would sin against an illuminated conscience.

Instantia II. Just as God does not restore sight to a man naturally dead, without the vivification of the whole body; so neither does He illuminate the intellect, without the total regeneration of the soul. Resp. This analogy is lame for this reason, that God raises a man naturally dead in one moment, but converts a man spiritually dead successively. But more on this below.

Latin:

Obs. VIII. Differt illuminatio, a regeneratione. Illa magis intellectum; hæc magis voluntatem respicit. Illa in informatione e verbo diuino de rebus sacris: hæc in donatione fidei formaliter consistit. Illius effectus est cognitio mysteriorum diuinorum: huius effectus est fiducia merito Christi innixa. Illa præcedit, hæc sequitur.

Obs. IX. Differt illuminatio, a sanctificatione, stricte dicta. Sanctificationem, sensu latiori sumtam, omnes actus gratiæ applicatricis complecti, inter omnes Christianos constat: eadem tamen, sensu strictiori accepta, ab illuminatione distinguitur 1) ratione subiecti partialis; quia per illuminationem proxime & formaliter intellectus, per sanctificationem voluntas perficitur: 2) ratione latitudinis; quia plures homines illuminantur, quam sanctificantur: 3) ratione effectus & termini proprii; quia effectus illuminationis est γνῶσις, siue cognitio supernaturalis Dei, & rerum diuinarum, Eph. I, 18. 2 Cor IV, 6. sed sanctificationis effectus est ἁγιοσύνη καὶ δικαιοσύνη, sanctitas & iustitia, Eph. IV, 24.

Β Ε Β Α Ι Ω Σ Ι Σ.

Posse illuminationem simplicem, vel imperfectam, esse in intellectu hominis, morose non obsistentis, absque sanctificatione voluntatis, probatur: 1) Quæ illuminatio diuina aliquo temporis interuallo maiori, vel minori, antecedit fidem saluisicam, illa potest esse sine sanctificatione: Atqui illuminatio diuina imperfecta &c. Ergo. Maior liquet: quia corda purificantur fide, Act. XV, 9. Ergo, vbi nulla fides in corde, ibi puritas aut sanctitas nulla. Minor probatur; quia ordinaria adultorum illuminatio est actus gratiæ successiuus, qui non vno absoluitur momento, sed fit per temporum interualla, per gradus, per actus repetitos, donec fidem plene & salutariter concipiant, adeo, vt nullus actus gratiæ diuinæ applicatricis magis opus habeat mora & tractu, quam illuminatio, iudice D. FECHTIO in eruditissimo tractatu de ordine, modoque gratiæ, §. 9. p. 19. Quam gradualem & successiuam hominum adultorum illuminationem docet a) Ipsa praxis. Etenim minister ecclesiæ, conuersurus Iudæum, omni conatu & studio eundem illuminare nititur. א. Conuincit Iudæum, Messiam, in V. T. promissum, iam dudum venisse, adhibitis luculentis scripturæ testimoniis, & excussis animo Iudæi dubiis. Interim tempus labitur. ב. Demonstrat, hunc Messiam, non esse nudum hominem, sed verum Deum, filiumque Dei Patris, ab æterno genitum. ג. Ostendit, hunc Messiam & θεάνθρωπον esse Iesum Nazarenum, filium virginis Mariæ, collatis oraculis propheticis cum natiuitate, doctrina, passione, resurrectione, euectione in cœlum, & miraculis Christi, vbi plurima dubia Iudæo eximenda sunt. Interea vna & altera hora effluit. ד. Probat ex veteri testamento, in vna essentia diuina esse tres personas, Deum Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum, vbi non solum veritas asserenda, sed & scrupuli animo Iudæi iniecti euellendi sunt: qui labor sacer certum temporis spatium requirit. ה. Instillat Iudæo doctrinam de officio Christi sacerdotali, prophetico & regio: quæ illuminatio moram temporis exigit. ו. Inculcat conuertendo salutis media δοτικὰ, verbum Dei & sacramenta, per quæ Deus hodie cum homine agit, ut ipsum convertat, regeneret, justificet, salvet.

I. Ostendit, ex parte nostri, ad remissionem peccatorum & vitam aeternam consequendam requiri veram fidem, meritum Christi apprehendentem, adeoque peccatorem justificari non per bona opera sed per fidem.

Mouebit Judaeus dubia, quae resoluenda sunt, procedente tempore.

II. Docet, fidem, quae justificauit, se per sanctimoniam vitae exserere, ceteroqui eam non viuam, sed mortuam esse.

Quam informationem Judaeus recipiens jam demum sufficienter illuminatus, convertitur, regeneratur & baptizatur, tanquam sigillum regenerationis, accipit.

Ex hac praxi, junctisque ei exemplis singularibus, perspicere licet, illuminationem non momento, sed diuturniori temporis tractu absolui.

Confideremus illuminationem & conversionem Gersonis Judaei, quam D. CalixTVS in tractatu de auctoritate scripturae sacrae p. 36. recenset, & ipsa verba Gersonis adducit; Paupercula quaedam Christiana femina, inquit Gerson, vicina mea, tradebat pignori mihi codicem novi testamenti germanici, a Luthero conversi: cui ego mutuo dabam octo solidos, ut usuram meo more lucrarer, & librum interim euoluerem; non quidem, quod de veritate Judaicae religionis dubitarem, aut ullum Christianae fidei articulum rectum crederem, sed ut cognoscerem, quisnam ille tantopere efficax error, qui tot animarum myriades seducebat, & in exitium praecipites daret.

Praesentibus igitur meis duobus affinibus, Lazaro & Simeone, totum perlegi, non sine blasphemiis. Interim vero cor meum percellebatur, & cum animaduertissem, Evangelistas & Apostolos, & Christum ipsum toties ad vetus testamentum prouocare, & subinde loca ex eo alia post alia adducere: illectus fui, ut denuo legerem, & clanculum quidem, nemine conscio, nequidem uxore mea, & ut loca adducta cum ipso veteris testamenti textu contenderem. Quod ubi feci, tanta mihi lux illuxit, ut eo nomine aeternas Deo debeam gratias.

Ecquis non videt, imperfectam Gersonis illuminationem ad tempus absque regeneratione & sanctificatione fuisse?

Eximium est exemplum AVGVSTINI, qui in libris confessionum fuse exponit, quomodo a Deo fuerit illuminatus & conversus: vbiis autem testatur, Spiritum S. longo temporis tractu in ipso operatum fuisse, priusquam plene illuminatus & conversus sit.

Libr. V. confess. c. 14. commemorat, quid sibi contigerit, cum aliquando audiuisset AMBROSIVM, verbum Dei praedicantem: nempe gradatim ea, quae proponebantur, intrasse mentem, & sibi verisimilia fuisse visa, cum non haberet, quid iis reponeret: Putabam tamen, ait, eruditiores ea posse refutare.

Ipsam ergo fidem nondum habebat, sed haerebat adhuc dubius.

Postea libr. VI. tentationes & dubitationes exponit, quibuscum aliquando conflictatus fuerit.

Libro VIII. c. 2. recenset, quid contigerit, cum accessisset ad SIMPLICIANVM, qui ambrosio post modum in episcopatu Mediolanensi successit: nempe Simplicianum narrasse de VICTORINO Rhetore converso, quod ex scripturae lectione a Spiritu Sancto fuerit illuminatus, quod idem ecclesiam ingressus, & fidem Christianam publice professus fuerit. Haec vbi narrari audiuisset a Simpliciano AVGVSTINVS, dicit c.

5. Exarsi ad imitandum Victorini exemplum. Neque tamen tunc potuit eo vsque eniti, ob validas dubitationes, quae animo inhaerebant.

Cui rei, inquit, ego suspirabam, ligatus non ferro alieno, sed mea ferrea voluntate.

Velle meum tenebat inimicus, & inde mihi catenam fecerat, & constrinxerat me. Vbi sane intellectus AVGVSTINI successive fuit illuminatus, quamuis ferrea ipsius voluntas gratiae convertenti & regeneranti ad tempus oblitteret. b) Si illuminatio ordinaria actio instantanea esset, foret irresistibilis; nam actioni divinae instantaneae nullum potest obiici impedimentum.

Creatio est actio instantanea, quia est irresistibilis actio divina.

Cum Deus dicebat: Fiat lux! eodem momento lux aderat, Gen. 1, 3. Nemo creationi diuinae potuit obsistere.

Quod si Deus per potentiam absolutam & irresistibilem vellet hominem peccatorem illuminare, vtique illa foret momentanea, & semper cum sanctificatione voluntatis coniuncta. At vero testatur experientia, quod plurimi mortalium gratiæ diuinæ, per ordinaria media operanti, obluctentur. Scite inquit AVGVSTINVS tract. XXVII. in Ioann. Qui resistit, quomodo viuificatur? Aduersarius est radio lucis, quo penetrandus est. Non aduertit aciem, sed claudit mentem.

c) Quomodo Spiritus S. nos per scripturam S. informat, capita doctrinæ Christianæ intellectui nostro proponendo & inculcando, eodem modo nos S. scripturam legentes, vel audientes illuminat: Atqui Spiritus S. nos per S. scripturam informat successiue, alia post alia capita doctrinæ Christianæ intellectui nostro proponendo & inculcando: Ergo.

d) Seminator bonus semen in agrum suum spargit, vt primum herbam, deinde spicas, postea plenum fructum ferat, Marc. IV, 28. Ita Deus bonum semen, verbum suum, in corda hominum spargens, ordinarie ac semper intendit ac vult abundantiorem gratiæ gradum, usque ad complementum, auditoribus conferre. Ex quo Christus nos compellat: Videte, quomodo audiatis! Quicunque enim habet (recipit & retinet primum illuminationis gradum) ei dabitur, Luc. VIII, 18.

e) Exemplum symbolicum illuminationis successiuæ cernere licet in sanatione cœci illius, cuius S. scriptura mentionem iniicit, Marc. VIII, 22. seqq. Hunc Christus, immisso in oculos ipsius sputo, sanauit, non momento perfectum restituendo visum; sed sensim & gradatim oculos eius aperiendo, vt primum tenuiter videret, cerneretque homines ambulantes, velut arbores; deinde, cum Christus manum oculis eius imponeret, is visu plene reddito, omnes dilucide intueretur: Sic Deus oculos mentis hominis irregeniti per verbum suum magis magisque aperit, vt ipsius notitia de Deo & rebus diuinis initio sit tenuis & exilis, progressu temporis autem incrementa capiat, si verbum diuinum meditari pergat.

f) Apostolus Paullus extraordinarie per immediatam Christi reuelationem, & apparitionem illuminatus est. Attamen illuminatio ipsius non fuit momentanea. Nam cum insolita de cœlo radiante luce circumfusus, in terram præceps rueret, audiebat cœlestem vocem: Saul, Saul, quare persequeris me? Saul, ignorans auctorem vocis cœlestis, dixit: Quis es, Domine? At Dominus dixit: Ego sum Iesus, quem tu persequeris; durum tibi contra stimulum calcitrare. Ecce initium supernaturalis illuminationis, ex qua Paullus Dominum Iesum, eiusque voluntatem, quod desistendum esset a persecutione Christianorum, agnoscebat. At nondum eo temporis articulo plene conuersus erat, quamuis voluntati ipsius iniectum esset desiderium conuersionis. Idcirco tremens ac pauens dixit: Domine, quid me vis facere? Dominus autem ad ipsum: Surge & intra in vrbem; tum dicetur tibi, quid te oporteat facere? Idcirco ingressus vrbem Damascum, illuminatus plenius ab Anania, & Spiritu S. impletus est, Act. IX.

Prob. 2) Si illuminatio intellectus non potest esse sine sanctificatione voluntatis, nullus Iudæus, nullus Turca hodie successiue illuminari potest: At Iudæi, Turcæ, gentiles hodienum successiue haud raro illuminantur: E. Consequentia patet; quia, vbi homo peccator successu temporis illuminatur, ibi non statim conuersio voluntatis plena adest.

3) Quodcunque lumen lucet in corde irregenito, velut loco tenebricoso, donec dies plenæ cognitionis exoriatur, & phosphorus Christus, per fidem in eodem corde exsplendescat, illud lumen ad tempus irradiat cor, sanctitatis expers: Atqui lumen propheticum & apostolicum &c. 2 Petr. I, 19. E. Verba Apostoli Petri sunt ἐμφατικώτατα. Sic enim inquit: Habemus firmius propheticum verbum, cui recte facitis, quod attenditis, tanquam lumini, lucenti in loco tenebricoso, vsque dum dies illucescat, & phosphorus oriatur in cordibus nostris. Non vacat, nec iuuat, in præsenti singula Apostoli verba excutere, sed obseruamus tantum a) per

τόπον ἀυχμηρὸν, locum squalidum & caliginosum, intelligi cor humanum, interprete B. CALOVIO, absque verbo Dei tenebricosum, quod opposita lux, quæ effulget in cordibus nostris, discuslis ignorantiæ & errorum tenebris, ostendit, quæque sermoni prophetico tribuitur. b) Particulam, ἕως, donec, vsque dum, successiuam indigitare illuminationem. Nam iterum, iterumque attendendum est, monente S. Petro, verbo prophetico, tanquam lumini, in tenebris fulgenti, vsque dum dies illucescat. Quem ad modum enim in diluculo umbræ noctis gradatim dispelluntur, & lumen crescit, donec plena dies illucescat: Ita per lumen prophetici & apostolici verbi tenebræ ignorantiæ ex corde irregenito expelluntur, vsque dum dies salutaris notitiæ exoriatur & Christus per fidem in corde habitet, atque splendorem gratiæ suæ in eodem vberius diffundat. Ex hoc effato Petrino colligimus: a) cor irregenitum per lumen verbi diuini successiue illuminari, atque adeo quandam illuminationem esse imperfectam. b) Illuminationem præcedere regenerationem, siue accensionem fidei, non tantum ordine naturæ, sed etiam ordine temporis. Frustra igitur sunt, qui asserere audent, nullam dari veram intellectus illuminationem, quæ sit absque conuersione & regeneratione voluntatis; siquidem prima & præcipua illuminationis ratio in præparando hominem ad conuersionem consistit. Ideo enim naturales tenebræ, ignorantia mysteriorum, & errores iis oppositi, ex intellectu humano per gratiam expelluntur, & ille cognitione Dei, & rerum sacrarum imbuitur, & tanquam luce quadam illustratur, vt ad recipiendam gratiam iustificantem aptus reddatur. Antecedit itaque illuminans gratia conuersionis, complementum, iudice D. FECHTIO, intractatu de ordine, modoque gratiæ, aphorismo IX. p. 18.

4) Probamus assertionem nostram ex oraculo Christi, Luc. XII, 47. 48. Seruus ille, qui scit voluntatem domini, sed neque parat se, neque facit voluntatem eius, percutietur multis. Scire voluntatem Domini, illuminationis, parare se facere eandem, renouationis effečtus est. Cum autem, teste Christo, quidam serui Dei voluntatem domini sciant, neque tamen se parent, nec voluntatem eius faciant; consequitur, quandam illuminationem intellectus absque conuersione & renouatione voluntatis exsistere.

5) Si nulla existit illuminatio mentis sine sanctificatione voluntatis; nemo peccabit contra conscientiam, verbo Dei illuminatam, nulli exsistent apostatæ, nulli peccatores in Spiritum S. Atqui multi peccant contra conscientiam illuminatam, multi existunt apostatæ, & peccatores in Spiritum S. E. Consequentia est firma: nam, qui contra conscientiæ illuminatæ dictamen delinquit, is eo momento, quo peccat, adhuc illuminatus est. Neque post commissum contra conscientiam peccatum notitiam legis diuinæ amittit. Antecedens liquet: quia protoplasti, Aaron sacerdos, rex Dauid, Petrus Apostolus, contra conscientiam illuminatam grauissime deliquerunt. Apostatæ autem graphice delineantur a Petro, 2 ep. II, 20. 21. Si qui effugerant pollutiones mundi per cognitionem Domini & Saluatoris, Iesu Christi, his vero rursus impliciti vincuntur, facta sunt illis postrema peiora primis. Melius enim esset illis, non agnouisse viam iustitiæ, quam, postquam agnouerant, relapsos esse ex tradito illis verbo. Peccatores vero in Spiritum S. viuis quasi coloribus depinxit Apostolus Paullus, Hebr. VI, 4. 5. 6. Impossibile est, eos, qui semel illuminati sunt, & gustauerunt donum supracæleste, & participes facti sunt Spiritus S., & qui bonum gustauerunt Dei verbum, virtutesque venturi sæculi, & prolapsi sunt, iterum renouari in pœnitentiam, denuo crucifigentes sibi ipsis Filium Dei, & ludibrio exponentes.
