E quibus dispalefcit, apostatarum intellectum tam insigni lumine collustratum fuisse, vt viam iustitiæ cognouerint, virtutesque futuri sæculi degustauerint, quorum tamen voluntas a sancto præcepto tantopere desciuit, vt Filium Dei denuo crucifigere, & ludibrio habere ausi sint.

6) Quicunque per peccatum proæreticum e statu gratiæ prolabuntur in statum iræ, & tantum tamen lumen supernaturalis notitiæ retinent, vt per illud in statum gratiæ redire queant, illorum illuminatio est absque sanctificatione: Atqui homines destinata malitia peccantes &c. E. Minor probatur ex Apoc. III, 3. vbi Ioannes Episcopo Sardensi scribere iubetur: Recordare, quomodo acceperis & audiueris, & tene, & pœnitentiam age. Hic Episcopus describitur, quod nomen habuerit, quod viuat, re autem vera mortuus sit, i. e. quod gratia regenerante, iustificante & inhabitante destitutus sit. Ex quo concludit B. DANNHAV. in hodof. phænom. p. 878. Aliqui peccatores reuocantur per illud lumen supernaturale, quod adhuc in lapsis est. Et in lacte catechet. P. IV. conc. XXIII. p. 285. Etliche durch schwere Sünden gefallene haben noch das übernatürliche licht des Glaubens, was anlanget die Wissenschaft, und bleibet noch ein Glanz davon.

Instantia I. Per peccatum proæreticum excutitur Spiritus S. adeoque & supernaturale notitiæ lumen. Resp. Peccato proæretico excutitur gratia Spiritus S. inhabitans, non autem assistens, a qua est illuminatio. Peccatum voluntarium non expellit actutum supernaturale lumen; alias nemo peccaret aduersus conscientiam illuminatam.

Instantia II. Sicut Deus homini naturaliter mortuo non restituit visum, fine totius corporis viuificatione; ita nec intellectum illuminat, fine omnimoda animæ regeneratione. Resp. Hoc simile ideo claudicat, quod Deus hominem naturaliter mortuum resuscitat vno momento, hominem autem spiritualiter mortuum conuertit successive. Sed de hoc infra plura.


### Quest. IX. What men does God illuminate?: 7) There exist examples of those who were illuminated by the divine word, and yet were not holy A) The Bishop of Sardis, of whom we have already spoken

7) There exist examples of those who were illuminated by the divine word, and yet were not holy.

a) The Bishop of Sardis, of whom we have already spoken.

b) Balaam was a man stained with lethal crimes, namely idolatry, Apoc. II, 14, injustice and avarice, 2 Petr. II, 15, Iud. v. 11, whose way was evil before the angel of Jehovah, Num. XXII, 32, &c. yet God put His word into his mouth, Num. XXIII, 5, and opened the eyes of his mind, c. XXIV, so that even the prophet might hear, 2 Petr. II, 16.

c) Christ called Judas Iscariot a devil, Io. VI, 70, and yet sent him with the rest of the Apostles to preach the gospel, Matth. X, 17. But if Judas had not been illuminated, he would not have been sent by Christ to illuminate others through the preaching of the gospel.

d) Those workers of iniquity were illuminated who address Christ: Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? Matth. VII, 22. 23. A man destitute of supernatural illumination cannot prophesy in the name of Christ.

e) Those Scribes and Pharisees, whose precepts the Jews were commanded to observe and do, Matth. XXIII, 1. 2. 3, were not destitute of all supernatural light; otherwise the most wise Lord, Jesus, would not have gravely exhorted not only the crowds indiscriminately, whom He seriously wished to arrive at the acknowledgment of the truth, but also His own disciples, that they should observe and express in deeds all things which those [Scribes and Pharisees] enjoined to be observed from Moses and the prophets.

You object: Those Pharisees are called blind guides, Matth. XXIII, 24. Resp. They are called blind comparatively and in a certain respect; because they had not directed the knowledge of spiritual things, which they had drawn from the word of God, to a living practice, which the Savior objects to them, saying: They say, but do not. But relative blindness can consist with imperfect illumination. Which is evident from the example of the disciples of Christ, Luc. XVIII, 34. f) The teachers who were rivals of Paul were illuminated, who, to depress him, preached Christ out of envy and contention; in whose preaching, however, the Apostle, held in bonds, rejoiced, Phil. I, 16. g) The supernatural light irradiated the mind of the prophet of Bethel, who led another innocent prophet, circumvented by fraud, away from the path by which he was going according to the will of God: for the word of God came to him, by which he predicted sudden destruction to this man. You object: The illumination of Balaam, and of this prophet of Bethel, was extraordinary, which does not make a common rule.

Resp. From that extraordinary illumination it may be gathered that sometimes the illumination of the intellect occurs without the sanctification of the will.

Latin:

7) Exstant exempla eorum, qui e verbo diuino illuminati, neque tamen sancti fuerunt.

a) Episcopus Sardensis, de quo iam egimus.

b) Bileamus fuit homo lethalibus maculatus flagitiis, scilicet idololatria, Apoc. II, 14. iniustitia & auaritia, 2 Petr. II, 15. Iud. v. 11. cuius via fuit mala coram angelo Iehouæ, Num. XXII, 32. &c. tamen Deus verbum suum in os eius posuit, Num. XXIII, 5. & oculos mentis ei aperuit, c. XXIV. vt etiam propheta audiat, 2 Petr. II, 16.

c) Iudam Ischariothem Christus appellauit diabolum, Io. VI, 70. & tamen cum reliquis Apostolis misit ad prædicandum euangelium, Matth. X, 17. At si Iudas non fuisset illuminatus, a Christo non fuisset missus ad illuminandum alios per prædicationem euangelii.

d) Illuminati fuerunt illi operatores iniquitatis, qui Christum compellant: Domine, Domine, nonne in nomine tuo prophetauimus? Matth. VII, 22. 23. In nomine Christi prophetare nequit homo supernaturalis illuminationis expers.

e) Scribæ & Pharisæi illi, quorum præcepta seruare, & facere iubebantur Iudæi, Matth. XXIII, 1. 2. 3. non omnis luminis supernaturalis expertes fuerunt; ceteroqui sapientissimus Dominus, Iesus, non tantum populos promiscue, quos ad veritatis agnitionem peruenire serio volebat, sed & discipulos suos grauiter adhortatus esset, vt omnia, quæ illi ex Mose & prophetis seruanda iniungerent, seruarent, factisque exprimerent.

Excipis: Pharisæi illi dicuntur duces cæci, Matth. XXIII, 24. Resp. Dicuntur cæci comparate & certo respectu; quia notitiam rerum spiritualium, quam e verbo Dei hauserant, non ad viuam praxin direxerant, quod ipsis obiicit Saluator inquiens: Dicunt, sed non faciunt. At respectiua cæcitas cum illuminatione imperfecta consistere potest. Id quod patet exemplo discipulorum Christi, Luc. XVIII, 34. f) Illuminati erant doctores æmuli Paulli, qui, vt hunc deprimerent, ex inuidia & contentione Christum prædicabant; quorum tamen prædicatione Apostolus in vinculis detentus gaudebat, Phil. I, 16. g) Lumen supernaturale irradiabat mentem prophetae Bethelensis, qui alium prophetam innocentem, fraude circumuentum ex via, qua ex voluntate Dei ibat, reducebat: factum est enim ad illum verbum Dei, quo huic repentinum interitum praedicebat. Excipis: Illuminatio Bileami, & huius prophetae Bethelensis, fuit extraordinaria, quae non facit regulam communem.

Resp. Ex illa extraordinaria illuminatione colligere licet, quod aliquando illuminatio intellectus fit sine sanctificatione voluntatis.


### Quest. IX. What men does God illuminate?: Resolution

RESOLUTION

The opponents object.

I. Whoever maliciously resists divine grace, they are not illuminated: But unregenerate men, etc.

Therefore. Resp.

Resp. Whoever maliciously resists the illuminating divine grace, they are undoubtedly not illuminated. For the subject of illumination is a teachable man, called to the church, admitting the illuminating grace of the Holy Spirit, and attentively hearing, reading, and meditating upon the divine word. Nevertheless, it is also true that many admit the illuminating grace, but resist the converting and regenerating grace.

II. That conversion happens in an instant is taught by theologians of great name, among whom is also Dr.

CALOVIUS, who in system. theolog. vol. X. p. 16. writes: Conversion happens in a moment of time, once and for all, and as if in the twinkling of an eye, so that we may speak here of God anthropopathically. Resp.

The form of conversion specially so called consists in the translation of an unregenerate man from the state of wrath and sin into the state of grace and faith, and from the kingdom of darkness into the kingdom of light, which has its preparatory acts, in respect of which it is said to happen successively. For preparation has its degrees; and it happens successively.

But the translation itself from the state of wrath into the state of grace happens in an instant and a moment, since it is impossible that any subject should be, even for a moment, simultaneously in the state of wrath and in the state of grace, simultaneously under life and under death, as taught by the most accurate theologians, Dr. KOENIG in theol. positiua §. 502. and Dr. QVENSTED. in system. theol. P. III. c. VII. p. 493.

Now, however, the illumination of adult men (we are not speaking here of the illumination of infants) is imperfect and pedagogical, belongs to the preparatory acts of conversion, and happens successively.

The most memorable words of Dr. SONTAG in fanaticismo §. 62 pertain here: Since the whole conversion of man (and that taken not terminatively or exclusively, but cumulatively) happens successively, Mark

IV, 28. and does not consist in a mathematical point (which the blessed

Martin Chemnitz said); it is not surprising if that economy of divine grace, which we call the illumination of the intellect, and which God works resistibly through the preached word, does not happen in an instant. There are, indeed, many impulses of assisting grace, among which is also that by which the Holy Spirit works the perception of the literal biblical sense.

Objection: If illumination is imperfect and pedagogical, it will be natural. For pedagogical actions happen with nature as a guide. Resp.

Pedagogy is one thing, general; another, special.

The former happens through natural powers; the latter happens through the elevation of the intellect above natural powers. The illumination of the intellect pertains here, preparing man from the divine word to conceive faith in Christ. III.

There is one soul in man, whose faculties (intellect and will) are distinguished not essentially, but virtually, or by operation.

Since, therefore, there is a perpetual and intimate conspiracy of intellect and will, the intellect cannot be illuminated without the will being simultaneously improved, nor the will healed without the intellect being simultaneously illuminated. For they perpetually conspire from one and into one. Resp.

1) The conspiracy of intellect and will after the fall is not necessary and perpetual. For the will is a free power, which, with all things required for acting present, among the number of which is also the dictate of the intellect, can act and not act, this or or to act in another way.

A very violent impulse of the passions often boils over, which drags the will away from the judgment of reason, so that it obeys not the intellect, but a depraved appetite: This is what Ovid’s Medea openly confesses in book 7 of the Metamorphoses. But a new force drags me, unwilling, and desire persuades me of one thing, the mind of another: I see better things, and I approve of them, I follow the worse.

2) If, upon the intellect being illuminated, the will were immediately converted, the illumination would be momentary; that this is false, we have abundantly proven. Counter-argument: If, upon the intellect being illuminated, the will is not converted at the same time, in the same instant of time, there would be authority over the human intellect for God, and over the human will for the devil, which is absurd.

Resp. If God wished to exert an absolute and irresistible force, He would indeed cast the devil out of the human soul in one moment; but He uses an ordered and resistible power in converting man. Therefore, He illuminates the intellect gradually, so that in the progress of time the will may be liberated from the captivity of the devil.

3) If the intellect is illuminated, without the will being amended, that illumination will be vain and devoid of all fruit: The consequent is absurd: Therefore, the antecedent is also. The consequence is proven; because the will of man, not being amended but enslaved to a depraved appetite, drags the intellect into consent by its own force and vehemence, and imbues it with foul errors, which hinder the illumination.

Resp. I deny the consequence, because only this follows: If the intellect is illuminated, without the will being amended, that illumination is not perfect and completely salvific, but imperfect and pedagogical. The will, serving a depraved appetite, hinders the completion, not the beginning and any sort of progress of the illumination.

Nor, however, should an imperfect illumination be considered vain and sterile; since it is divinely ordained for correcting the will. Which it would also accomplish, were the will not maliciously and stubbornly resisting.

IV. Where the Holy Spirit is present, there He is whole, not half, there He also works as a whole, and exercises all His acts: Therefore, whatever human heart the Holy Spirit illuminates, that He simultaneously converts, regenerates, justifies, and renews.

Resp. Distinguish between the essence of the Holy Spirit and His operations. Where the Holy Spirit is present, there His whole essence is present, since He is indivisible, or invisible; but He does not exercise all His operations at once and in the same moment; He does not pour out all the riches of His goodness at once and in the same moment, nor does He make a holy person out of a most wicked man in one moment.

V. Whoever cannot receive the Holy Spirit, they cannot be illuminated: But the unregenerate, etc.

Therefore. The minor is proven from John.

XIV, 17. The world cannot receive the Spirit of truth.

Distinguish between the assisting grace of the Holy Spirit and the indwelling grace. Whoever cannot receive the Holy Spirit, neither assisting nor indwelling, they cannot be illuminated; I concede this. But although the unregenerate do not receive the indwelling grace of the Holy Spirit within a moment of time, they can nevertheless receive the assisting grace of the Holy Spirit, through which they are prepared and disposed to conceive faith in Christ, so that through this the Holy Spirit may dwell in their hearts.

Counter-argument: Assisting grace is for helping a renewed man, and cooperating with him; which does not precede indwelling grace, but follows it. Resp. By assisting grace here is not understood grace helping a renewed man, but grace is called assisting when the Holy Spirit moves externally around the heart of man, not only by proposing a salvific object and showing what ought to be done, but also by effectively touching, knocking, and exciting, so that he may know the will of God, even if he does not always do it, Rev.

III, 20. VI. He who does not love his brother, ...he is not illuminated.

But a man devoid of holiness does not love his brother. Therefore.

The major is proven from 1 John II, 9. 10. 11. He who says he is in the light, but hates his brother, is in darkness even until now.

But he who loves his brother, in [He] remains in the light, and there is no scandal in him. But he who hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going: because the darkness has blinded his eyes. Response: He who does not love his brother, he is not illuminated by an illumination that is perfect and completely salvific. Nevertheless, he can be imperfectly and pedagogically illuminated through divine grace. Perfect illumination suffices for generating faith, which is effective through charity, Gal. V, 6. But through imperfect illumination, the Holy Spirit intends to prepare and dispose a man so that he may believe in Christ and love his neighbor; although this intended effect does not always follow because of the contumacy by which a sinful man resists the regenerating and renewing grace.

VII. He who does not love God has not known Him, 1 John IV, 8, and therefore is not illuminated: A man devoid of holiness does not love God: Therefore. Response: He who does not love God does not know Him with a practical and effective knowledge; nevertheless, having been anticipated and excited by the Holy Spirit, he can know God with a theoretical and literal knowledge.

VIII. He in whom there is no true knowledge of God is not truly illuminated by the Holy Spirit: But in a man devoid of holiness there is no true knowledge of God. Therefore. The minor is proved from 1 John II, 4: He who says, "I have known Him," and does not keep His commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him. Response: He in whom there is no knowledge of God that is either logically or ethically true, he is not illuminated by the Holy Spirit. But in an unregenerate man, insofar as he is imperfectly illuminated by the Holy Spirit, there can be a knowledge of God that is logically and formally true, even if the same is not true ethically and finally, i.e., even if it has not been brought to the true practice and end intended by the Holy Spirit. He who, from the light of supernatural revelation, knows that God is one in essence and three in persons, his *theognosia* (knowledge of God) is true logically and formally; but if he does not apply the same to placing trust in Christ the mediator, to loving and venerating the triune God, his knowledge is not true ethically and finally.

IX. He who is not light in the Lord is not illuminated: But an unregenerate man, etc., Eph. V, 8. Therefore. Response: He who is not light in the Lord is not perfectly illuminated; I grant it. For in order for a man to be light in the Lord, it is required that, for the state of this life, he be adequately illuminated, converted, reborn, justified, and renewed.

X. That soul which is not capable of heavenly wisdom is not illuminated by the Holy Spirit: But a malevolent soul, etc., Wis. I, 4. Therefore. That soul which is capable of wisdom neither theoretically nor practically is not illuminated by the Holy Spirit; I grant it. From imperfect illumination comes theoretical wisdom, by which God is simply apprehended and known, but not practical wisdom, by which God is so known that He is loved and worshipped.

XI. He who, under the condition of doing the divine will, knows that the doctrine of Christ is divine, he cannot be illuminated without sanctification: But a sinful man, etc. Therefore. The minor is proved from John VII, 16-17: Jesus answered them and said: My doctrine is not mine, but His who sent me. If anyone wills to do His will, he shall know concerning the doctrine, whether it is from God, or whether I speak from myself. Response: 1) To do the will of the Father in the cited place does not mean to live holily. For who, being blind, will walk holily? Must not the intellect first be illuminated? Must not the doctrine first be judged, whether it is divine or not? Must not those things be done only then, to which the intellect, enlightened by the knowledge of the doctrine, directs? And therefore, since the object of the dispute between Christ and the Jews is the doctrine of Christ, whether it is the doctrine of the heavenly Father: "to do the will of the Father" must be taken here not absolutely, but restrictively, according to the underlying subject matter, so that it signifies: to search the Scriptures of the Old Testament out of the will of the heavenly [Father], and to compare the doctrine of Christ with them, whether this is consonant with them. 2) By "knowledge" in the cited place is understood a richer, fuller, and more illustrious awareness of the doctrine of Christ.

Whoever is dead in sins, he cannot be an illuminated man. Yet the unregenerate man is dead in sins; Therefore. The major is proved: because, just as a naturally dead man does not see with his bodily eyes, so one spiritually dead sees nothing with the eyes of his mind; but he would see, if he were illuminated. The minor is clear: because man receives through regeneration the life of faith, Gal. II, 20. but before he was dead in sins, Eph. II, 5. Resp. Whoever is dead in sins, he cannot be illuminated with an illumination that is perfect and completely salutary: for this is sufficient for exciting faith. A man, however, though spiritually dead, but constituted under the dispensation of assisting grace and divine impulse, can be illuminated imperfectly and pedagogically. For although he does not yet have an internal vital principle in his soul, the Holy Spirit nevertheless moves and occupies himself extrinsically around his soul, by touching, knocking, exciting, and instilling the light of literal knowledge through the preached or read word. I prove this assertion of mine by the example of the Bishop of Sardis, mention of whom is made in Rev. III, 3. He is called dead, and yet is commanded to remember how he had received and heard: From this I argue validly: Whoever is spiritually dead, and yet can remember what kind of doctrine he received from the Lord through the ministry of the word, he is imperfectly illuminated: But a certain man, though spiritually dead, yet constituted under the dispensation of assisting grace and divine impulse, can remember what doctrine he received from the Lord through the ministry of the word: Therefore. I would compare such unregenerate persons to those dead bones which the Prophet Ezekiel saw in chapter XXXVII, 7. which were moved from the outside by the wind, were bound by sinews, and were covered with flesh and skin, with no spirit existing within them. Thus the assisting grace of the Holy Spirit touches, knocks, and moves the hearts of the unregenerate from the outside, instills into them a literal knowledge of things to be believed, although they are destitute of the life of faith.

Latin:

ΔΙΑΛΥΣΙΣ

Obiiciunt oi ἐξ ἐναντίας.

I. Quicunque malitiose resistunt gratiae diuinae, illi non illuminantur: Atqui homines irregeniti &c.

Ergo. Resp.

Resp. Quicunque malitiose resistunt gratiae diuinae illuminanti, illi haud dubie non illuminantur. Nam subiectum illuminationis est homo docilis, ad ecclesiam uocatus, gratiam Spiritus S. illuminatricem admittens, verbumque diuinum attente audiens, legens, meditans. Nihilo tamen minus & hoc uerum est, quod multi gratiam illuminantem admittant, gratiae autem conuertenti & regeneranti obsistant.

II. Conuersionem fieri in instanti, magni nominis Theologi docent, quos inter etiam est D.

CALOVIVS, qui in system. theolog. tom. X. p. 16. scribit: Conuersio temporis momento fit, simul ac semel, & ueluti ἐν ῥιπῇ ὄμματος, ut hic ita de Deo κατ’ ἄνθρωποπάθειαν loquamur. Resp.

Forma conuersionis specialiter dictae consistit in hominis irregeniti e statu irae & peccati in statum gratiae & fidei, et regno tenebrarum in regnum lucis translatione, quae habet actus suos praeparatorios, respectu quorum fieri dicitur successiue. Praeparatio enim suos habet gradus; & fit successiue.

Ipsa uero ex statu irae in statum gratiae translatio fit in instanti & momento, cum impossibile sit, ut subiectum aliquod uel per momentum fit simul in statu irae, & in statu gratiae, simul sub uita, & sub morte, docentibus Theologis accuratissimis, D. KOENIGIO in theol. positiua §. 502. & D. QVENSTED. in system. theol. P. III. c. VII. p. 493.

Iam uero illuminatio hominum adultorum (de infantum illuminatione nobis hic non est sermo) imperfecta atque paedagogica pertinet ad actus conuersionis praeparatorios, & fit successiue.

Spectant huc uerba memoratu dignissima D. SONTAGII in fanaticismo §. 62. Cum tota hominis conuersio (eaque non terminatiue, aut exclusiue, sed cumulative sumta) fiat successiue, Marc.

IV, 28. & non in puncto mathematico (quod dixit B.

Martinus Chemnitius) consistat; mirum non est, si illa diuinae gratiae oeconomia, quam uocamus illuminationem intellectus, quamque Deus resistibiliter operatur per uerbum praedicatum, non fiat in instanti. Dantur nimirum plures gratiae assistentis pulsus, quos inter & ille est, quo Spiritus S. perceptionem sensus biblici litteralis operatur.

Instantia: Si illuminatio imperfecta est paedagogica, erit naturalis. Nam actiones paedagogicae fiunt duce natura. Resp.

Paedagogia alia est generalis, alia specialis.

Illa fit per uires naturales; haec fit per eleuationem intellectus supra uires naturales. Huc spectat illuminatio intellectus, e uerbo diuino praeparans hominem ad fidem in Christum concipiendam. III.

Vna est in homine anima, cuius facultates (intellectus & uoluntas) non essentialiter, sed virtualiter, siue operatione distinguuntur.

Cum itaque perpetua sit, & intima conspiratio intellectus & uoluntas, non potest illuminari intellectus, quin simul emendetur uoluntas, nec sanari uoluntas, quin simul illuminetur intellectus. Ex uno enim & in unum perpetuo conspirant. Resp.

1) Non necessaria & perpetua est intellectus & uoluntas post lapsum conspiratio. Nam uoluntas est potentia libera, quae omnibus ad agendum requisitis praesentibus, e quorum censu etiam est dictamen intellectus, potest agere & non agere, hoc uel vel alio modo agere.

Perquam vehemens saepe exaestuat affectuum impetus, qui voluntatem a iudicio rationis transuersam rapit, vt non intellectui, sed prauo appetitui obtemperet: Id quod aperte fatetur Medea Ouidiana libr. 7. metamorph. Sed trahit inuitam noua vis, aliudque cupido, Mens aliud fuadet: Video meliora, proboque, Deteriora sequor.

2) Si illuminato intellectu, confestim converteretur voluntas, illuminatio esset momentanea; quod falsum esse, abunde probauimus. Instantia: Si illuminato intellectu, non simul convertitur voluntas, eodem temporis articulo, Deo in intellectum, diabolo in voluntatem hominis esset imperium, quod est absurdum.

Resp. Si Deus vim absolutam et irresistibilem exserere vellet, vtique vno momento diabolum ex anima humana eiiceret; at vtitur potentia ordinata et resistibili in convertendo homine. Idcirco gradatim intellectum illuminat, vt progressu temporis voluntas a captiuitate diaboli liberetur.

3) Si intellectus illuminatur, non emendata voluntate, illa illuminatio erit vana et omnis frugis expers: Consequens est absurdum: E. et antecedens. Consequentia probatur; quia voluntas hominis non emendata, sed prauo appetitui mancipata intellectum vi et vehementia sua in consensum trahit, et foedis erroribus imbuit, qui illuminationem impediunt.

Resp. Neg. consequentiam, quia hoc tantum sequitur: Si intellectus illuminatur, non emendata voluntate, illa illuminatio non est perfecta et complete salutaris, sed imperfecta et paedagogica. Seruiens prauo appetitui voluntas complementum, non initium et qualemcunque progressum illuminationis impedit.

Neque tamen imperfecta illuminatio censenda est vana et sterilis; siquidem ad voluntatem corrigendam diuinitus ordinata est. Quod etiam praestaret, nisi voluntas malitiose et morose obluctaretur.

IV. Vbi Spiritus S. adest, ibi est totus, non dimidius, ibi totus etiam operatur, omnesque suos actus exercet: Ergo quodcunque cor humanum Spiritus S. illuminat, illud insimul convertit, regenerat, iustificat et renouat.

Resp. Dist. inter essentiam Spiritus S. et eius operationes. Vbi Spiritus S. adest, ibi tota eius essentia adest, cum fit ἀμερίσως, siue inuisibilis; at non simul et semel omnes suas operationes exercet; non simul et semel omnes diuitias bonitatis suae profundit, neque vno momento ex homine sceleratissimo sanctum efficit.

V. Quicunque Spiritum S. non possunt accipere, illi nequeunt illuminari: Atqui irregeniti etc.

Ergo. Minor probatur ex Io.

XIV, 17. Mundus spiritus veritatis non potest accipere.

Disting. inter gratiam Spiritus S. assistentem, et inhabitantem. Quicunque Spiritum S. neque assistentem, neque inhabitantem possunt accipere, illi nequeunt illuminari; concedo. At licet irregeniti non intra momentum temporis accipiant gratiam Spiritus S. inhabitantem, possunt tamen accipere gratiam Spiritus S. assistentem, per quam praeparantur et disponuntur ad fidem in Christum concipiendam, vt per hanc Spiritus S. in cordibus habitet.

Instantia: Gratia assistens est adiuuans hominem renouatum, et cum eo cooperans; quae gratiam inhabitantem non praecedit, sed sequitur. Resp. Per gratiam assistentem heic non intelligitur gratia hominem renouatum adiuuans, sed gratia assistens dicitur, cum Spiritus S. externe circa cor hominis versatur, non tantum obiectum salutificum proponendo, et ostendendo, quid fieri debeat, sed etiam efficaciter tangendo, pulsando, et excitando, vt voluntatem Dei cognoscat, licet eam non semper faciat, Apoc.

III, 20. VI. Qui non amat fratrem suum, ...is non est illuminatus.

Atqui homo sanctitatis expers non amat fratrem suum. E.

Maior prob. ex 1 Io. II, 9. 10. 11. Qui dicit, in luce se esse, at fratrem suum odit, in tenebris est vsque nunc.

Qui vero diligit fratrem suum, in luce manet, & scandalum in ipso non est. Qui vero odit fratrem suum, in tenebris est, in tenebris ambulat, & non scit, quo abeat: quia tenebræ cæcos reddiderunt oculos eius. Resp. Qui non amat fratrem suum, ille non est illuminatus illuminatione perfecta & complete salutari. Potest tamen per gratiam diuinam imperfecte & pædagogice illuminatus esse. Perfecta illuminatio sufficit ad generandam fidem, quæ per caritatem efficax est, Gal. V, 6. Per illuminationem autem imperfectam intendit Spiritus S. hominem præparare & disponere, vt in Christum credat, & proximum amet; quamuis hic intentus effectus non semper sequatur per contumaciam, qua homo peccator gratiæ regeneranti & renouanti obsistit.

VII. Qui non diligit Deum, non cognouit eum, 1 Io. IV, 8. adeoque non est illuminatus: Homo expers sanctitatis, non diligit Deum: Ergo. Resp. Qui non diligit Deum, non cognoscit eum notitia practica & effectiua; potest tamen, a Spiritu S. præuentus & excitatus, Deum cognoscere notitia theoretica & litterali.

VIII. In quo non est vera Dei cognitio, is a Spiritu S. non est vere illuminatus: Atqui in homine sanctitatis experte non est vera Dei cognitio. Ergo. Minor probatur ex 1 Io. II, 4. Qui dicit, cognoui illum, & mandata illius non seruat, mendax est, & in hoc non est veritas. Resp. In quo non est notitia Dei neque logice, neque ethice vera, ille non est a Spiritu S. illuminatus. At vero in homine irregenito, quatenus a Spiritu S. imperfecte illuminatus est, potest esse cognitio Dei logice & formaliter vera, licet eadem non fit vera ethice & finaliter, i. e. licet ad veram praxin & finem a Spiritu S. intentum non fit traducta. Qui e lumine supernaturalis reuelationis cognoscit Deum esse in essentia vnum, & in personis trinum, illius θεογνωσία est vera logice & formaliter; at, si eandem non applicet ad fiduciam in Christo mediatore collocandam, ad Deum triunum amandum, venerandum, notitia illius non est vera ethice & finaliter.

IX. Qui non est lux in domino, is non est illuminatus: Atqui homo irregenitus &c. Eph. V, 8. Ergo. Resp. Qui non est lux in domino, is non perfecte illuminatus est; concedo. Nam vt homo fit lux in domino, requiritur, vt pro statu huius vitæ sit adequate illuminatus, conuerfus, renatus, iustificatus, & renouatus.

X. Quæ anima non est capax cœlestis sapientiæ, illa a Spiritu S. non illuminatur: Atqui anima maleuola &c. Sap. I, 4. Ergo. Quæ anima neque theoretica, neque practica sapientiæ capax est, illa a Spiritu S. non illuminatur; concedo. Ex illuminatione imperfecta est sapientia theoretica, qua Deus simpliciter apprehenditur & cognoscitur, sed non sapientia practica, qua Deus sic cognoscitur, vt ametur & colatur.

XI. Qui sub conditione voluntatis diuinæ faciendæ cognoscit, doctrinam Christi esse diuinam, ille absque sanctificatione non potest illuminari: Atqui homo peccator &c. Ergo. Minor prob. ex Io. VII, 16. 17. Respondit illis Iesus, & dixit: Mea doctrina non est mea, sed eius, qui misit me. Si quis voluerit voluntatem illius facere, cognoscet de doctrina, vtrum a Deo fit, an a me ipso loquar. Resp. 1) Voluntatem Patris facere l. c. non significat, sancte viuere. Qui enim cæcus sancte ambulabit? Annon intellectus prius est illuminandus? Annon de doctrina primum iudicandum, vtrum ea diuina fit, nec ne? Annon ea tunc demum facienda, ad quæ intellectus collustratus, cognitione doctrinæ, dirigit? Ideoque cum obiectum disputationis, Christum inter & Iudæos, fit doctrina Christi, an fit Patris cœlestis doctrina: τὸ facere voluntatem Patris non absolute, sed restrictine hic accipiendum est, secundum substratam materiam, vt significet, ex voluntate cœlestis scrutari scripturas V. T., & cum iis doctrinam Christi conferre, an hæc illis fit consona. 2) Per cognitionem l. c. intelligitur notitia de doctrina Christi vberior, plenior & illustrior.

Quicumque est in peccatis mortuus, ille non potest esse homo illuminatus. Atqui homo irregenitus est in peccatis mortuus; Ergo. Maior probatur: quia, sicut homo naturaliter mortuus oculis corporeis non cernit; ita spiritualiter mortuus nil videt oculis mentis; videret autem, si esset illuminatus. Minor claret: quia homo per regenerationem accipit vitam fidei, Gal. II, 20. ante autem erat mortuus in peccatis, Eph. II, 5. Resp. Quicumque est in peccatis mortuus, ille non potest esse illuminatus illuminatione perfecta & complete salutari: nam hæc ad excitandam fidem sufficiens est. Potest tamen homo, spiritualiter mortuus quidem, sub dispensatione autem gratiæ assistentis, & pulsu divino constitutus, imperfecte & pædagogice illuminari. Nam licet in anima nondum habeat internum principium vitale, Spiritus tamen sanctus extrinsece circa animam eius versatur & occupatur, tangendo, pulsando, excitando, & lucem notitiæ litteralis per verbum prædicatum aut lectum immittendo. Hanc meam assertionem probo exemplo Episcopi Sardensis, cuius mentio iniicitur Apoc. III, 3. Hic vocatur mortuus, & tamen iubetur recordari, quomodo acceperit & audiverit: Hinc valide argumentor: Quicumque est spiritualiter mortuus, & tamen recordari potest, qualem doctrinam a Domino per ministerium verbi acceperit, ille imperfecte est illuminatus: Atqui quidam homo, spiritualiter quidem mortuus, at sub dispensatione gratiæ assistentis, pulsuque divino constitutus, recordari potest, quam doctrinam a Domino per ministerium verbi acceperit: Ergo. Comparauerim eiusmodi irregenitos mortuis illis ossibus, quæ vidit Propheta Ezechiel cap. XXXVII, 7. quæ a vento extrinsecus mouebantur, neruis ligabantur, carne & cuti obtegebantur, nullo in ipsis exsistente spiritu. Sic gratia Spiritus S. assistens corda irregenitorum forinsecus tangit, pulsat, mouet, notitiam credendorum litteralem ipsis instillat, quamuis vita fidei destituantur.


### Quest. IX. What men does God illuminate?: Q. XI

Q. XI.

Illumination with respect to man, receiving heavenly doctrine, is either literal and pedagogical, or spiritual and completely salutary. The former is an operation of the Holy Spirit, by which He, through His externally assisting and preparing grace, instructs the intellect of a man who is indeed unregenerate, yet tending toward generation, with a literal knowledge of things to be believed, and produces a historical assent to the Gospel, so that he may be more and more disposed to receive saving faith: The latter is an operation of the Holy Spirit, by which He, entering and inhabiting the contrite heart of man, kindles in it a salutary knowledge of divine mercy founded on the merit of Christ, produces a fiducial assent to the Gospel, and confirms and seals the same with His internal testimony.

Obs. The distinction of illumination into literal and spiritual is used by orthodox Theologians. D. DANNHAEVER, about to judge accurately concerning the sin against the Holy Spirit, says in Hodof. phaenom. XI. p. 1419: The sin against the Holy Spirit is prohairetic (deliberate) unbelief in a man sufficiently illuminated, Heb. 6:4, ch. 10:26, 29. For he would not have spoken reproach against the king, unless he had known him to be king. I say, sufficient, because ἄπαξ [once], i.e., perfectly, Heb. 9:26. Whether that illumination was pedagogical, and of the letter only, or spiritual, joined with a γεῦσις [tasting] of heavenly things, which, if neglected, turns into blindness by a later divine judgment.

D. Quenstedt explains this solid distinction more clearly in his Systhem. theol., Part II, p. 77. Φωτισμὸς [Illumination], or illumination, is either παιδαγωγικὴ καὶ γραμματικὴ [pedagogical and grammatical], pedagogical, merely literal and external, when someone is instructed in the knowledge of divine truth, and convinced of its certainty in his own conscience, yet does not yet have this knowledge sealed in his heart by the seal of the Spirit, or confirmed by the gracious indwelling of the Holy Spirit; or πνευματικὴ [spiritual], spiritual, gracious, and internal, when, namely, one who is truly reborn not only has a literal understanding of evangelical doctrine, but is at the same time a temple of the Holy Spirit, whom He graciously inhabits, or when the truth is not only known and acknowledged, but is at the same time corroborated and sealed by the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit graciously inhabiting the heart.

D. Seb. Schmid supports the same in his Colleg. bibl. post., writing thus on p. 164: Subjectively, he can be ψυχικὸς [natural/soulish], animal, who understands something of those things which are of the Spirit of God; not as such, but as one already imperfectly illuminated by the Spirit of God.

This illumination, which D. Dannhauer and Quenstedt called pedagogical and literal, D. Schmid calls imperfect.

To these, D. Johann Adam Osiander adds his vote in his Theol. positiua, Part III, p. 19. Grace is distinguished into assisting and indwelling; and indeed, that which is assisting is that which still operates from without, not that it does not touch the heart of man itself, but because, while the Spirit still lingers externally and does not dwell within, it exerts its power, to which is assigned the preventing [grace], which removes the natural incapacity innate in all: the preparing [grace], which restrains the natural and actual resistance adverse to spiritual things: Finally, the exciting [grace], which instructs the mind in the literal sense, works assent, and crushes the heart: But it is called indwelling when the Holy Spirit Himself enters the heart, changes it, and dwells within.

And in his Colleg. systhem., Part IV, p. 335: The first degree of preventing and assisting grace is objective illumination, in the preaching of the Word, whether strictly or analogically so called, with the application of a special object, revealed through grace, to the individual: The second degree of the same is the inhibition and restraint of actual and natural repugnance: The third, finally, is the dispensation of literal knowledge and historical assent to the Gospel, as well as general trust in God, and, through the law, contrition.

D. Osiander therefore attributes to assisting grace both objective illumination and the dispensation of literal knowledge and historical assent.

Of the more recent ones, I add D. Fecht in his Tr. de ordine modoque gratiæ, p. 21: The Holy Spirit illuminates and exercises His actions not only in the faithful, but also in the unfaithful, in preparing them for faith.

Prob. Pedagogical illumination of the unregenerate 1) From John 1:9: Christ is the true light, illuminating every man coming into this world. D. Fecht clearly explains these words in the same place, p. 21: Christ, as much as in Him lies, through the ministry of the Word, implants true knowledge of God with all zeal and effort, and thus by repeated acts, as often as all those who admit Him working, as far as they admit Him. For the generality of the expression does not permit it to be understood only of that illumination which attains its completion in the plenary conversion of man. For was the young man not informed by Christ; is he not, because after the information ἀπῆλθε λυπούμενος [he went away grieved], he departed sadly from Christ, because he could not retain his riches? Matt. 19:21. Is he therefore not illuminated by the Holy Spirit who has received some light, although he has not admitted all through his own fault? Does the sun not illuminate a room because it either does not illuminate it entirely, or does not illuminate all its parts equally? Balaam, taught by God concerning the Savior of the world, about to arise long ago from Jacob, although he was unfaithful, nevertheless calls himself שְׁתֻם הָעַיִן [open of eye], open of eye, or, which is the same thing, illuminated, who has heard the words of God and seen the visions of the Almighty.

We argue: Whatever light shines in a dark place until the day of the knowledge of Christ dawns, that illuminates the unregenerate man: But the light of the divine word &c.

Therefore. 3) From Ps. XXV, 8: Good and upright is Jehovah, therefore He will teach sinners in the way. God is the highest good, and thus communicative of Himself: He is upright and just in Himself, and most willingly desires to draw His creatures to righteousness: and therefore He informs sinners (I speak with D. GEIER) both by the external prescription of the word, and by internal prevenient and subsequent grace, as to what way they ought to enter, i.e., what is to be believed, done, and omitted by them.

4) From Eph. III, 9, where the Apostle asserts that he illuminates all men. Therefore, he illuminated even the unregenerate successively and through repeated acts, until they might fully and savingly conceive faith.

5) If no unregenerate person can be illuminated, no Jew, no Turk, no gentile can be converted: But they are not rarely converted: Therefore, they are truly illuminated. Since this illumination is not completed in one moment, but by degrees, by turns, and by many acts, it disposes and prepares the Jew or Turk to conceive saving faith; certainly, a certain pedagogical illumination of a man not yet fully converted, but established in the way of conversion, must be granted.

You say: I. The distinction of illumination into literal and spiritual does not seem to be accurate, since literal illumination draws its origin from the grace of the Holy Spirit assisting and preparing. I answer with the words of OSIANDER: Although the powers of assisting grace are new and spiritual: they are not, however, such except with respect to the efficient cause, the divine intention, and the end to be attained, insofar as they proceed from the Holy Spirit and are directed to a spiritual end, although they do not yet constitute the man spiritually alive. See OSIANDER, colleg. systemat. part. IV, p. 335.

Therefore, spiritual illumination is said here in a stricter sense, which makes a man spiritually alive, exerts itself more and more in him as in a temple of the Holy Spirit, and is sealed by the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit.

You say: II. There is no illumination of an unregenerate man, because the god of this age has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, so that the illumination of the glory of Christ might not shine for them, 2 Cor. IV, 3. I answer: We are not speaking of an unregenerate man who is stubbornly contumacious, who, because he loves darkness more than light, by God’s permission, has been so blinded by the devil that he maliciously closes the eyes of his mind to the light of the divine word; but of a sinner, unregenerate indeed, yet docile, and admitting the light of the divine word, established in the way of conversion, and thus prevented by the Holy Spirit. This one is illuminated pedagogically, until the day of the spiritual knowledge of Christ dawns in his heart.

Latin:

Quæst. XI. Quotuplex est illuminatio respectu subiecti, siue hominis peccatoris?

Illuminatio respectu hominis, doctrinam cœlestem recipientis, est vel litteralis & pædagogica, vel spiritualis & complete salutaris. Illa est operatio Spiritus sancti, qua is per gratiam suam externe assistentem & præparantem intellectum hominis irregeniti quidem, ad generationem tamen tendentem, litterali credendorum notitia instruit, & assensum euangelii historicum producit, vt ad suscipiendam fidem saluificam magis magisque disponatur: Hæc est operatio Spiritus Sancti, qua is cor hominis contritum ingrediens & inhabitans, saluificam misericordiæ diuinæ in merito Christi fundatæ cognitionem in eodem accendit, assensum euangelii fiducialem producit, eundemque interno suo testimonio confirmat & obsignat.

Obs. Distinctio illuminationis in litteralem, & spiritualem a Theologis orthodoxis vsurpatur . D. DANNHAVERS, de peccato in Spiritum S. accurate iudicaturus, inquit in hodof. phænom. XI. p. 1419. Peccatum in Spiritum S. est ἀπιστία proæretica in homine satis illuminato, Hebr. VI, 4. c. X, 26. 29. Regi enim conuitium non dixerit, nisi qui sciuerit esse regem. Satis, inquam, quia ἄπαξ, i. e. perfecte, Hebr. IX, 26. Siue pædagogica illa fuerit illuminatio, & litteræ tantum, siue spiritualis cum γεῦσις cœlestium coniuncta, quæ neglecta diuino post iudicio vertit in excæcationem.

Quam solidam distinctionem clarius exponit D. QVENSTEDIVS systhem. theol. part. II. p. 77. Φωτισμὸς, siue illuminatio, vel est παιδαγωγικὴ καὶ γραμματικὴ, pædagogica, mere litteralis & externa, quando quis veritatis diuinæ cognitione est instructus, deque eius certitudine in conscientia sua conuictus, nondum tamen cognitionem hanc nec sigillo Spiritus in corde suo obsignatam, aut, per gratiosam Spiritus S. inhabitationem, confirmatam habet; vel πνευματικὴ, spiritualis, gratiosa & interna, quando scilicet quis vere renatus non tantum habet litteralem doctrinæ euangelicæ intelligentiam, sed simul est templum Spiritus S., quod ipse gratiose inhabitat, fue quando veritas non modo scitur & agnoscitur, sed simul a Spiritu S. in corde gratiose inhabitantis interno testimonio corroboratur & obsignatur.

Suffragatur iisdem D. SEB. SCHMIDIVS in colleg. bibl. post. ita scribens p. 164. Subiectiue potest esse ψυχικὸς, animalis, qui aliquid intelligit eorum, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei; non qua talis, sed qua iam a Spiritu Dei imperfecte illuminatus.

Quam illuminationem D. DANNHAV. & QVENSTED. vocarunt pædagogicam & litteralem, eandem D. SCHMID. appellat imperfectam.

Quibus calculum suum addit D. IOANN. ADAMVS OSIANDER, in theol. positiua, Part. III. p. 19. Distinguitur gratia in assistentem, & inhabitantem; Et quidem assistens illa est, quæ extrinsecus adhuc operatur, non quod non ipsum cor hominis tangat, sed quia adhuc Spiritu exterius versante, nec inhabitante, suam vim exserit, cui assignatur præueniens, quæ incapacitatem naturalem, omnibus connatam, aufert: præparans, quæ naturalem & actualem resistentiam spiritualibus aduersam cohibet: Denique excitans, quæ mentem litterali sensu instruit, assensum operatur, atque cor conterit: Inhabitans vero dicitur, cum ipse Spiritus S. cor ingreditur, illud immutat atque inhabitat.

Et in colleg. systhem. Part. IV. p. 335. Gradus primus gratiæ præuenientis & assistentis est illuminatio obiectiua, in verbi prædicatione, vel stricte, vel analogice sic dicta, cum obiecti specialis, per gratiam reuelati, ad indiuiduum applicatione: Alter gradus eiusdem est actualis & naturalis repugnantiæ inhibitio & refrænatio: Tertius denique est dispensatio litteralis notitiæ, & historici assensus in euangelium, nec non generalis fiducia in Deum, & mediante lege, contritio.

Tribuit itaque D. OSIANDER gratiæ assistenti tum illuminationem obiectiuam, tum dispensationem litteralis notitiæ & assensus historici.

Ex recentioribus addo D. FECHTIVM in Tr. de ordine modoque gratiæ, p. 21. Spiritus S. illuminat & actiones suas exercet non in fidelibus tantum, sed etiam in infidelibus ad fidem præparandis.

Prob. Illuminatio pædagogica irregenitorum 1) ex Io. I, 9. Christus vera lux, illuminans omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum. Quæ verba luculenter exponit D. FECHTIVS l. c. p. 21. Christus, quantum in se est, per verbi ministerium veram Dei cognitionem omni studio & conatu, adeoque repetitis sæpe actibus omnibus, qui se operantem admittunt, quousque admittunt, implantat. Nec enim generalitas locutionis permittit, vt de ea tantum illuminatione accipiatur, quæ complementum in plenaria hominis conuersione assequitur. An enim ideo a Christo informatus iuuenis; ille non est, quia post informationem ἀπῆλθε λυπούμενος, tristis a Christo discessit, eo, quod diuitias suas retinere non posset? Matth. XIX, 21. An ideo illuminatus a Spiritu S. non est, qui aliquid accepit luminis, licet omne culpa sua non admiserit? An ideo fol non illuminat conclaue, quia vel non totum illuminat, vel non omnes eius partes æqualiter illuminat? Bileam, a Deo de seruatore mundi, olim ex Iacob orituro, edoctus, quanquam infidelis esset, tamen semet appellat שְׁתֻם הָעַיִן apertum oculo, seu, quod idem est, illuminatum, qui audiuerit verba Dei, videritque visiones omnipotentis.

Arguimus: Quodcunque lumen lucet in loco tenebroso, vsque dum dies cognitionis Christi illucescat, illud illuminat hominem irregenitum: Atqui lumen verbi diuini &c. Ergo.

3) E Ps. XXV, 8. Bonus & rectus est Iehouah, propterea docebit peccatores in via. Deus est summum bonum, adeoque communicatiuum sui: Est rectus & in se iustus, suasque creaturas ad iustitiam libentissime vult pertrahere: ideoque peccatores (loquor cum D. GEIERO) tum externo verbi praescripto, tum interna praeueniente ac subsequente gratia informat, quam viam debeant ingredi, h. e. quid ipsis sit credendum, agendum, omittendum.

4) Ex Eph. III, 9. vbi Apostolus asserit, se illuminare omnes homines. E, illuminauit etiam irregenitos successive & per actus repetitos, donec fidem plene & salutariter conciperent.

5) Si nullus irregenitos illuminari potest, nullus Iudaeus, nullus Turca, nullus gentilis conuerti potest: Sed haud raro conuertuntur: E. vere illuminantur. Quae illuminatio cum non vno absoluatur momento, sed per gradus, per vices, per plures actus, Iudaeum vel Turcam disponat ac praeparet ad fidem saluificam concipiendam, vtique concedenda est quaedam illuminatio paedagogica hominis nondum plene conuersi, sed in via conuersionis constituti.

Dicis: I. Distinctio illuminationis in litteralem, & spiritualem non videtur esse accurata, cum illuminatio litteralis originem suam ducat e gratia Spiritus S. assistente & praeparante. Respondeo verbis OSIANDRI: Quanquam vires gratiae assistentis sint nouae & spirituales: non sunt tamen tales, nisi respectu efficientis causae, intentionis diuinae & finis consequendi, quatenus scilicet a Spiritu S. proficiscuntur, & ad spiritualem finem diriguntur, quanquam nondum hominem spiritualiter viuum constituunt. Vid. OSIANDRI colleg. systemat. part. IV. p. 335.

Illuminatio itaque spiritualis sensu strictiori hic dicitur, quae hominem spiritualiter viuum efficit, in eodem, tanquam templo Spiritus S. magis magisque se exserit, atque interno Spiritus S. testimonio obsignatur.

Dicis: II. Non datur illuminatio hominis irregeniti, eo, quod Deus huius saeculi excaecauit sensus infidelium, vt non splendeat illis illuminatio gloriae Christi, 2 Cor. IV, 3. Resp. Non loquimur de homine irregenito praefracte contumaci, qui ideo, quod tenebras magis amat, quam lucem, permittente Deo, a diabolo sic occaecatus est, vt ad lumen verbi diuini oculos mentis malitiose occludat; sed de peccatore, irregenito quidem, docili tamen, & lumen verbi diuini admittente, in via conuersionis constituto, atque adeo praeuento a Spiritu S. Hic illuminatur paedagogice, donec dies spiritualis cognitionis Christi in ipsius corde illucescat.


### Quest. XII

The sinner, established in the way of conversion and pedagogically illuminated, should assiduously and attentively read, hear, and meditate upon the divine word, and permit himself entirely to the illuminating grace of the Holy Spirit, until the light of spiritual wisdom, which can stand before the judgment of God, arises in his soul.

Proved 1) From 2 Pet. I, 19: We have the more sure prophetic word, to which you do well to pay attention, as to a light shining in a dark place, until the day dawns, and the morning star rises in your hearts. As Peter warns, one must attend to the divine word until the illumination of faith follows, and Christ, dwelling in the heart, suffuses it, like a most brilliant phosphorus, with a richer light of saving knowledge. 2) By

2) To this end, the sinner is pedagogically illuminated, so that he may be disposed and prepared for spiritual illumination, which not only illuminates the intellect but also directs the will toward the love of God and neighbor.

If the sinner to be converted does not attain this spiritual illumination, his literal knowledge is not sufficient, not fruitful, not salutary, because it is not translated into due use, and thus can finally be called false; for the reason that it is frustrated of the true end intended by God. Cf. D. FECHT. l. c. p. 22. & 46. To this point look the words of St. John, 1 Ep. II, 4: He who says: I have known him, and does not keep his commandments, is a liar, and in him the truth is not: And the words of St. Paul, 1 Cor. VIII, 2. 3: If anyone thinks that he knows anything, he does not yet know anything as he ought to know; but if anyone loves God, this one is known by him.

3) Literal knowledge, which is the effect of pedagogical illumination, cannot stand before the judgment of God.

This is what Christ points out, Matt. VII, 22: Many will say to me in that day: Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in your name? But then I will confess to them: I do not know you, depart from me, you who work iniquity! And Luke XII, 47: The servant who knows the will of his master, but neither prepares himself nor does his will, shall be beaten with many [stripes].

4) Spiritual knowledge, which is the fruit of spiritual illumination, is effectively and completely salutary; whence it is called the knowledge of salvation, Luke I, 77. For when this becomes the beginning of saving faith, it makes one not only wise but also righteous before God. By his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many, says Jehovah, Es. VIII, 11. From which it is concluded that the sinner, established in the way of conversion, ought not to acquiesce or stop in literal and pedagogical illumination, but ought to tend and strive toward spiritual and salutary illumination.

You say: Literal knowledge of things to be believed is 1) true; because it is conformable to Holy Scripture: 2) salutary; for the reason that it flows from the word of salvation, and is ordained to salvation by divine intention: Therefore, the sinner can acquiesce in it.

I answer to I. with the words of D. BREITHAUPT, ex instit. theol. p. 263: Knowledge among the unregenerate can be true by logical and literal truth, or by reason of the doctrine and the credible object; but not by reason of the disposition and divine efficacy, under which the Holy Spirit wills the objects of Scripture to be known to the intellect and will; which, unless He is able to effect, it happens indeed that what is truth according to the letter is not truth according to the spirit.

To II. Something is called salutary in two ways: a) by reason of ordination, or destination to salvation: in which sense a medicine is in itself salutary, which is destined to repair the health of the body: b) by reason of the actual conferring of salvation: in which sense a medicine is called salutary, which actually repairs health. Literal knowledge is indeed divinely ordained for procuring salvation: but it does not actually confer salvation. Although, therefore, it may be said to be pedagogically salutary, it is not, however, effectively or completely salutary. Cf. D. FECHT. l. c. p. 22. & D. BREITHAUPT. in thesib. credend. p. 133. 134 (*).

XIII. What aids must a sinner use in order to be spiritually enlightened? To obtain spiritual illumination, three aids are required: Prayer, meditation, and temptation.

Proof a. From Luke 11:13. The Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask.

Since the saving understanding of the divine word is not obtained without the grace of the Holy Spirit, one must pray assiduously that God may give us the Spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of Him, and the enlightened eyes of the intellect, Eph. 1:17, 18. Thus King David prays: Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things from your law, Ps.

119:18. Proof b. From John 5:39. Search the scriptures, for you think that in them you have eternal life, and they are those which testify of me.

Just as miners of metals search the innermost caverns of the earth, and hunters track wild beasts in the hidden recesses of the forests: so the Holy Scripture must be inspected not cursorily, but most deeply, so that we may find the way to eternal life (which is Christ, John 14:6). Proof c. From Ps. 119:71. It is good for me that I have been afflicted, that I may learn your statutes.

Afflictions open the way to a practical and experimental knowledge of divine statutes. Question XIV. Is the illumination and regeneration of a sinner through purification, or the abstraction of the soul from creatures, and conversion into itself?

The illumination and regeneration of a sinner does not occur through purification, or the abstraction of the soul from creatures, and conversion into itself. This is the antithesis of 1) the Pythagoreans and Platonists, who maintained that before the soul can arrive at true wisdom, it has need of κάθαρσις (katharsis), that is, a certain purification, by which the filth of the body and of material senses might be cleansed from it: to this purification they joined a certain conversion of the mind into itself, which they wished to be as it were an approach and door to true wisdom; for they thought that the mind, conscious of its own powers and liberated from the bonds and filth of the body and matter, should above all things turn into itself, with other things that are outside being as it were consigned to oblivion, and, as pertaining nothing to itself, cast out from memory (they called this ἐπιστροφὴν εἰς ἑαυτὸν [epistrophēn eis heauton]).

Finally, they added the last duty of the mind, which they called ἄνοδον (anodon), or ascent. For they wanted the mind, pure from all contagion of the body and liberated, with its powers as it were collected into itself, to desert these inferior things, and be carried upward, and seek celestial and divine things, and strive to return to its own principle, and this they named its ascent.

See SCHEFFER'S Italian philosophy, ch. IX, p. 74 et seq.

2) The Mystics, who embrace the dogmas of the Pythagoreans and Platonists. MICHAEL DE MOLINOS inculcates this introversion most frequently in his Spiritual Guide, book III, ch. 2, p. 270.

It is the continuous exercise of spiritual men to enter into themselves, into God, with quiet and silence, because there is His center, dwelling, and delights; they esteem this interior retreat more than discourse about God; they withdraw into that interior and secret center of the soul, to know God and to receive His divine influence with fear and most loving reverence. But from what things the soul must be abstracted, the same author teaches in the same place on page 379, saying: Know that he who desires to arrive at mystical knowledge ought to deny himself and alienate himself from five things: 1. from creatures, 2. from temporal things, 3. from the very gifts of the Holy Spirit, 4. from himself, [the] nature of a man not yet born again, as soon as he reads, hears, or perceives the word, is true, is divine, is efficacious, and not void of all effect, although only begun, to be continued daily, and to be perfected with the whole effect, which is entirely saving. in itself, and 5. must lose itself in God. This last is the most perfect, because only that soul which can so alienate itself, is the one that arrives at the point of losing itself in God.

He calls this κάθαρσιν [catharsis] also annihilation, by which a man makes himself and all things in the world nothing, ibid. p. 382. as well as interior solitude, which consists in the oblivion of all creatures, in alienation, and perfect nakedness of all affections, desires, and thoughts, and of one's own will, ibid. p. 304. concerning which he philosophizes thus: You will never taste the delicious Manna Ap. 2. which no one knows, except he who receives it, unless you perfectly conquer yourself, until you die within yourself; therefore resign yourself, and deny yourself totally.

Introversion is also called by MOLINOS, recollection of one's interior, book 1. ch. 11. p. 92.

WEIGELIUS greatly commends this introversion (Einkehr, or Einkehrung) in Part II. of his postil, p. 62.

Latin:

Peccator, in via conuersionis constitutus, & paedagogice illuminatus, verbum diuinum assidue attenteque legat, audiat, meditetur, atque se totum gratiae Spiritus S. illuminatrici permittat, donec lux sapientiae spiritualis, quaeque coram iudicio Dei consistere potest, in animo illius exoriatur.

Prob. 1) Ex 2 Petr. I, 19. Habemus firmius propheticum verbum, cui, recte facitis, quod attenditis, tanquam lumini lucenti in loco tenebroso, vsque dum dies illucescat, & lucifer oriatur in cordibus vestris. Monente Petro, eo vsque attendendum est verbo diuino, donec sequatur illuminatio fidei, & Christus, habitans in corde, id ipsum, lucidissimi instar phosphori, vberiori saluificae cognitionis luce perfundat. ipsum, lucidiffimi instar phofphori, vberiori falutificæ cognitionis luce perfundat. 2) Eo

2) Eo fine paedagogice illuminatur peccator, vt disponatur & praeparetur ad illuminationem spiritualem, quae non tantum illustrat intellectum, sed dirigit etiam voluntatem ad amorem Dei & proximi.

Quam illuminationem spiritualem si non assequitur peccator convertendus, notitia illius litteralis non est sufficiens, non fructuosa, non salutaris, quia ad debitum usum non traducitur, adeoque finaliter falsa vocari potest; ideo, quod fine vero, a Deo intento frustratur. Conf. D. FECHT. l. c. p. 22. & 46. Quo spectant verba S. Ioannis, 1 ep. II, 4. Qui dicit: Cognoui illum, & mandata illius non seruat, mendax est, & in hoc veritas non est: Et verba S. Pauli, 1 Cor. VIII, 2. 3. Si quis videtur sibi scire aliquid, nondum quidquam scit, sicut decet cognoscere; sed si quis amat Deum, hic cognitus est ab ipso.

3) Notitia litteralis, quae illuminationis paedagogicae effectus est, coram iudicio Dei consistere nequit.

Id quod indigitat Christus, Matth. VII, 22. Multi dicent mihi in illa die: Domine, Domine, nonne per nomen tuum prophetavimus? Sed tum confitebor iis: non noui vos, discedite a me operantes iniquitatem! Et Luc. XII, 47. Seruus, qui scit voluntatem domini, sed neque parat se, neque facit voluntatem eius, percutietur multis.

4) Notitia spiritualis, quae illuminationis spiritualis fructus est, effective & complete salutaris est; ex quo dicitur scientia salutis, Luc. I, 77. Cum enim isthaec fit initium fidei salutificae, coram Deo non tantum sapientes, sed etiam iustos facit. Per scientiam sui iustificabit iustus seruus meus multos, inquit Iehouah, Es. VIII, 11. Ex quibus conficitur, quod peccator, in via conuersionis constitutus, in illuminatione litterali & paedagogica non acquiescere, sed subsistere, sed tendere & conniti debeat ad illuminationem spiritualem & salutarem.

Dicis: Notitia credendorum litteralis est 1) vera; quia S. Scripturae est conformis: 2) salutaris; propterea, quod e verbo salutis fluit, & ad salutem diuina intentione ordinata est: E. peccator in eadem acquiescere potest.

Respondeo ad I. verbis D. BREITHAVPTI, ex instit. theol. p. 263: Vera esse potest notitia apud irregenitos veritate logica & litterali, seu ratione doctrinae & obiecti credibilis; non autem ratione indolis & efficaciae diuinae, sub qua Spiritus S. obiecta scripturae intellectui & voluntati cognita esse vult; id quod nisi is possit efficere, fit sane, ut quae secundum litteram est veritas, secundum spiritum non sit veritas.

Ad II. Salutare aliquid bifariam dicitur: a) ratione ordinationis, vel destinationis ad salutem: quo sensu medicamentum in se salutare est, quod ad sanitatem corporis reparandam destinatum est: b) ratione actualis collationis salutis: quo sensu medicamentum salutare dicitur, quod actu valetudinem reparat. Notitia litteralis ad salutem procurandam diuinitus quidem ordinata est: actu autem salutem non confert. Quamuis itaque dici queat paedagogice salutaris, non tamen effective aut complete salutaris est. Conf. D. FECHT. l. c. p. 22. & D. BREITHAVPT. in thesib. credend. p. 133. 134 (*).

XIII. Quibus adminiculis uti debet peccator, ut spiritualiter illuminetur? Ad obtinendam illuminationem spiritualem tria requiruntur adminicula: Oratio , meditatio , tentatio .

Prob. a. Ex Luc. XI, 13. Dabit Pater Spiritum S. petentibus.

Quoniam salutaris intelligentia verbi divini non obtinetur sine gratia Spiritus S., assidue orandum est, ut Deus det nobis Spiritum sapientiæ & revelationis in agnitionem ipsius, atque illuminatos oculos intellectus, Eph. I, 17. 18. Sic precatur rex Dauid: Revela oculos meos; ut videam mirabilia e lege tua, Ps.

CXIX, 18. Prob. b. Ex Io. V, 39. Scrutamini scripturas, quia vos putatis in ipsis habere vitam æternam, & illæ sunt, quæ de me testantur.

Quemadmodum fossores metallorum intimas terræ cavernas rimantur, & venatores feras in abstrusis siluarum recessibus indagant: Ita non obiter, sed penitissime inspicienda est S. Scriptura, ut viam ad vitam æternam, (quæ est Christus, Io. XIV, 6.) inveniamus. Prob. c. Ex Ps. CXIX, 71. Bonum est mihi, quod afflictus sum, ut discam statuta tua.

Afflictiones pandunt viam ad practicam & experimentalem statutorum divinorum notitiam. Quæst. XIV. Sitne illuminatio & regeneratio peccatoris per purgationem, sive abstractionem animæ a creaturis, & conversionem in seipsam?

Illuminatio & regeneratio peccatoris non fit per purgationem, sive abstractionem animæ a creaturis, & conversionem in seipsam. Antithesis est 1) Pythagoræorum, & Platonicorum, qui statuebant, priusquam anima pervenire valeat ad veram sapientiam, opus habere καθάρσεως, hoc est, purgatione quadam, qua ei sordes corporis, sensuumque materialium detergerentur: Purgationi iungebant mentis in seipsam veluti conversionem aliquam, quam volebant esse ad veram sapientiam quasi aditum, ostiumque; nam putabant, animum conscium suarum virium, & a vinculis, sordibusque corporis, materiæque liberatum ante omnia in se verti, ceteris, quæ extra sunt, oblivioni velut traditis, &, ut ad se nil pertinentibus, memoria eiectis (ἐπιστροφὴν εἰς ἑαυτὸν hoc appellabant).

Tandem ultimum adiiciebant mentis officium, quod vocabant ἄνοδον, seu ascensum. Volebant enim mentem puram ab omni corporis contagione, liberatamque, collectis quasi in se viribus, deserere hæc inferiora, ferrique sursum, & cœlestia divinaque petere, & ad ipsum suum studere principium reuerti, hocque ascensum eius nominabant.

Vid. SCHEFFERI philosoph. Italicam c. IX. p. 74 sqq.

2) Mysticorum, dogmata Pythagoræorum & Platonicorum amplectentium. Inculcat hanc introuersionem frequentissime MICHAEL DE MOLINOS in manuduct. spirituali libr. III. c. 2. p. 270.

Continuum hominum spiritualium exercitium est, intrare in se, in Deum, cum quiete & silentio, quia ibi eius est centrum, habitatio & deliciæ, maiores æstimant interiorem hunc secessum, quam sermonem de Deo; secedunt in illud interius, & secretum animæ centrum, ad cognoscendum Deum, & accipiendam divinam eius influentiam cum timore & amantissima reverentia. A quibus rebus autem anima abstrahenda sit, idem ibidem pagina 379. docet, inquiens: Scias, quod abnegare se debeat, & a quinque rebus abalienare ille, qui pervenire cupit ad scientiam mysticam; 1. a creaturis, 2. a rebus temporalibus, 3. ab ipsis donis Spiritus S. 4. a semetipso, natio hominis, nondum denuo nati, simul atque is verbum legit, audit, percipit, est vera, est divina, est efficax, nec omni effectu vacua, quamuis incepta tantum, in dies continuanda, ac toto effectu, omnino salutari, perficienda. semetipso, et 5. perdere se debeat in Deo. Hæc vltima est perfectissima, quia tantum ea anima, quæ ita se alienare potest, illa est, quæ eo peruenit, ut in Deo se perdat.

Hanc κάθαρσιν vocat etiam annihilationem, qua homo seipsum, & omnia in mundo nihili facit, ibid. p. 382. nec non interiorem solitudinem, quæ consistit in obliuione omnium creaturarum, in alienatione, & perfecta nuditate omnium affectuum, desideriorum, & cogitationum, ac propriæ voluntatis, ibid. p. 304. de qua sic philosophatur: Nunquam gustabis deliciosum Manna Ap. 2. quod nemo nouit, nisi qui accipit, nisi te perfecte vincas, donec in te ipso moriaris; ideo resigna te, & abnega totaliter.

Introuersionem dicitur etiam a MOLINOSIO recollectio sui interior, libr. 1. c. 11. p. 92.

Hanc introuersionem (Einkehr, oder Einkehrung) magnopere commendat WEIGELIVS Part. II. postillæ p. 62.


### Quest. XII: Could we turn inward, and hear God within ourselves, we would come to an excellent Light, & p

Could we turn inward, and hear God within ourselves, we would come to an excellent Light, & p.

67. We in the New Testament are ourselves the temple, into which we should turn through fasting, watching, and prayer, so shall we also learn the things which no book nor man can teach us, until the last day.

3) Of the Quakers, whose leader writes in Apol. p. 226: souls must turn to that internal principle within themselves, as if to a most excellent teacher, who can never be removed into a corner.

EXPOSITION

Obf. I. We do not disapprove of every abstraction of the mind from foreign matters and secular cares during the actual use of the word, and pious meditations and prayers.

For those prayers are not devout which the mouth of a man recites, while his heart is distracted by foreign and widely wandering thoughts. See Is. XXIX, 13. We reject that abstraction, or annihilation, by which the mind is abstracted from all creatures and from divine gifts, and loses its being in God.

Obf. II. We do not criticize every resignation, since our own Theologians also teach a moderate and pious resignation (die Gelassenheit), which the blessed

SCRIVERIUS described elegantly in the spiritual treasury of the soul, Part III. p. 1390. Resignation is a fruit of faith, and a childlike confidence of the soul in God, through which it leaves and surrenders itself wholly and entirely to his holy and gracious will, willingly and humbly submits itself to his fatherly providence and all-wise government, and seeks and desires nothing else than that it may be, everywhere and at all times, in love and suffering, in fortune and misfortune, in wealth and poverty, in life and death, a work of his grace and a vessel of his honor.

But we do disapprove of that resignation which denotes the stripping away of all affections, desires, and thoughts, which WEIGELIUS wishes to be the entrance and way to illumination, saying: If I could be a child, or work as much as a lump of clay, for only half an hour, I would be a prophet and apostle, Part II. postill. p. 229.

Obf. III. A distinction must be made between a descent into the heart or soul that is commemorative of sin or a state of misery and exploratory of repentance and faith, and one that is apprehensive of an internally and immediately revealing light.

Who would dare to criticize a descent of the soul into itself that is commemorative of sin? The prodigal son, ἑαυτὸν ἐλθὼν, returning to himself, said: How many of my father's hired servants have bread enough! but I perish with hunger! This return of the soul to itself pertains to the recognition of sin, without which there is no true repentance.

God exhorts the Israelites to this descent into the heart, Is. XLVI, 8. Return, you transgressors, to your heart. But the descent into the soul that is δοκιμασμός, or exploratory, belongs to all Christians, that they may test themselves, whether they have true faith, to which all the requirements of true faith apply.

To this δοκιμασίαν [testing] we deservedly let the Pauline exhortation move you, 2 Cor. XIII, 5. Test yourselves, whether you are in the faith; prove yourselves. At present, the controversy is about ἐπιστροφῇ εἰς ἑαυτὸν, or the introversion of the soul into itself, in order to await & observe & apprehend an internal light, revealing immediately.

Latin:

Könnten wir einkehren, und Gott in uns selber hören, wir kämen zu einem treflichen Licht, & p.

67. Wir im neuen Testament sind selbst der Tempel, darein sollen wir kehren durch Fasten, Wachen und Beten, so werden wir auch lernen die Dinge, die uns kein Buch, noch Mensch lehren mag, bis an den jüngsten Tag.

3) Quackerorum, quorum Antefignanus in Apol. p. 226. scribit: debent animæ ad internum illud in semetipsis principium conuertere, quasi ad doctorem excellentissimum, qui nunquam in angulum remoueri potest.

ΕΚΘΕΣΙΣ

Obf. I. Non improbamus omnem abstractionem animi a rebus peregrinis, & curis sæcularibus in actuali verbi vsu, piisque meditationibus & precationibus.

Neque enim deuotæ sunt preces, quas os hominis recitat, cuius cor in peregrinas, & longe lateque euagantes cogitationes distrahitur. Vid. Es. XXIX, 13. Auerfamur eam abstractionem, aut annihilationem, qua mens ab omnibus creaturis, atque a donis diuinis abstrahitur, & esse suum in Deo perdit.

Obf. II. Non reprehendimus omnem resignationem, cum & nostri Theologi moderatam pianque resignationem (die Gelassenheit) doceant, quam eleganter descripsit B.

SCRIVERIVS in spirituali thesauro animæ, Part. III. p. 1390. Die Gelassenheit ist eine Frucht des Glaubens, und eine kindliche Zuversicht der Seelen zu Gott, dadurch sie sich ganz und gar seinem heiligen und gnädigen Willen überlässet und ergiebet, seiner väterlichen Vorsorge und allweisen Regierung sich willig und demüthig unterwirft, und nichts anders suchet und wünschet, als daß sie allenthalben und allezeit in Lieb und Leid, in Glück und Unglück, in Reichthum und Armuth, im Leben und Sterben, ein Werk seiner Gnaden und Gefäß seiner Ehren seyn möge.

Illam vero resignationem improbamus, quæ notat exspoliationem omnium affectuum, desideriorum & cogitationum, quam WEIGELIVS aditum & viam ad illuminationem esse vult, inquiens: Möchte ich ein Kind seyn, oder so viel würken als ein Kloß, nur eine halbe Stunde, ich würde ein Prophet und Apostel, Part. II. postill. p. 229.

Obf. III. Distinguendum est inter descensum in cor, vel animam commemoratiuum peccatus vel status miseriæ & exploratiuum pœnitentiæ & fidei, atque apprehensiuum luminis interni immediate reuelantis.

Descensum animi in seipsum commemoratiuum peccati quis ausit reprehendere? Filius acolastus eis ἑαυτὸν ἐλθὼν, ad se rediens, dixit: Quot mercenarii patris mei abundant pane! ego vero fame pereo! Qui reditus animi ad seipsum pertinet ad agnitionem peccati, sine qua nulla est vera pœnitentia.

Ad hunc descensum in cor cohortatur Deus Israëlitas, Es. XLVI, 8. Redite præuaricatores ad cor. Descensus autem in animam δοκιμασμός, siue exploratiuus, Christianorum omnium est, vt seipsos probent, an veram habeant fidem, cui omnes veræ fidei requisita competunt.

Ad hanc δοκιμασίαν nos merito moueat adhortatio Paullina, 2 Cor. XIII, 5. Vos ipsos tentate, num sitis in fide; vos ipsos probate. In praesentiarum controvertitur de ἐπιστροφῇ εἰς ἑαυτὸν, sive de introuersione animi in seipsum, ad expectandum & obseruandum & apprehendendum lumen internum, immediate reuelans.


### Quest. XII: Confirmation

CONFIRMATION

I. Whatever dogma rests upon a false hypothesis, that is to be rejected: But the dogma concerning introversion into the innermost center of the soul, in order to observe & apprehend an internal light, revealing immediately (without the concurrence of Holy Scripture), rests upon a false hypothesis: Therefore.

The minor premise is evident from the previous question: because we have most clearly demonstrated that there is not given at the present time in the human soul an internal light, teaching immediately. II. Whoever finds the densest darkness in his heart, he cannot be illuminated through introversion into the innermost recesses of the heart: But the Gentile, destitute of the light of Scripture, &c.

The minor premise is proved from Eph.

V, 8. 18. III. Whatever doctrine calls a man away from the ordinary means of illumination, that is not to be tolerated in the orthodox church: But the doctrine of the mystics, concerning introversion into the heart, in order to await & observe an internal light &c.

The minor premise is proved: because the ordinary means of illumination is Holy Scripture, 2 Pet. I, 19. To this external light the sinner who is to be illuminated ought to turn the eyes of his body and mind.

IV. Whatever opinion introduces enthusiasm into the church, that becomes alien to us: But the opinion concerning introversion into the heart, in order to await an internal light &c. The major premise is confirmed from the epitome of the Form.

Conc. p 581.; We also reject and condemn the error of the Enthusiasts, who imagine that God draws men to Himself, illuminates, justifies, and saves them immediately without the hearing of the Word of God and the use of the sacraments. But the mystics, turning the soul into the innermost depth of the heart, wish to be illuminated immediately. V.

Abstraction from all creatures is impious: Therefore, it is unbecoming to a pious Christian. The antecedent is clear: because even the human nature of Christ, Holy Scripture, with respect to the material of its letters and syllables, and the sacraments, with respect to their external elements, are of the category of creatures. VI. Mystical resignation is opposed both to divine worship and to the rational nature of man: Therefore,

it is unbecoming to a Christian. The antecedent is evident: because God demands worship not ἄλογον (irrational), but λογικὸν (rational), not ἀπαθῆ (devoid of affections), but παθητικὸν (ardent with pious affections), Rom. XII, 2. 11. But the resignation of the mystics is a stripping away of all senses, thoughts, and affections, and changes man into a log, lacking rational sense.

SOLUTION

The adversaries object: I. A descent into the soul is commanded by the divine Word, Is.

XLVI, 8. But a descent into the soul is an introversion of the soul into itself. Therefore. Resp. That a descent into the soul which is done for the purpose that a man may be immediately illuminated is commanded by the divine Word; I deny.

In the cited passage, a descent into the soul is understood as a remembrance of sins and misery. II. Self-denial is commanded, Matt.

XVI, 24. Abstraction from all external things is self-denial. Therefore. Resp. I deny the minor. For self-denial is an act of the will, by which we postpone our own honor and advantage to the divine glory.

But abstraction is an act of the intellect, by which the Mystics abstract the mind from the consideration of all creatures. III. Those whose duty it is to test and prove themselves, they ought to turn their soul into themselves.

But it is the duty of Christians &c. 2 Cor. XIII, 5. Resp. Those whose duty it is to test and prove themselves, Resp.

Those whose duty it is to test and prove themselves, that with the end in view, that they may be illuminated and regenerated, it is their duty to turn the soul into itself; I concede this. But true Christians are not to be illuminated or regenerated, but are already illuminated and regenerated; and thus their δοκιμασία (testing) is not a means of illumination and regeneration, but is instituted by those who are illuminated and reborn for the purpose that they may be rendered more certain that they possess a true and living faith.
