Therefore, having instituted an examination within themselves, they subject their faith to the touchstone of the divine word, to see whether it provides the conditions, parts, and virtues required therein, and whether it manifests itself by the true fruits of a living faith? For which reason the δοκιμασία of Christians differs most widely from the Pythagorean ἐπιστροφῇ εἰς ἑαυτὸν (turning to oneself). The former is of a man who is illuminated; the latter is of a man who is to be illuminated. The former is done according to the external word of God; the latter observes an internal and immediate light. The former is done by a reflex act of the mind, by which a man reflects upon his own cognition and knows that he truly knows God and believes in Him; the latter is done by a direct act of the mind, which is as it were an approach and a way to knowing God.

IV. Whoever is a temple of God, he can turn himself into the innermost depth of his heart, to seek God dwelling within him: But indeed a Christian, etc.

The major premise is confirmed by MICHAEL DE MOLINOS, book I of the Manuductio spiritualis, ch. III, p. 52, from the soliloquies of AUGUSTINE, who addresses God thus: I was wandering, O Lord, like a straying sheep, seeking Thee by an industrious search outside, when Thou wert within me. I was greatly fatigued in seeking Thee outside of myself; and Thou hast Thy habitation within me, while I desire and pant for Thee. I was going around the streets and squares of the city of this world, seeking Thee, and I did not find Thee, because I was seeking Him in vain outside, who was within myself. Resp.

1) An ignoratio elenchi (ignorance of the point at issue) is committed. For the question is whether a sinful man is illuminated and regenerated through the turning of the mind into itself. But a true Christian, who is the temple of God, is already illuminated and regenerated. 2) A man who is a wayfarer, by a direct act of the mind, seeks and finds God a) in the kingdom of nature, by observing the natural light implanted within, and the proofs of divine beneficence so clear that they can be felt even by the blind, Acts 17:28. b) in the kingdom of grace, by meditating on the Scripture, which testifies of Christ, John 5:39, and in which are found the saving counsel of God, Acts 20:27, the mysteries of God revealed for our salvation, Rom. 16:25, and the riches of Christ, Eph. 3:8.

But by a reflex act of the mind, a true Christian tests his faith, whether it be true and living? and thus inquires whether God dwells in him through the same? to which b. AUGUSTINE seems to have looked.

Quest. XV. Is the supernatural and saving light of God to be awaited in silence? So far is it from the case that the supernatural divine light is to be awaited in silence, that rather the external word of God, which is the clearest light, is to be preached seriously, heard diligently, read frequently, and pondered attentively, just as pious prayers, mixed with sacred hymns, are to be sent to heaven, so that the saving light of knowledge may arise in our hearts and subsequently take on greater increments.

The antithesis is that of the Mystics, Weigelians, and Quakers. MOLINOS, the author of QUIETISM, especially commends silence in book I of De spirit. manud., ch. XVII, p. 146, saying:

There is a triple kind of silence. The first is of words, the second of desires, the third of thoughts. The first is perfect, the second more perfect, the third most perfect. By the first, which is of words, virtue is acquired: by the second, which is of desires, rest is obtained: by the third, which is of thoughts, interior recollection. By not speaking, not desiring, not thinking, one arrives at the true and perfect mystical silence, in which God speaks with the soul, communicates Himself to it, and teaches it in its innermost depth the most perfect and most sublime wisdom. The same WEIGELIUS urges the same silence in his Postill, Part II, p. 230: "Everything must come into a stillness, if I am to hear or perceive the divine speaking-in; that is, if I am to be enlightened or made a believer, I must go into my little chamber, and go into a corner, and in a stillness wait upon God; which waiting in a stillness is called literal enthusiasm, or fanaticism."

The Quakers in their public meetings love silence, which CATON does not deny in his Simple Inquirer, p. 8: "When the Quakers meet, they look to the Lord in his light, sometimes for an hour or two, in silence."

Sometimes, however, before it passes by, some are moved by the Lord to say more or less, for the edification of others, in the most holy faith. This silence the Quakers call the internal sabbath of the soul, of which GEORG.

KEITH, in his friendly response to D. BAIER, p. 14, writes: "From the exercise and use of the words of scripture, the faithful soul, following its internal teacher, the Holy Spirit, turns for a time to another kind of nobler exercise and life, as if from labor into rest, and as if from a six-day work into this most delightful sabbath; indeed, it is snatched away from all its exercises (both external and internal, where scripture has its own excellent place) into this leisure, sabbath, and, as it were, spiritual sleep with Jacob, where it sees the heavens opened, and as it were the angels of God ascending and descending." WEIGELIUS is wonderfully pleased with this internal sabbath, who, in part

II. of his Postill, p. 86, says: "Give yourself often after your inward prayer into a silence, let God entirely and completely [work] from within and from without, come into a forgetting of yourself, so that God may find room and place to work, and to enlighten you." ΕΚΘΕΣΙΣ (Exposition) Obf. I. Since the mystics distinguish between the silence of words, of thoughts, and of desires, we certainly approve of the first, the silence of words; for meditations on the divine word love silence within private walls; but we disapprove of the silence of desires and thoughts.

Obf. II. It indeed befits true Christians to have an expectation of divine help joined with silence, but not a silent expectation of light, revealing immediately.

Obf. III. The doctrine concerning the internal sabbath of the soul, insofar as it denotes 1) a cessation from the works of the flesh, 2) the rest of the soul in God, 3) meditation on divine benefits, 4) the desire and expectation of the eternal sabbath, is retained and inculcated in our churches.

See GERHARD in Schola Pietatis, Part III, ch. 28. But the internal sabbath is rejected insofar as it denotes the silence not only of words, but also of all thoughts and senses.

Latin:

ΒΕΒΑΙΩΣΙΣ

I. Quodcunque dogma falsa nititur hypothesi, illud est reiiciendum: Atqui dogma de introuersione in intimum animae centrum, ad obseruandum & apprehendendum lumen internum, immediate (absque concursu S. scripturae) reuelans, falsa nititur hypothesi: Ergo.

Minor e superiori quaestione patet: quia luculentissime demonstrauimus, non dari praesenti tempore in anima humana lumen internum, immediate docens. II. Quicunque in corde suo densissimas inuenit tenebras, is per introuersionem in intima cordis penetralia non potest illuminari: Atqui gentilis, lumine scripturae destitutus, &c.

E. Minor probatur ex Eph.

V, 8. 18. III. Quaecunque doctrina hominem ab ordinario illuminationis medio auocat, illa in ecclesia orthodoxa non est toleranda: Atqui doctrina mysticorum, de introuersione in cor, ad expectandum & obseruandum lumen internum &c.

E. Minor probatur: quia ordinarium illuminationis medium est S. scriptura, 2 Petr. I, 19. Ad hoc lumen externum oculos corporis & mentis conuertere debet peccator illuminandus.

IV. Qua opinione enthusiasmus in ecclesiam inuehitur, illa a nobis fit aliena: Atqui opinione de introuersione in cor, ad expectandum lumen internum &c. E. Maior confirmatur ex epitome Form.

Conc. p 581.; Reiicimus etiam, damnamusque Enthusiastarum errorem, qui fingunt, Deum immediate absque verbo Dei auditu, & sacramentorum usu homines ad se rapere, illuminare, iustificare & saluare. Atqui mystici, conuertentes animum in intima cordis fundum, volunt immediate illuminari. V.

Abstractio ab omnibus creaturis est impia: E. pio christiano indecora. Antecedens liquet: quia etiam humana Christi natura, S. scriptura, ratione materialis fui litterarum & syllabarum, atque sacramenta, respectu elementorum externorum, sunt e censu creaturarum. VI. Resignatio mystica tum cultui diuino, tum rationali hominis naturae aduersatur: E.

Christianum dedecet. Antecedens patet: quia Deus cultum postulat non ἄλογον, sed λογικὸν, seu rationalem, non ἀπαθῆ, affectibus destitutum, sed παθητικὸν, affectibus piis ardentem, Rom. XII, 2. 11. At resignatio mysticorum est exspoliatio omnium sensuum, cogitationum & affectuum, atque commutat hominem in truncum, fana ratione carentem.

ΔΙΑΛΥΣΙΣ

Obiiciunt aduersarii: I. Descensus in animum verbo diuino praecipitur, Es.

XLVI, 8. Atqui descensus in animum est introuersio animi in seipsum. E. Resp. Descensus in animum qui eo fine fit, vt homo immediate illuminetur, verbo diuino praecipitur; nego.

In loco citato intelligitur descensus in animum commemoratiuus peccatorum & miseriae. II. Abnegatio sui est praecepta, Matth.

XVI, 24. Abstractio ab omnibus externis est abnegatio sui. E. Resp. Neg. Min. Nam abnegatio sui est actus voluntatis, quo nostrum honorem & commodum gloriae diuinae postponimus.

At abstractio est actus intellectus, quo mentem a consideratione omnium creaturarum abstrahunt Mystici. III. Quorum est, seipsos tentare & probare, illos oportet conuertere animum in seipsum.

Atqui Christianorum est &c. 2 Cor. XIII, 5. Resp. Quorum est tentare & probare seipsos, Resp.

Quorum est tentare & probare seipsos, eum cum in finem, ut illuminentur, & regenerentur, illorum est convertere animam in seipsum; concedo. At veri Christiani non sunt illuminandi, aut regenerandi, sed sunt illuminati & regenerati, adeoque δοκιμασία illorum non est medium illuminationis & regenerationis, sed ab illuminatis & renatis eo fine instituitur, ut certiores reddantur, se habere veram vivamque fidem. Idcirco, instituto intra seipsos examine, fidem suam ad verbi divini obrussam exigunt, num requisitas in eo conditiones, partes, virtutesque præstet, verisque fidei vivæ fructibus se exserat? Quam ob rem δοκιμασία Christianorum, a Pythagorica ἐπιστροφῇ εἰς ἑαυτὸν longissime differt. Illa est hominis illuminati; hæc hominis illuminandi. Illa fit secundum verbum Dei externum; hæc obseruat lumen internum & immediatum. Illa, fit actu mentis reflexo, quo homo se reflectit supra cognitionem suam, & cognoscit, se vere Deum cognoscere, & in ipsum credere; hæc fit actu mentis directo, qui est quasi aditus & via ad Deum cognoscendum.

IV. Quicunque est templum Dei, ille potest se convertere in intimum cordis fundum, ad quærendum Deum in se habitantem: At vero Christianus &c. E.

Maiorem confirmat MICHAEL DE MOLINOS, libr. I. manud. spirit. c. III. p. 52. ex soliloquiis AVGVSTINI Deum ita compellantis: Ego, Domine, errabam, ut ouis errabunda, te industrioſo discursu quærens foris, cum esses intra me. Magnopere fatigatus sum, ut quærerem te extra me; tuque habes habitationem tuam intra me, cum ego te desidero & anhelo. Circumibam plateas, & fora ciuitatis huius mundi, quærens te, & non inueniebam te, quia eum frustra quærebam foris, qui erat in me ipso.

Resp. 1) Committitur ignorantia elenchi. Nam quæstio est, an homo peccator illuminetur & regeneretur per conversionem mentis in seipsam. At verus Christianus, qui est templum Dei, iam illuminatus & regeneratus est. 2) Homo viator, actu mentis directo, quærit & inuenit Deum a) in regno naturæ, obseruando lumen naturale insitum, & documenta beneficentia divinæ tam luculenta, vt vel a cæco palpari queant, Act. XVII, 28. b) in regno gratiæ, meditando scripturam, quæ de Christo testatur, Io.

V, 39. & in qua reperiuntur consilium Dei salutiferum, Act. XX, 17. mysteria Dei, propter salutem nostram reuelata, Rom. XVI, 25. & diuitiæ Christi, Eph. III, 8. Actu vero mentis reflexo verus Christianus suam probat fidem, an sit vera & viua? atque adeo inquirit, an per eundem Deus in se habitet? quo b. AVGVSTINVS spectasse videtur.

Quæst. XV. An cum silentio exspectandum est lumen Dei supernaturale & salutiferum? Tantum abest, vt lumen diuinum supernaturale cum silentio sit exspectandum, vt potius verbum Dei externum, quod est lumen clarissimum, serio sit prædicandum, sedulo audiendum, frequenter legendum, attenteque pensitandum, iuxta atque piæ preces, sacris hymnis mixtæ, in cœlum mittendæ sint, quo lux salutifera cognitionis in cordibus nostris suboriatur, & subinde maiora incrementa sumat.

Antithesis est Mysticorum, Weigelianorum, & Quackerorum. Præcipue silentium commendat MOLINOSVS, auctor QVIETISMI, in libr. I. de spirit. manud. c.

XVII. p. 146. inquiens: Triplex silentii genus est. Primum verborum, secundum desideriorum, tertium cogitationum. Primum est perfectum, perfectius secundum, perfectissimum tertium. Primo, quod est verborum, acquiritur virtus: secundo, quod est desideriorum, obtinetur quies: tertio, quod est cogitationum, interior recollectio. Non loquendo, non desiderando, non cogitando peruenitur ad verum & perfectum silentium mysticum, in quo Deus loquitur cum anima, ipsi se communicat, eamque maxime docet in intimo fundo suo perfectissimam, maximeque sublimem sapientiam. Idem silentium urget WEIGELIVS in postill. P. II. p. 230. Es muß alles in eine Stille kommen, soll ich das göttliche Einsprechen hören, oder vernehmen, das ist, soll ich erleuchtet, oder gläubig gemacht werden, so muß ich in mein Kämmerlein gehen, und auf einen Winkel gehen, und in einer Stille auf GOtt warten; welches Warten in einer Stille die buchstäbische Enthusiasterey, oder Schwärmerey heisset.

Quackeri in publicis suis conuentibus amant silentium, quod non diffitetur CATON in simplici inquisitore, p. 8. Quando Quackeri conueniunt, conspectant dominum in lumine suo, interdum ad alteram, tertiamue horam, in silentio.

Nonnunquam tamen, antequam præterlabatur, aliqua domino mouentur, ut plus, minusue dicant, ad ædificationem aliorum, in sanctissima fide. Silentium hoc Quackeri vocant internum animæ sabbathum, de quo GEORG.

KEITHVS, amica resp. ad D. BAIERVM p. 14. scribit: Ab exercitio & vsu verborum scripturæ anima fidelis, sequendo internum suum doctorem Spiritum S. ad tempus in aliud genus nobilioris exercitii & vitæ, tanquam a labore in quietem, & veluti a sextiduo opere in iucundissimum hoc sabbathum diuertit, immo ab omnibus suis exercitiis (tum externis, tum internis, vbi scriptura locum suum habeat præclarum) in hoc otium, sabbathum, & veluti somnum spiritualem cum Iacobo rapitur, vbi videt cælos apertos, & quasi angelos Dei ascendentes, & descendentes. WEIGELIO mire placet hoc sabbathum internum, qui part.

II. postill. p. 86. inquit: Gib dich nach deinem innigen Gebet oftmals in ein Silentium, laß dich GOtt ganz und gar von innen und von außen, komme in ein Vergessen diener selbst, auf daß GOtt Raum und Statt finde zu würken, und dich zu erleuchten. ΕΚΘΕΣΙΣ Obf. I. Cum mystici distinguant inter silentium verborum, cogitationum & desideriorum, nos primum silentium verborum certo approbamus; amant enim meditationes verbi diuini intra priuatos parietes silentium; at silentium desideriorum & cogitationum improbamus.

Obf. II. Veros christianos decet quidem cum silentio coniuncta exspectatio auxilii diuini, non autem tacita exspectatio luminis, immediate reuelantis.

Obf. III. Doctrina de interno animæ sabbatho, quatenus notat 1) cessationem ab operibus carnis, 2) quietem animæ in Deo, 3) meditationem beneficiorum diuinorum, 4) æterni sabbathi desiderium & exspectationem, in ecclesiis nostris retinetur, & inculcatur.

Vid. GERHARD. in schol. pietatis P. III. c. 28. At reiicitur sabbathum internum, quatenus non verborum tantum, sed & omnium cogitationum & sensuum silentium notat.


### Quest. XII: ΒΕΒΑΙΩΣΙΣ (Confirmation)

ΒΕΒΑΙΩΣΙΣ (Confirmation)

We confirm our assertion: 1) It is not for those who are not illuminated by immediate divine revelations to wait, with silence, for the divine light revealing immediately, having set aside external means: But men living in the present time, etc.

Therefore, we have demonstrated the major and minor premises above.

2) It is not for those whose duty it is to meditate day and night in the law, Ps.

I, 2, to hear the word of God attentively, Matt. XI, 15, so that they may conceive faith from it, Rom.

X, 14, to pray always and incessantly, Luke XVIII, 1,

1 Thess. V, 17, to give thanks always for all things, Eph.

V, 20, to converse about divine things, Col. III, 16,

1 Thess. IV, 18, to wait with silence for a supernatural light teaching immediately: But true Christians, etc.

Therefore. 3) By the same reason that the Savior, teaching in person, and his Apostles celebrated sacred assemblies, by that same reason we ought today to institute ecclesiastical assemblies and perform public exercises of piety: But Christ was preaching, Mark

I, 39, with Peter preaching, three thousand auditors were converted, Acts II, 41. The remaining Apostles also applied themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word, Acts VI, 4. Therefore, their assemblies were not silent.

4) Whatever silence excludes both a perennial meditation on God and a perpetual desire for divine grace, that is impious: But the silence of the mystics, etc. Therefore. The major is established: because it is our duty to always meditate on God and to pant for His grace. See Ps. LXIII, 7. Is. XXVI, 8, 9. The minor is proven: because the mystical authors demand of the spiritual man silence not only of words, but also of all desires and thoughts, so that he even interrupts actual cognition of God for a time; BONAVENTURE, citing and approving MOLINOS, l. c. p. 55, teaches that no thing is to be thought of, not even of God Himself; since it is an imperfection to hold forms, images, and species, however subtle they may be, whether of will, or goodness, of trinity and unity, or even of the divine essence itself; since all those species and images, although they may seem deiform, are nevertheless not God Himself, who does not admit any image or form. The same author, l. c. p. 53, adduces THOMAS Aquinas, who persuades the silence of desires: Great blindness, says THOMAS, is in many who always seek God, continually sigh for God, frequently desire God, daily cry out to God in prayer, and knock, when they themselves, according to the word of the Apostle, are the temple of the living God, and God truly dwells in them, since their soul is the seat of God, in which He continually rests.

5) Mystics and Quakers, waiting in silence for an immediately revealing light, cannot escape the mark of Enthusiasm; because they feign that God illuminates men immediately without the hearing of the divine word and the use of the sacraments. Conf. F. Conc. p. 58. D I S S O L U T I O N

Latin:

ΒΕΒΑΙΩΣΙΣ

Affertum nostrum confirmamus: 1) Qui per immediatas reuelationes diuinas non illuminantur, illorum non est, sepositis externis mediis, cum silentio lumen diuinum immediate reuelans exspectare: Atqui homines tempore præsenti viuentes &c.

E. Maiorem & minorem demonstrauimus supra.

2) Quorum est, diu & noctu meditari in lege, Pf.

I, 2. verbum Dei attente audire, Matth. XI, 15. vt fidem ex eo concipiant, Rom.

X, 14. semper & indefinenter orare, Luc. XIIX, 1.

1 Thess. V, 17. gratias agere semper de omnibus, Eph.

V, 20. de rebus diuinis colloqui, Col. III, 16.

1 Thess. IV, 18. illorum non est, lumen supernaturale immediate docens cum silentio exspectare: Atqui verorum christianorum &c.

Ergo. 3) Qua ratione Saluator αὐτοπροσώπως docens, eiusque Apostoli conuentus sacros celebrarunt, eadem ratione hodienum nos oportet conuentus ecclesiasticos instituere, & publica pietatis exercitia peragere: Atqui Christus erat prædicans, Marc.

I, 39. Petro concionante, ter mille auditores convertebantur, Act. II, 41. Reliqui etiam Apostoli orationi & ministerio verbi incumbebant, Act. VI, 4. E. eorum conuentus non fuerunt muti.

4) Quodcunque silentium tum perennem de Deo cogitationem, tum perpetuum gratiae divinae desiderium excludit, illud est impium: Atqui mysticorum silentium &c. E. Maior constat: quia nostrum est, semper de Deo cogitare, eiusque gratiam anhelare. Vid. Ps. LXIII, 7. Es. XXVI, 8. 9. Minor prob. quia auctores mystici ab homine spirituali exigunt silentium non solum verborum, verum etiam omnium desideriorum & cogitationum, vt etiam actualem de Deo cognitionem ad tempus intermittat, BONAVENTVRA citante & approbante MOLINOSIO l. c. p. 55. docet, nullam rem cogitandam esse, ne quidem de ipso Deo; cum imperfectio sit, tenere formas, imagines ac species, quam etiam sint subtiles, tam voluntatis, quam bonitatis, trinitatis & unitatis, ipsius etiam essentiae divinae; quando quidem omnes illae species ac imagines, quanquam deiformes videantur, ipsae tamen non sint Deus, qui non admittat imaginem, aut formam ullam. Adducit idem l. c. p. 53. THOMAM Aquinatem, silentium desideriorum suadentem: Magna caecitas, inquit THOMAS, est in multis, qui semper Deum quaerunt, continue ad Deum suspirant, frequenter Deum desiderant, quotidie in oratione ad Deum clamant, & pulsant, cum ipsi secundum verbum Apostoli sint templum Dei vivi, & Deus veraciter habitet in eis, cum anima ipsorum sedes Dei sit, in qua continue requiescit.

5) Non possunt Mystici & Quackeri cum silentio exspectantes lumen immediate revelans, notam Enthusiasmi effugere; quia fingunt, Deum immediate absque verbo diuini auditu, & sacramentorum vsu, homines illuminare. Conf. F. Conc. p. 58. Δ Ι Α Λ Υ Σ Ι Σ


### Quest. XII: D I S S O L U T I O N

D I S S O L U T I O N

X, 39. Therefore an argument can be formed: Whose duty it is to learn in silence, it is his duty to wait for an immediately illuminating light: But it is the duty of a woman, etc. E. Resp. I deny the major. For it is indeed the duty of a woman to learn in silence, by reading or hearing the word of God consigned to letters; which is what Mary of Bethany did, since she is said to have sat at the feet of Jesus, not in some fanatical quiet, but so that she might hear His sermon, l. c. v. 39: But it is not the duty of a woman to wait for illumination immediately in silence.

II. Jeremiah, Lam. III, 26. It is good, he says, to wait with silence for the salvation of God. Therefore, let a man silently wait for the internal illumination of God. Resp. The prophet’s discourse in the cited place is not about a silent expectation of light, but a patient expectation of help.

III. The Apostles were commanded to wait for the promise of the Father, Acts I, 4. Who also, Acts II, 1, are said to have all been in one place, with no one speaking; and then suddenly the Holy Spirit arrived: Therefore, it is the duty of Christians today to wait for the illuminating Holy Spirit with silence. Resp. 1) The example of the Apostles is extraordinary; since they were illuminated by the Holy Spirit immediately, for the purpose of teaching all nations. But just as not all believers ought to be apostles, 1 Cor. XII, 28; so not all are illuminated immediately. 2) The Apostles waited for the promise of the Father not by keeping silence, but by praying and preaching incessantly. Acts I, 14. 15.

Instance: It is not necessary for those who are temples of the living God, and in whom God truly dwells and rests, to continually sigh to God and cry out to God in prayer. For God knows their needs, and speaks in their hearts. Resp. Christ commands us to pray always, Luke XVIII, 1, and Paul persuades us to pray without ceasing, 1 Thess. V, 17. Moreover, to the present God, who inhabits our hearts and is omniscient, we set forth our desires, not

not to inform the omniscience of the most present Deity, but to testify to our faith, that every good and perfect gift descends from the Father of lights, Jas. 1:17.

IV. The friends of Job sat silent for seven days and as many nights. This was a long silent convention, Job 2:13. Cf. Ezra 9:4.

Resp. Job with his friends, and also Ezra, were silent for a time, not suspended by the expectation of light, but struck and stupefied by immense grief, Quest.

Latin:

I. Mulier discat in silentio, 1 Tim. II, 11. 12. Id quod fecit Maria Bethaniensis, Luc.

X, 39. Formari itaque potest argumentum: Cuius est, in silentio discere, illius est exspectare lumen immediate illuminans: Atqui mulieris est &c. E. Resp. Neg. Maior. Nam mulieris quidem est, discere in silentio, verbum Dei litteris consignatum legendo, vel audiendo; id quod fecit Maria Bethaniensis, quippe quae ad pedes Iesu assedisse dicitur, non in fanatica quadam quiete, sed vt audiret sermonem eius l. c. v. 39.: At non est mulieris, immediate in silentio exspectare illuminationem.

II. Ieremias, Thren. III, 26. Bonum est, inquit, exspectare cum silentio salutare Dei. E. homo tacitus exspectet internam Dei illuminationem. Resp. L. c. prophetae sermo est non de tacita exspectatione luminis, sed patienti exspectatione auxilii.

III. Apostolis praecipiebatur, vt exspectarent promissionem Patris, Act. I, 4. Qui etiam Act. II, 1. dicuntur omnes vno loco fuisse, nullo loquente; & tunc repente Spiritus S. aduenit: E. hodienum Christianorum est, cum silentio Spiritum S. illuminantem exspectare. Resp. 1) Exemplum Apostolorum est extraordinarium; siquidem illi a Spiritu S. illuminati sunt immediate, ad docendum omnes gentes. At sicut non omnes fideles debent esse apostoli, 1 Cor. XII, 28.; sic non omnes immediate illuminantur. 2) Apostoli exspectarunt promissionem Patris non silentium tenendo, sed iugiter precando, & concionando. Act. I, 14. 15.

Instantia: Non necesse est, continue ad Deum suspirare, in oratione ad Deum clamare illos, qui sunt templa Dei vivi, & in quibus Deus veraciter habitat & quiescit. Nam Deus nouit illorum necessitates, & in cordibus ipsorum loquitur. Resp. Christus nobis praecipit, vt semper precemur, Luc. XVIII, 1. & Paulus suadet, vt indefinenter oremus, 1 Thess. V, 17. Praesenti autem, corda nostra inhabitanti, & omniscio Deo exponimus desideria nostra, non Thess. V, 17. Præfenti autem, corda nostra inhabitanti, & omniscio Deo exponimus desideria nostra, non

omniscientiam praesentissimi Numinis informaturi, sed fidem nostram testaturi, quod omnia dona bona & perfecta a Patre luminum descendant, Iac. I, 17.

IV. Amici Iobi septem dies, & noctes totidem taciti confidebant. Haec erat longa silens conuentio, Iob. II, 13. Conf. Esdr. IX, 4.

Resp. Iobus cum amicis suis, nec non Esdra, ad tempus silebant, non suspensi expectatione luminis, sed ingenti moerore perculsi & obstupefacti, Quaest.


### Q. XVI. What is the terminus of illumination from which, and to which?

The terminus a quo of illumination is the blindness of the intellect, covered with the darkness of ignorance and errors. The terminus ad quem is the light of saving knowledge.

Prob. a. Men, not illuminated, are darkened in mind, alienated from the life of God, because of the ignorance that is in them, because of the hardening of their heart, Eph. 4:18.

Obs. I. In an unilluminated man there is not only ignorance *kat' apophasin* (by way of negation), of simple negation, but also ignorance *kata diathesin* (by way of disposition), or of a depraved disposition, which is error, contrary to true knowledge; for the reason that the *psychikos*, or natural man, not only does not apprehend the things that are of the Spirit of God; but also judges them to be absurd, 1 Cor. 2:14. Therefore, not only simple ignorance is opposed to saving knowledge, but also the *phronema tes sarkos*, the mind of the flesh, Rom. 8:6, and the wisdom of this world, 1 Cor. 1:20. For the world has its own wisdom, but immersed in the darkness of arrogance, so that it may exalt itself against divine wisdom, 2 Cor. 10:4.

II. The innate and affected ignorance of the intellect is followed by the impiety of life and *porosis*, or the hardening of the will.

Prob. b. Through the law comes the knowledge of sin, Rom. 3:20. From the gospel proceeds the knowledge of the glorious grace of God in the unveiled face of Jesus Christ, 2 Cor. 4:6. This knowledge is accompanied by assent, by which the illuminated man holds as certain and indubitable all that which has been revealed in the word of God, and especially the gospel concerning the remission of sins and eternal salvation to be obtained through Christ: Which indubitable assent is called *elenchos*, the conviction of the intellect, Heb. 11:1.

Quest. XVII. In what, therefore, does illumination formally consist?

Divine illumination formally consists in the information of the Holy Spirit through the divine word read or preached, not only externally, but also internally, and effectively penetrating the innermost recesses of the human heart, so that the darkness of ignorance and errors may be expelled from it, and the light of supernatural knowledge may be infused into it.

Prob. 1) Because God ordinarily illuminates the sinful man, brought to the church, through the ministry of the word. This is evident from Eph. 3:8-9: To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given, that I should preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, and enlighten all. Paul enlightened the Gentiles, not by immediately infusing the light of knowledge into them, but by informing them through the preaching of the gospel. Whence H. GROTIUS, commenting on the cited passage, explains: *photizein*, [Hebrew word], is to teach.

2) From Ps. 119:130: The hearing of your words gives light: It makes the simple understand. Explaining these words, D. GEIER says: The preceding figurative expression is explained by its proper voice, "gives light." For [Hebrew word], taken transitively, signifies "made to understand," "instructed." Therefore, to illuminate is the same as to instruct, and illuminating grace is teaching, as DANNHAV. says in *Hodof. phanom.*

IX. p. 938. Furthermore, when we describe illumination as information, we do not understand it as merely external, which is done by the tongue or pen of a minister of the church, but also as internal, by which the Holy Spirit, by His special and gracious concurrence, in the hearts of the hearers or readers who do not maliciously resist, kindles the light of supernatural wisdom through the divine word preached or read. Illumination is therefore an internal information of the Holy Spirit, but not immediate; because it does not exclude the external ministry, but graciously concurs with it, and being inseparably united with the word preached and read, it communicates to the same the power of penetrating and illuminating hearts.

Latin:

Terminus illuminationis a quo, est caecitas intellectus, oppleti tenebris ignorantiae & errorum . Terminus ad quem, est lux salutaris cognitionis .

Prob. a. Homines, non illuminati, sunt obscurati mente, alienati a vita Dei, propter ignorantiam, quae est in illis, propter obdurationem cordis ipsorum, Eph. IV, 18.

Obs. I. In homine non illuminato non datur tantum ignorantia κατ' ἀπόφασιν, simplicis negationis, sed etiam ignorantia κατὰ διάθεσιν, seu prauae dispositionis, quae est error, verae scientiae contrarius; eo, quod homo ψυχικός, siue animalis, non tantum non apprehendit, ea, quae sunt Spiritus Dei; sed iudicat etiam ea esse absurda, 1 Cor. I, 14. Opponitur itaque salutari notitiae non solum ignorantia simplex, sed etiam φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς, prudentia carnis, Rom. VIII, 6. & sapientia huius mundi, 1 Cor. I, 20. Habet enim mundus suam sapientiam, sed tenebris arrogantiae immersam, vt sese contra sapientiam diuinam efferat, 2 Cor. X, 4.

II. Ignorantiam intellectus connatam, & affectatam, sequitur vitae impietas, & πώρωσις, seu obduratio voluntatis.

Prob. b. Ex lege est agnitio peccati, Rom. III, 20. Ex euangelio proficiscitur agnitio gloriosae gratiae Dei in retecta facie Iesu Christi, 2 Cor. IV, 6. Quam cognitionem comitatur assensus, quo homo illuminatus cum id omne, quod in verbo Dei patefactum est, tum inprimis euangelium de remissione peccatorum & aeterna salute, per Christum impetranda, pro certo & indubitato habet: Qui assensus indubitatus vocatur ἔλεγχος, conuictio intellectus, Hebr. XI, 1.

Quaest. XVII. In quo igitur formaliter consistit illuminatio?

Illuminatio diuina formaliter consistit in informatione Spiritus Sancti per verbum diuinum lectum, aut praedicatum, non tantum externa, sed etiam interna, & efficaciter penetrante intimos recessus cordis humani, vt ex eo tenebrae ignorantiae & errorum expellantur, & lumen supernaturalis cognitionis ipsi infundatur.

Prob. 1) Quia Deus hominem peccatorem, ad ecclesiam perductum, ordinarie illuminat per ministerium verbi. Id quod patet ex Eph. III, 8. 9. Mihi, minimo omnium sanctorum, data est gratia haec, vt inter gentes euangelizarem inuestigabiles diuitias Christi, & illuminarem omnes. Illuminauit Paullus gentes, non immediate lumen notitiae ipsis infundendo, sed per praedicationem euangelii eas informando. Vnde H. GROTIVS ad locum citatum exponendum commentatur: φωτίζειν, הָאִיר, est docere.

2) E Ps. CXIX, 130. Auditus verborum tuorum illuminat: Intelligentes reddit simplices. Quae verba explanaturus D. GEIERVS inquit: Voce propria exponitur praecedens figurata, illuminat. Nam הָאִיר, tranfitiue sumtum, significat, intelligere fecit, instruxit. Ergo illuminare idem est, quod instruere, & gratia illuminatrix est docens, dicente DANNHAV. in hodof. phanom.

IX. p. 938. Ceterum quando illuminationem describimus per informationem, non intelligimus tantum externam, quæ fit lingua, aut calamo ministri ecclesiæ, sed etiam internam, qua Spiritus S. concursu suo speciali ac gratioso, in cordibus auditorum, vel lectorum, malitiose non obsistentium, per verbum divinum prædicatum, aut lectum, lucem supernaturalis sapientiæ accendit. Est igitur illuminatio informatio Spiritus S. interna, sed non immediata; quia ministerium externum non excludit, sed cum eodem gratiose concurrit, & cum verbo prædicato & lecto indiuulse vnitus, eidem vim penetrandi & illuminandi corda communicat.


### Question XVIII

Is the illumination of a sinner, called to the church, completed in one moment? Ordinary illumination is not completed in one moment, but occurs through intervals of time, through degrees, through acts often repeated, so that man may be disposed and prepared successively to admit the greater light of truth by and by, so that, if he rejects the first degree of illumination, the Holy Spirit may deny the second to him; for it cannot have a place without the first.

Obj. I. Our discourse is concerning ordinary illumination, not extraordinary. That God, by singular and extraordinary grace, and by absolute power, can fully illuminate a man in one moment, so that he may have all articles of faith known, we doubt not: since it is certain to us that the Holy Spirit infused the gift of tongues to the Apostles in one moment, Acts

II. Obs. II. Nor do we here treat of the illumination of infants by baptism, which the Greek Fathers called φωτισμὸν [illumination], since the manner by which the light of knowledge and saving faith is kindled by the Holy Spirit in infants through baptism can neither be comprehended nor explained by us, as CHEMNITIUS says, in Exam. Conc. Trid. fol. m. 247. We assert that the ordinary illumination of adult men is not instantaneous, but successive.

Proof 1) Every instantaneous action is irresistible: But the ordinary illumination of adult men is not irresistible: Therefore. The major is clear; because no impediment can be opposed to an instantaneous action, e.g., Creation is an instantaneous action, since nothing can hinder it. The minor is evident; because men of stiff neck resist the Holy Spirit, Acts VII, 51. They resist the ray of light by which they are to be penetrated. They do not turn their mind, but close their intellect.

2) The nature of the seed and the intention of the sower is that not only the herb should sprout, but also that after the herb the ear, and after the ear the full corn in it should grow, Mark IV, 28. Thus God, sowing the good seed through His ministers into the hearts of men, ordinarily and always intends to confer upon the hearers a more intense degree of grace, even unto completion.

3) When Christ had finished His discourse concerning the efficacious operation of the divine word by the institution of God, but with a diverse effect according to the diversity of the hearers, He exclaimed with a loud voice: Take heed how you hear! For whoever has [receives and retains the first degree of illumination], to him shall be given [a further and more intense degree of light]: but whoever has not [does not receive and retain a more intense degree of knowledge], even what he thinks he has [of the first degree of illumination] shall be taken away from him [by the judicial will of God]. Luke VIII, 18. Thus illumination occurs not in an instant, but by degrees. Cf. the brief enucleation of HULSEMANN, ch. VIII, p.

456. 4) The gradual and successive illumination of adult men is most clearly evident from practice. A minister of the church, about to convert a Jew, strives with all effort and study to illuminate him. a) He teaches that the Messiah has already come: b) He demonstrates that this Messiah is not a mere man, but true God and the Son of God the Father, begotten from eternity: c) He convinces that this Messiah

that Jesus of Nazareth, the son of the virgin Mary, is the Messiah and the God-man: d) Having obtained the duality of the divine persons, he proves that the Holy Spirit is also the true God: e) He instills into the Jew the doctrine concerning the priestly, prophetic, and kingly office of Christ: f) He shows that, on our part, true faith is required to obtain the remission of sins and eternal life, apprehending the satisfaction of Christ: g) He inculcates to him that justifying faith manifests itself through the holiness of life. Therefore, the Jew is not illuminated in one moment; but through intervals of time, by degrees, and by repeated acts. But if it should happen that the Jew stubbornly resists the final act of information, by the just judgment of God even the previous degrees of light will be taken away from him.

Quest. XIX.

What is the end of illumination? The proximate end of illumination is the conversion and regeneration of the sinner a). The ultimate end, on our part, is immediate illumination, to be obtained in the kingdom of glory b). The ultimate end, on the part of God, is the glory of the divine illuminating grace c).

Proof a. For this end, through the ministry of the word, the eyes of sinful men are opened, that they may turn themselves from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God, Acts XXVI, 18. Proof b.

Proof b. The servants of God (who have been spiritually illuminated in this life) shall serve Him (in the city of God), they shall see His face, and His name shall be on their foreheads: And there shall be no night there, and they need no lamp nor light of the sun; for the Lord God illuminates them, Rev. XXII, 4, 5.

I, 12. Thanks are to be given to the most merciful Father, who, when we were by nature blind and inept for every good, made us fit for the participation of the heavenly inheritance promised to the saints, through the evangelical light, by which He kindles the light of saving knowledge in this age, intending to bestow a more brilliant light in the future age.

SIGH

Praise thy God, O my soul! with whom is the fountain of spiritual life, which all faithful souls live, tasting the sweetness of the divine goodness. Therefore they rejoice wondrously, because, O God, author of light, in Thy light they see light, while they are advanced from grace to grace. Through the light of Thy revealed word they reach the light of faith, through the light of faith they aspire to the light of glory. Shine forth, O Jesus, most splendid morning star, in my soul! Expel from it the mist of ignorance! Dispel the darkness of vices! Pour forth a clearer light of knowledge, a purer light of holiness, so that, having beheld Thee through the mirror of the word in the way of this life, I may one day see Thee face to face in the heavenly fatherland!

Latin:

Illuminatio ordinaria non absoluitur vno momento, sed fit per temporum interualla, per gradus, per actus sæpe repetitos, vt homo disponatur ac præparetur successiue. ad maiorem subinde veritatis lucem admittendam, adeo, vt, si primum illuminationis gradum repellat, alterum ipsi Spiritus S. deneget; quippe qui sine primo locum habere nequit.

Obs. I. Sermo nobis est de illuminatione ordinaria, non de extraordinaria. Quin Deus gratia singulari & extraordinaria, potentiaque absoluta, vno momento plene illuminare possit hominem, vt omnes articulos fidei cognitos habeat, nulli dubitamus: cum nobis constet, quod Spiritus S. donum linguarum Apostolis vno momento infuderit, Act.

II. Obs. II. Non etiam hic agimus de illuminatione infantum per baptismum, quem græci Patres φωτισμὸν vocarunt, cum modus, quo per baptismum lux agnitionis & fidei salutificæ a Spiritu S. in infantibus accenditur, a nobis nec comprehendi, nec explicari possit, dicente CHEMNITIO, in exam. Conc. Trid. fol. m. 247. Ordinariam hominum adultorum illuminationem non esse instantaneam, sed successiuam, afferimus.

Prob. 1) Omnis actio instantanea est irresistibilis: Sed ordinaria hominum adultorum illuminatio non est irresistibilis: E. Maior est clara; quia actioni instantaneæ nullum obiici potest impedimentum, v. gr. Creatio est actio instantanea, quoniam eam nihil sufflaminare potest. Minor liquet; quia Spiritui S. homines duræ ceruicis resistunt, Act. VII, 51. Resistunt radio lucis, quo penetrandi sunt. Non aduertunt animum, sed claudunt mentem.

2) Seminis natura & feminatoris intentio est, vt non solum herba propullulet, sed etiam vt post herbam spica, post spicam plenum in ea frumentum enascatur, Marc. IV, 28. Ita Deus bonum semen per ministros suos in corda hominum spargens, ordinarie ac semper intendit intensiorem gratiæ gradum, vsque ad complementum, auditoribus conferre.

3) Quando Christus de verbi diuini operatione efficaci ex instituto Dei, effectu vero diuerso, pro diuersitate auditorum, sermonem finiuerat, exclamauit voce magna: Videte, quomodo audiatis? Quisquis enim habet (recipit & retinet primum illuminationis gradum), ei dabitur (vlterior & intensior lucis gradus): qui vero non habet (non recipit ac retinet intensiorem notitiæ gradum), etiam quod putat se habere, (de primo illuminationis gradu) auferetur ab eo (voluntate Dei iudiciaria). Luc. VIII, 18. Fit itaque illuminatio non in instanti, sed per gradus. Conf. d. HVLSEMANNI breu. enucl. c. VIII. p. 456.

4) Gradualis & successiua hominum adultorum illuminatio clarissime patescit e praxi. Minister ecclesiæ, conuerfurus Iudæum, omni conatu & studio eundem illuminare annititur. a) Docet Messiam iam venisse: b) Demonstrat, hunc Messiam non esse nudum hominem, sed verum Deum Filiumque Dei Patris, ab æterno genitum: c) Conuincit, hunc

Messiam & θεάνθρωπον esse Iesum Nazarenum, filium virginis Mariae: d) Obtenta personarum divinarum dualitate, probat, Spiritum S. etiam esse verum Deum: e) Instillat Iudaeo doctrinam de officio Christi sacerdotali, prophetico, & regio: f) Ostendit, ex parte nostri ad remissionem peccatorum & vitam aeternam consequendam requiri veram fidem, apprehendentem satisfactionem Christi: g) Inculcat ipsi, fidem iustificantem se exferere per sanctimoniam vitae. Proinde illuminatur Iudaeus non uno momento; sed per temporum intervalla, per gradus, per actus repetitos. Quod si contigerit, ut Iudaeus ultimo informationis actui praefracte obstiterit, iusto Dei iudicio etiam priores lucis gradus ei auferentur.

Quaest. XIX.

Quis est finis illuminationis? Finis proximus illuminationis est conversio & regeneratio peccatoris a). Finis ultimus, ex parte nostri, est illuminatio immediata, in regno gloriae obtinenda b). Finis ultimus, ex parte Dei, est gloria gratiae divinae illuminatricis c).

Prob. a. Eo fine per ministerium verbi aperiuntur oculi hominum peccatorum, ut convertant se, a tenebris ad lucem, & e potestate Satanae ad Deum, Act. XXVI, 18.

Prob. b. Servi Dei (qui in hac vita spiritualiter illuminati fuerunt) ministrabunt illi (in civitate Dei), videbunt faciem eius, & nomen eius erit in frontibus ipsorum: Et nox non erit ibi, neque opus habent lucerna & luce solis; quia Dominus Deus illustrat illos, Apoc. XXII, 4. 5.

Prob. c. Gratias agite Patri, qui idoneos fecit nos in partem fortis sanctorum in luce, Col. I, 12. Agendae sunt gratiae Patri misericordissimo, qui nos, natura caecos, & ad omne bonum ineptos, ad participationem hereditatis coelestis, sanctis promissae, idoneos fecit, per lumen evangelicum, quo lumen salutiferae cognitionis in hoc saeculo accendit, in futuro saeculo lucem fulgentiorem largiturus.

SUSPIRIUM

Collauda anima mea Deum tuum! quem penes est fons vitae spiritualis, quam vivunt omnes fideles animae, suavitatem bonitatis divinae degustantes. Proinde mirifice laetantur, quod, o Deus, auctor lucis, in tuo lumine vident lumen, dum de gratia in gratiam provehuntur. Per lumen verbi tui revelati pertingunt ad lumen fidei, per lumen fidei adspirant ad lumen gloriae. Illucefce, o Iesu, phosphore splendidissime, in anima mea! Expelle ex eadem caliginem ignorantiae! Discute tenebras vitiorum! Affunde lucem clariorem notitiae, puriorem sanctimoniae, vt per speculum verbi in via huius vitae conspicatus, aliquando videam te a facie ad faciem in patria coelesti!


## 21 On Converting Grace, and Conversion


### Quest. I

Whether conversion is taken here in a transitive or intransitive sense? Conversion is taken in the present instance in a transitive sense, and denotes an act of grace by which the Holy Spirit is said to convert the sinner, and the sinner is said to be converted a).

Intransitively taken conversion signifies an immanent and reciprocal act of the will, by which a sinner is denominated to convert himself . Prob. a. Since at present we are engaged in unfolding the acts of divine grace that applies itself, it is easily evident that we are not here considering the intransitive conversion of the sinner, or his repentance, by design.

Moreover, that gracious action by which God converts the sinner is not inappropriately called transitive conversion, in that it does not terminate in God the agent himself, but passes from Him into another subject, namely, into the human sinner: To this action corresponds a passion, by which the sinner, not stubbornly rejecting but passively admitting and receiving the converting grace, is said to be converted by the Lord according to that saying in Jeremiah ch.

XXXI, 28. Convert me, O Lord, and I shall be converted.

God converts actively, the sinner is passively converted by God; but the active conversion of God and the passive conversion of the sinner are, as to the thing itself, one and the same conversion; which, when the agent God is connoted, and insofar as it proceeds from Him, is called active; when the subject, or man, is connoted, and insofar as it is received by him, it is called passive.

Prob. b. Intransitive conversion is the terminus and effect of transitive conversion, and it is repentance itself, by which a sinner, through powers conferred by converting grace and received in small measure, is said to convert himself, just as a ship is said to turn itself not by its own powers, but by the powers of the sailors. But the sinner's repentance is rightly called intransitive conversion; for this reason, that it does not pass into another subject, but is terminated in the sinner himself. Concerning intransitive conversion, the words of Peter are worth noting, Acts III, 19. Repent, and convert yourselves, that your sins may be blotted out. For which reason the sinner, by doing penance, converts himself by powers not native, but given.

Latin:

Utrum conversio hic fumitur significatu transitivo, an intransitivo? Conversio in praesenti sumitur significatu transitivo, & notat actum gratiae, quo Spiritus S. peccatorem convertere, & peccator converti dicitur a).

Intransitiue accepta conuersio significat actum voluntatis immanentem & reciprocum, quo peccator seipsum conuertere denominatur . Prob. a. Cum in praesentiarum versemur in actibus diuinae gratiae applicatricis euoluendis, ex facili patet..., nos hic nondum ex professo considerare intransitiuam peccatoris conuersionem, siue ipsius resipiscentiam.

Ceterum gratiosa illa actio, qua Deus peccatorem conuertit, haud incommode dicitur conuersio transitiua, eo, quod non in ipso agente Deo terminatur, sed ab ipso in aliud subiectum, nempe in hominem peccatorem transit: Cui actioni respondet passio, qua peccator gratiam conuertentem morose non reiiciens, sed passiue admittens & recipiens a domino conuerti dicitur iuxta illud Ieremiae cap.

XXXI, 28. Conuerte me, domine, & conuertar.

Deus actiue conuertit, peccator passiue a Deo conuertitur; sed conuersio actiua Dei, & passiua peccatoris, quoad rem, vna eademque conuersio est; quae cum connotato agente Deo, & quatenus ab eo procedit, actiua; cum connotato subiecto, siue homine, & quatenus ab illo recipitur, passiua appellatur.

Prob. b. Conversio intransitiva est terminus et effectus conversionis transitivae, estque ipsa poenitentia, qua peccator per vires, a gratia convertente collatas, et paullue receptas, seipsum convertere dicitur, sicut navis se vertere dicitur non viribus propriis, sed viribus nautarum. Recte autem peccatoris resipiscentia vocatur conversio intransitiva; ideo, quod non in aliud transit subiectum, sed in ipso peccatore terminatur. De conversione intransitiva notari merentur verba Petri, Act. III, 19. Agite poenitentiam, et convertite vos, ut deleantur peccata vestra. Quam ob rem peccator, poenitentiam agendo, se convertit viribus non nativis, sed dativis.


### Q. II. In how many senses is transitive conversion understood?

Transitive conversion, by which God converts the sinner, is taken in a general, special, and most special sense.

Latin:

Conversio transitiva, qua Deus peccatorem convertit, sumitur sensu generali, speciali et specialissimo.


### Q. III. What divine action is denoted by general conversion?

Transitive conversion, by which the sinner is converted by God, taken in a general sense, embraces in its scope illumination, turning away from sin, regeneration, justification, and renewal.

Prob. It is taken in the general meaning of conversion in the Solid Declaration of the Formula of Concord, p. 675. This is most certain, that in true conversion there must occur a change, renewal, and movement in man's intellect, will, and heart; so that, namely, man's mind may acknowledge sins, fear the wrath of God, turn itself away from sin, acknowledge and apprehend the promise of grace in Christ, stir up pious thoughts in the mind, have a good purpose, and apply diligence in regenerating his own morals, and fight against the flesh. For where none of these things happens, there is without doubt no true conversion to God. But since the question is about the efficient cause, that is, who it is that works these things in us, whence man has this very thing, and how he can attain it: This pious doctrine shows the source of these goods, namely in this way. Since man's natural powers can contribute nothing to true conversion, nor bring any help, God in His ineffable goodness and mercy prevents us, and takes care that the gospel (through which the Holy Spirit wills to work and perfect conversion and regeneration in us) be announced. And through the preaching and meditation of His word, He kindles faith and other virtues of piety in us. Most theologians abstain from this broader meaning of conversion, since from the same, confusion and error can easily creep into incautious minds; inasmuch as in this way distinct acts of grace are joined together by one word.

Latin:

Conversio transitiva, qua a Deo peccator convertitur, sensu generali sumta, ambitu suo complectitur illuminationem, aversionem a peccato, regenerationem, iustificationem et renovationem.

Prob. Conversionis significatu generali sumitur in solida declar. Form. conc. p. 675. Hoc certissimum est, in vera conversione immutationem, renovationem, et motum fieri oportere in hominis intellectu, voluntate et corde; ut nimirum hominis mens peccata agnoscat, iram Dei metuat, a peccato sese avertat, promissionem gratiae in Christo agnoscat, et apprehendat, pias cogitationes animo agitet, bonum propositum habeat, atque diligentiam in moribus suis regenerandis adhibeat, et contra carnem pugnet. Ubi enim nihil horum fit, ibi procul dubio non est vera ad Deum conversio. Cum autem quaestio sit de causa efficiente, hoc est, quisnam haec in nobis operetur, unde homo hoc ipsum habeat, et quomodo id consequi possit: Haec pia doctrina ostendit horum bonorum fontem, hoc videlicet modo. Cum naturales hominis vires ad veram conversionem nihil conferre, aut quidquam adiuventi adferre possint, Deus ineffabili bonitate et misericordia nos praevenit, et evangelion (per quod Spiritus S. conversionem, et regenerationem in nobis operari, et perficere vult) annuntiari curat. Et per verbi sui praedicationem et meditationem, fidem aliasque pietatis virtutes in nobis accendit. Abstinent ab hoc latiori conversionis significatu plerique Theologi, cum ex eodem incautis mentibus facile confusio et error obrepere queat; siquidem sic una voce distincti actus gratiae coniunguntur.


### Q. IV. What is transitive conversion, taken in a special meaning?

Transitive conversion, taken in a special sense, is an act of grace by which the Holy Spirit excites in the sinful man serious sorrow for sins through the word of the law, but through the word of the gospel kindles true faith in Christ, so that he may obtain the remission of sins and eternal salvation. Obs.

I. The terminus a quo of conversion, taken in a special sense, is the state of sin, which is the most miserable condition of the sinner, who has neither morally retracted sin, nor obtained pardon, or remission of sin: The terminus ad quem is the state of faith, which is the better condition of the sinner, who indeed seriously detests his sins with sorrow of soul, but flees to Christ, the sole mediator of God and men, and apprehends His merit and satisfaction,

Latin:

Conversio transitiva, sensu speciali sumta, est actus gratiae, quo Spiritus S. in homine peccatore serium de peccatis dolorem verbo legis excitat, verbo evangelii autem veram in Christum fidem accendit, vt remissionem peccatorum aeternamque salutem consequatur.

Obs. I. Conversionis, sensu speciali acceptae, terminus a quo est status peccati, qui est miserrima conditio peccatoris, qui neque peccatum moraliter retractavit, neque veniam, sive remissionem peccati, impetravit: Terminus ad quem est status fidei, qui est melior conditio peccatoris, qui peccata sua serio cum animi dolore detestatur quidem, ad Christum vero, unicum mediatorem Dei et hominum, confugit, eius meritum et satisfactionem apprehendit,


### Question V. Prob. 1) The strictest meaning of conversion is conformable to scripture, inasmuch as it is accustomed to call that act, by…

it, and to God, the most just judge, as a ransom (ἀντίλυτρον) for his own sins and those of the whole world, he presents it most validly, and, raised up by trust in Him, he seeks from Him the forgiveness of sins.

Obs. II. The medium of conversion, taken in a special sense, is the divine word, and that both the word of the law, by which contrition is excited, and the word of the gospel, by which faith in Christ the mediator is kindled.

Obs. III. Regeneration is commonly held to be a synonym for conversion when spoken of specifically.

However, D. Koenigius observed in his Theol. posit., Part III, § 451, that there is some difference between conversion and regeneration. According to his opinion, these two differ:

1) by reason of the subjects: for regeneration is of adults and infants; but conversion is at least of adults; since infants are indeed said to be regenerated, but not as commonly said to be converted (unless one perhaps wishes, with the blessed Dannhauer, to attribute to them some analogy (ἀνάλογόν τι) of conversion and repentance. See Hodof., p. 1269): 2) by reason of the media: regeneration is done through the word and sacraments, conversion through the word alone. One could add: 3) conversion is done through the law and the gospel; regeneration only through the gospel.

The special acceptance of conversion is proven: 1) because God, opening the eyes of sinners through the ministry of the word (illuminating them), converts them from darkness to light, Acts 26: 18. Where by darkness we do not precisely understand the ignorance of the mind, nor by light knowledge, so that a fuller description of illumination might be exhibited in those words; for the reason that the tables of the Pauline vocation, succinctly delineated, do not admit of redundancy (περισσολογίαν), but rather by darkness (σκότος) are designated the works of darkness, Rom. 13:12, Eph. 5:11; but by light is denoted the light of faith, which not rarely comes in the sacred scriptures under the name of light, Matt. 5:16, Eph. 5:8, 1 John 2:9, 11, and believers are called children of light, Luke 16:8, John 12:36, 1 Thess. 5:5.

Conversion is therefore transitive, and specifically so called, by which God converts the sinner, an act of grace by which the Holy Spirit turns the sinner away from the works of darkness, by working a detestation of sins, and suffuses him with the light of faith. Prob. 2) Man is converted so that his sins may be blotted out, Acts 11:19. And to the Gentiles God gives repentance unto life, Acts 11:18. Therefore, through converting grace, besides active contrition, faith in Christ is conferred, without which neither the remission of sins nor any spiritual life is obtained.

Question V.

Prob. 1) The strictest meaning of conversion is conformable to scripture, inasmuch as it is accustomed to call that act, by which the heart of the sinner is crushed, conversion.

Thus the Israelite people pray:

Convert me, O Lord, and I shall be converted (by passive conversion): for after I have been converted (passively), I will do penance (taken as μετάνοια, for contrition), and after it has offended me, I struck my thigh: I am ashamed and blushed (lo! still an act of contrition) because I have borne the reproach of my youth, Jer. 31:19. And God, exhorting the Israelites to repentance, says: Be converted to me with all your heart, and in fasting, and in weeping and mourning. So that you may rend your hearts, and not your garments: So (I say) be converted to the Lord your God, Joel 2:12, 13.

2) Just as one act of applying grace is that by which God works contrition, and another act of grace is that by which He grants to the contrite sinner confidence, leaning upon the merit of Christ: so the former act is conveniently called conversion (taken in the strictest sense), and the latter act of grace is called regeneration. God converts the sinner through the law; He regenerates through the gospel. Contrition is the effect of converting grace; faith is the effect of regenerating grace. Repentance, taken *ἐκλῶς* [in a broad sense] (consisting of contrition and faith), is the effect of both acts of grace, namely, of conversion and regeneration, flowing together to produce one *ἀποτέλεσμα* [result]. For repentance is indeed a divine *ἀποτέλεσμα*. Nor is it properly a virtue or a habit, but an act, composed of contrition and faith, and therefore an *ἀποτέλεσμα*, a salutary theriac against the plague of sin, as D. DANNHAV. says, *hodof.* p. 1265.

3) In the order of nature, conversion precedes, and regeneration follows; Scripture retains this order, while it describes conversion through the removal of the heart of stone, but regeneration through the bestowing of a heart of flesh, Ezek. XI, 19; ch. XXXVI, 26. It expresses the former through the rending of the heart, Joel II, 13; Ps. LI, 19, but the latter through the healing of the broken heart in the prophetic style, Is. LXI, 1.

4) Practice itself shows this order of the acts of grace. God, most wise, having converted the fallen first parents of the human race, preached the law to them, so that, struck by this thunderbolt, they might tremble and grieve: to the fearful and contrite He preached the gospel, so that He might regenerate and justify them, Gen. III, 7, 8, ff. The listeners of Peter, having heard the apostolic sermon, were pricked in their heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the Apostles: "What shall we do, men and brethren?" (behold the grace of conversion through the law!) Peter says to them: "Repent" (behold the active contrition, which followed passive conversion!), "and let every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ" (by which words regeneration through baptism is expressed), "for the remission of sins" (thus justification immediately follows regeneration). Acts II, 38.

5) The Formula of Concord accurately distinguishes the converting and regenerating grace of God, p. 662. Man is illuminated, converted, and regenerated by the Holy Spirit. And p. 681: The intellect and will of man, not yet reborn, are only the subject to be converted. For they are the intellect and will of a man spiritually dead, in which man the Holy Spirit works conversion and renewal. To which work the will of the man being converted contributes nothing: but he suffers, so that God may work in him (now regeneration follows as the terminus of conversion) until he is regenerated. In this strictest signification, D. CARPZOV. in *isagog.* p. 1244, B. HOEPFNERVS *loc. theol.* p. 451, and D. NEVMANN in *disput. de nexu & discrimine donorum gratiæ* §. 13, use the word "conversion."

You say: Conversion through the law is not an act of grace, but of vindictive justice, for the reason that the law works wrath, Rom. IV, 15. I reply: The law, in itself good and holy, works wrath because of the fault of men who transgress the precepts of the law, by accusing and condemning their sins; but this operation of the law is directed by the most merciful God toward a salutary end for man. D. IO. MVSÆVS teaches this excellently in *disput. II. de convers. c. III.*, Iena edition, p. 80. The law is a certain organ of divine grace, working in the sinful man, softening his hard heart, preparing and disposing him for faith, to be kindled in him by the voice of the gospel.

Quest. VI. How manifold is conversion? Conversion is twofold: ordinary and extraordinary. The former is that by which God, through the medium of the word of the law, in the usual manner and way, leads the sinful man to the detestation of sins a). The latter is that by which God, either immediately or through miracles, so strikes the sinner that he seriously grieves for the sins he has committed b).

Prob. a. Ordinarily, God crushes men with the hammer of the law, Jer. XXIII, 29, and he hews them through the Prophets, or ministers of the church, duly called and ordained, Hos. VI, 5; Acts XXVI, 17, 18. Prob. b. Extraordinarily, God converts sinful men, either immediately themselves, or without the intervention of his ministers by speaking: by which manner Abraham was converted, Gen. XII, 1; the thief on the cross, Luke XXIII, 42; Paul, Acts IX, 3, 4: or by accompanying his word and the ministers of the word with miracles and signs, where, however, that power of converting is to be ascribed not to the miracles and signs, but to the divine word. Thus, the miracles which accompanied the death of Christ struck the centurion and others standing by the cross, so that they beat their breasts, Luke XXIII, 48.

Latin:

Deoque, justissimo iudici, tanquam ἀντίλυτρον pro suis & totius mundi peccatis validissimum sistit, atque eius fiducia erectus, ab ipso peccatorum veniam petit.

Obs. II. Medium conversionis, sensu speciali acceptae, est verbum divinum, idque cum verbum legis, quo excitatur contritio, tum verbum evangelii, quo accenditur fides in Christum mediatorem.

Obs. III. Conversionis speciatim dictae synonymum communiter habetur regeneratio.

Observauit tamen D. KOENIGIVS in theol. posit. Part. III. §. 451. nonnihil discriminis inter conversionem, & regenerationem. Ex huius sententia haec duo differunt 1) ratione subiectorum: Regeneratio enim est adultorum & infantum; conversio vero adultorum saltem est; quum infantes regenerari quidem, non autem aeque vsitate converti dicantur, (nisi quis forte cum B.

DANNHAV. ἀνάλογόν τι conversionis & poenitentiae iisdem tribuere velit. Vid. hodof. p. 1269.): 2) ratione mediorum: Regeneratio fit per verbum & sacramenta, conversio per verbum solum. Posset quisquam addere 3) conversio fit per legem & evangelium; regeneratio tantum per evangelium.

Probatur speciatis conversionis acceptio: 1) quia Deus, per ministerium verbi aperiens oculos peccatorum (illuminans eosdem), convertit ipsos a tenebris ad lucem, Act. XXVI, 18. Vbi per tenebras non intelligimus praecise ignorantiam mentis, neque per lucem agnitionem, vt verbis illis exhibeatur vberior illuminationis descriptio; propterea, quod tabulae vocationis Paullinae succincte delineatae non admittunt περισσολογίαν, sed potius per σκότος, tenebras, designantur opera tenebrarum, Rom. XIII, 12. Eph. V, 11. per lucem autem denotatur lux fidei, quae haud raro in sacris litteris nomine lucis venit, Matth. V, 16. Eph. V, 8. 1 Ioann. II, 9. 11. atque credentes dicuntur filii lucis, Luc. XVI, 8. Io. XII, 36. 1 Thess. V, 5. Est itaque conversio transitiva, & specialiter sic dicta, qua Deus peccatorem convertit, actus gratiae, quo Spiritus S. peccatorem auertit ab operibus tenebrarum, detestationem peccatorum operando, atque eundem luce fidei perfundit.

Prob. 2) Convertitur homo, vt deleantur peccata ipsius, Actor. XI, 19. Et gentibus Deus dat poenitentiam ad vitam, Act. XI, 18. E. per gratiam convertentem, praeter contritionem activam, confertur fides in Christum, sine qua nec remissio peccatorum, nec vlla vita spiritualis obtinetur.

Quaest. V. Quid est conversio sensu specialissimo sumta?

Conversio sumta sensu specialissimo est actus gratiae, quo Spiritus Sanctus voluntatem & cor hominis peccatoris in medio peccati statu inhibet, frangitque ac conterit, vt cum dolore animi peccata detestetur, atque adeo praeparetur ad salvificam in Christum fidem concipiendam.

Prob. 1) Strictissima conversionis significatio conformis est scripturae, quippe quae actum illum, quo cor peccatoris conteritur, conversionem appellare consueuit.

Sic precatur populus Israëliticus: Converte me, Domine, & convertar (conversione passiva): nam postquam conversus fuero (passive), agam poenitentiam (μετὰς sumtam, pro contritione), ac postquam offensum est mihi, percussi femur: Pudet me & erubui (en! adhuc actus contritionis) quia sustinui opprobrium adolescentiae meae, Ier. XXXI, 12. Et Deus, exhortans Israëlitas ad poenitentiam, inquit: Convertimini ad me toto corde vestro, & in ieiunio, & in fletu ac planctu. Ita vt scindatis corda vestra, & non vestes vestras: Sic (inquam) convertimini ad Iehouam Deum vestrum, Ioel. II, 12. 13.

2) Sicut alius actus gratiæ applicatricis est, quo Deus contritionem operatur, alius actus gratiæ, quo peccatori contrito fiduciam donat, merito Christi innixam: Ita prior actus conversio (strictissime sumta), posterior actus gratiæ regeneratio, commode appellatur. Convertit Deus peccatorem per legem, regenerat per euangelium. Contritio est effectus gratiæ convertentis, fides est effectus gratiæ regenerantis. Pœnitentia, ἐκλῶς sumta (constans ex contritione & fide), est effectus utriusque actus gratiæ, scilicet conversionis & regenerationis, ad unum ἀποτέλεσμα producendum confluentis. Pœnitentia quippe est ἀποτέλεσμα diuinum. Neque enim proprie virtus est, aut habitus, sed actus, e contritione & fide compositus, ideoque ἀποτέλεσμα, theriacum contra pestem peccati salutare, dicente D. DANNHAV. hodof. p. 1265.

3) Ordine naturæ præcedit conversio, sequitur regeneratio; quem ordinem retinet scriptura, duin conversionem per remotionem cordis lapidei, regenerationem vero per collationem cordis carnei describit, Ezech. XI, 19. c XXXVI, 26. Illam per scissionem cordis, Ioel. II, 13. Ps. LI, 19. hanc vero per fracti cordis fanationem stilo prophetico exprimit, Es. LXI, 1.

4) Hunc ordinem actuum gratiæ ostendit ipsa praxis. Deus sapientissimus, lapfos generis humani primos parentes converterus, prædicauit ipsis legem, vt, hoc fulmine perculfi, contremiscerent & dolerent: pauidis & contritis prædicauit euangelium, vt ipsos regeneraret & iustificaret, Gen. III, 7. 8. feqq. Auscultatores Petri, audita concione apostolica, compuncti sunt corde, & dixerunt ad Petrum & reliquos Apostolos: Quid facimus, viri fratres? (en gratiam conversionis per legem!) Petrus ait ad illos: Pœnitentiam agite (en contritionem actiuam, quæ conversionem passiuam insequebatur!), & baptizetur unusquisque vestrum in nomine Iesu Christi (quibus verbis regeneratio per baptismum exprimitur), in remissionem peccatorum (sic immediate regenerationem excipit iustificatio). Act. II, 38.

5) Formula Concordiæ gratiam Dei convertentem, & regenerantem accurate distinguit p. 662. Homo per Spiritum S. illuminatur, convertitur, regeneratur. Et p. 681. Hominis, nondum renati, intellectus & voluntas tantum sunt subiectum convertendum. Sunt enim hominis spiritualiter mortui intellectus & voluntas, in quo homine Spiritus S. conversionem & renouationem operatur. Ad quod opus hominis convertendi voluntas nihil confert: Sed patitur, vt Deus in ipsa operetur (iam regeneratio vt terminus conversionis sequitur) donec regeneretur. In strictissima hac significatione vocem, conversio, usurpant D. CARPZOV. in isagog. p. 1244. B. HOEPFNERVS loc. theol. p. 451. D. NEVMANN. in disput. de nexu & discrimine donorum gratiæ §. 13.

Dicis: Conversio per legem non est actus gratiæ, sed iustitiæ vindicatiæ, ideo, quod lex iram operatur, Rom. IV, 15. Resp. Lex, per se bona & sancta, iram operatur culpa hominum, præcepta legis transgredientium, peccata eorum accusando & condemnando; sed hæc operatio legis a Deo misericordiffimo in finem homini salutarem dirigitur. Præclare hoc docet D. 10. MVSÆVS disput. II. de convers. c. III. edit. Ien. p. 80. Lex est organon quoddam gratiæ diuinæ, in homine peccatore operantis, eius cor durum emollientis, præparantis & disponentis ad fidem, voce euangelii in eo accendendam.

Quæst. VI. Quotuplex est conversio? Donuersio est duplex, ordinaria, & extraordinaria. Illa est, qua Deus, mediante verbo legis, more modoque vfitato, hominem peccatorem ad detestationem peccatorum perducit a). Hæc est, qua Deus vel immediate, vel per miracula, peccatorem fic percellit, vt admissa peccata serio doleat b).

Prob. a. Ordinarie Deus homines conterit malleo legis, Ier. XXIII, 29. eosque dolat per Prophetas, sive ministros ecclesiae, rite vocatos & ordinatos, Hos. VI, 5. Act. XXVI, 17. 18. Prob. b. Extraordinarie Deus homines peccatores convertit, vel ipsos immediate, sive citra interventum ministrorum suorum alloquendo: qua ratione conversus est Abrahamus, Gen. XII, 1. latro in cruce, Luc. XXIII, 42. Paullus, Act. IX, 3. 4: vel verbum suum, verbique ministros miraculis & signis stipando, ubi tamen vis illa convertendi non miraculis & signis, sed verbo divino adscribenda est. Sic miracula, quae mortem Christi comitata sunt, perculerunt centurionem, aliosque, cruci adstantes, ut pectora pulsarent, Luc. XXIII, 48.


### Quest. VII

How manifold is ordinary conversion? Ordinary conversion is twofold: first and second. The former is the action of the Holy Spirit, by which he crushes and softens the hearts of men who are unbelieving and established outside the church, through the word of the law, in order to kindle in them, by the voice of the gospel, a saving faith in Christ a). The latter is that by which the Holy Spirit recalls to repentance sinful men who indeed live in the bosom of the church, but who, by committed proaeretic sins, have fallen from the state of regeneration b).

Prob. a. God also gave repentance unto life to the Gentiles, Acts XI, 18. God calls Gentiles, Turks, Tartars, and Jews to the church of Christ, and in this workshop the Holy Spirit illuminates them and breaks their ferocity with the hammer of the law, so that they may be prepared to receive faith in Christ.

Prob. b. Men living within the boundaries of the church make shipwreck of the faith by sins that devastate the conscience, 1 Tim. I, 19, and fall from the grace of God, Rev. II, 5. These God recalls to repentance: "Return, backsliding Israel! says Jehovah. I will not cause my face to fall upon you (in anger); for I am merciful, says Jehovah. I will not hold (anger) forever. Only acknowledge that you have transgressed against Jehovah your God," Jer. III, 12, 13. The conversion of these is called second, likewise the conversion of the relapsed.

Latin:

Conversio ordinaria est duplex, prima, & secunda. Illa est actio Spiritus Sancti, qua corda hominum infidelium, & extra ecclesiam constitutorum, per verbum legis conterit & emollit, ad fidem in Christum salvificam in ipsis voce evangelii accendendam a). Haec est, qua Spiritus Sanctus homines peccatores, qui in gremio ecclesiae quidem degunt, sed commissis peccatis proaereticis e statu regenerationis exciderunt, ad poenitentiam revocat b).

Prob. a. Deus etiam gentibus poenitentiam dedit ad vitam, Act. XI, 8. Deus gentiles, Turcas, Tartaros, Iudaeos ad ecclesiam Christi vocat, & in hac officina Spiritus S. illuminat, eorumque ferociam malleo legis frangit, ut ad fidem in Christum suscipiendam praeparentur.

Prob. b. Homines, intra pomoeria ecclesiae viventes, peccatis conscientiam vastantibus naufragium fidei faciunt, 1 Tim. I, 19. & gratia Dei excidunt, Apocal. II, 5. Hos Deus ad poenitentiam revocat, Reuertere, auersa Israël! dictum Iehouae. Non (enim) faciam cadere facies super vos (iratas) meas; quoniam misericors ego sum: dictum Iehouae. Non tenebo (iram) in aeternum. Tantummodo agnosce, quod contra Iehouam Deum tuum praevaricata sis. Ier. III, 12. 13. Horum conversio dicitur secunda, item relapsorum conversio.


### Quest. VIII

Who converts man? God a), the Father b), the Son c), and terminatively the Holy Spirit d).

Prob. a. Conversion, on the part of God who works, is active; on the part of the man who is converted, it is merely passive. For God alone circumcises the heart, Deut. XXX, 6; takes away the heart of stone, Ezek. XI, 19; c. XXXVI, 26; and gives repentance unto the acknowledging of the truth, 2 Tim. II, 25. Therefore, God alone actively converts, so that man is passively converted, Jer. XXXI, 18; Lam. V, 21.

Prob. b. God the Father commands all men everywhere to repent; for this reason, because he has appointed a day in which he will judge the world in righteousness by the man whom he has ordained, Acts XVII, 30. Obj. When God the Father commands sinners to repent, he at the same time offers and confers the efficacy of converting, unless they maliciously resist.

Prob. c. Christ is said to turn away ungodliness from Jacob, Rom. XI, 26. Who, having performed the prophetic office in the flesh, began to preach: "Repent and believe the gospel!" Mark I, 15. Christ stands before the door of the heart and knocks, by exciting the sinner to repentance with the hammer of the law, Rev. III, 20.

Proof. The Holy Spirit convicts the world of sin, He convinces [it] that ἀπισίαν, or unbelief, by which Christ the mediator is rejected, is the greatest sin, John XVI, 9. (*).

Latin:

Deus a), Pater b), Filius c), & terminative Spiritus Sanctus d).

Prob. a. Conversio, ex parte Dei operantis, activa; ex parte hominis conversi, mere passiva est. Etenim solus Deus cor circumcidit, Deut. XXX, 6. cor lapideum aufert, Ezech. XI, 9. c. XXXVI, 26. & dat poenitentiam in cognitionem veritatis, 2 Tim. II, 25. Ergo solus Deus active convertit, ut homo passive convertatur, Ier. XXXI, 18. Thren. V, 21.

Prob. b. Deus Pater praecipit hominibus omnibus ubique, ut poenitentiam agant; propterea, quod constituit diem, in quo iudicaturus est orbem in iustitia, per virum, quem destinauit, Act. XVII, 30. Obs. Quando Deus Pater peccatoribus praecipit, ut poenitentiam agant, simul etiam convertendi efficaciam, nisi malitiose restiterint, offert & confert.

Prob. c. Christus auertere impietatem a Iacobo dicitur, Rom. XI, 26. Qui, functus in carne munere prophetico, praedicare exorsus est: Poenitentiam agite & credite evangelio! Marc. I, 15. Stat Christus ante ostium cordis, & pulsat, malleo legis ad poenitentiam peccatorem excitando, Apocal. III, 20. Christus ante ostium cordis, & pulsat, malleo legis ad pœnitentiam peccatorem excitando, Apoc. III, 20.

Prob. d. Spiritus S. arguit mundum de peccato, conuincit, ἀπισίαν, siue incredulitatem, qua Christus mediator reiicitur, esse peccatum maximum, Io. XVI, 9. (*).


### Quest. IX. By what means does God convert the sinner, so that he may detest his sins?

God converts the sinner by the word of the law, so that with serious sorrow of heart he may detest his sins a), and be prepared for conceiving faith in Christ from the word of the gospel b).

Proof. a. 1) Just as from the law is the knowledge of sin, Rom. III, 20: so also is sorrow for sin, following the knowledge of sin.

2) The law works wrath, Rom. IV, 15, by accusing sins, by denouncing the curse to the transgressors of the law, and thus by striking terror into them. For which reason it is also said to kill and to condemn, 2 Cor. III, 6. But the law kills, not so much by way of a physical cause, as by way of a moral cause; not so much by destroying us, as by adjudging and condemning us to death; although it is also said to kill in that manner as a physical cause, because it crushes and mortifies our hearts, so that they feel nothing but death and that we must perish eternally, being struck down by the blow and lightning of the law, unless grace comes to our aid. Thus D. CALOVIVS aptly says, explaining the cited passage in bibl. illustr. fol. 443.

Proof. b. The law is a schoolmaster unto Christ, Gal. III, 24, inasmuch as He is said to be the end of the law, Rom. X, 4. God has ordained this order, that the stony and iron hearts of sinful men should be crushed by the divine law, as if by a hammer, and softened, as if by fire, see Jer. XXIII, 29, and be prepared for conceiving faith in Christ, and through Him obtaining the remission of sins. D. CHEMNIT. inculcates this order in exam concil. Trid. fol. m. 155. There is altogether a certain order, or mode, designated and prescribed in the word of God, which God uses when He wishes to lead a man to justification, so that he may receive reconciliation, remission of sins, adoption, etc. And those who do not wish to accommodate themselves to that mode, or order, divinely prescribed, under the guidance of the Spirit, but neglect and trample upon it, these do not arrive at justification: for God wishes us to begin from the knowledge and assent of His word. And before justification, contrition must precede, i.e., a serious acknowledgment of sins, the terrors of a conscience recognizing the wrath of God against our sins, and grieving on account of sin; in which contrition the purpose of persevering and continuing in wickedness is not retained, but cast away

ribes. To these terrors, however, it is necessary that faith be added, which, by the recognition and trust of the mercy of God, promised on account of the mediator Son, may again raise up and comfort the soul, lest, oppressed by despair, we rush into eternal destruction; but let faith approach God, seek, desire, ask, apprehend, and receive the remission of sins. And in this way, or order designated in the word of God, that the way is prepared for the Lord, so that in Him, through and on account of Him, we may by faith attain and receive justification, Scripture itself teaches.
