For thus the voice cries: Prepare the way of the Lord, And concerning the ministry of the Baptist, preaching the baptism of repentance, Gabriel says, Prepare for the Lord a people prepared. This order Dannhauer rightly explains in his Hodof. phaenom. The divine order on our part requires repentance, first requested in the preaching of Christ and the apostles, to level the way for God. This order, divinely intimated in the first sermon of Christ: Repent and believe the gospel! is on the part of man not dispositive, much less meritorious, but pedagogical and in a healthy sense preparatory, by which the way is prepared and leveled for the Lord, and privative, removing, prohibiting, as in surgical medicine the removal of pus precedes; removing, I say, the incapacity and obstacles to the remission of sins, namely the opinion of non-need, and the desire to continue in sins,

Latin:

Deus verbo legis peccatorem conuertit, vt cum serio animi dolore peccata detesteur a), & præparetur ad concipiendam ex verbo euangelii fidem in Christum b).

Prob. a. 1) Quemadmodum ex lege est agnitio peccati, Rom. III, 20: ita & dolor de peccato, agnitionem peccati consequens.

2) Lex iram operatur, Rom. IV, 15. peccata accusando, transgressoribus legis maledictionem denunciando, atque adeo ipsis terrorem incutiendo. Qua de caussa etiam occidere & condemnare dicitur, 2 Cor. III, 6. Occidit autem lex, non tam per modum caussæ physicæ, quam vt caussa moralis; non tam nos perimendo, quam morti adiudicando & condemnando; quamquam & ea ratione occidere caussa physica dicitur, quod corda nostra conterat & mortificet, vt nil nisi mortem sentiant & æternum pereundum nobis sit, ictu & fulmine legis prostratis, nisi gratia succurrat. Sic scite ait D. CALOVIVS, locum citatum exponens in bibl. illustr. fol. 443.

Prob. b. Lex est pædagogus ad Christum, Gal. III, 24. quippe qui finis legis dicitur, Rom. X, 4. Hunc ordinem Deus sanciuit, vt saxea & ferrea hominum peccatorum corda lege diuina, velut malleo, conterantur, &, velut igne, emolliantur, vid. Ier. XXIII, 29. atque præparentur ad concipiendam fidem in Christum, & per hunc impetrandam remissionem peccatorum. Inculcat hunc ordinem D. CHEMNIT. in exam concil. Trid. fol. m. 155. Omnino est certus ordo, siue modus, in verbo Dei designatus & præscriptus, quo Deus vtitur, quando vult hominem ad iustificationem deducere, vt accipiat reconciliationem, remissionem peccatorum, adoptionem &c. Et qui ad modum, siue ordinem illum, diuinitus præscriptum, non volunt se ductu Spiritus accommodare, sed negligunt & conculcant illum, hi ad iustificationem non perueniunt: vult enim Deus a notitia & assensu verbi sui nos ordiri. Et ante iustificationem oportet præcedere contritionem, h. e. seriam agnitionem peccatorum, pauores conscientiæ, agnoscentis iram Dei aduersus peccata nostra, & dolentis propter peccatum; in qua contritione non retinetur, sed abiicitur propositum perseuerandi & pergendi in scele-

Ad hos vero terrores necesse est accedere fidem, quae agnitione et fiducia misericordiae Dei, promissae propter filium mediatorem, rursus erigat et consoletur animum, ne, oppressa desperatione, ruamus in aeternum exitium; sed fides accedat ad Deum, quaerat, desideret, petat, apprehendat, accipiat remissionem peccatorum. Et hoc modo, seu ordine in verbo Dei designato, viam parari Domino, vt in ipso, per et propter ipsum fide consequamur et accipiamus iustificationem, ipsa scriptura tradit. Ita enim vox clamat: Parate viam Domino, Et de ministerio baptistae, praedicantis baptismum poenitentiae, dicit Gabriel, Parate Domino plebem praeparatam. Quem ordinem dextre explicat Dannhav. in hodof. phaenom. Ordo diuinus ex parte nostri exigit poenitentiam, primum in praedicatione Christi et apostolorum requisitam, ad viam Deo complanandam. Hic ordo, diuinitus intimatus in prima Christi concione: Resipiscite et credite euangelio! est ex parte hominis non dispositivus, nedum meritorius, sed paedagogicus et sano sensu praeparatorius, quo praeparatur et complanatur via Domino, ac priuatiuus, remouens, prohibens, vt in medicina chirurgica puris remotio praecedit; remouens, inquam, incapacitatem, et obstacula remissionis peccatorum, scilicet opinionem non-indigentiae, et studium pergendi in peccatis,


### Quest. IX. By what means does God convert the sinner, so that he may detest his sins?: Q. X

Q. X.

What ministers does God use in the conversion of sinners? God in the conversion of sinful men ordinarily uses holy heralds, decently called a): extraordinarily, any pious Christian can recall an erring one to the way b).

Prob. a. From 1 Cor. III. 9. We are God's fellow workers. Holy heralds are called fellow workers, not from an innate faculty, but from grace granted by God, 1 Cor. XV, 10. They are fellow workers of God, not in such a way as if they were associate causes with God in the business of conversion, but because they are subordinate and less principal, or ministerial, causes.

Prob. b. Jas. V, 20. Know that he who converts a sinner from the error of his way will save a soul from death, and will cover a multitude of sins.

There is an antithesis of the Schwenckfeldians, who derogate the efficacy of converting both from the divine word and from the ministers of the word. They strive to strengthen their opinion with the following two arguments.

I. God works all things in all, 1 Cor. XII, 6. Therefore, He does not need fellow workers. Resp. In the business of conversion, God works all things not immediately, but through the mediation of the holy ministry, to which He has granted the gifts of ministering.

II. Neither he who plants, nor he who waters, is anything, but God who gives the increase, 1 Cor. III, 7. Therefore, in the business of conversion, the minister of the church is worth nothing. Resp. a) Ministers of the church are worth nothing outside their office, insofar as they are not subordinate to Christ. b) In their office, indeed, they are worth something, since they are stewards of the mysteries of God, 1 Cor. IV, 1. Yet they refer that worth to Christ, as to the head and source. Whence, in their office, comparatively (a comparison being made to Christ) they are worth nothing.

Q. XI.

Who is to be converted? He who is to be converted is an adult man, turned away from God by deadly sins a), whose will, prone to sins, is struck by the lightning of the law, so that he may detest them; b) the sensitive appetite, however, is so pricked by the sword of the law that it is moved to serious sorrow for sins c). An adult is properly said to be converted; for he is capable of listening to, reading, and meditating upon the divine law, as well as of detesting sin: since infants are destitute of this capacity by reason of their age, they are indeed said to be regenerated through baptism, but not equally said to be converted in a living manner.

Moreover, an adult human is either joined to God through faith and reborn; or he is turned away from God through infidelity and mortal sins and is unregenerate. Speaking Ἀκριβῶς (precisely), a person who is turned away, whom iniquity has separated from God, is said to be converted, Is.

LIX, 2. There is indeed also the repentance of those who stand, that is, of reborn and faithful men who still persist in the state of rebirth and grace: because, however, they have sins which they must daily acknowledge, detest, and grieve over; therefore they are also rightly said to be capable of conversion from sins in this respect.

But it must be admitted that the name of conversion is then taken more generally, which in a more special meaning has as its subject only the wicked man, who is constituted in potentiality for his union with God, but is not actually joined.

See BAIER, Comp. Part. III. c. IV. p. 729. Prob. b. The will of an unregenerate man is carried so headlong into evil, prohibited by divine law, that it cannot be subjected to the law even by natural passive power, Rom.

VIII, 7. Yet the will of an unregenerate man is the subject quo (by which) of conversion; because in it there is given an obediential passive power, by which it is fit for receiving converting grace, supernatural powers for morally retracting sin, and for casting off the purpose of continuing in illicit acts.

Prob. c. The sensitive appetite rages, indulging in inordinate affections, unless it is divinely pricked.

The hearers of Peter κατενύγησαν τῇ καρδίᾳ, they were pricked in their heart, Acts II, 37. Their heart, the seat of the affections, was lacerated with such pain as if it had been pricked by a needle or pierced by a lance.

Latin:

Quast. X. Quibus ministris Deus in conuersione peccatorum utitur?

Deus in conuersione hominum peccatorum ordinarie utitur praeconibus sacris, decenter vocatis a): extra ordinem quilibet pius christianus errantem in viam reuocare potest b).

Prob. a. Ex 1 Cor. III. 9. Sumus Dei cooperarii. Dicuntur praecones sacri cooperarii, non ex facultate innata, sed ex gratia a Deo concessa, 1 Cor. XV, 10. Sunt cooperarii Dei, non perinde, ac si in negotio conuersionis essent cum Deo causae sociae, sed quia sunt causae subordinatae et minus principales, siue ministeriales.

Prob. b. Iac. V, 20. Cognoscito, quod, qui conuertit peccatorem ex errore viae ipsius, seruabit animam ex morte, et obteget multitudinem peccatorum.

Antithesis est Schwenckfeldianorum, efficaciam conuertendi et verbo diuino et ministris verbi derogantium. Qui sequentibus duobus argumentis suam opinionem firmare nituntur.

I. Deus omnia in omnibus operatur, 1 Cor. XII, 6. E. non indiget cooperariis. Resp. In negotio conuersionis Deus omnia operatur non immediate, sed mediante ministerio sacro, cui ministrantia concessit dona.

II. Neque qui plantat, neque qui rigat, est aliquid, sed Deus dans incrementum, 1 Cor. III, 7. E. in negotio conuersionis minister ecclesiae nihil valet. Resp. a) Ministri ecclesiae nihil valent extra officium, quatenus Christo non subordinantur. b) In officio quidem aliquid valent, quoniam sunt dispensatores mysteriorum Dei, 1 Cor. IV, 1. Valorem tamen illum Christo, tanquam capiti et fonti, acceptum referunt. Vnde in officio comparatiue (facta comparatione ad Christum) nihil valent.

Quast. XI. Quis est conuertendus?

Conuertendus est homo adultus, per peccata mortifera a Deo auersus a), cuius voluntas, ad peccata proclius, fulmine legis percellitur, vt ea detestetur; b) appetitus vero sensitivus gladio legis sic compungitur, vt ad serium de peccatis dolorem commoueatur c). Proprie converti dicitur homo adultus; quippe qui auscultationis, lectionis & meditationis legis divinae, iuxta atque detestationis peccati capax est: qua capacitate cum per aetatem destituantur infantes, per baptismum quidem regenerari, non autem aeque vivitate converti dicuntur.

Ceterum homo adultus vel est per fidem cum Deo coniunctus, & renatus; vel est per infidelitatem & peccata mortifera a Deo aversus & irregenitus. Ἀκριβῶς loquendo converti dicitur homo aversus, quem iniquitas a Deo separavit, Es.

LIX, 2. Datur quidem & poenitentia stantium, seu hominum renatorum & fidelium, qui in statu renascentiae & gratiae adhuc persistunt: quia tamen peccata habent, quae quotidie agnoscere, detestari & dolere debent; ideo & conversionis a peccatis hac ratione capaces recte dicuntur.

Sed fatendum est, conversionis nomen tunc accipi generalius, quod specialiorem significatu pro subiecto habet solum hominem improbum, qui ad coniunctionem sui cum Deo in potentia constitutus, non actu coniunctus est.

Vid. BAIERI Comp. Part. III. c. IV. p. 729. Prob. b. Voluntas hominis irregeniti adeo praeceps fertur in malum, lege divina prohibitum, ut nec per potentiam quidem passivam naturalem legi subiici queat, Rom.

VIII, 7. Est tamen voluntas hominis irregeniti subiectum quo conversionis; quia in eadem datur potentia passiva obedientialis, qua apta est ad recipiendum gratiam convertentem, vires supernaturales ad peccatum moraliter retractandum, & abiiciendum propositum pergendi in actibus illicitis.

Prob. c. Ferocit appetitus sensitivus inordinatis affectibus indulgens, nisi divinitus compungatur.

Auditores Petri κατενύγησαν τῇ καρδίᾳ, compuncti sunt corde, Act. II, 37. Tanto dolore ipsorum cor, sedes affectuum, laceratum est, ac si acu punctum, aut lancea perfoffum esset.


### Quest. IX. By what means does God convert the sinner, so that he may detest his sins?: Obs

Obs.

Some authors refer also the intellect of the unregenerate man to the subject quo of conversion; who do not distinguish the act of illumination from the act of conversion.

But since illumination becomes for us a peculiar act of applying grace, we suppose in the present case that the intellect, illuminated by the word of God, acknowledges the foulness of sin and holds a torch before the will, which is blind in itself.

The antithesis is that of the Pelagians, Papists, Socinians, and Arminians, who attribute to the human will the actual power of converting; most of whose arguments we considered in Part II. c. VI. A few remain to be weighed here.

I. Whoever converts himself, to him belong actual powers for eliciting his own conversion:

But the unregenerate man, etc. Therefore. The major is evident; because to convert oneself denotes an immanent and reciprocal act, which presupposes actual power. The minor is proved from Acts

III, 19. Repent and convert yourselves. Resp.

Whoever converts himself by natural and …proper powers, to him belong actual powers for eliciting his conversion. But the unregenerate man does not convert himself by natural or proper powers, but by supernatural powers, granted through the converting grace of the Holy Spirit, and passively received by the unregenerate man, just as a ship is said to turn itself not by its own powers, but by the powers of the sailors and the winds. II. Whoever is converted, not necessarily, but freely, his will can actively determine itself to conversion: But a sinful man is not necessarily, but freely converted: Therefore. The major is proved: because, if a man were determined to his conversion by another principle than his own will, he would not be converted freely, but necessarily. For whatever is determined to one of opposites is no longer free, but necessary. The minor is evident: because a sinful man is not converted by necessitating grace, or by bringing in any violence, and therefore [is converted] freely. Resp. I deny the major; because a sinful man is indeed converted freely in a negative sense, insofar as he can prevent himself from being converted; not positively, as if his will could dispose or determine itself to conversion by its own powers; for a sinner is spiritually dead before he is regenerated, Eph. II, 5, and therefore destitute of active powers. Then, to the proof we say that a man is indeed determined by converting grace, but by grace acting through a resistible power, which has no necessity accompanying it, except a hypothetical one. But this does not take away liberty, but can consist with it.

III. God converts man in such a way that, nevertheless, not God, but man performs repentance: Therefore, the provision of powers is indeed from God, but the exercise of them is of man, who as a particular cause actively determines himself to the act of conversion; because otherwise it would follow, if both the powers and the exercise of them were ascribed to God, that man would be denominated by such an exercise. Resp. Repentance is considered either by reason of its origin or by reason of the receiving subject. Repentance by reason of origin is from transitive conversion, by which God gives not only the powers of repenting, but also repentance itself, Acts XI, 18. The subject suffering and receiving supernatural powers is the sinful man, who, being passively converted by God, performs repentance by exerting, exercising, and clearly showing the supernatural powers received. It is illustrated by a simile. Christ, raising the dead Lazarus, bestowed upon him both the powers of living and life itself; and yet, because of this bestowed life, not Christ, but Lazarus was said to be living, because he used the granted powers of living. Thus the Holy Spirit both confers the powers of repenting and, by a special influx, leads the conferred powers into act, so that, nevertheless, not the Holy Spirit, but the sinner is said to repent; because he uses the conferred powers of repenting.

Latin:

Obs.

Nonnulli auctores ad subiectum quo conversionis referunt etiam intellectum hominis irregeniti; qui actum illuminationis ab actu conversionis non distinguunt.

Cum autem illuminatio nobis fit peculiaris actus gratiae applicatricis, in praesenti supponimus, intellectum, ex verbo Dei illuminatum, foeditatem peccati agnoscere, & voluntati, per se caecae, facem praeferre.

Antithesis est Pelagianorum, Pontificiorum, Socinianorum & Arminianorum, voluntati humanae actuam convertendi vim tribuentium; quorum pleraque argumenta Part. II. c. VI. consideravimus. Restant pauca hic expendenda.

I. Quicunque seipsum convertit, illi suppetunt vires actuae ad eliciendam sui ipsius conversionem:

Atqui homo irregenitus &c. E. Maior constat; quia seipsum convertere, notat actum immanentem & reciprocum, qui potentiam actuam supponit. Minor prob. ex Act.

III, 19. Agite poenitentiam & convertite vos. Resp.

Quicunque viribus naturalibus & propriis seipsum convertit, illi suppetunt vires actuae ad eliciendam sui conversionem. At homo irregenitus seipsum non convertit viribus naturalibus, aut propriis, sed viribus supernaturalibus, per gratiam Spiritus Sancti convertentem concessis, & ab homine irregenito passive receptis, sicut navis dicitur seipsam vertere non propriis, sed nautarum ventorumque viribus. II. QuiII. Quicunque conuertitur non necessario, sed libere, illius voluntas ad conuersionem actiue se determinare potest: Atqui homo peccator non necessario, sed libere conuertitur: Ergo. Maior probatur: quia, si homo ab alio principio, quam a voluntate sua determiharetur ad conuersionem sui, non libere, sed necessario conuerteretur. Quidquid enim determinatum est ad vnum oppositorum, non amplius liberum, sed necessarium est. Minor constat: quia homo peccator non conuertitur gratia necessitante, aut vllam violentiam inferente, adeoque libere. Resp. Neg. maiorem; quia homo peccator libere quidem conuertitur negatiue, quatenus potest impedire, ne conuertatur; non positiue, quasi voluntas eius seipsam disponere, aut determinare ad conuersionem viribus propriis possit; est enim peccator spiritualiter mortuus, antequam regeneretur, Eph. II, 5. adeoque viribus actiuis destitutus. Deinde ad probationem dicimus, quod homo a gratia conuertente determinetur quidem, sed per potentiam resistibilem agente, quæ nullam necessitatem comitem habet, nisi hypotheticam. At hæc libertatem non tollit, sed cum eadem consistere potest.

III. Deus ita conuertit hominem, vt tamen non Deus, sed homo pœnitentiam agat: E. virium quidem suppeditatio est a Deo, exercitium vero illarum est hominis, qui tanquam caussa particularis ad actum conuersionis actiue se determinat; quia alias sequeretur, si & vires, & exercitium illarum Deo adscriberetur, hominem denominari ab istiusmodi exercitio. Resp. Pœnitentia consideratur vel ratione originis, vel ratione subiecti recipientis. Pœnitentia ratione originis est a conuersione transitiua, qua Deus non tantum vires pœnitendi, sed & ipsam pœnitentiam dat, Act. XI, 18. Subiectum patiens viresque supernaturales recipiens est homo peccator, qui a Deo passiue conuersus pœnitentiam agit, vires supernaturales receptas exserendo, exercendo, & luculenter ostendendo. Illustratur simili. Christus, Lazarum mortuum resuscitans, huic & vires viuendi, & ipsam vitam largiebatur; neque tamen ab hac collata vita Christus, sed Lazarus viuus dicebatur, quia concessis viribus viuendi vtebatur. Ita Spiritus S. & vires pœnitendi confert, & collatas vires speciali influxu in actum deducit, vt tamen non Spiritus Sanctus, sed peccator pœnitere dicatur; quia is collatis pœnitendi viribus vtitur.


### XII. Does God wish to convert all men, even the hardened?

The most merciful God wishes to convert all men, even the hardened, by his antecedent will a), from whom by his consequent judicial will he indeed withdraws regenerating, justifying, and sanctifying grace, but does not cut off the grace common to all b), by which, during the whole space of time in which they run the course of this life, he invites them to repentance and effectively calls them back c), so that not a few hardened ones are converted d). But those who maliciously resist the Holy Spirit until the end of life, and die in impenitence, rush into eternal destruction from their own voluntary guilt, not from a divine decree absolutely denying converting grace e).

Obs. I. When we assert the universal converting grace of the Holy Spirit, we are not speaking of the consequent will of God, by which he has decreed to save those who finally believe and to condemn those who are finally impenitent: but of the antecedent will of God, by which God offers to all men the sufficiency and efficacy of conversion, both by inviting sinners, established outside the church, to the kingdom of grace, and thus to repentance, and by calling back those living in the external communion of the church, who have slipped from the state of regeneration by deliberate sins, to repentance.

Obj. II. Revoking grace is that which, after the first grace has been worn away by relapse, the Holy Spirit having been driven out, faith lost, and an obsession of Satan that blinds and hardens having been admitted, recalls the man—who is most miserable, having fallen of his own accord, and being unable to rise of his own accord, and being ensnared in diabolical shackles—as if by a postliminy, to repentance, to the means of salvation, and to salvation, as defined by Dannhauer in Hodof. phænom. IX, p. 877.

Obj. III. Revoking grace is dispensed by the antecedent will of God. For the Father of compassions is equally affected by the misery of the man who has relapsed as by the one who is to be converted for the first time, in the judgment of Dannhauer, l. c.

Obj. IV. We are speaking here of hardened men, established in the way of this life, whom the universal grace of God seriously intends to convert: after this life, the door of indulgence, the door of mercy, the door of hope, the door of consolation, and the door of good works will be closed, as D. Quistorp holds in Annotat. bibl. ad Matth. XXV, p. 71. D. Pol. Lyserus agrees with him in Harmon. c. 117, p. 1264. When is the door of salvation closed? For individuals, at the hour of death; for all, at the final judgment of the world. For then there will no longer be a place for repentance or a time for procuring salvation, but the exact justice of God or paternal consolation must be expected; while this door of the kingdom of heaven, which is otherwise open to whomsoever lives, and in general stands open even to all men, remains so until the consummation of the age.

Prob. a. 1) From the classic saying: "When the wicked man shall have turned away from all his sins which he has committed, and shall have kept all my statutes, and shall have done judgment and justice, by living he shall live and shall not die. All his transgressions which he has committed shall not come into remembrance, but in his justice which he has done, he shall live. For do I desire the death of the wicked, says the Lord Jehovah? Is it not that he should turn from his ways and live?" Ezek. 18:21-22. With which agrees that divine oath, Ezek. 33:11: "As I live, says the Lord Jehovah, I do not desire the death of the wicked, but that the wicked should turn from his way and live: turn (therefore), turn from your evil ways; for why will you die, O house of Israel?"

Latin:

Deus misericordissimus omnes homines, etiam induratos, voluntate antecedente vult conuertere a), quibus voluntate consequente iudiciaria gratiam quidem regenerantem, iustificantem & sanctificantem subtrahit, non autem communem omnibus gratiam præcidit b), qua toto temporis spatio, quo viam huius vitæ decurrunt, eosdem ad pœnitentiam inuitat, & efficaciter reuocat c), vt haud pauci indurati conuertantur d). Qui autem Spiritui S. vsque ad finem vitæ malitiose resistunt, & in impœnitentia decedunt, ex voluntaria culpa, non ex decreto diuino, gratiam conuertentem absolute denegante, in æternum ruunt exitium e).

Obs. I. Quando gratiam Spiritus S. conuertricem vniuersalem asserimus, non loquimur de voluntate Dei consequente, qua is finaliter credentes saluare, finaliter impœnitentes condemnare decreuit: sed de voluntate Dei antecedente, qua Deus omnibus hominibus sufficientia & efficacia conuersionis media offert, tum peccatores, extra ecclesiam constitutos, ad regnum gratiæ, atque adeo ad pœnitentiam inuitando, tum in ecclesiæ externa communione degentes, peccatis autem proæreticis e statu regenerationis elapsos, ad pœnitentiam reuocando.

Obs. II. Gratia reuocatrix est, quæ, prima gratia per relapsum decocta, pulso Spiritu S., fide amissa, admissa contra obsessione Satanica excæcatrice & induratrice, postliminio quasi hominem miserrimum, ex se lapsum, ex se resurgere impotentem compedibus diabolicis irretitum, ad pœnitentiam, ad media salutis, ad salutem reuocat, definiente DANNHAV. in hodof. phænom. IX. p. 877.

Obs. III. Gratia reuocatrix dispensatur voluntate Dei antecedente. At æque enim Patrem οἰκτιρμῶν afficit miseria hominis relapsi, ac primum conuertendi, iudice DANNHAV. l. c.

Obs. IV. Sermo nobis est de hominibus induratis, in via huius vitæ constitutis, quos gratia Dei vniuersalis conuertere serio intendit: post hanc vitam clausa erit ianua indulgentiæ, ianua misericordiæ, ianua spei, ianua consolationis, ianua bonæ operationis, censente D. QVISTORPIO in annotat. bibl. ad Matth. XXV. p. 71. Cui suffragatur D. POL. LYSERVS c. 117. harmon. p. 1264. Quando porta salutis clauditur? singulis in hora mortis, vniuersis in nouissimo post vniuersale iudicium mundi. Tum enim non amplius erit locus pœnitentiæ, aut tempus salutis procurandæ, sed expectanda exacta iustitia Dei, vel paterna consolatio; dum hæc porta regni cælorum alias cuius patet, quamdiu viuit, & in genere etiam omnibus hominibus aperta stat, vsque ad consummationem sæculi.

Prob. a. 1) E dicto classico: Quando impius auersus fuerit ab omnibus peccatis suis, quæ fecerat, & custodierit omnia statuta mea, feceritque iudicium & iustitiam, viuendo vinet & non morietur. Omnes præuaricationes, quas fecit, non in recordationem venient, sed in iustitia sua quam fecit, viuet. Num enim volendo volo mortem impii? dictum Adonai Iehouah: Nonne vt conuertatur a viis suis & viuat? Ezech. XVIII, 21. 22. Cum quo conuenit illud iuramentum diuinum, Ezech. XXXIII, 11. Viuus ego, dictum Iehouah, si velim mortem impii, sed vt conuertatur impius a via sua, & viuat: conuertimini (ergo), conuertimini a viis vestris malis: quare enim moriemini, o domus Israëlis?


### XII. Does God wish to convert all men, even the hardened?: Obj. I

Obj. I.

The prophet is speaking of the most wicked sinners, indeed of those who, from a perverse habit of sin, ferociously perpetrate whatever is permitted, who practice robbery, shed blood, contaminate themselves with idolatry, defile the wife of their neighbor, and oppress the needy and the poor, v. 14, 15, 16. And yet God nonetheless offers them revoking grace in most significant words, even bringing forth the religion of an oath by His own life, and furthermore with such a serious and ready declaration of a benevolent mind, that He indicates, not obscurely, that the doors of converting grace are not closed up to that time, at which the obstinate sinner, stubbornly opposing the revoking grace of God, dies in his sins—that is, by temporal and eternal death, according to the parallel passage, 1 Chron. 10:13. 2) When God says: "Do I desire the death of the wicked?" Hugo Grotius understands those words comparatively, saying: This does not prevent there being some limit of mercy with God, as appeared in Pharaoh, the Canaanites, and others. To whom B. Calovius responds: These things are not to be understood absolutely. God simply wills that man should be converted and live. He does not merely prefer life to death. But there is nothing in the Scriptures about a limit of mercy; they proclaim everywhere the supreme mercy of God, which has no end: nowhere is a limit set for it, but we are commanded to hear the voice of Him who graciously calls us, the end of which is our gracious conversion. "Exhort yourselves every day, while it is called today, that none of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin," Heb. 3:13. Pharaoh was moved by God by a living voice and by miracles to repentance, up to the very end of his life. For even then, when he saw the Israelites crossing the Red Sea on dry ground, there was still time to return to a sounder mind, to desist from persecuting them, and not to wage war against God. Nor were the Canaanites excluded from mercy by any absolute decree, such that they could not, having seen and heard the miracles, humble themselves and obtain grace, which is evident from the example of Rahab and the Gibeonites. Whence the argumenwe argue: Whoever does not desire the death of the sinner or the most wicked person, but seriously intends his conversion, he wills by an antecedent will that all who are hardened be converted: But God &c. Therefore.

2) From 2 Pet. III, 9. God is patient toward us, not willing that any should perish, but that all should return to repentance. From this apostolic statement we conclude: Toward those sinners toward whom God shows Himself long-suffering, to the end that they may not perish, but return to repentance, them He seriously and effectively wills to convert. But toward hardened sinners &c. Therefore.

But toward hardened sinners &c. Therefore. 3) From 1 Tim. II, 4. For whom Christ has died, them He wills to convert. But Christ has died for all, even the hardened. Therefore. The major and minor are clear from the Pauline testimony. God wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God, and one mediator of God and men, the man Jesus Christ, who gave himself a ransom ἀντίλυτρον for all.

4) From Acts XVII, 30. God commands all men everywhere to repent: because He has appointed a day in which He is to judge the world in righteousness. We conclude: Whoever are to be judged on the final day of the universal judgment, them God wills to convert: But all men, even the most obstinate &c. Therefore.

Prob. b. That the consequent will of God, or of justice, does not rescind, expunge, or overturn the consequent will of God, or of mercy, is the common opinion of theologians. D. BALTH. MEISNER writes considerately in anthropol. decad. II. p. 108: "The judgment of the consequent will cannot remove the universal vocation, which God antecedently willed." To this D. DANNH. adds his calculation in hodom. Calu. p. 1447: "The consequent will of showing mercy to a few does not overturn the antecedent will of showing mercy to all." Nor does D. HENRIC. MVLLER dissent in femicentur. quaest. theol. p. 52: "The consequent will of God does not remove or rescind the antecedent." Likewise p. 53: "The antecedent will does not define, as if the consequent were expunged: The same affection of saving remains, which was before, the condition not yet being fulfilled." This is confirmed from Holy Scripture: 1) By an antecedent will God does not desire the death of the impious man, established in the way of this life, but that he be converted and live, Ezek. XXXIII, 11. This universal will of God is not rescinded or removed by the consequent or judiciary will, so that it might be permissible to assert that 'God by a consequent will does not desire that a hardened sinner be converted and live.' Let us listen to D. RVLSEMANN and the concurring D. CALOV in bibl. illustrat. in h. l. f. 550: "It is not necessary, for the exposition of this passage, to have recourse to the distinction of the divine will into antecedent and consequent. For neither by a consequent will does God delight in the destruction of the impious, as the Jews calumniated, but out of the necessity of the office of judge, and He is compelled against His will to pass sentence. See Lam. III, 33.

2) If all converting grace were utterly removed by a consequent will from hardened sinners, while they are still wayfarers, they would be like the devils, and would have sustained the execution of judgment in this life: Therefore, converting grace is not utterly removed from hardened wayfarers. The connection of the major is proved: because no converting grace is promised to devils; who have also long since sustained the execution of the judgment begun. Conf. 2 Pet. II, 4. Jude v. 6. The consequent is evident from Heb. IX, 27. It is appointed for men once to die, but after this the judgment. After death, judgment befalls those finally hardened, by which all converting grace is simply rescinded. But those who walk in the way of this life, they have Moses and the Prophets, whom they hear, so that through their word, with the Holy Spirit concurring, they may repent, Luke XVI, 31.

3) Whoever are delivered by a consequent will into the power of the devil, so that the flesh indeed may be afflicted, but the Spirit may be saved in the day of Jesus Christ, from them grace, calling back to repentance, ...consequent will is not simply subtracted: But hardened sinners, etc. Therefore. The minor premise is clear from 1 Cor. V, 5.

4) Whoever, by a consequent will, has been given over to a reprobate sense, and yet is invited to repentance by the kindness of God, for them the revoking grace is not cut off by a consequent will: But hardened wayfarers, etc. Therefore. The minor premise is evident from Rom. I, 28, compared with Rom. II, 4. For at Rom. I, 28, the despisers of the saving knowledge of God are said to have been delivered into a reprobate mind. The Apostle addresses these gravely in Rom. II, 4: "Do you despise the riches of God's kindness, and patience, and longsuffering? Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance?" The same is gathered from Ps. LXXXI, 12, 13, 14: "My people did not obey my voice, and Israel did not acquiesce to me: Therefore I dismissed them into the hardness of their hearts; that they might walk in their own counsels. Oh that my people would obey me, and Israel would walk in my ways!" etc. God dismissed the Israelite people, who were ill-disposed, into the hardness of their hearts, yet with a sincere vow He wished that they would cease from their malicious and stubborn resistance, and admit medicinal grace.

Proved 1) From Is. LXV, 2, 3: "I have spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, after their own thoughts; a people who provoke me to anger before my face continually, who sacrifice in gardens, and burn incense upon bricks." Whoever, throughout the day of life, spreads out gracious hands to rebellious sinners, who are continually provoking divine wrath and serving idols, he wishes to convert hardened sinners throughout the whole time of their life: But the most merciful God, etc. Therefore.

2) From Lam. III, 21, compared with Rom. II, 4: "The mercies of Jehovah are not finished; His compassions are not consumed: They become new every morning." Whatever mercy is not finished, nor consumed, but is new every morning, that is not terminated by any limit in the way of this life, but is limitlessly universal: But the beneficent mercy of God, inviting to repentance, etc. Therefore. That the minor proposition may be more fully understood, let the words of D. SEBAST. SCHMID in his commentary on Jer. V, 24 be observed: "The benefits of God also invite men to perform repentance daily, while He preserves the whole orb of nature with His beneficent longsuffering."

3) From Ps. XCV, 8: "Today, if you will hear His voice, do not harden your heart!" Compare Heb. III, 13: "Exhort yourselves καθ' ἑκάστην ἡμέραν, every day, as long as it is called 'today,' lest any of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin!" We argue: The present day is destined by God for every sinner to perform repentance: Every present day of life is 'today': Therefore.

4) From Ps. XXIII, 6: "Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life." Which words D. GEIER explains concisely: "Indicated in this place is the ardor of divine grace, which eagerly follows us who are careless, nay, even averse and fleeing; which prevents the unwilling, that he may will well; assists the willing, that he may perfect; follows the working, that he may persevere; and does not desert the sinner on any day."

You say: These words are understood of the penitent sinner, not of the hardened one. Resp. We have brought forward these words to show that the universal grace of God accompanies the sinner throughout the whole time of his life: We note, however, that God exhorts even contumacious sinners to repentance, which we learn

5) from Jer. III, 1: "They (are wont to) say: Behold! If a man puts away his wife, and she goes from him and becomes another man's: will he return to her again? Shall not that land be polluted by profaning? But you have played the harlot with many companions! Yet return to me! The saying of Jehovah." So unusual and stupendous is the clemency of God, that He calls back to Himself a soul, polluted by repeated deadly sins just as an adulteress who has played the harlot with many lovers, and stimulates it to repentance.

Latin:

Obs. I.

Sermo est prophetæ de peccatoribus maxime sceleratis, immo illis, qui ex peruerso peccati habitu, quidquid licet, ferociter patrant, qui latrocinia exercent, sanguinem effundunt, qui se idololatria contaminant, vxorem proximi polluunt, egenum & pauperem opprimunt, v. 14. 15. 16. Et hisce Deus nihilominus gratiam reuocantem offert verbis maxime significantibus, exserta etiam iuramenti per vitam suam religione, atque insuper tam feria ac propensa mentis beneuolæ contestatione, vt fores gratiæ conuertentis non esse præclusas ad id vsque tempus, haud obscure innuat, quo peccator obstinatus, & diuinæ gratiæ reuocanti præfracte se opponens, in peccatis moritur, morte scil. temporali & æterna, iuxta locum parall. 1 Paral. X, 13. 2) Quando Deus dicit: Num volendo volo mortem impii? HVGO GROTIVS verba illa comparate intelligit, inquiens: Hoc non obstat, quin fit apud Deum limes aliquis misericordiæ, vt apparuit in Pharaone, Cananæis & aliis. Cui respondet B. CALOVIVS: Non absolute hæc intelligenda sunt. Simpliciter Deus vult, vt homo conuertatur & viuat. Non tantum mauult vitam, quam mortem. De limite autem misericordiæ nihil in scripturis; quæ vndiquaque misericordiam Dei summam, nullumque finem habentem prædicant: nuspiam ei limites figitur, sed vocem gratiose nos vocitantis audire iubemur, cuius finis est gratiosa nostra conuersio. Adhortamini vosmet ipsos per singulos dies, donec hodie cognominatur, vt non obduretur quis ex vobis fallacia peccati, Hebr. III, 13. Pharao inotus a Deo viua voce & miraculis ad pœnitentiam fuit, vsque ad extremum vitæ terminum. Nam etiam tunc, vbi transire per mare rubrum sicco pede videbat Israëlitas, adhuc tempus erat ad faniorem mentem redeundi, a persecutione eorum desistendi, nec contra Deum belligerandi. Neque Cananæi absoluto aliquo decreto a misericordia exclusi erant, quin potuerint visis & auditis miraculis sese humiliare & gratiam consequi, quod exemplo Rahabi & Gibeonitarum constat. Vnde argumentamur: Quicunque non vult mortem peccatoris vel sceleratissimi, sed serio conversionem eius intendit, is vult voluntate antecedenti, vt omnes indurati convertantur: Atqui Deus &c. Ergo.

2) Ex 2 Petr. III, 9. Deus est patiens erga nos, non vult ullos perire, sed omnes ad poenitentiam reuerti. Ex quo effato apostolico colligimus: Erga quos peccatores se Deus longanimum praebet, eum in finem, vt non pereant, sed ad poenitentiam reuertantur, illos serio & efficaciter vult conuertere. Atqui erga peccatores induratos &c. Ergo.

3) Ex 1 Tim. II, 4. Pro quibus Christus est mortuus, illos vult conuertere. Sed pro omnibus, etiam induratis, Christus est mortuus. E. Maior & minor liquet e testimonio Paullino. Deus vult omnes homines saluari & ad agnitionem veritatis peruenire. Vnus enim est Deus, & vnus mediator Dei & hominum, homo Iesus Christus, qui dedit seipsum pretium redemptionis ἀντίλυτρον pro omnibus.

4) Ex Act. XVII, 30. Deus praecipit hominibus omnibus vbique, vt poenitentiam agant: propterea, quod constituit diem, in quo iudicaturus est orbem in iustitia. Colligimus: Quicunque sunt iudicandi in extremo vniuersalis iudicii die, illos Deus vult conuertere: Atqui omnes homines, etiam obstinatissimi &c. Ergo.

Prob. b. Voluntatem Dei consequentem, siue iustitiae, non rescindere, expungere, aut euertere voluntatem Dei consequentem, siue misericordiae, communis est Theologorum sententia. Considerate scribit D. BALTH. MEISNERVS in anthropol. decad. II. p. 108. Voluntatis consequentis iudicium non potest tollere vniuersalem vocationem, quam Deus antecedenter voluit. Cui calculum adiicit D. DANNH. in hodom. Calu. p. 1447. Voluntas miserendi paucorum consequens non euertit voluntatem miserendi omnium antecedentem. Nec dissentit D. HENRIC. MVLLER. in femicentur. quaest. theol. p. 52. Voluntas Dei consequens non tollit, aut rescindit antecedentem. Item p. 53: Non definit voluntas antecedens, quasi expuncta consequente: Manet idem affectus saluandi, qui fuit antea, conditione nondum impleta. Id quod confirmatur e S. scriptura: 1) Voluntate antecedente Deus non vult mortem hominis impii, in via huius vitae constituti, sed vt conuertatur & viuat, Ezech. XXXIII, 11. Hanc voluntatem Dei vniuersalem non rescindit aut tollit voluntas consequens, aut iudiciaria, vt asserere liceat, 'Deum voluntate consequente nolle, vt peccator induratus conuertatur & viuat'. Auscultemus D. RVLSEMANN. & suffragantem D. CALOV. in bibl. illustrat. in h. l. f. 550. Non necessum est, pro expositione huius loci, decurrere ad distinctionem voluntatis diuinae in antecedentem & consequentem. Nam neque consequente voluntate Deus delectatur interitu impii, quomodo Iudaei calumniabantur, sed ex necessitate officii iudicis, & innuitus cogitur ad ferendam sententiam. Vid. Thren. III, 33.

2) Si peccatoribus induratis, etiamnum viatoribus, omnis gratia conuertrix voluntate consequente penitus esset sublata; similes forent diabolis, & iudicii executionem in hac vita sustinuissent: E. gratia induratis viatoribus conuertrix non est penitus sublata. Connexio maioris probatur: quia diabolis nulla gratia conuertens est promissa; qui etiam iudicii inchoati executionem iam dudum sustinuerunt. Conf. 2 Petr. II, 4. Iud. V, 6. Consequens patet ex Hebr. IX, 27. Positum est hominibus semel mori, post hoc vero iudicium. Post mortem hominibus finaliter obduratis obtingit iudicium, quo omnis gratia conuertens simpliciter rescinditur. Sed qui via huius vitae incedunt, illi habent Mosen & Prophetas, quos audiunt, vt per illorum verbum, concurrente ...Spiritu S., resipiscant, Luc. XVI, 31.

3) Quicunque voluntate consequente traditi sunt in potestatem diaboli, ut caro quidem affligatur, sed Spiritus saluetur in die Iesu Christi, illis gratia, ad poenitentiam reuocans, tate consequente non simpliciter subtracta est: Sed peccatores indurati, &c. Ergo. Minor liquet, ex 1 Cor. V, 5.

4) Quicunque voluntate consequente in sensum reprobum sunt dati, & tamen benignitate Dei ad poenitentiam inuitantur, illis voluntate consequente gratia reuocatrix non est praecisa: Sed viatores indurati &c. Ergo. Minor patescit ex Rom. I, 28. collat. cum Rom. II, 4. Nain ad Rom. I, 28. contemtores salutiferae Dei cognitionis dicuntur esse traditi in mentem reprobam. Hos Apostolus Rom. II, 4. grauiter alloquitur: An diuitias bonitatis Dei & patientiae & longanimitatis contemnis? Ignoras, quod bonitas Dei te ad poenitentiam ducat? Idem colligitur e Ps. LXXXI, 12. 13. 14. Non obediuit populus meus voci meae, & Israel non acquieuit mihi: Ideo dimisi eum in duritie cordis eorum; vt irent in consiliis suis Vtinam populus meus esset obediens mihi, & Israel in viis meis ambularet! &c. Populum Israeliticum malefanum Deus dimisit in duritie cordis sui, sincero tamen voto exoptauit, vt a malitiosa & pertinaci repugnantia cessaret, & gratiam medicinalem admitteret.

Prob. c. 1) Ex Es. LXV, 2. 3. Expandi manus meas toto die ad populum rebellem, qui ambulant in via non bona post cogitationes suas; populum, qui ad iram prouocant me coram faciebus meis iugiter, qui sacrificant in hortis, & suffiunt super lateribus. Quicunque toto vitae die manus gratiofas expandit ad peccatores rebelles, iram diuinam iugiter prouocantes, idolisque feruientes, is toto vitae tempore induratos peccatores vult conuertere: Atqui Deus misericordissimus &c. Ergo.

2) Ex Thren. III, 21. collat. cum Rom. II, 4. Misericordiae Iehouae finitae non sunt; non sunt consumtae miserationes eius: Nouae fiunt omni mane. Quaecunque misericordia non est finita, neque consumta, sed omni mane noua, illa in via huius vitae nullo terminatur limite, fed illimitate vniuerfalis est: Atqui misericordia Dei benefica, ad poenitentiam inuitans &c. Ergo. Vt minor propositio plenius intelligatur, obseruentur verba D. SEBAST. SCHMID. in comment. Ier. V, 24. Ad poenitentiam agendam homines etiam quotidianis beneficia Dei inuitant, dum naturae vniuerfum orbem benefica sua longanimitate conferuat.

3) Ex Ps. XCV, 8. Hodie, si vocem eius audueritis, ne obdurate cor vestrum! Confer. Hebr. III, 13. Exhortamini vos ipsos καθ' ἑκάστην ἡμέραν, quolibet die, quamdiu hodie vocatur, ne quis ex vobis induretur fraude peccati! Arguimus: Hodiernus dies ad poenitentiam agendam cuilibet peccatori a Deo est destinatus: Omnis praesens vitae dies est hodiernus: Ergo.

4) Ex Ps. XXIII, 6. Profecto bonitas & misericordia insequentur me omnibus diebus vitae meae. Quae verba concinne exponit D. GEIER. Indicatur h. l. gratiae diuinae ardor, quae nos incuriosos, immo auerfantes ac fugientes, auide insequitur, quae praeuenit nolentem, vt bene velit, volentem adiuuat, vt perficiat, operantem subsequitur, vt perseueret; neque vllo die peccatorem destituit.

Dicis: Verba haec intelliguntur de peccatore poenitente, non de indurato. Resp. Adduximus haec verba, vt ostendamus, gratiam Dei vniuerfalem comitari peccatorem toto vitae tempore: Notamus tamen Deum vel contumacifluos peccatores ad poenitentiam cohortari, quod discimus

5) ex Ierem. III, 1. Dicere (solent): En! (Si) dimiserit vir uxorem suam, & haec abiuerit ab eo fueritque viro alii: num reuertetur ad eam denuo? Nonne profanando profanabitur terra illa? Sed tu scortata es cum fociis multis! Reuertere tamen ad me! Dictum Iehouae. Tam inusitata & stupenda est clementia Dei, vt animam, iteratis peccatis mortiferis aeque pollutam, ac adulteram, cum multis amafiis scortatam, ad se reuocet, & ad resipiscentiam stimulet.


### XII. Does God wish to convert all men, even the hardened?: Even though the hearers of Etsiæ were blinded and hardened

Even though the hearers of Etsiæ were blinded and hardened. See Ef. VI, 9. Nevertheless, he cried out with a clear voice:

Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: then let him return to Iehouam, who will have mercy on him, and to our Lord, who will multiply to pardon.

Proof. 1) From I Cor. VI, 9. Do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived! Neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor effeminate, nor abusers of themselves with mankind, nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners will inherit the kingdom of God. And such indeed you were: but you were washed, but you were sanctified, and you were justified in the name of the Lord Iesu, and by the Spirit of our God.

By these words the Apostle teaches that the most wicked sinners, anticipated by the mercy of God and brought to repentance, were translated from a state of wrath to a state of grace.

2) The Iudæi, in their cruelty, like barren branches, were broken off from the olive tree, Christ, Rom. XI, 19. Yet God is able to graft them in again, v. 23. Many of them were converted, and even exploded, Actor. II, 42. 3) The Niniuita, whose wickedness had ascended before God, repented at the preaching of Iona, and obtained forgiveness of sins, Ion.

III, 10. 4) The most obstinate sinners were converted: Manasses, hardened to the extreme; Dauid, having fallen enormously twice, obtained pardon twice; Salomo, enticed to idolatry; Nabuchodonosor, a seducer of others; the most vile harlot, Luc. VII. and many, many others.

The example of Paulli should not be passed over in silence, who says of himself in I Tim. I, 15:

I am the chief of sinners: But for this reason I obtained mercy, that in me first Iesus Christus might show all longsuffering as an example to those who would believe in Him for eternal life. Proof. e.

That sinful man falls into eternal destruction by voluntary fault, and not by a decree of God absolutely denying converting grace, the most merciful God teaches everywhere in the sacred scriptures, Ier. XXXII, 33. They turned their back to me, and not their face, so that, although I taught them, teaching them, rising early and teaching, yet they were not obedient to receive instruction, Matth. XXIII, 37. O Ierusalem! Ierusalem! who kills the prophets (now and formerly) and stones those sent to you! How often I wanted to gather your children in the way a hen gathers her chicks under her wings! but you were not willing! God, having sent sacred heralds, earnestly and intensely desires to convert the most wicked sinners: but the obstinacy of many is so malicious that they reject the word of God and despise medicinal grace.

The Antithesis was formerly that of the Nouatianorum, who decreed that there was no return to repentance for those who had fallen after baptism; today, however, it is that of the Socinianorum, who deny that a sinful man, who has once shaken off the yoke of sin, and has fallen into mortal sin and is entangled in it, so that he has contracted a habit of sinning, can be renewed to repentance. Let us examine their arguments.

I. Whoever hardens malicious sinners, does not want to convert them.

But God &c. Therefore. The minor is evident from Ef. VI, 10. and the example of Pharao, Exod. X, 1. Response.

1) Whoever effectively hardens sinful men, by injecting hardness into their hearts, does not want to convert them; I concede. But God is said to harden partly permissively, by just judgment permitting that the sinner, who does not allow himself to be softened, being left to himself, remains hard: partly negatively, by withdrawing regenerating and justifying grace, as a punishment for preceding sins.

2) Pharao hardened himself, Exod. VII, 15. namely, actively.

Therefore, God concurs in hardening in another way, namely, Pharao effectively and directly, God permissively and indirectly.

Conf. PFEIFFERI dubia vexat. p. 250 (*).

II. Who- ((*)) To explain the matter a little more fully, these are primarily to be considered: 1) The effect that God willed must be accurately distinguished from the contrary event that God foresaw, just as to say PARS III. SECT. I. Rrr rr con-

SECT. I. Rrr rr conWhoever abandons a sinful man, and withdraws his grace from him, he does not will to convert the same; But God [does abandon] the hardened sinner, etc. Therefore.

The minor is evident 1) by the example of Pharaoh; 2) from 2 Chron. XII, 5. You have abandoned me; therefore I also have abandoned you into the hand of Shishak; likewise 2 Chron. XV, 2. If you abandon Jehovah, he will abandon you.

Response 1) Although God withdrew from Pharaoh the indwelling grace, he did not however deprive him of assisting grace, as long as he was on the way; since through the word and miracles he reminded him of his duty, and exhibited his grace to him. 2) D. Hulsemann discourses excellently on the withdrawal of divine grace in his dissertation on sin, § 5. By no means does God so withdraw his grace that he leaves none at all, or that he removes every sin-prohibiting [influence]: because he left the law, by which it is prohibited, both inscribed upon nature and prescribed to all; also by the threat of punishment, as well as by the examples of his judgment against sins, he recalls all, and finally, to those falling into sins, even against conscience, he leaves exciting grace, which warns that one must return to the grace of original sonship.

This is gathered from the very context of 2 Chron. XII, 6: But the princes of Israel and the king humbled themselves; and they said: Jehovah is just. When therefore Jehovah saw that they had humbled themselves, the word of Jehovah came to Shemaiah saying: They have humbled themselves, therefore I will not destroy them.

The same can be shown from 2 Chron. XV, 3.

III. He who does not will to hear crying sinners, does not intend their conversion: God does not will to hear hardened sinners crying out: Therefore. The minor is proved from Prov. I, 28. They will cry to me, but I will not hear; in the morning they will seek me, but they will not find me.

Response. The impious, with calamity pressing, cry out from impatience, not from a serious purpose of converting themselves to God. They seek God, that they may be freed from punishment, not from guilt.

A cry, proceeding from a penitent heart, is heard by God. For everyone who shall call upon the name of Jehovah, shall be delivered, Joel III, 5.

IV. Whom God has delivered into a reprobate sense, him he does not will to convert: Hardened sinners etc. Rom.

I, 28. Ps. LXXXI, 12. 13. Therefore.

Response. Those sinners whom God has delivered into a reprobate sense by a consequent judicial will, them he invites to repentance by an antecedent will of his most benign divinity, Rom. II, 4. For neither is the antecedent will, or that of mercy, extinguished by the consequent will, or that of justice.

V. God takes away the talent from the useless servant, Matth. XXV, 28. Therefore he denies him converting grace.

Response. By the talent in the cited place is understood an increase of grace, or a more intense and abundant [one] we are accustomed: I will increase this man with benefits, and I will leave nothing untried; but I already sense that it will happen that the ungrateful man will become the more impudent, the more kind I shall have been toward him: I will only harden him with that.

2) It stands clearly written that this most sad outcome was by no means God's counsel and determining will, Rom. XI, 11, where the little word, ἵνα, without doubt denotes the end, which the Ambassador of Christ denies that God had proposed to himself.

3) God condemns hardness of heart, and warns men to flee from it, Hebr. III, 8.

12. 13. IV, 7.

11. add. Ps.

XCV, 8. Therefore he himself does not effect it.

4) The cause of a hardened heart is expressly said to be the deceitful persuasion of sin, and the malignant Spirit, Hebr. III, 13.

2 Cor. IV, 4. coll. with Eph. II, 2.

Therefore to attribute the same effect to God is truly the greatest injury.

5) Man hardens himself, as even now, so before, and more often, Ex. VIII, 32. Jerem.

V, 3. Zachar.

VII, 11. 12.

6) Before God abandons and punishes a hardened man, he tolerates him with slowness of anger and great leniency, Rom. IX, 17. coll. with the following v. 22. By what counsel, however?

Surely a most excellent one, that the wicked man may use the space for repenting, 2 Petr. III, 9. 7) Sometimes he is said to do something, who predicts that it will happen.

Behold a clear example! Jerem. I, 10. And so God is said to have hardened Pharaoh's mind, not because he himself effected it, but because he certainly predicted that it would so happen, and by the clearest documents of his kindness and leniency, and power, and severity, he openly signified that he had left nothing undone which pertained to correcting Pharaoh, but that Pharaoh himself was the author and effector of such obstinacy of mind.

rior degree of grace, not the first assisting grace, i.e., standing before the door of the heart and knocking, so that it may be opened, Apoc. III, 20.

VI. God is weary of repenting, Ier. XV, 6. E. He does not wish to give repentance to disobedient sinners. Resp. In the cited place, the discourse is not about the denial of repentance, but about the retraction of the decree concerning the temporal punishments to be inflicted. God did not wish to show mercy any longer, and to take away the punishments, says VATABLVS in this place, p. 293. This is evident from the following words, v. 7. Therefore I will winnow them with a winnowing fan in the gates of the land; I will bereave, I will destroy my people: because they have not turned from their ways. Meanwhile, many are stirred to repentance through temporal punishments. This is what we learn from Ier. XVIII, 7. 8. At the moment I speak against a nation, or against a kingdom, to pluck up and to destroy and to ruin. But if that nation has turned from its malice, on account of which I spoke against it; I will repent of the evil that I thought to do to it.

VII. For whom one must not pray, they cannot be converted: For the hardened, etc. Ier. VII, 16. c. XI, 14. c. XIV, 11. Resp. God does not forbid praying for the conversion of sinners, and for the forgiveness of guilt through faith in the Messiah, for God wills this to be done and has promised to hear it, Ier. XXIX, 12. 13.; but He forbids praying for the temporal punishment, the deportation to Babylon, to be remitted for the obstinate Jews. But this temporal [punishment] is a sermon of real repentance. See Lev. XXVI, 41. 42.

Objection: But temporal punishment rarely has eternal punishment as a companion, because they are extinguished in flagrant sin, as Zimri and Cozbi, Num. XXV, 6. Resp. Our discourse is about sinners established in the way of life, whom the long-suffering of God entices to repentance, not about the finally impenitent, who die in impenitence, or are snatched away by sudden death in an illicit act: for that the door of mercy and indulgence is closed to sinners at the hour of death is an established truth (ἐξαγώνιον).

Latin:

Esaiæ auditores erant occæcati & obdurati. Vid. Ef. VI, 9.

Nihilominus clara voce clamitabat: Deferat impius viam suam, & vir iniquitatis cogitationes suas: tum reuertatur ad Iehouam, qui miseribitur eius, & ad Dominum nostrum, qui multiplicabit condonare.

Prob. d. 1) Ex I Cor. VI, 9. Annuon scitis, quod iniusti regnum Dei pro hæreditate non possidebunt? Ne errate! Neque scortatores, neque idololatræ, neque machi, neque molles, neque concumbentes cum maribus, neque fures, neque auari, neque ebriosi, neque calumniatores, neque raptores regnum Dei in hæreditatem possidebunt. Et hæc quidem eratis: Sed abluti estis, sed sanctificati estis, & justificati estis in nomine Domini Iesu, & per Spiritum Dei nostri.

Quibus verbis Apostolus docet, peccatores sceleratissimos misericordia Dei præuentos, & ad pœnitentiam reductos, e statu iræ in statum gratiæ translatos esse.

2) Iudæi incrudelitate sua, velut steriles rami, effracti sunt ex olea Christo, Rom. XI, 19. potens tamen Deus est, vt eos rursus inserat, v. 23. quorum plurimi conuersi sunt, etiam explodebant, Actor. II, 42. 3) Niniuita, quorum malitia ascenderat coram Deo, prædicante Iona, resipuerunt, & veniam peccatorum consecuti sunt, Ion.

III, 10. 4) Conuersi sunt peccatores obstinatissimi, Manasses, extremo gradu induratus, Dauid, bis enormiter lapsus, bis veniam adeptus, Salomo, ad idololatriam pellectus, Nabuchodonosor, aliorum seductor, fædissima meretrix, Luc. VII. & alii longe plurimi.

Silentio prætermittendum non est exemplum Paulli, qui I Tim.

I, 15. de seipso inquit: Peccatorum primus sum ego: Sed propterea misericordiam consecutus sum, vt in me primo demonstraret Iesus Christus omnem longanimitatem ad exemplar illorum, qui credituri erant in ipsum in vitam æternam. Prob. e.

Quod homo peccator ex voluntaria culpa, non autem ex decreto Dei, gratiam conuertentem absolute denegantis, in æternum ruat exitium, Deus misericordissimus in facris litteris passim docet, Ier. XXXII, 33. Obuerterunt mihi ceruicem, & non facies, vt, licet, (docuerim) docendo eos, matutinando & docendo, non tamen illi fuerint audientes, ad admittendum disciplinam, Matth. XXIII, 37. O Ierusalem! Ierusalem! quæ occidis prophetas (nunc & olim) & lapidas missos ad te! quoties volui congregare liberos tuos eo modo, quo congregat gallina pullos suos sub alas! sed non voluistis! Deus, missis præconibus sacris, peccatores sceleratissimos conuertere serio impenseque cupit: at tam malitiosa multorum est contumacia, vt verbum Dei repellant, gratiamque medicinalem contemnant.

Antithesis fuit olim Nouatianorum, qui lapsis post baptifmum reditum ad pœnitentiam minime patere statuebant; hodie autem est Socinianorum, negantium, hominem peccatorem, qui semel ingem peccati excussit, in peccatum mortiferum prolapsum, eidemque implicitum, vt peccandi habitum contraxerit, renouari posse ad pœnitentiam. Quorum argumenta expendamus.

I. Quicunque peccatores malitiosos indurat, is non vult eosdem conuertere.

Atqui Deus &c. Ergo. Minor patet ex Ef. VI, 10. & exemplo Pharaonis, Exod.

X, 1 Respo. 1) Quicunque homines peccatores effective indurat, duritiem cordibus ipsorum immittendo, is non vult eos conuertere; concedo. At Deus indurare dicitur partim permissiue, iusto indicio permittendo, vt peccator, qui se molliri non patitur, sibi permissus, durus maneat: partim negatiue, gratiam regenerantem & iustificantem subtrahendo, in pœnam antegressorum peccatorum. 2) Pharao seipsum indurauit, Exod.

VII, 15. scil. actiue. E.

Deus alio modo concurrit ad indurationem, scil. Pharao effective & directe, Deus permissiue & indirecte. Conf.

PFEIFFERI dubia vexat. p. 250 (*).

II. Qui- (*) Vt rem paullo vberius explicemus, hæc sunt in primis consideranda: 1) Accurate discernendus est effectus, quem Deus voluit, ab euentu contrario, quem Deus præuidit, sicut dicere PARS III.

SECT. I. Rrr rr conII. Quicunque hominem peccatorem deserit, & gratiam suam illi subtrahit, is non vult eundem convertere; Atqui Deus peccatorem induratum &c. Ergo.

Minor patet 1) exemplo Pharaonis; 2) ex 2 Chron. XII, 5. Vos deseruistis me; ideo etiam deserui vos in manu Schischacki; item 2 Chron. XV, 2. Si deserueritis Iehouam, deseret vos.

Resp. 1) Licet Deus subtraxerit Pharaoni gratiam inhabitantem, non tamen ipsum destituit gratia assistente, quoad in via fuit; quum per verbum & miracula ipsum officio commonefecerit, gratiamque suam ipsi exhibuerit. 2) De gratiæ divinæ subtractione præclare disserit D. Hvlsemann. in differt. de peccato §. 5. Nequaquam Deus ita gratiam suam subtrahit, vt nullam plane relinquat, vel vt omne prohibens peccatum subducat: quia legem, qua prohibetur, tum inscriptam naturæ, tum præscriptam omnibus reliquit; pœnæ etiam comminatione, vt & exemplis iudicii sui aduersus peccata omnes reuocat, & denique labentibus in peccata, etiam contra conscientiam, relinquit gratiam excitantem, quæ monet redeundum in pristinæ filiationis gratiam.

Id quod ex ipso contextu 2 Chron. XII, 6. colligitur: Humiliarunt vero se principes Isräelis, & rex; dixeruntque: Iustus est Iehouah. Cum ergo videret Iehouah, quod humiliassent se, factum est verbum Iehouæ ad Schemaiam dicendo: Humiliarunt se, ideo non perdam eos.

Idem ostendi potest ex 2 Chron. XV, 3.

III. Qui peccatores clamantes non vult audire, is illorum conuersionem non intendit: Deus peccatores induratos clamantes non vult audire: E. Minor probatur e Prou. I, 28. Clamabunt ad me, sed non exaudiam; mane quærent me, sed non inuenient me.

Resp. Impii, vrgente calamitate, clamant ex impatientia, non ex ferio proposito conuertendi se ad Deum. Quærunt Deum, vt liberentur a pœna, non a culpa.

Clamor, e corde pœnitenti profectus, a Deo exauditur. Omnis enim, qui inuocauerit nomen Iehouæ, eripietur, Ioel. III, 5.

IV. Quem Deus tradidit in sensum reprobum, illum non vult conuertere: Peccatores induratos &c. Rom. I, 28. Ps.

LXXXI, 12. 13. E.

Resp. Quos peccatores Deus tradidit in sensum reprobum voluntate consequente iudiciaria, illos voluntate antecedente benignissimum numen ad pœnitentiam inuitat, Rom. II, 4. Neque enim voluntas antecedens, siue misericordiæ, expungitur voluntate consequente, siue iustitiæ.

V. Deus talentum seruo inutili aufert, Matth. XXV, 28. E. denegat ipsi gratiam verticordiam.

Resp. Per talentum l.c. intelligitur augmentum gratiæ, siue intensior & vberior confueuimus: hunc ego hominem beneficiis augebo, nihilque intentatum relinquam; sed iam præsentio, fore, vt eo impudentior fiat ingratus ille, quo benignior in illum fuero: Ich werde ihn nur damit verhærten.

2) Perspicue scriptum exstat, tristissimum huncce euentum neutiquam fuisse Dei consilium ac determinantem voluntatem, Rom. XI, 11. vbi vocula, ἵνα, haud dubie denotat finem, quem Deum sibi propositum habuisse, Legatus Christi pernegat.

3) Deus damnat duritiem animi, hominesque admonet de ea fugienda, Hebr. III, 8.

12. 13. IV, 7.

11. add.

Ps. XCV, 8. Ergo eam ipse non efficit.

4) Caussa obdurati animi diserte dicitur esse fraudulenta peccati persuasio, & malignus Spiritus, Hebr. III, 13.

2 Cor. IV, 4. coll. cum Eph. II, 2.

Ergo eundem effectum Deo tribuere, est profecto maxima iniuria.

5) Homo semet ipse indurat, vt etiam nunc, ita ante, & sæpius, Ex. VIII, 32.

Ierem. V, 3.

Zachar. VII, 11. 12.

6) Prius, quam Deus induratum hominem deferat puniatque, tolerat eum tarditate iræ & magna lenitudine, Rom. IX, 17. coll. cum seqq. v. 22. Quo nam autem consilio?

Sane optimo, vt improbus spatio resipiscendi vtatur, 2 Petr. III, 9. 7) Facere aliquid interdum is dicitur, qui illud futurum prædicit.

Luculentum en! exemplum, Ierem. I, 10. Itaque Deus Pharaonis animum indurasse dicitur, non quod ipse id effecerit, sed quod certe ita euenturum prænuntiauerit, clarissimique documentis suæ & benignitatis lenitudinisque, & potentiæ, & seueritatis, aperte significarit, se nihil fecisse reliqui, quod ad corrigendum Pharaonem pertineret, ipsum vero Pharaonem esse tantæ obstinationis animi auctorem atque effectorem.

rior gratiae gradus, non gratia prima assistens, i. e. stans ante ostium cordis & pulsans, vt aperiatur, Apoc. III, 20.

VI. Deus est fessus poenitendo, Ier. XV, 6. E. immorigeris peccatoribus non vult dare poenitentiam. Resp. Loco citato non est sermo de denegatione poenitentiae, sed de retractatione decreti de committendis poenis temporalibus. Deus nolebat amplius misereri, & poenas auferre, inquit VATABLVS in h. l. p. 293. Patet id e verbis sequentibus v. 7. Quare ventilabo eos ventilabro in portis terrae; orbabo, perdam populum meum: quia a viis suis non sunt conuersi. Interim per poenas temporales multi ad poenitentiam excitantur. Id quod discimus e Ier. XVIII, 7. 8. Momento loquor contra gentem, aut contra regnum ad euellendum & ad destruendum & ad perdendum. Quod si conuersa fuerit gens ista a malitia sua, propter quam locutus sum contra eam; poenitebit me mali, quod cogitaui facere illi.

VII. Pro quibus non est orandum, illi non possunt conuerti: Pro induratis &c. Ier. VII, 16. c. XI, 14. c. XIV, 11. Resp. Deus non vetat orare pro conuersione peccantium, & pro culpae condonatione per fidem in Messiam, id enim Deus vult fieri & exauditionem promisit, Ier. XXIX, 12. 13.; sed vetat orare pro poena temporali, deportatione in Babyloniam obstinatis Iudaeis remittenda. Sed haec temporalis est concio poenitentiae realis. Vid. Leu. XXVI, 41. 42.

Instantia: Sed poena temporalis haud raro comitem habet poenam aeternam, propterea, quod in flagranti peccato exstinguuntur, vt Simri & Chasbi, Num. XXV, 6. Resp. Sermo nobis est de peccatoribus in via vitae constitutis, quos longanimitas Dei ad poenitentiam allicit, non de finaliter impoenitentibus, qui in impoenitentia decedunt, aut subita morte in actu illicito rapiuntur: nam in hora mortis ianuam misericordiae & indulgentiae peccatoribus occludi, ἐξαγώνιον est.


### XII. Does God wish to convert all men, even the hardened?: Even though the hearers of Etsiæ were blinded and hardened (continued)

VIII. Whoever swears that those who are always erring will not enter into the heavenly rest, he does not wish to convert them: But God, etc. Hebr. III, 11. 12. Resp. Those who are always erring are the finally impenitent, whom God rejects by a judicial will; whom, however, as long as they were in the way of life, He stimulated to repentance by an antecedent will.

IX. Whoever is already judged and condemned, to him the door of grace is closed; but everyone who does not believe is already judged: E. The minor is clear from Io. III, 18. Resp. 1) He who does not believe finally, or until the end of life, he is already judged, by reason of the divine reprobatory decree, made from eternity. But we are not dealing with the finally incredulous in the present. 2) He who does not believe for a time is already judged by the law; because the judgment, already passed by the law, presses upon him, nor is he liberated from it as long as he is an unbeliever (ἄπισος). For although liberation from the curse of the law has been obtained for him through Christ the redeemer; whence he could and ought to have applied it to himself through faith in Christ: yet he does not enjoy it, because he does not embrace with faith the liberation acquired by the redeemer and offered by the word of the gospel. But indeed, a sinner who is incredulous for a time can be converted and led to faith, which the examples of David, Peter, Thomas, Paul, and others teach.

X. That divine grace is denied to those who repent late, the example of the five foolish virgins shows, to whom, coming late, the door was closed, Matth. XXV, 10. I will answer with the words of GERHARD in his Harmony, c. 163, p. 836. Primarily and especially, Christ speaks here of the state in the future day of judgment, where the time of repentance and grace will have completely passed by. But if we should wish to accommodate this member of the parable to the death of man, it must be established that then at last the door is closed, and the time of repentance, grace and pardon punished, when the soul has been separated from the body.

XI. That converting grace is not offered to all hardened sinners is clear from the example of the sons of Eli, who did not listen to the voice of their father: because the Lord willed to slay them, 1 Sam. II, 25. And of Saul, whom God utterly deserted, so that He did not answer him either through dreams, or through Urim, or through the prophets, 1 Sam. XXVIII, 6. Resp. 1) God did not simply cut off recalling grace from the sons of Eli, since He earnestly intended to recall them to repentance through His word, announced by the ministry of their father: However, the words of the cited text, rendered simply from the Hebrew source by D. SEB. SCHMID, are as follows: The sons of Eli did not listen to the voice of their father, because Jehovah willed to slay them. 2) Saul remained under the shadow of the visible church, and thus was excited to repentance by the continuous voice of the law and the offering of light; although that special grace, by which God in the O.T. revealed future things, was not divinely granted to him.

XII. Esau did not find a place for repentance, even though he sought it with tears, Hebr. XII, 16. Therefore, God does not wish to give repentance to all sinners. Resp. In the cited passage, the discourse is not about the repentance of Esau (that Esau repented of his rash deed, his own tears testify); but about the repentance of Isaac, that even though Esau sought it with tears, he did not find a place for repentance, namely, so that the parent might repent of the blessing conferred by right of primogeniture upon Jacob, and revoke it.

Instance: Yet Esau, seeking the repentance of his father, but in vain, is a type of a sinner seeking the remission of sins from God the Father, but not finding it. Resp. Esau typically represents not every fallen man, but one sinning against the Holy Spirit, from whom the consequence of having fallen mortally is denied. Cf. SEBAST. SCHMID. in h. l. p. 1355.

XIII. God denies recalling grace to those sinning against the Holy Spirit, Hebr. VI, 6. c. X, 26. Therefore, He does not wish to convert all hardened sinners. Resp. Those sinning against the Holy Spirit are finally impenitent not because of denied recalling grace, but because of the voluntary and persevering rejection of the ordinary medium, i.e., the divine word, by which they were to be converted. Wherefore DANNHAV. says gravely in hodof. phænom. XI p. 1420: It is impossible that those sinning against the Holy Spirit be renewed to repentance, not by the impossibility of a reprobatory decree, but by human vice.

XIV. Sinners living outside the church are not recalled to repentance through the ordinary medium: Therefore, the converting grace of God is not universal. Resp. That nations living outside the church are not recalled to repentance through the solemn preaching of the divine word, they can accuse not the most merciful God, who intensely desires the repentance of all men; but their ancestors, who did not faithfully preserve the precious deposit of the evangelical lamp, as was fitting. Furthermore, they are called to the church, the workshop of grace, by the voice of nature, of conscience, and of the fame of the Christian religion scattered throughout the world, so that in it they may be converted through the ordinary medium of salvation.

XV. The authority of LUTHER seems to stand against us, saying: Although God promised pardon, as Augustine says, yet He did not promise this, that you will certainly return after a fall, just as Saul and Judas did not return. Resp. a) If God promised pardon to a sinner, He did not deny all converting grace to him. For the evangelical promise, by which pardon is offered to the sinner, is an efficacious medium of conversion. b) God did not promise that the sinner will certainly return: because He converts the sinner not by irresistible grace, but by resistible grace through ordinary media; which the sinner can reject.

Quest. XIII. What is the terminus a quo, and the terminus ad quem, of conversion, strictly so called? The terminus a quo of conversion, taken most strictly, is actual sins, insofar as, after they have been committed, they morally remain as ratified, or not retracted stated a), then habitual, insofar as they not only imply the lack of habitual perfection, which is due to be present, but also a propensity to all evils, which is the fountain and cause of actual sins b). The term to which it is nearest is contrition c): the remote term is faith in Christ d). Obf.

Obs. I. Sins can be viewed in two ways: 1) Physically, insofar as they are actions, and depend efficiently upon man: 2) Morally, insofar as they are actions against the law, and concern the right of some third party. Viewed in the former way, they have in common with all other actions that, because they imply man in respect to him, as an effect to his cause, they denominate him as sinning in the present when they are done, but as having sinned in the past after they have passed. Viewed in the latter way, however, they have this peculiar feature in common with other moral actions, which besides the agent also concern the right of some third party, that they induce an obligation in the agent, and hold the sinner, even after they have passed, as if bound under the action, or rather under the state resulting from the action; e.g., just as in civil matters a contract once entered into induces an obligation in the contracting parties, and holds them as if bound under the state of the contract, even if the act of contracting has long since passed; so a sin once committed induces an obligation in the sinner, and holds him as if bound under the state of sin, even though the act of sinning has long since passed.

But since the will of men is mutable, and they are accustomed to retract what they have once done, once the will is changed, and, as far as in them lies, to render it morally void; therefore, in order for past sins to remain morally, and to hold a man in the state of sin, it is required further that they be held as ratified by subsequent acts of the will, or at least that they not be retracted by acts of the subsequent will, just as for a contract once entered into, if it is to endure morally, it is required that it be held as ratified afterwards by the contracting parties, or at least that it not be retracted by either of the contracting parties. Obf.

II. Not only ratification, or non-retraction, is the cause why sins, after they have passed, remain morally, and hold the sinner in the state of sin. For since sins are forbidden by divine law, and by this very fact, that they violate the divine law, they most gravely offend God, they induce in the sinner the guilt of fault, and an obligation to make satisfaction for the offense and injury brought upon God. Whence they do not have it from the mere ratification, or non-retraction, of the sinner that they remain morally, nor can they be abolished by his mere retraction.

For even if the sinner should most seriously retract within himself his past sins, he will still remain guilty of fault on account of the violated law of God, and obligated to make satisfaction for the offense and injury brought upon God. But as long as the guilt of fault and the obligation to make satisfaction remain, so long do sins remain morally and the man in the state of sin. Wherefore, in order that sins may be morally abolished, and the sinner be transferred from the state of sin into the state of grace, two things are required: 1) That sins be no longer held as ratified, but be retracted: 2) That to God, the supreme Lord and legislator, for the offense and injury brought upon Him, full satisfaction be exhibited, and thus God who was offended be reconciled.

Prob. a. Actual sins are held as ratified as long as they so please the unconverted sinner that he indulges in them and acts upon them, either because he is ignorant that they are forbidden by divine law, or because they flatter him under the appearance of an apparent good, e.g.,

The enemies of the gospel, by killing the Apostles, thought they were offering a holy service to God, John XVI, 2. To not a few, avarice is pleasing on account of the useful good, fornication on account of the pleasant good, etc.

XVI, 2. Not a few are pleased with avarice on account of the useful good, with fornication on account of the pleasant good &c. As long as the sinner does not hate these vices, or detest them, but rather takes such delight in them, that in the very proposes to himself to continue and persevere in them, those actual sins remain morally for as long (even if physically or really they do not survive), and man is detained in a state of sin.

Proof b. Actual sins are the immediate and proximate terminus a quo (starting point) of conversion; habitual sin is the mediate and remote terminus a quo. For since actual sins, when they have been committed, present themselves to the sinner's mind by their own nature and immediately, and burden and torment his conscience; but the habit of sinning becomes known only a posteriori and from the actual sins, of which it is the principle and cause: conversion is indeed directed in its acts toward them, and tends toward their abolition primarily, proximately, and immediately, yet in such a way that consequently and through the mediation of the acts of sinning it is also directed toward this [habit], as toward a more remote terminus, and one which is connoted in actual sins, as the proximate terminus, through the movement of the principle.
