Thus David, repenting after the committed crimes of adultery and murder, besides the crimes actually committed and now past, also seriously disapproved of and with much sorrow detested his innate malice, as the cause and source of the committed crimes: Behold! I was shaped in iniquity, and in sin did my mother warm me! Ps. LI, 7.

Proof c. Just as it is the office of the law to break and crush hearts of stone like a hammer, Jer. XXIII, 29, to denounce the wrath of God to transgressors of the law, Rom. IV, 15, and to adjudge them to death, 2 Cor. III, 6: So the terminus ad quem (end point) and the proximate and immediate effect of conversion through the law is CONTRITION, by which the sinful man, having recognized his sins from the divine law, seriously detests them with sorrow. Since, therefore, the Holy Spirit leads the sinner to contrition through the divine law, he no longer holds his past sins as valid, but retracts them; which retraction is completed by two acts, one of which pertains to the intellect, the other to the will. To the intellect pertains the recognition of sins, which is required as a necessary condition, without which the retraction of sins finds no place. Whence David: I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin (as a thing to be abhorred, detested, and retracted) is ever before me, Ps. LI, 5. This recognition of sin is an effect of illuminating grace. On the part of the will, there is required for the retraction of sins a displeasure toward them, which is either simple or efficacious. Simple displeasure is that by which something displeases the will according to some known reason of evil, without the intention of fleeing it. Efficacious displeasure is that by which a thing known as evil so displeases the will that it simultaneously intends to flee it. For the retraction of sins, any simple displeasure does not suffice; since it is also found in the impenitent, who see and approve better things, but follow the worse: but an efficacious displeasure is also required, joined with a serious purpose of fleeing sins; by which, indeed, we so turn away from sins that not only do we wish to render those committed undone, if it were possible, but we also abhor with our whole heart all others to be committed in the future: which displeasure we are accustomed to call, specifically, the detestation of sin. Furthermore, this detestation or efficacious displeasure (by which sins, even if they were voluntary while they were being committed, take on the nature of involuntary actions) is usually followed by pain and sadness of mind (to which pertain the stings and terrors of conscience), usually the more severe the more deeply the sinner considers his sins, God offended, and the punishments of this life and the next deserved. From which it shines forth that the retraction of sin becomes the detestation of the same, recognized from the law, joined with sorrow of mind.

Proof d. Just as the law is a schoolmaster unto Christ, Gal. III, 24, so contrition is a certain useful and necessary disposition for kindling faith in the sinner and obtaining salvation by faith, as MUSAUS says in disp. II. de convers. §. 60. To which D. FECHT. agrees in sylloge controv. disp. XXIX. §. 1. Theologians do not fear to call repentance, taken partially (contrition), in a sound sense, a disposition and preparation for faith, and a means of arriving at the end, from Matthew

Certainly, contrition is not a positive or causal medium for the kindling of faith, but is only a privative medium (such as the removal of impurities for the healing of a wound), by which the incapacity of the subject and the obstacles that would otherwise hinder the kindling of faith are removed. For God looks to the miserable and contrite in spirit, Ps. LXVI, 2. Faith in Christ is therefore the terminus of conversion to which it is remote; for this reason, that the Holy Spirit, by working contrition through the law, intends to dispose the heart of the sinner for the kindling of saving faith within him through the word of the gospel. However, when I call it remote, I would not have anyone think that faith is to be removed further from contrition, or to be separated: for contrition is joined with faith in the confessions of Christ by a most tight bond: repent and believe the gospel, Mark I, 15. Acts II, 38. 2 Cor. VII, 10; but by this very thing it is at least indicated that the light of faith does not arise through conversion from the law, but elsewhere through regeneration from the gospel, 1 Pet. I, 23. James I, 18.

Latin:

VIII. Quicunque iurat, semper errantes non venturos esse in requiem coelestem, ille non vult eos conuertere: Atqui Deus &c. Hebr. III, 11. 12. Resp. Semper errantes sunt finaliter impoenitentes, quos Deus voluntate iudiciaria reprobat; quos tamen, quoad fuerunt in via vitae, voluntate antecedente ad poenitentiam exstimulauit.

IX. Qui iam iudicatus & condemnatus est, illi porta gratiae occlusa; sed omnis, qui non credit, iam iudicatus est: E. Minor liquet ex Io. III, 18. Resp. 1) Qui non credit finaliter, siue vsque ad finem vitae, ille iam iudicatus est, ratione decreti diuini reprobatorii, ab aeterno facti. At de finaliter incredulis in praesenti non agimus. 2) Qui ad tempus non credit, iam iudicatus est per legem; eo, quod iudicium, a lege iam latum, ipsum premit, nec ab illo, quamdiu est ἄπισος, liberatur. Quamuis enim per Christum redemptorem ipsi parta sit liberatio a maledictione legis; -vnde illam sibi applicare poterat & debebat per fidem in Christum: ea tamen non fruitur, quia liberationem a redemptore acquisitam, & verbo euangelii oblatam, fide non amplectitur. At vero peccator ad tempus incredulus, conuerti & ad fidem perduci potest, quod exempla Dauidis, Petri, Thomae, Paulli, & aliorum docent.

X. Sero poenitentibus denegatam esse gratiam diuinam, ostendit exemplum quinque virginum fatuarum, quibus sero venientibus porta clausa erat, Matth. XXV, 10. Respondebo verbis GERHARDI in harmon. c. 163. p. 836. Primario ac praecipue Christus hic loquitur de statu in die iudicii futuro, vbi iam tempus poenitentiae & gratiae prorsus erit praeterlapsum. Quod si ad mortem hominis hoc parabolae membrum accommodare velimus, statuendum est, tum demum ianuam claudi, & tempus poenitentiae, gratiae ac veniae puniri, quando anima a corpore fuerit separata.

XI. Gratiam conuertentem non offerri omnibus peccatoribus induratis claret exemplo filiorum Eli, qui non audiuerunt vocem Patris sui: quia voluit Dominus occidere eos, 1 Sam. II, 25. & Saulis, quem Deus penitus deseruit, vt ipsi non responderit siue per somnia, siue per Vrim, siue per prophetas, 1 Sam. XXVIII, 6. Relp. 1) Filiis Eli Deus gratiam reuocatricem non simpliciter præcidit, quippe quos per verbum suum, ministerio patris annuntiatum, ad pœnitentiam reuocare serio intendit: Verba autem citati textus ex fonte hebræo a D. SEB. SCHMIDIO simpliciter reddita ita se habent: Filii Eli non audiuerunt vocem patris sui, quod vellet Iehouah eos occidere. 2) Saul mansit sub vmbraculo ecclesiæ visibilis, adeoque continua legis voce & luminis oblatione ad pœnitentiam excitatus est; quamuis ipsi gratia illa specialis, qua Deus in V. T. futura reuelabat, non fuerit diuinitus concessa.

XII. Esauus pœnitentiæ locum non inuenit, etsi cum lacrymis eam exquifiuerit, Hebr. XII, 16. E. Deus pœnitentiam omnibus peccatoribus dare non vult. Resp. Loco citato non est sermo de pœnitentia Esaui (Esauum temerarii facinoris pœnituisse, testantur ipsius lacrymæ); sed de pœnitentia Isaaci, quod etiamsi eam cum lacrymis quæsierit Esauus, pœnitentiæ tamen locum non inuenerit, vt nempe parentem benedictionis de iure primogenituræ in Iacobum collatæ pœniteret, eamque reuocaret.

Instantia: Esauus tamen, pœnitentiam patris, sed frustra, quærens, typus est peccatoris, remissionem peccatorum apud Deum Patrem quærentis, fed non inuenientis. Resp. Esauus typice repræsentat non quemuis hominem lapsum, sed peccantem in Spiritum S., a quo adqueinuis mortaliter lapsum negatur consequentia. Conf. SEBAST. SCHMID. in h. l. p. 1355.

XIII. Deus peccantibus in Spiritum S. gratiam reuocatricem denegat, Hebr. VI, 6. c. X, 26. E. non vult omnes peccatores induratos conuertere. Resp. Peccantes in Spiritum S. funt finaliter impœnitentes non ob denegatam gratiam reuocatricem, sed ob voluntariam & perseuerantem reiectionem ordinarii medii, h. e. verbi diuini, quo conuertendi erant. Quare grauiter inquit DANNHAV. hodof. phænom. XI p. 1420. Impossibile est, vt peccantes in Spiritum S. renouentur ad pœnitentiam, non impossibilitate decreti reprobatorii, sed vitii humani.

XIV. Peccatores, extra ecclesiam degentes, per ordinarium medium non reuocantur ad pœnitentiam: E. gratia Dei conuertrix non est vniuerfalis. Resp. Quod gentes extra ecclesiam degentes per solemnem verbi diuini prædicationem non reuocantur ad pœnitentiam, accusare possunt non Deum misericordissimum, omnium hominum resipiscentiam impense cupientem; fed maiores suos, qui lampadis euangelicæ pretiosum depositum non fideliter, vt par erat, seruarunt. Cæterum vocantur illi per vocem naturæ, conscientiæ, & famæ de religione christiana passim terrarum sparsæ, ad ecclesiam, officinam gratiæ, vt in illa per ordinarium salutis medium conuertantur.

XV. Obstare nobis videtur auctoritas LVTHERI, inquitentis: Quamquam Deus promisit veniam, sicut ait Augustus, tamen non promisit hoc, quod certo fis rediturus post lapsum, sicut Saul & Iudas non redierunt. Resp. a) Si Deus veniam peccatori promisit, non omnem gratiam conuertentem ipsi denegauit. Nam promissio euangelica, qua venia peccatori offertur, est efficax conuertendi medium. b) Non promisit Deus, quod peccator certo fit rediturus: quia peccatorem conuertit non gratia irresistibili, fed resistibili per media ordinaria; quæ peccator potest reiicere.

Quæst. XIII. Quis est conuersionis, strictissime dictæ, terminus a quo, & ad quem? Conuersionis, strictissime sumtæ, terminus a quo funt peccata cum actualia, quatenus, postquam admissa sunt, moraliter manent velut rata, aut non retrata etata a), tum habitualia, quatenus non solum important carentiam perfectionis habitualis, inesse debitae, sed etiam propensionem ad omnia mala, quae peccatorum actualium fons & causa est b). Terminus ad quem proximus est contritio c): remotus est fides in Christum d).

Obs. I. Peccata dupliciter spectari possunt: 1) Physice, in quantum sunt actiones, & ab homine efficienter dependent: 2) Moraliter, in quantum sunt actiones contra legem, & ius cuiusdam tertii concernunt. Priori modo spectata, commune habent cum aliis quibusvis actionibus, cum hominem ob respectum, quem ad eum, tanquam effectus ad suam causam, important, tum peccare in praesenti denominent, cum fiunt, peccasse autem in praeterito, postquam praeterierunt. Posteriori autem modo considerata, cum aliis actionibus moralibus, quae praeter agentem etiam ius cuiusdam tertii concernunt, hoc peculiare habent, vt in agente obligationem inducant, & peccantem, etiam postquam praeterierunt, sub actione, vel potius sub statu ex actione resultante, quasi constrictum teneant, v. gr. vt in ciuilibus contractus semel initus in contrahentibus obligationem inducit, eosque sub statu contractus quasi constrictos tenet, etiamsi actus contrahendi dudum praeterierit; ita peccatum semel patratum inducit in peccante obligationem, & tenet eum sub statu peccati quasi constrictum, licet actus peccandi dudum praeterierit.

Cum vero hominum voluntas mutabilis sit, & quae semel egerunt, postea mutata voluntate, retractare, &, quantum in ipsis est, moraliter irrita reddere soleant; ideo, vt peccata praeterita moraliter maneant, & hominem in statu peccati detineant, requiritur insuper, vt postea per subsequentes voluntatis actus habeantur rata, vel certe, vt non per actus voluntatis subsequentis retractentur, perinde vt ad contractum semel initum, si moraliter durare debeat, requiritur, vt postea a contrahentibus ratus habeatur, vel certe vt a neutro contrahentium retractetur.

Obs. II. Non sola ratihabitio, aut non-retractio, in causa est, cur peccata, postquam praeterierunt, moraliter maneant, & hominem peccatorem in statu peccati detineant. Cum enim peccata lege diuina interdicta sint, & per hoc ipsum, quod legem diuinam violant, Deum grauissime offendant, inducunt in peccante reatum culpae, & obligationem ad satisfaciendum pro offensione ac iniuria Deo illata. Vnde nec a sola peccantis ratihabitione, seu non-retractione habent, quod moraliter manent, nec etiam per solam eius retractionem aboleri possunt.

Nam si vel maxime peccator serio retractet secum peccata praeterita, adhuc manebit reus culpae ob violatam legem Dei, & obligatus ad satisfaciendum pro offensione & iniuria Deo illata. Quamdiu autem manet reatus culpae & obligatio ad satisfaciendum, tamdiu moraliter manent peccata & homo in statu peccati. Quamobrem vt peccata moraliter aboleantur, & homo peccator e statu peccati in statum gratiae transferatur, duo requiruntur: 1) Vt peccata non amplius habeantur rata, sed retractentur: 2) Vt Deo, supremo Domino & legislatori, pro offensione & iniuria illata, plena satisfactio exhibeatur, adeoque Deus offensus reconcilietur.

Prob. a. Peccata actualia tamdiu habentur rata, quamdiu peccatori non converso sic placent, vt ipsis indulgeat & operetur, vel quia ignorat, ea lege diuina esse prohibita, vel quia specie boni apparentis ipsi abblandiuntur, v. gr.

Gentiles nesciebant, suam idololatriam esse lege diuina interdictam (quamuis isthac ignorantia esset supina, crassa & affectata). Hostes euangelii Apostolos occidendo putabant, se cultum Deo sacrum offerre, Ioann.

XVI, 2. Haud paucis placet auaritia ob bonum vtile, scortatio ob bonum iucundum &c. Quamdiu peccator haec vitia non odit, aut detestatur, sed potius illis ita delectatur, vt in ips ipsis pergere ac perfeuerare sibi proponat, tamdiu peccata illa actualia moraliter manent (licet physice, aut realiter non supersint), & homo in statu peccati detinetur.

Prob. b. Peccata actualia sunt terminus conuersionis a quo immediatus & proximus; peccatum habituale est terminus a-quo mediatus & remotus. Cum enim peccata actualia, vbi patrata sunt, peccatoris animo per ſe ipsa & immediate obuersentur, eiusque conscientiam onerent & angant; habitus vero peccandi a posteriori demum & ex actualibus peccatis, quorum principium & caussa est, innotelcat: fertur conuersio quidem suis actibus in illa, & tendit ad illorum abolitionem primo, proxime & immediate, ita tamen, vt consequenter & mediantibus actibus peccandi etiam in hunc feratur, tanquam in terminum remotiorem, & qui in peccatis actualibus, tanquam termino proximo, per motum principii-connotatur. Ita Dauid, post patrata adulterii & homicidii scelera resipiscens, præter scelera actu commissa, & iam præterita improbauit etiam serio, ac multo cum dolore detestatus est suam connatam malitiam, tanquam patratorum scelerum caussam & fontem: Ecce! in iniquitate formatus sum, & in peccato calefecit me mater mea! Pf. LI, 7.

Prob. c. Quemadmodum officium legis est, corda saxea instar mallei frangere & conterere, Ier. XXIII, 29. transgressoribus legis iram Dei denuntiare, Rom. IV, 15. eosque morti adiudicare, 2 Cor. III, 6: Ita conuersionis per legem terminus ad quem & effectus proximus, atque immediatus est CONTRITIO, qua homo peccator agnita ex lege diuina peccata serio cum dolore detestatur. Cum igitur Spiritus S. per legem diuinam ad contritionem perducit peccatorem, hic peccata præterita non amplius habet rata, sed eadem retractat: quæ retractatio duobus actibus, quorum vnus ad intellectum, alter ad voluntatem pertinet, absoluitur. Ad intellectum pertinet agnitio peccatorum, quæ tanquam necessaria conditio, sine qua peccatorum retractatio locum haud inuenit, prærequiritur. Vnde Dauid: Præuaricationes meas agnosco: & peccatum meum (tanquam res abominanda, detestanda, retractanda) coram me est iugiter, Pf. LI, 5. Hæc peccati agnitio est effectus gratiæ illuminantis. Ex parte voluntatis requiritur ad peccatorum retractationem eorum displicentia, quæ est vel simplex, vel efficax. Simplex displicentia est, quæ secundum aliquam rationem mali cognitam voluntati aliquid displicet, sine intentione illud fugiendi. Efficax displicentia est, qua res cognita, tanquam mala, ita voluntati displicet, vt simul illam fugere intendat. Ad peccatorum retractationem non sufficit quæuis displicentia simplex; quippe quæ datur etiam in impœnitentibus, qui meliora vident probantque, deteriora sequuntur: sed requiritur etiam displicentia efficax, cum serio peccata fugiendi proposito coniuncta; qua nimirum peccata ita auersamur, vt non solum commissa, ſi fieri posset, velimus reddere infecta, sed etiam ab aliis omnibus in posterum committendis toto pectore abhorremus: quam displicentiam, speciatim peccati detestationem nuncupare solemus. Porro hanc detestationem fiue displicentiam efficacem (qua peccata, etsi, dum patrarentur, voluntaria essent, inuitarum actionum, naturam induunt) dolor ac tristitia animi (quo pertinent morsus ac pauores conscientiæ) insequi solet, tanto plerumque grauior, quanto penitius peccator peccata, Deum offensum, pœnas huius & alterius vitæ promeritas considerat. E quibus elucescit, quod retractatio peccati fit eiusdem ex lege agniti detestatio, cum dolore animi coniuncta.

Prob. d. Sicut lex est pædagogus ad Christum, Gal. III, 24. ita contritio est dispositio quædam vtilis & necessaria ad fidem in peccatore accendendam & salutem fide obtinendam, dicente MVSÆO disp. II. de conuers. §. 60. Cui suffragatur D. FECHT. in sylloge controu. disp. XXIX. §. 1. Pœnitentiam pàrtialiter acceptam (contritionem) sano sensu dispositionem & præparationem ad fidem, mediumque perueniendi ad finem vocare non verentur Theologi ex Matth.

Nimirum contrititio non est medium positivum, aut causale accendendæ fidei, sed est tantum medium privativum (quale est puris remotio ad sanandum vulnus), quo removetur incapacitas subiecti & obstacula, quæ alias impedirent accensionem fidei. Ad miseruni enim & contritum spiritu respicit Deus, Ps. LXVI, 2. Est itaque fides in Christum terminus conversionis ad quem remotus; ideo, quod Spiritus S., per legem contritionem operando, intendit cor peccatoris disponere ad accendendam in ipso per verbum evangelii fidem salvificam. Cum autem remotum appello, nolim aliquis existimet, fidem a contritione longius removendam, aut seiungendam esse: arctissimo quippe nexu contritio cum fide in confessionibus Christi copulatur: resipiscite & credite evangelio, Marc. I, 15. Act. II, 38. 2 Cor. VII, 10; verum hoc ipso saltem indigitatur, non per conversionem ex lege, sed aliunde per regenerationem ex evangelio lucem fidei oriri, 1 Petr. I, 23. Iac. I, 18.


### Q. XIV. In what does conversion, taken in the most special sense, formally consist?

Conversion, taken in the strictest sense, formally consists in the excitation of contrition, through the word of the law, by which the hard heart of the sinner is softened, prepared, and disposed by the Holy Spirit for faith to be kindled in him by the voice of the gospel.

Proof. These things are evident from what has already been said, and also from Apol. A. C. p. 86. That faith, of which we speak, exists in penitence, that is, it is conceived in the terrors of the conscience, which feels the wrath of God against our sins, and seeks the remission of sins, and to be freed from sin. And in such terrors, and other afflictions, this faith ought to grow and be confirmed. Wherefore it cannot exist in those who live according to the flesh, who delight in their own desires, and obey them.

Latin:

Conversio strictissime sumta formaliter consistit in excitatione contritionis, per verbum legis, quo a Spiritu S. cor durum peccatoris mollitur, præparatur & disponitur ad fidem voce evangelii in eo accendendam.

Prob. Patent hæc e iam dictis, nec non ex Apol. A. C. p. 86. Fides illa, de qua loquimur, exsistit in pænitentia, hoc est, concipitur in terroribus conscientiæ, quæ sentit iram Dei aduersus nostra peccata, & quærit remissionem peccatorum, & liberari a peccato. Et in talibus terroribus, & aliis afflictionibus debet hæc fides crescere & confirmari. Quare non potest exsistere in his, qui secundum carnem vivunt, qui delectantur cupiditatibus suis, & obtemperant eis.


### Q. XV. What is the end of conversion?

The proximate end of conversion is regeneration a): the ultimate, on the part of men, is eternal life b); on the part of God, the glory of the divine name c).

Proof. a. Since conversion through the law excites in the heart of the sinner contrition, which is a disposition for the kindling of faith, it clearly appears that the Holy Spirit, by crushing the hard heart, intends to tend toward the regeneration of the contrite sinner: this is what we have clearly shown above from Acts 2:38. Proof b.

Sorrow, which is according to God, works repentance unto salvation, not to be repented of, 2 Cor. VII, 10. God, through converting grace, by making the sinner sorrowful through the law, works repentance unto salvation, namely, so that repentance taken μερικῶς [partially], or contrition, is not indeed a causal means of salvation, yet it is a means of the divine order. Which divine order we explained above in qu.

IX. Proof c. When the apostles and the brethren who were throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God, they praised God, saying: then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance unto life, Acts XI, 18. The goodness of God is to be praised, who seeks him who is bleating, and entices the recidivist harlot to Himself, Jer. III, 1.

Latin:

Finis proximus conversionis est regeneratio a): ultimus, ex parte hominum, vita æterna b); ex parte Dei, gloria nominis diuini c).

Prob. a. Cum conversio per legem excitet in corde peccatoris contritionem, quæ est dispositio ad fidem accendendam, liquido patet, Spiritum S. cor durum conterendo intendere tendere regenerationem peccatoris contriti: id quod supra dilucide ostendimus ex Act. 11, 38.

Prob. b. Tristitia, quæ secundum Deum est, pænitentiam ad salutem non pænitendam operatur, 2 Cor. VII, 10. Deus, per gratiam convertentem, peccatorem ex lege contristando operatur pænitentiam ad salutem, nimirum ut pænitentia μερικῶς accepta, sive contritio, non quidem sit medium salutis causale, attamen ut sit medium ordinis divini. Quem ordinem divinum supra qu. IX. exposuimus.

Prob. c. Cum apostoli & fratres, qui erant per Iudæam, audiverunt, quod etiam gentes accepissent verbum Dei, laudaverunt Deum, dicentes: ubique ergo, etiam ethnicis Deus pænitentiam dedit ad vitam, Act. XI, 18. Laudanda est bonitas Dei, qui quem balantem quærit, & scortatricem recidivam ad se allicit, Ier. III, 1.


### Q. XVI. Does God convert the sinner with irresistible grace?

Men can resist converting grace.

Obs. I. Distinguish between natural and malicious resistance. The former is otherwise called congenital, and flows immediately from the corrupted nature of man, and is common to all men, which, through preparing grace joined to the word of God, is indeed diminished and inhibited, but not rooted out. For there is a struggle of the flesh against the spirit, even in the regenerate. See Rom. VII, 23. Gal. V, 17. Therefore, since man, through the corruption of nature, cannot but resist the divine law, because the flesh does not submit to the law, nor indeed can it, Rom. VIII, 7; converting grace breaks this necessity of resisting, and causes man to be able to admit the means, but not that he must necessarily and irresistibly admit them; rather, he retains the liberty to resist these means. The latter is otherwise called voluntary, affected, and morose, and is sought out by the peculiar fault and deliberate effort of man, and thus proceeds from malice, contracted of one's own accord: which in some is more stubborn, in others less stubborn, in some temporary, in others final. For the Savior teaches that it is harder for the rich to enter the kingdom of heaven than for the poor, Matt. XIX, 23. The same teaches that publicans and harlots can be converted and saved more easily than the Pharisees, since these were inflated by the persuasion of their own righteousness, Matt. XXI, 31. Indeed, we also learn by experience that those occupied with false opinions, inflamed with preposterous zeal, immersed in graver vices, and frequently relapsing into heretical sins, resist converting grace more vehemently than those who avoid such dangerous reefs of salvation. Those who are finally impenitent resist most stubbornly, among whom those who sin against the Holy Spirit stand out.

Obs. II. Some authors believe that extraordinary conversion was irresistible: a point which others call into doubt. We gather that Paul’s extraordinary conversion was not simply irresistible from Acts XXVI, 19, where the Apostle says: I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision. By which words he implies that he could have resisted, had he wished. Such a powerful calling did not take away from him the power of resisting, as HUGO GROTIUS judges in this place. Moses also resisted the heavenly apparition and calling, until the anger of Jehovah was kindled, Ex. IV, 14. D. HULSEMANN in brev. enucl. c. VI thef. XV, distinguishes between the calling and the conversion of Paul. Paul’s calling was indeed done irresistibly: but his conversion and regeneration were not done irresistibly, Acts IX, 4 seqq. For the former was done as if in an instant: but the latter (within three days) successively. Whence the consequence from the extraordinary and miraculous to the irresistible is not valid. For many resist miracles.

Latin:

Gratia convertenti homines peccatores resistere possunt.

Obs. I. Dist. inter repugnantiam naturalem, & malitiosam. Illa dicitur alias congenita, proximeque fluit ex natura hominis corrupta, & est communis omnibus hominibus, quæ per gratiam præparantem, verbo Dei coniunctam, imminuitur quidem & inhibetur, non autem radicitus tollitur. Datur enim lucta carnis adversus spiritum, etiam in renatis. Vid. Rom. VII, 23. Gal. V, 17. Idcirco, cum homo per naturæ corruptionem non possit non legi divinæ resistere, eo, quod caro legi non subiicit, neque enim potest, Rom. VIII, 7; gratia convertens hanc repugnandi necessitatem infringit, facitque, ut homo quidem admittere media possit, non autem ut necessario & irresistibiliter admittat, verum ut retineat libertatem mediis istis refragandi. Hæc dicitur alias voluntaria, affectata & morosa, estque peculiari hominis culpa & dedita opera accersita, atque adeo ex malitia, sponte contracta, profecta: quæ in aliis pertinacior, in aliis minus pertinax est, quorundam temporaria, quorundam finalis est. Docet enim Salvator, divites difficilius ingredi regnum cælorum, quam pauperes, Matth. XXIX, 23. Docet idem, publicanos & meretrices facilius posse converti & salvari, quam Pharisæos, quoniam hi persuasione propriæ iustitiæ inflati erant, Matth. XXI, 31. Quin experimento etiam discimus, vehementius resistere gratiæ convertenti homines, falsis occupatis opinionibus, zelo præpostero inflammatos, grauioribus vitiis immersos, fæpius relabentes in peccata præterita, quam declinantes istiusmodi periculosos salutis scopuli. Pertinacissime resistunt finaliter impoenitentes, quos inter eminent peccantes in Spiritum Sanctum.

Obs. II. Conversionem extraordinariam fuisse irresistibilem, censent nonnulli auctores: id quod alii in dubium vocant. Paulli conversionem extraordinariam non fuisse simpliciter irresistibilem, colligimus ex Act. XXVI, 19. vbi Apostolus dicit: Non fui incredulus cælesti visioni. Quibus verbis innuit, potuisse se, si voluisset, refragari. Tam potens vocatio non adimebat ei obsistendi potentiam, censente HVGONE GROTIO in h. l. Cælesti apparitioni ac vocationi resistebat etiam Moses, vsque dum furor Iehovæ accenderetur, c. IV, 14. D. HVLSEM. in breu. enucl. c. VI thes. XV, distinguit inter vocationem, & conversionem Paulli. Paulli vocatio quidem facta est irresistibiliter: sed non irresistibiliter facta est eius conversio & regeneratio, Act. IX, 4. seqq. Illa enim facta est quasi in instanti: hæc autem (intra triduum) successiue. Vnde ab extraordinario & miraculoso ad irresistibile non valet consequentia, Miraculis enim multi resistunt.


### Q. XVI. Does God convert the sinner with irresistible grace?: Obf. III

Obf. III.

Dist. between actual and possible irresistibility. Grace is called resistible to which one can by nature resist, whether one actually resists it or not: irresistible, to which one cannot by nature resist.

Obf. IV.

When a man lies dead in sins, and lives securely from day to day, thinking nothing of his own conversion, the most benevolent God prevents him, and by means of the Word, whether heard or read, and retained within the mind, presently excites good motions in him, which Theologians call inevitable, because their presence and sense cannot be avoided: which also can in a certain way be called irresistible, by reason of their origin and sense, since the sinner man can by no means oppose himself to the suggestion of them through the Word, and to their sense, but only to the consent.

The first motions, says D. IOAN. MVSÆVS, can be called irresistible, insofar as they anticipate our deliberation, so that it is not in our power to prevent them from arising; although, after they have arisen, they can be resisted, and prevented from taking root, or even entirely suffocated, in *tract. de convers. c.

V. §. XLVIII. But those good motions, which preventing grace kindles in a sinner man within the church, by means of the Word, consist in κατανύξεως τῆς καρδίας, in the compunction of the heart, Acts

II, 3. or in the injection of a certain stimulus, and an internal admonition arising beyond all intention concerning the immense danger and atrocious misery to which the sinner spontaneously exposes himself through crimes committed daily against his conscience, so that at times, by the example of the prodigal son, he descends into himself, Luke 15:17, and ἔμφοβος γενόμενος, Acts 24:25, compunctious and terrified, he begins to repeat that, Jer. ch. 8:6: What have I done? Whither do I rush? Whither am I carried headlong?

Why do I not rather consult for eternal salvation than for the fleeting pleasure of the body, joined with the danger of eternal torments? God has disposed it so for His immense grace, that no place for excuse is left to any man.

Indeed, the most obstinate atheists, who have hardened their minds against all the objections of Christians, yet presently, against their own will, when they are as it were struck by the proposition of the divine Word, feel such prickings within themselves.

Obf. V.

Non-resistance is twofold, pedagogical & spiritual.

Pedagogical non-resistance is in the power of the sinner man in external matters inviting to the church.

E.g. Some unregenerate men refuse to go on foot to the temple, some do not refuse.

This pedagogical non-resistance responding to external hearing is of free will.

But spiritual non-resistance, responding to internal hearing or assent, is from the assisting and preparing grace of the Holy Spirit, inasmuch as it breaks and inhibits the natural and actual simple repugnance, lest it become malicious, affected, and morose; although through the extreme malice of men it does not always attain this intended end.

Prob. 1) From Acts 7:51. Σκληροτράχηλοι καὶ ἀπερίτμητοι τῇ καρδίᾳ καὶ τοῖς ὠσίν, ὑμεῖς τῷ πνεύματι ἁγίῳ ἀντιπίπτετε, you stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit.

This heavenly oracle is ἐμφατικώτατον.

The first emphasis is on the word σκληροτράχηλοι, i.e., stiff-necked, ihr Halsstarrige, oder Hartnäckige.

The metaphor is taken from calves impatient of the yoke, and petulantly shaking off that which is imposed.

The second is on the word ἀπερίτμητοι, i.e., uncircumcised spiritually.

Indeed, the Jews had the foreskin of the genitals circumcised outwardly, but they unseemly nourished the foreskin of the heart inwardly.

They are uncircumcised in heart who indulge in the vicious affections of the heart, Jer. 9:26. They are uncircumcised in ears whose ears itch to hear either new dogmas, discordant with the divine Word, or obscene and flagitious words.

The third is on the word ἀντιπίπτετε, i.e.,

you oppose yourselves to the Holy Spirit as if crosswise, and obstruct the entrance into your heart.

2) From Isa. 65:2. coll. with Rom.

10:21. All day long I have stretched out my hands to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, after their own thoughts.

They are accustomed to expand their hands, who after their thoughts. They are accustomed to expand their hands, who they offer benefits to others of their own accord, they invite and entice them to themselves, intending to receive them into their embrace or bosom. God does this all day long, i.e., at all times, by offering assisting grace even to the refractory, who walk in the way of impiety after their own thoughts, pleasing themselves in their own inventions, and not restraining their senses under the obedience of God.

Latin:

Obs. III.

Dist. inter irrefistentiam actualem, & possibilem. Gratia resistibilis dicitur, cui per naturam resisti potest, sive actu ei resistatur, sive non: irresistibilis, cui per naturam resisti non potest.

Obs. IV.

Cum homo in peccatis mortuus iacet, & secure in diem vivit, de conversione sui nequicquam cogitans, prævenit eundem benignissimus Deus, & mediante verbo, sive audito, sive lecto, ac intra mentem retento, subinde bonos in eo motus excitat, quos inevitabiles Theologi appellant, quia eorum præsentia & sensus evitari nequit: qui etiam quodammodo irrefistibiles dici possunt, ratione originis & sensus, cum eorumdem suscitationi per verbum, ac sensui nequaquam, sed tantum consensui opponere se homo peccator possit.

Primi motus, inquit D. IOAN. MVSÆVS, dici possunt irrefistibiles, quatenus nostram deliberationem antevertunt, ut in nostra potestate non sit impedere, ne oriantur; quamvis, postquam exorti sunt, resisti iis, & ne radices agant, impediri, vel plane suffocari possint, in tract. de convers. c.

V. §. XLVIII. Consistunt autem illi boni motus, quos gratia præveniens in homine peccatore intra ecclesiam, mediante verbo, accendit, in κατανύξεως τῆς καρδίας, in compunctione cordis, Act.

II, 3. sive in iniectione quadam stimuli, & exorta præter omnem intentionem interna commonitione de ingenti periculo & atroci miseria, cui se per crimina, quotidie contra conscientiam commissa, peccator sponte obiicit, vt quandoque exemplo filii perditi in semetipsum descendat, Luc. XV, 5. & ἔμφοβος γενόμενος, Act. XXIV, 25. compunctus & conterritus, incipiat ingeminare illud, Ier. c. VIII, 6. Quid feci? quo ruo? quo præceps feror?

Cur non potius æternæ saluti, quam fluxæ corporis voluptati, cum periculo æternorum cruciatuum coniunctæ, consulo? Id ita pro immensa sua gratia disposuit Deus, quo minus vlli homini locus ad excusationem relictus sit.

Sane obstinatissimi athei, qui animum suum aduersus omnes christianorum obiectiones obdurarunt, tamen subinde contra voluntatem suam, vbi verbi diuini propositione quasi siderantur, vellicationes intra se tales sentiunt.

Obs. V.

Non resistentia est duplex, pædagogica & spiritualis.

Pædagogica non-resistentia est penes hominem peccatorem in rebus externis, ad ecclesiam inuitantibus.

V. gr. Quidam homines irregeniti renuunt ire pedibus in templum, quidam non recusant.

Hæc pædagogica non-resistentia auditui externo respondens est liberi arbitrii.

Spiritualis autem non-resistentia auditui interno, sive assensui respondens, est a gratia Spiritus S. assistente & præparante, quippe quæ repugnantiam naturalem & actualem simplicem frangit & inhibet, ne fiat malitiosa, affectata & morosa; quamvis per extremam hominum malitiam intentum hunc finem non semper assequatur.

Prob. 1) Ex Act. VII, 51. Σκληροτράχηλοι καὶ ἀπερίτμητοι τῇ καρδίᾳ καὶ τοῖς ὠσίν, ὑμεῖς τῷ πνεύματι ἁγίῳ ἀντιπίπτετε, vos duri ceruice, & incircumcisi corde atque auribus, semper Spiritui S. resistitis.

Oraculum hoc cœleste est ἐμφατικώτατον.

Prima emphasis est in voce σκληροτράχηλοι, q. d. ceruice duri, ihr Halsstarrige, oder Hartnäckige.

Metaphora sumta est a vitulis iugi impatientibus, illudque impositum petulanter excutientibus.

Altera est in voce ἀπερίτμητοι, i. e. incircumcisi spiritualiter.

Erat quidem Iudæis exterius genitalis præputium circumcisum, sed interius cordis præputium indecore alebant.

Sunt autem corde incircumcisi, qui vitiosis cordis affectibus indulgent, Ier. IX, 26. Incircumcisi auribus sunt, quorum aures pruriunt ad audiendum vel dogmata noua, verbo diuino difformia, vel verba obscœna & flagitiosa.

Tertia est in voce ἀντιπίπτετε, i. e.

Spiritui S. vos quasi transfuerfos opponitis, & aditum in cor vestrum obstruitis.

2) Ex Es. LXV, 2. coll. cum Rom.

X, 21. Tota die expandi manus meas ad populum rebellem, qui ambulant in via non bona post cogitationes suas.

Manus expandere solent, qui bene. post cogitationes suas. Manus expandere solent, qui beneficia aliis vltro offerunt, eos ad se inuitant & alliciunt, in complexum aut sinum eosdem recepturi. Hoc facit Deus, tota die, i. e. omni tempore gratiam assistentem offerendo etiam refractariis, qui ambulant in via impietatis post cogitationes suas, sibi ipsis in inuentionibus suis placentes, nec sensus suos sub obsequio Dei frenantes.


### Q. XVI. Does God convert the sinner with irresistible grace?: 3) From

3) From

Matth. XXIII, 37. O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you! How often have I wanted to gather your children in the way that a hen gathers her chicks under her wings! But you (you and your children) would not. By which words Christ most openly testifies to his most earnest will to gather and convert the Jews. For just as there is an ardent and most tender affection in a hen, by which she desires the safety of her chicks to be promoted: so Christ inclined with true and sincere benevolence toward the citizens of Jerusalem, to be gathered under the wings of his grace. He complains of the same voluntary stubbornness of the Jews, who morosely repudiated the grace offered to them.

The antithesis is that of certain Scholastics, Jansenists, and others asserting that the converting grace of God is irresistible.

Whose stronger arguments are:

I. Paul says explicitly: Who resists the divine will? Rom. IX, 19. Resp.

Paul speaks these words not from his own mind, but from the mind of an antagonist speaking against him: to whom the apostle replies a) indirectly by rebuke, that man ought not to answer against God: b) directly by information, that God does not harden positively, by injecting hardness into hearts with an irresistible will, but invites to repentance, bearing with much gentleness and patience the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction by their own fault.

II. Whatever power is no less effective and potent than that which exerted itself in raising Christ from the dead, that is insuperable and irresistible. But the power of the Holy Spirit converting us, etc. Therefore. The major is proven, because the divine power by which Christ was raised from the dead was clearly irresistible and insuperable, and once it was put into action, the effect could not but follow: The minor is evident from Col. II, 12. Eph. I, 19. 20. Resp.

The power raising the body of Christ from the dead agrees with converting grace, as regards the substance of the divine virtue considered in itself; in that a) both are supernatural, b) both give life. The former gives the life of a body to be glorified, the latter the life of a soul to be converted. However, it differs by reason of the subject; because the dead body of Christ, as such, or precisely considered, was destitute of all life: but the soul, dead in sins, is indeed destitute of the life of grace, but it lives the life of this world, it is devoid of spiritual life, but a participant in natural life.

Whence the dead body of Christ did not struggle against the divine raising virtue, but the soul, satiated and as it were drunk with the love of this world, does struggle. III. Whatever power is far superior to human powers, no one can resist it. But the divine converting power, etc. Therefore. The major is certain: because a lesser power is forced to yield to a greater. The minor is evident; because the divine power that turns the heart is infinite, but human power is finite.

Resp. Whatever power is far superior to human powers, and operates absolutely, no one can resist it: I concede. But the divine converting power is not absolute, but ordered, operating through ordinary means, which man can reject.

Instance. By this reasoning, man resisting divine power will be either more powerful than God, or at least equally powerful as God. Resp. a) If man were to resist through greater or equal perfection, that would follow; but man resists through blindness of intellect, and foolish concepts, through the disorder of appetite and the malice of the will; which do not argue for perfection, but for impotence.

It is illustrated by a simile. God sustains natural life not by absolute power, but by ordered power, through bread. But if anyone has proceeded to such madness that he would refuse to eat bread, he [violates] the order...

resisting the divinely constituted order through his own folly, yet he is not more powerful than God. b) Even then, when the power of God is hindered, He is able to act in such a way that He would not be hindered, if indeed He wished to act with irresistible power. Therefore, it is not permissible to infer that there is anything more powerful than God. For just as God permits His ordained power to be overcome by a malicious obstacle being placed in the way, so His absolute power is insuperable.

IV. He in whose hand are the hearts of men, so that He Himself may bend them whithersoever He wills, to Him men cannot offer resistance: But the hearts of men are in the hand of God, so that He Himself may bend them whithersoever He wills: Therefore. The major premise is proven; because he who bends something according to his own will attains the goal of the bending without any resistance. The minor premise is proven from Prov. XXI, 1 The king's heart is in the hand of God, as the rivers of waters; to everything that He wills, He inclines it: Resp. In the cited passage, Solomon's discourse is not about converting grace, but about divine providence concerning the affairs of kings, in respect to whom God inclines their hearts as often as it seems good to Him. Although even this bending of the royal mind is not simply irresistible, which is evident from the example of Saul, who resisted the divine command, 1 Sam. XV, 23.

V. He whom God the Father draws to the Son, he does not struggle against it: For God does not draw the unwilling: But sinners &c. John VI, 44 . Therefore. Resp. God does not indeed draw the unwilling; but He makes the unwilling by nature willing by grace. Nevertheless, since that drawing is not a violent abduction, but is carried out by the ordinary cords of grace, it is not simply irresistible: for it requires a tractable subject, not morosely resisting, or shaking off the cords of grace.

VI. If man can resist converting grace, and not resist, contrition and faith depend on the natural powers of free will: The latter is Pelagian: Therefore, so is the former. The consequence of the major premise is proven: because not to resist is the same as to repent and believe. Resp. a) We deny the consequence of the major. To the proof we say that non-resistance becomes only a condition, without which contrition and faith are not produced in the heart of the sinner, but it is not repentance and faith itself. b) Pedagogical non-resistance in external ecclesiastical matters is from the powers of free will; spiritual non-resistance is from the grace of God.

VII. If man can resist converting grace, God will be frustrated in His end: But God is never frustrated in His end: Therefore. The major premise is clear: because resistance hinders the end of the agent. The consequent is proven: because no wise and powerful person intends an end which he knows to be void: But God is most wise and most powerful, and therefore He foreknows the outcome of conversion, and by acting can attain the same: Therefore, He is never frustrated in His end. Resp. God always attains the ultimate and general end, i.e., the manifestation of His glorious grace, although He does not always obtain the intermediate and special end, i.e., the repentance of the sinner; nevertheless, divine wisdom reduces this frustration of the special end to the ultimate end, namely, to the glory of severe justice, which the man who stubbornly resists has provoked.

Latin:

3) Ex

Matth. XXIII, 37. O Ierusalem, Ierusalem, quæ occidis prophetas & lapidas missos ad te! Quoties volui congregare liberos tuos eo modo, quo congregat gallina pullos suos sub alas! Sed non voluistis (tu & liberi tui). Quibus verbis Christus apertissime testatur voluntatem suam maxime feriam congregandi & conuertendi Iudæos. Sicut enim ardens tenerrimusque gallinæ inest affectus, quo incolumitatem pullorum suorum promotam cupit: ita Christus vera & sincera beneuolentia propendebat in ciues Hierosolymitanos, sub alas gratiæ suæ congregandos. Idem conqueritur de voluntaria contunacia Iudæorum, oblatam gratiam morose repudiantium.

Antithesis est quorundam Scholasticorum, Iansenistarum & aliorum asserentium, gratiam Dei conuertentem esse irresistibilem.

Quorum potiora sunt argumenta:

I. Paullus diserte dicit: Voluntati diuinæ quis resistit? Rom. IX, 19. Resp.

Hæc verba loquitur Paullus non ex sua mente, sed ex mente antagonistæ obloquentis: cui apostolus respondet a) indirecte per obiurgationem, quod homo non debeat ex aduerso Dei respondere: b) directe per informationem, quod Deus non induret positiue, voluntate irresistibili duritiem cordibus immittendo, sed ad pœnitentiam inuitet, multa lenitate & patientia vasa iræ ad interitum propria culpa coagmentata, perferendo.

II. Quæ vis non minus efficax & potens est, quam quæ se exseruit in Christo a mortuis excitando, illa est insuperabilis & irresistibilis. Atqui vis Spiritus S. nos conuertentis &c. E. Maior probatur, quia vis diuina, qua Christus e mortuis excitatus est, plane irresistibilis & insuperabilis fuit, qua posita in actu non potuit non sequi effectus: Minor patet e Col. II, 12. Eph. I, 19. 20. Resp.

Vis resuscitans corpus Christi e mortuis conuenit cum gratia conuertente, quoad substantiam diuinæ virtutis in se consideratæ; eo, quod a) vtraque est supernaturalis, b) vtraque dat vitam. Illa dat vitam corporis glorificandi, hæc vitam animæ conuertendæ. Differt autem ratione subiecti; quia corpus Christi mortuum, vt tale, vel præcise consideratum, omni vita fuit destitutum: anima autem, in peccatis mortua, destituta quidem est vita gratiæ, viuit autem vitam huius sæculi, expers est vitæ spiritualis, sed particeps vitæ naturalis.

Vnde corpus Christi mortuum non fuit obluctatum virtuti diuinæ resuscitanti, obluctatur autem anima amore huius sæculi infatiata & quasi ebria. III. Quæcunque vis longe superior est viribus humanis, illi nemo potest resistere. Atqui vis diuina conuertens &c. E. Maior constat: quia vis minor cedere cogitur maiori. Minor est euidens; quia vis diuina verticordia est infinita, vis autem humana finita.

Resp. Quæcunque vis longe superior est viribus humanis, atque absolute operatur, illi nemo potest resistere: concedo. At vis diuina conuertens non est absoluta, sed ordinata, operans per ordinaria media, quæ homo reiicere potest.

Instantia. Hac ratione homo potentiæ diuinæ obsistens erit vel Deo potentior, vel saltim æque potens, ac Deus. Resp. a) Si homo obsisteret per perfectionem maiorem, aut parem, id sequeretur; sed resistit homo per cœcitatem intellectus, stolidofque conceptus, per ἀταξίαν appetitus & malitiam voluntatis; quæ non arguunt perfectionem, sed impotentiam.

Illustratur simili. Deus sustentat vitam naturalem non potentia absoluta, sed ordinata, mediante pane. Quod si quis eo vecordiæ processerit, vt pane vesci detrectaret, is ordini si quis eo vecordiæ procefferit, vt pane vesci detrectaret, is

ordini divinitus constituto reniteretur per stultitiam suam, neque tamen Deo potentior est. b) Etiam tum, cum potentia Dei impeditur, ita agere potest, ut non impediretur, si nimirum agere vellet potentia irresistibili. E. inferre haud licet, dari aliquid Deo potentius. Nam sicut Deus permittit, ut potentia sua ordinata, obiecto malitioso obice, vincatur; ita potentia eius absoluta insuperabilis est.

IV. In cuius manu sunt hominum corda, ut ipse ea flectat, quo vult, illi homines non possunt resistere: Sed corda hominum sunt in manu Dei, ut ipse ea flectat, quo vult: E. Maior probatur; quia, qui aliquid flectit pro arbitratu suo, flexionis scopum sine ulla resistentia assequitur. Minor probatur ex Prou. XXI, 1 Cor regis est in manu Dei, sicut riui aquarum; ad omne, quod vult, illud inclinat: Resp. L. c. Salomoni sermo est non de gratia conuertente, sed prouidentia diuina, circa regum negotia, quorum respectu Deus corda eorum inclinat, quoties ipsi visum fuerit. Quamuis neque haec flexio animi regii sit simpliciter irresistibilis, quod patet exemplo Saulis, praecepto diuino resistentis, 1 Sam. XV, 23 .

V. Quem Deus Pater trahit ad Filium, ille non reluctatur: Deus enim non trahit inuitum: Atqui peccatores &c. Io. VI, 44 . E. Resp. Deus non trahit quidem inuitum; sed non volentem per naturam, volentem per gratiam facit. Attamen quoniam tractus ille non est raptus violentus, sed ordinariis gratiae funibus peragitur, simpliciter irresistibilis non est: requirit enim subiectum tractabile, morose non repugnans, aut gratiae funes non excutiens.

VI. Si homo gratiae conuertenti potest resistere, & non resistere, contritio & fides pendent a viribus naturalibus liberi arbitrii: Posterius est Pelagianum: E. & prius. Consequentia maioris probatur: quia non resistere est idem, quod poenitere & credere. Resp. a) Neg. consequ. maior. Ad probationem dicimus, quod non-resistentia fit tantum conditio, sine qua non producitur in corde peccatoris contritio & fides, sed non est ipsa poenitentia & fides. b) Non-resistentia paedagogica in rebus ecclesiasticis externis est a viribus liberi arbitrii, non-resistentia spiritualis est a gratia Dei.

VII. Si homo gratiae conuertenti potest resistere, Deus fine suo frustrabitur: Sed Deus nunquam fine suo frustratur: E. Maior liquet: quia resistentia finem agentis impedit. Consequens prob. quia nemo sapiens & potens eum intendit finem, quem nouit esse irritum: Sed Deus est sapientissimus & potentissimus, adeoque praenouit conuersionis exitum, eundemque agendo assequi potest: E. nunquam fine suo frustratur. Resp. Deus semper attingit finem ultimum & generalem, i. e. manifestationem gloriosae gratiae suae, licet non semper obtineat finem medium & specialem, i. e. poenitentiam peccatoris; attamen sapientia diuina hanc frustrationem finis specialis ad finem vltimum, nempe ad gloriam seuerae iustitiae, quam homo pertinaciter resistens prouocauit, reducit.


### Q. XVI. Does God convert the sinner with irresistible grace?: S I G H

S I G H.

Convert, O most benign God, sinners turned away from You, prostrate the fierce, bend the contumacious, raise up the fallen! Recall, O most mild Father, the disobedient children, gather the scattered doves, bring back the bleating sheep! Soften iron hearts with the fire of Your word, break the stony ones with the hammer of the law, so that they may be prepared and disposed to receive by true faith Jesus, the King of souls, the asserter and defender of our salvation! Restrain my will, prone to sin, support it when it wavers, confirm it when it is weak, so that I may be and remain established in the constant exercise of repentance, a hater of all baseness, a cultivator of true piety!

Latin:

S V S P I R I V M.

Conuerte, o Deus benignissime, peccatores a te auersos, prosterne feroces, flecte contumaces, erige lapsos! Reuoca, o Pater mitissime, filios immorigeros, collige columbas dispersas, reduce oues balantes! Igni verbi tui emolli corda ferrea, saxea malleo legis frange, vt praeparentur & disponantur ad suscipiendum vera fide Iesum, animarum regem, salutis nostrae assertorem & vindicem! Voluntatem meam ad peccandum procliuem prohibe, nutantem suffulci, imbecillem confirma, vt sim maneamque in iugi poenitentiae exercitio constitutus, omnis turpitudinis osor, verae pietatis cultor!


## 22 On Regenerating Grace, and Regeneration

I. What is regeneration?

Regeneration is an act of grace, by which the Holy Spirit endows a sinful man with saving faith, so that, with sins forgiven, he may be rendered a son of God and an heir of eternal life. It is more fully defined: Regeneration is an act of applying grace, by which the Holy Spirit endows a sinful man, lacking the powers of believing, but not stubbornly resisting, out of mercy founded on the merit of Christ, with true faith in Christ, kindled through the Gospel and baptism, so that he may be justified, adopted as a son of God, renewed, and eternally saved.

Obs.

I. Regeneration is called in Greek παλιγγενεσία, from πάλιν, again, and γένεσις, generation, and therefore by the force of the word it is a new or repeated generation.

Moreover, παλιγγενεσία has a double meaning; for it denotes either rebirth to the life of grace, or spiritual life, Tit. III, 5, or rebirth to the life of glory, or eternal life, Matth. XIX, 28.

Obs.

II. The word, regeneration, insofar as it denotes rebirth to spiritual life, is taken either in a broader and general sense, or in a stricter and special sense.

Taken broadly, regeneration comprises a) regeneration strictly so called, b) justification, c) and renewal. In which comprehensive sense the Formula of Concord, p. 686, accepts it.

The term regeneration is sometimes taken in that sense so that it comprises both the remission of sins and the subsequent renewal. Sometimes it also signifies only the remission of sins and adoption as sons of God. And in this latter meaning that word is often and much used in the Apology of the Augsburg Confession.

Furthermore, regeneration is also often used for sanctification, in which meaning LUTHER used this word much, both in his book on the Church and Councils, and elsewhere. Taken strictly, it denotes the donation of faith; which stricter meaning we shall prove below.

Obs.

III. Regeneration is active on the part of God, and passive on the part of the sinful man.

For just as no son of man generates himself; so no son of God regenerates himself. Therefore, just as natural generation is active only for the father, and passive only for the begotten; so active regeneration is attributed only to God, and passive regeneration to man. Add that while conversion is indeed taken in the Holy Scriptures now transitively, now intransitively: yet regeneration is always taken transitively; for nowhere in Holy Scripture is it said that a man regenerates himself, or ought to regenerate himself.

Obs.

IV. Synonyms of regeneration are:

1) Vivification, Eph. II, 5. For just as generation is the communication of natural life; so regeneration is the communication of spiritual life.

2) New creation, Ps. LI, 12. Whence also the regenerated are called a new creature, 2 Cor. V, 17.

Gal. VI, 15. The first creation was made by the infinite power of the Creator; so regeneration is done by the infinite power of God. The difference is that God created the world by absolute power; but He regenerates the sinner by ordained power.

3) Resuscitation, Eph. II, 6. For just as the resuscitation of the dead is a translation from death to life; so regeneration is the translation of the sinner from the death of sin into state of living faith. 4) Conversion, as it is accepted in a special sense, not a most special one. See: above c. VI. quest. IV. obs.

Latin:

I. Quid est regeneratio?

Regeneratio est actus gratiae, quo Spiritus Sanctus hominem peccatorem salvifica fide donat, vt remissis peccatis filius Dei & haeres aeternae vitae reddatur. Uberius definitur: Regeneratio est actus gratiae applicatricis, quo Spiritus Sanctus hominem peccatorem, viribus credendi carentem, sed contumaciter non repugnantem, ex misericordia, in merito Christi fundata, vera in Christum fide, per euangelium & baptismum accensa, donat, vt iustificetur, in filium Dei adoptetur, renouetur & aeternum saluetur.

Obs.

I. Regeneratio graece vocatur παλιγγενεσία, ex πάλιν, rursus, & γένεσις, generatio, ideoque vi vocis est noua, vel iterata generatio.

Habet autem παλιγγενεσία duplicem significatum; denotat enim vel renascentiam ad vitam gratiae, siue spiritualem, Tit. III, 5. vel renascentiam ad vitam gloriae, siue aeternam, Matth. XIX, 28.

Obs.

II. Vox, regeneratio, quatenus notat renascentiam ad vitam spiritualem, sumitur vel in significatione latiori & generali, vel in significatione strictiori & speciali.

Late sumta regeneratio complectitur a) regenerationem stricte dictam, b) iustificationem, c) & renouationem. Quo sensu complexiuo Form. Conc. p. 686. accipit.

Vocabulum regenerationis interdum in eo sensu accipitur, ut simul & remissionem peccatorum, & subsequentem renouationem complectatur. Quandoque etiam solam remissionem peccatorum & adoptionem in filios Dei significat. Et in hoc posteriori significatu saepe multumque id vocabulum in August. confess. apol. ponitur.

Deinde etiam regeneratio saepe pro sanctificatione usurpatur, in qua significatione LVTHERVS hac voce tum in libro de eccl. & conciliis, tum alibi multum usus est. Stricte sumta notat donationem fidei; quam strictiorem significationem infra probabimus.

Obs.

III. Regeneratio ex parte Dei actiua, ex parte hominis peccatoris passiua est.

Vti enim nullus filius hominis seipsum generat; ita nullus filius Dei seipsum regenerat. E, vti naturalis generatio actiua solius patris, passiua solius geniti est; ita generatio actiua soli Deo, regeneratio passiua homini tribuitur. Adde, quod conuersio quidem in sacris litteris iam transitiue, iam intransitiue sumatur: at regeneratio semper transitiue sumitur; nuspiam quippe in S. Scriptura dicitur, quod homo se regeneret, aut se regenerare debeat.

Obs.

IV. Regenerationis synonyma sunt:

1) Viuificatio, Eph. II, 5. Sicut enim generatio est communicatio vitae naturalis; ita regeneratio est communicatio vitae spiritualis.

2) Noua creatio, Ps. LI, 12. Vnde etiam regenerati vocantur noua creatura, 2 Cor. V, 17.

Gal. VI, 15. Prima creatio facta est vi infinita creatoris; ita regeneratio fit infinita Dei potentia. Id discriminis est, quod Deus mundum condiderit potentia absoluta; peccatorem vero regeneret potentia ordinata.

3) Resuscitatio, Eph. II, 6. Sicut enim resuscitatio mortuorum est translatio e morte ad vitam; ita regeneratio est translatio peccatoris ex morte peccati in statum vivae fidei. 4) Conversio, prout illa accipitur in sensu speciali, non specialissimo. Vid: supra c. VI. quaest. IV. obs.


### III. Quest. II. Who regenerates sinful man?

God the triune regenerates the sinner, the Father , the Son of God , and the Holy Spirit, to whom regeneration is attributed appropriatively and terminatively .

Prob. a. From John 1, 12. 13. Who believe in his name, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but are born of God. John teaches by these words that the origin of regeneration is not to be attributed to blood, i.e., to natural generation from faithful parents (just as the Jews thought themselves to be children of God, since they drew their origin from the blood of Abraham), nor to the will of the flesh, i.e., to the natural powers of free will, nor to the will of man, i.e., not to the efforts or noble deeds of any outstanding and strenuous man, but solely to God, the parent and author of spiritual generation. Moreover, regeneration is common to the three persons of the divinity; therefore, because it is an action ad extra, and is terminated at an effect really produced within man.

Prob. b. That God the Father regenerates us, Peter affirms 1 ep. I, 3. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his abundant mercy has regenerated us unto a living hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead. The efficacious grace of God the Father excites faith in Christ. No one can come to me, unless the Father, who sent me, has drawn him, says the Savior, John VI, 44. Prob. c.

The Son of God, by reason of spiritual generation unto eternal life, is called the Father of eternity, Is. IX, 5. The Father of many children, Is. VIII, 18. Heb. II, 13. to whom a most numerous multitude of children is generated just as dew is born most copiously from the womb of the dawn, Ps. CX, 3. Prob. d.

Regeneration is appropriated to the Holy Spirit, because he is the spirit of faith, 2 Cor. IV, 3. who kindles and gives faith. He is the spirit of υἱοθεσίας, or adoption, in which we cry: Abba, Father, Rom. VIII, 15. He is the author of regeneration, to whom it is vindicated by Christ himself, John III, 3. 5. 6. Unless one has been generated of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God. That which is born of the flesh is flesh; but that which is generated of the Spirit is spirit: and by Paul, Tit. III, 5. calling baptism the laver of regeneration of the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

Peccatorem regenerat Deus triunus , Pater , Filius Dei , & Spiritus Sanctus, cui regeneratio appropriative & terminative tribuitur .

Prob. a. Ex Io. I, 12. 13. Qui credunt in nomen ipsius, non ex sanguinibus, neque ex voluntate carnis, neque ex voluntate viri, sed ex Deo nati sunt. Docet his verbis Ioannes, quod regenerationis origo non tribuenda sit sanguinibus, i. e. naturali generationi, ex fidelibus parentibus (sicut Iudaei se filios Dei esse putabant, quoniam e sanguine Abrahami ducerent originem), neque voluntati carnis, i. e. naturalibus viribus liberi arbitrii, neque voluntati viri, i. e. non conatibus aut rebus praeclare gestis alicuius viri praestantis & strenui, sed vnice Deo spiritualis generationis parenti & auctori. Ceterum regeneratio est communis tribus personis diuinitatis; ideo, quod est actio ad extra, & terminatur ad effectum intra hominem realiter productum.

Prob. b. Deum Patrem nos regenerare, affirmat Petrus 1 ep. I, 3. Benedictus Deus & Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui iuxta multam suam misericordiam regenerauit nos in spem viuam per resurrectionem Iesu Christi ex mortuis. Efficax Dei Patris gratia excitat fidem in Christum. Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi Pater, qui misit me, traxerit illum, ait Saluator, Io. VI, 44.

Prob. c. Filius Dei ratione spiritualis generationis ad vitam aeternam appellatur Pater aeternitatis, Es. IX, 5. Pater multorum filiorum, Es. VIII, 18. Hebr. II, 13. cui numerosissima filiorum frequentia perinde generatur, ac ex vtero aurorae ros copiosissime nascitur, Ps. CX, 3.

Prob. d. Spiritui S. appropriatur regeneratio, quia is est spiritus fidei, 2 Cor. IV, 3. qui fidem accendit & donat. Est spiritus υἱοθεσίας, siue adoptionis, in quo clamamus: Abba, Pater, Rom. VIII, 15. E. est auctor regenerationis, cui vindicatur ab ipso Christo, Io. III, 3. 5. 6. Nisi quis generatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest ingredi in regnum Dei. Quod natum est e carne, caro est; sed quod generatum est e Spiritu, spiritus est: & a Paullo, Tit. III, 5. appellante baptismum, lauacrum regenerationis Spiritus S.


### Quest. III. What moves God to regenerate sinful men?

To regenerate sinful men, mercy most prone toward the fallen human race moves God internally . Externally, the satisfaction and merit of Christ the mediator impelled him .

Prob. a. From 1 Pet. I, 3. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his abundant mercy has regenerated us. To regenerate sinful man, the natural aptitude of man, or capacity, did not move God, much less his own merit; since there was none; but mere mercy; although the most profound misery of man dead in sins provided God with an occasion for showing mercy. This is what Paul inculcates in us, Eph. II, 4. God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, has quickened us together with Christ. James hints at the same, c. I, 18. The Father of lights βουληθεὶς ἀπεκύησεν ἡμᾶς, i.e., by his beneficent and gracious will he brought us forth.

Prob. b. Christ by his obedience most fully satisfied divine justice, so that, this being saved, God might exert his mercy upon man dead in sins, and to him life anew can confer it anew. Paul intends to indicate this, 1 Cor. IV, 15: In Christ Jesus, he says, I have begotten you through the gospel. Expounding these words, D. CALOV. in Bibl. illustrat. on this passage says: Paul begat the Corinthians in Christ Jesus, i.e., by the merit and efficacy of Christ, as mediator and redeemer, through and on account of whom we are regenerated unto spiritual and eternal life. Therefore Peter asserts, 1 Ep. 1, 3, that God has regenerated us unto a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead. The Apostle attributes our regeneration to the resurrection of Christ, a) because this, taken complexly, as it includes the death of Christ, is the meritorious cause of regeneration; b) because the same merits of Christ are sealed; c) because Christ was therefore raised and exalted into heaven, that He might pour the spirit of faith into our hearts, John XVI, 7.

Latin:

Ad regenerandum homines peccatores interne mouet Deum misericordia in genus humanum lapsum propensissima . Externe ipsum impulit satisfactio & meritum Christi mediatoris .

Prob. a. Ex 1 Petr. I, 3. Benedictus Deus & Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui iuxta multam suam misericordiam regenerauit nos. Ad regenerandum hominem peccatorem Deum non mouit naturalis aptitudo hominis, aut capacitas, molto ininus ipsius meritum; quippe quod nullum fuit; sed mera misericordia; quamuis Deo occasionem miserefcendi praebuerit miseria hominis in peccatis mortui profundissima. Id quod nobis inculcat Paulus, Eph. II, 4. Deus, qui diues est misericordia, propter multum amorem suum, quo dilexit nos, & nos, quum essemus mortui peccatis, viuificauit cum Christo. Idem innuit Iacobus, c. I, 18. Pater luminum βουληθεὶς ἀπεκύησεν ἡμᾶς, i. e benefica & gratiosa sua voluntate progenuit.

Prob. b. Christus obedientia sua plenissime satisfecit iustitiae diuinae, vt, hac salua, Deus misericordiam suam in hominem mortuum in peccatis exserere, eidemque vitam denuo conferre possit. Id indicaturus Paullus, 1 Cor IV, 15: In Christo, inquit, Iesu per euangelium ego vos generaui. Quæ verba expositurus D. CALOV. in bibl. illustrat. in h. l. inquit: Paullus in Christo Iesu genuit Corinthios, i. e. merito & efficacia Christi, ceu mediatoris & redemptoris, per & propter quem regeneramur ad vitam spiritualem & æternam. Idcirco asserit Petrus, 1 ep. 1, 3. quod Deus nos regenerauerit in spem viuam per resurrectionem Iesu Christi ex mortuis. Tribuit Apostolus regenerationem nostri resurrectioni Christi, a) quia hæc, complexe sumta, prout mortem Christi includit, est causa meritoria regenerationis; b) quia eadem merita Christi sunt obsignata, c) quia Christus ideo resuscitatus & in cœlum euectus est, vt spiritum fidei in corda nostra effunderet, Io. XVI, 7.


### Q. IV. By what means does the Holy Spirit regenerate the sinner?

The means by which the Holy Spirit regenerates the sinner, and with which He concurs to produce faith, are the word of the gospel a) and the sacrament of baptism b).

Proof a. 1) Paul expressly says: In Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel, 1 Cor. IV, 15. The Apostle begat the Corinthians, under the leadership and auspices of Christ, not through the law, by which contrition and sorrow for sins are excited, but through the gospel, by which trust in Christ is excited.

2) From 1 Pet. I, 23. You have been regenerated not of corruptible seed, but incorruptible, through the living word of God, and abiding forever. The Apostle distinguishes between the corruptible seed of earthly fruits, and the incorruptible seed of the divine word, which is incorruptible both formally, insofar as it is the eternal concept of the divine mind; and effectively, because it leads to eternal life. The Word of God is also a living seed, because it is a seed fruitful and efficacious for producing living faith in Christ.

3) From James I, 18. It pleased Him (the Father of lights) to beget us with the word of truth. That the gospel is the word of truth, we learn from Eph. I, 13, where the Apostle says: You heard the word of truth, the gospel of our salvation. Not without emphasis is the gospel called the word of truth, because it is not only true in itself, just as the word of the law is, but because it also truly regenerates, and the life of grace and glory which it promises, it actually confers.

Proof b. That baptism is the ordinary medium of regeneration is clearly evident from John III, 5, where Christ, about to open the way to heaven to Nicodemus, says: Unless one has been born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven. By water in the cited place, the Holy Spirit is not understood; because otherwise a tautology would be committed, but true and natural water, united with the Holy Spirit, who makes the baptismal water a saving medium of regeneration. Whence baptism is called λουτρὸν παλιγγενεσίας, the washing of regeneration, Tit. III, 5. The antithesis is that of the Schwenckfeldians, who deny that the word of God and baptism are efficacious media of regeneration.

Their arguments are: I. Regeneration is an action of the Holy Spirit, by whom it is performed by infinite power: Therefore, it is not to be attributed to the word of God. Resp. Regeneration is an action of the Holy Spirit as the principal cause, and of the word of God, as the efficacious medium of regeneration.

II. Whatever is a creature, that cannot regenerate a sinner: But Holy Scripture, etc. Therefore. The major is clear: because for regeneration an infinite power is required, which does not fall to a creature. I answer with the words of D. CALOV. in System. theol. tom I. p. 717. The word of God, considered formally, is not to be reckoned in the catalog of creatures: since it is the divine concept, the mind of God, the counsel of God, as it is described in the sacred writings. For who would reckon the divine concept, who the mind of God and counsel of God among creatures? the counsel of God among creatures?

III. The Word of God is the letter that killeth, 2 Cor. 3:6: Therefore it does not regenerate or vivify. Resp. In the cited passage, the word of the law is understood, denouncing temporal and eternal death to the disobedient; but the seed of regeneration is the gospel.

IV. Baptism is an external element: Therefore it cannot internally and spiritually regenerate the soul. Resp. Baptism is an external element, joined with the divine word and the name of the Most Holy Trinity, from which it has the efficacy of regenerating.

V. Adults are not regenerated by the water of baptism; because they were reborn by the divine word, by which they had been previously informed: nor are infants; because in succeeding years they turn out malicious; which is an indication that they were not reborn through baptism. Resp. In the baptism of adults, regeneration is confirmed: infants are truly regenerated in the laver of baptism; but, if in the passage of time they become malicious, by their own fault they fall from the state of regeneration, because they allow themselves to be overcome by the flesh and the devil.

VI. If baptism truly regenerates us, trust can be placed in it: which, however, is idolatrous. Resp. Trust is to be placed in God, not in the means.

Latin:

Media, per quæ Spiritus S. peccatorem regenerat, & cum quibus ad producendum fidem concurrit, sunt verbum euangelii a) & sacramentum baptismi b).

Prob. a. 1) Paullus diserte dicit: In Christo Iesu per euangelium vos generaui, 1 Cor. IV, 15. Apostolus generauit Corinthios, duce & auspice Christo, non per legem, qua excitatur contritio & dolor de peccatis, sed per euangelium, quo excitatur fiducia in Christum.

2) Ex 1 Pet. I, 23. Regenerati estis non ex semine corruptibili, sed incorruptibili, per verbum viuens Dei, & manens in æternum. Distinguit Apostolus inter semen corruptibile frugum terrestrium, & incorruptibile verbi diuini, quod est incorruptibile tum formaliter, quatenus est conceptus mentis diuinæ æternus; tum effectiue, quia ad vitam æternam perducit, Verbum Dei etiam est semen viuum, quia est semen fœcundum & efficax ad producendum viuam in Christum fidem.

3) Ex Iac. I, 18. Placuit ipsi (Patri luminum) generare nos verbo veritatis. Euangelium esse verbum veritatis, discimus ex Eph. I, 13. vbi Apostolus inquit: Audiuistis verbum veritatis, euangelium salutis nostræ. Non sine emphasi euangelium dicitur verbum veritatis, quia non tantum in se verum est, æque ac verbum legis, sed quia etiam vere regenerat, & quam vitam gratiæ & gloriæ promittit, reuera confert.

Prob. b. Baptismum esse ordinarium regenerationis medium, liquido patet ex Io. III, 5. vbi Christus, Nicodemo viam ad cœlum patefacturus, inquit: Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest ingredi in regnum cœlorum. Per aquam l. c. non intelligitur Spiritus Sanctus; quia ceteroqui tautologia committeretur, sed aqua vera & naturalis, vnita cum Spiritu Sancto, qui aquam baptismalem salutare regenerationis medium efficit. Vnde baptismus dicitur λουτρὸν παλιγγενεσίας, lauacrum regenerationis, Tit. III, 5. Antithesis est Schwenckfeldianorum, negantium, verbum Dei & baptismum esse efficacia regenerationis media.

Quorum argumenta sunt: I. Regeneratio est actio Spiritus S., a quo peragitur virtute infinita: E. non est tribuenda verbo Dei. Resp. Regeneratio est actio Spiritus S. vt causæ principali, & verbo Dei, tanquam efficaci regenerationis medio.

II. Quidquid est creatura, illud non potest peccatorem regenerare: Atqui scriptura S. &c. E. Maior liquet: quia ad regenerationem requiritur vis infinita, quæ non cadit in creaturam, Respondeo verbis D. CALOVII in system. theol. tom I. p. 717. Verbum Dei formaliter consideratum creaturarum catalogo accensendum non est: quum fit conceptus diuinus, mens Dei, consilium Dei, prout in sacris litteris describitur. Quis enim conceptum diuinum, quis mentem Dei & consilium Dei creaturis accenseret? consilium Dei creaturis accenseret?

III. Verbum Dei est littera occidens, 2 Cor. III, 6: E. non regenerat aut vivificat. Resp. Loco citato intelligitur verbum legis, mortem temporalem & aeternam denuntians inobedientibus; at regenerationis semen est evangelium.

IV. Baptismus est externum elementum: E. interne & spiritualiter non potest animam regenerare. Resp. Baptismus est externum elementum, cum verbo divino & nomine SS. Trinitatis coniunctum, ex quo efficaciam regenerandi habet.

V. Baptismi aqua non regenerantur adulti; quia illi verbo divino, quo antea informati erant, renati sunt: neque infantes; quia illi succedentibus annis evadunt malitiosi; quod indicio est, illos per baptismum non fuisse renatos. Resp. Adultorum baptismo regeneratio confirmatur: infantes lavacro baptismi vere regenerantur; at, si successu temporis malitiosi fiant, propria culpa e statu regenerationis excidunt, propterea, quod patiuntur, se a carne & diabolo vinci.

VI. Si baptismus nos vere regenerat, in eodem fiducia collocari potest: quod tamen idololatricum est. Resp. Fiducia collocanda est in Deo, non in mediis.


### Q. V. What ministers does God use in the regeneration of men?

The ministers whom God uses in the ordinary act of regeneration are sacred heralds, who are said to generate spiritually, insofar as they apply the Word of God and baptism to men to be regenerated, not by their own authority, but by God’s, and according to divine institution.

Prob. Paul in the epistle to Philemon v. 10 asserts that he had begotten Onesimus in his bonds. And to the Galatians 4:19 the Apostle writes: My little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you. Certainly, the ministers of the church generate, not as principal causes; but as subordinate ones, insofar as they scatter the seed of the gospel into hearts and duly apply baptism. But the supereminent power of regenerating is not from men, but from God alone, 2 Cor. 4:7. This is what the Apostle points out, 1 Cor. 4:15: In Christ through the gospel I have begotten you, i.e., the Lord Jesus by His infinite virtue has regenerated you through the gospel preached by me among you, so that from heathens you were born Christians, from infidels believers, from children of wrath children of grace, and heirs of the heavenly kingdom.

Latin:

Ministri, quibus Deus in ordinaria regenerationis actu utitur, sunt praecones sacri, qui spiritualiter generare dicuntur, quatenus verbum Dei & baptismum hominibus regenerandis auctoritate non sua, sed Dei, & iuxta institutionem divinam applicant.

Prob. Paullus in epist. ad Philem. v. 10. asserit, se in vinculis suis genuisse Onesimum. Et ad Galat. IV, 19. scribit Apostolus: Filioli mei, quos iterum parturio, dum formetur Christus in vobis. Nimirum ministri ecclesiae generant, non ut causae principales; sed ut subordinatae, quatenus semen evangelii in corda spargunt, & baptismum rite applicant. At vis regenerandi supereminens non est ex hominibus, sed solius Dei, 2 Cor. IV, 7. Id quod indigitat Apostolus, 1 Cor. IV, 15. In Christo per evangelium vos generavi, q. d. Dominus Iesus infinita sua virtute vos per evangelium, a me inter vos praedicatum, regenuit, ut ex ethnicis Christiani, ex infidelibus fideles, ex filiis irae nasceremini filii gratiae, & regni coelestis heredes.


### Q. VI. What men are regenerated?

Men lacking spiritual life are regenerated a), but not those who pertinaciously resist b), as much infants c), as adults informed by the Word of God, and struck and contrite by the thunderbolt of the divine law d).

Prob. a. Men living in the faith which is in the Son of God, as the reborn are described by Paul, Gal. 2:20, are not, properly speaking, the subject of regeneration. For just as those who are not living, but dead, are resurrected from temporal death to the life of glory: so those who are not reborn, but lacking the life of faith, are resurrected from spiritual death to the life of grace.

Prob. b. Prevenient and preparing grace indeed diminishes and breaks natural repugnance, lest it impede regenerating grace; but a sinner opposing himself to the means of grace by voluntary and pertinacious resistance is not a subject capable of regeneration through the word ἄκυσον καὶ ὀρατόν, i.e., through the gospel and baptism. This assertion of ours is clear from examples. The Pharisees and lawyers rejected the will of God against themselves, and therefore were not baptized by John, Luke 7:30. Paul and Barnabas said to the Jews: It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you: but seeing ye put it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life; lo, we turn to the Gentiles. For thus the Lord commanded us: I have set thee to be a light of the Gentiles, that thou shouldest be for salvation unto the ends of the earth.

When therefore the Gentiles heard this, they were glad and glorified the word of the Lord, as many as were ordained to eternal life, Acts XIII, 46, 47, 48. From these things it is clearly evident that neither are those unregenerated by baptism who reject the counsel of God concerning the communication of eternal salvation through ordinary means against themselves, that is, to their own greatest harm, nor are those led to faith through the Gospel who maliciously repel it.
