IV, 19, where the Apostle says: My little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you. Resp. 1) I deny the major. For we receive our form and image in a mirror and on a painter's tablet, yet we are not generated there. The image of Christ is imprinted on our souls first through faith, by which we thus know the face and form of Christ, just as he is prescribed before our eyes in the Holy Scriptures: secondly, through the likeness and conformity of the life and holiness of Christ. 2) The object to be generated in the Pauline parturition is not Christ, but the Galatians: My little children, he says, of whom I travail in birth again. Therefore, Christ is not generated in us, but he is formed (μορφοῦται), or he imparts his form (μορφίαν) to us, so that in this life we may become like his image, just as we are to bear the same image in the other life, 1 Cor. XV, 49.

II. Apoc. XII, 5. A woman clothed with the sun (by whom the church is understood) brought forth a man child, who was to rule all nations with a rod of iron (by whom Christ is denoted). But if the church brings forth Christ, why not also the faithful? For the church is the assembly of the faithful. Resp. In that place, by the son, Christ, the son of Mary, is represented only by a phraseological allusion, but directly the spiritual sons are represented, whom the church militant, which is treated of there, brings forth to God with pain and amidst the straits of perfections.

III. Christ lives in us, Gal. II, 20. Therefore he is also generated in us. Resp. Christ lives in us, not as the new man, but as the author of the new life; since we are created in him unto good works, Eph. II, 10. Nor is he generated in us, but, like a Father, he regenerates us.

IV. Everyone who does the will of Christ is his mother, Matth. XII, 19. E. He generates Christ. Resp. He who does the will of Christ is called his mother, not on account of generation, but on account of love. For a man does not generate Christ like a mother; but Christ loves him most ardently, just as a son loves his mother.

V. Orthodox theologians have used that phrase, that Christ is generated in us through faith. Resp. Those theologians spoke more securely before the controversies were stirred up, intending to express our most intimate union with Christ: but as Quakerism has grown prevalent, we rightly and deservedly abstain from that catachrestic allegory. Moreover, no orthodox theologian has asserted that Christ is generated in us as the new man in us, and as flesh of our flesh.

Quest. XXIII. How do regeneration, justification, and renewal differ?

Regeneration, justification, and renewal differ: a) In order of nature: b) In respect of the subjects: c) In respect of the term from which, and to which: d) In respect of the internal form: e) In respect of the mode of acting.

Prob. a. In order of nature, regeneration, or the donation of faith, precedes justification and renewal, without which we do not please God, Heb. XI, 6. thus neither are we justified, nor renewed, unless we are regenerated.

Prob. b. The subject of regeneration is a sinner converted and contrite through the divine law, but lacking the life of faith, and thus spiritually dead: The subject of justification is a sinner converted and reborn, or contrite and believing in Christ: The subject of renewal is a man converted, reborn, and justified.

Prob. c. The term from which of regeneration is spiritual death, insofar as this denotes a lack of the powers of believing, the term to which is saving faith: The term from which of justification is the guilt of fault and punishment, the term to which is the remission of sins, and the imputed righteousness of Christ: The term from which of renewal is the dominion and remnants of sin, the term to which is the image of God, and inherent holiness.

Prob. d. Regeneration consists formally in the donation of faith, justification in the remission of sins and the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, renewal in the liberation from the dominion and stains of sin, and the restoration of the divine image.

Prob. e. Regeneration is an action of God alone, bringing about an intrinsic denomination of the subject which is regenerated, since in his heart trust in Christ is excited by the Holy Spirit, so that the sinner who is regenerated behaves himself merely passively.

Justification is an action of God alone, bringing about an extrinsic denomination of the subject which is justified; for to him, by the estimation of God, his own injustice is not imputed, but another's (namely, Christ's) righteousness is imputed or adjudged. Whence in the business of justification the sinner also behaves himself merely passively, since no one can absolve himself before the divine judgment.

Renewal is indeed an action of God, but not of Him alone, for the reason that the justified man concurs toward the same, not by his own powers, but by those bestowed from above, as a subordinate cause.

Conf. D. CALOV. in bibl. illustrat. in Io. III. fol. 692. SIGH.

By your singular benefit, O heavenly Father, I live reborn. What do I say, I live? Christ lives in me. For what I live in the flesh, I live in faith, which is in your only-begotten Son, who loved me, and gave himself for me.

O grace without my merit! O love without example! Relying on this, I live tranquil and cheerful among the fiery darts of the devil, among the cunning machinations of men. Live, I beseech you, O Jesus, author of the blessed life, perpetually in my soul, and most clemently grant that it may live eternally in the bosom and embrace of your mercy!

Latin:

Proprie loquendo neque Christus in nobis nascitur a), neque nouus in nobis est homo b), neque beneficio regenerationis fit caro de carne nostra c).

Prob. a. 1) Quia assertum illud, quod Christus in nobis generetur, est ἀγεωμετρητον. Perspicue docet S. Scriptura, quod Deus Pater nos regenerauerit per resurrectionem Iesu Christi, 1 Petr. I, 3. & quod in Christo Iesu per euangelium generati simus, 1 Cor. IV, 15. Quae eloquia Spiritus S. sunt clara & perspicua; at obscura & intricata loquendi ratio est, qua ipse Christus in nobis generari dicitur. 2) Christus est pater regenerationis, Es. VIII, 18. Hebr. II, 13. qui nos spiritualiter generat, non autem in nobis generatur. 3) Filius Dei ab aeterno generatur in sinu Patris coelestis, Io. I, 18. non in sinu nostro. Est generatio Filii Dei actio immanens, non emanans, aut transiens.

4) Iesus noster, qua homo, natus est in & ex Maria virgine, Luc. I, 35. non autem nascitur in, aut e nobis; caeteroqui proueniret ex essentia hominis fidelis. Nam generatio est communicatio essentiae. 5) Assertione illa, quod Christus in nobis generetur, vtuntur Quackeri, ad corrumpendum articulum de iustificatione peccatoris. Neque enim erubescit ROBERTUS BARCLAIVS in Apol. §. 7. p. 141. asserere: peccatorem iustificari, quando Christus in ipso formetur, generetur, & in lucem edatur. Quin & Mysticorum absurdissimum dogma est, generationem Christi in nobis fieri per introuersionem ad Deum. Verbum Patris caelestis effeetine toties in nobis generatur, quoties perfecte nos ad Deum introuertimus, inquit GERLACVS PETRI, citante D. LOESCHERO in praefat. theol. myst. orthod.

§. 8. Prob. b. 1) Nullibi docet S. Scriptura, Christus esse nouum hominem. Non autem docet nos sapere supra id, quod scriptum est, 1 Cor. IV, 6.

Christus est causa novi hominis. At causa de causato, & causatum de causa nunquam praedicatur in casu recto.

3) Novus homo, formaliter & abstractive consideratus, est accidens, scilicet agnitio Dei, Col. III, 10. iustitia & sanctitas vera, Eph. IV, 24. At quam impossibile est substantiam transmutari in accidens; tam impossibile etiam est, Christum mutari in novas qualitates, novas vires, novosque motus, quos verbo Dei conformiter novum hominem (abstractive suntum) appellamus.

4) Novus homo, concretive acceptus, est ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος, novis viribus a Deo instructus: At Christus est θεάνθρωπος. E. non est novus homo.

Prob. c. Christus factus est caro de carne nostra tum per incarnationem, Hebr. II, 14. tum etiam per vnionem & communicationem mysticam fideles redduntur participes carnis & sanguinis Christi, Eph. V, 30. & fiunt viva membra corporis Christi mystici, sive ecclesiae. Per regenerationem autem fides in Christum accenditur.

Antithesis est Weigelianorum & Quackerorum, statuentium, Christum generari in nobis, esseque novum hominem, & fieri in regeneratione carnem de carne nostra. Quorum argumenta potiora sunt:

I. Quicunque in nobis formatur, in nobis regeneratur (formatio quippe generationem supponit): Atqui Christus &c. E. Minor prob. ex Gal. IV, 19. vbi Apostolus inquit: Filioli mei, quos iterum parturio, vsque dum formetur Christus in vobis. Resp. 1) Neg. mai. Nam formam & imaginem nostri accipimus in speculo atque tabella pictoris, neque tamen ibi generamur. Nostrae animae imprimitur imago Christi primo per fidem, qua Christi faciem & formam sic cognoscimus, quemadmodum in sacris litteris ante oculos nostros praescriptus est: secundo per similitudinem & conformitatem vitae & sanctitatis Christi. 2) Obiectum in parturitione Paulina generandum non est Christus, sed Galatae: Filioli, inquit, quos iterum parturio. Non itaque Christus in nobis generatur, sed μορφοῦται, sive μορφίαν suam nobis impertitur, vt hac in vita similes evadamus imagini ipsius, perinde ac gesturi sumus in altera vita eiusdem imaginem, 1 Cor. XV, 49.

II. Apoc. XII, 5. Mulier amicta sole (per quam ecclesia intelligitur) peperit filium masculum, qui pasturus erat omnes gentes virga ferrea (per quem denotatur Christus). Quod si ecclesia Christum parit, quidni & fideles? Est enim ecclesia coetus fidelium. Resp. L. c. per filium allusione tantum phraseologica Christus Mariae filius, directe autem filii spirituales, quos ecclesia militans, de qua ibidem agitur, Deo cum dolore & inter angustias perfectionum enititur, repraesentantur.

III. Christus in nobis vivit, Gal. II, 20. E. etiam in nobis generatur. Resp. Christus in nobis vivit, non vt novus homo, sed vt auctor novae vitae; siquidem in ipso creati sumus ad bona opera, Eph. II, 10. Neque in nobis generatur, sed, velut Pater, nos regenerat.

IV. Omnis faciens voluntatem Christi, est ipsius mater, Matth. XII, 19. E. Christum generat. Resp. Faciens voluntatem Christi dicitur ipsius mater, non ob generationem, sed ob dilectionem. Neque enim homo matris instar Christum generat; sed Christus ipsum, perinde ac filius matrem, ardentissime diligit.

V. Orthodoxi Theologi phrasi illa, quod Christus in nobis generetur per fidem, vsi sunt, Resp. Theologi illi ante mota certamina locuti sunt fecurius, arctissimam nostram cum Christo vnionem expressuri: inualescente autem Quackerianismo, ab allegoria illa catachrestica iure meritoque abstinemus. Nullus autem Theologus orthodoxus asseruit, Christum in nobis generari, vt novus in nobis homo, & caro de carne nostra.

Quest. XXIII. Quomodo regeneratio, iustificatio & renouatio differunt?

Regeneratio, iustificatio & renouatio differunt: a) Ordine naturae: b) Ratione subiectorum: c) Ratione termini a quo, & ad quem: d) Ratione formae internae: e) Ratione modi agendi.

Prob. a. Ordine naturae iustificationem & renouationem praecedit regeneratio, sius donatio fidei, fine qua vti Deo non placemus, Hebr. XI, 6. ita nec iustificamur, nec renouamur, nisi simus regeniti.

Prob. b. Subiectum regenerationis est peccator per legem diuinam conuersus & contritus, sed vita fidei carens, adeoque spiritualiter mortuus: Subiectum iustificationis est peccator conuersus & renatus, seu contritus & credens in Christum: Subiectum renouationis est homo conuersus, renatus & iustificatus.

Prob. c. Regenerationis terminus a quo est mors spiritualis, prout haec notat carentiam virium credendi, terminus ad quem est fides saluifica: Iustificationis terminus a quo est reatus culpae & poenae, terminus ad quem est remissio peccatorum, & iustitia Christi imputata: Renouationis terminus a quo est dominium & reliquiae peccati, terminus ad quem est in ago Dei, & sanctitas inhaerens.

Prob. d. Regeneratio in donatione fidei, iustificatio in remissione peccatorum, & imputatione iustitiae Christi, renouatio in liberatione a dominio, maculisque peccati, & instauratone imaginis diuinae formaliter consistit.

Prob. e. Regeneratio est actio solius Dei, denominationem inferens intrinsecam subiecti, quod regeneratur, cum in corde ipsius a Spiritu S. excitetur fiducia in Christum, vt peccator, qui regeneratur, se mere passiue habeat.

Iustificatio est actio solius Dei, denominationem inferens extrinsecam subiecti, quod iustificatur; quippe cui aestimatione Dei propria iniustitia non imputatur, aliena autem (scil. Christi) iustitia imputatur, vel adiudicatur.

Vnde in negotio iustificationis peccator se etiam mere passiue habet, cum nemo coram iudicio diuino seipsum possit absoluere.

Renouatio est quidem actio Dei, sed non solius, ideo, quod ad eandem homo iustificatus viribus non propriis, sed superne collatis, tanquam causa subordinata, concurrit. Conf. D. CALOV. in bibl. illustrat. in Io. III. fol. 692.

SVSPIRIVM. Singulari tuo beneficio, o Pater coelestis, renatus viuo. Quid dico, viuo? viuit in me Christus. Nam quod viuo in carne, viuo in fide, quae est in Filium tuum vnigenitum, qui dilexit me, & tradidit se ipsum pro me.

O gratiam sine meo merito! O dilectionem sine exemplo! Hac fretus viuo tranquillus & hilaris inter ignita diaboli tela, inter callida hominum machinamenta. Viue, obsecro, o Iesu, auctor vitae beatae, perpetuo in anima mea, clementissimeque concede, vt haec aeternum viuat in sinu atque complexu misericordiae tuae!


## 23 On Justifying Grace, and the Justification of the Sinner


### Of Justifying Grace, and the Justification of the Sinner Before God

Quest. I. What is justification?

Justification is an act of grace, by which God, the most just and most merciful judge, to a sinful man, guilty of fault and punishment, but converted and reborn, out of mere mercy on account of the satisfaction and merit of Christ, through true faith apprehending, remits sins, and imputes the righteousness of Christ, so that, adopted as a Son of God, he becomes an heir of eternal life.

Latin:

Quest. I. Quid est iustificatio?

Iustificatio est actus gratiae, quo Deus, iudex iustissimus & misericordissimus, homini peccatori, culpae & poenae reo, sed conuerso & renato, ex mera misericordia fericordia propter satisfactionem & meritum Christi, vera fide apprehendium, peccata remittit, & iustitiam Christi imputat, vt in Filium Dei adoptatus, hæres fit vitæ æternæ. Quæst.


### Q. II. What does this 'to justify' signify?

The verb, to justify, in the present case, where the sinner is considered, guilty of fault and punishment, insofar as he is to be justified before the divine judgment, is not taken in a physical sense, but in a forensic or judicial one. For it does not signify to infuse a habit of righteousness into someone, or to make someone just by infused qualities; but to absolve a sinner from the guilt of fault and punishment for certain causes, and to esteem, declare, and pronounce him just.

Obs. The Latin verb, iustificare, is not read among profane authors: wherefore its meaning must be sought from the Scriptures alone. Unfolding these, we discover that the Latin word, iustificare, is expressed by the Hebrew הַצְדִּיק, and the Greek δικαιοῦν, & δικαιοῦσθαι. Which words never and nowhere in the entire code, even outside the business of the justification of a sinful man before God, signify the infusion of new qualities, but denote: a) The acknowledgment and celebration of divine righteousness, Ps. 51:6. Luke 7:29. Matt. 11:35. b) The showing and manifestation of accepted justification, James 2:12. c) Comparative justification, Ezek. 16:51. or even vain, by which one deems himself just, Luke 10:29. d) Liberation from sin, Rom. 6:7. e) They are also used of civil judgments in a forensic sense, concerning which it may suffice to have noted these few things. Deut. 25: 1. When there shall be a dispute between men, they shall come to judgment, that they may judge them: where they shall justify the just, and condemn the wicked. Prov. 17: 15. He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, are both an abomination to Jehovah. Isa. 5: 23. Woe to those who justify the wicked for a bribe.

Prob. That the Hebrew verb הַצְדִּיק, and the Greek δικαιοῦν and δικαιοῦσθαι, from which the Latin iustificare comes, designate a judicial act in the article of justification, is confirmed

1) From all the requirements of a judicial process, where we note a) A judgment rigid according to the norm of the law, concerning which Ps. 143:2. Enter not into judgment with thy servant: for no one living shall be just before thee. b) A most just judge, who is God, the judge of all the earth, Gen. 18:25. c) The defendant, who is every man a sinner. For the whole world becomes guilty before God. Rom. 3:19. By the whole world is understood the entire human race, liable to punishment on account of the transgression of the law. From which also sins are called debts, Matt. 6:12. d) The plaintiff or accuser, who is partly Moses the legislator, or the Mosaic law: There is one who accuses you, Moses, John 5:45; partly the devil, Rev. 12:10. e) The witness, who is the conscience. Their conscience bears witness to them, Rom. 2:15. f) The handwriting, which is the binding of the conscience through the moral law, Col. 2:14. (*).

g) The condemnatory sentence, which is held in the Mosaic law. Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things which are written in the book of the law, Deut. XXVII, 26.

h) The Mediator and advocate, who is Christ. There is one mediator of God and men, the man Jesus Christ, 1 Tim. II, 5. If anyone has sinned, we have an advocate (paracletum) with the Father, Jesus Christ, the righteous, 1 John II, 1.

i) The satisfaction of the Mediator. For this mediator gave himself as an ἀντίλυτρον, a price of redemption for all, 1 Tim. II, 6. by whose death we have been reconciled to God, Rom. V, 10. and by whose obedience we are constituted righteous, Rom. V, 16.

k) The non-imputation of sin, and the judicial imputation of the righteousness of Christ. Concerning which Paul says in 2 Cor. V, 19: God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, while not imputing their sins to them, and Rom. IV, 5: To him who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, faith is imputed for righteousness.

1) The absolutory sentence, then generally pronounced through the gospel: Let everyone who believes in him receive remission of sins through the name of Jesus Christ, Acts X, 43.; then specifically applied to a certain individual: Your sins are forgiven you, Matt. IX, 2.

2) Condemnation is not an infusion of sin: Therefore, the opposite, justification, is not an infusion of righteousness. For the logic of opposites is the same. The antecedent is clear from Rom. VIII, 33.

3) Justification is opposed to the imputation of iniquities, Ps. XXXII, 2. Rom. IV, 8. Therefore, it signifies absolution from guilt.

The consequence is evident. Just as the imputation of iniquity is an act of a judge, who recognizes, estimates, and determines iniquity to pertain to the delinquent, so that he is obligated to punishment: so the non-imputation of iniquity is an act of a judge, who for grave reasons absolves a man from the obligation to punishment, or from guilt.

4) Justification consists in absolution from things from which we cannot be justified by the law of Moses, and are justified through Christ, Acts XIII, 38. Therefore, justification does not denote the infusion of righteousness, but absolution from guilt.

5) The forensic meaning of justification is taught by equivalent phrases and periphrases, all of which are judicial, e.g., to impute righteousness, Rom. IV, 3, 5; to remit sins, Rom. III, 25; John XX, 23; to be reconciled to God, 2 Cor. V, 19; not to be judged, John III, 18. (*).

Antithesis (*)

The antithesis is that of the Papists, for whom to justify is to infuse a habit of justice, and of the Anabaptists, Schwenckfeldians, and Weigelians, for whom to justify is to make a man just and upright by renewing him, or by giving a new heart and a new spirit. Who impugn the evangelical doctrine of justification with the following arguments:

I. The word to justify, by the force of the voice, signifies to make someone just: for it is composed of the words, just and to make. To esteem and pronounce as just does not signify to make just. R. a) Arguments from etymology and the grammatical composition of a word are invalid. We sanctify the name of the Lord, not by making it holy, but by acknowledging its holiness and esteeming it most highly. b) The composition of a Latin word does not constitute a rule and measure for investigating the genuine meaning of justification; since it must be deduced from the Hebrew and Greek language, which the Holy Spirit used. Among the Hebrews, צדק in Kal signifies to be just, in Piel צדק to attribute the praise of justice to someone, in Hiphil הצדיק to pronounce just, with which the Greek δικαιοῦν corresponds.

II. Dan. XII, 3. מצדיקים are called those who instruct unto justice, not those who absolve from sins, or declare just: R. to justify does not signify to absolve from sins. R. a) To instruct unto justice is not the same as to infuse a habit of justice. b) The Vulgate version indeed rendered the Hebrew word in that way, but according to the source, the Hebrew word must be translated: Justifying, namely the doctors of the church, διακονικῶς, or ministerially absolving from sins, and announcing the word of reconciliation.

III. Whatever justification admits of degrees, that does not denote absolution from sins: But the justification of a sinner before God &c. Therefore. The major shines with its own light; because absolution from sins is perfect, so that it can neither be diminished nor increased. The minor is evident from Apoc. XXII, 11. Ὁ δίκαιος δικαιωθήτω ἔτι, let the just be justified still. R. L. c. is understood as the continuation of justification through the perseverance of faith and the flight from proaeretic sin. For the adverb ἔτι nowhere signifies the intension of quality, but the continuation of time; for it does not mean the same as μᾶλλον, more, but ποῤῥώτερον, let him be justified further.

Instance: But the penitent publican is said to be more justified than the Pharisee, Luc. XVIII, 14. R. Luke imitates the Hebrews, who use a comparative particle for a negative adverb. The sense is: The publican went down justified, but not the Pharisee.

IV. Whatever justification follows sanctification, that is not absolution from sins: But the justification of a sinner &c. Therefore. The major is evident; because absolution from sins precedes sanctification. The minor is proved from 1 Cor. VI, 11. You are washed, you are sanctified, you are justified. R. a) Distinguish between the order of words and of things. One must not always attend to the order of words, where divine benefits are exchanged, but to the order of things, which is otherwise held in sacred matters (*). d) The Apostle speaks with the converted Corinthians, adult baptized in their maturity. These, before receiving baptism, were informed by the divine word, and justified through faith in Christ, i.e., having obtained the remission of sins, then renewed and sanctified, and finally washed by baptism. The Apostle recalls these three things to the memory of the Corinthians, although in reverse order, so that, mindful of their washing in baptism, the holiness conferred, and the remission of sins received, they might not relapse into their former sins. Wherefore, in this place, justification is taken in a forensic sense, and does not denote sanctification, since it is distinguished from the same in the cited text.

Latin:

Verbum, iustificare, in præsenti, vbi consideratur peccator, reus culpæ & pœnæ, quatenus coram iudicio diuino iustificandus est, non sumitur sensu physico, sed forensi, siue iudiciali. Neque enim significat, habitum iustitiæ alicui infundere, aut infusis qualitatibus aliquem iustum facere; sed peccatorem a reatu culpæ & pœnæ certis de caussis absoluere, & iustum æstimare, declarare, pronuntiare.

Obs. Verbum latinum, iustificare, apud profanos auctores non legitur: quare eius significatio petenda est ex solis Scripturis. Quas euoluentes deprehendimus, vocem latinam, iustificare, per hebræum הַצְדִּיק, atque græcum δικαιοῦν, & δικαιοῦσθαι exprimi. Quæ verba nunquam & nusquam in vniuerso codice, etiam extra negotium iustificationis hominis peccatoris coram Deo, infusionem nouarum qualitatum significant, sed notant: a) Iustitiæ diuinæ agnitionem, & celebrationem, Ps. LI, 6. Luc. VII, 29. Matth. XI, 35. b) Acceptæ iustificationis ostensionem & manifestationem, Iac. II, 12. c) Iustificationem comparatiuam, Ezech. XVI, 51. vel etiam vanam, qua quis seipsum iustum reputat, Luc. X, 29. d) Liberationem a peccato, Rom. VI, 7. e) De iudiciis etiam ciuilibus in sensu forensi vsurpantur, de quibus pauca hæc dicta notasse sufficiat. Deut. XXV, 1. Cum fuerit lis inter viros, accedent ad iudicium, vt iudicent eos: vbi iustificabunt iustum, & condemnabunt impium. Prou. XVII, 15. Iustificans impium, & condemnans iustum, abominatio-Iehouæ simul sunt. Es. V, 23. Væ iustificantibus impium propter munus.

Prob. Quod verbum hebræum הַצְדִּיק, & græcorum δικαιοῦν καὶ δικαιοῦσθαι, vn de latinorum iustificare est, designent in articulo iustificationis actum iudicialem, confirmatur

1) Ex omnibus requisitis processus iudicialis, vbi notamus a) Iudicium secundum normam legis rigidum, de quo Ps. CXLIII, 2. Ne intra in iudicium cum seruo tuo: quia non iustus erit coram te vllus viuens. b) Iudicem iustissimum, qui est Deus iudex vniuersæ terræ, Gen. XVIII, 25. c) Reum, qui est omnis homo peccator. Totus namque mundus reus fit Deo. Rom. III, 19. Per totum mundum intelligitur vniuersum genus humanum, ob transgressionem legis pœnæ obnoxium. Ex quo etiam peccata debita appellantur, Matth. VI, 12. d) Actorem siue accusatorem, qui est partim Moses legislator, siue lex Mosaica: Est, qui vos accusat, Moses, Io. V, 45.; partim diabolus, Apoc. XII, 10. e) Testem, qui est conscientia. Testimonium ipsis perhibet conscientia illorum, Rom. II, 15. f) Chirographum, quod est coniunctio conscientiæ per legem moralem, Col. II, 14. (*).

g) Sententiam condemnatoriam, quæ habetur in lege Mosaica. Maledictus omnis, qui non permanet in omnibus, quæ scripta sunt in libro legis, Deut. XXVII, 26.

h) Mediatorem & advocatum, qui est Christus. Vnus est mediator Dei & hominum, homo Iesus Christus, 1 Tim. II, 5. Si quis peccaverit, paracletum habemus apud Patrem Iesum Christum, iustum, 1 Io. II, 1.

i) Mediatoris satisfactionem. Hic enim mediator dedit seipsum ἀντίλυτρον, pretium redemptionis pro omnibus, 1 Tim. II, 6. per cuius mortem Deo reconciliati sumus, Rom. V, 10. & per cuius obedientiam iusti constituimur, Rom. V, 16.

k) Non-imputationem peccati, & imputationem iustitiæ Christi iudicialem. De qua Paulus 2 Cor. V, 19. Deus erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi ipsi, dum non imputabat illis peccata illorum, & Rom. IV, 5. Ei, qui non operatur, credit vero in eum, qui iustificat impium, imputatur fides in iustitiam.

1) Sententiam absolutoriam, tum generatim per evangelium pronuntiatam: Remissionem peccatorum accipiat per nomen Iesu Christi omnis, qui credit in ipsum, Act. X, 43.; tum sigulatim applicatam ad certum individuum: Remissa sunt tibi peccata tua, Matth. IX, 2.

2) Condemnatio non est peccati infusio: E. Opposita iustificatio non est iustitiæ infusio. Oppositorum enim eadem est ratio. Antecedens liquet ex Rom. VIII, 33.

3) Iustificatio opposita est imputationi iniquitatum, Ps. XXXII, 2. Rom. IV, 8. E, significat absolutionem a reatu.

Consequentia est evidens. Sicut imputatio iniquitatis est actus iudicis, qui iniquitatem cognoscit, æstimat, & statuit, eandem pertinere ad delinquentem, vt obligatus sit ad pœnam: ita non imputatio iniquitatis est actus iudicis, qui gravibus de caussis hominem ab obligatione ad pœnam, sive reatu absoluit.

4) Iustificatio consistit in absolutione ab aliis, a quibus per legem Mosis iustificari non possumus, & per Christum iustificamur, Actor. XIII, 38. Ergo iustificatio non denotat infusionem iustitiæ, sed absolutionem a reatu.

5) Significatum iustificationis forensem docent æquipollentes phrases & periphrases, quæ omnes sunt iudiciales, v. gr. imputare iustitiam, Rom. IV, 3. 5. peccata remittere, Rom. III, 25. Io. XX, 23. Deo reconciliari, 2 Cor. V, 19. non iudicari, Io. III, 18. (*).

Antithesis (*)

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, quibus iustificare est, habitum iustitiae infundere, & Anabaptistarum, Schwenckfeldianorum atque Weigelianorum, quibus iustificare est, hominem iustum & probum facere renouando, siue nouum cor & nouum spiritum dando. Qui sequentibus argumentis doctrinam euangelicam de iustificatione impugnant:

I. Verbum iustificare, vi vocis, significat aliquem iustum facere: componitur enim ex vocibus, iustus & facere. Iustum aestimare & pronuntiare non significat iustum facere. E. Resp. a) Argumenta ab etymologia, & compositione vocis grammatica sunt inualida. Nos sanctificamus nomen Domini, illud non sanctum faciendo, sed eius sanctitatem agnoscendo, & maximi aestimando. b) Compositio vocis latinae non constituit regulam & mensuram inuestigandi genuinum significatum iustificationis; quippe qui ex lingua hebraea & graeca, qua vsus est Spiritus S., deducendus est. Apud Hebraeos צדק in Kal significat iustum esse, in Piel צדק iustitiae laudem alicui tribuere, in Hiphil הצדיק iustum pronuntiare, cui graecorum δικαιοῦν consonat.

II. Dan. XII, 3. מצדיקים dicuntur erudientes ad iustitiam, non a peccatis absoluentes, aut iustos declarantes: E. iustificare non significat, a peccatis absoluere. Resp. a) Erudire ad iustitiam non est idem, quod habitum iustitiae infundere. b) Vulgata quidem versio vocem hebraeam ita reddidit, sed secundum fontem vox hebraea vertenda est: Iustificantes, nempe doctores ecclesiae, διακονικῶς, siue ministerialiter a peccatis absoluentes, & verbum reconciliationis annuntiantes.

III. Quaecunque iustificatio gradus admittit, illa non notat absolutionem a peccatis: Atqui iustificatio peccatoris coram Deo &c. Ergo. Maior sua luce radiat; quia absolutio a peccatis est perfecta, vt neque minui, neque intendi possit. Minor constat ex Apoc. XXII, 11. Ὁ δίκαιος δικαιωθήτω ἔτι, iustus iustificetur adhuc. Resp. L. c. intelligitur continuatio iustificationis per fidei perseuerantiam & fugam peccati proaeretici. Aduerbium enim ἔτι nuspiam significat qualitatis intensionem, sed temporis continuationem; non idem quippe valet, quod μᾶλλον, magis, sed ποῤῥώτερον, vlterius iustificetur.

Instantia: Sed publicanus poenitens dicitur magis iustificatus, quam Pharisaeus, Luc. XVIII, 14. Resp. Imitatur Lucas hebraeos, pro negatiuo aduerbio particula comparatiua vtentes. Sensus est: Publicanus descendit iustificatus, non autem Pharisaeus.

IV. Quaecunque iustificatio sequitur sanctificationem, illa non est absolutio a peccatis: Atqui iustificatio peccatoris &c. Ergo. Maior est euidens; quia absolutio a peccatis sanctificationem antecedit. Minor probatur ex 1 Cor. VI, 11. Abluti estis, sanctificati estis, iustificati estis. Resp. a) Distingu. inter ordinem verborum & rerum. Non semper attendendum est ad ordinem verborum, vbi commutantur beneficia diuina, sed ad ordinem rerum, qui alias in sacris tenetur (*). d) Loquitur Apostolus cum conuersis Corinthiis, adulta ætate baptizatis. Hi ante susceptum baptismum e verbo diuino erant informati, & per fidem in Christum iustificati, h. e. remissionem peccatorum indepti, dein renouati & sanctificati, denique baptisimo abluti. Hæc tria Apostolus, ordine quamuis retrogrado, Corinthiis in memoriam reuocat, vt memores ablutionis suæ in baptisino, collatæ sanctimoniæ, & acceptæ remissionis peccatorum, in pristina peccata ne relabantur. Quare h. l. iustificatio in sensu forensi sumitur, neque sanctificationem notat, cum ab eadem in textu citato distinguatur.


### Question III. Who justifies the sinner?

God the triune justifies the sinner a), the Father b), the Son of God c), and the Holy Spirit d).

Proof a. From Mark II, 8. Who can forgive sins, but God alone? God alone forgives sins αὐτοκρατορικῶς, principally; the legates of Christ [forgive] διακονικῶς, ministerially, John XX, 23. Furthermore, since justification is indeed an immanent action of God, insofar as it occurs within the mind and will of God, yet it tends toward an object outside of God, and thus far is an action ad extra; it is common to all three persons of the divinity, saving, however, the order of these, according to that trite saying: Divine works ad extra are undivided, i.e., common.

Proof b. From Rom. VIII, 33. Who shall lay anything to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth. Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died. Where the word God is taken ὑποστατικῶς and denotes God the Father, because he is distinguished from Christ in verse 34, of whom the Apostle had also said in verse 32: God spared not his own Son.

Proof c. From Is. LIII, 11. By his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many. Where note a) Christ is called the servant of God, according to his human nature, considered in the state of humiliation. For Christ, when exalted, does not work servilely regarding the business of our salvation. b) He is called righteous not only in himself, but because he also procured righteousness for us by his most perfect obedience. c) Christ justifies by his knowledge, i.e., by faith, by which he is known and apprehended. d) The Son of God is the efficient cause of justification; insofar as he justifies us in one act with the Father and the Holy Spirit: he is also the meritorious cause of justification, insofar as he has merited righteousness for us by his active and passive obedience: he is furthermore the material cause of justification, insofar as the merit of Christ is the very thing which is offered to be apprehended by converted and reborn sinners, and is imputed for righteousness: he is finally the formal cause in application, insofar as we are justified by the imputed righteousness of Christ.

Proof d. From 1 Cor. VI, 11. Ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God. The Holy Spirit justifies by offering the righteousness acquired by the merit of Christ to sinners through the evangelical promise, and by conferring and sealing it to the faithful.

Latin:

Peccatorem iustificat Deus triunus a), Pater b), Filius Dei c), & Spiritus Sanctus d).

Prob. a. Ex Marc. II, 8. Quis potest peccata remittere, nisi vnus Deus? Solus Deus peccata remittit αὐτοκρατορικῶς, principaliter, legati Christi διακονικῶς, ministerialiter, Io. XX, 23. Ceterum cum iustificatio sit actio Dei quidem immanens, quatenus intra mentem & voluntatem Dei fit, in obiectum tamen extra Deum tendat, atque hactenus actio ad extra sit; omnibus tribus personis diuinitatis, saluo tamen harum ordine, communis est, iuxta tritum illud: Opera diuina ad extra sunt indiuisa, i. e. communia.

Prob. b. Ex Rom. VIII, 33. Quis accusabit electos Dei? Deus est, qui iustificat. Quis est, qui condemnet? Christus est, qui mortuus est. Vbi vox Deus, sumitur ὑποστατικῶς atque denotat Deum Patrem, quia a Christo v. 34. distinguitur, de quo etiam Apostolus v. 32. dixerat: Deus proprio Filio non pepercit.

Prob. c. Ex Es. LIII, 11. Per scientiam sui iustificabit iustus seruus meus multos. Vbi obs. a) Christus dicitur seruus Dei, secundum humanam naturam, in statu exinanitionis consideratam. Christus namque exaltatus non operatur seruiliter circa salutis nostræ negotium. b) Dicitur iustus non solum in se, sed quia etiam nobis iustitiam perfectissima sua obedientia peperit. c) Iustificat Christus per scientiam sui, i. e. per fidem, qua agnoscitur & apprehenditur. d) Filius Dei est caussa iustificationis efficiens; quatenus vno actu cum Patre & Spiritu S. nos iustificat: est etiam caussa iustificationis meritoria, quatenus obedientia sua actiua & passiua iustitiam nobis promeritus est: est præterea caussa iustificationis materialis, quatenus meritum Christi est res ipsa, quæ peccatoribus conuersis & renatis apprehendenda offertur, & ad iustitiam imputatur: est denique caussa formalis in applicatione, quatenus imputata Christi iustitia iustificamur.

Prob. d. Ex 1 Cor. VI, 11. Iustificati estis in nomine Domini Iesu, & per Spiritum Dei nostri. Spiritus S. iustificat, acquifitam merito Christi iustitiam per promissionem euangelicam peccatoribus offerendo, fidelibus conferendo & obsignando.


### Question IV. What is the internal impulsive cause of justification?

To justify the sinner, God is internally moved by his most abundant grace, by which is understood in the present case benevolence, mercy, and the gratuitous favor of God, with which he embraces those who believe in Christ.

…Proof 1) From Rom. III, 24. We are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. St. Paul does not simply say that we are justified by the grace of God, but with the addition of the particle, freely, so that we may understand that there is no cause in us which moved God to justify us.…

2) From Eph. II, 8. By grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not of yourselves, it is the gift of God; not of works, lest anyone should boast. Here the Apostle ascribes all salvation, as much of grace, which consists in the remission of sins, as of divine glory, to God, and opposes this to every quality inherent in us, so that all glorying in vain things may be cut off from us.

2) Synonyms of justifying grace are χρηστότης καὶ φιλανθρωπία, kindness and love of mankind, as is evident from Tit. III, 4. The antithesis is that of the Papists, who posit that justifying grace is not the gratuitous favor of God outside of us, but grace infused, and like a quality inherent in us: Who rely upon the following arguments:

I. Justifying grace is said to be given by measure, Eph. IV, 7. The benevolence of God is not given by measure, because it is immense and infinite. E. Resp. The Apostle in the cited place does not understand justifying grace, but the gifts of the Holy Spirit, both sanctifying and ministering, which are called grace metonymically, because they are the effects of grace.

II. Justifying grace is shed abroad in our hearts through the Holy Spirit. Divine benevolence is not charity shed abroad, etc. Therefore. The major premise is Paul's, Rom. V, 5. The minor is evident; because benevolence is in God, not in our hearts. Resp. a) By charity in the cited place is not understood the charity by which we love God, but by which God embraces us; that charity which God declared toward us while we were yet sinners, v. 8, which is certainly God's, not ours. b) It is not said to be charity infused, but shed abroad in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, i.e., most bountifully declared, and confirmed and sealed by the efficacious operation of the Holy Spirit. It is therefore in us not by way of subjective inhesion, but by way of termination toward us, of operation, and of sense through faith, through which we taste the sweetness of divine charity.

III. The grace of God is said to be a gift abounding unto us, Rom. V, 15. The benevolence of God is not a gift abounding unto us, because it is the cause of gifts. Therefore. Resp. The words of the Pauline text are: much more the grace and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ has abounded unto many. The Apostle speaks accurately, and distinguishes grace from the gift of righteousness and salvation: just as eternal life is also called χάρισμα, Rom. VI, 23. Grace and the gift of righteousness are said to abound unto us, not by reason of subjective inhesion, but by reason of the most liberal declaration and bestowal.

IV. Of the benevolence of God it is not correctly said that it was made, because it is eternal and independent: It is said of the grace of God that it was made. E. The minor is proved from John I, 17. The law was given through Moses: grace and truth came [was made] through Jesus Christ. Resp. The grace of God is said to be made with respect to us, i.e., meritoriously acquired for us through Jesus Christ.

Latin:

Ad iustificandum peccatorem Deus interne motus est gratia sua vberrima, per quam in præsenti intelligitur beneuolentia, misericordia, & gratuitus Dei fauor, quo credentes in Christum complectitur.

Prob. 1) Ex Rom. III, 24. Iustificamur gratis gratia ipsius per redemtionem, quæ est in Christo Iesu. S. Paullus non simpliciter dicit, nos iustificari gratia Dei, sed cum adiene particulae, gratis, vt intelligamus, nullam in nobis esse caussam, quae Deum ad iustificandum nos permouerit.

2) Ex Eph. II, 8. Gratia saluati estis per fidem; & hoc non ex vobis, Dei donum est; non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur. Hic Apostolus omnem salutem, tam gratiae, quae consistit in remissione peccatorum, quam gloriae diuinae adscribit, & hanc opponit omni qualitati nobis inhaerenti, vt omnis gloria inania nobis praecidatur.

2) Gratiae iustificantis synonyma sunt χρηστότης καὶ φιλανθρωπία, benignitas & amor hominum, vt patet ex Tit. III, 4. Antithesis est Pontificiorum, statuentium, gratiam iustificantem non esse fauorem Dei gratuitum extra nos, sed gratiam infusam, & instar qualitatis nobis inhaerentem: Qui sequentibus argumentis innituntur:

I. Gratia iustificans dicitur dari ad mensuram, Eph. IV, 7. Beneuolentia Dei non datur ad mensuram, quia est immensa & infinita. E. Resp. Apostolus l. c. non intelligit gratiam iustificantem, sed dona Spiritus S. tum sanctificantia, tum ministrantia, quae dicuntur gratia metonymice, quia sunt effecta gratiae.

II. Gratia iustificans est diffusa in cordibus nostris per Spiritum S. Beneuolentia diuina non est caritas diffusa &c. E. Maior est Paulli, Rom. V, 5. Minor constat; quia beneuolentia est in Deo, non in cordibus nostris. Resp. a) Per caritatem l. c. non intelligitur caritas, qua nos Deum diligimus, sed qua Deus nos complectitur; illa caritas, quam Deus erga nos declarauit, cum adhuc essemus peccatores, v. 8. quae vtique est Dei, non nostra, b) Non dicitur caritas infusa, sed diffusa in cordibus nostris per Spiritum S. i. e. largiffune declarata, & efficaci Spiritus S. operatione confirmata & obsignata. Est itaque in nobis non per modum subiectiuae inhaesionis, sed per modum terminationis ad nos, operationis, & sensus per fidem, per quam dulcedinem caritatis diuinae degustamus.

III. Gratia Dei dicitur donum in nos abundans, Rom. V, 15. Beneuolentia Dei non est donum in nos abundans, quia est caussa donorum. E. Resp. Verba textus Paullini sunt: multo magis gratia & donum in gratia vnius hominis Iesu Christi in multos superabundauit. Apostolus loquitur accurate, & gratiam a dono iustitiae & salutis distinguit: sicut etiam vita aeterna dicitur χάρισμα, Rom. VI, 23. Dicitur autem gratia & donum iustitiae in nos abundare, non ratione subiectiuae inhaesionis, sed ratione liberalissimae declarationis & collationis.

IV. De beneuolentia Dei non recte dicitur, quod facta sit, quia est aeterna & independens: De gratia Dei dicitur, quod facta sit. E. Minor probatur e Io. I, 17. Lex per Mosen data est: gratia & veritas per Iesum Christum facta est. Resp. Gratia Dei respectu nostri dicitur facta, i. e. per Iesum Christum meritorie acquisita nobis.


### Q. V. What is the external impulsive cause of justification?

The external impulsive cause of justification is the satisfaction and merit of Christ, comprising the active and passive obedience of Christ, both satisfactory and meritorious a). By passive obedience, Christ of his own accord transferred to himself and suffered the punishments of sins, which were to be inflicted upon the violators of the law, so that sins might not be imputed as a punishment to converted and reborn sinners b). By active obedience, Christ most perfectly fulfilled the divine law in the place of the fallen human race, so that that vicarious fulfillment of the law might be imputed as righteousness to sinners believing in Christ c).

Obs. I. The meritorious cause is contained under the impulsive, as a species under a genus. For the meritorious cause is that which, by a good deed worthy of reward, impels the efficient cause to bestow the reward. Therefore, the merit of Christ impelled the will of God to justify the believing sinner.

Obs. II. The satisfaction and merit of Christ are indeed most closely connected, yet they differ in a certain respect. The former is the payment of our debts, by which we were bound to God; through that satisfactory payment of our debts, Christ merited for us immunity from guilt and punishment. Therefore, satisfaction stands in relation to merit as a cause, and merit as an effect. Christ satisfied the Holy Trinity, not us, although for us; but He merited not for the Holy Trinity itself, but for us. Satisfaction implies a respect for compensating the injury done to God; merit implies a respect for acquiring gratuitous reward for sinners. Hence it is that some Theologians call only the active obedience of Christ, in a stricter sense, merit.

Prob. a. By His passive obedience, Christ satisfied the threat of the law, expressed in Mosaic words: "You shall surely die," Gen. II, 17, by undergoing voluntary death for the sins of men: Gal. I, 4; by His active obedience, He satisfied the law itself, by fulfilling it most exactly, Matth. V, 17. Passive obedience satisfied for the punishment; active for the guilt of the sinner. Passive obedience merited absolution from the guilt of punishment; active, righteousness valid before God.

Prob. b. 1) From Rom. III, 25. 26. We are justified freely by His grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus; whom God set forth as a propitiation by faith in His blood, to demonstrate His righteousness, because of the passing over of sins previously committed. In these words, the Apostle presents to us all the causes of justification for consideration. He expresses the efficient cause by the pronoun αὐτῆς, "His," namely, God's. He calls the internal impulsive cause the grace of God, i.e., the effect of benevolence; from which, by the particle "freely," He removes all our merit, all cause existing in us. But to show clearly that the grace of God, by which we are justified, is not absolute, but founded in the merit of Christ, He subjoins the meritorious, or external impulsive cause, which He calls ἀπολύτρωσιν, the redemption of Christ. He aptly calls this ἱλαστήριον, propitiation. Just as the cover placed on the ark of the covenant covered the tablets of the law; so Christ covers the lightning bolt of the law with His obedience, Rom. IV, 7. The Apostle adds ἐν αὐτῷ αἵματι, "in His blood." In the Old Testament, the propitiatory was sprinkled with the blood of victims to reconcile the people to God, Lev. XVI, 14. 15. So Christ was sprinkled with His own blood, without which there is no remission, Hebr. IX, 22. He names the mediating offering cause πρόθεσιν, "proposition," i.e., the preaching of the gospel; by which Christ with His benefits is proposed and offered. The receiving medium is faith, or the trust of the repentant sinner, fixed in the blood of Christ. The final cause is the demonstration of divine vindicative justice, which had to be satisfied by the blood of Christ, so that the sinner might be absolved from the guilt of punishment while it remained intact. The formal cause is the transmission, that is, the forgiveness of past sins.

2) From Rom. V, 8. God commends His love toward us, in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Much more then, having now been justified in His blood, Christ died for us. Much more then, having now been justified in His blood him, we shall be saved by him from wrath. For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son; much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved in his life.

The Apostle asserts that we are justified in his blood, i. e., on account of the blood of Christ, through which justification is acquired for us; which assertion he explains by an equivalent phrase when he says that we are reconciled to God by the death of his Son.

To be justified by Paul is the same as for a sinful man to be reconciled to God, or, having obtained the remission of offenses, to return to grace with God through the death of the Son of God, by which the vindictive divine justice has been satisfied, on account of the supreme dignity of the Mediator, the God-man (θεανθρώπου), who died.

Latin:

Caussa impulsiva externa iustificationis est satisfactio & meritum Christi, complectens obedientiam Christi actiuam & passiuam, vtramque satisfactoriam & meritomiam a). Obedientia passiva Christus poenas peccatorum, violatoribus legis infligendas, sponte sua in se transtulit ac perpessus est, ne peccatoribus conuersis & renatis peccata in poenam imputarentur b). Obedientia actiua Christus legem diuinam vice generis humani lapsi perfectissime impleuit, vt illa impletio legis vicaria peccatoribus in Christum credentibus ad iustitiam imputaretur c).

Obs. I. Causa meritoria continetur sub impulsiva, ut species sub genere. Nam causa meritoria est, quae benefacto, quod praemio dignum fit, efficientem ad praemium conferendum impellit. Impulit ergo meritum Christi voluntatem Dei ad peccatorem credentem justificandum.

Obs. II. Satisfactio & meritum Christi sunt quidem conjunctissima, certo tamen respectu differunt. Illa est nostrorum debitorum, quibus Deo obstricti eramus, exsolutio; per illam satisfactoriam debitorum nostrorum exsolutionem Christus nobis meruit immunitatem a culpa & poena. Quare satisfactio in ordine ad meritum se habet instar causae, meritum instar effectus. Christus satisfecit SS. Trinitati, non nobis, licet pro nobis; at non ipsi SS. Trinitati, sed nobis meruit. Satisfactio respectum infert ad injuriam, Deo illatam, compensandam; meritum importat respectum ad mercedem gratuitam acquirendam peccatoribus. Inde fit, ut nonnulli Theologi solam obedientiam Christi activam sensu strictiori vocent meritum.

Prob. a. Obedientia passiva Christus satisfecit comminationi legis, verbis expressae Mosaicis: Morte morieris, Gen. II, 17. pro peccatis hominum voluntariam mortem subeundo: Gal. I, 4: obedientia activa satisfecit ipsi legi, eam exactissime implendo, Matth. V, 17. Obedientia passiva satisfecit pro poena; activa pro culpa peccatoris. Meruit obedientia passiva absolutionem a reatu poenae; activa justitiam, coram Deo valentem.

Prob. b. 1) Ex Rom. III, 25. 26. Justificamur gratis gratia ipsius, per redemptionem, quae est in Christo Iesu; quem proposuit Deus propitiatorium per fidem in ipsius sanguine, in demonstrationem justitiae suae, propter transmissionem prius factorum peccatorum. Quibus verbis Apostolus considerandas nobis exhibet omnes justificationis causas. Causam efficientem exprimit pronomine αὐτῆς, ipsius, nempe Dei. Causam impulsivam internam vocat gratiam Dei, i. e. effectum benevolentiae; a qua per particulam, gratis, removet omne nostrum meritum, omnem causam, in nobis existentem. Vt vero perspicue ostendat, gratiam Dei, qua justificamur, non esse absolutam, sed in merito Christi fundatam, subnectit causam meritoriam, vel impulsivam externam, quam vocat ἀπολύτρωσιν, redemptionem Christi. Hunc concinne appellat ἱλαστήριον, propitiatorium. Quem ad modum operculum, arcae foederis inpositum, tegebat tabulas legis; ita Christus fulmen legis obedientia sua obtegit, Rom. IV, 7. Addit Apostolus ἐν αὐτῷ αἵματι, in ipsius sanguine. In V. T. propitiatorium victimarum sanguine aspergebatur, ad populum Deo reconciliandum, Leu. XVI, 14. 15. Ita Christus aspersus est suo ipsius sanguine, fine quo nulla fit remissio, Hebr. IX, 22. Causam mediam offerentem nominat πρόθεσιν, propositionem, i. e. praedicationem euangelii; qua Christus cum beneficiis suis proponitur & offertur. Medium recipiens est fides, sive fiducia peccatoris poenitentis, defixa in sanguine Christi. Causam finalem est demonstratio justitiae divinae vindicativae, cui satisfaciendum erat sanguine Christi, vt eadem salua peccator reatu poenae absolueretur. Causa formalis est transinissio, id est, condonatio peccatorum praeteritorum.

2) Ex Rom. V, 8. Commendat suam dilectionem erga nos Deus, quod, adhuc peccatoribus existentibus nobis, Christus pro nobis mortuus est. Multo magis ergo justificati nunc in sanguine existentibus nobis, Christus pro nobis mortuus est. Multò magis ergo iustificati nunc in sanguine illius, saluabimur per ipsum ab ira. Si enim, cum essemus hostes, reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem filii ipsius; multo magis reconciliati saluabimur in vita eius.

Apostolus asserit, nos esse iustificatos in sanguine, i. e. propter sanguinem Christi, per quem nobis iustificatio est acquisita; quam suam assertionem exponit per phrasin aequipollentem, cum ait, nos esse Deo reconciliatos per mortem filii ipsius.

Paullo iustificari idem est, atque hominem peccatorem reconciliari Deo, siue impetrata offensarum remissione, redire cum Deo in gratiam per mortem Filii Dei, per quam iustitiae diuinae vindictiuae satisfactum est, ob summam mediatoris θεανθρώπου, qui mortuus est, dignitatem.


### Q. V. What is the external impulsive cause of justification?: 3) From

3) From

Eph. I, 7. In Christ we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins.

Cf. Col. I, 14. God remits sins to believers in Christ, therefore through the bloody death of Christ, as a ransom (λύτρον), they are redeemed from the guilt of sin.

Proof. c. 1) From Rom. X, 14. Τὸ τέλος νόμῳ, Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.

Obs. a) Τὸ τέλος νόμῳ does not denote the abrogation or cessation of the law, but its complement, consummation, or perfect fulfillment.

b) The righteousness of Christ is understood not as essential, common to God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, which is incommunicable externally, nor as habitual, by which Christ excelled as man from the first moment of conception, but as the active obedience acquired for us, rendered in our place to the divine law.

For the effect of vicarious fulfillment of the law is righteousness, which indeed is Christ's causally, but the believing sinner's terminatively, or, to speak more clearly, righteousness acquired by Christ for the sinful man through the most exact fulfillment of the law.

It pertains to Christ as the meritorious cause; it also pertains to the converted and reborn sinner as the subject in whom it terminates by Christ's intention, and to whom it is imputed by God's gracious estimation.

Therefore, the sinner believing in Christ is called righteous by the imputed righteousness of Christ. c) The Apostle adds: Παντὶ πιστεύοντι, to everyone who believes; because the righteousness acquired for us by Christ the mediator must be apprehended by true faith and applied to us, so that it may become and remain ours.

2) From

Rom. V, 19. For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners; so also by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.

Adam, by active disobedience, by which he transgressed the divine law, devolved unrighteousness upon the entire human race:

Therefore, Christ the mediator, by active obedience, by which he fulfilled the divine law, derived righteousness upon the entire human race; for the reason of opposites is the same. 3) If Christ by his active obedience had not fulfilled the divine law for righteousness to the believing man, every sinner would be cursed:

But not every sinner is cursed: Therefore, Christ by his active obedience fulfilled the divine law for righteousness to the believing man.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, who deny that we are justified by God on account of the satisfaction and merit of Christ; their arguments have been refuted above in the section on Christ.

We repeat one, which brings no small moment to explaining the nature of justification: Whatever justification is not only gracious, but also gratuitous, that does not occur on account of the merit of Christ: The justification of the sinner before God, etc.

Therefore, the major premise is established: because gratuitous justification excludes all merit.

The minor premise is Paul's teaching, Rom. III, 24, that men are justified freely (δωρεὰν), gratis, by the grace of God, and by alien merit; or that of Christ the mediator.

The former, not the latter, is excluded by gratuitous justification.

That the merit of Christ and the grace of God perfectly consist and conspire in the act of justification, the Apostle indicates,

Justice, when it teaches that sinners are justified freely, by the grace of God through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus; whom God set forth as ἱλαστήριον, a propitiation, through his own blood. Thus, the tempering of divine justice shines forth.

To divine grace it must be attributed that God a) did not wish to leave the human race, immersed in sins, in the state of sin, and (which he could have done by just judgment) to adjudge it to eternal damnation. For he embraced in his mercy sinful men, not as such, but as his own creatures. b) That for sinful men, who were properly unequal to the satisfaction that had to be performed for their sins, he destined and gave a mediator, and him his only-begotten son, who might fulfill the law for all sinners, and pay the vicarious penalties of transgressions, and thus took from his own what was paid for our sins, by whose merit we are justified. For he did not spare his own son but delivered him up to death for us, Rom. VIII, 32. c) That the merit of Christ, since it was not the property of the sinful man, and its effect, which is both the remission of sins and perfect justice, he imputes and attributes to every penitent sinner who by true faith applies the satisfaction of Christ to himself. d) That he justifies us not through and because of our works, but in view of faith in Christ δωρεὰν, freely, without the intervention of our own merit.

It belongs to divine justice to demand satisfaction for the injury and offense brought upon God. For by the very fact that sins violate the internal and immutable law of God, they induce on the part of the sinner guilt and the liability to divine punishment; but they affect God with injury and offend him. They indeed induce guilt and the liability to divine punishment: because he who sins deviates from the rule of rectitude, and through this contracts guilt upon himself, and the guilt born from the deviation from the rule of rectitude is accompanied by the liability to divine punishment, by itself and by its own nature. But they affect God with injury, and offend him, because they violate his law. For the violation of divine law is a certain violation of divine right, and thus an injury redounding upon God, by which God cannot but be most gravely offended. As long, therefore, as guilt and the liability to punishment remain on the part of the sinner, so long does injury, brought upon him by the past act of sinning, and offense remain on the part of God. It is also repugnant that someone should be culpable and worthy of punishment on account of a past act of sinning, and yet not be unjust toward God, and, because of his violated right, be constituted in offense and hatred before him. Whence, to expiate sins, it is required that both the guilt and the obligation to punishment, on the part of the sinner, and the injury and offense, on the part of God, be removed. The latter is removed through the satisfaction of Christ, apprehended by true faith; which indeed God procured out of mere grace, and which he benevolently accepts.

Latin:

3) Ex

Eph. I, 7. In Christo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ipsius, remissionem peccatorum.

Conf. Col. I, 14. Deus credentibus in Christum peccata remittit, ideo per cruentam Christi mortem, velut λύτρον, a reatu peccati redempti sunt.

Prob. c. 1) Ex Rom. X, 14. Τὸ τέλος νόμῳ, finis legis Christus in iustitiam omni credenti.

Obs. a) Τὸ τέλος νόμῳ non notat abrogationem aut desitionem legis, sed eius complementum, consummationem, aut perfectam impletionem.

b) Iustitia Christi intelligitur non essentialis, Deo Patri, Filio, & Spiritui S. communis, quae ad extra est incommunicabilis, neque habitualis, qua eminuit Christus, qua homo, a primo conceptionis momento, sed acquisita nobis obedientia actiua, nostro loco legi diuinae praestita.

Nam impletionis legis vicariae effectus est iustitia, quae quidem Christi est causaliter, sed peccatoris credentis terminatiue, siue, vt clarius loquar, iustitia, per exactissimam legis impletionem a Christo homini peccatori acquisita.

Pertinet ea ad Christum, tanquam caussam promerentem; pertinet etiam ad peccatorem conuersum & renatum, tanquam subiectum, in quo ex intentione Christi terminatur, & cui per gratiosam Dei aestimationem imputatur.

Dicitur itaque peccator, in Christum credens, iustus, a iustitia Christi imputata. c) Addit Apostolus: Παντὶ πιστεύοντι, omni credenti; quia iustitia a Christo mediatore nobis acquisita, vera fide apprehendenda applicanda nobis est, vt fiat, & maneat nostra.

2) Ex

Rom. V, 19. Sicut per vnius hominis inobedientiam peccatores constituti sunt multi; ita etiam per obedientiam vnius iusti constituentur multi.

Adamus inobedientia actiua, qua legem diuinam trangressus est, iniustitiam in vniuersum genus humanum deuoluit: E.

Christus mediator obedientia actiua, qua legem diuinam impleuit, iustitiam in vniuersum genus humanum deriuauit; oppositorum quippe eadem est ratio. 3) Si Christus obedientia sua actiua legem diuinam ad iustitiam homini credenti non impleuisset, omnis peccator esset maledictus:

Sed non omnis peccator est maledictus: E. Christus obedientia sua actiua legem diuinam ad iustitiam homini credenti impleuit.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, negantium, nos propter satisfactionem & meritum Christi a Deo iustificari; quorum argumenta supra in loco de Christo sunt confutata.

Vnum repetimus, haud parum momenti afferens ad indolem iustificationis explicandam: Quaecunque iustificatio non tantum est gratiosa, sed etiam gratuita, illa non fit propter meritum Christi: Iustificatio peccatoris coram Deo &c.

E. Maior constat: quia iustificatio gratuita omne meritum excludit. Minor est Paulli docentis, Rom.

III, 24. homines iustificari δωρεὰν, gratis, gratia Dei, & meritum alienum; siue mediatoris Christi.

Illud, non hoc, excludit gratuita iustificatio.

Quod meritum Christi, & gratia Dei, in actu iustificationis optime consistant & conspirent, indicat Apostolus,

Ius, cum docet, quod peccatores iustificentur gratis, gratia Dei per redemptionem, quæ est in Christo Iesu; quem proposuit Deus ἱλαστήριον, propitiatorium, per ipsius sanguinem. Elucescit igitur e iustitiæ divinæ temperamentum.

Gratia divinæ tribuendum est, quod Deus a) genus humanum peccatis immersum noluit in statu peccati relinquere, & (quod iusto iudicio facere poterat) æternæ damnationi adiudicare. Complexus enim misericordia sua est homines peccatores, non qua tales, sed qua creaturas suas. b) Quod hominibus peccatoribus, qui præstandæ pro peccatis suis satisfactioni proprie impares erant, destinauit & dedit mediatorem, eumque filium suum vnigenitum, qui pro peccatoribus omnibus legem impleret, & pœnas transgressionum vicarias folueret, adeoque de suo sumsit, quod pro peccatis nostris persolutum est, cuius merito iustificamur. Suo enim filio non pepercit sed eum pro nobis in mortem tradidit, Rom. VIII, 32. c) Quod meritum Christi, cum non esset hominis peccatoris proprium, eiusque effectum, qui est tum remissio peccatorum, tum perfecta iustitia, omni peccatori pœnitenti, qui vera fide satisfactionem Christi sibi applicat, imputat & attribuit. d) Quod non per & propter opera nostra, sed intuitu fidei in Christum δωρεὰν, gratis, citra interuentum meriti proprii, nos iustificat.

Iustitiæ divinæ est, pro illata Deo iniuria & offensa satisfactionem exigere. Eo ipso enim, quod peccata legem Dei internam & immutabilem violant, inducunt ex parte peccantis culpam & reatum pœnæ divinæ; Deum vero afficiunt iniuria offenduntque. Culpam quidem & reatum pœnæ divinæ inducunt: quia is, qui peccat, a regula rectitudinis exorbitat, & per hoc culpam sibi contrahit, natam vero ex exorbitantia a regula rectitudinis culpam comitatur reatus pœnæ divinæ, per se & natura sua. Deum autem afficiunt iniuria, offenduntque, quia legem eius violant. Violatio enim legis divinæ est quædam iuris divini violatio, atque adeo iniuria in Deum redundans, qua non potest non Deus grauissime offendi. Quamdiu igitur manet ex parte peccantis culpa & reatus pœnæ, tamdiu manet ex parte Dei etiam iniuria, per actum peccandi præteritum ei illata, & offensa. Repugnat etiam, aliquem esse ob actum peccandi præteritum culpabilem, pœnaque dignum, nec tamen esse iniustum in Deum, & ob violatum eius ius in offensa & odio apud eum constitutum. Vnde ad expianda peccata requiritur, vt tum culpa & obligatio ad pœnam, ex parte peccatoris, tum iniuria & offensa, ex parte Dei, tollatur. Tollitur illa per satisfactionem Christi, vera fide apprehensam; quippe quam Deus ex mera gratia procurauit, eamque beneuole acceptat.


### Q. VI. What man does God justify?

God justifies man a) as a sinner b), guilty of guilt and punishment before divine judgment c), but converted d), and reborn e).

Prob. a. Not the good angels are justified by God, who, since they have persisted in concrete holiness, do not need the remission of sins, nor the evil angels, who have been held by divine judgment to be unpitiable; but men. This we prove: Those whose nature Christ assumed are justified through faith in Christ, and no others: But Christ assumed the nature of men only, not of angels. Therefore, Τὸ γὰρ ἀπρόσληπτον, ἀθεράπευτον. That which is not assumed by Christ is not healed by him. Therefore, man the wayfarer, or he who is constituted in the way of this life, is curable. He who dies with sins not remitted departs in a state of wrath, not of grace. For since he has maliciously repudiated the grace offered in the course of life, the wrath of God remains upon him perpetually, John 3:16.

Prob. b. God justifies the ungodly, Rom. IV, 5. Those who have sinned, and are destitute of the glory of God, are justified freely, by the grace of God, through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus, Rom. III, 23. 24

Prob. c. A sinner, by transgressing the divine law, contracts guilt, and this obligation to punishment follows. Whence every man, examined by the standard of the divine law, is ὑπόδικος to God, i. e., liable to God the judge, to eternal death, Rom. III, 19. Therefore, the sinner stands before the divine throne not as Mephibosheth innocent, or Barzillai beneficent before David, but as the cupbearer before Pharaoh, or Shimei before Solomon.

For the sinner has been accused by Moses, John V, 45, and by the devil, Apoc. XII, 10, convicted by the witness of conscience, Rom. II, 15, so that the conviction of conscience is a handwriting against him, Col. II, 14.

Prob. d. God justifies the ungodly not while they persist in impiety, or retain the purpose of sinning, but when they are converted and contrite through the divine law, so that they may acknowledge the baseness of their sins from the law, feel the wrath of God, dread divine punishments, and thus not ratify the sins committed, but retract them, and seriously detest them with sorrow, and cast away the purpose of sinning. Which sorrow for sins, and their displeasure and detestation, is not indeed a positive and causal medium of justification; yet it is a condition required on the part of the sinner to be justified, and a privative medium of order, removing the incapacity and obstacles to the remission of sins, to wit, the false opinion of non-need, and the zeal for continuing in sins. For he who does not acknowledge and detest his sins, but rather is prepared to continue in them maliciously, he will neither seek nor find the remission of sins. God himself hints at this, Jer. III, 4. 5. Hast thou not from this time called me, My father, thou (art) the guide of my youth? Will he keep it for ever (wrath?) Will he keep it to the end? Behold thou hast spoken, and done evil things, and hast prevailed, q. d. I shall not be able to be a gracious Father, or to remit sins to thee, unless thou ceasest to sin by choice. Conf. HVLSEM. breu. enucl. c. IX, p. 501. 523.

Prob. e. From Rom. IV, 4. To him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, faith is counted for righteousness. It is required of the ungodly that he detest his impiety with sorrow of mind, but this does not suffice; but it is necessary that he believe also in God, who justifies the ungodly. God is indeed a just judge and a severe avenger of crimes; but by the satisfaction of Christ, who died for the ungodly, Rom. V, 8, he is appeased. This the penitent sinner acknowledges from the gospel, which promises grace and remission of sins on account of the merit of Christ apprehended by true faith; who gives undoubted assent to the evangelical promise, and thus by singular confidence accepts the satisfaction of Christ, applies it to himself, exhibits it to God the judge, and on account of the same seeks and finds grace and remission of sins, and, like the repenting publican, departs justified, Luc.

Latin:

Deus iustificat hominem a) peccatorem b), coram iudicio diuino reum culpæ & pœnæ c), sed conuersum d), & renatum e).

Prob. a. Iustificantur a Deo non angeli boni, qui cum in sanctitate concreta perstiterint, remissione peccatorum non indigent, neque angeli mali, qui iudicio diuino habiti sunt immiferabiles; sed homines. Id quod probamus: Quorum naturam Christus assumsit, ii per fidem in Christum iustificantur, & non alii: Atqui Christus solorum hominum, non angelorum naturam assumsit. E. Τὸ γὰρ ἀπρόσληπτον, ἀθεράπευτον. quod a Christo non est assumtum, ab eodem non est sanatum. Sanabilis igitur est homo viator, siue in via huius vitæ constitutus. Qui cum, peccatis non remissis, moritur, is decedit in statu iræ, non gratiæ. Cum enim gratiam in cursu vitæ oblatam malitiose repudiauerit, ira Dei super ipsum perpetuo manet, Io. III, 16.

Prob. b. Deus iustificat impium, Rom. IV, 5. Qui peccarunt, & destituuntur gloria Dei, iustificantur gratis, gratia Dei, per redemptionem, quæ est in Christo Iesu, Rom. III, 23. 24

Prob. c. Peccator transgrediendo legem divinam, contrahit culpam, & hanc obligationem ad pœnam sequitur. Vnde omnis homo, ad normam legis divinæ examinatus, est ὑπόδικος Deo, i. e. obnoxius Deo iudici, ad mortem æternam, Rom. III, 19. Stat igitur peccator coram throno divino non vt Mephibofet innocens, aut Barfillai beneficus coram Dauide, sed vt pincerna coram Pharaone, aut Simei coram Salomone.

Peccator enim accusatus est a Mose, Io. V, 45. & diabolo, Apoc. XII, 10. conuictus a teste conscientia, Rom. II, 15. ita vt conuictio conscientiæ sit chirographum contra ipsum, Col. II, 14.

Prob. d. Iustificat Deus impium non persistentem in impietate, aut propositum peccandi retinentem, sed per legem divinam conuersum & contritum, vt turpitudinem peccatorum suorum ex lege agnoscat, iram Dei sentiat, supplicia divina expauefcat, atque adeo commissa peccata non rata habeat, sed retractet, & serio cum dolore detestetur, atque peccandi propositum abiiciat. Qui dolor de peccatis, eorumque displicentia & detestatio non est quidem medium positivum & causale iustificationis; conditio tamen est, requisita ex parte peccatoris iustificandi, & medium ordinis priuatiuum, remouens incapacitatem & obstacula remissionis peccatorum, scil. opinionem falsam non-indigentiæ, & studium pergendi in peccatis. Nam qui non agnoscit & detestatur peccata sua, sed potius paratus est ea malitiose continuare, is nec quæret, nec inueniet remissionem peccatorum. Innuit hoc ipse Deus, Ier. III, 4. 5. Nonne abhinc vocasti me, Pater mi, ductor iuuentutis meæ tu (es). Num seruabit in æternum (iram?) Num retinebit eam in perpetuum? Ecce locuta es, & fecisti mala, ac præualuisti, q. d. non potero esse gratiosus Pater, aut peccata tibi remittere, nisi proæretice peccare desinas. Conf. HVLSEM. breu. enucl. c. IX, p. 501. 523.

Prob. e. Ex Rom. IV, 4. Ei, qui non operatur, credit vero in eum, qui iustificat impium, fides imputatur in iustitiam. Requiritur ab impio, vt suam impietatem cum dolore animi detestetur, sed hoc non sufficit; verum necesse est, vt credat etiam in Deum, qui iustificat impium. Est quidem Deus iudex iustus & scelerum vindex seuerus; at satisfactione Christi, qui pro impiis mortuus est, Rom. V, 8. placatus. Hoc peccator pœnitens agnoscit ex euangelio, quod promittit gratiam & remissionem peccatorum propter meritum Christi vera fide apprehensum; qui promissioni euangelicæ indubitatum præbet assensum, atque adeo singulari fiducia satisfactionem Christi acceptat, sibi applicat, Deo iudici exhibet, & propter eandem gratiam & remissionem peccatorum quærit, inuenit, atque, ad instar publicani resipiscentis, iustificatus abit, Luc.


### XVIII. Quæst. VII. Are also repenting sinners of the Old Testament justified through faith in Christ?

Penitent sinners, who lived in the times of the Old Testament, were reconciled to God and justified through faith in Christ. Prob. 1)

All the prophets testify of Christ, that everyone who believes in him receives remission of sins, Acts X, 43.

2) We all believe that we are saved through the grace of Christ, even as they (our Fathers), Acts XV, 11. (*).

The antithesis is of the Socinians, who maintain that justification through faith in Christ was first promulgated and announced in the New Testament. They urge: I. Christ the mediator did not exist in the times of the Old Testament, nor was his satisfaction rendered then: therefore, the Israelites could not believe in Christ. Response: Although Christ's satisfaction for sins was rendered at an appointed time, it is nevertheless universal in value, and extends itself to all men of all times and ages. For it relates to the remission of sins by way of a meritorious cause. This, before it exists, can exercise its power of causing by the value of the merit foreseen, and can move the will of the efficient cause to act. That the satisfaction of Christ was known to God before it was rendered is beyond doubt. See Acts 2:33; ch. 4:28. But that the same was also foreknown by sinful men, or at least was so revealed that, if it had been without the negligence, malice, and contempt of the divine word of men, it could have been known to all at any time, is easily understood. For first, God announced it to the protoplasts while they were still in paradise, when, having promulgated the protoevangelium, He predicted that the seed of the woman would crush the head of the serpent, Gen. 3:15. Then He repeated this prediction to the patriarchs, and afterwards through prophets taught by Him to the holy Israelite people, with fuller declarations added, until that promised seed, born of the Virgin Mary, was actually exhibited. To this Peter refers when he says that God sent the foretold Jesus Christ, Acts 3:20, and that all the prophets from Samuel and onwards, as many as have spoken, foretold those days in which, namely, Christ was exhibited in the flesh, v. 24.

II. They urge the passages of Scripture Rom. 3:21; Gal. 3:23. To which we have responded above, Part

Latin:

Peccatores pœnitentes, qui temporibus veteris testamenti vixerunt, per fidem in Christum Deo reconciliati & iustificati sunt.

Prob. 1) Omnes prophetæ testantur de Christo, omnem, qui credit in eum, remissionem peccatorum accipere, Act. X, 43.

2) Omnes credimus per gratiam Christi saluari, sicut & illi (Patres nostri), Act. XV, 11. (*).

Antithesis est Socinianorum, statuentium, iustificationem per fidem in Christum primum in N. T. promulgatam atque annuntiatam esse. Urgent illi I. Christus mediator non exstitit temporibus V. T. nec eius satisfactio tunc praestita est: E. non potuerunt Israelitae in Christum credere. Resp. Quamuis Christi satisfactio pro peccatis constituto tempore praestita sit, quoad valorem tamen vniuersalis est, & ad omnes omnium temporum & aetatum homines se extendit. Habet enim se ad remissionem peccatorum per modum causae meritoriae. Haec prius, quam existat, valore meriti praecogniti suam causandi vim exercere, & voluntatem causae efficientis ad agendum mouere potest. Deo cognitam fuisse satisfactionem Christi, quam praestaretur, dubio vacat. Vid. Act. II, 33. c. IV, 28. Quod vero eadem hominibus peccatoribus etiam praecognita, vel certe ita patefacta fuerit, vt, si absque hominum negligentia, malitia & contemptu verbi diuini fuisset, omnibus quouis tempore nota esse potuisset, facile intelligitur. Primum enim Deus exstentibus adhuc in paradiso protoplastis eam praenuntiauit, quando promulgato proteuangelio, semen mulieris caput serpentis contriturum esse, praedixit, Gen. III, 15. Deinde praedictionem hanc patriarchis, & postea per edoctos a se prophetas sancto populo Israelitico subinde, adiectis declarationibus vberioribus, repetiit, donec semen illud promissum, ex Maria virgine natum, reapse exhiberetur. Quo respicit Petrus, quando Deum dicit misisse praenuntiatum Iesum Christum, Act. III, 20. & omnes prophetas a Samuele & deinceps eos, qui fuerint, quotquot locuti sint, praenuntiasse dies illos, quibus scilicet Christus in carne exhibitus est, v. 24.

II. Urgent loca scripturae Rom. III, 21. Gal. III, 23. Ad quae supra respondimus, Part. I. Quaest.


### I. Quest. VIII. By what means does God justify the sinner?

Means of bestowing [δοτικά], or on the part of God offering the grace of God and the satisfaction and merit of Christ, for obtaining the remission of sins and justification, are and finally the reason for the thing. To what end also so many and such illustrious prophecies about the future Christ, both those that are literal and those that are typical, but especially the piacular sacrifices, which of themselves had no power of expiating, as also the lustrations—to what end, I ask, unless they had availed to this, that all might place their trust in the future Christ, just as all did; see John 8:56, coll. with v. 52, 53, and Heb. 11:17 & 19. For which reason our Jesus is called the author [ἀρχηγὸς τῆς πίστεως] of faith in the Old Testament and its finisher [τελειωτής] in the New Testament, Heb. 12:2; the same yesterday in the Old Testament who is today in the New Testament, Heb. 13:8. But this principle: that a satisfaction once rendered was always valid, or, as they commonly say, the merit of Christ avails forward no less than backward—this, I say, as it is most plainly signified in this place, Heb. 9:26, so it must be most firmly opposed not only to the Socinians, but also to the Roman Catholics, who, although they do not entirely deny the merits of Christ to men who died happily before He was born, yet opine that they did not perceive the fruit of them until Christ suffered death, and that in the meantime they were held as captives in a certain limbo and affected by the punishment of loss. From the same principle proceeds the argumentation against the Cocceians, who are in this heresy: that Christ, while the common sponsor of all men, is now at last in the New Testament an expromissor [surety], but in the Old Testament was only a fideiussor [guarantor]; and therefore they think that ἄφεσιν must be defined in one way, and πάρεσιν in another, namely, that the former is the remission of sin, never to be punished, but the latter is the toleration of it for a time, by winking at it and deferring the punishment, not yet taken away. They appeal first of all to Rom. 3:25, 26.
