Response: 1) ἀνοχή τῶ Θεῶ is expressly distinguished from what is called πάρεσις; 2) this πάρεσιν is nothing other than ἄφεσιν, and that this very ἄφεσιν, or remission of sins, befell David and those like him equally as us in the New Testament, appears from Rom. 4:6, 7 & Heb. 9:15, coll. with v. 22.

are the word of the gospel a), and the sacraments b): the medium ληπτικόν [receptive], or that which on the part of the sinful man receives the merit of Christ, and the grace of God founded therein, is faith c).

Prob. a. From 2 Cor. V, 19. God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, while he did not impute their sins to them, and has placed in us the word of reconciliation. The Apostle teaches: a) That God, offended by the sins of men, out of immense grace, having pitied the inescapable misery of men, procured καταλλαγήν [reconciliation]: b) That this reconciliation is acquired through Christ the mediator, who made satisfaction for divine justice: c) That the actual non-imputation of sins flows from the reconciliation acquired through the satisfaction of Christ: d) That reconciliation and the remission of sins are announced, promised, and offered through the word of reconciliation, i.e., the gospel. Prob. b.

That through the sacrament of initiation, or baptism, the justice of Christ is offered and applied, we learn from Gal. III, 27. As many of you as have been baptized into Christ, have put on Christ. The Apostle does not mean a legal putting on, or one of imitation; since in this way we could also put on St. Paul, but an evangelical putting on, or one of faith. The blessed LUTHER concisely explains this putting on in this place. To put on Christ is to put on justice, truth, all grace, and the fullness of the whole law.

That the Eucharist is a medium for the exhibition of justifying grace is clear from the fact that the pouring out of the eucharistic cup is said to be done for the remission of sins, Luke XXII, 20. Obs. Through the sacrament of the supper, justification is continued rather than begun; for this reason, that no one becomes a partaker of the body and blood of the Lord with saving fruit, unless he has first examined himself, to wit, whether he is in the faith, 1 Cor. XI, 28, and thus is a believer, and has already been justified and was in a state of reconciliation: meanwhile, however, justifying faith is confirmed and preserved through the sacrament of the supper; and thus justification is continued.

Prob. c. Faith justifies not by itself, by its own dignity or value, by moving God to justify the believing man; but because as an instrument, or medium ληπτικόν [receptive], it apprehends the merit of Christ, by the intuition of which God is moved, so that he may absolve the penitent sinner, and the one believing in Christ, from the guilt of sin, while his justice remains intact, out of grace, and account him just. For the ἐνέργεια [energy], or internal force, of justifying faith is λαμβάνειν [to receive], to receive Christ, the grace of God founded in Christ, which forgives sins, offered in the evangelical promise, and the remission of sins dependent upon this. This is what can be perceived from the clearest sayings of scripture, John I, 12. But as many as ἔλαβον [received] him, to them he gave power to become the sons of God, to them that believe on his name. In this place, to believe in the name of Christ is explained as receiving him, as the author of divine υἱοθεσίας [adoption], Rom. V, 17. For if by the sin of one death reigned by one: much more they, who receive (λαμβάνοντες) the abundance of grace and of the gift of justice, shall reign in life through him. Paul describes faith excellently, in that it receives the abundance of grace and of the gift of justice, Gal. III, 14. That we might receive (λαμβῶμεν) the promise of the Spirit through faith. The promise of grace is received and applied to us by no other medium than faith, Acts X, 43. To him (Christ) all the prophets give testimony, that through his name whosoever believeth in him shall receive (λαβεῖν) remission of sins. Faith accepts the effect of the satisfaction of Christ, the remission of sins. From these heavenly oracles we conclude that faith is the receptive medium by which the satisfaction of Christ, and the grace of God obtained thereby, are accepted.

The antithesis is of the Papists, Socinians, and Arminians, who deny that faith justifies by way of an instrument, or medium, receiving the merit of Christ . They rely on the same following arguments:

I. If faith justifies instrumentally, it justifies as a work: The Evangelicals concede the antecedent: E. and the consequent. The consequence of the major is proven. For if the causality of an efficient cause is an operation, and an instrument enjoys the causality of an efficient cause; then the causality of faith will be an operation, and thus faith will justify as a work, or operation.

Resp. Distinguish between an active and a receptive instrument. Faith does not justify as an agent, but as a patient, or passively receiving.

To justify instrumentally, predicated of faith, denotes passion, and thus faith can be called an instrument of justification, but a passive one, as D. Osiander excellently says in colleg. systemat. part. V. p. 3.

Instance: Faith formally considered is a fiducial apprehension of the merit of Christ and the grace of God promised in the gospel: E. Faith formally is an action, not a passion.

Resp. 1) Apprehension is an act, if I may say so, passive.

Dannhaverus says, explained indeed by an active voice (grammatically), yet in reality passive, which suffers itself to be benefited, Hodof. p. 1340. For as the hand of a beggar receives alms, the mouth of a sick person medicine, a mirror an image passively: so faith is an organ for those spiritually begging, who spiritually receive the grace of God and the merit of Christ.

2) Faith justifies, not insofar as it is an apprehension and our act, but insofar as it embraces the justifying object.

II. Whatever consists in knowledge, assent, and trust, that is not an instrument: But justifying faith, etc. E. The major is proven: because knowledge, assent, and trust are acts of the intellect and will, which cannot be called instruments.

The minor is conceded by the Evangelicals.

Resp. Distinguish between the faith that justifies, and insofar as it justifies. The former consists in knowledge, assent, and trust.

The latter is the medium receiving the satisfaction of Christ. Faith is called an instrument, not univocally and in the philosophical rigor, but by analogy, insofar as an instrument denotes a medium, or principle, by which an object is apprehended, or accepted.

III. Whatever action of God is immanent, immediate, and inorganic, that is not done through the faith of man, as a medium, or instrument: But justification is an action of God immanent, immediate and inorganic: The major premise is established; because an immanent and inorganic action does not occur through an instrument. The minor premise is clear in itself; because justification is carried out within the very bosom of the Godhead, without the intervention of any instrument. Response: Faith is called an instrument, not as if the act of justification itself were produced by faith as an instrument, but because it behaves by way of an instrument, by which that for which we are justified, namely the merit of Christ, is apprehended and applied to us. In relation to the act of justification itself, however, faith in Christ behaves by way of a cause, or a less principal impulsive reason; because it does not move God to justify the penitent sinner who believes in Christ by itself, not by its own power or value, but by the power of the merit of Christ, which it embraces. Cf. D. MVSAEVS in dissert. de praedest. §. 75.

Latin:

Media δοτικά, seu ex parte Dei offerentia gratiam Dei & satisfactionem atque meritum Christi, ad impetrandam remissionem peccatorum & iustitiam, sunt demque rei rationem. Quorsum etiam tot, tamque illustres vaticinationes de futuro Christo, cum litterales illae, tum typicae, praesertim vero sacrificia piacularia, quae per se nullam habebant vim expiandi, vt & lustrationes, quorsum, quaeso! nisi eo valuissent, vt omnes in futuro Christo, ita omnes collocarent fiduciam; Vid. Io. VIII, 56. coll. cum v. 52. 53. & Hebr. XI, 17. & 19. Quam ob rem Iesus noster dicitur ἀρχηγὸς τῆς πίστεως in V. T. eiusdemque τελειωτής in N. T. Hebr. XII, 2. idem heri in V. T. qui hodie in N. T. Hebr. XIII, 8. Principium vero hoc: satisfactio semel praestita, semper valida fuit, seu, vt vulgo loquuntur, meritum Christi valet antrorsum non minus, quam retrorsum, hoc, inquam, vt planissime significatum est in hoc loco, Hebr. IX, 26. ita firmissime opponendum est non solum Socinianis, verum etiam Romanocatholicis, qui, quamuis Christi promerita hominibus, ante eum natum beate defunctis, non omnino denegent, fructum tamen eorum non prius, quam Christus mortem oppetiit, illos percepisse, opinantur, interea illos velut captiuos in limbo quodam detentos fuisse, & poena damni adfectos. Ab eodem principio proficitur argumentatio aduersus Cocceianos, qui in ea sunt haeresi: Christum, communem quidem omnium hominum sponsorem, nunc demum in N. T. esse expromissorem, sed in V. T. non nisi fideiussorem fuisse; ideoque putant aliter definiendam esse ἄφεσιν, aliter πάρεσιν, ita nimirum, vt illa quidem sit remissio peccati, nunquam vindicandi; haec autem toleratio eius ad tempus, conniuendo ac poenam, nondum ablatam, differendo. Prouocant in primis ad Rom. III, 25. 26. Resp. 1) Diserte discernitur ἀνοχή τῶ Θεῶ ab eo, quod dicitur πάρεσις, 2) hancce πάρεσιν nihil esse aliud, quam ἄφεσιν, atque hanc ipsam ἄφεσιν, siue remissionem peccatorum Dauidi, eiusque similibus aeque, ac nobis in N. T. contigisse, adparet ex Rom. IV, 6. 7. & Hebr. IX, 15: coll. cum v. 22.

sunt verbum evangelii a), & sacramenta b): medium ληπτικόν, seu ex parte hominis peccatoris recipiens meritum Christi, & in eo fundatam Dei gratiam, est fides c).

Prob. a. Ex 2 Cor. V, 19. Deus erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi ipsi, dum non imputabat illis peccata illorum, & posuit in nobis verbum reconciliationis. Docet Apostolus: a) Quod Deus, peccatis hominum offensus, ex immensa gratia, ineluctabilis hominum miseriæ misertus, καταλλαγήν, seu reconciliationem procuraverit: b) Quod hæc reconciliatio acquisita fit per Christum mediatorem, qui iustitiæ divinæ fecit satis: c) Quod actualis non-imputatio peccatorum ex acquisita reconciliatione per satisfactionem Christi fluat: d) Quod reconciliatio & remissio peccatorum per verbum reconciliationis, i. e. evangelium, annuntietur, promittatur & offeratur.

Prob. b. Per sacramentum initiationis, sive baptismum, iustitiam Christi offerri & applicari, discimus ex Gal. III, 27. Quotquot in Christum baptizati estis, Christum induistis. Non intelligit Apostolus inductionem legalem, sive imitationis; siquidem hac ratione etiam S. Paullum possemus induere, sed inductionem evangelicam, sive fidei. B. LVTHERVS concinne explicat hanc inductionem h. l. Induere Christum est iustitiam, veritatem, omnem gratiam, totiusque legis plenitudinem induere.

Eucharistiam esse medium exhibitivum gratiæ iustificantis, liquet ex eo, quia effusio poculi eucharistici dicitur fieri in remissionem peccatorum, Luc. XXII, 20. Obs. Per sacramentum cænæ continuatur potius, quam inchoatur iustificatio; propterea, quod nemo cum salutari fructu corporis & sanguinis dominici fit particeps, nisi qui seipsum prius probauerit, scil. num sit in fide, 1 Cor. XI, 28. adeoque fidelis, & iam ante iustificatus & in statu reconciliationis fuerit: interim tamen fides iustifica per sacramentum cænæ confirmatur & conferuatur; atque adeo iustificatio continuatur.

Prob. c. Fides iustificat non per se, propria dignitate aut valore, mouendo Deum ad iustificandum hominem credentem; sed quia tanquam instrumentum, aut medium ληπτικόν, sive receptiuum, apprehendit meritum Christi, cuius intuitu Deus impellitur, vt peccatorem pœnitentem, & in Christum credentem, salua iustitia sua, ex gratia a reatu culpæ absoluat, & iustum reputet. Fidei enim iustificantis ἐνέργεια, sive vis interna est, λαμβάνειν, recipere Christum, in Christo fundatam gratiam Dei, peccata condonantem, oblatam in promissione euangelica, & ab hac dependentem remissionem peccatorum. Id quod e clarissimis scripturæ dictis perspicere licet, Io. I, 12. Quotquot vero ἔλαβον, receperunt eum, dedit illis potestatem, vt essent filii Dei, credentibus in nomen ipsius. H. l. credere in nomen Christi exponitur per recipere ipsum, tanquam auctorem τῆς υἱοθεσίας divinæ, Rom. V, 17. Si namque unius peccato mors regnauit per unum: multo magis ii, qui abundantiam gratiæ & doni iustitiæ, (λαμβάνοντες) accipiunt in vita, regnabunt per eum. Paullus egregie describit fidem, quod abundantiam gratiæ & doni iustitiæ accipiat, Gal. III, 14. Vt promissionem Spiritus fidei accipiamus (λαμβῶμεν). Promissio gratiæ non alio medio, quam fide recipitur nobisque applicatur, Act. X, 43. Huic (Christo) omnes prophetæ testimonium perhibent, quod remissionem peccatorum (λαβεῖν) accipiat omnis, qui credit in ipsum. Fides acceptat effectum satisfactionis Christi, remissionem peccatorum. Ex his oraculis cœlestibus colligimus, fidem esse medium receptiuum, quo satisfactio Christi, & ea parta gratia Dei acceptatur.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, Socinianorum, & Arminianorum, negantium, fidem iustificare per modum instrumenti, aut medii, meritum Christi accipientis . Nituntur iisdem sequentibus argumentis:

I. Si fides iustificat instrumentaliter, iustificat ut opus: Antecedens concedunt Evangelici: E. & consequens. Consequentia maioris prob. Si enim causalitas causae efficientis est operatio, instrumentum autem causalitate, causae efficientis gaudet; utique causalitas fidei erit operatio, adeoque fides ut opus, seu operatio iustificabit.

Resp. Dist. inter instrumentum activum, & receptivum. Fides non iustificat ut agens, sed ut patiens, aut passive recipiens.

Instrumentaliter iustificare, de fide enuntiatum, notat passionem, & ita fides instrumentum iustificationis dici potest, sed passivum, ut praeclare ait D. Osiander in colleg. systemat. part. V. p. 3.

Instantia: Fides formaliter considerata est fiducialis apprehensio meriti Christi & gratiae Dei in evangelio promissae: E. Fides formaliter est actio, non passio.

Resp. 1) Apprehensio est actus, ut sic dicam, passivus.

Dannhaverus inquit, activa quidem voce (grammatice) explicatus, reuera tamen passivus, qui sibi patitur benefieri, Hodof. p. 1340. Vt enim manus mendici eleemosynam, os aegroti medicamen, speculum imaginem passive recipit: ita fides est organon spiritualiter mendicantium, qui gratiam Dei & meritum Christi spiritualiter recipiunt.

2) Iustificat fides, non quatenus est apprehensio & actus noster, sed quatenus obiectum iustificum amplectitur.

II. Quidquid consistit in notitia, assensu & fiducia, illud non est instrumentum: Atqui fides iustificans &c. E. Maior probatur: quia notitia, assensu & fiducia sunt actus intellectus & voluntatis, qui non possunt instrumenta appellari.

Minor est concessa ab Evangelicis.

Resp. Dist. inter fidem, quae iustificat, & quatenus iustificat. Illa consistit in notitia, assensu & fiducia.

Haec est medium satisfactionem Christi recipiens. Dicitur fides instrumentum, non univoce & rigore philosophico, sed per analogiam, quatenus instrumentum notat medium, vel principium, quo obiectum apprehenditur, vel acceptatur.

III. Quaecunque actio Dei est immanens immediata & inorganica, illa non fit per fidem hominis, tanquam medium, aut instrumentum: Atqui iustificatio est actio Dei immanens, inimeimmediata & inorganica: E. Maior constat; quia actio immanens & inorganica non sit per instrumentum. Minor per se clara est; quia iustificatio peragitur intra ipsum deitatis sinum, citra interuentum alicuius instrumenti. Resp. Fides dicitur instrumentum, non quasi ipse actus iustificationis per fidem, tanquam instrumentum producatur, sed quia se habet per modum instrumenti, quo id, propter quod iustificamur, scilicet meritum Christi, apprehenditur, nobifque applicatur. In ordine vero ad ipsum actum iustificationis fides in Christum se habet per modum caussae, vel rationis impulsiuae minus principalis; quia non per se, non vi aut valore proprio, sed vi meriti Christi, quod ea amplectitur, Deum mouet ad iustificandum peccatorem poenitentem & in Christum credentem. Conf. D. MVSAEVS in dissert. de praedest. §. 75.


### I. Quest. VIII. By what means does God justify the sinner?: Question IX. Does faith alone justify?

Question IX. Does faith alone justify?

Faith alone is the divinely ordained medium by which we apprehend and apply to ourselves the satisfaction of Christ, performed in our stead and offered in the evangelical promise, by whose intuition we are justified by God; good works, however, do not enter the circle of justification.

Observation I. Nowhere in the Holy Scriptures is faith said to justify in the nominative case, but it is always said in the oblique case: We are justified by faith, Gal. II, 16; a man is justified by faith, Rom. III, 28. God, however, is said to justify in the nominative case, Rom. III, 30; c. IIX, 33. Whence it is not in vain that D. OSIANDER says in colleg. system. P. V. p. 96: If we wish to speak accurately and according to Scripture, it should be said that God alone justifies (for it is the action of God alone); but that man is justified by faith. For faith itself does not justify, for the very reason that it behaves merely apprehensively. However, the mode of speaking, because it has prevailed so that it is said 'faith alone justifies,' can be retained if the mode of speaking is rightly applied from scriptural usage. It is therefore explained in the Solid Declaration of the Formula of Concord, p. 684: Faith does not justify because it is such a good work and such an excellent virtue, but because it apprehends and embraces the merit of Christ in the promise of the Gospel. Which D. AEG. HVNNIVS sets forth more broadly in epist. ad Rom. III, 164: "Faith does not justify because it is considered absolutely and in itself as a certain virtue. For in this respect it is a work of only one commandment of the Decalogue, namely the first: whereas, however, the fulfillment of the whole law is required to complete justification. Furthermore, because faith, considered in itself, is imperfect: whence it rather needs the mercy of God, by which its imperfection is covered, than that it should merit that mercy of God. Thirdly, because, even if it were most perfect, it would still be owed, because it is commanded in the law. That, however, to which we are held by debt merits nothing for us before God. Faith justifies, however, insofar as it is considered relatively, i.e., insofar as it looks to Christ and apprehends his merit. For in this way it diffuses itself through the whole Decalogue, i.e. includes the obedience of all the commandments of the Decalogue, performed for us by Christ, and that perfect and unowed, since Christ was not subject to the law by himself, but performed it for us." D. MVSAEVS in disp. de iustif. §. 38: "When it is said of faith in the nominative case that it justifies, the locution seems to be metonymical. For the sense is not that faith absolves a man from sins and reckons him righteous; but faith is said to justify because, by its intuition, God reckons us righteous, or because faith (not indeed by its own dignity, but by the dignity of the merit of Christ) moves God to justify us."

Observation II. When faith alone is said to justify, the grace of God, the merit of Christ, the Word, and the sacraments are not excluded; for the reason that exclusive particles exclude that which is opposite. But the grace of God, the merit of Christ, the Word, the sacraments, and faith are not opposed, but subordinated and consonant. For the grace of God is the internal impulsive cause of justification; the merit of Christ is the meritorious and external impulsive cause; the word and the sacraments are the offering media, faith is the receiving medium. It remains, therefore, that faith and the works of man are opposed to each other in relation to justification, and that faith in Christ, but not good works, is said to justify before the divine tribunal.

Obs. III. Distinction between faith considered with respect to justification itself, and then it alone is the instrument apprehending the merit of Christ, and it alone justifies: and [faith] viewed in the person of the justified, or after justification, and in this way it is never alone, but is always accompanied by the remaining virtues, nay, it is the root and mother of them all. This is what the epitome of the F. C. p. 586 asserts: We believe, teach, and confess, that although preceding contrition and subsequent new obedience do not pertain to the article of justification before God; yet such a justifying faith is not to be feigned, which could exist and stand together with an evil purpose, namely, of sinning and acting against conscience. But after a man is justified through faith, then that true and living faith is effective through charity, and good works always follow justifying faith, and together with it, if only it is true and living, are most certainly perceived. For true faith is never alone, but that it always has charity and hope with it. Which words are explained by D. MVSÆUS in his lectures on the F. Conc. p. 177, in the following manner: “Good works follow justification finally, not by reason of time, but by order of nature. By order of nature, justification is prior to renewal and new obedience, and thus good works can rightly be said to follow justification; because they are by nature posterior to justification and justifying faith: but by reason of time, faith is never without all good works, but always has some works, either external or internal, or interior motions of love, hope, etc., joined to it.”

Prob. 1. From Rom. IV, 5. To him who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is imputed for righteousness. Whoever, being ungodly, obtains righteousness through faith without the influx of good works, he is justified by faith alone: But the ungodly, believing in Christ, etc. Therefore.

2) From the denomination of justifying faith alone, Rom. III, 28. We conclude therefore, that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law: and Gal. II, 16. Since we know that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but through the faith of Jesus Christ. Whoever is not justified by the works of the law, but through faith without works, is justified by faith alone: But a sinner believing in Christ etc. Therefore.

3) From the exclusion of works, Rom. III, 20. By the works of the law shall no (any) flesh be justified before God.

You say: …The Apostle understands the works of the natural and ceremonial law, from which no one is justified; yet we are justified from works that proceed from grace. Resp. a) The Apostle does not treat of the works of the ceremonial or natural law, but of the works of the moral law, from which is the knowledge of sin, in the same verse (*). b) Works proceeding from faith and grace follow the justified and do not precede those to be justified: for they are the fruits of righteousness, Phil. I, 22. c) Paul also removes the works of righteousness, Tit. III, 5. Not by works, (which were done) in righteousness he saved us.

4) From the opposition of grace and works: we are justified freely by his grace, Rom. III, 24. Whatever happens by grace, that by no reason can happen through any work: But justification &c.: Therefore. The Apostle proves the major premise in Rom. XI, 6. If by grace, then it is no longer of works, otherwise grace would not be grace.

5) From the imperfection of our own righteousness. All our righteousnesses are as filthy rags, Is. LXIV, 6. We all stumble often, James III, 2. Whatever is unclean and imperfect, that cannot justify a man before God.

6) By the example of Abraham, who was not justified by works, Rom. IV, 2. 3. Abraham, when he received the testimony of imputed righteousness, had long since been received into grace (compare Gen. XII, 1. c. XV, 6.); nor yet was he justified by the works of grace.

The antithesis is I. of the Papists, II. of the Anabaptists, III. of the Socinians and Arminians, who deny that we are justified by faith alone, as the medium apprehending the merit of Christ. Whose arguments are.

I. By the same reason that Abraham was justified, by the same reason we also are justified (for Abraham is the Father of believers, Rom. IV, 11. and an example proposed to all who are to be justified): But Abraham was justified not only by faith, but also by good works. Therefore. The minor premise is of the Apostle James, ch. II, 21. Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he offered his son upon the altar? Do you see that faith was perfected by works? Resp. a) Distinguish between the justification of a sinner before God, and the showing or notification of faith and righteousness accepted by God before men (*). St. James does not speak of the justification of a sinner before God, but of the showing and notification of faith and righteousness before men, through good works, as signs and testimonies of true faith and fruits of righteousness. Therefore he says v. 18. Δείξόν μοι τὴν πίσιν σε ἐκ τῶν ἔργων σε, show me your faith from your works. The sense therefore is; Was not Abraham, our Father, justified, i. e. acknowledged and manifested as righteous by works, especially those which shone openly, when he offered Isaac his son upon the altar? b) The Apostle speaks of the external profession of faith. For he says v. 14. What profit (is there) my brethren, if someone says he has faith, but does not have works. Can (that) faith save him? The external profession of faith is sometimes true, if it exerts itself through charity and other virtues; sometimes false, when it is destitute of the company of good works, and is commonly called the vain boasting of faith.

Latin:

Quaest. IX. An sola fides iustificat?

Sola fides est medium diuinitus ordinatum, quo apprehendimus, nobísque applicamus satisfactionem Christi, vice nostri praestitam, & in euangelica promissione oblatam, cuius intuitu a Deo iustificamur; bona opera autem circulum iustificationis non ingrediuntur.

Obs. I. Nuspiam in sacris litteris in casu recto fides dicitur iustificare, sed semper in casu obliquo dicitur: Fide iustificamur, Gal. II, 16. fide homo iustificatur, Rom. III, 28. Deus autem in casu recto iustificare dicitur, Rom. III, 30. c. IIX, 33. Vnde haud ex vano inquit D. OSIANDER in colleg. system. P. V. p. 96. Si accurate & secundum scripturam loqui velimus, dicendum esset, solum Deum iustificare (est enim actio solius Dei); fide autem hominem iustificari. Non enim ipsa fides iustificat, eo ipso, quod se habet mere apprehensiue. Modus autem loquendi quia ita inualuit, vt dicatur, sola fides iustificat, retineri potest, si modus loquendi ex vsu scripturario dextre applicetur. Explicatur igitur in solid. declar. F. C. p. 684. Fides non iustificat, quod ipsa tam bonum opus, tamque praeclara virtus sit: sed quia in promissione euangelii meritum Christi apprehendit & amplectitur. Quae latius diducit D. AEG. HVNNIVS in epist. ad Rom. III, 164. "Fides non iustificat, quod absolute & in se, tanquam virtus quaedam consideratur. Hoc enim respectu est opus unius tantum praecepti decalogi, nempe primi: cum tamen ad perficiendam iustificationem totius legis impletio requiratur. Deinde, quia fides, in se considerata, imperfecta est: vnde potius indiget Dei misericordia, qua tegatur eius imperfectio, quam vt illam misericordiam Dei promereatur. Tertio, quia, si maxime perfecta esset, tamen esset debita, quia in lege est praecepta. Id autem, ad quod ex debito tenemur, nihil meretur nobis coram Deo. Iustificat autem fides, quatenus consideratur relate, h. e. quatenus Christum aspicit, eiusque meritum apprehendit. Hoc enim modo diffundit se per totum decalogum, i. e. includit obedientiam omnium praeceptorum decalogi, a Christo pro nobis praestitam, eamque perfectam, & indebitam, cum Christus per se legi non fuerit obnoxius, sed pro nobis eam praestiterit.,, D. MVSAEVS in disp. de iustif. §. 38. "Quando de fide dicitur in casu recto, quod iustificet, locutio videtur esse metonymica. Non enim sensus est, fidem absoluere hominem a peccatis, & reputare eum iustum; sed dicitur fides iustificare, quia eius intuitu Deus nos iustos reputat, seu quia fides (non sua quidem, sed meriti Christi dignitate) Deum mouet, vt nos iustificet.,,

Obs. II. Quando sola fides iustificare dicitur, non excluduntur gratia Dei, meritum Christi, verbum & sacramenta; ideo, quod particulae exclusiuae excludunt id, quod est oppositum. At gratia Dei, meritum Christi, verbum, sacramenta & fides non sunt opposita, sed subordinata & consentanea. Nam gratia Dei est caussa iustificationis impulsiua interna; meritum Christi caussa meritoria & impulsiua externa; verbum & sacramenta sunt media offerentia, fides medium recipiens. Relinquitur ergo, quod fides & hominis opera in ordine ad iustificationem sibi opponantur, & fides in Christum, non autem bona opera, coram tribunali diuino iustificare dicatur.

Obs. III. Dist. inter fidem consideratam respectu ipsius iustificationis, & tum sola est instrumentum apprehendens Christi meritum, solaque iustificat: & spectatam in persona iustificati, siue post iustificationem, & hoc modo nunquam est sola, sed semper reliquis virtutibus stipata, immo earum omnium est radix & genitrix. Id quod asserit epitome F. C. p. 586. Credimus, docemus, & confitemur, etsi antecedens contritio & subsequens noua obedientia ad articulum iustificationis coram Deo non pertinent; non tamen talem fidem iustificantem esse fingendam, quæ vna cum malo proposito, peccandi videlicet, & contra conscientiam agendi, esse & stare possit. Sed postquam homo per fidem est iustificatus, tum veram illam & viuam fidem esse per caritatem efficacem, & bona opera semper fidem iustificantem sequi, & vna cum ea, si modo vera & viua est, certissime deprehendi. Fides enim vera nunquam sola est, quin caritatem & spem semper secum habeat. Quæ verba a D. MVSÆO in prælect. in F. Conc. p. 177. sequenti ratione explicantur: „Bona opera sequuntur demum iustificationem non ratione temporis, sed ordine naturæ. Ordine naturæ iustificatio est prior renouatione & noua obedientia, & ita recte dici possunt B. O. sequi iustificationem; quia sunt natura posteriora iustificatione & fide iustificante: temporis autem ratione fides nunquam est absque omnibus operibus bonis, sed semper aliqua opera vel externa, vel interna, siue interiores motus dilectionis, spei, &c. habet coniunctos.“

Prob. 1. Ex Rom. IV, 5. Ei, qui non operatur, credit vero in eum, qui iustificat impium, imputatur fides in iustitiam. Quicunque impius per fidem sine confluxu bonorum operum iustitiam consequitur, is iustificatur sola fide: Atque impius, in Christum credens, &c. Ergo.

2) Ex solius fidei iustificantis denominatione, Rom. III, 28. Concludimus ergo, fide iustificari hominem sine operibus legis: & Gal. II, 16. Cum sciamus, quod non iustificetur homo ex operibus legis, sed per fidem Iesu Christi. Quicunque non iustificatur ex operibus legis, sed per fidem sine operibus, iustificatur sola fide: Atqui peccator in Christum credens &c. Ergo.

3) Ex operum exclusione, Rom. III, 20. Ex operibus legis non iustificabitur omnis (vlla) caro coram Deo.

Dicis: Apostolus intelligit opera legis naturalis & cærimonialis, ex quibus nemo iustificatur; iustificamur tamen ex operibus, profectis e gratia. Resp. a) Non de operibus legis cærimonialis, aut naturalis agit Apostolus, sed de operibus legis moralis, ex qua est agnitio peccati, eodem versu (*). b) Opera ex fide & gratia profecta sequuntur iustificatos non præcedunt iustificandos: sunt enim fructus iustitiæ, Phil. I, 22. c) Paullus etiam opera iustitiæ remouet, Tit. III, 5. Non ex operibus, (quæ facta) in Iustitia saluauit nos.

4) Ex oppositione gratiæ, & operum: iustificamur gratis gratia ipsius, Rom. III, 24. Quidquid contigit ex gratia, illud nulla ratione potest contingere per aliquod opus: Atqui iustificatio &c.: Ergo. Maiorem probat Apostolus Rom. XI, 6. Si per gratiam, iam non ex operibus, alias gratia non esset gratia.

5) Ex propriæ iustitiæ imperfectione. Omnes nostræ iustitiæ sunt velut pannus menstruatæ, Es. LXIV, 6. Sæpe labimur omnes, Iac. III, 2. Quidquid immundum & imperfectum est, illud non potest hominem coram Deo iustificare.

6) Exemplo Abrahami, qui non iustificatus est ex operibus, Rom. IV, 2. 3. Abrahamus cum testimonium imputatæ iustitiæ accepit, iamdudum in gratiam receptus fuit (confer. Gen. XII, 1. c. XV, 6.); neque tamen operibus gratiæ iustificatus est ex.

Antithesis est I. Pontificiorum, II. Anabaptistarum, III. Socinianorum & Arminianorum, negantium, nos sola fide, vt medio, meritum Christi apprehendente, iustificari. Quorum argumenta sunt.

I. Qua ratione Abrahamus iustificatus est, eadem ratione & nos iustificamur (Abrahamus quippe est Pater credentium, Rom. IV, 11. & exemplum omnibus iustificandis propositum): Atqui Abrahamus non tantum fide, sed & bonis operibus iustificatus est. E. Minor est Apostoli Iacobi, c. II, 21. Abrahamus, pater noster, nonne ex operibus iustificatus est, dum obtulit filium suum super altare? Videsne, quod fides per opera consummata sit? Resp. a) Dist. inter iustificationem peccatoris coram Deo, & inter ostensionem vel notificationem fidei & iustitiæ a Deo acceptæ coram hominibus (*). Non loquitur S. Iacobus de iustificatione peccatoris coram Deo, sed de ostensione & notificatione fidei ac iustitiæ coram hominibus, per bona opera, tanquam signa & testimonia veræ fidei & fructus iustitiæ. Idcirco inquit v. 18. Δείξόν μοι τὴν πίσιν σε ἐκ τῶν ἔργων σε, ostende mihi fidem tuam ex operibus tuis. Sensus itaque est; Nonne Abrahamus, Pater noster, iustificatus, i. e. iustus agnitus & manifestatus est ex operibus, inprimis illis, quæ palam effulgebant, cum offerret Isaacum filium suum super altare? b) Loquitur Apostolus de externa fidei professione. Dicit enim v. 14. Quænam vtilitas (est) fratres mei, si fidem dicat quis se habere, opera vero non habeat. Poteritne fides (ista) eum saluare? Externa fidei professio interdum vera est, si per caritatem aliasque virtutes se exserat; interdum falsa, quando comitatu bonorum operum destituitur, & vocatur communiter vana fidei iactantia.


### I. Quest. VIII. By what means does God justify the sinner?: [[Instantia I]] But the example of Abraham is brought forward, justified by works

[[Instantia I]] But the example of Abraham is brought forward, justified by works. [[Resp.]]

It is brought forward in opposition, to refute hypocrites, who are content with the mere external profession of faith; i.e., you hypocrites, boasting of faith, can be refuted by the example of Abraham. He was found, held, and acknowledged by men to be just, and called the friend of God, not so much by an external profession of faith as by works and most humble obedience (of which the offering of his son for sacrifice was an illustrious specimen).

[[Instantia II]] Whatever faith cooperates with works for justification, that alone does not suffice to obtain righteousness: But the faith of Abraham and of all believers, etc.

Therefore.

[[Resp.]] Faith, strengthening the heart of Abraham in most humble obedience, cooperated to show and notify justification before men, not to obtain it from God.

[[Instantia III]] Whatever faith is perfected by works, that alone does not suffice to obtain righteousness: But the faith of Abraham and of all believers, etc.

Therefore.

[[Resp.]] Faith is perfected by works not intrinsically, by reason of itself and its essential perfection; but extrinsically, by reason of others and of manifestation; thus the faith of Abraham became perfectly known to others from the offering of Isaac, as a stupendous deed.

[[II]] Faith alone justifies:

Faith alone is a dead thing: Therefore, a dead thing justifies. [[Resp.]]

In this paralogism there are four terms. For the word "alone" in the major premise excludes the confluence of good works in the apotelesma (result) of justification, while in the minor premise it excludes the coexistence of good works and denotes solitary faith. By the same reasoning, one might perhaps conclude: The eye alone sees: The eye alone is a dead thing: Therefore, a dead thing sees.

[[III]] Whatever faith is never alone, that never justifies alone: Justifying faith is never alone: Therefore.

[[Resp.]]

I deny the major and distinguish between the existence of faith and its office, or energeia (activity) and justifying power. Faith justifies alone, even though it is never alone, but joined with charity, hope, and other internal motions. Thus the intellect alone understands, although it is joined with the will: the eyes alone see, although ears and nostrils coexist with them: the taste of an apple alone affects the palate, however much the odor and color of the same apple accompany it.

Cf. DANNHAV. hodof. phaenom. XI. p. 1389.

[[IV]] Faith justifies either without charity, or with charity: Not without charity; because, as Paul testifies, it always works through this,

Gal. V, 6. Therefore with charity, and consequently not alone.

[[Resp.]] Faith, viewed within the sphere of justification, justifies without charity, i.e., faith, and not charity, is the medium apprehending the merit of Christ, by whose intuition God absolves the sinner believing in Christ from the debt of guilt and punishment. But faith considered outside the sphere of justification works through charity as the queen of the other virtues. But indeed, in this respect, faith does not flow into justification, but into sanctification and the production of good works.

[[Instantia]] But the power of justifying is attributed to charity 1) by Christ himself,

Luc. VII, 47. Her many sins are forgiven; for she loved much; 2) by John, 1 ep. III, 14. We have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren.

[[Resp.]] To 1): In the words of Christ, the particle ὅτι is not causal, but argumentative; for it does not denote the cause of the remission of sins, but an argument taken from the effect and external sign, by which the remission of sins is proved a posteriori; just as we argue a posteriori: This woman was pregnant, because (therefore) she gave birth; there is fire in this house, because (therefore) smoke has ascended. The true cause of the remission of sins is expressed in v. 50. Thy faith hath saved thee.

To 2): John says: we know that we have passed from death unto life; because we love the brethren. From which words it is clear that the love of the brethren is not the cause of the transition from spiritual death to life, but a principle of knowing a posteriori.

V. Maxima

V. The greatest virtue justifies most: Charity is the greatest virtue, 1 Cor. XIII, 13. Obj. No virtue justifies, whether it be small or great, because by the law, which is the norm of virtues, there is no justification, Rom. III, 20.

VI. The fear of the Lord expels sins; because he who is without fear cannot be justified, Sir. I, 25. 26. Resp. a) The fear of the Lord expels future sins, so that we may avoid them: faith cleanses the heart from past sins by the benefit of the blood of Christ, apprehended by singular trust. b) The Greek text stands thus: ὁ δυνήσεται θυμώδης ἀνὴρ δικαιωθῆναι, a wrathful man will not be able to be justified. A man indulging in wrath will be able to stand neither in the judgment of this world, nor before the divine tribunal; he will be condemned everywhere.

VII. Faith is imputed for righteousness, Rom. IV, 5. Faith is a virtue: for it is commanded in the first precept of the decalogue. Obj. A certain virtue, and consequently a certain good work, justifies. Resp. Faith is imputed for righteousness not absolutely and by itself, insofar as it is a virtue, but relatively and on account of Christ, whom it embraces; just as a hand enriches a beggar not by itself, but on account of the treasure offered by a rich man, which it accepts.

VIII. Repentance is not faith alone; because it embraces contrition and faith: Repentance justifies: Obj. a certain justifying thing is not faith alone. The minor is proved from Acts III, 19. Repent, and convert yourselves, that your sins may be blotted out for you. Resp. Repentance justifies by reason of faith alone in Christ, although it is joined with contrition. For contrition is necessary for those to be justified, not by the necessity of a means, but of order. Contrition does not concur positively to justification, but only removes the obstacle to the remission of sins, namely, the malicious purpose of sinning.

IX. Certain good works seem to precede faith and justification, namely the acknowledgment of sins, their detestation, and sorrow for sins, which are necessary for a man to be justified: Obj. faith alone does not justify. Resp. The acknowledgment of sins, their detestation, as also sorrow for sins, are indeed movements of the mind, excited by the divine law through the Holy Spirit, but they are not good works, speaking accurately. For good works proceed from faith, and are fruits of righteousness. But those movements precede regeneration, faith, and justification, and pertain to the conversion of the sinner. However, it is not one and the same thing to treat of the conversion of a man and of his justification. For not all those things which are required for true conversion also pertain to justification. For to justification only the grace of God, the merit of Christ, and faith, which embraces these very benefits of God in the promise of God, are required and necessary, as the Form. Concord. p. 687 says. (*).

Latin:

Instantia I Sed adducitur exemplum Abrahami, per opera iustificati. Resp.

Adducitur in contrarium, ad redarguendum hypocritas, sola externa fidei professione contentos; q. d. vos hypocritae, fidem iactantes, exemplo Abrahami potestis refutari. Ille non tam externa fidei professione, quam operibus & obedientia humillima (cuius illustre specimen erat oblatio filii ad sacrificium) iustus deprehensus, habitus & agnitus est ab hominibus, & amicus Dei vocatus.

Instantia II Quaecunque fides cooperatur cum operibus ad iustificationem, illa sola non sufficit ad consequendam iustitiam: Atqui fides Abrahami & omnium credentium &c.

E.

Resp. Fides, in humillimo obsequio cor Abrahami confortans, cooperata est ad iustificationem ostendendam & notificandam coram hominibus, non impetrandam a Deo.

Instantia III Quae fides ex operibus consummatur, illa sola non sufficit ad consequendam iustitiam: Atqui fides Abrahami & omnium credentium &c.

E.

Resp. Fides ex operibus consummatur non intrinsece, ratione sui & perfectionis essentialis; sed extrinsece, ratione aliorum & innotescentiae; sic fides Abrahami perfecte innotuit aliis ex oblatione Isaaci, tanquam facto stupendo.

II Sola fides iustificat:

Sola fides est res mortua: E. res mortua iustificat. Resp.

In hoc paralogismo sunt quatuor termini. Nam vox, sola, in maiori excludit bonorum operum confluentiam in ἀποτέλεσμα iustificationis, in minori excludit bonorum operum coexistentiam & notat fidem solitariam. Eadem ratione forte quis colligeret: Solus oculus videt: Solus oculus est res mortua: E. res mortua videt.

III Quaecunque fides nunquam est sola, illa nunquam sola iustificat: Fides iustificans nunquam est sola: Ergo.

Resp.

Neg. mai. & dist. inter fidei existentiam, & officium, seu ἐνέργειαν & vim iustificam. Fides iustificat sola, tametsi nunquam fit sola, sed cum caritate, spe & aliis internis motibus coniuncta. Sic solus intelligit intellectus, licet cum voluntate fit coniunctus: soli vident oculi, quamuis ipsis coexistlant aures & nares: solus sapor pomi afficit gustum, quantumuis ipsum comitetur odor & color eiusdem pomi.

Conf. DANNHAV. hodof. phaenom. XI. p. 1389.

IV Fides iustificat aut absque caritate, aut cum caritate: Non absque caritate; quia teste Paulo per hanc semper operatur,

Gal. V, 6. E. cum caritate, & consequenter non sola.

Resp. Fides, spectata intra sphaeram iustificationis, absque caritate iustificat, h. e. fides, non autem caritas, est medium apprehendens meritum Christi, cuius intuitu Deus peccatorem in Christum credentem absoluit a reatu culpae & poenae. At fides extra sphaeram iustificationis considerata operatur per caritatem tanquam reginam ceterarum virtutum. At vero hac ratione fides non influit in iustificationem, sed in sanctificationem, & bonorum operum productionem.

Instantia Sed caritati tribuitur vis iustificandi 1) ab ipso Christo,

Luc. VII, 47. Remissa sunt illi peccata multa; quoniam multum amauit; 2) a Ioanne, 1 ep. III, 14. Translati sumus de morte ad vitam, quoniam diligimus fratres.

Resp. Ad 1): In verbis Christi particula ὅτι non est causalis, sed ratiocinatiua; neque enim denotat caussam remissionis peccatorum, sed argumentum sumtum ab effectu & signo externo, quo remissio peccatorum a posteriori probatur; sicut a posteriori argumentamur: Haec mulier fuit grauida, quia (ideo) peperit; in his aedibus est ignis, quia (ideo) sumus ascendit. Vera remissionis peccatorum caussa exprimitur v. 50. Fides tua te saluam fecit.

Ad 2): Ioannes inquit: nos scimus, quod transiuerimus ex morte in vitam; quia amamus fratres. E quibus verbis patet, quod amor fratrum non fit caussa transitus e morte spirituali ad vitam, sed principium cognoscendi a posteriori. caussa transitus e morte spirituali ad vitam, sed principium cognoscendi a posteriori.

V. Maxima

V. Maxima virtus maxime iustificat: Caritas est maxima virtus, 1 Cor. XIII, 13. E. Resp. Nulla virtus iustificat, siue parua sit, siue magna, quia ex lege, quæ norma virtutum est, nulla est iustificatio, Rom. III, 20.

VI. Timor Domini expellit peccata; quia qui sine timore est, is non potest iustificari, Sir. I, 25. 26. Resp. a) Timor Domini expellit peccata futura, vt ea euitemus: fides purgat cor a peccatis præteritis beneficio sanguinis Christi, singulari fiducia apprehensi. b) Textus græcus ita se habet: ὁ δυνήσεται θυμώδης ἀνὴρ δικαιωθῆναι, non poterit iracundus homo iustificari. Homo iræ indulgens neque in iudicio huius mundi, neque coram tribunali diuino subsistere poterit, vbique damnabitur.

VII. Fides imputatur ad iustitiam, Rom. IV, 5. Fides est virtus: præcipitur enim in primo decalogi præcepto. E. Quædam virtus, & consequenter quoddam bonum opus iustificat. Resp. Fides imputatur ad iustitiam non absolute & per se, quatenus est virtus, sed relate & propter Christum, quem amplexatur; sicut manus mendicum ditat non per se, sed propter thesaurum, a viro diuite oblatum, quem acceptat.

VIII. Pœnitentia non est sola fides; quia contritionem & fidem complectitur: Pœnitentia iustificat: E. quoddam iustificans non est sola fides. Minor prob. ex Act. III, 19. Agite pœnitentiam, & conuertite vos, vt deleantur vobis peccata vestra. Resp. Pœnitentia iustificat ratione solius fidei in Christum, licet cum contritione sit coniuncta. Contritio enim necessaria est iustificandis, non necessitate medii, sed ordinis. Non concurrit contritio positiue ad iustificationem, sed remouet tantum obstaculum remissionis peccatorum, videlicet malitiosum peccandi propositum.

IX. Quædam bona opera videntur antecedere fidem & iustificationem, scilicet peccatorum agnitio, eorum detestatio, & dolor de peccatis, quæ homini iustificando necessaria sunt: E. non sola fides iustificat. Resp. Agnitio peccatorum, eorum detestatio, vt & dolor de peccatis sunt quidem motus animi, per legem diuinam a Spiritu S. excitati, sed non sunt bona opera, accurate loquendo. Nam bona opera proficiscuntur ex fide, & sunt fructus iustitiæ. At illi motus regenerationem, fidem & iustificationem antecedunt, & pertinent ad conuersionem peccatoris. Non autem vnum idemque est, de conuersione hominis, & de iustificatione eius agere. Non enim omnia illa, quæ ad veram conuersionem requiruntur, etiam ad iustificationem pertinent. Ad iustificationem enim tantum requiruntur, atque necessaria sunt gratia Dei, meritum Christi & fides, quæ hæc ipsa Dei beneficia in promissione Dei amplectitur, dicente Form. Concord. p. 687. (*).


### X. Does faith justify completely?

Faith justifies not dispositively , nor initially imperfectly, but completely & perfectly .

Proof a. Faith in the act of justification is not considered absolutely, as our quality or disposition, but relatively, as it looks upon Christ the ἱλαστήριον (propitiation), and relies upon his blood, Rom. III, 25. so that through his name it may receive the remission of sins, Acts X.

X. Proof b. Faith is the sole medium, embracing divine grace; and apprehending Christ with all his benefits. It does not, therefore, justify initially, but completely & perfectly. This is evident from the clearest sayings of Scripture.

For thus says the Apostle, Heb. IV, 16. Let us therefore approach with confidence to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy, and find grace for timely help. And John I, 12. As many as received Christ, to them he gave the power to be children of God, (namely) to those believing in his name.

The antithesis is 1) of the Papists, asserting that faith justifies only initially or dispositively, but not perfectly: 2) of the Socinians, maintaining that sins will be perfectly remitted only in the future life.

Their arguments are: I. Whatever is described by access to the throne of grace, that is only the beginning of justification: But faith, etc. Heb. IV, 16. Therefore. The major is clear: since access is the first motion, by which he who was far off begins to draw near. Resp. a) To approach to God, or to come to Christ, is the same as to believe, John VI, 35. b) Faith not only approaches the throne of grace, but also receives mercy, and finds help.

II. Whoever through faith only receive the power to become children of God, they are not by faith actually rendered children of God; the power of becoming differs greatly from actual existence: But those believing in Christ, etc. John I, 12. Therefore. Resp. ἐξουσία (power) in the cited place does not denote a power opposed to the act or state of filiation, but the right of those who are already reborn of God, v. 13. The word γενέσθαι (to become) signifies not only to be made, but also to be.

Latin:

Fides iustificat non dispositive , neque initialiter imperfecte, sed complete & perfecte .

Prob. a. Fides in actu iustificationis non consideratur absolute, ut qualitas aut dispositio nostra, sed relate, prout Christum ἱλαστήριον intuetur, eiusque sanguine nititur, Rom. III, 25. ut per nomen ipsius remissionem peccatorum accipiat, Act. X.

Prob. b. Fides est unicum medium, gratiam diuinam amplectens; & Christum cum omnibus beneficiis apprehendens. Non igitur initialiter, sed complete & perfecte iustificat.

Patet hoc e clarissimis scripturae dictis. Sic enim ait Apostolus Hebr. IV, 16. Accedamus itaque cum fiducia ad thronum gratiae, ut accipiamus misericordiam, & gratiam inueniamus in opportunum auxilium. Et Io. I, 12. Quotquot receperunt Christum, dedit illis potestatem, ut filii Dei essent, (nempe) credentibus in nomen ipsius.

Antithesis est 1) Pontificiorum, afferentium, fidem tantum initialiter aut dispositive, non autem perfecte iustificare: 2) Socinianorum, statuentium, in futura demum vita peccata perfecte remissum iri.

Quorum argumenta sunt: I. Quidquid describitur per accessum ad thronum gratiae, illud est tantum initium iustificationis: Atqui fides &c. Hebr. IV, 16. E. Maior liquet: quoniam accessus est primus motus, quo ille, qui procul erat, incipit appropinquare. Resp. a) Accedere ad Deum, aut venire ad Christum est idem, quod credere, Io. VI, 35. b) Fides non tantum accedit ad thronum gratiae, sed & misericordiam accipit, & auxilium inuenit.

II. Quicunque per fidem tantum accipiunt potestatem, ut fiant filii Dei, illi per fidem non actu redduntur filii Dei; potestas fiendi ab actuali existentia maxime differt: Atqui credentes in Christum &c. Io. I, 12. E. Resp. ἐξουσία l. c. non notat potestatem, attui, vel statui filiationis oppositam, sed ius eorum, qui iam ex Deo sunt regeniti v. 13. Verbum γενέσθαι significat non tantum fieri, sed etiam esse.


### Q. XI. Does God also use ministers in the justification of a sinner?

God in the business of justification uses holy heralds, duly called & ordained, who by the power of the keys of loosing remit sins.

Proof. The ministers of the word are called הרבים מצדיקי (those who justify many), Dan. XII, 3. The minister of the church does not only declare who receives the remission of sins, but also, by applying the word of reconciliation to repenting sinners, really, organically & ministerially remits sins, in the name of the principal cause.

VIII. Therefore, the suretyship of a certain mediator (μεσίτης) is necessary, who by expiating the sins of all men would fully satisfy the avenging justice, c. III, 25. (Δικαιοσύνη [righteousness] in this place is not that righteousness of God which he himself bestows upon us, but is the righteousness natural in God, and that indeed judging and punishing, which God wished to declare by a singular example, for ἔνδειξις [demonstration] is a declaration; he declared it, however, in that he constituted Christ a ἱλαστήριον [propitiation], understand ϑῦμα [victim], a piacular sacrifice, indeed ἐν τῷ αἵματι αὐτῦ [in his blood], from which it appears that God is so just that he cannot himself, his justice being safe, forgive sins to men, unless satisfaction has been rendered; add c. V, 8. & 9.). IX. The properties and perfections of that sponsor are necessary, namely three: that he should be 1) one, making satisfaction for all, c. V, 18. 19.: 2) innocent, and contaminated by no sin, ibid. v. 15. 19.: 3) one man, and the same true God, so that he himself might be able both to sustain the place of men, and to reconcile God, who has been appeased, to men, c. I, 3. VIII, 3. X. The imputation of vicarious righteousness, rendered by this sponsor, is necessary, as well as its application, which cannot be done otherwise than by confidence placed in him, c. III, 24. IV, 24. 25. V, 18.

Question XII. In what act does justification formally consist?

Justification is completed by two acts, a privative and a positive one. The former is the non-imputation, or remission of sins a): the latter is the imputation of the righteousness of Christ b). (*).

Observation I. Why our justification formally consists in a privative and a positive act, D. Hutterus teaches excellently in his Loci Communes, art. III, on justification, fol. 477. In the act of our justification there are two terms; one is of the evil from which we are freed, the other is of the good to which we are transferred. Thus, a twofold form of this imputation is also given: one privative, by which that which is inherent is not imputed; the other positive, by which that which is not inherent is imputed. Hence likewise emerge two parts of one and the same formal cause in justification: one privative, which is and is called the remission of sins, such that iniquities and inherent sins are not imputed to those being justified in the act of justification; the other part is positive, which is called the donation or imputation of the righteousness of Christ, such that an alien righteousness—namely, Christ's—is imputed to those being justified, not that eternal and essential one, but ἐπίκτητος, that is, acquired by the merits of obedience. Of which two foundations are to be noted. The first is taken from the condition of that state from which we are transferred through justification to a better state. For outside of justification we dwell in a state of corruption, in which a twofold evil lies upon us: one θετικὸν, or positive, namely the damnable guilt of our sins; the other στερητικὸν, privative, namely the lack of righteousness which ought to have been present. The formal cause of our justification brings a remedy to both this evils: for the remission of sins removes the former, and the donation or imputation of the righteousness of Christ compensates for the latter. The second foundation is sought from the parts of the mediation by which righteousness and salvation have been restored to us by Christ. For this mediation consists of 1) the obedience of Christ, performed for us to the divine law; 2) satisfaction, by which Christ paid the penalties due to our sins by his passion and death. but the latter of these [provides] the remission of both sins and the penalties due to them. By both of which merits our justification is completed.

Observation II. The sinner appears before the divine tribunal not only naked, but also defiled. And therefore, both the filthy garments must be removed, which is done through the death and satisfaction of Christ; and the white garments must be applied, which is done through the imputation of the obedience of Christ. The act concerning Joshua the priest, exhibited in a vision to Zechariah, expressed this very thing most elegantly in a typical way, from whom the filthy garments were first removed, and with them removed, clean garments were put on, Zech. III, 4.

Proof a. 1) From Rom. IV, 7. Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered! Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute sin! The Apostle took these words from Ps. XXXII, 1-2. Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered! Blessed is the man to whom Jehovah does not impute iniquity! To King David and the Apostle Paul, to forgive transgression, to cover sin, and not to impute iniquity are synonyms. The sins of believers are covered before God, not as if they escape His knowledge, but because He is no more offended by them, as if they were nothing. Not badly

AUGUSTINE in Ps. 32. If God covered sins, He did not wish to notice; if He did not wish to notice, He did not wish to take note; if He did not wish to take note, He did not wish to punish; if He did not wish to punish, He did not wish to acknowledge; if He did not wish to acknowledge, He wished to forgive. Furthermore, for a deeper understanding of the remission of sins, it must be observed: In original sin there is a) an inherent root; b) a relation to the person, insofar as it designates a certain person and contracts the guilt of sin to him, for the reason that it is ἀνομία, or a habit discrepant from the divine law; c) the guilt of punishment, or an obligation to punishment. Actual sins, however, are considered either physically, insofar as they are actions and depend efficiently upon man: or morally, insofar as they are actions against the law, and concern the right of some third party. Considered in the former way, they are transient acts; but in the latter way, after they have been committed, and as regards their real being have passed away, they remain morally, as regards the guilt of sin and punishment. The guilt of sin is that by which a man is held as if bound under sin, committed through a past act, just as, for example, he who has once committed adultery is called guilty of adultery, i.e., as if bound under the sin of adultery, so that he truly is and is called an adulterer, even if he is no longer committing adultery. The guilt of punishment is the obligation to undergo punishment for the committed sin. Wherefore, in order that the bond of guilt, by which the sinner is held bound, may be relaxed, both contrition and faith in Christ are necessary for him. Contrition is necessary by necessity of order, so that the sinner, according to divine law, may morally retract, disapprove of, and seriously detest with sorrow his acknowledged sins. Faith in Christ is necessary by necessity of means; for the reason that faith is the only medium by which the satisfaction of Christ, performed for the sins of the whole world, is apprehended, and is applied and united to the contrite soul, so that by the intuition of this, God may be moved to remove the guilt of sin and punishment. The guilt of sin is removed, by the gracious estimation of God, so that the repenting David before the divine tribunal is not considered an adulterer, Paul is not held as a persecutor of the church, Peter is not judged as a denier of Christ. The guilt of punishment is also removed, so that God does not inflict punishment upon the sinner believing in Christ, as an angry judge.

2) From 2 Cor. 5:19. God was in Christ, reconciling the world to Himself, while He did not impute their sins to them. The Apostle hints that the non-imputation of sins flows from the satisfaction of Christ, concerning which his own words in v. 14, 15 are to be understood. If one died for all, then all are dead. And He died for all, so that, while they live, they should no longer live for themselves, but for Him who died and was resurrected for all, i.e., the death of Christ, performed in the vicarious place of all men, is not otherwise estimated or accepted in the judgment of God than if all had died, i.e., by dying they had themselves expiated their sins; since the death of Christ is entirely ours through faith, as He did not die for Himself, but for us, indeed for all men, so that, bound by such a great benefit, they might henceforth also adapt themselves for the sake of gratitude to the will of the Redeemer. From which the Apostle in v. 18 concludes that God, through the satisfactory death of Christ, has been reconciled, so that, with His justice saved, He does not impute sins to believers for punishment, but forgives them, and receives them into grace.

3) That justification consists formally in the non-imputation, or remission of sins, is clear from Acts 13:38. Be it known therefore to you, men and brethren, that through this Jesus the remission of sins is announced to you, and from all things, from which you could not be justified in the law of Moses; in Him everyone who believes is justified. The word, δικαιωθῆναι, to be justified, constructed with the preposition ἀπὸ, from, or by, has a forensic meaning, and denotes to absolve someone in judgment from those things of which he is guilty and of which he is accused. Therefore, justification is formally the absolution from sins, or the remission of sins. For this reason also the penitent publican, having obtained the remission of sins, is said to have gone down to his house justified, Luke 18:14.

Prob. b. 1) From Rom. 5:19. Just as through the disobedience of one man many were constituted sinners; so also through the obedience of one many will be constituted just. Just as descendants of Adam are constituted sinners by the imputation of Adam’s disobedience; so we are constituted righteous by the imputation of Christ’s obedience.…

2) From 2 Cor. 5:21: "Him who knew no sin, He made to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in Him." Whence arises the argument: By the same reason that Christ was made sin for us, by that same reason are we rendered the righteousness of God on account of Christ; i.e., perfectly righteous before God. But Christ was made sin for us not inherently, but imputatively. Therefore, we also are rendered the righteousness of God on account of Christ not inherently, but imputatively.

3) Gal. 3:6: "Abraham believed God, and it was imputed to him for righteousness." St. Paul adds in v. 13: "Christ redeemed us from the curse, having become a curse for us." The faith of Abraham, therefore, looked to the Redeemer Christ, who was made a curse for us, whose righteousness was imputed to him out of divine mercy.

4) From Phil. 3:9: "That I may be found in Him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ; the righteousness which is given from God by faith." Paul appears before the most rigid divine judgment, relying not on his own righteousness, but on an alien one, which is from faith in Christ, to whom, as a branch to the vine, he was grafted.

5) From Rom. 4:5: "To him who does not work, but believes in Him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is imputed for righteousness." Faith is imputed for righteousness, not because it itself becomes such a good work and of such great value, but because it is borne toward the merit of Christ, which it involves by way of an object. For neither faith alone, nor the merit of Christ alone is imputed for righteousness, but faith apprehending the merit of Christ, or, as to the thing itself, it coincides: the merit of Christ, apprehended by faith. The mode of preaching is merely different. For when I say: "The merit of Christ, apprehended by faith, is imputed for righteousness," the effect is predicated of the subject to which it belongs by itself, and flows from its intrinsic value. But when I say: "Faith, leaning upon the merit of Christ, is imputed for righteousness," the effect is predicated of the subject to which it accrues from elsewhere. For faith is not imputed for righteousness insofar as it is our act; but solely insofar as it receives the merit of Christ. Therefore, all the imputability of faith is from nowhere else than from the object apprehended.

6) Whatever a man is blessed with in this life, in that his justification formally consists: By the imputation of the righteousness of Christ a man is blessed in this life. Therefore. The major is proved; because the blessedness of man in this life is his justification. The minor is proved from Rom. 4:6: "Just as David also speaks of the μακαρισμὸν [blessedness], the beatification of the man to whom God imputes righteousness apart from works." This righteousness which is imputed apart from works is not a proper righteousness inherent in us, since this would consist in works, but an alien one, which is none other than the righteousness of Christ, inasmuch as He has been made righteousness for us by God, 1 Cor. 1:30.

Latin:

Deus in iustificatione negotio utitur preconibus sacris, rite vocatis & ordinatis, qui vi clauis soluentis peccata remittunt.

Prob. Ministri verbi dicuntur הרבים מצדיקי iustificantes multos, Dan. XII, 3. Minister ecclesiae non declarat tantum, quinam remissionem peccatorum accipiat, sed etiam, verbum reconciliationis peccatoribus resipiscentibus applicando, realiter, organice & ministerialiter peccata remittit, nomine causae principalis.

VIII. Necessaria igitur sponsio μεσίτης cuiusdam, qui peccata hominum omnium expiando iustitiae vindici satis omnino faceret, c. III, 25. (Δικαιοσύνη hoc in loco non est ea Dei iustitia, quam nobis ipse tribuit, sed est iustitia in Deo naturalis, & ea quidem iudicans ac puniens, quam Deus singulari quodam exemplo declarare voluit, namque ἔνδειξις est declaratio; declaravit autem eo, quod Christum constituit ἱλαστήριον, subintellige ϑῦμα, piaculare sacrificium, quippe ἐν τῷ αἵματι αὐτῦ, ex quo adparet, Deum tam iustum esse, vt non possit ipse, salua iustitia sua, hominibus delicta condonare, nisi praestita satisfactione; add. c. V, 8. & 9.). IX. Necessariae sponsoris illius proprietates perfectionesque, nimirum tres: vt is esset 1) unus, pro omnibus satis faciens, c. V, 18. 19.: 2) innocens, nulloque peccato contaminatus, ibid. v. 15. 19.: 3) unus homo, idemque verus Deus, vt valeret ipse, & hominum vicem sustinere, & Deum placatum hominibus reconciliare, c. I, 3. VIII, 3. X. Necessaria imputatio iustitiae vicariae, ab hoc sponsore praestita, atque adplicatio, quae aliter fieri non potest, nisi fiducia in ipso posita, c. III, 24. IV, 24. 25. V, 18.

Quæst. XII. In quo actu formaliter consistit iustificatio?

Iustificatio absoluitur duobus actibus, priuatiuo, & positiuo. Ille est non-imputatio, seu remissio peccatorum a): hic est imputatio iustitiæ Christi b). (*).

Obs. I. Quare iustificatio nostri formaliter consistat in actu priuatiuo & positiuo, præclare docet D. HVTTERVS in loc. com. art. III. de iustificat. fol. 477. In actu iustificationis nostræ duo sunt termini; vnus est mali, a quo liberamur, alter vero est boni, ad quod transferimur. Ita gemina etiam datur forma imputationis huius: vna priuatiua, qua non imputatur id, quod inest; altera positiua, qua imputatur, quod non inest. Hinc emergunt itidem partes duæ vnius & eiusdem caussæ formalis in iustificatione: vna priuatiua, quæ est ac dicitur remissio peccatorum, ita, vt iustificandis in actu iustificationis non imputentur iniquitates & peccata inhærentia; altera pars est positiua, quæ dicitur donatio, siue imputatio iustitiæ Christi, ita, vt iustificandis imputetur aliena, Christi nimirum, iustitia, non æterna illa & essentialis, sed ἐπίκτητος, h. e. obedientiæ meritis acquisita. Cuius notanda sunt duo fundamenta. Primum sumitur a conditione illius status, ex quo per iustificationem ad statum meliorem transferimur. Nam extra iustificationem versamur in statu corruptionis, in quo duplex malum nobis incumbit, vnum θετικὸν, siue positiuum, nempe damnabilis peccatorum nostrorum reatus, alterum στερητικὸν, priuatiuum, nempe defectus iustitiæ, quæ inesse debebat. Vtrique huic malo medicinam affert caussa formalis iustificationis nostræ: nam prius illud tollit remissio peccatorum, posterius compensat donatio, siue imputatio iustitiæ Christi. Alterum fundamentum petitur a partibus mediationis, qua iustitia & salus a Christo nobis reparata est. Constat enim mediatio hæc 1) obedientia Christi, legi diuinæ pro nobis præstita; 2) satisfactione, qua pœnas, peccatis nostris debitas, Christus sua passione & morte exsoluit. Prior illa promeruit nobis imputationem iustitiæ; posterior vero hæc remissionem & peccatorum & pœnarum illis debitarum. Quo vtroque merito iustificatio nostra absoluitur.

Obs. II. Comparet peccator coram tribunali diuino non solum nudus, sed etiam sordidatus. Ideoque tum sordidæ vestes sunt tollendæ, quod fit per mortem & satisfactionem Christi; tum candidæ vestes sunt applicandæ, quod fit per imputationem obedientiæ Christi. Elegantissimæ hoc ipsum expressit typice actus circa Iosuam sacerdotem, in visione exhibitus Zachariæ, a quo primum ablatæ sunt vestes immundæ, ipsisque ablatis, vestes mundæ sunt indutæ, Zach. III, 4.

Prob. a. 1) Ex Rom. IV, 7. Beati, quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates & quorum occultata sunt peccata! Beatus vir, cui Dominus non imputat peccatum! Apostolus hæc verba transsumsit e Ps. XXXII, 12. Beatus, cui remissa est præuaricatio, tectum peccatum! Beatus homo, cui non imputat Iehouah iniquitatem! Regi Dauidi & Apostolo Paullo remittere præuaricationem, tegere peccatum, non imputare iniquitatem, sunt synonyma. Peccata credentium Deo tecta sunt, non quasi ipsius scientiam fugiant, sed quia illis non magis offenditur, quasi nulla essent. Haud male

AVGVSTINVS in Pf. XXXII. Si texit peccata Deus, noluit aduertere; fi noluit aduertere, noluit animaduertere; si noluit animaduertere, noluit punire; si noluit punire, noluit agnoscere; si noluit agnoscere, voluit ignoscere. Ceterum ad penitius cognoscendum peccatorum remissionem, obseruandum est: In peccato originali esse a) radicem inhærentem; b) relationem ad personam, quatenus certam denominat personam, & reatum culpæ ei contrahit, ideo, quod est ἀνομία, seu habitus a lege diuina discrepans; c) reatum pœnæ, siue obligationem ad pœnam. Peccata autem actualia considerantur vel physice, in quantum sunt actiones & ab homine efficienter dependent: vel moraliter, in quantum sunt actiones contra legem, & ius cuiusdain tertii concernunt. Priori modo considerata sunt actus transeuntes; posteriori autem modo, postquam patrata sunt, & quoad suum esse reale præterierunt, manent moraliter, quoad reatum culpæ & pœnæ. Reatus culpæ est, quo homo sub peccato, per actum præteritum patrato, tenetur quasi constrictus, quomodo v. gr. qui semel commisit adulterium, reus dicitur adulterii, i. e. sub adulterii peccato quasi constrictus, vt vere sit & dicatur adulter, etiamsi iam non adulteretur. Reatus pœnæ est obligatio ad subeundam pro commisso peccato pœnam. Quare vt relaxetur vinculum reatus, quo obstrictus tenetur peccator, huic necessaria est tum contritio, tum fides in Christum. Contritio necessaria est necessitate ordinis, vt peccator ex lege diuina sua peccata agnita moraliter retractet, improbet, & serio cum dolore detestetur. Fides in Christum necessaria est necessitate medii; ideo, quod fides vnicum medium est, quo satisfactio Christi, pro peccatis totius mundi præstita, apprehenditur, & animæ contritæ applicatur atque vnitur, vt huius intuitu Deus moueatur ad tollendum reatum culpæ & pœnæ. Tollitur reatus culpæ, gratiosa Dei æstimatione, vt resipiscens Dauid coram tribunali diuino non censeatur adulter, Paullus non habeatur persecutor ecclesiæ, Petrus non iudicetur abnegator Christi. Tollitur etiam reatus pœnæ, vt Deus peccatori in Christum credenti non irroget pœnam, vt iratus iudex.

2) Ex 2 Cor. V, 19. Deus erat in Christo, mundum reconcilians sibi ipsi, dum non imputabat peccata illorum. Apostolus innuit, non-imputationem peccatorum fluere ex satisfactione Christi, de qua intelligenda sunt ipsius verba v. 14. 15. Si vnus pro omnibus mortuus est, omnes igitur mortui sunt. Et ipse pro omnibus mortuus est, vt, dum viuunt, non amplius sibi ipsis viuant, sed ipsi, qui pro omnibus mortuus est & resuscitatus, q. d. Mors Christi, vicario loco omnium hominum præstita, in iudicio Dei non aliter æstimatur, vel acceptatur, quam si omnes mortui essent, h. e. moriendo ipsi peccata sua expiassent; quandoquidem Christi mors tota est nostra per fidem, cum non pro se mortuus sit, sed pro nobis, immo pro omnibus hominibus, vt, deuincti tanto beneficio, posthac gratitudinis caussa etiam sese attemperent voluntati redimentis. E quibus Apostolus v. 18. concludit, quod Deus per mortem Christi satisfactoriam reconciliatus sit, vt salua sua iustitia peccata credentibus ad pœnam non imputet, sed condonet, eosque in gratiam recipiat.

3) Quod in non imputatione, seu remissione peccatorum formaliter consistat iustificatio, liquet ex Act. XIII, 38. Notum ergo esto vobis, viri fratres, quod per hunc Iesum vobis remissio peccatorum annuntiatur, & ab omnibus, quibus non poteritis in lege Mosis iustificari; in hoc omnis, qui credit, iustificatur. Verbum, δικαιωθῆναι, iustificari cum præpositione ἀπὸ, a, vel ab, constructum, habet significationem forensem, notatque absoluere aliquem in iudicio ab illis, quorum est reus & quorum accusatur. E. iustificatio formaliter est absolutio a peccatis, vel remissio peccatorum. Idcirco etiam publicanus pœnitens, impetrata remissione peccatorum, in domum suam iustificatus descendisse dicitur, Luc. XVIII, 14.

Prob. b. 1) Ex Rom. V, 19. Sicut per vnius hominis inobedientiam peccatores constituti sunt multi; ita etiam per obedientiam vnius iusti constituentur multi. Quemadmodum posteri Adami constituuntur peccatores imputatione inobedientiae Adami; ita nos iusti constituimur imputatione obedientiae Christi.

2) Ex 2 Cor. V, 21. Eum, qui non nouerat peccatum, pro nobis peccatum fecit, vt nos fieremus iustitia Dei in ipso. Vnde nascitur argumentum: Qua ratione Christus factus est pro nobis peccatum, eadem ratione nos reddimur propter Christum iustitia Dei; i. e. coram Deo perfecte iusti. Sed Christus factus est pro nobis peccatum non inhaesiue, sed imputatiue. E. & nos propter Christum reddimur iustitia Dei non inhaesiue, sed imputatiue.

3) Gal. III, 6. Abraham credidit Deo, & imputatum est ipsi in iustitiam. Addit S. Paulus v. 13. Christus nos redemit a maledictione, factus pro nobis maledictio. Respexit ergo fides Abrahami redemtorem Christum, qui est factus pro nobis maledictio, cuius iustitia ipsi ex misericordia diuina est imputata.

4) Ex Phil. III, 9. Vt inueniar in Christo, non habens meam iustitiam, quae ex lege (fit) sed eam, quae ex fide Christi; iustitiam, quae ex Deo datur, fidei. Comparet Paullus coram rigidissimo iudicio diuino, fretus non iustitia propria, sed aliena, quae est ex fide Christi, cui, vt palmes viti, insitus erat.

5) Ex Rom. IV, 5. Ei, qui non operatur, credit vero in eum, qui iustificat impium, imputatur fides in iustitiam. Fides imputatur in iustitiam, non quod ipsa tam bonum opus fit, tantique valoris, sed quia fertur in meritum Christi, quod per modum obiecti inuoluit. Neque enim fides sola, nec meritum Christi solum ad iustitiam imputatur, sed fides meritum Christi apprehendens, seu, quoad, quod rem, coincidit, meritum Christi, fide apprehensum. Modus praedicandi tantum diuersus est. Nam cum dico: Meritum Christi, fide apprehensum ad iustitiam imputatur, effectus praedicatur de subiecto, cui per se competit, & ex intrinseco eius valore fluit. At cum dico: Fides, merito Christi innixa, imputatur ad iustitiam, effectus praedicatur de subiecto, cui aliunde accrescit. Non enim imputatur fides ad iustitiam, quatenus est actus noster; sed vnice, quatenus Christi meritum recipit. Omnis itaque fidei imputabilitas haud aliunde, quam ex obiecto apprehenso est.

6) Quocunque homo in hac vita beatus est, in eo ipsius iustificatio formaliter consistit: Imputatione iustitiae Christi homo in hac vita beatus est. E. Maior probatur; quia beatitudo hominis in hac vita est ipsius iustificatio. Minor prob. ex Rom. IV, 6. Quem ad modum etiam Dauid dicit, μακαρισμὸν, beatificationem esse hominis, cui Deus imputat iustitiam sine operibus. Quae iustitia sine operibus imputatur, non est propria iustitia nobis inhaerens, cum haec in operibus consistat, sed aliena, quae nulla alia est, quam iustitia Christi, quippe qui nobis a Deo factus est iustitia, 1 Cor. I, 30.


### Q. XI. Does God also use ministers in the justification of a sinner?: Q

Q.

Imputation, considered generally, is an act of the intellect and will of him who exercises judgment, by which the voluntary action of some person is recognized and estimated to pertain, with the effect redundant from it, either to the person acting himself, or to another in whose stead that action was undertaken. Imputation occurs, however, sometimes by debt, sometimes by grace. A voluntary action is imputed by debt when its effect is attributed to the acting person, as the moral cause, by the estimation and decree of the judge . A voluntary action is imputed by grace when the effect is reckoned not to the agent, but to that person in whose favor the action undertaken is directed, by the gracious estimation of the judge .

Obf. I. Obf. I. To impute in the article of justification is not taken in a physical sense, so as to signify to infuse, to implant, einpflanßen, or to graft in, but in a moral, judicial, and declarative sense, by which voluntary actions are said to be imputed to the agent when he, especially, who has disposed concerning them by law, declares the agent to be the author of the same, and at the same time determines that the effects of them actually redound to him, or reside in him, as Samuel Pufendorf defines in *De I. N. & G.*, ch. IX, p. 125. To impute here signifies to adjudge, to reckon, to attribute, by one's own estimation and judgment to transfer, derive, or devolve the effect of a voluntary action to someone.

Obf. II. Obf. II. An impossible, involuntary, and merely natural action is imputed to no one, but a voluntary action, depending on the powers of the agent and his own intention.

Therefore, a moral cause is commonly described as that which becomes a cause because it concurs with an efficacious intention, on account of which the effect is imputed to it. Obf. III. Obf. III. In every imputation, three things are strictly to be considered: 1) the voluntary action, 2) the estimation and judgment concerning the voluntary action, 3) the effect of the action, which is adjudged to someone.

The voluntary action is the foundation of the imputation, in consideration of which the judge renders judgment: if this foundation is true, certain, and real, the imputation is true, real, and just.
