But if no voluntary action has been performed, no foundation is present, and thus the effect cannot be imputed; or, if it is imputed, the imputation is vain, fictitious, false, and unjust, e.g., when guilt is imputed to an innocent person. Furthermore, the voluntary action which is imputed passes away, but the effect redounding from the action remains. Obf. IV. Obf. IV. A voluntary action is either good or evil.

The effect of a good action is praise, reward, wages; the effect of an evil action is guilt, offense to the judge, and punishment. Obf. V. Obf. V. A voluntary action, whether our own or another's, is imputed to us for grave and just causes.

When our own action is imputed to us, the foundation of the imputation is in us; when another's action is imputed to us, the foundation is indeed in another, yet there are grave and just causes on account of which it is imputed to us. E.g., the first sin of Adam is truly and really imputed to the whole human race; for the reason that he is the head of all men, inasmuch as they are joined to him by the bond of blood (*): the vicarious fulfillment of the law of Christ is also imputed by the true and real judgment of God to all believers; for the reason that he is the head of all believers, inasmuch as they are united to him by the bond of faith. Prob. a. Prob. a. From Rom. 4:4. To him who works, the reward is not imputed of grace, but of debt. To a hireling, his own voluntary action is imputed for wages by the master, and thus the foundation of the imputation is in the hireling himself: but if a friend labors for a friend, and the master benevolently accepts that labor, the reward is imputed not to the one laboring, but to him for whose benefit the labor was undertaken, out of grace. Then the foundation of the imputation is not in the person who receives the reward, but in that person who labored for another. Imputation according to debt, therefore, is that whose foundation exists in the worker himself, to whom the imputation is made.

Imputation according to grace is that whose foundation is not in him to whom the imputation is made, but in another, who directed his operation for his benefit, the effect of which the master or judge attributes to him out of grace, e.g., the obedience of Christ is reckoned to the believing sinner for righteousness by God out of grace.

Prob. b. Prob. b. Paul himself provides a very clear example of gracious imputation, who writes to Philemon, v. 17, 18, 19: If you count me as a partner, receive him (Onesimus)

...as me. But if he has done you any injury, or owes you anything, charge this to me. I, Paul, have written it with my own hand; I will make satisfaction. Onesimus had done an injury to Philemon, and was his debtor. Paul was the mediator, satisfier, and intercessor, who asked that every injury which Onesimus had done to Philemon be charged to himself. Philemon acknowledged this satisfaction to be valid and accepted it, and he adjudged its fruit, or the remission of the debt and injury, to Onesimus, and thus received him back into favor. So the sinner, by violating the law of God, has done an injury to His majesty and has contracted the debts of sins. The mediator, satisfier, and intercessor is Jesus Christ, who willed that the debts of all sinners be charged to Himself, by offering a most full satisfaction to God. God judges by grace that this satisfaction pertains to the sinner believing in Christ, and in view of this, He absolves him from guilt and punishment. There are also many examples of gracious imputation. King Pharaoh imputed the merits of Joseph to his father and brothers for a convenient dwelling in Egypt; King David imputed the merits of Jonathan to Mephibosheth for the enjoyment of the royal table. Indeed, we learn from many experiences that even today the merits of husbands are imputed to wives, so that they may shine with their rays, and the merits of parents are imputed to children for honor and dignity.

Question XIV. Can you now clearly explain the non-imputation or remission of sins, and the imputation of the righteousness of Christ?

God, the most just but placable judge, so hears the case of a sinful man accused by the law and convicted of sins, yet at the same time believing in Christ, that He finds him indeed guilty of fault and eternal punishment, and destitute of his own righteousness, but judges the satisfaction and merit of the mediator Christ to pertain to him in such a way that, on account of Christ’s satisfactory passion (*) apprehended by true faith, He absolves him from guilt and punishment, and on account of the fulfillment of the divine law performed by Christ in the place of the human race, and applied by singular trust, He reputes and pronounces him righteous by a gracious estimation.

You say: The remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness are equipollent terms according to Paul, Rom. IV, 6, 7. Resp. The remission of sins and the imputation of the righteousness of Christ are acts inseparable and intimately conjoined, yet formally distinct, since the former is privative and the latter is positive: the former proceeds immediately from the passive obedience of Christ, the latter from His active obedience. We do not deny, meanwhile, that one is rightly inferred from the other; since there is no sinner to whom sins have been remitted, and yet the righteousness of Christ has not been imputed, and vice versa.

The antithesis is I. of the Papists, who teach that we are justified through an infused habit of righteousness; II. of the Socinians, who teach that we are justified through obedience performed to the precepts of Christ; III. of the Arminians, who teach that we are justified through faith as our act or work; IV. of the Weigelians, who teach that we are justified through the imitation of Christ; V. of the Osiandrians, who teach that we are justified through the essential righteousness of God. Their principal arguments are:

I. Whatever righteousness is alien, that cannot be our own: But the righteousness of Christ is alien: Therefore. Resp. 1) Whatever righteousness is alien cannot be our own by inherence; yet it can be our own... ours imputatively. 2) That in human judgment the justice of one person is not estimated or considered the justice of another, arises from the fact that in common life one person is not made united to another, just as those believing in Christ not only receive this their mediator within the chamber of their heart, as a guest, John 1:22 but also put him on, Gal. 3:28 and through faith are as it were glued to him, 1 Cor. 6:17 so that they may be found in Christ, no differently than branches in the vine, Phil. 3:9 add. John 15:1 sqq. Hence it happens that believers apply, appropriate, and make the justice of Christ their own through faith.

3) If the injustice of Adam could be imputed to all who were begotten from him: why could the justice of Christ not be imputed to those who are spiritually born from him?

II. Whoever are denominated just through the intrinsic justice of Christ, they are not truly, but only reputatively just: But penitent sinners are called just truly, and not reputatively: Therefore. Resp. 1) Extrinsic denomination is not opposed to the truth of the thing. A wall is said to be seen by extrinsic denomination, and yet it is truly seen. Someone is called my friend from my love, which is in me, and outside of him. A debtor is said to be freed extrinsically from a foreign debt, for whom another has dissolved the debt. Which extrinsic denomination does not take away the truth of the thing. 2) Although in the very act of justification the extrinsic justice of Christ is imputed to the repenting sinner; yet that is received by the believing sinner within the mind, so that justification in man becomes and remains not by way of inherence, but of appropriation and union.

III. Whoever is not equally just as Christ, his justice cannot be the justice of Christ: But the penitent sinner etc. Therefore. The major is proven; because Christ is justice itself, Jer. 23:6 But the penitent sinner and one believing in Christ, although he is justified on account of the merit of Christ, yet complains with Paul that no good dwells in him, Rom. 7:18 Resp. Distinguish between the essential, habitual, and mediatorial justice of Christ. There is a huge difference between the justice of Christ and the justified sinner; so that the latter is not to be compared to the former at all. For Christ, as God, is just essentially; as man, he is just habitually, from the first moment of conception: which can by no means be asserted of the justified sinner. Furthermore, if Christ, the mediator, according to both natures, by his merit produced justice not for himself, but for the sinful man, it is derivatively terminated not in Christ but in the sinner, receiving him by true faith; and this is the mediatorial justice of Christ. Whence not Christ, but the sinful man believing in Christ is denominated just from the merited justice.

IV. Whoever are said to be truly just from the imputed justice of Christ, they are not only equally just among themselves, but also more just than the heavenly beings: But not all Christians are equally just among themselves, nor more just than the heavenly beings: Therefore. The major is clear; because Christians are denominated just from the one justice of Christ, which will cease in heaven; for the reason that knowledge (faith) will be abrogated there. Resp. By reason of the imputed justice of Christ, man is not more just than man; for the reason that justice, brought forth by the merit of Christ, admits no degrees; but man is said to be more just than man by reason of inherent justice. Furthermore, the imputed justice of Christ will not indeed cover any sins in heaven, because there will be none; yet it will endure eternally, as the excellent splendor of the heavenly beings and the basis of all holiness, of all glorious rectitude.

V. If through the imputation of the justice of Christ we are truly just, Christ through the imputation of our sin will truly be a sinner: The consequent is false: Therefore, the antecedent also. The consequence of the major is proven: because our sins are thus imputed to Christ, as the justice of Christ is imputed to …us, 2 Cor. 5:21. That the consequent is false, is evident: because a sinner is a son of the devil. Resp. a) CHRYSOSTOM and other Greek Fathers call Christ the greatest sinner, such imputatively; because he was held guilty of the sins of the whole world in the divine judgment. Jehovah made to fall upon him the iniquity of all of us, says Is. 53:6. b) It remains yet there is a huge difference between us and Christ. For Christ not only ascribes and imparts his righteousness to us, but also endows us with inherent righteousness; we, however, do not infect him with the contagion of the unrighteousness inherent in us. Whence our sin does not inhere in him. c) He is called a son of the devil who commits sins against his conscience with deliberate counsel of mind, and indulges in them. Therefore, not even the pious, to whom sin inheres, and who not infrequently fall out of human infirmity, are to be called sons of the devil: much less Christ.

VI. If through the inherent disobedience of Adam all men are constituted unrighteous, then certainly through the inherent obedience of Christ all believing men are constituted righteous: The antecedent is true: Therefore also the consequent. The consequence of the major is clear: because the reason for opposites is the same. The antecedent is clear from the Pauline testimony Rom. V, 19. Resp. The disobedience of Adam and the obedience of Christ are proper, personal, and individual acts, which cannot be common to others unless they are imputed to them by divine judgment. Hence it happens that, although disobedience inheres in Adam, and obedience in Christ; yet the disobedience of Adam is reckoned to his descendants, and the obedience of Christ to believers, by divine estimation and declaration, so that the former are reputed guilty of death, the latter righteous and heirs of eternal life.

Instance: But the disobedience of Adam also inheres in his descendants; because through carnal generation it is implanted in them: Therefore, the obedience of Christ also inheres. Resp. It is said incorrectly that the disobedience of Adam inheres in his descendants. For the disobedience of Adam was the first and originating sin, which could not be attributed to his descendants except by imputation; but original, or originated, sin is that which has arisen from it, which indeed inheres in the descendants of Adam, but only consequently flows from the disobedience of Adam.

VII. Faith is not the righteousness of Christ (because they differ as the medium and the form of justification): Faith is imputed for righteousness, Rom. IV, 5. Therefore, something which is imputed for righteousness is not the righteousness of Christ. Resp. In the major, faith is taken absolutely and abstractly, insofar as it is the receiving medium; in the minor, relatively and concretely, insofar as it is the medium receiving the merit of Christ, which is imputed to the believer for righteousness by divine estimation. This diverse consideration of faith produces a quaternio terminorum.

VIII. The satisfaction of Christ is either imputed before we have it, or when we have it: But not before we have it; because it was performed long ago, so that we might most certainly have it: nor when we have it; because what a man has is not imputed to him: Therefore, it is never imputed. Resp. Distinguish a) between satisfaction and its effect; b) between satisfaction performed by Christ and applied by man to himself. The satisfaction of Christ was performed long ago; but we do not have its effect, which is the remission of sins, before we apply the universal satisfaction of Christ to ourselves and make it our own through faith. For in order that a gracious imputation may be correctly made, there must be present in the agent the intention of procuring some good for another by his action; in the recipient, an express or presumed will to receive that from him. For the imputation of a service which is forced upon an unwilling person is rightly repelled, says SAM. PVFEND. in L. de I. N. & G. p. 128.

IX. The righteousness which we lost through Adam, that is restored through Christ: Inherent righteousness etc. Therefore. The major is clear: because whatever was lost through Adam was restored through Christ, Rom. V, 15. Resp. The conclusion can be granted in a conclusive sense; because righteousness inherent in the reborn is to be credited to the merit of Christ. If it is understood in an exclusive sense, that inherent righteousness was restored only through Christ, we deny the major. To its proof we say that Christ did not only restore that which was lost through Adam, but also acquired for us other goods or benefits, e.g., penitential conversion, faith resting on Christ, imputed righteousness, brotherhood with Christ, which were not lost. Conversely, certain goods, lost through Adam, Christ did not restore, namely: immortality in this life, full dominion over living creatures, the inhabitation of paradise, etc.

X. To whom the righteousness of God is given, and that eternal, so that they may become partakers of the divine nature, to them is conferred not the righteousness of Christ, but the essential righteousness of God: Yet to believers, etc.

E. The major premise is established: because the eternal righteousness of God is not the righteousness of Christ, since the latter was brought forth in the fullness of time, and through it we are not rendered partakers of the divine nature.

Resp. The imputed righteousness of Christ is the righteousness of God, in that, by the gracious estimation of God, it is reckoned to those who believe in Christ; it is eternal, both by reason of the divine decree and by reason of its value and efficacy; however, we are rendered partakers of the divine nature through the mystical union, which follows justification.

Quæst. XV. Is the doctrine of the imputed righteousness of Christ not only true, but also useful for piety?

The evangelical doctrine of the imputed righteousness of Christ is not only true and solid a), but also most useful for exercising true piety, which is free from hypocrisy b).

Antithesis is 1) that of the Papists, whose canon X in the Council of Trent, Sess. V, stands thus: If anyone shall say that men are formally righteous through the righteousness of Christ, let him be anathema.

2) That of the Socinians, who deny that the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us.

OSTORODVS in his German Instantia, ch. XXXIV, fol. 304, writes: Not the slightest little verse can be shown in Holy Scripture concerning the righteousness of Christ imputed to us.

3) That of the Arminians, who contend that faith as an act or our work, not the righteousness, merit, or obedience of Christ, is imputed to us for righteousness, in Apol. f. 112. 4) That of the Weigelians and Mystics, who, as much as in them lies, undermine the imputed righteousness of Christ.

For thus WEIGELIVS in part III of his Postilla, p. 15, says: They must have the death and resurrection of Christ within them, and not impute it from without.

This is not better, but much worse, CHRIST. HOBVRG. says in his mystical Postilla, p. 190: If your imputation can accomplish everything and justify us before God, what need have we of union with Christ?

5) The Quakers support these. ROBERT BARCLAY in Apol. ad thef. 7, n. 7, says: The imputative righteousness of Christ is not found in the Holy Scriptures.

Latin:

Quæst. XIII. Quid est imputatio generatim considerata?

Imputatio, generatim considerata, est actus intellectus & voluntatis illius, qui iudicium exercet, quo voluntaria alicuius personae actio cognoscitur & aestimatur pertinere, cum effectu ex ea redundante, vel ad ipsam personam agentem, vel ad aliam, cuius vice illa actio suscepta est. Fit autem imputatio alia ex debito, alia ex gratia. Ex debito imputatur actio voluntaria, quando illius effectus personae agenti, vt causae morali, aestimatione & decreto iudicis attribuitur . Ex gratia imputatur actio voluntaria, quando effectus non agenti, sed illi personae, in cuius commodum actio suscepta dirigitur, gratiosa aestimatione iudicis accensetur .

Imputare in articulo iustificationis non sumitur in sensu physico, vt significet inferere, implantare, einpflanßen, oder einpfropffen, sed in sensu morali, iudiciali ac declaratiuo, quo actiones voluntariae imputari agenti dicuntur, quando ille potissimum, qui circa eas lege disposuit, agentem earundem auctorem declarat, simulque effectus ipsarum in ipsum actu redundare, aut in eodem haerere statuit, definiente Samuele Pufendorfio de I. N. & G. c. IX. p. 125. Imputare hic significat adiudicare, accensere, attribuere, aestimatione & iudicio suo effectum actionis voluntariae ad aliquem transferre, deriuare, deuoluere.

Obs. II. Obs. II. Nemini imputatur actio impossibilis, inuita, & mere naturalis, sed actio voluntaria, a viribus agentis, ipsiusque intentione dependens.

Idcirco causa moralis vulgo describitur, quod fit causa, quae efficaci concurrit intentione, propter quam effectus illi imputatur. Obs. III. Obs. III. In omni imputatione tria oppido consideranda sunt: 1) actio voluntaria, 2) aestimatio & iudicium de actione voluntaria, 3) effectus actionis, qui alicui adiudicatur.

Actio voluntaria est fundamentum imputationis, cuius intuitu iudex fert iudicium: quod fundamentum si fuerit verum, certum & reale, imputatio vera, realis & iusta est. Sed si nulla actio voluntaria patrata est, nullum adest fundamentum, adeoque effectus non potest imputari; aut, si imputatur, vana, fictitia, falsa & iniqua est imputatio, v. gr. cum culpa imputatur innocenti. Ceterum actio voluntaria, quae imputatur, transit, effectus autem ex actione redundans permanet. Obs. IV. Obs. IV. Actio voluntaria vel est bona, vel mala.

Actionis bonae effectus est laus, praemium, merces; actionis malae effectus est culpa, offensa iudicis, & poena. Obs. V. Obs. V. Imputatur nobis actio voluntaria vel propria, vel aliena, grauibus & iustis de causis.

Cum propria actio nobis imputatur, fundamentum imputationis est in nobis; cum actio aliena nobis imputatur, fundamentum est in alio quidem, sunt tamen graues & iustae causae, propter quas nobis imputetur. V. gr. Peccatum primum Adami imputatur vere & realiter vniuerso generi humano; ideo, quod est caput omnium hominum, quippe qui vinculo sanguinis cum ipso sunt coniuncti (*): imputatur etiam iudicio Dei vero & reali omnibus credentibus impletio legis Christi vicaria; propterea, quod est caput omnium credentium, quippe qui vinculo fidei cum ipso sunt vniti. Prob. a. Prob. a. Ex Rom. IV, 4. Ei, qui operatur, merces non imputatur ex gratia, sed ex debito. Mercenario actio voluntaria propria imputatur ad mercedem a domino, adeoque imputationis fundamentum est in ipso mercenario: sed si amicus laboret pro amico, & dominus illum laborem beneuole accepet, praemium non laboranti, sed illi, in cuius commodum labor susceptus est, imputatur ex gratia. Tunc fundamentum imputationis non est in persona, quae praemium accipit, sed in illa persona, quae pro altero laborauit. Est igitur imputatio secundum debitum, cuius fundamentum exstat in ipso operante, cui fit imputatio.

Imputatio secundum gratiam est, cuius fundamentum non est in eo, cui fit imputatio, sed in alio, qui in ipsius commodum suam direxit operationem, cuius effectum dominus, vel iudex eidem ex gratia attribuit, v. gr. obedientia Christi peccatori credenti ad iustitiam a Deo ex gratia accensetur. Prob. b. Prob. b. Perquam luculentum imputationis gratiosae exemplum praebet ipse Paullus, qui ad Philemonem scribit, v.

17. 18. 19. Si me habes pro consorte, suscipe eum (Onesimum) consorte, suscipe eum (Onesimum)

mum) ficut me. Si vero quid iniuriæ tibi fecit, aut debet, hoc mihi imputa. Ego Paullus fcripfi manu mea, ego fatisfaciam. Onefimus fecerat iniuriam Philemoni, eiusque erat debitor. Mediator, fatisfactor & interceffor erat Paullus, qui petebat, omnem iniuriam, quam Onefimus Philemoni fecerat, fibi imputari. Philemon hanc fatisfactionem validam effe agnofcebat, & acceptabat, eiusque fructum, fiue remiffionem debiti & iniuriæ, Onefimo adiudicabat, atque adeo eundem in gratiam recipiebat. Ita peccator, violando legem Dei, huius maieftati iniuriam fecit, & debita peccatorum contraxit. Mediator, fatisfactor & interceffor eft Iefus Chriftus, qui voluit omnium peccantium debita fibi imputari, offerendo pleniffimam Deo fatisfactionem. Deus hanc fatisfactionem ad peccatorem in Chriftum credentem pertinere ex gratia iudicat, & huius intuitu eundem a culpa & pœna abfoluit. Dantur etiam plura exempla gratiofæ imputationis. Rex Pharao merita Iofephi ipfius patri & fratribus ad commodam in Ægypto habitationem, rex Dauid merita Ionathanis Mephibofetho ad fruendum menfa regali imputauit. Quin & hodie merita maritorum imputari vxoribus, vt hæ illorum radiis corufcent, & merita parentum imputari filiis ad honorem & dignitatem, plurimis experimentis difcimus.

Quæft. XIV. Potesne iam non imputationem feu remiffionem peccatorum, & imputationem iuftitiæ Chrifti perfpicue explicare?

Deus, iudex iuftiffimus, fed placabilis, hominis peccatoris a lege accufati, & peccatorum conuicti, fimul tamen in Chriftum credentis, cauffam fic cognofcit, vt eundem quidem culpæ, æternæque pœnæ reum, propriaque iuftitia deftitutum deprehendat, mediatoris Chrifti autem fatisfactionem & meritum ita ad eum pertinere iudicet, vt ipfum propter fatisfactoriam Chrifti paffionem, (*) vera fide apprehenfam, a culpa & pœna abfoluat, & propter impletionem, legi diuinæ a Chrifto vice generis humani præftitam, fingularique fiducia applicatam, eundem gratiofa æftimatione iuftum reputet atque pronunciet.

Dicis: Remiffio peccatorum & imputatio iuftitiæ funt termini æquipollentes apud Paullum, Rom. IV, 6. 7. Refp. Remiffio peccatorum & imputatio iuftitiæ Chrifti funt actus indiuulfi & intime coniuncti, formaliter tamen diftincti, cum ille priuatiuus, hic potitiuus fit: ille ex obedientia Chrifti paffiua, hic ex obedientia actiua immediate proficifcatur. Non diffitemur interim, vnum ex altero recte inferri; cum nullus detur peccator, cui remiffa fint peccata, & tamen non imputata fit iuftitia Chrifti & vice verfa.

Antithefis eft I. Pontificiorum, qui per infufum iuftitiæ habitum, II. Socinianorum, qui per obedientiam præceptis Chrifti præftitam, III. Arminianorum, qui per fidem, vt actum vel opus noftrum, IV. Weigelianorum, qui per imitationem Chrifti, V. Ofiandristarum, qui per iuftitiam Dei effentialem nos iuftificari docent. Quorum præcipua funt argumenta:

I. Quæcunque iuftitia eft aliena, illa non poteft effe noftra: Atqui iuftitia Chrifti eft aliena: E. Refp. 1) Quæ iuftitia eft aliena, non poteft effe noftra inhæfue; poteft tamen effe noftra nostra imputatiue. 2) Quod in humano iudicio vnius personae iustitia non aestimetur, aut censeatur alterius iustitia, inde prouenit, quod in vita communi vna persona alteri non fit vnita, sicut in Christum credentes hunc suum mediatorem non tantum intra conclaue cordis sui recipiunt, vt hospitem, Io. I, 22. sed etiam induunt, Gal. III, 28. & per fidem ei quasi agglutinantur, 1 Cor. VI, 17. vt in Christo inueniantur, haud secus ac palmites in vite, Phil. III, 9. add. Io. XV, 1. sqq. Inde fit, vt iustitiam Christi credentes sibi applicant, approprient, & suam faciant per fidem.

3) Si iniustitia Adami potuit imputari omnibus, qui ex ipso geniti sunt: quidni iustitia Christi imputari queat illis, qui spiritaliter ex ipso nati sunt?

II. Quicunque per intrinsecam iustitiam Christi denominantur iusti, illi non sunt vere, sed tantum putatiue iusti: Atqui peccatores poenitentes dicuntur iusti vere, & non putatiue: E. Resp. 1) Extrinseca denominatio non opponitur veritati rei. Paries dicitur visus per extrinsecam denominationem, & tamen vere visus est. Dicitur aliquis amicus meus ab amore meo, qui in me, & extra ipsum est. Debitor dicitur, ab aere alieno extrinsece liberatus, pro quo alius debitum dissoluit. Quae extrinseca denominatio non tollit veritatem rei. 2) Quamuis in ipso actu iustificationis peccatori resipiscenti extrinseca Christi iustitia imputetur; illa tamen, a peccatore credente intra animum accipitur, vt in homine iustificatio fit & maneat non per modum inhaesionis, sed appropriationis, & vnionis.

III. Quicunque non aeque iustus est, ac Christus, illius iustitia non potest esse iustitia Christi: Atqui peccator poenitens &c. E. Maior probatur; quia Christus est iustitia ipsa, Ier. XXIII, 6. Peccator vero poenitens & in Christum credens, licet propter meritum Christi iustificetur, conqueritur tamen cum Paulo, quod nihil boni in ipso habitet, Rom. VII, 18. Resp. Dist. inter iustitiam Christi essentialem, habitualem, & mediatariam. Ingens est discrimen inter iustitiam Christi & peccatoris iustificati; vt hic illi plane non sit conferendus. Nam Christus, qua Deus, est iustus essentialiter, qua homo, iustus est habitualiter, inde a primo conceptionis momento: quod de peccatore iustificato nequaquam afferi potest. Ceterum si Christus, mediator, secundum vtramque naturam, merito suo peperit iustitiam non sibi, sed homini peccatori, terminatiue deriuatur non in Christum sed in peccatorem, vera fide eum recipientem; atque haec est iustitia Christi mediatoria. Vnde a iustitia promerita iustus denominatur non Christus, sed homo peccator in Christum credens.

IV. Quicunque a iustitia Christi imputata dicuntur vere iusti. illi non tantum inter se sunt aequaliter iusti, sed etiam iustiores coelitibus: Sed non omnes Christiani inter se sunt aequaliter iusti, neque iustiores coelitibus: E. Maior claret; quia Christiani iusti denominantur ab vna iustitia Christi, quae in coelo cessabit; ideo, quod cognitio (fides) ibi abrogabitur. Resp. Ratione iustitiae Christi imputatae homo homine non est iustior; eo, quod iustitia, merito Christi parta, nullos admittit gradus; dicitur autem homo homine iustior ratione iustitiae inhaerentis. Deinde iustitia Christi imputata non quidem in coelo vlla peccata teget, quia nulla erunt; aeternum tamen durabit, tanquam eximius coelitum splendor & basis omnis sanctitatis, omnis rectitudinis gloriosae.

V. Si per imputationem iustitiae Christi nos vere iusti sumus, Christus per imputationem nostri peccati vere erit peccator: Consequens est falsum: E. & antecedens. Consequentia maioris probatur: quia nostra peccata sic imputata sunt Christo, vti nobis imputatur iustitia Christi, 2 Cor. V, 21. Consequens esse falsum, constat: quia peccator est filius diaboli. Resp. a) CHRYSOSTOMVS & alii graeci Patres vocant Christum peccatorem maximum, imputatiue talem; quia peccatorum totius mundi reus in iudicio diuino habitus est. Iehouah incurrere fecit in eum iniquitatem omnium nostrum, ait Es. LIII, 6. b) Manet nostrum, ait Es. c. LIII, 6. b) Manet tamen ingens discrimen nos inter, & Christum. Nam Christus non suam tantum nobis adscribit ac impertitur iustitiam, sed & iustitia inhærente nos donat; nos vero iniustitiæ nobis inhærentis contagio eundem non inficimus. Vnde peccatum nostrum ipsi non inhæret. c) Filius diaboli dicitur, qui deliberato animi consilio contra conscientiam peccata patrat, illisque indulget. Idcirco ne pii quidem, quibus peccatum inhæret, & qui ex infirmitate humana haud raro labuntur, filii diaboli dicendi sunt: multo minus Christus.

VI. Si per inhærentem Adami inobedientiam omnes homines constituuntur iniusti, vtique per inhærentem obedientiam Christi omnes homines fideles constituuntur iusti: Antecedens est verum: Ergo & consequens. Consequentia maioris patet: quia oppositorum eadem est ratio. Antecedens claret testimonio Paullino Rom. V, 19. Resp. Inobedientia Adami & obedientia Christi sunt actus proprii, personales ac indiuiduales, qui aliis non possunt esse communes, nisi iudicio diuino ipsis imputentur. Inde fit, vt licet inobedientia Adamo, & obedientia Christo inhæreat; tamen inobedientia Adami posteris, & obedientia Christi credentibus per æstimationem & declarationem diuinam accenseatur, vt illi rei mortis, hi iusti & hæredes vitæ æternæ reputentur.

Instantia: Sed inobedientia Adami etiam posteris inhæret; quia per generationem carnalem iisdem est insita: E. etiam obedientia Christi inhæret. Resp. Perperam dicitur, quod inobedientia Adami posteris inhæreat. Nam inobedientia Adami erat peccatum primum & originans, quod posteris non potuit tribui, nisi per imputationem; peccatum autem originale, siue originatum, est ex illo ortum, quod posteris Adami quidem inhæret, sed consequenter tantum ex Adami inobedientia fluit.

VII. Fides non est iustitia Christi (quia differunt vt medium, & forma iustificationis): Fides imputatur ad iustitiam, Rom. IV, 5. E. quoddam, quod imputatur ad iustitiam, non est iustitia Christi. Resp. In maiori fides sumitur absolute & abstractiue, quatenus est medium recipiens, in minori relate & concretiue, quatenus est medium recipiens meritum Christi, quod credenti per æstimationem diuinam ad iustitiam imputatur. Quæ diuersa consideratio fidei parit quaternarium terminorum.

VII. Satisfactio Christi aut imputatur, antequam eam habemus, aut cum habemus: Sed non ante, quam habemus; quia dudum est præstita, vt eam certissime habeamus: neque cum habemus; quia quod homo habet, ipsi non imputatur: E. nunquam imputatur. Resp. Dist. a) inter satisfactionem, & eius effectum; b) inter satisfactionem a Christo præstitam, & ab homine sibi applicatam. Satisfactio Christi dudum est præstita; sed eius effectum, qui est remissio peccatorum, non habemus prius, quam satisfactionem Christi vniversalem nobis applicamus, & nostram facimus per fidem. Etenim vt imputatio gratiosa recte fieri possit, in agente quidem adesse debet intentio, alteri sua actione aliquid boni conciliandi; in recipiente voluntas expressa, aut præsumta ab isto illud recipiendi. Nam operæ, quæ inuito obtruditur, imputatio recte repellitur, ait SAM. PVFEND. in L. de I. N. & G. p. 128.

IX. Quam iustitiam per Adamum amisimus, illa per Christum est reparata: Iustitiam inhærentem &c. E. Maior liquet: quia quidquid per Adamum est amissum, per Christum est restitutum, Rom. V, 15. Resp. Conclusio potest concedi in sensu conclusiuo; quia iustitia renatis inhærens merito Christi accepta ferenda est. Sin intelligatur sensu exclusiuo, quod per Christum tantum iustitia inhærens sit reparata, negamus maiorem. Ad eius probationem dicimus, quod Christus non id tantum restituerit, quod amissum est per Adamum, sed etiam alia bona, vel beneficia nobis acquifiuerit, v. gr. conuersionem pœnitentialem, fidem Christi innixam, iustitiam imputatam, confraternitatem cum Christo, quæ non fuerunt amissa. Contra, quædam bona, per Adamum amissa, Christus non restituit, scil. immortalitatem in hac vita, plenum dominium in animantia, inhabitationem paradisi, &c.

X. Quibus donatur iustitia Dei, eaque æterna, vt fiant consortes diuinæ naturæ, illis non iustitia Christi, sed essentialis Dei iustitia confertur: Atqui credentibus &c.

E. Maior constat: quia iustitia Dei æterna non est iustitia Christi, quippe quæ in plenitudine temporis parta, & per quam naturæ diuinæ participes non reddimur.

Resp. Iustitia Christi imputata est iustitia Dei, eo, quod gratiosa Dei æstimatione credentibus in Christum accensetur; est æterna, tum ratione decreti diuini, tum ratione valoris & efficaciæ; participes autem reddimur diuinæ naturæ per vnionem mysticam, quæ iustificationem sequitur.

Quæst. XV. An doctrina de iustitia Christi imputata non tantum vera, sed & ad pietatem vtilis est?

Doctrina euangelica de imputata Christi iustitia non tantum vera, & solida a), sed etiam ad exercendam veram, fucique expertem pietatem vtilissima est b).

Antithesis est ) Pontificiorum, quorum canon X. in Concil. Trident. Sess. V. ita se habet: Si quis dixerit, homines per Christi iustitiam formaliter iustos esse, anathema fit.

2) Socinianorum, iustitiam Christi nobis imputari negantium.

OSTORODVS in instant. german. c. XXXIV. fol. 304. scribit: Von der uns zugerechneten Gerechtigkeit Christi kann nicht das geringste Sprüchlein in der h. Schrift gezeiget werden.

3) Arminianorum, contendentium, fidem vt actum, vel opus nostrum, non Christi iustitiam, meritum, vel obedientiam nobis imputari ad iustitiam, in Apol. f. 112. 4) Weigelianorum, & Mysticorum, imputatam Christi iustitiam, quantum in ipsis, labefactantium.

Sic enim WEIGELIVS in part. III. postill. p. 15. inquit: Sie müssen den Tod, und die Auferstehung Christi in ihnen haben, und nicht von aussen imputiren.

Hoc non melior, sed multo peior, CHRIST. HOBVRG. in postilla mystica ait p. 190. So eure imputation alles ausrichten, und uns vor Gott rechtfertigen kann, was bedürfen wir der Vereinigung mit Christo?

5) His suffragantur Quackeri. ROBERTVS BARCLAIVS in Apol. ad thef. 7. n. 7. inquit: Imputatiua Christi iustitia in sacris litteris non inuenitur.


### Q. XI. Does God also use ministers in the justification of a sinner?: Ε Κ Θ Ε Σ Ι Σ. (Exposition.)

Ε Κ Θ Ε Σ Ι Σ. (Exposition.)

The Dissenters , who traduce the most true doctrine of the Protestants concerning the imputed righteousness of Christ, labor under either most foul ignorance or clearly detestable malice; since they judge of it no differently than the blind do of colors, and attribute to Protestants those things which never even in a dream entered their minds. Wherefore, this dogma, most firmly founded in the Holy Scriptures, must first be elucidated, then solidly proven, and finally applied to the practice of piety.

Observe , however, benevolent reader, I. that for the present the sophistries of the Weigelians, Mystics, and Quakers are primarily to be discussed: we examined the objections of the Papists and Socinians in the preceding question 14 of this chapter VIII. Obs.

II. Protestants, with the Holy Scripture shining before them, take the word "to justify" in a forensic or judicial sense, so that it signifies to absolve a penitent sinner from the guilt of sin and punishment for certain reasons, and to esteem, repute, declare, and pronounce him righteous.

This judicial meaning of the word "to justify" we proved above, question 2 of this chapter VIII.

Obs. III. For how the word "to impute" is taken here, see the preceding question.

XIII. Obs.

XIII. Obs. I.

Obs. IV. In every imputation, three things must be strictly considered: a) An action, or voluntary passion. For involuntary actions, or those which proceed from physical necessity, or which exceed our powers, are imputed to no one. b) The estimation and judgment concerning the voluntary action. The lord, or judge, who possesses the power of judging, estimates the goodness or malice of the action. c) The effect of the action, which is adjudged to someone. The voluntary action acts by way of matter, and is the foundation of the imputation, in view of which the judge renders judgment: the effect acts by way of form, and redounds either to the acting person himself, or to another, in whose stead or for whose benefit that action was undertaken. Obs.

V. Imputation is made either by debt or by grace, a distinction which Paul uses, Rom. IV, 4: To him who works, the wages are not imputed by grace, but by debt. Both can be described, either with respect to the foundation or with respect to the effect. Our CHEMNITIUS looked primarily to the foundation in loc. theol. part. II. p. 294. There is a certain imputation which has and looks to a foundation in the agent to whom the imputation is made, and this is not done according to grace, but according to debt. But there is another imputation which does not have, nor look to, a foundation in the one to whom it is made, by reason and respect of which it is imputed, but the foundation is in the grace and mercy of God justifying the ungodly.

Obs. VI. If, however, imputation by grace and debt is to be described with respect to the effect which redounds from a voluntary action, it can be defined in the following manner: Imputation by debt is when the effect of a voluntary action is attributed to the acting person, as a moral cause, by the estimation and decree of a judge. Imputation by grace is when the effect is reckoned not to the agent, but to that person for whose benefit the voluntary action is directed, by the gracious estimation of the judge. In which manner VASQUEZ , the most learned of the Jesuits, cited by D.

CALOVIUS in bibl. illustrat. in c. IV. Rom. f. 73, judged not badly concerning the nature of imputation: We concede that even extrinsic things, such as the merit and obedience of Christ, are imputed to us for some effect; because not only those things which are in us, but also the things of others, in view of which something is given to us, are said to be reckoned as ours for some effect, as if they were truly our own.

Obs. VII. In order that gracious imputation (of which we are presently treating) may be rightly performed, there must be present in the agent the intention of procuring some good for another by his action: and in the recipient, an expressed or presumed will to receive that from him: for the imputation of a service that is forced upon an unwilling person is rightly rejected, as PUFENDORF judges, de I. N. et G. c. IX. p. 128.

Obs. VIII. The lord, or judge, who imputes in a gracious imputation, for the most part kindly regards and estimates the union, whether natural or moral, which intervenes between the acting person and that person for whose benefit the voluntary action was undertaken. A natural union exists between father and children; a moral one between husband and wife, between friends, acquaintances, and colleagues. Communion, or communication, follows union. Wherefore the judge in a gracious imputation, in view of a natural or moral union, gives and communicates the effect of the voluntary action, which the acting person performs, to another person who is joined to the acting person by some bond of union.

Obs. IX. Imputation is either privative or positive. The former is when a debt, on account of satisfaction provided by the acting person, is not imputed to another non-acting person, in view of that impotence and indigence, or is remitted. The latter is when a reward, on account of a voluntary action which the agent performed for the benefit of another, is given and communicated in view of a natural or moral union.

Obs. X. Although imputation, considered generally, is an act of the intellect and will of him who exercises judgment, by which the voluntary action of some person is known, estimated, and judged— is judged to pertain with effect, redundant from it, either to the acting person himself, or to another, in whose stead, or for whose benefit that action was undertaken; yet that imputation is not fictitious or fabricated, but true and real: 1. on account of a true and real foundation, which is a voluntary action; 2. in respect of a true and real intention, which intervenes between the acting person and the one who receives the reward; 3. by reason of a true and real effect, which follows the voluntary action.

Obl. XI. This moral doctrine, which is most excellent and useful, though it seems difficult to understand for the unskilled, must be illustrated by examples. In the sacred code there exist examples of gracious imputation. Pharaoh, King of Egypt, imputed the good deeds of Joseph both to his father and to his brothers, as well as a comfortable habitation in Egypt. King David imputed the merits of Jonathan to Mephibosheth, for the enjoyment of the royal table, regarding the bond of natural union that existed between son and father. Philemon imputed the satisfaction offered by Paul to Onesimus, for immunity from debt. Furthermore, in military and civil life, it is not rare for the noble deeds performed by a parent to be graciously imputed by a prince to his children, so that, the former being ennobled, these also are considered noble: the merits of husbands are imputed to wives, so that these may shine with their rays. It often happens that a colleague labors for another who is sick, and the reward is imputed and conferred by the master, the employer, not to the one who did not labor, but to the one who is sick.

Obl. XII. Having generally unfolded moral imputation, we now prepare ourselves to consider, and piously weigh, the much more gracious divine imputation: where we note a) The Judge, who is the triune God. This judge is most just, a most bitter hater and avenger of all sin, of whom the royal Psalter, Ps. 5:5, 6, 7. "You are not a God who approves wickedness: the evil man shall not dwell with you. The boastful shall not stand before your eyes: you hate all workers of iniquity. You shall destroy those who speak lies; the man of blood and deceit Jehovah will abhor." Whose

Whose b) Judgment according to the norm of the law is most rigid, of which Ps. 143:2. "Do not enter into judgment with your servant: for no one living will be righteous before you."

c) The defendant is every sinful man. For the whole world becomes guilty before God, Rom. 3:19.

d) The actor, or accuser, is partly Moses the lawgiver, John 5:45, partly the devil, Rev. 12:10.

e) The witness is the conscience, Rom. 2:15, Col. 2:14.

f) The condemnatory sentence is held in the law of Moses. "Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things which are written in the book of the law," Deut. 27:26.

g) But there intervenes a mediator, advocate, and sponsor, Christ, who gave himself for all εἰς ἀντίλυτρον, as a price of redemption, 1 Tim. 2:6. He reconciled sinners by his death, Rom. 5:10, and fulfilled the law in their stead, Gal. 4:5, Matt. 5:17, Rom. 10:4.

h) On account of this satisfaction, sin is not imputed to those who believe in Christ, 2 Cor. 5:18, and on account of his vicarious fulfillment of the law, righteousness is imputed to all who truly believe in him, Rom. 4:5.

Because God regards the union of believers with Christ the satisfier and mediator, who labored for sinners by acting and suffering, Is. 43:24, 25, therefore that union is made through faith, which not only apprehends Christ, John 1:12, but also puts him on, Gal. 3:24, adheres to him, 1 Cor. 6:17, and is found in him, as a branch in the vine, Phil. 3:9, John 15:5.

Here one must accurately distinguish between the formal or relative union of faith and the mystical or sanctifying union. The latter follows justification in the order of nature: for sins, unless they are remitted, impede the gracious union by which God dwells and works in the soul, Is. 59:2. But the formal and relative union of faith (which is also apprehensive, appropriative and adhesive, one may call it) precedes justification in the order of nature. This is what the most accurate theologians confirm from the Holy Scriptures. D. BROCHMAND, tom. II. system. p. 485, says: But if regeneration is taken for that spiritual birth from God, which consists primarily in our union, because we are from God, or, because we are in Christ, according to that of Paul, Rom. VIII, 1: There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. D. QUENSTED supports this, part. III. system. fol. 523, intending to explain the apostolic utterance, Phil. III, 9: That I may be found in Christ, not having my own righteousness, etc., he says: The sense of the words is: When God shall inquire into the righteousness of each one, and shall demand it according to the most exact and most severe norm of His judgment, that I may then be found engrafted into Christ, as a branch in the vine, and a bough in the olive tree, or, as it is in Gal. III, 17. clothed in Christ, joined by an intimate and most close union with Christ; for thus it will happen through this conjunction, that what is Christ's may also be mine. The same is asserted by D. WILHELMUS LYSERUS in system. p. 1548. Imputation is founded upon the spiritual union of faith, by which we are made the flesh of the mediator Christ himself, and we find his operation, through the mirror of faith, communicating all his deeds and merits to us, so that we may be found in Christ, Phil. III, 9, and thus, as his members, we may be rendered participants of all the labors performed for our sake. Conf. D. NEVMANN, disputat. de nexu & ordine donorum gratiæ §. XV.

Latin:

Ε Κ Θ Ε Σ Ι Σ.

Dissidentes doctrinam verissimam Protestantium de imputata Christi iustitia traducentes, aut fœdissima ignorantia, aut malitia plane detestabili laborant; cum de ea iudicent haud secus, ac cœci de coloribus, ac Protestantibus ea affingant, quæ ne per somnium quidem ipsis in mentem venerunt. Quare hoc in sacris litteris fundatissimum dogma primum enucleandum, deinde solide probandum, & ad vsum denique pietatis transferendum est.

Obferues autem, lector beneuole, I. impræsentiarum strophas Weigelianorum, Mysticorum & Quackerorum potissimum discutiendas esse: obiectiones Pontificiorum & Socinianorum examinauimus præcedenti quæst. 14. cap. huius VIII. Obf.

II. Protestantes, prælucente S. scriptura, verbum, iustificare, sumunt in sensu forensi, aut iudiciali, vt significet, peccatorem pœnitentem a reatu culpæ & pœnæ certis de caussis absoluere, & iustum æstimare, reputare, declarare, pronuntiare.

Hunc significatum verbi iustificare iudicialem probauimus supra, quæst. 2. cap. huius VIII.

Obf. III. Verbum, imputare, quomodo hic sumatur, vide præcedentem quæst.

XIII. Obf.

XIII. Obf. I.

Obs. IV. In omni imputatione tria oppido consideranda sunt: a) Actio, vel passio voluntaria. Nam actiones invitae, aut quae proveniunt ex necessitate physica, aut quae vires nostras excedunt, nemini imputantur. b) Aestimatio et iudicium de actione voluntaria. Aestimat autem actionis bonitatem aut malitiam dominus, vel iudex, qui iudicandi potestate pollet. c) Effectus actionis, qui alicui adiudicatur. Actio voluntaria habet se per modum materiae, et est fundamentum imputationis, cuius intuitu iudex fert iudicium: effectus habet se per modum formae, et redundat vel ad ipsam personam agentem, vel ad aliam, cuius vice vel in cuius commodum illa actio suscepta est. Obs.

V. Imputatio alia fit ex debito, alia ex gratia, qua distinctione utitur Paullus, Rom. IV, 4. Ei qui operatur, merces, non imputatur ex gratia, sed ex debito. Vtraque describi potest, vel respectu fundamenti, vel respectu effectus. Fundamentum respexit potissimum noster CHEMNITIVS in loc. theol. part. II. p. 294. Est quaedam imputatio, quae habet et respicit fundamentum in operante, cui fit imputatio, et haec non fit secundum gratiam, sed secundum debitum. Est vero alia imputatio, quae in eo, cui fit, non habet, nec respicit fundamentum, cuius ratione et respectu imputetur, sed fundamentum est in gratia, et misericordia Dei iustificantis impium.

Obs. VI. Si autem imputatio ex gratia et debito, respectu effectus, qui ex actione voluntaria redundat, describenda sit, sequenti ratione definiri poterit: Imputatio ex debito est, cum effectus actionis voluntariae personae agenti, ut causae morali, aestimatione et decreto iudicis attribuitur. Imputatio ex gratia est, quando effectus non agenti, sed illi personae, in cuius commodum actio voluntaria dirigitur, gratiosa aestimatione iudicis accensetur.

Qua ratione de imputationis indole haud male iudicavit VASQVEZIVS , Iesuitarum doctissimus, allegatus a D. CALOVIO in bibl. illustrat. in c. IV. Rom. f. 73. Imputari nobis ad aliquem effectum, etiam aliqua extrinseca, ut meritum et obedientiam Christi, concedimus; quia non modo ea, quae nobis insunt, sed etiam aliena, quorum intuitu nobis aliquid donatur, computari dicuntur nostra ad aliquem effectum, ac si reuera nostra essent. Obs.

VII. Vt imputatio gratiosa (de qua in praesenti agimus) recte fieri possit, in agente quidem adesse debet intentio, alteri sua actione aliquid boni conciliandi: in recipiente voluntas expressa, aut praesumta, ab isto illud recipiendi: nam operae, quae invito obtruditur, imputatio recte repellitur, censente PVEENDORFIO , de I. N. et G. c. IX. p. 128. Obs.

VIII. Dominus, vel iudex, imputans in gratiosa imputatione, plerumque benigne respicit et aestimat vnionem vel naturalem, vel moralem, quae inter personam agentem et eam personam, in cuius commodum actio voluntaria suscepta est, intercedit. Datur vnio naturalis inter patrem et liberos; moralis inter maritum et vxorem, inter amicos, familiares et collegas. Vnionem communio, vel communicatio consequitur. Quamobrem iudex in gratiosa imputatione, intuitu vnionis naturalis, vel moralis, effectum actionis voluntariae, quam persona agens expedit, alteri personae, quae vnionis quodam vinculo cum persona agente coniuncta est, donat et communicat. Obs.

IX. Imputatio est vel priuatiua, vel positiua. Illa est, cum debitum, propter satisfactionem, a persona agente praestitam, alteri non agenti, intuitu illius impotentiae et indigentiae non imputatur, sive remittitur. Haec est, cum praemium propter actionem voluntariam, quam agens in alterius commodum fecit, intuitu vnionis naturalis, vel moralis donatur et communicatur. Cbf.

X. Quamuis imputatio generatim considerata sit actus intellectus et voluntatis illius, qui iudicium exercet, quo voluntaria alicuius personae actio cognoscitur, aestimatur, et iudicatur pertinere cum effectu, ex ea redundante, vel ad ipsam personam agentem, vel ad aliam, cuius vice, aut in cuius commodum illa actio suscepta est, tamen illa imputatio non ficta, aut commentitia, sed vera & realis est; 1. ob verum & reale fundamentum, quod est actio voluntaria; 2. respectu verae & realis intentionis, quae inter agentem personam, & eam, quae praemium recipit, intercedit; 3. ratione veri & realis effectus, qui actionem voluntariam consequitur.

Obl. XI. Exemplis haec doctrina moralis longe praestantissima & utilissima, cum imperitis difficilis cognitu videatur, illustranda est. In codice sacro exstant exempla gratiosae imputationis. Rex Aegypti Pharao benefacta Iosephi tam patri, quam fratribus eius, & commodam in Aegypto habitationem imputavit. Rex Dauid merita Ionathanis imputavit Mephibosetho, ad fruendum mensa regali, respiciendo vinculum unionis naturalis, quod erat inter filium & patrem. Philemon oblatam a Paulo satisfactionem imputabat Onesimo, ad immunitatem a debito. Ceterum in vita militari & civili haud raro a principe facta praeclara parentis gratiose imputantur liberis, vt, illo nobilitato, & hi censeantur nobiles: merita maritorum imputantur uxoribus, vt hae illorum radiis coruscent. Saepe usu venit, vt collega laboret pro altero aegrotante, & praemium a domino collatore non laboranti, sed aegrotanti imputetur ac conferatur.

Obl. XII. Generatim euoluta imputatione morali, iam nos accingimus ad considerandam, pieque expendendam imputationem diuinam multo gratiosissimam: vbi notamus a) Iudicem, qui est Deus triunus. Hic iudex est iustissimus, omni peccato osor & vltor acerrimus, de quo regius Psalter, Ps. V, 5, 6, 7. Non Deus approbans impietatem tu es: non manebit apud te malus. Non consistent glorabundi coram oculis tuis: odisti omnes operatores iniquitatis. Perdes loquentes mendacium; virum sanguinum & doli abominabitur Iehouah. Cuius

b) Iudicium secundum normam legis est rigidissimum, de quo Ps. CXLIII, 2. Ne intra in iudicium cum seruo tuo: quia non iustus erit coram te ullus viuens.

c) Reus est omnis homo peccator. Totus namque mundus reus fit Deo, Rom. III, 19.

d) Actor, siue accusator, est partim Moses legislator, Ioann. V, 45. partim diabolus, Apoc. XII, 10.

e) Testis est conscientia, Rom. II, 15. Col. II, 14.

f) Sententia condemnatoria habetur in lege Mosis. Maledictus est omnis, qui non permanet in omnibus, quae scripta sunt in libro legis, Deuter. XXVII, 26.

g) At interuenit mediator, aduocatus & sponsor Christus, qui se pro omnibus dedit εἰς ἀντίλυτρον, in pretium redemptionis, 2 Tim. II, 6. Hic morte sua peccatores reconciliauit, Rom. V, 10. & eorum vice legem impleuit, Gal. IV, 5. Matth. V, 17. Rom. X, 4.

h) Propter huius satisfactionem peccatum credentibus in Christum non imputatur, 2 Cor. V, 18. & propter ipsius impletionem legis vicariam iustitia imputatur omnibus, in ipsum vere credentibus, Rom. IV, 5.

Quia Deus respicit unionem credentium cum Christo satisfactore & mediatore, qui pro peccatoribus laborauit agendo & patiendo, Es. XLIII, 24, 25. idcirco fit illa vnio per fidem, quae Christum non tantum apprehendit, Io. I, 12. fed etiam induit, Gal. III, 24. ipsi adhaeret, 1 Cor. VI, 17. & in ipso inuenitur, vt palmes in vite, Phil. III, 9. Io. XV, 5.

Accurate hic distinguendum est inter unionem fidei formalem, siue relatiuam; & unionem mysticam, siue sanctificantem. Haec ordine naturae iustificationem sequitur: peccata namque, nisi remittantur, vnionem gratiosam, qua Deus in anima habitat & operatur, impediunt, Es. LIX, 2. Vnio autem fidei formalis & relatiua (quam etiam apprehensiuam, appropriatiuam & adhæsiuam appellare licet) iustificationem ordine naturæ præcedit. Id quod accuratissimi Theologi e sacris litteris confirmant. D. BROCHMAND. tom. II. system. p. 485. inquit: Quod si sumatur regeneratio pro spirituali illa e Deo natiuitate, quæ potissimum constit in vnione nostri, quia ex Deo sumus, siue, quia in Christo sumus, iuxta illud Paulli, Rom. VIII, 1. Nihil condemnationis est in his, qui sunt in Christo Iesu. Suffragatur D. QVENSTED. part. III. system. fol. 523. enucleaturus eloquium apostolicum, Phil. III, 9. Vt inueniar in Christo, non habens meam iustitiam &c. ait: Sensus verborum est: Quando Deus in vnius cuiusque iustitiam inquiret, & ad exactissimam, seuerissimamque iudicii sui normam exiget, vt tunc inueniar Christo insitus, tanquam palmes in vite, & ramus in olea, siue, vt est Gal. III, 17. Christo indutus, intima & arctissima vnione cum Christo coniunctus; ita enim per hanc coniunctionem fiet, vt, quod Christi est, meum quoque sit. Idem asserit D. WILHELMVS LYSERVS in system. p. 1548. Imputatio fundatur in vnione spirituali fidei, qua ipsius mediatoris Christi caro efficimur, & nos reperimus eiusdem operationem, per fidei speculum, omnia sua facta & merita nobis communicantis, vt in Christo inueniamur, Phil. III, 9. & ita, tanquam membra eius, omnium nostri caussa peractorum laborum participes reddamur. Conf. D. NEVMANN. disputat. de nexu & ordine donorum gratiæ §. XV.


### Q. XI. Does God also use ministers in the justification of a sinner?: Ε Κ Θ Ε Σ Ι Σ. (Exposition.) (continued)

Obs. XII. Gracious imputation is distinguished into privative and positive. Privative imputation is that by which, on account of the spontaneous and satisfactory passion of Christ, which he underwent for us, sins are not imputed to believers for punishment. Positive is that by which, on account of the voluntary obedience of Christ, by which he willingly subjected himself to the law in place of the human race, and fulfilled it, the righteousness of Christ is imputed, so that they may be constituted righteous before the divine tribunal.

Both are real 1) by reason of the foundation, which is the real passion of Christ and the vicarious fulfillment of the law; 2) by reason of the serious and real intention of Christ to procure many goods for sinners; 3) by reason of the true and real union with Christ, which is effected through faith; 4) by reason of the effect, which is the true and real remission of sins, the true and real righteousness of Christ imputed.

Yet neither is simple, by which the subject is considered in itself, and thus an estimation is instituted; but permutatory, by which the subject is considered in the vicarious sponsor and satisfier. Indeed, the sins and punishments of men were imputed to the sponsor Christ. He himself paid the penalties in his passion, so that sins might not be imputed to believers for punishment: he transferred the sins onto himself, so that on account of the most consummate obedience rendered to the divine law, the righteousness of Christ might be imputed to believers. Both imputations are to be confirmed in the present, and subsequently this doctrine is to be applied to the exercises of piety.

Β Ε Β Α Ι Ω Σ Ι Σ.

Privative imputation is proved 1) from 2 Cor. V, 19: God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, while he did not impute their sins to them. The Apostle implies that the non-imputation of sins flows from the satisfaction of Christ, concerning which his words are to be understood. v. 14, 15: If one died for all, then all died, i.e., the vicarious death of Christ, performed in the place of all men, is estimated in the judgment of God no otherwise than if all had died, i.e., had paid the penalties of sins by a most bitter death.

2) From Rom. IV, 7: Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute sin! Confer. Ps. XXXII, 12. From these two classic sayings we argue: Whoever are therefore considered blessed because they have been reconciled to God through the death of Christ, they are reputed righteous before the divine tribunal, and therefore are considered blessed: But those to whom sins have been forgiven, they are therefore, etc.: Therefore.

…3) From Eph. I, 7: In Christ we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins. Whoever have the forgiveness of sins through the blood of Christ the redeemer, they are justified before the divine judgment on account of the bloody passion of Christ: But believers in Christ &c: Therefore.

Positive imputation is also proved from Rom. IV, 6. Just as David also speaks of the μακαρισμὸν, the beatification of the man to whom God imputes righteousness without works. From this apostolic utterance we conclude: That righteousness which is imputed by God without works is not inherent in us, but is the righteousness of Christ imputed to us: But the righteousness which makes us blessed in the kingdom of grace is the righteousness which is imputed to us without works: Therefore.

You say: In the major proposition there is more contained than in the apostolic utterance. For the Apostle indeed affirms that we are blessed through righteousness imputed without works, but he does not add that we are blessed through the imputed righteousness of Christ.

Resp. 1) The imputed righteousness opposed to the righteousness of works is the righteousness of faith in Christ, as Paul teaches, Phil. III, 9, seeing that he was made righteousness for us by God, 1 Cor. I, 30.

2) Which righteousness Paul wishes to be understood, he himself explains in Rom. V, 18. As through the sin of one (Adam) it resulted in condemnation for all men: So through the righteousness of one (Christ) it results in justification of life for all men.

2) From Rom. IV, 5. To him who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, faith is imputed for righteousness.

Obs. Faith is imputed for righteousness not absolutely, insofar as it is from the census of virtues or works; for it is expressly opposed to works in this place and elsewhere: but relatively, on account of Christ, whom it receives and contains; just as a hand enriches a beggar not by itself, but on account of the treasure which it accepts.

We conclude: To whom, not working but believing in Christ, faith is imputed for righteousness, he is judged righteous before the divine tribunal not on account of his own righteousness, but on account of the righteousness of Christ apprehended by true faith: But to the ungodly man not working, but believing in Christ &c. Therefore.

3) From Gal. III, 6. Abraham believed God, and it was imputed to him for righteousness. Paul adds, v. 13. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us. Therefore, the faith of Abraham looked to the redeemer Christ, who was made a curse for us, so that to us, redeemed from the curse, the righteousness of Christ might be divinely imputed. We argue: In the same manner that Abraham, the father of all believers, was justified, in the same manner all believers are justified: But Abraham was justified; because the righteousness of Christ was imputed to him: Therefore all believers are justified for the reason that the righteousness of Christ is imputed to them.

4) From 2 Cor. V, 21. Him who knew no sin, he made sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in him. By the same reason that Christ was made sin for us, by the same reason we are rendered the righteousness of God on account of Christ (i.e., perfectly righteous before God): But Christ was made sin for us not inherently, as if any sin had inhered in him; but imputatively, because by divine judgment our sin was imputed to him: Therefore also we, on account of Christ, are rendered the righteousness of God not inherently, as if a perfect righteousness of works inhered in us; but imputatively, because the most perfect righteousness of Christ is imputed and reckoned to us.

5) From Phil. III, 9. That I may be found in Christ, not having my own righteousness, which (is) from the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ; the righteousness which is given from God, by faith. Whoever appears before the most rigid divine judgment relying not on his own righteousness, but on an alien one, which is through the faith of Christ, to whom also the branch is engrafted into the vine, him God most graciously esteems righteous with the righteousness of Christ apprehended by true faith. But Paul, and every converted and regenerated sinner &c. Therefore.

6) From Rom. V, 19. As through the disobedience of one man (Adam) many were constituted sinners: so also through the obedience of one (Christ) many will be constituted righteous. I subjoin: But through the disobedience of Adam imputed to all men, connected by the bond of blood with Adam, connected by the bond of blood with

in Adam, are constituted sinners. Therefore, also through the obedience of Christ imputed, all the reborn, joined to Him by the bond of faith, are constituted righteous.

You say: The disobedience of Adam is not only imputed to his descendants, but also inheres in them. I answer: The disobedience of Adam is his own proper, personal, and individual act, which cannot be common to his descendants except by imputation. For it is the transgression of the paradisiacal law, and thus the first and originating sin, which is imputed to his descendants; but original sin, or originated sin, is the sin arisen from the first, which indeed inheres in the descendants of Adam, but flows consequently only from the disobedience of Adam.

7) Τὸ τέλος νόμου, the end, or fulfillment of the law is Christ for righteousness to everyone who believes, Rom. 10, 4. If Christ fulfilled the law for righteousness to everyone who believes, that vicarious fulfillment of the law is imputed to the reborn man for righteousness. The antecedent, as Paul testifies, is true. Therefore, the consequent also.

8) Two enormous absurdities press upon the hypothesis of the adversaries. For 1) they dare to appear before the rigid judgment of God relying on their own righteousness, which in the Old Testament David, most adorned with virtues, did not dare, see Ps. 143, 2., nor under the new covenant did Paul, see 1 Cor. 4, 4. Phil. 3, 9., since the righteousness inherent in us is imperfect and impure, and cannot sustain the examination of divine judgment. 2) They likewise deny the satisfactory passion and death of Christ, and also the fulfillment of the law, performed by Christ in place of the whole human race, the effect of which cannot redound to the human race except through the most gracious imputation of God. But in denying this, they go about undermining the very foundation of faith, as much as lies in them.

Prob. b. That the evangelical doctrine concerning the divine imputation of the active and passive obedience of Christ for righteousness and the remission of sins is most useful for promoting piety is easy to demonstrate. For 1) by privative imputation, on account of the satisfactory passion of Christ, sin is not imputed for condemnation, 2 Cor. 5, 19. But the Apostle Paul joins immunity from condemnation and the holiness of life, Rom. 8, 1. There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who walk not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit. And the Apostle Peter teaches 1 Pet. 2, 24. that the end of the satisfactory passion of Christ is twofold: the remission of sins and the holiness of life: Christ Himself bore our sins in His body upon the tree, that, being dead to sins, we might live to righteousness, by whose wounds you have been healed. Reborn men, to whom sins are not imputed for condemnation, do not indulge the lusts of the flesh, but having obtained the Holy Spirit, they obey His motions, lest they fall from the blessedness of grace and glory. To this point tend the words of the royal Prophet, Ps. 130, 4. For with You is forgiveness, that You may be feared.

The fruits of imputed righteousness are generally good works, Phil. 1, 11.; specifically, however:

a) Ardent love of God, and of Christ the mediator. For faith, by whose regard the obedience of Christ is imputed for righteousness, works through love, Gal. 5, 6. Indeed, the reborn and justified man is kindled with the love of God, pondering within himself the ineffable mercy of God, which imputes faith for righteousness even to an impious man, provided he is penitent and believes in Christ. He burns with love for Christ, whoever piously considers that he is adorned as if with the garment of Christ's righteousness, or is surrounded as if by most splendid light, Isa. 61, 10. Rev. 12, 1.

b) Love toward one's neighbor, which justifying faith produces. Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God: and everyone who loves Him who begat him, loves also him who is born of Him, says John in Christ, who was made unto us righteousness, 1 Cor. I, 30., but testifies to faith with sincere love, both toward God and toward one's neighbor. c) Obedience rendered to divine precepts.

Let Abraham be an example to us, who declared his faith by works and especially by most prompt obedience, having complied with the divine command concerning offering his son as a burnt offering, Gen. XXII, 1. Iac. II, 21. d) True submission of the soul, and spiritual self-denial.

For whoever, after the likeness of Paul, is found in Christ, not having his own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, he truly does not swell up in the manner of the Pharisees, but conducts himself submissively; he is not puffed up, but refers whatever he has of divine blessing to his Savior. e) Spiritual joy, which the Israelite church, about to express it, sings: I will greatly rejoice in Jehovah: my soul shall exult in my God: for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, he has covered me with the robe of righteousness, Is. LXI, 10. f) Thanksgiving, to which we are stirred as much by the non-imputation of sins as by the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, as Paul warns, Col. I, 12. sqq. Give thanks to the Father, who has made us fit for the portion of the inheritance of the saints in light; who has delivered us from the power of darkness, and has translated us into the kingdom of the Son of his love; in whom we have redemption through his blood, the remission of sins.

Wherefore we do not side with the enemies of the truth, who deny that the imputed righteousness of Christ contributes anything of importance to the pursuit of sincere piety, but with Paul, who gravely says: Being made free from sin, and become servants to God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, Rom. VI, 22.

Latin:

Obs. XII. Imputatio gratiosa distinguitur in priuatiuam, & positiuam. Imputatio priuatiua est, qua propter spontaneam & satisfactoriam Christi passionem, quam is pro nobis subiuit, credentibus peccata ad pœnam non imputantur. Positiua est, qua propter obedientiam Christi voluntariam, qua vice generis humani vltro legi se subiecit, eamque impleuit, iustitia Christi imputatur, vt ea coram tribunali diuino iusti constituantur.

Vtraque est realis 1) ratione fundamenti, quod est realis Christi passio & impletio legis vicaria; 2) ratione seriæ & realis Christi intentionis, plurima bona peccatoribus conciliandi; 3) ratione veræ & realis vnionis cum Christo, quæ fit per fidem; 4) ratione effectus, qui est vera & realis remissio peccatorum, vera & realis iustitia Christi imputata.

Vtraque tamen non est simplex, qua subiectum in se consideratur, & ita æstimatio instituitur; sed permutatoria, qua subiectum consideratur in vicario sponsore & satisfactore. Nimirum sponsori Christo imputata sunt hominum peccata & pœnæ. Pœnas ipse luit in passione, vt ne peccata credentibus in pœnam imputarentur: peccata in se transtulit, vt propter consummatissimam obedientiam legi diuinæ præstitam, iustitia Christi credentibus imputaretur. Vtraque imputatio in præsenti confirmanda, & deinceps ad exercitia pietatis hæc doctrina applicanda est.

Β Ε Β Α Ι Ω Σ Ι Σ.

Probatur imputatio priuatiua 1) ex 2 Cor. V, 19. Deus erat in Christo, mundum reconcilians sibi, dum non imputabat peccata illorum. Apostolus innuit, non imputationem peccatorum fluere ex satisfactione Christi, de qua intelligenda sunt ipsius verba. v. 14. 15. Si vnus pro omnibus mortuus est, omnes mortui sunt, q. d. Mors Christi vicaria, loco omnium hominum præstita, in iudicio Dei non aliter æstimatur, quam si omnes mortui essent, i. e. pœnas peccatorum morte acerbissima luissent.

2) E Rom. IV, 7. Beati, quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates, & quorum occultata sunt peccata. Beatus vir, cui non imputat Deus peccatum! Confer. Ps. XXXII, 12. Ex his duobus dictis classicis argumentamur: Quicunque ideo beati censentur, quod per mortem Christi Deo reconciliati sunt, illi coram tribunali diuino iusti reputantur, & ideo beati censentur: Atqui quibus remissa sunt peccata, illi ideo &c: Ergo.

3) Ex Eph. I, 7. In Christo habemus redemtionem per sanguinem ipsius, remissionem peccatorum. Quicunque per sanguinem Christi redemtoris remissionem peccatorum habent, illi propter cruentam passionem Christi coram iudicio diuino iustificantur: Atqui credentes in Christum &c: Ergo.

Probatur etiam imputatio positiua ex Rom. IV, 6. Quemadmodum etiam Dauid dicit, μακαρισμὸν, beatificationem esse hominis, cui Deus imputat iustitiam sine operibus. Ex quo effato apostolico colligimus: Quæ iustitia sine operibus a Deo imputatur, illa non est nobis inhærens, sed iustitia Christi nobis imputata: Atqui iustitia, quæ in regno gratiæ nos beatos reddit, est iustitia, quæ sine operibus nobis imputatur: Ergo.

Dicis: In maiori propositione plus habetur, quam in effato apostolico. Nam affirmat quidem Apostolus, quod beati sumus, per iustitiam, sine operibus imputatam, sed non addit, quod beati sumus per imputatam iustitiam Christi.

Resp. 1) iustitia imputata opposita iustitiæ operum est iustitia fidei in Christum, docente Paulo, Phil. III, 9. quippe qui a Deo factus est nobis iustitia, 1 Cor. I, 30.

2) Quam iustitiam Paullus intellectam velit, ipsemet exponit Rom. V, 18. Sicut per vnius (Adami) peccatum in omnes homines in condemnationem (res cessit): Ita per vnius (Christi) iustitiam in omnes homines in iustificationem vitæ.

2) Ex Rom. IV, 5. Ei, qui non operatur, credit vero in eum, qui iustificat impium, fides imputatur in iustitiam.

Obs. Fides imputatur ad iustitiam non absolute, quatenus est e censu virtutum, aut operum; operibus enim diserte hoc loco, & alibi opponitur: sed relate, propter Christum, quem recipit & continet; sicut manus mendicum ditat non per se, sed propter thesaurum, quem acceptat.

Colligimus: Cui non operanti, sed credenti in Christum fides ad iustitiam imputatur, ille coram tribunali diuino iustus censetur non ob iustitiam propriam, sed propter iustitiam Christi vera fide apprehensam: Atqui homini impio non operanti, credenti vero in Christum &c. Ergo.

3) Ex Gal. III, 6. Abraham credidit Deo, & imputatum ipsi est in iustitiam. Addit Paullus, v. 13. Christus nos redemit a maledictione legis, factus pro nobis maledictio. Respexit ergo fides Abrahami redemptorem Christum, qui est factus pro nobis maledictio, vt nobis, a maledictione redemtis, iustitia Christi diuinitus imputaretur. Arguimus: Quo pacto Abrahamus, pater omnium credentium, iustificatus est, eodem pacto omnes credentes iustificantur: Atqui Abrahamus iustificatus est; quia iustitia Christi ei est imputata: E. omnes credentes ideo iustificantur, quod iustitia Christi ipsis imputatur.

4) Ex 2 Cor. V, 21. Eum, qui non nouerat peccatum, pro nobis peccatum fecit, vt nos fiamus iustitia Dei in ipso. Qua ratione Christus factus est pro nobis peccatum, eadem ratione nos reddimur propter Christum iustitia Dei (i. e. coram Deo perfecte iusti): Sed Christus factus est pro nobis peccatum non inhæsive, quasi vllum peccatum ipsi inhæsisset; sed imputatiue, quia iudicio diuino peccatum nostrum ipsi est imputatum: Ergo & nos propter Christum reddimur iustitia Dei non inhæsive, quasi perfecta operum iustitia nobis inhæreat; sed imputatiue, quia perfectissima iustitia Christi nobis imputatur & accensetur.

5) Ex Phil. III, 9. Vt inueniar in Christo, non habens meam iustitiam, quæ ex lege (fit), sed eam, quæ ex fide Christi; iustitiam, quæ ex Deo datur, fidei. Quicunque coram rigidissimo iudicio diuino comparet fretus non iustitia propria, sed aliena, quæ est ex fide Christi, cui & palmes viti insitus est, illum Deus gratiosissime æstimat iustum iustitia Christi, vera fide apprehensa. Atqui Paullus, & omnis peccator conuersus & renatus &c. Ergo.

6) Ex Rom. V, 19. Sicut per vnius hominis (Adami) inobedientiam peccatores constituti sunt multi: ita etiam per obedientiam vnius (Christi) iusti constituentur multi. Subsumo: Atqui per Adami inobedientiam imputatam omnes homines, vinculo sanguinis connexi, cum Adamo. sanguinis connexi, cum

Adamo, peccatores constituuntur. E. etiam per obedientiam Christi imputatam omnes renati, vinculo fidei cum ipso coniuncti, iusti constituuntur.

Dicis: Inobedientia Adami posteris non tantum imputatur, sed etiam inhaeret. Resp. Inobedientia Adami est actus proprius, personalis & individualis, qui posteris non potest esse communis, nisi per imputationem. Est quippe transgressio legis paradisiacae, adeoque peccatum primum & originans, quod posteris imputatur; peccatum vero originale, seu originatum est peccatum a primo ortum, quod posteris quidem Adami inhaeret, sed consequenter tantum ex inobedientia Adami fluit.

7) Τὸ τέλος νόμου, finis, vel complementum legis est Christus in iustitiam omni credenti, Rom. X, 14. Si Christus legem implevit in iustitiam omni credenti, illius impletio legis vicaria homini renato ad iustitiam imputatur. Antecedens, teste Paulo, est verum. E. & consequens.

8) Hypothesin aduersariorum duo absurda enormia premunt. Nam 1) audent coram rigido Dei iudicio comparere freti propria iustitia, quod in V. T. non ausus est Dauid, virtutibus ornatissimus, vid. Ps. CXLIII, 2., nec sub nouo foedere Paullus, vid. 1 Cor. IV, 4. Phil. III, 9., cum iustitia nobis inhaerens sit imperfecta & impura, atque examen iudicii divini sustinere nequeat. 2) Idem negant satisfactoriam Christi passionem & mortem, nec non impletionem legis, a Christo loco totius generis humani praestitam, cuius effectus non, nisi per gratiosissimam Dei imputationem, in genus humanum redundare potest. At isthanc negantes, ipsum fundamentum fidei, quantum in ipsis est, labefactatum eunt.

Prob. b. Doctrinam euangelicam de imputatione diuina obedientiae Christi actiuae & passiuae ad iustitiam & remissionem peccatorum, ad promouendam pietatem utilissimam esse, demonstratu facile est. Nam 1) imputatione priuatiua, propter satisfactoriam Christi passionem, peccatum non imputatur ad condemnationem, 2 Cor. V, 19. At immunitatem a condemnatione, & vitae sanctimoniam Apostolus Paullus coniungit Rom. VIII, 1. Nihil ergo nunc condemnationis iis est, qui in Christo Iesu non secundum carnem ambulant, sed secundum spiritum. Et Apostolus Petrus docet 1 epist. II, 24. satisfactoriae passionis Christi finem geminum esse, remissionem peccatorum, & sanctitatem vitae: Christus ipse peccata nostra pertulit in corpore suo super lignum, vt, peccatis mortui, iustitia viueremus, cuius vulneribus sanati estis. Homines renati, quibus peccata ad condemnationem non imputantur, non indulgent cupiditatibus carnis, sed Spiritum S. adepti, eius motibus obsequuntur, ne beatitudine gratiae & gloriae excidant. Quo spectant verba regii Prophetae, Ps. CXXX, 4. Nam tecum est remissio, vt timearis.

2) Iustitiae imputatae fructus sunt generatim bona opera, Phil. I, 2.; speciatim vero

a) Ardens dilectio Dei, & mediatoris Christi. Nam fides, cuius intuitu obedientia Christi ad iustitiam imputata est, per dilectionem operatur, Gal. V, 6. Sane homo renatus & iustificatus accenditur amore Dei, secum expendens misericordiam Dei ineffabilem, quae etiam homini impio, sed poenitenti & in Christum credenti, fidem ad iustitiam imputat. Exardescit amore in Christum, quotusquisque pie considerat, quod iustitia Christi vel tanquam veste ornetur, vel tanquam luce splendidissima circumfundatur, Es. LXI, 10. Apoc. XII, 1.

b) Amor erga proximum, quem parit fides iustificans. Omnis, qui credit, quod Iesus fit Christus, ex Deo natus est: & omnis, qui diligit eum, qui generauit ipsum, diligit etiam eum, qui natus est ex illo, ait Ioannes 1 ep. V, 1. Homo a Deo renatus est, qui credit in Christum, qui ipsi factus est in iustitiam, 1 Cor. I, 30., fidem autem sincero amore tum in Deum, tum in proximum testatur. c) Obsequium praeceptis diuinis praestitum.

Exemplo nobis sit Abrahamus, qui operibus & inprimis promptissima obedientia fidem declarauit, mandato diuino de offerendo in holocaustum filio, obsecutus, Gen. XXII, 1. Iac. II, 21. d) Vera animi submissio, & spiritualis sui abnegatio.
