Conc. p. 675: "This is most certain, that in true conversion a change, renovation, and motion must take place in man's intellect, will, and heart: so that, namely, the mind may acknowledge sins, fear the wrath of God, turn itself away from sin, acknowledge and apprehend the promise of grace, stir up pious thoughts in the soul, etc." Where the name of both conversion and renovation is taken in a general meaning. That this loose signification of renovation is not unusual in Holy Scripture is clearly demonstrated by D. SEB. SCHMID, in Commentar. in ep. ad Hebr. c. VI, 6. p. 663. Ἀνακαινισμὸς, renovation in Scripture is twofold. For there is one renovation εἰς μετάνοιαν, into or unto repentance, which precedes repentance itself; but another is through repentance and from repentance, which follows repentance as an effect. This is proved partly from this verse 6 of ours, partly from the rest of Scripture. For when the Apostle says that it is impossible ἀνακαινίζειν to renew those who have fallen away (scil. by sin against the Holy Spirit) εἰς μετάνοιαν, into or unto repentance, it is clear that he wishes ἀνακαινισμὸν, renovation, to be understood as that which precedes repentance and terminates in it: for ἀνακαινισμὸς is the renovation by which a man becomes penitent, and thus a believer. But there is another ἀνακαινισμὸς, another renovation, to which our Apostle exhorts the Romans who are already believers, to whom he writes, c. XII. 2: "And be not conformed to this world, ἀλλὰ μεταμορφοῦσθε τῇ ἀνακαινώσει τοῦ νοὸς ὑμῶν, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind." That this follows repentance and faith is plain and evident. Whence, if we wish to describe ἀνακαινισμὸν from Scripture in general, we can describe it thus: Ἀνακαινισμὸς of man, or renovation, taken generally, is the divine donation of new motions and spiritual powers, for producing spiritual acts, which man, left to the oldness of his corruption by nature, can produce neither in part nor in whole by himself and from himself. At present, renovation taken strictly imports a certain real and intrinsic change in the converted, reborn, and justified man; by which from an old man he becomes a new one, from a sinner a saint.

Obs. II. Renovation strictly so-called is taken either transitively or intransitively: whence it is described by authors in a twofold manner. Renovation taken transitively is an act of the applying grace of the Holy Spirit, by which He, with the Father and the Son, by virtue of the merit of Christ, so changes a sinful man that his intellect is illuminated with the darkness of errors dispelled, his will is amended and coerced from inclining toward depravity, and the members of his body become weapons of righteousness to the praise of God and the obedience owed to Him. Concerning this transitive renovation, the heavenly oracle deserves to be noted, Ezek. XXXVI, 26, where Jehovah says: "I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will give in the midst of you, and I will remove the stony heart from your flesh; for I will give you a heart of flesh. My Spirit, I say, I will give in the midst of you, and I will cause that you walk in my statutes, and keep and do my judgments." Renovation taken intransitively is a real and intrinsic change of the converted, reborn, and justified man, is taken as a real and intrinsic change of the converted, reborn, and justified

mutation, by which that man, instructed by powers divinely conferred, having shaken off the dominion of sin, purifies himself from the defilements of the flesh and spirit, and conforms his internal and external motions, as far as is possible in this life, to the divine will, expressed in the word of the law. Of which intransitive renovation the Apostle speaks, Col. III, 9. 10. Put off the old man with his deeds, and put on the new, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of him who creates him.

Synonymy Obj. III. Renovation is otherwise called sanctification, which is likewise taken either broadly, so that in its scope it embraces vocation, illumination, conversion, regeneration, justification, and renovation, or it is taken strictly, insofar as it coincides with renovation strictly so called. Furthermore, sanctification is accustomed, by the guidance of Scripture, to be distinguished into external and internal. The former is that by which something is separated from common and profane use and destined for a sacred use, pleasing to God. Thus the Sabbath is sanctified, Exod. XX, 8; the tabernacle is sanctified, and all its vessels, the altar, the priests, Exod. XL, 9. 10; food, 1 Tim. IV, 5. The latter is that by which sin is expelled from the justified man, and inherent holiness is granted to him. We make mention of inherent holiness for this reason, that we may distinguish it from imputed holiness, which God, out of mercy in view of the merit of Christ, apprehended by true faith, attributes to converted and reborn sinners by a gracious estimation: this is granted to them through justifying grace, by which the holiness of Christ is imputatively ours, so that we dare to say with the Apostle, from 1 Cor. I, 10, Christ has been made for us sanctification from God. We have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once performed, Hebr. X, 10. At present, our discourse is concerning holiness not imputed, but inherent.

Latin:

Quæst. I. Quid est renouatio?

Renouatio est actus gratiæ, quo Spiritus S. hominem iustificatum, expulsis vitiis, sanctitate inhærente donat.

Vberius definitur: Renouatio est actus gratiae applicatricis, quo Spiritus S. inhaerentes homini iustificato reliquias peccati, ne dominetur, abolet, motusque internos & externos voluntati diuinae conformes, adeoque spiritualiter bonos, in eodem parit, vt, imagine diuina instaurata donatus, sobrie, iuste & pie viuat in laudem Dei sanctissimi.

Obs. I. Renouatio in genere denotat quamlibet actionem, qua ea, quae vetustate detrita, infirmata, aut corrupta sunt, restaurantur. Atque ita in renouatione hominis spirituali, latius sumta, vetus homo secundum omnem suam rationem, i. e. carentiam virium spiritualium omnimodam, reatum & dominium peccati, aboleri, & nouus homo secundum suam latitudinem, i. e. ipsas vires spirituales, absolutionem a reatu, & donum habituale, quo supprimatur dominium peccati, produci intelligitur. Quo sensu latiori vox, renouatio, accipitur in Declar. Form. Conc. p. 675. Hoc certissimum est, in vera conuersione immutationem, renouationem, & motum fieri oportere in hominis intellectu, voluntate & corde: vt nimirum mens peccata agnoscat, iram Dei metuat, a peccato sese auertat, promissionem gratiae agnoscat & apprehendat, pias cogitationes animo agitet &c. Vbi tam conuersionis, quam renouationis nomen significatu generali sumitur. Laxam hanc renouationis significationem S. scripturae non esse inusitatam, dilucide demonstrat D. SEB. SCHMID, in Commentar. in ep. ad Hebr. c. VI, 6. p. 663. Ἀνακαινισμὸς, renouatio in scriptura duplex est. Est namque renouatio vna εἰς μετάνοιαν, in, vel ad paenitentiam, quae ipsam paenitentiam praecedit; altera vero per paenitentiam & ex paenitentia, quae paenitentiam vt effectus sequitur. Probatur hoc partim ex nostro hoc versu 6. partim ex reliqua scriptura. Quando namque Apostolus dicit, impossibile esse ἀνακαινίζειν renouare eos, qui prolapsi sunt, (scil. peccato in Spiritum S.) εἰς μετάνοιαν, in vel ad paenitentiam, clarum est, quod ἀνακαινισμὸν, renouationem intelligi velit eam, quae paenitentiam antecedat, & in eam terminetur: est namque ἀνακαινισμὸς, renouatio, qua homo fit paenitens, atque adeo fidelis. Est vero alius ἀνακαινισμὸς, alia renouatio, ad quam Apostolus noster Romanos iam fideles adhortatur, ad quos scribit, c. XII. 2. Et ne configuremini saeculo huic, ἀλλὰ μεταμορφοῦσθε τῇ ἀνακαινώσει τοῦ νοὸς ὑμῶν, sed transformamini renouatione mentis vestrae. Hanc namque sequi paenitentiam & fidem, planum est & perspicuum. Vnde si ἀνακαινισμὸν ex scriptura in genere describere voluerimus, ita describere poterimus: ’Ἀνακαινισμὸς hominis, seu renouatio, generaliter sumta, est diuina donatio nouorum motuum & virium spiritualium, ad producendos actus spirituales, quos homo, suae naturae vetustate corruptionis relictus, per se & ex se nec ex parte, nec ex toto producere potest. Impraesentiarum renouatio stricte sumta importat realem quandam & intrinsecam mutationem in homine conuerso, renato & iustificato; qua ex homine vetere fit nouus, ex peccatore sanctus.

Obs. II. Renouatio stricte dicta sumitur vel transitiue, vel intranfitiue: vnde ab auctoribus duplici ratione describitur. Renouatio transitiue sumta est actus gratiae Spiritus S. applicatricis, quo is cum Patre & Filio, vi meriti Christi, hominem peccatorem ita immutat, vt intellectus pulsis errorum tenebris illuminetur, voluntas emendetur, ad praua inclinans coercetur, & membra corporis arma iustitiae fiant in laudem Dei, & debitum eidem praestandum obsequium. De hac renouatione transitiua notari meretur oraculum coeleste, Ezech. XXXVI, 26. vbi Iehouah inquit: Dabo vobis cor nouum, & spiritum nouum dabo in medio vestri, ac remouebo cor lapideum e carne vestra; dabo enim vobis cor carnis. Spiritum, inquam, meum dabo in medio vestri, faciamque, vt in statutis meis ambuletis, ac iudicia mea custodiatis ac faciatis, Renouatio intranfitiue sumta est realis & intrinseca hominis conuersi, renati ac iustificati mutatio, sumta est realis & intrinseca hominis conuersi, renati ac iustificati

mutatio, qua is viribus divinitus collatis instructus, excusso peccati dominio, ab inquinamentis carnis & spiritus se purificat, motusque internos & externos, quantum in hac vita possibile est, ad voluntatem divinam, verbo legis expressam, conformat. De qua renovatione intransitiva loquitur Apostolus, Col. III, 9. 10. Exuite veterem hominem cum actionibus eius, & induite novum, qui renovatur in cognitionem secundum imaginem eius, qui creat illum.

Synonymia Obi. III. Renovatio dicitur alias sanctificatio, quae itidem vel late accipitur, vt ambitu suo vocationem, illuminationem, conversionem, regenerationem, iustificationem & renovationem complectatur, vel stricte sumitur, prout cum renovatione stricte sic dicta coincidit. Ceterum consuevit sanctificatio, ductu scripturae, distingui in externam, & internam. Illa est, qua aliquid ab usu communi & profano segregatum ad usum sacrum, Deoque gratum destinatur. Sic sanctificatur sabbathum, Exod. XX, 8. sanctificatur habitaculum, & omnia eius vasa, altare, sacerdotes, Exod. XL, 9. 10, cibus, 1 Tim. IV, 5. Haec est, qua ex homine iustificato peccatum expellitur, & sanctitas inhaerens ipsi donatur. Sanctitatis inhaerentis mentionem ideo facimus, vt eam distinguamus a sanctitate imputata, quam Deus ex misericordia intuitu meriti Christi, vera fide apprehensi, peccatoribus conversis & renatis gratiosa aestimatione attribuit: haec ipsis donatur per gratiam iustificantem, qua Christi sanctitas imputative nostra est, vt cum Apostolo dicere audimus, ex 1 Cor. I, 10. Christus nobis a Deo factus est sanctificatio. Sanctificati sumus per oblationem corporis Iesu Christi semel peractam, Hebr. X, 10. In praesenti nobis sermo est de sanctitate non imputata, sed inhaerente.


### Q. II. Who renews and sanctifies us?

The principal efficient cause of renovation is the triune God a), the Father b), the Son c), and terminatively and appropriatively the Holy Spirit d), who renews and sanctifies justified men.

Proof a. From 1 Thess. V, 23. May the God of peace himself sanctify you wholly, and may your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Spirit in the loc. cit. denotes the superior faculty of the soul, which distinguishes men from brutes, viz., the mind and will. Soul denotes the inferior faculties, to which belong the external and internal senses with the sensitive appetite. Body is the domicile and organ of the spirit and soul. The sense, therefore, is: May God, the author and vindicator of temporal, spiritual, and eternal peace, illuminate the spirit, i.e., the intellect and will, lest it be filled with the darkness of errors or diffidence: may he renew the soul, i.e., wipe away every stain or blemish from external and internal affections: may he purify the body, and render it immune from every pollution, lest you incur the reproach of God and men.

Proof b. God the Father, the heavenly vinedresser, purges every spiritual branch remaining in Christ, that it may bear more fruit, John XV, 2. God purges the reborn soul, joined to Christ by the bond of faith, both by removing the impediments of spiritual fructification from it, and by rendering it more fruitful through divine power, so that it may bear more fruits of righteousness (good works).

Proof c. From John XV, 5. I am the vine; you are the branches. He who remains in me, and I in him, he bears much fruit; because without me you can do nothing. The Son of God is united mystically with justified men, as the vine with the branches, and bestows upon them all vigor, all faculty of bearing fruits of righteousness by spiritual communication. From which Paul attributes the sanctification of the church to Christ, Eph. V, 25. Christ loved the church, and gave himself for it, that he might sanctify it and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word.

Proof d. The work of sanctification is attributed to the Holy Spirit κατ' ἰδιοποίησιν, or by a certain appropriation. For we are said to be sanctified by the Holy Spirit, Rom. XV, 16. And baptism it is called the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Spirit, Tit. III, 5. He dwells in the regenerate, as in temples, 1 Cor. III, 16. He leads them, Rom. VIII, 14. He helps their infirmities, ibid. v. 26.

Latin:

Causa efficiens renovationis principalis Deus trinus a), Pater b), Filius c), atque terminative & appropriative Spiritus Sanctus d), homines iustificatos renovat & sanctificat.

Prob. a. Ex 1 Thess. V, 23. Ipse Deus pacis sanctificet vos integros, & integer vester spiritus & anima & corpus irreprehenfibiliter in aduentum Domini nostri Iesu Christi servetur. Spiritus l. c. notat superiorem animae facultatem, quae homines a brutis discernit, scil. mentem & voluntatem. Anima denotat facultates inferiores, ad quas pertinent sensus externi & interni cum appetitu sensitivo. Corpus est spiritus & animae domicilium atque organon. Sensus itaque est: Deus auctor & vindex pacis temporalis, spiritualis & aeternae, illuminet spiritum, i. e. intellectum & voluntatem, ne errorum aut diffidentiae tenebris oppleatur: renouet animam, h. e. ab affectibus externis & internis omnem maculam aut labem abstergat: corpus purificet, atque ab omni pollutione immune praestet, ne Dei hominumque reprehensionem incurratis.

Prob. b. Deus Pater, vinitor caelestis, omnem palmitem spiritualem in Christo manentem purgat, vt plures fructus ferat, Io. XV, 2. Deus animam renatam & vinculo fidei cum Christo coniunctam purgat, tum impedimenta spiritualis fructificationis ab ea remouendo, tum virtute diuina foecundiorem eandem reddendo, vt plures fructus iustitiae (bona opera) ferat.

Prob. c. Ex Io. XV, 5. Ego sum vitis; vos palmites. Qui manet in me, & ego in illo, hic fert fructum multum; quia sine me non potestis facere quidquam. Filius Dei vnitur mystice cum hominibus iustificatis, vt vitis cum palmitibus, iisdemque omnem vigorem, omnem facultatem ferendi fructus iustitiae communicatione spirituali dilargitur. Ex quo Paullus sanctificationem ecclesiae Christo tribuit, Eph. V, 25. Christus dilexit ecclesiam, & seipsum tradidit pro illa, vt sanctificaret illam & mundaret lauacro aquae in verbo.

Prob. d. spiritui S. opus sanctificationis κατ' ἰδιοποίησιν, seu per appropriationem quandam tribuitur. Dicimur enim sanctificati Spiritu Sancto, Rom. XV, 16. Et baptismus nominatur lauacrum regenerationis atque renouationis Spiritus Sancti, Tit. III, 5. Hic habitat in renatis, tanquam templis, 1 Cor. III, 16. agit eos, Rom. VIII, 14. coadiuuat infirmitates eorum, ibid. v. 26.


### Quest. III. Does a justified man cooperate with God in the business of sanctification?

A regenerate and justified man concurs in the work of sanctification, as a secondary, subordinate cause, moved by God, so that through the powers received from above he may renew him-self dai-

Obf. I. The Holy Spirit effects the faculty of acting well and the first act of satisfaction in man without the concurrence of man, but to the second act of sanctification, or the exercises and continuation of sanctification once introduced by the Holy Spirit, man concurs, not by natural powers, but by supernatural ones. Obf.

Obs. II. A regenerate man does indeed cooperate with God in the business of sanctification, yet not by an equal action, but by subordination and dependence upon the Holy Spirit, in that he operates not by native, but by given powers (*). This is gathered from the words of the Apostle, Phil. II, 12. 13. Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling! For it is God who works in you both to will and to do for his good pleasure. If a justified man were to concur in his own renewal in the same way that God does, the mere εὐδοκία (good pleasure) of God could not be alleged as the reason why it is right for a man, inflamed with the zeal of seeking salvation, to tremble, since the good pleasure of God does not of itself terrify the conscience of man, but calms it. But man trembles whenever he contemplates his own imperfect mode of acting in the business of renewal, and God’s most perfect one. Therefore, having made a comparison of himself with the most perfect God, Matth. V, 45, he cannot but shudder, being conscious of his own imperfection.

Prob. 1) From Ezech. XVIII, 31. Make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. Regenerate men make for themselves a new heart and spirit, not by their own powers, but by powers divinely granted, through which they concur, as subordinate causes, to the continued amendment of life, Jer. XII, 2.

2) From 2 Cor. VII, 1. Having therefore these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God. By which words the Apostle

Latin:

Homo renatus atque iustificatus ad opus sanctificationis, tanquam causa secundaria, subordinata, motaque a Deo, concurrit, vt per acceptas superne vires seipsum in dies renouet.

Obs. I. Facultatem bene operandi, & actum primum satisfactionis efficit Spiritus S. in homine, sine concursu hominis, sed ad sanctificationis actum secundum, siue exercitia & continuationem sanctificationis, per Spiritum S. semel introductae, homo concurrit, non per vires naturales, sed supernaturales.

Obs. II. Cooperatur quidem homo renatus Deo in negotio sanctificationis, attamen non aequali actione, sed subordinatione ac dependentia a Spiritu S. eo, quod non per vires nativas, sed datiuas operatur (*). Id quod colligitur e verbis Apostoli, Phil. II, 12. 13. Cum pauore & tremore vestram salutem operamini! Deus enim est, qui operatur in vobis tam velle, quam perficere pro beneplacito. Si homo iustificatus eodem, quo Deus, modo ad renouationem sui concurreret, non posset sola εὐδοκία Dei pro ratione allegari, ob quam aequum sit, hominem studio quaerendae salutis incensum tremere, siquidem beneplacitum Dei conscientiam hominis per se non terret, sed tranquillat. Tremit autem homo, quoties in negotio renouationis suum imperfectum, Dei autem perfectissimum agendi modum intuetur. Facta igitur comparatione sui cum Deo perfectissimo, Matth. V, 45. non potest non suae imperfectionis conscire cohorrescere.

Prob. 1) Ex Ezech. XVIII, 31. Facite vobis cor nouum, & spiritum nouum. Homines renati faciunt sibi cor & spiritum nouum, non per vires proprias, sed per vires diuinitus concessas, per quas ad continuatam vitae emendationem, velut causa subordinatae, concurrunt, Ier. XII, 2.

2) Ex 2 Cor. VII, 1. Has igitur cum habeamus promissiones, dilecti, mundemus nos ab omni inquinatione carnis & spiritus, perficientes sanctitatem in timore Dei. Quibus verbis


### Quaest. V. By what means does God renovate us?

looks back to the divine promises, of which he had made mention in the previous chapter, namely that God, as if in dedicated temples, is about to dwell in the faithful, and is about to embrace them as children with fatherly love. From which promises he validly concludes: that it is the duty of Christians to purge the dwellings of the divine majesty from all defilement of flesh and spirit, and to pursue the holiness of life after the example of the heavenly Father.

Obs. Renovation is therefore an action of God, as the principal cause, renovating the justified man, both by conferring sanctifying powers upon him, and by concurring with the act of renovation by a special and gracious influx. The same renovation is an action of the justified man, as a secondary and subordinate cause, renovating himself intransitively, not by native powers, but by given ones, or those divinely bestowed. However, renovation, whether called transitive or intransitive, does not differ in reality; for this reason, that a) it denotes the same change, by which one becomes new from an old man, and holy from a sinner: which, with the connoted dependence on God, as an agent in another, is called transitive renovation; but viewed from the side of the subject, by way of an immanent act, it is called intransitive renovation. b) Both are accomplished by the same powers, namely, not human, but divine, which the Holy Spirit has originally and independently, but the reborn man has dependently and because of his mystical union with God.

Quaest. IV.

What impelled God to renovate the justified man? God was internally impelled to renovate man by mercy , and externally by the merit of Christ .

Prob. a. From Tit. III, 5. According to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Spirit. Just as his mercy, most inclined toward the human race, moved God to regenerate and save the sinner: so the same mercy led him to renovate man, infected by the oldness of sin, which shone most clearly in the work of sanctification, as Paul testifies, Tit. II, 12. The grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men, teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world.

Prob. b. From Tit. II, 14. Jesus Christ gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works. The effect of Christ's redemption is the purification of men who have fallen into sin, which happens partly by faith through the sprinkling and cleansing of the blood of Christ, 1 Pet. I, 1. 1 John I, 7. and partly by the consecration of the faithful into a people περιούσιον, a peculiar people, zealous of good works.

Quaest. V.

By what means does God renovate us? The means of renovation, on the part of God, are the word of the law and of the gospel , baptism and the eucharist

of faith, or through the gospel, Gal. III, 2. The gospel also produces faith, the mother of good will, as AMBROSIUS thinks, and of just action. Prob. c.

Baptism is the washing of regeneration, Tit. III, 5. For baptism is not a bare sign of our sanctification, but an active and communicative (ἐνεργητικὸν καὶ μεταδοτικὸν) medium, productive and collative, by which sanctifying powers are conferred by God, and the act of sanctification itself is perfected. Add that the sanctifying powers, conferred in baptism, contribute and provide not a little to subsequent spiritual acts. Prob. d.

The Eucharist is a valid medium of our union with Christ, in whom we bear much fruit, Io. XV, 5. It is also a symbol and bond of our mutual charity, 1 Cor. X, 16, 17. Prob. e.

Faith works through charity, Gal. V, 6. i. e. it exerts itself actively, and through charity, the queen of virtues, it pours itself into external works. Where a) it is to be observed, that the energy (ἐνέργεια) of faith is twofold, the first is internal, or formal, when it extends itself to Christ, and apprehends his satisfaction and merit: the other is external, or effective, when it exerts itself through charity toward God and neighbor. b) It is to be noted, that faith in order to renovation performs a double duty. One indeed, that it determines the intellect to assent both to the word of the law, the norm of holiness, and to the gospel, the principle of spiritual powers, collative to doing good. Whence, from the practical conclusions deduced, it dictates what things are to be done, and what things are to be avoided. In another way, it inclines the will, in which it likewise subjectively resides, to resist depraved concupiscence, and to do that which the intellect, concerning any spiritual object already believed, prescribes by way of practical judgment. From which faith is called the victory that overcomes the world, 1 Io. V, 4. Faith overcomes the world within us and outside us. For faith indeed subdues within us the inordinate love of the world, and outside us the riches, honors, and delights of the flattering world, and the envy, hatred, and persecution of the afflicting world.

Latin:

Apostolus respicit promissiones diuinas, quarum capite superiori mentionem iniecerat, nimirum quod Deus in fidelibus, velut dedicatis templis, habitaturus, eosque velut liberos paterno amore complexurus sit. E quibus promissis valide colligit: Christianorum esse, ab omni inquinatione carnis & spiritus domicilia maiestatis diuinae repurgare, & ad exemplar Patris caelestis sanctitatem vitae sectari.

Obs. Est itaque renouatio actio Dei, tanquam causae principalis, renouantis hominem iustificatum, tum vires sanctificas ipsi conferendo, tum ad actum renouationis speciali & gratioso influxu concurrendo. Eadem renouatio est actio hominis iustificati, tanquam causae secundariae & subordinatae, seipsum intransitiue renouantis, non per vires natiuas, sed datiuas, siue diuinitus collatas. Non differt autem renouatio transitiva, & intransitiue dicta, realiter; ideo, quod a) eandem notat mutationem, qua ex vetere homine nouus, ex peccatore fit sanctus: quae cum connotata dependentia a Deo, tanquam ab agente in alio, transitiva; ex parte subiecti vero, per modum actus immanentis spectata, intransitiva renouatio dicitur. b) Vtraque iisdem perficitur viribus, scil. non humanis, sed diuinis, quas Spiritus S. habet originaliter & independenter, homo renatus autem dependenter & propter vnionem cum Deo mysticam.

Quaest. IV. Quid impulit Deum ad renouandum hominem iustificatum?

Ad hominem renouandum Deum interne impulit misericordia , externe meritum Christi .

Prob. a. Ex Tit. III, 5. Iuxta misericordiam saluauit nos, per lauacrum regenerationis & renouationis Spiritus Sancti. Quem ad modum Deum ad regenerandum & saluandum peccatorem permouit misericordia sua, in genus humanum propensissima: ita ad renouandum hominem, vetustate peccati infectum, eadem misericordia adduxit, quae in opere sanctificationis clarissime refulsit, teste Paulo, Tit. II, 12. Apparuit gratia Dei salutaris omnibus hominibus, erudiens nos, ut abnegemus impietatem, & mundanas concupiscentias, ac sobrie & iuste & pie viuamus in praesenti saeculo.

Prob. b. Ex Tit. II, 14. Iesus Christus dedit seipsum pro nobis, ut liberaret nos ab omni iniquitate, & purificaret sibi ipsi populum peculiarem, aemulum bonorum operum. Effectus redemptionis Christi est purificatio hominum, in peccatum prolapsorum, quae fit partim fide per aspersionem & emundationem sanguinis Christi, 1 Petr. I, 1. 1 Io. I, 7. partim consecratione fidelium in populum περιούσιον, peculiarem, aemulum bonorum operum.

Quaest. V. Quibus mediis Deus nos renouat?

Media renouationis, ex parte Dei sunt verbum legis & euangelii , baptismus & eucharistia

trinam fidei, seu per evangelium, Gal. III, 2. Producit etiam evangelium fidem, bonae voluntatis, censente AMBROSIO, & iustae actionis genitricem.

Prob. c. Baptismus est lavacrum renovationis, Tit. III, 5. Neque enim nudum sanctificationis nostrae signum est baptismus, sed medium ἐνεργητικὸν καὶ μεταδοτικὸν productivum & collativum, quo vires sanctificantes a Deo conferuntur, & ipse sanctificationis actus perficitur. Adiice, quod vires sanctificae, in baptismo collatae, ad actus sequentes spirituales haud parum praestent, & contribuant.

Prob. d. Eucharistia est validum medium unionis nostrae cum Christo, in quo multum fructum ferimus, Io. XV, 5. Est etiam mutuae nostrae caritatis symbolum & vinculum, 1 Cor. X, 16, 17.

Prob. e. Fides per caritatem operatur, Gal. V, 6. i. e. active se exserit, & per caritatem, reginam virtutum, in opera externa se effundit. Ubi a) observandum, quod gemina sit fidei ἐνέργεια, prima est interna, sive formalis, cum se extendit ad Christum, eiusque satisfactionem & meritum apprehendit: altera est externa, sive effectiva, cum se per caritatem erga Deum & proximum exserit. b) Notandum, quod fides in ordine ad renovationem duplici munere fungatur. Vno quidem, quod intellectum determinat ad assentien-dum tum verbo legis, sanctitatis normae, tum evangelio, principio virium spiritualium, ad bene operandum collativo. Vnde deductis conclusionibus practicis dictat, quae agenda, quaeque fugienda sint. Altero modo voluntatem, cui itidem subiective inest, inclinat ad resistendum prauae concupiscentiae, & agendum id, quod intellectus circa quodlibet obiectum spirituale iam creditum, per modum iudicii practici praescribit. Ex quo fides dicitur victoria vincens mundum, 1 Io. V, 4. Vincit fides mundum intra nos & extranos. Debellat quippe fides intra nos inordinatum mundi amorem, extra nos mundi blandientis opes, honores, delicias, mundi affligentis invidiam, odium, persecutionem.


### Quaest. VI. What are the secondary aids of renovation?

The secondary aids of renovation are the afflictions of the flesh a), and the temptations of the soul b), which to men reborn and justified are not punishments; but paternal castigations c).

Prob. a. From 1 Petr. IV, 1, 2. He who suffers in the flesh, abstains from sin: that he may no longer live the rest of his time in the flesh to the concupiscences of men, but to the will of God. Through divine providence by adverse things and afflictions, as if by a certain medicine, man is rendered sounder, having been freed from his destined malice, says IVSTINVS Martyr, quaest. 137. Prob. b.

From 2 Cor. XII, 7. By the excellence of the revelations, that I might not be puffed up, a thorn was given to my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me, lest I should be exalted. Concerning which I besought the Lord four times, that it might depart from me: but he said to me: My grace is sufficient for thee; for my power is perfected in infirmity. From this example of Paul it is to be learned that the internal temptation of the soul brings much moment a) to the submission of the mind, b) to the ardor of prayers, c) to the experimental knowledge of the grace and power of Christ, which is perfected in infirmity, i. e. it exerts itself perfectly, is illustrated, and is clearly known. Prob. c.

From Hebr. XII, 11. All castigation for the present does not seem to be of joy: but afterwards it renders the peaceful fruit of justice to those exercised by it. If you look at the judgment of reason left to itself, all divine castigation is exceedingly troublesome and bitter; but the more grievous the beginning, the more pleasant is the end: the more bitter the root, the sweeter the fruit. For the fruit of castigation is justice, or holiness, which is the peaceful fruit, i. e. tranquilizing and soothing the conscience.

Latin:

Adminicula renovationis secundaria sunt afflictiones carnis a), & tentationes animae b), quae hominibus renatis & iustificatis non sunt poenae; sed castigationes paternae c).

Prob. a. Ex 1 Petr. IV, 1, 2. Qui patitur carne, abstinet a peccato: ut non amplius hominum concupiscentiis, sed voluntati Dei reliquum in carne vivat tempus. Per divinam providentiam rebus adversis & afflictionibus, tanquam medicina quadam, a destinata sua malitia liberatus homo sanior redditur, ait IVSTINVS Martyr, quaest. 137.

Prob. b. Ex 2 Cor. XII, 7. Excellentia revelationum ut non efferar, datus est mihi stimulus carni angelus satanae, ut me colaphis excipiat, ne me extollam. Super quo quater Dominum rogavi, ut a me desisteret: sed dixit ad me: Sufficit tibi gratia mea; nam virtus mea in infirmitate perficitur. Ex hoc exemplo Paulli discere est, internam animae tentationem multum momenti afferre a) ad submissionem animi, b) ad precum ardorem, c) ad experimentem notitiam gratiae & potentiae Christi, quae infirmitate perficitur, i. e. se perfecte exserit, illustratur & liquido cognoscitur.

Prob. c. Ex Hebr. XII, 11. Omnis castigatio ad praesens non videtur esse gaudii: postea vero fructum pacificum per eam exercitatis reddit iustitiae. Si spectes iudicium rationis sibi relictae, omnis castigatio divina est perquam molesta & amara; sed quo grauius initium, eo iucundior est finis: quo acerbior radix, eo dulcior fructus. Fructus namque castigationis est iustitia, sive sanctitas, quae est fructus pacificus, h. e. tranquillans & permulcens conscientiam.


### Q. VII. What is the term from which and to which of renewal?

The term from which of renewal is the old man, the term to which is the new man.

Prob. 1) From Eph. IV, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24. But you have not so learned Christ, if indeed you have heard him and have been taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus; that you put off, according to your former conversation, the old man, who is corrupted according to the desires of deceit; and be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who according to God is created in justice and holiness.

2) From Col. III, 10. Strip yourselves of the old man with his deeds, and put on the new, who is renewed unto knowledge according to the image of him that created him. Obs. a) The old and new man are not distinguished essentially, but accidentally; because in the present case, the old and new man are not understood physically, by reason of a diverse substance, but mystically, by reason of distinct qualities. Tertullian says excellently: We maintain that the moral oldness and newness of man does not pertain to a substantial difference. b) The old and new man are explained partly concretely, partly abstractly.

Viewed concretely, the old man is the corrupted nature of man, or to speak more distinctly, it is the mind of man blinded and prone to pass rash judgments on spiritual matters, a will turned away from the good and inclined to evil, a sensitive appetite deviating from the rule of rectitude and prone to desire goods pleasing to the senses, even if forbidden: on the contrary, the new man is a new mind illuminated by the light of knowledge, a will amended, an appetite corrected. Considered abstractly, the old man is a horrendous corruption in the intellect, will, and sensitive appetite, namely, ignorance of spiritual things and a proneness to rash judgments in the intellect, an inclination of the will toward temporal and fleeting goods, to be preferred over spiritual and eternal ones, a rebellion of the sensitive appetite: it therefore denotes original sin, with actual sins connoted. Conversely, the new man is the restored image of God, which is conformity with God by reason of wisdom in the intellect, justice in the will, and purity in the sensitive appetite. c) Man is called old from his origin, both from the first seduction of the protoplasts and from the derived conception and carnal birth, through which sin is propagated. Man is called new from the renewed image of God. Therefore he is said to be created according to God in justice and holiness of truth.

Latin:

Terminus a quo renouationis est homo vetus, terminus ad quem est homo nouus.

Prob. 1) Ex Eph. IV, 20. 21. 22. 23. 24. Vos vero non ita didicistis Christum, si modo ipsum audiuitis, in ipso edocti estis, sicut veritas est in Iesu; quod vos deponere debeatis iuxta priorem conuersationem veterem hominem, qui se corrumpit iuxta concupiscentias fraudis; renouari vero spiritu mentis vestræ, & induere nouum hominem, qui secundum Deum creatus est in iustitia & sanctitate.

2) Ex Col. III, 10. Exuite veterem hominem cum actionibus eius, & induite nouum, qui renouatur in cognitionem secundum imaginem eius, qui creat illum. Obs. a) Vetus & nouus homo non distinguuntur essentialiter, sed accidentaliter; quia in præsenti non intelligitur vetus & nouus homo physice, ratione substantiæ diuersæ, sed mystice, ratione distinctarum qualitatum. Præclare inquit TERTULLIANUS: Vetustatem & nouitatem hominis moralem non ad substantialem differentiam pertinere, defendimus. b) Vetus & nouus homo explicantur partim concretie, partim abstractiue.

Concretie spectatus vetus homo est natura hominis corrupta, siue distinctius loquendo, est mens hominis occæcata, & prona ad ferendum temeraria de rebus spiritualibus iudicia, voluntas a bono auersa, ad malum propensa, appetitus sensitivus a regula rectitudinis exorbitans, & procliuis ad appetendum bona sensibus grata, etsi prohibita: contra nouus homo est mens noua cognitionis luce collustrata, voluntas emendata, appetitus correctus. Abstractiue consideratus vetus homo est horrenda corruptio in intellectu, voluntate & appetitu sensitivo, scilicet ignorantia rerum spiritualium & pronitas ad iudicia temeraria in intellectu, inclinatio voluntatis ad bona temporalia & caduca, spiritualibus atque æternis præferenda, rebellio appetitus sensitivi: notat igitur peccatum originale, connotatis peccatis actualibus. Ex aduerso nouus homo est reparata imago Dei, quæ est confornitas cum Deo ratione sapientiæ in intellectu, iustitiæ in voluntate, puritas in appetitu sensitivo. c) Vetus dicitur homo ab origine tum prima protoplastorum seductionis, tum deriuata conceptionis & natiuitatis carnalis, per quam peccatum propagatur. Nouus dicitur homo a renouata imagine Dei. Idcirco dicitur esse creatus secundum Deum in iustitia & sanctitate veritatis.


### Q. VIII. Is the old man, according to his whole reason, the term from which, and the new man, according to his whole breadth, the term to…

Although through illumination, conversion, regeneration, and justification, not a little is taken away from the old man, and some powers for putting on the new man are divinely bestowed a): nevertheless, there remain in illuminated, converted, and reborn men the remnants of sin, or of the old man, which, so that they may not grow strong and obtain dominion, are diminished and abolished through successive renewal b).

Prob. a. By the benefit of illumination, the darkness of the intellect is dispersed, and supernatural powers are conferred for knowing sin from the law, and Christ from the gospel, and the grace of God founded in this. By the benefit of conversion, contrition is excited through the law, or displeasure and detestation of sin joined with sorrow of heart, bringing about the extermination of an evil purpose. By the benefit of regeneration, through the gospel, unbelief (ἀπισία) is abolished and faith in Christ is kindled. By the benefit of justification, the guilt of sin is removed. Therefore, through illumination, conversion, regeneration, and justification, not a little is taken away from the old man.

Prob. b. In men who are illuminated, converted, reborn, and justified, the flesh, the old man, or the depravity of original nature lusts, and by lusting struggles against the spirit, the new man, or those new and supernatural powers which the Holy Spirit bestowed in the act of illumination, conversion, and regeneration, Gal. V, 17. The flesh must therefore be suppressed, lest it gain the mastery.

Latin:

Quamuis per illuminationem, conuersionem, regenerationem & iustificationem veteri homini haud parum detractum fit, viresque nonnullæ ad induendum nouum hominem diuinitus collatæ sint a): remanent tamen in hominibus illuminatis, conuersis & renatis reliquiæ peccati, siue veteris hominis, quæ ne inualescant & dominium obtineant, per successiuam renouationem imminuuntur & abolentur b).

Prob. a. Beneficio illuminationis discuritur caligo intellectus, & conferuntur vires supernaturales ad cognoscendum ex lege peccatum, & ex euangelio Christum, & in hoc fundatam gratiam Dei. Beneficio conuersionis per legem excitatur contritio, siue displicentia & detestatio peccati cum cordis dolore coniuncta, exterminium mali propositi inferens. Beneficio regenerationis per euangelium aboletur ἀπισία & accenditur fides in Christum. Beneficio iustificationis tollitur reatus peccati. Ergo per illuminationem, conuersionem, regenerationem & iustificationem veteri homini haud parum detrahitur.

Prob. b. In hominibus illuminatis, conversis, renatis & justificatis caro, vetus homo, sive pravitas naturae originalis concupiscit, & concupiscendo reluctatur adversus spiritum, novum hominem, seu novas & supernaturales illas vires, quas Spiritus S. in actu illuminationis, conversionis & regenerationis contulit, Gal. V, 17. Opprimenda igitur est caro, ne praedominetur.


### Quest. IX. Can you distinctly explain the term from which and the term to which of renovation?

The term from which of renovation are the remnants of sin remaining in justified men after illumination, conversion, and regeneration, which are to be abolished by daily renovation, so that they may be diminished and suppressed, although they are not rooted out in this life; namely, some defect of spiritual powers on the part of the intellect indeed for knowing, on the part of the will for pursuing spiritual good; on the part of the sensitive appetite for obeying the superior faculties; at the same time also the proneness of these same faculties of the soul toward evil.

Latin:

Terminus a quo renovationis sunt reliquiae peccati post illuminationem, conversionem & regenerationem in hominibus justificatis remanentes, quae quotidiana renovatione abolendae sunt, vt imminuantur & opprimantur, licet in hac vita non radicitus evellantur; nempe defectus aliquis virium spiritualium ex parte intellectus quidem ad cognoscendum, ex parte voluntatis ad prosequendum bonum spirituale; ex parte appetitus sensitivi ad obsequendum superioribus facultatibus; simul etiam pronitas earundem facultatum animae ad prava. Terminus ad quem renovationis sunt maiores illae vires, quae post illuminationem, conversionem & regenerationem hominibus justificatis a Spiritu S. conferuntur, videlicet clarior & plenior intellectus cognitio rerum spiritualium, inhaerens voluntati justitia & sanctitas, promptum appetitus sensitivi obsequium, superioribus facultatibus praestandum; quibus conjunctis imago Dei instauratur.


### Quest. X. What man is renewed?

A sinful man is renewed by the Holy Spirit, but one who is illuminated, converted, reborn, and justified , insofar as he is infected by the remnants of indwelling sin and is destitute of inherent righteousness .

Prob. a. 1) From the harmony of apostolic doctrine. The Apostle Paul had taught, in chapters III, IV, V to the Romans, that a converted and reborn man is justified by faith alone without the concurrence of works; but in chapter VI he shows that it is the duty of justified men to walk in newness of life.

2) Sanctification is called the fruit of freedom from sin, Rom. VI, 22.

3) The Apostle exhorts the converted and reborn Ephesians and Colossians to put off and lay aside the old man, and likewise to put on the new man, Eph. IV, 22; Col. III, 10.

4) Good works, which are produced through renewing grace, are fruits of repentance, Matt. III, 8; fruits of righteousness, Phil. I, 11. Therefore, a man must be converted, reborn, and justified first, namely by priority of order, before he is renewed.

Prob. b. 1) The reborn and justified have sin, 1 John I, 8; they often fall, James III, 2; their flesh lusts against the spirit, Gal. V, 17. Sin dwells in them, Rom. VII, 17. Hence it happens that with the mind they serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin, ibid. v. 25.

2) No one is adorned with inherent righteousness who is not renewed. We must therefore be renewed in the spirit of our mind; and put on the new man, which is created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth, i.e., true and sincere, Eph. IV, 24.

Latin:

Renovatur a Spiritu S. homo peccator, sed illuminatus, conversus, renatus & justificatus , quatenus reliquiis inhabitautis peccati infectus & inhaerente justitia quod destitutus est .

Prob. a. 1) Ex harmonia doctrinae apostolicae. Docuerat Apostolus Paullus, c. III. IV. V. ad Romanos, sola fide fine confluentibus operibus hominem conversum & renatum justificari; capite vero VI. ostendit, hominum justificatorum officium esse, in novitate vitae ambulare.

2) Libertatis a peccato fructus dicitur sanctificatio, Rom. VI, 22.

3) Apostolus conversos atque renatos Ephesios & Colossenses adhortatur, vt exuant & deponant veterem hominem, iuxta atque induant novum hominem, Eph. IV, 22. Col. III, 10.

4) Bona opera, quae per gratiam renovantem producuntur, sunt fructus poenitentiae, Matth. III, 8. fructus iustitiae, Phil. I, 11. Oportet igitur hominem conversum, renatum & justificatum esse prius, prioritate sc. ordinis, quam renouetur.

Prob. b. 1) Renati & justificati peccatum habent, 1 Io. I, 8. saepe labuntur, Iac. III, 2. caro ipsorum concupiscit adversus spiritum, Gal. V, 17. Habitat in ipsis peccatum, Rom. VII, 17. Inde fit, vt mente quidem serviant legi Dei, carne vero legi peccati, ibid. v. 25.

2) Justitia inhaerente nemo exornatus est, qui non est renovatus. Debemus igitur renovari spiritu mentis nostrae; & induere novum hominem, qui secundum Deum creatus est in iustitia & sanctitate veritatis, i. e. vera & sincera, Eph. IV, 24.


### Quest. XI. Is the whole man, consisting of soul and body, renewed?

Primarily the soul is renewed, and its faculties corrupted by sin: the mind, the will, and the sensitive appetite . Secondarily, the members of the body are renewed, by wh. which were the weapons of righteousness, as they are the instruments and, as it were, the weapons of the sanctified soul, necessary for carrying out holy actions b).

Objection: This doctrine is proposed in philosophical terms as follows: The subject of renewal, that is, the whole suppositum which is said to be renewed, is man, by reason of his past state, a sinner; by reason of his present state, renewed and justified. The subject by which is either primary or secondary. The primary is either remote or proximate. The remote is the soul; the proximate is partly the intellect, partly the will, partly the sensitive appetite. The secondary is the body and its members. Compare KOENIG, Theol. Positiv., p. 215.

Proof a & b From Rom. XII, 1, 2. "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service. And be not conformed to this world: but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, that you may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God." From these words of St. Paul, a concise description of intransitive renewal can be formed in the following manner: Renewal is the spiritual μεταμόρφωσις (metamorphosis), or reformation, of a justified man, by which he, having renounced conformity to the world, with a renewed mind, knows and strives to do the good will of God, and whatever is acceptable and perfect to God, and presents his body as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, in order to worship Him religiously according to the prescription of the divine word.

Latin:

Primario renovatur anima, eiusque per peccatum corruptae facultates, mens, voluntas & appetitus sensitivus . Secundario renovantur membra corporis, quo. quae fuerunt arma iustitiae, vt sunt organa & quasi arma animae sanctificatae, ad expediendas actiones sanctas necessaria b).

Obiectio Terminis philosophicis haec doctrina ita proponitur: Subiectum renouationis quod, seu totum suppositum, quod renouari dicitur, est homo, ratione status praeteriti, peccator, ratione status praesentis, renatus & iustificatus. Subiectum quo vel primarium, vel secundarium est. Primarium est vel remotum, vel proximum. Remotum est anima, proximum est partim intellectus, partim voluntas, partim appetitus sensitivus. Secundarium est corpus, eiusque membra. Confer, KOENIGII theol. positiu. p. 215.

Probatio a & b Ex Rom. XII, 1, 2. Hortor itaque vos, fratres, per miserationes Dei, vt sistatis corpora vestra sacrificium viuum, sanctum, acceptum, Deo nempe, vestrum secundum verbum cultum. Et ne conformemini mundo huic, sed transformemini renouatione mentis vestrae, vt probetis vos quanam voluntas Dei bona, quodnam acceptum ac perfectum. Ex his verbis S. Pauli concinna renouationis intranfitiuae descriptio sequenti ratione formari potest: Renouatio est spiritualis hominis iustificati μεταμόρφωσις, reformatio, qua is, abnegata conformatione mundi, renouata mente, bonam Dei voluntatem, & quidquid Deo acceptum perfectumque est, cognoscit & facere nititur, atque corpus suum sistit sacrificium viuum, sanctum, Deo que gratum, ad eundem, secundum praescriptum verbi diuini, religiose colendum.


### Question XII. In what does renewal formally consist?

The form of renewal is completed by a twofold act, privative and positive. The privative consists in the dissipation of the darkness of the intellect, in the aversion of the will from evil, in the restraint of the ferocity of the sensitive appetite, and in the abstraction of the members of the body from forbidden use, lest sin obtain dominion in it a). The positive consists in the richer illumination of the intellect for knowing, in the amendment of the will for choosing, and the correction of the sensitive appetite for desiring the spiritual good, and also in the direction of the members of the body to a use pleasing and approved by God, and thus in the restoration of the divine image b).

Proof a: The privative act of renewal, Holy Scripture calls the putting off of the old man, Col. III, 10, and the laying aside of the same, Eph. IV, 22, by a metaphor taken from worn-out, torn, and defiled garments, which we put off and do not resume. We put off the old man, however, when, instructed by the powers of grace, we cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, 2 Cor. VII, 1. By the filthiness of the flesh, every sin is understood which is consummated by the pleasure of the flesh and the senses; such as are not only unchastities, promiscuity, and drunkenness, but also injuries, rapine, thefts, and the like: but the filthiness of the spirit is heresy, idolatry, emulation, dissension, and others, the consummation of which consists without the pleasure of the senses.

Proof b: The positive act of renewal, Holy Scripture calls the putting on of the new man, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of the Creator, Col. III, 10. Wherefore we put on the new man, by following the holiness of life after the example of the heavenly Father and Jesus Christ, so that the image of divine holiness may shine forth in us.

Objection: Dr. Dannhauer most beautifully represents the parts of sanctification when, in Hodof. Phaen. IX, p. 703, he shows it to be accomplished by a) sacrificing the body and all its members, abstracting them from all injustice and vanity of this age, Rom. XII, 1: b) mortifying and crucifying the old Adam, and our own flesh, which always desires evil, by afflicting it with trouble, Gal. of which Christ prescribed the formula, Matt. VI, 5; d) Adorning themselves with the fruits of righteousness, which are produced through Jesus Christ to the glory and praise of God, Phil. I, 11.

Quest. XIII.

Is renewal instantaneous, or successive? Just as the body of sin is weakened more and more by the reborn man as time progresses a): so the reborn man is transformed into the image of God by the Holy Spirit from glory to glory b).

Obs. The body of sin is called the old man metaphorically by Paul in Rom. VI, 6; because it is a complex of many sins, like parts and members. Whence also the various species of sins are called earthly members, Col. III, 5.

Prob. a. Just as in former times those condemned to the cross were affixed to the cross, their limbs were crushed, mortified, and buried: so the old man is successively crucified Rom. VI, 6. when the desires of the flesh are suppressed and as it were constrained; he is crushed, 1 Cor. IX, 27. insofar as the flesh, with the external delights of this world removed, is chastised; he is mortified, Rom. VIII, 13. in that the powers of emerging into sin are taken away from him; once mortified he is buried, Rom. VI, 4. while the memory and thoughts of illicit things are put aside; once buried he is corrupted, so that the whole body of sin may be abolished here incipiently and continuously, and in the other life consummately, Rom. VI, 6.

Prob. b. 1) From 2 Cor. III, 18. We, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, are transformed (μεταμορφούμεθα) into that same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord. Just as Moses of old indeed covered his face when he went out into the assembly of the people; but returning to the tabernacle, and turning himself to the Lord, he beheld the glory of the Lord with unveiled face: so Paul says that we do not, after the manner of the Jews, over whose heart a veil lies, become blind, but with unveiled face behold the glory of the Lord shining in the gospel. And just as Moses had attained this from his secret conversation with God, that his face radiated with a new light: so we, while we contemplate the face of the heavenly Father with the eyes of the mind in the most limpid mirror of the gospel, are illuminated by certain rays, as it were, of wisdom and holiness, and are renewed into the image of God, which from glory to glory, i.e., by new increments, reveals itself more clearly day by day. And this is done by the Spirit of the Lord, who repairs in us by his grace the image of God lost through sin.

2) From 2 Cor. IV, 16. Even though our external man is corrupted: yet the internal is renewed day by day (ἡμέρᾳ καὶ ἡμέρᾳ). Obs. a) The internal and external man, as to substance, is the same; but with respect to carnal desires he is called the external man, and with respect to inherent holiness the internal man. b) The external man is corrupted and mortified by calamities, which withdraw the delights of this world, and apply a bridle, so that he may not exercise his powers. But the internal man grows and is strengthened daily by continued exercises of piety, which burn more fervently under the cross.

Quest. XIV.

What is the end of renewal? The ultimate end of renewal is the glory of God. a) The intermediate end is both the image of God, or inherent righteousness b), and good works c).

Prob. a. Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father, who is in heaven. Matt. V, 16. The ultimate end of renewal, from which good works proceed, is the glory of God.

Prob. b. Put on the new man, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of him who creates him, Col. III, 10. Man is renewed to this end, that the image of God may be repaired in him, which, on the part of the intellect, consists in the true knowledge of the creator, and on the part of the will, in true righteousness and holiness, Eph. IV, 24.

However, righteousness is understood as universal, or complete. Righteousness as universal, or a complex of all virtues, which pertain to Christian morals, and are otherwise wont to be distributed variously according to the two tables of the decalogue. Prob. c.

Latin:

Forma renouationis absoluitur duplici actu, priuatiuo, & positiuo. Priuatiuus consistit in discussione tenebrarum intellectus, in auersione voluntatis a malo, in cohibitione ferociae appetitus sensitui, & in abstractione membrorum corporis ab vsu prohibito, ne peccatum in eodem dominium obtineat a). Positiuus consistit in uberiori illuminatione intellectus ad cognoscendum, in emendatione voluntatis ad eligendum, & correctione appetitus sensitui ad expetendum bonum spirituale, nec non in directione membrorum corporis ad vsum Deo gratum probatumque, atque adeo in imaginis diuinae instauratione b).

Probatio a Actum priuatiuum renouationis S. scriptura vocat exuitionem veteris hominis, Col. III, 10. & eiusdem depositionem, Eph. IV, 22. per metamorphoram petitam a vestibus detritis, laceris & conspurcatis, quas exuimus, & non resumimus. Exuimus autem veterem hominem, cum viribus gratiae instructi mundamus nos ab inquinatione carnis & spiritus, 2 Cor. VII, 1. Per carnis inquinamentum omne peccatum intelligitur, quod voluptate carnis & sensuum consummatur; vti non tantum sunt impudicitiae, commixtiones, ebrietates, sed etiam iniuriae, rapinae, furta & similia: Spiritus vero inquinamentum est haeresis, idolatria, aemulatio, dissensio & alia, quorum consummatio fine voluptate sensuum consistit.

Probatio b Actum positiuum renouationis S. scriptura appellat inductionem noui hominis, qui renouatur in cognitionem secundum imaginem Creatoris, Col. III, 10. Quamobrem induimus nouum hominem, sanctimonia vitae ad exemplar Patris caelestis & Iesu Christi sectando, vt sanctitatis diuinae imago in nobis resplendeat.

Obiectio Sanctificationis partes pulcerrime repraesentat D. DANNH. dum in hodof. phaen. IX. p. 703. eandem fieri ostendit a) sacrificando corpus omniaque membra ipsius, abstrahendo eadem ob omni iniustitia & vanitate... huius saeculi, Rom. XII, 1: b) mortificando & crucifigendo veterem Adamum, carnemque propriam, semper mala concupiscentem, molestia afficiendo, Gal. V, 24.: c) thurificando, vel offerendo Deo thymiama ardentissimarum precum, quarum formulam praescripsit Christus, Matth. VI, 5; d) Exornando semet fructibus iustitiae, quae fiunt per Iesum Christum in gloriam & laudem Dei, Phil. I, 11.

Quaest. XIII.

Sitne renovatio in momento, an successive? Sicut corpus peccati progressu temporis ab homine renato magis magisque eneruatur a): ita homo renatus ad imaginem Dei per Spiritum S. de gloria in gloriam transformatur b).

Obs. Corpus peccati a Paulo Rom. VI, 6. dicitur vetus homo metaphorice; quia est complexus plurium peccatorum, velut partium & membrorum. Vnde & variae peccatorum species, membra terrestria appellantur, Col. III, 5.

Prob. a. Quem ad modum olim cruciarii affigebantur cruci, artus ipsorum contundebantur, mortificabantur, sepeliebantur: ita successive vetus homo crucifigitur Rom. VI, 6. cum desideria carnis comprimuntur & quasi constringuntur; contunditur, 1 Cor. IX, 27. quatenus caro, remotis externis deliciis huius saeculi, castigatur; contulus mortificatur, Rom. VIII, 13. in quantum vires emergendi peccato adimuntur; mortificatus sepelitur, Rom. VI. 4. dum memoria & cogitationes rerum illicitarum seponuntur; sepultus corrumpitur, vt totum corpus peccati, hic inchoate & continuate, in altera vita consummate aboleatur, Rom. VI, 6.

Prob. b. 1) Ex 2. Cor. III, 28. Nos revelata facie gloriam Domini introspicientes, in eam imaginem μεταμορφούμεθα, transformamur a gloria in gloriam, tanquam a Domini Spiritu. Sicut olim Moses obtegebat quidem faciem, cum prodiret in concionem populi; reversus autem ad tabernaculum, & ad Dominum se vertens, facie retecta gloriam Domini aspiciebat: sic ait Paullus, nos non ad modum Iudaeorum, super quorum corde velamen iacet, caecutire, sed retecta facie gloriam Domini in evangelio relucentem intueri. Et quem ad modum Moses ex arcana cum Deo conversatione hoc adeptus erat, vt nova luce radiaret ipsius facies: ita nos, dum in limpidissimo evangelii speculo Patris coelestis faciem oculis mentis contemplamur, illustramur quibusdam quasi radiis sapientiae & sanctitatis, & renouamur ad imaginem Dei, quae de gloria in gloriam, h. e. nouis incrementis de indies clariorem exserit. Idque fit a Domini Spiritu, qui amissam per peccatum imaginem Dei gratia sua in nobis reparat.

2) Ex 2 Cor. IV, 16. Etiamsi externus noster homo corrumpitur: internus tamen renovatur ἡμέρᾳ καὶ ἡμέρᾳ, de die in diem. Obs. a) Internus & externus homo, qua substantiam, est idem; sed respectu desideriorum carnalium externus, respectu inhaerentis sanctitatis internus homo appellatur. b) Externus homo corrumpitur & mortificatur calamitatibus, quae delicias huius mundi subtrahunt, & frenum iniiciunt, ne vires suas exerceat. Internus autem continuatis pietatis exercitiis, quae sub cruce magis fervent, quotidie crescit & corroboratur.

Quaest. XIV.

Quis est finis renovationis? Finis renovationis ultimus est gloria Dei. a) Finis intermedius est tum imago Dei, siue iustitia inhaerens b), tum bona opera c).

Prob. a. Luceto lux vestra coram hominibus, vt videant vestra bona opera, & glorificent Patrem vestrum, qui in caelis est. Matth. V, 16. Renovationis, e qua bona opera proficiscuntur, finis ultimus est gloria Dei.

Prob. b. Induite novum hominem, qui renovatur in cognitionem secundum imaginem eius, qui creat illum, Col. III, 10. Eum in finem renovatur homo, vt in eo reparetur imago Dei, quae, ex parte intellectus, consistit in vera agnitione creatoris, ex parte voluntatis, in vera iustitia & sanctitate, Eph. IV, 24.

Intelligitur autem iustitia velut vniuersalis, seu completa. iustitia velut vniuerfalis, feu complexus omnium virtutum, quae ad mores christianos pertinent, & alias iuxta duas decalogi tabulas varie dispesci solent. Prob. c.


### Q. XVI

Just as the immediate effect of renewal is inherent holiness: so the mediate effect is the zeal and exercise of good works. For inherent holiness is the root of good works, which, by reason of execution, are the effects of renewal; by reason of intention, they are its end: for we are renewed for this reason, that we may perform good works. We learn this from the words of Christ: Every branch that abideth in me, my heavenly Father will purge, i.e., will renew, that it may bring forth more fruit, John XV, 2. And from the words of Paul, Eph. IV, 24. Put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness. Wherefore put away lying and speak every man truth with his neighbor. Where the Apostle connects the external exercise of good works with inherent righteousness.

Quest. XV. Is a renewed man to be proclaimed holy? A renewed man is holy, not of himself, but by grace

Quest. XVI. How manifold is the renewal, or sanctification, of a justified man? The sanctification of a reborn and justified man is threefold: begun, continued, and consummated.

It is begun, whereby the Holy Spirit, through baptism, begins to break the powers of original sin, lest it predominate, to wash away vicious impurity, and to introduce holiness to the baptized. It is continued, whereby the Holy Spirit, by means of the divine word and the use of the Supper, confers immunity from the dominion of sin, successively abolishes the remnants of the old man more and more, and makes the image of God clearer with new increments. It is consummated, whereby the Holy Spirit most fully adorns the blessed, who are freed from the sense and root of sin, with the divine image.

Latin:

Sicut effectus renovationis immediatus est sanctitas inhaerens: ita effectus mediatus est studium & exercitium bonorum operum. Sanctitas quippe inhaerens est radix bonorum operum, quae ratione executionis sunt effectus renovationis; ratione intentionis sunt ipsius finis: ideo enim renovamur, vt bona opera praestemus. Discimus id e verbis Christi: Omnem palmitem, in me manentem, Pater meus caelestis purgabit, i. e. renovabit, vt plures fructus ferat, Io. XV, 2. Et e verbis Pauli, Eph. IV, 24. Induite novum hominem, qui secundum Deum creatus est in iustitia & sanctitate veritatis. Quare deponite mendacium & loquimini veritatem quilibet cum proximo suo. Vbi Apostolus cum iustitia inhaerente externum bonorum operum exercitium connectit.

Quaest. XV. Estne homo renovatus sanctus praedicandus? Homo renovatus est sanctus, non ex se, sed ex gratia

Quaest. XVI. Quotuplex est renovatio, vel sanctificatio hominis iustificati? Sanctificatio hominis renati & iustificati triplex est, inchoata, continuata & consummata.

Inchoata est, qua Spiritus S. per baptismum vires peccati originalis, ne hoc praedominetur, frangere, impuritatem vitiosam abluere, & sanctitatem baptizato introducere incipit. Continuata est, qua Spiritus S. immunitatem a dominio peccati, mediante verbo diuino, & vsu coenae conferat, reliquias veteris hominis successive magis magisque abolet, & imaginem Dei nouis incrementis clariorem efficit. Consummata est, qua Spiritus S. beatos, sensu & radice peccati liberatos, imagine diuina plenissime exornat.


### Q. XVII. Is the renewed man to be called spiritual, or carnal?

The renewed man is spiritual not in whole, but in part, in that he knows, chooses, and does the spiritual good under the guidance of the Holy Spirit ). The same is called carnal not in whole, but in part, not simply and absolutely, but in a certain respect and comparatively, insofar as he has the remnants of sin, and feels the goads of the recalcitrant flesh, with which he must struggle daily ). Moreover, the renewed man is compared partly with Christians who are more advanced in knowledge and holiness ), and partly with the divine law, which he does not perfectly fulfill ).

Obs. When the renewed man is called spiritual, the reason for the denomination is taken from the stronger part, namely, from the prevailing spirit; but when the same is called carnal [*], the reason for the denomination is taken from the weaker part, namely, from the flesh, which is indeed subdued, yet rebellious and resisting, with which the justified man, established in the way of life, wages continuous wars.

Prob. a. 1) From Gal. VI, 1. Brethren, if a man be even overtaken in any fault, you, who are spiritual, restore such a one in the spirit of meekness, considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted. Obs. a) By the Apostle, not presbyters, but all brethren are called spiritual, joined by the bond of faith, whom the Apostle describes in ch. V, 24. 25. as having crucified the flesh, and as living and walking in the spirit. But since renewal admits of degrees, those who are stronger in the spirit are called spiritual, Rom. XV, 1. b) Not in vain does the Apostle say: considering thyself; lest thou also be tempted. If spiritual men were empty of all temptation of the flesh, and of all inclination to sin, that exhortation would be of no use at all.

2) From Rom. VIII, 9. You are not in the flesh, but in the spirit; if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. The regenerate are not in the flesh, i.e., in the power of the flesh, but in the kingdom of the Holy Spirit, in that the Holy Spirit is not only a guest, but also the master of his dwelling. As He dwells in the regenerate, so He also powerfully reigns.

Prob. b. The regenerate are called carnal in a certain respect, 1 Cor. III, 1. 2. Rom. VII, 14. furthermore, because they have sin, and struggle daily with the flesh. That they have sin, St. John teaches, 1 Ep. 1, 8. If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. The regenerate have and feel sin, but they do not commit sin by proairesis, or by deliberate counsel of the mind. D. Chemnitz inculcates this distinction, loc. theol. P. III. p. 104. John shows that there is a difference between having sin and doing sin: and the latter is graver than the former; although sometimes they are taken for one. For sin inheres in all, nor can anyone say that he is entirely clean from all sin. Nevertheless, the pious resist through the grace of the Holy Spirit. But he who completes it by action, translates depraved concupiscences into work, and thus as it were practices the art of sinning, of him Christ pronounces, Jo. VIII, 33: Everyone who does sin is the servant of sin. And Matth. VII, 13: Depart from me all you who work iniquity. That the regenerate struggle daily with the flesh, St. Paul asserts, Gal. V, 16. 17. But I say, walk in the spirit, and you shall not fulfill the lust of the flesh. For the flesh lusts against the spirit: but the spirit against the flesh.

But these things are contrary to one another, so that you do not do the things that you wish. Which words of Paul in the Apol. A. C. p. 91, are explained thus: The flesh distrusts God, trusts in present things, seeks human aids in calamity, even against the will of God, flees afflictions which it ought to bear on account of the command of God, doubts the mercy of God, etc. With such affections the Holy Spirit struggles in the hearts, that He may repress and mortify them, and bring in new spiritual motions.

Prob. c. From I Cor. III, 1. 2. Furthermore I, brethren, could not speak to you as to spiritual, but as to carnal, as to infants in Christ. I gave you milk, and not food. For you were not yet able to digest it, indeed you are not yet able; for you are still carnal. Carnal in that place are not for Paul men unregenerate or unbelieving, but the regenerate, who are beginning to learn the first principles and mysteries of the faith, and to become accustomed to the struggle against the affections, such as are the more unlearned and weaker catechumens, to whom, as to infants, the milk of the Gospel must be instilled in a most simple and catechetical manner, because they are not yet capable of solid food, that is, of the mysteries of the faith, delivered in a more accurate manner.

Prob. d. From Rom. VII, 14. For we know that the law is spiritual; but I am carnal. The law is called spiritual, not only because it has proceeded from the Holy Spirit, but also because, not content with external obedience, it requires internal, perfectly spiritual obedience, which, because of the adhering oldness of sin, the Apostle cannot perform, he professes that he is, not indeed absolutely, but comparatively to the divine law, carnal.

There is an antithesis of the Socinians, who maintain that the struggle of the flesh against the spirit ceases in some, and that Paul in Rom. VII, 14 did not call himself carnal, but assumed the person of a man constituted under the law, not yet regenerate by the Spirit of Christ, and sustains it in that complaint. They rely on the following arguments:

I. To the carnal man, described in Rom. VII, 14 ff., are attributed those predicates which can be said of no regenerate person. For he is said 1) to be sold under sin. But the regenerate person has been freed from sin, Rom. VI, 18: 2) to be captivated by the law of sin, from which the regenerate person has likewise been loosed, Rom. VIII, 2: 3) to serve the law of sin with the flesh. But the regenerate person is a servant of righteousness, Rom VI, 18. 4) He is said to do what he does not wish, v. 20. But the regenerate person has the Holy Spirit and with Him the freedom of acting, I Cor. III, 17. Resp. to I. Distinguish between active and passive selling. Whoever sells himself actively, to the full obedience of predominating sin, like King Ahab, I Kings XXI, 2, he is unregenerate; I concede. But he who is sold passively, like Joseph, submitting to a foreign master with a reluctant mind, he remains regenerate. This one is sold under sin, as regards the evident sense of indwelling sin, but not as regards its full dominion. To II. Distinguish between voluntary and involuntary captivity. The regenerate man is snatched away and captivated against his will, like Samson, to do that toward which he is not moved with full intention. To III. The Apostle serves the law of God with an enlightened mind, he serves the law of sin with the flesh (insofar as he is infected by the stain of indwelling sin), with a servitude not spontaneous, but involuntary. To IV. Distinguish between freedom from the dominion and from the sense of sin. Although the renewed man has been freed from the dominion of sin, he is not yet immune from the sense and root of sin.

II. Whoever has crucified the flesh, he does not have to struggle with the flesh. Who would fight with a man affixed to a cross? But the regenerate man, etc. Gal. V, 24. E. Resp. Whoever has crucified the flesh by a crucifixion not only begun and continued, but also consummated, he does not have to struggle with the flesh. But the regenerate are commanded daily to crucify and mortify the flesh, Rom. VIII, 13. E. their crucifixion of the flesh is not consummated.

III. Whoever conquers the world, they no longer have to struggle with the flesh. But the regenerate, etc. I John V, 4. E. Resp. Whoever conquers the world with a full victory, by which the enemy is eradicated, they do not have to struggle with the flesh. But the regenerate conquer, as Joshua conquered the Canaanites, nay, not that the carnal desires of the world should be extirpated, but that these spiritual enemies should be placed under the yoke, although, impatient of the yoke, they may from time to time affect dominion.

Latin:

Homo renovatus est spiritualis non ex toto; sed ex parte, in quantum duce Spiritu S. bonum spirituale cognoscit, eligit, facit ). Idem carnalis dicitur non ex toto, sed ex parte, non simpliciter, & absolute, sed certo respectu & comparate, quatenus reliquias peccati habet, stimulosque carnis recalcitrantis, cum qua ipsi quotidie decertandum est, sentit ). Comparatur autem homo renovatus partim cum Christianis cognitione & sanctitate provectioribus ), partim cum lege divina, quam non perfecte implet ).

Obs. Quando homo renovatus dicitur spiritualis, denominationis ratio sumitur a potiori, scil. a praevalente spiritu; at quando idem carnalis appellatur [*], ratio denominationis sumitur a sequiori, nimirum a carne subacta quidem, rebellante tamen & obluctante, cum qua homo iustificatus, in via vitae constitutus, continua bella gerit.

Prob. a. 1) Ex Gal. VI, 1. Fratres, si etiam praeoccupatus fuerit homo in aliquo lapsu, vos, qui spirituales (estis) restaurate talem spiritu mansuetudinis, respiciens teipsum, ne & tu tenteris. Obs. a) Spirituales vocantur ab Apostolo non presbyteri, sed omnes fratres, fidei vinculo coniuncti, quos describit Apostolus c. V, 24. 25. quod carnem crucifixerint, quod spiritu vivant & ambulent. Cum autem renovatio gradus admittat, spirituales dicuntur, qui spiritu sunt robustiores, Rom. XV, 1. b) Non frustra dicit Apostolus: respiciens te ipsum; ne & tu tenteris. Si homines spirituales vacui essent ab omni tentatione carnis, ab omni ad peccandum proclivitate, ista paraneesi opus minime foret.

2) Ex Rom. VIII, 9. Vos non estis in carne, sed in spiritu; siquidem Spiritus Dei habitat in vobis. Renati non sunt in carne, i. e. in potestate carnis, sed in regno Spiritus S. eo, quod Spiritus S. non hospes tantum, sed & dominus fui domicilii est. Vt ille in renatis habitat, ita & valide regnat.

Prob. b. Renati certo respectu dicuntur carnales, 1 Cor. III, 1. 2. Rom. VII, 14. praeterea, quod peccatum habent, & cum carne quotidie conflictantur. Quod peccatum habeant, docet S. Ioannes, 1 Ep, 1, 8. Si dixerimus, quod peccatum non habeamus, nos ipsos seducimus, & veritas non est in nobis. Renati peccatum habent & sentiunt, sed ex proaeresi, sive deliberato animi consilio peccatum non faciunt. Inculcat hanc distinctionem D. Chemnit. loc. theol. P. III. p. 104. Ioannes ostendit, discrimen esse, inter habere peccatum, & facere peccatum: & grauius hoc est, quam illud; licet interdum pro vno accipiantur. Nam peccatum omnibus inhaeret, nec quisquam dicere potest, se prorsus mundum esse ab omni peccato. Attamen pii per gratiam Spiritus S. resistunt, Qui autem opere complet, in opus prauas concupiscentias traducit, & sic quasi artem peccandi exercet, de eo Christus pronuntiat, Io. VIII, 33: Omnis faciens peccatum, servus est peccati. Et Matth. VII, 13: Discedite a me omnes, qui operamini peccatum. Quod renati quotidie cum carne conflictentur, asserit S. Paullus, Gal. V, 16. 17. Dico autem, spiritu ambulate, tum concupiscentiam carnis non perficietis. Nam caro concupiscit aduersus spiritum: sed spiritus aduersus carnem.

Hæc autem aduersantur inuicem, vt non, quæ vultis, ea faciatis. Quæ verba Paulli in Apol. A. C. p. 91. ita explicantur: Caro diffidit Deo, confidit rebus præsentibus, quærit humana auxilia in calamitate, etiam contra voluntatem Dei, fugit afflictiones, quas debebat tolerare propter mandatum Dei, dubitat de Dei misericordia &c. Cum talibus affectibus luctatur Spiritus S. in cordibus, vt eos reprimat ac mortificet, & inferat nouos spirituales motus.

Prob. c. Ex I Cor. III, 1. 2. Præterea ego, fratres, non poteram vobiscum loqui vt spiritualibus, sed vt carnalibus, vt infantibus in Christo. Lac vobis dedi, & non cibum. Nondum enim poteratis digerere, immo neque adhuc potestis; adhuc enim carnales estis. Carnales l. c. non sunt Paullo homines irregeniti aut increduli, sed renati, qui primum & mysteria fidei incipiunt addiscere, & luctæ contra affectus assuescere, quales sunt catechumeni rudiores & infirmiores, quibus velut infantibus lac euangelii modo simplicissimo & catechetico instillandum est, eo, quod cibi solidi h. e. mysteriorum fidei, modo accuratiori traditorum, nondum sunt capaces.

Prob. d. Ex Rom. VII, 14. Scimus namque, quod lex spiritualis fit; ego vero carnalis sum. Lex spiritualis dicitur, non tantum quia a Spiritu S. est profecta, sed & quia non contenta externa obedientia, internum, perfecte spirituale obsequium requirit, quod cum ob adhærentem vetustatem peccati, præstare nequeat Apostolus, profitetur, se non quidem absolute; sed comparate ad legem diuinam carnalem esse.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, statuentium, luctam carnis contra spiritum in quibusdam cessare, neque Paullum Rom. VII, 14. seipsum carnalem vocare, sed personam hominis sub lege constituti, necdum Spiritu Christi renati, sumsisse, & in illa querela sustinere. Nituntur sequentibus argumentis:

I. Carnali homini, Rom. VII, 14. seqq. descripto ea tribuuntur prædicata, quæ de nullo renato dici possunt. Dicitur enim 1) venundatus sub peccatum. Sed renatus liberatus est a peccato, Rom. VI, 18: 2) captiuatus lege peccati, a qua renatus itidem solutus est, Rom. VIII, 2: 3) carne seruiens legi peccati. Sed renatus est seruus iustitiæ, Rom VI, 18. 4) Dicitur facere, quæ non vult, v. 20. Sed renatus habet Spiritum S. & cum eo libertatem agendi, I Cor. III, 17. Resp. ad I. Dist. inter venditionem actuam, & passiuam. Quicunque se actiue vendit, ad plenum obsequium peccati prædominantis, instar regis Achabi, I Reg. XXI, 2. ille est irregenitus; concedo. Sed qui passiue venditur, ad instar Iosephi, dominum alienum animo reluctante subeuntis, ille manet renatus. Hic venundatus est sub peccatum, quoad peccati inhabitantis euidentem sensum, non autem quoad plenum eius dominium. Ad II. Dist. inter captiuitatem voluntariam, & inuoluntariam. Homo renatus inuitus abripitur & captiuatur, Simsonis instar, ad faciendum id, in quod plena intentione non fertur. Ad III. Apostolus feruit mente illuminata legi Dei, feruit carne (quatenus labe inhærentis peccati infectus est) legi peccati, seruitute non spontanea, sed inuoluntaria. Ad IV. Dist. inter libertatem a dominio, & sensu peccati. Quamuis homo renouatus liberatus sit a dominio peccati, non tamen a sensu & radice peccati immunis est.

II. Quicunque crucifixit carnem, illi cum carne non est confligendum. Quis cum homine cruci affixo decertaret? Atqui homo renatus &c. Gal. V, 24. E. Resp. Quicunque crucifixit carnem crucifixione non tantum inchoata & continuata, sed etiam consummata, illi cum carne non est confligendum. At renati iubentur quotidie carnem crucifigere & mortificare, Rom. VIII, 13. E. illorum crucifixio carnis non est consummata.

III. Quicunque vincunt mundum, illis non amplius luctandum est cum carne. Atqui renati &c. I Io, V, 4. E. Resp. Quicunque vincunt mundum victoria plena, qua hostis eradicatur, illis non est luctandum cum carne.
