The triune God a), the Father b), the Son of God c), and the Holy Spirit d).

Proof a. From Rom. 8:30: Whom God justified, them He also glorified. Obj. a) Δοξάζειν, to glorify, here does not signify to celebrate the glory of someone, in the way that creatures glorify God glorify, Matt. V, 16; ch. IX, 8; ch. XV, 31; but to confer glory and excellence upon someone: in which signification it is also used of the Redeemer himself, John XII, 16; ch. XIII, 32;

ch. XVII, 5. b) Paul says that God has glorified those who are justified, which is in no way to be understood of any glorification of this world, since Scripture does not attribute δοξασμὸν [glorification] to the elect in this life; but it must be taken concerning the δοξασμῷ [glorification] that is future after this life. Cf. Rom. VIII, 17, 18. However, the past tense is used because of the certainty of future glorification.

Proof b. God the Father is to bring many sons into glory. Heb. II, 10.

Proof c. Christ, the righteous judge, will give the crown of righteousness to all who love his appearing, 2 Tim. IV, 8.

Proof d. The Holy Spirit is called the spirit of glory, 1 Pet. IV, 14, because he is not only glorious in himself, but also confers glory upon us, and renders us certain of the same in the sufferings of this world.

Question III.

What impelled God to glorify men who had fallen into sin? Internally, goodness and mercy impelled God [a)]; externally, the merit [b)] and intercession of Christ [c)].

Proof a. God saved us according to his mercy, Tit. III, 5. Obj. a) It was not the merits of works of righteousness, which are none, that provoked God to save us sinners, but mercy, elicited by no merits of men, impelled him. b) God is said to have saved in the past not only because of the certainty of future blessedness, but also because of the foretaste of the same in this life.

Proof b. The external and meritorious impulsive cause is the merit of Christ, by which satisfaction was made to divine justice, which had been injured by the sins of men. Therefore, the merit of Christ accomplishes this, that God may save man while his justice remains intact. Paul inculcates this, Rom. V, 10: If, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son; much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved in his life.

Proof c. Christ, by virtue of his merit, intercedes with God the Father to obtain for us eternal glory. Father, those whom you have given me, I will that, where I am, they also may be with me, that they may see my glory, which you have given me, John XVII, 24.

Question IV.

By what means does God glorify us? The means offering and exhibiting salvation are the word of the Gospel [a)] and the sacraments [b)]. The receiving medium is faith in Christ [c)]. The executive means, and those introducing into glory, are death, the resurrection of the dead, the consummation of this age, and the final judgment [d)].

Proof a. The word of the Gospel is the word of salvation, Acts XIII, 26. It is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes, Rom. I, 16.

Proof b. God saved us according to his mercy, through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, Tit. III, 5. And in the Eucharist we receive the body and blood of Christ for the remission of sins, Matt. XXVI, 27. But where there is remission of sins, there is life and salvation, as regards the προποτισμὸν [foretaste], and the certain hope of consummated blessedness.

Proof c. We are saved through faith, Eph. II, 8. And we live by faith, Rom. I, 16.

Proof d. Through death, resurrection, and the final judgment we are introduced into heavenly glory, concerning which [we shall speak] below.

Q.

V. What is the end and effect of glorification? The end of glorification, on the part of God, is the praise of divine grace ; on the part of man, the end and effect of glorification is eternal beatitude .

Proof a. For just as the end of election to eternal life is the glory of divine grace, Eph. 1:6, so also is it the same end for the actual bestowal of eternal life. Therefore, the angels and blessed men, falling down before the throne of God and worshipping Him, say: Amen! Blessing, and glory, and wisdom, and thanksgiving, and honor, and power, and might be to our God forever and ever. Amen!

Rev. 7:11, 12. Proof b. The end and effect of glorification is glory, and that eternal, 1 Pet. 5:10. It is called otherwise beatitude, and eternal life, and the salvation of souls, 1

Pet. 1:9. Q.

VI. Who are glorified by God? Sinners who are justified , who persevere in faith until the end of life , and who have departed from this life , are glorified by God. Proof a. Those whom God justified, them He also glorified, Rom. 8:30. Proof b.

From Matt. 10:22: He who shall have persevered until the end, he shall be saved. And to the faithful even unto death is given the crown of life, Rev. 2:10.

Proof c. In this life, no one is in possession of consummated beatitude. St. John hints at this, 1 Ep. ch. 3:2: Beloved, now we are the children of God, but it has not yet been manifested what we shall be. We know, however, that if it shall be manifested, we shall be like Him,

because we shall see Him as He is.

Q. VII. Is both the soul and the body a participant in eternal beatitude? Primarily the soul , secondarily the body, enjoys eternal beatitude .

Proof a. The end of faith is the salvation of souls, 1 Pet. 1:9. Christ came to save souls, Luke 9:56. The Word of God makes souls saved, James 1:21. Obs. It is called the salvation of souls, not because it will be of souls alone, but because it happens partly to the soul, which is to enjoy it immediately as soon as it has departed from the body, partly it happens to the soul as the most important part, and partly it is to come to the body not without the soul, and in a certain way through the soul. Conf. D. Seb. Schmid, aphorism. theol. p. 198.

Proof b. The body of the faithful will be resurrected in glory, 1 Cor. 15:43, and will be transformed by the Lord Jesus Christ, so that it becomes conformed to His glory, Phil.

3:21. Q. VIII. In what does the salvation of souls formally consist?

The salvation of souls formally consists in the beatific vision and fruition of God, which is accompanied by the love of God, most abundant joy, and the perfect holiness of life.

Obs. We treated of the beatific vision and fruition of God, as the formal end of theology,

above in Book I. Q. IX.

In what does the future beatitude of bodies consist? The beatitude of bodies consists in the complex of those perfections with which the bodies of the elect will be divinely adorned in the

kingdom of glory. Q.

X. What will be the perfections of the glorified bodies? With Holy Scripture shining the way, the perfections of the glorified bodies will be principally three: a) spirituality, b) clarity, c) impassibility, from which other endowments of glorified bodies flow, and are elicited by consequence.

Prob. a. From 1 Cor. XV, 44. It is sown an animal body, it shall be raised a spiritual body. The ψυχικὸν or animal body is that which in this life is subject to animal affections and actions, to generation, nutrition, augmentation, motion, needing food, drink, clothing, air, external heat, and is governed by the soul as an internal principle. The body is called spiritual not by reason of substance, because it is not changed into spirit; but by reason of qualities, inasmuch as it will be free from spiritual operations, and will be moved by the spirit of God: not that the soul will then cease to move, but that it itself, also full of spiritual light, will move the body spiritually, nor will it need food or drink, sleep, or marriage, but will serve heavenly and isangelic functions. Since, therefore, a spiritual body will rise, it follows that it will be: 1) Invisible, in relation to eyes not glorified. Nevertheless, glorified bodies can be seen by eyes not yet glorified, if divine dispensation should occur. Let the saints be an example to us, who rose with Christ, and appeared not to all, but to many, whose eyes were opened, Matth. XXVII, 53. 2) Impalpable: for palpability is a property of an animal body, not a spiritual one. Nevertheless, the blessed will be able to present their bodies to be touched, when they themselves wish; just as Christ presented his glorious body to the disciples to be touched, Jo. XX, 20. Luc. XXIV, 39. 3) Subtle, i.e., apt for penetrating solid bodies. Thus Christ penetrated closed doors with his glorified body, to which our bodies in the heavenly fatherland will be conformed, Jo. XX, 19. Phil. III, 21. 4) Illocal, which will not be in a circumscriptive where, but a definitive one. It will not be circumscribed by an ambient body, but will define some πõ for itself at will. 5) Agile, which will be able to be moved most easily and most quickly, where the spirit, or soul, wishes to be.

Prob. b. The glorified body will be clear, and shining like the sun, Matth. XIII, 43. Yet it will not for that reason be transparent like glass. It will shine forth, as the face of Christ, of Moses and of Elias on Mount Tabor, Matth. XVII, 1. 2. From this it follows that it will be beautiful and most fair. It is sown in ignominy, it will rise in glory, 1 Cor. XV, 44.

Prob. c. The glorified body will be impassible; for the reason that it will be subject to no corruptive passion arising either from internal or from external causes. For it will neither hunger, nor thirst; nor will the sun fall upon it, nor any heat, Apocal. VII, 16. It follows from this that it will be immortal and incorruptible, and thus always healthy and firm. It is sown in corruptibility, it will rise in incorruptibility, 1 Cor. XV, 42. Adam, whole, was able not to die; the blessed will not be able to die, the power of dying being removed as much as the proximity, Luc. XX, 36.

Latin:

Deus trinus a), Pater b), Filius Dei c), & Spiritus S. d).

Prob. a. Ex Rom. VIII, 30. Quos Deus iustificauit, eos etiam glorificauit. Obs. a) Δοξάζειν, glorificare, hic non significat gloriam alicuius celebrare, quomodo creaturae Deum glorificant, Matth. V, 16. c. IX, 8. c. XV, 31. sed gloriam atque excellentiam alicui conferre: qua in significatione etiam de ipso redemptore usurpatur, Io. XII, 16. c. XIII, 32. c.

XVII, 5. b) Paullus dicit, quod Deus iustificatos glorificaverit, quod nullo modo de glorificatione aliqua huius mundi intelligendum, cum scriptura δοξασμὸν, electis in hac vita non tribuat; sed de δοξασμῷ, futuro post hanc vitam accipi debet. Conf. Rom. VIII, 17. 18. Ponitur autem præteritum ob futuræ glorificationis certitudinem.

Prob. b. Deus Pater multos filios in gloriam adducturus est. Hebr. II, 10.

Prob. c. Christus, iustus iudex, dabit coronam iustitiæ omnibus, qui amant apparitionem ipsius, 2 Tim. IV, 8.

Prob. d. Spiritus S. dicitur spiritus gloriæ, 1 Petr. IV, 14. quia non tantum in se est gloriosus, sed etiam gloriam nobis confert, & eiusdem in passionibus huius mundi nos certos reddit.

Quæst. III. Quid impulit Deum ad glorificandum homines in peccatum prolapsos?

Interne Deum impulit bonitas & misericordia a); externe meritum b) & intercessio Christi c).

Prob. a. Deus iuxta misericordiam suam saluavit nos, Tit. III, 5. Obs. a) Non operum iustitiæ merita, quæ nulla sunt, Deum ad saluandum nos peccatores prouocarunt, sed impulit eum misericordia nullis hominum meritis elicita. b) Deus in præterito saluasse dicitur non tantum ob certitudinem futuræ beatitudinis, sed etiam ob eiusdem prægustum in hac vita.

Prob. b. Caussa impulsiva externa & meritoria est meritum Christi, quo satisfactum est iustitiæ diuinæ, peccatis hominum læsæ. Id ergo præstat meritum Christi, vt Deus salua iustitia sua hominem saluet. Inculcat hoc Paullus, Rom. V, 10. Si, cum essemus hostes, reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem Filii ipsius; multo magis reconciliati saluabimur in vita eius.

Prob. c. Christus, vi meriti sui, apud Deum Patrem interpellat ad impetrandam nobis æternam gloriam. Pater, quos dedisti mihi, volo, vt, vbi sum ego, etiam illi sint mecum, vt videant gloriam meam, quam dedisti mihi, Io. XVII, 24.

Quæst. IV. Quibus mediis Deus nos glorificat?

Media salutis offerentia & exhibentia sunt verbum euangelii a) & sacramenta b). Medium recipiens est fides in Christum c). Media exsecutiva, & in gloriam introducentia, sunt mors, resurrectio mortuorum, consummatio huius sæculi, & extremum iudicium d).

Prob. a. Verbum euangelii est verbum salutis, Act. XIII, 26. Est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti, Rom. I, 16.

Prob. b. Deus iuxta misericordiam suam saluavit nos, per lauacrum regenerationis & renouationis Spiritus S. Tit. III, 5. Et in eucharistia accipimus corpus & sanguinem Christi in remissionem peccatorum, Matth. XXVI, 27. Sed vbi est remissio peccatorum; ibi est vita & salus, quoad προποτισμὸν, & certam spem consummatæ beatitudinis.

Prob. c. Saluamur per fidem, Eph. II, 8. Et viuimus ex fide, Rom. I, 16.

Prob. d. Per mortem, resurrectionem & iudicium extremum introducimur in gloriam cœlestem, de quibus infra. cæleftem, de quibus infra.

Quaest. V. Quis est finis & effectus glorificationis?

Finis glorificationis, ex parte Dei, est laus gratiae divinae ; ex parte hominis, glorificationis finis & effectus est aeterna beatitudo .

Prob. a. Prout enim electionis ad vitam aeternam finis est gloria gratiae divinae, Eph. I, 6. ita & actualis collationis vitae aeternae idem finis est. Idcirco angeli & homines beati, procumbentes ante thronum Dei, eunque adorantes dicunt: Amen! Benedictio, & gloria, & sapientia, & gratiarum actio, & honor, & potentia, & robur Deo nostro in saecula saeculorum. Amen! Apoc. VII, 11. 12.

Prob. b. Finis & effectus glorificationis est gloria, eaque aeterna, 1 Petr. V, 10. Vocatur alias beatitudo, & vita aeterna, & salus animarum, 1 Petr. I, 9.

Quaest. VI. Quinam a Deo glorificantur?

Glorificantur a Deo peccatores iustificati , in fide usque ad finem vitae perseverantes , & ex hac vita egressi .

Prob. a. Quos Deus iustificavit, hos glorificavit, Rom. VIII, 30.

Prob. b. Ex Matth. X, 22. Qui perseveraverit usque ad finem, iste servabitur. Et fideli usque ad mortem datur corona vitae, Apoc. II, 10.

Prob. c. In hac vita consummatae beatitudinis nemo est compos. Innuit hoc S. Ioannes, 1 ep. c. III, 2. Dilecti, iam filii Dei sumus, sed nondum manifestatum est, quid futuri simus. Scimus tamen, quod, si manifestabitur, similes ipsi futuri simus, quia videbimus ipsum, sicuti est.

Quaest. VII. Num tam anima, quam corpus, aeternae beatitudinis particeps est?

Primario anima , secundario corpus aeterna potitur beatitudine .

Prob. a. Finis fidei est salus animarum, 1 Petr. I, 9. Christus venit ad servandum animas, Luc. IX, 56. Verbum Dei salvas facit animas, Iac. I, 21. Obs. Dicitur salus animarum, non quod solarum animarum futura fit, sed quod partim fit animae, statim ea fruiturae, quam primum a corpore discesserit, partim animae fit potissima ex parte, partim corpori non sine anima, & per animam quodammodo obventura fit. Conf. D. Seb. Schmidii aphorism. theol. p. 198.

Prob. b. Corpus fidelium resuscitabitur in gloria, 1 Cor. XV, 43. & transformabitur a Domino Iesu Christo, ut fit conforme gloriae ipsius, Phil. III, 21.

Quaest. VIII. In quo formaliter consistit salus animarum?

Salus animarum formaliter consistit in visione & fruitione Dei beatifica, quam comitatur amor Dei, gaudium cumulatissimum, & sanctitas vitae perfecta.

Obs. De visione & fruitione Dei beatifica, tanquam fine theologiae formali, supra libr. I. egimus.

Quaest. IX. In quo consistit futura corporum beatitudo?

Beatitudo corporum consistit in complexu perfectionum illarum, quibus hominum electorum corpora in regno gloriae divinitus exornabuntur.

Quaest. X. Quae erunt perfectiones corporum glorificatorum?

Praelucente S. scriptura perfectiones corporum glorificatorum praecipue tres erunt; a) spiritualitas, b) claritas, c) impassibilitas, e quibus aliae corporum glorificatorum dotes fluunt, & per consequentiam eliciuntur. consequentiam eliciuntur. consequentiam eliciuntur.

Prob. a. Ex 1 Cor. XV, 44. Seminatur corpus animale, resuscitabitur corpus spirituale. Corpus ψυχικὸν seu animale est, quod in hac vita animalibus subiectum est affectionibus, & actionibus, generationi, nutritioni, augmentationi, motui, indigens cibo, potu, vestitu, aëre, calore externo, & anima, vt principio interno, regitur. Corpus spirituale dicitur non ratione substantiae, quia non mutatur in spiritum; sed ratione qualitatum, quippe quod operationibus spiritualibus vacabit, & mouebitur spiritu Dei: non quod anima tunc cessabit mouere, sed quod ipsa quoque plena luce spirituali corpus spiritualiter motura est, nec cibo aut potu, somno, aut matrimonio indigebit, sed coelestibus & isangelicis functionibus inseruiet. Quoniam itaque resurget corpus spirituale, sequitur, vt illud futurum sit: 1) Inuisibile, in relatione ad oculos non glorificatos. Possunt tamen ab oculis nondum glorificatis corpora glorificata videri, si diuina accesserit dispensatio. Exemplo sint nobis sancti, qui cum Christo resurrexerunt, & apparuerunt non omnibus, sed multis, quibus oculi fuerunt aperti, Matth. XXVII, 53. 2) Impalpabile: nam palpabile est proprietas corporis animalis, non spiritualis. Nihilo tamen minus beati poterunt corpora sua palpanda exhibere, quando ipsi voluerint; perinde, vt Christus corpus suum gloriosum discipulis exhibuit palpandum, Io. XX, 20. Luc. XXIV, 39. 3) Subtile, i. e. aptum ad penetrandum corpora solida. Sic Christus ianuas clausas penetrauit suo corpore glorificato, cui nostra corpora in patria cœlesti erunt conformia, Io. XX, 19. Phil. III, 21. 4) Illocale, quod non in vbi circumscriptiuo, sed definitiuo erit. Non circumscribetur corpore ambiente, sed pro lubitu aliquod πõ sibi definiet. 5) Agile, quod facillime ac celerrime moueri poterit, vbi volet esse spiritus, siue anima.

Prob. b. Clarum erit corpus glorificatum, & lucens instar solis, Matth. XIII, 43. Neque tamen ideo instar vitri pellucidum futurum est. Refulgebit, vt facies Christi, Mosis & Eliae in monte Thabor, Matth. XVII, 1. 2. Ex hoc sequitur, quod futurum sit formosum & pulcerrimum. Seminatur in ignominia, resurget in gloria, 1 Cor. XV, 44.

Prob. c. Impassibile erit corpus glorificatum; propterea, quod nulli passioni corruptiuae siue ab internis, siue ab externis caussis prouenienti obnoxium erit. Neque enim esuriet, neque sitiet; neque cadet super illud sol, neque vllus æstus, Apocal. VII, 16. Consequitur ex hoc, quod futurum sit immortale & incorruptibile, adeoque semper sanum & firmum. Seminatur in corruptibilitate, resurget in incorruptibilitate, 1 Cor. XV, 42. Adamus integer poterat non mori, beati non poterunt mori, potentia moriendi tam remota, quam proxima sublata, Luc. XX, 36.


### Quest. XI. What perfections will the whole man have in eternal beatitude?

The whole man will shine forth in the future life with the image of God most perfectly restored a), and will celebrate God with all the powers of soul and body b).

Prob. a. The image of God consists in the conformity of man with the knowledge, justice, purity, and immortality of God. Which gifts will be most abundantly conferred upon the blessed. That which John indicates, 1 ep. c. III, 22. We know, if he shall be manifested, that we shall be like him; because we shall see him, as he is. The light of glory will manifest and represent God, to be seen by the eyes of the intellect (*). But the vision of God will illuminate the mind with wisdom, it will perfect the will with love

of God and holiness, He will adorn the body with immortality, so that between God and the blessed there may be a visible ὁμοίωσις, or likeness, and a κοινωνία τῆς θείας φύσεως [communion of the divine nature].

Prob. b. From Apoc. V, 9. The blessed sing a new song, saying with a loud voice: Worthy is the Lamb that was slain, to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and glory, and blessing.

Latin:

Totus homo imagine Dei perfectissime instaurata in futura vita resplendescet a), & cunctis animæ corporisque viribus Deum celebrabit b).

Prob. a. Imago Dei consistit in conformitate hominis cum scientia, iustitia, puritate & immortalitate Dei. Quae dotes in beatos vberrime conferentur. Id quod indicat Ioannes, 1 ep. c. III, 22. Scimus, si manifestabitur, quod similes ipsi futuri simus; quia videbimus ipsum, sicut est. Lumen gloriae manifestabit atque repraesentabit Deum, oculis intellectus videndum (*). Visio autem Dei illustrabit mentem sapientia, voluntatem perficiet amore

Dei & sanctitate, corpus ornabit immortalitate, vt inter Deum & beatos conspicua sit ὁμοίωσις, siue similitudo, & κοινωνία τῆς θείας φύσεως.

Prob. b. Ex Apoc. V, 9. Canunt beati canticum nouum, dicentes magna voce: Dignus est agnus occisus, qui accipiat potentiam, & diuitias, & sapientiam, & robur, & gloriam, & benedictionem.


### Q. XII. What will be the external goods of the blessed?

The external goods of the blessed will be a) most sweet conversation, b) most pleasant habitation.

Prob. a. The blessed will converse 1) with God and Christ, to be with whom, while afflicted in this mortal life, they desired, Phil. I, 23; 2) with angels and elect men. For they have come to myriads of angels and to the church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, Hebr. XII, 22, 23. Than which association nothing is sweeter, nothing more lovely.

Prob. b. The dwelling of the blessed will shine with brightness, will flourish with pleasantness, will thrive with perpetuity, Apoc. XXI, 10.

Latin:

Bona externa beatorum erunt a) dulcissima conuersatio, b) amœnissima habitatio.

Prob. a. Conuersabuntur beati 1) cum Deo & Christo, cum quo esse, in hac vita mortali afflicti, desiderarunt, Phil. I, 23; 2) cum angelis & electis hominibus. Accesserunt enim ad myriades angelorum & ad ecclesiam primogenitorum in cœlis conscriptorum, Hebr. XII, 22. 23. Qua consuetudine nihil dulcius, nihil amabilius.

Prob. b. Domicilium beatorum fulgebit claritate, florebit amœnitate, wigebit perennitate, Apoc. XXI, 10.


### Q. XIII. When will these perfections befall the blessed?

The mentioned perfections will befall the blessed as soon as the soul has been separated from their body a). But on the last day those gifts will be more conspicuous and more abundant, the soul being reunited with the body b). Prob.

a. Prob. a. 1) From Apoc. XIV, 13. Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord, ἀπ' ἄρτι from now, i.e., from that instant in which they die. 2) Souls after death sing, Apoc. IV, 8. They glorify Him who sits upon the throne, v. 9. They adore the same, having cast down their crowns, v. 10. They have vials, cap. VIII. They cry with a loud voice, cap. VI, 10. They follow the Lamb whithersoever He goes, cap. XI, 4. They enjoy eternal happiness before the resurrection of the flesh. 3) The same is evident by examples. Moses, dead and buried, was seen in heavenly glory, Luc. IX, 31. Christ promised the converted thief: today you will be with me in paradise, Luc. XXIII, 3. Paul desired to be dissolved and to be with Christ, Phil. I, 24. To be with Christ signifies to enjoy the same happiness which He enjoys.

There is an antithesis of the Psychopannychians, Anabaptists, and Socinians, who maintain that separated souls do nothing or suffer nothing, but lie immersed in deep sleep. Their stronger arguments are:

I. The piously deceased are said to sleep, Matth. IX, 24. Io. XI,

1. Therefore, the souls of the fallen feel no joys before they are reunited with their bodies. Resp.

The piously deceased sleep only as regards the body; because their souls enjoy the blessed vision of God in heaven, Act. XIV,

13. more-as regards the nature of God Himself.

For the body, although most subtle and adorned with certain perfections of spirit, nevertheless retains its corporeal nature; which we constantly defend against the Socinians.

But it cannot be that corporeal eyes should see a spirit, clothed with no form of body, nay, a most perfect spirit:

wherefore God is excellently named ὁ ἀόρατος [the invisible], 1 Tim. I,

17. and indeed so significantly, that no man has seen Him, nor will ever see Him, and not even then, when eternal praises are decreed to Him, 1 Tim. VI, 16. and are to be considered as watching more, than they ever watched in the body: for they have no rest from celebration, neither by night, nor by day, Apoc.

IV, 8. II. Faithful souls enter into rest, Hebr. IV, 3. and rest under the heavenly altar, Apoc. VI, 9. 11. Therefore, they do not enjoy heavenly pleasure.

Resp.

1) Faithful souls rest from the works, labors, and troubles of this life, Apoc.

XIV, 13. but they do not rest from heavenly operations, nor are they buried in sleep.

For God also is said to have rested on the seventh day, Gen.

II, 1. who nevertheless does not sleep, but works perpetually. 2) Blessed souls are under the altar, i.e., under the protection and fellowship of Christ, and they rest, i.e., they patiently await the final liberation of the church and the reunion with the bodies to be resurrected; but they are not seized by inert sleep; because they cry out with a loud voice, v. 9. III. Christians persevering in faith receive the crown of righteousness on the last day, 2 Tim.

IV, 8. when the pious shall first appear with Christ in glory, Col. III, 4. Therefore, before the last day they are not partakers of eternal glory.

Resp.

2 Tim.

IV, 8. the Apostle speaks of the crown of righteousness to be given not to the soul, which has already received it, but to be given to the whole supposit, consisting of soul and body, i.e., Paul, and all faithful worshippers of Christ.

IV. Whoever maintains that souls have entered into eternal life before the day of the last judgment, from their opinion flows this absurdity, that there is no need for a last judgment: But the evangelical doctors etc.

Therefore.

The major is proven: because in their view they are to be adjudged to eternal joys on the day on which they are separated from the body.

What need then is there for a last judgment?

Resp.

Distinguish between the particular judgment and the universal.

The former is instituted on the day of death, the latter on the last day.

Yet there is need for a universal judgment, 1) for the public recognition of the judge and redeemer Christ; 2) for the manifestation of divine glory, justice, and mercy; 3) for the consummation of rewards and punishments with respect to the whole man; 4) for the greater exaltation of the pious and the confusion of the impious, so that the former may be publicly crowned, and the latter, on the contrary, may be confounded in the most illustrious assembly, Sap. III, 10.

V. If the souls of the pious separated from their bodies enjoyed heavenly happiness, the souls of the holy fathers would possess consummated blessedness without us: But the consequent is false: Therefore, the antecedents are also.

The falsity of the consequent is proven from Hebr. XI, 39.

40. The holy fathers did not obtain the promise (the consummated blessedness promised to the faithful); because God provided something better for us, lest they should be consummated without us (enjoying consummated blessedness).

The holy fathers did not receive the promise (the consummated blessedness promised to the faithful); because God provided something better for us, so that they might not be perfected without us (might not enjoy the consummated blessedness).

Resp.

Blessedness is either consummated in a certain respect, such as befits the separated soul; or it is absolutely consummated, which is that of the whole supposit after the reunion of the soul with the body.

The Apostle speaks of the consummated blessedness of body and soul together, insofar as it is to be given with the end of the world at the last judgment of all.

If the ancients had obtained this consummation without us, the world would have ceased before we were born, and thus we would never have been heirs of eternal life.

VI. The dead do not praise God, Ps CXV, 17.

There is no remembrance of God in death.

Ps. VI, 6. Resp. 1) The Psalmist speaks of those proclamations of divine praises which are made in the militant church with a bodily tongue.

2) He speaks of the grateful remembrance of God, by which divine benefits are preached, so that in this life other men also may be invited to conversion and the celebration of the divine name.

2) He speaks of the grateful memory of God, by which divine benefits are proclaimed, so that in this life other men also may be invited to conversion and to the celebration of the divine name.

Souls released from their bodies praise God with the angels, in a spiritual manner.

Prob. b.

On the last day the blessedness of the faithful will be more cumulative; because then we shall be consummated with the holy fathers, Hebr.

XI, 40. i.e., we shall obtain the most full and most consummated blessedness of soul and body together, it will also be more conspicuous; for when Christ shall be manifested, then also we shall be manifested with him in glory, Col. III, 4.

III, 4.

Conf.

1 Io.

III, 2.

Q. XIV. Is heavenly beatitude losable?

The beatitude of the heavenly fatherland is not losable, but eternal.

Prob. 1) The elect shall go into eternal life, just as the damned into eternal disgrace, Dan. XII, 2. 2) No one shall take our joy from us, John XV, 22. because we shall always be with the Lord, 1 Thess. IV, 17.

Latin:

Obtingent commemoratæ perfectiones beatis, simulatque anima a corpore eorum separata fuerit a). In nouissimo vero die dotes illæ conspectiores erunt & cumulatiores, anima cum corpore redunita b).

Prob. a. 1) Ex Apoc. XIV, 13. Beati mortui, qui in domino, ἀπ' ἄρτι a nunc, i. e. ab instanti illo, quo moriuntur. 2) Animæ post decessum canunt, Apoc. IV, 8. sedentem super thronum glorificant. v. 9. eundem, abiectis coronis, adorant, v. 10. phialas habent, cap. VIII. magna voce clamant, cap. VI, 10. agnum, quocunque ierit, sequuntur, cap. XI, 4. Eterna felicitate ante resurrectionem carnis fruuntur. 3) Patet idem exemplis. Moses mortuus & sepultus in cœlesti gloria visus est, Luc. IX, 31. Latroni conuerso promittebat Christus: hodie mecum eris in paradiso, Luc. XXIII, 3. Paullus dissolui, & cum Christo esse desiderauit, Phil. I, 24. Cum Christo esse significat eadem frui felicitate, qua ille perfruitur.

Antithesis est Psychopannychitarum, Anabaptistarum & Socinianorum statuentium, animas separatas nihil agere aut pati, sed alto sopore mersas iacere. Quorum potiora sunt argumenta:

I. Pie defuncti dicuntur dormire, Matth. IX, 24. Io. XI, 1. E.

animæ lapsorum nulla sentiunt gaudia prius, quam corporibus redunitæ sunt. Resp.

Pie defuncti dormiunt, quoad corpus solum; quia animæ eorum beata visione Dei in cœlis fruuntur, Act. XIV,

13. magisquod ad ipsam Dei naturam attinet.

Corpus enim, quamuis subtilissimum, & quibusdam spiritus perfectionibus exornatum, corpoream tamen naturam suam retinet; id quod aduersus Socinianos constanter tuemur.

Fieri autem non potest, vt corporei oculi videant spiritum, nulla corporis forma indutum, immo perfectissimum spiritum:

quo circa Deus excellenter nominatur ὁ ἀόρατος, 1 Tim.

I, 17. & ita quidem significanter, vt eum nec viderit ullus homo, nec visurus sit vnquam, ac ne tunc quidem, cum æternæ ei laudes decernuntur, 1 Tim. VI, 16. magisque vigilare censendae sunt, quam unquam in corpore vigilarant: non enim requiem a celebratione habent, nec nocte, nec die, Apoc.

IV, 8. II. Animae fideles ingrediuntur in requiem, Hebr. IV, 3. & requiescunt sub altari caelesti, Apoc. VI, 9. 11. E. nulla voluptate caelesti fruuntur.

Resp.

1) Animae fideles requiescunt ab operibus, laboribus & molestiis huius vitae, Apoc.

XIV, 13. non autem requiescunt ab operationibus caelestibus, neque somno sepultae sunt.

Nam & Deus dicitur septimo die requievisse, Gen.

II, 1. qui tamen non dormit, sed perpetuo operatur. 2) Animae beatae sunt sub altari, i. e. sub protectione & consortio Christi & requiescunt, i. e. patienter exspectant finalem liberationem ecclesiae & coniunctionem cum corporibus resuscitandis; sed inerti somno non sunt correptae; quia clamant voce magna, v. 9. III. Christiani in fide perseverantes accipiunt coronam iustitiae extremo die, 2 Tim.

IV, 8. quo pii cum Christo in gloria primum apparebunt, Col. III, 4. E. ante diem extremum non sunt participes aeternae gloriae.

Resp.

2 Tim.

IV, 8. loquitur Apostolus de corona iustitiae danda non animae, quae iam illam accepit, sed danda toti supposito, anima & corpore constanti, i. e.

Paullo, & omnibus fidelibus Christi cultoribus. IV. Quicunque statuunt, ante diem extremi iudicii animas ingressas esse vitam aeternam, ex illorum sententia fluit hoc absurdum, quod non opus sit extremo iudicio: Atqui doctores euangelici &c.

Ergo.

Maior probatur: quia ex illorum mente aeternis gaudiis adiudicanda est eo die, quo separata est a corpore.

Quid igitur opus est extremo iudicio?

Resp.

Resp. Dist. inter iudicium particulare, & universale.

Illud in die mortis, hoc in extremo die instituitur.

Opus tamen est iudicio universali, 1) ob agnitionem publicam iudicis & redemptoris Christi; 2) ob manifestationem gloriae, iustitiae & misericordiae divinae, 3) ob consummationem praemiorum & suppliciorum respectu totius hominis; 4) ob maiorem piorum exaltationem, & impiorum confusionem, ut illi publice coronentur, hi contra in illustrissima panegyri confundantur, Sap.

III, 10. V. Si animae piorum a corporibus separatae caelesti felicitate fruerentur, sanctorum patrum animae fine nobis consummatam possiderent beatitudinem: Sed consequens est falsum: E. & antecedentes.

Consequentis falsitas probatur ex Hebr.

XI, 39. 40.

Sancti patres non reportarunt promissionem (promissam fidelibus beatitudinem consummatam); quia Deus pro nobis melius quid providit, ne fine nobis consummarent (consummatate beatitudine fruerentur).

Resp.

Resp. Beatitudo est vel secundum quid consummata, qualis animae separatae competit; vel est absolute consummata, quae est totius suppositi post animae cum corpore redunitionem.

Loquitur Apostolus de consummata beatitudine corporis simul & animae, quatenus illa cum fine mundi danda est in ultimo omnium iudicio.

Quam consummationem si veteres sine nobis obtinuissent, defuisset mundus prius, quam nos essemus nati, adeoque nunquam fuissemus haeredes vitae aeternae.

VI. Mortui Deum non laudant, Ps CXV, 17.

Non est in morte memoria Dei.

Ps. VI, 6. Resp.

1) Loquitur Psaltes de illis laudum diuinarum praeconiis, quae in ecclesia militante fiunt lingua corporea.

2) Loquitur de grata Dei memoria, qua beneficia diuina depraedicantur, vt in hac vita alii quoque homines ad conversionem, & nominis diuini celebrationem inuitentur.

Animae a corporibus solutae laudant Deum cum angelis, modo spirituali.

Prob. b.

In die novissimo beatitudo fidelium erit cumulatior; quia tunc cum sanctis patribus consummabimur, Hebr.

XI, 40. i. e. plenissimam & consummatissimam animae simul, atque corporis beatitudinem obtinebimus, erit etiam conspectior; nam quando Christus manifestabitur, tunc etiam nos cum ipso manifestabimur in gloria, Col.

III, 4.

Conf.

1 Io.

III, 2.

Quaest. XIV. Estne beatitudo caelestis amissibilis?

Beatitudo patriae caelestis non est amissibilis, sed aeterna.

Prob. 1) Ibunt electi in vitam aeternam, sicut damnati in aeternum opprobrium, Dan. XII, 2. 2) Gaudium nostrum nemo de nobis tollet, Io. XV, 22. quia semper erimus cum Domino, 1 Thess. IV, 17.


### Q. XV. Will eternal beatitude be equal?

Essential beatitude will indeed be the same for all without distinction. But the accessory rewards of beatitude will admit of different degrees, according to more or fewer works, promised and compensated by God, out of liberal grace and unmerited favor, to those working unequally.

Prob. a. 1) Essential beatitude is equal; because all the pure in heart shall see God, Matt. V, 8. The beatific vision, in which beatitude formally consists, does not admit of more and less.

2) If any were less blessed regarding essential things, these would not yet be enjoying the highest good perfectly or completely, but only imperfectly, which imperfection fights diametrically against consummated beatitude, which excludes every essential defect according to the definition of Boethius: Beatitude is a state of life, perfect by the aggregation of all goods.

Prob. b. 1) From Dan. XII, 3. Then the wise shall shine like the splendor of the firmament, and those who justify many, like the stars forever and ever. The chief splendor in the kingdom of glory will be of the teachers who justify, the lesser of those who learn. The former approaches the likeness of the firmament, the latter of the stars. And just as the splendor of the firmament is not as great as that of the stars: so neither will the glory be as great, [Hebrew: משכילים] as [Hebrew: מציקים].

2) From the apostolic suffrage of Paul, 1 Cor. XV, 41. 42. There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, another glory of the stars: for star differs from star in glory. So also is the resurrection of the dead. Star surpasses star in brightness: so the resurrected bodies will radiate more or less splendor from themselves.

3) From comparison with the angels, In the resurrection of the dead the elect will be [Greek: ἰσάγγελοι] (like the angels), Matt. XII, 30. But among the angels there are given distinct orders and degrees, as to excellence and glory: Therefore, blessed men also will be reduced into certain orders after the manner of the angels.

4) All the saints indeed are to judge the world, 1 Cor. VI, 3. and to sit on a throne, Apoc. III, 21. But the Apostles, by a peculiar prerogative over the tribes of Israel, which they shall judge, are to sit upon XII thrones, Matt. XIX, 28. Luke XXII, 30. But of those sitting on a judicial throne, there is great eminence over those who are judged.

5) He who sows sparingly, shall reap also sparingly: he who sows bountifully, shall reap also bountifully, 2 Cor. IX, 6. Doubtless each one according to his own labor, 1 Cor. III, 8. shall report a greater or lesser reward. e.g. Paul, having suffered so many labors, so many sorrows for the glory of Christ, will obtain greater glory; the thief converted in the last hour of life will obtain a lesser reward.

Prob. c. Works are not the meritorious causes of either eternal life or accidental rewards. For although we have done all things which we ought to have done, we are nevertheless unprofitable servants; because we have not done except what we were bound to do, Luke XVI, 19. But merit, properly speaking, is a work perfectly performed by our own powers, unowed, and equal or proportioned to the reward.

Antithesis 1) Of the Socinians, denying degrees of divine rewards, 2) Of the Papists, attributing a diversity of degrees to the merits of works. Whose arguments are: 1. All the bodies of the just will shine in eternal life like the sun, Matt. XIII, 43, and will be conformed to the glorified body of Christ, Phil. III, 21. Therefore, they do not differ in brightness.

Resp.

1) Speaking absolutely, all the bodies of the just will shine in eternal life like the sun, Matt. XIII, 43. But where a comparison is instituted between them, an inequality of brightness is detected, as the sun has one splendor, the moon another, and the rest of the stars another, 1 Cor. XV, 42. 2) All the bodies of the blessed will be [conformed] to the body of Christ, but not in terms of degrees of brightness, Dan. XII, 13.

II. All laborers, whether they have worked more or less, receive the denarius equally, Matt. XX, 10. Therefore, rewards are not dispensed as greater or lesser according to the labor performed.

Resp.

By the denarius in the parable, it is not precisely understood as the blessedness of the heavenly fatherland, but any reward whatsoever, whether it be temporal or eternal, corporal or spiritual: which, considered absolutely, all receive equally, but considered comparatively, one reward is greater and another is lesser.

III. Those to whom God is all in all are equally blessed: But the inhabitants of heaven, etc., 1 Cor. XV, 28.

Therefore. Resp.

Those to whom God is all in all are equally blessed in objective blessedness (which is God Himself); I concede: in formal and accidental blessedness, I deny. A prince in his court is all in all to his ministers, yet he confers greater dignity upon one minister and lesser upon another.

God is all in all to the blessed angels, whose orders are nevertheless distinct.

IV. The greatest promises have been given to all Christians in common, 2 Pet. I, 4. Therefore, neither greater nor lesser promises have been given to these or those.

Resp.

The greatest promises have been given to all Christians concerning the κοινωνίᾳ τῆς θείας φύσεως, the communion of the divine nature, of which we shall be participants, incipiently in this life, and consummately in the future life. But the inequality of rewards consists in accidental dignity, in the greater brightness of bodies, and in the special revelation made to blessed minds.

V. Inequality of rewards implies an imperfection of blessedness: Therefore, it should not be asserted. Resp.

It does not imply imperfection, but a lesser and a greater accidental perfection.

VI. The Apology of the Augsburg Confession, p. 96, claims degrees of heavenly rewards for the merits of works, of which these are the words: We teach that good works are meritorious, not of the remission of sins, of grace, or of justification (for these we obtain by faith); but of other corporal and spiritual rewards in this life and after this life; because Paul says: Each one will receive his reward according to his own labor.

Resp.

Merit in the Apology of the Augsburg Confession is not taken properly or univocally, but analogically. For just as in common life a laborer who works more deserves a greater wage than one who works less: so he who, presupposing faith in Christ, has performed more works, will obtain more reward than he who has performed fewer.

The former indeed from merit, the latter from the liberal promise of God (*).

Quest.

(*) No one receives rewards, whether greater or lesser, by his own merit; but each one XVI. What will be the seat or dwelling of the blessed? the dwelling of the blessed is the heaven of glory ), most distinct from hell ).

But what that is, and where it may be, is not clear to us in this life ).

Prob. a. The seat of the blessed is called the third heaven, 2 Cor. XII. 2. The first heaven is of nature (the airy and starry), the second of grace, the third of glory, in which are the angels, Matth.

XVIII, 10. It is surnamed the kingdom of heaven, Matth.

XVIII, 3. Paradise, Luc.

XXIII. 43. the fatherland of the faithful, Hebr.

XI, 14. the city of the living God, Hebr. XII, 22. the city to come, Hebr.

XIII, 14. Jerusalem, which is above, Gal.

IV, 26. the heavenly Jerusalem, Hebr.

XII, 22. (*). the house of the heavenly Father, in which there are many mansions, Io.

XIV, 2. Prob. b. Between heaven and hell a great gulf is fixed, Luc.

XVI, 26. Prob. c. Whether this heaven was created within the six days, or not, the sacred scriptures do not record.

Neither has eye seen, nor ear heard, nor have they ascended into the heart of man, the things which God has prepared for those who love him, 1 Cor. II, 9. Wherefore it is not for us to discuss the secrets of heaven, as Augustine judges in De fide et symbolo c. 17.

Q. XVII. What is opposed to eternal beatitude? To eternal beatitude is opposed death, or eternal damnation.

OF DEATH OR ETERNAL DAMNATION. Q. XVIII. What is death, or eternal damnation? Eternal death is a state, most miserable by the aggregation of many evils, which will endure eternally.

It is defined more fully: Eternal death is a complex of many evils, which God the triune, the most just judge, on account of final infidelity and sins committed against conscience, will inflict upon the souls and bodies of reprobate men who have departed from this life, to be endured eternally, to the glory of his justice, truth, and divine power.

Obs. I. Eternal damnation denotes ) the act of damnation, and thus includes both the sentence passed by the judge Christ upon the impious, and the execution, by which the impious are thrust into hell. ) It designates a most unhappy and most sad state, which will endure eternally.

The latter acceptance is of this place: for it is treated here of damnation, as it is eternal.

But the act, by which Christ will pass sentence upon the impious, and the act of execution does not endure eternally, but passes.

Obs. II. merits may be over and above for themselves, which they might be able to bestow upon others.

By which very thing they declare, that it is generally false, if anyone dares to attribute any dignity of merit, properly so called, whether abundant, or sufficient for himself, to his own good works.

Obj. II. Death in the Holy Scriptures is opposed to life, either natural or spiritual. In the former way, death is the separation of the soul from the body. In the latter way, spiritual death, just as spiritual life, is twofold: a) it is understood in respect of this life: as spiritual life consists in the mystical union of the soul justified by faith with God, who is as it were the soul of the soul, the life of our life, in this way spiritual death is the separation of the infidel soul from the gracious fellowship of God: b) It is understood in respect of the other life: in which sense eternal spiritual life consists in the intuitive vision of God, and the beatific fruition of God through communion with God, most intense love, and perennial joy. By which reason, eternal death is the separation of the infidel soul from the beatific vision of God and eternal fruition.

Obj. III. Eternal death is also called the second death, Apoc. II, 11. chap. XX, 6. for the reason that it imports the privation of the other life, which man could have attained once this life was completed; it is called furthermore corruption, ep. Jude v. 12. Matt. VII, 13. eternal destruction, 2 Thess. I, 9. not in such a way as if eternal death were the annihilation of substance, but because it is a privation, or lack of happiness, everlasting reproach and ignominy, Dan. II, 2. for to the damned there will be nothing more contemptible before the eyes of God, the angels, and the blessed, for they will be an abomination to all flesh, Is. LXVI, 24. eternal punishment, Matt. XXV, 46. affliction and anguish, Rom. II, 9.

Latin:

Beatitudo essentialis omnibus quidem sine discrimine eadem erit . At praemia beatitudinis accessoria admittent diversos gradus , secundum plura vel pauciora opera, a Deo, ex gratia liberali, & favore indebito inaequaliter operantibus promissa & compensata .

Prob. a. 1) Beatitudo essentialis aequalis est; quia omnes mundi corde Deum videbunt, Matth. V, 8. Visio beatifica, in qua beatitudo formaliter consistit, non recipit maius & minus.

2) Si qui circa essentialia minus beati essent, hi nondum perfecte aut complete, sed imperfecte tantum summo bono fruerentur, quae imperfectio cum beatitudine consummata e diametro pugnat, quae defectum essentialem omnem excludit iuxta definitionem Boethii: Beatitudo est status vitae, bonorum omnium aggregatione perfectus.

Prob. b. 1) Ex Dan. XII, 3. Tum intelligentes splendebunt, sicut splendor expansi, & iustificantes multos, sicut stellae in saeculum & aeternatem. Praecipuus in regno gloriae splendor erit doctorum iustificantium, minor discentium. Horum ad firmamenti, illorum ad stellarum similitudinem accedit. Et quemadmodum splendor firmamenti tantus non est, quantus stellarum: ita nec tanta erit gloria, משכילים quanta מציקים.

2) Ex suffragio apostolico Paullino, 1 Cor. XV, 41. 42. Alia gloria solis, & alia gloria lunae, alia gloria stellarum: stella namque a stella differt in gloria. Sic etiam resurrectio mortuorum se habet. Stella stellam claritate superat: ita corpora resurgentia alia plus, alia minus splendoris ex se fundent.

3) Ex comparatione cum angelis, In resurrectione mortuorum erunt electi ἰσάγγελοι, Matth. XII, 30. At inter angelos dantur distincti ordines & gradus, quantum ad excellentiam & gloriam: E. & homines beati ad angelorum modum in certos redigentur ordines.

4) Omnes quidem sancti mundum sunt iudicaturi, 1 Cor. VI, 3. & in throno sessuri, Apoc. III, 21. Apostoli vero peculiari prae tribubus Israëlis, quas iudicabunt, praerogativa super XII thronos sessuri sunt, Matth. XIX, 28. Luc. XXII, 30. At sedentium in throno iudiciali magna est prae iis, qui iudicantur, eminentia.

5) Parce seminans, parce metet: largiter seminans, largiter etiam metet, 2 Cor. IX, 6. Nimirum unusquisque iuxta suum laborem, 1 Cor. III, 8. reportabit mercedem maiorem, vel minorem. v. gr. Paullus tot labores, tot dolores pro gloria Christi perpessus, maiorem gloriam; latro in ultima vitae hora conversus, praemium minus nanciscetur.

Prob. c. Opera nec vitae aeternae, nec praemiorum accidentalium sunt causae meritoriae. Nam licet omnia fecerimus, quae fecisse oportuit, servi tamen inutiles sumus; quia non fecimus, nisi quae debebamus facere, Luc. XVI, 19. At meritum proprie loquendo est opus perfecte praestitum viribus nostris, indebitum, & mercedi aequale, vel proportionatum.

Antithesis 1) Socinianorum, gradus praemiorum diuinorum negantium, 2) Pontificiorum diuersitatem graduum meritis operum tribuentium. Quorum argumenta sunt: 1. Omnia iustorum corpora in vita aeterna fulgebunt, ut sol, Matth. XIII, 43. & erunt conformia glorificato corpori Christi, Phil. III, 21. E. non differunt claritate.

Resp.

1) Absolute loquendo omnia corpora iustorum in vita aeterna fulgebunt, ut sol, Matth. XIII, 43. Sed ubi comparatio inter eadem instituitur, deprehenditur claritatis inaequalitas, ut alia solis, alia lunae, alia reliquarum stellarum splendorem referant, 1 Cor. XV, 42. 2) Omnia beatorum corpora erunt corpori Christi, non autem ratione graduum claritatis, Dan. XII, 13.

II. Omnes operarii, sive plus, sive minus laboraverint, pariter denarium accipiunt, Matth. XX, 10. E. non secundum praestitum laborem praemia plura, aut pauciora dispensantur.

Resp.

Per denarium in parabola praecise non intelligitur beatitudo patriae coelestis, sed quodcunque praemium, temporale, an aeternum, corporale, an spirituale fuerit: quod absolute consideratum omnes pariter accipiunt, comparate autem unum praemium maius, alterum minus est.

III. Quibus Deus est omnia in omnibus, illi ex aequo sunt beati: At incolis coeli &c. 1 Cor. XV, 28.

E. Resp.

Quibus Deus est omnia in omnibus, illi ex aequo sunt beati beatitudine obiectiva (quae est ipse Deus); concedo: formali, eaque accidentali, nego. Princeps in aula ministris est omnia in omnibus, uni tamen ministro, alteri minorem dignitatem confert.

Deus omnia in omnibus est beatis angelis, quorum tamen distincti sunt ordines.

IV. Omnibus Christianis communiter maxima promissa donata sunt, 2 Petr. I, 4. E. nec his maiora, nec illis minora donata sunt promissa.

Resp.

Omnibus Christianis maxima promissa sunt donata de κοινωνίᾳ τῆς θείας φύσεως, communione naturae divinae, cuius inchoate in hac vita, consummate in futura vita erimus participes. At inaequalitas praemiorum consistit in dignitate accidentali, in maiori claritate corporum, in speciali revelatione mentibus beatis facta.

V. Inaequalitas praemiorum imperfectionem beatitudinis infert: E. non est afferenda. Resp.

Non imperfectionem infert, sed minorem, maioremque perfectionem accidentalem.

VI. Apol. Aug. Confess. p. 96. gradus praemiorum coelestium meritis operum vindicat, cuius haec sunt verba: Docemus, bona opera meritoria esse non remissionis peccatorum, gratiae aut iustificationis (haec enim fide consequimur); sed aliorum praemiorum corporalium & spiritualium in hac vita & post hanc vitam; quia Paullus inquit: Unusquisque accipiet mercedem iuxta suum laborem.

Resp.

Meritum in Apol. Aug. Conf. non sumitur proprie, aut univoce, sed analogice. Sicut enim in vita communi operarius, qui plus laborat, maiorem mercedem meretur, quam qui minus laborat: ita qui praesupposita fide in Christum plura opera praestitit, plus praemii consequetur, quam qui pauciora praestitit.

Ille quidem ex merito, hic ex liberali Dei promisso (*).

Quaest.

(*) Suo quidem merito praemia, sive maiora, sive minora, nemo accipit; unus autem quique XVI. Quae erit sedes aut domicilium beatorum? Domicilium beatorum est caelum gloriae ), distinctissimum ab inferno ).

Quid vero illud, & ubi sit, nobis in hac vita non liquet ).

Prob. a. Vocatur sedes beatorum caelum tertium, 2 Cor. XII. 2. Primum caelum est naturae (aereum & sidereum), alterum gratiae, tertium gloriae, in quo sunt angeli, Matth.

XIIX, 10. Cognominatur regnum caelorum, Matth.

XIIX, 3. Paradisus, Luc.

XXIII. 43. fidelium patria, Hebr.

XI, 14. ciuitas Dei viuentis, Hebr. XII, 22. ciuitas futura, Hebr.

XIII, 14. Hierosolyma, quae sursum est, Gal.

IV, 26. Hierusalem caelestis, Hebr.

XII, 22. (*). domus Patris caelestis, in qua multae sunt mansiones, Io.

XIV, 2. Prob. b. Inter caelum & infernum ingens hiatus firmatus est, Luc.

XVI, 26. Prob. c. Sitne hoc caelum conditum intra hexaëmeron, an minus, sacrae litterae non commemorant.

Neque oculus vidit, neque auris audiuit, neque super cor hominis ascenderunt, quae Deus praeparauit iis, qui diligunt ipsum, 1 Cor. II, 9. Quare nostrum non est caeli secreta discutere, iudice AVGVSTINO de fide & symbolo c. 17.

Quaest. XVII. Quid opponitur aeternae beatitudini? Aeternae beatitudini opponitur mors, seu damnatio aeterna.

DE MORTE SEV DAMNATIONE AETERNA. Quaest. XVIII. Quid est mors, seu damnatio aeterna? Mors aeterna est status, plurium malorum aggregatione miserrimus, aeternum duraturus.

Vberius definitur: Mors aeterna est complexus plurium malorum, quae Deus trinus, iudex iustissimus, ob infidelitatem finalem & peccata contra conscientiam patrata, hominum reprobarum ex hac vita egrefforum animabus & corporibus aeternum toleranda infliget, ad iustitiae, veracitatis & potentiae diuinae gloriam.

Obs. I. Aeterna damnatio notat ) damnationis actum, & sic includit tum sententiam iudicis Christi in impios latam, tum executionem, qua impii in infernum detrudentur. ) Designat statum infelicissimum tristissimumque, aeternum duraturum.

Posterior acceptio huius loci est: agitur enim hic de damnatione, vt aeterna est.

Actus vero, quo Christus sententiam feret in impios, & actus executionis non durat in aeternum, sed transit. Obs.

II. merita super sint sibi, quae aliis donare queant.

Quo ipso declarant, generatim falsum esse, si quis ullam dignitatem meriti, proprie sic dicti, siue abundantis, siue sibi sufficientis, suis operibus bonis tribuere ausit.

Obi. II. Mors in sacris litteris opponitur vitæ vel naturali, vel spirituali. Priori modo mors est separatio animæ a corpore. Posteriori modo mors spiritualis, sicut & vita spiritualis, est duplex: a) intelligitur ratione huius vitæ: quomodo vita spiritualis consistit in vnione mystica animæ iustificatæ per fidem cum Deo, qui est quasi anima animæ, vita vitæ nostræ, hoc modo mors spiritualis est separatio animæ infidelis a gratioso Dei consortio: b) Intelligitur hoc ratione alterius vitæ: quo sensu vita spiritualis æterna consistit in intuitiva Dei visione, & fruitione Dei beatifica per communionem cum Deo, amorem intensissimum & gaudium perenne. Qua ratione mors æterna est separatio animæ infidelis a beatifica Dei visione & fruitione æterna.

Obi. III. Mors æterna dicitur etiam mors secunda, Apoc. II, 11. cap. XX, 6. ideo, quod priuationem vitæ alterius, quam expleta hac vita homo consequi poterat, importat; vocatur præterea corruptio, ep. Iud. v. 12. Matth. VII, 13. interitus æternus, 2 Thess. I, 9. non perinde, ac si mors æterna sit annihilatio substantiæ, sed quia est priuatio, seu defectus felicitatis, opprobrium & ignominia sempiterna, Dan. II, 2. dammatis quippe nihil erit contemptius coram oculis Dei, angelorum & beatorum, erunt enim nausea omni carni, Es. LXVI, 24. pœna æterna, Matth. XXV, 46. afflictio & angustia, Rom. II, 9.


### Q. XV. Will eternal beatitude be equal?: II, 9. Q. XIX. Can the existence of eternal death be validly proven from the Holy Scriptures?

II, 9. Q. XIX. Can the existence of eternal death be validly proven from the Holy Scriptures?

The existence of eternal death is clearly proven from the most evident sayings of both the Old and New Testament . is proven. Prob. a. From the sayings of the O.T., it suffices to have adduced that classic dictum, Dan. XII, 2. Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake; some to the life of the age, but others to the reproach and ignominy of the age. The Prophet asserts that very many shall rise again to eternal reproach and ignominy, which shall be the punishment of the impious. For those who are thus awakened by God the judge, so that they bear away ignominy, for them ignominy is punishment.

Prob. b. From the N.T. there occurs to us that memorable Pauline testimony 2 Thess. I, 6. 7. 8. 9. It is just before God to repay with affliction those who afflict you; and to you who are afflicted, relief with us at the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven, with the angels of his power in a flame of fire; who will give vengeance to those who do not know God, and who have not obeyed the gospel of our Lord, Jesus Christ: who shall pay the penalty, eternal destruction, from the face of the Lord, and from the glory of his power. The Apostle teaches a) that the judge inflicting the eternal punishment of death upon the damned is God, whose vindictive justice he praises v. 7. b) He inculcates that the meritorious causes are deliberate sins, cruelty toward the pious, affected ignorance, disobedience. c) He calls eternal death now affliction, now punishment, now eternal destruction to designate the most grievous mass of perpetual torments. d) He ascribes the torments not to the devil, but to the face of the judge; for whose sight will not shine upon them favorably, like the radiance of the rising sun, but like a lightning bolt will strike the impenitent, cast them down, and drive them headlong into unquenchable fire.

Latin:

Quæst. XIX. An existentia æternæ mortis e sacris litteris valide probari potest?

Existentia æternæ mortis e clarissimis dictis tam veteris , quam noui Testamenti , liquido probatur. Prob. a. Ex dictis V. T. adduxisse sufficiat illud dictum classicum, Dan. XII, 2. Multi de dormientibus in puluere terræ euigilabunt; hi ad vitam sæculi, reliqui vero in opprobrium & ignominiam sæculi. Affert Propheta, quod plurimi resurrecturi sint in opprobrium & ignominiam æternam, quæ impiorum erit pœna. Nam qui adeo a Deo iudice excitantur, vt reportent ignominiam, illis ignominia est pœna.

Prob. b. Ex N. T. nobis occurrit memorabile illud testimonium Paullinum 2 Thess. I, 6. 7. 8. 9. Iustum est apud Deum, retribuere affligentibus vos afflictionem; at vobis, qui affligimini, recreationem nobiscum in reuelatione Domini Iesu de cælo, cum angelis potentiæ ipsius in flamma ignis; qui dabit vindictam iis, qui non norunt Deum, & qui non obedierunt euangelio Domini nostri, Iesu Christi: qui pœnam luent, interitum æternum, a facie Domini, & gloriæ roboris ipsius. Docet Apostolus a) iudicem infligentem damnatis pœnam æternam mortis esse Deum, cuius dilaudat iustitiam vindicatiuam v. 7. b) Inculcat, caussas meritorias esse peccata proæretica, fauitiam in pios, affectatam ignorantiam, inobedientiam. c) Mortem æternam iam afflictionem, iam pœnam, iam interitum æternum appellat ad designandam cruciatuum molem perpetu grauissimam. d) Cruciatus adscribit non diabolo, sed faciei iudicis; quippe cuius conspectus non affulgebit ipsis fauiter, vt exorientis solis iubar, sed fulminis instar impœnitentes percellet, prosternet, & in ignem inexstinguibilem præcipites aget.


### Q. XX. Who, therefore, is the judge who will inflict the punishment of eternal death?

God will inflict the punishment of eternal death, by a decree not absolute, but ordained .

Prob. 1) God has threatened eternal death to disobedient men, Gen. II, 17. Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, of this (I say) you shall not eat; for, in the day that you eat of it, you shall die the death. AUGUSTINE, L. XIII. de C. D. 12, aptly explains these words of the heavenly judge. When God said to that first man, whom he had placed in paradise, concerning the forbidden food: on whatever day you eat of it, you shall die the death, not only the former part of the first death, where the soul is deprived of God, and not only the later [death], where the body is deprived of the soul, not only the first one itself in its entirety, where the soul is punished, separated both from God and from the body, but whatever there is of death, up to the last, which is called the second, and than which there is none later, that threat has encompassed.

2) God the judge will pronounce the sentence, Matth. XXV, 41. Depart from me, ye cursed, into eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels. 3) The omnipotent Judge will execute the pronounced sentence. For the execution follows immediately, v. 46. And these shall go away into eternal punishment.

Quest. XXI. Will God use ministers in the execution of the sentence? Quest. XXII. For what meritorious causes does God adjudge a reprobate man to eternal death? (*) The cause meriting condemnation is remote, as one whose effect is indeed certainly to be, but yet on that condition, unless something contrary intervenes. The cause bringing about condemnation is proximate, by which name we signify that which produces an effect so necessary that it cannot be avoided by the intervention of some other salutary cause contrary to it. Any sin whatsoever is of such a kind that a man is justly to be condemned on account of it. But there is something intervening, namely, the satisfaction provided by Christ alone for all. If anyone embraces it with true and constant trust, he will be saved, and freed from all guilt and punishment, Rom. VIII, 1. If not: there will be nothing left that can avert the condemnation, long since merited. Therefore, any sin whatsoever is a remote cause of condemnation; but unbelief (ἀπισία), continued even unto death, and that indeed by which the merits of Christ are rejected, is the proximate cause.

It will be helpful to have illustrated the matter with one or two comparisons. 1) A criminal man, who has already been condemned to punishment, has indeed merited death by his crime. But what happens in the meantime? The grace of the Prince is announced to him. What does he do? He spurns the grace offered to him. What will finally happen? Certainly, he must be given over to punishment. But why? Not because of the crime, but because of the rejected grace, which was prepared to pardon it. 2) A disease, even if most serious, or a lethal wound, does not yet bring death; since indeed a medicine is prepared, which, if it be sufficient for healing the wound, and also rightly applied, truly frees the wounded and sick person from the danger of death. If it happens otherwise; then indeed it is not the death-dealing force of the wound or disease, but the contempt, or neglect, and perverse use of the medicine, which makes the condition of the sick person utterly desperate.

In exactly that way must the meaning of the words of Christ be understood, 1 Jo.

III, 18. coll. with v. 36.: the vengeance of the judge remains upon him, as that which he had indeed merited by his sins, which however could have been taken away, if he, repenting, had wished to trust wholly in Christ.

God will use the ministry of angels in the execution. Proof. From Matth. XIII, 41. The Son of man shall send forth his angels, and they shall gather out of his kingdom all things that offend, and them which do iniquity (with them). And shall cast them into a furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth.

The causes meriting eternal death are both all unexpiated sins a), and especially actual proeretic sins b). Final infidelity, however, insofar as it is a sin against the first commandment, is reckoned among the causes of eternal death; but insofar as final unbelief (ἀπισία) is diametrically opposed to saving faith, it is the immediate and proximate cause of eternal damnation c) (*).

Proof. a. Every sin is either the first, or has arisen from the first. The first is the disobedience of the protoplasts, to whom the punishment of eternal death was denounced, Gen. II, 17. Conf. Rom. V, 12.

Prob. b. Every sin, from its first origin, is by its own nature mortal, since it is ἀνομία (lawlessness), 1 John III, 4. Ἀνομία has a curse as its companion, Deut. XXVII, 29. Sin is either involuntary or voluntary. The former can consist with the grace of God and saving faith: the latter drives out the grace of the Holy Spirit and extinguishes faith: from which in a special sense it is said to bring forth death. Concerning which James c. I, 15. When concupiscence has conceived, it brings forth sin; but sin, when it is finished, brings forth death. Obs. Sin is finished, which, having arisen from evil concupiscence, with the full consent of the will added, is as it were cherished and brought forth into the light.

Prob. c. He who does not believe is already judged, John III, 18. He is judged, not according to the promulgation and publication of a final damnatory sentence, but because of the certainty of the divine decree made from eternity, and by reason of the judgment, manifested in the Word and denounced to the unbelievers, the execution of which will follow on the last day. Moreover, that sins merit damnation is established: and thus also unbelief, as a sin against the first commandment, merits death, and in this sense it is true that not only unbelief, but also other sins, are the cause of damnation, namely, the meritorious cause. But when unbelief is directly opposed to faith, as an organic cause, or instrument of application, then just as a man is justified only by faith, and by no other organ, apprehending the remission of sins in the promise of the gospel: so he is damned only by unbelief not applying, or rejecting, the promise of the gospel, Mark XV, 16, 18, 56. Conf. D. MENZERUS, resp. to def. II. Part. Conuersat. Pruten. c. IX. Quæst.

Conf. D. MENZERUS, resp. to def. II. Part. Conuersat. Pruten. c. IX. Quæst. XXIII. Which men will be adjudged to eternal death?

All reprobate men a), or the impious b), the finally impenitent c), and the unbelievers d). Obs. We do not treat here of the damnation of the apostate angels.

Prob. a. From Rev. XX, 15. If anyone was not found written in the book of life, he was cast into the lake of fire.

Prob. b. The impious are called those who, with a deliberate purpose of mind to sin, perform the works of the flesh, of whom Paul says, 1 Cor. VI, 9, 10. Do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners will inherit the kingdom of God.

Prob. c. The finally impenitent are those who die in their sins without a practical recognition and detestation of sin, as is evident from the example of Saul, 1 Chron. XI, 13. Who, since they do not acknowledge their misery, neither seek nor find mercy.

Prob. d. The finally unbelieving stubbornly reject the grace offered in the gospel, just as the phrenetic reject medicine. By the phrase of Scripture they are called those who do not obey the gospel, and therefore they will pay the penalty of eternal destruction, 2 Thess. I, 8.

Latin:

Pœnam æternæ mortis infliget Deus, ex decreto non absoluto, sed ordinato .

Prob. 1) Deus mortem æternam hominibus immorigeris interminatus est, Genes. II, 17. De arbore scientiæ boni & mali, de hac (inquam) non comedes; quia, quo die comedes de ea, morte morieris. Concinne hæc verba iudicis cœlestis exponit AVGVSTINVS L. XIII. de C. D. 12. Quando dixit Deus illi homini primo, quem in paradiso constituerat, de cibo vetito: quocunque die ederis ex eo, morte moriemini, non tantum mortis primæ partem priorem, vbi anima priuatur Deo, nec tantum posteriorem, vbi corpus priuatur anima, non solum ipsam totam primam, vbi anima & a Deo, & a corpore separata punitur, sed quidquid mortis est, vsque ad nouissimam, quae secunda dicitur, & qua nulla posterior, comminatio illa complexa est.

2) Deus iudex sententiam pronuntiabit, Matth. XXV, 41. Discedite a me, maledicti, in ignem aeternum, qui paratus est diabolo, & eius angelis. 3) Iudex omnipotens pronuntiatam sententiam exsequetur. Nam exsecutio statim subsequitur, v. 46. Et ibunt hi in poenam aeternam.

Quaest. XXI. Num Deus in exsecutione sententiae ministris utetur? Quaest. XXII. Propter quas causas meritorias Deus hominem reprobum aeternae morti adiudicat? (*) Causae damnationem promerens est remota, vtpote cuius effectus certo quidem futurus est, at ea tamen conditione, nisi intercedat aliquid contrarium. Causa adferens damnationem est proxima, quo nomine eam significamus, quae effectum profert ita necessarium, vt is non possit evitari interventu alius cuiusdam causae salutaris, illi contrariae. Peccatum quoduis est eiusmodi, vt homo propter illud iuste fit damnandus. Est vero aliquid interveniens, nimirum satisfactio, a Christo vno pro omnibus praestita. Si quis eam vera & constante fiducia amplectatur, saluus erit, omnique culpa ac poena liberatus, Rom. VIII, 1. Sin minus: nihil erit reliquum, quod damnationem, dudum promeritam, auertere queat. E. peccatum quoduis est causa damnationis remota; ἀπισία autem, ad mortem vsque continuata, & ea quidem, qua Christi promerita reiiciuntur, est causa proxima.

Iuuabit, rem similitudine vna atque altera illustrasse. 1) Facinorosus homo, qui iam ad supplicium damnatus est, delicto suo est sane mortem promeritus. Quid vero accidit interea? Gratia Principis ipsi nunciatur. Quid ille? Aspernatur gratiam, sibi oblatam. Quid tandem eueniet? Certe ad supplicium dandus est. Quare autem? Non propter delictum, sed ob repudiatam gratiam, ad condonandum illud paratam. 2) Morbus, tametsi grauissimus, aut vulnus lethale, nondum tamen mortem adfert; quando quidem medicina parata est, quae, si sufficiens fuerit vulneri sanando, recte etiam adhibita, profecto liberat vulneratum atque aegrotantem mortis periculo. Si aliter fit; tum vero non vulneris, aut morbi vis mortifera, sed medicamenti aut contemtio, aut neglectio & sinistra vsurpatio est, quod statum aegroti prorsus desperatum efficit.

Plane eum ad modum percipienda est sententia verborum Christi, 1 Io.

III, 18. coll. cum v. 36.: manet super eo iudicis vindicta, vtpote quam peccatis quidem suis erat promeritus, quae tamen poterat auferri, si, ipse reprehendens, totus Christo confidere voluisset.

Deus in exsecutione vtetur ministerio angelorum. Prob. Ex Matth, XIII, 41. Mittet filius hominis angelos suos, qui colligent e regno illius omnia offendicula, & eos, qui faciunt iniquitatem (cum illis). Et mittent eos in caminum ignis, vbi erit ploratus, & stridor dentium.

Causae, aeternam mortem promerentes, cum omnia peccata non expiata a), tum imprimis peccata actualia proeretica sunt b). Infidelitas autem finalis, in quantum est peccatum contra primum praeceptum, causis aeternae mortis accensetur; at quatenus fidei saluificae e diametro opponitur ἀπισία finalis, immediata & proxima aeternae damnationis causa est c) (*).

Prob. a. Omne peccatum vel primum est, vel a primo ortum. Primum est inobedientia protoplastorum, cui denuntiata est poena aeternae mortis, Gen. II, 17. Conf. Rom. V, 12.

Prob. b. Omne peccatum, a primo ortum, natura sua mortale est, cum sit ἀνομία, 1 Io. III, 4. 'Aνομία maledictionem habet comitem, Deut. XXVII, 29. Peccatum ortum est vel involuntarium, vel voluntarium. Illud cum gratia Dei & fide salvifica consistere potest: hoc gratiam Spiritus S. excutit, fidemque exstinguit: ex quo speciali sensu dicitur parere mortem. De quo Iacobus c. I, 15. Concupiscentia postquam concepit, parit peccatum; peccatum vero, quando consummatum est, parturit mortem. Obs. peccatum consummatum est, quod, ex prava concupiscentia ortum, accedente pleno voluntatis consensu, quasi fouetur & in lucem editur.

Prob. c. Qui non credit, iam iudicatus est, Io. III, 18. Iudicatus est, non secundum finalis damnatoriæ sententiæ promulgationem & publicationem, sed propter decreti diuini ab æterno facti certitudinem, & ratione iudicii, in verbo manifestati & incredulis denuntiati, cuius exsecutio sequetur in die nouissimo. Ceterum peccata mereri damnationem, ratum est: & sic etiam incredulitas, tanquam peccatum contra primum præceptum, meretur mortem & in hoc sensu verum est, non solum incredulitatem, sed etiam cetera peccata, damnationis esse caussam, nempe meritariam. Quando autem incredulitas directe opponitur fidei, tanquam caussæ organicæ, seu instrumento applicandi, tunc vti homo tantum iustificatur fide, & nullo alio organo, remissionem peccatorum in euangelii promissione apprehendente: sic tantum incredulitate euangelii promissionem non applicante, vel repellente damnatur, Marc. XV, 16. 18. 56. Conf. D. MENZERI resp. ad des. II. Part. Conuersat. Pruten. c. IX. Quæst.

XXIII. Quinam homines æternæ morti adiudicabuntur?

Omnes homines reprobi a), siue impii b), finaliter impœnitentes c), & increduli d). Obs. De damnatione angelorum apostatarum in præsenti non agimus.

Prob. a. Ex Apoc. XX, 15. Si quis non inuentus est in libro vitæ scriptus, eiectus est in stagnum ignis.

Prob. b. Impii dicuntur, qui deliberato peccandi animi proposito opera carnis perficiunt, de quibus Paullus, 1 Cor. VI, 9, 10. Annon scitis, quod iniusti regnum Dei pro hereditate non possidebunt. Ne errate: neque scortatores, neque idololatræ, neque mæchi, neque molles, neque concubentes cum maribus, neque fures, neque auari, neque ebriosi, neque calumniatores, neque raptores regnum Dei in hereditatem possidebunt.

Prob. c. Finaliter impœnitentes sunt, qui sine practica peccati agnitione & detestatione in peccatis suis moriuntur, vt patet exemplo Saulis, 1 Chron. XI, 13. Qui cum non agnoscant suam miseriam, nec quærunt, nec inueniunt misericordiam.

Prob. d. Finaliter increduli oblatam in euangelio gratiam pertinaciter respuunt, sicut phrenetici medicinam reiiciunt. Phrasi scripturæ dicuntur euangelio non obedientes, ideoque pœnam luent interitum æternum, 2 Thess. I, 8.


### Quæst. XXIV. Whether the soul only, or also the body will undergo infernal punishments?

Both the soul and the body of the impious will pay eternal punishments. Prob. 1) From Matt. X, 28. Fear him, says the Savior, who can destroy both body and soul in Gehenna (not by killing, but by tormenting).

2) The same is taught by the example of those who went down alive together with body and soul into hell, Num. XVI, 33. Rev. XIX, 20.

3) Soul and body were joined in guilt, Rom. VI, 13. 1 Cor. VI, 18.

E. and in punishment. 4) Therefore the impious will be resurrected, that they may render an account of whatever they committed through the body, united to the soul, 2 Cor. V, 10.

Latin:

Tam anima, quam corpus impiorum pœnas æternas luet. Prob. 1) Ex Matth. X, 28. Timete eum, inquit Saluator, qui potest & corpus, & animam perdere in Gehenna (non necando, sed cruciando).

2) Idem docet exemplum eorum, qui viui vna cum corpore & anima descenderunt in infernum, Num. XVI, 33. Apoc. XIX, 20.

3) Anima & corpus coniuncta fuerunt in culpa, Rom. VI, 13. 1 Cor. VI, 18. E. & in pœna.

4) Propterea resuscitabuntur impii, vt referant, quæcunque per corpus, animæ vnitum, patrarunt, 2 Cor. V, 10.


### Q. XXV. In what does death, or eternal damnation, formally consist?

In a complex of many evils, both privative and positive. Proof: For eternal damnation is opposed to eternal beatitude 1) privatively, and thus it consists in the punishment of loss, or the forfeiture of all perfection and happiness; 2) positively, and thus it brings about the punishment of sense, or most exquisite torments, which the damned will feel. Therefore, there will be in hell the absence of all good, and the presence of all evil.

Question XXVI. What privative evils will the damned suffer?

The soul of the damned will lack the beatific vision of God and the light of glory a), the enjoyment of the highest good, the love of God, and joy b); their bodies will be destitute of all brightness and beauty c). Furthermore, the damned will be excluded from all fellowship with the holy angels and blessed men d). Proof a: The soul of the damned, on the part of the intellect, will lack the intuitive knowledge of God. For he who does not believe in the Son will not see life, i.e., God and Christ, who is the life of the soul, John 3:36. Jesus, the light of the world, will gravely compel them: depart from me! Matthew 25:41. That is to say, get away from here, you cursed! You are unworthy of all light of grace and glory, but rather worthy to be cast into outer darkness, Matthew 8:12. To be cast into outer darkness will be nothing else than to be expelled from the Lord, who is the light of minds, says PROSPER, Book III, On the Contemplative Life, ch. 12. Proof b. On the part of the will, the soul of the damned will lack the enjoyment and love of God, and all joy. For whoever does not see the gracious face of God does not enjoy the sweetness of His goodness, is not admitted to the marriage of the heavenly bridegroom, Matthew 25:10, does not taste the supper of the Lord, Luke 14:24. But he is tormented by hunger, Luke 6:25, and all water of comfort, joy, and pleasure fails him, Zechariah 9:11. Proof c: The beauty of resurrected bodies flows from the συμμορφίᾳ with the body of Christ, Philippians 3:21, and since the bodies of the damned are destitute of this, they will have no beauty, no noble appearance, but will be an abhorrence to all flesh, Isaiah 66:24. Proof d: The holy angels and blessed men are in the heavenly Jerusalem, into which nothing defiled shall enter, Revelation 21:27. Whence the damned are dogs outside, ch. 22:15; the angels stand before the throne of God, Daniel 7:10, and always behold His face, Matthew 18:10. Wherefore, since the damned are separated from the sight and throne of God, they are excluded from the fellowship of the angels. Where the grace of God has no place, there the gracious presence of the angels does not obtain. They will also be deprived of the society of the pious; because these will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven: but the impious will be cast out into outer darkness, Matthew 8:11, 12.

Question XXVII. What positive evils will afflict the damned?

Positive evils will afflict the souls and bodies of the damned. Their intellect will know God as the most just judge and the most bitter avenger of sins a). The will will be tormented by hatred of God, extreme sadness, and furious impatience b). The bodies will be tormented by fire, material indeed, but singular c). Proof a: The damned will know the face of God, but threatening adversity and sad thunderbolts: which face of divine wrath the damned will not escape, Psalm 139:7. For they will pay the penalty from the face of God, 2 Thessalonians 1:9. Therefore, the damned will know God, but abstractively from the sense of punishments (and in this way they will in a certain manner see the face of God, even against their will); but they will not know Him except as angry and most hostile to themselves. From this θεογνωσίᾳ, a most sad ἑαυτογνωσία will be born, in which the damned will contemplate themselves in such a way that they will reckon with themselves the multitude of their sins, the gravity of the punishments which they sustain, and their merit, Sap. V, 3. Nay, and they will know the blessed, not without anxiety, as participants of beatitude and exempt from calamity, Sap. V, 5.
