Prob. b. The damned will wish to be hidden from the face of God, but they will not be able to, Apoc. VI, 16. They will not be able to bear the face of God, but will shudder; they will not love God as a good to them, but will pursue Him with hatred as their adversary; they will envy other possessors of eternal felicity, and thus will be tormented by immense pain, they will be filled with θλῖψις καὶ στενοχωρία [tribulation and anguish], Rom. II, 9. they will groan because of the anguish of spirit, Sap. V, 3. they will feel the worm of conscience gnawing without intermission, Es. LXVI, 24. which will be accompanied by dire despair, when they know that the door of grace will never be opened to them, so that they would prefer to be torn into pieces, nay, to be reduced to nothing, than to live in this way.

Prob. c. The bodies of the damned will be tormented by hellfire properly so called, and therefore material. For the sentence of the judge denounces fire, Matth. XXV, 41. from which smoke ascends, Apoc. XIV, 10 whose flames burn, Luc. XVI, 14. To which, therefore, the Holy Spirit attributes the name of the property and effect of true fire, that is not metaphorical, but fire properly so called: But to hellfire etc. Therefore. But it will not be elemental fire, but altogether singular. Ordinary fire only burns bodies; hellfire would also act upon souls. The former, when fuel is lacking, ceases; the latter does not need food properly so called. Moreover, to wish to explain the nature of hellfire more distinctly is more curious than useful (*).

Question (*)

Latin:

In complexu plurimorum malorum, tum priuatiuorum, tum positiuorum. Prob. Nam damnatio æterna beatitudini æternæ opponitur 1) priuatiue, atque sic consistit in pœna damni, seu iactura omnis perfectionis & felicitatis; 2) positiue, atque sic infert pœnam sensus, siue cruciatus exquisitissimos, quos damnati persentiscent. Erit igitur in inferno absentia omnis boni, & præsentia omnis mali.

Quæst. XXVI. Quæ mala priuatiua patientur damnati?

Carebit anima damnatorum visione Dei beatifica & lumine gloriæ a), fruitione summi boni, amore Dei & gaudio b); Corpora destituentur omni claritate & venustate c). Præterea exclusi erunt damnati ab omni consortio sanctorum angelorum & hominum beatorum d). Prob. a. Anima damnatorum, ex parte intellectus, carebit cognitione Dei intuitiua. Nam qui non credit Filio, non videbit vitam, i. e. Deum & Christum, qui est vita animæ, Io. III, 36. Grauiter ipsos compellabit Iesus, lux mundi: discedite a me! Matth. XXV, 41. q. d. procul hinc facessite, maledicti! indigni estis omni lumine gratiæ & gloriæ, contra digni, qui proiiciamini in tenebras exteriores, Matth. VIII, 12. In tenebras exteriores mitti, nil aliud erit, nisi a Domino, qui est mentium lumen, expelli, ait PROSPER L. III. de vita contemplatiua, c. 12. Prob. b. Ex parte voluntatis carebit anima damnatorum fruitione & amore Dei, atque omni gaudio. Quicunque enim gratiosam Dei faciem non videt, non fruitur suauitate ipsius bonitatis, non admittitur ad nuptias sponsi cœlestis, Matth. XXV, 10. non gustat cœnam domini, Luc. XIV. 24. Sed torquetur fame, Luc. VI, 25. & deficit ipsum omnis aqua solatii, gaudii, voluptatis, Zach. IX, 11. Prob. c. Pulcritudo corporum resuscitatorum manat e συμμορφίᾳ cum corpore Christi, Phil. III, 21. qua cum destituantur corpora damnatorum, nulla ipsis erit venustas, nulla facies liberalis, sed erunt fastidium omni carni, Es. LXVI, 24. Prob. d. Angeli sancti, beatique homines sunt in Hierosolyma cœlesti, quam non intrabit aliquid inquinatum, Apoc. XXI, 27. Vnde foris sunt canes damnati, c.XXII, 15. angeli adstant coram throno Dei, Dan. VII, 10. faciemque eius semper intuentur, Matth. XVIII, 10. Quare, cum damnati separati sint a conspectu & throno Dei, exclusi sunt ab angelorum consortio. Vbi non habet locum gratia Dei, ibi nec obtinet gratiosa angelorum præsentia. Priuabuntur etiam societate piorum; quia hi cum Abrahamo, Isaaco & Iacobo accumbent in regno cœlorum: impii vero eiicientur in tenebras exteriores, Matth. VIII, 11. 12.

Quæst. XXVII. Quæ mala positiua damnatos affligent?

Mala positiua damnatorum animas & corpora affligent. Intellectus ipsorum cognoscet Deum iudicem iustissimum, & vindicem peccatorum acerrimum a). Voluntas torquebitur odio Dei, tristitia summa & impatientia furibunda b). Corpora cruciabuntur igni materiali quidem, sed singulari c). Prob. a. Cognoscent damnati faciem Dei, sed aduersum & tristia fulmina minitantem: quam faciem iræ diuinæ damnati non effugient, Ps. CXXXIX, 7. Luent enim pœnam a facie Dei, 2 Thess. I, 9. Cognoscent ergo damnati Deum, sed abstractiue ex sensu pœnarum (& hoc modo Dei faciem quodammodo videbunt, etiam inuiti); sed non, nisi iratum, & maxime sibi aduersarium cognoscent. Ex hac θεογνωσίᾳ, tristissima nascetur ἑαυτογνωσία, qua damnati seipsos ita contemplabuntur, ut peccatorum suorum multitudinem, poenarum, quae sustinent, gravitatem & meritum secum reputent, Sap. V, 3. Quin & beatos non sine anxietate cognoscent participes beatitatis, expertes calamitatis, Sap. V, 5.

Prob. b. Abscondi volent damnati a facie Dei, sed non poterunt, Apoc. VI, 16. Faciem Dei ferre non poterunt, sed exhorrescent; non amabunt Deum, tanquam sibi bonum, sed odio prosequentur sibi adversarium; aliis aeternae felicitatis possessoribus invidebunt, atque adeo immani dolore torquebuntur, opplebuntur θλῖψις καὶ στενοχωρία, Rom. II, 9. gement propter angustiam spiritus, Sap. V, 3. sentient vermem conscientiae sine intermissione rodentem, Es. LXVI, 24. quem comitabitur dira desperatio, cum sciant, januam gratiae sibi nunquam apertum iri, vt in partes discerpi, immo in nihilum redigi, quam sic vivere, malint.

Prob. c. Corpora damnatorum cruciabuntur igni infernali proprie dicto, adeoque materiali. Nam sententia iudicis denuntiat ignem, Matth. XXV, 41. a quo sumus ascendit, Apoc. XIV, 10 cuius flammae vrent, Luc. XVI, 14. Cui igitur Spiritus S. nomen proprietatis & effectus veri ignis attribuit, ille non est metaphoricus, sed proprie dictus ignis: Atqui igni infernali &c. E. Non autem erit ignis elementaris, sed prorsus singularis. Ignis vulgaris tantum corpora vrit; ignis infernalis etiam ageret in animas. Ille, deficiente pabulo, cessat, hic alimento proprie dicto non indiget. Ceterum distinctius naturam ignis infernalis velle exponere, curiosum magis, quam vtile est (*).

Quæst. (*)


### Q. XXVIII

What external evils will surround the damned? The external evils that will surround the damned are a) the detestable fellowship with demons, b) the most squalid dwelling, which is hell.

Prob. a. The decretory sentence of the judge stands: Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire, prepared for the devil and his angels! Matt. XXV, 41. As the sight of God and the angels wonderfully refreshes men made blessed: so the gaze of the devil and of malignant angels torments them to an immense degree. Therefore, the demons will torment the damned objectively, i.e., by their foul and horrible appearance; but that they will torment them effectively, like executioners, does not seem probable. For a) as God blesses the elect in heaven without the ministry of angels: so He torments the reprobate in hell without the ministry of devils, b) It is not consistent that God, most just, should constitute the seducer of men their torturer. For thus the lot of the seducer would perhaps be better than that of the seduced, which seems repugnant to justice. c) The devils themselves will be tormented: therefore men will not be tormented. d) The Holy Scriptures testify that it will come to pass that the damned will pay the penalty, eternal destruction from the face of the Lord, 2 Thess. I, 9. Therefore not from the devil.

You say: I. Matt. XVIII, 34. The angry Lord delivered the wicked servant to the torturers, i.e., to the demons. Resp. a) A parable is not an argument. b) The torturers are the torments which the angry face of God sends, 2 Thess. I, 9. You say: II. Devils are the torturers of men in this life: therefore also in the life to come. Resp. Many things are permitted in this age which, as if the doors of long-suffering [μακροθυμίας] were closed, cannot be granted in the other.

Prob. b. The most squalid dwelling of the damned is hell, which is succinctly defined by τόπον βασάνου, a place of torment, Luke XVI, 28. It is metaphorically depicted as a lake in which there is no water (of solace and refreshment), Zech. IX, 11; as a prison in which the last farthing must be paid, Matt. V, 26; 1 Pet. III, 19; as a furnace of fire, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, Matt. XIII, 42; as a lake of fire burning with sulfur, Rev. XIX, 20.

Latin:

Externa mala, quae damnatos circumstabunt, sunt a) detestabile cum cacodaemonibus consortium, b) domicilium squalidissimum, quod est infernus.

Prob. a. Stat sententia decretoria iudicis: Discedite a me, maledicti, in ignem aeternum, paratum diabolo & eius angelis! Matth. XXV, 41. Vt aspectus Dei & angelorum homines beatos mirifice recreat: ita intuitus diaboli, & malignorum angelorum inmane quantum cruciat. Torquebunt ergo daemones damnatos obiective, i. e. foedo & horrendo aspectu; quod autem hos effective, carnificum instar, sint cruciaturi, non videtur probabile. Nam a) vt Deus electos sine ministerio angelorum beat in coelis: ita reprobos sine ministerio diabolorum torquet in inferno, b) Non est vero consentaneum, Deum iustissimum, seductorem hominum constituturum esse horum tortorem. Sic enim seductoris fors melior foret forte seducti, quod iustitiae repugnare videtur. c) Diaboli ipsi torquebuntur: E. homines non torquebunt. d) Sacrae litterae testantur, futurum esse, ut damnati poenam luant, interitum aeternum a facie domini, 2 Thess. I, 9. E. non a diabolo.

Dicis: I. Matth. XVIII, 34. Dominus iratus feruum scelestum tradidit tortoribus, i. e. daemonibus. Resp. a) Parabola non est argumentatio. b) Tortores sunt cruciatus, quos immittit irata Dei facies, 2 Thess. I, 9. Dicis: II. Diaboli tortores hominum sunt in hac vita: ergo & in vita futura. Resp. Multa in hoc saeculo permittuntur, quae, quasi clausis μακροθυμίας foribus in altero concedi nequeunt.

Prob. b. Domicilium squalidissimum damnatorum est infernus, qui succincte definitur per τόπον βασάνου, locum tormenti, Luc. XVI, 28. Metaphorice depingitur vt lacus, in quo non est aqua (solatii & refrigerii), Zach. IX, 11. vt carcer, in quo nouissimus quadrans soluendus, Matth. V, 26. 1 Petr. III, 19. vt caminus ignis, vbi erit fletus ac stridor dentium, Matth. XIII. 42. vt stagnum ignis ardens sulphure, Apoc. XIX, 20.


### Q. XXIX. Where is hell?

It is certain that the infernal prison is in a real place a), distinct from the seat of the blessed b). It is also probable that it is outside this habitable world c). But where that place is definitely, is unknown to men who are wayfarers d).

Prob. a. 1) Hell is explicitly called τόπον βασάνου, a place of torment, Luke XVI, 28. 2) Hell was a real terminus, to which the descent of Christ, 1 Pet. III, 19, was made. But Christ did not descend into some imaginary space.

Prob. b. 1) Without are dogs, Rev. XXII, 15, i.e., outside the heavenly Jerusalem. 2) They were cast into a place, most distinct from the seat of the blessed by a great chasm, Luke XVI, 23. Prob. ought to be understood; or both improperly; or one or the other.

If both are to be understood properly, there will be an open contradiction (for extreme darkness to be, and at the same time the greatest fire, and flame, is surely something repugnant to itself): If you think both are said in an improper sense, I have what I want: If one or the other, why not also the other? Where there is an equal reason, there is also an equal consequence.

Indeed, the greatest men, who hold the contrary opinion, reason from the properties of the judicial style, from which all metaphors ought to be absent. But it must be considered, 1) that the metaphorical expressions which I have now brought forward are also in the judicial style: 2) that that judicial style is at the same time prophetic, to which, by customary usage, metaphorical expressions are mixed, just as in Isa. VII, 18. 19. 20.

Prob. c. 1) The whole orb of the earth with all its elements will burn up, 2 Pet. III, 10. If, therefore, hell were contained within the circumference of the elements, it would be burned up and perish on the last day.

2) The prince of the world is said to be about to be cast out, John XII, 31. i. e. outside this world into the outer darkness, Matt. VIII, 12. i. e. outside the darkness of this world.

Prob. d. Holy Scripture has not revealed the place of hell to us. Therefore, the modesty of St. Chrysostom is to be praised, homil. XXXI. on the epistle to the Romans, ch. XVI. Let us not ask where Gehenna is, but how we may escape it. And Augustine, lib. XX. de C. D. c. 16. That infernal fire, in what part of the world or of things it may be, I believe no man knows, unless perhaps he to whom the divine Spirit shows it.

The antithesis of the Papists, who maintain that hell is in the center of the earth. Their stronger arguments are:

I. Hell, by the force of the word, denotes a lower place, by which reasoning it is also described in Matt. XI, 23. Resp. Something is said to be lower either by reason of place or by reason of status. Hell, compared with heaven, is called lower, not so much by reason of place as by reason of a lower status.

II. Devils are called subterranean creatures, Phil. II, 10. E. hell is a subterranean place. Resp. Devils and damned men are called subterranean, not precisely by reason of place, but of status. For in the phraseology of Scripture, whatever is honorable is called heavenly; and whatever is despised is called earthly, or subterranean.

III. Whoever, by descending into the earth, descended into hell, they by this very fact showed that hell is in the earth: But Core, Dathan, and Abiram, etc., Num. XVI, 33. E. Resp. 1) I deny the consequence of the major premise. For I argue by the same reasoning: Whoever by descending into the sea descends into the belly of the whale, he by this very fact shows that the sea is in the belly of the whale: But the prophet Jonah, etc. E. 2) We do not deny that the factious, as regards their soul, descended to the state of the damned; but indeed by the word שְׁאוֹל in the cited place, the hell of the damned is not denoted proximately and immediately, but that word designates the chasm of the earth, an analogue of the sepulcher, which, namely, they were forced to seek, having been swallowed alive by the earth. For since otherwise only the dead were accustomed to be brought into the earth, here the living (not indeed into hell, but) were forced to seek subterranean places and the chasm of the earth, which devoured and buried them with this chasm. Conf. D. Pfeiffer, dub. vexata p. 330.

IV. Christ, by descending into hell, descended into the lower parts of the earth, Eph. IV, 9. E. hell is situated in the lower parts of the earth. Resp. 1) The lower parts of the earth are called hell not properly, but metaphorically, in respect to the highest heavens, to which they are opposed: but this opposition is not in respect of place, but in respect of condition; because the heaven of the blessed, to which Christ ascended, is not defined even by physical place. 2) The Holy Spirit not rarely condescends to the infirmity of our intellect, and describes the things of the future age with the words of the present age, e.g., celestial beatitude is called paradise, likewise a rich banquet; because we cannot conceive the delights of heaven otherwise than by imagining in our minds the innocent and most sweet pleasures of some garden, or a rich banquet; so also hell is described through the lower parts of the earth, so that its squalor and most filthy face may be placed before our eyes. 3) Our D. Dannhauer explains these words neatly in hodof. phænom. XVIII. p. 736. He descended into the very lower places of the earth, i. e., into the infernal prison, to the τὰ κατώτερα τῆς γῆς; certainly not a sepulcher, because burial is not in the heart of the earth; but this descent is to the τὰ κατώτερα, nay, to the τὰ κατώτατα τῆς γῆς, or by the nature of the Grecism into places which are lower than the earth itself, and are not contained within the body of the earth; which truly is the lowest of all lowest things, not geometrically, but mystically.

Latin:

Certum est, carcerem infernalem esse in loco reali a), a beatorum sede distincto b). Probabile etiam est, eumdem esse extra hunc mundum habitabilem c). At vbi locus ille definite sit, hominibus viatoribus est incognitum d).

Prob. a. 1) Infernus diserte vocatur τόπον βασάνου, locus tormenti, Luc. XVI, 28. 2) Fuit infernus terminus realis, ad quem descensus Christi 1 Petr. III, 19. factus. At Christus non descendit in spatium aliquod imaginarium.

Prob. b. 1) Foris sunt canes, Apoc. XXII, 15. i. e. extra coelestem Hierosolymam. 2) Proiecti sunt in locum, per magnum hiatum a beatorum sede distinctissimum, Luc. XVI. 23. Prob. debet intelligi; aut vtrumque improprie; aut alterutrum.

Si vtrumque fit proprie intelligendum; aperta erit repugnantia (caliginem enim extremam esse, ignemque simul maximum, & flammam, et profecto aliquid sibi repugnans): Si vtrumque sensu improprio dictum putes; habeo, quod volo: Si alterutrum; quidni etiam alterum? Vbi par ratio est, ibi est etiam par consequutio.

Summi quidem Viri, qui contrariam tuentur sententiam, ratiocinantur ex proprietatibus styli iudiciarii, a quo omnes abesse debent metaphora. Sed cogitandum est, 1) quod metaphoricae loquutiones, quas iam in medium protuli, etiam sint in stylo iudiciario: 2) quod stylus ille iudiciarius sit simul propheticus, cui, vsitato more, admiscentur loquutiones metaphoricae, quem ad modum, Ies. VII, 18. 19. 20.

Prob. c. 1) Totus terrarum orbis cum omnibus elementis conflagrabit, 2 Petr. III, 10. Quod si igitur infernus intra ambitum elementorum contineretur, in die extremo combureretur & periret.

2) Princeps mundi dicitur ejiciendus foras, Io. XII, 31. i. e. extra hunc mundum in tenebras exteriores, Matth. VIII, 12. i. e. extra hujus mundi tenebras.

Prob. d. Locum inferni S. scriptura nobis non revelavit. Laudanda ergo est modestia S. Chrysostomi homil. XXXI. in epist. ad Rom. c. XVI. Non quæramus, ubi sit gehenna, sed quomodo illam effugiamus. Et Augustinus lib. XX. de C. D. c. 16. Ille ignis infernalis, in qua mundi, vel rerum parte sit, hominem scire arbitror neminem, nisi forte, cui Spiritus divinus ostendit.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, statuentium, infernum esse in centro terræ. Quorum argumenta potiora sunt:

I. Infernus, vi vocis, notat locum inferiorem, qua ratione etiam describitur Matth. XI, 23. Resp. Inferius aliquid dicitur vel ratione loci, vel ratione status. Infernus, comparatus cum cælo, dicitur inferior, non tam ratione loci, quam ratione status inferioris.

II. Dicuntur diaboli creaturæ subterraneæ, Phil. II, 10. E. infernus est locus subterraneus. Resp. Diaboli & homines damnati dicuntur subterranei, non præcise ratione loci, sed status. Nam phrasi scripturæ quidquid honorabile est, dicitur cæleste; & quidquid contemptum est, vocatur terrestre, aut subterrrestre.

III. Quicunque, descendendo in terram, descenderunt in infernum, illi hoc ipso ostenderunt, infernum esse in terra: Atqui Core, Dathan & Abiram &c. Num. XVI, 33. E. Resp. 1) Neg. consequens. majoris. Nam eadem ratione argumentor: Quicunque descendendo in mare descendit in ventrem ceti, ille hoc ipso ostendit, mare esse in ventre ceti: Atqui propheta Ionas &c. E. 2) Non negamus, factiosos, quoad animam, descendisse ad statum damnatorum; at vero per vocem שְׁאוֹל l. c. non denotatur proxime & immediate infernus damnatorum, sed designat vox illa hiatum terræ, analogon sepulcri, quod scilicet terra absorpti vivi petere coacti sunt. Cum enim alias non nisi mortui terris inferri consueverint, hic viui (non utique infernum, sed) loca subterranea ac voraginem terræ petere coacti sunt, quæ eos huo hiatu devoravit & sepelivit. Conf. D. Pfeiffer. dub. vexata p. 330.

IV. Christus, descendendo in infernum, descendit in inferiora terræ, Eph. IV, 9. E. infernus situs est in inferioribus terræ. Resp. 1) Inferiores partes terræ dicuntur infernus non proprie, sed metaphorice, respectu supremorum cælorum, quibus opponuntur: hæc autem oppositio non est respectu loci, sed respectu conditionis; quia cælum beatorum, ad quod Christus ascendit, loco etiam physico non definitur. 2) Condescendit haud raro Spiritus S. ad infirmitatem nostri intellectus, & res futuri sæculi describit verbis præsentis sæculi, v. gr. beatitudo cœlestis vocatur paradisus, item convivium pingue; quia nos delicias cœli aliter concipere nequimus, quam animis nostris fingendo innoxias voluptates suavissimas cujusdam horti, aut pinguis convivii; sic etiam infernus describitur per inferiora terræ, vt squalor eius & fordidissima facies nobis ob oculos ponatur. 3) Concinne explicat hæc verba noster D. Dannhav. in hodof. phænom. XVIII. p. 736. Descendit in loca ipsa terra inferiora, h. e. in carcerem infernalem, eis τὰ κατώτερα τῆς γῆς; non sane sepulcrum, quia sepultura non est in corde terræ; sed descensus hic est eis τὰ κατώτερα, immo eis τὰ κατώτατα τῆς γῆς, vel ex Græcismi indole in loca, quæ ipsa terra sunt inferiora, & terræ corpore non continentur; quod vere est omnium infimorum infimum, non geometrice, sed mystice.


### Q. XXX. What will be the beginning of the infernal torments?

Infernal torments will befall the souls of the damned at the same time as they depart from the body.

Proof 1) Souls released from bodies immediately descend into the place of torments: this is what the soul of the rich man testifies, crying out in the flames, Luke 16. 2) Just as those who die in the Lord, ἀπ’ ἄρτι (from now on), from the time of departure from this life, are blessed; so also, those who die in sins are immediately, as to the soul, miserable.

3) Christ preached to the spirits detained in prison, 1 Pet. 3:19. By spirits in that place are understood the separated souls of those who were incredulous in the days of Noah, and had already perished in the flood in the days of Noah. To these spirits Christ preached not the gospel, but the law, and convicted them that they were most justly condemned to eternal torments. And those spirits were tormented before their reunion with their bodies.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, who deny that separated souls are truly tormented before their reunion with their bodies.

Their arguments are: I. The soul after the death of man does not live before reunion with the body: Therefore it feels no torments. The antecedent is clear: because life consists in the conjunction of the soul with the body. Therefore the whole man lives, not the body, not the soul. Response: The whole man lives the life of the composite, the soul lives the life of the part; for it is the breath of life, Gen. 2. Counter-argument: It is said of the dead that they are not; Jer. 31:15, Matt. 2:18. Therefore they do not live. Response: It is said of the dead that they are not, namely in this life.

II. Just as the body without the spirit is a corpse; so the soul without the body does nothing and suffers nothing. For the ratio of the parts composing a whole is the same. Response: The ratio is different. For the body is a material principle, ἄεργον (inactive), or in itself inefficacious; the soul is a formal principle, ἐνεργητικόν (active), and the fountain of life.

Latin:

Cruciatus infernales animabus damnatorum simul, atque illae a corpore discesserint, obtingent.

Prob. 1) Animæ a corporibus solutæ statim descendunt in locum tormentorum: id quod testatur anima epulonis in flammis vociferans, Luc. XVI. 2) Sicut qui in Domino moriuntur, ἀπ’ ἄρτι, a tempore discessus ex hac vita, sunt beati; ita etiam, qui in peccatis moriuntur, statim qua animam sunt miseri.

3) Christus prædicauit spiritibus in carcere detentis, 1 Petr. III, 19. Per spiritus l. c. intelliguntur animæ separatæ eorum, qui in diebus Noæ erant increduli, ac iam in diebus Noæ diluuio perierant. His spiritibus Christus prædicauit non euangelium, sed legem, eosque conuicit, quod iure iustissimo æternis cruciatibus sint addicti. E illi spiritus ante redunitionem cum corporibus suis sunt cruciati.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, negantium, animas separatas ante redunitionem cum corporibus uere cruciari.

Quorum argumenta sunt: I. Anima post mortem hominis ante redunitionem cum corpore non uiuit: Ergo nullos cruciatus sentit. Antecedens patet: quia uita consistit in coniunctione animæ cum corpore. E. totus homo uiuit, non corpus, non anima. Resp. Totus homo uiuit uitam compositi, anima uiuit uitam partis; est enim spiraculum uitæ, Gen. II. Instantia: De mortuis dicitur, quod non sint; Ier. XXXI, 15. Matth. II, 18. Ergo nec uiuunt. Resp. De mortuis dicitur, quod non sint, scilicet in hac uita .

II. Quemadmodum corpus sine spiritu cadauer est; ita anima sine corpore nil agit aut patitur. Est enim partium, totum aliquod componentium, par ratio. Resp. Est dispar ratio. Nam corpus est principium materiale ἄεργον, siue per se inefficax; anima est principium formale, ἐνεργητικόν, & fons uitæ.


### Q. XXXI. Will the torments of the damned be eternal?

The torments of the damned are eternal, destined to have no end.

Proof 1) From Matt. 25:4. And these (the cursed) shall go away into eternal punishment; but the just into eternal life. By the same reason that the life of the blessed is eternal, by the same reason the punishment of the damned is eternal: but the former is eternal absolutely: Therefore the latter is too.

2) The worm of the damned shall not die and the fire shall not be quenched, Isa. 66:24. Therefore the worm of conscience will gnaw the damned without intermission, and the infernal fire will torment them without end.

3) He that believeth in the Son, hath everlasting life: but he that believeth not the Son, shall not see life, but the wrath of God abideth upon him, John III, 36. Upon whom the wrath of God abideth, from them it never departeth.

4) It is agreeable to divine justice that they who know not God, and have not obeyed the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, should suffer punishment, eternal destruction from the presence of the Lord, 2 Thess. I, 9. For they have sinned against an eternal and infinite God, and have rejected the merit of Christ, which is of infinite value. (*)

Antithesis (*) When we dispute concerning the eternity of punishments, first, as it pertains to the constitution of the cause, we say they are eternal not only as continuous and lasting for a long time without any intermission (unceasing); but also as perpetual and infinite, never to be ended (endless). Next, as to the proof, our opinion is I. Abundantly confirmed by the most ample testimonies of Scripture. There are two kinds of these: α) Κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν (According to the letter), testimonies expressed in the clearest words, which S. V. IO. GEORG. WALCHIVS distributes into various classes, Einleit. in die Streitigk. in der Evang. Kirche, P. III. p. 277. sqq. Generally there are three things to be duly considered.

1) Divine writers, as often as they denounce eternal damnation to the impious, speak without any limitation, which certainly would have been necessary, especially in the principal passages, if any liberation were ever to be expected. For the rich glutton, no hope was provided, Luke XVI, 25. 26. 2) Damnation is called eternal in opposition to eternal blessedness: and it is necessary that this adjunct, αἰώνιος (eternal), in both parts of the opposites, should obtain the same power. 3) Eternal damnation is described in words much more significant than blessedness and its eternal duration; because the Holy Spirit foresaw that this would not be brought into dispute in the same way as that, and that hardly anyone who believes in blessedness would doubt its eternity. Therefore, this expression is used concerning it: εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας αἰώνων (for ever and ever), Apoc. XIV, 11. XX, 10. which manner of speaking has such force that it is never used otherwise than of perpetual and infinite eternity. β) Κατὰ τὴν διάνοιαν (According to the sense),

by necessary and open consequence. Such sayings of Scripture, and also the principles of revealed Theology, from which this corollary is derived, the celebrated WALCHIVS presents to you, collected with great study and in due order, l. c. p. 294. sqq.

II. Most agreeable to Reason, illuminated by the divine word. The argumentation is threefold, upon which our people chiefly rely. 1) Such and so great as the fault is, such and so great also must the punishment be, if it is just. But every fault, and its gravity, is to be estimated and weighed chiefly from the violated Object. Since in sin this is the eternal God, Ps. LI, 6, and also the eternal Son of God, and his αἰώνια λύτρωσις (eternal redemption), Hebr. IX, 12: it follows that the punishment of man, being just and divine, and properly so called, cannot but be eternal. For thus, and not otherwise, is the punishment of retaliation, which is properly called punishment. Therefore, it is of no value, the opposition of the adversaries, one of the principal ones in which they place the most confidence: that there will be no just proportion and comparison between a temporal offense and an eternal vengeance. For it is false what they assume, that in weighing the gravity of a fault, the duration of the action, and its brevity or long duration, is chiefly to be considered. Who would doubt that the crime of high treason, committed in one point of time, is to be punished much more severely than a manifold insult and accumulated injury by which someone has afflicted a man of the lowest rank for a long space of time? We shall also dispute κατ' ἄνθρωπον (as a man). Those who deny the perpetuity of punishments nevertheless all confess with one mouth their longest continuation through many centuries. Let them therefore explain themselves, what proportion and equality there may be between sins completed in a brief life, and a long-lasting punishment? 2) Such and so great as is the proportion between temporal virtue and perpetual remuneration, on account of the justice of Christ bestowed upon man, perfect in all respects, such and so great also is the proportion between temporal viciousness and perpetual punishment, on account of the rejected justice of Christ. Equal on both sides is the reason: equal therefore the consequence. — Nay, the damned will never cease sinning, nor can it ever come about that they repent, Luc. XVI, 26. seqq. 3) Such and so great as is the relation, as it is commonly said, τῆς πίστεως (of faith) to eternal salvation, such and so great also is the relation τῆς ἀπιστίας (of unbelief) to eternal damnation, by force of opposition. Mare. XVI, 16. Io. III, 36.

The antithesis was 1) of the Origenists, 2) of the Anabaptists, whose mention is made in the Augsburg Confession, art. XVII. It condemns the Anabaptists, who think that for damned men and devils there will be an end of punishments. 3) Of the Socinians, who maintain that the damned are to be annihilated. Their arguments are:

I. The mercy of God is infinite, as the Hieropsalmist testifies, Ps. LXXVII, 9. Does his mercy fail forever? But it would not be infinite if God were to be angry without end. Resp. 1) The cited Psalm deals with the church militant in these lands; therefore it is wrongly transferred to the damned, and to the devil himself. 2) God embraces penitent sinners, and those who with persevering faith embrace the merit of Christ, with His infinite mercy. But upon impenitent sinners, and those who by final ἀπιστία (unbelief) reject the merit of Christ, the wrath of God remains, John III, 36. For just as the mercy of God is infinite; so also is His justice infinite. The redemption of Christ does not pertain to the devil. Therefore, neither does liberation from hell.

II. If no grace were to be hoped for by the damned; then grace would not be greater than sin; nor would all who die in Adam be made alive through Christ: But grace is greater than sin, and all who die in Adam are made alive through Christ: Therefore, for the damned, the grace of God is to be hoped for. The antecedent is evident from Rom. V, 18, 1 Cor. XV, 22. Resp. Grace is greater than sin, as recognized by the law in penitent hearts. But for the damned, no return to repentance is open. For the time of repentance is not the future, but the present age, 2 Cor. VI, 2. Furthermore, those who die in Adam are made alive through Christ, namely those who have fallen asleep through faith in Christ, and in Christ. For although Christ acquired life for all by His most precious merit, yet not all apply it to themselves through faith, and thus not all see life, John III, 36.

III. Christ is the Savior of all, especially of the faithful, 1 Tim. IV, 10. Therefore, the faithful will be saved first; but eventually even the unfaithful. Resp. Christ is the Savior of all men, as to merit; but especially of the faithful, as to the actual outcome, not pertaining to the unfaithful, because of their final infidelity.

IV. Christ preached in hell to the spirits who were once disobedient, 1 Pet. III, 19, 20. Therefore, He wished to convert them. Resp. The sermon of Christ made to the spirits detained in the infernal prison was not evangelical, leading to faith and salvation, but legal, convicting and striking terror. Christ preached more in reality than in words, by showing Himself alive and triumphant to the damned spirits.

V. The liberation of the damned and of the evil spirits themselves is the ἀποκατάστασις πάντων (restoration of all things); of which there is discourse in St. Peter, Acts III, 21. For if all things are to be restored, then both demons and damned men must be raised to their original state. Resp. The restoration of all things, of which Peter speaks, is universal, not absolutely, but limitedly; since the Apostle himself adds a limitation: which God spoke through the mouth of all his holy prophets from of old.

But of the restoration of the damned to a happy state, neither a trace nor a footprint is found in the writings of the prophets. VI.

Whoever imposes an eternal and infinite punishment upon a sinner for a temporal offense is not just: But it is the opinion of the evangelical doctors that God, etc.

E.

The major is proven; because where there is no proportion between the offense and the punishment, there no justice of the judge shines forth; but rather his supreme injustice appears.

Now, however, between a temporal and finite offense and an infinite and eternal punishment, there is no proportion given.

Resp.

I deny the major.

For between a temporal sin and an eternal punishment there is a proportion, not indeed by reason of the act, which is transitory, but by reason of the guilt, which is infinite and eternal, 1) because of the infinite object injured, which is the infinite majesty of the eternal Divinity, 2) because of the rejected infinite price of the Redeemer Christ.

VII. If sins are infinite by reason of guilt, because by them the infinite majesty of God is violated, all sins will be equal; which is absurd.

Resp.

Although sins agree in this, that they are all committed against the infinite majesty of God: they do not, however, agree by reason of malice, which is in the subject, and hence an inequality of sins results.

VIII. Whoever are dead eternally are not tormented eternally: But the damned, etc.

E.

The major is evident; because no one feels torments unless he lives.

Resp.

Eternal death is spoken of in opposition to the eternal life of the blessed.

The damned will be dead eternally; because neither God, the life of the soul, dwells in them, nor will He offer to them the most full face of grace and glory to be beheld.

Yet the damned do not die in such a way that they do not live at all, nor feel any torments; which life of theirs, because of extreme misery, is to be considered death rather than life.

IX. Those whom infernal fire devours, so that it brings upon them eternal destruction, they are utterly annihilated: But finally the infidels, etc.

Therefore.

The minor is clear from Heb.

X, 27.

2 Thess.

I, 9.

Resp.

In Heb.

X, the word ἐσθίειν is used, which signifies to eat, not to consume utterly.

Whatever unquenchable fire eats, it always eats, it never eats up.

The word ὄλεθρος, which is read in 2 Thess.

I, does not signify total annihilation, but a change of state tending toward the worse.

Thus also God will destroy the soul in Gehenna, Matt.

X, 28, not by destroying it utterly, but by disturbing it into a most wretched state.

X. Christ will destroy every principality, every power, and every virtue, 1 Cor. XV, 24.

E. He is clearly about to annihilate all princes of angels and men.

Resp.

The word καταργεῖν, which is read in the sources, does not signify to annihilate, but to enervate; to render void, to take away the state, use, and efficacy.

Confer.

Luke.

Luke XIII, 7.

Rom.

III, 3.

31. Gal.

III, 17. Eph. II, 15. Christ, therefore, will cut the strength and sinews of princes; He will not abolish their essence. (*)

Latin:

Cruciatus damnatorum sunt æterni, nullum habituri finem.

Prob. 1) Ex Matth. XXV, 4. Et abibunt (hi maledicti) in pœnam æternam; iusti uero in uitam æternam. Qua ratione uita beatorum est æterna, eadem ratione pœna damnatorum æterna est: sed illa est æterna absolute: E. hæc.

2) Vermis damnatorum non morietur & ignis non exstinguetur, Es. LXVI, 24. E. uermis conscientiæ sine intermissione damnatos rodet, & ignis infernalis sine fine eos torquebit.

3) Qui credit in Filium, habet vitam aeternam: qui vero non credit Filio, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super ipsum, Io. III, 36. Super quos ira Dei manet, ab illis nunquam recedit.

4) Iustitiae divinae consentaneum est, vt, qui non norunt Deum, nec obediverunt evangelio Domini nostri Iesu Christi, poenam luant, interitum aeternum a facie Domini, 2 Thess. I, 9. Peccarunt enim in Deum aeternum & infinitum, ac meritum Christi, quod valoris infiniti est, reiecerunt. (*)

Antithesis (*) Cum de aeternitate poenarum disputamus, primum, quod ad causae constitutionem adtinet, aeternas dicimus non solum continuas, ac sine vlla intermissione diu duraturas (unaufhörliche); sed etiam perpetuas infinitasque, nunquam terminandas (unendliche). Deinde, quantum ad probationem, nostra sententia est I. Scripturae testimoniis amplissimis abunde confirmata. Horum duo sunt genera: α) Κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν, verbis longe clarissimis expressa testimonia, quae in varias classes distribuit S. V. IO. GEORG. WALCHIVS, Einleit. in die Streitigk. in der Evang. Kirche, P. III. p. 277. sqq. Generatim tria sunt, probe consideranda.

1) Diuini scriptores, quoties damnationem impiis denuntiant aeternam, toties loquuntur sine vlla limitatione, qua certe opus fuisset, praesertim in locis praecipuis, si qua esset liberatio vnquam exspectanda. Diuiti epuloni nulla spes facta fuit, Luc. XVI, 25. 26. 2) Aeterna dicitur damnatio, in oppositione aeternae beatitatis: E necesse est, adiunctum hoc, αἰώνιος, in vtraque parte oppositorum, eamdem obtinere potestatem. 3) Damnatio aeterna describitur verbis multo significantioribus, quam beatitas, eiusque aeterna duratio; quoniam Spiritus S. praeuidebat, hanc non similiter, ac illam, in disceptationem adductum iri, & neminem fere vnquam, qui beatitudinem esse credat, de eius autem aeternitate dubitet. De illa igitur adhibetur haec loquutio: εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας αἰώνων, Apoc. XIV, 11. XX, 10. quae dicendi ratio tantam vim habet, vt nusquam aliter, quam de aeternitate perpetua atque infinita vsurpetur. β) Κατὰ τὴν διάνοιαν,

per necessariam atque apertam consequentiam. Eiusmodi dicta scripturae, atque etiam principia Theologiae revelatae, ex quibus efficitur hoc consectarium, magno studio & iusto ordine collecta tibi exhibet celeb. WALCHIVS l. c. p. 294. sqq.

II. Rationi, verbo diuino illuminatae, maxime consentanea. Argumentatio triplex est, qua potissimum freti sunt Nostrates. 1) Qualis & quanta est culpa, talem ac tantam quoque poenam, si iusta fit ea, fieri oportet. Omnis autem culpa, eiusque gravitas, maxime ex Obiecto violato aestimanda est, ac ponderanda. Quod quum in peccato fit aeternus Deus, Ps. LI, 6. aeternus etiam Dei filius, eiusque αἰώνια λύτρωσις, Hebr. IX, 12.: efficitur, vt poena hominis iusta, eaque diuina, & proprie sic dicta, non possit non aeterna esse. Ita enim non aliter, est poena talionis, quae est proprie sic dicta poena. Ergo ne quidquam valet aduersariorum oppositio, vna ex praecipuis, cui illi plurimum confidunt: Nullam fore proportionem & comparationem iustam delicti temporalis, ac vindictae aeternae. Falsum est enim, quod adsumunt, in ponderanda gravitate culpae considerandam maxime esse actionis durationem, eiusque aut breuitatem, aut diuturnitatem. Quis dubitet, quin crimen laesae Maiestatis, vno temporis puncto commissum, multo acerbius vindicandum sit, quam contumelia multiplex, atque iniuria cumulata, qua quis hominem de infima plebe per longum temporis spatium adfecerit? Disputabimus etiam κατ' ἄνθρωπον. Qui negant poenarum perpetuitatem, omnes tamen vno ore fatentur, longissimam earum per plura saecula continuationem. Explicent igitur ipsi, quae intercedat proportio atque aequalitas inter peccata brevi vita consummata, & poenam diuturnam? 2) Qualis & quanta est proportio inter virtutem temporalem, & remunerationem perpetuam, propter tributam homini iustitiam Christi, omnibus numeris absolutam, talis ac tanta etiam est proportio inter vitiositatem temporalem, & poenam perpetuam, propter reiectam iustitiam Christi. Par vtrimque est ratio: par igitur consecutio. - Immo nunquam definent peccare damnati, nec fieri vnquam poterit, vt resipiscant, Luc. XVI, 26. seqq. 3) Qualis & quanta est relatio, vt dici solet, τῆς πίστεως ad salutem aeternam, talis ac tanta quoque est relatio τῆς ἀπιστίας ad damnationem aeternam, vi oppositionis. Mare. XVI, 16. Io. III, 36.

Antithesis fuit 1) Origenistarum 2) Anabaptistarum, quorum mentio fit in Augustana Confess. art. XVII. Damnat Anabaptistas, qui sentiunt, hominibus damnatis ac diabolis finem pœnarum futurum esse. 3) Socinianorum, statuentium damnatos annihilatum iri . Quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Misericordia Dei est infinita, teste Hieropsalte, Ps. LXXVII, 9. Num desit in perpetuum misericordia eius? Non esset autem infinita, si Deus sine fine irasceretur. Resp. 1) Psalmus citatus agit de ecclesia in his terris militante; ad damnatos ergo, atque ipsum diabolum male transfertur. 2) Deus infinita sua misericordia complectitur peccatores pœnitentes, & perseverante fide meritum Christi amplectentes. At super peccatores impœnitentes, & ἀπιστία finali meritum Christi repudiantes manet ira Dei, Io. III, 36. Sicut enim infinita est Dei misericordia; ita & infinita est eius iustitia. Ad diabolum non pertinet Christi redemtio. E. nec liberatio ex inferno.

II. Si nulla gratia speranda esset damnatis; neque gratia maior foret peccato; nec omnes, qui in Adamo moriuntur, per Christum vivificarentur: At gratia est maior peccato, & omnes, qui in Adamo moriuntur, per Christum vivificantur: E. damnatis gratia Dei speranda est. Antecedens patet ex Rom. V, 18. 1 Cor. XV, 22. Resp. Gratia est maior peccato, ex lege in cordibus pœnitentibus agnito. At damnatis nullus patet reditus ad pœnitentiam. Tempus enim pœnitentiæ non est futurum, sed præsens sæculum, 2 Cor. VI, 2. Ceterum, qui in Adamo moriuntur, per Christum vivificantur, nempe qui per fidem in Christo, & in Christo obdormiverunt. Nam quamvis Christus omnibus vitam acquisiverit merito suo pretiosissimo, non tamen omnes per fidem sibi illud applicant, adeoque non omnes vident vitam, Io. III, 36.

III. Christus est Salvator omnium, maxime fidelium, 1 Tim. IV, 10. E. fideles primo saluabuntur; tandem vero etiam infideles. Resp. Christus est Salvator omnium hominum, qua meritum; maxime fidelium, qua actualem euentum, ad infideles, propter infidelitatem finalem, non spectantem.

IV. Christus spiritibus, qui aliquando increduli fuerunt, in inferno prædicauit, 1 Petr. III, 19, 20. E. voluit eos conuertere. Resp. Concio Christi facta spiritibus, in carcere infernali detentis, non fuit euangelica ad fidem & salutem perducens, sed legalis conuincens & terrorem intutiens. Prædicauit Christus realiter magis, quam verbaliter, se viuum & triumphantem spiritibus damnatis ostendendo.

V. Liberatio damnatorum & ipsorum cacodæmonum est ἀποκατάστασις πάντων, restitutio omnium; de qua S. Petro sermo est, Act. III, 21. Si enim omnia sunt restituenda, & dæmones & homines damnati in pristinum statum euehendi sunt. Resp. Restitutio omnium, de qua loquitur Petrus, est vniuersalis, non absolute, sed limitate; siquidem ipse Apostolus limitationem deferte addit: quae locutus est Deus per os omnium sanctorum suorum prophetarum a saeculo.

Sed de restitutione damnatorum in statum felicem nec vola, nec vestigium invenitur in scriptis prophetarum. VI.

Quicunque propter delictum temporale peccatori irrogat poenam aeternam & infinitam, ille non est iustus: Atqui doctorum evangelicorum sententia Deus &c.

E.

Maior probatur; quia, ubi nulla est proportio inter delictum & poenam, ibi nulla elucet iustitia iudicis; sed potius summa ipsius iniustitia apparet.

Iam vero inter temporale finitumque delictum & poenam infinitam atque aeternam nulla datur proportio.

Resp.

Neg. maior.

Nam inter peccatum temporale & poenam aeternam datur proportio non quidem ratione actus, qui transitorius est, attamen ratione reatus, qui infinitus & aeternus est, 1) propter laesum obiectum infinitum, quod est infinita aeterni Numinis maiestas, 2) ob reiectum infinitum pretium redemptoris Christi.

VII. Si peccata ratione reatus sunt infinita, quia iisdem violatur infinita Dei maiestas, omnia peccata erunt aequalia; quod est absurdum.

Resp.

Licet peccata in hoc conveniant, quod omnia committantur contra infinitam Dei maiestatem: non tamen conveniunt ratione malitiae, quae est in subiecto, atque hinc peccatorum resultat inaequalitas.

VIII. Quicunque aeternum mortui sunt, non aeternum torquentur: Atqui damnati &c.

E.

Maior constat; quia nemo tormenta sentit, nisi vivat.

Resp.

Mors aeterna dicitur in oppositione ad beatorum vitam aeternam.

Damnati aeternum erunt mortui; quia nec Deus, vita animae, in illis habitat, neque faciem gratiae & gloriae plenissimam illis conspiciendam praebebit.

Non tamen ita moriuntur damnati, vt plane non vivant, neque ulla tormenta sentiant; quae vita illorum ob extremam miseriam mors potius, quam vita censenda est.

IX. Quos ignis infernalis devorat, vt aeternum illis afferat interitum, illi penitus annihilantur: Atqui finaliter infideles &c.

Ergo.

Minor liquet ex Hebr.

X, 27.

2 Thess.

I, 9.

Resp.

Hebr.

X. habetur verbum ἐσθίειν, quod significat, edere, non penitus depascere.

Quidquid ignis inextinguibilis edit, semper edit, nunquam exedit.

Vox ὄλεθρος, quae legitur 2 Thess.

I. non significat totalem annihilationem, sed mutationem status vergentem in deterius.

Sic & Deus animam perdet in Gehenna, Matth.

X, 28. eam non prorsus destruendo, sed in statum perditissimum disturbando.

X. Christus destruet omnem principatum, omnem potestatem, omnemque virtutem, 1 Cor. XV, 24.

E. plane annihilaturus est omnes principes angelorum & hominum.

Resp.

Verbum καταργεῖν, quod legitur in fontibus, non significat annihilare, sed enervare; irritum reddere, statum, vsum, efficaciam tollere.

Confer.

Luc.

XIII, 7.

Rom.

III, 3.

31. Gal.

III, 17. Eph. II, 15. Christus itaque vires & neruos principum incidet, non essentiam eorum abolebit. (*)


### Q. XXXI. Will the torments of the damned be eternal?: Quest. XXXII. Are there degrees of punishments in hell?

Quest. XXXII. Are there degrees of punishments in hell?

Infernal punishments differ in degrees, according to the quality and measure of sins.

Proof 1) It will be more tolerable on the final day for the Sodomites than for the inhabitants of Chorazin and Bethsaida, Matt. XI, 24.

2) The servant who knew the will of his master and does not do it will be beaten with many [stripes]; but he who did not know, and did things worthy of stripes, will be beaten with few, Luke XII, 47.

3) You make, says the Savior to the Pharisees, a son of Gehenna twice as much as you yourselves are, Matt. XXIII, 15.

The Socinians object: Whoever are equally rejected from the face of God, and are equally dead in sin, they undergo equal punishments: But the damned, etc. Therefore. The major is evident: because rejection from the divine face is the root of all the torments which the damned sustain. Response: Distinguish between the punishment of loss and the punishment of sense. All the damned agree equally in the punishment of loss, by which they are deprived of the beatific vision of God; but they differ in the punishment of sense; inasmuch as those who have sinned more gravely and more frequently will feel greater torments.

(*) Besides these statements, and many more of this kind which the adversaries abuse, there are certain false principles and foundations of error, which have been overturned by invincible arguments in the place concerning God, concerning Christ, and concerning the means of grace. 1. They rashly separate divine love and benevolence from the vindicatory justice of God, and they think that this [justice] is not as natural, necessary, and infinite in God as that [love]. 2. They confuse the power by which God is able—what is accustomed to be called absolute and ordained—and they dare to separate that from the remaining properties and perfections of God. For they attack us with this dilemma: God either does not want, or cannot, eventually at some time extirpate sin from the world. But why do they say: "eventually at some time," after a long series of years and centuries? Why not quickly and suddenly? What if someone were to argue thus: God either does not want, or cannot, take away and destroy evil without delay in the present? Nay, did He either not want, or could He not, prevent evil from arising in the first place? What, we ask, will they be able to answer? They will have the same answer for themselves. 3. They indeed make much of salvation itself, to be imparted to all by the propitious will of God; but they do not consider the order of salvation, holily established by God. 4. They either entirely deny or diminish the necessity of satisfaction to be rendered to God as judge and avenger for the sake of dignity, thinking, namely, that it is a finite satisfaction. 5. They opine that that satisfaction, which Christ rendered most perfectly, pertains to all the damned, and even to the malignant demons themselves, nor do they accurately weigh the distinction between acquisition and application. 6. They invent that a reversion from sins to God can happen after the final fates, without the use of the means of grace. 7. They posit the fire, to which demons and men have been adjudged, not so much as punishing (a vengeance-fire), but as purging (a cleansing-fire). This is opposed by the clearest pronouncements, Ps. II, 12; 2 Thess. I, 8. It is also contrary to sound reason, which can teach anyone that punishment, properly so called, must be distinguished from judicial chastisement. Underlying this false principle of theirs is another certain error: namely, that the bitterness of torments is a medium sufficient for amendment.

Furthermore, the importance of this controversy is truly most grave. For the opinion of the adversaries 1) detracts much from the highest perfections of God, specifically from His vindicatory justice; 2) either removes or diminishes the necessity of vicarious satisfaction to be applied in this life; 3) perverts the order of salvation; 4) contributes not a little to the security of an impious life. Rightly, therefore, it was disapproved in our Aug. Confess. art. 17.

XXXIII. What is the end of eternal damnation? The end of eternal damnation is the glory of the vindicatory justice ), of the truthfulness ), and of the power of God the judge ).

Proof a. From the vindicatory justice of God proceeds the act of punishing, directed toward the glory of God the judge. The Apostle proclaims this justice, 2 Thess. 1:6. It is just before God to repay with affliction those who afflict you.

Proof b. The truthfulness of God will shine forth on the day of judgment, when God will actually fulfill the threats made to the ungodly. The King sitting upon the throne says to John: Write, for these words are true and faithful. For the cowardly, and the unfaithful, and the abominable, and murderers, and fornicators, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, their portion shall be in the lake burning with fire and sulfur; which is the second death, Apoc. XXI, 8.

Proof c. The judge must be most powerful, who is able to subject all the ungodly to eternal punishments. Whence the heavenly hosts sing: Hallelujah! Salvation, and honor, and glory, and power (ἡ δύναμις) to the Lord our God: for His judgments are true and just, Apoc. XIX, 1, 2.

SIGH. My heart, Lord Jesus, strives to ascend to you into heaven, but of itself it cannot! Do you what it cannot do itself! Draw me, through you, to you! Lead me into the heavenly life, which never ends, into the fatherland, which is never disturbed, to the fountains of waters, which never dry up, but always abound! My soul languishes for love of you! Grant, I beseech you, that your sweetness may soothe it, your goodness may satisfy it, your wisdom may enlighten it, and your love may occupy it entirely and possess it entirely, because you are with the Father and the Holy Spirit God alone blessed for ever and ever, Amen!

Latin:

Quæst. XXXII. Danturne gradus pœnarum in inferno?

Pœnæ infernales differunt gradibus, pro peccatorum qualitate & mensura.

Prob. 1) Tolerabilius erit in die extremo Sodomitis, quam incolis Chorazim & Bethsaida, Matth. XI, 24.

2) Seruus, qui cognouit voluntatem domini, & non facit eam, vapulabit multis; qui autem non cognouit, & fecit plagis digna, vapulabit paucis, Luc. XII, 47.

3) Facitis, inquit Saluator ad Pharisaos, filium Gehennæ duplo magis, quam vos estis, Matth. XXIII, 15.

Obiiciunt Sociniani: Quicunque pariter sunt reiecti a facie Dei, pariterque mortui in peccato, illi pares subeunt pœnas: Atqui damnati &c. E. Maior patet: quia reiectio a facie diuina est radix omnium cruciatuum, quos damnati sustinent. Resp. Dist. inter pœnam damni & sensus. Omnes damnati pariter conueniunt pœna damni, qua visione Dei beatifica priuati sunt; at differunt pœna sensus; siquidem maiores cruciatus persentifcent, qui grauius & fæpius peccarunt.

(*) Præter dicta hæc, & quæ plura sunt huiusmodi, quibus aduersarii abutuntur, sunt quædam falsa principia ac fundamenta erroris, quæ inuictis argumentis euersa sunt in loco de Deo, de Christo, & de mediis gratiæ. 1. Amorem ac beneuolentiam diuinam a iustitia Dei vindicante temere seiungunt, & hanc non æque, ac illam, in Deo naturalem, necessariam atque infinitam esse existimant. 2. Potentiam, qua Deus valet, absolutam, quæ vocari solet, & ordinatam, inter se confundunt, illamque a reliquis Dei proprietatibus ac perfectionibus separare audent. Hoc enim nos impugnant dilemmate: Deus peccatum ex mundo tandem aliquando exstirpare aut non vult, aut non potest. Quare autem dicunt: tandem aliquando, post longam annorum ac sæculorum seriem? Cur non cito subitoque? Quid? si quis ita argumentaretur: Deus malum sine mora in præsens tollere ac delere aut non vult, aut non potest? immo impedire, quæ minus exoriretur malum, aut nolebat, aut non poterat? Quid quæsumus, valebunt respondere? Id idem fibi responsum habebunt. 3. Salutem quidem ipsam, propitia Dei voluntate omnibus impertiendam, magni faciunt; ordinem vero salutis, sancte a Deo constitutum, non considerant. 4. Satisfactionis, Deo iudici ac vindici præstandæ, necessitatem ad dignitatem aut omnino negant, aut extenuant, finitam scilicet satisfactionem putantes. 5. Eam satisfactionem, quam Christus perfectissimam præstitit, ad omnes damnatos, ipsosque adeo dæmones malignos, pertinere opinantur, nec distinctionem acquisitionis, & adplicationis, adcurate ponderant. 6. Reuersionem a peccatis ad Deum, fine vsu mediorum gratiæ, post suprema fata fieri posse comminiscuntur. 7. Ignem, cui adiudicati sunt dæmones & homines, non tam punientem statuunt (ein Rachfeuer), quam purgantem (ein Reinigungsfeuer). Id quod aduersatur clarissimis effatis, Ps. II, 12. 2 Thess. I, 8. Contrarium est etiam sanæ rationi, quæ potest quemque docere, pœnam, proprie ita dictam, discernendam esse a castigatione iudiciaria. Huic falso illorum principio subest alius quidam error: nimirum quod cruciatuum acerbitas fit medium, ad emendationem sufficiens:

De cætero, momentum huius controuersiæ est sane grauissimum. Aduersariorum enim sententia 1) summis Dei perfectionibus, sigillatim iustitiæ vindicanti, multum detrahit; 2) satisfactionis vicariæ, in hac vita adplicandæ, necessitatem aut tollit, aut minuit; 3) ordinem salutis peruertit; 4) impiæ vitæ securitati haud parum conducit. Iure igitur improbata est in nostra Aug. Confess. art. 17.

XXXIII. Quis est finis aeternae damnationis? Finis aeternae damnationis est gloria iustitiae vindicativae ), veracitatis ) & potentiae Dei iudicis ).

Prob. a. A iustitia Dei vindicativa procedit actus puniendi, directus in gloriam Dei iudicis. Depraedicat hanc iustitiam Apostolus, 2 Thess. 1, 6. Iustum est apud Deum, retribuere affligentibus vos afflictionem.

Prob. b. Veracitas Dei elucescet in die iudicii, quando Deus comminationes impiis factas reapse implebit. Rex sedens super throno dicit Ioanni: Scribe, quia haec verba vera & fidelia sunt. Timidis, & infidelibus, & abominabilibus, & homicidis, & scortatoribus, & incantatoribus, & idolatris, & omnibus mendacibus pars futura est in stagno ardenti igne & sulphure; quae est altera mors, Apoc. XXI, 8.

Prob. c. Potentissimum oportet esse iudicem, qui omnes impios poenis aeternis subiicere valet. Vnde coelites canunt: Hallelujah! Salus, & honor, & gloria, & virtus (ἡ δύναμις) Domino Deo nostro: quia vera & iusta iudicia eius, Apoc. XIX, 1, 2.

SVSPIRIVM. Cor meum, Domine Iesu, conatur ad te conscendere in coelum, sed per se non potest! Fac tu, quod ipsum non potest! Trahe me, per te, ad te! Duc me in vitam coelestem, quae nunquam terminatur, in patriam, quae nunquam inquietatur, ad fontes aquarum, qui nunquam inarescunt, sed semper abundant! Languet anima mea amore tui! Fac, obsecro, vt illam permulceat dulcedo tua, satiet bonitas tua, illustret sapientia tua, dilectio tua occupet eam totam & possideat totam, quia es tu cum Patre & Spiritu S. Deus solus benedictus in saecula saeculorum, Amen!


## 28 On the Means of Salvation in General, and the Law


### Concerning the Means of Salvation in General, and Concerning the Word of the Law in Specific

Question I. What are the means of salvation? The means of salvation are the means divinely ordained, through which God, out of grace, offers to all men, who have fallen into sin, the salvation acquired by the mediator Christ, and grants and preserves true faith, and likewise introduces all who embrace the merit of Christ with final faith into the kingdom of glory. )

Question II. How many are the means of salvation? The means of salvation are of a twofold order: Some are called means of salvation more strictly and more properly, others more broadly and less properly. The means strictly so called, on the part of God, δοτικά (giving), or exhibiting salvation, are the word and the sacraments ); on our part, the medium ληπτικόν (receiving), or apprehending the offered salvation, is faith resting on the merit of Christ ).

The means of salvation broadly so called are εἰσαγωγικά (introductory), or executive and introducing into the kingdom of glory, namely death, the resurrection of the dead, the final judgment, and the consummation of the age ). consummation of the age c). consummation of the age c).

Obs. In a stricter sense, the means of salvation are called exhibitive and receptive, because they are causal. For although they are not the principal causes of salvation, they are nevertheless the organic causes of salvation. But the isagogic means are only conditions, without which there is no entry into the kingdom of glory, and thus they are called means of salvation ὡς ἐν πλάτει (in a broad sense).

Prob. a. The Word of God and the sacraments are exhibitive means of salvation: because through them the most merciful God offers, applies, and seals grace and salvation to men.

Prob. b. Faith is the apprehensive medium: because it receives the grace of God founded upon the merit of Christ, and offered by the evangelical promise, by which eternal salvation is bestowed.

Prob. c. Death, the resurrection of the dead, the final judgment, and the consummation of the age are called executive means of salvation, as well as isagogic, or introductory. They are called executive, insofar as through them God executes the sentence of glorification and damnation: they are called isagogic, insofar as by their immediate intervention men, finally persevering in faith, are introduced into the kingdom of glory. Concerning these

Latin:

Quaest. I. Quid sunt media salutis? Media salutis sunt media diuinitus ordinata, per quae Deus acquisitam a mediatore Christo salutem omnibus hominibus, in peccatum prolapsis, ex gratia offert, veramque fidem donat & conseruat, iuxta atque omnes, meritum Christi finali fide amplectentes, in regnum gloriae introducit. )

Quaest. II. Quotuplica sunt media salutis? Media salutis duplicis sunt ordinis: Quaedam strictius magisque proprie, quaedam latius & minus proprie media salutis dicuntur. Media stricte dicta, ex parte Dei, δοτικά, seu salutem exhibentia, sunt verbum & sacramenta ); ex parte nostri, medium ληπτικόν, seu oblatam salutem apprehendens, est fides merito Christi innixa ).

Media salutis late dicta sunt εἰσαγωγικά, siue exsecutiua & in regnum gloriae introducentia, scilicet mors, resurrectio mortuorum, extremum iudicium & consummatio saeculi ). consummatio fæculi c). consummatio fæculi c).

Obs. Strictiori sensu media salutis dicuntur exhibitiva & receptiva, quia sunt causalia. Quamvis enim non sint causae salutis principales; sunt tamen causae salutis organicae. At media isagogica sunt tantum conditiones, sine quibus non fit ingressus in regnum gloriae, adeoque ὡς ἐν πλάτει media salutis appellantur.

Prob. a. Verbum Dei & sacramenta sunt media salutis exhibitiva: quia per eadem Deus misericordissimus gratiam & salutem hominibus offert, applicat & obsignat.

Prob. b. Fides est medium apprehensum: quia recipit gratiam Dei in merito Christi fundatam, & evangelica promissione oblatam, qua aeterna salus donatur.

Prob. c. Mors, resurrectio mortuorum, iudicium extremum, & consummatio saeculi vocantur media salutis executiva, atque isagogica, vel introductoria. Executiva dicuntur, quatenus per ea Deus sententiam glorificationis & damnationis exsequitur: Isagogica vocantur, quatenus eorum proximo interventu homines, in fide finaliter perseverantes, in regnum gloriae introducuntur. De his


### III. In what mode of consideration is the Word of God treated here?

The Word of God is not considered here as a principle of γνώσεως, or of knowing, but as a medium of πράξεως, or of acting, by whose intervention the sinful man is led by God to eternal salvation.

Prob. The Word of God, considered as a principle of knowing God and divine things, pertains to the prolegomena of theology; in the present [context] it is weighed as a medium of calling, illuminating, converting, etc.

Quest. IV. Is the Word of God an efficacious medium of salvation? The Word of God is a most efficacious medium of salvation; indeed, its power and efficacy is not only objective, but also effective a); not consisting in moral persuasion, but in supernatural operation b); not external, or supervening in human use, but intrinsic to the word; not accidental, but necessary from the necessity of divine ordination, and thus not separable, but perpetual, belonging to the divine word, as a primary act, even outside of use c).

This efficacy is truly divine, producing the same effect as the Holy Spirit, who is perpetually united with the word, into which the Spirit flows together with the word through a divine power, which belongs to the Holy Spirit originally and independently, and to the Word of God communicatively and dependently, on account of the mystical, intimate, and indivisible union of the word with the Holy Spirit d).

Prob. a. The efficacy of the divine word is not only objective, or significative, such as that of a statue of Mercury, which shows the way but does not cause the traveler to walk; but effective, since the Word of God does not merely show the way of salvation, but also saves souls, Jas. 1:21.

Prob. b. That the efficacy of the divine word does not consist in moral persuasion, such as that of rhetoricians, persuading by the splendor of speech, the gravity of sentiments, and the weight of arguments, Paul teaches, 1 Cor. 2:4. My speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power. The same, v. 13. Which things also we speak, not in the words which man's wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth; comparing spiritual things with spiritual.

Prob. c. Divine power does not belong to the written Word of God through mere παράστασιν (presentation) and external assent, in such a way that, viewed in itself and outside of use, Scripture [has] the power of illuminating, converting and deprived of the power of regenerating the souls of men, it becomes ineffective and a dead letter. For it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth, Rom. 1:16, and the seed of regeneration, 2 Pet. 1:19. Therefore, it has and retains its internal power and efficacy even outside of use (just as the sun’s power of illuminating remains, even if, with the moon’s shadow intervening, no one perceives it, and just as a seed possesses internal efficacy, even though it has not been sown in a field), but it brings forth and exerts its efficacy in the second act when it is rightly used, attentively read, heard, and pondered.

Proof: Divine power is communicated to the Word by the Holy Spirit, who is inseparably joined with it.

For this reason:

1) The Word of God is called spirit and life, John 6:63, because it is instructed and animated by spirit and life.

2) The Word of God is living and powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword, and piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart; because it is joined with Christ, before whom no creature is invisible, Heb.

4:12, 13. 3) Supernatural and divine effects are attributed to the Word of God, which in the Holy Scriptures are also claimed for the Holy Spirit.

For indeed, by the Word of God we are called to the church, 2 Tim.

2:14, illuminated, 2 Pet.

1:19, converted, Jer.

23:29, regenerated, 1 Pet.

1:23, justified, 2 Cor.

3:9, renewed, John 17:17, preserved, Ps.

119:11, saved, James 1:21.

Therefore, these apotelesmata, or effects, concur as common to the Holy Spirit and the Word of God, not as associate causes, but the Holy Spirit produces the same as the principal cause, to which the Word of God is subordinated as an intermediate cause, and the power of illuminating, converting, regenerating, etc., belongs to the Holy Spirit originally and independently, and to the Word of God communicatively and dependently, through dependence upon the concurring Holy Spirit.

For it pleased the Father of lights to beget us with the word of truth, James 1:18.

4) The Word of God, as such, cannot be imagined without divine virtue, or without the Holy Spirit, who is inseparable from His Word.

For if the Holy Spirit were separated from the Word of God, it would not be that Word of God, or the Word of the Spirit, but it would be a human word.

Nor is the Word of God, which is in God, or which was inspired to the men of God, anything other than that which is handed down in Scripture, or preached, or stored in the human mind.

Now, that it is the divine sense, counsel, mind, and wisdom of God, as it cannot be denied, so it cannot be deprived of divine virtue.

The antithesis is that of the Schwenckfeldians and Weigelians, in whose opinion Holy Scripture has no efficacy outside of use.

Their arguments are: I.

No instrument has efficacy outside of use: The Word of God is an instrument: Therefore.

The major is evident: because the entire power of an instrument consists in its use.

Resp. 1) The Word of God is not so much an instrument as it is a medium, since not every medium is an instrument.

The Word of God is too eminent to be expressed by the name of an instrument; for it is the power of God, the counsel of God, the concept of the divine mind, etc.

Meanwhile, it is called an instrument, as in a broad sense, and primarily by reason of writing, preaching, economy, and ministry; but it is not properly called an instrument by reason of the internal virtue of the Holy Spirit with which it is endowed.

2) Distinguish between an instrument joined with a principal cause and one separated from it (a hammer, an axe, a writing pen, etc.) which has no efficacy outside of use; but an instrument, always joined with the principal cause, possesses its efficacy even outside of use, e.g., the ear outside of use enjoys the powers of hearing.

3) Distinguish between use and the ordination to actual use. The power of an instrument consists in its ordination to use, even if it is not actually employed. The eye, outside of the external act of vision, is a visual instrument; for the reason that it is ordained for seeing. II. Whatever word effects nothing outside of use, its efficacy depends upon use: But the divine word, etc. Therefore. The major is proved; because efficacy is for the sake of an effect, which, if it does not produce it, is in vain. But God did not bestow efficacy upon His Word in vain.

The minor is clear; because the word of God, outside of use, on paper or parchment, is like a dead letter, accomplishing nothing.

Resp. 1) Distinguish between the efficacy of the divine word viewed as a first act and as a second act. Outside of use, the word of God does not exercise its efficacy as a second act, yet it retains the same as a first act.

2) Although the word of God accomplishes or performs nothing outside of use; it is nevertheless destined for a salutary effect and operation, and thus its power is not in vain, nor is it to be called dead. The hand of a sleeping man performs nothing; yet the power of acting is not put into it in vain, nor is the hand, performing nothing, dead.

III. Whoever attributes divine power to a created thing, they are idolaters: But Evangelical Doctors &c. do so: Therefore.

The major is evident: because divine power is God himself. If, therefore, divine power belonged to Holy Scripture, it would be God himself. The minor is proven; because scripture is either creator or creature: It is not creator: Therefore, it is a creature.

Resp. 1) Whoever attributes divine power to a created thing, just as if it belonged to the thing originally and independently, they are idolaters; I concede this. But Evangelical Doctors maintain that the power of illuminating, regenerating, and renewing belongs to Holy Scripture dependently, communicatively, and by divine ordination.

2) Although Holy Scripture, viewed materially, as letters, syllables, and sounds, is from the sense of creatures; yet considered formally, as a θεόπνευστον (God-breathed) sense, it is wrongly reckoned among creatures, since it is the mind of God, the counsel of God, the wisdom of God, etc.

IV. If divine power is intrinsically in the word of God, it will also be in it outside of legitimate use, when applied by magicians and sorcerers for incantation: The consequent is false: Therefore, the antecedent is also.

Resp. Distinguish between use and abuse. Abuse, when it happens against the nature of the divine word, does not take away from it the intrinsic power which, though not physically affixed or included in it, is nevertheless supernaturally joined with it.

Furthermore, the word of God, outside of use, has an intrinsic efficacy which, by virtue of divine ordination, respects and requires legitimate use, so that a salutary effect may follow.

V. If the sacraments, outside of use, have no efficacy, neither will the word of God have any outside of use: But the former is true: Therefore, the latter is also. The consequence of the major is proven: because the sacraments, no less than the word of God, are means of salvation.

The assumption is evident from the trite axiom: let use be added to the element, and it becomes a sacrament.

Resp. The reason for the word and the sacraments is different. For the sacraments formally consist in action: Therefore, outside of use, they enjoy no efficacy.

But who would say that the word of God is formally an action; since the act of preaching, reading, and meditation only happens to it.

VI. Whatever is a sign of the divine will, that does not have an intrinsic power of working: But the word of God &c. is such. Therefore. The major is clear: because no sign, as such, works, but only represents the power of knowing something.

The minor is clear: because by the word of God, as a sign, the will of God is manifested.

Resp. The word of God considered materially, by reason of the sounds, is a sign; but viewed formally, by reason of the sense and dogmas, it is not a sign, but an efficacious means of salvation; nor does it only signify the mysteries of faith, but it also effectively converts the sinner.

VII. If the word of God has a native faculty of acting, then it exercises it either physically or morally. Not physically; for thus no one could resist it: Not morally; for thus it would not differ from the words of Demosthenes or Cicero.

Therefore, it does not have a native efficacy.

Resp. A third is given: The word of God exercises its power supernaturally.

For the power of the divine word is not physical (strictly speaking; because it does not happen through physical and quantitative contact); nor merely moral, such as is in the persuasive words of rhetoricians; but hyperphysical, however, through physical actions explained in the scriptures. For it is compared with seed bearing fruit, Mark IV, 25; with rain moistening, Isa. LV, 10; with honey refreshing, Ps. CXIX, 103. Therefore, the power of the divine word is hyperphysical, analogous to physical efficacy, i.e., true and real. Add that not every physical action is irresistible. Seed fructifies physically, but not irresistibly.

VIII. With whom the divine power of the Holy Spirit is perpetually joined, his operation is irresistible: But the operation of the divine word is not irresistible: Therefore, the divine power is not perpetually joined with it. The major is evident: because no one can resist the power of the Holy Spirit. The minor is proved from Heb. IV, 2: The word heard did not profit them, not being mixed by faith with those who heard. Resp. 1) I deny the major. For the divine power of the Holy Spirit joined with the word is not absolute, but ordered, to which an impediment can be opposed by the voluntary repugnance of man. 2) From the negation of the effect to the negation of the power of operating is a bad conclusion. For the word of God produces faith, through which it is mixed with hearts, in men who do not resist.

IX. If efficacy is intrinsic to the word of God; why do we sing: Deinen Geist und Krafft zum Worte geben? Resp. By the word in the litany is understood the external preaching and reading of the word, for which, so that it may attain the desired effect in the minds of the hearers and readers, the grace of God is implored, that it may remove impediments and open hearts (*).

Latin:

Verbum Dei hic non consideratur vt principium γνώσεως, siue cognoscendi, sed vt medium πράξεως, siue operandi, cuius interventu homo peccator a Deo ad aeternam salutem perducitur.

Prob. Verbum Dei, consideratum vt principium cognoscendi Deum & res diuinas, pertinet ad prolegomena theologiae; in praesenti pensitatur vt medium vocandi, illuminandi, conuertendi &c.

Quaest. IV. Estne verbum Dei efficax medium salutis? Verbum Dei est medium salutis efficacissimum; quippe cuius vis & efficacia non est tantum obiectiva, sed etiam effectiva a); non consistens in morali persuasione, sed in supernaturali operatione b); non externa, aut in vsu humano superueniens, sed verbo intrinseca; non accidentalis, sed necessaria ex necessitate ordinationis diuinae, atque adeo non separabilis, sed perpetua, extra vsum quoque, verbo diuino, qua actum primum, competens c).

Est haec efficacia vere diuina, eundem cum Spiritu S., qui perpetuo cum verbo vnitus est, producens effectum, in quem Spiritus influit vna cum verbo per vim diuinam, quae Spiritui S. originaliter & independenter, verbo Dei, communicatiue & dependenter, propter mysticam verbi cum Spiritu S. vnionem intimam & indiuiduam, competit d).

Prob. a. Efficacia verbi diuini non est tantum obiectiva, aut significativa, qualis est statuae Mercurialis, quae viam ostendit, sed non efficit, vt viator ambulet; sed effectiva, quoniam verbum Dei non ostendit duntaxat viam salutis, sed & saluas facit animas, Iac. I, 21.

Prob. b. Efficaciam verbi diuini non consistere in morali persuasione, qualis est rhetorum, orationis splendore, sententiarum gravitate, rationum pondere persuadentium, docet Paullus, 1 Cor. II, 4. Sermio meus & praeconium meum non fuit in persuasoriis humanae sapientiae verbis f.d in demonstratione spiritus & virtutis. Idem v. 13. Quae loquimur non doctis sapientiae humanae verbis, sed doctis Spiritus S., spiritualibus spiritualia componentes.

Prob. c. Non competit vis diuina verbo Dei scripto per nudam παράστασιν, & assientiam externam, ita, vt in se, & extra vsum spectata, Scriptura vi illuminandi, conuertendi & regenerandi hominum animas destituta, inefficax & littera mortua fit. Est enim potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti, Rom. I, 16. & semen regenerationis, 2 Pet. I, 19. Ergo internam suam vim, & efficaciam habet & retinet etiam, extra usum (sicut soli vis illuminandi constat, licet, obiecta lunæ umbra, nemo ipsum conspiciat, & sicut semen interna pollet efficacia, quamuis in agrum non sit sparsum), actu secundo autem suam efficaciam profert & exserit, cum recte usurpatur, attente legitur, auditur, pensitatur.

Vis diuina communicata est verbo a Spiritu S. cum eodem indiulse coniuncto.

Ideo enim 1) Verbum Dei dicitur spiritus & vita, Io.

VI, 63. quia spiritu & vita instructum atque animatum est.

2) Verbum Dei est viuum & efficax, & secantius omni gladio ancipiti, & pertingens usque ad diuisionem animæ & spiritus, compagum quoque ac medullarum, & discretor cogitationum & intentionum cordis; quia coniunctum est cum Christo, coram quo nulla creatura est inuisibilis, Hebr.

IV, 12. 13. 3) Tribuuntur verbo Dei effectus supernaturales & diuini, qui in sacris litteris etiam Spiritui S. vindicantur.

Etenim verbo Dei ad ecclesiam vocamur, 2 Tim.

II, 14. illuminamur, 2 Petr.

I, 19. conuertimur, Ier.

XXIII, 29. regeneramur, 1 Petr.

I, 23. iustificamur, 2 Cor.

III, 9. renouamur, Io. XVII, 17. conseruamur, Ps.

CXIX, 11. saluamur, Iac. I, 21.

Concurrunt ergo ad hæc ἀποτελέσματα, siue effecta communia Spiritus S. & verbum Dei non vt causæ sociæ, sed Spiritus S. eadem producit, vt causa principalis, cui verbum Dei subordinatur, vt causa intermedia, & competit vis illuminandi, conuertendi, regenerandi &c.
