Spiritui S. originaliter & independenter, verbo Dei communicatiue & dependenter, per dependentiam a Spiritu S. concurrente.

Placuit enim Patri lumen, generare vos verbo veritatis, Iac. I, 18.

4) Verbum Dei, qua tale, non potest fingi sine diuina virtute, aut sine Spiritu S., qui a verbo suo est inseparabilis.

Nam si a verbo Dei separetur Spiritus S. non esset id Dei verbum, vel verbum Spiritus, sed esset verbum humanum.

Nec vero aliud est Dei verbum, quod in Deo est, vel quod inspiratum est viris Dei, quam quod in scriptura traditur, aut prædicatur, vel mente humana reconditur.

Illud autem diuinum sensum, consilium, mentem, sapientiam Dei esse, vti negari nequit, ita virtute diuina destitui non potest.

Antithesis est Schwenckfeldianorum & Weigelianorum, quorum mente S. Scriptura extra vsum nullam habet efficaciam.

Quorum argumenta sunt: I.

Nullum instrumentum extra vsum habet efficaciam: Verbum Dei est instrumentum: Ergo.

Maior patet: quia tota vis instrumenti consistit in vsu.

Resp. 1) Verbum Dei non tam instrumentum est, quam medium, cum non omne medium sit instrumentum.

Eminentius est verbum Dei, quam vt nomine instrumenti exprimatur; est enim potentia Dei, consilium Dei, conceptus mentis diuinæ &c.

Vocatur interim instrumentum, ὡς ἐν πλάτει, & in primis ratione scriptionis, prædicationis, οἰκονομίας & ministerii; non autem proprie vocatur instrumentum ratione internæ virtutis Spiritus S. qua præditum est.

2) Dist. inter instrumentum cum causa principali coniunctum, & ab ea separatum (malleus, securis, calamus scriptorius &c.) extra vsum nullam habet efficaciam; At instrumentum, cum causa principali semper coniunctum, sua pollet efficacia, etiam extra vsum, v. gr. auris extra vsum gaudet viribus audiendi.

3) Dist. inter vsum, & ordinationem ad vsum actualem. Vis instrumenti consistit in ordinatione ad vsum, licet actu non vsurpetur. Oculus extra externum visionis actum instrumentum est visiuum; ideo, quod ad videndum est ordinatus. II. Quodcunque verbum extra vsum nil efficit, illius efficacia ab vsu pendet: Atqui verbum diuinum &c. Ergo. Maior probatur; quia efficacia est propter effectum, quem nisi producat, frustranea est. At Deus efficaciam verbo suo non frustra impertivit. suo non frustra impertivit.

Minor liquet; quia verbum Dei, extra usum, in charta, aut membrana, est instar litteræ mortuæ, nil efficientis.

Resp. 1) Dist. inter efficaciam verbi diuini spectatam qua actum primum, & secundum. Extra usum verbum Dei non exercet suam efficaciam, qua actum secundum, retinet tamen eandem, qua actum primum.

2) Quamuis verbum Dei extra usum nil efficiat, aut operetur; ad salutarem tamen effectum & operationem destinatum est, adeoque vis eius non est frustranea, nec illud mortuum dicendum est. Manus hominis dormientis nil operatur; neque tamen operandi vis ei frustra indita est, nec manus, nil operans, mortua est.

III. Quicunque rei creatæ virtutem diuinam attribuunt, illi sunt idololatræ: Atqui Doctores Euangelici &c: Ergo.

Maior constat: quia virtus diuina est ipse Deus. Quod si itaque S. scripturæ competeret vis diuina, esset ipse Deus. Minor probatur; quia scriptura aut est creator, aut creatura: Non est creator: E. est creatura.

Resp. 1) Quicunque rei creatæ attribuunt virtutem diuinam, perinde, ac si rei competeret originaliter & independenter, illi sunt idololatræ; concedo. At Doctores Euangelici statuunt, virtutem illuminandi, regenerandi, renouandi, competere S. scripturæ dependenter, communicatiue, & ex ordinatione diuina.

2) Tametsi S. scriptura spectata materialiter, qua litteras, syllabas & voces, sit e sensu creaturarum; considerata tamen formaliter, qua sensum θεόπνευστον, male creaturis accenfetur, cum sit mens Dei, consilium Dei, sapientia Dei &c.

IV. Si vis diuina intrinsece inest verbo Dei, etiam extra legitimum usum, eidem inerit adhibito a magis & veneficis ad incantationem: Consequens est falsum: E. & antecedens.

Resp. Dist. Inter usum & abusum. Abusus, cum fit contra naturam verbi diuini, huic intrinsecam non adimit virtutem, quæ ipsi non physice affixa, aut inclusa, supernaturaliter tamen cum eodem coniuncta est.

Ceterum verbum Dei, extra usum, habet intrinsecam efficaciam, quæ vi ordinationis diuinæ legitimum usum respicit & requirit, vt salutaris effectus sequatur.

V. Si sacramenta, extra usum, nullam habent efficaciam, neque verbum Dei extra usum vllam habebit: Atqui prius est verum: E. & posterius. Consequentia maioris probatur: quia sacramenta haud secus, ac verbum Dei, sunt media salutis.

Assumtio constat ex trito axiomate: accedat usus ad elementum, & fit sacramentum.

Resp. Dispar est ratio verbi & sacramentorum. Sacramenta enim formaliter in actione consistunt: E. extra usum nulla gaudent efficacia.

At quis diceret, verbum Dei formaliter esse actionem; quippe cui actus prædicationis, lectionis & meditationis tantum accidit.

VI. Quidquid est signum voluntatis diuinæ, illud non habet vim intrinsecam operandi: Atqui verbum Dei &c. E. Maior patet: quia nullum signum, vt tale, operatur, sed tantum potentiam cognoscendi aliquid repræsentat.

Minor claret: quia verbo Dei, velut figno, voluntas Dei manifestatur.

Resp. Verbum Dei materialiter consideratum, ratione vocum, est signum; sed formaliter spectatum, ratione sensus & dogmatum, non est signum, sed medium salutis efficax; neque etiam tantum mysteria fidei significat, sed etiam peccatorem efficaciter conuertit.

VII. Si verbum Dei natiuam habet agendi facultatem, tum illam exercet vel physice, vel moraliter. Non physice; sic enim nemo ei posset resistere: Non moraliter; sic enim a verbis Demosthenis, aut Ciceronis non differret.

E. non habet natiuam efficaciam.

Resp. Datur tertium: Verbum Dei suam vim exercet supernaturaliter.

Etenim vis verbi diuini non est physica (stricte loquendo; quia non fit per contactum physicum & quantitatiuum); neque mere moralis, qualis est in persuasoriis rhetorum verbis; fed hyperphysica, per physicas tamen actiones in scripturis exposita. Comparatur enim cum semine fructificante, Marc. IV, 25. cum pluuia humectante, Es. LV, 10. cum melle recreante, Ps. CXIX, 103. Est ergo vis verbi diuini hyperphysica, analoga efficaciæ physicæ, i. e. vera & realis. Adiice, quod non omnis actio physica sit irresistibilis. Semen physice fructificat, sed non irresistibiliter.

VIII. Cum quo virtus diuina Spiritus S. perpetuo coniuncta est, illius operatio est irresistibilis: Sed operatio verbi diuini non est irresistibilis: E. virtus diuina cum eo non est perpetuo coniuncta. Maior est euidens: quia virtuti Spiritus S. nemo potest resistere. Minor probatur ex Hebr. IV, 2. Non profuit illis sermo auditus, non admistus per fidem cum iis, qui audiuerunt. Resp. 1) Neg. maior. Virtus quippe diuina Spiritus S. cum verbo coniuncta non est absoluta, sed ordinata, cui a voluntaria hominis repugnantia impedimentum obiici potest. 2) A negatione effectus ad negandum vim operandi male concluditur. Producit enim verbum Dei fidem, per quam cum cordibus commiscetur, in hominibus non obsistentibus.

IX. Si verbo Dei intrinseca est efficacia; quare canimus: Deinen Geist und Krafft zum Worte geben? Resp. Per verbum in litania intelligitur externa verbi prædicatio & lectio, quæ vt in animis auditorum & lectorum optatum assequatur effectum, gratia Dei imploratur, vt impedimenta remoueat, & corda aperiat (*).


### Q. V. How is the word of God divided?

The word of God is divided into the word of the law, and the word of the gospel. The former excites contrition; the latter kindles saving faith by divine intention.

Prob. 1) John the Baptist inculcates the distinction of the divine word into law and gospel, John I, 17. The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. The law was given through Moses, not as the author, but as a minister. But the truest grace came to us through Jesus Christ the mediator; which is the sum of the evangelical proclamation: which the Son of God himself brought forth from the bosom of the Father, and manifested to us. Paul hands down the same distinction, 2 Cor. III, 6. The letter kills, but the spirit gives life. The law is called the letter, because it was not only once inscribed in letters on stone tablets, but because it also, like a letter, prescribes and demands things to be done, but confers no powers for doing them. The gospel, however, is spirit; in that it gives the spirit, which, by graciously uniting itself with the word of the gospel, bestows upon it the spiritual power to illuminate, regenerate, justify, and save our hearts.

2) The law detects and convicts sin, Rom. II, 19; it works wrath, c. IV, 15; it announces a curse, Deut. XXVII, 27; it kills, 2 Cor. III, 6. The Gospel, however, covers sins, Rom. IV, 7; and teaches absolution from sins, Matt. IX, 2; it works salvation, Rom. I, 17; it brings a blessing, Gal. III, 14; and it gives life, 2 Cor. III, 6. Therefore, contrition is excited through the law, but faith, righteousness, and salvation are given through the Gospel.

Latin:

Verbum Dei diuiditur in verbum legis, & verbum euangelii. Illud excitat contritionem; hoc accendit fidem saluificam ex intentione diuina.

Prob. 1) Distinctionem verbi diuini in legem & euangelium inculcat Ioannes baptista, Io. I, 17. Lex per Mosen data est; gratia & veritas per Iesum Christum facta est. Lex per Mosen data est, non vt auctorem, sed vt ministrum. At gratia verissima nobis obtigit per Iesum Christum mediatorem; quæ summa est præconii euangelici: quod ipse Filius Dei e sinu Patris protulit, & nobis manifestauit. Eandem distinctionem tradit Paullus, 2 Cor. III, 6. Littera occidit, spiritus autem viuificat. Lex dicitur littera, quia non tantum olim litteris inscripta fuit tabulis lapideis, sed quia etiam velut littera, præscribit & exigit agenda, sed nullas agendi vires confert. Euangelium autem est spiritus; eo, quod dat spiritum, qui, se gratiose vniendo cum verbo euangelii, largitur ei vim spiritualem corda nostra illuminandi, regenerandi, iustificandi, saluandi.

2) Lex peccata detegit & arguit, Rom. II, 19. operatur iram, c. IV, 15. annuntiat maledictionem, Deut. XXVII, 27. occidit, 2 Cor. III, 6. Evangelium vero peccata tegit, Rom. IV, 7. docetque absolutionem a peccatis, Matt. IX, 2. operatur salutem, Rom. I, 17. affert benedictionem, Gal. III, 14. ac vivificat, 2 Cor. III, 6. Excitatur itaque contritio per legem, datur vero fides, iustitia & salus per evangelium.


### Of the Word of the Law

Quest. VI. Is the divine law a means of salvation? The divine law is not a causal and contributing means of salvation for fallen man, but is only a pedagogical means for the sinful man who is seeking a causal means of salvation.

Proof a. The divine law does indeed promise eternal life, but under the condition of perfect fulfillment, Lev. XVIII, 5; Ezek. XX, 11. But since after the fall no one provides the law with perfect obedience in all respects; because it is weakened by the flesh, Rom. VIII, 3; it happens accidentally that the law works wrath, Rom. IV, 15; and kills, 2 Cor. III, 6. Proof b. The law is our schoolmaster unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith, Gal. III, 24. The law leads to Christ not directly, but just as a disease leads to a physician, and by the occasion of the demonstrated inability (ἀδυναμία) to obtain salvation through the law. Blessed LUTHER explains this pedagogy of the law excellently in vol. III of the Jena edition, fol. 29. The law prepares for grace while it reveals and increases sin, humbling the proud, so that they desire the help of Christ.

Quest. VII. What is law? Law is the command of a superior, by which he dictates to his subject what is to be done and what is to be omitted, and binds the same to obedience, or, this failing, to punishment.

Obs. I. SAMUEL PUFFENDORF, in Book I of De Jure Naturae et Gentium, p. 81, defines law in general as a decree by which a superior binds his subject so that he may compose his actions according to the prescription of that [superior]. Where it is strictly to be noted that a decree commanding and a command are the same thing. Therefore, whether you define law by a decree and precept, or by the command of a superior, the matter comes to the same thing. For "command" is taken so broadly here that it even includes the impression of natural law.

Obs. II. Since, however, the command of a superior binding an inferior to himself is either of God or of man, therefore law is divided into divine and human. For us at present, the discourse is about divine law, which God gave to men.

Quest. VIII. What is divine law? Divine law is the command of God, by which this supreme Lord and legislator commands men what is to be done and forbids what is to be avoided, binding the same to provide perfect obedience, or, this failing, to punishment.

Note. Divine law in the Holy Scriptures is taken a) most generally, for the entire heavenly doctrine, Ps. I, 2; b) more specially, for the scriptures of the O.T., John XV, 25; 1 Cor. XIV, 21; c) most specially, for the Mosaic Pentateuch, Luke XXIV, 44. Here, however, the terms of law and gospel are taken insofar as they are adequately contrasted with one another, and law denotes the norm of things to be done and avoided, the gospel the norm of things to be believed. The sum of the law is: Do this, and you shall live, Luke X, 28; Gal. III, 12. The sum of the Gospel is: Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you shall be saved, Acts XVI, 31.

Latin:

Quaest. VI. Estne lex diuina medium salutis? Lex diuina homini lapso non est medium causale & collatiuum salutis , sed est tantum medium paedagogicum, homini peccatori, causale salutis medium quaerenti .

Prob. a. Promittit quidem lex diuina vitam aeternam, sed sub conditione perfectae impletionis, Leu. XVIII, 5. Ezech. XX, 11. At quoniam post lapsum nemo legi omnibus numeris perfectam praestat obedientiam; propterea, quod a carne infirmatur, Rom. VIII, 3. ex accidenti fit, vt lex iram operetur, Rom. IV, 15. & occidat, 2 Cor. III, 6. Prob. b. Lex est paedagogus noster ad Christum, vt ex fide iustificemur, Gal. III, 24. Ducit lex ad Christum non directe, sed sicut morbus ad medicum ducit, & per occasionem monstratae ἀδυναμίας, salutem obtinendi per legem. Egregie hanc paedagogiam legis explicat B. LVTHERVS, in tom. III. Ienens. fol. 29. Lex ad gratiam praeparat, dum peccatum reuelat & auget, humilians superbos, ad auxilium Christi desiderandum.

Quaest. VII. Quid est lex? Lex est iussum superioris, quo sibi subiecto agenda & omittenda dictat, eumdemque obligat ad obsequium, aut hoc deficiente, ad poenam .

Obs. I. SAMVEL PVFFENDORFF. in L. I. de I. N. & G. p. 81. in genere definit legem, quod fit decretum, quo superior sibi subiectum obligat, vt ad istius praescriptum actiones suas componat. Vbi oppido notandum, quod decretum praecipiens, & iussum idem fit. Idcirco siue per decretum & praeceptum, siue per iussum superioris definias legem, res eodem recidit. Iussum enim tam late hic sumitur, vt etiam impressionem legis naturalis includat.

Obs. II. Cum autem iussum superioris, inferiorem sibi obligantis, vel Dei sit, vel hominis: ideo lex in diuinam & humanam diuiditur. Nobis in praesenti sermo est de lege diuina, quam Deus dedit hominibus.

Quaest. VIII. Quid est lex diuina? Lex diuina est iussum Dei, quo summus hic Dominus & legislator hominibus facienda praecipit, & fugienda prohibet, eosdem obligans ad praestandam perfectam obedientiam, aut, hac deficiente, ad poenam .

Obs. Lex diuina in sacris litteris sumitur a) generalissime, pro vniuersa doctrina coelesti, Ps. I, 2; b) specialius, pro scripturis V. T. Io. XV, 25. 1 Cor. XIV, 21; c) specialissime pro pentateucho Mosaico, Luc. XXIV, 44. Hic autem accipiuntur voces legis & euangelii, quatenus adaequate sibi contradistinguuntur, denotatque lex normam faciendorum & fugiendorum, euangelium normam credendorum. Summa legis est: Fac hoc, & viues, Luc. X, 28. Gal. III, 12. Euangelii summa est: Crede in Dominum Iesum, & saluaberis, Act. XVI, 31.


### Quest. X

The divine law is either universal and perpetual, or particular and temporary. The universal and perpetual law is the immutable rule of all moral acts, by which God obliges all men to do that which is honest and right, and to flee that which is base and unjust. It is also called the moral law. The particular and temporary law is that which God gave to the Israelites alone, and bound them to obedience: which, upon the fall of the Hebrew polity, itself fell, and is either ceremonial or forensic.

Obs. We are speaking at present of the law of God not as archetypal, but as ectypal. The archetypal law is the eternal and immutable justice, holiness, wisdom, and judgment of God concerning the honest and the base, joined with the will that the honest be done by the rational creature, and the base be omitted. Whence God is said to be law unto Himself. Against this eternal law God can in no way act; because He cannot deny Himself, 1 Tim. II, 13. But He would deny Himself if He were to act against the eternal law, i.e., against Himself. The ectypal is every law given to the rational creature by God; for it is derived from the law of God, which was born with God, as MARCUS TULLIUS says in book II of the Laws.

Ques. X. How is the perpetual and moral law of God, spoken of generally, divided?

The perpetual law of God is divided into natural law and moral law specifically so called (*). Natural law is the command of God, naturally impressed upon the minds of all, by which they are informed and obliged to do those things which are in themselves right and honest, and to flee those things which are in themselves iniquitous and base, for the praise of God the Creator and the preservation of civil society.

Obs. I. The law of nature here does not denote the law of nature prescribed by the Creator, by virtue of which every creature maintains its own order, nor the right common to man and beast, which is defined by ULPIAN in book I of the Institutes, tit. 2: Natural law is that which nature has taught all animals, and is improperly called the law of nature; but here the law of nature denotes the right divinely implanted in man and impressed through nature (**).

Obs. II. The natural law is also called moral in a general sense; because it directs morals, or the manner of living, which befits a rational creature. Obs.

from his very fingernails to his final breath needs the work and benevolence of others: Finally, the third is the scope of the sciences, arts, and various kinds of life, along with a certain natural inclination of minds. Yet there would not be even the least use of all these without the closest bond of society. To this third part of human nature are to be referred those duties which contribute much to living tranquilly and well in society and the commonwealth. These foundations having been laid, I trust it will be clear that there are altogether three kinds of natural laws, and consequently different principles for each. Indeed, there is one general principle, which extends so broadly that it pertains to that entire threefold nature of man, namely this: Live conveniently and congruently with nature. But there are also Special principles

I. Of animal nature; namely this: One must live conveniently for the preservation of life and the perception of the senses.

From this principle proceed these laws, and those which are of this kind: Seek food and shelter: Decline harmful things: Dare nothing against the affection of love, called στοργὴν [storgēn], which is present even in brute animals, by which they are carried toward their young, and which is by no means to be confused with the virtue of love, ἀγάπης [agapēs], which must always be directed by the use of reason. These are indeed a certain necessity and natural instinct for brute animals, the cause and reason of which they themselves do not know; but for man, they are laws, properly so called, inasmuch as he is capable of their knowledge.

II. The principle of rational nature is this: Know thyself.

For from this one [principle] all laws are made, looking toward this most noble nature of man. Namely, man, when he turns his mind to himself, easily understands the origin of human nature, because it depends entirely on the will of one Creator and Preserver; its constitution, nay even its excellence, but at the same time its corruption and misery, although he has an obscure and insufficient knowledge of it, until he is illuminated by revelation.

Therefore, the natural laws that pertain to this are especially these: 1) From the known dependence, to use a common word, of human nature: Remember your Creator and Preserver, and rightly know and worship Him: Use created things, and moderately, according to what is right, and wisely, that is, for the just ends of each thing, established by the Creator Himself.

2) From the known constitution, and also the excellence of human nature: Undertake nothing without counsel and deliberation: Always set for yourself an end, good and salutary: Discern the truly good from the false and specious, the greater from the lesser, the certain from the uncertain: Value the happiness of the soul more than the care of the body, though the latter is not to be treated negligently: Of two evils, if you cannot avoid both at once, choose the lesser: It is better to suffer evil than to do it, nor are evils to be done so that goods may result from the accident: The necessary is to be preferred to the useful, the useful to the pleasant: Compare means with ends, and do not consider only what is present, but also anticipate in thought what will be: Choose the best, most certain, and safest medium from among many.

3) From the known corruption and misery of human nature: Explore the defects of your intelligence and will, but especially of your religion and reverence toward God: Hear the voice of your conscience: Reprove yourself: Desire and seek the restoration and perfection of your happiness: Bear with an even mind the evils that might happen to you, and do not attribute any blame for them to God, the author of all good things.

In these is discerned the use which is called pedagogical, of nature to grace, of reason to revelation.

III. The principle of social nature is that which a man once great, PVFENDORFIVS, held as the general principle of the entire law of nature: Behave conveniently and decently toward society.

From this source have flowed the special laws, the chief of which are: Exercise public worship of God with others, so that there may be both a mutual stirring of minds and a common profession of the highest duty, by which we are all alike bound to God: Harm no one: Render to each his own: What you wish to be done to you, that do in turn to another, and what you do not wish done to you, do not do to another: Regard is to be had for those joined to you by near kinship and relationship, more than for others: Each according to his own reason: Pro sua quem.

Obs. III. Things are honest by themselves and by nature, which are suitable to a rational creature, as such. Conversely, things are base by themselves, which are unsuitable to a rational creature, as such.

Latin:

Lex diuina est vel vniuersalis & perpetua, vel particularis & temporaria. Lex vniuersalis & perpetua est immutabilis omnium actuum moralium regula, qua Deus omnes homines obligat ad faciendum id, quod honestum & rectum, fugiendum id, quod turpe & iniustum est. Vocatur etiam lex moralis. Lex particularis & temporaria est, quam Deus solis dedit Israëlitus, eosque ad obedientiam obstrinxit: Quæ cadente Hebræorum politia, & ipsa cecidit, estque vel cæremonialis vel forensis.

Obs. Loquimur in præsenti de lege Dei non archetypa, sed ectypa. Lex archetypa est æterna & immutabilis Dei iustitia, sanctitas, sapientia & iudicium de honestis & turpibus coniunctum cum voluntate, vt honesta a creatura rationali fiant, & turpia omittantur. Vnde Deus sibi ipsi lex esse dicitur. Contra hanc æternam legem Deus nullo modo facere potest; quia seipsum abnegare nequit, 1 Tim. II, 13. Abnegaret autem seipsum, si contra æternam legem, i. e. seipsum faceret. Ectypa est omnis lex creaturæ rationali a Deo data; ea enim deriuatur a lege Dei, quæ nata est cum Deo, dicente MARCO TVLLIO libr. II. de legibus.

Quæst. X. Quomodo diuiditur lex Dei perpetua & moralis, generatim dicta?

Lex Dei perpetua diuiditur in legem naturalem & moralem specialiter sic dictam (*). Lex naturalis est iussum Dei, omnium mentibus naturaliter impressum, quo informantur, & obligantur ad faciendum ea, quæ per se sunt recta & honesta, & ad fugiendum ea, quæ per se sunt iniqua & turpia, in laudem Dei creatoris & societatis ciuilis conseruationem.

Obs. I. Lex naturæ hic non notat legem naturæ a conditore præscriptam, vi cuius quælibet creatura ordinem suum tuetur, neque ius homini & bruto commune, quod ab VLPIANO libr. I. instit. tit. 2. definitur: Ius naturale est, quod natura omnia animalia docuit, & ius naturæ improprie vocatur; sed denotat hic lex naturæ ius, homini diuinitus inditum, & per naturam impressum (**).

Obs. II. Lex naturalis dicitur etiam moralis sensu generali; ideo, quòd dirigit mores, seu rationem viuendi, quæ rationalem creaturam decet. Obs.

vnguiculis vsque ad extremum spiritum eget aliorum opera ac beneuolentia: Tertium denique est ambitus scientiarum, artium, variorumque vitæ generum, cum naturali quadam animorum inclinatione. Eorum autem omnium ne minimus quidem vsus esset sine arctissimo societatis vinculo. Ad tertiam hanc humanæ naturæ partem referenda sunt ea officia, quæ multum conferunt ad tranquille bonefque viuendum in societate reque publica. Iactis his fundamentis, perspicuum fore, confido, legum etiam naturalium omnino tria esse genera, ac proinde singulorum diuersa quoque principia. Vnum quidem est principium generale, quod ita latissime patet, vt ad vniuersam illam triplicem hominis naturam pertineat, nimirum hoc: Naturæ conuenienter congruenterque viue. Sunt vero etiam principia Specialia

I. Naturæ animalis; quippe hoc: Vitæ conseruationi, sensuumque perceptioni conuenienter viuendum est.

Ab hoc principio proficiscuntur hæ leges, & quæ sunt huiusmodi: Quære alimenta & latibula: Declina nocitura: Nihil aude contra adfectum amoris, στοργὴν dictum, qui in brutis etiam animantibus inest, quo erga pullos suos feruntur, & qui cum virtute amoris, ἀγάπης, semper rationis vsu dirigenda, neutiquam confundendus est. Hæc sunt brutis quidem animantibus necessitas quædam, ac naturalis instinctus, cuius caussam rationemque ipsa nesciunt; homini autem leges, propriæ sic nominatæ, vtpote quarum cognitione ipse capax est.

II. Naturæ rationalis principium hoc est: Nosce te ipsum.

Ex hoc enim vno omnes efficiuntur leges, ad hanc nobilissimam hominis naturam spectantes. Scilicet homo, cum animum ad se aduertit, facile intelligit naturæ humanæ originem, quod ea tota ex vnius Creatoris & Conseruatoris arbitrio pendeat; constitutionem, immo & excellentiam, at simul tamen corruptionem ac miseriam, quamuis obscuram eius, nec sufficientem, notitiam habeat, donec reuelatione illuminetur.

Ergo, quæ huc pertinent, leges naturales sunt hæ potissimum: 1) Ex cognita dependentia, vt vulgari verbo vtar, humanæ naturæ: Memento Creatoris & Conseruatoris tui, recteque cum cognosce & cole: Vtere rebus creatis, & modice, pro eo, ac par est, & sapienter, hoc est, propter iustos rei cuiusque fines, ab ipso Creatore constitutos.

2) Ex cognita constitutione, atque etiam præstantia humanæ naturæ: Nil fine consilio ac deliberatione suscipe: Semper tibi finem constitue, bonum ac salutarem: Discerne vere bonum a falso ac specioso, maius a minori, certum ab incerto: Beatitatem animi fac pluris, quam corporis curam, non negligenter quidem tractandam: Ex duobus malis, si vtrumque simul euitare non queas, minus elige: Præstat malum perpeti, quam operari, nec facienda sunt mala, vt ex accidente eueniant bona: Necessarium anteferendum est vtili, vtile iucundo: Media cum finibus compara, nec id, quod præsens est, solum considera, verum etiam quid futurum sit, cogitatione præcipe: Elige medium ex pluribus optimum, certissimum, tutissimum.

3) Ex cognita corruptione ac miseria humanæ naturæ: Explora defectus tuæ intelligentiæ ac voluntatis, in primis vero tuæ religionis ac reuerentiæ aduersus Deum: Audi vocem tuæ conscientiæ: Te ipse reprehende: Restitutionem ac perfectionem tuæ felicitatis exopta & quære: Mala, quæ tibi acciderent, æquo fer animo, neque vllam eorum culpam Deo omnium bonorum auctori, tribue.

In his cernitur vsus, qui vocatur, pædagogicus naturæ ad gratiam, rationis ad reuelationem.

III. Naturæ socialis principium est, quod vir quondam summus, PVFENDORFIVS, pro generali principio vniuersi iuris naturæ habuit: Societati conuenienter decenterque se gere.

Ex hoc fonte manarunt speciales leges, quarum præcipuæ sunt: Cultum Dei publicum cum aliis exerce, vt & mutua animorum incitatio sit, & communis professio officii summi, quo omnes pariter Deo deuincti sumus: Neminem læde: Suum cuique tribue: Quod tibi vis fieri, id tu alteri vicissim præsta, & quod tibi non vis fieri, alteri ne feceris: Propinqua cognatione ac necessitudine tecum coniunctorum, magis, quam aliorum, habenda est ratio: Pro sua quem est ratio: Pro sua quem.

Obs. III. Per se & natura honesta sunt, quae creaturae rationali, ut tali, conveniunt. Contra per se turpia sunt, quae creaturae rationali, ut tali, disconveniunt.


### XI. Is there a law of nature in man after the fall?

The law of nature, indeed, through the fall of the first men and the infection of the fall's sins, has been greatly obliterated; yet certain traces of it have remained, namely universal principles, from which the distinction between honest and base things is naturally known.

Prob. 1) From the testimony of Paul, Rom. 2:15. Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature the things that are of the law: These, although they do not have the law, are a law unto themselves, (inasmuch as) they demonstrate the work of the law written in their hearts, while their conscience bears witness to them, and their thoughts will accuse or even excuse them among themselves. The Gentiles do not indeed have the Mosaic law, proposed or prescribed to them by divine revelation; yet they have a law, written by the finger of nature, by the force of which they descend into themselves after their actions, and now accuse themselves as violators of the law given by God, now excuse, defend, and praise themselves as observers of the law.

2) There exist in the practical intellect of man first and universal principles, such as: Good is to be done, and evil is to be avoided: God is to be worshipped: The advantages of civil society are to be promoted: What you wish that another should do to you, do you to him: Live honestly: Injure no one: Give to each his own: Commit nothing of which you might be ashamed or repent. The habit of these practical principles is called in the schools συντήρησις (synderesis).

3) There is given also after the fall the faculty of applying first practical principles to singular actions, e.g., It is not permitted for me today to beat Sempronius; because no one is to be injured. Which faculty of applying practical principles here and now is called φρόνησις (phronesis), or prudence.

4) The natural law reveals and exerts itself naturally, which seizes the mind with horror and shame, e.g., it testifies that intercourse with a mother or with a beast is wicked, horror before the act, and shame after the act.

5) The natural law is confirmed by the suffrage of all more cultured nations. Moreover, it is an argument of truth that something seems so to all, says SENECA, epist. 117.

Latin:

Lex naturae quidem per lapsum primorum hominum, & infecta lapsum peccata, valde oblitterata est; remanserunt tamen quaedam eiusdem vestigia, nempe universalia principia, ex quibus discrimen honestorum & turpium naturaliter innotescit.

Prob. 1) Ex testimonio Pauli, Rom. II, 15. Gentiles, qui legem non habent, natura ea, quae legis sunt, faciunt: Hi, licet legem non habeant, sibi ipsis lex sunt, (quippe) qui demonstrant, opus legis scriptum in cordibus suis, dum illis testimonium perhibet conscientia illorum, & inter sese cogitationes accusabunt, vel etiam excusabunt. Gentiles non habent quidem legem Mosaicam, per revelationem divinam sibi propositam, aut praescriptam; habent tamen legem, digito naturae scriptam, cuius vi post actiones suas in se descendunt, & seipsos iam ut violatores legis a Deo latae accusant, iam ut servatores legis excusant, defendunt, laudant.

2) Exstant in intellectu hominis practico principia prima & universalia, qualia sunt: Bonum est faciendum, & malum est fugiendum: Deus est colendus: Commoda societatis civilis sunt promovenda: Quod vis, ut alius tibi faciat, tu ipsi fac: Honeste vive: Neminem laede: Unicuique suum tribue: Nihil committe, cuius te pudeat, aut paeniteat. Horum principiorum practicorum habitus in scholis vocatur συντήρησις.

3) Datur etiam post lapsum facultas applicandi prima principia practica ad actiones singulares, v. gr. Non licet mihi hodie verberare Sempronium; quoniam nemo est laedendus. Quae facultas, hic & nunc applicandi principia practica, appellatur φρόνησις, seu prudentia.

4) Lex naturalis se prodit & exserit naturali, qui animum capit, horrore & pudore, v. gr. concubitum cum matre, cum bestia, iniquum esse, horror ante factum, & pudor post factum testatur.

5) Lex naturalis omnium gentium cultiorum suffragio comprobatur. Argumentum autem veritatis est, omnibus aliquid videri, ait SENECA epist. 117.


### XII. What are the causes of the natural law?

The efficient cause of the natural law is God a). The exemplary cause is the justice and holiness of God b). The matter from which it is made are common notions, or practical principles, and honor them with dignity: Apply your mind to a certain kind of life, to which you have understood yourself to be most apt and as if born, so that you may be for the benefit of the republic: Take care of the function of the office entrusted to you diligently and faithfully, and do not involve yourself in the business of others: The safety of the many is to be preferred to the safety of one individual: Keep faith, but see to whom: Pacts and promises are to be kept: Observe all duties which pertain to the use of speech. (*)

lic, known by nature c). The matter in which, or the subject which, is man, not a brute d). The subject by which is man's intellect, will, and sensitive appetite e). The matter about which, or the personal object, is God, one's neighbor, and man himself f). The real object is things to be done and things to be avoided g). The form is the directive and obligatory power h). The end intended in itself is the glory of God i), and the preservation of civil society k). The accidental end, or outcome, is ἀναπολόγησις, or the lack of excuse l).

Prob. a. The efficient cause of natural law is God, who 1) by the very fact that He gave man reason, by which he strives to discern good from evil, simultaneously willed that man should do the good he knows and omit the evil. Hence, when Paul in Rom. 2:15 asserts that the Gentiles show the work of the law written in their hearts, he understands the inscription made by God through natural propagation. 2) The obligation of natural law is from God Himself, the Creator and supreme governor of the human race, because He has bound men to observe it by His authority. The sense of conscience, very tender in the minds of men who are not completely savage, testifies to this, by which they are convinced that by sinning against the law of nature, they offend Him who has authority over the minds of men, and who is to be feared even where no fear threatens from men.

Prob. b. The law as an imprint (ἔκτυπος) has its archetype (ἀρχέτυπον) in the very holiness and justice of God, which natural law reflects just as rays, scattered into water, reflect their source, the sun; as an image reflects its exemplar. Therefore, the ultimate root of the law of nature does not reside in the divine will, but in the holiness and justice of God; and God forbade sin not because He willed it, but because it is contrary to the very injustice and holiness of God.

Prob. c. The practical principles known by nature, which we reviewed above, are as it were the constituent parts of the law of nature; when these are posited, the law of nature is posited, and when they are removed, it is removed—the light of truth and the seed of goodness.

Prob. d. Man, a participant in reason and free will, is capable of natural law. Hence, the law of nature, properly so called, does not apply to brutes: Because 1) due to a lack of reason, they cannot compose their actions to the norm of law: 2) Because they lack free will, which is constrained by law. Analogically, however, and by way of similarity, it is attributed to them; insofar as they, just like man, intend their own preservation, repel injury, and nourish and defend the offspring they have generated.

Prob. e. Natural law illuminates the intellect of man, like a mirror, so that he may know and judge good and evil; it directs the will so that it may choose the good proposed by the intellect and reject the evil shown to it: but the sensitive appetite is kept within certain bounds by the law of nature, lest it go astray or overstep the laws of honesty.

Prob. f. The law of nature teaches one to worship God, not to harm one's neighbor, to give everyone his due, to defend oneself, and to keep one's soul sober and chaste.

Prob. g. The law of nature is concerned directly with things to be done, which are in themselves due, convenient to a rational creature, and thus by nature right and honest: Conversely, it is concerned indirectly with things to be avoided, which are in themselves illicit, inconvenient to a rational creature, and thus by intrinsic reason evil and base. By this very fact, the law of nature differs not only from human law, but also from divine voluntary or positive law, which does not command or forbid those things which are in themselves and by their own nature either due or illicit, but makes them so by forbidding the illicit and commanding the due. Conf. GROT. de I. B. ac P. book I, ch. I, p. 7.

Conf. GROT. de I. B. ac P. book I, ch. I, p. 7. Prob. h. The form of natural law consists in directive and obligatory power. For the law of nature directs all the moral acts of men, insofar as it is an immutable rule, from which human life

honesty and turpitude is known, estimated, discerned, and examined. It obligates to obedience, and, if this is not rendered, to punishment, insofar as it is a bond of law, by which a certain necessity is imposed upon the liberty of the human will, and man is bound to do that which is in itself right, and to flee that which is in itself base. Which obligation proceeds from the eminence, beneficence, and power of God, the supreme legislator, to whom we are bound to render homage on account of natural subjection. For God is most just, most wise, most good, and most powerful, to whom we owe ourselves and all that is ours; who both can and will render the greatest rewards to those who obey Him, and inflict the most grievous punishments upon the disobedient. Therefore, we are bound necessarily and without exception to obey the law inscribed by God upon our minds.

Proof i. God willed that in the human intellect after the fall there should exist common practical notions, as relics of the divine image, by which all men might know, worship, and celebrate God, on account of the supreme eminence and authority of the divine nature, and its beneficence toward all creatures: But many Gentiles, who knew God from the light of nature, did not glorify Him as God, nor gave Him thanks, Rom.

Proof k. God created man for civil society, instructed him by nature, led him by reason, and joined him by speech. That this society might be kept tranquil, ordered, and honest, God implanted in the minds of men the law of nature, which dictates that one must live honestly, harm no one, render to each his own, and promote the advantages of the republic.

Proof l. From Rom. 1:20. The invisible things of God are manifested to the Gentiles, that they may be without excuse. The Gentiles knew from the dictate of the implanted law what ought to be done and what ought to be omitted in external action: Nevertheless, many of them fell into the most grievous crimes against their conscience. By reason of these, the accidental end of the natural law is ἀναπολογία, or that they may be without excuse, because they were convicted in their conscience that such crimes ought not to be committed, Question

Latin:

Legis naturalis causa efficiens est Deus a). Causa exemplaris est iustitia & sanctitas Dei b). Materia ex qua sunt notiones communes, seu principia practica, que dignitate honora: Aplica animum ad quoddam vitae genus, ad quod maxime aptum & quasi natum te esse intellexeris, vt fis rei publicae emolumento: Functionem muneris, tibi mandati, cura diligenter ac fideliter, neque alienis te negotiis immisce: Salus plurium communis saluti vnius singulari anteponenda est: Fide, sed cui, vide: Pacta & promissa sunt feruanda: Officia, quae ad vsum sermonis pertinent, omnia obferua. (*)

lica, natura nota c). Materia in qua, sive subiectum quod, est homo non brutum d). Subiectum quo est hominis intellectus, voluntas & appetitus sensitivus e). Materia circa quam, sive obiectum personale est Deus, proximus & homo ipse f). Obiectum reale sunt facienda & fugienda g). Forma est vis directiva & obligativa h). Finis per se intentus est gloria Dei i), & societatis civilis conservatio k). Finis accidentarius, seu eventus est ἀναπολόγησις, seu defectus excusationis l).

Prob. a. Causa efficiens legis naturalis est Deus, qui 1) eo ipso, quod homini dedit rationem, per quam bonum a malo discernere satagit, simul voluit, vt homo bonum cognitum faceret, & malum omitteret. Proinde cum Paullus Rom. II, 15. asserit, gentiles ostendere opus legis scriptum in cordibus suis, intelligit inscriptionem factam a Deo, mediante naturali propagatione. 2) Obligatio legis naturalis est ab ipso Deo, Creatore ac summo generis humani moderatore, quia homines ad istam observandam pro imperio suo adstrinxit. Testatur de eo tener admodum conscientiae sensus in animis hominum, non penitus efferatorum, quo convincuntur, in legem naturae peccando, offendi illum, cui in animos hominum imperium est, & qui metuendus fit, etiam ubi ab hominibus metus non impendeat.

Prob. b. Lex ἔκτυπος habet suam ideam ἀρχέτυπον in ipsa Dei sanctitate & iustitia, quam ita lex naturalis refert, ut radii, in aquam sparsi, suum fontem, solem; ut imago suum exemplar. Radix igitur iuris naturae ultima non in voluntate divina, sed in sanctitate & iustitia Dei residet, & prohibuit Deus peccatum, non quia voluit, sed quia id ipsum iniustitiae & sanctitati divinae aduerfatur.

Prob. c. Principia practica natura nota, quae supra recensuimus, sunt quasi partes constituentes legem naturae; quibus positis ponitur, & sublatis tollitur lex naturae, lumen veri, & semen boni.

Prob. d. Homo, particeps rationis & liberi arbitrii, capax est legis naturalis. Proinde lex naturae, proprie dicta, in bruta non cadit: Quia 1) ob defectum rationis actiones suas ad normam legis componere nequeunt: 2) Quia carent libero arbitrio, quod per legem constringitur. Analogice tamen & per similitudinem iis tribuitur; quatenus perinde, ac homo, conservationem sui intendunt, iniuriam propulsant, foetum, quem progenerarunt, alunt & defendunt.

Prob. e. Lex naturalis intellectum hominis, velut speculum, illustrat, vt bonum & malum cognoscat atque diiudicet; voluntatem dirigit, vt bonum ab intellectu propositum eligat, & malum sibi ostensum reiiciat: appetitus vero sensitivus per legem naturae intra certos continetur cancellos, ne exorbitet, aut leges honestatis tranfiliat.

Prob. f. Ius naturae docet Deum colere, proximum non laedere & unicuique suum tribuere, seipsum defendere, & animam sobriam castamque servare.

Prob. g. Lex naturae versatur directe circa facienda, quae per se sunt debita, creaturae rationali convenientia, atque adeo natura recta & honesta: Contra versatur indirecte circa fugienda, quae per se sunt illicita, creaturae rationali disconvenientia, atque adeo intrinseca ratione mala & turpia. Quo ipso differt ius naturae non tantum ab humano iure, sed & a divino voluntario, vel positivo, quod non ea praecipit, aut vetat, quae per se ac suapte natura aut debita sunt, aut illicita, sed vetando illicita, praecipiendo debita facit. Conf. GROT. de I. B. ac P. libr. I. c. I. p. 7.

Prob. h. Forma legis naturalis consistit in vi directiva & obligativa. Dirigit enim lex naturae omnes actus hominum morales, in quantum est immutabilis regula, ex qua vitae humanae

honestas & turpitudo cognoscitur, aestimatur, discernitur atque examinatur. Obligat ad obedientiam, &, si haec non praestetur, ad poenam, quatenus est vinculum iuris, quo libertati voluntatis humanae necessitas quaedam imponitur, & homo obstringitur ad faciendum id, quod per se rectum, & fugiendum id, quod per se turpe est. Quae obligatio proficiscitur ab eminentia, beneficentia & potentia Dei, summi legislatoris, cui ob naturalem subiectionem obsequium praestare tenemur. Est enim Deus iustissimus, sapientissimus, optimus & potentissimus, cui nos & nostra omnia debemus; qui sibi obedientibus praemia reddere maxima, inobedientibus poenas infligere gravissimas & potest, & vult. Ergo legi, a Deo mentibus nostris inscriptae, necessario & sine exceptione parere tenemur.

Prob. i. Voluit Deus, vt in humano intellectu post lapsum exstarent communes notiones practicae, velut reliquiae imaginis divinae, quo omnes homines ex iisdem Deum cognoscerent, colerent, celebrarent, ob summam naturae divinae eminentiam & imperium, atque beneficentiam in omnes creaturas: At multi gentiles, qui ex lumine naturae Deum cognoverunt, eundem non vt Deum glorificarunt, nec ipsi gratias egerunt, Rom. I, 21.

Prob. k. Ad societatem civilem Deus hominem condidit, natura instruxit, ratio deduxit, oratio copulavit. Vt haec societas tranquilla, ordinata, & honesta servaretur, Deus insevit mentibus hominum legem naturae, quae dictat, honeste esse vivendum, neminem laedendum, vnicuique suum tribuendum, & commoda reipublicae esse promovenda.

Prob. l. Ex Rom. I, 20. Invisibilia Dei gentilibus manifestata sunt, ut sint inexcusabiles. Sciuerunt gentiles ex dictamine legis insitae, quid externo opere agi & intermitti oporteat: Nihilominus tamen multi ex illis contra conscientiam lapsi sunt in scelera gravissima. Horum ratione legis naturalis finis accidentarius est ἀναπολογία, siue, ut sint inexcusabiles, quia in conscientia conuicti erant, eiusmodi scelera non esse committenda, Quaest.


### Question XIII. What are the properties of the natural law?

The properties of the natural law are that it a) is σύμφυτος, or connate to all men, b) immutable, c) indispensable, d) imperfect after the fall, e) insufficient for salvation.

Proof a. The natural law is connate to all men and inscribed by the finger of God, Rom. 2:15, by an inscription 1) actual, not merely potential, which only then comes into act when reason begins to assert and exert itself. For it is called the ἔργον νόμου (work of the law) inscribed: E Actu. 2) By an inscription analogous to that by which the law was inscribed upon the first man: Just as once the image was concreated in man, of which this writing is as it were a certain sacred relic. 3) By an inscription different from the inscription of the supernatural light kindled in regeneration. 4) By an indelible inscription, although it may be obscured and captivated. The examples of barbarous nations, who have used vices against nature as virtues, prove that the fire is covered by ashes, not utterly extinguished, Conf. DANNHAV. in hodof. phan. VI. p. 467.

Proof b. If the law of nature could be changed, it would be changed either by God Himself or by man. But it cannot be changed by God Himself; because God can do nothing against His own justice, of which the law of nature is an express and infallible image: nor by man; because he who does not have the power to make a law, cannot change it either. And what man, who is inferior, would dare to change the law of God, who is far superior? Here one must rightly distinguish between a true change and an apparent one. The law of nature, by reason of the most common principles of which it consists, is not truly and in itself changed; but often the thing about which the natural law constitutes something receives a change: When this happens, not indeed the natural right is changed, but the matter to which it is subtracted, e.g., If a creditor acknowledges receipt of what is owed to him, the debtor is no longer bound to pay, not because the law of nature has ceased to command that what one owes should be paid; but because what he owed has ceased to be owed. Thus, when God commanded Isaac to be killed..., He did not wish to change the law of nature by decreeing that homicide is licit, but the slaughter of Isaac would not have been prohibited by the law of nature as homicide, because it would have been done by the will of Him who is the Lord of life and death.

Proof c.

The law of nature is indispensable, i.e., no one can be excepted from its obligation. For since God cannot change the law of nature, neither can He remove its obligation, in which the law formally consists. 2) If God were to exempt man from the obligation of natural law, then He would grant with impunity and with approval that which is base by intrinsic reason, which is repugnant to divine justice. God can indeed permit and approve an act which seems contrary to the law of nature, yet in reality it is not, if the circumstances are considered, e.g., When the Israelites took the vessels of the Egyptians, that act was not theft; because it was not the handling of another’s property, but of their own wages, earned by the most grievous labors endured in Egypt, not against the will of the master, but by the command of the supreme Lord of all goods, God.

Proof d.

The law of nature before the fall and after the fall does not differ φύσει (by nature), essentially, but by perfection, or gradually. For it illustrated the mind of integral man more clearly and perfectly than it does today the intellect of man corrupted by sin. Hence it happens that we know neither original sin, nor the first and indeliberate motions of depraved concupiscence from the law of nature. Paul teaches this, Rom. VII, 7. I had not known sin, but by the law (Mosaic). For I had not known concupiscence, unless the law had said: thou shalt not covet.

Proof e.

The law of nature indeed dictates that God is to be worshipped: But since in this state of corrupted nature we offend God daily with our sins, the law of nature does not teach what satisfaction for sins committed can or ought to be offered to God. But unless satisfaction has been rendered to God, the most just avenger of sins, we can neither place our trust in God, nor sincerely love Him, nor perform works pleasing to Him. It remains, therefore, fixed and settled that outside of Christ the mediator, of whom the law of nature knows nothing, there is no salvation, Acts IV, 12.

Latin:

Proprietates legis naturalis sunt, quod illa a) est σύμφυτος, siue omnibus hominibus connata, b) immutabilis, c) indispensabilis, d) imperfecta post lapsum, e) insufficiens ad salutem.

Prob. a. Lex naturalis omnibus hominibus est connata & inscripta digito Dei, Rom. II, 15. inscriptione 1) actuali, non solum potentiali, quae tum demum in actum prodeat, cum ratio se vindicare & exserere incipit. Dicitur enim ἔργον νόμου inscriptum: E Actu. 2) Inscriptione analoga illa, qua primo homini lex est insculpta: Sicut olim homini imago concreata erat, cuius haec scriptura est quasi quoddam sacrum lipfanum. 3) Inscriptione diuersa ab inscriptione luminis supernaturalis in regeneratione accensi. 4) Inscriptione indelebili, quamuis obscurabili & captiuabili. Exempla barbararum gentium, quae vitiis contra naturam pro virtutibus vsae sunt, probant ignem cineribus obrutum, non penitus exstinctum, Conf. DANNHAV. in hodof. phan. VI. p. 467.

Prob. b. Si lex naturae mutari posset, mutaretur vel ab ipso Deo, vel ab homine. At non mutari potest ab ipso Deo; quia Deus nihil facere potest contra iustitiam suam, cuius expressa & infallibilis imago lex naturae est: neque ab homine; quia quam quis legem fanciendi potestatem non habet, eam nec mutare potest. Et quis auderet homo, qui est inferior, Dei longe superioris legem mutare? Probe hic distinguendum est inter mutationem veram, & apparentem. Lex naturae ratione communissimorum principiorum, e quibus constat, vere & per se non mutatur; fed saepe res, de qua lex naturalis aliquid constituit, mutationem recipit: Quod cum fit, non quidem ius naturale mutatur, sed materia ei subtrahitur, v. g. Si creditor, quod ei debetur, acceptum ferat, iam solvere debitor non tenetur, non quia ius naturae desierit praecipere soluendum, quod quis debet; sed quia, quod debebat, deberi desiit. Ita cum Deus occidi praecipit Isaacum..., non mutare voluit ius naturae, decernendo, homicidium esse licitum, sed non fuisset homicidium iure naturae prohibitum caedes Isaaci, quia facta esset ex voluntate illius, qui Dominus vitae & necis est.

Prob. c.

Lex naturae est indispensabilis, h. e. ab eius obligatione nemo excipi potest. Cum enim Deus legem naturae non possit mutare, neque obligationem illius, in qua lex, formaliter consistit, tollere potest. 2) Si Deus hominem ab obligatione iuris naturalis eximeret, tum id, quod intrinseca ratione turpe est, impune & cum appropriatione concederet, quod iustitiae divinae repugnat. Potest quidem Deus permittere & approbare actum, qui videtur legi naturae contrarius, re vera tamen non est, si circumstantiae considerentur, v. gr. Quando Israelitae secum abstulerunt vasa Aegyptiorum, factum illud non fuit furtum; quia non fuit contrectatio rei alienae, sed propriae mercedis, gravissimis laboribus in Aegypto exantlatis promeritae, non invito domino, sed iubente supremo omnium bonorum Domino, Deo.

Prob. d.

Lex naturae ante lapsum, & post lapsum non differt φύσει, essentialiter, sed perfectione, seu gradualiter. Clarius enim & perfectius illustrabat mentem hominis integri, quam hodie intellectum hominis peccato corrupti. Inde fit, vt neque peccatum originis, neque primos & indeliberatos prauae concupiscentiae motus ex lege naturae cognoscamus. Docet id Paullus, Rom. VII, 7. Peccatum non novissem, nisi per legem (Mosaicaim). Nam etiam concupiscentiam non noueram, nisi lex dixisset: non concupisces.

Prob. e.

Dictat quidem lex naturae, Deum esse colendum: At cum in hoc corruptae naturae statu Deum peccatis nostris quotidie offendamus, non docet lex naturae, quae satisfactio offenso peccatis Deo exhiberi possit aut debeat. At nisi Deo, iustissimo peccatorum vindici, praestita sit satisfactio, neque fiduciam in Deo collocare, neque eundem sincere amare, neque opera ipsi grata praestare possumus. Ratum igitur fixumque manet, quod extra Christum mediatorem, de quo lex naturae nihil nouit, non sit salus, Act. IV, 12.


### Question XIV. What is the moral law specifically called?

The moral law, specifically so called, is a command of God, superadded to the natural law by divinely revealed word, repeated more often from the origin of the world, and finally solemnly promulgated on Mount Sinai, and committed to writing, distinctly commanding and forbidding base things, directing all external and internal motions, and obliging all men to most perfect obedience, or, this failing, to most exquisite punishments. Obs.

The natural law in a general sense is also a moral law, because it directs the morals of men toward honesty; nor does it differ from the moral law, specifically so called, materially, since the sum of the natural law is contained in the decalogue: But it differs from it formally. For a) the natural law is inscribed in the innermost souls of men by nature, the moral law is extrinsically promulgated, revealed by the voice of God, and committed to writing: b) The natural law is more imperfect and obscure, the moral law is more perfect and clearer. The former directs external discipline: the latter rules and tempers both the internal and external motions of men (). () And indeed the natural law also directs the internal motions of the soul and the external actions of man, as is plainly apparent, both from the great power of conscience and from the very sentiment of almost all natural laws. See the notes on page 998. Civil laws, however, are those laws which

Latin:

Lex moralis, specialiter dicta, est iussum Dei, legi naturali verbo diuino revelato superadditum, inde ab origine mundi saepius repetitum, & tandem in monte Sinai solemniter promulgatum, atque in litteras relatum, distincte praecipiens, & prohibens turpia, omnes motus externos & internos dirigens, omnesque homines obligans ad obedientiam perfectissimam, vel hac deficiente, ad poenas exquisitissimas.

Obs. Lex naturalis sensu generali etiam est lex moralis, quia mores hominum ad honestatem dirigit; neque differt a lege morali, specialiter dicta, materialiter, siquidem summa legis naturalis continetur in decalogo: Sed distat ab eadem formaliter. Nam a) lex naturalis est intimis hominum animis per naturam inscripta, lex moralis est extrinsece promulgata, voce Dei patefacta & in litteras relata: b) Lex naturalis est imperfectior & obscurior, lex moralis perfectior & clarior est. Illa dirigit externam disciplinam: hac tam internos, quam externos motus hominum regit & temperat (*).


### Q. XV. How manifold is the moral law specially so called?

The moral law, specially so called, is either primordial or Sinaitic. The primordial moral law is that which was both set before our first parents and revealed to their descendants by the voice of God, and was further expounded and declared through the patriarchs, up to that solemn promulgation of the law on Mount Sinai; which instructed them to live piously toward God, justly toward their neighbor, and temperately toward themselves, and bound them to perfect obedience.

Objection. The primordial and Sinaitic moral law do not differ in the substance of their dogmas, but in one mode of revelation and another. For the primordial law had its beginning in paradise, when God commanded the protoplasts to abstain from the fruits which the tree of the knowledge of good and evil bore. But after the fall, both before and after the flood, the doctrine of the law, being proposed immediately by God and further expounded through the ministry of the God-inspired (θεοπνεύστων) patriarchs, flourished among the people of God until God solemnly promulgated the law on Mount Sinai. How the doctrine of the law flourished in the church of God before the times of Moses, and how it comprised the individual precepts of the decalogue, is shown by Chemnitius in Loc. theol., Part II, t. VI, fol. 21, and Gerhardus in Loco de lege,

§ 15. Q. XVI. What is the Sinaitic moral law?

The Sinaitic moral law is a divine command, solemnly promulgated on Mount Sinai in the presence of and with the ministry of angels, consisting of ten precepts, inscribed by God himself on stone tablets, and transmitted by Moses to the Israelites, and frequently declared in Holy Scripture, so that it might be a perfect and perpetual norm of things to be done and to be avoided for all men, binding them to most consummate obedience, and promising rewards to those who comply, and denouncing temporal and eternal punishments to the disobedient.

Latin:

Lex moralis, specialiter dicta, est vel primordialis, vel Sinaitica. Primordialis lex moralis est, quae tum primis parentibus praefixa, tum posteris eorum voce Dei patefacta, & per patriarchas vlterius exposita atque declarata fuit, vsque ad solemnem illam legis in monte Sinai promulgationem; quae ipsos ad viuendum pie erga Deum, iuste erga proximum, & temperanter erga se ipsos informauit, & ad perfectam obedientiam eosdem obligauit.

Obs. Lex moralis primordialis, & Sinaitica non differunt dogmatum substantia, sed alio atque alio reuelationis modo. Nam lex primordialis fuinsit initium in paradiso, cum Deus protoplastis praecepit abstinentiam a fructibus, quos ferebat arbor scientiae boni & mali. Post lapsum vero ante & post diluuium, doctrina legis, tum immediate a Deo proposita, tum, mediante patriarcharum θεοπνεύστων ministerio, vlterius exposita, viguit in populo Dei, vsque dum Deus solemniter promulgaret legem in monte Sinai. Quomodo autem ante Mosis tempora doctrina legis in ecclesia Dei sonuerit, & singula decalogi praecepta complexa sit, ostendit CHEMNITIVS in loc. theol. Part. II. t. VI. fol. 21. & GERHARDVS in loco de lege,

§. 15. Quaest. XVI. Quid est lex moralis Sinaitica?

Lex moralis Sinaitica est iussum diuinum, solemniter in monte Sinai, praesentibus & ministrantibus angelis, promulgatum, constans decem praeceptis, ab ipso Deo tabulis lapideis inscriptum, & per Mosen ad Isrélitas translatum, atque in scriptura S. saepius declaratum, vt esset omnibus hominibus perfecta & perpetua faciendorum atque fugiendorum norma, obligans eosdem ad obedientiam consummatissimam, & promittens obsequentibus praemia, poenasque temporales & aeternas inobedientibus denuntians.


### Q. XVII. Who is the author of the Sinaitic moral law?

The author of the Sinaitic moral law is the Triune God.

Proof. From Exod. 20:1: "Then Elohim spoke all these words." Objection 1) By "these words" are understood the ten precepts, which are called the ten words of the covenant, Exod. 34:28, whence the name Decalogue (δεκαλόγος). 2) Elohim spoke the ten precepts, i.e., God, one in essence and three in persons. The unity of the divine essence is indicated by the Hebrew word ברא, which is placed in the singular: the plurality of the divine persons, and consequently the trinity, is denoted by the word אלהים, which divine name we have demonstrated (Part I, cap. I, q. 14) to be plural not only in formation and termination, but also in sense and signification, and thus to imply a plurality of persons. Therefore, God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is the one legislator, James 4:12. Moreover, the promulgation of the law by a sonorous and audible voice is appropriated to God the Son; for he is that uncreated angel who spoke with Moses on Mount Sinai, as Stephen testifies, Acts 7:38.

Latin:

Auctor legis moralis Sinaiticae est Deus trinus.

Prob. Ex. Exod. XX, 1. Deinde locutus est Elohim omnia verba haec. Obs. 1) Per verba haec intelliguntur decem praecepta, quae vocantur verba foederis decem, Exod. XXXIV, 28. vnde nomen δεκαλόγος. 2) Decem praecepta locutus est Elohim, i. e. Deus in essentia vnus, & in personis trinus. Essentiae diuinae vnitas indicatur voce Hebraea ברא, quae ponitur in singulari: Personarum diuinarum pluralitas, & consequenter trinitas, denotatur voce אלהים, quod nomen diuinum non tantum formatione & terminatione, sed etiam sensu & significatione esse plurale, atque adeo pluralitatem personarum inferre, demonstrauimus part. I. cap. I. quaest. 14. Est ergo Deus Pater, Filius & Spiritus S. vnus legislator, Iac. IV, 12. Promulgatio autem legis per vocem sonoram & audibilem Filio Deo appropriatur; quippe qui est angelus ille increatus, qui locutus est cum Mose in monte Sinai, teste Stephano, Act. VII, 38.


### Question XV. How many kinds of moral law are there, considered specifically?

God in the promulgation of the Sinaitic law used the ministry of angels a), and Moses b).

Proof. which moderate only the external discipline. That which the blessed man calls the moral law, I have briefly noted at page 997 that it is more correctly called "revealed" when it is distinguished from the natural [law].

Prob. a. That God the legislator was attended by hosts of angels in the promulgation of the law, we gather from Deut. XXXIII, 2. God came from Sinai, with myriads of holy ones. By those holy ones are designated the angels, as Stephen explains, Acts VII, 53, who asserts that the Jews received the law as διαταγὰς ἀγγέλων, among the dispositions of the angels, i.e., among the arranged and well-ordered hosts of the angels, standing by their emperor, and attending him for the sake of majesty.

Paul supports this, who says that the law was disposed through angels in the hand of a mediator, Gal. III, 19, where δι' ἀγγέλων is the same as among the angels, just as the particle διὰ is taken in 2 Tim. II, 2: but the hand of the mediator denotes the power and authority of the mediator Christ, so that the sense is: The law was ordained, commanded, and proclaimed through the power of the mediator Christ among the angels, who were attending their Lord for the sake of honor and duty, and congratulating him with the voice of a trumpet.

Prob. b. The law was given through Moses, John I, 17, not as the author, but as the minister, inasmuch as he carried the tablets of the law written by the finger of God to the Israelites, Exod. XXXIV, 29, and inculcated and expounded the divine law to them.

Latin:

Deus in promulgatione legis Sinaiticae vsus est ministris angelis a), & Mose b).

Prob. quae externam duntaxat disciplinam moderantur. Quam Vir beatus moralem adpellat legem, eam, cum a naturali distinguitur, rectius dici patefactam, breuiter adnotaui ad pag. 997.

Prob. a. Deum legislatorem in promulgatione legis stipasse angelorum agmina, colligimus ex Deut. XXXIII, 2. Deus de Sinai venit, cum myriadibus sanctorum. Per sanctos illos designantur angeli, exponente Stephano, Act. VII, 53. qui asserit, Iudaeos legem accepisse eis διαταγὰς ἀγγέλων, inter dispositiones angelorum, i. e. inter disposita beneque collocata angelorum agmina, imperatori suo adstantia, eumque maiestatis causa stipantia.

Cui suffragatur Paullus, qui dicit, legem dispositam esse per angelos in manu mediatoris, Gal. III, 19. vbi δι' ἀγγέλων idem est, ac inter angelos, vti particula διὰ 2 Tim. II, 2. accipitur: manus mediatoris autem notat potentiam & auctoritatem mediatoris Christi, vt sensus sit: Lex per potentiam mediatoris Christi inter angelos, Dominum suum honoris & officii causa stipantes, & voce tubae congratulantes, ordinata, imperata & edicta est.

Prob. b. Lex per Mosen data est, Io. I, 17. non vt auctorem, sed vt ministrum, quippe qui scriptas digito Dei tabulas legis ad Israelitas transtulit, Exod. XXXIV, 29. & legem diuinam illis inculcauit & exposuit.


### Question XIX. What causes impelled God to the solemn promulgation of the moral law?

God solemnly promulgated the moral law, a) so that greater authority, clarity, and perfection might be added to the natural law: b) so that the moral law might be a valid medium by which the Holy Spirit might break, soften, and convert the hearts of men: c) so that men, corrupted by sin, recognizing their internal uncleanness from the divine law, might be compelled to seek the true physician of souls, Christ.

Prob. a. God willed, 1) that there should exist a manifest divine testimony that the natural notions of the law concerning the distinction between honorable and base things are divinely implanted in human minds, and that they are consonant with the idea of holiness and justice which is in God, so that men might be validly obligated to provide assent and render obedience to the dictate of the natural law. 2) The most benign Deity willed to add clearer light to the natural law, which had been greatly obliterated by the sins of men, and to supply its defect. For the natural law after the fall does indeed direct discipline from the internal part of men, but it does not teach the internal holiness of the soul, nor does it prohibit the indeliberate acts of depraved concupiscence.

Hence it happens that neither original sin nor the first motions of evil are recognized from the law of nature, but many men, in the manner of the Pharisees, fascinated by the admiration of external discipline, strive to establish their own righteousness before God, Rom. X, 3. . Which defect of the inscribed law has been supplied by the most holy God by the light of the prescribed law. Prob. b. God, in the solemn promulgation of the word of the law, which went forth from His own mouth, infused a supernatural power, so that it might be an efficacious organ of the Holy Spirit, working in sinful man, softening his hard heart, preparing and disposing him for faith, to be kindled in him by the voice of the gospel. For the Holy Spirit convicts the world through the law concerning sin, John XVI, 8. Prob. c. Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick, says Christ, Matt. IX, 12. Those who do not acknowledge their internal misery do not seek mercy.

The divine law was therefore promulgated so that, acknowledging our internal disease of original sin and our misery from it, we, as sick persons, might sigh for the physician, the redeemer and deliverer, Christ. Quest. XX. Which men are bound by the Sinaitic moral law? All men without exception are bound by the Sinaitic moral law. 1) The moral law comprises the sum of the natural law, which is inscribed upon the minds of all men, and is the express image of the eternal law existing in God. 2) Just as God is the creator of all men, so all are obligated to keep the moral law, by which God commands those things which He judged to be fitting for them as rational creatures, and to be observed on account of the authority of the creator and most wise and powerful Lord. 3) The Sinaitic moral law was in force among the people of God as to the substance of its dogmas before its solemn promulgation, and it has not been abrogated by Christ, but declared, and diligently inculcated by the Apostles, who were teachers of all nations. Therefore, the binding force of the Sinaitic moral law is both greatest and most universal, which no man can escape. 4) The Apostle testifies that by the moral law every mouth is stopped, and the whole world becomes guilty before God, Rom. III, 19.

This would not be the case if the Mosaic law bound only the Jews. The antithesis is that of certain Scholastics, and of Pererius, disp. VI. on chap. II of Romans, who maintain that the law promulgated on Mount Sinai bound only the Israelites.

Their arguments, contracted into a summary, are: 1) The Sinaitic law was promulgated only to the Israelites, to whom 2) it was delivered solely through the ministry of Moses. 3) There are contained in the Sinaitic law some things which pertain specifically to no other nations than the Israelitic people. Therefore, the law promulgated on Mount Sinai binds only the Israelites.

Resp. to 1. The promulgation of the Sinaitic law was indeed made only to the Israelites, but not for the sake of the Israelites alone: just as many prophetic promises concerning Christ were made to the Israelites, but not for their sake alone. But just as Holy Scripture, which is divided into law and gospel, pertains to all, so also the moral law, not [only] that which pertains to rational nature: God is to be worshipped with the whole soul and all strength.

Revealed laws, however, are the norm of those actions which pertain to certain surrounding circumstances to be observed by men, and the reason for which can be known from nowhere else than from divine revelation. No one will deny that the natural law was perfect in the state of integrity. Yet there were even then certain revealed laws, concerning the forbidden tree and the Sabbath. And the reason for the former was dominion over the earth, granted to man by the benefit of God, which, so that man might confess it to be circumscribed by limits, and that he was as it were a vassal, God prohibited him from this fruit by His own will. The reason for the latter, however, was this singular circumstance of creation, to be known from revelation alone: that all kinds of created things were completed on the seventh day.

The origin of evil, and the imputation as well as the propagation of the first sin, the intimate corruption of the soul and the propensity toward every evil, is truly the most sorrowful of the circumstances and changes that have happened to human nature, and which revelation alone teaches us must be known with the greatest sorrow.

no less than the Gospel concerns all men.

Therefore, in the N.T., moral laws are not promulgated anew to the Gentiles, but are repeated from the writings of Moses, and prescribed to all.

To II. Distinguish between Moses the minister and God the author. We keep the Sinaitic law, not because of the ministry of Moses, but because of the authority of God the legislator.

To III. Distinguish between ουσιωδη [essential], or the substantials of the moral law, and περιστατικα [circumstantial], or the accidentals of the commandments. The substantial dogmas of the moral law are fitting for man as a rational creature, from whose obligation no one is exempt; the accidental appendices specifically concern the Israelites.

Latin:

Deus legem moralem solemniter promulgauit, a) vt legi naturali adderetur maior auctoritas, claritas & perfectio: b) vt esset lex moralis validum medium, quo Spiritus S. corda hominum frangeret, emolliret & conuerteret: c) vt homines, peccato corrupti, ex lege diuina internam suam immunditiem agnoscentes, compellerentur ad quaerendum verum animarum medicum, Christum.

Prob. a. Voluit Deus, 1) vt exstaret manifestum testimonium diuinum, naturales notitias legis de discrimine honestorum & turpium esse diuinitus insitas mentibus humanis, easque ideae sanctitatis & iustitiae, quae est in Deo, esse consentaneas, vt homines valide obligarentur ad praebendum assensum & praestandum obsequium dictamini legis naturalis. 2) Voluit Numen benignissimum legi naturali, peccatis hominum valde oblitteratae, clarius addere lumen, eiusque supplere defectum. Etenim lex naturalis post lapsum dirigit quidem ex interna hominum disciplinam, sed non docet interiorem animae sanctitatem, neque prohibet indeliberatos prauae concupiscentiae actus.

Inde fit, vt ex lege naturae neque peccatum originis, neque primi motus mali agnoscantur, sed multi homines, Pharisaeorum more, externa disciplina admiratione fascinati, propriam iustitiam coram Deo constituere satagant, Rom. X, 3. . Qui defectus legis inscriptae a Deo sanctissimo suppletus est lumine legis praescriptae. Prob. b. Deus in solemni promulgatione verbo legis, quod ex ore ipsius exiuit, vim supernaturalem indidit, vt sit efficax organon Spiritus S., in homine peccatore operantis, eius cor durum emollientis, praeparantis & disponentis ad fidem, voce euangelii in eo accendendam. Arguit enim Spiritus S. mundum per legem de peccato, Io. XVI, 8. Prob. c. Non opus habent validi medico, sed male habentes, ait Christus, Matth. IX, 12. Qui non agnoscunt internam miseriam, non quaerunt misericordiam.

Promulgata ergo est lex diuina, vt internum peccati originalis morbum & miseriam nostram ex eadem agnoscentes, aegroti suspiremus ad medicum, redemptorem & liberatorem, Christum. Quaest. XX. Quinam homines lege morali Sinaitica obligantur? Lege morali Sinaitica obligantur omnes omnino homines, nemine excepto. 1) Lex moralis complectitur summam legis naturalis, quae omnium hominum mentibus inscripta, atque aeternae legis in Deo exsistentis expressa imago est. 2) Sicut Deus omnium hominum est creator: ita omnes obstricti sunt ad seruandum legem moralem, qua Deus praecipit ea, quae ipsis, vt creaturis rationalibus, conuenientia iudicauit, & obseruanda ob auctoritatem creatoris, & sapientissimi potentissimi domini. 3) Lex moralis Sinaitica viguit in populo Dei, qua substantiam dogmatum, ante solemnem promulgationem, neque est a Christo abrogata, sed declarata, & ab Apostolis, qui omnium gentium doctores erant, sedulo inculcata. E. legis moralis Sinaiticae vis obligandi & maxima & vniuersalissima est, quam nemo hominum effugere potest. 4) Testatur Apostolus, per legem moralem omnium os obstrui, & reum fieri totum mundum Deo, Rom. III, 19.

Quod non esset, si lex Mosaica solos Iudaeos obligaret. Antithesis est Scholasticorum quorundam, & Pererii, disp. VI. in cap. II. ad Rom. statuentium, solos Israelitas legem, in monte Sinai promulgatam, obligasse.

Quorum argumenta, in summam contracta, sunt: 1) Lex Sinaitica promulgata est solis Israelitis, quibus 2) solis ministerio Mosis est tradita. 3) Continentur in lege Sinaitica nonnulla, quae nullis aliis gentibus, quam populo Israelitico specialiter conueniunt. E. Lex in monte Sinai promulgata solos Israelitas obligat.

Resp. ad I. Promulgatio legis Sinaiticae solis quidem facta est Israelitis, sed non propter solos Israelitas: Quemadmodum etiam promissiones propheticae de Christo plurimae ad Israelitas, non autem propter eos solos factae sunt. Sed vti scriptura sacra, quae in legem & euangelium dispescitur, ad omnes pertinet: ita etiam lex moralis non quae ad naturam rationalem spectant: Deus toto animo omnibusque viribus colendus est.

Patefactae autem leges sunt norma earum actionum, quae ad certas quasdam res circumstantes, ab hominibus obseruandas, pertinent, & quarum ratio non aliunde, quam ex patefactione diuina potest cognosci. In statu integritatis perfectam fuisse legem naturalem, nemo abnuet. At erant tamen etiam tunc leges quaedam patefactae, de arbore vetita, & de Sabbatho. Et illius quidem ratio erat dominium in terram, Dei beneficio homini concessum, quod vt homo fateretur terminis circumscriptum, & se velut Vasallum esse, suo Deus arbitrio eum ab hoc fructu prohibuit. Huius autem ratio erat singularis haec circumstantia creationis, ex sola patefactione cognoscenda: quod omnia rerum creatarum genera septimo die consummata fuerunt.

Origo mali, & peccati primi tum imputatio, tum propagatio, intima animi corruptio & ad quoduis malum propensio, est profecto tristissima rerum circumstantium ac mutationum, quae humanae naturae acciderunt, & quas cum summo dolore cognoscendas sola nos reuelatio edocet.

non minus, quam evangelium omnes homines concernit. Ideo in N. T. leges morales non de nouo promulgantur gentibus, sed e scriptis Mosis repetuntur, & omnibus praescribuntur.

Ad II. Dist. inter Mosen ministrum, & Deum auctorem. Seruamus legem Sinaiticam, non ob ministerium Mosis, sed ob auctoritatem Dei legislatoris.

Ad III. Dist. inter ουσιωδη, siue substantialia legis moralis, & περιστατικα, siue accidentalia praeceptorum. Substantialia dogmata legis moralis conueniunt homini, vt creaturae rationali, a quorum obligatione nemo exemptus est; appendices accidentales specialiter concernunt Israelitas.


### Quest. XXI

In what does the moral law formally consist?

The form of the moral law consists in a directive a) and an obligatory b) force.

Prob. a. The moral law is a perfect and adequate norm, directing all moral acts, internal and external, from which everything honest and holy, everything base and iniquitous is known, judged, and discerned. Every word that I command you, this you shall keep by doing; you shall not add to it, nor take away from it, says Jehovah, Deut. XII, 32.

Prob. b. The moral law is a bond by which God, our most wise, best, and most powerful Creator and Lord of all, constrains our freedom of action, so that we cannot rightly tend in a direction different from that to which it leads; although our will in fact not rarely departs into different directions. Therefore, God the legislator threatens and inflicts the most grave punishments upon transgressors, Exod. XX, 5.

Latin:

Forma legis moralis consistit in vi directiua a), & obligatiua b).

Prob. a. Lex moralis est perfecta & adaequata norma, dirigens omnes actus morales, internos & externos, ex qua omne honestum & sanctum, omne turpe & iniquum cognoscitur, diiudicatur & discernitur. Omne verbum, quod ego praecipio vobis, hoc custodietis faciendo, non addetis super illud, nec diminuetis de eo, inquit Iehouah, Deut. XII, 32.

Prob. b.
