Lex moralis est vinculum, quo Deus nostrum omnium Creator & Dominus sapientissimus, optimus & potentissimus, nostram agendi libertatem constringit, vt in diuersam, quam quo illa ducit, partem tendere recte non possimus; quamuis voluntas nostra de facto in diuersa haud raro abeat. Idcirco Deus legislator poenas grauissimas transgressoribus comminatur & infligit, Exod. XX, 5.


### Quest. XXII

To what kind of obedience does the moral law obligate us? The moral law obligates us to the most consummate obedience, which is perfect: a) with an intensively highest perfection, by reason of degrees; b) with an extensively most ample perfection, by reason of parts; c) with a protensively longest perfection, by reason of perseverance.

Prob. a. The moral law demands from us today a perfection in the highest degree, just as much as Adam had while still innocent. For whatever talent God first gave to man, that He demands back. Thus the law commands that we love Jehovah our God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our strength, Deut. VI, 5.

Prob. b. The law demands perfect obedience according to all the commandments of the Decalogue; he who does not provide this is condemned by the law just as much, having transgressed a single commandment, as he who has violated the whole law. Whoever shall have kept the whole law, but has stumbled in one, has become guilty of all, by the judgment of James, ch. II, 10.

Prob. c. The moral law requires perseverance in obedience. For cursed is everyone who does not remain in all things which are written in the book of the law, to do them, Gal. III, 10. Where the Greek word, εμμενει [remain], designates permanence and perseverance in the observance of the law.

A distinction is made here between affirmative and negative commandments. Affirmative ones obligate indeed always, but not to the doing of them at all times; e.g., the fourth commandment: Honor your parents, does not obligate at all times; for it can happen that parents command things contrary to God, or that they have ceased to be alive. Negative ones obligate always, and to the fleeing of them at all times; e.g., these prohibitions, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, obligate perpetually, at all times and simply [*]. XXIII. Does the moral law bind us equally to punishment as to obedience? The moral law binds men primarily to obedience, and secondarily and consequently to punishment.

Proof. God, by virtue of His supreme authority over men, demands from them due obedience by commanding through the moral law what is fitting for rational creatures. But if they refuse the divine command and decline to live in a manner consistent with their rational nature, God eventually inflicts a most just punishment, through which they are not freed from the debt of obedience. Therefore, the debt of obedience remains essential and principal, which the law demands; however, punishment is accidental to the law that has been enacted.

Question XXIV. Does human law bind the conscience just as divine law does? Divine law binds the conscience immediately and absolutely; human law, enacted by legitimate authority, binds mediately and hypothetically, provided, that is, it is just, derived from the divine moral law.

Proof a. God is the Lord of consciences: Therefore, He binds them immediately and absolutely by His most holy law, so that conscience accuses those who transgress it, Rom. II, 15. Proof b. A law enacted by a magistrate for subjects binds consciences mediately, through these principles: What the magistrate, who is the ordinance of God, prescribes to those whose magistrate he is, must be done; and what the magistrate forbids them, must be avoided. Since these are eternal truths and are implicitly contained in the Decalogue, no one can act against a law enacted by a superior without at the same time acting against the eternal law of God.

2) It binds hypothetically, if it is just; for thus it is a ray of divine justice, and he who violates it violates the sun. If it is clearly and simply unjust, it does not bind.

For everywhere that saying must hold true, Acts V, 29: We must obey God rather than men.

Question XXV. What is the end of the moral law? The end of the moral law is a) the glory of the legislator, b) eternal life, promised under the condition of perfect obedience.

The accidental outcome is eternal death. Proof: where there is a limitation and determination of an action, as to the manner of acting, if there is any exception, either of time, or of place, or of a certain thing in which the action is engaged; the same determination and exception is in the law itself, and in its meaning and binding force.

For example: In the fourth commandment, "Honor your parents," there is initially no exception of time, for they are to be honored by perpetual remembrance of their benefits as well as by the observance of their commands, even if they have long since ceased to be among the living: furthermore, this limitation and determination of the action, in a just cause and not contrary to divine commands, is contained in the very meaning of the law and its obligation, inasmuch as it does not extend further.

3) In every affirmative law there is an inherent negation of the opposite, and in the same way in every negative law there is a precept of the contrary. E.g., in this affirmative law, "Render due honor to your parents," this prohibition is contained: "Do not deny your parents their due." Therefore, whatever limitation and determination of action is in an affirmative law, the same must be in the contrary negative one.

4) There are certain affirmative laws without any exception, and without limitation and determination of action, and thus binding one to always act, such as these: "Strive for your own preservation, always using legitimate means": "Give to each his own"; which affirmative laws surely extend just as widely as the negative ones: "Do not harm yourself": "Harm no one."

Indeed, this affirmative law, the first and chief of all, binds most of all to always act: "Worship God, and never cease to pursue Him with the most perfect love."

Prob. a. From the promulgation of the Sinaitic law shines forth the wisdom, justice, and power of the supreme Lord and legislator, to be celebrated eternally.

Prob. b. From Lev. XVIII, 5. Keep my laws and judgments, which if a man do, he shall live in them. The law was given so that it might lead all who keep it perfectly to eternal life, not indeed by the merit of the law, because God owes nothing to anyone; but from the promise and ordination of God.

Prob. c. From Rom. VII, 10. The commandment, which (was given) unto life, the same (was found) to be unto death. The law, beatific in itself, becomes mortiferous by accident, on account of the defect of receptive power; because it is weakened through the flesh, Rom. VIII, 3. Hence it works wrath, denounces a curse, and adjudges to eternal condemnation all who do not fulfill the law.

Latin:

Lex moralis nos obligat ad obedientiam consummatissimam, quae sit perfecta, a) perfectione intensiue summa, ratione graduum, b) extensiue amplissima, ratione partium, c) protensiue longissima, ratione perseuerantiae.

Prob. a. Lex moralis tantam in summo gradu hodie poscit a nobis perfectionem, quantam habuit Adamus adhuc innocens. Quod enim talentum homini Deus primum dedit, illud reposcit. Praecipit itaque lex, vt diligamus Iehouam Deum nostrum ex toto corde, tota anima, & ex omnibus viribus nostris, Deut. VI, 5.

Prob. b. Postulat lex perfectam secundum omnia praecepta decalogi obedientiam; quam qui non praestat, per legem aeque condemnatur, vnicum transgressus praeceptum, ac is, qui totam legem violauit. Quisquis totam legem seruauerit, lapsus vero fuerit in vno, factus est omnium reus, iudice Iacobo, c. II, 10.

Prob. c. Requirit lex moralis obedientiae perseuerantiam. Nam maledictus omnis, qui non manet in omnibus, quae scripta sunt in libro legis, vt ea facias, Gal. III, 10. Vbi graecum verbum, εμμενες, designat in legis obseruantia permanentiam & perseuerantiam.

Dist. hic est inter praecepta affirmatiua & negatiua. Affirmatiua obligant quidem semper, sed non ad semper faciendum, v. gr. praeceptum quartum: Honora parentes, non obligat ad semper; fieri enim potest, vt parentes Deo aduersa imperent, aut viui esse desierint. Negatiua obligant semper, & ad semper fugiendum, v. gr. haec indicta, non moechaberis, non occides, obligant perpetuo, ad semper & simpliciter []. semper & simpliciter (). XXIII. An lex moralis peraeque ad poenam, ac ad obedientiam nos obligat? Lex moralis homines primario ad obedientiam, secundario & consequenter ad poenam obligat.

Prob. Deus, vi summi imperii in homines, ab ipsis exigit debitam obedientiam, lege morali praecipiendo, quae creaturis rationalibus conveniunt. Quod si iussum divinum abnuant, & naturae suae rationali convenienter vivere detrectent, tandem Deus iustissimam irrogat poenam, per quam a debito obedientiae non liberantur. Manet ergo debitum obedientiae essentiale & principale, quod lex exigit; poena autem latae legi est accidentaria.

Quaest. XXIV. An lex humana conscientiam, perinde ac lex divina obligat? Lex divina obligat conscientiam immediate & absolute ); lex humana, a legitima potestate lata, obligat mediate & hypothetice, si scilicet fuerit iusta, ex lege divina morali derivata ).

Prob. a. Deus est Dominus conscientiarum: E. easdem lege sua sanctissima immediate & absolute obligat, vt illius transgressores conscientia accuset, Rom. II, 15. Prob. b. Lex magistratu subditis lata obligat conscientias ) mediate, mediantibus his principiis: Quae magistratu, qui Dei ordinatio est, his, quorum magistratus est, praescribit, ea sunt facienda: quaeque magistratus his prohibet, ea sunt fugienda. Quae cum aeternae sint veritates, & in decalogo implicite contineantur, nemo potest contra legem a superiore latam agere, quin simul etiam contra aeternam Dei legem agat.

2) Obligat hypothetice, si fuerit iusta; nam sic est iustitiae divinae radius, quem qui violat, solem violat. Si contra clare & simpliciter iniusta est, non obligat.

Vbique enim valere debet illud, Act. V, 19. Obedire oportet Deo magis, quam hominibus.

Quaest. XXV. Quis est finis legis moralis? Finis legis moralis est a) gloria legislatoris, b) vita aeterna, sub conditione perfectae obedientiae promissa.

Eventus accidentalis est mors aeterna ). Prob. qua est limitatio ac determinatio actionis, quantum ad modum agendi, si qua exceptio, aut temporis, aut loci, aut rei cuiusdam, in qua versatur actio; eadem determinatio atque exceptio est in ipsa lege, eiusque sententia ac vi obligante.

V. gr. In lege quarta honora parentes tuos, primum nulla est exceptio temporis, honorandi enim sunt illi perpetua tum recordatione beneficiorum, tum observatione mandatorum, tametsi dudum in vivis esse desierint: deinde haec actionis limitatio ac determinatio, in causa iusta, divinisque imperatis non contraria, continetur in ipsa sententia legis, eiusque obligatione, vtpote quae non latius patet.

3) In omni lege aiente inest negatio oppositi eundemque ad modum in omni lege negante inest praeceptio contrarii. E. g. in hac lege adfirmante, parentibus tuis debitum honorem defer, continetur hoc interdictum: Noli parentibus denegare officium. Ergo, quae determinatione limitatioque actionis est in lege adfirmante, eandem oportet esse in contraria negante.

4) Sunt quaedam leges adfirmantes, sine vlla exceptione; actionifique limitatione ac determinatione, adeoque ad semper faciendum obligantes, cuiusmodi sunt illae: Tui conservationi stude, adhibitis semper mediis legitimis: Suum cuique tribue; quae leges adfirmantes aeque profecto late patent, ac negantes: Ne tibi ipse noceas: Neminem laede.

Immo semper & ad semper faciendum maxime obligat haec lex adfirmans, omnium prima ac praecipua: Deum cole, & amore perfectissimo prosequi nunquam define. perfectissimo profequi nunquam define.

Prob. a. Ex promulgatione legis Sinaiticae elucescit sapientia, iustitia & potestas summi Domini & legislatoris aeternum celebranda.

Prob. b. Ex Lev. XVIII, 5. Custodite leges meas & iudicia, quae faciens homo vivit in eis. Data est lex, vt ad vitam aeternam perduceret omnes eam perfecte servantes, non quidem ex merito iuris, quia Deus nemini quidquam debet; sed ex promissione & ordinatione Dei.

Prob. c. Ex Rom. VII, 10. Praeceptum, quod in vitam mihi (datum), idem (factum) in mortem. Lex, per se beatifica, per accidens fit mortifera, ob defectum potentiae receptivae; quia per carnem infirmatur, Rom. VIII, 3. Hinc operatur iram, denuntiat maledictionem, & adiudicat aeternae damnationi omnes, legem non implentes.


### Quest. XXII: Q

Q.

XXVI. From how many commandments does the Sinaitic law consist? The moral law promulgated on Mount Sinai consists of ten commandments, which were inscribed by God on two stone tablets . The sum of them is the love of God and neighbor , not excluding the love of ourselves .

Prob. a. From Exod. XXXIV, 28. He wrote (Jehovah) upon the tablets the words of the covenant, דברי הברית, ten words (a decade of words). The Greeks call it δεκάλογον and δεκαλόγιον. However, the words are understood not as bare, but as commanding. Cf. Deut. IV, 13. A distinction must be made here between general divine mandates and special ones. Special ones are far more numerous than ten, which nevertheless are contained under the decade of commandments. For the decalogue is an epitome of all moral laws, to which, as to a fountain, all laws directing the morals of men are to be referred. From which, to the Hebrews, they are called the ten mothers of the law and its roots.

Prob. b. Christ testifies that in the two mandates concerning loving God and neighbor, the law and the prophets hang, i.e., are contained in summary, Matth. XXII, 38.

Prob. c. In the mandate concerning the love of neighbor, the love of ourselves is also involved. For God commands: Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself, Lev. XIX, 18. so that the love of ourselves may be the measure of the love of our neighbor.

Q.

Bipartitely, into two tablets. The first deals immediately with the love of God, the second with the love of neighbor. To the first tablet we refer the three prior commandments, to the second the seven posterior commandments.

Prob. 1) They are called the two tablets of testimony, tablets of stone, written by the finger of God, Exod. XXXI, 18. Christ calls the first tablet the first and greatest commandment, concerning loving God; the same calls the second tablet the second commandment, like unto the first, concerning loving one's neighbor, Matth. XXII, 37. Paul names the commandment concerning honoring parents the first commandment with promise, Eph. VI, 2. Therefore the second tablet of the law begins from the IV commandment. Moreover, that there are ten commandments of the moral law, Moses writes explicitly, Exod. XXXIV, 28. Deut. IV, 13. and X, 4. But he does not record which is to be established as the second, which as the third commandment. It has been customary in almost all churches that sincerely embrace the Augsburg Confession and the catechism of LUTHER, to reckon three commandments to the first tablet, and to refer the mandate concerning graven images to the first concerning not having strange gods, to refer seven commandments to the second tablet, and to divide the mandate concerning coveting into two commandments; which division we retain as indifferent.

2) Images and graven things, made for worship, are strange gods. Therefore they are prohibited by the first commandment, and the mandate concerning graven things is not distinct from the first commandment, but only an appendix and explanation of the first commandment, containing a special example of the same.

3) In the Hebrew codex, each commandment is concluded with a distinctive sign ס, or ם; the former signifies a closed ס, the latter an open ם. But neither in Exodus, nor in Deuteronomy, is such a distinctive sign found between v. 3 and 4. Yet in Deuteronomy, between the ninth commandment, which we make, and the tenth, it is expressly placed.

4) That the mandate concerning graven images and the mandate concerning strange gods constitute one commandment, the Decalogue's accentuation teaches, concerning which see D. PFEIFFER in dub. vex. p. 268.

5) In the ninth commandment, actual concupiscence is forbidden; in the tenth, original. This is evident a) from the double repetition of חמד, Exod. XX, 17, so that two acts are signified; b) from the subsequent interpretation לא תתאוה, Deut. V, 21, which verb in Hithpaël denotes 'to act so that you covet,' because even the first motions are forbidden here; c) from the diverse declaration of the object, since by the ninth commandment actual concupiscence related to a vague, particular concupiscible object is forbidden, but by the tenth commandment, original concupiscence related to a universal concupiscible object.

There is an antithesis from Piscator, Keckermann, Socinus, and others, in whose opinion the mandate concerning strange gods and the mandate concerning graven images are two commandments. Their arguments are:

I. God's Spirit forbids the worship of strange gods and of images in distinct sentences: And they are two distinct things. Resp. God's Spirit subjects the prohibition of graven images to the mandate of not having strange gods, so that the general commandment may be illustrated by a special example, and one that most strikes the senses. If the diversity of periods introduced a diversity of commandments, more commandments would arise from the one commandment of sanctifying the Sabbath.

II. Two commandments are proposed in two verses in the sacred codex: But the ninth and tenth of the Lutherans are not, etc. Therefore. The minor is evident from Exod. XX, 17, where the commandment concerning concupiscence is comprised in only one verse, and indeed with one root. Resp. The ninth and tenth commandments of Exod. XX are uttered in one verse, but are nevertheless distinguished by a distinctive accent, Atnachum, and in Deut. V by the ס, as a distinctive mark. Furthermore, a double verb is employed there.

III. Paul embraces actual and original concupiscence in one commandment, Rom. XIII, 19. Rom. VII, 7. Resp. Distinguish between the implicit and explicit mode of proposing divine commandments. Paul had not taken up the plan of explicitly recounting individual commandments; but he makes mention of them summarily and generally. Meanwhile, he indicates the distinction between actual and original concupiscence not obscurely, Rom. VII, 7.

IV. If concupiscence made diverse commandments, there would be far more commandments than ten: But there are not more: Therefore. The consequence of the major is proven: because there would be one commandment about not coveting a house, another about not coveting a servant, another about not coveting cattle. Resp. The commandments are distinguished not according to objects, but according to the diverse modes of tending toward objects. Although the objects of concupiscence may be diverse; the mode of tending toward those objects is nevertheless twofold, actual and habitual, or original.

Latin:

Quaest. XXVI. Ex quot praeceptis constat lex Sinaitica?

Lex moralis in monte Sinai promulgata constat ex decem praeceptis, quae a Deo duabus tabulis lapideis inscripta sunt . Summa eorum est dilectio Dei & proximi , non exclusa dilectione nostri .

Prob. a. Ex Exod. XXXIV, 28. Scripsit (Iehovah) super tabulas verba foederis, דברי הברית, decem verba (decadem verborum). Graeci vocant δεκάλογον καὶ δεκαλόγιον. Intelliguntur autem verba non nuda, sed praecipientia. Conf. Deut. IV, 13. Distinguendum est hic, inter mandata divina generalia, & specialia. Specialia sunt longe plura, quam decem, quae tamen sub decade praeceptorum continentur. Est enim decalogus omnium legum moralium epitome, ad quam, tanquam fontem, omnes leges, dirigentes mores hominum, sunt referendae. Ex quo hebraeis decem audiunt matres legis & radices eius.

Prob. b. Testatur Christus, in duobus mandatis de diligendo Deo & proximo legem & prophetas pendere, i. e. summatim contineri, Matth. XXII, 38.

Prob. c. In mandato de dilectione proximi, etiam dilectio nostri involvitur. Praecipit enim Deus: Diliges proximum tuum, sicut teipsum, Lev. XIX, 18. vt dilectio nostri sit mensura dilectionis proximi.

Quaest. XXVII. Quomodo distinguuntur praecepta decalogi?

Bipartito, in duas tabulas. Prima immediate agit de dilectione Dei, secunda, de dilectione proximi. Ad tabulam primam referimus tria praecepta priora, ad secundam septem praecepta posteriora.

Prob. 1) Vocantur tabulae duae testimonii, tabulae lapidis, scriptae digito Dei, Exod. XXXI, 18. Primam tabulam Christus vocat primum & maximum praeceptum, de diligendo Deo, tabulam secundam idem appellat praeceptum secundum, primo simile, de diligendo proximo, Matth. XXII, 37. Paullus praeceptum de honorandis parentibus nominat praeceptum primum cum promissione, Eph. VI, 2. Ergo tabula secunda legis a praecepto IV. incipit. Ceterum decem esse praecepta legis moralis, Moses diserte scribit, Exod. XXXIV, 28. Deut. IV, 13. & X, 4. At non commemorat, quodnam sit statuenduni secundum, quod tertium praeceptum. Visitatum est in Ecclesiis fere omnibus, Aug. confessionem & catechesin LUTHERI sincere amplectentibus, tria primae tabulae accensere praecepta, & mandatum de sculptilibus referre ad primum de non habendis diis alienis, in secundam tabulam septem referre praecepta, & mandatum de concupiscendo in duo dividere praecepta; quam divisionem nos vt adiaphoram retinemus.

2) Imagines & sculptilia, ad cultum facta, sunt dii alieni. E. primo praecepto prohibentur, estque mandatum de sculptilibus non distinctum a primo praecepto, sed tantum appendix & explicatio primi praecepti, eiusdem speciale exemplum continens.

3) In codice hebræo vnum quodque præceptum absoluitur signo discretiuo ס, vel ם, illud significat ס clausum, hoc ם apertum. At nec in Exodo, nec in Deuteronomio, eiusmodi signum discretiuum inuenitur inter v. 3. & 4. At in Deuter. inter præceptum nonum, quod nos facimus, & decimum expresse ponitur.

4) Mandatum de sculptilibus cum mandato de diis alienis vnum constituere præceptum, docet accentuatio decalogica, de qua vid. D. PFEIFFER in dub. vex. p. 268.

5) In præcepto nono prohibetur concupiscentia actualis, in præcepto decimo originalis. Id quod patet a) e bina repetitione חמד, Exod. XX, 17. vt duo significentur actus; b) ex secuta interpretatione לא תתאוה, Deut. V, 21. quod verbum in Hithpaël notat, facere, vt concupiscas, quia etiam primi motus hic prohibentur; c) e diuersa declaratione obiecti, cum præcepto nono prohibeatur concupiscentia actualis relata ad obiectum concupiscibile vagum particulare, præcepto vero decimo concupiscentia originalis relata ad obiectum concupiscibile vniuerfale.

Antithesis est Piscatoris, Keckermanni, Socini & aliorum, quorum opinione mandatum de diis alienis, & mandatum de sculptilibus sunt duo præcepta. Quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Spiritus Dei distinctis sententiis prohibet Deorum alienorum, & imaginum cultum: Et sunt duo distincta. Resp. Spiritus Dei sculptilium prohibitionem subiicit mandato de non habendis diis alienis, vt præceptum generale speciali exemplo, eoque in sensus maxime incurrente, illustretur. Si periodorum diuersitas introduceret diuersitatem præceptorum, ex vno præcepto de sanctificando sabbatho plura exsurgerent præcepta.

II. Duo præcepta duobus versibus in sacro codice proponuntur: At præceptum nonum & decimum Lutheranorum non &c. Ergo. Minor patet ex Exod. XX, 17. vbi præceptum de concupiscentia vno tantum versu, & quidem vna radice comprehenditur. Resp. Præceptum nonum & decimum Exod. XX. efferuntur vno versu, sed tamen per accentum distinctiuum, Atnachum, Deut. V. per ס, tanquam notam distinctiuam discernuntur. Præterea duplex verbum ibi adhibetur.

III. Paullus concupiscentiam actualem & originalem vno complectitur præcepto, Rom. XIII, 19. Rom. VII, 7. Resp. Dist. inter modum proponendi præcepta diuina implicitum & explicitum. Non ceperat Paullus consilium, singula præcepta explicite recensendi; sed summatim & generaliter eorum facit mentionem. Haud obscure interim discrimen inter concupiscentiam actualem, & originalem indicat, Rom. VII, 7.

IV. Si concupiscentia diuersa præcepta faceret, longe plura essent præcepta, quam decem: Sed non sunt plura: Ergo. Conseq. mai. probatur: quia aliud esset præceptum de non concupiscenda domo, aliud de non concupiscendo seruo, aliud de non concupiscenda pecude. Resp. Distinguuntur præcepta non secundum obiecta; sed secundum diuersos modos tendendi in obiecta. Licet obiecta concupiscentiæ sint diuersa; modus tamen tendendi in illa obiecta est duplex, actualis & habitualis, seu originalis .


### Q. XXVIII. How is the decalogue to be explained?

The decalogue is to be explained in such a way that both all virtues and works worthy of a Christian, and all vices and illicit works, may be reduced to it.

Prob. The decalogue is an epitome of all moral laws, succinctly comprising all things to be done and to be avoided; and therefore the precepts of the decalogue are synecdochical, i.e., more things are commanded and prohibited than are expressly named in the decalogue. Wherefore, in the explanation of the Sinaitic law, certain rules are to be observed.

I. Negative precepts include the contrary affirmative ones, and affirmative ones the contrary negative ones.

II. In the decalogue, both external and internal obedience is commanded: conversely, not only external but also internal sins, along with original sin itself, the root of all evils, are prohibited.

III. In the explanation of the law, the distinction must be accurately held and inculcated between mortal sins, or proæretic [deliberate] ones, which cast out the grace of the Holy Spirit, extinguish faith, and devastate the conscience, and venial sins, or involuntary ones, which, although they consist with faith in the regenerate, must nevertheless be more and more diminished and abolished.

IV. That the law may be fully explained, punishments and rewards, promises and threats, must be added. But the promises are to be understood with the exception of the cross, and the threats with the exception of repentance .

V. In the decalogue, the moral [part], which binds all men, must be diligently distinguished from the ceremonial [part], which bound only the Jews while the Mosaic polity stood. Whatever, therefore, agrees with the law of nature is shown to pertain to all nations by Moses and the Prophets , in a certain way, distinguished above others. To this, as a certain species, it ought to be referred as to its genus. But these two, the ninth and the tenth, as various genera, although closely coupled, differ among themselves in such a way that the nature and definition of the things are different. Namely, hereditary concupiscence is a most powerful propensity of the mind to think, desire, and do everything that is not in accordance with divine laws. Actual concupiscence, as it is called, is a motion of the mind not consenting to the law, and the very thought and appetite, and its determination now to this, now to that forbidden thing, born from that innate and perverse inclination and alacrity of mind in every man, prone to any forbidden thing. Therefore, hereditary concupiscence is the first principle of all actions not in accordance with the law; actual [concupiscence] then is the second principle of the same, arising from the first. But when the cause is pleaded against the Socinians, one must encounter them with this theological argument above all. For they do not want the division of the ninth and tenth precepts because they are ignorant of the true and real reason for the concupiscence innate in us, and in this place, concerning hereditary sin, they wander into a most grave error.

in the N. T. by Christ and the Apostles it is repeated and enjoined, that is moral, obligating all men: the rest are ceremonial, or special appendices pertaining only to the Israelites.

VI. The effect being prohibited, the cause is prohibited: In the relative, the correlate is understood: Precepts or prohibitions of some special species, even a related species, or the whole genus is commanded, or prohibited.

VII. The precepts of the second table yield to the precepts of the first table. The neighbor is to be loved; but God is to be loved more.

VIII. For different ends and respects the same virtue can be referred to different precepts of the decalogue.

IX. To explain the precepts of the decalogue, all those things which are contained in Moses, the Prophets, as well as the writings of the N. T. as moral, are useful.

Latin:

Decalogus ita explicandus est, vt ad illum tum omnes virtutes & opera, Christiano digna, tum omnia vitia & opera illicita reducantur.

Prob. Est decalogus epitome omnium legum moralium, omnia facienda & fugienda succincte complectens; ideoque præcepta decalogi sunt synecdochica, h. e. plura præcipiuntur & prohibentur, quam quæ expresse in decalogo nominantur. Quo circa in explicatione legis Sinaiticæ regulæ quædam observandæ sunt.

I. Præcepta negativa includunt contraria affirmativa, & affirmativa contraria negativa.

II. In decalogo tum externa, tum interna præcipitur obedientia: contra non exteriora tantum, sed & interiora peccata, cum ipso peccato originali, omnium malorum radice, prohibentur.

III. In explicatione legis accurate tenendum & inculcandum est discrimen inter peccata mortalia, sive proæretica, quæ gratiam Spiritus S. excutiunt, fidem exstinguunt, & conscientiam vastant, & inter peccata venialia, sive involuntaria, quæ licet in renatis cum fide consistant, magis magisque tamen imminuenda & abolenda sunt.

IV. Vt lex plene explicetur, addendæ sunt pænæ & præmia, promissiones & comminationes. Sunt autem promissiones cum exceptione crucis, comminationes cum exceptione pænitentiæ intelligendæ .

V. In decalogo diligenter discernendum est morale, quod omnes homines obligat, a cærimoniali, quod solos Judæos, stante politia Mosaica, obstringebat. Quidquid itaque cum lege naturæ conuenit, a Mose & Prophetis ad omnes gentes pertinere ostenditur , in quadam, præ cæteris insigni. E. hoc, tanquam species aliqua, ad illud, vtpote genus suum, debet referri. Hæc duo autem, IXnum ac Xmum, vt varia genera, quamuis arcte copulata, ita inter se differunt, vt alia atque alia sit rerum natura ac definitio. Scilicet cupiditas hereditaria est validissima animi propensio ad cogitandum, desiderandum, agendumque omne id, quod legibus diuinis non est conueniens. Cupiditas actualis, vti dicitur, est motus animi legi non consentaneus, ipsaque cogitatio atque adpetitio, & eius modo ad hoc, modo ad illud vetitum determinatio, enata ex illa homini cuique innata ac perversa inclinatione atque alacritate animi, ad quoduis vetitum propensi. Itaque hereditaria cupiditas est principium primum omnium actionum legi non conuenientium; actualis deinde est principium earundem secundum, ex primo ortum. Cum vero causa agitur contra Socinianos, his potissimum theologico argumento obuiam erit eundum. Hi enim diuisionem præcepti IXni ac Xmi propterea nolunt, quod innata nobis cupiditas vim veramque rationem ignorant, atque in loco hoc, de peccato hereditario, in grauissimo errore versantur.

in N. T. a Christo & Apostolis repetitur & praecipitur, illud est morale, omnes homines obligans: reliqua sunt caerimonialia, aut appendices speciales ad solos Israelitas pertinentes.

VI. Prohibito effectu, prohibetur causa: In relato intelligitur correlatum: Praecepta aut prohibita specie aliqua praecipua, etiam cognata species, sive totum genus praecipitur, aut prohibetur.

VII. Praecepta secundae tabulae cedunt praeceptis primae tabulae. Diligendus est proximus; sed magis diligendus est Deus.

VIII. Ob diversos fines & respectus eadem virtus ad diversa praecepta decalogi referri potest.

IX. Ad explicanda praecepta decalogi faciunt omnia ea, quae in Mose, Prophetis, ut & scriptis N. T. continentur moralia.


### Q. XXVIII. How is the decalogue to be explained?: Decalogi Praeceptvm Primvm. I am Jehovah thy God: Thou shalt have no other Gods before me

DECALOGI PRAECEPTVM PRIMVM. I am Jehovah thy God: Thou shalt have no other Gods before me.

Obs. Those words: I am thy God, some, with Lucas Brugensis, make the general preface of the decalogue, others claim them for the first precept, with the Targum of Jonathan, the Hebrews, Josephus, and Philo; but they are more correctly held as the affirmative part of the first precept, as to who is to be worshipped as the true God, to which the negative is subjoined concerning not having other gods. For a) the decalogic accentuation (which is twofold, namely the accentuation of the verse, and of the precept) begins from the same words; b) Christ, being asked which was the first precept, answered: The first precept is: Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one, Matt. XII, 29.

You say: I. Those words: I am thy God, are indicative, not preceptive: Therefore they do not make the first precept. Resp. That those words have the force of commanding, the subjoined words teach: Thou shalt have no other before me. For not the affirmative part alone, but that which is joined to it, the negative, renders the full sense of the precept.

You say: II. Those words contain a general reason, impelling to the observation of all the precepts: Therefore they do not make a special precept. Resp. The first precept concerning it is effected, that, as widely as the reason of the law extends, so widely also its meaning and obligation extend. Therefore, if the reason of the law becomes so general and perpetual, that that reason pertains to all men and all ages of the world: the law, and its power of obligating, becomes no less general and perpetual, it is necessary. So also in the contrary part the argumentation is valid. II. Since there can be many and various reasons for one thing; therefore, if the reasons of a certain law are many, and indeed so diverse, that some of them are general and perpetual, inasmuch as they are to be referred to the whole human race, and all times; others special and temporary, suitable only to the Jews and the age of the O. T.: it is effected, that that law is mixed, partly common to all men and times, partly special to the Jews and times, according to the condition which existed before Christ was born and finished. E.g. Of the law concerning the Sabbath, by acting holily, the first and chief reason is of such a kind, the remembrance of which religion demands from all nations and men, until the end of the ages, Gen. II, 2. Ex. XX, 11. Therefore by this reason this law is common and perpetual. Then there is added one and another special reason, proper both to the Jews and the times of the O. T.; one indeed sacred and typical, Heb. IV, 9.; the other however forensic, which looked to the Jewish nation and commonwealth, Deut. V, 15. Therefore by this double reason this law is special and proper to the Jews. Therefore in the Christian state of the N. T. not this whole law is abrogated, but that only which pertains to the Jews and the age of the O. T. is derogated: for always there remains one reason, and that indeed the first and chief. directs all the remaining precepts to fearing and loving God. Whence B. LUTHER in his exposition of the same deliberately prefaced these words: We ought to fear and love God. You say: III. Those words regard the Israelites, for God adds: who brought you out of the land of Egypt. Resp. One must distinguish the τὰ συςατικὰ, the substantial dogmas, from the circumstances and appendages, which concern the Israelites alone.

Latin:

DECALOGI PRAECEPTVM PRIMVM. Ego sum Iehouah Deus tuus: Non habebis Deos alienos coram me.

Obs. Verba illa: Ego sum Deus tuus, alii, cum LVCA BRVGENSI faciunt prooemium generale decalogi, alii pro primo praecepto venditant, cum Targum IONATHANIS, Hebraeis, 10-SEPHO & PHILONE; sed rectius habentur pro parte affirmativa primi praecepti, quis pro vero Deo colendus sit, cui negativa subiicitur de non habendis diis alienis. Etenim a) accentuatio decalogica (quae est duplex, scilicet accentuatio versus, & praecepti) ab iisdem verbis incipit; b) Christus interrogatus, quodnam primum esset praeceptum, respondit: Primum praeceptum est: Audi, Israel, Dominus Deus noster, Dominus vnus est, Matth. XII, 29.

Dicis: I. Verba illa: Ego sum Deus tuus, sunt indicativa, non praeceptiva: Non faciunt igitur primum praeceptum. Resp. Verba illa habere vim praecipiendi, docent verba subiuncta: Non habebis alienos coram me. Plenum enim sensum praecepti reddit non sola pars affirmativa, sed, quae ei iungitur, negativa.

Dicis: II. Verba illa continent rationem generalem, impellentem ad observationem omnium praeceptorum: E. non faciunt praeceptum speciale. Resp. Praeceptum primum de efficitur, vt, quam late pateat legis ratio, tam late pateat eius etiam sententia atque obligatio. E. si ratio legis fit adeo generalis ac perpetua, vt ea ratio ad omnes homines omnesque mundi aetates pertineat: lex, eiusque vis obligandi, non minus generalis ac perpetua fit, necesse est. Ita quoque in contrariam partem valet argumentatio. II. Quum vnius rei plures ac variae possint esse rationes; idcirco, si cuiusdam legis rationes sint plures, & ita quidem diuersae, vt earum aliae sint generales ac perpetuae, quippe ad vniuersum hominum genus, omniaque tempora referendae; aliae speciales ac temporariae, solis Iudaeis atque aetati V. T. conuenientes: efficitur, eam legem esse mixtam, partim communem omnium hominum ac temporum, partim specialem Iudaeorum ac temporum, pro ea, quae erant ante Christum natum & consummatum, conditione. V. g. Legis de Sabbatho, sancte agendo, ratio prima ac praecipua est eiusmodi, cuius recordationem religio ab omnibus postulat gentibus atque hominibus, ad finem vsque saeculorum, Genes. II, 2. Ex. XX, 11. E. hac ratione haec lex est communis ac perpetua. Deinde accedit vna atque altera ratio specialis ac propria tum Iudaeorum, tum temporum V. T.; vna quidem sacra ac typica, Hebr. IV, 9.; altera autem forensis, quae ad Iudaeicam gentem remque publicam spectabat, Deut, V, 15. E. hac duplici ratione haec lex est specialis ac Iudaeorum propria. E. in Christiana ciuitate N. T. non tota haec lex abrogata est, sed id solum, quod ad Iudaeos atque aetatem V. T. pertinet, derogatum: semper enim permanet vna ratio, & ea quidem prima ac praecipua. de timendo & diligendo Deo dirigit præcepta reliqua omnia. Vnde B. LVTHERVS in expositione eorundem consulto præmisit hæc verba: Debemus Deum timere & diligere. Dicis: III. Verba illa respiciunt Israëllitas, addit enim Deus: qui eduxit te e terra Ægypti. Resp. Discernenda sunt τὰ συςατικὰ, substantialia dogmata, a circumstantiis & appendicibus, solos Israëllitas concernentibus.


### Q. XXVIII. How is the decalogue to be explained?: Quæst. XXIX. What does the first commandment comprise?

Quæst. XXIX. What does the first commandment comprise?

The first commandment comprises a divine edict, or command a), and a divine interdict, or prohibition b).

Prob. a. When God says: I am Jehovah, your God, He commands us the true worship of God, consisting in fear, love, and sincere trust. This commandment demands of us a) reverential and filial fear, excited by His supreme majesty, justice, and power. From the fear of God flows sincere, prompt, and constant obedience, to be rendered to God: submission of the mind, born from the consideration of divine majesty and our own infirmity: as well as patience, when we are chastised by God. b) The love of God, not only on account of divine benefits, but for His own sake, because He is the supreme good, and therefore worthy of love in Himself. From the love of God follows the denial of ourselves and the world. c) Trust, to be placed in God, on account of divine goodness, power, wisdom, and truth, by which He fulfills His promises. From trust is born hope and joy in God. The foundation of these virtues is θεογνωσία, or the knowledge of God.

Prob. b. When God says: You shall have no other gods before me, He prohibits all idolatry, which 1) is either grosser or more subtle. The former is when a man considers that which is not God to be the true God, and worships it, or if he otherwise exhibits religious worship to those who are not gods. To this belongs the religious worship of images (the use of images can sometimes be lawful and useful for the sake of memory). The latter is that by which we worship something that we know is not God, and yet we exhibit to it some worship which is owed to God alone. Thus avarice is called idolatry, Col. III, 5. 2) Idolatry is divided into that by which that which is not the true God is worshipped divinely, and that by which the true God is not worshipped divinely, i.e., when the true God is worshipped otherwise than He has commanded Himself to be worshipped in His word.

THE SECOND COMMANDMENT.

You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain. For the Lord will not hold him guiltless who takes His name in vain.

Quæst. XXX. What is commanded and prohibited by this commandment?

The abuse of the divine name is prohibited a), and its genuine use is commanded b).

Obs. I. The first commandment directs the heart of man to the fear of God: the second forms the tongue for the celebration of the divine name (*): the third moderates the public worship of God.

…Obs. II. The name of God is God Himself, insofar as He is revealed in the divine word, and from the same it is acknowledged, and it denotes God's essence, majesty, all His attributes and works, and whatever praise can be spoken of the Triune God.…

Prob. a. When God says: Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain, the light and profane taking of the most glorious name of God into the mouth of man is understood. Thus Elohim says to the impious: What hast thou to do to declare my statutes, and that thou shouldest take my covenant in thy mouth? Therefore, there is forbidden a) generally, the abuse of the divine name, i.e., profane use without due devotion, light, unworthy, prayers blathered without attention, the reading of scripture, or the hearing of the word, without devotion and reverence. b) Specifically: 1) Execrations, to which blasphemies also pertain. 2) Light, or futile, and false oaths. Here one must distinguish between an illicit and a licit oath. The former fights against the word of God and is undertaken regarding things false, uncertain, impossible, or futile. The latter does not fight against the word of God, and is undertaken regarding things true, certainly known, licit, possible, and grave. If the glory of God requires this, if our salvation and that of our neighbor demands it, if the magistrate commands it, and the necessity of duty insists upon it, it can be performed for the confirmation of truth with a safe conscience, Prob. b.

Conversely, there is commanded a) in general, the genuine and holy use of the divine name, in the devout preaching, hearing, reading, meditation, and confession of the divine word, and in prayers and vows. b) Specifically: 1) Invocation, by which we seek benefits from divine power and goodness, in our infirmity, indigence, and necessity, from God. 2) Adoration, by which we humble ourselves before God, and venerate His power and eternal majesty above us with internal reverence of the heart and external gesture, 3) Laudation, or glorification, by which we not only feel magnificently about God in our heart, but also celebrate His goodness, power, wisdom, justice, and general and special providence with tongue and words. To this pertain all the Psalms, all sacred music. 4) Thanksgiving for all spiritual and corporal benefits, which God has exhibited to us and to others, whoever they may be, not only to those of our own household, but also to strangers, whether friends or enemies.

Latin:

Quæst. XXIX. Quid complectitur primum præceptum?

Primum præceptum complectitur diuinum edictum, siue mandatum a), & divinum interdictum, siue prohibitionem b).

Prob. a. Cum Deus dicit: Ego sum Iehouah, Deus tuus, mandat nobis verum Dei cultum, consistentem in timore, dilectione & fiducia sincera. Exigit hoc præceptum a nobis a) timorem reuerentialem & filialem, excitatum summa eius maiestate, iustitia, potentia. Ex timore Dei fluit obedientia sincera, promta, constans, Deo præstanda: animi submissio, ex consideratione diuinæ maiestatis & nostræ infirmitatis nata: nec non patientia, cum a Deo castigamur. b) Dilectionem Dei, non tantum ob beneficia diuina, sed propter ipsummet, quia ipse est summum bonum, adeoque per se amore dignus. Consequitur ex dilectione Dei abnegatio nostri & mundi. c) Fiduciam, in Deo collocandam, ob diuinam bonitatem, potentiam, sapientiam, veritatem, qua promissa sua implet. Nascitur ex fiducia spes & lætitia in Deo. Fundamentum harum virtutum est θεογνωσία, siue agnitio Dei.

Prob. b. Cum Deus dicit: Non habebis alienos Deos coram me, prohibet omnem idololatriam, quæ 1) est vel crassior, vel subtilior. Illa est, cum homo id, quod Deus non est, pro vero Deo reputat, & colit, vel si alioqui cultum religiosum iis, qui non sunt dii, exhibet. Huc pertinet cultus religiosus imaginum (vsus imaginum licitus & vtilis aliquando memoriæ caussa esse potest). Hæc est, qua colimus aliquid, quod scimus non esse Deum, & tamen aliquem cultum ei exhibemus, qui soli Deo debetur. Sic auaritia vocatur idololatria, Col. III, 5. 2) Diuiditur idololatria, in eam, qua diuine colitur id, quod non est verus Deus, & eam, qua verus Deus non colitur diuine, h. e. cum verus Deus aliter colitur, quam se in verbo coli præcepit.

PRAECEPTVM SECVNDVM.

Non assumes nomen Domini Dei tui in vanum. Non enim habebit insontem Dominus eum, qui assumserit nomen eius in vanum.

Quæst. XXX. Quid præcipitur & prohibetur hoc præcepto?

Prohibetur nominis diuini abusus a), & præcipitur eiusdem genuinus vsus b).

Obs. I. Præceptum primum dirigit cor hominis ad timorem Dei: secundum format linguam ad celebrationem nominis diuini (*): tertium moderatur cultum Dei publicum.

Obs. II. Nomen Dei est Deus ipse, quatenus in verbo diuino reuelatus, & ex eodem agnitus est, & notat Dei essentiam, maiestatem, omnia ipsius attributa & opera, & quidquid elogii de Deo trinuno dici potest.

Prob. a. Cum Deus dicit: Non assumes nomen Domini Dei tui in vanum, leuis & profana assumtio gloriosissimi nominis Dei in os hominis intelligitur. Sic impio dicit Elohim: Quid tibi, ut enarres statuta mea, & assumas fœdus meum super os tuum? Interdicitur ergo a) generatim abusus nominis diuini, h. e. vsus profanus sine denotione debita, leuis, indignus, preces sine attentione deblateratæ, lectio scripturæ, vel auditus verbi, sine deuotione & reuerentia. b) In specie: 1) Exsecrationes, quo etiam blasphemiæ pertinent. 2) Iuramenta leuia, siue futilia, & falsa. Distinguendum hic est inter iuramentum illicitum & licitum. Illud cum verbo Dei pugnat & suscipitur de rebus, falsis, incertis, impossibilibus, futilibus. Hoc non pugnat cum verbo Dei, & suscipitur de rebus veris, certo cognitis, licitis, possibilibus & grauibus. Hoc si gloria Dei requirat, salus nostra & proximi exigat, magistratus mandet, & officii necessitas efflagitet, ad confirmationem veritatis salua conscientia præstari potest, Prob. b.

E contrario mandatur a) in genere genuinus & sanctus nominis diuini vsus, in deuota verbi diuini prædicatione, auditione, lectione, meditatione, confessione, in precibus & votis. b) In specie: 1) Invocatio, qua beneficia a diuina potentia & bonitate, in infirmitate, indigentia & necessitate nostra, a Deo petimus. 2) Adoratio, qua nos coram Deo humiliamus, eiusque supra nos potestatem & æternam maiestatem veneramur interna cordis reuerentia & exteriori gestu, 3) Laudatio, siue glorificatio, qua non tantum in corde magnifice de Deo sentimus, sed etiam lingua & verbis eius bonitatem, potentiam, sapientiam, iustitiam, prouidentiam generalem & specialem celebramus. Huc spectant omnes Psalmi, omnis musica sacra. 4) Gratiarum actio pro omnibus beneficiis spiritualibus & corporalibus, quæ Deus nobis & aliis quicunque sint illi, non solum domesticis, sed etiam peregrinis, siue amicis, siue inimicis, exhibuit.


### Q. XXVIII. How is the decalogue to be explained?: Praeceptvm Tertivm (the Third Commandment)

PRAECEPTVM TERTIVM (THE THIRD COMMANDMENT).

Remember, that thou keep holy the sabbath day. Quæst. XXXI. What is commanded and forbidden by this commandment? By this third commandment is commanded the sanctification of the sabbath a): The profanation of the seventh day is forbidden b).

Prob. a. When God commands: Remember, that thou keep holy the sabbath day, the object to be sanctified is the sabbath day. It must be well observed here that the third commandment contains something moral, to the obligation of which all men are bound: and something ceremonial, which is proper to the Israelite people. The former is perpetual, the latter is temporary. It is moral that some day of the week should be destined for sacred worship; it is ceremonial that precisely the seventh day of the week should be dedicated to the exercise of divine worship, or, as others like to speak, the moral element in the sabbath is the indefinite septenary and cardinal number, or that some seventh day is to be destined for divine worship; but the ceremonial element is the definite septenary and ordinal number, or that this day, precisely the seventh in order, is to be sanctified. There was in this commandment something ceremonial, the rigor of leisure, or rest prescribed to the Jews; namely, the divine interdict by which one was forbidden to travel for the sake of expediting private business, the kindling of fire, the carrying of a burden. The moral element still endures, the ceremonial has been abrogated. For nature stands firm that some time must be given to divine worship: the divine constitution in paradise defined the seventh day, ordained, Gen. II, 2, 3. Which sanctification was observed before the promulgation of the Sinaitic law, Exod. XVI, 5, and was repeated in the decalogue, Exod. XX, with certain circumstances added, Exod. XXXV, 3.

In the New Testament those circumstances, together with the circumstance of the seventh day specifically, were abrogated by Christ through the Apostles, and in place of the seventh day was substituted the first day of the week, called κυριακὴ ἡμέρα, the Lord's day, Apoc. I, 10, which Christ consecrated by his own authority and example; for he rose again on that same day, appeared to the gathered disciples, Thomas excepted, and afterwards, a week later, after eight days, he showed himself with Thomas present, John XX, 19, 26. On the same day also he poured out the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles, Acts II. The Apostles thereafter sanctified this first day of the week and instituted it as the ordinary Sabbath of Christians.

For the Apostles used the same for public assembly, Acts XX, 7, and ordained that it should be so done, 1 Cor. XVI, 2. The antithesis is that of the Anabaptists and Socinians, who maintain that Christ entirely abolished the third commandment concerning the sanctifying of the Sabbath day.

Who object: I. Distinctions of days are forbidden to Christians in the N. T., Gal. IV, 10. Response: Levitical distinctions of days are forbidden to Christians, especially insofar as the observance of those days is believed in the N. T. to be necessary for salvation.

Response: Levitical distinctions of days are forbidden to Christians, especially insofar as the observance of those days is believed to be necessary for salvation in the New Testament. II. The Sabbath is referred to among the shadows of things to come, Col. II, 16. Response: Paul is speaking of the Jewish observance of feasts and Sabbaths, which were shadows of things to come.

To the Jews, the observance of Sabbaths was a part of sacred worship; to Christians, it is a part of order and a circumstance of worship. Sanctification of the Sabbath a) in general is a setting apart from profane use, and a consecration to sacred uses. The Sabbath is therefore sanctified when it is separated from common works and dedicated to divine worship and holy operations, for which our rest is necessary, so that the mind, wearied by cares and labors on the remaining days, may rest in God.

Moreover, because the divine word is the means of sanctification, it is commanded b) in particular: 1) the public preaching of the divine word and the administration of the sacraments, Acts XX, 7; 1 Cor. XI, 20. 2) the devout listening to the preached word, its manifest reception, and pious meditation, Luke X, 16; 1 Thess. II, 13; James I, 21. 3) public prayer and thanksgiving, 1 Tim. II, 1; Acts II, 42.; 4) private worship of God, consisting in the repetition of the word heard, pondering it, rumination on divine benefits, catechetical instruction, examination of conscience, and confirmation of good purpose; 5) the exhibition of works of charity toward one's neighbor, and the distribution of alms, 1 Cor. XVI, 1. Prob. b. The profanation of the Sabbath is forbidden in general, when public and private divine worship is interrupted, and works that impede sacred worship are performed. In particular, there are forbidden: 1) Sinful works, by which one sins not only on other days but especially on the Sabbath day, such as drinking bouts, gluttony, luxury in dress, obscene conversations, etc. 2) Civil and servile works, and those for gain, such as commerce, agriculture, and manual crafts, by which both the body is wearied and the mind is disquieted. 3) Works of recreation that are untimely or disorderly, by which the devotion of public or private worship is hindered. However, those works are lawful which are not only formally divine worship, but also works of charity, necessity, and those which pertain to the sustenance of life.

Latin:

PRAECEPTVM TERTIVM. Memento, ut diem sabbathi sanctifices. Quæst. XXXI. Quid mandatur & interdicitur hoc præcepto?

Mandatur hoc præcepto tertio sanctificatio sabbathi a): Interdicitur profanatio diei septimi b).

Prob. a. Cum Deus præcipit: Memento, ut diem sabbathi sanctifices, obiectum sanctificandum est dies sabbathi. Probe obseruandum hic est, quod præceptum tertium contineat aliquid morale, ad cuius obligationem omnes homines obligantur: & aliquid cærimoniale, quod populo Israëlitico proprium est. Illud perpetuum, hoc temporarium est. Morale est, quod aliquis dies septimanæ cultui sacro sit destinandus; cærimoniale est, quod præcise septimus septimanæ dies exercitio cultus diuini dicandus sit, siue, ut alii loqui amant, morale in sabbatho est septenarius indefinitus & numerus cardinalis, siue septimum aliquem diem cultui diuino esse destinandum; cærimoniale vero est septenarius definitus & numerus ordinalis, siue hunc præcise in ordine septimum diem esse sanctificandum. Fuit in hoc præcepto aliquid cærimoniale, rigor otii, siue quietis Iudæis præscriptus; nimirum interdictum diuinum, quo vetabatur iter negotii priuati expediundi caussa, accensio ignis, portatio oneris, Morale adhuc durat, cærimoniale est abrogatum, Etenim natura constat, aliquod tempus cultui diuino esse dandum: diuina constitutio in paradiso septimum diem definauit, gnauit, Gen. II, 2. 3. quæ sanctio observata est ante promulgationem legis Sinaiticæ, Exod. XVI, 5. repetita est in decalogo, Exod. XX, additis quibusdam circumstantiis, Exod. XXXV, 3.

In N. T. illæ circumstantiæ, vna cum circumstantia diei definite septimi, abrogatæ sunt a Christo per Apostolos, & surrogatus est in locum diei septimi dies septimanæ primus, dictus κυριακὴ ἡμέρα, dies dominica, Apoc. I, 10. quam Christus auctoritate & exemplo suo consecrauit; quippe qui eadem die resurrexit, congregatis discipulis, excepto Thoma, apparuit, & postmodum altera septimana post octiduum, Thoma præsente, se exhibuit, Ioann. XX, 19. 26. eadem etiam die Spiritum S. in Apostolos effudit, Act. II. Apostoli deinceps primum hunc hebdomadæ diem sanctiuerunt, & instituerunt in sabbathum Christianorum ordinarium.

Eundem quippe Apostoli ad publicum conuentum vsurparunt, Act. XX, 7. &, vt ita fieret, ordinarunt, 1 Cor. XVI, 2. Antithesis est Anabaptistarum & Socinianorum, statuentium, Christum præceptum tertium de sanctificando die sabbathi plane sustulisse.

Qui obiiciunt: I. Discrimina dierum Christianis in N. T. prohibentur, Gal. IV, 10. Resp. Prohibentur Christianis discrimina dierum Leuitica, præcipue quatenus obseruantia illorum dierum creditur in N. T. necessaria ad salutem.

II. Sabbathum inter vmbras rerum futurarum refertur. Col. II, 16. Resp. Paullus loquitur de Iudaica obseruatione festorum & sabbathorum, quæ erant vmbræ rerum futurarum. At dies dominica non est vmbra rerum futurarum, sed sancta habetur ob gloriose resurrectionis Christi ex mortuis gratam recordationem.

Iudæis obseruatio sabbathorum erat pars cultus sacri, Christianis est pars ordinis & circumstantia cultus. Sanctificatio sabbathi a) in genere est segregatiua ab vsu profano, & consecratiua ad vsus sacros. Sanctificatur igitur sabbathum, cum a communibus operibus segregatur, & cultui diuino, sanctisque operationibus dicatur, ad quod nostra quiete opus est, vt animus curis laboribusque reliquis diebus defatigatus in Deo quiescat.

Ceterum quia verbum diuinum medium sanctificationis est, præcipitur b) in specie: 1) publica verbi diuini prædicatio & sacramentorum dispensatio, Act. XX, 7. 1 Cor. XI, 20. 2) deuota verbi prædicati auscultatio, manifesta susceptio, & pia meditatio, Luc. X, 16. 1 Thess. II, 13. Iac. I, 21. 3) publica precatio & gratiarum actio, 1 Tim. II, 1. Act. II, 42.; 4) priuatus cultus Dei consistens in verbi auditi repetitione, pensitatione, beneficiorum diuinorum ruminatione, catechetica informatione, scrutinio conscientiæ, boni propositi confirmatione; 5) operum caritatis erga proximum exhibitio, & eleemosynarum erogatio, 1 Cor. XVI, 1. Prob. b. Prohibetur in genere profanatio sabbathi, cum cultus diuinus publicus & priuatus intermittitur, & opera sacri cultus impeditiua patrantur. In specie prohibentur: 1) Opera peccaminosa, quibus cum aliis diebus, tum maxime peccatur die sabbathi, qualia sunt compotationes, comessationes, luxus in vestitu, colloquia obscoena &c. 2) Opera ciuilia, seruilia, lucrosa, qualia sunt commercia, agricultura, opificia manuaria, quibus & corpus delassatur, & animus inquietatur. 3) Opera recreationis intempestiue, aut inordinate, quibus deuotio cultus publici, aut priuati impeditur. Licita autem sunt non tantum opera, quæ formaliter sunt cultus diuini, verum etiam opera caritatis, necessitatis, & quæ ad vitæ sustentationem pertinent.


### Q. XXVIII. How is the decalogue to be explained?: Praeceptvm Qvartvm

PRAECEPTVM QVARTVM.

Honor thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be prolonged upon the earth, and it may be well with thee.

XXXII. What is commanded and forbidden by this precept?

By this precept is commanded the honor and obedience to be rendered to parents, and those who are in their place . Forbidden is the contempt and offense of the same .

Parents, and those like them, are at the same time obligated to provide for the comforts of their children, and those who are in their place .

Obl. By parents here are understood all superiors whom God has set over others to be ruled and defended, such as natural parents, tutors and curators, magistrates, ministers of churches, teachers, and those senior in age.

For precepts, either by one principal species prohibited, also cognate species, or the whole genus is commanded or forbidden. Conversely, by children are understood inferiors whom God has subjected to others to be ruled and defended, such as natural children, wards, hearers of the divine word, disciples, servants, and juniors.

Prob. a. When God commands: Honor thy father, in the general name of honor are comprehended all duties which children owe to parents: b) in particular it is required of children, that they 1) honor them, because of the divine character impressed upon them, because in them God himself is honored.

That honor consists in the estimation of the heart, reverence of gesture and words, and the defense of their reputation. 2) That they serve them, by promoting their comforts, and by relieving the poverty of the aging; which the Greeks call ἀντιπελαργεῖν (to requite parents). 3) That they obey them, by doing their commands promptly, unless they command things contrary to God, the supreme Father. 4) That they love them; since from them they derive both their blood and receive very many benefits. This love is the foundation of honor and obedience, and at the same time the root of patience, by which the defects of parents are to be borne.

Sir. III, 11. Prob. b. To the honor which children owe to parents is opposed 1) contempt of parents, when they are vilified in heart, mouth, or gestures; 2) offense, by which children, refusing the commands of their parents, provoke their anger.

Prob. c. By the fourth precept it is not only prescribed to children what is to be done by them toward their parents, but also to parents in turn their own duties are demanded.

Whence the Apostle joins both, Eph. VI, 4. Namely, parents are bound to provide for their children all things which pertain to their comforts, 1) sustenance, 1 Tim.

V, 8. 2) education in piety and morals, Eph.

VI, 4. joined with discipline, even more severe where necessity has required it, Prov. XIII, 24. THE FIFTH PRECEPT. Thou shalt not kill. Q. XXXIII. What is forbidden and commanded by this precept? By the fifth precept homicide is forbidden , and the preservation of our own life and that of our neighbor is commanded .

Prob. a. God, the Lord of life and death, expressly forbids the killing not of beasts (which from the foundation of the world were granted to man not only for service, but also for food, Gen.

I, 28.) but of men. Homicide is committed 1) by deed, to wit, by hand, instrument, or poison; 2) by mouth, by betrayal, insults, or imprecations; 3) by an irascible and cruel gesture, Gen.

IV, 5; 4) by heart, by anger, hatred, or private vengeance, Matth. V, 22. 1 John III, 15. Homicide is forbidden both against our neighbor, whether he be a friend or an enemy, whose body or soul (by giving scandal) it is not lawful to kill: and against ourselves, lest we become αὐτόχειρες (suicides), by laying violent hands upon ourselves, by indulging in gluttony, anger, or sadness, or by enervating ourselves with wicked labors. However, capital punishments, which the magistrate inflicts upon evildoers, are not prohibited here, nor are just and necessary wars, which are waged by public authority. God has prohibited that we should kill, but He has not bound His own hands, who is the Lord of life and death; indeed, the magistrate uses His ministry, Rom. XIII, 4. Proof b. Opposed to homicide is the preservation of our own life and that of our neighbor. We preserve our life and that of our neighbor 1) through meekness, by restraining our anger; 2) through mercy, by succoring our neighbor in necessity; 3) through humanity, by speaking kindly, consoling, and informing.

Latin:

PRAECEPTVM QVARTVM.

Honora patrem tuum & matrem tuam, vt prolongentur dies tui super terra, & bene fit tibi.

XXXII. Quid mandatur & interdicitur hoc praecepto?

Mandatur hoc praecepto honor & obsequium praestandum parentibus, & qui eorum sunt loco a). Interdicitur eorundem contemtus & offensa b).

Parentes, & his similes, simul obligantur ad commoda liberorum, & qui horum sunt loco, procuranda c).

Obl. Per parentes hic intelliguntur omnes superiores, quos Deus aliis regendis & defendendis praefecit, quales sunt parentes naturales, tutores & curatores, magistratus, ecclesiarum ministri, praeceptores, seniores aetate.

Praecepta enim, aut prohibita una specie praecipua, etiam cognatae species, sive totum genus praecipitur, aut prohibetur. E regione per liberos intelliguntur inferiores, quos regendos ac defendendos Deus aliis subiecit, quales sunt liberi naturales, pupilli, auditores verbi divini, discipuli, servi, iuniores.

Prob. a. Cum Deus praecipit: Honora patrem tuum, a) in genere nomine honoris comprehenduntur omnia officia, quae liberi parentibus debent: b) in specie exigitur a liberis, vt parentes 1) honorent, ob divinum characterem, iis impressum, quia in illis ipse Deus honoratur.

Constat ille honor aestimatione cordis, reverentia gestus & verborum, defensione famae illorum. 2) Vt ipsis feruiant, commoda eorum promouendo, & senescentium inopiam subleuando; quod Graeci vocant ἀντιπελαργεῖν. 3) Vt ipsis obediant, imperata eorum promte faciendo, nisi Deo, supremo Patri, aduersa praecipiant. 4) Vt ipsos diligant; quoniam ab illis & sanguinem ducunt, & plurima beneficia accipiunt. Haec dilectio est fundamentum honoris & obedientiae, & simul radix patientiae, qua ferendi sunt parentum defectus.

Sir. III, 11. Prob. b. Honori, quem liberi parentibus debent, contrariatur 1) contemtus parentum, cum iidem corde, ore, gestibus vilipendentur; 2) offensa, qua parentum iussa abnuentes filii ipsorum iram prouocant.

Prob. c. Praecepto quarto non solum praescribitur liberis, quid faciendum illis sit erga parentes, sed & parentibus vicissim sua demandantur officia.

Vnde vtrumque iungit Apostolus, Eph. VI, 4. Scil. tenentur parentes filiis praestare omnia, quae ad eorum commoda pertinent, 1) sustentationem, 1 Tim.

V, 8. 2) educationem in pietate & moribus, Eph.

VI, 4. iuncta disciplina etiam seueriori, vbi requisiuerit necessitas, Prouerb. XIII, 24. PRAECEPTVM QVINTVM. Non occides. Quaest. XXXIII. Quid hoc praecepto prohibetur & mandatur? Praecepto quinto prohibetur homicidium a), & mandatur conseruatio vitae nostrae & proximi b).

Prob. a. Deus, dominus vitae & necis, diserte vetat occisionem non bestiarum, (quae inde ab orbe condito homini concessae sunt non solum ad seruitium, sed & ad alimentum Gen.

I, 28.) sed hominum. Committitur homicidium 1) opere, scil. manu, instrumento, veneno; 2) ore, proditione, conuitiis, imprecationibus; 3) gestu iracundo & crudeli, Genes.

IV, 5; 4) corde, ira, odio, vindicta priuata, Matth V, 22. 1 Io. III, 15. Homicidii prohibitum est tum proximus, siue amicus, siue inimicus sit, cuius neque corpus, neque animum (dato scandalo) occidere licet: tum nos ipsi, ne fiamus αὐτόχειρες, violentas manus nobis inferendo, crapulae, irae, tristitiae indulgendo, aut improbis laboribus nos enervando. Non autem hic prohibentur supplicia capitalia, quae magistratus maleficis infert, neque bella iusta & necessaria, quae publica auctoritate geruntur. Deus prohibuit, ne nos occidamus, sibi vero, qui dominus vitae & mortis est, manus non ligauit; vtitur vero magistratus ministerio, Rom. XIII, 4. Prob. b. Homicidio opponitur conseruatio vitae nostrae & proximi. Conseruamus vitam nostram & proximi 1) per mansuetudinem, nostram iram cohibendo; 2) per misericordiam in necessitate proximo succurrendo; 3) per humanitatem, blande alloquendo, consolando, informando.


### Q. XXVIII. How is the decalogue to be explained?: The Sixth Commandment

THE SIXTH COMMANDMENT.

Thou shalt not commit adultery. Question XXXIV. What is commanded and forbidden by the sixth commandment? By the sixth commandment, chastity is commanded a), and impurity is forbidden b). Proof a. When God prohibits adultery, He commands us chastity, which preserves both an uncontaminated body and a pure soul. Chastity is either virginal, by which the unmarried preserve the true purity of body and heart undefiled, without the uncleanness of the flesh, 1 Cor. VII, 34, to which also widowly chastity is to be referred: or conjugal, by which spouses living together, according to the dictate of the Holy Spirit and conscience, not only abstain from all foreign and adulterous commixtion, but also observe moderation in the use of their own marriage, having regard for the primary purpose of matrimony, and for health and time, and restrain their concupiscence.

The aids for acquiring and preserving chastity are the frequent reading and meditation of the divine word, devout prayers, temperance, and sometimes fasting, assiduity in labor, and abstinence from all things that provoke lust. Pray, read chaste things, fast, avoid idleness: If you wish to keep your bodies chaste for God. Proof b. By the sixth commandment, adultery is prohibited, and all impurity related to it, or uncleanness 1) of deed, fornication, concubinage, incest, Sodomy; 2) of speech, obscene jokes, filthy language, immodest poems, amorous songs; 3) of gestures, lasciviousness of the eyes, harlot-like adornment, denudation, embraces, kissing; 4) of heart, impure thoughts, and delight in them.

The enticements and occasions of impurity, which are also forbidden by this commandment, are drunkenness and revelling, Rom. XIII, 14. Eph. V, 18. idleness, the pillow of Satan, wicked company, and lascivious dances, light clothing, and especially that which excessively uncovers parts of the body, obscene pictures and images.

THE SEVENTH COMMANDMENT.

Thou shalt not steal. Question XXXV. What is interdicted and commanded by the seventh commandment? By the seventh commandment, theft is interdicted a), and justice is commanded b). Proof a. Theft is expressly forbidden, by which here a) is generally designated every unjust acquisition, possession, and usurpation of temporal faculties, and the taking away of the wealth of others. b) Specifically, every theft is prohibited which is committed 1) by deed, whether it happens more manifestly or more secretly.

It is more manifest; which is commonly so held, and is punished by the political magistrate, is punished by the political magistrate, is punished by the political magistrate,

is punished, such as theft strictly defined, which is the handling of another’s property, against the will of the owner, with the intention of depriving him: robbery, which is the violent and manifest carrying away of another’s goods: sacrilege, the unjust carrying away of ecclesiastical goods: peculation, theft regarding matters pertaining to the republic: kidnapping, the theft of a human being. More hidden or subtle is every injustice whereby we attribute to ourselves more, and to our neighbor less, than is proper: to which pertains injustice in contracts, double measures, excessive prices, biting usury, the detention of that which we owe, dishonest arts, prodigality.

2) It is committed by the tongue, or by fraudulent words, by which the neighbor is defrauded, Jer. IX, 4. It is committed 3) by the heart and an inconvenient appetite for the faculties of others, avarice and trust in temporal goods.

Prob. b. By the seventh commandment, justice is commanded, diligent in seeking temporal goods, upright in exchanging them, frugal in protecting them, liberal in bestowing them, rendering to each his own. Specifically, therefore, it is commanded 1) diligence in the works of one’s office, that we may acquire temporal goods decently: 2) sincerity in contracts, observing proportion and equality: 3) parsimony, that we may prudently protect acquired goods: 4) liberality, that we may give what is fitting and to whom it is fitting.

Latin:

PRAECEPTVM SEXTVM.

Non moechaberis. Quaest. XXXIV. Quid praecepto sexto mandatur & vetatur? Praecepto sexto mandatur castitas a), & vetatur impudicitia b). Prob. a. Cum Deus prohibet adulterium, praecipit nobis castitatem, quae & corpus incontaminatum, & animam puram seruat. Castitas est vel virginalis, quae coelibes veram corporis & cordis puritatem citra carnis immunditiem illibatam conseruant, 1 Cor. VII, 34. ad quam etiam referenda est castitas vidualis: vel coniugalis, qua coniuges cohabitantes, secundum Spiritus S. & conscientiae dictamen, non solum ab omni aliena & adulterina commixtione abstinent, sed in proprii etiam coniugii vsu moderationem seruant, praecipui in matrimonio scopi, & sanitatis & temporis rationem habent, & concupiscentiam suam coërcent.

Subsidia conciliandae & conseruandae castitatis sunt frequens lectio & meditatio verbi diuini, preces deuotae, temperantia, & aliquando ieiunium, laboris assiduitas, & ab omnibus rebus libidinem prouocantibus abstinentia. Ores, casta legas, ieiunes, otia vites: Si seruare voles corpora casta Deo. Prob. b. Praecepto sexto prohibetur adulterium, & omnis ei cognata impudicitia, vel impuritas 1) operis, scortatio, concubinatus, incestus, Sodomia; 2) oris, ioci obscoeni, turpiloquia, carmina impudica, cantica amatoria; 3) gestuum, oculorum lasciuia, ornatus meretricius, denudatio, amplexus, deosculatio; 4) cordis, impurae cogitationes, & in iis delectatio.

Illecebrae & occasiones impudicitiae, quae hoc praecepto etiam vetantur, sunt ebrietas & comesatio, Rom. XIII, 14. Eph. V, 18. otium, puluinar satanae, praua societas, & lasciuiae saltationes, vestitus leuis, & in primis corporis partes nimium renudans, picturae & imagines obscoenae.

PRAECEPTVM SEPTVMVM.

Non furtum facies. Quaest. XXXV. Quid praecepto septimo interdicitur & praecipitur? Praecepto septimo interdicitur furtum a), & praecipitur iustitia b).

Prob. a. Furtum expresse vetatur, quo hic a) generatim designatur omnis iniusta facultatum temporalium acquisitio, possessio & vsurpatio, atque alienarum opum ablatio. b) Speciatim prohibetur omne furtum, quod committitur 1) opere, siue illud manifestius, siue occultius fit. Manifestius est; quod communiter ita habetur, & a magistratu politico punitur, magistratu politico punitur, magistratu politico

punitur, quale est furtum stricte dictum, quod est contrectatio rei alienae, inuito domino, cum animo priuandi: rapina, quae est violenta & manifesta bonorum alienorum ablatio: sacrilegium, iniqua ablatio bonorum ecclesiasticorum: peculatus, furtum in re ad rempublicam spectante: plagiatus, furtum hominis. Occultius vel subtilius est omnis iniustitia, quae nobis plus, proximo minus, quam decet, tribuinus: quo pertinet iniustitia in contractibus, mensura duplex, pretium immodicum, usurae mordaces, detentio eius, quod debemus, inhonestae artes, prodigalitas.

2) Committitur lingua, siue verbis fraudulentis, quibus proximus defraudatur, Ier. IX, 4. Committitur 3) corde & appetitu alienarum facultatum inconuenienti, auaritia & fiducia in bona temporalia.

Prob. b. Mandatur praecepto septimo iustitia, in bonis temporalibus quaerendis diligens, in commutandis recta, in tuendis parca, in largiendis liberalis, vnicuique suum tribuens. In specie itaque praecipitur 1) diligentia in operibus officii, vt bona temporalia decenter acquiramus: 2) iustitia in contractibus sincera, proportionem & aequalitatem obseruans: 3) parsimonia, vt bona acquisita prudenter tueamur: 4) liberalitas, vt demus, quae & quibus oportet.


### Q. XXVIII. How is the decalogue to be explained?: The Eighth Commandment. Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbor

THE EIGHTH COMMANDMENT. Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbor.

Latin:

PRAECEPTVM OCTAVVM. Non loqueris falsum testimonium contra proximum tuum.


### Q. XXXVI. What is prohibited and commanded by this eighth commandment?

By the eighth commandment, every lie and every indecorous use of the tongue, contrary to truth and charity, is prohibited ). But γλωσσαρχία [tongue-governance], or the legitimate use of the tongue in speaking what is true and what is useful to one’s neighbor, is commanded ).

Prob. a. Since God, the supreme Lord and Lawgiver, forbids false witness against one’s neighbor, the order of judgments is indeed regarded, but under one species of forensic lying (which is more pestilential than the rest) is contained in general the detestation of every lie. Whence Paul explains the eighth commandment thus: Put away lying, and speak every man truth with his neighbor, Eph. IV, 25. Now a lie, strictly defined, is an external speech contradictorily opposed to an internal speech, directed toward deceiving someone; but if it is taken more broadly, it is described as that which is done by a malicious contradiction of an external sign and an internal concept. Therefore, every lie is prohibited 1) in judgment, in which a lie is committed by a witness who either keeps silent the truth or harms the truth by speaking, Exod. XXIII, 1.; by a plaintiff, accusing unjustly, Mic. VII, 23.; by a defendant, denying against his conscience or weaving delays; by an advocate, attacking a good cause with evil arts and defending a bad cause; by a judge, not having sufficiently known the cause, or pronouncing an unjust sentence according to inordinate affections. 2) Outside of judgment, when false or uncertain things are said about a neighbor, and those things are eagerly heard and spread further, which bring detriment to the reputation of another; or when, conversely, the unworthy are praised or commended. Therefore, every defamation of a neighbor is prohibited, when those things are said about a neighbor which harm his reputation. Nor does it excuse one from this sin that what was said was true. To this also pertain insults, stinging jests, libelous pamphlets, every betrayal of a secret or of a matter that ought to have been kept silent, every vain garrulity. Indeed, even sinister judgments about another, contrary to the laws of charity. However, the concealment of truth, which I am not bound to reveal to a neighbor, nor which would be useful to him, is not prohibited. Nor is the correction of a sinning neighbor forbidden, if it be done modestly and out of charity.

Prob. b. There is commanded 1) truth, or veracity, which is the harmony of the mouth and the heart; for it is diametrically opposed to lying, Eph. IV, 25. Truth must be spoken in judgments, in counsels, in doctrines and arts, and in the whole of civil society. 2) Glossarchy, or the moderate use of the tongue, consisting in prudent taciturnity, a just measure of speech, and the utility and sweetness of words. Wherefore, he uses his tongue moderately who interprets in a fairer light those things which are doubtful, who covers or excuses the errors and infirmities of his neighbor, which is permitted, and hopes for his amendment, and procures it by correcting him fraternally, or by causing him to be corrected by others.

THE NINTH COMMANDMENT Thou shalt not covet thy neighbor's house.

THE TENTH COMMANDMENT

Thou shalt not desire thy neighbor's wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor anything that is his.

Latin:

Praecepto octauo prohibetur omne mendacium, & omnis indecorus linguae vsus, contra veritatem & caritatem ). Praecipitur autem γλωσσαρχία siue legitimus linguae vsus in dicendis veris, & quae proximo vtilia sunt ).

Prob. a. Cum Deus, summus dominus & legislator, interdicit falsum testimonium contra proximum, respicitur quidem ordo iudiciorum, sed sub vna specie mendacii forensis (quod reliquis est pestilentius) continetur in genere detestatio omnis mendacii. Vnde Paulus octauum praeceptum ita explicat: Deponite mendacium, & loquimini veritatem quilibet cum proximo suo, Eph. IV, 25. Est autem mendacium, stricte dictum, oratio externa contradictorie opposita orationi internae ad aliquem fallendum directa; si autem latius sumatur, describitur, quod fit malitiosa signi externi & conceptus interni contradictio. Prohibetur itaque omne mendacium 1) in iudicio, in quo mendacium committitur testis, qui vel veritatem reticet, vel loquendo veritatem laedit, Exod. XXIII, 1.; actor, iniuste accusans, Mich. VII, 23.; reus, negans contra conscientiam, vel moras nectens; aduocatus, bonam caussam malis artibus impugnans, & malam caussam defendens; iudex, non satis cognita caussa, vel secundum inordinatos affectus iniustam sententiam pronuntians. 2) Extra iudicium, cum falsa, vel incerta, dicuntur de proximo, eaque cupide audiuntur & latius sparguntur, quae detrimentum famae alterius afferunt; vel cum ex aduerso laudantur, aut commendantur indigni.
