Prohibetur itaque omnis infamatio proximi, cum ea de proximo dicuntur, quae famae ipsius nocent. Nec excusat ab hoc peccato, quod, quae dicta sunt, vera fuerint. Huc spectant etiam conuitia, ioci aculeati, libelli famosi, omnis proditio secreti, vel rei, quae taceri debebat, omnis inanis garrulitas. Quin etiam iudicia sinistra de altero, contra leges caritatis. Non autem prohibetur occultatio veritatis, quam proximo reuelare non teneor, nec quae illi vtilis foret. Neque interdicitur correctio proximi peccantis, si fiat modeste & ex caritate.

Prob. b. Praecipitur 1) veritas, sive veracitas, quae est concordia oris & cordis; quippe quae mendacio e diametro opponitur, Eph. IV, 25. Dicenda autem est veritas in iudiciis, in consiliis, in doctrinis & artibus, in tota civili societate. 2) Glossarchia, sive moderatus linguae usus, consistens in prudenti taciturnitate, iusta sermonis mensura, verborum utilitate, suavitate. Quare moderate lingua utitur, qui aequiorem in partem interpretatur, quae dubia sunt, errores & infirmitates proximi, quod licet, tegit aut excusat, atque emendationem eius sperat, eamque procurat, fraterne illum corripiendo, aut, vt ab aliis corripiatur, efficiendo.

PRAECEPTVM NONVM Non concupisces domum proximi tui.

PRAECEPTVM DECIMVM

Non desiderabis vxorem proximi tui, non seruum, non ancillam, non asinum, nec omnia, quae illius sunt.


### Quest. XXXVII. What is prohibited and commanded by the ninth and tenth commandments?

By the ninth commandment, actual depraved concupiscence joined with delight and deliberate consent is prohibited ; but spiritual fortitude is commanded, by which the old Adam is subdued and natural desires are tempered . By the tenth commandment, original concupiscence is forbidden , and original righteousness is commanded .

Obs. I. There is no discussion here of natural concupiscence, e.g., for food, drink, sleep, etc., which, if ἀταξία (disorder) be absent, is not condemned; nor of the holy concupiscence for eternal things: but of depraved concupiscence, which is an inclination and motion of the mind, discordant with the divine law.

Obs. II. Deut. V, 21, a transposition of the objects of depraved concupiscence occurs: for the wife is listed in the first place, the house in the second. From which it appears that the distinction of these commandments cannot be sought primarily and properly from the objects.

Obs. III. Concupiscence does not contain itself within those objects which are enumerated in these commandments, but wanders more widely: therefore a general clause is added: Thou shalt not covet anything of those things which are thy neighbor's.

Prob. a. That actual concupiscence is prohibited by the ninth commandment, and original concupiscence by the tenth, Moses indicates when, in Deut. V, 18, he expresses the divine interdict concerning concupiscence with a double Hebrew word, not without emphasis. First he says: לֹא תַחְמֹד, which denotes the second act, or actual concupiscence. Then he says: לֹא תִתְאַוֶּה, which denotes the first act, by which one makes himself to covet. Therefore, by the ninth commandment, actual concupiscence is forbidden, which is placed first as being better known: By the tenth commandment, original concupiscence is prohibited, the knowledge of which philosophers have not attained by the light of nature. Of which Paul speaks, Rom. VII, 7. I had not known concupiscence (to be sin), unless the law had said: Thou shalt not covet. The Apostle James, ch. I, 15, calls actual concupiscence συλλαβοῦσαν καὶ τίκτουσαν, conceiving and bringing forth, which conceives delight and the consent of the will, and breaks forth into an external act; but he calls original concupiscence in v. 14.

abstracting and enticing, which turns the heart of man away from God and the rule of righteousness, and invites it to evil by any allurements whatsoever. Therefore, by the ninth commandment, all depraved affections and evil thoughts are forbidden, in which man indulges and in which he takes delight, especially against his neighbor, an example of which matter is brought forward. Specifically, there is forbidden 1) envy, Prov. XXI, 10.; 2) the desire to do harm, Mic. II, 1. 2.: 3) avarice, Eccl. V, 9.: 4) ambition, or the inordinate desire for honor, Gal. V, 26.: 5) the concupiscence of pleasures, and the love of the world, 1 John II, 16. Prob. b.

Depraved concupiscence is resisted by spiritual fortitude, which both subdues, overcomes, and mortifies carnal or depraved desires, and moderates natural desires so that they do not exceed, and finally adds a spur to the desire for eternal things. Therefore, specifically, there are commanded: 1) the daily struggle against the flesh, Gal. V, 24.: 2) temperance in food, drink, and recreations: 3) modesty in seeking honors: 4) αὐτάρκεια [self-sufficiency/contentment], or equanimity of mind: 5) the desire for spiritual and heavenly goods. Prob. c.

By the tenth commandment, original concupiscence is forbidden, which is a congenital inclination toward evil, and the root of all other desires and sins. To this pertain the first evil motions, or depraved acts of the will that are indeliberate, to which neither delight nor consent is added. Prob. d.

In the tenth commandment, God demands from us original righteousness, which He rightly claims from us because He had co-created it, and the putting on of the new man, by which that is gradually repaired, Eph.

IV, 24. Quest. XXXVIII. Is the Sinaitic moral law a perfect norm of things to be done and to be avoided; or was it augmented by Christ, as a new legislator, and completed with new precepts?

The Sinaitic moral law is a perfect norm of things to be done and to be avoided, nor was it augmented by Christ with new precepts or additions, but only more fully declared and purged of Pharisaical corruptions.

Prob. 1) The divine law is perfect, Ps. XIX, 8. and therefore suffers neither addition nor diminution, Deut. XIII, 1. 2) The moral law is not repeated in the New Testament otherwise than it was delivered in the Old Testament. The compendium of both is the doctrine of loving God and neighbor, which exists in Deut. VI, 5. Lev. XIX, 18. Which compendium of the law is repeated for the same reason in Matt. XXII, 27. and Luke X, 27. 3) All virtues worthy of a Christian are commanded in the Mosaic law, and all vices are forbidden in the same: Therefore, it is perfect. 4) Christ, the God-man (θεάνθρωπος), is not a new legislator, but an interpreter, teacher, and vindicator of the law. For the law was given through Moses, grace and truth came through Christ, John I, 17.

5) Although Christ in His prophetic office inculcated, expounded, and purged the divine law of the corruptions of the Pharisees; yet the principal part and end of Christ’s prophetic office was that He might lift up the poor in spirit and the contrite and broken in heart with the sweetest doctrine of the Gospel, Isa. LXI, 1. Luke IV, 18.

The antithesis is that of the Anabaptists, Socinians, and Arminians, asserting that Christ is a new legislator who rendered the moral law more perfect and completed it with new precepts.

Their stronger arguments are: I. Christ and Moses, as two legislators, are opposed to each other, Heb. III, 5. 6.

Resp. They are opposed to each other as master and servant, as a son in the house of God and a domestic.

II. Christ is expressly called a legislator, Isa. XXXIII, 22. Resp. The words of the text are: Jehovah is our judge: Jehovah is our legislator: Jehovah is our king: He will save us.

Resp. The sense is: The Holy Trinity preserves us. God the Father is our judge and avenger. The Holy Spirit is our lawgiver and teacher. The Son of God is our king. Cf. CALOVIUS, Bibl. Illustr. on this passage, fol. 151.

III. Christ gave a new law, John XIII, 34. Therefore, He was a new legislator. Resp. Distinguish between a law that is simply new, and one that is new in a certain respect, or comparatively new. The law of Christ is called new not absolutely and simply, because it is the same law as the Sinaitic law, but it is called new in a certain respect and comparatively, because it was renewed by Christ, vindicated from the false interpretations of the Pharisees, and confirmed by Christ's new example.

IV. He who opposes his precepts to the Mosaic precepts is a new legislator: But Christ, etc. Matt. V, 21. 22.

Resp. Christ opposed His precepts not to the Mosaic laws, but to the corruptions of the Pharisees, who thought that murder was committed only by external act, not by the heart, not by gesture, not by word .

V. Whoever fulfilled the law, augmented it: But Christ, etc.

Therefore, the Major is proven: because something is fulfilled when something is added to its completion, just as a vessel is filled with oil when more oil is poured in.

The Minor is clear from Matt. V, 17.

Resp. Christ speaks of the fulfillment of the law through the most perfect obedience rendered in our stead, not of the fulfillment of the law through addition. For πληροῦν νόμον nowhere signifies an augmentation of the law . Cf. Rom. VIII, 8. 10. Gal. V, 14. Gal. VI, 2.

VI. Christ gave three moral precepts which are not found in the Mosaic law: 1) To deny oneself, 2) to take up, or endure, one's cross, and 3) to imitate Christ. Matt. XVI, 24. Resp. Self-denial pertains to the first commandment, which deals with loving God with all one's heart and all one's soul. For he denies himself who postpones self-love to the love of God. The endurance of the cross is patience, commended to us in the first commandment; because it flows from filial fear of God. The imitation of Christ (as explained by the Racovian Catechism, c. II. concerning the precepts of Christ, quest. 8.) consists in trust toward God, perfect charity, humility, and perseverance in prayers, and thus it pertains both to the first and to the second commandment of the decalogue. Moreover, that the imitation of God and Christ was not unknown to the fathers and prophets, we learn from Lev.

XI, 44. I am the Lord, your God: Be holy, for I am holy. Which is repeated in Matt. V, 48. 1 Pet. I, 15. And lest anyone think that the imitation of God prescribed to the fathers is one thing, and the imitation of Christ prescribed to us is another, let him hear Paul, Eph.

V, 1. 2. Be imitators of God, as beloved children; and walk in love, just as Christ also loved us. Q. XXXIX. How manifold is the use of the moral law? The use of the moral law is fourfold: a) political, b) elenchtic, c) pedagogical, d) & didactic .

Prob a. The political use of the law consists in the preservation of external discipline, so that fierce and untamed men may be turned away from more serious crimes by the proposal of punishments and rewards. According to this use, the law is a bridle or barrier by which sinners are restrained. Prob b. The elenchtic use consists in the manifestation and reproof of sins, as well as in the demonstration of the most severe divine judgment, Rom.

III, 2. According to this use, the law is the mirror of sin. Prob c. The pedagogical use consists in an indirect compulsion toward Christ.

For although the law formally and directly neither knows nor teaches Christ; yet by accusing, convicting, and terrifying, it obliquely compels the sinner to seek solace and help in Christ the redeemer. Thus the law is a pedagogue to Christ, Gal. III, 24 . Prob d. The didactic use consists in the information and direction of all moral acts, both internal and external.

Thus the law is the perpetual rule of living, Matt. V, 17.

Latin:

Praecepto nono prohibetur concupiscentia praua actualis cum delectatione & deliberato consensu coniuncta ; praecipitur autem fortitudo spiritualis, qua vetus Adamus debellatur, & naturales cupiditates temperantur . Praecepto decimo interdicitur concupiscentia originalis , & praecipitur iustitia originalis .

Obs. I. Non est hic sermo de concupiscentia naturali, v. gr. cibi, potus, somni &c. quae, si absit ἀταξία, non damnatur; neque de concupiscentia sancta rerum aeternarum: sed de concupiscentia praua, quae est inclinatio & motus animi, legi diuinae difformis.

Obs. II. Deut. V, 21. fit transpositio obiectorum prauae concupiscentiae: vxor enim primo loco, domus secundo recensetur. Ex quo apparet, distinctionem horum praeceptorum non posse ex obiectis primo ac proprie peti.

Obs. III. Concupiscentia non continet se in illis obiectis, quae in his praeceptis enumerantur, sed latius vagatur: ideo additur generalis clausula: Non concupisces quidquam eorum, quae sunt proximi.

Prob. a. Praecepto nono concupiscentiam actualem, & decimo concupiscentiam originalem prohiberi, indigitat Moses, quando Deut. V, 18. non sine emphasi interdictum diuinum de concupiscentia duplici verbo hebraeo exprimit. Primo dicit: לֹא תַחְמֹד, quod notat actum secundum, siue concupiscentiam actualem. Deinde dicit: לֹא תִתְאַוֶּה, quod notat actum primum, quo quis seipsum facit concupiscere. Nono itaque praecepto interdicitur concupiscentia actualis, quae tanquam notior praemittitur: Praecepto decimo prohibetur concupiscentia originalis, cuius notitiam philosophi ex lumine naturae non sunt assecuti. De qua Paullus loquitur, Rom. VII, 7. Concupiscentiam (peccatum esse) non noueram, nisi lex dixisset: Non concupisces. Apostolus Iacobus c. I, 15. concupiscentiam actualem vocat συλλαβοῦσαν καὶ τίκτουσαν, concupiscentiam concipientem & parientem, quae concipit delectationem & consensum voluntatis, atque in actum externum erumpit; concupiscentiam originalem autem appellat v. 14.

abstrahentem & inescantem, quae a Deo & regula rectitudinis cor hominis avertit, & quibusvis illecebris ad malum invitat. Prohibentur itaque praecepto nono omnes affectus pravi & cogitationes malae, quibus homo indulget, & quibus delectatur, in primis adversus proximum, cuius rei exemplum adducitur. In specie prohibetur 1) invidia, Prov. XXI, 10.; 2) nocendi cupiditas, Mich. II, 1. 2.: 3) avaritia, Eccl. V, 9.: 4) ambitio, sive honoris inordinata cupiditas, Gal. V, 26.: 5) concupiscentia voluptatum, & amor saeculi, 1 Io. II, 16.

Prob. b. Concupiscentiae pravae resistitur fortitudine spirituali, quae tum cupiditates carnales, sive pravas debellat, vincit, mortificat, tum cupiditates naturales, ne excedant, moderatur, ad cupiditatem denique rerum aeternarum calcar addit. In specie itaque praecipiuntur: 1) quotidiana lucta adversus carnem, Gal. V, 24.: 2) temperantia cibi, potus & recreationum: 3) modestia, in appetendis honoribus: 4) αὐτάρκεια, sive aequitas animi: 5) desiderium bonorum spiritualium & caelestium.

Prob. c. Praecepto decimo prohibetur concupiscentia originalis, quae est congenita inclinatio ad malum, & radix omnium aliarum cupiditatum & peccatorum. Huc spectant primi motus mali, sive pravi voluntatis actus indeliberati, ad quos non accedit delectatio aut consensus.

Prob. d. In praecepto decimo Deus a nobis exigit iustitiam originalem, quam iure a nobis poscit, quia concreaverat, & indutionem novi hominis, qua illa paullatim reparatur, Eph. IV, 24.

Quaest. XXXVIII. Estne lex moralis Sinaitica perfecta faciendorum & fugiendorum norma; an a Christo, tanquam novo legislatore, aucta, & novis praeceptis completa fuit?

Lex moralis Sinaitica est perfecta faciendorum & fugiendorum norma, neque eadem a Christo novis praeceptis, aut additamentis aucta, sed tantum uberius declarata, & a corruptelis pharisaicis repurgata est.

Prob. 1) Lex divina perfecta est, Ps. XIX, 8. adeoque nec additionem, neque diminutionem patitur, Deut. XIII, 1. 2) Lex moralis non aliter repetitur in novo testamento, quam tradita fuit in V. T. Compendium utriusque est doctrina de diligendo Deo & proximo, quae exstat Deut. VI, 5. Leu. XIX, 18. Quod compendium legis eadem ratione repetitur Matth. XXII, 27. & Luc. X, 27. 3) Omnes virtutes, Christiano dignae, in lege Mosaica praecipiuntur, & omnia vitia in eadem prohibentur: E. est perfecta. 4) Christus θεάνθρωπος, non est novus legislator, sed legis interpres, doctor & vindex. Lex enim per Mosen data est, gratia & veritas per Christum facta, Io. I, 17.

5) Quamuis Christus in officio prophetico legem divinam inculcauerit, exposuerit, & a corruptelis Pharisaeorum repurgauerit; praecipua tamen pars & finis officii Christi prophetici fuit, vt dulcissima euangelii doctrina pauperes spiritu & contritos, confractosque corde erigeret, Ies. LXI, 1. Luc. IV, 18.

Antithesis est Anabaptistarum, Socinianorum & Arminianorum, afferentium, Christum esse novum legislatorem, qui legem moralem perfectiorem reddiderit, & novis praeceptis compleuerit.

Quorum potiora argumenta sunt: I. Christus & Moses, tanquam duo legislatores, sibi opponuntur, Hebr. III, 5. 6.

Resp. Opponuntur sibi, vt dominus & servus, vt filius in domo Dei & famulus.

II. Christus diserte dicitur legislator, Es. XXXIII, 22. Resp. Verba textus sunt: Iehouah est iudex noster: Iehouah est legislator noster: Ille saluabit nos. Christus diserte dicitur legislator, Es. XXXIII, 22. Resp. Verba textus sunt: Iehouah est iudex noster: Iehouah est legislator noster: Iehouah est rex noster: Ille saluabit nos.

Resp. Sensus est: SS. Trinitas conferuat nos. Deus Pater est iudex & vindex noster. Spiritus S. est legifer & doctor noster. Filius Dei est rex noster. Confer. CALOVII bibl. illustr. in h. l. fol. 151.

III. Christus dedit nouam legem, Io. XIII, 34. E. fuit nouus legislator. Resp. Dist. inter legem simpliciter nouam, & secundum quid, seu comparate nouam. Lex Christi noua dicitur non absolute & simpliciter, quia est eadem lex cum lege Sinaitica, sed dicitur noua secundum quid & comparate, quia est a Christo renouata, a falsis interpretationibus Pharisaeorum vindicata, & nouo Christi exemplo confirmata.

IV. Qui praecepta sua Mosaicis praeceptis opponit, ille est nouus legislator: Atqui Christus &c. Matth. V, 21. 22.

Resp. Christus praecepta sua opposuit non legibus Mosaicis, sed corruptelis Pharisaeorum, qui putabant, homicidium tantum fieri opere externo, non corde, non gestu, non ore [*].

V. Quicunque impleuit legem, eandem auxit: Atqui Christus &c.

E. Maior probatur: quia tunc aliquid impletur, quando ad ipsius complementum aliquid adiicitur, sicut vas oleo impletur, quando plus olei infunditur.

Minor patet ex Matth. V, 17.

Resp. Loquitur Christus de impletione legis per consummatissimam obedientiam nostri vice praestitam, non de impletione legis per additionem. Nam πληροῦν νόμον nullibi legis auctionem significat []. Conf. Rom. VIII, 8. 10. Gal. V, 14. Gal. VI, 2.

VI. Christus tria dedit praecepta moralia, quae non exstant in lege Mosaica: 1) Seipsum abnegare, 2) crucem suam tollere, siue tolerare, & 3) Christum imitari. Matth. XVI, 24. Resp. Abnegatio sui pertinet ad praeceptum primum, quod agit de Deo diligendo ex toto corde & ex tota anima. Nam seipsum abnegat, qui amorem sui postponit amori Dei. Crucis tolerantia est patientia, commendata nobis in praecepto primo; quia fluit ex timore Dei filiali. Imitatio Christi, (exponente catech. Racov. c. II. de praecept. Christi, quaest. 8.) consistit [*] Id sistit in fiducia erga Deum, caritate perfecta, humilitate ac perseverantia in precibus, adeo que tum ad primum, tum ad secundum decalogi præceptum pertinet. Ceterum imitationem Dei & Christi non fuisse ignotam patribus & prophetis, discimus ex Leu.

XI, 44. Ego sum Dominus, Deus vester: Sancti estote, quia ego sanctus sum. Quod repetitur Matth. V, 48. 1 Petr. I, 15. Et ne quis opinetur, aliam esse Dei, patribus præscriptam, & aliam esse Christi, nobis præscriptam, imitationem, audiat Paullum, Eph.

V, 1. 2. Estote imitatores Dei, sicut liberi dilecti; & ambulate in dilectione, sicut etiam Christus dilexit nos. Quæst. XXXIX. Quotuplex est usus legis moralis? Usus legis moralis est quadruplex: a) politicus, b) elenchticus, c) pædagogicus, d) & didacticus .

Prob a. Usus legis politicus consistit in conservatione externæ disciplinæ, vt feri & indomiti homines a sceleribus grauioribus, propositis pænis & præmiis, auertantur. Iuxta hunc usum lex est frenum aut repagulum, quo peccatores coërcentur. Prob b. Usus elenchticus consistit in peccatorum manifestatione & redargutione, iuxta atque seuerissimi iudicii diuini demonstratione, Rom.

III, 2. Iuxta hunc usum lex est speculum peccati. Prob c. Usus pædagogicus consistit in compulsu indirecto ad Christum.

Quamuis enim lex formaliter directeque Christum nec sciat, nec doceat; attamen accusando, conuincendo, terrendo, oblique compellit peccatorem ad quærendum solatium & auxilium in Christo redemptore. Itaque lex est pædagogus ad Christum, Gal. III, 24 . Prob d. Usus didacticus consistit in informatione & directione omnium actuum moralium internorum & externorum.

Sic lex est perpetua viuendi regula, Matth. V, 17.


### Q. XL. Are the reborn liberated and exempted from this fourfold use of the law, so that the doctrine of the law is not to be preached to

The moral law, because of the fourfold use which it provides, must be preached and inculcated even to the reborn.

Prob. 1) By the political use of the law, Christians are contained in discipline, so that they may avoid vices and grow in virtues; because they are not fully renewed in this life, but struggle assiduously with their old Adam: for that old Adam (as an untamed and stubborn ass) is still also some part of them, which must be coerced not only by the doctrine of the law, by exhortations, impulse, and threats, but even as if by a club, stripes, and punishments, and must be compelled into the obedience of Christ, as the Form. Conc. p. 723 teaches.

2) The law exercises an elenchtic use in the reborn, as often as they, looking into the mirror of the law, are led to the knowledge of indwelling sin and their own imperfection, Rom. VII, 18.

3) The law is also a schoolmaster to Christ for the reborn. This is what the Blessed Luther teaches excellently in his later commentary on Galatians, p. 94. Insofar as the flesh remains, to that extent the law also remains a schoolmaster, which is accustomed to terrify and sadden the conscience from time to time by the showing of sin and the threat of death. Yet it is always raised up by the daily coming of Christ.

4) The law is a necessary rule of life for believers, lest they devise a kind of religion of their own choosing by some peculiar holiness of their own, and under the pretext of the Spirit of God, institute elective worship without the word and command of God, as the Form.

Conc. p. 722 warns. The antithesis is that of the Arminians and Anabaptists, who contended that the Mosaic law does not pertain to Christians.

Their arguments are:

I. The law is not laid down for the just; 1 Tim. I, 9. Resp. The words of Paul are: Δικαίῳ νόμος οὐ κεῖται, the law does not lie upon the just as a heavy burden. Which is accurately explained in the Form. Concord. p. 719: The law can neither overwhelm those who have been reconciled with God through Christ, nor can it be troublesome to the reborn by its coercion: since they delight in the law of God according to the inner man.

Latin:

Lex moralis ob quadruplicem, quem præstat usum, etiam renatis prædicanda & inculcanda est,

Prob. 1) Usu legis politico Christiani continentur in disciplina, ut vitia vitent, & virtutibus crescant; propterea, quod in hac vita non plene renouantur, sed assidue cum veteri suo Adamo luctentur: Vetus enim ille Adam (quasi asinus indomitus & contumax) est adhuc etiam aliqua pars ipsorum, quæ non modo legis doctrina, exhortationibus, impulsu & comminationibus, verum etiam quasi fuste, plagis & pænis coercenda, & in obedientiam Christi cogenda est, docente Form. Conc. p. 723.

2) Usum elenchticum lex exercet in renatis, quoties speculum legis intuentes perducuntur ad peccati inhabitantis & imperfectionis suæ cognitionem, Rom. VII, 18.

3) Lex etiam renatis est pædagogus ad Christum. Id quod eximie docet B. Lutherus in comment. poster. ad Gal. p. 94. Quatenus manet caro, eatenus etiam manet lex pædagogus, qui subinde perterrefacere & contristare solet conscientiam, ostensione peccati & comminatione mortis. Ipsa tamen semper erigitur quotidiano aduentu Christi.

4) Lex credentibus est regula vitæ necessaria, ne propria quadam sanctimonia religionis genus de suo ingenio excogitent, & sub prætextu spiritus Dei electitios cultus sine verbo & mandato Dei instituant, monente Form.

Conc. p. 722. Antithesis est Arminianorum & Anabaptistarum, qui contendebant, legem Mosaicam ad Christianos non pertinere.

Quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Lex iusto non est posita; 1 Tim. I, 9. Resp. Verba Pauli sunt: Δικαίῳ νόμος οὐ κεῖται, iusto lex non incumbit, velut graue onus. Quod in Form. Concord. p. 719. accurate exponitur: Lex neque eos, qui per Christum cum Deo reconciliati sunt obruere, neque renatis coactione sua molesta esse potest: Quandoquidem illi secundum interiorem hominem lege Dei delectantur.


### Q. XIV. Are also infants foundlings, to be baptized?

Resp. The reborn are not under the curse and burdensome coercion of the law; they are, however, under the obligation of the law to provide obedience.

Quaest. XLI. Is the Sinaitic moral law abrogated?

The moral law, promulgated by God on Mount Sinai, cannot be abrogated.

Proof 1) The moral law was promulgated immediately by the Son of God, inscribed by Him on stone tablets, and preserved in the ark of the covenant, so that it might be the most certain rule and norm according to which life is to be piously instituted in accordance with the immutable will of God. Therefore, it cannot be abrogated.

2) The moral law comprises the natural law, which refers to justice itself in God, and is a certain ray of it. Therefore, just as this is immutable, so is that.

The antithesis is that of Rivet, Pareus, and others, who assert that the moral law, insofar as it was delivered through the ministry of Moses, has been abrogated for Christians. Their arguments are:

I. Those who have nothing in common with Moses, but everything in common with Christ, are not bound to keep the law of Moses: But Christians, etc. Therefore. Resp. The moral law is called the law of Moses as the minister, but it is the law of God as the author, from whom it retains the communicated perpetual power of obligating. Moses did not promulgate the moral law, nor did he inscribe it with his own hand on stone tablets, but the Son of God did.

II. Some Lutheran theologians teach that the moral law is abrogated regarding justification, the curse, and the rigor of exaction. Conf. Dieterici, Inst. Catechet. p. 73; Quensted, Syst. part. IV, fol. 11. Resp. Other Lutheran theologians have judged that one should abstain from that manner of speaking, namely D. Calov in Bibl. Illustratis on Exod. c. XX, fol. 98, on Gal. III, f. 591; D. Osiander in Typo Legis Moralis, p. 83; D. Rudrauff in Syll. Controu. p. 362; D. Bayer in Comp. p. 817. I shall append here the judgment of D. Gerhard, which is read in the locus on the ceremonial and forensic law, c. IV, § 43: "That the law is invalid for men regarding justification and life after the fall, that brings no change or abrogation to the law, but argues that a great change has been made in us; for it is because of this that justification and salvation cannot be hoped for from the law, because it is weakened through the flesh, Rom. VIII, 3. By the same reasoning, that believers in Christ are not actually subject to the curse of the law, from that likewise no change or abrogation can be attributed to the law, since the voice of the law retains its property and efficacy of accusing, cursing, and condemning perpetually; that it does not actually exert this power against believers happens by accident, namely because the shield of divine grace and the cloak of the righteousness of Christ covers them. The same judgment is made concerning the rigor of the judgment of exaction, which remains perpetual and inviolate for the law, which even believers themselves and their works would be forced to experience, were they not believers, i.e., were they not reconciled to God through faith in Christ, because of whom even their works, although they are in many ways unclean and imperfect, please God." Rightly, therefore, does D. Chemnitius warn, in the locus on the law, c. V, p. 18, that Scripture does not say that the moral law is dead, abrogated, or evacuated, but that we are said to be dead and abrogated to the law, to signify that the change occurs not in that rule of justice in God, but in us, Rom. III, 21. We do not καταργοῦμεν (nullify) the law, but we κατηργήθημεν ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου (have been nullified from the law), having died. Therefore, a distinction must be made here between accurate speech and common or popular speech: the latter is to be understood according to the sense rather than the words. For it is customary that, when through grace the transgression of the law is not punished with rigor but is pardoned, we say in common parlance that the legislator himself does not require it; especially if that happens ordinarily.

III. Christ abrogated the third commandment concerning the sanctification of the Sabbath day, when through the Apostles He ordered the first day of the week to be kept as a holiday, Acts XX, 7; 1 Cor. XVI, 2.

Resp. The third commandment contains within itself something moral and ceremonial. The moral part is divine worship, on the seventh day. to be celebrated on some day: The ceremonial is precisely the seventh day of the week.

The moral regards the indefinite septenary and the cardinal number, or one of the seven days of the week: The ceremonial regards the definite septenary and the ordinal number, i.e., precisely the seventh day of the week. The moral still endures, the ceremonial has been abrogated.

Latin:

Resp. Renati non sunt sub maledictione et molesta coactione legis; sunt tamen sub obligatione legis ad praestandam obedientiam.

Quaest. XLI. Estne lex moralis Sinaitica abrogata?

Lex moralis, in monte Sinai a Deo promulgata, abrogari nequit.

Prob. 1) Lex moralis, immediate per Filium Dei promulgata, ab ipso tabulis lapideis inscripta, et in arca foederis asseruata est, vt esset certissima regula et norma, ad quam vita secundum immutabilem voluntatem Dei fit pie instituenda. E. abrogari nequit.

2) Lex moralis complectitur legem naturalem, quae refert ipsam iustitiam in Deo, et quidam huius radius est. Vt itaque haec est immutabilis; ita et illa.

Antithesis est Riveti, Parei et aliorum, asserentium, legem moralem, quatenus ministerio Mosis est tradita, abrogatam esse Christianis. Quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Quibus nihil est commune cum Mose, sed omnia communia sunt cum Christo, illi ad legem Mosis seruandam non sunt adstricti: Atqui Christianis etc. E. Resp. Lex moralis dicitur lex Mosis, tanquam ministri, est autem lex Dei, tanquam auctoris, a quo perpetuam vim obligandi communicatam retinet. Moses non promulgauit legem moralem, neque manu sua eandem tabulis lapideis inscriptit, sed Filius Dei.

II. Nonnulli Theologi Lutherani docent, legem moralem abrogatam esse quoad iustificationem, maledictionem et rigorem exactionis. Conf. Dieterici inst. catechet. p. 73. Qvensted. syst. part. IV. fol. 11. Resp. Alii Theologi Lutherani ab ea loquendi ratione abstinendum esse censuerunt, nominatim D. Calov. in bibl. illustratis ad Exod. c. XX. fol. 98. ad Gal. III. f. 591. D. Osiander in typo legis moralis, p. 83. D. Rvdravff in syll. controu. p. 362. D. Bayer. in comp. p. 817. Adscribam hic iudicium D. Gerhardi, quod legitur in loco de lege carimon. et forenf. c. IV. §. 43. Quod ad iustificationem et vitam hominibus, post lapsum lex inualida est, illud nullam affert legi mutationem vel abrogationem, sed in nobis grandem mutationem factam esse arguit; ideo enim ex lege non potest sperari iustificatio et salus, quia per carnem infirmatur, Rom. VIII, 3. Pari ratione, quod credentes in Christum non sunt actu obnoxii maledictioni legis, ex eo itidem nulla potest mutatio, vel abrogatio legi tribui, siquidem proprietatem et efficaciam suam accusandi, maledicendi et damnandi vox legis obtinet perpetuam; quod hanc vim suam non actu exserat aduersus credentes, ex accidenti prouenit, nimirum quia scutum diuinae gratiae ac pallium iustitiae Christi eos tegit. Idem iudicium fit de rigore iudicii exactionis, qui legi manet perpetuus ac inuiolatus, quem ipsi etiam credentes et eorum opera experiri cogerentur, nisi credentes essent, h. e. nisi per fidem in Christum Deo reconciliati essent, propter quem etiam opera ipsorum, licet multis modis immunda et imperfecta sint, Deo placent. Recte igitur monet D. Chemnitivs, loco de lege c. V. p. 18. Scripturam non dicere, quod lex moralis sit mortua, abrogata vel euacuata, sed nos dici mortuos et abrogatos legi, vt significet, fieri mutationem non in illa regula iustitiae in Deo, sed in nobis, Rom. III, 21. Legem non καταργοῦμεν, sed nos κατηργήθημεν ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου, ἀπεθα νόντες. Distinguendum itaque hic est inter locutionem accuratam et vulgarem, siue popularem: Haec secundum sensum potius, quam secundum verba intelligenda est. Consuetum enim est, vt, cum ex gratia transgressio legis non rigore reficitur, sed condonatur, ipsum legislatorem hoc non requirere, in sermone vulgari dicamus; imprimis si id ordinarie fiat.

III. Christus abrogauit praeceptum tertium de sanctificando die sabbathi, dum per Apostolos feriari iussit diem primum septimanae, Act. XX, 7. 1 Cor. XVI, 2.

Resp. Praeceptum tertium continet in se aliquid morale et carimoniale. Morale est cultus diuinus, septimo die Resp. Præceptum tertium continet in se aliquid morale & cærimoniale. Morale est cultus diuinus, septimo die aliquo celebrandus: Caerimoniale est praecise septimus septimanae dies.

Morale respicit septenarium indefinitum & numerum cardinalem, sive unam e septem septimanae diebus: Caerimoniale respicit septenarium definitum, & numerum ordinarium, i. e. praecise septimum septimanae diem. Morale adhuc durat, caerimoniale est abrogatum.


### Q. XLII

Can the regenerate perfectly fulfill the law?

No regenerate person in this life perfectly fulfills the law of God ; however, there is imputed to the regenerate for righteousness the perfect obedience which Christ the mediator, in place of the human race, rendered to the divine law . And there are conferred upon them by the Holy Spirit through the grace of regeneration supernatural powers, so that by a deliberate purpose of the will they do not violate the law of God, as long as they remain in the state of regeneration .

Obj. I. Dr. Chemnitius warns gravely, in the place on the law, ch. VIII, fol. 99. In individual precepts this doctrine must be diligently inculcated, both how the law is impossible, and how we can have the fulfillment of it. For on both sides one errs dangerously, and often not from ignorance, but from petulance.

The Pharisees, because it is written in Ezek. 36:27: "I will cause you to walk in my statutes," feign that they can satisfy every precept with perfect obedience. The Epicureans, when they hear that no one in this life can satisfy the law of God with perfect obedience, excuse all lapses against conscience under this veil, and feign, believing that they can and ought to keep nothing in the commandments of God. But this is just as false of men as the delirium of the Pharisees.

Obj. II. There is no question here about the unregenerate, who can perform external discipline in some way, which Scripture calls the righteousness of the flesh, Heb. 9:10, but the interior obedience of the heart cannot be performed or fulfilled by them without faith and the Holy Spirit, nor can their external discipline please God. The question here is about the regenerate.

Obj. III. One must distinguish accurately between absolute perfection, or of consummation, and comparative, or of sincerity. The regenerate in this life never attain absolute perfection; yet they are called perfect comparatively, in respect to others, who are either hypocrites or commit proaeretic sins without any shame . But the regenerate serve the law of God sincerely, and do not sin from proaeresis, but strive for perfection with the utmost zeal.

Prob. a. 1) From Acts 15:10, where Peter says in the Apostolic college: "Now therefore why do you tempt God, to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers (Abraham, Moses, etc., who could be seen as most perfect), nor we have been able to bear." Obj.

1) That the controversy was stirred up against the Apostles by false teachers not only about circumcision, but about the whole law, of which that was as it were the first door and token, is clear from the distinction in v. 5, the mention of fornication in v. 20, and the inference in Gal. 5:13.

2) This moral law is a yoke not only δυσβάστακτον, difficult to bear (just as Christ says that the legal ceremonies are φορτία βαρέα καὶ δυσβάστακτα, heavy and difficult-to-bear burdens, and difficult to bear but utterly impossible, because it cannot be perfectly fulfilled by any mortal.

2) From Rom. VIII, 3. For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God, by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh, in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us. The Apostle teaches that the law cannot justify and save, not by itself (for it is a perfect standard of righteousness, and promises salvation to those who observe it), but because man, corrupted by sin, cannot perfectly fulfill it.

3) From Rom. VII, 14. For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal. The reborn are carnal not entirely, but in part, not because of the dominion of the flesh, but its sensation. They are carnal compared to the law, which demands obedience not only external, but also internal. Therefore, since the reborn are carnal in part, they cannot exactly fulfill the whole spiritual law.

4) The moral law obliges the reborn to perfect obedience in terms of degrees, parts, and perseverance, which no mortal can achieve after the fall. See above, question XXI. Prob. b. From Rom. X, 14. Christ is the end (fulfillment) of the law for everyone who believes. Those who repent and apprehend Christ the mediator with true faith, to them is imputed the perfect obedience of the law, which Christ performed, as if they themselves had satisfied the law. And in this way they have full, perfect, and complete obedience to the law, by imputation through faith, as CHEMNITIUS teaches in l.c.

Prob. c. The obedience of Christ is not given to the reborn so that they may live freely according to the flesh, Rom. VIII, 12. but the spirit of renewal is also given, which causes them to walk in the statutes of God, Jer. XXXI, 33. and writes the law in their heart, Ezek. XXXVI, 27.: strengthened by its powers, they mortify the deeds of the flesh, Rom. VIII, 13. nor do they sin voluntarily, as long as the seed of regeneration is vigorous in them, 1 Jn. III, 9.

The antithesis is that of the Pontificians, Socinians, Arminians, and Anabaptists, who maintain that the reborn can perfectly fulfill the law of God.

They rely on the following arguments: I. Christ says: My yoke is easy and my burden is light. Matt. XI, 30. Therefore, it can be easily fulfilled. Response: Christ speaks of the evangelical doctrine, which, although it has the attached weight of the cross and temptations, quite heavy for the carnal man, is nevertheless sweet to the reborn, both because of the sweetest consolation blossoming from the evangelical promises and the remission of sins, and because of the grace and presence of the Holy Spirit, and the certain hope of gratuitous remission.

II. God's commandments are not burdensome, 1 Jn. V, 3. Therefore, they can be easily fulfilled. Response: They are not burdensome to the believer in Christ, who, by the Spirit of God, delights in the law of God by a spontaneous act according to the inner man; although he sees another law in his members, which wars against the law of his mind, Rom.

VII, 22. 23. III. Christ died so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, Rom. VIII, 4. Response: The Apostle notably says "in us," not "by us": namely, the righteousness of the law is fulfilled in us when the obedience of Christ is imputed to us.

IV. He who loves Christ keeps his word. But the reborn, etc. Therefore, the major premise is clear from Jn. XIV, 23. Response: Just as the reborn in this life do not love Christ perfectly, but according to the measure of their strength: so they keep his word imperfectly: they will love and keep it perfectly in the homeland.

V. The Lord your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you will love the Lord your God with all your heart. Deut. XXX, 6. Response: "Whole heart" is opposed either to a double and divided heart, or to a defective and mutilated heart: In the former sense, it denotes a sincere heart; in the latter sense, it designates a perfectly renewed heart. The reborn love God with a sincere heart, and acknowledge and grieve over their imperfection in loving.

VI. I can do all things through him who strengthens me, Christ, Phil. IV, 13. Therefore, I can perfectly fulfill the law.

Response: 1) These words are to be understood reduplicatively: All things that I can

Latin:

XLII. Possuntne renati legem perfecte implere?

Nullus renatus in hac vita legem Dei perfecte implet a); imputatur autem renatis ad iustitiam perfecta obedientia, quam Christus mediator, vice generis humani, legi divinae praestitit b). Et conferuntur illis a Spiritu S. per gratiam renovationis vires supernaturales, ut deliberato voluntatis proposito legem Dei non violent, quamdiu in statu regenerationis permanent c).

Obs. I. Grauiter monet D. Chemnitius, loco de lege c. VIII. fol. 99. In singulis praeceptis haec doctrina diligenter inculcanda est, & quomodo lex sit impossibilis, & quomodo impletionem eius habere possimus. Utrinque enim periculose, & saepe non ex ignorantia, sed ex petulantia erratur.

Pharisaei, quia scriptum est Ezech. XXXVI, 27.: Faciam, ut in praeceptis meis ambuletis, fingunt, se posse singulis praeceptis perfecta obedientia satisfacere. Epicuraei, quando audiunt, neminem in hac vita posse legi Dei satisfacere perfecta obedientia, hoc velamine excusant omnes lapsus contra conscientiam, & fingunt, credentes nihil nec posse nec debere in mandatis Dei servare. Sed hoc hominum aeque falsum est, ac Pharisaeorum delirium.

Obs. II. Non est quaestio de irregenitis, qui externam disciplinam utcunque praestare possunt, quam scriptura vocat iustitiam carnis, Hebr. IX, 10. (*), sed interior obedientia cordis sine fide & Spiritu S. non potest ab iisdem praestari, aut impleri, nec externa illorum disciplina Deo placere. Quaeritur hic de renatis.

Obs. III. Accurate distinguendum est inter perfectionem absolutam, sive consummationis, & comparatam, sive sinceritatis. Renati in hac vita nunquam assequuntur perfectionem absolutam; comparate tamen dicuntur perfecti, respectu aliorum, qui vel hypocritae sunt, vel sine ullo pudore peccata proaeretica committunt (**). At renati fincere legem Dei servant, nec ex proaeretic peccant, sed summo studio ad perfectionem contendunt.

Prob. a. 1) Ex Act. XV, 10. ubi Petrus in collegio Apostolico inquit: Nunc ergo quid tentatis Deum, ad ponendum iugum super cervicem discipulorum, quod neque patres nostri (Abraham, Moses &c. qui poterant videri perfectissimi), neque nos valuimus portare.

Obs. 1) Non de circumcisione tantum, sed de universa lege, cuius illa quasi prima ianua & tessera erat, controversia Apostolis a pseudo-doctoribus mouebatur, nec tantum de caerimoniali, sed & morali lege agi ex distinctione v. 5., fornicationis nominatione v. 20., & illatione Gal. V, 13. liquet.

2) Lex haec moralis iugum est non tantum δυσβάστακτον, portatu difficile (sicut Christus dicit, quod legales caerimoniae sint φορτία βαρέα καὶ δυσβάστακτα, onera gravia & portatu difficilia sed prorsus ἀδύνατον, quia a nullo mortalium perfecte impleri potest.

2) Ex Rom. VIII, 3. Quod impoffibile erat legi, dum per carnem infirmatum est, Deus, qui sui ipfius filium mifit in fimilitudinem carnis peccati (præstitit) & pro peccato condemnavit peccatum in carne, ut iustificatio legis impleretur in nobis. Docet Apostolus, legem iustificare & faluare non posse, non per fe (est enim perfecta iustitiæ norma, fuique obfervatoribus salutem promittit), sed quia homo peccato corruptus eam perfecte implere nequit.

3) Ex Rom. VII, 14. Scimus, quod lex spiritualis fit: ego vero carnalis fum. Renati sunt carnales non ex toto, sed ex parte, non ob carnis dominium, sed sensum. Carnales sunt comparate ad legem, quæ exigit obedientiam non tantum exteriorem, sed etiam interiorem. Cum ergo renati ex parte carnales sint, legem totam spiritualem exacte implere nequeunt.

4) Lex moralis obligat renatos ad obedientiam perfectam ratione graduum, partium, perfeuerantiæ, quam nemo mortalium post lapsum præstare potest. Vide supra quæst. XXI. Prob. b. Ex Rom. X, 14. Christus est finis (impleto) legis omni credenti. Qui agunt pænitentiam, & vera fide apprehendunt Christum mediatorem, illis imputatur perfecta obedientia legis, quam Christus præstitit, ac fi ipsi fati fecissent legi. Et hoc modo habent plenam, perfectam & integram obedientiam legis, imputatione per fidem, docente CHEMNITIO l.c.

Prob. c. Non donatur renatis obedientia Christi, vt libere fecundum carnem viuant, Rom. VIII, 12. sed datur etiam spiritus renovationis, qui facit, vt in præceptis Dei ambulant, Ier. XXXI, 33. & scribit legem in cor eorum, Ezech. XXXVI, 27.: cuius viribus instructi mortificant actiones carnis, Rom. VIII, 13. nec peccant voluntarie, quamdiu femen regenerationis in illis est vegetum, 1 Io. III, 9.

Antithefis est Pontificiorum, Socinianorum, Arminianorum, & Anabaptistarum, statuentium, renatos posse legem Dei perfecte implere.

Qui fequentibus nituntur argumentis: I. Christus dicit: Iugum meum est fuaue & onus meum est leue. Matth. XI, 30. E. facile impleri potest. Resp. Loquitur Christus de doctrina euangelica, quæ, licet adiunctum habeat crucis & tentationum pondus, fatis graue carnali homini, tamen renatis est fuaue, tum ob dulcissimam confolationem ex promissis euangelicis & remissione peccatorum efflorescentem, tum ob Spiritus S. gratiam & præfentiam, & spem certam gratuitæ remissionis.

II. Mandata Dei sunt grauis, 1 Io. V, 3. E. facile impleri poffunt. Resp. Non sunt grauis credenti in Christum, quippe qui Spiritu Dei spontaneo actu delectatur lege Dei fecundum internum hominem; quamuis videat aliam legem in membris suis, quæ repugnat legi mentis suæ, Rom.

VII, 22. 23. III. Christus mortuus est, ut iustificatio legis in nobis impleretur, Rom. VIII, 4. Resp. Notanter dicit Apostolus in nobis, non a nobis: nimirum τὸ δικαίωμα τῶ νόμω in nobis impletur, cum obedientia Christi nobis imputatur.

IV. Qui Christum diligit, fermonem eius feruat. Atqui renati &c. E. Maior patet ex Io. XIV, 23. Resp. Sicut renati in hac vita Christum non perfecte, sed pro modulo fuarum virium diligunt: ita fermonem eius imperfecte feruant: diligent & seruabunt perfecte in patria.

V. Circumcidet Deus cor tuum, & cor femini tui, ut diligas Deum, Dominum tuum, ex toto corde tuo. Deut. XXX, 6. Resp. Cor totum opponitur vel cordi duplici & diuerfo, vel cordi manco & mutilo: Priori sensu notat cor fincerum, posteriori sensu defignat cor perfecte renouatum. Renati Deum diligunt corde fincero, & imperfectionem suam in diligendo agnoscunt & dolent.

VI. Omnia possum per eum, qui me perficit, Christum Phil. IV, 13. E. perfecte implere legem possum.

Resp. 1) Reduplicatiue hæc verba intelligenda sunt: Omnia, quæ


### Q. XLII: Part III, Sec

PART III, SEC. I can through the grace of Christ, who strengthens me, not by my own powers: 2) Restrictively, according to the underlying subject matter: I know how to be humble, I know also how to excel. VII. The commandment, which I command you, is not above you, i.e., above your powers, Deut. XXX, 11. Resp. Paul explains this word not concerning the word of the law, but concerning the word of the gospel, Rom. X, 6. VIII. God commands nothing impossible, or He is unjust. Resp. God commands nothing simply and at all times impossible. For 1) the fulfillment of the instituted law of nature was possible: Therefore, God is not unjust if He demands it from us, who are weak by our own fault. A creditor uses his right, demanding a debt even from him who, by his own fault, is not able to pay. 2) The fulfillment of the law is not in itself impossible, but κατ' ἄλλο, because of something else, insofar as it is weakened by the flesh, Rom. VIII, 3. 3) God, out of grace, imputes the obedience of Christ to believers for righteousness; and accepts their begun and sincere obedience, although it may be imperfect, with the imperfection pardoned.

CONCERNING THE CEREMONIAL LAW.

Question XLIII. What is the ceremonial law? The ceremonial law is a command of God, by which this supreme Lord and legislator obligated the people of the Old Testament, and through Moses prescribed to them a certain form of external worship, so that He might remind men of their sins, show the contrite a redeemer from afar, and apply and seal federal grace through two sacraments and various sacrifices.

Question XLV. In what did the external worship prescribed by the ceremonial law consist? The external worship, prescribed to the people of God in the Old Testament, consisted in certain rites to be observed concerning sacred persons a), things b), places c), and times d).

Proof a. Sacred persons in the O.T. destined for ecclesiastical functions were divided into three orders, namely, the high priest, the priests, and the Levites strictly so-called: Concerning whom see Exod. XXVIII, 29. Lev. IV, 8. Lev. VIII. To these add the Nazarites, Num. VI. Proof b. The ceremonial laws deal 1) with abstinence from certain foods and the eating of certain animals, Lev. XI, 2. c. XVII, 11. 2) with the use of certain garments, Deut. XXII, 11. 3) with the structure of houses, Lev. XIV, 34. 4) With sowing, trees, and brute animals, Deut. XXII, 9. Lev. XIX, 9. Deut. XXII, 6. 5) With sacred vessels and utensils, or instruments of external divine worship. 6) With the two sacraments of the O.T., circumcision and the paschal lamb, concerning which below: 7) With sacrifices. A sacrifice is an external sacred action, by which some visible thing is offered to God by a priest, by a rite prescribed in the law, to remind men of the gravity of sin, and of the future sacrifice of the Messiah to be offered on the altar of the cross for sins (*). A sacrifice, by reason of its matter, was one thing, מנחה δῶρον, which was a food sacrifice: another, זבח, θυσία, a bloody sacrifice from animals slaughtered in honor of God: by reason of its form, one was expiatory, another pacific, and that either eucharistic or votive: by reason of time, one was daily, another sabbath-related, another anniversary. Concerning these see GERH. in the place concerning the ceremonial law, ch. I, p. 163.

Prob. c. The sacred places, concerning which the ceremonial law was occupied, were two; the tabernacle, or portable Mosaic temple, concerning which see Exod. XXV, 9. & XL. and the Solomonic temple, fixed in one place, concerning which see 1 Reg VI, 36.

Prob. d. Sacred time comprises the legal festivities. Now the feasts of the Hebrews were various: 1) the weekly, which is the sabbath, to be celebrated on the last day of the week, Gen. II, 3. 2) the monthly, which was νουμηνία, or the new moon, Num. X, 10. 3) The anniversary feasts were the feast of the passover, or of unleavened bread; Exod. XII, 34. the feast of pentecost, or of weeks, Lev. XXIII, 15. the feast of tabernacles, Lev. XXIII, 34. the feast of the blowing of trumpets, Num. XXIX, 1. the feast of atonement, Lev. XVI, & XXIII, the sabbatical year, Exod. XXIII, 10. the jubilee year, Lev. XXV, 8. 9. [*].

Latin:

PARS III, SECT. possum per gratiam Christi, qui me corroborat, non ex meis viribus: 2) Restricte, secundum substratam materiam: Noui esse humilis, noui & excellere. VII. Mandatum, quod præcipio tibi, non est supra te, i. e. supra vires tuas, Deut. XXX, 11. Resp. Paullus verbum hoc non de verbo legis, sed de verbo euangelii exponit, Rom. X, 6. VIII. Nihil impossibile Deus præcipit, aut est iniquus. Resp. Deus nihil simpliciter & omni tempore impossibile præcipit. Etenim 1) impletio legis naturæ institutæ fuit possibilis: E. Deus non iniustus est, si eam a nobis, nostra culpa infirmis, exigat. Vtitur iure suo creditor, repetens debitum etiam ab eo, qui propria culpa non est soluendo. 2) Impletio legis non est in se impossibilis, sed κατ' ἄλλο, propter aliud, quatenus per carnem infirmatur, Rom. VIII, 3. 3) Deus ex gratia credentibus obedientiam Christi ad iustitiam imputat; eorumque inchoatam & sinceram obedientiam, licet imperfecta sit, acceptat, condonata imperfectione.

DE LEGE CÆRIMONIALI.

Quæst. XLIII. Quid est lex cærimonialis? Lex cærimonialis est iussum Dei, quo summus hic dominus & legislator populum veteris testamenti obligauit, & per Mosen certam formam externi cultus ei præscripsit, vt homines peccatorum commonefaceret, contritis redemtorem eminus ostenderet, & gratiam fœderalem per duo sacramenta & varia sacrificia applicaret & obsignaret.

Quæst. XLV. In quo consistebat cultus externus lege cærimoniali præscriptus? Cultus externus, populo Dei in veteri testamento præscriptus, consistebat in certis ritibus obseruandis circa personas a), res b), loca c), & tempora sacra d).

Prob. a. Personæ sacræ in V. T. ecclesiasticis functionibus destinatæ, in tres dispescebantur ordines, scil. summi pontificis, sacerdotum, & leuitarum stricte dictorum: De quibus vide Exod. XXVIII, 29. Leu. IV, 8. Leu. IIX. his adde Nazaræos, Num. VI. Prob. b. Agunt leges cærimoniales 1) de abstinentia a certis cibis & quorundam animalium esu, Leu. XI, 2. c. XVII, 11. 2) de vsu certarum vestium, Deut. XXII, 11. 3) de ædium structura, Leu. XIV, 34. 4) De satione, arboribus, animalibus brutis, Deut. XXII, 9. Leu. XIX, 9. Deut. XXII, 6. 5) De vasis & vtensilibus sacris, siue instrumentis externi cultus diuini. 6) De duobus sacramentis V. T. circumcisione & agno paschali, de quibus infra: 7) De sacrificiis. Sacrificium est externa sacra actio, qua res aliqua visibilis Deo per sacerdotem, ritu in lege præscripto, offertur, ad commonefaciendum homines de peccati grauitate, & futuro sacrificio Messiæ in ara crucis pro peccatis offerendo (*). Sacrificium, ratione materiæ, aliud erat מנחה δῶρον, quod erat sacrificium cibarium: aliud זבח, θυσία, sacrificium sanguineum ex animalibus in honorem Dei mactatis: ratione formæ, aliud expiatiuum, aliud pacificum, idque vel eucharisticum, vel votiuum: ratione temporis, aliud quotidianum, aliud sabbatharium, aliud anniuersarium. De his vid. GERH. loco de lege cerem. c. I. p. 163.

Prob. c. Loca sacra, circa quæ occupabatur lex cærimonialis, duo erant; tabernaculum, seu templum Mosaicum portatile, de quo vide Exod. XXV, 9. & XL. & templum Salomonæum, in vno loco fixum, de quo vide 1 Reg VI, 36.

Prob. d. Tempus Sacrum complectitur festiuitates legales. Erant autem festa Hebræorum varia: 1) hebdomadarium, quod est sabbathum, vltimo septimanæ die celebrandum, Gen. II, 3. 2) menstruum, quod erat νουμηνία, siue nouilunium, Num. X, 10. 3) Festa anniuersaria erant festum pascha, siue azymorum; Exod. XII, 34. festum pentecostes, siue hebdomadum, Leu. XXIII, 15. festum tabernaculorum, Leu. XXIII, 34. festum clangoris tubarum, Num. XXIX, 1. festum expiationis, Leu. XVI, & XXIII, annus sabbathicus, Exod. XXIII, 10. annus iubilæus, Leu. XXV, 8. 9. [*].


### Q. XLV

What is the end of the ceremonial law? The principal end of the ceremonial law is both the signification and adumbration of the benefits of Christ, and the application of the same through sacraments and sacrifices a). The less principal end is the reminder of sin b), εὐταξία in ecclesiastical assemblies and actions c), and the segregation of the Jewish church from all the gatherings of the nations d).

Prob. a. The constitutions and observations concerning food, drink, and the distinctions of feasts are called shadows of things to come, but the body is Christ, Col. II, 16. therefore, because they prefigured Christ. Nor were the benefits of Christ only adumbrated in those Levitical ceremonies, but they were also applied and sealed to believers through the use of sacraments and sacrifices. Whence circumcision is called a seal of the righteousness of faith, Rom. IV, 11. And the blood of sacrifices is said to atone for souls, Lev. XVII, 11. not in itself, but by reason of the merit of Christ, availing forward and back, whose fruit it offered.

Prob. b. Through the ceremonial laws a remembrance of sins is made every year, Heb. X, 3.

Prob. c. God had ordained ecclesiastical rites, so that all things in the church might be done in order and decently, 1 Cor XIV, 40.

Prob. d. By sacrifices and other Levitical ceremonies, the Israelites were distinguished from other nations. That which Moses hints at, Deut. IV, 8. What great nation is there, that hath God so nigh unto them; as all this law, which I set before you this day?

Latin:

Quis est finis legis cærimonialis? Finis legis cærimonialis principalis est tum beneficiorum Christi significatio & adumbratio, tum eorundem per sacramenta & sacrificia applicatio a). Finis minus principalis est commonefactio de peccato b), εὐταξία in conuentibus & actionibus ecclesiasticis c), ecclesiæ iudaicæ ab omnibus gentium cœtibus segregatio d).

Prob. a. Constitutiones & obseruationes circa cibum, potum, festorum discrimina, dicuntur vmbræ futurorum, corpus autem Christus, Col. II, 16. ideo, quod Christum præfigurabant. Neque solum adumbrabantur in Leuiticis illis cærimoniis beneficia Christi, sed & credentibus per sacramentorum & sacrificiorum vsum applicabantur & obsignabantur. Vn-de circumcisio appellatur sigillum iustitiæ fidei, Rom. IV, 11. Et sanguis sacrificiorum animas expiare dicitur, Leu. XVII, 11. non in se, sed ratione meriti Christi, ante & retro valentis, cuius fructum offerebat.

Prob. b. Per leges cærimoniales singulis annis fit recordatio peccatorum, Hebr. X, 3.

Prob. c. Ritus ecclesiasticos Deus ordinauerat, vt omnia in ecclesia fierent ordine & decenter, 1 Cor XIV, 40.

Prob. d. Sacrificiis, aliisque cærimoniis Leuiticis Israëlitæ ab aliis gentibus discernebantur. Id quod innuit Moses, Deut. IV, 8. Quæ est gens magna, cui Deus propinquus apud ipsam; sicut omnis lex hæc, quam ego daturus sum coram vobis hodie?


### Q. XLVI

Is the ceremonial law abrogated? The ceremonial laws were abrogated by the advent, passion, and death of Christ, as to the necessity of observing them and the utility of their observation; but with the Jerusalem temple destroyed, they were utterly abolished.

Prob. 1) The Levitical ceremonies were shadows, prefiguring the benefits of Christ, which vanished upon the arrival of the body, Christ, Col. II, 14.

2) Sacrifice and oblation had to cease, upon the arrival of the Messiah, Dan. IX, 27. and the justifications of the flesh (Levitical ceremonies, which were for the most part occupied with the flesh) were imposed until the time of reformation, Heb. IX, 10.

3) The ceremonial law was abrogated by the public decree of the Holy Spirit in the council of the Apostles, Acts XV, 6, and with the destruction of the Jerusalem temple, the Levitical priesthood was abolished.

The antithesis is that of the Jews, who deny that the ceremonial laws have been abrogated. Their arguments are:

I. The ceremonial laws were promulgated by the eternal Deity no differently than the moral law: therefore, they are to be observed perpetually, just as the moral law. Resp. There is a great difference between the moral law and the ceremonial law. For 1) God gave the moral law immediately, Exod. XX, 1, and He wrote it with His own fingers, Exod. XXXIV, 1, and commanded that it be kept in the ark of the covenant, Hebr. IX, 4. But He did not promulgate the ceremonial law immediately, but through the intervention of Moses' work, Deut. V, 31, nor did He write it Himself, but Moses did, Exod. XXIV, 4, nor were the ceremonial laws placed in the ark of the covenant, but committed to the custody of the priests, Deut. XVII, 19. 2) The moral law is universal; because it is materially the same as the natural law inscribed in the minds of all men: the ceremonial law, however, is particular, which expired when the Jerusalem temple collapsed.

II. If the ceremonial law was abrogated in the N. T., the will of God would be mutable (because it proceeded from the will of God): But the consequent is false: therefore, the antecedent is as well. Resp. Through the abrogation of the ceremonial law, the will of God is not changed; because God willed that it should only last until the times of διορθώσεως, or correction, Hebr. IX, 10.

III. The ceremonial law still flourishes in the N. T.: for Paul circumcised Timothy, Acts XVI, 3, and the Apostles commanded abstinence from blood and from things strangled, Acts XV, 29, which pertain to the ceremonial law. Resp. 1) Paul willed that Timothy be circumcised, not out of necessity, but out of charity toward the weak Jews, who were not yet sufficiently instructed regarding the purpose of circumcision, which was given for a time. 2) The Apostles commanded abstinence from blood and from things strangled, not by the force of a law that is in effect and binding; but to avert every scandal. For the Jews did not want to approach the Christian church: because they saw Christians eating things strangled and blood, from which the Jews recoiled. Therefore, so that the Apostles might remove this obstacle, they commanded Christians to abstain from blood and things strangled: which command, however, was not perpetual, but temporary; until, namely, the Jews and the Gentiles should coalesce into one body.

Quæst. XLVII. Did the sacrifices of the O. T. have the power of expiating sins, both voluntary and involuntary?

The sacrifices of the O. T. had the power of expiating sins, both voluntary and involuntary a), not of themselves, but typically and organically b).

Objection. The use of the sacrifices of the O.T. was twofold, legal and evangelical. The legal use was ἀνάμνησις ἁμαρτιῶν, a remembrance of sins, Heb. X, 3, so that, namely, sinful men might be admonished of the gravity and guilt of sin, and thus they were means of exciting contrition. The evangelical use was that they might show from afar the one expiatory sacrifice of Christ, and reconcile the sinful man to God, on account of that future sacrifice of Christ prefigured and apprehended by faith.

Proof a. From Lev. XVII, 11: The soul of the flesh is in the blood: therefore I have given it to you upon the altar, to expiate your souls; for the reason that the blood itself expiates for the soul. To which the Apostle looks, saying Heb. IX, 22: Almost all things are purged by blood according to the law, and without the shedding of blood there is no remission.

2) Expiated by the sacrifices were חַטָּאת & אָשָׁם, i.e., from the LXX version, ἀδικία, ἀσέβεια, iniquity and impiety, Lev. XVI, 22; c. VII, 2: Therefore also voluntary sins.

3) The blood of the antitype, Christ, cleanses us from all sin and iniquity, 1 John I, 7. Therefore the typical blood of the sacrifices also cleansed from all sin.

Proof b. The Levitical sacrifices had the power of expiating sins not from themselves, or by their own virtue. Therefore Paul says, Heb. X, 4: It is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins: They expiated, therefore, by the power of the antitype, or the sacrifice of Christ, which they shadowed forth; for the law had shadows of good things to come, Heb. X, 1. Yet the sacrifices of the O.T. did not exist as mere signs σημαντικὰ (significant), but they were also organs divinely ordained, which proposed to sinners the Messiah, God to be incarnate, in his assumed humanity in his own time to offer himself as a sacrifice to the Father for the sins of the whole world, and offered, applied, and sealed to them the fruits of his bloody obedience.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, who deny that the sacrifices truly expiated sins, and that they did not even typically expiate voluntary sins. Their arguments are:

I. No creature can be offered to God as a price of ransom for sin: But all cattle, etc. Therefore. The major is evident: because creatures are God's. But whatever is already God's cannot be offered to Him as a price for sins. Resp. I limit the major: unless God has so ordained. One must look here to the will and ordination of the Creator, not, however, to the judgment of human reason.

II. Whatever typically expiates, does not expiate truly (for the type is opposed to the true). But the sacrifices of the O.T., etc. Therefore. Resp. The true is opposed a) to the feigned, b) to shadows, 1 John I, 17. If it is taken in the former sense; they certainly expiated truly and really, according to the true and real divine estimation: If it is taken in the latter sense; the truth of proper expiation is in Christ, the typical adumbration in the legal sacrifices.

III. Legal sacrifices are rejected by God as useless, Ps. L, 8. Therefore they did not truly expiate. Resp. The sacrifices of the impenitent man are rejected; those which are offered from a penitent and faithful heart are benevolently accepted.

IV. It is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins, Heb. X, 4. Resp. Of themselves, or by their own virtue and dignity.

V. The anniversary offering was made ὑπὲρ τῶν τῦ λαῦ ἀγνοημάτων, for the ignorances of the people, Heb. IX, 7. Therefore not for sins committed against conscience. Resp. 1) The position of one is not the exclusion of another.

Latin:

Estne lex cærimonialis abrogata? Leges cærimoniales per Christi aduentum, passionem & mortem abrogatæ sunt, quantum ad necessitatem obseruandi ad obseruationis vtilitatem; euerso autem templo Hierosolymitano penitus abolitæ sunt.

Prob. 1) Cærimoniæ Leuiticæ erant vmbræ, beneficia Christi præfigurantes, quæ superueniente corpore, Christo, euanuerunt, Col. II, 14.

2) Sacrificium & oblatio cessare debuit, adueniente Messia, Dan. IX, 27. & iustificationes carnis (cærimoniæ Leuiticæ, quæ circa carnem maxima ex parte occupabantur) vsque ad tempus correctionis impositæ fuerunt, Hebr. IX, 19.

3) Lex caerimonialis publico Spiritus S. decreto in concilio Apostolorum est abrogata Act. XV, 6. & everso templo Hierosolymitano sacerdotium Leviticum deletum est.

Antithesis est Iudaeorum, negantium, leges caerimoniales esse abrogatas. Quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Leges caerimoniales haud secus, ac lex moralis, ab aeterno Numine sunt promulgatae: E. perinde, ac lex moralis, perpetuo sunt observandae. Resp. Magna est differentia inter legem moralem, & caerimonialem. Nam 1) Deus immediate dedit legem moralem, Exod. XX, 1. idemque suis digitis eam scripsit, Exod. XXXIV, 1. & vt in arca foederis asservaretur, mandauit, Hebr. IX, 4. Sed legem caerimonialem non immediate, verum interveniente Mosis opera, promulgauit, Deut. V, 31. nec eandem scripsit ipse, sed Moses, Exod. XXIV, 4. nec in arca foederis repositae sunt leges caerimoniales, sed sacerdotum custodiae commissae, Deut. XVII, 19. 2) Lex moralis est vniuersalis; quia materialiter eadem est cum lege naturali omnium hominum mentibus inscripta: lex autem caerimonialis est particularis, quae collapso templo Hierosolymitano expirauit.

II. Si lex caerimonialis in N. T. est abrogata, voluntas Dei erit mutabilis (quia a voluntate Dei profecta est): At consequens est falsum: E. & antecedens. Resp. Per abrogationem legis caerimonialis voluntas Dei non est mutata; quia Deus voluit, vt tantum duraret vsque ad tempora διορθώσεως, siue correctionis, Hebr. IX, 10.

III. Lex caerimonialis viget adhuc in N. T.: nam Paullus Timotheum circumcidit, Act. XVI, 3. & Apostoli praeceperunt abstinentiam a sanguine & suffocato, Act. XV, 29. quae pertinent ad legem caerimonialem. Resp. 1) Paullus voluit Timotheum circumcidi, non ex necessitate, sed ex caritate erga Iudaeos infirmos, nondum satis de fine circumcisionis, ad tempus datae, institutos. 2) Apostoli praeceperunt abstinentiam a sanguine & suffocato, non vi legis vigentis & obligantis; sed ad auertendum omne scandalum. Nolebant enim Iudaei accedere ad ecclesiam christianam: quia videbant, Christianos edere suffocatum & sanguinem, a quo abhorrebant Iudaei. Vt igitur Apostoli hunc amouerent obicem, praeceperunt Christianis abstinentiam a sanguine & suffocato: Quae tamen praeceptio non fuit perpetua, sed temporaria; quousque scil. Iudaei & gentes in vnum corpus coalescerent

Quæst. XLVII. An sacrificia V. T. habuerunt vim expiandi peccata tam voluntaria, quam inuoluntaria?

Sacrificia V. T. habuerunt vim expiandi peccata tam voluntaria, quam inuoluntaria a), non ex se, sed typice & organice b).

Obf. Vsus sacrificiorum V. T. duplex erat, legalis & euangelicus. Vsus legalis erat ἀνάμνησις ἁμαρτιῶν, recordatio peccatorum, Hebr. X, 3. vt scil, homines peccatores de peccati gravitate & reatu admonerentur, & sic erant media excitandæ contritionis. Vsus euangelicus erat, vt vnicum expiatorium Christi sacrificium eminus ostenderent, & hominem peccatorem Deo, propter illud futurum sacrificium Christi præfiguratum, & fide apprehensum, reconciliarent.

Prob. a. Ex Leuit. XVII, 11. Anima carnis in sanguine est: ideo dedi eum vobis super altare, ad expiandum animas vestras; eo, quod sanguis ipse pro anima expiet. Quo respicit Apostolus, inquiens Hebr. IX, 22. Prope per sanguinem omnia mundantur iuxta legem, & sine sanguinis effusione non fit remissio.

2) Expiata sunt sacrificiis חַטָּאת & אָשָׁם, i. e. ex versione LXX. ἀδικία, ἀσέβεια, iniquitas & impietas, Leu. XVI, 22. c. VII, 2: E. etiam peccata voluntaria.

3) Sanguis antitypi, Christi, mundat nos ab omni peccato & iniquitate, 1 Io. I, 7. E. etiam ab omni peccato mundauit sanguis typicus sacrificiorum.

Prob. b. Sacrificia Leuitica habuerunt vim expiandi peccata non ex se, aut virtute propria. Ideo Paullus dicit, Hebr. X, 4. Impossibile est, sanguinem taurorum & hircorum auferre peccata: Expiarunt ergo vi antitypi, siue sacrificii Christi, quod adumbrarunt; habuit enim lex vmbras futurorum bonorum, Hebr. X, 1. Neque tamen habebant se sacrificia V. T. vt nuda signa σημαντικὰ, sed etiam erant organa diuinitus ordinata, quæ Messiam, Deum incarnandum, in assumta humanitate suo tempore pro peccatis totius mundi in sacrificium Patri se oblaturum, peccatoribus proponerent, ipsiusque obedientiæ cruentæ fructus iis offerrent, applicarent & obsignarent.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, negantium, sacrificia vere expiasse peccata, eademque ne typice quidem expiasse peccata voluntaria. Quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Nulla creatura potest Deo offerri, tanquam pretium solutionis pro peccato: Atqui omnes pecudes &c. Ergo. Maior patet: quia creaturæ sunt Dei. Quidquid autem antea est Dei, non potest ipsi offerri, tanquam pretium pro peccatis. Resp. Limito maiorem: nisi Deus ita ordinauerit. Respicienda hic est voluntas & ordinatio creatoris, non autem rationis humanæ iudicium.

II. Quidquid typice expiat, non expiat vere (nam typus vero opponitur). Atqui sacrificia V. T. &c. Ergo. Resp. Verum opponitur a) ficto, b) vmbris, 1 Io. I, 17. Si priori sensu sumatur; vtique expiarunt vere & realiter, secundum veram & realem æstimationem diuinam: Sin posteriori accipiatur sensu; veritas propriæ expiationis est in Christo, typica adumbratio in legalibus sacrificiis.

III. Sacrificia legalia a Deo reiiciuntur, vt inutilia, Ps. L, 8. E. non vere expiarunt. Resp. Reiiciuntur sacrificia hominis impænitentis; beneuole acceptantur, quæ offeruntur a corde pænitenti & fideli.

IV. Impossibile est, sanguinem taurorum & hircorum auferre peccata, Hebr. ...X, 4. Resp. Ex se, aut propria virtute & dignitate.

V. Oblatio anniuersaria facta est ὑπὲρ τῶν τῦ λαῦ ἀγνοημάτων, pro populi ignorantiis, Hebr. IX, 7. E. non pro peccatis contra conscientiam patratis. Resp. 1) Vnius positio non est alterius exclusio.


### Q. XLVIII. Do sacrifices have their origin from the light of nature, or from divine revelation?

The light of nature does not dictate that God is to be worshipped with sacrifices; but they have their origin from supernatural revelation and ordination.

Proof. The law of nature dictates in general that God is to be worshipped, but it does not reveal the determination of the worship, nor does reason find any analogy between God, who is spirit, and corporal sacrifices; indeed, reason left to itself would persuade the contrary, that the most blessed God neither needs nor is delighted by the shed blood of animals and bodies burning with a foul odor.

There is an antithesis of certain Jews and Papists, who maintain that the rite of sacrificing proceeds from the light of nature. They object:

I. The Gentiles by common consent used sacrifices for the worship of God. E. Therefore, the rite of sacrificing proceeds from the light of nature. Resp. The Gentiles did not offer sacrifices to the gods except from the κακοζηλίᾳ [misguided zeal] of the Jews; for the rest, they knew neither the matter, nor the form, nor the final cause of them. Whence they were even precipitated into human sacrifice (ἀνθρωποθυσίαν).

II. Abel sacrificed without a prescribed divine command: Therefore, from the instinct of reason and the dictate of natural law. Resp. Although a prescribed command to Abel concerning sacrificing is not read in the sacred code, yet it is not to be denied. For the Apostle testifies, Hebr. XI, 4, that by faith Abel offered a more excellent sacrifice to God than Cain. But faith is not from the instinct of nature, but from the hearing of the word of God, Rom. X, 17.

Latin:

Lumen naturae non dictat, Deum esse colendum sacrificiis; sed habent illa originem suam ex supernaturali revelatione & ordinatione.

Prob. Lex naturae dictitat in genere, Deum esse colendum, determinationem autem cultus non patefacit, neque invenit ratio ullam analogiam inter Deum, qui spiritus est, & inter sacrificia corporalia; immo ratio sibi relicta contrarium suaderet, Deum beatissimum nec indigere, nec delectari fuso animalium sanguine, & combustis corporibus grave olentibus.

Antithesis est quorundam Iudaeorum & Pontificiorum, statuentium, ritum sacrificandi proficisci ex lumine naturae. Obiiciunt:

I. Gentiles communi consensu ad cultum Dei adhibuerunt sacrificia. E. ritus sacrificandi proficiscitur ex lumine naturae. Resp. Gentiles non, nisi ex κακοζηλίᾳ Iudaeorum, sacrificia Diis obtulerunt, de cetero nec materiam, nec formam, nec caussam finalem eorum nouerunt. Vnde etiam in ἀνθρωποθυσίαν praecipitati sunt.

II. Habel sacrificauit sine praescripto mandato diuino: E. ex instinctu rationis & dictamine legis naturalis. Resp. Quamuis non legatur in sacro codice mandatum praescriptum Habeli, de sacrificando, id tamen non negandum est. Testatur quippe Apostolus, Hebr. XI, 4. fide praestantius sacrificium Habelem prae Caino obtulisse Deo. At fides non est ex instinctu naturae, sed ex auditu verbi Dei, Rom. X, 17.


### Of the Forensic, or Judicial Law


### Q. XLIX. What is the forensic, or judicial law?

The forensic, or judicial law, is a command of God, by which He bound the Israelites in the times of the Old Testament, and prescribed to them a form of political government through Moses, so that external discipline might be preserved in civil society, and the Jewish polity, in which Christ was to be born, might be distinguished from the polities of other nations.

Obs. It is called forensic and judicial; because it directed the forum, both criminal and civil, and the judgment.

Latin:

Lex forensis, siue iudicialis, est iussum Dei, quo is Israëliitas temporibus veteris testamenti obligauit, & iisdem formam gubernationis politicae per Mosen praescripsit, vt externa disciplina in societate ciuili conseruaretur, & politia iudaica, in qua Christus nasciturus erat, ab aliarum gentium politiis discerneretur.

Obs. Dicitur lex forensis & iudicialis; quia forum tum criminale, tum ciuile, iudicium dirigebat.


### Q. L. Concerning what matters does the forensic law provide precepts?

The forensic law provides precepts concerning all those things which pertain to the administration of the Israelite republic, and fall under the forum or judgment of the Jews.

Proof. Contained in the forensic law are precepts concerning kings, Deut. XVII, 14; concerning the waging of wars, Deut. XX, 1; concerning marriage, Lev. XVIII, 19; Deut. XXV, 5; concerning servants, Deut.

concerning hired servants, strangers, the poor, orphans & widows, Lev. XIX, 13. concerning homicides, Lev. XXIV, 17. concerning thefts, Exod. XXI, 16. concerning deposits, Exod. XX, 7. concerning loans, Exod. XXII, 6. concerning damages inflicted, Exod. XXI, 35. concerning weights & measures, Lev. XIX, 35. concerning not moving boundaries, Deut. XXVII, 17. concerning avoiding inordinate usury, Exod. XXII, 25.

Latin:

Lex forensis tradit praecepta de omnibus iis rebus, quae ad administrationem reipublicae Israëliticae pertinent, & sub forum, aut iudicium Iudaeorum cadunt.

Prob. Continentur in lege forensi praecepta de regibus, Deut. XVII, 14. de gerendis bellis, Deut. XX, 1. de matrimonio, Leu. XVIII, 19. Deut. XXV, 5. de feruis, Deut.

XXIII, 15. de mercenariis, peregrinis, pauperibus, pupillis & viduis, Lev. XIX, 13. de homicidiis, Lev. XXIV, 17. de furtis, Exod. XXI, 16. de depositis, Exod. XX, 7. de commodatis, Exod. XXII, 6. de damnis illatis, Exod. XXI, 35. de ponderibus & mensuris, Lev. XIX, 35. de limitibus non transferendis, Deut. XXVII, 17. de usuris inordentibus vitandis, Exod. XXII, 25.


### Quest. LI. What is the end of the judicial law?

The end of the forensic law is a) the preservation of external discipline in civil society, b) the distinction of the Jewish polity from the polities of other nations.

Proof a. Just as no nation can be contained within the limits of honesty and justice without external discipline: so the Israelite people had to be coerced by a more rigid polity, lest they take for themselves unbridled license to sin, and cast off all shame.

Proof b. It pleased the most holy God to distinguish the Israelite republic, in which the true worship of God & the genealogy of the Messiah were to be preserved, by most equitable laws from the remaining peoples, among whom grave sins were committed with impunity, by a particular forensic law, as if marked by a certain charac-

Latin:

Finis legis forensis est a) conservatio externae disciplinae in societate civili, b) discretio politiae iudaicae ab aliarum gentium politiis.

Prob. a. Sicut nulla gens sine externa disciplina intra honestatis iustitiaeque limites contineri potest: ita populus Israëliticus rigidiori politia coercendus erat, ne effrenatam peccandi licentiam sibi sumeret, omnemque pudorem exueret.

Prob. b. Placuit Deo sanctissimo, rempublicam Israëliticam, in qua verus Dei cultus & genealogia Messiae conservanda erant, aequissimis legibus a reliquis populis, in quibus gravia peccata impune fiebant, particulari iure forensi, velut certo charactere signatam, distinguere.


### Quest. LII. Is the forensic law of the Jews abrogated?

The precepts of the forensic law are twofold. Some are of common law, and are deduced as easy consequences from the moral law a). Some are of particular law, which respect the circumstances of the Israelite republic b). Not the former, but the latter are abrogated.

Proof a. Precepts concerning the office of a king, concerning servants, & rebellious children, are reduced to the fourth precept of the moral law: Concerning homicide, war, injury to a neighbor, to the fifth: Concerning marriage, rape, adultery, to the sixth: Concerning theft, deposit, loan, usury, to the seventh: Concerning witnesses, concerning slanders, to the eighth. These precepts, as to their substance, are in force among all.
