Their circumstances, peculiar to the Jews alone, have been abrogated in most Christian polities: yet it is free for the Christian magistrate to retain them.

Proof b. The precepts of the forensic law, concerning marriage with the wife of a brother who has no children, Deut. XXV, 5. concerning the water of jealousy, Num. V, 11. concerning those who are to be barred from honors & public offices, Deut. XXIII, 1. 2. 3. have been abrogated, since they were enacted by God for just reasons for the Israelites alone [*].

SIGH.

Upon the tablets of my heart, most holy God, You have inscribed Your law, the express image of Your holiness and justice, to which You added more abundant light and greater weight by Your precepts promulgated on Mount Sinai, so that it might perpetually be before my mind and eyes. But I confess that I have too often forgotten it, so that I have deviated from that perfect rule of living, and have offended Your majesty. Grant me, Your most humble servant, most clement Father, remission of my crimes, on account of the most consummate obedience of my Redeemer, performed in my place, which I apprehend, and I doubt not to make its fruit my own. Furthermore, I humbly venerate and pray that You may govern me with Your divine Spirit, so that my thoughts, counsels, undertakings, words, and deeds may never stray from Your law! Q. I. What is the Gospel?

Latin:

Praecepta legis forensis sunt duplicia. Quaedam sunt iuris communis, & prona consequentia e lege morali deducuntur a). Quaedam sunt iuris particularis, quae respiciunt circumstantias reipublicae Israëliticae b). Non priora, sed posteriora sunt abrogata.

Prob. a. Praecepta de officio regis, de servis, & liberis contumacibus, reducuntur ad legis moralis praeceptum quartum: De homicidio, bello, laesione proximi, ad quintum: De coniugio, stupro, adulterio, ad sextum: De furto, deposito, commodato, usura, ad septimum: De testibus, de calumniis, ad octavum. Quae praecepta, qua substantiam, vigent inter omnes. Circumstantiae eorum, solis Iudaeis peculiares, in plerisque Christianorum politiis abrogatae sunt: liberum tamen est magistratui christiano, eas retinere.

Prob. b. Praecepta legis forensis, de coniugio cum uxore fratris, cui non sunt liberi, Deut. XXV, 5. de potu zelotypiae, Num. V, 11. de illis, qui ab honoribus & muneribus publicis sunt arcendi, Deut. XXIII, 1. 2. 3. abrogata sunt, cum a Deo iustis de causis solis Israëlitis lata sint [*].

SVSPIRIVM.

Tabulis cordis mei, Deus sanctissime, inscriptisti legem tuam, expressam sanctitatis & iustitiae tuae effigiem, cui uberius lumen, maiusque pondus promulgatis in monte Sinai praeceptis tuis addidisti, vt illa perpetuo animo oculisque meis obuersetur. At fateor, me saepius illius cepisse obliuionem, vt ab illa perfecta viuendi regula deflexerim, & maiestatem tuam laeserim. Da mihi, seruo tuo humillimo, Pater clementissime, remissionem criminum meorum, propter consummatissimam redemptoris mei obedientiam, meo loco praestitam, quam apprehendo, & illius fructum meum facere nullus dubito. Ceterum supplex veneror & precor, vt diuino tuo spiritu me gubernes, ne a lege tua mea cogitata, consilia, coepta, dicta, facta vnquam aberrent!


## 29 On the Gospel

is a proclamation of purely gratuitous grace, offering the merit of Christ and the benefits procured to all men, and by the faith which it kindles, conferring them in act; for the glory of God and the eternal salvation of men.

Obs. The Gospel, by the force of the word, denotes good news, or a joyful and desired announcement.

Q. II. In how many ways is the name of the Gospel taken? The name of the Gospel is taken in three ways: a) Generally, and less properly, for the entire doctrine of the N.T. which was proposed by Christ and the Apostles, and is found handed down in the writings of the evangelists and apostles: b) Specially, for the doctrine of grace concerning the gratuitous remission of sins, to be obtained through faith in Christ, whether it be held in the New or in the O.T.: c) Most specially, for the proclamation, or doctrine, concerning the Messiah already exhibited.

The doctrine which was proposed by Christ and the Apostles, and is found delivered in the writings of the evangelists and apostles: b) Specifically, for the doctrine of grace concerning the gratuitous remission of sins, to be obtained through faith in Christ, whether it be held in the New or in the Old Testament: c) Most specifically, for the proclamation, or doctrine, concerning the Messiah already exhibited.

Proof a. The name of the Gospel is taken generally, Mark I, 1, in the words: The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ. Where the beginning of the gospel denotes the same as the beginning of the doctrine handed down by Christ.

But Christ not only handed down the doctrine of the gospel, strictly so called, but also the doctrine of the law; which is evident partly from the various sermons of Christ; and partly also from the doctrine of John the Baptist, who is said immediately in the same place, v. 4, to have preached the baptism of repentance.

In the same sense it is also taken in Mark XVI, 15, where Christ sends forth his disciples equipped with this instruction: Go into all the world, preach the gospel, etc. But it is certain that the Apostles not only preached the gospel, strictly called, but also the law.

Proof b. In the special sense, the gospel is adequately distinguished from the law. For just as the law is the norm of things to be done and things to be avoided: so the gospel is the norm of believing in Christ, and is the doctrine concerning the gratuitous remission of sins, to be obtained from God on account of the merit of Christ, whether they be proposed in the N. or in the O.T.

Thus it is taken in Is.

LII, 7: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news?

Which words Paul cites in Rom.

X, 15: How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of peace?

Add Heb. IV, 2.

Proof c. The name of the gospel is used in the most special sense, Rom. I, 1, where Paul affirms that he was set apart to preach the gospel, which he had promised before.

Therefore, a distinction must be made here between εὐαγγέλιον strictly so called, and ἐπαγγελίαν. The preaching concerning the Messiah not yet exhibited, but to be exhibited, is called ἡ πρὸς τοὺς πατέρας ἐπαγγελία, the promise made to the fathers, Acts XIII, 32.

But Εὐαγγέλιον, in the most special sense, denotes the public proclamation concerning the Messiah exhibited [*].

Latin:

Quæst. I. Quid est euangelium? Euangelium est concio gratiæ mere gratuitæ, meritum Christi & parta beneficia omnibus hominibus offerens, & per fidem, quam accendit, actu conferens; in Dei gloriam, & æternam hominum salutem.

Obs. Euangelium, vi vocis, notat bonum nuntium, siue lætam & optatam annuntiationem.

Quæst. II. Quot modis sumitur nomen euangelii? Nomen euangelii sumitur tribus modis: a) Generaliter, minusque proprie, pro vniuersa doctrina N.

T. quæ a Christo & Apostolis proposita est, inque scriptis euangelistarum & apostolorum tradita inuenitur: b) Specialiter, pro doctrina gratiæ de gratuita peccatorum remissione, per fidem in Christum impetranda, siue ea in Nouo, siue in V. T. habeatur: c) Specialissime, pro præconio, siue doctrina de Messia iam exhibito.

Prob. a. Generaliter accipitur nomen euangelii, Marc. I, 1. in verbis: Initium euangelii Iesu Christi. Vbi initium euangelii idem notat, quod initium doctrinæ, a Christo traditæ.

Christus autem non solum tradidit doctrinam euangelii, stricte sic dicti, sed etiam doctrinam legis; quod partim ex diuersis Christi concionibus patet; partim etiam ex doctrina Ioannis baptistæ, qui statim l. c. v. 4. dicitur prædicasse baptismum pænitentiæ.

Eodem sensu accipitur etiam Marc. XVI, 15. vbi Christus discipulos suos hac instructione munitos dimittit: Ite in vniuersum mundum, prædicate euangelium &c. At vero constat, Apostolos non solum prædicasse euangelium, stricte dictum, sed quoque legem.

Prob. b. Speciali sensu euangelium adæquate legi contradistinguitur. Sicut enim lex est norma faciendorum & fugiendorum: ita euangelium est norma credendi in Christum, estque doctrina de gratuita remissione peccatorum, propter meritum Christi a Deo impetranda, siue in N. siue in V.

T. proponantur. Sic sumitur Es.

LII, 7. Quam speciosi sunt super montes pedes euangelizantium?

Quæ verba Paullus citat Rom. X, 15.

Quam pulcri pedes euangelizantium pacem? Add.

Hebr. IV, 2.

Prob. c. Specialissimo sensu vsurpatur nomen euangelii, Rom. I, 1. vbi Paullus affirmat, se esse segregatum ad prædicandum euangelium, quod prius promissum.

Distinguendum igitur hic est inter εὐαγγέλιον strictissime dictum, & ἐπαγγελίαν. Prædicatio de Messia nondum exhibito, sed exhibendo vocatur ἡ πρὸς τοὺς πατέρας ἐπαγγελία, promissio patribus facta, Act.

XIII, 32. Εὐαγγέλιον vero, in sensu specialissimo, notat publicum de Messia exhibito præconium [*].


### On the Gospel: Is the Gospel a sermon of repentance?

Is the Gospel a sermon of repentance? The Gospel, in a general and less proper sense, is rightly called a sermon of repentance, spoken of in a generic way ): But the Gospel, taken in a special and proper sense, insofar as it is opposed to the Law, is not a sermon of repentance accusing and condemning sins ).

Proof a. The Gospel, in a generic and looser sense, designates the whole Christian doctrine comprised in the writings of the Evangelists and Apostles, which consists in the preaching of repentance and the remission of sins, by the command of Christ, Luke 24:44. And repentance, taken generally, embraces contrition and faith. The Gospel, taken in the looser sense, certainly preaches this, as theologians addicted to the Augsburg Confession do not deny.

For this form of speaking is used in the Apology of the Augsburg Confession, p. 165: "The sum of the preaching of the Gospel is to reprove sins, and to offer the remission of sins, and righteousness for Christ's sake."

And in the Epitome of the Formula of Concord, p. 592: "We believe, teach, and confess that if the word 'Gospel' is taken for the whole doctrine of Christ, which He Himself (as did His Apostles) professed in His ministry, it is rightly said and taught that the Gospel is a sermon concerning repentance and the remission of sins." Proof b. The Gospel, taken in a stricter sense, insofar as it is distinguished from the Law, is not a sermon of repentance specifically or partially spoken, and indeed by reason of the former part of repentance, i.e., contrition, or sorrow for sin.

We confirm this assertion of ours 1) From the doctrine of the Gospel, proposed from the first time of the fall. For the protoevangelium concerning the seed of the woman, who would crush the head of the serpent, Gen. 3:15; the promise concerning the seed of Abraham, in whom all the nations of the earth would be blessed, Gen. 12:3; concerning the son of David, who ought to restore the kingdom of David and continue it eternally, 2 Sam. 7:12 seqq.; the prediction concerning the Messiah being wounded for our iniquities, Is. 53: is the true Gospel, but most different from a sermon of repentance accusing, terrifying, and condemning the sins of men.

2) A sermon of repentance terrifies the sinner, saddens him, and denounces to him the wrath of God and eternal death. But the Gospel is described in the Holy Scriptures as being the Gospel of peace, Eph. 2:17; the Gospel of joy, Luke 2:10; the Gospel of the grace of God, Acts 20:24; the word of reconciliation, 2 Cor. 5:18; the Gospel of salvation, Rom. 1:16. Therefore, the Gospel formally is not a sermon of repentance.

3) A sermon of repentance aims at this, that the hearts of men may be broken and crushed: But the Gospel is preached to the poor and the contrite in heart, that they may be raised up and refreshed, Is. 61:1, Matt. 11:5. 4) A sermon of repentance leads men to the acknowledgment and detestation of sin. But this is not from the Gospel, but from the Law, Rom. 3:20.

From which the Declaration of the Formula of Concord, p. 717, concludes: "It is joined with great danger, and cannot be approved, that it is asserted that the Gospel (properly so called, and when it is distinguished from the Law) is a sermon of repentance, reproving sins." The antithesis is that of the Papists and Antinomians, who maintain that the Gospel is more rightly described by a sermon of repentance than by a sermon of grace.

They confirm their opinion with the following arguments: I.

Which in the future, now present, are the three principal parts of which this doctrine of the Gospel consists. First: Christ, whom the Prophets foretold would come, has long since come. Second: He is no other than Jesus of Nazareth. Third: In Him alone have been completed and consummated all things which the divine Prophets predicted concerning Christ who was to come.

I. Whatever sermon terrifies the consciences of men, that is a sermon of repentance: But the evangelical sermon &c. Therefore. The minor is proved by the examples of Peter, Acts II, 37, and Paul, Acts XXIV, 25. Resp. The Apostles preached not only the gospel, but also the law. II. In the gospel there exist many threatenings. See Matt. V, 22, ch. VII, 19, and elsewhere passim. Therefore, the gospel terrifies the minds of men. Resp. Threatenings exist in the gospel taken generally, but they are not of the gospel taken specifically, as it is opposed to the law.

III. Whatever doctrine reproves & accuses sins, that is a sermon of repentance: But the evangelical doctrine &c. Therefore. The minor is proved: because the Holy Spirit reproves the sin of ἀπιστίας (unbelief) in Christ, by which the redeemer of the world is despised and rejected: But the Holy Spirit does not reprove that ἀπιστίαν (unbelief) through the law, which knows nothing of Christ.

Therefore, through the gospel. Resp. 1) Distinguish between the law alone, and that which is illuminated by the light of the gospel. The law alone, or taken separately, knows nothing of faith or ἀπιστία (unbelief) in Christ; yet, when illuminated by the light of the gospel, it reproves and condemns unbelief in Christ. 2) Unbelief is considered either by reason of its genus, or by reason of its object.

In the former way, it can and must be referred to nothing but the law: since by reason of its genus it is a sin, and consequently it reproves and condemns it just as it does other sins. In the latter way, by reason of the object, it looks either to God as legislator, or, according to the gospel, it has Christ the mediator in the place of the object. This respect does not change the genus of unbelief, but only varies the object, so that unbelief, although it is borne directly toward Christ, nevertheless strikes against the first commandment of the decalogue, and thus is subject to the law.

For this commandment in general commands one to believe in God, in whatever way He is considered, whether as creator and preserver, or as legislator, or as redeemer: and thus the law in general reproves and condemns all unbelief. On the contrary, the gospel, although it manifests and declares a certain object of unbelief, yet, properly speaking, it does not reprove or condemn the ἀπιστίαν (unbelief) itself.

IV. Every sermon concerning the passion & death of Christ is a sermon of repentance: But the gospel &c. Therefore. The major is clear: the passion and death of Christ is a real sermon of repentance, full of the severity and wrath of God. Resp. The passion and death of Christ is considered in two ways: 1) as a mirror of the justice, severity, and divine wrath toward sinners, and thus it pertains reductively to the law: 2) Insofar as it is a mirror of the ineffable mercy of God toward the miserable human race; and a most full satisfaction for sins, and thus it pertains to the gospel.

V. Whatever reveals the wrath of God is a sermon of repentance: But the gospel &c. Therefore. The minor is proved from Rom.

I, 18. The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness &c. But the wrath of God is revealed through the gospel, of which the Apostle had spoken before. Resp. The Apostle does not say that the wrath of God is revealed in the gospel, but in the preceding verse he had said that the righteousness by which man is justified is revealed in the gospel; to which is opposed the wrath, which the Apostle asserts is revealed from heaven, viz., through the natural and moral law, through the judgments of God, through examples, and through one's own experience.

VI. Whatever contrition is salutary, that flows from the gospel: But the contrition of the faithful &c. Therefore. The major is evident: because without the gospel, the greater the contrition, the more effectively it leads a man to despair. The minor is clear; because it is a spiritual sacrifice, Ps. LI, 19, and repentance unto salvation, 2 Cor.

VII, 10. Resp. God, through the grace converting the sinner by making him sorrowful through the law, works repentance unto salvation, so that repentance taken μερικῶς (partially), or contrition, does not indeed become a causal means of salvation, but a means of the divine order, by which man is disposed and prepared through the Holy Spirit to conceive from the gospel a saving faith in Christ, with which salutary contrition is conjoined.

Despair is not to be attributed to contrition itself viewed in its essence; because contrition in itself is a work of the Holy Spirit through the law. But the Holy Spirit does not work despair, nor does the divine law command it. But it is that vicious act of man, who makes the mercy of God smaller than his sin, and knows not how to flee from the law of Moses to the gospel of Christ. VII.

VII. Whatever doctrine excludes all boasting, that most effectively convicts of sins: But the gospel &c. Rom. III, 27. Resp. The gospel excludes all boasting, not by convicting of sins, which is the work of the law; but by referring every beginning, progress, and end of salvation to the grace of God alone.

VIII. Whatever doctrine is not only a fragrance of life to life, but also a fragrance of death to death, that is not only a sermon of grace, but also of repentance: But the gospel &c. 2 Cor. II, 15. Resp. The gospel in itself is a fragrance of life; it becomes a fragrance of death accidentally to those who either despise the gospel or abuse it for security: just as the scent of sweet ointment refreshes doves, but kills beetles.

IX. The gospel is proposed with saving fruit only to the penitent: Therefore, it is rightly called a sermon of repentance. Resp. We assert that the gospel, strictly and properly speaking, is not formally a sermon of repentance or contrition. But if anyone wishes to call the gospel a sermon of repentance objectively, because it is fruitful only to the contrite, and declaratively, insofar as it declares what infidelity is, the object of which is unknown to the law, we allow him to abound in his own sense. Conf. DANNH. in hodof. phanom. VI. p. 484.

Latin:

Estne evangelium concio poenitentiae? Evangelium, sensu generali, minusque proprio, recte vocatur concio poenitentiae, generatim dicta ): Evangelium vero, acceptum sensu speciali & proprio, quatenus legi opponitur, non est concio poenitentiae accusans & damnans peccata ).

Prob. a. Evangelium, in sensu generico & laxiori, designat totam doctrinam christianam in scriptis Evangelistarum & Apostolorum comprehensam, quae consistit in praedicatione poenitentiae & remissionis peccatorum, iubente Christo, Luc. XXIV, 44. & poenitentia, generatim sumta, complectitur contritionem & fidem. Hanc vtique praedicant evangelium, sensu laxiore acceptum, non diffitentibus Theologis, Augustanae confessioni addictis.

Vsurpatur enim haec loquendi forma in Apologia Aug. Conf. p. 165. Summa praedicationis evangelii est, arguere peccata, & offerre remissionem peccatorum, & iustitiam propter Christum.

Et in Epitome Form. Concord. p. 592. Credimus, docemus & confitemur, si vocabulum evangelii de tota Christi doctrina accipiatur, quam ipse in ministerio suo (quem ad modum & eius Apostoli) professus est, recte dici & doceri, evangelium esse concionem de poenitentia & remissione peccatorum. Prob. b. Evangelium, sumtum sensu strictiori, quatenus legi contradistinguitur, non est concio poenitentiae specialiter, aut partialiter dictae, & quidem ratione prioris partis poenitentiae, i.e. contritionis, sive doloris de peccato.

Quam assertionem nostram firmamus 1) E doctrina evangelii, a primo lapsus tempore proposita. Nam proteuangelium de semine mulieris, contrituro caput serpentis, contrituro caput serpentis, Gen. III, 15. promissio de semine Abrahami, in quo benedicendae essent omnes gentes terrae, Gen. XII, 3. de filio Dauidis, qui regnum Dauidis restaurare & aeternum continuare debeat, 2 Sam. VII, 12. seqq. praedictio de Messia vulnerando propter iniquitates nostras, Es. LIII: verum est evangelium, diversissimum autem a concione poenitentiae accusante, terrente, condemnante hominum peccata.

2) Concio poenitentiae peccatorem terret, contristat, iram Dei aeternamque mortem ipsi denuntiat. At evangelium in sacris litteris describitur, quod sit evangelium pacis, Eph. II, 17. evangelium gaudii, Luc. II, 10. evangelium gratiae Dei, Act. XX, 24. verbum reconciliationis, 2 Cor. V, 18. evangelium salutis, Rom. I, 16. E. evangelium formaliter non est concio poenitentiae.

3) Concio poenitentiae eo collineat, vt hominum corda frangantur & conterantur: At evangelium praedicatur pauperibus & contritis corde, vt erigantur & reficiantur, Es. LXI, 1, Matth. XI, 5. 4) Concio poenitentiae perducit homines ad agnitionem & detestationem peccati. At haec non est ex evangelio, sed ex lege, Rom. III, 20. E quibus concludit Declarat.

Form. Concord. p. 717. Magno cum periculo coniunctum est, neque approbari potest quod asseritur, evangelium (proprie sic dictum, & cum a lege discernitur) esse concionem poenitentiae, arguentem peccata. Antithesis est Pontificiorum & Antinomorum, statuentium, evangelium rectius per concionem poenitentiae, quam per concionem gratiae describi.

Qui suam opinionem sequentibus firmant argumentis: I.

Quae futuro, nunc praesente, tres sunt partes praecipuae, ex quibus haec Evangelii doctrina constat. Prima: Christus, quem Vates venturum praenuntiarunt, iam dudum venit. Secunda: Is nemo est alius, quam Iesus Nazarenus. Tertia: In eo vno completa & consummata sunt vniuersa, quae Vates diuini predixerunt de Christo aduenturo. quæ Vates diuini prædixerunt de Christo aduenturo.

I. Quae concio terret conscientias hominum, illa est concio poenitentiae: Atqui concio evangelica &c. E. Minor probatur exemplis Petri, Act. II, 37. Pauli, Act. XXIV, 25. Resp. Apostoli non tantum evangelium, sed etiam legem praedicarunt. II. In evangelio multa extant comminationes. Vid. Matth. V, 22. c. VII, 19. & alibi passim. E. evangelium animos hominum terret. Resp. Comminationes extant in evangelio generaliter dicto, sed non sunt de evangelio specialiter sumpto, prout legi opponitur.

III. Quaecunque doctrina arguit & accusat peccata, illa est concio poenitentiae: Atqui doctrina evangelica &c. Ergo. Minor probatur: quia Spiritus S. arguit peccatum ἀπιστίας in Christum, quo redemptor orbis contemnitur & reiicitur: At illam ἀπιστίαν Spiritus S. non arguit per legem, quae de Christo nihil novit.

E. per evangelium. Resp. 1) Dist. inter legem solam, & luce evangelii illustratam. Lex sola, sive feortim sumpta, nihil novit de fide, aut ἀπιστία in Christum, collustrata tamen lumine evangelii incredulitatem in Christum arguit & condemnat. 2) Incredulitas consideratur vel ratione sui generis, vel ratione sui obiecti.

Priori modo non, nisi ad legem referri potest ac debet: siquidem ratione generis est peccatum, & per consequens aeque, ac reliqua peccata arguit & damnat. Posteriori modo obiecti loco respicit vel Deum tanquam legislatorem, vel iuxta evangelium obiecti loco habet Christum mediatorem. Hic respectus non mutat genus incredulitatis, sed tantum obiectum variat ita, vt incredulitas, licet directe in Christum feratur, tamen impingat in primum praeceptum decalogi, & sic legi subiaceat.

Praeceptum enim hoc in genere iubet credere Deo, quocunque modo, sive vt creator & conservator, sive vt legislator, sive vt redemptor consideretur: & sic in genere arguit & damnat lex omnem incredulitatem. Contra evangelium licet quoddam incredulitatis obiectum manifestet ac declaret, ipsam tamen ἀπιστίαν proprie loquendo non arguit aut damnat.

IV. Omnis concio de passione & morte Christi est concio poenitentiae: Atqui evangelium &c. Ergo. Maior liquet: passio & mors Christi est realis concio poenitentiae, plena severitatis & irae Dei. Resp. Passio & mors Christi consideratur dupliciter: 1) vt speculum iustitiae, severitatis & irae divinae erga peccatores, & sic reductive ad legem pertinet: 2) Quatenus est speculum ineffabilis Dei misericordiae, erga miserum genus humanum; & plenissima pro peccatis satisfactio, & sic ad evangelium spectat.

V. Quidquid revelat iram Dei, est concio poenitentiae: Atqui evangelium &c. Ergo. Minor probatur ex Rom. I, 18. Revelatur ira Dei de caelo super omnem impietatem &c.

Revelatur autem ira Dei per evangelium, de quo Apostolus antea locutus erat. Resp. Apostolus non dicit, iram Dei revelari in evangelio, sed versu praecedente dixerat, in evangelio revelari iustitiam, qua iustificatur homo; cui opponitur ira, quam Apostolus a caelo revelari asserit, scil. per legem naturalem & moralem, per iudicia Dei, per exempla, & propriam experientiam.

VI. Quaecunque contritio est salutaris, illa fluit ex evangelio: Atqui contritio fidelium &c. Ergo. Maior constat: quia sine evangelio contritio, quo maior est, eo efficacius perducit hominem ad desperationem. Minor liquet; quia est sacrificium spirituale, Ps. LI, 19. & poenitentia ad salutem, 2 Cor. VII, 10. Resp. Deus per gratiam convertentem peccatorem ex lege contristando operatur poenitentiam ad salutem, vt poenitentia μερικῶς accepta, sive contritio, non quidem fit medium salutis causale, sed medium ordinis divini, quo homo per Spiritum S. disponitur & praeparatur ad concipiendam ex evangelio fidem in Christum salutificam, cum qua coniuncta est salutaris contritio.

Desperatio non est tribuenda ipsi contritioni in essentia sua spectatae; quia contritio in se est opus Spiritus S. per legem.

At desperationem neque Spiritus S. operatur, neque lex divina iubet. Sed est illa actus vitiosus hominis, qui misericordiam Dei minorem facit peccato, nec a lege Mosis ad evangelium Christi confugere novit. Mosis ad euangelium Christi confugere nouit. VII.

VII. Quaecunque doctrina excludit omnem gloriationem, illa efficacissime arguit peccata: Atqui euangelium &c. Rom. III, 27. Resp. Euangelium excludit omnem gloriationem, non peccata arguendo, quod est legis; sed omne salutis initium, progressum & finem soli gratiae Dei acceptum referendo.

VIII. Quaecunque doctrina non tantum est odor vitae ad vitam, sed etiam odor mortis ad mortem, illa non tantum est concio gratiae, sed etiam poenitentiae: Atqui euangelium &c. 2 Cor. II, 15. Resp. Euangelium per se est odor vitae; per accidens fit odor mortis illis, qui vel contemnunt euangelium, vel eodem abutuntur ad securitatem: sicut suauis unguenti odor columbas recreat, scarabaeos perimit.

IX. Euangelium solis poenitentibus cum salutari fructu proponitur: E. recte dicitur concio poenitentiae. Resp. Asserimus, euangelium, stricte & proprie dictum, formaliter non esse concionem poenitentiae, siue contritionis. Quod si autem quis euangelium velit vocare concionem poenitentiae obiective, quia non nisi contritis fructuosum est, & declaratiue, quatenus declarat, quid sit infidelitas, cuius obiectum legi ignotum est, illum suo sensu abundare patimur. Conf. DANNH. in hodof. phanom. VI. p. 484.


### On the Gospel: Quæst. IV. What is the principal efficient cause of the gospel?

Quæst. IV. What is the principal efficient cause of the gospel?

The Cause efficient of the gospel, both by reason of the decree and of the revelation, is the whole Holy Trinity, God the Father, the Son of God, and the Holy Spirit.

Prob. a. God the Father with the Son and the Holy Spirit decreed from eternity: a) That as a remedy for the Adamic fall and the sin which He foresaw, the second person of the Trinity, the Son of God, in the fullness of time should assume a true human nature, and in it, by fulfilling the law, suffering, and dying, should make satisfaction for the sins of men, and merit eternal salvation for the whole human race. b) He decreed that the merit of Christ, and His benefits, should be offered, exhibited, and distributed to all through the word of the gospel. With respect to this decree, the gospel is called the mystery hidden in God from the ages, Eph. III, 9.

Prob. b. God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by His Son, Hebr. I, 1. God, who spoke in the Son, is God the Father, who already long ago in the O.T. spoke to the fathers by the prophets, that through His name whosoever believeth in Jesus Christ shall receive remission of sins, Act. X, 43. Which is the sum of the gospel.

Prob. c. From Jo. I, 18. The law was given by Moses: Grace and truth came by Jesus Christ. No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared (it to us). Just as the law was given to us by Moses, through which our injustices are convicted: so through Jesus Christ the truest grace was not only acquired for us, but also clearly explained to us by evangelical preaching, since this eternal Son of God, existing in the bosom of the Father, knows most perfectly the divine decree concerning our salvation, which this Word of God announced to the first-formed in paradise, Gen. III, 15.

Prob. d. From Eph. III, 5. Which in other ages was not made known unto the sons of men, as it is now revealed unto his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit, that the Gentiles should be fellowheirs, and of the same body, and partakers of his promise in Christ by the gospel. The mystery concerning Christ and the calling of all Gentiles to His church was revealed more clearly to the Apostles through the Holy Spirit in the N.T. than to the men of God in the O.T., who nevertheless also spoke of Christ, moved by the Holy Spirit, 2 Petr. I, 21.

Latin:

Quæst. IV. Quae est causa efficiens principalis euangelii?

Causa efficiens euangelii, tam ratione decreti, quam patefactionis est tota SS. Trinitas , Deus Pater , Filius Dei , & Spiritus S. .

Prob. a. Deus Pater cum Filio & Spiritu S. ab aeterno decreuit: a) Vt in remedium lapsus Adamitici & peccati, quod praeuidit, secunda persona Trinitatis, Filius Dei, in plenitudine temporis veram humanam naturam assumeret, ac in ea legem implendo, patiendo & moriendo, pro peccatis hominum satisfaceret, ac toti humano generi aeternam salutem promereretur. b) Decreuit, vt Christi meritum, eiusque beneficia, per verbum euangelii omnibus offerrentur, exhiberentur, & distribuerentur. Respectu huius decreti euangelium vocatur mysterium absconditum in Deo ἀπὸ τῶν αἰώνων, Eph. III, 9.

Prob. b. Multis vicibus multisque modis olim Deus locutus patribus in prophetis, vltimis diebus locutus est nobis in Filio, Hebr. I, 1. Deus, qui locutus est in Filio, est Deus Pater, qui iam olim in V. T. locutus est patribus in prophetis, quod remissionem peccatorum accipiat omnis, qui credit in Iesum Christum, Act. X, 43. Quae est summa euangelii.

Prob. c. Ex Io. I, 18. Lex per Mosen data est: Gratia & veritas per Iesum Christum facta est. Deum nemo vidit vnquam; nisi vnigenitus filius, qui in sinu Patris est, ille exposuit (nobis). Sicut per Mosen data est nobis lex, per quam nostrae iniustitiae conuincimur: ita per Iesum Christum verissima gratia nobis est acquilita haud tantum, sed & praedicatione euangelica dilucide nobis exposita, cum hic aeternus Dei Filius, in sinu Patris existens, decretum diuinum de nostra salute perfectissime sciat, quod protoplastis hic λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ in paradiso enuntiauit, Gen. III, 15.

Prob. d. Ex Eph. III, 5. Nunc reuelatum est sanctis Apostolis Christi & Prophetis in Spiritu, quod sint gentes cohaeredes, & concorpores & participes promissionis ipsius in Christo per euangelium. Mysterium de Christo & vocandis ad ecclesiam ipsius gentibus omnibus, clarius Apostolis per Spiritum S. reuelatum est in N. T. quam viris Dei in V. T. qui tamen etiam de Christo locuti sunt, impulsi a Spiritu S. 2 Petr. I, 21.


### Q. V. By whose ministry was the Gospel preached?

The Gospel was preached by the ministry of the holy men of God, both in the Old and the New Testament . Indeed, even angels, by the command of God, joyfully and willingly expounded the Gospel concerning Christ . Proof a. The protoevangelium concerning the seed of the woman, who would crush the head of the serpent, was without doubt handed down by Adam and the remaining patriarchs and repeated until the flood. After the flood, Noah was a preacher of righteousness, 2 Pet. II, 5, along with his descendants. The most illustrious evangelical promise was made to Abraham concerning the Messiah, the seed of Abraham, in whom all nations were to be blessed, Gen. XII, 3, which was repeated to Isaac, Gen. XXVI, 3, from whom that promise was propagated until Moses, whose ministry, although it is distinguished from the ministry of the Gospel, finally points to and shows Christ. "Moses wrote of me," says the Savior, John V, 46. Memorable is the passage concerning the great Prophet, Deut. XVIII, 15, which is cited in Acts III, 22. The Levitical priests, moreover, described and prefigured the promise of the Messiah the Redeemer, as it were, in sacrifices. After Moses, all the Prophets bore witness to Christ, Acts X, 43. Cf. Ps. II, VII, XXII, XLV, CX. Is. VII, LIII, LXI. Jer. XXIII. Dan. IX. Hos. XIII. Mich. V. Hag. II. Zach. IX, XIII. Mal. I, III, IV. Proof b.

In the N. T., the Gospel of Christ was preached by the shepherds of Bethlehem, Luke II, 10; Simeon, Luke II, 29; John the Baptist, John I, 9; the Apostles, Mark XVI, 15; and their successors, or all faithful heralds of the Gospel, in whom God placed the word of reconciliation, 2 Cor. V, 19. Proof c.

It was a singular pleasure for the angels to propose and narrate to men the Gospel concerning Christ’s conception, Luke I, 26; birth, Luke II, 10; resurrection, Luke XXIV, 4; ascension into heaven, and return for judgment, Acts I, 1. The Antithesis is 1) of certain Scholastics, who contend with Pelagius that men before Moses were justified and saved by the law of nature alone, and after Moses by the law of Moses alone; but in the N. T. are justified and saved by the Gospel: 2) of the Anabaptists, who assert that the Fathers of the O. T. knew nothing of the promises of the Gospel and eternal life: 3) of the Socinians, who maintain that the Gospel began with Christ and is proper only to the N. T. They fortify their opinion with the following arguments:

I. Whatever was silent from eternal times, and finally manifested in the N. T., was not in the V. T. But the Gospel concerning Jesus Christ, etc., Rom. XVI, 25. Therefore. Resp. Distinguish between the τὰ ουσιατικά (essential things), or the substantials, and the περιστατικά (circumstantial things), or the circumstantials of the Gospel. The same evangelical doctrine concerning Christ the Mediator, as to its substance, was proposed in the O. T.; but that Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Mary, is the promised Messiah was not known except in the N. T.: which is also occupied in explaining this doctrine more abundantly and illustrating it more clearly, and thus far that mystery was hidden in ancient times, because it was not so fully handed down, nor so fully proposed: therefore it is said to be made manifest διὰ γραφῶν προφητικῶν (through prophetic writings), with the addition, namely, of a more abundant apostolic explanation and a more diffuse promulgation among the nations.

II. The joyful message concerning Christ born is called the Gospel, Luke III, 10; Rom. I, 1. But in the O. T. there was no joyful message concerning Christ born. Resp. Distinguish between the Gospel taken in a special sense, insofar as it is opposed to the law, and taken in the most special sense, insofar as it is distinguished from the promise and denotes the proclamation concerning Christ exhibited: The Gospel was in the O. T. not in the latter, but in the former sense.

III. If the law was given through Moses, but grace and truth were made and expounded through Christ; the Gospel was not yet known in the times of Moses: But the former is true, and the latter. The consequence of the major is evident, because the Gospel is a sermon of grace, contrasted with the law. The antecedent is clear from John I, 17. Resp. Distinguish between Moses the ministerial legislator and the prophet. or teacher. Moses was not only a minister of the law, but also a Prophet, who wrote about Christ, John 5:46. Furthermore, grace is considered, partly by reason of the promise concerning Christ to be incarnated, and partly by reason of its fulfillment.

That grace which God had promised concerning Christ, who was to assume flesh and reconcile the human race, He fulfilled, with Christ exhibited in the flesh. IV. If the discourse concerning the coming Messiah is called ἐπαγγελία, or promise, but not εὐαγγέλιον, it follows that in the O.T. the fathers did not rejoice in the gospel. The antecedent is true, therefore the consequent is also.

The antecedent is clear from Acts 13:32, Gal. 3:18. Resp. The distinction between ἐπαγγελία and εὐαγγέλιον in the sacred scriptures is frequent, but not perpetual.

For Paul says Rom. 10:15: It is written (Is. 52:7): How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the gospel of good things! But not all have obeyed the gospel. And Heb. 4:2: To us the gospel was preached, just as also to them (the fathers). Objection: But the gospel is said to have been promised through the prophets, Rom.

1:2. Therefore it was not preached by them. Resp.

By the name of the gospel in the cited place is understood the public proclamation concerning the Messiah exhibited, which began to be preached only in the N.T., Mark 1:1, 2. Meanwhile, the doctrine concerning grace and the remission of sins on account of the Messiah in the O.

T. promised, and in the N.T. exhibited, is in both cases one and the same. Quæst.

VI. By what means is the gospel accepted? The gospel is accepted and retained by faith, which it kindles a), together with all the benefits which it offers b).

Obs. Faith has a twofold relation to the gospel: a) as an effect, because it is produced through the gospel: b) as an organ, by which the evangelical promise and all the goods offered by it are apprehended, so that there is a perpetual relation between the offering organ and the apprehending organ, between the promise of grace and the fiducial apprehension.

Prob. a. The Holy Spirit in regeneration kindles faith through the word of the gospel. For faith is from hearing, and hearing through the word of God.

Whence we are said to believe through the word of the Apostles, John 17:20. Prob. b.

From Mark 1:14, 15. Jesus came into Galilee, preaching the gospel of the kingdom of God, and saying: Because the time is fulfilled and the kingdom of God has drawn near. Repent and believe in the gospel.

Penitent and contrite sinners receive with fiducial assent the implanted word, which is able to save their souls, James

1:21. Quæst. VII. To what men is the gospel to be preached?

The gospel, by the intention of God, is to be preached to all men a). But it is applied specially and with saving fruit to the penitent and believers b). Prob. a. 1) Christ commanded the Apostles to preach the gospel to every creature, Mark 16:15. 2) The gospel has been preached to every creature which is under heaven, Col. 1:23. 3) God wills all men to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth, 1 Tim. 2:3. Therefore God wills that the means of faith and salvation be proposed to all men.

Prob. b.

A special application of the gospel is made to penitent sinners who do not maliciously resist; for God does not pour the oil of mercy except into a contrite vessel.

Whence Christ is said to have been sent to preach the gospel to the poor, Is. 61:1, and πτωχοὶ εὐαγγελίζονται, the poor hear the gospel, Matt. 11:5. It is necessary, however, that faith be added to contrition, which is as it were a hand, receiving the goods offered in the evangelical promise.

does not receive the gospel by faith, hears and reads it without fruit. The word heard does not profit, not being mixed by faith with those who heard it, Hebr.

Latin:

Evangelium praedicatum est ministerio sanctorum Dei virorum, tam in veteri , quam novo testamento . Quin angeli etiam ex mandato Dei evangelium de Christo laeti lubentesque exposuerunt . Prob. a. Protenangelium de semine mulieris, caput serpentis contrituro, dubio procul Adamus et reliqui patriarchae tradiderunt et repetiverunt usque ad diluvium. Post diluvium praeco iustitiae fuit Noachus, 2 Petr. II, 5. cum posteris suis. Maxime illustris promissio evangelica facta est Abrahamo, de Messia, semine Abrahami, in quo omnes gentes benedicendae essent, Gen. XII, 3. quae repetita Isaaco, Gen. XXVI, 3, a quibus illa promissio propagata est usque ad Mosen, cuius ministerium licet a ministerio evangelii distinguatur, finaliter monstrat et ostendit Christum. De me Moses scripsit, inquit Salvator Io. V, 46. Memorabilis est locus de Propheta magno, Deut. XVIII, 15. qui citatur Actor. III, 22. Sacerdotes autem Levitici promissionem de Messia redemptore in sacrificiis quasi descripserunt et praefigurarunt. Post Mosen omnes Prophetae de Christo testimonium perhibuerunt, Act. X, 43. Conf. Ps. II, VII. XXII, XLV. CX. Es. VII. LIII. LXI. Ier. XXIII. Dan. IX. Hos. XIII. Mich. V. Hag. II. Zach. IX. XIII. Mal. I. III. IV. Prob. b.

In N. T. evangelium Christi praedicarunt pastores Bethlehemitici, Luc. II, 10. Simeon, Luc. II, 29. Ioannes baptista, Io. I, 9. Apostoli, Marc. XVI, 15. et illorum successores, sive omnes fideles evangelii praecones, in quibus Deus posuit verbum reconciliationis, 2 Cor. V, 19. Prob. c.

Angelis singulari voluptate fuit, proponere et enarrare hominibus evangelium de Christi conceptione, Luc. I, 26. natiuitate, Luc. II, 10. resurrectione, Luc. XXIV, 4. ascensione in caelum et reditu ad iudicium, Act. I, 1. Antithesis est 1) quorundam Scholasticorum, cum Pelagio contendentium, homines ante Mosen sola lege naturae, post Mosen sola lege Mosis iustificatos et salvatos esse; in N. T. autem iustificari et salvari evangelio: 2) Anabaptistarum, afferentium, Patres V. T. de evangelii ac vitae aeternae promissionibus nihil scivisse: 3) Socinianorum, statuentium, evangelium coepisse cum Christo, esse solius N. T. proprium. Qui suam opinionem sequentibus muniunt argumentis:

I. Quidquid ab aeternis temporibus fuit tacitum, et demum in N. T. manifestatum, illud non fuit in V. T. Atqui evangelium de Iesu Christo etc. Rom. XVI, 25. E. Resp. Dist. inter τὰ ουσιατικά, seu substantialia, et περιστατικά, seu circumstantialia evangelii. Eadem doctrina evangelica de Christo mediatore, quantum ad substantiam, proposita est in V. T.; sed Iesum Nazarenum, Mariae filium, esse Messiam promissum, non, nisi in N. T. cognitum est: quod etiam in hac doctrina uberius explicanda et clarius illustranda occupatur, et hactenus antiquis temporibus mysterium illud absconditum fuit, quod non ita plene traditum, nec adeo plene propositum fit: ideo dicitur, patefactum διὰ γραφῶν προφητικῶν, accedente scil. explicatione apostolica uberiori, et diffusiori promulgatione inter gentes. II.

Laetus nuntius de Christo nato dicitur evangelium, Luc. III, 10. Rom. I, 1. Sed in V. T. non fuit laetus nuntius de Christo nato. E Resp. Dist. inter evangelium sumtum in sensu speciali, quatenus legi opponitur, et acceptum sensu specialissimo, quatenus a promissione discernitur, et notat praeconium de Christo exhibito: Non posteriori, sed priori sensu evangelium fuit in V. T. III.

Si lex per Mosen est data, gratia vero et veritas per Christam facta et exposita est; evangelium temporibus Mosis nondum innotuit: Atqui verum prius est, et posterius. Consequentia maioris est euidens, quia evangelium est concio gratiae, legi contradistincta. Antecedens patet ex Io. I, 17. Resp. Dist. inter Mosen legislatorem ministerialem, et prophetam seu doctorem. Fuit Moses non tantum minister legis, sed etiam Propheta, qui de Christo scripsit, Io. V. 46. Ceterum consideratur gratia, partim ratione promissionis de Christo incarnando, partim ratione complementi.

Quam gratiam de Christo, carnem assumpturo & genus humanum reconciliaturo, Deus promiserat, illam complevit, Christo in carne exhibito. IV. Si concio de venturo Messia vocatur ἐπαγγελία, sive promissio, non autem εὐαγγέλιον, sequitur, quod in V. T. patres non gavisi sint euangelio. Antecedens est verum, E. & consequens.

Antecedens liquet ex Act. XIII, 32. Gal. III, 18. Resp. Distinctio inter ἐπαγγελίαν & εὐαγγέλιον in sacris litteris est frequens, sed non perpetua.

Dicit enim Paullus Rom. X, 15.: Scriptum est (Es. LII, 7.): Quam pulcri pedes euangelizantium bona! Sed non omnes obedierunt euangelio. Et Hebr. IV, 2. Nobis euangelizatum est, sicut & illis (patribus.) Instantia: Sed euangelium dicitur per prophetas promissum, Rom.

I, 2. E. non est per ipsos prædicatum. Resp.

Euangelii nomine l. c. intelligitur publicum de Messia exhibito præconium, quod in N. T. demum prædicari cœpit, Marc. I, 1. 2. Interim doctrina de gratia & remissione peccatorum propter Messiam in V.

T. promissum, & in N. T. exhibitum vtrobique vna & eadem est. Quæst.

VI. Quo medio euangelium acceptatur? Euangelium per fidem, quam accendit a), vna cum omnibus beneficiis, quæ offert, acceptatur & retinetur b).

Obs. Fides duplicem habet respectum ad euangelium: a) effectus, quia per euangelium producitur: b) organi, quo euangelica promissio, & omnia ab ipso oblata bona apprehenduntur, vt fit perpetua relatio inter organum offerens, & organum apprehendens, inter promissionem gratiæ & fiducialem apprehensionem.

Prob. a. Spiritus S. in regeneratione per verbum euangelii fidem accendit. Fides enim est ex auditu, auditus autem per verbum Dei.

Vnde per verbum Apostolorum credere dicimur, Io. XVII, 20. Prob. b.

Ex Marc. I, 14. 15. Venit Iesus in Galilæam, prædicans euangelium regni Dei, & dicens: Quia impletum est tempus & appropinquauit regnum Dei. pænitentiam agite & credite euangelio.

Peccatores pœnitentes & contriti assensu fiduciali recipiunt verbum implantatum, quod potest saluas facere animas ipsorum, Iac.

I, 21. Quæst. VII. Quibus hominibus prædicandum est euangelium?

Euangelium ex intentione Dei prædicandum est omnibus hominibus a). Specialiter vero & salutari cum fructu applicatur pœnitentibus & credentibus b). Prob. a. 1) Christus præcepit Apostolis, prædicare euangelium omni creaturæ, Marc. XVI, 15. 2) Euangelium prædicatum est omni creaturæ, quæ sub cœlo est, Col. I, 23. 3) Deus vult omnes homines saluos fieri, & ad agnitionem veritatis venire, 1 Tim. II, 3. E. Deus vult, vt omnibus hominibus medium fidei & salutis proponatur.

Prob. b.

Specialis applicatio euangelii fit peccatoribus pœnitentibus & malitiose non obsistentibus; neque enim infundit Deus misericordiæ oleum, nisi in vas contritum.

Vnde Christus ad euangelizandum pauperibus missus esse dicitur, Es. LXI, 1. & πτωχοὶ εὐαγγελίζονται, pauperes euangelium audiunt, Matth. XI, 5. Necesse autem est, vt ad contritionem accedat fides, quæ est quasi manus, oblata in promissione euangelica bona recipiens.

fide non suscipit evangelium, sine fructu illud audit & legit. Non prodest sermo auditus non commixtus per fidem cum iis, qui audierunt, Hebr. IV, 2.


### Q. V. By whose ministry was the Gospel preached?: IV, 2. Q. VIII. What does the gospel preach and offer to us?

IV, 2. Q. VIII. What does the gospel preach and offer to us?

The gospel preaches and offers to us the grace of God, the merit of Christ, and all the benefits obtained by the same .

Prob. 1) The author of salvation himself declares the compendium of the gospel, John III, 6. God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life. From which the gospel is called the grace of God, Acts XX, 24.

2) The gospel of God treats of the Son of God, born of the seed of David, according to the flesh, Rom. I, 3. It is the preaching of Jesus Christ, Rom. XVI, 25. We preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness; but unto them which are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God, 1

Cor. I, 23. 24. 3) The benefits obtained by the merit of Christ are various, which the Holy Spirit offers to us through the gospel, as a most efficacious medium. For that we are called by the gospel to the church, in it are enlightened, converted, regenerated, made children of God, gifted with the peace of conscience, justified, united with God, renewed, sanctified, preserved in faith, and glorified, we have shown through all the heads in the preceding section.

Q. IX.

In what does the gospel formally consist? The gospel formally consists in a gratuitous promise , and ordained to the obtaining of blessedness, in the kingdom of grace and glory .

Prob. a. The Apostle teaches that the evangelical promise is gratuitous, Rom. III, 23. 24. All have sinned, and come short of the glory of God, while they are justified (δωρεὰν) freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. The evangelical promise is called gratuitous, on our part, because we have not merited the benefits offered in the gospel by our works; not on the part of Christ, who merited them for us at the highest price of his blood and life, 1 Cor. VI, 20. 1 Pet. I, 19. Prob. b. Blessedness in the kingdom of grace is the remission of sins and righteousness availing before God.

Blessedness of the kingdom of glory consists in the full fruition of God and heavenly goods. To both, as an end, the evangelical promise is divinely ordained. For which cause it is called the evangelium of the kingdom of God, Mark 1:14.

The gospel of our salvation, Eph. 1:13. The word of reconciliation, 2 Cor. 5:18. The word of eternal life, John 6:68.

Q. X. What is the end of the gospel?

The ultimate end of the gospel, on the part of God, is the glory of God's mercy, wisdom, power, and truth . The ultimate end, with respect to men, is the beatitude of glory, or eternal life . The intermediate end is the beatitude of grace, or the remission of sins and the righteousness of faith .

Prob. a.

In the gospel the bowels of God's mercy are opened, for the sake of Christ who remits sins to us and accepts us unto eternal life.

Luke 1: 7. In it is revealed the manifold wisdom of God, by which He found a temperament of justice and mercy, having destined and sent Christ as mediator, Eph.

3: 10. By the same is preached the divine virtue and power, 1 Cor. 1:24, because Christ most powerfully crushed the head of the infernal serpent, destroyed the works of the devil, and swallowed up death into victory.

Finally, there shines forth in the gospel the immutable and infallible truth of God, who, having exhibited His Son in the flesh, fulfilled the promise made to the fathers.

Prob. b.

The gospel is the power unto salvation to every one that believeth, Rom. 1:

16. For it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe, 1 Cor. 1:

31. The preaching of the gospel seems absurd to the incredulous; because it teaches one to seek salvation in the crucified, and life in the dead; but to believers, the preaching of the gospel is most wise and most salutary. Prob. c.

The righteousness of God is revealed in the gospel from faith to faith: As it is written: The just shall live by faith, Rom. 1:17.

By this is understood in this place imputed righteousness, which is through faith in Christ, Phil. 3:9.

It is called the righteousness of God, because it is imputed by the most merciful God to those believing in Christ unto salvation, Rom. 4:6.

In this consists the beatitude in the kingdom of grace.

Latin:

Quaest. VIII. Quid praedicat & offert nobis evangelium?

Evangelium praedicat & offert nobis gratiam Dei, meritum Christi, & parta ab eodem beneficia omnia .

Prob. 1) Compendium evangelii enuntiat ipse salutis auctor, Io. III, 6. Adeo dilexit Deus mundum, ut Filium suum vnigenitum daret, vt omnis, qui credit in ipsum, non pereat, sed vitam aeternam habeat. Ex quo evangelium gratia Dei appellatur, Act. XX, 24.

2) Evangelium Dei agit de Filio Dei, nato ex semine Dauidis, secundum carnem, Rom. I, 3. Est praedicatio Iesu Christi, Rom. XVI, 25. Praedicamus Christum crucifixum, Iudaeis quidem scandalum, Graecis vero stultitiam, ipsis vero vocatis tam Iudaeis, quam Graecis, Christum, Dei virtutem & sapientiam, 1 Cor. I, 23. 24.

3) Beneficia merito Christi parta varia sunt, quae Spiritus S. per evangelium, velut efficacissimum medium, nobis offert. Quod enim per evangelium vocemur ad ecclesiam, in eadem illuminemur, convertamur, regeneremur, Filii Dei reddamur, pace conscientiae donemur, iustificemur, cum Deo vniamur, renouemur, sanctificemur, in fide conferuemur, & glorificemur, in sect. praecedente per omnia capita ostendimus.

Quaest. IX. In quo formaliter consistit evangelium?

Evangelium formaliter consistit in promissione gratuita , & ordinata ad beatitudinem, in regno gratiae & gloriae obtinendam .

Prob. a. Gratuitam esse promissionem evangelicam, docet Apostolus, Rom. III, 23. 24. Omnes peccauerunt, & destituuntur gloria Dei, dum iustificantur (δωρεὰν) gratis gratia ipsius per redemptionem, quae est in Christo Iesu. Gratuita dicitur promissio evangelica, ex parte nostri, ideo, quod beneficia, in evangelio oblata, operibus nostris non sumus promeriti; non ex parte Christi, qui ea nobis promeritus est summo pretio sanguinis & vitae, 1 Cor. VI, 20. 1 Petr. I, 19.

Prob. b. Beatitudo in regno gratiae est remissio peccatorum & iustitia coram Deo valens. Beatitudo regni gloriae in plena Dei bonorumque coelestium fruitione consistit. Ad utramque, velut finem, divinitus ordinata est promissio evangelica. Qua de causa dicitur Evangelium regni Dei, Marc.

Evangelium regni Dei, Marc. I, 14. evangelium salutis nostrae, Eph. I, 13. verbum reconciliationis, 2 Cor. V, 18. verbum vitae aeternae. Io. VI, 68.

Quæst. X. Quis est finis evangelii?

Finis ultimus evangelii, ex parte Dei, est gloria misericordiae, sapientiae, potentiae & veritatis Dei . Finis ultimus, ratione hominum, est beatitudo gloriae, sive vita aeterna . Finis intermedius est beatitudo gratiae, sive remissio peccatorum & iustitia fidei .

Prob. a.

In evangelio aperiuntur viscera misericordiae Dei, propter Christum peccata nobis remittentis, & ad vitam aeternam nos acceptantis.

Luc. I, 7. Revelatur in illo multifaria sapientia Dei, qua invenit temperamentum iustitiae & misericordiae, destinato & misso mediatore Christo, Eph.

III, 10. Praedicatur eodem divina virtus & potentia 1 Cor. I, 24. quod Christus caput serpentis infernalis potentissime contriverit, opera diaboli destruxerit, & mortem in victoriam absorpserit.

Relucet denique in evangelio immutabilis & infallibilis veritas Dei, qui, exhibito filio suo in carne, promissionem factam patribus implevit.

Prob. b.

Evangelium est potentia in salutem omni credenti, Rom.

I, 16. Complacuit enim Deo per stultitiam praeconii salvare credentes, 1 Cor.

I, 31. Praedicatio evangelii incredulis videtur absurda; quia docet salutem in crucifixo, vitam in mortuo quaerere; at credentibus praedicatio evangelii est sapientissima & saluberrima. Prob. c.

Iustitia Dei in evangelio revelatur ex fide in fidem: Sicut scriptum est: Iustus vero ex fide vivet, Rom.

I, 17. Intelligitur h. l. iustitia imputata, quae est per fidem in Christum, Phil.

III, 9. Vocatur iustitia Dei, quia a Deo misericordissimo credentibus in Christum ad salutem imputatur, Rom.

IV, 6. In hoc consistit beatitudo in regno gratiae.


### On the Difference and Agreement of the Law and the Gospel

Note. The law and the gospel are distinct as the whole heaven in respect of nature (φύσεως); but in respect of practice (πράξεως) they are more conjoined than any mathematical point: and therefore here it is necessary to ὀρθοτομεῖν, to rightly divide the word of truth, 2 Tim.

2:15. Q.

XI. How do the law and the gospel differ? The moral law and the gospel differ: a) in the mode of manifestation and cognition: b) in respect of the object: c) in the diversity of promises: d) in the subject to whom they are to be proposed: e) in the disparity of their effects.

Prob. a. The law is in a certain way known from the light of nature; since it is implanted in the minds of men in the first creation, and not entirely extinguished by the fall, Rom.

2:15. The Gentiles show the work of the law written in their hearts; although a fuller knowledge of it, because of the corruption of the human intellect after the fall, must be sought from revelation, comprised in the scriptures.

But the gospel is a mystery, entirely hidden from human reason, brought forth by the Son of God from the bosom of the eternal Father, and revealed to us, John 1:18, Rom. 16:25.

Prob. b. The Law is the doctrine of works; for it prescribes and commands things to be done and things to be avoided.

Whence it is called the law of works, Rom. III, 27. The Gospel, however, is the doctrine of faith; for it proposes Christ the mediator, his merit, and the righteousness and salvation obtained by him to be embraced by faith; therefore it is called the law (doctrine) of faith, Rom. III, 27. the hearing of faith, Gal. III, 2. Prob. c. The promises of the Law are conditional and compensatory; which indeed promise life, but under the condition of personal, perfect, and perpetual obedience. The evangelical promises, however, are gratuitous; because they promise life not on account of personal obedience, but the obedience of another, namely Christ, apprehended by true faith. The evangelical promises are therefore absolute and unconditioned, not simply, but with respect to the legal and meritorious condition; although they do not exclude the evangelical condition, or faith, which lacks all merit, and the use of the means of faith .

Prob. I. Whatever pertains to the duties of man to be performed, insofar as they are duties, all that is to be attributed to the Law, which is the most perfect norm of all things, whether to be done or to be avoided; although the most valid moving arguments are to be drawn from the Gospel: for nothing moves and bends minds more to perform obedience willingly than the perception and grateful remembrance of the highest benefits, Luke I, 74. 75. John XIII, 34. 2 Cor. VII, 1. Tit. II, 11. 12. 1 John III, 16. IV, 11. 19. Whatever, however, is to be referred to the benefits of God reconciled, obtained by the merits of Christ, all that is to be brought to the Gospel (by definit

II. Whatever must be referred to promises, given the condition of obedience to be performed by man himself, and indeed perfect and perpetually continued, that is proper to the Law; Do this, and you shall live. Whatever on the contrary is of the kind of those promises which exhibit to every faithless man, provided he repents, the grace of God, reconciled to men through the vicarious obedience of Christ, to be received by true trust placed in Christ, that is proper to the Gospel: Believe, and you shall be saved. Concerning this significant difference of legal and evangelical promises, a most clear testimony exists Rom. X, 5. seqq.

III. Whatever pertains to convicting and knowing sins, insofar as they are sins, that is of the Law. Rom. III, 20. And indeed the thing itself speaks. For since the Law is the most perfect norm of all duties: it follows that the same is also the norm for knowing the neglect of all duties. Every ἀμαρτία (sin) is ἀνομία (lawlessness). 1 John III, 4. Scholion: The nature of sin, insofar as it is sin, must be distinguished from the Object, either in whom, or against whom one sins. Having observed this distinction, the answer to this opposition of the Antinomians is easy: does the Gospel convict of ἀπιστία (unbelief), and indeed that ἀπιστία, if anyone does not trust in Christ? I interpret that passage, John XVI, 9. not of the sin itself, but of the cause of all sins: ὅτι, because they do not wish to trust in me, therefore they cannot be freed from sin. See the opposite 2 Pet. I, 5.: ἐν τῇ πίστῃ τὴν ἀρετήν (in faith virtue). Whatever, however, pertains to the remission of sins and liberation, that is of the Gospel, Luke XXIV, 47. Acts X, 37. add. Rom. V, 1.

IV. Whatever looks to threatenings and punishments, denounced and to be inflicted upon man, that is of the Law. Rom. IV, 15. Gal. III, 10. Whatever, however, looks to grace and salvation, to be imparted to man, guilty of damnation, on account of Christ, that is of the Gospel. Acts XX, 24. Rom. I, 16. Scholion: The endurance of evils, which Christ bore for us, must be considered in a different way: Otherwise indeed in itself, insofar as it was a vicarious punishment; and this must be referred entirely to the Law: Otherwise, however, as to the end and use, that it might be the means of recovering grace and salvation, by which we might be freed from all punishment; and in this way it pertains entirely to the Gospel.

Proof d. The Law must be proposed and sharply inculcated to the impious and stubborn sinners, so that they may be led to contrition; the Gospel must be applied to the contrite, so that they may conceive faith in Christ.

Proof e. The Law accuses, convicts, condemns, and terrifies the delinquent of disobedience, as Paul testifies, Rom. III, 20; IV, 15; 2 Cor. III, 3; the Gospel, however, shows the Mediator, consoles, absolves, and gives life, as the angel testifies, Luke II, 10; and Christ, Luke IV, 18; and Paul, 2 Cor. III, 6.

Latin:

Observes. Lex & evangelium ratione φύσεως toto caelo sunt distincta; ratione πράξεως quovis puncto mathematico coniunctiora: adeoque hic oportet ὀρθοτομεῖν, recte secare verbum veritatis, 2 Tim.

II, 15. Quæst.

XI. Quomodo differunt lex & evangelium? Lex moralis & evangelium differunt: a) patefactionis & cognitionis modo: b) ratione obiecti: c) promissionum diversitate: d) subiecto, cui proponenda sunt: e) effectorum disparitate.

Prob. a. Lex ex lumine naturae quodammodo nota est; cum mentibus hominum in prima creatione sit insita, nec per lapsum prorsus exstincta, Rom.

II, 15. Gentes ostendunt opus legis scriptum in cordibus suis; quamvis plenior eius notitia, ob corruptionem intellectus humani post lapsum, ex revelatione, in scripturis comprehensa, petenda sit.

Evangelium autem mysterium est, humanae rationi plane absconditum, per Filium Dei ex sinu aeterni Patris prolatum, & nobis revelatum, Io. I, 18. Rom. XVI, 25.

Prob. b. Lex est doctrina operum; praescribit enim et praecipit facienda et fugienda.

Unde lex operum dicitur, Rom. III, 27. Evangelium vero est doctrina fidei; proponit enim Christum mediatorem, ipsius meritum, et eo partam iustitiam et salutem fidei amplectendam; idcirco dicitur lex (doctrina) fidei, Rom. III, 27. auditus fidei, Gal. III, 2. Prob. c. Promissiones legis sunt conditionales et compensatoriae; quae promittunt quidem vitam, sed sub conditione obedientiae propriae, perfectae et perpetuae. Promissiones autem evangelicae sunt gratuitae; quia promittunt vitam non ob obedientiam propriam, sed alienam, nempe Christi, vera fide apprehensam. Sunt igitur promissiones evangelicae absolutae et inconditionatae, non simpliciter, sed respectu conditionis legalis et meritoriae; licet non excludant conditionem evangelicam, sive fidem, quae omni caret merito, atque usum mediorum fidei .

Prob. I. Quidquid pertinet ad officia hominis praestanda, quatenus sunt officia, id omne tribuendum est legi, quae est perfectissima norma omnium, sive faciendorum, sive fugiendorum; licet argumenta moventia omnium validissima ex evangelio depromenda fiat: etenim nihil magis movet flectitque animos ad obsequium libenter praestandum, quam summorum beneficiorum perceptio et grata recordatio, Luc. I, 74. 75. Ioann. XIII, 34. 2 Cor. VII, 1. Tit. II, 11. 12. 1 Ioann. III, 16. IV, 11. 19. Quidquid vero referendum est ad beneficia Dei placati, promeritis Christi parta, id omne adferendum est Evangelio (per definit).

II. Quidquid referri debet ad promissiones, posita conditione obedientiae, ab homine ipso praestandae, et quidem perfectae ac perpetuo continuatae, illud est legis proprium; Fac hoc, et vives. Quidquid contra est ex genere earum promissionum, quae homini perfido cuique, modo resipiscat, gratiam Dei, per vicariam Christi obedientiam hominibus reconciliati, exhibent, accipiendam vera fiducia in Christo collocanda, illud est Evangelii proprium: Crede, et salvus eris. De hac insigni differentia promissionum legalium, et evangelicarum, clarissimum testimonium exstat Rom. X, 5. seqq.

III. Quidquid pertinet ad peccata arguenda et cognoscenda, quatenus sunt peccata, illud est legis. Rom. III, 20. Et profecto res ipsa loquitur. Quum enim lex sit perfectissima norma omnium officiorum: consequens est, ut eadem sit etiam norma cognoscendi neglectionem omnium officiorum. Omnis ἀμαρτία est ἀνομία. 1 Io. III, 4. Scholion: Natura peccati, quatenus est peccatum, distinguenda est ab Obiecto, vel in quo, vel in quod peccatur. Obferuata hac distinctione facilis est responsio ad hanc Antinomorum oppositionem: an ne evangelium arguat ἀπιστίαν, et eam quidem ἀπιστίαν, si quis Christo non confidit? Locum equidem illum, Ioann. XVI, 9. interpretor non de ipso peccato, sed de causa omnium peccatorum: ὅτι, quia nolunt mihi confidere, ideo non possunt peccato liberari. Oppositum vide 2 Pet. I, 5.: ἐν τῇ πίστῃ τὴν ἀρετήν. Quidquid autem pertinet ad peccatorum remissionem ac liberationem, illud est evangelii, Luc. XXIV, 47. Act. X, 37. add. Rom. V, 1.

IV. Quidquid spectat ad comminationes ac poenas, homini denuntiatas atque irrogandas, illud est legis. Rom. IV, 15. Gal. III, 10. Quidquid vero spectat ad gratiam ac salutem, homini, damnationis reo, propter Christum impertiendam, illud est evangelii. Act. XX, 24. Rom. I, 16. Scholion: Perpetio malorum, quae Christus pro nobis pertulit, diversa ratione est consideranda: Aliter quidem in se ipsa, quatenus fuit poena vicaria; atque haec omnino ad legem referri debet: Aliter autem, quantum ad finem atque usum, vt ea esset medium gratia et salutis recuperandae, quo nos omni poena liberaremur; atque hac ratione prorsus ad evangelium pertinet.

Prob. d. Lex proponenda & acriter inculcanda est impiis & contumacibus peccatoribus, vt ad contritionem perducantur; euangelium applicandum est contritis, vt fidem in Christum concipiant.

Prob. e. Lex delinquentes accusat inobedientiae, conuincit, damnat, terret, teste Paulo, Rom. III, 20. c. IV, 15. 2 Cor. III, 3; euangelium vero ostendit mediatorem, solatur, absoluit, viuificat, teste angelo, Luc. II, 10. & Christo, Luc. IV, 18. & Paulo, 2 Cor. III, 6.


### XII. How do the Law and the Gospel agree?

The Law and the Gospel agree in a) their author, b) the universality of their subject, c) the end intended in themselves, d) their duration.

Proof a. God is the author of the Law no less than of the Gospel.

Proof b. Just as the Law binds all men whatsoever to obedience, or, this failing, to punishment; so the Gospel proposes to all men the satisfaction and merit of Christ, to be apprehended by faith, for the obtaining of the remission of sins and eternal life, 1 Tim. II, 5, 6.

Proof c. The end of the Law and the Gospel, intended in themselves, is eternal life.

The Law promises eternal life under the condition of perfect obedience, Lev. XVIII, 5; Ezek. XX, 11; Luke X, 25, 28; Rom. X, 5.

The Gospel promises eternal life under the condition of faith, apprehending the satisfactionary obedience of Christ, Rom. X, 9, 10.

The accidental event of the Law is death.

The commandment, which was given to me for life, the same was found to be unto death, Rom. VII, 10.

By the same reasoning, the Gospel to some is a savor of death unto death, 2 Cor. II, 16.

Proof d. The moral Law is a perpetual norm of things to be done and things to be avoided, never abrogated, nor to be abrogated: And that the Gospel is to be preached in the Church until the end of the world is expressly stated in Matt. XXVIII, 20. Question

Latin:

Lex & euangelium conueniunt a) auctore, b) subiecti vniuersalitate, c) fine per se intento, d) duratione.

Prob. a. Deus est auctor legis non minus, quam euangelii.

Prob. b. Quemadmodum lex omnes omnino homines obligat ad obedientiam, vel hac deficiente, ad poenam; ita euangelium omnibus hominibus proponit satisfactionem & meritum Christi, fide apprehendendum, ad impetrandam remissionem & vitam aeternam, 1 Tim. II, 5. 6.

Prob. c. Finis legis & euangelii, per se intentus, est vita aeterna.

Lex promittit vitam aeternam sub conditione perfectae obedientiae, Leu. XVIII, 5. Ezech. XX, 11. Luc. X, 25. 28. Rom. X, 5.

Euangelium promittit vitam aeternam sub conditione fidei, obedientiam Christi satisfactionariam apprehendentis, Rom. X, 9. 10.

Euentus legis accidentalis est mors.

Praeceptum, quod mihi datum ad vitam, idem factum in mortem, Rom. VII, 10.

Pari ratione euangelium quibusdam est odor mortis ad mortem, 2 Cor. II, 16.

Prob. d. Lex moralis est norma faciendorum & fugiendorum perpetua, nunquam abrogata; nec abroganda: Et euangelium vsque ad finem mundi in ecclesia praedicandum esse, expresse dicitur Matth. XXVIII, 20.


### XIII. Are the Law and the Gospel joined in practice?

The Law and the Gospel are joined in practice at every mathematical point.

For they flow together a) toward the repentance of the sinner, b) toward the renewal of the justified man, c) toward the preservation of the renewed man in the perseverance of faith and piety.

Proof a. Repentance consists of two parts, contrition and faith, and thus is an apotelesma, or common effect of converting and regenerating grace.

The Law, in converting man, does what is its own by exciting or working contrition.

The Gospel, in regenerating man, also does what is its own by kindling faith in Christ.

Repentance, therefore, results as an apotelesma from the confluence of the Law and the Gospel.

Proof b. In sanctifying man, the Law is present as a normative principle, or as a rule of a holy life; for it prescribes and teaches what is to be done and what is to be omitted, and binds to obedience: but it does not confer new strength for a spiritual and holy life.

Therefore, the Gospel assists as a productive principle, which supplies the faculty and strength to man to walk rightly in the ways of the Lord.

Wherefore, the Law and the Gospel concur in one holy action in the business of renewal.

Proof c. The Law, with its comminations, moves the renewed man to suppress the desires of the flesh more strongly, lest, overcome by the flesh, he fall into mortal sin and fall away from faith.

The Gospel, with new strength conferred from time to time, confirms and increases faith, so that the renewed man may persevere in faith and holiness.

Add that only the Gospel shows the distinction between mortal and venial sin, as judged by Dr. Chemnitz, part II, loc. f. 225. Both forbid

law, so that the renewed man, acknowledging his own imperfection, may continue in daily repentance.

The Gospel raises up his soul, which is shaken by a sense of imperfect obedience and sin, by teaching that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who walk not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit, Rom. VIII, 1.

Latin:

Lex & euangelium in praxi quouis puncto mathematico sunt coniunctiora.

Confluunt enim ad paenitentiam peccatoris a), ad renouationem hominis iustificati b), ad conseruationem hominis renouati in perseuerantia fidei & pietatis c).

Prob. a. Paenitentia constat e duabus partibus, contritione & fide, adeoque est ἀποτέλεσμα, siue communis effectus gratiae conuertentis & regenerantis.

Lex in conuertendo homine agit, quod suum est, excitando vel operando contritionem.

Euangelium in homine regenerando etiam agit, quod suum est, accendendo fidem in Christum.

Resultat igitur paenitentia, tanquam ἀποτέλεσμα, ex confluxu legis & euangelii.

Prob. b. In sanctificando homine lex praesto est vt principium normatiuum, siue vt regula vitae sanctae; praescribit enim & docet, quae agenda, quaeque omittenda sint, & obligat ad obedientiam: non autem confert nouas vires ad vitam spiritualem & sanctam.

Succurrit igitur euangelium, vt principium productiuum, quod facultatem & vires homini suppeditat in viis Domini recte incedendi.

Quare ad vnam actionem sanctam concurrit lex & euangelium in negotio renouationis.

Prob. c. Lex comminationibus suis mouet hominem renouatum, vt desideria carnis comprimat fortius, ne a carne victus in peccatum mortale prolabatur, & fide excidat.

Euangelium collatis subinde nouis viribus fidem confirmat & auget, vt homo renouatus in fide & sanctitate perseueret.

Adiice, quod solum euangelium commonstret discrimen inter peccatum mortale & veniale, iudice D. Chemnitio part. II. loc. f. 225. Vtrumque prohibet

lex, vt renouatus, suam imperfectionem agnoscens, quotidianam pœnitentiam continuet.

Evangelium animum ipsius, imperfectæ obedientiæ ac peccati sensu labefacentem, erigit docendo, quod nihil condemnationis sit in iis, qui in Christo Iesu sunt, non secundum carnem ambulantes, sed secundum spiritum, Rom. VIII, 1.


### Q. XIV. Are all evangelical promises suspended upon the condition of faith?

Some evangelical promises, namely those concerning the remission of sins and the bestowing of eternal life, are suspended upon the condition of faith . However, other evangelical promises are given which are not made under the hypothesis of faith, but some regard and promise acts of grace which, by divine ordination, are directed toward the excitation of faith .

Proof a. If you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God has raised Him from the dead, it shall come to pass that you will be saved, Rom. X, 9. The evangelical promise is suspended upon the condition of faith, not as a work and merit, but as an ἀντιληπτικῆς (apprehensive) medium, or receptive organ, by which salvation procured by the merit of Christ is accepted.

Proof b. The calling to the church, illumination, conversion, and regeneration are acts of applying grace, which do not presuppose the condition of faith, but which precede faith in the order of nature, though not in time, and are directed and terminated toward its generation by divine τάξει (order). Cf. D. Calov. in synopsi controu. p. 625.

Latin:

Promissiones euangelicæ quædam, nimirum de remissione peccatorum & largienda vita æterna, suspensæ sunt a conditione fidei a). Dantur autem promissiones euangelicæ aliæ, quæ non sub hypothesi fidei factæ sunt, sed nonnullæ respiciunt & pollicentur actus gratiæ, qui ex ordinatione diuina ad excitationem fidei terminantur b).

Prob. a. Quod si confessus fueris ore tuo Dominum Iesum, & credideris in corde tuo, quod Deus ipsum resuscitauerit ex mortuis, futurum est, vt salueris, Rom. X, 9. Suspensa est promissio euangelica a conditione fidei, non vt operis & meriti, sed vt medii ἀντιληπτικῆς, siue organi receptiui, quo parta merito Christi salus acceptatur.

Prob. b. Vocatio ad ecclesiam, illuminatio, conuersio, regeneratio sunt actus gratiæ applicatricis, qui non præsupponunt conditionem fidei, sed qui fidem ordine naturæ, non tempore antecedunt, & ad illius generationem ex τάξει diuina diriguntur atque terminantur. Conf. D. Calov. in synopsi controu. p. 625.


### Q. XV. Are evangelical promises suspended upon the condition of works, or the perfect observance of the divine commandments?

Evangelical promises concerning the obtaining of the blessedness of grace and glory are not suspended upon the condition of works.

Proof 1) The Gospel is a proclamation of grace, Acts XX, 24. But grace is opposed to good works. For Paul writes explicitly, Rom. XI, 6: If by grace, then it is no longer of works: otherwise work is no longer work. Therefore, evangelical promises are gratuitous.

2) The moral law is a law of works; but the Gospel is a law (doctrine) of faith, Rom. III, 27. The sum of the moral law, therefore, is: Do! Gal. III, 12. The sum of the Gospel, however, is: Believe in Christ! Acts XVI, 31.

3) Therefore it is of faith, that it might be according to grace, that the promise might be sure to all the seed, Rom. IV, 16. If the evangelical promise were made under the condition of works, it would not be sure, by reason of us; because we would always have to doubt whether our works were so pure, holy, and perfect that through them righteousness and salvation could be obtained by us.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, who assert that evangelical promises require the condition of works.

Their arguments are: I. Christ says to the lawyer aspiring to eternal life: Do this, and you shall live! Luke X, 28. Therefore, Christ in His Gospel requires the condition of works from a man about to obtain eternal life. Resp. The question of the lawyer was legal, proposed in these words: What shall I do to inherit eternal life? But such as the question was, such was the answer. Hence Christ says: You shall love the Lord your God, etc.

Instance: The answer of Christ exists in the Gospel: Therefore it is evangelical. Resp. The Gospel is taken here in a special sense, insofar as it is opposed to the law.

II. The Gospel requires faith: Therefore also good works. The reason for the consequence is that faith is the mother of good actions. Resp. That faith generates good works in the justified, we readily grant;

ciles: but it is asked, whether the remission of sins and eternal life is promised under the condition of good works? Which we deny. Good works pertain to the renewal of man, not to justification or beatification: And the norm of good works is the law, not the gospel.

III. Whatever is promised under the condition of the mortification of the flesh, that is promised under the condition of a good work: But eternal life &c. E. The major is clear: because the mortification of the flesh is a good work, commanded by the ninth precept of the decalogue. The minor is proved from Rom. VIII, 13. If by the spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, you shall live. Resp. I distinguish between the condition of the subject, to whom the possession of eternal life happens, and between the condition of the thing, under which eternal life is promised. The mortification of the flesh is a condition of the subject, preceding eternal life in the order of antecedence, not of causality; since it becomes neither a means of salvation, nor a meritorious cause of eternal life.

Latin:

Promissiones euangelicæ de obtinenda beatitudine gratiæ & gloriæ non sunt suspensæ a conditione operum.

Prob. 1) Euangelium est concio gratiæ, Act. XX, 24. Sed gratia bonis operibus opponitur. Etenim Paullus diserte scribit, Rom. XI, 6. Si ex gratia, iam non ex operibus: fin ex operibus, iam non ex gratia: alioquin opus iam non est opus. Sunt ergo promissiones euangelicæ gratuitæ.

2) Lex moralis est lex operum; euangelium autem est lex (doctrina) fidei, Rom. III, 27. Legis itaque moralis summa est: Fac! Gal. III, 12. Euangelii vero summa est: Crede in Christum! Act. XVI, 31.

3) Propterea ex fide, vt fit iuxta gratiam, vt fit firma promissio omni semini, Rom. IV, 16. Si promissio euangelica facta esset sub conditione operum, illa non esset firma, ratione nostri; quia nobis semper ambigendum foret, an nostra opera adeo pura, sancta & perfecta sint, vt per ea nobis iustitia & salus obtingere queat.
