Temporibus veteris testamenti promissa est vita aeterna, sed minus clare, & innotuit tantum populo Israëlitico; at Christus per evangelium viam ad vitam aeternam manifestavit clarius, remotis umbris figurarum, eamque notificavit toti mundo.

S V S P I R I V M.

Aduolutus ad pedes misericordiae tuae, o Deus aeterne, Pater clementissime, gratias tibi ago tantas, quantas mente capere possum maximas, pro patefacto evangelio tuo de conferenda nobis aeterna salute, propter merita Christi.

Hoc verbum gratiae docet me tremefactum, comparatione æterna salute, propter merita Christi. Hoc verbum gratiæ docet me tremefactum, comparatione mei cum praeceptis divinis, & haud ignarum imperfectionis meae, confugere in sinum Christi, & sub ipsius bonitate, tanquam firmissimo clypeo, tutum aduersus ea, quae lex minatur, supplicia delitescere.

Hoc euangelium pacis confirmat, Christum nobis, qui certa in ipsum fide nitimur, iustitiam sua obedientia, quietem suis laboribus, solatium suis cruciatibus, vitam denique sua morte peperisse. Proinde euangelio Christi nullus mihi thesaurus est pretiosior, nullus cibus dulcior, nullum medicamen salubrius, nulla lux serenior. Etenim hac luce tendentibus ad patriam caelestem via expedita ostenditur: Hoc medicamine vulnera conscientiae sanantur: Hoc cibo esurientes iustitiam reficiuntur: Hoc thesauro pauperes spiritu ditantur. Reconde, o Spiritus Sancte, hunc thesaurum in anima mea, quo, opibus huius saeculi spretis calcatisque, unice bona caelestia desiderem, quaeram, inueniam, possideam. Et tu, o anima mea, Iesum, salutis tuae auctorem & vindicem, vera fide apprehende, apprehensum retine, retentum cole sanctis cogitationibus, piis precibus, & actionibus euangelio dignis.


## 30 On the Sacraments in General, and of the Old Testament


### Q. XIV. Are also infants foundlings, to be baptized?

II. CAPVT III. ON THE SACRAMENTS IN GENERAL, AND ON THE SACRAMENTS OF THE OLD TESTAMENT IN SPECIE.

Q. I. What is a sacrament?

A sacrament is a sacred and solemn action, divinely instituted, by which God, through the intervening ministry of man, by an external and visible element, joined with the word of institution, exhibits a heavenly thing to each one using it, for the purpose of offering to all men, and conferring upon believers, and sealing the evangelical grace .

Obj. I. Varro, in book IV of the Latin language, derives sacramentum from sacrum, so that it denotes a sacred thing; Vegetius, however, in book II of military affairs, ch. 5, derives it from sacrando, i.e., from dedicating and consecrating.

Obj. II. The name of sacramentum among profane authors sustains a double meaning. a) It signifies money deposited with the pontiff in a sacred place, so that when the lawsuit was finished, the victor might reclaim his own intact, but the money of the vanquished would yield to the treasury, to be spent on sacred uses, as Varro notes in book IV of the Latin language; although afterwards the word sacramentum was used more loosely for any pledge, as Cicero testifies in book I of the Orator. b) It denotes an oath, especially a military one.

Obj. III. The word sacramentum is not explicitly read in the sacred code; but just as it is of Latin origin, so in the Hebrew and Greek language of the Old and New Testament, no certain word is found that corresponds exactly to it. Tertullian was the first, in his book On the Soldier's Crown, to use the word sacramentum to denote the act by which those to be baptized bind themselves to God, and religiously promise that they will strenuously fight under the banner of Christ against Satan, the world, and the flesh.

Whence it came about that not only the whole rite of baptism, but also the sacred supper was called a sacrament.

Obj. IV. The word sacramentum in the ecclesiastical sense is taken a) most generally, b) more specially, c) most specially. It is taken most generally for hidden and secret things; as it is used in the Latin version, 1 Tim. 3:16, Eph. 5: 32.

It is taken more specially for an external sign of a sacred and heavenly thing, e.g., the rainbow in the clouds, the fleece of Gideon, the sun moving backward can be called sacraments. It is taken most specially for a sign and means of conferring and sealing divine grace; and in this last meaning, which belongs to this place, it denotes either ὅλικῶς (wholly) the entire sacramental action, encompassing both the earthly and heavenly thing, or μερικῶς (partially), the other essential part, namely the external symbol, or the earthly thing, e.g., water in baptism, bread and wine in the sacred supper.

Obj. V. Sacramentum is called in Greek μυστήριον. The name μύσης, from which it is immediately derived, denotes a man initiated into sacred rites; μύω signifies to initiate into sacred rites. See Phil. 4:12. μύω descends from μύω, to close; because among the Greeks, the mystae were bound μύειν τὸ στόμα, to close the mouth, and to say nothing of those things which they had perceived, lest the authority of the sacred rites should become cheap.

Moreover, it is very much to be noted that while every sacrament is a mystery, not every mystery is a sacrament properly so called.

The spiritual marriage of Christ and the church is a μέγα μυστήριον, Eph. 5:32, but not a sacrament properly so called.

Q.

It is required for a sacrament, properly so called: a) That it be an action divinely instituted and commanded: b) That it have an external and visible element, united with a heavenly thing, by means of the word of institution: c) That it have the promise of evangelical grace.

Obj. These general requirements of the sacraments are to be deduced from those things which are handed down in Holy Scripture specifically concerning individual sacraments.

Q.

III. Is a sacrament to be defined by an action? A sacrament is rightly defined by an action a) sacred b) and solemn c).

Proof a. All preceptive words concerning the sacraments conceived in the Holy Scriptures 1) command an action, e.g., Circumcise, Gen. 17:11; take the lamb, slaughter it, Exod. 12:3; baptize, Matt. 28:19; take, eat, drink, do this, Matt. 26:26.

2) The form of the sacrament consists in δόσει καὶ λήψει, in distribution and reception, and therefore in action.

3) Outside of use, i. e., sacramental use, it is not a sacrament.

Prob. b. A sacrament is a sacred action: because 1) it has as its author the most holy God, by whose word it is consecrated, and 2) it is destined for a sacred use.

Prob. c. A sacrament is a solemn action, i. e., serious, clear, certain, not ludic, jocular, or mimic; just as Sozomen, book II, ch. 16, commemorates that Athanasius as a boy baptized little children not yet initiated into the sacred rites.

An antithesis is that of the Anabaptists, Schwenckfeldians, and Weigelians, for whom the sacraments are only external signs; to whom the Papists partly accede, in whose opinion the sacraments of the Old Testament were only signs. Their principal arguments are: I. All types are signs; because they signify and prefigure the antitype: But the sacraments of the O. T. are types. Therefore, the minor is evident: because circumcision prefigured the shedding of Christ's blood, the paschal lamb his death, 1 Cor. 5:7. Resp. Distinguish between theoretical and practical signs. The former signify and of themselves effect nothing: The latter not only signify, but also effect something, and of this class are the sacraments, and therefore they formally consist in action.

II. Whatever seals federal grace, that is a sign: But the sacraments, etc. Therefore. Resp. To seal federal grace pertains to the end, or use of the sacraments, not to their essential constitution.

Instance. But Augustine defines sacraments by visible signs of invisible grace. Resp. That description, taken from the final cause, is not an adequate definition .

Latin:

II. CAPVT III. DE SACRAMENTIS IN GENERE, ET DE SACRAMENTIS VETERIS TESTAMENTI IN SPECIE.

Quæst. I. Quid est sacramentum?

Sacramentum est sacra & solemnis actio, diuinitus instituta, qua Deus interueniente hominis ministerio, per externum & visibile elementum, cum verbo institutionis coniunctum, rem caelestem singulis vtentibus exhibet, ad offerendam omnibus hominibus, & conferendam credentibus, atque obsignandam gratiam euangelicam .

Obs. I. Sacramentum VARRO libr. IV. de lingua latina deriuat a sacro, vt notet rem sacram; VEGETIVS vero libr. II. de re milit. c. 5. deducit a sacrando, i. e. dedicando & consecrando.

Obs. II. Nomen sacramenti apud auctores profanos duplicem sustinet significationem. a) Significat pecuniam, apud pontificem in loco sacro depositam, vt lite finita victor suam integram repeteret, victi autem pecunia ærario cederet, vsibus sacris impendenda, monente VARRONE, libr. IV. de latina lingua; quamuis postea laxius usurpata sit vox sacramenti pro quouis pignore, teste CICERONE libr. I. de oratoribus. b) Notat iuramentum, præcipue vero militare.

Obs. III. Vox, sacramentum, in codice sacro expresse non legitur; sed sicut origine latina est, ita in hebræo atque græco sermone V. & N. T. non reperitur vox certa, quæ illi exacte respondeat. Primus TERTULLIANUS L. de corona militis vocem, sacramentum, adhibuit ad denotandum actum, quo baptizandi Deo se obligant, ac religiose promittunt, se sub vexillo Christi contra Satanam, mundum & carnem strenue pugnaturos esse.

Vnde factum est, vt non tantum totus ritus baptismi, sed & cœna sacra sacramentum diceret.

Obs. IV. Vox, sacramentum, in sensu ecclesiastico sumitur a) generalissime, b) specialius, c) specialissime. Generalissime accipitur pro requais arcana & secreta; quomodo usurpatur in versione latina, 1 Tim. III, 16. Eph. V, 32. Specialius accipitur pro signo externo rei sacræ & cœlestis, v. gr.

Iris in nubibus, vellus Gideonis, sol retrogradus sacramenta vocari possunt. Specialissime accipitur pro signo & medio conferendæ & obsignandæ gratiæ diuinæ; atque in hac postrema significatione, quæ huius loci est, notat vel ὅλικῶς totam actionem sacramentalem, complectentem utramque rem terrenam & cœlestem, vel μερικῶς, alteram partem essentialem, videlicet symbolum externum, seu rem terrenam, v. gr. aquam in baptismo, panem & vinum in sacra cœna.

Obs. V. Sacramentum græce appellatur μυστήριον. Nomen μύσης, a quo proxime deriuatur, notat hominem sacris initiatum, μύω significat sacris initio, instituo. Vid. Phil. IV, 12. Descendit μύω a μύω, claudo; quia apud Græcos mystæ tenebantur μύειν τὸ στόμα, os claudere, & nihil eorum dicere, quæ ipsi perceperant, ne sacrorum auctoritas vilesceret.

Ceterum oppido notandum est, quod omne quidem sacramentum fit mysterium, sed non omne mysterium sacramentum proprie dictum.

Spirituale coniugium Christi & ecclesiæ est μέγα μυστήριον, Eph. V, 32. sed non sacramentum proprie dictum.

Quæst. II. Quænam sunt requisita sacramenti proprie dicti essentialia?

Requiritur ad sacramentum, proprie dictum: a) Vt fit actio diuinitus instituta & mandata: b) Vt habeat elementum externum & visibile, cum re cœlesti, mediante verbo institutionis, vnitum: c) Vt habeat promissionem gratiæ euangelicæ.

Obs. Requisita hæc generalia sacramentorum deducenda sunt ex iis, quæ in specie de singulis sacramentis in scriptura S. traduntur.

Quæst. III. Estne sacramentum definiendum per actionem?

Sacramentum recte definitur per actionem a) sacram b) & solemnem c).

Prob. a. Omnia verba præceptiua de sacramentis in sacris litteris concepta 1) actionem imperant, v. gr. Circumcidite, Gen. XVII, 11. agnum tollite, mactate, Exod. XII, 3. baptizate, Matth. XXVIII, 19. accipite, edite, bibite, hoc facite, Matth. XXVI, 26.

2) Forma sacramenti consistit in δόσει καὶ λήψει, in distributione & acceptione, adeoque in actione.

3) Extra usum, i. e. sacramentalem, non est sacramentum.

Prob. b. Sacramentum est actio sacra: quia 1) auctorem habet Deum sanctissimum, cuius verbo consecratur, & 2) ad sacrum usum destinatur.

Prob. c. Sacramentum est actio solemnis, i. e. feria, clara, certa, non ludicra, iocosa, aut mimica; sicut Sozomenus libr. II. c. 16. commemorat, Athanasium puerum baptizasse puerulos, nondum sacris initiatos.

Antithesis est Anabaptistarum, Schwenckfeldianorum & Weigelianorum, quibus sacramenta sunt tantum externa signa; quibus ex parte accedunt Pontificii, quorum opinione sacramenta veteris Testamenti fuerunt tantum signa. Praecipua eorum argumenta sunt: I. Omnes typi sunt signa; quia signant & praefigurant antitypum: Atqui sacramenta V. T. sunt typi. E. Minor patet: quia circumcisio praefiguravit effusionem sanguinis Christi, agnus paschalis ipsius mortem, 1 Cor. V, 7. Resp. Dist. inter signa theoretica, & practica. Illa signant & per se nihil efficiunt: Haec non tantum signant, sed etiam aliquid efficiunt, e quorum censu sunt sacramenta, adeoque formaliter in actione consistunt.

II. Quidquid gratiam foederalem obsignat, illud est signum: Atqui sacramenta &c. E. Resp. Obsignare gratiam foederalem pertinet ad finem, sive usum sacramentorum, non ad eorum essentialem constitutionem.

Instantia. Sed Augustinus definit sacramenta per signa visibilia invisibilis gratiae. Resp. Descriptio illa a causa finali petita non est adaequata definitio .


### Quaest. IV. Who instituted the sacraments?

Who instituted the sacraments? God instituted the sacraments a) and our Lord Jesus Christ, who also established the sacraments of the N. T. as man b) .

Prob. a. 1) God alone is the author of salvation and the fountain of grace. Therefore, God alone possesses the authority and power of ordaining the means of salvation and the seals of grace.

2) By induction of all the sacraments. For God himself prescribed circumcision as a sacrament to be observed by Abraham, Gen. 17:10, and likewise Moses that other sacrament of the O.T., Exod. 12:3. In the N.T. the institution of baptism is expressly attributed to God, John 1:33, as is the institution of the Holy Supper, 1 Cor. 11:23.

Prob. b. 1) In general. According to the same nature by which our Christ is mediator, according to that same nature he ordained the sacraments as means of salvation. But he is our mediator also according to his human nature. Therefore, he also ordained the sacraments as means of salvation according

2) In particular: a) Concerning baptism, from Matt. 28:19, where Christ says: Go, teach, and baptize all nations. He who said this was Christ resurrected from the dead, and the disciples appearing to the disciples, v. 17. to whom all power has been given in heaven and on earth, v. 18. But indeed he was resurrected, appeared to the disciples, and received power in time, according to his human nature. Concerning the holy supper from Matth. XXVI, 26. where Christ says: Take, eat my body, and drink my blood. The God-man has body and blood, according to his human nature. Therefore, also according to his human nature, he is the author and institutor of the holy supper.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, who deny that Christ, as man, is the primary author of the sacraments. Who argue: Whoever does not have divine power, he cannot principally establish sacraments: But Christ is man &c. Therefore. Resp. I deny the minor; because Christ, as man, has divine power, not indeed of himself, but yet by the grace of the personal union. The institution of the sacraments belongs to Christ, as God, and as man: as God indeed, by divine authority, and that essential; but as man, by the same authority and power, but communicated to him by virtue of the personal union.

Quæst. V. What impelled God to the institution of the sacraments? Internally, mercy moved God to establish the sacraments, to which the infirmity and misery of fallen man provided the occasion for showing mercy ). Externally, the merit of Christ the mediator impelled him ).

Prob. a. It is of the most liberal divine goodness that God ratified a covenant with sinful man, and annexed to this covenant the sacraments, the seals of grace, Gen. XVII, 10. Matth. XXVI, 28. 1 Petr. III, 21. The propitious Deity went to consult the infirmity of fallen man, whose will, manifested by audible word, he captured, which he strengthened with visible words, so that the promise of grace which man received with his ears, he might behold the pledges and seals of it with his eyes. Chrysostom says excellently in homil. LX to the people of Antioch: If you were incorporeal, God would hand over incorporeal gifts to you nakedly: but because your soul is united to a body, those things are handed over to you to be understood in corporeal things. Thus, after the fall, sacrifices immediately followed the gospel, the rainbow the Noachic covenant, circumcision the Abrahamic covenant, the paschal lamb and many sacrifices the Mosaic covenant: Thus, in the evangelical covenant in the new Testament, the sacraments, baptism and the Lord's supper, have been added.

Prob. b. In Christ the mediator we are blessed with every spiritual blessing, Eph. I, 3. which blessing the sacraments offer, confer, and seal.

Quæst. VI. To whom did God entrust the dispensing of the sacraments? God entrusted the right of dispensing the sacraments to the church ), which, for the sake of observing order and decency (εὐσχημοσύνης), has commended the execution or exercise of this right to the called and ordained ministers of the divine word ). In the case, however, of extreme necessity, where the sacrament is necessary, and cannot be omitted except at the peril of salvation, any Christian man can validly celebrate the sacrament of initiation ).

Prob. a. 1) Because the church is the bride of Christ, John III, 29, whose ornaments are the sacraments. 2) Because the church is the house of God, and the pillar and foundation of the truth, 1 Tim. III, 14. This house manages the treasure of the sacraments: This pillar guards the heavenly truth, and its seals, namely the sacraments.

Prob. b. 1) Because the ministers of the church are stewards, or dispensers of the mysteries of God, 1 Cor. IV, 1. The sacraments also pertain to the divine mysteries.

2) Because no one (in ecclesiastical matters) takes this honor to himself, but he who is called, like Aaron, Heb. V, 4. 3) Because Christ specifically instructed the Apostles: Baptize! Matt. XXVIII, 39. Do this! Luke XXII, 19. Prob. c. Because all Christians are spiritual kings and priests, 1 Pet. II, 9. Rev. I, 5. Therefore, with necessity pressing, they use the right of the spiritual priesthood, which the faithful possess as members by the priestly office of their head, Jesus Christ, Eph. I, 22. IV, 16. V, 25, 26.

Latin:

Sacramenta instituit Deus a) & Dominus noster Iesus Christus, qui sacramenta N. T. etiam qua homo condidit b) .

Prob. a. 1) Solus Deus est auctor salutis & fons gratiae. E. solus Deus pollet auctoritate & potestate ordinandi media salutis, & figilla gratiae.

2) Inductione omnium sacramentorum. Deus enim ipse circumcisionem sacramentum Abrahamo praescripsit obferuandum, Gen. XVII, 10. nec non Mosi alterum illud V. T. sacramentum, Exod. XII, 3. In N. T. baptismi institutio diserte tribuitur Deo, Io. I, 33. vt & institutio S. coenae, 1 Cor. XI, 23.

Prob. b. 1) In genere. Secundum quam naturam Christus noster est mediator, secundum eandem sacramenta salutis media ordinavit. Atqui etiam secundum humanam naturam noster est mediator. E. etiam secundum naturam humanam sacramenta salutis media ordinavit.

2) In specie: a) De baptismo, ex Matth. XXVIII, 19. vbi Christus inquit: Euntes docete, & baptizate omnes gentes. Qui hoc dixit, fuit Christus a mortuis resuscitatus, & discipulis apparens, v. 17. cui est data omnis potestas in caelo & in terra, v. 18. At vero resuscitatus est, apparuit discipulis, & potestatem accepit in tempore, secundum humanam naturam. De s. coena ex Matth. XXVI, 26. vbi Christus dicit: Accipite, edite corpus meum, & bibite sanguinem meum. Corpus & sanguinem habet θεάνθρωπος, secundum humanam naturam. E. etiam secundum humanam naturam est auctor & institutor s. coenae.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, negantium, Christum, qua hominem, esse primarium auctorem sacramentorum. Qui argumentantur: Quicunque non habet potestatem diuinam, ille non potest principaliter condere sacramenta: Atqui Christus homo &c. E. Resp. Neg. minorem; quia Christus, qua homo, habet potestatem diuinam non quidem per se, attamen per unionis personalis gratiam. Competit institutio sacramentorum Christo, qua Deo, & qua homini: qua Deo quidem, auctoritate diuina, ipsique essentiali; qua homini autem, auctoritate & potestate eadem, sed vi unionis personalis ipsi communicata.

Quæst. V. Quid impulit Deum ad institutionem sacramentorum? Deum ad condendum sacramenta interne mouit misericordia, cui miserendi occasionem praebuit hominis lapsi infirmitas & miseria ). Externe impulit ipsum meritum Christi mediatoris ).

Prob. a. Liberalissima bonitatis diuinae est, quod Deus cum homine peccatore foedus sanciuit, & huic foederi sacramenta, sigilla gratiae, annexuit, Gen. XVII, 10. Matth. XXVI, 28. 1 Petr. III, 21. Propitium Numen consultum iuit infirmitati hominis lapsi, cui voluntatem suam verbo audibili manifestatam capiiuit, quam verbis visibilibus firmauit, vt quam promissionem gratiae auribus acciperet homo, illius pignora & sigilla oculis conspiceret. Praeclare inquit Chrysostomus homil. LX. ad pop. Antiochen. Si incorporeus esses, Deus tibi dona incorporea nude traderet: sed quia anima tua corpori est unita, in rebus corporeis ea tibi intelligenda traduntur. Sic post lapsum euangelio statim accessere sacrificia, pacto Noachico iris, pacto Abrahamico circumcisio, pacto Mosaico agnus paschalis, & sacrificia plura: Sic pacto euangelico in nouo Testamento addita sunt sacramenta, baptismus & coena dominica.

Prob. b. In Christo mediatore benedicimur omni benedictione spirituali, Eph. I, 3. quam benedictionem sacramenta offerunt, conferunt & obsignant.

Quæst. VI. Cui dispensanda sacramenta Deus concredidit? Ius dispensandi sacramenta Deus concredidit ecclesiae ), quae executionem aut exercitium huius iuris, obseruandi ordinis & εὐσχημοσύνης caussa, commendauit ministris verbi diuini vocatis & ordinatis ). In casu autem extremae necessitatis, vbi sacramentum est necessarium, nec nisi periculo salutis omitti potest, quilibet homo christianus sacramentum initiationis valide celebrare potest ).

Prob. a. 1) Quia ecclesia est sponsa Christi, Ioann. III, 29. cuius ornamenta sunt sacramenta. 2) Quia ecclesia est domus Dei, & columna & firmamentum veritatis, 1 Tim. III, 14. Haec domus affertuat thesaurum sacramentorum: Haec columna custodit veritatem caelestem, eiusque signacula, nempe sacramenta.

Prob. b. 1) Quia ministri ecclesiae sunt oeconomi, siue dispensatores mysteriorum Dei, 1 Cor. IV, 1. Ad mysteria diuina pertinent etiam sacramenta. mysteria diuina pertinent etiam sacramenta.

2) Quia nemo (in ecclesiasticis) sibi sumit honorem, nisi qui vocatus est, instar Aaronis, Hebr. V, 4. 3) Quia Christus peculiariter instruxit Apostolos: Baptizate! Matth. XXVIII, 39. Hoc facite! Luc. XXII, 19. Prob. c. Quia omnes Christiani sunt spirituales reges & sacerdotes, 1 Petr. II, 9. Apoc. I, 5. Vrgente igitur necessitate vtuntur iure spiritualis sacerdotii, quod habent fideles, tanquam membra ex officio sacerdotali capitis sui, Iesu Christi, Eph. I, 22. IV, 16. V, 25. 26.


### Q. VII. Can the church change anything in the sacraments?

The church can change nothing in the substantial parts of the sacraments . It enjoys, however, the liberty of changing something in the circumstances of the sacraments .

Prob. a. Because the church is not the master of the sacraments, and therefore cannot change the essence of the sacraments (which consists in the indivisible), e.g., it cannot take away the cup instituted by Christ from the supper. But Christ uses the church, 1) as a messenger and promulgator of the institution, once made by God, and as a treasurer, which only preserves the treasure (κειμήλιον) and transfers it to posterity, 3) as an effective minister and steward, through whom Christ works, 1 Cor. I. 4) as an arranger and decorator, as far as external solemnity and circumstantial ceremonies are concerned. Cf. D. DANNHAUER in hodof. p. 1008. Prob. b.

The church has the power of arranging that all things be done decently and in order, 1 Cor. XIV, 40. Thus the Christian church, for the sake of the sick, whose infirmity does not support baptismal immersion, changed immersion into aspersion. While SABELLIUS was raging, who attacked the Most Holy Trinity, the rite of triple immersion was observed with singular care; but while ARIUS was raging, who denied the unity of the Father and the Son, baptism was performed by one immersion. Against EBION, who urged unleavened bread, leavened bread was used by the church; against the Greeks, who fought fervently for leavened bread, unleavened bread was received. Cf. B. BROCHMAND in loc. de sacrament. p. 1039.

Latin:

Ecclesia nihil mutare potest in substantialibus sacramentorum a). Gaudet tamen libertate aliquid mutandi in circumstantiis sacramentorum b).

Prob. a. Quia ecclesia non est domina sacramentorum, ideoque essentiam sacramentorum (quae consistit in indiuisibili) mutare non potest, v. gr. calicem a Christo institutum non potest coenae adimere. Sed vtitur Christus ecclesia, 1) vt nuntia ac promulgatrice institutionis, semel a Deo factae, & thesauraria, quae κειμήλιον tantum conferuat, & ad posteritatem transfert, 3) vt ministra & oeconoma efficace, per quam Christus operatur, 1 Cor. I. 4) vt ordinatrice & ornatrice, quod ad externam solemnitatem & caerimonias circumstantiales attinet. Conf. D. DANNHAVERVS in hodof. p. 1008.

Prob. b. Ecclesia habet potestatem disponendi, vt omnia decenter & secundum ordinem fiant, 1 Cor. XIV, 40. Sic ecclesia Christiana in gratiam aegrotorum, quorum infirmitas immersionem baptismalem non sustinet, immersionem in aspersionem mutauit. Grafante SABELLIO, qui S. S. Trinitatem impugnabat, trinae immersionis ritus singulari cura obseruatus fuit; at furente ARIO, qui vnitatem Patris & Filii negabat, vna immersio baptismus peragebatur. Contra EBIONEM, qui panem azymum vrgebat, adhibitus est ab ecclesia panis fermentatus; contra Graecos pro fermentato feruide pugnantes, azymus receptus. Conf. B. BROCHMAND. in loc. de sacrament. p. 1039.


### Q. VIII. Is a sacrament effective, administered by a minister of the church whose life is impure?

By reason of propriety (τῆς εὐσχημοσύνης), or decorum, sincere piety is required in a minister of the church . However, the efficacy of the sacrament does not depend on the minister, or steward, but on the master, or author, God.

Prob. a. 1) Because it is necessary for a bishop to be blameless (δεῖ τὸν ἐπίσκοπον ἀνεπιλήπτον εἶναι), 1 Tim. III, 3. 2) Because the minister is an ambassador of Christ, whom he ought to imitate, and a vicar of the whole church, whose ornaments he ought to reflect. Prob. b.

1) Because neither he who plants, nor he who waters, is anything, but God, who gives the increase, 1 Cor. III, 7. Therefore, the efficacy of the sacraments does not depend on the minister of the church planting or watering, but on God, who bestows the increase. The reason is: because the minister in the order toward the effect of the sacrament does not act, except instrumentally. But every instrument acts, not according to its own form, but according to the virtue of him by whom it is moved. 2) Just as the unbelief of men cannot make the faith of God of no effect, Rom. III, 3: So the malice of the minister cannot hinder the goodness of God, who infuses the sacraments. The Augsburg Confession teaches this, Art. VIII. Although the church is properly the congregation of saints and true believers; yet since in this life many hypocrites and evil men are mixed in, it is permitted to use the sacraments. which are administered by the wicked according to the voice of Christ, Matt. XXIII, 2. The scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses' seat, etc. And the sacraments and the word are effective because of the ordination and command of Christ, even if they are exhibited by the wicked.

The antithesis is that of the Donatists and Anabaptists, who ascribe the efficacy of the sacraments to the piety of the ministers.

They rely chiefly on this argument: Whoever does not have the Holy Spirit cannot confer the benefits of the Holy Spirit upon another: But a wicked minister, etc.

Therefore. The major premise is proven: because what one does not have, one cannot give to another.

Response.

Distinguish between the principal cause and the instrumental cause. What the principal cause does not have (formally or eminently), it cannot impart to another.

But through an instrumental agent, that which is not in the agent itself can be conferred: for example, air is a vehicle of speech to a friend standing far away; yet the air itself is devoid of speech.

Question IX.

Is the intention of the minister required for the integrity and efficacy of the sacraments?

Proof a. Because external intention is legitimate administration and formal use, outside of which there is no sacrament.

For it is an instrument of grace and salvation, and thus consists in use, in conformity with divine institution.

Proof b. It is the duty of the minister of the church, τὴν διακονίαν αὐτοῦ πληροφορεῖν, to fulfill his ministry, 2 Tim.

IV, 5. which requires accurate intention.

Proof c.

1) If the integrity and efficacy of the sacrament were to be judged by the intention of the minister, every consolation to be drawn from the sacraments would completely expire, and the entire efficacy of the sacraments would be uncertain, contrary to the manifest utterances of the Holy Spirit, John III, 5.

Gal. III, 27.

Matt. XXVI, 28.

John VI, 51.

For since it is not given to man to penetrate the recesses of another's breast, how could anyone be certain of the intention of the baptizer, and consequently of the efficacy of the baptism?

2) Just as the unbelief of men cannot make the faith of God void, Rom. III, 3: so a defect of good intention in the minister does not make the divine intention void.

3) The audible word, in the absence of the minister's good intention, is effective; since some preach Christ even out of envy and strife, Phil. I, 15.

Therefore, the visible sacrament is effective in the absence of good intention.

4) Zipporah, out of anger, without due intention, circumcised her son, Exod.

IV, 26. and that circumcision was valid.

Therefore.

The sacrament is valid without the due intention of the minister.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, who suspend the efficacy of the sacrament upon the good intention of the minister.

Their arguments are: I. Every proairetic (deliberate) action is done with the intention of acting (for it proceeds from one who knows and wills): The administration of the sacrament is a proairetic action: Therefore.

Response.

Distinguish between the internal intention of the minister and the external. Every proairetic action requires the external intention of the minister, conformable to the will of the Lord, although the internal intention of the minister is not always good: e.g.

If a servant of some liberal master were to pursue you with hatred, and were ordered by

External intention, which consists in the application of all the sacramental words and actions, for this end and in the manner which Christ instituted, is entirely necessary for the essential integrity of the sacrament a).

Internal intention is indeed required for the decorum of the minister, so that he may bring an attentive and present mind to his office, not a sleepy one, not one wandering elsewhere b).

If, however, either out of negligence or out of malice he is not intent, the defect of internal intention does not hinder the salutary effect of the sacrament c).

to the master to hand over to you a hundred gold pieces, he might bring the money with an external intention, conforming to the master's command, even if his internal intention were not good.

II. In every faithful and prudent servant a good intention is required: Every minister of the sacraments is a faithful and prudent servant, Matt. 24:45. Therefore. Resp. A good intention is required by reason of decorum and office, but not by reason of absolute necessity for the integrity and efficacy of the sacrament.

III. If the intention of the minister were not necessary for the integrity of the sacrament, baptism in a bath, and the eucharist at a banquet, or otherwise conferred through play and jest, would be legitimate sacraments: The consequent is absurd: Therefore the antecedent is also. Resp. I deny the consequent. Jocular baptism and ludic eucharist are not sacraments, not because the intention of the minister is lacking, but because it pertains to the essence of the sacrament that it be a sacred and solemn action, to be administered with the reverence due in ecclesiastical use, such as an ironic, mimic, jocular, and ludic action is

not. Quaest. X. What is the matter of the sacraments?

Since the sacraments are actions instituted by God, it is clear that there is no matter of them, properly so called . Analogously, however, their earthly matter is called an element, or external symbol, which is a corporeal, visible thing, analogous to its signified, expressly determined by the word of divine institution, and ordered to this end, that it may be the ὄχημα (vehicle), vehicle and medium of exhibition of the heavenly thing . The heavenly matter is an invisible and intelligible thing, exhibited by the earthly visible thing as a medium divinely ordained, upon which the fruit of the sacrament principally depends .

Prob. a. Matter properly so called belongs to corporeal substances, which are composed of matter and form as parts. Since therefore a sacrament is not a corporeal substance, it is easy to conclude that it does not consist of matter properly so called: Analogously, however, the matter about which it is concerned is assigned to it.

Prob. b. & c. 1) Going inductively through the individual sacraments. In circumcision the earthly and visible thing was the foreskin, cut off and cast away not without the shedding of blood: typically the Messiah was present, to be born from the blood of Abraham, to be sprinkled with his own blood in the passion, to be cut off and cast away.

In the Passover the earthly and visible thing was the lamb to be slaughtered: typically the Messiah was present to be sacrificed for us, 1 Cor. 5:7. In baptism the visible symbol is water: the heavenly thing is the Holy Spirit. In the Holy Supper the external elements are bread and wine, the invisible and heavenly matter is the body and blood of the Lord.

2) God acts in the sacraments with the external and internal man; therefore He willed that there be two parts of the sacraments, suitable for the consideration of each man, of which the heavenly would be concerned with the faith of the internal man, but the earthly with the senses of the external man. 3) The effect of the sacraments (regeneration, justification, renewal, and glorification) cannot proceed from the earthly matter alone, nor can it be attributed to it without the appearance of idolatry. Therefore, the effect of the sacraments proceeds principally from the heavenly thing, with which the earthly matter is sacramentally united, as a vehicle and medium of exhibition of the heavenly thing.

4) The Word ἄσχετον (unbound), by the power of divine ordination, is united with the Holy Spirit, so that it can produce supernatural effects: Thus, since spiritual and divine power is attributed to the sacrament, it is necessary that the heavenly matter be sacramentally bound to the external element, by the power of which it produces heavenly ἐνεργήματα (energies/effects), as a medium instructed by divine power, Conf. D. CALOVIUS, vol. IX, system, p. 175.

5) The same is proved from the end of the sacraments, which, since they are sensible signs, require some intelligible thing signified. For a sign is, in the definition of AUGUSTINE, L. II. de doctrin. Christ. c. 2. thing, which beyond the appearance that it brings to the senses, makes something else from itself come into thought. Since, furthermore, the sacraments are effective organs for supernatural acts: Therefore they require some, if I may so say, internal and heavenly nucleus, from which such great efficacy can proceed through an external element. Cf. DANNHAV. in hodof. p. 1006. You say: The sacramental matter must be present in the sacramental act. But the Messiah to be born and sacrificed was not present to the sacramental actions of the O.T. Therefore the Messiah to be born and sacrificed was not the heavenly matter of the sacraments of the O.T. I respond: The Word (ὁ λόγος), because He is eternal and omnipresent, was indeed really present in the sacramental actions of the O.T., in that He was morally present as the one to be incarnated and sacrificed, which concerns the foreknowledge and decree, as well as the evangelical promise and efficacy, so that He could be apprehended and applied by faith. For Christ is yesterday and today, and the same forever, Heb. XIII, 8. and the Lamb of God was slain from the foundation of the world, Apoc. XIII, 8.

Latin:

Ratione τῆς εὐσχημοσύνης, siue decori, requiritur in ministro ecclesiae sincera pietas a). Efficacia autem sacramenti non a ministro, siue oeconomo, sed a magistro, siue auctore Deo pendet b).

Prob. a. 1) Quia δεῖ τὸν ἐπίσκοπον ἀνεπιλήπτον εἶναι, oportet episcopum esse inculpatum, 1 Tim. III, 3. 2) Quia minister est legatus Christi, quem imitari, & ecclesiae totius vicarius, cuius ornamenta referre debet.

Prob. b. 1) Quia neque qui plantat, neque qui rigat, quidquam est, sed Deus, qui dat incrementum, 1 Cor. III, 7. E. efficacia sacramentorum non dependet a ministro ecclesiae plantante aut rigante, sed a Deo, incrementum largiente. Ratio est: quia minister in ordine ad effectum sacramenti non agit, nisi instrumentaliter. Omne autem instrumentum agit, non secundum propriam formam, sed secundum virtutem eius, a quo mouetur. 2) Sicut incredulitas hominum non potest irritam facere fidem Dei, Rom. III, 13: Ita malitia ministri non potest impedire bonitatem Dei, sacramenta influentis. Docet hoc Augustana confessio, Art. VIII. Quanquam ecclesia proprie sit congregatio sanctorum & vere credentium; tamen cum in hac vita multi hypocritae & mali admixti sint, licet vti sacramentis. quae per malos administrantur iuxta vocem Christi, Matth. XXIII, 2. Sedent scribae & Pharisaei in cathedra Mosis &c. Et sacramenta & verbum propter ordinationem & mandatum Christi sunt efficacia, etiamsi per malos exhibeantur.

Antithesis est Donatistarum & Anabaptistarum, efficaciam sacramentorum pietati ministrorum adscribentium.

Nituntur potissimum hoc argumento: Quicunque non habet Spiritum S., alteri beneficia Spiritus S. conferre nequit: Atqui minister improbus &c.

E. Maior probatur: quia quod quis non habet, alteri dare nequit.

Resp.

Dist. inter caussam principalem, & instrumentalem. Quod caussa principalis non habet (formaliter aut eminenter), alteri non potest impertiri.

Sed per agens instrumentale potest conferri, quod ipsi non inest: v. gr. aër est vehiculum loquelae ad amicum longe stantem; ipse tamen aër est loquelae expers.

Quaest. IX.

Num ad integritatem & efficaciam sacramentorum requiritur intentio ministri?

Prob. a. Quia externa intentio est legitima administratio & formalis vsus, extra quem non datur sacramentum.

Est enim organon gratiae & salutis, adeoque consistit in vsu, institutioni diuinae conformi.

Prob. b. Ministri ecclesiae est, τὴν διακονίαν αὐτοῦ πληροφορεῖν, ministerium suum adimplere, 2 Tim.

IV, 5. quod accuratam requirit intentionem.

Prob. c.

1) Si sacramenti integritas & efficaciam aestimanda esset intentione ministri, omnis plane consolatio ex sacramentis haurienda exspiraret, & vniuersa efficacia sacramentorum incerta foret, contra manifesta Spiritus S. effata, Io. III, 5.

Gal. III, 27.

Matth. XXVI, 28.

Io. VI, 51.

Cum enim alieni pectoris recessus penetrare non sit datum homini, quomodo poterit quisquam de baptizantis intentione, & consequenter de baptismi efficacia certus esse?

2) Sicut incredulitas hominum non potest fidem Dei facere irritam, Rom. III, 3.: ita defectus bonae intentionis in ministro non facit diuinam intentionem irritam.

3) Verbum audibile, absente bona ministri intentione, est efficax; siquidem nonnulli per inuidiam & contentionem Christum praedicant, Phil. I, 15.

E. & sacramentum visibile, absente bona intentione est efficax.

4) Zippora ex iracundia, sine debita intentione, filium circumcidit, Exod.

IV, 26. & illa circumcisio rata fuit.

E.

Sacramentum sine debita ministri intentione ratum est.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, efficaciam sacramenti a bona ministri intentione suspendentium.

Quorum argumenta sunt: I. Omnis actio proairetica fit cum intentione agendi (proficiscitur enim a sciente & volente): Administratio sacramenti est actio proairetica: Ergo.

Resp.

Dist. inter intentionem ministri internam, & externam. Omnis actio proairetica requirit intentionem ministri externam, conformem voluntati Domini, quamuis interna ministri intentio non semper fit bona: v. gr.

Si famulus alicuius domini liberalis te prosequeretur odio, & iuberetur a

Intentio externa, quae consistit in adhibitione omnium verborum & actionum sacramentalium, hoc fine & modo, quo Christus instituit, omnino ad integritatem essentialem sacramenti necessaria est a).

Interna intentio requiritur quidem ad decorum ministri, vt attentum praesentemque, non somnolentum, non peregrinantem animum ad officium suum afferat b).

Si tamen vel ex negligentia, vel ex malitia non fit intentus, defectus internae intentionis salutarem sacramenti effectum non impedit c).

domino centum tibi tradere aureos, afferret ille pecuniam intentione externa, mandato domini conformi, licet interna ipsius intentio non esset bona.

II. In omni fideli prudenti servo requiritur bona intentio: Omnis minister sacramentorum est fidelis & prudens servus, Matth. XXIV, 45. Ergo. Resp. Requiritur bona intentio ratione decori & officii, non autem ratione absolutae necessitatis ad integritatem & efficaciam sacramenti.

III. Si non necessaria esset intentio ministri ad integritatem sacramenti, baptismus in balneo, & eucharistia in convivio, vel alias per ludum & iocum collata, legitima forent sacramenta: Consequens est absurdum: E. & antecedens. Resp. Neg. conseq. Baptismus iocularis & eucharistia ludicra non sunt sacramenta, non ideo, quod desit intentio ministri, sed quod ad essentiam sacramenti pertineat, ut sit actio sacra & solemnis, usu ecclesiastico debita reverentia administranda, qualis non est actio ironica, mimica, iocularis & ludicra.

Quaest. X. Quae est materia sacramentorum?

Cum sacramenta sint actiones divinitus institutae, liquet, eorum non dari materiam, proprie dictam . 'Ανάλογως tamen eorum materia terrestris dicitur elementum, sive symbolum externum, quod est res corporea, visibilis, suo signato analoga, expresse verbo institutionis divinae determinata, & ordinata ad hoc, ut sit rei coelestis ὄχημα, vehiculum & medium exhibitivum . Materia coelestis est res invisibilis & intelligibilis, re terrena visibili, tanquam medio divinitus ordinato exhibita, a qua fructus sacramenti principaliter dependet .

Prob. a. Materia proprie dicta competit substantiis corporeis, quae ex materia & forma, velut partibus, componuntur. Cum itaque sacramentum non sit substantia corporea, collectu proclive est, illud non constare ex materia proprie dicta: Analogice tamen ei materia, circa quam versatur, assignatur.

Prob. b. & c. 1) Inductive eundo per singula sacramenta. In circumcisione res terrena & visibilis fuit praeputium, non fine sanguinis effusione recisum & abiectum: typice praesto fuit Messias, e sanguine Abrahami nascendus, sanguine suo in passione conspergendus, excidendus & abiiciendus.

In Paschate res terrena & visibilis erat agnus mactandus: typice aderat Messias pro nobis immolandus, 1 Cor. V, 7. In baptismo symbolum visibile est aqua: res coelestis est Spiritus S. In S. coena externa elementa sunt panis & vinum, invisibilis & coelestis materia est corpus & sanguis Domini.

2) Agit Deus in sacramentis cum externo & interno homine; ideo duas etiam partes, cuilibet hominis considerationi convenientes, sacramentorum esse voluit, quarum coelestis circa hominis interni fidem, terrena vero circa externi hominis sensus versaretur. 3) Effectus sacramentorum (regeneratio, iustificatio, renovatio & glorificatio) non potest provenire a sola materia terrestri, neque citra speciem idolatriae ei tribui. Prodit igitur effectus sacramentorum principaliter a re coelesti, cum qua sacramentaliter unita est materia terrestris, ceu vehiculum & medium exhibitivum rei coelestis.

4) Verbum ἄσχετον, vi ordinationis divinae, vnitum est cum Spiritu S., vt effectus supernaturales producere queat: Ita cum sacramento tribuatur vis spiritualis & divina, necesse est, vt elemento externo sacramentaliter vinita fit materia coelestis, vi cuius coelestia ἐνεργήματα producat, ceu medium, divina vi instructum, Conf. D. CALOVII tom. IX. system. p. 175.

5) Probatur idem ex fine sacramentorum, quae cum sint signa sensibilia, requirunt aliquod signatum intelligibile. Est enim signum, definiente AVGVSTINO, L. II. de doctrin. Christ. c. 2. res, quae praeter speciem, quam sensibus ingerit, aliud aliquid ex se facit in cogitationem venire. Quia porro sacramenta sunt organa efficacia ad actus supernaturales: Ergo requirunt aliquem, ut sic dicam, nucleum internum & caelestem, a quo tanta per externum elementum efficacia prodire queat. Conf. DANNHAV. in hodof. p. 1006. Dicis: Materia sacramentalis debet esse praesens in actu sacramentali. Sed Messias nascendus & immolandus non fuit actionibus sacramentalibus V. T. praesens. Ergo Messias nascendus & immolandus non fuit materia caelestis sacramentorum V. T. Resp. ὁ λόγος, quia aeternus & omnipraesens est, utique realiter praesens fuit in actionibus sacramentalibus V. T., qua incarnandus & immolandus praesto fuit moraliter, quod praevisionem & decretum, nec non quod promissionem evangelicam & efficaciam, ut fide apprehendi & applicari posset. Est enim Christus heri & hodie, & idem in saecula, Hebr. XIII, 8. & agnus Dei occisus est ab origine mundi, Apoc. XIII, 8.


### Q. XI. Is there a union of earthly and heavenly things in the sacraments?

There is a union of earthly and heavenly things in the sacraments , not indeed essential, nor personal, nor accidental by reason of the terms to be united , but unusual, mystical, symbolic, and sacramental .

Prob. a. Because by the confession of all, one sacrament is made from the earthly and the heavenly, this cannot happen unless some union intervenes; for it is the formal principle of one composite.

Prob. b. The sacramental union is not an essential union, such as is the conjunction of two incomplete substances to constitute one thing in itself; for neither the Messiah to be born and killed, nor the Holy Spirit is an incomplete being, nor do they coalesce to constitute one essence: Nor is it personal, whose term is one intelligent supposit, or one composite (σύνθετος) person. Who would dare to say that the Holy Spirit coalesces with baptismal water into one person? Nor is it accidental by reason of the terms to be united, for the reason that in the sacraments the earthly substance is united with the heavenly substance. We concede, meanwhile, that it can be referred to an accidental union, by reason of the term to which, as it is called. Cf. D. CALOV. metaphys. diu. p. 317.

Prob. c. The sacramental union is called unusual, by reason of the united matter; because a similar account of sacramental union is not found in the whole of nature, and thus it becomes known solely from the light of supernatural revelation: It is called mystical, by reason of the arcane and unsearchable mode: But it is called sacramental and symbolic, by reason of the end; because it effects that the external symbol signifies the heavenly thing and exhibits the thing signified. By the power of this mystical and symbolic union, the sacrament is a mystery, consisting of shell and nucleus, casket and jewel, the receiving shell and the precious water, or (to speak more clearly) of the external and internal thing, the earthly and the heavenly.

Latin:

Datur rei terrestris & caelestis in sacramentis unio , non quidem essentialis, neque personalis, neque ratione terminorum unibilium accidentalis , sed inusitata, mystica, symbolica, & sacramentalis .

Prob. a. Quia e terrena & caelesti omnium confessione unum fit sacramentum, non potest id fieri, nisi intercedente aliqua unione; quippe quae est principium formale unius compositi.

Prob. b. Unio sacramentalis non est unio essentialis, quales est duarum substantiarum incompletarum coniunctio ad unum per se constituendum; neque enim Messias nascendus & occidendus, neque Spiritus S. est ens incompletum, neque coalescunt ad unam essentiam constituendam: Neque est personalis, cuius terminus est unum suppositum intelligens, sive una persona σύνθετος. Ecquis dicere ausit, Spiritum S. cum aqua baptismali coalescere in unam personam? Neque est unio ratione extremorum unibilium accidentalis, ideo, quod in sacramentis substantia terrena cum substantia caelesti unitur. Concedimus interim, quod ad unionem accidentalem, ratione termini ad quem, sic dictam, referri queat. Conf. D. CALOVII metaphys. diu. p. 317.

Prob. c. Unio sacramentalis dicitur inusitata, ratione materiae unitae; quia unionis sacramentalis consimilis ratio non invenitur in universa natura, adeoque e lumine supernaturalis revelationis unice innotescit: Dicitur mystica, ratione modi arcani & imperuestigabilis: Sacramentalis autem & symbolica appellatur, ratione finis; propterea, quod efficit, ut symbolum externum rem caelestem signet, signatam exhibeat. Vi huius unionis mysticae & symbolicae sacramentum est mysterium, constans ex putamine & nucleo, scrinio & clinodio, concha excipula & aqua pretiosa, sive (ut clarius loquar) re externa & interna, terrestri & caelesti.


### Q. XII. What is the form of the sacrament?

The form of the sacrament is the external action, and that entirely occupied with the earthly and heavenly thing of any sacrament, which is constituted by formal acts, succeeding one another without distinction, which are three: I. Recitation of the words of institution: II. Δόσις (Giving), or sacramental dispensation: III. Λῆψις (Taking), or reception of the sacrament.

The assertion is proved by induction. Δόσις in circumcision is to amputate the foreskin: Λῆψις is to undergo the amputation of the foreskin. In the Passover, Δόσις is to slaughter the paschal lamb, to roast it, and to offer it for eating: Λῆψις is to eat the slaughtered and roasted lamb.

In baptism, the *dosis* [giving] is to pour water upon a person, or to immerse them in water in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: the *lepsis* [receiving] is to admit the affusion or immersion. In the Holy Supper, the *dosis* is to distribute the blessed bread, which is the *koinonia* [communion] of the body of Christ, and the blessed wine, which is the *koinonia* of the blood of Christ, for eating and drinking: the *lepsis* is to eat the body of Christ with the eucharistic bread, and to drink His blood with the blessed wine. Everywhere the word of institution or ordination is added, which is also called the consecratory [word], by which the elements or external symbols are separated from profane use and effectively dedicated to a sacred use, so that heavenly things may be distributed, exhibited, and received with them. Thus, individual sacraments have their own word of institution, Gen. XVII, 10. Exod. XII, 3. Matth. XXVIII, 19. Matth. XXVI, 26. Concerning which AUGUSTINE, tract. LXXX in John: Let the word be added to the element, and it becomes a sacrament.

Obs. I. In the administration of any sacrament, antecedent, formal, and consequent acts converge. Those that are antecedent are also called preparatory and pedagogical, e.g., exhortation, prayer, confession of faith: The formal [acts] are those which constitute the sacraments and distinguish them from other actions: The consequent and final [acts] are the application and sealing of evangelical grace.

Obs. II. A threefold word concurs with the sacramental act: a) The word of command, by which we are divinely bound to the use of the sacrament: b) The word of institution, or consecratory [word], which is fittingly applied to the sacramental action so that earthly symbols may be transferred and dedicated to a mystical and sacred use: c) The word of promise, by which the saving effect is promised. The word of invocation may be added, which contributes not a little to the solemn signification of the sacrament.

Quest. XIII. To what men are the sacraments to be dispensed?

The sacraments are to be dispensed to all and only those men who are capable of their formal and final use.

Proof. Only living men receive the formal acts of the sacraments, as is evident from the response to the preceding question. Only living men are capable of the end of the sacraments, namely, regeneration, justification, and renewal. However, the sacraments of initiation are dispensed to infants as well as adults, the sacraments of confirmation to adults only.

Quest. XIV. Does faith also pertain to the integrity of a sacrament?

Faith is indeed necessarily required for grasping the saving fruit of the sacrament. a) But it is not required for the substantial integrity of the sacrament b.

Proof. a. 1) Without faith no one can please God, Heb. XI, 6.

2) The promise annexed to the sacraments is received by faith, Rom. IV, 26. ch. III, 14.

Proof. b. 1) The sacrament depends on the will and institution of God, which is not rendered void by the unbelief of men, Rom. III, 3.

2) If faith were to enter into the substance of the sacrament, the circumcision and baptism of infants would not be complete sacraments, for the reason that infants lack faith before the sacrament is conferred, Eph. III, 3. John III, 6. The faith of adults is indeed confirmed by the sacrament: however, that which confirms and that which is confirmed differ.

3) Just as the word of God is true, which hypocrites hear: so the sacrament is true, which adult hypocrites receive, though destitute of faith.

You say: I. Whatever is not a true means of salvation outside of use, faith pertains to the constituting of its integrity: But a sacrament outside of use, etc. Therefore. The major is evident: because when faith is lacking, the saving use of the sacrament is lacking. The minor is clear; because the whole being of the sacrament consists in its use. Response. Distinguish between the external or formal use of the sacrament, and the internal or

Latin:

Forma sacramenti est externa actio, eaque integre circa rem terrestrem & caelestem cuiuslibet sacramenti occupata, quam constituunt actus formales, sibi indistricte succedentes, qui sunt tres: I. Recitatio verborum institutionis: II. Δόσις, sive dispensatio sacramentalis: III. Λῆψις, sive sacramenti receptio.

Probatur assertum per inductionem. Δόσις in circumcisione est, amputare praeputium: Λῆψις est amputationem praeputii sustinere. In paschate δόσις est, agnum paschalem mactare, affare & ad manducandum offerre: Λῆψις est, agnum mactatum & affatum manducare.

ptisimo δόσις est, aquam affundere homini, vel in aquam immergere in nomine Patris, Filii & Spiritus S.: λῆψις est, admittere affusionem vel immersionem. In S. cœna δόσις est, panem benedictum, qui est κοινωνία corporis Christi, & vinum benedictum, quod est κοινωνία sanguinis Christi, ad manducandum & bibendum distribuere: λῆψις est, corpus Christi cum pane eucharistico edere, & sanguinem ipsius cum vino benedicto bibere. Accedit vbique verbum institutionis, siue ordinationis, quod etiam consecratorium vocatur, quo elementa, siue symbola externa ab vsu profano segregantur, & ad vsum sacrum efficaciter dedicantur, vt cum illis res cœlestes distribuantur, exhibeantur & sumantur. Sic singula sacramenta habent suum verbum institutionis, Gen. XVII, 10. Exod. XII, 3. Matth. XXVIII, 19. Matth. XXVI, 26. De quo AVGUSTIN. tract. XXC. in Ioannem: Accedat verbum ad elementum, & fit sacramentum.

Obf. I. In administratione cuiuslibet sacramenti confluunt actus antecedentes, formales & consequentes. Antecedentes dicuntur etiam præparatorii & pædagogici, v. gr. exhortatio, precatio, fidei confessio: Formales sunt, qui sacramenta constituunt, & ab aliis actionibus distinguunt: Consequentes & finales sunt gratiæ euangelicæ applicatio & obsignatio.

Obf. II. Ad actum sacramentalem triplex concurrit verbum: a) Verbum mandati, quo ad vsum sacramenti diuinitus adstringimur: b) Verbum institutionis, siue consecratorium, quod actioni sacramentali decenter applicatur, vt symbola terrena ad vsum mysticum & sacrum transferantur ac dedicentur: c) Verbum promissionis, quo salutaris effectus promittitur. Addi potest verbum inuocationis, quod haud parum facit ad solemnem sacramenti significationem.

Quæst. XIII. Quibus hominibus sacramenta sunt dispensanda?

Sacramenta dispensanda sunt omnibus & solis hominibus, vsus formalis & finalis capacibus.

Prob. Soli homines viuentes, recipiunt actus formales sacramentorum, vt patet ex responsione ad quæstionem præcedentem. Soli homines viuentes capaces sunt finis sacramentorum, nempe regenerationis, iustificationis & renouationis. Dispensantur autem sacramenta initiationis tam infantibus, quam adultis, sacramenta confirmationis solis adultis.

Quæst. XIV. An ad integritatem sacramenti etiam fides pertinet?

Fides quidem necessario exigitur ad capiendum salutarem sacramenti fructum. a) Sed non requiritur ad substantialem sacramenti integritatem b.

Prob. a. 1) Sine fide nemo potest Deo placere, Hebr. XI, 6.

2) Promissio, sacramentis annexa, fide recipitur, Rom. IV, 26. c. III, 14.

Prob. b. 1) Sacramentum pendet a voluntate & institutione Dei, quæ incredulitate hominum non fit irrita, Rom. III, 3.

2) Si fides ingrederetur substantiam sacramenti; circumcisio & baptismus infantum non forent sacramenta integra, propterea, quod infantes ante collatum sacramentum fide carent, Eph. III, 3. Io. III, 6. Adultorum fides quidem sacramenti confirmatur: Differunt autem confirmans & confirmandum.

3) Sicut verum Dei est verbum, quod audiunt hypocritæ: Ita verum est sacramentum, quod accipiunt adulti hypocritæ, fide destituti.

Dicis: I. Quidquid extra vsum non est verum salutis medium, ad illius integritatem constituendam pertinet fides: Atqui sacramentum extra vsum &c. E. Maior patet: quia deficiente fide deficit salutaris sacramenti vfus. Minor liquet; quia totum esse sacramenti conglit in vsu. Resp. Dist. inter vsum sacramenti externum, siue formalem, & internum,


### Quest. XVI

or the final and saving one. Faith is required not for that, but for this. AUGUSTINE also looked to this saving use, or fruit, of the sacrament, tract. 80 on John, speaking thus: Let the word be added to the element, and it becomes a sacrament. But whence such great power of water, that it washes the heart? Unless by the acting word, not because it is spoken, but because it is believed.

You say: II. Paul says, 1 Cor. X, 21: You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons, by which words he indicates that infidels cannot receive the sacrament of the Supper. Whence arises the argument: Without which the cup of the Lord cannot be drunk, without that the true sacrament cannot be received: Without faith, etc. Therefore. Resp. The Apostle is speaking of moral impossibility, in this sense: it is not decorous, it is not convenient, that those who drink the cup of the Lord should be present at feasts prepared from sacrifices which had been offered to idols.

Quest. XV. What is the primary end of the sacraments? The primary end of the sacraments is the offering, conferring, application, and sealing of evangelical grace.

Obs. I. By evangelical grace is understood the grace of the Holy Spirit that applies, obtained by the merit of Christ, and promised in the gospel, namely, grace that is calling, illuminating, regenerating, justifying, indwelling, renewing, and glorifying.

Obs. II. Through the sacraments, evangelical grace is offered to all who use them, conferred upon those who use them worthily, applied, and sealed to believing adults.

Proof. 1) To circumcision is annexed the promise: I will be your God, and of your seed, Gen. XVII, 7. By which promise, grace that is regenerating, justifying, indwelling, renewing, and glorifying is offered. Therefore it is called σφραγὶς δικαιοσύνης, a seal of righteousness, Rom. IV, 11.

2) The paschal lamb confirmed faith in Christ, who is called the passover sacrificed for us, 1 Cor. V, 7.

3) Baptism is the washing of regeneration and renewal, Tit. III, 5.

4) In the Holy Supper we receive the body given for us, and the blood of the N. T. which is shed for us for the remission of sins, Matth. XXVI, 26. 27. 28. Therefore, through the sacrament of the Supper, evangelical grace concerning the remission of sins is confirmed and sealed.

Quest. XVI. Which are the secondary ends of the sacraments? The secondary ends of the sacraments are: a) That they may be marks of the church, by which it is distinguished from the infidel people: b) That they may be monuments of the benefits of Christ: c) That they may be bonds of charity and sinews of public gatherings: d) That they may be incitements to the exercises of virtues.

Proof. a. The Israelite church was distinguished from the assembly of infidels by circumcision and the paschal lamb, as if by marks and tokens. By baptism and the eucharist duly administered, the Christian church is distinguished both from the Jewish synagogue and from heathens and sectarians.

Proof. b. The paschal lamb [commemorates] the miraculous leading out of the Israelites from Egypt, Exod. XII, 14. The Lord's Supper recalls the death of Christ to the memory of Christians, Luc. XXII, 19.

Proof. c. Paul shows that one baptism is a bond of charity and peace, Eph. IV, 5. By equal reasoning, the Holy Supper is a means of our conjunction with Christ the head and his mystical members. For we being many are one bread, one body, 1 Cor. X, 17.

Proof. d. Circumcision admonished the Israelites of spiritual circumcision, Deut. X, 16; the paschal lamb of gratitude toward God, Exod. XII, 26; Ps. CXI, 4. Baptism signifies the submersion of the old Adam, which occurs through repentance and daily renewal, Rom. VI, 4. The Holy Supper excites us to a grateful remembrance of the death of Christ, 1 Cor. XI, 25.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, Arminians, Anabaptists, Schwenckfeldians, and Weigelians, who deny the primary end of the sacraments. The Papists, however, detract not a little from the efficacy of the sacraments of the O.T.

They rely on the following arguments:

I. God confers evangelical grace: Therefore, not the sacraments. Resp. God confers grace principally; the sacraments (taken as external symbols) instrumentally. The sacraments are media or organs through which God the Father wills to exhibit, bestow, and apply His grace; the Son of God to communicate His merit; the Holy Spirit to exert His efficacy for salvation to every believer.

II. Whatever we are justified by instrumentally, that is faith; Rom. III, 28. The sacraments are not faith: Therefore, we are not justified by the sacraments. Resp. We are justified by faith as the receptive instrument; by the sacraments as the exhibitive and sealing instruments. Faith is as it were our hand, by which we apprehend and receive the benefits of the Gospel as our own: The Word and sacraments are as it were the hand of God, by which the benefits of Christ are offered, applied, and sealed to us.

III. An instrument has no efficacy: The sacrament is an instrument: Therefore. Resp. I distinguish between the efficacy of an instrument separated and one conjoined. An instrument separated from the principal cause has no efficacy. But the sacraments are instruments conjoined with the heavenly thing, from which so great an efficacy proceeds through the external element.

IV. No external thing can penetrate into the soul and produce spiritual motions within it: The sacrament is an external thing: Therefore. Resp. No merely external and natural thing can penetrate into the soul; I concede. But the sacrament is not a merely natural or external thing; rather, it is conjoined with the heavenly thing and the word of institution. Its efficacy depends upon the heavenly thing with which it is conjoined, and upon the divine ordination.

V. Whatever is a sign has no power except the power of signifying: But the sacraments are signs: Therefore. Resp. Whatever is a theoretical sign, and one that merely signifies, that has only the power of signifying; I concede. But the sacraments are practical and exhibitive signs, which, by exhibiting the thing signified, effect something by the covenant, institution, and promise of God.

VI. The sacraments of the Old Testament were not exhibitive signs, because they did not exhibit the body of Christ: Therefore, they were signs that merely signified. Resp. The sacraments of the Old Testament are signifying and exhibitive in different respects. They are signifying, insofar as they prefigured the Messiah who was to come and suffer: They are exhibitive, insofar as they made the Messiah present in the efficacious divine promise.

VII. A shadow has no efficacy: The sacraments of the O.T. are shadows: Therefore, the sacraments of the O.T. have no efficacy. Resp. The sacraments of the O.T. are partly shadows, partly means of grace. They are shadows with respect to the future incarnation, passion, and death of Christ, which they adumbrated from afar. They are means of grace insofar as the external elements, with the word of institution added, being conjoined with the heavenly thing, regenerated, justified, sanctified, and saved by the force of the divine federal promise.

VIII. If the sacraments, applied outwardly, purge inwardly, Judaism will be introduced into the church. But Judaism is not to be introduced into the church. Therefore, the sacraments do not purge inwardly. The consequence of the major is proven: because the Jews believed that they could expiate and, as it were, redeem their crimes by various victims and offerings, Ps. XL, 7. Ps. LI, 8. Is. XI, 11. Amos V, 22.

Resp. 1) The cited passages deal with the sacrifices of the Jews, which differ greatly from the sacraments. Those are from the people to God; these are from God to the people. In the sacraments, men receive something from God: In the sacrifices, men offer something to God.

Furthermore 2) The Jews without repentance and faith,

that God's grace can be obtained through external rites and sacrifices: we require repentance and faith to receive the saving fruit of the sacraments.

IX. Whatever is most certain does not need sacramental confirmation: But divine promises etc. E. Response. Divine promises are considered either absolutely and in themselves, or in relation to us. Considered absolutely and in themselves, they do not need confirmation, but in relation to us, so that they may be effectively applied to us and approved by us with solid assent.

X. Whatever excludes all doubt does not need confirmation: But faith, according to the mind of the Lutherans, etc. E. Response. Faith excludes the doubt of unbelief, not of weakness, because faith is not always equally robust; but sometimes weak and languid, like a bruised reed or a smoldering wick, Es. XLII, 3.

Latin:

siue finalem ac salutarem. Non ad illum, sed ad hunc requiritur fides. Hunc salutarem sacramenti vfum, vel fructum respexit etiam AVGVSTINVS, tract. 80. in Ioannem sic fatus: Accedat verbum ad elementum, & fit sacramentum. Vnde autem tanta virtus aquæ, vt cor abluat? Nisi faciente verbo, non quia dicitur, sed quia creditur.

Dicis: II. Paullus inquit, 1 Cor. X, 21. Non potestis poculum Domini bibere, & poculum dæmoniorum, quibus verbis indicat, infideles non posse accipere sacramentum cœnæ. Vnde nascitur argumentum: Sine quo non potest bibi poculum Domini, fine illo non potest accipi verum sacramentum: Sine fide &c. E. Resp. Sermo est Apostolo de impossibilitate morali, hoc sensu: non est decorum, non est conueniens, vt, qui poculum Domini bibunt, interfint conuiuiis, apparatis de sacrificiis, quæ idolis immolata erant.

Quæst. XV. Quis est finis primarius sacramentorum? Finis primarius sacramentorum est oblatio, collatio, applicatio & obsignatio gratiæ euangelicæ.

Obf. I. Per gratiam euangelicam intelligitur gratia Spiritus S. applicatrix, merito Christi parta, & in euangelio promissa, nempe gratia vocans, illuminans, regenerans, iustificans, inhabitans, renouans, glorificans.

Obf. II. Per sacramenta gratia euangelica omnibus vtentibus offertur, digne vtentibus confertur, applicatur, & adultis credentibus obfignatur.

Prob. 1) Circumcisioni annexa est promissio: Ero Deus tuus, & feminis tui, Gen. XVII, 7. Qua promissione offertur gratia regenerans, iustificans, inhabitans, renouans, glorificans. Idcirco vocatur σφραγὶς δικαιοσύνης, figillum iustitiæ, Rom. IV, 11.

2) Agnus paschalis confirmabat fidem in Christum, qui dicitur pascha pro nobis immolatum, 1 Cor. V, 7.

3) Baptismus est lauacrum regenerationis & renouationis, Tit. III, 5.

4) In S. cœna accipiamus corpus pro nobis traditum, & fanguinem T. N. qui pro nobis effunditur in remissionem peccatorum, Matth. XXVI, 26. 27. 28. E. per sacramentum cœnæ gratia euangelica de remissione peccatorum confirmatur & obfignatur.

Quæst. XVI. Quinam sunt fines sacramentorum secundarii? Fines sacramentorum secundarii sunt: a) Vt sint notæ ecclesiæ, quibus a populo infideli distinguitur: b) Vt sint monumenta beneficiorum Christi: c) Vt sint vincula caritatis & nerui publicorum congressuum: d) Vt sint incitamenta ad virtutum exercitia.

Prob. a. Ecclesia Ifraëlitica circumcifione & agno paschali, velut notis ac tefferis, a cœtu infidelium discernebatur. Baptismo & eucharistia rite administratis ecclesia Christiana tum a synagoga iudaica, tum ab ethnicis & sectariis distinguitur.

Prob. b. Agnus paschalis miraculosam eductionein Ifraëlitarum ex Ægypto, Exod. XII, 14. Cœna dominica mortem Christi Christianis in memoriam reuocat, Luc. XXII, 19.

Prob. c. Vnum baptisma esse vinculum caritatis & pacis, ostendit Paullus. Eph. IV, 5. Pari ratione S. cœna est medium coniunctionis nostræ cum Christo capite & membris eius mysticis. Vnus enim panis, vnum corpus multi fumus, 1 Cor. X, 17.

Prob. d. Circumcifio admonebat Ifraëlitas circumcifionis spiritualis, Deut. X, 16. agnus paschalis gratitudinis erga Deum, Exod. XII, 26. Pf. CXI, 4. Baptismus fignificat submersionem veteris Adami, quae fit per poenitentiam & quotidianam renovationem, Rom. VI, 4. S. coena excitat nos ad gratam mortis Christi memoriam, 1 Cor. XI, 25.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, Arminianorum, Anabaptistarum, Schwenckfeldianorum & Weigelianorum, finem primarium sacramentorum negantium. Pontificii autem efficaciae sacramentorum V. T. haud parum derogant.

Nituntur sequentibus argumentis:

I. Deus confert gratiam evangelicam: E. non sacramenta. Resp. Deus confert gratiam principaliter, sacramenta (sumta pro symbolis externis) instrumentaliter. Sacramenta sunt media vel organa, per quae Deus Pater suam gratiam vult exhibere, donare & applicare, Filius Dei meritum suum communicare, Spiritus S. suam efficaciam exserere ad salutem omni credenti.

II. Quocunque instrumentaliter iustificamur, illud est fides; Rom. III, 28. Sacramenta non sunt fides: E. sacramentis non iustificamur. Resp. Fide iustificamur, vt instrumento receptivo; sacramentis, vt instrumentis exhibitivis & obsignationis. Fides est quasi manus nostra, qua beneficia evangelii propria apprehendimus & accipimus: Verbum & sacramenta sunt quasi manus Dei, qua nobis offeruntur, applicantur & obsignantur beneficia Christi.

III. Instrumenti nulla est efficacia: Sacramentum est instrumentum: E. Resp. Dist. inter efficaciam instrumenti separati, & coniuncti. Instrumenti separati a causa principali nulla est efficacia. At sacramenta sunt instrumenta coniuncta cum re caelesti, a qua tanta per elementum externum prodit efficacia.

IV. Nulla res externa potest penetrare in animam, & motus spirituales in ea producere: Sacramentum est res externa: E. Resp. Nulla res mere externa & naturalis potest penetrare in animam; concedo. Sed sacramentum non est res mere naturalis aut externa; sed est cum re caelesti & verbo institutionis coniuncta. Pendet eius efficacia a re caelesti, cum qua coniungitur, & ordinatione divina.

V. Quidquid est signum, nullam nisi vim signandi habet: Atqui sacramenta sunt signa: E. Resp. Quidquid est signum theoreticum, & nude signans, illud habet tantum vim signandi; concedo. At sacramenta sunt signa practica & exhibitiva, quae rem signatam exhibendo aliquid efficiunt ex pacto, instituto & promissione Dei.

VI. Sacramenta vet. testam. non fuerunt signa exhibitiva, quia non exhibuerunt corpus Christi: E. fuerunt signa nude signantia. Resp. Sacramenta vet. testam. diverso respectu sunt signantia & exhibitiva. Signantia sunt, quatenus venturum & passurum Messiam praefigurarunt: Exhibitiva sunt, quatenus Messiam in efficaci promissione divina praesentem fecerunt.

VII. Vmbrae nulla est efficacia: Sacramenta V. T. sunt vmbrae: E. sacramentorum V. T. nulla est efficacia. Resp. Sacramenta V. T. partim sunt vmbrae, partim media gratiae. Sunt vmbrae, respectu futurae incarnationis, passionis & mortis Christi, quam eminus adumbrarunt. Sunt media gratiae, quatenus externa elementa, accedente verbo institutionis, cum re caelesti coniuncta, regenerarunt, iustificarunt, sanctificarunt, salvarunt, vi foederalis promissionis divinae.

VIII. Si sacramenta, exterius adhibita, interius purgant, introducetur in ecclesiam Iudaismus. Sed Iudaismus non est in ecclesiam introducendus. E. Sacramenta interius non purgant. Consequentia maioris probatur: quia Iudaei credebant, se variis victimis & oblationibus posse scelera sua expiare, & velut redimere, Ps. XL, 7. Ps. LI, 8. Es. XI, 11. Amos V, 22.

Resp. 1) Dicta citata agunt de sacrificiis Iudaeorum, quae maxime differunt a sacramentis. Illa sunt populi ad Deum, haec sunt Dei ad populum. In sacramentis homines aliquid a Deo accipiunt: In sacrificiis homines Deo aliquid offerunt.

Ceterum 2) Iudaei sine poenitentia & fide, Iudæi fine pœnitentia & fide,

& fide, ritibus externis & sacrificiis gratiam Dei esse comparabilem, sibi ex vano persuasere runt: nos pœnitentiam & fidem ad percipiendum salutarem sacramentorum fructum requirimus.

IX. Quidquid est certissimum, illud non indiget sacramentali confirmatione: Atqui promissiones divinæ &c. E. Respo. Promissiones divinæ considerantur vel absolute & in se, vel respectu nostri. Absolute, & in se consideratæ, non indigent confirmatione, sed respectu nostri, vt nobis efficaciter applicentur, & a nobis solido assensu comprobentur.

X. Quidquid excludit omnem dubitationem, illud non indiget confirmatione: Atqui fides ex mente Lutheranorum &c. E. Respo. Fides excludit dubitationem incredulitatis, non infirmitatis, eo, quod fides non semper ex æquo robusta est; sed interdum infirma & languida, instar calami contusi, aut ligni fumigantis, Es. XLII, 3.


### Quest. XVI: XLII, 3. Quæst. XVII. Do the sacraments confer divine grace ex opere operato, without the faith of the recipient?

XLII, 3. Quæst. XVII. Do the sacraments confer divine grace ex opere operato, without the faith of the recipient?

Sacraments confer no grace on adults unless they receive that grace, offered with true faith, which pre-exists in their hearts a). In infants, the Holy Spirit ignites faith through the sacraments of initiation, by which infants accept covenantal grace b). The dogma concerning opus operatum is not in conformity with the hypotyposis sanorum verborum c).

Prob. a. 1) Because sacraments have an attached promise of grace, Marc. XVI, 16. Luc. XXII, 19, 20. But the promise of grace must be received by faith; because promise and faith are correlatives. 2) Because just as the verbum aoraton, or audible word, is of no benefit unless it is mixed with faith, Hebr. IV, 2: so neither is the sacrament, which is called the verbum horaton, or visible word, beneficial without the faith of those using it. 3) In the sacraments, a covenant is established with God: but for the establishment of a covenant, two hands are required, embracing each other. In the establishment of the divine covenant, God's hand is the word and sacrament; the hand, on our part, is faith. 4) For an adult, dokimasia, or self-examination, is necessary, so that he may test himself, whether he is in the faith, 1 Cor. XIII, 5. Prob. b.

Prob. b. Because, before infants are baptized, they lack faith; since they are not flesh of flesh, Ioann. III, 6. but are reborn of water and Spirit, Io. III, 5. through which regeneration faith is ignited and Christ is put on, Gal. III, 27. From this it follows that baptism is such an efficacious means by which the Holy Spirit excites faith in infants, and also a saving instrument by which justifying grace is offered, which is accepted by faith ignited in baptism.

DANNHAV. excellently says in hodof. phænom. X. p. 1007.: Faith is both an effect of the sacraments and their receiving organ. In the same moment of time that faith is given, it also receives; however, moments of nature must be distinguished. Faith is given before it embraces grace; yet both acts of giving and embracing occur almost in the same moment of time.

Prob. c. 1) Because that phrase, opus operatum, is barbaric; since, contrary to the rule of grammar, operatum is taken passively, just as if you were to say opus perpetratum, peractum, perfectum [a deed perpetrated, carried out, perfected].

2) Because the opinion concerning opus operatum in the sacraments of the N. T. invents a giving hand without a receiver, a correlative without a correlate, a saving promise without faith. 3) Because

3) Because by this device those using them worthily and unworthily are confounded; although, as St. Paul testifies, those who eat unworthily eat judgment to themselves, 1 Cor. XI, 29.

Latin:

Quæst. XVII. Conferuntne sacramenta gratiam divinam ex opere operato, sine fide vtentis?

Sacramenta nullam gratiam conferunt adultis, nisi eam oblatam vera fide, quæ in cordibus eorum præexistit, recipiant a). In infantibus Spiritus S. per sacramenta initiationis fidem accendit, qua infantes gratiam fœderalem acceptant b). Dogma vero de opere operato ὑποτυπώσεως sanorum verborum non est conforme c).

Prob. a. 1) Quia sacramenta annexam habent promissionem gratiæ, Marc. XVI, 16. Luc. XXII, 19, 20. Sed promissio gratiæ fide recipienda est; quia promissio & fides sunt relata, 2) Quia sicut verbum ἀόρατον, siue audibile, non prodest, nisi sit mixtum fide, Hebr. IV, 2: ita nec sacramentum, quod dicitur verbum ὁρατὸν, siue visibile, sine fide vtentis prodest, 3) In sacramentis fœdus cum Deo sancitur: sed ad sanctionem fœderis duæ exiguntur manus, se invicem complectentes. In sanctione fœderis divini manus Dei est verbum & sacramentum; manus, ex parte nostri, est fides, 4) Homini adulto necessaria est δοκιμασία, siue probatio sui, vt testet seipsum, an sit in fide, 1 Cor. XIII, 5. Prob. b.

Quia, antequam infantes baptizantur, fide carent; siquidem caro de carne non sunt, Ioann. III, 6. renascuntur autem ex aqua & Spiritu, Io. III, 5. per quam regenerationem fides accenditur & Christus induitur, Gal. III, 27. Ex quo conficitur, quod baptismus sit tam efficax medium, per quod Spiritus Sanctus fidem in infantibus excitat, tum salutare organon, per quod gratia iustifica offertur, quæ fide in baptismo accensa acceptatur.

Egregie inquit DANNHAV. in hodof. phænom. X. p. 1007. Fides est & effectus sacramentorum, & eorundem organum recipiens.
