The time of administration varies according to the different acts: for the separation took place on the tenth day of the month Nisan, the slaughter on the fourteenth day, and the roasting and eating on the night following the fourteenth day, and indeed in the first watch, Exod. 12:8. The sacrament of the paschal lamb was abrogated by the institution of the Lord's Supper: for when the body is present, the shadow ceases, Col. 2:17. Furthermore, the solemn celebration of the Passover was restricted to the Jerusalem temple, and upon its collapse, its solemnity expired.

SIGH.

The weakness of the human intellect is most clearly evident to You, O omniscient God. It does not acquiesce to promises, even the most truthful ones, but demands signs and pledges that strike the eyes. Intending to provide for the infirmity of the human intellect, You, most merciful Father, have most wisely ordained visible signs of Your invisible grace. Recalling this with grateful memory of soul, I pray most humbly that by the salutary use of the sacraments You may confirm me in my infirmity, rouse me in my languor, and sustain me in my wavering, so that I may stand unmoved in the doctrine of faith and the piety of life, and likewise fight strenuously against the devil, the world, and the flesh! Finally, out of grace, eternal God, grant to me, who am fighting for You alone under the sun, the crown of righteousness and glory!

Latin:

Sacramentum agni paschalis fuit necessarium, necessitate præcepti & medii. Prob. Deus manducationem agni paschalis instituit & mandavit, Exod. XII. E. illa necessaria est necessitate præcepti. Neglecta manducatio agni paschalis damnauit.

Exod. XI, 15. E. obseruata saluauit atque adeo necessaria fuit necessitate non tantum præcepti, sed & medii.

Quæst. XLII. Quæ circumstantiæ obseruandæ sunt ad plenius cognoscendum sacramentum agni paschalis?

Vt plenius intelligamus hoc sacramentum, obseruandæ sunt circumstantiæ loci a), & temporis b).

Prob. a. Locus celebrati paschatis fuit vel extraordinarius, vel ordinarius. Extraordinarius primus erat Ægyptus, & in specie domus cuiusque patrisfamilias, Exod. XII, 46. alter desertum Sina, Num. IX. 2. Tertius Gilgal, Ios. V, 10. Ordinarius erat Hierosolyma; quippe quæ erat locus ille, quem delegerat Deus ad collocandum ibi nomen suum, Deut. XVI, 5. 6. Expressa illa loci denominatione 1) obuian ibatur cultibus electitiis, 2) concordia inter confessores vnius veræ religionis alebatur, 3) sacrificium Messiæ, in vrbe Hierosolyma offerendum, præfigurabatur. Extra hunc locum vero Hebræi extorres & dispersi pascha quidem mnemoneuticum, non autem panegyricum & solemne celebrarunt.

Prob. b. Tempus huius sacramenti aliud est institutionis, aliud administrationis, aliud abrogationis. Tempus institutionis incidit in annum mundi 2513. iuxta calculum D. CALOVII. Vid. ipsius chronicon biblicum fol. 80. Tempus administrationis variat, iuxta diuersos actus: nam segregatio fiebat die decimo mensis Nisan, mactatio vero die decimo quarto, assatio vero & manducatio nocte, diem decimum quartum insecuta, & quidem vigilia prima, Exod. XII, 8. Abrogatum autem sacramentum agni paschalis est institutione cœnæ dominicæ: præsente enim corpore cessat vmbra, Col. II, 17. Accedit, quod celebratio solemnis paschatis adstricta fuerit ad templum Hierosolymitanum, quo collapso, ipsius solemnitas exspirauit.

SVSPIRIVM.

Humani intellectus imbecillitas tibi, o Deus omniscie, constat liquidissime. Non acquiescit ille promissionibus vel verissimis, sed signa & pignora, in oculos incurrentia, postulat. Consulturus tu, Pater clementissime, infirmitati humani intellectus, signa visibilia inuisibilis gratiæ tuæ ordinasti sapientissime. Id quod grata animi memoria recolens, precor humillime, vt sacramentorum salutari vsu me infirmum confirmes, languentem excites, vacillantem sustentes, quo stem immotus in doctrina fidei & pietate vitæ, iuxta atque strenuus pugnem aduersus diabolum, mundum & carnem! Dispensa tandem ex gratia, æterne Deus, mihi, sub sole tibi soli militanti, coronam iustitiæ & gloriæ!


## 31 On the Sacraments of the New Testament, and Baptism

Question 1. How many are the sacraments of the New Testament?

The sacraments of the N.T. are two, baptism and the Lord's Supper, or the Eucharist.

Proof 1) From the requirements of the sacraments of the N.T. How many are the sacred and solemn actions, instituted by Christ, proper to the N.T., consisting of an external visible element defined by Christ Himself, and dispensing with the same the heavenly thing, likewise determined by Christ in the words of institution, for the purpose of conferring and sealing grace, comprehended in the word of promise, so many there are so many sacraments of the N. T.: But there are only two such sacred and solemn actions, namely baptism and the eucharist: Therefore. 2) If, besides the Spirit, the witness of our salvation, there are only two earthly witnesses in the N. T. concerning divine grace and our salvation, namely water and blood; more than two sacraments of the N. T. are not to be established: But the former is true, as John testifies, 1 ep. c. V, 6. Therefore also the latter. 3) Primitive… true, as John testifies, 1 ep. c. V, 6. Therefore the latter is also. 3) The primitive church had only two sacraments, concerning which Paul 1 Cor. XII, 13. We have all, he says, been baptized in one spirit, and have been made to drink into one spirit. 4) Those are the only sacraments of the N. T. whose matter flowed from the side of Christ hanging on the cross. But the matter of baptism and the eucharist &c. Therefore. The major is clear from a comparison of the Johannine passage 1 ep. c. V, 6. and the gloss. ordin. which is from AVGVSTINE, praises this opinion: Just as Eve is made from the side of Adam while he sleeps: So when Christ is dead, his side is pierced by a lance, so that the sacraments may flow forth, by which the church is formed. The minor is evident from John XIX, 34. 5) Just as in the O. T. there were only two, not more, properly called sacraments, circumcision and the paschal lamb: so also in the N. T. the sacraments, properly and strictly called, are none but those two which were substituted in their place, baptism, which is also called περιτομὴ ἀπειρίτμητος thence, Col. II, 11. and the S. eucharist, which for that reason was instituted after the eating of the paschal lamb on the very night in which Christ was betrayed, at the same table, Matthew XXVI, 18. 6) Because these two sacraments suffice for spiritual life. There are four things which man needs for the constitution and preservation of life. Birth, clothing, food, and medicine. Man receives the birth and clothing of spiritual life in baptism, food and medicine in the S. supper. What is there that he could further desire? 7) The remaining sacraments, which are feigned by the adversaries, are not properly called sacraments of the N. T. For matrimony is not proper to the N. T., because it had long since been instituted in paradise. Penance flourished as much in the times of the old as of the new testament, nor does it have a visible element defined by Christ himself. Extreme unction was not instituted by Christ, but according to the mind of LOMBARD it is owed to S. James; nor did it always endure in the new testament. Order indeed has the promise of the efficacy of the ministry, but that is not connected with an external visible element. Confirmation was not instituted by Christ, whether you look at its matter or its form. The antithesis is that of the Papists, whose opinion is that there are seven sacraments: baptism, the Lord's supper, confirmation, penance, unction, the order of the ministers of the church, matrimony *). Since their arguments are weak, we shall touch upon at least a few of them: I. How many

I. As many as are the necessary supports of the spiritual life, so many are the sacraments. But there are seven, etc. E. The major premise is established: because the sacraments were divinely instituted so that they might confer, strengthen, and increase spiritual life, and preserve it from diseases. The minor is proven; because through baptism spiritual generation occurs, through confirmation augmentation, through the eucharist nourishment, through penance a remedy against sin, through extreme unction a remedy against the remnants of sin, through matrimony men are propagated to be deputed to the worship of God, and through holy order they are governed and ordained. Resp. 1) If it is permitted to argue thus, there will be more sacraments than seven, namely the blood of Christ, the preaching of the divine word, and daily prayer, which contribute much of moment to the spiritual life. 2) Neither extreme unction nor marriage generates spiritual life, or preserves it once generated.

II. Marriage is called a great sacrament, Eph. V, 32, and is an efficacious medium of divine grace; since the woman is saved through the generation of children, if she has remained in faith, 1. Tim. II, 15. Resp. 1) In the text there is μυςήριον, which extends more broadly than sacrament. 2) The spiritual marriage of Christ and the church, adumbrated by the marriage of husband and wife, is called μυςήριον. 3) Τεκνογονία is neither a cause of salvation nor an impediment to salvation.

III. Extreme unction is a sacrament: for it has the word of command and promise, and a visible element, Iac. V, 14. Resp. Distinguish between corporal and spiritual unction. The place cited concerns corporal unction, and that miraculous, which had a place in the primitive church. But sacraments strictly so called confer and bind evangelical grace concerning the remission of sins and connected spiritual benefits.

IV. Penance is a sacrament properly so called, insofar as it is joined with absolution: for it has a divine command, an annexed promise of grace, Io. XX, 23, and an external symbol, viz. χειροθεσίαν, or the imposition of hands. This is what the Apology of the A. C. p. 200 observed. Baptism, the Lord's supper, and absolution, which is the sacrament of penance, are truly sacraments. For these rites have the command of God and the promise of grace, which is proper to the N. T. Resp. Penance, joined with absolution, approaches closely to the nature of sacraments properly so called; for through it the benefits of Christ are dispensed to penitents according to the command of God, evangelical promises are applied in particular, and the gratuitous remission of sins is announced: but it does not have an external and visible element, expressly determined in the word of institution; concerning which AUGUSTIN. tract. 80. in Io. Let the word be added which they observe, and which is accustomed to be performed with many superstitious rites (for requisites 1, 2, 3 are missing): It is not 2) Order and the consecration of ministers of the church (for requisites 2, 3, 4 are missing): Nor 3) matrimony (likewise requisites 2, 3, 4 are missing) and behold! a wondrous contradiction, and a doubled one at that: by what pact, we ask, will this opinion of theirs concerning the sacrament of matrimony be able to be reconciled with another decree of theirs concerning celibacy, as if its dignity and excellence were greater than that of marriage? Can anything be holier and more excellent than a sacrament? How unjustly also is it dealt with the priests! Is it right and fair to deprive men, consecrated to a holy business, of the grace of the sacrament? What further? If someone, in their usual manner, argues thus: that which one does not have, one cannot give to another?): Nor 4) absolution of sins (for requisites 2 and 4 are missing): Finally, least of all 5) extreme unction, as if it were extreme superstition (all four enumerated requisites are missing). What the Apostles did, Marc. VI, 13, and what for some time was the custom under the auspices of the church of the N. T., Iac. V, 14, 15, that 1) was something singular and extraordinary, just like miracles; let them therefore perform today, if their powers are worth anything, even those things attributed to the first legates of Christ, Marc. XVI, 17, 18: 2) it pertained to healing the sick: therefore it was the least thing like extreme unction, a cause of death, as is evident in both cited places: 3) it carried with it nothing of the many and so superstitious rites which are thought necessary for this action in the Roman assembly.

to the element, and it becomes a sacrament. Χειροθεσία (laying on of hands) is not expressly defined by the word of institution (which, according to the mind of the Papists, is held in John 20:23), nor is it essential to repentance and absolution. Add that repentance also existed in the O.T. Therefore, it is not a sacrament of the N.T. strictly so called.

Latin:

Quæst. I. Quot sunt sacramenta noui testamenti?

Sacramenta N. T. sunt duo, baptismus & cœna dominica, siue eucharistia.

Prob. 1) a requisitis sacramentorum N. T. Quot sunt actiones sacræ & solemnes, a Christo institutæ, N. T. propriæ, externo visibili elemento, a Christo ipso definito, constantes, & cum eodem dispensantes rem cœlestem, itidem a Christo in verbis institutionis determinatarn, ad conferendam & obsignandam gratiam, verbo promissionis comprehenfam, tot tot sunt sacramenta N. T.: Atqui duæ tantum sunt eiusmodi actiones sacræ & solennes, nimirum baptismus & eucharistia: Ergo. 2) Si præter Spiritum, nostræ salutis testem, duo tantum sunt in N. T. testes terrestres de gratia diuina & salute nostra, scilicet aqua & sanguis; plura non sunt statuenda sacramenta N. T., quam duo: Atqui prius est verum, teste Ioanne, 1 ep. c. V, 6. Ergo & posterius. 3) Primitiua ecclesia duo tantum habuit sacramenta, de quibus Paullus 1 Cor. XII, 13. Omnes, inquit, vno spiritu baptizati, & ad vnum spiritum potati sumus. 4) Illa sunt tantum sacramenta N. T. quorum materia e latere Christi pendentis in cruce fluxit. At baptismi & eucharistiæ materia &c. E. Maior liquet e collatione loci Ioannæi 1 ep. c. V, 6. & glossæ ordin. quæ est ex AVGVSTINO hanc laudat sententiam: Sicut dormiente Adamo fit Eua de latere: Sic mortuo Christo lancea percutitur latus, vt profluant sacramenta, quibus formetur ecclesia. Minor patet ex Io. XIX, 34. 5) Quemadmodum in V. T. duo tantum, non plura fuere proprie dicta sacramenta, circuncisio & agnus paschalis: ita & in N. T. sacramenta, proprie & stricte dicta, non, nisi duo illa sunt, quæ in istorum locum surrogata sunt, baptismus, qui & περιτομὴ ἀπειρίτμητος inde dicitur, Col. II, 11. & S. eucharistia, quæ ideo post agni paschalis comestionem in ipsa nocte, qua Christus traditus est, in eadem mensa instituta est, Matth. XXVI, 18. 6) Quia hæc duo sacramenta ad vitam spiritualem sufficiunt. Quatuor sunt, quibus homo ad vitæ constitutionem & conseruationem eget. Natiuitas, vestimentum, alimentum & medicamentum. Natiuitatem & vestimentum vitæ spiritualis accipit homo in baptismo, alimentum & medicamentum in S. cœna. Quid est, quod porro desiderare queat? 7) Sacramenta reliqua, quæ ab aduersariis finguntur, non sunt proprie dicta sacramenta N. T. Nam matrimonium non est proprium N. T., quia iamdudum in paradiso institutum erat. Pœnitentia viguit tam temporibus veteris, quam nou. test., neque habet elementum visibile, a Christo ipso definitum. Extrema vnctio non est a Christo instituta, sed ex mente LOMBARDI ea debetur S. Iacobo; neque semper durauit in nou. test. Ordo habet quidem efficaciæ ministerii promissionem, sed illa non est connexa cum externo elemento visibili. Confirmatio a Christo non est instituta, siue eius materiam, siue formam spectes. Antithesis est Pontificiorum, quorum sententia septem sunt sacramenta: baptismus, cœna dominica, confirmatio, pœnitentia, vnctio, ordo ministrorum ecclesiæ, matrimonium *). Quorum argumenta cum infirma sint, nos pauca saltem ex iisdem attingemus: I. Quot

I. Quot sunt vitæ spiritualis necessaria adminicula, tot sunt sacramenta. Atqui septem sunt &c. E. Maior constat: quia sacramenta diuinitus instituta sunt, vt vitam spiritualem conferant, roborent, augeant, a morbis præseruent. Minor probatur; quia per baptismum fit generatio spiritualis, per confirmationem augmentatio, per eucharistiam nutritio, per pœnitentiam remedium contra peccatum, per vnctionem extremam remedium contra reliquias peccati, per matrimonium propagantur homines, ad cultum Dei deputandi, per ordinem sacrum reguntur ac ordinantur. Resp. 1) Si sic argumentari liceat, plura erunt sacramenta, quam septem, nempe sanguis Christi, prædicatio verbi diuini, & quotidiana oratio, quæ ad vitam spiritualem multum conferunt momenti. 2) Nec extrema vnctio, nec coniugium vitam spiritualem generat, aut generatam conferuat.

II. Coniugium dicitur sacramentum magnum, Eph. V, 32. & est efficax gratiæ diuinæ medium; siquidem mulier saluatur per filiorum generationem, si manserit in fide, 1. Tim. II, 15. Resp. 1) In textu habetur μυςήριον, quod latius patet, quam sacramentum. 2) Spirituale coniugium Christi & ecclesiæ adumbratum per coniugium mariti & vxoris dicitur μυςήριον. 3) Τεκνογονία neque salutis caussa, neque salutis impedimentum est.

III. Extrema vnctio est sacramentum: habet enim verbum mandati & promissionis, atque elementum visibile, Iac. V, 14. Resp. Dist. inter vnctionem corporalem & spiritualem. L. c. de vnctione corporali, eaque miraculosa, quæ in ecclesia primitiua locum habebat, agitur. At sacramenta stricte dicta conferunt & oblignant gratiam euangelicam de remissione peccatorum, & beneficiis connexis spiritualibus.

IV. Pœnitentia est sacramentum proprie dictum, quatenus cum absolutione coniuncta est: habet enim mandatum diuinum, annexam promissionem gratiæ, Io. XX, 23. atque symbolum externum, scil. χειροθεσίαν, siue impositionem manuum. Id quod obseruauit Apologia A. C. p. 200. Vere sunt sacramenta baptismus, cœna domini & absolutio, quæ est sacramentum pœnitentiæ. Nam hi ritus habent mandatum Dei & promissionem gratiæ, quæ est propria N. T. Resp. Pœnitentia, cum absolutione coniuncta, proxime ad naturam sacramentorum proprie dictorum accedit; per illam enim pœnitentibus iuxta mandatum Dei dispensantur beneficia Christi, promissiones euangelicæ in specie applicantur, & gratuita peccatorum remissio annuntiatur: at non habet externum & visibile elementum, in verbo institutionis expresse determinatum; de quo AVGVSTIN. tract. 80. in Io. Accedat verbum quem illi seruant, & multis cum superstitiosis ritibus peragi solita (deest enim requis. 1. 2. 3.): Non est 2) Ordo & consecratio ministrorum ecclesiæ (deest enim requis. 2. 3. 4.): Nec 3) matrimonium (deest enim itidem requis. 2. 3. 4.) & en! miram repugnantiam, eamque geminatam: quo pacto, quæsumus, hæc illorum sententia de sacramento matrimonii poterit conciliari cum alio quodam illorum decreto de cælibatu, quasi eius maior sit dignitas ac præstantia, quam coniugii? Num quid esse queat sacramento sanctius ac præstabilius? Quam inique etiam cum sacerdotibus agitur! An fas & æquum est, homines, sacro negotio consecratos, sacramenti gratia priuare? Quid porro? si quis, illorum quidem vsitato more, ita argumentetur: quod quis non habet, alteri dare non potest?): Neque 4) absolutio peccatorum (deest enim requis. 2. & 4.): Omnium tandem minime 5) extrema vnctio, velut extrema superstitio (desunt enim omnia quatuor numerata). Quod Apostoli fecerunt, Marc. VI, 13. & quod sub auspicium ecclesiæ N. T. aliquo tempore moris fuit, Iac. V, 14. 15. id 1) erat aliquid singulare atque extraordinarium, quem ad modum miracula; præstent igitur hodieque, si quid valeant vires, etiam illa, primis Christi legatis tributa, Marc. XVI, 17. 18: 2) ad sanandos ægrotos pertinebat: ergo nihil minus erat, quam extrema vnctio, mortis caussa, prout patet in vtroque loco citato: 3) ne quidquam secum ferebat ex tot, tamque superstitiosis ritibus, qui in cœtu Romano ad hanc actionem necessarii putantur.

ad elementum, & fit sacramentum. Χειροθεσία non est verbo institutionis (quæ ex mente Pontificiorum habetur Io. XX, 23.) expresse definita, neque pœnitentiæ & absolutioni essentialis. Adiice, quod pœnitentia etiam fuerit in V. T. E. non est sacramentum N. T. stricte dictum.


### II. What is baptism?

Baptism is a sacred and solemn action, divinely instituted, by which a human sinner, living and born, without distinction of sex and age, is washed with water, in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so that through this washing of water, the divine grace, promised by the word of the gospel, may be applied, conferred, and sealed to him.

Obs. I. Baptism is derived from the verb βαπτίζειν, which properly signifies to wash, either by immersing or by sprinkling. It signifies immersion indeed more often, but sprinkling more rarely. The meaning of sprinkling occurs in Mark 7:34, where the Jews are said not to have eaten unless they were baptized, i.e., washed their hands with water, and Luke 11:38, the Pharisees are said to have wondered that Christ had sat down not baptized, i.e., with unwashed hands (*).

Obs. II. The word baptism is taken either improperly or properly. Improperly it denotes a) the baptism of blood, i.e., the cross, calamity, a bloody and bitter death. In which sense the Savior says, Luke 12:50, I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how am I constrained until it be accomplished! Cf. Matt. 20:22. Thence it happened that in the primitive church martyrdom was called the baptism of blood, when catechumens were snatched away by a bloody death before they were dipped in baptismal water; to which, however, the remission of sins is wrongly attributed by the Papists; since Christ procured this with his own blood, which he confers and applies to believers through the sacraments. b) The baptism of the Spirit, or fire, that is, the miraculous outpouring of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, concerning which John says in Matt. 3:12: I baptize you with water, but Christ will baptize you with the Spirit and with fire; by which words are indicated the gifts of tongues, miraculously bestowed upon the Apostles, and represented by fiery tongues, Acts 2:16. c) The baptism of the journey, through the Red Sea, and the cloud, 1 Cor. 10:2. Our fathers were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, i.e., the Israelites crossed the Red Sea, with Moses and the shining cloud as their leader. For just as the Israelites were liberated from Egyptian slavery through this crossing: so we are asserted by the benefit of baptism from the slavery of the Stygian Pharaoh. And as Pharaoh with his entire army was swallowed by the waves of the Erythraean Sea: so the old Adam, surrounded by an army of vices, is submerged in baptism. Properly it denotes a) generally every washing, or cleansing of filth. b) Specifically it designates the legal and Levitical washings, handed down to the Israelites by the law of Moses, which in Heb. 9:10 are called διάφοροι βαπτισμοὶ. c) Most specifically it designates the evangelical baptism, proper to the new testament, and is commonly called the baptism of water.

Obs. III. Some add the baptism of light, i.e., doctrine. But the sayings of scripture which are cited, Matt. 21:25, Acts 18:25, Acts 19:3, are to be understood concerning the baptism of water.

Latin:

Baptismus est sacra & solemnis actio, diuinitus instituta, qua homo peccator, viuils & natus, sine discrimine sexus & ætatis, abluitur aqua, in nomine Patris, Filii & Spiritus S., vt per hoc lauacrum aquæ gratia diuina, verbo euangelii promissa, ipsi applicetur, conferatur & obsignetur.

Obs. I. Baptismus, deriuatur a verbo βαπτίζειν, quod proprie significat lauare, aut immergendo, aut aspergendo. Immersionem quidem sæpius, aspersionem autem rarius significat. Occurrit aspersionis significatus Marc. VII. 34. vbi Iudæi dicuntur non comedisse, nisi baptizarentur, i. e. manus abluerent aqua, & Luc. XI, 38. Pharisæi dicuntur mirati, accubuisse Christum non baptizatum, i. e. manibus non ablutis (*).

Obs. II. Vox baptismi sumitur vel improprie, vel proprie. Improprie notat a) baptismum sanguinis, i. e. crucem, calamitatem, cruentam & acerbam mortem. Quo sensu inquit Saluator, Luc. XII, 50. Baptismo opus habeo baptizari, & quomodo coarctor, donec perficiatur! Conf. Matth. XX, 22. Exinde factum, vt in primitiua ecclesia martyrium baptismus sanguinis diceretur, quando catechumeni cruenta rapiebantur morte prius, quam aqua baptismali tingerentur; Cui tamen remissio peccatorum male a Pontificiis tribuitur; siquidem hanc Christus sanguine suo peperit, quam credentibus per sacramenta confert & applicat. b) Baptismum flaminis, siue ignis, hoc est miraculosam effusionem donorum Spiritus S., de qua Ioannes Matth. III, 12. inquit: Ego baptizo vos aqua, Christus autem baptizabit vos Spiritu & igne; quibus verbis indigitantur dona linguarum, in Apostolos mirifice collata, & ignitis linguis repræsentata, Act. II, 16. c) Baptismum itineris, per mare rubrum, & nubem, 1 Cor. X, 2. Patres nostri in Mosen baptizati sunt in nube & mari, i. e. transiuerunt Israëlitæ mare rubrum, duce Mose & nube lucida. Sicut enim Israëlitæ per hunc transitum ex Ægyptiaca seruitute liberati sunt: ita nos beneficio baptismi a seruitute stygii Pharaonis asserimur. Et vt Pharao cum vniuerso exercitu fluctibus maris Erythræi haustus est: ita vetus Adam, exercitu vitiorum stipatus, in baptismo submergitur. Proprie notat a) generatim omnem lotionem, vel sordium ablutionem. b) Speciatim designat lauacra legalia & Leuitica, Israëlitis lege Mofis tradita, quæ Hebr. IX, 10. dicuntur διάφοροι βαπτισμοὶ. c) Specialissime designat baptismum euangelicum, noui testamenti proprium, & dicitur communiter baptismus fluminis.

Obs. III. Addunt nonnulli baptismum luminis, i. e. doctrinam. Sed dicta scripturæ, quæ citantur, Matth, XXI, 25. Act. XVIII, 25. Act. XIX, 3. de baptismo fluminis intelligenda sunt.


### Q. III. Who instituted baptism?

The Triune God instituted the sacrament of baptism a). Christ the θεάνθρωπος, revived from the dead, repeated the command to baptize, and extended it to all nations b); yet he himself baptized no one with his own hands c).

Proof a. God sent John, that he might baptize with water, Jo. I, 33. To which command he most promptly obeyed. For the word of the Lord came to John, and he came (about to obey the divine command) preaching baptism, Luc. III, 2.

Proof b. Christ after the resurrection did not first institute the sacrament of baptism, but repeated the institution, extended the command to baptize to all nations and men, and prescribed a universal and perpetual norm and formula of administering baptism to the Apostles and their successors, saying: All power is given to me in heaven and in earth. From which it is concluded that the authority to institute baptism belongs to Christ, even according to his human nature, according to which all power was given to him in heaven and in earth, Matth. XXVIII, 18.

Proof c. Jo. IV, 2. Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples. But when in Jo. III, 22. & 26. Christ is said to have baptized, that is to be understood of the ministry of the Apostles, through whom Christ baptized; just as King Solomon is said to have built the temple, Act. VII, 21. not immediately, but through architects. The cause, why Christ did not baptize αὐτοχειρὶ, because scripture has not revealed it, we do not clearly know. The ancients, however, have brought forward the following reasons: 1) That Christ might remove the false persuasion of those being baptized, lest those who had been baptized immediately by Christ might seem to have received a greater benefit than those who had been baptized by the disciples: 2) That Christ might show the distinction between himself and the ministers, that the ministers might baptize only with water, but he himself with the Spirit: 3) That he might indicate that baptism is not to be estimated from the dignity of the minister.

Latin:

Sacramentum baptismi instituit Deus triunus a). Christus θεάνθρωπος, rediviuus ex mortuis, mandatum baptizandi repetiuit, & ad omnes gentes extendit b); ipse tamen manibus propriis neminem baptizauit c).

Prob. a. Deus misit Ioannem, vt baptizaret aqua, Io. I, 33. Cui mandato hic promtissime obtemperauit. Nam ad Ioannem factum est verbum Domini, & venit (mandato diuino pariturus) prædicans baptismum, Luc. III, 2.

Prob. b. Christus post resurrectionem sacramentum baptismi non primum instituit, sed institutionem repetiuit, mandatum baptizandi ad omnes nationes & homines extendit, & vniversalem perpetuamque administrandi baptismi normam ac formulam Apostolis eorumque successoribus præscripsit, inquiens: Mihi data est omnis potestas in cælo & in terra. Ex quo conficitur, Christo competere auctoritatem instituendi baptismum, etiam secundum humanam naturam, secundum quam ipsi omnis potestas data est in cælo & in terra, Matth. XXVIII, 18.

Prob. c. Io. IV, 2. Iesus ipse non baptizauit, sed discipuli eius. Quando autem Io. III, 22. & 26. Christus baptizasse dicitur, id intelligendum est de ministerio Apostolorum, per quos Christus baptizauit; sicut rex Salomo ædificasse dicitur templum, Act. VII, 21. non immediate, sed mediantibus architectis. Caussam, cur Christus αὐτοχειρὶ non baptizauerit, quia scriptura non reuelauit, liquido non cognoscimus. Veteres tamen sequentes adduxerunt rationes: 1) Vt Christus falsam amoliretur persuasionem baptizandorum, ne illi, qui a Christo immediate baptizati essent, maius accepisse viderentur beneficium, quam qui a discipulis baptizati erant: 2) Vt ostenderet Christus discrimen inter se & ministros, quod ministri tantum aqua, ipse autem Spiritu baptizaret: 3) Vt indigitaret, baptismum non esse æstimandum ex ministri dignitate.


### Q. IV. Who ordinarily administers baptism?

Ordinarily, the ministers of the church, legitimately called and ordained a), orthodox and blameless in life b), administer baptism. Extraordinarily, however, and in a case of necessity, any pious Christian who is knowledgeable in sacred rites, whether male or female, can administer baptism c).

Proof a. Only the ministers of the church are the ordinary dispensers of the mysteries of God, 1 Cor. IV, 1. They are the same as the ambassadors of God, sent to the ministry of reconciliation, 2 Cor. V, 18. 20. which consists in the preaching of the word, and the administration of the sacraments.

Proof b. From 2 Tim. II, 15. Be diligent to present yourself approved to God, a worker who does not need to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth. Where note, that piety of life is required of a minister of the church for the sake of decorum, but the efficacy of baptism does not depend on his probity; since it flows from God the author. Whence there is no doubt at all concerning the validity of baptism dispensed by an impure minister.

Proof c. 1) Laymen in a case of necessity can preach the word of God (which is evident from the example of Aquila and Priscilla, Act. XVIII, 26. Rom. XVI, 3.). But whose it is to teach; his it is also to baptize.

2) Every Christian is a spiritual priest before God, Apoc. I, 6. Wherefore by virtue of the spiritual priesthood he can baptize, if he is knowledgeable in sacred rites.

…3) Laymen administered circumcision, in whose place baptism has succeeded. Zippora circumcised her son, Exod. IV, 24. 25. which the Maccabean women also did in a case of necessity, 1 Maccab. I, 36. book II, c. 10. Which circumcision God himself approved.

You say: I. To whom it is not permitted to teach in the church, to him it is not permitted to baptize, (because the office of teaching and baptizing is of equal dignity): But it is not permitted to a woman to teach in the church, 1 Tim. II, 12. Therefore. Resp. Just as it is not appropriate for women to teach solemnly and publicly; so the solemn use of baptizing does not befit them. But just as in urgent necessity they can teach privately, so also they can baptize.

You say: II. Women are not called to teach and baptize. Resp. They are not called by a special and economic vocation; they are, however, called by a general vocation to the spiritual priesthood, and by a vocation of charity, to be exercised in a case of necessity.

You say: III. To whom it is not permitted to dispense the Holy Supper, to them it is not permitted to administer baptism: But it is not permitted to women to dispense the Holy Supper. Therefore. The major premise is evident: because the utility and necessity of baptism and the Lord's Supper are equal. Resp. I deny the major.

To the proof we say that the necessity of baptism is greater than that of the Lord's Supper. For concerning baptism the Savior says: Unless one has been born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven, John III, 5. But he does not say the same concerning the Lord's Supper. Confirmation of faith is had from the Holy Supper, but not from it alone; rather, it can also be obtained and had from the pious remembrance of baptism, the announcement of absolution, and the evangelical promise.

Quest. V. Was the baptism of John and that of Christ, administered by the Apostles, the same?

The baptism of John and of Christ was one and the same, by reason of origin and efficacy, although accidentally the former differs from the latter.

Proof a. Because the baptism of John was instituted by God just as much as that of the Apostles, John I, 33. Luke III, 2.

Proof b. 1) Because John baptized a baptism of repentance and faith in Christ. This is what Paul inculcates to the Ephesian disciples, Acts XIX, 4. John indeed baptized a baptism of repentance, but he told the people that they should believe in him who was to come, namely in Jesus Christ.

2) John baptized for the remission of sins. But that does not occur except through faith in the name of Jesus Christ. Acts X, 43.

Proof c. 1) John baptized into Christ ἐρχόμενον, the one to come, i.e., born indeed, but not yet suffered and dead, nor yet glorified, and announced to the whole world, Matt. III, 11. Acts XIX, 4. John I, 29. The Apostles, however, although they baptized in the beginning into Christ not yet suffered or dead; later, however, they administered baptism into Christ suffered, dead, glorified, and known to the whole world, Acts II, 36. Rom. VI, 3.

2) Through the Johannine baptism, no visible gifts of the Holy Spirit were conferred upon any man. For John performed no sign, John X, 41. The Apostles, however, after the ascension of Christ into heaven, not always indeed, but very often, conferred the visible gifts of the Holy Spirit through baptism, as can be read in Acts XIX, 2. 3.

Antithesis of the Papists and Socinians, who deny the identity of the baptism of John and the Apostles.

Who object to us: 1. John himself distinguishes his baptism from the baptism of Christ, when he says that he baptizes with water, but Christ will baptize with the Spirit and fire, Matt. III, 11. Resp. The baptism of Christ is taken in two ways: a) For the sacrament of initiation, which is otherwise called the baptism of water: b) For the visible outpouring of the Holy Spirit, and it is called the baptism of fire. When it is asked: whether the baptism of John is of the same efficacy as the baptism of Christ? It is accepted in the former sense, insofar as it is a sacrament of initiation; by which reason it is the same as the baptism of John, since by it also an initiation into Christianity was effected.

II. Certain disciples baptized by John were baptized again by Paul, namely with the baptism of Christ, Acts XIX, 3. seqq. Resp. Those disciples were not dipped twice, but once by John the proto-baptist, v. 3. But when it is said in verse 5: Having heard these things, they were baptized in the name of Jesus, these words are not those of Luke the historian, who wrote the Acts of the Apostles, but the words of Paul the teacher still speaking, and explaining the baptism of John.

Indeed, when the disciples in v. 3 had said that they had been baptized with the baptism of John, Paul begins to explain how and in what order John baptized, and shows that the baptism of John was a baptism of repentance, and that John spoke of the coming Christ, so that they might believe in him. The Apostle continues by teaching, v. 5: Having heard these things, they were baptized (namely by John, not by Paul), the hearers of John in the name of the Lord Jesus.

The reason is at hand: because it is a continued speech of Paul, and in the Greek text (ἀκούσαντες δὲ) the particle δὲ corresponds to the preceding particle μὲν (Ἰωάννης μὲν).

From which series of the text it is clear that Paul did not re-baptize them, but only laid hands upon them, so that by a visible sign, of which they had heard nothing before, they might receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

For by the Holy Spirit is understood the miraculous spirit, or the miraculous outpouring of the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

See Acts X, 44. 45. 46. III. Whoever is not said to have baptized in the name of Christ, his baptism is not the same as the baptism of the Apostles: because the Apostles are said to have baptized in the name of Christ: But John &c.

E. Resp. I deny the minor: for according to the testimony of Paul, Acts

XIX, 4. John baptized a baptism of repentance, and said to the people that they should believe in him who was to come, namely in Jesus Christ.

IV. John is not said to have baptized in the name of the Most Holy Trinity. Resp. Although it may not be said αὐτολεξεὶ (word for word), or found κατὰ τὸ γράμμα (according to the letter), that John baptized in the name of the Most Holy Trinity; yet because John was sent by God to baptize, John

I, 33. it is validly concluded that he baptized in the name of the Most Holy Trinity; since this formula of baptizing is handed down by Christ, Matt.

XXVIII, 19. Nor is it probable that God instituted baptism with one form and then another.

And how would he not baptize in the name of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, to whom the whole Most Holy Trinity appeared under visible signs while he was baptizing?

V. The baptism of John pertained to the Jews alone: for we do not read that John baptized other nations than the Jews: The baptism of Christ did not pertain to the Jews alone: Therefore, the baptism of John is not the same as that of Christ.

Resp. a) John did not baptize only Jews: because all Judea and the whole region situated around the Jordan, Matt.

III, 5. was baptized by John, in which tract there were many Gentiles.

Conf. Matt.

IV, 15. b) John preached the baptism of repentance, Acts

XIX, 4. whoever stood in need of repentance, to them the baptism of John pertained. But not only Jews, but also Gentiles stand in need of repentance.

VI. Whoever by baptizing prepared the way for Christ, his baptism does not agree with the baptism of Christ: But John &c.

Luke

I, 76.

John

I, 23.

Therefore.

Resp. That preparation detracts nothing from the efficacy of John's ministry.

But just as his doctrine and preaching was effective for converting men, Luke

I, 16. and for giving the knowledge of salvation, which is in the remission of sins, Luke

I, 77.: so his baptism also did not lack spiritual virtue and efficacy.

VII. The baptism of Christ is the baptism of regeneration, Tit.

III, 6.

But the baptism of John was not the baptism of regeneration: Therefore.

The minor is proven: because the baptism of John is called only the baptism of repentance, Matt.

III, 11.

Resp. By the very fact that the baptism of John is a baptism of repentance, it is a baptism of regeneration.

For regeneration formally consists in the gift of faith, which, as a principal part, saving repentance embraces within itself.

Objection: But by the very fact that it is called the baptism of John, it differs from the baptism of Christ. Resp. It is called the baptism of John, as of a minister, whose author and master is God. John baptized diakonikos (ministerially); the autokratoria (sovereign authority) resides with Christ. See John I, 6; III, 27.

Latin:

Ordinarie baptismum administrant ministri ecclesiæ, legitime vocati & ordinati a), orthodoxi & vita inculpati b). Extraordinarie vero, & in casu necessitatis, quiuis Christianus pius & rituum sacrorum gnarus, siue sit mas, siue fœmina, baptismum administrare potest c).

Prob. a. Soli ministri ecclesiæ sunt ordinarii dispensatores mysteriorum Dei, 1 Cor. IV, 1. Sunt iidem legati Dei, missi ad ministerium reconciliationis, 2 Cor. V, 18. 20. quod in prædicatione verbi, & administratione sacramentorum consistit.

Prob. b. Ex 2 Tim. II, 15. Diligens esto, vt teipsum sistas probatum Deo operarium, non pudendum, qui recte secet verbum veritatis. Vbi notes, quod pietas vitæ ratione decori a ministro ecclesiæ requiratur, efficacia autem baptismi a probitate eius non dependeat; quippe quæ ab auctore Deo manat. Vnde de valore baptismi, ab impuro ministro dispensati, minime dubitandum est.

Prob. c. 1) Laici in casu necessitatis possunt prædicare verbum Dei (quod constat exemplo Aquilæ & Priscillæ, Act. XVIII, 26. Rom. XVI, 3.). Sed cuius est, docere; illius etiam est, baptizare.

2) Omnis Christianus est spiritualis sacerdos coram Deo, Apoc. I, 6. Quo circa vi spiritualis sacerdotii baptizare potest, si rituum sacrorum sit gnarus.

3) Laici circumcisionem, in cuius locum baptismus successit, administrarunt. Zippora circumcidit filium, Exod. IV, 24. 25. quod etiam mulieres Maccabaeae in casu necessitatis fecerunt, 1 Maccab. I, 36. libr. II, c. 10. Quam circumcisionem ipse Deus approbavit.

Dicis: I. Cui non permittitur docere in ecclesia, illi non permittitur baptizare, (quia munus docendi et baptizandi est paris dignitatis): Sed mulieri non permittitur docere in ecclesia, 1 Tim. II, 12. E. Resp. Uti mulieribus non competit docere solemniter et publice; ita usus baptizandi solemnis ipsis non convenit. Sed sicut urgente necessitate possunt docere privatim, ita et baptizare.

Dicis: II. Mulieres ad docendum et baptizandum non sunt vocatae. Resp. Non sunt vocatae vocatione speciali et economica; sunt tamen vocatae vocatione generali ad spirituale sacerdotium, et vocatione caritatis, in casu necessitatis exercenda.

Dicis: III. Quibus non licet dispensare S. coenam, illis non licet administrare baptismum: Atqui mulieribus non licet dispensare S. coenam. E. Maior constat: quia par est utilitas et necessitas baptismi et coenae dominicae. Resp. Neg. maior.

Ad probationem dicimus, quod necessitas baptismi maior sit, quam coenae dominicae. Nam de baptismo inquit Salvator: Nisi quis natus fuerit ex aqua et Spiritu, non potest ingredi in regnum caelorum, Io. III, 5. At non idem dicit de coena dominica. Confirmatio fidei habetur e S. coena, sed non sola, verum etiam ex pia baptismi recordatione, annuntiatione absolutionis, et promissione evangelica obtineri et haberi potest.

Quaest. V. Fuitne idem baptismus Ioannis, et Christi, ab Apostolis administratus?

Vnus idemque fuit baptismus Ioannis et Christi, ratione originis , et efficaciae , licet accidentaliter ille ab hoc differat .

Prob. a. Quia baptismus Ioannis aeque, ac Apostolorum a Deo fuit institutus, Io. I, 33. Luc. III, 2.

Prob. b. 1) Quia Ioannes baptizavit baptismum poenitentiae et fidei in Christum. Id quod Paulus discipulis Ephesinis inculcat, Act. XIX, 4. Ioannes baptizavit quidem baptismum poenitentiae, sed dixit populo, ut crederent in eum, qui venturus erat, nempe in Iesum Christum.

2) Ioannes baptizavit in remissionem peccatorum. At illa non contingit, nisi per fidem in nomine Iesu Christi. Act. X, 43.

Prob. c. 1) Ioannes baptizavit in Christum ἐρχόμενον, venturum, i. e. natum quidem, sed nondum passum et mortuum, nec dum glorificatum, totique mundo annuntiatum, Matth. III, 11. Act. XIX, 4. Io. I, 29. Apostoli vero licet baptizauerint initio in Christum nondum passum aut mortuum; postea tamen administrauerunt baptismum in Christum passum, mortuum, glorificatum, et toti mundo notum, Act. II, 36. Rom. VI, 3.

2) Per baptismum Ioanneum non sunt collata vlli homini visibilia Spiritus S. dona. Ioannes enim signum non edidit vllum, Io. X, 41. Apostoli vero post ascensionem Christi in coelum, non semper quidem, saepissime tamen per baptismum contulerunt dona Spiritus S. visibilia, sicut legere est Act. XIX, 2. 3.

Antithesis Pontificiorum et Socinianorum, identitatem baptismi Ioannis et Apostolorum negantium.

Qui obiiciunt nobis: 1. Ioannes ipse baptismum suum distinguit a baptismo Christi, quando dicit, se baptizare aqua, Christum vero baptizaturum esse Spiritu et igne, Matth. III, 11. Resp. Baptismus Christi dupliciter accipitur: a) Pro sacramento initiationis, quod alias baptismus fluminis dicitur: b) Pro visibili effusione Spiritus S., et dicitur baptismus flaminis. Cum quaeritur: an baptismus Ioannis eiusdem efficaciae sit cum baptismo Christi? accipitur priori modo, quatenus est sacramentum initiationis; qua ratione idem est cum baptismo Ioannis, quippe quo etiam facta est initiatio ad Christianismum.

II. Discipuli quidam baptizati a Ioanne iterum baptizati sunt a Paulo, nempe baptismo Christi, Act. XIX, 3. seqq. Resp. Discipuli illi non bis, sed semel tincti sunt a Ioanne protobaptista, v. 3. Cum autem versu 5. dicitur: His auditis baptizati sunt in nomine Iesu, verba haec non sunt Lucae historici, qui acta apostolica conscripsit, sed verba Pauli doctoris adhuc loquentis, & baptismum Ioannis explicantis.

Nimirum cum discipuli v. 3. dixissent, se baptismo Ioannis baptizatos esse, Paullus incipit explicare, quomodo & quo ordine Ioannes baptizauerit, & ostendit, quod baptismus Ioannis fuerit baptismus poenitentiae, & quod Ioannes locutus sit de venturo Christo, vt crederent in eum. Pergit Apostolus docendo, v. 5. His auditis baptizati sunt (scilicet a Ioanne, non a Paulo) auditores Ioannis in nomine Domini Iesu.

Ratio est in promptu: quia est continuata oratio Paulli, & in textu graeco (ἀκούσαντες δὲ) particula δὲ respondet praecedenti particulae μὲν (Ἰωάννης μὲν).

Ex qua serie textus perspicuum est, Paullum hos non rebaptizasse, sed tantum imposuisse manus, vt visibili specie, de qua nihil auduerant antea, dona Spiritus S. acciperent.

Per Spiritum S. enim intelligitur spiritus mirificus, siue miraculosa donorum Spiritus S. effusio.

Vid. Act. X, 44. 45. 46. III. Quicunque non dicitur baptizasse in nomine Christi, illius baptisma non est idem cum baptismo Apostolorum: quia Apostoli dicuntur baptizasse in nomine Christi: Atqui Ioannes &c.

E. Resp. Neg. minor: nam teste Paulo Act.

XIX, 4. Ioannes baptizauit baptismum poenitentiae, & dixit populo, vt crederent in eum, qui venturus erat, nempe in Iesum Christum.

IV. Ioannes non dicitur baptizasse in nomine SS. Trinitatis. Resp. Licet non αὐτολεξεὶ dicatur, siue κατὰ τὸ γράμμα inueniatur, Ioannem baptizasse in nomine SS. Trinitatis; quia tamen Ioannes a Deo ad baptizandum missus est, Io.

I, 33. valide colligitur, eum in nomine SS. Trinitatis baptizasse; quippe quae baptizandi formula a Christo traditur, Matth.

XXVIII, 19. Neque enim probabile est, Deum alia atque alia forma baptismum instituisse.

Et quomodo non baptizaret in nomine Dei Patris, Filii & Spiritus S., cui baptizandi sub signis visibilibus tota SS. Trinitas apparuit?

V. Baptismus Ioannis ad solos pertinuit Iudaeos: neque enim legimus, Ioannem alias nationes, quam Iudaeos baptizasse: Baptismus Christi non ad solos Iudaeos pertinuit: E. baptismus Ioannis non est idem, qui Christi.

Resp. a) Ioannes non solos baptizauit Iudaeos: quia tota Iudaea & vniuersa regio, circa Iordanem sita, Matth.

III, 5. baptizata est a Ioanne, in quo tractu multi erant gentiles.

Conf. Matth.

IV, 15. b) Praedicauit Ioannes baptismum poenitentiae, Act.

XIX, 4. quicunque poenitentia indiguerunt, ad illos baptismus Ioannis pertinuit. Sed indigent poenitentia non tantum Iudaei, verum etiam gentiles.

VI. Quicunque baptizando praeparauit viam Christo, illius baptismus non conuenit cum baptismo Christi: Atqui Ioannes &c.

Luc.

I, 76.

Io.

I, 23.

E.

Resp. Praeparatio illa nihil derogat efficaciae ministerii Ioannis.

Verum sicut doctrina & praedicatio eius fuit efficax ad conuertendum homines, Luc.

I, 16. & dandam scientiam salutis, quae est in remissione peccatorum, Luc.

I, 77.: ita baptismus quoque ipsius virtute & efficacia spirituali non caruit.

VII. Baptismus Christi est baptismus regenerationis, Tit.

III, 6.

At baptismus Ioannis non fuit baptismus regenerationis: E.

Minor probatur: quia baptismus Ioannis dicitur tantum baptismus poenitentiae, Matth.

III, 11.

Resp. Eo ipso, quod baptismus Ioannis est baptismus poenitentiae, est baptismus regenerationis.

Nam regeneratio formaliter consistit in donatione fidei, quam, velut partem praecipuam, salutaris poenitentia in se complectitur.

Instantia: Sed eo ipso, quod dicitur baptismus Ioannis, differt a baptismo Christi. Resp. Dicitur baptismus Ioannis, ceu ministri, cuius auctor & magister Deus est. Baptizavit Ioannes διακονικῶς, αὐτοκρατορία est penes Christum. Vid. Io. I, 6. III, 27.


### Q. VI. Is baptism conferred by a heretic efficacious and valid?

If baptism is conferred by a heretic who retains the substantials of baptism, there is no reason to doubt its efficacy . But if it is to be conferred in a flourishing church, where an orthodox minister can be had, it cannot be sought from a heterodox person without great sin . However, in a church under pressure, when necessity urges, it is sought and accepted without fault from a heretic who observes the customary formula of baptism; provided that a protestation is added, that the infant is not bound by this baptism to accept false doctrine .

Proved a. Because the efficacy of baptism rightly performed does not depend on the ministerial cause, but on the principal cause, 1 Cor. III, 7.

Proved b. Because we are forbidden to be unequally yoked with unbelievers, 2 Cor. VI, 14. Conversely, we are commanded to come out of the malignant church, lest we partake of the plagues of the malignant assembly, Rev. XVIII, 4.

Proved c. Because Christ commanded that the Pharisees be heard, sitting in the seat of Moses, insofar as they proposed the doctrine of Moses (for the seat of Moses is understood as vocal, not local; since Moses never crossed the Jordan, nor ever lived in Jerusalem), Matt. XXIII, 2. If, therefore, the circumcision of the heterodox Pharisees was not held to be invalid, certainly the baptism of heretics is not inefficacious.

Latin:

Si baptismus ab haeretico, substantialia baptismi retinente, collatus fit, de eius efficacia non est dubitandum . Sin conferendus est in ecclesia florente, vbi orthodoxus haberi potest minister, sine grandi peccato ab heterodoxo non potest peti . In ecclesia autem pressa, vrgente necessitate, ab haeretico consuetam formulam baptismi obseruante, sine vitio petitur & assumitur; modo adiiciatur protestatio, infantem hoc baptismo ad suscipiendam falsam doctrinam non adstringi .

Prob. a. Quia efficacia baptismi rite peracti non pendet a causa ministeriali, sed a principali, 1 Cor. III, 7.

Prob. b. Quia prohibemur trahere iugum cum infidelibus, 2 Cor. IV, 14. Contra iubemur exire ex ecclesia maligna, ne de plagis coetus maligni participemus, Apoc. XVIII, 4.

Prob. c. Quia Christus audire inffit Pharisaeos, sedentes in cathedra Mosis, quatenus doctrinam Mosis proposuerunt (intelligitur enim cathedra Mosis vocalis, non localis; siquidem Moses Iordanem nunquam est transgressus, neque vnquam Hierolymis vixit), Matth. XXIII, 2. Quod si itaque heterodoxorum Pharisaeorum circumcisio non est habita inualida, vtique haereticorum baptismus non est inefficax.


### Q. VII. What is the matter of baptism?

The matter of baptism is twofold, earthly and heavenly. The earthly matter is natural, pure water, everywhere available, established in legitimate use. Obs.

I. By natural water, artificial, distilled, medicated, rose water, etc., are excluded; by pure water, mixed, muddy, and feculent water—such as lye, broth mixed with parts of bread and meat, salt water, and the like—is excluded. However, purity is not understood as exact and absolute, to which no foreign element adheres, but common or natural purity is understood. Whence baptismal water is to be separated from dregs with as much diligence as men are accustomed to avoid feculent waters used for washing and drinking. By water everywhere available, common water is indicated, whatever that may be. There is no distinction, says TERTULLIAN, De Baptismo c. VI, whether one is washed in the sea, or a pool, a river, or a fountain, a lake, or a channel. Nor does it differ at all between those whom John dipped in the Jordan, and those whom Peter dipped in the Tiber. Obs.

II. The proximate matter of baptism is water placed in legitimate use, inasmuch as it touches the body of the one being baptized. If any droplets of water flow past the body of the infant being baptized, they are not the proximate matter of baptism. Obs.

III. The reason why God destined water for the sacrament of baptism has not been revealed in the written Word of God. It is certain, however: a) That water is a polykoinon (common) medium, available to all nations. Everywhere among the nations there is as much water as suffices for baptism. b) That there is no clearer symbol of the Holy Spirit and the efficacy of baptism than water.

The Father is the fountain, the Son of God is the mouth of the fountain, the crystalline river flowing forth from both is the Holy Spirit. Water cleanses the body: baptism, the vehicle of the Holy Spirit, purges the soul. Water refreshes the thirsty, vivifies drooping plants, and makes trees fruitful: baptism, called to memory, settles the thirst of the soul, which it vivifies when sad, and brings forth the fruits of repentance. Water cools: baptism provides refreshment against the heat of concupiscence.

Proof. Our assertion 1) Because Christ was baptized with water, and commanded to baptize with water, Matt. III, 11. Matt. XXVIII, 19. 2) Because baptism is called the washing of water by the word, Eph. V, 26. 3) Because we are born again of water and the spirit, John III, 5. 4) Because the Apostles baptized with water, Acts VIII, 36. ch. X, 47. The antithesis is that of the Papists and Socinians, who maintain that another liquid than water can be used for baptizing. Who object: I. Such a necessity can arise that another liquid, in the absence of water, must necessarily be used for baptizing: but necessity has no law. Resp. One should not feign such a necessity by which the substance of baptism is changed. II. The Lutherans do not reject the baptism of the Papists, who add something of the chrism of the priests and the oil of the catechumens to the baptism of water. Why then could not lye, rose water, or another liquid be used? Resp. We certainly blame that mixture in the Papists. Since, however, water preponderates in that Papal baptismal act, we maintain that an infant baptized by the Papists is not deprived of the saving effect on account of that mixture.

Latin:

Materia baptismi est duplex, terrestris & coelestis. Materia terrestris est aqua naturalis, pura, passim obuia, in vsu legitimo constituta.

Obs. I. Per aquam naturalem artificialis, destillata, medicata, rosacea &c.; per aquam puram mixta, lutosa & feculenta, qualis est lixiuium, iusculum cum partibus panis & carnis mixtum, aqua salsa, similisque excluditur. Puritas autem non intelligitur exacta & omnimoda, cui nihil alieni elementi adhaereat, sed intelligitur puritas communis, siue naturalis. Vnde tanta diligentia a fecibus segreganda est aqua baptismalis, quanta diligentia solent homines vitare aquas feculentas, ablutioni & potui inferuientes. Per aquam passim obuiam indicatur aqua vulgaris, qualiscunque illa fuerit. Nulla distinctio est, inquit TERTULLIANUS L. de baptismo c. VI., mari quis, an stagno, flumine, an fonte, lacu, an alueo diluatur. Neque quidquam differt inter eos, quos Ioannes in Iordane, & quos Petrus in Tiberi tinxit.

Obs. II. Materia proxima baptismi est aqua in vsu posita legitimo, quippe quae corpus baptizandi tangit. Si quae guttulae aquae in baptizando praeterfluunt corpus infantis baptizandi, non sunt materia proxima baptismi.

Obs. III. Causa, cur Deus sacramento baptismi aquam destinauerit, verbo Dei scripto reuelata non est. Certum tamen est: a) Quod aqua sit medium πολύκοινον, omnibus nationibus obuium. Vbiuis gentium tantum datur aquae, quantum baptismo sufficit. b) Quod nullum sit clarius symbolum Spiritus S. & efficaciae baptismi, quam aqua.

Pater est fons, fontis os Filius Dei, fluuius crystallinus ex vtroque profluens est Spiritus Sanctus. Aqua emundat corpus: baptismus, vehiculum Spiritus Sancti, purgat animam. Aqua recreat sitientem, viuificat plantas flaccidas arboresque fœcundat: baptismus in memoriam reuocatus sedat sitim animæ, quam tristem vitificat, & fructus pœnitentiæ parit. Aqua refrigerat: baptismus præstat refrigerium contra concupiscentiæ ardorem.

Prob. Assertio nostra 1) Quia Christus aqua baptizatus est, & aqua baptizare iussit, Matth. III, 11. Matth. XXVIII, 19. 2) Quia baptismus vocatur lauacrum aquæ in verbo, Eph. V, 26. 3) Quia ex aqua & spiritu renascimur, Io. III, 5. 4) Quia Apostoli aqua baptizarunt, Act VIII, 36. c. X, 47. Antithesis est Pontificiorum & Socinianorum, statuentium, alium liquorem, quam aquam ad baptizandum posse adhiberi. Qui obiiciunt: I. Tanta potest dari necessitas, vt alius liquor, absente aqua, ad baptizandum necessario sit adhibendus: necessitas autem non habet legem. Resp. Non fingenda est necessitas tanta, qua substantia baptismi mutetur. II. Lutherani non reiiciunt baptismum Pontificiorum, qui baptismo aquæ de chrismate sacerdotum, & oleo catechumenorum nonnihil affundunt. Quidni igitur lixiuium, aqua rosacea, aut alius liquor-adhiberi queat? Resp. Vtique vitio vertimus Pontificiis illam mixturam. Quoniam tamen aqua præponderat in illo actu baptismali pontificio, statuimus, infantem a Pontificiis baptizatum, ob mixtionem illam, salutari effectu non priuari.


### Q. VIII. What is the heavenly matter of baptism?

The heavenly matter of baptism is analogically said to be the whole Most Holy Trinity a); peculiarly and terminatively the Holy Spirit b).

Obs. We take the name of heavenly matter here not in the ἀκριβείᾳ of the philosophers, but in a certain latitude for a heavenly thing. Strictly speaking, neither the Holy Spirit nor the venerable Trinity is, or can be called, a material cause. Therefore, by matter we understand nothing other than the thing itself. See D. SCHERZER in breuiar. Hulsein. p. 588.

Proof. a. 1) From divine institution. Matt. XXVIII, 19. Whatever, by virtue of divine institution, is most presentially united to the baptismal water and conferred upon the infant being baptized, that is the matter or heavenly thing of baptism: But the name of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, etc. Therefore. Where note that, according to the interpretation of GERHARD, by the name of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, is understood the infinite majesty, ineffable holiness, inenarrable goodness, admirable virtue and grace of the whole Most Holy Trinity, which is present with all its virtue and benefits, and through which, united to the word and sanctified, it works efficaciously.

2) From Gal. III, 27. He whom we put on in baptism, he is the heavenly matter united with the earthly matter; But we put on Christ, etc. Therefore.

Proof. b) 1) Whatever is poured out upon us in baptism, that is the matter of baptism: But water and the Holy Spirit are poured out upon us in baptism: Therefore they are the matter of baptism; the former indeed earthly, the latter heavenly. The major is evident: because baptism is a spiritual washing, the matter of which is that which is poured out upon the one being washed.

2) By whatever we are washed in the sacrament of baptism, that is its matter: But we are washed by the Holy Spirit in the sacrament of baptism, 1 Cor. VI, 11. Therefore.

…3) From that from which we are regenerated, that is the matter of baptism: We are regenerated from water and the Holy Spirit, John III, 5. Where note that just as the particle, from, joined to water, denotes the matter or earthly thing; so the same particle, from, joined to the Spirit, denotes the matter or thing heavenly of baptism.

For no suitable reason can be opposed to the contrary, why, to wit, to be born again of water should signify the visible thing of baptism; but to be born again of the Spirit (in the same phrase, in the same clause) should not denote the invisible thing of baptism.

You say: The cited passage cannot be understood of the material cause; because, although the water of baptism is a material cause; yet it is not the material cause of regeneration, but the instrumental: because regeneration is not something consisting of water and Spirit, as of matter, but is an action and mutation of the spiritual man, efficiently depending on the Holy Spirit and water; on the Holy Spirit, indeed, as the principal efficient [cause], but on the water, as on the instrumental cause.

Resp. 1) By regeneration in the cited place is understood baptism, which is the efficacious medium of regeneration. 2) Since baptism is a divine action, just as regeneration is; it does not have matter from which, properly so called, but that thing is called its matter, about which it is occupied, and from which its efficacy flows. 4) To water alone, as to terrestrial matter, spiritual and truly divine effects (such as are regeneration, justification, renovation, salvation) cannot be attributed without idolatry; just as neither to the mere sound of the word ἀκοῆς [of hearing], unless the Holy Spirit were united to it, who makes it so that the word, whether ἀκοὴν [hearing] or ὁρατὸν [visible], becomes spirit and life.

Antithesis is 1) of the Socinians, who deny the heavenly thing of baptism, 2) of certain of our own [theologians], who indeed do not deny that the Holy Spirit or the most holy Trinity is present to the baptismal water, but doubt whether it can therefore be called the matter of baptism. Their arguments are:

I. The most pure Spirit cannot be called matter: The Holy Spirit is the most pure spirit: Therefore. Resp. The most pure Spirit cannot be called matter univocally; I concede. But it is called [matter] analogically, and by heavenly matter is understood that supernatural thing which, united with water, is conferred in baptizing, and which bestows efficacy upon baptism.

II. The efficient cause of baptism is wrongly held to be its matter: But the triune God, etc. Therefore. Resp. The triune God is the efficient cause of baptism, by reason of institution; yet he is the matter of baptism, by reason of sacramental union and communication, by which the triune God most presentially unites himself to the water of baptism, and by this means communicates himself to us, as our most present good, with all spiritual benefits.

III. Whatever doctrine is explained in diverse ways by evangelical doctors; nothing certain is to be asserted concerning it: the doctrine concerning the heavenly matter of baptism, etc., Therefore. The minor is proved: because D. LUTHER teaches that the heavenly thing is the word of God, whom D. BALDUINUS follows: D. HUTTER judges that the heavenly thing of baptism is the blood of Christ; D. DANNHAV. [judges it to be] the Holy Spirit, D. AFFELMANN, the whole most holy Trinity. Resp. This diverse manner of speaking is not difficult to reconcile by D. CALOVIUS, who excellently teaches, tom. IX. of his system, p. 166. The heavenly matter of baptism, if it is to be defined integrally, is the most holy Trinity, God the Father, the Son of God, Christ the θεάνθρωπος [God-man], to whose integrity not only the divine, but also the human nature pertains, just as the blood also pertains to this entirely, of which he was made a participant for our sake, and also the Holy Spirit: Which heavenly thing is univocally called the word and name of God, that is, God himself triune and one, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Instance I. The word of institution is not God himself. Resp. The word of institution, when it is called the heavenly thing of baptism, is to be understood not without connection, incomplexly, simply & nakedly, as if it were the mere external word, but with connection, complexly with the name, i. e. with the very thing expressed by that most holy name: Father, Son, & Holy Spirit, or unitedly & conjointly: because just as the bare word, apart from the Holy Spirit, is not the power of God; so the word of God always has united to itself the Holy Spirit & the whole Trinity, John VI, 63. 68.

Whence its efficacy, which it also exerts in baptism, which is the washing in the word, for our regeneration and salvation, Eph. V, 26.

Instance II. The blood of Christ is the meritorious cause of baptism. Resp. The blood of Christ is present in the sacrament of baptism, 1) by reason of merit; because the fruit of baptism was brought forth by the blood of Christ, shed on the altar of the cross for our sins, Heb. IX, 28. 2) by reason of substance; because the Son of God assumes flesh and blood into the unity of his person, and now, after the union has been effected, performs all the works of the mediator in, with, and through the human nature; therefore the whole Christ, θεάνθρωπος (God-man), is present to this sacrament: 3) by reason of efficacy; because in baptism we are cleansed from our sins through the blood of Christ, 1 John I, 7. And St. Peter, 1 Ep. I, 2, teaches that we are sprinkled no less by the blood of Christ than by water, while he commemorates the ῥαντισμὸν αἵματος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ). Our mind, therefore, is that Christ is present to baptism ἐκ ἀναίματος (not without blood) by a substantial and efficacious presence, and communicates the efficacy brought forth by his blood to the person being baptized, through the medium of the washing of water. For which reason it is called the heavenly matter of baptism.

Furthermore, when some of our own deny that the blood of Christ is the heavenly matter of baptism, they take the word "blood" distinctly and with a specific difference from the body and divinity of Christ, as is done in the Eucharist; yet they concede that the blood of Christ is the heavenly thing, if it is taken conjunctively, as blood is an internal part of the body of Christ. Instance III. But why is the Holy Spirit peculiarly called the heavenly thing of baptism, when the baptismal act is nevertheless an external work, and therefore a work common to all three persons of the Godhead? Resp. Although the works of the Trinity ad extra (outwardly) are undivided; yet the order and distinction of the persons must be maintained. Scripture itself attributes the effect of baptism, namely regeneration and renewal, in a peculiar way to the Holy Spirit, Tit. III, 6. And therefore the Holy Spirit is called the heavenly thing of baptism by appropriation, because the Holy Spirit is present to baptism, administered according to the institution of Christ, 1) by reason of essence, just as the other persons of the Trinity are also present; 2) as the offering and collation of evangelical grace: 3) as the sealing of the covenant initiated between God and the baptized, ratified at any time.

Latin:

Materia cœlestis baptismi analogice dicta est tota SS. Trinitas a); peculiariter & terminatiue Spiritus Sanctus b).

Obs. Materiæ cœlestis nomen h. l. non in ἀκριβείᾳ Philosophorum, sed in latitudine quadam pro re cœlesti accipimus. Stricte loquendo neque Spiritus Sanctus, neque venerabilis Trinitas caussa materialis est, aut dici potest. Igitur per materiam nihil aliud, quam rem intelligimus. Vid. D. SCHERZER in breuiar. Hulsein. p. 588.

Prob. a. 1) Ex institutione diuina. Matth. XXVIII, 19. Quidquid, vi institutionis divinæ aquæ baptismali præsentissime vnitum, confertur infanti baptizando, illud est materia, siue res cœlestis baptismi: Atqui nomen Dei Patris, Filii & Spiritus sancti &c. Ergo. Vbi notes, quod, interprete GERHARDO, per nomen Dei Patris, Filii & Spiritus Sancti, intelligatur infinita maiestas, ineffabilis sanctitas, inenarrabilis bonitas, admiranda virtus & gratia totius SS. Trinitatis, quæ cum omni virtute sua & beneficiis adest, & per quam, verbo vnitam & sanctificatam, efficaciter operatur.

2) Ex Gal. III, 27. Quem in baptismo induimus, ille est materia cœlestis cum materia terrestri vnita; Atqui Christum &c. Ergo.

Prob. b) 1) Quidquid in baptismo in nos effunditur, illud est materia baptismi: Atqui aqua & Spiritus S. in baptismo in nos effunditur: Ergo sunt inateria baptismi; illa quidem terrena, hic cœlestis. Maior constat: quia baptismus est spirituale lauacrum, cuius materia est id, quod in lauandum effunditur.

2) Quocunque abluimur in sacramento baptismi, illud est eius materia: Atqui Spiritu S. in sacramento baptisini abluimur, 1 Cor. VI, 11. Ergo.

3) Ex quo regeneramur, illud est materia baptismi: Ex aqua & Spiritu S. regeneramur, Io. III, 5. Vbi notes, quod sicut particula, ex, iuncta aquæ, notat materiam, siue rem terrenam; ita eadem numero particula, ex, iuncta Spiritui, notet materiam, siue remcaelestem baptismi.

Neque enim vlla idonea ratio opponi potest in contrarium, cur scil. τὸ renasci ex aqua visibilem quidem rem baptismi significet; renasci vero ex Spiritu (eadem phrasi, eodem commate) invisibilem rem baptismi non denotet.

Dicis: Locus citatus non potest de causa materiali intelligi; quia, licet aqua baptismi sit causa materialis; non tamen materialis causa est regenerationis, sed instrumentalis: quia regeneratio non est aliquid ex aqua & Spiritu, velut ex materia, constans, sed actio & mutatio hominis spiritualis, a Spiritu sancto & aqua efficienter dependens; a Spiritu S. quidem, vt efficiente principali, ab aqua vero, vt a causa instrumentali.

Resp. 1) Per regenerationem l.c. intelligitur baptismus, qui est medium efficax regenerationis. 2) Quum baptismus sit actio diuina aeque, ac regeneratio; materiam ex qua, proprie dictam, non habet, sed materia eius dicitur res illa, circa quam occupatur, & a qua eius efficacia fluit. 4) Soli aquae, tanquam materiae terrestri, effectus spirituales & vere diuini (quales sunt regeneratio, iustificatio, renouatio, saluatio) citra idololatriam tribui nequeunt; vti nec soli sono verbi ἀκοῆς, nisi vnitus eidem esset Spiritus Sanctus, qui facit, vt verbum, siue ἀκοὴν siue ὁρατὸν, spiritus & vita sit.

Antithesis est 1) Socinianorum, rem caelestem baptismi negantium, 2) quorundam nostratium, qui quidem non negant praesentem aquae baptismali esse Spiritum S. aut sacro-sanctam Trinitatem, sed dubitantium, an ideo materia baptismi vocari queat. Quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Spiritus purissimus non potest vocari materia: Spiritus S. est spiritus purissimus: Ergo. Resp. Spiritus purissimus non potest vocari materia vniuoca; concedo. Vocatur autem analogice, & intelligitur per materiam caelestem ea res supernaturalis, quae cum aqua vnita baptizando confertur, & quae baptismo efficaciam largitur.

II. Causa efficiens baptismi male habetur eius materia: Atqui Deus triunus &c. Ergo. Resp. Deus triunus est causa efficiens baptismi, ratione institutionis; est tamen materia baptismi, ratione sacramentalis vnionis & communicationis, qua Deus triunus sese praesentissime vnit aquae baptismi, & hac mediante sese nobis, vt praesentissimum nostrum bonum, cum omnibus beneficiis spiritualibus communicat.

III. Quaecunque doctrina a doctoribus euangelicis diuerfimode explicatur; de ea nil certi est afferendum: doctrina de materia caelesti baptismi &c, Ergo. Minor probatur: quia D. LVTHERVS docet, rem caelestem esse verbum Dei, quem sequitur D. BALDVINVS: D. HVTTERVS censet, rem caelestem baptismi esse sanguinem Christi; D. DANNHAV. Spiritum sanctum, D. AFFELMANNVS, totam sacrosanctam Trinitatem. Resp. Haec diuersa loquendi ratio haud difficulter conciliatur a D. CALOVIO, praeclare docente, tom. IX. system. p. 166. Materia baptismi caelestis, si integre definienda fit, est SS. Trinitas, Deus Pater, Filius Dei, Christus θεάνθρωπος, ad cuius integritatem non diuina tantum, sed etiam humana natura spectat, quemadmodum ad hanc omnino pertinet etiam sanguis, cuius particeps factus est nostri causa, nec non Spiritus Sanctus: Quae res caelestis vniuoce dicitur verbum & nomen Dei, hoc est ipse Deus trinus & vnus, Pater, Filius & Spiritus Sanctus.

Instantia I. Verbum institutionis non est Deus ipse, Resp. Verbum institutionis, cum baptismi res caelestis dicitur, accipiendum est non ἄνευ συμπλοκῆς, incomplexe, simpliciter & nude, veluti solum externum est verbum, sed μετὰ συμπλοκῆς, complexe cum nomine, i. e. cum ipsa re, nomine illo sanctissimo expressa: Patre, Filio, & Spiritu sancto, seu ἡνωμένως & coniunctim: quia vti non nudum verbum, absque Spiritu S. est potentia Dei; sic verbum Dei semper vnitum sibi habet Spiritum S. & totam Trinitatem, Io. VI, 63. 68.

Vnde eius est efficacia, quam etiam in baptismo, qui est lauacrum in verbo, exserit, ad nostri regenerationem & salutem, Eph. V, 26.

Instantia II. Sanguis Christi est causa meritoria baptismi. Resp. Sanguis Christi adest in sacramento baptismi, 1) ratione meriti; quia fructus baptismi partus est sanguine Christi, in ara crucis pro nostris peccatis effuso, Hebr. IX, 28. 2) ratione substantiae; quia Filius Dei carnem & sanguinem in vnitatem personae suae assumit iamque post factam vnionem in, cum, & per naturam humanam omnia opera mediatoris perficit; ideo totus Christus θεάνθρωπος huic sacramento adest: 3) ratione efficaciae; quia in baptismo per sanguinem Christi a peccatis nostris mundamur, 1 Io. I, 7. Et S. Petrus 1 ep. I, 2. docet, quod non minus sanguine Christi, quam aqua conspergamur, dum ῥαντισμὸν αἵματος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ commemorat. Mens itaque nostra est, quod Christus ἐκ ἀναίματος (non fine sanguine) praesentia substantiali, eaque efficaci, baptismo adsit, & partam sanguine efficaciam, mediante lauacro aquae, homini baptizando communicet. Qua ratione materia baptismi caelestis dicitur. Ceterum quando nonnulli ex nostratibus negant, sanguinem Christi esse materiam caelestem baptismi, sumunt vocabulum, sanguis, distincte & cum differentia specifica a corpore & diuinitate Christi, quemadmodum in eucharistia fit; concedunt tamen, sanguinem Christi esse rem caelestem, si sumatur coniunctim, vt sanguis est pars interna corporis Christi.

Instantia III. Sed cur Spiritus S. peculiariter dicitur res caelestis baptismi, cum tamen actus baptismalis sit opus ad extra, adeoque opus commune omnibus tribus deitatis personis? Resp. Quamuis opera Trinitatis ad extra sint indiuisae; seruandas tamen est ordo & discrimen personarum. Ipsa scriptura effectum baptismi, nempe regenerationem & renovationem peculiari ratione tribuit Spiritui S. Tit. III, 6. Ideoque Spiritus S. dicitur res caelestis baptismi appropriatiue, eo, quod Spiritus S. baptismo, iuxta institutionem Christi administrato, adest, 1) ratione essentiae, sicut etiam reliquae Trinitatis personae adsunt; 2) qua oblationem & collationem gratiae euangelicae: 3) qua obsignationem foederis inter Deum & baptizatum initi, quouis tempore rati.


### Quest. IX. What is the union of the earthly and heavenly thing in the sacrament of baptism?

The sacramental union of the water, constituted in the legitimate use of baptism, and the word of institution, which embraces the glorious name of the Most Holy Trinity, is not typical or relative a);

but real and exhibitive, bringing about both the substantial presence of the Triune God and the communication of supernatural efficacy b).

Obs. From the preceding question it is clear that baptism consists not only of earthly matter, but also of heavenly matter, spoken of analogically (which can also be called the other intrinsic constituent of the sacrament), which heavenly matter is called by some the word of institution, by others the name of the Most Holy Trinity, and by others the Holy Spirit. The word of institution, however, is taken here not abstractly, but complexly, insofar as it embraces the glorious name of the Most Holy Trinity: but the name of God here denotes the majesty, goodness, wisdom, power, and holiness of God. The Holy Spirit is called the heavenly thing of the sacrament of baptism in a peculiar and singular way, because the effects of baptism are appropriated to the Holy Spirit. If, therefore, you should assert that the water in the baptismal act is united with the word of institution, or with the name of the Most Holy Trinity, or with the Holy Spirit, you would not err, because those formulas of speaking agree in reality.

Prob. a. In the sacraments of the O. T., the earthly thing only prefigured the heavenly, typically shadowed it forth, and presented it as morally present: But in the sacraments of the N. T., the earthly thing presented the heavenly substance as present: But in the sacraments of the N. T. the earthly thing [presented] the heavenly substan substantially present.

Hence, the union of the earthly and heavenly thing in the sacrament of baptism is not typical, or relative, but real and exhibitive. Proof b. 1) The washing of water is called the medium of our purification and sanctification not simply, but in the word, Eph. V, 26. Therefore, the washing of water is mystically united with the word of institution. 2) There is one baptism, which is done by water in the name of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I.e., in the act, the baptismal water is sacramentally united with God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. 3) One ἀποτέλεσμα (result) of regeneration proceeds from water and the Spirit, John III, 5. Water, therefore, placed in legitimate use is mystically joined with the Holy Spirit, from whom the power of regenerating primarily proceeds.

Latin:

Vnio sacramentalis aquae in legitimo baptismi vsu constitutae, & verbi institutionis, gloriosum SS. Trinitatis nomen complectentis, non est typica, aut relatiua a);

sed realis & exhibitiva, tum substantialem Dei triunius praesentiam, tum communicationem efficaciae supernaturalis inferens b).

Obs. Ex praecedente quaestione liquet, baptismum constare non tantum ex materia terrestri, sed etiam ex materia caelesti, analogice dicta (quae etiam constituentem intrinsecum sacramenti alterum dici potest), quae materia caelestis a quibusdam verbum institutionis, ab aliis nomen SS. Trinitatis, ab aliis Spiritus S. dicitur. Verbum institutionis autem hic sumitur non abstractiue, sed complexe, prout nomen gloriosum SS. Trinitatis complectitur: Nomen Dei vero in praesenti maiestatem, bonitatem, sapientiam, potentiam & sanctitatem Dei notat. Spiritus S. peculiari & singulari ratione dicitur res caelestis sacramenti baptismi, ideo, quod effectus baptismi, Spiritui S. appropriantur. Quod si itaque assuerueris, aquam in actu baptismali esse vnitam cum verbo institutionis, vel cum nomine SS. Trinitatis, vel cum Spiritu S., non erraueris, ideo, quod illae loquendi formulae reapse conueniunt.

Prob. a. In sacramentis V. T. res terrestris caelestem tantum praefigurabat, typice adumbrabat & moraliter praesentem sistebat: At in sacramentis N. T., res terrestris caelestem substantialiter præsentem sistebat: At in sacramentis N. T. res terrestris cœleftem substantialiter praesentem exhibet.

Proinde unio rei terrestris & caelestis in sacramento baptismi non est typica, aut relativa, sed realis & exhibitiva. Prob. b. 1) Medium purificationis & sanctificationis nostrae dicitur lavacrum aquae non simpliciter, sed in verbo, Eph. V, 26. Ergo lavacrum aquae mystice unitum est cum verbo institutionis. 2) Unus est baptismus, qui fit aqua in nomine Dei Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. E. in actu, baptismali aqua cum Deo Patre, Filio & Spiritu S. sacramentaliter vnita est. 3) Unum ἀποτέλεσμα regenerationis proficiscitur ab aqua & spiritu, Io. III, 5. Aqua igitur posita in vsu legitimo mystice coniuncta est cum Spiritu S., a quo vis regenerandi principaliter prodit.


### Quest. X. What is the form of baptism?

Form of baptism
