The form of baptism comprises both the washing by water, which is done either by the immersion of the whole body into water , or by the continuous sprinkling, or pouring of water upon the more important part of the body , and the pronunciation of the words of institution , so that there may be a distinct mention, confession, and invocation of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit .

Proof a. Βαπτίζειν (to baptize) in general signifies washing, or ablution, whether it be done by the pouring of water, or by immersion. At the beginning of the primitive church, baptism was performed by immersion. The one to be baptized, having laid aside his garments, descended into the river, and naked was immersed in the water: for which reason Christ, Matt. III, 13, 26, is said to have immediately ascended from the Jordan. Therefore, he had previously descended, and it is probable that the whole body of Christ was submerged, so that by his purification he might sanctify the waves, as GREGORY NAZIANZEN states, Orat. 34. For thus Philip and the eunuch both descended into the water, and he baptized him, Acts VIII, 38. To this point the words of Paul, Rom. VI, 4, look: By baptism we are buried with Christ into death, and Col. II, 12, we are buried with him in baptism. For by these phrases reference is made to this rite of the primitive church, where those to be baptized, being wholly immersed in water, were as it were buried. Which custom of baptizing the church long cherished and used. For that it had not yet become obsolete in the third century after Christ was born, CYPRIAN is witness, who in Book IV, epist. 7, raises the question concerning those who obtain grace in infirmity, that is, are regenerated, and yet because of adverse health cannot be thoroughly immersed in water, but can only be sprinkled with water; whether they are to be held as true Christians? From which collection it is clear that, while CYPRIAN was alive in the third century, baptism was performed by immersing the whole body; yet, necessity stimulating, because of the infirmity of the body, it was customary for baptism to be performed by the sprinkling of water. And CYPRIAN reports in the same place that some did not wish to count such, who were only sprinkled with water, as true Christians, but called them Clinici, because they were sprinkled with water while lying in bed. To whom he replies in the cited epistle that it does not hinder those lying in bed that they could not be baptized by the customary rite, namely immersion, because they were excluded by necessity, but that it is sufficient that they were washed with water in the name of the Holy Trinity.

Proof b. 1) The washing of hands and feet, which is done even by sprinkling alone, is called βαπτισμὸς (baptism), Mark VII, 4; Luke XI, 38. Therefore, sprinkling alone also satisfies the meaning of the word Βαπτίζειν; just as the βαπτισμὸς (baptism) of the cloud and the sea, 1 Cor. X, 2, denotes a lightly performed sprinkling. 2) In one day within the city of Jerusalem, three thousand are read to have been baptized, Acts II, 38. But who would believe that so many men, as many as had flocked together in that place in the city, were washed by Peter alone by the immersion of the whole body into water?

3) Who could persuade themselves that such a multitude of men and women, Matth. III, 5, was immersed by John in the Jordan, completely naked and with clothes (with all modesty) laid aside, in the eyes of so many spectators, in broad daylight?

3) The baptism of the clinicorum provides a manifest example of baptismal sprinkling. However, the custom of baptizing by sprinkling prevailed in the Western church after the age of GREGORY, around the year 875, and gradually the rite of immersion died out throughout almost the entire West: a) Because of the tender bodies of infants, which cannot be exposed to cold air and totally immersed in regions situated to the north, especially in the wintertime, without present danger to their health: b) Because of honesty and modesty, for which reason it is more decent today to sprinkle or pour over adults, especially women, than to immerse them with their whole body naked in the presence of men.

Prob. c. The form of baptism consists not only in things done, but also in things said. The τὸ μαθητεῦον and the τὸ βαπτισέον pertain to baptism, on account of the words of institution: μαθητεύσατε βαπτίζοντες, Matth. XXVIII, 19. Therefore, the form of baptism consists both in action and in diction. The imperative introduces the diction: μαθητεύσατε. Which word indeed signifies generally to make disciples, but at the same time connotes the τὸ dicere. For disciples are made both by words, or information, and by ritual initiation; which initiation, however, requires words of peculiar institution through the rite. For it is not a rite that is as it were mute, and to be performed by gestures alone, or by mute actions. The action, however, is clear from the imperative: baptize, which is hinted at by the participle. For the words, teach baptizing, are to be resolved thus: Teach and baptize. Conf. HVLSEM. breu. cap. X. p. 595.

Prob. d. That the customary formula of baptizing in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is to be retained is validly gathered: 1) Because Christ himself prescribed this formula, Matth. XXVIII, 19. One must not rashly depart from the prescription of Christ for Christians.

2) Because by this formula of baptizing, both the ὁμοοσία, or the same essence, of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and their personal distinction are indicated. For we are baptized not into the names, but into the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, because their name is one, i.e., one authority, majesty, and essence. Furthermore, the Son is distinguished personally from the Father in the words of institution: Therefore, in the same way, the Holy Spirit is distinguished from the Father and the Son.

3) By this formula of baptizing, the confession and invocation of the Most Holy Trinity is comprehended. We are baptized into the name of him in whom we are bound to believe and whom we are bound to invoke: for by the sacrament of baptism we are bound to the faith, profession, worship, and obedience of him who is the author of baptism. Therefore, baptism is called the interrogation of a good conscience toward God, 1 Petr. III, 21. We must believe as we have been baptized, and adore as we believe, says BASILIVS M. ep. LXXIIX.

4) By this formula of baptizing, the benefits are indicated which all and each of the three persons of the divinity dispense to the baptized through baptism. God the Father receives him as a son, the Son as a brother, the Holy Spirit as a temple or dwelling place. For which reason, in baptism, a distinct mention of the three persons of the Divinity must be made.

Obs. Although the passive formula of the Greeks is sufficient: Let the servant (handmaid) of Christ be baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit: nevertheless, the active formula of the Latins: I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, is plainer and more emphatic; for by it the principal and organic cause, the Holy Spirit and the minister, are comprehended at the same time. Add that, by natural sense, it is perceived that the practical imperative of the formula, baptize, is to be changed in practice into the indicative: I baptize. For in this way the conformity of the command and the execution becomes more evident.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, who deny that baptism is rightly performed by sprinkling, and that the formula of baptism in the name of the three persons of the Godhead must be rigidly observed.

They contend for immersion with the following arguments: I. They bring forward the examples of Christ and others, of those baptized by the submersion of the whole body, Matt. III, 16; Acts VIII, 36. Response: Those examples show that such immersion is lawful, and was used in ancient times, especially in warmer regions, but they do not prove that it is absolutely and everywhere necessary.

E. βαπτισμὸς (baptismos) denotes immersion. Response: Βαπτίζειν (baptizein) signifies to wash, either by immersion into water, or by the pouring of water.

III. The Apostle of the Gentiles institutes a comparison between baptism and the death and resurrection of Christ, Rom. VI, 3. 4. namely, that by immersion we are buried with Christ, but by emersion we rise again. This adumbration can in no way be had by sprinkling, which is done with a little water. Response: 1) Significations and adumbrations pertain to the secondary end of baptism, not the primary. For this is regeneration and renewal, Tit. III, 5. 2) The analogy of Christ's burial can have a place, even if only the head is bathed with water; for he whose head is sprinkled or bathed with waters is, as it were, buried by those waters. 3) Although sprinkling does not so manifestly signify our spiritual burial with Christ, it does signify the ῥαντισμὸν αἵματος (rhantismon haimatos), the sprinkling of the blood of Christ, 1 Petr. I, 2, and the form of establishing a covenant, which was performed by the sprinkling of blood, Exod. XXIV, 8; Heb. IX, 19.

They argue against the rigid observation of the customary formula of baptizing:

I. The Apostles baptized in the name of Christ, Acts II, 38; ch. X, 48; ch. XIX, 5. Therefore, we are not necessarily bound to baptize in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Response: 1) Some Fathers maintain that those who are baptized in the name of Christ are implicitly baptized also in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, according to that of BASIL, in his book On the Holy Spirit, ch. XII. The appellation of Christ is a profession of the whole Most Holy Trinity; because it simultaneously declares the Father, who anointed, and the Son, who was anointed, and the Holy Spirit, who is the anointing. And IRENAEUS, in book IV against Valentinus, says: In the name of Christ three persons are understood, the anointed, the anointer, and the anointing. For which reason some maintain that this formula is not to be rejected: in the name of Jesus Christ; provided it is not understood exclusively: which baptism HUGO and LOMBARD acknowledge as valid, according to D. CALOV, vol. X, system, p. 288. 2) When the Apostles are said to have baptized in the name of Christ, the formula of baptism is not indicated, but the efficient cause, or the author instituting baptism, so that the sense is: The Apostles baptized by the authority, will, and command of Christ. For it is in no way probable that the Apostles did anything contrary to the institution of Christ, which is of strict observation.

II. We are also baptized into the death of Christ, Rom. VI, 5. But death is not the name of God: Therefore, we are not baptized in the name of God alone. Response: We are baptized into the death of Christ not formally, but finally; because through baptism we are made partakers of the efficacy of Christ's death, by which we obtain the freedom from the guilt and dominion of sin, which Christ procured for us by his death.

III. The Israelites were baptized into Moses, 1 Cor. X, 2. Therefore, men are not baptized in the name of God alone. Response: a) Paul speaks of a typical baptism, not a proper one. b) The Israelites were baptized not into the name or person of Moses, but into Moses, that is, into the profession and ratification of the doctrine which Moses had professed: which doctrine was not so much of Moses as of God. If one could be baptized into the name of Moses, why not also into the name of Paul? But the Apostle rejects this, 1 Cor. I, 13.

Latin:

Forma baptismi

Forma baptismi tum ablutionem per aquam, quae fit vel per immersionem totius corporis in aquam , vel per aspersionem continuam, sive affusionem aquae in potiorem corporis partem , tum verborum institutionis pronuntiationem , ita, vt distincta fiat mentio, confessio & invocatio Dei Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. complectitur.

Prob. a. Βαπτίζειν in genere lotionem, vel ablutionem significat, sive ea fiat affusione aquae, sive fiat immersione. Initio primitivae ecclesiae baptismus peragebatur immersione. Baptizandus, depositis vestimentis, in flumen descendebat, & nudus aquae immergebatur: Qua ratione Christus Matth. III, 13, 26. dicitur protinus ascendisse ex Iordane. E. prius descenderat, & probabile est, totum corpus Christi fuisse submersum, vt sua purificatione undas sanctificaret, cesente GREGOR. NAZIANZENO Orat. 34. Sic enim Philippus & Eunuchus descenderunt ambo in aquam, baptizavitque ille hunc, Act. VIII, 38. Quo spectant verba Paulli, Rom. VI, 4. Per baptismum cum Christo sepulti sumus in mortem, & Col. II, 12. consepulti cum Christo sumus. His quippe phrasibus respicitur ad hunc ritum primitivae ecclesiae, vbi baptizandi, toti aquae immersi, quasi sepeliebantur. Quem morem baptizandi diu coluit & vsurpavit ecclesia. Nam quod nondum obsoleuerit saeculo III. a nato Christo, testis est CYPRIANUS, qui L. IV. epist. 7. movet quaestionem de iis, qui in infirmitate gratiam consequuntur, hoc est, regenerantur, nec tamen per valetudinem aduersam aquae penitus immergi, sed tantum aqua conspergi possunt; an habendi sint veri Christiani? Ex quo collectu proclive est, saeculo III. superstite CYPRIANO, baptismum immergendo toto corpore peractum fuisse; stimulante tamen necessitate, ob infirmitatem corporis, baptismum peragi consueuisse aspersione aquae. Et refert ibidem CYPRIANUS, quosdam noluisse tales, aqua tantum aspersos, veris Christianis accensere, sed vocasse eos Clinicos, quod lecto decumbentes aqua conspersi sint. Quibus ille respondet in citata epistola, decumbentibus nil obesse, quod necessitate exclusi non potuerint ritu consueto, nempe immersione baptizari, sed sufficere, quod aqua perfusi sint in nomine SS. Trinitatis.

Prob. b. 1) Ablutio manuum & calcium, quae sola etiam aspersionem fit, dicitur βαπτισμὸς, Marc. VII, 4. Luc. XI, 38. Ergo significationi verbi, Βαπτίζειν, fatsit etiam sola aspersio; sicuti nubis ac maris βαπτισμὸς 1 Cor. X, 2. leuiter factam aspersionem notat. 2) Vna die intra vrbem Hierolymam tria millia baptizata leguntur, Act. II, 38. At quis credat, tot homines eo loco, quot in vrbe confluxerant, a solo Petro totius corporis in aquam immersione ablutos fuisse? immersione ablutos fuisse? immersione ablutos fuisse?

3) Quis sibi persuadeat, tantam virorum mulierumque multitudinem, Matth. III, 5. totam nudam, ac vestibus (cum omni pudore) depositis in oculis tot empectarum, claro die Iordani a Ioanne immersam fuisse?

3) Baptismus clinicorum manifestum præbet exemplum baptismalis aspersionis. Inualuit autem mos baptizandi per aspersionem in ecclesia occidentali post ætatem GREGORII circa annum 875., & paullatim per vniuersum pene occidentem ritus immersionis exoleuit: a) Ob infantum tenella corpora, quæ aëri frigido exponi, & tota immergi in regionibus ad septentrionem sitis, præsertim tempore hyberno, sine præsente valetudinis periculo non possunt: b) Propter honestatem & verecundiam, propter quam decentius est, hodie adultos, præsertim fœminas aspergere, vel perfundere, quam coram viris nudatas toto corpore immergere.

Prob. c. Forma baptismi non tantum in faciendis, sed & dicendis consistit. Pertinet ad baptismum τὸ μαθητεῦον, & τὸ βαπτισέον, propter verba institutionis: μαθητεύσατε βαπτίζοντες, Matth. XXVIII, 19. E. Forma baptismi tum in actione, tum in dictione consistit. Dictionem infert imperatiuus: μαθητεύσατε. Quod verbum quidem generaliter discipulos facere significat, sed simul τὸ dicere connotat. Discipuli enim fiunt tum verbis, siue informatione, tum rituali initiatione; quæ initiatio tamen per ritum verba peculiaris institutionis correquirit. Non enim est ritus quasi mutus, & solis gestibus, aut mutis actionibus peragendus. Actio vero patet ex imperatiuo: baptizate, qui innuitur participio. Verba enim, docete baptizantes, ita resoluenda sunt: Docete & baptizate. Conf. HVLSEM. breu. cap. X. p. 595.

Prob. d. Retinendam esse consuetam baptizandi formulam in nomine Patris, Filii & Spiritus S., valide colligitur: 1) Quia Christus ipse hanc formulam præscripsit, Matth. XXVIII, 19. A præscripto Christi Christianis temere non est recedendum.

2) Quia hac baptizandi formula tum Dei Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. ὁμοοσία, siue eadem essentia, tum personalis distinctio indigitatur. Baptizamur enim non in nomina, sed in nomen Patris, Filii & Spiritus S., quia eorum vnum est nomen, i. e. vna auctoritas, maiestas & essentia. Ceterum Filius a Patre in verbis institutionis distinguitur personaliter: Ergo eodem modo Spiritus S. a Patre & Filio distinguitur.

3) Hac baptizandi formula comprehenditur confessio & inuocatio SS. Trinitatis. In illius nomen baptizamur, in quem credere, & quem inuocare tenemur: nam sacramento baptismi ad fidem, professionem, cultum & obsequium illius, qui auctor est baptismi, adstringimur. Ideo baptismus dicitur interrogatio bonæ conscientiæ ad Deum, 1 Petr. III, 21. Oportet nos credere, vt baptizati sumus, adorare, vt credimus, ait BASILIVS M. ep. LXXIIX.

4) Hac baptizandi formula indicantur beneficia, quæ omnes & singulæ tres diuinitatis personæ per baptismum dispensant in baptizatum. Deus Pater ipsum recipit in filium, Filius in fratrem, Spiritus S. in templum, vel habitaculum. Quam ob rem in baptismo distincta trium personarum Diuinitatis mentio facienda est.

Obs. Licet sufficiens sit Græcorum formula passiua: Baptizetur seruus (serua) Christi in nomine Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus S.: Latinorum tamen formula actiua: Ego baptizo te in nomine Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus S. planior & magis emphatica est; quippe qua comprehenditur simul caussa princeps & organica, Spiritus S. & minister. Adiice, quod naturali sensu deprehendatur, imperatiuum formulæ practicum, baptizate, in praxi mutandum esse in indicatiuum: Ego baptizo. Hoc enim modo mandati & exsecutionis conformitas fit euidentior.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, negantium baptismum rite peragi aspersione, formulam baptismi in nomine trium deitatis personarum rigide observandum esse. Pro immersione dimicant sequentibus argumentis:

I. Adducunt exempla Christi & aliorum, submersione totius corporis baptizatorum, Matth. III, 16. Act. VIII, 36. Resp. Exempla illa ostendunt, immersionem illam esse licitam, & antiquitus, in locis praesertim calidioribus, usurpatam, sed non euincunt, eam esse absolute & ubique necessariam. II. Βαπτίζειν significat immergere.

E. βαπτισμὸς notat immersionem. Resp. Βαπτίζειν significat abluere, vel per immersionem in aquam, vel per aquae affusionem.

III. Gentium Apostolus instituit comparationem inter baptismum, & inter mortem ac resurrectionem Christi, Rom. VI, 3. 4. siue quod per immersionem Christo consepeliamur, per emersionem vero consurgamus. Quae adumbratio nullo modo per aspersionem, quae paucula fit aqua, haberi potest. Resp. 1) Significationes & adumbrationes pertinent ad finem baptismi secundarium, non primarium. Hic enim est regeneratio & renouatio, Tit. III, 5. 2) Analogia sepulturae Christi locum habere potest, etiamsi solum caput unda perfundatur; Cuius enim caput aquis aspergitur, vel perfunditur, is aquis istis quasi sepelitur. 3) Licet aspersio non adeo manifeste significet spiritualem nostram cum Christo consepulturam, significat tamen ῥαντισμὸν αἵματος, aspersionem sanguinis Christi, 1 Petr. I, 2. & formam pangendi foederis, quae sanguinis aspersione peragebatur, Exod. XXIV, 8. Hebr. IX, 19.

Contra rigidam observationem usitatae baptizandi formulae argumentantur:

I. Apostoli baptizarunt in nomine Christi, Act. II, 38. c. X, 48. c. XIX, 5. E. non necessario obligamur ad baptizandum in nomine Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. Resp. 1) Nonnulli Patres statuunt, quod, qui baptizantur in nomine Christi, implicite baptizentur quoque in nomine Patris, Filii & Spiritus S., iuxta illud BASILII, libro de Spiritu S. c. XII. Christi appellatio est totius SS. Trinitatis professio; quia simul & declarat Patrem, qui unxit, & Filium, qui unctus est, & Spiritum S., qui est unctio. Et IRENAEUS libr. IV. contra Valentin. inquit: In nomine Christi tres personae intelliguntur, unctus, ungens & unctio. Quae causa nonnulli statuunt, non esse reprobandam formulam hanc: in nomine Iesu Christi; modo non exclusive intelligatur: Quem baptismum ratum agnoscunt HUGO & LOMBARDS apud D. CALOV. tom. X. system. p. 288. 2) Quando Apostoli dicuntur baptizasse in nomine Christi, non indigitatur baptismi formula, sed causa efficiens, vel auctor baptismum instituens, vt sensus fit: Apostoli baptizarunt auctoritate, voluntate, & iussu Christi. Nullo enim modo probabile est, Apostolos contra institutionem Christi, quae stricta observationis est, quidquam fecisse.

II. Baptizamur etiam in mortem Christi, Rom. VI, 5. At mors non est nomen Dei: E. non in solo nomine Dei baptizamur. Resp. Baptizamur in mortem Christi non formaliter, sed finaliter; quia per baptismum participes reddimur efficaciae mortis Christi, qua libertatem a reatu & dominio peccati, quam Christus morte sua nobis peperit.

III. Israelitae in Mosen baptizati sunt, 1 Cor. X, 2. E. non in solo nomine Dei homines baptizantur. Resp. a) Loquitur Paulus de baptismo typico, non proprio. b) Israelitae baptizati sunt non in nomen, siue personam Mosis, sed in Mosen, hoc est, in professionem & ratihabitionem doctrinae, quam Moses professus erat: Quae doctrina non tam Mosis, quam Dei erat. Si in nomen Mosis quis baptizari potuit, cur non etiam in nomen Pauli? Sed hoc reicit Apostolus, 1 Cor. I, 13.


### Q. XI. Who is to be baptized?

He who is to be baptized is a true human (Subiectum baptizandi), carnally begotten, and brought into the light, whether he be male or female, or an adult, not resisting, or an infant.

Proof a. From Matt. 28:19. Therefore, he who is to be baptized is a true human, not a bell, not a monster, incapable of regeneration.

Proof b. From John 3:5-6. Unless one has been begotten of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven. That which is born of the flesh is flesh. The reason why men are in need of baptism is that they are flesh of flesh, i.e., conceived in original sin.

You say: Christ was baptized, who nevertheless was not flesh of sinful flesh. Resp. Christ was baptized by the same economy, or peculiar dispensation, by which he was circumcised; namely, that by the contact of his body he might sanctify the baptismal waters, and apply to us through the baptism of water the righteousness procured by his blood, Matt. 3:16.

Proof c. No one can be reborn unless he has been born. Hence an embryo is by no means capable of baptism.

Proof d. We read that Lydia the woman was baptized, Acts 16: 15. There is here neither male nor female: for we are all one in Christ, Gal. 3: 17.

Proof e. History teaches that at the beginning of the nascent church many adults were dipped in the sacred wave. The distinction between infants and adults is that infants indeed cannot be instructed beforehand; but adults must be taught first, and baptized afterwards, so that from the hearing of the word they may conceive both hatred of sin and faith in Christ, Matt. 28:19; Matt. 3:6; Acts 8: 27. Wherefore, through baptism, faith, and the justification and renewal which follow it, are not first conferred upon adults, but are sealed and increased.

Proof f. That infants are capable of baptism is evident 1) from universal necessity. Whatever is born flesh of flesh, that must be regenerated under peril of salvation from water and the Spirit, John 3:5-6. But infants are born flesh of flesh. Therefore.

2) From the universal command of Christ, Matt. 28:19. Where Christ commands to baptize all nations. Under all nations, infants are also included.

3) From the universal promise, Acts 2:38-39, collated with Gen. 17:7, from which we gather: To whom the promise of grace and the evangelical covenant has been made, they are to be baptized, so that through baptism they may be constituted heirs of eternal salvation: But the promise has also been made to infants. Therefore.

4) From the parity of circumcision. To whom the circumcision of the Old Testament pertained, to them also pertains the baptism of the New Testament (because the latter succeeded into the place of the former, Col. 2:11. For the grace of the Old Testament is not greater than that of the New Testament): But circumcision also pertained to infants: Therefore.

5) From aptitude for the kingdom of heaven. To whom the kingdom of heaven belongs, to them pertains baptism as a means of arriving at that kingdom. The kingdom of heaven belongs to infants, Mark 10:14. Therefore.

6) From the practice of the primitive church; since the Apostles baptized whole houses and families (to which infants also belong), Acts 16:15; ch. 18:8; 1 Cor. 1:16.

The Antithesis is that of the Anabaptists and Socinians, who impugn infant baptism with the following arguments:

I. We do not have an explicit divine command to baptize infants: Therefore, we are not obligated to infant baptism. Resp. The universal command suffices for us, which admits of descent to infants.

Otherwise, by the same reasoning we conclude: There is no explicit divine command of baptizing Transylvanians: Therefore, no Transylvanian is to be baptized. There is no explicit command that the Eucharist must be offered to women. Therefore, should it not be offered to them? Just as from the words "drink all of you," we rightly conclude; so, because of the words "baptize all nations," we argue invincibly regarding infants.

II. Christ was baptized in the thirtieth year of his age: Therefore, baptism today must be deferred until the thirtieth year of age. Resp. Christ was circumcised at an infantile age; at which time baptism had not yet been instituted, since John the Baptist administered the first baptism in the 29th year of Christ. Add that the baptism of the most holy Jesus (which he undertook out of a free economy) could be deferred without danger: but our infants, conceived in sin, are subject to various dangers.

III. If infants are fit to receive baptism, they will also be fit to receive the preaching of the divine word (because both baptism and the preaching of the word are a means of regeneration): The consequent is false: Therefore, so is the antecedent. Resp. I deny the consequence of the major; because to receive the preaching of the word with fruit, listening and meditation are required, of which infants are not capable due to the lack of the full use of reason. However, nothing prevents them from being baptized.

IV. If infants are capable of baptism, they will also be capable of the Lord's Supper (for both are sacraments of the N.T.): The consequent is false: Therefore, so is the antecedent. Resp. I deny the consequence of the major; because he who is to approach the Lord's Supper, δοκιμαζέτω ἑαυτὸν, let him examine himself, 1 Cor. XI, 28. But such a δοκιμασία (examination) does not fall upon infants, nor is it required of those to be baptized.

V. Whoever’s baptism is not voluntary, that is not legitimate: The baptism of infants is not voluntary: Therefore. The major is evident, because the entire Christian religion is voluntary. Therefore, so is baptism, a significant part of the Christian religion. The minor is proven: because προαίρεσις, or the purpose of the will, does not yet fall upon infants. Resp. Something is called voluntary either because it is elicited by the will, or because it is admitted by a will that does not resist. Although infants do not actively choose baptism, they do not resist it; but they admit it spontaneously.

VI. Whoever cannot enter into a covenant with God, they are not to be admitted to baptism: For in baptism a pact or covenant is entered into with God: Infants cannot enter into a covenant with God: Therefore. The minor is clear: because a covenant is entered into between those who possess the use of reason, of which infants are destitute. Resp. On the part of the one who makes a covenant with another, the full use of reason is not always necessary, which is evident from the example of circumcised infants. Not rarely are covenants ratified among men in which parents pledge in place of infants, and thus the covenant also embraces infants not yet possessing the use of reason. The same happens in baptism, where, when infants are received into the covenant, others pledge for them, namely those who offer them for baptism.

VII. Infants are not capable of faith: Therefore, they are not fit to receive baptism. Resp. That infants are capable of regeneration and faith, we have proven in the previous section, ch. IV, on regeneration.

Latin:

Baptizandus est verus homo a), carnaliter genitus b), & in lucem editus c), sive fuerit masculus, sive foemina d), sive adultior, non repugnans e), sive infans f).

Prob. a. Ex Matth. XXVIII, 19. E. baptizandus est verus homo, non campana, non monstrum, regenerationis incapax.

Prob. b. Ex Io. III, 5. 6. Nisi quis generatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest ingredi in regnum caelorum. Quod natum est e carne, caro est. Causa, cur homines indigeant baptismo, est, quia sunt caro de carne, i. e. in peccato originali concepti.

Dicis: Christus baptizatus est, qui tamen non fuit caro de carne peccaminosa. Resp. Christus eadem oeconomia, sive peculiari dispensatione baptizatus est, qua circumcisus est; nimirum ut contactu corporis sui aquas baptismales sanctificaret, & iustitiam, sanguine suo partam, per baptismum aquae nobis applicaret, Matth. III, 16.

Prob. c. Nemo potest renasci, nisi sit natus. Hinc embryo baptismi minime capax est.

Prob. d. Lydiam foeminam baptizatam esse, legimus Act. XVI, 15. Non est hic mas neque foemina: Omnes enim unus sumus in Christo, Gal. III, 17.

Prob. e. Sub exordium nascentis ecclesiae multos adultos sacra unda tinctos esse, docet historia. Id discrimen est inter infantes, & adultos, quod infantes quidem non possunt ante institui; adulti autem prius docendi, & postea baptizandi sunt, ut ex auditu verbi tum odium peccati, tum fidem in Christum concipiant, Matth. XXVIII, 19. Matth. III, 6. Act. VIII, 27. Quocirca per baptismum fides, & quae hanc sequitur, iustificatio & renovatio non primum adultis confertur, sed obsignatur & adaugetur.

Prob. f. Infantes capaces esse baptismi, patet 1) ex universali necessitate. Quicquid de carne caro natum est, illud sub periculo salutis ex aqua & Spiritu regenerandum est, Io. III, 5. 6. Atqui infantes caro de carne nati sunt. E.

2) Ex universali mandato Christi, Matth. XXVIII, 19. Ubi Christus omnes gentes baptizare iubet. Sub omnibus gentibus etiam infantes comprehenduntur.

3) Ex promissione universali, Act. II, 38. 39. coll. cum Gen. XVII, 7. ex qua colligimus: Quibus facta est promissio gratiae & foederis evangelici, illi sunt baptizandi, ut per baptismum constituantur heredes salutis aeternae: Atqui infantibus etiam facta est promissio. E.

4) Ex circumcisionis paritate. Ad quos pertinuit circumcisio veteris testamenti, ad eos etiam spectat baptismus novi testamenti (quia hic in illius locum successit, Col. II, 11. Neque enim amplior gratia vet. testam. quam novi testamenti): Atqui etiam ad infantes pertinuit circumcisio: E.

5) Ex aptitudine ad regnum caelorum. Quorum est regnum caelorum, ad illos pertinet baptismus tanquam medium perveniendi in illud regnum. Infantum est regnum caelorum, Marc. X, 14. E.

6) Ex praxi primitivae ecclesiae; siquidem Apostoli integras domos & familias (ad quas etiam pertinent infantes) baptizarunt, Act. XVI, 15. c. XVIII, 8. 1 Cor. I, 16.

Antithesis est Anabaptistarum & Socinianorum, paedobaptismum impugnantium sequentibus argumentis:

I. Non habemus mandatum explicitum divinum, baptizandi infantes: E. non obligamur ad paedobaptismum. Resp. Sufficit nobis mandatum universale, quod descensum ad infantes admittit.

Ceteroqui eadem ratione concludimus: Non datur explicitum mandatum divinum baptizandi Transylvanos: E. nullus Transylvanus est baptizandus. Non datur mandatum explicitum, foeminis porrigendam esse eucharistiam. Ergone illis porrigenda non est? Sicut autem ex vocibus: bibite omnes, recte colligimus; Ita ad infantes propter voces; baptizate omnes gentes, invicte argumentamur.

II. Christus trigesimo aetatis anno baptizatus est: E. vsque ad trigesimum aetatis annum hodiernum baptismus differendus est. Resp. Christus circumcisus est in aetate infantili; quo tempore baptismus nondum erat institutus; siquidem Ioannes baptista anno Christi 29. primum baptismum administravit. Adde, quod sanctissimi Iesu baptismus (quem ille ex libera oeconomia suscepit) sine periculo potuit differri: nostri autem infantes, in peccato concepti, variis periculis subiacent.

III. Si infantes apti sunt ad recipiendum baptismum, apti etiam erunt ad recipiendam praedicationem verbi divini (quia & baptismus & praedicatio verbi est medium regenerationis): Consequens est falsum: E. & antecedens. Resp. Neg. consequentiam maioris; quia ad praedicationem verbi cum fructu recipiendam requiritur auscultatio & meditatio, cuius infantes ob defectum pleni vsus rationis non sunt capaces. Nihil autem impedit, quo minus baptizentur.

IV. Si infantes capaces sunt baptismi, capaces etiam erunt coenae dominicae (vtrumque enim est sacramentum N. T.): Consequens est falsum: E. & antecedens. Resp. Neg. consequentiam maioris; quia aditurus coenam dominicam, δοκιμαζέτω ἑαυτὸν, probet seipsum, 1 Cor. XI, 28. At in infantes eiusmodi δοκιμασία non cadit, neque a baptizandis exigitur.

V. Quicunque baptismus non est voluntarius, ille non est legitimus: Baptismus infantum non est voluntarius: E. Maior constat, quia tota religio christiana est voluntaria. E. &, baptismus, insignis pars religionis christianae. Minor probatur: quia in infantes nondum cadit προαίρεσις, sive propositum voluntatis. Resp. Voluntarium aliquid dicitur, vel quod a voluntate est elicitum, vel quod a voluntate non repugnante admissum. Licet infantes non active eligant baptismum, non tamen repugnant; sed ipsum sponte admittunt.

VI. Quicunque cum Deo non possunt foedus inire, illi non sunt admittendi ad baptismum: Nam in baptismo initur pactum, vel foedus cum Deo: Infantes non possunt inire foedus cum Deo: E. Minor claret: quia foedus initur inter illos, qui vsu rationis pollent, quo infantes destituuntur. Resp. Ex parte eius, qui cum altero foedus pangit, non semper necessarius est plenus vsus rationis, quod liquet exemplo infantum circumcisorum. Haud raro inter homines foedera fanciuntur, in quibus infantum loco parentes spondent, adeoque foedus complectitur etiam infantes, vsu rationis nondum pollentes Idem contingit in baptismo, vbi cum in foedus recipiuntur infantes, alii pro ipsis spondent, qui scilicet ipsos ad baptismum offerunt.

VII. Infantes non sunt capaces fidei: E. nec apti sunt ad recipiendam baptismum, Resp. Quod infantes regenerationis, fideique sint capaces, sect. superiori c. IV. de regeneratione probatum dedimus.


### Quest. XII

Are the infants of Jews and Gentiles to be washed in the sacred laver? The infants of Jews and Gentiles who resist are not to be snatched to baptism by violent attempt a). If, however, they come into our power through legitimate means, baptism is not to be denied to them b).

Prob. a. 1) Because to baptize a little child, while the parents object, is an injury to paternal authority. The power of disposing of the religion of children is and remains with the parents, 2) Because the Apostle says: What have I to do to judge them that are without? i.e., no right over these belongs to me. 3) The violent abduction of children from the hand of infidel parents is repugnant to divine and natural law, as kidnapping, severely prohibited: but the Gospel does not abolish right and equity. 4) Such a baptism is joined with the manifest danger of apostasy and the profanation of baptism. Prob. b.

Infants of Jews and Gentiles, coming into our power through legitimate means, e.g., through victory, through liberation from shipwreck, etc., are from the census of our goods, and thus subject to our command and disposal. For which reason, if danger of life threatens them, they are to be baptized immediately. But if God prolongs their life, baptism is to be deferred until they become catechumens, so that they themselves may render an account of their faith before they are baptized.

Latin:

Infantes Iudaeorum & gentilium reluctantium, violento ausu ad baptismum rapiendi non sunt a). Si tamen per legitima media in nostram venerint potestatem, baptismus ipsis non est denegandus b).

Prob. a. 1) Quia baptizare parvulum, contradicentibus parentibus, est iniuria in potestatem patriam. Est et manet penes parentes omnes, facultas disponendi de religione liberorum, 2) Quia Apostolus inquit: Quid ad me, iudicare de his, qui foris sunt? q. d. nullum mihi in hos ius competit. 3) Raptus liberorum violentus e manu parentum infidelium iuri divino ac naturali, tanquam plagium, severe prohibitum, repugnat: Evangelium autem ius et aequitatem non tollit. 4) Eiusmodi baptismus cum manifesto periculo apostasiae et profanationis baptismi coniunctus est. Prob. b.

Infantes Iudaeorum et gentilium, per legitima media v. gr. per victoriam, per liberationem e naufragio etc. in nostram potestatem pervenientes, e censu bonorum nostrorum sunt, adeoque nostro imperio et dispositioni subiecti. Quam ob rem, si illis immineat vitae periculum, statim baptizandi sunt. At si Deus ipsis proroget vitam, differendus est baptismus, usque dum catechumeni fiant, ita ut ipsi fidei suae, antequam baptizentur, rationem reddant.


### Quest. XIII. Are the children of harlots, and of other men excommunicated by the church, to be baptized?

The infants of harlots, and of other men excommunicated by the church, are rightly baptized, with the consent of the parents.

Prob. 1) Because the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, Because it is the will of God that not one of the infants should perish, Hence Christ invites all infants to himself, 3) Illegitimates are capable of salvation: Therefore also of the means of salvation. Jephthah was illegitimate, yet not uncircumcised, whom the Apostle deigns to introduce into the catalog of the saints,

You say: The author of the book of Wisdom condemns the illegitimate, ch. III, 16. 17. Resp. a) That book is apocryphal. b) Those illegitimates are understood who press the footsteps of impious parents,

Objection: But the illegitimate is prohibited from entering the congregation of the Lord, even to the tenth generation, Resp. To enter the congregation of the Lord in the cited place signifies to perform an ecclesiastical office, from which the illegitimate are barred, lest the authority of the ecclesiastical office become cheapened.

Latin:

Meretricum, et aliorum hominum, ab ecclesia excommunicatorum, infantes, consentientibus parentibus, recte baptizantur.

Prob. 1) Quia filius non portabit delictum patris, Quia Dei voluntas est, ne unus ex infantibus pereat, Hinc Christus omnes infantes ad se invitat, 3) Spurii sunt capaces salutis: Ergo et mediorum salutis. Iephta spurius fuit, non tamen incircumcisus, quem inferre catalogo sanctorum dignatur Apostolus,

Dicis: Auctor libri Sapientiae damnat spurios, c. III, 16. 17. Resp. a) Liber ille apocryphus est. b) Intelliguntur illi spurii, qui impiorum parentum premunt vestigia,

Instantia: Sed prohibetur spurius ingredi ecclesiam Domini, etiam decima generatione, Resp. Ingredi ecclesiam Domini l. c. significat officio ecclesiastico fungi, a quo arcentur spurii, ne auctoritas officii ecclesiastici evilescat.


### Q. XIV. Are also infants foundlings, to be baptized?

Baptism is not to be denied to foundling infants.

Prob. 1) From the universal will of God; because he does not will that any of the little ones should perish, 2) From supreme necessity; because unless they are born again of water and the Spirit, they cannot enter the kingdom of heaven, But Paul teaches that the salvation of others is to be procured

You say: If that foundling infant had been baptized before, it would become an ἀναβαπτισμός (rebaptism). Resp. That cannot be called repeated, which is not known to have been done.

Objection I. But if a note is attached to the foundling infant, testifying that he has been baptized, must it then be repeated? Resp. That note does not deserve faith, inasmuch as it arises from a woman, worse than beasts, which cherish their own offspring.

Objection II. But could one be baptized conditionally, in this manner: If you are baptized, I do not baptize you; but if you are not baptized, I baptize you in the name of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Resp. That hypothetical baptism of the Papists produces perpetual doubt, both in him who administers the baptism and in him who receives this sacrament conditionally; whether the baptism was conferred once or twice, rightly or wrongly. For this reason, that conditional baptism is not to be tolerated in the church.

Latin:

Infantibus exposititiis non est denegandus baptismus.

Prob. 1) A voluntate Dei universali; quia non vult, ut ullus ex parvulis pereat, 2) Ex summa necessitate; quia nisi renascantur ex aqua et Spiritu, non possunt ingredi regnum caelorum, Salutem autem aliorum procurandam esse, docet Paullus

Dicis: Si ille infans exposititius antea fuisset baptizatus, fieret ἀναβαπτισμός. Resp. Non potest dici iteratum, quod nescitur factum.

Instantia I. Sed si schedula infanti exposito affixa sit, testificans, ipsum baptizatum esse, num tunc iterandus est? Resp. Schedula illa non meretur fidem, utpote quae oritur a femina, peiore bestiis, suos foetus foventibus. quæ oritur a fœmina, peiore bestiis, suos fœtus fouentibus.

Instantia II. Sed posset conditionate baptizari, hoc modo: Si baptizatus es, ego te non baptizo; sed si non baptizatus, ego te baptizo in nomine Dei Patris, Filii & Spiritus S. Resp. Hypotheticus ille Pontificiorum baptismus parit perpetuam dubitationem tum in eo, qui baptismum administrat, tum in eo, qui percipit conditionaliter hoc sacramentum; semel, an bis, recte, an male, collatus sit baptismus. Quam ob rem conditionalis ille baptismus non est tolerandus in ecclesia.


### Quest. XV. Are the infants of Christians holy before the reception of baptism, and in the divine covenant?

The infants of Christians before the reception of baptism are holy with an external holiness, or that of the church , but they are not holy with an internal holiness, or that of faith . The promise of the covenant pertains to them, but they are not yet in the exhibited covenant .

Proof a. From 1 Cor. VII, 14. But now your children are holy. External or ecclesiastical holiness is understood, which consists in this, that the infants of believers have near access to divine grace and thus to the participation of the means through which, by divine ordination, eternal salvation is conferred. For they are born within the camp of the church, and they have the right to the thing (ius ad rem), although they do not yet have the right in the thing (ius in re), i.e., they have immediate access to the divine federal grace; but they are not yet actually participants of the divine federal grace. It is called ecclesiastical holiness, not as if unbaptized (ἀβάπτιστοι) infants of Christians were citizens or members of the church, but because they have the right and power of obtaining the privileges of the citizens of the church, which are not so easily granted to others who are outside. This external holiness is called by Dr. GALOV. in bibl. illustr. on 1 Cor. VII, f. 317, a merely relative holiness, and such according to extrinsic denomination. By Dr. BALDVIN it is called Levitical and legal; by Dr. DANNHAV. it is said to correspond to Levitical purity, in hodof. p. 1093.

Proof b. 1) Because infants before the reception of baptism are flesh of flesh, John III, 6, children of wrath, Eph. II, 3, unclean, conceived from unclean seed, Job XIV, 4, Ps. LI, 7. 2) Because through baptism we are cleansed from sins, Eph. V, 26. Therefore, before baptism we were unclean and not holy.

3) Because through baptism the first access into the kingdom of heaven is opened to us, John III, 5, whence by the confession of all, baptism is the sacrament of initiation. Hence TERTULLIAN says: Christians are not born, but made.

Proof c. To the infants of believers the divine covenant is indeed promised, but its application is not yet exhibited, Gen. XVII, 10. Acts II, 39, 41. For since the promise of the covenant is made conditional, or determined by the condition of receiving circumcision or baptism: Infants before the reception of the sacrament of initiation are not yet actually grafted into the divine covenant.

The Antithesis is that of the Anabaptists, asserting that the infants of believers are holy before the reception of baptism, and co-opted into the divine covenant. Their arguments are: I. The infants of believers are expressly called holy, Rom. II, 16 [sic]; 1 Cor. VII, 14. Resp. The infants of believers before the reception of baptism are holy with an external holiness, or that of the church, but they are not yet holy with an internal holiness, or that of faith.

II. Those to whom the divine covenant pertains are holy: But it pertains to the infants of believers, etc. Therefore. The minor is evident from Gen. XVII, 19; Acts II, 38. Resp. Those to whom the divine covenant pertains through the means of grace (circumcision and baptism) exhibited and applied, they are holy with an internal and spiritual holiness; but indeed to the infants of believers not yet circumcised, or bapti-circumcised, or bapti-circumcised, or bapti-

to the baptized, belongs only the promise of the covenant, determined by the condition of receiving circumcision, or baptism.

III. Many unbaptized have believed, e.g., Cornelius, Acts X, 47; the Eunuch, Acts VIII, 37. And before receiving baptism they were holy with the holiness of faith.

In infants, with the intervention of baptism, faith is kindled; in adult catechumens, through the mediation of baptism, faith is increased and confirmed.

IV. If those born of Jews are called Jews by nature, those born of Christians will also be Christians by nature. The antecedent is true, witness Paul, Gal. II, 5. And the consequent.

Resp. Distinguish between Jews according to the flesh and according to the spirit. Jews according to the flesh are those who are born of Israelites, and they are opposed to the Gentiles, just as Germans are distinguished from the French, Spaniards, etc. Such a gentilic name is not "Christian," but he who is anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit is called truly Christian, who is not born as such, but is made so through baptism; just as a Jew according to the spirit is one who, through circumcision, has been grafted into the divine covenant, and remains in the same covenant through true faith.

Instance: If the infants of Christians are not Christians by nature, there will be no difference between the infants of Gentiles and Christians; since both the former and the latter are devoid of holiness. Resp. There is indeed a difference. For the infants of Christians enjoy external and ecclesiastical holiness; since they are born in the church from faithful parents and have an immediate, or proximate, right to the means of grace, so that a certain prerogative belongs to them over those who are outside, 1 Cor. V, 12. Therefore, they are wrongly called by the common people, junge Heyden (young heathens).

Latin:

Infantes christianorum ante perceptum baptismum, sunt sancti sanctitate externa, sive ecclesiae , sed non sunt sancti sanctitate interna, sive fidei . Competit illis promissio foederis, sed nondum sunt in foedere exhibito .

Prob. a. Ex 1 Cor. VII, 14. Nunc autem liberi vestri sancti sunt. Intelligitur sanctitas externa, seu ecclesiastica, quae consistit in hoc, quod infantes fidelium proximum aditum habent ad gratiam divinam atque adeo ad participationem mediorum, per quae ex ordinatione divina confertur salus aeterna. Sunt enim intra castra ecclesiae nati, & habent ius ad rem, licet nondum habeant ius in re, i. e. habent immediatum aditum ad gratiam divinam foederalem; sed actu nondum sunt participes gratiae divina foederalis. Dicitur sanctitas ecclesiastica, non quasi infantes Christianorum ἀβάπτιστοι sint ciues, aut membra ecclesiae, sed quia habent ius & potestatem consequendi priuilegia ciuium ecclesiae, quae aliis, qui foris sunt, non tam facile conceduntur. Dicitur haec sanctitas externa a D. GALOV. in bibl. illustr. in 1 Cor. VII. f. 317. sanctitas mere relativa, & secundum extrinsecam denominationem talis. A D. BALDVINO appellatur leuitica & legalis, a D. DANNHAV. leuiticae puritati respondens, in hodof. p. 1093.

Prob. b. 1) Quia infantes ante susceptum baptismum sunt caro de carne, Io. III, 6. filii irae, Eph. II, 3. immundi, de immundo semine concepti, Iobi XIV, 4. Ps. LI, 7. 2) Quia per baptismum emundamur a peccatis, Eph. V, 26. E. ante baptismum fuimus immundi & non sancti.

3) Quia per baptismum nobis patet primus aditus in regnum caelorum, Io. III, 5. vnde omnium confessione baptismus est sacramentum initiationis. Hinc TERTVLLIANVS inquit: Non nascuntur, sed fiunt Christiani.

Prob. c. Infantibus fidelium foedus divinum quidem est promissum, sed nondum exhibitum eius applicatum, Gen. XVII, 10. Act. II, 39. 41. Cum enim promissio foederis fit conditionata, sive determinata conditione suscipiendae circumcisionis, aut baptismi: Infantes ante acceptum initiationis sacramentum foederi divino actu non sunt insiti.

Antithesis est Anabaptistarum Asserentium, infantes fidelium ante susceptum baptismum esse sanctos, & in foedus divinum cooptatos. Quorum argumenta sunt: I. Infantes fidelium diserte dicuntur sancti, Rom. II, 16. 1 Cor. VII, 14. Resp. Infantes fidelium ante susceptum baptismum sunt sancti, sanctitate externa, sive ecclesiae, sed nondum sunt sancti sanctitate interna, sive fidei.

II. Ad quos pertinet foedus divinum, illi sunt sancti: Sed ad infantes fidelium &c. E. Minor patet ex Gen. XVII, 19. Act. II, 38. Resp. Ad quos pertinet foedus divinum per media gratiae (circumcisionem & baptismum) exhibitum & applicatum, illi sunt sancti sanctitate interna & spirituali; at vero ad infantes fidelium nondum circumcisos, aut baptizacircumcisos, aut baptizacircumcisos, aut

baptizatos, pertinet tantum promissio foederis, determinata conditione suscipiendae circumcisionis, aut baptismi.

III. Multi non baptizati crediderunt, v. gr. Cornelius, Act. X, 47. Eunuchus, Act. VIII, 37. E ante susceptum baptismum fuerunt sancti sanctitate fidei. Resp. Dist. inter infantes, & adultos catechumenos.

In infantibus, interveniente baptismo, fides accenditur, in adultis catechumenis, mediante baptismo, fides augetur & confirmatur.

IV. Si nati ex Iudaeis dicuntur natura Iudaei, etiam nati ex Christianis, natura erunt Christiani. Antecedens est verum, teste Paulo, Gal. II, 5.

E & consequens. Resp. Dist. inter Iudaeos secundum carnem, & secundum spiritum. Iudaei secundum carnem sunt, qui ex Israelitis nati sunt, & oppontuntur ethnicis, sicut Germani Gallis, Hispanis &c. contradistinguuntur. Eiusmodi nomen gentilitium non est Christianus, sed qui oleo Spiritus S. unctus est, ille dicitur vere Christianus, qui non nascitur talis, sed fit per baptismum; sicut Iudaeus secundum spiritum est, qui per circumcisionem foederi divino est insitus, & in eodem foedere per veram fidem manet.

Instantia: Si infantes Christianorum non sunt natura Christiani, inter infantes gentilium & Christianorum nullum erit discrimen; quoniam tam illi, quam hi, sunt sanctitatis expertes. Resp. Vtique datur discrimen. Nam infantes Christianorum gaudent sanctitate externa & ecclesiastica; quoniam in ecclesia ex fidelibus parentibus sunt prognati & habent ius immediatum, sive proximum ad media gratiae, vt ipsis conpetat praerogativa quaedam prae his, qui foris sunt, 1 Cor. V, 12. Itaque male dicuntur a vulgo, junge Heyden.


### Q. XVI. What is the end of baptism?

The primary end of baptism is the offering, application, conferral, and sealing of evangelical grace . The secondary ends are: the distinction of Christians from Gentiles, and the union into the body of the church , and the obligation to true faith and piety of life .

Prob. a. Evangelical grace in this place is the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is applicative. The Holy Spirit applies this grace to us as the principal cause through baptism, as an organ, or a divinely ordained medium. For through baptism there is applied to us 1) the calling grace; therefore, through baptism, as a door, we enter into the kingdom of grace, or the church, John III, 5. 2) The illuminating grace; because through baptism we are imbued with that light of knowledge so that we put on Christ, Gal. III, 27. From which the Greek Fathers call baptism φωτισμόν (illumination), from Heb. VI, 4. See GREGOR. NAZIANZ. orat. 40. in baptism. 3) The regenerating grace, by which we are gifted with faith; for baptism is the washing of regeneration, Tit. III, 5. In infants, the regenerating grace divinely implanted is excited and kindled. 4) The justifying grace: for the reason that we are baptized for the remission of sins, Acts II, 38. 5) The indwelling grace; since through baptism we put on Christ, Gal. III, 27, and are grafted into His mystical body, 1 Cor. XII, 13. 6) The renewing grace; for baptism is indeed the washing of renewal, Tit. III, 5. 7) The preserving and sealing grace. Just as circumcision was to Abraham a seal of the righteousness of faith, Rom. IV, 11, so baptism, which succeeded into the place of circumcision, is today for adults, who have been reborn through the preaching of the gospel, a seal by which both faith and the righteousness of faith are confirmed and sealed. 8) The glorifying grace. For God saves us through the washing of regeneration, witness Paul, Tit. III, 5, to which Peter gives his suffrage, 1 ep. III, 22.

The water of baptism makes us safe, just as the water of the flood saved Noah.

For example b. By one Spirit we are all baptized into one body, 1 Cor. XII, 13. By the Holy Spirit as the principal cause, and by baptism as the divinely ordained medium, we are united and grow together into one mystical body, which is the church.... Men are members of this, reborn through baptism, but Christ is its head, Eph. I, 22. As therefore we are baptized to that end, that we may be grafted into one body: so by baptism, as a sign and token, we are distinguished from men not baptized: Prob. c. From 1 Pet. III, 21. Baptism is συνειδήσεως ἀγαθῆς ἐπερώτημα εἰς Θεόν, the interrogation of a good conscience toward God. This apostolic oracle is learnedly explained by DANNHAV. in hodof. p. 1107. The word, ἐπερώτημα immediately and formally denotes the interrogation, formerly customary in baptism: Do you believe? I believe: Do you renounce? I renounce. Cf. Act. VIII, 37. and therefore baptism is called a stipulation. Now a stipulation, by the authority of POMPONIUS, is a conception of words, by which he who is interrogated answers that he will give and do what he has been asked. This is followed by another interrogation of the baptized, a confessional one, responding to a certain assertion: Abba Father! am I your son? 2) It denotes by metonymy a certain proof and demonstration. In which sense the word of God is called ἐρώτημα δῆλον, a clear speech, Sir. XXXIII, 4. 3) It designates complexly the federal act of the stipulators, born from mutual interrogations and responses. God therefore makes a pact in baptism with the baptized, and by the pact gives him a good conscience, that is, the remission of sins, righteousness, and eternal life; furthermore, He promises that He will be his God, father, provider, and protector. Conversely, the baptized promises that he will be a faithful servant and son to God, and that he will enter upon a new life, will preserve the good conscience received from Him, even to the last breath of life, and will obey His law and commandments in all things. For this reason, those who were formerly to profess the Christian faith publicly in baptism used to look up to heaven, and raise their right hands on high, with an oath taken before witnesses; and the oath, subscribed by the hand of the baptized and sealed with his ring, was recorded in the registers. See D. CALOV. in bibl. illustratis on 1 Pet. III. fol. 1508.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, Arminians, Anabaptists, and Weigelians; who deny that baptism is an efficacious medium for conferring grace and binding [the conscience], whose arguments see refuted in the previous section, chap. IV, on regeneration.

Latin:

Finis baptismi primarius est gratiae evangelicae oblatio, applicatio, collatio & obsignatio . Fines secundarii sunt: discretio Christianorum a gentilibus, & adunitio ad corpus ecclesiae , obligatio ad veram fidem & pietatem vitae .

Prob. a. Gratia evangelica hoc loco est gratia Spiritus S. applicatrix. Applicat nobis hanc gratiam Spiritus S. tanquam causa principalis per baptismum, velut organon, aut medium divinitus ordinatum. Etenim per baptismum nobis applicatur 1) gratia vocans, ideo per baptismum velut ianuam in regnum gratiae, sive ecclesiam ingredimur, Io. III, 5. 2) Gratia illuminans; quia per baptismum ea cognitionis luce imbuimur, vt Christum induamus, Gal. III, 27. Ex quo Patres Graeci baptismum vocant φωτισμόν, illuminationem, ex Hebr. VI, 4. Vid. GREGOR. NAZIANZ. orat. 40. in baptism. 3) Gratia regenerans, qua fide donamur; est enim baptismus lavacrum regenerationis, Tit. III, 5. Infantes gratiam regenerantem diuinitus inditam excitatur & accenditur. 4) Gratia iustificans: propterea, quod baptizamur in remissionem peccatorum, Act. II, 38. 5) Gratia inhabitans; quoniam per baptismum Christum induimus, Gal. III, 27. & corpori ipsius mystico inferimur, 1 Cor. XII, 13. 6) Gratia renouans; est quippe baptismus lavacrum renovationis. Tit. III, 5. 7) Gratia conferuans & obsignans. Sicut Abrahamo circumcisio erat sigillum iustitiae fidei, Rom. IV, 11. ita baptismus, qui in locum circumcisionis successit, hodie adultis, qui per praedicationem evangelii renati sunt, est sigillum, quo tum fides, tum iustitia fidei confirmatur & obsignatur. 8) Gratia glorificans. Deus enim nos saluat per lavacrum regenerationis, teste Paulo, Tit. III, 5. cui suffragatur Petrus, 1 ep. III, 22.

Baptismi aqua saluos nos reddit, sicut aqua diluvii servauit Noachum.

Prob. b. Per unum Spiritum nos omnes in unum corpus baptizati sumus, 1 Cor. XII, 13. Per Spiritum S. tanquam caussam principalem, & per baptismum, tanquam medium divinitus ordinatum, unimur & coalescimus in unum corpus mysticum, quod est ecclesia. Huius membra sunt homines, per baptismum renati, Christus autem ipsius caput est, Eph. I, 22. Sicut igitur eo fine baptizamur, vt uni corpori inferamur: ita per baptismum, velut notam ac tesseram, ab hominibus non baptizatis discernimur: Prob. c. Ex 1 Petr. III, 21. Baptismus est συνειδήσεως ἀγαθῆς ἐπερώτημα εἰς Θεόν, bonae conscientiae interrogatio erga Deum. Quod oraculum apostolicum scite enucleat DANNHAV. in hodof. p. 1107. Vox, ἐπερώτημα immediate ac formaliter notat interrogationem, in baptismo olim usitatam: Credis? Credo: Renuntias? Renuntio. Conf. Act. VIII, 37. ac ideo baptismus stipulatio vocatur. Est autem stipulatio, auctore POMPONIO, verborum conceptio, quibus is, qui interrogatur, daturum facturumque se, quod interrogatus est, respondet. Quam sequitur alia baptizati interrogatio παρρησιασική, respondens certae asseverationi: Abba pater! num ego sum filius tuus? 2) Notat μεταληπτικῶς certam ἀπόδειξιν ac demonstrationem. Quo sensu verbum Dei ἐρώτημα δῆλον, eine klare Rede, appellatur, Sir. XXXIII, 4. 3) Designat complexe actum stipulatorum foederalem, ex mutuis interrogationibus & responsionibus natum. Paciscitur itaque Deus in baptismo cum baptizato, eique ex pacto dat bonam conscientiam, puta, remissionem peccatorum, iustitiam & vitam aeternam; insuper promittit, se ei fore Deum, patrem, provisorem & protectorem. Vice versa promittit baptizatus, se Deo fore fidelem famulum & filium, & novam vitam initurum, bonam conscientiam ab eo acceptam conferuaturum, vsque ad extremum vitae spiritum, eiusque legi & mandatis in omnibus obediturum. Hac de caussa olim in baptismo fidem christianam publice professuri in coelum suspiciebant, ac manus dextras in altum erigebant, adhibito iureiurando coram testibus; ac iusiurandum manu baptizati subscriptum, eiusque annulo obsignatum, in tabulas referebatur. Vid. D. CALOV. in bibl. illustratis in 1 Petr. III. fol. 1508.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, Arminianorum, Anabaptistarum & Weigelianorum; negantium, baptismum esse efficax gratiae conferendae & obligandae medium, quorum argumenta confutata vide sectione superiori cap. IV. de regeneratione.


### Quaest. XVII. Is the root of sin destroyed by baptism?

By baptism the guilt and dominion of sin are removed, not the root, or the tinder of sin.

Prob. 1) From the presence of depraved concupiscence in the reborn. Paul, baptized and reborn, complains, Rom. VII, 14. I am carnal, sold under sin. I perpetrate evil because of the sin inhabiting me. St. John pours forth similar complaints, 1 ep. I, 8. If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.

2) From the propagation of original sin. For the saints propagate sin into their children, Ps. LI, 7. Therefore sin still inheres in them.

3) From actual sins, which the reborn commit after baptism. For there is no man who does not sin. 1 Kings VIII, 46.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, who maintain that sin is destroyed by baptism, so that it is no longer present. Who rely on the following arguments:

I. Whatever is washed away is no longer present. In baptism sin is washed away, Acts XXII, 16. Therefore.

Resp. I deny the major. Sin is washed away in baptism, not so that it does not exist, but so that it is not imputed, nor does it rule.

II. Whoever cleanses the church through the washing of water in the word, he takes away every sin. But Christ &c. Eph. V, 26. E. Resp. Christ cleanses the church by remitting sins and washing away stains, which cleansing, however, is imperfect due to the incapacity of the subject. Instantia: But Christ so sanctifies the church, that it may not have a stain or wrinkle. Resp. The Apostle does not say that the church is already without stain or wrinkle, but that it is to be presented without stain or wrinkle, glorious. That which will come to pass in the future life, where the triumphant church will be free from all defilement.

III. Through baptism we die to sin, Rom. VI, 4. E. in us who are baptized there is nothing of sin remaining. Resp. We die to sin, not so that it is extirpated through baptism, but so that it may not rule.

Latin:

Tollitur per baptismum reatus & dominium peccati, non radix, aut fomes peccati.

Prob. 1) Ex prauae concupiscentiae praesentia in renatis. Paullus baptizatus & renatus conqueritur, Rom. VII, 14. Ego carnalis sum, venundatus sub peccatum. Perpetro malum propter inhabitans peccatum. Similes querelas S. Ioannes effundit, 1 ep. I, 8. Si dixerimus, quod peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos seducimus, & veritas non est in nobis.

2) Ex peccati originalis propagatione. Sancti enim peccatum in liberos propagant, Ps. LI, 7. E. peccatum ipsis adhuc inest.

3) Ex peccatis actualibus, quae renati post baptismum patrant. Neque enim est homo, qui non peccet. 1 Reg. VIII, 46.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, statuentium, peccatum per baptismum deleri, vt non amplius adsit. Qui sequentibus innituntur argumentis:

I. Quidquid abluitur, non amplius adest. In baptismo peccatum abluitur, Act. XX, 11.

E. Resp. Neg. maiorem. Abluitur peccatum in baptismo, non vt non sit, sed vt non imputetur, neque dominetur.

II. Quicunque per lauacrum aquae in verbo mundat ecclesiam, ille omne peccatum tollit. Atqui Christus &c. Eph. V, 26. E. Resp. Mundat Christus ecclesiam peccata remittendo & maculas abstergendo, quae tamen abstersio, ob incapacitatem subiecti, imperfecta est. Instantia: Sed Christus ita sanctificat ecclesiam, vt non habeat maculam, aut rugam. Resp. Non dicit Apostolus, quod ecclesia iam sit sine macula aut ruga, sed quod fit sistenda sine macula, aut ruga, gloriosa. Id quod fiet in futura vita, vbi ecclesia triumphans ab omni inquinamento libera erit.

III. Per baptismum morimur peccato, Rom. VI, 4. E. in nobis baptizatis nihil peccati reliquum est. Resp. Morimur peccato, non vt illud per baptismum exstirpetur, sed ne dominetur.


### Quaest. XVIII

Does the efficacy of baptism extend even to future sins? Baptism possesses such remarkable efficacy by divine ordination, that God both calls the sinner back to Himself in view of the baptismal covenant, and remits the sin to him as he repents , and the sinner, contrite and longing for the grace of God, can raise himself up by the remembrance of his baptism .

Prob. a. Baptism is a sin and a divine covenant, 1 Petr. III, 21. But the divine covenant, on the part of God, is eternal, Es. LIV, 10. it is ἀμεταμέλητον (irrevocable), Rom. XI, 29. since the infidelity of men does not make the faith of God void, Rom. III, 3. Hence it comes about that God calls the sinner back to Himself, and to the covenant entered into with him, Ier. III, 22.

Prob. b. Just as in the Old Testament Jonathan, 1 Sam. XIV, 6, and David, 1 Sam. XVII, 26, drew most efficacious consolations from circumcision: so the most sorrowful sinners receive solid comforts from baptism, when called to memory.

Peter certainly, after his most grave fall, sustains himself by the remembrance of baptism, saying: Baptism saves us, 1 ep. III, 21. The Corinthians had sinned not lightly, to whose minds the Apostle applies baptism, 1 Cor. VI, 11.: You were washed, namely in baptism, and 1 Cor. XII, 13. In one spirit we were all baptized into one body.

St. Paul raises up the fallen Galatians, Gal. III, 27. As many of you as have been baptized, have put on Christ.

There is an antithesis of the Papists, who deny that the efficacy of baptism extends to future sins.

I. Whoever are baptized for the remission of future sins, their sins are remitted before they are committed: But no sins are remitted before they are committed. Therefore.

Resp. Distinguish between sin remitted and sin remissible. By virtue of the baptismal covenant, future sin is remissible, not actually remitted. For baptism does not delete future sins by a complete act, but by virtue, when the sinner is reborn through repentance to the baptismal covenant, as if to a ship.

Instantia: But the ship of the baptismal covenant is broken by a proaretic (deliberate) sin: therefore repentance is called the second plank after shipwreck, by TERTULLIAN, lib. de poenitentia fol. 553. and JEROME, ep.

VIII. Resp. 1) Repentance is called the second plank after shipwreck, not as if the ship of baptism were completely shattered by sin, or the covenant which God entered into with us in baptism becomes fragile and temporary (which is against Hos. II, 13. Rom. XI, 29.); but because it becomes the second plank after the shipwreck of faith & a good conscience, 1 Tim. I, 19. 2) From the shipwreck. shipwreck of faith, on the part of man, to the shipwreck of the baptismal covenant on the part of God, N. V. C. because the unbelief of men does not make the faith of God of no effect, Rom. III, 3.

II. Circumcision did not avail for the future: therefore, neither does baptism. The antecedent is evident: because the Israelites, having fallen into sin after circumcision, obtained the remission of sins not through circumcision, but through repentance. Resp. 1) That the Israelites sought very sweet consolations from circumcision is clear from the examples of Jonathan and David adduced above. 2) We do not separate repentance from circumcision and baptism, but we join it with this sacrament. 3) God promises that He will circumcise the heart of the Israelites, when they have repented of the sins committed after circumcision, Deut. XXX, 6. Which promise rests upon the covenant of circumcision availing for the future.

III. Those who have relapsed after baptism cannot be recalled through baptism, Hebr. VI, 6. 1) We do not assert that a sinner who has relapsed after baptism is recalled through a repeated baptism, but that God, in view of the baptismal covenant, recalls the sinner to Himself and forgives him his sin. 2) In that place, the Apostle speaks of the sin against the Holy Spirit; which is irremissible, not on the part of God absolutely reprobating, or simply denying the means of grace; but on the part of man, who stubbornly and perseveringly rejects the offered means of salvation.

Latin:

Tam insigni efficacia pollet baptismus ex ordinatione diuina, vt tum Deus intuitu foederis baptismalis peccatorem ad se reuocet, & ipsi resipiscenti peccatum remittat , tum peccator contritus & gratiam Dei anhelans recordatione baptismi se erigere possit .

Prob. a. Baptismus est peccatum ac foedus diuinum, 1 Petr. III, 21. At foedus diuinum, ex parte Dei, est aeternum, Es. LIV, 10. est ἀμεταμέλητον, Rom. XI, 29. siquidem infidelitas hominum non irritam facit fidem Dei, Rom. III, 3. Inde fit, vt Deus peccatorem ad se, & ad foedus cum ipso initum reuocet, Ier. III, 22.

Prob. b. Quemadmodum in veteri testamento Ionathan, 1 Sam. XIV, 6. Dauid, 1 Sam. XVII, 26 ex circumcisione efficacissimas hauserunt consolationes: ita tristissimi peccatores e baptismo, in memoriam reuocato, solida capiunt solatia.

Petrus certe, post grauissimum lapsum, se recordatione baptismi sustentat, inquiens: Baptismus nos saluat, 1 ep. III, 21. Corinthii haud leuiter peccauerant, quorum animis Apostolus baptismum subiicit, 1 Cor. VI, 11.: Abluti estis, nimirum in baptismo, & 1 Cor. XII, 13. In vno spiritu in vnum corpus baptizati sumus.

Lapsos Galatas S. Paullus erigit, Gal. III, 27. Quotquot baptizati estis, Christum induistis.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, negantium, efficaciam baptismi ad futura peccata se extendere. Quorum praecipua sunt argumenta:

I. Quicunque baptizantur in remissionem peccatorum futurorum, illorum peccata sunt remissa prius, quam commissa: Sed nulla peccata sunt remissa prius, quam commissa. Ergo.

Resp. Dist. inter peccatum remissum, & remissibile. Vi foederis baptismalis peccatum futurum est remissibile, non actu remissum. Neque enim baptismus delet peccata futura actu completo, sed virtute, cum peccator per poenitentiam ad foedus baptismale, velut ad nauem, renatat.

Instantia: Sed nauis foederis baptismalis per peccatum proareticum frangitur: ideo poenitentia vocatur secunda post naufragium tabula, a TERTULLIANO, lib. de poenitentia fol. 553. & HIERONYMO, ep.

VIII. Resp. 1) Poenitentia appellatur secunda post naufragium tabula, non quasi per peccatum nauis baptismi plane disiliat, seu foedus, quod Deus nobiscum in baptismo iniuit, fragile atque temporarium fit (quod est contra Hos. II, 13. Rom. XI, 29.); sed quod fit secunda tabula post naufragium fidei & bonae conscientiae, 1 Tim. I, 19. 2) A naufragio. fragio fidei, ex parte hominis, ad naufragium foederis baptismalis ex parte Dei, N. V. C. quia infidelitas hominum non irritam facit fidem Dei, Rom. III, 3.

II. Circumcisio non valuit in futurum: E. nec baptismus. Antecedens constat: quia Israëlitae, post circumcisionem in peccatum prolapsi, non per circumcisionem, sed per poenitentiam remissionem peccatorum consecuti sunt. Resp. 1) Israëlitas ex circumcisione perquam dulcia petiisse solatia, ex supra adductis exemplis Ionathanis & Dauidis liquet. 2) Poenitentiam a circumcisione & baptismo non seiungimus, sed cum hoc sacramento coniungimus. 3) Promittit Deus, se circumcisurum esse cor Israëlitarum, cum respuerint de peccatis post circumcisionem commissis, Deut. XXX, 6. Quae promissio foedere circumcisionis in futurum valente nititur.

III. Relapsi post baptismum non possunt revocari per baptismum, Hebr. VI, 6. 1) Non asserimus, peccatorem relapsum post baptismum per repetitum baptismum reuocari, sed Deum intuitu foederis baptismalis peccatorem ad se reuocare, & ipsi peccatum remittere. 2) L. c. loquitur Apostolus de peccato in Spiritum S.; quod est irremissibile, non ex parte Dei absolute reprobantis, aut media gratiae simpliciter denegantis; sed ex parte hominis, oblata salutis media praefracte & perseueranter repudiantis.


### Q. XIX. Is baptism necessary?

Baptism is necessary by necessity of precept , and of means , and indeed by an ordered necessity, not an absolute one; since we believe that infants of Christians dying without baptism are saved .

Prob. a. The precept of Christ exists, Matth. XXVIII, 19. Teach all nations, and baptize them. Cf. Acts II, 38.

Prob. b. 1) From John III, 5. Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven. Which exception is resolved into this exponent: No unbaptized person (ἀβάπτισος) shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but baptism is the ordinary medium, and as it were the way, by which we enter the kingdom of God. 2) From Mark XVI, 16.

He who believes and is baptized shall be saved: but he who does not believe shall be condemned. As faith is a necessary medium, receiving the offered salvation: so baptism is an instrument offering salvation, and conferring it upon believers, by virtue of divine ordination.

Prob. c. 1) Because the promise of the divine covenant pertains to the infants of Christians, although they are not yet in the covenant exhibited or applied, Gen. XVII, 7. Acts II, 39. Wherefore, without doubt, God, mindful of His promise, is propitious to the infants of Christians who have departed from this life without baptism.

2) Because God does not will that one of the little ones should perish, Matth. XVIII, 14.

3) Because just as it is harsh and cruel to condemn infants who either were born and died in the desert within the forty years of pilgrimage before they were circumcised, Josh. V, 4, or were destroyed in the persecution of Pharaoh, with the foreskin not yet removed, Exod. I, 22, or were killed by the satellites of Herod before the sacrament of circumcision was received, Matth. II, 16: so the opinion by which the infants of the faithful who are unbaptized (ἀβάπτισος) are adjudged to eternal damnation is harsher than is just.

4) God has not bound His grace to the sacraments, as THOMAS holds, P. III. qu. 64. We indeed are bound to the use of the means, but God can act extraordinarily, just as we ordinarily use food in hunger and medicines in sickness: but God can nourish without food, and restore health without medicine, in an extraordinary way.

5) Not the privation, but the contempt of baptism damns, as AUGUSTINE says, L. IV. against the Donatists, c. 32.

The antithesis is 1) of the Socinians, who maintain that baptism is a rite merely arbitrary, used by the Apostles around the beginnings of the church, today no longer necessary. 2) Of the Papists generally, who maintain that infants not baptized are excluded from the kingdom of heaven, and suffer the punishment of loss, not of sense.

The Socinians argue: I. Whatever is not numbered among the rudiments of celestial doctrine, that is not necessary for Christians: The baptism of water is not numbered &c. Therefore. The minor is proved from Heb. VI, 2, where mention is made of βαπτισμῶν διδαχῆς (baptisms of doctrine), not of τοῦ ὕδατος (of water). Resp. The Apostle understands baptism properly so-called, concerning which catechumens were to be informed. He speaks, however, in the plural, to indicate that the doctrine concerning baptisms can be so instituted that it may be inculcated to catechumens, that there is a great difference between the ceremonial baptisms of the Old Testament, and the sacramental baptism of the New Testament. For we learn from Heb. IX, 10, that the Jews had various ceremonial baptisms.

II. If John baptized with water, but Christ with the Spirit and fire, it follows that in the present-day church of Christ no one is necessarily to be baptized with water. The antecedent is true, by the testimony of John, Luke III, 17. Therefore, the consequent also. Resp. In that place is understood the baptism of the Spirit, which does not take away the baptism of the river.

III. The Apostles are not read to have been baptized: Therefore, baptism is not necessary. Resp. In historical matters, from an argument from the negative, or rather from silence, a firm consequence is not drawn. For it does not follow: We do not read that the Apostles were baptized: Therefore, they were not baptized. If all things were written, the world could not have contained the mass of books, John XXI, 25.

IV. Whatever doctrine is entirely spiritual, and regards the inner man, that does not prescribe an external rite of baptism to be necessarily observed: But the evangelical doctrine of the New Testament &c. Therefore. The minor is proved from 2 Cor. III, 6. God made us fit ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter, but of the spirit, where the doctrine of the New Testament is called spirit, i.e., spiritual. Resp. 1) I deny the major. For spiritual doctrine does not simply exclude external rites, otherwise it would also exclude the external rite of the Lord's Supper, which is absurd. 2) Baptism is not a rite merely external, but is the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Spirit, who is poured out upon us abundantly, Tit. III, 5.

The Papists argue: I. Whoever is not born again of water and the Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven, John III, 5. Infants ἀβάπτιστοι (unbaptized) &c. Therefore. Resp. I limit the major; Whoever is a contemner of baptism is not born again of water and the Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven; I concede: But the infants of the faithful, whether they perish in the maternal womb, or are snatched away by sudden death before baptism, are not contemners of baptism. They are indeed ἀβάπτιστοι negatively, but not privatively such. Those dead in the mother's womb did not have to be baptized: but those deceased by sudden fate before baptism was received could not be bathed in the sacred washing. Therefore, they are not ἀβάπτιστοι privatively such, and thus are not excluded from entry into heaven.

II. Those who do not believe are damned: Infants ἀβάπτιστοι (unbaptized) do not believe: Therefore. The minor is proved: because in infants not baptized, neither through the sacrament of baptism, nor through the preaching of the gospel, faith is kindled. Resp. God kindles faith in the infants of the faithful in an extraordinary way.

III. The infants of the faithful are unbaptized [ἀβάπτιστοι] and conceived in original sin, the remission of which they have not obtained: Therefore, they are not partakers of eternal salvation.

Resp: Christ has acquired by His merit the remission of sins for unbaptized infants, which they apply to themselves by faith kindled in an extraordinary way.

Latin:

Baptismus necessarius est necessitate praecepti , & medii , & quidem necessitate ordinata, non absoluta; siquidem infantes Christianorum sine baptismo decedentes saluari credimus .

Prob. a. Praeceptum Christi exstat, Matth. XXVIII, 19. Docete omnes gentes, & baptizate eas. Conf. Act. II, 38.

Prob. b. 1) Ex Io. III, 5. Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest ingredi in regnum caelorum. Quae exceptiua in hanc exponentem resoluitur: Nullus ἀβάπτισος introibit in regnum caelorum; sed baptismus est ordinarium medium, & quasi via, qua renum Dei intramus.

2) Ex Marc. XVI, 16. Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, saluabitur: Qui vero non crediderit, condemnabitur. Vt fides est necessarium medium, salutem oblatam recipiens: ita baptismus est organon salutem offerens, & credentibus conferens, vi ordinationis diuinae.
