Prob. c. 1) Quia ad infantes Christianorum pertinet promissio foederis diuini, licet nondum sint in foedere exhibito, aut applicato, Gen. XVII, 7. Act. II, 39. Quare dubio procul Deus, recordatus suae promissionis, propitius est infantibus Christianorum, sine baptismo ex hac vita egressis.

2) Quia Deus non vult, vt unus e paruulis pereat, Matth. XVIII, 14.

3) Quia sicut durum & crudele est damnare infantes, qui aut in deserto intra quadraginta peregrinationis annos nati & denati prius, quam circumcisi sunt, Ios. V, 4. aut in persecutione Pharaonis exstincti, praeputio nondum refecto, Exod. I, 22. aut a satellitibus Herodis sunt occisi ante susceptum cicumcisionis sacramentum, Matth. II, 16.: ita iusto durior est sententia, qua infantes fidelium ἀβάπτισος aeternae damnationi adiudicantur.

4) Deus non alligauit gratiam suam sacramentis, censente THOMA, P. III. qu. 64. Nos quidem ad mediorum vsum adstricti sumus, sed Deus extraordinarie agere potest, sicut ordinarie vtimur cibo in fame, & medicamentis in morbis: at Deus fine cibo alere, sine medicamine sanitatem restituere potest modo extraordinario.

5) Non priuatio, sed contemptus baptismi damnat, dicente AVGVSTINO L. IV. contra Donatist. c. 32.

Antithesis est 1) Socinianorum, statuentium, baptismum esse ritum mere arbitrarium, usurpatum ab Apostolis circa primordia ecclesiae, hodie non amplius necessarium. 2) Pontificiorum plerumque, statuentium, infantes non-baptizatos exclusos esse regno caelorum, & pati poenam damni, non sensus.

Sociniani argumentantur: I. Quidquid non annumeratur rudimentis doctrinae caelestis, illud Christianis non est necessarium: Baptismus aquae non annumeratur &c. E. Minor prob. ex Hebr. VI, 2. vbi mentio fit βαπτισμῶν διδαχῆς, non τοῦ ὕδατος. Resp. Apostolus intelligit baptismum proprie dictum, de quo catechumeni erant informandi . Loquitur autem in plurali, vt indicet, doctrinam de baptismis ita posse institui, vt inculcetur catechumenis, magnam esse differentiam inter baptismos caerimoniales veteris testamenti, & inter baptismum sacramentalem noui testamenti. Iudaeos namque varia habuisse baptisata caeremonialia, discimus ex Hebr. IX, 10.

II. Si Ioannes baptizauit aqua, Christus autem Spiritu & igne, sequitur, quod in hodierna ecclesia Christi nemo necessario baptizandus sit aqua. Antecedens est verum, teste Ioanne, Luc. III, 17. E. & consequens. Resp. L. c. intelligitur baptismus flaminis, qui non tollit baptismum fluminis.

III. Apostoli non leguntur baptizati: E. Baptismus non est necessarius. Resp. In historicis ab argumento negativo, siue potius a silentio, non firma ducitur consequentia. Neque enim sequitur: Non legimus, Apostolos esse baptizatos: E. non fuerunt baptizati. Si omnia scripta essent, mundus molem librorum capere non potuisset, Io. XXI, 25.

IV. Quaecunque doctrina tota spiritualis est, & interiorem respicit hominem, illa non praescribit ritum externum baptismi necessario obseruandum: Atqui doctrina euangelica noui testamenti &c. Ergo. Minor probatur ex 2 Cor. III, 6. Deus nos idoneos fecit ministros noui testamenti, non littera, sed spiritus, vbi doctrina noui test. vocatur spiritus, i. e. spiritualis. Resp. 1) Neg. mai. Nam doctrina spiritualis non simpliciter excludit externos ritus, ceteraqui excluderet etiam ritum externum coenae domini, quod est absurdum. 2) Baptismus non est ritus mere externus, sed est lauacrum regenerationis & renouationis Spiritus S. qui in nos opulenter effunditur, Tit. III, 5.

Pontificii argumentantur: I. Quicunque non est renatus ex aqua & Spiritu, is non introibit in regnum caelorum, Io. III, 5. Infantes ἀβάπτιστοι &c. Ergo. Resp. Lim. maiorem; Quicunque contemtor baptismi non est renatus ex aqua & Spiritu, ille non introibit in regnum caelorum; concedo: At infantes fidelium, vel extincti in vtero materno, vel subita morte rapti ante baptismum, non sunt contemtores baptismi. Sunt quidem ἀβάπτιστοι negatiue, sed non priuatiue tales. Mortui in vtero matris non debuerunt baptizari: subito autem fato ante susceptum baptismum defuncti non potuerunt sacro lauacro tingi. E. non sunt ἀβάπτιστοι priuatiue tales, adeoque ab ingressu in caelum non exclusi.

II. Qui non credunt, damnantur: Infantes ἀβάπτιστοι non credunt: Ergo. Minor probatur: quia in infantibus non-baptizatis neque per sacramentum baptismi, neque per praedicapradicationem evangelii fides est accensa. Resp. Deus in infantibus fidelium modo extraordinario fidem accendit.

III. Infantes fidelium ἀβάπτιστοι sunt in peccato originali concepti, cuius remissionem non sunt consecuti: E. non sunt consortes aeternae salutis.

Resp: Remissionem peccatorum infantibus non-baptizatis Christus merito suo acquisivit, quam fide extraordinarie accensa sibi applicant.


### Q. XX. Is baptism to be repeated?

Baptism performed rightly ought not to be repeated.

Proof 1) Because in baptism God establishes a covenant with us, which is not momentary or temporary, but eternal and irrevocable [ἀμεταμέλητον].

2) Just as circumcision could not be repeated: so neither can baptism.

3) As natural generation is one, so is spiritual regeneration.

4) Baptism is a sacrament of initiation and spiritual investiture. Now, in truth, there is need for initiation and entry into the church only once.

Latin:

Baptismus rite peractus non debet repeti.

Prob. 1) Quia in baptismo Deus nobiscum sancit foedus, quod non est momentaneum aut temporarium, sed aeternum & ἀμεταμέλητον .

2) Sicut circumcisio non potuit repeti: ita nec baptismus.

3) Vt generatio naturalis, ita spiritualis regeneratio una est, .

4) Baptismus est sacramentum initiationis & spiritualis investitura. Iam vero semel tantum opus est initiatione, & ingressu in ecclesiam.


### Q. XXI. Is baptism twofold, internal & external?

There is not given by the very act and time a twofold baptism, internal and external baptism, but baptism is one, and by one and an undivided action the Holy Trinity, as the principal cause, and the minister of the church, as the ministerial cause, dispense in baptism, by means of the exterior washing of water, to those who do not resist the divine operation, the remission of sins and renewal by virtue of divine institution.

Proof 1) From "One Lord, one faith, one baptism." As truly as there is only one Lord and one faith, so truly is there only one baptism: But those are monadic, so that they cannot be doubled: Therefore, neither can baptism be doubled.

2) From the nature of baptism, inasmuch as it consists of water and the Spirit. Whoever’s baptism is true and complete, that consists of water and the Spirit: But external baptism separated from internal does not consist of water and the Spirit: Therefore, external baptism, separated from internal, is not a true and complete baptism.

3) From the subordination of the minister. Baptism is dispensed by God as the principal cause, to whom the baptizing minister is subordinated: Therefore, it is one and an individual act, which God dispenses through the minister.

You say I. Whoever distinguishes baptism, which washes away the filth of the body, from the baptism of the conscience, he establishes a double baptism, one external, the other internal. But St. Peter, etc. Therefore. Resp. St. Peter denies that the putting away of the filth of the flesh is baptism; on the contrary, he affirms that baptism is the interrogation of a good conscience, in that it washes away the filth of the soul, or confers the remission of sins, from which arises a good and tranquil conscience.

You say II. If external and internal baptism could not be separated, all the baptized would be regenerated: But not all the baptized are regenerated, which is evident from the example of Simon Magus. Therefore. Resp. Distinguish between the offering of regenerating grace and the conferring of it. God offers regenerating grace, by which faith is kindled, to all, but confers it only upon those who do not resist: the reason is that regeneration is not an irresistible action, but a resistible one. Although, therefore, God intends to regenerate all the baptized, yet because of malicious resistance [malicious resistance, malicious resistance] gnancy of adult humans it happens that not all are actually regenerated; infants, however, since they do not place a malicious obstacle before the Holy Spirit, are all truly regenerated through baptism.

Latin:

Non datur actu ipso & tempore baptismus duplex, baptismus internus & externus, sed baptismus est unus, unaque ac indivisa actione dispensat in baptismo & SS. Trinitas, ceu causa principalis, & minister ecclesiae, ceu ministerialis causa, mediante exteriori lavacro aquae, illis, qui divinae non resistunt operationi, remissionem peccatorum, & renovationem vi institutionis divinae.

Prob. 1) Ex Vnus dominus, una fides, unum baptisma. Quam vere unus tantum est Dominus & una fides, tam vere unus tantum est baptismus: Sed illa sunt monadica, ut non possint geminari: Ergo nec baptismus geminari potest.

2) Ex natura baptifini, quippe qui constat ex aqua & Spiritu . Quicunque baptismus est verus & integer, ille constat ex aqua & Spiritu: Sed baptismus externus separatus ab interno, non constat ex aqua & Spiritu: E. baptismus externus, separatus ab interno, non est verus & integer baptismus.

3) A subordinatione ministri. Baptismus dispensatur a Deo ceu causa principali, cui subordinatur minister baptizans: Proinde unus & individuus actus est, quem dispensat Deus per ministrum.

Dicis I. Quicunque baptismum, abluentem sordes corporis, a baptismo conscientiae distinguit, ille statuit duplicem baptismum, alium externum, alium internum. Atqui S. Petrus &c. . Ergo. Resp. S. Petrus negat, depositionem sordium carnis esse baptismum; contra affirmat, baptismum esse interrogationem bonae conscientiae, eo, quod abluit sordes animae, sive confert remissionem peccatorum, ex qua oritur bona & tranquilla conscientia.

Dicis II. Si baptismus externus & internus non possent separari, omnes baptizati regenerarentur: Sed non omnes baptizati regenerantur, quod constat exemplo Simonis Magi, . Ergo. Resp. Dist. inter gratiae regenerantis oblationem, & collationem. Deus gratiam regenerantem, qua fides accenditur, omnibus offert, solis autem non resistentibus confert: ratio est, quia regeneratio non est actio irresistibilis, sed resistibilis. Quamvis itaque Deus intendat, omnes baptizatos regenerare, ob malitiosam tamen repugnantiam malitiosam tamen repugnantiam malitiosam tamen repugnantiam gnantiam hominum adultorum evenit, ut non omnes actu regenerentur; infantes autem, cum non ponant Spiritui S. malitiosum obicem, omnes per baptismum vere regenerantur.


### Q. XXII. Can the exorcism, which is accustomed to be placed before baptism, be tolerated in the church?

The exorcism, which in our churches is accustomed to be placed before baptism, is a Christian Exorcism, and indifferent, and thus it is not retained in vain for the purpose of shadowing forth the spiritual dominion of the devil over the unregenerate, and the salutary effect of baptism, by which they are liberated from the same. Obs.

I. We are not speaking at present of the miraculous exorcism, by which at the beginnings of the apostolic church some cast out devils from the possessed, but of the exorcism shadowing forth the efficacy of baptism. Obs.

II. A distinction must be made between an exorcism that is σημαντικὸν, or significative, and ἐνεργητικὸν, or effective. The Papists ascribe to exorcism the power of expelling the devil from those corporally possessed: We, however, assert that by exorcism it is only signified or shadowed forth the tyranny and dominion of the devil, which he exercises over the unregenerate: which dominion of the devil over the unregenerate is called by some authors in a broader sense spiritual obsession, who nevertheless confess that the subject of spiritual obsession, strictly and properly so called, is a man who is stubbornly and contumaciously impious. From which it follows that the infants of believers, strictly and properly speaking, are not spiritually obsessed. Obs.

III. Exorcism is retained by us not from the necessity of a precept or as a means; since exorcism is neither divinely commanded, nor a means of salvation, nor a part of religious worship; but from Christian liberty: because it is a certain adiaphoron, and a free ceremony, neither commanded nor prohibited. Obs.

Obs. IV. Ἐξορκίζειν, and ὁρκίζειν means a) to exact an oath from someone; b) to command, to order, or to impose something upon someone, by the authority of God the supreme judge, or by the threat of divine judgment, e.g. 1 Sam. XIV, 24. Saul is said to have adjured the people, that no one should take food before evening, before he had taken vengeance on his enemies, i.e. he had commanded the people under the most grave threat of divine judgment. Thus Paul writes, 1 Thess. V, 27. ὁρκίζω ὑμᾶς τὸν Κύριον, I adjure you by the Lord. to read this epistle to all the holy brethren, i.e. I command you by the authority of the Lord. In the latter sense it is taken at present, and thus the minister of the divine word adjures the devil, i.e. he commands the devil, by the authority of the Triune God, and under the threat of the most just divine judgment, that he should let the one to be baptized go, and should not claim for himself any right or power over him, but should leave room for the divine operation.

The assertion is proved: 1) The significative exorcism, which in our churches is placed before baptism, signifies and shadows forth: a) The state of sin, in which we are constituted outside the state of regeneration, which is done through baptism; that we are by nature children of wrath, and under the power, captivity, and dominion of the devil, b) The efficacy of baptism, that now such a one, who is to be offered to Christ in baptism, by the power of Christ's institution and the divine promise, is to be liberated from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of Christ the redeemer: c) The stipulation, that these things are to be performed to God alone, and that one must renounce the devil and his works in opposition. From which arises the argument: That rite which shadows forth both the state of sin, in which infants are conceived and born, and the efficacy of baptism, and the stipulation to be performed to God, is usefully retained in the church by Christian liberty: But the exorcism, which in our churches is placed before baptism, is such a rite, &c. Therefore.

2) Exorcism is a most ancient Christian rite, used in the church in the times of Cyprian, who lived in the 3rd century, as is evident from his

L. IV. Ep. VII. The following doubts may be raised against this ceremony:

I. Whoever demands an oath from the devil acts wrongly: But Lutherans, etc., do so. Therefore. The major is evident; because an oath is not to be demanded from the devil, a most lying impostor. The minor is manifest: since Lutheran pastors adjure the devil. Resp. The prelates of the Lutheran church do not demand an oath from the devil, but they command him by authority and under the threat of divine judgment, that he should let the one to be baptized go, and leave the place to the Holy Spirit working through baptism.

II. Whoever is not possessed by the devil, neither corporally nor spiritually, from them the devil is not to be cast out: But the infants of the faithful, etc. Therefore. Resp. This argument does not strike us; because a) we deny that the infants of the faithful are corporally possessed by the devil. b) Spiritual obsession, however, is spoken of either broadly or strictly. In the stricter sense, it denotes the indwelling and operation of the devil in a man who is stubbornly and contumaciously impious: In which sense we deny that the infants of the faithful are spiritually possessed by the devil. In the broader sense, however, spiritual obsession denotes power and dominion over an unregenerate man: In which broader sense, by some authors, the infants of the faithful, not yet reborn through baptism, are said to be spiritually obsessed by the devil. c) Lutherans do not cast the devil out of infants by exorcism; since their exorcism is not effective, but significative and adumbrative of sin, the power of the devil, and the efficacy of baptism.

III. Why then do the baptizers say, Daß du ausfahrest und weichest ? Resp. These words are understood regarding abstinence from dominion, as if the baptizers were saying: Satan, do not claim for yourself power or dominion over this infant; seeing that he will now be snatched from your kingdom of darkness and brought into the kingdom of Christ through baptism.

IV. Whoever is called a servant of Christ does not need exorcism: The infant to be baptized is called a servant of Christ by the baptizer: Therefore. Resp. He is called a servant of Christ not in state, but by anticipation, just as one who is to be girded is held as girded.

V. Whoever are holy from the maternal womb in the divine covenant, they do not need exorcism: The infants of Christians, etc. Therefore. The minor is clear from the testimony of Paul, 1 Cor. VII, 14. Compare Acts II, 39. Resp. 1) The infants of Christians before receiving baptism are holy with an external holiness, or that of the church: but they are not holy with an internal holiness, or that of faith; since they are not yet reborn.

2) The promise of the covenant pertains to the unbaptized infants of the faithful, but they are not yet in the exhibited and applied covenant; for application is made through baptism.

VI. Whatever belongs solely to Christ, that cannot be attributed to exorcism: To liberate from the power of Satan, etc. 1 John III, 8. Therefore.

Resp. Distinguish between the acquisition of spiritual liberation and its application. Christ by His merit acquired for us freedom from enemies, which He applies to us through the Word and sacraments; by exorcism the same is signified and adumbrated.

VII. Exorcists fare badly, Acts XIX, 14. 15.

Resp. Infidel exorcists, who attempt to use effective and therefore miraculous exorcism in the name of Jesus, fare badly: But evangelical doctors truly believe in Christ, and their exorcism is not ἐνεργητικὸς [effective], but σημαντικός [significative].

VIII. Exorcism has neither a divine command nor a promise: Therefore it is not to be tolerated in the church. Resp.

If exorcism had a divine command and promise, it would not be an indifferent rite, but would be a necessary part of religious worship. We use exorcism as an adiaphoron, out of Christian liberty.

VIII. What is Christian. VIII. What VIII. Whatever tends to the contempt of matrimony, that is to be removed by the church: Exorcism etc. Therefore.

The minor is proven; because it results in the contempt of matrimony, if it be said that spouses beget children possessed by the devil. Resp. We do not maintain that the infants of Christians are corporally possessed by the devil. But as for the spiritual dominion of Satan concerning the unregenerate, that cannot be denied by Christian parents, no less than the propagation of sin itself. The infants of Christians are gifts of God, but before they are brought into the divine covenant through baptism, they are in a state of sin and under the power of Satan.

X. It cannot be denied that the sound of the words of exorcism is rather harsh: and therefore this rite is to be abrogated.

Resp. The sense of the words is more convenient, although the sound may be harsher. This rite, since it is an adiaphoron, can be abrogated with the consent of the church, provided it be done without prejudice to the heavenly doctrine concerning the state of sin and the efficacy of baptism. It can also be converted into a formula of prayer, or even be proposed and explained in words more agreeable to scripture.

Compare D. CHEMNITII loc. theol. P. III. fol. 161. & D. CALOVII synops. controu. p. 785.

SIGH.

But if, O God, best in holiness, greatest in virtue, most blessed in life, I were to bury in oblivion or dissimulate your benefits, most wisely instituted from baptism and bestowed upon me, overflowing in me, I would be a most wicked impious man. But rather, with a grateful mind I venerate and with a full mouth I praise your mercy most inclined toward me, that you have deigned to sprinkle, wash, regenerate, and renew me, infected with the stain of congenital sin, with the sacred water. By the intervention of this saving bath I have become, O most indulgent Father, a partner of your covenant, a son of grace, a brother of Christ, a temple of the Holy Spirit, a citizen of the church, an heir of heaven. In every fall, in every temptation, in the very article of death, no consolation will be more present, sweeter, or more solid to me than the remembrance of baptism. Strengthen me, I beseech you, with power, that I may continually reflect upon my baptismal covenant, commit nothing unworthy of it, crucify the concupiscences of the old Adam, and walk in newness of life!

Latin:

Exorcismus, qui in ecclesiis nostris baptismo praemitti solet, est christianus Exorcismus, & indifferens, atque adeo ad adumbrandum spirituale diaboli in non-renatos dominium, & salutarem baptismi, quo ab eodem liberantur, effectum, haud ex vano retinetur.

Obs. I. Non est nobis in praesenti sermo de exorcismo miraculoso, quo circa primordia ecclesiae apostolicae nonnulli ex obsessis diabolos eiiciebant, sed de exorcismo adumbrativo efficaciae baptismi.

Obs. II. Distinguendum est inter exorcismum σημαντικὸν, sive significativum, & ἐνεργητικὸν, sive effectivum. Pontificii adscribunt exorcismo vim expellendi diabolum a corporaliter obsessis: Nos autem afferimus, exorcismo tantum significari, vel adumbrari tyrannidem & dominium diaboli, quod ille exercet in non-renatos: quod dominium diaboli in non-renatos a nonnullis auctoribus sensu latiori dicitur obsessio spiritualis, qui tamen fatentur, spiritualis obsessionis, stricte & proprie dictae, subiectum esse hominem praefracte & contumaciter impium. Ex quo consequitur, infantes fidelium, stricte & proprie loquendo, non esse spiritualiter obsessos.

Obs. III. Retinetur a nobis exorcismus non ex necessitate praecepti, aut medii; siquidem exorcismus neque divinitus mandatus est, neque medium salutis, neque pars cultus religiosi; sed ex libertate christiana: quia est quoddam adiaphoron, & libera caerimonia, neque praecepta, neque prohibita.

Obs. IV. Ἐξορκίζειν, & ὁρκίζειν significat a) iuramentum ab aliquo exigere; b) praecipere, imperare, vel imponere alicui aliquid, auctoritate Dei summi iudicis, vel comminatione iudicii diuini, v. gr. 1 Sam. XIV, 24. Saul dicitur adiurasse populum, ne quis ante vesperam cibum capiat, priusquam de hostibus vindictam sumserit, i. e. sub grauissima comminatione iudicii diuini populo praecepisse. Sic Paullus scribit, 1 Thess. V, 27. ὁρκίζω ὑμᾶς τὸν Κύριον, adiuro vos per Dominum. legi hanc epistolam, omnibus sanctis fratribus, i. e. praecipio vobis auctoritate Domini. Posteriori sensu in praesenti accipitur, adeoque minister verbi diuini diabolum adiurat, i. e. praecipit diabolo, auctoritate Dei triunius, & sub comminatione iustissimi iudicii diuini, ut missum faciat baptizandum, neque vullum ius aut potestatem in ipsum sibi vindicet, sed locum relinquat operationi diuinae.

Probatur assertum: 1) Exorcismus significativus, qui in nostris ecclesiis baptismo praemittitur, significat & adumbrat: a) Statum peccati, in quo constituti sumus extra statum regenerationis, quae fit per baptismum; quod simus natura filii irae, & sub potestate, captiuitate & dominio diaboli, b) Efficaciam baptismi, quod iam talis, qui Christo offerendus est in baptismo, vi institutionis Christi & promissionis diuinae, fit liberandus ex potestate tenebrarum & transferendus in regnum Christi redemptoris: c) Stipulationem, quod haec soli Deo praestanda, & renuntiandum fit ex aduerso diabolo, eiusque operibus. E quibus nascitur argumentum: Qui ritus adumbrat tum statum peccati, in quo concipiuntur & nascuntur infantes, tum efficaciam baptismi, tum stipulationem, Deo praestandam, ille ex libertate Christiana in ecclesia utiliter retinetur: Atqui exorcismus, qui in ecclesiis nostris baptismo praemittitur, est eiusmodi ritus, &c. Ergo.

2) Exorcismus est ritus christianus antiquissimus, temporibus Cypriani, qui vixit saeculo III, in ecclesia vsitatus, vti patet ex ipsius L. IV. Ep. VII.

Dubia sequentia moueri possunt aduersus hanc caerimoniam:

I. Quicunque a diabolo exigunt iuramentum, perperam faciunt: Atqui Lutherani &c. Ergo. Maior est euidens; quia a diabolo impostore mendacissimo non est exigendum iuramentum. Minor est manifesta: quoniam pastores Lutherani diabolum adiurant. Resp. Antistites ecclesiae Lutheranae non exigunt iuramentum a diabolo, sed ipsi praecipiunt auctoritate & sub comminatione iudicii diuini, vt missum faciat baptizandum, & locum relinquat Spiritui S. per baptismum operanti.

II. Quicunque a diabolo non sunt obsessi, neque corporaliter, neque spiritualiter, ex illis diabolus non est eiiciendus: Atqui infantes fidelium &c. E. Resp. Argumentum hoc nos non ferit; propterea, quod a) negamus, infantes fidelium a diabolo esse corporaliter obsessos. b) Obsessio autem spiritualis dicitur vel late, vel stricte. Sensu strictiori notat inhabitationem & operationem diaboli in homine praefracte & contumaciter impio: Quo sensu negamus, infantes fidelium esse a diabolo spiritualiter obsessos. Sensu autem latiori obsessio spiritualis notat potestatem & dominium in hominem irregenitum: Quo sensu latiori a nonnullis auctoribus infantes fidelium, per baptismum nondum renati, a diabolo spiritualiter obsideri dicuntur. c) Lutherani per exorcismum diabolum non eiiciunt ex infantibus; siquidem illorum exorcismus non est effectiuus, sed significatiuus & adumbratiuus peccati, potestatis diaboli, & efficaciae baptismi.

III. Quare igitur baptistae dicunt, Daß du ausfahrest und weichest? Resp. Hae verba intelliguntur de abstinentia a dominio, quasi dicant baptistae: Satana, ne vindices tibi potestatem, aut dominium in hunc infantem; quippe qui per baptismum iamiam tuo regno tenebrarum eripietur, & regno Christi inferetur.

IV. Quicunque dicitur seruus Christi, non indiget exorcismo: Infans baptizandus a baptista dicitur seruus Christi: E, Resp. Dicitur seruus Christi non in statu, sed ampliatione, sicut cingendus habetur pro cincto.

V. Quicunque ab vtero materno sunt sancti in foedere diuino, illi non indigent exorcismo: Infantes christianorum &c. Ergo. Minor claret testimonio Pauli, 1 Cor. VII, 14. Confer. Act. II, 39. Resp. 1) Infantes christianorum ante susceptum baptismum sunt sancti sanctitate externa, siue ecclesiae: at non sunt sancti sanctitate interna, siue fidei; quoniam nondum sunt renati.

2) Pertinet ad infantes fidelium non-baptizatos promissio foederis, sed nondum sunt in foedere exhibito & applicato; applicatio enim fit per baptismum.

VI. Quidquid soli competit Christo, illud neque exorcismo potest tribui: Liberare a potestate Satanae &c. 1 Io. III, 8. Ergo. Resp. Dist. inter liberationis spiritualis acquisitionem, & applicationem.

Christus merito suo nobis libertatem ab hostibus acquisiuit, quam per verbum & sacramenta nobis applicat; per exorcismum eadem significatur & adumbratur.

VII. Exorcistae male audiunt, Act. XIX, 14.

15. Resp. Exorcistae infideles, qui conantur in nomine Iesu vti exorcismo effectiuo, eoque miraculoso, male audiunt: At doctores euangelici in Christum vere credunt, eorumque exorcismus non ἐνεργητικὸς est, sed σημαντικός.

VIII. Exorcismus neque habet mandatum, neque promissionem diuinam: Ergo non est tolerandus in ecclesia. Resp.

Si haberet exorcismus mandatum & promissionem diuinam, non esset ritus indifferens, sed esset pars cultus religiosi necessaria. Nos vtimur exorcismo, tanquam adiaphoro, ex libertate christiana. christiana.

VIII. Quid christiana. VIII. Quid VIII. Quidquid vergit in contemptum matrimonii, illud ab ecclesia est removendum: Exorcismus &c. Ergo.

Minor probatur; quia cedit in contemptum matrimonii, si dicantur coniuges gignere liberos, a diabolo obsessos. Resp. Non statuimus, infantes Christianorum a diabolo corporaliter esse obsessos. Quod vero spirituale dominium Satanae in irregenitos concernit, illud non minus, quam ipsa peccati propagatio, a christianis parentibus negari nequit. Sunt infantes Christianorum dona Dei, sed antequam per baptismum foederi divino inferuntur, sunt in statu peccati & sub potestate Satanae.

X. Negari non potest, sonum verborum exorcismi esse asperiorem: ideoque abrogandus est hic ritus.

Resp. Sensus verborum est commodior, licet sonus sit asperior. Ritus hic, cum sit adiaphorus, abrogari potest consentiente ecclesia, modo fiat citra praeiudicium doctrinae coelestis, de statu peccati & efficacia baptismi. Potest etiam converti in formulam precationis, vel etiam verbis scripturae magis consentaneis proponi & explicari.

Confer. D. CHEMNITII loc. theol. P. III. fol. 161. & D. CALOVII synops. controu. p. 785.

SVSPIRIVM.

Quod si; o Deus, sanctitate optime, virtute maxime, vita beatissime, beneficia tua, e baptismo sapientissime instituto, & mihi collato, in me redundantia, oblivione sepelirem, aut dissimularem, profligatissime impius forem. Quin potius & grata mente veneror & pleno ore collaudo misericordiam tuam in me propensissimam, me, congeniti peccati labe infectum, sacro latice perfundere, abluere, regenerare, renovare dignatus sis. Interuentu salutaris huius lauacri factus sum, o Pater indulgentissime, consors foederis tui, filius gratiae, frater Christi, templum Spiritus S. ciuis ecclesiae, heres caeli. In omni lapsu, in omni tentatione, in ipso mortis articulo, nulla consolatio recordatione baptismi mihi erit praesentior, dulcior, solidior. Validis, quaeso, me viribus in-brae, ut foedus meum baptismale subinde recogitem, nihil ipso indignum committam, veteris Adami concupiscentias crucifigam, & in nouitate vitae ambulem!


## 32 On the Eucharist, or the Lord's Supper


### Of the Eucharist, or the Lord's Supper

Quest. I. What is the eucharist, or the Lord's supper? The Eucharist is a sacrament of the N. T., or a sacred and solemn action; instituted by Christ the God-man (θεανθρώπῳ), in which the true and substantial body of Christ, to be eaten with the blessed bread, and the true and substantial blood of the same, to be drunk with the blessed wine, is given to communicating Christians, and both are received by them, and in a supernatural manner are eaten and drunk, in commemoration of the death of Christ, and for the confirmation of evangelical grace.

Obj. I. Just as baptism is the sacrament of initiation, and as it were the gate of grace, through which we enter into the kingdom of God; so the Lord's supper is the sacrament of confirmation, and as it were the food and medicine by which the faithful soul is refreshed, and is confirmed in faith and in the hope of eternal life. Obj. II. This sacrament of confirmation is distinguished by various names. 1) The most ancient church, and especially the Greek, called it eucharist (εὐχαριστίαν), i. e. thanksgiving; because Christ [gave] thanks (εὐχαρι-)

having given thanks, Matt. XXVI, 27. He instituted this sacrament, and we ought to announce the death of the Lord, 1 Cor. XI, 26, with thanksgiving. For just as our redemption and salvation through the passion and death of Christ is the greatest of all benefits, so also the greatest thanks are to be given to God and our Savior when, in the reception of the body and blood of Christ, we celebrate His solemn memorial. 2) It is called εὐλογία, or blessing, likewise from the words of institution, Matt. XXVI, 26. Jesus took bread, καὶ εὐλογήσας, and having blessed it, He broke it, and gave it to the disciples, etc. Whence also the cup is called τῆς εὐλογίας, 1 Cor. X, 16, because the external symbols (bread and wine) are blessed, i.e., consecrated, and unless they are blessed, they are not exhibitive of the Lord’s body and blood.

3) It is named κυριακὸν δεῖπνον, the Lord’s Supper, 1 Cor. XI, 20. The Greek, δεῖπνον, denoted a banquet to the ancient Greeks, whether it was instituted at midday or in the evening.

See HOMER, Iliad. B. Whence it is called by TERTULLIAN the Lord’s banquet, book 1 to his wife. Interpreters have rendered it cœna [supper]; the Germans, des Herrn Nachtmahl , des Herrn Abendmahl , because our Lord Jesus Christ, on that night in which He was betrayed, took bread, and the cup likewise, after He had supped, when He instituted this sacred banquet.

Although we ordinarily celebrate the Eucharist in the morning and fasting, we commonly call it the Holy Supper; either in honor of the first institution, performed in the evening at the beginning of the night, or because it is made κοινή, whence it is called cœna by the Latins, because the ancients ate lunch alone, but had the cœna [supper] with guests as a κοινήν, i.e., a common meal: Thus the Eucharist in public sacred rites, although it is performed in the morning, is nevertheless a cœna , i.e., to many a κοινή, a common meal. 4) It is called τράπεζα τοῦ Κυρίου, the table of the Lord, 1 Cor. X, 21, because in the time of the Apostles it was celebrated at a table. The Greeks used two tables in the Eucharist; one they called the table of the προθέσεως, of proposition, on which the bread and wine were placed before consecration; the other they called ἱερατεῖον, the sanctuary, where the consecration took place. Cf. METROPHANES, Confess. Orient. c. IX, on the Lord’s Supper.

5) It is called ἀρτοκλασία, the breaking of bread, because Christ, blessing it, broke the bread, Matt. XXVI, 26. Cf. 1 Cor. X, 16. 6) It is called ἡ κοινωνία, communion; because 1) the blessed bread is the communion of the body, and the blessed cup is the communion of the blood of Christ, and 2) by means of this communion we are joined with Christ and among ourselves by a closer faith and love.

Hence those who approach the sacrament are called communicants, from 1 Cor. X, 17. 7) Καινὴ διαθήκη, the new testament; because Christ, offering the blessed cup, said: This cup is the new testament in my blood, Luke XXII, 20, i.e., this, which is in the cup, is the foundation and support of the new covenant of grace sanctioned in my blood.

Therefore, the testator is Christ, sealing the testament with His death; the heirs, all believers; the witnesses, the Apostles; the notaries, the Evangelists and Paul; the good legacy, the golden key to the kingdom of heaven and the heavenly treasures; the seal, the body of Christ in the bread, the blood in the wine. 8) It is called σύναξις, a gathering or congregation, having respect to the sacred assemblies in which it is accustomed to be celebrated. Cf. 1 Cor.

XI, 20. 9) Λειτουργία, which word, taken generally, denotes the administration of a public office; taken specifically, it designates the sacred and solemn action by which the body of Christ is dispensed to be eaten by means of the bread, and the blood of Christ to be drunk by means of the wine. 10) ’Αγάπη, charity. For in the primitive church, the more affluent brought bread and wine to the table of the Lord, so that a part might be used for the sacrament, and whatever remained would go to the ministers of the church and the poor.

This was a sign of charity; hence the Holy Supper was called ἀγάπη, charity. 11) Θυσία καὶ προσφορά, sacrifice and oblation, not by reason of a sacrificial act, as if the priest were sacrificing: but partly by reason of the matter, because that which was once sacrificed on the cross is distributed; partly by reason of the end, because the sacrament of the Supper is dispensed and received in commemoration of the sacrifice once performed on the cross. 12) Μυστήριον, and with the addition Φρικτόν, Φρικῶδες, Φρικοδέστατον μυστήριον, a tremendous mystery. JUSTIN, Apol. II, for the Christians. CHRYSOSTOM, Homily 38 on Matthew. For the Eucharist is an admirable mystery: a) because it was revealed by God alone, b) on account of the mode of union between the heavenly and earthly thing, which is not merely significative, or that the earthly thing signifies the heavenly, but is a real exhibition, through which the heavenly thing is communicated to those eating and consuming no less than the earthly thing: c) on account of the mode of the presence of the body and blood of Christ, which is substantial and real, not virtual, not objective, or intentional: d) on account of the mode of union with us, by which the heavenly things, the body and blood of Christ, are more closely united with the faithful communicants in the sacrament than outside the sacrament. Cf. HULSEM. Brev. c. XIII. p. 819.

13) The Mass, the abuse of which name is very frequent in the papacy, where they make the hearing of mass the beginning and end of their sacred rites; and what is more well-known than the sacrifice of the mass? The word "missa" (mass) has a Latin origin, and is so called from the dismissal of the people. However, as CASAUBON explains, there was a twofold ἄφεσις (aphesis), dismissal, or missa: the former, when, with the readings of Holy Scripture and those prayers finished, in which catechumens, energumens, and others not initiated could participate, the deacon would cry out: "Go, catechumens, in peace: it is the dismissal!" (i.e., you shall have dismissal, for it was not permitted to witness the sacred liturgy); the latter, when the sacred rites were performed and the celebration of the Eucharist finished, after the εὐχὴν ἀπολυτικήν (euchēn apolytikēn), i.e., the dismissal prayer, the deacon, toward the end of all the sacred rites, would cry out again: "Go, faithful, in peace! it is the dismissal!" i.e., now you also are dismissed, so that everyone has the free power of departing.

14) Today it is called the sacrament of the altar. For when Christian temples were built under Constantine the Great, stone tables were erected and called altars, which we still freely use in the public administration of the Eucharist. *

Latin:

Quæst. I. Quid est eucharistia, siue cœna domini? Eucharistia est sacramentum N. T., siue sacra & solemnis actio; a Christo θεανθρώπῳ instituta, in qua verum & substantiale corpus Christi, cum pane benedicto manducandum, verusque & substantialis ipsius sanguis, cum vino benedicto bibendus, datur communicantibus Christianis, & vtrumque ab his accipitur, modoque supernaturali editur & bibitur, in commemorationem mortis Christi, & gratiae euangelicae confirmationem.

Obs. I. Sicut baptismus est sacramentum initiationis, & quasi porta gratiae, per quam in regnum Dei intramus; ita cœna Domini est sacramentum confirmationis, & quasi alimentum & pharmacum, quo fidelis anima reficitur, & in fide atque spe aeternae vitae confirmatur. Obs. II. Hoc sacramentum confirmationis variis insignitur nominibus. 1) Ecclesia antiquissima, & inprimis graeca, vocauit εὐχαριστίαν, i. e. gratiarum actionem; quia Christus εὐχαρι-

εὐχαριστήσας, Matth. XXVI, 27. hoc sacramentum instituit, & nos mortem Domini, 1 Cor. XI, 26. cum gratiarum actione annuntiare debemus. Sicut enim beneficiorum omnium maximum est redemptio nostra & salvatio, per passionem & mortem Christi: Sic gratiæ etiam maximæ Deo & Salvatori nostræ agendæ sunt, quando in sumtione corporis & sanguinis Christi solemnem eius memoriam celebramus. 2) Appellatur εὐλογία, sive benedictio, itidem ex verbis institutionis, Matth. XXVI, 26. Accepit Iesus panem, καὶ εὐλογήσας, & cum benedixisset, fregit, deditque discipulis &c. Vnde etiam calix τῆς εὐλογίας dicitur, 1 Cor. X, 16. quia symbola externa (panis & vinum) benedicuntur, i. e. consecrantur, & nisi benedicantur, corporis & sanguinis dominici exhibitiva non sunt.

3) Nominatur κυριακὸν δεῖπνον, cœna dominica, 1 Cor. XI, 20. Græcum, δεῖπνον, priscis Græcis denotabat convivium, sive meridiano, sive vespertino tempore institueretur.

Vid. HOMER. Iliad. B. Vnde a TERTULLIANO vocatur convivium dominicum, libr. 1. ad uxor. Interpretes reddiderunt cœnam; Germani, des Herrn Nachtmahl, des Herrn Abendmahl, quia D. N. I. C. in ea nocte, qua tradebatur, accepit panem, & calicem similiter, postquam cœnavit, cum sacrum hoc convivium institueret.

Nos licet mane & ieiuni eucharistiam ordinarie celebremus, communiter tamen S. cœnam vocamus; vel in honorem primæ institutionis, vesperi sub noctis initium peractæ, vel quod fit κοινή, unde cœna latinis dicta, quia veteres foli prandebant, cœnam cum convivis κοινήν, h. e. communem habebant: Sic eucharistia in sacris publicis, licet mane peragatur, est tamen cœna, h. e. multis κοινή, communis. 4) Dicitur τράπεζα τῦ Κυρίο, mensa Domini, 1 Cor. X, 21. quia tempore Apostolorum in mensa celebrabatur. Græci in eucharistia duas adhibebant mensas, alteram vocabant mensam προθέσεως, propositionis, in qua panis & vinum reposita erant ante consecrationem; alteram appellabant ἱερατεῖον, sacrarium, ubi fiebat consecratio. Conf. METROPHANIS confeff. orient. c. IX. de cœna domini.

5) Vocatur ἀρτοκλασία, panifragium, quia Christus benedicens, panem fregit, Matth. XXVII, 26. Conf. 1 Cor. X, 16. 6) Appellatur ἡ κοινωνία, communio; quia 1) panis benedictus est communio corporis, & calix benedictus est communio sanguinis Christi, & 2) mediante hac communione nos cum Christo inter nos arctiori fide & amore coniungimur.

Hinc qui ad sacramentum accedunt, adhuc communicantes audiunt, ex 1 Cor. X, 17. 7) Καινὴ διαθήκη, novum testamentum; quia Christus porrigens calicem benedictum aiebat: Hic calix novum testamentum est in meo sanguine, Luc. XXII, 20. i. e. hoc, quod est in calice, fundamentum & firmamentum est noui gratiæ fœderis in sanguine meo sanciti.

Est itaque testator, Christus, morte sua testamentum obsignans; heredes, omnes credentes; testes, Apostoli; notarii, Evangelistæ & Paullus; bonum legatum, clauis aurea ad regnum cœlorum & thesauros cœlestes; sigillum, corpus Christi in pane, sanguis in vino. 8) Dicitur σύναξις, conuentus vel congregatio, habito respectu ad conuentus sacros, in quibus celebrari solet. Conf. 1 Cor. XI, 20.

9) Λειτουργία, quæ vox, generatim sumta, notat administrationem muneris publici; speciatim accepta designat sacram & solemnem actionem, qua corpus Christi mediante pane manducandum, & sanguis Christi mediante vino bibendum dispensatur. 10) ’Αγάπη, caritas. Opulentiore enim in primitiua ecclesia ad mensam Domini panem & vinum afferebant, vt pars adhiberetur ad sacramentum, & quidquid residuum erat, ministris ecclesiæ & pauperibus cederet. Hoc fuit indicium caritatis; inde S. cœna ἀγάπη, caritas dicta est.

11) Θυσία καὶ προσφορά, sacrificium & oblatio, non ratione actus sacrificialis, quasi facerdos sacrificet: sed partim ratione materiæ, quia distribuitur id, quod in cruce semel sacrificatum fuit; partim ratione finis, quia sacramentum cœnæ dispensatur & accipitur in commemorationem sacrificii, in cruce semel peracti. 12) Μυστήριον, & cum adiectione Φρικτόν, Φρικῶδες, Φρικοδέσατον μυστήριον, tremendum mysterium. IVSTINVS apol. II, pro Christianis. CHRYSOST. homil. 38. in Matth. Est enim eucharistia mysterium admirandum: a) quia a solo Deo est revelatum, b) propter modum unionis inter rem caelestem & terrestrem, qui non tantum est significativus, seu, quod res terrena significet caelestem, sed realis exhibitivus, per quem res caelestis non minus communicatur edentibus & comedentibus, quam res terrena: c) propter modum praesentiae corporis & sanguinis Christi, qui est substantialis & realis, non virtualis, non obiectivus, aut intentionalis: d) propter modum unionis nobiscum, quo res caelestes, corpus & sanguis Christi, propius uniuntur cum communicantibus fidelibus in sacramento, quam extra sacramentum. Conf. HULSEM. breu. c. XIII. pag. 819.

13) Missa, cuius vocis abusus in papatu creberrimus est, vbi in audienda missa sacrorum suorum propam & puppim constituunt; & quid notius sacrificio missae? Habet vox, missa, originem latinam, & ita dicitur a dimissione populi. Fuit autem, explicante CASABONO, duplex ἄφεσις, dimissio, vel missa: prior, cum finitis lectionibus S. scripturae & precibus illis, quibus catechumeni, energumeni & alii, non initiati, interesse poterant, diaconus clamaret: Ite catechumeni in pace: missa est! h. e. dimissionem habebitis (enim sacram liturgiam spectare fas non erat); posterior, dum sacris peractis, & eucharistiae celebratione finita, post εὐχὴν ἀπολυτικήν, h. e. precationem dimissoriam, diaconus sub finem sacrorum omnium denuo clamasset: Ite fideles in pace! missa est! h. e. iam & vos dimissi estis, vt cuilibet discedendi libera sit potestas.

14) Hodie dicitur sacramentum altaris. Exstructis quippe christianorum templis sub Constantino M., erectae sunt mensae lapideae & dictae altaria, qualibus in publica eucharistiae administratione adhuc libere vtimur.


### Quest. II

Who instituted the Eucharist?.* The principal efficient cause of the Sacrament of the Supper is God alone, one in essence and three in persons a).

Proof a. The sacrament of the Supper is an efficacious means of salvation and a seal of grace: Therefore, the institution of the sacred Supper depends on the authority and power of the Triune God, who is the author of salvation and the fountain of grace.

Proof b. By a special reason, the institutor of the sacred Supper, according to the unanimous testimony of the evangelists, Matt. XXVI, 26, Mark XIV, 22, Luke XXII, 19, and the Apostle Paul, 1 Cor. XI, 23, is our Lord, Jesus Christ, as our μεσίτης (mesitēs), according to both natures, both divine and human. For according to whichever nature Christ could say: "This is my body, this is my blood," according to that same nature He also ordained His body to be eaten and His blood to be drunk. Now, it is most certain that Christ could say "This is my body, this is my blood" not only according to His divine nature, but altogether according to His human nature as well. Wherefore, the human nature of Christ is in no way to be excluded from the institution of the Eucharist.

The author and founder of this sacrament is called Lord Jesus in 1 Cor. XI, 23. For He is the Lord of lords and King of Kings, Rev. XIX, 6, according to both natures: as God, born from eternity; as man, made in the fullness of time, by the grace of the personal union. In the institution of the sacred Supper, He showed Himself by the very act to be Jesus, i.e., the Savior, outside of whom there is no salvation. For the Eucharist was founded by Him as a sacrament of salvation, as GREGORY THE GREAT says in his Paschal Homily.

This sacrament is described through the communication of the body and blood of Christ, 1 Cor. X, 6. Christ denotes the Priest, King, and Prophet. The founder of the sacrament of the Supper is our most loving Priest, who [gives] His body and blood... his own blood sacrificed on the altar of the cross he exhibits to us to be eaten & drunk: He is a Prophet πανσοφος, or most wise, who most rightly knows what and how he ought to speak, and by what reason he can fulfill his promises, since he knows how to do more than we understand, Eph. III, 20.: He is a most truthful Prophet, and truth itself, and thus he will not deceive us: He is an omnipotent King, and thus he will perform what he has promised: He is an omnipresent King, who is now also present at all συναξεσι, or sacred assemblies, Matt. XVIII, 20.: He is a most opulent King, who feeds his subjects with himself and specifically with his body and blood, and thus is also the host of the banquet. He was indeed then, when he instituted this sacrament, in a state, though not in the act of emptying, but he displayed the splendor of his majesty, if anywhere, most clearly.

Latin:

Causa efficiens Sacramenti coenae principalis est solus Deus, vnus in essentia & trinus in personis a). Speciali autem ratione Dominus noster, Iesus Christus, sacrae coenae auctor & institutor est b).

Prob. a. Sacramentum coenae est efficax medium salutis & sigillum gratiae: E. institutio sacrae coenae dependet ab auctoritate & potestate Dei triunius, qui auctor salutis & fons gratiae est.

Prob. b. Speciali ratione institutor sacrae coenae ex vnanimi testimonio euangelistarum, Matth. XXVI, 26. Marc. XIV, 22. Luc. XXII, 19. & Apostoli Paulli, 1 Cor. XI, 23. est Dominus noster, Iesus Christus, tanquam μεσίτης noster, secundum vtramque naturam, tam divinam, quam humanam. Nam secundum quam naturam Christus dicere potuit: hoc est corpus meum, hoc est sanguis meus, secundum eam quoque corpus suum manducandum, & sanguinem suum bibendum ordinauit. Iam vero certissimum est, Christum non tantum secundum divinam, sed omnino secundum humanam etiam naturam dicere potuisse: hoc est corpus meum, hoc est sanguis meus. Quare ab institutione eucharistiae humana Christi natura nullo modo excludenda est.

Auctor & fundator huius sacramenti 1 Cor. XI, 23. dicitur Dominus Iesus. Est enim Dominus dominorum, & Rex Regum, Apoc. XIX, 6. secundum vtramque naturam, qua Deus, ab aeterno natus, qua homo, in plenitudine temporis factus, ex vnionis personalis gratia. In institutione sacrae coenae se Iesum, h. e. saluatorem, extra quem salus nulla est, opere ipso ostendit. Eucharistia quippe ab ipso condita est sacramentum salutis, dicente GREGORIO M. in homil. paschal. Describitur hoc sacramentum per communicationem corporis & sanguinis Christi, 1 Cor. X, 6.

Christus notat Sacerdotem, Regem & prophetam. Conditor sacramenti coenae est Sacerdos nostri amantissimus, qui corpus & sanguinem suum in ara crucis sacrificatum nobis edendum & bibendum exhibet: Est Propheta πανσοφος, seu sapientissimus, qui rectissime novit, quid & quomodo loqui debeat, & qua ratione suas promissiones implere possit, cum plura facere sciat, quam nos intelligimus, Eph. III, 20.: Est Propheta veracissimus, & ipsa veritas, adeoque nos non fallet: Est Rex omnipotens, adeoque praestabit; quod promisit: Est Rex omnipraesens, qui nunc omnibus quoque συναξεσι, sive sacris conventibus praesto adest, Matth. XVIII, 20.: Est Rex opulentissimus, qui subditos seipso ac sigillatim corpore & sanguine suo pascit, adeoque & hospes convivii. Fuit quidem tunc, cum condidit hoc sacramentum, in statu, non tamen actu exinanitionis, sed maiestatis suae splendorem, si vspiam, luculentissime exseruit.


### Quest. III. Who today dispense the sacrament of the supper?

Ministers.

The present-day dispensers of the sacrament of the supper are ordained ministers of the church ), who consecrate the external elements, with prayers poured out to God, and the words of institution pronounced in the name of Christ ), and distribute them to the communicants ).

Prob. a. 1) Although Christ himself αυτοπροσωπως distributed the first supper to his disciples; yet today he does not dispense this sacrament to us except through the mediation of the ministers of the church. For upon them, through the conferring of holy orders, the public and ordinary power of teaching the word of God in the church, and thus also of administering the sacraments, baptism and the holy supper, has been conferred. For the word and the sacraments are so connected that without the word of God there can be no true and formal sacrament.

2) The ministers of the church are stewards or dispensers of the mysteries of God, 1 Cor. IV, 1. among which mysteries the sacrament of the Lord's supper stands out.

3) Not even in a case of necessity is the administration of the holy supper to be committed to a lay or private person; because in this part there is a distinction between baptism, which is the sacrament of initiation, and the eucharist, which is the sacrament of confirmation. Concerning the necessity of baptism Christ testifies: Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven, John III, 5. But one is not placed in equal necessity by the use of the holy supper; and therefore when there is no abundance of an ordinary minister, then that saying of AUGUSTINE has place: Believe, and you have eaten. For it is better, for a man anxiously desiring the sacrament of the supper, when a minister is lacking, to persuade him in any way of the sufficiency of spiritual eating, and to show the danger of other temptations, which could arise if the sacrament were administered by another, without a legitimate calling, and thus with a doubtful mind and uncertain outcome.

Prob. b. It belongs to the ministers of the church to consecrate the elements of bread and wine.

For no one can rightly enjoy the eucharist unless the consecration of the bread and wine has preceded, on account of the command of Christ in the institution: Do this: namely, what you saw me do in the distribution, while I blessed the bread and wine, and gave them blessed to you, and what you did by eating and drinking, the same I enjoin you, distributing or receiving these same symbols, to do hereafter. But consecration is one thing total, another partial. The latter is twofold, namely of destination, and of union; which two, joined together, are called total consecration. The consecration of destination destines the symbols for sacred use: The consecration of union is performed through the testamentary and dispositive words, not as merely historical, nor by reason of letters and syllables, but as they are operative, by reason of the divine sense (this is my body, which voice retains its efficacy, just as that: increase and multiply). Mention of both these consecrations is made in these words: Christ took (i.e., separated from profane use) the bread, gave thanks (destined for sacred use), desti- [sic] destined), and said: this is my body (i.e., he united it sacramentally to his own body).

Matt. XXVI, 26. Whence the consecrated cup is called the communion of the blood, 1 Cor. X, 16. Conf. SCHERZER, system. theol. p. 380. Prob. c. The ministers of the church distribute the bread and blood to the communicants, through whose ministry Christ, the author of the supper, offers his body to be eaten and his blood to be drunk. Which exhibition of body and blood is not done by a distinct and separate act, but by a joined one; therefore, because Christ, not immediately, but through the ministry of the word, presents his body and blood as really present in the Holy Supper for true eating and drinking with the earthly symbols.

Quæst. IV. Can a minister of the church lawfully dispense the eucharist to himself? A minister of the church should ordinarily receive the sacrament of the supper from a neighboring fellow-minister ; but in a case of necessity, where another minister is away abroad, or cannot be had so suddenly, and there is danger in delay, he may lawfully offer the sacrament to himself .

Prob. a. 1) The closer the dispensation of the sacrament approaches its first institution, the better and safer it is. But in the first institution, the person dispensing, who was Christ, and the persons receiving, who were the disciples, were distinct. 2) Just as no one ordinarily absolves himself from sins; so no one gives the sacrament to himself. 3) The sacrament of the supper is a symbol of charity and brotherly love (φιλαδελφίας): wherefore let him seek and employ a neighboring fellow-minister as a witness of faith and charity.

Prob. b. 1) All things yield to necessity which are not divinely commanded or prohibited. Nowhere, however, is it commanded that distinct persons must always perform the parts of the communicant and the receiver of the sacrament of the supper; nor is it forbidden anywhere that a pastor, in time of necessity, should offer the supper to himself. 2) Just as a minister of the divine word can and ought to console himself with the divine word; so nothing prevents him from refreshing himself by the taking of the sacrament, which he himself dispenses.

Quæst. V. What is the norm of the whole doctrine concerning the sacrament of the supper? The norm of the whole doctrine concerning the sacrament of the eucharist is the words of the institution of the Holy Supper, which are read in Matt.

XXVI, 26 ff., Mark XIV, 22, Luke XXII, 19, 1 Cor. XI, 23 a); but by no means is the norm or foundation for knowing and confirming this doctrine the Capernaitic sermon of Christ, which is read in John VI, 26 ff. b).

Prob. a. 1) One must judge the nature of any sacrament from its institution, as from its proper seat, where it is proposed and explained not incidentally or in passing, but directly and accurately. 2) The Apostle of the Gentiles himself, Paul, in 1 Cor. XI, 23, in bringing forward the orthodoxy concerning the Holy Supper, appealed to the words of the institution as the proper seat of this doctrine. 3) The sacrament of the supper is called a testament, Luke XXII, 20. Therefore its norm and foundation is the will and ordinance of the testator.

Prob. b. The Capernaitic sermon, John VI, does not formally include the sacramental eating of the body of Christ. For 1) sacramental eating was only required as it was instituted on the last night of Christ; but that eating, which is treated in John chapter VI, [was] long before is required, therefore, because the Capernaitic discourse was held a full year before the Holy Supper was instituted by the Lord Jesus.

2) Sacramental eating takes place by means of symbols, bread and wine: spiritual eating, which is enjoined in John chapter VI, requires no such symbol in itself; because Christ can be perceived spiritually through faith, without any symbol.

3) The former is eating properly so-called, and distinct from drinking; for neither is the blood offered to us to be eaten with the wine, nor the body to be drunk with the bread: the latter is metaphorical, and not distinct in reality from drinking.

4) The former is done by the mouth of the body; the latter by the mouth of faith.

5) The former can be done unto judgment and death, 1 Cor. XI, 29; the latter is always done unto life, John VI, 50.

6) The former is not absolutely necessary for salvation: the latter is absolutely necessary, even for infants, v. 53.

Therefore, John VI does not treat of the substance of the Holy Supper, although the fruit of every spiritual eating, whether it be symbolic or asymbolic, is set forth in the same chapter.

Latin:

Ministri.

Hodierni sacramenti caenae dispensatores sunt ordinati ecclesiae ministri ), qui elementa externa, fusis ad Deum precibus, & verbis institutionis nomine Christi pronuntiatis, consecrant ), & communicantibus distribuunt ).

Prob. a. 1) Licet Christus ipse αυτοπροσωπως suis discipulis primam caenam distribuerit; nobis tamen hodie non, nisi mediantibus ministris ecclesiae, hoc sacramentum dispensat. His enim, per collationem sacri ordinis, publica & ordinaria potestas docendi verbum Dei in ecclesia, atque adeo administrandi etiam sacramenta, baptismum & sacram caenam, collata est. Verbum enim & sacramenta ita sunt connexa, vt verum & formale sine verbo Dei sacramentum esse nullum possit.

2) Ministri ecclesiae sunt oeconomi vel dispensatores mysteriorum Dei, 1 Cor. IV, 1. inter quae mysteria eminet sacramentum caenae Domini.

3) Ne in casu quidem necessitatis homini laico, sive privato, committenda est sacrae caenae administratio; quia hac in parte discrimen est inter baptismum, qui est sacramentum initiationis, & inter eucharistiam, quae est sacramentum confirmationis. De baptismi necessitate Christus testatur: Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest ingredi regnum caelorum, Io. III, 5. Sed vsu sacrae caenae non est in pari necessitate constitutus; ideoque quando non est copia ordinarii ministri, tunc locum habet illud AVGVSTINI; Crede, & manducasti. Praestat enim, homini anxie desideranti sacramentum caenae, deficiente ministro, quomodocunque persuadere sufficientiam manducationis spiritualis, & ostendere periculum aliarum tentationum, quae nasci possent, si sacramentum ab alio, citra vocationem legitimam, adeoque dubia mente incertoque eventu administretur.

Prob. b. Ministrorum ecclesiae est, consecrare elementa panem & vinum.

Nemo quippe eucharistia rite frui potest, nisi consecratio panis & vini praecesserit, ob mandatum Christi in institutione: Hoc facite: nimirum, quod me in distributione facere vidistis, dum pani & vino benedixi, & benedicta vobis dedi, & quod vos comedendo & bibendo fecistis, idem vobis, eadem haec symbola distribuentibus, vel accipientibus, postera faciendum injungo. Est autem consecratio alia totalis, alia partialis. Hac duplex est, scilicet destinationis, & vnitionis; qua dua, simul iunctae, consecratio totalis appellantur. Consecratio destinationis symbola ad sacrum vsum destinat: Vnitionis consecratio, per verba testamentaria & dispositiva, non vt nude historica, nec ratione litterarum & syllabarum, sed vt operativa sunt, ratione sensus divini (hoc est corpus meum, quae vox efficaciam suam retinet, sicut illa: crescite & multiplicamini) peragitur. Vtriusque huius consecrationis mentio fit in his verbis: Christus accepit, (i. e. a profano vsu separauit) panem, gratias egit, (ad sacrum vsum destinavit), facrum vfum deftinauit), facrum vfum destinauit), & dixit: hoc est corpus meum (i. e. corpori suo sacramentaliter vniuit).

Matth. XXVI, 26. Vnde poculum consecratum, κοινωνία τοῦ αἵματος, 1 Cor. X, 16. dicitur. Conf. SCHERZERI system. theol. p. 380. Prob. c. Ministri ecclesiæ communicantibus distribuunt panem & sanguinem, per quorum ministerium Christus, auctor cœnæ, corpus suum manducandum, & sanguinem suum bibendum præbet. Quæ exhibitio corporis & sanguinis non fit actu distincto & separato, sed coniuncto; ideo, quod Christus non immediate, sed per ministerium verbi, corpus & sanguinem suum in S. cœna realiter præsentia sistit ad veram cum symbolis terrenis manducationem & bibitionem.

Quæst. IV. An minister ecclesiæ sibi ipsi eucharistiam licite dispensare potest? Minister ecclesiæ a vicino symmysta sacramentum cœnæ ordinarie accipiat ; at in casu necessitatis, vbi alius minister peregre abest, vel tam subito haberi nequit, & periculum in mora est, licite porrigit sibi sacramentum .

Prob. a. 1) Quo propius dispensatio sacramenti ad primam ipsius institutionem accedit: eo melior illa est, ac tutior. At in prima institutione persona dispensans, quæ erat Christus, & personæ sumentes, quæ erant discipuli, distinctæ erant. 2) Sicut nemo ordinarie seipsum a peccatis absoluit; ita nemo sibi ipsi dat sacramentum. 3) Sacramentum cœnæ est caritatis & φιλαδελφίας symbolum: Quare testem fidei & caritatis expetat & adhibeat vicinum symmystam.

Prob. b. 1) Necessitati cedunt omnia, quæ diuinitus non sunt præcepta, vel prohibita. Nuspiam autem præceptum est, vt distinctæ personæ semper obeant partes communicantis & accipientis sacramentum cœnæ; nec vllibi interdictum est, ne pastor tempore necessitatis cœnam sibi porrigat. 2) Sicut minister verbi diuini seipsum a verbo diuino consolari potest & debet; ita nil impedit, quo minus seipsum sumtione sacramenti, quod ipse dispensat, reficiat.

Quæst. V. Quæ est norma totius doctrinæ de sacramento cœnæ? Norma totius doctrinæ de sacramento eucharistiæ sunt verba institutionis S. cœnæ, quæ leguntur, Matth.

XXVI, 26. seqq. Marc. XIV, 22. Luc. XXII, 19. 1 Cor. XI, 23. a); nequaquam vero norma, aut fundamentum cognoscendæ & confirmandæ huius doctrinæ est concio Christi Capernaitica, quæ legitur Io. VI, 26. seq. b).

Prob. a. 1) Ex cuiuslibet sacramenti institutione, tanquam sede propria, vbi non incidenter, aut obiter, sed directe & accurate proponitur atque explicatur, de eius natura iudicandum est. 2) Ipse gentium Apostolus, Paullus, 1 Cor. XI, 23. in afferenda orthodoxia de S. cœna ad verba institutionis, tanquam sedem propriam huius doctrinæ, prouocauit. 3) Sacramentum cœnæ dicitur testamentum, Luc. XXII, 20. E. ipsius norma & fundamentum est voluntas & ordinatio testatoris.

Prob. b. Concio Capernaitica, Io. VI. formaliter non complectitur manducationem corporis Christi sacramentalem. Nam 1) manducatio sacramentalis tantum in vltima nocte Christi, vt instituta, ita requisita fuit; sed manducatio illa, de qua Ioannu. VI. cap. agitur, diu ante requisita est, ideo, quod concio Capernaitica integro anno prius habita, quam sacra coena a Domino Iesu instituta est.

2) Manducatio sacramentalis fit mediantibus symbolis, pane & vino: spiritualis, quae Io. VI. cap. praecipitur, nullum eiusmodi symbolum per se postulat; quia spiritualiter percipi potest Christus per fidem, citra ullum symbolum.

3) Illa est manducatio proprie dicta, & distincta a bibitione; neque enim praebetur nobis sanguis cum vino edendus, neque corpus cum pane bibendum: haec est metaphorica, neque secundum rem distincta a bibitione.

4) Illa fit ore corporis; haec ore fidei.

5) Illa potest fieri ad iudicium & mortem, 1Cor. XI, 29.; haec semper fit ad vitam, Io. VI, 50.

6) Illa non est absolute ad salutem necessaria: haec absolute necessaria, etiam infantibus, v. 53.

Non ergo Io. VI. agitur de substantia sacrae coenae, quamuis fructus ex omni spirituali manducatione, siue symbolica sit, siue asymbolica, eodem capite exponatur.


### Quest. VI. What is the literal sense of the words of institution: This is my body: This is my blood?

In the former proposition, the demonstrative pronoun, THIS, denotes the whole sacramental complex, consisting of bread and the body of Christ: In the latter proposition, it likewise denotes the whole complex, consisting of wine and the blood of Christ, mystically united . The substantive verb, IS, connects the predicate with the subject, and denotes that what is offered in the Holy Supper is truly and really not only bread, but also the body of Christ . BODY and BLOOD OF CHRIST denote the true and substantial body of Christ, and the true and substantial blood of Christ .

Obj. Tò ῥητὸν, the letter, the literal sense, are spoken of in two ways: 1) in the comparison of different interpretations of scripture; for one interpretation of scripture is literal, another is mystical. The literal sense is that which the words themselves immediately yield, all circumstances being considered, and it is distinguished into the literal sense proper, and figurative.

The proper sense is that which the Holy Spirit intends with the words taken in their native signification, e.g., God is a spirit. The figurative sense is that which is proximately intended by the Holy Spirit with words affected by some trope, e.g., God is our shield. The mystical sense is said to be that which is not signified proximately by the θεόπνευσα (God-breathed) words, but which flows and is deduced from the thing signified by the θεοπνεύσοις (God-breathed) words.

2) Tò ῥητὸν, the letter, the literal sense is spoken of with respect to the different use of words, proper and tropical. Where there is the letter, it is when words are used properly and without any trope: the literal sense, indeed, is that which is generated from words taken properly and outside of any trope. In this latter signification, τὸ ῥητὸν, the letter, and the literal sense are taken in the present case.

Proof a. 1) That the pronoun τοῦτο, THIS, denotes the whole sacramental complex, we learn from the Greek construction. Ἐσθιόντων δὲ αὐτῶν, λαβὼν ὁ Ἰησοῦς τὸν ἄρτον, καὶ εὐλογήσας ἔκλασε, καὶ ἐδίδου τοῖς μαθηταῖς, καὶ εἶπε· λάβετε, φάγετε, τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ σῶμά με, Matth. XXVI, 26. Where the demonstrative pronoun, τοῦτο, does not precisely or solely denote τὸν ἄρτον, or the bread; because the Greek construction stands in the way: nor precisely or solely the body; because the proposition would be identical and tautological. Therefore it denotes the whole sacramental complex.

We conclude: The pronoun, THIS, either denotes precisely the body of Christ, or the bread, or precisely the body of Christ, or the bread, or the whole

sacramental [entity], consisting of earthly and heavenly matter. But it does not denote precisely the body of Christ; because thus the predication would be identical and tautological: Nor does it denote precisely the bread; because the Greek construction stands in the way, which does not allow us to say ἄρτον τοῦτο. Therefore, the demonstrative HOC denotes the whole sacramental complex.

2) From the context itself. What the demonstrative pronoun, HOC, demonstrates, the context of the words of institution teaches. Taking bread, and blessing, Jesus broke and gave to the disciples, and said: Take, eat, this is my body. From which words we conclude: 1) Whatever Christ, instituting his most holy supper, took from the table, broke, and gave to his disciples, that is demonstrated by the demonstrative pronoun, hoc.

But bread, etc. E. 2) The Lord Jesus added, when he took bread, broke it, and gave it to the disciples: τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ σῶμά με, this is my body, so that he might demonstrate that he, by the bread being offered, was also offering his own body.

If he had said: This is bread; the demonstrative pronoun would precisely and solely demonstrate the bread: But Christ said, τοῦτο, this is my body, so that he might indicate that he was giving not only bread to be eaten, but also his own body.

3) The pronoun, HOC, which is of the singular number, embraces two things, namely bread and the body of Christ. It is necessary, therefore, that these two come into a certain union, so that they can be signified and called by one singular [pronoun], hoc, not haec.

4) Bread is demonstrated not only as present, but also as visible. And this is the reason why bread is not placed in the predicate; nor was it said: This is bread and my body; or: this is bread with my body. For that which is demonstrated and exhibited to the eye has no need of exposition, which is wont to be done through the predicate. But the body is demonstrated, as invisibly present; and therefore it is expressly named, so that it may be known.

3) The rationale of exhibitive propositions is that, with diverse things shown to be united among themselves, the whole complex is demonstrated in the subject, [and] that which is more worthy and less obvious to the senses is expressed in the predicate, e.g. If a bridegroom, having offered to his bride a skillfully made box as a sign of his love, were to say: Take, this is a gem; the demonstrative particle, HOC, demonstrates both the box and the gem. When a host at a banquet, having offered you a goblet, says: Take, this is wine, the demonstrative, HOC, denotes both the goblet and the wine. If a physician were to offer a noble medicine to a sick person in a small vessel, and were to say to him: Take, this is a noble alexipharmic; by the demonstrative pronoun both the vessel and the alexipharmic are comprehended. By the same reasoning, when Christ, the physician of souls, having offered bread, says: Take, eat, this is my body, the little deictic word denotes both the eucharistic bread and the body of Christ.

4) In exhibitive propositions the demonstrative, HOC, is not taken adjectivally, but substantively, involving a substantive noun, and signifying the same thing as 'this thing'. It has, therefore, a general signification, and is apt for demonstrating every being, and therefore whatever it signifies, it signifies not distinctly and according to its own specific notion, but confusedly and generally, under the concept of 'this thing'. But what thing 'this' (tò hoc) placed in the position of the subject designates, is to be gathered from the predicate. For such are the subjects as are permitted to be by their predicates. Hence it happens that the more noble thing, and the one less obvious to the senses, is noted principally and in the nominative case, [while] the more ignoble thing is connoted in the oblique case, e.g. When a bridegroom hands a box to his bride, and has said: Take, this is a gem; the pronoun HOC in the nominative case, although confusedly and under the concept of 'this thing', denotes the gem, [while] in the oblique case it connotes the box, and can be explained: This thing, which I hand or exhibit to you in and with the box, is a gem. Thus the sacramental proposition, by which Christ says to his disciples, having offered bread: Take, eat, this is my body; has this sense: Take, eat, this thing, which I hand to you to be eaten with the bread, is my body.

Conf. D. DANNH. in hodof. phanom. X. p. 1178. & D. MVSAEVS in controu. theol. p. 365.

5) Sacramental propositions: this is my body, this is my blood, are explained by the exegetical particles, in, with, and under. This is evident: a) Because the pronoun, this, intended the whole sacramental complex, consisting of the earthly and heavenly thing, and indeed denotes this in the nominative case, and connotes that in the oblique case; but the oblique case is conveniently explained by the particles, in, with, and under. b) Pious antiquity used those particles. AUGUSTINE in a sermon to the neophytes says: Receive this IN the bread, which hung on the cross. AMBROSE on the mysteries, ch. 9. What we see is the species of bread and wine: What we believe UNDER that species is the true body and true blood of Christ. And CHRYSOSTOM, book 3 on the priesthood, says: WITH those things which are seen, the body and blood of the Lord is believed to be present. c) The sacramental union and communion is explained by those particles, just as personal propositions concerning the personal union conceived in Holy Scripture are explained by such particles. Paul, 1 Tim. III, 16, explains the personal proposition which John has in ch. I, 14, The Word was made flesh, thus: God was manifested IN flesh. He explains the proposition which the Apostle uses in Rom. IX, 5, Christ is God, the same in 2 Cor. V, 19, by this proposition: God was IN Christ, and Peter in Acts X, 38, by this: God was WITH Christ. However, sacramental propositions can also be explained by other particles, e.g., This proposition: Take, eat, this is my body, is declared: this thing, which I exhibit to you to be eaten, is not only bread, but also my body; or: this, which I exhibit to you by means of the bread, is my body.

Prob. b. The substantive verb, IS, according to its literal meaning and proper use, denotes the existence, nature, state of a thing, or what the thing becomes, and of what kind it is. Wherefore the verb, IS, taken properly, as a copula, connects the predicate with the subject, and indicates that that which is given to be eaten in the Holy Supper is truly and really not only bread, but also the body of Christ.

Prob. c. BODY literally signifies the essential body, or the very substance of the body, for it is expressly added: which is given for you, Luke XXII, 19, which is broken for you, 1 Cor. XI, 24. The BLOOD of Christ is the true and substantial blood, by which the new testament was sanctioned and confirmed: but the new testament has no types or shadows: therefore, not a typical, but the true and substantial blood of Christ is present in the Holy Supper, which was shed for us for the remission of sins, Matt. XXVI, 28.

You say: I. That Christ, instituting the Holy Supper, took from the table, broke, and distributed to his disciples, is demonstrated only by the pronominal particle, THIS, when he says, offering it: this is my body.

But Christ, instituting the Holy Supper, took bread from the table, broke it, and distributed it to his disciples. Therefore. Resp. We deny 1) the major, taken in an exclusive sense. For nothing more follows than this: it is demonstrated by the pronominal particle, THIS; which is true. For in reality the pronoun demonstrates the bread, but not solely, nor precisely, but in the complex, of which it is a part, and that the more ignoble one. 2) The thing which, in the dispensation of the sacrament, is designated by Christ through the little word, THIS, in the proposition, this is my body, is to be taken in the nominative case not from the preceding words, by which what Christ did before he ordered the disciples to take and eat is described, but from the predicate is: for such are the predicates as are permitted to be by their subjects. Since, therefore, the predicate of this proposition is the body of Christ: it is evident that the THIS in the nominative case signifies the body of Christ, or the concept of this thing, which was offered to the disciples to be eaten with the bread, with the bread thus simultaneously connoted in the oblique case.

You say: II. Paul explains the particle, THIS, concerning the bread, saying: The bread, which we break, is the κοινωνία [communion] of the body of Christ, 1 Cor. X, 16. Resp. Paul's proposition: The bread is the communion of the body of Christ, is different from this: This is my body. For in this latter, the body of Christ is predicated in the nominative case: in the former, it is connoted at least in the predicate, in the oblique case. Whence it is not necessary that the subjects be the same in both, or that the same thing be denoted by the subject in both. Paul elicits his proposition from the proposition of Christ. For if that which He gave to His disciples was the Body of Christ: it follows that the bread is the communion of the body of Christ, or is therefore used by Christ, so that it becomes the medium through which we might be made partakers of the body of Christ, not so that we might fill our belly.

III. If the pronoun, THIS, denotes the body of Christ; the proposition of Christ will be tautological, just as if He had said: My body is my body. Resp. We assert that the pronoun, THIS, denotes the sacramental complex, the principal part of which is the body of Christ, which is denoted by the pronoun, THIS, confused under the concept of this thing. Whence no ταυτολογία [tautology] is inferred.

IV. If by the δεικτικόν [demonstrative], τοῦτο [this], Christ had understood the complex of bread and the body of Christ, mystically united, the sense of the words of Christ would be this: Bread together with my body is my body; or: bread and my body are my body, or the communion of my body: How absurd this is, no one fails to understand. Resp. We indeed understand by τὸ HOC [the THIS] the complex of bread and the body of Christ; but we maintain at the same time that in the signifying of the two complex parts, some inequality intervenes; that the body of Christ is designated principally, or in the nominative case, under the most general notion of this thing, but the bread less principally, or in the oblique case, so that the sense becomes: This thing, which is handed over to be eaten with the bread, is my body.

V. Ecclesiastical doctors have used this proposition: The eucharistic bread is the body of Christ. Resp. That proposition is not ἔγγραφος [written/scriptural], or biblical, but ἄγραφος [unwritten/extra-biblical], and ecclesiastical. We are investigating in the present the sense of the biblical proposition, which Christ Himself used. Quæst.

Latin:

In priori propositione pronomen demonstratiuum, HOC, denotat totum complexum sacramentale, constans ex pane & corpore Christi: In posteriori propositione itidem notat totum complexum, constans ex vino & sanguine Christi, mystice vnitis . Verbum substantiuum, EST, connectit praedicatum cum subiecto, & denotat, id, quod in sacra coena porrigitur, vere & realiter esse non tantum panem, sed etiam corpus Christi . CORPVS & SANGVIS CHRISTI verum & substantiale Christi corpus, verum & substantialem Christi sanguinem notant .

Obs. Tò ῥητὸν, littera, litteralis sensus, bifariam dicuntur: 1) in collatione diuersarum interpretationum scripturae; est namque interpretatio scripturae alia litteralis, alia mystica. Litteralis sensus est, quem verba ipsa immediate, consideratis omnibus circumstantiis, reddunt, & distinguitur in sensum litteralem proprium, & figuratum.

Sensus proprius est, quem verbis sumtis in natiua significatione Spiritus S. intendit, v. gr. Deus est spiritus. Sensus figuratus est, qui proxime intenditur a Spiritu S. verbis tropo aliquo affectis, v. gr. Deus est clypeus noster. Sensus mysticus dicitur, qui non significatur proxime per verba θεόπνευσα, sed qui ex re, verbis θεοπνεύσοις significata, fluit atque deducitur.

2) Tò ῥητὸν, littera, litteralis sensus dicitur respectu diuersi vsus vocabulorum, proprii & tropici.
