Vbi littera est, quando verba proprie, & sine vllo tropo vsurpata stant: litteralis vero sensus est, qui, ex verbis proprie & extra omnem tropum acceptis gignitur. Posteriori hac significatione τὸ ῥητὸν, littera, & litteralis sensus in praesenti accipitur.

Prob. a. 1) Pronomen τοῦτο, HOC, denotare totum complexum sacramentale, discimus ex constructione graeca. Ἐσθιόντων δὲ αὐτῶν, λαβὼν ὁ Ἰησοῦς τὸν ἄρτον, καὶ εὐλογήσας ἔκλασε, καὶ ἐδίδου τοῖς μαθηταῖς, καὶ εἶπε· λάβετε, φάγετε, τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ σῶμά με, Matth. XXVI, 26. Vbi pronomen demonstratiuum, τοῦτο, non praecise aut solum notat τὸν ἄρτον, siue panem; quia obstat constructio graeca: neque praecise aut solum corpus; quia propositio foret identica & tautologica. Ergo notat totum complexum sacramentale.

Colligimus: Pronomen, HOC, aut notat praecise corpus Christi, aut panem, aut præcife corpus Christi, aut panem, aut

totum sacramentale, ex re terrena & caelesti constans. At non denotat praecise corpus Christi; quia sic esset praedicatio identica & tautologica: Neque denotat praecise panem; quia obstat constructio graeca, quae non admittit, vt dicamus ἄρτον τοῦτο. E. demonstrativum HOC notat totum complexum sacramentale.

2) Ex ipso contextu. Quid pronomen demonstrativum, HOC, demonstret, docet contextus verborum institutionis. Accipiens Iesus panem, & benedicens, fregit & dedit discipulis, & dixit: Accipite, comedite, hoc est corpus meum. Ex quibus verbis concludimus: 1) Quidquid Christus, coenam suam sacro-sanctam instituens, de mensa sumsit, fregit, discipulisque suis dedit, illud pronomine demonstrativo, hoc, demonstratur.

Atqui panem &c. E. 2) Addidit Dominus Iesus, cum panem sumsit, fregit, discipulisque dedit: τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ σῶμά με, hoc est corpus meum, vt demonstraret, se porrecto pane, porrigere etiam corpus suum.

Si dixisset: Hic est panis; pronomen demonstrativum praecise & vnice demonstraret panem: Sed dixit Christus, τοῦτο, hoc est corpus meum, vt indigitaret, se comedendum dare non solum panem, sed etiam corpus suum.

3) Pronomen, HOC, quod singularis numeri est, complectitur duo, nimirum panem & corpus Christi. Oportet itaque haec duo in vnionem quandam venire, vt vno singulari significari, dicique possit, hoc, non, haec.

4) Panis demonstratur non tantum vt praesens, sed etiam vt visibilis. Atque haec est ratio, quare panis in praedicato positus non fit; nec dictum: Hoc est panis & corpus meum; aut: hoc est panis cum corpore meo. Nam id, quod ad oculum demonstratur & exhibetur, non opus habet expositione, quae per praedicatum fieri solet. Corpus autem demonstratur, vt inuisibiliter praesens; ideoque expresse nominatur, vt innotescat.

3) Exhibitiuarum propositionum ratio communis est, vt, ostensis rebus diuersis, inter se vnitis, in subiecto demonstretur totum complexum, in praedicato exprimatur id, quod dignius, minusque sensui obvium est, v. gr. Si sponsus sponsae, affabre facta pyxide in signum amoris sui oblata, diceret: Accipe, hoc est gemma; particula demonstratiua, HOC, & pyxidem & gemmam demonstrat. Cum tibi in conuiuio hospes, porrecto cantharo, dicit: Accipe, hoc est vinum, demonstratiuum, HOC, & cantharum & vinum notat. Si medicus in vasculo offerret aegroto nobile pharmacum, & ipsi diceret: Accipe, hoc est nobile alexipharmacum; pronomine demonstrativo & vasculum & alexipharmacum comprehenditur. Pari ratione cum animarum medicus Christus, porrecto pane, dicit: Accipite, comedite, hoc est corpus meum, vocula δεικτική, & panem eucharisticum, & corpus Christi notat.

4) In propositionibus exhibitiuis demonstrativum, HOC, non sumitur adiectiue, sed substantive, inuoluendo nomen substantivum, idemque significando, quod hac res. Habet itaque significationem generalem, & ad omne ens demonstrandum aptum est, ideoque quidquid significat, non distincte & iuxta rationem suam specificam, sed confuse & generaliter, sub conceptu huius rei significat. Quam rem autem τὸ hoc subiecti loco positum designet, ex praedicato desumendum est. Talia enim sunt subiecta, qualia permittuntur esse a suis praedicatis. Inde fit, vt res nobilior, minusque obuia sensibus, notetur praecipue & in casu recto, res ignobilior connotetur in obliquo, v. gr. Cum sponsus sponsae tradit pyxidem, & dixit: Accipe, hoc est gemma; pronomen HOC in casu recto, quamuis confuse & sub conceptu huius rei, notat gemmam, in casu obliquo connotat pyxidem, & exponi potest: Hac res, quam tibi in & cum pyxide trado, vel exhibeo, est gemma. Ita propositio sacramentalis, qua Christus discipulis suis, porrecto pane, dicit: Accipite, comedite, hoc est corpus meum; hunc sensum habet: Accipite, comedite, hac res, quam cum pane comedendam vobis trado, est corpus meum.

Conf. D. DANNH. in hodof. phanom. X. p. 1178. & D. MVSAEVS in controu. theol. p. 365.

5) Propositiones sacramentales: hoc est corpus meum, hoc est sanguis meus, particulis exegeticis, in, cum, & sub exponuntur. Id quod patet: a) Quia pronomen, hoc, involuit totum complexum sacramentale, constans ex re terrena & cœlesti, & hanc quidem in casu recto notat, illam in casu obliquo connotat; casus autem obliquus commode per particulas, in, cum, & sub exponitur. b) Pia antiquitas illis particulis vsa est. AVGVSTINVS in sermone ad neophytos inquit: Hoc accipite IN pane, quod pependit in cruce. AMBROS. de myst. c. 9. Quod videmus, species est panis & vini: Quod SVB illa specie credimus, verum corpus & verus sanguis Christi est. Et CHRYSOST. l. 3. de sacerdot. inquit: CVM illis rebus, quæ videntur, simul adesse creditur corpus & sanguis Domini . c) Vnio & communio sacramentalis illis particulis explicatur, sicut propositiones personales de vnione personali conceptæ in S. scriptura per eiusmodi particulas exponuntur. Propositionem personalem, quam habet Ioannes c. I, 14. Verbum caro factum est, Paullus 1 Tim. III, 16. sic explanat: Deus manifestatus est IN carne. Propositionem, qua vtitur Apostolus Rom. IX, 5. Christus est Deus, idem 2 Cor. V, 19. per hanc propositionem: Deus erat IN Christo, & Petrus Act. X, 38. per hanc: Deus erat CVM Christo, exponit. Poslunt tamen propositiones sacramentales etiam aliis particulis explicari, v. gr. Hæc propositio: Accipite, comedite, hoc est corpus meum, declaratur: hæc res, quam vobis comedendam exhibeo, non est tantum panis, sed etiam corpus meum; vel: hoc, quod mediante pane vobis exhibeo, est corpus meum.

Prob. b. Verbum substantivum, EST, secundum litteram suam, propriumque vsum, notat rei exsistentiam, naturam, statum, siue quod res fit, & cuiusmodi sit. Quare verbum, EST, proprie sumtum, vt copula, prædicatum cum subiecto connectit, & indicat, id, quod in S. cœna comedendum datur, vere & realiter non tantum panem, sed etiam corpus Christi esse.

Prob. c. CORPVS litteraliter significat corpus essentiale, seu ipsam corporis substantiam, diserte enim additur: quod pro vobis datur, Luc. XXII, 19. quod pro vobis frangitur, 1 Cor. XI, 24. SANGVIS Christi est verus & substantialis sanguis, quo nouum testamentum sancitum & confirmatum est: nouum testamentum autem non typos aut vmbras habet: ergo sanguis non typicus, sed verus & substantialis Christi sanguis in sacra cœna adest, qui pro nobis effusus est in remissionem peccatorum, Matth. XXVI, 28.

Dicis: I. Quod Christus sacram cœnam instituens, de mensa sumsit, fregit, discipulisque suis distribuit, id solum demonstratur particula pronominali, HOC, cum dicit porrigens: hoc est corpus meum. Atqui panem, Christus sacram cœnam instituens, de mensa sumsit, fregit discipulisque suis distribuit.

E. Resp. Negamus 1) maiorem, sumtam in sensu exclusiuo. Neque enim plus sequitur, quam hoc: id demonstratur particula pronominali, HOC; quod verum est. Nam reuera pronomen demonstrat panem, sed non solum, nec præcise, sed in complexo, cuius pars, eaque ignobilior est. 2) Quæ res in sacramenti dispensatione per voculam, HOC, in propositione, hoc est corpus meum, a Christo designata fit, in casu recto non ex antecedentibus verbis, quibus, quid fecerit Christus, antequam accipere & comedere iussit discipulos, describitur, sed ex prædicato est desumendum: nam talia sunt prædicata, qualia permittuntur esse a suis subiectis. Cum ergo huius propositionis prædicatum sit corpus Christi: patet, τὸ HOC in casu recto significare corpus Christi, siue conceptum huius rei, quæ cum pane comedenda porrigebatur discipulis, sic simul connotato pane in obliquo.

Dicis: II. Paullus particulam, HOC, de pane explicat, dicens: Panis, quem frangimus, est κοινωνία corporis Christi, 1 Cor. X, 16. Resp. Propositio Paulli: Panis est communicatio corporis Christi, diversa est ab hac: Hoc est corpus meum. In hac enim prædicatur corpus Christi in casu recto: in illa connotatur saltem in prædicato, in casu obliquo. Unde non necesse est, ut vtrobique eadem sint subiecta, sive ut eadem res per subiectum vtrobique denotetur. Paullus suam propositionem ex propositione Christi elicit. Si namque id, quod discipulis suis dedit, fuit Corpus Christi: sequitur, quod panis sit communio corporis Christi, seu propterea a Christo vsurpatus, ut fit medium, per quod corporis Christi redderemus participes, non ut ventrem impleremus.

III. Si pronomen, HOC, notat corpus Christi; propositio Christi erit tautologica, perinde ac si dixisset: Corpus meum est corpus meum. Resp. Asserimus, pronomen, HOC, notare complexum sacramentale, cuius pars præcipua est corpus Christi, quod pronomine, HOC, confuso sub conceptu huius denotatur. Unde nulla infertur ταυτολογία.

IV. Si per δεικτικόν, τοῦτο, Christus intellexisset complexum ex pane & corpore Christi, mystice vnitis, sensus verborum Christi hic esset: Panis una cum corpore meo est corpus meum; seu: panis & corpus meum sunt corpus meum, vel communio corporis mei: Quod quam sit absonum, nemo non intelligit. Resp. Intelligimus quidem per τὸ HOC complexum ex pane & corpore Christi; sed statuimus simul, in significandis duabus complexis partibus inæqualitatem aliquam intercedere; quod corpus Christi principaliter, sive in casu recto, sub ratione generalissima huius rei, at panis minus principaliter, sive in obliquo designetur, ut sensus fit: Hæc res, quæ cum pane comedenda traditur, est corpus meum.

V. Doctores ecclesiastici hac propositione vsi sunt: Panis eucharisticus est corpus Christi. Resp. Propositio illa non est ἔγγραφος, aut biblica, sed ἄγραφος, & ecclesiastica. Nos inuestigamus in præsenti sensum propositionis biblicæ, qua ipse Christus vsus est. Quæst.


### VII. Is the ῥητόν [literal sense], or the literal sense of the words of the sacred supper to be retained?

One must not depart from the propriety of the words of the sacred supper, but they are, as they lie and sound, to be understood most simply according to the letter. Obf.

I. We are not at present discussing all the words of the institution of the sacred supper whatsoever, but the οὐσιατικοῖς καὶ διαθετικοῖς [substantial and dispositive] words: this is my body: this is my blood. Obf.

II. A trope is a change of a proper and native signification into an alien one, made in a word resolvable to a topical place by the intellect freely, for the sake of necessity, or perspicuity, or decency. From which it is evident that a periphrasis is not a trope, since the same signification of the word is not changed, but only illustrated. Our assertion is proved: 1) In the exposition and consideration of any passage of Scripture, one must not depart from the letter, where the sense of the letter is good, and no most grave and perspicuous reasons persuade the contrary: But of this our scripture, i.e., the words of the sacred supper, the letter has a good sense, and no grave reasons are present which urge a trope: Therefore, in the exposition of the words of the supper, one must not depart from the letter.

The major premise is a hermeneutical rule and self-evident. For the literal sense has a certain natural prerogative, from which it cannot be driven, except by some great right. It is prior by nature, as the simple stands before the composite, the direct before the oblique, the naked before the colored. It is also prior by cognition; when I hear: Herod is a fox, first the image of a fox occurs to the concept, and only later by the mind's negotiation and consideration of the absurdity am I carried into the cognition of the trope. It is prior by doctrine, and thus always clearer and better known by nature, even if sometimes later in time. The minor premise will be made more clear from what is to be said below.

2) The author and institutor of the Holy Supper is our Lord, Jesus, the most truthful, most benevolent, and most authoritative teacher. He is most truthful, and therefore deceives no one, but speaks the truth so openly that it can be recognized by men. He is most benevolent, because out of love and benevolence towards the human race He instituted the sacrament of the Supper, and at the Last Supper, if ever, He attested His benevolence towards His disciples. Who then will deny that He dealt clearly with them? He is most authoritative. Therefore, all ought to revere the words of this supreme teacher in such a way that in their interpretation one should in no way rashly depart from the letter, but diligently retain it. (*)

3) The institution of the Lord's Supper, after Christ's ascension into heaven, was repeated by various writers in various places and committed to writing. However, just as sacred writers otherwise undertook these mutual labors among themselves, so that what one might have written less fully, or in less proper words, another might express more fully, or in more proper words: so these, with these words: "This is My body: This is My blood," did not mean what they properly import, but that the Lord wished to signify this, that the bread is a sign of His body, and the wine is a sign of His blood; it is not credible that the sacred writers, who described the history of the institution with all due care, all kept silent about this. But they all kept silent about it, nor did any of them indicate by a single word that what is offered for eating and drinking are not the very body and blood of Christ, but only their signs.

4) The Lord Jesus spoke the words of the Supper when He was near death, and was not going to speak much more with His disciples: And so He truly acted as a testator, who bequeathed His body and blood to His church. And at this very time, when anyone is near death, he speaks most clearly and plainly. For everyone prudently avoids the disputes of heirs, which necessarily follow when a testament suffers from obscurity due to tropes. Since this is the case, the heirs must certainly adhere to the words of the testator as much as possible. For if one were to depart from the proper meaning of the speech, the testator would undoubtedly have indicated it clearly. Since such prudence is found among men: how much more in the Savior!

5) The Lord's Supper is a sacred feast: But convivial words never suffer the metonymy of the sign for the thing signified. Because no one offering the sign of bread, flesh, wine, says without ridicule: "Take, eat, this is bread, flesh: Drink, this is wine."

6) That it is dangerous to rashly depart from the letter of the words, Eve learned by experience, Gen. III, 6. Abraham, on the other hand, constantly adhered to the letter with great fruit, Gen. XXII, 2.

7) The individual words of the institution are so clear that they reject a trope. For the demonstrative particle, THIS, indeed demonstrates the whole complex, namely the blessed bread and at the same time the body of Christ, yet in such a way that the body of Christ is denoted in the nominative case, but the bread in the oblique case; which usually happens in all exhibitive propositions, in which we exhibit two conjoined things to someone. The verbal copula, IS, is not capable of a trope. For if the copula, IS, loses its meaning of coupling, or uniting the predicate with the subject, and assumes another; then it would also destroy the proposition itself, so that it is no longer a proposition. But if the verb IS means the same as "signifies," it will not be a copula, but part of the predicate. For if the verb "signifies" is resolved, it is the same as if you said: "Is signifying": whence what from the resolution the solution comes, the word, EST, will finally be the copula; but the participle signifying can be referred to nothing other than the predicate. Nor does a trope fall upon the body or blood, on account of the προσδιορισμὸν [specification], which is given for us. For that is designated by the name of body and blood, which is given for us into death, and which is poured out for us for the remission of sins. But now, not a sign of the body, not tropical, not figurative, but the true and proper body of Christ is given for us into death, and not tropical, not figurative, but the true and proper blood of Christ is poured out for us for the remission of sins: Therefore.

8) The New Testament differs from the old in this, that there the shadow is exhibited, here the body; in the former signs are proposed, in the latter the things signified. Therefore, a merely metonymical and significative theology has no place here. For if the Lord had wished to institute signs of things, He would have retained the paschal lamb, which far more evidently figured the death and promise of Christ, and in the paschal feast He would have said thus: Eat, this, noting the lamb, is my body, i. e., it signifies my body for you, as it was once to be given, so now it is given.

Latin:

A proprietate verborum sacræ cænæ recedendum non est, sed sunt illa, ut iacent & sonant, simplicissime ad litteram intelligenda. Obs.

I. Non est nobis in præsenti sermo de omnibus omnino institutionis sacræ cænæ verbis, sed de verbis οὐσιατικοῖς καὶ διαθετικοῖς, substantialibus & dispositivis: hoc est corpus meum: hoc est sanguis meus. Obs.

II. Tropus est mutatio significationis propriæ ac nativæ in alienam, in voce resolubili ad locum topicum ab intellectu libere facta, vel necessitatis, vel perspicuitatis, vel honestatis gratia. Ex quo dispalescit, periphrasin non esse tropum, cum eadem significatio vocis non mutetur, sed tantum illustretur. Probatur assertio nostra: 1) In expositione & consideratione cuiuscunque loci scripturæ a littera non est recedendum, ubi litteræ sensus bonus est, nec rationes gravissimæ & perspicuæ contrarium suadent: Atqui huius nostræ scripturæ, h. e. verborum sacræ cænæ, littera bonum sensum habet, nec rationes graues adsunt, quæ tropum vrgeant: E. in expositione verborum cænæ a littera recedendum non est.

Maior est regula hermeneutica & per se euidens. Habet enim sensus litteralis naturalem quandam prærogativam, a qua non, nisi magno aliquo iure, depelli potest. Est ille prior natura, qua simplex composito, rectum obliquo, nudum colorato antestat. Est etiam prior cognitione; cum audio: Herodes est vulpes, primum occurrit conceptui vulpis imago, altera demum mentis negotiatione & consideratione absurditatis feror in cognitionem tropi. Est prior doctrina, adeoque semper clarior & notior natura, etsi tempore aliquando posterior. Minor ex infra dicendis conflabit luculentius.

2) Auctor & institutor sacræ cœnæ est Dominus noster, Iesus, doctor veracissimus, beneuolentissimus, & auctoritate validissimus. Veracissimus est, adeoque neminem fallit, seu veritatem dicit tam aperte, vt ab hominibus agnosci queat. Beneuolentissimus est, quia ex amore & beneuolentia erga genus humanum sacramentum cœnæ instituit, & in vltima cœna, si vnquam, erga discipulos suam beneuolentiam contestatus est. Qui ergo negabimus, quin perspicue cum illis egerit? Est auctoritate validissimus. Huius itaque summi doctoris verba ita reuereri omnes debent, vt in interpretatione eorum a littera temere nullo modo discedatur, sed eadem follicite retineatur. (*)

3) Institutio cœnæ dominicæ, post ascensionem Christi ad cœlos, a diuersis scriptoribus in locis diuersis repetita & in litteras redacta est. Quem ad modum autem alias sacri scriptores has mutuas operas in se susceperunt, vt quod aliis forte minus plene, vel verbis minus propriis scripsisset, alius plenius, vel verbis magis propriis exprimeret: ita hi his verbis: Hoc est corpus meum: Hoc est sanguis meus, non id, quod proprie accepta important, sed hoc significare Dominus voluisset, panem esse signum corporis est, & vinum esse signum sanguinis sui; credibile non est, scriptores sacros, qui historiam institutionis omni adhibita cura descripserunt, omnes id tacuisse. Tacuerunt autem de eo omnes, nec quisquam illorum non ipsum corpus & sanguinem Christi, sed signa illorum tantum esse, quæ ad edendum & bibendum porriguntur, vel verbo indicauit.

4) Verba cœnæ locutus est Dominus Iesus, cum morti vicinus esset, & multa amplius cum discipulis suis non locuturus: Atque adeo reuera testatorem egit, qui ecclesiæ suæ corpus & sanguinem suum legauit. Ithoc vero tempore, quo morti quisque vicinus est, maxime perspicue & clare loquitur. Vnusquisque enim prudenter vitat lites heredum, quæ necessario consequuntur, vbi testamentum obscuritate per tropos laborat. Quod cum ita se habeat, vtique heredes verbis testatoris inhærere debent, quantum fieri potest. Nam si a proprietate sermonis recedendum foret, testator sine dubio id manifeste indicasset. Ea cum apud homines inueniatur prudentia: quanto magis in Saluatore!

5) Cœna dominica est sacrum conuiuium: At verba conuiuialia nunquam metonymiam signi pro signato patiuntur. Quia nemo exhibens signum panis, carnis, vini, absque ludibrio dicit: Accipe, ede, hoc est panis, caro: Bibe, hoc est vinum.

6) A littera verborum temere recedere, periculosum esse, didicit experimento Eua, Gen. III, 6. Contra litteræ constanter inhæsit magno cum fructu Abrahamus, Genes. XXII, 2.

7) Singula verba institutionis adeo clara sunt, vt tropum respuant. Nam particula demonstratiua, HOC, demonstrat quidem totum complexum, nempe panem benedictum & simul corpus Christi, ita tamen, vt corpus Christi in casu recto, panis vero in casu obliquo denotetur; quod in omnibus propositionibus exhibituiis, in quibus duo coniuncta exhibemus alicui, vsu venire solet. Copula verbalis, EST, non est capax tropi. Si enim copula, EST, amiserit suam significationem copulandi, vel vniendi prædicatum cum subiecto, ac induerit aliam; tum ipsam quoque propositionem destruxerit, ne amplius fit propositio. Si autem verbum EST idem valet, quod significat, non erit copula, sed pars prædicati. Nam si resoluatur verbum, significat, idem est, ac si dixeris: Est significans: vnde quod ex resolutione solutione provenit, verbum, EST, demum copula erit; participium vero significans non alio, quam ad prædicatum referri potest. Neque cadit tropus in corpus aut sanguinem, propter προσδιορισμὸν, quod pro nobis traditum. Nam id designatur nomine corporis & sanguinis, quod pro nobis in mortem est traditum, & qui in remissionem peccatorum pro nobis effusus est. Iam vero non signum corporis, non tropicum, non figuratum, sed verum & proprium Christi corpus pro nobis in mortem est traditum, & non tropicus, non figuratus, sed verus & proprius Christi sanguis pro nobis in peccatorum remissionem est effusus: Ergo.

8) Testamentum novum in eo differt a veteri, quod illic umbra, hic corpus exhibeatur; in illo signa, in hoc signata proponantur. Idcirco mere metonymica & significatiua theologia hic locum non habet. Nam si Dominus figuras rerum instituere voluisset, agnum paschalem retinuisset, longe evidentius mortem & promissionem Christi figurantem, ac in convivio paschali sic dixisset, Edite, hoc, notando agnum, est corpus meum, i. e. significat corpus meum pro vobis, vt olim tradendum, ita nunc traditum.


### VII. Is the ῥητόν [literal sense], or the literal sense of the words of the sacred supper to be retained?: Certain doubts are moved against our assertion

Certain doubts are moved against our assertion.

I. The sense of the words of Christ is: This bread is my body, this wine is my blood: But bread is not properly called the body of Christ, for it would follow that bread was crucified for us: Therefore, bread is metonymically and sacramentally called the body of Christ, because it is a symbol and seal of the body of Christ.

Response: The sense of the words of Christ: This is my body, this is my blood, is not: This bread is my body, this wine is my blood; but this is the literal sense: This, which I offer to you, which you are about to receive and eat, is not only bread, but is moreover my body: This, which I offer to you, and which you are about to receive and drink, is not only wine, but is moreover my blood.

II. In the words of the Holy Supper recounted from Luke, ch. XXII, 20, and Paul, 1 Cor. XI, 25, This cup is the N. T. in my blood, a figurative expression must necessarily be admitted. For cup, by metonymy, whereby the container is put for the contained, is taken for wine, and testament for the sign or seal of the testament.

Resp. 1) Distinguish between that which is not inconvenient, and that which is necessary. The sense would not be inconvenient: That which is contained in this cup is the testament in my blood; which trope would not destroy the presence of Christ, but would support it. But it is not necessary to establish that trope, because cup is taken complexly, and denotes a cup filled with wine; since Christ did not bless an empty vessel. Here the cup is considered not by way of subtraction (ἐξ ἀφαιρέσεως), but by way of addition (ἐκ προσθέσεως), insofar as it is constituted in order, office, and mystical union. The same is said to be poured out for us, 1 Cor. X, 21. and capable of blessing (εὐλογίας), 1 Cor. X, 16. 2) Nor would you inconveniently say that testament, by metonymy of the effect for the cause, denotes the cause of the testament, so that the sense may be: That which is drunk from the cup, namely my blood, is the foundation and cause of the N. T. Yet it is not necessary to explain the words of the Holy Supper by that trope. For διαθήκη not only signifies a covenant, but also, equally with the Hebrew word ברית the medium by which the covenant and pact is established, and grace and peace are granted: of which kind of media the divinely instituted sacraments are the principal ones.

Therefore, the cup taken, when spoken of in a complex way as containing both the container and the content, is properly called a new medium of divine grace and peace in the blood of Christ, that is, in respect of the blood of Christ.

3) If there is any obscurity in the words of Luke and Paul, Matthew and Mark nevertheless express the words of Christ clearly: This is my blood N., which anyone who has merely compared the words of the former part—This is my body, which all the Evangelists together with Paul retain with the highest consensus—would recognize as the very words of the Savior.

III. The body of Christ is said to be broken metaphorically, 1 Cor. XI, 24. Therefore, there is a trope in the words of the Holy Supper.

Resp. Distinguish between the ουσιατικὰ (substantial) words of the Holy Supper, and the περιστατικὰ (circumstantial) ones.

The breaking of the body of Christ denotes a circumstance and is taken improperly; because the history of the passion clearly teaches that no bone of Christ was broken, John XIX, 33. A most weighty reason therefore urges us to depart from the literal sense.

IV. The substantive verb, IS, must be explained as meaning "signifies"; because the bread is not properly or substantially the body of Christ, but its memorial, sign, and seal.

Resp.

1) No weighty reason urges us to explain IS as "signifies," since according to its literal and proper use it denotes the essence and existence of a thing.

2) The words of the Holy Supper: This is my body, do not mean the same as these: Bread is my body.

V. The proposition: This is my body, must be understood sacramentally. It is, however, a sacramental phrase, by which the names of the things signified are attributed to external symbols, because they signify and seal the things signified.

Such sacramental propositions are: 1) Circumcision is the covenant of God, Gen.

XVII, 10. 13. because it is the sign and seal of the covenant, v. 11. 2) The lamb is the passover, or the passing over, Exod.

XII, 11. i.e., it signifies the passing over of the Lord.

Resp.

1) Just as sacraments are formally not signs, but media, and such sacred actions by which God, through an earthly thing joined with the word of institution, exhibits a heavenly thing, in order to offer, confer, and seal evangelical grace: So sacramental propositions are not merely significative, but express the mystical union which exists between the earthly and the heavenly thing, and show that, through the earthly thing as a symbol and medium, the heavenly thing is truly and really exhibited.

2) Circumcision considered εὐνῶς [sic], insofar as it denotes the whole sacramental action, is properly and without any trope בְּרִית, i.e., a medium of grace and peace: since the Hebrew word denotes both a covenant and the medium by which the covenant of grace is sanctioned: But circumcision viewed μερικῶς, by reason of the external amputation of the foreskin, is a sign of the covenant. 3) Nowhere in scripture is it read: The lamb is the passing over of the Lord; but it is written: פֶּסַח הוּא, which words some render in Latin: It is the passing over of Jehovah.

For the Israelites are commanded to eat the paschal lamb in haste.

And it is added as a reason: It is the passing over of Jehovah, namely, it is near, or it is at hand, the passing over of the Lord is imminent, it is approaching.

Others, however, understand the paschal lamb as having derived its name from the passing over of the Lord, whence D.

VARENIUS in his commentary on Exodus translates: The lamb of the passing over before the Lord, that is and is called then a true Passover-lamb before the Lord, and thus the sense is: The lamb set apart, to be slaughtered and eaten at the appointed time, is the paschal lamb consecrated to God and destined for a sacrifice spoken of analogically.

From which D.

SEB.

SCHMIDIUS translates Pesach in Latin as "sacrificium praeterificum" (a sacrifice of passing over): All of which are said without any trope.

VI.

Latin:

Dubia quædam aduersus nostram assertionem mouentur.

I. Sensus verborum Christi est: Hic panis est corpus meum, hoc vinum est sanguis meus: Sed panis non dicitur proprie corpus Christi, sequeretur enim, panem pro nobis crucifixum esse: E. panis metonymice & sacramentaliter dicitur corpus Christi, quia est symbolum & sigillum corporis Christi.

Resp. Sensus verborum Christi: Hoc est corpus meum, hoc est sanguis meus, non est: Hic panis est corpus meum, hoc vinum est sanguis meus; sed hic est sensus litteralis: Hoc, quod vobis porrigo, quod vos accepturi & comesturi estis, non est tantum panis, sed est insuper corpus meum: Hoc, quod vobis porrigo, & vos accepturi bibiturique estis, non est solum vinum, sed est insuper sanguis meus.

II. In verbis S. cœnæ recensitis e Luca, c. XXII, 20. & Paulo, 1 Cor. XI, 25. Hoc poculum est N. T. in meo sanguine, necessario admittenda est figurata dictio. Nam poculum per metonymiam, qua continens ponitur pro contento, sumitur pro vino, & testamentum pro signo vel sigillo testamenti.

Resp. 1) Dist. inter id, quod non incommodum, & quod necessarium est. Non incommodus sensus esset: Id, quod in hoc poculo continetur, est testamentum in meo sanguine; qui tropus præsentiam Christi non destrueret, sed adstrueret. Sed illum tropum constituere non est necesse, quia poculum sumitur complexe, & notat poculum vino impletum; siquidem Christus non vacuo benedixit vasi. Consideratur hic poculum non ἐξ ἀφαιρέσεως, sed ἐκ προσθέσεως, quatenus in ordine, officio & vnione mystica constitutum est. Idem dicitur pro nobis effusum, 1 Cor. X, 21. & capax εὐλογίας, 1 Cor. X, 16. 2) Neque incommode dixeris, testamentum per metonymiam effecti pro caussa notare caussam testamenti, vt sensus sit: Id, quod ex poculo bibitur, nimirum sanguis meus, est fundamentum & caussa N. T. Neque tamen necesse est, per tropum illum verba S. cœnæ explicare. Nam διαθήκη non solum significat pactum, sed etiam, peræque ac vox Hebræa ברית medium, quo foedus & pactum erigitur, & gratia atque pax conceditur: cuiusmodi media praecipue sunt sacramenta divinitus instituta.

Proprie itaque poculum sumtum complexe pro continente & contento dicitur novum medium gratiae & pacis divinae in sanguine Christi, hoc est, respectu sanguinis Christi.

3) Si quidquam obscuritatis fit in verbis Lucae & Pauli, Matthaeus tamen & Marcus verba Christi clare exprimunt: Hic est sanguis meus N. , quae pro ipsis Salvatoris verbis quilibet agnoscat, qui modo contulerit verba prioris partis: Hoc est corpus meum, quae summo consensu omnes Evangelistae cum Paulo retinent.

III. Corpus Christi dicitur fractum metaphorice, 1 Cor. XI, 24. E. datur tropus in verbis S. coenae.

Resp. Dist. inter verba S. coenae ουσιατικὰ, sive substantialia, & περιστατικὰ, sive circumstantialia .

Fractio corporis Christi notat circumstantiam, & sumitur improprie; quia historia passionis clare docet, quod os nullum Christi fractum sit, Io. XIV, 33. Gravissima itaque ratio urget, ut a sensu litterali discedamus.

IV. Verbum substantivum, EST, exponendum est per significat; quia panis non proprie, aut substantialiter est corpus Christi, sed eius memoriale, signum & sigillum.

Resp.

1) Nulla nos urget gravis ratio, quare EST exponamus per significat, cum secundum litteram propriumque usum notet essentiam & existentiam rei.

2) Verba S. coenae: Hoc est corpus meum, non idem valent, ac haec: Panis est corpus meum.

V. Propositio: Hoc est corpus meum, sacramentaliter est intelligenda. Est autem phrasis sacramentalis, qua externis symbolis tribuuntur nomina rerum signatarum, quia signant & obsignant res signatas.

Eiusmodi propositiones sacramentales sunt: 1) Circumcisio est foedus Dei, Gen.

XVIII, 10. 13. quia est signum & sigillum foederis, v. 11. 2) Agnus est pascha, seu transitus, Exod.

XII, 11. i. e. significat transitum Domini.

Resp.

1) Sicut sacramenta formaliter non sunt signa, sed media, & eiusmodi actiones sacrae, quibus Deus per rem terrestrem, cum verbo institutionis coniunctam, rem coelestem exhibet, ad offerendam, conferendam & obsignandam gratiam evangelicam: Ita propositiones sacramentales non sunt mere significativae, sed exprimunt unionem mysticam, quae datur inter rem terrenam & coelestem, & ostendunt, per rem terrestrem, tanquam symbolum & medium, rem coelestem vere & realiter exhiberi.

2) Circumcisio εὐνῶς considerata, prout totam actionem sacramentalem notat, proprie & fine vllo tropo est בְּרִית, i. e. medium gratiae & pacis: siquidem vox hebraea tum foedus, tum medium, quo foedus gratiae sancitur, notat: At circumcisio spectata μερικῶς, ratione externa amputationis praeputii, est signum foederis. 3) Nuspiam in scriptura legitur: Agnus est transitus Domini; sed scriptum est: פֶּסַח הוּא, quae verba nonnulli latine reddunt: Transitus est Iehovae.

Iubentur enim Israelitae comedere agnum paschalem festinanter.

Et additur pro ratione: Transitus Iehovae est, nempe in proximo, seu prae manibus iamiam erit, instat, imminet transitus Domini.

Alii autem intelligunt agnum paschalem, a transitu Domini nomen sortitum, unde D.

VARENIVS in comm. ad Exod. vertit: Agnus transitionis coram Domino, das ist und heisst alsdenn ein recht Spring-oder Oster-lamm vor dem HErrn, adeoque sensus est: Agnus segregatus, stato tempore mactandus & comedendus, est agnus paschalis Deo consecratus & in sacrificium analogice dictum destinatus.

Ex quo D.

SEB.

SCHMIDIVS Pesach latine vertit sacrificium praeterificum: Quae omnia sine vllo tropo dicuntur.

VI.


### VII. Is the ῥητόν [literal sense], or the literal sense of the words of the sacred supper to be retained?: The substantive verb, IS, is also taken for "signifies" in other places of scripture, e.g

The substantive verb, IS, is also taken for "signifies" in other places of scripture, e.g.

The rock was Christ, 1 Cor.

X, 4.

The Apostle speaks of the rock from which water flowed in the desert, which was not Christ, except σημαντικῶς, significatively, because it signified Christ.

The seven cows are seven years, Gen.

XLI, 26.

Resp.

1) The Apostle speaks of the rock, accompanying the Israelites in the desert: Such was not that natural and properly so-called [rock], from which water flowed; but metaphorical and spiritual, namely Christ, as God, whom we also read in v. 9 was tempted by some of the people. But the spiritual rock, accompanying the Israelites everywhere, did not signify Christ, but in reality was Christ himself. Therefore, the word, IS, is not taken there σημαντικῶς [significatively], but ὑπαρκτικῶς [existentially]. 2) Seven cows are not cows properly so-called, but seen in a dream: and years by the same reasoning are years not real, but visionary. The sense is therefore: The seven dreamed cows are the seven years prefigured in the dream. 3) Those are extrasacramental propositions, the sense of which to investigate anxiously contributes little or nothing to our purpose.

VII. Such as is Paul's expression: Bread is κοινωνία, or communion of the body of Christ; such also is the expression of Christ: bread is my body. But that one is sacramental, of which this is the sense: bread is a sacrament, or a sacred sign of the communion of the body of Christ: Therefore this one also is such. Resp. 1) Christ does not say: Bread is my body. 2) The expression of Paul is not similar to the expression of Christ, but differs from this in subject and predicate. 3) Bread is not a sign, but a medium communicating the body of Christ, or a medium by which, when taken and eaten, we take and eat the body of Christ.

VIII. Whoever explains the words of the Holy Supper far otherwise than they were uttered by Christ, they explain the same by a trope: But Lutheran doctors etc. do so. Therefore. The minor is proved: because Christ said: This is my body, which the Lutherans explain: In, with and under the bread is my body. But this explanation differs much from the expression of Christ. Resp. 1) Distinguish between a periphrastic explanation and a tropical one. A periphrasis is not a trope, but only a more copious description of a thing, or a fuller explanation. 2) When in exhibitive propositions the demonstrative pronoun, THIS, demonstrates two things joined together, the exegetical particles, in, with and under, are conveniently employed for a clearer periphrasis, nor yet are they simply necessary, as was shown above.

IX. LUTHER explained the words of Christ by a synecdoche, which is indeed a trope. Resp. Distinguish between a rhetorical synecdoche and a grammatical one. LUTHER understands not the former, but the latter, and indeed not that figure which in grammar is called synecdoche; but because synecdoche, by the force of the word, denotes a complex, LUTHER rightly posits that the word τοῦτο, or THIS, is to be understood complexly, so that it may denote the body of Christ in the nominative case, but connote the bread in the oblique case.

Instance: By this reasoning the ecclesiastical proposition: Bread is the body of Christ, will be plainly rejected. Resp. That ecclesiastical proposition rightly explained is not entirely rejected, but tolerated; because the bread is understood as consecrated, and constituted in a sacramental union with the body of Christ, and so the sense is: Bread is the body of Christ sacramentally, that is, bread is a symbol, or a medium, with which the body of Christ is exhibited. For the sacramental union is more intimate and closer, although it be mystical, than that we might attain it with our senses. That this closest union might be signified, it is said: Bread is the body of Christ, i.e., the union of the bread and the body of Christ is so close that, where the sacramental bread is, there is the body of Christ, and if I take the sacramental bread, I truly also take the body of Christ. Compare SEB. SCHMIDT's treatise on the foundations of the presence of the body and blood of Christ in the Holy Supper p. 24.

Latin:

Verbum substantivum, EST, etiam in aliis scripturae locis pro significat accipitur, v. gr.

Petra erat Christus, 1 Cor.

X, 4.

Loquitur Apostolus de petra, ex qua in deserto fluxit aqua, quae non erat Christus, nisi σημαντικῶς, significative, quia significavit Christum.

Septem vacca sunt septem anni, Gen.

XLI, 26.

Resp.

1) Loquitur Apostolus de petra, comitante Israëlitas in deserto: Qualis non erat naturalis illa & proprie dicta, ex qua fluxit aqua; sed metaphorica & spiritualis, nempe Christus, vt Deus, quem etiam a quibusdam e populo tentatum legimus v. 9. Petra autem spiritualis, vbique Israëlitas comitans, non significabat Christum, sed reuera erat ipse Christus. Non ergo sumitur ibi verbum, EST, σημαντικῶς, sed ὑπαρκτικῶς. 2) Septem vaccæ non sunt vaccæ proprie dictæ, sed visæ in somnio: & anni pari ratione sunt anni non reales, sed visionales. Est igitur sensus: Septem vaccæ somniatæ sunt septem anni in somnio præfigurati. 3) Sunt propositiones illæ extrasacramentales, quarum sensum sollicite indagare, parum aut nihil facit ad nostrum institutum.

VII. Qualis est Paulli locutio: Panis est κοινωνία, vel communio corporis Christi; talis quoque est locutio Christi: panis est corpus meum. Atqui illa est sacramentalis, cuius hic est sensus: panis est sacramentum, vel sacrum signum communionis corporis Christi: Ergo & hæc talis est. Resp. 1) Non dicit Christus: Panis est corpus meum. 2) Locutio Paulli non est similis locutioni Christi, sed differt ab hac, subiecto & prædicato. 3) Panis non est signum, sed medium communicans corpus Christi, siue medium, quo sumto & manducato sumimus & manducamus corpus Christi.

VIII. Quicunque verba S. cœnæ longe aliter explicant, quam prolata sunt a Christo, illi explicant eadem per tropum: Atqui doctores Lutherani &c. Ergo. Minor probatur: quia Christus dixit: Hoc est corpus meum, quod Lutherani exponunt: In, cum & sub pane est corpus meum. Sed hæc explicatio multum differt a locutione Christi. Resp. 1) Dist. inter explicationem periphrasticam, & tropicam. Periphrasis non est tropus, sed tantum copiosior rei descriptio, aut vberior explicatio. 2) Quando in propositionibus exhibitiuis pronomen demonstratiuum, HOC, duas res coniunctas demonstrat, particulæ exegeticæ, in, cum & sub, ad luculentiorem periphrasin commode adhibentur, neque tamen simpliciter sunt necessariæ, vti supra ostensum est.

IX. LVTHERVS verba Christi exposuit per synecdochen, quæ vtique tropus est. Resp. Dist. inter synecdochen rhetoricam, & grammaticam. Non illam, sed hanc intelligit LVTHERVS, & quidem non figuram illam, quæ in grammatica vocatur synecdoche; sed quia synecdoche, vi vocis, complexionem denotat, recte statuit LVTHERVS, vocabulum τοῦτο, siue HOC, complexe intelligendum esse, vt corpus Christi in casu recto notet, panem autem in casu obliquo connotet.

Instantia: Hac ratione propositio ecclesiastica: Panis est corpus Christi, plane reiicietur. Resp. Propositio illa ecclesiastica recte exposita non prorsus reiicitur, sed toleratur; quia panis intelligitur consecratus, & in vnione sacramentali cum corpore Christi constitutus, adeoque sensus est: Panis est corpus Christi sacramentaliter, hoc est, panis est symbolum, seu medium, cum quo exhibetur corpus Christi. Vnio enim sacramentalis intimior & arctior est, licet mystica sit, quam vt nos sensibus nostris eam assequamur. Ista vnio arctissima vt significaretur, dicitur: Panis est corpus Christi, q. d. Vnio panis & corporis Christi adeo arcta est, vt, vbi est panis sacramentalis, ibi sit corpus Christi, & si ego panem scramentalem accipiam, reuera etiam accipiam corpus Christi. Confer. SEB. SCHMIDII tractat. de fundamentis præsentiæ corp. & sang. Chr. in S. cœna p. 24.


### Q. VIII. How manifold is the matter of the Lord's Supper?

…The matter of the Holy Supper is twofold, earthly, and heavenly. Prob. 1) From the nature of all sacraments, which require some external, visible, tangible element, analogous to its signatum, determined by the express word of institution, and ordained to this, that it may be an ὄχημα, a vehicle and exhibitive medium of the heavenly thing: requir ing moreover also the heavenly and intelligible thing, exhibited by the earthly visible thing as a divinely ordained medium, from which the fruit of any sacrament principally depends and flows.…

2) The heavenly thing is proposed in no sacrament more clearly than in the sacrament of the Supper by the words of institution. Wherefore, consider what IRENAEUS says, L. IV. advers. haer. c. 34: "The bread which is from the earth, receiving the invocation of God, is no longer common bread, but the Eucharist, consisting of two things, an earthly and a heavenly."

Quest. IX. What is the earthly matter of the Holy Supper? The earthly matter of the Holy Supper is, in part, bread, true in respect of substance ), concerning which, in respect of quantity—whether greater or smaller, round or oblong; in respect of quality—whether unleavened or leavened; in respect of flour—whether wheat, rye, or barley, it matters not ): In part, wine, true in respect of substance ), concerning which, whether it be red or white, pure or diluted slightly with water, it makes no difference ).

Now, bread and wine have the character of matter in the Holy Supper, insofar as they are dispensed and received, eaten and drunk ).

Prob. a. Christ, instituting the Holy Supper, took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to the disciples, Matt. XXVI, 26. Which bread is not abolished by consecration, but retains its substance.

For thus in 1 Cor. X, 25, communicants are said to eat bread, and that too already blessed or consecrated. Prob. b.

In the description of the Holy Supper, mention is made of bread, without a description of quantity or quality. The quantity of the Eucharistic bread is therefore arbitrary: yet a smaller is preferred to a larger, so that 1) men may be reminded that that bread does not serve to feed the belly, but to sanctify the soul and body: 2) that it may be distributed more conveniently among many, and 3) because of the most ancient practice of the church.

Round breads, or small cakes, which they call hosts and oblations, are rightly used in our churches.

For they are, as to matter and form, and thus as to substance, true bread; because they consist of purer wheat flour, mixed with water, and are baked by the heat of fire. Add that they have been used in the church for over 1000 years.

For by EPIPHANIUS, who lived toward the end of the IV century, in the Ancoratus, the Eucharistic bread is called στρογγυλοειδής, having a round figure. Moreover, they seem more suitable for distribution and consumption, especially for the elderly, the toothless, and the sick, than common and coarse bread.

The quality of the Eucharistic bread is also arbitrary, and it is the same whether leavened or unleavened bread is used for the distribution of the Holy Supper.

Christ indeed used unleavened bread in the first Holy Supper; because He celebrated the Supper in the days of the τῶν ἀζύμων [unleavened bread], and after the eating of the paschal lamb, at which time, according to the law of God, no bread other than unleavened was in use among the Jews.

See Exod. XII, 18;

Lev. XXIII, 6. Yet He did not institute that either unleavened or leavened bread must be used, but simply instituted bread, whatever it may be, provided it has the true nature of bread.

Whence, although Christ used unleavened bread, it is nevertheless probable that the primitive church, even in the time of the Apostles themselves, used leavened bread.

For we read in Acts XX, 6, that Paul sailed away from Philippi after the days of unleavened bread, and within five days came to Troas, and on the first day of the week the disciples came together to break bread.

But the days of unleavened bread having passed, leavened bread was in use among the Jews.

From which we probably conclude that the Apostle also used it in the celebration of the Holy Supper.

c. The other symbol and visible element is wine. For when Christ, having offered the cup, had said: Drink ye all of this, Matt. XXVI, 27. he adds in v. 29. that he would not henceforth drink ἐκ τοῦ γεννήματος τῆς ἀμπέλου, of this fruit of the vine; which is an elegant periphrasis for wine.

Prob. d. Christ determined the substance, not the quality of the wine. It is indeed made similar, that the Lord used wine tempered with water, because in the hottest regions (in which is Palestine) wines are born more generous, or stronger, than those which can be drunk comfortably without the tempering of water. But in these northern regions, where wines are not so strong, there is no necessity for water to be poured in. We distinguish between a light mixture, or the pouring of water in small quantity, and a heavy mixture or the pouring of water in large quantity. We concede that the former is lawful; but we say that the latter is not even lawful. Thus one must judge concerning the mixture, so that the odor, color, and taste may prevail.

Prob. e. Bread and wine, considered generally and in themselves, are the remote matter of the Holy Supper: But the same, viewed in sacramental use, insofar as they are consecrated and dispensed among communicants, and are received, eaten, and drunk by them, are the proximate matter of the eucharist.

Obs. The causes why Christ wished to use these symbols in particular are: 1) Because they are almost the most common, and are available at all times and everywhere: 2) These are almost the principal nutritive things in every kind of food and drink, Ps. CIV, 25: 3) The union of food and drink with our bodies is a symbol of our closest union with Christ: 4) A reminder of charity, 1 Cor. X, 17. Antithesis

Antithesis is 1) Of the Greeks, who contend sharply that leavened bread must be used in the dispensation of the Holy Supper; who call the Latins 'azymites' because of the use of unleavened bread in the eucharist, while they themselves are called 'fermentarians' by the Latins. 2) Of the Socinians, who deny that round breads, which we commonly call hosts or oblations, are to be used in the eucharist. 3) Of the Pontificians, who assert that crama, or wine mixed with water, must necessarily be used.

The Greeks' principal argument is that Christ did not celebrate the passover at the same time as the Jews, but anticipated it. Whence they conclude that leavened bread was used.

Resp. We concede that Christ did not celebrate the passover at the same time as the Jews; because on the same day that Christ had eaten the passover, they killed him, and they would not enter the praetorium, lest they be defiled so as not to eat the passover, John XVIII, 28. But Christ observed the time of the passover according to the divine institution, the Jews according to human tradition. There was a tradition among them that, if the passover fell on a προσάββατον, or the day of preparation, it should be put off to the next sabbath. For which reason the day of the sabbath (on account of the concurrence of feasts, of course) is called 'great' at that time, John XIX, 31. That Christ ate the passover on the 14th day of the first month according to the divine institution, we prove from the fact that he was otherwise most tenacious of divine commandments, and held the δευτερώσεις (secondary traditions) of the Jews in contempt; partly because in Luke XXII, 7, when the day of unleavened bread had come, in which ἔδει, i.e., it was necessary to sacrifice the passover, Christ sent Peter and John to prepare the passover: partly from the Jews' own confession concerning that translation, about which let the Chronologists be consulted. Socinians object

The Socinians object I. That bread is to be used in the administration of the Holy Supper which has the power of nourishing and strengthening the body: But hosts do not have the power of nourishing, etc. Therefore. Resp. 1) Round breads have the power of nourishing: 2) Taken in greater quantity they actually nourish: 3) We do not take much, but little, that we may acknowledge that these are not a filling from them, πλησμονὴν, ἀλλ' ἁγιασμόν, but a sanctification (as the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea speak). II. Between which bread there is no analogy with the body of Christ, that is not to be used in the eucharist: But between the hosts & the body of Christ etc.

Therefore. Resp.

1) The sacrament of the supper was not instituted primarily because of the analogy of the bread with the body of Christ, but as eucharistic bread, and κοινωνία [communion], i.e., a medium for the exhibition of the body of Christ, 1 Cor. 10, 16. 2) A greater analogy is given of thin and subtle breads with the glorified body of Christ, than of thicker breads.

III. Christ used a larger bread: Therefore let us also use the same.

Resp. Distinguish between that which is lawful, and that which is necessary. We lawfully use larger bread, but not necessarily; otherwise by the same reasoning someone might perhaps infer: Christ used unleavened bread: Therefore unleavened bread must necessarily be used in the dispensation of the supper.

IV. One bread is to be used, of which many may partake, 1 Cor.

10, 17. But hosts are not one bread etc. Therefore.

Resp. Distinguish between the unity of bread by reason of one mass, or substance, and the unity of bread by reason of sacramental office. There is one eucharistic bread, according to Paul l. c. in the whole Christian world, by reason of the sacramental duty, not by reason of mass and substance. It is one not in number, but in species, in all churches.

V. True bread is to be used in the eucharist: Hosts are not etc.

Therefore. The minor is proved: True bread has an outer crust and an inner marrow: Which cannot be said of hosts.

Resp. 1) Hosts have an outer crust, and an inner marrow, but a subtle one: 2) A toothless old woman eating the marrow eats true bread.

VI. Hosts draw their origin from the papacy.

Resp. Neg. They were in use in the time of EPIPHANIUS.

Latin:

Materia sacræ cœnæ est duplex, terrena, & cœlestis. Prob. 1) Ex natura omnium sacramentorum, quæ requirunt aliquod elementum externum, visibile, tractabile, suo signato analogum, expresso verbo institutionis determinatum, & ordinatum ad hoc, vt sit rei cœlestis ὄχημα, vehiculum & medium exhibitiuum: Requiinsuper etiam rem caelestem, & intelligibilem, re terrena visibili tanquam medio divinitus ordinato exhibitam, a qua fructus alicuius sacramenti principaliter dependet & fluit.

2) Res caelestis in nullo sacramento clarius, quam in sacramento coenae verbis institutionis proponitur. Quocirca considerate inquit IRENAEUS L. IV. aduers. haer. c. 34. Qui est a terra panis, percipiens invocationem Dei, tam non communis panis est, sed eucharistia, ex duabus rebus constans, terrena & caelesti.

Quaest. IX. Qua est materia terrena sacrae coenae? Materia terrestris sacrae coenae est partim panis, ratione substantiae verus ), qui ratione quantitatis, maior, an minor, rotundus, an oblongus; ratione qualitatis, azymus, an fermentatus; ratione farinae, triticeus, filigineus, an hordeaccus fuerit, nihil refert ): Partim vinum ratione substantiae verum ), quod rubrum, an album, merum, an aqua paulisper dilutum sit, nil interest ).

Habent autem panis & vinum rationem materiae in S. coena, quatenus dispensantur & accipiuntur, manducantur & bibuntur ).

Prob. a. Christus instituens S. coenam accepit panem, benedixit, fregit, & dedit discipulis, Matth. XXVI, 26. Qui panis per consecrationem non aboletur, sed retinet substantiam suam.

Sic enim 1 Cor. X, 25. communicantes dicuntur edere panem adeoque iam benedictum, aut consecratum. Prob. b.

In sacrae coenae descriptione panis fit mentio, sine quantitatis, aut qualitatis descriptione. Est igitur quantitas panis eucharistici arbitraria: minor tamen praefertur maiori, quo 1) homines commonefiant, panem illum non inferuire pascendo ventri, sed sanctificandae animae ac corpori: 2) vt eo commodius inter plures possit distribui, & 3) ob praxin antiquissimam ecclesiae.

Panes orbiculares, seu placentulae, quas hostias & oblatas appellant, in nostris ecclesiis recte adhibentur.

Sunt enim, quoad materiam & formam, adeoque quoad substantiam, verus panis; quia constant ex farina triticea puriore, aqua permixta, & calore ignis cocti sunt. Adiice, quod vltra 1000. annos visitati fuerint in ecclesia.

Etenim ab EPIPHANIO, qui vixit sub finem saeculi IV. in Ancorato panis eucharisticus στρογγυλοειδής rotundam figuram habens appellatur. Quin etiam ad distributionem & sumtionem praesertim senum, edentulorum & aegrotorum, videntur aptiores, quam panis vulgaris & cibarius.

Arbitraria etiam est qualitas panis eucharistici, & perinde est, siue adhibeatur ad distributionem sacrae coenae panis fermentatus, siue azymus.

Christus quidem in prima sacra coena vsus est pane azymo; quia celebravit coenam in diebus τῶν ἀζύμων, & post manducatum agnum paschalem, quo tempore, iuxta legem Dei, apud Iudaeos non alius panis, quam azymus in vsu fuit. Vid.

Exod. XII, 18. Leu.

XXIII, 6. Non tamen instituit, vt vel azymus, vel fermentatus panis adhibeatur, sed simpliciter instituit panem, qualiscunque ille fit, modo veram naturam panis habeat.

Vnde licet Christus pane azymo vsus sit, vero tamen simile est, primitivam ecclesiam, ipso Apostolorum quoque tempore, fermentato pane vsam esse.

Legimus quippe Act. XX, 6. Paullum post dies azymorum abnauigasse Philippis, & intra quinque dies Troadem venisse, vno autem sabbathorum die convenisse discipulos ad frangendum panem.

Praeterlapsis autem diebus azymorum apud Iudaeos in vsu erat panis fermentatus.

Ex quo probabiliter colligimus, eo vsum etiam esse Apostolum in celebratione sacrae coenae.

Prob. c. Alterum symbolum & elementum visibile est vinum. Cum enim Christus porrecto poculo dixisset: Bibite ex hoc omnes, Matth. XXVI, 27. subiungit v. 29. se posthac non bibiturum ἐκ τοῦ γεννήματος τῆς ἀμπέλου, ex hoc germine vitis; quæ est elegans periphrasis vini.

Prob. d. Substantiam, non qualitatem vini Christus determinavit. Vero quidem fit simile, Dominum usum esse vino aqua temperato, quod in calidissimis regionibus (in quibus est Palæstina) vina nascuntur generofiora, aut fortiora, quam quæ sine aquæ temperamento commode bibantur. Sed in his septentrionalibus regionibus, vbi vina adeo fortia non sunt, nulla aquæ affundendæ est necessitas. Distinguimus inter mixturam levem, sive affusionem aquæ in exigua copia, & inter mixtionem gravem sive affusionem aquæ in magna copia. Priorem esse licitam, concedimus; posteriorem autem ne quidem licitam esse dicimus. Ita iudicandum est de mixtura, vt odor, color & sapor prævaleat.

Prob. e. Panis & vinum, generatim & per se considerata, sunt materia remota S. cœnæ: At eadem spectata in usu sacramentali, quatenus consecrantur & dispensantur inter communicantes, & ab his accipiuntur, manducantur & bibuntur, sunt materia proxima eucharistiæ.

Obs. Causæ, cur Christus his inprimis symbolis vti voluerit, sunt: 1) Quia fere communissima, & omni tempore ac vbique parabilia sunt: 2) Præcipua hæc fere sunt in omni genere cibi & potus nutritiva, Ps. CIV, 25: 3) Vnio cibi & potus cum corporibus nostris symbolum est arctissima nostræ cum Christo vnionis: 4) Commonefactio caritatis, 1 Cor. X, 17. Antithesis

Antithesis est 1) Græcorum, qui acriter contendunt, in dispensatione S. cœnæ adhibendum esse panem fermentatum; qui Latinos ob vsum panis azymi in eucharistia azymitas vocant, ipsi autem a Latinis fermentarii appellantur. 2) Socinianorum, negantium, in eucharistia vsurpandos esse panes orbiculares, quos hostias, vel oblatas communiter nominamus. 3) Pontificiorum, afferentium, crama, sive vinum aqua mixtum, necessario adhibendum esse.

Græcorum præcipuum argumentum est, quod Christus non eodem, quo Iudæi, tempore pascha celebraverit, sed anticipaverit. Vnde fermentato pane vsum esse, colligunt.

Resp. Concedimus, Christum cum Iudæis non eodem tempore pascha celebrasse; quia eodem die, quo Christus pascha comederat, ipsum occiderunt, & prætorium, ne confeluri pascha inquinarentur, intrare noluerunt, Io. XVIII, 28. Sed Christus secundum divinam institutionem, Iudæi secundum traditionem humanam, tempus paschatis obseruarunt. Erat apud eosdem traditio, vt, si pascha incideret in προσάββατον, vel diem παρασκευῆς, in proximum sabbathum reiiceretur. Quam ob causam dies sabbathi (propter concursum scilicet festorum) magnus tunc temporis dicitur, Io. XIX, 31. Christum secundum institutionem divinam pascha 14. die primi mensis comedisse, probamus ex eo, quod alias tenacissimus fuerit mandatorum divinorum, δευτερώσεις autem Iudæorum susque deque habuerit; partim, quod Luc. XXII, 7. Christus, cum venisset dies azymorum, in quo ἔδει, i. e. oportebat mactare pascha, Petrum & Ioannem miserit, vt pascha pararent: partim ex propria Iudæorum de translatione illa confessione, de qua videantur Chronologi.

Sociniani obiiciunt I. Ille panis adhibendus est in administratione sacræ cœnæ, qui habet vim nutriendi & corpus corroborandi: Atqui hostiæ non habent vim nutriendi &c. E. Resp. 1) Habent panes orbiculares vim nutriendi: 2) Sumti in maiori copia actu nutriunt: 3) Non sumimus multum, sed parum, vt agnoscamus, hæc fumi ἐκ eis πλησμονὴν, ἀλλ' ἁγιασμόν (vt Patres Concil. Nican. loquuntur). II. Inter quem panem non datur analogia cum corpore Christi, ille in eucharistia non est adhibendus: Sed inter hostias & corpus Christi &c.

E. Resp.

1) Sacramentum coenae non primario ob analogiam panis cum corpore Christi institutum est, sed ut panis eucharisticus, & κοινωνία, i.e. medium exhibitivum corporis Christi, 1 Cor. X, 16. 2) Maior datur analogia tenuium & subtilium panium cum corpore Christi glorificato, quam panium crassiorum.

III. Christus usus est pane grandiore: E. eodem & nos utamur.

Resp. Dist. inter id, quod licitum, & quod necessarium est. Licite utimur pane grandiore, sed non necessario; ceteroqui eadem ratione quispiam forte colligeret: Christus usus est pane azymo: E. panis azymus necessario adhibendus est in dispensatione coenae.

IV. Unus adhibendus est panis, de quo plures participare queant, 1 Cor.

X, 17. Sed hostiae non sunt panis unus &c. E.

Resp. Dist. inter unitatem panis ratione unius massae, aut substantiae, & unitatem panis ratione officii sacramentalis. Unus est panis eucharisticus, iuxta Paullum l. c. in toto christiano orbe, ratione muneris sacramentalis, non ratione massae & substantiae. Unus est non numero, sed specie, in omnibus ecclesiis.

V. Verus panis adhibendus est in eucharistia: Hostiae non sunt &c.

E. Minor probatur: Verus panis habet corticem exteriorem & medullam interiorem: Quod de hostiis dici nequit.

Resp. 1) Hostiae habent corticem exteriorem, & medullam interiorem, sed subtilem: 2) Anus edentula medullam edens verum comedit panem.

VI. Hostiae e papatu trahunt originem.

Resp. Neg. Fuerunt in usu tempore EPIPHANII.


### Q. VIII. How manifold is the matter of the Lord's Supper?: Papists argue: I

Papists argue: I.

Christ in the institution of the holy supper used cramum [mixed wine], or wine tempered with water: Therefore that must be used today in the dispensation of the holy supper.

Resp. It is indeed probable that Christ, according to the custom of the region, used wine tempered with water, but it is not infallibly certain. The example of Christ can show that it is lawful to use mixed wine; but necessity is not inferred from it, since a commandment is lacking, and Christ only makes mention of the fruit of the vine.

II. Whatever was foreshadowed by the flow of blood and water from the side of Christ, that must be used in the administration of the H. supper: But wine tempered with water etc.: Therefore.

Resp. 1) We are speaking of the mixing of water and wine, not of the flow of water and blood. 3) By the flow of blood and water two sacraments of the new testament were foreshadowed, baptism and the Lord's supper.

III. The mixing of wine and water in the eucharist has many good significations, e.g., of the union of two natures in Christ, of the union of Christ with the church.

Resp. Not for the sake of signification, but for the sake of κοινωνίαν [communion] and exhibition, were the external symbols instituted by Christ.

Quaest. X. What is the heavenly matter of the holy supper?

The heavenly matter of the Lord's supper is the true & substantial body of Christ a), and likewise the true & substantial blood of Christ b).

Prob. a. That the true & substantial body of Christ is given to us in the H. supper to be eaten with the blessed bread, is most clearly evident from the unanimous & unvaried description of the H. supper made by the three Evangelists, Matt.

26, 25. Mark 14, 22. Luke 22, 19. And Paul's repetition, 1 Cor. 11, 24.: This is my body, which is given for you.

But since the true body of Christ was delivered for us unto death; it is easy to conclude that in the eucharist, with the consecrated bread, there is given to be eaten not a typical or figurative body, such as was the body of the paschal lamb, insofar as it foreshadowed or prefigured the body of Christ; not the mystical body, which is the church, Eph. 1, 23., not a sign of the body, seeing that it was not crucified for us: crucified: but the true and personal body of Christ, proper to the Son of God, and therefore full of God and majestic, in which the fullness of the divinity dwells as in its own temple, Col. II, 3. From which it follows that this body is truly life-giving, John VI, 51. The body of Christ is now glorified and most glorious. For although we always enjoy the body of Christ crucified and dead, as regards merit; yet it is no longer in that state now, but we enjoy it in the state in which it now is. Therefore it is not to be circumscribed by the rules of nature. The flesh of Christ could exist without its own hypostasis; why not also without quantitative extension? Glorified bodies are affected by the angelic duration of the aeon; why not also by an angelic 'where'? Confer DANNHAV. in Hodosoph. phænom. X. p. 1197.

Prob. b. The other part of the heavenly matter in the Holy Supper is the true and substantial blood of Christ. For by the testimony of the Evangelists, Matt. XXVI, 27-28 & Mark XIV, 23-24, Christ, having taken, consecrated, and offered the cup to be drunk, said: This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins. Wherefore, since the true blood of Christ was shed for us, it is easily evident that in the Eucharist, with the consecrated wine to be drunk, there is given not a typical or figurative blood, not a sign of blood, not the efficacy of blood, but the true blood of Christ, contained in his own veins, shed in the passion, but assumed again by the resurrected one; the blood proper to the Son of God, Acts XX, 28, and therefore most precious, ἱλαστικός [propitiatory] & λυτρωτικός [redemptive], sacrificial and redemptive, 1 Pet. I, 19, Heb. IX, 12, the federal blood, Zech. IX, 11, by which the new testament was sanctioned and confirmed; blood cleansing by sprinkling, 1 John I, 7. From which we collect: Whatever is exhibited in the Holy Supper to be eaten with the blessed bread and to be drunk with the consecrated wine, that is the heavenly matter of this holy banquet: But the true and substantial body of Christ is exhibited in the Holy Supper to be eaten with the blessed bread, and the true and substantial blood of Christ to be drunk with the consecrated wine: Therefore. The major premise is evident in itself: for whatever is exhibited in a banquet, or offered to be eaten and drunk, that is the matter of the banquet. But the body and blood of Christ is the heavenly matter; because it is the body and blood proper to the Son of God, and is distinguished from earthly matter, namely bread and wine.

Dicis: I. When Christ said: This is my body, he did not wish to designate his body as the heavenly matter in this sacrament, under the aspect of exhibition; because 1) he himself sat at the table, and 2) if he himself ate of this bread, he would have eaten himself, and also 3) when he spoke, he would have been simultaneously mute and speaking; which is contradictory and absurd.

Resp. To I. Christ sat at the table in a natural manner: but he gave his body to be eaten sacramentally. To II. Christ indeed ate the paschal bread, but not the eucharistic bread; just as he also did not drink the eucharistic wine. For Mark c. XIV, 23 testifies that all drank from the blessed cup, but the Apostles, to whom the command of eating the body of Christ with bread, and drinking his blood with wine, pertained. To III. Christ was speaking according to the natural condition, and simultaneously was not speaking according to the supernatural condition; which are not contradictory.

Dicis: II. The blood of Christ is not the heavenly matter of the Holy Supper, for the reason that, as Luke XXII, 20 and Paul, 1 Cor. XI, 25 report, Christ, instituting the Eucharist, said: This cup is the new testament in my blood. Resp. Distinguish between a real proposition and a customary one. In the former, a thing is predicated of a thing; in the latter, the use is predicated of a thing. Luke and Paul in the cited words refer to the use of the Lord's Supper: of which kind a customary proposition also is, when baptism is called the stipulation of a good conscience, 1 Pet. III, 21.

Latin:

Pontificii argumentantur: I.

Christus in institutione sacrae coenae usus est cramate, sive vino aqua temperato: E. illud hodie in dispensatione sacrae coenae usurpandum est.

Resp. Probabile quidem est, Christum ex more regionis usum esse vino aqua temperato, sed non infallibiliter certum est. Exemplum Christi ostendere potest, cramate esse licitum; sed necessitas ex eo non infertur, cum desit praeceptum, & Christus tantum mentionem faciat germinis vitis.

II. Quidquid adumbratum est fluxu sanguinis & aquae e latere Christi, illud adhibendum est in administratione S. coenae: Sed vinum aqua temperatum &c.: Ergo.

Resp. 1) Sermo nobis est de mixtione aquae & vini, non de confluxu aquae & sanguinis. 3) Fluxu sanguinis & aquae adumbrata sunt duo sacramenta novi testamenti, baptismus & coena dominica.

III. Mistio vini & aquae in eucharistia multas bonas habet significationes, v. gr. unionis duarum naturarum in Christo, unionis Christi cum ecclesia.

Resp. Non propter significationem, sed propter κοινωνίαν & exhibitionem, symbola externa a Christo sunt instituta.

Quaest. X. Quae est materia caelestis sacrae coenae?

Materia caelestis coenae dominicae est verum & substantiale Christi corpus a), verus item & substantialis Christi sanguis b).

Prob. a. Verum & substantiale Christi corpus in S. coena nobis cum pane benedicto manducandum dari, luculentissime patet ex unanimi & invariata S. coenae descriptione facta a tribus Euangelistis, Matth.

XXVI, 25. Marc. XIV, 22. Luc. XXII, 19. Paullique repetitione, 1 Cor. XI, 24.: Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis datur.

Cum autem verum Christi corpus pro nobis in mortem traditum sit; collectu proclive est, quod in eucharistia cum pane consecrato manducandum detur non corpus typicum, aut figurativum, quale erat corpus agni paschalis, quatenus adumbrabat, aut praefigurabat corpus Christi; non corpus mysticum, quod est ecclesia, Eph. I, 23., non signum corporis, quippe quod pro nobis non est crucifixum: sed corpus Christi verum & personale, Filii Dei proprium, adeoque Deo plenum & maiestaticum, in quo plenitudo divinitatis, velut in proprio templo habitat, Col. II, 3. Ex quo consequitur, quod hoc corpus sit vere vivificum, Io. VI, 51. Est corpus Christi nunc glorificatum & gloriosissimum. Etsi enim corpore Christi crucifixo ac mortuo semper fruamur, quoad meritum; non tamen nunc est amplius in illo statu, sed in quo statu nunc est, eo fruimur ipso. Non ergo circumscribendum est naturæ regulis. Potuit caro Christi esse sine propria ὑποστάσει; quidni etiam sine extensione quantitativa? Afficiuntur corpora gloriosa duratione angelica ævi; quidni etiam ubi angelico? Confer. DANNHAV. in hodosoph. phænom. X. pag. 1197.

Prob. b. Altera pars materiæ cœlestis in S. cœna est verus & substantialis Christi sanguis. Etenim testibus Evangelistis, Matth. XXVI, 27. 28. & Marc. XIV, 23. 24. Christus accepto, consecrato & exhibito ad bibendum poculo, dixit: Hoc est sanguis meus ille novi testamenti, qui pro multis effunditur in remissionem peccatorum. Quare cum verus Christi sanguis pro nobis effusus sit, ex facili patet, quod in eucharistia cum vino consecrato bibendus non detur non sanguis typicus, aut figurativus, non signum sanguinis, non efficacia sanguinis, sed verus Christi sanguis, in venis ipsius contentus, in passione effusus, sed a resurgente iterum assumtus; sanguis Filii Dei proprius, Act. XX, 28. ideoque pretiosissimus, ἱλαστικός & λυτρωτικός, sacrificialis & redemptorius, 1 Petr. I, 19. Hebr. IX, 12. sanguis fœderalis, Zach. IX, 11. quo novum testamentum sancitum & confirmatum est; sanguis aspersione mundans, 1 Io. I, 7. Ex quibus colligimus: Quidquid cum pane benedicto comedendum, & cum vino consecrato bibendum in S. cœna exhibetur, illud est materia cœlestis sancti huius convivii: Atqui corpus Christi verum & substantiale, cum pane benedicto comedendum, & sanguis Christi verus & substantialis, cum vino consecrato bibendum, in S. cœna exhibetur: E. Maior est per se evidens: quidquid enim in convivio exhibetur, aut porrigitur comedendum & bibendum, illud est materia convivii. Est autem corpus & sanguis Christi materia cœlestis; quia est corpus & sanguis Filii Dei proprius, & distinguitur a materia terrena, scilicet pane & vino.

Dicis: I. Cum Christus dixit: Hoc est corpus meum, non voluit corpus suum designare, tanquam materiam cœlestem in hoc sacramento, sub ratione exhibitionis; quia 1) ipse assedit mensæ, & 2) cum ipse ederet de pane hoc, semetipsum comedisset, nec non 3) cum locutus fuerit, simul fuerit mutus & loquens; quod contradictorium & absurdum est.

Resp. Ad I. Christus assedit mensæ modo naturali: sed corpus suum manducandum dedit sacramentaliter. Ad II. Christus comedit quidem panem paschalem, sed non panem eucharisticum; sicut etiam non bibit vinum eucharisticum. Testatur enim Marcus c. XIV, 23. bibisse ex poculo benedicto omnes, sed Apostolos, ad quos mandatum edendi cum pane corpus Christi, & bibendi cum vino sanguinem ipsius spectabat. Ad III. Christus loquebatur, secundum conditionem naturalem, & simul non loquebatur, secundum conditionem supernaturalem; quæ non sunt contradictoria.

Dicis: II. Sanguis Christi non est materia cœlestis sacræ cœnæ, ideo, quod referente Luca XXII, 20. & Paullo, 1 Cor. XI, 25. Christus eucharistiam instituens dixit: Hoc poculum est novum testamentum in meo sanguine. Resp. Dist. inter propositionem realem, & vsualem. In illa res de re, in hac vsus de re prædicatur. Lucas & Paullus verbis citatis respiciunt vsum cœnæ dominicæ: cuiusmodi vsualis propositio etiam est, cum baptismus dicitur stipulatio bona conscientiæ, 1 Petr. III, 21.


### Q. VIII. How manifold is the matter of the Lord's Supper?: Q. XI

Q. XI.

The sacramental union in the use of the Holy Supper is a true and real conjunction of the earthly and heavenly matter, by which, from the will and power of Christ the institutor, the external elements, bread and wine, being consecrated, are united with the heavenly thing expressed by the word of institution, namely the body and blood of Christ, into one sacrament, so that on account of this union, in the very use of this sacrament, the body and blood of Christ are exhibited to all communicants to be eaten and drunk orally with the bread and wine, in commemoration of the death of Christ.

Obj. I. We are not here speaking of the personal union of the divine and human nature in Christ, the God-man (θεανθρώπῳ), nor of the spiritual union of the souls of the faithful with Christ; but of the sacramental union, which is not merely significative (σημαντική), or significative, nor typical (τυπική), prefigurative, nor only operative (ἐνεργητική), or operative, nor relative (σχετική), or relative, nor natural (φυσική) or local; but it is substantial, by reason of the extremes, even if it is sacramental by reason of the mode, through a true and real conjunction, and the simultaneous exhibition of the body of Christ with the blessed bread, and of the blood of Christ with the blessed wine, in the use of the sacrament of the Supper.

Obj. II. The mathematical point of time, when precisely the earthly and heavenly thing are united in the Eucharist, cannot be defined; because the Lord promised the presence of his body and blood not for the execution of one, but of several required actions, which require some latitude of time, and among which actions the last are the eating and drinking. For he said: Take, eat, this is my body, Matt. XXVI, 26. Therefore, to take the bread, to bless, to distribute, to eat, are required together, so that the body of Christ united with the bread may exist. In the same manner, it is to be understood concerning the wine, when it is to be joined with the blood of Christ. Cf. Hulsem. breu. c. XIII. p. 858.

Obj. III. The sacramental union of the earthly and heavenly thing brings about a mutual presence and communication of the bread and the body, and likewise of the wine and the blood of Christ, so that the blessed bread is the vehicle of the body, and the blessed wine is the vehicle of the blood of Christ.

The assertion is proved: 1) Whatever Christ offers to us in the Holy Supper to be eaten with the blessed bread, and to be drunk with the blessed wine, that must be joined and united with the eucharistic bread and wine in the use of this sacrament: But he offers his body and blood &c. Therefore.

2) From the Apostolic testimony. Paul says distinctly: The cup of blessing, which we bless, is it not (is) the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? 1 Cor. X, 16. Where a true and real communion is given, there a true and real union is given, and communion (κοινωνία) cannot have any place without union; because communion is the effect of union.

3) Because from the earthly and heavenly thing one sacrament is made, it cannot be made without some intervening union.

Latin:

Quaest. XI. Qualis est unio materiae terrenae & caelestis in usu S. cenae?

Vnio sacramentalis in usu S. cenae est vera & realis materiae terrenae & caelestis coniunctio, qua, ex voluntate & virtute Christi instituentis, externa elementa, panis & vinum, consecrata, cum re caelesti, verbo institutionis expressa, corpore videlicet & sanguine Christi, ad unum sacramentum uniuntur, ut propter hanc unionem, in ipso sacramenti huius usu, corpus & sanguis Christi cum pane & vino oraliter manducanda & bibenda exhibeantur omnibus communicantibus, in commemorationem mortis Christi.

Obs. I. Non est nobis in praesenti sermo de unione personali divinae & humanae naturae in Christo θεανθρώπῳ, neque de unione spirituali animarum fidelium cum Christo; sed de unione sacramentali, quae non est mere σημαντική, aut significatiua, neque τυπική, prefiguratiua, neque tantum ἐνεργητική, seu operatiua, neque σχετική, seu relatiua, φυσική naturalis aut localis; sed est substantialis, ratione extremorum, etsi sacramentalis sit ratione modi, per veram & realem coniunctionem, & simultaneam exhibitionem corporis Christi cum pane benedicto, & sanguinis Christi cum vino benedicto, in sacramenti cenae usu.

Obs. II. Punctum temporis mathematicum, quando praecise uniantur res terrena ac caelestis in eucharistia, definiri nequit; propterea, quod non ad unius, sed plurium correquifitarum actionum exsecutionem, quae aliquam temporis latitudinem requirit, & inter quas actiones ultimae sunt comestio ac bibitio, Dominus praesentiam corporis & sanguinis sui promisit.
