Dixit enim: Accipite, edite, hoc est corpus meum, Matth. XXVI, 26. Accipere igitur panem, benedicere, distribuere, edere, simul correquiruntur, ut existat corpus Christi unitum cum pane. Eundem ad modum de vino, cum sanguine Christi coniungendo, sentiendum est. Conf. Hvlsem. breu. c. XIII. p. 858.

Obs. III. Vnio sacramentalis rei terrenae & caelestis infert mutuam praesentiam & communicationem panis & corporis, vini itidem & sanguinis Christi, ut panis benedictus sit vehiculum corporis, & vinum benedictum sit vehiculum sanguinis Christi.

Probatur assertum: 1) Quidquid Christus cum pane benedicto manducandum, & cum vino benedicto bibendum in sacra cena nobis porrigit, illud in usu huius sacramenti oportet esse cum pane & vino eucharistico coniunctum atque unitum: Atqui corpus & sanguinem suum &c. Ergo.

2) Ex testimonio Apostolico. Paullus diserte dicit: Poculum benedictionis, cui benedicimus, nonne (est) communicatio sanguinis Christi? Quem panem frangimus, nonne is communicatio corporis Christi est? 1 Cor. X, 16. Vbi vera & realis datur communicatio, ibi vera & realis datur unio, neque κοινωνία locum ullum habere potest sine unione; quia communicatio est effectus unionis.

3) Quia e re terrena & caelesti fit unum sacramentum, non potest fieri sine intercedente aliqua unione.


### Q. XII

Are the substantial body of Christ, and the substantial blood of Christ, truly present in the sacrament of the Supper? The true and substantial body and blood of Christ are really present in the use of the Holy Supper.

Obj. I. Distinguish between physical presence, and hyperphysical. Physical presence is local and circumscriptive, proper to bodies naturally behaving themselves. The mode of hyperphysical, or supernatural presence (i.e., which we cannot attain by natural perception), is twofold, definitive, and repletive. A finite being is definitively present, which without local occupation of space in a certain way . In this manner angels are present, who, since they are spiritual essences, cannot be measured by an interval of place. This definitive mode of presence will also be common to our own bodies in eternal life. In this manner Christ also acted, when he went forth from the tomb through the sepulchral stone, and when he entered to the disciples through closed doors. In which manner the body of Christ is also not inconveniently posited to be present to the elemental bread in the use of the Holy Supper: although, furthermore, there is added a sacramental union of the bread with the body of Christ, which does not depend precisely or simply upon this definitive mode of presence, but upon a special divine promise.

Repletive presence is omnipresence, which belongs to God alone by himself and essentially, and to the human nature of Christ through union with the divine, and personally.

Objection II. Distinction between objective, or intentional, presence, and true and real presence. Something is said to be objectively present by this, that it is actually an object of our cognition, or that it is known by a cognitive power, such as our intellect. But that which is present only by this, that it is known by the intellect, is not really present: For that which is present really, is present without this, that it is known by the intellect. Therefore, that which is only objectively present, is present only through its species, not in itself. But that which is not present in itself, but only through a species impressed upon the intellect, how can it be truly and really present? If in a common banquet conversation should fall upon the King of France, and upon the exquisite delicacies of food and drink with which the royal table is furnished; it is rightly said that the King of France and his dishes are present there objectively, while they are known through their species impressed upon the intellect: But who would bear someone saying that the King of France and the royal dishes are truly and really present at that banquet? Furthermore, it is certain that even those beings of reason, which are feigned to be, when they neither are nor can be, have their own objective presence: as when I conceive a chimera, or a goat-stag, which nevertheless are not truly and really present to the one conceiving them. That which is present to someone truly and really, is present according to its true and real being: Who therefore becomes truly and really present to someone, which neither has, nor can have, its own true and real being, but consists entirely in fiction?

Obf. III. The body of Christ is present distinctly to the eucharistic bread, and the blood of Christ to the blessed wine; because Christ willed that the distribution be made through distinct symbols. But that discrete exhibition does not entail separation, so that the body is really separated from the blood. Whence we distinguish between material, personal, and sacramental presence; in which last mode alone the body of Christ, and his blood, is present in the use of the Holy Supper. Thus, although the blood is inseparable from the body of Christ, as regards natural and personal presence, yet by sacramental presence they can be distinctly present and exhibited; because this sacrament does not result from nature, by the force of which the body of Christ is not without blood; nor from personal union, according to which the blood, just as the body, is assumed into the hypostasis of the Son of God; but solely from the ordination and institution of Christ, by which these things were ordered to the distinct distribution and eating of the body of Christ with the blessed bread, and the drinking of the blood of Christ with the blessed wine.

Obf. IV. The question is not about the virtual or operative presence of Christ, i.e., whether Christ is present in the Holy Supper through effect or operation, as the sun is present to us through light and heat; nor about significative or prefigurative presence, as the body of the paschal lamb in the Old Testament foreshadows the body of Christ; but about the sacramental, real, and substantial presence of the body and blood of Christ in the action of the Holy Supper.

Our assertion is proven: 1) From the words of institution. Whatever is exhibited in the Holy Supper to be eaten and drunk by the mouth of the body, that is substantially and undistantly present to the communicants in the Holy Supper: But the body and blood of Christ is that which is exhibited in the Holy Supper to be eaten and drunk by the mouth of the body: Therefore, the body and blood of Christ are substantially and immediately present to those communicating in the Holy Supper. The major premise is evident in itself, unless you wish to say that what is exhibited to the communicants to be eaten and drunk is not eaten and drunk by them in the Holy Supper. For it implies a contradiction that something should be eaten or drunk by the mouth of the body which is not substantially and immediately present to the one eating and drinking. The minor premise is also manifest from the words of institution. For, having exhibited the blessed bread, the Savior says to His disciples: Take, eat, this is my body. Likewise, having exhibited the blessed cup: Drink from it, all of you. For this is my blood, that blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins, Matt. XXVI, 26. 27. 28. Where the words of the command, "eat, drink," are undoubtedly to be understood concerning oral eating and drinking, which is the only eating and drinking properly so called. Which drinking Mark also commemorates as having been performed immediately at the Lord's command, ch. XIV, 23: And they all drank of it. The word "drank" designates an external act, concerning which testimony could be borne. Now, that the body and blood of Christ itself is that which is exhibited to be eaten and drunk by the mouth of the body in the Holy Supper is likewise clear from the words of institution. For when Christ commanded the disciples, He immediately adds, explaining the object which must be eaten: This is my body. And when He had commanded them to drink, He adds, explaining the object which must be drunk: This is my blood. What else is this than Christ commanding His body to be eaten and His blood to be drunk?

2) From the periphrasis of the blood of Christ. For as Matthew reports, ch. XXVI, 28, Christ described the object of the drinking thus: This is my blood, that blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins. Indeed, just as when the law had been promulgated, and the people had bound themselves by its religion, Moses, sprinkling it with the blood of victims, spoke thus: Behold the blood of the covenant, which Jehovah has made with you concerning all these words, Exod. XXIV, 8; so Christ, exhibiting His own blood—than which nothing is more precious—soon to be shed on the altar of the cross, in the newly instituted sacrament, says: This is my blood, etc. From which we gather: In the same sense that the blood of bulls is called the blood of the O.T., in that same sense the blood of Christ is called the blood of the N.T. But the blood of bulls is called the blood of the O.T. not significantly, but effectively and constitutively, through real presence; Therefore. In particular, the words of Luke, ch. XXII, 20, This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you, most clearly demonstrate the virtue of the blood of Christ present in the chalice. For nothing is more certain than that the cup is shed for us not by reason of the matter, nor by reason of the wine contained, but solely in respect of the blood of Christ. For either wine is present in the cup without blood, or the blood of Christ with the wine. Not the former; because that which is present is the basis of the ratified new testament, and which is shed for us. But wine alone is not the basis of the new testament, nor was wine shed for us. Therefore, the blood is present with the wine.

3) From the true and real κοινωνίᾳ [communion], which is between the eucharistic bread and the body of Christ, and likewise between the wine and the blood of Christ, as Paul testifies, 1 Cor. X, 16. Where there is a true and real communication of the distributed bread with the body, and of the consecrated wine with the blood of Christ, there is a true and real presence of the body and blood of Christ with the blessed bread and wine: But in the eucharist, etc.

4) From the guilt of the body and blood of the Lord, of which Paul speaks, 1 Cor. XI, 27. Those who incur guilt against the body and blood of the Lord by unworthily eating and drinking it must have the body and blood of the Lord really present to them: But impenitent sinners &c. E.

5) From the necessary discernment of the Lord’s body, of which Paul speaks in 1 Cor. XI, 29. For if the body of Christ in the Eucharist must be discerned from common food, it must certainly be present truly and really: But the antecedent is true: Therefore, also the consequent.

6) From the testimony of the blood of Christ concerning our salvation in these lands, of which John speaks in 1 Ep. c. V, 8. There are three that bear witness on earth, the Spirit, the water, and the blood. He who bears witness on earth must be present on earth: But the blood of Christ, etc. Therefore.

7) From the absurdities that follow the contrary opinion. If the body and blood of Christ are not truly and really present in the Holy Supper, it follows: 1) that only naked sacramental symbols are left: 2) that the sacramental signs of the N.T. are more obscure than the signs of the O.T.; for indeed the paschal lamb represented the death of Christ more clearly than the eucharistic bread: 3) that Christ is no more present in the Eucharist than He was present to the fathers of the O.T.

8) Christ, who is the only-begotten Son of God, and Himself true God and omnipotent, can easily perform this through His omnipotent power, so that He may cause His body and blood, endowed with divine subsistence, to be present in that divine subsistence in the H.

Latin:

Verum & substantiale Christi corpus atque sanguis in usu S. cenae realiter praesto est.

Obs. I. Distingue inter praesentiam physicam, & hyperphysicam. Praesentia physica est localis & circumscriptiva, corporum naturaliter se habentium propria. Praesentiae hyperphysicae, siue supernaturalis (h. e. quem nos naturali perceptione adsequi non possumus), modus est duplex, definitiuus, & repletiuus, Definitiue praesens est ens finitum, quod citra localem spatii occupationem in certo vi est. Hoc modo praesentes sunt angeli, qui cum sint essentiae spirituales, loci intercapedine mensurari nequeunt. Hic modus adessendi definitiuus nostris etiam corporibus in vita aeterna erit communis. Hoc modo Christus quoque vsus est, quando per lapidem sepulcralem egressus est monumento, quando per clausas ianuas introiuit ad discipulos. Quo modo corpus Christi etiam pani elementari in vsu sacrae coenae adesse haud incommode statuitur: licet insuper etiam accedat vnio sacramentalis panis cum corpore Christi, quae non ex modo isto praesentiae definitiuo praecise, aut simpliciter, sed ex peculiari promissione diuina dependet.

Praesentia repletiva est omnipraesentia, quae soli Deo competit per se & essentialiter, humanae Christi naturae per vnionem cum diuina, & personaliter.

Obs. II. Dist. inter praesentiam obiectiuam, siue intentionalem, & praesentiam veram atque realem. Obiectiue praesens aliquid dicitur per hoc, quod actu est obiectum nostrae cognitionis, siue quod a potentia cognoscente, veluti ab intellectu nostro, cognoscitur. Quod vero tantum per hoc praesens est, quod ab intellectu cognoscitur, id realiter praesens non est: Nam quod praesens est realiter, id praesens est citra hoc, quod ab intellectu cognoscitur. Ergo quod tantum obiectiue praesens est, tantum per sui speciem, non in seipso praesens est. Quod autem non in seipso praesens est, sed tantum per speciem impressam intellectui, quomodo id vere & realiter praesens esse queat? Si in conuiuio vulgari sermo incidat de rege Galliae, deque ciborum potusque exquisitis deliciis, quibus mensa regia instruitur; recte dicitur, regem Galliae eiusque dapes ibidem praesentes esse obiectiue, dum, per species eorum, intellectui impressas, cognoscuntur: Sed quis ferat dicentem, regem Galliae dapesque regias in conuiuio isto vere & realiter praesentes esse? Praeterea constat, etiam illis entibus rationis, quae finguntur esse, cum nec sint, nec esse possint, suam esse praesentiam obiectiuam: veluti cum chimaeram concipio, aut hircoceruom, quae tamen concipienti vere & realiter praesentia non sunt. Quod alicui praesens est vere & realiter, secundum esse suum verum & reale praesens est: Qui ergo vere & realiter praesens fit alicui, quod esse suum verum & reale nec habet, nec habere potest, sed totum fictione constat? *

Obs. III. Distincte adest corpus Christi pani eucharistico, & sanguis Christi vino benedicto; quia per distincta symbola distributionem fieri voluit Christus.* Illa autem discreta exhibitio non infert separationem, vt corpus realiter separetur a sanguine. Vnde distinguimus inter praesentiam materialem, personalem, & sacramentalem; quo vltimo tantum modo corpus Christi, & sanguis eius vino adest in S. coena vsu. Ita, etsi sanguis a corpore Christi, qua praesentiam naturalem & personalem, inseparabilis fit, sacramentali tamen praesentia distincte adesse & exhiberi possunt; quia hoc sacramentum non redundat e natura, vi cuius corpus Christi non est sine sanguine; nec ex vnione personali, iuxta quam aeque sanguis, ac corpus in hypostasin Filii Dei assumptus est; sed vnice ex ordinatione & institutione Christi, qua haec ordinata sunt ad distinctam distributionem, & manducationem corporis Christi cum pane benedicto, & bibitionem sanguinis Christi cum vino benedicto. *

Obs. IV. Non est quaestio de praesentia Christi virtuali, aut operativa, h.* e. an Christus adsit in S. coena per effectum vel operationem, quomodo sol nobis praesens est per lumen & calorem; nec de praesentia significativa, aut prefiguratiua, quomodo corpus agni paschalis in V. T. adumbrat corpus Christi; sed de praesentia sacramentali, reali & substantiali corporis & sanguinis Christi in actione S. coenae.

Probatur assertio nostra: 1) Ex verbis institutionis. Quidquid in sacra coena exhibetur ore corporis manducandum & bibendum, illud in S. coena communicantibus substantialiter & indistanter praesens est: Atqui corpus & sanguis Christi est illud, quod in S. coena exhibetur ore corporis manducandum & bibendum: E. corpus & sanguinis Christi in S. cœna communicantibus substantialiter & instanter præsens est. Maior ex se est evidens, nisi dicere velis, non manducari bibique a communicantibus in S. cœna, quod manducandum & bibendum illis exhibetur. Nam manducari aliquid aut bibi ore corporis, quod manducanti & bibenti non substantialiter & indistanter præsens fit, contradictionem implicat. Minor quoque manifesta est ex verbis institutionis. Nam, exhibito pane benedicto, ait Servator discipulis suis: Accipite, comedite, hoc est corpus meum. Similiter, exhibito poculo benedicto; Bibite ex eo omnes. Hoc enim est sanguis meus, sanguis ille novi testamenti, qui pro multis effunditur in remissionem peccatorum, Matth. XXVI, 26. 27. 28. Vbi verba mandati: comedite, bibite, de manducatione & bibitione orali, quæ sola proprie dicta manducatio & bibitio est, haud dubie sunt accipienda: Quam bibitionem etiam statim ad mandatum Domini peractam commemorat Marcus, c. XIV, 23. Et biberunt ex eo omnes. Verbum, biberunt, externum actum designat, de quo testimonium perhiberi poterat. Iam ipsum corpus & sanguinem Christi esse illud, quod ore corporis manducandum & bibendum exhibetur in S. cœna, perinde ex verbis institutionis perspicuum est. Nam cum Christus discipulos iussit statim addit, exponens obiectum, quod comedi debet: Hoc est corpus meum. Et cum iussisset ipsos bibere, addit, exponens obiectum, quod bibi debet: Hoc est sanguis meus. Quod ipsum quid aliud est, quam Christum corpus suum comedendum, & sanguinem suum bibendum præcipere?

2) Ex periphrasi sanguinis Christi. Referente enim Matthæo, c. XXVI, 28. Christus obiectum bibitionis sic descripsit: Hoc est sanguis meus ille novi testamenti, qui pro multis effunditur in remissionem peccatorum. Nempe quemadmodum, cum lex esset promulgata, eiusque religione se obstrinxisset populus, Moses illum sanguine victimarum aspergens, sic allocutus est: Ecce sanguis fœderis, quod pepigit Iehouah vobiscum super omnibus verbis his, Exod. XXIV, 8. ita Christus, proprium sanguinem suum, quod nihil pretiosius, mox in ara crucis fundendum, instituto novo sacramento exhibens, inquit: Hoc est sanguis meus &c. Ex quibus colligimus: Quo sensu sanguis taurorum sparsus dicitur sanguis V. T. eo sensu sanguis Christi dicitur sanguis N. T. Atqui sanguis taurorum dicitur sanguis V. T. non significatve, sed effective & constitutive, per realem præsentiam; E. Inprimis verba Lucæ, c. XXII, 20. Hoc poculum est novum testamentum in meo sanguine, quod pro vobis effunditur, virtutem sanguinis Christi, in calice præsentis, clarissime demonstrant. Nihil enim certius est, quam poculum non ratione materiæ, nec ratione vini contenti, sed solius sanguinis Christi respectu, pro nobis effusum esse. Aut enim in poculo præsens est vinum sine sanguine, aut sanguis Christi cum vino. Non illud; quia id præsens est, quod est basis sanciti novi testamenti, quodque pro nobis effunditur. Vinum autem tantum non est basis novi testamenti, nec vinum pro nobis effusum est. Sanguis igitur cum vino præsto est.

3) E vera & reali κοινωνίᾳ, quæ est inter panem eucharisticum & corpus Christi, inter vinum itidem & sanguinem Christi, teste Paulo, 1 Cor. X, 16. Vbi est vera & realis communicatio panis distributi cum corpore, & vini consecrati cum sanguine Christi, ibi est vera & realis præsentia corporis & sanguinis Christi cum pane & vino benedicto: Atqui in eucharistia &c. E.

4) E corporis & sanguinis Domini reatu, de quo Paullus 1 Cor. XI, 27. Qui reatum incurrunt corporis & sanguinis Domini, indigne illud manducando & bibendo, illis corpus & sanguinem Domini realiter adesse oportet: At impœnitentes peccatores &c. E.

5) Ex necessaria corporis Domini discretione, de qua Paulus 1 Cor. XI, 29. Si enim discernendum est corpus Christi in eucharistia, a cibo vulgari, oportet utique id vere & realiter adesse: Atqui verum est antecedens: E. & consequens.

6) Ex testimonio sanguinis Christi de nostra salute in his terris, de quo Ioannes 1 Ep. c. V, 8. Tres sunt qui testantur in terra, Spiritus, aqua & sanguis. Qui testatur in terra, illum in terra oportet esse praesentem: Atqui sanguis Christi &c. E.

7) Ex absurdis, quae contrariam sententiam sequuntur. Si corpus & sanguis Christi vere & realiter non adsunt in sacra coena, sequitur: 1) nuda tantum relinqui symbola sacramentalia: 2) signa sacramentalia N. T. esse obscuriora signis V. T.; clarius quippe agnus paschalis mortem Christi repraesentabat, quam panis eucharisticus: 3) Christum non magis esse praesentem in eucharistia, quam fuit praesens patribus V. T.

8) Christus, qui unigenitus Filius Dei est, & ipse verus Deus atque omnipotens, per omnipotentem suam virtutem praestare hoc facile potest, ut corpus & sanguinem suum, divina subsistentia praedita, in ista divina subsistentia sistat praesentia in S. coena, ubicunque illa & quandocunque celebratur.


### Q. XII (continued)

Supper, wherever and whenever it is celebrated. If anyone denies this, we oppose to him the divine omnipotence, by which the angel Gabriel once confirmed the virgin Mary, saying, Luke I, 37: Nothing shall be impossible with God.

The Antithesis is that of the Anabaptists, Arminians, Socinians, and Schwenkfeldians, who deny the true and real presence of the body and blood of Christ in the H. Supper.

Their arguments are: I. Every natural body is in a certain and determined place, and therefore not in many places where the sacrament of the Supper is administered: But the body of Christ, etc. Therefore.

Resp. 1) Distinguish between a body called natural by reason of substance, and by reason of affections, or qualities. The body of Christ is a true and natural body by reason of substance, but by reason of affections it is glorified and majestic, and therefore supernatural. 2) No natural body can be in several places by the powers of nature, yet the presence of some body can be multiplied by the omnipotence of God, without its essence being multiplied. What is impossible to nature is possible to God. Let us grant, therefore, that God can do something which we confess we cannot understand.

3) Suppose that no body, subsisting in a finite and created subsistence, can be in several places; yet it is otherwise with the body of Christ, which is assumed into the infinite ὑπόστασιν τοῦ λόγου [hypostasis of the Word]: This the Son of God can and will cause to be present through His omnipotent power, wherever and whenever the Holy Supper is celebrated. Instance: Christ assumed a human body, the same in species as our body, Hebr. II, 14. Therefore, it enjoys the same affections. Resp. As close as the body of Christ the θεανθρώπου [God-man] approaches the condition of a body ψιλῶς ἀνθρώπου [merely human] regarding essence, by so long an interval does it differ from the same regarding subsistence, and the consequence of this, the participation of divine majesty, so that all the fullness of the divinity dwells in Him σωματικῶς [bodily], Col. II, 9.

II. Whatever doctrine overturns the truth of Christ’s human nature, that is not to be asserted: But the doctrine of the substantial presence of the body of Christ in the Holy Supper overturns, etc. Therefore. The minor is proved: because every true human body is visible, palpable, and circumscribed in a certain place; such is not the body which is said to be under the hosts in several places.

Resp. Every body is visible, palpable, and circumscribed in a certain place according to its natural condition; I concede. But by divine omnipotence it becomes invisible, impalpable, and not actually circumscribed by place, if it is established divinely in a supernatural state. For glorified bodies, endowed with spiritual qualities, are not seen, touched, and circumscribed by physical place. circumscribed by physical place. circumscribed by physical place.

III. If the body of Christ is co-present with the eucharistic bread, there will be as many bodies of Christ as there are hosts distributed: The consequent is absurd: Therefore the antecedent. Resp. By denying the consequence. For by the same reasoning someone might perhaps conclude: If God is mystically united with all Christian believers, there will be as many Gods as there are Christian believers. This therefore only follows, that the body of Christ is under as many breads as are distributed in the holy supper. Furthermore, all the breads in the holy supper are for one bread, as the Apostle teaches, 1 Cor. 10:17, we who are many partake of one bread. It must therefore be concluded rather: Although there are many breads, since they are nevertheless for one, it will be one body.

IV. If the body of Christ were present distinctly in the holy supper under the bread, and the blood under the wine; the body of Christ would be separated from his own blood: The consequent is absurd: Therefore the antecedent. Resp. Distinguish between union and sacramental presence, and union and natural presence. The body of Christ is under the bread sacramentally; because the body is under the bread, as under its sacramental symbol, and the blood is under the wine, as under its sacramental symbol: For the bread in the sacrament was instituted by Christ, that it might be a symbol of his body; and the wine was instituted, that it might be a symbol and vehicle of his blood. By this very fact the natural union of the body and blood of Christ is not broken; since the Son of God through his omnipotence can present his body and blood in various ways, while its nature remains intact.

V. If the body of Christ were in, with, and under the bread; it would certainly have to be adored in, with, and under the bread. The consequent is false: Therefore the antecedent. The consequence is evident: because Christ is to be adored there, where he exhibits his gracious presence to us. The falsity of the consequent is manifest, because those who adore Christ in, or under the bread, adore the bread itself at the same time. Resp. 1) Not everything with which Christ is united is to be adored. For he is united with believers: are believers therefore to be adored? 2) The object of adoration is one thing, the place of adoration is another. Where the eucharistic bread is distributed, there Christ is to be adored; but the eucharistic bread is not the object of adoration.

VI. Whoever does not wish to assert consubstantiation in the holy supper, they ought not to assert that the body of Christ is in, with, and under the bread: But the Lutherans do not wish to assert consubstantiation: Therefore. The major is clear; because he who says that the body of Christ is in, with, and under the bread, by this very fact indicates that the body of Christ is mixed with the bread, or impanated. Resp. Those explanatory particles imply not a physical presence, but a hyperphysical one; not a local inclusion, but a singular union; not a carnal impanation, or consubstantiation, but a mutual presence and sacramental communion of the blessed bread and the body of Christ, of the blessed wine and the blood of Christ.

VII. Whatever body is subject to the heavens, that is not present on earth: But the body of Christ &c. Therefore. Resp. 1) Christ ascended into heaven, that he might fill all things, Eph. 4:10, that is, that he might be omnipresent, Jer. 23:23. He was exalted to the right hand of the omnipresent God, which permeates, encompasses, and exceeds all places: Therefore by virtue of this exaltation he can present his body in a special way, where and when he wills. After the ascension Christ was seen several times by Paul, Acts 9, 22, 23, 26. 2) By the ascension indeed the mode of visible presence was removed; but not the invisible and sacramental one.

By the ascension indeed the mode of visible presence was removed; but not the invisible and sacramental one. VIII. Substantial presence in the eucharist conflicts with the end of the instituted supper, which Paul says is, that we may remember Christ, and proclaim his death, until he comes to judgment. But if he is already present in his body, the proclamation of his death will cease; for commemoration is of things not present, but absent. Resp. It is denied that it conflicts. For 1) we remember him who is not seen, even if he were present: 2) Indeed, we remember him, who visibly to us present presents it; if we have previously forgotten it. 3) Christ is present, and comes with his body in the holy supper, but he does not come for judgment. Whence the announcement of his death, desired for so many centuries, and thus now by no means present, does not cease, even if the body of Christ is now present, but invisibly. In the other life, the announcement of the death of Christ will not cease among the elect, when they shall see the body of Christ present in glory, Apoc. V, 9.

IX. The substantial presence of the body of Christ in, with, & under the bread conflicts with the first institution and administration of the supper. For when Christ took bread from the table, broke and distributed it, he sat together with the disciples at the table: But he was not in, with, & under the bread, nor did he break himself in, with, & under the bread, nor did he carry himself with his hands. Resp. It does not conflict with the first institution and administration of the supper. When Christ took bread from the table, broke and distributed it, he sat naturally at the table together with the disciples; and when he distributed the bread, he acted at the same time so that his body was in, with, or under the bread sacramentally, not by removing the sitting at the table, but by multiplying the presence of his body through divine omnipotence.

X. The substantial presence of the body of Christ in, with, & under the bread conflicts with the purpose and intention of Christ. For Christ wished his body to be eaten by the faithful principally insofar as it is delivered and crucified for us. Whence he says: This is my body, which is delivered for you. But those who assert a substantial presence in the bread, they exhibit for eating only a glorious and impassible body. Resp. It does not conflict with the purpose and intention of Christ. For he wished his body to be eaten, which was to be delivered and crucified for us: Not insofar as it is delivered and crucified for us. Christ in the first supper exhibited a body soon to be delivered, not yet delivered: Now he exhibits to us the delivered body.

XI. Whatever body is omnipresent, that is exhibited to be eaten not only under the blessed bread; but under all bread: But the opinion of the Lutherans is that the body of Christ is omnipresent. Therefore. Resp. Distinguish between general and special presence. It is not contradictory to be omnipresent, and nevertheless to be exhibited to someone in a certain special mode of presence. For thus we read that the omnipresent Holy Spirit descended upon Christ in the form of a dove, Matth. III, 6; was given to the disciples by an external breath, Io. XX; was communicated to the Apostles in the form of fiery tongues, Act. II, 3; and truly dwells in the bodies of the pious through a gracious presence, 1Cor. III, 6. Although, therefore, through the grace of the personal union, a general omnipresence was communicated to the assumed flesh of Christ, that presence of the body of Christ does not nevertheless remove or destroy the special and sacramental one.

XII. The substantial presence of the body of Christ in the eucharist conflicts with the express testimonies of scripture, which deny that Christ is always with his body in these lands, such as: 1) I came into the world, I leave the world again, i.e., the earth, Io. XVI, 28. 2) You do not always have me with you, Io. XII, 8. 3) The angel said concerning Christ, who had risen: He has risen, he is not here, Matth. XXVIII, 6. 4) If he were still on earth, he would not be a Priest, Hebr. VIII, 4. Resp. These and similar places of scripture do not simply deny the presence of the body of Christ in these lands, but a certain mode of presence. For 1) when the Lord says: I leave the world, the leaving of the world is to be understood according to the ordinary and visible conversation, according to which the Word made flesh had hitherto dwelt among men. But nothing prevents Christ, according to that visible presence, having left the world, from nevertheless being present in the Holy supper by his body according to the promise in another way, namely invisibly. 2) Thus the Savior denies only a certain mode of presence, Io. XII, 8. You do not always have me with you, namely in such a way that you may be able to do good to me, just as you do to the poor. 3) Similarly, when the angel says in Matt. XXVIII, 6: He is not here; namely, dead, lying in the sepulcher, whom you might be able to anoint, such as you are seeking. 4) In Heb. VIII, concerning our High Priest, Christ, it is written: If he were on earth, namely in that manner in which other priests are, who offer gifts according to the law and serve the shadows of heavenly things, he would not even be that true priest prefigured by the Levitical priests in the O.T.; and therefore it was not fitting for him to remain on earth after the manner of priests serving shadows, but to penetrate into heaven itself and sit at the right hand of God. But the ascension of Christ into heaven and his session at the right hand of God the Father do not destroy the invisible presence of Christ in the Holy Supper, although they do remove his visible, ordinary, humble, and local presence.

XIII. Such as is the union of the members, i.e., of the believers, with Christ the head, such also is the presence: But the union of believers with Christ is only spiritual: Therefore, the presence is also only spiritual. The major premise is evident: because the presence of Christ in the Supper is on account of our union with Christ. The minor premise is proven: because the union is effected through faith, Eph. III, 7.

Resp. The union of believers with Christ in the Holy Supper is twofold, one bodily, the other spiritual. It is called bodily by reason of the substance united, not by reason of the mode of uniting; by which, indeed, not in a bodily, natural, and sensible mode, but truly, nevertheless, the very substance of Christ’s body is present and united or joined to the believers by substantial proximity in, with, or under the bread. The spiritual union is effected through faith, of which John VI, 36 speaks. Unbelievers in the Holy Supper do not have a spiritual union with Christ, but only a bodily union: which, however, does not profit them, but rather harms them and results in greater condemnation. 1 Cor. XI, 29. Objection: If the presence of the body and blood of Christ in the Holy Supper is not spiritual, it will be bodily, and will take place through the physical contact of Christ’s body, which is absurd. Resp. The presence of Christ’s body in the Holy Supper is not merely spiritual, which might occur through the mere representation of faith, nor is it bodily by reason of the mode, or physical; but it is true, real, and substantial, yet supernatural, incomprehensible, and known to God alone.

Latin:

Si quis hoc negaverit, opponimus illi omnipotentiam divinam, per quam quondam angelus Gabriel Mariam virginem confirmavit, dicens, Luc. II, 37: Non impossibile est apud Deum quodcunque verbum.

Antithesis est Anabaptistarum, Arminianorum, Socinianorum & Schwenkfeldianorum, veram & realem corporis & sanguinis Christi praesentiam in S. coena negantium. Quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Omne corpus naturale est in certo & determinato loco, adeoque non in multis locis, ubi sacramentum coenae administratur: Atqui corpus Christi &c. E.

Resp. 1) Dist. inter corpus, naturale dictum ratione substantiae, & ratione affectionum, seu qualitatum. Corpus Christi est verum & naturale corpus ratione substantiae, sed ratione affectionum est glorificatum & maiestaticum, adeoque supernaturale. 2) Nullum corpus naturale per vires naturae potest esse in pluribus locis, potest tamen per omnipotentiam Dei alicuius corporis praesentia multiplicari, non multiplicata eius essentia. Quae impossibilia sunt naturae, possibilia sunt Deo. Demus igitur, Deum aliquid posse, quod nos fateamur, intelligere non posse.

3) Fac, nullum corpus, finita & creata subsistentia subsistens, in pluribus locis esse posse; aliter tamen comparatum est cum corpore Christi, quod in infinitam ὑπόστασιν τοῦ λόγου cunctum est: Hoc Filius Dei per omnipotentem suam virtutem praesens sistere potest & vult, ubicunque & quandocunque sacra coena celebratur. Instantia: Assumsit Christus corpus humanum, specie idem cum nostro corpore, Hebr. II, 14. E. iisdem gaudet affectionibus. Resp. Quam prope accedit corpus Christi θεανθρώπου ad conditionem corporis ψιλῶς ἀνθρώπου, qua essentiam, tam longo interuallo ab eodem differt, qua subsistentiam, & huius consequens, maiestatis divinae participationem, ut omnis plenitudo diuinitatis in eo ipso habitet σωματικῶς, Col. II, 9.

II. Quacunque doctrina euertitur veritas humanae Christi naturae, illa non est asserenda: Atqui doctrina de substantiali praesentia corporis Christi in sacra coena euertitur &c. E. Minor probatur: quia omne verum corpus humanum est visibile, palpabile, & certo loco circumscriptum; quale corpus non est, quod sub hostiis in pluribus locis esse dicitur.

Resp. Omne corpus est visibile, palpabile, & certo loco circumscriptum secundum naturalem suam conditionem; concedo. At per omnipotentiam diuinam fit inuisibile, impalpabile & actu non circumscriptum loco, si diuinitus constituatur in statu supernaturali. Nam corpora glorificata, spiritualibus qualitatibus praedita, non videntur, palpantur, & loco physico circumscribuntur. physico circumscribuntur. physico circumscribuntur.

III. Si corpus Christi compræsens est cum pane eucharistico, tot erunt corpora Christi, quot hostiæ distribuuntur: Consequens est absurdum: Ergo & antecedens. Resp. negando consequentiam. Nam eadem ratione quispiam forte colligeret: Si Deus mystice vnitus est cum omnibus fidelibus christianis, tot erunt Dii, quot sunt fideles christiani. Hoc igitur tantum sequitur, corpus Christi esse sub tot panibus, quot in sacra cœna distribuuntur. Deinde omnes panes in S. cœna pro vno pane sunt, docente Apostolo, 1 Cor. X, 17. de vno pane multi participamus. Concludendum itaque potius: Licet multi panes sint, cum tamen pro vno sint, erit & vnum corpus.

IV. Si corpus Christi distincte adesset in S. cœna sub pane, & sanguis sub vino; corpus Christi ab ipsius sanguine separaretur: Consequens est absurdum: E. & antecedens. Resp. Dist. inter vnionem atque præsentiam sacramentalem, & vnionem atque præsentiam naturalem. Corpus Christi sub pane est sacramentaliter; quia corpus sub pane est, tanquam sub suo symbolo sacramentali, & sanguis sub vino est, tanquam sub suo symbolo sacramentali: Nam panis in sacramento institutus est a Christo, vt esset symbolum corporis sui; & vinum institutum est, vt esset symbolum & vehiculum sanguinis sui. Hoc ipso non rumpitur vnio naturalis corporis & sanguinis Christi; cum Filius Dei per omnipotentiam suam variis modis præsens sistere queat corpus & sanguinem suum, salua manente ipsius natura.

V. Si corpus Christi esset in, cum, & sub pane; vtique in, cum, & sub pane esset adorandum. Consequens est falsum: E. & antecedens. Consequentia est euidens: quia Christus ibi est adorandus, vbi suam præsentiam gratiosam nobis exhibet. Consequentis falsitas est manifesta, quia adorantes Christum in, aut sub pane, ipsum panem simul adorant. Resp. 1) Non id semper, cum quo Christus vnitus est, adorandum est. Nam vnitus est cum fidelibus: ergone fideles adorandi sunt? 2) Aliud est obiectum adorationis, aliud locus adorationis. Vbi distribuitur panis eucharisticus, ibi Christus est adorandus; at panis eucharisticus non est obiectum adorationis.

VI. Quicunque nolunt asserere consubstantiationem in S. cœna, illos non oportet asserere, corpus Christi esse in, cum, & sub pane: Atqui Lutherani nolunt asserere consubstantiationem: E. Maior claret; quia qui dicit, in, cum & sub pane, corpus Christi esse, hoc ipso indicat, corpus Christi commixtum esse cum pane, vel impanatum. Resp. Particulæ illæ explicatuæ non præsentiam physicam, sed hyperphysicam; non localem inclusionem, sed singularem vnionem; non carnalem impanationem, aut consubstantiationem, sed præsentiam mutuam & sacramentalem communionem panis benedicti & corporis Christi, vini benedicti & sanguinis Christi inferunt.

VII. Quodcunque corpus subiectum est in cœlos, illud non est præsens in terra: Atqui corpus Christi &c. Ergo. Resp. 1) Ascendit Christus in cœlum, vt omnia impleret, Eph. IV, 10. h. e. vt esset omnipræsens, Ier. XXIII, 23. Exaltatus est ad dextram Dei omnipræsentem, quæ omnia loca immeat, ambit & excedet: E. vi huius exaltationis corpus suum speciali ratione præsens sistere potest, vbi & quando vult. Post ascensionem Christus aliquoties visus est a Paulo, Actor. IX. XXII. XXIII. XXVI. 2) Per ascensionem quidem sublatus est modus præsentiæ visibilis; non vero inuisibilis & sacramentalis.

VIII. Præsentia substantialis in eucharistia pugnat cum fine institutæ cœnæ, quem Paulus ait esse, vt recordemur Christi, & mortem eius annuntiemus, dum venerit ad iudicium. Quod si vero iam adest suo corpore, cessabit annuntiatio mortis eius; commemoratio enim est rerum non præsentium, sed absentium. Resp. Negatur pugnare. Nam 1) recordamur eius, qui non videtur, etiamsi præsens fuerit: 2) Immo recordamur eius, qui visibiliter se nobis præsentem fistit; si prius eius obliti fuimus. 3) Adest, venitque Christus corpore suo in sacra cœna, sed non venit ad iudicium. Vnde non cessat annuntiatio mortis eius, ante tot sæcula appetitæ, adeoque iam minime præsentis, etsi iam adsit corpus Christi, sed inuisibiliter. In altera vita non cessabit annuntiatio mortis Christi inter electos, quando corpus Christi præsens conspicient in gloria, Apoc. V, 9.

IX. Substantialis præsentia corporis Christi in, cum, & sub pane pugnat cum prima cœnæ institutione & administratione. Cum enim Christus de mensa panem sumeret, frangeret & distribueret, assedit vna cum discipulis mensæ: Non autem fuit in, cum, & sub pane, nec seipsum fregit in, cum, & sub pane, nec manibus gestauit. Resp. Non pugnat cum prima cœnæ institutione & administratione. Cum Christus de mensa panem sumeret, frangeret & distribueret, assedit naturaliter mensæ vna cum discipulis; & cum distribueret panem, fecit simul, vt corpus suum esset in, cum, vel sub pane sacramentaliter, non sublata assessione ad mensam, sed multiplicata per omnipotentiam diuinam corporis sui præsentia.

X. Substantialis præsentia corporis Christi in, cum, & sub pane pugnat cum scopo & intentione Christi. Voluit enim Christus a fidelibus principaliter manducari corpus suum, quatenus pro nobis est traditum & crucifixum. Vnde ait: Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis traditur. Qui vero præsentiam substantialem in pane adstruunt, ii manducandum exhibent tantum corpus gloriosum & impatibile. Resp. Non pugnat cum scopo & intentione Christi. Voluit namque manducari corpus suum, quod pro nobis traderetur, & crucifigeretur: Non quatenus pro nobis traditum & crucifixum est. Christus in prima cœna exhibuit corpus mox tradendum, nondum traditum: Nunc traditum nobis ipse exhibet.

XI. Quodcunque corpus est omnipræsens, illud non tantum sub pane benedicto; sed sub pane omni manducandum exhibetur: Atqui sententia Lutheranorum corpus Christi est omnipræsens. E. Resp. Dist. inter præsentiam generalem & specialem. Non sunt opposita, omnipræsentem esse, & nihilominus certo præsentiæ modo speciali alicui exhiberi. Sic enim omnipræsentem Spiritum S. descendisse super Christum in specie columbæ, Matth. III, 6. flatu externo datum discipulis, Io. XX. specie ignitarum linguarum Apostolis communicatum, Act. II, 3. in corporibus piorum vere & per gratiosam præsentiam habitare, 1Cor. III, 6. legimus. Quamuis itaque per vnionis personalis gratiam assumtæ carni Christi communicata fit omnipræsentia generalis, non illa tamen præsentia corporis Christi specialem & sacramentalem tollit, aut destruit.

XII. Substantialis præsentia corporis Christi in eucharistia pugnat cum expressis scripturæ testimoniis, quæ negant, Christum semper corpore suo in hisce terris esse, qualia sunt: 1) Veni in mundum, iterum relinquo mundum, i. e. terram, Io. XVI, 28. 2) Me non semper habetis vobiscum, Io. XII, 8. 3) Angelus de Christo, qui resurrexerat, dixit: Surrexit, non est hic, Matth. XXVIII, 6. 4) Si adhuc in terris esset, Sacerdos non esset, Hebr. VIII, 4. Resp. Hæc & similia loca scripturæ non simpliciter negant præsentiam corporis Christi in hisce terris, sed certum præsentiæ modum. Nam 1) cum Dominus ait: Relinquo mundum, intelligenda est relictio mundi secundum ordinariam & visibilem conuersationem, secundum quam Verbum caro factum hucusque habitauerat inter homines. At nil obstat, quo minus Christus secundum visibilem illam præsentiam, relicto mundo, tamen ex promissione alio modo, nempe inuisibiliter, corpore suo adsit in S. cœna. 2) Sic certum duntaxat præsentiæ modum negat Seruator, Io. XII, 8. Me non semper habetis vobiscum, nempe tali modo, vt benefacere mihi, sicut pauperibus, queatis. 3) Similiter cum angelus, Matth. XXVIII, 6. inquit: Non est hic; nempe mortuus, in sepulcro iacens, quem vngere queatis, qualem vos queritis. 4) Hebr. VIII, de Pontifice nostro, Christo, scriptum est: Si esset in terra, scilicet eo modo, quo alii pontifices, qui secundum legem offerunt dona, & vmbræ seruiunt rerum cœlestium, ne esset quidem sacerdos ille verus, per sacerdotes Leuiticos in V. T. præfiguratus; ideoque non opportuit ipsum in terra manere ad morem sacerdotum, vmbræ seruientium, sed in ipsum cœlum penetrare & ad dextram Dei sedere. At ascensio Christi in cœlum, & sessio ad dextram Dei Patris, non destruunt præsentiam Christi inuisibilem in sacra cœna, licet tollant præsentiam visibilem, ordinariam, humilem & localem.

XIII. Qualis est vnio membrorum, h. e. fidelium, cum Christo capite, talis quoque est præsentia: Atqui vnio fidelium cum Christo non est, nisi spiritualis: E. & præsentia non est, nisi spiritualis. Maior constat: quia præsentia Christi in cœna est propter vnionem nostri cum Christo. Minor probatur: quia vnio fit per fidem, Eph. III, 7.

Resp. Vnio fidelium cum Christo in S. cœna duplex est, vna corporalis, altera spiritualis. Corporalis dicitur ratione substantiæ vnite, non ratione modi vniendi; qua nimirum non corporali quidem, naturali & sensibili modo, sed vere tamen ipsa corporis Christi substantia propinquitate substantiali, in, cum, vel sub pane præsens vnitur, seu coniungitur fidelibus. Spiritualis vnio fit per fidem, de qua Io. VI, 36. Infideles in S. cœna vnionem spiritualem cum Christo non habent, sed tantum vnionem corporalem: Quæ tamen ipsis non prodest, sed obest potius, & cedit in maiorem condemnationem. 1 Cor. XI, 29. Instantia: Si præsentia corporis & sanguinis Christi in S. cœna non est spiritualis, erit corporalis, & fiet per contactum corporis Christi physicum, quod est absurdum. Resp. Præsentia corporis Christi in S. cœna non est mere spiritualis, quæ per solam fidei repræsentationem fiat, neque est corporalis ratione modi, siue physica; sed est vera, realis & substantialis quidem, attamen supernaturalis, incomprehensibilis, folique Deo cognita.


### Quest. XIII. What is the form of the Eucharist?

The form of the Holy Supper is completed by the formal acts of this sacrament, following one another without interruption: a) εὐλογία, blessing, or consecration of the symbols: b) δόσις, or the distribution of the consecrated symbols; c) λῆψις, the reception of the distributed symbols, consisting in the eating of the body of Christ with the blessed bread, and the drinking of the blood of Christ with the blessed wine.

Prob. a. We learn that the first formal act of this sacrament is εὐλογία from the words of institution. For, as Matthew testifies, c. XXVI, 26, Jesus took bread, καὶ εὐλογήσας, blessing, he broke it, and gave it to the disciples, and v. 27, and taking the cup, καὶ εὐχαριστήσας, and giving thanks, he gave it to them. εὐλογία, or blessing, differs from εὐχαριστία, if not really, yet objectively and formally; in that the former was directed to the external symbols, bread and wine; the latter to the heavenly Father. Cf. 1 Cor. X, 16, where Paul makes mention of the cup of blessing. Now, the blessing, or consecration, is performed by a) prayer, b) the repetition of the words of institution. For whatever is sanctified, is sanctified by the word of God and prayer, 1 Tim. IV, 5. We do not find in the sacred code a certain formula of prayers for consecrating the Eucharist, described by Christ or by the Apostles. Since, therefore, it is not certain what kind of prayer Christ used in blessing the symbols, we conclude that the Savior left the form of prayer to the discretion of the Church, so that consequently not even the Lord’s Prayer is simply necessary by divine right for this act, provided that such forms of prayer are to be employed, which are full of devotion, and are more accommodated than others to the consecratory act. Meanwhile, since Christ prescribed this formula of prayer elsewhere: Our Father, who art in heaven, nay, commanded us to pray thus, and no better prayer can be given, the church from the beginning rightly and piously established this prayer in the consecration of the eucharist.

But consecration is indeed performed by the Lord's Prayer in a general sense, but by the addition of the words of institution that generic consecration is determined to this act in specie, which is proper to the eucharist, so that it is not just any consecration, but a consecration in the species of the eucharist.

Moreover, the repetition of the words of institution is not a merely historical recitation of the words of institution, or a doctrinal review directed toward informing the people; but it is a) ἁγιαστική (sanctifying), or separative of the symbols from natural and profane use: b) effectively elevative and destinative, to a holy and supernatural use, so that the consecrated bread and blessed wine may be the adequate matter of this sacrament; c) exhibitive of the body of Christ in many πᾶσι (all), and unitive of the same with the bread and wine, insofar as it is joined with δόσις καὶ λῆψις (giving and receiving): for the εὐλογία (blessing) alone is not the cause of the sacramental union; insofar as Christ gave, and said: Take, and only then uttered these words: THIS IS MY BODY. Therefore, unless the eucharistic bread is offered and received at the same time, it cannot be said: this is the body of Christ.

Conf. D. Hulsem. brev. cap. XIII. p. 675. It is to be observed here carefully that the threefold effect of consecration here does not depend on some magical incantation, which inheres in the consecratory words according to the tips of the letters, or according to the bark of the syllables, or from a created virtue which might have been given to the presbyter through an indelible character. Far be it that we should think such things about this venerable sacrament! But we distinguish between the efficient cause and the impulsive cause of the sacramental union. The efficient cause is the sole omnipotent virtue of Christ, through which he makes his body and blood present, and unites them sacramentally with the bread and wine, whenever and wherever the Lord's Supper is duly celebrated. The impulsive cause is the benevolent will of Christ, which pleased him, and he also promised to make his body and blood present, and to unite them with the bread and wine, wherever his supper is rightly celebrated. The words of institution contain this will and promise of Christ, the recitation of which is necessary on account of this, and is required by way of an impulsive cause. Which the solid declaration of the Form of Concord does not deny. Form. Concord. p. 747. We believe, teach, and confess that neither the word, nor the work, dignity, or merit of any man, nor the pronunciation of the minister, nor the eating, nor the faith of the communicants effects the true presence of the body and blood of Christ in the supper. None of these makes the body and blood of Christ present for us. But all this, that we have the body present in the supper of Christ, is to be ascribed simply and entirely to the virtue and word of the omnipotent God, and to the institution and ordination of the Lord Jesus Christ.

Prob. b. The second formal act of this sacrament is δόσις (giving), or the distribution of the H. Supper, by which the consecrated symbols are distributed among the communicants according to the dominical institution. However, it is the same whether these holy symbols are given into the hands of the recipients, or are moved immediately to their mouths by the church minister. For since the mode of distribution is not expressed in Holy Scripture, it is left to the discretion of the church.

Prob. c. The third formal act of this sacrament is λῆψις (receiving), or the acceptance, by which with the consecrated bread the body of Christ is received and eaten, and with the consecrated wine the blood of Christ is received and drunk, according to the dominical institution, Matt.

Latin:

Forma S. cœnæ

Formam eucharistiæ absoluunt actus formales huius sacramenti, indistracte se inuicem subsequentes: a) εὐλογία, benedictio, siue consecratio symbolorum: b) δόσις, siue symbolorum consecratorum distributio; c) λῆψις, symbolorum distributorum acceptio, consistens in manducatione corporis Christi cum pane benedicto, & bibitione sanguinis Christi cum vino benedicto. Prob. a. Primum actum formalem huius sacramenti esse εὐλογίαν, discimus ex verbis institutionis. Etenim, teste Matthæo, c. XXVI, 26. accepit Iesus panem, καὶ εὐλογήσας, benedicens, fregit, deditque discipulis, & v. 27. & accipiens calicem, καὶ εὐχαριστήσας, & gratias agens dedit illis. Differt εὐλογία, seu benedictio ab εὐχαριστίᾳ, si non realiter, tamen obiectiue formaliter; eo, quod illa ad symbola externa, panem & vinum; hæc ad patrem cœlestem directa fuit. Confer. 1 Cor. X, 16. vbi Paullus mentionem facit poculi benedictionis. Fit autem benedictio, seu consecratio, a) precatione, b) repetitione verborum institutionis. Quidquid enim sanctificatur, per verbum Dei & preces sanctificatur, 1 Tim. IV, 5. Certain precum formulam in consecranda eucharistia, a Christo, vel ab Apostolis descriptam, in sacro codice non inuenimus. Cum igitur non constet, quali precatione Christus symbolis benedicens vsus sit, colligimus, Saluatorem precationis formam in arbitrio ecclesiæ reliquisse, vt proinde ne oratio quidem dominica ad hunc actum simpliciter iure diuino sit necessaria, modo eiusmodi precum formulæ adhibeantur, quæ devotionis plenæ, & actui consecratorio præ ceteris sint accommodatæ. Interim cum Christus hanc orandi formulam: Pater noster, qui es in cælis, alibi præscripserit, immo sic orare nos iusserit, nec oratio melior detur, ecclesia ab initio hanc precationem in consecranda eucharistia recte & pie sanxit.

Ceterum consecratio per orationem dominicam quidem fit in genere, sed accessu verborum institutionis generica illa consecratio ad hunc in specie actum, qui est eucharistiæ proprius, determinatur, vt non fit qualiscunque, sed in specie eucharistiæ consecratio.

Repetitio autem verborum institutionis non est nude historica recitatio verborum institutionis, aut recensio doctrinalis, ad populum informandum directa; sed est a) ἁγιαστική, sive separativa symbolorum ab usu naturali & profano: b) efficaciter elevativa & destinativa, ad usum sanctum & supernaturalem, vt consecratus panis, vinumque benedictum sit materia adæquata huius sacramenti; c) exhibitiva corporis Christi in multis πᾶσι, ac eiusdem cum pane & vino unitiva, quatenus cum δόσις καὶ λῆψις est coniuncta: sola namque εὐλογία non est causa unionis sacramentalis; quatenus Christus dedit, & dixit: Accipite, & tum demum hæc verba protulit: HOC EST CORPUS MEUM. Ergo nisi porrigatur & accipiatur simul panis eucharisticus, non potest dici: hoc est corpus Christi.

Conf. D. Hvlsem. breu. cap. XIII. p. 675. Probe hic obseruandum est, quod triplex hic effectus consecrationis non dependeat a magica quadam incantatione, quæ verbis consecratoriis secundum apices litterarum, vel iuxta corticem syllabarum infit, vel a virtute creata, quæ data sit sacerdoti per indelebilem characterem. Absit, vt de venerabili hoc sacramento ista cogitemus! Sed distinguimus inter caussam efficientem, & impulsivam unionis sacramentalis. Efficiens est sola omnipotens virtus Christi, per quam corpus & sanguinem suum præsentia sistit, & sacramentaliter cum pane & vino vnit, quandocunque & ubicunque cœna Domini rite celebratur. Impulsiva est beneuola Christi voluntas, quæ placuit ipsi, & promisit etiam corpus & sanguinem suum præsentia sistere, & cum pane & vino vnire, ubicunque cœna eius recte celebratur. Hanc voluntatem & promissionem Christi continent verba institutionis, quarum recitatio propter ea necessaria est, & requiritur per modum caussæ impulsivæ. Quod non diffitetur solida declarat. Form. Concord. p. 747. Credimus, docemus & confitemur, quod veram præsentiam corporis & sanguinis Christi in cœna non efficiat ullius hominis vel verbum, vel opus, dignitas, seu meritum, sive pronuntiatio ministri; seu manducatio, seu fides communicantium. Horum nullum nobis corpus & sanguinem Christi præsentia facit. Sed hoc totum, quod in cœna Christi corpus præsens habemus, simpliciter & in solidum omnipotentis Dei virtuti & verbo, institutioni atque ordinationi Domini Iesu Christi est adscribendum.

Prob. b. Secundus actus formalis huius sacramenti est δόσις, seu distributio S. cœnæ, qua consecrata symbola iuxta institutionem dominicam inter communicantes distribuuntur. Perinde autem est, sive sacræ hæc symbola in manus accipientium dentur, sive ab ecclesia ministro ori eorum immediate admoueantur. Cum enim modus distributionis in S. scriptura non sit expressus, in arbitrio ecclesiæ relictus est.

Prob. c. Tertius actus formalis huius sacramenti est λῆψις, seu acceptio, qua cum consecrato pane accipitur & comeditur corpus Christi, cum vino consecrato accipitur & bibitur sanguis Christi, iuxta institutionem dominicam, M.tth.


### Quest. XIII. What is the form of the Eucharist?: XXVI, 26. 27. Quæst. XIV. Is the breaking of bread necessary in the administration of the H

XXVI, 26. 27. Quæst. XIV. Is the breaking of bread necessary in the administration of the H.

Supper? The breaking of bread in the administration of the H. Supper is indeed free and lawful, in those places in which it has obtained a), but it is not simply necessary b).

Obs. I. The term "fraction" is sometimes taken broadly for distribution, Is. LVIII, 7, sometimes strictly for the breaking into parts.

Obs. II. The question is not: whether the bread must be broken before distribution? but: whether it must necessarily be broken in the very act of distribution? Among us, the mass of bread is broken before distribution; but the breaking of bread in the very act of distribution is an adiaphoron, or indifferent.

Prob. a. That the breaking of bread is free and lawful in the act of distribution is taught by the example of Christ, Matt. XXVI, 26.

Prob. b. 1) The breaking of the Eucharistic bread was accidental to the first supper, on account of the larger loaves, and because, as was the custom among the Hebrews, they were fragile. The breaking of bread was therefore an action παρασκευαστικὴ (preparatory), and a servant to the principal action, i.e., the distribution.

2) If the breaking of bread is necessary: it must be done necessarily either for the sake of distribution, or for the sake of the representation of the broken body of Christ. If for the sake of distribution; it will be a ministerial act serving the principal one, and thus left to the discretion of the church. If for the sake of representation; it is necessary that a certain analogy exist between the sign and the thing signified. But the body of Christ, strictly speaking, was not broken, John XIX, 36.

You say: I. Whatever Christ himself did, and commanded us to do, that must necessarily be done by us: But Christ himself broke the bread, and commanded the breaking of bread to us: Therefore.

Resp. 1) Distinguish between formal acts and ministerial or concomitant ones. In the formal acts of the Holy Supper, we always imitate Christ, the author of the Holy Supper. But concomitant acts can be in some way different by reason of circumstances. For Christ distributed the sacrament of the supper a) in Jerusalem, b) at evening time, c) after the common supper, d) in an upper room of a house, e) among the disciples reclining. Just as we do not necessarily imitate Christ in these circumstances, so neither in the breaking of bread. For the Jews, at the time when Christ was instituting the supper, did not use loaves as thick as we do, but broad and less thick loaves, or cakes, which could be broken by hand more conveniently than cut with a knife. 2) What Christ commanded is clear from the words of institution: Take, eat: This is my body. Do this in remembrance of me. There is no mention of breaking there.

II. The Apostles broke bread, Acts II, 42 [sic]. Acts XX, 7. Therefore we must necessarily break bread. Resp. 1) The question is not: whether the breaking of bread was customary in the apostolic church? but: whether it was performed under the opinion of a command? 2) The Apostles, according to the custom of the Jews, even when they were about to eat outside the Eucharist, are read to have broken the bread which we cut.

III. Whatever action is most full of comfort, that is necessary: But the breaking of bread, etc. Therefore. The minor is proven; because ἀρτοκλασία (breaking of bread) shows and represents Christ broken for us, 1 Cor. XI, 24. Resp. 1) Christ, strictly speaking, was not broken, John XIX, 36. 2) Paul, in the cited place, understands a metaphorical breaking, i.e., the passion or crucifixion of Christ; if the breaking of bread in the Eucharist referred to this, it would have to be not a metaphorical, but a true and properly so-called breaking, since every type is more obscure than its antitype; which does not happen in this case, since the breaking of bread is literal, but the breaking of the body of Christ, which is posited as the antitype, is metaphorical.

Latin:

XXVI, 26. 27. Quæst. XIV. An fractio panis in S. cœnæ administratione necessaria est?

Fractio panis in administratione S. cœnæ libera quidem & licita est, in iis locis, in quibus obtinuit a), sed non est simpliciter necessaria b).

Obs. I. Fractionis vocabulum interdum sumitur late pro distributione, Es. LVIII, 7. interdum stricte pro comminutione in partes.

Obs. II. Non quaeritur: an frangendus sit panis ante distributionem? sed: an necessario frangendus sit in ipso distributionis actu? Frangitur apud nos massa panis ante distributionem; at panifragium in ipso distributionis actu est adiaphorum, sive indifferens.

Prob. a. Panifragium liberum licitumque esse in distributionis actu, docet exemplum Christi, Matth. XXVI, 26.

Prob. b. 1) Fractio panis eucharistici accidentalis fuit primae coenae, occasione panium grandiorum, & ut apud Hebraeos in usu erant fragilium. Fuit itaque fractio panis actio παρασκευαστικὴ, & ministra actionis principalis, i. e. distributionis.

2) Si fractio panis necessaria est: aut propter distributionem, aut propter repraesentationem fracti corporis Christi necessario fieri debet. Si propter distributionem; erit actus ministerialis principali inferuiens, adeoque in arbitrio ecclesiae relictus. Si propter repraesentationem; analogia quaedam inter signum & signatum intercedat, necesse est. Sed corpus Christi proprie loquendo fractum non est, Io. XIX, 36.

Dicis: I. Quidquid Christus ipse fecit, & fieri nobis praecepit, illud necessario nobis faciendum est: Atqui Christus ipse panem fregit, & fractionem panis nobis praecepit: E.

Resp. 1) Dist. Inter actus formales, & ministeriales, sive concomitantes. In actibus formalibus S. coenae semper imitamur Christum auctorem S. coenae. Actus autem concomitantes possunt esse quodammodo diversi ratione circumstantiarum. Nam Christus distribuit sacramentum coenae a) Hierosolymis, b) tempore vespertino, c) post coenam vulgarem, d) in contignatione superiori aedium, e) inter discipulos accumbentes. Sicut his circumstantiis Christum necessario non imitamur: ita nec in fractione panis. Iudaei enim tempore eo, quo Christus coenam instituebat, non ita spissis ut nos, sed latis, & minus crassis panibus, vel placentis utebantur, quae manu commodius frangi, quam cultro scindi poterant. 2) Quid Christus praeceperit, patet e verbis institutionis: Accipite, edite: Hoc est corpus meum. Hoc facite in mei commemorationem. Ibi nulla fit mentio fractionis.

II. Apostoli fregerunt panem, Act. II, 24. Act. XX, 7. E. & nos necessario panem frangamus. Resp. 1) Non quaeritur: an fractio panis usitata fuerit in ecclesia apostolica? sed: an sub opinione mandati sit peracta? 2) Apostoli more Iudaeorum, etiam extra eucharistiam cibaturi, panem, quem nos scindimus, fregisse leguntur.

III. Quaecunque actio solatii est plenissima, illa est necessaria: Atqui fractio panis &c. Ergo. Minor probatur; quia ἀρτοκλασία ostendit & repraesentat Christum pro nobis fractum, 1 Cor. XI, 24. Resp. 1) Christus proprie loquendo fractus non est, Io. XIX, 36. 2) Paullus l. c. intelligit fractionem metaphoricam, h. e. passionem vel crucifixionem Christi; quam si fractio panis in eucharistia referret, haec non metaphorica, sed vera & proprie dicta fractio esse debebat, cum omnis typus antitypo suo sit obscurior; quod h. l. non fit, cum fractio panis fit propria, sed eius, qui statuitur antitypus, fractio corporis Christi sit metaphorica.


### Quest. XIII. What is the form of the Eucharist?: Quest. XV. Whether

Quest. XV. Whether

through consecration the bread and wine are essentially changed into the body and blood of Christ, or transubstantiated? Through consecration, the bread and wine are not essentially changed into the body and blood of Christ.

Obs. Dist. between essential and accidental change. When the holy Fathers wrote that bread and wine in the Eucharist are changed or trans-elemented through consecration, they did not understand an essential change, but an accidental one, namely by reason of office and mystical use, i.e., the elevation of the elements into a nobler state, so that the bread becomes and remains by reason of essence the same that it was before consecration, but according to the institution and promise of Christ, by His own omnipotent power, it becomes a symbol communicative of the body of Christ, whereas before consecration it was common bread.

Prob. 1) Because transubstantiation, or the essential change of the blessed bread and wine, cannot be demonstrated from the words of the institution of the Holy Supper: since in the words of Christ there is an exhibitive locution, by which two things accidentally united are exhibited, of which one, the nobler and less obvious to the senses, is expressed in the predicate, the other not expressed, without any change of one thing into the other. See above, qu. 5.

See above, qu. 5. 2) Whatever Christ took, consecrated, broke, and distributed in the institution of the Supper, this same thing He commanded to be eaten: But He took, consecrated, broke, and distributed the substance of bread, not mere accidents.

3) The Eucharistic bread is called by Paul κοινωνία, the communion of the body of Christ, 1 Cor. X, 16, which would be taken away if one of those things between which the κοινωνία must exist were taken away and ceased to be.

X, 16, ch. XI, 26, 27. 5) Every sacrament, and the Eucharist in particular, as IRENAEUS teaches L. III. c.

34, consists of two things, the earthly and the heavenly.

6) If a mouse were to eat the consecrated bread, it would eat the body of Christ itself; which is most absurd.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, who maintain that through consecration the substance of bread and wine is changed and converted into the substance of the body and blood of Christ, so that after the blessing only the external species and accidents of bread and wine remain. Their principal arguments are:

I. The words of institution: Take, this is my body, either denote only a significative representation of the body of Christ, or an essential change of the blessed bread into the body of Christ: But they do not denote only a significative representation: Therefore, they imply an essential change. Resp. A third option is given. The words of Christ denote a sacramental union, or two things sacramentally united.

II. If the Eucharistic bread is not changed essentially into the body of Christ, it follows that that proposition: Bread is the body of Christ, is false. But that proposition is true and used by the holy Fathers and LUTHER. Therefore. Resp. Dist. between the biblical and ecclesiastical proposition, to be understood by reason of the sacramental union.

III. Whoever cannot simultaneously receive the food of the mind and of the belly, they must explain the words of institution not by sacramental union, but by transubstantiation: But communicants &c.: Therefore. The major is evident: because the sacramental union joins the food of the belly, viz. bread, and the food of the mind, namely the body of Christ. Resp. Dist. Inter Christi. Resp. Dist. Inter

the primary and secondary use or end of the body of Christ. Primarily, indeed, the body of Christ confirms faith and refreshes the soul: the secondary use consists in this, that the life-giving flesh of Christ confers a blessed resurrection upon our bodies.

Latin:

Quaest. XV. An

per consecrationem panis & vinum in corpus & sanguinem Christi essentialiter mutantur, sive transubstantiantur? Per consecrationem panis & vinum in corpus & sanguinem Christi essentialiter non mutantur. sanguinem Christi essentialiter non mutantur.

Obs. Dist. inter mutationem essentialem & accidentalem. Quando sancti Patres scripserunt, quod panis & vinum in eucharistia per consecrationem mutantur, aut transelemententur, non intellexerunt mutationem essentialem, sed accidentalem, nempe ratione officii & usus mystici, i. e. evectionem elementorum in nobiliorem statum, ita, vt panis fit & maneat ratione essentiæ idem, qui ante consecrationem fuit, sed iuxta institutionem atque promissionem Christi omnipotente ipsius virtute fiat symbolum corporis Christi communicatiuum, cum ante consecrationem esset panis vulgaris.

Prob. 1) Quia transubstantiatio, aut essentialis mutatio panis & vini benedicti e verbis institutionis S. cœnæ demonstrari nequit: siquidem in verbis Christi est locutio exhibitiva, qua duæ res accidentaliter vnitæ exhibentur, quarum vna nobilior, sensibusque minus obuia in prædicato exprimitur, altera non expressa, fine omni mutatione vnius rei in alteram. Vide supra, qu. 5.

2) Quidquid Christus in institutione cœnæ accepit, consecrauit, fregit ac distribuit, hoc ipsum manducare iussit: At substantiam panis, non accidentia nuda accepit, consecrauit, fregit atque distribuit. Ergo.

3) Panis eucharisticus a Paullo vocatur κοινωνία, communio corporis Christi, 1 Cor. X, 16. quæ tolleretur, altero eorum sublato & desinente, inter quæ κοινωνία esse debet.

4) Panis consecratus dicerte vocatur panis 1 Cor. X, 16. cap. XI, 26. 27.

5) Omne sacramentum, & in specie eucharistia, docente IRENAEO L. III. c. 34. constat duabus rebus, terrena & cœlesti.

6) Si mus comederet panem consecratum, ipsum corpus Christi comederet; quod est absurdissimum.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, statuentium, per consecrationem substantiam panis & vini in substantiam corporis & sanguinis Christi mutari atque conuerti, vt post benedictionem tantum externæ species & accidentia panis & vini remaneant. Quorum præcipua argumenta sunt:

I. Verba institutionis: Accipite, hoc est corpus meum, aut notant tantum significatiuam repræsentationem corporis Christi, aut essentialem mutationem panis benedicti in corpus Christi: At non notant tantum significatiuam repræsentationem: E, inferunt essentialem mutationem. Resp. Datur tertium. Verba Christi notant sacramentalem vnionem, siue duas res sacramentaliter vnitas.

II. Si panis eucharisticus non mutatur essentialiter in corpus Christi, sequitur, quod illa propositio: Panis est corpus Christi, sit falsa. At illa propositio est vera & usurpata a sanctis Patribus & LYTHERO. Ergo. Resp. Dist. inter propositionem biblicam & ecclesiasticam, ratione vnionis sacramentalis intelligenda.

III. Quicunque non possunt simul accipere cibum mentis & ventris, illos oportet verba institutionis explicare non per sacramentalem vnionem, sed per transubstantiationem: Atqui communicantes &c.: Ergo. Maior constat: quia vnio sacramentalis coniungit cibum ventris, scil. panem, & cibum mentis, nempe corpus Christi. Resp. Dist. Inter Christi. Resp. Dist. Inter

vsum vel finem corporis Christi primarium, & secundarium. Primario quidem corpus Christi confirmat fidem & reficit animam: secundarius vsus consistit in hoc, quod viuifica caro Christi corporibus nostris beatam confert resurrectionem.


### Q. XVI. Do we eat and drink the body and blood of Christ not only by the mouth of faith, but also by the mouth of the body?

The body and blood of Christ are received, eaten, and drunk by communicants in the legitimate use of the holy supper not only by the mouth of faith, but also by the mouth of the body. Obs.

I. Eating is formally the reception of a thing, offered under the aspect of food, through the mouth into the body, for the nourishment of man. Obs.

II. Eating is threefold: one is natural, another spiritual, another sacramental. The former is done by the bodily mouth, and is instituted for the nourishment and refreshment of natural powers: the latter is done by the mouth of faith, and tastes Christ with all his merits and benefits, offered in the gospel, for the refreshment of soul and conscience: by this [latter] it can be done by the mouth of the body, but in a supernatural manner, for spiritual refreshment. Obs.

III. Spiritual and sacramental eating differ. The former is of all times; the latter is proper to the N. T. The former [can be] even outside the supper: the latter has a place only in the supper itself. The former can also be done without symbols; the latter is performed only by means of external symbols. The former always profits unto salvation: the latter sometimes is done even unto judgment. The former apprehends the whole Christ with all his benefits; the latter only the body of Christ in and under the bread. The former is metaphorical; the latter is proper by grammatical property, though not by physical property. Obs.

IV. Distinction between oral eating that is physical, or natural, and hyperphysical, or supernatural. The former is that by which food taken by the mouth is sent into the stomach, digested, and ejected: the latter is that by which food, though offered through the mouth, is received into the body, but is not digested and ejected in a natural manner. The angels ate, Gen. 18:8, and Christ after the resurrection, Luke 24:42, which eating, however, was not of the natural order, nor was the food digested in a natural manner. But just as the earth absorbs water in one way, and the sun in another: so also that food is not digested by a physical reason. D. DANNHAVER in Hodof. phanom. X, p. 1233, subdistinguishes proper supernatural eating into economic and sacramental. Obs.

V. Sacramental eating and drinking is one and an undivided action, by which at one and the same moment we eat the eucharistic bread, and the body of Christ sacramentally united to it, and drink the same wine and with it the blood of the Lord sacramentally united [to it] from the eucharistic cup. But of that one eating and drinking there is a twofold mode. For although the earthly and heavenly thing is taken by one and the same organ, yet it is not [taken] in the same mode. Bread and wine are received by the mouth immediately and naturally, the body and blood of Christ mediately and supernaturally. It can be declared by similarities. Into an infant to be baptized, water is poured immediately, the Holy Spirit mediately. The disciples immediately received the breath of Christ's mouth, with which he breathed upon them, mediately the Holy Spirit. The Apostles immediately saw the Son of the Virgin Mary with bodily eyes, and touched him with their hands; mediately they saw and touched the Word of life, 1 John 1:1, on account of the personal union. The whale immediately swallowed the body of Jonah, mediately his soul on account of the natural union. Thus in the legitimate use of the eucharist we immediately eat and drink the blessed bread and wine, mediately the body and blood of Christ on account of the sacramental union.

The assertion is proved: 1) Whatever is eaten by the same eating with the blessed bread, that is eaten by the mouth of the body: But the body of Christ, etc. Therefore. The minor is proved, because one in number

word, EDITE, is predicated of the bread and the body simultaneously. Therefore, it will enjoy only one signification in the same proposition. Therefore, it will signify either only oral eating, or only spiritual, or both simultaneously. If the former: Therefore, both bread and the body of Christ will be eaten by the mouth simultaneously, which is what we want. If the latter: Therefore, we will believe in the bread simultaneously, which is idolatrous. If both simultaneously: Therefore, one word, in the same place, and in the same member of the proposition, will have a double literal sense, which is false.

2) The word, EDITE, joined with τῷ ACCIPITE, in a convivial proposition signifies properly. But τὸ EDITE in this place is joined with τῷ ACCIPITE, in a convivial proposition. Therefore, τὸ EDITE in this place is taken properly. But all proper eating is oral.

3) Whatever things are united sacramentally in the same sacrament and in the same action, they are also received by the same organ. Now, in the use of the Holy Supper, the bread and the body of Christ, the wine and the blood of Christ are united sacramentally. Therefore, in the use of the sacrament, the bread and the body, the wine and the blood of Christ are also received by the same organ. The major premise is evident: because one and undivided action cannot be performed by a double instrument.

4) Every eating, distinct from drinking, is oral eating: But sacramental eating is distinct from drinking. Therefore. The major premise is evident: because spiritual eating, which is done by the mouth of faith, does not differ from spiritual drinking.

5) Whoever distinctly eat the body of Christ with the blessed bread, and distinctly drink the blood of Christ with the blessed wine, they eat the body and drink the blood of Christ with the mouth of the body: But communicants &c. Therefore. The major premise is evident: because spiritual eating and drinking regards the whole Christ with all his benefits. Therefore, that eating, by which the body of Christ is distinctly eaten with the blessed bread, and the drinking, by which the blood of Christ is distinctly drunk with the blessed wine, is not a merely spiritual eating and drinking, which might be done by the mouth of faith.
