Thee, Jesus Christ, almighty Lord, fountain of life and immortality, as most devoutly as can be, I pray and beseech, that with thy most holy Spirit thou mayest illuminate my mind, filled with innate darkness, so that concerning the sublime mystery of the holy supper I may think, feel, speak, or write nothing that is either alien to thy majesty, or abhorrent from the truth, or deviates from the words of thy testament! And as often as I am about to approach thy holy table, for the sake of refreshing my soul, I beseech thee, make me, unworthy, worthy through thy grace, cleanse me, impure, clothe me, naked, so that thy body, full of divine virtue, and thy most precious blood, may not result in judgment or punishment for me, thy lowest servant, but into a monument of thy death, sought for my sake, into a strengthening of my faith, into a pledge of the remission of my sins, into a bond of closer union with thee, into an increase of holiness, into a root of blessed resurrection, into an earnest of eternal life!

Latin:

S V S P I R I V M.

Te, Iesu Christe, omnipotens Domine, fons vitae & immortalitatis, quam devotissime fieri potest, precor & obtestor, vt Spiritu tuo sanctissimo mentem meam, connatis tenebris oppletam, illustres, quo de sublimi sacrae cenae mysterio nil cogitem, sentiam, loquar, aut scribam, quod vel a maiestate tua sit alienum, vel a vero abhorreat, vel a verbis testamenti tui deflectat! Et quotiescunque ad sanctam tuam mensam sum accessurus, animae meae reficiendae causa, indignum me, obsecro, per gratiam tuam fac dignum, me impurum repurga, me nudum vesti, vt corpus tuum virtute divina plenum, & sanguis tuus pretiosissimus mihi, servo tuo infimo, non cedat in iudicium, aut poenam, sed in monumentum mortis tuae, pro me appetitae, in firmamentum fidei meae, in pignus remissionis peccatorum meorum, in vinculum arctioris tecum unionis, in incrementum sanctitatis, in radicem beatae resurrectionis, in arrabonem vitae aeternae!


## 33 On the Penitence of the Sinner


### Quest. I. What is penitence?

Penitence is a movement of the soul, excited by the converting and regenerating grace of the Holy Spirit, by which a sinful man, having acknowledged his sins from the divine law, seriously detests them with sorrow, while at the same time he apprehends by true faith the satisfaction and merit of the mediator Christ, and the mercy of God thereby obtained, promised in the gospel apprehends, and applies to himself, so that by the obtained gratuitous remission of sins he may be eternally saved.

Obs. I. Repentance can be succinctly described as a movement of the soul, seriously detesting its sins with sorrow, and apprehending by true faith the grace of God, founded upon the merit of Christ.

Obs. II. Repentance is an ἀποτέλεσμα, or the common effect of divine grace converting and regenerating; for this reason, because through conversion strictly so-called, contrition is divinely excited, and through regeneration, faith in Christ: Since this was demonstrated in the previous section, ch.

III and IV, it is unnecessary to treat of the efficient cause of repentance. Obs. III. Repentance is also called intransitive conversion, by which the sinner, anticipated by the Holy Spirit and instructed with supernatural powers, is said to convert himself; likewise, a change of mind, by which the sinner returns to a better state of mind. In Greek it is called μετάνοια, μεταμέλεια. The former denotes a change of mind, by which we disapprove of the evil that we previously approved, and approve of the opposite good: the latter denotes a change of will, by which we grieve on account of the memory of the evil perpetrated, and are solicitous about obtaining the good. The former can be rendered in German as die Nachwih; the latter as die Nachforge. In Hebrew it is called תשובה, which word generally designates a return, specifically the return of the sinner to God: The same is נחם, which denotes displeasure.

Latin:

Paenitentia est motus animi, per gratiam Spiritus S. convertentem & regenerantem excitatus, quo homo peccator agnita ex lege divina peccata sua serio cum dolore detestatur, simul vero satisfactionem & meritum mediatoris Christi, eoque partam misericordiam Dei, in evangelio promissam, vera fide apprehendit, sibique applicat, vt impetrata gratuita peccatorum remissione aeternum saluus fiat.

Obs. I. Succincte describi potest paenitentia, quod fit motus animi, peccata sua serio cum dolore detestantis, & gratiam Dei, in merito Christi fundatam, vera fide apprehendentis.

Obs. II. Paenitentia est ἀποτέλεσμα, seu communis effectus gratiae diuinae conuertentis, & regenerantis; propterea, quod per conuersionem strictissime dictam contritio, per regenerationem fides in Christum diuinitus excitatur: Quod cum superiori sectione c. III. & IV. demonstratum sit, de caussa efficiente paenitentiae agere, nil attinet.

Obs. III. Paenitentia vocatur etiam conuersio intransitiua, qua peccator, a Spiritu S. praeuentus, & supernaturalibus viribus instructus, se conuertere dicitur; item resipiscentia, qua peccator ad meliorem mentem redit. Graece appellatur μετάνοια, μεταμέλεια. Illa notat mutationem mentis, qua malum, quod antea probauimus, improbamus, & oppositum bonum approbamus: haec notat mutationem voluntatis, qua ob memoriam mali perpetrati dolemus, & de obtinendo bono solliciti sumus. Illa germanice die Nachwih; haec die Nachforge reddi potest. Hebraice dicitur תשובה, quae vox generatim reditum, speciatim reditum peccatoris ad Deum designat: Idem נחם, quod notat displicentiam.


### Quest. II. In how many ways is the name of repentance taken?

Homonymy of repentance The name repentance is used in either a general or a special signification.

The name of repentance is used in either a general or a special signification. In a general signification, repentance denotes a change of mind, by which those things which we have done begin to displease us, and to affect and vex our mind with sorrow a). In a special and proper signification, repentance denotes the internal change of the sinful man, by which the sins with which he is polluted displease him, and affect his mind with sorrow, so that he meditates on offering satisfaction to God, whom he has offended, to obtain the remission of sins; in which special sense repentance is taken either μερικῶς, partially, for contrition, which is a change of mind toward sorrow b), or ὁλικῶς, totally, for the whole intransitive conversion, which is a change of mind toward sorrow and trust simultaneously c). In an improper signification, it designates an external change, or one declared by external signs d).

Prob. a. Repentance formally is displeasure of a deed joined with sorrow, and thus denotes any change of mind by which a deed displeases and affects the mind with sorrow. In this sense the name of repentance is taken in Heb. XI, 17. Where Esau is said not to have found a place of repentance, although he sought it, i.e., Esau could not move his father Isaac with his tears to change his mind and to revoke, retract, and render void the blessing by which he had transferred the right of primogeniture to Jacob.

Prob. b. When faith, or a cognate word, to believe, is annexed to repentance, then in Holy Scripture repentance is not understood as the whole intransitive conversion, but only contrition. This is evident from Mark I, 15: μετανοεῖτε καὶ πιστεύετε ἐν εὐαγγελίῳ, repent, and believe the gospel. Where by repentance the whole intransitive conversion of man cannot be understood; because to repentance is expressly annexed τὸ πιστεύειν.

…Prob. c. When an express denomination of faith is not added to repentance, and nevertheless a salutary effect is attributed to it, by repentance the whole intransitive conversion of man is denoted: This is evident from Luke XXIV, 47, where our Savior says: It behooved Christ to suffer, and to rise again from the dead, on the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name. Here the salutary effect is annexed to repentance, namely the remission of sins, which is not obtained without faith in Christ, Acts 10:43. By repentance in the cited place is understood the entire intransitive conversion, which is completed by contrition and faith, as essential parts.

Proof d. External repentance is also called ecclesiastical. Because penitent sinners are accustomed to testify to their inner sorrow, which has arisen in the mind from acknowledged sins, by weeping, fasts, sordid garments, ashes cast upon the head, and other gestures and actions, and to reveal them openly by these, as signs; therefore the name of repentance has become accustomed to be transferred to those actions and external signs as well, by the metonymy of the sign for the thing signified. To which can be referred the oracle of Christ, Matthew 11:21. If the mighty works which were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.

Latin:

Homonymia paenitentiae

Nomen paenitentia usurpatur significatu vel generali, vel speciali. Significatu generali paenitentia denotat mutationem animi, qua quae egimus, post displicere, animumque nostrum moerore afficere & angere incipiunt a). Significatu speciali & proprio notat paenitentia internam hominis peccatoris mutationem, qua ipsi peccata, quibus pollutus est, displicent, animumque ipsius moerore afficiunt, vt satisfactionem Deo, quem laesit, offerre meditetur ad impetrandam peccatorum remissionem; quo sensu speciali paenitentia sumitur vel μερικῶς, partialiter, pro contritione, quae est mutatio animi ad dolorem b), vel ὁλικῶς, totaliter, pro tota conuersione intransitiua, quae est mutatio animi ad dolorem & fiduciam simul c). Significatu improprio designat mutationem externam, siue externis signis declaratam d).

Prob. a. Paenitentia formaliter est displicentia facti cum dolore coniuncta, adeoque quamlibet mutationem animi; qua factum displicet, animumque dolore afficit, denotat. Quo sensu sumitur nomen paenitentiae, Hebr. XI, 17. Vbi Esauus dicitur non inuenisse locum paenitentiae, quamuis quaesita, h. e. Esauus lacrymis suis non potuit permouere Isaacum patrem, ut animum mutaret, & benedictionem, qua ius primogeniturae in Iacobum transtulerat, reuocaret, retractaret, irritamque redderet.

Prob. b. Quando paenitentia annectitur fides, aut cognatum verbum, credere, tunc in S. scriptura per paenitentiam non intelligitur tota conuersio intransitiua, sed tantum contritio. Patet hoc ex Marc. I, 15. μετανοεῖτε καὶ πιστεύετε ἐν εὐαγγελίῳ, paenitentiam agite, & credite euangelio. Vbi per paenitentiam non potest tota conuersio hominis intransitiua intelligi; quia paenitentiae expresse annectitur τὸ πιστεύειν. pœnitentiam non potest tota conuersio hominis intranfitiua intelligi; quia pœnitentiæ expreffe annectitur τὸ πιστεύειν.

Prob. c. Quando pœnitentiæ non additur expressa fidei denominatio, & nihilo tamen minus salutaris tribuitur effectus, per pœnitentiam tota hominis conuersio intranfitiua denotatur: Id quod constat ex Luc. XXIV, 47. vbi Seruator nofter inquit: Oportebat Christum Prob. c. Quando paenitentiae non additur expressa fidei denominatio, & nihilo minus salutaris tribuitur effectus, per paenitentiam tota hominis conuersio intransitiua denotatur: Id quod constat ex Luc. XXIV, 47. vbi Seruator noster inquit: Oportebat Christum pati, & resurgere a mortuis, tertia die, & prædicari in nomine eius pœnitentiam & remissionem peccatorum. Hic pœnitentiæ annectitur salutaris effectus, nempe remissio peccatorum, quæ sine fide in Christum non impetratur, Act. X, 43. E. per pœnitentiam l. c. intelligitur tota conuersio intransitiua, quæ contritione ac fide, tanquam partibus essentialibus, absoluitur.

Prob. d. Pœnitentia externa dicitur etiam ecclesiastica. Quia peccatores pœnitentes interiorem suum dolorem, ex agnitis peccatis in animo obortum, planctu, ieiuniis, vestibus sordidis, cinere capiti iniecto, aliisque gestibus & actionibus solent contestari, iisque, ceu signis, palam prodere; ideo pœnitentiæ nomen ad illas quoque actiones & externa signa consueuit transferri, per metonymiam signi pro signato. Quo referri potest oraculum Christi, Matth. XI, 21. Si in Tyro & Sidone factæ fuissent virtutes, quæ factæ sunt in vobis, olim in sacco & cinere pœnitentiam egissent.


### Quest. III. How manifold is repentance?

Repentance by reason of the subject, or the penitent man, is twofold: of those who have fallen, and of those who stand a). Those who have fallen are either infidels, who have never been reborn through baptism or circumcision, and yet are converted from idols to the true God by the grace of the Holy Spirit b); or malicious sinners, who indeed were reborn through baptism, or in the Old Testament through circumcision, but having fallen into deliberate sins are illuminated by the lightning of the law and the light of the gospel, so that they may repent c). The repentance of those who stand is the daily sorrow for sins of infirmity, and the daily fiducial embrace of divine grace, obtained by the merit of Christ d).

Proof a. Paul makes mention of those who stand and those who have fallen, 1 Corinthians 10:12. He who thinks he stands, let him take heed lest he fall. Those who stand are those who persist through faith in the covenant of grace: Those who fall are those who fall away from grace through voluntary sins.

Proof b. From 1 Thessalonians 1:9. You turned to God from idols, to serve the living and true God. The Thessalonians, having turned from the worship of idols to the worship of the true God, performed the first repentance.

Proof c. From Revelation 2:5. Remember from where you have fallen and repent. By which words Christ addresses the bishop of Ephesus, whose ardor for converting the Ephesians had grown cold, on account of the stubborn resistance of the Jews and Gentiles. But since he is cursed who does the work of the Lord negligently, Jeremiah 48:10, this bishop who has fallen gravely is stimulated to perform repentance.

Proof d. Christians who stand through faith pray daily, Matthew 6:12. Father, forgive us our debts. For there is no man who does not sin, 1 Kings 8:46. Christians who stand do not indeed sin by deliberate purpose; yet they do so out of infirmity and ignorance. *).

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, who maintain that perfect Christians, as they call them, have no need of repentance. Who fortify their opinion with the following arguments:

I. Christ says explicitly: The righteous do not need repentance, Luke 15:7. Resp. AUGUSTINE, in Ps. 61, understands the words of Christ as referring to the righteous κατὰ δόξαν, according to opinion, such as the Pharisees were. But a more accurate distinction is made between the repentance of those who stand and those who have fallen, in this sense: the righteous have no need of such repentance as those who have been led astray into mortal sins require.

II. Matt. 9:13. The Savior says: I came to call sinners to repentance, and not the righteous. Resp. All men are sinners, 1 Kings 8:46. But those who are righteous by opinion, i.e., swollen with the persuasion of their own righteousness, think that they do not need the call of Christ to repentance.

III. Certain men are called perfect, such as Josiah, 2 Chron. 34:2. But those who are perfect do not fall into sins, and therefore do not need repentance.

Resp. Distinguish between comparative perfection and absolute perfection, not only of parts, but also of degrees.

Josiah was not perfect in all respects, which is evident from the useless war which, to his own detriment and that of his people, he waged against Pharaoh Necho, 2 Chron. 35:3. He also performed repentance; for he is said to have turned to God with all his heart, 2 Kings 23:25. Furthermore, all men are commanded to repent, Acts 17:30. Observe here the distinction between men as wayfarers and angels. Good angels do not need repentance: evil angels are neither called to repentance nor can they hope for the grace of conversion: but all men as wayfarers are in need of repentance, and are called to it by God.

Quæst. James 3:2. That he himself has sin, and feels its enticements within himself most unwillingly, although he himself commits no sin knowingly and consenting, Rom. 7:15 et seq. coll. with 8:1. 1 John 1:8, 9; 3:9. There is therefore a great necessity for this matter as a consequence.

Nor is the necessity of the precept any less, as is commonly said.

The name of the repentance of those who stand exists in writing in Rev. 2:16: μεταvόησον (repent). Christ commands this to a man born again, and even one persisting in faith, but who in a certain matter sins out of ignorance and a set purpose, v. 13, 14, 15. As far as the matter itself is concerned, the formula of prayer commanded to us by Christ provides us with a most valid argument. He himself taught us, nay, commanded us, to pray to God, as a Father reconciled and kind to us, in this way: Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors!

But to whom does this pertain? Certainly not to the impious, who have not yet repented of their evil deeds, who neither want nor are able to offer prayers pleasing to God, in whose souls also no vice is usually more tenaciously fixed than implacable hatred, so that they are unwilling to forgive debts to their brothers and to forget injuries.

Christ addressed men who were devoted to his discipline in this way.

Let us also consider both the connection and the order of the words and things.

Whatever precedes the fifth petition, all of it judges the good disposition of a renewed mind. Whatever follows it, these two things signify the imperfect condition of the same, not to be perfected until we have departed from this life in a blessed transition.

From this bond of prayer a twofold argument is made.

One: Since we are in such a condition that we hallow the name of God, perpetually desire the kingdom of God, piously revere the will of God, and receive our bread with a grateful mind (petit.

I, II, III, IV); then it is our duty to ask for the forgiveness of sins from God.

The other is this: As long as we are subject to many and various vexations and incitements to evil, and are not yet freed from all evil (petit.

VI & VII); so long must this deprecation be continued: Father, be propitious! Forgive us our debts!

We have as adversaries in this cause not only the Socinians, but also the Pseudo-mystics and fanatical men, and all those who, with rash audacity, attribute legal perfection, both of parts and of degrees, to a man who is renewed and, as it were, adult.

Latin:

Pœnitentia ratione subiecti, siue hominis pœnitentis, est duplex, lapsorum, & stantium a). Lapsi sunt vel infideles, qui per baptismum vel circumcisionem nunquam sunt renati, & gratia tamen Spiritus S. conuertuntur ab idolis ad verum Deum b); vel peccatores malitiosi, qui per baptismum, aut in V. T. per circumcisionem quidem renati fuerunt, sed in proæretica peccata prolapsi fulmine legis & luce euangelii illuminantur, vt resipiscant c). Pœnitentia stantium est quotidianus dolor de peccatis infirmitatis, & quotidianus amplexus fiducialis gratiæ diuinæ, merito Christi partæ d).

Prob. a. Paullus stantium & lapsorum mentionem facit, 1 Cor. X, 12. Qui sibi videtur stare, videat, ne cadat. Stantes sunt, qui per fidem in fœdere gratiæ persistunt: Cadentes, qui per voluntaria peccata gratia excidunt.

Prob. b. Ex 1 Thess. I, 9. Conuersi estis ad Deum ab idolis, ad seruiendum Deo viuo & vero. Thessalonicenses, a cultu idolorum ad cultum veri Dei conuersi, primam egerunt pœnitentiam.

Prob. c. Ex Apoc. II, 5. Recordare, vnde excideris & pœnitentiam age. Quibus verbis Christus episcopum Ephesinum, cuius ardor conuertendi Ephesios intepuerat, ob pertinacem Iudæorum & gentilium reluctationem, compellat. Cum autem maledictus sit, qui opus Domini negligenter facit, Ier. XLVIII, 10. ad agendam pœnitentiam hic Episcopus grauiter lapsus exstimulatur.

Prob. d. Stantes per fidem Christiani quotidie suspirant, Matth. VI, 22. Pater, dimitte nobis debita nostra. Neque enim est homo, qui non peccet, 1 Reg. VIII, 46. Stantes christiani non peccant quidem ex deliberato proposito; ex infirmitate tamen & ignorantia. *).

Antithesis est Socinianorum, statuentium, Christianos perfectos, quos vocant, poenitentia non indigere. Qui sequentibus argumentis suam opinionem muniunt:

I. Christus diserte dicit: Iusti non indigent poenitentia, Luc. XV, 7. Resp. AVGVSTINVS in Ps. LXI, verba Christi intelligit de iustis κατὰ δόξαν, secundum opinionem, quales erant Pharisaei. Sed accuratius distinguitur inter poenitentiam stantium, & lapsorum, hoc sensu: iustis non opus est tali poenitentia, quali indigent abrepti in deuia peccatorum immortalium .

II. Matth. IX, 13. Saluator inquit: Veni ad poenitentiam vocatum peccatores. & non iustos. Resp. Homines omnes sunt peccatores, 1 Reg. VIII, 46. At iusti opinione, i. e. persuasione propriae iustitiae tumidi, existimant, se vocatione Christi ad poenitentiam non indigere.

III. Quidam homines dicuntur perfecti, vt Iosias, 2 Paral. XXXIV, 2. Sed qui perfecti sunt, non prolabuntur in peccata, adeoque poenitentia non indigent.

Resp. Distingu. inter perfectionem comparatam, & absolutam, non tantum partium, sed & graduum.

Iosias non fuit omnibus numeris perfectus, quod patet ex bello inutili, quod suo fuorumque damno Pharaoni Necho, 2 Paral. XXXV, 3. intulit. Egit etiam poenitentiam; nam toto corde ad Deum conuersus dicitur 2 Reg. XXIII, 25. Ceterum iubentur omnes homines resipiscere, Act. XVII, 30. Obserues hic discrimen inter homines viatores, & angelos. Angeli boni non indigent poenitentia: angeli mali nec ad poenitentiam vocantur, nec gratiam conuersionis sperare possunt: at homines viatores omnes poenitentiae sunt indigi, & ad eam a Deo vocantur.

Quæst. Iac. III, 2. quod peccatum ipse habeat, eiusque illecebras maxime inuitus in se sentiat, licet peccatum nullum ipse faciat sciens & consentiens, Rom. VII, 15. seq. coll. cum VIII, 1. 1 Io. I, 8. 9 III, 9. Est igitur magna huius rei necessitas consequentia.

Nec minor est necessitas praecepti, vt dici solet.

Nomen poenitentiae stantium scriptum exstat Apoc. II, 16.: μεταvόησον. Id Christus imperat homini denuo nato, atque etiam in fide persistenti, sed quadam in re ex ignorantia ac fine proposito peccanti, v. 13. 14. 15. Quod ad rem ipsam attinet, argumentum nobis validissimum praebet formula precationis, a Christo nobis praecepta. Ipse nos docuit, immo iussit, ita Deum, vt Patrem nobis reconciliatum ac benignum, precari: Remitte nobis debita nostra, quem ad modum nostris nos debitoribus remittimus!

Ad quosnam vero hoc pertinet? Certe non ad impios, quos male factorum nondum paenituit, qui nec volunt, nec possunt preces Deo gratas fundere, quorum etiam in animis nullum vitium tenacius infixum haerere solet, quam implacabile odium, vt nolit fratribus debita condonare atque iniuriarum obliuisei.

Disciplinae suae addictos homines Christus ita affatus est.

Consideremus etiam verborum rerumque & copulationem, & ordinem.

Quae precationem quintam praecedunt, ea vniuersa iudicant bonam indolem renouati animi. Quae eam sequuntur, haec bina significant imperfectam eiusdem conditionem, non prius, quam beato transitu ex hac vita discesserimus, perficiendam.

Ex hoc orationis vinculo duplex efficitur argumentum.

Vna: Quando ea sumus conditione, vt nomen Dei sancte colamus, regnum Dei perpetuo exoptemus, voluntatem Dei pie veneremur, panem nostrum grato animo accipiamus (petit.

I. II. III. IV.); tunc nostri est officii, vt veniam peccatorum a Deo petamus.

Altera haec est: Quam diu multis ac variis vexationibus ac malorum irritamentis obnoxii sumus, nondumque omni malo liberati (petit.

VI. & VII.); tam diu continuanda est haec deprecatio: Pater propitie! remitte nobis debita nostra!

Aduersarios in hac caussa habemus non Socinianos solum, sed etiam Pseudomysticos ac fanaticos homines, omnesque eos, qui homini renouato, & quasi adulto, perfectionem legalem. & partium, & graduum, temeraria audacia adferunt.


### IV. How many are the parts of repentance?

The parts of repentance are two, contrition & faith.

This bipartition is proved: 1) From the nature of repentance. For since repentance is the intransitive conversion of a sinner, it moves between two terms; namely, between the term from which, and the term to which. The term from which is the sin committed, from the recognition of which contrition is born: The term to which is God, to whose mercy for Christ’s sake the sinner flees by faith, Acts XIV, 15.

2) From the principal efficient cause. The justice & mercy of God show that there are two parts of repentance. From the consideration of justice arises contrition, from the meditation of mercy springs up trust, Dan. IX, 15. We have sinned, we have acted iniquitously, we have been impious: v. 18. But yours, O Lord, is mercy & remission.

3) From the twofold intermediate cause of repentance. Since there is a twofold kind of doctrine by which God effects repentance in us, the law & the gospel; and it is the work of the law to crush sinners; but of the gospel to kindle living faith: it is clearly evident that contrition & faith are the two parts of repentance.

4) From the effect. Repentance is a spiritual motion by which sins are abolished, and we are reconciled to God who was offended by the sins. For the abolition of sins there is required 1) a moral retraction of sins, which is performed by contrition, & 2) an offering of satisfaction for the injury & offense brought upon God, by which we are freed from the debt of undergoing punishment, or from the guilt of punishment, which is not performed except by faith, apprehending the satisfaction of Christ, applying it to us, & offering it to God.

5) In Holy Scripture repentance is described as being a conversion to the living God, Acts XIV, 14. into God c. XX, 21. repentance unto life, c. XI, 18. repentance & conversion for the τὸ ἐξαλειφθῆναι τὰς ἁμαρτίας, that sins may be blotted out, c. III, 19. conversion from darkness to light, c. XXVI, 18. But without faith in Christ, it is impossible for there to be repentance, or conversion to God, to life, to light, to the remission of sins. Through faith in Christ we obtain the remission of sins, Acts X, 43. through faith, saving repentance is distinguished from destructive [repentance], as the example of Peter & Judas shows. If faith did not enter into the essence of repentance, the whole of repentance would be a work of the law; from which there is no consolation, no justification: Nay, repentance would also be destitute of the term to which.

6) From the examples of true penitents, the first parents, David, the hearers of John the Baptist, the sinful woman, the prodigal son, the thief on the cross, in whose repentance two things are discerned, contrition & faith.

Antithesis 1) Of the Papists, whose opinion is that there are three parts of repentance, contrition of heart, confession of mouth, & satisfaction of work. 2) Of the Arminians, asserting that repentance is the correction of life. 3) Of the Socinians, from whose mind new obedience is almost the sole part of repentance.

Their arguments are: I. Faith is contradistinguished from repentance, Mark I, 15: Repent, & believe the gospel.

Resp. Then repentance is understood μερικῶς, or partially, and denotes contrition.

Faith pertains to the whole scope of saving repentance.

II. Faith precedes repentance: Therefore it is not a part of repentance. The antecedent is evident from Jonah III, 5. The Ninevites believed in God, and proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth.

Resp. Historical faith precedes repentance; because no one seriously grieves for sins unless he believes that God is a severe hater & avenger of sinners: But saving faith constitutes repentance.

III. Faith, which is required for repentance, cannot be a certain trust in the remission of sins; because the Ninevites believed in God, and yet they doubted concerning the remission of sins; which is evident from their words, Jonah III, 9:

"Who knows? God may turn and relent, that He may turn from the fierceness of His anger, so that we may not perish?" Resp.

1) The Ninevites did not doubt concerning the remission of guilt, but concerning the condonation of temporal punishment and affliction; since God sometimes inflicts temporal afflictions even upon truly faithful penitents who are certain of the gratuitous remission of sins. David, Job, and others are examples to us.

2) The particle, "who knows," is not always that of one doubting, but sometimes also that of one hoping well. See 1 Sam.

XIV, 6; 2 Sam. XII, 22.

IV. Repentance, or contrition, is a moral virtue, faith is a theological virtue, which cannot concur to constitute one essential thing. Resp.

Contrition is not an active virtue, but a sorrow and passion of the soul: Nor is faith considered here as a theological virtue, but as an ὄργανον (instrument), or a medium receptive of divine grace and the merit of Christ. V.

Repentance, by the force of the word, denotes a displeasure at some deed joined with sorrow, but it does not signify faith or trust: Therefore, faith is not a part of repentance. Resp.

Although among profane authors of the Latin language repentance denotes displeasure joined with sorrow; yet among sacred and ecclesiastical authors it is taken with such breadth that it designates the whole conversion to God and the abolition of sins.

VI. Repentance (pœnitentia) is deduced from punishment (pœna), and "it repents me" (pœnitet) signifies the same as "punishment holds me" (pœna me tenet). Therefore, repentance denotes a certain external punishment for sins, which ecclesiastical authors commonly call satisfaction.

Resp. To Erasmus, "to repent" (pœnitere) is the same as "to hold punishment" (pœna tenere); because later thoughts are better: but to us, the verb "to repent" seems to be primitive, not derivative.

However, what "to repent" signifies according to the usage of the Latin language, Gallus Asinius and Largius Licinius, ancient writers, teach in A. Gellius, book XVII, Noct.

Att. ch. I, when they say:

"We are accustomed to say 'it repents' (pœnitere) then, when those things which we ourselves have done, or which have been done by our will and our counsel, begin afterwards to displease us, and we change our opinion concerning them."

Instance: If the name of repentance in its meaning includes sorrow for past life, it follows certainly that it includes a certain punishment.

Resp. Punishment is taken in two ways: 1) In a general and improper meaning, by which it denotes an evil, or damage, uncongenial to an intelligent nature, contracted on account of guilt. 2) In a special and most proper meaning, by which it designates an evil, or damage, by which guilt is avenged and an injury inflicted upon someone is compensated.

In the general and improper sense, repentance with respect to the former part, or contrition, can be called a punishment: for it is a certain evil, uncongenial to the nature and will of man, and that contracted on account of guilt, namely an evil placed in the lack of delight and tranquility of soul, which is also commonly held to be like a punishment. But in the special sense, contrition is not a punishment, but only a certain disposition toward faith, to be kindled by the voice of the Gospel; for by contrition man does not compensate for the injury inflicted upon God, but is only disposed toward conceiving faith in Christ.

Confer Musaeus, disp.

II, de convers. p. 78 seqq.

VII. The true parts of repentance are salutary to man: Contrition is not salutary to man.

Therefore, the major is clear: because repentance is given unto life, Acts XI, 18. The minor is proved from 2 Cor.

VII, 10, and the example of Judas, whose contrition was not salutary. Resp.

1) In general. Something is said to be salutary either remotely or positively.

Contrition is salutary partly remotely, insofar as it removes the purpose of sinning, which is an obstacle to faith and the remission of sins, and exterminates it; partly positively, not indeed effectively, as if it produced salvation by itself, but yet pedagogically, insofar as through it the way is prepared and leveled for the Lord, by receiving Him with true faith, Matt. III, 3. 2) Specifically, to 2 Cor. VII, 10. The sorrow of the world, conceived from impatience of punishments and the loss of earthly goods, works death, but not the sorrow according to God excited by the Holy Spirit through the moral law, and conceived from the offense of the most good Divinity and the loss of divine grace. 3) The repentance of Judas was not joined with faith in Christ, by which it ought to be tempered, so that it may be not only pedagogically, but also effectively and thus completely salutary.

VIII. Whatever works repentance, that is not a part of repentance. But contrition etc. Therefore. The major is clear; because nothing works itself. If therefore contrition were repentance, or a part of repentance, it could not work repentance. The minor is proved from 2 Cor. VII, 10. Sorrow, which is according to God, works repentance to salvation not to be repented of. Resp. Sorrow according to God is that which God not only commands or approves, but also excites by the word of the law, by saddening the heart of man, and thus works repentance to salvation, insofar as through contrition it softens the hard heart of man, prepares and disposes it to receive saving faith from the gospel, by which repentance may be salutary.

IX. Contrition precedes repentance: Therefore it is not a part of repentance. The antecedent is clear from Acts II, 37. 38. where St. Peter inculcates to those who were already pricked in their heart, that repentance must be done; and thus compunction of heart precedes repentance. Resp. 1) By denying the consequence; because parts by nature precede the whole. 2) More is required for contrition than compunction of heart, namely detestation of sin and faith in Christ.

Latin:

Partes poenitentiae sunt duae, contritio & fides.

Probatur haec bipartitio: 1) Ex natura poenitentiae. Cum enim poenitentia sit intransitiva peccatoris conversio, inter duos versatur terminos; nempe inter terminum a quo, & ad quem. Terminus a quo est peccatum admissum, ex cuius agnitione nascitur contritio: Terminus ad quem est Deus, ad cuius misericordiam propter Christum peccator fide confugit, Act. XIV, 15.

2) A causa efficiente principali. Duas esse poenitentiae partes, ostendit iustitia & misericordia Dei. Ex consideratione iustitiae suboritur contritio, e meditatione misericordiae suppullulat fiducia, Dan, IX, 15. Peccavimus, inique egimus, impii fuimus: v. 18. Tua vero, Domine, est misericordia & remissio.

3) A duplici poenitentiae causa intermedia. Cum duplex fit doctrinae genus, quo Deus in nobis poenitentiam efficit, lex & evangelium; & legis quidem fit, peccatores conterere; evangelii autem, vivam fidem accendere: constat liquido, contritionem & fidem esse duas poenitentiae partes.

4) Ab effectu. Poenitentia est motus spiritualis, quo peccata abolentur, Deoque peccatis offenso reconciliamur. Ad abolitionem vero peccatorum requiritur 1) peccatorum moralis retractatio, quae contritione peragitur, & 2) oblatio satisfactionis pro iniuria & offensa Deo illata, qua a debito subeundi poenam, sive a reatu poenae liberamur, quae non, nisi fide, satisfactionem Christi apprehendente, nobisque applicante & Deo offerente, peragitur.

5) In S. scriptura poenitentia describitur, quod sit conversio ad Deum vivum, Actor. XIV, 14. in Deum c. XX, 21. poenitentia ad vitam, c. XI, 18. resipiscentia & conversio eis τὸ ἐξαλειφθῆναι τὰς ἁμαρτίας, ut deleantur peccata, c. III, 19. conversio a tenebris ad lucem, c. XXVI, 18. Sed absque fide in Christum poenitentiam, seu conversionem ad Deum, ad vitam, ad lucem, ad remissionem peccatorum dari, impossibile est. Per fidem in Christum impetramus remissionem peccatorum, Act. X, 43. per fidem poenitentia salutaris ab exitiosa distinguitur, vt ostendit exemplum Petri & Iudae. Si fides essentiam poenitentiae non ingereret, tota poenitentia esset opus legis; e qua nulla consolatio, nulla iustificatio est: Quin poenitentia etiam termino ad quem destitueretur.

6) Ab exemplis vere poenitentium, primorum parentum, Dauidis, auditorum Ioannis baptistae, mulieris peccatricis, filii prodigi, latronis in cruce, in quorum poenitentia cernuntur duo, contritio & fides.

Antithesis 1) Pontificiorum, quorum sententia tres sunt poenitentiae partes, contritio cordis, confessio oris, & satisfactio operis. 2) Arminianorum, asserentium, poenitentiam esse correctionem vitae. 3) Socinianorum, ex quorum mente nova obedientia fere sola est pars poenitentiae.

Quorum argumenta sunt: I. Fides poenitentiae contradistinguitur, Marc. I, 15: Poenitentiam agite, & credite evangelio.

Resp. Tunc intelligitur poenitentia μερικῶς, sive partialiter dicta, & notat contritionem.

Fides ad totum poenitentiae salutaris ambitum pertinet.

II. Fides poenitentiam antecedit: E. non est pars poenitentiae. Antecedens patet ex Ion. III, 5. Crediderunt Niniuitae in Deum, & praedicaverunt ieiunium, & induti sunt cilicio.

Resp. Fides historica praecedit poenitentiam; quia nemo serio de peccatis dolet, nisi credat, Deum esse peccatorum severum osorem & vltorem: Fides autem salutifica poenitentiam constituit. faluifica pœnitentiam constituit. faluifica pœnitentiam constituit. faluifica pœnitentiam constituit.

III. Fides, quæ ad pœnitentiam requiritur, non potest esse certa fiducia remissionis peccatorum; quia Niniuitæ crediderunt in Deum, & tamen de remissione peccatorum dubitarunt; quod constat ex eorum verbis, Ion. III, 9.

Quis scit? Reuertetur & pœnitentia ducetur Deus, ut reuertatur ab ardore iræ suæ, ne pereamus?

Resp. 1) Non dubitarunt Niniuitæ de remissione culpæ, sed de condonatione pœnæ temporalis & afflictionis; quum etiam pœnitentibus vere fidelibus, & certis de gratuita peccatorum remissione, afflictiones temporales Deus quandoque immittat. Exemplo nobis sunt Dauid, Iobus, & alii.

2) Particula, quis scit, non est semper dubitantis, sed quandoque etiam bene sperantis. Vid. 1 Sam.

XIV, 6. 2 Sam. XII, 22.

IV. Pœnitentia, siue contritio, est virtus moralis, fides virtus theologica, quæ non possunt concurrere ad vnum essentiale constituendum.

Resp. Contritio non est virtus actiua, sed dolor & passio animi: Neque h. l. fides consideratur, vt virtus theologica, sed vt ὄργανον, vel medium gratiæ diuinæ & meriti Christi receptiuum.

V. Pœnitentia, vi vocis, notat displicentiam alicuius facti cum dolore coniunctam, non autem significat fidem aut fiduciam: Ergo fides non est pars pœnitentiæ.

Resp. Quamuis apud auctores latinæ linguæ profanos pœnitentia denotet displicentiam cum dolore coniunctam; apud auctores tamen sacros & ecclesiasticos ea latitudine accipitur, vt designet totam conuersionem ad Deum, & abolitionem peccatorum.

VI. Pœnitentia deducitur a pœna, & pœnitet significat idem, quod pœna me tenet. E. pœnitentia denotat quandam peccatorum pœnam externam, quam auctores ecclesiastici satisfactionem vulgo vocant.

Resp. Erasmo pœnitere idem est, quod pone tenere; ideo, quod cogitationes posteriores sunt meliores: nobis autem videtur verbum pœnitere esse primitiuum, non deriuatiuum.

Quid autem pœnitere ex vsu latinæ linguæ significet, docent Gallus Asinius & Largius Licinius, scriptores veteres, apud A. Gellium, libr.

XVII. Noct.

Att. c. I. quando, pœnitere, inquiunt, tum dicere solemus, cum, quæ ipsi fecimus; aut quæ de nostra voluntate, nostroque consilio facta sunt, ea nobis post displicere incipiunt, sententiamque in iis nostram demutamus.

Instantia: Si pœnitentiæ nomen in suo significatu includit dolorem de vita præterita, sequitur vtique, quod pœnam quandam includat.

Resp. Pœna sumitur bifariam: 1) in significatu generali & improprio, quo notat malum, siue damnum naturæ intelligenti disconueniens ob culpam contractum. 2) In significatu speciali & maxime proprio, quo designat malum, siue damnum, quo vindicatur culpa, & iniuria cuipiam illata compensatur.

Sensu generali & improprio pœnitentia respectu prioris partis, siue contritionis, dici potest pœna: est enim quoddam malum, hominis naturæ & voluntati disconueniens, idque ob culpam contractum, nempe malum positum in carentia delectationis, & tranquillitatis animi, quod etiam vulgo instar pœnæ haberi solet. Sensu autem speciali contritio non est pœna, sed tantum dispositio quædam ad fidem, voce euangelii accendendam; neque enim per contritionem homo compensat iniuriam Deo illatam, sed disponitur tantum ad concipiendam fidem in Christum.

Confer. Musaei disp. II. de conuerf. p.

78. seqq.

VII. Veræ partes pœnitentiæ homini sunt salutares: Contritio non est homini salutaris.

E. Maior liquet: quia pœnitentia datur ad vitam, Act. XI, 18. Minor probatur ex 2 Cor.

VII, 10. & exemplo Iudæ, cuius contritio non erat salutaris. Resp.

1) in genere. Salutare aliquid dicitur vel remotiue, vel positiue.

Contritio est salutaris partim remotiue, quatenus peccandi propositum, quod obstaculum fidei & remissionis peccatorum, remouet propositum, quod est obstaculum fidei & remissionis peccatorum, remouet mouet atque exterminat; partim positiue, non quidem effectiue, quasi per se salutem efficiat, at tamen pædagogice, quatenus per eam præparatur & complanatur via Domino, vera fide recipiendo, Matth. III, 3. 2) In specie, ad 2 Cor. VII, 10. Dolor mundi, conceptus ex impatientia pœnarum & iactura bonorum terrestrium mortem operatur, non autem dolor secundum Deum excitatus a Spiritu S. per legem moralem, & conceptus ex offensa Numinis optimi & iactura gratiæ diuinæ. 3) Pœnitentia Iudæ non erat cum fide in Christum coniuncta, qua temperata esse debet, vt sit non solum pædagogice, sed etiam effectiue adeoque complete salutaris.

VIII. Quidquid pœnitentiam operatur, illud non est pars pœnitentiæ. Atqui contritio &c. E. Maior claret; quia nil seipsum operatur. Quod si itaque contritio esset pœnitentia, aut pars pœnitentiæ, non posset pœnitentiam operari. Minor probatur ex 2 Cor. VII, 10. Tristitia, quæ secundum Deum est, pœnitentiam ad salutem non pœnitendam operatur. Resp. Tristitia secundum Deum est, quam Deus non solum iubet aut approbat, sed etiam verbo legis excitat, cor hominis contristando, adeoque operatur pœnitentiam ad salutem, quatenus per contritionem cor hominis durum emollit, præparat & disponit ad fidem salificam ex euangelio suscipiendam, quo pœnitentia sit salutaris.

IX. Contritio pœnitentiam antecedit: E. non est pars pœnitentiæ. Antecedens liquet ex Act. II, 37. 38. vbi S. Petrus illis, qui iam compuncti corde erant, inculcat, agendam esse pœnitentiam; adeoque compunctio cordis præcedit pœnitentiam. Resp. 1) Negando consequentiam; quia partes natura totum præcedunt. 2) Plus requiritur ad contritionem, quam compunctio cordis, nimirum detestatio peccati & fides in Christum.


### IV. How many are the parts of repentance?: Quæst. V. Is new obedience a part of repentance?

Quæst. V. Is new obedience a part of repentance?

New obedience is not a part, but an effect of repentance.

Obs. New obedience is the pursuit of good works, or a serious and indefatigable pursuit of keeping the commandments of God, and of living soberly, justly, and piously, and it is distinguished into new internal obedience, and external. The former is the internal purpose of the mind and will to obey divine precepts promptly; the latter is the external execution of the internal purpose. Confer. D. HULSEM. breuiar. c. IX. p. 526.

Prob. 1) From Matt. III, 18. where the pursuit of good works is called the fruit of repentance. Just as therefore the fruit of a tree is not its part: so new obedience is not a part of repentance.

2) Scripture describes the pursuit of good works as a consequence of conversion. Christ warns the Ephesian bishop: Repent, and do the first works, Apoc. II, 5. where good works are distinguished from repentance, and are placed after it.

3) Repentance is divinely ordained for the remission of sins, Acts III, 18. Luke XXIV, 47. But new obedience is the fruit of the remission of sins. The Apostle of the Gentiles says gravely: But now being made free from sin, and servants to God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end life everlasting. Rom. VI, 22.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, who opine that new obedience is the most essential part of repentance. Who rely on the following arguments: 1. Repentance in Greek is called μετάνοια, i.e. a change of mind and of all actions flowing from it, and thus μετάνοια denotes the whole reformation of man. Resp. Μετάνοια is a change of mind either only to sorrow for committed sins, and is called contrition, and is repentpenitence in a partial sense; or to sorrow, and at the same time to trust resting in Christ, and it is penitence understood in a whole sense. But μετάνοια [repentance] in Holy Scripture is not used for sanctification, which is the fruit of the remission of sins. Rom. VI, 22. II. Holy Scripture describes penitence through the pursuit of good works. Therefore, new obedience is a part of penitence.

The antecedent is clear from Ps. XXXIV, 15. Depart from evil, and do good. Ezech. XVIII, 27. Turn from impiety and practice justice.

Response: In the cited passages, the conversion of the sinner is not described according to its essential parts, but rather the renewal, which follows conversion, and notifies and declares it a posteriori.

III. The Apology of the Augsburg Confession, art. XII, reckons new obedience among the parts of penitence. You see, here two parts are joined, contrition, when sins are reproved, and faith, when it is said: Believe the gospel. If anyone here says that Christ also includes the fruits of penitence, we will not disagree. For it suffices for us that these are named as the principal parts, contrition and faith. Response: 1) The Apology of the Augsburg Confession expressly calls new obedience the fruit of penitence: therefore it is not a principal part of penitence. 2) If penitence is taken broadly, as it immediately includes its effect, neither will we disagree.

Latin:

Quæst. V. Estne noua obedientia pars pœnitentiæ?

Noua obedientia non est pars, sed effectus pœnitentiæ.

Obs. Noua obedientia est studium bonorum operum, siue serium & indefessum studium seruandi præcepta Dei, & sobrie, iuste pieque viuendi, & distinguitur in nouam obedientiam internam, & externam. Illa est internum mentis voluntatisque propositum præceptis diuinis promte obediendi; hæc est externa interni propositi exsecutio. Confer. D. HVLSEM. breuiar. c. IX. p. 526.

Prob. 1) Ex Matth. III, 18. vbi studium bonorum operum dicitur fructus pœnitentiæ. Quem ad modum igitur fructus arboris non est eius pars: ita noua obedientia non est pars pœnitentiæ.

2) Scriptura describit studium bonorum operum, tanquam consequens conuersionis. Christus monet episcopum Ephesinum: Age pœnitentiam, & fac priora opera, Apoc. II, 5. vbi bona opera a pœnitentia distinguuntur, & ei postponuntur.

3) Pœnitentia diuinitus ordinata est ad remissionem peccatorum, Actor. III, 18. Luc. XXIV, 47. At noua obedientia est fructus remissionis peccatorum. Grauiter gentium Apostolus inquit: Iam vero liberi facti a peccato, & Dei serui, habetis fructum vestrum in sanctificationem, finem autem vitam æternam. Rom. VI, 22.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, opinantium, nouam obedientiam esse partem pœnitentiæ maxime essentialem. Qui sequentibus innituntur argumentis: 1. Pœnitentia græce dicitur μετάνοια, i. e. mutatio mentis & omnium inde manantium actionum, adeoque μετάνοια totam hominis reformationem denotat. Resp. Μετάνοια est mutatio mentis vel tantum ad dolorem de admissis peccatis, & dicitur contritio, estque pœnitentia μερικῶς dicta; vel ad dolorem, & simul fiduciam in Christo recumbentem, & est pœnitentia ὁλικῶς intellecta. Sed μετάνοια in S. scriptura non usurpatur pro sanctificatione, quæ est fructus remissionis peccatorum. Rom. VI, 22. II. S. scriptura pœnitentiam per studium bonorum operum describit. E. noua obedientia est pars pœnitentiæ.

Antecedens liquet ex Ps. XXXIV, 15. Recedite a malo, & facite bonum. Ezech. XVIII, 27. Reuertimini ab impietate & exercete iustitiam.

Resp. Locis citatis non describitur conuersio peccatoris secundum partes ipsius essentiales, sed renouatio, quæ conuersionem consequitur, eamque a posteriori notificat & declarat.

III. Apologia August. confess. art. XII. nouam obedientiam partibus pœnitentiæ accenset. Videtis, hic duas partes coniungi, contritionem, cum arguuntur peccata, & fidem, cum dicitur: Credite euangelio. Si quis hic dicat, Christum complecti etiam fructus pœnitentiæ, non diffintiemus. Nam hoc nobis sufficit, quod hæ partes præcipuæ nominantur, contritio & fides. Resp. 1) Apolog. August. confess. diserte nouam obedientiam vocat fructum pœnitentiæ: non igitur pars pœnitentiæ præcipua est. 2) Si pœnitentia sumatur late, prout immediate suum effectum includit, neque nos dissentiemus.


### Question VI. Is new obedience a necessary and inseparable consequence of penitence?

New obedience follows penitence in an indissoluble bond, and cannot be separated from it, not even in those who are in their death throes.

Proof: 1) Penitence, or new obedience, is like a tree not bearing good fruit, and to be cast into the fire, Matt. III, 10. 2) Faith without good works (at least internal ones) is dead, James II, 20. For which reason, those who in the agony of death do not seriously propose to themselves that they wish to practice new obedience, it cannot be said of them that they truly repent.

Latin:

Noua obedientia indiuulso nexu pœnitentiam sequitur, & ab ea ne in agonizantibus quidem separari potest.

Prob. 1) Pœnitentia, siue noua obedientia, est funilis arbori, bonos fructus non ferenti, & in ignem proiiciendæ, Matth. III, 10. 2) Fides sine bonis, operibus (saltim internis) est mortua, Iac. II, 20. Quam ob rem qui in agone mortis non serio sibi proponunt, se velle nouæ obedientiæ illudere, de illis non potest dici, quod vere resipiscant.


### Question VII. Are mortification and vivification true parts of penitence?

If by mortification is understood passive mortification, by which our hearts are crushed and mortified by God through the law; and by vivification, living faith, by which our hearts are raised up and sustained: this bipartition is conformable to orthodoxy . But if by mortification is understood the active putting off of the old man, and by vivification the putting on of the new man: this dichotomy is to be referred not to conversion, but to renewal.

Proof: a. The Apology of the Augsburg Confession, p. 160, admits these parts of penitence, namely mortification and vivification; but by mortification it understands the serious sorrow of heart and conscience, excited by legal sermons concerning committed sins by the power of the Holy Spirit; but by vivification it understands the immovable trust of the heart, by which we are fully certain of the remission of sins through and because of Christ. Proof: b.

Active mortification and vivification belong to the reborn and justified man: which we learn from Rom. VIII, 12, 13. Therefore, brethren, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh; for if you live according to the flesh, you will die: but if by the Spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, you will live. The Apostle addresses the brethren, who are inhabited by the Holy Spirit, v. 11. But spiritual brethren are men reborn and justified, who in continued renewal mortify the flesh by subduing its desires.

VIII. What is the end of repentance? The ultimate end of repentance simply is the glory of God ), with respect to man the ultimate end is eternal life ).

The intermediate and proximate end is the remission of sins ).

Proof a. Penitents give to God the honor of omniscience, justice, and mercy.

See the example of Achan, Jos. VII, 19.

Proof b. God gave repentance unto life, Acts

XI, 18.

Proof c. From Acts III, 19.

Repent, and convert yourselves, that your sins may be blotted out for you. However, the remission of sins is the end and effect of repentance, not by reason of contrition, but by reason of faith, which is as it were the soul of repentance.

Latin:

Si per mortificationem intelligatur mortificatio passiua, qua corda nostra a Deo per legem conteruntur & mortificantur; per viuificationem autem viua fides, qua corda nostra eriguntur & sustentantur: hæc bipartitio orthodoxiæ est conformis a). Sin per mortificationem intelligatur actiua depositio veteris hominis, & per viuificationem induitio noui hominis: hæc διχοτομία non ad conuersionem, sed ad renouationem referenda est b).

Prob. a. Apologia August. confess p. 160. admittit has pœnitentiæ partes, mortificationem scilicet & viuificationem; sed per mortificationem intelligit serium cordis conscientiæque dolorem, e legalibus concionibus ob admissa peccata virtute Spiritus S. excitatum; per viuificationem autem intelligit immotam cordis fiduciam, qua de remissione peccatorum per & propter Christum plane certi sumus.

Prob. b. Actiua mortificatio & viuificatio est hominis renati & iustificati: Id quod discimus ex Rom. VIII, 12. 13. Quare, fratres, debitores sumus non carni, ut secundum carnem viuamus; si enim secundum carnem viuitis, moriemini: Si vero Spiritu actiones carnis mortificatis, viuetis. Compellat Apostolus fratres, qui a Spiritu S. inhabitantur, v. 11. Fratres autem spirituales sunt homines renati & iustificati, qui in continuata renouatione carnem mortificant, eius cupiditates subigendo.

VIII. Quis est finis poenitentiae? Finis poenitentiae simpliciter ultimus est gloria Dei ), respectu hominis finis ultimus est vita aeterna ).

Finis intermedius & proximus est remissio peccatorum ).

Prob. a. Poenitentes dant Deo honorem omniscientiae, iustitiae, misericordiae.

Vid. exemplum Achanis, Ios. VII, 19.

Prob. b. Deus dedit poenitentiam ad vitam, Act.

XI, 18.

Prob. c. Ex Act. III, 19.

Agite poenitentiam, & convertite vos, ut deleantur vobis peccata vestra. Est autem remissio peccatorum finis & effectus poenitentiae, non ratione contritionis, sed ratione fidei, quae velut anima poenitentiae est.


### Of Contrition

Question IX. What is contrition? Contrition is a serious and holy sorrow of the heart, by which a sinner, having acknowledged his sins from the divine law, detests them ).

Note. Not a feigned or painted sorrow, such as that of hypocrites and Pharisees, Matth. VI, 18. nor a worldly sorrow, conceived from impatience of punishments or the loss of earthly things, such as that of Pharaoh and the Egyptians, Exod. XII, 30. but a serious and holy one, i.e., one excited by the most Holy Spirit through the divine law, illuminated by the radiance of the gospel, is true contrition.

Question X. Is contrition a meritorious cause of salvation, or at least a causal medium of salvation? Contrition is neither a meritorious cause of salvation ), nor a causal and positive medium of salvation ).

But it is only a medium of order, and that a privative one, removing the impediments to the remission of sins and eternal salvation ). Proof a. 1). Merit is an undue work, perfect, proceeding from one's own powers, equal and proportionate to its reward.

But the contrition of a sinner is due, imperfect, proceeding from supernatural powers bestowed by the Holy Spirit, and in no way equal or proportionate to meriting eternal life. Therefore, contrition is not a meritorious cause of salvation.

2) The one and only meritorious cause of the remission of sins is the satisfaction and merit of Christ.

For what was impossible for the law (from which contrition comes), while it was weakened by the flesh, God, who sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh, that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us, as Paul teaches, Rom. VIII, 3.

4. Proof b.

The causal, exhibitive media of salvation are the word of God and the sacraments: The apprehensive, or receptive, medium of salvation is faith resting on the merit of Christ. He who believes in the Son has eternal life, John

III, 36. Contrition, however, is destitute of the faculty of apprehending Christ the mediator.

Proof c. Although contrition is not a causal and positive medium of obtaining salvation: It is nevertheless a medium of the order established by God: Just as the transit along a road is an ordinal medium, but not the cause of the journey.

For thus said Jehovah: I look to the poor and contrite in spirit, and who trembles at my word, Is. LXVI, 2.

Truly God has sanctioned this order, that the sinner should acknowledge his miserable state, dread the wrath and punishments of God the judge, bitterly grieve for his sins, and detest them with his whole heart; for this reason, that He does not will to remit sins unless the acknowledgment and detestation of them precedes in the subject being justified and saved. Nowhere, however, in the sacred code is it said that the acknowledgment and detestation of sins merits remission. For which reason, contrition is not a meritorious cause, or a causal and positive medium of the remission of sins and eternal salvation, but only a privative medium, removing and prohibiting, just as in surgical medicine the removal of pus precedes; because the wound cannot be healed or close as long as the pus is not removed. But just as the removal of pus is not a positive cause of healing, but only a privative medium and a removal of an obstacle, without the removal of which healing could not follow: so sorrow for sin is not a cause of remission, but only a medium removing obstacles which would otherwise impede the remission from following; for it removes the opinion of non-indigence and the purpose of continuing in sins. The antithesis is that of the Papists, who assert that contrition is necessary for obtaining the remission of sins and salvation, and that it merits the remission of sins in its own way.

Their arguments are: I. Sorrow that is according to God works repentance unto salvation, 2 Cor. VII, 10. Sorrow that is according to God is contrition: Therefore. Resp. Sorrow according to God is that which God Himself excites, so that a preparation and disposition may be made for conceiving faith, with which repentance, when joined, becomes salutary.

II. If contrition did not merit the remission of sins, God would not look upon the contrite sinner with propitious eyes: But He does look upon him, etc. Therefore. The reason for the consequence is: because man is looked upon with a serene countenance on account of his own merits. The truth of the consequent is evident from Is. LXVI, 2. Resp. God does not look upon contrition itself as a merit of remission, but upon the contrite man, who acknowledges his misery and flees to the mercy of God with true faith: for there is in the penitent heart contrition, tempered by faith.

III. That to which spiritual vivification is attributed has the power of justifying (because justification is spiritual vivification): But it is attributed to contrition, etc. Therefore. The minor is evident from Ezek. XVIII, 27. When the wicked turns from his wickedness that he has committed, and does judgment and justice, he shall save his soul. Resp. By conversion is understood not only contrition, but also faith, from which the whole conversion consists in transition. Faith vivifies not ἐνεργητικῶς, by effecting, by producing spiritual life, but ληπτικῶς, by receiving the life of grace and glory: Contrition, however, removes the obstacles to spiritual life.

IV. Whatever is a sacrifice, that placates God and is a meritorious cause of the remission of sins: But contrition is a sacrifice, Ps. LI, 19: Therefore. Resp. 1) Whatever is a sacrifice ἱλασμὸν (propitiatory), that placates God; I concede. But the contrition of those standing is a sacrifice εὐχαρισμὸν (eucharistic). 2) The cited passage speaks of the subject that is pleasing to God, not indeed of the cause from which that favor is obtained by us. 3) Contrition is a sacrifice pleasing to God, not insofar as it is separated from faith, but insofar as it is tempered by faith resting in the merit of Christ.

Latin:

Quaest. IX. Quid est contritio? Contritio est serius & sanctus dolor cordis, quo peccator agnita ex lege diuina peccata sua detestatur ).

Obs. Non dolor simulatus, aut fucatus, qualis est hypocritarum, & Pharisaeorum, Matth. VI, 18. neque dolor mundanus, conceptus ex impatientia poenarum, aut iactura rerum terrestrium, qualis erat Pharaonis & Aegyptiorum, Exod. XII, 30. sed serius & sanctus, i.e. a Spiritu sanctissimo per legem diuinam, euangelii iubare collustratam, excitatus, est vera contritio.

Quaest. X. Estne contritio causa salutis meritoria, aut saltem medium salutis causale? Contritio neque est causa salutis meritoria ), neque medium salutis causale & positivum ).

Sed est tantum medium ordinis, idque priuatiuum, remouens impedimenta remissionis peccatorum aeternaeque salutis ). Prob. a. 1). Meritum est opus indebitum, perfectum, ex propriis viribus profectum, mercedi suae aequale & proportionatum.

At contritio peccatoris est debita, imperfecta, profecta ex viribus supernaturalibus a Spiritu S. collatis, minimeque aequalis aut proportionata promerendae vitae aeternae. E. contritio non est meritoria salutis causa.

2) Una & sola causa meritoria remissionis peccatorum est satisfactio & meritum Christi.

Nam impossibile legis (e qua est contritio), dum infirmatum est per carnem, Deus, qui sui ipsius filium misit in similitudine carnis peccati, & pro peccato, condemnauit peccatum in carne, ut iustificatio legis impleretur in nobis, docente Paulo, Rom. VIII, 3.

4. Prob. b.

Media salutis causalia exhibitiva verbum Dei & sacramenta sunt: Medium salutis apprehensiuum, seu receptiuum, est fides merito Christi innixa. Qui credit in Filium, habet vitam aeternam, Io.

III, 36. Contritio autem destituitur facultate apprehendendi Christum mediatorem.

Prob. c. Quamuis contritio non sit medium obtinendae salutis causale & positivum: Est tamen medium ordinis, a Deo constituti: Sicut transitus per viam est medium ordinale, non autem causa itineris.

Sic enim dixit Iehouah: Respicio ad miserum, & afflictum spiritu, & timentem sibi super verbo meo, Es. LXVI, 2.

Nimirum hunc ordinem sanciuit Deus, vt peccator statum suum miserum agnoscat, Dei iudicis iram poenasque expauescat, peccata sua acerbe doleat, totoque pectore detestetur; propterea, quod non vult remittere peccata, nisi agnitio & detestatio eorum in subiecto iustificando & saluando antecedat. Nullibi vero in sacro codice dicitur, quod agnitio & detestatio peccatorum mereatur remissionem. Quam ob rem contritio non est causa meritoria, aut medium remissionis peccatorum, aeternaeque salutis causale & positivum, sed tantum medium priuatiuum, remouens, prohibens, vt in medicina chirurgica puris remotio praecedit; eo, quod vulnus sanari, aut coire nequit, quamdiu pus non remouetur. At sicut remotio puris non est causa positiva curationis, sed tantum medium priuatiuum & remotium obstaculi, quo non remoto curatio sequi non posset: Ita dolor de peccato non est causa remissionis, sed tantum medium remouens obstacula, quae alias impedirent, ne sequeretur remissio; remouet enim opinionem non-indigentiae, & propositum pergendi in peccatis. Antithesis est Pontificiorum, afferentium, contritionem ad remissionem peccatorum & salutem consequendam necessariam esse, eamque suo modo mereri remissionem peccatorum.

Quorum argumenta sunt: I. Tristitia, quae secundum Deum est, operatur paenitentiam ad salutem, 2 Cor. VII, 10. Tristitia, quae secundum Deum est, est contritio: Ergo. Resp. Tristitia secundum Deum est, quam ipse Deus excitat, vt praeparatio & dispositio fiat ad concipiendam fidem, cum qua coniuncta paenitentia fit salutaris.

II. Si contritio non mereretur remissionem peccatorum, Deus oculis propitiis non respiceret peccatorem contritum: Sed respicit &c. Ergo. Ratio consequentiae est: quia homo ob merita sua fronte serena respicitur. Consequentis veritas patet ex Es. LXVI, 2. Resp. Deus non respicit ipsam contritionem, vt meritum remissionis, sed hominem contritum, qui suam miseriam agnoscit, & ad misericordiam Dei vera fide confugit: est enim in corde paenitente contritio, fide temperata.

III. Cui tribuitur viuificatio spiritualis, illud habet vim iustificandi (quia iustificatio est spiritualis viuificatio): Atqui contritioni &c. Ergo. Minor constat ex Ezech. XVIII, 27. Quando conuertitur impius ab impietate sua, quam fecerat, facitque iudicium & iustitiam, ille animam suam iustificabit. Resp. Per conuersionem intelligitur non tantum contritio, sed & fides, ex quibus tota conuersio in transitua constat. Viuificat fides non ἐνεργητικῶς, efficiendo, vitam spiritualem producendo, sed ληπτικῶς, vitam gratiae & gloriae recipiendo: Contritio autem obstacula vitae spiritualis remouet.

IV. Quidquid est sacrificium, illud Deum placat, & causa meritoria est remissionis peccatorum: Atqui contritio est sacrificium, Ps. LI, 19: Ergo. Resp. 1) Quidquid est sacrificium ἱλασμὸν, illud Deum placat; concedo. At contritio stantium est sacrificium εὐχαρισμὸν. 2) Dictum citatum de subiecto, quod Deo placet, non vero de causa, vnde fauor ille nobis obtingat, loquitur. 3) Contritio est gratum Deo sacrificium, non quatenus seiuncta est a fide, sed quatenus temperata fide in meritum Christi recumbente.


### Q. XI. Is contrition a good work?

The contrition of the fallen is not a good work, properly so called.

Obs. 1) The contrition of one kind is that of the fallen, who live in a state of wrath: of another kind is that of those standing, who through regeneration & justification have been translated into a state of grace. The question is understood concerning the contrition of fallen men. For the contrition of those standing, which follows faith, and of sin

concerns the remnants, can come into the reckoning of good works, we readily grant, as D. KROMAIER holds in his theol. positivo-polem. p. 382 (*).

2) Good works are usually understood in two ways: 1) generally; and thus good works are said to be all movements of the soul which are commanded in the Word of God, whether they be internal or external acts, and whether they be formally free actions, or passions and movements excited by the Holy Spirit, without the free consent of man. 2) Specifically and properly: Thus good works are free actions of man, which he, as a new creature, performs through powers bestowed by the Holy Spirit. Cf. D. MUSAEUS's praelect. in Form. Concord. p. 177.

Our assertion is proven: 1) Every good work proceeds from justifying faith, Phil. 1:11, Rom. 14:23. But contrition precedes faith.

Prob. 2) Every good work is a free action of a regenerate and justified man, performed by the grace of renovation according to the prescription of the divine law. But the contrition of the fallen a) is not an action, but partly a passive movement, inasmuch as it is sorrow for sins, partly a privative movement, inasmuch as it is displeasure with sins. b) It is not free; for the reason that fallen man, before he is transferred into a state of grace, enjoys no liberty in spiritual matters, whence the sorrow for sins, which is λύπη κατὰ Θεὸν, is not placed in the will of the penitent, but is on his part an involuntary passion of the soul, or one contrary to the nature and will of man, since by contrition he is deprived of his delight and tranquility of mind. c) Contrition precedes regeneration, justification, and renovation. Therefore, contrition is not a good work.

The antithesis is that of the Pontificians, who assert that contrition is to be reckoned among good works. They seek to strengthen their opinion with the following arguments: I. Whatever is a work of the Holy Spirit, which He works in us through the word of the law, that is a good work: But contrition etc. Jer. 23:23. Therefore. Resp. Whatever is a work of the Holy Spirit dwelling in us, that is a good work properly so called; I grant. But contrition is an effect of the externally assisting grace of the Holy Spirit, striking and breaking the heart with the hammer of the law: and therefore it is not a good work properly so called.

II. Every action commanded in the Word of God is a good work: Contrition is an action etc.: Therefore. Resp. 1) For a good work, the command of God is not sufficient, but grace is also required for it

The Spirit of the Holy One inhabiting, and faith, without which it is impossible to please God, Hebr. XI, 6. 2) If in a general and improper sense a good work is called that which is commanded in the divine word, we readily grant that contrition can be called a good work. 3) Contrition is not an action, but an involuntary passion of the soul. For God actively crushes the sinner, the sinner is passively crushed.

Instance I. To full contrition pertains the acknowledgment of sin, meditation on the divine law, and the detestation of sins, which are true actions. Resp. The acknowledgment of sin and meditation on the law concur to contrition not formally or constitutively, but antecedently and efficiently. But the detestation of sins is an efficacious displeasure, which is a privative motion. Instance

II. If contrition is not voluntary, it will be coerced: The consequent is absurd; since God does not force a reluctant man to repentance. Therefore, it is voluntary. Resp. Contrition, by reason of its cause, is not voluntary; because it does not proceed from the natural powers of free will; nor is it coerced; since God does not convert man by an irresistible force: but it is excited through the law, by a cause acting supernaturally, namely by the Holy Spirit, whose grace bends the mind of man, and finally overcomes his repugnance.

III. Contrition is either good or evil. If it is good; why can it not be called a good work? If it is evil; it is prohibited by the divine word, which is false. Resp. The contrition of the fallen is indeed pedagogically good; because through it man is divinely prepared for faith in Christ; but it is not a free action of a man reborn and justified, performed through the grace of renewal.

Latin:

Contritio lapsorum non est bonum opus, proprie dictum.

Obs. 1) Contritio alia est lapsorum, qui viuunt in statu irae: Alia est stantium, qui per regenerationem & iustificationem in statum gratiae sunt translati. Quaestio intelligitur de contritione hominum lapsorum. Nam contritionem stantium, quae fidem sequitur, & peccati

reliquias concernit, in censum bonorum operum venire posse, non illibenter damus, censente D. KROMAIERO in theol. postiuo-polem. p. 382 (*).

2) Bona opera accipi solent dupliciter: 1) generaliter; & sic bona opera dicuntur omnes motus animi, qui in verbo Dei praecipiuntur, sive sint interni, sive externi actus, & sive sint formaliter actiones liberae, sive sint passiones & motus a Spiritu S. excitati, absque hominis consensu libero. 2) Specialiter & proprie: Sic bona opera sunt actiones hominis liberae, quas ipse tanquam nova creatura per vires a Spiritu Sancto donatas exercet. Confer. D. MUSAEI praelect. in Form. Concord. p. 177.

Probatur assertio nostra: 1) Omne bonum opus proficiscitur ex fide iustificante, Phil. I, 11, Rom. XIV, 23. At contritio fidem antecedit.

Prob. 2) Omne bonum opus est actio hominis renati & iustificati libera, per gratiam renovationis iuxta legis divinae praescriptum praestita. Sed contritio lapsorum a) non est actio, sed partim motus passivus, quatenus est dolor de peccatis, partim motus privativus, in quantum est displicentia peccatorum. b) Non est libera; ideo, quod homo lapsus, antequam in statum gratiae transferatur, in rebus spiritualibus nulla gaudet libertate, vnde dolor de peccatis, qui est λύπη κατὰ Θεὸν, non est in arbitrio poenitentis posita, sed est ex parte ipsius passio animi involuntaria, sive disconueniens naturae & voluntati hominis, quippe qui per contritionem sua delectatione & tranquillitate animi priuatur. c) Contritio antecedit regenerationem, iustificationem & renovationem. E. contritio non est bonum opus.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, statuentium, contritionem esse e censu bonorum operum. Qui suam opinionem sequentibus argumentis firmatum eunt: I. Quidquid est opus Spiritus S. quod ille per verbum legis in nobis operatur, illud est bonum opus: Atqui contritio &c. Ier. XXIII, 23. Ergo. Resp. Quidquid est opus Spiritus S. in nobis habitantis, illud est bonum opus proprie dictum; concedo. At contritio est effectus gratiae Spiritus S. externe assistentis, cor per malleum legis pulsantis & conterentis: adeoque non est bonum opus proprie dictum.

II. Omnis actio, in verbo Dei praecepta, est bonum opus: Contritio est actio &c: Ergo. Resp. 1) Ad bonum opus non sufficit mandatum Dei, sed requiritur ad illud etiam

Spiritus S. inhabitans, & fides, sine qua impossibile est Deo placere, Hebr. XI, 6. 2) Si sensu generali & improprio bonum opus dicatur, quod in verbo divino præceptum est, faciles largimur, contritionem posse bonum opus vocari. 3) Contritio non est actio, sed passio animi involuntaria. Deus enim active peccatorem conterit, peccator passive conteritur.

Instantia I. Ad contritionem plenam pertinet agnitio peccati, meditatio legis divinæ, detestatio peccatorum, quæ sunt veræ actiones. Resp. Agnitio peccati & meditatio legis concurrunt ad contritionem non formaliter aut constitutive, sed antecedenter & efficienter. Detestatio autem peccatorum est efficax displicentia, quæ est motus privativus.

Instantia II. Si contritio non est voluntaria, erit coacta: Consequens est absurdum; siquidem Deus hominem reluctantem ad pœnitentiam non cogit. E. est voluntaria. Resp. Contritio, ratione causæ, non est voluntaria; quia non proficiscitur a viribus naturalibus liberi arbitrii; neque coacta est; quoniam Deus hominem vi irresistibili non convertit: sed est excitata per legem, a causa supernaturaliter agente, nempe a Spiritu Sancto, cuius gratia flectit hominis animum, tandemque vincit eius repugnantiam.

III. Contritio aut est bona, aut est mala. Si est bona; cur non dici possit bonum opus? Si est mala; prohibita est verbo divino, quod est falsum. Resp. Contritio lapsorum est quidem pædagogice bona; quia per eandem homo divinitus præparatur ad fidem in Christum; sed non est actio hominis renati & iustificati libera, per gratiam renovationis præstita.


### Quæst. XII. What are the requirements of true contrition?

To true contrition, as the prior part of repentance, by which sins are morally retracted, there antecedently pertains and is required the acknowledgment of sin a), not only theoretical, but also practical b): Formally, an efficacious displeasure, or detestation of sins, joined with serious sorrow, constitutes it c). Proof a.

Repentance, or transitive conversion, is directed toward abolishing past sins, so that they do not remain morally. They have, however, that they remain morally, partly from the fact that, after sins are committed, they are held as ratified, or at least that they are not retracted; partly from the fact that the offense and injury brought upon God, and the obligation born thence to make satisfaction to God for it, is not removed by performed satisfaction, nor is the anger of God against sins appeased. Whence repentance, or intransitive conversion, is also directed toward that twofold reason: one, by which it causes that they are no longer held as ratified; the other, by which it offers satisfaction to God for the offense and injury brought upon Him, and appeases the offended God through it. That sins may not be ratified after they are committed, conversion effects this through their retraction, which is opposed to ratification, and which is commonly called by ecclesiastical writers CONTRITION; to which various acts pertain, some of which look to the intellect of the man to be converted, others to his will. To the intellect pertains ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF SINS, which as a necessary condition, and without which the retraction of sins finds no place, is a prerequisite; since the will, to which it formally pertains to retract what once pleased, is a blind power, and in its acts so depends upon the prior cognition of the intellect, that it can render nothing void unless it has first been known by the intellect. Which the practice of the scriptures also proves, in which, when sinners were to be led to conversion through the ministry of the word, we always find that the beginning was made from the manifestation of sins, by which they might be led into the acknowledgment of them. See the example of David, 2 Sam. XII, 7. seq. Ps. LI, 5. This acknowledgment of sins is made a) by the speculative judgment of the intellect, by which sins, whether presenting themselves to the mind by themselves (when they are more grave), or or having entered into a more diligent examination, or an investigation of one's life previously led, and a more accurate comparison instituted with the norm of divine law, they are known to be contrary to divine law, hateful to God, and worthy of temporal and eternal punishments; just as in Rom. III, 20, the recognition of sin is said to be through the law: b) by the practical judgment of the intellect, which dictates that the sinner must not proceed or persevere in his sins, but must diligently apply himself to their abolition, and anxiously look into how and by what means they can be abolished.

It is evident, however, from the examples of penitents in scripture, how, once sins were known, they anxiously sought by what means their sins could be abolished, e.g., Josiah, 2 Kings XXII, 11 ff., and certain Jews in the time of John the Baptist, Matt. III, 6, Mark I, 5.

Prob. b. On the part of the will, there is required for contrition, or the retraction of sins: DISPLEASURE and detestation of them. For even if the intellect were to know all sins to the greatest degree, and were to dictate that one must not persist in them; yet they would not be retracted unless they were displeasing to the will. Displeasure, however, is twofold: one is simple, by which sins, known according to some notion of evil, are displeasing to the will, without that intention of fleeing them; the other is efficacious, by which the thing, known as evil, is so displeasing that the will simultaneously intends to flee it, and it is otherwise called DETESTATION. For contrition, or the retraction of sins, simple displeasure is not sufficient, such as exists even in the impenitent, who see and approve of better things, but follow the worse; but there is required efficacious displeasure, or detestation, by which we turn away from sins entirely, being willing, if it were possible, to render them undone, and abhorring the perpetrating of such foul deeds.

Through efficacious displeasure, or detestation, sins cease to be voluntary, and take on the nature of involuntary actions. But involuntary actions are accompanied by an inseparable bond of PAIN, which is a passion, perturbation, and restlessness of the soul, arising from the apprehension of sin as a present evil, and the cause of many evils to be endured in this life and the next. And this pain is indeed the more grievous, the more deeply the sinner considers the foulness of sins, the offense to God, and the punishments of this and the future life deserved. Whence it is clear that the stings of conscience and fears are contained under this pain. Obs.

Obs.
