These requirements of true contrition are recounted and explained otherwise by other authors. proposes them in the following manner: It pertains to contrition: 1) That the mind of the sinner, from the judgment of the law, understands, acknowledges, and seriously considers the manifold uncleanness and abomination of sin before God: 2) From the doctrine concerning the wrath, indignation, and judgment against sins, the conscience, understanding how seriously and horribly God is angered by sins and wishes to punish them, acknowledges that it is ensnared by sins and held by the bonds of the wrath and judgment of God unto eternal condemnation: 3) Thence arises in the conscience fear, terror, and dread of the wrath and judgment of God against sins: 4) Hence follows the pain of a conscience grieving gravely that it has sinned and has offended God by its sins: It begins, therefore, to hate and detest sin, and to cast off the purpose of it: 5) This very recognition, this dread and pain, excites and urges the conscience to think and seek whether, and how, it can escape the wrath of God and the judgment of condemnation, as the Baptist says: Who has shown you to flee from the wrath to come? writes concerning the requirements of true contrition: Although five things occur in contrition: 1) In the memory, the recollection of sins, 2) in the mind, the consideration of the divine offense, 3) in the will, the detestation of sins acknowledged, 4) in the heart, fear of vengeance and of the future judgment: 5) In the conscience, wounded by the sting of the law, horror, pain, bite and compunction: yet in the first two degrees, which are internal acts, contrition does not consist alone, but rather in the three subsequent ones. For those do not so much constitute contrition as they effect it: They relate to it προκαταρκτικῶς (preparatorily) rather than ὡσιωδῶς (essentially). They are the efficient, not the formal, cause of contrition; since it is properly a passion of the heart.

Latin:

Ad veram contritionem, tanquam priorem partem pœnitentiæ, qua peccata moraliter retractantur, antecedenter pertinet & requiritur agnitio peccati a), non tantum theoretica, sed etiam practica b): Formaliter eam constituit efficax displicentia, seu detestatio peccatorum, cum serio dolore coniuncta c).

Prob. a. Fertur pœnitentia, seu conversio transitiva, in peccata præterita abolenda, ne moraliter maneant. Habent autem, vt moraliter maneant, partim ex eo, quod, postquam peccata sunt, habentur rata, vel certe quod non retractantur; partim ex eo, quod offensio & iniuria Deo illata, & hinc nata obligatio ad satisfaciendum Deo pro illa, non est per præstitam satisfactionem sublata, neque ira Dei aduersus peccata placata. Vnde pœnitentia, siue conversio intransitiva, etiam fertur in illa ratione duplici: una, qua facit, ne amplius habeantur rata; altera, qua satisfactionem Deo pro offensa & iniuria ipsi illata exhibet, Deumque offensum per illum placat. Vt non ratahabeantur peccata, postquam patrata sunt, efficit conversio per ipsorum retractionem, ratihabitioni oppositam, quæ a scriptoribus ecclesiasticis communiter vocatur CONTRITIO; ad quam diuersi actus pertinent, quorum alii ad hominis convertendi intellectum, alii ad eius voluntatem spectant. Ad intellectum pertinet AGNITIO PECCATORVM, quæ tanquam conditio necessaria, & sine qua peccatorum retractatio haud inuenit, prærequiritur; cum voluntas, ad quam formaliter pertinet, retractare, quod semel placuit, si potentia cæca, & in actibus suis a præuia intellectus cognitione ita dependeat, vt nihil irritum reddere possit, nisi prius ab intellectu fuerit cognitum. Quod & scripturarum praxis exincit, in quibus, cum per ministerium verbi peccatores securi ad conversionem fui perducendi fuerunt, semper a peccatorum manifestatione, qua in illorum agnitionem deducerentur, initium factum esse, deprehendimus. Vide exemplum Dauidis, 2 Sam. XII, 7. seq. Ps. LI, 5. Fit hæc agnitio peccatorum a) iudicio intellectus speculatiuo, quo peccata siue per se animo obuerfantia (quando grauiora sunt), sive inito diligentiore examine, aut excussione vitae ante actae, & collatione accuratiore cum norma legis divinae instituta, cognoscuntur esse adversa legi divinae, Deo exosa, & poenis temporalibus atque aeternis digna; prout Rom. III, 20. agnitio peccati per legem esse dicitur: b) iudicio intellectus practico, quod dictitat, non pergendum, aut perseverandum esse peccatori in suis peccatis, sed in illorum abolitionem sedulo incumbendum, & follicite dispiciendum, quomodo & quibus mediis aboleri possint.

Constat autem exemplis poenitentium in scriptura, quomodo, cognitis peccatis, follicite quaesiverint, quo pacto possent peccata sua aboleri, v. gr. Iosiae, 2 Reg. XXII, 11. seq. Iudaeorum quorundam tempore Ioannis baptistae, Matth. III, 6. Marc. I, 5.

Prob. b. Ex parte voluntatis requiritur ad contritionem, seu peccatorum retractationem: DISPLICENTIA ac detestatio illorum. Nam si vel maxime intellectus peccata omnia cognosceret, & in iis non persistendum esse dictitaret; non tamen ea retractarentur, nisi voluntati displicuerint. Est autem displicentia duplex: una simplex, qua peccata secundum aliquam rationem mali cognita, voluntati displicent, fine intentione illa fugiendi; altera efficax, qua res, cognita tanquam mala, ita displicet, ut simul illam fugere intendat voluntas, & dicitur alias DETESTATIO. Ad contritionem, sive peccatorum retractationem, non sufficit displicentia simplex, qualis est etiam in impoenitentibus, qui meliora vident probantque, deteriora sequuntur; sed requiritur displicentia efficax, sive detestatio, qua peccata prorsus aversamur, quippe ea, si fieri posset, infecta reddere volentes, & a funilibus patrandis abhorrentes.

Prob. c. Per displicentiam efficacem, seu detestationem, desinunt peccata esse voluntaria, & inuitarum actionum naturam induunt. Inuitas autem actiones nexu indiuideo comitatur DOLOR, qui est passio, perturbatio & inquietudo animi, oborta ex apprehensione peccati, tanquam mali praesentis, & causae malorum plurium, in vita hac & altera luendorum. Atque hic quidem dolor tanto grauior est, quanto penitius peccator foeditatem peccatorum, offensam Dei, poenas huius & futurae vitae promeritas considerat. Vnde patet, conscientiae morsus & pauores sub isto dolore contineri.

Obs. Haec requisita verae contritionis aliter ab aliis auctoribus recensentur & exponuntur. sequenti ratione ea proponit: Pertinet ad contritionem: 1) Vt mens peccatoris ex iudicio legis intelligat, agnoscat, & serio consideret multiplicem immunditiem & abominationem peccati coram Deo: 2) Ex doctrina de ira, indignatione & iudicio aduersus peccata, conscientia intelligens, quam serio & horribiliter Deus peccatis irascatur, & ea punire velit, agnoscit, se propter peccata irretitam teneri nexibus irae & iudicii Dei ad aeternam condemnationem: 3) Inde oritur in conscientia timor, terror, pauor irae & iudicii Dei aduersus peccata: 4) Hinc sequitur dolor conscientiae grauiter dolentis, se peccasse, & peccatis offendisse Deum: Incipit igitur peccatum odisse & detestari, atque eius propositum abiicere: 5) Haec vero agnitio, hic pauor & dolor excitat & vrget conscientiam, vt cogitet & quaerat, an, & quomodo effugere possit iram Dei, & iudicium condemnationis, sicut Baptista inquit: Quis monstravit vobis effugere venturam iram? de requisitis verae contritionis scribit: Quamuis quinque in contritione occurrant: 1) In memoria peccatorum recordatio, 2) in mente offensae divinae consideratio, 3) in voluntate peccatorum agnitorum detestatio, 4) in corde timor vindictae, & futuri iudicii: 5) In conscientia legis aculeo vulnerata horror, dolor, morsus & compunctio: tamen in prioribus duobus gradibus, qui sunt actus interni, non consistit sola contritionis, sed potius in tribus posterioribus. Illi enim contritionem non tam constituunt, quam efficiunt: Habent se ad eam προκαταρκτικῶς magis, quam ὡσιωδῶς. Sunt causa efficiens non formalis contritionis; quippe quæ est proprie cordis passio.


### Quæst. XII. What are the requirements of true contrition?: D Dannhaverus in hodof. phæn

D.

DANNHAVERUS in hodof. phæn.

XI. p. 1281. judges thus concerning the requirements of contrition: Formal contrition consists in sadness on account of good omitted, and pain on account of evil committed, as great as is wont to be in the loss of friends and offspring through death.

This sadness is not worldly, which flows from the consideration of the loss of temporal things, from impatience, from melancholy excited by Satan, from bites of conscience, of which kind was the sadness of Judas, such as was also in Cain, in Ahab on account of Naboth's vineyard, in incestuous Ammon; but divine, from the loss of spiritual good and the foulness of sin, as such: a serious and sincere sadness, not of an ἰσόρροπον (equal) weight, most perfect, so that God desires nothing in it. For who understands his errors? much less that he should grieve exactly for all.

Sin like indigestible food, creates torments in the stomach far more bitter and longer-lasting than the delay of pleasure was in the eating. 2) By hatred, aversion, and detestation, 3) By fear and terror, which although it may turn one away from God by itself, yet accidentally works for good, and leads to God by another way, and is salutary by the intention of God, 4) By shame, on account of God offended. Finally 5) by the real desertion of sin.

Hating and leaving belong together. From these requirements of true contrition, a fuller definition of the same can be deduced: Contrition is a passive movement of the soul, excited by the Holy Spirit through converting grace, by which a man, a sinner, having recognized his sins from the divine law, feels the wrath of God, dreads His temporal and eternal punishments, is tormented with heavy pain on account of the foulness of sin, the offense of God, and the loss of divine grace, is affected with shame, and so detests both original evil and actual sins that he casts away the purpose of sinning and exterminates it from his heart.

Quæst. XIII. Do the terrors of conscience sent by the law also pertain to contrition?

Terrors, struck into the conscience by the divine law, pertain to the essence of contrition.

Proof. 1) Every pain injected into the soul, on account of the offense of the supreme Lord and Judge, is joined with terror and dread in the conscience. But contrition is such a pain. Therefore.

The Apology of the Augsburg Confession, p. 165, explains the minor premise. We say: that contrition is the true terrors of conscience, which feels that God is angry at sin; and grieves that it has sinned.

2) The examples of penitent sinners teach this. King David, repenting, says, I am feeble and sore broken: I have roared by reason of the disquietness of my heart.

Conf. The antithesis is that of the Papists, who deny that terrors struck into the conscience by the law enter into the essential constitution of contrition.

Whose arguments are: I. Terrors struck into the soul are natural affections, which are detected both in children and in beasts, which are not capable of repentance.

Resp. Contrition is not called simply terror, but terror arising from the recognition of sins and the intuition of divine wrath, which is a movement of the soul excited by the Holy Spirit, and therefore is not by nature in children and beasts.

II. Terrors are also given in devils, who nevertheless do not repent.

Resp. The terrors of evil spirits are joined neither with an efficacious displeasure of sins, nor with the hope of pardon, and therefore they are not penitential.

III. Repentance flows from love, not from terror, as the example of the harlot shows, Luke 7:47. Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much. Resp. 1) Christ does not speak in that place of repentance, but of the remission of sins, which is the effect of repentance. 2) The particle 'for' (quia) is not taken aitiologikos (causally), as if love were the cause of the remission of sins, but syllogistikos (by way of reasoning), so that the ground of the consequence is indicated a posteriori. This is abundantly clear from a comparison of this verse 47 with those verses 42 and 43. 3) The terrors and pains of conscience of that harlot are abundantly testified to by her tears.

Latin:

D.

DANNHAVERVS in hodof. phæn.

XI. p. 1281. de requisitis contritionis ita iudicat: Contritio formalis consistit in tristitia ob bonum omissum, ac dolore ob malum commissum tanto, quantus esse solet in iactura amicorum ac prolis per mortem.

Tristitia isthæc non est mundana, quæ fluit ex consideratione iacturæ rerum temporalium, ex impatientia, a Satana excitata melancholia, conscientiæ morsibus, cuiusmodi fuit Iudæ tristitia, qualis etiam fuit in Caino, in Achabo ob vineam Nabothi, in Ammone incestuoso; sed divina, ex iactura boni spiritualis & peccati, qua talis, fœditate: tristitia feria ac sincera, non ad ἰσόρροπον pondus perfectissima, ut Deus nihil in ea desideret. Nam delicta quis intelligit? nedum ut exacta de omnibus doleat.

Peccatum cibo simile indigestibili, cruciatus in stomacho creant longe acerbiores, & diuturniores, quam mora voluptatis fuit in comestione. 2) Odio, auerfatione ac detestatione, 3) Timore ac terrore, qui tametsi per se auertat a Deo, per accidens tamen operatur in bonum, & alia via ad Deum ducit, ac ex intentione Dei est salutaris, 4) Pudore, ob Deum offensum. Denique 5) reali peccati desertione.

Hassen und lassen gehören zusammen. Ex his requisitis veræ contritionis vberior eiusdem definitio deduci potest: Contritio est motus animi passivus, a Spiritu S. per gratiam conuertentem excitatus, quo homo peccator, agnitis ex lege diuina peccatis, iram Dei sentit, ipsius pœnas temporales & æternas expauescit, ob fœditate peccati, offensam Dei, & iacturam gratiæ diuinæ graui dolore angitur, pudore afficitur, & tum malum originale, tum actualia peccata adeo detestatur, vt peccandi propositum abiiciat, & ex corde exterminet.

Quæst. XIII. An etiam terrores conscientiæ per legem immissi pertinent ad contritionem?

Terrores, per legem diuinam conscientiæ incussi, pertinent ad essentiam contritionis.

Prob. 1) Omnis dolor animo iniectus, propter offensam summi Domini & Iudicis, cum terrore ac pauore in conscientia est coniunctus. Atqui contritio est eiusnodi dolor. E.

Minorem explicat Apol. Aug. confess. p. 165. Dicimus: contritionem esse veros terrores conscientiæ, quæ Deum sentit irasci peccato; & dolet, se peccasse.

2) Docent hoc exempla pœnitentium peccatorum. Rex Dauid resipiscens inquit, Debilitatus sum usque valde, rugiui præ rugitu cordis mei.

Conf. Antithesis est Pontificiorum, negantium, terrores per legem conscientiæ incussos essentialem contritionis constitutionem ingredi.

Quorum argumenta sunt: I. Terrores animo incussi sunt affectiones naturales, quæ & in pueris, & in bestiis, pœnitentiæ haud capacibus, deprehenduntur.

Resp. Contritio non dicitur simpliciter terror, sed terror ex agnitione peccatorum, & intuitu iræ diuinæ ortus, qui est motus animi per Spiritum S. excitatus, adeoque non est per naturam in pueris & bestiis.

II. Terrores dantur etiam in diabolis, qui tamen non resipiscunt.

Resp. Terrores cacodæmonum neque cum efficaci displicentia peccatorum, neque cum spe veniæ sunt coniuncti, adeoque non sunt pœnitentiales.

III. Pœnitentia ex amore, non ex terrore fluit, sicut ostendit exemplum meretricis, Luc. VII, 47. Remissa sunt ei peccata multa; quia amauit multum. Resp. 1) Non loquitur Christus l. c. de pœnitentia, sed de remissione peccatorum, quæ est effectus pœnitentiæ. 2) Particula, quia, non sumitur αἰτιολογικῶς, causaliter, perinde ac si amor esset causa remissionis peccatorum, sed συλλογιστικῶς, ratiocinatiue, vt indicetur ratio consequentiæ a posteriori. Id abunde patet ex comparatione versus huius 47. cum illis, 42. 43. 3) Peccatricem illam terrores ac dolores conscientiæ, abunde testantur ipsius lacrymæ.


### Q. XIV. Are only actual sins retracted through contrition, or habitual ones as well?

Through contrition, actual sins are retracted proximately and immediately a). Consequently, and through the acts of sinning, habitual ones are also retracted b). Prob. a.

Actual sins, when they have been committed, present themselves to the sinner's mind by themselves and immediately, and they burden and distress his conscience: therefore, the intransitive conversion toward their abolition tends to them primarily, proximately, and immediately. Prob. b.

King David, repenting after the crimes of adultery and murder had been committed, besides the sins committed in act and already past, also disapproved of and with much sorrow detested his innate malice, as the cause and fountain of the crimes committed, Ps. 51:7. And although original sin cannot be completely extirpated in this life, yet the inordinate motions erupting from it against the will can be restrained and checked by the regenerate, so that it may not beget voluntary and mortally active sin.

Latin:

Per contritionem proxime & immediate retractantur peccata actualia a). Consequenter & mediantibus actibus peccandi etiam habitualia b).

Prob. a. Peccata actualia, vbi patratæ sunt, peccatoris animo per se ipsa & immediate obuerfantur, eiusque conscientiam onerant & angunt: ideoque conuersio intransitiua ad eorum abolitionem primo, proxime & immediate tendit.

Prob. b. Rex Dauid, post patratæ adulterii & homicidii scelera resipiscens, præter peccata actu commissa & iam præterita, improbauit etiam, ac multo cum dolore detestatus est suam connatam malitiam, tanquam patratorum scelerum causam & fontem, Ps. LI, 7. Et quamuis peccatum originale in hac vita penitus exstirpari nequeat, motus tamen inordinati, ex eo præter voluntatem erumpentes, compefci & cohiberi possunt a renatis, ne gignat peccatum voluntarium, & actu mortiferum.


### Q. XV. What are the reasons impelling a fallen sinner to contrition?

There are very many and most grave causes which move a fallen sinner to sincere contrition.

Prob. The following impel a sinner, constituted outside the state of grace, to serious contrition: 1) the offense of the divine majesty: 2) the rupture of the baptismal covenant, on the part of the malicious sinner: 3) the foulness of the deliberate sin: 4) the shipwreck of faith, which is inconsistent with deliberate sins: 5) the lack of the consolation of the Holy Spirit: 6) the gravity of temporal and eternal punishments: 7) the scandal given to the weak: 8) the lack of angelic protection: 9) the rigor of divine judgment: 10) the loss of eternal life.

Latin:

Dantur plurimæ atque grauissimæ causæ, quæ peccatorem lapsum ad contritionem sinceram permoueant.

Prob. Peccatorem, extra statum gratiæ constitutum, ad seriam contritionem impellunt 1) offensa maiestatis diuinæ: 2) ruptura fœderis baptifinalis, ex parte malitiosi peccatoris: 3) peccati proæretici fœditas: 4) naufragium fidei cum peccatis proæreticis inconstibilis: 5) defectus solatii Spiritus S.: 6) pœnarum temporalium & æternarum grauitas: 7) scandalum infirmis datum: 8) carentia præfidii angelici: 9) iudicii diuini rigor: 10) vitæ æternæ iactura.


### Q. XVI. What is the end of contrition?

The end of true contrition is preparation for faith in Christ, to be conceived from the Gospel. Prob. 1)

Just as the law is a schoolmaster unto Christ, Gal. 3:24: so contrition, which is from the law, is a pedagogical means for kindling faith in Christ by the word of the Gospel.

2) By contrition the way is made level for the Lord, Matt. 3:3, insofar as by it those obstacles are removed which would otherwise prevent faith in Christ from being generated. Whence the Formula of Concord, p. 688: True and saving faith is not in those who lack contrition and have the intention of continuing and persevering in sins.

Latin:

Finis veræ contritionis est præparatio ad fidem in Christum, ex euangelio concipiendam.

Prob. 1) Sicut lex est pædagogus ad Christum, Gal. III, 24: ita contritio, quæ est ex lege, est medium pædagogicum ad fidem in Christum verbo euangelii accendendam.

2) Contritione complanatur via Domino, Matth. III, 3. quatenus ea remouentur obstacula, quæ alias impedirent, ne fides in Christum generaretur. Vnde Form. Conc. p. 688: Vera ac saluans fides in iis non est, qui contritione carent & propositum in peccatis pergendi & perseuerandi habent.


### Q. XVII. What are the signs of true contrition?

The signs of true contrition are some internal and certain, others external and probable. The internal are: a) the renunciation of evil intention, and the omission of deliberate sin: b) the desire for internal [renewal].

desire, legal and pedagogical, of the most approved physician, or of the most benign and most powerful liberator.

a. Contrition is formally a serious sorrow for sins committed, joined with an efficacious displeasure or detestation of sins. But it cannot happen that sins should seriously displease someone, or that one should seriously detest sins, and yet have a purpose of sinning. But here one must accurately distinguish between the purpose of amending one's life, and the renunciation of an evil purpose. The former follows justifying faith as an internal work: the latter precedes faith, and is not a good work; because it does not consist in a positive action, or commission, but only in the omission of an evil work, the cessation of morose resistance, and the removal of acts impeding regeneration. Prob. b.

From Acts 2:37: When they heard this (the Jews), they were pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter and the rest of the Apostles: What shall we do, men and brethren? The hearers of Peter's preaching of the divine word were pricked in their heart no otherwise than if their hearts had been pierced or stabbed by sharp swords. This compunction of heart excited a general and confused desire, which they express with the question: What shall we do? Here one must distinguish between legal and evangelical desire. The former presupposes knowledge of the disease, the latter knowledge of the physician. The former is pedagogical, the latter is actually salutary: the former is a consequence and testimony of contrition, the latter is an act of faith, seeking efficacious medicine in the wounds of Christ.

Q.

XVIII. What are the external and probable signs of contrition? External and probable signs of contrition are detected in the sinner's mouth, in his face and habit, and in external work.

Latin:

Indicia veræ contritionis alia sunt interna & certa, alia externa & probabilia. Interna sunt: a) abnegatio mali propositi, & omissio peccati proæretici: b) desiderium internæ.

THEOL. PART. III. SECT.Ú. CAP. VI. 1156 fiderium legale & pædagogicum medici probatissimi, sive liberatoris benignissimi & potentissimi.

Prob. a. Contritio formaliter est serius dolor de peccatis admissis, cum efficaci displicentia sive detestatione peccatorum conjunctus. Fieri autem nequit, ut serio alicui displiceant peccata, aut ut quis serio detestetur peccata, & tamen habeat propositum peccandi. Accurate autem hic distinguendum est inter propositum emendandæ vitæ, & abnegationem mali propositi. Illud tanquam opus internum fidem iustificantem sequitur: Hæc fidem antecedit, neque bonum opus est; quia non consistit in positiva factione, aut commissione, sed tantum in omissione mali operis, cessatione morosæ repugnantiæ, & remotione actuum regenerationem impedientium.

Prob. b. Ex Act. II, 37: Cum autem audirent (Iudæi), compuncti sunt corde, dixeruntque ad Petrum & reliquos Apostolos: Quid faciemus, viri fratres? Auditores Petri prædicatione verbi divini corde erant compuncti haud aliter, ac si gladiis acutis corda ipsorum puncta, aut perfoffa essent. Quæ compunctio cordis excitavit desiderium generale & confusum, quod exprimunt quæstione: Quid faciemus? Distinguendum hic est inter desiderium legale & evangelicum. Illud supponit cognitionem morbi, hoc cognitionem medici. Illud pædagogicum, hoc actu salutare est: Illud contritionis consequens & testimonium, hoc est actus fidei, in vulneribus Christi efficacem medicinam quærens.

Quæst. XVIII. Quæ sunt indicia contritionis externa & probabilia?

Indicia contritionis externa & probabilia deprehenduntur in peccatoris ore, in facie & habitu ipsius, & in opere externo.


### Q. XIX. What external sign of contrition is observed in the mouth of a penitent sinner?

The external and probable sign of true contrition, which is observed in the mouth of the sinner, is the confession of sins, which is either of the whole church, inasmuch as it confesses its sins both ordinarily in public prayers, and extraordinarily in public calamities a); or it is of a private man, who confesses his sins, immediately before God b), before the church c), before a minister of the church d), before his neighbor e). Prob. a. That a general confession of sins of the whole church is necessary and useful, is evident among other things from Lev. 16:21. Aaron shall lay both his hands upon the head of the live goat, and confess over him all the iniquities of the children of Israel, and all their transgressions in all their sins: He shall put them upon the head of the goat and shall send him away by the hand of a man appointed into the wilderness. We observe here: 1) That a public confession of the whole church is made, with the voice of the minister of God leading, such as the priest Aaron was of old. Conf. 1 Sam. 7:5. Neh. 9:1. Judg. 10:10. 2) That public confession is joined with faith in Christ, whose type of old was the goat ἀποπομπαῖος, or scapegoat: for Christ is the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, John 1:29, upon whom we lay the hand of faith.

Prob. b. From Ps. 51:4. Against thee only have I sinned, and done evil before thee. King David confesses his sin to God, as to the supreme legislator, judge, and καρδιογνώστῃ (knower of hearts), inasmuch as he had violated His law. He had indeed sinned also against his neighbor, but principally and ultimately against God the legislator. This confession, which is made immediately to God, is called by LUTHER the confession of faith.

Proof c. Achan confessed his theft before the face of the entire Israelite assembly, Josh. 7:19. This confession before the church was formerly called ἐξομολόγησις, and it was either voluntary, by which the sinner of his own accord published his transgression, or involuntary, to the rendering of which he was compelled by the church. Proof d.

From Matt. 3:6. And they were baptized in the Jordan by him (John), confessing their sins. John’s hearers, before this herald, testified to the internal contrition of their hearts by the external confession of their mouths, and received baptism as an efficacious means of regeneration and justification. Proof e.

From Jas. 5:15. Where the Apostle says: Confess your lapses one to another, and pray one for another, that you may be healed. The Apostle James is not speaking of a confession to be rendered to a priest; because this is not mutual. St. James says: Ἐξομολογεῖσθε ἀλλήλοις, i.e., mutually and reciprocally. Now, a neighbor confesses his fault to a neighbor, either for the sake of reconciliation, when he has inflicted an injury upon his neighbor, see Matt. 5:23; or for the sake of seeking counsel, when a hidden transgression has wounded the conscience; or even for the sake of mutual prayers, so that one may pour out pious prayers to God for the safety and salvation of the other. This confession, which is made to a neighbor, is commonly called the confession of charity. Quest.

Latin:

Indicium veræ contritionis externum & probabile, quod in ore peccatoris animadvertitur, est confessio peccatorum, quæ vel est totius ecclesiæ, quippe quæ tum ordinarie in publicis precibus, tum extraordinarie in publicis calamitatibus peccata sua confitetur a); vel est hominis priuati, qui sua peccata confitetur, immediate coram Deo b), coram ecclesia c), coram ecclesiæ ministro d), coram proximo e) Prob. a. Confessionem peccatorum generalem totius ecclesiæ esse necessariam & utilem, inter alia patet ex Leu. XVI, 21. Imponet Aaron ambas manus suas super caput hirci uiui, & confitebitur super illum omnes iniquitates filiorum Israëlis, ac omnes præuaricationes eorum quoad omnia peccata eorum: Dabit illa super caput hirci imittetque per manum viri destinati in desertum. Obseruamus hic: 1) Confessionem publicam totius ecclesiæ fieri, præeunte voce ministri Dei, qualis olim erat sacerdos Aaron. Conf. 1 Sam. VII, 5. Neh. IX, 1. Iud. X, 10. 2) Confessionem publicam coniunctam esse cum fide in Christum, cuius typus olim erat hircus ἀποπομπαῖος, siue emissarius: Christus enim est agnus Dei, tollens peccata mundi, Io. I, 29. cui manum fidei imponimus.

Prob. b. Ex Ps. LI, 6. Tibi soli peccaui, & malum coram te feci. Confitetur rex Dauid peccatum suum Deo, tanquam summo legislatori, iudici & καρδιογνώστῃ, vipote cuius legem violauerat. Peccauerat quidem etiam in proximum, sed principaliter & ultimo in Deum legislatorem. Hæc confessio, quæ inmediate fit Deo, a LVTHERO vocatur confessio fidei.

Prob. c. Achan coram facie totius ecclesiae Israeliticae furtum suum confessus est, Ios. VII, 19. Quae confessio coram ecclesia olim dicebatur ἐξομολόγησις, & erat vel voluntaria, qua peccator vltro delictum suum publicabat, vel involuntaria, ad quam edendam ab ecclesia compellebatur.

Prob. d. Ex Matth. III, 6. Et baptizati sunt in Iordane ab ipso (Ioanne), confitentes peccata sua. Auditores Ioannis coram hoc praecone facram internam cordis contritionem externa oris confessione testati, baptismum tanquam efficax medium regenerationis & iustificationis accipiebant.

Prob. e. Ex Iac. V, 15. Vbi Apostolus: Confitemini, inquit, alter alteri lapsus, & precamini alter pro altero, ut sanemini. Non est Apostolo Iacobo sermo de confessione edenda sacerdoti; quia haec non est mutua. S. Iacobus inquit: Ἐξομολογεῖσθε ἀλλήλοις, i. e. mutuo & invicem. Confitetur autem proximus proximo culpam, vel reconciliationis causa, cum proximum iniuria affecit, vid. Matth. V, 23; vel petendi consilii causa, cum delictum occultum conscientiam vulneravit; vel etiam mutuarum precum causa, ut alter pro alterius incolumitate & salute pias ad Deum fundat preces. Haec confessio, quae fit proximo, communiter vocatur confessio caritatis.


### XX. What signs of contrition are detected in the face and external habit of the sinner?

In the face and habit of the sinner, certain external signs of contrition are observed: a) tears:

b) haircloth and sackcloth: c) the sprinkling of ashes: d) the beating of the breast and thigh: e) the rending of garments: f) squalid lying on the ground.

Proof a. Tears, shed without hypocrisy, are the ambassadors of grief and the blood of a wounded heart. The penitent Israelites shed tears, Exod. 33: 4. David, Ps. 6: 7. Peter, Matt. 26: 75. The sinful woman, Luke 7:38. Proof b.

The King of Nineveh, about to declare his repentance with external signs, arose from his throne, and laid aside his robe from him, and covered himself with sackcloth, Jonah 3:6. Sackcloth is also called haircloth, and it is a mournful, vile, rough garment, woven from the hair of wild beasts, narrow, pricking and lacerating the skin, an index of a mourning, humiliated, suppliant mind. Proof c.

The repenting Israelites sprinkled themselves with ashes, 2 Sam. 13:19; Neh. 9:1, by which act they both testified that they were nothing but ash and dust, and intended to invite God to commiseration toward His fragile work, fashioned from dust. Proof d. The penitent publican beat his breast, saying: Lord, be merciful to me a sinner, Luke 18:13.

To beat the breast is, by an evident blow, to chastise a hidden sin, says AUGUSTINE, serm. 8 de verbis dom. Proof e. The Hebrews rent their garments in the height of mourning and in more vehement commotions of the mind.

See Gen. 37:34; 2 Sam. 3:31. That the rending of garments is a sign of repentance is evident from Joel 2:13. Proof f.

King David, struck by heavy grief, lay upon the earth, 2 Sam. 12:16; which χαμευνία, or lying on the ground, is a sign of a submissive mind. Quest.

Latin:

In facie & habitu peccatoris animadvertuntur quaedam externa contritionis signa: a) lacrymae:

b) cilicium & saccus: c) cineris aspersio: d) percussio pectoris & femoris: e) scissio vestium: f) humicubatio squalida.

Prob. a. Lacrymae, fine hypocrisi effusae, sunt legati doloris, & vulnerati cordis sanguis. Fuderunt lacrymas poenitentes Israelitae, Exod. XXXIII, 4. Dauid, Ps. VI, 7. Petrus, Matth. XXVI, 75. Peccatrix, Luc. VII, 38.

Prob. b. Rex Niniues, poenitentiam suam externis signis declaraturus, surrexit de throno suo, & deposuit chlamydem suam desuper se, obduxitque saccum, Ion. III, 6. Saccus dicitur etiam cilicium, estque vestis lugubris, vilis, hirta, ex pilis ferarum contexta, angusta, cutim pungens & lacerans, index animi lugentis, humiliati, supplicis.

Prob. c. Cinere se consperferunt Israelitae resipiscentes, 2 Sam. XIII, 19. Neh. IX, 1. quo ipso tum testatum iuerunt, se nil, nisi cinerem & pulverem esse, tum inuitaturi fuerunt Deum, ad commiserationem erga opus suum fragile, ex pulvere conflatum.

Prob. d. Percussit poenitens publicanus pectus suum dicens: Domine, propitius esto mihi peccatori, Luc. XVIII, 13. Tundere pectus, est, evidenti pulsu occultum castigare peccatum, ait AVGVSTINVS ferm. 8. de verbis dom.

Prob. e. Hebraei vestes suas lacerabant in summo luctu, & in vehementioribus animi commotionibus. Vid. Gen. XXXVII. 34. 2 Sam. III, 31. Scissionem vestium esse poenitentiae indicium, patet ex Ioël II, 13.

Prob. f. Rex Dauid, graui dolore perculsus, iacuit super terram, 2 Sam. XII, 16. quae χαμευνία, sive humicubatio, est animi submissi signum.


### XXI. What external signs of contrition are detected in the work itself?

Externally, a) fasting and b) satisfaction testify to internal contrition. Proof a.

Fasting is a voluntary abstinence from food, so that the flesh may be restrained and the mind humbled. When Ezra had undertaken the journey from Babylon to Jerusalem, he immediately proclaimed fasting to that end, that the flesh might be afflicted, and the Israelites might be more apt to seek the right way from the Lord. See Ezra VIII, 21. Thus fasted the Ninevites, Jon. III, 5. Jehoshaphat, 2 Chron. XX, 3. Nehemiah, ch. I, 4. Daniel, ch. X, 3. Prob. b....

Satisfaction is here understood as that which is rendered to a neighbor who has been harmed, or to the church, offended by a public scandal. Thus the penitent Zacchaeus said, Luke XIX, 8: If I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold. Zacchaeus therefore made satisfaction not to God, but to the neighbor who had been defrauded . That incestuous man, of whom the Apostle makes mention, 1 Cor. V, 1, was delivered unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit might be saved. Concerning this, the Apostle writes 2 Cor. II, 6: Sufficient to such a one is this ἐπιτιμία, that rebuke which was made by many. The Corinthian church, warned by St. Paul, had gravely rebuked (for ἐπιτιμία denotes a rebuke joined with infamy) the incestuous man, and had shunned his company; afterwards, by the will of the Apostle, it forgave the crime to this repenting sinner, and comforted him, lest he should rush headlong into despair, but it imposed no penalty by which he might make satisfaction to God for a temporal punishment. Conf. CHEMNITIUS, Examen Concilii Tridentini, fol. 711, where also this most weighty author shows that the Greeks' ἐπιτιμία is more rightly suited to the church than the satisfaction of the Latins; since that word is more inconvenient and arrogant.

Latin:

De interna contritione externe testantur a) ieiunium, b) satisfactio.

Prob. a. Ieiunium est voluntaria abstinentia cibi, vt caro coerceatur, & animus humilietur. Cum Esdra suscepisset iter e Babylonia Hierosolymam, confestim proclamauit ieiunium eum in finem, vt caro affligeretur, & Israëlitae aptiores essent ad petendum viam rectam a Domino. Vid. Esdrae VIII, 21. Sic ieiunarunt Niniuitae, Ion. III, 5. Iosaphat, 2 Paral. XX, 3. Nehemias, c. I, 4. Daniel, c. X, 3.

Prob. b.... Satisfactio hic intelligitur ea, quae praestatur proximo laeso, vel ecclesiae, publico scandalo offensae. Ita Zachaeus poenitens dicebat, Luc. XIX, 8: Si quem de aliquo defraudaui, reddo quadruplum. Satisfecit igitur Zachaeus non Deo, sed proximo defraudato . Incestuosus ille, cuius meminit Apostolus, 1 Cor. V, 1. tradebatur Satanae in perditionem carnis, vt spiritus saluaretur. De hoc scribit Apostolus 2 Cor. II, 6: Sufficit tali ἐπιτιμία, reprehensio illa, quae a pluribus facta est. Ecclesia Corinthiaca, monita a S. Paullo, grauiter increpauerat (ἐπιτιμία enim notat increpationem cum infamia coniunctam) incestuosum, & eius consortium declinauerat; postea, ex voluntate Apostoli, huic peccatori resipiscenti condonabat crimen, cumque solabatur, ne in desperationem praeceps rueret, nullam autem mulctam imponebat, qua pro poena temporali Deo satisfaceret. Conf. CHEMNITII ex. concil. Trident. fol. 711. vbi etiam hic auctor grauissimus ostendit, graecorum ἐπιτιμίαν rectius conuenire ecclesiae, quam satisfactionem latinorum; quippe quae vox est incommodior & arrogantior.


### Q. XXII

Are the mentioned signs of contrition infallible? They are probable, but not infallible.

Prob. Those external signs of contrition sometimes do not proceed from serious sorrow, but are assumed by art, and for this reason are hateful to God. See Is. LVIII, 5. Luke XVIII, 12.

Latin:

Sunt probabilia, sed non infallibilia.

Prob. Externa illa contritionis signa interdum non ex serio dolore proficiscuntur, sed ex arte assumuntur, & hac ratione Deo sunt exosa. Vid. Es. LVIII, 5. Luc. XVIII, 12.


### Q. XXIII. Is

special enumeration of all and singular sins to be required in confession? A special enumeration of all and singular sins according to circumstances is not necessary in confession before a minister of the church.

Prob. 1) An enumeration of all and singular sins according to circumstances is impossible. Who understands his errors? Cleanse me from secret faults, O Lord, says King David, Ps. XIX, 13. This King was of a most perspicacious mind, yet he did not have all his שגיאות, errors, known. Therefore he sought purification from secret sins, which escape the memory.

2) That articular, special, and circumstantial confession is a torture of consciences, and a path nearest to despair. For sinners are deterred by shame, or fear of punishment, from revealing all and singular sins; indeed, many are even obliterated by forgetfulness when the confession is issued. A snare is truly woven for consciences, because there is no remission for sins not expressed in confession.

3) That special confession is superstitious; for it is considered to be meritorious, upon which absolution is to be suspended.

4) It is hostile to honesty and modesty, pernicious to the secret counsels of Princes and private individuals, and a machine of avarice .

This is the antithesis of the Papists, who demand a special enumeration of all and individual sins in confession before a priest. They rely on the following arguments:

I. Whatever is enjoined upon us by God, that is necessary by virtue of divine command: But special confession of sins is [enjoined] etc.: Therefore. The minor is proved from James 5:16. Confess your faults one to another.

Instantia: Christ commanded the leper to show himself to the priests, Matt. 8:4. Therefore, special confession of sins is necessary by virtue of divine command. Resp. The cause of the sending away to the Levitical priests was not a special confession of sins, but the showing of the cleansing already performed.

II. Whatever has a divine promise annexed to it, that is necessary for Christians: Special confession of sins [has this] etc.: Therefore. The minor is proved from 1 John 1:9. Resp. St. John in that place treats of confession to be rendered before God, not before a priest.

III. Whoever must remit sins, to them sins must be recounted: But priests [must remit sins] etc.: Therefore. The major is evident: because to remit and to confess sins are relatives. But with one of the relatives posited, the other is also posited. The minor is proved from Matt. 16:19, Matt. 18:18, John 20:22. Resp. A general confession suffices; a special and circumstantial confession is not necessarily required.

Instantia: The key of loosing and binding denotes the power of judging: But to a judge, a deed must be recounted with all its circumstances: Resp. The key of loosing and binding does not imply the power of judging, but of discerning sinners, and of decently applying promises and threats to certain individuals. God is the omniscient judge; priests are ministers and messengers. He remits sins αὐτοκρατορικῶς (autocratically), or principally; these remit sins διακονικῶς (ministerially), or ministerially.

IV. In the same way that Christians in the Apostolic church confessed their sins, let us also confess our sins: But in the Apostolic church Christians confessed their sins specifically and individually. Therefore. The minor is proved from Acts 19:18. Many also of them that believed came, and confessed, and showed their deeds. Resp. 1) CHRYSOSTOM takes this passage to refer to miracles; because the word ἀναγγέλλειν (to report/announce) is never used for the confession of sins. 2) Be it so, that evil deeds are understood, yet that confession was not private and auricular, but public, before the whole assembly of believers. 3) They did not recount all and individual sins with every circumstance, but the more atrocious ones, primarily acts of curious vanity and the magic art. See the following verse, 19.

Latin:

specialis omnium & singulorum peccatorum enumeratio in confessione exigenda? Specialis omnium & singulorum peccatorum secundum circumstantias enumeratio in confessione coram ministro ecclesiae non est necessaria.

Prob. 1) Enumeratio omnium & singulorum peccatorum secundum circumstantias est impossibilis. Delicta quis intelligit? Ab occultis munda me, Domine, ait Rex Dauid, Ps. XIX, 13. Erat hic Rex perspicacissimi ingenii, neque tamen omnia sua שגיאות, errata, cognita habebat. Idcirco expetebat purgationem a peccatis occultis, memoriam fugientibus.

2) Confessio illa articularis, specialis & circumstantialis est carnificina conscientiarum, & proxima ad desperationem via. Deterrentur enim peccatores pudore, aut metu poenae, quo minus omnia & singula peccata detegant; quin obliuione etiam pleraque sunt oblitterata, cum confessio editur. Nectitur vero conscientiis laqueus, quod peccatorum in confessione non expressorum nulla fit remissio.

3) Confessio illa specialis est superstitiosa; censetur enim esse meritoria, a qua absolutio fit suspendenda.

4) Est honestati & pudori inimica, arcanis consiliis Principum & priuatorum perniciosa, & auaritiae machina .

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, exigentium specialem enumerationem omnium & singulorum peccatorum in confessione coram sacerdote. Qui sequentibus nituntur argumentis:

I. Quidquid a Deo nobis est iniunctum, illud vi mandati diuini est necessarium: Atqui specialis peccatorum confessio est &c: E. Minor probatur ex Iac. V, 16. Confitemini alter alteri lapsus. Resp. Apostolus Iacobus loquitur de confessione caritatis fraternae, non de confessione ecclesiastica.

Instantia: Christus mandabat leproso, vt se ostenderet sacerdotibus, Matth. VIII, 4. Ergo specialis peccatorum confessio est necessaria vi mandati diuini. Resp. Causa ablegationis ad sacerdotes leuiticos non erat specialis confessio peccatorum, sed mundationis iam factae ostensio.

II. Quidquid habet annexam promissionem diuinam, illud Christianis est necessarium: Specialis peccatorum confessio &c. E. Minor probatur ex 1 Io. I, 9. Resp. Agit S. Ioannes l. c. de confessione edenda coram Deo, non coram sacerdote.

III. Quicunque peccata debent remittere, illis peccata sunt recensenda: Atqui sacerdotes &c. E. Maior constat: quia remittere & confiteri peccata sunt relata. Sed posito vno relatorum ponitur etiam alterum. Minor prob. ex Matth. XVI, 19. Matth. XVIII, 18. Io. XX, 22. Resp. Sufficit confessio generalis, non necessario requiritur confessio specialis, & circumstantialis.

Instantia: Clauis soluendi & ligandi notat potestatem iudicandi: Iudici autem factum cum omnibus circumstantiis est recensendum: Resp. Clauis soluendi & ligandi non infert potestatem iudicandi, sed peccatores discernendi, & decenter applicandi promissiones & comminationes ad certa indiuidua. Deus est iudex omniscius, sacerdotes sunt ministri & nuntii. Ille αὐτοκρατορικῶς, siue principaliter, hi διακονικῶς, ministerialiter peccata remittunt.

IV. Quomodo in ecclesia Apostolica Christiani peccata sua confessi sunt, eodem modo & nos peccata confiteamur: Sed in ecclesia Apostolica Christiani peccata sua speciatim & sigillatim confessi sunt. E. Minor probatur ex Act. XIX, 18. Multi etiam eorum, qui crediderunt, veniebant, confitebantur ac annuntiabant facta sua. Resp. 1) CHRYSOSTOMVS hunc locum accipit de miraculis; quia verbum ἀναγγέλλειν nunquam de peccatorum confessione vsurpatur. 2) Esto, intelligi facta mala, non tamen illa confessio erat priuata & auricularis, sed publica, coram vniuerso credentium coetu. 3) Non recensebant peccata omnia & singula cum singulis circumstantiis, sed atrociora, in primis actus curiosae vanitatis & artis magicae. Vid. versum sequ. 19.


### Question XXIV. Whether private confession before a minister of the church is rightly retained in the orthodox church?

Private confession, by which sins in general and, in particular, those that are more atrocious and stinging to the conscience are recounted before a minister of the church, is rightly retained in the orthodox church, not under the condition of absolute necessity for salvation, but on account of its most abundant utility.

Proved: 1) From the general command of God, Lev. 5:5, "He shall confess that in which he has sinned," and Num. 5:7, "They shall confess their sin." Every Israelite who had sinned brought sacrifices and confessed his transgressions privately to the priest before the slaughtering and offering of the sacrifices, especially the more atrocious ones; which is gathered from Lev. ch. 4, 5, and 6.

2) From the rite of private absolution. The power of absolving privately has been divinely granted to the minister of the church, Matt. 16:19, 18:18, John 20:22. Therefore, the power of hearing the confession of sins privately has been granted to the same.

3) From the examples of David, 2 Sam. 12:13; the sinful woman, Luke 7:38; and those baptized by John, Matt. 3:5.

4) Because confession and absolution contribute much: a) to the instruction of the young, b) to the correction of dissolute behavior, c) to the probation and preparation of communicants who are about to enjoy the Lord’s Supper, d) to the special application of the remission of sins, e) to the consolation of afflicted consciences.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, Anabaptists, and Weigelians, who abhor private confession and absolution. They impugn our assertion with the following arguments:

I. Whatever weakens and overturns ecclesiastical confession must be abrogated: Private confession of sins before a minister of the church, etc. Therefore. The minor is proved: because formerly malicious sinners, when they had once turned away from grave sins and returned to their vomit, were exterminated from the fellowship of the church. Resp. Ecclesiastical discipline is not removed by the private confession of sins, but only the degrees of ecclesiastical censure are observed, according to the admonition of Christ, Matt. 18:15. Public ecclesiastical censure, by which sinners are barred from the use of the sacraments, is to be used modestly and prudently.

II. Whatever pertains to the relics of the papacy must be abrogated: Private confession of sins, etc. Therefore. Resp. A huge difference exists between the confession visited among the Papists and the Evangelicals. The former is a confession of sins, special and circumstantial; the latter is a general confession of all sins and only relatively special, viz., with respect to a sin stinging the conscience. The former is considered absolutely necessary; the latter is decorous by reason of order, useful by reason of solace, and just by reason of the scandalized neighbor. The former is held to be meritorious; the latter is declarative of internal repentance. The former is a path to despair; the latter to consolation and the δοκιμασίαν (testing) of the conscience.

III. Whatever confession draws many inconveniences with it must be abrogated: Private confession, etc. Therefore. The minor is proved: because the special confession of a more atrocious sin a) casts a man into the most present danger of fame and life; b) establishes the avarice of ministers of the church, who greedily accept penitential monies; c) stirs up envy among them, while one has a smaller and another a larger number of those confessing. Resp. a) Special confession of an enormous transgression is not held by us as simply necessary, but only hypothetically, for the fuller exoneration and instruction of the conscience, and the confessor should press the seal of silence upon his mouth [[p. 1190]]. b) Penitential monies have been abrogated in some orthodox churches; in others, they are offered to the ministers of the divine word as gratuitous gifts, not as prices by which the remission of sins is venal. c) The envy is of dogs, not of ministers of the church; but if it should arise by accident, nothing is detracted from confession itself.

Latin:

Confessio privata, qua recensentur coram ministro ecclesiae peccata in genere ac in specie atrociora & conscientiam pungentia, recte retinetur in orthodoxa ecclesia, non sub conditione absolutae necessitatis ad salutem, sed ob utilitatem vberrimam.

Prob. 1) Ex mandato Dei generali, Lev. V, 5. Confiteatur, in quo peccauit, & Num. V, 7. Confitebuntur peccatum suum. Vnusquisque Israelita, qui peccauerat, adducebat sacrificia, & confitebatur sacerdoti priuatim delicta sua ante mactationem & oblationem sacrificiorum, praesertim atrociora; quod ex Lev. c. IV. V. & VI. colligitur.

2) Ex ritu absolutionis privatae. Diuinitus concessa est ministro ecclesiae potestas priuatim absoluendi, Matth. XVI, 19. XVIII, 18. Io. XX, 22. Ergo eidem concessa est potestas priuatim audiendi confessionem peccatorum.

3) Exemplis Dauidis, 2 Sam. XII, 13. peccatricis, Luc. VII, 38. baptizatorum a Ioanne, Matth. III, 5.

4) Quia confessio & absolutio plurimum facit; a) ad iuniorum informationem, b) ad dissolutionum correctionem, c) ad probationem & praeparationem conuiuarum, qui coena dominica sunt fruituri, d) ad specialem remissionis peccatorum applicationem, e) ad conscientiarum afflictarum consolationem.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, Anabaptistarum & Weigelianorum, confessionem & absolutionem priuatam abominantium. Qui sequentibus nostram assertionem argumentis impugnant:

I. Quaecunque confessionem ecclesiasticam eneruat & euertit, illa est abroganda: Confessio peccatorum priuata coram ministro ecclesiae &c. Ergo. Minor probatur: quia olim malitiosi peccatores, quando semel a grauibus peccatis auersi resipuerant, & ad vomitum redibant, e complexu ecclesiae exterminabantur. Resp. Non tollitur per confessionem peccatorum priuatam disciplina ecclesiastica, sed gradus tantum censurae ecclesiasticae obseruantur, iuxta monitum Christi, Matth. XVIII, 15. Publica censura ecclesiastica, qua peccatores ab vsu sacrorum arcentur, modeste & prudenter usurpanda est.

II. Quidquid pertinet ad reliquias papatus, illud est abrogandum: Confessio peccatorum priuata &c. Ergo. Resp. Ingens datur discrimen inter confessionem visitatam apud Pontificios, & Euangelicos. Illa est confessio peccatorum, specialis & circumstantialis; haec est generalis omnium peccatorum & respective tantum specialis, scil. respectu peccati conscientiam pungentis. Illa censetur absolute necessaria; haec ratione ordinis decora, ratione solatii utilis, ratione proximi scandalizati iusta est. Illa habetur meritoria; haec declaratina internae poenitentiae. Illa est via ad desperationem; haec ad consolationem & conscientiae δοκιμασίαν.

III. Quaecunque confessio plurima secum trahit incommoda, illa est abroganda: Confessio priuata &c. Ergo. Minor probatur: quia atrocioris peccati specialis confessio hominem a coniicit in praesentissimum famae vitaeque discrimen; b) stabiliit ministrorum ecclesiae, nummos poenitentiales auide accipientium, auaritiam; c) inuidiam inter eos conflat, dum vni minor, alteri maior est confitentium numerus. Resp. a) Confessio specialis enormis delicti a nobis non habetur simpliciter, sed tantum hypothetice necessaria, ad pleniorem exonerationem & informationem conscientiae, confessionarius autem sigillum silentii ori imprimat. b) Nummi pænitentiales, in quibusdam ecclesiis orthodoxis sunt abrogati, in quibusdam offeruntur ministris verbi divini, tanquam dona gratuita, non tanquam pretia, quibus remissio peccatorum sit venalis. c) Inuidia canum, non ministrorum ecclesiæ est; quod si ea per accidens suboriatur, confessioni ipsi nil derogatur. *


### Q. XXV. Does a temporal punishment remain after the guilt is remitted, to be redeemed by one's own satisfactions?

After the guilt is remitted, no τιμωρία (punishment), or punishment properly so called, threatens converted and justified sinners a): yet there remains sometimes παιδεία (discipline), or fatherly chastisement and medicinal affliction b).

Proved: a. 1) From the perfect remission of guilt: To whomsoever all guilt is remitted, in them no liability to punishment remains. But to all believers guilt is remitted, Acts 10:43. Therefore. The major is confirmed from the relation of guilt and punishment. Where there is no guilt, there punishment has no place: since it is the vindication of guilt.

2) From the express testimony of the Apostle, who says, Rom. 8:1, "There is no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus." Where there is no condemnation, there is no liability to punishment.

3) From the parabolic illustration. The heavenly King not only remits the debts to the servant burdened with the greatest debts, but also the punishments, Matt. 18:32.

4) Christ most fully satisfied divine justice, not only by taking our sins upon Himself, but also by deriving the punishments of sins upon Himself, Ps. 53:5. For which reason, with the persuasion of one's own satisfaction, much is detracted from the most abundant satisfaction of Christ.

5) From the lack of our own powers to satisfy God. To render satisfaction to God requires infinite virtue, which no sluggish man possesses. For which reason it was necessary for our Redeemer to be God, so that He could pay the λύτρον ἰσάξιον (equivalent ransom), the most sufficient price of redemption, to divine justice. Proved: b.

Proved: b. Whom the Lord loves, He παιδεύει (disciplines), corrects, Heb. 12:6, and 1 Cor. 11:32. We are παιδευόμεθα (disciplined) by the Lord, chastised, that we may not be condemned with the world. Therefore there is imposed upon the faithful παιδεία (discipline), chastisement, which arises not from an angry God, but from a placated one, and does not result in condemnation, but in the amendment of the one chastised.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, who impose various satisfactions upon penitents for temporal punishments ( ). Furthermore, they assign three kinds of satisfactory works: prayer, fasting, and alms. They recall to prayer those things which are exhibited immediately to God, such as praises, acts of thanksgiving, contrition, and confession: To fasting, those which afflict the body and resist the concupiscence of the flesh, such as hairshirts, ashes, and flagellations: To alms, all works of mercy, which resist avarice and yield to the utility of one's neighbor. They rely on the following arguments:

I. To King David, after his sin was forgiven, a punishment was denounced, Resp. Distinguish between τιμωρίαν, or punishment, inflicted by an angry God, and παιδείαν, or chastisement sent by a placated God. Not the former, but the latter was denounced to David, so that it might be both a memorial of his most grave past lapse and a medicine προφυλακτική, preserving from sins. Elegantly says AUGUSTINE: Calamities before forgiveness are punishments; after forgiveness they are struggles and exercises of the pious.

II. The prophet Daniel gave counsel to King Nebuchadnezzar: Redeem your sins with alms, Resp. In the original text is the word פְּרַק, which signifies, break off. Whence in the source the words flow thus: Wherefore, O king, let my counsel be pleasing to you, that you may break off (change) your sins into righteousness, and your iniquities into mercy for the afflicted. From these it is clear that in the cited place, it is not understood as a satisfactory redemption, but an emendatory change.

III. Tob. XII, 9. The Angel Gabriel says: Alms deliver from death, and it is that which purges sins, and makes one find mercy and life. Resp. 1) The Book of Tobit is apocryphal. b) Liberation from untimely death is understood, which God often averts from those who are beneficent out of true charity toward the poor, not as if beneficence were satisfactory for punishment, but because God compensates the same out of grace. c) Alms purge sins not past, but future, by inducing a habit opposite to the former. For while a man strives for beneficence, he avoids avarice, rapacity, inhumanity, and similar vices. d) The last words in the source sound thus: Those who do alms and righteousness shall be filled with long and lasting life. IV. is fought, and of satisfaction, for averting it.

But they also wish to appear very liberal and merciful. Namely, they say that it is not so simply necessary that each person make satisfaction for himself; but that it is permitted to the wretched, whose flesh and skin perhaps might be very tender, that it is permitted, therefore, to redeem this burden imposed upon himself with a certain price. You ask, in what way? They respond: by the benefit of indulgences. By whose authority? Indeed of the Roman Pontiff, as if he were truly the vicar of Christ. Whence are those? From the treasury of the church, and indeed the Roman one. But what is that treasury? It is, of course, that in which the merits of holy men, collected from many centuries and increased more cumulatively every year, are preserved with the greatest care. Who are those holy men? Not all who have died blessedly, but only those whom the Roman Prelate has judged worthy, whom he himself, moved by political reasons, would refer into the number of saints, who are barbarously called canonized, and to whom others are thought inferior, whom they are accustomed to call beatified. Concerning those blessed and saints, the matter is very uncertain, whether they are blessed and saints even in divine judgment; indeed, that some of them never even existed as men is today agreed upon by all. What, finally, are their merits? Namely, as they say, works that are absolutely excellent and abundant, or, as they love to speak barbarously, works of supererogation, which exceed the whole number of precepts, and which might suffice not only for the saints themselves who are thought so, but also bring forgiveness of sins and salvation to many others. I pass over more. What or who the Doctors were at that time, when a stricter ecclesiastical discipline lived, who were accustomed to signify by the name of both satisfactions and indulgences, and how far their mind was from the sense of the Roman Catholics, that escapes no one today, except him who has brought a mind that is a total stranger to the monuments of sacred history.

IV. The penitent Ninevites fasted, clothed themselves in sackcloth, sprinkled themselves with ashes, etc., so that they might make satisfaction for temporal punishments. Jonah III, 5. Resp. Those were not satisfactory works, but external signs and testimonies of internal penitence. Instance: In the primitive church, canonical satisfactions were received by custom. Resp. They were imposed upon sinners who had fallen into more serious crimes, not to satisfy God for the punishment, but a) for the exercise and probation of the season of penitence: b) for the example and terror of others: c) for the authority and reconciliation of the scandal given to the church, to which satisfaction had to be made by an external declaration of penitence.

SIGH.

By the powers of grace, O most holy God, instruct and strengthen me, the most miserable of sinners, that I may restrain and curb the vicious motions of my soul, lest they break out into grave crimes! Give me, heavenly Father, true and sincere penitence, give me a contrite heart, give water to my head, and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that by temporal weeping I may forestall the weeping and gnashing of teeth! Slay, I beseech thee, my flesh prone to evil, break and crush my hard heart, that, the obstacle being removed, the spirit of faith may dwell, live, and reign in me!

Latin:

Post remissam culpam nulla τιμωρία, siue pæna, proprie dicta, peccatoribus conuersis & iustificatis imminet a): manet tamen interdum παιδεία, siue paterna castigatio & afflictio medicinalis b).

Prob. a. 1) E perfecta culpæ remissione: Quibuscunque culpa omnis remittitur, in illis nullus remanet pænæ reatus. At omnibus credentibus remittitur culpa, Act. X, 43. Ergo. Maior confirmatur e relatione culpæ & pænæ. Vbi nulla est culpa, ibi nec locum habet pæna: quippe quæ est vindicta culpæ.

2) A diserta Apostoli testificatione, inquitentis, Rom. VIII, 1. Nihil condemnationis iis est, qui in Christo Iesu sunt. Vbi nulla est condemnatio, ibi nullus est reatus pænæ.

3) E parabolica illustratione. Rex cœlestis seruo, debitis maximis onerato, non tantum remittit debita, sed etiam pænas, Matth. XVIII, 32.

4) Christus plenissime satisfecit iustitiæ diuinæ, non tantum peccata nostra, sed & peccatorum pænas in se deriuando, Ps. LIII, 5. Quam ob rem cumulatissime Christi satisfactioni persuasione propriæ satisfactionis plurimum derogatur.

5) A defectu virium nostrarum ad satisfaciendum Deo. Ad satisfactionem Deo præfandam requiritur infinita virtus, qua nullus homo iners pollet. Quam ob causam redemptorem nostrum oportuit esse Deum, vt λύτρον ἰσάξιον, pretium redemptionis sufficientissimum, iustitiæ diuinæ persoluere posset.

Prob. b. Quem Dominus diligit, παιδεύει, corrigit, Hebr. XII, 6. & 1 Cor. XI, 32. A Domino παιδευόμεθα, castigamur, ne cum mundo condemnemur. Imponitur itaque fidelibus παιδεία, castigatio, quæ oritur non a Deo irato, sed placato, neque cedit in condemnationem, sed castigati emendationem.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, pænitentibus varias satisfactiones pro pænis temporalibus imponentium (*). Ceterum tria assignant operum satisfactorum genera: Orationem, ieiunium, & eleemosynas. Ad orationem revocant ea, quæ Deo immediate exhibentur, vt laudes, gratiarum actiones, contritionis & confessionis actus: Ad ieiunium, quæ corpus affligunt, & concupiscentiæ carnis repugnant, vt sunt cilicia, cineres, flagellationes: Ad eleemosynas omnia opera misericordiæ, quæ repugnant auaritiæ, & cedunt in proximi vtilitatem. Nituntur sequentibus argumentis:

I. Regi Dauidi post remissam culpam pœna denuntiabatur, Resp. Dist. inter τιμωρίαν, siue pœnam, inflictam a Deo irato, & inter παιδείαν, siue castigationem immissam a Deo placato. Non illa, sed hæc Dauidi denuntiabatur, vt esset tum memoriale præteriti lapsus grauissimi, tum medicina προφυλακτική, præseruans a peccatis. Eleganter inquit AVGVSTINVS: Calamitates ante remissionem sunt supplicia, post remissionem sunt certamina, exercitationesque piorum.

II. Propheta Daniel regi Nabuchodonofari dabat consilium: Peccata tua redime eleemosynis, Resp. In textu originali habetur verbum פְּרַק, quod significat, abrupit. Vnde in fonte sic fluunt verba. Quare, rex, consilium meum placeat tibi. vt peccata tua in iustitiam abrumpas (mutes), & iniquitates tuas in miserationem afflictorum Ex his patet, quod l. c. non intelligatur redemptio satisfactoria, sed mutatio emendatoria.

III. Tob. XII, 9. Angelus Gabriel infit: Eleemosyna a morte liberat, & ipsa est, quæ purgat peccata, & facit inuenire misericordiam & vitam. Resp. 1) Liber Tobiæ est apocryphus. b) Intelligitur liberatio a morte immatura, quam sæpe Deus auertit ab iis, qui ex vera caritate erga pauperes sunt benefici, non quasi beneficentia sit satisfactoria pro pœna, sed quia Deus eandem ex gratia compensat. c) Eleemosyna purgat peccata non præterita, sed futura, habitum priori oppositum inducendo. Dum enim homo studet beneficentia, auaritiam, rapacitatem, inhumanitatem & similia vitia vitat. d) Vltima verba in fonte sic sonant: Qui faciunt eleemosynas & iustitias, implebuntur vita longa & diuturna.

IV. Pugnatur, & satisfactionis, pro illa auertenda. Sed videri etiam cupiunt admodum liberales ac misericordes. Scilicet dicunt, non ita simpliciter necesse esse, vt pro se quisque satis faciat; sed licere misero, cuius forsitan tenerrima caro & cutis sit, licere igitur hoc onus, sibi impolitum, pretio quodam redimere. Quæris, quo pacto? Respondent: beneficio indulgentiarum. Cuiusnam auctoritate? Quippe Pontificis Romani, tanquam is vere Christi vicarius fit. Vndenam illæ? Ex thesauro ecclesiæ, & quidem Romanæ. Ecquis vero thesaurus ille? Is nimirum, in quo merita sanctorum hominum, inde a multis sæculis collecta, & quotannis cumulatius aucta, cum cura maxima adseruantur. Quinam sunt illi homines sancti? Non omnes beate defuncti, sed illi tantum, quos Præsul Romanus dignos iudicauit, quos ipse, rationibus politicis motus, in numerum sanctorum referret, qui barbare vocantur canonisati, & quibus inferiores putantur alii, quos solent beatificatos appellare. De illis quidem beatis & sanctis res valde incerta est, vtrum diuino etiam iudicio beati sint, & sancti, immo quosdam eorum ne homines quidem nunquam fuisse, hodie inter omnes constat. Quæ tandem illorum promerita? Nempe, vt aiunt, opera prorsus eximia atque abundantia, seu, vt barbare loqui amant, opera supererogationis, quæ totum numerum præceptorum superent, & quæ non ipsis solum sanctis putatis sufficiant, sed multis etiam aliis veniam peccatorum, salutemque adferre possint. Taceo plura. Quid aut qui Doctores eo tempore, quo seuerior disciplina ecclesiastica viuit, nomine & satisfactionum & indulgentiarum significare soliti sint, & quam longe illorum mens a sensu Romano-Catholicorum abfuerit, id hodie præterit neminem, nisi eum, qui ex sacra historiæ monumentis prorsus hospitem retulit animum.

Poenitentes Ninivitae ieiunarunt, cilicio se induerunt, cinere se consperserunt &c. vt pro poenis temporalibus satisfacerent. Ionae III, 5. Resp. Non fuerunt illa opera satisfactoria, sed externa signa & testimonia internae poenitentiae. Instantia: In primitiva ecclesia usu receptae fuerunt satisfactiones canonicae. Resp. Imponebantur illae peccatoribus, in graviora prolapsis crimina, non ad satisfaciendum Deo pro poena, sed a) ob feriae poenitentiae exercitium & probationem: b) ob aliorum exemplum & terrorem: c) ob ecclesiae scandalo offensae auctoritatem & reconciliationem, cui externa poenitentiae declaratione satisfaciendum erat.

SUSPIRIUM.

Viribus gratiae, o Deus sanctissime, instrue & robora me, peccatorum miserrimum, vt motus animi mei vitiosos compescam & cohibeam, ne in gravia scelera erumpant! Da mihi, Pater caelestis, veram & sinceram poenitentiam, da cor contritum, da capiti meo aquam, & fontem lacrymarum oculis meis, vt fletu temporali praeveniam fletum & stridorem dentium! Iugula, quaeso, carnem meam ad mala proclivem, frange & contere cor meum durum, vt, remoto obice, spiritus fidei in me habitet, vivat, regnet!


## 34 On Faith in Christ


### Q. I. What is faith in Christ?

Faith in Christ is a gift of the Holy Spirit, by which the converted and reborn sinner salutarily acknowledges the evangelical promise concerning the grace of God and the remission of sins and eternal salvation, to be obtained on account of the satisfaction and merit of Christ, approves it with firm assent, and applies it to himself with singular trust, so that he may be justified and saved eternally. Obs.

Faith is said to be from trusting [fidendo], and therefore, by the force of the word, it is trust. Cicero indeed, in Book 1 of his Etymology of Offices, ch. 7, brings forward another etymology of faith, saying: We believe, because it is done, which is said to be called faith. But this is an allusion, not a genuine derivation.

Latin:

Fides in Christum est donum Spiritus S., quo peccator conversus & renatus promissionem evangelicam de gratia Dei & remissione peccatorum aeternaque salute, propter satisfactionem & meritum Christi impetranda, salutariter agnoscit, solido assensu comprobat, & singulari fiducia sibi applicat, vt iustificetur, & aeternum salvetur. Obs.

Fides dicitur a fidendo, adeoque, vi vocis, est fiducia. Cicero quidem L. 1. de Etymologia. Offic. c. 7. aliam adducit etymologiam fidei, inquiens: Credimus, quia fiat, quod dictum est, appellatam esse fidem. Sed haec allusio, non genuina derivatio est.


### Q. II. What kind of faith is understood here?

Faith is not understood here as objective, or that which is believed; but subjective, by which one believes a): not false, or dead, but true and living b): not another's, but one's own c): not historical, or dogmatic, nor miraculous, but justifying d): not general, but special e): not absolutely, but relatively considered f). Prob. a. Objective faith, or that which is believed, is the doctrine of faith; which is improperly called faith, because it is the object of faith. Cf. Acts VI, 7; ch. XIII, 8; ch. XVI, 5; Rom. XII, 6. But subjective faith, or that by which one believes, is faith properly so called, which is in the believing man as in a subject. Prob. b.

False faith, or vain and dead, is equivocally called faith, since it is only an empty persuasion and boasting of faith, or a rash presumption concerning the mercy and grace of God, on account of the merit of Christ, in an impenitent man who indulges in sins, concerning which James ep. ch. II, 20.

Do you truly wish to know, O vain man, that faith without works is dead and not saving?

Our discourse here is of faith that is true and living, which receives its life from Christ, and when it has justified the sinner, it exerts and shows itself to be living through charity and the pursuit of good works. Prob. c. We are not dealing at present with alien faith, by which the needs of a neighbor are commended to God, and temporal and spiritual goods are obtained for him, Matt.

IX, 2, but with proper faith, of which the Prophet Habakkuk, ch.

II, 4, and with him Paul, Gal.

III, 11: The just shall live by his own faith.

As everyone naturally lives by his own soul, so everyone spiritually lives by his own faith.

You should observe that by 'proper faith' here is not understood the proper faith of our words and deeds, which is called fidelity, integrity of mind, and candor; but faith receiving the word of the Gospel and the merit of Christ.

Prob. d. Historical faith, which is also called dogmatic, is twofold; one rests on human authority; the other on divine revelation.

That the former is different from justifying faith is beyond doubt; saving faith embraces the latter: just as the rational soul embraces the vegetative and sensitive soul.

But just as the vegetative soul exists in plants, and the sensitive in brutes without the rational soul, so historical faith exists without saving faith in hypocrites.

For these know the documents of divine grace and the deeds of Christ externally and historically, not so as to place trust in Christ, the author of salvation.

But trust is the complement, soul, and life of faith in Christ.

Historical faith is found even in devils, James II, 19.

Furthermore, historical faith of impious men differs from the faith of demons; not indeed essentially, but accidentally: 1) In the principle of cognition, because in impious men it is only scripture, in demons it is additionally αὐτοψία (direct vision).

2) In the applicability of the object believed, which demons lack, but men do not.

The faith of miracles, or miraculous faith, is that by which we firmly establish that what God has either foretold or willed to happen, either by us or by others, for our benefit or that of others, will come to pass from the infinite and absolute power of God, Matt. XVII, 20.

It is subdistinguished into active and passive.

The former is that by which one is divinely endowed with the peculiar gift of performing miracles, Matt. XVI, 17.

The latter is that by which a man firmly establishes that he will be a participant in the individual benefits that occur through miracles, Matt. IX, 27.

But the faith of miracles differs from justifying faith.

The former is an extraordinary and periodic gift; the latter is ordinary and perpetual.

Without the former, many are saved; without the latter, no one.

The former is given to hypocrites and the impious, Matt.

VII, 22; the latter is possessed only by the truly converted and reborn.

The object of the former is the omnipotence of God; of the latter, His mercy.

Yet miraculous faith is 1) a certain image, as it were, of saving faith.

For Christ in visible miracles shadowed forth His invisible grace, in healing the saving grace, in resuscitation the life-giving grace, which the healed and resurrected one received, without any cooperation of his own good work.

2) The end of this same miraculous faith is saving faith, which if it be present, makes one saved, not because that faith which is saving was excited by a miracle.

Cf.

D.

DANNHAV. in hodof. phænom.

XI. p.

1302.

Prob. e. General faith is that by which a man to be saved believes that all things are true which have been revealed by the divine word; of which general faith we are not now speaking, because it considers faith.

we had considered as a means of salvation, and thus in order to a special, or peculiar object, which has the power of recovering salvation, lost through sin, and by whose regard faith can be enumerated among the means of salvation. Faith is therefore special, by which the converted and reborn sinner applies to himself individually the universal promises concerning Christ the mediator and the grace of God to be obtained through Him, and believes that God wills to be propitious even to him, and to forgive his sins on account of the satisfaction of Christ, performed for his sins and those of all men. It is therefore called special faith, not because it has as its object some special promise which was made peculiarly to the believer, but because of the application, through which it descends to him individually under the universal promise concerning the grace of God and the merit of Christ.

Thus Job, issuing a profession of his faith, said: I know that my redeemer liveth, Job XIX, 25. And Paul, Gal. II, 20: The Son of God loved me, and gave himself for me.

Proof. Faith is not viewed for the present absolutely, as it is a good work pertaining to the first commandment of the decalogue; but relatively, insofar as it looks upon Christ and apprehends His merit. To justify relatively is nothing other than to justify by the power of its correlate. Faith therefore justifies relatively, i.e., the thing believed, the merit of Christ apprehended by faith, justifies.

Faith, WHICH justifies, is knowledge, assent, and trust, etc., but faith, INSOFAR AS it justifies, is the bare passive reception of the benefits of the Messiah, admitting the motion of the Holy Spirit, reclining and resting in the merits of Christ.

Conf. D. DANNHAV. l. c. p. 1305.

Question III. In how many ways is the word "to believe" taken?

The word "to believe" is taken in three ways.

Proof. For it is one thing to believe God [credere Deum]; another to believe to God [credere Deo]; another to believe into God [credere in Deum]. We believe that God is, through knowledge; we believe God, through assent; we believe into God through trust.

Question IV. What are the causes of faith?

The cause and means of kindling faith are the same as those of regeneration.

Proof. Regeneration formally is the conferring of the powers of believing and the donation of faith itself. Therefore, it is of no use to treat here of the causes and means of kindling faith.

Question V. Who believes in Christ?

Men believe in Christ: a) sinners, b) both converted and reborn adults, c) and infants reborn through baptism d).

Proof. a. Only men are capable of faith in Christ, of whom He is the mediator, 1 Tim. II, 5. Devils believe that Christ is the Son of God and the supreme judge (see Matth. VIII, 29): but they tremble, James II, 19.

Therefore they do not place trust in Christ as their mediator and the author of their salvation.

Proof. b. Just as Christ was given as mediator not to whole men, but to fallen men, Matth. I, 21: so faith in Christ was not in man when whole, but is given only in man as a sinner.

Prob. c. True and saving faith is not in those who lack contrition and have the intention of continuing and persevering in sins, says the Form. concord. p. 688. Wherefore it is necessary that the sinner, indulging in the desires of the flesh, be converted from the darkness of sin to the light of faith, Acts 26:16. But the light of faith is kindled by the grace of regeneration: For everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, 1 John 5:1.

Prob. d. Baptized infants put on Christ, Gal. 3:27. Therefore, they believe in Christ. But we have dealt more fully with the faith of infants in the previous section, ch.

Latin:

Non intelligitur hic fides obiectiva, sive quae creditur; sed subiectiva, qua creditur a): non falsa, aut mortua, sed vera & viva b): non aliena, sed propria c): non historica, sive dogmatica, neque miraculosa, sed iustificans d): non generalis, sed specialis e): non absolute, sed relate spectata f). Prob. a. Fides obiectiva, seu quae creditur, est doctrina fidei; quae improprie dicitur fides, quia est obiectum fidei. Conf. Act. VI, 7. c. XIII, 8. cap. XVI, 5. Rom. XII, 6. Fides autem subiectiva, seu qua creditur, est fides proprie dicta, quae inest homini credenti, tanquam subiecto. Prob. b.

Fides falsa, sive vana ac mortua, aequivoce dicitur fides, cum tantum sit inanis persuasio ac iactantia fidei, aut temeraria praesumtio de Dei misericordia & gratia, propter meritum Christi, in homine impoenitente, peccatisque indulgente, de qua Iacobus epist. cap. II, 20.

Visne vero scire, o homo vane, quod fides sine operibus mortua sit & non salvifica?

Nobis hic sermo est de fide vera & viva, quæ vitam suam accipit a Christo, & cum iustificavit peccatorem converti, per caritatem & studium bonorum operum se vivam exserit & ostendit. Prob. c. Non agimus in præsenti de fide aliena, quæ necessitates proximi Deo commendant, & ipsi bona temporalia & spiritualia impetrantur, Matth.

IX, 2. sed de fide propria, de qua Propheta Habacuc, c.

II, 4. & cum eo Paullus, Gal.

III, 11: Iustus sua fide vivet.

Vt quilibet naturaliter propria vivit anima: ita quilibet propria fide spiritualiter vivit.

Obferues, quod per fidem propriam hic non intelligatur fides propria nostrorum dictorum & factorum, quæ fidelitas, integritas animi & candor appellatur; sed fides verbum euangelii, meritumque Christi recipiens.

Prob. d. Fides historica, quæ etiam dogmatica appellatur, est duplex; una auctoritati humanæ; altera revelationi divinæ innititur.

Illam a fide iustificante esse diversam, extra dubium est; hanc fides salvifica complectitur: sicut anima rationalis complectitur animam vegetiuam & sensitivam.

At vero quem ad modum anima vegetativa in plantis, & sensitiva in brutis sine anima rationali existit: ita fides historica est sine salvifica in hypocritis.
