Etenim hi documenta gratiæ divinæ & gesta Christi externe & historice cognoscunt, non vt fiduciam in Christo, auctore salutis, collocent.

Fiducia autem est fidei in Christum complementum, anima & vita.

Fides historica deprehenditur etiam in diabolis, Iac. II, 19.

Ceterum differt fides historica hominum impiorum a fide dæmonum; non quidem essentialiter, sed accidentaliter: 1) In principio cognitionis, quod in hominibus impiis sola est scriptura, in dæmonibus insuper αὐτοψία.

2) In obiecti crediti applicabilitate, qua carent dæmones, non item homines.

Fides miraculorum, sive miraculosa est, qua firmiter statuimus, euenturum ex infinita & absoluta Dei potentia, quod Deus vel prædixit, vel fieri voluit, aut a nobis, aut ab aliis, in nostrum aliorumue commodum, Matth. XVII, 20.

Subdistinguitur in actuam, & passiuam.

Illa est, qua quis peculiari dono miracula faciendi divinitus præditus est, Matth, XVI, 17.

Hæc est, qua homo certo statuit, se fore participem singularum beneficiorum, quæ per miracula contingunt, Matth. IX, 27.

Differt autem fides miraculorum a fide iustificante.

Illa est donum extraordinarium, & periodicum; hæc ordinarium & perpetuum.

Sine illa multi sunt saluati; sine hac nemo.

Illa datur in hypocritis & impiis, Matth.

VII, 22. hanc habent tantum vere conuersi & renati.

Illius obiectum est omnipotentia Dei; huius, misericordia.

Est tamen fides miraculosa 1) quædam quasi imago fidei salvificæ.

Etenim Christus in miraculis visibilibus invisibilem suam gratiam adumbravit, in sanatione salvificam, in resuscitatione vivificam, quam sanatus, & exsuscitatus accepit, nulla sua cum cooperatione boni operis.

2) Eiusdem fidei miraculosæ finis est fides salvifica, quæ si adsit, saluum facit, non quia miraculum excitata est ea fides, quæ salvifica est.

Conf.

D.

DANNHAV. in hodof. phænom.

XI. p.

1302.

Prob. e. Fides generalis est, qua homo saluandus credit, omnia vera esse, quæ verbo divino reuelata sunt; de qua fide generali iam nobis sermo non est, propterea, quod fidem considerat.

fideramus ut medium salutis, adeoque in ordine ad speciale, seu peculiare obiectum, quod habet vim recuperandi salutem, per peccatum amissam, & cuius intuitu fides inter media salutis recenseri potest. Est igitur fides specialis, qua peccator conuersus & renatus promissiones vniuersales de Christo mediatore & gratia Dei, per ipsum impetranda, sibi in indiuiduo applicat, & credit, Deum velle sibi etiam propitium esse, & peccata remittere propter Christi satisfactionem, pro suis & omnium hominum peccatis praestitam. Dicitur itaque fides specialis, non quod specialem aliquam promissionem pro obiecto habeat, quae credenti peculiariter sit facta, sed ob applicationem, per quam sub promissione vniuersali de gratia Dei & merito Christi ad se in indiuiduo descendit.

Sic Iobus, professionem fidei suae edens, dixit: Scio, quod redemtor meus viuit, Iob. XIX, 25. & Paullus, Gal. II, 20. Filius Dei dilexit me, & tradidit semetipsum pro me.

Prob. f. Fides impraesentiarum non spectatur absolute, prout est bonum opus, ad primum decalogi praeceptum pertinens; sed relate, quatenus Christum aspicit, eiusque meritum apprehendit. Relatiue iustificare, nihil aliud est, quam vi sui correlati iustificare. Fides itaque iustificat relate, i. e. res credita, meritum Christi fide apprehensum, iustificat.

Fides, QUAE iustificat, est notitia, assensus & fiducia &c. sed fides, QUATENUS iustificat, est nuda receptio beneficiorum Messiae passiua, admissiua motum Spiritus sancti, recubitoria, resquietoria in meritis Christi.

Conf. D. DANNHAV. l. c. p. 1305.

Quæst. III. Quot modis sumitur verbum, credere?

Verbum, credere, sumitur tribus modis.

Prob. Aliud enim est, credere Deum; aliud, credere Deo; aliud, credere in Deum. Credimus esse Deum, per notitiam; credimus Deo, per assensum; credimus in Deum per fiduciam .

Quæst. IV. Quæ sunt cauffæ fidei?

Causa & media accendendæ fidei, eadem sunt, quæ regenerationis.

Prob. Regeneratio formaliter est collatio virium credendi, & ipsius fidei donatio. Proinde de causis & mediis fidei accendendæ hic agere nil attinet.

Quæst. V. Quis credit in Christum?

In Christum credunt homines a) peccatores b), tum adulti conuersi & renati c), tum infantes per baptismum regeniti d).

Prob. a. Fidei in Christum capaces sunt soli homines, quorum is mediator est, 1 Tim. II, 5. Diaboli credunt, Christum esse Filium Dei & summum iudicem (vid. Matth. VIII, 29): sed contremiscunt, Iac. II, 19.

Non ergo fiduciam collocant in Christo, tanquam suo mediatore & auctore salutis suae.

Prob. b. Quemadmodum Christus non integris, sed lapsis hominibus datus est mediator, Matth. I, 21: ita fides in Christum non fuit in homine integro, sed tantum in homine peccatore datur.

Prob. c. Vera ac salvans fides in iis non est, qui contritione carent, & propositum in peccatis pergendi & perseverandi habent, ait Form. concord. p. 688. Quare necesse est, ut peccator, desideriis carnis indulgens, convertatur a tenebris peccati ad lucem fidei, Actor. XXVI, 16. Accenditur autem lux fidei per gratiam regenerationis: Nam omnis, qui credit, quod Iesus fit Christus, ex Deo natus est, 1 Io. V, 1.

Prob. d. Infantes baptizati Christum induunt, Gal. III, 27. E. in Christum credunt. Sed de fide infantum sectione superiori c. IV. fusius egimus.


### IV. Q. VI. Is faith in the intellect or in the will of man?

Faith is in the intellect, by reason of knowledge and assent; in the will, by reason of trust.

Prob. 1) The converted and regenerate sinner not only believes that Jesus is the Christ, 1 John 5:1, by an act of knowledge and assent, which is in the intellect; but he also believes in Christ, John 3:36, by an act of trust, which is in the will.

2) The evangelical promise, which is the object of faith, proceeds not only from the knowledge, but also from the will of God: Therefore, the acceptance of the promise is not only an act of the intellect, but also of the will.

3) The converted and regenerate sinner receives the evangelical promise as true, with the intellect; as good for himself, with the will. With the intellect he knows and approves the truth of the promise; with the will he embraces it, and by a singular trust appropriates its goodness to himself.

The antithesis is that of Bellarmine, who asserts, book I de iustificat. ch. 6, that faith cannot exist simultaneously in the intellect and the will, because one virtue cannot exist in two powers that are distinct in kind. But Bellarmine’s hypothesis, that one virtue cannot be in two powers, fails in a composite unity, through collection and subordination.

Suarez, vol. II, disp. 44, sect. 4, no. 4, says: The one virtue of faith is fashioned from a habit of the intellect and a pious affection in the will.

THOMAS AQUINAS, cited by D. GERHARD in confess. cathol. f. m. 1459, says: Something is said to be in two principles first in this way: that it is equally in both: Thus it is impossible for one virtue to be in two powers. Secondly, by a certain order; and thus one virtue can pertain to several powers, so that it is in one principally and extends itself to others by way of diffusion or disposition. Thus the image of God consists in the concreated wisdom of the intellect and the integrity of the will. Free will is in the intellect, by reason of judgment, in the will, by reason of freedom. Heresy looks partly to the intellect, partly to the affection, says ALEXANDER of HALES, cited by D. SCHERZER in system. p. m. 300.

Prudence is in the intellect, by reason of consultation; in the will, by reason of election. Prayer, as defined by THOMAS in 2, q. 83, art. 1, is an act of practical reason, explaining the desire of the will, and asking something from another.

Which BELLARMINE himself, book I de bonis operibus ch. 1, explains thus: The intellect and the affection concur in praying. The affection concurs by desiring that good which it lacks: the intellect, however, by explaining and proposing that desire. From which it is clear that one must distinguish between a simple habit, which cannot be in different powers, and an aggregated habit, or one composed of different acts terminated at the same object, and indeed having an order among themselves toward one and the same object, which can reside in distinct faculties.

Latin:

Fides est in intellectu, ratione notitiae & assensus; in voluntate, ratione fiduciae.

Prob. 1) Peccator conversus & renatus non tantum credit, Iesum esse Christum, 1 Io. V, 1. actu notitiae & assensus, qui est in intellectu; sed etiam credit in Christum Io. III, 36. actu fiduciae, quae est in voluntate.

2) Promissio evangelica, quae est obiectum fidei, non proficiscitur tantum a scientia, sed & a voluntate Dei: E. acceptio promissionis non est tantum actus intellectus, sed & voluntatis.

3) Peccator conversus & renatus recipit promissionem evangelicam, ut veram, intellectu; ut sibi bonam, voluntate. Intellectu cognoscit & approbat promissionis veritatem; voluntate amplectitur, & singulari fiducia sibi appropriat eius bonitatem.

Antithesis est Bellarmini, statuentis, libr. I. de iustificat. c. 6. fidem non posse simul in intellectu & voluntate existere, eo, quod una virtus in duabus potentiis, genere distinctis, esse nequeat. Sed hypothesis Bellarmini, quod una virtus non possit esse in duabus potentiis, fallit in unitate composita, per collectionem & subordinationem.

Svarez. tom. II. disp. 44. sect. 4. num. 4. inquit: Una virtus fidei conflatur ex habitu intellectus & piae affectionis in voluntate.

THOMAS AQVINAS, citante D. GERHARDO in confess. cathol. f. m. 1459. ait: Dicitur aliquid esse in duobus principiis primo fic. quod ex aequo fit in vtroque: Sic impossibile est, vnam virtutem esse in duabus potentiis. Secundo, ordine quodam; & sic vna virtus potest pertinere ad plures potentias, ita, vt in vna sit principaliter & se extendat ad alias per modum diffusionis, aut dispositionis. Sic imago Dei consistit in concreata sapientia intellectus, & integritate voluntatis. Liberum arbitrium est in intellectu, ratione arbitrii, in voluntate, ratione liberi. Haeresis respicit in parte intellectum, in parte affectum, inquit ALEXANDER ab ALES, citante D. SCHERZERO in system. p. m. 300.

Prudentia est in intellectu, ratione consultationis; in voluntate, ratione electionis. Oratio, definiente THOMA in 2. quaest. 83. art. 1. est actus rationis practicae, voluntatis desiderium explicans, & ab alio aliquid postulantis.

Quod ipse BELLARMINVS lib. I. de bonis operibus c. 1. ita explicat: Intellectus & affectus ad orandum concurrunt. Affectus concurrit desiderando id bonum, quo caret: intellectus vero, id desiderium explicando & proponendo. Ex quibus dispalescit, distinguendum esse inter habitum simplicem, qui in diversis potentiis esse nequit, & inter habitum aggregatum, sive compositum ex diversis actibus ad idem obiectum terminatis, & ordinem quidem inter se ad vnum idemque obiectum habentibus, qui in distinctis facultatibus residere potest.


### Q. VII. What is the object of faith, which it itself regards?

The object of general, or dogmatic, faith is every word of God revealed a). The object of special, or saving, faith is Christ the mediator, insofar as he is offered to us by the evangelical promise as the meritorious cause of God’s grace and the remission of sins b). which is the same thing, the grace of God, remitting sins on account of the satisfaction of Christ, and promised in the gospel c); or, which comes to the same, the evangelical promise concerning the grace of God and the remission of sins, to be obtained on account of the satisfaction of Christ d). Obs.

One thing, as regards the matter, is signified as the object of trust, whether in Christ the mediator, or in the grace of God, or in the promise of grace made on account of Christ the mediator, that it consists in this, you might say. The diversity is only in the manner of conceiving and speaking. For by the first manner of speaking, the notion of the object is constituted in Christ the mediator, as the meritorious cause of the grace repaired and promised to us, and the grace of God repaired to us through him is connoted. By the second, however, the notion of the object is constituted in the grace of God repaired through Christ, remitting sins, as in the internal impulsive cause of God; but Christ, as its meritorious cause, if not expressed in words at the same time, is nevertheless tacitly understood. By the third manner of speaking, finally, the notion of the object is constituted in the promises concerning the remission of sins on account of Christ, which proceeds from the satisfaction of Christ and the grace of God, and by which both, namely the merit of the mediator and the mercy of God, are offered to us.

In whatever way, therefore, you speak, the trust of a man about to obtain the remission of sins before God will always return to one and the same object, namely Christ the mediator, insofar as he is the cause of the mercy of God repaired to us, and of the remission of sins to be obtained before God. Prob. a. Dogmatic, or general, faith is directed toward every word of God, insofar as it is God's, 1 Thess. II, 13, to which, on account of the authority of God who reveals, an undoubted assent must be given. Prob. b.

Special, or justifying, faith is directed toward Christ, as the meritorious cause of the remission of sins and of eternal salvation: concerning which John, 1 ep. II, 2: Christ is the propitiation for our sins, and Paul, Rom. III, 25: God set forth Christ ἱλαστήριον, a propitiatory, through faith in his blood, i.e., because Christ by his satisfaction for our sins has rendered God propitious to us, let us fix our trust of obtaining the remission of sins in the blood of Christ.

This object of faith is such that, when it is posited and applied, justification itself is posited, and the question is satisfied: on account of what are we justified and saved? This is evident from Acts XVI, 31, where we read that to the question of the jailer among the Philippians: What must I do to be saved? the Apostles answered roundly: Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, and your house.

Whence we argue: In whom we must believe, for the reason that he is the cause of the remission of sins and of eternal salvation, he is the object of saving faith, which it regards. But we must believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, etc. Prob. c.

We are justified freely by his (God's) grace, through the redemption in Christ Jesus.

Whence we argue: In whatever we are justified, toward that, as an object, justifying faith is directed: But we are justified by the grace of God, reconciled to us by the redemption of Christ: Therefore. Prob. d. 1) From Rom. IV, 16.

Therefore righteousness is by faith, that it might be by grace, that the promise might be firm. That upon which faith firmly relies is its object: Faith firmly relies upon the promise of divine grace: Therefore. 2) From Gal. III, 22.

The scripture has concluded all under sin, that the promise by faith might be given to those who believe. The Apostle understands the federal, or testamentary, promise concerning the seed of Abraham, which is Christ, v. 16 & 19. Just as this promise was given to those who believe: so it is to be received by true faith for salvation, which the Apostle teaches, 1 Tim. I, 15. Faithful is the saying and worthy of all acceptance, that Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners.

it is gathered from these things that the promise concerning Christ, the author of salvation, was given so that it might be accepted by believers for eternal salvation. Whatever is given to a believer so that he may apprehend salvation by faith, that is the object of saving faith. The antithesis is that of the Pontificians, who state that the object of faith extends as widely as the word of God extends.

They object to us: I. Whatever must be believed on account of the authority of God revealing, that is the object of justifying faith: But every word of God &c: E.

Resp. Distinguish between general, or dogmatic, faith and special, or saving, faith.

The object of the former is every word of God, even the word of the law, from which, however, there is no justification, Gal. III, 22. The object of the latter is the evangelical promise, Gal. III, 22.

II. The object of faith, comprehended in the Apostolic Creed, is the object of justifying faith: The object of faith, comprehended in the Apostolic Creed, is not only mercy in Christ: E.

Resp. Distinguish between the common and proper object of justifying faith. Justifying faith does not exclude the common object, namely, the doctrine of faith concerning the Holy Trinity, creation, preservation, and governance; but it presupposes or includes it.

But just as the sum, scope, end, and goal of the entire scripture is Christ in His mediatorial office, John XX, 31: so saving faith, although it generally assents to the entire word of God, nevertheless specially regards the scope of the entire scripture, and refers all other articles to the promise of grace, on account of Christ the mediator. Just as Augustine in book II. on the Trinity distinguishes the faith of Christians from the faith of demons by the last articles: I believe in the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the body, and life everlasting.

And faith is in vain concerning the other objects of scripture if it does not hold the head of scripture, Christ, Col. II, 19. as Chemnitz says, in loc. theol. de iustific. f. m. 268. Instance: In the Apostolic Creed not even a word is found about the special mercy of God.

Resp. The name of Father, Savior, sanctifier, forgiveness of sins, breathes pure grace and mercy. When I confess: I believe in the forgiveness of sins, I apply God's universal mercy, founded on the merit of Christ, to myself individually. For this is not the meaning: I believe that the gift of forgiveness is in the church; since even demons believe this; but this is the meaning: I believe that God wills to forgive my sins.

III. Whatever faith regards the power of Christ, its adequate object is not the mercy of God, proposed to us in Christ: But the faith of penitent men &c. E. The major is evident: because the power of Christ and the mercy of God differ greatly.

Christ also exerts His power in the impious, on whom God does not have mercy. The minor is evident from the example of the blind men, Matt. IX, 28. Do you believe that I am able to do this? The blind men answered: Yes, Lord.

Resp. 1) L. c. the discourse is about miraculous faith, not justifying faith. 2) Faith, which justifies, regards the power of Christ as a common object: but insofar as it justifies, it is specially directed to the mercy of God, on account of the satisfaction of Christ forgiving sins.

Christ exercises His power in many who are not justified. IV. Whatever faith is directed to the divinity of Christ, its object is not the special mercy of God: But justifying faith &c.

E. The minor is proven by the example of Simon Peter, Matt. XVI, 18. saying: You are the Christ, the Son of the living God. Where Peter's faith did not regard the mercy of God, but the divinity of Christ.

Resp. The divinity of Christ, the God-man, is not to be opposed to the mercy of God, because this is founded in the merit of Christ, but to be joined with it. The grace of God would not have been restored unless Christ, God and man, had merited it for us by His merit.

V. Luke XVIII, 11. The Pharisee confessed that he was righteous, and therefore praying said: I thank you, Lord, that I am not as other men. Here he placed his trust in the mercy of God, and yet he was not justified.

Resp. The trust of the Pharisee was hypocritical & was justified. Resp. The trust of the Pharisee was hypocritical & mercenary, relying on one's own works, not on the merit of Christ. For he stood in the temple, as if proudly and arrogantly arguing with God about his own righteousness; he did not, however, like the publican, flee with a contrite heart to the mercy of God restored by the merit of Christ.

Objection: The publican does not mention Christ in his penitential vow. Resp. The publican prays: God ἱλάσθητί μοι (be merciful to me), as if to say: because of the ἱλαστήριον (propitiation), which is Christ, in whom I trust, have mercy on me.

VI. The object of justifying faith is the resurrection of Christ, as Paul teaches, Rom. X, 9: Therefore, it is not the mercy of God. Resp. The Papists play with the fallacy of opposites: for the resurrection of Christ does not exclude the mercy of God. Christ rose again as our sponsor, by which, having been released from the prison of death, it was most clearly revealed that the grace of God has been reconciled to us.

See Rom. IV, 25.

VII. Whatever object was not of Abrahamic faith, that is not the object of our justifying faith (for Abraham is the father of believers, Rom. IV, 11): But the mercy of God, obtained by the merit of Christ, was not the object of Abrahamic faith. Therefore. The minor premise is evident: because Abraham believed that he would be the father of many nations from a ninety-year-old and barren woman, Rom. IV, 11.

Resp. Distinguish between the primary and secondary object of Abrahamic faith. The former was the promise of mercy, because of Christ, that blessed seed, Gal. III, 16; the latter was the promise concerning the bodily fecundity of Sarah.

For since all promises of other goods are ratified and firm in Christ, according to 2 Cor. I, 20, Abraham could not have believed that he would be the possessor of the promised son from Sarah, and of other bodily goods, unless he had first had faith in the Messiah, or Christ the mediator, and had believed that he had a propitious God because of His satisfaction, to be performed for his sins in the fullness of time.

Quest. VIII. Is Christ the mediator the primary or secondary object of faith?

Christ is true God a), and for all who believe in Him the cause of the remission of sins b) and of eternal life c), and therefore He is not a secondary object of justifying faith, but a primary one. Proof a. From 1 John

V, 20. This (Jesus Christ) is the true God and eternal life. Proof b.

From Acts X, 43. To Christ all the Prophets bear witness, that through His name everyone who believes in Him receives remission of sins.

Proof c. From John III, 16. Whoever believes in Him does not perish, but has eternal life.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, who maintain that trust must be placed in God as the primary object, but in Christ as a secondary object (*).

Who argue: I.

Who

I. He who is not the ultimate scope of faith, he is not the primary object of trust: But Christ, etc. Therefore. They attempt to prove the minor premise from John 12:44: "He who believes in me, does not believe in me; but in him who sent me." Resp. The cited words are to be understood not in an opposite or exclusive sense; but in a composite and inclusive sense, thus: He who believes in me, does not believe in me only; but also in him who sent me.

II. He through whom we believe in God, he is not the primary object of faith: But through Christ, etc. Therefore. The major premise is evident: because in him through whom we believe in God, our trust does not rest, but through him it tends toward the ultimate end, namely God. The minor is proved from 1 Pet. 1:21: "Through Christ you believe in God, who raised him from the dead." Resp. Peter, in the cited place, considers Christ by reason of his prophetic office, and in view of that, says that through him, informing us of the will of God, we believe in God. Which notwithstanding, it is also rightly said that we believe in Christ, the true God, John 5:20, the author of salvation, Acts 4:12, the leader and perfecter of faith, Heb. 12:2, to be honored equally as the Father, John 5:23.

Latin:

Obiectum fidei generalis, sive dogmaticae, est omne verbum Dei revelatum a). Obiectum fidei specialis, sive salvificae, est Christus mediator, quatenus vt caussa meritoria Dei & remissionis peccatorum nobis evangelica promissione offertur b). quod idem est, gratia Dei, propter satisfactionem Christi remittens, & in euangelio promissa c); vel, quod eodem recidit, promissio euangelica de gratia Dei & peccatorum remissione, propter satisfactionem Christi impetranda d). Obs.

Vnum, quoad rem, significatur obiectum fiduciae, siue in Christo mediatore, siue in gratia Dei, siue in promissione gratiae, propter Christum mediatorem facta, id consistere dicas. Tantum in modo concipiendi & loquendi est diuersitas. Per primum enim modum loquendi constituitur ratio obiecti in Christo mediatore, vt reparatae & promissae nobis gratiae causa meritoria, & gratia Dei per ipsum nobis reparata connotetur. Per secundum autem constituitur obiecti ratio in reparata per Christum gratia Dei, peccata remittentis, tanquam in causa impulsina Dei interna, Christus autem, tanquam eius causa meritoria, si non simul verbis exprimitur, tacite tamen subintelligitur. Per tertium denique modum loquendi constituitur ratio obiecti in promissionibus de peccatorum remissione propter Christum, quae a Christi satisfactione & gratia Dei proficiscitur, & qua vtrumque, scilicet meritum mediatoris & misericordia Dei, nobis offertur.

Quocunque igitur modo loquaris, hominis apud Deum remissionem peccatorum impetraturi fiducia semper ad vnum & idem redibit obiectum, Christum mediatorem scilicet, quatenus reparatae nobis misericordiae Dei, & impetrandae apud Deum remissionis peccatorum causa est. Prob. a. Fides dogmatica, siue generalis, fertur in omne verbum Dei, quatenus Dei est, 1 Thess. II, 13. cui propter auctoritatem Dei reuelantis indubitatus assensus praebendus est. Prob. b.

Fides specialis, siue iustifica, fertur in Christum, vt caussam meritoriam remissionis peccatorum, aeternaeque salutis: de quo Ioannes, 1 ep. II, 2: Christus est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, & Paullus, Rom. III, 25: Deus Christum proposuit ἱλαστήριον, propitiatorium per fidem in sanguine ipsius, q. d. Quia Christus satisfactione pro nostris peccatis Deum nobis reddidit propitium, fiduciam impetrandae remissionis peccatorum in sanguine Christi defigamus.

Hoc obiectum fidei ita se habet, vt, eo posito & applicato, ponatur ipsa iustificatio & satisfiat quaestioni: propter quid iustificamur & saluamur? Id quod patet ex Act. XVI, 31. vbi legimus, quod ad quaestionem custodis vinctorum apud Philippenses: Quid me oportet facere, vt saluus fiam? rotunde responderent Apostoli: Crede in Dominum Iesum Christum, & saluus eris tu, & domus tua.

Vnde argumentamur: In quem nos oportet credere, ideo, quod est caussa remissionis peccatorum aeternaeque salutis, ille est obiectum fidei saluificae, quod ipsa respicit. Atqui in Dominum Iesum Christum &c. E. Prob. c.

Ex Rom. III, 24. Iustificamur gratis gratia ipsius (Dei), per redemptionem in Christo Iesu.

Vnde arguimus: Quocunque iustificamur, in illud, tanquam obiectum, fertur fides iustificans: Atqui gratia Dei, redmtione Christi nobis conciliata, iustificamur: E. Prob. d.

1) Ex Rom. IV, 16. Propterea iustitia est ex fide, vt fit ex gratia, vt firma sit promissio. Cui fides firmiter innititur, illud est eius obiectum: Promissioni gratiae diuinae fides firmiter innititur: E.

2) Ex Gal. III, 22. Conclusit scriptura omnia sub peccatum, vt promissio ex fide daretur credentibus. Intelligit Apostolus promissionem foederalem, siue testamentariam de semine Abrahae, quod est Christus, v. 16. & 19. Sicut haec promissio data est credentibus: ita vera fide recipienda est ad salutem, quod docet Apostolus, 1 Tim. I, 15. Fidelis est sermo & omni acceptatione dignus, quod Iesus Christus venit in mundum, vt peccatores saluet.

ligitur ex his, quod ideo data fit promissio de Christo, salutis auctore, ut a credentibus ad æternam salutem acceptetur. Quidquid autem datur credenti, ut salutem fide apprehendat, illud est obiectum fidei salvificæ. Antithesis est Pontificiorum, statuentium, tam late patere obiectum fidei, quam late patet verbum Dei.

Qui obiiciunt nobis: I. Quidquid propter auctoritatem Dei revelantis credendum est, illud est obiectum fidei iustificantis: Sed omne verbum Dei &c: E.

Resp. Dist. inter fidem generalem, sive dogmaticam, & specialem, sive salvificam.

Illius obiectum est omne verbum Dei, etiam verbum legis, ex quo tamen non est iustificatio, Gal. III, 22. Huius obiectum est promissio evangelica, Gal. III, 22.

II. Obiectum fidei, symbolo apostolico comprehensæ, est obiectum fidei iustificantis: Obiectum fidei, symbolo apostolico comprehensæ, non est tantum misericordia in Christo: E.

Resp. Dist. inter obiectum fidei iustificantis commune, & proprium. Fides iustificans non excludit obiectum commune, nempe doctrinam fidei de SS. Trinitate, creatione, conservatione & gubernatione; sed illud supponit, aut includit.

At sicut summa, scopus, finis & meta totius scripturæ est Christus in officio mediatorio, Io. XX, 31: ita fides salvifica, quamvis generatim universo Dei verbo assentiat, speciali tamen ratione respicit ad scopum totius scripturæ, & omnes alios articulos refert ad promissionem gratiæ, propter Christum mediatorem. Sicut Augustinus libr. II. de trinit. fidem christianorum discernit a fide dæmonum per ultimos articulos: Credo remissionem peccatorum, corporum resurrectionem, & vitam æternam.

Et frustra fides circa reliqua obiecta scripturæ versatur, si non caput scripturæ teneat, Christum, Col. II, 19. dicente Chemnitio, in loc. theol. de iustific. f. m. 268. Instantia: In symbolo apostolico ne verbum quidem habetur de speciali misericordia Dei.

Resp. Nomen Patris, Servatoris, sanctificatoris, remissionis peccatorum, meram gratiam & misericordiam spirat. Quando confiteor: Ego credo remissionem peccatorum, misericordiam Dei universalem, fundatam in merito Christi, mihi in individuo applico. Neque enim hic est sensus: Credo, remissionis donum esse in ecclesia; siquidem etiam dæmones hoc credunt; sed hic est sensus: Credo, velle Deum mihi peccata remittere.

III. Quæcunque fides respicit potentiam Christi, illius obiectum adæquatum non est misericordia Dei, in Christo nobis proposita: Atqui hominum pœnitentium fides &c. E. Maior constat: quia potentia Christi & misericordia Dei maxime differunt.

Potentiam suam Christus etiam exserit in impios, quorum Deus non miseretur. Minor constat exemplo cæcorum, Matth. IX, 28. Creditis, quod hoc possim facere? Responderunt cæci: Utique.

Resp. 1) L. c. sermo est de fide mirifica, non iustifica. 2) Fides, quæ iustificat, respicit potentiam Christi tanquam obiectum commune: at quatenus iustificat, speciali ratione fertur in misericordiam Dei, propter satisfactionem Christi peccata remittentis.

In multos Christus potentiam suam exercet, qui non iustificantur. IV. Quæcunque fides fertur in divinitatem Christi, illius obiectum non est specialis Dei misericordia: Atqui fides iustificans &c.

E. Minor probatur exemplo Simonis Petri, Matth. XVI, 18. dicentis: Tu es Christus, Filius Dei viventis. Vbi fides Petri non respiciebat misericordiam Dei, sed divinitatem Christi.

Resp. Divinitas Christi θεανθρώπης misericordiæ Dei non est opponenda, quia hæc in merito Christi est fundata, sed coniungenda. Non reparata esset gratia Dei, nisi Christus Deus & homo eam nobis merito suo peperisset.

V. Luc. XVIII, 11. Pharisaeus confitebatur, se esse iustum, ideoque orans dicebat: Gratias tibi ago, Domine, quia non sum, sicut ceteri homines. Hic fiduciam suam locabat in misericordia Dei, & tamen non iustificabatur.

Resp. Fiducia Pharisaei erat hypocritica & mercenaria, propriis operibus, non merito Christi innixa. Stabat enim in templo, quasi superbe & arroganter de propria iustitia cum Deo differens; non autem perinde, atque publicanus, corde contrito ad misericordiam Dei merito Christi reparatam confugiebat.

Instantia: Publicanus in voto suo poenitentiali Christi mentionem non iniicit. Resp. Publicanus precatur: Deus ἱλάσθητί μοι, quasi dicat: propter ἱλαστήριον, quod est Christus, in quo confido, mei miseraris.

VI. Obiectum fidei iustificantis est resurrectio Christi, docente Paulo, Rom. X, 9: Ergo non misericordia Dei. Resp. Ludunt Pontificii elencho oppositorum: neque enim resurrectio Christi excludit misericordiam Dei. Resurrexit Christus, vt sponsor noster, quo e carcere mortis dimisso, clarissime patuit, gratiam Dei nobis esse conciliatam.

Vid. Rom. IV, 25.

VII. Quodcunque obiectum non fuit fidei Abrahamicae, illud non est obiectum fidei nostrae iustificantis (est enim Abraham pater credentium, Rom. IV, 11): Sed misericordia Dei, merito Christi parta, non fuit obiectum fidei Abrahamicae. E. Minor constat: quia Abraham credebat, se futurum e foemina nonagenaria & sterili patrem multarum gentium, Rom. IV, 11.

Resp. Dist. inter obiectum fidei Abrahamicae primarium, & secundarium. Illud fuit promissio misericordiae, propter Christum, semen illud benedictum, Gal. III, 16; hoc fuit promissio de corporali foecunditate Sarae.

Cum enim omnes ceterorum bonorum promissiones in Christo sint ratae & firmae, iuxta 2 Cor. I, 20. non potuisset Abraham promissi ex Sara filii, & aliorum bonorum corporalium se compotem futurum credere, nisi prius fidem in Messiam, sive Christum mediatorem habuisset, seque propter eius satisfactionem, pro peccatis suis in plenitudine temporis praestandam, Deum propitium habere, creduisset.

Quæst. VIII. Estne Christus mediator obiectum fidei primarium, an secundarium?

Christus est verus Deus a), & omnibus in ipsum credentibus causa remissionis peccatorum b) vitaeque aeternae c), adeoque non est obiectum fidei iustificae secundarium, sed primarium. Prob. a. Ex 1 Io.

V, 20. Hic (Iesus Christus) est verus Deus & vita aeterna. Prob. b.

Ex Act. X, 43. Christo omnes Prophetae testimonium perhibent, quod remissionem peccatorum accipiat per nomen ipsius omnis, qui credit in ipsum.

Prob. c. Ex Io. III, 16. Qui credit in ipsum, non perit, sed habet vitam aeternam.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, statuentium, collocandam esse fiduciam in Deo, vt obiecto primario, in Christo autem, tanquam obiecto secundario (*).

Qui argutantur: I.

Qui

I. Qui non est scopus fidei ultimus, ille non est obiectum fiduciae primarium: Atqui Christus &c. E. Minorem probare conantur ex Io. XII, 44. Qui credit in me, non credit in me; sed in eum, qui misit me. Resp. Verba citata intelligenda sunt non in sensu opposito, aut exclusiuo; sed composito & inclusiuo hoc sensu: Qui credit in me, non credit in me tantum; sed etiam in eum, qui misit me.

II. Per quem credimus in Deum, ille non est obiectum fidei primarium: Atqui per Christum &c. E. Maior patet: quia per quem in Deum credimus, in illo fiducia nostra non conquiescit, sed per ipsum ad ultimum finem, scilicet Deum tendit. Minor probatur ex 1 Petr. I, 21. Per Christum creditis in Deum, qui suscitatit ipsum ex mortuis. Resp. Petrus l. c. considerat Christum ratione officii prophetici, & eius intuitu dicit, quod per eum, de voluntate Dei nos informantem, credamus in Deum. Quo non obstante, recte etiam dicitur, quod credamus in Christum, verum Deum, Io. V, 20. auctorem salutis, Act. IV, 12. fidei ducem & consummatorem, Hebr. XII, 2. aeque honorandum, ac Patrem, Io. V, 23.


### Quest. IX. Does justifying faith revolve around universal promises, or special or singular ones?

To justifying faith, before the act of justification, there are presented universal promises concerning the mercy of God, forgiving sins for the sake of Christ a), which the converted and regenerate sinner in the very act of justification applies to himself individually and specifically, and relies upon them with firm trust b).

Which application the absolving key of the ministry c), the sacrament of baptism d), and of the Lord’s Supper e) perfect and strengthen.

Prob. a. The divine promises concerning the grace of God and the remission of sins, to be obtained for the sake of Christ, are universal, and promise eternal salvation to all who accept them with true faith, e.g., "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life," John 3:16. "Whoever believes in him will not be put to shame," Rom. 10:11. "To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name." These universal promises are laid under justifying faith, like a solid foundation, so that it may be able to rely upon them validly. Prob. b.

The converted sinner, about to obtain the remission of sins and eternal salvation, descends from universal propositions to himself individually, and believes with certainty that for him also in particular the grace of God and the remission of sins has been restored through Christ, and that God now wills to forgive his sins also. For this is the way of universal signs, that when added to some common term, they signify that what is said of the common term applies to all singulars contained under it: Which also in the present matter are read as being added and inculcated so often in the Scriptures for this end, that sinners, anxious and solicitous about their sins, may be able and ought to raise themselves by the universality of the satisfaction rendered by Christ for all sins, and hence of the restored grace of the remission of sins, and to believe safely and firmly that they pertain to them also individually. Thus says the royal Prophet: "God forgives me all my sins," Ps. 103:3, and Paul: "Christ loved me, and gave himself for me," Gal. 2:20, "therefore I have obtained mercy," 1 Tim. 1:16.

Prob. Of this, Rom. 5:1, 2, 3, that I may now pass over in silence several modes of difference. As far as obedience is concerned, they refer it to the commands of God, not only the ancient ones, and those not abrogated by Christ, but also the new ones, by which they claim the moral law to have been increased by Christ.

The absolving key of the ministry contributes much to individual application. For when the minister of the Word compels the penitent sinner with a solemn formula of words: I absolve thee from thy sins in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; the contrite sinner receives this absolution by special faith: I am now absolved from my sins in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Prob. d. From Gal. III, 27. As many as have been baptized have put on Christ. In baptism, everyone who is baptized apprehends the righteousness of Christ, as a most beautiful garment, with the hand of faith, and puts it on himself. Prob. e. In the dispensation of the Holy Supper, individual communicants eat the body of Christ and drink his blood for the remission of sins. From which the penitent sinner gathers and believes: As truly as I eat the body of Christ and drink his blood, so truly do I receive the remission of sins.

There is an antithesis of the Papists, who maintain that no one can believe, by virtue of divine promises, that God wills to be propitious to him even in particular and to remit sins on account of Christ .

Latin:

Fidei iustificae, ante actum iustificationis, obuersantur promissiones vniuersales de misericordia Dei, propter Christum peccata remittentis a), quas peccator conuersus & renatus in ipso actu iustificationis sibi in indiuiduo sigillatim applicat, iisque firma fiducia innititur b).

Quam applicationem perficiunt & roborant clauis soluens ministerii c), sacramentum baptismi d), & coenae dominicae e),

Prob. a. Promissiones diuinae de gratia Dei & remissione peccatorum, propter Christum impetranda, sunt vniuersales, & pollicentur omnibus, qui eas vera fide acceptant, aeternam salutem, v. gr. Sic Deus dilexit mundum, vt filium suum vnigenitum daret, vt omnis, qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed vitam aeternam habeat, Io. III, 16. Omnis, qui credit in eum, non pudefiet, Rom. X, 11. Christo omnes prophetae testimonium perhibent, quod remissionem peccatorum accipiat per nomen ipsius omnis, qui credit in ipsum. Hae promissiones vniuersales fidei iustificanti, solidi instar fundamenti, substernuntur, vt iis valide inniti queat.

Prob. b. Peccator conuersus, remissionem peccatorum aeternamque salutem adepturus, sub vniuersalibus propositionibus ad se in indiuiduo descendat, & certo credat, sibi quoque in particulari reparatam esse per Christum gratiam Dei & remissionem peccatorum, & Deum velle nunc sibi quoque peccata remittere. Haec enim signorum vniuersalium via est, vt termino alicui communi addita, quae de termino communi dicuntur, omnibus sub eo contentis singularibus conuenire significent: Quae etiam in praesenti materia, eo fine in scripturis toties adiecta & inculcata leguntur, vt peccatores, de suis peccatis anxii & solliciti, vniuersitate satisfactionis, pro omnibus peccatis a Christo praestita, & hinc reparatae gratiae remissionis peccatorum sese erigere, eaque ad se etiam in indiuiduo pertinere, tuto ac firmiter credere possint & debeant. Sic inquit Propheta regius: Deus mihi omnia peccata remittit, Ps. CIII, 3. & Paullus: Christus me dilexit, & seipsum pro me tradidit, Gal. II, 20. propterea ego misericordiam consecutus sum, 1 Tim. I, 16.

Prob. Eius, Rom. V, 1. 2. 3. vt plures differentiae modos nunc silentio transeam. Quod ad obedientiam attinet, eam referunt ad imperata Dei, non solum antiqua, & a Christo non abrogata, sed & noua, quibus legem moralem a Christo auctam fuisse conniant. Christo auctam fuisse fomiant.

Ad applicationem individualem plurimum confert clavis soluens ministerii. Cum enim minister verbi peccatorem poenitentem compellat solemni verborum formula: Ego te absoluo a peccatis tuis in nomine Dei Patris, Filii & Spiritus sancti; peccator contritus hanc absolutionem fide speciali recipit: Ego nunc absoluor a peccatis meis in nomine Dei Patris, Filii & Spiritus sancti.

Prob. d. Ex Gal. III, 27. Baptizati Christum induerunt. In baptismo iustitiam Christi quilibet, qui baptizatur, vt vestem pulcherrimam, manu fidei apprehendit, & sibi induit. Prob. e. In dispensatione S. coenae singuli communicantes edunt corpus Christi, & bibunt eius sanguinem in remissionem peccatorum. Ex quo colligit & credit peccator poenitens: Quam vere edo corpus Christi & bibo ipsius sanguinem, tam vere accipio remissionem peccatorum.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum statuentium, neminem credere posse, vi promissionum divinarum, Deum velle sibi etiam in particulari esse propitium & peccata remittere propter Christum .


### Quest. IX. Does justifying faith revolve around universal promises, or special or singular ones?: Their arguments are: I

Their arguments are: I.

Whatever is not revealed by God, that is not an object of justifying faith: The special promise that God wills to remit sins to me, to you, to CHRISTOPHER, to MARTIN, etc., is not divinely revealed: Therefore that special promise is not an object of justifying faith.

Resp. 1) Distinguish between the object of faith and its act. Faith in Christ, which is also called special faith, has for its proper object the promises concerning the grace of God and the remission of sins on account of Christ, and these not as peculiar and to each one individually, but universal, made to all universally. The proper act of faith on the part of the intellect is a special assent, by which the penitent sinner is so carried into the universal promises that, under their universality, he descends to himself, applies them to himself in the individual, and believes that in them grace from God and remission of sins on account of Christ are offered and promised to him also in particular.

This is what our D. CHEMNITIUS teaches excellently in exam. conc. Trid. fol. m. 163. Knowledge must be joined with assent, not indeed merely general, but by which every believer, with firm persuasion, determines that the universal promise pertains privately (individually) to himself also, that he himself is also included and comprehended in that universal promise.

2) God himself applies the universal promise to me: I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins, Is. XLIII, 25. which divine promise I dare to accept, and I believe it pertains to me.

3) God offers and exhibits to me the indeterminate promise of grace, determinately and in the individual, through the absolving key and through the sacraments, so that I may boldly say: I believe the remission of my sins.

II. To whom it is not divinely revealed that he has true faith in Christ, he cannot, under the universal promises of grace, descend by the assent of faith and believe that God wills to be propitious to him and to remit sins on account of Christ.

To no sinner is it divinely revealed, etc.

E.

The major is established: because the promises concerning the grace of God and the remission of sins them include faith itself, John 3:16, Acts 10:43.

Resp. 1) I deny the major, because although it may not be divinely revealed to anyone that he has true faith, nevertheless the converted and reborn sinner is certain of his faith, a) from the witness (συμμαρτυρίᾳ) of the divine Spirit with our spirit, Rom. 8:16. b) From the testing (δοκιμασίᾳ), 2 Cor. 13:5. 2) For special faith it suffices that the penitent sinner believes in Christ his mediator, who for his sake in particular merited the grace of God and the remission of sins by his satisfaction, nor is it required that he believe that he believes by an assent resting upon divine revelation.

For faith, which is included in those promises, does not relate to special faith by way of an object to be believed, but is itself special faith. III. Justifying faith precedes the remission of sins; special faith, by which one believes that his sins have been remitted for him on account of Christ, does not precede the remission of sins: Therefore. The major is proven: because justifying faith is the cause of the remission of sins. But a cause is prior to its effect. The minor is clear: because, when one believes that his sins have been remitted for him, he is already justified, and thus this act of faith is posterior to justification. Resp. Special faith is not correctly explained. For special faith is that by which one descends under the promise of universal grace to himself individually and believes that God wishes to be propitious to him also in particular, and to remit his sins now, on account of Christ's satisfaction, performed for his sins and the sins of the whole world. But that act of faith, by which one believes that his sins have been remitted for him, is not faith formally justifying, but an act of faith, which has justified.

Latin:

Quorum argumenta sunt: I.

Quidquid a Deo non est reuelatum, illud non est obiectum fidei iustificantis: Promissio specialis, Deum mihi, tibi, CHRISTOPHORO, MARTINO, &c. peccata velle remittere, non est diuinitus reuelata: Ergo illa promissio specialis non est obiectum fidei iustificantis.

Resp. 1) Dist. inter fidei obiectum, & ipsius actum. Fides in Christum, quae etiam dicitur fides specialis, pro obiecto proprio habet promissiones de gratia Dei, & remissione peccatorum propter Christum, easque non peculiares, & vnicuique singulatim, sed vniuersales, omnibus vniuerse factas. Actus fidei proprius ex parte intellectus est assensus specialis, quo peccator poenitens ita fertur in promissiones vniuersales, vt sub illarum vniuersalitate ad se descendat, easque sibi in individuo applicet, & in iis sibi in peculiari quoque gratiam Dei & remissionem peccatorum propter Christum offerri & promitti credat.

Id quod praeclare docet noster D. CHEMNITIVS in exam. conc. Trid. fol. m. 163. Notitia oportet coniunctam esse assensionem, non quidem generalem tantum, sed qua firma persuasione quisque credens statuat, vniuersalem promissionem privatim (singulatim) ad se quoque pertinere, se quaque includi, & comprehendi in vniuersali illa promissione.

2) Pro immissionem vniuersalem Deus ipse mihi applicat: Ego, ego ipse deleo iniquitates tuas propter me, & peccatorum tuorum non recordor, Es. XLIII, 25. quam promissionem diuinam aude accedo, & ad me pertinere credo.

3) Deus promissionem gratiae indeterminatam mihi determinate & in individuo offert & exhibet per clauem soluentem, & per sacramenta, vt intrepide dicere queam: Ego credo remissionem peccatorum meorum.

II. Cui diuinitus reuelatum non est, quod veram fidem habeat in Christum, ille sub promissionibus gratiae vniuersalibus assensu fidei ad se descendere & credere nequit; Deum velle sibi esse propitium, & propter Christum peccata remittere.

Nulli peccatori diuinitus reuelatum est &c.

E.

Maior constat: quia promissiones de gratia Dei & remissione peccatorum ipsam fidem includunt, Io. III, 16. Act.

X, 43. Resp. 1) Neg. mai. quia licet nemini divinitus revelatum sit, quod veram fidem habeat, certus tamen est peccator conversus & renatus suae fidei, a) ex συμμαρτυρίᾳ spiritus divini cum spiritu nostro, Rom. VIII, 16. b) Ex δοκιμασίᾳ, 2 Cor. XIII, 5. 2) Ad fidem specialem sufficit, quod peccator poenitens credit in Christum mediatorem suum, qui sibi in particulari gratiam Dei & remissionem peccatorum satisfactione sua promeruit, neque requiritur, vt credat, se credere assensu, divinae revelationi innixo.

Nam fides, quae in promissionibus illis includitur, non habet sese ad fidem specialem per modum obiecti credendi, sed est ipsa fides specialis. III. Fides iustifica remissionem peccatorum antecedit; fides specialis, qua quis credit, peccata sibi propter Christum esse remissa, non antecedit peccatorum remissionem: E. Maior probatur: quia fides iustifica est causa remissionis peccatorum. Causa autem prior est effectu. Minor est clara: quia, cum quis credit, peccata sibi esse remissa, iam iustificatus est, adeoque hic actus fidei posterior est iustificatione. Resp. Fides specialis non recte explicatur. Nam fides specialis est, qua quis sub promissione gratiae vniversali ad se in individuo descendit & credit, Deum velle sibi in particulari etiam esse propitium, & peccata sua nunc remittere, propter Christi satisfactionem, pro suis & totius mundi peccati praestitam. At ille actus fidei, quo quis credit, peccata sibi esse remissa, non est fides formaliter iustificans, sed actus fidei, quae iustificavit.


### Quest. IX. Does justifying faith revolve around universal promises, or special or singular ones?: Question X

Question X.

How manifold is the energy (ἐνέργεια), power, and office of faith in Christ? The power and energy (ἐνέργεια) of faith is twofold: receptive, or apprehensive, and operative. The former is that by which faith passively receives Christ and all the benefits obtained by his merit a). The latter is that by which faith actively exerts itself through works of charity and other virtues b).

Prob. a. The places of Scripture testify concerning the taking (λῆψες), or apprehension of Christ and his benefits, John 1:12, ch. 17:8, Col. 2:6, 1 Tim. 1:15, Rom. 5:17, Acts 10:43, James 1:12, Gal. 3:14.

Prob. b. From Gal. 5:6. Faith works through charity. Which words Dr. Hülsemann skillfully elucidates, as cited by Calov in the Illustrated Bibles on this passage, fol. 624. That epithet, to work through charity, is attributed to the faith which has justified, not attributed to the faith which is yet to justify, much less is it the form or essence of justifying faith, insofar as it justifies. For the Apostle does not describe the office of justifying faith, insofar as it justifies, but another office of faith, namely to work through charity, for the praise of God and the utility of one's neighbor. Obf.

I. The distinction of the twofold energy (ἐνεργείας) of faith is of no small moment; since the same twofold office of faith, and the twofold effect redundant from this, is expressed. Dr. Brentz in the Apology of the Confession of Württemberg, p. 319, explains this distinction thus: Faith, so to speak, has two hands: One, which it extends upward; and it apprehends Christ with all his benefits, and in this part we are said to be justified: The other, which it extends downward to exercise works of charity and other virtues, and in this part we indeed testify to the truth of faith, but we are not justified. Dr. Calov in System of Theology, vol. X, p. 326, says: The Holy Scriptures attribute a twofold act to saving faith: 1) the formal, as it is called in the schools, which is the apprehension of divine grace founded in the merit of Christ, or, which is the same thing, of the merit of Christ, insofar as divine grace is reconciled to us by it: 2) they speak of the effects, by which it extends itself now not to Christ the mediator, but to God and one's neighbor, and embraces them with charity.

II. Although by reason of a twofold activity and effect, faith can be distinguished into justifying and operating, or sanctifying: yet essentially faith is one; just as in man the rational, sensitive, and vegetative soul is one in itself.

Ques. XI. In what does justifying faith formally consist? The form of faith, which justifies, consists in the taking, apprehension, reception, and special application of the justifying object, which is the satisfaction of Christ, and that grace of God procured thereby, which forgives sins, promised in the gospel. For justifying faith receives the evangelical promise, in the promise Christ, in Christ divine grace, from the grace of God the remission of sins, and eternal life.

Latin:

Quaest. X. Quotuplex est ἐνέργεια, vis & officium fidei in Christum?

Vis & ἐνέργεια fidei duplex est: receptiva, sive apprehensiva, & operativa. Illa est, qua fides Christum, & omnia merito ipsius parta beneficia passive recipit a). Haec est, qua fides per opera caritatis & reliquarum virtutum actiue se exserit b).

Prob. a. De λῆψες, sive apprehensione Christi, & beneficiorum ipsius testantur loca scripturae, Ioann. I, 12. c. XVII, 8. Col. II, 6. 1 Tim. I, 15. Rom. V, 17. Act. X, 43. Iac. I, 12. Gal. III, 14.

Prob. b. Ex Gal. V, 6. Fides per caritatem operatur. Quae verba scite enucleat D. Hvlsemannvs, citante Calovio in bibliis illustrat. in h. l. fol. 624. Epitheton illud, operari per caritatem, attributum est fidei, quae iustificauit, non attributum fidei, quae adhuc iustificatura est, multo minus forma, aut essentia fidei iustificantis, quatenus iustificat. Neque enim describit Apostolus officium fidei iustificantis, quatenus iustificat, sed aliud fidei officium, nempe operari per caritatem, ad laudem Dei & vtilitatem proximi.

Obs. I. Distinctio duplicis fidei ἐνεργείας haud leuis momenti est; quoniam eadem geminum fidei officium, & hinc redundans geminus effectus exprimitur. D. Brentivs in apol. conf. Wurtenberg. p 319. hanc distinctionem ita exponit: Fides, vt ita dicam, duplices habet manus: Vnam, quam extendit sursum; & apprehendit Christum cum omnibus ipsius beneficiis, & hac parte nos dicimur iustificari: Alteram, quam protendit deorsum ad exercenda opera caritatis & reliquarum virtutum, & hac parte testificamur quidem veritatem fidei, sed non iustificamur. D. Calovivs in system. theol. tom. X. p. 326. inquit: Geminum actum fidei salvificae tribuunt S. litterae: 1) formalem, vt in scholis dicitur, qui est apprehensio gratiae divinae in merito Christi fundatae, vel, quod idem est, meriti Christi, quatenus eo gratia diuina nobis conciliata est: 2) effectuum dicunt, quo se extendit iam non ad Christum mediatorem, sed ad Deum & proximum, eosque caritate complectitur.

II. Quamuis ratione duplicis ἐνεργείας & effectus, fides distingui possit in iustificantem, & operantem, siue sanctificantem: essentialiter tamen una est fides; sicut in homine anima rationalis, sensitiva & vegetatiua per se una est.

Quaest. XI. In quo formaliter consistit fides iustificans? Forma fidei, quae iustificat, consistit in λῆψει, apprehensione, receptione & speciali applicatione obiecti iustifici, quod est satisfactio Christi, & ea parta gratia Dei, peccata remittentis, in euangelio promissa. Recipit enim fides iustificans promissionem euangelicam , in promissione Christum , in Christo gratiam diuinam , ex gratia Dei remissionem peccatorum , & vitam aeternam .


### Quest. IX. Does justifying faith revolve around universal promises, or special or singular ones?: Obs

Obs.

I. Apprehension or reception is understood here, not as bodily, but spiritual, which takes place by the intellect and will of the converted sinner, and is therefore metaphorical, drawn from the likeness of a hand apprehending a friend or another thing, e.g., an alms. For justifying faith is a receptive organ, and as it were the hand of the miserable sinner, by which he applies to himself, and receives into himself, embraces, and possesses those things which are offered in the gratuitous promise of the gospel. God, the supreme King, reaches out and offers from heaven the hand of grace, procured by the merit of Christ, and in it salvation: the sinner, established in the abyss of misery, receives with the begging hand of faith what is offered. Offering and reception are correlates. Wherefore, to the hand of grace, which offers the treasure of righteousness and salvation, let the hand of faith respond, which apprehends and receives the offered treasure.

Obs.

II. Intellectual apprehension among philosophers, used in a stricter sense, is referred to the first operation of the mind, and is truly called simple apprehension, or apprehension of simple things, with the addition. But in this place, to apprehend is the same as, on the part of the intellect, to transfer a thing to oneself by knowing it, and on the part of the will, to be carried toward the thought-of thing as being good for oneself, and to accept it, and to hold it as if enclosed in the hand, lest it be snatched away, e.g., King David promised Mephibosheth the sustenance of life and a royal table to be taken daily, 2 Sam. IX, 7. Mephibosheth apprehended the promise with his intellect, as true; with his will, as good. He apprehended it with his intellect by knowing it; with his will, by desiring it and adhering to it.

Obs.

III. The reception of Christ through faith is also called in the Holy Scriptures the putting on of Christ, Gal. III, 27; the spiritual tasting, eating, and drinking of Christ, Ps. XXXIV, 9; Jn. VI, 50; nay, even the cleaving, or agglutination with Christ into one Spirit, 1 Cor. VI, 17; and thus it implies a certain union, such as is between the apprehending hand and the apprehended treasure, and it is called the formal union of faith, distinct from the mystical union, or the effect of it.

Opposed to the reception of Christ through faith is the rejection of Christ, of grace, and of the gospel. Proved a. From Gal. III, 13-14, where Paul teaches that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, that we might receive (λάβωμεν) the promise of the Spirit through faith. Surely the promise of the Holy Spirit concerning the remission of sins, to be obtained on account of the redemption of Christ, is not accepted except by faith.

Prob. b. From Jn. I, 12. But as many as received (ἔλαβον) him, to them he gave the power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name. By this Johannine statement, to believe in the name of Christ is explained by receiving him as a most welcome guest and a most great King.

Paul agrees, Col. II, 6. As therefore you have received (παρελάβετε) Christ, so walk in him.

Prob. c. From Rom. V, 17. For if by one man's offence death reigned by one: much more they which receive (λαμβάνοντες) abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness shall reign in life.

St. Paul excellently describes faith, that it receives the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness, and therefore he admonishes, Heb. IV, 16, Let us come with confidence to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy.

Proof d. From Acts 10:43. To Him (Christ) all the prophets bear witness, that through His name everyone who believes in Him receives forgiveness of sins.

Proof e. From Rev. 2:10. Be faithful unto death: Then I will give you the crown of life. The crown of life is given to the faithful, that they may receive and carry it away, as the end of faith, 1 Pet. 1:9.

Latin:

Obs.

I. Intelligitur hic apprehensio, vel receptio, non corporalis, sed spiritualis, quae fit intellectu & voluntate peccatoris conuersi, adeoque metaphorica, similitudine arcessita a manu, amicum, aut rem aliam, v. gr. eleemosynam, apprehendente. Est enim fides iustificans organon receptiuum, & quasi manus miseri peccatoris, qua sibi applicat, & ad se recipit, complectitur & possidet ea, quae in gratuita promissione euangelii offeruntur. Deus, Rex summus, e caelo manum gratiae, merito Christi partae, & in ea salutem porrigit & offert: peccator, in abysso miseriae constitutus, manu fidei mendica accipit, quod offertur. Oblatio & receptio sunt correlata. Quare manui gratiae, quae thesaurum iustitiae & salutis offert, respondeat manus fidei, quae thesaurum oblatum apprehendit & recipit.

Obs.

II. Apprehensio intellectualis apud Philosophos, sensu strictiori usurpata, ad primam mentis operationem refertur, ac vere cum apposito apprehensio simplex, aut simplicium dicitur. Sed hoc loco apprehendere idem est, atque, ex parte intellectus, cognoscendo rem ad se transferre, ex parte voluntatis autem, in rem cogitatam, tanquam sibi bonam, ferri, eamque acceptare, & velut manu conclusam tenere, ne eripiatur, v. gr. Rex Dauid promittebat, Mephibosetho alimenta vitae & regia mensa quotidie capienda, 2 Sam. IX, 7. Mephibosethus promissionem apprehendebat intellectu, vt veram; voluntate, vt bonam. Intellectu eam apprehendebat cognoscendo; voluntate, appetendo & ei adhaerendo.

Obs.

III. Vocatur receptio Christi per fidem in sacris litteris etiam induitio Christi. Gal. III, 27. spiritualis gustus, manducatio & bibitio Christi Psal. XXXIV, 9. Io. VI. 50. quin & κόλλησις, seu agglutinatio cum Christo in vnum Spiritum, 1 Cor. VI, 17. adeoque infert vnionem quandam, qualis est inter manum apprehendentem, & thesaurum apprehensum, & dicitur vnio fidei formalis, distincta ab vnione mystica, seu illius effectu.

Receptioni Christi per fidem opponitur reiectio Christi, gratiae, euangelii. Prob. a. Ex Gal. III, 13. 14. vbi Paullus docet, Christum nos redemisse a maledictione legis, vt promissionem Spiritus per fidem accipiamus (λάβωμεν.) Nimirum promissio Spiritus S. de remissione peccatorum, propter redemptionem Christi impetranda, non, nisi fide, acceptatur.

Prob. b. Ex Io. I, 12. Quotquot vero (ἔλαβον) receperunt eum, dedit illis potestatem, vt filii Dei essent, credentibus in nomen eius. Quo effato Ioanneo, credere in nomen Christi, per recipere ipsum, vt hospitem exoptatissimum & Regem maximum exponitur.

Consentit Paullus, Col. II, 6. Quemadmodum itaque (παρελάβετε) accepistis Christum: ita in eo ambulate.

Prob. c. Ex Rom. V, 17. Si namque unius peccato mors regnauit per vnum: multo magis ii, qui abundantiam gratiae, & doni iustitiae (λαμβάνοντες) accipiunt, in vita regnabunt.

S. Paullus egregie describit fidem, quod abundantiam gratiae & doni iustitiae accipiat, ideoque monet, Hebr. IV, 16, Accedamus cum fiducia throno gratiae, vt misericordiam accipiamus. gratiæ, vt misericordiam accipiamus.

Prob. d. Ex Act. X, 43. Huic (Christo) omnes prophetae testimonium perhibent, quod remissionem peccatorum accipiat per nomen ipsius omnis, qui credit in ipsum.

Prob. e. Ex Apoc. II, 10. Esto fidelis usque ad mortem: Tum dabo tibi coronam vitae. Corona vitae datur fidelibus, vt eam accipiant & reportent, tanquam finem fidei, 1 Petr. I, 9.


### Q. XII. How manifold is the apprehension or reception of the merit of Christ and the mercy of God founded therein?

The apprehension or reception of the merit of Christ, and of the mercy of God founded therein, is threefold: cognitive, which occurs through knowledge; approbative, which occurs through assent; and appropriative or adhesive, through trust.

Proof. We apprehend Christ the mediator, by knowing His universal merit, by applying it to ourselves with special assent, and by embracing it with singular trust, and firmly adhering to the same.

The antithesis is that of BELLARMINE, who in Book I de iustific. c. XVI, denies that apprehension formally belongs to faith, moving the following little arguments:

1. Whatever does not pertain to the first operation of the mind, to it intellectual apprehension does not belong: Faith is not, etc.: Therefore. The major is evident: because apprehension is commonly referred to the first operation of the mind. The minor: because faith is assent, which is in the judgment, which does not apprehend the thing, but discerns whether it be true or false? Resp. 1) Faith is not assent only, but also knowledge and trust. 2) All cognition of the intellect is apprehension, although it is not simple apprehension, but judicial or discursive. By judgment we know and apprehend the union of one thing with another, or its division from another. 3) To apprehend here signifies, on the part of the intellect, to transfer some thing to oneself by knowing it, or to know a thing with the application of it to the knower, which occurs through special assent.

II. To trust is not to apprehend, but to adhere firmly: Therefore, apprehension does not belong to trust, but firm adhesion. Resp. Apprehension and firm adhesion are not opposites; Joab 1 Kings 2:28 was apprehending the horns of the altar, and so strongly was he adhering to them that he could not be torn away from them.

III. If Christ is not set forth as objectively present through trust, He is not apprehended by it: The antecedent is true: Therefore also the consequent. The reason for the consequence is: because the intellect indeed apprehends Christ, while by knowing Him it sets Him forth as objectively present to itself: but trust rests in Christ present. But to rest in something does not signify to apprehend something. Resp. Distinguish between the apprehension of the intellect and of the will. The intellect apprehends Christ the mediator when it not only sets Him forth as objectively present by knowing Him, but also applies His universal merit to the converted sinner; the will, however, embraces Christ the mediator, already present, with singular trust, and firmly adheres to Him.

IV. Whatever apprehends Christ, that by the opinion of the Lutherans is faith: But love and joy apprehend Christ: Therefore love and joy, if the opinion of the Lutherans is true, is faith. The Cardinal proves the minor from AUGUSTINE, L. VIII. confess. c. 2. They all wanted to snatch Him into their heart, and they were snatching Him by loving and rejoicing. These were the hands of those snatching. Resp. 1) Trust embraces Christ as a present good, related by way of a cause to obtaining for us another arduous and difficult good, namely the grace of God and the remission of sins. Love, however, does not apprehend Christ under the relation causes for us to obtain grace and remission of sins, but absolutely as the highest good: Nor is love an act of concupiscence, by which we desire Christ as a good suitable for us, and in Him other goods for ourselves, which is required for fiducial apprehension; but it is an act of benevolence towards Christ, by which we wish well to Christ Himself, and are aroused by the fruit of His benefits to a sign of gratitude, and to the right uses of accepted grace. 2) Joy does not have Christ the Mediator as its object, as the cause of grace and remission of sins yet to be obtained: but as all other joy is concerning a good obtained and possessed; so joy concerning Christ has Christ the Mediator as its object, as the cause of grace and remission of sins actually obtained, now apprehended and possessed, and is a complacency, or a certain spiritual delight in Christ the Mediator, now fiducially apprehended, and in the remission of sins obtained through Him.

Latin:

Apprehensio, vel receptio meriti Christi, & in eo fundatae misericordiae Dei, est triplex: cognititia, quae fit per notitiam: approbativa, quae fit per assensum: appropriativa, vel adhaesiva, per fiduciam.

Prob. Apprehendimus Christum mediatorem, meritum ipsius universale cognoscendo, speciali assensu nobis applicando, & singulari fiducia illud amplectendo, eidemque firmiter inhaerendo.

Antithesis est BELLARMINI, qui lib. I. de iustific. c. XVI. negat, apprehensionem formaliter competere fidei, motus sequentibus ratiunculis:

1. Quidquid non pertinet ad primam mentis operationem, illi non competit apprehensio intellectualis: Fides non &c.: Ergo. Maior constat: quia apprehensio communiter refertur ad primam mentis operationem. Minor: quia fides est assensus, qui est in iudicio, quod rem non apprehendit, sed discernit, verane, an falsa sit? Resp. 1) Fides non assensus tantum, sed etiam notitia & fiducia est. 2) Omnis cognitio intellectus est apprehensio, licet non sit apprehensio simplex, sed diiudicativa, aut discursiva. Iudicio cognoscimus & apprehendimus unionem rei unius cum altera, vel eius ab altera diuisionem. 3) Apprehendere hic significat, ex parte intellectus, rem aliquam cognoscendo ad se transferre, vel cognoscere rem cum applicatione eius ad cognoscentem, quod fit per assensum specialem.

II. Confidere non est apprehendere, sed firmiter adhaerere: Ergo fiduciae non competit apprehensio, sed firma adhaesio. Resp. Apprehensio & firma adhaesio non sunt opposita, Ioab 1 Reg. II, 28. cornua altaris apprehendebat, & ita fortiter illis adhaerebat, vt ab illis avelli non posset..

III. Si Christus per fiduciam non sistitur obiective praesens, per eam non apprehenditur: Antecedens est verum: Ergo & consequens. Ratio consequentiae est; quia intellectus Christum quidem apprehendit, dum cognoscendo illum sibi obiective praesentem sistit: fiducia autem in Christo praesente acquiescit. Sed acquiescere in aliqu, non significat, aliquem apprehendere. Resp. Dist. inter apprehensionem intellectus & voluntatis. Intellectus apprehendit Christum mediatorem, cum non tantum cognoscendo eum obiective praesentem sistit, sed etiam eius universale meritum peccatori converso applicat; voluntas autem Christum mediatorem iam praesentem singulari fiducia amplectitur, & ipsi firmiter adhaeret.

IV. Quidquid apprehendit Christum, illud Lutheranorum sententia est fides: Atqui dilectio & gaudium apprehendit Christum: E. dilectio & gaudium, si vera est Lutheranorum sententia, est fides. Minorem probat Cardinalis ex AUGUSTINO L. VIII. confess. c. 2. Volebant eum omnes rapere intra in cor suum, & rapiebant amando & gaudendo. Hae rapientium manus erant. Resp. 1Fiducia amplectitur Christum, vt bonum praesens, per modum causae relatum ad impetrandum nobis aliud bonum arduum & difficile, gratiam Dei scilicet & remissionem peccatorum. Amor autem non apprehendit Christum sub relatione causae ad impetrandam nobis gratiam et remissionem peccatorum, sed absolute ut summum bonum: Neque amor est actus concupiscentiae, quo Christum ut bonum nobis conveniens, et in eo bona alia nobis velimus, quod ad fiducialem apprehensionem requiritur.equiritur; sed est actus benevolentiae erga Christum, quo ipsi Christo bene cupimus, ipsiusque beneficiorum fructu excitamur ad grati animi significationem, rectosque usus gratiae acceptae. 2) Gaudium non habet pro obiecto Christum mediatorem, ut causam impetrandae adhuc gratiae ac remissionis peccatorum: sed ut alias omne gaudium est de bono obtento, et possesso; ita gaudium de Christo habet pro obiecto Christum mediatorem, ut causam gratiae ac remissionis peccatorum actu impetrata, iam apprehensum et possessum, estque complacentia, sive delectatio quaedam spiritualis in Christo mediatore, iam fiducialiter apprehenso, et in impetranda per ipsum remissione peccatorum.


### Quaest. XIII. How many acts, degrees, or parts are there of justifying faith?

The acts, degrees, or parts of justifying faith, by which it apprehends the justifying object, are three: Knowledge, assent, and trust . Obs.

Theologians adhering to the Augsburg Confession differ in enumerating the acts of faith.

To some a bipartition is pleasing, among whom is D. Musaeus in his lectures on the Formula of Concord, p. m. 168. Justifying faith consists in a special assent, both in respect of the object and in respect of the subject, and this assent always has a conjoined trust of the will, so that it can rightly be called fiducial assent: This author refers the knowledge of Christ and the desire for grace among the presuppositions of justifying faith, insofar as it justifies. D. Fridem. Becmann follows him, in his institutes, p. 417. Nor does D. Baier seem to dissent from him, in his compendium, p. 642, by whom faith is called assensual trust.

To others, a quadripartition seems more convenient, among whom D. Chemnitz stands out, who thus delineates the degrees or acts of justifying faith: By what movements faith apprehends and receives the promise of the Gospel is understood in the true exercises of justifying faith. For there such movements and degrees are observed, as are described in Scripture. I. Knowledge or science, thought and meditation on God's promise concerning the benefits of Christ the Mediator, concerning God's mercy, concerning gratuitous reconciliation, etc. II. To this knowledge must be conjoined assent, not indeed merely general, but by which every believer firmly determines that the universal promise pertains privately to himself also, that he also is included and comprehended in that universal promise, Rom. IV. It is written not for Abraham's sake only, but for ours also, to whom it shall be imputed, if we believe. III. From that knowledge, or assent, the heart, or will, through the operation of the Holy Spirit, conceives a desire, so that, because it seriously feels itself burdened with sins and the wrath of God, it seeks, wills, asks, petitions that the benefit of justification, which is proposed in the promise of the Gospel, be given and communicated to it, and it apprehends that by faith, so as to receive it for itself. IV. When in this way, from the sentence of condemnation, which is denounced to us by the law on account of sins, faith flees to the throne of grace and to the propitiatory, which the Heavenly Father proposes in the blood of Christ, trust is added, Eph. III., which from the promise determines that God then gives, communicates, and applies to it the benefits of the promise: And that in this way it truly receives those things which the gratuitous promise of the Gospel offers, righteousness, salvation, and eternal life. From this trust follows παρρησία, which has access to God, Eph. III. peace of conscience, Rom. V. joy of the Spirit, Rom. XIX. so that the heart may rest in the promise of mercy, even in the cross, in temptation, and finally in death itself, retaining the hope of the glory of God, Rom. V. in exam. concil. Trid. fol. 163. & loc. theolog. part. II. fol. 270. D. GERHARD in disput. acad. P. I. p. 289. D. HOEPFNER, in tract. de actibus fidei iustif. p. 140. D. DANNHAU. in hodos. p. 1317. D. BREITHAVPT. in institut. theol. p. 338. support this. Most Theologians commemorate three acts, or parts, of faith: knowledge, assent, and trust; who under trust include the desire for grace. I bring forward as witnesses D. CALOVIVM, and D. QVENSTEDIVM. The former, tom. X. system. p. 303. says: Trust is to seek Christ, Is. LV, 6. to desire him greedily, Ps. LXXIII, 28. to pant for him, Ps. XLII, 2. 3. to desire his attraction. Cant. I, 3. John IV, 44. The latter, in system. Part. IV. p. 291. writes: Trust denotes desire and access to Christ, and the application and appropriation of his merit.

Ques. XIV. What is the knowledge of faith?

The knowledge of faith is a supernatural, evangelical, explicit knowledge, kindled by the Holy Spirit through illuminating grace, concerning all things to be believed, primarily concerning Christ, and his merit and the grace of God, concerning the remission of sins and eternal salvation, to be obtained through the mediator Christ.

Proof 1) The knowledge of faith is not natural (*); because Christ and the grace of God, founded in the merit of Christ, is not known from the light of nature: It is therefore kindled by the Holy Spirit through the grace of supernatural illumination. 2) This justifying knowledge is not legal; because there is no justification from the law, Gal. II, 11. but evangelical, the scope and nucleus of which is Christ. Whence it is called the faith of Christ, or that whose object is Christ, Gal. II, 16. But the grace of God is founded in the merit of Christ, remitting sins, or justifying and saving, Rom. III, 24. 3) That implicit knowledge, by which one says that he believes what the church believes, is not sufficient for obtaining the remission of sins and eternal salvation, is evident, because it is the duty of the faithful to search the scriptures, John V, 39. to meditate in the law of the Lord, Ps. I, 2. to follow the voice of Christ alone, the ἀρχιποίμέ- νος, John X, 4. to beware of false prophets, Matt. VII, 15. to test the spirits, 1 John IV, 10. to test all things, and to hold fast to what is good, 1 Thess. V, 21. Which duties of the faithful cannot be performed by implicit knowledge. Furthermore, although the knowledge of the reborn concerning the obtaining of the remission of sins and eternal salvation is explicit; it is nevertheless not perfect, 1 Cor. XIII, 9. nor equal in all, but in some it is fuller, in others it is thinner.

4) That the knowledge of Christ is to be kindled by the acts and parts of faith is evident: a) Because to believe is explained by to know, John 6:69. We have believed and known that you are the Christ, the Son of God. b) Because unbelief, which is opposed to faith, is called ignorance, Acts 17:23, 30. Therefore faith is knowledge. c) Whatever, on our part, we are justified and saved by, that is justifying and saving faith: But on our part we are justified and saved by the knowledge of Christ: Therefore the knowledge of Christ is justifying faith. The minor premise is proved from Isaiah 53:11. By his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many. Where the knowledge of the righteous servant is not active, by which he knows us, but passive, by which he is known: for it is knowledge concerning the most bitter sufferings of the Messiah and his bloody passion, explained in chapter 53 of Isaiah. To this prophetic oracle we add that saying of Christ, John 17:3. This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom you have sent. Whence saving faith is not inappropriately described by the knowledge of salvation, Luke 1:77.

There is an antithesis of the Papists, who deny that knowledge is an act or part of faith .

I. Whatever is above the grasp of reason, that is not known, but believed: But the mysteries of faith, etc., 1 Cor. 2:13. Therefore. The major premise is evident: because we only know those things which do not exceed the grasp of reason. I answer: 1) Whatever is above the grasp of reason, that is not known by natural knowledge; I concede this, but the same can be known by supernatural knowledge, kindled by the grace of illumination, from the Holy Spirit through the word written, read, and heard. 2) Distinguish between reason left to itself, and reason illuminated by the light of the divine word. The mysteries of faith exceed the grasp of reason left to itself; yet illuminated reason receives them, as an instrument and subject, although it is not the judge or norm of the articles of faith.

II. Whatever is a step toward understanding is not understanding itself: But faith is, etc. Therefore. The major premise is proved: because a prior disposition precedes a thing, it does not constitute it. The minor premise is proved from Isaiah 7:9. If you will not believe, you shall not understand. I answer: a) The Vulgate version renders the original text poorly. The source flows thus: If you will not believe; surely you shall not be established. b) There is no consequence: If you will not believe, you shall not understand.
