Therefore faith is a step toward understanding; just as it does not follow: If it is not a rational animal, it is not a man: Therefore a rational animal is a step toward man: If it does not have a principle of motion, it does not have a soul: Therefore the principle of motion is a step toward the soul. Trifles!

III. If the intellect is to be taken captive under the obedience of faith; faith is not knowledge: The antecedent is true: Therefore the consequent is also. The reason for the consequence is: because where the knowledge of truth shines in the intellect, there the intellect is not to be taken captive. The truth of the antecedent is clear from 2 Cor. 10:5.

Resp. The natural intellect is ferocious and rebellious and must be taken captive: The illuminated intellect submits itself with sweet and prompt obedience to the prescription of the divine word.

IV. Whatever falls to impious men and devils, that is not an act of justifying faith: But knowledge about Christ, etc.: Therefore. The major is proven: because by a justifying act converted men are justified. But the impious and devils are not converted, and therefore by their knowledge they are not justified. The minor is clear from James II, 19, and daily experience. Resp. Theoretical knowledge about Christ falls to the impious and evil spirits, not practical knowledge, which is joined with trust in Christ.

V. Paul distinguishes knowledge from faith, 1 Cor. XII, 8, 9; 1 Cor. XIII, 2. Therefore, knowledge is not faith. Resp. In both cited places, miraculous faith is understood, which is distinct from justifying γνῶσις (knowledge), not in species, but certainly in degree.

Latin:

Actus, gradus, aut partes fidei iustificae, quibus haec obiectum iustificum apprehendit, sunt tres: Notitia, assensus, et fiducia .

Obs. Theologi Augustanae confessioni addicti in recensendis actibus fidei differunt.

Quibusdam placet bipartitio, quos inter est D. Musaeus in praelect. in Formul. Concord. p. m. 168. Fides iustificans consistit in assensu speciali, tum ratione obiecti, tum ratione subiecti, et hic assensus semper coniunctam habet fiduciam voluntatis, ut recte dici possit assensus fiducialis: Qui auctor notitiam Christi et desiderium gratiae refert inter praesupposita fidei iustificantis, quatenus iustificat. Hunc sequitur D. Fridem. Becmann, in institut. p. 417. Neque ab hoc dissentire videtur D. Baier. in compend. p. 642. a quo fides dicitur fiducia assensualis.

Aliis commodior videtur quadripartitio, quos inter eminet D. Chemnitius, qui gradus, vel actus fidei iustificantis ita delineat: Quibus motibus fides apprehendat et accipiat promissionem evangelii, in veris fidei iustificantis exercitiis intelligitur. Ibi enim animadvertuntur tales motus et gradus, sicut in scriptura describuntur. I. Notitia seu scientia, cogitatio et meditatio promissionis Dei de beneficiis Christi mediatoris, de misericordia Dei, de gratuita reconciliatione etc. II. Huic notitiae oportet coniunctam esse assensionem, non quidem generalem tantum, sed qua firma persuasione quisquis credens statuat, universalem promissionem privatim ad se quoque pertinere, se quoque includi et comprehendi in universali illa promissione, Rom. IV. Scriptum est non propter Abrahamum tantum, sed propter nos, quibus imputabitur credentibus. III. Ex illa notitia, seu assensione, cor, seu voluntas, per operationem Spiritus S. concipit desiderium, ut, quia serio sentit, se onera um peccatis et ira Dei, expetat, velit, quaerat, petat sibi donari et communicari beneficium iustificationis, quod in promissione evangelii proponitur, et illud fide apprehendit, ut ad se recipiat. IV. Quando hoc modo a sententia damnationis, quae per legem propter peccata nobis denuntiatur, fides confugit ad thronum gratiae et ad propitiatorium, quod Pater caelestis proponit in sanguine Christi, accedit fiducia, Eph. III. quae ex promissione statuit, Deum tunc sibi donare, communicare et applicare beneficia promissionis: Et se hoc modo vere accipere ea, quae gratuita evangelii promissio offert, iustitiam, salutem et vitam aeternam. Ex hac fiducia sequitur παρρησία, quae habet accessum ad quæ gratuita euangelii promissio offert, iustitiam, salutem & vitam æternam. Ex hac fiducia sequitur παρρησία, quæ habet accessum ad Deum, Eph. III. pax conscientiæ, Rom. V. gaudium Spiritus, Rom. XIX. ut cor acquiescat in promissione misericordiæ, etiam in cruce, in tentatione, ipsa denique morte, retinens spem gloriæ Dei, Rom. V. in exam. concil. Trid. fol. 163. & loc. theolog. part. II. fol. 270. Suffragantur D. GERHARD. in disput. acad. P. I. p. 289. D. HOEPFNER, in tract. de actibus fidei iustif. p. 140. D. DANNHAU. in hodos. p. 1317. D. BREITHAVPT. in institut. theol. p. 338. Plerique Theologi tres commemorant fidei actus, vel partes, notitiam, assensum & fiduciam; qui sub fiducia desiderium gratiæ complectuntur. Testes adduco D. CALOVIVM, & D. QVENSTEDIVM. Ille tom. X. system. p. 303. inquit: Fiducia est Christum quærere, Es. LV, 6. auide appetere, Ps. LXXIII, 28. anhelare ipsum, Ps. XLII, 2. 3. attractionem eius desiderare. Cant. I, 3. Io. IV, 44. Hic in system. Part. IV. p. 291. scribit: Fiducia notat desiderium & accessum ad Christum, eiusque meriti applicationem & appropriationem.

Quæst. XIV. Quid est notitia fidei?

Notitia fidei est notitia supernaturalis, euangelica, explicita, a Spiritu S. per gratiam illuminantem accensa, de omnibus credendis, in primis de Christo, eiusque merito & gratia Dei, de remissione peccatorum & salute æterna, per mediatorem Christum obtinenda.

Prob. 1) Notitia fidei non est naturalis (*); quia Christus & gratia Dei, in merito Christi fundata, ex lumine naturæ non innotescit: Accensa itaque est a Spiritu S. per supernaturalis illuminationis gratiam. 2) Notitia hæc iustificans non est legalis; quia ex lege nulla est iustificatio, Gal. II, 11. sed euangelica, cuius scopus, & nucleus est Christus. Vnde vocatur fides Christi, seu cuius obiectum est Christus, Gal. II, 16. In merito Christi autem fundatur gratia Dei, peccata remittens, siue iustificans & saluans, Rom. III, 24. 3) Quod non sufficiat notitia implicita, qua quis dicit, se credere id, quod ecclesia credit, ad impetrandam remissionem peccatorum & æternam salutem, patet, quia fidelium est, scrutari scripturas, Io. V, 39. meditari in lege Domini, Ps. I, 2. solius Christi ἀρχιποίμένος vocem sequi, Io. X, 4. cauere sibi a pseudoprophetis, Matth. VII, 15. probare spiritus, 1 Io. IV, 10. omnia probare, &, quod bonum est, tenere, 1 Thess. V, 21. Quæ officia fidelium notitia implicita præstari nequeunt. Ceterum, quamuis notitia renatorum de impetranda remissione peccatorum æternaque salute sit explicita; non tamen est perfecta, 1 Cor. XIII, 9. neque in omnibus æqualis, sed in quibusdam plenior, in quibusdam tẹnuior est.

4) Notitiam Christi accendendam esse actibus, partibusque fidei, constat: a) Quia credere per cognoscere exponitur, Io. VI, 69. Nos credimus & cognouimus, quod tu sis Christus, Filius Dei. b) Quia incredulitas, fidei opposita, vocatur ignorantia, Act. XVII, 23. 30. Ergo fides est notitia. c) Quocunque, ex parte nostri, iustificamur & saluamur, id est fides iustifica & saluifica: Atqui ex parte nostri iustificamur & saluamur cognitione Christi: Ergo cognitio Christi est fides iustifica. Minor probatur ex Es. LIII, 11. Scientia sui iustificabit seruus meus multos. Vbi scientia iusti serui non est actiua, qua ille noscit, sed passiua, qua ille cognoscitur: est enim notitia de acerbissimis Messiae passionibus atque cruenta passione, c. LIII. Es. expositis. Huic oraculo prophetico addimus illud effatum Christi, Io. XVII, 3. Haec est vita aeterna, ut cognoscant te, solum illum verum Deum, &, quem misisti, Iesum Christum. Vnde non incongrue fides saluifica describitur per cognitionem salutis, Luc. I, 77.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, negantium, notitiam esse actum, aut partem fidei . Qui obiiciunt:

I. Quidquid est supra captum rationis, illud non cognoscitur, sed creditur: Atqui mysteria fidei &c. 1 Cor. II, 13. E. Maior constat: quia illa tantum cognoscimus, quae captum rationis non excedunt. Resp. 1) Quidquid est supra captum rationis, illud non cognoscitur cognitione naturali; concedo, at idem cognosci potest cognitione supernaturali, per gratiam illuminationis, a Spiritu S. per verbum scriptum, lectum & auditum, accensa. 2) Dist. inter rationem sibi relictam, & lumine verbi diuini illustratam. Excedunt mysteria fidei captum rationis sibi relictae; ratio tamen illustrata illa recipit, vt instrumentum & subiectum, quamuis non sit iudex aut norma articulorum fidei.

II. Quidquid est gradus ad intelligentiam, non est ipsa intelligentia: Atqui fides est &c. E. Maior probatur: quia praeuia dispositio rem antecedit, non constituit. Minor probatur ex Es. VII, 9. Si non credideritis, non intelligetis. Resp. a) Versio vulgata textum originalem male reddit. Fons ita fluit: Si non credideritis; certe non stabiles eritis. b) Nulla est consequentia: Si non credideritis, non intelligetis. Ergo fides est gradus ad intelligentiam; sicut non sequitur: Si non est animal rationale, non est homo: E. animal rationale est gradus ad hominem: Si non habet principium motus, non habet animam: E. principium modus est gradus ad animam. Nugae!

III. Si intellectus captiuandus est sub obsequium fidei; fides non est notitia: Antecedens est verum: E. & consequens. Consequentiae ratio est: quia, vbi notitia veritatis fulget in intellectu, ibi intellectus non est captiuandus. Antecedentis veritas liquet ex 2 Cor. X, 5.

Resp. Intellectus naturalis ferociens & rebellis est captiuandus: Intellectus illuminatus obsequio suaui & promto se submittit praescripto verbi diuini.

IV. Quidquid cadit in homines impios & diabolos, illud non est actus fidei iustificantis: Atqui notitia de Christo &c: E. Maior probatur: quia actu iustifico homines conuersi iustificantur. Sed impii & diaboli non sunt conuersi, adeoque sua notitia non iustificantur. Minor liquet ex Iac. II, 19. & quotidiana experientia. Resp. Notitia theoretica de Christo cadit in impios & cacodaemones, non practica, cum fiducia in Christum coniuncta.

V. Paullus scientiam a fide distinguit, 1 Cor. XII, 8. 9. 1 Cor. XIII, 2. E. scientia non est fides. Resp. Vtroque loco citato intelligitur fides miraculosa, quae a γνῶσις iustifica non specie, certe gradu distincta est.


### Q. XV. What is the assent of faith?

The assent of faith is a judgment of the intellect approving, by which those things which the Holy Scripture hands down concerning Christ the mediator, and the divine grace restored through him, as well as the obtaining of the remission of sins and eternal salvation, are judged to be true. The assent of faith is distinguished into general and special. By general assent, the universal promises concerning the grace of God and the merit of Christ are judged to be true. By special assent, the converted and regenerate sinner determines that those general promises pertain to himself individually.

Prob. From 1 Tim. I, 15. The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost. But for this reason I received mercy, that in me as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life. In this Pauline utterance, the general and special assent of faith are joined. By general assent, this sentence is to be approved, that Jesus Christ came into the world to save all sinners. From this universal proposition, the Apostle descends to himself individually, and believes that, on account of Christ, he has obtained the mercy of God unto salvation. From which it is clear that the merit of Christ is universal, and the promises concerning the gratuitous remission of sins to be obtained on account of Christ are indeterminate. However, when they ought to profit this or that man in act, it is necessary that the universal merit of Christ and the indeterminate promises be applied and determined to this or that penitent sinner through special assent.

Obj. Special assent is spoken of in a twofold respect. 1) With respect to the object, which are the merit of Christ and the divine promises concerning the gratuitous remission of sins on account of Christ. These promises, which include the merit of Christ, are the proper object of justifying faith. 2) By reason of the subject; and thus the special assent of faith is called that by which the converted sinner believes that the merit of Christ also pertains to himself individually, and that he has God in heaven propitious to him, and the remission of sins on account of Christ.

Latin:

Assensus fidei

Assensus fidei est iudicium intellectus approbans, quo ea, quae de Christo mediatore, & per eum reparata gratia diuina, nec non impetranda remissione peccatorum & aeterna salute sacra scriptura tradit, vera esse iudicantur. Distinguitur assensus fidei in generalem, & specialem. Assensu generali promissiones vniuersales de gratia Dei & merito Christi verae esse iudicantur. Assensu speciali statuit peccator conuersus & renatus, illas promissiones generales ad se in individuo pertinere.

Prob. Ex 1 Tim. I, 15. Fidelis est sermo, & omni acceptione dignus, quod Christus Iesus venerit in mundum, ut peccatores saluaret, quorum primus sum ego. Sed propterea misericordiam consecutus sum, ut in me primo demonstraret Iesus Christus omnem longanimitatem ad exemplar eorum, qui credituri erant in ipsum in vitam aeternam. In hoc effato Paullino coniungitur assensus fidei generalis & specialis. Assensu generali comprobanda est haec sententia, quod Iesus Christus venerit in mundum, ut omnes peccatores saluaret. Ab hac propositione vniuersali descendit Apostolus ad se in individuo, & credit, propter Christum se ad salutem consecutum esse misericordiam Dei. Ex quo patet, meritum Christi esse vniuersale, & promissiones indeterminatas de gratuita remissione peccatorum propter Christum impetranda. Quando autem huic aut illi homini actu prodesse debent, necesse est, ut meritum Christi vniuersale & promissiones indeterminatae per assensum specialem, applicentur ac determinentur ad hunc illumue peccatorem poenitentem.

Obs. Assensus specialis duplici dicitur respectu. 1) Respectu obiecti, quod sunt meritum Christi, & promissiones diuinae de gratuita peccatorum remissione propter Christum. Hae promissiones, quae meritum Christi includunt, sunt proprium fidei iustificantis obiectum. 2) Ratione subiecti; atque sic specialis fidei assensus dicitur, quo peccator conuersus credit, Christi meritum etiam ad se pertinere in individuo, & se habere Deum in coelis sibi propitium, & remissionem peccatorum propter Christum. sic specialis fidei assensus dicitur, quo peccator conuersus credit, Christi meritum etiam ad se pertinere in indiuiduo, & se habere Deum in cœlis sibi propitium, & remissionem peccatorum propter Christum. Quæft. XVI. Quid est fiducia defixa in Christo? Fiducia est actus voluntatis, quo peccator, conuersus & renatus, auide expetit & quærit misericordiam Dei, partam merito Christi, & hunc, tum vt præfens


### Q. XVI. What is trust fixed in Christ?

Fiducia (Trust) is an act of the will, by which the converted and regenerate sinner greedily seeks and searches for the mercy of God, obtained by the merit of Christ, and this [mercy], both as a present its present good, as well as the cause of the remission of sins and eternal salvation, it embraces, leans upon Him against all terrors, and securely rests and acquiesces in the same.

Obs. I. We have described trust, fixed upon Christ, in a broader sense, in which it includes the desire for divine grace; since trust is an act of desire, by which we wish for and seek after a good suitable to us, and other goods in it. However, express mention of the desire for grace ought to be made in enumerating the acts of faith: a) On account of the testimony of Christ, by which righteousness and blessedness are attributed to this evangelical desire (we dealt with legal desire in the preceding chapter), Matt. V, 6: "Blessed are they who hunger and thirst for righteousness; for they shall be satisfied." For here the hunger and thirst for righteousness is the desire for the imputative righteousness of Christ; since by it sinners, who are needy and greedy for spiritual food and drink, are fully satisfied. b) On account of hypocrites, who maintain that God is propitious to them; whose most vain dream is validly refuted by the fact that they truly desire neither the grace of God, nor the remission of sins, nor eternal life; otherwise, they would remove the obstacles to salvation—the opinion of non-neediness and the purpose of continuing in sins—and would duly use the means of salvation. c) On account of the tempted, whom this hunger and thirst urges the more, the less trust is perceived in them. Those infirm brothers not rarely sigh: "Would that we had the faculty of believing! Give us faith, O God! Relieve the infirmity of believing!" This desire of faith is true faith, even if it does not exert itself in firm trust. D. Chemnitius rightly says: "When the true object is in the Word, and the aforementioned movements follow, or at least the endeavor and desire, then it is true faith," in loc. theol. part. II. de iustific. fol. 271. It can, however, be referred to trust, because this also is indeed an act of desire, as we said above. Obs.

II. What trust is will be clear to us by considering generally both the object and the form of trust. Trust has for its object a) a present good. For we are not said to trust in future things, just as we do not hope for them. The impious trust in riches, which they possess, or in men and their power; but the pious trust in the present God, and in His goodness, truthfulness, and power. By a present good, however, is understood that which is present, or is apprehended as present, either really and physically, or only morally, by reason of promise, merit, and value. Thus, the pious in the O.T. rightly trusted in the coming Messiah, and in the satisfaction for sins to be performed by Him at some time; and we trust in the same satisfaction performed long ago through His passion and death. For Christ, and His passion and death, extend themselves morally, and by reason of their merit, to all past ages, as well as present and future, and were at all times the cause for believers of obtaining the remission of sins and salvation. For Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today, and forever, Heb. XIII, 8. b) Our good, or that which in some way pertains to us. For because we trust in those goods which are an aid to us for obtaining some effect, it is necessary that they be ours, or at least, on account of friendship or a covenant which intervenes between us and Him to whom they belong, that they in some way pertain to us, and in this regard be esteemed as our own. Whence we rightly trust in the merit and satisfaction of Christ, as in some good of our own; because it was performed for us and in our place. From which also Theologians call the fiducial apprehension "appropriative." c) A related good, by way of a cause for obtaining another good, and that an arduous and difficult one, or that which is known as the cause of obtaining another good; e.g., an Emperor places trust in an army, insofar as it is the cause of obtaining victory...: A miser trusts in money, insofar as it is conceived by him as the cause of obtaining help in harsh times: A student trusts in learning, as the cause of obtaining promotion. Thus, the regenerate fix their trust in Christ the mediator, as the cause of obtaining grace, the remission of sins, and eternal salvation before God. The form of trust consists in the embrace, adherence, and acquiescence of the will. For trust eagerly embraces and holds a present good, which is known as the cause of obtaining another, adheres to it, and leans upon it against all terrors; and thus it securely rests and acquiesces in it. E.g., A miser embraces his money with singular trust, as the cause of providing aid, leans upon it against harsh circumstances, and securely acquiesces in it. Trust is therefore formally the acquiescence of the will in some present good, which is referred by way of cause to obtaining another good, and consequently includes a certain security about obtaining a future good, opposed to fear, since it is a rest from the disturbance of fear. Confer D. MVSAEI disput. III. de conuers. p. 172. In which sense MELANCHTHON in loc. theol. describes trust, that it is the will acquiescing in the promise of mercy, granted on account of the mediator. Trust adds to assent the rest of the will acquiescing in the promise, says D. DANNHAVER in hodof. p. 1322, who delineates justifying faith thus: Faith, WHICH justifies, is knowledge, assent, trust & πληροφορία: Faith, BY WHICH, or INSOFAR AS it justifies, is a bare apprehension of the benefits of the Messiah, passive, admitting the motions of the Holy Spirit, resting, quieting in the merits of Christ, in hodof. p. 1305. And KOENIG. in theol. posit. §. 899. While we call justifying trust an apprehension, we understand an apprehension not theoretical, barely assenting, when someone in his intellect holds it as indubitable that Christ died not only for all, but also for him individually, (for thus even the impious themselves, who do not desire that salvation should come to them on account of Christ's merit, can infer): But practical, which involves the resting of the whole heart and will in the merit of Christ.

Obs. III. The distinction between trust, hope, and love is manifest. 1) Trust is concerned with a present good; hope with a future good. The former acquiesces in our good, or that which pertains to us; the latter tends toward a future good, so that it may become ours. Trust is about a present good, related by way of cause to obtaining another good: hope is simply about obtaining a good, and is born from trust. Whence the latter is prior, the former posterior: The former has the nature of a cause, the latter of an effect. 2) Love embraces Christ absolutely, as a good: trust embraces Christ, with a relation to another good, known as a cause. The former [relates] to an act of benevolence, by which we wish all best things for Christ (*): the latter to an act of concupiscence, by which we desire Christ, as a good suitable to us, and in Him other goods for ourselves. (**).

…It is proven that faith in Christ formally and intrinsically includes trust leaning upon the merit of Christ: 1) Because faith in Christ is not only an act of the intellect, or knowledge and assent but also an act of the will. This is confirmed a) by the very phrase: TO BELIEVE IN CHRIST; which, by the force of the preposition IN, constructed with the accusative case, insinuates a certain act of the believer, tending into Christ, by which the believing man is, as it were, carried out of himself into Christ, or adheres to Him: b) by the custom of speaking, which AUGUSTINE rightly urges, tract. XXIX. on John. For demons are said to believe Christ, as also to believe [that there is] Christ; yet they are not said to believe in Christ. And we are said to believe Paul; to believe Peter; we also believe that Paul and Peter exist; yet we are not said to believe in Paul and Peter. Therefore, to believe in someone, besides the act of believing, or assenting, imports some act concerning the believed object, which neither falls upon demons, nor has Peter, Paul, or any creature as its object: Namely, an act by which the believer tends into the object, known and believed under a certain and peculiar aspect, which falls upon no creature. Which certainly must be an act of the will. For it is of the will to be carried out of itself into an object; just as, on the contrary, it is of the intellect to know an object within itself through species impressed upon it. c) The condition of the object proves the same. For Christ is not proposed in the Scriptures to the human race, fallen into sins, to be known for the sake of speculation, but as mediator and cause of the remission of sins and eternal life. See 1 Tim. II, 5. John I, 29. ch. III, 16. These goods of ours, redundant from Christ into us, are proposed in the Scriptures to be known and believed, not so that the intellect may stop in the knowledge and assent of them, but so that, once known and believed, they may be represented and exhibited to the will, so that the will may be carried into them, may rest in them, and by the confidence of them the sinner may raise and console himself against the wrath of God and the terrors of conscience. We conclude: Every act of the will, concerning a present good, related by way of cause to the obtaining of another arduous and difficult good, is formally trust: But that act, which faith in Christ includes on the part of the will, is an act of the will concerning a present good, related by way of cause to the obtaining of other arduous and difficult goods: Therefore.

Latin:

Fiducia

Fiducia est actus voluntatis, quo peccator, conuersus & renatus, auide expetit & quaerit misericordiam Dei, partam merito Christi, & hunc, tum vt præsens suum bonum, tum vt caussam remissionis peccatorum, æternæque salutis amplectitur, aduersus omnes terrores ipsi innititur, atque in eodem secure recumbit & acquiescit.

Obs. I. Fiduciam in Christo defixam, sensu latiori, quo desiderium gratiæ diuinæ includit, descripsimus; quoniam fiducia est actus concupiscentiæ, quo bonum nobis conueniens, & in eo bona alia nobis volumus & expetimus. Expressa autem mentio desiderii gratiæ in recensendis actibus fidei fieri debet: a) ob testimonium Christi, quo desiderio huic euangelico (de desiderio legali capite præcedenti egimus) tribuitur iustitia & beatitudo, Matth. V, 6. Beati, qui esuriunt & sitiunt iustitiam; hi enim ipsi saturabuntur. Vbi fames & sitis iustitiæ est desiderium iustitiæ Christi imputativæ; quippe qua plene satiantur peccatores, spiritualis cibi potusque indigi & auidi. b) Propter hypocritas, statuentes, Deum sibi esse propitium; quorum vanissimum somnium valide refutatur eo, quod nec gratiam Dei, nec remissionem peccatorum, nec vitam æternam vere desiderant; Ceteroqui obstacula salutis opinionem non-indigentiæ & propositum pergendi in peccatis remouerent, mediisque salutis rite vterentur. c) Propter tentatos, quos vrget fames sitisque hoc maior, quo minor in ipsis deprehenditur fiducia. Infirmi illi fratres haud raro suspirant: Vtinam nobis esset credendi facultas! Da Deus fidem! Subleua infirmitatem credendi! Quod desiderium fidei est vera fides, licet firma fiducia se non exserat. Recte inquit D. Chemnitius: Quando obiectum verum est in verbo, & sequuntur motus prædicti, vel saltem conatus & desiderium, tunc vera fides est, in loc. theol. part. II. de iustific. fol. 271. Potest tamen ad fiduciam referri, quia & hæc actus quidem concupiscentiæ est, prout supra diximus.

Obs. II. Quid sit fiducia, patebit nobis generatim considerando tum obiectum, tum formam fiduciæ. Fiducia pro obiecto habet a) bonum præsens. Non enim vt futura sperare, ita in futuris confidere dicimur. Impii confidunt in diuitiis; quas possident, vel in hominibus, illorumque potentia: pii vero confidunt in præsente Deo, eiusque bonitate, veracitate, potentia. Per bonum præsens autem intelligitur, quod vel realiter & physice, vel tantum moraliter, ratione promissionis, meriti & valoris, præsens est, aut vt præsens apprehenditur. Ita pii in V. T. recte confidebant in venturo Messia, & in satisfactione pro peccatis, ab ipso aliquando præstanda; & nos confidimus in eadem satisfactione olim per eius passionem & mortem præstita. Christus enim, eiusque passio & mors, extendit sese moraliter, & ratione sui meriti, ad omnia retro sæcula, præsentia item & futura, fuitque omni tempore credentibus remissionis peccatorum & salutis obtinendæ caussa. Est enim Iesus Christus heri & hodie, idem & in sæcula, Hebr. XIII, 8. b) Bonum nostrum, aut quod ad nos quodammodo pertinet. Nam quia confidimus in iis bonis, quæ ad obtinendum aliquem effectum nobis adiumento sunt, necesse est, vt illa sint nostra, vel saltim ob amicitiam, aut pactum, quod cum eo, cuius sunt, nobis intercedit, ad nos quodammodo pertineant, & hoc intuitu tanquam nostra æstimentur. Vnde in Christi merito & satisfactione recte confidimus, tanquam in nostro quodam bono; quia pro nobis & nostro loco præstita est. Ex quo etiam Theologi apprehensionem fiducialem vocant appropriatiuam. c) Bonum relatum, per modum caussæ ad obtinendum aliud bonum, idque arduum & difficile, siue quod cognoscitur vt caussa alterius boni impetrandi, v. gr. Imperator fiduciam collocat in exercitu, quatenus est caussa impetrandæ victoriæ...: Confidit auarus pecunia, in quantum concipitur ab ipso, vt caussa obtinendi auxilii temporibus asperis: Confidit studiosus eruditione, tanquam caussa consequendæ promotionis. Ita renati fiduciam defigunt in Christo mediatore, tamquam caussa impetrandæ apud Deum gratiæ, remissionis peccatorum, æternæque salutis. Forma fiduciæ consistit in amplexu, adhæsione & acquiescentia voluntatis. Fiducia enim bonum præsens, quod est cognitum vt caussa alterius obtinendi, cupide amplectitur & tenet, eidem adhæret, & aduersus omnes terrores innititur; atque adeo in eodem secure recumbit & acquiescit. V. gr. Auarus singulari fiducia suam amplectitur pecuniam, vt caussam præstandi auxilii, eidem aduersus asperos casus innititur, & in ipsa secure acquiescit. Est itaque fiducia formaliter, acquiescentia voluntatis in bono aliquo præsente, quod per modum caussæ refertur ad aliud bonum obtinendum, & includit proinde securitatem quandam de assequendo bono futuro, formidini oppositam, quippe quæ est quies a perturbatione timoris. Confer. D. MVSAEI disput. III. de conuers. p. 172. Quo sensu MELANCHTHON in loc. theol. describit fiduciam, quod ea voluntas acquiescat in promissione misericordiæ, propter mediatorem donatæ. Fiducia assensui addit quietem voluntatis acquiescentis in promisso, ait D. DANN HAVER. in hodof. p. 1322. qui fidem iustificantem sic delineat: Fides, QVAE iustificat, est notitia, assensus, fiducia & πληροφορία: Fides, QVA, vel QVATENVS iustificat, est nuda apprehensio beneficiorum Messiæ passiua, admissua motuum Spiritus Sancti, recubitoria, requietoria in meritis Christi, in hodof. p. 1305. Et KOENIG. in theol. posit. §. 899. Dum apprehensionem dicimus fiduciam iustificantem, intelligimus apprehensionem non theoreticam, nude assensiuam, cum quis in intellectu suo pro indubitato habet, Christum non tantum pro omnibus, sed etiam pro se in indiuiduo esse mortuum, (ita enim vel ipsi impii, qui non desiderant, vt propter Christi meritum sibi obtingat salus, inferre possunt): Sed practicam, quæ totius cordis & voluntatis in merito Christi recumbentiam inuoluit.

Obs. III. Manifestum est discrimen inter fiduciam, spem, & dilectionem. 1) Fiducia versatur circa bonum præsens; spes circa bonum futurum. Illa acquiescit in bono nostro, aut ad nos pertinente; hæc tendit ad bonum futurum, vt nostrum fiat. Fiducia est de bono præsente, per modum caussæ relato ad aliud bonum obtinendum: spes, simpliciter est de bono obtinendo, & nascitur ex fiducia. Vnde hæc prior, illa posterior est: Illa caussa, hæc effectus rationem habet. 2) Dilectio amplectitur Christum absolute, vt bonum: fiducia amplectitur Christum, cum relatione ad aliud bonum, tanquam caussam, cognitum. Illa ad actum beneuolentiæ, quo Christo optima quæque volumus (*): hæc ad actum concupiscentiæ, quo Christum, vt bonum nobis conueniens, & in eo alia bona nobis cupimus. (**).

Probatur, fidem in Christum formaliter & intrinsece includere fiduciam merito Christi innixam: 1) Quia fides in Christum non est tantum actus intellectus, siue notitia & assensus; fus; sed etiam actus voluntatis. Id quod confirmatur a) ex ipsa phrasi: CREDERE IN CHRISTVM; quæ vi præpositionis, IN, cum casu quarto constructæ, insinuat actum quendam credentis, in Christum tendentem, quo homo credens quasi extra se in Christum feratur, aut ipsi adhæreat: b) ex consuetudine loquendi, quam recte urget AVGVSTINVS, tract. XXIX. in Ioannem. Nam dæmones dicuntur credere Christo, vt & Christum; nec tamen credere dicuntur in Christum. Et nos credere dicimur Paullo; credere Petro; credimus etiam Paullum & Petrum esse; nec tamen in Paullum & Petrum credere dicimur. Ergo credere in aliquem, præter actum credendi, siue assentiendi, importat actum aliquem circa obiectum creditum, qui nec in dæmones cadit, nec Petrum, Paullum, aut vllam creaturam habeat pro obiecto: Neimpe actum, quo credens in obiectum, sub certa quadam & peculiari ratione, quæ in nullam cadat creaturam, cognitum & creditum tendit. Quem certe voluntatis actum esse oportet. Voluntatis enim est, extra se ferri in obiectum; sicut contra intellectus est, obiectum per species sibi impressas in se cognoscere. c) Idem euincit obiecti conditio. Christus enim non proponitur in scripturis prolapso in peccata mortalium generi cognoscendus speculationis caussa, sed tanquam mediator & caussa remissionis peccatorum & vitæ æternæ. Vid. 1 Tim. II, 5. Io. I, 29. c. III, 16. Quæ bona nostra, ex Christo in nos redundantia, proponuntur in scripturis cognoscenda & credenda, non vt in illorum cognitione & assensu intellectus sistat, sed vt cognita & credita voluntati repræsententur & exhibeantur, vt voluntas in illa feratur, in iis recumbat, & illorum fiducia peccator aduersus iram Dei & conscientiæ pauores sese eriget ac consoletur. Colligimus: Omnes actus voluntatis, circa bonum præsens, ad obtinendum aliud bonum arduum & difficile, per modum caussæ relatum, est formaliter fiducia: Atqui actus ille, quem ex parte voluntatis fides in Christum includit, est actus voluntatis circa bonum præsens, ad obtinenda alia bona ardua & difficilia, per modum caussæ relatum: Ergo.


### Q. XVI. What is trust fixed in Christ?: 2) From the names attributed to faith in the Holy Scripture

2) From the names attributed to faith in the Holy Scripture.

For it is described by Paul a) by ὑπόστασιν, Heb. XI, 1. which word signifies trust, confidence, or (as ERASMUS SCHMIDIUS translates) an undaunted consistency of mind, yielding to no dangers. It is said from ὑφίστασθαι, which signifies to stand, to subsist, to consist; because faith does not flee from the sight of God, does not fall, but stands unmoved, consists, and acquiesces in divine promises, like a thing subsisting by itself. Both the name ὑπόστασις and ὑφίστασθαι is military. See CRAUSERUS, Phosph. p. 310. b) By πληροφορίαν, Rom. IV, 21. Col. II, 2. Heb. VI, 11. Πληροφορία is said ἀπὸ τῆς πλήγεος, full, and φέρεσθαι, to be carried, by which through it the mind of the believer is fully carried into the object, just as a ship is carried into port with full sails. But the mind is then fully carried into the object, when it is carried into it according to every aspect under which it is presented to it; the intellect indeed, insofar as it is presented under the aspect of truth; but the will, insofar as it is presented under the aspect of good and desirable. Therefore, πληροφορία is not of the intellect alone, but most especially of the will, and of trust, which is carried into the good object with full impetus, represented by the intellect, illuminated by divine revelation. c) By πεποίθησιν, Rom. VIII, 38. 2 Tim. I, 12. Πεποίθησις derives its origin from the verb πείθω, I persuade. Therefore, πεποίθησις is a persuasion of the mind and will. The former is a certain assent; the latter is unmoved trust. Thus Paul says: Πέποιθα δὲ ἐν κυρίῳ, but I trust in the Lord, Phil. II, 24. d) by παρρησίαν, Heb. IV, 16. which word taken strictly denotes liberty of speech, sometimes taken more broadly it denotes trust of heart, with alacrity and firmness of believing connoted

3) From a collation of passages of the Old and New Testaments. What is attributed to those who trust and to trust in the O.T., that is attributed to those who believe and to faith in the N.T. What is said in Ps. II, 12: Blessed are they who trust in him, that is said in Mark XVI, 16: he who believes will be saved. 4) From exegetical declaration.

For the Holy Spirit explains faith through trust in 1 John V, 13: These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God: And this is the trust that we have toward him. 5) From the object; which Paul explains thus, Rom.

III, 25. God set forth Christ as ἱλαστήριον, a propitiatory, through faith in his blood, i.e., a mediator and appeaser of divine wrath, by reason of his satisfaction and merit, rendered by the shedding of his blood for our sins, to be apprehended by faith. From which it is concluded: Whoever has as the object of an act of will Christ, as the meritorious cause of appeasing divine wrath, that is formally and intrinsically trust; But that act, which faith in the blood of Christ includes on the part of the will, is an act of the will, which has as its object Christ, as the meritorious cause of appeasing divine wrath: Therefore. 6) From the opposite.

Fear of the heart is opposed to faith: Therefore faith is trust. The reason for the consequence is; because trust struggles against fear. The antecedent is proved from Luke VIII, 50: Do not fear, only believe. 7) From the justification of the ungodly man.

Whoever is an ungodly man justified by faith, he is justified, with trust placed in the satisfaction of the mediator: But the penitent ungodly man &c. Rom. IV, 5. Therefore. The major is of immovable truth: because God, the most just and most severe avenger of crimes, cannot justify the ungodly without rendered satisfaction (one's own, or vicarious), Prov. XVII, 15. But the ungodly man himself is not equal to satisfying: Therefore it is necessary that he fix his trust in the vicarious satisfaction of Christ, who died for the ungodly, Rom. V, 6. 8) From the effects of faith.

Whoever by their faith resist the devil, overcome the world, obtain peace, pray with salutary fruit, their faith is trust: But converted and reborn sinners &c. The major is evident: because those effects proceed from trust. For strong men by trust in their strength and arms resist enemies, and extort from them victory and peace. A son by trust in paternal benevolence implores the father's help. The minor is clear from the testimonies of scripture, 1 Pet. V, 9: Resist the devil, steadfast in faith. 1 John V, 4: This is the victory that has overcome the world, our faith. Rom. V, 1: Having been justified by faith we have peace toward God. James I, 6: Let him ask in faith, doubting nothing! The antithesis is that of the Papists, who deny that justifying faith is trust.

Latin:

2) A nominibus, fidei in S. scriptura tributis.

Describitur enim a Paullo a) per ὑπόστασιν, Hebr. XI, 1. quæ vox significat fiduciam, confidentiam, vel (vt ERASM. SCHMIDIVS vertit) imperterritam animi consistentiam, nullis periculis cedentem. Dicitur ab ὑφίστασθαι, quod significat stare, subsistere, consistere; quia fides non fugit a conspectu Dei, non cadit, sed immota in promissis diuinis stat, consistit, & acquiescit instar rei, per se subsistentis. Tam nomen ὑπόστασις, quam ὑφίστασθαι militare est. Vid. CRAVSERI phosph. p. 310. b) Per πληροφορίαν, Rom. IV, 21. Col. II, 2. Hebr. VI, 11. Πληροφορία dicitur ἀπὸ τῆς πλήγεος, plenus, & φέρεσθαι, ferri, quo per eam animus credentis plene feratur in obiectum, sicut nauis plenis velis in portum inuehitur. Tunc autem plene animus in obiectum fertur, cum secundum omnem rationem, secundum quam ei obiicitur, in illud fertur; intellectus quidem, in quantum sub ratione veri; voluntate autem, in quantum sub ratione boni & appetibilis obiicitur. Non igitur πληροφορία solius est intellectus, sed vel maxime voluntatis, & fiduciæ, quæ fertur in obiectum bonum toto impetu, repræsentatum ab intellectu, diuina reuelatione illuminato. c) Per πεποίθησιν, Rom. VIII, 38. 2 Tim. I, 12. Πεποίθησις originem ducit a verbo πείθω, persuadeo. Est igitur πεποίθησις persuasio mentis & voluntatis. Illa est certus assensus; hæc immota fiducia. Sic Paullus inquit: Πέποιθα δὲ ἐν κυρίῳ, confido autem in Domino, Phil. II, 24. d) per παρρησίαν, Hebr. IV, 16. quæ vox stricte sumta notat libertatem dicendi, aliquando latius accepta notat fiduciam cordis, connotata alacritate & firmitate credendi

3) A collatione locorum veteris & novi testamenti. Quae in V. T. confidentibus & fiduciae, ea in N. T. credentibus & fidei tribuuntur. Quod Ps. II, 12. dicitur: Beati, qui confidunt in eo, id Marc. XVI, 16. dicitur: qui crediderit, salvus erit. 4) Ab exegetica declaratione.

Spiritus S. enim fidem per fiduciam exponit 1 Io. V, 13. Haec scripsi vobis, qui creditis in nomen Filii Dei: Et haec fiducia est, quam habemus apud illum. 5) Ab obiecto; quod Paullus sic explicat, Rom.

III, 25. Christum Deus proposuit ἱλαστήριον, propitiatorium per fidem in ipsius sanguine, i. e. mediatorem & placatorem irae divinae, ratione satisfactionis & meriti sui, effuso sanguine suo pro peccatis nostris praestiti, fide apprehendendi. Ex quibus concluditur: Quicunque voluntatis actus pro obiecto habet Christum, vt caussam meritoriam placandae irae divinae, ille formaliter & intrinsece est fiducia; Atqui actus ille, quem fides in sanguine Christi ex parte voluntatis includit, est actus voluntatis, qui pro obiecto habet Christum, vt caussam meritoriam placandae irae divinae: Ergo. 6) Ab opposito.

Fidei opponitur cordis timor: E. fides est fiducia. Ratio consequentiae est; quia fiducia timori obluctatur. Antecedens probatur ex Luc. VIII, 50. Ne timeto, crede modo. 7) A iustificatione hominis impii.

Quicunque impius fide iustificatur, ille iustificatur, fiducia posita in satisfactione mediatoris: Atqui impius poenitens &c. Rom. IV, 5. Ergo. Maior est immotae veritatis: quia Deus, iustissimus & severissimus scelerum vindex, impium sine praestita satisfactione (propria, aut vicaria) iustificare non potest, Prov. XVII, 15. Sed impius ipse non est par satisfaciendo: E. necesse est, vt fiduciam suam defigat in satisfactione vicaria Christi, qui pro impiis mortuus est, Rom. V, 6. 8) Ab effectis fidei.

Quicunque fide sua resistunt diabolo, vincunt mundum, obtinent pacem, salutari cum fructu precantur, illorum fides est fiducia: Atqui peccatores conversi & renati &c. Maior constat: quia effecta illa proficiscuntur a fiducia. Nam viri fortes fiducia virium armorumque suorum resistunt hostibus, iisque victoriam & pacem extorquent. Filius fiducia paternae benevolentiae implorat patris opem. Minor claret testimoniis scripturae, 1 Petr. V, 9. Diabolo resistite, stabiles fide. 1 Io. V, 4. Haec est victoria, quae vicit mundum, fides nostra. Rom. V, 1. Iustificati fide pacem habemus erga Deum. Iac. I, 6. Petito in fide, nil addubitans! Antithesis est Pontificiorum, negantium, fidem iustificantem esse fiduciam.


### Q. XVI. What is trust fixed in Christ?: Who object

Who object:

I. The effect of faith is not faith itself: But trust is an effect of faith: Therefore. The minor is proved from Eph. III, 12: In whom we have trust and access in confidence through faith in him. Where Paul distinguishes trust from faith, and teaches that we have trust through faith, and thus that trust stands in relation to faith as an effect to a cause.

Resp. 1) The words in the source flow thus: In whom we have παρρησίαν, boldness of speech and access in confidence through faith in him. Boldness of speech is indeed an effect of faith, according to Ps. CXVI, 10: I believed, therefore I speak. 2) Trust is an effect of faith, taken as assenting knowledge; for by knowing, it represents that Christ the mediator is for us the cause of obtaining grace and remission of sins before God, with the most certain persuasion, which is πληροφορία, as a double effect from its cause.

Eph. III, 12. For from this is effected first προσαγωγή, access to the appeased God, and to the θρόνον τῆς χάριτος, throne of grace, without any trembling, Heb.

IV, 16.; then παρρησία, prayer without any doubt. presents Christ the mediator to the will, as the cause of obtaining a certain difficult and arduous good, and as much as is in itself, directs it through the representation of the Object to elicit an act of trust; but trust is not an effect of faith in Christ; for faith in Christ, or to believe in Christ, in its formal concept includes and embraces knowledge, assent, and trust. 3) Dist. between the trust of a man to be justified, and one who is justified. The former is fixed on the merit of Christ, as the cause of obtaining grace and the remission of sins: The latter is placed in the grace of God obtained, as the cause of peace and of conscience, and of spiritual joy, which trust is indeed an effect of faith in Christ. The sense of the Pauline statement is: We, having been reconciled with God, have the liberty of speaking with God, and access to him joined not with trembling, but with trust placed in the grace of God, which we have received through faith in Christ.

II. Whatever is joined with fear, that is not trust (because trust is opposed to fear): But faith &c: Therefore. The minor is evident from Hebr. XI, 7. By faith Noah, being moved with fear, prepared an ark. Resp. The fear of Noah was not servile, but filial; not of flight, such as was Adam's upon committing sin; but of caution, such as was Joseph's, guarding himself from adultery. Filial fear consists well with trust (*).

III. The object of trust is not every word of God: The object of faith is every word of God: Therefore faith is not trust. The major is clear: since the object of trust is the promise of grace concerning obtaining the remission of sins and eternal life on account of the merit of Christ. But the promise of grace is not every word of God. The minor is evident: because every word of God is to be received with firm faith on account of the authority of the speaker. Resp. Dist. between general, or dogmatic faith, and special, or justifying faith. The object of the former is every word of God; the object of the latter is the word of promise concerning the gratuitous remission of sins and eternal salvation, to be obtained on account of the merit of Christ.

IV. Trust is hope strengthened, as defined by THOMAS Aquinas II. III. q. 129. a. VI. Faith is not hope strengthened (because it is distinguished from hope, 1 Cor. XIII, 13.): Therefore faith is not trust. Resp. We disapprove of the definition of THOMAS; for trust acquiesces in a present good: but hope tends toward a future good. See Obs. III.

Instance: Trust also is concerned with a future good. For the patriarchs of the O.T. placed their trust in the coming Christ. Resp. Christ the Mediator was present to the patriarchs morally, by reason of the promise, merit, and value, although, as to his human nature, he was not present physically or really.

V. If faith were trust; its act in the Holy Scriptures would be expressed not by believing, but by trusting: But it is not expressed by trusting: Therefore Faith is not trust. The reason for the consequence is: because conjugates explain one another. Resp. 1) Neg. the antecedent: because in the O.T. the act of faith is for the most part expressed by trusting. See Ps. II, 12. That in the N.T. it is for the most part expounded by believing, the reason is; because besides trust it also embraces assent. 2) Dist. between believing someone, and in someone. The former denotes assent, the latter denotes trust joined with assent. But trust is as it were the soul and complement of faith, so that, if it be absent, the naked assent is not a complete, not a living and efficacious, but a dead faith.

VI. Justifying faith precedes the remission of sins: Trust in sin remitted on account of Christ does not precede the remission of sins: Therefore trust in sin remitted on account of Christof sin is not justifying faith. Resp. We concede the whole argument. For we maintain that justifying faith is a trust fixed upon the merit of Christ, as the cause of obtaining grace and the remission of sins before God: but trust in the remission of sins obtained on account of Christ is an effect of justifying faith.

Latin:

Qui obiciunt:

I. Effectus fidei non est fides ipsa: Atqui fiducia est effectus fidei: Ergo. Minor prob. ex Eph. III, 12. In quo habemus fiduciam & accessum in confidentia per fidem illius. Vbi Paullus fiduciam contradistinguit fidei, & docet, nos habere fiduciam per fidem, adeoque fiduciam in ordine ad fidem se habere, vt effectum ad caussam.

Resp. 1) Verba in fonte ita fluunt: In quo habemus παρρησίαν, loquendi fiduciam & accessum in confidentia per fidem eius. Fiducia loquendi vtique est effectus fidei, secundum Ps. CXVI, 10. Credidi, ideo loquor. 2) Fiducia est effectus fidei, sumta pro notitia assensitiva; quippe qua cognoscendo, Christum mediatorem esse nobis caussam impetrandae apud Deum gratiae & remissionis peccatorum, repraesentat certissima persuasione, quae est πληροφορία, tanquam duplex effectus a sua caussa.

Eph. III, 12. Ex hoc enim efficitur primum προσαγωγή, accessus ad Deum placatum, ac θρόνον τῆς χάριτος, sine vllo tremore, Hebr.

IV, 16.; deinde παρρησία, precatio sine vlla dubitatione. præsentat voluntati Christum mediatorem, vt caussam obtinendi cuiusdam boni difficilis & ardui, & quantum in ipsa est, dirigit eam per repræsentationem Obiecti ad eliciendum fiduciæ actum; at fiducia non est effectus fidei in Christum; nam fides in Christum, siue credere in Christum, in conceptu suo formali includit & complectitur notitiam, assensum, & fiduciam. 3) Dist. inter fiduciam hominis iustificandi, & iustificati. Illa figitur in merito Christi, vt caussa impetrandæ gratiæ & remissionis peccatorum: Hæc collocatur in gratia Dei impetrata, vt caussa pacis & conscientiæ, & spiritualis lætitiæ, quæ fiducia vtique est effectus fidei in Christum. Sensus effati Paullini est: Nos cum Deo reconciliati habemus libertatem loquendi cum Deo, & aditum ad ipsum coniunctum non cum tremore, sed fiducia posita in gratia Dei, quam per fidem in Christum accepimus.

II. Quidquid coniunctum est cum metu, id non est fiducia (quia fiducia metui opponitur): Atqui fides &c: E. Minor patet ex Hebr. XI, 7. Fide Noë metuens aptauit arcam. Resp. Metus Noachi non erat seruilis, sed filialis; non fugæ, qualis erat Adami commisso peccato; sed cautelæ, qualis erat Iosephi, ab adulterio sibi cauentis. Filialis metus cum fiducia bene consistit (*).

III. Fiduciæ obiectum non est omne verbum Dei: Fidei obiectum est omne verbum Dei: E. fides non est fiducia. Maior est clara: quoniam obiectum fiduciæ est promissio gratiæ de impetranda propter meritum Christi remissione peccatorum & vita æterna. At promissio gratiæ non est omne verbum Dei. Minor liquet: quia omne verbum Dei ob auctoritatem dicentis firma fide recipiendum est. Resp. Dist. inter fidem generalem, siue dogmaticam, & specialem, siue iustificam. Illius obiectum est omne Dei verbum; huius obiectum est verbum promissionis de gratuita peccatorum remissione æternaque salute, propter meritum Christi obtinenda.

IV. Fiducia est spes roborata, definiente THOMA Aquinate II. III. q. 129. a. VI. Fides non est spes roborata (quia a spe distinguitur, 1 Cor. XIII, 13.): E. fides non est fiducia. Resp. Improbamus definitionem THOMÆ; nam fiducia in bono præsenti acquiescit: spes autem ad bonum futurum tendit. Vid. Obs. III.

Instantia: Etiam fiducia versatur circa bonum futurum. Nam patriarchæ V. T. fiduciam suam collocarunt in Christo venturo. Resp. Christus Mediator patriarchis fuit præsens moraliter, ratione promissionis, meriti & valoris, licet, qua humanam naturam, non fuerit præsens physice aut realiter.

V. Si fides esset fiducia; actus eius in S. litteris non per credere, sed per fidere exprimeretur: At non exprimitur per fidere: E. Fides non est fiducia. Ratio consequentiæ est: quia coniugata se mutuo explicant. Resp. 1) Neg. antecedens: quia in V. T. actus fidei plerumque exprimitur per confidere. Vid. Ps. II, 12. Quod in N. T. plerumque exponatur per credere, ratio est; quia præter fiduciam etiam assensum complectitur. 2) Dist. inter credere alicui, & in aliquem. Illud assensum, hoc fiduciam cum assensu coniunctam denotat. At fiducia est fidei quasi anima & complementum, vt, si ea absit, assensus nudus non sit completa, non viua & efficax, sed mortua fides.

VI. Fides iustificans remissionem peccatorum antecedit: Fiducia remissi propter Christum peccati non antecedit remissionem peccatorum: E. fiducia remissi propter Christumpeccati non est fides iustificans. Resp. Concedimus totum argumentum. Nam nos statuimus, fidem iustificantem esse fiduciam defixam in merito Christi, vt caussa impetrandæ apud Deum gratiæ & remissionis peccatorum: at fiducia impetratæ propter Christum remissionis peccatorum est effectus fidei iustificantis.


### Q. XVII. Is faith to be defined by obedience?

Obedience is twofold, evangelical, and legal a). The obedience of the gospel b) and of the doctrine of faith c) is faith itself, by which a repenting sinner admits, approves, and applies to himself the evangelical doctrine not unwillingly. The obedience of the law, however, or of works, is a virtue; conformable to the divine law, not essentially constituting faith d), but following the same as its fruit and effect e).

Proof a. From 1 John III, 23. This is his commandment, that we should believe on the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another. St. John joins the evangelical commandment concerning faith in Christ, and the legal one concerning charity; just as the evangelical will of God is also described, John VI, 40. This is the will of him that sent me, that every one which seeth the Son, and believeth on him, may have everlasting life. The legal will of God, however, is our sanctification, 1 Thess. IV, 3. Our obedience ought to respond to both divine commandments.

Proof b. From 2 Thess. I, 8. God will give vengeance to them that know not God, and that have not obeyed the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, 2 Thess. I, 8. To obey the gospel signifies to offer it a fiducial assent. For St. Peter also calls assent the obedience of the truth, 1 Petr. I, 22. Conversely, not to obey the truth, Gal. III, 1. is the same as not to believe.

Proof c. From Rom. I, 5. By Christ we have received grace and Apostleship, for obedience to the faith among all nations, for his name. By faith the Apostle understands objective faith, or that which is believed. St. Paul therefore received the apostolic office, that he might preach the doctrine of faith and that the nations might accept the same with fiducial assent.

Proof d. From Rom. III, 28. Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith, without the works of the law. Whatever is opposed to the office and nature of justifying faith, that does not enter into its essence. But the obedience of the law is opposed to the office and nature of justifying faith. Therefore.

Proof e. From Matt. III, 8. Bring forth fruits meet for repentance. The fruits of repentance are good works, Acts XXVI, 20. of the census of which is obedience (*).

The antithesis is that of the Socinians and Arminians, who define faith by obedience under the hope of obtaining eternal life. Their stronger arguments are:

I. The obedient are blessed, Hebr. V, 9. The believers are blessed. Therefore, believers are obedient, and consequently faith and obedience are one and the same. Resp. 1) In the major, either the obedience of the gospel is understood, or the obedience of the law. The former is faith itself; the latter is a sign of faith, by which the subject to be saved is specified, yet the causal reason for salvation is not rendered. The obedient are blessed, but not through obedience. 2) Distinguish between subjective and formal identity. Faith and obedience meet in one subject, so that believers are called obedient; but they do not meet formally. Although therefore believers are obedient; faith nevertheless is not obedience: Just as a certain philosopher is a theologian, yet philosophy is not theology.

II. The faith of the Ninevites was obedience, Jon. III, 5. The Ninevites believed in God, and proclaimed a fast, and were clothed in sackcloth. Resp. From the words of Jonah, you will gather in vain that faith is obedience. For the faith of the Ninevites is distinguished from the obedience of works.

III. The faith of Daniel was obedience, Dan. VI, 23. compared with v. 21. Resp. You gather poorly: Daniel served God obediently: Daniel believed God: Therefore, to believe God, and to obey Him, is ταὐτό [the same]. Otherwise, by the same reasoning I argue: David believed: David spoke, Ps. CXVI, 10. Therefore, to speak, and to believe is ταὐτό. Things which are conjoined meet in one subject, but formally they are not the same.

IV. If unbelief is disobedience, faith will be obedience. The former is true: Therefore also the latter. The consequence is manifest: because the reason of opposites is opposite. The antecedent is evident from Ps. LXXVIII, 22, in which the Israelites are accused of unbelief, because they did not render the due obedience to God. Resp. The Israelites are accused a posteriori, or by gathering from the effect to the cause; because disobedience is the effect and indication of unbelief.

V. Paul, 1 Thess. I, 9, makes two parts of the Christian religion, and thus also of faith, one of which is to obey God, the other to await His Son from heaven. What else is this, than to obey God and Christ under the hope of obtaining the life of immortality? Resp. Religion and justifying faith are not synonyms; since religion, besides faith in Christ, requires the whole choir, or concert, of virtues worthy of a Christian.

VI. That without which faith is dead, that is its internal form: Without obedience and the pursuit of good works, faith is dead: Therefore. The major is proved: As a body is dead without the soul, as an internal form: so faith is dead without obedience. The minor is evident from Jas. II, 26. Resp. The major is not universally true. For as a body is dead without respiration, yet respiration is not the internal form of the body: so faith is dead without the pursuit of good works, yet the pursuit of good works is not the internal form of saving faith.

Latin:

Obedientia est duplex, euangelica, & legalis a). Obedientia euangelii b) & doctrinæ fidei c) est ipsa fides, qua peccator resipiscens doctrinam euangelicam haud inuitus admittit, approbat, sibique applicat. Obedientia autem legis, siue operum, est virtus; legi diuinæ conformis, fidem essentialiter non constituens d), sed eandem tanquam fructus & effectus consequens e).

Prob. a. Ex 1 Io. III, 23. Hoc est mandatum illius, vt credamus nomini Filii eius Iesu Christi, & diligamus nos inuicem. S. Ioannes coniungit mandatum euangelicum de fide in Christum, & legale de caritate; prout etiam voluntas Dei euangelica describitur, Io. VI, 40. Hæc est voluntas eius, qui misit me, vt omnis, qui videt filium, & credit in ipsum, habeat vitam æternam. Legalis autem Dei voluntas est nostra sanctificatio, 1 Thess. IV, 3. Vtrique mandato diuino obedientia nostra respondere debet.

Prob. b. Ex 2 Thess. I, 8. Deus dabit vindictam iis, qui non norunt Deum, & qui non obediuerunt euangelio Domini nostri Iesu Christi, 2 Thess. I, 8. Euangelio obedire significat, ipsi assensum fiducialem præbere. Nam & S. Petrus assensum vocat obedientiam veritatis, 1 Petr. I, 22. Contra, veritati non obedire, Gal. III, 1. idem est, quod non credere.

Prob. c. Ex Rom. I, 5. Per Christum accepimus gratiam & Apostolatum in obedientiam fidei inter omnes gentes super nomine ipsius. Per fidem Apostolus intelligit fidem obiectiuam, siue quæ creditur. Accepit igitur S. Paullus munus apostolicum, vt doctrinam fidei prædicaret & gentes eandem assensu fiduciali acceptarent.

Prob. d. Ex Rom. III, 28. Concludimus ergo, hominem iustificari fide, sine operibus. Quidquid officio & naturæ fidei iustificantis opponitur, illud eius essentiam non ingreditur, Sed obedientia legis officio & naturæ fidei iustificantis opponitur. E.

Prob. e. Ex Matth. III, 8. Facite fructus dignos pœnitentia. Fructus pœnitentiæ sunt bona opera, Act. XXVI, 20. e quorum censu est obedientia (*).

Antithesis est Socinianorum & Arminianorum, fidem per obedientiam sub spe consequendæ vitæ æternæ definientium. Quorum potiora sunt argumenta:

I. Beati sunt obedientes, Hebr. V, 9. Beati sunt credentes. E. Credentes sunt obedientes, & consequenter fides & obedientia sunt vnum idemque, Resp. 1) In maiori intelligitur vel obedientia euangelii, vel obedientia legis. Illa est ipsa fides; hæc est signum fidei, a quo subiectum saluandum specificatur, neque tamen caussalis ratio salutis redditur. Beati sunt obedientes, sed non per obedientiam. 2) Dist. inter identitatem subiectiuam & formalem. Fides & obedientia conueniunt in vno subiecto, vt credentes dicantur obedientes; sed non conueniunt formaliter. Quamuis igitur credentes sint obedientes; fides tamen non est obedientia: Sicut quidam philosophus est theologus, neque tamen philosophia est theologia.

II. Niniuitarum fides erat obedientia, Ion. III, 5. Crediderunt Niniuitæ in Deum, & prædicauerunt ieiunium, & vestiti sunt saccis. Resp. Ex verbis Ionæ frustra colliges, fidem esse obedientiam. Nam Niniuitarum fides ab obedientia operum distinguitur.

III. Danielis fides erat obedientia, Dan. VI, 23. collat. cum v. 21. Resp. Male colligis: Daniel Deo seruiuit obedienter: Daniel credidit Deo: E. credere Deo, & ipsi obedire, est ταὐτό. Alias eadem ratione argumentor: Dauid credidit: Dauid locutus est, Ps. CXVI, 10. E. loqui, & credere est ταὐτό. Quæ coniuncta sunt, conueniunt in vno subiecto, sed formaliter eadem non sunt.

IV. Si incredulitas est inobedientia, fides erit obedientia. Prius est verum: Ergo & posterius. Consequentia est manifesta: quia oppositorum opposita est ratio. Antecedens patet ex Ps. LXXVIII, 22. in quo Israëlitæ arguuntur incredulitatis, quod debitam Deo obedientiam non præstiterint. Resp. Arguuntur Israëlitæ a posteriori, siue colligendo ab effectu ad caussam; quia inobedientia incredulitatis effectus & indicium est.

V. Paullus 1 Thess. I, 9. duas partes religionis christianæ, adeoque & fidei facit, quarum vna est obedire Deo, altera Filium eius expectare e caelo. Quod quid aliud est, quam sub spe inmortalitatis vitæ consequendæ Deo & Christo obedire? Resp. Religio & fides iustificans, non sunt synonyma; siquidem religio præter fidem in Christum requirit totum virtutum Christiano dignarum chorum, vel concentum.

VI. Sine quo fides est mortua, illud est eius forma interna: Sine obedientia & studio bonorum operum fides est mortua: Ergo. Maior probatur: Sicut corpus mortuum est sine anima, tanquam forma interna: ita mortua est fides sine obedientia. Minor patet ex Iac. II, 26. Resp. Maior non est vniuersaliter vera. Nam sicut corpus sine respiratione mortuum est, respiratione tamen non est forma interna corporis: ita fides sine studio bonorum operum est mortua, neque tamen studium bonorum operum est forma interna fidei saluificæ.


### Q. XIX. What is the end of faith?

The intermediate end of faith is justification a) and renewal b). The ultimate end, on the part of man, is eternal life c); on the part of God, it is the glory of divine mercy d).

Prob. a. From Gal. II, 16. We believe in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law. But we are justified by the faith of Christ, i.e., in Christ ὀργανικῶς [organically/instrumentally]: because faith is the instrument, or medium, receiving the merit of Christ, and the grace of God obtained thereby, which forgives sins and is offered by the evangelical promise, just as the hand receives alms, the mouth food, the eye light. For faith is not viewed here as a good work, by which righteousness availing before God is acquired, but as the organ of a beggar, by which the merit of Christ is apprehended. The Apostle of the Gentiles inculcates the very same, Rom. IX, 30, 31, 32. The Gentiles, which followed after righteousness, have attained to righteousness, even the righteousness which is of faith: But Israel, which followed after the law of righteousness, hath not attained to the law of righteousness. Wherefore? Because they sought it not by faith, but as it were by the works of the law.

Prob. b. Faith worketh by love, Gal. V, 6. And he who remains in Christ through faith, this one bears much fruit, John XV, 5. Faith indeed flows into the production of good works as an emanating efficient cause, as we shall show more clearly in the following chapter.

Prob. c. The end of faith is the salvation of souls, 1 Pet. I, 9. Faith is therefore the medium of salvation.

Prob. d. Abraham was confirmed by faith, giving glory to God, Rom. IV, 20. Abraham, confirmed by faith, gave glory to God for his grace, truth, and power: because he was fully persuaded that whatever God had promised, he was able to perform. So far is the faithful man from hunting after his own glory, that he denies himself, and celebrates the riches of divine mercy, obtained by the satisfaction of Christ, by which he is justified and saved.

Q. XIX. How manifold is justifying faith?

Justifying faith, considered essentially and absolutely, is one: Accidentally and respectively it is distinguished: a) by reason of degree, into small and great: b) by reason of duration, into temporary and final: c) by reason of the mode of knowing, into direct and reflex: d) by reason of exercise, into habitual and actual.

Prob. a. Small, or weak faith (in Greek ὀλιγοπιστία) is when either a thin light of the knowledge of Christ glimmers in the intellect, or the promise of grace is received with a weak and languid assent, or trust struggles with the fear of conscience. Thus the father of the lunatic said, Mark IX, 24. Lord, I believe; help my unbelief. Yet weak faith is also true: just as a spark lying under ashes is true fire, and a tender infant is a true human. Great, or firm faith (in Greek πληροφορία) is a clear knowledge of divine mercy proposed in Christ, a solid assent, a fearless trust that overcomes all terrors. Firm faith is compared to the pulse of an artery in a healthy man, weak faith to the movement of a weak artery in a sick man. Concerning the πληροφορία of Abraham, see Rom. IV, 18. ff. Prob. b.

Temporary faith is that by which a man believes for a certain time, but afterwards, either fascinated by false opinions, or overcome by the desires of the flesh, or by the adversities of the world, falls away from true faith. It is called in Greek faith πρόσκαιρος, from Luke VIII, 13. Final faith is that which perseveres until the last breath of life, Matt. X, 22. Prob. c.

Simple and direct faith is that which is directed straight to Christ, and the grace of God obtained by him, e.g., infants believe, Matt. XIX, 6, but cannot yet examine their own faith due to a lack of full judgment. Reflex and discursive faith is that by which a reborn man believes and feels that he believes, so that he can say with Paul, from 2 Tim. I, 12. I know whom I have believed.

Prob. d. Actual faith is an act of the human intellect and will, by which a man so knows the doctrine concerning Christ the mediator, and concerning the grace of God and the remission of sins to be obtained from God through his merit, that by divine power joined to that doctrine, he not only judges, being fully persuaded, that it is true, and that Christ has merited grace for him before God; but also rests in Christ as the cause of obtaining grace before God; for the sake of obtaining righteousness and salvation. Habitual faith is a habit of the intellect and will of knowing those things which are divinely revealed and to be believed; especially concerning Christ the mediator and the grace of God and salvation to be obtained through Christ, and of assenting to the same by and for the sake of divine revelation, and of resting trustfully in Christ, divinely bestowed, for the sake of obtaining righteousness and salvation.

Q.

The distinction of faith into unformed and formed is destitute of a solid foundation, and therefore is to be rejected.

Prob. 1) Truly justifying faith is always formed; because by its form (which is the special application of the mercy of God remitting sins, founded in the merit of Christ, and promised in the gospel) it is what it is.

2) Fides informis (unformed faith) is vain, not true: dead, not living, and therefore not justifying. For according to the mind of the adversaries, fides informis can consist with proæretic (deliberate) sins: But true faith does not consist with voluntary sins. For he who is born of God does not commit sin, 1 John III, 9.

3) It is absurd for faith to be moved by charity, as if it were a superior directive principle, since charity is an effect of faith, and faith is rather operative through charity, as Paul testifies, Gal. V, 6. The antithesis is that of the Papists, who posit that charity is the form of faith; on the contrary, they hold that informis faith, devoid of charity and joined with mortal sins, is true. Their principal arguments are:

I. Faith is acted upon and moved through charity, as Paul testifies, Gal. V, 6. Therefore, charity is the essential form of faith. Resp. The words of the text are: Πίστις δι' ἀγάπης ἐνεργουμένη, faith working through charity. The participle, ἐνεργουμένη, is of the middle voice and has an active meaning. Confer. Rom. VII, 5. 2 Cor. IV, 12. The sense is: Faith works through charity, as some consequence, and as if through an accidental form, just as fire is said to act through heat.

II. James says c. II, 15. What will it profit, my brethren, if a man says he has faith, but does not have works? Can this faith save him? Resp. St. James is speaking not of true faith, but of hypocritical faith, or a vain boast of faith.

III. Paul says 1 Cor. XIII, 2. If I have all faith, so that I remove mountains, but have not charity, I am nothing. Resp. The Apostle is speaking of miraculous faith, which it is established can sometimes exist without charity, from Matt. VII, 22.

IV. John XII, 42. Many of the rulers believed in him: But because of the Pharisees they did not confess him, lest they should be put out of the synagogue. For they loved the glory of men more than the glory of God. Resp. Those rulers had historical faith, but not salvific faith: Which is evident a) from the lack of confession, as a necessary fruit of true faith: b) from the pursuit of human glory, to which divine glory was subordinated.

Latin:

Finis fidei intermedius est iustificatio a) & renouatio b). Finis vltimus, ex parte hominis, est vita æterna c); ex parte Dei, est gloria misericordiæ diuinæ d).

Prob. a. Ex Gal. II, 16. Nos in Christum Iesum credimus, vt iustificemur ex fide Christi, & non ex operibus legis. Iustificamur autem ex fide Christi, i. e. in Christum ὀργανικῶς: quia fides est instrumentum, vel medium, meritum Christi, & eo partam gratiam Dei, peccata remittentis, promissione euangelica oblatam, recipiens, perinde, ac manus eleemosynam, os cibum, oculus lucem recipit. Neque enim fides hic spectatur, vt bonum opus, quo iustitia coram Deo valens acquiritur, sed vt organon mendici, quo meritum Christi apprehenditur. Id ipsum inculcat gentium Apostolus, Rom. IX, 30. 31. 32. Gentes, quæ persequebantur iustitiam, apprehenderunt iustitiam; iustitiam vero, quæ ex fide: Israël vero persequens legem iustitiæ, ad legem iustitiæ non peruenit. Quare? Quod non ex fide, sed quasi ex operibus legis.

Prob. b. Fides per caritatem operatur, Gal V, 6. Et qui per fidem in Christo manet, hic fert fructum multum, Io. XV, 5. Influit vero fides in productionem bonorum operum tanquam caussa efficiens emanatiua, vti capite sequenti luculentius ostendemus:

Prob. c. Finis fidei est salus animarum, 1 Petr. I, 9. Est itaque fides salutis medium. Est itaque fides salutis medium.

Prob. d. Abraham confirmatus est fide, dans gloriam Deo, Rom. IV, 20. Abraham fide confirmatus dedit Deo gloriam gratiae, veritatis & potentiae: quia plane persuasus erat, quod, quidquid Deus promisit, facere possit. Tantum abest, vt homo fidelis suam aucupetur gloriam, vt seipsum abneget, & diuitias misericordiae diuinae, satisfactione Christi partae, qua iustificatur & saluatur, celebret.

Quaest. XIX. Quotuplex est fides iustificans?

Fides iustificans, essentialiter & absolute considerata, est vna: Accidentaliter & respective distinguitur: a) ratione gradus, in paruam & magnam: b) ratione durationis, in temporariam & finalem: c) ratione modi cognoscendi, in directam & reflexam: d) ratione exercitii, in habitualem & actualem.

Prob. a. Fides parua, vel infirma (graece ὀλιγοπιστία) est, cum vel tenuis lux notitiae Christi in intellectu gliscit, vel assensu debili & languido recipitur promissio gratiae, vel fiducia cum pauore conscientiae luctatur. Sic pater lunatici dicebat, Marc. IX, 24. Credo, Domine; iuuua meam incredulitatem. Est tamen fides infirma etiam vera: sicut scintilla sub cinere latens est verus ignis, & tenellus infans verus homo est. Fides magna, vel firma, (graece πληροφορία) est clara notitia misericordiae diuinae, in Christo propositae, assensus solidus, fiducia intrepida & omnes terrores vincens. Comparatur fides firma pulsui arteriae in homine sano, infirma motui arteriae debilis in aegro. De πληροφορίᾳ Abrahami vid. Rom. IV, 18. seqq.

Prob. b. Fides temporaria est, qua homo ad certum tempus credit, at postea vel fascinatus falsis opinionibus, vel victus desideriis carnis, aut mundi aduersitatibus, a vera fide defiscit. Vocatur graece fides πρόσκαιρος, ex Luc. VIII, 13. Fides finalis est, quae vsque ad nouissimum vitae halitum perseuerat, Matth. X, 22.

Prob. c. Fides simplex & directa est, quae recta fertur in Christum, & eo conciliatam gratiam Dei, v. gr. infantes credunt, Matth. XIX, 6. sed nondum fidem suam propter defectum pleni iudicii explorare queunt. Fides reflexa & discursiva est, qua homo renatus credit & sentit, se credere, vt cum Paulo dicere possit, ex 2 Tim. I, 12. Scio, cui crediderim.

Prob. d. Fides actualis est actus intellectus & voluntatis humanae, quo homo doctrinam de Christo mediatore, deque gratia Dei, remissione peccatorum, per illius meritum a Deo impetranda, ita cognoscit, vt virtute diuina, doctrinae illi coniuncta, non solum plene persuasus iudicet, eam esse veram, & Christum sibi promeruisse gratiam apud Deum; verum etiam in Christo, tanquam causa impetrandae gratiae apud Deum, acquiescat; consequendae iustitiae & salutis caussa. Fides habitualis est habitus intellectus & voluntatis cognoscendi ea, quae diuinitus reuelata & credenda sunt; praesertim de Christo mediatore & gratia Dei ac salute, per Christum impetranda, eidemque per & propter reuelationem diuinam assentienti, & fiducialiter in Christo acquiescendi, diuinitus collatus, consequendae iustitiae & salutis caussa.

Quaest. XX. Estne distinctio fidei in informem & formatam admittenda?

Distinctio fidei in informem, & formatam solido destituitur fundamento, adeoque reiicienda est.

Prob. 1) Fides vere iustificans semper est formata; quia per formam suam (quae est specialis applicatio misericordiae Dei peccata remittentis, fundatae in merito Christi, & in euangelio promissae) est id, quod est.

2) Fides informis est vana, non vera: mortua, non viua, adeoque non iustifica. Nam ex mente aduersariorum fides informis cum peccatis proæreticis consistere potest: At vera fides non consistit cum peccatis voluntariis. Nam qui ex Deo natus est, peccatum non facit, 1 Io. III, 9.

3) Absurdum est, fidem moueri per caritatem, tanquam principium superius directiuum, cum caritas sit effectus fidei, & fides potius per caritatem operosa sit, teste Paulo, Gal. V, 6. Antithesis est Pontificiorum, statuentium, fidei formam esse caritatem; contra, informem fidem caritatis expertem, & cum peccatis mortalibus coniunctam esse veram. Quorum præcipua sunt argumenta:

I. Fides per caritatem agitur & mouetur, teste Paulo, Gal. V, 6. Ergo caritas est fidei forma essentialis. Resp. Verba textus sunt: Πίστις δι' ἀγάπης ἐνεργουμένη, fides per caritatem operans. Participium, ἐνεργουμένη, est mediæ vocis, & habet significationem actiuam. Confer. Rom. VII, 5. 2 Cor. IV, 12. Eph. III, 20. Sensus est: Fides operatur per caritatem, tanquam aliquod consequens, & velut per formam accidentalem, vt ignis per calorem agere dicitur.

II. Iacobus dicit c. II, 15. Quid proderit, fratres mei, si fidem quis dicat se habere, opera vero non habeat? Num potest eum hæc fides seruare? Resp. S. Iacobus loquitur non de fide vera, sed de hypocritica, aut vana fidei iactantia.

III. Paullus inquit 1 Cor. XIII, 2. Si habuero omnem fidem, adeo, vt montes transferam, caritatem autem non habuero, nihil sum. Resp. Sermo est Apostolo de fide miraculosa, quam aliquando sine caritate esse posse constat ex Matth. VII, 22.

IV. Io. XII, 42. Multi ex principibus crediderunt in eum: Sed propter Pharisaeos non confitebantur, ne synagoga mouerentur. Dilexerunt enim magis gloriam hominum, quam gloriam Dei. Resp. Principes illi habuerunt fidem historicam, sed non saluificam: Quod patet a) e defectu confessionis, tanquam veræ fidei necessarii fructus: b) e gloriæ humanæ aucupio, cui gloria diuina est posthabita.


### Quest. XXI. What are the affections, or properties, of true faith?

The affections of faith are: a) certainty, b) fruitfulness, by which it produces good works.

Prob. a. Certainty belongs to faith in Christ: a) On the part of the object, which is believed, to which it is repugnant that falsehood should underlie it. For the Word of God, which is received by the assent of faith, is most certain, because of the authority of God who reveals it. b) On the part of the subject, or he who believes, and most tenaciously adheres to and leans upon the divine promises. For faith is ἔλεγχος πραγμάτων οὐ βλεπομένων, i.e., the demonstration and conviction of those things which are not seen, Heb. XI, 1. The mind is convinced both by the authority of God promising and by the efficacy of the Gospel unto indubitable assent.

Faith is ὑπόστασις, undaunted confidence of mind, ibid.; it is πληροφορία, full assurance (which word is frequent in Ulpian), certain assent and full trust, Rom. IV, 21. Col. II, 2. Heb. VI, 11.; it is πεποίθησις, firm persuasion, or the unmoved adherence of the mind to divine promises, Eph. III, 12. by which the believer is glued to the Lord, 1 Cor. VI, 17. all of which designate the certainty of faith in the subject. Prob. b.

Prob. b. Faith is a good tree producing good fruits, Matt. VII, 7. and bearing the fruits of righteousness, Phil. I, 11. Which generous fruits are either immanent, such as purity of heart and body, Acts XV, 9. 2 Cor. VII, 1. peace of conscience, Rom. V, 1. spiritual joy, Is. LXI, 10. or transient, such as charity toward God and neighbor, hope of heavenly goods, and access to

God through sighs and prayers, patience victorious over evils, etc.

Lacking these fruits, faith is dead, Iac. II, 7.

Certainty of faith. Question XXII. Can a converted sinner be certain of his faith?

Converted and reborn people can and usually do know with infallible certainty that they truly believe, both from the συμμαρτυρία, or attestation of the Holy Spirit with the testimony of their own spirit, or the soul illuminated and reborn [a)]; and from the δοκιμασία, examination or proof of faith [b)].

Proof [a]. Regarding the συμμαρτυρία of the Holy Spirit with our spirit, Paul says, Rom. VIII, 16. The Spirit itself (συμμαρτυρεῖ) testifies with our spirit that we are children of God: and John, 1 Ep. V, 9. If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater: For this is the testimony of God, which he has testified concerning his Son: He who believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. Here the testimony of the Holy Spirit and our spirit concur. The testimony of the Holy Spirit is revealed, applied, and sealed, and effective in our hearts.
