It is revealed by the word of the gospel: He who believes in Christ is a Son of God, Gal. III, 26. has remission of sins, Act. X, 23. eternal life, Io. III, 16. This testimony of the Holy Spirit is applied and sealed through individual absolution and the dispensation of the sacraments. It is effective through spiritual movements. The testimony of our spirit, or of the illuminated and reborn soul, is this: I know and believe that the Holy Spirit dwells in me through faith. For thus says John, 1 Ep. IV, 13. By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit. This testimony of our spirit is experimental, concerning which AUGUSTINE in book XIII. de trinit. c. 1. says: Everyone sees his own faith in himself, and holds it with the most certain knowledge.

Proof [b]. Regarding the δοκιμασία, or examination and proof of faith, the Apostle says, 2 Cor. XIII, 5. Examine yourselves, whether you are in the faith: Prove yourselves: Do you not know that Jesus Christ is in you? Unless you are reprobates, i.e., you can feel and experience the power of Christ, who dwells in the hearts of the faithful, within yourselves. For he works faith in you; which you can perceive and prove from the movements of the Holy Spirit, from the love of God, from prayers, from effective consolation, and living hope, from peace of conscience, and spiritual joy: unless you have become utterly reprobate, i.e., unless through your impenitence you have lost faith and the Holy Spirit; for in these, Christ also has ceased to work. This δοκιμασία of faith can be instituted from the antecedents, constituents, and consequents of faith.

We prove our faith 1) from the antecedents of faith. Whoever has seriously and sorrowfully detested his committed sins, so as to abandon the purpose of sinning, and has diligently listened to, read, and meditated on the word of the gospel, him the Holy Spirit has regenerated and endowed with true faith: But I have seriously and sorrowfully detested my sins, etc. Therefore. The Major premise is evident from 1 Petr. I, 23. where the word of the gospel is called the seed of regeneration; which certainly regenerates contrite hearts, in which stubborn resistance has ceased. The Minor premise is established by the testimony of my spirit, or by the feeling of my heart.

We prove our faith 2) from the constituents of faith. I acknowledge the evangelical promise of obtaining God's grace through the satisfaction of Christ, and I approve it with my consent as most true, and therefore I accept the offered grace with ardent desire and singular trust: Therefore I have true faith. The reason for the consequence is: because the acts of faith are knowledge, assent, and trust. Our intellect, reflecting upon its own acts, knows that it knows, assents, and inclines the will to trust; from which mental reflection arises the experience of faith. Prove-

We prove our faith from the consequences of faith. Whoever loves God and his neighbor, confesses his Jesus, adores the Father in His name, crucifies his flesh, does not commit prohairetic sin; but strives to overcome the divine law, as much as can be done in this infirmity of life, he is certain of his faith: But I love God and my neighbor, etc. Therefore. The most true biblical sayings confirm the major premise, Gal.

V, 6. 1 John IV, 13. John XVI, 23. collated with James I, 6. Gal. V, 24. 1 John III, 9. 1 John II, 3. The minor premise consists of the testimony of my spirit, or from the sense and experience of my heart, excited by the Holy Spirit dwelling in me, so that I can truly say with those blind men, Matt. IX, 28. with the father of the lunatic, Mark IX, 24. with the disciples of Christ, John VI, 69. with the eunuch, Acts VIII, 37.

I BELIEVE; nay, even with Paul: I KNOW WHOM I HAVE BELIEVED, 2 Tim. I, 12. and also with John: We have known and believed the love that God has toward us, 1 Ep. IV, 16. Which examples are virtually universal, according to that of Paul, Rom. XV, 4. There is an antithesis of the Papists, who deny that any man can be infallibly certain of his own faith, unless by a new revelation, a faith which they call privileged and special, it is manifested to him by God Himself.

Who object: I. Whatever is not revealed in the Holy Scriptures, that no one can infallibly believe: But to no man is it revealed in the Holy Scriptures that he truly believes: Therefore. The major is evident: because divine revelation is the formal object of faith. Resp. It is said to be revealed in two ways: a) explicitly and formally: b) implicitly and virtually.

If the major is understood in this way, that nothing is to be infallibly believed which is not expressly, formally, and in so many letters revealed, the same is false; because, when God has revealed something universally, He has virtually included the singulars. Whence a singular statement, which is elicited from a universal proposition, formally and explicitly revealed, by good and easy consequence, is virtually revealed.

I conclude: That every man, receiving Christ the mediator with fiduciary assent, truly believes, is divinely revealed, John I, 12. I receive Christ the mediator with fiduciary assent: Therefore, that I truly believe is divinely revealed, not by formal and explicit revelation, but by virtual and implicit. You say: I.

The minor is not revealed, but depends on human sense. Resp. It does not depend on human sense, but on the sense of the heart reborn and excited by the grace of indwelling. For he who believes in the Son has the testimony of the Holy Spirit in himself, 1 John V, 10. Its conclusion is of the same nature as the major proposition, which contains the principle of believing. You say: II. Even a hypocrite could appeal to the sense of his heart, and say: I believe.

Resp. The subject of faith is not a hypocrite, but a converted sinner, seriously detesting his sins with sorrow, and casting away the purpose of sinning. When a hypocrite says he believes, he lies, and is like a man dreaming of golden mountains, who when he wakes up, is a beggar. II. Whoever does not feel faith, does not believe: A tempted man does not believe. The conclusion is absurd, the absurdity of which flows from the major.

For the Evangelicals wish to know the presence of faith from the sense of the heart. Resp. From the sense of faith to faith itself, with Holy Scripture shining as a light, one is rightly concluded affirmatively, but not negatively, since in the heavy heat of temptations faith lies as if in a swoon. For which reason, although a tempted man does not feel fiduciary assent, he nevertheless feels the hunger and thirst for justice, and the desire for faith and grace: Which desire in the tempted heart is faith, although it be small and weak, such as was that of the afflicted father: Lord, I believe: Help my unbelief! Mark IX, 24. who doubted not of the sincerity of his faith, but of its perfection.

Faith therefore struggles in the tempted soul with unbelief.

SIGH

To thee, Lord Jesus, throne of grace and fountain of salvation, I approach with filial confidence, that I may receive mercy, and find grace in timely aid, while the door of salvation stands open! I, a most sorrowful sinner, look upon thee, who art the Lamb of God, taking away the sins of the world: I come to thee, poor, because thou art my most precious treasure; I flee to thee, because thou art my safest asylum: I recline upon thee, as the firmest rock of salvation: I rest in thee, as in the most tranquil harbor. My faith seeks, desires, and pants for thee, as my mediator, and the cause of restored divine grace, and of the remission of my sins to be obtained! Forgive me, most merciful God, my sins for the sake of my Jesus, and endow me with eternal salvation, which is the end of my faith!

Latin:

Affectiones fidei sunt: a) certitudo, b) fœcunditas, qua bona parit opera.

Prob. a. Competit fidei in Christum certitudo: a) Ex parte obiecti, quod creditur, cui falsum subesse repugnat. Verbum quippe Dei, quod fidei assensu recipitur, est certissimum, ob auctoritatem Dei reuelantis. b) Ex parte subiecti, siue eius, qui credit, & promissionibus diuinis tenacissime adhæret atque innititur. Etenim fides est ἔλεγχος πραγμάτων οὐ βλεπομένων, i. e. demonstratio & conuictio de his, quæ non videntur, Hebr. XI, 1. Conuincitur etiam animus tum auctoritate Dei promittentis, tum efficacia euangelii ad indubitatum assensum.

Fides est ὑπόστασις, imperterrita animi confidentia, ibid.; est πληροφορία, certioratio (quæ vox Vlpiano frequens), certa assensio & plena fiducia, Rom. IV, 21. Col. II, 2. Hebr. VI, 11.; est πεποίθησις, firma persuasio, vel immota animi ad diuinas promissiones adhæsio, Eph. III, 12. qua credens Domino agglutinatur, 1 Cor. VI, 17. quæ omnia certitudinem fidei in subiecto designant.

Prob. b. Fides est bona arbor faciens bonos fructus, Matth. VII, 7. & ferens fructus iustitiæ, Phil. I, 11. Qui generosi fructus sunt vel immanentes, vt puritas cordis & corporis, Act. XV, 9. 2 Cor. VII, 1. pax conscientiæ, Rom. V, 1. lætitia spiritualis, Es. LXI, 10. vel transeuntes, quales sunt caritas in Deum & proximum, spes bonorum cœlestium, accessus ad

Deum per suspiria & preces, patientia malorum victrix &c.

Quibus fructibus destituta fides mortua est, Iac. II, 7.

Certitudo fidei. Quæst. XXII. Potesne peccator conuerfus fidei suæ certus esse?

Poffunt & folent homines conuerfi & renati certitudine infallibili cognoscere, quod vere credant, tum e συμμαρτυρία, siue contestatione Spiritus S. cum testimonio spiritus sui, siue animæ lux illuminata & renata a); tum e δοκιμασία, examine aut probatione fidei b).

Prob. a. De συμμαρτυρία Spiritus S. cum spiritu nostro inquit Paullus, Rom. VIII, 16. Ipse Spiritus (συμμαρτυρεῖ) testatur cum spiritu nostro, quod fimus filii Dei: & Ioannes, 1 ep. V, 9. Si testimonium hominum accipimus, testimonium Dei maius est: Quia hoc est testimonium Dei, quod testificatus est de filio suo: Qui vero credit in filium Dei, habet testimonium in feipfo. Concurrit hic testimonium Spiritus Sancti & spiritus nostri. Testimonium Spiritus S. est reuelatum, applicatum & obsignatum, atque efficax in cordibus nostris. Reuelatum est verbo euangelii: Qui credit in Christum, est Filius Dei, Gal. III, 26. habet remissionem peccatorum, Act. X, 23. vitam æternam, Io. III, 16. Applicatur & obfignatur hoc testimonium Spiritus S. per indiuidualem abfolutionem & sacramentorum dispensationem. Est efficax per spirituales motus. Testimonium spiritus nostri, siue animæ illuminatæ & renatæ, est hoc: Ego cognosco & credo, quod Spiritus S. per fidem in me habitat. Ita enim ait Ioannes, 1 ep. IV, 13. In hoc cognoscimus, quod in ipso maneamus, & ipse in nobis, quia ex spiritu suo dedit nobis. Est hoc testimonium spiritus nostri experimentale, de quo AVGUSTINVS libr. XIII. de trinit. c. 1. Suam quisque fidem in fe videt, eamque tenet certissima scientia.

Prob. b. De δοκιμασία, siue examine & probatione fidei inquit Apostolus, 2 Cor. XIII, 5. Tentate vos ipfos, num fitis in fide: Vos ipfos probate: Aut non cognoscitis, quod Iefus Christus in vobis fit? Nisi reprobi estis, q. d. Virtutem Christi, qui in cordibus fidelium habitat, in vobis ipfis fentire & experiri potestis. Is enim fidem in vobis operatur; quam ex motibus Spiritus S., ex amore Dei, ex precibus, ex consolatione efficaci, & spe viua, ex pace conscientiæ, & lætitia spirituali animaduertere & probare potestis: nisi prorsus reprobi facti estis, i. e. nisi per impœnitentiam vestram fidem & Spiritum S. amisistis; in his enim Christus quoque operari defiit. Potest hæc δοκιμασία fidei institui ex antecedentibus, constituentibus & consequentibus fidei.

Probamus fidem nostram 1) ex antecedentibus fidei. Quicunque peccata sua admiffa ferio cum dolore detestatus est, vt peccandi propofitum abiecerit iuxta, atque verbum euangelii attente auscultauit, legit & meditatus est, illum Spiritus S. regenerauit, veraque fide donauit: Atqui ego peccata mea ferio cum dolore detestatus &c. E. Maior patet ex 1 Petr. I, 23. vbi verbum euangelii dicitur femen regenerationis; quod vtique regenerat corda contrita, in quibus morosa cessauit repugnantia. Minor constat e testimonio spiritus mei, feu e sensu cordis mei.

Probamus fidem nostram 2) ex constituentibus fidei. Ego promissionem euangelicam de impetranda propter fatisfactionem Christi gratia Dei agnosco, eamque confenfu meo approbo, vt verissimam, atque ideo oblatam gratiam ardenti defiderio, singularique fiducia accepto: Ergo ego habeo veram fidem. Ratio confequentia est: quia actus fidei sunt notitia, affenfus & fiducia. Intellectus noster, reflectens fe fuper actus suos, cognoscit, fe cognoscere, affentiri, & voluntatem ad fiduciam inclinare; e qua reflexione mentis oritur expe-rimentum fidei.

Probamus fidem nostram e consequentibus fidei. Quicunque Deum & proximum suum diligit, Iesum suum confitetur, in nomine ipsius Patrem adorat, carnem suam crucifigit, peccatum proareticum non committit; sed legem divinam, quantum in hac vitae infirmitate fieri potest, vincere servat, is fidei suae certus est: Atqui Ego Deum & proximum meum diligo &c. E. Maiorem confirmant dicta biblica verissima, Gal.

V, 6. 1 Io. IV, 13. Io. XVI, 23. collat. cum Iac. I, 6. Gal. V, 24. 1 Io. III, 9. 1 Io. II, 3. Minor constat e testimonio spiritus mei, sive e sensu & experimento cordis mei, a Spiritu S. in me habitante excitato, vt vere dicere possim cum caecis illis, Matth. IX, 28. cum patre lunatici, Marc. IX, 24. cum discipulis Christi, Io.

VI, 69. cum eunucho, Act. VIII, 37. EGO CREDO; quin etiam cum Paulo: SCIO, CVI CREDIDERIM, 2 Tim. I, 12. nec non cum Ioanne: Cognouimus & credimus dilectionem, quam habet Deus erga nos, 1 ep. IV, 16. Quae exempla virtualiter vniversalia sunt, iuxta illud Pauli, Rom. XV, 4. Antithesis est Pontificiorum, negantium, vllum hominem fidei suae infallibiliter certum esse, nisi noua reuelatione, fides, quam privilegiatam & specialem vocant, a Deo ipsi manifestetur.

Qui obiiciunt: I. Quidquid in sacris litteris non est reuelatum, illud nemo infallibiliter credere potest: Atqui nulli homini in S. litteris reuelatum est, quod vere credat: E. Maior patet: quia reuelatio diuina est obiectum formale fidei.

Resp. Reuelatum dicitur duobus modis: a) explicite, & formaliter: b) implicite & virtualiter. Si maior intelligatur hoc modo, quod nihil infallibiliter credendum sit, quod expresse formaliter & totidem litteris non reuelatum est, eadem falsa est; quia, cum Deus aliquid vniuersaliter reuelauit, virtualiter complexus est singularia. Vnde enuntiatio singularis, quae ex propositione vniuersali, formaliter & explicite reuelata, per bonam & pronam consequentiam elicitur, est virtualiter reuelata.

Colligo: Omnem hominem, assensu fiduciali recipientem Christum mediatorem, vere credere, diuinitus reuelatum est, Io. I, 12. Ego assensu fiduciali recipio Christum mediatorem: Ergo me vere credere, diuinitus reuelatum est, non reuelatione formali & explicita, sed virtuali & implicita.

Dicis: I. Minor non est reuelata, sed pendet a sensu humano. Resp. Non pendet a sensu humano, sed a sensu cordis renati per gratiam inhabitationis excitato. Nam qui credit in Filium, habet testimonium Spiritus S. in seipso, 1 Io. V, 10. Conclusio eius est naturae cuius est propositio maior, quae continet principium credendi. Dicis: II.

Etiam hypoerita posset prouocare ad sensum cordis sui, & dicere: Ego credo. Resp. Subiectum fidei non est hypocrita, sed peccator conuersus, serio cum dolore peccata sua detestans, & peccandi propositum abiiciens. Cum hypocrita dicit, se credere, mentitur, & similis est homini somnianti aureos montes, qui cum furgit, mendicus est. II. Quicunque fidem non sentit, non credit: Homo tentatus non credit.

Conclusio est absurda, cuius absurditas fluit a maiori. Etenim Euange'ici praesentiam fidei e sensu cordis cognoscere volunt. Resp. A fidei sensu ad fidem ipsam, praelucente S. Scriptura, recte concluditur affirmative, non item negative, cum in graui tentationum aestu fides quasi in deliquio lateat. Quam ob rem licet homo tentatus non sentiat fiduciam assensualem, sentit tamen famem & sitim iustitiae, & desiderium fidei atque gratiae: Quod desiderium in corde tentato fides est, licet sit parua & infirma, qualis erat illa patris afflicti: Credo, Domine: Iuua meam incredulitatem! Marc.

IX, 24. qui dubitabat non de fidei suae sinceritate, sed perfectione. Luctatur igitur fides in anima tentata cum incredulitate.

SUSPIRIUM

Ad te, Domine Iesu, throne gratiae & fons salutis, filiali fiducia accedo, ut accipiam misericordiam, & inveniam gratiam in auxilium opportunum, dum patet ianua salutis! Ego peccator moestissimus intueor te, qui es agnus Dei, tollens peccata mundi: Venio ad te, pauper, quia es thesaurus meus pretiosissimus; Confugio ad te, quia meum es asylum tutissimum: Recumbo in te, ut petra salutis firmissima: Acquiesco in te, ut portu tranquillissimo. Fides mea te quaerit, expetit & anhelat, tanquam mediatorem meum, caussamque reparatae gratiae divinae, & impetrandae remissionis peccatorum meorum! Remitte mihi, Deus misericordissime, peccata mea propter Iesum meum, & dona me aeterna salute, quae est fidei meae finis!


## 35 On Good Works, the Effects of Faith


### On the Effects of Faith, or Good Works, and Their Exercise

Q. I.

What are good works? Good works are the free acts of justified men, performed through the grace of the Holy Spirit renewing them, according to the prescription of the divine law, with true faith in Christ shining before them, for the honor of God and the edification of men.

I. The works of regenerated and justified men are called good not absolutely, as if they were perfectly good; but in their own kind, because a) they derive their origin from the good Spirit of God, Ps. 143:10; b) they proceed from a good heart, Matt. 12:35; c) they are in some measure conformable to the good will of God, expressed in the law, Rom. 12:2; and d) they intend a good end, the glory of God. Obj.

Obj. II. By works here are understood not only external actions that strike the eyes, but the internal affections of the heart, and the motions of the will, and thus the whole obedience and inherent justice of the regenerated. Therefore, a distinction must be made between internal and external good works. The former are obvious to the eyes of God alone, and embrace the thoughts of the interior mind, the motions of the will, and the good affections of the heart: The latter are those which, conspicuous not only to the eyes of God but also of men, manifest themselves through exterior gestures, words, and external actions.

Q. II.

What is the efficient cause of good works? The principal efficient cause of good works is God a), the Father b), the Son c), and by a peculiar reason, or appropriatively, the Holy Spirit d). The subordinate secondary cause, and the subject of the denomination, is the man who is regenerated, justified, and renewed, who produces good works not by natural powers, but by supernatural ones, received in regeneration and renewal from the Holy Spirit e).

Prob. a. From Phil. 2:13. It is God who works in you both to will and to perform: Which words AUGUSTINE explains excellently, in the book on grace and free will, ch. 17. That we may will, God works without us: But when we will, that we may do, He cooperates with us: Yet without Him either working, that we may will, or cooperating, when we will, we are able to do nothing toward good works of piety.

Prob. b. God the Father works even until now, not only in the kingdom of power, but also in the kingdom of grace and glory, John 15:17. He purges the branches in Christ, that they may bear more fruit, John 15:2. We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath prepared that we should walk in them, Eph. 2:10. Prob. c.

Christ says, John 15:5. I am the vine, ye are the branches. He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: For without me ye can do nothing. Christ flows into the renewed man, as the vine into the branch. Whence what species of works does not proceed from Christ, as the vine, through a gracious influx into the branch, is not reckoned by the name of a good work. Prob. d.

Good works are the fruits of the Spirit, Gal. 5:22. who dwells in the regenerate, as in a temple, 1 Cor. 3:16. He moves them, that they may act, Rom. 8:14. He helps their infirmities, ibid. v. 26. Prob. e. The secondary cause of good works is the man who is regenerate, justified, and renewed. For the man regenerate in Christ Jesus is created unto good works, Eph. 2: 10. The Apostle speaks of regeneration, which is as it were a new creation. The justified man shows his faith by good works, James 2: 19. The renewed man crucifies his flesh with its passions and concupiscences. Whence living by the Spirit, he walks in the Spirit, Gal. 5: 25. To walk in the Spirit signifies to exercise the works of the spiritual life, and by them to testify to the grace of the indwelling Spirit. But the renewed man is the secondary cause of good works; because he is subordinated to God, and the grace of God moves the man before he, moved by grace, acts. AUGUSTINE teaches this in his book on Correction and Grace, ch. 2. Let them understand, if they are children of God, that they are moved by the Spirit of God, so that they may do what is to be done, and when they have done it, they may give thanks to Him by whom they are moved: for they are moved, that they may act, not that they themselves do nothing. Meanwhile, however, that synergy of the regenerate in good works is by no means excluded, but requires the perpetual aid of the Holy Spirit. Quæst.

Latin:

Quaest. I.

Quid sunt bona opera? Bona opera sunt actus hominum iustificatorum liberi, per gratiam Spiritus S. renouantem, ad praescriptum legis divinae, praelucente vera in Christum fide, praestiti, in honorem Dei & hominum aedificationem. Obs.

I. Opera hominum renatorum & iustificatorum dicuntur bona non absolute, quasi perfecte bona sint; sed in suo genere, quia a) originem ducunt a bono Dei Spiritu, Ps. CXLIII, 10; b) ex corde bono proueniunt, Matth. XII, 35; c) bonae Dei voluntati, lege expressae, quadantenus sunt conformia, Rom. XII, 2. & d) bonum intendunt finem, gloriam Dei. Obs.

II. Per opera hic intelliguntur non tantum externae in oculos incurrentes actiones, sed interni affectus cordis, motusque voluntatis, adeoque tota renatorum obedientia & iustitia inhaerens. Distinguendum igitur est inter bona opera interna, & externa. Illa solins Dei oculis sunt obuia, & interioris mentis cogitationes, voluntatis motus, cordisque affectus bonos complectuntur: Haec sunt, quae non solum Dei, sed hominum etiam oculis conspicua, per exteriores gestus, verba ac actiones externas se exserunt.

Quaest. II.

Quae est caussa efficiens bonorum operum? Caussa efficiens bonorum operum principalis est Deus a), Pater b), Filius c), & peculiari ratione, seu appropriatiue, Spiritus S. d). Caussa subordinata secundaria, & subiectum denominationis est homo renatus, iustificatus & renouatus, qui bona opera producit non per vires naturales, sed per supernaturales, in regeneratione & renouatione a Spiritu Sancto acceptas e).

Prob. a. Ex Phil. II, 13. Deus est, qui operatur in vobis tam velle, quam perficere: Quae verba praeclare explicat AUGUSTINUS, libr. de gratia & lib. arb. c. 17. Vt velimus, Deus fine nobis operatur: Cum autem volumus, ut faciamus, nobiscum cooperatur: Tamen fine illo vel operante, ut velimus, vel cooperante, cum volumus, ad bona pietatis opera nihil valemus.

Prob. b. Deus Pater usque adhuc operatur, non tantum in regno potentiae, sed etiam in regno gratiae & gloriae, Io. XV, 17. Ille palmites in Christo purgat, ut plures fructus ferant Io. XV, 2. Illius factura sumus, creati in Christo Iesu ad bona opera, quae praeparavit Deus, ut in iis ambulemus, Eph. II, 10.

Prob. c. Christus ait, Io. XV, 5. Ego sum vitis, vos palmites. Qui manet in me, & ego in illo, hic fert fructum multum: Quia sine me non potestis facere quidquid. Christus influit in hominem renovatum, ut vitis in palmitem. Vnde quae species operum non proficiscitur a Christo, tanquam vite, per gratiosum influxum in palmitem, boni operis nomine non censetur.

Prob. d. Bona opera sunt fructus Spiritus, Gal. V, 22. qui in renatis, tanquam in templo habitat, 1 Cor. III, 16. agit eos, ut agant, Rom. VIII, 14. auxiliatur infirmitatibus eorum, ibid. v. 26. Prob. e. Causa secundaria bonorum operum est homo renatus, iustificatus & renovatus. Etenim homo renatus in Christo Iesu creatus est ad bona opera, Eph. II, 10. Loquitur Apostolus de regeneratione, quae nova quasi creatio est. Homo iustificatus fidem suam bonis operibus ostendit, Iac. II, 19. Homo renovatus crucifigit carnem suam cum passionibus & concupiscentiis. Vnde spiritu vivens spiritu ambulat, Gal. V, 25. Spiritu ambulare significat opera vitae spiritualis exercere, iisque gratiam inhabitantis Spiritus testari. Est autem homo renovatus causa secundaria bonorum operum; quia Deo subordinatur, & gratia Dei prius movet hominem, quam is per gratiam motus agat. Docet hoc AVGVSTIN. in libr. de corrept. & grat. c. 2. Intelligant, si filii Dei sunt, Spiritu Dei se agi, ut, quod agendum est, agant, & cum egerint, illi, a quo aguntur, gratias agant: aguntur enim, ut agant, non ut ipsi nihil agant. Interim tamen synergia illa renatorum in operibus bonis nequaquam excludit, sed requirit perpetuum Spiritus S. auxilium.


### III. By what intervening principle does the renewed man produce good works?

The principle by which the renewed man performs good works is true and living faith in Christ , which is called the cause of good works by emanation . Obf.

The words of D. SEB. SCHMIDT in his Collegium Biblicum Posterius, p. 258, deserve to be noted here. The regenerate man, or the believer, is the principle 'Which' of good works: but his faith is the principle 'By Which' primarily. I say the principle 'By Which' primarily, that I may distinguish it from the principle 'By Which' secondarily and proximately, which are the Christian virtues, e.g., charity, in respect to the acts of charity. For faith does not produce the act of charity immediately, but mediately through charity; according to that of the Apostle: In Christ Jesus faith avails, which works through charity. Prob. a. Prob. a. From Gal.

5:6. Faith works through charity. Where it is to be accurately observed that faith, in order to the production of good works, performs a double duty. One indeed, that it determines the intellect to assent, both in general to all things which have been revealed in the sacred scriptures, and in particular to the promises concerning the gratuitous remission of sins for Christ's sake: For thus, with practical conclusions deduced, it prescribes what things are to be done and what are to be avoided, with reasons and motives added, by which the will is impelled to the pursuit of piety. In the other way, faith inclines the will itself, in which it likewise resides subjectively, to resist the depraved concupiscence of the flesh, and to do that which the intellect, concerning any spiritual object already believed, prescribes by way of a practical judgment. See BAYER in Compend. p. 780.

Prob. b. From Matt. V, 16: "Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven." Just as the sun radiates its rays, the soul its faculties, and the tree its fruits—spontaneously and without laborious effort scattering, pouring forth, and producing them from itself—so the sun of faith spontaneously emits from itself the rays of good works. For faith is something living, efficacious, and powerful, such that it is impossible for it not to be always working well. Nor does faith ask whether good works ought to be done; but before that question is even raised, it has already performed many works and is always occupied in acting, as the words of LUTHER in his preface to the Epistle to the Romans are read in Latin translation in the Formula of Concord , p. 701. Hence AMBROSE calls faith the mother of good will and just action, cited in the Augsburg Confession, Art. XX; and AUGUSTINE calls it the root and mother of good works, Epist. 143. D. KOENIG says vigorously in Theol. Posit. de fide , § 908: Regarding the influx into the production of good works, faith stands in the analogy of a form to its properties, of which it is the cause through emanation.

Latin:

Principium, quo homo renovatus bona opera patrat, est vera & viva in Christum fides , quae bonorum operum causa per emanationem dicitur .

Obs. Notari hic merentur verba D. SEB. SCHMIDII in colleg. bibl. poster. p. 258. Homo renatus, sive fidelis, est principium Quod bonorum operum: Fides autem ipsius est principium Quo primum. Dico principium Quo primum, ut distinguam a principio Quo secundo & proximo, quod sunt virtutes Christianae, v. gr. caritas, respectu actuum caritatis. Nam fides actus caritatis non producit immediate, sed mediate per caritatem; iuxta illud Apostoli: In Christo Iesu valet fides, quae per caritatem operatur.

Prob. a. Ex Gal. V, 6. Fides per caritatem operatur. Vbi accurate observandum est, quod fides, in ordine ad productionem bonorum operum, duplici munere fungatur. Vno quidem, quod intellectum determinat ad assentiendum, tum in genere omnibus, quae in scripturis sacris revelatae sunt, tum in specie promissionibus de gratuita remissione peccatorum propter Christum: Sic enim deductis conclusionibus practicis praescribit, quae agenda, quae fugienda sint, additis rationibus ac motiuis, quibus voluntas ad sectandum pietatis studium impellitur. Altero modo fides voluntatem ipsam, cui itidem subiectine inest, inclinat ad resistendum pravae concupiscentiae carnis, & agendum id, quod intellectus circa quodlibet obiectum spirituale, iam creditum, per modum iudicii practici praescribit. Vid. BAYER in Compend. p. 780.

Prob. b. Ex Matth. V, 16. Luceto lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant vestra bona opera, et glorificent Patrem vestrum, qui in caelis est. Sicut sol radios, anima facultates, arbor fructus, ultro et citra laboriosum conatum ex se spargit, fundit, profert: ita sol fidei sponte sua radios bonorum operum ex se emittit. Fides enim est quidquam vivum, efficax, potens, ita ut fieri non possit, quin semper bene operetur. Neque fides quaerit demum, an bona opera sint facienda; sed priusquam ea de re inquiratur, iam multa opera efficit, et semper in agendo est occupata, prout verba LUTHERI praefat. in epist. ad Rom. latine reddita leguntur in Form. Concord. p. 701. Proinde fidem AMBROSIUS, citante Augustana conf. artic. XX. vocat bonae voluntatis et iustae actionis genitricem: et AUGUSTINUS eam appellat bonorum operum radicem et matrem. epist. 143. Neruose inquit D. KOENIG in theol. posit. de fide. §. 908. Quoad influxum in productionem bonorum operum, habet se fides ad analogiam formae ad sua propria, quorum causa per emanationem est.


### Quaest. IV. What is the norm of good works?

The adequate and infallible norm of good works is the divine law, comprised in the Decalogue, which perfectly and sufficiently commands what is to be done and forbids what is to be avoided.

Prob. From Deut. XIII, 1: "Everything that I am commanding you, that you shall keep by doing: you shall not add to it, nor take away from it." In performing good works, one must perpetually look to the divine law, as to a mirror of the divine will and an express image of divine justice.

Latin:

Norma bonorum operum adequata, eaque infallibilis est lex divina, decalogo comprehensa, quae perfecte et sufficienter praecipit facienda, et prohibet fugienda.

Prob. Ex Deut. XIII, 1. Omne verbum, quod ego sum praecipiens vobis, hoc custodietis faciendo: Non addes super illud, neque diminishes de eo. In faciendos bonis operibus perpetuo aspicienda est lex divina, velut voluntatis divinae speculum et expressa iustitiae divinae imago.


### Quaest. V. Is conscience the norm of good works?

The conscience of a renewed man is not, indeed, the primary and simply infallible norm of good works a). It can, however, be called a secondary norm of good works, insofar as it applies the divine law to a particular or singular action, and shows what is to be done here and now b).

Prob. a. Conscience is not a norming norm, because it is normed by the divine law; nor is it an infallible norm, because due to original sin and the lapses of infirmity, the judgment of conscience is dulled even in the regenerate. Therefore the Apostle says, 1 Cor. IV, 4: "I am conscious of nothing against myself; yet I am not justified by this," i.e., the heavenly Judge is so sharp-sighted or keen that He discerns many defects in us that escape the eye of conscience. But the norm of what is to be done and what is to be avoided must be infallible.

Prob. b. "The end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and faith unfeigned," 1 Tim. I, 5. Love is born from a pure heart, i.e., one justified and renewed; from a good conscience, which, as POLE notes on this passage, is not poorly described as the conformity between the law of the mind and the law of God; and from faith that is not hypocritical, but true, which is the mother of good will and just action.

Latin:

Conscientia hominis renouati non est quidem norma bonorum operum primaria et simpliciter infallibilis a). Potest tamen dici norma secundaria bonorum operum, quatenus legem divinam actioni particulari, aut singulari applicat, et ostendit, quid hic et nunc agendum fit b).

Prob. a. Conscientia non est norma normans, quia normatur a lege divina: neque est norma infallibilis, quia a peccato originali et lapsibus infirmitatis etiam in renatis iudicium conscientiae hebetatur. Idcirco inquit Apostolus, 1 Cor. IV, 4. Nihil mihi conscius sum; sed in hoc non sum iustificatus, q. d. Iudex caelestis adeo oculatus, aut perspicax est, ut multos in nobis cernat defectus, qui conscientiae oculum fugiunt. Normam autem faciendorum et fugiendorum oportet esse infallibilem.

Prob. b. Finis praecepti est caritas ex puro corde, et conscientia bona, et fide non hypocritica, 1 Tim. I, 5. Nascitur caritas ex corde puro, i. e. iustificato et renouato; ex conscientia bona, quae, notante POLO in h. l., haud male describitur, quod fit conformitas inter legem mentis et legem Dei; ex fide non hypocritica, sed vera, quae bonae voluntatis et iustae actionis genitrix est.


### Quaest. VI. Is the Gospel the norm of good works?

The Gospel is not a norm or directive principle of good works, but is a conferring and productive principle: Conferring, because it confers the Spirit; and productive: Conferring, because it confers the Spirit

the Holy Spirit, by whose impulse, bestowing of strength, and cooperation we do good works; Productive; because it produces faith, the foundation of every good action.

I seek the proof of the assertion from the solid Declaratio Formulae Concordiae, p. 720. It must be distinctly explained what the gospel does toward the new obedience of believers, and what (as regards the works of believers) is the office of the law. For the law indeed inculcates that it is the will and commandment of God that we should walk in new life; but it does not bestow the strength and faculty by which we can begin and perform new obedience. But the Holy Spirit, who is given and received not through the preaching of the law but of the gospel, Gal. III, 5, renews the heart of man. Then the same Spirit uses the ministry of the law, that through it He may teach the regenerate, and in the decalogue show them what is the good and pleasing will of God, Rom. XII, 2, that they may know to what works they should apply themselves, which God has prepared that we should walk in them, Eph. II, 10.

Latin:

Evangelium non est norma, aut principium directiuum bonorum operum, sed est principium collatiuum, et productiuum: Collatiuum, quia confert Spiritum

Sanctum, quo impellente, vires largiente & cooperante bene operamur; Productivum; quia producit fidem, omnis bonae actionis fundamentum.

Probationem assertionis peto e solida declarat. Form. Concord. p. 720. Distincte explicandum est, quid evangelium ad novam obedientiam credentium faciat, & quodnam (quoad opera credentium) sit legis officium. Lex enim inculcat quidem, esse voluntatem & mandatum Dei, ut in nova vita ambulemus; At vires & facultatem non donat, quibus novam obedientiam inchoare & praestare possumus. Spiritus S. autem, qui non per legis, sed evangelii praedicationem datur & accipitur, Gal. III, 5. cor hominis renovat. Deinde idem Spiritus ministerio legis utitur, ut per eam renatos doceat, atque in decalogo ipsis monstret, quae sit voluntas Dei bona & ipsi placens, Rom. XII, 2. ut noverint, quibus operibus opera danda sit, quae Deus praeparavit, ut in ipsis ambulemus, Eph. II, 10.


### Q. VII. What is the form of good works?

The form, or formal notion of good works, when they are considered absolutely and in themselves, is ἐννομία [legality], or conformity with the law of God a): but when they are viewed in relation to the special complacency of God, insofar as, although they do not exactly conform to the law, they nevertheless please God, their form is faith in Christ b).

Prob. a. The goodness of every work, to be done according to the prescription of a certain norm, consists in its agreement with its norm.

Prob. b. By the very fact that good works do not exactly agree with the law, they cannot, as if by agreement with the norm, simply and absolutely please God: and therefore the form, by whose intuition they please God, is not that imperfect ἐννομία [legality], but faith in Christ. For 1) believers please God, and are not under the law, but under grace, Rom. VI, 14. Whence 2) their good works, as spiritual sacrifices, are accepted through faith in Christ, without which no one can please God, Hebr. XI, 6. And although 3) those works are imperfect and impure, they are nevertheless pleasing to God; because their stains are covered by the veil of the most perfect obedience of Christ, which the regenerate apply to themselves through faith, and make their own, and the same 4) do not do them out of the coercion of the law, but out of the renewal of the Holy Spirit, from the heart, promptly and spontaneously, Ps. CX, 3. 2 Cor. IX, 5.

Latin:

Forma, seu formalis ratio bonorum operum, quando absolute & in se considerantur, est ἐννομία, seu conformitas cum lege Dei a): quando autem relate ad specialem complacentiam Dei spectantur, quatenus, licet legi exacte non conveniant, Deo tamen placent, forma eorum est fides in Christum b).

Prob. a. Bonitas omnis operis, ad praescriptum certae normae faciendi, in convenientia ipsius cum sua norma consistit.

Prob. b. Eo ipso quod bona opera non exacte conveniunt cum lege, non possunt Deo, velut ob convenientiam cum norma, simpliciter & absolute placere: Adeoque forma, cuius intuitu Deo placent, non est ἐννομία illa imperfecta, sed fides in Christum. Nam 1) fideles placent Deo, & non sunt sub lege, sed sub gratia, Rom. VI, 14. Unde 2) bona opera ipsorum, tanquam spiritualia sacrificia, accepta sunt per fidem in Christum, sine qua Deo nemo placere potest, Hebr. XI, 6. Et licet 3) opera illa sint imperfecta & impura, Deo tamen grata sunt; quia maculae eorum velamine perfectissimae Christi obedientiae, quam renati per fidem sibi applicant, suamque faciunt, obteguntur, & iidem 4) non ex coactione legis, sed ex renovatione Spiritus S. ex animo promte & sponte ea faciunt, Ps. CX, 3. 2 Cor. IX, 5.


### Q. VIII. Are the honest works of the unregenerate truly good and do they please God?

The honest works of unregenerate men, which contribute to external discipline and the preservation of human society, are in a civil and moral sense good in some way a): yet they are not theologically and spiritually good, nor do they please God b), and thus, insofar as they are destitute of the requirements of truly good works, they are rightly called splendid sins c).

Obs. The virtues and excellent deeds of the Gentiles, e.g., the liberality of Cimon, the fortitude of Alexander, the continence of Scipio, the justice of Aristides, etc., are considered good before the human forum; but before the divine forum they are not truly good, nor do they please God.

Prob. a. From Rom. II, 14. The Gentiles, who do not have the law, τὰ τοῦ νόμου [the things of the law], those things which are of the law, they do. The Gentiles have a law not prescribed divinely, but inscribed by nature. Wherefore, with nature as their guide, τὰ τοῦ νόμου, they were able to do certain (not all) things which are of the law. Which works, though they are not renewed, even if, as regards the substance of the act, they import some conformity with the law and right reason; yet in their circumstances they fail in many ways from the rule of rectitude.

For the human will (of the unregenerate) can in some way effect civil righteousness, or that of works: It can speak about God, exhibit to God a certain worship by external work, obey magistrates and parents in choosing an external work, and can restrain its hands from murder, from adultery, from theft, as the Apology of the Augsburg Confession teaches, p.

218. Prob. b. Spiritually good works, and those acceptable to God, are 1) the fruit of the Holy Spirit, Gal. V, 22, of whose grace the unregenerate are destitute.

2) They are performed by friends of God, or by persons reconciled to God through Christ, John XV, 14; Rom. V, 10. But the unregenerate are enemies of God, Col. I, 21.

3) Good works proceed from a pure heart, a good conscience, and faith unfeigned, 1 Tim. 1, 5. But to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure, but even their mind and conscience are defiled, Tit. 1, 15. The mind of the infidel is defiled, because they do not acknowledge the true God unto salvation. Their conscience is defiled, in that they do not correctly apply the norm of the divine law to things to be done, nor do they judge incorruptly concerning things already done. Finally, they are destitute of saving faith, without which nothing pleases God, Heb. XI, 6.

4) Good works are spontaneous and free actions, 2 Cor. IX, 5. But the honest works of the Gentiles and the unregenerate are either extorted by the fear of punishment, or elicited by love and the hope of reward.

5) Truly good works are directed to the glory of God, Matt. V, 16; the unregenerate hunt for their own glory in their honest deeds: for they are proud and boastful, Rom. 1, 30.

Prob. c. The honest works of the unregenerate are called sins, because they are destitute of the requirements of truly good works. And indeed, this defect of actions is not supplied by the imputation of alien righteousness; since the unregenerate do not accept the vicarious obedience of Christ and apply it to themselves by faith, but repudiate it by their ἀπιστία [unbelief]. Now truly, whatever is not of faith is sin.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, Socinians, and Arminians, who assert that unbelieving men can perform truly good works. They argue: I. Whoever do τὰ τοῦ νόμου [the things of the law], they do good works (because ὁ νόμος, or the law, is the norm of good works): But the Gentiles, etc., Rom. II, 14. Therefore. Resp. a) Whoever do perfectly all things that are of the law, they do truly good works(*): But the Gentiles from the rule of the law

That indeed will not overcome that opposition, since something can be truly good, even if it is not perfectly good, and b. have deviated enormously from the law. b) Distinguish between a work that is civilly, or morally, good in some way, and a work that is theologically, spiritually, and evangelically good, which is the fruit of the Holy Spirit and is done while true faith in Christ shines forth. The honest works of the Gentiles are not good before the forum of heaven, but are contaminated by sins, even if they are esteemed morally good before the forum of earth.

II. If the honest works of the Gentiles are not good because they are imperfect, then neither will the works of Christians be good, because they are likewise imperfect: But the works of Christians are good, notwithstanding their imperfection: Therefore, the works of the Gentiles are also good, even if they are imperfect. I respond: I deny the consequence: because the works of Christians are called good not on account of their perfection, but because they are done sincerely to the glory of God, according to the prescription of the law, by the leading of the Holy Spirit, by persons reconciled to God through faith in Christ, from a free spirit: The works of the unregenerate lack these requirements.

III. Are the virtuous works of the unregenerate good or evil? They are not evil; because they are not discordant with the law of nature: Therefore they are good. I respond: I concede the whole argument, that they are good 1) morally to a certain extent, 2) as regards the substance of the act, which is to a certain extent conformable to the law , 3) before human judgment. But they are evil 1) spiritually, 2) as regards the circumstances, 3) before divine judgment.

IV. As to what is usually said, that one proceeds, just as a sanguine person, although he thinks neither of God nor of divine laws, is by his own nature inclined and prone to compassion and liberality: β) distinguish between moral virtue, which is the highest pursuit of obedience toward God, from the reason of conscience, illuminated by the Word of God (because God commanded this, forbade that), and civil virtue, from no other reason than political, by which a man, prudent indeed, but not religious and loving of God, regards men and the bond of human society. 3) Beware, lest you confuse these two among themselves: It is one thing to make a law, νόμον; another to do it in a legitimate way, ποιήσας, 1 Tim. 1:8, 2 Tim. 2:5. Namely, in every action that is agreeable to the law, there are joined several surrounding things, determined by laws, of which if you neglect even one, the action is not the very one which the Legislator commanded you. Therefore, it is not truly good, but that which seems good is evil, and thus a specious and splendid cause is sin. V. e.g., one must labor diligently; but if you exceed the measure, if arrogance or avarice has inflamed your mind with the pursuit of assiduous labor, if you have consumed with labor the time holy and destined for the public worship of God and for the tranquility of your own mind, you have indeed sinned greatly. This distinction of the action viewed in itself, and of the surrounding circumstances which pertain to it so that it may be truly good, declares the truth of this most certain statement: When two do the same thing, it is not the same thing. The chief of these surrounding things are: right principles, namely, trust in the grace of God reconciled through Christ, and love toward God, 1 John 5:3: the manner of acting, and finally, just ends. But the principle of every action, even if it seems most good, which a man not yet renewed undertakes and performs, is always false: Therefore, it is necessary that the whole action be false. He always acts, whatever he does, impelled by self-love (φιλαυτία), which is for him the first, indeed the only, principle of acting, and therefore a perverse self-love (φιλαυτία). From which 1) he does only that which is agreeable to his natural propensity or political reason, 2) only that which seems pleasant and profitable to him. In other things he knowingly and willingly deviates from the law, and the φρόνημα of one not yet reconciled to God cannot but be ἔχθρα εἰς Θεόν. Rom. 8:7.

Whatever is affected by rewards from God, that is good: But the honest works of the Gentiles &c. Therefore. The major is evident: because God never affects that which is evil with rewards. The minor is proved by the example of the midwives in Egypt, Exod. I, 20. Resp. 1) Those midwives were either Hebrews, as most Rabbis agree, or Egyptians by origin, yet converted to the faith of the Israelites; otherwise the Hebrew women would not have so easily entrusted themselves to them. 2) God affects the virtues of the Gentiles directed toward honesty with temporal rewards, but He does not deign to grant them eternal rewards.

V. Cornelius the Gentile performed good works. For he was religious and fearing God with all his house, and doing many alms to the people, and praying to God always, Acts X, 2. Resp. Cornelius was a proselyte, who, having rejected idolatry, had been converted and justified. He believed in the Messiah with a saving faith, but he was destitute of this dogmatic, or rather historical, faith, that Jesus of Nazareth was the Messiah, the gospel concerning Christ having not yet been widely propagated [*].

Latin:

Honesta hominum irregenitorum opera, quae ad externam disciplinam & tuendam generis humani societatem faciunt, civiliter & moraliter aliquivo modo bona sunt a): non tamen theologice & spiritualiter bona sunt, neque Deo placent b), atque adeo, quatenus requisitis operum vere bonorum destituuntur, splendida peccata recte appellantur c).

Obs. Virtutes & facta excellentia gentilium, v. gr. liberalitas Cimonis, fortitudo Alexandri, continentia Scipionis, iustitia Aristidis &c. coram foro humano bona censentur; at coram foro divino non sunt vere bona, neque Deo placent.

Prob. a. Ex Rom. II, 14. Gentes, quae legem non habent, τὰ τοῦ νόμου, ea, quae legis sunt, faciunt. Habent gentes legem non praescriptam divinitus, sed natura inscriptam. Quare natura duce τὰ τοῦ νόμου, quaedam (non omnia) quae legis sunt, facere potuerunt. Quae non renouatur opera, etsi, quoad substantiam actus, importent aliquam conformitatem cum lege & ratione recta; in circumstantiis tamen a regula rectitudinis multis modis deficiunt.

Potest enim humana voluntas (non-renatorum) aliquo modo efficere iustitiam civilem, seu operum: Potest loqui de Deo, exhibere Deo certum cultum externo opere, obedire magistratibus, parentibus, in opere externo eligendo, potest continere manus a caede, ab adulterio, a furto, docente Apol.

Aug. Conf. p. 218. Prob. b. Opera spiritualiter bona, & Deo accepta sunt 1) fructus Spiritus Sancti, Gal. V, 22. cuius gratia inregeniti desituuntur.

2) Fiunt ab amicis Dei, sive a personis, per Christum Deo reconciliatis, Io. XV, 14. Rom. V, 10. At inregeniti sunt hostes Dei, Col. I, 21.

3) Bona opera proficiscuntur ex corde puro, conscientia bona, & fide non hypocritica, 1 Tim. 1, 5. At pollutis & incredulis nihil mundum est, sed pollutae sunt illorum mens & conscientia, Tit. 1, 15. Infidelium mens est polluta, quia verum Deum salutariter non agnoscunt. Polluta est eorum conscientia, eo, quod normam legis divinae rebus agendis non recte applicant, neque de rebus actis incorrupte iudicant. Expertes denique sunt fidei faluae, sine qua Deo nihil placet, Hebr. XI, 6.

4) Bona opera sunt actiones spontaneae & liberae, 2 Cor. IX, 5. At honesta gentilium & inregenitorum opera, aut poenae formidine extorquentur, aut amore & spe mercedis eliciuntur.

5) Opera vere bona diriguntur ad gloriam Dei, Matth. V, 16. inregeniti honestis factis suam aucupantur gloriam: sunt enim superbi & gloriosi, Rom. 1, 30.

Prob. c. Honesta inregenitorum opera dicuntur peccata, quia requisitis operum vere bonorum destituuntur. Atque hic quidem defectus actionum non suppletur per imputationem iustitiae alienae; cum inregeniti obedientiam Christi vicariam non acceptent, fibique applicant fide, sed ἀπιστία sua repudient. Iam vero, quidquid non est ex fide, peccatum est.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, Socinianorum & Arminianorum, afferentium, homines infideles opera vere bona praestare posse. Qui argumentantur: I. Quicunque faciunt τὰ τοῦ νόμου, illi faciunt bona opera (quia ὁ νόμος, sive lex est norma bonorum operum): Atqui gentiles &c. Rom. II, 14. Ergo. Resp. a) Quicunque faciunt perfecte omnia, quae legis sunt, illi faciunt opera vere bona(): At gentiles a regula legis ()

Id quidem non vincet illam oppositionem, quando legis enormiter deflexerunt. b) Dist. inter opus civiliter, sive moraliter aliquo modo bonum, & opus theologice, spiritualiter & evangelice bonum, quod est fructus Spiritus Sancti & fit prælucente vera in Christum fide. Honesta gentilium opera coram foro poli non sunt bona, sed peccatis contaminata, licet coram foro soli moraliter bona æstimentur.

II. Si opera honesta gentilium non sunt bona ideo, quod sunt imperfecta, neque Christianorum opera bona erunt, quia itidem imperfecta sunt: Sed opera Christianorum sunt bona, non obstante imperfectione: Ergo & gentilium opera bona sunt, licet sint imperfecta. Resp. Neg consequentiam: quia Christianorum opera bona dicuntur non ob perfectionem, sed quia ad præscriptum legis ductu Spiritus S a personis Deo per fidem in Christum reconciliatis, ex animo libero, in gloriam Dei sincere fiunt: Quibus requisitis carent opera irregenitorum.

III. Virtuosa irregenitorum opera aut sunt bona, aut mala: Non sunt mala; quia legi naturæ non sunt difformia: Ergo sunt bona. Resp. Concedo totum argumentum, quod sint bona 1) moraliter quadantenus, 2) quoad substantiam actus legi quadantenus conformis , 3) coram iudicio humano. Sed mala sunt 1) spiritualiter, 2) quoad circumstantias, 3) coram iudicio divino.

IV. Quidquod dici solet, proficiscitur, velut sanguineus, quamvis nec de Deo, nec de legibus divinis cogitet, natura sua proclivis ac pronus est ad miserationem ac liberalitatem: β) inter virtutem moralem, quæ est summum studium obedientiæ erga Deum, ex ratione conscientiæ, verbo Dei illuminatæ (quia Deus hoc præcepit, illud vetuit), & virtutem civilem, ex ratione haud alia, quam politica, qua homo prudens quidem, at non religiosus Deique amans, respicit homines, & humanæ vinculum societatis. 3) Caue, inter se confundas hæc duo: Aliud est, νόμον, legem facere; aliud, ποιήσας, legitimo modo facere, 1 Tim. I, 8. 2 Tim. II, 5. Scilicet in omni actione, legi conveniente, coniundæ sunt plures res circumstantes, legibus determinatæ, quarum si vel unam neglexeris, actio non est ipsa, quam Legislator tibi imperavit. E. non est vere bona, sed quæ videtur bona, mala est, adeoque speciosa causa & splendida peccatum. V. g. diligenter laborandum est; sed si modum excesseris, si arrogantia, aut avaritia animum tuum studio labori assidui incenderit, si tempus sanctum, cultuique Dei publico, ac tui animi tranquillati destinatum, labore consumferis, multum sane deliquisti. Hæc distinctio actionis in se spectatæ, &, quæ ad eam, vt vere bona sit, pertinent, rerum circumstantium, declarat veritatem certissimi huius enuntiati: Cum duo faciunt idem, non est idem. Earum vero rerum circumstantium præcipuæ sunt: recta principia, nimirum fiducia in Dei reconciliati gratia per Christum, & amor in Deum, 1 Io. V, 3.: modus agendi, iustæ denique fines. Atqui principium actionis cuiusque, si ea vel maxime bona esse videatur, quam homo nondum renovatus suscipit ac perficit, semper est falsum: Falsam igitur totam actionem esse, necesse est. Agit semper, quidquid agit, φιλαυτία impulsus, quæ ipsi est primum, immo unicum agendi principium, ideoque perversa φιλαυτία. Ex quo 1) agit id solum, quod suæ propensioni naturali, aut rationi politicæ est conueniens, 2) id dumtaxat, quod ipsi gratum ac fructuosum videtur. In aliis rebus deflectit a lege sciens volensque, & nondum Deo reconciliati φρόνημα non potest non esse ἔχθρα εἰς Θεόν. Rom. VIII, 7.

IV. Quidquid praemiis a Deo afficitur, illud est bonum: Atqui honesta gentilium opera &c. Ergo. Maior est evidens: quia Deus nunquam id, quod malum est, praemiis afficit. Minor probatur exemplo obstetricum in Aegypto, Exod. I, 20. Resp. 1) Obstetricae illae vel fuerunt Hebraeae, consentibus plerisque Rabbinis, vel Aegyptiacae origine, conversae tamen ad fidem Israelitarum; alias mulieres Hebraeae illis se non ita facile credidissent. 2) Virtutes gentilium ad honestatem directas Deus praemiis temporalibus afficit, non autem dignatur illas praemiis aeternis.

V. Cornelius gentilis bona patrauit opera. Erat enim religiosus & timens Deum cum tota domo sua, faciensque eleemosynas multas populo, & orans ad Deum semper, Act. X, 2. Resp. Cornelius erat proselytus, qui reiecta idololatria conversus & iustificatus erat. Credebat in Messiam fide saluifica, sed fide hac dogmatica, fine historica, quod Iesus Nazarenus esset Messias, destituebatur, euangelio de Christo exhibito nondum late propagato [*].


### Quest. IX. Are elective works truly good works, acceptable to God?

Elective works, which each person devises for himself with a good intention, or which are done according to human traditions, are not truly good works, pleasing and approved by God.

Prob. 1) Because the adequate norm of good works is the divine law, Ps. XIX, 9. Deut. IV, 2. Therefore, whatever is commanded by divine law neither immediately and formally, nor mediately and virtually, that is not a good work, pleasing to God.

2) Because elective works are vain, and destitute of all fruit. In vain do they worship me with the commandments of men, Matt. XV, 9. Who has required these things from your hands? Is. I, 12. 3) They are expressly forbidden and rejected. Every plant, which my heavenly Father has not planted, shall be rooted up, Matt. XV, 13. By a plant not planted by God, Christ understands a work not commanded by God.

Conf. Ezech. XX, 18.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, who maintain that worship chosen at one's own discretion pleases God: whence so many elective works flourish among them, fasts, vows, brotherhoods, the worship of saints, monasticism.

I. The Patriarchs, Abel, Gen. IV, 4. Noah, Gen. VIII, 20. and others offered sacrifices to God, to which they were bound by no divine command. Therefore, the divine law does not command all good works. Resp. a) With the words of BELLARMINE from L. I. de missa cap. 2. God undoubtedly first inspired the use of sacrifices to Abel and other holy men. Divine inspiration is an internal command. b) The sacrifices offered were by faith, Heb. XI, 4. Therefore they pleased God. But sacrifices which God has not required do not please Him, Is. I, 22. From which we gather that the sacrifices had been required by God and commanded.

II. The ordinances of the church, of councils, and of bishops are to be duly observed: although they do not have an express command of God. He who hears you, says Christ, hears me, Luke X, 16. Obey your leaders, Heb. XIII, 16. Resp. Christ granted to the church, to councils, and to the Apostles themselves a power not absolute, but circumscribed by the limits of the commandments, Matt. XXVIII, 10. And St. Paul expressly testifies that it is not lawful for himself, nor for the other Apostles, to propose anything beyond the gospel received from Christ, Gal. I, 8. They are observed nevertheless those things which have been sanctioned and handed down by sincere and more ancient councils, or by the pious leaders of churches with wise counsel; not under the opinion of worship, but for the sake of εὐσχημοσύνης (decency): they are observed as adiaphora, not as necessary requirements of divine worship.

III. Whatever things are directed toward a good end with a good intention, those are truly good and pleasing to God. Elective acts are directed toward a good end with a good intention: Therefore. The major premise shines by its own light: because the goodness of an action is judged from the goodness of the end. The minor is proved by example: If someone were to piously meditate on a pilgrimage to the sepulcher of Christ, that work would not be divinely commanded, and yet it is good.

Resp. 1) A good intention, looking toward a good end, does not suffice in spiritual matters, unless that end is intended through means ordained by God. 2) A pilgrimage to the sepulcher of Christ is not evil in itself, provided that there is no added opinion of worship pleasing to God in itself, or trust in some merit, by which the grace of God and righteousness availing before God is acquired.

IV. Whatever holy men have done, that is imitable (because they provide examples of virtues): Holy men have done elective works: Therefore. The minor is proved a) by the example of the Rechabites, Jer. XXXV, 5, to whom their father Jonadab had commanded abstinence from wine, from agriculture, and from the habitation of houses. b) The Apostles commanded the Gentiles to abstain from things strangled and from blood, Acts XV, 20, which Christ, however, had never commanded.

Resp. Whatever good work holy men have done according to the prescription of the divine word, that is imitable. Thus, with the major premise limited, the minor is denied. For a) abstinence from wine, from agriculture, and from the habitation of houses are not, strictly speaking, good works, because they are nowhere prescribed in the law; but at least secondary aids, by which the sons of Jonadab were called away from drunkenness, avarice, and pride. Meanwhile, however, the Rechabites were bound to obedience by the fourth commandment of the decalogue. Their obedience was therefore not ἐθελοθρησκεία (will-worship). Nor is b) abstinence from blood and things strangled a good moral work, but it was sanctioned by the Apostles so that the Jews and converted Gentiles might the better coalesce into one body: for the Jews were greatly offended by the eating of blood and things strangled.

Latin:

Opera electitia, quae quisque bona intentione ipsemet excogitat, aut quae secundum traditiones humanas fiunt, non sunt opera vere bona, Deo grata & probata.

Prob. 1) Quia adequata norma bonorum operum est lex diuina, Ps. XIX, 9. Deut. IV, 2. Ergo quidquid lege diuina neque immediate & formaliter, neque mediate & virtualiter iubetur, id non est bonum opus, Deo placens.

2) Quia opera electitia sunt vana, & omnis frugis expertia. Frustra me colunt mandatis hominum, Matth. XV, 9. Quis requisiuit haec de manibus vestris? Es. I, 12. 3) Diserte prohibentur & reiiciuntur. Omnis planta, quam non plantauit Pater caelestis, eradicabitur, Matth. XV, 13. Per plantam a Deo non plantatam intelligit Christus opus a Deo non mandatum.

Conf. Ezech. XX, 18.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, statuentium, Deo placere cultum pro arbitratu electum: vnde tot electitia apud illos vigent, ieiunia, vota, fraternitates, cultus sanctorum, monachatus. Qui sequentibus nituntur argumentis:

I. Patriarchae, Abel, Gen. IV, 4. Noachus, Gen. VIII, 20. & alii obtulerunt Deo sacrificia, ad quae nullo mandato diuino adstricti fuerunt. E. Lex diuina non omnia bona opera praecipit. Resp. a) Verbis BELLARMINI ex L. I. de missa cap. 2. Deus primum sine dubio inspirauit Abeli, & aliis sanctis viris vsum sacrificiorum. Inspiratio diuina est mandatum internum. b) Sacrificia oblata fuerunt fide, Hebr. XI, 4. E. placuerunt Deo. Sacrificia autem, quae Deus non requisiuit, ipsi non placent, Es. I, 22. Ex quo colligimus, sacrificia fuisse requisita a Deo & mandata.

II. Ordinationes ecclesiae, conciliorum & episcoporum rite sunt obseruandae: quamuis expressum Dei mandatum non habeant. Qui vos audit, inquit Christus, me audit, Luc. X, 16. Obedite praepositis vestris, Hebr. XIII, 16. Resp. Christus ecclesiae, conciliis, ipsisque Apostolis concessit potestatem non absolutam, sed mandatorum, finibus circumscriptam, Matth. XXVIII, 10. Et S. Paullus neque sibi, neque ceteris Apostolis fas esse, praeter euangelium a Christo acceptum quidquid proponere, expresse testatur, Gal. I, 8. Obseruantur [*] ur nihilominus ea, quae vel sinceris & antiquioribus conciliis, vel a piis ecclesiarum praepositis sapienti consilio sancita & tradita sunt; non sub opinione cultus, sed εὐσχημοσύνης ergo: Observantur tanquam adiaphora, non tanquam necessaria cultus divini requisita.

III. Quaecunque bona intentione ad bonum diriguntur finem, illa sunt vere bona & Deo placentia. Actus electitii bona intentione ad bonum diriguntur finem: Ergo. Maior sua luce radiat: quia bonitas actionis ex bonitate finis diiudicatur. Minor probatur exemplo: Si quis peregrinationem ad sepulcrum Christi pie meditaretur, illud opus non esset divinitus mandatum, & tamen bonum.

Resp. 1) Bona intentio, bonum respiciens finem, in spiritualibus non sufficit, nisi per media a Deo ordinata ille finis intendatur. 2) Peregrinatio ad sepulcrum Christi per se non est mala, modo non accedat opinio cultus per se Deo grati, aut fiducia alicuius meriti, quo gratia Dei & iustitia coram Deo valens acquiratur.

IV. Quidquid fecerunt viri sancti, illud est imitabile (quia suppeditant exempla virtutum): Opera electitia fecerunt sancti: Ergo. Minor probatur a) exemplo Rechabitarum, Ier. XXXV, 5. quibus pater Ionadabus praeceperat abstinentiam a vino, ab agricultura, ab inhabitatione domuum. b) Apostoli iusserunt gentiles abstinere a suffocato & sanguine, Act. XV, 20. quod Christus tamen nunquam praeceperat.

Resp. Quodcunque bonum opus fecerunt viri sancti ad verbi divini praescriptum, illud est imitabile. Sic limitata maiore negatur minor. Nam a) abstinentia a vino, ab agricultura, a domuum inhabitatione non sunt proprie loquendo opera bona, quia nullibi in lege praescripta; sed saltim adminicula secundaria, quibus filii Ionadabi ab ebrietate, auaritia, & superbia auocarentur. Interim tamen quarto decalogi praecepto Rechabitae ad obsequium obstringebantur. Non erat itaque eorum obedientia ἐθελοθρησκεία. Neque b) abstinentia a sanguine & suffocato est bonum opus morale, sed sancita est ab Apostolis, ut Iudaei & conuersi gentiles eo melius in vnum corpus coalescerent: Iudaei enim esu sanguinis & suffocati valde offendebantur.


### Q. X. How are good works to be distinguished?

Good works are to be distinguished by reason of the object, which is God, the neighbor, and the acting man himself.

Prob. Some works pertain immediately to the love of God, others to the love of the neighbor, others to the love of ourselves, which must be considered distinctly according to the individual commandments of both tables of the decalogue. See above in this section, chapter I, Q. XXVII, and following. The Apostle Paul, having regard to the triple object of good works, gravely admonishes that we live εὐσεβῶς, piously and holily toward God: δικαίως, justly toward the neighbor: σωφρόνως, modestly, chastely, soberly toward ourselves, Tit. II, 12. For by these three adverbs the Apostle has encompassed all the duties of the Christian life. Furthermore, good works, which are comprehended by the individual commandments of the decalogue, are either internal or external. See

Latin:

Bona opera distinguenda sunt ratione obiecti, quod est Deus, proximus, & ipse homo operans.

Prob. Alia opera immediate pertinent ad dilectionem Dei, alia ad dilectionem proximi, alia ad dilectionem nostri, quae distincte consideranda sunt iuxta singula praecepta vtriusque tabulae decalogi. Vid. supra sect. huius caput I. Qv. XXVII. sqq. Apostolus Paullus habeto respectu ad triplex bonorum operum obiectum, grauiter monet, vt viuamus εὐσεβῶς pie & sancte erga Deum: δικαίως, iuste erga proximum: σωφρόνως, pudice, caste, sobrie erga nos ipsos, Tit. II, 12. His enim tribus aduerbiis Apostolus omnia vitae christianae officia complexus est. Ceterum bona opera, quae singulis decalogi praeceptis comprehenduntur, sunt vel interna, vel externa. Vid. qu. I.


### Q. I. Q. XI. Are some works of the law, others of grace, or of the spirit?

In a general sense, all good works of the regenerate and the unregenerate, considered by reason of their norm, are works of the law; but the same works, viewed by reason of the efficient cause, differ. For thus the works of the regenerate are the fruits of the spirit; but the works of the unregenerate are absolutely called works of the law.

721. There is a distinction in works because of the difference of men who strive to live according to the law and will of God. For a man not yet regenerate lives in some way according to the law of God, and therefore does the works of the law, because are mandates in this manner; And he performs such obedience out of fear of punishment, or hope of some reward: He is still under the law, as a servant, and his works are properly called works of the law by ST. PAUL; because such works have arisen from the law: And these are Cainite little saints (i.e., hypocrites).

But when a man is reborn through the Holy Spirit, and has been freed from the law, i.e., from the coercion of the law, and is now led by the Spirit of God; then he lives according to the immutable will of God revealed in the law; and all things, insofar as he is reborn, he does with a free and prompt spirit, 1 Tim. 1. 8. And such works are properly not works of the law, but works and fruits of the Spirit: Or as Paul calls them, they are called the law of the mind and the law of Christ, Rom. VI, 8. 14. For these men are no longer under the law, but under grace.

And although they are in the law, and live and walk according to the law of God, they are nevertheless not under the law, that is, they do not perform good works out of the coercion of the law.

Quest. XII. Is a good intention also to be counted among the census of good works? A good intention is to be reckoned among internal good works.

Prob. 1) A good intention is an inclination of the will, conformable to the divine law; since the law concerns not only external acts, but also most especially the internal acts of the mind and will, a good intention conformable to the divine law is a good work, not indeed external, but internal. 2) Just as an evil intention, arising from depraved desire, is a sin: So a good intention is a good work.

Quest. XIII. For what ends do we perform good works? The End of G. W. Since our good works are concerned with God, our neighbor, and ourselves, good works vary in respect to this triple object.

The ultimate and principal end of our good works is the glory of God a).

The end secondary is the edification of our neighbor b) and ourselves c). Prob. a. From Matth. V, 16. Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father, who is in heaven.

We glorify God, a) by performing prompt obedience to His will and command, 1 Thess. IV, 3. b) by declaring our gratitude, Col. III, 17. c) by imitating the holiness of God, as far as it can be done in this way of life, Levit. XIX, 2.

1 Petr. I, 15.

Prob. b. We perform good works for the sake of our neighbor, so that we may 1) love him, Levit. XIX, 18. and by loving him, relieve the afflicted, Matth.

XXV, 23.

2) scandalize no one, 1 Cor. X, 32. 3) either win over the impious with good deeds, or, if they remain obstinate, put them to shame, 1

Petr. III, 16. Tit.

II, 8. 4) confirm and edify the pious more and more, 1

Thess. V, 11. Prob. c. We perform good works for our own sake: 1) That we may declare our faith through good works, Iac.

II, 18. 2) That we may make our calling and election (insofar as it can be known, and a posteriori) firm, 2

Petr. I, 10. 3) That we may lead a life worthy of Christians who are enlightened, converted, reborn, justified, mystically united with God, and renewed, Eph.

IV, 1. Phil. I, 27.

Col. I, 10. 4) That we may obtain gratuitous, spiritual, corporal, and eternal rewards from the most benign God.

For godliness is profitable for all things, having promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come.

To the exercises of godliness are promised the corporal goods of this present life, Deut. XXVIII, 1. seqq. spiritual increases and strengthenings of grace and justice, Eph.

IV, 15. Phil. I, 6.

Eternal rewards are degrees of heavenly glory, not the common and essential glory itself, which is called χάρισμα Rom. VI, 23. 5) Lest by the omission of good works we act evilly, and bring upon ourselves temporal and eternal punishments, Matth.

III; 6. Rom.

VIII, 15. End of G. W. End of Good Works.

Latin:

Sensu generali omnia bona opera renatorum & irregenitorum, ratione normae suae considerata, sunt opera legis; sed eadem spectata ratione causae efficientis differunt. Sic enim opera regenitorum fructus spiritus; opera autem irregenitorum absolute opera legis dicuntur.

Probatioem assertionis denuo peto e solid. decl. Form. Conc. p. 721. Est discrimen in operibus propter differentiam hominum, qui secundum legem & voluntatem Dei viuere student. Homo enim nondum renatus utcunque secundum legem Dei viuit, & opera legis ideo facit, quia ad eum modum sunt mandata; Eamque obedientiam formidine poenae, aut spe praemii alicuius praestat: Is adhuc sub lege est, tanquam servus, & opera eius proprie a D. PAVLLO legis opera vocantur; quia talia opera a lege exorta sunt: Et hi sunt Cainici sanctuli (h, e. hypocritae).

Cum autem homo per Spiritum S. renatus, atque a lege, h. e. a coactione legis liberatus est, iamque a spiritu Dei agitur; tum secundum immutabilem Dei voluntatem in lege revelatam vivit; & omnia, quatenus renatus est, libero & prompto spiritu agit, 1 Tim. 1. 8. Et talia opera proprie non sunt opera legis, sed opera & fructus spiritus: Aut ut Paullus ea vocat, dicuntur lex mentis & lex Christi, Rom. VI, 8. 14. Hi enim homines non amplius sub lege sunt, sed sub gratia.

Et quamvis in lege sint, & secundum legem Dei vivant & ambulent, non tamen sub lege sunt, hoc est, bona opera ex coactione legis faciunt.

Quæst. XII. Estne bonum propositum etiam e censu bonorum operum? Bonum propositum accensendum est bonis operibus internis.

Prob. 1) Bonum propositum est intentio voluntatis, legi divinae conformis; siquidem lex non tantum actus externos, sed etiam maxime actus mentis & voluntatis internos legi divinae conformis est bonum opus non quidem externum, sed internum. 2) Sicut malum propositum, ortum e prava cupiditate, est peccatum: Ita bonum propositum est bonum opus.

Quæst. XIII. Propter quos fines bona opera facimus? Cum bona opera nostra versentur circa Deum, proximum & nosmet ipsos, respectu triplicis huius obiecti bona opera variant.

Finis ultimus & principalis nostrorum bonorum operum est gloria Dei a).

Finis secundarius est proximi b) & nostri c) aedificatio. Prob. a. Ex Matth. V, 16. Luceto lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant vestra bona opera, & glorificent Patrem vestrum, qui est in caelis.

Glorificamus Deum, a) promptam obedientiam ipsius voluntati ac mandato praestando, 1 Thess. IV, 3. b) gratitudinem nostram declarando, Col. III, 17. c) sanctitatem Dei, quoad eius in hac via vitae fieri potest, imitando, Leuit. XIX, 2.

1 Petr. I, 15.

Prob. b. Propter proximum facimus bona opera, vt eum 1) diligamus, Leuit. XIX, 18. & diligendo afflictum sublevemus, Matth.

XXV, 23.

2) neminem scandalizemus, 1 Cor. X, 32. 3) impios benefactis aut lucrifaciamus, aut, si obstinati fuerint, pudefaciamus, 1

Petr. III, 16. Tit.

II, 8. 4) pios magis magisque confirmemus & aedificemus, 1

Thess. V, 11. Prob. c. Propter nos ipsos bona opera facimus: 1) Vt fidem nostram per bona opera declaremus, Iac.

II, 18. 2) Vt vocationem & electionem nostram (quoad cognosci, & a posteriori firmam faciamus, 2

Petr. I, 10. 3) Vt dignam Christianis illuminatis, conversis, renatis, iustificatis, cum Deo mystice unitis & renovatis vitam agamus, Eph.

IV, 1. Phil. I, 27.

Col. I, 10. 4) Vt praemia gratuita, spiritualia, corporalia & aeterna a Deo benignissimo impetremus.

Nam pietas ad omnia utilis est, promissionem habens vitae praesentis & futurae.

Exercitiis pietatis promissa sunt bona praesentis huius vitae corporalia, Deut. XXVIII, 1. seqq. spiritualia augmenta & firmamenta gratiae atque iustitiae, Eph.

IV, 15. Phil. I, 6.

Aeterna praemia sunt gradus gloriae coelestis, non ipsa gloria communis & essentialis, quae χάρισμα Rom. VI, 23. dicitur. 5) Ne omissione bonorum operum male operemur, & temporales atque aeternas poenas nobis accersamus, Matth.

III; 6. Rom.

VIII, 15. Finis Bonorum Operum.


### Quest. XIV. What are the affections of good works?

Good works are, as many as there are, a) imperfect actions; b) free and spontaneous; c) necessary for those being saved.

Quest. XV. Are the works of renewed and reborn men imperfect?

The good works of reborn and renewed men neither rise to that degree of perfection that they cannot grow a); nor do they correspond entirely to the norm of the divine law b); nor are they so consummate that they can sustain the rigid examination of divine justice c); but they are imperfect d).

Proof a. From Eph. IV, 15. Being sincere in love, let us grow up in all things into Him who is the head, Christ. The scope of the Pauline apostolic institution is a more abundant progress in the minds of the hearers or readers, not only of knowledge, but also of love and good works, so that under Christ the head, to whom they are joined by faith, they may grow like members and aspire to perfection. However, as long as a member is growing, it has not yet reached the highest degree of perfection.

Proof b. From Rom. VII, 14. For we know that the law is spiritual; but I am carnal. Renewed men, being carnal in part, do not provide to the law, which demands spiritual, i.e., internal and full obedience of the heart, an obedience perfect in all numbers, because the law is weakened by the flesh, Rom.

VIII, 3. Proof c. From Ps. CXLIII, 2. Do not enter into judgment with your servant; for no one living is righteous before you. The works of the most pious King David did not shine with such purity that they could sustain the censorious examination of divine judgment.

Proof d. From Jas. III, 2. In many things we all stumble. LACTANTIUS aptly says in book IV of his Institutes, ch. 13: The mortal condition does not allow a man to be pure from every stain.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, Socinians, Schwenckfeldians, and Anabaptists, who assert the perfection of good works.

Whose principal arguments are: I. Whatever works are not perfect, they cannot be called good: But the works of the reborn are called good, Tit. III, 8. Therefore. The major premise shines with its own light; because a good thing is judged from the whole cause, an evil thing from any defect.

Response Whatever works are not perfect, they cannot be called good absolutely and simply; I concede. But the works of the reborn are called good not absolutely or simply, but in a certain way and in a certain respect, namely κατὰ τὸ ἐπικρατὲν (according to what prevails), from the stronger, or from the prevailing quality. For if a work is good in its own kind, and the spirit prevails, it will be a good work: But if a work is good in its own kind, and yet the flesh prevails (as if someone should distribute alms to a poor person, or pour out prayers, only so that he may be seen by men and receive praise from it), it will be an evil work. Nevertheless, even in that first work, if God were willing to act rigidly and judge strictly, some imperfection would be found; which, while it is not imputed to the reborn person who believes in Christ, the work is accepted by God as good on account of Christ, by whose benefit whatever stain remains in it is covered. Cf. DANNHAUER in Hodom. Pap. phantasiae IX, p. 175.

II. No good tree can bear bad fruit, says Christ, Matt. VII, 18. But a reborn man is a good tree, Ps. I, 3. Therefore. Response: 1) No perfectly good tree can bear bad fruit; I concede: But a reborn man is not perfectly good. 2) The major premise must be taken in the composite sense, or formally and reduplicatively, in this way: No good tree, in so far as it is good, can bear bad fruit; otherwise, if it is taken in the divided and material sense, -ated, that is false.

For the righteous, who are good trees, can sin venially, as adversaries admit. But venial sins are not good fruits, but evil. Furthermore, the righteous are not yet so confirmed in good that, overcome by the flesh, they cannot sin mortally.

Instance: If the works of the regenerate are evil fruits, they will not be good works, but sins, filth, and defilements. Resp.
