We do not say that the good works of the regenerate are evil fruits, or sins, per se and formally, but that they are imperfectly good works, to which some stain of sin adheres.

III. Every branch grafted into Christ bears perfect fruit, or a perfectly good work: But the regenerate are etc.

John XV, 2. E.

The Major is proven from the requisites of perfect fruits.

For spiritual branches are in Christ the vine, John XV, 4. they draw from Him the sap of grace, John IV, 14. they have sufficient warmth, Luke XXIV, 32. No impediment is present, neither internal, Rom.

VIII, 1. nor external, Rom. VIII, 38. E. nothing is lacking to regenerate men, so that they cannot bear perfectly good fruits.

Resp.

Indeed, an internal impediment is present, namely, original evil concupiscence; which, although it does not actually condemn the regenerate, yet tempts them to sin. From it, spiritual branches draw a certain vicious sap, whence they do not bear perfectly good fruits. IV.

Whatever works are like gold, silver, and precious stones remaining in the fire, and receiving a reward, those are perfect: But the works of some regenerate etc.

1 Cor. III, 12.

13. E. The Major is clear; because gold, silver, and precious stones have significant perfection compared to wood, hay, and stubble:

They are proven by fire; because they endure the fire of divine judgment: They receive a reward; because they have a proportion sufficient for reward.

Resp.

The Apostle in the cited passage does not treat of the life and works of the regenerate, but of teachers and their doctrine; which, if it is pure and uncorrupted, and consistent with the Word of God as a dogmatic foundation, is compared to gold because of its purity, preciousness, and durability.

But the work of a regenerate man (e.g., almsgiving) is a work commanded by God, and is done with a good intention, namely, to relieve an afflicted neighbor: Therefore.

The Major is established from Matt. VI, 22. If your eye is simple; your whole body will be luminous, i.e., if your intention is good, your whole work will be good.

Resp. a) Intention makes a work laudable to some extent, but not perfect; because for perfection, exact conformity with divine law is required. b) By a simple eye is not understood a right intention, but the light of the mind kindled by the Holy Spirit through the word (*); if the heart follows its guidance in desiring, the hands in doing, the tongue in speaking, the whole 1. 2 5. 16. But 1) it is most true that the right one is like the eye of an enlightened mind; the false, on the contrary, like the eye of a mind darkened by the shadows of errors.

2) If it is truly made right and consistent with the divine will, it will indeed come about that the renewed man uses means that are none other than just, and also observes with as much care as he can the manner of acting prescribed by God.

For just ends to be obtained, sufficiently apt means cannot be employed unless they are just; since indeed human wisdom will never be able to find anything better or more apt than what the most wise legislator has prescribed: Nor can there be any just means, except those destined by God for seeking and attaining some just end, or several. body is luminous, but not immediately in its totality; just as the moon in the full moon is said to be luminous, yet nonetheless joined with spots, opacity, and parallax.

VI. Whatever works are imperfectly good, on account of the adhering stain of sin, those do not please God: But the works of the regenerate please God: Therefore, they are not imperfect on account of the adhering stain of sin. The major premise is established: because the stain of sin does not please God, and therefore neither do those works infected by that stain. Response: The good works of the regenerate are considered either νομικῶς (nomikos) and legally, in so far as they are required according to the law as a norm; or εὐαγγελικῶς (euangelikos), in so far as they are considered as the works of the regenerate who believe in Christ. Viewed legally, they do not please God absolutely and simply; but secundum quid (in a certain respect), and in so far as they are conformable to the law and good: but considered evangelically, they please God absolutely and simply. For although they are imperfect in themselves, and the adhering imperfections cannot please God; yet because they proceed from faith in Christ, and are done by those who are in Christ Jesus, and in whom there is no κατάκριμα (katakrima), Rom. VIII, 1: the adhering imperfections are freely forgiven to the doers, on account of the merit of Christ, apprehended by faith, and therefore their works please God simply, as if they were entirely and in all ways perfect, on account of the merit of Christ, apprehended by faith.

VII. If anyone, with the intention that he might worship God in some singular way, performs an action that does not accord with the divine law, he himself finds a foolish means, indulging his own ingenuity; which he certainly would not have found, had not a false opinion of the end he set for himself—namely, what divine worship is and what it ought to be—deceived him. For there cannot be other means for the true manner of worshipping God, besides those which have been destined for this end by divine authority; if it were otherwise, this absurdity would follow, that there was some defect in the divine laws regarding the means commanded to us, and that man could supply that defect by his own wisdom. Likewise, if someone, with the mind that he himself might be liberal and munificent toward the poor, should steal a great sum of wealth from a rich man, since that most ample means is entirely unjust, the end itself is not truly good. For nothing is less than true liberality, to be liberal with another’s property. Besides this, there is something to be weighed accurately, which I shall briefly explain. For a man’s intention, as it is called, to be truly good, two things are required. It is not sufficient, 1) that the end which he proposes to himself be commanded by God; but it is also necessary, 2) that this commandment be known by the man, and that the man be zealous for that end for that very reason, because the divine constitution demands it so. For there can be no observance of the law and agreement of action with the law without a right and sufficient knowledge and consciousness of it. But he who has the mind to obey God in one thing, and to do that which has been commanded by God, and to do it for the reason that God has so commanded it; he will certainly burn with no less zeal to obey in all things also, led by the same reason, since God has equally commanded all those actions; by the force of this axiom: Where the reason is equal, there cannot but be an equal consequence. See James II, 10, 11. I will complete the argumentation: The end is that to which the whole action with all its surrounding circumstances pertains, nor would that action be commanded if the ends were opposed: Therefore, he who pursues a truly good and truly known end with the highest zeal, because God established it, and takes care that nothing in seeking that end is inconsistent with the divine will: he, for the same reason, will equally take care that nothing be committed by him in the whole action that does not accord with the divine will. This I take to be the meaning of Christ’s words, and this their rationale: that it is one thing when we say: if you have proposed to yourself an end truly good, as we have now explained, you will strive for the whole action to be good; but quite another thing, which the Roman Catholics, above all the Doctors of the Society of Jesus, put forward: that a good intention (which, if separated from the other things pertaining to the action, and from those commanded by God, can never be good) suffices for the whole action to be good. How absurd this is, and opposed to all reason, the necessity of the conjunction of ends and means, and of all the surrounding circumstances that constitute an integral action, can teach anyone by itself alone.

If the good works of the just were sins, God himself would sin: The consequent is a blasphemous statement: And the antecedent. The consequence is proven: because God himself works in us both to will and to do, Phil. 2:13. Resp. 1) We do not assert that the good works of the just are in themselves and formally sins, but that they are indeed good, yet vitiated by certain circumstances. 2) The defect adhering to the good works of the regenerate is not to be attributed to the first cause, which influences and operates perfectly; but to the second cause, or man, who does not perfectly receive the influx and operation of God: Just as the generation of animals is attributed to the sun, but not their vice or defect.

Latin:

Bona opera sunt, quotquot sunt, a) actiones imperfectae; b) libera & spontaneae; c) necessaria saluandis.

Quaest. XV. Suntne opera hominum renouatorum & renatorum imperfecta?

Bona opera hominum renatorum & renouatorum neque eo perfectionis gradu assurgunt, quin possint crescere a); neque ex asse normae legis diuinae respondent b); neque adeo consummata sunt, vt rigidum iustitiae diuinae examen sustineant c); sed imperfecta sunt d).

Prob. a. Ex Eph. IV, 15. Sine fuco existentes in dilectione, crescamus in ipsum (quoad omnia), qui est caput, Christus. Scopus institutionis apostolicae Paullinae est vberior in animis auditorum, aut lectorum profectus non tantum cognitionis, sed & dilectionis, atque bonorum operum, vt sub capite Christo, cui per fidem iuncti sunt, membrorum instar, crescant, & ad perfectionem adpirent. Quamdiu autem membrum crescit, tamdiu summum perfectionis gradum nondum attigit.

Prob. b. Ex Rom. VII, 14. Scimus namque, quod lex spiritualis sit; ego vero carnalis sum. Homines renouati ex parte carnales obedientiam omnibus numeris perfectam non praestant legi, spirituale i. e. internum & plenum cordis obsequium exigenti, eo quod lex per carnem infirmatur, Rom.

VIII, 3. Prob. c. Ex Ps. CXLIII, 2. Ne intra in iudicium cum seruo tuo; quia non est iustus coram te vllus viuens. Piissimi regis Dauidis opera non ea fulgebant puritate, vt examen censori iudicii diuini sustinerent.

Prob. d. Ex Iac. III, 2. In multis labimur omnes. Concinne ait LACTANTIVS libr. IV. instit. c. 13. Mortalis conditio non patitur esse hominem ab omni macula purum.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, Socinianorum, Schwenckfeldianorum & Anabaptistarum, perfectionem bonorum operum afferentium.

Quorum praecipua sunt argumenta: I. Quaecunque opera non sunt perfecta, illa non possunt vocari bona: Atqui renatorum opera dicuntur bona, Tit. III, 8. E. Maior sua luce radiat; quia bonum iudicatur ex integra causa, malum e quouis defectu.

Resp. Quaecunque opera non sunt perfecta, illa non possunt absolute & simpliciter bona vocari; concedo. Renatorum autem opera dicuntur bona non absolute, aut simpliciter, sed secundum quid & certo respectu, nempe κατὰ τὸ ἐπικρατὲν, a potiori, siue a praualente qualitate. Si enim opus fit suo genere bonum, & praualeat spiritus; erit bonum opus: Si autem fit opus suo genere bonum, & praualeat tamen caro (vt si quis eleemosynam eroget pauperi, aut preces fundat, tantum vt ab hominibus videatur, & inde laudem reportet); erit malum opus. Nihilominus etiam in illo primo opere, si rigide Deus agere vellet, & stricte iudicare, reperietur imperfectio & imperfectio nonnulla; quae dum renato, in Christum credenti, non imputatur, opus acceptum est Deo, tanquam bonum propter Christum, cuius beneficio tegitur, quidquid maculae in eo reliquum est. Conf. DANNHAUER. in hodom. Pap. phantasiae IX. p. 175.

II. Nulla bona arbor potest facere malos fructus, ait Christus, Matth. VII, 18. Atqui homo renatus est bona arbor, Ps. I, 13. E. Resp. 1) Nulla arbor perfecte bona potest facere malos fructus; concedo: At homo renatus non est perfecte bonus. 2) Maior accipienda est in sensu composito, siue formaliter & reduplicatiue, hoc modo: Nulla arbor bona, in quantum bona est, potest facere malos fructus; alias si in sensu diuiso & materialiter accipisi in sensu diuifo & materialiter accipiatur, atur, ea est falla.

Iusti enim, qui sunt arbores bonae, possunt peccare venialiter, fatentibus aduersariis. Peccata venialia autem non sunt fructus boni, sed mali. Praeterea iusti nondum sunt in bono adeo confirmati, ut a carne victi mortaliter peccare nequeant.

Instantia: Si renatorum opera sunt fructus mali, non erunt bona opera, sed peccata, sordes & inquinamenta. Resp.

Non dicimus, bona opera renatorum esse fructus malos, aut peccata, per se & formaliter, sed esse opera imperfecte bona, quibus aliqua peccati labes adhaereat.

III. Omnis palmes Christo insitus fert fructum perfectum, siue opus perfecte bonum: Atqui renati sunt &c.

Io. XV, 2. E.

Maior probatur ex requisitis perfectorum fructuum.

Nam spirituales palmites sunt in vite Christo, Io. XV, 4. trahunt ab illo succum gratiae, Io. IV, 14. habent sufficientem calorem, Luc. XXIV, 32. Nullum adest impedimentum, neque internum, Rom.

VIII, 1. neque externum, Rom. VIII, 38. E. nihil deest hominibus renatis, quo minus possint ferre fructus perfecte bonos.

Resp.

Vtique adest impedimentum internum, nempe concupiscentia praua originalis; quae licet renatum actu non damnet, tentat tamen ad peccandum. Trahunt ex illa spirituales palmites succum quendam vitiosum, vnde non ferunt fructus perfecte bonos.

IV. Quaecunque opera sunt similia auro, argento & lapidibus pretiosis in igne manentibus, & mercedem accipientibus, illa sunt perfecta: Sed quorundam renatorum opera &c.

1 Cor.

III, 12. 13. E.

Maior claret; quia aurum, argentum & lapides pretiosi prae ligno, foeno & stipula insignem habent perfectionem: Probantur igne; quia ignem iudicii diuini sustinent: Accipiunt mercedem; quia sufficientem mercedi proportionem habent.

Resp.

Apostolus l. c. non agit de vita & operibus renatorum, sed de doctoribus, eorumque doctrina; quae si pura est & incorrupta, verboque Dei, vt fundamento dogmatico, consentanea, propter puritatem, pretiositatem & durabilitatem auro comparatur.

V. Quodcunque opus a Deo praeceptum bona fit intentione, illud est perfectum: Atqui hominis renati opus (v. gr. eleemosyna) est opus a Deo praeceptum, & bona fit intentione, nimirum ad subleuandum proximum afflictum: Ergo.

Maior constat ex Matth. VI, 22. Si oculus tuus fuerit simplex; totum tuum corpus erit lucidum, i. e. si intentio tua sit bona, totum opus tuum erit bonum.

Resp. a) Intentio facit opus quadantenus laudabile, sed non perfectum; quia ad perfectionem requiritur exacta conformitas cum lege diuina. b) Per oculum simplicem non intelligitur intentio recta, sed mentis lumen a Spiritu S. per verbum accensum (); cuius ductum si sequatur cor in appetendo, manus in faciendo, lingua in dicendo, totum () Adparet quidem ex verborum cohaerentia ac scopo, similitudine ab oculo arcessita, hoc in loco, significari consilium ac propositum rectum, siue, vt vulgo dicitur, intentionem rectam; ea enim opponitur falsae, vt moris erat Pharisaeorum, v. 1. 2 5. 16. Sed 1) veridimum est, rectam illam esse velut oculum mentis illuminatae; falsam contra, tamquam oculum mentis, errorum tenebris obscurata.

2) Si vere fit recta ac voluntati diuinae consentanea, fiet profecto, vt homo renouatus mediis vtatur haud aliis, quam iustis, atque etiam modum agendi, diuinitus praescriptum, quanta potest adcuratione obseruet.

Vt rem exemplo vno atque altero illustrem: Si quis sibi videatur actionem quamdam suscepisse totum corpus est lucidum, sed non statim totaliter; sicut luna in plenilunio dicitur lucida, nihilo tamen minus coniuncta cum maculis, opaco, parallaxi,

VI. Quaecunque opera imperfecte bona sunt, propter adhaerentem peccati labem, illa Deo non placent: Sed renatorum opera Deo placent: E. non sunt imperfecta propter adhaerentem peccati labem. Maior constat: quia labes peccati Deo non placet, adeoque nec opera illa labe infecta. Resp. Bona opera renatorum considerantur vel νομικῶς & legaliter, in quantum ad legem, velut normam, exiguntur; vel εὐαγγελικῶς, in quantum considerantur, vt opera renatorum in Christum credentium. Legaliter spectata, non placent Deo absolute & simpliciter; sed secundum quid, & in tantum, in quantum legi conformia & bona sunt: euangelice autem considerata placent Deo absolute & simpliciter. Quamuis enim in se imperfecta sint, & imperfectiones adhaerentes Deo placere nequeant; quia tamen ex fide in Christum procedunt, & ab iis fiunt, qui sunt in Christo Iesu, & in quibus non est κατάκριμα, Rom. VIII, 1: imperfectiones adhaerentes condonantur operantibus gratis, propter Christi meritum, fide apprehensum, & proinde opera illorum Deo placent simpliciter, ac si prorsus & omnibus modis perfecta essent, propter meritum Christi, fide apprehensum.

VII. Si pisse eo consilio, vt Deum singulari quadam ratione colat, ea vero actio non congruat cum lege diuina, fatuum ipse medium, suo ingenio indulgens, reperit; quod certe non reperisset, nisi falsa ipsum fefellisset opinio finis sibi constituti, nimirum cultus diuini, quis & qualis esset debeat. Ad veram enim Deum colendi rationem non possunt esse alia media, praeter ea, quae diuina auctoritate ad hunc finem destinata sunt; quod si aliter esset, consequens foret hoc absurdum, vt defectus quidam esset in legibus diuinis, quantum ad media nobis praecepta, illumque defectum sua homo sapientia supplere valeret. Ita pariter, si quis ea mente, vt liberalis ipse sit & munificus erga pauperes, diuiti homini magnam opum vim furto furripiat, quum amplissimum illud medium omnino iniustum sit, etiam finis non est vere bonus. Nihil enim minus est, quam vera liberalitas, de alieno liberalem esse. Praeter ea est aliquid, adcurate ponderandum, quod breuiter explanabo. Ad hominis intentionem, quae dicitur, vt vere bona sit, ea duo requiruntur. Non sufficit, 1) eum finem, quem sibi ipse propositum intuetur, a Deo praeceptum esse; sed necesse est etiam, 2) hanc eius praeceptionem ab homine cognitam esse, eiusque finis hominem studiosum esse ob eam ipsam caussam, quoniam diuina constitutio id ita postulat. Nulla enim potest esse legis obseruantia & conuenientia actionis cum lege, fine recta ac sufficiente eius cognitione & conscientia. Atqui, cui animus est, Deo in vna re obtemperandi, atque id faciendi, quod a Deo imperatum est, & propterea faciendi, quia Deus id ita imperauit; is certe non minori ardebit studio, in omnibus etiam rebus obtemperandi, eadem ratione ductus, quoniam Deus eas actiones omnes pariter imperauit; vi huius axiomatis: Vbi par ratio est, ibi non potest non esse par quoque consequentio. Vid. Iac. II, 10. 11. Perficiam argumentationem: Finis est id, ad quod tota actio cum omnibus rebus circumstantibus pertinet, neque esset illa actio praecepta, nisi fines essent offositi: Ergo, qui finem vere bonum, vereque cognitum, ideo, quod Deus eum constituit, summo studio consectatur, ac prouidet, ne quid in eo fine quaerendo sit, voluntati diuinae non consentaneum: is profecto, ob eamdem rationem, aeque cauebit, ne quid in tota actione a se committatur, quod cum voluntate diuina non congruat. Hanc puto verborum Christi sententiam, atque hanc eius rationem esse; vt aliud quidem sit, cum dicimus: si finem tibi vere bonum, prout iam explicauimus, proposueris, toti actioni bona studebis; multo autem aliud, quod Romanocatholici, in primis ex societate Iesu Doctores, prae se ferunt: bonam intentionem (quae, si separata sit a reliquis, ad actionem pertinentibus, atque a Deo praeceptis, nunquam potest esse bona) ad bonam actionem totam sufficere. Quod quam sit absonum, omnique ratione aduersarium, vel vna quemque docere potest necessitas copulationis finium ac mediorum, omniumque, quae actionem integram constituunt, rerum circumstantium.

Si bona opera iustorum essent peccata, Deus ipse peccaret: Consequens est dictum blasphemum: Et antecedens. Consequentia probatur: quia Deus ipse in nobis operatur tam velle, quam perficere, Phil. II, 13. Resp. 1) Non afferimus, bona iustorum opera per se et formaliter esse peccata, sed esse quidem bona, circumstantiis tamen quibusdam vitiari. 2) Defectus, bonis renatorum operibus adhaerens, non est tribuendus causae primae, perfecte influenti et operanti; sed causae secundae, sive homini, influxum Dei et operationem perfecte non recipienti: Sicut soli animalium generatio, non illorum vitium, aut defectus attribuitur.


### Quaest. XVI. Are there works of supererogation?

Since the regenerate do not perform perfectly the works which they are bound by divine law to perform; much less will they perfectly execute those which they are not bound to do.

Prob. Because the divine law demands from us the highest perfection, Deut. 6:5. Matt. 22:37. Mark 12:30. Rom. 7:14. but no mortal in the infirmity of this life attains that apex of perfection; since there is no man who does not sin, 1 Kings 8:46: it is easy to conjecture that we, as wayfarers, cannot attain a degree of perfection higher than, and transcending, the precepts of God .

The antithesis is that of the Papists, who dream of works of supererogation; to whom works of supererogation are undue works, to which man is not obligated by divine precept. The Papists object:

I. Paul testifies in 1 Cor. 9:15 that he preached the gospel for free, who nevertheless could have demanded with the most equitable right compensation for his labors: Therefore the preaching of the gospel, done for free by Paul, was a work of supererogation.

Resp. According to the reason of circumstances, it is not always expedient that we do that which is permitted. Sometimes regard must be had for weak brethren, and indeed for detractors, lest anyone be offended. Paul, intending to refute the opinion of those who thought he was greedy for temporal goods, preached the gospel for free. But we are commanded by the divine word to avoid stumbling blocks or scandals for the weak, Matt. 18:7. 1 Cor. 8: 13.

II. The Samaritan says to the innkeeper, Luke 10: 35. If you spend anything more, I will repay you. Resp. a) Allegorical theology is not argumentative. b) The Greek source flows thus: Whatever else you spend, I, when I have returned, will repay you. The Samaritan is an example of a beneficent and merciful man; whatever good he confers upon the afflicted and the sick, he does according to the prescription of the divine law, Lev. 19:18. The innkeeper also does not exceed the perfection of the commandment. For while the Samaritan says: Take care of him; he certainly commands the innkeeper to see to it that nothing is lacking to the sick man. If the innkeeper, having spent two denarii, had afterwards neglected the sick man, and had not spent anything more for him, would he not have openly transgressed the commandment: Take care of him ?

Quest. XVII. Are the good works of the reborn free actions?

Good works are not actions free from the necessity of obligation or debt a); but they are called actions free from the necessity of coercion b) and immutability c), and are performed by the reborn, who have been freed from the slavery of sin by the Holy Spirit d).

Proof a. Since all men, and especially those who have been regenerated and renewed by the Holy Spirit, are debtors to perform good works; as the Epit. Form. Conc. p. 589 teaches. For good works, which are commanded in the decalogue, are not to be considered arbitrary or indifferent; so that they can be performed or omitted, or their opposites performed, without sin; but all are obligated to perform or omit those things which the law commands to be performed or omitted, and those who do otherwise sin gravely. By reason of this obligation, good works, which are commanded in the decalogue, are rightly called necessary in the reborn; which we shall show more clearly in the following question.

…Proof b. The good works of the reborn are free actions; because they are not coerced, or extorted by threats of punishment, or performed externally and indeed in appearance against the will (*). For God does not approve of such hypocritical works: But He wills that the people of the new testament be a spontaneous people, Ps. CX, 3. (*) and that they may offer spontaneous sacrifices, Ps. LIV, 8. and may perform obedience not unwillingly, or compelled, but from the heart. For God loves a cheerful giver, 2 Cor. IX, 7. Proof c. After conversion and regeneration, man is free from the necessity of immutability; since his will is no longer determined to always think and do evil, as before conversion; but he can freely choose and do good works through supernatural powers, received from the Holy Spirit; he can also choose evil works through the remnants of the flesh still clinging to him, since he is not determined toward the good in the same way as the angels. Proof d. After conversion and regeneration, there is in man freedom from the servitude of sin; because he is no longer a slave of sin, but has been liberated from that captivity and servitude through the Holy Spirit, Jo. VIII, 36. Rom. VI, 18. 2 Cor. III, 17. He can therefore, through spiritual powers received in renewal, freely cooperate with the Holy Spirit, Rom. VIII, 14. 1 Cor. XV, 10.

Latin:

Cum renati opera, ad quae praestanda lege divina adstringuntur, non obeant perfecte; multo minus ea, quae facere non tenentur, perfecte exequentur.

Prob. Quia lex divina summam a nobis exigit perfectionem, Deut. VI, 5. Matth. XXII, 37. Marc. XII, 30. Rom. VII, 14. nemo autem mortalium in hac vita infirmitate illum perfectionis apicem attingit; cum non sit homo, qui non peccet, 1 Reg. VIII, 46: coniectare facile est, quod gradum perfectionis altiorem, transcendentem praecepta Dei, nos viatores assequi nequeamus .

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, opera supererogationis somniantium; quibus opera supererogationis sunt opera indebita, ad quae homo praecepto divino non obligatur. Obiiciunt Pontificii:

I. Paullus testatur 1 Cor. IX, 15. se gratis evangelium praedicasse, qui tamen iure aequissimo laborum compensationem poscere potuit: Ergo praedicatio evangelii, facta gratis a Paulo, fuit opus supererogationis.

Resp. Pro ratione circumstantiarum non semper conducit, ut faciamus id, quod concessum est. Interdum fratrum infirmorum, quin et obtrectatorum habenda est ratio, ne quisquam offendatur. Paullus refutaturus opinionem eorum, qui existimabant, ipsum temporalibus inhiare bonis, evangelium gratis praedicabat. Sed infirmorum offendicula, aut scandala declinare verbo divino iubemur, Matth. XVIII, 7. 1 Cor. VIII, 13.

II. Samaritanus dicit hospiti, Luc. X, 35. Si quid supererogaueris, reddam tibi. Resp. a) Theologia allegorica non est argumentativa. b) Fons graecus ita fluit: Quodcunque praeterea insumseris, ego, quando reuersus fuero, restituam tibi. Samaritanus est exemplum hominis beneficii et misericordis; quidquid boni is confert in afflictum et aegrotum, facit ad praescriptum legis divinae, Leu. XIX, 18. Hospes etiam non supergreditur perfectionem mandati. Nam dum ait Samaritanus: Curam illius age; certe praecipit hospiti, vt det operam, ne quid aegro desit. Si hospes consumtis duobus denariis, postea neglexisset aegrum, nec quid amplius pro eo expendisset, nonne palam transgressus fuisset mandatum: Curam illius habe ?

Quæst. XVII. Suntne bona renatorum opera actiones liberæ?

Bona opera non sunt actiones liberæ a necessitate obligationis vel debiti a); sed dicuntur actiones liberæ a necessitate coactionis b) & immutabilitatis c), & fiunt a renatis, per Spiritum S. a seruitute peccati liberatis d).

Prob. a. Cum omnes homines, tum præcipue ii, qui per Spiritum S. regenerati sunt & renouati, ad bona opera facienda debitores sunt; docente Epit. Form. Conc. p. 589. Etenim bona opera, quæ in decalogo sunt præcepta, non sunt censenda arbitraria, aut indifferentia; vt absque peccato possint fieri, vel omitti, vel eorum opposita fieri; sed quæ agenda, vel omittenda lex præcipit, ad ea agenda, vel omittenda omnes obligantur, & qui secus faciunt, grauiter peccant. Ratione huius obligationis bona opera, quæ in decalogo sunt præcepta, recte dicuntur necessaria in renatis; id quod in sequenti quæstione clarius ostendemus.

Prob. b. Sunt bona opera renatorum actiones liberæ; quia non sunt coactæ, aut comminationibus pœnarum extortæ, vel externe, & quidem in speciem contra voluntatem factæ (*). Talia enim hypocritica opera Deus non probat: Sed vult, vt populus noui testamenti sit populus spontaneus, Pf. CX, 3. (*) & vt spontanea sacrificia offerat, Pf. LIV, 8. atque obedientiam non inuitus, aut coactus, sed ex animo præstet. Hilarem enim datorem diligit Dominus, 2 Cor. IX, 7. Prob. c. Post conuersionem & regenerationem homo liber est a necessitate immutabilitatis; cum ipsius voluntas non amplius sit determinata ad malum semper cogitandum & agendum, sicut ante conuersionem; sed potest libere eligere & facere bona opera per vires supernaturales, a Spiritu S. acceptas, potest etiam mala opera eligere per carnis reliquias adhuc in ipso hærentes, cum ad bonum non perinde, atque angeli, determinatus sit. Prob. d. Post conuersionem & regenerationem est in homine libertas a seruitute peccati; quia non amplius est seruus peccati, sed a captiuitate & seruitute illa per Spiritum S. liberatus, Io. VIII, 36. Rom. VI, 18. 2 Cor. III, 17. Potest itaque per vires spirituales, in renouatione acceptas, Spiritui S. libere cooperari, Rom. VIII, 14. 1 Cor. XV, 10.


### Quaest. XVI. Are there works of supererogation?: Question XVIII. Are good works necessary?

Question XVIII. Are good works necessary?

Good works in the regenerate are necessary by the necessity of a) command, b) debt, c) order, d) presence, e) and consequence after faith and justification (**).

Proof a. From Is. I, 17. where Jehovah says: Learn to do good. Lev. XIX, 2. You shall be holy: For I (am) holy, Jehovah, your God. Therefore, the command of God imposes upon us the necessity of doing good works.

Proof b. Since every creature owes obedience and gratitude to its Creator, especially man, who is a participant in reason, he is bound by the immense benefits of many things, namely creation, Acts XVII, 24. redemption, Luke I, 72. vocation, 1 Thess. IV, 7. regeneration, Eph. II, 10. justification, Rom. VIII, 1. to the pursuit of good works, by which God is glorified.

Proof c. From Rom. VIII, 13. If by the Spirit you mortify the deeds of the body, you shall live. God has established this order, that those who are to live eternally should, with the concurrence of the Holy Spirit, mortify the deeds of the flesh. To mortify the flesh is a noble work.

Prob. d. Good works in those who are reborn and to be saved are necessary by reason of presence, lest they lose the grace of God and faith, and fall from the hope of inheritance, although not by reason of efficacy for obtaining righteousness and salvation.

Prob. e. The pursuit of good works follows justifying faith by a necessary and inseparable bond. Paul inculcates this very thing, Tit. III, 8. This is a faithful saying, and concerning these things I want you to be confirmed, that those who have believed in God should be careful to excel in good works. The mind of the Apostle is, Those who have been gifted with true faith by the grace of the Holy Spirit, and justified by it, must necessarily walk in the way of good works, so that they may shine before others by the example of piety.

Question XIX. Are good works necessary for justification?

Good works are not necessary for justification a), because they are its effects b).

Prob. a. From Rom. III, 28. We conclude therefore, that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law.

Prob. b. Good works are the fruits of righteousness, Phil. I, 11. Fruit neither makes nor constitutes the nature of the tree, but follows it. AUGUSTINE says skillfully in the book On Faith and Works, ch. 4. Good works do not precede those who are to be justified, but follow those who have been justified.

Question XX. Are good works necessary for men who are to be saved?

Good works are necessary for men who are to be saved, that is, for those who are to be saved, as proper adjuncts of the heirs of eternal salvation a): they are not necessary for those to be saved, insofar as they are to be saved, as causes and means of salvation b).

Obs. That proposition: Good works are necessary for men who are to be saved, is true in the specificative, or material sense, by which the quality of the subject is noted; not in the reduplicative, or formal sense, by which the cause, on account of which the predicate is attributed to the subject, is indicated.

Prob. a. Blessed are the merciful; for they themselves shall receive mercy, Matt. V, 7. 8. The subject of blessedness is described in these words by a proper adjunct, which is mercy, not by the cause on account of which we receive mercy or shall see God; and therefore the words of the Savior are to be understood in the specificative, or material sense, not the reduplicative, or formal.

Prob. b. From Rom. IV, 6. Blessedness is of the man to whom God imputes righteousness without works. Paul excludes good works not only from the justification of the sinner, but also ἀπὸ τοῦ μακαρισμοῦ, from beatification. He adds the reason in v. 16, so that the promise might be firm. For the promise of blessedness would not be firm, as far as we are concerned, if it depended in any way on the condition of works.

Latin:

Quæst. XVIII. Suntne bona opera necessaria?

Bona opera in renatis sunt necessaria necessitate a) mandati, b) debiti, c) ordinis, d) præsentiæ, e) & consequentiæ post fidem & iustificationem (**).

Prob. a. Ex Es. I, 17. vbi Iehouah inquit: Discite bonum facere. Leu. XIX, 2. Sancti eritis: Nam sanctus (sum) ego Iehouah, Deus vester. Proinde mandatum Dei nobis necessitatem faciendi bona opera imponit.

Prob. b. Cum omnis creatura Creatori suo debet obsequium & gratitudinem, tum in primis homo rationis particeps ingentibus plurimorum beneficiorum, scilicet creationis, Act. XVII, 24. redemptionis, Luc. I, 72. vocationis, 1 Thess. IV, 7. regenerationis, Eph. II, 10. iustificationis, Rom. VIII, 1. nominibus, ad studium bonorum operum, quibus Deus glorificatur, obstrictus est.

Prob. c. Ex Rom. VIII, 13. Si spiritu actiones corporis mortificaueritis, viuetis. Hunc ordinem Deus sanciuit, vt æternum victuri concurrente Spiritu S. actiones carnis mortificent. Mortificare carnem insigne est opus.

Prob. d. Bona opera in renatis & saluandis sunt necessaria ratione præsentiæ, ne gratiam Dei, & fidem amittant, & spe hereditatis excidant, licet non ratione efficaciæ ad consequendam iustitiam & salutem.

Prob. e. Fidem iustificantem necessario & indiuulso nexu sequitur studium bonorum operum. Hoc ipsum inculcat Paullus, Tit. III, 8. Fidelis hic est sermo, circa hæc volo te confirmari, vt curent bonis operibus præire ii, qui crediderunt Deo. Mens Apostoli est, Qui gratia Spiritus S. donati sunt vera fide, eaque iustificati, iis necessario ambulandum est in via bonorum operum, vt aliis exemplo pietatis præluceant.

Quæst. XIX. Suntne bona opera necessaria ad iustificationem?

Bona opera ad iustificationem non sunt necessaria a), quia eiusdem sunt effecta b).

Prob. a. Ex Rom. III, 28. Concludimus ergo, fide iustificari hominem sine operibus legis.

Prob. b. Bona opera sunt fructus iustitiæ, Phil. I, 11. Fructus naturam arboris nec efficit, nec constituit, sed sequitur. Scite inquit AVGVSTIN. libr. de fide & oper. c. 4. Bona opera non præcedunt iustificandos, sed sequuntur iustificatos.

Quæst. XX. An bona opera hominibus saluandis sunt necessaria?

Bona opera necessaria sunt hominibus saluandis, hoc est, iis, qui saluandi sunt, tanquam adiuncta propria hæredum salutis æternæ a): non sunt necessaria salvandis, quatenus sunt saluandi, vt caussæ & media salutis b).

Obs. Propositio illa: Hominibus saluandis necessaria sunt bona opera, vera est in sensu specificatiuo, seu materiali, quo notatur qualitas subiecti; non in sensu reduplicatiuo, siue formali, quo caussa, propter quam prædicatum subiecto attribuitur, indigitatur.

Prob. a. Beati misericordes; quia hi ipsi misericordiam accipient, Matth. V, 7. 8. Describitur his verbis subiectum beatitudinis ab adiuncto proprio, quod est misericordia, non a caussa, propter quam misericordiam accipimus, aut Deum videbimus; adeoque verba Saluatoris intelligenda sunt in sensu specificatiuo, seu materiali, non reduplicatiuo, aut formali.

Prob. b. Ex Rom. IV. 6. Beatitudo est hominis, cui Deus imputat iustitiam sine operibus. Paullus excludit bona opera non tantum a iustificatione peccatoris, sed etiam ἀπὸ τοῦ μακαρισμοῦ, a beatificatione. Rationem addit v. 16. vt firma sit promissio. Neque enim firma, quoad nos, foret promissio beatitudinis, si hæc vlla ratione ab operum conditione penderet.


### Quaest. XVI. Are there works of supererogation?: Question XXI. Are good works necessary for salvation?

Question XXI. Are good works necessary for salvation?

Good works are not necessary for obtaining eternal salvation by necessity of means to acquire it a), nor by necessity of merit to deserve it b), nor by necessity of a condition without which it is not, to obtain it c). And therefore that phrase: Good works are necessary for salvation, is neither to be used, nor to be defended d).

Obs. One must accurately distinguish between a necessary requirement of a subject, absolute and respective. The former is that which is necessarily connected with the subject not with respect to causal efficiency, but only by reason of existence, e.g., for tasting an apple, color is necessary, but not for the tasting of the apple. For a painter, as an upright man, ears are necessary, but not for painting. Thus, for a man who is to be saved, G. W. are necessary, but not for salvation. This is that which, being necessarily connected with the subject, directly and in itself brings in a relation to a particular office, and proper effect, e.g., Diligence is necessary for the novice and the learner, and for learning. Fortitude is necessary for the soldier and for living, and for obtaining victory. Thus, Christ's active and passive obedience is necessary both for saving man and for the attainment of salvation, by necessity of merit. True faith in Christ is necessary both for saving and for salvation, by necessity of means.

Prob. a. Because faith alone is the necessary means for receiving salvation, John III, 15. He who believes in the Son of God does not perish, but has eternal life. Conf. Mark XVI, 16.

Prob. b.

Eternal life is χάρισμα, Rom. VI, 23: Χάρισμα is a gratuitous gift, obtained by no merit. Eternal life is a promised inheritance, not merited by works of the law, as Paul teaches, Gal. III, 18.: If the inheritance is from the law, it is no longer from promise. But God gratified Abraham through promise, he gave by grace. Here, the emphasis of the words must be observed. For inheritance is not obtained by merits, but accrues gratuitously. Promise is not apprehended by merits, but by faith. And what God κεχάρισαι, gave by grace, works contributed nothing to it, Rom. XI, 6. Prob. c. From Eph. II, 8. For by grace you have been saved through faith:

And this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest anyone should boast. From this arises the argument: Whoever are saved by faith through the liberality of God giving (both faith and salvation), and not by works, their salvation is not suspended on the condition of works: But the regenerate &c: Therefore. Prob. d.

That phrase: Good works are necessary for salvation, is 1) ἄγραφος, nowhere expressed in the sacred scriptures. 2) It establishes other causes of salvation than of justification, and thus conflicts with the whole apostolic doctrine, because good works are excluded from the business of both beatification and justification, Rom. IV, 6. Eph. II, 8. Tit. III, 5. 3) It deprives disturbed and afflicted consciences of the true gospel consolation, and offers an occasion for doubting God's grace. For faith cannot validly rely on our imperfect works. 4) It confirms presumption and a false opinion of one's own righteousness, and confidence in one's own dignity. For as much as we attribute to works in the matter of salvation, so much we ascribe to our own righteousness and dignity. 5) It overturns the distinction between law and gospel: Which is evident from Gal. III, 21. For if a law had been given that could make alive, then righteousness would indeed have been by the law. But the Scripture has confined all under sin, that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe. 6) It detracts from the praise of Christ's absolute perfection of merit. For if our salvation consists in Christ alone, and in no one else, Acts IV, 12. then surely our works are associated with Christ's merit in vain. 7) It has enemies of the truth as its authors, and favors their heterodox opinion. 8) It is obscure, ambiguous, slippery, and fallacious.

The antithesis is of the Papists, Socinians, Arminians, and Anabaptists, who assert the necessity of good works for obtaining eternal salvation . Who contend with us with the following arguments:

I. Whoever will not see the Lord without holiness, for them holiness is necessary to see the Lord. But regenerate man &c. Heb. XII, 14. Therefore. Resp. a) In the original text, the word ἁγιοσύνη, which denotes our work, is not found, but ἁγιασμὸς, which word signifies the operation of the Holy Spirit, and sometimes denotes the gift of holiness, Rom. VI, 19. sometimes the application of the merit of Christ through the Holy Spirit in the word of the gospel, 2 Thess. II, 13. 1 Pet. I, 2. Heb. X, 10. Both meanings fit this passage of ours very well. For we must pursue both the sanctification of the Holy Spirit, which is the application of the merit of Christ through the gospel, by which faith is not only excited, but also confirmed; and that which is the donation and augmentation of holiness, when in the order of salvation we conduct ourselves in such a way that the Holy Spirit can duly perform this work of sanctification, and is not hindered.

Therefore, one may not conclude: Without sanctification, by which God sanctifies us, no one shall see the Lord: Therefore, our good works are necessary for salvation. For if sanctification is taken as the application of the merit of Christ, the sense will be this: that no one shall see the Lord unless the application of the merit of Christ through the Holy Spirit and the gospel, by which faith is kindled, takes place. But if sanctification is taken as the donation of holiness, can we not say that the Apostle means this, that no one shall enter into eternal life and to the beatific vision unless in the perfect resurrection he is clothed with holiness? May we not argue thus: Without which no one in the other life shall see the Lord, that we must pursue also in this life: But without sanctification &c. Therefore. From which it certainly does not follow that the holiness of this life is necessary for salvation, as a condition without which not.

Conf. D. Seb. Schmid, in commentar. in h. l. p. 1349. b) Suppose, by ἁγιασμὸν (sanctification) our work is understood; yet there is no power of proof in the argument. For whoever without holiness, as a respective requirement of the man to be saved, shall not see God, to him holiness is necessary for seeing God; I concede. But whoever without holiness, as an absolute requirement of the man to be saved, shall not see God, to him holiness is necessary for seeing God; I deny. Otherwise, by the same reasoning I argue: Without risibility no one shall dispute: Therefore, risibility is necessary for disputing: Without innate gravity baptismal water shall not regenerate: Therefore, the gravity of water is necessary for regeneration. Trifles! The words: Without holiness, pertain to the description of the subject, not to the modification of the predicate, in this sense: He who is not holy shall not see the Lord; because God has established this order, that the reborn man, about to obtain through faith the beatific vision of God, should strive for holiness of life.

II. Patience is necessary to obtain the promise of salvation, Heb. X, 36. Patience is a good work: Therefore, a certain good work is necessary to obtain the promise of salvation. Resp. In the source is the word, ὑπομονή (patience/endurance). The Apostle understands in the l. c. (loco citato) the patience of light, i. e., persevering faith, or the perseverance of faith: which is clear a) from the conjugated verb, ὑπομένειν (to endure), Matt. X, 22. ὁ ὑπομείνας εἰς τέλος (he who endures to the end), whoever shall have persevered to the end, this one shall be saved: b) From the context. For the Apostle understands that ὑπομονή which he calls in v. 35 παρρησίαν (confidence), and in v. 38 πίστιν (faith), and to which he opposes ὑποστολὴν (withdrawal), or defection from the faith: c) From the purpose of the Apostle, who argues thus: Ὑπομονὴ (patience) is necessary for you. Therefore, do not cast away the confidence of faith. Which how does it proceed more conveniently than if ὑπομονὴ be the perseverance of faith?

But be it that the patience of the cross is understood, or patience, having applied an accurate analysis, two statements will emerge. The former is: The reborn have need of patience, that they may do the will of God. The latter is: Those doing the evangelical will of God, i. e., believing in Christ John VI, 28, obtain the promise.

III. Whoever by mortifying the flesh live eternally, to them good works are necessary for eternal life: But justified men &c. Rom. VIII, 13.: Therefore. The major is established: because Paul wishes the promise of eternal life to be suspended from the condition of the mortification of the flesh.

Resp. I deny the major, because for the justified and those who are to live eternally, the mortification of the flesh is indeed an absolute requirement, but not a respective one, i. e., bringing a causal relation to eternal life, as its proper effect.

Instance I. Instance I. The conditional particle, IF, denotes a condition, without which not. Resp. The particle, IF, in the cited place denotes the condition of the subject, and connects the mortification of the flesh with eternal life, not by reason of influence, merit, or means, but by reason of the order established by God, so that the proposition may be understood in a specificative, material, or subjective sense, not in a reduplicative, formal, or causal sense. Instance II. Instance

Instance II. Because good works precede eternal salvation, by an antecedence of order, they can be called necessary for salvation, as a condition without which not, which is not a cause properly so called. Resp. a) There is no positive and active condition without which not, which is not a cause. b) A virtuous moral action, such as a good work is, necessary for obtaining an effect, is not only a condition without which not, but a meritorious cause.

IV. IV. Confession is made with the mouth unto life, Rom. 10:10. Confession, which is made with the mouth, is a good work: Therefore, a certain good work is made unto life. Resp. a) An ignorance of the refutation is committed. For it is one thing to be made unto salvation; another, to be necessary for salvation. The former implies merit and means: the latter implies some sort of antecedence. Thus, the title of Doctor contributes to the estimation of a learned man, but it is not simply necessary. b) By confession is understood either faith declared by the mouth, or an adjunct of faith, and a work, pertaining to the second commandment of the decalogue. If the former opinion is assumed, the sense will be: Faith kindled in the heart receives the righteousness obtained by the merit of Christ, and afterwards with the mouth celebrates salvation, received from the Savior, and glories in the same. If the latter pleases, the mind of the Apostle is: Confession is made with the mouth unto salvation, which is in Christ, to be attested and declared.

V. V. Whoever works out their own salvation with fear and trembling, to them good works are necessary for salvation: But the regenerate do so, etc.: Therefore. The major is evident: because no one can work out their own salvation, unless the work itself is a cause of salvation. The minor is proved from Phil. 2: 12. Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. Resp. Whoever works out their own salvation by a positive and efficacious influence, to them good works are necessary for salvation; I concede. But the regenerate work out their own salvation only by the diligent use of the means of salvation; just as a sick man works out his own health not efficiently, but by admitting or receiving remedies. The Greek word, ἐργάζεσθαι, does not always signify the same thing as to effect. See Apoc. 18: 17. John 6:27. where it denotes the same thing, namely, to bestow diligent effort, or to be occupied in some matter. The Apostle therefore warns that the Philippians and all the regenerate should be occupied in the causes of salvation, in receiving and retaining the word and sacraments, not without the fear of caution, so that, to wit, they may beware of and flee from deliberate sins, by which faith is extinguished and salvation is lost.

VI. VI. For that for which faith is required, for that good works are required. But saving faith is required for obtaining salvation: Therefore. The major is clear: because those things which are conjoined, they look to the same effect. Resp. a) By denying the major, and arguing by a similar reason: For that for which eyes are required, for that ears conjoined with eyes are required: But eyes are required for seeing: Therefore also ears. b) Distinguish between the requirement of the subject absolute, and respective. Not all things, which are conjoined with the subject absolutely, as to existence, are the same regard the end. The intellect is joined with the will. The former regards and intends the cognition of the true, but the latter the appetite for the good.

VII. Good works for the obtaining of salvation are either necessary or arbitrary: But they are not arbitrary, because by omitting them man falls from salvation: Therefore, they are necessary for the obtaining of salvation.

Resp. A third option is given. Good works are neither necessary nor arbitrary for the obtaining of salvation, because they bring no causal respect to the attainment of salvation; they are, however, necessary by the necessity of command, of debt, of order, of presence, and of consequence.

VIII. If the end of the study of good works is eternal life, then certainly good works regard this end: The antecedent is true.

Therefore, the consequent is also. The consequence of the major is clear: because the end is that for whose sake the efficient cause uses means regarding the end.

The truth of the antecedent is evident from Rom. 6: 22. Resp. τὸ τέλος, the end, is spoken of ambiguously. Sometimes it denotes the end of intention, which means regard. Sometimes the end of termination, or the outcome. The Apostle wished to teach that, just as the outcome and final clause of sins is death and destruction; so eternal life follows good works, as a desired clause, since works of piety precede eternal life by order, not by causal influx.

IX. If good works precede eternal life necessarily, by the necessity of order, like a way, then certainly good works are necessary for salvation: The antecedent is true: Therefore, the consequent is also.

The reason for the consequence is: because the way by which we reach the goal necessarily regards this goal. The truth of the antecedent is manifest: because the study of good works is the path of divine commandments, Ps. 119:35.

It is the way of the Lord, by which the regenerate must walk, Ps. 143:8. BERNARD, in his book On Grace and Free Choice, says: Good works are the way of the kingdom, not the cause of reigning.

Resp. Distinguish between the way in the kingdom and to the kingdom of God. The way to the kingdom is Christ, John 14:6. Through Christ, who is the way effective by doctrine, example, and merit, we reach the goal, namely, eternal life. Good works are the way in the kingdom of grace, not regarding the goal by themselves, immediately, and causally. Although this phrase: "Good works are necessary for salvation by the necessity of order," can be excused in some part, so that the words "for salvation" do not denote an effect to be produced through works, but only the terminus of the way: it is nevertheless an ambiguous phrase, obscure, and hardly accessible to the learned.

For in the whole universe of things, there is no virtuous moral action necessary for obtaining an effect by reason of order, which is not at the same time a meritorious or moral cause of that effect. Therefore, we rightly abstain from the ambiguous phrase, and we say: Good works, by reason of order, are necessary for a man being saved, or for one who is about to attain eternal salvation.

Resp. Whatever is necessary for a man being saved, insofar as he is such, in the reduplicative sense, that is necessary for salvation. But good works are necessary for a man being saved, not insofar as he is such, but for one who is about to attain salvation, in the specificative sense.

X. It is necessary, that you have faith, that you have good works; because true faith is not without good works: Instance: Whatever is necessary for a man being saved, that is also necessary for salvation.

It is necessary, that you be justified, or attain salvation, that you have true faith: Therefore, it is necessary, that you be justified, or attain salvation, that you have good works. Resp. I deny the major, because that is just as inept as if you were to say: It is necessary, that I have a good tree, that I have fruits.

The major can be inverted: It is necessary, that you have good works, that you have true faith.

Meanwhile, good works are not necessary for having faith, but for declaring and showing it, so that it may become known, James 2:18.

Latin:

Quæst. XXI. Suntne bona opera ad salutem necessaria?

Bona opera neque necessitate medii ad acquirendam a), neque necessitate meriti ad promerendam b), neque necessitate conditionis sine qua non, ad consequendam æternam salutem sunt necessaria c). Ideoque phrasis illa: Bona opera ad salutem sunt necessaria, neque vsurpanda, neque defendenda est d).

Obs. Accurate distinguendum est inter requisitum subiecti necessarium absolutum, & respectiuum. Illud est, quod cum subiecto non respectu caussalis efficientiæ, sed tantum ratione exsistentiæ necessario connexum est, v. gr. Pomo degustando necessarius est color, sed non ad degustationem pomi. Pictori, tanquam homini integro, aures sunt necessariæ, sed non ad pingendum. Ita homini saluando B. O. sunt necessaria, sed non ad salutem. Hoc est, quod cum subiecto necessario connexum proxime & per se respectum infert ad pecumunus, propriumque effectum, v. gr. Diligentia tironi & discenti, & ad discendum est necessaria. Fortitudo militi & victuro, & ad victoriam consequendam est necessaria. Sic obedientia Christi activa & passiva tam homini salvando, quam ad consecutionem salutis est necessaria, necessitate meriti. Vera in Christum fides & salvando & ad salutem necessaria est, necessitate medii.

Prob. a. Quia sola fides est medium ad accipiendam salutem necessarium, Io. III, 15. Qui credit in Filium Dei, non perit, sed habet vitam aeternam. Conf. Marc. XVI, 16.

Prob. b. Vita aeterna est χάρισμα, Rom. VI, 23: Χάρισμα est donum gratuitum, nullo merito partum.

Vita aeterna est haereditas promissa, non operibus legis promerita, docente Paulo, Gal. III, 18.: Si ex lege est haereditas, non amplius est ex promissione. Atqui Deus Abrahamo per promissionem gratificatus est, ex gratia donauit. Vbi, obseruanda est vocum emphasis. Nam haereditas non obtinetur meritis, sed gratis obtingit. Promissio non apprehenditur meritis, sed fide. Et quod Deus κεχάρισαι, ex gratia donauit, ad id nil contulere opera, Rom. XI, 6.

Prob. c. Ex Eph. II, 8. Gratia saluati estis per fidem: Et hoc non ex vobis, Dei donum est: Non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur. Vnde nascitur argumentum: Quicunque saluantur per fidem ex liberalitate Dei donantis (tam fidem, quam salutem), non vero ex operibus, illorum salus a conditione operum suspensa non est: Atqui renati &c: Ergo.

Prob. d. Phrasis illa: Bona opera sunt ad salutem necessaria, est 1) ἄγραφος, nullibi in sacris litteris expressa. 2) Alias constituit causas saluationis, quam iustificationis, atque adeo pugnat cum tota doctrina apostolica, quia B. O. a negotio tam beatificationis, quam iustificationis excluduntur, Rom. IV, 6. Eph. II, 8. Tit. III, 5. 3) Perturbatis & afflictis conscientiis veram euangelii consolationem eripit, occasionemque praebet dubitationi de gratia Dei. Neque enim imperfectis nostris operibus fides valide inniti potest. 4) Praesumtionem & falsam opinionem de propria iustitia, & fiduciam propriae dignitatis confirmat. Quantum enim tribuimus operibus in negotio salutis, tantum adscribimus propriae iustitiae & dignitatis. 5) Discrimen legis & euangelii conuellit: Quod patescit ex Gal. III, 21. Si data esset lex, quod posset viuificare, reuera ex lege esset iustitia. Atqui concludit scriptura omnia sub peccatum, vt promissio ex fide Iesu Christi detur credentibus. 6) Merito Christi absolutae perfectionis laudem derogat. Si enim in solo Christo nostra salus, neque in alio quopiam consistit, Act. IV, 12. vtique frustra merito Christi nostra associantur opera. 7) Hostes veritatis auctores habet, eorumque heterodoxae opinioni fauet. 8) Obscura, ambigua, lubrica & fallax est.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, Socinianorum, Arminianorum & Anabaptistarum, necessitatem bonorum operum ad obtinendam aeternam salutem afferentium . Qui sequenti bus argumentis nobiscum confligunt:

I. Quicunque sine sanctimonia non videbit Dominum, illi sanctimonia ad videndum Dominum est necessaria. Atqui homo renatus &c. Hebr. XII, 14. Ergo. Resp. a) In textu originali non habetur vox ἁγιοσύνη, quae notat opus nostrum, sed ἁγιασμὸς, quae vox significat operationem Spiritus S., & interdum notat donationem sanctitatis, Rom. VI, 19. interdum applicationem meriti Christi per Spiritum S. in verbo evangelii, 2 Thess. II, 13. 1 Petr. I, 2. Hebr. X, 10. Vtraque significatio huic loco nostro optime quadrat. Nam prosequi debemus tum sanctificationem Spiritus S., quae est meriti Christi per evangelium, per quod fides non tantum excitatur, sed & confirmatur, applicatio; tum eam, quae est sanctitatis donatio & augmentatio, quando in ordine salutis nos ita gerimus, vt Spiritus S. opus sanctificationis huius rite peragere possit, nec impediatur.

Non itaque concludere licet: Sine sanctificatione, qua Deus nos sanctificat, nemo videbit Dominum: E. nostra bona opera sunt necessaria ad salutem. Nam si sanctificatio sumitur de applicatione meriti Christi; sensus hic erit: quod nemo visurus sit Dominum, nisi applicatio meriti Christi per Spiritum S. & evangelium, quo fides accenditur, fiat. Si autem sanctificatio sumatur de donatione sanctitatis; nonne dicere possumus, Apostolum hoc velle, quod nemo in vitam aeternam & ad beatificam visionem ingressurus sit, nisi in resurrectione perfecta fit indutus sanctitate? Nonne liceat nobis sic argumentari: Sine quo in altera vita nemo visurus est Dominum, id nos hac quoque in vita prosequi debemus: Atqui fine sanctificatione &c. Ergo. Vnde sane non sequitur, sanctitatem huius vitae esse ad salutem necessariam, esse conditionem fine qua non.

Conf. D. Seb. Schmid, in commentar. in h. l. p. 1349. b) Fac, per ἁγιασμὸν intelligi opus nostrum; nulla tamen vis probandi inest argumento. Nam quicunque sine sanctimonia, tanquam requisito hominis saluandi respectivo, Deum non videbit, illi sanctimonia, ad videndum Deum est necessaria; concedo. Sed quicunque sine sanctimonia, vt requisito hominis saluandi absoluto, Deum non videbit, illi sanctimonia ad videndum Deum est necessaria; nego. Alias eadem ratione argumentor: Sine risibilitate nemo disputabit: E. risibilitas ad disputandum est necessaria: Sine connata gravitate aqua baptismalis non regenerabit: E. gravitas aquae ad regenerationem est necessaria. Nugae! Verba: Sine sanctimonia, pertinent ad descriptionem subiecti, non ad modificationem praedicati, hoc sensu: Qui non est sanctus, non videbit Dominum; quia Deus hunc constituit ordinem, vt homo renatus, consecuturus per fidem visionem Dei beatificam, sanctitati vitae studeat.

II. Patientia necessaria est ad reportandam promissionem salutis, Hebr. X, 36. Patientia est bonum opus: E. quoddam bonum opus ad reportandam promissionem salutis est necessarium. Resp. In fonte est vox, ὑπομονή. Intelligit Apostolus l. c. ὑπομονὴν lucis, h. e. perseuerantem fidem, seu perseuerantiam fidei: quod liquet a) ex verbo coniugato, ὑπομένειν, Matth. X, 22. ὁ ὑπομείνας εἰς τέλος, quisquis perseuerauerit in finem, hic seruabitur: b) E contextu. Nam illam ὑπομονὴν intelligit Apostolus, quam v. 35. παρρησίαν, & v. 38. πίστιν appellat, & cui ὑποστολὴν, subductionem, vel defectionem a fide opponit: c) E scopo Apostoli, qui sic argumentatur: Ὑπομονὴ vobis est necessaria. E. nolite abiicere confidentiam fidei. Quod quomodo procedit commodius, quam si ὑπομονὴ sit perseuerantia fidei? Sed esto, quod intelligatur ὑπομονὴ crucis, siue patientia, adhibita accurata analysi duae emergent enuntiationes.

Prior est: Renatis opus est patientia, vt voluntatem Dei faciant. Posterior est: Facientes voluntatem Dei euangelicam, i. e. credentes in Christum Io. VI, 28. promissionem reportant.

III. Quicunque mortificando carnem aeternum viuunt, illis bona opera ad vitam aeternam sunt necessaria: Atqui homines iustificati &c. Rom. VIII, 13.: Ergo. Maior constat: quia Paullus promissionem vitae aeternae a conditione mortificationis carnis vult suspensam esse.

Resp. Neg. mai. quia iustificatorum & aeternum victurorum requisitum absolutum quidem est mortificatio carnis, sed non respectiuum, h. e. inferens causalem relationem ad vitam aeternam, tanquam proprium effectum. suspensam esse. Resp. Neg. mai. quia iustificatorum & æternum victurorum requisitum absolutum quidem est mortificatio carnis, sed non refpectiuum, h. e. inferens caussalem relationem ad vitam æternam, tanquam proprium effectum.

Instantia I. Instantia I. Conditionalis particula, SI, notat conditionem, sine qua non. Resp. Particula, SI, l. c. notat conditionem subiecti, & connectit mortificationem carnis cum vita æterna, non ratione influxus, meriti, aut medii, sed ratione ordinis, a Deo constituti, vt propositio intelligatur in sensu specificatiuo, materiali, vel subiectiuo, non reduplicatiuo, formali aut causali. Instantia

II. Instantia II. Quia bona opera æternam salutem antecedunt, antecessu ordinis, possunt dici necessaria ad salutem, tanquam conditio sine qua non, quæ non est causa proprie dicta. Resp. a) Non datur conditio positiua & actiua sine qua non, quæ causa non sit. b) Actio moralis virtuosa, qualis est bonum opus, ad obtinendum effectum necessaria, non est tantum conditio sine qua non, sed causa meritoria.

IV. IV. Confessio ore fit ad vitam, Rom. X, 10. Confessio, quæ ore fit, est bonum opus: E. quoddam bonum opus fit ad vitam. Resp. a) Committitur ignoratio elenchi. Nam aliud est, fieri ad salutem; aliud, esse necessarium ad salutem. Hoc infert meritum & medium: illud infert qualemcunque antecessum. Sic ad existimationem viri docti facit titulus Doctoris, sed non est simpliciter necessarius. b) Per confessionem intelligitur aut fides ore declarata, aut adiunctum fidei, & opus, ad secundum decalogi præceptum pertinens. Si prior sententia assumatur, sensus erit: Fides in corde accensa recipit iustitiam merito Christi partam, & postea ore salutem, a Salvatore acceptam, celebrat, & de eadem gloriatur. Sin posterior placeat, mens Apostoli est: Ore fit confessio ad salutem, quæ in Christo est, contestandam & declarandam .

V. V. Quicunque operantur suam salutem cum timore & tremore, illis bona opera sunt necessaria ad salutem: Atqui renati &c: Ergo. Maior constat: quia nemo salutem suam potest operari, nisi opus ipsius sit causa salutis. Minor probatur ex Phil. II, 22. Cum timore & tremore vestram salutem operamini. Resp. Quicunque salutem suam operatur positiuo & efficaci influxu, illi bona opera sunt necessaria ad salutem; concedo. At renati suam salutem operantur tantum sedula mediorum salutis usurpatione; sicut ægrotus operatur sanitatem suam non efficienter, sed admittendo, aut recipiendo remedia. Græcum verbum, ἐργάζεσθαι, non semper significat idem, quod efficere. Vid. Apoc. XVIII, 17. Io. VI, 27. vbi idem notat, quod sedulam nauare operam, vel re aliqua occupatum esse. Monet igitur Apostolus, vt Philippenses & omnes renati occupentur, in causis salutis, verbo & sacramentis recipiendis & retinendis, non fine timore cautelæ, vt scil. caueant & fugiant peccata proæretica, quibus exstinguitur fides, & salus amittitur.

VI. VI. Ad quod requiritur fides, ad id requiruntur bona opera. Sed fides saluifica requiritur ad salutem consequendam: Ergo. Maior patet: quia quæ coniunctæ sunt, ea eundem effectum respiciunt. Resp. a) Negando maiorem, & simili ratione argumentando: Ad quod requiruntur oculi, ad id requiruntur aures cum oculis coniunctæ: Sed oculi requiruntur ad videndum: Ergo & aures. b) Dist. inter requisitum subiecti absolutum, & respectiuum. Non omnia, quæ cum subiecto absolute, qua existentiam, sunt coniuncta, eundem respiciunt finem. Intellectus cum voluntate est coniunctus. Ille cognitionem veri, at hic appetitionem boni respicit & intendit.

VII. Bona opera ad salutem consequendam aut sunt necessaria, aut arbitraria: Sed non sunt arbitraria, quia iis omissis homo salute excidit: E. ad salutem consequendam sunt necessaria.

Resp. Datur tertium. Bona opera neque sunt necessaria, neque arbitraria ad salutem consequendam, quia ad consecutionem salutis nullum respectum causalem inferunt; sunt tamen necessaria necessitate mandati, debiti, ordinis, praesentiae & consequentiae.

VIII. Si studii bonorum operum finis est vita aeterna, utique bona opera hunc finem respiciunt: Antecedens est verum.

E. & consequens. Consequentia maioris est clara: quia finis est, cuius gratia causa efficiens mediis finem respicientibus utitur.

Antecedentis veritas liquet ex Rom. VI, 22. Resp. τὸ τέλος, finis, ambigue dicitur. Interdum notat finem intentionis, quem media respiciunt. Interdum finem terminationis, sive exitum. Docere voluit Apostolus, quod, quem ad modum peccatorum exitus & clausula finalis est mors atque interitus; ita bona opera sequatur vita aeterna, tanquam exoptata clausula, quoniam opera pietatis vitam aeternam ordine, non causali influxu antecedunt.

IX. Si bona opera vitam aeternam antecedunt necessario, necessitate ordinis, instar viae, utique bona opera sunt necessaria ad salutem: Antecedens est verum: E. & consequens.

Ratio consequentiae est: quia via, per quam metam attingimus, hanc metam necessario respicit. Veritas antecedentis patet: quia studium bonorum operum est semita mandatorum diuinorum, Ps.

CXXIX, 35. Est via Domini, qua renatis ambulandum est, Ps. CXLIII, 8. BERN-HARD. l. de grat. & arbitr. inquit: Bona opera sunt via regni, non causa regnandi. Resp. Dist. inter viam in regno, & ad regnum Dei.

Via ad regnum est Christus, Io. XIV, 6. Per Christum, qui est via efficax doctrina, exemplo & merito, attingimus metam, scil. vitam aeternam. Bona opera sunt via in regno gratiae, per se, proxime & causaliter metam non respiciens. Licet haec phrasis: Bona opera ad salutem sunt necessaria necessitate ordinis, aliqua ex parte excusari possit, ut verba, ad salutem, non effectum producendum per opera, sed tantum terminum viae notent: est tamen phrasis ambigua, obscura & vix eruditis pervia.

Nam in tota rerum vniversitate non datur actio moralis virtuosa ad consequendum effectum ratione ordinis necessaria, quae non simul sit causa meritoria, aut moralis illius effectus. Idcirco a phrasi ambigua merito abstinemus, & dicimus: Bona opera, ratione ordinis, necessaria sunt homini saluando, sive aeternam salutem adepturo.

Resp. Quidquid necessarium est homini saluando, quatenus tali, in sensu reduplicativo, id necessarium est ad salutem. At bona opera necessaria sunt homini saluando, non quatenus, sed qui adepturus est salutem, in sensu specificativo.

X. Necesse est, ut habeas fidem, te habere bona opera; quia vera fides non est sine bonis operibus: Instantia Quidquid necessarium est homini saluando, id etiam necessarium est ad salutem.

Necesse est, ut iustificeris, vel salutem adipiscaris, te veram fidem habere: E, necesse est, ut iustificeris, vel salutem adipiscaris, te habere bona opera. Resp. Neg. mai. quia illa perinde inepta est, ac si diceres: Necesse est, vt habeam bonam arborem, me habere fructus.

Maior inuerti potest: Necesse est, vt habeas bona opera, te habere veram fidem. Interim bona opera non sunt necessaria ad fidem habendam, sed ad declarandam & ostendendam, vt ea innotescat, Iac.

II, 8. sunt necessaria ad fidem habendam, sed ad declarandam & ostendendam, vt ea innotescat, Iac. II, 8.


### Q. XXII. Are good works necessary for the preservation of righteousness and salvation?

Our righteousness and salvation are preserved not by good works, but by the grace of God, through the Word and sacraments confirming our faith, which apprehends righteousness and salvation, and retains them once apprehended.

Proof: 1) From 1 Pet. 1:5. "You are kept by the power of God through faith for salvation." God keeps us (fortifies us with protection) by His gracious power through faith, which, as a means of grace, looks toward salvation, so that it may not be intercepted from us by the force or fraud of enemies.

2) From Rom. 5:1-2. "Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ: through whom also we have had access into this grace, in which we stand and rejoice in the hope of the glory of God." Christians, through faith, not only have access to grace, but also stand in faith, conferred out of the grace of regeneration, in the manner of sturdy soldiers who persist unmoved in the battle line, so that they do not yield even a hair's bre-

Latin:

Conservatur iustitia & salus nostra non bonis operibus, sed gratia Dei, per verbum & sacramenta confirmante fidem nostram, quae iustitiam & salutem apprehendit, apprehensam retinet.

Prob. 1) Ex 1 Petr. I, 5. Virtute Dei custodimini per fidem in salutem. Deus gratiosa sua virtute nos custodit (praesidio nos munit) per fidem, quae media gratiae respicit ad salutem, vt ne illa per vim, aut fraudem hostium nobis intercipiatur.

2) Ex Rom. V, 1. 2. Iustificati itaque fide pacem habemus cum Deo, per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum: Per quem & aditum habuimus in gratiam hanc, in qua stamus & gloriamur super spe gloriae Dei. Christiani per fidem non tantum aditum habent ad gratiam, sed etiam in fide, ex gratia regenerationis collata, stant strenuorum ritu militum, qui in acie immoti persistunt, vt ne latum quidem vnguem cedant.


### Q. XXIII. Are good works meritorious of eternal life?

The good works of reborn men, properly speaking, do not merit eternal life; because God gives this to the reborn by way of the decree of predestination a), in respect to both the right b) and the full possession, out of grace founded upon the merit of Christ d), to whom e) the requirements of merit, both all and singular, do not apply to their works.

Obj. The term "merit" is taken either properly or improperly. Merit properly so-called is an undue work, which the worker performs by his own powers for the benefit of another, so that a reward equal to the labor may correspond to it. Improperly, it signifies that which, by way of a bare antecedent and by reason of order, not by the dignity of the work, obtains or attains something. In this sense, one is said to merit who obtains or attains something from someone, even if he obtains it out of grace, or liberality, or a similar manner; e.g., a beggar merits alms by his prayers, i.e., he obtains them. In this looser sense, ecclesiastics have often used this word, merit.

AUGUSTINE, bk. 1, de grat. & libero arbitr., says: "The waters above the firmament merited so sublime a place." We, at present, use the name of merit in its proper signification.

Proof a. God "predestined us to adoption as sons by Jesus Christ to Himself, according to the good pleasure of His will," Eph. 1:5. The good pleasure of the divine will is the most merciful and most gracious will of God.

Whence arises the argument: Whoever are predestined to eternal life by the most merciful and most gracious will of God, to them eternal life is given out of grace, without the merits of works: But the reborn, etc. Therefore. The major is clear: because there is a most exact consensus and harmony between the decree and its execution.

Proof b. "We are justified freely by His grace," Rom. 3:24. In justification, the right to eternal life is conferred upon us.

I argue: Whoever are justified by divine grace, provoked by no merits of their own works, they are saved without any merits of works. But the reborn, etc. Therefore. The major is liquid: because for the same causes for which the right to eternal life is conferred upon us, for the same causes the possession of eternal life is granted to us.

Proof c. 2 Tim. 1:9. "He saved us, and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to His own purpose, and grace given to us in Christ Jesus before time began." By these words, the Apostle wishes every respect of our merit to be excluded from our salvation and calling, and only the purpose and grace of God to be considered. Christ Jesus before time began. By these words, the Apostle wishes every respect of our merit to be excluded from our salvation and calling, and only the purpose and grace of God to be considered.

Prob. d. Eternal life is called χάρισμα, a gratuitous gift, Rom. VI, 23. It is also called an inheritance, Gal. III, 18. But an inheritance is given without regard to merits.

Prob. e. Merit properly so called is an undue work, which a worker performs by his own powers for the benefit of another, so that he may receive a reward equal to his labor. But our works are due, to which we are obligated by the right of creation, redemption, vocation, regeneration, justification & renovation. Luke XVII, 10. When you have done all those things which are commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants; for we have done what we were bound to do. They are not so much our works as the works of God, working in us.

Christ says, John XV, 5. Without me you can do nothing. They procure no utility for God, Job XXXV, 7. If you are righteous, what will you give Him? Or what will He receive from your hand? They are unequal to the heavenly kingdom, just as a draught of water is unequal to meriting the kingdom of France, or of Spain.

Added to this is the fact that the lesser the perfection of our good works, the lesser becomes the συμμετρία & proportion of our impure works to the most consummate glory of heaven. Rom. VIII, 18. I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, who posit that a man not yet justified, by the natural powers of free will, can merit justification by merit of congruity; but that a justified man, by good works, as by merit of condignity, merits eternal life.

Merit of congruity, or by congruity, is so called: because it becomes congruous, and it befits God, to confer the first grace of justification upon a man working according to human virtue. Some more recent Papists reject the merit of congruity.

STAPLETON, tom. II. oper. libr. II. de iustif. c. 16. p. 265. says: Merit of congruity, with respect to first grace, has already been exploded from the Catholic schools. They call merit of condignity a work proceeding from the grace of the Holy Spirit, by which a justified person merits eternal life.

It is called of condignity, because it becomes worthy that eternal life be repaid to this person. That of the Arminians, who posit that good works indeed do not have a proportion with eternal life, if they are considered in themselves; yet they do have it, if they are accepted by God out of grace, & are considered according to evangelical moderation.

They strive to defend their opinion with the following arguments: I. The sacred pages testify that works of mercy merit some retribution. Sirach says, c. XVI, 14. All mercy will make a place for everyone according to the merit of his works. And the Apostle Heb. XIII, 16. Do not forget beneficence & communion. For with such sacrifices God is merited. The Vulgate version does not flow purely from the Greek source.

Sirach says: Πᾶση ἐλεημοσύνη ποιήσον τόπον, ἕκασος γὰρ κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ εὑρήσει. Make a place for every alms: For everyone shall find according to his works. No mention of merit is made here. Εὑρίσκειν does not mean to merit, but to find.

You say: Yet Sirach brings forward: But everyone shall find according to his works. Resp. It is one thing to find a reward according to works; it is another to find it because of works. We obtain rewards according to the qualities of the works, not because of merits.

The Apostolic passage is likewise poorly translated. The original text reads thus: Τοιαύταις γὰρ θυσίαις εὐαρεσθεῖται ὁ Θεός, for with such sacrifices God is well pleased. The Vulgate renders it barbarously: God is merited, in a passive sense, although the verb promereor is a deponent, which does not have a passive meaning.

II. Whoever are worthy of eternal life, merit it: But justified men &c. Therefore. The major is established from Luke X, 7. The laborer is worthy of his hire, i.e., he merits his hire. The minor is clear from Luke XX, 35. 2 Thess. I, 5. Apoc. III, 4. Resp. Worthiness is one thing

legal, the other evangelical. Legally, no one is worthy of the kingdom of heaven who has not rendered perfect obedience to the divine law in all respects; which, however, in this infirmity of nature, no one can render, Rom. VIII, 3. Evangelically, they are worthy, not those who have actively rendered themselves worthy of the kingdom of glory by their own merits, but those who are passively esteemed worthy out of grace on account of the merit of Christ, apprehended by true faith.

III. Every reward is acquired by the merits of works: for a reward is a recompense equal to the labor: Eternal life is a reward, Matt. V, 12; c. X, 42. Resp. a) Distinguish between eternal life considered essentially, insofar as it consists in the beatific vision of God, and considered accidentally, insofar as it denotes the accidental rewards of eternal life, or greater degrees of celestial glory. Eternal life, common to all the blessed, is nowhere called a reward, but χάρισμα (gift), Rom. VI, 23. The Savior indicates this, Matt. V, 12, when He does not say: Heaven will be the reward; but: In heaven the reward will be great. b) Distinguish between a reward acquired by debt, and one imputed by grace, Rom. IV, 4. Eternal life, considered accidentally, is called a reward promised by grace, not reckoned by debt. In the phraseology of Scripture, a reward denotes a recompense, sometimes corresponding to the merits of works, sometimes gratuitous and liberally promised. Thus, children are called a reward, Ps. CXXVII, 3. God Himself is called the reward of Abraham, Gen. XV, 1.

Instance I. Eternal life, as a reward, is rendered on account of labor performed, Matt. XX, 9. Call the laborers, and give them their reward: Where by reward is understood eternal life. Resp. The denarius and the reward, Matt. XX, do not denote eternal life: because it is given even to those who murmur and are envious, who are not heirs of eternal life.
