It is also given to the last, who had labored only one hour: Therefore not by condignity. For if the master had wished to reckon a reward proportionate to the labor by the rigor of the law, he would certainly have had to distribute more to one and less to another according to the measure of the labor exhausted. He renders, therefore, a reward promised by covenant, not one owed by the rigor of justice.

Instance II. Every promise falls into debt: Therefore, eternal life belongs to us by debt. Resp. a) A debt strictly and properly so called arises from the dignity of the work, to the performance of which someone is obligated by a certain right according to the rule of proportion and the law of commutative justice: A debt spoken of broadly and improperly arises from a gratuitous promise. AUGUSTINE indicates this distinction, lib. II. confess. c. 4. God renders debts, owing them to no one. b) Moralists warn that not every promise confers upon another a right to the thing, as if it were to be demanded as a debt. For powerful and gracious men sometimes seriously promise their recommendation, intercession, promotion, or suffrage; which, however, they do not wish to be demanded of them by any right, but wish to be imputed entirely to their humanity and truthfulness. As regards divine promises, it is indeed impossible for the immutable and most truthful God to revoke them; yet it seems too arrogant to say that a mortal seeks for himself a right against God from a promise, as SAM. PUFFENDORF judges, lib. III. de I. N. & G. c. 5. §. 6. & 7. And not even a son can sue his father if a promise is not kept, according to the judgment of DANNHAV. hodom. pap. post p. 201.

IV. Whoever will render to everyone according to works, he looks to the dignity of works in distributing rewards: But God, etc. Rom. II, 5. Matt. XVI, 27. The major premise is established: because to render according to works pertains to distributive justice, by virtue of which a reward is rendered according to the proportion of labor: Resp. a) God will render to everyone according to works, not on account of the merits of works. He will render according to the qualities of works, but not on account of works, as meritorious causes of eternal life. b) From the quality of works arises their difference. If therefore the faithful are compared with the faithful, God will render greater rewards according to purer and more numerous works: But if they are compared with unbelievers, to these, as they deserve, punishments, to those, as they are esteemed worthy out of grace, He will distribute accidental rewards, not eternal life itself.

c) When the particle, ACCORDING TO, takes on the nature of a cause, Paul expressly denies that we are saved according to our works, 2 Tim. I, 9. V. Good works are the cause of eternal life: Therefore, they merit it. The reason for the consequence is: because every virtuous moral action, which is the cause of an effect, is meritorious. The antecedent is proved from Matt. XXV, 34, 35, where Christ says: Possess the kingdom as an inheritance: For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat. Resp. 1) An inheritance is not acquired by the merits of works. 2) The particle, γὰρ, in this place is not causal, or does not denote the cause of the thing, but is argumentative and eventual, designating the reason for the consequence, or the inference a posteriori, taken from works, as fruits and testimonies of faith, which is the true cause of obtaining life.

Instance: The particle, THROUGH, is also used, which is causal, 1 Tim. II, 15. The woman shall be saved through the childbearing, if she continues in faith and charity, Acts XIV, 22. Through many afflictions we must enter into the kingdom of God. Resp. a) The particle, THROUGH, in the cited passages is not designative of a cause, but of an order divinely constituted, so that the sense may be: The woman shall be saved through childbearing, i. e., in the state divinely ordained, in which she bears children: We must enter into the kingdom of heaven amidst afflictions sent by God. b) The bearing of children is a natural work, and therefore not a merit of eternal life: And afflictions are not good works.

VI. Whatever God renders to man out of justice, He renders to him on account of the merits of works: Eternal life, etc. Therefore. The major is proved: because rewards, rendered out of justice, presuppose merits, and are equal to them. The minor is clear from 2 Thess. I, 6, 7. It is just before God to repay with affliction those who afflict you; but to you who are afflicted, rest with us. Furthermore, 2 Tim. IV, 8, eternal life is called a crown of righteousness, which God the just judge gives to those who love Him. Resp. 2 Thess. I, 7 is understood of the justice of God not commutative, founded on the merits of men, but remunerative, founded on the love of God and gratuitous divine promises. Eternal life is called a crown of righteousness, partly imputed on account of the merit of Christ, partly of the righteousness, truthfulness, and constancy with which God fulfills His promises. This crown is given to those who love Christ, not because love is the meritorious cause of salvation, but because love is a mark and testimony of saving faith.

VII. Whoever distributes rewards without regard for merits, he is a προσωπολήπτης. God is not a προσωπολήπτης (respecter of persons): Therefore, He does not distribute rewards without regard for merits. The major is proved: because he is a προσωπολήπτης who, in distributing rewards, looks to the person whom he favors, without observing merits. The minor is evident from Acts X, 34. Resp. Whoever distributes rewards, which he ought to render by right, without regard for merits, he is a προσωπολήπτης. But God owes man nothing: He regards merits not our own; since they are none, but Christ's.

VIII. Whoever lends to the Lord, he can demand the loan back by his own right. But the merciful man, etc. Prov. XIX, 17. Therefore. Resp. Distinguish between a loan properly so called, and one spoken of analogically. Speaking properly, man can lend nothing to God. Divine gratuitous compensation is called a loan analogically: For just as a man pays a loan, to which he is obligated, by right: so God repays alms out of grace.

IX. Whoever enters into eternal life through the observation of the divine commandments, his good works are meritorious of eternal life: But the reborn man, etc. Matt. XIX, 17. Therefore. The major is proved: because the observation of the divine commandments is the pursuit of good works, through which no one can enter into eternal life, unless he merits it. Resp. Neg. major. For every merit is owed by no obligation and equal to its reward. But the observation of the divine commandments is owed to those about to enter into eternal life, and unequal to the heavenly kingdom.

At the cited place the question is proposed by a young man: the observation of the divine commandments is owed to those about to enter eternal life, and unequal to the heavenly kingdom.

legal. Therefore, it is solved by Christ not from the gospel, but from a legal hypothesis. The mind of the Savior is: If by doing good you wish to enter into eternal life, keep the divine commandments perfectly; the δοκιμασία (test) of which perfection will be the selling of goods, which are to be distributed to the poor. The young man went away sorrowful, convicted of his own imperfection. For which reason, the admonition of Christ was not confirmatory, but refutatory and corrective.

X. Evil works merit eternal condemnation: Therefore, good works merit eternal salvation. The reason for the consequence is: because the reason for opposites is opposite. Resp. Paul denies the consequence, Rom. 6:23. The wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life, in Christ Jesus, our Lord. The Gentiles were being cast out of Palestine on account of injustice, yet the Israelites were not being introduced into it on account of their own justice, Deut. 9:4. The argument from opposites is therefore invalid; because evil works are evil in a perfect or intense degree, [while] good works are imperfectly good.

Latin:

Bona opera hominum renatorum, proprie loquendo, non merentur vitam aeternam; quia Deus hanc vi decreti praedestinationis a), ratione tam iuris b), quam plenae possessionis, ex gratia in merito Christi fundatae d), donat renatis e), quorum operibus etiam omnia & singula meritorum requisita non competunt.

Obi. Nomen meriti sumitur vel proprie, vel improprie. Meritum proprie dictum est opus indebitum, quod operarius propriis viribus in alterius commodum facit, vt par labori praemium respondeat. Improprie significat, quod per modum nudi antecedentis & ratione ordinis, non operis dignitate aliquid impetrat, aut consequitur. Hoc sensu mereri dicitur, qui aliquid ab aliquo impetrat, seu consequitur, etiam si id ex gratia, aut liberalitate, similive modo obtineat, v. gr. mendicus precibus eleemosynas meretur, i. e. impetrat. Quo laxiori sensu ecclesiastici saepe vsi sunt verbo hoc, meriti.

AVGVSTINVS l. 1. de grat. & libero arbitr. inquit: Aquae supra firmamentum tam sublimem locum meruerunt. Nos in praesentia nomine meriti in propria significatione vtimur.

Prob. a. Deus praedestinavit nos in adoptionem filiorum per Iesum Christum in seipsum, iuxta beneplacitum voluntatis suae, Eph. I, 5. Beneplacitum voluntatis diuinae est misericordissima & gratiosissima Dei voluntas.

Vnde nascitur argumentum: Quicunque misericordissima & gratiosissima Dei voluntate ad vitam aeternam sunt praedestinati, illis ex gratia, sine operum meritis, vita aeterna donatur: Atqui renati &c. Ergo. Maior claret: quia decreti & ipsius exsecutionis exactissimus est consensus & harmonia.

Prob. b. Iustificamur gratis gratia ipsius, Rom. III, 24. In iustificatione confertur nobis ius ad vitam aeternam.

Argumentor: Quicunque gratia diuina, nullis suorum operum meritis prouocata, iustificantur, illi sine vllis operum meritis saluantur. Atqui renati &c. Ergo. Maior est liquida: quia quibus de caussis ius ad vitam aeternam nobis confertur, iisdem de caussis possessio vitae aeternae nobis conceditur.

Prob. c. 2 Tim. I, 9. Saluos fecit nos, & vocauit nos vocatione sancta, non secundum opera nostra, sed iuxta proprium propositum, & gratiam datam nobis in Christo Iesu ante tempora saecularia. His verbis vult Apostolus omnem meriti nostri respectum a salute & vocatione nostra excludi, & solum cogitari propositum & gratiam Dei. Christo Iesu ante tempora secularia. His verbis vult Apostolus omnem meriti nostri respectum a salute & vocatione nostra excludi, & solum cogitari propositum & gratiam Dei.

Prob. d. Vita aeterna dicitur χάρισμα, donum gratuitum, Rom. VI, 23. Vocatur etiam haereditas, Gal. III, 18. Sed haereditas datur citra intuitum meritorum.

Prob. e. Meritum proprie dictum est opus indebitum, quod operarius propriis viribus in alterius commodum facit, ut par labori praemium reportet. Sed opera nostra sunt debita, ad quae iure creationis, redemptionis, vocationis, regenerationis, iustificationis & renovationis obligamur. Luc. XVII, 10. Cum feceritis omnia, quae mandata sunt vobis, dicite: Servi inutiles sumus; quia, quod debebamus facere, fecimus. Non tam sunt nostra, quam opera Dei, in nobis operantis.

Christus inquit, Io. XV, 5. Sine me nihil potestis facere. Nihil utilitatis Deo conciliant, Iob. XXXV, 7. Si iustus sis, quid dabis illi? Aut quid e manu tua accipiet? Sunt imparia regno caelesti, perinde, ac haustus aquae impar est promerendo regno Galliae, aut Hispaniae.

Accedit, quod quo minor perfectio bonorum operum nostrorum est, eo minor fit συμμετρία & proportio impurorum nostrorum operum ad consummatissimam caeli gloriam. Rom. VIII, 18. Arbitror, quod non dignae sint passiones praesentis temporis, gloria quae revelabitur in nobis.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, statuentium, hominem nondum iustificatum, naturalibus viribus liberi arbitrii, merito de congruo iustificationem posse promereri; iustificatum autem bonis operibus, tamquam merito de condigno, vitam aeternam promereri.

Dicitur autem meritum congrui, vel de congruo: quia congruum fit, Deumque deceat, homini operanti secundum virtutem humanam primam gratiam iustificationis conferre. Recentiores nonnulli Pontificii meritum congrui reiiciunt.

STAPLETONVS tom. II. oper. libr. II. de iustif. c. 16. p. 265. ait: Meritum de congruo, respectu primae gratiae, iam ex scholis catholicis explosum est. Meritum condigni vocant opus procedens ex gratia Spiritus Sancti, qua iustificatus meretur vitam aeternam.

Dicitur de condigno, quia dignum fit, huic vitam aeternam rependere. Arminianorum, statuentium, bona opera quidem non habere proportionem cum vita aeterna, si ex se considerentur; habere tamen, si ex gratia a Deo acceptentur, & secundum moderationem evangelicam considerentur. Qui opinionem suam tueri nituntur sequentibus argumentis:

I. Sacrae paginae testantur, opera misericordiae aliquam retributionem promereri. Siracides inquit, c. XVI, 14. Omnis misericordia faciet locum unicuique secundum meritum operum suorum. Et Apostolus Hebr. XIII, 16. Beneficentiae & communionis nolite oblivisci. Talibus enim hostiis promeretur Deus. Vulgata versio non fluit pure ex fonte graeco.

Siracides inquit: Πᾶση ἐλεημοσύνη ποιήσον τόπον, ἕκασος γὰρ κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ εὑρήσει. Omni eleemosynae fac locum: Vnusquisque enim secundum opera sua inveniet. Nulla hic fit mentio meriti. Εὑρίσκειν non significat mereri, sed invenire.

Dicis: Affert tamen Siracides: Sed unusquisque inveniet secundum opera sua. Resp. Aliud est, invenire praemium secundum opera; aliud est, invenire propter opera. Consequimur praemia secundum qualitates operum, non propter merita.

Locus Apostolicus itidem male versus est. Textus originalis ita sonat: Τοιαύταις γὰρ θυσίαις εὐαρεσθεῖται ὁ Θεός, talibus enim sacrificiis delectatur Deus. Vulgata barbare reddit: promeretur Deus, sensu passivo, cum tamen verbum promereor sit deponens, quod non habet significationem passivam.

II. Quicumque sunt digni vita aeterna, illam merentur: Atqui homines iustificati &c. E. Maior constat ex Luc. X, 7. Dignus est operarius mercede sua, i. e. meretur suam mercedem. Minor liquet ex Luc. XX, 35. 2 Thess. I, 5. Apoc. III, 4. Resp. Dignitas alia est Resp. Dignitas alia est

legalis, alia euangelica. Legaliter nemo dignus est regno caelorum, qui non numeris omnibus perfectam obedientiam legi diuinae praestitit; quam tamen in hac infirmitate naturae nemo praestare potest, Rom. VIII, 3. Euangelice digni sunt, non qui se meritis suis actiue reddiderunt dignos regno gloriae, sed qui passiue aestimantur digni ex gratia ob meritum Christi, vera fide apprehensum.

III. Omnis merces acquiritur meritis operum: nam merces est praemium labori aequale: Vita aeterna est merces, Matth. V, 12. c. X, 42. Resp. a) Dist. inter vitam aeternam essentialiter consideratam, prout consistit in visione Dei beatifica, & consideratam accidentaliter, prout praemia accidentalia vitae aeternae, seu maiores gradus gloriae coelestis notat. Vita aeterna omnibus beatis communis nusquam dicitur merces, sed χάρισμα, Rom. VI, 23. Indicat hoc Saluator, Matth. V, 12. dum non dicit: Caelum erit merces; sed: In caelo merces copiosa erit. b) Dist. inter mercedem ex debito adquisitam, & ex gratia imputatam, Rom. IV, 4. Vita aeterna, accidentaliter considerata, dicitur merces ex gratia promissa, non ex debito annumerata. Phrasi scripturae merces notat praemium, interdum meritis operum respondens, interdum gratuitum & liberaliter promissum. Sic liberi dicuntur merces, Ps. CXXVII, 3. Ipse Deus vocatur Abrahami merces, Gen. XV, 1.

Instantia I. Vita aeterna, tanquam merces, ob praestitum laborem redditur, Matth. XX, 9. Voca operarios, & redde illis mercedem: Vbi per mercedem intelligitur vita aeterna. Resp. Denarius & merces, Matth. XX. non notat vitam aeternam: quia datur etiam murmurantibus & inuidis, qui non sunt haeredes vitae aeternae. Datur quoque nouissimis, qui vnam tantum horam laborauerant: Ergo non ex condigno. Nam si ex rigore legis labori proportionatam annumerare voluisset dominus mercedem, vtique secundum mensuram exhausti laboris vni plus, alteri minus distribuere debuisset. Reddit ergo mercedem ex pacto promissam, non ex rigore iustitiae debitam.

Instantia II. Omne promissum cadit in debitum: E. vita aeterna ex debito nobis competit. Resp. a) Debitum stricte & proprie dictum, oritur ex dignitate operis, ad quod perfoluendum aliquis iure quodam ex regula proportionis & lege iustitiae commutatiuae obligatur: Late & improprie dictum debitum nascitur ex gratuita promissione. Indicat hanc distinctionem AVGVSTINVS. libr. II. confess. c. 4. Deus reddit debita nulli debens. b) Monent Moralistae, non omnem promissionem alteri ius conferre ad rem, velut debitam exigendam. Nam viri potentes & gratiosi interdum serio promittunt suam commendationem, intercessionem, promotionem, aut suffragium; quae tamen nolunt iure quodam abs se exigi, sed in solidum volunt humanitati ac veracitati suae imputari. Quod attinet ad promissa diuina, impossibile quidem est, Deum immutabilem & veracissimum esse reuocare; nimis tamen superbum videtur dicere, mortalem sibi ex promisso aduersus Deum ius quaerere, censente SAM. PVFFENDORE. libr. III. de I. N. & G. c. 5. §. 6. & 7. Ac ne filius quidem conuenire potest patrem, si non feruetur promissum, iudice DANNHAV. hodom. pap. post p. 201.

IV. Quicunque reddet vnicuique secundum opera, ille in distribuendis praemiis dignitatem operum respicit: Atqui Deus &c. Rom. II, 5. Matth. XVI, 27. Maior constat: quia reddere secundum opera, pertinet ad iustitiam distributiuam, vi cuius praemium secundum proportionem laboris redditur: Resp. a) Reddet Deus vnicuique secundum opera, non propter operum merita. Secundum operum qualitates reddet, sed non propter opera, tanquam caussas meritorias vitae aeternae. b) Ex qualitate operum nascitur eorum differentia. Si itaque fideles comparentur cum fidelibus, Deus reddet secundum opera puriora & plura, maiora praemia: Sin comparentur cum infidelibus, his, vt merentur, poenas, illis, vt ex gratia digni reputantur, praemia distribuet accidentalia, non ipsam vitam aeternam.

c) Quando particula, SECVNDVM, rationem causae induit, expresse negat Paullus, nos secundum opera nostra saluari, 2 Tim. I, 9. V. Bona opera sunt causa vitae aeternae: E. eam promerentur. Ratio consequentiae est: quia omnis actio moralis virtuosa, quae est causa effectus, meritoria est. Antecedens probatur ex Matth. XXV, 34, 35. vbi Christus dicit: Tanquam hereditatem possidete regnum: Nam esurivi, & dedistis mihi, quod ederem. Resp. 1) Hereditas non acquiritur operum meritis. 2) Particula, γὰρ, h. l. non est causalis, seu non denotat caussam rei, sed ratiocinatiua & eventualis, designans rationem consequentiae, vel illationis a posteriori, ab operibus, velut fructibus & testimoniis fidei, quae vera consequenda vitae causa est, petitam.

Instantia: Adhibetur etiam particula, PER, quae causalis est, 1 Tim. II, 15. Mulier saluabitur per generationem liberorum, si manserit in fide & caritate, Act. XIV, 22. Per multas afflictiones oportet nos ingredi in regnum Dei. Resp. a) Particula, PER, locis citatis non est designativa causae, sed ordinis divinitus constituti, vt sensus sit: Mulier per generationem, i. e. in statu divinitus ordinato, quo generat liberos, saluabitur: Oportet nos inter afflictiones a Deo immissas ingredi in regnum caelorum. b) Generatio liberorum est opus naturale, adeoque non meritum vitae aeternae: Et afflictiones non sunt bona opera.

VI. Quidquid Deus homini reddit ex iustitia, illud reddit ipsi propter merita operum: Vitam aeternam &c. E. Maior probatur: quia praemia, ex iustitia reddita, praesupponunt merita, & his aequantur. Minor liquet ex 2 Thess. I, 6, 7. Iustum est apud Deum, retribuere affligentibus vos, afflictione; at vobis, qui affligimini, recreationem nobiscum. Porro 2 Tim. IV, 8. vita aeterna dicitur corona iustitiae, quam Deus iustus iudex dat diligentibus se. Resp. 2 Thess. I, 7. intelligitur iustitia Dei non commutativa, fundata in meritis hominum, sed remunerativa, fundata in amore Dei & promissionibus divinis gratuitis. Vita aeterna dicitur corona iustitiae, partim imputatae propter meritum Christi, partim iustitiae, veracitatis & constantiae, qua Deus promissa sua implet. Haec corona datur diligentibus Christum, non quod dilectio sit causa meritoria salutis, sed quia dilectio est nota & testimonium fidei saluificae.

VII. Quicunque praemia distribuit citra intuitum meritorum, ille est προσωπολήπτης. Deus non est προσωπολήπτης (personarum acceptor): E. non distribuit praemia citra intuitum meritorum. Maior probatur: quia ille est προσωπολήπτης, qui respicit in distribuendis praemiis personam, cui fauet, non obseruatis meritis. Minor constat ex Act. X, 34. Resp. Qui praemia, quae reddere ex iure debet, distribuit citra intuitum meritorum, ille est προσωπολήπτης. At Deus homini nihil debet: Respicit merita non nostra; quippe quae nulla sunt, sed Christi.

VIII. Quicunque Domino faeneratur, ille faenus iure suo repetere potest. Atqui homo misericors &c. Prou. XIX, 17. E. Resp. Dist. inter faenus proprie, & analogice dictum. Proprie loquendo homo Deo nihil faenerari potest. Compensatio divina gratuita analogice dicitur faenus: Sicut enim homo faenus, ad quod obligatus est, soluit ex iure: ita Deus eleemosynas repensat ex gratia.

IX. Quicunque per obseruationem mandatorum divinorum vitam aeternam ingreditur, illius bona opera sunt vitae aeternae meritoria: Atqui homo renatus &c. Matth. XIX, 17. E. Maior probatur: quia obseruatio mandatorum divinorum est studium bonorum operum, per quod nemo potest vitam aeternam ingredi, nisi eam mereatur. Resp. Neg. mai. Nam omne meritum est indebitum & par mercedi. At obseruatio mandatorum divinorum est debita ingressuris vitam aeternam, & impar regno caelesti.

Loco citato quaestio a iuvene proponitur. observatio mandatorum diuinorum est debita ingressuris vitam æternam, & impar regno cœlesti.

batur legalis. Idcirco solvitur a Christo non ex euangelio, sed ex hypothesi legali. Mens Salvatoris est: Si bona faciendo vis vitam aeternam ingredi, serua perfecte mandata diuina; cuius perfectionis δοκιμασία erit venditio bonorum, quae pauperibus eroganda sunt. Abiit iuuenis contristatus, imperfectionis suae conuictus. Quam ob rem admonitio Christi non confirmatoria, sed refutatoria & correctoria fuit.

X. Mala opera merentur aeternam condemnationem: E. bona opera merentur aeternam salutem. Ratio consequentiae est: quia oppositorum opposita est ratio. Resp. Consequentiam Paulus negat, Rom. VI, 23. Stipendia peccati mors; donum autem Dei vita aeterna, in Christo Iesu, Domino nostro. Gentiles propter iniustitiam ex Palaestina eiiciebantur, neque tamen Israelitae propter iustitiam suam in eam introducebantur, Deut. IX, 4. Inualidum igitur est argumentum ab oppositis; quia mala opera in gradu perfecto, vel intenso mala, bona opera imperfecte bona sunt.


### Quest. XXIV. Are good works pernicious to salvation?

So far are good works from being pernicious to believers that, when considered in themselves, they are rather most useful ; however, confidence of salvation, placed in the merits of works, is harmful .

Prob. a. From 1 Tim. 4:8. Godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come. Neither this life nor the future life is owed to godliness, but the accidental rewards of the present and future life are promised to pious men from the benevolent disposition of God. Excellently says LUTHER in ch. 3 of Galatians: Outside the cause of justification, no one can commend true good works magnificently enough. Who can sufficiently proclaim the utility and fruit of even one good work, which a Christian does from faith and in faith? For it is more precious than heaven and earth.

Prob. b. From the Solid Declaration of the Formula of Concord, p. 708. If anyone wishes to mix good works into the article of justification, to place his own justice or confidence of his salvation in them, to merit the grace of God by them, and to obtain salvation through them; we answer, not indeed we, but St. Paul himself, and he repeats it three times (Phil. 3:7), that for such a man his works are not only useless and an impediment to salvation, but even pernicious: the fault of which thing, however, is not of good works in themselves, but of that vain confidence which is placed in them against the express word of God.

Latin:

Tantum abest, vt bona opera credentibus perniciosa sint, vt potius per se considerata sint vtilissima ; fiducia autem salutis, in meritis operum collocata, est noxia .

Prob. a. Ex 1 Tim. IV, 8. Pietas ad omnia vtilissima est, promissionem habens vitae praesentis & futurae. Neque haec, neque futura vita pietati debetur, sed praemia praesentis & futurae vitae accidentalia ex beneuola Dei dispositione promissa sunt hominibus piis. Praeclare inquit LVTHERVS in c. III. Gal. Extra caussam iustificationis nemo potest vera bona opera satis magnifice commendare. Quis vel vnius boni operis, quod Christianus ex fide & in fide facit, vtilitatem & fructum satis praedicare potest? Est enim pretiosius, quam caelum & terra.

Prob. b. Ex solid. declarat. Form. concord. p. 708. Si quis bona opera articulo iustificationis immiscere, iustitiam suam, aut fiduciam salutis suae in ea reponere, gratiam Dei iis promereri, & per ea salutem consequi velit; respondemus non quidem nos, sed S. Paullus ipse, idque tertio repetit (Phil. III, 7.), quod tali homini opera sua non tantum sint inutilia, atque ad salutem impedimento; verum etiam perniciosa: Cuius tamen rei culpa non est bonorum operum per se, sed vanae illius fiduciae, quae contra expressum Dei verbum iis collocatur.


### Quest. XXV. Is confidence of justice and salvation to be placed in good works?

Our confidence of obtaining justice and salvation does not rest upon our good works , but upon the mercy of God alone , proposed to us in Christ the mediator .

Prob. a. From Rom. 4:6. Blessedness is of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works.

Prob. b. From Dan. 9:18. We do not present our supplications before thee for our righteousnesses, but for thy great mercies.

As an exposition, one may take the testimony of BELLARMINE, book 5, de iustific., ch. 7: On account of the uncertainty of one's own justice, and the danger of vainglory, it is safest to place one's whole confidence in the mercy and kindness of God alone.

Prob. c. From 1 John 2:1-2. My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. And he is the propitiation for our sins. Which words GREGORY THE GREAT explains elegantly, homily 7 on Ezekiel: Our righteous advocate will not defend [us] in judgment; because we also know and accuse ourselves as unrighteous. Therefore, let us not confide in our weeping, nor in our acts, but in the allegation of our advocate.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, who rely on the merits of their own works. Their stronger arguments are: I. King David relied on his own righteousness, to which he appeals, Ps. 7:9: "Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness." Resp. Distinguish between the righteousness of the cause and of the person. David, in that cause which he had against King Saul, and in which he was accused of sedition and of aspiring to the kingdom, was innocent before God: Otherwise, he acknowledges his own great sins, Ps. 130:3. II. King Hezekiah relied on his works, by commemorating them before God, Ps. 38:3. Resp. 1) Hezekiah commemorates his works as effects and testimonies of sincere faith, not as the foundations of his confidence. 2) Hezekiah, by commemorating his works, seeks a corporal benefit, namely, deliverance from his present sickness and the danger of death. Now, it is not denied that God, in such goods, also regards the innocence of life. See Ps. 41:1 et seqq. Yet it does not follow from this that the confidence of obtaining righteousness and salvation rests upon the merits of works.

Latin:

Fiducia nostra consequendi iustitiam & salutem non nititur nostris bonis operibus , sed sola Dei misericordia , in Christo mediatore nobis proposita .

Prob. a. Ex Rom. IV, 6. Beatitudo est hominis, cui Deus imputat iustitiam sine operibus.

Prob. b. Ex Dan. IX, 18. Non super iustitiis nostris deponimus nos preces nostras coram te, sed super miserationibus tuis multis.

Expositionis instar esse potest testimonium BELLARMINI libr. V. de iustific. c. 7. Propter incertitudinem propriae iustitiae, & periculum inanis gloriae tutissimum est, fiduciam totam in sola Dei misericordia & benignitate reponere.

Prob. c. Ex 1 Io. II, 1. 2. Filioli mei, haec scribo vobis, vt non peccetis. Quod si quis peccauerit, paracletum habemus apud Patrem, Iesum Christum, iustum. Et ille est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris. Quae verba eleganter explicat GREGOR. M. homil. 7. in Ezech. Iustus aduocatus noster non defendet in iudicio; quia & nos ipsos cognoscimus & accusamus iniustos. Non ergo fletibus nostris, non in actibus nostris, sed in aduocati nostri allegatione confidamus.

Antithefis est Pontificiorum, meritis operum fuorum confidentium. Quorum potiora argumenta sunt: I. Rex Dauid confidebat propriæ iustitiæ, ad quam prouocat, Pf. VII, 9. Iudica me, Domine, fecundum iustitiam meam. Resp. Dist. inter iustitiam caussæ, & perfonæ. Dauid in illa caussa, quam aduerfus regem Saulem habebat, & in qua feditionis & affectati regni accusabatur, coram Deo innocens erat: Ceteroqui grandia sua peccata agnoscit, Pf. CXXX, 3. II. Rex Hiskias nitebatur operibus suis, ea coram Deo commemorando, Pf. XXXVIII, 3. Resp. 1) Commemorat Hiskias opera sua, vt fidei finceræ effecta & testimonia, non vt fiduciæ suæ fundamenta. 2) Hiskias commemorando opera sua, expetit beneficium corporale, nempe liberationem ex præfenti morbo & periculo mortis. Iam vero non negatur, quod Deus in huiusmodi bonis respiciat etiam vitæ innocentiam. Vid. Pf. XLI, 1. feqq. Neque tamen ex eo fequitur, fiduciam consequendi iustitiam & salutem niti operum meritis.


### Question XXVI. Is it lawful to perform good works with a view to a reward?

The regenerate, in the exercise of good works, primarily regard the glory of God (a), but secondarily, and with a filial affection, they may regard the rewards of this and the future life, not as a due reward or as the wages of a master, but as gratuitous gifts and divine benefits, to be ultimately terminated in the glory of God (b). Proof a.

"Do all to the glory of God," 1 Cor. 10: 31. Proof b.

Because godliness is profitable unto all things, and has promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come, 1 Tim. 4:8; effort must be made that we may obtain the rewards promised to the pious. Conf. Heb. 11:26.

They object: I.

I. That the promises of retribution were not made by God in vain, and recorded in Holy Scripture, but so that the regenerate might regard them in the practice of piety. See Gal. 6:8, 9; 1 Cor. 9:24; Matt. 6:33. Resp. For the regenerate who work well, the glory of God is primarily before their eyes; secondarily, they regard the promised rewards, which they do not demand by right, but expect from the grace of God.

II. They object the examples: a) Of Moses, who looked to the μισθαποδοσίαν (recompense of reward), Heb. 11:26. b) Of Paul, striving with the greatest zeal for the brabeum (prize), Phil. 3:14. Resp. to a): Moses looked not to the reward of debt, but of grace. For God, who in the future life is all in all to the blessed, 1 Cor. 15:28, was his reward, Gen. 15:1. To b): Paul looked to the prize, not as wages to be imputed by debt, but as a gift and benefit of God, promised out of grace: He looked to it with an affection not servile or mercenary, but filial.

Question XXVII.

The work most pleasing to God, by which the true faith of regenerate men and the interior worship of God is most especially exerted and exercised, is prayer or supplication.

Proof. From Gal. 4:6: "Because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father!" The regenerate are sons of God through faith in Christ, Gal. 3:26. They exert this faith of theirs with a filial cry, excited by the Holy Spirit; for the Holy Spirit cries when He makes us cry. The regenerate call upon and address God: "Abba, Father!" By which very act they testify to their filial confidence fixed in the paternal benevolence of God. We are therefore treating here of prayer, as a signal

Generally, it will still be for me to discuss this: that, and by what reason, all good works, with none excepted, are the necessary fruits and effects of saving trust, and are not I call a necessary effect that which is brought forth from a certain cause, and that alone, and always, so that it can never be without this cause, and always cannot not be through this cause. That this necessary manner of consequence, what and in what way good works are effected from true faith in Christ, could ever be explained and proved by clear arguments, that masked MELODIUS too confidently denied, who at the same time harshly criticized the words of our blessed LUTHER, in his golden preface sent before the letter to the Romans, which very words were deservedly approved in our Declar. Form. Conc. c. IV. p. 701. The demonstration a priori, which he indeed thought could never be done, I shall complete by the man of three principles.

Nor shall I bring forth anything new. Our theologians have long since argued from the very nature of saving trust. Principle I. Saving trust, placed in the merits of Christ, and that indeed alone, instructs us with all powers sufficient for every good work. 2 Pet. 1:3. Explanation.

In every moral action, insofar as it is moral, the powers suitable for acting are the principles and arguments, both teaching the intellect and moving the will, sufficiently known and perceived. The principles of man's duties toward God are all the benefits bestowed upon us by God, and the right and complete knowledge of them. The grace of God reconciled to us, and our salvation recovered through Christ, is indeed the greatest benefit of all, as much in dignity as in amplitude.

And the knowledge of saving truths, which pertain to faith in Christ, if it be true, certain, and complete, contains in itself the knowledge also of our obligation toward God and Christ most of all, Rom. 8:12, especially since this obligation is a certain end of the benefits of God through Christ, Luc. 1:74-75, and thus a necessary condition, joined with such great benefits well placed, 2 Pet. 1:4. To this theological principle must be added two philosophical axioms: 1) The intellect, endowed with true, certain, and complete knowledge of the principles and arguments pertaining to actions, so that no error, no doubt, no prejudiced opinion intervenes, therefore determines the will to act by moral necessity.

Nothing can be done without a reason: Reasons are in the intellect: Therefore there can never be any determination of the will to act, therefore no action, without the knowledge and judgment of the intellect, whether true or false, whether entirely or in some part. Nor can an action be done otherwise than consistently with the knowledge of the principles and arguments. Such and so great as the knowledge is in the intellect, such and so great cannot but be the determination of the will to act.

2) Whoever vehemently desires a certain great benefit, nay even rejoices in it already bestowed upon himself, he also willingly and with the highest zeal observes the conditions attached, the order established, and his own duty arising from the fruit of the benefit.

And whoever ardently desires and seeks an end, he no less ardently desires and greedily seizes all those things which pertain to that end, and are tightly coupled with it. Assumption: But, that we may enjoy the greatest benefit of God, by receiving saving trust, which our Jesus liberally promises to us: "Come to me all," here this order is prescribed to us: what must precede, namely that we be "laboring and burdened," what must follow: "take my yoke upon you and learn from me."

Conclusion: Therefore, the true, certain, and complete knowledge of such a benefit makes the mind, by moral necessity, prompt and prepared to perform all duties most willingly.

Principle II. True, firm, and complete knowledge of the benefit with which God has enriched us, the greatest of all, cannot but inflame the mind with most ardent love toward God, 1 Jo. 4:19. And such is the nature of this love toward God, that it is able to excite and increase the highest zeal for pleasing God, and for always performing our business consistently with the divine will; so that it also makes the mind prompt and cheerful, by which we do what is commanded not unwillingly, 1 Jo. 5:3.

Principle III. True trust in Christ conquers all impediments of virtues, and the enticements of evils, 1 Io. V, 4.

Latin:

Renati in exercitio bonorum operum primario gloriam Dei respiciunt a), fecundario autem & filiali affectu præmia huius & futuræ vitæ, non vt mercedem debitam, aut herilia falaria, sed vt dona gratuita & beneficia diuina, ad gloriam Dei vltimate terminanda, respicere poffunt b).

Prob. a. Omnia ad gloriam Dei facite, 1 Cor. X, 31. Prob. b.

Quia pietas ad omnia vtilis est, & habet promissionem huius & futuræ vitæ, 1 Tim. IV, 8. danda est opera, vt promissa piis præmia consequamur. Conf. Hebr. XI, 26.

Antithefis est Pontificiorum, afferentium, mercedis debitæ intuitu bona opera esse facienda. Qui obiiciunt:

I. Promissiones retributionum non esse frustra factas a Deo; & consignatas in S. scriptura, sed vt renati in praxi pietatis ea respiciant. Vid. Gal. VI, 8. 9. 1 Cor. IX, 24. Matth. VI, 33. Resp. Renatis bene operantibus primario ob oculos verfatur gloria Dei, fecundario respiciunt promissa præmia, quæ non poscunt ex iure, sed exspectant a gratia Dei.

II. Obiiciunt exempla: a) Mofis, qui respexit μισθαποδοσίαν, Hebr. XI, 26. b) Pauli, summo studio contendentis ob brabeum, Phil. III, 14. Resp. ad a): Mofes respexit non mercedem debiti, sed gratiæ. Etenim Deus, qui in futura vita beatis est omnia in omnibus, 1 Cor. XV, 28. merces ipfius erat, Gen. XV, 1. Ad b): Paullus respexit brabeum, non vt falarium ex debito imputandum, sed vt donum & beneficium Dei, ex gratia promissum: Respexit illud affectu non feruili, aut mercenario, sed filiali.

Quæst. XXVII. In quo opere potiffimum conspicitur exercitium fidei & praxis pietatis?

Opus Deo gratissimum, quo hominum renatorum vera fides & cultus Dei interior potiffimum exseritur & exercetur, est oratio, siue precatio.

Prob. Ex Gal. IV, 6. Quia estis filii, emifit Deus Spiritum filii sui in corda vestra, clamantem, Abba! Pater! Renati sunt filii Dei per fidem in Christum, Gal. III, 26. Hanc suam fidem exserunt clamore filiali, a Spiritu S. excitato; clamat enim Spiritus S. cum nos clamare facit. Renati Deum inclamant & compellant: Abba! Pater! Quo ipso filialem suam fiduciam in paterna Dei beneuolentia defixam testantur. Agimus itaque hic de oratione, vt

Generatim mihi differendum adhuc erit de eo: quod, & qua ratione, bona opera omnia, nullo demto, sint necessarii fructus atque effectus fiduciae salutaris & haud fueat, Necessarium effectum dico eum, qui a certa quadam causa & sola, & semper profertur, vt is nunquam possit esse sine hac causa, semper non possit non esse per hanc causam. Necessariam hanc consequutionis rationem, quod, & quo modo, bona opera ex vera in Christum fide efficiantur, perspicuis argumentis explicari ac probari vnquam posse, nimium confidenter negauit perfonatus ille MELODIVS, qui simul acerbe perstrinxit verba b. LVTHERI nostri, in aurea ipsius praefatione, litteris ad Romanos praemissa, quae ipsa verba merito adprobata sunt in nostra Declar. Form. Conc. c. IV. p. 701. Demonstrationem a priori, quam ille quidem fieri nunquam posse ratus est, perficiam vir trium principiorum.

Nec noui aliquid proferam. Theologi nostrates dudum argumentati sunt ex ipsa natura fiduciae salutaris. Principium I. Fiducia salutaris in Christi promeritis posita, & ea quidem vna, viribus nos instruit omnibus, bono operi cuique sufficientibus. 2 Petr. 1, 3. Explicatio.

In omni actione morali, quatenus est moralis, vires ad agendum idoneae sunt principia atque argumenta, & intellectum docentia, & voluntatem mouentia, satis cognita ac percepta. Principia officiorum hominis erga Deum omnium sunt beneficia, diuinitus in nos collata, eorumque recta atque integra cognitio. Gratia Dei nobis reconciliati, ac salus nostra per Christum recuperata, est profecto beneficium omnium maximum, tam dignitate, quam amplitudine.

E cognitio veritatum salutarium, quae ad fidem in Christum pertinent, si ea sit vera, certa atque integra, continet in se cognitionem etiam nostrae erga Deum & Christum obligationis maxime, Rom. VIII, 12. praesertim quum haec obligatio sit finis quidam beneficiorum Dei per Christum, Luc. I, 74. 75. atque adeo conditio necessaria, cum tantis beneficiis bene locatis coniuncta, 2 Petr. I, 4. Explicatio huic principio theologico adiungenda sunt duo axiomata philosophica: 1) Intellectus, cognitione principiorum atque argumentorum, ad actiones spectantium, vera, certa atque integra praeditus, vt nullus intercedat error, nulla dubitatio, nulla praeiudicata opinio, is igitur necessitate morali voluntatem ad agendum determinat.

Nil potest fieri sine ratione: Rationes sunt in intellectu: Nulla igitur vnquam esse potest voluntatis ad agendum determinatio, nulla igitur actio, sine cognitione ac iudicatione intellectus, aut vera, aut falsa, siue omnino, siue aliqua ex parte. Nec aliter fieri potest actio, quam cognitioni principiorum atque argumentorum conuenienter. Qualis & quanta cognitio in intellectu est, talis ac tanta non potest non esse voluntatis ad agendum determinatio.

2) Quicunque vehementer adpetit finnum quoddam beneficium, immo etiam eo iam sibi impertito gaudet, is libenter quoque ac summo studio obseruat conditiones adiunctas, ordinem, constitutum, suumque officium ex beneficii fructu exortum.

Et quicunque ardenter cupit optatque finem, is non minus ardenter adpetit auideque arripit ea omnia, quae ad illum finem pertinent, arcteque cum eo copulata sunt. Adsumtio: Atqui, vt fruamur summo Dei beneficio, fiducia salutari accipiendo, quod Iesus noster liberaliter nobis pollicetur: δεῦτε πρός με πάντες, hic nobis ordo praescriptus est: quid debeat praecedere, nimirum vt simus κοπιῶντες καὶ πεφορτισμένοι, quid debeat subsequi: ἄρατε τὸν ζυγόν με ἐφ' ὑμᾶς καὶ μάθετε ἀπ' ἐμοῦ.

Consequutio: Ergo tanti beneficii cognitio vera, certa atque integra, necessitate morali animum efficit promptum paratumque ad omnia officia libentissime praestanda.

Principium II. Cognitio vera, firma atque integra beneficii, quo Deus nos auxit, omnium maximi, non potest non animum incendere ardentissimo in Deum amore, 1 Io. IV, 19. Ea vero natura huius in Deum amoris, vt is valeat summum excitare atque augere studium, Deo placendi, ac rem nostram semper diuinae voluntati congruenter peragendi; vt promptum etiam hilaremque efficiat animum, quo imperata haud inuiti faciamus, 1 Io. V, 3.

Principium III. Vera in Christo fiducia vincit omnia impedimenta virtutum, atque irritamenta malorum, 1 Io. V, 4.


### Q. XXVIII. What is prayer considered generally?

Prayer is a religious act, by which a man converted and reborn, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, calls upon the triune God with true confidence of heart, leaning upon the merit and intercession of Christ the mediator, as a suppliant, for the glory of God and for his own salvation and that of others.

Latin:

Oratio est actus religiosus, quo homo conversus & renatus, ductu Spiritus S. Deum vnitrinum vera cordis fiducia, Christi mediatoris merito & intercessione innixa, supplex compellat, ad Dei gloriam & suammet ac aliorum salutem.


### Q. XXIX. How is prayer divided?

Prayer is divided by St. Paul into δέησιν, or deprecation, προσευχὴν, precation, ἐντευξιν, interpellation, and εὐχαρισίαν, or thanksgiving. Proof. From 1 Tim. II, 1. I exhort therefore that, first of all, supplications (δεήσεις), prayers (προσευχὰς), intercessions (ἐντεύξεις), and giving of thanks (εὐχαρισίας) be made for all men. Δέησις, or deprecation, is that by which we seek the turning away of some evil, which either presses upon us or hangs over us: Προσευχὴ, or precation, is that by which we seek that bodily and spiritual goods be conferred upon us: Ἔντευξις, interpellation, or intercession, is that by which we intercede for others, that God may either bestow some good upon them, or turn away some evil from them: Ἐυχαρισία, or thanksgiving, is that by which we give thanks to God for benefits conferred upon us or others.

Latin:

Oratio dividitur a S. Paullo in δέησιν, sive deprecationem, προσευχὴν precationem, ἐντευξιν, interpellationem, & εὐχαρισίαν, sive gratiarum actionem. Prob. Ex 1 Tim. II, 1. Hortor igitur primo omnium fieri δεήσεις, deprecationes, προσευχὰς obsecrationes, ἐντεύξεις, interpellationes, εὐχαρισίας, gratiarum actiones pro omnibus hominibus. Δέησις, sive deprecatio est, qua petimus aversionem alicuius mali, quod aut nos premit, aut nobis imminet: Προσευχὴ, sive precatio est, qua petimus nobis conferri bona corporalia & spiritualia: Ἔντευξις, interpellatio, sive intercessio est, qua pro aliis intercedimus, vt Deus ipsis vel bonum aliquod impertiat, vel malum aliquod ab ipsis avertat: Ἐυχαρισία, sive gratiarum actio est, qua Deo pro beneficiis, in nos vel alios collatis, gratias agimus.


### Q. XXX. In what does prayer formally consist?

Prayer formally consists in the fiducial calling upon God.

Proof. The form of prayer comprises 1) confidence, fixed in the merit of Christ and the mercy of God obtained thereby, according to that of James I, 6. Let him ask in faith, nothing wavering: 2) the reverent calling upon the eternal Deity, not indeed that words must always be sent forth from the mouth, and pro-

Explanation: Κόσμος, in this place, is the lust of sinning, and thus the whole genus of depraved desires (per loc. parall. 1 John II, 16.). The reason for the name lies in this: that in every allurement of sin, to which a man indulges and yields, his mind turns away entirely from the Creator, and, shamefully forgetful of Him, seeks in vain all pleasure of the soul in created things, nay, in the perverse use of them. But forbidden desire is always the cause of every voluntary sin committed, James I, 14. Therefore, by the power of saving confidence, which far and greatly surpasses all lust of sinning, there cannot but be produced a zeal for virtue and the exercise of all good works. Illustration from this axiom: We always judge that a certain greater good, which is at once more certain, sufficiently known, and thus accepted with firm confidence, is to be preferred to a lesser and very uncertain one. Assumption: But the saving knowledge of Christ brings us the highest good, greater and more excellent than all earthly pleasures (Rom. VIII, 32.) and far more certain (ibid. v. 38, 39. add. 1 John II, 17; 2 Tim. IV, 8 & 18.). That is, what PAUL says, the excellency of the knowledge (ὑπερέχον τῆς γνώσεως) (Phil. III, 8.), and therefore concludes: we are more than conquerors (ὑπερνικῶμεν ἐν τέτοις πᾶσιν) (Rom. VIII, 37.). Consequence: Therefore, the saving knowledge of Christ, provided it be true, certain, and integral, so surpasses all earthly pleasures and allurements of sin, that no more excellent victory is ever reported anywhere. Completion of the argument: When all things required for acting are present, the action is now morally necessary. There are altogether three things which are required for any one action: 1) sufficient powers: 2) zeal and inclination of the will: 3) the destruction of all impediments. But saving confidence placed in the merits of Christ, and that alone, 1) confers upon us all powers sufficient for all good works (per princip. I.): 2) incites the highest zeal and a most prompt will to perform obedience to God, and increases it more cumulatively day by day (per princip. II.): 3) overcomes all impediments to good works (per princip. III.): Therefore, the necessary effects of saving confidence, or of faith in Christ, are all good works without exception.

must be brought forth, but also the word formed in the heart of the believer through sighs alone sometimes suffices. For prayer consists chiefly in the elevation of the heart to God: which, however, is not to be taken exclusively, but since the tongue has been granted by God as an organ both of praises and also of complaints, it is to be referred to God for that reason of the assigned end. Confer. LYSER. l. c.

Latin:

Oratio formaliter consistit in fiduciali compellatione Dei.

Prob. Forma orationis complectitur 1) fiduciam, in merito Christi, & eo parta misericordia Dei defixam, iuxta illud Iacobi I, 6. Petito in fide, nihil addubitans: 2) venerandam æterni Numinis compellationem, non quidem quod semper verba ex ore emittenda, & profe-

Explicatio: Κόσμος, hoc in loco, est libido peccandi, atque adeo vniversum genus pravarum cupiditatum (per loc. parall. 1 Io. II, 16.). Ratio nominis sita est in eo: quod in omni illecebra peccandi, cui homo indulget atque obtemperat, mens ipsius tota a Creatore deflectit, eiusque turpiter oblita, omnem animi voluptatem in rebus creatis, immo in perverso earum vsu, frustra quærit. Atqui vetita cupiditas semper est caussa consummati peccati cuiusque voluntarii, Iac. I, 14. E. vi salutaris fiduciæ, quæ peccandi libidinem longe omnem multumque superat, non potest non effici virtutis studium, ac bonorum operum omnium exercitatio. Illustratio ex hoc axiomate: Bonum quoddam maius, simul certius, satis cognitum, atque adeo firma fiducia acceptum, semper iudicamus anteferendum minori, valdeque incerto. Adsumtio: Atqui salutaris cognitio Christi nobis adfert bonum summum, omnibus terrenis voluptatibus & multo maius ac præstabilius (Rom. VIII, 32.) & longe certius (ibid. v. 38. 39. add. 1 Io. II, 17: 2 Tim. IV, 8. & 18.). Id est, quod PAVLLVS dicit, ὑπερέχον τῆς γνώσεως (Phil. III, 8.), ideoque concludit: ὑπερνικῶμεν ἐν τέτοις πᾶσιν (Rom. VIII, 37.). Consequutio: Ergo salutaris cognitio Christi, modo vera fit ea, certa, atque integra, voluptates terrenas ac peccandi illecebras omnes ita superat, vt nulla vsquam reportata fit excellentior victoria. Argumentationis consummatio: Cum adsunt omnia, ad agendum requisita, actio nunc est moraliter necessaria. Omnino tria sunt, quæ ad actionem vnam quamque requiruntur: 1) vires sufficientes: 2) studium ac voluntatis inclinatio: 3) impedimentorum omnium destructio. Atqui salutaris fiducia in Christi promeritis collocata, & sola quidem ea, 1) vires in nos confert omnes, bonis operibus vniuersis sufficientes (per princip. I.): 2) studium summum ac voluntatem promptissimam ad præstandum Deo obedientiam incitat, in diesque cumulatius auget (per princip. II.): 3) impedimenta bonorum operum vincit omnia (per princip. III.): E. fiducia salutaris, seu fidei in Christum, necessarii effectus sunt bona opera ad vnum omnia.

THEOL. PART. IILL SECT. II. CAP. VIII. 1218 proferenda sint, sed & verbum in corde credentis formatum per sola quandoque suspiria sufficit. Precatio enim praecipue in elevatione cordis ad Deum consistit: quod tamen non est exclusive accipiendum, sed cum lingua a Deo ut organum tum laudum, tum etiam querelarum concessa sit, & illa ratione assignati finis ad Deum referenda est. Confer. LYSER. l. c.


### Q. XXXI. What is the efficient cause of prayer?

The principal efficient cause of prayer is the Holy Spirit ). The subordinate cause and subject of the denomination is a man converted and reborn not by natural powers but by supernatural ones, received from the Holy Spirit in regeneration, pouring forth prayers pleasing to God ).

Prob. a. The Holy Spirit is the spirit of prayers, Zech. XII, 11. not only because He teaches and compels us to pray rightly, but also because He excites and forms the prayers themselves within us. For through the Holy Spirit we cry out: Abba! Father! Rom. VIII, 15.

Prob. b. The subordinate, or secondary, cause of prayer, and the subject of the denomination, or the worshiper, is a man converted and reborn, who seriously detests sins with sorrow, and adheres to Christ with true faith. Such a true worshiper worships God in spirit and truth, John IV, 24. where the Savior opposed spirit to hypocrisy, and truth to shadows and Levitical ceremonies. The worship of God must be done in the Spirit, so that it is commanded by the Holy Spirit, and defined in the word of the Spirit, and does not consist in external manners, or in appearance and external simulation; but in true internal motions of the faithful heart, excited by the Holy Spirit, which the flesh or the reason of man cannot effect or elicit, but they must be the fruits of the Spirit, who illuminates the mind, creates a clean heart, and works in us the internal motions of the heart, devotion, groans, and prayers. Confer. D. CALOVIVS in bibl. illustrat. on this passage, fol. 716.

Latin:

Causa efficiens principalis orationis est Spiritus S. ). Causa subordinata & subiectum-denominationis est homo conversus & renatus non per vires naturales sed supernaturales, a Spiritu S. in regeneratione acceptas, preces Deo gratas fundens ).

Prob. a. Spiritus S. est spiritus precum, Zach. XII, 11. non solum, quia nos recte orare docet & compellit, sed etiam quia ipsas preces in nobis excitat & format. Per Spiritum S. enim clamamus: Abba! Pater! Rom. VIII, 15.

Prob. b. Causa subordinata, sive secundaria orationis, & subiectum denominationis, sive adorator, est homo conversus & renatus, qui peccata serio cum dolore detestatur, & vera fide Christo adhaeret. Eiusmodi verus adorator Deum in spiritu & veritate adorat, Io. IV, 24. ubi Salvator spiritum hypocrisi, veritatem umbris & caerimoniis Leviticis opposuit. In Spiritu fieri debet cultus Dei, ita ut a Spiritu S. mandatus, & in verbo Spiritus definitus sit, neque in externis moribus, aut specie ac simulatione exteriore consistat; sed in veris internis, a Spiritu S. excitatis, fidelis cordis motibus, quos caro, aut ratio hominis non potest efficere, aut elicere, sed oportet esse fructus Spiritus, qui mentem illuminat, cor mundum creat, & in nobis interiores motus cordis, devotionem, gemitus, preces operatur. Confer. D. CALOVIVS in bibl. illustrat. in h. l. fol. 716.


### Q. XXXII. Who is to be invoked and worshiped?

Only the triune God is to be invoked and worshiped ), the Father ), the Son of God, who is Christ the God-man (θεάνθρωπος) ), and the Holy Spirit ).

Prob. a. From Matt. IV, 10. You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him only shall you serve. Confer. Deut. VI, 13. Is. XLII, 8. Prob. b.

From John XVI, 23. Amen, Amen I say to you: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, He will give you.

Prob. c. From John V, 23. That all may honor the Son, as they honor the Father. The human nature of Christ is not excluded from the worship of adoration, but the same, in personal union with the divine nature itself of the Word (τοῦ λόγου), is to be honored and worshiped with one and the same adoration, Phil. II, 9. Rev. V, 12. Prob. d. From 2 Cor. XIII, 13.

The communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all!

Latin:

Invocandus & adorandus est solus Deus triunus ), Pater ), Filius Dei, qui est Christus θεάνθρωπος ) & Spiritus S. ).

Prob. a. Ex Matth. IV, 10. Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, & illi soli servies. Confer. Deut. VI, 13. Es. XLII, 8.

Prob. b. Ex Io. XVI, 23. Amen, Amen dico vobis: Quaecunque petieritis a Patre in nomine meo, dabit vobis.

Prob. c. Ex Io. V, 23. Omnes honorent Filium, sicut honorant Patrem. A cultu adorationis non excluditur humana Christi natura, sed eadem, in unione personali cum ipsa natura divina τοῦ λόγου, una eademque adoratione colenda & adoranda est, Phil. II, 9. Apoc. V, 12.

Prob. d. Ex 2 Cor. XIII, 13. Communicatio Spiritus S. sit vobiscum!


### Q. XXXIII. Are the deceased saints also to be invoked?

The deceased saints are not to be invoked.

Objection. We do not withhold due honor from the deceased saints, nor do we treat them with contumely, but we deny that they are to be religiously honored, invoked, and worshiped. For one kind of worship is religious, which belongs to God alone, on account of His independent, omnipotent, omnipresent, omniscient, and most merciful essence: Another is non-religious, belonging to creatures dependent on God, to whom, by reason of greater excellence, greater honor is due, but not religious [honor].

Our Augsburg Confession, Art. XXI, pays the honor due to the saints who have died in the Lord: concerning the worship of saints, they (our churches) teach that the memory of the saints may be set forth, so that we may imitate their faith and good works according to our calling.

We therefore approve that [statement] of AUGUSTINE, book on true religion, ch. 55: The saints are to be honored for the sake of imitation, not adored for the sake of religion.

*Proof. 1) God alone is to be religiously invoked, Deut. VI, 3. Matth. IV, 10. Exod. XX, 3. Is. XLII, 8. Therefore, deceased saints are not to be religiously invoked.* The Papists object, and say that a distinction must be made between latria and dulia.

The former [is due] to God alone; the latter also to deceased saints. They even add hyperdulia, which they assign to the human nature of Christ and to the Blessed Virgin Mary. But we respond that the dulia of the first table is nothing other than latria, by which God is to be served, Matth.

IV, 10. But dulia pertaining to the second table of the Decalogue is either official, which is shown to the living, or memorial, which we do not deny to the deceased saints. Hyperdulia, however, is a monster of a word and a thing, devised by the Scholastics.

2) He who is religiously invoked must be a) omniscient and a knower of hearts, so that he may hear our prayers and groans,

Ps. XVIII, 20. and b) omnipotent, so that he may be able to bring aid to the afflicted, Exod. XV, 2. Ps. LXII, 9. But the saints are not omniscient and knowers of hearts, 1 Kings

VIII, 39. Is. LXIII, 16. nor omnipotent, Gen. XVII, 1. Therefore, deceased saints are not to be religiously invoked.

The Papists object: a) That the saints, in the essence of God, as in a mirror, see creatures clearly and distinctly, and thus our prayers. b) That God reveals our groans to them.

Resp. to a): The saints, by virtue of the beatific vision, see that which is in God actually and formally, but they do not know that which is in God virtually and eminently.

To b): If God reveals our prayers and groans, how do the deceased saints carry our prayers to God?

3) In whom we do not believe, him we ought not to religiously invoke, as Paul teaches,

Rom. X, 14. But we do not believe in deceased saints: for we believe in God alone: Therefore.

*4) The invocation of saints is not commanded in the word of God, but rather prohibited by the first commandment: Therefore, it is will-worship, condemned by God,

Col. II, 23. Matth. XV, 13.* 5) Christ alone is to be invoked, as our mediator and intercessor before God, 1 Tim. II, 5.

1 John

II, 1. The antithesis is that of the Papists, who maintain that deceased saints can be usefully invoked.

Who argue: I.

If we call upon living saints to pray for us, we can also call upon deceased saints to intercede for us: The antecedent is true: Therefore, the consequent.

The reason for the consequence is: because deceased saints are nearer to God, and thus can intercede for us better than living men. Resp.

Distinguish between the official calling upon of the living, and the religious invocation of deceased saints.

The calling upon of the living does not proceed from a religious cult of adoration, but from brotherly affection. Living saints know our needs, but the deceased do not know them specifically. The calling upon of the living has a foundation in Holy Scripture, viz., command and example. See 1 Thess. V, 25. James V, 16.

The religious invocation of deceased saints is destitute of both.

Latin:

Sancti demortui non sunt invocandi.

Obs. Debitum honorem non detrahimus sanctis defunctis, neque eos contumelia afficimus, sed eosdem religiose colendos, invocandos & adorandos esse, negamus. Alius enim cultus est religiosus, qui competit soli Deo, ob essentiam independentem, omnipotentem, omnipraesentem, omnisciam, misericordissimam: Alius est non-religiosus, competens creaturis a Deo dependentibus, quibus ob maiorem quidem excellentiam maior competit honos, at non-religiosus.

Augustana nostra confessio artic. XXI. debitum sanctis in Domino demortuis honorem defert: de cultu sanctorum docent (ecclesiae nostrae), quod memoria sanctorum proponi possit, ut imitemur fidem eorum, & bona opera iuxta vocationem.

Approbamus igitur illud AVGVSTINI libr. de vera relig. c. 55. Honorandi sunt sancti propter imitationem, non adorandi propter religionem.

*Prob. 1) Solus Deus religiose invocandus est, Deut. VI, 3. Matth. IV, 10. Exod. XX, 3. Es. XLII, 8. E. sancti defuncti religiose invocandi non sunt.* Excipiunt Pontificii, & dicunt distinguendum esse inter λατρείαν & δουλείαν.

Illam soli Deo; hanc etiam sanctis demortuis competere. Addunt etiam ὑπερδουλείαν, quam humanae Christi naturae assignant & B. virgini Mariae. Sed respondemus, quod δουλείας primae tabulae nihil aliud fit, quam λατρεία, qua Deo serviendum est, Matth.

IV, 10. At δουλεία ad secundam tabulam decalogi pertinens est vel officiosa, quae exhibetur superstitibus, vel memorialis, quam defunctis sanctis non detrahimus. Ὑπερδουλεία autem est monstrum vocabuli & rei, a Scholasticis excogitatum.

2) Is, qui religiose invocatur, debet esse a) omnisciis & καρδιογνώστης, vt preces nostras & gemitus exaudire queat,

Ps. XVIII, 20. & b) omnipotens, vt afflictis opem ferre queat, Exod. XV, 2. Ps. LXII, 9. At sancti non sunt omniscii & καρδιογνώσται, I Reg.

VIII, 39. Es. LXIII, 16. neque omnipotentes, Gen. XVII, 1. Ergo sancti demortui non sunt religiose invocandi.

Excipiunt Pontificii: a) Quod sancti in essentia Dei, velut speculo, videant clare atque distincte creaturas, atque adeo nostras preces. b) Quod Deus nostros gemitus illis reuelet.

Resp. ad a): Sancti, vi beatificae visionis, id, quod in Deo est, actu & formaliter vident, non autem cognoscunt id, quod in Deo est virtualiter & eminenter.

Ad b): Si Deus preces & gemitus nostros reuelat, quomodo sancti demortui preces nostras ad Deum perferunt?

3) In quem non credimus, illum non debemus religiose invocare, docente Paulo,

Rom. X, 14. Atqui in sanctos demortuos non credimus: credimus enim in solum Deum: Ergo.

*4) Invocatio sanctorum in verbo Dei non praecepta, sed potius praecepto primo prohibita est: E. est ἐθελοθρησκεία, a Deo damnata,

Col. II, 23. Matth. XV, 13.* 5) Solus Christus invocandus est, vt mediator & intercessor noster apud Deum, I Tim II, 5.

I Io.

II, 1. Antithesis est Pontificiorum, statuentium, sanctos defunctos utiliter invocari posse.

Qui argumentantur: I.

Si compellamus sanctos vivos, vt pro nobis orent, compellare etiam possumus sanctos demortuos, vt pro nobis intercedant: Antecedens est verum: E. consequens.

Ratio consequentiae est: quia sancti demortui Deo sunt propiores, atque adeo melius pro nobis intercedere possunt, quam homines vivi. Resp.

Dist. inter compellationem viventium officiosam, & invocationem sanctorum defunctorum religiosam.

Compellatio viventium non procedit ex religioso adorationis cultu, sed ex fraterno affectu. Sancti viventes norunt nostras necessitates, sed defuncti eas in specie non norunt. Compellatio viventium in S. Scriptura habet fundamentum, scil. mandatum & exemplum. Vid. I Thess, V, 25. Iac. V, 16.

Vtroque destituitur religiosa sanctorum demortuorum invocatio. destituitur religiosa sanctorum demortuorum inuocatio.


### Quæst. XXXIV. The images of Christ and the saints are not to be venerated with religious worship that is direct and terminative, nor with…

II. We dare not approach any Prince or King without a secretary or other intercessor: Therefore, much less should we attempt to approach God without some holy intercessor. Resp. We distinguish between the mystical or spiritual kingdom of Christ and any political or temporal kingdom. In a political kingdom, it is customary not to approach the king or prince immediately, but to use the intercession of someone, namely a counselor or secretary. But in the mystical Kingdom of Christ, everyone can appear before the heavenly Father without the intercession of saints: for we rely on the intercession of Christ, our only mediator.

III. Whoever intercedes for us can be invoked by us as intercessors: But the dead saints, etc. Therefore. The major premise is certain: because the help of a good intercessor can be usefully implored. The minor premise is conceded by the Apology of the Augsburg Confession, p. 224, and can be confirmed from Jer. 15:1, Rev. 5:8. Resp. 1) We distinguish between general and special intercession. The Apology of the Augsburg Confession concedes that the deceased saints pray in general for the whole church: but just as they are ignorant of the groans of individuals, so they do not intercede for individuals specifically. 2) Even if the blessed in heaven pray for the church; they are not therefore to be invoked. For Christians living in Asia or Africa also pray for the church of Christ: yet it is not right to address them by invocation.

Quæst. XXXIV.

The images of Christ and the saints are not to be venerated with religious worship that is direct and terminative, nor with religious worship that is analogical and reductive.

Prob. a. Direct religious worship belongs to God alone, who is omnipresent, omniscient, omnipotent, and infinitely merciful.

Prob. b. 1) The analogical and reductive worship of images (which ought to redound, be ultimately referred, and terminated not to the image, but to the prototype itself) has no divine command, nor any example in the Holy Scriptures. Therefore, it is ἐθελοθρησκεία (will-worship), a self-chosen worship.

2) The worship of the omnipresent and omniscient God is not to be bound to an image or statue, since we can venerate Him in all places without the sight of images.

3) The reductive worship of images savors of paganism. For, as LACTANTIUS testifies (Inst. lib. II, c. II), the pagans excused their idolatry with this pretext, that they did not adore the idols themselves, but God through them: to whom LACTANTIUS replies: Why then do you not lift your eyes to heaven? When the Israelites formed a golden calf for themselves, they did not attribute worship directly to the calf, but intended this to be a type moving them to a more devout worship of God.

There is an antithesis from the Papists, who defend the analogical and reductive worship of images, whose trivial arguments we shall summarize.

They object: I) The Israelites adored the ark, upon which were the Cherubim, Exod. 25:22. II) They looked upon the bronze serpent, that they might be healed, Num. 21:8. Therefore, it is permitted for us also to look upon images in our worship. III) Miracles have been performed through images, as EUSEBIUS testifies (Hist. Eccl. lib. VII, c. 14). IV) The images of princes are honored: Therefore, the images of Christ and the saints are to be honored. Resp. to I): The Israelites did not adore the ark of the covenant, but [prayed] toward the ark. The ark was not the object of adoration, but the place of the manifestation of the gracious divine presence. To II): Not everything that those who are adoring look upon, when it is placed on high, is an object of adoration. For those who adore usually look toward heaven: do they therefore adore heaven? To III): Not everything through which miracles are performed is to be adored: otherwise, the staff of Moses, through which many miracles were performed, would also have been adored. To IV): The images of princes are honored civilly: But we do not deny civil or external honor to the images of Christ and the saints either.

Latin:

II. Nullum Principem, aut Regem audemus adire, fine secretario, aut alio intercessore: Ergo multo minus conemur adire Deum, sine intercessore quodam sancto. Resp. Dist. inter regnum Christi mysticum, sive spirituale, & regnum aliquod politicum, sive temporale. In regno politico vlitatum est, non flatim adire regem, vel principem, sed vti alicuius intercessione, nempe consiliarii aut secretarii. Sed in Regno Christi mystico vnusquisque apparere potest coram Patre coelesti, fine intercessione sanctorum: nitimur enim intercessione Christi, vnici nostri mediatoris.

III. Quicunque pro nobis intercedunt, illi tanquam intercessores possunt a nobis inuocari: Atqui sancti demortui &c. Ergo. Maior constat: quia boni intercessoris auxilium vtiliter implorari potest. Minorem concedit Apolog. August. Confess. p. 224. & potest confirmari ex Ier. XV, 1. Apoc. V, 8. Resp. 1) Dist. inter intercessionem generalem, & specialem. Apol. Aug. Confess. concedit, quod sancti defuncti orent in genere pro vniuersa ecclesia: sed sicut singulorum ignorant gemitus; ita pro singulis in specie non intercedunt. 2) Etiamsi beati in coelo orent pro ecclesia; non tamen ideo inuocandi sunt. Nam & Christiani viuentes in Asia, aut Africa pro ecclesia Christi orant: neque tamen fas est inuocando eos compellare.

Quæst. XXXIV. Suntne imagines Christi & sanctorum religioso cultu venerandæ?

Imagines Christi & sanctorum neque cultu religioso directo & terminatiuo , neque cultu religioso analogico & reductiuo venerandæ sunt .

Prob. a. Cultus religiosus directus competit soli Deo omnipræsenti, omniscio, omnipotenti & infinite misericordi.

Prob. b. 1) Cultus imaginum analogicus & reductiuus (qui redundare, vltimate referri & terminari debet non ad imaginem, sed ad ipsum prototypum) nullum habet mandatum diuinum, neque vllum exemplum in sacris litteris. E. est ἐθελοθρησκεία, cultus electitius.

2) Dei omnipræsentis & omniscit cultus imagini, aut statuæ non est alligandus, cum in omnibus locis citra intuitum imaginum eundem venerari possimus.

3) Cultus imaginum reductiuus sapit gentilismum. Nam teste LACTANTIO lib. II. instit. c. II. gentiles idololatriam hoc prætextu excusaverunt, quod non adorent ipsa idola, sed per illa Deum: Quibus respondet LACTANTIUS: Cur igitur oculos in cœlum non tollitis? Cum Israëlitæ aureum vitulum sibi formarent, vitulo cultum directe non tribuebant, sed volebant hunc esse typum permouentem in deuotiorem Dei cultum.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, cultum imaginum analogicum & reductiuum defendentium, quorum argumenta leuicula in summam contrahemus.

Obiiciunt: I) Israëlitæ adorarunt arcam, super quam erant Cherubin, Exod. XXV, 22. II) Iidem aspexerunt serpentem æneum, vt sanarentur, Num. XXI, 8. E. & nobis licet in cultu nostro aspicere imagines. III) Per imagines miracula facta sunt, teste EVSEBIO libr. VII. histor. Ecclesiast. c. 14. IV) Principum imagines honorantur: E. honorandæ sunt imagines Christi & sanctorum. Resp. ad i): Israëlitæ non adorarunt arcam fœderis, sed ad arcam. Fuit arca non obiectum adorationis, sed locus manifestationis gratiosæ præsentiæ diuinæ. Ad II): Non omne, quod in sublimi positum adorantes aspiciunt, est adorationis obiectum. Nam adorantes plerumque cœlum intuentur: Ergone cœlum adorant? Ad III): Non omne, per quod miracula fiunt, adorandum est: ceteroqui etiam baculus Mosis fuisset adorandus, per quem multa sunt facta miracula. Ad IV): Imagines principum honorantur ciuiliter: At cultum ciuilem, siue externum, neque nos imaginibus Christi & sanctorum detrahimus.


### XXXV. What causes move and impel men to pray?

The impulsive causes of prayer are: a) the will of God declared by divine command and promise: b) our indigence and necessity: c) the utility of prayers.

Proved a. We read the threefold command of Christ, Matt. VII, 7. Ask, seek, knock. A threefold promise is also added: You shall receive, you shall find, it shall be opened.

Proved b. From Is. XXVI, 16. Jehovah, in distress they sought thee.

Proved c. From John XVI, 23. Amen, Amen I say to you, that whatsoever you shall ask the Father in my name, he will give you.

Latin:

Causae impulsivae orationis sunt: a) voluntas Dei declarata mandato et promisso divino: b) nostra indigentia et necessitas: c) precum utilitas.

Prob. a. Tergeminum mandatum Christi legimus, Matth. VII, 7. Petite, quaerite, pulsate. Tergeminum etiam additur promissum: Accipietis, invenietis, aperietur.

Prob. b. Ex Es. XXVI, 16. Iehouah, in angustia quaesiverunt te.

Prob. c. Ex Io. XVI, 23. Amen, Amen dico vobis, quod, quaecunque petieritis Patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis.


### Q. XXXVI. What things are to be asked of God?

Bodily and spiritual goods are to be asked of God. Bodily goods are to be asked and expected from God with the condition of the divine will, and without the prescription of manner or time a). But spiritual and heavenly goods are to be sought simply and without condition b).

Proved a. From 1 John V, 14. This is the παρρησία, confidence, which we have toward God, that, if we ask anything according to his will, he hears us. Wherefore the will of God must always be regarded in the petition of bodily goods; because God knows better what profits us than we ourselves.

Thus David permitted himself wholly to the divine will, 2 Sam. XV, 25; that leper, Matt. VIII, 2; nay, even Christ himself in the state of deepest humiliation, Matt. XXVI, 39.

Proved b. Spiritual and heavenly goods are promised to us in the divine word simply, absolutely, and without condition.

1 Tim. II, 4. Luke XI, 13. Therefore the same are to be sought without condition.

Latin:

Petenda sunt a Deo bona corporalia et spiritualia. Bona corporalia a Deo petenda et expectanda sunt cum conditione divinae voluntatis, et sine praescriptione modi, aut temporis a). Bona autem spiritualia et coelestia simpliciter et sine conditione expetenda sunt b).

Prob. a. Ex Io. V, 14. Haec est παρρησία, fiducia, quam habemus apud Deum, quod, si quid petamus secundum voluntatem eius, audiat nos. Quare semper respicienda est voluntas Dei in petitione bonorum corporalium; quia Deus melius novit, quid profit nobis, quam nos ipsi.

Sic voluntati divinae se totum permisit Dauid, 2 Sam. XV, 25. leprosus ille, Matth. VIII, 2. quin et ipse Christus in statu profundissimae exinanitionis, Matth. XXVI, 39.

Prob. b. Bona spiritualia et coelestia simpliciter, absolute et absque conditione in verbo divino nobis promissa sunt.

1 Tim. II, 4. Luc. XI, 13. E. eadem sine conditione expetenda sunt.


### Q. XXXVII. For whom is one to pray?

We are to pray both for ourselves a), and for other men, and indeed in general for all b), in particular for the faithful c).

Proved a. From Ps. L, 15. Call upon me in the day of distress: I will deliver thee and thou shalt honor me.

Proved b. From 1 Tim. II, 1. I exhort, that first of all supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks be made for all. We pray for infidels and enemies, that God may enlighten and convert them.

Proved c. Spiritual brothers pray for one another, 1 Thess. V, 25, that they may persevere in the faith.

Latin:

Orandum nobis est tum pro nobis ipsis a), tum pro aliis hominibus, et quidem in genere pro omnibus b), in specie pro fidelibus c).

Prob. a. Ex Ps. L, 15. Invoca me in die angustiae: Eripiam te et honorabis me.

Prob. b. Ex 1 Tim. II, 1. Adhortor, ut ante omnia fiant deprecationes, obsecrationes, interpellationes, gratiarum actiones pro omnibus. Pro infidelibus et inimicis precamur, vt Deus illos illuminet et convertat.

Prob. c. Spirituales fratres pro se invicem orant, 1 Thess. V, 25. vt in fide perseverent.


### Q. XXXVIII. Is one to pray for the dead?

For men who have died piously, there are not to be poured forth prayers that are meritorious, or satisfactory, nor impetratory, on account of which God might grant grace after this life for punishment remaining after the guilt has been remitted.

Obj. We do not disapprove of all prayers for the dead with Aerius. We (the words are from the Apol. Aug. Conf. p. 274) do not prohibit prayers for the dead, nor do we patronize Aerius. Truly we do not reject, but we retain an encomiastic commemoration of the piously deceased, as well as eucharistic prayers for a blessed departure from this life, and votive prayers, by which souls released from the body [are granted] blessed rest in the heavens, the body [is granted] a tranquil resting place in the bosom of the earth, and for both the bosom of the earth, & for both on the last day we pray for a glorious reunion. We vow, however, a blessed rest for the soul, not because it has not yet attained it, but because we desire a sweet rest for the pious soul, and we wish for it the perpetuity of joys. Therefore, eucharistic and votive prayers are clear symbols of our charity toward the deceased.

Prob. 1) From the lack of a divine mandate and promise and an approved example. For in the entire canonical scripture of the Old and New Testament, we find no mandate, no divine promise, no example of prayer for the dead. Whatever of sacred worship is undertaken for the sake of being exhibited without a divine mandate and promise, that is will-worship (ἐθελοθρησκεία).

2) From the analogy of faith. For the deceased are either blessed, and thus do not need our prayers; or damned, and thus cannot be helped by our prayers: For the wrath of God remains upon them, John 3:36.

3) Only the intercession of Christ is meritorious and satisfactory; our prayers have no power of meriting and satisfying.

4) Those who die in the faith of Christ are absolved both from guilt and from punishment: once guilt is remitted, no punishment is to be feared.

The antithesis of the Papists, asserting that one must pray for the deceased, so that they may be freed from the temporal punishment remaining after the guilt is remitted. They urge most strongly the example of Judas Maccabeus, who is said to have sent 2000 drachmas of silver to be spent for the dead, and to have commanded that prayer be made for the deceased, 2 Maccab. 12:42 ff. Resp. 1) The books of the Maccabees are not in the canon. 2) Judas Maccabeus ordered to sacrifice and pray for the dead (ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν), on account of the dead, so that the particle 'for' (ὑπὲρ) might denote the cause of the prayers, lest, namely, the sin of the dead be imputed to the surviving people. For he knew very well that certain enormous sins are sometimes imputed to the whole people; just as God once in the times of Joshua punished the whole people on account of the sin of Achan, Josh. 7:11. 3) Even if Judas had sacrificed and ordered prayer for the dead; this example would prove nothing, because it is destitute of a divine mandate.

Latin:

Pro hominibus pie defunctis non sunt fundendae preces meritoriae, aut satisfactoriae, neque impetratoriae, propter quas Deus poenae, post culpam remissam residuae, gratiam faciat post hanc vitam.

Obs. Non omnes preces pro defunctis cum Aerio improbamus, Nos (verba sunt Apolog. Aug. Conf. p. 274.) orationes pro mortuis non prohibemus, nec Aerio patrocinamur. Nimirum non reiicimus, sed retinemus commemorationem pie defunctorum encomiasticam, nec non preces eucharisticas pro beato decessu ex hac vita, et votivas, quibus animae a corpore solutae requiem in coelis beatam, corpori tranquillam in terra gremio cubationem, et utrique terræ gremio cubationem, & utrique in extremo die redunitionem gloriosam apprecamur. Vovemus autem, animæ requiem beatam, non quia eam nondum adepta est, sed quia dulcem requiem animæ piæ fincere cupimus, & gaudiorum perpetuitatem ipsi optamus. Sunt ergo preces eucharisticæ & votivæ caritatis nostræ erga defunctos luculenta symbola.
