Prob. 1) A mandati promissique divini & approbati exempli defectu. In tota quippe scriptura canonica V. & N. T. nullum mandatum, nullum promissum divinum, nullum exemplum de oratione pro mortuis invenimus. Quidquid autem sacri cultus exhibendi caussa fine mandato promissoque divino suscipitur, illud est ἐθελοθρησκεία.

2) Ab analogia fidei. Defuncti enim vel sunt beati, & sic precibus nostris non indigent; vel damnati, & sic precibus nostris iuvari non possunt: Manet enim ira Dei super ipsos, Io. III, 36.

3) Sola Christi intercessio est meritoria & satisfactoria; Preces nostræ merendi & satisfaciendi vim non habent.

4) Qui in fide Christi decedunt, absolvuntur tam a culpa, quam a pœna: remissa culpa, nulla metuenda est pœna.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, asserentium, orandum esse pro defunctis, ut a pœna post remissam culpam temporali residua liberentur. Urgent potissimum exemplum Iudæ Maccabæi, qui misisse dicitur 2000 drachmas argenti pro mortuis expendendas, & mandasse, ut pro defunctis oraretur, 2 Maccab. XII, 42. seq. Resp. 1) Libri Maccabæorum non sunt in canone. 2) Iudas Maccabæus sacrificare & orare iussit ὑπὲρ νεκρῶν, propter mortuos, ut vocula ὑπὲρ denotet caussam precum, ne scil. peccatum mortuorum populo superstiti imputaretur. Optime enim noverat, quod enormia quædam peccata interdum toti populo imputentur; quomodo Deus olim temporibus Iosuæ propter peccatum Achanis totum populum puniuit, Ios. VII, 11. 3) Si vel maxime Iudas pro mortuis sacrificasset, & orare iussisset; hoc tamen exemplum nihil probaret, quia destituitur mandato divino.


### Quest. XXXIX. What is the end of prayer?

The end of prayer is both the glory of God a), and our own and others' temporal and eternal salvation b).

Prob. a. True worshippers attribute to God alone the glory of omnipotence, omniscience, omnipresence, and infinite mercy, Isa. 42:8.

Prob. b. On our part, the ends and effects of prayers are various: the obtaining of the Holy Spirit and spiritual gifts, the attainment of temporal aid, and eternal rewards.

SIGH

Without your guidance and auspices, most holy God, I think, plan, or accomplish nothing good. You command what you will, and you give what you command. By grace you give the will, you give the working, and whatever you work in us and through us, you crown. Give me, I beseech you, your Spirit, the author of holiness. Give me the faculty of working well, so that by detesting evil works and cultivating virtues worthy of a Christian, I may serve you, cling to you, and set sail for your glory!

Latin:

Finis orationis est tum gloria Dei a), tum nostræ & aliorum salus temporalis & æterna b).

Prob. a. Veri adoratores tribuunt soli Deo gloriam omnipotentiæ, omniscientiæ, omnipræsentiæ, infinitæ misericordiæ, Es. XLII, 8.

Prob. b. Ex parte nostri, fines & effectus precum sunt varii: Spiritus S. & donorum spiritualium impetratio, auxilii temporalis consecutio, & æterna præmia.

SUSPIRIUM

Sine ductu & auspiciis tuis, Deus sanctissime, nihil boni cogito, molior, expedio. Tu iubes, quod vis, & das, quod iubes. Ex gratia das velle, das operari, & quidquid in nobis, ac per nos operaris, coronas. Da, quæso, mihi Spiritum tuum, sanctitatis auctorem. Da bene operandi facultatem, vt mala opera detestando, & virtutes Christiano dignas excolendo tibi seruiam, tibi adhæream, tuæ gloriæ velificer!


## 36 On Death, and the Resurrection of the Dead

Ques.

The executive and isagogic means of salvation are means divinely ordained, without the precedence of which God does not execute the sentence of glorification, and by the immediate intervention of which men, perseveringly faithful, are introduced into supreme blessedness, which are: death a), the resurrection of the dead b), the final judgment c), and the consummation of the age d).

Obs. I. The means of salvation in the stricter sense are called causal means, such as both the exhibiting means, the Word of God and the sacraments, and the receiving medium, which is faith in Christ. But death, the resurrection of the dead, the final judgment and the consummation of the age are called means of salvation in the broader sense; because they are means of an order, divinely constituted, without the precedence of which no one is admitted into eternal glory. For just as a way is something intermediate between the term of motion from which, and the term to which; so death, the resurrection of the dead, the final judgment and the consummation of the age are intermediates between this temporal life and the eternal. For which reason, eternal life does not relate to death, etc., as an effect to causes, but as a terminus to antecedent means of order.

Obs. II. For the faithful, death, the resurrection of the dead, the final judgment, and the consummation of the age are executive means of glorification; for the unfaithful, they are executive means of condemnation.

Obs. III. Among the isagogic means of salvation, there exists some distinction, inasmuch as some precede the glorification of the elect more remotely, others more proximately. It is especially to be noted that the consummation of the age is not required for the execution of the sentence of glorification with the same necessity as death, resurrection, and judgment. For God could glorify the pious and condemn the impious, even if the world were not to burn. Yet He could not, while preserving His decrees and His justice, glorify the impious, unless death (whether properly or ἀναλόγως [analogously] spoken) and resurrection and judgment were to precede. Wherefore we call the consummation of the age an executive medium because God has freely decreed not to execute the final sentence until this age is consummated. Compare D. HULSEM. breuiar. cap. 16. p. 1127. and D. OSIANDER colleg. system. part. VI. p. 278.

Proof a. The faithful groan and desire through dissolution to be more present with the Lord, 2 Cor. V, 4. Therefore, for the faithful, death is a means leading to life. The consequence is proven: Unless glorification were consequent to death, by divine institution as to an antecedent medium; there would not be among the faithful a desire for dissolution, but rather for the continuation of union.

Prob. b. From Dan. XII, 2. Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake: These (indeed) to eternal life, but the others to disgrace, to eternal ignominy. Therefore the resurrection of the bodies of the faithful is a means of promoting glory; but of the unfaithful, a means of calling forth to punishment.

Prob. c. On the day of the last judgment the King will praise those who shall be placed on the right, and will say: Come, ye blessed, etc. But to those who shall stand on the left, he will say: Depart, ye cursed, etc. Matth. XXV, 34. 41. Therefore the final judgment is a means of commending and admitting the faithful into blessedness; but of convicting the unfaithful, and publicly condemning them to eternal punishment.

Prob. d. The consummation of the age serves the acceleration of the faithful to glory: for unless those days (of the final tribulation) were shortened, no flesh would be saved: But for the sake of the elect they will be shortened, Matth. XXIV, 22.

Obs. Although these words immediately regard the destruction of Jerusalem, because however the destruction of Jerusalem is a type of the destruction of the world, they are rightly referred to the consummation of the age.

Latin:

Quaest. I. Quid sunt media salutis exsecutiva & isagogica?

Media salutis exsecutiva & isagogica sunt media divinitus ordinata, sine quo-rum antecessu Deus glorificationis sententiam non exsequitur, & quorum interventu proximo homines, perseveranter fideles, in summam beatitudinem introducuntur, quae sunt: mors a), resurrectio mortuorum b), extremum iudicium c), & consummatio saeculi d).

Obs. I. Media salutis in sensu strictiori dicuntur media causalia, qualia sunt tum exhibentia, verbum Dei & sacramenta, tum medium recipiens, quod est fides in Christum. At mors, resurrectio mortuorum, extremum iudicium & consummatio saeculi, dicuntur media salutis in sensu latiori; quia sunt media ordinis, divinitus constituti, sine quorum antecessu nemo in aeternam gloriam immittitur. Vt enim via est aliquid intermedium inter terminum motus a quo, & terminum ad quem; ita mors, resurrectio mortuorum, extremum iudicium & consummatio saeculi sunt intermedia inter hanc vitam temporalem, & aeternam. Quam ob rem vita aeterna ad mortem &c, se non habet ut effectus ad causas, sed ut terminus ad antecedentia media ordinis.

Obs. II. Fidelibus mors, resurrectio mortuorum, extremum iudicium & consummatio saeculi sunt media exsecutiva glorificationis; infidelibus media exsecutiva condemnationis.

Obs. III. Inter media salutis isagogica datur nonnihil discriminis, propterea, quod quaedam remotius, quaedam propius glorificationem electorum antecedant. Inprimis notandum, quod consummatio saeculi non ea necessitate, qua mors, resurrectio & iudicium, ad exsecutionem sententiae glorificationis requiratur. Posset enim Deus glorificare pios, ac damnare impios, etsi mundus non conflagraret. Non posset tamen, salvis decretis & iustitia sua, glorificare impios, nisi mors (vel proprie, vel ἀναλόγως dicta), & resurrectio, iudicium praecederent. Quare consummationem saeculi ideo medium exsecutivum dicimus, quia Deus sententiam ultimam non nisi consummato hoc saeculo exsequi libere decrevit. Confer, D. HVLSEM. breuiar. cap. 16. p. 1127. & D. OSIANDRI colleg. system. part. VI. p. 278.

Prob. a. Fideles ingemiscunt & volunt per dissolutionem fieri praesentiores Domino, 2 Cor. V, 4. Ergo mors fidelibus est medium ad vitam ducens. Consequentia probatur: Nisi glorificatio esset consequens ad mortem, ex instituto divino tanquam ad medium antecedaneum; non esset apud fideles desiderium dissolutionis, sed potius continuandae unionis.

b. Ex Dan. XII, 2. Multi de dormientibus in pulvere terrae evigilabunt: Hi (quidem) ad vitam aeternam, reliqui vero in opprobria, in ignominiam aeternam. Ergo resurrectio corporum fidelium est medium promovendae gloriae; infidelium vero, medium evocandi ad supplicium.

Prob. c. In die extremi iudicii Rex laudabit eos, qui a dextris collocabuntur, & dicet: Venite benedicti &c. Illis autem, qui a sinistris stabunt, dicet: Discedite, maledicti &c. Matth. XXV, 34. 41. Ergo extremum iudicium est medium commendandi & immittendi fideles in beatitudinem; infideles autem convincendi, & publice condemnandi ad aeternum supplicium.

Prob. d. Consummatio saeculi feruit accelerationi fidelium ad gloriam: nam nisi abbreviarentur dies isti (vltimae tribulationis), non servaretur ulla caro: Sed propter electos abbreviabuntur, Matth. XXIV, 22.

Obs. Quamuis haec verba immediate respiciant excidium Hierosolymitanum, quia tamen excidium Hierosolymitanum est typus excidii mundani, recte ad consummationem saeculi referuntur,


### Of Death


### Q. II, What is temporal death?

Definition of death Temporal death is the privation of the natural life of men, proceeding from the dissolution of soul and body.

It is defined more fully: Homonymy Temporal death is the privation of natural life, proceeding from the dissolution of soul and body, committed by the first-formed humans through sin, at the instigation of the devil, to be ordinarily undergone by all sinful men, by the decree of God, the most just judge, in the justice of divine glory.

Obs. The name of death is used in sacred scripture both in a proper sense and in an improper sense. We have already described death properly so-called, which they also call the death of the body. Improperly, death is taken either metonymically or metaphorically. Metonymically, death denotes a deadly thing, 2 Kings IV, 40. Exod. X, 17. Metaphorically, it signifies spiritual death, which is either of the unfaithful or of the faithful. The spiritual death of the unfaithful is the privation of spiritual life, proceeding from the separation of the impenitent and unfaithful soul from God, and is theirs both in this age and the future age. The spiritual death of the unfaithful in this age is the privation of the life of grace. Thus a wanton and forward widow is said to be dead in sins, 1 Tim. V, 6. i. e. destitute of the life of grace, since Christ, the life of the soul, does not live in her through faith. The spiritual death of the unfaithful in the future age is the privation of the life of glory, arising from the lack of the vision and fruition of the beatific God, joined with the suffering of most monstrous torments in hell. It is called the second death, Apocal. XX, 14.

The faithful are dead 1) to sin, partly through justification, insofar as sin, on account of the merit of Christ apprehended by faith, is not imputed to them by God out of grace, Rom. VI, 7. partly through renovation, by which the reborn and justified man is freed from the dominion of sin, so that he does not indulge it or enslave himself to it, but renounces it, 1 Pet. II, 24. 2) The faithful are dead to the world, insofar as they renounce the pleasures of this world, Gal. VI, 14. 3) The faithful are dead to the law, both ceremonial and moral, being utterly freed from the obligation of the former, and immune from the coercion, accusation, and condemnation of the latter; inasmuch as they have been gifted with a spontaneous spirit, and freed from the condemnation of the law by the grace of justification, Rom. VII, 1. 2.

Ques. III. In what does the death of the body formally consist?

The death of the body formally consists in the privation of natural life.

Proof. Because death is privatively opposed to life, and thus denotes the absence of animal life from a subject apt to possess it.

You say; Bodily death formally consists in the dissolution of soul and body, or in the separation of the soul from the body. Resp. The formal reason of death consists in the privation of life, which the dissolution of soul and body precedes; just as natural life is not the union of body and soul itself, but follows the same.

Ques. IV. What are the efficient causes of temporal death?

Temporal death, considered formally as the privation of natural life, strictly speaking does not have an efficient cause a): but viewed μεταληπτικῶς, as it is the dissolution of soul and body, its efficient causes are some moral, to which the dissolution of body and soul is imputed; others are physical, which really destroy the bond of union by which body and soul are joined. The moral causes are: the devil, by instigating to sin, directly intending the death of man b), and man, by obeying the devil's instinct, meriting death by his sin c). But death, considered as an evil of punishment, arises from a decreeing and inflicting cause, namely from God, the most just judge d).

Proof. a. Since death formally is a privation, or defect, it cannot be an effect produced by a positively acting cause.

Proof. b. The devil is the moral cause of death; because by giving the most crafty counsel about eating the forbidden fruit, he directly intended the temporal, spiritual, and eternal death of man. Therefore he is called a murderer from the beginning, John VIII, 44.

Proof. c. Eve, embracing the counsel of the demon and enticing Adam into the society of sin, and Adam, listening to the blandishments of his wife and violating the divine law, drew upon themselves the guilt of fault and punishment, and subjected not only themselves, but also their descendants to the necessity of dying, Rom. V, 12.

Proof. d. God indeed did not make death, Wis. I, 13. and thus by antecedent will did not will the death of man: yet by consequent will, on account of the preceding sin, He decreed to inflict death as a punishment upon man, and executes His decree. Therefore He threatens the punishment of death, Gen. II, 17. He defines the limit of life and death, Job XIV, 5. and finally commands man to depart from this mortal station, Ps. XC, 3.

Ques. V. What are the physical causes of temporal death?

The physical causes of death are some natural, some preternatural, some violent. The natural cause is the consumption of the radical moisture and the extinction of the innate heat a). The preternatural causes are more serious diseases b). The violent causes are external things, inflicting such force upon the body that the bond of natural union, by which body and soul are joined, is broken c).

…Proof. a. For since the innate heat and the radical moisture (which we posit to coincide in substance, but to differ in qualities) are most closely joined to the soul, it is easily gathered that when this is consumed, death invades man. Therefore, those die a natural death whose innate heat is gradually weakened, and the radical moisture with the progress of time, apart from any more serious disease, dries up more and more.…

Prob. b. More violent diseases, for example, malignant fevers, dropsy, consumption, plague, destroy the powers of the native heat, so that it is overturned not by successive consumption, but by a just and more violent concussion.

Prob. c. He who pierces the heart of a man with a sword, casts him out of life by the application of external force .

Latin:

Definitio mortis Mors temporalis est privatio vitae naturalis hominum, ex dissolutione animae & corporis proveniens.

Plenius definitur: Homonymia Mors temporalis est privatio vitae naturalis, ex dissolutione animae & corporis, per peccatum ab hominibus protoplastis, instigante diabolo, commissum, proveniens, omnibus hominibus peccatoribus, decernente Deo, iustissimo iudice, ordinarie obeunda in iustitia divinae gloriam.

Obs. Nomen mortis usurpatur in sacris litteris tum in sensu proprio, tum in sensu improprio. Proprie dictam mortem, quam etiam mortem corporis vocant, iam descripsimus. Improprie mors sumitur vel metonymice, vel metaphorice. Metonymice mors notat rem mortiferam, 2 Reg. IV, 40. Exod. X, 17. Metaphorice significat mortem spiritualem, quae vel est infidelium, vel fidelium. Mors spiritualis infidelium est privatio vitae spiritualis, ex separatione animae impoenitentis & infidelis a Deo proveniens, eisque tum huius, tum futuri saeculi. Mors spiritualis infidelium in hoc saeculo est privatio vitae gratiae. Sic vidua lasciva & procax dicitur in peccatis mortua, 1 Tim. V, 6. i. e. destituta vita gratiae, quoniam Christus vita animae in ea per fidem non viuit. Mors spiritualis infidelium in futuro saeculo est privatio vitae gloriae, orta ex carentia visionis & fruitionis Dei beatificae, coniuncta cum perpessione immanissimorum cruciatuum in inferno. Dicitur mors secunda, Apocal. XX, 14.

Fideles mortui sunt 1) peccato, partim per iustificationem, quatenus peccatum propter meritum Christi, fide apprehensum, a Deo ex gratia ipsis non imputatur, Rom. VI, 7. partim per renovationem, qua homo renatus & iustificatus liberatur a dominio peccati, vt huic non indulgeat, aut se mancipet, sed eidem nuntium remittat, 1 Petr. II, 24. 2) Fideles mortui sunt mundo, in quantum voluptatibus huius mundi renuntiant, Gal. VI, 14. 3) Fideles mortui sunt legi, & caerimoniali, & morali, ab illius quidem obligatione penitus liberati, ab huius autem coactione, accusatione & condemnatione immunes; quippe qui donati sunt spiritu spontaneo, & a condemnatione legis gratia iustificationis liberati, Rom. VII, 1. 2.

Quæst. III. In quo formaliter consistit mors corporis?

Mors corporis formaliter consistit in priuatione vitæ naturalis.

Prob. Quia mors priuatiue opponitur vitæ, adeoque notat absentiam vitæ animalis a subiecto, ad eam habendam apto.

Dicis; Mors corporalis formaliter consistit in dissolutione animæ & corporis, siue in separatione animæ a corpore. Resp. Mortis ratio formalis consistit in priuatione vitæ, quam dissolutio animæ & corporis antecedit; sicut vita naturalis non est ipsa vnio corporis & animæ, sed eandem consequitur.

Quæst. IV. Quæ sunt caussæ mortis temporalis efficientes?

Mors temporalis, considerata formaliter, vt priuatio vitæ naturalis, proprie loquendo non habet caussam efficientem a): at spectata μεταληπτικῶς, prout est dissolutio animæ & corporis, eiusdem caussæ efficientes aliæ sunt morales, quibus solutio corporis & animæ imputatur; aliæ sunt physicæ, quæ vinculum vnionis, qua corpus & anima coniunguntur, realiter destruunt. Caussæ morales sunt: diabolus, instigando ad peccatum mortem hominis directe intendens b), & homo, diaboli instinctui parendo, mortem peccato suo promerens c). At mors, considerata vt malum pœnæ, oritur a caussa decernente & infligente, scilicet a Deo, iudice iustissimo d).

Prob. a. Cum mors formaliter sit priuatio, aut defectus, non potest esse effectus a caussa positiue agente productus.

Prob. b. Diabolus est caussa moralis mortis; quia dato vaferrimo consilio de comedendo fructu vetito mortem hominis temporalem, spiritualem & æternam directe intendit. Idcirco dicitur homicida ab initio, Io. VIII, 44.

Prob. c. Euæ consilium dæmonis amplectens, atque Adamum in societatem peccati pelliciens, & Adamus, vxoris blanditiis auscultans, legemque diuinam violans, sibi ipsis reatum culpæ & pœnæ attraxerunt, & non se tantum, sed posteros etiam moriendi necessitati subiecerunt, Rom. V, 12.

Prob. d. Non fecit quidem Deus mortem, Sap. I, 13. atque adeo voluntate antecedente mortem hominis non voluit: voluntate tamen consequente, ob antegressum peccatum, mortem, vt pœnam, homini infligere decreuit, & decretum suum exsequitur. Ideo pœnam mortis comminatur, Gen. II, 17. vitæ mortisque terminum definit, Iob. XIV, 5. & tandem hominem ex hac statione mortali decedere iubet, Ps. XC, 3.

Quæst. V. Quæ sunt caussæ physicæ mortis temporalis?

Caussæ physicæ mortis aliæ sunt naturales, aliæ præternaturales, aliæ violentæ. Caussa naturalis est humidi radicalis absumtio, & calidi natiui exstinctio a). Caussæ præternaturales sunt morbi grauiores b). Caussæ violentæ sunt res externæ, tantam vim corpori inferentes, vt vinculum vnionis naturalis, qua corpus & anima iunguntur, rumpatur c).

Prob. a. Cum enim calidum innatum, humidumque radicale (quod, qua substantiam, coincidere, sed qua qualitates differre statuimus) proxime iungatur animæ, eo depasto mortem inuadere hominem, ex facili colligitur. Defunguntur ergo morte naturali, quorum calidum innatum sensim debilitatur, & humidum radicale progressu temporis citra graviorem morbum magis magisque inarescit.

Prob. b. Morbi vehementiores v. gr. febres malignae, hydrops, phthisis, pestis, vires calidi nativi pessundant, ut non successiva absumtione, sed iusto vehementiore concussione evertatur.

Prob. c. Qui cor hominis gladio transfodit, eundem adhibita vi externa e vita eiicit .


### Q. VI. To which men must death be undergone?

Subject. Temporal death must ordinarily be undergone by all sinful men

Latin:

Subiectum. Mors temporalis ordinarie obeunda est omnibus hominibus peccatoribus


### Q. VII. What is the end of death?

End. The end of death, on the part of the devil, is the manifestation of hatred and envy toward God and men

Latin:

Finis. Finis mortis, ex parte diaboli, est manifestatio odii invidiaeque erga Deum atque homines


### VIII. How is death distinguished with respect to men emigrating from this life?

Death is either of the pious and faithful, or of the impious and unfaithful. The death of the pious is a local separation of the soul from the body, acting as a means, on the part of God, leading man to glorification. The death of the impious is a local separation of the soul from the body, acting as a means, on the part of God, disposing man to undergo the punishment he has merited.

Latin:

Mors est vel piorum & fidelium, vel impiorum & infidelium. Mors piorum est separatio animae a corpore localis, instar medii, ex parte Dei, hominem ad glorificationem ducens. Mors impiorum est separatio animae a corpore localis, instar medii, ex parte Dei, disponens hominem ad subeundum poenam promeritam.


### On the State of Souls After Death

Quest. IX. Is the soul immortal, and does it truly live after separation from the body?

The soul is immortal, and when released from the body, it performs its actions separately. Proof: 1) From the testimony of Christ, Matt. X, 28. Fear not those who can kill the body; but they cannot kill the soul. That which can be killed by no one is immortal: But the soul, etc. Therefore.

2) From the testimony of Solomon, Eccl. XII, 7. The spirit shall return to God, who gave it. Whoever has a spirit that, separated from the body, returns to God, that spirit lives after separation from the body: But the human soul is a spirit, etc. Therefore.

3) From the testimony of John, Rev. VI, 9. I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held, who cried with a loud voice. Those souls that cry out, they live: The souls of the slain cry out: Therefore.

4) From the light of reason: No spirit is mortal: But the soul is a spirit: Therefore. I prove the minor premise from the spiritual operations of the soul; such as: to contemplate God and eternal things, to abstract universals from particulars, to infer the future from the past, to desire eternal happiness, etc. These actions are independent of matter, and producible without any cooperation of an organic body, and therefore are spiritual. But the soul that produces spiritual operations is a spirit; for the effect is never more excellent than its cause.

The antithesis is the body, from which the soul, having been separated, has passed into another dwelling, Eccl. XII, 7. Luke XVI, 22, 23. It is evident that the comparison of death to sleep does not in any way pertain to the soul.

II. The truth is entirely twofold, and both parts pertain to the body. Namely, in sleep, properly so called, there are two things chiefly to be considered, of which one constitutes the nature of sleep, and the other happens to it as a consequence and event. 1) Sleep is the rest of the body, with the cessation of the operation of the external senses and of the movements of the mind, insofar as it uses reason in communication with the body. Regarding this, Isaiah, LVII, 2, transferred this name, sleep, to signify the state of death. 2) In sleep there is an expectation of the time when the sleeping man will wake up. We, however, who are dying, rely on the firmest hope of the awakening of the body. Thus Christ compared death to sleep, John XI, 11.

Conclusion: Since pleasant rest cannot exist without the consciousness of well-performed tasks, and that becomes the property of the blessed deceased; but the future recall to life of the examined body is common to all men: it follows that, for the former reason, death is compared to sleep only for blessed men, but for the latter reason, the death of all is compared to sleep.

Concerning the former, see Is. LVII, 2. Concerning the latter, Dan. XII, 2, just as it has been handed down in memory concerning the impious Kings: that they slept, e.g., 1 Kings XIV, 20, 31.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians, who assert that the soul is indeed incorruptible, but not properly immortal, or living after its separation from the body.

Latin:

Quaest. IX. Estne anima immortalis, vereque vivens post separationem a corpore?

Anima est immortalis, & soluta a corpore actionibus suis seorsum fungitur. Prob. 1) E testimonio Christi, Matth. X, 28. Ne timete vobis ab iis, qui occidere corpus possunt; animam vero occidere nequeunt. Quod a nemine potest occidi, illud est immortale: Atqui anima &c. E.

2) E testimonio Salomonis, Eccl. XII, 7. Spiritus reuertetur ad Deum, qui dedit eum. Quicunque spiritus a corpore separatus redit ad Deum, ille post separationem a corpore viuit: Atqui anima humana est spiritus &c. E.

3) E testimonio Ioannis, Apoc. VI, 9. Vidi sub altari animas, occisorum propter verbum Dei, & propter testimonium, quod habebant, quae clamarunt voce magna. Quae animae clamant, illae viuunt: Animae occisorum clamant: E.

4) E lumine rationis: Nullus spiritus est mortalis: Atqui anima est spiritus: E. Minorem probo ex operationibus animae spiritualibus; quales sunt: contemplari Deum & res aeternas, abstrahere vniversalia a singularibus, colligere futura ex praeteritis, desiderare felicitatem aeternam, &c. Quae actiones sunt independentes a materia, & sine vlla corporis organici cooperatione producibiles, ideoque spirituales. At quae anima spirituales edit operationes, illa est spiritus; effectus quippe nunquam praestantior est sua causa.

Antithesis iacet corpus, a quo seiunctus animus in aliud domicilium transiit, Cohel. XII, 7. Luc. XVI, 22, 23. Euidens est, mortis ac somni comparationem neutiquam ad animum pertinere.

II. Vera omnino est duplex, quae vtraque ad corpus spectat. Scilicet in somno, proprie ita nominato, duo sunt potissimum consideranda, quorum quidem alterum naturam somni constituit, alterum ei accidit, tanquam consequens atque euentus. 1) Somnus est quies corporis, cessante sensuum externorum operatione, motuumque animi, quatenus is quidem ratione vtitur, cum corpore communicatione. Id respiciens Iesaias, LVII, 2. nomen hoc, somnus, ad significandum mortis statum transtulit. 2) In somno est exspectatio temporis, quo dormiens homo evigilabit. Nos vero morientes firmissima nitimur spe expergefaciendi corporis. Ita Christus mortem cum somno contulit, Io. XI, 11.

Confectar: Quum requies iucunda non possit esse sine conscientia bene actorum negotiorum, eaque beate defunctorum propria fit; corporis autem examinati futura in vitam reuocatio communis sit omnium hominum: efficitur, ut priore ratione mors dumtaxat beatorum hominum, posteriore autem mors omnium cum somno comparetur.

De illa, vid. Ies. LVII, 2. De hac, Dan. XII, 2. quem ad modum de impiis Regibus memoriae proditum est: eos obdormiisse, e. g. 1 Reg. XIV, 20, 31.

Antithesis est Socinianorum, afferentium, animam quidem incorruptibilem, at non proprie immortalem, aut viuentem post solutionem a corpore esse .


### On the State of Souls After Death: Their arguments are

Their arguments are:

I. Whatever soul truly lives, it is united with the body: But the separated soul is not united with the body: Therefore. The major is proven: because the union of body and soul is required for life.

Resp.

1) This syllogism at first glance seems to be in the second figure; but in reality it is in the first figure because of the transposed terms, and then the minor premise is viciously negative.

2) Distinguish between the life of the composite, and of the part, which lives by itself and originally.

For the life of a man, or of the whole composite, the union of body and soul is required. But the soul is the nobler part of man, living by itself and originally, from which the body has its life communicated. Hence it happens that the soul separated from the body truly lives.

II. The soul in operating needs bodily members as organs: Therefore, outside the body it performs no operations, and consequently does not live. The antecedent is clear; because the soul needs eyes to see, and ears to hear.

Resp.

Distinguish between material human actions and immaterial ones.

To see and to hear are material actions, depending on the cooperation of the organic body. But there are other immaterial and spiritual actions, for which the concurrence of bodily members is not required, e.g., to understand, to contemplate, to reason, to will, to choose, to trust, to love, etc. The soul, released from the body, performs these operations, which are truly vital.

III. King Solomon says: As the beast dies, so also dies man. And there is one spirit for all, nor is there a prerogative of man over the beasts; because all is vanity. All go to one place: Eccl. III, 19, 20. From this statement of Solomon, one may conclude that the soul of man perishes just as the souls of beasts.

Resp.

1) There are those who persuade themselves that Solomon assumed the persona of some Epicurean, or of a profane man, philosophizing crudely about the death of man, and comparing it with the death of beasts.

2) Others respond more correctly with the blessed

LUTHER, that Solomon is reasoning about man and beasts from the principles of reason, with respect had to external events, common to man and beasts, in respect to which the entry of man into this world and his exit does not seem to differ from the entry and exit of beasts. But sound reason truly gathers the immortality of the human soul from another principle, namely from the spiritual operations of the soul; which Solomon expressly affirms in the same little book, ch. XII, 7: The spirit returns to God.

Question X. What is the state of souls separated from the body? (The quality of this state.) The state of souls that are perseveringly faithful, and separated from the body, is blessed in heaven a).

The state of unfaithful souls, released from the body, is damned in hell b).

Proof a. & b.

We showed this clearly in the previous section, ch. IX; we did not wish to do the work twice.

Question XI. Is there an intermediate state in purgatory between the blessed and damned state of certain separated souls? (Concerning the intermediate state.) There is no intermediate state after this life between the state of eternal blessedness and eternal condemnation a).

Therefore, purgatory is a most vain invention of men b).

Proof a. 1) Holy Scripture divides all men into believers and non-believers, or into the faithful and the unfaithful.

Whoever truly believes while dying is saved; those who do not believe are condemned.

Latin:

Quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Quaecunque anima vere viuit, illa cum corpore est vnita: Atqui anima separata, non est cum corpore vnita: E. Maior probatur: quia ad vitam requiritur vnio corporis & animae.

Resp.

1) Hic syllogismus primo intuitu videtur esse in secunda figura; at reuera est in prima figura ob terminos transpositos, atque tunc minor vitiose negans est.

2) Dist. inter vitam compositi, & partis, quae per se & originaliter viuit.

Ad vitam hominis, siue totius compositi, requiritur vnio corporis & animae. At anima est pars nobilior hominis, per se & originaliter viuens, a qua corpus vitam habet communicatam. Inde fit, vt anima a corpore separata vere viuat.

II. Anima in operando indiget membris corporeis velut organis: E. extra corpus nullis operationibus fungitur, & consequenter non viuit. Antecedens patet; quia anima ad videndum oculis, ad audiendum auribus indiget.

Resp.

Dist. inter actiones humanas materiales, & immateriales.

Videre & audire sunt actiones materiales, a cooperatione corporis organici dependentes. At dantur aliae actiones immateriales & spirituales, ad quas non requiritur concursus membrorum corporeorum, v. gr. intelligere, contemplari, discurrere, velle, eligere, confidere, amare &c. His operationibus, vere vitalibus, fungitur anima a corpore soluta.

III. Rex Salomo dicit: Sicut moritur bestia; ita & moritur homo. Ac spiritus vnus omnibus, nec praerogatiua hominis est prae bestiis; eo quod omnia vanitas. Omnia abeunt ad locum vnum: Eccl. III, 19, 20. Ex quo effato Salomonis colligere licet, animam hominis aeque, ac bestiarum animas interire.

Resp.

1) Sunt, qui sibi persuadent, Salomonem induisse personam alicuius Epicuraei, aut profani hominis, de interitu hominis crasse philosophantis, & cum interitu bestiarum comparantis.

2) Rectius alii respondent cum b.

LVTHERO, Salomonem de homine & bestiis discurrere ex principiis rationis, respectu habito ad euentus externos, homini & bestiis communes, quorum respectu hominis ingressus in hunc mundum & egressus non videtur differre ab ingressu & egressu bestiarum. At vero sana ratio immortalitatem animae humanae colligit ex alio principio, scilicet ex operationibus spiritualibus animae; quod expresse affirmat Salomo eodem libello, c. XII, 7. Spiritus reuertitur ad Deum.

Quaest. X. Qualis est status animarum separatarum a corpore? (Qualitas huius status.) Animarum perseueranter fidelium, & a corpore separatarum, status est beatus in caelo a).

Animarum infidelium, a corpore solutarum, status est damnatus in inferno b).

Prob. a. & b.

Dilucide ostendimus sectione superiori c. IX; noluimus hic actum agere.

Quaest. XI. Datur ne inter statum beatum & damnatum quarundam animarum separatarum status intermedius in purgatorio? (De statu intermedio.) Non datur post hanc vitam status intermedius inter statum aeternae beatitudinis, & aeternae condemnationis a).

Proinde purgatorium vanissimum hominum commentum est b).

Prob. a. 1) S. scriptura omnes homines diuidit in credentes, & non credentes, siue in fideles & infideles.

Quicunque morientes vere credunt, saluantur; qui non credunt, condemnantur.


### On the State of Souls After Death: The author of salvation, Jesus

The author of salvation, Jesus, Matt. VII, 13. 14. shows two paths, which men run in this life toward two places after this life; he makes no mention of a third path to a third place.

The words of the Savior are: Enter through the narrow gate; for the gate is wide and the way is spacious, which leads to destruction; and there are many who enter through it.

For the way is narrow and straight; which leads to life, and there are few who find it. As many men, therefore, as run the spacious, beaten path, with sinners who know not how to repent and believe, they rush into eternal destruction: those who walk the narrow way of faith, go into eternal life.

3) Whoever are blessed from the first moment of their departure from this world, they are not thrust down into purgatory: But all and every one who have died piously in the Lord, etc.

Rev. XIV, 13. The major premise is proven: because, according to the mind of the Roman Catholics, there are burning flames and most intense torments in purgatory, which cannot consist with blessedness.

Proof 1. In the most holy assertion of Christ, John

V, 24. there is a threefold nerve of proof: 1) There is no medium that intervenes between temporal death and everlasting life: μεταβέβηκεν ἐκ τοῦ θανάτου εἰς τὴν ζωήν (he has passed from death into life). This blessed lot is common to all, whoever, dying, cling to Christ with true trust; ὁ πιστεύων (he who believes), ὁ πιστεύων (he who believes), i.e., every single one. 3) The cause of this transition from death into life, with no delay interposed, the cause, I say, is said to be none other than saving trust: ὁ τὸν λόγον μου (he who hears my word, i.e., Christ’s own voice, which is evangelical), καὶ πιστεύων τῷ πέμψαντί με (and believes in Him who sent me).

But with the efficient cause present, and that indeed the only one, there is nothing left why the effect should be deferred and retarded:

2. This saying, 2 Corinthians V, 8. in its whole scope contains these propositions: 1) The soul, separated from the body, remains surviving: 2) It passes to blessedness: 3) That transition happens, without any delay, after the departure from this mortal body, and from this life, as if from an inn, so that nothing intervenes as a medium, v. 1. 6. 8. so that there is also no desire for a better lot, no expectation of it, as those who have it while we are in the body, v. 4. & 6.: 4) That blessedness, therefore, to be obtained immediately after death, is eternal, v.

1.: 5) It is also perfect, as far as the soul is concerned, namely, an intimate union with God, v.

8. and thus the contemplation of God, so that nothing becomes a medium between αἴσῳ (sight) and ἄδος (hades); v. 7.: 6) This benefit is common to all, nor does Paul arrogate excellence to himself, v. 1. 7. 10. Roman Catholics are asked: whether they think Paul also felt the power of the fire of purgatory? They respond by denying: for they wish for Martyrs, and especially the Apostles, to be excepted; they also except two other kinds of men, whose estimation, however, is so great and so singular with no one except themselves. But, what Paul professes about himself, he promises the same to all true Christians.

Add. 2 Tim. IV, 8.

7) It is also a great comfort: θαῤῥοῦμεν (we are confident), v. 8. You see, therefore, how great is the weight of the cause about which we are disputing.

Latin:

Salutis auctor, Iesus, Matth. VII, 13. 14. duas ostendit vias, quas decurrunt homines in hac vita ad duo loca post hanc vitam; tertiae viae ad tertium locum non meminit.

Verba Salvatoris sunt: Intrate per angustam portam; quia lata porta & spatiosa via, quae abducit ad interitum; & multi sunt, qui intrant per eam.

Quia angusta & stricta via; quae ducit ad vitam, & pauci sunt, qui inveniunt eam. Quotquot igitur homines decurrunt viam spatiosam, tritam, cum peccatoribus poenitere & credere nesciis, illi ruunt in interitum aeternum: qui angusta incedunt via fidei, eunt in vitam aeternam.

3) Quicunque a primo momento decessus ex hoc mundo sunt beati, illi non detruduntur in purgatorium: Atqui omnes & singuli in Domino pie defuncti &c.

Apoc. XIV, 13. E. Maior probatur: quia ex mente Pontificiorum in purgatorio dantur flammae aestuantes & cruciatus intensissimi, qui cum beatitudine consistere nequeunt .

Prob. 1. In sanctissima Christi adseveratione, Ioann.

V, 24. triplex est nervus probationis: 1) Nequidquam intercedit medium, inter mortem temporalem, vitamque sempiternam: μεταβέβηκεν ἐκ τοῦ θανάτου εἰς τὴν ζωήν. Beata haec fors communis est omnium, quicunque morientes Christo vera fiducia adhaerescunt; ὁ πιστεύων, ὁ πιστεύων, i. e. unus quisque. 3) Causa huius transitus ex morte in vitam, nulla interiecta mora, causa, inquam, non alia esse dicitur, quam fiducia salutaris: ὁ τὸν λόγον μου (Christi propriam vocem quae est evangelica, καὶ πιστεύων τῷ πέμψαντί με.

Atqui praesente causa efficaci, & ea quidem unica, nihil est reliquum, quare effectus differendus sit, ac retardandus:

2. Dictum hoc, 2 Corinth. V, 8. toto suo ambitu has continet propositiones: 1) Animus, a corpore separatus, manet superstes: 2) Is ad beatitudinem transit: 3) Transitus ille fit, sine ulla mora, post discessionem ex hoc mortali corpore, atque ex hac vita, tamquam ex hospitio, vt nihil intersit medium, v. 1. 6. 8. vt nullum quoque sit melioris fortis desiderium, nulla eius exspectatio, vtpote quam habentibus, dum in corpore sumus, v. 4. & 6.: 4) Ista igitur beatitas, continuo post obitum impetranda, est aeterna, v.

1.: 5) Est etiam perfecta, quod ad animum attinet, nimirum intima cum Deo coniunctio, v.

8. atque adeo Dei contemplatio, vt nihil fit medium inter αἴσῳ, & ἄδος; v. 7.: 6) Hoc beneficium est commune omnium, neque vitam sibi excellentiam Paullus arrogat, v. 1. 7. 10. Interrogati Romano catholici: vtrum putent etiam Paullum vim ignis purgatorii sensisse? respondent negando: Martyres enim, in primisque Apostolos, exceptos esse volunt; excipiunt etiam duo alia hominum genera, quorum vero apud neminem, nisi apud ipsos, tanta, tamque singularis est existimatio. Atqui, quod Paullus de se profitetur, id idem omnibus vere christianis promittit.

Add. 2 Tim. IV, 8.

7) Est etiam magnum solatium: θαῤῥοῦμεν, v. 8. Vides igitur, quantum sit momentum causae, de qua disputamus.


### On the State of Souls After Death: 3) From that discourse of Christ

3) From that discourse of Christ,

Luke XVI, 22. seqq. three truths shine forth: 1) That the souls of the departed, whether blessed or damned, are always conscious of themselves, thinking and feeling (i.e., they do not lie asleep, as the Psychopannychites dream): 3) Immediately after they have emigrated from their bodies, without delay, they are placed in that state in which they are to remain perpetually (i.e., there is no intermediate breath at all).

You say: That is indeed a parable.

Let it be so; although it is probable that a thing truly done is being commemorated by Christ. But, you ask, a firm argument cannot be made from parables. This, indeed, I know well. But do you not know that even in a similitude nothing should ever be brought forward that does not agree either with its scope or with any part of true doctrine? 4) That this promise of Christ, Luke XXIII, 43. also has great force for proof is apparent even from the fact that that thief, hanging on the cross, in such a short time was not able to make satisfaction for sins to be expiated, nor was he of the number of those for whom, as they say, the fire of purgatory is not to be feared. Nor was he a Martyr; nor a Doctor who had deserved well of the Roman church; To these arguments must be added more, in which there is certainly very much weight:

Prob. b. The founders of purgatory have placed as a foundation the venial sins of many faithful souls, with which they departed from this life contaminated. But since nothing defiled shall enter into heaven, Apoc. XXI, 27, they conclude that faithful souls, being thus impure, must be purified by purgatorial fire for a certain time, so that they may subsequently enter into heavenly glory. But this foundation is ruinous. For faithful men are purified partly in this life, partly after this life, yet so that a purgatory, such as the Papists imagine, does not exist. In this life, indeed, they are purified, as regards the formal aspect of sin, namely the debt of guilt and punishment, through justification. For in those who are by faith in Christ Jesus, there is no κατακριμα (condemnation), or anything that is imputed to condemnation, Rom. VIII, 1. They are purified through renewal, as regards the dominion of sin, so that they may be holy in Christ, Phil. I, 1. Moreover, the imperfection adhering to incipient holiness is covered by the veil of Christ's obedience, which the reborn apply to themselves by faith, and which they perform. But after this life they are purified, as regards the material aspect of sin, in death itself, and after death they are divinely adorned with such perfection that they are devoid of every stain. For in death, together with the body, depraved concupiscence is destroyed; which, on the part of the sensitive appetite, used to adhere. After death they are purified 1) on the part of the soul, by the infused light of glory, by which the intellect is elevated to know God intuitively, is purified from all ignorance, blindness, and error, and the will is elevated by the intuitive knowledge of God and directed into the most intense love of God, so that it loves nothing except in order to God and for the sake of God, devoid of inordinate love and depraved concupiscence. 2) On the part of the body, however, they are entirely purified in the resurrection of the dead. For the bodies of men dying in the faith of Christ will be resurrected, and spiritual and glorious bodies will be returned to the souls, 1 Cor. XV, 42 ff., and conformed to the glorious body of Christ, Phil. III, 21, so that without any inordinate concupiscence, the glorified souls may be perfectly subjected to perform perfectly holy actions. Therefore, there is no need for purgatory, nor does it rest on a solid foundation.

Antithesis rite; nor a monk, or any other holy man, conspicuous for the form of works of supererogation.

5. From the volumes of the Old Testament, among many documents, one stands out, this clear and significant description, frequently visited: The gathering of the dead, and the union with their people. I shall premise a definition: A people is a multitude of those men who live in one society. There are, therefore, three things which are required for the notion of a people: 1) a multitude of men, 2) of the living, 3) joined together in a certain society. And our people is a multitude of societies, not of strangers and guests, but of citizens, with whom we have always been accustomed to associate. These are citizens of the heavenly fatherland, as Paul interprets, Hebr. XI, 13--16. For our πολιτευμα is in heaven, Phil. III, 23, since in this mortality we are not so much citizens as guests, 2 Cor. V, 6; 1 Petr. II, 11. That gathering of the dying with their people is therefore opposed to 1) ejection from the number of citizens, 2) pilgrimage, which is called a sojourn on earth, Hebr. XI, 9, 10, 13, 14; 1 Chron. XXX, 15. Indeed, Paul manifestly looked to that manner of speaking of the O.T., 2 Corinth. V, 6, ενδημευμεν, that is, we are absent from our people while abroad, and only during the time that we are enclosed in these bonds of the mortal body; to which is contrary v. 8, ενδημησας προς Κυριον, that is, to associate with our people, and indeed with the Lord. Therefore 1) the gathering of those dying blessedly with their people is nothing else than accession to perpetual habitation in the heavenly fatherland: 2) It takes place as soon as the soul departs from the body; wherefore this manner of speaking, he was gathered to his people, is closely coupled with the commemoration of death: 3) Nothing intervenes between death and the eternal beatitude of the soul of the saint. If you should think that burial is designated by that sacred manner of speaking; if you should dare to confirm this with sayings of this kind, 2 Reg. XXII, 20: the arguments already set forth will teach you that by those two manners of speaking not one and the same thing, but distinct things are signified, of which one pertains to the departing soul, the other to the body.

The antithesis is that of the Papists (*), who invent a purgatory in which the souls of the just, which have not been sufficiently purged in this life, may be purged after this life, before they are admitted to heaven and the clear vision of God. We shall examine their arguments: I. Whoever dies in a state of grace with venial sins, their souls must be purified after their departure from this life through purgatorial fire; otherwise, they shall not enter into the kingdom of glory; Apoc. [He] himself confesses that for a blessed death nothing more is required than this one thing: that we believe in Christ. There is a profound silence there regarding satisfaction to be performed by man himself, regarding purgation after death, and regarding sacrifice for the deceased.

CLASS V consists of those who say that souls, as soon as they depart from their bodies, do indeed pass into that state in which they are to remain eternally, yet one that is not yet perfect, nor to be consummated before the day of the final judgment.

The ambiguity of the term must be noted. When beatitude—or its opposite, damnation—is called perfect, it can be understood in two ways: Either subjectively, as is the custom of speaking, which pertains to the whole man; in which sense there is no doubt that it is imperfect until the resurrection of the soul into its own body, awakened from the ashes, see 2 Tim. IV, 8. Or formally, in which nothing is lacking as far as the soul is concerned, especially the principal part of beatitude, namely, the perfect knowledge and contemplation of God; in this sense, we deny and utterly reject that the beatitude of the soul is imperfect before it has been joined with the resurrected body. As soon as it ceased to be seen, it begins to be present, 2 Cor.

V, 7. Finally, in CLASS VI we count those who indeed concede that the souls of all damned men are sent without any delay into eternal destruction, and that some of the blessed are admitted immediately to the perception of eternal joy; but they say that the rest, not yet sufficiently purged, are detained in a certain middle state, so that they are subjected to great torments therein, until their purgation is consummated.

But even they depart into factions, and although they all agree in the fact that they invent some purgation of separated souls to be necessary, they differ much among themselves in defining the mode. The Jews imagined the matter one way, and among the profane nations, the Platonic philosophers, from whom the Pseudo-mystics and fanatical men are not far removed; the Greeks think of it one way, the Roman Catholics another, in whose minds the opinion of a certain purgatorial fire, distinct from hell, is deeply fixed. The false principles of this are: 1) That Christ made satisfaction only for eternal punishments, not likewise for temporal ones, for which every person must make satisfaction himself, either in life or after death. 2) That satisfaction is a certain part of penance, indeed the principal one. From which it ought to be understood by what reasoning they attempt to derive their purgatorial fire from this precept: μετανοεῖτε [repent]. Which argumentation, as most absurd, our Apology of the Augsburg Confession, cap. VI, p. 186, refutes, and not without cause. See how they connect their reasons: Penance is necessary for salvation (correct!): But it consists of three parts: contrition of heart, confession of mouth, satisfaction of work (false!): Therefore, satisfaction must be performed by everyone who repents of their sins: Therefore, if he did not make sufficient satisfaction while alive, the deceased will have to supply this defect in purgatory.

3) That punishment is not entirely remitted, even though all guilt has been pardoned. 4) That faith in Christ is not the sole and perfect cause of salvation, but that there is also a great necessity of good works for salvation.

I pass over more. But behold! A manifest contradiction. This intolerable error of the Roman Catholics contradicts 1) another error in which they are involved, namely, concerning extreme unction, which they say is the sacrament that consummates penance, to which they attribute such power that it wipes away faults, if any are still to be expiated, and all remnants of sin, see Concil. Trident. Sess. XIV. Yet all, when they are at the point of death, must become participants in extreme unction. Who, therefore, are to be purged thereafter? Or what remains in them, after death, to be expiated, purged, and wiped away?

What need is there, therefore, for purgatorial fire? Or, if there is need, what is the value of extreme unction? It contradicts 2) the truth, which they profess with us, concerning the final judgment and the continuously following entry of the blessed into the eternal home prepared for them, Matt. XXV, 46; 1 Thess. IV, 17, in which place the word ἅμα [together] carries much weight, together with them, with no interval of time interposed.

But what, we ask, will become of those who will still be among the living on the very day of judgment? By what reasoning will they finally be purged, or be able to make satisfaction for punishments to be endured in purgatorial fire? Is it credible that they will all, to a man, be so perfect that they will need no purgation or satisfaction?

But a certain difficulty remains. The question is about these dead? concerning whom it is not certain that they died a second time, since it could have happened that they were caught up as living into the blessed seat.

Whatever the case may be, this one thing is at issue in the discussion: where in terms of place they will have resided

Apoc. XXI, 27. But many just [men] &c. E. The minor is evident: because in many things we all stumble, Iac. III, 2. Resp. I deny the minor. For venial sins are so called, because they are not actually imputed to condemnation, on account of the satisfaction for sins performed by Christ, and apprehended by true faith by the repenting sinner. But whatever is not imputed, is morally held as not done. Whence the scriptures teach that God so remits sins, that He wills to remember them no more, Ezech. XVIII, 22. that He casts them into the depth of the sea, Mich. VII, 19. that He blots them out like a cloud, Es. XLIV, 22. Hence the just do not die with venial sins.

Instance: When the guilt is remitted, sometimes a temporal punishment remains. Resp. That openly fights with the formal notion of the remission of sins. For to remit a sin signifies, not to impute the sin to punishment: Whatever is not imputed to punishment, on account of that no punishment is to be undergone. God sometimes reserves to Himself paternal chastisements, the guilt being remitted; but not punishments, which must necessarily proceed from a judge who is still angry; but the penitent are chastised in this life.

II. Whose works are tested by fire, the same are tested by purgatorial fire. But the works of the dead &c. 1 Cor. III, 13. E. The major is evident: because purgatorial fire is ordained to test the works of men. Resp. 1) The whole context of Paul is allegorical, and therefore the fire is understood not as material, or properly so called, such as purgatorial fire is considered to be; but metaphorical, and so called by way of similitude, which the little word ὡς, as, also hints. But it does not designate a fire of repurgation, or of the expiation of sin, but of probation, of examination, or of the exploration of doctrine, exerting itself by the virtue of the Holy Spirit through the written word of God, not without the fire of the cross and of temptation, either in the danger of persecutions and of life, or in the final moment of the struggle, by which true doctrine is tested and perfected, erroneous [doctrine] is consumed, and hay. For also scripture, Ier. XXIII, 29. and the temptation of the cross, 1 Petr. I, 7. is compared to fire. But the truth of doctrine is tested in this, not in the future age, to which purgatory is referred by the Papists. 2) That phrase, σώζεσθαι ὡς διὰ πυρὸς, is proverbial, and signifies the highest danger, as GROTIUS judges in this place, so that the sense becomes: That teacher, who builds hay and stubble upon the foundation of faith, will be in the highest danger of salvation, and will be saved, as if through fire, as if snatched from a dangerous conflagration, the stubble of errors also being burned up. Confer. ep. Iude v. 23.

Confer. ep. Iude v. 23. III. Those whom Christ is about to purge with fire as if with a refining furnace, He will send into purgatorial fire: But many sinners &c. Mal. III, 2. E. Resp. The prophet speaks of the purgation which is done in this life by fire not proper, but metaphorical, such as is the word of God, joined with the cross, or affliction.

Instance: Sinners are said to enter into fire and waters, and yet to be led out into a broad place, Ps. LXVI, 12. by which words is indicated a thrusting into purgatorial fire, and a completed purification.

were the souls during that time, in which each one was separated from his own body? Whether in heaven? It seems harsh to us, and unworthy of the kindness of God, nor convenient to the consummated order of salvation, to thrust souls, already perfectly blessed, again into this calamitous life. Or in hell? From hell there is no redemption. What then is to be thought? Is there a third place and state, intermediate between both? That there is absolutely none, we have brought to a clear conclusion. Among so many and so discrepant opinions, I understand this one, both to be safer, and more probable: that they were in heaven indeed, but as guests, not yet as citizens, that they might delight in the singular and exceptional foretaste of eternal beatitude. To the illustration of this matter serves [the fact] that Paul, still alive, but caught up outside himself, experienced something most similar to this. 2 Corinth. XII, 2. 3. 4. future purification, liberation.

Resp. The passage cited is understood as the fire of the cross, or of temptation. This is evident from the preceding v. 10, 11: "You have tested us, O God; you have refined us as silver is refined; you brought us into the net; you laid oppression upon our loins."

IV. Whatever sins are forgiven to men in the future age, from them they are to be repurified by purgatorial fire: But certain sins, etc.

Therefore. The major is clear: because God does not forgive sins to the impure, insofar as they perseveringly follow impurity.

The minor is proved from Matt. XII, 32:

"The sin against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the future." Resp. The words of Christ imply an absolute negation, so that the sense is: the sin against the Holy Spirit is not forgiven εἰς αἰῶνας, unto eternity, as interpreted by Mark, c. III, 29. But that Christ uses a distributive expression, and says: "neither in this, nor in the future age," this is done to exaggerate the sin against the Holy Spirit, as if He were to say: If it were possible that any sin could be forgiven even after this life, yet the sin against the Holy Spirit is such that it cannot be forgiven even after this life.

V. Whoever are brought out of the pit in which there is no water, they are brought out of purgatory: But certain sinners, etc.

Zech. IX, 11. Therefore. The major is evident; because a pit without water is not given in this world: nor are we brought out of hell, because from it there is no liberation.

Therefore we are brought out of purgatory. Resp.

The passage cited is understood as the pit of extreme misery, such as is, in the first place, infernal misery. We have been brought out of the pit of extreme misery, in which there is not even a drop of consolation, through the liberation made by the blood and death of Christ, not because we were actually cast into the infernal pit, or damned, but because we were damnable and guilty of eternal punishment.

Latin:

3) Ex illa oratione Christi,

Luc. XVI, 22. seqq. tres elucent veritates: 1) Animos defunctorum, sive beatorum, sive damnatorum, non semper sui conscios esse, cogitantes ac sentientes (E. non iacent somno consopiti, vt somniant Psychopannychitae): 3) Continuo post, quam ex suis corporibus emigrarunt, sine mora, in eo collocari statu, in quo perpetuo permansuri (E. medius flatus omnino nullus est).

Dicis: Id vero est parabola.

Sit ita; quamuis probabile fit, rem vere gestam a Christo commemorari. At, inquis, ex parabolis non potest effici firma argumentatio. Hoc equidem probe scio. At tu nescis, etiam in similitudine nihil vnquam proferendum esse, quod vel cum scopo eius, vel cum vlla parte doctrinae gerae non conveniat? 4) Magnam quoque vim ad probationem habere hoc promissum Christi, Luc. XXIII, 43. vel ex eo adparet, quod latro ille, in cruce pendens, tam brevi tempore non valuit satis facere pro peccatis expiandis, nec fuit ex eorum numero, quibus vt aiunt, non metuendus est ignis purgatorius. Nec Martyr fuit; nec Doctor, de Romana ecclesia praeclare meritus; His argumentis adjungenda sunt plura, in quibus plurimum sane ponderis inest:

Prob. b. Conditores purgatorii loco fundamenti posuerunt multarum animarum fidelium peccata venialia, quibus contaminatae ex hac vita emigrarunt. Cum autem nihil inquinatum ingressurum sit in caelum, Apoc. XXI, 27. colligunt, animas fideles, ita impuras, igne purgatorio ad certum tempus esse purificandas, ut deinceps in gloriam caelestem intrent. Sed hoc fundamentum ruinosum est. Purgantur enim homines fideles partim in hac vita, partim post hanc vitam, ut tamen purgatorium, quale Pontificii fingunt, non detur. In hac vita quidem purgantur, quoad formale peccati, reatum scilicet culpae & poenae, per iustificationem. In iis enim, qui sunt per fidem in Christo Iesu, non est κατακριμα, sive aliquid, quod imputetur ad condemnationem, Rom. VIII, 1. Purgantur per renovationem, quoad dominium peccati, ut sint sancti in Christo, Phil. I, 1. Adhaerens autem inchoatae sanctitati imperfectio tegitur velamine obedientiae Christi, quam renati per fidem sibi applicant, quamque faciunt. Post hanc vitam autem purgantur, quoad materiale peccati, in ipsa morte, & post mortem ea perfectione divinitus ornantur, ut sint omnis maculae expertes. In morte enim destruitur cum corpore prava concupiscentia; quae ex parte appetitus sensitivi adhaerebat. Post mortem purgantur 1) ex parte animae, per infusum lumen gloriae, quo intellectus ad Deum intuitive cognoscendum elevatur, purgatur ab omni ignorantia, caecitate, errore, & voluntas per intuitiuam Dei cognitionem elevatur & dirigitur in Dei amorem intensissimum, ut nihil, nisi in ordine ad Deum, & propter Deum, amet, inordinati amoris & concupiscentiae prauae expers. 2) Ex parte corporis autem, in mortuorum resurrectione omnino purgantur. Corpora enim hominum, in fide Christi decedentium, resuscitabuntur, & animabus rediunentur spiritualia & gloriosa, 1 Cor. XV, 42. seqq. atque glorioso corpori Christi conformia, Phil. III, 21. ut absque ulla inordinata concupiscentia animae glorificatae perfectae subiiciantur ad actiones perfecte sanctas obeundas. E. non opus est purgatorio, neque illud solido nititur fundamento.

Antithesis ritus; nec monachus, aliusve vir sanctus, operum supererogationis scilicet forma conspicuus.

5. Ex voluminibus veteris Testamenti, inter plura documenta una eminet haec dilucida significansque descriptio, crebro visitata: Congregatio defunctorum, coniunctioque cum suo populo. Premittam definitionem: Populus est multitudo eorum hominum, qui in una societate vivunt. Tria igitur sunt, quae ad notionem populi requiruntur: 1) multitudo hominum, 2) viventium, 3) in quadam societate coniunctorum. Et populus noster est multitudo societates que non peregrinorum ac hospitum, sed civium, quibus cum semper versari consueuimus. Hi sunt ciues caelestis patriae, interprete Paulo, Hebr. XI, 13--16. Nostrum enim πολιτευμα est in caelo, Phil. III, 23. quando quidem in hac mortalitate non tam ciues sumus, quam hospites, 2 Cor. V, 6. 1 Petr. II, 11. Illa igitur morientium congregatio cum populo suo opponitur 1) eiectioni ex numero ciuium, 2) peregrinationi, quae dicitur commoratio in terra, Hebr. XI, 9. 10. 13. 14. 1 Chron. XXX, 15. Immo Paullus manifesto ad illam dicendi rationem V. T. respexit, 2 Corinth. V, 6. ενδημευμεν, hoc est, a populo nostro peregre absumus, nec nisi eo tempore, quo sumus in his inclusi compagibus mortalis corporis; cui contrarium est v. 8. ενδημησας προς Κυριον, id est, versari cum populo nostro, & quidem apud Dominum. Ergo 1) congregatio beate morientium cum populo suo nihil est aliud; quam accessio ad perpetuam habitationem in caelesti patria: 2) Ea fit, quam primum animus e corpore emigrat; quam ob rem loquitio haec, congregatus est cum gente sua, arcte copulatur cum mortis commemoratione: 3) Nihil intercedit medium inter mortem, sanctique animam beatitatem aeternam. Si putaueris, sacra illa dicendi ratione sepulturam designari; si id confirmare ausis dictis huiusmodi, 2 Reg. XXII, 20: argumenta iam prolata te docebunt, binis illis loquutionibus non unam eandemque rem, sed distinctas res significari, quarum altera ad animum discedentem, altera ad corpus pertineat.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum (*), fingentium purgatorium, in quo animæ iustorum, quæ in hac vita sufficienter purgatæ non sunt, purgentur post hanc vitam, antequam ad cœlum & claram Dei visionem admittantur. Quorum expendemus argumenta: I. Quicunque iusti cum peccatis venialibus moriuntur, illorum animæ post decessum ex hac vita per ignem purgatorium sunt purificandæ, alias non intrabunt in regnum gloriæ; Apoc. fitetur ipse, ad beatam mortem nihil requiri amplius, quam hoc vnum, vt in Christum credamus. Altum ibi est silentium de satisfactione, ab homine ipso præstanda, de purgatione post mortem, de sacrificio pro defunctis.

CLASSIS V. est eorum, qui dicunt, animos simul atque e suis corporibus egrediuntur, in eum quidem transire statum, in quo æternum sunt permansuri, nondum tamen perfectum, neque ante diem supremi iudicii consummandum.

Notanda est vocis ambiguitas. Perfecta cum dicitur beatitudo, aut et opposita damnatio, id potest dupliciter intelligi: Aut subiectiue, vt moris est loqui, quod ad totum hominem attinet, qua quidem ratione non est dubium, quin imperfecta sit, vsque ad resurrectionem animi in suum corpus, ex cineribus excitatum, vid. 2 Tim. IV, 8. Aut formaliter, in qua nihil deest, quantum ad animum, præfertim vero pars præcipua beatitatis, nimirum perfecta Dei cognitio & contemplatio; hoc sensu negamus ac pernegamus, imperfectam esse animi prius, quam cum corpore rediuiuo coniunctus fuerit, beatitatem. Quam primum uisis esse desiit, ados incipit, 2 Cor. V, 7.

Denique in CLASSE VI. illos numeramus, qui concedunt quidem, animos damnatorum hominum omnes, sine vlla mora, in æternum exitium amandari, quosdam etiam beatorum protinus admitti ad æterni gaudii perceptionem; reliquos autem, nondum fatis purgatos, aiunt, in statu quodam medio detineri, vt magnis in eo cruciatibus adficiantur, vsque ad consummatam ipsorum purgationem. Sed & illi in partes abeunt, & quamuis in eo conueniant omnes, quod purgationem aliquam animorum separatorum necessariam esse fabulantur, in modo tamen definitione explicando multum inter se differunt.

Aliter rem finxerunt Iudæi, &, inter gentes profanas, Platonici Philosophi, a quibus prope abfunt Pseudomystici & fanatici homines; aliter de ea sentiunt Græci, aliter Romanocatholici, quorum animis penitus infixa hæret opinio ignis cuiusdam purgatorii, ab inferno distincti. Huius falsa principia hæc sunt: 1) Quod Christus pro pænis dumtaxat æternis fatis fecerit, non item pro temporalibus, pro quibus fatis facere quilibet ipse debeat, aut in vita, aut post mortem. 2) Quod satisfactio sit pars quædam pænitentiæ, imo præcipua. Ex quo debet intelligi, qua ratione ignem suum purgatorium conentur efficere ex hoc præcepto: μετανοεῖτε. Quam argumentationem, tanquam absurdissimam, exagitat, nec immerito, nostra Apol. Aug. Conf. cap. VI. p. 186. Vide, quo modo rationes colligant: Pænitentia est fumine necessaria (recte!): Ea vero ex tribus constat partibus; contritione cordis, confessione oris, satisfactione operis (falso!): E. satisfactionem præstare oportet vnum quemque, quem peccatorum pænitet: E. si viuus non fatis ex affe fecerit, debebit defectum hunc supplere mortuus in purgatorio.

3) Quod pæna non omnino remittatur, tametsi culpa omnis condonata sit. 4) Quod fides in Christum non sit vnica ac perfecta salutis causa, sed bonorum etiam operum magna fit ad salutem necessitas.

Taceo plura. Sed en! manifestam repugnantiam. Repugnat hic Romano-Catholicorum error intolerabilis 1) alii cuidam errori, in quo illi verfantur, nimirum de extrema vnctione, quam dicunt sacramentum esse pænitentiæ consummatinum, cui tantam illi vim afferunt, vt delicta, si qua sint adhuc expianda, omnefque peccati reliquias abstergat, Vid. Concil. Trident. Sess. XIV. Atqui omnes, cum animam agunt, debent extremæ vnctionis participes fieri. Quinam igitur sunt deinceps purgandi? aut quidnam in iis remanet, post fata expiandum, purgandum, abstergendum?

Quid igitur opus est igne purgatorio? aut, si opus fit, quid valet extrema vnctio? Repugnat 2) veritati, quam nobiscum profitentur, de iudicio supremo, & continuo subsequente introitu beatorum in æternum domicilium, iis paratum, Matth. XXV, 46. 1 Thess. IV, 17. quo in loco multum sane ponderis fecum fert vocabulum, ἅμα, vna cum eis, nullo interiecto temporis-interuallo.

Quid vero, quæsumus, fiet de illis, qui ipso iudicii die adhuc in viuis erunt? Qua demum ratione illi purgabuntur, aut pro pænis in igne purgatorio perferendis satisfacere valebunt? An est credibile, eos ad vnum omnes ita fore perfectos, vt nulla purgatione, aut satisfactione indigeant?

Sed restat quædam difficultas. Quæritur de bis mortuis? de quibus quidem non constat, eos iterum mortem oppetiisse, quum fieri potuerit, vt viui deinceps in sedem beatam adfumerentur.

Quidquid fit; hoc vnum in disceptatione versatur: vbi locorum commorati fuerint

Sed multi iusti &c. E. Minor patet: quia in multis labimur omnes, Iac. III, 2. Resp. Neg. minor. Nam peccata venialia ita dicuntur, quia actu non imputantur ad condemnationem, propter satisfactionem Christi pro peccatis praestitam, & vera fide a peccatore resipiscente apprehensam. Quidquid autem non imputatur, moraliter habetur pro non facto. Unde scripturae docent, Deum ita remittere peccata, ut eorum nolit amplius recordari, Ezech. XVIII, 22. ut demergat ea in profundum maris, Mich. VII, 19. ut deleat ea instar nubis, Es. XLIV, 22. Proinde iusti non moriuntur cum peccatis venialibus.

Instantia: Remissa culpa interdum remanet poena temporalis. Resp. Id aperte pugnat cum formali ratione remissionis peccatorum. Nam remittere peccatum significat, peccatum non imputare ad poenam: Quidquid ad poenam non imputatur, propter illud nulla poena subeunda est. Castigationes paternas Deus sibi aliquando reservat, culpa remissa; at non poenas, quas a iudice ad huc irato proficisci necesse est; castigantur autem poenitentes in hac vita.

II. Quorum opera probantur igne, eadem probantur igne purgatorio. Atqui opera mortuorum &c. 1 Cor. III, 13. E. Maior constat: quia ignis purgatorius ordinatus est ad probanda opera hominum. Resp. 1) Totus contextus Pauli allegoricus est, & proinde intelligitur ignis non materialis, aut proprie sic dictus, qualis censetur esse ignis purgatorius; sed metaphoricus, & per similitudinem sic dictus, quod & vocula ὡς, quasi, innuit. Non autem designatur ignis repurgationis, vel expiationis peccati, sed probationis, examinis, vel explorationis doctrinae, virtute Spiritus S. sese exserens per verbum Dei scriptum, non fine igne crucis & tentationis, vel in persecutionum & vitae periculo, vel in extremo agonis articulo, quo vera doctrina probatur & perficitur, erronea consumitur, et foenum. Nam & scriptura, Ier. XXIII, 29. & tentatio crucis, 1 Petr. I, 7. igni comparatur. Probatur autem veritas doctrinae in hoc, non futuro saeculo, ad quod purgatorium a Pontificiis refertur. 2) Phrasis illa, σώζεσθαι ὡς διὰ πυρὸς, est proverbialis, & significat summum periculum, censente GROTIO in h. l. vt sensus fit: Ille doctor, qui foenum & stipulas superaedificat fundamento fidei, in summo salutis periculo versabitur, & fiet saluus, quasi per ignem, tanquam ex periculoso incendio, conflagratis etiam errorum stipulis, ereptus. Confer. ep. Iudae v. 23.

III. Quos Christus purgaturus igne quasi conflatorio est, illos mittet in ignem purgatorium: At multos peccatores &c. Mal. III, 2. E. Resp. Loquitur propheta de purgatione, quae fit in hac vita per ignem non proprium, sed metaphoricum, qualis est verbum Dei, cum cruce, seu afflictione, coniunctum.

Instantia: Peccatores dicuntur intrare in ignem & aquas, & educi tamen in latitudinem, Ps. LXVI, 12. quibus verbis indicatur detrusio in ignem purgatorium, & peracta purificatio.

erint animi per illud tempus, quo a suo quisque corpore disiunctus fuit? Virum in caelo? Durum nobis videtur, ac Dei benignitate indignum, neque ordini salutis consummato conveniens, animos, perfecte iam beatos, denuo in calamitosam hancce vitam detrudere. An in inferno? Ex inferno nulla redemtio. Ecquid igitur erit existimandum? Tertius ne quidam locus ac status est, inter utrumque medius? Eum vero omnino nullum esse, ad liquidum perduximus. Inter tot, tamque discrepantes sententias, hanc intelligo, & magis tutam esse, & magis probabilem: fuisse eos in caelo quidem, sed tamquam hospites, nondum velut ciues, vt in singulari atque eximio praegustu aeternae beatitatis delectarentur. Illustrationi huius rei servit, quod Paullus adhuc vivus, sed extra se raptus, aliquid, huic simillimum, est expertus. 2 Corinth. XII, 2. 3. 4. purificatione futura liberatio.

Resp. Intelligitur l. c. ignis crucis, sive tentationis. Id quod patet e præcedente v. 10. 11. Probasti Deus, purgasti nos, sicut purgatur argentum; induxisti nos in rete; posuisti oppressionem super lumbos nostros.

IV. Quæcunque peccata hominibus in futuro sæculo remittuntur, ab illis igne purgatorio sunt repurgandi: Atqui quædam peccata &c.

Ergo. Maior claret: quia Deus impuris, quatenus perfeueranter sectantur impuritatem, peccata non remittit.

Minor prob. ex Matth. XII, 32. Peccatum in Spiritum S. neque in hoc, neque in futuro sæculo remittitur: Resp.

Verba Christi absolutam negationem important, vt sensus sit: peccatum in Spiritum S. non remittitur eis αἰῶνας, in æternum, interprete Marco, c. III, 29. Quod autem Christus distributiva locutione vtitur, & dicit: neque in hoc, neque in futuro sæculo, id fit ad exaggerandum peccatum in Spiritum S., quasi dicat: Si possibile esset, vt aliquod peccatum etiam post hanc vitam remitteretur, tamen peccatum in Spiritum S. tantum est, vt ne quidem post hanc vitam remitti queat.

V. Quicunque educuntur ex lacu, in quo non est aqua, illi educuntur ex purgatorio: Atqui quidam peccatores &c.

Zach. IX, 11. Ergo. Maior patet; quia lacus sine aqua non datur in hoc mundo: neque ex inferno educimur, quia ex illo non est liberatio.

Ergo educimur e purgatorio. Resp.

L. c. intelligitur lacus extremæ miseriæ, qualis in primis est miseria infernalis. Educti sumus e lacu extremæ miseriæ, in quo ne guttula quidem solatii est, per liberationem factam sanguine & morte Christi, non ideo, quod actu fuerimus proiecti in lacum infernalem, aut damnati, sed quoniam fuimus damnabiles & rei æterni supplicii.


### On the Burial of the Body

Quest. XII. Are the bodies of Christians to be buried?

Proved 1) By examples: The first mention of burial is made in the history of Abraham, of whom Moses, the most ancient of all writers, reports that he bought a field from the Hittites with a cave, in which he buried his deceased wife Sarah, Gen.

XXIII, 4. God Himself honored the body of Moses with burial in the land of Moab, Deut.

XXXIV, 6. The men of Jabesh are praised because they committed the bodies of Saul and Jonathan to the earth, 2 Sam.

II, 4, 5. Christ Himself, having expired on the cross, was brought by Joseph of Arimathea into an honorable monument.

2) Inhumation is a most beautiful type of our future resurrection.

For our body is sown, or committed to the earth like seed, 1 Cor. XV, 37, so that it may rise again on the day of universal judgment; it sleeps in the dust of the earth, Dan.

XII, 2, to be awakened by the voice of Christ, John V, 28. Therefore, the lifeless bodies of Christians are not to be cremated by fire, not to be thrown to beasts, not to be cast into the water.

Quest. XIII. Are the infants of Christians, not baptized, to be buried with solemn rites?

The bodies of infants, born of Christian parents, who are snatched away by sudden death before receiving baptism, are to be interred with solemn rites. born of Christians, who are snatched away by sudden death before receiving baptism, are to be interred with solemn rites.

Burial of the body. The lifeless bodies of the pious, who have departed from this life in communion with the church, are to be hidden in the earth honorably, but without luxury and immoderate pomp.

Prob. For they are born in the bosom of the church, and commended to God by the prayers of their parents and are thus holy (by external holiness), 1 Cor. VII, 14. inasmuch as sudden fate, not contempt, deprived them of baptism.

Latin:

Quæst. XII. Suntne corpora Christianorum sepelienda?

Prob. 1) Exemplis: Prima sepulturæ mentio fit in historia Abrahami, de quo Moses scriptorum omnium antiquissimus, refert, quod ab Hethitis agrum emerit cum spelunca, in qua defunctam coniugem Saram sepelivit, Gen.

XXIII, 4. Corpus Mosis Deus ipse sepultura honestavit in terra Moabi, Deut.

XXXIV, 6. Viri Iabes laudantur, quod corpora Saulis & ionathanis terræ mandauerint, 2 Sam.

II, 4. 5.

Christus ipse, in cruce exanimatus, a Iosepho Arimathæo in honorificum monumentum illatus est. 2) Inhumatio est typus pulcherrimus nostræ futuræ resurrectionis.

Corpus enim nostrum seminatur, sive feminis instar terræ committitur, 1 Cor. XV, 37. vt in die vniuersalis iudicii resurgat; dormit in pulvere terræ, Dan.

XII, 2. voce Christi excitandum, Io. V, 28. Proinde exanimata Christianorum corpora non sunt igne cremanda, non bestiis obiicienda, non in aquam mittenda.

Quæst. XIII.

An infantes christianorum, non baptizati, solemnibus ritibus humandi sunt? Corpora infantum, ex parentibus christianorum natorum, qui ante susceptum baptismum subita morte rapiuntur, solemnibus ritibus contumulanda sunt. christianis natorum, qui ante susceptum baptismum subita morte rapiuntur, folemnibus ritibus contumulanda sunt.

Sepultura corporis. Exanimata corpora piorum, qui in communione cum ecclesia ex hac vita decesserunt, honeste, sed sine luxu & pompa immoderata, in terram recondenda sunt.
