Prob. Sunt enim nati in gremio ecclesiae, precibusque parentum Deo commendati atque adeo sancti (sanctitate externa), 1 Cor. VII, 14. quippe quos repentinum fatum, non contemptus, baptismo priuauit.


### Quaest. XIV. Should honorable burial be granted to obstinate heretics and extremely wicked men?

Honorable burial should not be granted to obstinate heretics, who lead others away from orthodoxy, nor to men who are stubbornly malicious.

Prob. The Holy Scriptures show us the examples of Jeroboam, 1 Reg XIV, 11. Ahab and Jezebel, 1 Reg. XXI, 23. Jehoiakim, Jer. XXII, 19. who, having harmed others either by introducing heterodoxy or by evil example, were buried like asses.

Latin:

Neque pertinacibus haereticis, alios ab orthodoxia abducentibus, neque hominibus praefracte malitiosis, honorifica concedenda est sepultura.

Prob. Sacrae litterae ostendunt nobis exempla Ieroboami, 1 Reg XIV, 11. Achabi et Iezabelis, 1 Reg. XXI, 23. Ioiakimi, Ier. XXII, 19. qui cum aliis vel introducta heterodoxia, vel malo exemplo nocuissent, vel ut asini sepulti sunt.


### Quaest. XV. Must we despair of the salvation of those who are not buried?

If they die in the true faith, there is no reason to doubt their salvation.

Prob. Burial is a matter of decency, if it can be had, not of the necessity of salvation; otherwise, one would have to despair of the salvation of very many martyrs: of whom Augustine writes, L. I. de C. D. c. 12. The earth did not cover many bodies of Christians, but no one separated any of them from heaven and earth: which the presence of Him who knows from where He may resurrect what He created, fills entirely.

Latin:

Si in vera fide moriuntur, de illorum salute non est dubitandum.

Prob. Sepultura est de honestate, si haberi possit, non de necessitate salutis; alioqui de plurimorum martyrum salute desperandum fuerit: de quibus Augustinus scribit, L. I. de C. D. c. 12. Multa corpora Christianorum terra non texit, sed nullum eorum quisquam a caelo et terra separauit: quam totam implet praesentia sui, qui nouit, vnde resuscitet, quod creauit.


### On the Resuscitation and Resurrection of the Dead


### Quaest. XVI. What is the resuscitation of the dead?

The resuscitation of the dead is the action of the Triune God, by which He, by the power of His justice, will reproduce the bodies of all the deceased, and will unite them with their souls for the participation of eternal beatitude, or eternal damnation. Obs.

Resuscitation and resurrection differ as cause and effect. The former is the cause of the latter, since they do not rise again unless they are resuscitated. Resuscitation is the action of God, resurrection is the end-point of that action, and thus a divine work.

Latin:

Resuscitatio mortuorum est actio Dei triunius, qua is, vi iustitiae suae, omnium defunctorum corpora reproducet, et cum animabus vniet ad participationem aeternae beatitudinis, aut aeternae damnationis.

Obs. Resuscitatio, et resurrectio differunt, vt causa, et effectus. Illa huius causa est, cum non, nisi resuscitati, resurgant. Resuscitatio est actio Dei, resurrectio est terminus illius actionis, adeoque opus diuinum.


### Quaest. XVII. What is the resurrection of the dead?

The resurrection of the dead is the work of the Triune God, by which all deceased men will receive the same bodies in number which they had in this life, raised from death and reunited with their souls, for the full participation of eternal beatitude or damnation, and for the manifestation of divine justice, both remunerative and vindicative. Obs.

The resurrection of the dead is taken either in the proper sense or in the improper sense. Properly, it denotes the resurrection of bodies from natural death. Improperly, it is taken either metonymically; thus Christ is called the resurrection, i.e., the cause of the resurrection, John XI, 25. or metaphorically, both for liberation from adversities, Ps. XLI, 9. and for the conversion of a sinner, which is otherwise called the first resurrection, Apoc. XX, 5. Conf. Eph. V, 14.

Latin:

Resurrectio mortuorum est opus Dei triunius, quo defuncti homines omnes eadem numero corpora, quae in hac vita habuerunt, e morte excitata, et cum animabus suis redunita recipient, ad plenam beatitudinis, aut damnationis aeternae participationem, et ad manifestationem iustitiae diuinae remuneratoriae et vindicatiuae.

Obs. Resurrectio mortuorum sumitur vel in sensu proprio, vel in sensu improprio. Proprie notat resurrectionem corporum a morte naturali. Improprie sumitur vel metonymice; sic Christus dicitur resurrectio, i. e. causa resurrectionis, Io. XI, 25. vel metaphorice, tum pro liberatione ex aduersitatibus, Ps. XLI, 9. tum pro conuersione peccatoris, quae alias dicitur resurrectio prima, Apoc. XX, 5. Conf. Eph. V, 14.


### Question XVIII. Whether the resurrection of the dead is to be proven from the light of nature or from the light of scripture?

Although the possibility of the resurrection of the dead can be shown probably from the light of nature a) (*): yet its certainty is validly demonstrated from the prophetic writings of the Old b) and the apostolic writings of the New Testament c) alone.

Proof a. If human reason can to some extent investigate the creation of man: why not also the resurrection of men? For thus sound human reason concludes probably: he who could create from nothing the heaven, the earth, and whatever things are in them, he can also reproduce the bodies of men that have died and turned to ashes, and unite them with their souls: especially because the soul is immortal, and naturally desires the body to which it was united. That this natural desire should be in vain, and never fulfilled by God, is not at all likely; since in that way the soul would be left in an imperfect and preternatural state. Added to this is that divine providence and justice require that it be well for the good and ill for the bad. Since this often does not happen in this life: reason concludes that it will happen in the other life, so that the body which was the instrument of the soul in good and evil works may also become a participant in rewards and punishments. Whence it truly seems consistent that the dead body will at some time be resurrected.

Proof b. From Dan. XII, 2. Many of those sleeping in the dust of the earth shall awake: these to eternal life: but the others to reproach, to eternal ignominy. From this prophetic oracle we learn that some resurrection will certainly happen, not only of the pious, but also of the impious: for the former, the resurrection is a way to a glorious life; for the latter, a passage into ignominy.

Prob. c. From John V, 28. 29. The hour is coming, in which all who are in the graves will hear the voice of the Son of God, and will come forth; those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment. Which words of Christ are not to be understood concerning a spiritual resurrection through repentance. For those who rise again spiritually do not come forth from the sepulchers of sins to a resurrection of condemnatory judgment, which is asserted concerning certain ones who, upon hearing the voice of Christ, come forth from the graves. Therefore, the universal resurrection of bodies is understood. For the Savior speaks of all lying in the graves, and divides them into those to be saved and those to be damned (*).

Antithesis is that of the Atheists, Sadducees, and Epicureans (**), who deny the universal resurrection of bodies. Who object:

Giant-

is he himself finally going to destroy the bodies of brute animals, or rather everything in which there is nothing but matter? If you should think the former, it behooves you to posit a huge miracle, since this miracle, confirmed by the authority of divine revelation, seems to you utterly incredible only because it is a miracle. From this principle of reason has sprung the distinction of a twofold matter, which pertains to this mortal body with which we are now clothed. One is indeed constant, or, as is commonly said, essential, namely necessary for the nature and constitution of the body, so that it may truly be a human body, composed of its members, connected and fitted together: but the other is mutable, which is accustomed to be called accidental, and this pertains to the nourishment and preservation of the body, insofar as the body is mortal. Make it so, therefore, that the lifeless body of a man is devoured and consumed by living creatures, whether brute or rendered savage by ferocity. Its constant and natural matter is not consumed, nor indeed can it be by this principle: The nature and natural parts of no thing can, except by the will, power, and authority of the one Creator, be utterly converted into another nature). Daily, indeed, a continuous change of the body happens to man, by the departure of some particles and the accession of others. Yet the very nature of the body is always one and the same, neither ever increased nor diminished. With this distinction applied, the specious defense of the adversaries, in which alone they have trusted, collapses entirely.

II. That the thing will truly come to pass, a man, following nature alone as his guide, will never be able to know with any certain reasoning of the matter, especially for this reason, that no one, unless revelation shines before him, can be able to perceive the intimate corruption of human nature, and its restoration to integrity, whether it be, and what sort it is. But yet he concludes by probable argumentation from this, that 1) the body of man is the other part of human nature, and therefore the soul, unless it be altogether brutalized, burns with a most ardent desire for perpetual conjunction with its body; this indeed, since it tends not to destruction, but to perfection, is to be attributed not to the corruption, but to the constitution of human nature; nor is it credible that it was naturally implanted in every man in vain, and without a most wise counsel befitting it: 2) that the whole man, and not the soul alone, was given over either to virtue or to vice, for which reason it seems consistent with justice that the whole man also should be affected either by rewards or by punishments: especially if we consider 3) that the remuneration of virtue in this life often and greatly fails, where it goes ill with the good and well with the evil, Cohel. VIII, 14. IX, 2. nay 4) that this whole life is destined not so much for the completion of remuneration as for the consummation of labor; for the perfect reward is bestowed upon each one when labors are entirely finished: but as long as we shall dwell on earth, we must labor continuously, and the parts of earthly happiness are one and all means for laboring more, and incitements to greater zeal. Experience is also a witness, when we read what is related, Act. XVII, 32, that some of the Athenian citizens indeed held Paul’s assertion about the dead being recalled to life in derision, but the rest did not reject it, as being not improbable, being vehemently desirous of hearing more about this subject, and not from a desire for novelty (which you might perhaps suspect from v. 21), but from a zeal for knowing the truth with certainty, v. 34.

I. The giants shall not rise again, Resp. The giants shall not rise again to this temporal life, they shall not rise to the height of their former power. For the prophet adds: Thou hast destroyed them, and hast destroyed all their memory.

II. He who, when he has slept, has not revived, he does not rise again: But man &c. Therefore. Resp. Job does not deny the resurrection absolutely, but with a limitation. For he adds this limitation: until the heaven be worn away. For the universal resurrection shall be deferred until the day of the last judgment, when the heaven itself shall be worn away,

III. Whomever God resurrects, He remembers them: But He does not remember many men, Therefore. Resp. Distinguish between simple memory and benevolent memory. God forgets no man, but He does not remember the wicked benevolently after death, so as to affect them with eternal benefits.

IV. Those whose end is like the end of beasts, they shall not rise again: But the end of certain men &c. Therefore. Resp. King Solomon speaks of the necessity of dying, by which both beasts and men are bound, not of the state after death.

Instance: But King Solomon adds: Who knows if the spirit of man ascends upward, and the spirit of beasts downward? Resp. From external events, which happen as much to beasts as to men, reason left to itself does not certainly know the blessed immortality of souls: but from the word of God Solomon knows, and any reborn man knows, that the spirit returns to God,

V. The wicked shall not stand in judgment, Therefore they shall not rise again. Resp. The wicked shall not stand well in judgment, they shall not ll, but deprived of the goodness of their cause they shall fall into destruction.

VI. Whoever rise again to eternal life, praise God: The dead do not praise God, Therefore they rise again to eternal life. Resp. The dead, insofar as and as long as they are dead, do not praise God with bodily members, although their soul celebrates God: but when the bodies of the pious are resurrected, both their bodies and souls shall sing the praises of God.

Latin:

Quamvis possibilitas resurrectionis mortuorum e lumine naturæ probabiliter ostendi queat a) (*): illius tamen certitudo ex solis scriptis propheticis veteris b) & apostolicis novi Testamenti c) valide demonstratur.

Prob. a. Si ratio humana quadantenus investigare potest hominis creationem: quidni etiam hominum resurrectionem? Sic enim colligit probabiliter sana hominis ratio: qui e nihilo condere potuit cœlum, terram, & quæcunque in illis sunt, is potest etiam hominum demortua & in cineres versa corpora reproducere, & cum animabus vnire: inprimis quia anima immortalis est, & naturaliter corpus appetit, cui vnita fuit. Quod naturale desiderium frustraneum esse, & nunquam a Deo impleri, haud verisimile est; siquidem ita relinqueretur anima in statu imperfecto & præternaturali. Accedit, quod diuina prouidentia & iustitia requirat, vt bonis bene, malis male sit. Quod cum sæpe in hac vita non eueniat: colligit ratio, id in altera vita euenturum esse, vt quod corpus animæ in operibus bonis & malis fuit organon, præmiorum quoque ac pœnarum fiat particeps. Vnde vero consentaneum videtur, corpus mortuum aliquando resuscitatum iri.

Prob. b. E Dan. XII, 2. Multi de dormientibus in puluere terræ evigilabunt: hi ad vitam æternam: reliqui vero in opprobria, in ignominiam æternam. Ex hoc oraculo prophetico discimus, certo futuram esse aliquam resurrectionem non tantum piorum, sed & impiorum: illis resurrectionem esse viam ad vitam gloriosam; his transitum in ignominiam.

Prob. c. Ex Io. V, 28. 29. Venit hora, in qua omnes, qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem Filii Dei, & exibunt; qui bona fecerunt, in resurrectionem vitæ; qui mala fecerunt, in resurrectionem iudicii. Quæ verba Christi non intelligenda sunt de resurrectione spirituali per pœnitentiam. Nam qui spiritualiter resurgunt, non exeunt de sepulcris peccatorum ad resurrectionem iudicii condemnatorii, quod asseritur de quibusdam, qui ad auditam vocem Christi e monumentis prodeunt. Ergo intelligitur resurrectio corporum vniuersalis. Loquitur quippe saluator de omnibus iacentibus in sepulcris, eosque in saluandos & damnandos diuidit (*).

Antithesis est Atheorum, Sadducæorum & Epicuræorum (**), resurrectionem corporum vniuersalem negantium. Qui obiiciunt:

I. Gigan-

tentiam tandem destructurus ipse est corpora brutorum animantium, immo omnia, in quibus nil est, nisi materia? Si illud superius opineris, oportet te ingens statuere miraculum, quum tibi miraculum hoc, diuinæ patefactionis auctoritate confirmatum, tantum propter ea, quod sit miraculum, prorsus incredibile videatur. Ex hoc rationis principio enata est distinctio duplicis materiæ, quæ pertinet ad hoc corpus mortale, quo nunc induti sumus. Alia quidem est constans, seu, vt vulgo dicitur, essentialis, nimirum necessaria ad corporis naturam & constitutionem, vt vere sit humanum corpus, ex membris suis, inter se connexis atque aptis, compositum: Alia vero est mutabilis, quæ adpellari solet accidentalis, atque hæc ad alimentum & conseruationem corporis spectat, quoad mortale est corpus. Fac ergo, corpus hominis exanime ab animantibus, siue brutis, siue immanitate efferatis, deuoratum consumi. Non constans & naturalis eius materia consumitur, ac ne potest quidem per hoc principium: Nullius rei natura, ac partes naturales, possunt, nisi vnius Creatoris voluntate, potentia ac potestate, prorsus in aliam naturam conuerti). Quotidie quidem homini accidit continua corporis mutatio, particularum aliarum decessione, aliarum accessione. At ipsa tamen corporis natura semper vna est eademque, nec aucta vnquam, nec imminuta. Adhibita hac distinctione, speciosum aduersariorum præsidium, quo vno freti sunt, totum corruit.

II. Vere rem futuram esse, non quidem cum certa rei ratione homo, naturam solum ducem sequutus, cognoscere vnquam poterit, præsertim hanc ob caussam, quod nemo, nisi prælucente reuelatione, corruptionem naturæ humanæ intimam, atque eius in integrum restitutionem, an, & qualis sit ea, perspicere valeat. At probabili tamen argumentatione concludit ex eo, quod 1) corpus hominis est pars altera naturæ humanæ, ideoque animus, nisi plane efferatus sit, ardentissimo flagrat desiderio perpetuæ cum corpore suo coniunctionis; id vero, quum non ad destructionem, sed ad perfectionem tendat, non corruptioni, sed constitutioni naturæ humanæ tribuendum est; nec est credibile, illud frustra, ac sine sapientissimo consilio, illi conveniente, naturaliter homini cuique insitum esse: 2) quod homo totus, nec animus solum, aut virtuti, aut vitiositati deditus fuit, quam ob rem iustitiæ consentaneum videtur, vt totus etiam homo aut præmiis, aut pœnis adficiatur: in primis si cogitemus 3) remunerationem virtutis in hac vita sæpe multumque deficere, vbi cum bonis male, cum malis bene agitur, Cohel. VIII, 14. IX, 2. immo 4) vniuersam hancce vitam non tam ad perficiendum remunerationem, quam ad consummandum laborem destinatam esse; etenim perfectum præmium cuique tribuitur, laboribus omnino peractis: atqui quoad in terra commorabimur, continuo laborandum est, & partes terrestris felicitatis ad vnum omnes sunt media ad plus laborandum, & maioris studii incitamenta. Testis est etiam experientia, cum relatum legimus, Act. XVII, 32, non nullos quidem ciuium Atheniensium Paulli adseuerationem de mortuis in vitam reuocandis ludibrio habuisse, reliquos autem eam, vtpote non improbabilem, non reiecisse, vehementer cupidos, plus de hoc argumento audiendi, nec cupiditate nouitatis (quod forsitan suspiceris ex v. 21.), sed studio veritatis, certo cognoscendæ, v. 34.

I. Gigantes non resurgent, Resp. Gigantes non resurgent ad hanc vitam temporalem, non assurgent ad prioris potentiæ fastigium. Addit enim propheta: Dissipasti eos, & perdidisti omnem eorum memoriam.

II. Qui, cum dormiuit, non reuiuit, ille non resurgit: Sed homo &c. Ergo. Resp. Iobus non negat resurrectionem absolute, sed limitate. Addit enim hanc limitationem: donec atteratur cœlum. Differetur enim resurrectio vniuersalis vsque ad diem extremi iudicii, quo ipsum cœlum atteretur,

III. Quoscunque Deus resuscitat, illorum recordatur: Sed multorum hominum non recordatur, Ergo. Resp. Dist. inter memoriam simplicem, & beneuolam. Deus nullius hominis obliuiscitur, sed impiorum, post mortem, non recordatur beneuole, vt beneficiis æternis illos afficiat.

IV. Quorum exitus similis est egressui iumentorum, illi non resurgent: Sed quorumdam hominum exitus &c. Ergo. Resp. Loquitur Rex Salomo de moriendi necessitate, qua tam iumenta, quam homines obstringuntur, non de statu post mortem.

Instantia: Sed addit Rex Salomo: Quis scit, an Spiritus hominis ascendat sursum, & Spiritus iumentorum deorsum? Resp. Ex euentibus externis, qui tam iumentis, quam hominibus obtingunt, ratio sibi relicta beatam animarum immortalitatem certo non cognoscit: at ex verbo Dei nouit Salomo, & quilibet homo renatus, spiritum redire ad Deum,

V. Impii in iudicio non stabunt, E. non resurgent. Resp. Impii in iudicio non bene stabunt, non llent, sed bonitate causæ destituti ruent in interitum.

VI. Quicunque ad æternam resurgunt, Deum laudant: Mortui Deum non laudant, E. ad vitam æternam resurgunt. Resp. Mortui, quatenus & quam diu mortui sunt, Deum non laudant membris corporeis, licet eorum anima Deum celebret: at cum corpora piorum resuscitabuntur, eorum & corpora & animæ laudes Dei canent.


### Quæst. XIX. Who shall resurrect the dead?

Who shall resurrect the dead? The triune God shall resurrect the dead, the Father , the Son of God , and the Holy Spirit . Yet in a singular way the resurrection of the dead is appropriated to Christ, the God-man .

Prob. a. From 2 Cor. IV, 14. He who raised up Jesus, the same shall also raise us up through Jesus. But God the Father raised up Jesus, .

Prob. b. From Job V, 25. The dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God, and they who hear, shall live.

Prob. c. From Rom. VIII, 11. If the Spirit of him who raised up Jesus from the dead, dwells in you: he who raised up Christ from the dead, shall also quicken your mortal bodies because of his Spirit that dwells in you. The Holy Spirit preserves in us spiritual life. that they dared to deny the calling back of the dead into life, not in its entirety, but as something to happen at some time. It is not clear what both of them intended, putting this forward: that it had already been done entirely. Many think the cause of the error was this: that they interpreted the resurrection of the dead (ἀνάστασιν νεκρῶν) entirely improperly, either as the spiritual resurrection of men converted to Christ, or as the civil resurrection of the Jewish republic, restored to its pristine integrity after the bonds of the Babylonian captivity were loosed, . But to me those heretics seem to have understood the calling back of the dead into life in the proper sense of the word, but to have thought that it was all to be attributed to Christ alone, not wishing to perceive the force and necessity of the consequence. I shall produce that very testimony, 1 Cor. XV, 12. from which words it is apparent that no Christian doubted that Christ's body was called back into life, but that many only denied this, that it would follow that our bodies also would be raised from the underworld.

them, and if we constantly follow his guidance, he guards us for the obtaining of eternal life, into which we enter through the resurrection.

Prob. d. In a singular way the resurrection of the dead is appropriated to Christ the God-man (θεανθρώπῳ); because 1) just as God the Father gave to Christ the power of executing judgment, because he is the son of man, John 5:27, so also to Christ, as man, he committed the power of raising the dead. 2) It is a fruit of the glorious resurrection of Christ, that he might rule over the dead and the living, Rom. 14:9. Which universal dominion King Jesus will exert in the resuscitation of the dead. 3) Christ with a sensible voice and visible in the clouds will call the dead from the tombs to judgment. Matt. 25:31; 1 Thess. 4:16. 4) Because Christ is the cause of the resurrection not only efficient, but also meritorious, with respect to the glorious resurrection of the faithful. Which the author of life himself hints at John 11:25: I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live: and whoever lives and believes in me shall never die.

Latin:

Mortuos resuscitabit Deus triunus, Pater , Filius Dei , & Spiritus Sanctus . Singulari tamen ratione resuscitatio mortuorum appropriatur Christo, θεανθρώπῳ .

Prob. a. Ex 2 Cor. IV, 14. Qui suscitauit Iesum, idem & nos suscitabit per Iesum. At Deus Pater Iesum suscitauit, .

Prob. b. Ex Iob. V, 25. Mortui audient vocem Filii Dei, & qui audient, viuent.

Prob. c. Ex Rom. VIII, 11. Si Spiritus eius, qui suscitauit Iesum ex mortuis, habitat in vobis: is, qui suscitauit Christum ex mortuis, viuificabit etiam mortua corpora vestra propter inhabitantem suum Spiritum in vobis. Spiritus S. conferuat in nobis vitam spiritualem. que mortuorum in vitam reuocationem non omnem, sed aliquando futuram infitiari ausi sunt. Non liquet, quid sibi voluerint ambo, hoc præ se ferentes: eam omnino iam factam esse. Causam erroris putant plerique hanc fuisse: quod ἀνάστασιν νεκρῶν illi omnem improprie sint interpretati, vel de spirituali hominum, ad Christum conuersorum, vel de ciuili rei publicæ Iudaicæ, solutis vinculis captiuitatis Babylonicæ, in pristinam integritatem restitutæ, . Sed mihi videntur illi hæretiçi reuocationem mortuorum in vitam proprie quidem ita dictam intellexisse, eam vero omnem Christo vni adferendam putasse, nolentes perspicere consequentis vim ac necessitatem. Producam illud ipsum testimonium, 1 Cor. XV, 12. quibus ex verbis adparet, de Christi corpore in vitam reuocato, Christianorum neminem dubitasse, hoc tantum multos negatum iuisse, consequens fore, vt nostra quoque corpora ab inferis excitentur.

lem, & si ductum eius constanter sequimur, custodit nos ad obtinendam vitam aeternam, in quam per resurrectionem ingredimur.

Prob. d. Singulari modo resurrectio mortuorum Christo θεανθρώπῳ appropriatur; quia 1) sicut Deus Pater Christo dedit potestatem iudicii faciendi, quia filius hominis est, Io. V, 27. ita & Christo, qua homini, commisit potestatem mortuos resuscitandi. 2) Fructus gloriosae resurrectionis Christi est, vt mortuis & viventibus dominetur, Rom. XIV, 9. Quod dominium vniversale Rex Iesus in mortuorum resuscitatione exseret. 3) Christus sensibili voce & in nubibus conspicuus mortuos e tumulis evocabit ad iudicium. Matth. XXV, 31. 1 Thess. IV, 16. 4) Quia Christus est causa resurrectionis non tantum efficiens, sed etiam meritoria, respectu gloriosae resurrectionis fidelium. Id quod ipse auctor vitae innuit Io. XI, 25. Ego sum resurrectio & vita, qui credit in me, etsi moriatur, vivet: omnis vero, qui vivit & credit in me, non morietur in aeternum.


### XX. Will all men rise again?

All men will rise again, who have been dead, as well the pious as the impious.

Prob. a. The universal resurrection of the dead is established from Dan. 12:2 and John 5:29, which classic sayings we adduced above, qu.

XVIII. Prob. b. From Isa. 26:19: Thy dead shall live, and with their bodies they shall rise. From which prophetic utterance we gather two things: 1) That the subject of the resurrection is dead men; wherefore Enoch and Elias, who have never died, and those men whom the last day of the world, with Christ the judge appearing, shall find alive, will not rise again from natural death; because their soul was not separated from the body, yet they will be changed by the heavenly judge: concerning which change Paul informs us, 1 Cor. 15:51: Behold! I tell you a mystery: we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. Paul calls the doctrine concerning this change a mystery; since that ἀλλαγή, or change, will be singular, miraculous, unsearchable, and ineffable; the same says that it will not come to pass that we shall all sleep. Therefore this miraculous change will not be substantial, bringing about either the dissolution of soul and body, or another substance of the body; but accidental, as regards state and qualities, so that the corruptible body of the living may on the last day suddenly put on incorruptibility, whereby neither the bodies of the impious may be annihilated by flames, nor the bodies of the pious undergo any alteration before the throne of God. 2) We gather that the subject of the resurrection is not the soul, but the body of the deceased man, for the prophet says: with their bodies they shall rise. The soul, since it is immortal, as it does not die, so it does not rise again. For resurrection is formally the repeated standing of the same thing that fell: Only the body, not the soul, fell: Therefore only the body, not the soul, will rise again.

Prob. c. From the testimony of Christ saying, John 11:25: He who believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live. From which Paul, 1 Thess. 4:14, says: God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus.

Prob. d. 1) From Acts 24:15: I have hope in God, which these themselves also expect, that there will be a future resurrection of the dead, both of the just and the unjust. You say: The resurrection of the unjust, since it is not good, cannot be hoped for.

I answer: It can be hoped for secondarily, in so far as the innocence of a just man accused and oppressed by the calumnies of the unjust, such as Paul was, becomes most clearly known in the resurrection and judgment of the unjust.

2) From 2 Cor. V, 10. For we must all be manifested before the judgment seat of Christ, that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to what he hath done, whether it be good or evil. Whoever are the architects of crimes in the body will pay the penalty in the body; their body will also rise again for punishment. For once the consequent is posited, namely, judgment divinely exercised upon the body, the antecedent, the resurrection of the body, must be posited.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians (*), who deny the resurrection of the impious. Who object:

I. The impious die eternally, 2 Thess. I, 9: Therefore they do not rise again. Resp. The impious die eternally because they will be deprived of the glorious life of the elect, yet they will live eternally the ignominious life of the reprobate; which life is called death, because it is bereft of all happiness and all consolation.

II. The impious shall not rise in judgment, Ps. I, 5. Resp. The word קום signifies not only to rise again, but also to stand. The impious shall not stand in judgment; they will not be able to sustain the rigor of the divine examination. Cf. Is. VII, 12.

III. The resurrection is a huge benefit, Phil. III, 9, of which the impious are unworthy. Resp. The resurrection to eternal life is a huge benefit: but the resurrection to eternal condemnation is a huge punishment.

IV. God will bring back with Him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus, 1 Thess. IV, 14. Therefore only Christians finally believing will rise again. Resp. Paul, in the cited place, deals with the glorious resurrection of the just; he does not speak exclusively, he does not exclude the resurrection of the unjust, of which he makes mention in Acts XXIV, 15.

Latin:

Resurgent omnes homines a), qui fuerunt mortui b), tam pii c), quam impii d).

Prob. a. Resurrectio mortuorum vniversalis constat e Dan. XII, 2. & Io. V, 29. quae dicta classica adduximus supra, qu.

XVIII. Prob. b. Ex Es. XXVI, 19. Viuent mortui tui, & cum corporibus resurgent. Ex quo eloquio prophetico colligimus duo: 1) Subiectum quod resurrectionis esse homines mortuos; quare Enoch & Elias, qui nunquam sunt mortui, & homines illi, quos extremus mundi dies, apparente iudice Christo, viuos deprehendet, non resurgent a morte naturali; quia anima eorum a corpore non fuit separata, immutabuntur tamen a iudice coelesti: de qua immutatione nos informat Paullus, 1 Cor. XV, 51. Ecce! mysterium vobis dico: omnes quidem non obdormiemus, omnes tamen immutabimur in momento, in ictu oculi, in extrema tuba. Paullus doctrinam de ista immutatione vocat mysterium; quoniam illa ἀλλαγή, siue mutatio, erit singularis, miraculosa, impervestigabilis & ineffabilis; dicit idem, quod non futurum sit, vt omnes obdormiamus. Ergo mutatio haec miraculosa non erit substantialis, inferens vel dissolutionem animae & corporis, vel aliam substantiam corporis; sed accidentalis, quoad statum & qualitates, vt corpus viventium corruptibile in extremo die subito induat incorruptibilitatem, quo nec corpora impiorum flammis annihilentur, nec corpora piorum coram throno Dei vllam subeant alterationem. 2) Colligimus, subiectum quo resurrectionis non esse animam, sed corpus hominis defuncti, dicit enim propheta: cum corporibus resurgent. Anima, cum sit immortalis, vt non moritur, ita non resurgit. Resurrectio enim formaliter est eiusdem, quod cecidit, iterata statio: Solum corpus, non anima, cecidit: Ergo solum corpus, non anima resurget.

Prob. c. Ex testimonio Christi dicentis, Io. XI, 25. Qui credit in me, etsi moriatur, vivet. Ex quo Paullus, 1 Thess. IV, 14. inquit: Deus eos, qui obdormierunt per Iesum, reducet cum ipso.

Prob. d. 1) Ex Act. XXIV, 15. Spem habeo erga Deum, quam etiam hi ipsi exspectant, resurrectionem futuram esse mortuorum, iustorum & iniustorum. Dicis: Resurrectio iniustorum, cum non sit bona, sperari nequit.

Resp. Sperari potest secundario, in quantum innocentia hominis iusti ab iniustis accusati & calumniis oppressi, qualis erat Paullus, in resurrectione & iudicio iniustorum clarissime innotescit.

2) Ex 2 Cor. V, 10. Oportet nos omnes manifestari coram tribunali Christi, vt reportet quilibet ea, quæ per corpus (facta), prout ea fecit, siue bonum, siue malum quodlibet fuerit. Quicunque scelerum architecti in corpore supplicium luent, eorum corpus etiam ad supplicium resurget. Nam posito consequente, scil. iudicio in corpus diuinitus exercendo, ponenda est antecedens corporis resurrectio.

Antithesis est Socinianorum (*), impiorum resurrectionem infitiantium. Qui obiiciunt:

I. Impii æternum moriuntur, 2 Thess. I, 9: E. non resurgunt. Resp. Impii æternum moriuntur, quia priuati erunt vita gloriosa electorum, æternum tamen viuere vitam ignominiosam reproborum; quæ vita mors dicitur, quia omni felicitate, omni solatio orbata est.

II. Impii non resurgent in iudicio, Ps. I, 5. Resp. Verbum קום non tantum resurgere, sed & stare significat. Impii non consistent in iudicio, non poterunt sustinere rigorem examinis diuini. Conf. Es. VII, 12.

III. Resurrectio est ingens beneficium, Phil. III, 9. quo indigni sunt impii. Resp. Resurrectio ad vitam æternam est ingens beneficium: at resurrectio ad condemnationem æternam est ingens supplicium.

IV. Deus eos, qui obdormierunt per Iesum, reducet cum ipso, 1 Thess. IV, 14. E. soli Christiani finaliter credentes resurgent. Resp. Paullus l. c. agit de resurrectione gloriosa iustorum; non autem loquitur exclusiue, non excludit resurrectionem iniustorum, cuius mentionem iniicit, Act. XXIV, 15.


### XX. Will all men rise again?: Question XXI. Are the impious to rise again by virtue of the merit of Christ?

Question XXI. Are the impious to rise again by virtue of the merit of Christ?

Christ will not raise the unjust to eternal condemnation as a gracious mediator, but as an omnipotent and severe judge; and thus the impious will not rise by virtue of the merit of Christ a), but by virtue of the divine decree and vindicatory justice b).

Obs. Here one must accurately distinguish between the merit of Christ considered in terms of acquisition and application. By His universal merit, Christ has merited and acquired the resurrection to eternal life for all, and thus even for the impious: but the impious, due to a lack of application, do not enjoy that acquired and merited resurrection to life. Hence it happens that they do not rise to eternal condemnation by virtue of the merit of Christ, but by virtue of divine justice.

Proof a. 1) From 1 Cor. XV, 23, where those who are to rise by virtue of the merit of Christ are said to be His members. Hence arises the argument: Those to whom the resurrection belongs, to be future by virtue of the merit of Christ, are members of Christ: But the impious are not members of Christ: Therefore the future resurrection by virtue of the merit of Christ does not belong to the impious.

You say: The impious are not spiritual members of Christ, but natural: for they are bone of His bones and flesh of His flesh, Eph. V, 30. Resp. Christ is called our head not naturally, but spiritually; therefore His members are not natural, but spiritual, because of the spiritual union through faith, Gal. II, 20; Eph. III, 17. Whence the members of Satan cannot be members of Christ; for he who does not have the Spirit of Christ is not His, Rom. VIII, 9.

Prob. b. 2) The resurrection, which happens on account of the merit of Christ, is a huge benefit (For it is ordained unto eternal life, John 11:25, John 14:19): But the resurrection of the wicked is not a benefit, but a huge punishment: Therefore, the resurrection of the wicked does not happen on account of the merit of Christ. The minor is proven: because the resurrection of the wicked is ordained unto eternal condemnation, and thus is not a benefit, but a huge punishment. From this argument flows that other one: No fruit of the merit of Christ reaches a man without faith in Christ: But the resurrection reaches the wicked, men without faith in Christ: Therefore, the resurrection of the wicked is not a fruit of the merit of Christ.

Prob. c. That the wicked rise again by the force of the decree and divine justice, is evident from the divine oracle, Gen. 2:17. In whatsoever day you eat of the fruit of that tree, you shall die the death. By which oracle is contained the decree of God the most just judge, encompassing temporal and eternal death, and thus the punishment of this and the future age. But the body, a companion of sins, cannot pay the eternal punishment unless it be raised from the dust of the earth to endure perpetual torments in hell. Wherefore, even if Christ had never come in the flesh, nor had ever merited any good for men; yet sinful men would have had to rise again, that they might pay the eternal punishment of sins, by the force of divine vindictive justice. We conclude: Whatever would have happened to men without the intervention of the merit of Christ, that is not a fruit of the merit of Christ: But the resurrection unto punishment for the wicked would have happened without the intervention of the merit of Christ. Therefore.

You say: The resurrection unto punishment is indeed not an effect of the merit of Christ; but the resurrection, considered generally and formally, as it is distinguished from the resurrection unto glory and ignominy, is an effect of the merit of Christ. Hence the wicked will indeed rise again by the force of the merit of Christ, but not unto punishment.

Resp. The merit of Christ of itself looks to an end beneficial to man. And therefore the resurrection, considered abstractly and formally, is an action of divine omnipotence, but the resurrection unto salvation is a fruit of the merit of Christ.

The antithesis is that of Benedictus Aretius, Henricus Boëthius, and others, who maintain that even the wicked rise again by the force of the merit of Christ. Who argue:

I. That the resurrection of the pious and the wicked depends on the resurrection of Christ, Paul shows not obscurely, 1 Cor. 15:12 up to v. 34. For in that place he argues on purpose that men will rise again because Christ rose again. But the Pauline inference would not suffice to solve the raised question, unless the resurrection of Christ is the cause why the pious and the wicked rise again. For the question was not asked about the resurrection of the pious only, but the question was moved generally about the resurrection of all the dead. Resp. 1) The Apostle's inference does not tend to demonstrate the necessity of a universal resurrection; but to refute the alleged impossibility and to defend its truth, taking the argument from the truth of the resurrection of Christ, and the power of the one rising, 1 Cor. 15 from v. 3 to 12, and also by a reduction to the absurd, from v. 12 to 20 and from v. 29 to 33. 2) Although the Apostle in the cited place directly and immediately proves only the resurrection of the pious, yet from it the resurrection of the wicked is afterwards indirectly and mediately deduced because of the necessary connection of the resurrection of the pious and the wicked, which depends on the divine decree.

II. Paul says, 1 Cor. 15: 22. As in Adam all die: So in Christ shall all be made alive. And from which they collect: Whoever die in Adam, are made alive through Christ: But all men &c. Therefore. Resp. The universal sign in the latter part of the Pauline proposition is to be taken restrictively, so that it refers to those who are members of Christ, v. 23, and rise again unto eternal life. But not it follows: All rising to eternal life rise by the power of the merit of Christ: Therefore also the reprobate. For these do not rise to eternal life. For it is just as if you were to infer; Rom. 5, 18. As by the sin of one man into all men unto condemnation (the matter resulted): so by the righteousness of one man into all men unto justification of life. Therefore all men, elect and reprobate alike, are actually saved. It is not absolutely necessary that the parts of the opposition be of equal breadth.

III. The merit of Christ is universal, 1 Tim. 2, 6. Therefore it looks also to the impious. Resp. The merit of Christ in itself is universal, as the acquisition of benefits; but that anyone may possess them, application through faith is required, which the impious lack. Whence the resurrection of them is not a benefit, but a punishment.

IV. Whoever are raised from the dead by the voice of Christ the mediator, they rise by the power of the merit of Christ: But the impious also are awakened from the dead by the voice of Christ the mediator, Io. 5, 28. Therefore. Resp. Whoever are raised by the voice of Christ to eternal life, they rise by the virtue of the merit of Christ; I concede: But the impious rise to eternal ignominy, which does not descend from the merit of Christ. The impious are therefore raised by the voice of Christ, as of an angry judge, not as of a mediator, or a gracious head, since they were never joined and incorporated to him through faith.

Latin:

Quæst. XXI. An impii resurrecturi sunt vi meriti Christi?

Christus iniustos ad æternam condemnationem non resuscitabit vt gratiosus mediator, sed vt omnipotens & seuerus iudex; adeoque impii non resurgent vi meriti Christi a), sed vi decreti diuini, & iustitiæ vindicatiuæ b).

Obs. Accurate hic distinguendum est inter meritum Christi consideratum ratione acquisitionis, & applicationis. Christus vniuersali suo merito omnibus, atque adeo etiam impiis resurrectionem ad vitam æternam promeruit & acquisiuit: at impii, propter defectum applicationis, acquisita & promerita illa resurrectione ad vitam non potiuntur. Inde fit, vt ad æternam condemnationem non resurgant vi meriti Christi, sed vi iustitiæ diuinæ.

Prob. a. 1) Ex 1 Cor. XV, 23. vbi illi, qui resurrecturi sunt vi meriti Christi, dicuntur esse ipsius membra. Hinc oritur argumentum: Ad quos pertinet resurrectio, virtute meriti Christi futura, illi sunt membra Christi: Impii autem non sunt membra Christi: Ergo ad impios non pertinet resurrectio futura virtute meriti Christi.

Dicis: Impii non sunt membra Christi spiritualia, sed naturalia: sunt enim os de ossibus eius & caro de carne eius, Eph. V, 30. Resp. Christus dicitur caput nostrum non naturaliter, sed spiritualiter; ergo membra ipsius non sunt naturalia, sed spiritualia, ob spiritualem vnionem per fidem, Gal. II, 20. Eph. III, 17. Vnde membra Satanæ non possunt esse membra Christi; qui enim Spiritum Christi non habet, non est ipsius, Rom. VIII, 9.

Prob. b. 2) Resurrectio, quae fit propter meritum Christi, est ingens beneficium (Ordinatur enim ad vitam aeternam, Io. XI, 25. Io. XIV, 19.): At resurrectio impiorum non beneficium est, sed ingens supplicium: E. resurrectio impiorum non fit propter meritum Christi. Minor probatur: quia resurrectio impiorum ordinatur ad aeternam condemnationem, adeoque non est beneficium, sed ingens supplicium. Ex hoc argumento fluit alterum illud: Nullus fructus meriti Christi sine fide in Christum homini obtingit: At resurrectio impiis, sine fide in Christum hominibus, obtingit: E. resurrectio impiorum non est fructus meriti Christi.

Prob. c. Quod impii vi decreti & iustitiae divinae resurgant, patet ex oraculo divino , Gen. II, 17. Quacunque die de fructu illius arboris comedes, morte morieris. Quo oraculo continetur decretum Dei iustissimi iudicis, complectens mortem temporalem & aeternam, atque adeo poenam huius & futuri saeculi. Non autem potest corpus, peccatorum socium, aeternam luere poenam, nisi e pulvere terrae excitetur ad sustinendum perpetuos in inferno cruciatus. Quare, etiamsi Christus nunquam venisset in carnem, nec unquam hominibus quidquam boni meruisset; tamen hominibus peccatoribus fuisset resurgendum, ut luerent poenam peccatorum aeternam, vi iustitiae divinae vindicativae. Colligimus: Quidquid sine interventu meriti Christi hominibus evenisset, illud non est fructus meriti Christi: Atqui resurrectio ad poenam impiis sine interventu meriti Christi evenisset. Ergo.

Dicis Resurrectio ad poenam non quidem est effectus meriti Christi; at resurrectio γενικῶς & formaliter spectata, prout praecindit a resurrectione ad gloriam & ignominiam, est effectus meriti Christi. Vnde impii vi meriti Christi quidem resurgent, sed non ad poenam.

Resp. Meritum Christi per se respicit finem homini salutarem. Ideoque resurrectio abstracte & formaliter considerata est actio omnipotentiae divinae, resurrectio autem ad salutem est fructus meriti Christi.

Antithesis est Benedicti Aretii, Henrici Boëthii & aliorum, statuentium, etiam impios vi meriti Christi resurgere. Qui argumentantur:

I. Piorum ac impiorum resurrectionem pendere a resurrectione Christi, non obscure monstrat Paullus, 1 Cor. XV, 12. usque ad v. 34. Isthic enim loci ex professo urget, ideo resurrecturos homines, quia Christus resurrexit. Non autem sufficeret illatio Paullina motae quaestioni soluendae, nisi resurrectio Christi caussa sit, cur pii & impii resurgant. Non enim quaerebatur de piorum tantum resurrectione, sed generatim mouebatur quaestio de omnium mortuorum resurrectione. Resp. 1) Apostoli illatio non tendit ad demonstrandam necessitatem resurrectionis vniversalis; sed ad refutandam praetensam impossibilitatem & defendendam eius veritatem, sumto argumento a veritate resurrectionis Christi, & resurgentis potentia, 1 Cor. XV, a v. 3. ad 12. nec non deductione ad absurdum, a v. 12. ad 20. & a v. 29. ad 33. 2) Quamuis Apostolus l. c. directe & immediate probet duntaxat piorum resurrectionem, ex ea tamen indirecte & mediate postea impiorum resurrectio deducitur ob necessariam piorum & impiorum resurrectionis connexionem, a divino decreto dependentem.

II. Paullus inquit, 1 Cor. XV, 2. Quem ad modum per Adamum omnes moriuntur: Ita per Christum omnes vivificantur. Et quibus colligunt: Quicunque in Adamo moriuntur, per Christum vivificantur: Atqui omnes homines &c. Ergo. Resp. Signum vniversale in posteriori parte propositionis Paullinae restricte accipiendum est, vt scilicet referatur ad illos, qui sunt membra Christi, v. 23. & resurgunt ad vitam aeternam. Non autem sequitur: Omnes ad vitam aeternam resurgentes resurgunt vi meriti Christi: E. etiam reprobi. Nam hi non resurgunt ad vitam aeternam. Perinde enim est, ac si inferres; Rom. V, 18. Sicut per unius hominis peccatum in omnes homines in condemnationem (res cessit): ita per unius hominis iustitiam in omnes homines in iustificationem vitae. Ergo omnes homines, electi & reprobi simul actu saluantur. Non absolute necessarium est, vt partes oppositionis sint aequalis latitudinis.

III. Meritum Christi est vniuersale, 1 Tim. II, 6. E. spectat etiam ad impios. Resp. Meritum Christi in se est vniuersale, qua acquisitionem beneficiorum; sed vt iis quispiam potiatur, requiritur applicatio per fidem, qua impii carent. Vnde resurrectio illorum non est beneficium, sed supplicium.

IV. Quicunque voce Christi mediatoris a morte resuscitantur, illi vi meriti Christi resurgunt: Atqui impii etiam voce Christi mediatoris a morte excitantur, Io. V, 28. Ergo. Resp. Quicunque voce Christi resuscitantur ad vitam aeternam, illi virtute meriti Christi resurgunt; concedo: At impii resurgunt ad aeternam ignominiam, quae non descendit ex merito Christi. Resuscitantur igitur impii voce Christi, tanquam iudicis irati, non vt mediatoris, aut capitis gratiosi, cum huic nunquam per fidem fuerint iuncti & incorporati.


### XX. Will all men rise again?: Quest. XX. Do the same bodies in number, which fell, rise again?

Quest. XX. Do the same bodies in number, which fell, rise again?

The same bodies in number, which men carried about in this mortal life, are to rise again on the last day , but clothed with new qualities .

Prob. a. 1) Resurrection formally is the repeated standing of the same thing which fell through death. Wherefore, those who deny the resurrection of the same body in number, utterly deny the true resurrection.

2) Paul 1 Cor. 15, 53. It is necessary, he says, for this corruptible to put on incorruptibility. Not without cause does the Apostle employ the pronoun of demonstration, τοῦτο, this, but to show that this body, which in this life is corruptible, is to be rendered incorruptible by God in the resurrection (*).

3) Everyone shall report what he did in his body, good or evil, 2 Cor. 5, 10. The same body, therefore, which was a companion of the struggle in this age, shall be crowned in the future age, and that which was a participant of evils, shall not be devoid of ignominy by the power of divine vindictive justice. 4) Is

4) He who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to our bodies, because of His Spirit dwelling in us, as Paul testifies, Rom. VIII, 10.

Whatever bodies have been the dwellings of the Holy Spirit in this life, those will be given life by God: But the same bodies which the pious bear in this life have been the dwellings of the Holy Spirit. Therefore.

5) Job, broken by many evils, raises himself up with the hope of his body, clearly worn out, being divinely resurrected c.

XIX, 26. After my skin, these shall be surrounded; and from my flesh I shall see God. The meaning is: after my skin has been reduced to dust, these bones of mine shall be surrounded by skin, and with these bodily eyes of mine I shall see God incarnate.

*Prob. b. 1) The bodies of the faithful, glorified in the resurrection, will be similar to the glorified body of Christ, Phil. III, 21. But this was adorned with new qualities. Therefore, those too will shine with new ornaments (*).

2) Paul, describing the accidental change which occurs by the benefit of the resurrection, says: 1 Cor. XV, 42. It is sown in corruptibility, it is raised in incorruptibility: It is sown in dishonor, it will be raised in glory: It is sown an animal body, it will be raised a spiritual body.

Therefore, the bodies which we carry about in this life differ from the resurrected bodies not by reason of substance, but 1) by reason of duration: Those are corrupted and perish, these, immune from corruption, endure forever. 2) By reason of external form.

Those become deformed, pale, foul-smelling corpses: These will be graceful, radiant, most beautiful: 3) By reason of strength. Those are sown into the earth flaccid, destitute of sense and motion: These will be vigorous, robust, endowed with excellent senses, subject to no defect.

4) By reason of operation and passion. Those are subject to generation, nutrition, augmentation, local progress, they need drink, food, marriage: These will be entirely free from these, occupied with spiritual actions, nor will they need nourishment or conjugal society.

The antithesis is that of the Socinians (**) who deny that the bodies will rise again numerically the same.

Latin:

Quaest. XX. An eadem numero corpora, quae ceciderunt, resurgent?

Eadem numero corpora, quae homines in hac vita mortali circumtulerunt, in die extremo resurrectura sunt , sed nouis qualitatibus vestita .

Prob. a. 1) Resurrectio formaliter est eiusdem, quod per mortem cecidit, iterata statio. Quare, qui negant eiusdem numero corporis resurrectionem, veram resurrectionem penitus infitiantur.

2) Paullus 1 Cor. XV, 53. Oportet, inquit, corruptibile hoc induere incorruptibilitatem. Non sine caussa Apostolus adhibet pronomen demonstrationis, τοῦτο, hoc, sed vt ostendat, hoc corpus, quod in hac vita corruptibile est, in resurrectione a Deo redditum iri incorruptibile (*).

3) Vnusquisque reportabit, quae in corpore suo gessit, bonum, aut malum, 2 Cor. V, 10. Idem igitur corpus, quod socium fuit certaminis in hoc saeculo, coronabitur in saeculo futuro, & quod fuit malorum particeps, non erit expers ignominiae vi iustitiae diuinae vindicatiuae. 4) Is

4) Is, qui resuscitavit Christum ex mortuis, vivificabit etiam corpora nostra, propter inhabitantem suum Spiritum in nobis, teste Paulo, Rom. VIII, 10.

Quaecunque corpora fuerunt domicilia Spiritus S. in hac vita, illa a Deo vivificabuntur: Atqui eadem corpora, quae pii gerunt in hac vita, fuerunt domicilia Spiritus S. E.

5) Iobus se plurimis fractum malis erigit spe corporis sui plane eneruati, divinitus resuscitandi c.

XIX, 26. Post cutem meam circumdabuntur haec; & ex carne mea videbo Deum. Sensus est: post cutem meam in puluerem redactam haec mea ossa cute circumdabuntur, & his meis oculis corporeis Deum incarnatum videbo.

*Prob. b. 1) Corpora fidelium glorificata in resurrectione similia erunt clarificato corpori Christi, Phil.* III, 21. At hoc novis qualitatibus erat exornatum. E. & illa novis ornamentis refulgebunt (*).

2) Paullus accidentalem, quae beneficio resurrectionis contingit, mutationem describens ait: 1 Cor. XV, 42. Seminatur in corruptibilitate, resuscitatur in incorruptibilitate: Seminatur in ignominia, resuscitabitur in gloria: Seminatur corpus animale, resuscitabitur spirituale.

Differunt itaque corpora, quae in hac vita circumferimus, a corporibus resuscitatis non ratione substantiae, sed 1) ratione durationis: Illa corrumpuntur, & intereunt, haec immunia a corruptione semper durant. 2) Ratione formae externae.

Illa fiunt cadauera deformia, pallida, foetida: Haec erunt gratiosa, fulgida, pulcerrima: 3) Ratione roboris. Haec seminantur in terram flaccida, sensu motuque destituta: Illa erunt vegeta, robusta, sensibus eximiis pollentia, nulli defectui obnoxia.

4) Ratione operationis & passionis. Illa subiecta sunt generationi, nutritioni, augmentationi, progressui locali, indigent potu, cibo, matrimonio: Haec tota vacabunt actionibus spiritualibus, nec egebunt nutrimento, aut societate coniugali.

Antithesis est Socinianorum negantium (**), corpora numero eadem resurrectura esse.


### XX. Will all men rise again?: Their arguments are: I

Their arguments are: I.

The resurrected body is called spiritual, 1 Cor. XV, 44. Therefore, it differs essentially from this animal body.

Resp. It is called spiritual by reason of qualities and operations, not by reason of substance.

For it is not converted into spirit through the resurrection. The Galatians are πνευματικοὶ (spiritual), Gal.

VI, 1. and yet they are not spirit. II.

We shall be ἰσάγγελοι (like the angels) after the resurrection

Luc. XX, 36. But angels are spirits. Ergo, we too shall be blessed spirits.

Resp.

We shall be like the angels, not by an absolute similarity, but a respective one. We shall not be the same as the angels, but similar to them, not through the essence of nature, but through the suitability of quality and glory.

III. God will destroy the belly and foods, 1 Cor. VI, 13. Ergo, the same body in number will not rise again.

Resp.

The belly will be destroyed in respect of its use, in that there will be neither food, nor appetite, nor the use of food: thus the belly, as far as the use of foods is concerned, will be destroyed. Yet the substance of the belly will not be abolished for that reason.

Christ, raised from the dead, to whom our body will be σύμμορφον (conformed), Phil.

III, 19. did not lack a belly, Luc. XXIV, 43.

IV. Flesh and blood will not inherit the kingdom of God, 1 Cor. XV, 50. Ergo, the same body in number, as far as substance is concerned, will not rise again.

Resp.

Animal flesh and blood, in so far as it prevails only with natural qualities, with supernatural axioms excluded, or is even subject to sins, will not inherit the kingdom of God. For it is necessary that, having put off natural and vicious qualities and infirmities, it be clothed with spiritual qualities, so that it requires neither the use of foods, nor the procreation of offspring, nor is subject to sin or any infirmity.

Instance: The substance of flesh and blood consists of elements that are by nature contrary to one another. But all these things are corruptible. Flesh can be bruised, blood can flow away, and be corrupted by other violent means.

Resp. a) The conflict of elements falls upon an animal body, not a spiritual one. b) Even in the unfallen Adam, the conflict of elements, insofar as it brings about destruction, had no place.

Quest. XXIII. Will there be a distinction of sex in the resurrection? Men awakened from the dust of the earth will come forth with diverse sex, male and female. Proof: 1) The bodies that rise are the same as those that fell. But if a man comes forth in place of a woman, the same body that fell through death does not rise again. 2) Christ, when questioned by the Sadducees, Matt. XXII, 16, as to whose wife the woman would be, did not answer that the distinction of sex would be removed in the other life, but that there would be no place for marriage there, because the saints would be ἰσάγγελοι (like unto the angels). Indeed, while Christ said that men in the other life neither take wives nor are given in marriage, he clearly asserts the distinction of sex; for to take a wife is for men, and to be given in marriage is for women.

Antithesis is that of certain Fathers and Scholastic doctors, who deny that there will be a distinction of sex in the resurrection.

Whose arguments are:

I. Men in the resurrection will be like the angels, Luke XX, 36. But there is no sex in the angels.

Resp.

They will be like the angels not absolutely, but in a certain respect, namely in respect of spiritual qualities, not in respect of the substantial members of the body.

II. Every faithful man in the resurrection of the dead will be a perfect man to the measure of the stature of Christ, Eph. IV, 13.

And in the other life there will be no women.

Resp.

Paul in the cited place does not treat of the resurrection of the dead, but of the progress of the reborn in this life.

III. The female sex is an imperfection of man: But every imperfection will slip away from those rising in glory.

Resp.

Woman was created in the state of integrity, in which all things were most perfect.

Quest. XXIV. In what does the resurrection of the dead formally consist? The resurrection of the dead formally consists a) in the reproduction, or restoration of the same body that fell through death, from the atoms, or particles of that body, scattered and dissipated here and there; b) in the reunion of the same with the soul. Proof a.

Resurrection differs from creation: since creation is made from nothing, or from unsuitable matter, from which a body such as is first produced never comes into being; but resurrection presupposes matter, from which it is reproduced through the infinite power of God.

Proof b.

A living body cannot be made unless it is united with the soul, the breath of life.

Wherefore, in order for the body to resume life, it is required that 1) it be reproduced from its original matter, 2) that it be united with the soul.

Quest. XXV. What is the end of the resurrection? The end of the resurrection, with respect to God who resurrects, is the glory of divine remunerative and vindictive justice a).

But the end of the resurrection with respect to the men to be resurrected is either common or proper. The common end for all who are to be resurrected is the appearance before the tribunal of Christ ...the judge b): The proper end with respect to

SSS SSS S 3 the faithful, of the faithful, is the consummated participation of eternal blessedness ); with respect to the unfaithful, the consummation of eternal damnation ).

Prob. a. For just as God is moved to resurrect men by His justice, partly remunerative, by which... He rewards the good, and partly vindicatory, by which He punishes the wicked, so that each one may receive τὰ διὰ τοῦ σώματος, the things done through his body, 2 Cor.

V, 10: so He is rightly said to intend the glory of both justices by resurrecting the dead. Prob. b. To this end all men shall be resurrected, that they may be set before the tribunal of Christ, Rom. XIV, 10. This is what the Apostle hints at, Hebr. IX, 27.

Prob. c. & d. From Acts XXIV, 15. There shall be a resurrection of the just and the unjust: of the former indeed to eternal life, of the latter to eternal ignominy, Dan. XII, 2. Therefore, by reason of the end, the resurrection can be distinguished into the glorious one of the just, and the ignominious one of the unjust.

Latin:

Quorum argumenta sunt: I.

Corpus resuscitatum vocatur spirituale, 1 Cor. XV, 44. E. essentialiter differt ab hoc corpore animali.

Resp. Dicitur spirituale, ratione qualitatum & operationum, non ratione substantiae.

Neque enim in spiritum per resurrectionem convertitur. Galatae sunt πνευματικοὶ, Gal.

VI, 1. neque tamen spiritus. II.

Futuri sumus post resurrectionem ἰσάγγελοι

Luc. XX, 36. Angeli autem sunt spiritus. E. & nos beati spiritus erimus.

Resp.

Futuri sumus angelis similes similitudine non absoluta, sed respectiva. Non erimus cum angelis iidem, sed iis similes, non per essentiam naturae, sed per convenientiam qualitatem & gloriae.

III. Deus ventrem & escas destruet, 1 Cor. VI, 13. E. idem numero corpus non resurget.

Resp.

Destruetur venter ratione usus, in quantum nec cibus, nec appetitus aut usus cibi erit: ita venter qua usum ciborum destruetur. Neque tamen ideo substantia ventris abolebitur.

Christus resuscitatus ex mortuis, cui corpus nostrum erit σύμμορφον, Phil.

III, 19. ventre non caruit, Luc. XXIV, 43.

IV. Caro & sanguis non possidebunt haereditate regnum Dei, 1 Cor. XV, 50. E. idem numero corpus qua substantiam non resurget.

Resp.

Caro & sanguis animalis, in quantum pollet tantum qualitatibus naturalibus, exclusis axiomatibus supernaturalibus, aut etiam peccatis obnoxius est, regnum Dei hereditate non possidebit. Necesse quippe est, ut exutis qualitatibus & infirmitatibus naturalibus atque vitiosis vestiatur qualitatibus spiritualibus, ut neque usum ciborum, neque procreationem sobolis requirat, neque peccato, aut ulli infirmitati sit subiectus .

Instantia: Carnis et sanguinis substantia ex elementis inter se natura contrariis constat. Haec vero omnia sunt corruptibilia. Caro potest contundi, sanguis diffluere, ac aliis violentis modis corrumpi.

Resp. a) Elementorum pugna in corpus animale, non spirituale cadit. b) Etiam in Adamo integro pugna elementorum, quatenus illa infert interitum, locum non habuit.

Quaest. XXIII. An in resurrectione futurum est sexus discrimen? Homines e pulvere terrae excitati prodibunt diverso sexu, virili et muliebri. Prob. 1) Eadem resurrectione sunt corpora, quae ceciderunt. At si loco mulieris prodeat vir, non idem resurgit corpus, quod per mortem cecidit. 2) Christus interrogatus a Sadducaeis, Matth. XXII, 16. cuius uxor futura esset mulier, non respondit, sublatum iri in altera vita discrimen sexus, sed nuptiis ibi non futurum locum, eo, quod sancti futuri sint ἰσάγγελοι. Immo dum Christus dixit, quod homines in altera vita neque ducant uxores, neque nubant, discrimen sexus clare adstruit; nam ducere, virorum, nubere, autem mulierum est.

Antithesis est quorundam Patrum, et doctorum Scholasticorum, sexus discrimen in resurrectione futurum negantium.

Quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Homines in resurrectione erunt angelis similes, Luc. XX, 36. At in angelis non est sexus.

Resp.

Erunt angelis similes non absolute, sed certo respectu, nempe respectu spiritualium qualitatum, non respectu substantialium corporis membrorum.

II. Quilibet homo fidelis in resurrectione mortuorum erit vir perfectus ad mensuram staturae Christi, Eph. IV, 13.

Et in altera vita nullae erunt feminae.

Resp.

Paullus l. c. non agit de resurrectione mortuorum, sed de renatorum profectu in hac vita.

III. Foemineus sexus est imperfectio hominis: At omnis imperfectio a gloriosae resurgentibus exlabit.

Resp.

Condita est foemina in statu integritatis, ut quo omnia erant perfectissima.

Quaest. XXIV. In quo formaliter consistit resurrectio mortuorum? Resurrectio mortuorum formaliter consistit a) in reproductione, seu reparatione eiusdem, quod per mortem cecidit, corporis, ex atomis, seu particulis illius corporis, hinc inde disiectis atque dissipatis; b) in redunitione eiusdem cum anima. Prob. a.

Differt resurrectio a creatione: quoniam creatio fit ex nihilo, aut materia inhabili, ex qua nunquam enterfit corpus, quale primum producitur; at resurrectio prae-supponit materiam, ex qua per infinitam Dei potentiam reproducitur.

Prob. b.

Non potest fieri corpus vivum, nisi unitur cum anima, vitae spiraculo.

Quare, ut corpus vitam resumat, requiritur, ut 1) e pristina materia reproducatur, 2) ut cum anima uniatur.

Quaest. XXV. Quis est finis resurrectionis? Finis resurrectionis, respectu Dei resuscitantis, est gloria iustitiae divinae remuneratoriae et vindicativae a).

At finis resurrectionis respectu hominum resuscitandorum, est vel communis, vel proprius. Finis communis omnibus resuscitandis est apparitio coram tribunali Christi ...iudicis b): Finis proprius respectu

SSS SSS S 3 fidelium, est consummata aeternae beatitudinis participatio ); respectu infidelium, aeternae damnationis consummatio ).

Prob. a. Quem ad modum enim Deus ad resuscitandum homines movetur per iustitiam suam partim remuneratoriam, qua... bonos remuneratur, partim vindicatiuam, qua malos punit, vt vnusquisque accipiat τὰ διὰ τοῦ σώματος, quae per corpus ipsius facta, 2 Cor. V, 10: ita gloriam vtriusque iustitiae mortuos resuscitando intendere recte dicitur.

Prob. b. Eum in finem resuscitabuntur omnes homines, vt statuantur ante tribunal Christi, Rom. XIV, 10. Id quod innuit Apostolus, Hebr. IX, 27. Statutum est hominibus semel mori; post hoc, iudicium, h. e. postquam ex mortuis fuerunt resuscitati, stentur ad iudicium.

Prob. c. & d. Ex Act. XXIV, 15. Futura est resurrectio iustorum & iniustorum: illorum quidem ad vitam aeternam, horum ad ignominiam aeternam, Dan. XII, 2. Proinde, ratione finis, distingui potest resurrectio in gloriosam iustorum, & ignominiosam iniustorum.


### XX. Will all men rise again?: S I G H

S I G H.

Thee, Lord Jesus, Savior of the world, Victor of death, Leader of life, I pray and beseech as devoutly as can be done, that through Thy most holy Spirit Thou mayest make me a partaker of the first resurrection, that the second death may have no power over me! Arouse my sluggish soul to frequent and pious meditation on the future resurrection, so that, whether I drink, or eat, or do anything else, Thy divine voice may always resound in my ears: Arise, ye dead, come to judgment! Grant me, I beseech Thee, a peaceful death, a glorious resurrection, eternal life!

CHAPTER X. CONCERNING THE LAST JUDGMENT AND THE CONSUMMATION OF THE AGE.

Q. I. What is the last universal judgment?

The last universal judgment is a solemn act, by which the Triune God, through the Lord Jesus Christ, appearing in visible form and supreme glory, shall set angels and all men before the tribunal, and by judging all thoughts, words, and deeds—those of the pious according to the norm of the Gospel, but those of the impious according to the prescription of the Law—shall assign and confer upon the former eternal joys, and upon the latter eternal torments, to the glory of His mercy and of His remunerative and vindicatory justice.

Obs. The last judgment is twofold: one is particular, and as it were private, by which at the hour of death the state of glory or of ignominy is adjudged to every man: the other is universal and ecumenical, by which on the last day of the world an absolutory or condemnatory sentence shall be pronounced and solemnly promulgated to all men. It is of the latter that we are speaking at present.

Latin:

S V S P I R I V M.

Te, Domine Iesu, Seruator orbis, Victor mortis, Dux vitae, quam deuotissime fieri potest oro, obtestor, ne per Spiritum tuum sanctissimum consortem facias resurrectionis primae, ne secunda mors vllam in me potestatem habeat! Torpentem meum animum excita ad crebram & piam resurrectionis futurae meditationem, vt, siue bibam, siue comedam, siue aliud quid agam, semper in auribus meis vox tua diuina perfonet: Surgite mortui, venite ad iudicium! Da mihi, obsecro, obitum placitum, resurrectionem gloriosam, vitam aeternam!

CAPVT X. DE IVDICIO EXTREMO ET CONSVMMATIONE SAECVLI.

Quæst. I. Quid est extremum iudicium vniuersale?

Extremum iudicium vniuersale est actus solemnis, quo Deus vnitrinus, per Dominum Iesum Christum, in visibili forma summaqve gloria apparentem, angelos, omnesque homines ad tribunal sistet, & cogitata, dicta, factaque omnia, piorum quidem ad normam euangelii, impiorum autem ad praescriptum legis diiudicando, illis aeterna gaudia, his aeternos cruciatus assignabit & conferet, ad misericordiae atque iustitiae suae remuneratoriae & vindicatiuae gloriam.

Obs. Iudicium extremum est duplex: aliud particulare, & quasi priuatum, quo in hora mortis vnicuique homini status gloriae, aut ignominiae adiudicatur: aliud est vniuersale & oecumenicum, quo in nouissimo mundi die omnibus hominibus sententia absolutoria, aut condemnatoria pronuntiabitur & solemniter promulgabitur. De posteriori nobis in praesenti sermo est.


## 37 On the Last Judgment and the Consummation of the Age


### Q. I. What is the last universal judgment?

II. Is it certain that a universal judgment will take place? That a universal judgment will take place, in which, at the time divinely appointed, all men shall be set before the tribunal of Christ, is established from the Scriptures of the Old and New Testament, all men of the same shall be set before the tribunal of Christ, from the Scriptures of the Old and New Testament

it is certainly established a). It is also certain that the resurrection of the dead and the final judgment will take place on one and the same day b). However, when the day of the great judgment is to come, it is clear to no mortal c).

Prob. a. The prophetic writings of the Old Testament testify that God has prepared His throne for judgment, and that He will judge the world in righteousness, Ps. 9:8-9. Let us all hear the sum of the word!

Fear God, and keep His commandments; for this is the whole of man. For God will bring every work into judgment, even every secret thing, whether it be good, or whether it be evil, Eccl. 12:13-14.

In the New Testament, the prophecy of Enoch, the seventh from Adam, is cited, who said: Behold, the Lord cometh with ten thousands of His saints, to execute judgment upon all, and to convince all that are ungodly among them of all their ungodly deeds which they have ungodly committed, and of all their hard speeches which ungodly sinners have spoken against Him, Jude v. 15. Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said: God hath appointed a day, in the which He will judge the world in righteousness by that man whom He hath ordained; Acts 17:31. Moreover, the process of the final judgment is described in Matt. 25:31. Prob. b.

The coming of Christ to judgment is joined with the last day of the world, 1 Thess. 4:16. The Lord Himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God, and the dead in Christ shall rise first. Therefore, the last day of the created world will be the great day of judgment, Jude v. 6. Prob. c.

Which day will be the last day of the world is not clearly established, and therefore no mortal can know exactly and precisely in what year, day, and hour Christ is to come to judgment. For thus the Savior says in Mark 13:31 ff.: Heaven and earth shall pass away: but My words shall not pass away. But of that day and that hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels which are in heaven, neither the Son, but the Father (alone). Take ye heed, watch and pray: for ye know not when the time is.

The antithesis is that of the Epicureans and the Scoffers, who deny the coming of Christ to judgment. Their arguments are:

I. If the world has remained unmoved and invariable for so many centuries, it is consistent with truth that it will continue to be such in the future, and that Christ will not come to judge and destroy the world: The antecedent is true. Therefore, the consequent is also true, see 2 Pet. 3: 4. Resp. What is deferred is not taken away. The long passage of time does not abolish the most true promise and threatening of God, but testifies to the longsuffering of God; for He grants time to the ungodly to repent, whose duty it was to rightly use the concession of the time of grace for repentance. See ibid., v. 9.

II. Now is the judgment of this world, now shall the prince of this world be cast out, as Christ testifies, John 12: 31. Therefore, there will be no judgment on the last day of the world. Resp. In the cited passage, judgment is taken metonymically, by the metonymy of the cause for the effect, and denotes the vindication from the unjust possessor, the devil. For the fruit of the passion of Christ is that the souls of men are vindicated into liberty from the unjust possessor, the devil, in that Christ by His passion and death conquered this tyrant, and having conquered him, cast him out of the hearts of men through the word of the Gospel. But we are here dealing with judgment properly so called.

III. If all men are to be judged on the last day of the world, they are either believers or unbelievers who are to be judged: Not unbelievers; for they are already judged, John 3:18: Nor believers; because he that believeth is not judged, John 3:18. Therefore, no men are to be judged on the last day. to be judged. Resp. to be judged. Resp.

Latin:

Futurum esse iudicium vniuersale, in quo, tempore diuinitus statuto, omnes homines stentur ad tribunal Christi, e scripturis veteris & noui testamenti ftatuto, omnes eiusdem. homines sistentur ad tribunal Christi, e scripturis veteris & noui testamenti

certo constat a). Certum etiam est, uno & eodem die simul & resurrectionem mortuorum & iudicium extremum fore b). Quando autem dies magni iudicii venturus sit, nemini mortalium liquet c).

Prob. a. Prophetica scripta veteris testamenti testantur, Deum ad iudicium praeparasse thronum suum, & eundem iudicaturum esse orbem in iustitia, Ps. IX, 8. 9. Summam verbi omnes audiamus!

Deum time, & praecepta eius custodi; hoc namque omnis hominis est. Nam omnis opus Deus producet in iudicium, etiam omne occultum, sive bonum, sive malum, Eccl. XII, 13. 14.

In nouo testamento adducitur prophetia Enochi septimi ab Adamo, qui dixit: Ecce venit Dominus, cum myriadibus sanctis suis, ad faciendum iudicium contra omnes & ad redarguendum omnes impios illorum, de omnibus operibus impietatis illorum, quibus impie egerunt, & de omnibus duris, quae locuti sunt contra ipsum peccatores impii, ep. Iud, v. 15. Paullus constitutus in medio Areopagi, dixit: Deus constituit diem, in quo iudicaturus est orbem in iustitia per virum, quem destinauit; Act. XVII, 31. Quin & processus extremi iudicii describitur Matth. XXV, 31.

Prob. b. Aduentus Christi ad iudicium cum vltimo mundi die coniungitur, 1 Thess. IV, 16. Ipse Dominus cum celeusmate, in voce archangeli, & tuba Dei descensurus est de caelo, & mortui in Christo resurgent primo. Nouissimus itaque orbis conditi dies erit magnus dies iudicii, epist. Iud. v. 6.

Prob. c. Quis vltimus mundi dies futurus sit, non liquido constat, ac proinde quo anno, die & hora Christus ad iudicium sit venturus, nemo mortalium exacte & praecise scire potest. Sic enim Saluator Marc. XIII, 31. seqq. Caelum & terra transibunt: Verba autem mea non transibunt. De die tamen ista & hora nemo scit, neque angeli, qui in caelo, neque Filius, sed Pater (solus). Videte itaque, vigilate, & orate: non enim scitis, quando tempus futurum sit.

Antithesis est Epicuraeorum & Empaetarum, aduentum Christi ad iudicium negantium. Quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Si mundus per tot saecula immotus & inuariabilis perstitit, vero consentaneum est, quod etiam in posterum talis duraturus, neque Christus ad mundum iudicandum & destruendum venturus sit: Antecedens est verum. Ergo & consequens, vid. 2 Petr. III, 4. Resp. Quod differtur, non aufertur. Diuturnum temporum tractus non tollit verissimam Dei promissionem & comminationem, sed testatur de longanimitate Dei; quippe qui fat temporis concedit impiis ad resipiscendum, quorum erat concessio tempore gratiae ad poenitentiam recte vti. Vid. ibid, v. 9.

II. Nunc est iudicium mundi, nunc princeps huius mundi eiicietur foras, teste Christo, Io. XII, 31. Ergo non habebitur iudicium in vltimo mundi die. Resp. L. c. Iudicium sumitur metonymice, per metonymiam causae pro effectu, & notat vindicationem ab iniusto possessore diabolo. Fructus quippe passionis Christi est, vt animae hominum ab iniusto possessore diabolo in libertatem vindicentur, eo, quod Christus passione & morte sua hunc tyrannum vicit, victum ex cordibus hominum per verbum euangelii eiecit. At nos hic agimus de iudicio proprie sic dicto.

III. Si in extremo mundi die iudicandi sunt... omnes homines, aut credentes, aut infideles sunt iudicandi: Non infideles; nam illi iam sunt iudicati, Io. III, 18: Neque credentes; quia qui credit, non iudicatur, Io. III, 18. E, nulli homines in extremo die sunt iudicandi. sunt iudicandi. Resp. sunt iudicandi. Resp.


### Quest. III. Do certain signs precede the coming of the Lord, from which it can be known when the last day is to come?

Resp. Infidels are said to be judged by reason of the decree and judgment manifested concerning them in the divine word; but the solemn promulgation and execution of this judgment is deferred to the last day of the world. Believers shall not come into the judgment of condemnation, although they are not exempt from the judgment of appearance and discussion.

IV. To whom the definitive sentence is promulgated at the hour of death, to him it is not to be promulgated on the last day of the world (for it is not probable that the same sentence will be pronounced twice by the heavenly judge): But a definitive sentence, whether absolutory or condemnatory, is promulgated at the hour of death: Therefore. The minor is evident: because to souls released from the body, the heavenly paradise or hell is assigned immediately, Luke XVI. Resp. Distinguish between particular and universal judgment. The former is to be undergone by everyone separately at the hour of death: the latter will be published on the last day of the world, so that then the justice of God may be openly acknowledged and celebrated by all, and the whole man, consisting of soul and body, may be judged and receive, according to what he did in the body, whether good or evil, 1 Cor. IV, 5.

III. Do certain signs precede the coming of the Lord, from which it can be known when the last day is to come?

By the will and ordination of God, signs divinely revealed precede the supreme day, from which it is permitted to know that that great day is approaching.

Obs. Prognostic signs of the last day are distinguished into remote, or common, and proximate, or proper. The former occur not in one century, and often recur or are continued. The latter are those which, as the judgment finally draws nearer, are not to be seen equally in previous centuries.
