The church is absolutely universal, as much in respect to place as in respect to time, and is described by Dr. Hülsemann in Breviar. c. 17. §. 9. as being the church taken collectively, consisting of the universality of believers, both teachers and hearers, of the present, future, and past time. For the church of the Old and New Testaments has one head, Christ. "But we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they [the fathers of the Old Testament]," Acts 15: 11. Prob. b.

Prob. b. The apostolic church was universal secundum quid [in a certain respect] and by reason of places, because "their sound went into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world," Rom. 10: 18. And even today the assembly of all men who truly believe in Christ and are holy is universal secundum quid and in respect.

The church of Christ, diffused throughout the orb of the earth, contains many particular assemblies, which themselves also claim for themselves the name and definition of the church. Whence they are spoken of in the plural number, "churches," Acts 15:41; 1 Cor. 16: 19. There are, therefore, many particular churches distinct among themselves. Furthermore, even in the singular number, a certain particular church is spoken of with some added restriction, e.g., "the church which is at Jerusalem," Acts 8:1; "the church of God which is at Corinth," 1 Cor. 1:2; "the church of the Thessalonians," 1 Thess. 1:1.

Latin:

Ecclesia synthetica militans vtriusque testamenti distinguitur in vniuersalem, & particularem. Ecclesia vniuersalis est, vel absolute, vel respectiue vniuersalis. Ecclesia absolute vniuersalis est coetus constans ex fidelibus omnium locorum & temporum, quos Deus ad actualem spiritualium bonorum communionem, inde a mundi initio, per verbi sui praeconium vocauit, atque hodienum vocat, & vsque ad consummationem saeculi vocabit a). Secundum quid & respectiue vniversalis ecclesia est coetus omnium fidelium eodem tempore, vbiuis terrarum in vna eademque fidei & caritatis communione interna persistentium b). Ecclesia particularis est coetus non omnium, sed quorundam fidelium in loco certo ad salutem participandam vocatorum, & in communione spirituali interna persistentium c).

Prob. a. Ecclesia absolute vniversalis, tam ratione loci, quam ratione temporis vniversalis est, & describitur a D. Hvlsemanno in breviar. c. 17. §. 9. quod sit ecclesia collective sumta, constans ex vniversitate fidelium, tam doctorum, quam auditorum, præsentis, futuri & præteriti temporis. Etenim ecclesia vet. & nou. testam. vnum habet caput Christum. Exinde per gratiam Domini nostri Iesu Christi credimus saluari, quemadmodum & patres veteris testamenti, Actor. XV, 11.

Prob. b. Ecclesia apostolica erat secundum quid & ratione locorum vniversalis, propterea, quod in omnem terram exiit sonus apostolorum, & in fines orbis terrarum verba illorum, Rom. X, 18. Et hodienum cœtus omnium hominum in Christum vere credentium & sanctorum secundum quid & respectus vniversalis est.

Prob. c. Ecclesia Christi, per terrarum orbem diffusa, plures continet cœtus particulares, qui & ipsi nomen ac definitionem ecclesiæ sibi vendicant. Vnde in numero plurali dicuntur ecclesiæ, Actor. XV, 41. 1 Cor. XVI, 19. Sunt itaque plures ecclesiæ particulares inter se distinctæ. Quin etiam in numero singulari, particularis quædam ecclesia cum adiecta aliqua restrictione dicitur, v. gr. ecclesia, quæ est Hierosolymis. Actor. VIII, 1. ecclesia Dei, quæ est Corinthi, 1 Cor. I, 2. ecclesia Thessalonicensium, 1 Thess. I, 1.


### Q. VIII. How is a particular church divided?

A particular church is divided into composite and simple. The former is that which consists of other churches: the latter is that which is not composed of other churches.

Obs. A certain particular church is called simple, not absolutely, as if it were devoid of all composition (for thus it would not be a church, since it is formally an assembly of many faithful men); but secundum quid [in a certain respect], and in a certain genus: because it does not consist of several smaller churches.

Prob. A composite particular church is distinguished 1) by reason of secular government. Thus, when once the supreme empire was divided into eastern and western, the church itself was also bipartite into eastern and western, or, which amounts to the same thing, into Greek and Latin. 2) By reason of ecclesiastical government. Thus, one is the church which is constituted under one ecclesiastical government: there are many, whose government is diverse, or as they speak today, whose consistories are diverse. Formerly, in the ancient church, a Bishop resided in the major city of a province, to whom the inspection of the surrounding churches [belonged], and this was a diocesan church. The Bishop who presided over sacred matters in the metropolis of a province, called a Metropolitan, cared for the churches of the whole province, and had the bishops themselves committed to his inspection and trust, and this was a provincial church, just as the Saxon church, the Pomeranian church, etc., are. 3) By reason of nation. Thus, formerly one church was Asian, another African, etc. Today one is German, another Swedish, another Danish, etc. 4) By reason of the unity of doctrine which otherwise distinct churches profess. A simple church does not consist of other smaller churches; such was the Paradisiacal, the Noachic, etc. Today all smaller churches, which are not composed of others, are simple, to which are also to be referred domestic churches.

Latin:

Ecclesia particularis diuiditur in compositam, & simplicem. Illa est, quæ ex Ecclesia particularis aliis constat ecclesiis: hæc est, quæ ex aliis ecclesiis non componitur.

Obs. Ecclesia quædam particularis dicitur simplex, non absolute, quod omnis compositionis sit expers (sic enim non esset ecclesia, quippe quæ formaliter est cœtus plurium hominum fidelium); sed secundum quid, & in certo genere: quoniam ex pluribus minoribus non constat ecclesiis.

Prob. Ecclesia particularis composita, distinguitur 1) ratione regiminis sæcularis. Sic cum olim imperium summum in orientale & occidentale diuideretur, ipsa quoque ecclesia in orientalem, & occidentalem, vel quod eodem recidit, in græcam, & latinam fuit bipartita. 2) Ratione regiminis ecclesiastici. Sic vna est ecclesia, quæ sub vno regimine ecclesiastico est constituta: plures, quarum diuersum est regimen, vel vt hodie loquuntur, quarum diuersæ sunt consistoria. Olim in veteri ecclesia in maiori prouinciæ vrbe Episcopus residebat, cui circumiacentes ecclesias inspectio, & hæc erat ecclesia diœcesana. Episcopus, qui in prouinciæ metropoli sacris præerat, Metropolitanus dictus, totius prouinciæ ecclesias curabat, ipsosque episcopos inspectioni suæ ac fidei habebat commissos, atque hæc ecclesia erat prouincialis, sicut est ecclesia Saxonica, Pomeranica &c. 3) Ratione nationis. Sic olim alia ecclesia erat Asiatica, alia Africana &c. Hodie alia est Germanica, alia Suecica, alia Danica &c. 4) Ratione vnitatis doctrinæ, quam ecclesiæ alias distinctæ profitentur. Ecclesia simplex non constat ex aliis ecclesiis minoribus; qualis erat Paradisiaca, Noachica, &c. Hodie omnes ecclesiæ minores, quæ ex aliis non componuntur, sunt simplices, ad quas referendæ sunt etiam ecclesiæ domesticæ.


### Q. IX. Is the church rightly divided into visible and invisible?

The church of Christ, which is on earth, strictly and properly taken for the assembly of true believers and saints, diffused far and wide throughout the orb of the earth, is not visible and conspicuous distinctly a), but only confusedly b). But taken broadly and improperly... III. An assembly of men can be seen: properly, for the promiscuous assembly of the called, it is visible in such a way that it can be recognized distinctly as true, and as far as its members are concerned, and can be discerned from other false or corrupted churches c). It may happen, however, God permitting, that the true church is in no part of itself visible, with the conspicuous and illustrious assembly of men, which publicly professes the true doctrine, failing, and with heretics and schismatics predominating everywhere d). Obs.

I. We do not assert that the visible and invisible church are two churches different in species, or contrarily opposed; but we say that one and the same church is visible and invisible under different respects: visible, with respect to the called; invisible, with respect to the reborn and the elect; visible, with respect to a flourishing and free state; invisible, with respect to a pressed and corrupted state; which different ways of considering and respects neither constitute different species, nor imply a contrary or contradictory opposition; because the invisible assembly of the reborn is contained under the visible assembly of the called, and lies hidden in time of persecution. Obs.

II. Visible here is the same as that which is subject to our sensual and intellectual cognition, or that which is obvious to the eyes of the body and mind.

Since, however, our cognition is twofold, either confused or distinct, the church can also be denominated visible, or cognizable, either in relation to our confused or in relation to our distinct knowledge. Wherefore the question can be understood in a twofold sense. One: whether the church of Christ is invisible, or confused in its cognizable aspects? The other: whether it is visible, or cognizable by us distinctly?

Obs. III. A distinction is made between the external and internal form of the church. The former consists in the harmony, or public society, of the same doctrine of faith: the latter consists in the union of called men and spiritual communion with Christ through faith. By reason of the internal form, the church is invisible; but by reason of the external form, the same is visible. Obs.

Obs. IV. The members of the church are considered either materially or formally. Considered materially, the members of the church are called men, professing the heavenly doctrine and using the sacraments, who are indeed visible. Viewed formally, the members of the church are reborn, holy, and elect men; these, by reason of faith, internal holiness, and election, are invisible.

V. We distinguish between the free and flourishing state of the church, and the corrupted and pressed state. The state of the church is flourishing and free when no impediment is placed in the way of the public ministry of the Word and the exercise of true religion. But the corrupted and pressed state varies according to the different degrees of pressure and corruption. For sometimes heretics emerge and predominate, and the true church is so pressed by tyrants that a conspicuous assembly of those who externally profess the true heavenly doctrine is scarcely found. Obs.

VI.

The church is called invisible, partly negatively, partly comparatively. The church is called negatively invisible by reason of its internal form, i.e., by reason of its spiritual union with Christ through faith. It is called comparatively invisible by reason of its external splendor; which, just as the flourishing church has it in the public ministry of the Word and the external profession of faith, so the pressed church loses it in a corrupted state, where, with heretics and schismatics prevailing, the church is so pressed that there is no conspicuous, illustrious assembly of those who externally profess the true heavenly doctrine that strikes human eyes, but rather the true doctrine and its confessors lie hidden, being pressed. Prob. a. Prob. a. 1) From clear sayings of Scripture: God alone ...knows the hearts of men, 1 Kings 8:39, and those who are his, 2 Tim. 2:19, and Christ alone, the supreme shepherd, infallibly knows his sheep, John 10:14. Therefore we do not distinctly know holy hearts, elect men, and souls the faithful. 2) From the Apostles' Creed, in which we profess: I believe the church. Whence we argue: Whatever we believe, that we do not see: But the church, etc. Therefore. The major premise is evident from Heb. XI, 3. From the internal form of the church, which is internal union with the head, Christ, through faith. But no one sees that, because no one is a καρδιογνώστης [knower of hearts]. We conclude: That whose essential form is invisible, that very thing is, by reason of its essential form, invisible: But the essential form of the church is invisible. Therefore. 4) Just as Judas, the betrayer of Christ, was visible materially, as regards the being of a man, but not formally, as regards the being of a betrayer (for the disciples were asking, Lord, who is it? John XIII, 2.): So believers are seen materially, as regards their existence and human presence, but formally, as regards the faith fixed in their hearts, they cannot be infallibly known and discerned from hypocrites.

Proof b. The church of Christ, which is on earth, taken properly and principally for the assembly of the reborn and the elect, can be said to be conspicuous and visible only in a confused manner. For wherever there are congregations in which the word of God is taught and the sacraments are administered, we conclude from divine promises that there are some truly believing and holy persons who constitute a part of the church, Is. LV, 10; Matt. XIII, 8, although we cannot know certainly and distinctly who those truly believing and holy persons are. For from the certainty of the coexistence of the faithful with the unfaithful in some assembly, the consequence does not hold for the discernment of individual faithful from the unfaithful.

Proof c. The church is visible, taken more broadly for the promiscuous assembly of the called, both by reason of the men who externally profess the internal and uncorrupted catholic faith, and by reason of the means through which the church is gathered on earth: As also with respect to the external exercises of religion, which are the profession of doctrine, the use of the sacraments and ecclesiastical discipline, the preaching of the word and the administration of the sacraments, as well as the remaining external exercises of religion, which strike the eyes and ears. With respect to these, therefore, the church is visible.

Proof d. It can happen that everywhere, with eminent and prevailing teachers professing false doctrines, the true church lies oppressed and as if covered by clouds, and thus is comparatively invisible and inconspicuous.

For 1) Elijah, a most clear-sighted prophet, instructed by the greatest divine gifts, could not see the oppressed church, 1 Kings XIX, 14. Therefore, the church, when oppressed and deprived of external splendor, which consists in the public exercise of the true religion, is comparatively invisible.

2) Whatever church hides in solitudes, mountains, caves, and caverns of the earth, that is comparatively invisible: But the oppressed church, etc. Heb. XI, 38. Therefore.

3) At the time of the passion and resurrection of Christ, the Christian church was invisible. For the apostles, fearing the force and threats of the Jews, fled the sight of men, John XX, 19.

The antithesis is a) of the Papists, who maintain that there is no invisible church. b) of the Weigelians, who deny that there is a true visible church.

The Papists object: I. Whatever opinion involves a contradiction, that is to be rejected: But the opinion of the Lutherans concerning the visible and invisible church, etc. Therefore. The minor is evident: because it involves a contradiction to be at once visible and invisible. Resp. We distinguish between a true and an apparent contradiction. The contradiction which is objected to us by our adversaries is only apparent, because it is not according to the same thing. For the flourishing church, according to its external form, is visible; according to its internal form, the same is invisible.

II. Whatever church is one, that cannot be double: Visible and invisible. The church of Christ is one, Therefore. Resp. The church is essentially one; but according to a diverse mode of consideration, it is distinguished into visible and invisible: Which diverse modes of consideration, or respects, do not constitute specifically diverse churches; just as the moon, conspicuous and inconspicuous, is not essentially twofold.

III. A gathering of men can be seen: The Church is a gathering of men: Therefore. Resp. The Church is a gathering of faithful men, who can be seen materially, as men, not formally, insofar as they are faithful; just as Judas, the betrayer of Christ, was visible to the apostles as a man, but invisible as a betrayer.

IV. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden: The Church of Christ is a city set on a hill, Matt. 5: 14. Therefore. Resp. L. c. does not concern the Church, but the apostolic office, and it is taught that the apostles, by reason of the office which they discharge, ought not to lie hidden, just as a city set on a hill cannot lie hidden; since they ought to preach the Gospel with the greatest freedom.

Otherwise, it is possible for a city to be covered by a dense fog or the darkness of night and not be seen.

V. Whatever is placed in the sun is absolutely visible: But the Church, etc. Therefore. The minor is proved from Ps. 19:5. "In the sun," i.e., in a conspicuous place, "he has set his tabernacle," i.e., his Church. Which words Augustine explains thus: He has set his Church in the manifest, so that just as the sun cannot be entirely hidden, so neither can the Church be concealed. Resp. 1) The sun is most visible; yet it can also be called invisible, both because of the interposition of the moon, as happens in eclipses, and because of its recession from our horizon, as happens at night. 2) In the original text, the words are otherwise, namely in this way: "He has set a tabernacle for the sun in them," i.e., in the heavens. The Psalmist shows how, even by the guidance of the light of nature, God and His glory can be known from creatures, but especially from the heaven and the celestial bodies. It is said, therefore, that God has prepared a tabernacle for the sun in the heavens, i.e., a certain space within which it completes its course, so that even from the sun the divine glory and majesty may be naturally known. The Psalmist in the cited passage does not treat of the Church and its absolute visibility, but compares Christ, who dwells in the heaven of grace, to the sun.

VI. If the Church were invisible, access to it would be open to no one: But access to the Church is open to all men (because the calling to the Church is universal, Matt. 28:19): Therefore the Church is not invisible. Resp. If the Church were always oppressed, so that it was never seen; if it were invisible both by reason of its external form and its internal form; access to it would never be open. Thus, the whole argument is indeed conceded, but it does not strike our thesis: because we maintain that the Church sometimes flourishes, sometimes lies hidden while oppressed; that it is seen by reason of its external form, not by reason of its internal form.

Instance I. The Church, which is pressed by heresy and external persecution, is certainly visible; because persecution requires a visible object, falling into the senses of heretics and tyrants. Resp. It is one thing for tyrants to persecute the Church as a visible object; it is another for persecution to prevail to such an extent that there is no conspicuous gathering of those who publicly profess the true doctrine.

Instance II. It is repugnant to divine mercy if He permits even a small amount of time for the Church to become invisible. For, given such a state, a Gentile will have no source from which to be converted: he will perish not by his own fault, but by God’s; which is foreign to the mercy of God. Resp. 1) The Church will never be led into that state of invisibility by the promise and consequent will of God, such that the way of salvation is closed to Gentiles: For a Gentile approaching the Church, where the ministry of the Word is corrupted, is regenerated by the power of the preached Word and the administered baptism. 2) A Gentile, regenerated by the ministry of the Word and baptism, is endowed with the spirit of discernment and becomes a sheep of Christ.

…But he who is endowed with the spirit of discernment can distinguish the prophet from the deceiver, and he who is a sheep of Christ hears the voice of Christ, not of a stranger, John 10:27. And if, therefore, a Gen tile perishes, having once imbibed the poison of errors, not by the fault of God, who works effectively through His word, but perishes by his own vice, insofar as he prefers to attend to the spirits of error rather than to follow the light of regeneration once bestowed.…

VII. Just as three things can be observed in a civil republic: 1) a multitude of men, 2) an external government, 3) the internal affection of citizens, by which citizens are united among themselves: So the same can be observed in the church: 1) a multitude of men, 2) an external ecclesiastical government, 3) the internal faith and charity of Christians, by which they are united among themselves. The first two are visible both in a civil republic and in the church. The third is invisible in both. But just as a republic is absolutely visible, even though the affection of the citizens is not visible: So the church is visible, even though internal faith and charity are not visible. Resp. It is not permitted to argue from a civil republic to the church, because there is a huge difference between the two. For the whole republic is an external society, placed in a conspicuous order of rulers and subjects, which therefore in itself falls entirely under the senses, so that its citizens are known to all and can be pointed out with a finger. Although citizens are indeed accustomed to embrace one another with an internal and mutual affection, which is not accessible to the eyes of men: that internal affection, however, is not of the formal nature of citizens, and if someone is not well-disposed toward his fellow citizens, he does not cease to be a citizen on account of this. But the church, taken strictly and properly, is formally and essentially an internal society of true believers and saints, joined to Christ the head by the bond of faith, and to one another by the bond of charity, which in itself does not fall under the senses, but is believed by faith.

VIII. The faith of Christians is seen and known from their works, James II, 18. Therefore, the Christian church, by reason of its internal form, which is founded on faith, is not invisible. Resp. The faith of Christians is indeed known to a certain extent from good works, but that knowledge is not certain and infallible; rather it is uncertain, probable, and conjectural, to which falsehood can be subject; since hypocrites also perform good external works, just as the Pharisees of old seemed to be famous for their zeal for good works (*).

Latin:

Ecclesia Christi, quæ in terris est, stricte & proprie sumta, pro cœtu vere Ecclesia visibilis & inuisibilis. credentium & sanctorum, per terrarum orbem longe lateque diffuso, non est visibilis & conspicua distincte a), sed tantum confuse b). At sumta late & improprie proprie, pro coetu vocatorum promiscuo, ita visibilis est, vt tanquam vera, & quoad membra sua distincte agnosci, & ab aliis ecclesiis falsis, seu corruptis discerni queat c). Fieri tamen potest, permittente Deo, vt ecclesia vera nulla sui parte sit visibilis, deficiente coetu hominum conspicuo & illustri, veram doctrinam publice profitente, & vbique locorum haereticis atque schismaticis praedominantibus d).

Obs. I. Non afferimus, ecclesiam visibilem, & invisibilem, esse duas ecclesias specie diversas, aut contrarie oppositas; sed vnam eamdemque ecclesiam diverso respectu dicimus visibilem, & invisibilem: visibilem, respectu vocatorum, invisibilem, respectu renatorum & electorum; visibilem, respectu status florentis & liberi, invisibilem, respectu status pressi & corrupti; qui diversi considerandi modi & respectus, nec constituunt diversas species, nec inferunt oppositionem contrariam, aut contradictoriam; quia coetus invisibilis renatorum sub visibili coetu vocatorum continetur, & tempore persecutionis delitescit.

Obs. II. Visibile hic idem est, quod cognitioni nostrae sensuali & intellectuali subest, siue quod oculis corporis & mentis obvium est.

Cum autem cognitio nostra duplex, aut confusa, aut distincta fit, potest ecclesia etiam visibilis, seu cognoscibilis denominari, vel in ordine ad confusam, vel in ordine ad distinctam nostram notitiam. Quare quaestio duplici sensu intelligi potest. Vno: an ecclesia Christi sit invisibilis, siue cognoscibilibus confusa? altero: an visibilis, siue cognoscibilis sit a nobis distincte?

Obs. III. Distinguitur inter formam ecclesiae externam, & internam. Illa consistit in harmonia, siue societate publica eiusdem doctrinae fidei: haec consistit in vnione hominum vocatorum, & communione spirituali cum Christo per fidem. Ratione formae internae ecclesia est invisibilis; ratione autem formae externae eadem est visibilis.

Obs. IV. Membra ecclesiae considerantur vel materialiter, vel formaliter. Materialiter considerata membra ecclesiae sunt homines vocati, doctrinam coelestem profitentes, & sacramentis vtentes, qui vtique sunt visibiles. Formaliter spectata ecclesiae membra sunt homines renati, sancti & electi; hi ratione fidei, sanctitatis internae & electionis, sunt invisibiles.

Obs. V. Distinguimus inter statum ecclesiae liberum florentemque, & statum corruptum atque pressum. Florens & liber est status ecclesiae, cum publico verbi ministerio & verae religionis exercitio nullum obiicitur impedimentum. Status autem corruptus & pressus variat, pro diuersis pressurae & corruptionis gradibus. Interdum enim eminent & praedominantur haeretici, & vera ecclesia a tyrannis tantopere premitur, vt vix inueniatur coetus conspicuus eorum, qui veram doctrinam coelestem externe profitentur.

Obs. VI. Ecclesia dicitur invisibilis, partim negative, partim comparative. VI. Si ecclesia esset invisibilis, nemini ad eam pateret aditus: Negative invisibilis dicitur ecclesia ratione formae internae, i.e. ratione spiritualis vnionis cum Christo per fidem. Comparative invisibilis dicitur, ratione externi splendoris; quem vt ecclesia florens habet in publico verbi ministerio, & externa fidei professione, ita ecclesia pressa amittit in statu corrupto, vbi praeualentibus haereticis & schismaticis ecclesia ita premitur, vt non detur coetus conspicuus, illustris, & in oculos humanos incurrens eorum, qui veram doctrinam coelestem externe profitentur, sed vt vera doctrina eiusque confessores pressi lateant.

Prob. a. 1) Ex claris scripturae dictis: Solus Deus ...nouit corda hominum, 1 Reg. VIII, 39. & eos qui sui sunt, 2 Tim. II, 19. & solus Christus, pastor supremus, infallibiliter nouit suas oues, Io. X, 14. Ergo nos distincte non cognoscimus corda sancta, homines electos & animas fideles. 2) Ex symbolo apostolico, in quo profitemur: Credo ecclesiam. Vnde arguemur: Quidquid credimus, illud non videmus: Atqui ecclesiam, &c. Ergo. Maior constat ex Hebr. XI, 3. Ex forma interna ecclesiae, quae est interna vnio cum capite e Christo, per fidem. At illam nemo videt, quia non est καρδιογνώστης. Colligimus: Cuius forma essentialis est invisibilis, illud ipsum est ratione formae essentialis invisibile: Atqui ecclesiae forma essentialis est invisibilis. Ergo. 4) Sicut Iudas proditor Christi materialiter, quoad esse hominis, erat visibilis, non vero formaliter, quoad esse proditoris (quaerebant enim discipuli, Domine, quis est? Io. XIII, 2.): Ita credentes materialiter, quoad existentiam & praesentiam humanam videntur, formaliter autem, quoad fidem cordibus infixam, infallibiliter cognosci & discerni ab hypocritis nequeunt.

Prob. b. Ecclesia Christi, quae in terris est, proprie & principaliter sumta pro coetu renatorum & electorum, dici potest conspicua & visibilis esse confuse tantum. Vbicunque enim dantur congregationes, in quibus verbum Dei docetur & sacramenta administrantur, ibi dari aliquos vere credentes & sanctos, qui ecclesiae partem constituant, colligimus ex promissionibus diuinis, Es. LV, 10. Matth. XIII, 8. quamuis quinam illi vere credentes & sancti sint, certo & distincte cognoscere nequeamus. Nam a certitudine coexistentiae fidelium cum infidelibus in aliquo coetu, ad discretionem individuorum fidelium ab infidelibus non valet consequentia.

Prob. c. Visibilis est ecclesia, latius accepta pro coetu vocatorum promiscuo, cum ratione hominum, fidem catholicam internam & incorruptam exterius profitentium, tum ratione mediorum, per quae in terris colligitur ecclesia: Vti etiam respectu externorum religionis exercitiorum, quae sunt professio doctrinae, vsus sacramentorum ac disciplina ecclesiastica, praedicatio verbi & administratio sacramentorum, nec non reliqua externa religionis exercitia, quae in oculos & aures incurrunt. Horum igitur respectu ecclesia est visibilis.

Prob. d. Fieri potest, vt vbique locorum, eminentibus & praevalentibus doctoribus falsas doctrinas profitentibus, vera ecclesia pressa & velut nubibus tecta lateat, adeoque comparative invisibilis & inconspicua fit.

Nam 1) Elias, Propheta oculatissimus, maximis donis diuinis instructus, ecclesiam pressam videre non potuit, 1 Reg. XIX, 14. Ergo ecclesia pressa & splendore externo, qui consistit in publico verae religionis exercitio, orbata, comparative invisibilis est.

2) Quaecunque ecclesia delitescit in solitudinibus, montibus, speluncis & cauernis terrae, illa comparative est invisibilis: Atqui ecclesia pressa, &c. Hebr. XI, 38. Ergo.

3) Tempore passionis & resurrectionis Christi ecclesia christiana erat invisibilis. Nam apostoli, Iudaeorum vim & minas reformidantes, conspectum hominum fugiebant, Io. XX, 19.

Antithesis est a) Pontificiorum, statuentium, non dari ecclesiam invisibilem. b) Weigelianorum, negantium, veram dari ecclesiam visibilem.

Obiiciunt Pontificii: I. Quaecunque sententia inuoluit contradictionem, illa est reiicienda: Atqui sententia Lutheranorum de ecclesia visibili & invisibili, &c. Ergo. Minor est euidens: quia contradictionem inuoluit, esse simul visibile, & invisibile. Resp. Disting. inter contradictionem veram, & apparentem. Contradictio, quae ab aduersariis nobis obiicitur, est tantum apparens, quia non fit secundum idem. Nam ecclesia florens, secundum formam externam, est visibilis, secundum formam internam eadem est invisibilis.

II. Quaecunque ecclesia est vna, illa non potest ...esse duplex: Visibilis & invisibilis. Ecclesia Christi est vna, Ergo. Resp. Ecclesia essentialiter est vna; at pro diuerso considerandi modo, in visibilem & invisibilem distinguitur: Qui diuersi considerandi modi, aut respectus, non constituunt specie diversas ecclesias; sicut luna conspicua, & inconspicua non est essentialiter duplex.

III. Coetus hominum potest videri: Ecclesia est coetus hominum: Ergo. Resp. Ecclesia est coetus hominum fidelium, qui possunt ...videri materialiter, ut homines, non formaliter, quatenus sunt fideles; sicut Iudas Christi proditor apostolis visibilis erat, ut homo, invisibilis, ut proditor.

IV. Urbs, in monte constituta, non potest esse occulta: Ecclesia Christi est urbs in monte constituta, Matth. V, 14. Ergo. Resp. L. c. non de ecclesia, sed de munere apostolico agitur & docetur, apostolos, ratione muneris, quo funguntur, non debere latere, sicut ciuitas in monte constituta latere nequit; cum summa libertate praedicare debeant euangelium.

Ceterum fieri potest, ut urbs, vel densa nebula, vel caligine nocturna obtecta, non videatur.

V. Quidquid in sole positum est, illud absolute est visibile: Atqui ecclesia &c. Ergo. Minor probatur ex Ps. XIX, 5. In sole, i. e. loco conspicuo, posuit tabernaculum suum, h. e. ecclesiam suam. Quae verba AVGVSTINVS sic exponit: In manifesto posuit ecclesiam suam, ut sicut sol non potest omnino latere, ita nec ecclesia possit abscondi. Resp. 1) Sol est maxime visibilis; potest tamen etiam dici invisibilis, cum ob interpositionem lunae, ut fit eclipsibus, tum ob recessum ex nostro horizonte, ut fit tempore nocturno. 2) In textu originali verba aliter se habent, nempe hoc modo: Soli posuit tabernaculum in illis, scil. coelis. Ostendit Psalmista, quomodo etiam ductu luminis naturae, ex creaturis, inprimis autem ex caelo & corporibus coelestibus Deus, eiusque gloria cognosci possit. Dicitur itaque, Deum soli in coelis parauisse tabernaculum, i. e. certum spatium, intra quod cursum absoluit, ut etiam ex sole diuina gloria & maiestas naturaliter innotescat, De ecclesia, eiusque absoluta visibilitate Psalmista l. c. non agit, sed Christum, in caelo gratiae habitantem, soli confert.

VI. Si ecclesia esset invisibilis, nemini ad eam pateret aditus: Sed omnibus hominibus ad ecclesiam patet aditus (quia vocatio ad ecclesiam est vniuersalis, Matth. XXVIII, 19.): Ergo ecclesia non est invisibilis. Resp. Si ecclesia semper esset pressa, ut nunquam videretur; si esset invisibilis tam ratione formae externae, quam internae; nunquam ad eam pateret aditus. Ita conceditur quidem totum argumentum, sed non ferit nostram thesin: quia nos statuimus, ecclesiam aliquando florere, aliquando pressam latere; videri eandem ratione formae externae, non ratione formae internae.

Instantia I. Ecclesia, quae haeresi & persecutione externa premitur, utique visibilis est; quia persecutio requirit obiectum visibile, in sensus haereticorum & tyrannorum incurrens, Resp. Aliud est, tyrannos persequi ecclesiam, ut obiectum visibile; aliud, persecutionem ita inualescere, ut non detur coetus conspicuus eorum, qui veram doctrinam publice profitentur.

Instantia II. Repugnat misericordiae diuinae, si vel exiguum temporis permittat, ut ecclesia fiat invisibilis. Posito enim tali statu, gentilis non habebit, vnde conuertatur: peribit non sua, sed Dei culpa; quod a misericordia Dei est alienum. Resp. 1) Nunquam ecclesia in illum statum invisibilitatis ex promissione & voluntate Dei consequente deducetur, ut via salutis praeclusa sit gentilibus: Nam gentilis accedens ecclesiae, vbi ministerium verbi est corruptum, ille regeneratur vi verbi praedicati, & baptismi administrati. 2) Gentilis. ministerio verbi & baptismo regeneratus, donatur spiritu discretionis, & fit ouis Christi.

Qui autem spiritu discretionis praeditus est, ille discernere potest prophetam a deceptore, & qui ouis Christi est, vocem Christi audit, non peregrini, Io. X, 27. Quodsi itaque gentilis Quodfi itaque gentilis Quodfi itaque gentilis tilis pereat, imbibito semel errorum veneno, non is culpa Dei, qui verbo suo efficaciter operatur, sed suo perit vitio, quatenus mauult attendere spiritus errorum, quam vi semel collatæ regenerationis lucem sectari.

VII. Quemadmodum tria spectari possunt in republ. ciuili, 1) hominum multitudo, 2) externum regimen, 3) interna ciuium affectio, qua ciues inter se vniuntur: Ita eadem spectari possunt in ecclesia, 1) hominum multitudo, 2) externum regimen ecclesiasticum, 3) interna fides & caritas christianorum, qua inter se vniuntur. Duo priora cum in republ. ciuili, tum in ecclesia sunt visibilia. Tertium vtrobique est inuisibile. Sicut autem respubl. absolute visibilis est, licet ciuium affectio non sit visibilis: Ita visibilis est ecclesia, licet visibilis non sit interna fides & caritas. Resp. A republ. ciuili ad ecclesiam non licet argumentari, quia ingens inter vtranque est discrimen. Nam tota republ. est societas externa, in imperantium & subditorum ordine conspicuo posita, quæ proinde secundum se tota in sensus cadit, ita, vt ciues eius noti sint omnibus, digitoque ostendi possint. Licet vero etiam interno ac mutuo affectu, qui hominum oculis peruius non est, se complecti ciues soleant: ille tamen affectus internus non est de ratione formali ciuium, & si quis non bene affectus sit erga suos conciues, per hoc non desinit esse ciuis. At ecclesia, stricte & proprie sumta, formaliter & per essentiam est vere credentium & sanctorum societas interna, fidei vinculo Christo capiti, & caritatis vinculo inter se coniuncta, quæ secundum se sub sensus non cadit, sed fide creditur.

VIII. Fides christianorum videtur & cognoscitur ex operibus ipsorum, Iac. II, 18. Ergo ecclesia christiana, ratione formæ internæ, quæ fundatur in fide, non est inuisibilis. Resp. Innotescit quidem quadantenus fides christianorum ex bonis operibus, sed illa cognitio non est certa & infallibilis; verum incerta, probabilis & coniecturalis, cui falsum subesse potest; siquidem hypocritæ etiam bona opera externa patrant, sicut olim Pharisæi studio bonorum operum clari esse videbantur (*).


### Quæst. X. What is the principal efficient cause of the church?

The principal efficient cause of the church is God a) triune b).

Prob. a. The church is the people of God, whom He has called into His marvelous light, 1 Pet. II, 9. 10. God has called the human race from the state of sin and wrath into the kingdom of grace, which is the church.

Prob. b. The calling, gathering, and governing of the church, since it is a divine action ad extra, is common to all three Persons of the Divinity. God the Father brings the church, as a bride, to His Son, and prepares the wedding for Him, Matt. XXII, 2. The Son of God is the bridegroom, to whom the church is betrothed, 2 Cor. XI, 2. The Holy Spirit, through the ministry of the word and sacraments, cleanses and adorns the church, as a bride for her husband, Eph. V, 27. God the Father is the architect of the church, as a spiritual house, 1 Tim. III, 15. The Son of God is the cornerstone and foundation of this house, by which it is sustained, 1 Petr. II, 7. 1 Cor. III, 11. The Holy Spirit is the principal dispenser and steward, in this house opening and distributing through the ministers of the word the treasures, merited by the passion and death of Christ, and stored up in it, Act. XX, 18. 1 Cor. IV, 1. God the Father bears a providential and truly paternal care for the church, as his daughter, Ps. XLV, 14. The Son of God graciously flows into the church by way of a head, and rules it as Lord, Eph. I, 22. 23. The Holy Spirit by way of a soul moves, informs, and perfects this mystical body, Eph. IV, 3. 4.

XI. What impulsive cause moved God to gather the church to himself?

Prob. a. That God called the human race to his kingdom out of mere grace, Paul teaches clearly, 2 Tim. I, 9. God called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose, and grace, given to us in Christ Jesus. He also regenerated those called out of mercy, and endowed them with faith, through which men become true members of the church. See 1 Petr. I, 3. Iac. I, 18. Prob. b.

The merit of Christ is the external impulsive cause, which moved God to gather the church. For just as by the power and value of the merit of Christ all the gifts of grace come to us from above, according to that of Paul: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavens, in Christ Jesus, Eph. I, 3: So Christ by his satisfactory obedience, both active and passive, merited before God the Father, that he might gather a church to himself from all nations, and offer the benefits of the redeemer to them; for which reason Christ is said to have acquired the church for himself with his own blood, Act. XX, 28. Prob. c.

Human misery could not causally move God to gather the church, since it was contracted by man's own fault, and therefore unless the satisfaction and merit of Christ had intervened, God, the most just avenger of sins, would have turned away and condemned men who had fallen into sins, just as [he did] the apostate angels. It does not happen, therefore, of itself, but accidentally, that the compassion of God arises from the misery of man, who from deep misery; from which man could not emerge by his own powers, took for himself the occasion of having compassion and doing good.

Q. XII. What ministers does God use in gathering the church? Prob. a. Heralds of the divine word are συνεργοὶ, or co-workers of God in the gathering of the church; since it is their task to plant and to water, but God makes it grow, 1 Cor. III, 6. 9. For God does not always and everywhere call men immediately, but for the most part mediately through his ministers, through whom also those called believe, 1 Cor. III, 5. insofar as by their work the gospel is applied to the hearers by the authority and command of Christ. Prob. b.

From Hebr. I, 1. At many times and in many ways God spoke to the fathers by the Prophets. That God might gather the church to himself from the human race, gratuitous favor moved him internally, [and] the merit of Christ the mediator moved him externally . Moreover, the misery of men, having fallen into sins, provided God with an occasion for having compassion .

God in gathering the church uses heralds of the divine word, as co-workers , such as in the O.T. were the Patriarchs and Prophets , in the N.T. the Apostolic [men], and today are all duly called and ordained doctors and pastors .

Prob. c. Christ, being about to gather the Church of the New Testament, called the Apostles, Matth. XXVIII, 19, 20. Go, make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things, whatsoever I have commanded you: And behold, I am with you all days even unto the consummation of the age. From this mandate and promise of Christ we gather: 1) That the Apostles were the planters of the Church: 2) That Christ provided a gracious and efficacious influence for the planting of the Apostles: 1) That the presence and influence of Christ is promised to all teachers of the Church, even unto the end of the world.

Prob. d. From Eph. IV, 2. Christ gave some indeed as Apostles, and others as Prophets, and others as Evangelists, and others as Pastors and Doctors, for the restoration of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edification of the body of Christ, until we all arrive at the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God. From this apostolic oracle we learn that the Church is not a confused confluence of men (as the Arminians would have it), but an ordered congregation; because it is described by the Apostle as a body, consisting of distinct members, and duly coordinated and subordinated.

Latin:

Caussa efficiens principalis ecclesiæ est Deus a) triunus b).

Prob. a. Ecclesia est populus Dei, quem is vocauit in admirabilem suam lucem, 2 Petr. II, 9. 10. Vocauit Deus genus humanum e statu peccati & iræ in regnum gratiæ, quod est ecclesia.

Prob. b. Vocatio, collectio & gubernatio ecclesiæ, cum sit actio diuina ad extra, omnibus tribus diuinitatis Personis communis est. Deus Pater ecclesiam, vt sponsam, filio suo adducit, ac nuptias ipsi apparet, Matth. XXII, 2. Filius Dei est sponsus, cui ecclesia despondetur, 2 Cor. XI, 2. Spiritus S. per ministerium verbi & sacramentorum ecclesiammundat et ornat, tanquam sponsam viro suo, Eph. V, 27. Deus Pater est architectus ecclesiae, tanquam spiritualis domus, 1 Tim. III, 15. Filius Dei est lapis angularis et fundamentum huius domus, quo sustentatur, 1 Petr. II, 7. 1 Cor. III, 11. Spiritus S. est dispensator ac oeconomus principalis, in hac domo per ministros verbi recludens et distribuens thesauros, Christi passione et morte promeritos, et in eam repositos, Act. XX, 18. 1 Cor. IV, 1. Deus Pater curam providam vereque paternam gerit ecclesiae, tanquam filiae suae, Ps. XLV, 14. Filius Dei per modum capitis in ecclesiam gratiose influit, eamque ut Dominus regit, Eph. I, 22. 23. Spiritus S. per modum animae hoc corpus mysticum agitat, informat et perficit, Eph. IV, 3. 4.

XI. Quae causa impuluit Deum ad colligendam sibi ecclesiam?

Prob. a. Deum ex mera gratia humanum genus ad regnum suum vocasse, perspicue docet Paulus, 2 Tim. I, 9. Deus vocauit nos vocatione sancta, non secundum opera nostra, sed iuxta proprium propositum, et gratiam, datam nobis in Christo Iesu. Vocatos etiam ex misericordia regenerauit, et fide donauit, per quam homines fiunt verae ecclesiae membra. Vid. 1 Petr. I, 3. Iac. I, 18.

Prob. b. Meritum Christi est causa impulsiva externa, quae Deum mouit ad colligendam ecclesiam. Sicut enim vi et valore meriti Christi nobis omnia gratiae dona superne obueniunt, iuxta illud Pauli: Benedictus Deus et Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui benedixit nobis omni benedictione spirituali in caelis, in Christo Iesu, Eph. I, 3: Ita Christus sua obedientia satisfactoria, tam actiua, quam passiua, meruit apud Deum Patrem, vt sibi ex omnibus gentibus colligeret ecclesiam, et beneficia redemptoris ipsis offerret; qua ratione Christus proprio sanguine ecclesiam sibi acquisivisse dicitur, Act. XX, 28.

Prob. c. Ad colligendam ecclesiam miseria humana Deum causaliter mouere non potuit, quippe quae propria hominis culpa est contracta, adeoque nisi satisfactio et meritum Christi interuenisset, Deus, peccatorum vindex iustissimus, homines in peccata prolapsos, perinde, atque angelos apostatas, auerfatus damnasset. Non igitur per se, sed per accidens fit, vt ex miseria hominis oriatur commiseratio Dei, qui e profunda miseria; ex qua homo propriis viribus emergere non poterat, commiserescendi et benefaciendi occasionem ipse sibi sumpsit.

Quaest. XII. Quibus ministris Deus in colligenda ecclesia vtitur? Prob. a. Praecones verbi diuini sunt συνεργοὶ, seu cooperarii Dei in collectione ecclesiae; quippe quorum est plantare et irrigare, sed Deus facit crescere, 1 Cor. III, 6. 9. Neque enim Deus semper et vbique immediate homines vocat, sed plerumque mediate per suos ministros, per quos etiam vocati credunt, 1 Cor. III, 5. quatenus illorum opera euangelium auditoribus ex auctoritate et mandato Christi applicatur.

Prob. b. Ex Hebr. I, 1. Multis vicibus, multisque modis Deus locutus est patribus in Prophetis. Vt Deus ex genere humano sibi colligeret ecclesiam, ipsum interne mouit fauor gratuitus a), externe ipsum impulit meritum Christi mediatoris b). Miseria autem hominum, in peccata prolapsorum, praebuit Deo occasionem commiserescendi c).

Deus in colligenda ecclesia vtitur praeconibus verbi diuini, tanquam cooperariis a), quales in V. T. fuerunt Patriarchae et Prophetae b), in N. T. Apostolici, et hodienum sunt omnes rite vocati et ordinati doctores atque pastores d).

Prob. c. Christus collecturus ecclesiam N. T. compellauit Apostolos, Matth. XXVIII, 19, 20. Fontes facite discipulos omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomine Patris, Filii, & Spiritus Sancti, docentes eos seruare omnia, quaecunque mandaui vobis: Et ecce, ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus vsque ad consummationem saeculi. Ex hoc mandato & promisso Christi colligimus: 1) Apostolos fuisse plantatores ecclesiae: 2) Christum in plantationem Apostolorum gratiosum & efficacem praebuisse influxum: 1) praesentiam & influentiam Christi promissam esse omnibus doctoribus ecclesiae, vsque ad finem mundi.

Prob. d. Ex Eph. IV, 2. Christus dedit alios quidem Apostolos, alios vero Prophetas, alios vero Euangelistas, alios vero Pastores & Doctores, in instaurationem sanctorum, in opus ministerii, in aedificationem corporis Christi, vsque dum perueniamus omnes in vnitatem fidei & cognitionis Filii Dei. Ex hoc oraculo apostolico discimus, ecclesiam non esse confusum hominum confluxum (quod volunt Arminiani), sed congregationem ordinatam; quia describitur ab Apostolo, tanquam corpus, ex membris distinctis, riteque coordinatis & subordinatis constans.


### Q. XIII. By what means does God gather the Church?

God gathers the Church to Himself, and grants the life of faith through the word of the gospel a), and baptism b). Prob. a. 1) From 2 Thess. II, 14. God called us through the gospel to the possession of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. God called us to the kingdom of grace and glory through the word of the gospel, as through the word of reconciliation, 2 Cor. V, 19. The Law after the fall is the word of wrath, Rom. IV, 15. and therefore it is not a means of grace calling to the Church.

2) By the word of the gospel the Church is not only gathered, but also vivified, or granted the life of faith. For the assembly of the called is regenerated not from corruptible seed, but from incorruptible, through the living word of God which remains forever, 1 Pet. I, 25. In Christ Jesus through the gospel I have begotten you, says Paul, 2 Cor. IV, 15.

Prob. b. He who is not generated from water and the Spirit does not enter into the kingdom of God, Jo. III, 5. For they become disciples of Christ through baptism, Matth. XXVIII, 19. by which men who are called are regenerated and renewed, Tit. III, 5.

Q. XIV.

What are the parts and members of the Church? The constitutive parts of the Church, and its true and spiritually living members, are men a) who are truly believing and holy b), as long as they are such c).

Prob. a. The true members of the Church are men, not angels; because the Church is the society of those whom God has acquired with His own blood, Acts XX, 28. But He acquired only men, and not angels, with His blood.

Prob. b. That men who are truly believing and holy are the living and properly so-called members of the Church is evident: 1) because the Church is the congregation of the saints, a pure virgin and the spouse of Christ, the mother of the children of God, and the kingdom of God, to which men devoid of true faith and holiness do not belong. See Q. III. 2) From Rom. VIII, 9. He who does not have the spirit of Christ is not His. Which words THOMAS Aquinas skillfully expounds in his commentary on ch. VIII of Romans. Just as that is not a member of the body which is not vivified by the spirit of the body: So he is not a member of Christ who does not have the spirit of Christ. From which we argue: Whoever does not have the spirit of Christ is not a true and living member of the Church: But a hypocritical and unholy man does not have the spirit of Christ: Therefore. The major premise is established: because he who is not a true member of Christ the head, he also is not member of the church, which is the mystical body of Christ. 3) Whoever does not truly believe in Christ, he cannot be a living member of the church: But a hypocrite does not truly believe in Christ: Therefore. The major premise is proved from Habakkuk II, 4; Galatians III, 11.

Proof of the chapter: Truly believing and holy persons, insofar as and as long as they are such, are living members of the church. If by deliberate sins they cast off the Holy Spirit, they become from members of Christ members of a harlot, 1 Corinthians VI, 15; nor do they remain in the vine, John XV, 4 ff., but are dead members; just as David, from being a man according to God's heart, or a true and living member, became a son of death, or a dead member, 2 Samuel XII, 5; and the faithful city became a harlot, Isaiah I, 21.

There is an antithesis from the Papists, who acknowledge as true members of the church all persons universally who dwell in her visible communion, even though they may be great sinners and secret infidels. Their stronger arguments are:

I. Whoever, just as believers do, hear the word of God and use the sacraments, they are true members of the church: But hypocrites and the unholy, etc. Therefore. The major premise is proved: because hypocrites hearing the word and using the sacraments are either in the church or are outside the church. They are not outside the church. Therefore they are in the church and consequently are its members.

Response: The major premise is denied. Regarding the proof, we say that hypocrites are in the church, but not of the church. For they are in the church in name, not in reality itself. They are in that assembly in which the church is, but they are not that assembly which is the church, for the reason that they are not united by faith with the head, Christ, although they externally profess the doctrine of Christ. They are therefore in the church as morbid humors, not as true parts of the body.

Instance: Those who by external profession of the same doctrine of faith are joined to the faithful are true external parts, and thus even members, although arid and dead, of the body of the church.

Response: Just as members, although arid and dead, are not called members of a living body except equivocally, for the reason that they are not informed or governed by the soul: so hypocrites belong to the church, not truly and univocally by reason of a spiritual union with Christ, but equivocally and putatively, in respect of external profession and society with the faithful, to whom they adhere accidentally and contrary to the intention of Christ.

II. The church is compared to a threshing floor, in which there is wheat and chaff, Matthew III, 12; to a net or seine, by which are caught fish not only good, but also rotten, Matthew XIII, 47. By these likenesses it is indicated that hypocrites and the unholy are mixed in with truly believing and holy persons in the church.

Resp. Hypocrites are mixed with truly believing persons, just as chaff adheres to wheat. But just as chaff, on account of this admixture, is not called a part of the wheat: so by the fact that the unholy are mixed with the church, which is the mystical body of Christ, they are not true parts or living members of the church. And just as bad fish, although they are mixed with the good, are cast out: so it shall be, that the unbelieving shall be cast out and excluded from the kingdom of God. But if they are to be excluded from the kingdom of God, it follows that they are not living members of the church.

Some teachers and pastors are hypocrites: Therefore some hypocrites are true members of the church. The major premise is proven: because teachers and pastors are constituted by Christ, as Paul testifies, 1 Cor. XII, 27. 28. You are the body of Christ, and members in particular. And God has indeed placed these in the church, first Apostles, second Prophets, third teachers, Eph. IV, 11. But who would believe that Christ constituted teachers and pastors in the church as organs, ordained for a sacred function and operation, and for this end granted them ministering gifts: He also willed, and seriously intends, that teachers should be true and living members of the church, through faith and sanctifying gifts. But when teachers of the church allow themselves to be overcome by the flesh, so that by indulging in deliberate sins they shake off the Holy Spirit and extinguish faith, they are not members of the true, living, and univocal church, but rotten, dead, and equivocal, although they may be operative organs.

Confer. D. Gerhard, Confess. Cathol. Book II, Art. V, c. 1, fol. 712. XIII, 18. If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone. He who sins in such a way that he must be rebuked is certainly an impious man: But a certain brother sins in this way: Therefore a certain brother is impious, etc. The consequence is proven: because a brother of believers is a son of God, and therefore a true member of the church. Response: He is called impious who indulges in sins and perseveres in them. A brother of believers and saints can be overcome by the flesh and fall into sins, but he does not continue or persevere in sins; rather, he rises again through repentance. For which reason he is held to be a brother as long as any hope of amendment shines forth; when this vanishes, he is to be cast out like a Gentile from the holy society.

Some impious men are baptized: Therefore. Response: Every baptized person is a true member of the church as long as he leads a life worthy of baptism. Since an impious man does not do this, he becomes a dead member.

Whoever maintains that only holy men are true members of the church, they are rushed into the heresy of the Donatists and Anabaptists: But the Lutherans, etc. Therefore. Response: The Donatists and Anabaptists assert that true members of the church are men perfectly holy and marked by no stain; but we acknowledge and maintain the imperfection of human holiness in the way of this life, and hold that for believers who have fallen into mortal sins, a return to repentance and the state of grace lies open.

Latin:

Deus ecclesiam sibi colligit, vitamque fidei donat per verbum euangelii a), & baptisimum b). Prob. a. 1) Ex 2 Thess. II, 14. Deus vocauit nos per euangelium ad possessionem gloriae Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Deus ad regnum gratiae & gloriae nos vocauit per verbum euangelii, tanquam per verbum reconciliationis, 2 Cor. V, 19. Lex post lapsum est verbum irae, Rom. IV, 15. adeoque non est medium gratiae vocantis ad ecclesiam.

2) Verbo euangelii ecclesia non colligitur tantum, sed etiam viuificatur, seu vita fidei donatur. Coetus namque vocatorum non ex semine corruptibili, sed incorruptibili per verbum viuens Dei & manens in aeternum regeneratur, 1 Petr. I, 25. In Christo Iesu per euangelium ego vos generaui, ait Paullus 2 Cor. IV, 15.

Prob. b. Qui non generatur ex aqua & Spiritu, non ingreditur in regnum Dei, Io. III, 5. Fiunt enim discipuli Christi per baptisimum, Matth. XXVIII, 19. quo homines vocati regenerantur & renouantur, Tit. III, 5.

Quæst. XIV. Quænam sunt partes & membra ecclesiæ?

Partes ecclesiae constitutiuae, & vera atque spiritualiter viua ipsius membra sunt homines a) vere credentes & sancti b), quamdiu tales sunt c).

Prob. a. Vera ecclesiae membra sunt homines, non angeli; quia ecclesia est societas eorum, quos Deus proprio suo sanguine acquisiuit, Act. XX, 28. At solos homines, non autem angelos sanguine suo acquisiuit.

Prob. b. Quod homines vere credentes & sancti sint viua & proprie dicta membra ecclesiae, patet: 1) quia ecclesia est congregatio sanctorum, virgo pura & sponsa Christi, mater filiorum Dei, atque regnum Dei, ad quod non pertinent homines verae fidei sanctitatique expertes. Vide quaest. III. 2) Ex Roman. VIII, 9. Qui spiritum Christi non habet, non est ipsius. Quae verba scite exponit THOMAS Aquinas commentar. in c. IIX. Rom. Sicut non est membrum corporis, quod per spiritum corporis non viuificatur: Ita non est membrum Christi, qui spiritum Christi non habet. E quibus argumentamur: Quicunque non habet spiritum Christi, non est membrum verum & viuum ecclesiae: Atqui homo hypocrita & non sanctus non habet spiritum Christi: Ergo. Maior constat: quia qui non est verum membrum Christi capitis, ille etiam non est rum membrum ecclesiae, quae est corpus Christi mysticum. 3) Quicunque non vere credit in Christum, is non potest esse vivum ecclesiae membrum: Atqui hypocrita non vere credit in Christum: Ergo. Maior probatur ex Habac. II, 4. Gal. III, 11.

Prob. c. Vere credentes & sancti, quatenus & quamdiu tales sunt, viva membra ecclesiae sunt. Si peccatis proareticis Spiritum sanctum excutiunt, ex membris Christi fiunt membra scorti, 1 Cor. VI, 15. nec manent in vite, Io. XV, 4. seqq. sed sunt membra mortua; quem ad modum David ex viro secundum cor Dei, seu vero ac vivo membro, factus est filius mortis, seu membrum mortuum, 2 Sam. XII, 5. & urbs fidelis scortum facta est, Esai. I, 21. .

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, qui pro veris ecclesiae membris agnoscunt omnes in universum, qui in visibili eius communione versantur, quamvis sint magni peccatores & infideles occulti. Quorum argumenta potiora sunt:

I. Quicunque aeque, ac credentes, verbum Dei audiunt & sacramentis utuntur, illi sunt vera membra ecclesiae: Atqui hypocritae & non sancti &c. Ergo. Maior probatur: quia hypocritae audientes verbum, & sacramentis utentes, aut sunt in ecclesia, aut sunt extra ecclesiam. Extra ecclesiam non sunt. Ergo sunt in ecclesia & consequenter eius membra.

Resp. Negatur maior. Ad probationem dicimus, quod hypocritae sint in ecclesia, sed non de ecclesia . Sunt enim in ecclesia nomine, non re ipsa. Sunt in coetu illo, in quo est ecclesia, sed non sunt coetus ille, qui est ecclesia, ideo, quod per fidem cum capite Christo non sunt uniti, licet externe doctrinam Christi profiteantur. Sunt igitur in ecclesia ut praevi humores, non ut verae corporis partes.

Instantia: Qui externa professione eiusdem doctrinae fidei coniuncti sunt fidelibus, sunt verae partes exteriores, atque adeo etiam membra, licet arida & mortua corporis ecclesiae.

Resp. Sicut membra, licet arida & mortua, non, nisi aequivoce, membra corporis vivi dicuntur, ideo, quod ab anima non informantur, aut reguntur: ita hypocritae ad ecclesiam pertinent, non vere & univoce, ratione spiritualis cum Christo coniunctionis, sed aequivoce & putative, respectu externae professionis & societatis cum fidelibus, quibus per accidens, & praeter intentionem Christi adhaerent.

II. Ecclesia comparatur areae, in qua datur triticum & palea, Matth. III, 12. reti, vel sagenae, qua capiuntur pisces non tantum boni, sed etiam putres, Matth. XIII, 47. Quibus similibus indicatur, vere credentibus & sanctis admixtos esse hypocritas & non sanctos in ecclesia.

Resp. Hypocritae admixti sunt vere credentibus, sicut palea adhaeret tritico. Quem ad modum vero palea ob hanc admixtionem non dicitur pars tritici: ita per hoc, quod non sancti admixti sunt ecclesiae, quae est corpus Christi mysticum, non sunt verae partes, aut viva membra ecclesiae. Et sicut pisces mali, licet admixti sint bonis, foras proiiciuntur: ita futurum est, ut increduli foras proiiciantur & e regno Dei excludantur. Sed si excludendi sunt e regno Dei, sequitur, quod non sint vivae ecclesiae membra.

Quidam doctores & pastores sunt hypocritæ: Ergo quidam hypocritæ sunt vera ecclesiæ membra. Maior probatur: quia doctores & pastores a Christo sunt constituti, teste Paulo, 1 Cor. XII, 27. 28. Vos estis corpus Christi, & membra ex parte. Et hos quidem posuit Deus in ecclesia, primo Apostolos, secundo Prophetas, tertio doctores, Eph. IV, 11. Ecquis autem credat, Christum constituisse doctores & pastores in ecclesia vt organa, ad sacram functionem & operationem ordinata, & hunc in finem ipsis concessit dona ministrantia: Voluit etiam, & serio intendit, vt essent doctores vera & viua ecclesiæ membra, per fidem & dona sanctificantia. Quando autem doctores ecclesiæ a carne se vinci patiuntur, vt peccatis proæreticis indulgendo Spiritum S. excutiant & fidem exstinguant, non sunt membra ecclesiæ veræ, viuæ & vniuoca, sed putida, mortua & æquiuoca, quamuis esse queant organa operatiua. Confer. D. Gerhardi confess. cathol. libr. II. art. V. c. 1. fol. 712. Ergo homo impius potest esse verum & viuum ecclesiæ membrum: Antecedens probatur ex Matth.

XIII, 18. Si peccauerit in te frater tuus, abi & argue eum inter te & ipsum solum. Qui ita peccat, vt arguendus sit, vtique homo impius est: Sed quidam frater ita peccat: E. quidam frater impius est &c. Consequentia probatur: quia frater credentium est filius Dei, adeoque verum ecclesiæ membrum. Resp. Impius dicitur, qui peccatis indulget, & in iisdem perseuerat. Frater credentium & sanctorum potest a carne vinci, & in peccata prolabi, sed non pergit, aut perseuerat in peccatis; verum resurgit per pœnitentiam. Quam ob rem tamdiu habetur frater, quamdiu spes vlla emendationis affulget; hac euanescente, tanquam ethnicus extra societatem sanctam eiiciendus est.

V. Omnis baptizatus est membrum ecclesiæ: Quidam homines impii sunt baptizati: E. Resp. Omnis baptizatus est verum membrum ecclesiæ, quamdiu vitam baptismo dignam agit. Quod cum non faciat impius, fit membrum mortuum. VI.

Quicunque statuunt, vera ecclesiæ membra esse tantum homines sanctos, illi in hæresin Donatistarum & Anabaptistarum præcipites feruntur: Atqui Lutherani &c. Ergo. Resp. Donatistæ & Anabaptistæ asserunt, vera ecclesiæ membra esse homines perfecte sanctos, nullaque macula notatos; nos autem sanctitatis humanæ in via huius vitæ imperfectionem agnoscimus & statuimus, credentibus, prolapsis in peccata mortifera, reditum patere ad pœnitentiam & statum gratiæ.


### Q. XV. Are catechumens before receiving baptism true members of the church?

Catechumens, imbued with the knowledge of the Christian religion, even before receiving baptism, are true and living members of the church.

Proof 1) Because catechumens, informed by Christian doctrine, have received faith from the preaching of the gospel, Rom. X, 17. But through faith they are sons of God, and thus also sons of the church. For those who are spiritually regenerated, their Father is God, the church is their mother, Gal. IV, 26.

2) Likewise, they are partakers of the goods of the church, namely, the remission of sins and the renewal of the Holy Spirit. 3) The thief on the cross, Emperor Valentinian, and martyrs snatched to torments before receiving baptism, became citizens of the church triumphant. Therefore they were also citizens of the church militant.

Latin:

Catechumeni, notitia Christianæ religionis imbuti, etiam ante perceptum baptismum, sunt vera & viua ecclesiæ membra.

Prob. 1) Quia catechumeni doctrina Christiana informati, ex prædicatione euangelii fidem acceperunt, Rom. X, 17. per fidem autem sunt filii Dei, atque adeo etiam filii ecclesiæ. Nam qui spiritualiter regenerantur, eorum Pater est Deus, ecclesia mater, Gal. IV, 26.

2) Item participes sunt bonorum ecclesiæ, scilicet remissionis peccatorum & renouationis Spiritus S. 3) Latro in cruce, Valentinianus Imperator, & martyres ante susceptum baptismum ad tormenta rapti, facti sunt ciues ecclesiæ triumphantis. Ergo etiam fuerunt ciues ecclesiæ militantis.


### Q. XVI. Are excommunicated men members of the church?

Men excommunicated for just causes are not members of the church a). But those unjustly excommunicated do not cease to be members of the catholic church, even if they are cast out from a visible and particular church b).

Proof a. 1) A man excommunicated for just causes is impenitent, and lacks faith, as the formal reason for members of the church. Wherefore, with Christ as judge, he is to be held as a heathen, Matt. XVIII, 17, and with Paul as monitor, he is to be taken away from the midst of the church, 1 Cor. V, 13. 2) Excommunication is therefore nothing other than an ejection outside the church, similar to death, through which men are plainly separated from the whole commonwealth (*).

Proof b. An illicit excommunication does not harm the one marked, but condemns the one excommunicating. For he cannot be separated from the catholic church by the judgment of men, who has not separated himself from it by impenitence and incredulity. Christ foretold to the Apostles: Ἀποσυνάγωγες ποιήσεσιν ὑμᾶς, they will make you excluded from the synagogues, John XVI, 2. But the Apostles, through the illicit excommunication of the Jews, did not cease to be members of the church; for Christ raised them up with most effective consolation, saying: Blessed are you when men shall hate you, and shall separate you, Luke VI, 22.

Question XVII. Are schismatics true members of the church?

Those who, knowingly and willingly, out of mere malice against conscience, instigated by admiration of their own virtues and a spirit of causing trouble for others, stir up disturbances in the church, they are not true members of the church a). But those who depart from some church having been unjustly excommunicated, and cease to communicate with it, just as the guilt of schism cannot be imputed to them, so they do not cease to be true members of the church b).

Observation I. By schism here is denoted a division of the church into parts, with mutual charity and peace removed, regarding actual ecclesiastical communication, which ought to exist between spiritual brothers and the household of faith (**).

Observation II. Schism arises a) from a dissension of doctrine in the foundation of faith. For with the union of faith failing through a disparity of external profession of faith, actual ecclesiastical communion fails, and the stubborn defense of an error fighting against the foundation of faith necessarily also brings about the guilt of schism: just as also formerly heretics were excommunicated from the orthodox church, who, having obtained a crowd of followers, constituted peculiar assemblies for the sake of religion. b) From dissension in less necessary parts of doctrine. Such was the schism between the Roman and African church, in the time of STEPHEN, Bishop of Rome, and CYPRIAN, Bishop of Africa. For CYPRIAN determined that heretics, and those baptized by heretics, if they wished to return to the bosom of the church, were to be rebaptized: STEPHEN, on the contrary, asserted that they were to be received only by the imposition of hands. See EUSEB. book VI, hist. eccl. c. 1. From dissension in ceremonies. Thus VICTOR, the Roman Bishop, gave cause for schism between the Roman church and the Asiatic churches, dissenting concerning the day of Easter. See EUSEB. book V, hist. eccl. c. 1. From dissension in those things which pertain to ecclesiastical government. Such a schism or disagreement arose between the Eastern Bishops and JULIUS, the Roman Pope; the latter affecting dominion over them, while they manfully defended their own liberty. See SOZOM. book III, c.

Schismatics properly so called are those who of their own accord and by deliberate work tear themselves away from the church, and, rashly stirring up disturbances in it, look to nothing else in all their endeavor than to rend the unity of the church. In which class of schismatics MARCION can be reckoned; for he, according to EPIPHANIUS, heresy XLIII, is said to have said: Σχίσῳ τὴν ἐκκλησίαν ὑμῶν, καὶ βαλῶ σχίσμα ἐν αὐτῇ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα: I will rend your church, and I will cast a schism into it forever. Which kind of schismatics is by most just right denied to be a part of the church. For it is the duty of true members of the church both to be closely joined with the head, Christ, and to be connected by the bond of charity, Eph. IV, 16. Nay, even from the punishment by which God took note of this kind of schismatic, it is manifest that these schismatics are unworthy to be numbered among the members of the church. For the schism of Dathan, Korah, and Abiram was avenged by the opening of the earth, with the followers consumed by heavenly fire, Num. XVI, 32. seqq. Prob. b.

Those who are unjustly excommunicated because they refuse to receive errors thrust upon them as articles of faith, their conscience reclaiming, the guilt of schism is not to be imputed to them, for the reason that they do not turn themselves away from the church out of malice, but are expelled by superior force. Thus the Protestants addicted to the Augsburg Confession are not of the census of schismatics; because they did not make a schism, but suffered one: They did not of their own accord tear themselves away from the Roman church, but were ejected from it by the unjust excommunication of the Roman Pontiffs, and by the frauds and cruelty of teachers professing false doctrine. Although, therefore, they were compelled to depart from a particular church, they nevertheless remain true members of the catholic church.

The Antithesis is that of the Papists, who accuse the Protestants of heresy and schism, and deny that they are true members of the church. Their arguments are: I. No one can depart from the communion of the Roman apostolic see without the crime of heresy or schism, since the Roman church is commended for its true and catholic faith, Rom. I, 8. Resp. 1) Dist. between the Roman church pure, such as it was in the time of Paul, and the Roman church corrupt, such as it is in our times. Not from the former; but from the latter did the Protestants depart. Not all who are torn away from the communion of the Roman see are heretics or schismatics.

For VICTOR, the Roman Bishop, had excommunicated the Asiatic churches because they celebrated Easter on the fourteenth moon, as EUSEBIUS reports, book V, hist. eccl. c. 25, yet the holy Fathers who at that time held the care of souls did not charge them with the crime of heresy or schism. Pope STEPHEN excluded CYPRIAN, and all who acted with him, from fraternal communion, as witnessed by DIONYSIUS, Bishop of Alexandria, in Eusebius book VII, hist. eccl. c. 1, whom, however, other bishops did not condemn of heresy or schism. (*) II. Whoever dissolves the unity of the church is a schismatic: LUTHER, and those who stand by him, have dissolved it, etc.

Therefore. Resp. Not LUTHER, and those who stand by him, but the Roman Pontiffs and their parasites have dissolved the unity of the church, by excluding those addicted to the Augsburg Confession from Christian and fraternal communion, and by persecuting them with fire and sword.

Q. XVIII. Who is the head of the church? Christ is the head of the church, the God-man , not only because of his eminence and perfection above the members, but also especially because of the moral and physical, or real , influence which he provides to the members of his mystical body according to both natures . Obs.

The church is a being by aggregation with order, where someone is supreme, upon whom the others depend. He upon whom the church depends is called the head, metaphorically and by a likeness taken from the head of the human body, and here indeed not because of the material concept of the head, as it is an integral part of the body and has the same relation to the whole body as the other members (for Christ cannot be called a member of the church quite conveniently, since he does not depend on it at all); but formally, in so far as the head is the directive principle of the body, and by his influence rules, cherishes, and aids the whole body and all its members.

Prob. a. Christ is explicitly called the head of the body of the church, Col. 1:18, since God gave him as head over all things to the church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all, Eph.

1:22-23. Christ is the head: from whom the whole body, being fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part, maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love, Eph. 4:16.

Prob. b. The influence which Christ provides to the members of the church is twofold: 1) Moral, which consists in this, that Christ by the virtue of his merit has acquired all spiritual goods. The Apostle signifies this, Eph. 1:3, where he says: That God has blessed us with all spiritual blessing in heavenly places in Christ.

2) Physical, so called in opposition to moral; or it is real, which Christ provides to the members of the church effectively, by actions terminated in them, by kindling, increasing, and confirming faith, charity, and other Christian virtues, by cherishing anxious minds, sustaining the wavering, bringing back the erring, and governing each and every one in the course of life. This influence is supernatural in its substance, and can depend on none but him who possesses infinite power and is true God, as from the head and principal cause.

Prob. c. Christ is the head of the church according to both natures.

1) According to his human nature; because just as in the human body the head is conformed to the members, so in Christ's mystical body the head had to be conformed to the members in nature and be a true man. And just as in the human body the head is the first part and holds the supreme place, so Christ, not only as God but also as man, excels in dignity above others in his church and holds the primary place, which the Apostle hints at, Col. 1:18, saying: Christ is the head of the body of the church, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence. To this is added that, just as in the human body the head is more perfect than other parts because all the senses are in it and exert themselves, so Christ also according to his human nature surpasses in perfection all the members of the mystical body, therefore, because all the fullness of the Godhead dwells in him bodily (σωματικῶς), Col. 2:9.

2) According to his divine nature, however; because the influence which he provides as head to the members is of infinite virtue, which belongs to the divine nature formally, and to the human communicatively.

Christ provides this influence to the members of the mystical body. mystical through ordinary means, namely through the Word and the sacraments. For through these, the church was planted at the beginning, and afterwards propagated far and wide, and preserved to this very day; and thus also through those means of grace and salvation it will be illuminated, sanctified, and preserved until the end of the world.

Through the same means, the most abundant gifts flow from Christ the head into the church, both ministering and sanctifying, with which are adorned not only all the faithful, but especially the leaders of the church, Apostles, Prophets, Pastors, and Doctors, whose ministry Christ uses in diffusing his gracious influx, Eph. IV, 11. Q. XIX. Is there given, besides Christ, another and visible head, which in the place of Christ visibly governs the universal church? Besides Christ, another certain head of the church, which in the place of Christ visibly governs the universal church, is to be acknowledged neither by necessity , nor by the free will and institution of Christ . Obs.

The question is not: Whether there is given, besides Christ, another head of the church which provides to it an internal influx, from which it has spiritual life: for the sounder Papists acknowledge that, regarding internal influx, no other head of the church is given besides Christ. But the question is: Whether, by reason of external order and government, there is given some visible head of the church which holds the place of Christ on earth, and obtains supreme authority and power over the universal church diffused throughout the whole world, so that all the faithful are bound to hear its decrees and decisions in matters of the church, and to acquiesce in them without hesitation.

Prob. a. 1) A visible head is not required by necessity, by which it might be ruled as a certain sacred monarchy. For just as the forms of republics that are simple and upright are three—monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy—and any republic can be conveniently governed and preserved for the public welfare: so also the church, viewed from the side of external government, can be governed and preserved not only by one head, but also by several bishops equal in power among themselves, by way of an aristocratic form of government, so that it does not become a necessity that it be governed visibly by one visible head.

2) Christ, according to both natures, is the omnipotent, all-wise, and omnipresent head of the church, and therefore does not need a vicar. 3) A single mortal man cannot perform the functions that a head of the universal church has. For one human-loving [φιλάνθρωπος] person cannot rightly rule over all, nor institute sacraments, nor establish articles of faith, nor bestow the gifts [χαρίσματα] of the Holy Spirit, nor give motion and sense while absent, nor defend all the members of the church, nor unite them by a spiritual bond, nor be heard by all with divine infallibility.

Prob. b. 1) If Christ, about to ascend into heaven, entrusted the church to the Apostles to be planted and governed in such a way that he gave equal power to all: it follows that he constituted no visible head of the church to whom some singular power was granted over others: The antecedent is true: Therefore the consequent is also. The consequence is clear; for of those who received the same and entirely equal power from Christ, none received singular power over others, through which he was constituted the visible head of the church.

The antecedent is proved from Matt. XXVIII, 19.
