"Go, teach all nations," etc. Here the Savior, shortly before his ascension into heaven, instructs the Apostles concerning those things which they ought to observe in planting and governing the church after his ascension, and commands all equally to teach the nations, to baptize, and to warn men to observe all things which he had commanded them.

No mention is made here of a singular power granted to one of the Apostles over the others, through which he might have been constituted the visible head of the church. Then the antecedent

is proven from John 20:21, where Christ addresses the Apostles in general: As the Father has sent me, even so I send you. Here he sends the Apostles equally to plant and govern the church; nor does he say that he sends one of them in a more worthy manner than the others, who, forsooth, ought to be the visible head of the church. In verse 23, Christ says: Whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them. Here again, Christ commits the power of the keys to the Apostles equally, nor does he grant greater power to one than to another, through which he ought to be the visible head of the church.

2) Paul, in 1 Cor. 12:28 and Eph. 4:11, recounts the entire hierarchical order instituted by Christ; yet in neither place does he make any mention of a visible head to whom supreme power over the universal church might belong, but in the hierarchical order he assigns the first place to the Apostles, who are equal in power and office.

3) The same Apostle, when he distinguishes the body of the church from Christ the head, calls all the faithful, of whatever status and condition they may be, not only members in relation to Christ, but also says that when compared among themselves they are ἀλλήλων μέλη, that is, members one of another, Rom. 12:5. Therefore, none of those who are under Christ is the head of the others.

4) Although the praised Apostle speaks quite often of the head of the church, Col. 1:18, Eph.

1:21, ch. 4:15, he nowhere names any other head besides Christ. Certainly, if there were given some visible head in the church, the Apostle would have said that it was placed there by God or Christ. But he never says that a vicar head has a place in the church. 5) Neither in the time of the Apostles, nor for several centuries afterward, was anyone found who would take upon himself the superiority and roles of a visible head over the universal church, or say that it belonged to him by divine right. Not in vain did GREGORY THE GREAT write, book 6, epistle 30: Whoever calls himself universal priest, or desires to be called so, in his elation runs before Antichrist.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, who posit that besides Christ there is another head of the church, and that it is visible. Their arguments are:

I. Every visible body must have a visible head: The Church is, etc. Therefore. I respond: 1) The true and sincere church is invisible; because it is a mystical and spiritual body, joined to the head, Christ, by the bond of faith, which, considered formally, does not fall under the senses, but is believed by faith. Any particular church, insofar as it consists of true believers and hypocrites mixed in, is indeed visible; but the universal church cannot be seen, and thus does not require a visible universal head. 2) Although Christ has withdrawn his visible presence from the militant church until the last day of the world, he nevertheless governs it most presently through pastors and teachers as his organs and ministers. 3) It is not necessary that the head of a society always be seen. Charles V was not seen in Spain for many years, yet he governed it prosperously. Objection: When the King is not seen, a viceroy is needed.

Resp. 1) The reason secular kingdoms require viceroys is the king’s impotence, ignorance, and absence. But Christ is the head of his mystical body and the king of his spiritual kingdom, omnipotent, omniscient, and omnipresent. Therefore, he does not need a vicar head or a viceroy. 2) Secular kingdoms do not necessarily require a viceroy upon whom all the king’s ministers must depend.

II. Whatever government is best and most perfect, that belongs to the church by the will of the best and most perfect God: But monarchical government is best and most perfect: Therefore. Resp. 1) The whole argument can be conceded; because Christ is the hieromonarch governing the church through certain organs and ministers. 2) The consequence is invalid. For if you firmly conclude: the monarchical form of government is always and everywhere the best and most perfect: Therefore the same is owed to the Catholic church; by the same reasoning I would conclude: Therefore the same is owed of the Venetian, Swiss, and Dutch republics. Certainly, one must not look here at which form is more perfect or more excellent, but what the subject matter can bear. The form of a shoe suitable for robust men is most perfect, yet it is not suitable for boys or girls.

Latin:

Homines iustis de caussis excommunicati, non sunt membra ecclesiæ a). At vero iniuste excommunicati non desinunt esse membra catholicæ ecclesiæ, etiamsi ex visibili & particulari ecclesia eiiciantur b).

Prob. a. 1) Homo iustis de caussis excommunicatus est impœnitens, caretque fide, tanquam ratione formali membrorum ecclesiæ. Quocirca, iudice Christo, habendus est pro ethnico, Matth. XVIII, 17. & monitore Paullo, tollendus est de medio ecclesiæ, 1 Cor. V, 13.. 2) Est itaque excommunicatio nihil aliud, quam eiectio extra ecclesiam, similis morti, per quam homines plane separantur a tota republica (*).

Prob. b. Illicita excommunicatio non lædit notatum, sed condemnat excommunicantem. Neque enim hominum iudicio ab ecclesia catholica separari potest, qui per impœnitentiam & incredulitatem ab ipsa se non separauit. Prædixit Christus Apostolis: Ἀποσυναγώγες ποιήσεσιν ὑμᾶς, a synagogis alienos vos facient, Io. XVI, 2. Apostoli autem per illicitam Iudæorum excommunicationem non desierunt esse membra ecclesiæ; quippe quos Christus efficacissimo solatio erexit, inquiens: Beati estis, quando homines odio habebunt, & separabunt vos, Luc. VI, 22.

Quæst. XVII. Suntne schismatici vera ecclesiæ membra?

Qui scientes & volentes ex mera malitia contra conscientiam, propriarum virtutum admiratione, ac aliis ægre faciendi animo instigati, turbas in ecclesia excitant, illi non sunt vera ecclesiæ membra a). Sed qui ab aliqua ecclesia iniuste excommunicati discedunt, & cum ea communicare desinunt, illis sicut culpa schismatis imputari nequit, ita non desinunt esse vera ecclesiæ membra b).

Obs. I. Per schisma hic denotatur diuisio ecclesiæ in partes, sublata mutua caritate & pace, quoad actualem communicationem ecclesiasticam, quæ inter spirituales fratres & domesticos fidei esse debet (**).

Obs. II. Oritur schisma a) ex dissensu doctrinæ in fundamento fidei. Nam deficiente vnione fidei per disparitatem professionis fidei externæ, deficit actualis communio ecclesiastica, & pertinax defensio erroris cum fundamento fidei pugnantis, necessario etiam infert reatum schismatis: prout etiam olim hæretici ab ecclesia orthodoxa excommunicati fuerunt, qui turbam sectatorum nacti, peculiares cœtus religionis caussa constituerunt. b) Ex difsensu in partibus doctrinæ minus necessariis. Tale fuit schisma inter ecclesiam Romanam & Africanam, tempore STEPHANI, Episcopi Romani, & CYPRIANI, Episcopi Africani. Cyenim hæreticos, & ab hæreticis baptizatos, si ad ecclesiæ gremium redire vellent, rebaptizandos esse statuit: STEPHANVS contra tantum impositione manuum recipiendos esse asseruit. Vid. EVSEB. libr. VI. hist. eccles. c. 1. Ex dissensu in cærimoniis. Sic VICTOR, Episcopus Romanus, causam schismati dedit inter ecclesiam Romanam, & Asiaticas, de die paschatis dissentientes. Vid. EVSEB. libr. V. hist. eccles. c. 1. Ex dissensu in iis, quæ ad regimen ecclesiasticum pertinent. Quale schisma vel dissidium exortum est inter Episcopos orientales, & IVLIVM, Papam Romanum; hoc dominatum in illos affectante, illis autem libertatem suam masculè tuentibus. Vid. SOZOM. libr. III. c.

XIII. Prob. a. Propriè dicti schismatici sunt, qui suapte sponte & destinata opera se divellunt ab ecclesia, & in ea temere turbas excitantes, nihil aliud universo suo conatu spectant, quam ut unitatem ecclesiæ scindant. In quo schismaticorum genere censeri potest MARCION; quippe qui apud EPIPHANIVM, hæresi XLIII. dixisse fertur: Σχίσῳ τὴν ἐκκλησίαν ὑμῶν, καὶ βαλῶ σχίσμα ἐν αὐτῇ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα: Ego scindam vestram ecclesiam, & schisma mittam in eam in æternum. Quod genus schismaticorum iure iustissimo negatur esse pars ecclesiæ. Verorum enim ecclesiæ membrorum est, & cum capite Christo arctè coniungi, & vinculo caritatis connecti, Eph. IV, 16. Quin immo vel ex pœna, qua in hoc genus schismaticorum quodam animadvertit Deus; manifestum est, indignos esse hos schismaticos, qui inter membra ecclesiæ numerentur. Etenim schisma Dathanis, Corachi & Abirami hiatu terræ vindicatum est, sectatoribus igne cœlesti absumtis, Num. XVI, 32. seqq.

Prob. b. Qui iniuste excommunicantur, quod errores pro articulis fidei obtrusos recipere nolunt, conscientia reclamante, illis culpa schismatis non est imputanda, propterea, quod non ex malitia ab ecclesia se avertunt, sed per vim maiorem expelluntur. Sic Protestantes Augustanæ Confess. addicti, non sunt e censu schismaticorum; quia schisma non fecerunt, sed passi sunt: Non suapte sponte ab ecclesia Romana se divulserunt, sed per iniustam excommunicationem Pontificum Romanorum, & per fraudes atque sævitiam doctorum falsam doctrinam profitentium, ex eadem ejecti sunt. Quamvis itaque ab ecclesia particulari cedere coacti sint, manent tamen vera membra ecclesiæ catholicæ.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, Protestantes hæreseos & schismatis insimulantium, & negantium, eos esse vera ecclesiæ membra. Quorum argumenta sunt: I. A communione sedis apostolicæ Romanæ nemo discedere potest absque hæreseos, aut schismatis crimine, cum ecclesia Romana ob veram & catholicam fidem commendetur, Rom. I, 8. Resp. 1) Dist. inter ecclesiam Romanam puram, qualis erat tempore Pauli, & ecclesiam Romanam corruptam, qualis nostris est temporibus. Non ab illa; sed ab hac discesserunt Protestantes. Non omnes, qui a communione sedis Romanæ divelluntur, sunt, hæretici, aut schismatici.

Nam VICTOR, Episcopus Romanus excommunicaverat ecclesias Asiaticas, quod pascha decima quarta luna celebrarent, referente EVSEBIO libr. V. hist. eccles. c. 25. neque tamen Patres sancti, qui id temporis curam animarum gerebant, iisdem crimen hæreseos aut schismatis impegerunt. Papa STEPHANVS CYPRIANVM, & omnes, qui cum ipso faciebant, fraterna communione exclusit, teste DIONYSIO, Episcopo Alexandrino, apud Eusebium libr. VII. hist. eccles. c. 1. quos tamen alii episcopi hæreseos aut schismatis non damnarunt. (*) Quicunque dissoluit vnitatem ecclesiæ, is est schismaticus: LVTHERVS, & qui ab eo stant, dissoluerunt &c.

Ergo. Resp. Non LVTHERVS, & qui ab eo stant, sed Pontifices Romani & eorum parasiti, vnitatem ecclesiæ dissoluerunt, Protestantes Aug. Confess. addictos, christiana & fraterna communione excludendo, iuxta atque igne & ferro persequendo.

Quæst. XVIII. Quis est caput ecclesiæ? Caput ecclesiæ est Christus θεάνθρωπος , non solum ob eminentiam & perfectionem præ membris, verum etiam præcipue ob influxum moralem & physicum, siue realem , quem is secundum vtramque naturam in membra sui corporis mystici præbet.

Obs. Ecclesia est ens per aggregationem cum ordine, vbi aliquis summus est, a quo cæteri dependent. Is, a quo ecclesia dependet, dicitur caput, metaphorice & per similitudinem a capite corporis humani desumptam, & hic quidem non quod materiale conceptum capitis, prout est pars corporis integralis, atque eandem cum cæteris membris relationem ad totum corpus habet (non enim satis commode Christus membrum ecclesiæ dici potest, cum ab hac nullatenus dependeat); sed formaliter, in quantum caput principium directiuum corporis est, & influxu suo corpus totum & omnia ipsius membra regit, fouet & adiuuat.

Prob. a. Christus diserte dicitur caput corporis ecclesiæ, Col. I, 18. quippe quem Deus dedit caput super omnia ecclesiæ, quæ est corpus illius, plenitudo eius, qui omnia in omnibus implet, Eph.

I, 22. 23. Christus est caput: ex quo totum corpus probe coagimentatum, & cohærens per omnes iuncturas subministrationis, iuxta efficaciam in mensura vnius cuiusque partis augmentum corporis facit in ædificationem sui ipsius in dilectione, Eph. IV, 16.

Prob. b. Influxus, quem Christus præstat in membra ecclesiæ, est duplex: 1) Moralis, qui in eo consistit, quod Christus virtute meriti sui acquisifiuit omnia bona spiritualia. Hoc significat Apostolus, Eph. I, 3. vbi ait: Deum benedixisse nobis omni benedictione spirituali in supracælestibus in Christo.

2) Physicus, in oppositione ad moralem sic dictus; siue realis est, quem Christus præbet in membra ecclesiæ effectiue, per actiones in ipsis terminatas, fidem, caritatem & alias virtutes christianas accendendo, augendo, confirmando, mentes anxias fouendo, titubantes sustentando, errantes reducendo, omnes ac singulos in vitæ cursu gubernando. Qui influxus in substantia sua supernaturalis est, nec nisi ab eo, qui infinita pollet potentia, & verus Deus est, tanquam a capite & caussa principali dependere potest.

Prob. c. Christus est caput ecclesiæ secundum vtramque naturam.

1) Secundum humanam naturam; quia sicut in corpore humano caput conforme est membris, ita in Christi corpore mystico caput membris in natura conforne & verus homo esse debuit. Et sicut in corpore humano caput pars prima est, & supremum locum obtinuit, ita Christus non tantum qua Deus, sed etiam qua homo, in ecclesia sua dignitate præ aliis eminet & primarium obtinet locum, quod innuit Apostolus, Col. I, 18. inquiens: Christus est caput corporis ecclesiæ, qui est principium, primogenitus ex mortuis, vt fieret in omnibus ipse primatum habens, His accedit, quod sicut in corpore humano caput est perfectius aliis partibus, quia in eo omnes sensus sunt, & sese exerunt; ita Christus etiam secundum humanam naturam perfectione superat omnia corporis mystici membra, ideo, quod omnis plenitudo diuinitatis in eo habitat σωματικῶς, Col.

II, 9. 2) Secundum diuinam naturam vero; quia influxus, quem velut caput in membra præbet, virtutis infinitæ est, quæ diuinæ naturæ competit formaliter, adhumanæ communicatiue.

Præstat autem Christus hunc influxum in membra corporis mystici. per ordinaria media, scilicet per verbum & sacramenta. Per haec enim sub initio ecclesia est plantata, & postea longe lateque propagata, & in hunc usque diem conservata, adeoque etiam per illa media gratiae & salutis illuminabitur, sanctificabitur & conservabitur usque ad finem mundi.

Per eadem media a capite Christo in ecclesiam redundant dona uberrima, cum ministrantia, tum sanctificantia, quibus exornantur cum omnes fideles, tum in primis antistites ecclesiae, Apostoli, Prophetae, Pastores & Doctores, quorum ministerio Christus utitur in diffundendo gratioso suo influxu, Eph. IV, 11. Quaest. XIX. Daturne praeter Christum aliud, idque visibile caput, quod loco Christi universam ecclesiam visibiliter gubernet? Praeter Christum aliud quoddam ecclesiae caput, quod vice Christi universam ecclesiam visibiliter gubernet, neque ex necessitate , neque ex libera Christi voluntate & institutione agnoscendum est. Obs.

Non quaeritur: An detur praeter Christum aliud caput ecclesiae, quod in hanc praebeat internum influxum, a quo vitam spiritualem habeat: agnoscunt enim saniores Pontificii, quoad influxum interiorem, praeter Christum non dari aliud ecclesiae caput. Sed quaeritur: An ratione externi ordinis & gubernationis detur aliquod visibile ecclesiae caput, quod Christi vices in terris gerat, supremam auctoritatem & potestatem in universam per totum terrarum orbem diffusam ecclesiam obtineat, vt eius decreta ac decisiones in rebus ecclesiae fideles omnes audire, in iisque citra haesitationem acquiescere teneantur.

Prob. a. 1) Non ex necessitate requiritur visibile caput, a quo velut sacra quaedam monarchia regatur. Quemadmodum enim rerumpublicarum formae simplices, exque rectae, tres sunt, monarchia, aristocratia & democratia, & unaquaeque respublica convenienter ad salutem publicam gubernari & conservari potest: Ita & ecclesia, ex parte regiminis externi spectata, non solum per caput unum, sed etiam per plures episcopos potestate inter se pares, per modum regiminis aristocratici gubernari & conservari potest, vt de necessitate non fit, eam gubernari visibiliter per unum caput visibile.

2) Christus secundum utramque naturam est caput ecclesiae omnipotens, omnisapiens, omnipraesens, adeoque vicario non indiget. 3) Quas functiones habet caput, unus homo mortalis ecclesiae universae praestare nequit. Neque enim recte unus φιλάνθρωπος dominari omnibus potest, nec instituere sacramenta, nec condere articulos fidei, nec χαρίσματα Spiritus S. erogare, nec motum sensumque absens dare, nec defendere omnia ecclesiae membra, nec spirituali nexu vnire, nec ab omnibus infallibilitate divina audiri potest.

Prob. b. 1) Si Christus in coelum ascensurus ecclesiam Apostolis ita plantandam & gubernandam commisit, vt aequalem omnibus dederit potestatem: sequitur, quod nullum constituerit ecclesiae caput visibile, cui prae aliis singularis aliqua potestas fuerit concessa: Antecedens est verum: Ergo & consequens. Consequentia clara est; qui enim eandem & prorsus aequalem potestatem a Christo acceperunt, eorum nullus prae aliis singularem accepit potestatem, per quam visibile caput ecclesiae fit constitutus.

Antecedens probatur ex Matth. XXVIII, 19. Euntes docete omnes gentes &c. Hic Salvator breui ante ascensionem in coelum instruit Apostolos de iis, quae post ascensionem in ecclesia plantanda & gubernanda observare debeant, & omnibus aequaliter mandat, vt doceant gentes, vt baptizent; vt moneant homines servare omnia, quae praeceperat ipsis.

Nullias hic mentio fit singularis potestatis vni ex Apostolis prae aliis concessae, per quam visibile caput ecclesiae constitutus fuerit. Deinde antecedens feruare omnia, quæ præceperat ipsis. Nullius hic mentio fit singularis potestatis vni ex Apostolis præ aliis conceffæ, per quam visibile caput ecclefiæ constitutus fuerit. Deinde

antecedens probatur ex Io. XX, 21. vbi Christus in genere alloquitur Apostolos: Sicut misit me Pater, ita et ego mitto vos. Aequaliter hic mittit Apostolos ad plantandam et gubernandam ecclesiam; neque dicit, quod vnum ex illis digniori modo mittat, quam alios, qui scilicet visibile caput ecclesiae esse debeat. V, 23. dicit Christus: quorumcunque peccata remiseritis, remittuntur eis. Hic rursus aequaliter Christus Apostolis potestatem clauium committit, nec vni maiorem, quam alteri potestatem concedit, per quam ecclesiae caput visibile esse debeat.

2) Paullus I Cor. XII, 28. et Eph. IV, 11. totum a Christo institutum ordinem hierarchicum recenset; neutrubi tamen capitis visibilis, cui in vniuersam ecclesiam suprema conueniat potestas, vllam facit mentionem, sed in ordine hierarchico primum locum tribuit Apostolis potestate et officio paribus.

3) Idem Apostolus, quando corpus ecclesiae a Christo capite distinguit, fideles omnes, cuiuscunque sint status et conditionis; non solum in ordine ad Christum membra vocat, sed etiam inter se comparatos dicit esse ἀλλήλων μέλη, hoc est, sibi inuicem membra, Rom. XII, 5. E. nullus ex iis, qui sub Christo sunt, aliorum caput est.

4) Quamuis laudatus Apostolus saepius agat de capite ecclesiae, Col. I, 18. Eph. I, 21. c. IV, 15. nuspiam tamen aliud caput praeter Christum nominat. Sane si in ecclesia daretur caput aliquod visibile, Apostolus dixisset, illud a Deo vel Christo positum esse. At nusquam dicit, caput vicarium ecclesiae locum habere.

5) Nec Apostolorum tempore, nec postea, aliquot saeculis, quisquam inuentus fuit, qui superioritatem et partes capitis visibilis in ecclesiam vniuersam sibi sumeret aut sibi de iure diuino competere diceret. Haud ex vano scripsit GREGORIVS M. libr. 6. epist. 30. Quicunque se vniuersalem sacerdotem vocat, vel vocari desiderat, in elatione sua Antichristo praecurrit.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, statuentium, praeter Christum aliud caput ecclesiae, idque visibile dari. Quorum argumenta sunt:

I. Omne corpus visibile debet habere caput visibile: Ecclesia est etc. Ergo. Respond. 1) Ecclesia vera et sincera est inuisibilis; quia est corpus mysticum et spiritale, vinculo fidei capiti Christo coniunctum, quod formaliter consideratum non cadit sub sensus, sed fide creditur. Ecclesia quaelibet particularis, prout constat ex vere credentibus, et admixtis hypocritis, visibilis est quidem; sed ecclesia vniuersa videri nequit, adeoque caput vniuersale visibile non requirit. 2) Quamuis Christus vsque ad extremum mundi diem ecclesiae militanti praesentiam visibilem subtraxerit, praesentissime tamen eandem regit per pastores et doctores velut organa et ministros suos. 3) Non necesse est, vt caput societatis semper videatur. Carolus V. multis annis non visus est in Hispania, quam tamen prospere gubernauit.

Instantia. Cum Rex non videtur, prorege opus est. Resp. 1) Quod regna saecularia proreges requirunt, causa est regis impotentia, ignorantia et absentia. At Christus est caput sui corporis mystici et rex regni sui spiritualis omnipotens, omniscius, omnipraesens. Proinde non indiget capite vicario aut prorege. 2) Regna saecularia non necessario exigunt proregem, a quo omnes ministri regis dependeat.

II. Quodcunque regimen est optimum et perfectissimum, illud ex voluntate Dei optimi et perfectissimi competit ecclesiae: Atqui regimen monarchicum est optimum et perfectissimum: Ergo. Resp. 1) Concedi potest totum argumentum; quia Christus est hieromonarcha per certa organa et ministros ecclesiam gubernans. 2) Consequentia est inualida. Si enim firmiter concludis: forma regiminis monarchica semper et vbique est optima et perfectissima: E. eadem debetur ecclesiae catholicae; eadem ratione colligam: Ergo eadem debetur reipublicæ Venetæ, Helueticæ, Bataux. Sane non videndum est hic, quæ forma fit perfectior, aut præstantior, sed quam subjecta materia ferre possit. Forma calcei viris robustis æqua, est perfectissima, neque tamen apta pueris, aut puellis.


### Q. XVI. Are excommunicated men members of the church?: Question XX. Was the Apostle Peter the visible head of the church, and did he have the primacy of power and jurisdiction over the entire…

Question XX. Was the Apostle Peter the visible head of the church, and did he have the primacy of power and jurisdiction over the entire church of Christ?

Christ never constituted the Apostle Peter the head of his entire church, nor did he grant him the primacy of power and jurisdiction over the catholic church. Proof: 1) Christ, about to ascend into heaven, entrusted the church to be planted and governed not to Peter alone, but to all the Apostles, and he granted them equal power, John XX, 21. 23. Matthew XXVIII, 19.

2) So far is it from the case that Christ granted the primacy of power to Peter, that when the Apostles were arguing among themselves and contending about primacy, he said: You know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them. But it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister: and whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant, Matthew XX, 25.

3) If it was permitted for the disciples not only to send Peter into Samaria, but also to contend with him, so that he himself in his own person was subject to their accusation and examination, then he was certainly not the supreme monarch of the church: But the antecedent is true. See Acts VIII, 14. Galatians II, 11. Therefore, the consequent. Furthermore, no one can rebuke the ecumenical Bishop of the church and say: Pope, what are you doing? But Paul rebuked Peter and withstood him to his face, Galatians II, 11. seqq. Finally, the ecumenical Pontiff cannot err, if it is right to believe the Papists. But Peter erred, and therefore incurred the rebuke of Paul (*).

The antithesis is that of the Papists, asserting that Peter was constituted by Christ as the visible head of the church and the ecumenical Bishop. Who rely on the following arguments:

I. He upon whom the entire church is so solidly built that the gates of hell cannot prevail against it, he is the head and monarch of the church: But it is upon Peter &c. Matthew XVI, 18. Therefore. Resp. The words of the text are: Yea, truly I say to you: you are Peter, and upon this same rock I will build my church. From which words it is clear that Peter is not the rock, but that the confession which Peter issued, and which Christ still praises, is that rock from which Peter is named. For Christ does not say: You are the rock, and upon this rock I will build; but: You are Peter, καὶ ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ ὀικοδομήσω, and upon this same rock I will build. Christ had commended in v. 17 the confession of Peter, which he had issued concerning Christ: You are Christ, that Son of the living God. Christ had said that this confession is of divine revelation: he wished to add that the same is the foundation of Peter and the church. The sense of the words therefore is: You are πέτρος, a stony man, standing upon your confession as upon a rock, or a most firm stone: and upon this rock I will build my church, so that it may be stony, immovable, and impregnable, as long as it shall stand upon this confession or doctrine (that I am Christ, the son of the living God), as upon an immovable rock (**).

II. To Peter

II. The keys of the kingdom of heaven were entrusted to Peter, Matt. XVI, 19. Therefore, ecclesiastical supremacy was committed to him. The reason for the consequence is: because, when cities are surrendered to a prince, the keys are offered to him as a sign of subjection.

Resp. 1) Christ gave the keys to Peter, not as a prince, but as a minister and steward. Now, in truth, not only Peter, but also the remaining Apostles were constituted stewards by Christ, 1 Cor. IV, 1. Therefore, the keys promised here to Peter were also given to the remaining Apostles. Furthermore, the power of a steward is not autokratorikē (autocratic), monarchical, and absolute, but diakonikē (diaconal), ministerial, and restricted.

2) By the keys is designated the ordinary power of the ministry to loose and bind, or to remit and retain sins, which was both promised and conferred upon all the Apostles equally, but not supreme ecclesiastical power. Indeed, just as when all are questioned, one Peter answers, Matt. XVI, 15, 16: So in one, the keys were committed to all, and exercised by all equally, as the scripture testifies in Matt.

Latin:

Quæst. XX. An Apostolus Petrus fuit caput ecclesiæ visibile, & primatum potestatis ac iurisdictionis in vniuersam Christi ecclesiam habuit?

Christus nunquam constituit Apostolum Petrum caput, vniuersum suæ ecclesiæ, neque primatum potestatis ac iurisdictionis in ecclesiam catholicam ipsi concessit. Prob. 1) Christus in cælum ascensurus ecclesiam plantandam & gubernandam commisit non soli Petro, sed omnibus Apostolis, iisque parem tribuit potestatem, Io. XX, 21. 23. Matth. XXVIII, 19.

2) Tantum abest, vt Christus primatum potestatis Petro concesserit, vt Apostolis altercantibus inter se, & de primatu contendentibus dixerit: Scitis, quod principes gentium dominentur illis, & magnates potestatem habeant in eas. Verum non ita erit inter vos; sed quisquis voluerit inter vos magnus fieri, esse debebit vester minister: & quisquis voluerit esse primus, esse debet vester seruus, Matth. XX, 25.

3) Si licuit discipulis, Petrum non tantum mittere in Samariam, sed etiam cum ipso contendere, vt ipse in propria persona obnoxius fuerit eorum accusationi & examini, vtique non fuit summus ecclesiæ monarcha: At verum est antecedens. Vid. Act. VIII, 14. Gal. II, 11. E. & consequens. Præterea nemo œcumenicum ecclesiæ Episcopum reprehendere & dicere potest: Papa, quid facis? At Paullus Petrum reprehendit, eique in faciem restitit, Gal. II, 11. seqq. Denique œcumenicus Pontifex errare non potest, si Pontificiis credere fas est. At Petrus errauit, & ideo reprehensionem Paulli incurrit (*).

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, asserentium, Petrum a Christo constitutum fuisse caput ecclesiæ visibile, & Episcopum œcumenicum. Qui sequentibus innituntur argumentis:

I. Super quem vniuersa ecclesia tam solide ædificata est, vt portæ inferorum ipsi prævalere nequeant, is est caput & monarcha ecclesiæ: Atqui super Petrum &c. Matth. XVI, 18. Ergo. Resp. Verba textus sunt: Quinimo vere ego tibi dico: tu es Petrus, & super hanc eandem petram ædificabo ecclesiam meam. E quibus verbis patet, quod Petrus non sit petra, sed quod confessio, quam Petrus edidit, & Christus adhuc laudat, sit illa petra, a qua Petrus denominatur. Neque enim dicit Christus: Tu es petra, & super hac petra ædificabo; sed: Tu es Petrus, καὶ ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ ὀικοδομήσω, & super hac eadem petra ædificabo. Commendauerat Christus v. 17. confessionem Petri, quam ediderat de Christo: Tu es Christus, ille Filius Dei viuentis. Dixerat Christus, hanc confessionem esse diuinæ reuelationis: addere voluit, quod eadem sit fundamentum Petri & ecclesiæ. Sensus ergo verborum est: Tu es πέτρος, vir saxeus, stans super confessione tua velut super saxo, aut petra firmissima: & super hac petra ædificabo ecclesiam meam, vt sit saxea, immobilis & inexpugnabilis, quamdiu super hac confessione vel doctrina (quod ego sim Christus, filius Dei viuentis) stabit, velut super petra immobili (**).

II. Petro

II. Petro creditae sunt claves regni caelorum, Matth. XVI, 19. Ergo ipsi commissus est principatus ecclesiasticus. Ratio consequentiae est: quia, quando urbes deduntur alicui principi, offeruntur ipsi claves in signum subiectionis.

Resp. 1) Christus dedit claves Petro, non ut principi, sed ut ministro & oeconomo. Iam vero non solus Petrus, sed etiam reliqui Apostoli oeconomi a Christo fuere constituti, 1 Cor. IV, 1. Ergo etiam reliquis Apostolis claves Petro hic promissae fuere datae. Praeterea potestas oeconomi non est αὐτοκρατορική, monarchica & absoluta, sed διακονική, ministerialis & restricta.

2) Per claves designatur ordinaria ministerii potestas solvendi & ligandi, sive remittendi & retinendi peccata, quae omnibus Apostolis pariter cum promissa, tum collata est, non autem summa potestas ecclesiastica. Nempe sicut omnibus interrogatis, unus Petrus respondet, Matth. XVI, 15. 16: Ita in uno omnibus claves sunt commissae, & ab omnibus pariter gestae, teste scriptura Matth.


### Q. XVI. Are excommunicated men members of the church?: XVIII, 18

XVIII, 18.

John XX, 23.

III. Christ, after the resurrection, committed to Peter alone, as the ecumenical Pastor and head, not some, but all lambs and sheep to be fed, repeating it three times, John XXI, 15, 16, 17. Therefore, Christ constituted Peter the head and monarch of the universal church.

Resp. 1) Peter is called three times to feed the sheep, so that he might, as it were, wash away the stain of his triple denial with a triple confession, and thus, by the issuance of a triple profession of love for Christ, be restored to his sacred office. 2) The office of feeding was committed to Peter, not empire. The prelates of the church feed by the proclamation of the Word and the dispensation of the sacraments, but lordship is forbidden to them, Matt.

XX, 25. 3) Christ did not commend all sheep or lambs to Peter universally, but indefinitely; "feed," he says, "my sheep"; which is enjoined upon all pastors equally, Acts XX, 28; 1 Pet. V, 2.

IV. Luke XXII, 31, Christ says to Peter: I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. And you, when you have turned, strengthen your brothers. Therefore, Christ gave the primacy to Peter.

The reason for the consequence is: because while the Lord speaks singularly to Peter, and says that He prayed specifically for him, He sufficiently indicates that this man would be the head of the remaining Apostles.

And "strengthen your brothers" befits a man as he is the head and prince of others; for confirmation pertains to him who performs the duty of a superior.

Resp. 1) Christ prayed for all the Apostles, that their faith might not fail, John XVII, 20. That He prayed singularly for Peter does not argue for a monarchical eminence of Peter, but for a greater danger impending over Peter, and a more serious fall of his. Peter was, however, preserved by the prayers of Christ from a final defection of faith.

2) The confirmation of weak brothers does not infer ecclesiastical supremacy. For Paul also says in 1 Thess. III, 2, that he sent Timothy to confirm the Thessalonians, yet a monarchical primacy is not to be attributed to Timothy on that account.

V. The Apostle Peter has always been held as the prince of the apostles on account of the singular prerogatives by which he excels.

For this reason, the Evangelists, listing the Apostles, place Peter in the first position, Matt.

X; Mark III; Luke VI; Acts I. Resp. 1) We concede that Peter can be called first by priority of age, or vocation, or zeal, or order; but we deny that he is called first by reason of power or jurisdiction over the remaining Apostles. For he calls himself a sympresbyteros (fellow-elder), 1 ep. V, 1. 2) Galat. II, they are named pillars of the church, and the first place is attributed to James. It is also most worthy of great consideration that Paul, when he preaches that they are built upon the foundation (that is, the doctrine) of the Apostles and Prophets, assigns nothing singular and preeminent to Peter, Eph. II, 20.

Paul had many privileges before Peter. For Paul alone was called by Christ from heaven, Acts IX, 6. alone caught up into the third heaven, 2 Cor. XII, 2. alone sent to the Gentiles, Acts IX, 15. he wrote more than the other Apostles, planted more churches, labored more than the rest, 1 Cor. XV, 10. 2 Cor. XI, 23. He bore the care for all the churches, 2 Cor. XI, 28. Whence Paul profited the Christian church more than Peter, as BELLARMINE admits, Book I, On the Roman Pontiff, ch.

Latin:

XVIII, 18.

Io. XX, 23.

III. Christus uni Petro, tanquam oecumenico Pastori & capiti, post resurrectionem non aliquot, sed omnes agnos & oues, repetitis tribus vicibus pascendas commisit, Io. XXI, 15. 16. 17. Ergo Christus constituit Petrum universae ecclesiae caput & monarcham.

Resp. 1) Ter vocatur Petrus ad pascendas oues, ut maculam ternae abnegationis trina confessione quasi elueret, atque adeo edita trina amoris Christi professione in sacrum munus restitueretur. 2) Pascendi munus Petro commissum est, non imperium. Pascunt antistites ecclesiae praeconio verbi & sacramentorum dispensatione, dominatus autem illis interdictus est, Matth.

XX, 25. 3) Christus non universaliter oues aut agnos omnes commendauit Petro, sed indefinite, pasce, inquit, oues meas; quod omnibus pastoribus pariter iniungitur, Act. XX, 28. 1 Petr. V, 2.

IV. Luc. XXII, 31. dicit Christus ad Petrum: Ego rogaui pro te, ne deficiat fides tua. Tu autem conuerti confirma fratres tuos. Ergo Christus primatum dedit Petro.

Ratio consequentiae est: quia dum Dominus singulariter Petro loquitur, ac pro illo se peculiariter rogasse dicit, satis indicat, hunc futurum reliquorum Apostolorum caput.

Et confirma fratres conuenit homini, vt est caput & princeps aliorum; spectat enim confirmatio ad eum, qui maioris munere fungitur.

Resp. 1) Christus pro omnibus Apostolis rogauit, ne eorum fides deficeret, Ioan. XVII, 20. Quod autem singulariter orauit pro Petro, non arguit monarchicam Petri eminentiam, sed imminens Petro periculum mains, & lapsum ipsius graviorem. Praeferuatus autem est Petrus precibus Christi a defectione fidei finali.

2) Confirmatio fratrum infirmorum non infert principatum ecclesiasticum. Nam & Paullus dicit 1 Thess. III, 2. se misisse Timotheum ad confirmandos Thessalonicenses, nec tamen propterea monarchicus primatus Timotheo tribuendus est.

V. Apostolus Petrus semper habitus est princeps apostolorum ob singulares praerogatiuas, quibus eminet.

Propterea Evangelistae recensentes Apostolos Petrum primo loco ponunt, Matth.

X. Marc. III, Luc. VI. Act. I. Resp. 1) Petrum prioritate aetatis, aut vocationis, aut zeli, aut ordinis primum dici posse, concedimus; sed ratione potestatis, aut iurisdictionis in reliquos Apostolos primum dici, negamus. Vocat enim se συμπρεσβύτερον, 1 ep. V, 1. 2) Galat. II. nominantur columnae ecclesiae, primusque locus tribuitur Iacobo. Magna consideratione etiam hoc dignissimum est, quod Paullus, cum praedicat aedificatos super fundamento (hoc est, doctrina) Apostolorum & Prophetarum, nihil singulare ac praecipuum Petro adsignat. Eph. II, 20.

Paulus multa privilegia prae Petro habuit. Nam Paulus solus a Christo de caelo est vocatus, Act. IX, 6. solus in tertium caelum raptus, 2 Cor. XII, 2. solus ad gentes missus, Act. IX, 15. plura ceteris Apostolis scripsit, plures ecclesias plantavit, plus ceteris laboravit, 1 Cor. XV, 10. 2 Cor. XI, 23. Curam pro omnibus ecclesiis gessit, 2 Cor. XI, 28. Unde Paullus ecclesiae Christianae plus profuit, quam Petrus, fatente BELLARMINO L. I. de Rom. Pontif. c. 2.


### Q. XVI. Are excommunicated men members of the church?: 2. Question XXI. Is the Roman Pontiff the successor of Peter, and the visible head and Monarch of the Catholic church?

2. Question XXI. Is the Roman Pontiff the successor of Peter, and the visible head and Monarch of the Catholic church?

The Roman Pontiff is neither the successor of Peter in the Episcopate , nor the head or Monarch of the Catholic church . Proof 1. That Peter was in Rome cannot be evidently shown from the sacred scriptures. For a) Paul, writing to the Romans and greeting those known to him, ch. XVI, makes no mention at all of Peter: whom he surely would not have passed over, had he been in Rome. b) Paul, already arriving in Rome, and honorably received by the brethren, and living in his own rented lodging in Rome for two years, does not testify by even a single jot that Peter was seen by him in Rome, Acts XXVIII, v. 14, 15. c) Paul wrote certain epistles from Roman prison, namely to the Colossians, to Philemon, and the latter to Timothy. But in none of these epistles does he make mention of Peter; indeed, 2 Tim. IV, 16, he writes explicitly: In my first defense no one stood with me, but all deserted me. Peter would undoubtedly have stood with Paul, nor would he have deserted him, if he had been in Rome at that time.

2) Although we do not entirely deny that Peter was in Rome and taught there, since the Fathers testify to it, IRENAEUS, EUSEBIUS, ATHANASIUS, TERTULLIAN, LEO M., CYPRIAN, AUGUSTINE, LACTANTIUS, whom see cited in the ecclesiastical history of D. HORNEUS, p. 32 ff., they deny, however, that the Apostle Peter was the proper Bishop of the city of Rome, and that he erected a papal seat in that city. For a) St. Peter indeed calls himself an Apostle of Jesus Christ, 1 ep. I, 1, and a fellow-elder, ch. V, 1, but nowhere the Bishop of the Roman church. But an Apostle differs from a Bishop, as CHRYSOSTOM teaches in Matthew, Homily 19. For the Apostles were teachers of all nations, and bore the care of all the churches which they planted: But Bishops are fixed to certain places, and bear care particularly for particular churches. Whence only the care of the suburbicarian churches was assigned to the Roman Bishop by the ecumenical Council of Nicaea. The Apostle Peter was called immediately by Christ. The Roman Pontiff is destitute of immediate calling. Peter ordained bishops of Alexandria and Antioch: that which is not permitted to the Roman Pontiff. b) If Peter was Bishop of Rome, much more was Paul the Roman Bishop.

For Paul was the Apostle of the Gentiles, and therefore also the Bishop of the Gentile city of Rome. But Peter was the Apostle of the circumcision, Gal. II, 7. Paul taught the Romans in a most excellent epistle: Peter wrote his epistles to the dispersed brethren (Jews) in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia. Who therefore believes that St. Peter erected a chair of teaching in Rome, in which the Roman Bishop succeeds him? Grant that Peter had a chair in Rome; yet the Roman Pontiff never ascended it. For Peter was a herald of the gospel: the Roman Pontiff casts the duty of teaching onto the shoulders of others. Therefore the Roman Pontiff is not the successor of Peter in the chair of teaching.

For Peter commends the Holy Scripture because of its clarity, and exhorts to the reading of it, 2 Pet. I, 19. The Pope accuses Scripture of obscurity, and keeps the laity from reading it. Peter [placed] trust places salvation in one and only Christ, Acts IV, 12. The Pope teaches that salvation is to be sought not in Christ's merit alone, but also in the merits of the saints, in merits and one's own satisfactions, in monastic vows, in papal indulgences. Peter teaches that the remission of sins is received by faith in Christ, Acts X, 43. The Pope teaches that sins committed after baptism are redeemed by good works, and are not obtained by faith alone, but also by one's own satisfactions. Peter teaches that Christ alone is the foundation and cornerstone of the church, 1 Ep. II, 6. and the universal Bishop, v. 25. The Pope calls himself the foundation of the church, and the universal Bishop. Peter teaches that Christ, by dying once, perfected the offering for the sins of this world, 1 Ep. III, 18. The Pope teaches that Christ is daily immolated for our sins in the unbloody sacrifice of the mass. Peter teaches that our calling and election can be made firm, 2 Ep. I, 10. The Pope teaches that one must doubt concerning the grace of God and the remission of sins, and therefore also concerning election. Peter demands obedience toward magistrates, 1 Ep. II, 13. The Pope exempts his Clerics from the obedience of the magistrate, and teaches that Christians cannot tolerate an infidel or heretical magistrate.

4) The Roman Pontiff is not the successor of Peter in life and morals. Peter says: silver and gold I have none, Acts III, 6. of which the Pope is most greedy. Peter was not, like the Pope, adorned with gems, covered in gold, carried on a white horse, surrounded by soldiers, and hemmed in by clamoring ministers, as BERNARD says to Eugenius. Peter lived in marriage, Matt. VIII, 14. 1 Cor. IX, 5. But the Pope condemns the marriage of Clerics. Peter was pious, holy, chaste, honest. But how many Pontiffs have been impious, fornicators, and authors of slaughters and wars?

Prob. b. 1) That the Roman Pontiff is not the head of the catholic church is evident: because besides Christ, there is given no other, and that visible, head of the church. See above, question

XIX. 2) If the church, which is a mystical body, had two heads, namely Christ as the invisible head, and the Roman Pontiff as the visible head, the church would be a two-headed body, and therefore monstrous.

The Papists object: Not every body that is πολυκέφαλον (many-headed) is monstrous. For a man can have several heads, e.g. mystical, which is Christ; political, which is a King, Prince, or Magistrate; marital, if it be a woman: from which no monstrosity arises.

Resp. No man, and no body, can have several heads of the same order and respect without monstrosity. Thus, e.g., although a woman can have the three heads already mentioned, which are of different order and respect, yet in one and the same order she cannot have two heads, two marital heads; without ceasing to be a legitimate wife, and degenerating into a monstrous adulteress.

3) What no Apostle had or exercised, that the Roman Pope cannot arrogate to himself. But they never arrogated to themselves the primacy of the church, not even in title, much less did they usurp it in fact.

4) Whatever conflicts with the condition of the ecclesiastical ministry, that also the Roman Pontiff ought to judge to be foreign to himself: But primacy conflicts with the condition of the ecclesiastical ministry: Therefore. The minor is proved from Luke XXII, 25. and 1 Peter V, 3.

5) The true head of the church must be united to this mystical body and perpetually present to it, to bestow life, motion, and sense, to establish and protect the order of the spiritual members, to know their needs, to hear their prayers, and to provide for their difficulties. Such a true head of the church is Christ alone, not the Roman Pontiff. The Pope is not always is the unity of the church, but it can be taken away from it; indeed, the Roman see is often vacant of a Bishop: in which case the church would be bereft of a head, if he were a head in the true sense of the word.

6) After the times of the Apostles up to CONSTANTINE the Great, nothing is found in ecclesiastical history concerning a visible head of the church who was established as such and acknowledged by the church: in the first three centuries, when the church suffered severe persecutions, the Bishops acknowledged themselves as equals. From the time of CONSTANTINE the Great, however, when the state of the church was tranquil, the church was governed by Patriarchs, Metropolitans, and Bishops. Metropolitans presided over sacred matters in the metropolis of a province, and there were five: the Roman, Constantinopolitan, Alexandrian, Antiochene, and Hierosolymitan. The primacy of honor was granted to the Roman Bishop, on account of the eminence of the city of Rome, in which he held the bishopric: for Rome was the seat and mother of the Roman empire. But the primacy of power and jurisdiction does not belong to the Roman Bishop by right. We learn this from the 6th Canon of the Council of Nicaea, the words of which are: Let the ancient custom be preserved throughout Egypt, Libya, and Pentapolis, so that the Alexandrian bishop may have power over all these, because this is also customary for the Bishop of the city of Rome. Likewise in Antioch and the other provinces, let their privileges and dignities be preserved for the churches.

7) When ZOSIMUS, the Roman Pontiff, and his successors, BONIFACE I and CELESTINE, sought to affect dominion over the African churches, and under the pretext of a certain canon, which they feigned to be of the Council of Nicaea, claimed a certain right of appeal from the judgments of the Africans to the Roman see, the African Fathers resisted, and defended their rights and liberty so manfully that they openly rebuked the Pontiffs for their arrogance, and bitterly reproached them for having abused the authority of the Council of Nicaea to establish their dominion. Their letter to Pope CELESTINE is extant in ZONARAS and BALSAMON in the commentary on the canons of the councils.

8) From that time, however, the Roman Bishops did not cease to affect supreme power over the universal church, but other Bishops resisted them strongly, especially the Constantinopolitan. Finally, in the time of the Emperor PHOCAS, a most wicked man, BONIFACE III, the Roman Bishop, requested from the Emperor PHOCAS that the primacy of power over the universal church be confirmed to him, which happened at the beginning of the 7th century. BONIFACE III acted deceitfully in this matter, for it was known to him that PHOCAS had been sharply rebuked by the Bishop of Constantinople for the slaughter of the Emperor MAURITIUS, and that PHOCAS was hostile to him on that account. Therefore, BONIFACE approved the crime of PHOCAS and obtained the confirmation of the primacy. From these things it is clear that the Pope was constituted head and Monarch of the church not by Christ, but by a parricide.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, who contend most fiercely for the ecclesiastical principate of the Pope. Their arguments are: 1) The Roman Pontiff is the successor in the chair of Peter, who was constituted by Christ as the visible head of the church. Resp. 1) The Pope is the successor of Peter neither in the chair, nor in doctrine, nor in life and morals. 2)

2) The Apostle Peter neither had nor ever exercised an ecclesiastical principate. 2) From the times of CONSTANTINE the Great, the primacy has always been granted to the Roman Bishop: Therefore, the ecclesiastical principate cannot be derogated from him. Resp. The primacy was granted to the Roman Bishop not by divine right, but by ecclesiastical constitution. This is what the Canon Law inculcates, dist. 22, from the Council of Constantinople: It behooves the Bishop of the city of Constantinople to have the primacy of honor after the Roman bishop, for this reason, because it is new Rome. Therefore not by divine law, but by ecclesiastical constitution did the Roman Bishop obtain the primacy, and indeed not a primacy of monarchy, power, or jurisdiction, but merely of honor and of the see. For if the second place is attributed to the Bishop of Constantinople on account of new Rome, i.e., on account of the Roman empire transferred to Constantinople, it follows that the first place of honor was given to the Roman Bishop because old Rome is there, that is, the old seat of the empire. Whence also in the Second Council of Constantinople, can. 3, it was established that the Bishop of Constantinople should have equal privileges and an equal degree of dignity with the Roman.

3) By the same reason that the church of the Old Testament was governed, the church of the New Testament must be governed: But that was governed by one high priest, as a visible head: Therefore, this also must be so governed. Resp. I deny the major. For what kind of consequence is this: The Israelite synagogue, defined by narrow boundaries, was governed by one visible head. Therefore, the catholic church, diffused through the whole world, must likewise be governed by one visible head? Just as if you were to conclude: The village magistrate (I speak with DANN HAUER) can be sufficient for governing the whole village: therefore also for the whole city, therefore for the whole kingdom. Certainly, the Jewish people, as one people, could be ruled more conveniently and easily by one ruler than the catholic church, propagated far and wide through the whole world and all peoples. Moreover, the Pontiff of the O.T. did not have monarchical power, although he was the inspector of the other priests and the director of ecclesiastical affairs: nor was he a type of the Roman Pontiff, but of Christ alone, although the latter is far greater than the former, admitting no successor.

Latin:

Quaest. XXI. Estne Pontifex Romanus successor Petri, & caput visibile atque Monarcha catholicae ecclesiae?

Pontifex Romanus neque est successor Petri in Episcopatu , neque ecclesiae catholicae caput, aut Monarcha . Prob. a. Petrum Romae fuisse, e sacris litteris evidenter ostendi nequit. Nam a) Paullus ad Romanos scribens, atque sibi notos salutans, c. XVI. nullam plane iniicit mentionem Petri: quem sane haud praeteriisset, si Romae fuisset. b) Paullus Romam iam adveniens, & a fratribus honorifice exceptus, atque Romae in suo conducto biennium vivens, ne ullo quidem apice testatur, Petrum Romae sibi visum esse, Act. XXVIII, v. 14. 15. c) Scripsit Paullus ex carcere Romano epistolas quasdam, scilicet ad Colossenses, ad Philemonem & posteriorem ad Timotheum. At in nulla istarum epistolarum mentionem facit Petri; quinimmo 2 Tim. IV, 16. diserte scribit: In prima defensione nemo mihi adfuit, sed omnes me dereliquerunt. Petrus haud dubie adstitisset Paullo, neque eum deseruisset, si id temporis fuisset Romae.

2) Quamvis non penitus negemus, Petrum Romae fuisse & docuisse, cum id testentur Patres, IRENÆVS, EVSEBIVS, ATHANASIVS, TERTVLLIANVS, LEO M., CYPRIANVS, AVGVSTINVS, LACTANTIVS, quos citatos vide in hist. eccles. D. HORNEI. p. 32. seqq. infitiantur tamen, Apostolum Petrum proprium fuisse urbis Romanae Episcopum, & in illa urbe sedem papalem erexisse. Nam a) S. Petrus se quidem nominat Apostolum Iesu Christi, 1 ep. I, 1. & comprebyterum, c. V, 1. nusquam autem Episcopum ecclesiae Romanae. Differt autem Apostolus ab Episcopo, vt docet CHRYSOSTOMVS in Matth. Homil. 19. Nam Apostoli erant omnium gentium doctores, & curam omnium ecclesiarum, quas plantarunt, gerebant: At Episcopi certis affixi sunt locis, & curam peculiariter gerunt ecclesiarum particularium. Vnde Episcopo Romano tantum cura ecclesiarum suburbicarum ab oecumenico concilio Nicaeno assignata est. Apostolus Petrus immediate vocatus est a Christo. Pontifex Romanus immediate vocatione destituitur. Petrus Alexandriae & Antiochiae episcopos ordinavit: id quod Pontifici Romano non permittitur. b) Si Petrus fuit Episcopus Romae, multo magis Paullus Episcopus Romanus fuit.

Paullus namque fuit Apostolus gentium, adeoque etiam Episcopus urbis gentilis Romae. Petrus vero fuit Apostolus circumcisionis, Gal. II, 7. Paullus epistola praestantissima Romanos docuit: Petrus scripsit epistolas suas dispersis fratribus (Iudaeis) in Ponto, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia & Bithynia. Ecquis igitur credat, S. Petrum Romae erexisse cathedram docendi, in qua ipsi Episcopus Romanus succedat? Fac, Petrum Romae cathedram habuisse; illam tamen Pontifex Rom. nunquam ascendit. Nam Petrus fuit praeco euangelii: Pontifex Rom. docendi officium in aliorum humeros reiicit. Ergo pontifex Rom. non est successor Petri in cathedra docendi.

3) Pontifex Romanus non est successor Petri in doctrina. Petrus namque S. scripturam propter perspicuitatem commendat, & ad ipsius lectionem adhortatur, 2 Petr. I, 19. Papa scripturam obscuritatis accusat, & laicos ab ipsius lectione arcet. Petrus fiduciam salutis in vno & solo Christo collocat, Act. IV, 12. Papa docet, salutem quaerendam esse non in solo Christi merito, sed etiam in meritis sanctorum, in meritis ac satisfactionibus propriis, in votis monasticis, in papalibus indulgentiis. Petrus docet, remissionem peccatorum accipi fide in Christum, Actor. X, 43. Papa docet, peccata post baptismum commissa redimi operibus bonis, nec sola obtineri fide, sed & satisfactionibus propriis. Petrus docet, solum Christum esse ecclesiae fundamentum & lapidem angularem, 1 ep. II, 6. & vniuersalem Episcopum v. 25. Papa seipsum vocat fundamentum ecclesiae, & vniuersalem Episcopum. Petrus docet, Christum semel moriendo oblationem pro peccatis huius mundi perfecisse, 1 ep. III, 18. Papa docet, quod Christus quotidie in sacrificio missae non cruento pro peccatis nostris immoletur. Petrus docet, vocationem & electionem nostram posse fieri firmam, 2 ep. I, 10. Papa docet, de gratia Dei ac peccatorum remissione, adeoque etiam de electione esse dubitandum. Petrus obedientiam postulat erga magistratus, 1 ep. II, 13. Papa Clericos suos ab obedientia magistratus eximit iuxta, atque docet, Christianos non posse tolerare magistratum infidelem, vel haereticum.

4) Pontifex Rom. non est successor Petri in vita & moribus. Petrus dicit: aurum & argentum non habeo, Act. III, 6. cuius Papa est cupidissimus. Petrus non perinde, ac Papa fuit gemmis ornatus, auro tectus, vectus equo albo, stipatus milite, circumstrepentibus septus ministris, dicente BERNHARDO ad Eugenium. Petrus vixit in coniugio, Matth. VIII, 14. 1 Cor. IX, 5. Papa vero damnat coniugium Clericorum. Petrus fuit pius, sanctus, castus, honestus. At quot Pontifices fuere impii, scortatores, caedium & bellorum auctores?

Prob. b. 1) Pontificem Romanum non esse caput ecclesiae catholicae patet: quia praeter Christum, non datur aliud, idque visibile, ecclesiae caput. Vid. supra quaestio

XIX. 2) Si ecclesia, quae est corpus mysticum, haberet duo capita, videlicet Christum tanquam caput inuisibile, & Pontificem Rom. tanquam caput visibile, ecclesia foret corpus biceps, adeoque monstruosum.

Excipiunt Pontificii: Non omne corpus πολυκέφαλον esse monstruosum. Nam homo potest habere plura capita, v. g. mysticum, quod est Christus; politicum, quod est Rex, Princeps vel Magistratus; maritale, si sit foemina: vnde nulla monstruositas exsurgit.

Resp. Nullus homo, nullumque corpus potest habere plura capita eiusdem ordinis & respectus sine monstruositate. Sic v. g. quamuis foemina possit habere tria iam commemorata capita, quae sunt diuersi ordinis & respectus, in vno tamen eodemque ordine non potest habere duo capita, duo capita maritalia; quin desinat esse legitima vxor, & degeneret in adulteram monstruosam.

3) Quod nemo Apostolorum habuit vel exercuit, id Papa Rom. sibi arrogare nequit. At principatum ecclesiae sibi nunquam, ne titulotenus quidem, arrogarunt, multo minus facto vsurparunt

4) Quidquid pugnat cum conditione ministerii ecclesiastici, illud quoque Pontifex Romanus a se alienum iudicare debet: Atqui principatus pugnat cum conditione ministerii ecclesiastici: Ergo. Minor probatur ex Luc. XXII, 25. & 1 Petr. V, 3.

5) Verum caput ecclesiae, huic tanquam corpori mystico oportet esse vnitum perpetuoque praesens, vitam, motum sensumque largiri, membrorum spiritualium ordinem sancire & tueri, eorum necessitates cognoscere, preces exaudire, difficultatibus consulere. Eiusmodi verum ecclesiae caput est solus Christus, non Pontifex Romanus. Papa non semper per est ecclesiae vnitus, sed ab ea potest auferri; quinimmo saepe sedes Romana vacat Episcopo: quo quidem casu ecclesia orbata capite foret, si is veri nominis caput esset.

6) Post tempora Apostolorum vsque ad CONSTANTINVM M. in hist. ecclesiastica nihil reperitur de visibili capite ecclesiae, quod tale fuerit constitutum & ab ecclesia agnitum: prioribus tribus saeculis, vbi ecclesia graues perpessa est persecutiones, Episcopi se pro aequalibus agnouerunt. A tempore autem CONSTANTINI M. vbi tranquillus ecclesiae status fuit, ecclesia gubernata est per Patriarchas, Metropolitanos & Episcopos. Metropolitani sacris praeerant in prouinciae metropoli, & erant quinque: Romanus, Constantinopolitanus, Alexandrinus, Antiochenes & Hierosolymitanus. Primatus honoris concessus est Episcopo Romano, ob eminentiam vrbis Romae, in qua episcopatum gerebat: Roma quippe imperii Romani sedes & mater erat. At primatus potestatis ac iurisdictionis Episcopo Romano de iure non conuenit. Discimus hoc ex concilii Nicani Can. VI. cuius verba sunt: Antiqua consuetudo seruetur per Aegyptum, Libyam & Pentapolin, ita vt Alexandrinus episcopus horum omnium habeat potestatem, quia & vrbis Romae Episcopo hoc consuetum est. Similiter in Antiochia & cateris prouinciis sua priuilegia & dignitates ecclesiis seruentur.

7) Cum ZOSIMVS, Pontifex Romanus, eiusque successores, BONIFACIVS I. & COELESTINVS dominatum in ecclesias Africanas affectarent, & sub praetextu cuiusdam canonis, quem concilii Nicaeni esse fingebant, ius quoddam de appellando ab Africanorum iudiciis ad sedem Romanam praetenderent, Patres Africani repugnabant, fuaque iura & libertatem ita mascule defendebant, vt Pontifices ob fastum ipsorum palam increparent, & quod ad stabiliendum dominatum suum auctoritate concilii Nicaeni abusi essent, acerbe exprobrarent. Epistola illorum ad COELESTINVM Papam extat apud ZONARAM & BALSAMONEM in commentario in canones conciliorum.

8) Ab eo tempore autem Episcopi Romani non destiterunt affectare supremam potestatem in vniuersam ecclesiam, sed alii Episcopi fortiter restiterunt, maxime vero Constantinopolitanus. Tandem tempore Imperatoris PHOCAE, hominis sceleratissimi, BONIFACIVS III. Episcopus Rom. a PHOCA Imperatore petiit, sibi confirmari primatum potestatis in vniuersam ecclesiam, quod contigit sub initium saeculi VII. Subdole autem hac in re egit BONIFACIVS III. cui notum erat, PHOCAM ob caedem MAVRITII Imperatoris acriter fuisse correptum ab Episcopo Constantinopolitano, & huic PHOCAM eo nomine esse infensum. Quare BONIFACIVS facinus PHOCAE approbauit, primatusque confirmationem obtinuit. Ex his patet, quod Papa non a Christo, sed a parricida caput & Monarcha ecclesiae sit constitutus.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, pro principatu ecclesiastico Papae acerrime dimicantium. Quorum argumenta sunt: 1) Pontifex Romanus est successor in cathedra Petri, qui a Christo constitutus est visibile ecclesiae caput. Refp. 1) Papa neque in cathedra, neque in doctrina, neque in vita & moribus est successor Petri.

2) Apostolus Petrus principatum ecclesiasticum nec habuit, nec exercuit vnquam. 2) A temporibus CONSTANTINI M. Episcopo Romano semper primatus concessus est: Ergo non potest illi principatus ecclesiasticus derogari. Refp. Non iure diuino, sed ecclesiastica constitutione Episcopo Romano primatus concessus est. Id quod inculcat Ius canonicum dist. 22. ex concilio Constantinopolitano: Constantinopolitanae ciuitatis Episcopum oportet habere primatus honorem post Romanum episcopum, propterea, quod est noua Roma. Ergo non ex iure diuino, sed ex constitutione ecclesiastica Episcopus Romanus primatum obtinuit, & quidem non primatum monarchiæ, potestatis, aut iurisdictionis, sed duntaxat honoris, ac sedis. Quod si enim Episcopo Constantinopol. secundus tribuitur locus propter nouam Romam, h. e. propter imperium Romanum Constantinopolim delatum, sequitur, Romano Episcopo primum honoris locum esse datum, quia ibi est vetus Roma, hoc est vetus imperii sedes. Vnde etiam in concilio Constantinopolitano II. can. 3. constitutum est, vt Episcopus Constantinopolitanus æqualia priuilegia, & parem dignitatis gradum cum Romano habeat.

3) Qua ratione gubernata est ecclesia veteris testam. eadem gubernanda est ecclesia novi testamenti: Atqui illa gubernata est ab vno sacerdote summo, tanquam visibili capite: E. & hæc ita gubernanda est. Resp. Neg. maior. Quæ enim consequentia est: Synagoga Israëlitica, angustis pomœriis definita, gubernata est ab vno visibili capite. E. catholica ecclesia per totum orbem diffusa, itidem ab vno visibili capite gubernanda est? Perinde, ac si colligas: Scultetus pagi (cum DANN HAVERO loquor) potest toti pagi regendo par esse: ergo etiam toti ciuitati, ergo toti regno. Sane populus Iudaicus, tanquam populus vnus, ab vno rectore commodius & facilius regi potuit, quam ecclesia catholica per totum orbem, omnesque populos longe lateque propagata. Ceterum Pontifex V. T. monarchicam potestatem non habuit, licet ceterorum sacerdotum fuerit inspector, & negotiorum ecclesiasticorum director: neque fuit typus Pontificis Romani, sed solius Christi, quamuis hic illo sit longe maior, nullum admittens successorem.


### Quaest. XXII. What is the internal form, by which a gathering of men is constituted in the being of the church properly so called?

The internal and essential form of the church consists in the spiritual union of a) truly believing and holy persons, who are bound together as members of the church with Christ the head through true and living faith b), which is followed by the communion of mutual charity c).

Obs. I. D. HULSEM. in breviary c. XVII. §. 13. p. 124. expresses the essential form of the church thus: The internal form of the church is the communion of all the faithful, concerning the justifying and sanctifying grace of Christ through the same means, the communion of the same faith and profession concerning both those graces of Christ, and finally the communion of mutual charity. And for these reasons especially the church is called one, holy, catholic.

Obs. II. By union here is not understood an external and local conjunction of bodies, but an internal and spiritual conjunction of souls. For although the faithful also have local sacred assemblies; those, however, are not of the essence of the church (*).

…Prob. a. The church is a being by aggregation with order, where one, placed in the supreme position, rules the others who are inferior, and, as a head, gives life to the rest of the body and governs. Therefore it is necessary that this body be joined to its head with a firm bond.

Prob. b. Through faith, Christ is united with His mystical body and its members. For converted and reborn men receive Christ, John 1:12, put Him on, Galatians 3:27, and adhere to Him and are as it were glued to Him so closely that they are one spirit with Him, 1 Corinthians 6:17. However, it is understood in the present case not as general or historical faith, but as special and saving faith, which, besides knowledge and assent on the part of the intellect, also includes trust on the part of the will; or an act of such a kind by which the will acquiesces in Christ the mediator, as a present good and our own, and the cause of another good, namely the remission of sins and the attainment of eternal life.

Prob. c. Just as faith is by nature prior to charity, so it is necessary that the members of the church first have union in their head, Christ, through faith, and constitute one body of the church; then, however, they embrace one another with mutual love. But just as charity necessarily follows faith, so it is altogether required that the living members of the church pursue one another with mutual love. Therefore, mutual love is the character of a living member of the church. By this shall all men know that you are my disciples, if you have love one to another, says Christ, John 13:35.

Latin:

Forma ecclesiæ interna & essentialis consistit in vnione spirituali a) vere credentium & sanctorum, qui cum Christo capite per fidem veram ac viuam b), quam consequitur communio mutuæ caritatis, vt membra ecclesiæ, inter se devinciuntur c).

Obs. I. D. HVLSEM. in breuiar. c. XVII. §. 13. p. 124. formam ecclesiæ essentialem ita exprimit: Forma interna ecclesiæ est communio omnium fidelium, de gratia Christi iustificante & sanctificante per eadem media, communio eiusdem fidei & professionis circa vtramque illam Christi gratiam, & denique communio mutuæ caritatis. Atque his præcipue de caussis dicitur ecclesia vna, sancta, catholica.

Obs. II. Per vnionem hic non intelligitur externa & localis corporum, sed interna ac spiritualis animorum coniunctio. Quamquam enim fideles etiam locales congressus sacros habeant; illi tamen non sunt de essentia ecclesiæ (*).

Prob. a. Ecclesia est ens per aggregationem cum ordine, vbi vnus supremo loco constitutus, alios inferiores regit, &, tanquam caput, reliquum corpus vegetat & gu& gubernat. Proinde necesse est, vt corpus hoc cum capite suo firmo vinculo coniunctum fit.

Prob. b. Per fidem Christus caput cum corpore suo mystico, & ipsius membris vnitur. Nam homines conuersi & renati Christum recipiunt, Io. I, 12. induunt, Gal. III, 27. & ipsi tam arcte adhærent & quasi agglutinantur, vt sint cum ipso vnus spiritus, 1 Cor. VI, 17. Intelligitur autem in præsenti non fides generalis; aut historica; sed specialis & saluifica, quæ præter notitiam & assensum ex parte intellectus, includit etiam ex parte voluntatis fiduciam; seu actum eiusmodi, quo voluntas acquiescit in Christo mediatore, tamquam bono præsente atque nostro, & caussa alterius boni, nempe remissionis peccatorum, & vitæ æternæ consequendæ.

Prob. c. Sicut fides natura prior est caritate: ita necesse est, vt membra ecclesiæ prius in capite suo Christo habeant vnionem per fidem, & vnum corpus ecclesiæ constituant; deinde autem mutuo amore se inuicem complectantur. Sicut autem caritas necessario sequitur fidem: ita omnino requiritur, vt viua ecclesiæ membra se mutuo amore prosequantur. Est itaque amor mutuus character viui ecclesiæ membri. In hoc cognoscent omnes, quod mei discipuli sitis, si dilectionem habeatis inuicem, ait Christus, Io. XIII, 35.


### Question XXIII. What is the end of the church?

The proximate end of the church is edification, both of the whole body and of the individual members a). The ultimate end, on the part of the church, is eternal salvation b), on the part of God, the praise of His glorious divine grace c).

Prob. a. The most merciful God gathers and preserves the church to the end that its members may mutually edify one another by teaching, exhorting, correcting, and consoling. For He gave pastors and teachers for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ, Ephesians 4:12. Wherefore it is right that one Christian should exhort another with words and edify him by example, 1 Thessalonians 5:11.

Prob. b. Christ loved the church and gave Himself for it, that He might sanctify it and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word, that He might present it to Himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish. The church will be absolutely holy, blameless, and devoid of wrinkle and spot in the future state of glory, where it will be splendid not only internally but also externally, Ephesians 5:27.

Prob. c. Just as God finally chose those believing in Christ so that the glory of His grace might be praised, Ephesians 1:5, 6, so He has called together and preserves the church, or the assembly of believers, so that His most glorious grace may be celebrated in all places.

Latin:

Finis ecclesiæ proximus est ædificatio, cum corporis totius, tum singulorum membrorum a). Finis vltimus, ex parte ecclesiæ, est æterna salus b), ex parte Dei, laus gloriosæ gratiæ diuinæ c).

Prob. a. Deus misericordissimus eo fine ecclesiam colligit & conseruat, vt membra illius se mutuo ædificent docendo, exhortando, corrigendo, consolando. Dedit quippe pastores & doctores in instaurationem sanctorum, in opus ministerii, in ædificationem corporis Christi, Eph. IV, 12. Quare par est, vt vnus Christianus alterum hortetur verbis & ædificet exemplo, 1 Thess. V, 11.

Prob. b. Christus dilexit ecclesiam & seipsum tradidit pro illa, vt sanctificaret illam, & mundaret lauacro aquæ in verbo, ita vt sisteret eam sibi ipsi splendidam ecclesiam, non habentem maculam, aut rugam, aut quidquam talium; sed vt sit sancta & irreprehensibilis. Absolute sancta, irreprehensibilis & expers rugæ atque maculæ ecclesia erit in futuro statu gloriæ, vbi non tantum interne, sed etiam externe splendida erit, Eph. V, 27.

Prob. c. Sicut Deus finaliter in Christum credentes elegit, vt laudetur gloria gratiæ suæ, Eph. I, 5. 6. ita ecclesiam, siue cœtum credentium conuocauit & conseruat, vt gloriosissima gratia ipsius passim locorum celebretur.


### Question XXIV. What are the affections, or attributes, of the church properly so called?

The attributes of the church, properly so called, are commonly established as four: Unity a), holiness b), catholicity c), apostolicity d).

Prob. a. The church is one, partly absolutely and in itself, partly exclusively, or in opposition to many assemblies of the same species. For it must be noted here that "one" is taken in two ways. One 1) is the same as undivided: 2) is the same as unique. In both ways the church can be called one. For 1) the church is undivided; because all the members of the church are united in Christ, as the head, through faith in Christ, which is joined with the love not only of God, but also of the neighbor, by an indivisible bond. Moreover, brotherly and reciprocal love is understood, in such a way indeed, that union through charity in the first act, or Φιλαδελφία, may have a place among all Christians, as being altogether necessary. But as regards the second act of love, it is not always joined to faith, nor is it absolutely necessary that the members of the church should always mutually exhibit works of charity to one another. For the exercise of charity can be hindered by excessive distance of places, ignorance, or infirmity. 2) The church is also one: a) because it does not recognize several assemblies of the same species existing at the same time; since the catholic church is the assembly of all believers, united to Christ the head through faith. If, therefore, the church includes all believers, certainly no other church, or other assembly of believers, coexists with it, otherwise the universal church would not be an assembly including all believers. b) The catholic church is also one; because it does not recognize a succeeding church; since it never entirely perished, it will never entirely perish; but from its very beginning, through a perpetual succession of believers, it has lasted until these times, and will always last, until the consummation of the age.

Proof b. The church is holy: 1) on account of its most holy head, which is Christ. For such a High Priest it was fitting for us to have, holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, Hebr. VII, 27, who makes the church a participant in his holiness. For their sake I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified, John XVII, 19. 2) With respect to the members, who are holy: a) By imputed holiness, placed in the remission of sins and the righteousness of Christ, derived to the members of the church on account of the merit of Christ apprehended by faith; b) By inherent holiness, which consists in charity and the remaining Christian virtues. Which inherent holiness is indeed imperfect in this life: It is sufficient, however, that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh, but according to the spirit, Rom. VIII, 1. 3) The church is called holy on account of the word and sacraments, through which means it is sanctified by the divine Spirit, as well as on account of the holy worship to which it is devoted.

Proof c. The church is called catholic: which word is found in the Apostolic creed, but is not θεόπνευστος. Now καθολικόν signifies the same as καθ' ὅλον, according to the whole, or universal, and the church is called catholic, either by reason of quality, or by reason of quantity. By reason of quality; on account of doctrine and faith, insofar as it professes that faith which the universality of believers has always professed: by reason of quantity; on account of its diffusion throughout the whole world; insofar as it is not gathered, as was the church of the Old Testament, from one peculiar people or nation, but from all nations in the whole world. Other authors, intending to explain this notable distinction more clearly, distinguish between internal catholicism, which is of faith or doctrine, and external, which is of place, time, and persons. Indeed, that doctrine and faith is called catholic which is required of all those who are to be saved. Confer D. SCHERZERI system. pag. 708. Others observe that the church is sometimes called καθολική as it is opposed to heresy, i.e., to heterodox churches: sometimes it is said to be καθολική in respect and opposition to particular churches. In the former way, when the church is called καθολική, it is not the same as universal; but it is the same as the true and orthodox church, and it is so named from catholic doctrine, i.e., the orthodox doctrine of Christ and the Apostles, which, when heresies were spreading here and there in the church, was called catholic, insofar as it proceeded from Christ and the Apostles, was commended to all the faithful, and was received and believed by their unanimous consent. In this sense, even a particular church embracing catholic, or orthodox, doctrine is called catholic. Thus the Emperor CONSTANTIUS calls the Alexandrian church catholic, in SOCRATES Book II, c. 18. SOZOMEN calls Callinicus the Bishop of the catholic church which is in Pelusium, Book II, c. 24. In the latter way, when the church is called καθολική, namely in order to particular churches, it is the same as the universal church, and in this way it is not sufficient for the catholic church that it embraces the doctrine of Christ and the Apostles, because A particular church also receives this, but it is required furthermore for the catholic church that it include all believers of all places and times within its scope. Conf. D. HULSEM. manuale in A. C. p. 258. & D. BECHMANNI instit. theol. p. 575. Others note that the catholicism of the church is to be estimated primarily and in itself from the consensus with the doctrine of the Prophets and Apostles, and also from that conspiracy of faith which God uniformly works in all who adhere to the church: secondarily from the amplitude of places and diffusion through all peoples. Conf. D. IO. ADAMI OSIANDRI colleg. system. P. VII. p. 30. For by reason of actual diffusion through all places and peoples, not even the apostolic and primitive church was catholic, although it was to be diffused through all peoples, and thus prepared to receive all into its bosom, without distinction of nation, sex, or status.

Moreover, the catholicism of places, persons, and times is a property of the church of the New Testament, and indeed of the whole, through which it differs from the church of the Old Testament, which was restricted to the Jewish people, and from any particular congregations whatsoever.

Proof. The church is called Apostolic, partly because it was planted by the Apostles, partly because it has embraced the doctrine of salvation handed down by the Apostles and has been built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, indeed, with Jesus Christ being the cornerstone, Eph. II, 20.

Latin:

Attributa ecclesiæ, proprie dictæ, vulgo constituuntur quatuor: Vnitas a), sanctitas b), catholicismus c) apostolicismus d).

Prob. a. Vna est ecclesia, partim absolute & in se, partim exclusiue, siue in oppositione ad plures eiusdem speciei cœtus. Notandum enim hic est, quod vnum dupliciter accipiatur. Vnum 1) idem est, ac indiuisum: 2) idem est, ac vnicum. Vtroque modo ecclesia vna dici potest. Etenim 1) ecclesia est indiuisa; propterea, quod omnia membra ecclesiæ in Christo, tamquam capite, vniuntur per fidem in Christum, quæ cum dilectione non solum Dei, sed & proximi, nexu indiuiduo coniuncta est. Intelligitur autem dilectio fraterna & reciproca, ita quidem, vt vnio per caritatem in actu prima, seu, Φιλαδελφία, inter omnes Christianos locum habeat, tanquam omnino necessaria. Quod autem actum secundum dilectionis attinet, is non semper coniunctus est fidei, nec absolute necesse est, vt ecclesiæ membra sibi semper caritatis opera mutuo exhibeant. Exercitium quippe caritatis per nimiam locorum distantiam, ignorantiam, aut infirmitatem impediri potest. 2) Ecclesia etiam est vnica: a) quia non agnoscit plures eiusdem speciei cœtus simul existentes; siquidem ecclesia catholica est cœtus omnium credentium, Christo capiti per fidem vnitorum. Si ergo ecclesia, omnes includit credentes, vtique ei non coëxistit alia ecclesia, seu alius cœtus credentium, alias ecclesia vniuersalis non foret cœtus, omnes credentes includens. b) Vna etiam est ecclesia catholica; quia non agnoscit ecclesiam succedentem; siquidem nunquam tota periit, nunquam tota peribit; sed a primo sui initio, perpetua credentium successione, vsque ad hæc tempora durauit, semperque durabit, vsque ad consummationem sæculi.

Prob. b. Sancta est ecclesia: 1) propter caput sanctissimum, quod est Christus. Talis ettim debebat esse noster Pontifex, sanctus, innocens, impollutus, a peccatoribus segregatus, Hebr. VII, 27. qui sanctitatis suæ ecclesiam facit participem. Pro eis sanctifico me ipsum, vt sint & ipsi sanctificati, Io. XVII, 19. 2) Respectu membrorum, quæ sunt sancta: a) Sanctitate imputata, posita in remissione peccatorum & iustitia Christi, ob meritum Christi fide apprehensum, in membra ecclesiæ deriuata; b) Sanctitate inhærente, quæ in caritate & reliquis virtutibus christianis consistit. Quæ quidem inhærens sanctitas imperfecta est in hac vita: Sufficit autem, quod nulla condemnatio fit iis, qui sunt in Christo Iesu, qui non secundum carnem ambulant, sed secundam spiritum, Rom. VIII, 1. 3) Sancta dicitur ecclesia ob verbum & sacramenta, per quæ media a Spiritu diuino sanctificatur, iuxta, atque ob cultum sanctum, cui addicta est.

Prob. c. Ecclesia dicitur catholica: quæ vox habetur in symbolo Apostolico, sed non est θεόπνευστος. Valet autem καθολικὸν idem, quod καθ' ὅλον, secundum totum, vel vniuersum, & dicitur ecclesia catholica, vel ratione qualitatis, vel ratione quantitatis.
