Therefore it is very useful & necessary to seek diligently the assembly in which God ordinarily dispenses the means of salvation, and exhibits his gracious presence, and thus to associate oneself with the mystical body of Christ, the citizens of the kingdom of heaven, the household of God, the sheep of Christ, the spiritual mother, both in mind and body.

2) Christ commands us to avoid false prophets, and to turn away from them, Wherefore let us be as separated from heretics as they are fugitives from the church: on the authority of Cyprian, L. I. ep. 5. ad Cornel.

You say: Salvation is given in a false church; therefore it is not necessary to seek the true church. Resp. In a false church, considered reduplicatively; that is, insofar as it is false and contaminated with errors, no salvation is given. In a false church, viewed specifically, insofar as the word of God is publicly read in it, and baptism is administered whole in its essentials, regeneration and salvation are given: but not without great danger to souls: for they can be so darkened by false dogmas that either the light of faith is not kindled, or, if kindled in baptism, it is overwhelmed and extinguished by errors: just as a robust man in a house infected with a pestilential plague can be kept safe, but not without present danger to his life.

Latin:

Inquisitio verae ecclesiae homini, aeternam salutem adepturo, perquam utilis, & aliqua ratione necessaria est.

Obs. Fatemur, non esse ἁπλῶς, ac praecise ad salutem necessarium, nosse, quanam, & vbi sit vera ecclesia visibilis. Docemus enim ipsimet contra Papistas, id ordinaria tantum, non absoluta necessitate esse necessarium, hominemque posse saluari, etiam si ignoret, modo ecclesiae invisibilis membrum existat. Fieri enim potest, vt beate quis moriatur, etiam adultus, qui nondum novit, quid sit ecclesia.

Prob. 1) Ecclesia est corpus Christi, regnum caelorum, civitas Dei, domus Dei, ovile Christi, mater nostra, & communio, cui bona spiritualia (verbum, sacramenta, regeneratio &c.) ordinarie credita sunt, & promissio gratiae praesentiae facta est, Unde extra ecclesiam visibilem non est salus: Et qui non habet in his terris ecclesiam matrem, non habet Deum in caelis patrem, centente Cypriano, lib. de unit. eccles. Ergo perquam utile & necessarium est, sedulo quaerere coetum, in quo Deus ordinarie salutis media dispensat, & gratiosam suam praesentiam exhibet, atque adeo corpori Christi mystico, civibus regni caelorum, domesticis Dei, ovibus Christi, matri spirituali, & animo, & corpore se associare.

2) Christus vitare iubet falsos prophetas, & ab iis deflectere, Quapropter tam simus ab haereticis separati, quam illi ab ecclesia profugi: auctore Cypriano, L. I. ep. 5. ad Cornel.

Dicis: Datur salus in ecclesia falsa; E. non necesse est, veram ecclesiam inquirere. Resp. In ecclesia falsa, reduplicative considerata; sive quatenus est falsa, & erroribus contaminata, nulla datur salus. In ecclesia falsa, specificative spectata, quatenus in eadem verbum Dei publice praelegitur, & baptismus in substantialibus integer administratur, datur regeneratio & salus: at non sine ingenti periculo animarum: quippe quae dogmatibus falsis sic obtenebrari possunt, ut vel non accendatur lux fidei, vel in baptismo accensa, erroribus obruatur & extinguatur: sicut vir robustus in aedibus, pestifera lue infectis, servari potest incolumis, at non sine praesenti vitae discrimine.


### Quaest. XXXVI. Is the Roman church true & catholic?

The Roman, or Pontifical, church is neither true a), nor catholic b). Obf.

By the Roman church is not understood only that which is in the city of Rome, but all particular churches, addicted to the Roman Pontiff, wherever they are contained in the world.

Prob. a. The true church has one head, Christ, it has one adequate principle of faith, namely, Holy Scripture, it imparts the word of God as a clear light to all for reading & meditation, it religiously worships God alone, it frankly confesses the defect of free will in spiritual matters, it recognizes that the exact fulfillment of the law with respect to the flesh, by which it is weakened, is impossible in this life, it seeks and finds righteousness and eternal life only in the universal satisfaction and merit of Christ, it asserts the certainty of faith, it indicates that marriage is honorable for all suitable persons, it administers the sacraments rightly according to the institution of Christ, it teaches that believers are finally saved and that the unfaithful are perseveringly condemned, and it does not recognize an intermediate state between the state of glory and eternal ignominy, But the Roman, or Pontifical, church has two heads, Christ and the Roman Pontiff; it adds to Holy Scripture the consensus of the Fathers, the traditions of the church, and the decrees of the Pontiffs as principles of faith; it forbids the reading of Holy Scripture to the unlearned people; it transfers the religious worship due to God alone to the dead saints; it builds righteousness and eternal life upon the merits of one's own works; it vainly boasts of the powers of free will in spiritual matters; it impudently contends that the full fulfillment of the law is possible in this mortality; it disapproves of the certainty of faith, but it defends doubt regarding divine grace; it affirms that marriage is unbecoming for clerics, and on that account prohibits it; it mutilates the Sacrament of the Supper, by taking away the blessed cup from the laity, and transforms it into a sacrificial mass; it introduces an intermediate state between the state of glory and eternal ignominy: Therefore, the Roman church is not a true, but a false, impure, and corrupt church. Prob. b. The Roman church is not catholic, whether you look at the internal catholicity of faith and doctrine; or consider the external catholicity of places, persons, and times.

For it neither professes the catholic doctrine of faith, which the Prophets and Apostles taught and propagated: which we have already proven; nor does it embrace within its scope all particular churches and all true believers, saints, and elect.

For the Papists cannot deny that spiritual children and heirs of eternal life are born to God outside the Roman church, namely in the Greek, Lutheran, and Reformed churches.

Since, therefore, the Roman church is neither orthodox nor universal, it is not truly catholic, but a particular, and that an impure and corrupt church.

The Antithesis is that of the Papists, who maintain that the Roman church is true and catholic.

Their stronger arguments are:

I. The faith of the Roman church is announced in the whole world, Rom.

1:8. Therefore, the Roman church is true and catholic.

Resp. 1) Distinguish between the ancient Roman church, such as it was in the time of Paul, namely pure and orthodox; and the modern one, which is impure and so deformed that the epistle of Paul seems to have been written not to the Romans, but against the modern Romans.

2) There is no force of consequence in the argument.

For the ancient Roman church was not catholic because its faith was announced in the whole world; but it was particular, just as the Jerusalem, Antiochian, etc., churches were.

Indeed, the same praise that is attributed to the Roman church is given to the Thessalonian church, 1 Thess.

1:8: "For from you the word of the Lord has sounded forth, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but also in every place your faith toward God has gone out."

Yet the Thessalonian church is not catholic.

II. The gates of hell shall not prevail against the church, as Christ testifies, Matt.

16:18. Therefore, the Roman church could not fall into errors.

The Roman Church could not fall into errors.

Resp. The gates of hell shall not prevail against the universal church, so that it might utterly fail: but many particular churches have failed, e.g., that of the Corinthians.

Of the Corinthians.

III. Lutherans, who accuse the Papal church of having fallen away from the truth of the doctrine of faith, cannot judge the time when it fell away; therefore, they unjustly accuse it of defection.

Resp. 1) Lutherans are not obligated to indicate to the Papists the time when their church fell away; for it is sufficient that false dogmas are found in it, which testify that the Roman church is impure.

A gardener discovers weeds in a garden, but no one demands of him that he indicate the time when they began to grow.

A physician indicates to a sick person that he is suffering from consumption, yet there is no need for him to indicate the time when the patient began to suffer from this disease.

2) The errors by which the modern Roman church is defiled did not begin at one and the same time: and therefore one time for them cannot be indicated.

At one time the opinion regarding habitual righteousness, by which we are righteous before God, prevailed: at another time the dogma concerning the celibacy of priests, at another the dogma concerning transubstantiation, at another the erroneous doctrine concerning communion under only one kind, etc.

IV. Many Lutherans today call the Roman church catholic; which is a clear indication that it is truly catholic.

Resp. 1) The Roman church, in a contradictory state, or in a state of due confession, when we contradict those who err, is not to be called catholic, by the argument of the passage, 2 Cor.

11:12. 2) Lutherans, placed outside the state of confession, the Roman church placed outside the state of confession, the church

2) Lutherans, placed outside the state of confession, [the] Roman church

They call the Roman [church] catholic in the same sense and liberty with which we call the Jews Jews, who nevertheless are the synagogue of Satan, Apoc. II, 9. *).

Ques. XXXVII. Is the Lutheran church true and catholic?

The Christian church, addicted to the Unaltered Augsburg Confession, is true a), and embraces catholic doctrine, b); but by reason of quantity or amplitude it is not catholic, or universal, but particular c).

Proof a. The church addicted to the Augsburg Confession, which is commonly called Lutheran from the ministry of LUTHER, is true (**): because it embraces and teaches the truth revealed in Holy Scripture, John XVII, 17. For the Lutheran church has one mystical head, Christ; nor does it admit any other word as a suitable norm of faith and morals than that which the Prophets and Apostles left behind; nor does it acknowledge any other foundation of salvation than Jesus Christ; nor does it use any other sacraments than those which Christ himself instituted, namely baptism and the Lord's supper; nor does it attribute its righteousness and salvation to any of its own qualities, dispositions, and works, but solely to divine grace and the merit of Christ; meanwhile, it fervently contends that good works, prescribed by God, must be diligently performed: Therefore the Lutheran church is a true church.

Proof b. Catholic doctrine is that which, having proceeded from Christ and the Apostles, has been commended to all the faithful always and everywhere, and has been received and believed by their unanimous consent: The church addicted to the Augsburg Confession receives, believes, and professes that catholic doctrine. Therefore, by reason of doctrine, it is truly catholic.

Proof c. By reason of quantity or amplitude, the Lutheran church is not catholic, or universal; for the reason that it does not encompass within its scope all the reborn and elect of all places and times. Hence the Lutheran church is indeed orthodox, but particular.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, who deny that the Lutheran church is true and catholic. Who object:

I. The Lutheran church is not diffused throughout the whole world: Therefore it is not catholic. Resp. The Lutheran church is called catholic not by reason of amplitude or diffusion throughout the whole world (for we confess that it is particular): but by reason of catholic doctrine; because it is orthodox.

II. Whatever church began only in the previous century, that is a new, and therefore not a true church (for truth is most ancient): But the church of the Lutherans &c. Therefore. Resp. 1) I deny the major. In a similar way, someone could have argued in the 2nd century after the birth of Christ: Whatever church began only in the previous century, namely the first, that is a new, and therefore not a true [church]. church; But the church of Christ, etc. Therefore. Which argumentation is inept. It must be known, therefore, that the novelty which is objected by dissidents does not stand in the way of the truth of doctrine and the church. For it is said concerning the doctrine of Christ in Mark 1:27: "What is this new doctrine?" Cf. Acts 17:19. 2) The Lutheran church (not indeed under this name, but by reason of its doctrine) existed long before the Papacy, since it agrees exactly with the apostolic doctrine and church, and thus is prior to the papacy.

III. In the church of the Lutherans there is no union, nor consensus; but there are various dissensions and sects in it: Therefore, it is not the true church. The reason for the consequence is: because the members of the true church are joined by the bond of charity. Resp. 1) In the Roman church there are no fewer dissensions given than in the Lutheran church. 2) Those who dissent in fundamental dogmas of faith from the Augsburg Confession and the remaining symbolic books have departed from the church addicted to the A.C. But those who dissent in questions extra-fundamental agree on the foundation, and thus do not tear down the truth of the church.

Latin:

Ecclesia Romana, sive Pontificia, neque vera a), neque catholica est b).

Obs. Per ecclesiam Romanam non ea tantum intelligitur, quae est in urbe Roma, sed omnes ecclesiae particulares, Pontifici Romano addictae, ubicunque locorum continentur.

Prob. a. Vera ecclesia unum habet caput Christum, unum habet principium fidei adaequatum, scil. S. scripturam, verbum Dei tanquam claram lucem, omnibus ad lectionem & meditationem impertitur, solum Deum religiose veneratur, defectum liberi arbitrii in rebus spiritualibus ingenue fatetur, exactam impletionem legis respectu carnis, qua infirmatur, impossibilem in hac vita esse agnoscit, iustitiam & vitam aeternam tantum in universali Christi satisfactione atque merito quaerit & invenit, fidem certitudinem asserit, coniugium omnibus personis idoneis decorum esse indicat, sacramenta secundum institutionem Christi rite administrat, finaliter credentes salvari, perseveranter infideles condemnari docet, neque statum intermedium inter statum gloriae & aeternae ignominiae agnoscit, At ecclesia Romana, sive Pontificia, duo habet capita. Christum & Pontificem Romanum; S. scripturae addit consensum Patrum, traditiones ecclesiae & decreta Pontificum, tanquam principia fidei; lectionem S. scripturae rudi populo interdicit; cultum religiosum soli Deo debitum in sanctos demortuos transfert; iustitiam & vitam aeternam propriorum operum meritis superstruit; vires liberi arbitrii in rebus spiritualibus vane iactat; plenam legis impletionem in hac mortalitate possibilem esse, impudententer contendit; fidei certitudinem improbat, dubitationem autem de gratia divina propugnat; coniugium clericis indecorum esse affirmat, eoque nomine prohibet; Sacramentum coenae mutilat, demto laicis calice benedicto, idque in sacrificium missaticum transmutat; statum intermedium, inter statum gloriae & aeternae ignominiae affert: E. ecclesia Romana non est vera, sed falsa, impura & corrupta ecclesia. b. Ecclesia Romana non est catholica, sive spectes catholicismum internum fidei & doctrinae; sive consideres catholicismum externum locorum, personarum & temporum.

Neque enim profitetur doctrinam fidei catholicam, quam Prophetae atque Apostoli docuerunt & propagarunt: id quod iam probatum dedimus: neque ambitu suo omnes ecclesias particulares omnesque vere credentes, sanctos & electos complectitur.

Neque enim negare possunt Pontificii, extra Romanam ecclesiam Deo nasci spirituales filios & haeredes vitae aeternae, videlicet in ecclesia Graeca, Lutherana & Reformata.

Cum itaque ecclesia Romana neque orthodoxa, neque universalis sit, non est vere catholica, sed particularis, eaque impura & corrupta ecclesia.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, statuentium, ecclesiam Romanam esse veram & catholicam.

Quorum argumenta potiora sunt:

I. Ecclesiae Romanae fides annuntiatur in toto mundo, Rom.

I. Ecclesiae Romanae fides annuntiatur in toto mundo, Rom. I, 8. E. ecclesia Romana est vera & catholica.

Resp. 1) Dist. inter ecclesiam Romanam antiquam, qualis erat tempore Paulli, scil. pura & orthodoxa; & hodiernam, quae est impura adeoque deformata, ut epistola Paulli non ad Romanos, sed contra Romanos hodiernos scripta videatur.

2) Nulla argumento inest vis consequentiae.

Neque enim ideo ecclesia antiqua Romana fuit catholica, quoniam eius fides in toto mundo est annuntiata; sed fuit particularis, qualis erat Hierosolymitana, Antiochena &c.

Quin Thessalonicensi ecclesiae eadem laus, quae Romanae tribuitur, 1 Thess.

I, 8. A vobis non solum personuit sermo Domini in Macedonia & Achaia, verum etiam in omnem locum fides vestra, quae est in Deum, exiit.

Neque tamen ecclesia Thessalonicensis est catholica.

II. Portae inferorum non praevalebunt adversus ecclesiam, teste Christo, Matth.

II. Portae inferorum non prauelebunt aduersus ecclesiam, teste Christo, Matth. XVI, 18. E.

Romana ecclesia non potuit in errores prolabi.

Resp. Adversus ecclesiam universalem non praevalebunt portae inferorum, ut penitus deficiat: ecclesia autem particulares multae defecerunt, v. gr.

Corinthiorum.

III. Lutherani, qui pontificiam ecclesiam accusant, quod a veritate doctrinae fidei defecerit: non possunt iudicare tempus, quando defecerit, E. iniuste eam arguunt defectionis.

Resp. 1) Lutherani non obligati sunt, vt Pontificiis tempus indicent, quo eorum ecclesia defecerit; sufficit enim, quod in ea falsa inveniantur dogmata, quae testantur, quod ecclesia Romana fit impura.

Hortulanus zizania in horto deprehendit, nemo autem ab eo postulat, vt tempus, quo nasci coeperint, indicet.

Medicus indicat aegroto, quod phthisi laboret, neque tamen opus est, vt indicet tempus, quo aegrotus morbo hoc laborare coeperit.

2) Errores, quibus foedata est hodierna ecclesia Romana, non uno & eodem tempore coeperunt: ideoque unum eorum tempus indicari nequit.

Alio tempore inualuit opinio de iustitia habituali, qua coram Deo iusti sumus: alio tempore dogma de coelibatu sacerdotum, alio dogma de transubstantiatione, alio doctrina erronea de communione sub una tantum specie &c.

IV. Multi Lutherani hodienum ecclesiam Romanam vocant catholicam; quod luculento indicio est, eam esse vere catholicam.

Resp. 1) Ecclesia Romana in contradictorio, sive in statu confessionis debitae, cum errantibus contradicimus, non est dicenda catholica, argumento loci, 2 Cor.

XI, 12.

2) Lutherani, extra statum confessionis positi, ecclesiam Romana statum confessionis positi, ecclefiam

Romanam vocant catholicam eodem sensu & libertate, qua Iudæos appellamus Iudæos, qui tamen sunt synagoga Satanæ, Apoc. II, 9. *).

Quæst. XXXVII. Estne ecclesia Lutherana vera & catholica?

Ecclesia christiana, Augustanæ confessioni non variatæ addicta, est vera a), & catholicam amplectitur doctrinam, b); at ratione quantitatis vel amplitudinis non est catholica, siue vniuersalis, sed particularis c).

Prob. a. Ecclesia Augustanæ confessioni addicta, quæ a ministerio LVTHERI communiter Lutherana appellatur, est vera (**): quia amplectitur & docet veritatem in sacra scriptura reuelatam, Io. XVII, 17. Etenim habet ecclesia Lutherana vnum caput mysticum, Christum; nec admittit aliud verbum, tanquam aptam fidei & morum normam, quam quod Prophetæ & Apostoli reliquerunt; nec aliud agnoscit salutis fundamentum, quam Iesum Christum; nec alia vsurpat sacramenta, quam quæ ipse Christus instituit, videlicet baptismum & cænam dominicam; nec vllis suis qualitatibus, dispositionibus ac operibus, sed soli gratiæ diuinæ & merito Christi iustitiam & salutem suam acceptam refert; operibus interim bonis, a Deo præscriptis, operam sedulo dandam esse, feruide contendit: Ergo Lutherana ecclesia est vera ecclesia.

Prob. b. Doctrina catholica est, quæ a Christo & Apostolis profecta, omnibus fidelibus semper & vbique commendata, atque vnanimi eorum consensu recepta & credita est: Ecclesia Augustanæ confessioni addicta, catholicam illam doctrinam recipit, credit & profitetur. E. ratione doctrinæ vere catholica est.

Prob. c. Ratione quantitatis, vel amplitudinis ecclesia Lutherana non est catholica, siue vniuersalis; propterea, quod non omnes renatos & electos omnium locorum & temporum ambitu suo complectitur. Proinde ecclesia Lutherana est orthodoxa quidem, sed particularis.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, negantium, ecclesiam Lutheranain esse veram & catholicam. Qui obiiciunt:

I. Ecclesia Lutherana non est diffusa per totum terrarum orbem: E. non est catholica. Resp. Ecclesia Lutherana dicitur catholica non ratione amplitudinis, aut diffufsionis per totum terrarum orbem (fatemur enim, eam esse particularem): sed ratione doctrinæ catholicæ; quia est orthodoxa.

II. Quæcunque ecclesia superiori demum sæculo cœpit, ea est noua, adeoque non vera ecclesia (veritas enim est antiquissima): Atqui ecclesia Lutheranorum &c. Ergo. Resp. 1) Neg. mai. Simili modo potuisset quisquam sec. II. a nato Christo argumentari: Quæ ecclesia cœpit demum sæculo superiori, nempe primo, ea est noua, adeoque non vera ecclesia; Atqui ecclesia Christi &c. Ergo. Quae argumentatio inepta est. Sciendum ergo, quod novitas, quae a dissidentibus obiicitur, veritati doctrinae & ecclesiae non obstet. Etenim de Christi doctrina dicitur Marc. I, 27. Quae est nova haec doctrina? Conf. Act. XVII, 19. 2) Ecclesia Lutherana (non quidem sub hoc nomine, sed ratione doctrinae) dudum fuit ante Papatum, cum exacte consentiat cum doctrina & ecclesia apostolica, adeoque papatu prior fit.

III. In ecclesia Lutheranorum non datur unio, nec consensio; sed sunt in ea variae dissensiones & sectae: E, non est vera ecclesia. Ratio consequentiae est; quia membra verae ecclesiae vinculo caritatis coniuncta sunt. Resp. 1) In ecclesia Romana non minores dantur dissensiones, quam in ecclesia Lutherana. 2) Qui in dogmatibus fidei fundamentalibus ab Augustana confessione & reliquis libris symbolicis dissentiunt, ex ecclesia A. C. addicta exierunt. Qui autem dissentiunt in quaestionibus extra fundamentalibus, conveniunt in fundamento, atque adeo veritatem ecclesiae non convellunt.


### Q. XXXVIII. Do particular churches taken together constitute one catholic church?

Particular and visible churches, which exist today in the east and west, do not constitute one catholic church.

Prob. If all assemblies of the called, throughout the whole orb of the earth, were to profess the catholic faith purely and incorruptly, and were joined among themselves by the bond of charity and peace, we would not hesitate to assert that they, taken together, constitute the catholic or universal church, by a synecdoche so called, within the ambit of which the entire multitude of believers is contained, and outside of which there is no salvation. But truly, after particular churches have been so distracted by schisms that they neither profess the same doctrine of faith nor pursue one another with mutual love, they do not constitute one catholic church.

Latin:

Ecclesiae particulares & visibiles, quae hodie in oriente & occidente existunt, non constituunt unam ecclesiam catholicam.

Prob. Si omnes vocatorum coetus, per universum terrarum orbem, catholicam fidem pure & incorrupte profiterentur, & caritatis ac pacis vinculo inter se essent coniuncti, asserere haud dubitaremus, eos simul sumtos constituere ecclesiam catholicam, seu universalem, per synecdochen sic dictam, cuius ambitu universa credentium multitudo contineatur, & extra quam nulla sit salus. At vero postquam ecclesiae particulares per schismata ita distractae sunt, ut neque eandem doctrinam fidei profiteantur, neque mutuo amore se prosequantur, non constituunt unam ecclesiam catholicam.


### Q. XXXIX. Is the church indefectible, so that it cannot err, and indefectible, so that it cannot be cut off?

The catholic and invisible church, which embraces all and singular the reborn and elect, cannot err in the foundation of faith, nor fail entirely, but will endure until the consummation of the age ). However, any particular and visible church can be so contaminated by fundamental errors that they prevail, and teachers professing false doctrine constitute the public ministry, with the paucity of true believers lying hidden under the multitude of those erring ).

Obf. 1) The sense of our assertion is: that the whole catholic church never errs in such a way that there do not remain some who, following the simple leading of the Word, are sanctified and preserved in truth and faith by the direction of the Holy Spirit, so that, having retained the foundation of salvation, they are guarded by the power of God through faith unto salvation, although they may sometimes be few, and in the most disturbed times of the church lie hidden, so that the assembly of true believers is not illustrious and distinctly conspicuous: But that every particular and visible church can err in faith and has in fact sometimes erred, if it departs from the rule of the heavenly Word, from which danger of erring we do not except even the Roman church, from which alone they strive so greatly to remove it, as the blessed Dr. GERHARD says, in the locus on the church,

§. 107. Obs. 2) The church is called indefectible with a conditional ) indefectibility, because it adheres to its head, Christ, from whom nothing, except sin, can separate it ) except sin, can separate it (this indefectibility

common to the invisible church with the visible): b) catholic, regarding the whole (τὸ σύνολον), individual believers can fall away, but not the universal church, which indefectibility is proper to the invisible church: c) final, regarding the church of the elect.

Prob. a. 1) The gates of hell shall not prevail against the catholic church, Matt. XVI, 18. Therefore, the catholic church is indefectible from heavenly truth, and inexpugnable. For indeed πύλαι, gates, signify the place of councils and judgments, where the force and power of a city was situated. Wherefore the gates of hell are nothing other than the counsels, machinations, power, force, and strength of the devil and tyrants.

2) The spiritual kingdom of Christ (the church) is perennial in these lands, Luke I, 33. From which also Christ promised his gracious presence to the true members of this spiritual kingdom even unto the consummation of the age, Matt. XXVIII, 20. Therefore, the church of Christ is to endure until the end of the world.

3) The church is the house of God, the pillar and repository of truth, 1 Tim. III, 15. Therefore, it will stand inexpugnable as long as heavenly truth, or the word of God, which abides forever, shall remain, 1

Pet. I, 25. 4) The word of God shall always be preached, Isa. LIX, 21. Jer. XXX, 23. (though not always purely) and the guests of the eucharist shall announce the death of the Lord, until he comes (to judgment) 1 Cor. XI, 26. Therefore, there shall always be the reborn and the elect. For wherever the word of the Lord is preached, it always bears fruit in some, Isa. LV, 10. Matt. III, 24.

Prob. b. 1) From the Pauline warning, Rom. IX, 20, 21, 22. Do not think highly, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, lest perhaps he also not spare you. See therefore the kindness and severity of God: severity indeed in those who fell; but kindness in you, if you remain in kindness: otherwise you also shall be cut off. Whence an inexpugnable argument: That church which a) ought to beware of a fall; to which b) it can happen that God does not spare; which c) if it has not remained in faith, is to be cut off, that is defectible. But the particular and visible church is such.

2) Immunity from the danger of erring is not promised divinely, except to the true and living body of Christ, which those who externally prevail in the church and perform public ministry do not always constitute, but sometimes those constitute it who, pressed under the multitude of the erring, lie hidden and groan, whose splendor is not external, but they are like a small hut in the vineyards, or in the cucumber gardens, and like a devastated city, Isa. I, 8. like a woman left behind, ch. VI, 13. as a poor and needy people, Zeph. III, 12. as a little flock, Luke XII, 32.

3) Experience teaches that the particular and visible church has often defected from heavenly truth. For the Israelite church, contemporary with Moses, defected, which, with Aaron leading, adored the calf, Exod. XXXII. The church contemporary with Elijah defected, who thought himself alone to be a true believer, when yet there remained, by the grace of God, seven thousand true believers, who lay hidden under the multitude of the wicked, and had not bowed their knees to Baal, 1 Kings XIX, 10. The church contemporary with Christ defected, which was ignorant of the foundation of faith, to wit, the Messiah, the heavenly king, not a worldly one, the priest, to be offered as a most holy sacrifice for sins, the enemy and persecutor of Jesus of Nazareth, the true Messiah, made manifest by so many lights. The churches planted by Paul defected, the Ephesian, Philippian, Colossian, Corinthian, Galatian. With the Arian heresy predominating, the church was not to be sought in walls, not in roofs and buildings, but in mountains, in woods, in lakes, prisons, and chasms. Conf. AUGUSTIN. ep. XLVIII. SOZOM. lib. III. hist. eccles. c. XIII. In the time of the Anti-Christ, that everywhere the wicked and those addicted to the mendacious doctrines of Anti-Christ would be, and that the church of Christ would lie hidden under the immense throng of Anti-Christ's satellites, was foretold in the scriptures, Apoc. XII, 14. 2 Thess. II, 3.

1) Of the Papists, who deny that the Roman church can err in faith.

2) Of the Socinians and Arminians, who maintain that the catholic church can utterly fail.

The Papists object:

1. Against which church the gates of hell do not prevail, that church cannot err or fail: Against the church of Christ &c. Matt. XVI, 18. Therefore. Resp. The gates of hell do not prevail against the catholic, or universal church; but we have demonstrated that many particular churches have failed.

II. The pillar and foundation of truth does not slip. But the church is &c. I Tim. III, 15. E. Resp. The catholic and invisible church, which is the assembly of the reborn and the elect, is, firstly, in itself and properly called the pillar of truth, because it is firm, constant, and like an immovable pillar, stable in guarding and preaching the truth entrusted to it, and will never fail from it. Not that it cannot absolutely and considered in itself fail from the truth at all (for it consists of men, still exposed to manifold infirmity, and who individually can be deceived and can deceive); but that through the grace and assistance of Christ it cannot happen that it fails in things necessary for belief. Secondarily, improperly and by synecdoche of the part for the whole, the particular and visible church is called the pillar and foundation of truth, on account of the reborn and elect who are contained in it.

But when the wicked, having been admitted, obtain dominion in it and corrupt the public profession of faith, the visible assembly, whose public profession is corrupt, is not and is not called the pillar of truth; although a few, lurking within it, truly believing, are guardians and witnesses of the celestial truth: for the denomination is made from the more excellent part.

III. Whatever church is governed by Christ, as the supreme head, that church cannot err or fail: But the Christian church &c. Eph. I, 22. Therefore. Resp. Distinguish between the absolute and the ordered government of Christ. The latter occurs through ordinary means. The assembly of the called that abandons those means is abandoned and slips into errors.

IV. The church is led by the Holy Spirit into all truth, John XVI, 13. Therefore it is infallible. Resp. From the intention of Christ speaking, that promise primarily and proximately regards the instruction of the Apostles for the function of the Apostolic office, by which they had to serve by preaching the word of truth to all nations. Secondarily, that promise can be accommodated to the universal church: which is infallible conditionally, if it follows the Holy Spirit.

V. Christ prays for the church, John XVII, 17. Therefore it cannot fail. Resp. The intercession of Christ averts from the church total failure, not partial. That the assembly of true believers and saints does not cease to exist entirely is to be attributed to the grace and intercession of Christ: yet it is evident that very many assemblies of the called have shaken off faith in Christ.

VI. The church must be heard under penalty of anathema, Matt. XVIII, 17. Therefore it cannot err. The reason for the consequence is: because the church would never have to be heard under such a great penalty if it were liable to errors. Resp. 1) In the place cited, it is not a matter of articles of faith; but of ecclesiastical discipline, which even a corrupt church observes. 2) The church must be heard as long as it itself hears the voice of the shepherd Christ, and adheres to the divine word.

VII. Individual particular churches can fail: Therefore also the universal church. The consequence is proven: because the universal church is nothing other than the complex of churches.

of particular [churches]. Resp. Individual particular churches can fail separately, not jointly, or collectively; just as individual men die, but not the whole human species. The universal church is indefectible not absolutely and in itself, but on account of the grace, assistance, and governance of Christ, the spiritual head and king, who is not without a body and a spiritual kingdom .

Latin:

Ecclesia catholica & invisibilis, quae omnes singulosque renatos & electos complectitur, in fundamento fidei errare, penitusque deficere nequit, sed durabit usque ad consummationem saeculi ). Quaelibet autem ecclesia particularis & visibilis fundamentalibus erroribus adeo contaminari potest, ut praevaleant, publicumque ministerium constituant doctores fallam doctrinam profitentes, paucitate vere credentium sub multitudine errantium latente ).

Obs. 1) Assertionis nostrae sensus est: ecclesiam catholicam totam nunquam ita errare, ut non supersint aliqui, qui simplicem verbi ductum sequentes, Spiritus S. directione in veritate & fide sanctificentur, ac conferuentur, ut retento salutis fundamento virtute Dei per fidem custodiantur ad salutem, licet illi quandoque pauci sint, & perturbatissimis ecclesiae temporibus lateant, ut vere credentium coetus non sit illustris & distincte conspicuus: Ecclesiam autem particularem & visibilem unamquamque in fide posse errare & de facto aliquando errasse, si a regula verbi caelestis abeat, a quo errandi periculo nec Romanam ecclesiam, a qua sola tantopere illud amoliri conantur, excipimus, ut ait b. D. GERHARDVS, in loc. de ecclesia,

§. 107. Obs. 2) Indeficibilis dicitur ecclesia indeficibilitate ) conditionata, quod suo capiti Christo adhaeret, a quo illam nihil, nisi peccatum, separare potest ) nisi peccatum, separare potest (hæc indeficibilitas

ecclesiæ invisibili cum visibili communis est): b) catholica, quoad τὸ σύνολον, singuli fideles excidere possunt, non item universalis ecclesia, quæ indeficibilitas ecclesiæ invisibili est propria: c) finali, quoad ecclesiam electorum.

Prob. a. 1) Contra ecclesiam catholicam non sunt prævalituræ portæ inferorum, Matth. XVI, 18. E. Ecclesia catholica est indeficibilis a veritate cœlesti, & inexpugnabilis. Etenim πύλαι, portæ, locum consiliorum & iudiciorum, ubi vis ac potentia civitatis sita erat, significant. Quare portæ inferorum nil aliud sunt, quam consilia, molimina, potentia, vis ac robur diaboli & tyrannorum.

2) Regnum Christi spirituale (ecclesia) in his terris perenne est, Luc. I, 33. Ex quo etiam Christus veris huius spiritualis regni membris gratiosam suam præsentiam promisit usque ad consummationem sæculi, Matth. XXVIII, 20. E. ecclesia Christi usque ad finem mundi duratura est.

3) Ecclesia est domus Dei, columna & repositorium veritatis, 1 Tim. III, 15. E. tamdiu stabit inexpugnabilis, quamdiu supererit veritas cœlestis, seu verbum Dei, quod semper manet, 1 Petr. I, 25.

4) Semper prædicabitur verbum Dei, Es. LIX, 21. Ier. XXX, 23. (licet non semper pure) & conuiuæ eucharistiæ mortem Domini annuntiabunt, donec veniat (ad iudicium) 1 Cor. XI, 26. E. semper erunt renati & electi. Vbicunque enim prædicatur verbum Domini, semper in quibusdam fructificat, Es. LV, 10. Matth. III, 24.

Prob. b. 1) Ex monito Paullino, Rom. IX, 20. 21. 22. Nec altum sape, sed time. Si enim Deus naturalibus ramis non pepercit, ne forte etiam tibi non parcat. Vide ergo benignitatem ac severitatem Dei: in iis quidem, qui ceciderunt, severitatem; in te vero benignitatem, si manseris in benignitate: alioqui etiam exscinderis. Vnde argumentum inexpugnabile: Quæ ecclesia sibi a) cauere debet a lapsu; cui b) fieri potest, vt Deus non parcat; quæ c) si non permanserit in fide, exscindenda est, illa est deficibilis. Atqui ecclesia particularis ac visibilis sic se habet.

2) Immunitas ab errandi periculo non est promissa diuinitus, nisi vero & viuo Christi corpori, quod non semper constituunt, qui externe prævalent in ecclesia & ministerio publico funguntur, sed quandoque constituunt, qui sub errantium multitudine pressi latent & gemunt, quorum non est externus splendor, sed sunt instar tugurioli in vineis, aut in cucumerariis hortis, & sicut urbs vastata, Es. I, 8. instar feminis relicti, c. VI, 13. vt populus pauper & egenus, Zeph. III, 12. vt grex pusillus, Luc. XI, 32.

3) Experientia docet, ecclesiam particularem & visibilem sæpe defecisse a veritate cœlesti. Defecit quippe ecclesia Israëlitica, coætanea Mosi, quæ, præeunte Aarone, vitulum adorauit, Exod. XXXII. Defecit ecclesia coætanea Eliæ, qui se solum esse opinabatur vere credentem, cum tamen superessent, gratia Dei, septem millia vere credentium, qui sub improborum multitudine latebant, & genua sua Baali non flexerant, 1 Reg. XIX, 10. Defecit ecclesia coætanea Christo, quæ ignara erat fundamenti fidei, scil. Messiæ regis cœlestis, non mundani, sacerdotis, sanctissimo sacrificio pro peccatis offerendi, hostis, & persecutrix Iesu Nazareni, veri Messiæ, tot luminibus patefacti. Defecerunt ecclesiæ plantatæ a Paullo, Ephesina, Philippensis, Colossensis, Corinthiaca, Galatica. Prædominante hæresi Ariana non in parietibus, non in tectis & ædificiis quærenda erat ecclesia, sed in montibus, in sylvis, in lacubus, carceribus, voraginibus. Conf. AVGVSTIN. ep. XLVIII. SOZOM. lib. III. hist. eccles. c. XIII. Tempore Anti-Christi vbique improbos & Anti-Christi mendacibus doctrinis addictos, & ecclesiam Christi sub Anti-Christi satellitum ingenti caterua latituram esse, prædictum est in scripturis, Apoc. XII, 14. 2 Thess. II, 3.

1) Pontificiorum, negantium, ecclesiam Romanam posse in fide errare.

2) Socinianorum & Arminianorum, statuentium, ecclesiam catholicam penitus deficere posse.

Pontificii obiiciunt:

1. Contra quam ecclesiam portae inferorum non praevalent, illa non potest errare aut deficere: Contra ecclesiam Christi &c. Matth. XVI, 18. Ergo. Resp. Contra catholicam, siue vniuersalem ecclesiam non praevalent portae inferorum; ecclesias autem particulares multas defecisse, demonstravimus.

II. Columna & firmamentum veritatis non labitur. Atqui ecclesia est &c. I Tim. III, 15. E. Resp. Ecclesia catholica & inuisibilis, quae est coetus renatorum & electorum, primo, per se & proprie dicitur columna veritatis, quod firma, constans, & instar immobilis columnae stabilis sit in custodienda & praedicanda veritate, sibi concredita, neque vnquam ab ea defectura sit. Non quod absolute & in se spectata deficere a veritate prorsus nequeat (constat enim ex hominibus, multipli adhuc infirmitati expositis, & qui falli singuli, ac fallere possunt); sed quod per gratiam & assistentiam Christi fieri non possit, vt in creditu necessariis ab ea deficiat. Secundario, improprie & per synecdochen partis pro toto ecclesia particularis & visibilis dicitur columna & firmamentum veritatis, propter renatos & electos, qui in ea continentur.

Quando autem admixti mali in ea dominium consequuntur, & professionem fidei publicam corrumpunt, visibilis coetus, cuius professio publica corrupta est, non est & dicitur columna veritatis; quamuis pauci, in ea latentes, vere credentes, custodes & testes veritatis coelestis sint: fit enim denominatio a praestantiori.

III. Quaecunque ecclesia gubernatur a Christo, tanquam summo capite, illa non potest errare, aut deficere: Atqui ecclesia Christiana &c. Eph. I, 22. Ergo. Resp. Dist. inter gubernationem Christi absolutam, & ordinatam. Haec fit per ordinaria media. Qui coetus vocatorum illa media deserit, deseritur & labitur in errores.

IV. Ecclesia a Spiritu S. ducitur in omnem veritatem, Io. XVI, 13. Ergo est infallibilis. Resp. Ex intentione Christi loquentis promissio illa primario & proxime respicit instructionem Apostolorum ad functionem muneris Apostolici, quo omnibus gentibus praedicando verbum veritatis inferuire debuerunt. Secundario illa promissio accommodari potest ad ecclesiam vniuersam: quae est infallibilis conditionate, si Spiritum S. sequatur.

V. Christus precatur pro ecclesia, Io. XVII, 17. Ergo non potest deficere. Resp. Intercessio Christi auertit ab ecclesia defectionem totam, non partialem. Quod coetus vere credentium & sanctorum non penitus desinat esse, tribuendum est gratiae & intercessioni Christi: Plurimos tamen vocatorum coetus fidem in Christum excussisse, constat.

VI. Ecclesia sub anathematis poena audienda est, Matth. XVIII, 17. Ergo non potest errare. Ratio consequentiae est: quia nunquam sub tanta poena audienda esset ecclesia, si erroribus esset obnoxia. Resp. 1) L.c. non agitur de articulis fidei; sed de disciplina ecclesiastica, quam etiam ecclesia corrupta obseruat. 2) Audienda est ecclesia, quamdiu ipsa audit vocem pastoris Christi, & verbo diuino inhaeret.

VII. Singulae ecclesiae particulares possunt deficere: Ergo etiam ecclesia vniuersalis. Consequentia probatur: quia ecclesia vniuersalis nihil aliud est, quam complexus ecclesiarum.

particularium. Resp. Singulae ecclesiae particulares possunt deficere divisim, non coniunctim, aut collective; sicut singuli homines moriuntur, non autem tota species humana. Indeficibilis est ecclesia vniversalis non absolute & in se, sed ob gratiam, assistentiam & gubernationem Christi, spiritualis capitis & regis, qui non est sine corpore & regno spirituali .


### Of the Representative Church

Q. XL.

What is the representative church? The representative church is a congregation of doctors, representing the synthetic church in its own way. Prob. For the synthetic church is represented, both through the ecclesiastical ministry and through a council or synod. The profession of faith, which is issued by the voice of pastors when they inculcate the doctrine of Christ in public assemblies and explain it to the grasp of the hearers, is considered the common confession of the whole church and of individual members. Moreover, in councils, doctors and delegates of the church are gathered, to whom the power of recognizing and judging concerning the public interpretation of doctrine in doubtful and controversial matters, concerning ceremonies contributing to good order in the church, and also concerning the power of correcting public offenses, has been committed by the whole communion of believers.

Latin:

Quaest. XL.

Quid est ecclesia repraesentativa? Ecclesia repraesentativa est congregatio doctorum, ecclesiam syntheticam suo modo repraesentans. Prob. Repraesentatur enim ecclesia synthetica, cum per ministerium ecclesiasticum, tum per concilium, siue synodum. Professio fidei, quae editur voce pastorum, cum doctrinam Christi in conuentibus publicis inculcant, & ad auditorum captum declarant, communis confessio ecclesiae totius & singulorum membrorum censetur. In conciliis autem congregantur doctores & delegati ecclesiae, quibus a tota credentium communione commissa est potestas cognoscendi & iudicandi de publica interpretatione doctrinae in capitibus dubiis & controuersis, de caerimoniis ad bonum ordinem in ecclesia facientibus, vt & de potestate corrigendi publica delicta.


### Q. XLI

What is an ecclesiastical council? An ecclesiastical council is a solemn assembly of doctors and delegates of the church, gathered by the instigation and moderation of God, called together by public authority, for the purpose of duly weighing and judging questions that have arisen concerning the dogmas of faith, the morals of Christians, and the rites of the church, so that the glory of God may be propagated, concord in one faith may be established, and schisms, heresies, and public offenses may be averted. Obs. I. A council is not said to be from consulting, as the writing itself testifies; nor from reconciling discrepant opinions, which derivation is inadequate, but from 'concalando', i.e., calling together. For a council is a gathering of men called together to consult: whence also 'concilium' is as it were 'concalium' (which is from ἀπὸ τοῦ καλεῖν). In Greek it is called σύνοδος, or a congress of many. Obs. II. Although the name of a council, in its native signification and force of notation, designates any gathering, whether ecclesiastical or political, assembled for the sake of consultation: here, however, it is used in a stricter sense, so that it denotes a congregation of doctors and delegates of the church.

Latin:

Quid est concilium ecclesiasticum? Concilium ecclesiasticum est solemnis conuentus doctorum & delegatorum ecclesiae, instigante ac moderante Deo congregatorum, publica auctoritate conuocatorum, ad rite expendendum & diiudicandum quaestiones exortas de dogmatibus fidei, moribus Christianorum & ritibus ecclesiae, vt gloria Dei propagetur, concordia in vna fide stabiliatur, schismata, haereses & delicta publica auertantur. Obs. I. Concilium non dicitur a consulendo, vel ipsa scriptione teste; neque a conciliandis discrepantibus sententiis, quae deriuatio est inadaequata, sed a concalando, i. e. conuocando. Est enim concilium, coetus virorum ad consultandum conuocatus: vnde etiam concilium festo est quasi concalium (quod est ἀπὸ τοῦ καλεῖν). Graece dicitur σύνοδος, siue congressus plurium. Obs. II. Quanquam nomen concilii, natiua significatione & vi notationis, designet quemuis coetum, siue ecclesiasticum, siue politicum, consultationis caussa congregatum: hic tamen vsurpatur significatu strictiori, vt notet congregationem doctorum & delegatorum ecclesiae.


### Q. XLII

What is the principal efficient cause of councils? The cause and principal author of councils is God. Prob. The origin of councils is divine.

This is evident 1) from the councils of the Old Testament, which were called together by the command and moderation of God, Exod. XX, 20. Num. XI, 16. Deut. XVII, 9. Ps. CXXII.

From the apostolic council held at Jerusalem, in which, as in a most clear mirror, the genuine form and hypotyposis of a legitimate council is exhibited to us, whose president was the Holy Spirit, Acts XV, 28. For the Apostles say: It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us. 3) Christ himself refers us to the representative church, saying: Tell it to the church, Matt. XVIII, 17. Where by church is understood the judging assembly; but the promiscuous multitude does not judge: Therefore the representative church, which is the congregation of doctors. But Christ would not have referred [us] to the church, unless a tribunal had been divinely constituted in it.

Latin:

Quae est caussa efficiens principalis conciliorum? Conciliorum caussa & auctor principalis est Deus. Prob. Conciliorum origo diuina est.

Id quod patet 1) e conciliis vet. testam. quae iubente & moderante Deo sunt conuocata, Exod. XX, 20. Num. XI, 16. Deut. XVII, 9. Ps. CXXII.

Ex concilio apostolico Hierosolymis habito, in quo, ceu clarissimo speculo, concilii legitimi forma genuina, & hypotyposis nobis exhibetur, cuius praeses fuit Spiritus S. Act. XV, 28. Dicunt enim Apostoli: Visum est Spiritui S. & nobis. 3) Ipse Christus nos remittit ad ecclesiam repraesentativam, inquiens: Dic ecclesiae, Matth. XVIII, 17. Vbi per ecclesiam intelligitur coetus iudicans; multitudo autem promiscua non iudicat: Ergo ecclesia repraesentativa, quae est congregatio doctorum. Non autem remisisset Christus, ad ecclesiam, nisi divinitus tribunal in ea esset constitutum.


### Q. XLIII. With whom does the power of convening councils reside?

The power of proclaiming and convening councils resides with the political Magistrate (Power of convening councils); where he is deficient, the faithful themselves can, without injury to the heterodox lords of the territories, institute an ecclesiastical congregation .

Obs. I. It is not asked: whether some consensus of the political Magistrate is required for assembling councils? but the question is ventilated concerning the power of proclaiming and assembling councils. The Papists do not deny the consensus to the magistrate; but they concede that he can request a council and subsequently advise: however, they deny that the right and authority of assembling a council belongs to him.

Obs. II. Even if the Magistrate sometimes defers his right to Theologians, of proclaiming councils in his diocese; yet they use that right not as lords, but as ministers of a superior power, and therefore that power is not proper, but delegated.

Prob. a. 1) From the authority of the magistrate. The convocation of a council is an act of jurisdiction, implying some superiority, and therefore must always be instituted by him who has some jurisdiction, or authority, or superiority in the causes for which the convocation is made. But such jurisdiction does not reside with Bishops or Presbyters, 1 Pet. V, 3. but with the magistrate, Rom. XIII, 1.

2) From divine sanction.

To those to whom it is sanctioned and commanded that they kiss the Son of God, open the gates in the world to him, and promote the kingdom of the same and the increase of the church, it belongs, if it is expedient for the church, to assemble councils: But to the magistrate, as the guardian of both tables, this is sanctioned and commanded, Ps. II, 10. XXIV, 7. Is. XLIX, 18. Therefore.

3) From the custom of the Israelite church, in which Moses, Exod. XIX, Joshua, ch. XIX, David, 1 Chron. XIII, Solomon, 1 Kings VIII, Jehoshaphat, 2 Chron. XX, Hezekiah, ch. XXX, Josiah, ch.

4) From the practice of the primitive church of the new testament. The Nicene Council was assembled by CONSTANTINE THE GREAT: the First Constantinopolitan by THEODOSIUS the elder: the Ephesian by THEODOSIUS the younger: the Chalcedonian by the Emperor MARCIAN.

Prob. b. If the magistrate is heterodox and infidel, the right and power of convening councils does not however expire, if the orthodox themselves demand it. But if he does not grant the request, the Bishops themselves can, by the example of the Apostles, assemble councils as if by precarious right. Thus Acts XV, 2, when a dispute had been stirred up in the church at Antioch concerning the necessity of legitimate circumcision for salvation, the Apostles and elders assembled a council to discuss this controversy.

There is an Antithesis of the Papists, who maintain that the power of convening councils, especially general ones, resides with the Roman Pontiff.

Who object: I. Whatever council is not assembled in the name of Christ, that is not legitimate: Whatever council is assembled by a political magistrate, that is not assembled in the name in the name of Christ: Therefore. The minor is proved, because the Magistrate does not preside over the church in the name of Christ, but the Roman Pontiff, who is the vicar of Christ & the visible head of the church. Resp. 1) That council is gathered in the name of Christ which is convened for the sake of the doctrine & glory of Christ: which is also done by an orthodox Magistrate. 2) We deny that the Roman Pontiff is the ecumenical vicar of Christ and the visible head of the church.

II. Whoever are not shepherds in the sheepfold of Christ, but sheep, they do not have the power of compelling councils: But political Magistrates &c. Therefore. The major is proved: Just as it is not for the sheep to gather the shepherds: So it is not for Kings and secular Magistrates to convoke Bishops, as shepherds, to a council. Resp. Magistrates are considered in a twofold way: a) insofar as they are internally illuminated, converted, and sanctified through the means of salvation: b) insofar as they externally defend, confirm, and urge the Christian religion. In the former way they are to be considered as sheep; in the latter way they are guardians and defenders of the sheepfold of Christ.

III. Whoever does not have all the members of the universal church subject to him, he cannot call a general council: But the Emperor does not have all the members &c. Therefore. Resp. 1) Neither does the Roman Pontiff have all the members of the church subject to him. 2) The Emperor compels the Bishops subject to him to the council by authority; those who are outside his territory, he invites by courtesy. It suffices that the decrees of the council be transmitted to others and approved by them.

Latin:

Potestas indicendi & convocandi concilia est penes Magistratum politicum (Potestas convocandi concilia); quo deficiente, possunt ipsi fideles, citra injuriam in dominos territoriorum heterodoxos, congregationem ecclesiasticam instituere .

Obs. I. Non quaeritur: an consensus aliqualis Magistratus politici ad cogenda concilia requiratur? sed ventilatur quaestio de potestate indicendi & cogendi concilia. Non derogant Pontificii consensum magistratui; sed concedunt, quod hic concilium petere & deinceps consulere possit: negant autem, ipsi competere ius & auctoritatem cogendi concilium.

Obs. II. Etiam si Magistratus Theologis quandoque ius suum deferat, indicendi concilia in sua dioecesi; eo tamen iure utuntur non vt domini, sed vt potestatis superioris ministri, adeoque potestas illa non propria, sed delegata est.

Prob. a. 1) A magistratus auctoritate. Convocatio concilii est actus iurisdictionis, superioritatem aliquam importans, adeoque semper instituenda ab illo, qui habet aliquam iurisdictionem, vel auctoritatem, vel superioritatem in causis, ob quas fit convocatio. Eiusmodi autem iurisdictio non est penes Episcopos aut Presbyteros, 1 Petr. V, 3. sed penes magistratum, Rom. XIII, 1.

2) A divina sanctione.

Quibus sancitur & praecipitur, vt Filium Dei osculentur, eidem portas in mundo aperiant, regnum eiusdem, & incrementum ecclesiae promoveant, illorum est, si ecclesiae expedit, concilia cogere: At magistratui, ceu custodi utriusque tabulae, hoc sancitur & praecipitur, Ps. II, 10. XXIV, 7. Es. XLIX, 18. Ergo.

3) Ab ecclesiae Israeliticae consuetudine, in qua synodos convocarunt Moses, Exod. XIX, Iosua, c. XIX. Dauid, 1 Par. XIII. Salomo, 1 Reg. VIII. Iosaphat, 2 Par. XX. Ezechias, c. XXX. Iosias, c.

XXXIV. 4) Ex praxi ecclesiae primitivae novi testamenti. Concilium Nicaenum coactum est a CONSTANTINO MAGNO: Constantinopolitanum I, a THEODOSIO seniore: Ephesinum a THEODOSIO iuniore: Chalcedonense a MARCIANO Imperatore.

Prob. b. Si magistratus sit heterodoxus & infidelis, non tamen exspirat ius & potestas convocandi concilia, si id ipsum orthodoxi efflagitent. Quod si is petito non annuerit, possunt ipsi Episcopi exemplo Apostolorum quasi precario congregare concilia. Sic Act. XV, 2. cum disceptatio excitata esset in ecclesia Antiochena de circumcisionis legitimae necessitate ad salutem, concilium congregabant Apostoli & seniores ad discutiendam hanc controuersiam.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, statuentium, potestatem convocandi concilia, inprimis generalia, esse penes Pontificem Romanum.

Qui obiiciunt: I. Quodcunque concilium non congregatur in nomine Christi, illud non est legitimum: Quodcunque concilium congregatur a magistratu politica, id non congregatur in nomine Christi: Ergo. Minor probatur, quia Magistratus in nomine Christi non praeest ecclesiae, sed Pontifex Romanus, qui est Christi vicarius & visibile ecclesiae caput. Resp. 1) Illud concilium congregatur in nomine Christi, quod propter doctrinam & gloriam Christi convocatur: id quod etiam fit a Magistratu orthodoxo. 2) Pontificem Romanum esse oecumenicum Christi vicarium, & caput ecclesiae visibile, negamus.

II. Quicunque in ovili Christi non sunt pastores, sed oues, illi non habent potestatem cogendi concilia: Atqui Magistratus politici &c. Ergo. Maior probatur: Sicut ovium non est, congregare pastores: Ita Regum & Magistratuum saecularium non est, convocare Episcopos, tanquam pastores, ad concilium. Resp. Magistratus duplici modo considerantur: a) quatenus interne illuminantur, convertuntur, & sanctificantur per media salutis: b) quatenus externe defendunt, confernant & instant religionem Christianam. Priori modo considerandi sunt vt oues; posteriori modo sunt custodes & defensores ovilis Christi.

III. Quicunque non omnia membra vniversae ecclesiae subiecta habet, is non potest indicere concilium generale: Atqui Imperator non omnia membra &c. Ergo. Resp. 1) ne que Pontifex Romanus omnia membra ecclesiae subiecta habet. 2) Imperator subiectos sibi Episcopos ad concilium cogit imperio, qui extra ipsius territorium sunt, illos invitat comitate. Sufficit, quod decreta concilii aliis transmittantur, & ab illis approbentur.


### Quest. XLIV. Who is the president of a council?

The invisible president of a council is the Holy Spirit. The visible president is either political or ecclesiastical: The political president is the Emperor, King, or Christian Prince, or someone delegated by him . The ecclesiastical president is one or more Bishops, elected by the Emperor, King, or Prince, or by the common suffrage of the whole council .

Prob. a. The Holy Spirit is the supreme and infallible president of the council, Acts XV, 28, who, by means of the word contained in the sacred letters, speaks, teaches, illuminates, and directs the minds of the assessors of the council. Prob. b.

The political president moderates the external order of the council, provides security from external violence to those speaking, prevents tumults, restrains those quarreling, approves the decrees of the greater and better part, sanctions them by public edict, and delivers them for execution. Thus, CONSTANTINE THE GREAT governed the Council of Nicaea regarding external matters, THEODOSIUS the elder the Constantinopolitan, THEODOSIUS the younger the Ephesian, through legates, the Emperor MARCIAN the Chalcedonian, through consular men whom he himself had appointed as judges: as witnessed by EVAGRIUS, book II, ch. 4.

Prob. c. The ecclesiastical president moderates τὰ ἐσώτερα τῆς ἐκκλησίας, the internal matters of the church, or the ecclesiastical actions themselves, which concern the doctrine of faith, not with coercive authority, but with ordinary authority; he accurately proposes the questions about which deliberation is to be had, explains them candidly, asks for and collects suffrages and opinions, pronounces the definitive sentence, drafts the synodical acts, and delivers them to the whole congregation to be reviewed and confirmed. Sometimes several episcopal presidents have been elected, who presided over the synod either by turns or by common authority: In the Council of Nicaea, the Bishop of Corduba; in the Constantinopolitan Council, TIMOTHY of Alexandria, MELETIUS of Antioch, NECTARIUS of Constantinople, and CYRIL, Bishop of Jerusalem; in the Chalcedonian, ANATOLIUS of Constantinople, MAXIMUS of Antioch, and JUVENAL of Jerusalem, were the presiding Bishops:

were. Wherefore it is not necessary that the Roman Pontiff be the president of all councils, even general ones.

Latin:

Praeses concilii invisibilis est Spiritus S. Praeses visibilis est vel politicus, vel ecclesiasticus: Praeses politicus est Imperator, Rex, aut Princeps Christianus, aut aliquis ab illo delegatus . Praeses ecclesiasticus est vnus vel plures Episcopi, ab Imperatore, Rege, aut Principe, vel communi totius concilii suffragio electi .

Prob. a. Spiritus S. est summus & infallibilis praeses concilii, Act. XV, 28. qui mediante verbo in sacris litteris comprehenso loquitur, docet, illuminat & dirigit mentes assessorum concilii.

Prob. b. Praeses politicus ordinem concilii externum moderatur, colloquentibus securitatem a vi externa praestat, impedit tumultus, coercet rixantes, decreta maioris & melioris partis approbat, publico edicto sancit, & executioni tradit. Sic concilium Nicaenum, quoad externa gubernavit CONSTANTINVS MAGNVS, Constantinopolitanum THEODOSIVS senior, Ephesinum THEODOSIVS iunior, per legatos, Chalcedonense MARCIANVS Imperator, per viros consulares, quos iudices ipse constituerat: teste EVAGRIO, libr II. c. 4.

Prob. c. Praeses ecclesiasticus τὰ ἐσώτερα τῆς ἐκκλησίας, interna ecclesiae, seu ipsas actiones ecclesiasticas, quae circa doctrinam fidei sunt, moderatur, non cum auctoritate coactiva, sed ordinaria, quaestiones, de quibus deliberandum est, accurate proponit, candide explicat, suffragia & sententias rogat & colligit, definitiuam sententiam pronunciat, acta synodica concipit, eaque toti congregationi recensenda & confirmanda tradit. Interdum plures praesides episcopales electi sunt, qui vel per vices, vel communi auctoritate synodo praefuerunt: In concilio Nicaeno Episcopus Cordubensis, in concilio Constantinopolitano TIMOTHEVS Alexandrinus, MELETIVS Antiochenus, NECTATIVS Constantinopolitanus & CYRILLVS Hierosolymitanus Episcopus: In Chalcedonensi ANATOLIVS Constantinopolitanus, MAXIMVS Antiochenus, & IVVENALIS Hierosolymitanus, Episcopi praesides fuerunt: Hierosolymitanus, Episcopi praesides

fuerunt. Quare non necesse est, ut Pontifex Romanus sit praeses omnium conciliorum, etiam generalium.


### Q. XLV. Who are

the assessors and judges in councils? The assessors and judges in councils, besides the presidents, are not only Bishops, Doctors, and Pastors, but also laymen, skilled in the sacred letters, pious, lovers of truth and peace, delegated by the churches, so that they may deliver an opinion on the matters proposed.

Proof 1) From the solemn celebration of the Jerusalem council, described in Acts XV, in which not only the Apostles, but also the elders and the people gathered, and the votes of the whole church, consisting of clergy and laity, were heard. Wherefore also the decree of the synod was conceived in these words, Acts XV, 22: "It seemed good to the apostles and elders, with the whole church," and v. 25: "It seemed good to us, being assembled with one accord." 2) From the clear sayings of Scripture.

It is said to all the faithful that they should test the spirits, whether they are from God, 1 John IV, 1.

Paul compels the Corinthians: "Judge for yourselves what I say," 1 Cor.

X, 15. Cf. Rom. XIV, 12. We indeed grant to the doctors of the church the more important parts of deciding doubtful and controversial questions; but we deny that it is theirs to pass and publish an obligatory sentence without the consent of the laymen delegated by the churches, since it is their duty to consult together, to state opinions, and to define.

Latin:

Assessores & iudices in conciliis, praeter praesides, sunt non tantum Episcopi, Doctores & Pastores, sed etiam laici, litterarum sacrarum periti, pii, veritatis & pacis amantes, ab ecclesiis delegati, vt de rebus propositis sententiam ferant.

Prob. 1) Ex solemni concilii Hierosolymitani celebratione, descripta, Act. XV. in quo non tantum Apostoli, sed etiam presbyteri & populus convenerunt, auditaque sunt universae ecclesiae constantis ex clericis & laicis suffragia. Quare etiam decretum synodi his conceptum est verbis, Act. XV, 22. Visum est Apostolis & senioribus cum universa ecclesia, it. v. 25. Visum est nobis unanimiter congregatis.

2) E perspicuis dictis scripturae. Fidelibus omnibus dictum est, ut probent spiritus, an sint ex Deo, 1 Io.

IV, 1. Paullus compellat Corinthios: Iudicate vos, quae dico, 1 Cor. X, 15.

Conf. Rom. XIV, 12. Concedimus quidem doctoribus ecclesiae partes potiores decidendi quaestiones dubias & controversas; sed negamus, illorum esse, sententiam obligatoriam ferre & publicare, citra laicorum ab ecclesiis delegatorum consensum, quippe quorum est, una consultare, sententias dicere, definire.


### Q. XLVI. Concerning what matter do councils deal?

In councils, questions are weighed concerning the dogmas of faith, morals, and the ceremonies of the Christian church.

Proof. From Acts XV, 19. In the apostolic council (which exhibits the idea of a legitimate council) there was a question of faith: Whether eternal salvation could not be obtained without the reception of circumcision and the observation of the whole law? The question concerning the morals and ceremonies of the church was: Whether it is necessary to abstain for a time from the enjoyment of things prohibited by the ceremonial law, so that the church to be gathered from Jews and Gentiles might coalesce more easily?

Latin:

In conciliis expenduntur quaestiones de dogmatibus fidei, moribus, & caerimoniis ecclesiae Christianae.

Prob. Ex Act. XV, 19. In concilio apostolico (quod legitimi concilii ideam exhibet) erat quaestio de fide: An salus aeterna obtineri nequeat citra susceptionem circumcisionis & observationem universae legis? Quaestio de moribus & caerimoniis ecclesiae erat: An oporteat abstinere ad tempus a fruitione rerum lege caerimoniali prohibitarum, vt eo facilius coalesceret ecclesia ex Iudaeis & gentibus colligenda?


### Q. XLVII. What is the norm for deciding questions in a council?

The sole principle and norm for deciding controversial questions concerning dogmas and morals is the canonical Scripture.

Proof. The decisions of councils concern the faith and duties of Christians; which, just as they depend on Holy Scripture as the sole principle of knowing and acting: So also the decisions concerning these have solely Scripture as the perfect and adequate principle and norm of deciding. Cf. the sayings of Scripture, Deut. IV, 12; Is. VIII, 20; 2 Tim. III, 15; Gal. I, 8; c. VI, 16. In the first councils, the codex of the gospels was placed on a high throne, so that it might be exposed to the eyes of all.

Latin:

Vnicum principium & norma decidendi quaestiones controversas de dogmatibus & moribus est scriptura canonica.

Prob. Decisiones conciliorum concernunt fidem & officia Christianorum; quae sicut pendent a scriptura S. tanquam unico principio cognoscendi & operandi: Ita quoque decisiones, ista concernentes, habent unice scripturam, vt principium & normam decidendi perfectam & adaequatam. Conf. dicta scripturae, Deut. IV, 12. Es. VIII, 20. 2 Tim. III, 15. Gal. I, 8. c. VI, 16. In conciliis primis codex euangeliorum in excelso throno collocabatur, vt omnium oculis esset expositus. esset expositus. Quæft. XLVIII. Quæ est forma conciliorum? Forma est decens ordo concilii, feu legitimus proceffus, quoad fingula partiForma conum congregatarum munia. ciliorum.


### Q. XLVIII. What is the form of councils?

The form is the decent order of the council, or the legitimate process, regarding the individual duties of the gathered parties.

Prob. For a council is a being by aggregation with order, which cannot exist without a legitimate process of the parts. The presidents observe this by directing rightly, the assessors by deliberating, opposing, responding, and deciding.

Latin:

Forma est decens ordo concilii, seu legitimus processus, quoad singula partium congregatarum munia.

Prob. Est enim concilium ens per aggregationem cum ordine, qui sine legitimo processu partium esse nequit. Hunc observant praesides recte dirigendo, assessores deliberando, opponendo, respondendo, decidendo.


### Q. XLIX. What is the end of councils?

The end of councils is the propagation of divine glory a), the concord of the church b), and the avoidance of schisms, heresies, and scandals c) .

Prob. a. Councils are gathered in the name of Christ, Matt. XVIII, 20, i.e., for the sake of the glory of Christ.

Prob. b. The concord of the church is stabilized by the consensus of the profession of faith, for the sake of which, lest it be disrupted by heterodoxy, a council is convened. Thus, in the apostolic council, Acts XV, the Christian doctrine concerning the attainment of eternal salvation without the reception of circumcision was defended.

Prob. c. In the apostolic council, Acts XV, the true opinion concerning the Mosaic law was explained in such a way that the opinion of the pseudo-apostles concerning the necessity of observing Mosaic rites was solidly refuted and utterly extirpated; furthermore, an exhortation for all time, and the enjoyment of blood and things sacrificed to idols, were prohibited for a time.

Latin:

Finis conciliorum est propagatio gloriae divinae a), concordia ecclesiae b) schismatum, haeresium & scandalorum declinatio c) .

Prob. a. Concilia congregantur in nomine Christi, Matth. XVIII, 10. i. e. propter gloriam Christi.

Prob. b. Concordia ecclesiae stabilitur consensu professionis fidei, quae ne heterodoxia dirumpatur, concilium convocatur. Sic in concilio apostolico, Act. XV. doctrina Christiana de consecutione aeternae salutis citra susceptionem circumcisionis propugnata est.

Prob. c. Concilio apostolico, Act. XV. vera sententia de lege Mosaica sic explicata est, ut pseudo-apostolorum opinio de necessitate observationis rituum Mosaicorum solide confutata sit, & penitus exstirpata; quin & hortatio in perpetuum, & fruitio sanguinis atque idolothytorum ad tempus prohibita est.


### Q. L. How are councils divided?

Councils are divided into universal, or general (which are called in Greek οἰκουμενικά) and particular (in Greek μερικά, ἢ τοπικά).

Universal are those to which learned and pious men are called from either all or most parts of the Christian world a) . Particular are either national, to which learned and pious men of one nation are summoned: or provincial, in which the doctors of one province convene; or diocesan, which consist of religious men of one diocese b) .

Prob. a. Indeed, there has never existed in the whole world an absolutely universal council in which the bishops and delegates of the entire church militant have convened: therefore, councils are called universal, or ecumenical, οὐγκρίτως (comparatively), or respectively, in respect to national, provincial, and diocesan councils. Although, therefore, they are not simply universal, they are nevertheless held as such on account of the subsequent ratification of all the particular churches by which they have been approved. The first IV ecumenical councils are esteemed most highly: the Nicene, convened by the Emperor CONSTANTINE the Great in the year 325, in which, with 318 bishops present, the heresy of ARIUS, denying the divinity of Christ, was condemned: the First Council of Constantinople, proclaimed by THEODOSIUS the Elder in the year 381, in which MACEDONIUS and those who acted with him, the Pneumatomachi, were condemned by 150 bishops: the First Council of Ephesus, gathered by THEODOSIUS the Younger, in which they condemned NESTORIUS, who denied the communication of idioms: the Chalcedonian, held under the Emperor MARCIAN in the year 451, against EUTYCHES and DIOSCORUS, who confounded the two natures in Christ, who were condemned by 630 bishops.

Prob. b. A national council was held at Carthage in Africa, with CYPRIAN presiding. Against this, CORNELIUS, the Roman bishop, instituted a national council, in which the bishops of all Italy convened, as witnessed by EUSEBIUS, Hist. Eccl. Book II, c. 2. Provincial councils were the Moguntine, the Cologne, the Aachen, and many others held in Germany and described in Vol. IV of the Councils. Diocesan councils are synods, or assemblies of one diocese under one bishop, and therefore of lesser authority.

Question LI. What is the authority of councils?

Councils possess great authority, and that decretory a) and decisive b), which they do not have from the fact that they exactly represent the universal church c), but they have the same dependently upon sacred scripture and the agreement of their decrees with the same d): although a posteriori from the consent of the churches existing throughout the world a certain authority accrues to them e), which nevertheless is not infallible, or immune from the danger of erring f).

Proof a. A public Doctor of the church gains for himself no small authority through piety, erudition, and love of truth, so that his judgment is highly valued: and therefore the authority of many Doctors who are pious and outstanding in erudition, who, having conferred and examined the opinions of matters, decree unanimously, is far greater. But the decretory authority of councils is valued most highly in establishing good order, and sanctioning rites, and correcting the morals of the church, so that all things may be done εὐσχημόνως καὶ κατὰ τάξιν, decently and according to order, 1 Cor. XIV, 40.

Proof b. In dogmas of faith, concerning which a doubt and controversy has arisen, the decisive authority of councils is of no small value; whose decision, however, is not simply judicial, but diaconic and ministerial, restricted to the ordinary method of interpreting the sayings of scripture, and of eliciting theological conclusions from them.

Proof c. The authority of councils is not born from a perfect representation of the catholic church; since there is no council given that exactly represents the universal church, and thus no council is given that is absolutely universal and ecumenical. - In the Council of Nicaea I, from the west only two presbyters were sent from Italy, one Bishop from Gaul, one from Spain, one from Africa. In the Council II and III, there were none from the west; nevertheless, the Pontiffs DAMASUS and CELESTINE confirmed those councils, in their own name and that of other Bishops of the west, whom they themselves had gathered at Rome. In the Council IV, there were only the legates of LEO, and furthermore he himself sent the consent of other bishops of Spain, Gaul, and Italy, who, in councils celebrated in their own provinces, wrote to Leo that they followed his opinion in all things. See BELLARM. L. I. de concil. XVI.

Proof d. The unique norm of councils is Holy Scripture, from which they obtain all certainty. Wherefore councils, which follow the word of God, sincerely declare the catholic faith.

Proof e. Those councils which are received by many churches are judged to be of such authority that the doctrine of the true church may not invalidly be gathered from them.

Proof f. The decrees of councils, even if they have been confirmed by the Roman Pontiff, are not of absolute infallibility. For 1) those who are liable to error outside of a council, remain such when gathered in the council itself: But the doctors of the church are liable to error outside of a council, unless they follow scripture uniquely as a guide and light: Therefore. 2) From the sacred letters it is certain that the council of the Jewish church erred most gravely, in which, although the supreme Pontiff presided, with the whole synagogue and the entire sanhedrin sitting by, nevertheless the Savior Christ was condemned for blasphemy as a seducer, Matt. XXVI, 65. Which error was not only of fact, but also of faith. For Christ was condemned for this reason, because He said that He was the Son of God, and thus the sanhedrin stumbled into a fundamental article of faith. 3) That particular councils, whether they were national or provincial, have erred not lightly, is clearly evident: for CYPRIAN instituted three national councils in Africa, in which the dogma concerning rebaptizing those who had been baptized by heretics was confirmed, as witnessed by AUGUSTINE L. III. de bapt. contra Donatistas. But, you will say: - Particular councils, confirmed by the Roman Pontiff, do not err. Resp. The Roman Pontiff has no privilege of infallibility. That many Popes have been heretics, is clearly shown

D. GERHARD, in confess. catholica lib. I. part. II. cap. 2. fol. 77. That general councils are not immune from error, the example of the Second Council of Ephesus alone teaches, which was general , and yet confirmed the Eutychian heresy, as witnessed by BELLARMINE, L. I. de conciliis c. 6. fol. 10. The antithesis is that of the Papists, who deny that universal councils confirmed by the Roman Pontiff can err.

They object: I. Whatever represents the universal church is infallible: But a universal council, convoked and confirmed by the Pope, etc. Therefore. The major premise is certain: because the universal church, which is the pillar of truth, cannot err in the foundation of faith.

II. The supreme judgment of Christians ought to be infallible: But a legitimate council is the supreme judgment of Christians, Matt. XVIII, 17. E. Resp. The supreme judgment of Christians is infallible as long as it is consistent with its norm, or the divine word. But it can happen that Christian judges either do not interpret the word of God correctly, or do not accurately derive conclusions from it, and consequently fall into error.

III. Christ is in the midst of the Bishops gathered in his name, who gives them the light of wisdom which they seek, so that they cannot err, Matt. XVIII, 20. Resp. In the words of Christ there is a promise, given to all true Christians, concerning his gracious presence and the hearing of prayers. But if from this promise a privilege of infallibility could be inferred, it would be common to all the faithful gathered in the name of Christ.

Latin:

Concilia dividuntur in universalia, sive generalia (quae graece dicuntur οἰκουμενικά) & particularia (graece μερικά, ἢ τοπικά).

Universalia sunt, ad quae vel ex omnibus, vel ex plurimis orbis Christiani partibus viri docti & pii vocantur a) . Particularia vel sunt nationalia, ad quae viri docti & pii unius nationis evocantur: vel provincialia, in quibus doctores unius provinciae conveniunt; vel dioecesana, quae ex viris religiosis unius dioeceseos constant b) .

Prob. a. Nunquam quidem in toto orbe exstitit concilium absolute universale, in quo convenerint universae ecclesiae militantis Episcopi & delegati: dicuntur itaque concilia universalia, sive oecumenica οὐγκρίτως, sive respective, in respectu ad concilia nationalia, provincialia & dioecesana. Quamvis igitur non sint simpliciter universalia; habentur tamen talia ob fuissetam ratihabitionem omnium ecclesiarum particularium, a quibus approbata sunt. Maxime aestimantur priora IV. concilia oecumenica: Nicaenum, convocatum ab Imperatore CONSTANTINO M. An. 325. in quo praesentibus 318. Episcopis damnata est haeresis ARII, divinitatem Christi negantis: Concilium Constantinopolitanum I. indictum a THEODOSIO seniore, An. 381. in quo MACEDONIUS & qui cum ipso faciebant, pneumatomachi, ab Episcopis 150. condemnati sunt: Ephesinum I. coactum a THEODOSIO iuniore, in quo damnarant NESTORIUM, communicationem idiomatum negantem: Chalcedonense habitum sub MARCIANO Imperatore, An. 451. contra EVTYCHEN & DIOSCORUM, duas in Christo naturas confundentes, qui damnati sunt ab Episcopis 630.

Prob. b. Concilium nationale habitum est Carthagine in Africa, praeside CYPRIANO.
