Contra CORNELIUS, Episcopus Romanus, instituit concilium nationale, in quo convenerunt Episcopi totius Italiae, teste EUSEBIO hist. eccl. Libr. II. c. 2. Concilia provincialia fuerunt Moguntinum, Coloniense, Aquisgranense, aliaque plura habita, in Germania & descripta Tom. IV. Conciliorum. Concilia dioecesana sunt synodi, sive conventus unius dioeceseos sub uno Episcopo, adeoque minoris auctoritatis.

Quaest. LI. Quae est auctoritas conciliorum?

Concilia pollent auctoritate magna, eaque decretoria a), & decisiva b), quam non habent inde, quod ecclesiam universalem exacte repraesentent c), sed habent eandem dependenter a scriptura sacra & convenientia decretorum suorum cum eadem d): quamvis a posteriori ex consensu ecclesiarum per terrarum orbem existentium illis quaedam accedat auctoritas e), quae tamen non est infallibilis, aut immunis ab errandi periculo f).

Prob. a. Haud exiguam auctoritatem sibi conciliat Doctor ecclesiae publicus pietate, eruditione & amore veritatis, ut ipsius judicium magni fiat: ideoque longe maior est auctoritas plurium Doctorum piorum & eruditione praestantium, qui, collatis examinatisque rerum sententiis, unanimiter decernunt. Plurimi autem aestimatur auctoritas conciliorum decretoria in constituendo bono ordine, & sanciendis ritibus atque corrigendis moribus ecclesiae, ut omnia fiant εὐσχημόνως καὶ κατὰ τάξιν, decenter & secundum ordinem, 1 Cor. XIV, 40.

Prob. b. In dogmatibus fidei, de quibus exortum est dubium & controversia, haud parum valet auctoritas conciliorum decisiva; cuius tamen decisio non simpliciter iudicialis, sed diaconica & ministerialis est, adstricta ad methodum ordinariam interpretandi dicta scripturae, & eliciendi ex illis conclusiones theologicas.

Prob. c. Auctoritas conciliorum non nascitur ex perfecta repraesentatione ecclesiae catholicae; siquidem nullum datur concilium, quod ecclesiam universam exacte repraesentet, adeoque nullum datur concilium absolute universale & oecumenicum. - In concilio Nicaeno I. ex occidente solum fuerunt duo presbyteri missi ex Italia, unus Episcopus ex Gallia, vnus ex Hispania, vnus ex Africa. In Concilio II. & III. nulli fuerunt ex occidente; Pontifices tamen DAMASCUS & COELESTINUS concilia illa confirmarunt, nomine suo & aliorum Episcoporum occidentis, quos ipsi Romae collegerant. In concilio IV. solum fuerunt legati LEONIS, & praeterea misit ipse consensum aliorum episcoporum Hispaniae, Galliae & Italiae, qui in suis provinciis celebratis conciliis ad Leonem scripserunt, se in omnibus eius sententiam sequi. Vid BELLARM. L. I. de concil. XVI.

Prob. d. Conciliorum norma vnica est S. scriptura, a qua omnem certitudinem nanciscuntur. Quare concilia, quae dictum Dei sequuntur, fidem catholicam sincere declarant.

Prob. e. Quae concilia a pluribus ecclesiis recipiuntur, illa tantae auctoritatis esse censentur, ut ex illis verae ecclesiae doctrina haud inualide colligatur.

Prob. f. Decreta conciliorum, etiamsi a Romano Pontifice sint confirmata, non sunt absolutae infallibilitatis. Nam 1) qui extra concilium errori sunt obnoxii, in ipso concilio congregati tales manent: Sed ecclesiae doctores extra concilium errori sunt obnoxii, nisi scripturam velut ducem & lucem vnice sequantur: E. 2) Ex sacris litteris certum est, concilium eccles. Iudaicae gravissime errasse, in quo licet summus praesideret Pontifex, assidente tota synagoga, & vniuerso synedrio, tamen Salvator Christus, ut seductor, blasphemiae condemnatus est, Matth. XXVI, 65. Qui error non tantum fuit facti, sed etiam fidei. Ideo enim Christus condemnatus est, quia dixit, se esse Filium Dei, adeoque impegit synodrium in articulum fidei fundamentalem. 3) Concilia particularia, siue nationalia, siue prouincialia fuerint, haud leuiter errasse, liquido constat: tria enim concilia nationalia in Africa instituit CYPRIANUS, in quibus dogma de rebaptizandis, qui ab haereticis baptizati erant, confirmatum est, teste AUGUSTINO L. III. de bapt. contra Donatistas. At, inquies: - Concilia particularia, confirmata a Pontifice Romano non errant. Resp. Pontifex Rom. nullum habet priuilegium infallibilitatis. Multos Papas fuisse haereticos, dilucide ostendit

D. GERHARD, in confess. catholica lib. I. part. II. cap. 2. fol. 77. Concilia generalia non esse immunia ab errore, vel solum concilium Ephesinum II. suo docet exemplo, quod generale fuit , & tamen hæresin Eutychianam confirmauit, teste BELLARMINO L. I. de conciliis c. 6. fol. 10. Antithesis est Pontificiorum, negantium, concilia vniuersalia a Pontifice Romano confirmata posse errare.

Qui obiiciunt: I. Quidquid vniuersam repræsentat ecclesiam, illud est infallibile: Atqui concilium vniuersale, a Papa conuocatum & confirmatum, &c. Ergo. Maior constat: quia vniuersa ecclesia, quæ est firmamentum veritatis, in fundamento fidei errare nequit. Resp. Nullum vnquam fuit concilium absolute vniuersale, quod vniuersam ecclesiam militantem perfecte repræsentauerit.

II. Summum Christianorum iudicium debet esse infallibile: Atqui concilium legitimum est summum Christianorum iudicium, Matth. XVIII, 17. E. Resp. Summum christianorum iudicium est infallibile, quamdiu consentaneum est normæ suæ, siue verbo diuino. At fieri potest, vt christiani iudices verbum Dei vel non recte interpretentur, vel ex eo conclusiones non accurate eliciant, & consequenter in errorem incidant.

III. Christus est in medio Episcoporum in nomine ipsius congregatorum, qui illis dat lumen sapientiæ, quam expetunt, vt errare nequeant, Matth. XVIII, 20. Resp. In verbis Christi habetur promissio, omnibus vere christianis data, de gratiosa ipsius præsentia & exauditione precum. Quod si ex hac promissione inferri posset priuilegium infallibilitatis, illud commune foret omnibus fidelibus in nomine Christi congregatis.


### Q. LII. Are councils necessary?

Councils are necessary not absolutely ), but hypothetically ).

Prob. a. 1) Holy Scripture, without a numerous congregation of men, suffices both for ἔλεγχον (reproof), or the solid refutation of false dogmas, and for ἐπανόρθωσιν (correction), or the amendment of vicious morals, 2 Tim. III, 17. 2) God has given to every particular church also pastors and teachers, Eph. IV, 12, so that the hearers, imbued with their instruction, may grow in faith and piety. 3) Even by letters, with the presbyters absent, a controversy or schism can be settled, 1 Cor. V, 3. E. Councils are not absolutely necessary. Prob. b.

Councils are necessary for the well-being, so that heresies may be repressed with greater authority, and scandals may be removed by public censure, and ecclesiastical discipline may be solemnly sanctioned.

Latin:

Concilia sunt necessaria non absolute ), sed hypothetice ).

Prob. a. 1) Scriptura S. citra numerosam hominum congregationem sufficit, cum ad ἔλεγχον, seu falsorum dogmatum solidam refutationem, tum ad ἐπανόρθωσιν, seu morum vitiosorum emendationem, 2 Tim. III, 17. 2) Deus cuique etiam particulari ecclesiæ dedit pastores & doctores, Eph. IV, 12. vt illorum informatione imbuti auditores in fide & pietate crescant. 3) Etiam per litteras, absentibus presbyteris, componi potest controuersia, vel schisma, 1 Cor. V, 3. E. concilia non sunt absolute necessaria.

Prob. b. Necessaria sunt concilia ad bene esse, vt maiori auctoritate reprimantur hæreses, & censura publica scandala amoueantur, & disciplina ecclesiastica solemniter sanciatur.


### Of the Anti-christ, the Enemy of the True Church


### Q. LIII. Who is the chief enemy of the true church?

The chief invisible enemy of the church is the devil ), the visible is the Antichrist ). Prob.

Prob. a. From 1 Pet. V, 8. The chief adversary of true believers and saints is the devil, as a roaring lion walking about, and seeking whom he may devour among them. Cf. Eph. VI, 12. Prob. b. From 2 Thess. II, 3. where the Antichrist is called the man of sin, the son of perdition, and an adversary (ἀντικείμενος) for the reason that he is the slave and author of sin, guilty of the perdition which he brings upon himself and others, and an enemy of Christ; indeed, because without His authority and command he constitutes himself head, king, and monarch of the church.

Quest. LIV. Who is the Antichrist? The Antichrist is the great adversary of Christ, arrogating to himself universal rule over the church, exalting himself above Caesar, Kings, and Princes, having his seat especially in the city of Rome, introducing under the guise of singular holiness various corruptions of doctrine and public worship, and propagating them by fraud and violence against those who confess the true faith, to be manifested at a time divinely appointed, and to be destroyed by the spirit of the divine mouth, and to be utterly abolished by Christ coming to the final judgment.

Obs. I. The name of Antichrist is taken in two ways in the scriptures: a) Generally, for any heretics who disseminate false doctrines that oppose the doctrine of Christ, and who pertinaciously defend them. Of whom John says: even now, he says, there are many Antichrists, 1 ep. II, 18. who are commonly called little Antichrists. b) Specifically and κατ' ἐξοχήν (by way of eminence) for that notable adversary of Christ described in 2 Thess. II, whom, for the sake of distinction, we call the great Antichrist.

Obs. II. Some authors distinguish between an eastern and a western Antichrist. They posit the former to be Mahomet, the latter the Roman Pontiff. We admit that certain properties of the Antichrist apply to Mahomet, but not all taken together, or complexly. For the great Antichrist sits in the temple of God, 2 Thess. II, 4. that is: he rules in the midst of the church, which he does not wish to be utterly destroyed, as Mahomet does, but preserved and governed by himself with monarchical power. We describe that great Antichrist according to all the characters and properties which are attributed to him in the Holy Scriptures.

Prob. a. The Antichrist is ἀντικείμενος, that is: a great adversary, who opposes Christ not only in life and practice, but also in public doctrine, 2 Thess. II, 4. and sits in the temple of God. To sit, in sacred phrase, is the same as to reign. But the temple of God is the church, Eph. II, 20. in which the Antichrist sits not as to the position of his body, but as to the arrogation and usurpation of rule over the church. For he sits, and shows himself as if he were God, by arrogating to himself divine power, or supreme and monarchical power over the whole church, the power of making laws by which the consciences of Christians throughout the whole church are bound.

Prob. b. The Antichrist is described in 2 Thess. II, 4. as being ὑπεραιρόμενος ἐπὶ πάντα λεγόμενον θεὸν, ἢ σέβασμα, exalting himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped. Θεὸν λεγόμενοι are earthly gods, or magistrates, Ps. LXXXII, 1. Σέβασμα, according to the interpreter ERASMUS, is properly called that which we adore and venerate with the highest reverence, and which excels in majesty, and can be translated into Latin as Numen (Divinity). To such pride does the Antichrist proceed, that he exalts himself above all magistrates, above all that is to be venerated.

Prob. c. The general seat of the Antichrist is the church, the special one is the city of Rome. For the woman (that great harlot), Rev. XVII, 3. is said to sit upon the beast having seven heads; by which by which seven mountains are denoted, according to v. 9, which is a manifest description of Rome of the seven hills. And thus 2 Thess. II, 7 teaches Paul, that there is some κατέχον, or some κατέχοντα, i.e., an obstacle, or restrainer, by whose impediment the kingdom of the Anti-Christ cannot yet be erected, namely the empire (not the Roman of today, but that old one, to which Rome was subject), or the Emperors, who presided over Rome with power: but these being removed, that ἄνομον [lawless one] was to come, who until now, in the same seat which the Emperors actually held, could not have his throne.

Prob. d. To the Antichrist is attributed ἀποστασία, or a falling away from the heavenly truth, & the orthodox faith, 2 Thess. II, 7, where it is understood not as a common apostasy, but one horrible in respect of quality, and maximal in respect of quantity. The Anti-Christ does not wish this apostasy to be laid bare, but to be hidden, and therefore his mystery of iniquity is said to be effective, 2 Thess. II, 7. But the mystery of iniquity is impiety, cloaked under the guise of piety. To the establishing of which impiety the boasting of miracles contributes not a little. For the coming of the Anti-Christ is according to the working of Satan, in all power (miraculous) & signs, & lying wonders, 2 Thess. II, 9.

Prob. e. The Babylonian Harlot, who is the Anti-Christ, pours out the blood of the saints, & of the prophets (who contradict him). Apoc. XVI, 6. so that she becomes drunk with the blood of the saints & of the martyrs of Jesus, Apoc. XVII, 6.

Prob. f. The ὁ ἄνομος [lawless one] shall be revealed in his time, 2 Thess. II, 8. The Anti-Christ is ἄνομος, or lawless, who wishes to be restrained by no bonds of laws, whose pride, affected monarchy, force & frauds will be detected & argued at the time divinely constituted.

Prob. g. The Lord will destroy the Anti-Christ with the spirit of his mouth, & will abolish him by the appearance of his coming, 2 Thess. II, 8. Christ defeats the Anti-Christ with the spirit of his mouth, in that his wickedness is spiritual, and therefore to be destroyed not by corporal, but by spiritual weapons, until he is utterly abolished by the most glorious coming of Christ to the universal judgment.

Latin:

Præcipuus ecclesiæ hostis inuisibilis est diabolus ), visibilis est Antichristus ).

Prob. a. Ex 1 Petr. V, 8. Praecipuus vere credentium & sanctorum adversarius est diabolus, sicut leo rugiens circumiens, & quaerens, quem ex illis abforbeat. Conf. Eph. VI, 12. Prob. b. Ex 2 Thess. II, 3. ubi Antichristus dicitur homo peccati, filius perditionis & adversarius (ἀντικείμενος) ideo, quod est mancipium & auctor peccati, reus perditionis, quam sibi aliisque accersit, & hostis Christi; quippe qui sine illius auctoritate & iussu caput, regem & monarcham ecclesiae se constituit.

Quaest. LIV. Quis est Antichristus? Antichristus est magnus Christi adversarius, universale regimen in ecclesiam sibi arrogans , supra Caesarem, Reges, Principesque se extollens , sedem suam praecipue in urbe Roma habens , sub specie singularis sanctitatis varias doctrinae & sacrorum publicorum corruptelas invehens eaque, fraude & violentia oppressis verae fidei confessoribus, propagans , tempore divinitus statuto manifestandus , & spiritu oris diuini destruendus, atque a Christo, ad extremum iudicium veniente, penitus abolendus .

Obs. I. Nomen Antichristi in scripturis bifariam accipitur: a) Generatim, pro quibusvis haereticis, qui falsas & doctrinae Christi adversantes doctrinas disseminant, easque pertinaciter propugnant. De quibus Ioannes: etiam nunc, inquit, Anti-Christi multi sunt, 1 ep. II, 18. qui communiter dicuntur Anti-Christi parvi. b) Speciatim & κατ' ἐξοχήν pro insigni illo Christi adversario, 2 Thess. II. descripto, quem, differentiae causa Anti-Christum magnum vocamus.

Obs. II. Distinguunt nonnulli auctores inter Anti-Christum orientalem, & occidentalem. Illum statuunt esse Mahometum, hunc Pontificem Romanum. Fatemur, quasdam proprietates Anti-Christi competere Mahometo, sed non omnes coniunctim, sive complexe sumtas. Nam Anti-Christus magnus sedet in templo Dei, 2 Thess. II, 4. hoc est; in media ecclesia dominatur, quam non plane vult convulsum, ut Mahometus, sed conservatam, & a se potestate monarchica gubernatam. Anti-Christum illum magnum secundum omnes characteres & proprietates, quae in sacris litteris ipsi tribuuntur, describimus.

Prob. a. Anti-Christus est ἀντικείμενος, id est: magnus adversarius, qui non tantum vita & praxi, sed etiam doctrina publica Christo adversatur, 2 Thess. II, 4. & sedet in templo Dei. Sedere, phrasi sacra idem est, quod regnare. Templum Dei autem est ecclesia, Eph. II, 20. in qua Anti-Christus sedet non quoad situm corporis, sed quoad arrogationem & usurpationem regiminis in ecclesiam. Sedet enim, & ostentat se quasi sit Deus, arrogando tibi potentiam divinam, sive supremam ac monarchicam potestatem super universam ecclesiam, potestatem ferendi leges, quibus Christianorum conscientiae per totam ecclesiam obligentur.

Prob. b. Anti-Christus describitur 2 Thess. II, 4. quod sit ὑπεραιρόμενος ἐπὶ πάντα λεγόμενον θεὸν, ἢ σέβασμα, extollens se super omnem, qui dicitur Deus & cultus. Θεὸν λεγόμενοι sunt dii terrestres, sive magistratus, Ps. LXXXII, 1. Σέβασμα, interprete ERASMO, proprie dicitur id, quod adoramus, & summa reverentia veneramur, & quod maiestate praecellit, latineque verti potest Numen. Eo superbia procedit Anti-christus, vt se super omnes magistratus, super omnes venerandos efferat.

Prob. c. Sedes Anti-Christi generalis est ecclesia, specialis urbs Roma. Nam mulier (meretrix illa magna) Apoc. XVII, 3. dicitur sedere super bestiam habentem capita septem; quibus septem montes denotantur, iuxta v. 9. quae est manifesta descriptio Romae septicollis. Et sic 2 Thess. II, 7. docet Paulus, esse aliquod κατέχον, seu aliquem κατέχοντα, i.e. obstantem, vel detinentem, quo impediente regnum Anti-Christi nondum possit erigi, nempe imperium (Romanum non hodiernum, sed vetus illud, cui suberat Roma), sive Imperatores, qui Romae cum potestate praerant: His autem sublatis, venturum esse ἄνομον illum, qui hactenus in eadem sede, quam Imperatores actu tenerent, thronum suum habere non potuerit.

Prob. d. Tribuitur Antichristo ἀποστασία, sive defectio a veritate caelesti, & fide orthodoxa, 2 Thess. II, 7. ubi apostasia non vulgaris, sed respectu qualitatis horrenda, respectu quantitatis maxima, intelligitur. Hanc apostasiam Anti-Christus non vult denudari, sed occultari, ideoque ipsius mysterium iniquitatis efficax esse perhibetur, 2 Thess. II, 7. Mysterium autem iniquitatis est impietas, specie pietatis palliata. Ad quam impietatem fundandam haud parum facit iactantia miraculorum. Adventus enim Anti-Christi est iuxta operationem Satanae, in omni virtute (mirifica) & signis, & prodigiis mendacii, 2 Thess. II, 9.

Prob. e. Meretrix Babylonica, quae est Anti-Christus, effundit sanguinem sanctorum, & prophetarum (ipsi contradicentium) . Apoc. XVI, 6. vt ebria fit de sanguine sanctorum & martyrum Iesu, Apoc. XVII, 6.

Prob. f. Revelabitur ὁ ἄνομος suo tempore, 2 Thess. II, 8. Anti-Christus est ἄνομος, sive exlex, qui nullis legum vinculis vult coerceri, cuius superbia, affectata monarchia, vis & fraudes tempore divinitus constituto detegentur & arguentur.

Prob. g. Dominus Anti-Christum destruet spiritu oris sui, & abolebit apparitione adventus sui, 2 Thess. II, 8. Christus Anti-Christum debellat spiritu oris sui, eo, quod nequitia illius spiritualis est, adeoque non corporalibus, sed spiritualibus armis destruenda, donec gloriosissimo adventu Christi ad iudicium universale penitus aboleatur.


### Q. LIII. Who is the chief enemy of the true church?: Q

Q.

LV. Is the Anti-Christ a determined human individual? By the Anti-Christ in the sacred scriptures is not understood a determined human individual, or a single man lacking a successor, & fulfilling all his malice within the space of a few years.

Prob. 1) The Anti-Christ, as Paul teaches, 2 Thess. II, 6. 7. was then to come, when that which hindered his kingdom from being erected, namely the Roman empire, the western one, had been removed, & was to endure until the glorious coming of Christ, ibid. v. 8. but one human individual cannot survive for so many centuries, which intervene from the destroyed western Roman empire until the glorious coming of Christ. Therefore, by the Anti-Christ is not understood a determined human individual.

2) In the lifetime of one man, the kingdom of the Anti-Christ could neither be planted, nor can the things be accomplished which it is predicted in the scriptures will be done in it. Therefore the Anti-Christ is not one human individual. The consequence is evident, but the antecedent is proved: because, a) the kingdom of the Anti-Christ was to be planted not by open force & arms, but by false doctrines, yet speciously encrusted with manifold fraud, and also by lying signs & wonders, confirmed in appearance by the cooperation of Satan, 2 Thess. II, 9. 10. b) The fraud of the Anti-Christ was to wander far and wide through the world, so that peoples & nations everywhere might be induced to ἀποστασίαν, or to a falling away from the truth, Apoc. XVII, 1. all of which cannot happen in the lifetime of one man.

Q.

LVI. Is the Roman Pontiff the Anti-Christ? The Roman Pontiff is the great Anti-Christ.

Proof: Whoever is the ἀντικείμενος [adversary], or the great adversary of Christ, arrogating to himself universal rule over the Church, exalting himself above Kings, Princes, and the Roman Emperor himself, having his seat principally in the city of Rome, introducing under the guise of singular holiness various corruptions of doctrine and public worship, and propagating them by fraud and violence after suppressing the confessors of the true faith; manifested at a time divinely appointed, to be destroyed by the spirit of the divine mouth, and to be utterly abolished by Christ coming to the final judgment, he is the great Anti-Christ. But the Roman Pontiff is the ἀντικείμενος, etc. Therefore. We demonstrated the truth of the major premise in Question LIV. The individual members of the minor premise are validly proven. For: 1) The Roman Pontiff is the ἀντικείμενος; because without the command and authority of Christ he wishes to be the ecumenical Bishop, and an infallible one, the head, monarch, and spouse of the Church: and thus he arrogates to himself the honor proper to Christ. He sits, therefore, in the temple of God, and shows himself as if he were God.

2) The Roman Pontiffs learned from BONIFACE VIII to exalt themselves above the Emperor, the τὸν σεβασὸν [Augustus] (as he is called, Acts 25:25), as much as the sun is preferred to the moon. Whence they have dared more than once to cast Caesars, Kings, and Princes from their thrones, to transfer empires, kingdoms, and principalities to others, to absolve subjects from their oath of fidelity, and thus in reality to exalt themselves against everything that is called God or an Object of Worship.

3) The Pope has his seat in the seven-hilled city of Rome, once the τῷ κατέχοντι [the restrainer], the Roman Empire, was removed.

4) The apostasy of the Roman Pontiff from heavenly truth was shown above in Question XXXVI. 5) How much Christian blood has been shed at the instigation of the Roman Pontiff, Germany, France, Spain, Belgium, etc., have learned by many experiences.

6) The mystery of papal iniquity has been revealed through LUTHER and his followers.

7) Christ is progressively defeating his adversary, namely the Pope, with spiritual weapons, whom he will so abolish by the brightness of his coming to the universal judgment that an end will be put to his ecclesiastical monarchy.

Latin:

Quaest. LV. Estne Anti-Christus determinatum individuum humanum?

Per Anti-Christum in sacris litteris non intelligitur determinatum individuum humanum, aut vnicus homo carens successore, & intra spatium paucorum annorum omnem suam malitiam complens.

Prob. 1) Anti-Christus, docente Paulo, 2 Thess. II, 6. 7. tum erat venturus, cum id, quod obstabat eius regno erigendo, imperium Romanum, occidentale scilicet, sublatum fuerit, & duraturus vfque ad gloriosum Christi adventum, ibid. v. 8. sed vnum hominis individuum tot saeculis, quae a destructo imperio Romano occidentali ad Christi adventum gloriosum vfque intercedunt, superesse non potest. E. per Anti-Christum non intelligitur determinatum individuum humanum.

2) Vnius hominis aetate nec plantari potuit regnum Anti-Christi, nec peragi possunt res, quas in eo peractum iri in scripturis praedictum est. Ergo Anti-Christus non est vnum hominis individuum. Consequentia est euidens, Antecedens autem probatur: quia, a) regnum Anti-Christi plantandum erat non vi aperta & armis, sed doctrinis falsis, speciose tamen fraude multiplici incrustatis, nec non signis & prodigiis mendacibus, Satana cooperante in speciem confirmatis, 2 Thess. II, 9. 10. b) Fraus Anti-Christi peruagatura erat longe lateque per orbem, vt populi & gentes vbique ad ἀποστασίαν, siue ad defectionem a veritate inducerentur, Apoc. XVII, 1. quae omnia vnius hominis aetate fieri nequeunt.

Quaest. LVI. Estne Pontifex Romanus Anti-Christus?

Pontifex Romanus est Anti-Christus magnus.

Prob Quicumque est ἀντικείμενος, sive magnus Christi aduersarius, vniuersale regimen in ecclesiam sibi arrogans, supra Reges, Principes & ipsum Imperatorem Rom. se extollens, sedem suam præcipue in vrbe Roma habens, sub specie singularis sanctitatis varias doctrinæ & sacrorum publicorum corruptelas inuehens, easque, fraude & violentia oppressis veræ fidei confessoribus, propagans; tempore diuinitus statuto manifestatus, spiritu oris diuini destruendus, & a Christo, ad extremum iudicium veniente, penitus abolendus, ille est Anti-Christus magnus. Atqui Pontifex Romanus est ἀντικείμενος &c. Ergo. Maioris veritatem demonstrauimus Quæst. LIV. Minoris membra singula valide probantur. Nam: 1) Pontifex Romanus est ἀντικείμενος; quia sine iussu & auctoritate Christi vult esse Episcopus œcumenicus, isque infallibilis, caput, monarcha, & sponsus ecclesiæ: adeoque arrogat sibi honorem Christo proprium. Sedet igitur in templo Dei, & ostentat se, quasi fit Deus.

2) Didicerunt Pontifices Romani a BONIFACIO VIII. tantum se efferre supra Imperatorem τὸν σεβασὸν (vt vocatur, Act. XXV, 25.), quantum sol præfertur lunæ. Vn. de Cæsares, Reges, Principes de throno deiicere, imperia, regna & principatus ad alios transferre, subditos a iuramento fidelitatis absoluere, atque adeo reapse aduersus omne, quod Deus, aut Numen dicitur, se extollere plus vice simplici ausi sunt.

3) Papa sedem suam habet in vrbe septicolli Roma, sublato τῷ κατέχοντι, imperio Romano.

4) Apostasia Pontificis Rom. a veritate cœlesti supra ostensa est qu. XXXVI. 5) Quantum sanguinis christiani instinctu pontificis Rom. effusum sit, multis experimentis didicit Germania, Gallia, Hispania, Belgium &c.

6) Mysterium impietatis papalis reuelatum est per LVTHERVM, & eius asseclas.

7) Christus aduersarium suum, scil. Papam, pœcœssiue debellat armis spiritualibus, quem claritate aduentus sui ad vniuersale iudicium sic abolebit, vt ipsius monarchiæ ecclesiasticæ finis imponatur.


### Q. LIII. Who is the chief enemy of the true church?: The Antithesis is that of the Papists, who deny that the Pope is the Anti-Christ

The Antithesis is that of the Papists, who deny that the Pope is the Anti-Christ.

Their stronger arguments are:

I. The Anti-Christ is one, 2 Thess. 2:4. The Pope is not one; because many Roman Pontiffs are constituted. Therefore the Pope is not the Anti-Christ.

Resp. The Anti-Christ is one, not by numerical or monadic unity, in the manner in which the sun is one, but by successive unity in the manner in which the King of France is one, who has his successors.

II. The Anti-Christ departs from Christ, 2 Thess. 2:3. The Roman Pontiff does not depart from Christ. Therefore.

Resp. Distinguish between total and partial defection. The defection of the Roman Pontiff from the doctrine of Christ is not total, since he is said to sit in the temple of God; but it is partial, and that by reason of its quality, notable and horrible, and by reason of its quantity, or of accomplices, places, and times, it is the greatest.

III. The Anti-Christ denies Christ, 1 John 4:3. The Roman Pontiff does not, etc. Therefore.

Resp. The Roman Pontiff denies Christ not openly but consequentially, while he undermines the mediatorial office of Christ, and teaches that the merit of Christ does not suffice for our sins, but that the merits of the saints must be added to it, and that the indulgences for sins are to be bought for a certain sum of money.

IV. The Anti-Christ comes after the Roman Empire is overturned. But in these our times the Roman Empire has not yet been overturned. Therefore in these our times the Anti-Christ has not yet come.

The major premise is proved from 2 Thess. II, 6. Καὶ νῦν τὸ κατέχον οἴδατε, And now you know what withholds; so that he might be revealed in his time. For the mystery of iniquity is already at work: provided that he who now withholds is taken out of the way. The ancient Fathers agree that by τὸ κατέχον (that which withholds) is understood the Roman Empire, which stands in the way of the establishing of the kingdom of the Anti-Christ. Resp. Distinguish between the old Western Roman Empire and the modern Romano-Germanic Empire. It is not the latter, but the former, that stands in the way of the kingdom of the Anti-Christ. For since the seat of the Anti-Christ was to be fixed in the city of Rome, and this was subject to the old Roman Empire, and was its primary seat, it could not happen that the Anti-Christ would have his seat fixed in Rome. For two supreme empires, such as the old Roman one was, and such as the kingdom of the Anti-Christ was to be in its time, could not subsist together in one Rome.

V. Two witnesses are to come at the same time that the Anti-Christ will come, Apoc. XI, 3.

But these two witnesses (whoever they may be) have not yet come; therefore, neither has the Anti-Christ come.

Resp. All confessors of the truth and of the Anti-Christ are called two witnesses, both because of their fewness, and because according to the law of God every truth stands in the mouth of two or three witnesses. VI. The Anti-Christ is to cast fire from heaven onto the earth: the Roman Pontiff does not cast fire from heaven onto the earth. Therefore. The major premise is evident from Apoc. XIII, 13. Resp. Distinguish between literal and metaphorical fire. Although the Pope does not cast literal fire onto the earth, he does cast metaphorical fire, namely the lightning bolt of excommunication, upon all who oppose his superstition.

VII. The Anti-Christ will reign for 42 months. Apoc. XI, 2. The Pope has reigned for many centuries. Therefore, etc. Resp. Distinguish between lunar and mystical months. The cited passage cannot be understood as lunar months properly so called; because those unhappy works which the Anti-Christ will perform cannot be accomplished in so short a time. And therefore mystical months are noted. A mystical month, however, comprises 30 years, see Ezech. IV, 5. 6. Consequently, 42 mystical months become 1260 years. But since the year of the beginning of the Anti-Christ is not clearly known to us, the final year of the world cannot be certainly deduced from this term.

Latin:

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, negantium, Papam esse Anti-Christum.

Quorum potiora argumenta sunt:

I. Anti-Christus est unus, 2 Thess. II, 4. Papa non est unus; quia multi Pontifices Romani constituuntur. Ergo Papa non est Anti-Christus.

Resp. Anti-Christus est unus, non vnitate numerica, aut monadica, ad eum modum, quo sol vnus est, sed successiua ad eum modum, quo vnus est rex Galliæ, qui suos habet successores.

II. Anti-Christus deficit a Christo, 2 Thess. II, 3. Pontifex Romanus non deficit a Christo. Ergo.

Resp. Distingu. inter defectionem totalem, & partialem. Defectio pontificis Rom. a doctrina Christi non est totalis, cum in templo Dei sedere dicatur; sed partialis, eaque ratione qualitatis notabilis & horrenda, ratione quantitatis, seu complicum, locorum & temporum, maxima.

III. Anti-Christus abnegat Christum, 1 Io. IV, 3. Pontifex Rom. non &c. Ergo.

Resp. Pontifex Rom. Christum abnegat non aperte sed consequenter, dum labefactat officium Christi mediatorium, & docet, meritum Christi non sufficere pro nostris peccatis, sed eidem addenda esse merita sanctorum, & indulgentias peccatorum certa soluta pecunia esse emendas.

IV. Euerso imperio Rom. venit Anti-Christus. At his nostris temporibus imperium Rom. nondum est euersum. Ergo his nostris temporibus nondum venit Anti-Christus.

Maior probatur ex 2 Thess. II, 6. Καὶ νῦν τὸ κατέχον οἴδατε, Et nunc quid detineat, scitis; vi reueletur ille suo tempore. Nam mysterium iam efficax est iniquitatis: dummodo, qui detinet nunc, e medio fit (sublatus). Consentiunt Patres antiqui, per τὸ κατέχον intelligi imperium Romanum, quod erigendo regno Anti-Christi obstat. Resp. Disting. inter imperium Romanum occidentale vetus, & hodiernum imperium Romano-Germanicum. Non hoc, sed illud regno Anti-Christi obstat. Cum enim sedes Anti-Christi figenda esset in vrbe Roma, & hæc imperio Romano veteri subiecta, eiusque primaria sedes esset, fieri non poterat, vt Anti-Christus sedem suam Romæ defixam haberet. Neque enim duo imperia summa, quale fuit Romanum vetus, & quale Anti-Christi regnum suo tempore futurum erat, simul in vna Roma subsistere poterant.

V. Duo testes venturi sunt eodem tempore, quo Anti-Christus veniet, Apoc. XI, 3.

At hi duo testes (quicunque tandem illi sint) nondum venerunt; Ergo nec Anti-Christus venit.

Resp. Omnes veritatis confessores & Anti-Christi dicuntur duo testes, cum propter paucitatem, tum quòd iuxta legem Dei in ore duorum, aut trium testium consistit omne verum. VI. Anti-Christus ignem de cælo in terram deiecturus est: Pontifex Rom. non deiicit de cælo ignem in terram. Ergo. Maior patet ex Apoc. XIII, 13. Resp. Dist. inter ignem proprium, & metaphoricum. Licet Papa ignem proprium non deiiciat in terras, deiicit tamen ignem metaphoricum, nempe fulmen excommunicationis, in omnes superstitioni ipsius oblistentes.

VII. Anti-Christus regnabit mensibus 42. Apoc. XI, 2. Papa multis sæculis regnauit. Ergo. &c. Resp. Dist. inter menses lunares, & mysticos. Locus citatus de mensibus lunaribus proprie dictis intelligi nequit; quia infelicia illa opera, quæ præstabit Anti-Christus, non possunt tempore adeo breui expediri. Ideoque notantur menses mystici. Mensis autem mysticus complectitur 30. annos, vid. Ezech. IV, 5. 6. Proinde menses mystici 42. fiunt anni 1260. Cum autem annus initii Anti-Christi nobis haud liquido constet, ex hoc termino annus mundi finalis certo colligi nequit.


### Q. LIII. Who is the chief enemy of the true church?: A Sigh

A SIGH

To You, God the Father, Father of mercy, fountain of comfort, preserver of the works which You have created, be praise and immortal glory, because You have called me, redeemed by the most precious blood of Your only-begotten Son, to the fellowship of Your true church.

With a grateful heart I acknowledge that, with You as leader and patron, I have been made a member of that mystical body whose head is my Jesus, with whom it is my care and my heart's desire to be joined by the perpetual bond of faith. Preserve me, I beseech You, in the kingdom of grace, and at last transfer me into the kingdom of glory, so that in the triumphant church I may triumph full of joy, and sing Your praises eternally.

Latin:

SUSPIRIUM

Tibi, Deus Pater, Pater misericordiæ, fons solatii, conseruator operum, quæ condidisti, fit laus & gloria immortalis, quod me, pretiosissimo Filii tui vnigeniti sanguine redemptum, ad veræ ecclesiæ tuæ consortium vocasti.

Grato animo agnosco, quod te duce & auspice, factus sim membrum corporis illius mystici, cuius caput est Iesus meus, cum quo perpetuo vinculo fidei iungi, curæ mihi cordique est. Serua me, quæso! in regno gratiæ, & tandem me transfer in regnum gloriæ, vt in ecclesia triumphante plenus lætitiæ triumphem, tuasque laudes æternum canam.


## 39 On the Threefold Hierarchical State, and the Ministry

I. How many states or orders are divinely instituted in the church? The states or orders divinely instituted in the church are three: the ecclesiastical, the political, and the oecumenical state.

Proof. The ecclesiastical state serves the gathering and instruction of the church, and is opposed to heresies and corruptions of doctrine: The political state serves the defense and external governance of the church, and is opposed to tyranny and robbery: The oecumenical state serves the propagation of the church, and is opposed to wandering lusts. This triple state is also called the triple hierarchy.

Question II. What is the ecclesiastical ministry? The ecclesiastical ministry is a sacred and public office, divinely instituted, and entrusted to certain and suitable men through a legitimate calling, so that, instructed with peculiar power, they may teach the word of God, administer the sacraments, and preserve ecclesiastical discipline, for the glory of God and the promotion of the salvation of men.

Question III. What is the principal efficient cause of the ecclesiastical ministry? The principal efficient cause of the ecclesiastical ministry is God a), Father b), Son c), and Holy Spirit d). Proof. a. Just as God is the author of grace: so with Him lies the force and power of instituting and preserving the office by which the means of grace are applied to men.

Moreover, God is the author of the ecclesiastical ministry: 1) by promising teachers of the church, and by calling those promised to the sacred office, Jer.

III, 15. 1 Cor. XII, 28.: 2) by revealing what pertains to the right conduct of the sacred ministry. e.g., what doctrine is to be preached, Gal.

I, 8. what pertains to teaching, reproving, and exhorting, 2 Tim.

III, 14. what sacraments there are, and how they are to be administered, 1 Cor.

XI, 23.: 3) by instructing the teachers of the church with necessary gifts, 2 Cor.

III, 5. ch.

IV, 6.

4) by concurring with the actions of the ministers, and by granting a salutary success, Matt.

X, 20.

1 Cor.

III, 6.

Constitution of the ecclesiastical ministry, and the calling of certain persons to the sacred office, is a divine action ad extra, common to the three persons of the Godhead. Regarding God the Father, Paul says in Gal. I, 16: God called me, that he might reveal his son in me.

Proof c. Christ gave Apostles, Prophets, Evangelists, Teachers & Pastors, Eph. IV, 11. 12. who says expressly: John XX, 21: As the Father has sent me, so I send you.

Proof d. The Holy Spirit has appointed Bishops to feed the church, Acts XX, 28.

Question IV. What is understood here by divine calling?

Observation Hence, a distinction must be observed between the calling of all men to the church, and the calling of certain persons to a peculiar ecclesiastical state. The former is called general, the latter personal.

Question V. How manifold is the divine calling to the ecclesiastical ministry?

Proof a. God calls immediately in a threefold way. By divine calling here is understood the deputation of a certain and suitable person to the ecclesiastical ministry with the power of publicly teaching, administering the sacraments, and exercising ecclesiastical discipline, done by God either alone, or with the intervening arbitrary work of men.

The calling to the ecclesiastical ministry is twofold: one immediate, or extraordinary; the other mediate, or ordinary.

An immediate, or extraordinary, calling is that by which God alone calls, either by immediately addressing a certain person and sending him to teach, or by immediately commanding others to designate this or that teacher, or by showing [him] by an external sign which He Himself has chosen.

A mediate, or ordinary, calling is that by which God calls a certain person to the ecclesiastical ministry, with the intervening arbitrary work of those men who are members of the church.

you to Pharaoh, Exod. III, 10. Jeremiah: I have appointed you a Prophet to the nations themselves, Jer. I, 5. And Christ αὐτοπροσώπως called the Apostles, Matth. X, 1. 2) By immediately commanding others, that they might designate this or that teacher. Thus God immediately commanded Moses, that he should declare Aaron the priest; Elijah, that he should declare Elisha the Prophet of the Lord, Exod. XXVIII, 1. 1 Reg. XIX, 16. 3) By showing a sign external, which God himself has chosen. By this pact we read that Matthias the Apostle was called & elected, Acts I, 14., seq. where the Apostles having prayed said: You, Lord, the heart-knower of all, demonstrate (by an external sign, which was the lot), whom you have chosen. God therefore by the lot, as an external sign, showed that he himself had chosen Matthias v. 20. and so this calling also was immediate; otherwise Matthias could not have been held a true Apostle, since for the Apostolate is required most especially a divine, and that an immediate, calling *).

Prob. b. Although a mediate calling, which happens with God moderating through the church, or the members of the church, does not obtain an equal degree of dignity with an immediate one, nevertheless its principal cause is God, so that even a mediate calling must be judged divine. For 1) The Lord of the harvest sends laborers into his harvest, Matth. IX, 38. Therefore he sends, as long as the harvest lasts: but it lasts until the consummation of the age. But he does not always send immediately, but mediately: Therefore those who are sent through the mediation of men, are also sent by God. 2) The Ephesian presbyters, called mediately, are said to have been constituted by the Holy Spirit himself to shepherd the church of God, Acts XX, 28. Sylvanus and Timothy were approved by God, so that the gospel might be entrusted to them (mediately), 1 Thess. II, 4. col. c. I. 1. Archippus, though not called immediately, received his ministry from the Lord (viz. through the mediation of men), Col. IV, 17. 3) A mediate calling happens according to an order divinely prescribed, 2 Tim. II, 2. Tit. I, 5. 9. Therefore it is divine. 4) God adorns those called mediately with excellent gifts. Let Stephen be an example, elected and called mediately, whom God instructed with wondrous gifts, so that no one could resist the wisdom & the spirit, with which he spoke, Acts VI, 10. 5) God grants a salutary success to ministers called mediately. For Timothy, ἐμμέσως called, was able to save both himself and those who heard him, 1 Tim. IV, 16.

You say: I. Besides an immediate & mediate calling, there is given a mixed one, such as was LUTHER'S for the purging of the doctrine of faith from the corruptions of the Papists, which was extraordinary, & yet mediate. Resp. The calling of LUTHER to the work of reformation was mediate, although in the work of reformation itself he was blessed by God with extraordinary grace & success.

You say: II. God does not accompany a mediate calling with special grace: because in it many arts, and many abuses intervene. Resp. As God does not cease to cooperate with created things by a general concurrence, although against his intention many things intervene in the action: so by a special concurrence God influences a mediate calling, even if arts, or abuses intervene. For one must always distinguish between a human work, & a divine one. When a King is to be elected, very many arts intervene, nor yet does the divine ordination cease, Rom. XIII, 4.

Latin:

I. Quot sunt status, sive ordines in ecclesia divinitus instituti? Status, sive ordines in ecclesia divinitus instituti sunt tres: Status ecclesiasticus, politicus & oecumenicus.

Prob. Status ecclesiasticus inferuit ecclesiae collectioni & informationi, atque opponitur haeresibus & doctrinae corruptelis: Status politicus inferuit ecclesiae defensioni, & externae gubernationi, atque opponitur tyrannidi & latrociniis: Status oecumenicus inferuit ecclesiae propagationi, atque opponitur vagis libidinibus. Triplex hic status dicitur etiam triplex hierarchia.

Quaest. II. Quid est ministerium ecclesiasticum? Ministerium ecclesiasticum est officium sacrum & publicum, divinitus institutum, & certis atque idoneis hominibus per legitimam vocationem commendatum, vt peculiari potestate instructi verbum Dei doceant, sacramenta administrent, & disciplinam ecclesiasticam conferuent, ad gloriam Dei, hominumque salutem promouendam.

Quaest. III. Quae est causa efficiens principalis ministerii ecclesiastici? Causa efficiens principalis ministerii ecclesiastici est Deus a), Pater b), Filius c) & Spiritus sanctus d). Prob. a. Quemadmodum Deus est auctor gratiae: ita penes eundem vis & potestas est instituendi & conferuandi officium, quo media gratiae hominibus applicantur.

Est autem Deus auctor ministerii ecclesiastici: 1) doctores ecclesiae promittendo, promissos ad officium sacrum vocando, Ier.

III, 15. 1 Cor. XII, 28.: 2) reuelando, quae ad ministerium sacrum recte gerendum spectant. v gr. quae doctrina praedicanda sit, Gal.

I, 8. quae ad docendum, arguendum, cohortandum pertineant, 2 Tim.

III, 14. quae sacramenta, & quomodo administranda sint, 1 Cor.

XI, 23.: 3) doctores ecclesiae necessariis donis instruendo, 2 Cor.

III, 5. c.

IV, 6.

4) cum actionibus ministrorum concurrendo, & successum salutarem largiendo, Matth.

X, 20.

1 Cor.

III, 6.

Constitutio ministerii ecclesiastici, & vocatio certarum personarum ad officium sacrum, est actio divina ad extra, tribus divinitatis personis communis. De Deo Patre inquit Paullus Gal. I, 16. Deus vocavit me, ut revelaret filium suum in me.

Prob. c. Christus dedit Apostolos, Prophetas, Evangelistas, Doctores & Pastores, Eph. IV, 11. 12. qui diserte inquit: Io. XX, 21. Sicut me misit Pater, ita ego mitto vos.

Prob. d. Spiritus S. constituit Episcopos ad pascendum ecclesiam, Act. XX, 28.

Quaest. IV. Quid hic per vocationem divinam intelligitur?

Obs. Proinde observanda distinctio inter vocationem omnium hominum ad ecclesiam, & vocationem certarum personarum ad peculiarem statum ecclesiasticum. Illa generalis, haec personalis vocatur.

Quaest. V. Quotuplex est vocatio divina ad ministerium ecclesiasticum?

Prob. a. Immediate vocat Deus triplici modo Per vocationem divinam hic intelligitur deputatio certae & idoneae personae ad ministerium ecclesiasticum cum potestate publice docendi, sacramenta administrandi, & disciplinam ecclesiasticam exercendi, facta a Deo vel solo, vel interveniente hominum opera arbitraria.

Vocatio ad ministerium ecclesiasticum est duplex, alia immediata, sive extraordinaria, alia mediata, sive ordinaria .

Vocatio immediata, sive extraordinaria est , qua solus Deus vocat, vel immediate alloquendo certam personam, eamque ad docendum mittendo, vel immediate praecipiendo aliis, ut hunc vel illum doctorem designent, vel signo externo, quem ipse elegerit, ostendendo .

Vocatio mediata, sive ordinaria est, qua Deus certam personam ad ministerium ecclesiasticum vocat, interveniente opera arbitraria illorum hominum, qui sunt membra ecclesiae .

te ad Pharaonem, Exod. III, 10. Jeremiam: Constitui te Prophetam ipsis gentibus, Ier. I, 5. Et Christus αὐτοπροσώπως vocauit Apostolos, Matth. X, 1. 2) Immediate præcipiendo aliis, vt hunc vel illam doctorem designent. Ita Deus immediate præcepit Mosi, vt Aaronem sacerdotem; Eliæ, vt Elisæum Prophetam Domini declararet, Exod. XXVIII, 1. 1 Reg. XIX, 16. 3) Signo externo, quem ipse Deus elegerit, ostendendo. Hoc pacto Matthiam Apostolum vocatum & electum esse legimus, Actor. I, 14., seq. vbi Apostoli precati dixerunt: Tu, Domine, cardiognosta omnium, demonstra (per signum externum, quod fuit sors), quem elegeris. Deus itaque per sortem, velut signum externum ostendit, quod elegerit ipse Matthiam v. 20. adeoque & hæc vocatio fuit immediata; alias Matthias non potuisset haberi verus Apostolus, cùm ad Apostolatum requiratur vel maxime diuina, eaque immediata vocatio *).

Prob. b. Quamuis vocatio mediata, quæ moderante Deo fit per ecclesiam, aut membra ecclesiæ, non parem cum immediata dignitatis gradum obtineat, eius tamen caussa princeps est Deus, vt etiam vocatio mediata censenda sit diuina. Nam 1) Dominus messis mittit operarios in messem, Matth. IX, 38. Ergo mittit, quamdiu messis durat: durat autem vsque ad consummationem sæculi. Non autem semper mittit immediate, sed mediate: Ergo qui mediantibus hominibus mittuntur, etiam a Deo mittuntur. 2) Mediate vocati Ephesini presbyteri ab ipso Spiritu S. ad pascendum ecclesiam Dei constituti dicuntur, Act. XX, 28. Syluanus ac Timotheus probati sunt a Deo, vt ipsis (mediate) crederetur euangelium, 1 Thess. II, 4. col. c. I. 1. Archippus, non immediate tamen vocatus, ministerium suum a Domino (scil. mediantibus hominibus) accepit, Col. IV, 17. 3) Vocatio mediata fit secundum ordinem diuinitus præscriptum, 2 Tim. II, 2. Tit. I, 5. 9. E. est diuina. 4) Deus mediate vocatos excellentibus donis exornat. Exemplo sit Stephanus, mediate electus ac vocatus, quem Deus instruxit donis mirificis, vt nemo potuerit resistere sapientiæ & spiritui, quo loquebatur, Act. VI, 10. 5) Deus ministris, mediate vocatis, salutarem largitur successum. Nam Timotheus, ἐμμέσως vocatus, poterat tam seipsum saluum facere, quam eos, qui audiebant ipsum, 1 Tim. IV, 16.

Dicis: I. Præter vocationem immediatam & mediatam, datur mixta, qualis fuit LVTHERI ad repurgandam doctrinam fidei a corruptelis Pontificiorum, quæ fuit extraordinaria, & tamen mediata. Resp. Vocatio LVTHERI ad opus reformationis fuit mediata, quamquam in ipso reformationis opere extraordinaria gratia & successu a Deo fuerit beatus.

Dicis: II. Deus non comitatur speciali gratia vocationem mediatam: quia in illa multæ artes, multique abusus interueniunt. Resp. Vt non desinit Deus cooperari rebus creatis concursu generali, quamquam contra intentionem ipsius actioni multa interueniant: ita speciali concursu Deus influit in vocationem mediatam, etsi artes, aut abusus interueniant. Semper enim distinguendum est inter opus humanum, & diuinum. Cum eligendus est Rex, interueniunt artes plurimæ, nec tamen cessat ordinatio diuina, Rom. XIII, 4.


### Question VI. Is immediate calling to be expected today?

Prob. 1. Those who after the Apostles are to teach publicly in the church, these ought to be suitable, & faithful, having obtained a commission to teach from other men. For thus Paul addresses

Latin:

Prob. 1. Qui post Apostolos publice in ecclesia docturi sunt, hos oportet esse idoneos, & fideles, commissionem docendi ab aliis hominibus nactos. Sic enim alloquitur-


### Question VII. What is the less principal efficient cause of ecclesiastical ministry?

Timothy: The things which you have heard from me before many witnesses, commit these to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also; 2. Where it is supposed that the fitness of the subject and the commission of the office on the part of others calling [takes place]; there a mediate calling, carefully attending to the qualities of the man, performed by men, has a place.

2) Titus had to appoint presbyters in Crete; and indeed such as were adorned with a good testimony of doctrine and life; Therefore an immediate calling after the times of the Apostles is no longer to be expected. The reason for the consequence is: because 1) Titus called mediately: 2) Paul prescribes to Titus certain laws of prudence, lest by error he appoint an unworthy man to the church. But to God calling immediately, or about to call, laws of prudence or caution cannot be prescribed, lest He err in calling, prefer the unworthy to the worthy, or thrust a flagitious man upon the church with scandal. Therefore all these things are prescribed to men, who could err in calling, and through whom God calls mediately.

Q.

VII. What is the less principal efficient cause of the ecclesiastical ministry? Obj. I. Distinguish between the right of calling ministers of the divine word, and the delegate. The former is with God, as the principal cause, calling by His own authority mediately or immediately; the latter is with the church, as the less principal cause, calling not by its own authority, but in the name of God. Whence we know that prayers were formerly joined with the act of calling, Acts VI, 6.

Obj. II. Distinguish between the right of calling ministers, and the exercise of the right.

The right of calling is with the whole church, and all its orders and members: but the exercise of the right varies, according to the convention and custom of the particular church, whose duty it is, however, to observe a decent order, and to avoid confusion.

Prob. a. 1) Whatever touches all, especially in a matter of salvation, that ought to be performed by the suffrages of all: But the calling of ministers, etc. Therefore. 2) Whoever are ministers of the church, they are to be called by the whole church: But the heralds of the divine word, etc. Therefore. The major is evident: because the church, as a mother of a family, cannot be deprived of the right of hiring ministers. 3) The church has for itself, as a bride, the keys of the kingdom of heaven given by the bridegroom Christ, Matt. XVI, 18. ch. XVIII, 17. and therefore just as it is hers to open and close the kingdom of heaven: so it is hers to appoint ministers, through whom she may close and open. 4) Whose duty it is to beware of false prophets, and to test the spirits, whether they are from God, without their consent a pastor of the church is not to be called: But it is the duty of all members of the church, even the laity, to beware, etc. Therefore. The minor is evident from Matt. VII, 15. Therefore. 5) This was the practice of the primitive church, from the time of the Apostles, that public ministers were appointed with the consent of all the members of the church. Thus the Apostles said to the multitude of the disciples, or the faithful: Look out, brethren, for men from among you, adorned with testimony, seven, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this necessity, Acts VI, 3. They were indeed deacons, peculiarly destined for the care of the ecclesiastical treasury, yet not alien from the office of teaching, but rather chosen for their skill in sacred doctrine above others, so that they might be able to teach. Cf. ch. XIV, 23, where Paul and Barnabas are said, having collected the suffrages of the faithful (χειροτονήσαντες, so that by outstretched hands each might cast their votes), to appoint presbyters in individual churches. And thus, that after the times of the Apostles, in the course of many centuries, it was customary for ministers of the church to be appointed, D. GERHARD shows at length loc. de minist. qu. 94. sqq. The less principal cause constituting the ministry is the church, to whom there has been granted by God the right of choosing, ordaining and calling suitable ministers of the divine word, provided nevertheless a decent order is observed in the exercise of this right.

Probab. The calling of ministers, taken generally and complexly, as it includes election, ordination, and the calling specifically so-called by the whole church and all three estates, is to be carried out in such a way that due order is preserved and confusion is avoided. For God is not the God of confusion, but of order, 1 Cor. XIV, 33. Therefore, examination, ordination, and inauguration belong to the presbytery; nomination, presentation, and confirmation by letters of call belong to the Christian magistrate; consent, suffrage, and approval belong to the people.

The antithesis is 1) of the Papists, who assert that the right of calling ministers of the divine word belongs solely to the presbytery; 2) of the Arminians, who assert it belongs solely to the magistrate; 3) of the Anabaptists, who assert it belongs solely to the laity. Their stronger arguments are (*):

I. In whatever way Aaron and the Apostles were once called, in the same way the heralds of the divine word are to be called today: But they were called without the suffrage of the magistrate and the people. Therefore. The major premise is proved: 1) From the express words of Paul, Heb. V, 4. 2) Because sacred heralds are successors of the Apostles. The minor premise is proved: 1) because Aaron was called through Moses, Exod. XXVIII. 2) The Apostles were called through Christ, without the consent of the magistrate and the people, John I, 21. Resp. 1) Distinguish between general and special agreement. Our calling ought to agree with the calling of Aaron and the Apostles in general, so that it may be a divine and legitimate calling: but not in species; because the calling of Aaron and the Apostles was immediate, ours is mediate. Immediate and mediate calling agree regarding the thing itself, or the office of teaching: but the mode of calling is different. 2) Moses was not the high priest, but a Prince and a distinguished Prophet: Nor was Aaron called by Moses, but was called immediately by God Himself, and was only declared by Moses.

II. The Apostles appointed Bishops without the suffrage of the magistrate and the people, e.g., Paul appointed Titus as Bishop in Crete, Tit. I, 5. Therefore, today bishops and pastors are to be called without the suffrage of the people. Resp. Distinguish between a church to be planted, or first to be constituted, and one that is planted, or constituted. When a church is first to be planted and constituted among infidel nations, the suffrage of the people is not to be awaited, nor is the authority of an infidel magistrate to be regarded. The Apostles sent Bishops and pastors to peoples yet to be converted, without requiring the consent of the hearers. But where the church was planted and constituted, they did not set ministers over churches without the consent of the people, Acts I, 24; VI, 3; XIV, 23.

III. Whoever are like sheep cannot call a shepherd: But the hearers &c. John XXI, 17. The major premise is proved: because the calling of a pastor pertains to the regimen and government of the church. But just as sheep do not rule, but are ruled: so the hearers cannot call a pastor. Resp. 1) Different times must be distinguished. When members of the church elect a pastor, they are not yet sheep; nor is the one to be elected to the sacred ministry actually a pastor. 2) It is poorly concluded from irrational sheep to rational ones. For they are not brute sheep, but rational, and they use reason illuminated by the word of God well, so that they do not elect a hireling or a wolf as pastor.

IV. Whoever cannot judge the doctrine of a pastor, they cannot call a pastor: But the laity &c. Therefore. Resp. 1) By denying …the major premise. Although the laity cannot judge exactly concerning doctrine, since that is the task of the presbytery; they can nevertheless judge concerning the external gifts and the life of the person to be elected, and ratify the judgment of the presbytery concerning doctrine. 2) The judgment concerning ὀρθοδοξίᾳ θεοφαντικὸν, or exact and solid, is indeed in the power of the presbytery; but the δοκιμαστικὸν (probationary) or discerning judgment is not to be denied to the laity. For Paul addresses all the Corinthians generally: Judge for yourselves what I say, 1 Cor.…

X, 15. V.

Latin:

Paullus Timotheum: Quae audivisti a me per plures testes, haec appone fidis hominibus, qui apti fuerint etiam alios docere; 2. Ubi supponitur, idoneitas subiecti & commissio muneris ex parte aliorum vocantium; ibi vocatio mediata, sollicite attendens ad qualitates hominis, ab hominibus facta locum habet.

2) Titus debuit constituere presbyteros in Creta; & quidem tales, qui bono testimonio doctrinae & vitae ornati erant; Ergo vocatio immediata post Apostolorum tempora non amplius est expectanda. Ratio consequentiae est; quia 1) Titus vocavit mediate: 2) Paullus praescribit Tito certas prudentiae leges, ne per errorem hominem indignum praeficiat ecclesiae. At Deo immediate vocanti, vel vocaturo, non possunt praescribi prudentiae aut cautionis leges, ne in vocando erret, indignum digno praeferat, aut flagitiosum ecclesiae cum scandalo obtrudat. Ergo haec omnia praescribuntur hominibus, qui in vocando errare possent, & per quos Deus vocat mediate.

Quaest. VII. Quae est causa efficiens minus principalis ministerii ecclesiastici?

Obs. I. Dist. inter ius vocandi ministros verbi divinum, & delegatum. Illud est penes Deum, tanquam caussam principalem, auctoritate propria mediate, vel immediate vocantem, hoc est penes ecclesiam, tanquam caussam minus principalem, non auctoritate propria, sed nomine Dei vocantem. Vnde preces cum actu vocationis olim coniunctas nonimus, Act. VI, 6.

Obs. II. Dist. inter ius vocandi ministros, & iuris exercitium.

Ius vocandi est penes universam ecclesiam, & omnes eius ordines atque membra: exercitium autem iuris variat, pro diversae conventione & consuetudine ecclesiae particularis, cuius tamen est servare ordinem decentem, & vitare confusionem.

Prob. a. 1) Quidquid omnes tangit, maxime in re salutari, illud omnium suffragiis peragi debet: Atqui vocatio ministrorum &c. Ergo. 2) Quicunque sunt ministri ecclesiae, a tota ecclesia sunt vocandi: Atqui praecones verbi divini &c. Ergo. Maior constat: quia ecclesia, tanquam materfamilias, iure conducendi ministros priuari nequit. 3) Ecclesia habet sibi, velut sponsae, datas a sponso Christo claues regni coelorum, Matth. XVI, 18. c. XVIII, 17. ideoque sicut ipsius est, aperire & claudere regnum coelorum: ita ipsius est, constituere ministros, per quos claudat & aperiat. 4) Quorum est, sibi cauere a pseudo-prophetis, & probare spiritus, an ex Deo sint, citra illorum consensum non est vocandus-pastor ecclesiae: Atqui omnium membrorum ecclesiae, etiam laicorum, est, cauere sibi &c. Ergo. Minor patet ex Matth. VII, 15. Ergo. 5) Haec fuit praxis primitivae ecclesiae, inde ab Apostolorum tempore, vt consentientibus omnibus ecclesiae membris ministri publici constituerentur. Sic dixerunt Apostoli ad multitudinem discipulorum, sive fidelium: Circumspicite, fratres, viros ex vobis, testimonio ornatos, septem, plenos Spiritu S. & sapientia, quos constituamus super necessitate hac, Act. VI, 3. Fuerunt illi quidem diaconi, curae fisci ecclesiastici peculiariter destinati, non tamen ab officio docendi alieni, sed potius ob peritiam doctrinae sacrae prae aliis eligendi, vt docere possent. Conf. c. XIV, 23. vbi dicuntur Paullus & Barnabas, collectis fidelium suffragiis (χειροτονήσαντες, ita vt porrectis manibus singuli suffragia ferrent), constituere presbyteros in singulis ecclesiis. Atque ita post Apostolorum tempora multorum saeculorum decursu, ministros ecclesiae constitui consueuisse, prolixe ostendit D. GERHARDVS loc. de minist. qu. 94. sqq. Causa minus principalis ministerium constituens est ecclesia, cui a Deo est ius concessum eligendi, ordinandi & vocandi idoneos verbi divini ministros , servato tamen in iuris huius exercitio ordine decente .

Probab. Vocatio ministrorum, generatim & complexe sumta, prout complectitur electionem, ordinationem & vocationem speciatim dictam a tota ecclesia, & omnibus tribus statibus, ita peragenda est, vt seruetur debitus ordo, & vitetur confusio. Deus enim non est Deus confusionis, sed ordinis, 1 Cor. XIV, 33. Competit itaque presbyterio examen, ordinatio & inauguratio; magistratui Christiano nominatio, præsentatio, confirmatio per litteras vocationis; populo consensus, suffragium, approbatio.

Antithesis est 1) Pontificiorum, qui soli presbyterio; 2) Arminianorum, qui soli magistratui; 3) Anabaptistarum, qui soli plebi ius vocandi ministros verbi diuini competere asserunt. Quorum potiora argumenta sunt (*):

I. Quomodo olim vocati sunt Aaron & Apostoli, eodem modo hodienum vocandi sunt præcones verbi diuini: Sed illi vocati sunt sine suffragio magistratus & populi. Ergo. Major probatur: 1) E disertis verbis Paulli, Hebr. V, 4. 2) Quia præcones sacri sunt successores Apostolorum. Minor probatur: 1) quia Aaron vocatus est per Mosen, Exod. XXVIII. 2) Apostoli vocati sunt per Christum, citra consensum magistratus & populi, Io. I, 21. Resp. 1) Dist. inter conuenientiam generalem, & specialem. Nostra vocatio conuenire debet cum vocatione Aaronis & Apostolorum in genere, vt sit diuina & legitima vocatio: non autem in specie; quia vocatio Aaronis & Apostolorum fuit immediata, nostra est mediata. Convenit vocatio immediata, & mediata, quoad rem ipsam, seu officium docendi: Modus vocationis autem diuersus est. 2) Moses non fuit Sacerdos summus, sed Princeps & Propheta insignis: Nec Aaron a Mose vocatus, sed ab ipso Deo immediatè vocatus, & a Mose tantum declaratus fuit.

II. Apostoli sine suffragio magistratus & populi constituerunt Episcopos, v. gr. Paullus Titum constituit Episcopum in Creta, Tit. I, 5. Ergo hodienum episcopi & pastores sine suffragio populi vocandi sunt. Resp. Dist. inter ecclesiam plantandam, siue primum constituendam, & plantatam, siue constitutam. Quando inter gentes infideles primum plantanda & constituenda est ecclesia, non exspectandum est populi suffragium, aut magistratus infidelis auctoritas respicienda est. Apostoli miserunt Episcopos & pastores ad populos infideles adhuc conuertendos, non requisito auditorum consensu. At vbi ecclesia fuit plantata & constituta, non præfecerunt ministros ecclesiis absque populi consensu, Act. I, 24. c. VI, 3. c. XIV, 23.

III. Quicunque sunt ouibus similes, non possunt pastorem vocare: Atqui auditores &c. Io. XXI, 17. Maior probatur: quia vocatio pastoris pertinet ad regimen & gubernationem ecclesiæ. At sicut oues non regunt, sed reguntur: ita auditores pastorem vocare non possunt. Resp. 1) Distinguenda sunt diuersa tempora. Cum membra ecclesiæ pastorem eligunt, nondum sunt oues; neque eligendus ad ministerium sacrum actu pastor est. 2) Ab ouibus irrationalibus ad rationales male concluditur. Nam ideo, quod non sunt oues brutæ, sed rationales, ratione e verbo Dei illuminata bene vtantur, ne pro pastore eligant mercenarium, aut lupum.

IV. Quicunque non possunt de doctrina pastoris iudicare, illi non possunt pastorem vocare: Atqui laici &c. Ergo. Resp. 1) Negando maiorem. Quamuis laici non exacte iudicare queant de doctrina, quippe quod est presbyterii; iudicare tamen possunt de donis externis & vita personæ eligendæ, & iudicium presbyterii de doctrina ratihabere. 2) Iudicium de ὀρθοδοξίᾳ θεοφαντικὸν, siue exactum & solidum, est quidem penes presbyterium; at indicium δοκιμαστικὸν, sive discretivum, non est denegandum laicis. Paullus enim generatim omnes Corinthios compellat: Iudicate vos; quod dico, 1 Cor.

X, 15. V.


### Question VII. What is the less principal efficient cause of ecclesiastical ministry?: Whatever mode of calling is prone to dissensions and tumults is not legitimate: But the mode of calling that pertains to the whole…

Whatever mode of calling is prone to dissensions and tumults is not legitimate: But the mode of calling that pertains to the whole church is, etc.

Therefore. The minor premise is proven; because it not infrequently happens that the presbytery disagrees with the magistrate, and the latter with the people, when a minister is to be called.

Resp.

Dist. between that which happens by itself, and that which happens by accident.

By accident, dissension can arise concerning the calling of a minister; nevertheless, by good methods, those seeds of dissension can be crushed. VI.

Ecclesiastical power does not belong to the political magistrate: The power of calling ministers of the divine word is ecclesiastical: Therefore.

Major is evident: because the political magistrate is concerned with civil matters, not with sacred or ecclesiastical ones. Resp.

The magistrate is concerned not only with civil matters, but also with external ecclesiastical ones, or the external disposition of sacred things. Internal ecclesiastical matters, or the internal and immediate administration of sacred things, are in the hands of the presbytery.

VII. The stronger part of the church is the laity: Therefore, the calling of ministers belongs most especially to them.

Resp.

The stronger part of the church is the laity, by reason of the multitude: the magistrate, by reason of external government: the presbytery, by reason of the internal administration of sacred things and judgment concerning orthodoxy.

Thus, the right of calling belongs to the whole church, but the exercise of the right must be done in due order. You say: The right of calling is in the hands of the patron.

Resp.

We take vocation here in a general sense, as it encompasses election, ordination, and vocation taken specifically.

Quest.

VIII.

Is a legitimate vocation necessary for every minister of the church?

For every minister, publicly and ordinarily teaching or about to teach in an established church, a legitimate vocation is necessary, not only by reason of εὐταξία (good order) or decorum, but also by reason of divine command, and that today is mediate. Obs.

I. The question is not about all who teach, but about those who perform the office of teachers in public assemblies of the church; that believers privately teach one another, admonish, and call back those who err into the way, we freely grant is not only lawful, but is also rightly reckoned among works of charity.

Obs.

Obs. II. We are speaking of a church rightly planted or constituted, not of a church to be planted or constituted.

In a church being gathered and constituted, where there are none who teach having been ordinarily called, nor are there any at hand to call, in this extreme case of necessity, where the glory of God and the salvation of one's neighbor must be uniquely regarded, we do not reluctantly concede that any Christian is bound to instill the catechetical milk of the word of righteousness into the ignorant.

Latin:

Quicunque vocandi modus dissensionibus & tumultibus est obnoxius, ille non est legitimus: Atqui modus vocandi, qui toti competat ecclesiæ, est &c.

Ergo. Minor probatur; quia haud raro usu venit, ut presbyterium a magistratu, & hic a populo dissentiat, cum minister vocandus est.

Resp.

Dist. inter id, quod fit per se, & quod fit per accidens.

Per accidens potest oriri dissensio de vocatione ministri; attamen bonis modis illa dissensionis semina elidi possunt. VI.

Potestas ecclesiastica non competit magistratui politico: Potestas vocandi ministros verbi divini est ecclesiastica: Ergo.

Maior constat: quia magistratus politicus versatur circa civilia, non circa sacra, aut ecclesiastica. Resp.

Magistratus versatur non tantum circa civilia, sed etiam circa ecclesiastica exteriora, sive externam dispositionem de rebus sacris. Ecclesiastica interiora, sive interna & proxima sacrorum administratio est penes presbyterium.

VII. Potior pars ecclesiæ est plebs: Ergo huic potissimum competit vocatio ministrorum.

Resp.

Potior pars ecclesiæ plebs est, ratione multitudinis: magistratus, ratione gubernationis externæ: presbyterium, ratione interioris administrationis sacrorum, & iudicii de orthodoxia.

Competit itaque ius vocandi toti ecclesiæ, sed exercitium iuris debito ordine fieri debet. Dicis: Ius vocandi est penes patronum.

Resp.

Nos vocationem hic sumimus sensu generali, prout electionem, ordinationem & vocationem specialiter acceptam complectitur.

Quaest.

VIII.

Estne legitima vocatio cuilibet ministro ecclesiæ necessaria?

Cuilibet ministro, in ecclesia constituta publice & ordinarie docenti, vel docturo, non tantum ratione εὐταξίας, sive decori , sed etiam ratione mandati divini, necessaria est vocatio legitima, eaque hodie mediata . Obs.

I. Non est quæstio de quibuscunque docentibus, sed de iis, qui in publicis ecclesiæ conuentibus docentium officio funguntur; privatim vero fideles se invicem docere, admonere, errantes in viam revocare; non solum licitum esse, sed etiam caritatis operibus recte accenseri, vltro largimur.

Obs.

Obs. II. Sermo nobis est de ecclesia rite plantata, sive constituta, non de ecclesia plantanda, aut constituenda.

In ecclesia colligenda & constituenda, vbi non adsunt, qui ordinarie vocati doceant, nec præsto sunt, qui vocent, in hoc extremo necessitatis casu, vbi gloria Dei, proximique salus, vnice spectanda, quemuis Christianorum teneri, vt imperitis sermonis iustitiæ lac catecheticum instillat, haud inviti concedimus.


### Question VII. What is the less principal efficient cause of ecclesiastical ministry?: Obs

Obs.

Obs. III. The question is not about immediate vocation, which is not to be expected in the church today, but about mediate.

Prob. a.

A legitimate vocation is necessary for those who wish to perform the office of teaching publicly in church assemblies, for the sake of preserving order, so that all things may be done in the church εὐσχημόνως καὶ κατὰ τάξιν; decently and in order, 1 Cor.

XIV, 40. For the church is not an ἄτακτος (disorderly) congregation, or a confused assembly, but one rightly ordered.

For there is an ecclesiastical hierarchy instituted by Christ himself, who gave some Apostles, some Prophets, some Evangelists, some Pastors and Teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ, Eph.

IV, 11, 12. minister, so that there may be in the church those who are for the care of souls, and for teach-

while they are bound to set times, to which it is permitted for all who are in need of doctrine and consolation to have recourse, since they possess the power of rebuking and arguing with secure sinners, of remitting and retaining sins etc., which parts are everywhere in the scriptures demanded of the called ministers of the church.

Proof 1) From the express command of the Holy Spirit speaking through Paul, Tit. I, 5. Leave thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee. See above quest.

VI. 2) From the universal axiom of the Holy Spirit, Hebr. V, 4. No man taketh this honour unto himself, but he that is called of God, as was Aaron. Obj. I. The Apostle speaks not of the fact, but of the right. Obj. II. His discourse is not only of the Aaronic priesthood, but generally also of the sacred ministry.

For the text is general: No man taketh this honour unto himself, to wit, of the sacred ministry, which is both worthy of honour and laborious, just as the priesthood of Aaron.

You say: He takes something who arrogates to himself that which is not owed to him: But the ecclesiastical office is owed to him who is apt to teach and of blameless life: Therefore it cannot be said that he who is apt to teach others and is of blameless life, takes to himself the office of teaching, or that honour which is in the office of teaching. Resp. This dignity is owed to the worthy, but orderly, i.e., with the order of vocation preserved. He who does not wait for this, takes and arrogates to himself that which, in this manner, is not owed to him. For to the person, suitability and integrity of life are required; but to the office, mission is required. Otherwise, whoever discovers political prudence in himself could lawfully rush into a senatorial, or even a royal office.

Certainly Aaron, nay Christ himself, most worthy of the office, awaited a vocation; much more, therefore, should ministers today await a vocation.

3) From apostolic authority, Rom. X, 15. How shall they preach, except they be sent? From which apostolic oracle we conclude: For the preaching of the word, a vocation is necessary: Therefore also for the undertaking of the ecclesiastical office. The consequence is proved: Preaching is a part of the ministry, with which the Apostle so joins a legitimate mission that, from the defect of mission, he concludes to an illicit work in the ministry. Observe here the apostolic gradation: Invocation requires faith, faith the hearing of the word, hearing the preaching of the gospel, preaching a divine mission; because without this, no one shall preach by right. For the Apostle speaks of moral impossibility, not physical. For physically, indeed, it is possible that one might preach without a vocation, but not morally, that is, not rightly, not decorously, not in the manner expressed in the scriptures.

You say: The Apostle 1) deals with an immediate vocation to the apostolate, not with a mediate vocation. For there is a twofold mode of being constituted: the one which is done by mission, the other by the acquisition of those things which Paul requires in a bishop, 1 Tim. III, 2. Which latter suffices here, and can be called an internal vocation. 2) The Apostle deals with a mission for the preaching of a new thing; which requires some vocation and external mission, but not for the divulging of doctrine in a planted church, for which an internal vocation suffices. Resp. To 1) An internal vocation is feigned in vain . For Paul, 1 Tim. III, does not deal with vocation, but with the qualities and adjuncts of a bishop already constituted, by which his ability or aptitude is declared. But another thing is declared. Another thing one is the aptitude of the subject for the ministry, the other is the calling properly so called.

The former consists in certain qualities, but it is not the calling itself, as a divine act, since the aptitude of the subject precedes it. Very many are fit for a magistracy, yet they do not assume the dignity of a magistrate unless a calling follows.

To 2) The necessity of a mission is not required because of the novelty of the doctrine, but for the reason of a peculiar status and order; because the ministry is a status and order established by God, in which no one can be, unless the divine will is presupposed, signified through a mission. For the Apostle does not connect the necessity of a mission with doctrine, whether it be new or ancient.

Add that the Apostles did not preach a doctrine new in terms of its essence, Acts

XXVI, 22. Paul clearly testifies that he said nothing beyond what is contained in the prophets, Acts XXVIII, 23. Nor does κηρύσσειν (to preach) always signify preaching a new thing.

For even a Jew is κηρύσσων (preaching), μὴ κλέπτων (not stealing), Rom.

II, 21. which is nevertheless most ancient. 4) From the condition of the ministry.

Ministers of the church are ambassadors of God, 2 Cor.

V, 20. But no one performs the duty of an ambassador unless he is sent by a prince. They are stewards of the mysteries of God, 1 Cor.

IV, 1. A steward cannot be established except by the master of the house. Therefore, without a legitimate calling, no one ought to preach the word of God and dispense the sacraments.

For Jehovah detests those who run, not having been sent, Jer.

XXIII, 21. The antithesis is that of the Anabaptists, Socinians, and Weigelians, who deny that a mediate calling is necessary for a minister of the church by reason of a divine mandate. Their principal arguments are:

I. Whatever is a good work, a special calling is not required for its performance: But to desire the Episcopate is a good work, 1 Tim.

III, 1. Therefore. Resp.

Distinguish between an ordered desire and an unordered running. To desire the Episcopate is altogether a good work; but it signifies offering one's service to the church modestly and decently for a legitimate calling: To run, however, signifies to intrude oneself into a sacred office without a peculiar calling.

This is called shameful, Jer. XXIII, 12. To these add that certain good works are special, for the performance of which a peculiar calling and ordination of God is required, e.g., to govern the republic well, to educate children honestly, etc., to which must be added the public preaching of the gospel.

II. Whatever is a work of charity, that belongs to all, because works of charity are to be exercised by all: But to teach others is a work of charity: Therefore, the minor is proved from James V, 19. Resp.

Distinguish between works of charity common to all, and those proper to certain specific persons. To teach in public assemblies is indeed a work of charity, but it is proper to certain specific persons called to a public office: Just as performing an embassy is a good work, if it concerns the safety of the republic; meanwhile, however, no one ought to take upon himself the name and role of an ambassador, unless it is imposed upon him by the one sending.

Latin:

Obs.

Obs. III. Non quæritur de vocatione immediata, quæ hodie in ecclesia non est exspectanda, sed de mediata.

Prob. a.
