Necessaria est vocatio legitima iis, quæ publice in ecclesiæ conuentibus officium docendi abire volunt, ordinis feruandi caussa, vt omnia fiant in ecclesia εὐσχημόνως καὶ κατὰ τάξιν; deventer & ordine, 1 Cor.

XIV, 40. Neque enim ecclesia est congregatio ἄτακτος, sive cœtus confusus, sed rite ordinatus.

Est enim hierarchia ecclesiastica instituta ab ipso Christo, qui dedit alios Apostolos, alios Prophetas, alios Euangelistas, alios Pastores & Doctores, in instaurationem sanctorum, in opus ministerii, in ædificationem corporis Christi, Eph.

IV, 11, 12. ministrum, vt sint in ecclesia, qui ad curam animarum, & ad docen-

dum statis temporibus obligati sint, ad quos recurrere liceat omnibus, qui doctrina & solatio egent, quippe potestate polleant corripiendi & arguendi peccatores securos, peccata remittendi ac retinendi etc. quae partes vocatis ecclesiae ministris passim in scripturis demandantur.

Prob. 1) A diserto mandato Spiritus S. per Paullum loquentis, Tit. I, 5. Relinque te in Creta, ut reliqua coordinares, & constitueres per urbes presbyteros, sicut ego tibi disposui. Vid. supra quaest.

VI. 2) Ab axiomate Spiritus S. universali, Hebr. V, 4. Non sibi ipsi quis sumit honorem, sed qui vocatus a Deo, quomodo & Aaron. Obs. I. Loquitur Apostolus non de facto, sed de iure. Obs. II. Non tantum de sacerdotio Aaronico sermo ipsi est, sed generatim etiam de ministerio sacro.

Textus enim generalis est: Nemo sibi sumit honorem, scilicet ministerii sacri, quod tum honore dignum, tum laboriosum est perinde, atque sacerdotium Aaronis.

Dicis: Is sumit aliquid, qui id, quod ei non debetur, sibi arrogat: At ei, qui est ad docendum aptus, & vitae inculpatae est, debetur munus ecclesiasticum: Ergo dici non potest, eum, qui aptus ad docendum alios, & vitae inculpatae est, fumere sibi munus docendi, vel honorem illum, qui est in munere docendi. Resp. Debetur haec dignitas digno, sed ordinate, i. e. ordine vocationis servato. Hanc qui non exspectat, sumit & arrogat sibi id, quod hoc pacto ei non debetur. Ad personam enim idoneitas, vitae integritas, ad officium vero missio requiritur. Alias quicumque politicam prudentiam apud se deprehendit, in munus senatorium, immo & regium licite irruere posset.

Sane Aaron, imo Christus ipse, munere dignissimi, vocationem exspectarunt; multo magis igitur ministri hodie vocationem exspectare debent.

3) Ab auctoritate apostolica, Rom. X, 15. Quomodo praedicabunt, nisi missi fuerint? Ex quo oraculo Apostolico concludimus: Ad praedicationem verbi necessaria est vocatio: Ergo etiam ad obeundum munus ecclesiasticum. Consequentia probatur: Praedicatio est pars ministerii, cum qua legitimam missionem ita coniungit Apostolus, ut ex defectu missionis ad illicitam operam inministerii concludat. Obferues hie gradationem apostolicam: Invocatio praerequirit fidem, fides auditum verbi, auditus praedicationem euangelii, praedicatio diuinam missionem; quia absque hac nemo iure praedicabit. Loquitur enim Apostolus de impossibilitate morali, non de physica. Etenim physice quidem possibile est, ut quis praedicet sine vocatione, at non moraliter, id est non recte, non decore, non modo in scripturis expresso.

Dicis: Apostolus 1) agit de vocatione immediata ad apostolatum, non de vocatione mediata. Duplex quippe est constituendi modus: alter, qui fit per missionem, alter per acquisitionem eorum, quae Paullus requirit in episcopo, 1 Tim. III, 2. Qui posterior hic sufficit, & vocatio interna dici potest. 2) Agit Apostolus de missione ad praedicationem rei novae; quae requirit aliquam vocationem & missionem externam, non autem doctrinae diuulgatae in ecclesia plantata, ad quam sufficit vocatio interna. Resp. Ad 1) Vocatio interna frustra fingitur . Paullus enim 1 Tim. III. non agit de vocatione, sed de qualitatibus & adiunctis episcopi iam constituti, quibus habilitas vel aptitudo ipsius declaratur. Aliud autem ipsius declaratur. Alind autem est aptitudo subiecti ad ministerium, aliud vocatio proprie sic dicta.

Illa consistit in quibusdam qualitatibus, sed non est vocatio ipsa, ut actus divinus, quippe quem aptitudo subiecti antecedit. Plurimi apti sunt ad magistratum, nec tamen, nisi vocatione subsequente, magistratus dignitatem capessunt.

Ad 2) Non ob novitatem doctrinae requiritur missionis necessitas, sed ob rationem peculiaris status & ordinis; quia ministerium est status & ordo a Deo constitutus, in quo nemo potest esse, nisi praesupposita voluntate divina, per missionem significata. Neque enim Apostolus necessitatem missionis connectit cum doctrina, sive sit nova, sive antiqua.

Adiice, quod Apostoli non praedicaverint doctrina ratione essentiae novam, Act.

XXVI, 22. Paulus diserte testatur, se praeter id, quod in prophetis contentum est, nihil dixisse, Act. XXVIII, 23. Neque κηρύσσειν semper significat rem novam praedicare.

Nam & Iudaeus est κηρύσσων, μὴ κλέπτων, Rom.

II, 21. quod tamen antiquissimum est. 4) A conditione ministerii.

Ministri ecclesiae sunt legati Dei, 2 Cor.

V, 20. At nemo fungitur munere legati, nisi fit a principe missus. Sunt oeconomi mysteriorum Dei, 1 Cor.

IV, 1. Oeconomus non, nisi ab hero domus, constitutus esse potest. Ergo absque legitima vocatione nemo verbum Dei praedicare & sacramenta dispensare debet.

Iehovah enim detestatur currentes, non missos, Ier.

XXIII, 21. Antithesis est Anabaptistarum, Socinianorum & Weigelianorum, negantium, vocationem mediatam ministro ecclesiae ratione mandati divini esse necessariam. Quorum praecipua sunt argumenta:

I. Quidquid est bonum opus, ad illius praestationem non requiritur specialis vocatio: Atqui desiderare Episcopatum est bonum opus, 1 Tim.

III, 1. Ergo. Resp.

Dist. inter desiderium ordinatum & cursum inordinatum. Desiderare Episcopatum omnino est bonum opus; sed significat, modeste & decenter operam suam ecclesiae deferre ad legitimam vocationem: Currere autem significat, in officium sacrum sine peculiari vocatione se ingerere.

Hoc turpe dicitur, Ier. XXIII, 12. His adde, quod quaedam bona opera sint specialia, ad quorum praestationem peculiari requiritur vocatio & ordinatio Dei, v. gr. bene gubernare rempublicam, honeste educare liberos &c. quibus accensenda est publica euangelii praedicatio.

II. Quidquid est opus caritatis, illud omnibus competit, quia opera caritatis ab omnibus sunt exercenda: Sed docere alios est opus caritatis: Ergo, Minor probatur ex Iac. V, 19. Resp.

Dist. inter opera caritatis omnibus communia, & certis quibusdam personis propria. In conuentibus publicis docere, est quidem opus caritatis, sed certis quibusdam personis ad publicum officium vocatis proprium: Sicut legatione fungi, est bonum opus, si reipublicae salutem concernat; interim tamen nemo debet legati nomen & partes sibi sumere, nisi a legante ipsi imponatur.


### Question VII. What is the less principal efficient cause of ecclesiastical ministry?: Furthermore, any pious Christian can inform his neighbor privately without a peculiar calling

Furthermore, any pious Christian can inform his neighbor privately without a peculiar calling.

III. Whoever are Priests before God, they can teach and inform others without a peculiar calling, for to teach others is the duty of priests: All Christians are priests before God, 1 Pet.

II, 2. Rev. I, 6. Therefore.

Resp.

Distinguish between Priests so called by reason of ecclesiastical office, and by reason of spiritual sacrifices.

All Christians are Priests by reason of spiritual sacrifices, such as: prayers, praises, alms, mortification of the body; but they are not all Priests by reason of a public ecclesiastical office.

For even to women belongs the Priesthood, with respect to spiritual sacrifices; but not by reason of an ecclesiastical office, 1 Tim.

II, 12. 2) Christians are not only called Priests; but even Kings before God. If therefore it is permitted to Christians, on account of the spiritual priesthood, outside the case of necessity, to perform acts belonging to the ecclesiastical priesthood; it follows that it is permitted to them, on account of the spiritual kingdom, to perform acts belonging to the political kingdom. From which a nefarious Anarchy will spring.

IV. If in the primitive church some taught without a special vocation, today Christians can publicly teach without it; The Antecedent is true: Therefore also the consequent. The consequence is evident: because the primitive church was most pure, and most orthodox. The antecedent is proven: because the Christians dispersed by the death of Stephen, Acts IV, 4. Philip, Acts VIII, 5. Apollo, Acts XIV, 4. taught the gospel in various places without a special vocation. Resp. 1) In historical matters from Holy Scripture, it is not always permitted to argue negatively. 2) Those dispersed were indeed called. For there was among them Philip the evangelist, Acts XXI, 8. But an evangelist cannot exist without a vocation. Therefore we doubt not that Apollo also was legitimately called.

Instance: The Fathers of the primitive church, namely ORIGEN, homil. II. on ch. 18 of Numbers, and AMBROSE, in his commentary on ch. IV to the Ephesians, testify that laymen preached the gospel among the Gentiles ignorant of the Christian faith. Resp. Distinguish between a church being constituted, and one already constituted. When a Christian man is among Gentiles ignorant of the Christian faith, then he can, to the best of his ability, teach others and propagate the doctrine of Christ, with charity and necessity urging; but where the church is constituted, let no one intrude himself into a public office without an ordinary vocation.

V. 1 Cor. XVI, 15. Concerning those who were of the household of Stephanas, it is said that they ordained themselves to the ministry of the saints. Resp. The Apostle implies that the household of Stephanas did not intrude themselves into the ecclesiastical ministry, which would be against Heb. V, 4, but that they devoted themselves with voluntary charity to ministering to the saints in those things which pertain to τὰ βιωτικὰ (the things of this life). They ordained themselves to the ministry of hospitality, not of preaching.

VI. Academic students are admitted without a special vocation to hold sacred sermons: Therefore an ordinary vocation to the ecclesiastical office is not necessary. Resp. Distinguish between exercises of preaching, and the solemn office of preaching. The sermons of students are exercises, by which they modestly offer their service to the church for the future, but they do not arrogate to themselves the solemn office of preaching.

Latin:

Ceterum priuatim informare proximum, quilibet pius Christianus sine peculiari vocatione potest.

III. Quicunque sunt Sacerdotes coram Deo, illi possunt alios docere & informare sine peculiari vocatione, nam docere alios, est sacerdotum: Omnes Christiani sunt sacerdotes coram Deo, 1 Petr.

II, 2. Apoc. I, 6. Ergo.

Resp.

Dist. inter Sacerdotes ita dictos, ratione muneris ecclesiastici, & ratione sacrificiorum spiritualium.

Omnes Christiani sunt Sacerdotes, ratione sacrificiorum spiritualium, qualia sunt: preces, laudes, eleemosynae, mortificatio corporis; sed non sunt omnes Sacerdotes, ratione muneris ecclesiastici publici.

Nam & foeminis competit Sacerdotium, respectu sacrificiorum spiritualium; non autem ratione muneris ecclesiastici, 1 Tim.

II, 12. 2) Christiani non tantum dicuntur Sacerdotes; sed etiam Reges coram Deo. Si itaque Christianis, propter sacerdotium spirituale, extra casum necessitatis, licet exsequi actus sacerdotio ecclesiastico competentes; sequitur, iisdem propter regnum spirituale, licitum esse exsequi actus regno politico competentes. Ex quo Anarchia nefanda pullulabit.

IV. Si in primitiva ecclesia quidam docuerunt sine peculiari vocatione, hodiernum Christiani fine illa publice docere possunt; Antecedens est verum: Ergo & consequens. Consequentia patet: quia ecclesia primitiva fuit purissima, & maxime orthodoxa. Antecedens probatur: quia Christiani dispersi a morte Stephani, Act. IV, 4. Philippus, Act. VIII, 5. Apollo, Act. XIV, 4. fine peculiari vocatione passim locorum evangelium docuerunt. Resp. 1) In historicis e S. scriptura negative argumentari non semper licet. 2) Dispersi illi utique vocati fuere. Fuit enim inter illos Philippus evangelista, Act. XXI, 8. Evangelista autem esse nequit sine vocatione. Nulli itaque dubitamus, quin & Apollo legitime vocatus fuerit.

Instantia: Patres primitivae ecclesiae, nominatim ORIGENES, homil. II. in c. 18. Numer. & AMBROSIVS, in comment. in c. IV. ad Eph. testantur, laicos praedicasse evangelium inter gentes fidei Christianae ignaras. Resp. Dist. inter ecclesiam constituendam, & constitutam. Quando homo Christianus versatur inter gentiles fidei Christianae ignaros, tunc pro parte virili alios docere, & doctrinam Christi propagare potest, urgente caritate & necessitate; at ubi ecclesia est constituta, citra vocationem ordinariam nemo in officium publicum se ingerat.

V. 1 Cor. XVI, 15. De illis, qui erant ex familia Stephanae, dicitur, quod se ipsos in ministerium sanctis ordinaverint. Resp. Familiares Stephanae non se ipsos in ministerium ecclesiasticum ingessisse, quod esset contra Hebr. V, 4. sed ad ministrandum sanctis in iis, quae ad τὰ βιωτικὰ spectant, vltronea caritate se addixisse, Apostolus innuit. Ordinarant se ipsos in ministerium hospitalitatis, non praedicationis.

VI. Studiosi academici absque peculiari vocatione admittuntur ad habendas conciones sacras: Ergo ordinaria vocatio ad munus ecclesiasticum non est necessaria. Resp. Dist. inter exercitia concionandi, & solemne concionandi officium. Studiosorum conciones sunt exercitia, quibus ecclesiae operam suam in posterum praestandam modeste offerunt, non autem solemne concionandi officium sibi arrogant.


### Quaest. IX

What is the ordination of a minister of the church? Ordination is a solemn act, by which a suitable person is declared in the sight of God and the church to have been examined and legitimately called , is separated from profane business, and a certain office to be performed in the church is commended to him , to which he is inaugurated by a Bishop, or Presbyter, through χειροθεσίαν (the laying on of hands) & solemn prayers , and is gravely admonished to perform his office rightly .

Prob. a. Ordination is nothing other than a public testimony, by which the vocation of a person suitable for the ministry is declared, in the sight of God and in His name, to be legitimate and divine, as CHEMNITZ says, part. III. loc. fol. 137. Although therefore ordination does not create the election and vocation, but presupposes it: if however someone is legitimately called, that ecclesiastical rite declares and publicly confirms that the vocation which preceded is legitimate. Thus Paul, although he was called immediately, yet Ananias is sent, who should lay hands upon him, so that the church might be certain of his vocation, Acts IX, 17. But since hands are not to be laid on anyone hastily, as Paul warns, 1 Tim. V, 22, the suitability of the subject must be explored through an examination, which is a diligent inquiry and testing, whether the person whom the church calls is fit, to whom the arduous ecclesiastical office may be committed. Let them be tested first, then let them serve, if they are blameless, says Paul 1 Tim. III, 10.

Prob. b. Ordination formally consists in the segregation of the called person from profane business, and his destination to a public ecclesiastical office. This we learn from 2 Tim. II, 4: Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ. No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier. But if the soldiers of this age are not occupied with merchandise, agriculture, or civil crafts: much less does it befit the soldiers of Christ to be immersed in civil affairs. On account of this, the Holy Spirit requires in pious ministers ἀφορισμὸν, or segregation from profane cares, saying: Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them. And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away, Acts XIII, 2.

Prob. c. That the minister of the cause of Ordination can be as well a Presbyter as a Bishop, is evident 1) from 1 Tim. IV, 14. Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. From which we gather: grace was conferred upon Timothy through the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. Ergo, ordination ought not necessarily to be performed exclusively by a Bishop, but can also be performed by presbyters. The consequence is proved a) What was the manner of Timothy’s ordaining can still obtain in the church. b) Presbytery is a collective noun, and signifies a multitude of elders concurring in the laying on of hands; but a Bishop is one and a singular individual. 2) By divine right a Bishop and a Presbyter do not differ, except in names alone, and therefore by divine right the power of ordaining belongs to both. To which assertion of ours we give credence, a) from Acts XX, 17. 18. where Paul, having summoned the presbyters, said: Take heed to yourselves, and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as Bishops. Therefore, in the apostolic church, Bishops and Presbyters were the same. b) From Phil. I, 1, where Paul and Timothy pray for grace and peace for all the saints, together with the Bishops and Deacons. But they would not have omitted the Presbyters if they had been distinct from the Bishops in the apostolic age. c) From Tit. I, 5, where Titus is said to have been left in Crete, that he might appoint Presbyters town by town, and it is added, v. 7: For a Bishop must be irreproachable. Which would cohere less, unless Bishops and Presbyters were the same by divine right. d) The Apostle Peter, by the opinion of the Papists, is the supreme Bishop. But he calls himself a συμπρεσβύτερον 1 Pet. V, 1, and addresses the Presbyters: Feed the flock, which is among you ἐπισκοπῦντες, overseeing, or (by the interpretation of HIERONYMUS) superintending. But those whose duty it is to ἐπισκοπεῖν (oversee), they are Bishops. By ecclesiastical custom, for the sake of εὐταξίας (good order) and maintaining concord, a distinction was introduced between Bishops and Presbyters. HIERONYMVS teaches this in his commentary on c. 1 of the epistle to Titus: "Formerly the same person was a Presbyter who was also a Bishop, and before, by the devil's instinct, factions or schisms were made in religion, and it was said among the people: 'I am of Paul, I am of Apollos, I am of Cephas,' the churches were governed by the common council of Presbyters. But after each one thought that those whom he had baptized were his own, and not Christ's, it was decreed throughout the whole world that one of the Presbyters should be placed over the others, and the seeds of schisms be removed." Conf. HIERON. ep. LXXXV to Euagrius. Therefore, a Bishop is superior to a presbyter not by divine law, but by ecclesiastical law; which subordination of hierarchical order we do not abolish, but retain. Ordination is performed by the bishop through χειροθεσίαν, or the imposition of hands: a) That it may be a solemn testimony that the person present is suitable, duly elected, and lawfully called: b) That it may be a sign of divine blessing, which the sacred person ought to expect from God in his office. For it was the custom of the ancients to bless by the imposition of hands. See Gen. XLVIII, 14. Matth. XIX, 15. c) That the called minister may be admonished that he is consecrated to God, and as it were enslaved to Him. For hands were formerly imposed upon victims, Lev. I, 4. d) That public prayers for the minister brought into the sight of God and the church may be more ardent.

Latin:

Ordinatio est actus solemnis, quo persona idonea in conspectu Dei & ecclesiae declaratur esse examinata & legitime vocata , a negotiis profanis segregatur, certumque in ecclesia obeundum munus ipsi commendatur , ad quod ab Episcopo, vel Presbytero, per χειροθεσίαν & solemnes preces inauguratur , atque officii sui rite faciendi graviter admonetur .

Prob. a. Ordinatio nihil aliud est, quam publica testificatio, qua vocatio personae ad ministerium idonea, in conspectu Dei, & ipsius nomine declaratur esse legitima & diuina, dicente CHEMNIT. part. III. loc. fol. 137. Licet ergo ordinatio non faciat electionem & vocationem, sed eam praesupponat: si tamen quis legitime vocatus fit, ritus ille ecclesiasticus declarat & publice confirmat, vocationem illam, quae praecessit, esse legitimam. Sic Paullus licet immediate vocatus esset, tamen Ananias mittitur, qui ipsi imponat manus, vt ecclesiae de eius vocatione constet, Act. IX, 17. Cum autem manus nemini cito imponendae sint, monente Paullo, 1 Tim. V, 22. idoneitas subiecti exploranda est per examen, quod est diligens inquisitio & probatio, an persona, quam ecclesia vocat, apta fit, cui arduum munus ecclesiasticum committatur. Probentur prius, deinde ministrent, si fuerint irreprehensibiles, inquit Paullus 1 Tim. III, 10.

Prob. b. Ordinatio formaliter consistit in segregatione personæ vocatæ a profanis negotiis, & destinatione ad publicum munus ecclesiasticum. Id quod discimus ex 2 Tim. II, 4. Tu sustine mala, tanquam bonus miles Iesu Christi. Nemo, qui militat, se implicat huius vitæ negotiis, vt ei, qui ipsum elegit, placeat. Quod si milites huius sæculi non occupantur mercatura, agricultura, aut opificiis ciuilibus: multo minus decet milites Christi negotiis ciuilibus immergi. Id propter requirit Spiritus S. in piis ministris ἀφορισμὸν, siue segregationem a curis profanis, inquiens: Separate mihi tam Barnabam, quam Saulum ad opus, ad quod vocaui illos. Tunc postquam ieiunauerunt, & orarunt, imposuerunt illis manus, & dimiserunt eos, Actor. XXII, 3.

Prob. c. Ordinationis caussam ministram tam Presbyterum, quam Episcopum esse posse, patet 1) ex 1 Tim. IV, 14. Ne neglige, quod in te est, donum, quod datum est tibi per prophetiam, cum impositione manuum Presbyterii. E quibus colligimus: Timotheo collata est gratia per impositionem manuum presbyterii. E. per Episcopum exclusiue non debet fieri necessario ordinatio, sed potest etiam fieri per presbyteros. Consequentia prob. a) Quæ fuit ratio ordinandi Timothei, potest adhuc obtinere in ecclesia. b) Presbyterium est nomen collectiuum, & dicit multitudinem seniorum concurrentium ad impositionem manuum; Episcopus autem est vnum & singulare indiuiduum. 2) De iure diuino Episcopus & Presbyter non differunt, nisi solis nominibus, & proinde de iure diuino vtrique competit potestas ordinandi. Cui nostræ assertioni fidem facimus, a) ex Act. XX, 17. 18. vbi Paullus accersitis presbyteris dixit: Attendite vobis ipsis, & toti gregi, in quo vos Spiritus S. posuit Episcopos. Ergo in ecclesia apostolica iidem fuere Episcopi & Presbyteri. b) Ex Phil. I, 1. vbi Paullus & Timotheus precantur gratiam & pacem omnibus sanctis, vna cum Episcopis & Diaconis. Non autem prætermisissent Presbyteros, si æuo apostolico ab Episcopis fuissent distincti. c) Ex Tit. I, 5. vbi Titus relictus dicitur in Creta, vt oppidatim constituat Presbyteros, & subiicitur, v. 7. Oportet enim Episcopum esse irreprehensibilem. Quæ minus cohærerent, nisi Episcopi & Presbyteri de iure diuino iidem essent. d) Apostolus Petrus, Pontificiorum sententia, est Episcopus summus. At is se vocat συμπρεσβύτερον 1 Petr. V, 1. & Presbyteros alloquitur: Pascite gregem, qui inter vos ἐπισκοπῦντες, inspicientes, vel (interprete HIERONYMO) superintendentes. At quorum est ἐπισκοπεῖν, illi sunt Episcopi. Consuetudine ecclesiastica, εὐταξίας & alendæ concordiæ caussa, introductum est discrimen inter Episcopos, & Presbyteros. Docet hoc HIERONYMVS in comment. c. 1. ep. ad Tit. Olim idem erat Presbyter, qui & Episcopus, & antequam diaboli instinctu studia vel schismata in religione fierent, & diceretur in populis: Ego sum Paulli, ego sum Apollinis, ego sum Cephæ, communi Presbyterorum consilio ecclesiæ gubernabantur. Postquam autem vnusquisque eos, quos baptizauerat, suos esse putabat, non Christi: in toto orbe decretum est, vt vnus de Presbyteris superponeretur omnibus, & schismatum semina tollerentur. Conf. ep. HIERON. LXXXV. ad Euagrium. Est itaque Episcopus presbytero superior non iure diuino, sed iure ecclesiastico; quam subordinationem hierarchici ordinis non tollimus, sed retinemus. Fit ordinatio ab episcopo per χειροθεσίαν, siue manuum impositionem: a) Vt sit folemnis testificatio, personam præsentem esse idoneam, rite electam & legitime vocatam: b) Vt sit signum benedictionis divinæ, quam sacra persona in officio suo a Deo exspectare debeat. Prisci quippe moris erat, imposita manu benedicere. Vid. Gen. XLVIII, 14. Matth. XIX, 15. c) Vt admoneatur minister vocatus, se Deo esse consecratum, & quasi mancipatum. Nam victimis olim imponebantur manus, Leu. I, 4. d) Vt preces publicæ pro ministro in conspectum Dei & ecclesiæ adducto sint ardentiores.


### Question X. Are Luther and the Lutheran ministers legitimately called and duly ordained?

Prob. d. In the very act of ordination, the designated minister is admonished regarding faithfulness in the office committed to him, with Paul leading the way, 1 Tim. IV, 14: "Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you by prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery! Meditate on these things; be in them, that your progress may be manifest to all! Pay attention to yourself and to the doctrine!"

Q. X.

Whether Luther and the Lutheran ministers were legitimately called and duly ordained?

Both Luther a) and the Lutheran ministers b) were legitimately called and duly ordained. Prob. a.

The blessed LUTHER was called and ordained to the ecclesiastical office by his Bishop as a Presbyter, in the year of Christ 1507, at the age of 24, having received the power of teaching the Word of God. In the year 1508, he was called by JOHANN VON STAUPITZ, General of the Augustinians, with the accompanying confirmation and consent of FREDERICK the Elector, to the presbyterate and theological profession in the church and Academy of Wittenberg: in which calling it was said to him, by virtue of the Academic statutes: "It is yours to interpret the divine law and to teach the book of life." His calling by the letters of the Wittenberg senate to the presbyterate exists in Vol. IX, Wittenberg, fol. 103. In the year 1512, on the 18th day of October, he was declared a Licentiate of Theology; on the following day, Oct. 19, he was created a Doctor in the Erfurt convent, where, by the consent of the entire Augustinian convent, he received the power of propagating the truth of heavenly doctrine by living voice, and of defending it against any adversaries whatsoever. Prob. b.

Whoever are called and ordained by the apostolic rite, and faithfully propagate the truth of heavenly doctrine, they enjoy a legitimate calling and are true ministers of the church: But the Lutheran ministers addicted to the Augsburg Confession, etc. [are such]. Therefore. The minor is proved: because the Lutheran ministers were called through the χειροτονίαν (collection of votes) of particular churches, while the right of every estate remained intact, and were ordained by a Bishop or Superintendent through the χειροθεσίαν (laying on of hands) of the presbytery.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, who maintain that neither LUTHER nor the Lutheran ministers were legitimately called and duly ordained. Their arguments are:

I. LUTHER was called neither mediately nor immediately by God. Not mediately; because he was not called by the church, nor ordained by a Bishop to reform religion and oppose the doctrine of the Catholics: nor immediately, or extraordinarily; because he could not confirm an immediate calling with the seal of miracles. Resp. LUTHER was called mediately to the presbyterate, that is, to the ecclesiastical ministry and theological profession. But it is the duty of true ministers of the church to teach the Word of God rightly and to stop the mouths of those who contradict, Tit. I, 11. It is the duty of a Professor of Theology to assert heavenly truth and to refute errors opposing it. We do not, however, deny that something extraordinary was joined with the ministry of the blessed LUTHER, as far as it pertains to the impugning of the Papacy, not indeed on the part of the calling, which was ordinary and mediate, but on the part of the gifts divinely granted to him. For his heroic spirit in impugning the Papacy indicates an extraordinary and special assistance of God.

Instance: To propagate a new doctrine, such as that of LUTHER was, an immediate and extraordinary calling is required, to be confirmed by the seal of miracles. Resp. a) The doctrine of LUTHER was not new, but renewed, and purged from the leaven of the Papists, having long since been confirmed by the miracles of Christ and the Apostles. b) John the Baptist did not perform miracles, although his calling was immediate and extraordinary. c) Not the glory of miracles, but the agreement of doctrine with the divine Word is the certain proof of a divine calling.

II. The Bishop who ordained LUTHER was either a true pastor or a wolf.

If he was a true pastor; LUTHER, by departing from him, became a most base apostate. If he was a wolf; LUTHER could not be inaugurated by him as a true pastor. Resp. 1) Generally: This argument could be objected against all who, having been ordained by heretics, return to the bosom of the church. Yet, pontifical laws assert that even those ordained by heretics are truly ordained and are not to be ordained again. 2) Specifically: The Bishop who ordained LUTHER was, in different respects, a true bishop and a false bishop, or a wolf. He was a true Bishop insofar as he taught certain things consonant with the divine word in his episcopal office, baptized, and commended the ministry to suitable persons through the rite of ordination. He was a false Bishop insofar as he corrupted the sincerity of the heavenly doctrine by mixing in the leaven of human traditions, celebrated the sacrifice of the mass in place of the Lord’s Supper, etc. Therefore, the essential must be accurately distinguished from the accidental, the divine from the human. Instance: LUTHER did not receive from the ordaining Bishop the power to oppose the pontifical church. Resp. LUTHER received from God, through the ordaining Bishop, the power to oppose all errors of doctrine. And he obtained the power to oppose the errors of the pontifical church.

III. Whoever are not ordained by a Bishop, they are not true ministers of the church: But Lutheran ministers &c. Therefore. The minor is evident: because LUTHER ordained ministers addicted to the Augsburg Confession, who nevertheless was not a Bishop, but only a Presbyter. Resp. a) By divine law, a Bishop does not differ from a Presbyter, and thus the power of ordaining also belongs to a Presbyter by divine law. b) Today, Lutheran ministers are ordained by a Superintendent, and consequently by a Bishop. For canon law teaches that a Superintendent is a Bishop in name and office, in cap. Cleric. Dist. 21. The term Episcopatus is derived from the fact that he who is made a Bishop, superintends (superintendant). AUGUSTINE inculcates the same, L. XIX. de Ciu. Dei c. 19. In Greek it is ἐπισκοπεῖν, and the word is derived from the fact that he who is set over others, superintends (superintendant) those over whom he is set. If we wish, we can call Bishops, in Latin, Superintendents. Conf. HULSEMANN. Manuale disp. XII. pag. 524.

Latin:

Prob. d. In ipso ordinationis actu minister designatus fidelitatis in munere commisso admonetur, praeunte Paulo, 1 Tim. IV, 14. Ne neglige, quod in te est, donum, quod datum est tibi per prophetiam cum impositione manuum presbyterii! Haec meditare, in his esto, ut tuus profectus manifestus fit in omnibus! Attende tibi ipsi, & doctrinae!

Quaest. X. An Lutherus, & ministri Lutherani legitime vocati & rite ordinati sunt?

Tam Lutherus a), quam Ministri Lutherani b) legitime vocati & rite ordinati sunt.

Prob. a. B.

LUTHERVS ad munus ecclesiasticum vocatus & ordinatus est ab Episcopo suo Presbyter, A. C. 1507. aetatis 24. accepta potestate docendi verbum Dei. An. 1508. vocatus est a IOANNE STAVPITIO, Augustinianorum Generali, accedente confirmatione & consensu FRIDERICI Electoris ad presbyterium & professionem theologicam in ecclesia & Academia Wittebergensi: in qua vocatione ipsi dictum est, vi statutorum Academicorum: Vestrum est, legem divinam interpretari, & librum vitae docere. Vocatio eius per litteras senatus Witteberg. ad presbyterium exstat tom. IX, Witteb. fol. 103. An. 1512. die 18. Octobr. renuntiatus est Licentiatus theologiae; die sequenti 19. Oct. creatus est Doctor in conventu Erfurtenfi, vbi consensu totius conventus Augustiniani potestatem accepit, veritatem doctrinae coelestis viua voce propagandi, & contra quosuis aduersarios propugnandi.

Prob. b. Quicunque ritu apostolico vocantur & ordinantur, atque veritatem doctrinae coelestis fideliter propagant, illi gaudent legitima vocatione, & sunt veri ecclesiae ministri: Atqui ministri Lutherani August. conf. addicti &c. Ergo. Minor probatur: quia ministri Lutherani per χειροτονίαν (collectionem suffragiorum) ecclesiarum particularium, falvo manente cuiuslibet flatus iure, sunt vocati, & ab Episcopo, vel Superintendente, per χειροθεσίαν presbyterii sunt ordinati.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, statuentium, nec LUTHERVM, nec Lutheranos ministros legitime vocatos & rite ordinatos esse. Quorum argumenta sunt:

I. LUTHERVS nec mediate, nec immediate a Deo vocatus est. Non mediate; quia ab ecclesia non est vocatus, nec ab Episcopo ordinatus ad reformandam religionem, & oppugnandam doctrinam catholicorum: nec immediate, vel extraordinarie; quia vocationem immediatam figillo miraculorum confirmare nequiuit. Resp. LUTHERVS vocatus est mediate ad presbyterium, sine ministerium ecclesiasticum & professionem theologicam. At veri ministri ecclesiae, verbum Dei recte docere, & contradicentibus os obstruere, Tit. I, 11. Professor Theologiae est, veritatem coelestem asserere, & errores ei aduersantes refutare. Non tamen negamus, aliquid extraordinarii cum B. LUTHERI ministerio, quod ad impugnationem Papatus attinet, coniunctum fuisse, non quidem ex parte vocationis, quae ordinaria & mediata fuit, sed ex parte donorum, ipsi diuinitus concessorum. Eius enim spiritus heroicus ad impugnandum Papattum, extraordinariam & specialem Dei assistentiam indicat.

Instantia: Ad propagandam doctrinam nouam, qualis fuit LUTHERI, requiritur vocatio immediata & extraordinaria, figillo miraculorum confirmanda. Resp. a) Doctrina LUTHERI non fuit noua, sed renouata, & a fermento Pontificiorum repurgata, Christi & Apostolorum miraculis dudum confirmata. b) Ioannes baptista non fecit miracula, cum tamen vocatio ipsius fuerit immediata & extraordinaria. c) Non miraculorum gloria, sed doctrinae cum verbo diuino consensus certum diuinae vocationis documentum est.

II. Episcopus, qui LUTHERUM ordinauit, aut verus pastor, aut lupus fuit.

Si verus pastor fuit; LUTHERUS ab eo fecedendo turpissimus factus est apostata. Si lupus fuit; LUTHERUS ab eo vt verus pastor, non potuit inaugurari. Resp. 1) Generatim: Hoc argumentum obiici posset omnibus, qui ab haereticis ordinati ad ecclesiae gremium redeunt. Iam vero iura pontificia asserunt, etiam ab haereticis ordinatos vere esse ordinatos, nec denuo ordinandos. 2) Speciatim: Episcopus, qui LUTHERUM ordinauit, diuerso respectu verus episcopus, & falsus episcopus, siue lupus fuit. Verus Episcopus fuit, quatenus in officio episcopali quaedam verbo diuino consentanea docebat, baptizabat, & per ritum ordinationis ministerium idoneis personis commendabat. Falsus Episcopus fuit, quatenus sinceritatem doctrinae coelestis admixto fermento traditionum humanarum corrupit, sacrificium missae loco coenae dominicae celebrauit &c. Quare essentiale ab accidentali, diuinum ab humano accurate discernendum est. Instantia: LUTHERUS non accepit ab Episcopo ordinante potestatem oppugnandi ecclesiam pontificiam. Resp. LUTHERUS a Deo per Episcopum ordinantem accepit potestatem omnes errores doctrinae oppugnandi. Et nactus est potestatem oppugnandi errores ecclesiae pontificiae.

III. Quicunque non sunt ordinati ab Episcopo, illi non sunt veri ecclesiae ministri: Atqui ministri Lutherani &c. Ergo. Minor patet: quia LUTHERUS ordinauit ministros Augustanae confessioni addictos, qui tamen non fuit Episcopus, sed tantum Presbyter. Resp. a) Iure diuino non differt Episcopus a Presbytero, adeoque etiam iure diuino competit Presbytero potestas ordinandi. b) Hodie ordinantur ministri Lutherani a Superintendente, & proinde ab Episcopo. Docet enim ius canonicum, Superintendentem nomine & officio esse Episcopum, in cap. Cleric. Dist. 21. Episcopatus vocabulum inde deductum, quod ille, qui efficitur Episcopus, superintendant. Idem inculcat AUGUSTIN. L. XIX. de Ciu. Dei c. 19. Graece est ἐπισκοπεῖν, atque inde ductum vocabulum, quod ille, qui praeficitur, eis, quibus praeficitur, superintendant. Episcopos, si volumus, latine Superintendentes possumus dicere. Conf. HULSEMANN. Manuale disp. XII. pag. 524.


### Question XI. Is the ordering of a called minister necessary?

The necessity of ordination is ordained on account of εὐταξίαν, or decorum ), and divine precept ), although the number and form of the rituals vary according to the judgment of the church ); yet it is not an absolute necessity ).

Prob. a. Ordination is necessary on account of εὐταξίαν, or decorum, viz., on account of the public declaration of capacity on the part of the called person, and his solemn segregation from the affairs of the world to the ecclesiastical office, as well as his commendation before God and in the presence of the church. Prob. b.

The imperative clearly implies a divine precept: ἀφορίσατε, separate to me both Barnabas and Saul, for the work to which I have called them, Acts XIII, 2. Separation, therefore, in general, by whatever rite it is done, is of the necessity of divine precept.

Prob. c. That the number and form of rituals vary according to the judgment of the church is evident from a comparison of Acts VI, 6; c. XIII, 3; 1 Tim. IV, 14; c. V, 22. For mention is made of prayer and χειροθεσίας (laying on of hands) in Acts VI, 6; of prayer, χειροθεσίας, and fasting in c. XIII, 3; but of χειροθεσίας alone in 1 Tim. IV, 14, V, 22. The Pontificials also add the sacrifice of the mass: but in vain, because besides the sacrifice performed once on the cross, none is given in the N. T. See Heb. VII, 27; c. X, 14. They also anoint the priests. But the ceremony of anointing does not descend from institution or example by the example of the Apostles, but from a kakozēlia [zeal without knowledge] of the Levitical cult, and was introduced into the church some centuries after the birth of Christ.

Proof d. Ordination is not simply and absolutely necessary. For without the rite of ordination, in a time of siege, plague, etc., where an abundance of ordaining presbytery cannot be had, one lawfully called by the church can perform his [duty], even before he is ordained and consecrated. Meanwhile, outside of such a case, it ought not to be omitted.

Latin:

Necessitas ordinationis est ordinata ob εὐταξίαν, siue decorum ), & praeceptum diuinum ), quamuis ritualium numerus & forma pro arbitrio ecclesiae varient ); non absoluta tamen est necessitas ).

Prob. a. Necessaria est ordinatio, ob εὐταξίαν, siue decorum, scil. ob publicam declarationem capacitatis ex parte personae vocatae, eiusque segregationem solemnem a negotiis saeculi ad munus ecclesiasticum, nec non commendationem apud Deum & coram ecclesia.

Prob. b. Praeceptum diuinum clare innuit imperatiuus: ἀφορίσατε, separate mihi tam Barnabam, quam Saulum, ad opus, ad quod vocaui illos, Actor. XIII, 2. Separatio itaque in genere, quocunque ritu fiat, est de necessitate praecepti diuini.

Prob. c. Ritualium numerum & formam pro arbitrio ecclesiae variare, ex collatione Act. VI, 6. c. XIII. 3. 1 Tim. IV, 14. c. V, 22. patet. Nam orationis & χειροθεσίας, Actor. VI, 6. orationis, χειροθεσίας & ieiunii, c. XIII, 3. solius vero χειροθεσίας, 1 Tim. IV, 14. V, 22. mentio fit. Pontificii etiam addunt sacrificium missae: sed frustra, quia praeter sacrificium, semel in cruce peractum, nullum in N. T. datur. Vid. Hebr. VII, 27. c. X, 14. lidem vngunt etiam sacerdotes. At caerimonia vnctionis non descendit ab institutione, vel exemplo Apostolorum, sed ex κακοζηλίᾳ cultus Levitici, & elapsis aliquot saeculis post Christum natum in ecclesiam introducta est.

Prob. d. Ordinatio non est simpliciter & absolute necessaria. Nam absque ritu ordinationis, tempore obsidionis, pestis &c. ubi presbyterii ordinantis copia fieri nequit, legitime ab ecclesia vocatus suo, etiam antequam ordinetur & consecretur, fungi potest. Interim extra eiusmodi casum omitti non debet.


### Question XII. What is the matter in which, or the subject of the ecclesiastical ministry?

The subject to whom the ecclesiastical office is committed is not an angel a), but a man who is suitable, capable, and lawfully called b); in respect of sex, not a woman, but a male c); in respect of doctrine, learned, orthodox, and instructed in the gifts of teaching d); in respect of life, irreproachable e).

Proof a. Although God, when about to manifest His will, has sometimes extraordinarily used the work of angels; yet He has not committed the ordinary ecclesiastical office to them. CHRYSOSTOM gives the reason, in Orat. de Elia: because angels, since by their nature they are immune from sin, would have avenged the sins of the people with sudden thunderbolts. Regard, therefore, was had for infirmity, and the priesthood was committed to men, who, admonished by their own example of human frailty, use greater gentleness toward those who are infirm in faith and preoccupied by some fall. From this we recognize both the philanthrōpia [love for mankind] of God, who has deemed men worthy of such honor that He desires to hear His voice through their mouths and tongues, and the power of God, who opposes to the devil not angels powerful in strength, but weak men, through whom He attacks the kingdom of Satan and destroys it in the hearts of many. Proof b.

Suitable and capable men are those who possess a sharp intellect, mature judgment, and bodily strength, so that they are not a subject of contempt to others due to dullness of intellect, immaturity of age, or defect of body: for whom a divine calling is to be awaited, and that today a mediate one, as we showed above.

Proof c. Paul removes the public and ordinary office of teaching in the church from the female sex in express words, 1 Cor. XIV, 34. Let your women keep silence in the churches: For it is not permitted unto them to speak; but they are commanded to be under obedience, as also saith the law. And if they will learn any thing, let them ask their husbands at home: for it is a shame for women to speak in the church. Compare 1 Tim. II, 12. Here one must distinguish accurately: 1) Between ecclesiastical offices in general, and the office of teaching in particular: 2) Between public or ecclesiastical information, and private or domestic. 3) Between the ordinary rule, and a case of extraordinary necessity, Rom. XVI, 1. Phoebe is called a diakonos, or minister, of the church at Cenchrea, because of her care for the sick and the poor. Paul calls Priscilla his helper in the Lord, Rom. XVI, 3, because of private and domestic information.

Proof d. It behooves a minister of the church to be didaktikon, apt to teach, 1 Tim. III, 2. antechomenon tou kata tēn didachēn pistou logou, holding fast the faithful word which is according to the doctrine, Tit. I, 9. hygiainonta tē pistei, sound in faith, Tit. II, 2.

Proof e. As regards the life of a minister of the church, it is required: 1) In general, that he be anepilēptos , irreproachable, 1 Tim. III, 2, and …anenkletos, unaccusable, Tit. I, 7. The minister is not indeed immune from every sin; yet he shows himself such that he cannot be justly accused and convicted of a proaretic [deliberate] and atrocious sin, by which the sacred office is dishonored. 2) In particular, a) in respect to God, he should be hosios, pious and holy, Tit. I, 8. b) Toward himself, sōphrōn, sober, doing all things moderately and circumspectly, Tit. I, 7. nēphalios, vigilant, as if placed on a watchtower, and foreseeing imminent evils, 1 Tim. III, 2. mē paroinos, not a follower of wine, but a hater of drunkenness, v. 3. enkratēs, abstaining from lust and all illicit movements and perturbations of the mind, Tit. I, 8. kosmios, composed, conducting all things ornately and decently, in gait and becoming attire, 1 Tim. III, 2. μὴ αὐθάδης, not stubborn, or too self-pleasing, Tit. I, 7. μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἀνὴρ, not a polygamist, but a man of one wife, 1 Tim. III, 2. 2) With respect to his own, let him be a good head of a household, who presides well over his own house, 1 Tim. III, 4. 5. and has children submissive in all honesty, Tit. I, 6. d) With respect to others, let him be just and equitable, not irascible, not a striker, but a stranger to fights, not making shameful gain, not avaricious, or a lover of money. Finally, let him be hospitable and a lover of good things. See 1 Tim. III, 2. seq. Tit. I, 7.

Ques. XIII. What is the matter about which, or the object of the ecclesiastical ministry?

The object of the ministry is either personal or real. The personal object is the flock of the Lord, or the assembly of those men who hear those teaching publicly, and are made participants through their ministry and the dispensation of the sacraments.

Proof 1) From Acts XX, 28. Take heed to yourselves, and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as Bishops, to feed the church of God. Therefore, the assembly of hearers is called the flock of the Lord, committed to the faith and care of the pastors.

2) From 1 Pet. V, 2. 3. 4. Feed the flock of God, which is among you, looking after it not by constraint, but willingly, nor with desire of gain, but readily; nor as being lords over the heritage, but as being examples to the flock. The rule of the ministers of the church is not royal, but pastoral, and requires vigilance and attentive care of the committed flock, so that they treat the hearers not harshly, as slaves, but kindly, as little sheep.

Ques. XIV. What are the duties of the hearers?

The duties of the hearers consist in the reverence which they owe to the ministers, as ambassadors of God a), and in beneficence, by which they bestow upon the sacred heralds the means for leading an honest life b).

Proof a. From 1 Tim. V, 17. Let the elders who rule well be counted worthy of double honor; especially those who labor in the word and doctrine. Teaching elders are honored when, as ambassadors of God, they are highly esteemed, their word is accepted as the word of God, and their actions in the sacred office are judged to be directed by the Holy Spirit.

Proof b. 1) Because the laborer is worthy of his hire, Luke X, 7.

2) Those who announce the gospel, let them live from the gospel, 2 Cor. IX, 9.

3) Let him who is instructed in the word share with him who instructs, in all good things. Gal. VI, 6.

The antithesis is that of the Anabaptists, who maintain that it is not lawful for ministers of the church to receive salaries. Who object:

I. Freely you have received, freely give, Matt. X, 18. Resp. Christ is not speaking about the salaries of those who teach, but about not making profit from miracles, as the context teaches.

II. The Apostles sought their living by the labor of their own hands, which is evident from the example of Paul, who was a σκηνοποιὸς, a tentmaker, Acts XVIII, 3. Resp. The Apostles were called immediately, and without prior labor obtained such wisdom from the Holy Spirit that they had extemporaneous sermons: Their successors from their tender years devote effort to the study of languages, instrumental disciplines, and theology itself, not without great expenditure of costs, to

which, once promoted to the Sparta of the church, they adorn with every fiber of their being, nor can they find time for other pursuits. What of the fact that Paul did not refuse to accept what was sent by the Philippians, Phil. IV, 18, although, led by his own counsel, he did not accept from the Corinthians.

Latin:

Subiectum, cui munus ecclesiasticum committitur, non est angelus a), sed homo idoneus, habilis & legitime vocatus b); ratione sexus, non foemina, sed masculus c); ratione doctrinae, eruditus, orthodoxus & docendi donis instructus d); ratione vitae, irreprehensibilis e).

Prob. a. Quamvis Deus, manifestaturus voluntatem suam, extraordinarie usus sit aliquando opera angelorum; ordinarium tamen munus ecclesiasticum ipsis non commisit. Rationem reddit CHRYSOSTOMUS, in Orat. de Elia: quia angeli, cum natura sua sint a peccato immunes, peccata populi repentinis fulminibus essent ulturi. Habita igitur est ratio infirmitatis, & commissum est sacerdotium hominibus, qui, proprio exemplo humanae fragilitatis admoniti, maiori lenitate erga infirmos in fide, & lapsu aliquo praeoccupatos utuntur. Ex quo agnoscimus cum φιλανθρωπίᾳ Dei, qui tanto dignatus est homines honore, vt per ora & linguas eorum vocem suam audire cupiat, tum potentiam Dei, qui diabolo opponit non angelos virtute potentes, sed infellos homines, per quos regnum Satanae aggreditur, & in multorum cordibus destruit.

Prob. b. Homines idonei & habiles sunt, qui perspicaci ingenio, maturo iudicio, viribusque corporis pollent, vt neque ob hebetudinem intellectus, neque ob immaturitatem aetatis, neque ob defectum corporis, aliis sint contemptui: quibus exspectandam esse vocationem diuinam, eamque hodie mediatam, supra ostendimus.

Prob. c. Publicum & ordinarium docendi munus in ecclesia a sexu foemineo disertis verbis removet Paullus, 1 Cor. XIV, 34. Mulieres vestrae in ecclesiis tacento: Non enim concessum est illis loqui, sed dicto audientibus esse; sicut etiam lex dicit. Si vero quid discere voluerint, in domo proprios maritos interroganto: Turpe enim est mulieribus, in ecclesia loqui. Confer. 1 Tim. II, 12. Accurate hic distinguendum est: 1) Inter officia ecclesiastica in genere, & officium docendi in specie: 2) Inter informationem publicam, sive ecclesiasticam, & priuatam, seu domesticam. 3) Inter regulam ordinariam, & casum necessitatis extraordinariae, Rom. XVI, 1. Phoebe vocatur ecclesiae Cenchreensis διάκονος, sive ministra, ob curam aegrotorum & pauperum. Priscillam vocat Paullus suam in Domino adiutricem, Rom. XVI, 3. ob informationem priuatam & domesticam.

Prob. d. Ministrum ecclesiae oportet esse διδακτικόν, aptum ad docendum, 1 Tim. III, 2. ἀντεχόμενον τῦ κατὰ τὴν διδαχὴν πισῦ λόγῦ, tenacem fidelis illius sermonis, qui ad doctrinam facit, Tit. I, 9. ὑγιαίνοντα τῇ πίσει, sanum fide, Tit. II, 2.

Prob. e. Quod ad vitam ministri ecclesiae attinet, exigitur: 1) In genere, vt sit ἀνεπιλήπτος, irreprehensibilis, 1 Tim. III, 2. & ἀνέγκλητος, inaccusabilis, Tit. I, 7. Non quidem ab omni peccato immunis est minister; eum tamen se praebet, vt iure accusari & convinci nequeat peccati proaretici & atrocis, quo officium sacrum dehonestatur. 2) In specie, a) respectu Dei, sit ὅσιος, pius & sanctus, Tit. I, 8. b) Erga seipsum, σώφρων, sobrius, modeseipsum, σώφρων, sobrius, moderate & circumspecte omnia agens, Tit. I, 7. νηφάλιος, vigilans, quasi in specula constitutus, & imminentia mala præuidens, 1 Tim. III, 2. μὴ πάροινος, non sectator vini, sed osor ebrietatis, v. 3. ἐγκρατὴς, abstinens a libidine & omnibus animi illicitis motibus atque perturbationibus, Tit. I, 8. κόσμιος, compositus, omnia ornate & decenter gerens, in incessu & decoro habitu, 1 Tim. III, 2. μὴ αὐθάδης non pertinax, aut sibi nimium placens, Tit. I, 7. μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἀνὴρ, non polygamus, sed vnius vxoris vir, 1 Tim. III, 2. 2) Respectu suorum, sit bonus paterfamilias, qui suæ domui bene præsit, 1 Tim. III, 4. 5. & liberos habeat subditos in omni honestate, Tit. I, 6. d) Respectu aliorum, sit iustus & æquus, non iracundus, non percussor, sed alienus a pugnis, non turpe lucrum faciens, non auarus, aut amans pecuniæ. Sit denique hospitalis & bonorum amans. Vid. 1 Tim. III, 2. seq. Tit. I, 7.

Quæst. XIII. Quæ est materia circa quam, siue obiectum ministerii ecclesiastici?

Obiectum ministerii est vel personale, vel reale. Obiectum personale est grex Domini, siue cœtus illorum hominum, qui publice docentes audiunt, eorumque ministerio & dispensatione sacramentorum redduntur participes.

Prob. 1) Ex Act. XX, 28. Attendite vobis ipsis, & toti gregi, in quo vos Spiritus S. posuit Episcopos, ad pascendum ecclesiam Dei. Cœtus itaque auditorum vocatur grex Domini, pastorum fidei ac curæ commissus.

2) Ex 1 Petr. V, 2. 3. 4. Pascite gregem Dei, qui inter vos inspicientes non coacte, sed libenter, neque cum cupidine lucri, sed promte; neque vt dominantes in sortes, sed vt exempla sitis gregis. Regimen ministrorum ecclesiæ est non regium, sed pastorale, & requirit vigilantiam & attentam curam commissi gregis, vt auditores tractent non duriter, vt seruos, sed comiter, vt ouiculas.

Quæst. XIV. Quæ sunt officia auditorum?

Officia auditorum consistunt in reuerentia, quam debent ministris, tanquam legatis Dei a), & beneficentia, qua præconibus sacris subsidia vitæ honeste agendæ largiuntur b).

Prob. a. Ex 1 Tim. V, 17. Qui bene præsunt presbyteri, duplici honore digni æstimantor; maxime qui laborant in verbo & doctrina. Honorantur presbyteri docentes, cum, velut legati Dei, magni æstimantur, verbum eorum acceptatur, tanquam verbum Dei, & actiones eorum in officio sacro a Spiritu S. dirigi censentur.

Prob. b. 1) Quia operarius dignus est mercede sua, Luc. X, 7.

2) Qui euangelium annuntiant, ex euangelio viuant, 2 Cor. IX, 9.

3) Communicato is, qui informatur in sermone, cum eo, qui informat, in omnibus bonis. Gal. VI, 6.

Antithesis est Anabaptistarum, statuentium, ministris ecclesiæ non licere salaria accipere. Qui obiiciunt:

I. Gratis accepistis, gratis date, Matth. X, 18. Resp. Christus non loquitur de salariis docentium, sed de quæstu non faciendo ex miraculis, docente contextu.

II. Apostoli labore manuum suarum victum quæsiuerunt, quod patet exemplo Paulli, qui fuit σκηνοποιὸς, tentoriorum confector, Act. XVIII, 3. Resp. Apostoli immediate erant vocati, & sine præuio labore tantam sapientiam a Spiritu S. nacti, vt extemporales haberent conciones: Successores eorum a teneris vnguiculis studio linguarum, disciplinis instrumentalibus, & ipsi theologiæ, non sine magno sumtuum impendio dant operam, ad

Spartam ecclesiae promoti omnibus animi nervis eam ornant, nec aliis rebus vacare possunt. Quid? quod Paullus a Philippensibus transmissa suscipere non recusauerit, Phil. IV, 18. licet suo ductus consilio a Corinthiis non acceperit.


### Q. XV. Can a minister of the church accept an honorarium, offered by a penitent, with a good conscience?

A minister of the church can accept an honorarium, offered by a penitent with a good intention, with an uninjured conscience . But if anywhere the custom of offering and receiving such an honorarium brings with it various inconveniences, it can be abrogated with the consent of the church, and the stipends of the ministers of the divine word can be increased in a more convenient manner .

Proof a. 1) In certain churches the honorarium, which after absolution is given by the penitent to the confessor, and is commonly called the confession-penny (der Beicht-Pfennig), is a part of the salary. For since sometimes the salary becomes small, it is supplemented by the confession-penny. That an honorable stipend must be provided for the ministers of the divine word, Christ teaches in Luke X, 7, and Paul in 1 Tim. V, 18.

V, 18. 2) He who is instructed in the word, let him communicate of his goods to him who instructs him, in every place and time, Gal. VI, 6. But the penitent is instructed in the divine word by the confessor. Therefore, it is lawful for him to communicate of his goods to the same person even in the place of confession.

3) In the Old Testament it was commanded that no one should appear empty-handed before the Priest, Deut. XVI, 16, 17. Therefore, neither in the New Testament is it illicit to appear before a minister of God with a confession-penny.

4) In the primitive church, agapae, or gifts of bread and wine, were brought, from which something was taken for the Holy Supper, but a part was offered in a sacred place to the ministers of the word. Why, therefore, cannot the confession-penny, as a sign of gratitude, be given and received in the temple?

Proof b. If anywhere quarrels arise among ministers of the church on account of the confession-penny, with one colleague being indignant that another has more penitents; if the poorer ones are deterred from private confession on account of a lack of money; if the sins of the rich are treated more leniently on account of larger gifts: the custom of giving the confession-penny can be abrogated, and the stipends of pastors, which in most places are meager, can be increased in another way. Whence it has been piously and prudently provided in Denmark that pastors should not accept any price for absolution from a penitent, as witnessed by D. BROCHMAND, Tom. II. system p. 1021.

The antithesis is that of the Anabaptists, who maintain that the confession-penny cannot be accepted by a confessor with a clear conscience. They object:

I. Whoever sells the spiritual gift of absolution, they commit the crime of Simony: But Lutheran ministers, etc., do this. Therefore.

Resp. I deny the minor. Simony is that by which a price is paid for acquiring a spiritual good: But the confession-penny is not paid for acquiring absolution; since that is obtained even by those who do not pay, but is given for the sake of gratitude.

II. It went badly for Gehazi, the minister of Elisha, because after the cleansing of Naaman the Syrian from leprosy he had accepted silver, 2 Kings V, 26: so for all who accept the confession-penny, a sad fate is to be expected.

Resp. Gehazi the minister, against the will of his Master, demanded silver: But the ministers of the church, against the will of Christ their Lord, do not demand or exact the confession-penny. See Luke X, 7.

III. Those who accept the confession-penny give scandal to the penitents, who are persuaded that absolution is sold for that penny. Resp. No scandal is to be feared: for the penitents know confessing that they are not buying absolution, but giving the confession-money as a sign of a grateful mind.

IV. The confession-money produces various inconveniences: for it nourishes rivalries among ministers; its lack keeps the poor away from confession; on the other hand, the sins of the rich, who offer a larger honorarium, are not rebuked. Resp. a) The abuse can be prudently abolished, so that the use is retained. b) Because of these inconveniences, if they occur, the confession-money can be abrogated, yet in such a way that the meager stipends of the pastors are increased by another method.

Latin:

Minister ecclesiae honorarium, a confitente bono animo oblatum illesa conscientia acceptare potest . Sicubi autem mos offerendi & accipiendi eiusmodi honorarium varia incommoda secum trahat, consentiente ecclesia abrogari, & stipendia ministrorum verbi diuini commodiori ratione augeri possunt .

Prob. a. 1) In quibusdam ecclesiis honorarium, quod post absolutionem confessionario datur a confitente, & vulgo nummus confessionis (der Beicht-Pfennig) vocatur, est pars falarii. Cum enim interdum salarium fit exiguum, per nummum confessionis suppletur. De honorifico autem stipendio prospiciendum esse ministris verbi diuini, docet Christus Luc. X, 7. & Paullus 1 Tim. V, 18.

2) Qui verbo instituitur, instituenti, quocunque loco & tempore, licite communicato de bonis suis, Gal. VI, 6. At confitens a confessionario verbo diuino instituitur. Ergo eidem etiam in loco confessionis licite communicato de bonis suis.

3) In vet. testam. iubebatur, ne quis vacuus coram Sacerdote compareret, Deut. XVI, 16. 17. Ergo nec in nouo testam. illicitum est, cum nummo confessionali comparere coram ministro Dei.

4) In primitiva ecclesia ἀγάπαι, seu donaria ex pane & vino afferebantur, e quibus sumebatur aliquid ad S. coenam, pars vero in loco sacro offerebatur ministris verbi. Cur igitur nummus confessionis, tanquam gratitudinis signum, non potest in templo tradi & accipi?

Prob. b. Sicubi oriuntur simultates inter ministros ecclesiae, ob nummum confessionis, indignante vno collega, quod alter plures habeat confitentes; si pauperiores absterrentur a confessione priuata ob defectum pecuniae; si ditiorum peccata mollius tractentur ob dona largiora: mos dandi nummum confessionis abrogari, & alia ratione stipendia pastorum, quae plurimis in locis sunt exigua, augeri possunt. Vnde pie & prudenter cautum est in Dania, ne pastores vllum absolutionis pretium a confitente accipiant, teste D. BROCHMANDO, Tom. II. system p. 1021.

Antithesis est Anabaptistarum, statuentium, nummum confessionis a confessionario falsa conscientia accipi non posse.

Qui obiiciunt: I. Quicunque vendunt donum spirituale absolutionis, illi committunt crimen Simoniae: Atqui ministri Lutherani &c. Ergo.

Resp. Neg. min. Simonia est, qua persoluitur pretium pro bono spirituali acquirendo: Nummus confessionis autem non soluitur pro absolutione acquirenda; quippe quae obtingit etiam non soluentibus, sed datur gratitudinis ergo.

II. Gehafi, ministro Elisae, male cessit, quod post emundationem Naamani Syri alepra argentum acceperat, 2 Reg. V, 26: ita omnibus, nummum confessionis accipientibus, triste fatum exspectandum est.

Resp. Gehafi minister, inuito suo Domino, postulauit argentum: At ministri ecclesiae, Christo Domino suo inuito, non postulant, aut exigunt nummum confessionis. Vid. Luc. X, 7.

III. Qui nummum confessionis accipiunt, scandalum dant confitentibus, persuasis, absolutionem vendi pro nummo illo. Resp. Nullum metuendum est scandalum: sciunt enim confitentes, se non emere absolutionem, sed nummum confessionis dare tanquam grati animi signum.

IV. Nummus confessionalis parit varia incommoda: Alit enim simultates inter ministros; ipsius defectus arcet pauperes a confessione; contra, non arguuntur peccata diuitum, honorarium maius offerentium. Resp. a) Abusus potest prudenter aboli, vt retineatur vsus. b) Ob hæc incommoda, sicubi contingant, nummus confessionis abrogari potest, ita tamen, vt alia ratione exigua stipendia pastorum augeantur.


### Q. XVI. What is the real object of the ecclesiastical ministry?

The real object of the ministry is both divine mysteries and ecclesiastical discipline .

Prob. a. Divine mysteries are the revealed word of God, and the sacraments, which the ministers of the church offer and dispense. For this reason they are called stewards of the mysteries of God (οἰκονόμοι μυστηρίων Θεῦ), 1 Cor. 4:1. Prob. b. Pastors exercise ecclesiastical discipline in such a way that they employ the degrees of admonition, Matt. 18:15-16, and observe the rules prescribed by St. Paul, 1 Tim. 5:1 ff.

Latin:

Obiectum ministerii reale sunt tum mysteria diuina , tum disciplina ecclesiastica .

Prob. a. Mysteria diuina sunt verbum Dei reuelatum, & sacramenta, quæ offerunt & dispensant ministri ecclesiæ. Id propter vocantur οἰκονόμοι μυστηρίων Θεῦ, 1 Cor. IV, 1. Prob. b. Disciplinam ecclesiasticam sic exercent Pastores, vt gradus admonitionum adhibeant, Matth. XVIII, 15. 16. & regulas a S. Paulo præscriptas obseruent, 1 Tim. V, 1. seq.


### Q. XVII. What is the form of the ministry?

The form of the ministry is the due, decent, and public execution of the power and office committed to it. But the power committed to the ministers of the church, and the office, is that of publicly teaching , and ordinarily dispensing the sacraments , just as also the power and duty of remitting and retaining sins . Obs. Commonly, the power committed to Pastors through vocation and ordination is divided into the power of order and of jurisdiction, which distinction the Apology of the Augsburg Confession explains on page 294. We approve of the old partition of power into the power of order and the power of jurisdiction. A Bishop has the power of order, the ministry of the word and of the sacraments: he also has the power of jurisdiction, that is, the authority to excommunicate those liable for public crimes, and again to absolve them, if, having been converted, they seek absolution. Nor indeed does he have tyrannical power, that is, without a certain law; nor royal, that is, above the law, but he has a certain mandate, the certain word of God, which he ought to teach, and according to which he ought to exercise his jurisdiction. Which distinction, however, is less accurate; because that which is called the power of jurisdiction is not judicial properly, on the part of the minister, who does not absolve as a judge, nor does he pass any sentence, but dispenses that which was passed by a superior. Confer D. SCHERZER in his breviary of Hulsemann, ch. 19, fol. 1506.

Prob. a. No one, unless sent by God, can lawfully preach in public assemblies, Rom. 10:15.

Prob. b. Those who are stewards of the mysteries of God, 1 Cor. 4:1, to them belongs the power of ordinarily dispensing the sacraments. Prob. c.

The power of the keys, binding and loosing, Christ committed to the Apostles, and to all duly called and ordained ministers of the church, Matt. 16:19, John 20:23.

Latin:

Forma ministerii est debita, decens & publica commissæ potestatis & officii exsecutio. Commissæ autem est ministris ecclesiæ potestas, & officium publice docendi , & sacramenta ordinarie dispensandi , iuxta atque potestas & munus remittendi & retinendi peccata . Obs. Vulgo potestas, per vocationem & ordinationem Pastoribus commissa, diuiditur in potestatem ordinis, & iurisdictionis, quam distinctionem explicat Apologia August. Conf. pag. 294. Placet nobis vetus partitio potestatis in potestatem ordinis, & potestatem iurisdictionis. Habet Episcopus potestatem ordinis, ministerium verbi, & sacramentorum: habet & potestatem iurisdictionis, hoc est, auctoritatem excommunicandi obnoxios publicis criminibus, & rursus absoluendi eos, si conuersi petant absolutionem. Neque vero habet potestatem tyrannicam, hoc est, sine certa lege; neque regiam, hoc est, supra legem, sed habet certum mandatum, certum verbum Dei, quod docere, iuxta quod exercere suam iurisdictionem debet. Quæ tamen distinctio minus accurata est; quia illa, quæ potestas iurisdictionis dicitur, non est iudicialis proprie, ex parte ministri, qui non tanquam iudex absoluit, nec vllam fert sententiam, sed a superiori latam dispensat. Confer. D. SCHERZER. in breuiar. Hulsem. cap. XIX. fol. 1506.

Prob. a. Nemo, nisi missus a Deo, in conuentibus publicis licite prædicare potest, Rom. X, 15.

Prob. b. Qui sunt œconomi mysteriorum Dei, 1 Cor. IV, 1. illis competit potestas sacramenta ordinarie dispensandi.

Prob. c. Potestatem clauium, soluentem & ligantem, Christus commisit Apostolis, & omnibus rite vocatis & ordinatis ecclesiæ ministris, Matth. XVI, 19. Io. XX, 23.


### Q. XVIII. How does a minister of the church rightly perform the office of teaching?

A minister of the church rightly performs the office of teaching: a) by accurately investigating, certainly eliciting, and perspicuously explaining the genuine sense of the divine word through legitimate means of interpretation: b) by applying the explained word to didactic use, and elentic, paedeutic, epanorthotic, and paracletic [methods] by applying them decently .

Prob. a. The minister of the church is a sacred interpreter, whose duty it is: 1) To weigh the force of meaning and the emphasis of the individual words that are in the original text, and to consider diligently the construction of the connected phrases according to the custom of the holy language; 2) To investigate and explain the mind of the speaker through the Prophets and Apostles of the Holy Spirit, from the antecedents and consequents, from the occasion, the scope, the impulsive cause, and the circumstances.

Prob. b. From 2 Tim. III, 16. All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable πρὸς διδασκαλίαν, for doctrine, by which the dogmas of the faith are clearly proposed and solidly confirmed: πρὸς ἔλεγχον, for reproof, by which errors opposing the doctrine of the faith are detected and refuted: πρὸς ἐπανόρθωσιν, for correction, by which the baseness of vices and the guilt of punishments are shown, and minds are called away from and amended of the same: πρὸς παιδείαν, for instruction, by which the duties of Christians in any state are clearly taught, and they are excited to perform them by solid arguments brought forward and by suitable arguments for persuasion. To these add παράκλησιν, or consolation

Latin:

minister ecclesiæ officio docendi recte fungitur? Minister ecclesiæ officio docendi recte fungitur: a) Genuinum verbi diuini sensum, per legitima interpretandi media, accurate inuestigando, certo eruendo & perspicue explicando: b) verbum explicatum ad vsum didascalicum, & elenticum, paedeuticum, epanorthoticum & paracleticum decenter applicando .

Prob. a. Minister ecclesiae est Hermeneuta sacer, cuius est: 1) Vocum singularum, quae sunt in textu originali, vim significandi atque emphasin ponderare, & phrasium coniunctarum constructionem iuxta consuetudinem linguae sanctae diligenter considerare; 2) Ex antecedentibus & consequentibus, ex occasione, scopo, causa impulsiva, & circumstantiis mentem loquentis per Prophetas & Apostolos Spiritus S. investigare & explicare.

Prob. b. Ex 2 Tim. III, 16. Omnis scriptura divinitus inspirata est, & utilis πρὸς διδασκαλίαν, ad doctrinam, qua dogmata fidei perspicue proponuntur, solideque firmantur: πρὸς ἔλεγχον, ad redargutionem, qua errores, doctrinae fidei adversantes, deteguntur & refutantur: πρὸς ἐπανόρθωσιν, ad correctionem, qua vitiorum turpitudo & reatus poenae ostenditur, & ab iisdem animi avocantur atque emendantur: πρὸς παιδείαν, ad disciplinam, qua officia Christianorum in quovis statu diserte docentur, & ad ea praestanda adductis solidis, & ad persuadendum idoneis argumentis excitantur. His adde παράκλησιν, sive consolationem


### Q. XIX. How does the minister of the church rightly use the power of dispensing the sacraments?

The minister of the church uses the power of dispensing the sacraments rightly by administering them according to the words of institution , by conferring them in a timely manner upon men who are in need of the sacraments, yet not upon the unworthy themselves , and by keeping the unworthy from the use of the sacraments .

Prob. a. To the form of the sacrament belongs the word of institution, by which the external symbol is consecrated, or separated from common use to sacred use. Hence AUGUSTINE, tract. 80 on John: Let the word be added to the element, and it becomes a sacrament.

Prob. b. A pious pastor, mindful of his office, does not suffer, through his own fault, an infant to depart from this life without baptism, or a penitent adult desirous of the eucharist to depart without participation of the body and blood of the Lord.

Prob. c. The unworthy are contumacious sinners and those who do not know how to repent. The sacraments are not dispensed to these, lest that which is holy be given to the dogs, and pearls be cast before swine. Matt. VII, 6.

Latin:

Minister ecclesiae potestate sacramenta dispensandi recte utitur, iuxta verba institutionis ea administrando , hominibus sacramentorum indigis, neque tamen ipsis indignis, tempestive ea conferendo , indignos a sacramentorum usu arcendo .

Prob. a. Ad formam sacramenti pertinet verbum institutionis, quo symbolum externum consecratur, sive ab usu communi ad usum sacrum segregatur. Hinc AVGVSTIN. tract. 80. in Ioann. Accedat verbum ad elementum, & fit sacramentum.

Prob. b. Pastor pius, suique officii memor, non patitur, sua culpa infantem absque baptismo, aut adultum poenitentem & eucharistiae cupidum, sine participatione corporis & sanguinis dominici ex hac vita decedere.

Prob. c. Indigni sunt peccatores contumaces & poenitere nescii. His non dispensantur sacramenta, ne, quod sanctum est, detur canibus, & margaritae ante porcos proiiciantur. Matth. VII, 6.


### Q. XX. What kind of power to remit sins has been committed to the ministers of the church?

The ministers of the church have the power of remitting sins, not αὐτοκρατορικὴν, or principal and independent a), but διακονικὴν, or ministerial and delegated b), by which they remit to contrite and penitent sinners all sins, without any reservation of guilt or punishment, not only ἱστορικῶς, or significantly and declaratively, but also effectively and really, yet ὀργανικῶς c) d):

Proof a. God alone remits sins αὐτοκρατορικῶς καὶ ἀυτεξυσίως, by a principal, magisterial, and independent power. I, I myself, blot out your iniquities for my own sake, says Jehovah, Is. XLIII, 25. Hence AMBROSE on 2 Cor. XII: To forgive sins and to give the Holy Spirit is of God alone, meanwhile, however, God in this his magisterial absolution ordinarily uses the ministry of men.

Proof b. Christ said to Peter: I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven. Matt. XVI, 19. He said the same also to all the Apostles: Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven; whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven, John XX, 20. Therefore, the power of remitting sins depends on Christ (not excluding God the Father and the Holy Spirit, because it is an external work) by reason of form, norm, exercise, and efficacy. 1) By reason of form; because it is a delegated power, and therefore such and so much only as God has delegated. 2) By reason of norm; since the minister of the church can absolve penitent sinners not according to his own will (which would be to abuse the power), but according to the norm of divine judgment. 3) By reason of exercise, because God concurs with the ministers in the act of absolution, and absolves through them. 4) By reason of efficacy; because the minister cannot absolve except by a delegated power, and therefore one subordinate to the principal cause. All of which teach quite openly that the ministry by nature absolves later in these lands than God absolves in heaven. For when the principal and instrumental cause concur at the same time for the same ἀποτέλεσ- μα, the principal cause, because it elevates the instrumental, is always understood to act prior by nature.

Proof c. 1) The ministers of the church have the keys of heaven, so that whatever they bind and loose on earth is also bound and loosed in heaven, Matt. XVI, 16. John XX, 23. Therefore, they really bind and loose, and do not merely announce a binding and loosing already done in heaven. The reason for the consequence is: because he who receives a key to loose and open, he does not signify that it is opened by another, but he himself opens. For a key is not the same thing as the announcement of an opening, and to loose is not the same thing as merely to declare a loosing done by another.

2) Such as is the solution of sins which is done by God in heaven, such is the solution which is done by the ministers on earth: But the solution in heaven is real and effective. Therefore, the solution on earth is also real and effective. The major premise is clear: because from the real identity of the objects (whatever you loose) and the subjects (whomever you loose), a real identity of the solution is also undoubtedly gathered.

3) Ministers do not loose sins in their own name, but in God's. Therefore, this solution is not a bare declaration, or a human action; but plainly divine, one in number and undivided, just as the power is one in number, namely divine, by which they loose sins. For there is one key of heaven by which they loose. The minister does not have one key, and God another. Whence, he who hears the ministers absolving, hears Christ himself: But he who hears Christ (absolving) is absolved effectively, not only declaratively: Therefore.

4) Ministers through the word of God really and effectively convert sinners, Luke I, 16, regenerate them, 1 Cor. IV, 15, save them, 1 Tim. IV, 16. Therefore, they also really and effectively remit sins.

Proof. That the ministers of the church remit all sins is clear: 1) from the unlimited universality both of the object: Whatsoever you shall loose on earth, Matt. XIX, 18. and of the subject: Whosesoever sins you remit, John XX, 23. 2) As widely as the merit of Christ extends, so widely extends the remission of sins obtained by the merit of Christ: But the merit of Christ extends to all sins, without any restriction: Therefore.

Latin:

Ministri ecclesiæ habent potestatem remittendi peccata, non αὐτοκρατορικὴν, siue principalem & independentem a), sed διακονικὴν, siue ministerialem & delegatam b), qua peccatoribus contritis & pœnitentibus non tantum ἱστορικῶς, siue significatiue & declaratiue, sed etiam effectiue & realiter, ὀργανικῶς tamen c), omnia peccata, sine vlla culpæ vel pœnæ reseruatione, remittunt d):

Prob. a. Solus Deus αὐτοκρατορικῶς καὶ ἀυτεξυσίως, potestate principali, magisteriali & independente peccata remittit. Ego, ego ipse deleo iniquitates tuas propter me, inquit Iehouah, Es. XLIII, 25. Hinc AMBROSIVS in 2 Cor. XII. Peccata dimittere, & Spiritum sanctum dare, solius Dei est, interim vero Deus in hac sua absolutione magisteriali ordinarie vtitur ministerio hominum.

Prob. b. Christus dixit Petro: Dabo tibi claues regni cælorum, & quidquid ligaueris in terra, erit ligatum in cælis, & quidquid solueris in terra, erit solutum in cælis. Matth. XVI, 19. Idem dixit quoque omnibus Apostolis: Quæcunque ligaueritis in terra, ligata erunt in cælo; quæcunque solueritis in terra, soluta erunt in cælo, Io. XX, 20. Dependet itaque potestas remittendi peccata a Christo (non excluso Deo Patre & Spiritu S. quia est opus ad extra) ratione formæ, normæ, exercitii, ac efficaciæ. 1) Ratione formæ; quia est potestas delegata, adeoque talis ac tanta solum, qualem, quantamque Deus delegauit. 2) Ratione normæ; cum minister ecclesiæ non ad proprium arbitrium (quod esset abuti potestate), sed iuxta normam iudicii diuini pœnitentes peccatores absoluere possit. 3) Ratione exercitii, quia Deus in actu absolutionis cum ministris concurrit, & per eos absoluit. 4) Ratione efficaciæ; quia non, nisi delegata, adeoque caussæ principali subordinata vi ac potestate, minister absoluere potest. Quæ omnia satis aperte docent, ministerium natura posterius absoluere in his terris, quam Deus absoluit in cælis. Nam quando principalis & instrumentalis caussa ad idem ἀποτέλεσμα tempore simul concurrunt, principalis caussa, quia instrumentalem eleuat, semper natura prius agere intelligitur.

Prob. c. 1) Ministri ecclesiæ habent claues cæli, vt, quidquid ligant ac soluunt in terris, etiam ligatum ac solutum sit in cælis, Matth. XVI, 16. Io. XX, 23. E. realiter ligant ac soluunt, non vero ligationem ac solutionem in cælis factam tantum annuntiant. Ratio consequentiæ est; quia qui clauem accipit, vt soluat & aperiat; ille non significat ab alio aperiri, sed ipse aperit. Neque enim clauis idem est, quod annuntiatio aperturæ, & soluere non est idem, atque solutionem ab alio factam duntaxat declarare.

2) Qualis est solutio peccatorum, quæ fit a Deo in cælis, talis est solutio, quæ fit a ministris in terris: At solutio in cælis est realis & effectiua. E. etiam solutio in terris est realis & effectiua. Maior patet: quia ex identitate reali obiectorum (quidquid solueritis) & subiectorum (quorumcunque solueritis) etiam identitas realis solutionis indubitato colligitur.
