3) Ministri non suo, sed Dei nomine peccata soluunt. E. hæc solutio non est nuda declaratio, aut humana actio; sed plane diuina, vna numero ac indiuisa, sicut vna numero potestas est, nempe diuina, qua peccata soluunt. Est enim vna clauis cæli, per quam solvunt. Non aliam clauem minister, aliam clauem Deus habet. Vnde, qui ministros absoluentes audit, ipsum Christum audit: At qui Christum audit (absoluentem), effectiue, non solum declaratiue absoluitur: Ergo.

4) Ministri per verbum Dei peccatores realiter & effectiue conuertunt, Luc. I, 16. regenerant, 1 Cor. IV, 15. saluant, 1 Tim. IV, 16. Ergo etiam realiter & effectiue peccata remittunt.

Prob. d. Ministros ecclesiæ omnia peccata remittere, liquet: 1) ex illimitata vniuersalitate cum obiecti: Quæcunque solueritis in terra, Matth. XIX, 18. tum subiecti: Quorumcunque remiseritis, Io. XX, 23. 2) Quam late se extendit meritum Christi, tam late se extendit remissio peccatorum merito Christi parta: Atqui meritum Christi se extendit ad omnia peccata, sine vlla restrictione: E.


### Q. XXI. What kind of power of retaining sins is granted to the ministers of the church?

The ministers of the church have the power of retaining sins, not as a principal or independent power, but as a ministerial and delegated one a), by which they deny the remission of sins to enormous, publicly flagitious, and notorious sinners b), and either exclude them only from the use of the Holy Supper c), or, with the consent of the ecclesiastical senate, actually cast them out from the society of the church, and by an effective declaration deliver them to Satan d), so that they may perform true repentance and be reconciled to God and the church e).

Proof. a. Christ delegated the right of the binding key to the church, the spiritual mother of the family. He committed the exercise of this right to the Apostles and their successors, Matt. XVIII, 18. John XX, 22. Since, therefore, the power of the binding key is delegated, the ministers of the church can bind impenitent sinners not according to their own whim, but according to the norm of divine judgment.

Proof. b. Remission of sins is denied not to sinners falling through ignorance or infirmity (for to them a gentle admonition with an exhortation to avoid future lapses suffices), but to manifest and obstinate ones, who give scandal to others. Since they cause harm by their example, they are to be rebuked before all, so that the rest also may have fear, 1 Tim. V, 20.

Proof. c. Binding is the denial of absolution, and is commonly called excommunication, which is usually distinguished into lesser and greater. The lesser excommunication is that by which a publicly flagitious sinner is excluded from the use of the Holy Supper; the foundation of which is the saying of Christ: do not give what is holy to the dogs, Matt. VII, 6. The greater excommunication is that by which a manifest and obstinate sinner is not only excluded from the participation of the sacraments, but is also cut off from the church like a rotten member, and delivered to Satan, until he repents: the foundation of which is: If he will not hear the church, let him be to you as a heathen and a publican, Matt. XVIII, 17.

Proof. d. The greater excommunication should not be performed by a pastor without the consent of the ecclesiastical senate, or Consistory, which is the representative church. For ecclesiastical censure has certain degrees, intimated by Christ, Matt. XVIII, 15. The first censure is private, secret, and fraternally gentle. The second is collegiate, either chosen by the judgment of the parties, or according to the order established among the colleges. The third is ecclesiastical, and that either before the Consistory, or, if the evil is epidemic, before a council of several churches. Which ecclesiastical censure is not only declarative, but also effectively binding and inclusive in the shackles of guilt; for that is what it means to bind, Matt. XXII, 13. delivering into the power of Satan, 1 Cor. V, 3. 4. 5. excluding from the society of the faithful, not those who are necessary or common to all men, but those who are free and specific, from whom contagion or irritation might be feared, 2 Thess. III, 14.

Proof. e. The end of excommunication is not the perdition of the soul, but conversion. For the enormous and notorious sinner is delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus, 1 Cor. V, 5. Through excommunication, the lustful flesh is crucified and mortified, but the soul is brought back from sin to repentance and eternal life. Therefore, excommunication does not bring about a mortal exclusion, such as that of Ananias and Sapphira, Acts V; nor a deprivation of goods, possessions, and dominion; nor capital punishment, since it is not a political, but an ecclesiastical penalty: and thus it implies suspension and deprivation of the benefits of the church, and then

Latin:

Ministri ecclesiæ habent potestatem retinendi peccata non principalem, aut independentem, sed ministerialem & delegatam a), qua peccatoribus enormibus, publice flagitiosis & notoriis, peccatorum remissionem denegant b), eosque vel ab vsu S. cœnæ tantum arcent c), vel ex consensu senatus ecclesiastici e societate ecclesiæ realiter eiiciunt, & efficaci declaratione Satanæ tradunt d), vt veram pœnitentiam agant, & Deo atque ecclesiæ reconcilientur e).

Prob. a. Ius clauis ligantis Christus delegauit ecclesiæ, spirituali matrifamilias. Exercitium huius iuris commisit Apostolis, & eorum successoribus, Matth. XVIII, 18. Io. XX, 22. Cum itaque potestas clauis ligantis sit delegata; ministri ecclesiæ non ad proprium arbitrium, sed iuxta normam iudicii diuini peccatores impœnitentes ligare possunt.

Prob. b. Denegatur remissio peccatorum non peccatoribus ex ignorantia, vel infirmitate labentibus (quippe quibus sufficit blanda admonitio cum exhortatione ad cauendos futuros lapsus), sed manifestis & obstinatis, qui aliis dant scandalum. Qui cum noceant exemplo, coram omnibus sunt arguendi, vt etiam reliqui timorem habeant, 1 Tim. V, 20.

Prob. c. Ligatio est denegatio absolutionis, diciturque vulgo excommunicatio, quæ in minorem, & maiorem distingui solet. Excommunicatio minor est, qua peccator publice flagitiosus ab vsu S. cœnæ arcetur; cuius fundamentum est effatum Christi: ne sanctum detis canibus, Matth. VII, 6. Excommunicatio maior est, qua peccator manifestus & obstinatus non tantum a participatione sacramentorum arcetur, sed etiam velut membrum putridum ab ecclesia rescinditur, & Satanæ traditur, vsque dum resipiscat: cuius fundamentum est: Si ecclesiam non audiuerit, sit tibi velut ethnicus & publicanus, Matth. XVIII, 17.

Prob. d. Excommunicatio maior non sit a pastore, absque consensu senatus ecclesiastici, siue Consistorii, quod est ecclesia repræsentatiua. Habet enim censura ecclesiastica certos gradus, insinuatos a Christo, Matth. XVIII, 15. Prima censura est singularis, secreta, fraterneque mansueta. Altera est collegialis, vel arbitrio partium electa, vel iuxta ordinem, inter collegia constitutum. Tertia est ecclesiastica, eaque vel coram Consistorio, vel, si malum fuerit epidemicum, coram plurium ecclesiarum concilio. Quæ censura ecclesiastica non est tantum declaratiua, sed etiam efficaciter ligatiua & inclusiua in compedes reatus; id enim est ligare, Matth. XXII, 13. traditiua in potestatem Satanæ, 1 Cor. V, 3. 4. 5. exclusiua a societate fidelium, non necessaria, aut communi omnibus hominibus, sed libera & propria, vnde contagium, vel irritatio timeri posset, 2 Thess. III, 14.

Prob. e. Finis excommunicationis non est perditio animæ, sed conuersio. Traditur enim peccator enormis & notorius Satanæ in perditionem carnis, vt spiritus saluetur in die Domini Iesu, 1 Cor. V, 5. Per excommunicationem libidinosa caro crucifigitur & mortificatur, anima vero a peccato ad resipiscentiam & vitam æternam reducitur. Infert itaque excommunicatio non mortalem exclusionem, qualis erat Ananiæ & Sapphiræ, Act. V.; non priuationem bonorum, possessionum & dominii; neque capitole supplicium, cum sit pœna non politica, sed ecclesiastica: adeoque importat suspensionem & priuationem beneficiorum ecclesiæ, atque tum anxi-


### Quæst. XXII

the anxiety of the soul, by which they are agitated by Satan, who are in his power, then sometimes the affliction of the body.…

The antithesis is 1) of the Socinians, who maintain that the ministers of the church do not remit sins really or effectively, but only declaratively. 2) Of Thomas Erastus, Doctor of Medicine, who denies that enormous and notorious sinners are to be barred from the use of the S. Supper. Their arguments are: I. God alone remits sins, Is. XLIII, 25. Therefore not the minister of the church. Resp. God alone remits sins αὐτοκρατορικῶς, by principal and independent power: the minister of the church remits διακονικῶς, or ὀργανικῶς, by subordinate and delegated power. II. Christ delegated to the Apostles the power of remitting and retaining sins: But that power expired with the Apostles. The reason for the consequence is: because no successors of the Apostles are given. For the Apostles were immediately called, instructed with the privilege of infallibility and the power of teaching in the whole world. Such Apostles are not given today. Resp. 1) Certain special axioms and extraordinary privileges belonged to the Apostles, in respect of which they have no successors: there belonged to them also, considering it generally, the power of teaching, of dispensing the sacraments, and of remitting and retaining sins, in respect of which all faithful ministers of the church are their successors. 2) The church is given today: therefore the keys of the kingdom of heaven given to the whole church are also given. The gospel is given: therefore also absolution from sins. The sacraments are given: therefore also the remission of sins. Timothy was able to save himself and those who heard him, 1 Tim. IV, 16. Therefore Timothy, who was not an Apostle, was able to remit sins. III. Whoever does not possess the gift of infallibility, he cannot remit sins. Ministers mediately called do not possess the gift of infallibility. Therefore. The major is evident; because those sinners are to be absolved, whose repentance and faith is certainly known. Resp. For the power of absolving, apostolic infallibility is not required, but an ordered knowledge, drawn from the θεοπνεύστῳ word, suffices. And although the ministers of the church are not searchers of hearts, nevertheless from external signs they gather the internal repentance of the heart. IV. Judas the traitor was admitted by Christ to the supper, even with the crime of betrayal revealed: Therefore, an enormous and notorious sinner is not to be repelled from the use of the S. supper. Resp. Christ did not bar Judas from the supper, for the reason that the betrayal, which Judas was plotting, was not yet completed. No one, therefore, is barred from the sacraments on account of a future crime, and one known only to God, but on account of a committed crime.

Ques. XXII. What is the end of the ecclesiastical ministry?

The ultimate end of the ecclesiastical ministry, on the part of God, is the glory of the divine name a), on the part of man the ultimate end is eternal salvation b), the intermediate ends are illumination & conversion c), regeneration d), reconciliation with God e).

Prob. a. Neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth, but God that giveth the increase, 1 Cor. III, 4. Faithful heralds do not attribute the success of their office to themselves, but to the power of God, by whose grace they are what they are, 1 Cor. XV, 10. Prob. b. From 1 Tim. IV, 16. Thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee. Prob. c. From Acts XXVI, 18. I send thee to open their eyes, that they may turn themselves from darkness to light. Prob. d. From 1 Cor. IV, 15. In Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel. Prob. e. The ecclesiastical ministry is the ministry of reconciliation, 2 Cor. V, 19. Obs. From these ends the necessity and utility of the ecclesiastical ministry is simultaneously distinguished.

Latin:

etatem animæ, qua exagitantur a Satana, qui in ipsius sunt potestate, tum afflictionem quandoque corporis.

Antithesis est 1) Socinianorum, statuentium, ministros ecclesiæ non realiter, aut effectiue, sed tantum declaratiue peccata remittere. 2) Thomæ Erasti, Doctoris Medici, negantis peccatores enormes & notorios ab vsu S. cœnæ arcendos esse. Quorum argumenta sunt: I. Solus Deus peccata remittit, Es. XLIII, 25. Ergo non minister ecclesiæ. Resp. Solus Deus peccata remittit αὐτοκρατορικῶς, potestate principali & independente: Minister ecclesiæ remittit διακονικῶς, vel ὀργανικῶς, potestate subordinata & delegata. II. Christus delegauit Apostolis potestatem remittendi & retinendi peccata: At illa potestas cum Apostolis exspirauit. Ratio consequentiæ est: quia nulli dantur Apostolorum successores. Nam Apostoli erant immediate vocati, priuilegio infallibilitatis & potestate docendi in toto orbe instructi. Tales Apostoli hodie non dantur. Resp. 1) Competierunt Apostolis quædam specialia axiomata, priuilegia extraordinaria, quorum respectu nullos habent successores: competiuit illis etiam generatim considerando potestas docendi, sacramenta dispensandi, & peccata remittendi atque retinendi, quorum respectu omnes fideles ecclesiæ ministri illorum successores sunt. 2) Datur hodienum ecclesia: E. etiam dantur claues regni cœlorum toti ecclesiæ datæ. Datur euangelium: E. etiam absolutio a peccatis. Dantur sacramenta: Ergo & remissio peccatorum. Timotheus poterat seipsum, & qui ipsum audiebant, saluos facere, 1 Tim. IV, 16. E. Timotheus, qui non erat Apostolus, poterat peccata remittere. III. Quicunque non pollet dono infallibilitatis, is non potest peccata remittere. Ministri mediate vocati non pollent dono infallibilitatis. E. Maior patet; quia absoluendi sunt peccatores, quorum pœnitentia & fides certo constat. Resp. Ad potestatem absoluendi non requiritur infallibilitas apostolica, sed ordinata sufficit scientia, ex verbo θεοπνεύστῳ hausta. Et quamuis ministri ecclesiæ non sint scrutatores cordium, tamen ex signis externis internam cordis pœnitentiam colligunt. IV. Iudas proditor a Christo ad cœnam admissus est, etiam patefacto proditionis crimine: E. Peccator enormis & notorius ab vsu S. cœnæ non est repellendus. Resp. Iudam non arcuit Christus a cœna, ideo, quod proditio, quam machinabatur Iudas, nondum completa erat. Nemo ergo a sacris arcetur, ob facinus futurum, & soli Deo notum, sed ob facinus commissum.

Quæst. XXII. Quis est finis ministerii ecclesiastici?

Finis vltimus ministerii ecclesiastici, ex parte Dei, est gloria nominis diuini a), ex parte hominis finis vltimus est æterna salus b), fines intermedii sunt illuminatio & conuersio c), regeneratio d), reconciliatio cum Deo e).

Prob. a. Neque qui plantat, est aliquid, neque qui rigat, sed qui incrementum dat, Deus, 1 Cor. III, 4. Præcones fideles successum muneris sui non tribuunt sibi, sed virtuti Dei, cuius gratia sunt, quod sunt, 1 Cor. XV, 10. Prob. b. Ex 1 Tim. IV, 16. Teipsum saluum facies, & qui te audiunt. Prob. c. Ex Act. XXVI, 18. Mitto te ad aperiendum oculos eorum, vt conuertant se la tenebris in lucem. Prob. d. Ex 1 Cor. IV, 15. In Christo Iesu per euangelium ego vos generaui. Prob. e. Ministerium ecclesiasticum est ministerium reconciliationis, 2 Cor. V, 19. Obs. Ex his finibus insimul necessitas & vtilitas ministerii ecclesiastici dispescit.


### Q. XXIII. Can an impious minister teach with fruit in the church?

It behooves a minister of the church to cultivate piety with his whole heart , and, if his impiety becomes notorious, ecclesiastical censure must be applied to him .

Yet his impiety does not detract from the efficacy of the doctrine which he proposes from the word of God .

Prob. a. It behooves a Bishop and any overseer of the church to be irreproachable, 1 Tim. 3:2, and ὅσιον, holy, Tit. 1:8, and an example of the faithful in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in chastity, 1 Tim. 4:12.

Prob. b. A publicly scandalous person must be rebuked before all, 1 Tim. 5:20. Wherefore the notorious impiety of a minister of the church must be punished, in proportion to the offenses.

Prob. c. 1) The efficacy of doctrine does not depend on the minister, but on the Holy Spirit, who is indivisibly joined with the word of God. Hence the divine word is and remains the power of God unto salvation to every believer, Rom. 1:16, by whomever it is preached. This is illustrated by an elegant simile by AUGUSTINE, lib. 3 contr. Cresc. c. 8. It matters nothing to the efficacy of the seed and the planting whether it be done with clean hands or dirty, provided the seed be good, and the earth fertile, and the heat of the sun and rain from heaven be not lacking. 2) Christ, Matt. 23:3, commands to hear the scribes and Pharisees sitting in the chair of Moses, whom nevertheless he convicts of being guilty of the gravest crimes. 3) The Augsburg Confession, art. 8, p. 12, says gravely: The sacraments and the word, because of the ordination and command of Christ, are efficacious, even if they are administered by evil men.

The antithesis is that of the Donatists, Anabaptists, and Schwenckfeldians, who maintain that a minister of the church who is not himself truly renewed, reborn, and truly just, cannot teach other men with fruit or dispense true sacraments. Their arguments are: I. Whoever is not himself converted and reborn cannot convert and regenerate other men: But an impious minister is such, etc. Therefore. The major is evident: because nothing can be in the effect which was not previously in the cause, and what one does not have, one cannot give to another. Resp. 1) By denying the major and arguing by a similar ratio: Whoever is deformed cannot paint a beautiful image: But Apelles is deformed. Therefore. 2) By distinguishing between the principal cause and the instrumental. The efficacy of doctrine does not depend on the minister of the church as an instrumental cause, but on the Holy Spirit as the principal cause.

II. All false prophets are to be fled: But impious ministers are such, etc. Therefore. The major is established from Matt. 7:16. The minor is proved because false prophets are to be known by their fruits, to which belongs the impiety of life. Resp. False prophets are teachers professing false doctrine; our discourse is about teachers whose doctrine is true, but life impious. False prophets are to be known by the fruits of their doctrine. But if their doctrine of itself generates despair, Pharisaism, or Epicureanism, they are to be avoided and deserted.

Latin:

Ministrum ecclesiae decet pietatem toto pectore colere , &, si impietas eius fit notoria, censura ecclesiastica in eundem adhibenda est .

Impietas tamen ipsius non derogat efficaciae doctrinae, quam e verbo Dei proponit .

Prob. a. Oportet Episcopum & quemlibet antistitem ecclesiae esse irreprehensibilem, 1 Tim. III, 2. & ὅσιον, sanctum, Tit. I, 8. & exemplum fidelium in verbo, in conversatione, in caritate, in spiritu, in fide, in castitate, 1 Tim. IV, 12.

Prob. b. Publice flagitiosus coram omnibus arguendus est, 1 Tim. V, 20. Quare notoria impietas ministri ecclesiae punienda est, pro ratione delictorum.

Prob. c. 1) Efficacia doctrinae non pendet a ministro, sed a Spiritu S. qui cum verbo Dei individue coniunctus est. Proinde est & manet verbum divinum potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti, Rom. I, 16. a quocunque praedicetur. Id quod eleganti simili illustrat AVGVSTINVS libr. III. contr. Cresc. c. 8. Nihil refert ad efficaciam sementis & plantationis, lotis ne manibus, an sordidis id fiat, modo bonum sit semen, & terra fertilis, nec desit calor solis, & pluvia de caelo. 2) Christus Matth. XXIII, 3. iubet audire scribas & Pharisaeos, in cathedra Mosis sedentes, quos tamen gravissimorum criminum peragit reos. 3) Grauiter inquit Augustana confessio, artic. VIII. p. 12. Sacramenta & verbum, propter ordinationem & mandatum Christi sunt efficacia, etiam si per malos exhibeantur.

Antithesis est Donatistarum, Anabaptistarum & Schwenckfeldianorum, statuentium, quod is ecclesiae minister alios homines cum fructu docere, aut vera sacramenta dispensare non possit, qui ipse non fit vere renovatus, renatus & vere iustus. Quorum argumenta sunt: I. Quicunque ipse conversus & renatus non est, alios homines convertere & regenerare nequit: Atqui minister impius &c. Ergo. Maior est evidens: quia nihil potest esse in effectu, quin prius fuerit in causa, & quod quis non habet, alteri dare nequit. Resp. 1) Negando maiorem & simili ratione argumentando: Quicunque deformis est, formosam imaginem pingere nequit: Atqui Apelles deformis est. Ergo. 2) Distinguendo inter causam principalem, & instrumentalem. Efficacia doctrinae non pendet ab ecclesiae ministro, tanquam causa instrumentali, sed a Spiritu S. tanquam causa principali.

II. Omnes pseudo-prophetae sunt fugiendi: Atqui ministri impii &c. Ergo. Maior constat ex Matth. VII, 16. Minor prob. quia pseudo-prophetae e fructibus sunt cognoscendi, ad quos pertinet impietas vitae. Resp. Pseudo-prophetae sunt doctores, falsam doctrinam profitentes, nobis est sermo de doctoribus, quorum doctrina est vera, vita impia. Pseudo-prophetae cognoscendi sunt e fructibus doctrinae. Quod si doctrina eorum per se generet desperationem, Pharisaismum, aut Epicureismum, vitandi & deserendi sunt.


### Q. XXIV. Are there given different degrees of dignity and authority among the ministers of the church?

On account of εὐταξίαν, or good order, likewise, and the disparity of gifts, it is useful and advisable that there be distinct degrees of dignity and authority among the ministers of the church.

Prob. 1) God wills that all things in the church be done εὐσχημόνως καὶ κατὰ τάξιν, decently and according to order, 1 Cor. 14:40. Now indeed, just as in a republic all things are thrown into confusion, unless there be one who commands, and those who obey: Thus the body of the ecclesiastical ministry will be disordered, unless the disparate dignity of orders and degrees be admitted.

2) There were distinct degrees of ministers in the church of the O. T., namely the high priest, Exod. XXVIII, 29. priests of the second order, Lev. XXI, 10. Levites, Num. VIII, 6. In the N. T. are recounted ministers of disparate dignity and authority. For Christ gave some indeed as Apostles, others as Prophets, others as Evangelists, others as Pastors and Teachers, Eph. IV, 11.

There is an antithesis of the Puritans in England, and of the Anabaptists, who do not admit distinct degrees of dignity among the ministers of the church.

Who object: I. The assertion concerning the disparity of dignity among the ministers of the word paves the way to papal tyranny, which the reformed churches long ago abjured.

Resp. We do not bring back papal tyranny into the reformed churches by right of postliminy, because we affirm a) that the prelate of sacred things must indeed be heard by ministers of an inferior order, but only so long as he commands nothing contrary to orthodoxy and good morals, Mal. II, 7. b) That the same is subject to the direction and censure of the supreme magistrate, 1 Petr. II, 13.

II. Christ expressly disapproves of this ὑπεροχήν, or eminence, among ministers, Matth. XXIII, 8. Luc. XXII, 25.

Resp. We disapprove of absolute dominion in the church with Christ; yet we preserve the disparity of degrees for the sake of εὐταξίας (good order).

SIGH.

Thee, O God, Father of all good order, author of the sacred ministry, I beseech with sincere and most humble prayers, that Thou wouldst preserve Thy ecclesiastical hierarchy, which Thou didst most wisely institute for the benefit of mortals, whole and uncorrupted against the roaring of the world and of hell!

Give to Thy ministers who plant and water the most abundant increase! Give also to me, Thy weak and lowest minister, a mouth and wisdom! Bestow sanctifying gifts! Add an undaunted spirit! Grant prosperous successes in my office! That according to the prescription of Thy word I may rightly teach, duly dispense the sacraments, live piously, and from this life, as from an inn, not as from a home, at Thy command, I may peacefully depart.

PART IV.

Latin:

Ob εὐταξίαν, sive bonum ordinem, pariter, atque donorum disparitatem utile & consultum est, distinctos esse gradus dignitatis & auctoritatis inter ministros ecclesiae.

Prob. 1) Deus vult, omnia in ecclesia fieri εὐσχημόνως καὶ κατὰ τάξιν, decore & secundum ordinem, 1 Cor. XIV, 40. Iam vero, veluti in republica turbantur omnia, nisi sit, qui imperet, & qui pareant: Ita inordinatum erit corpus ecclesiastici ministerii, nisi ordinum & graduum dispar dignitas admittatur.

2) Fuerunt distincti gradus ministrorum in ecclesia V. T. scilicet summus sacerdos, Exod. XXVIII, 29. sacerdotes secundi ordinis, Leu. XXI, 10. Levitae, Num. VIII, 6. In N. T. recensentur ministri disparis dignitatis & auctoritatis. Dedit enim Christus alios quidem Apostolos, alios vero Prophetas, alios vero Evangelistas, alios vero Pastores & Doctores, Eph. IV, 11.

Antithesis est Puritanorum in Anglia, & Anabaptistarum, distinctos gradus dignitatis inter ministros ecclesiae non admittentium.

Qui obiiciunt: I. Assertio de disparitate dignitatis inter ministros verbi sternit viam ad tyrannidem pontificiam, quam ecclesiae reformatae dudum eiurarunt.

Resp. Tyrannidem pontificiam non postliminio in ecclesias reformatas reducimus, quia afferimus a) ministris inferioris ordinis audiendum quidem esse sacrorum praesulem, sed quamdiu de orthodoxia & bonis moribus nil adversum praecipit, Mal. II, 7. b) Eundem subesse directioni & censurae supremi magistratus, 1 Petr. II, 13.

II. Christus diserte improbat hanc inter ministros ὑπεροχήν, siue eminentiam, Matth. XXIII, 8. Luc. XXII, 25.

Resp. Absolutum in ecclesia dominium cum Christo improbamus; disparitatem tamen graduum εὐταξίας caussa seruamus.

SVSPIRIVM.

Te, Deus, Pater omnis boni ordinis, auctor ministerii sacri, sinceris humillimisque precibus obtestor, vt hierarchiam tuam ecclesiasticam, quam mortalium commodo sapientissime instituisti, adversus fremitum orbis & orci integram & incorruptam conferues!

Da ministris tuis plantantibus & rigantibus incrementum vberrimum! Da etiam mihi, ministro tuo infirmo & infimo, os & sapientiam! Confer dona sanctificantia! adde animum imperterritum! largire prosperos officii successus! vt ad praescriptum verbi tui recte doceam, sacramenta rite dispensem, pie viuam, & ex hac vita, tanquam ex hospitio, non tanquam ex domo, te iubente, placide discedam.

PARTIS IV.


## 40 Of the Political Magistrate


### Of the Political Magistrate

Q. I. Whence is the political magistrate called?

Magistrate is derived from master a); political from polity, which he governs b).

Prob. a.

It is called magistrate from master; because, as COELIUS RHODIGINUS testifies, L. VII. antiq. lect. c. 17, among the Romans he who was Dictator, and held supreme power, was accustomed to be called master: Just as today in the city the consuls are called masters of the citizens, Bürgermeister, Rathsmeister, Stadtmeister, Amtmeister.

Proof b. The magistrate is called "political" not from political affairs, insofar as those are opposed to ecclesiastical and sacred ones; since indeed the latter also are subject to the direction of the magistrate: but from *politeia*, which, being derived *ἀπὸ τῆς πόλεως* [from the city], denotes either the republic, or the regimen, or the administration of the republic, in which, when it is Christian, there is given a church, in respect to which the political magistrate is here considered as a peculiar hierarchical status.

Question II. In how many ways is the name "magistrate" taken?

The name "magistrate" is taken in two ways: a) abstractly, for the power and authority itself, by which those to whom the regimen is committed are strong: b) concretely, for the persons who are furnished with the power of commanding.

Proof a. From Rom. XIII, 1. Let every soul be subject to *ἐξουσίαις ὑπερεχούσαις* [to the supereminent powers].

Proof b. Christ calls magistrates taken concretely *ἐξουσιάζοντας* [those having power], Luke XXII, 25.

Question III. What is the political magistrate taken abstractly?

The political magistrate, accepted abstractly, is a public office, ordained by God, in which certain persons, legitimately called and furnished with power concerning civil and sacred matters, make laws in the republic, exercise judgments, and punish transgressors, and defend it against external enemies, for the sake of propagating the glory of God and promoting the temporal and eternal salvation of the subjects.

Question IV. What is the political magistrate taken concretely?

The political magistrate, accepted concretely, is a person, or a multitude of persons, divinely called and furnished with power concerning civil and sacred matters, for the purpose of making laws and exercising judgments, for punishing transgressors and defending the republic from external enemies, so that God may be glorified, the church may flourish tranquilly with the republic, and the temporal and eternal salvation of the subjects may be promoted.

Question V. What is the efficient cause of the magistrate?

The principal efficient cause of the magistrate, viewed both abstractly a) and concretely b), is the Triune God c), who commits the office of magistrate to certain persons, either immediately d) or mediately e).

Proof a. 1) The magistrate viewed in the abstract, by reason of the office, or by reason of the legislative, judiciary, and vindicatory power, is immediately from God. Paul teaches this in Rom. XIII, 1: "Let every soul be subject to the supereminent powers: For there is no power but of God; but the powers that be are ordained of God." Whence we argue: Whatever power is not, except from God, that is immediately ordained by God: But political power, etc. Therefore. The major is clear: Whatever is not, except from God, that is said to be immediately from God, with the exclusion of every other concurrent and socially acting cause; just as if someone were to say: The Apostles were not, except constituted by God or Christ, it would be easily understood. themselves to be constituted immediately by Christ. 2) Jehoshaphat said to the judges: Take heed to yourselves, and do it; for you do not exercise the judgment of man, but of God, 2 Chron.

XIX, 6. From which we gather: Whoever exercises judgment not of man, but of God, their judicial power is immediately from God: But the magistrate &c.

Therefore. 3) Of the same opinion is August. Confess. art. XVI. Concerning civil matters they teach that legitimate civil ordinances are good works of God. And lest anyone should draw the manner of institution to the meditation of human ingenuity, the Apology declares the manner to Art. VIII. p. 156. That this nature of things, and these motions of the stars are truly the ordinance of God and are preserved by God against the devil. Whence we argue: By what causality God produced nature and the motions of the stars, by that same he also ordained polities: But by immediate causality &c.

Therefore. Prob. b. The magistrate, viewed in the concrete, is also from God. For thus says the uncreated and hypostatic Wisdom, or the Son of God: By me kings reign, and rulers decree justice: By me princes bear rule, and all the judges of the earth are magnates, Prov. VIII, 15. 16. If by uncreated wisdom kings reign, they do not reign through men, who are distinct from uncreated wisdom. From Rom.

XIII, 4. 5. The magistrate is God's minister, an avenger for wrath to him who does evil. Therefore it is necessary to be subject not only because of wrath, but also because of conscience. Every minister of God, whom one must obey because of conscience, is elected and called to his office by God: But the civil magistrate &c. Therefore.

Prob. c. The triune God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, instituted and ordained the magistrate: for the institution of the magistrate is indeed a work ad extra, drawing its origin from divine authority, power, goodness, and wisdom, and thus is common to all three persons of the divinity. Prob. d.

Immediately, and with no arbitrary work of men intervening, God committed the office of magistrate to Moses, Exod. III, 10. Joshua, Num. XXVII, 18. Saul, 1 Sam. IX, 15. David, 1 Sam. XVI, 12. You say: David was called to the empire mediately, with the work of Samuel intervening.

I answer: God had immediately commanded Samuel that he should anoint David, and no other, as king, 1 Sam. XVI, 12. Therefore his calling to the office of magistrate was immediate.

Prob. e. Today God commits the office of magistrate to certain persons mediately, or with the counsels and voluntary work of men intervening, which is evident: 1) because all powers are from God, Rom. XIII, 2. But truly today they are not ordained divinely immediately: Therefore mediately. 2) From 1 Pet.

II, 13. 14. Be subject to every human creature (or one chosen by men, as an instrumental cause) for the Lord's sake (who constitutes through men) whether to the king, or to governors. 3) Christ acknowledged that even Pilate's power was certainly mediately from God: You would have, he says, no power against me, unless it were given to you from above, John XIX, 11. 4) To Nebuchadnezzar the God of heaven had given the kingdom and power and empire, and majesty mediately, as Daniel testifies, c.

II, 37. Quaest. VI. By what means and ways do men attain to the office of magistrate?

Obf. We are not speaking for the present of illicit ways and means by which some seize empire, such as: violent occupation through illegitimate war and the tyrannical oppression of others, fraudulent invasion through tricks and the solicitation of minds; and acquisition through bribery, or through money and gifts.

Today, capable persons, with God moderating, legitimately attain to the office of magistrate either by election a), or by succession b), or by just occupation c).

Prob. a. The magistracy is obtained by election when those to whom the power of electing belongs, either by law or by custom, designate a magistrate. Thus, the elders of Gilead chose Jephthah for themselves and constituted him leader, Jud. XI, 5. The election of inferior magistrates by superiors pertains to this. Prob. b.

The office of magistrate is obtained by succession when children receive authority from their parents by hereditary right, or kinsmen from their agnates. Thus, Solomon succeeded David by hereditary right, Rehoboam succeeded Solomon, and Abijah succeeded Rehoboam. Prob. c.

The magistracy is obtained by legitimate occupation when enemies defeated in a just war are subjected to the victor, by whom they are preserved. For it is of natural law that whatever is captured from enemies is subjected to the dominion of the victor.

The antithesis is 1) of the Anabaptists and Weigelians, who deny that the magistracy is ordained by God: 2) of some Papists, who deny that the magistracy, considered abstractly, derives its immediate origin from God.

They rely upon the following arguments: I. Whatever draws its origin from the violent and tyrannical oppression of men cannot be constituted by God: But monarchical rule, etc. Therefore. The major is clear: because that which is from an evil principle cannot be from God. The minor is proven: because monarchical rule draws its origin from Nimrod, who is said to have been a mighty hunter before the Lord, Gen. X, 9, which phrase implies Nimrod’s tyrannical rule over the men of his time, which he exercised while having no regard for the presence of God. Resp. 1) In Nimrod, indeed, the Assyrian empire began, but not the magistracy absolutely as such; for God committed the right of the sword to it long before Nimrod, Gen. IX, 6. 2) Distinguish between the lawful power of commanding and the illicit mode of acquiring power. The former is from God, the latter from Nimrod, who originally occupied the magistracy through the violent and tyrannical oppression of men. Certainly, power is one thing, and the acquisition and usurpation of power is another. Power itself is always from God, Rom. XIII, 1 seq., but the illegitimate acquisition and usurpation of power is tyranny, which is considered 1) insofar as it is an evil of fault, 2) insofar as it is an evil of punishment. In the former way, it is not from God, as He does not will evil, Ps. V, 5. In the latter way, it is from God, not as its author, but as an angry judge, Amos III, 6. This is what AUGUSTINE acknowledged, book V of De Civitate Dei, ch. 21: He who gave the empire to the Christian Constantine, the same also gave it to the apostate Julian.

II. The magistrate is called κτίσις ἀνθρωπίνη, or human ordinance, 1 Pet. II, 13. Therefore, it is not from God. Resp. The magistrate is indeed called κτίσις ἀνθρωπίνη, but one to whom obedience is owed for the Lord’s sake. It is therefore a human ordinance on account of the instrumental cause; it is also a divine ordinance on account of the principal cause; for the reason that God established the magistracy through men, so that men might sustain its office and rule over men.

III. If the devil is the prince of the world and gives the kingdoms of the world to whom he wills, then secular rule cannot be from God: The antecedent is true. See John XII, 31; XVI, 11; Matt. IV, 8. Resp. The devil is called the prince of the world and of all kingdoms in the world, not according to truth, by reason of creation, preservation, government, and legitimate possession, but according to opinion, a) on the part of the devil, by reason of both false boasting and unjust usurpation, b) on the part of men, by reason of both perverse imagination and vicious and inordinate subjection.

IV. A tyrant is not from God: Some magistrate is a tyrant: Therefore. Resp. 1) A distinction is made between a tyrant by title and by exercise. A tyrant by title does not even deserve the name of magistrate. 2) A tyrant, insofar as he is a tyrant, or insofar as he abuses his power for cruelty, his own advantage, and other vices, is not from God. Meanwhile, however, a tyrant, by reason of the legislative, judicial, and punitive power which he received through election, succession, or legitimate occupation, is from God. It must therefore be distinguished between power and the abuse of power.

V. The Israelite people, by asking for a King, provoked God to anger, E. not all magistrates are constituted by God. Resp. God did not simply and absolutely disapprove that the Israelites had or sought a magistrate, but that they wished to change the form of government instituted by God Himself according to their own will, and indeed out of the κακοζηλίᾳ (evil emulation) of the Gentiles. See v. 5 & 20.

VI. That certain Kings and Princes are not constituted by God, God Himself testifies, They have reigned, and not from me: Princes have existed, and I have not known them. Resp. The words cited according to the Hebrew text are to be rendered thus: They have made a King, and not from me: they have made Princes, and I have not known (approved) them. The Prophet taxes the people's diffidence, because out of the preposterous fear of dangers they choose the kings of the Gentiles as tutors and patrons, without consulting God whether this pleases Him. For at one time they implored the help and aid of the Assyrians, at another of the Egyptians. Whence it is not permitted to infer that the magistrate is not an ordinance of God.

Latin:

Quaest. I. Vnde dicitur magistratus politicus?

Magistratus dicitur a magistro a); politicus a politia, quam gubernat b).

Prob. a.

A magistro dicitur magistratus; quia, teste COELLO RHODIGINO, L. VII. antiq. lect. c. 17. apud Romanos is, qui Dictator erat, ac supremam potestatem gerebat, magister appellari solebat: Sicut hodie in ciuitate consules magistri ciuium, Bürgermeister, Rathsmeister, Stadtmeister, Amtmeister appellantur.

Prob. b. Politicus dicitur magistratus non a negotiis politicis, quatenus illa ecclesiasticis & sacris opponuntur; siquidem & hæc directioni magistratus subsunt: sed a politia, quæ, ἀπὸ τῆς πόλεως dicta, notat vel rempublicam, vel regimen, siue administrationem reipublicæ, in qua, cum Christiana est, datur ecclesia, cuius respectu magistratus politicus tanquam peculiaris status hierarchicus hic consideratur.

Quæst. II. Quot modis sumitur nomen magistratus?

Nomen magistratus sumitur bifariam: a) abstracte, pro ipsa potestate & auctoritate, qua pollent ii, quibus regimen est commissum: b) concretiue, pro personis, quæ potestate imperandi sunt instructæ.

Prob. a. Ex Rom. XIII, 1. Omnis anima subdita sit ἐξουσίαις ὑπερεχούσαις, potestatibus supereminentibus.

Prob. b. Magistratus concretiue sumtos Christus ἐξουσιάζοντας potestatem habentes, Luc. XXII, 25. appellat.

Quæst. III. Quid est magistratus politicus abstractiue sumtus?

Magistratus politicus, abstractiue acceptus, est officium publicum, a Deo ordinatum, in quo certæ personæ, legitime vocatæ, & potestate circa res ciuiles atque sacras instructæ, in republica leges ferunt, iudicia exercent, & transgressores puniunt, eamque aduersus hostes externos defendunt, ad propagandam gloriam Dei, & subditorum salutem temporalem atque æternam promouendam.

Quæst. IV. Quid est magistratus politicus concretiue sumtus?

Magistratus politicus concretiue acceptus est persona, vel multitudo personarum, diuinitus vocata, & potestate circa res ciuiles atque sacras instructa, ad ferendum leges & exercendum iudicia, ad puniendum transgressores & defendendum rempublicam ab externis hostibus, quo Deus glorificetur, ecclesia cum republica tranquille floreat, & subditorum temporalis atque æterna salus promoueatur.

Quæst. V. Quæ est causa efficiens magistratus?

Causa efficiens principalis magistratus, tum abstractiue a), tum concretiue b) spectati, est Deus trinunus c), qui certis personis officium magistratus committit, vel immediate d), vel mediate e).

Prob. a. 1) Magistratus in abstracto spectatus, ratione officii, siue ratione potestatis legislatoriæ, iudiciariæ & vindicatiuæ, immediate a Deo est. Docet hoc Paullus Rom. XIII, 1. Omnis anima potestatibus supereminentibus subdita esto: Non enim est potestas, nisi a Deo; sed quæ sunt potestates, a Deo ordinatæ sunt. Vnde argumentamur: Quæcunque potestas non est, nisi a Deo, illa immediate est a Deo ordinata: Atqui potestas politica &c. Ergo. Maior est clara: Quidquid non est, nisi a Deo, illud dicitur immediate esse a Deo, cum exclusione omnis alterius causæ concurrentis, & socialiter agentis; quem ad modum si quis diceret: Apostoli non fuerunt, nisi a Deo siue Christo constituti, facile intelligeretur. ipsos a Christo immediate esse constitutos.

2) Iosaphatus dixit ad iudices: Cauete vobis, & facite; non enim hominis exercetis iuditium, sed Dei, 2 Chron. XIX, 6. E quibus colligimus: Quicunque exercent iudicium non hominis, sed Dei, illorum potestas iudiciaria immediate est a Deo: Atqui magistratus &c. Ergo.

3) Eiusdem sententiae est August. Confess. art. XVI. De rebus ciuilibus docent, quod legitimae ordinationes ciuiles sint bona opera Dei. Ac ne quis modum institutionis ad meditationem humani ingenii traheret, declarat Apolog. modum ad Art. VIII. p. 156. Vt haec rerum natura, & hi siderum motus vere sunt ordinatio Dei & conferuantur a Deo aduersus diabolum. Vnde arguimus: Qua causalitate produxit Deus naturam & siderum motus, ea etiam ordinauit politias: Atqui causalitate immediata &c. Ergo.

Prob. b. Magistratus, in concreto spectatus, etiam est a Deo. Sic enim inquit Sapientia increata & hypostatica, siue Filius Dei: Per me reges regnant, & dominatores decernunt iustitiam: Per me principes principatum gerunt, & omnes iudices terrae sunt magnates, Prou. VIII, 15. 16. Si per sapientiam increatam regnant reges, non regnant per homines, distinctos sapientiae increatae.

Ex Rom. XIII, 4. 5. Magistratus Dei minister est, vindex in iram malum facienti. Ideo necesse est, subditum esse non solum propter iram, sed etiam propter conscientiam. Omnis minister Dei, cui propter conscientiam parendum est, ad officium suum a Deo electus & vocatus est: Atqui magistratus ciuilis &c. Ergo.

Prob. c. Magistratum instituit & ordinauit Deus trinunus, Pater, Filius & Spiritus Sanctus: est quippe institutio magistratus opus ad extra, ab auctoritate, potentia, bonitate atque sapientia diuina originem trahens, adeoque communis omnibus tribus diuinitatis personis.

Prob. d. Immediate, & nulla hominum opera arbitraria interueniente, Deus magistratus officium commisit Mosi, Exod. III, 10. Iosuae, Num. XXVII, 18. Sauli, 1 Sam. IX, 15. Dauidi, 1 Sam. XVI, 12.

Dicis: Dauid ad imperium mediate vocatus est, interueniente opera Samuelis. Resp. Deus immediate praeceperat Samueli, vt Dauidem, & non alium vngeret regem, 1 Sam. XVI, 12.

Ergo illius vocatio ad officium magistratus immediata fuit. Prob. e. Hodie Deus officium magistratus certis personis mediate, siue interuenientibus hominum consiliis & opera voluntaria committit, Quod patet: 1) quia omnes potestates a Deo sunt, Rom. XIII, 2.

At vero hodie non sunt ordinatae diuinitus immediate: Ergo mediate. 2) Ex 1 Petr. II, 13. 14. Subiecti estote omni humanae creaturae (seu ab hominibus, vt caussa instrumentali, electa) propter Dominum (qui per homines constituit) siue regi, siue praesidibus. 3) Christus agnouit, etiam Pilati potestatem esse certe mediate a Deo: Non haberes, inquiens, potestatem aduersus me vllam, nisi esset tibi data desuper, Io. XIX, 11.

4) Nabuchodonosari Deus caeli regnum & potestatem & imperium, & maiestatem dederat mediate, teste Daniele, c. II, 37. Quaest. VI. Quibus mediis & modis homines pertingunt ad officium magistratus?

Obs. Non est nobis sermo impraesentiarum de modis & mediis illicitis, quibus nonnulli imperium rapiunt, qualia sunt: occupatio violenta per bellum illegitimum & tyrannicam aliorum oppressionem, inuasio fraudulenta per technas & sollicitationes animorum; & acquisitio per largitionem, siue per pecuniam & munera.

Hodie ad officium magistratus personae habiles, moderante Deo, legitime perueniunt vel per electionem a), vel per successionem b), vel per iustam occupationem c).

Prob. a. Per electionem obtinetur magistratus, quando illi, quibus potestas eligendi aut lege, aut consuetudine competit, magistratum designant. Sic seniores Gilead Iephtam sibi elegerunt & constituerunt ducem, Iud. XI, 5. Huc pertinet electio inferiorum magistratuum a superioribus.

Prob. b. Per successionem obtinetur officium magistratus, quando iure hereditario a parentibus liberi, aut ab agnatis consanguinei imperium accipiunt. Sic Dauidi iure hereditario Salomo, Salomoni Rechabeam, Rechabeamo Abiam successit.

Prob. c. Per occupationem legitimam obtinetur magistratus, quando bello iusto deuicti hostes subiiciuntur victori, a quo conferuantur. Est enim iuris naturalis, vt quodcunque, ex hostibus captum, dominio victoris subiiciatur.

Antithesis est 1) Anabaptistarum & Weigelianorum, negantium, magistratum a Deo esse ordinatum: 2) nonnullorum Pontificiorum, negantium, magistratum, abstractiue consideratum, immediatam originem ducere a Deo.

Qui sequentibus innituntur argumentis: I. Quidquid a violenta & tyrannica hominum oppressione trahit originem, illud non potest a Deo esse constitutum: Atqui imperium monarchicum &c. Ergo. Maior liquet: quia id non potest esse a Deo, quod est a malo principio. Minor probatur: quia imperium monarchicum trahit originem a Nimrodo, qui dicitur fuisse fortis venator coram Domino, Gen. X, 9. quæ phrasis infert tyrannicum Nimrodi imperium in homines sui temporis, quod Dei præsentiam minime reueritus exercuit. Resp. 1) In Nimrodo quidem cœpit imperium Assyricum, sed non magistratus absolute talis; quippe cui Deus commisit ius gladii dudum ante Nimrodum, Gen. IX, 6. 2) Dist. inter potestatem imperandi licitam, & illicitum modum imperii acquirendi. Illa est a Deo, hic a Nimrodo, qui violenta & tyrannica hominum oppressione magistratum primitus occupauit. Sane aliud est potestas, aliud potestatis acquisitio & vsurpatio. Ipsa potestas semper est a Deo, Rom. XIII, 1. seq. sed potestatis acquisitio & vsurpatio illegitima est tyrannis, quæ consideratur, 1) quatenus est malum culpæ, 2) quatenus est malum pœnæ. Priori modo non est a Deo, vtpote qui malum non vult, Ps. V, 5. Posteriori modo est a Deo, non tanquam auctore, sed tanquam irato iudice, Amos III, 6. Id quod agnouit AVGVSTINVS, libr. V. de C. D. cap. 21. Qui dedit imperium Constantino Christiano, ipse etiam dedit apostatæ Iuliano.

II. Magistratus dicitur κτίσις ἀνθρωπίνη, siue ordinatio humana, 1 Petr. II, 13. Ergo non est a Deo. Resp. Magistratus dicitur quidem κτίσις ἀνθρωπίνη, sed cui propter Dominum debetur obedientia. Est igitur ordinatio humana, propter caussam instrumentalem; est etiam ordinatio diuina, propter caussam principalem; propterea, quod Deus per homines fanciuit magistratum, vt huius officium sustineant homines, & hominibus imperent.

III. Si diabolus est princeps mundi, & dat regna mundi, cui vult, vtique imperium fæculare non potest esse a Deo: Antecedens est verum. Vid. Io. XII, 31. c. XVI, 11. Matth. IV, 8. Resp. Diabolus dicitur princeps mundi & omnium in mundo regnorum, non secundum veritatem, ratione creationis, conseruationis, gubernationis & legitimæ possessionis, sed secundum opinionem, a) ex parte diaboli, ratione tam falsæ gloriationis, tum iniustæ vsurpationis, b) ex parte hominum, tum ex parte peruersæ imaginationis, tum ratione vitiosæ & inordinatæ subiectionis.

IV. Tyrannus non est a Deo: Quidam magistratus est tyrannus: Ergo. Resp. 1) Distinguitur inter tyrannum titulo & exercitio. Tyrannus titulo ne nomen quidem magistratus meretur. 2) Tyrannus, quatenus tyrannus, siue quatenus potestate sua abutitur ad fæuitiam, proprium commodum & alia vitia, non est a Deo. Interim tamen tyrannus ratione potestatis legislatiuæ, iudiciariæ & punitiuæ, quam per electionem, successionem, aut occupationem legitimam accepit, est a Deo. Distinguendum itaque est inter potestatem, & potestatis abusum.

V. Populus Israeliticus, Regem postulando, Deum ad iram prouocauit, E. non omnes magistratus a Deo sunt constituti. Resp. Deus non simpliciter & absolute improbauit, quod Israelita magistratum haberent, vel expeterent, sed quod formam regiminis ab ipso Deo institutam proprio arbitrio, & quidem ex κακοζηλίᾳ gentilium mutatam vellent. Vid. v. 5. & 20.

VI. Quosdam Reges Principesque non esse constitutos a Deo, ipse testatur Deus, Ipsi regnauerunt, & non ex me: Principes exfiterunt, & non cognoui eos. Resp. Verba citata secundum textum Hebraeum ita reddenda sunt: Illi Regem fecerunt, & non a me: Principes fecerunt, & non noui (approbaui). Taxat Propheta populi diffidentiam, quod ex praeposterorum periculorum metu reges gentilium in tutores & patronos eligat, Deo non consulto, an ipsi hoc placeat. Modo enim Assyriorum, modo Aegyptiorum opem & auxilium implorabant. Vnde inferre non licet, quod magistratus non fit ordinatio Dei.


### Quaest. VII. Can a Christian in the New Testament discharge the office of magistrate with a safe conscience?

Magistracy is a state pleasing and approved by God, even in the New Testament, the office of which a Christian can administer with an unblemished conscience.

Prob. 1) Magistracy is an ordinance of God, which the Gospel does not abolish, but confirms. 2) It is the will of God Himself that we be subject to human ordinance even in the New Testament, 3) Christ Himself approves of magistrates in the New Testament, when He commands to give to Caesar, and He Himself paid tribute, 4) Many pious and faithful men in the New Testament have discharged the office of magistrate. Joseph of Arimathea, although he was a Friend of Christ, awaiting the kingdom of God; yet he performed the duty of a senator, Christ, praising the faith of the royal official, did not command him to lay down his magistracy. With the praise of piety flourished CONSTANTINE the Great, both THEODOSIUSES, MARCIAN, CHARLES the Great, and others.

There is an antithesis of the Anabaptists and Weigelians, whose opinion is that the office of a Christian magistrate in the New Testament is unbecoming.

Their stronger arguments are: I. Whatever fights against Christian liberty, that cannot please God: But the office of magistrate &c: Therefore. Resp. Distinguish between spiritual liberty and political liberty or license. Christians are free by spiritual liberty from sin, which internal liberty of the mind does not at all take away the external subjection due to the magistrate, but rather establishes it,

II. A Gentile office is unbecoming to a Christian: The office of magistrate is Gentile. Therefore. The minor is proved from Matt. XX, 25. You know that the Princes of the Gentiles lord it over them, and the great ones have power over them: it shall not be so among you. Resp. Christ, in the place cited, denies political rule to the Apostles and ministers of the church, but not to all Christians.

III. In the state of innocence there was no magistrate: Therefore neither should there be one in the state of grace. The consequence is proved: because in the state of grace we are renewed into knowledge according to the same image of God, with which man was endowed in the state of innocence. Resp. 1) If a multitude of men had been propagated in the state of innocence, it would not have been without order and government, although that government would not have been δεσποτικόν (despotic), or masterly, but πατρικόν (paternal), and the subjection would not have been servile, but filial. 2) We are indeed renewed in the state of grace to the image of God, but our renewal is imperfect, because of the remnants of sin: on account of which infirmity God also in the state of grace willed the Christian man to be ruled, and to be kept in decent order by the magistrate.

Latin:

Magistratus est status Deo, etiam in nouo testamento, gratus, probatusque, cuius officium Christianus illibata conscientia administrare potest.

Prob. 1) Magistratus est ordinatio Dei, quam euangelium non abolet, sed confirmat. 2) Ipsius Dei voluntas est, vt humanae ordinationi etiam in nouo testamento subiecti simus, 3) Ipse Christus magistratus in nouo testamento approbat, dum iubet dare Caesari, & tributum ipse soluit, 4) Officio magistratus multi pii & fideles in nouo testamento functi sunt. Iosephus Arimathaeus, licet Amicus Christi esset, exspectans regnum Dei; senatoris tamen munus obiuit, Christus officialis regii fidem laudans, non iussit eum magistratum deponere. Pietatis laude floruerunt CONSTANTINVS m. vterque THEODOSIVS, MARCIANVS, CAROLVS MAGNVS, & alii.

Antithesis est Anabaptistarum & Weigelianorum, quorum sententia officium magistratus Christianum in nouo testamento dedecet. Quorum potiora argumenta sunt:

I. Quidquid pugnat cum libertate Christiana, id Deo non potest placere: Atqui officium magistratus &c: Ergo. Resp. Dist. inter libertatem spiritualem, & libertatem vel licentiam politicam. Liberi sunt Christiani libertate spirituali a peccato, quae interna animi libertas exteriorem subiectionem magistratui debitam minime tollit, sed potius stabili,

II. Officium gentile Christianum dedecet: Magistratus officium est gentile. Ergo. Minor probatur ex Matth. XX, 25. Scitis, quod Principes gentium dominentur illis, & magnates potestatem habeant in eas: non sic erit inter vos. Resp. Christus l. c. Apostolis & ministris ecclesiae, non autem omnibus Christianis, regimen politicum denegat.

III. In statu innocentiae non erat magistratus: Ergo nec idem debet in statu gratiae. Consequentia probatur: quia in statu gratiae renouamur in cognitionem secundum eandem imaginem Dei, qua homo in statu innocentiae praeditus erat. Resp. 1) Si in statu innocentiae propagata fuisset hominum multitudo, non fuisset fine ordine & regimine, quamuis illud regimen non δεσποτικόν, siue herile, sed πατρικόν, paternum, & subiectio non seruilis, sed filialis fuisset. 2) Renouamur quidem in statu gratiae ad imaginem Dei, sed renouatio nostra est imperfecta, propter reliquias peccati: ob quam infirmitatem Deus etiam in statu gratiae hominem christianum voluit regere, & in decenti ordine continere per magistratum.


### Quaest. VII. Can a Christian in the New Testament discharge the office of magistrate with a safe conscience?: Q. VIII

Q. VIII.

What persons are to be chosen for the undertaking of the office of magistrate? For the office of magistrate, those persons are to be chosen who are capable according to the requirements prescribed in the divine word.

Obj. I. Our discourse is concerning that state of the republic in which the nobles, or the people, have free votes to choose a magistrate, but not concerning that state in which a Prince succeeds by hereditary right.

Obj. II. The requirements of a good magistrate are divided into primary and secondary. Primary are the internal goods of the soul; or virtues worthy of a magistrate, such as: a) piety toward God, b) justice and clemency toward citizens and subjects, c) temperance and chastity toward oneself, moderation in the cultivation of the body and other courtly apparatus, greatness of soul, and constancy tempered by reason in both fortunes. Secondary are the external goods of the body and fortune, such as: lineage, age, appearance, riches. These, political theorists pursue more broadly; we follow the guidance of Scripture.

Prob. 1) Jethro teaches Moses what kind of magistrates are to be chosen, Exod. 18: 21. You shall look out from all the people able men, fearing God, men of truth, hating covetousness: and place over them rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens, that they may judge the people at all times.

2) Moses sets forth the requirements of a good magistrate, Deut. 1:13. Give to yourselves wise and understanding men, and known according to your tribes, that I may place them as heads over you.

3) God himself requires in a King, Deut. 17:15. a) that he be a native, not a foreigner, b) not trusting in, or puffed up by, a multitude of horses, c) not womanizing or lustful, d) not φιλάργυρος (a lover of money), or thirsting for money, e) that he be a worshiper of the divine law, f) not a proud contemner of citizens, but gentle, merciful, and easy of access.

Q. IX.

In what does the office of magistrate formally consist? The office of magistrate formally consists in the due and decent execution of the power granted by God. Now, the power granted to the magistrate is a) συμβουλευτική, consultative, b) νομοθετική, legislative, c) δικαστική, judiciary, d) κολαστική, vindicative. Prob. a.

God has granted to the magistrate the power of well-counseling the republic, and of solicitously providing for all things, so that the poverty and calamity of subjects may be relieved as much as possible, and they themselves may be protected against external force. For the magistrate is indeed an eye to the blind, a foot to the lame, a father to the poor, Job 29:15, 16.

Prob. b. Legislative power belongs to the magistrate, because it is his to decree justice, Prov. 8:15. He decrees justice through law, inasmuch as it is an obligatory decree, made by the Prince, for the salvation of the whole community.

Prob. c. That judiciary power belongs to the magistrate is evident a) from the name. Kings are called judges of the earth, Ps. 148:11 ff. b) God expressly commands: Deut. 16:18. Judges and officers you shall give to yourself in all your gates, which Jehovah your God is about to give to you, according to your tribes: who shall judge the people with righteous judgment.

Prob. d. Power has been granted to the magistrate of avenging injuries and punishing transgressors of the laws. To which end the magistrate is armed with a sword, not metaphorical (as is the ecclesiastical ministry), but properly so-called, and that both judiciary, by which he can strike the wicked even unto death, or inflict capital punishment, and military, by which he may repel the unjust force of enemies from the republic, and can protect religion, and liberty, and goods. That the judicial sword belongs to the magistrate, we prove 1) from Gen. IX, 6. Whoever shall shed man's blood, by man (the legitimate avenger) let his blood be shed. The legitimate avenger is the magistrate; for he does not bear the sword in vain: for he is God's minister, an avenger in wrath, to him who does evil, Rom. XIII, 4. 2) From Exod. XXI, 12. He who strikes a man, so that he dies, shall die by dying. 3) From Matt. XXVI, 52. All who take the sword (by private rashness) must perish by the sword. That the military sword belongs to the magistrate, we learn both from the Old and from the New Testament. In the O. T. the right of war is sanctioned, a) by divine command, Num. XXXI, 2. Josh. I, 6. and elsewhere passim, b) by military laws, prescribed by God, Num. X, 9. Deut. XX, 19. c) by clear victories granted by God, Exod. XVII, 11. Judg. III, 10. Prov. XXI, 31. Whence also holy men, Abraham, Moses, Joshua, David, Hezekiah, Jehoshaphat, waged wars lawfully. In the N. T. war is nowhere prohibited. For 1) John, being seriously asked by the soldiers: what must be done by them, that they might escape the wrath of God? did not order them to leave the military service (which they ought to have done entirely, if that had been the will of the Lord), but said to the same: Do violence to no one, neither circumvent anyone deceitfully, and be content with your wages, Luke III, 14. John, another Elijah, and a great reformer of the church, would certainly have simply condemned the military state, if it could not consist with the attainment of salvation; but he dissuaded them not from the substance of war; for he does not say: throw away arms, desert the military service, etc., but from vicious circumstances, accidentally connected with war, viz., from violence, from fraud, and from rapine. 2) Christ, Matt. VIII, 9. 10. and Luke, Acts X, 1. sqq. praise the faith of the soldiers, and pronounce them, notwithstanding their military state, pleasing to God. Therefore, neither Christ, nor the Apostles forbade war in the N. T.

Obs. There is a distinction 1) between a just war, and an unjust one. The former is that which is undertaken when most serious causes urge it: the latter is that which is waged for slight and vain causes (for vain glory, the enlargement of boundaries, the fulfillment of lust, etc.). 2) Between a defensive war, and an offensive one. The former is always lawful, because defense is of natural right: the latter is not to be waged, unless extreme necessity stimulates it, a) when atrocious injuries are to be avenged, b) when goods unjustly snatched away are to be reclaimed (*). 3) Between the use of arms, and the abuse. The former consists in this, that an honest peace may be restored: the latter rages without a limit. 4) Between the substance of war itself, and its vicious accidents, such as: frauds, rapines, fornications, adulteries, etc. We speak of a just war, of a defensive and necessary offensive war, of the right use of arms, and of the substance of war itself.

The antithesis is that of the Anabaptists, Weigelians, and Socinians, who deny that judicial and vindicatory power belongs to the magistrate.

They impugn the judicial power with the following arguments:

I. Christ prohibits human judgments, Matt. VII, 1. saying: judge not. Resp. Christ prohibits private and rash judgments, not public and necessary ones. Conf. Matt. V, 22.

Objection I. Objection I. Charity covers all offenses, Prov. 10:12. Therefore, no judgments are necessary. Resp. Charity covers lighter offenses, not more atrocious ones and those joined with the scandal of others, which cannot be tolerated while preserving honesty and public tranquility.

Objection II. Objection II. God will judge fornicators and adulterers, Heb. 13:4. Therefore, they are not to be judged by the magistrate. Resp. God will judge fornicators and adulterers as the supreme and independent judge; the magistrate judges the same as a ministerial and subordinate judge.

For he is a minister of God, an avenger in wrath to him who does evil, Rom. 13:4. II. II. Whoever is about to litigate before a court, and is to have his tunic taken away, let him leave his cloak as well; it is not for him to contend before a human court: But a true Christian, etc. Therefore. The major is proved because otherwise one might contend before a judge to retain his tunic. The minor is proved from Matt. 5:40. Resp. The words of Christ are to be taken not ἁπλῶς (simply), absolutely, but συγκριτικῶς (comparatively), so that the sense becomes: If someone wishes to contend with you more bitterly in court, so as to satisfy his petulance and lust, and takes away your tunic through an unjust sentence of the magistrate, then do not return evil for evil, but be more prepared to bear the injury moderately than to avenge it or inflict it upon another. It is better to suffer an injury than to inflict one.

III. III. Whatever is listed among the defects of the church is to be removed: The exercise of political judgments is listed among the defects of the church: Therefore. The minor is proved from 1 Cor. VI, 7. There is a defect among you, that you have lawsuits with one another. Why do you not rather suffer wrong? Resp. The Apostle in the cited place does not reject the judgment of the magistrate, nor does he mean that it is altogether illicit for Christians to contend with an adversary before a magistrate; but he reproves only the immoderate lust for contending in the Corinthians, because they contended more frequently in causes before a pagan magistrate with others, whence a stain was sprinkled upon the church and Christians, and many were deterred from embracing the Christian religion.

IV. IV. Christ says in Matt. 5:39: Do not resist the evil person. Resp. Christ by these words does not reject the public office of the magistrate, but private vengeance.

They attack the vindicatory power, by which the wicked are punished with death, with the following arguments:

I. Whoever kills, sins against the fifth commandment: A pious magistrate does not sin against the fifth commandment. Therefore. Resp. Whoever as a private person kills out of a purpose of harming, he sins against the fifth commandment. But the magistrate is not a private man, nor does he kill a man out of a purpose of harming, but is divinely armed with the sword for vengeance, Rom. 13:4.

II. II. Whatever conflicts with Christian charity is not to be tolerated in the Christian church: Capital punishments conflict with Christian charity: Therefore. The major is certain: because even enemies are to be loved, Matt. 5:44. Resp. 1) To punish the wicked is also a work of charity: for a putrid limb must be cut off, lest the sound part be drawn in. 2) Enemies are to be loved as men, not as robbers or wicked persons.

III. III. Whatever conflicts with the new covenant is to be abrogated: Capital punishments, etc. Therefore. The minor is proved from John 1:17. The law was given through Moses, grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. Resp. Distinguish between the name of grace, taken theologically and politically. Theologically, it denotes the gratuitous favor of God, who for the sake of Christ, apprehended by true faith, forgives our sins, so that they are not imputed to eternal condemnation. Which grace reaches

Latin:

Quaest. VIII.

Quenam personae eligendae sunt ad obeundum officium magistratus? Ad officium magistratus eligendae sunt personae habiles iuxta requisita in verbo diuino praescripta.

Obi. I. Sermo nobis est de eo reipublicae statu, in quo optimates, vel populus libera habent suffragia magistratum eligendi, non autem de eo statu, in quo Princeps iure hereditario succedit. Obi.

II. Diuiduntur requisita boni magistratus in primaria, & secundaria. Primaria sunt bona animi interna; siue virtutes magistratu dignae, quales sunt: a) erga Deum pietas, b) erga ciues & subditos iustitia atque clementia, c) erga seipsum temperantia & castitas, moderatio in cultu corporis, & cetero aulico apparatu, animi magnitudo, & temperata per rationem in vtraque fortuna constantia. Secundaria sunt bona corporis & fortunae externa, vpote: genus, aetas, forma, diuitiae. Quae latius exsequuntur politici; nos ductum scripturae sequimur.

Prob. 1) Quales eligendi sint magistratus, Iethro Mosen docet, Exod. XVIII, 21. Tu circumspicies ex omni populo viros cordatos, timentes Dei, viros veracitatis, odientes lucri: ponesque super eos in Principes millium, Principes centenorum, Principes quinquagenorum, & Principes decadum, vt iudicent populum omni tempore.

2) Moses requisita boni magistratus exponit, Deut. I, 13. Date vobis viros sapientes & intelligentes, & notos iuxta tribus vestras, vt ponam eos in capita vestra.

3) Deus ipse in Rege requirit, Deut. XVII, 15. a) vt fit indigena, non alienigena, b) non confisus, aut elatus multitudine equorum, c) non mulierosus, aut libidinosus, d) non φιλάργυρος, aut sitiens pecuniae, e) fit cultor legis diuinae, f) non superbus contemptor ciuium, sed mansuetus, clemens, & accessu facilis.

Quaest. IX.

In quo formaliter consistit officium magistratus? Officium magistratus formaliter consistit in potestatis diuinitus concessae debita & decenti executione. Concessa autem est magistratui potestas a) συμβουλευτική, consultatoria, b) νομοθετική, legislatoria, c) δικαστική, iudiciaria, d) κολαστική, vindicatiua.

Prob. a. Concessit Deus magistratui potestatem bene consulendi reipublicae, omniaque sollicite prouidendi, vt subditorum, quantum fieri potest, inopiae & calamitati succurratur, ipsique contra vim externam protegantur. Est quippe magistratus oculus caecis, pes claudis, pater pauperibus, Iob. XXIX, 15. 16.

Prob. b. Potestas legislatoria magistratui competit, quia ipsius est, iustitiam decernere Prou. VIII, 15. Decernit iustitiam per legem, vtpote quae est decretum obligatorium, factum a Principe, ad salutem totius communitatis.

Prob. c. Quod potestas iudiciaria competat magistratui, patet a) ex nomine. Vocantur Reges iudices terrae, Ps. CXLVIII, 11. seqq. b) Expresse Deus praecipit: Deut. XVI, 18. Iudices & moderatores dabis tibi in omnibus portis tuis, quas Iehouah Deus tuus daturus est tibi, iuxta tribus tuas: qui iudicabunt populum iudicio iustitiae.

Prob. d. Concessa est magistratui potestas vindicandi iniurias, & puniendi transgressores legum. Quem in finem magistratus armatus est gladio non metaphorico (sicut ministerium ecclesiasticum), sed proprie dicto, eoque tum iudiciario, quo flagitiosos ad necem vsque ferire, seu capitali supplicio afficere potest, tum bellico, quo iniustam vim hostium a republica propulsare, religionemque, & libertatem, atque bona tueri potest. Gladium iudiciarium competere magistratui, probamus 1) ex Genes. IX, 6. Quisquis effuderit sanguinem hominis, per hominem (vindicem legitimum) sanguis eius effundatur. Vindex legitimus est magistratus; quippe qui non frustra gladium gerit: Dei enim minister est, vindex in iram, malum facienti, Rom. XIII, 4. 2) Ex Exod. XXI, 12. Qui percusserit virum, ut moriatur, moriendo morietur. 3) Ex Matth. XXVI, 52. Omnes accipientes gladium (priuata temeritate) per gladium perire debent. Gladium bellicum magistratui competere, tum ex veteri, tum ex nonuo testamento discimus. In V. T. ius belli sancitum est, a) mandato diuino, Num. XXXI, 2. Ios. I, 6. & alibi passim, b) legibus bellicis, a Deo præscriptis, Num. X, 9. Deut. XX, 19. c) luculentis victoriis a Deo concessis, Exod. XVII, 11. Iudic. III, 10. Prou. XXI, 31. Vnde etiam sancti viri, Abraham, Moses, Iosua, Dauid, Ezechias, Iosaphat, bella licite gesserunt. In N, T. bellum nullibi est prohibitum. Nam 1) Ioannes serio interrogatus a militibus: quid sibi faciendum esset, vt iram Dei effugerent? non eos militia abire (quod facere omnino debebant, si ea fuisset voluntas Domini) iussit, sed dixit ad eosdem: Neminem concutite, neque dolose quemquam circumuenite, contentique estote stipendiis vestris, Luc. III, 14. Ioannes, alter Elias, & magnus reformator ecclesiæ, vtique statum militarem, si non posset consistere cum consecutione salutis, simpliciter improbabset; at dehortatus est non a belli substantia; neque enim dicit: arma abiicite, militiam deserite &c. sed a vitiosis circumstantiis, cum bello per accidens connexis, sc. a violentia, a fraudulentia, & a rapina. 2) Christus, Matth. VIII, 9. 10. & Lucas, Act. X, 1. sqq. fidem militum laudant, eosque, non obstante militari statu, Deo gratos pronuntiant. Ergo neque Christus, neque Apostoli bellum in N. T. interdixerunt.

Obs. Dist. est 1) inter bellum iustum, & iniustum. Illud est, quod vrgentibus gravissimis caussis suscipitnr: hoc est, quod leuiculis vanisque de caussis (ob vanam gloriam, finium amplitudinem, impletionem libidinis &c.) geritur. 2) Inter bellum defensiuum, & offensiuum. Illud semper est licitum, quia defensio est iuris naturalis: hoc non est gerendum, nisi extrema necessitate stimulante, a) cum atroces iniuriæ sunt vindicandæ, b) cum bona iniuste erepta sunt repetenda (*). 3) Inter armorum vsum, & abusum. Ille consistit in hoc, vt pax honesta reducatur: hic fine termino grassatur. 4) Inter ipsam belli substantiam, & vitiosa eius accidentia, qualia sunt: fraudes, rapinæ, scortationes, adulteria &c. Loquimur de bello iusto, de bello defensiuo & offensiuo necessario, de recto armorum vsu, & ipsa belli substantia.

Antithesis est Anabaptistarum, Weigelianorum & Socinianorum, qui negant, magistratui potestatem iudiciariam & vindicatiuam competere.

Potestatem iudiciariam impugnant sequentibus argumentis:

I. Christus prohibet iudicia humana, Matth. VII, 1. inquiens: ne iudicate. Resp. Christus prohibet iudicia priuata & temeraria, non publica & necessaria. Conf. Matth. V, 22.

Instantia I. Instantia I. Caritas tegit omnia delicta, Prou. X, 12. Ergo nulla iudicia sunt necessaria. Resp. Caritas tegit delicta leuiora, non atrociora & cum scandalo aliorum coniuncta, quae salua honestate & tranquillitate publica tolerari nequeunt. Instantia

II. Instantia II. Scortatores & adulteros iudicabit Deus, Hebr. XIII, 4. E. non sunt iudicandi a magistratu. Resp. Scortatores & adulteros iudicabit Deus, tanquam iudex summus & independens, eosdem indicat magistratus tanquam iudex ministerialls & subordinatus. Est enim minister Dei, vindex in iram malum facienti, Rom. XIII, 4. II.

II. Quicunque litigaturo coram iudicio, & ablaturo tunicam, etiam pallium relinquat, illius non est contendere coram iudicio humano: Sed verus Christianus &c. Ergo. Maior prob. quia ceteroqui contendere quis possit coram iudice, vt tunicam retineat. Minor prob. ex Matth. V, 40. Resp. Verba Christi accipienda sunt non ἁπλῶς, absolute, sed συγκριτικῶς, comparate, vt sensus fit: Si quis acerbius tecum contendere velit in iudicio, vt expleat petulantiam & libidinem suam, tibique iniqua magistratus sententia laeso tunicam auferat, tunc ne feras malum pro malo, fed sis paratior ad iniuriam moderate perferendam, quam vindicandam, aut alteri inferendam. Satius est iniuriam pati, quam inferre.

III. III. Quidquid refertur inter defectus ecclesiae, illud est remouendum: Exercitium iudiciorum politicorum refertur inter defectus ecclesiae: Ergo. Minor prob. ex 1 Cor. VI, 7. Defectus inter vos est, quod iudicia habetis, vobiscum ipsis. Quare non potius iniuriam patimini? Resp. Apostolus l. c. non reiicit iudicium magistratus, neque hoc vult, quod plane illicitum fit Christianis, coram magistratu contendere cum aduersario; fed in Corinthiis reprehendit tantum immoderatam contendendi libidinem, quod crebrius iudicia de caussa coram magistratu ethnico cum aliis contenderent, vnde ecclesiae & Christianis macula aspergebatur, & multi a religione christiana amplectenda deterrebantur.

IV. IV. Christus dicit Matth. V, 39. Ne resistatis malo. Resp. Christus his verbis non publicum officium magistratus, fed vindictam priuatam reiicit.

Potestatem vindicatiuam, qua flagitiosi capite plectuntur, sequentibus impetunt argumentis:

I. I. Quicunque occidit, peccat contra quintum praeceptum: Magistratus pius non peccat contra quintum praeceptum. Ergo. Resp. Quicunque priuatus ex proaeresi nocendi occidit, is peccat contra quintum praeceptum. At magistratus non est homo priuatus, neque ex proaeresi hominem occidit, fed diuinitus armatus est gladio in vindictam, Rom. XIII, 4.

II. II. Quidquid pugnat cum caritate christiana, illud non est tolerandum in ecclesia christiana: Supplicia capitalia pugnant cum caritate christiana: E. Maior constat: quia etiam inimici sunt diligendi, Matth. V, 44. Resp. 1) Punire facinorosos etiam opus caritatis est: membrum quippe putridum resecandum est, ne pars sincera trahatur. 2) Diligendi sunt inimici, vt homines, non vt latrones, aut facinorosos.

III. III. Quidquid pugnat cum foedere nouo, illud est abrogandum: Capitalia supplicia &c. Ergo. Minor prob. ex Io. I, 17. Lex per Mosen data est, gratia & veritas per Iesum Christum facta est. Resp. Dist. inter nomen gratiae, theologice & politice sumtum. Theologice totat gratuitum fauorem Dei, qui propter Christum, vera fide apprehensum peccata nobis remittit, ne imputentur ad condemnationem aeternam. Quae gratia obtingit


### Quaest. VII. Can a Christian in the New Testament discharge the office of magistrate with a safe conscience?: Q. VIII (continued)

even to evildoers, who are punished with death, provided they perform true repentance. Politically, grace denotes the remission of offenses, so that it is not imputed for temporal punishment. In the former sense it is called the covenant of... grace, not in the latter.

IV. Whoever is not to be deprived of eternal life, is not to be punished with death: But a Christian man &c. Therefore. The minor is clear: because it is most contrary to Christian charity to deprive a man of eternal life. Nor is it obscure, since for a man who undergoes the penalty of death, the time for repentance is cut off. For true repentance must be declared by good works. Response: I deny the minor. To the proof we say that repentance can be declared by good works, whether internal or external. Although an evildoer, who is subjected to capital punishment, cannot always declare his repentance by external good works before the end of his life, he can nevertheless manifest it by internal good works, by love of God and neighbor, by patience and hope, by obedience toward the magistrate, by pious prayers, and by an internal purpose of amending his life, if it were to last longer.

V. If Christ did not condemn the wicked man, neither should the Christian magistrate condemn him: The antecedent is true: Therefore, the consequent also. Response: I distinguish between the political office of the magistrate and the spiritual office of Christ. Our Savior in the days of his flesh did not wish to perform the office of a political judge; hence he would neither decide civil cases nor condemn anyone to temporal punishment: but he had come into the world to teach the gospel as a Prophet, to expiate sins as a Priest, and to erect a kingdom of grace as a spiritual King. They go about to undermine the power of waging war with the following arguments:

I. Whoever sheds human blood sins gravely: The warring magistrate &c. Therefore. The major is proved from Response: I distinguish between shedding human blood in private murder or in a just war; I concede the former. But we are speaking of a just war and public execution.

II. Whoever is angry with his brother is liable to divine judgment: Whoever wages war is angry with his brother. Therefore. The major is clear from Response: I distinguish between rash anger and just indignation. Whoever is angry with his brother rashly is liable to divine judgment.
