But whoever burns with just indignation against an enemy who dares to undermine either the liberty of the citizens or religion, and ravages from the borders of the fatherland, does so justly.

III. The weapons of Christians are spiritual: Therefore, let them abstain from corporal weapons. The antecedent is evident from Response: Christians draw spiritual weapons against spiritual enemies, Satan, the world, and the flesh: the same people draw corporal weapons against corporal enemies who ravage the vitals of the fatherland.

IV. Whose duty it is to love enemies, it is not their duty to wage war: But it is the duty of Christians to love their enemies, Therefore. Response: Christ in that place instructs private individuals in love, he does not disarm the magistrate. We love private enemies because private vengeance is prohibited: the external enemy, who attacks the republic with manifest force, the magistrate repels with the sword divinely granted. We ought to love our enemies as ourselves, not above ourselves.

V. Whoever are one body should not wage war: But Christians &c. Therefore. Response: Enemies of the fatherland, who attempt to ruin either the liberty of the citizens or religion, are not true members of the mystical body, or the church, because they do not have true faith, which works through charity, fixed in their hearts, even though they profess the doctrine of faith with their mouths.

VI. In the times of the Messiah, most desired peace shall flourish: For the wolves shall dwell with the lambs, Is. XI, 6. Resp. In the cited place, peace is understood as spiritual and the public society of faith, by which Jews and Gentiles, being converted, shall coalesce into one mystical body.

VII. David could not build the temple of the Lord, because he was a warrior, and shed human blood, who nevertheless had waged no wars except the Lord's, 1 Paral. XXIX, 3. How then will they dare to stain their hands with blood, who ought to be the holy temple of God? Resp. 1) David also was the holy temple of God, and yet by divine command he waged wars lawfully. 2) He could not build the temple of the Lord, a) because he was hindered by concatenated wars; b) because wars were little suited to the type; since the builder of the temple had to bear the type of the peaceful Messiah.

VIII. War is the judgment of all evils: Therefore it is to be avoided. The antecedent is clear: because war is accompanied by rapine, rapes, adulteries, homicides. Resp. These pertain to the abuse of war, and vicious accidents, not to the genuine use of arms, and the substance of just war itself.

Quest. X. How manifold is the object, about which the magistrate is concerned? The object, in the directing of which the magistrate is occupied, is either real or personal. The real object is civil and sacred things, about which the magistrate is concerned not equally, but in a diverse manner.

The magistrate is occupied about sacred things: by solicitously observing and exercising those things which are to be believed and done for the salvation of all men a); by directing the church and the Christian religion through external government b); yet not by claiming for himself the internal government of sacred things, but by leaving it to the ministers of the church c); and by using the counsel of sincere doctors of the church in the external regimen of sacred things d).

Prob. a. From Ps. II, 10. 11. 12. Now therefore, O Kings, understand! be instructed, O Judges of the earth! serve Jehovah in fear, and exult in trembling! kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and you perish in the way. The magistrate is bound, by reason of himself, to know the true God, to venerate Christ with the kiss of faith, love, and subjection, and to serve the Lord in fear.

Prob. b. The magistrate directs the church by external government: a) Generally, by opening the gate to the Lord, Ps. XXIV, 7. i.e., by positively cooperating toward the introduction, constitution, and conservation of true divine worship, so that under his government they may lead a quiet life in all not only honesty, but also piety, 1 Tim. II, 2. 2) Specifically, 1) by constituting suitable ministers of the church. For the calling of the sacred ministers of the church also pertains to the magistrate, both by reason of his person, because he is a member of the church and indeed a chief one, and by reason of his office, because he is the nourisher of the church and the guardian of both tables of the decalogue, divinely constituted: let him beware, however, lest, with the presbytery and people excluded, he thrust pastors upon unwilling hearers.

2) By erecting temples and schools: for these serve for the exercise of divine worship in public assemblies. 3) By providing for honest sustenance for the doctors in the church and schools who perform a public duty. For Kings are the nourishers of the church, Is. XLIV, 23. who often reflect with themselves that the Lord has so ordained, that they who announce the gospel (since they cannot exercise manual arts) should live from the gospel, 1 Cor. IX, 14. 4) By instituting orders among the ministers of the church, by the example of David 1 Chron. XXIV. 5) By suspending or removing flagitious ministers of the church from office: just as Solomon removed Abiathar, the high priest, with Sadoc substituted in his place, 1 Reg. I, 27. 6) By enacting ecclesiastical laws concerning the external exercise of divine worship making for εὐσχημοσύνην καὶ τάξιν (decency and order), by the example of David, who promulgated a law concerning restoring the ark, 1 Chron. 12:5. concerning the duties of the Levites, chap. 22:6. of Jehoshaphat, who proclaimed a fast, 2 Chron. 20:3. 7) By lawfully dispensing ecclesiastical goods. Thus King Asa brought into the temple what his father had sanctified, 1 Kings 15:15. Hezekiah, establishing a salary for the priests, erected a sacred treasury in the temple, 2 Chron. 31:11. 8) By instituting visitations and councils, after the example of pious Kings in the Old Testament: Jehoshaphat, 2 Kings 16:7; Hezekiah, chap. 29:4. 9) By reforming religion contaminated by heresy, superstition, and idolatry, and even by inquiring into and punishing heretics and seducers, after the example of Jehu, 2 Kings 10:19, and CONSTANTINE THE GREAT in EUSEBIUS, Book I of the Life of Constantine, chap. 11, and by abolishing idolatrous cults, after the example of Asa, 1 Kings 15:12; Jehoshaphat, 2 Chron. 17:7; and Christian Emperors.

The internal economy and government of sacred things, consisting in the doctrine of the Word, absolution from sins, and the lawful administration of the sacraments, is proper to the ministers of the church. The magistrate cannot claim this for himself without sacrilege; when Uzziah, otherwise pious, arrogated this to himself, having entered the temple of Jehovah to burn incense upon the altar of incense, he was severely punished by leprosy arising in his forehead. See 2 Chron. 26:16 ff.

Proof d. The magistrate ought, in the very sacred matters which are subject to the ecclesiastical power itself, to use the counsel of sincere doctors and pastors, according to the divine command, Deut. 17:18, Josh. 1:7, and the examples of praised Kings: David, 1 Chron. 16; Asa, 1 Chron. 14; Jehoshaphat, chap. 17; Hezekiah, chap. 29; Josiah, chap. 34. To this end, in our churches, Kings and Princes have constituted an ecclesiastical senate, or Consistory, consisting of persons not only political, but also ecclesiastical.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, who deny that the care of religion pertains to the magistrate. Their chief argument is: Whoever attributes the care of religion to the magistrate introduces a confusion of ecclesiastical and political office: But Protestant doctors, etc. Therefore. Resp. Distinguish between the external government of religion and the internal economy of sacred things (which distinction is gathered from the words of CONSTANTINE, in EUSEBIUS, Book IV of the Life of Constantine, chap. 24, saying: "You are Bishops in the church, I am a Bishop constituted by God outside the church, or temple"). The former belongs to the magistrate, the latter to the ministers of the church. Others distinguish between ecclesiastical power and formally spiritual power. Ecclesiastical power consists in the external care and disposition of sacred things; this belongs to the magistrate. But power that is formally spiritual, which produces the salvation of the soul by public office and proximately on the part of the living instrumental cause, is proper to ordained pastors alone.

Latin:

etiam maleficis, qui capite plectuntur, modo veram agant poenitentiam. Politice gratia notat veniam delictorum, ne imputetur ad poenam temporalem. Priori sensu dicitur foedus gratiae, non posteriori.

IV. Quicunque non est priuandus vita aeterna, is capite non est plectendus: Atqui homo christianus &c. Ergo. Minor claret: quia maxime pugnat cum caritate christiana, hominem vita aeterna priuare. Neque obscura est, siquidem homini, qui capitis poenam subit, tempus resipiscendi praeciditur. Vera namque poenitentia per bona opera declaranda est. Resp. Neg. min. Ad probationem dicimus, quod poenitentia declarari queat per bona opera interna, vel externa. Licet maleficus, qui capitali supplicio afficitur, ante clausulam vitae suam poenitentiam declarare semper nequeat per bona opera externa, exserere tamen eam potest per bona opera interna, per amorem Dei & proximi, per patientiam & spem, per obsequium erga magistratum, per pias preces, per internum propositum emendandae vitae, si illa longior superfutura esset.

V. Si Christus non condemnauit hominem facinorosum, neque magistratus christianus eum condemnet: Antecedens est verum: E. & consequens. Resp. Dist. inter officium magistratus politicum, & officium Christi spirituale. Saluator noster in diebus carnis nolebat officio iudicis politico perfungi; hinc neque caussas ciuiles decidere, neque ad poenam temporalem quendam condemnare volebat: sed venerat in mundum, vt Propheta, euangelium docturus, vt Sacerdos, peccata expiaturus, vt Rex spiritualis, regnum gratiae erecturus. Potestatem belligerandi labefactatum eunt sequentibus argumentis:

I. Quicunque sanguinem humanum effundit, grauiter peccat: Magistratus belligerans &c. Ergo. Maior prob. ex Resp. Dist. inter caede priuata, vel in bello iusto sanguinem humanum effundit, is grauiter peccat; concedo. At nos loquimur de bello iusto, & caede publica.

II. Quisquis fratri suo irascitur, reus est iudicio diuino: Quicunque bella gerit, fratri suo irascitur. E. Maior liquet ex Resp. Dist. inter iram temerariam, & iustam indignationem. Quisquis fratri suo irascitur, temere, is reus est iudicio diuino. At quisquis hostem, qui vel libertatem ciuium, vel religionem labefactare audet, a finibus patriae populat, is iusta indignatione exardescit.

III. Christianorum arma sunt spiritualia: E. abstineant ab armis corporalibus. Antecedens patet ex Resp. Christiani stringunt arma spiritualia aduersus hostes spirituales, Satanam, mundum & carnem: stringunt iidem arma corporalia aduersus hostes corporales, qui in viscera patriae grassantur.

IV. Quorum est, diligere inimicos, illorum non est bella gerere: Atqui Christianorum est, inimicos diligere, E. Resp. Christus l. c. priuatos in dilectione informat, non magistratum exarmat. Priuatos inimicos diligimus, quia vindicta priuata est prohibita: hostem externum, qui manifesta vi rempublicam aggreditur, magistratus gladio diuinitus concesso repellit. Inimicos, vt nos ipsos, non supra nos ipsos, diligere debemus.

V. Quicunque sunt vnum corpus, bella non gerant: Atqui Christiani &c. E. Resp. Hostes patriae, qui vel libertatem ciuium, vel religionem pessundare conantur, non sunt vera membra corporis mystici, siue ecclesiae, quia veram fidem, quae per caritatem operatur, cordibus infixam non habent, licet doctrinam fidei ore profitentur.

VI. Temporibus Messiae exoptatissima pax vigebit: Lupi enim cum agnis habitabunt, Es. XI, 6. Resp. L. c. intelligitur pax spiritualis & publica societas fidei, qua Iudaei & gentiles conuerti in vnum corpus mysticum coalescent.

VII. Dauid Domini templum aedificare nequiuit, quia bellator fuit, & sanguinem humanum effudit, qui tamen non, nisi Domini, bella gesserat, 1 Paral. XXIX, 3. Quomodo igitur illi audebunt manus suas sanguine cruentare, qui sanctum Dei templum esse debent. Resp. 1) Etiam Dauid fuit sanctum Dei templum, & tamen iussu diuino bella licite gessit. 2) Nequiuit templum Domini aedificare, a) quia bellis concatenatis impediebatur; b) quia bella parum conuenientia erant typo; siquidem templi conditor typum gerere debuit Messiae pacifici.

VIII. Bellum est sententia omnium malorum: E. est fugiendum. Antecedens liquet: quia bellum comitantur rapinae, stupra, adulteria, homicidia. Resp. Haec pertinent ad belli abusum, & vitiosa accidentia, non ad genuinum armorum vsum, & ipsam belli iusti substantiam.

Quaest. X. Quotuplex est obiectum, circa quod magistratus versatur? Obiectum, in quo dirigendo occupatur magistratus, est vel reale, vel personale. Obiectum reale sunt res ciuiles & sacrae, circa quas magistratus versatur non aequaliter, sed diuerso modo.

Circa res sacras occupatur magistratus: follicite obseruando & exercendo, quae omnibus hominibus saluandis sunt credenda & agenda a); externa gubernatione ecclesiam & religionem christianam dirigendo b); internam vero sacrorum gubernationem sibi non vindicando, sed ministris ecclesiae relinquendo c); & in externo sacrorum regimine sincerorum ecclesiae doctorum consilio vtendo d).

Prob. a. Ex Ps. II, 10. 11. 12. Nunc ergo, Reges, intelligite! erudimini, Iudices terrae! seruite Iehouae in timore, & exultate in tremore! osculamini Filium, ne irascatur, & pereatis in via. Magistratus tenetur, ratione sui ipsius, verum Deum cognoscere, Christum osculo fidei amoris & subiectionis venerari, atque in timore Domino seruire.

Prob. b. Externa gubernatione magistratus ecclesiam dirigit: a) Generatim, portam Domino aperiendo, Ps. XXIV, 7. i. e. ad introductionem, constitutionem & conseruationem veri cultus diuini positiue cooperando, vt sub ipsius regimine vitam quietam agant in omni non solum honestate, sed & pietate, 1 Tim. II, 2. 2) Speciatim, 1) idoneos ministros ecclesiae constituendo. Vocatio namque ministrorum sacrorum ecclesiae etiam pertinet ad magistratum, tum ratione personae, quia est membrum ecclesiae & quidem praecipuum, tum ratione officii, quia est ecclesiae nutritius & vtriusque tabulae decalogi custos, diuinitus constitutus: caueat tamen, ne, excluso presbyterio & populo, pastores inuitis auditoribus obtrudat.

2) Templa & scholas erigendo: haec enim ad exercitium cultus diuini in publicis conuentibus seruiunt. 3) Doctoribus in ecclesia & scholis publicum munus obeuntibus, de honesta sustentatione prospiciendo. Sunt enim Reges nutritii ecclesiae, Es. XLIV, 23. qui subinde secum reputant, quod Dominus ita ordinauerit, vt, qui euangelium annuntiant (cum non possint manuarias artes exercere), ex euangelio viuant, 1 Cor. IX, 14. 4) Ordines inter ecclesiae ministros instituendo, exemplo Dauidis 1 Chron. XXIV. 5) Ministros ecclesiae flagitiosos ab officio suspendendo, aut remouendo: quemadmodum Salomo Abiatharem, summum sacerdotem, substituto in eius locum Sadoco, remouit, 1 Reg. I, 27. 6) Leges ecclesiasticas de externo cultus diuini exercitio ad εὐσχημοσύνην καὶ τάξιν facientes ferendo, exemplo Dauidis, promulgantis legem de reducenda arca, 1 Paral. XII, 5. de officiis Levitarum, cap. XXII, 6. Iosaphati, ieiunium indicentis, 2 Paral. XX, 3. 7) Bona ecclesiastica legitime dispensando. Sic rex Asa, quae pater sanctificauerat, templo intulit, 1 Reg. XV, 15. Ezechias sacerdotibus salarium constituens, aerarium sacrum in templo erexit, 2 Paral. XXXI, 11. 8) Visitationes & concilia instituendo, ad exemplum piorum Regum in vet. test. Iosaphati, 2 Reg. XVI, 7. Ezechiae, cap. XXIX, 4. 9) Religionem per haeresin, superstitionem & idololatriam contaminatam, reformando, atque adeo in haereticos & seductores inquirendo & animaduertendo, exemplo Iehu, 2 Reg. X, 19. & CONSTANTINI M. apud EUSEBIUM, Libr. I. de vita Constantini cap. XI. iuxta, atque cultus idololatricos abolendo, exemplo Asa, 1 Reg. XV, 12. Iosaphati, 2 Paral. XVII, 7. & Imperatorum christianorum.

Prob. c. Interna sacrorum oeconomia & gubernatio, consistens in doctrina verbi, absolutione a peccatis, & legitima sacramentorum administratione, propria est ministrorum ecclesiae. Hanc sine piaculo sibi vindicare nequit magistratus: quam cum sibi arrogaret Vsia, alias pius, ingressus in templum Iehouae ad suffiendum super altari suffitus, lepra in fronte ipsius exorta grauiter punitus est. Vid. 2 Paral. XXVI, 16. seqq.

Prob. d. Debet magistratus in ipsis sacris, quae potestati ipsae ecclesiasticae subsunt, vti consilio sincerorum doctorum ac pastorum, iuxta mandatum diuinum, Deut. XVII, 18. Ios. I, 7. & exempla laudatorum Regum, Dauidis, 1 Paral. XVI. Asae, 1 Paral. XIV. Iosaphati, cap. XVII. Ezechiae, c. XXIX. Iosiae, c. XXXIV. Eo fine in nostris ecclesiis Reges, Principefque constituerunt senatum ecclesiasticum, siue Consistorium, ex personis non solum politicis, verum etiam ecclesiasticis constans.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, negantium, curam religionis magistratui competere. Quorum palmarium argumentum est: Quicunque curam religionis tribuunt magistratui, illi muneris ecclesiastici & politici confusionem introducunt: Atqui doctores protestantes &c. E. Resp. Dist. inter gubernationem religionis externam, & oeconomiam sacrorum internam (quae distinctio colligitur ex verbis CONSTANTINI, apud EUSEBIUM, L. IV. de vita Constantini, c. 24. inquientis: Vos Episcopi in ecclesia, ego extra ecclesiam, siue templum, Episcopus a Deo constitutus sum). Illa magistratus est, haec ministrorum ecclesiae. Distinguunt alii inter potestatem ecclesiasticam, & formaliter spiritualem. Potestas ecclesiastica consistit in externa facrorum cura & dispositione, haec competit magistratui: Potestas autem formaliter spiritualis, quae salutem animae ex officio publico, & proxime ex parte causae instrumentalis viuae producit, folis ordinatis pastoribus propria est.


### Q. XI. Does the architectonic power of acting and working in sacred things, just as in secular ones, belong to the magistrate through

The political magistrate does not have architectonic power concerning sacred things equally and indifferently, as he does concerning civil ones. Obs. Architectonic power is called that which, by one habit and one faculty, influences through intermediate causes—of the same kind and order as itself—an effect common to the principle that and the principle by which. For thus is architectonic power described by ARISTOTLE, Book I of the Great Ethics, last chapter. Just as an architect, even if he has under him a builder of a house, and this one in turn other ministers and craftsmen—masons, carpenters, blacksmiths, etc.—who influence the structure itself more closely; yet the architect also influences, because he prescribes the method to all of these.

Proof 1) The political magistrate does not influence through intermediate causes of the same kind and order as himself into an effect common to the principle that and the principle by which: Therefore, he does not have architectonic [power] regarding sacred matters, just as [it does] civil ones. The antecedent is proven because the power of the magistrate is not formally spiritual; nor are the ministers of the same order and genus as the political magistrate; nor, finally, is salvation a common effect of the ministers of the church, as the principle quo (by which), and the magistrate, as the principle quod (that which). 2) If architectonic power in sacred matters belongs to the magistrate, it will follow that: a) he efficiently influences the conversion, regeneration, justification, sanctification, and glorification of Christians through the ministers of the church; b) it is lawful for the magistrate to preach the word, administer the sacraments, hear confession, and absolve those confessing, just as an architect, if he wishes to apply his hand, is permitted to do everything that belongs to the builders and craftsmen; c) the supreme priesthood on earth belongs to the magistrate in a subordinate way, and thus Kings are pastors of the church, and presbyters are the sheep. By which hypothesis καισαροπαπία (caesaropapism) is most strongly confirmed.

The antithesis is that of Paraeus, Vedelius, and others, who posit that architectonic power belongs to the magistrate regarding sacred matters just as much as civil ones. Their stronger arguments are: I. Legislative power regarding sacred matters is either in the presbytery or in the political magistrate: It is not in the presbytery; because it belongs to it to receive laws, not to give them. Therefore, it is in the political magistrate: but he who gives laws enjoys architectonic power. Resp. To give laws regarding interior sacred matters is neither in the power of the presbytery nor the political magistrate, but in the power of God, the supreme legislator. The magistrate does indeed have the right to enact laws concerning the external order of divine worship, concerning ceremonies and rites, yet not absolutely, but with the presbytery called into council.

II. If both ecclesiastical and political power are subordinate to the majesty of Kings, the architectonic power regarding sacred matters will belong to kings no less than regarding political ones: The antecedent is true: Therefore, the consequent [is also true]. The reason for the consequence is: because the architectonic power of Kings regarding political matters is manifest. Therefore, if sacred matters are subject to the majesty of kings in the same way that civil matters are subject to it, [the king] undoubtedly excels in architectonic power regarding sacred matters. The minor is proven from Rom. XIII, 1; 1 Pet. II, 13. Resp. Political and ecclesiastical power are subordinate to the majesty of Kings, but in a different way, not in an equal degree. For civil power is subordinate to the majesty of kings simply, but ecclesiastical power only secundum quid (in a certain respect), and by reason of the external exercise of religion.

Latin:

Magistratus politicus non habet potestatem architectonicam circa sacra aequaliter & indifferenter, vt circa ciuilia. Obs. Potestas architectonica dicitur, quae vno habitu, vnaque facultate influit per causas medias, eiusdem secum generis & ordinis, in effectum communem principio quod, & quo. Ita enim describitur potestas architectonica ab ARISTOTELE, L. I. magnorum moral. c. vlt. Quemadmodum architectus, etsi sub se habeat aedificatorem domus, & hic rursus alios ministros fabrosque caementarios, lignarios, ferrarios &c. qui propius influunt in ipsam structuram; tamen etiam architectus influit, quia in his omnibus modum praescribit.

Prob. 1) Magistratus politicus non influit per causas medias, eiusdem secum generis & ordinis, in effectum communem principio quod, & quo: E. non habet potestatem architectonicam circa sacra, æque vt ciuilia. Antecedens prob. quia potestas magistratus non est formaliter spiritualis; neque ministri sunt eiusdem ordinis & generis cum magistratu politico; neque tandem salus est effectus communis ministris ecclesiæ, tanquam principio quo, & magistratui, tanquam principio quod. 2) Si magistratui potestas architectonica in sacris competit; sequetur, a) eundem per ministros ecclesiæ efficienter influere in conuersionem, regenerationem, iustificationem, sanctificationem, & glorificationem Christianorum; b) licere magistratui verbum prædicare, sacramenta administrare, confessionem audire, confitentes absoluere, sicut architecto, si manum admouere velit, omne illud, quod ædificatorum, fabrorumque est, facere licet; c) magistratui summum in terris sacerdotium subordinatum competere, adeoque Reges esse pastores ecclesiæ, & presbyteros esse oues. Qua hypothesi καισαροπαπία validissime confirmatur.

Antithesis est Paræi, Vedelii & aliorum, statuentium, magistratui circa res sacras æque, ac ciuiles, potestatem architectonicam competere. Quorum potiora argumenta sunt: I. Potestas legislatiua circa sacra, aut in presbyterio, aut in magistratu politico est: Non est in presbyterio; quia illius est, leges accipere, non dare. E. est in magistratu politico: qui autem leges dat, architectonica gaudet potestate. Resp. Circa sacra interiora leges dare, neque penes presbyterium, neque penes magistratum politicum est, sed penes Deum, summum legislatorem. Est quidem magistratus, ferre leges de externo ordine cultus diuini, de cærimoniis & ritibus, non tamen absolute, sed vocato in consilium presbyterio.

II. Si maiestati Regum tam potestas ecclesiastica, quam politica subordinata est, penes reges erit potestas architectonica circa sacra non minus, quam circa politica: Antecedens est verum: E. & consequens. Ratio consequentiæ est: quia Regum potestas architectonica circa res politicas manifesta est. Proinde si res sacræ eadem ratione subiectæ sunt maiestati regum, qua subiacent eidem res ciuiles, haud dubie potestate architectonica circa res sacras eminet. Minor prob. ex Rom. XIII, 1. 1 Petr. II, 13. Resp. Regum maiestati subordinantur potestas politica & ecclesiastica, sed diuerso modo, non autem gradu æquali. Nam potestas ciuilis subordinata est maiestati regum simpliciter, potestas autem ecclesiastica secundum quid tantum, & ratione externi exercitii religionis.


### Q. XII. How does the magistrate conduct himself regarding civil matters?

Regarding civil matters, the supreme magistrate can exercise his consultative, legislative, judicial, and vindicatory power at will a), provided he commands or arranges nothing that is repugnant to natural and divine law b).

Prob. a. Regarding civil matters, the magistrate can dispose [of things] according to his own judgment, for the reason that he is released from human positive and merely civil laws, unless he has bound himself by an oath and promised that he will holily observe the fundamental laws of the republic. We are speaking of the supreme magistrate, whose majesty acknowledges no superior on earth. It belongs to him not to receive laws from men, but to give them to the same. Prob. b.

The supreme magistrate is not released from natural and divine law, but rather, both from the nature of the subject matter and from the will of God, as the supreme Lord, he is obligated—immediately indeed to obedience, but if obedience is lacking, to punishment, to be paid if not in this life, certainly after this life, unless earnest repentance has intervened.

Latin:

Circa res ciuiles magistratus summus potestatem suam consultatoriam, legislatiuam, iudiciariam, & vindicatiuam pro lubitu exercere potest a), modo nil præcipiat, aut disponat, quod iuri naturali ac diuino repugnet b).

Prob. a. Circa res ciuiles magistratus pro arbitrio suo disponere potest, propterea, quod legibus humanis posititiis, mereque ciuilibus solutus est, nisi iuramento se adstrinxerit & promiserit, se leges reipubl. fundamentales sancte seruaturum esse. Loquimur de magistratu supremo, cuius maiestas in terris superiorem non agnoscit. Huius est, leges ab hominibus non accipere, sed iisdem dare.

Prob. b. Lege naturali & diuina non solutus est magistratus supremus, sed potius cum ex ratione materiæ subiectæ, tum ex voluntate Dei, velut summi Domini, obligatus proxime quidem ad obsequium, deficiente autem obsequio ad pœnam, si non in hac vita, certe post hanc, luendam, nisi feria pœnitentia interuenerit.


### Q. XIII. What is the personal object of the magistrate?

The personal object is all persons subject to the power and government of the magistrate, and they are commonly called subjects, or citizens, of whom some are laity, or seculars , others clergy, or ecclesiastics .

Objection. The distinction of subjects into laity and clergy is indeed ecclesiastical, but not biblical. For Peter, 1 Ep. V, 3, calls the church κλῆρος (the lot). For God the Father gave the nations to the Messiah as an inheritance, Ps. II, 8. Yet it was already used long ago in the primitive church to call ministers clergy, because they received τὸν κλῆρον τῆς διακονίας, the lot of the ministry. Isidore, lib. VII. etymol. c. 2, judges that the clergy and clerics were so called from this, because Matthias was chosen by lot, whom we read was the first ordained by the Apostles. Conf. D. Gerhard. lib. de minist. ecclest.

§. 38. Proof a. The laity, who are contained within the sphere of the republic, do not unwillingly confess themselves to be subjects; because under the authority and protection of the magistrate they can pass a tranquil and quiet life in all piety and honesty, 1 Tim. II, 2.

Proof b. That the clergy, insofar as they are viewed as members of the republic, are subject to the civil magistrate in power and government, both regarding their persons and their goods, is proven: a) Generally: Whoever are members and parts of the republic, they must be referred either to the magistrate or to the order of subjects: But now the clergy neither hold nor ought to hold the civil magistracy: Therefore, in this respect, insofar as they are members of the republic, they ought to be referred to the order of subjects. b) Specifically 1) From the Old Testament: Moses was set over Aaron in the place of God, Exod. IV, 15, and corrected the same when he had fallen into sin, Exod. XXXII, 21. Solomon and Hezekiah spoke to the Priests and Levites, 1 Paral. XXIX, 15. Therefore the Priests of the Old Testament were subject to the power of the political magistrate. 2) From the New Testament: a) Paul says explicitly: Rom. XIII, 1. Let every soul be subject to the supereminent powers. We argue: Every human soul, which is contained in the republic, let it be subject to the power ὑπερεχούσῃ (that is over it): But the clerical soul is a human soul, which is contained in the republic: Therefore. b) Christ, the supreme Bishop both in personal and in real matters, rendered obedience to the civil magistrate: Therefore ministers ought to render the same. The former member of the assumption is confirmed from John XIX, 11, where Christ says to Pilate: You would have no power over me, unless it were given to you from above. The latter is proven from Matt. XVIII, 17, where Christ paid the tax for himself and for Peter, with the added reason, lest he should give offense. c) Paul, Acts XXV, 10, appealed from the Jerusalem Sanhedrin and the tribunal of Festus to Caesar: I stand at the tribunal of Caesar, where I ought to be judged. We conclude: To whose tribunal anyone appeals, to his power he submits himself: Paul appeals to the tribunal of Caesar: Therefore.

Objection I. Ministers of the church are considered either regarding the political bond by which they are bound to the republic; or regarding their office in actions formally spiritual, e.g., in the doctrine of the word, absolution from sins, administration of the sacraments. They are subject to the civil magistrate in the former respect, not the latter.

Objection II. Distinguish between the supreme civil magistrate and the inferior. The prelates of the church are subject to the supreme political magistrate, not always to the inferior. For the supreme magistrate has set Superintendents over the Pastors, and instituted ecclesiastical Consistories, in which both ecclesiastical and political persons preside, to whom jurisdiction over the clergy is attributed in a certain order and manner.

Obs. III. Clerics are exempt from personal burdens, lest their authority become cheapened, and the administration of their office be hindered. Goods consecrated to the church, which Clerics enjoy, are immune from real burdens, but not their own private goods, even if conferred upon Clerics by the benefit and privilege of pious Princes.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, who deny that Clerics are subject to civil power and jurisdiction: they fortify their opinion with the following arguments:

I. It is absurd that a sheep should presume to judge its shepherd: Now, Clerics are shepherds; the Prince and the magistrate are sheep: Therefore. Resp. A magistrate in a different respect is a sheep, and a shepherd. In spiritual matters the magistrate is a ovis, but in political matters he is a shepherd, Ps. LXXVIII, 71. 72. Is. XLIV, 28. As therefore in spiritual matters the magistrate ought to obey the shepherds, because in respect to them he is a sheep; so in political matters the ministers of the church ought to obey the magistrate, because in respect to them they are sheep.

II. In those things which are consecrated to God, the princes of this age have no right: Clerics are consecrated to God: Therefore. Resp. Clerics, by reason of their office, are consecrated to God; by reason of their person, they remain parts of the republic and possess earthly goods, in respect to which they remain subject to earthly Princes.

III. The flesh is subject to the spirit, not the contrary: Therefore secular power is subject to spiritual, not the contrary. Resp. I deny the consequence; because neither is ecclesiastical power merely spiritual; for it has much of the flesh; nor is secular power merely carnal; for it has much of the spirit.

IV. Christian princes are sons of the church, and doctors are shepherds: Therefore the former are inferior and subject to the latter. Resp. 1) The name of father does not exempt one from the power of any order; since even a private natural father ought to be subject to a son who is a consul. Magistrates are also called fathers: are they therefore exempt from ecclesiastical power? Princes are called sons of the church, in respect to their submission toward the religion and dogmas of the church, not regarding the deprivation of power. Solomon showed reverence to his mother, but he was superior in majesty and jurisdiction.

V. The lands of the Hierophants were exempted by Pharaoh from tributes: Therefore the maintenance and lands of sacred men are exempt from the payment of tributes. Gen. XLVII, 22. Resp. The lands of the priests were not their own, but were assigned to them by Pharaoh out of his liberality for the maintenance of their life

Latin:

Obiectum personale sunt omnes personae, potestati & regimini magistratus subiectae, & vulgo dicuntur subditi, aut ciues, quorum alii sunt laici, siue saeculares , alii clerici, siue ecclesiastici .

Obs. Distinctio subditorum in laicos & clericos ecclesiastica quidem, non autem biblica est. Nam Petrus 1 ep. V, 3. κλῆρος vocat ecclesiam. Dedit enim Deus Pater Messiae gentes in haereditatem, Ps. II, 8. Fuit tamen iam olim in primitiua ecclesia usitatum, ministros appellare clericos, quia τὸν κλῆρον τῆς διακονίας, sortem ministerii acceperunt. Isidorus, libr. VII. etymol. c. 2. censet, cleros & clericos hinc appellatos esse, quia Matthias sorte electus est, quem primum per Apostolos legimus ordinatum. Conf. D. Gerhard. libr. de minist. ecclest.

§. 38. Prob. a. Laici, qui in sphaera reipublicae continentur, haud inuiti fatentur, se esse subditos; quia sub imperio & tutela magistratus tranquillam & quietam vitam transigere possunt in omni pietate & honestate, 1 Tim. II, 2.

Prob. b. Clericos, quatenus spectantur ut membra reipublicae, potestati & regimini, tam quoad personas, quam quoad bona, subiectos esse magistratui ciuili, probatur: a) Generatim: Quicunque membra & partes reipublicae sunt, illos oportet vel ad magistratum, vel ad subditorum ordinem referri: Iam vero clerici ciuilem magistratum nec gerunt, nec gerere debent: Ergo hoc respectu, quo membra reipublicae sunt, ad subditorum ordinem referri debent. b) Speciatim 1) Ex veteri testamento: Moses Aaroni praefectus fuit in Deum, Exod. IV, 15. & eundem in peccatum prolapsum correxit, Exod. XXXII, 21. Salomo & Ezechias Sacerdotibus atque Leuitis iux dixerunt, 1 Paral. XXIX, 15. Ergo Sacerdotes vet. testamenti potestati magistratus politici subiecti fuerunt. 2) Ex nouo testamento: a) Paullus diserte dicit: Rom. XIII, 1. Omnis anima potestatibus supereminentibus subdita esto. Argumentamur: Omnis anima humana, quae continetur in republica, potestati ὑπερεχούσῃ subdita esto: Atqui anima clericalis est anima humana, quae continetur in republica: Ergo. b) Christus, summus Episcopus tum in personalibus, tum in realibus, obedientiam praestitit magistratui ciuili: Ergo ministri eandem praestare debent. Prius membrum assumptionis confirmatur ex Io. XIX, 11. vbi Christus ad Pilatum dicit: Non haberes potestatem super me ullam, nisi tibi datum esset desuper. Posterius probatur ex Matth. XVIII, 17. vbi Christus pro se & pro Petro censum soluit, addita ratione, ne scandalum praeberet. c) Paullus Act. XXV, 10. a synedrio Hierosolymitano ac tribunali Festi appellauit ad Caesarem: Sub tribunali Caesaris sto, vbi me oportet iudicari. Colligimus: Ad cuius tribunal aliquis appellat, eius potestati se submittit: Paullus appellat ad tribunal Caesaris: Ergo.

Obs. I. Considerantur ministri ecclesiae vel quoad vinculum politicum, quo reipublicae sunt obstricti; vel quoad officium in actionibus formaliter spiritualibus, v. gr. in doctrina verbi, absolutione a peccatis, administratione sacramentorum. Subiecti sunt magistratui ciuili, respectu priori, non posteriori.

Obs. II. Dist. inter magistratum ciuilem summum & inferiorem. Subiecti sunt antistites ecclesiae magistratui politico summo, non semper inferiori. Praefecit enim magistratus summus Pastoribus Superintendentes, & instituit Consistoria ecclesiastica, in quibus & ecclesiasticae & politicae personae praesident, quibus in clericos certo ordine ac modo iurisdictio est attributa.

Obs. III. Exempti sunt clerici ab oneribus personalibus, ne eorum auctoritas vilescat, & officii administratio impediatur. Ab oneribus realibus immunia sunt bona ecclesiae consecrata, quibus Clerici fruuntur, non bona propria, etsi ex piorum Principum beneficio & privilegio Clericis collata.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, negantium, Clericos potestati & iurisdictioni civili esse subiectos: qui suam opinionem sequentibus muniunt argumentis:

I. Absurdum est, ut ovis pastorem suum iudicare praesumat: Iam vero Clerici sunt pastores; Princeps & magistratus sunt oves: Ergo. Resp. Magistratus diverso respectu est ovis, & pastor. In spiritualibus magistratus est ois, sed in politicis est pastor, Ps. LXXVIII, 71. 72. Es. XLIV, 28. Vt ergo in spiritualibus magistratus debet obedire pastoribus, quia illorum respectu est ovis; ita in politicis ministri ecclesiae debent obedire magistratui, quia illorum respectu sunt oues.

II. In ea, quae Deo sunt consecrata, principes huius saeculi nullum ius habent: Clerici sunt Deo consecrati: Ergo. Resp. Clerici, ratione officii, Deo sunt consecrati, ratione personae, manent partes reipublicae & possident terrena bona, quorum respectu terrenis Principibus subiecti manent.

III. Caro subiecta est spiritui, non contra: Ergo saecularis potestas subiecta est spirituali, non contra. Resp. Neg. consequentiam; quia nec potestas ecclesiastica est mere spiritualis; multum enim habet carnis; nec potestas saecularis mere carnalis est; multum enim habet spiritus.

IV. Principes christiani sunt filii ecclesiae, & doctores sunt pastores: Ergo illi his sunt inferiores & subiecti. Resp. 1) Patris nomen non eximit a potestate alicuius ordinis; cum & pater naturalis privatus subesse debeat filio consuli. Etiam magistratus dicuntur patres: an ideo exempti sunt a potestate ecclesiastica? Principes dicuntur filii ecclesiae, qua submissionem erga religionem & dogmata ecclesiae, non quoad privationem potestatis. Reuerentiam matri exhibuit Salomo, sed superior fuit maiestate & iurisdictione.

V. Fundi Hierophantarum exempti fuerunt a Pharaone a tributis: Ergo alimenta, fundique hominum sacrorum exempta sunt a solutione tributorum. Genes. XLVII, 22. Resp. Fundi sacerdotum non erant proprii, sed a Pharaone ex liberalitate ipsis ad tuendam vitam assignati


### XIV. For what end was the magistrate ordained by God?

The ultimate and principal end of the magistrate is the glory of God ; the intermediate and less principal end is the public good . Prob. a.

Since the political magistrate is a divine ordinance, Rom. XIII, 1. by right and merit he looks to the glory of God in his entire rule, and citizens obey the magistrate διὰ τὸν Κύριον [for the Lord's sake], 1 Pet. II, 13.

Prob. b. The civil magistrate is ordained for the public good, and that in a fourfold way: 1) ecclesiastical, for Kings are nursing fathers of the church, and Bishops outside the temple; 2) civil, while he protects the interests of the citizens, and repels external enemies from the borders of the fatherland: 3) moral, insofar as honesty prescribes laws, by which subjects are kept in their duty, so that they may lead a tranquil life in piety and honesty, 1 Tim. II, 2. 4) natural, by which those in power provide for the subjects regarding provisions and other necessities, like Pharaoh, Gen. XLI, 34.

Question XV. What are the duties of subjects? The duties of subjects are: a) to obey the magistrate in all things which do not conflict with the divine word and natural law: b) to revere the magistrate: c) to pay tributes: d) to pour out prayers for the safety of the magistrate. Prob. a. From Rom. XIII, 1. Let every soul be subject to the higher powers; for there is no power but of God, v. 5. Therefore it is necessary to be subject, not only for wrath, but also for conscience sake.

The mandates of the magistrate which are contrary to the word of God and the moral law are excepted. For it is necessary to obey God rather than men.

Acts V, 29. Prob. b.

From Rom. XIII, 7. Render to him to whom you owe fear, fear; to him to whom you owe honor, honor. Prob. c.

From Rom. XIII, 7. Render to him to whom you owe tribute, tribute; to him to whom you owe custom, custom. Prob. d.

From 1 Tim. II, 1. 2. I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men; for kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty.

Protect, O immortal God, King of Kings, Lord of Lords, all Magistrates, who by your authority have been raised to that pinnacle of dignity, so that they may be able to give laws to the citizens! Protect our King, that he may consult for us for a very long time! Protect our Lord, that he may most mercifully protect us! Protect the common Father of all, that he may most kindly cherish all! Inspire him with salutary counsels, grant prosperous successes to his counsels, confirm, increase, and advance those successes, so that they may be stable and perpetual! Supported by your grace, may the pious one rule! May he rule happily! And while he performs this, may he make us, his citizens, pious, just, and happy! O blessed King of ours, to his obedient citizens! O blessed citizens, with a King best in virtue, greatest in power! Whose source of blessedness, you, O most holy Divinity, we worship eternally.

OF THE OECONOMIC STATE, AND SPECIFICALLY OF THE CONJUGAL, PATERNAL, AND MASTERLY STATE. Quaest. I. What is the oeconomic state? The oeconomic state is a society of men constituting one house or family, and it is divided into conjugal, paternal, and masterly society.

Latin:

Finis magistratus ultimus & principalis est gloria Dei ; intermedius & minus principalis est bonum publicum .

Prob. a. Cum magistratus politicus sit ordinatio divina, Rom. XIII, 1. iure meritoque in toto regimine gloriam Dei respicit, & ciues magistratui obediunt διὰ τὸν Κύριον, 1 Petr. II, 13.

Prob. b. Magistratus civilis ordinatus est ob bonum publicum, idque quadruplex: 1) ecclesiasticum, sunt enim Reges nutritii ecclesiae, & Episcopi extra templum; 2) civile, dum civium commoda tuetur, & hostes externos a finibus patriae propulsat: 3) morale, quatenus honestas praescribit leges, quibus subditi in officio continentur, ut vitam tranquillam agant in pietate & honestate, 1 Tim. II, 2. 4) naturale, quo imperantes prospiciunt subditis de commeatu, & aliis necessariis, instar Pharaonis, Gen. XLI, 34.

Quaest. XV. Quae sunt officia subditorum? Officia subditorum sunt: a) magistratui obedire in omnibus, quae verbo divino & legi naturali non repugnant: b) magistratum reuereri: c) tributa soluere: d) preces pro incolumitate magistratus fundere. Prob. a. Ex Rom. XIII, 1. Omnis anima potestatibus supereminentibus subdita esto; non enim est potestas, nisi a Deo, v. 5. Ideo necesse est, subditum esse, non solum propter iram, sed etiam propter conscientiam.

Excipiuntur mandata magistratus, quae verbo Dei, & legi morali aduersantur. Obedire namque oportet Deo magis, quam hominibus.

Act. V, 29.

Prob. b. Ex Rom. XIII, 7. Reddite ei, cui timorem debetis, timorem; ei, cui honorem debetis, honorem.

Prob. c. Ex Rom. XIII, 7. Reddite ei, cui tributum debetis, tributum; ei, cui vectigal debetis, vectigal.

Prob. d. Ex 1 Tim. II, 1. 2. Hortor primo omnium, fieri supplicationes, precationes, intercessiones, gratiarum actiones pro omnibus hominibus, pro regibus & omnibus, qui in supereminentia sunt, ut tranquillam & quietam vitam transigamus in omni pietate & gravitate.

Tuere, Deus immortalis, Rex Regum, Domine Dominorum, omnes Magistratus, te auctore ad id fastigium dignitatis prouectos, ut civibus dare iura queant! Tuere Regem nostrum, ut diutissime nobis consulat! Tuere Dominum nostrum, ut clementissime nos protegat! Tuere communem omnium Patrem, vt benignissime foueat omnes! Adspira ipsi salutaria consilia, consiliis largire prosperos successus, successus confirma, auge, prouehe, vt sint stabiles & perpetui! Tua gratia suffultus pius imperet! Felix imperet! Et hoc dum praestat, nos ciues suos pios, iustos, felices efficiat! O beatum Regem nostrum, civibus morigeris! O beatos ciues, Rege virtute optimo, potestate maximo! Cuius beatitatis fontem te, Numen sanctissimum, aeternum veneramur.

DE STATV OECONOMICO, ET SPECIATIM DE STATV CONIVGALI, PATERNO ATQVE HERILI. Quaest. I. Quid est status oeconomicus? Status oeconomicus est societas hominum, unam domum, vel familiam constituentium, & diuiditur in societatem coniugalem, paternam, & herilem.


### Quaest. II. What is marriage?

Marriage is the indissoluble union of one man and one woman, according to divine institution, made from the mutual consent of both, for the generation of offspring, and mutual aid in life.

Obi. I. Marriage (coniugium) is so called from the common yoke (communi iugo), by which husband and wife are coupled together.

Obi. II. It is also called matrimony ( matrimonium ), from the end of marriage, or the generation of offspring, through which a woman becomes a mother: Likewise wedlock ( connubium ), from the rite of the bride, who, being led into the house of the bridegroom, was covered by a veil, as if by a certain cloud ( nube ).

Obi. III. Marriage is taken a) abstractly, in itself and its own nature, insofar as it is an individual society of one man and one woman, without attending to whether it is the union of this man or this woman: b) concretely and in particular, insofar as it is contracted between certain specific persons, this man, this woman. Furthermore, matrimony can be considered, 1) as it is begun, through betrothal, 2) as it is consummated, through nuptials and carnal copulation.

Obi. IV. Marriage is defined by union, which here denotes not only the transient act by which a male and female are joined, but also the permanent state, or conjugal society, in which husband and wife remain joined by an inseparable covenant.

Latin:

Coniugium est vnius maris & vnius foeminae coniunctio indissolubilis, iuxta institutionem diuinam, ex mutuo vtriusque consensu facta, ad generationem sobolis, & mutuum vitae adiutorium.

Obi. I. Coniugium dicitur a communi iugo, quo maritus & vxor inter se copulantur.

Obi. II. Vocatur etiam matrimonium, a fine coniugii, siue generatione sobolis, per quam mulier fit mater: Item connubium, a ritu sponsae, quae, ducenda in domum sponsi, velamine, velut nube quadam, obtegebatur.

Obi. III. Coniugium sumitur a) abstractiue, in se & natura sua, prout est societas indiuidua vnius maris & vnius foeminae, non attendendo, an fit coniunctio huius maris, huius foeminae: b) concretiue & in particulari, quatenus inter certas quasdam personas, hanc marem, hanc foeminam contrahitur. Potest praeterea matrimonium considerari, 1) vt est inchoatum, per sponsalia, 2) vt est consummatum, per nuptias & carnalem copulam.

Obi. IV. Definitur coniugium per coniunctionem, quae hic non tantum notat actum transeuntem, quo mas & foemina coniunguntur, sed etiam statum permanentem, siue societatem coniugalem, in qua maritus & vxor foedere inseparabili iuncti permanent.


### Quaest. III. What is the principal efficient cause of marriage?

The first and highest efficient cause of matrimony is the Triune God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit a), inasmuch as He immediately instituted marriage abstractly, and considered generally in its own nature b). To marriage considered concretely and in particular, God sometimes concurs effectively c), sometimes permissively d). Prob. a. From Gen. I, 27. The Triune God (אלהים) created; for both the creation and the institution of matrimony is a divine action ad extra; common to all three persons of the Godhead, He created man male and female, and blessed them, saying: Increase, and multiply, and fill the earth.

Prob. b. That God immediately instituted marriage, considered abstractly and in its own nature, is clearly evident: because God 1) created the spouses, Gen. I, 27. 2) formed the woman to provide help to the man, Gen. II, 18. 3) coupled the first parents, Gen. II, 22. seqq. 4) promulgated matrimonial laws, e.g., concerning the constancy of the conjugal bond, Gen. II, 24. A man shall leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife, and they shall be one flesh (those words indeed Adam, as a prophet enlightened by the prophetic spirit, and truly θεόπνευσος [God-breathed], spoke, yet they are attributed to God Himself, Matt. XIX, 5, because God by supreme authority spoke those words through Adam): likewise laws concerning the degrees of consanguinity impeding marriage, Lev. XVIII, 7, concerning the penalty of adultery, Lev. XX, 10. 5) blessed the spouses, Gen. I, 28. Therefore marriage is a state immediately sanctioned by God.

Prob. c. To the marriage of pious spouses God concurs by a general and special influx: By a general influx; because all the actions of men, and thus also the contract of matrimony, depend on God as the first cause: By a special influx, insofar as gracious providence ordains and disposes which woman a man ought to marry, by bending and moving their hearts to mutual consent. Thus, He gives Isaac his spouse Rebecca, Gen. XXIV, 2. Proof d. God does not concur with the illicit marriage of the impious by a special influx, because God does not approve, but detests, an illegitimate marriage; yet He permits it. E.g., Esau took two wives against the will of his parents, Gen. XXVI, 34, which marriage God did not approve, but only permitted.

Latin:

Causa efficiens matrimonii prima & summa est Deus vnitrinus, Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanctus a), quippe qui coniugium abstractiue, & in natura sua generatim consideratum immediate instituit b). Ad coniugium concretiue & in particulari spectatum, Deus quandoque effectiue c), quandoque permissiue d) concurrit. Prob. a. Ex Gen. I, 27. Creauit אלהים Deus triunus; est enim tam creatio, quam institutio matrimonii actio diuina ad extra; omnibus tribus diuinitatis personis communis, hominem masculum & foeminam, benedixitque illis, dicens: Crescite, & multiplicamini, & implete terram.

Prob. b. Deum coniugium, abstractiue & in natura sua consideratum, immediate instituisse, liquido constat: quia Deus 1) coniuges creauit, Gen. I, 27. 2) mulierem formauit ad praestandum viro auxilium, Gen. II, 18. 3) primos parentes copulauit, Gen. II, 22. seqq. 4) leges matrimoniales promulgauit, v. g. de vinculi coniugalis constantia, Gen. II, 24. Derelinquet vir patrem suum, & matrem suam, & adhaerebit vxori suae, & erunt duo in carnem vnam (verba illa quidem Adamus, tanquam propheta spiritu prophetico illustratus, vereque θεόπνευσος, elocutus est, tribuuntur tamen ipsi Deo, Matth. XIX, 5. quia Deus summa auctoritate illa verba per Adamum dixit): item leges de gradibus consanguinitatis coniugium impedientibus, Leu. XVIII, 7. de poena adulterii, Leu. XX, 10. 5) coniugibus benedixit, Gen. I, 28. Ergo coniugium est status a Deo immediate sancitus.

Prob. c. Ad coniugium piorum coniugum Deus concurrit influxu generali & speciali: Influxu generali; quia omnes hominum actiones, adeoque etiam contractus matrimonii a Deo pendent, tanquam causa prima: Influxu speciali, quatenus prouidentia gratiosa caussa prima: Influxu speciali, quatenus prouidentia gratiosa ordinat & disponit, quæ fœmina, cui viro nubere debeat, flectendo & mouendo corda eorum ad mutuum consensum. Sic Isaacum dat coniugem Rebeccam, Gen. XXIV, 2. Prob. d. Ad coniugium impiorum illicitum Deus non concurrit influxu speciali, quia coniugium illegitimum Deus non approbat, sed detestatur; permittit tamen. V. g. Esauus duas duxit vxores, inuitis parentibus, Gen. XXVI, 34. quod matrimonium non approbavit, sed permisit tantum Deus,


### Question IV. What are the secondary and subordinate causes of marriage?

The secondary and subordinate causes of a marriage to be contracted are the spouses themselves a), and their parents, in whose power they are, consenting to the marriage b).

I.* Just as one who is to be girded is considered as girded, so those are called spouses here who are yet about to contract a marriage between themselves. Obs. II.

A male and female to be joined by the marriage bond are considered in two ways: 1) as contracting parties: 2) as the object about which the contract is made. In the latter way, they pertain to the matter; in the former sense, they pertain to the efficient cause of marriage. Their causality, insofar as they are viewed in the genus of efficient cause, is the mutual consent of the contracting parties, which, joined with the consent of the parents, constitutes the adequate and complete cause of marriage.

Proof a. That the consent of the contracting persons is required for a legitimate marriage is gathered 1) from the character and nature of matrimony. To contract a most intimate, and indeed voluntary, society of life, the consent of the contracting parties is required: Marriage is a most intimate, and indeed voluntary, society of life: Therefore. The minor is evident from Gen. II, 24. 2) From the first institution of marriage. God, bringing Eve to Adam, does not violently force her upon him, but inwardly kindles the flame of chaste love in his heart toward Eve, so that he may freely choose her as his spouse, and exultantly exclaim: This, at this time (brought), is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh. She shall be called woman (vira); because she was taken from man (viro), Gen. II, 23. 3) From approved examples. When the father and brother of Rebecca were dealing with Eleazar, the steward of Abraham, who was asking for her as a wife for Isaac, they said: Let us call the girl, and ask her mouth, Gen. XXIV, 57. Compare Tob. VII, 8. 4) From the consequence of inconveniences. Marriages that are reconciled against the will of the contracting persons draw many inconveniences with them. What one does not love, one easily despises; and it is a sad marriage to which a male or female is forced to enter.

Proof b. That the antecedent consent of parents—who use sound reason and do not labor under excessive avarice or immorality toward their children—where it can be had, or at least their subsequent consent, is required for the legitimate and firm marriage of children, not only for the sake of propriety but also of necessity, is proved: 1) From the fourth commandment, and its explanation, which the Apostle delivers, Col. III, 20. Children, obey your parents in all things. If children ought to obey their parents in all lawful things, it follows that they ought to obey them also in contracting marriage, so that they do not contract marriage without their will. 2) From the divine mandate by which they are ordered to give their children in marriage, Jer. XXIX, 6. Take wives for your sons; and give your daughters to husbands, that they may bear sons and daughters; and Deut. VII, 3. You shall not give your daughter to any son of the Gentiles, and you shall not take a daughter of a Gentile for your son. To this pertains the divine mandate concerning freely giving away a deflowered daughter, Exod. XXII, 16, 17. If a man persuades a virgin who is not betrothed, to lie with her; he shall endow her with a dowry for himself as a wife. If her father refusing refuses to give her to him; he shall pay silver, according to the dowry of virgins. 3) From the collation of examples, and the perpetual practice among the people of God. Hagar took a wife for her son Ishmael, Gen. XXI, 21.

Abraham sends away Eleazar to arrange a marriage for his son, Gen. 26:3. Bethuel betroths his daughter Rebekah to Isaac, v. 51. Isaac sends Jacob into Mesopotamia, that he might take a wife from the daughters of Laban, Gen. 28:1. And Laban gave his daughter to Jacob, ch. 29:19. Samson to his parents: I have seen, he says, a woman in Timnath, of the daughters of the Philistines, therefore get her for me as a wife. Judg. 14:2. 4) From natural law. Whatever offspring is not sui iuris [of its own right], but under the power of its parents: that offspring cannot contract marriage without the consent of the parents: But offspring not yet emancipated &c. Therefore. 5) From absurd consequences. In marriages contracted without the consent of parents, a) the authority of parents is undermined, b) an heir is born to a father against his will, c) divine, natural, and civil law is violated.

The antithesis is that of the Papists, who maintain that a marriage can be ratified and valid, even if the consent of the parents is not forthcoming.

I. If Esau could take two wives without the consent of his parents, it follows that today a marriage becomes valid without the consent of parents: The antecedent is true. See Gen. 26:34. Therefore, the consequent. Resp. 1) The example of Esau, a profane and obstinate man, since it is inconsistent with divine law, proves nothing. 2) Isaac could have prevented Esau’s marriage by his dissent, or made it void; yet he tolerated it out of paternal indulgence, though he did not approve it.

II. Jacob took one wife with his parents’ consent, yet he took more later, with his parents completely unaware, Gen. 29:30; ch. 30:4, 9. Resp. 1) The marriage of Jacob cannot be a norm which pious spouses may safely follow, for he was a polygamist, and was circumvented by Laban. 2) When he allowed two handmaids to be joined to him, he had long since been emancipated from paternal power.

III. Tobias took a wife in a foreign land, without his parents knowing. Resp. Tobias took the daughter of Raguel at the persuasion of an angel: both were certain of the parents’ subsequent consent. See Tob. 6: 17.

IV. That without which a marriage is perfect is not necessarily required for its perfection: Now, it is perfect without the consent of parents &c. Therefore. The minor is proved. Because, even if the consent of parents is lacking, yet 1) the matter of marriage is present, i.e., sociable persons, 2) the form, i.e., the consent of the contracting persons, 3) the end, i.e., the procreation of offspring. Resp. The form of marriage consists in the indissoluble bond of the spouses, arising from a legitimate, full, and sufficient consent. But the consent of those who are not yet sui iuris is not legitimate, full, and sufficient unless the consent of those in whose power they are is added.

V. The marriage of servants, against the will of their masters, is firm and valid: Therefore, much more will the marriage of children, against the will of their parents, be valid. Resp. I deny the consequence: because the relationship of a father to his children is very different from the relationship of a master to a servant. The father’s right over his children is much greater and holier than that of a master over his servants, unless they are slaves, who certainly are not free to take a wife without the knowledge and against the will of their masters. Through the marriage of a servant, where the master’s consent is lacking, an heir is not born to him against his will: but this happens in a marriage of children contracted without the consent of parents, by which an heir is begotten against the will of the father or grandfather.

VI. Whatever can object an impediment to an honest marriage is not necessarily required for entering into the marriage covenant: But the consent of parents &c. Therefore. The minor is proved, because it can easily happen that parents, moved by no grave cause, deny their consent out of custom, or disagree among themselves. Resp. 1) If parents are unwilling to consent out of obstinacy or avarice, the children should first bring the matter to their nearest agnates, so that they may persuade the father not to abuse his paternal power. If they obtain nothing, the matter is to be signified to the ministers of the church; if the father does not yield to their admonition, the matter is to be brought to the consistory, which

Latin:

Coniugii contrahendi causæ secundæ & subordinatæ sunt ipsi coniuges a), eorumque parentes, in quorum potestate ipsi sunt, in matrimonium consentientes b).

Obs. I. Sicut cingendus habetur pro cincto: ita coniuges hic dicuntur, qui matrimonium inter se adhuc contracturi sunt.

Obs. II. Mas & fœmina fœdere connubiali iungendi dupliciter considerantur: 1) vt contrahentes: 2) vt obiectum, de quo contrahitur. Posteriori modo ad materiam, priori sensu ad caussam efficientem coniugii pertinent. Caussalitas eorum, quatenus in genere caussæ efficientis spectantur, est mutuus contrahentium consensus, qui, coniunctus cum consensu parentum, caussam adæquatam & completam coniugii constituit.

Prob. a. Requiri ad legitimum coniugium personarum contrahentium consensum, colligitur 1) ex indole & natura matrimonii. Ad societatem vitæ arctissimam, eamque voluntariam, contrahendam, requiritur consensus partium contrahentium: Coniugium est arctissima, eaque voluntaria vitæ societas: Ergo. Minor patet ex Gen. II, 24. 2) Ex prima institutione coniugii. Deus, Euam Adamo adducens, non violenter eam ipsi obtrudit, sed casti amoris flamma interius cor ipsius erga Euam accendit, vt libere coniugem ipsam eligat, & ouans exclamet: Hæc, vice hac (adducta) est os de ossibus meis, & caro de carne mea. Vocabitur vira; quia de viro sumta est, Gen. II, 23. 3) Ex probatis exemplis. Cum pater & frater Rebeccæ cum Eleazaro, procuratore Abrahami, qui eam Isaaco in vxorem petebat, tractarent, dicebant: Vocemus puellam, & interrogemus os eius, Gen. XXIV, 57. Confer. Tob. VII, 8. 4) Ex incommodorum consecutione. Matrimonia, quæ inuitis personis contrahentibus conciliantur, multa secum trahunt incommoda. Quod quis non diligit, facile contemnit; & triste est coniugium, ad quod ineundum mas aut fœmina cogitur.

Prob. b. Parentum, fana ratione vtentium, nec nimia auaritia, aut imorofitate erga liberos laborantium, consensum antecedentem, vbi haberi potest, aut saltim consequentem, ad legitimum firmumque liberorum matrimonium, non solum de honestate, sed etiam de necessitate requiri, probatur: 1) Ex præcepto quarto, eiusque explicatione, quam Apostolus tradit, Col. III, 20. Liberi, obedite parentibus, iuxta omnia. Si liberi obedire debent parentibus in omnibus licitis, sequitur, quod iis obedire etiam debeant in contrahendo matrimonio, vt fine voluntate eorum matrimonium non contrahant. 2) Ex mandato diuino, quo iubentur liberos matrimonio elocare, Ierem. XXIX, 6. Accipite filiis vestris vxores; & filias vestras date viris, vt pariant filios & filias; & Deut. VII, 3. Filiam tuam non dabis filio alicui ex gentilibus, & filiam gentilis non accipies filio tuo. Huc pertinet mandatum diuinum de libere elocanda filia deflorata, Exod. XXII, 16. 17. Si persuaserit vir virgini, quæ non desponsata, vt cubet cum ea; dote dotabit eam sibi in vxorem. Si renuendo renuet pater eius dare eam illi; argentum pendet, quantum est dos virginum. 3) Ex collatione exemplorum, & perpetua praxi in populo Dei. Agar accepit Ismaëli filio suo vxorem, Gen. XXI, 21.

Abraham ablegat Eleazarum ad conciliandas filio suo nuptias, Gen. XXVI, 3. Bethuel Isaaco filiam Rebeccam despondet, v. 51. Isaac Iacobum, vt vxorem de filiabus Laban ducat, in Mesopotamiam mittit, Gen. XXVIII, 1. & Laban dedit Iacobo filiam, cap. XXIX, 19. Simson ad parentes: vidi, inquit, mulierem in Thimnat, de filiabus Philistaeorum, itaque accipite mihi istam in vxorem. Iudic. XIV, 2. 4) Ex lege naturali. Quaecunque soboles non est sui iuris, sed in potestate parentum: illa sine consensu parentum, matrimonium contrahere nequit: Atqui soboles nondum emancipata &c. Ergo. 5) Ex absurdis consequentibus. Matrimoniis sine consensu parentum contractis, a) auctoritas parentum labefactatur, b) patri inuito heres adnascitur, c) lex diuina, naturalis & ciuilis violatur.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, statuentium, coniugium posse ratum validumque esse, licet non accedat consensus parentum. Qui obiiciunt:

I. Si Esauus sine consensu parentum duas potuit ducere vxores, sequitur, quod hodienum matrimonium validum fit sine consensu parentum: Antecedens est verum. Vid. Gen. XXVI, 34. E. & consequens. Resp. 1) Exemplum Esaui, hominis profani & obstinati, cum sit legi diuinae difforme, nil probat. 2) Potuisset Isaacus dissensu suo matrimonium Esaui impedire, vel irritum facere; tolerauit tamen ex indulgentia paterna, licet non approbauerit.

II. Iacobus vnam vxorem duxit parentibus consentientibus, plures tamen postea duxit, parentibus plane insciis, Gen. XXIX, 30. c. XXX, 4. 9. Resp. 1) Coniugium Iacobi non potest esse norma, quam pii coniuges tuto sequantur, fuit enim Iacob πολυγαμος, & a Labano circumuentus. 2) Cum duas ancillas sibi iungi passus est, iam dudum e patria potestate emancipatus.

III. Tobias in terra peregrina duxit vxorem, parentibus ignorantibus. Resp. Tobias angeli suasu duxit Raguelis filiam: vterque certus fuit de consensu parentum consequente. Vid. Tob. VI, 17.

IV. Sine quo perfectum est coniugium, illud ad eius perfectionem necessario non requiritur: Iam vero sine consensu parentum &c. Ergo. Minor prob. Quia deficiente consensu parentum, tamen 1) adest materia coniugii, siue personae sociabiles, 2) forma, i. e. consensus personarum contrahentium, 3) finis, i. e. sobolis procreatio. Resp. Forma coniugii consistit in vinculo coniugum indissolubili, orto ex legitimo, pleno, & sufficienti consensu. Consensus autem eorum, qui nondum sui sunt iuris, non est legitimus, plenus & sufficiens, nisi accedat consensus eorum, in quorum sunt potestate.

V. Coniugium seruorum, inuitis dominis, firmum & ratum est: Ergo multo magis coniugium filiorum, inuitis parentibus erit ratum. Resp. Nego consequentiam: quia diuersissimus est respectus patris ad liberos, & respectus domini ad seruum. Patris ius in liberos multo maius & sanctius est, quam domini in seruos, nisi sint mancipia, quibus certe non integrum est, insciis atque inuitis dominis vxorem ducere. Per coniugium serui, vbi deest consensus domini, huic inuito non adnascitur heres: hoc autem fit in matrimonio liberorum sine consensu parentum contracto, quo inuito patri, aut auo, heres gignitur.

VI. Quidquid honesto matrimonio impedimentum obiicere potest, illud non necessario requiritur ad ineundum foedus coniugale: Atqui consensus parentum &c. E. Minor prob. quia facile fieri potest, vt parentes consensum suum, nulla graui causa permoti, more denegent, vel inter se discordent. Resp. 1) Si parentes ex morositate, vel auaritia, nolint consentire, liberi rem primo deferant ad proximos agnatos, vt patri persuadeant, ne potestate patria abutatur. Si nihil obtineant, ecclesiae ministris res significanda est, quorum admonitioni si pater locum non relinquat; res ad consistorium deferenda est, quod


### Question IV. What are the secondary and subordinate causes of marriage?: Locoparentum [in place of parents] can consent. 2) If parents disagree among themselves, the father prevails, both because the paternal…

locoparentum [in place of parents] can consent. 2) If parents disagree among themselves, the father prevails, both because the paternal power resides more with the father, and because he possesses a more solid judgment.

Q. V. What kind of consent of the persons contracting marriage ought there to be? Consent.

The consent of the persons contracting marriage ought to be a) true and pure from error, b) free, c) just, d) manifested by external words signifying [it], and by other signs and acts, by which betrothals are constituted and declared, which are a mutual promise of future nuptials.

Proof a. True consent is as it were the soul of the conjugal contract, and therefore it ought to be pure from error.

Furthermore, error, being repugnant to full consent, is not of the same nature: for there is error of person, of fortune, of quality, and of status. Error of person is when someone thinks they are contracting with this person whom they have conceived in their mind; when, however, through error they contract with another, or another is joined to them in place of the one with whom they had contracted: by which error of person marriage can be impeded, unless it be ratified by subsequent consent. Thus Jacob had contracted with Rachel, to whom, however, when the time for cohabitation came, Leah was brought in place of Rachel.

Error of fortune is said to occur when someone thinks they are marrying a wealthy person, whom they later discover to be destitute: by which error marriage is not impeded; since riches do not pertain to its substance.

Error of quality is either an error of simple quality or an error of substantial quality. Error of simple quality does not concern the substance and end of marriage, e.g., when someone thinks they are going to marry a well-mannered and beautiful person, when however they turn out to be ill-tempered, quarrelsome, or a drunkard.

Furthermore, neither does error of simple quality impede marriage.

Error of substantial quality is that which is committed regarding a quality that looks to the substance or end of marriage, for example: When someone thinks they are marrying a virgin, whom they nevertheless discover to be deflowered and pregnant: or when they think they are marrying someone capable of the procreation of offspring, when they nevertheless discover them to be entirely incapable: by which error marriage is impeded. Error of status is when a free or free-born person thinks they are marrying a free person, and marries a slave; or when a free-born woman marries a slave whom she thought to be free-born: by which error formerly, when slaves were chattels, the consent was rendered void; today, however, one must judge differently regarding servants hired for wages, who are held to be free-born, since they were born of free-born parents.

Wherefore, to avoid errors, integrity of judgment is required: but a man who is profoundly drunk, foolish, or perpetually insane is destitute of sound and uncorrupted judgment, and therefore cannot truly consent to marriage.

Proof b. Consent on both sides ought to be free.

For consent extorted by force or fear is not in reality consent, because it is not an elicited act of the will.

A distinction must be made here between just fear and vain fear. The former arises from the threat of those things which a prudent man rightly shudders at; the latter arises from trivial causes.

Betrothals are dissolved by just fear, not by vain fear.

Proof c. Just consent ought to be mutual, born of promise and counter-promise, joined with the consent of those in whose power either both of the contracting parties, or one or the other, is.

Proof d. Although it formally consists in internal acts of the will, and denotes the will of two or more, equally terminated upon the same thing: it must nevertheless be confessed that internal acts alone, without external declaration, do not suffice for contracting marriage, so that betrothals may be valid and ratified.

Quæst. VI. How are betrothals distinguished? Betrothals are distinguished: a) Into betrothals of the present, and of the future. The former are made by words of the present; the latter are made by words of the future: b) Into pure, or absolute, betrothals, and conditional ones. The former are made without express mention of any condition; the latter are made under a certain condition.

Proof a. If a betrothed man conceives his promise in these words: "I will take you as my wife," he contracts a betrothal of the future: if he says: "I take you as my wife," he contracts a betrothal of the present. You should observe well here that those are properly called betrothals which are made by words of the future: however, a promise of matrimony by words of the present constitutes the matrimony itself, and thus betrothals of the present are not distinct.

Proof b. We learn from Scripture that betrothals are to be distinguished into absolute and conditional.

For Rebekah was betrothed to Isaac absolutely and without an annexed condition. See Gen. XXIV. But Rachel was betrothed to Jacob under the condition of seven years of service, Gen. XXIX.

From absolute betrothals arises an obligation so effective that one party of the contracting parties, at the request of the other party, can be compelled to consummate the marriage. Betrothals contracted under a condition do not have an effect in the present, but are suspended until the added conditions are fulfilled.

Moreover, the annexed conditions are some honest, some base, some impossible. Concerning which see GERHARD in loc. de coniug. §. 132.

Quæst. VII. Does the priestly blessing also pertain to the efficient cause of marriage? The solemn blessing, or coupling, which is performed by a Priest according to the customary rite, pertains not to the contracting a), but to the consummating of a Christian marriage b).

Proof a. We have clearly shown that marriage is contracted through mutual and just consent.

Proof b. For the consummation of a Christian marriage, a priestly blessing is required: a) So that it may be publicly established that the marriage of the contracting parties is legitimate: b) so that the contracting parties may be admonished concerning the holy and indissoluble bond of matrimony, concerning conjugal duties, and concerning the endurance of hardships: c) so that the new spouses may be commended through solemn prayers to God, the author of marriage.

Quæst. VIII. What is the matter of marriage? The matter, or subject of marriage, are the persons who are coupled in marriage a), two in number, one male and one female b), capable of obtaining the ends of marriage c), and constituted outside the prohibited degrees of consanguinity and affinity d).

Proof a. Persons sociable in marriage, insofar as they are viewed as consenting and contracting the marriage, are the secondary efficient causes of matrimony: but insofar as they are considered as parts and members of the conjugal society, they are the matter of marriage.

Proof b. 1) From the primeval divine institution. For God created only two humans, and joined only two into one flesh, Gen. II, 24.

We argue: Marriage according to divine institution is the joining of two humans, a male and a female, into one flesh: But simultaneous polygamy is not the joining of two, but of many into one flesh. Therefore, polygamy is not marriage contracted according to divine institution. *).

You say: Moses in the Hebrew text did not expressly use a word expressing the dual number. Reply: That matters nothing, because at that time there were no more than two people. That marriage ought to consist of only two persons is clear: 2) From the repetition of the first institution made by Christ, Matthew XIX, 4. 5. Have you not read that He who made them from the beginning made them male and female? And said: Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh. Objection: 1) If God had wanted one man to have multiple wives, He would have made not just one, but multiple women. 2) God said: a man shall cling to his wife, not to his wives. 3) Christ expressly used a word expressing the dual number. For He said: and the two shall become one flesh.

You say: In fornication two become one flesh, even if the fornicator is joined with another woman, 1 Cor. VI, 16. Therefore, even if someone has multiple wives, it still remains that two are one flesh, because with each one they become one flesh. Reply: 1) He who clings to a harlot becomes one flesh with her, not legitimately, but in fact. 2) He who clings to a harlot does not become one flesh with her under the hypothesis of a unity enduring in legitimate marriage; but under the act of breaking the first bond and removing unity with the legitimate wife. Therefore, by the very act of someone becoming one flesh with a harlot, he ceases to be one flesh with his legitimate spouse; for he commits adultery, directly opposed to marriage.

3) From the apostolic instruction: Because of fornications (to be avoided) let each man have his own wife; and let each woman have her own husband. The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband: Likewise, the husband also does not have authority over his own body, but the wife, 1 Cor. VII, 2. 4. From these arises a twofold argument. a) Where each woman does not have her own husband, there is no legitimate marriage pleasing to God: But in polygamy she does not have &c: Therefore. b) That power which has already been transferred to the wife, and rightfully belongs to her, and is her own, the husband cannot grant to another or make common: But the power over the husband's body has already been transferred to the wife through marriage &c: Therefore.

4) From the custom of the primitive church. The Christian world from its earliest beginnings had no polygamist, but the primal monogamous law, which the Savior renewed, Christians constantly observed. Proof c.

Marriage is a means of generating offspring; Gen. I, 28. and a remedy for extinguishing lust, 1 Cor. VII, 9. We argue: Those who are naturally unfit to procreate children, and to extinguish the flames of lust for the other contracting party, are also naturally unfit for marriage: But the immature, eunuchs, castrati, frigid, &c. are naturally unfit &c. Therefore. Proof d.

From Levit. XVIII, 7. No man shall approach any of his own flesh to uncover nakedness: For I (am) JEHOVAH. Where it is prohibiwe are prohibited from joining to ourselves in marriage a person near in flesh, namely on account of the modesty and reverence founded in the nearness of flesh resulting from generation or marriage. But which degrees of consanguinity or affinity are prohibited, we are taught in the l. c. .

The antithesis is 1) of the Muhammadans and Chinese, whose polygamy is known. 2) Of the Anabaptists, to some of whom πολυγαμία (polygamy) was pleasing. 3) Of the Socinians, dreaming that polygamy was indeed prohibited in the New, but not in the Old Testament. 4) Of Bernardino Ochino, the masked Sincero de Warenberg, M. Johann Lyser, and others, who fervently contend that polygamy is lawful even in the New Testament. Whose (*) stronger arguments are:

I. Whoever imitates the patriarchs and pious kings of the Old Testament, they do not sin: But polygamists &c. Therefore. Resp.
