The polygamy of the patriarchs was tolerated by God as a blemish and a sin of infirmity, arising both from ignorance of the genuine sense of the first divine institution, that there ought to be two and not more in one flesh, and from a zeal for restoring the nativity of the Messiah.

Instantia: If the polygamy of the patriarchs was a sin, the patriarchs died in mortal sin; since they are not said in Holy Scripture to have done penance for polygamy. Resp. Distinguish between a sin actually deadly, and venial. The polygamy of the patriarchs was a sin not actually deadly, but venial, which God did not impute to condemnation by an actually second [act]; because He looked with eyes of mercy upon their general repentance, heroic faith, and ardent desire for the Messiah.

II. Concerning whatever matter God has sanctioned a law, He approves it: Concerning polygamy &c. Therefore. The major is evident: because the law is a mirror of the divine will. The minor is proved: because God sanctioned a law 1) concerning a hated and a beloved wife, and the children of both; which of them ought to enjoy the right of primogeniture, Deut. XXI, 15 . Resp. I deny the major: because God brings forth a law not only concerning those things which He approves, but also which He permits and tolerates, such as divorce, Matth. XIX, 7. 8 . See also Ex. XXII, 16 . In that place, therefore, Deut. XXI, 15, it treats of a human act and indeed an illegitimate one, or one committed against the divine rule (which God tolerated for a time), not of divine right, or the approving will of God. See Exod. XXII, 16 . 2) God gave a law, the law, concerning raising up seed for a brother, when his widow is left without offspring. Deut. XXV, 5. Resp. God speaks of a widow; therefore of successive polygamy, not simultaneous. The brother is to be understood as being unmarried. But if you urge that the brother must be understood as married, we reply that God, by this law, had regard for polygamy hitherto tolerated by Him, and directed it to some good end in a certain case, namely, for the inheritance or possession of the Jews, so that it might not be torn away. This, however, does not help the defenders of polygamy; for it is incumbent upon them first to prove that polygamy is not prohibited, and is consistent with the primary institution of marriage.

III. That by which man attains the intention of God, namely the multiplication of the human race, is not prohibited, but lawful: But by polygamy &c. Therefore. Resp. God does not intend the multiplication of the human race against the primeval institution of marriage, to which polygamy is opposed.

IV. That which God proposed as a sin neither by law nor by inflicted punishments, is not a sin: But polygamy &c. Therefore. Resp. The minor is denied. For while God promulgated the primeval institution of marriage, that male and female ought to be one flesh, by this very fact He laid down the law that marriage ought not to be contracted otherwise.

V. Whoever gave the wives of Saul into the bosom of David, he approved of polygamy: But God &c. Therefore. The major is evident: since wives, who are given into our bosom, are given to us in marriage. The minor is clear from 2 Sam. XII, 8. Resp. To give into the bosom of another is taken either generally or specially. In a general sense, something is said to be given into the bosom of another which is committed to his power. Confer. 1 Reg. I, 20. Ps. XXXV, 13. Specially, that is given into the bosom which is handed over in marriage. When the wives of Saul are said to have been given into the bosom of David, they are said to have been given not in a special sense, but a general one. For he could not lawfully take them in marriage, because Saul was David's father-in-law; therefore the wives of Saul, among whom was Michal, the mother of David's spouse, could not be handed over to him in marriage. Grant that marriage is understood; it still does not follow that God approved of that deed. For the word נתן often denotes only permission and tolerance. See Gen. XX, 6. Num. XXI, 23. Iud. XI, 9.

VI. Whatever is only forbidden to a Bishop is not prohibited to other men: Polygamy &c. 1 Tim. III, 2. Therefore. Resp. A Bishop is called the husband of one wife, not in an exclusive sense, as if he alone ought to be monogamous, but in an inclusive sense (*).

Latin:

locoparentum consentire potest. 2) Si parentes inter se discordent, præualet pater, tum quia patria potestas magis penes patrem est, tum quia solidiori pollet iudicio. Quæst. V.

Qualis consensus personarum matrimonium contrahentium esse debet?

Consensus. Consensus personarum matrimonium contrahentium esse debet a) verus & purus ab errore, b) liber, c) iustus, d) externis verbis significantibus, aliisque signis & actibus manifestatus, quibus constituuntur & declarantur sponsalia, quæ sunt promissio mutua futurarum nuptiarum.

Prob. a. Verus consensus est quasi anima coniugalis contractus, adeoque purus esse debet ab errore.

Ceterum error, pleno consensui repugnans, non eiusdem rationis est: datur enim error personæ, fortunæ, qualitatis, & status. Error personæ est, cum quis putat, se contrahere cum isthac persona, quam animo concepit; cum tamen ex errore contrahat cum alia, vel cum alia ipsi adiungitur loco eius, cum qua contraxerat: quo errore personæ coniugium impediri potest, nisi per consensum consequentem ratihabeatur. Sic Iacob contraxerat cum Rahele, cui autem, cum tempus concumbendi esset, loco Rahelis Lea adducta fuit.

Error fortunæ dicitur, cum quis putat, se ducere opulentam, quam postea inopem deprehendit: quo errore non impeditur coniugium; cum ad huius substantiam divitiæ non pertineant.

Error qualitatis, est vel error qualitatis simplicis, vel error qualitatis substantialis. Error qualitatis simplicis non concernit substantiam & finem matrimonii, v. g. cum quis putat, se ducturum esse moratam & formosam, cum tamen fit morosa, rixosa, ebriosa.

Ceterum neque error qualitatis simplicis matrimonium impedit.

Error qualitatis substantialis est, qui committitur circa qualitatem, quæ spectat ad substantiam, vel finem matrimonii, verbi gratia: Cum quis putat, se ducere virginem, quam tamen comperit esse compressam & grauidam: vel cum putat, se ducere habilem ad procreationem sobolis, cum tamen deprehendat, eam prorsus inhabilem esse: quo errore matrimonium impeditur. Error status est, cum liber, vel ingenuus putat, se ducere liberam, & ducit seruam; vel cum ingenua nubit seruo, quem ingenuum esse putauit: quo errore olim, cum serui essent mancipia, consensus fiebat irritus, hodie autem aliter iudicandum est de seruis mercede conductis, qui pro ingenuis habentur, cum ex ingenuis nati sint.

Quocirca ad cauendos errores requiritur iudicii integritas: destituitur vero sano & incorrupto iudicio homo profunde ebrius, fatuus, & perpetuo furiosus, adeoque in matrimonium vere consentire nequit.

Prob. b. Consensus ab utraque parte liber esse debet.

Nam consensus vi, aut metu extortus, reuera non est consensus, quia non est actus voluntatis elicitus.

Distinguendum hic est inter metum iustum, & vanum. Ille oritur ex comminatione eorum, quæ homo prudens merito exhorrescit; hic oritur ex causis leuiculis.

Soluuntur sponsalia metu iusto, non vano.

Prob. c. Consensus iustus debet esse mutuus, ex promissione & repromissione natus, cum consensu eorum, in quorum potestate vel uterque contrahentium, vel alteruter est, coniunctus.

Prob. d. Quamuis formaliter consistat in internis actibus voluntatis, atque denotet duorum aut plurium voluntatem, ad eandem rem æque terminatam: fatendum tamen est, solos actus internos, sine externa declaratione, non sufficere ad contrahendum coniugium, ut valida & rata sint sponsalia.

Quæst. VI. Quomodo distinguuntur sponsalia? Sponsalia distinguuntur: a) In sponsalia de præsenti, & de futuro. Illa fiunt per verba de præsenti; hæc fiunt per verba de futuro: b) In sponsalia pura, sive absoluta, & conditionalia......ata. Illa fiunt sine expressa mentione alicuius conditionis; hæc fiunt sub certa conditione.

Prob. a. Si sponsus promissionem suam concipiat his verbis: Accipiam te in uxorem, contrahit sponsalia de futuro: si dicat: Duco te uxorem, sponsalia contrahit de præsenti. Probe hic observes, quod proprie sponsalia dicantur, quæ fiunt per verba de futuro: promissio autem matrimonii, per verba de præsenti constituit ipsum matrimonium, adeoque sponsalia de præsenti non distincta sunt.

Prob. b. Sponsalia distinguenda esse in absoluta, & conditionata, e scriptura discimus.

Nam Rebecca Isaaco desponsata est absolute & citra annexam conditionem. Vid. Gen. XXIV. At Iacobo Rahel desponsata est sub conditione septennalis servitii, Gen. XXIX.

Ex sponsalibus absolutis tam efficax nascitur obligatio, vt pars vna contrahentium, ad petitionem alterius partis, compelli possit ad consummandum matrimonium. Sponsalia sub conditione contracta, non habent effectum de præsenti, sed suspenduntur, donec conditiones adiectæ impleantur.

Sunt autem annexæ conditiones aliæ honestæ, aliæ turpes, aliæ impossibiles. De quibus vid. GERHARD. in loc. de coniug. §. 132.

Quæst. VII. An ad causam efficientem coniugii pertinet etiam benedictio sacerdotalis? Solemnis benedictio, sive copulatio, quæ ritu consueto fit a Sacerdote, non ad contrahendum a), sed ad consummandum coniugium Christianum b), pertinet.

Prob. a. Coniugium contrahi per mutuum iustumque consensum, luculenter ostendimus.

Prob. b. Ad consummandum coniugium Christianum requiritur benedictio sacerdotalis: a) Vt de legitimo contrahentium coniugio publice constet: b) vt de sancto & indissolubili vinculo matrimonii, de officiis coniugalibus, de ærumnarum tolerantia contrahentes admoneantur: c) vt noui coniuges per solemnes preces commendentur Deo, coniugii auctori.

Quæst. VIII. Quæ est materia coniugii? Materia, sive subiectum coniugii sunt personæ, quæ coniugio copulantur a), numero duæ, mas vnus & vna foemina b), habiles ad obtinendas coniugii fines c), atque extra prohibitos consanguinitatis & affinitatis gradus constitutæ d).

Prob. a. Personæ in coniugio sociabiles, quatenus spectantur vt consentientes & contrahentes matrimonium, sunt causæ efficientes secundariæ matrimonii: at quatenus considerantur vt partes & membra societatis coniugalis, coniugii materia sunt.

Prob. b. 1) Ex primæva institutione diuina. Deus enim duos tantum homines creauit, & duos tantum in vnam carnem coniunxit, Gen. II, 24.

Argumentamur: Coniugium iuxta institutionem diuinam est duorum hominum, maris & fæminæ, in vnam carnem coniunctio: At polygamia simultanea non est duorum, sed plurium in vnam carnem coniunctio. E. polygamia non est coniugium, iuxta institutionem diuinam contractum. *).

Dicis: Moses in textu hebraeo non expresse posuit vocem, dualem numerum exprimentem; Resp. Ea nil refert, quia tunc temporis non extabant plures homines, quam duo. Quod vero ex duabus tantum personis conjugium constare debeat, patet: 2) Ex primae institutionis repetitione facta a Christo, Matth. XIX, 4. 5. Annon legistis, quod is, qui fecit, ab initio masculum & feminam fecit eos. Et dixit: Propterea deseret homo patrem & matrem, & adhaerebit uxori suae, & erunt duo in carnem unam. Obs. 1) Si Deus voluisset unum virum plures habere uxores, non unam tantum, sed plures feminas fecisset. 2) Dixit Deus: homo adhaerebit uxori suae, non uxoribus suis. 3) Christus expresse posuit vocem, dualem numerum exprimentem. Dixit enim: & erunt duo in carnem unam.

Dicis: In scortatione duo fiunt una caro, etsi scortator fit cum alia muliere conjunctus, 1 Cor. VI, 16. Ergo etsi quis plures uxores habeat, tamen manet illud, quod duo sint in unam carnem, quia cum singulis fit una caro. Resp. 1) Qui scorto adhaeret, fit una caro cum illa, non legitime, sed de facto. 2) Qui scorto adhaeret, non fit una caro cum illa sub hypothesi unitatis perdurantis in legitima conjugio; sed sub actu rumpentis primum vinculum & unitatem tollentis cum legitima uxore. Ergo eo ipso, quo aliquis cum scorto fit una caro, definit esse caro una cum conjuge legitima; committit enim adulterium, conjugio directe oppositum.

3) Ex apostolica instructione: Propter scortationes (vitandas) quilibet suam ipsius uxorem habeto; & quaelibet proprium virum habeto. Uxor proprii corporis potestatem non habet, sed maritus: Similiter vero etiam maritus proprii corporis potestatem non habet, sed uxor, 1 Cor. VII, 2. 4. Nascitur ex his geminum argumentum. a) Ubi unaquaeque mulier non habet proprium maritum, ibi non est legitimum Deo placens conjugium: Atqui in polygamia non habet &c: Ergo. b) Quae potestas jam translata est in uxorem, eique jure convenit, ac propria est, eam maritus non potest alteri concedere ac communem facere: Sed potestas corporis mariti jam per conjugium translata est in uxorem &c: Ergo.

4) Ex primitivae ecclesiae consuetudine. Orbis Christianus inde a primis incunabulis nullum habuit polygamum, sed legem primaeam monogamicam, quam Salvator renouauit, Christiani constanter feruarunt.

Prob. c. Conjugium est generandae prolis medium; Gen. I, 28. & restinguendae libidinis remedium, 1 Cor. VII, 9. Arguimus: Qui naturaliter inepti sunt ad procreandum liberos, & ad restinguendum alteri parti contrahenti flammas vltionum, illi etiam naturaliter inepti sunt ad matrimonium: Atqui impuberes, eunuchi, spadones, frigidi &c. naturaliter inepti sunt &c. Ergo.

Prob. d. Ex Levit. XVIII, 7. Quisquis virorum fuerit, ad vllas reliquias carnis suae non appropinquabitis, ad reuelandam nuditatem: Ego (enim sum) IEHOVAH. Vbi prohibiprohibemur, personam carne propinquam matrimonio nobis iungere, scilicet ob pudorem & reverentiam in propinquitate carnis ex generatione aut nuptiis resultante fundatam. Quinam autem gradus consanguinitatis aut affinitatis prohibiti sint, l. c. edocemur.

Antithesis est 1) Muhammedanorum & Chinensium, quorum polygamia nota est. 2) Anabaptistarum, quorum nonnullis πολυγαμία placuit. 3) Socinianorum, somniantium, polygamiam quidem in novo, sed non in vet. testamento prohibitam fuisse. 4) Bernardini Ochini, personati Sinceri de Warenberg, M. Ioan. Lyseri, & aliorum, polygamiam licitam esse etiam in novo testamento feruide contendentium. Quorum (*) potiora argumenta sunt:

I. Quicunque imitantur patriarchas & pios reges veteris testamenti, illi non peccant: Atqui polygami &c. Ergo. Resp. Polygamia patriarcharum tolerata est a Deo, tanquam naevus & peccatum infirmitatis, ortum tum ex ignorantia genuini sensus primae institutionis divinae, quod duo tantum & non plures debeant esse in carne una, tum ex zelo instaurandae natuitatis Messiae.

Instantia: Si polygamia patriarcharum fuit peccatum, patriarchae in peccato mortali decesserunt; cum non dicantur in S. Scriptura ob polygamiam poenitentiam egisse. Resp. Dist. inter peccatum actu mortiferum, & veniale. Polygamia patriarcharum fuit peccatum non actu mortiferum, sed veniale, quod Deus ad condemnationem actu secundo non imputavit; quia oculis misericordiae adspexit illorum poenitentiam generalem, fidem heroicam, & ardens desiderium Messiae.

II. De quacunque re Deus sanxiit legem, illam approbat: De polygamia &c. Ergo. Maior patet: quia lex est speculum voluntatis divinae. Minor probatur: quia Deus sanxivit legem 1) de vxore exosa & dilecta, & vtriusque liberis; quis eorum iure primogeniturae frui debeat, Deut. XXI, 15. Resp. Neg. maior: quia Deus legem fert non tantum de illis rebus, quas approbat, sed etiam, quas permittit & tolerat, sicut divortium, Matth. XIX, 7. 8. Vid. & Ex. XXII, 16. In illo igitur loco, Deut. XXI, 15. agitur de facto humano & quidem illegitimo, sive contra regulam divinam commisso (quod Deus ad tempus toleravit), non de iure divino, aut voluntate Dei adprobante. Vid. Exod. XXII, 16. 2) Dedit Deus legem, de semine excitando fratri, quando eius relicta vidua prole caret. Deut. XXV, 5. Resp. De vidua Deus loquitur; ergo de polygamia successiua, non de simultanea. Frater cælebs intelligendus esse videtur. At si intelligendum esse fratrem vxoratum vrgeas, respondemus, Deum respexisse hac lege polygamiam hactenus a se toleratam, eamque in finem aliquem bonum in certo casu direxisse, nempe ad hæreditatem, siue possessionem Iudæorum, ne illa diuelleretur. Hoc vero defensores polygamiæ non iuuat; quippe quibus in primis probandum incumbit, polygamiam non esse prohibitam, & primæ matrimonii institutioni consentaneam.

III. Per quod homo intentionem Dei, nempe multiplicationem generis humani assequitur, illud non est prohibitum, sed licitum: Atqui per polygamiam &c. Ergo. Resp. Deus non intendit multiplicationem generis humani contra primæuam coniugii institutionem, cui polygamia aduersatur.

IV. Quod Deus nec per legem, nec per inflictas pœnas proposuit vt peccatum, id non est peccatum: Atqui polygamiam &c. Ergo. Resp. Negatur minor. Dum enim Deus promulgauit primæuam coniugii institutionem, quod mas & fœmina debeant esse in vnam carnem, hoc ipso legem tulit, quod non aliter matrimonium debeat contrahi.

V. Quicunque vxores Saulis dedit in sinum Dauidis, is polygamiam approbauit: Atqui Deus &c. Ergo. Maior constat: quoniam vxores, quæ dantur in sinum nostrum, dantur nobis in matrimonium. Minor patet ex 2 Sam. XII, 8. Resp. Dare in sinum alterius, sumitur vel generaliter, vel specialiter. Generali sensu dicitur aliquid dari in sinum alterius, quod potestati eius committitur. Confer. 1 Reg. I, 20. Ps. XXXV, 13. Specialiter in sinum datur, quod in matrimonium traditur. Quando vxores Saulis dicuntur datæ in sinum Dauidis, non sensu speciali, sed generali datæ dicuntur. Nam in matrimonium eâs licite assumere nequiuit, quia Dauidis socer erat Saul, vxores itaque Saulis, quas inter erat Michalis, coniugis Dauidis mater, in matrimonium ipsi tradi non poterant. Fac, intelligi matrimonium; non tamen sequitur, Deum illud factum probasse. Nam verbum נתן sæpe permissionem & tolerantiam tantum notat. Vid. Gen. XX, 6. Num. XXI, 23. Iud. XI, 9.

VI. Quidquid tantum interdicitur Episcopo, reliquis hominibus non prohibetur: Polygamia &c. 1 Tim. III, 2. Ergo. Resp. Episcopus dicitur vnius vxoris vir, non sensu exclusiuo, quasi ille solus monogamus esse debeat, sensu inclusiuo (*).


### Question IV. What are the secondary and subordinate causes of marriage?: Quest. IX. Is it lawful for ministers of the church to enter into marriage? It is lawful for ministers of the church to enter into marriage, and…

Quest. IX. Is it lawful for ministers of the church to enter into marriage?

It is lawful for ministers of the church to enter into marriage, and to live in it.

Obs. I. It is not asked: whether all who are established in an ecclesiastical office ought to be married? if indeed church ministers who have the gift of continence are not blamed by usendowed [with the gift of continence] live holily and chastely in celibacy, since the unmarried, not being greatly distracted by the cares of this world, can perform their ecclesiastical office with ease, 1 Cor. VII, 1.

Obs. II. The question is not: whether the celibate life is good and useful, especially in a time of persecution? but: whether it is necessary?

Prob. a. 1) The Apostles granted marriage to the Clergy, or ministers of the church. Therefore, it is not prohibited to them, nor can it be prohibited to them by ecclesiastical constitution. The antecedent is proved from 1 Tim. III, 2. A bishop must be blameless, the husband of one wife. Where by "wife" is not understood the church, whose spouse is not the minister, but Christ himself; but a true wife, in his own house begetting children to be honestly educated, v. 4. Conf. Tit. I, 5. 6. The reason for the consequence is: because it is not fitting for the church to make laws or to constitute anything against the doctrine of the apostles.

2) The Apostles thought marriage to be lawful for themselves, some of whom lived in the same. Therefore, it is wrongly prohibited to the ministers of the church. The antecedent is proved from 1 Cor. IX, 5. Have we not power to lead about a sister, a wife? as well as other Apostles, and the brethren of the Lord, and Cephas.

3) Marriage is honorable in all, Hebr. XIII, 4. Therefore, it cannot be reprehended in the Clergy, much less prohibited to them.

4) Those who do not possess the gift of continence are commanded by the Apostle to contract marriage: But many ministers of the church &c. Therefore. The major is proved from 1 Cor. VII, 2. To avoid fornication, let every man have his own wife. The minor is clear, Matth. XIX, 11. All men cannot receive this saying, save they to whom it is given.

The Antithesis is that of the Papists, who deny that it is lawful for ministers of the church to take wives. Who object:

I. Everyone by right must be ἐγκρατὴς, or continent, and abstain from the embraces of a wife. Every Bishop is by right ἐγκρατὴς, or continent, Tit. I, 8. Therefore. Resp. 'Εγκράτεια, or continence, denotes temperance in food, drink, and sexual matters, and it also pertains to men living in marriage. For there is given, besides virgin and celibate chastity, also conjugal chastity.

II. No man that warreth for God entangleth himself with the affairs of this life, 2 Tim. II, 4. Every cleric warreth for God. Therefore. Resp. 1) In the place cited, it treats in general of a soldier, with whom any Christian warring under the banner of Christ is compared. 2) Distinguish between the moderate care of secular things and the immoderate. The Apostle does not prohibit the moderate care of secular things; otherwise no Bishop could rule his own house well, contrary to 1 Tim. III, 4: but he prohibits the immoderate and excessive solicitude by which one is ἐμπλέκεται, entangled and immersed in the affairs of this life, so that he cannot raise his mind to the love of God and divine things. Such immoderate care of this world disgraces the soldier of Christ.

III. It is the duty of those to pray always, it is their duty to abstain from marriage: But it is the duty of the Clergy to pray always: Therefore. The major is proved from 1 Cor. VII, 5, where the Apostle advises that pious men, for the sake of prayer, should abstain from conjugal use. The minor is proved: because the Clergy ought to pour out prayers for the church, for the magistrate, for the salvation of the hearers, 1 Tim. II, 2. Resp. 1) It is the duty of all Christians to pray without ceasing, 1 Thess. V, 17. Therefore, if this argument concludes validly, it is the duty of all Christians to abstain from marriage. 2) There is a …distinction between common or daily prayers, and solemn or public ones. The Apostle in the l.c. advises abstaining from conjugal use during the time of solemn prayers, which are poured out on account of public calamity or some very grave danger. This counsel (for it is no precept) is given to all, not to the ministers of the church alone. The reason for the persuasion is not the pollution of prayers by conjugal use, but greater rest and freedom from temporal affairs, so that the whole mind may be turned to God, and implore his aid for relieving public necessity.

IV. Whatever is not good, from that let Clerics abstain; to touch a woman is not good, 1 Cor. VII, 1. Therefore. Resp. Distinguish between moral good and useful good (*). When Paul in the l. c. says: It is good for a man not to touch a woman; then it is understood as useful good in a state of persecution, which he who has no wife or children can sustain more easily; but it is not understood as moral good, to which sin is opposed.

V. Those ministers of the church are praised by Christ who have castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven: Married ministers of the church have not castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven: Therefore. The major is evident from Matth. XIX, 12. Resp. 1) Not only celibacy is praised by Christ, but also marriage, as a state ordained by God v. 5. 6. Wherefore both the celibate and the married please God. 2) Those have castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of God who, endowed with a special gift of continence, abstain from marriage by a free and firm purpose, so that they may be able to be more expeditiously free for the propagation of the church, which is the kingdom of God. But from this a general rule is not to be established, according to which all Clerics are to be barred from marriage, since not all are continent, and it is better to marry than to burn.

VI. By marriage ecclesiastical duties are hindered: For marriage hinders a) the fervor of praying, in that it depresses the soul to earthly things; b) the efficacy of preaching; for how will he effectively exhort widows and virgins, who is perpetually occupied with children? c) the care of the poor; since the married look out only for their own children: d) the dispensation of the Sacraments; because between laymen and married Clerics there is no distinction. Resp. a) The impediments which are alleged are fictitious. For the Priests of the old testament were also married, and yet they poured out prayers, took care of the poor, and dispensed the sacraments. b) The distinction between laymen and Clerics does not consist in marriage and celibacy, but in the different office.

Latin:

Quæst. IX. An ministris ecclesiæ matrimonium inire licet?

Ministris ecclesiæ matrimonium inire, & in eo viuere licet.

Obs. I. Non quæritur: an omnes, qui in munere ecclesiastico constituti sunt, vxorati esse debeant? si quidem a nobis non vituperantur ecclesiæ ministri, qui dono continentiæpræditi in cælibatu sancte casteque vivunt, cum cælibes curis huius sæculi non valde distracti, officio ecclesiastico expedite perfungi queant, 1 Cor. VII, 1.

Obs. II. Non quæritur: an vita cælebs sit bona & utilis, præsertim tempore persecutionis? sed: an sit necessaria?

Prob. a. 1) Apostoli Clericis, sive ecclesiæ ministris, matrimonium concesserunt. Ergo illis non est prohibitum, neque constitutione ecclesiastica illis prohiberi potest. Antecedens probatur ex 1 Tim. III, 2. Oportet Episcopum esse irreprehensibilem, unius mulieris maritum. Vbi per mulierem non intelligitur ecclesia, cuius sponsus non est minister, sed ipse Christus; verum uxor, in propria domo gignens liberos honeste educandos, v. 4. Conf. Tit. I, 5. 6. Ratio consequentiæ est: quia ecclesiæ non convenit leges ferre, aut aliquid constituere contra doctrinam apostolorum.

2) Apostoli conjugium sibi licitum esse putarunt, quorum nonnulli in eodem vixerunt. Ergo illud ecclesiæ ministris perperam prohibetur. Antecedens probatur ex 1 Cor. IX, 5. Nonne habemus potestatem sororem uxorem circumducendi? sicut etiam reliqui Apostoli, & fratres Domini, etiamque Kephas.

3) Conjugium in omnibus honorabile est, Hebr. XIII, 4. Ergo in Clericis non potest reprehendi, multo minus iisdem prohiberi.

4) Qui dono continentiæ non pollent, ab Apostolo iubentur matrimonium contrahere: Atqui multi ministri ecclesiæ &c. Ergo. Maior probatur ex 1 Cor. VII, 2. Propter fornicationes (vitandas) habeat quisque uxorem. Minor clara est, Matth. XIX, 11. Non omnes capiunt verbum hoc, sed quibus datum est.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, negantium, licere ministris ecclesiæ uxores ducere. Qui obiiciunt:

I, Omnis de iure ἐγκρατὴς, sive continens, ab uxoris amplexibus abstineat. Omnis Episcopus est de iure ἐγκρατὴς, sive continens, Tit. I, 8. Ergo. Resp. 'Εγκράτεια, sive continentia, notat temperantiam in cibo, potu, & re venerea, & competit etiam hominibus in coniugio viventibus. Datur enim præter castitatem virginem & cælibem, castitas etiam coniugalis.

II. Nemo militans Deo implicat se huius vitæ negotiis, 2 Tim. II, 4. Omnis clericus militat Deo. Ergo. Resp. 1) Loco cit. in genere agitur de milite, cum quo quilibet Christianus sub vexillo Christi militans comparatur. 2) Dist. inter curam rerum sæcularium moderatam, & immoderatam. Apostolus non prohibet moderatam rerum sæcularium curam; alias nullus Episcopus domui suæ bene præesse posset, contra 1 Tim. III, 4: sed prohibet immoderatam & nimiam sollicitudinem, qua quis ἐμπλέκεται, implicatur & immergitur negotiis huius vitæ, vt ad amorem Dei, & rerum divinarum animum erigere nequeat. Immoderata eiusmodi cura huius sæculi militem Christi dedecet.

III. Quorum est, semper orare, illorum est, a coniugio abstinere: Atqui Clericorum est, semper orare: Ergo. Maior probatur ex 1 Cor. VII, 5. vbi Apostolus suadet, vt homines pii, propter preces, ab vsu coniugali abstineant. Minor probatur: quia Clerici preces fundere debent pro ecclesia, pro magistratu, pro salute auditorum, 1 Tim. II, 2. Resp. 1) Omnium Christianorum est, indesinenter orare, 1 Thess. V, 17. Ergo, si hoc argumentum valide concludit, omnium Christianorum est, a coniugio abstinere. 2) Dist. est inter preces communes, sive quotidianas, & solemnes, sive publicas. Suadet Apostolus l. c. abstinere ab vsu coniugali, tempore precum solemnium, quæ funduntur ob publicam calamitatem, vel gravissimum aliquod periculum. Hoc consilium (neque enim præceptum est) omnibus datur, non solis ecclesiæ ministris. Suasionis ratio non est precum pollutio per vsum coniugalem, sed maior quies & vacatio a rebus temporalibus, vt tota mens conuertatur ad Deum, & eius opem imploret ad subleuandam necessitatem publicam.

IV. Quidquid non est bonum, ab eo Clerici abstineant; Mulierem tangere, non est bonum, 1 Cor. VII, 1. Ergo. Resp. Dist. inter bonum morale, & vtile (*). Quando Paullus l. c. inquit: Bonum est homini, mulierem non tangere; tunc intelligitur bonum vtile in statu persecutionis, quam facilius sustinere potest, qui non habet vxorem, aut liberos; non autem intelligitur bonum morale, cui peccatum opponitur.

V. Illi ministri ecclesiæ laudantur a Christo, qui se castrarunt propter regnum cælorum: Ministri ecclesiæ vxorati se non castrarunt propter regnum cælorum: Ergo. Maior patet ex Matth. XIX, 12. Resp. 1) Laudatur a Christo non tantum cælibatus, sed etiam coniugium, tanquam status a Deo ordinatus v. 5. 6. Quare tam cælibes, quam vxorati Deo placent. 2) Illi seipsos castrarunt propter regnum Dei, qui speciali continentiæ dono præditi, libero firmoque proposito a coniugio abstinent, vt expeditius vacare queant ecclesiæ, quæ est regnum Dei, propagandæ. At exinde non est constituenda regula generalis, iuxta quam omnes Clerici a coniugio arceantur, cum non omnes sint continentes, & melius sit nubere, quam vri.

VI. Per coniugium impediuntur munera ecclesiastica: Impedit enim coniugium a) ardorem precandi, eo, quod animam deprimit ad terrena; b) efficaciam prædicationis; quomodo enim efficaciter viduas & virgines hortabitur, qui liberis perpetuo dat operam? c) curam pauperum; quoniam coniugati propriis liberis tantum prospiciunt: d) Sacramentorum dispensationem; quia inter laicos & Clericos vxoratos non datur discrimen. Resp. a) Quæ obtenduntur impedimenta, commentitia sunt. Nam & Sacerdotes veteris testamenti vxorati erant, & tamen fundebant preces, gerebant curam pauperum, dispensabant sacramenta. b) Discrimen inter laicos & Clericos non consistit in coniugio & cælibatu, sed in diuerso officio.


### Q. X. What is consanguinity, the closer degrees of which impede marriage?

Consanguinity is the bond of persons descending from the same stock, contracted by carnal propagation, of which there are distinct lines and diverse degrees.

Latin:

Consanguinitas est vinculum personarum, ab eodem stipite descendentium, carnali propagatione contractum, cuius distinctæ sunt lineæ, diuersique gradus.


### Q. XI. What is a line?

A line is a series of persons descending from one another, containing degrees and distinguishing numbers: It is divided into a direct line and a collateral or transverse one. The direct is between persons, one of whom descends from the other, and it is called now ascending, now descending. In the ascending there is a progression from the begotten to the begetters, in the descending from the begetters to the begotten. The collateral is between persons placed to the side, who are not generated from one another, yet meet in one stock: It is divided into equal, which is between persons equally distant from the common stock, and unequal, which is between related persons, one of whom stands closer, the other more remotely from the common stock. A degree is the distance of one person from another, made through generation.

Latin:

Linea est series personarum ab inuicem descendentium, gradus continens, numerosque distinguens: Diuiditur in lineam rectam, & collateralem, siue transversam. Recta est inter personas, quarum vna ab altera descendit, eaque nunc ascendens, nunc descendens vocatur. In ascendente fit progressus a genitis ad generantes, in descendente a generantibus ad genitos. Collateralis est inter personas e latere positas, quæ non ab inuicem generatæ, in vno tamen stipite concurrunt: Diuiditur in æqualem, quæ est inter personas æqualiter distantes a communi stipite, & inæqualem, quæ est inter personas cognatas, quarum vna proaltera remotius a communi stipite distat. Gradus est distantia vnius personae ab alia, per generationem facta.


### Q. XII. By what method is a degree counted?

The method of counting degrees is done either according to civil law, or according to canon law. The single and perpetual rule of civil law is: As many as are the generations, so many are the degrees a). But of canon law there are three rules. The first rule for the direct line is this: As many as are the persons (in the series of generation), so many are the degrees, one being subtracted b). The second rule for the equal collateral line is this: By as many degrees as persons stand from the common stock, by so many degrees do they stand from each other c). The third rule for the unequal collateral line is this: In an unequal transverse line, persons stand apart from each other by as many degrees as that person stands apart who is more remote from the stock d).

Prob. a. According to civil law, the method of computing in a direct line is brief and accurate, in which it agrees with canon law: but in a collateral line, the calculation of canon law is more accurate, because civil law in a transverse line posits a second degree without a first. The worn-out verses deserve to be noted here: Through the straight thread both laws agree: But through the transverse, the legal laws exceed.

It is illustrated by an example Of Terah: Abraham. Nahor. Isaac. Bethuel. Jacob. Rebecca. According to civil law, Rebecca stands from Terah in the third degree, but Jacob and Rebecca stand in the sixth degree.

Prob. b. According to canon law in a direct line, degrees are counted according to the persons considered not simply, but with respect to generation. For, the stock being posited, as many as are added to that person through generation, so many are the degrees. The rule of civil law means the same: as many as are the generations, so many are the degrees.

You say: It is like a monster, that in canonical calculation the common stock is subtracted, without which generations cannot exist. Resp. In the numbering of degrees, the common stock is subtracted, because a degree is the distance of one person from another. But the second person begins to stand apart first, and thus also makes the first degree. Wherefore between the first two persons there is the first and only one degree.

Prob. c. According to canon law, Jacob and Rebecca differ by the third degree, because in the numbering of degrees, persons are not to be considered among themselves and by themselves (as is done in civil calculation), but in order to the common stock, in which kinship is founded.

Prob. d. According to canonical computation, Rebecca and Abraham stand in the third degree in an unequal collateral line. The reason is: because it cannot happen that any person is closer to their blood relative than to their own stock: which, however, would happen, unless the denomination were made from the more remote one.

Latin:

Ratio numerandi gradus fit vel secundum ius ciuile, vel secundum ius canonicum. Iuris ciuilis regula vnica & perpetua est: Quot sunt generationes, tot sunt gradus a). Iuris vero canonici tres sunt regulae. Prima regula pro linea recta haec est: Quot sunt personae (in serie generationis), tot sunt gradus, vna demta b). Altera regula pro linea collaterali aequali haec est: Quot gradibus distant personae a communi stipite, tot gradibus inter se distant c). Tertia regula pro linea collaterali inaequali haec est: In linea transuersa inaequali tot gradibus personae inter se distant, quot gradibus distat illa, quae a stipite est remotior d).

Prob. a. Secundum ius ciuile breuis & accurata est computandi ratio in linea recta, in qua concordat cum iure canonico: in linea vero collaterali accuratior est supputatio iuris canonici, quia ius ciuile in linea transuersa ponit gradum secundum sine primo. Notari hic merentur triti versus: Per filum rectum concordant vtraque iura: At per transuersum superant legalia iura.

Illustratur exemplo Tharae: Abraham. Nahor. Isaac. Bethuel. Iacob. Rebecca. Secundum ius ciuile Rebecca a Thara distat tertio gradu, sed Iacob & Rebecca distant sexto gradu.

Prob. b. Secundum ius canonicum in linea recta numerantur gradus iuxta personas consideratas non simpliciter, sed respectu generationis. Supposito enim stipite, quot per generationem ipsi personae accedunt, tot sunt gradus. Idem vult regula iuris ciuilis: quot sunt generationes, tot sunt gradus.

Dicis: Monstro simile est, in supputatione canonica demi communem stipitem, sine quo generationes esse nequeant. Resp. In numeratione graduum communis stipes demitur, quia gradus est distantia vnius personae ab alia. Secunda autem persona primo incipit distare, adeoque etiam primum gradum facit. Quare inter duas primas personas est primus & vnus tantum gradus.

Prob. c. Secundum ius canonicum Iacob & Rebecca differunt tertio gradu, quia in numeratione graduum non considerandae sunt personae inter se & per se (sicut fit in supputatione ciuili), sed in ordine ad communem stipitem, in quo cognatio fundatur.

Prob. d. Secundum computationem canonicam Rebecca & Abraham distant tertio gradu in linea collaterali inaequali. Ratio est: quia fieri non potest, vt vlla persona sit propinquior suo consanguineo, quam suo stipiti: id quod tamen fieret, nisi a remotiore fieret denominatio.


### Q. XIII. What is affinity, and what are its kinds and degrees?

Affinity is the conjunction of different kinships arising from marriage, through which the blood relatives of the husband become the relatives by affinity of the wife, and the blood relatives of the wife become the relatives by affinity of the husband. The kinds of affinity are three: The affinity of the first kind is that which is contracted by means of one person joined through carnal copulation; of the second kind, that which is contracted by means of two persons, through as many marriages; of the third kind, that which is contracted by means of three persons, and as many marriages. Degrees in affinity, in and of themselves and properly speaking, do not exist; but there are only quasi-degrees, concerning which there is the rule: In whatever degree of kinship blood relatives are joined to the husband, in that same degree they are joined to his wife, and vice versa.

Proof a. My brother-in-law, i.e., the husband of my sister, is my relative by affinity in the first kind. But if my brother-in-law, after my sister is deceased, marries another wife, she becomes my relative by affinity in the second kind. And if the other wife of my brother-in-law, after this husband has died (who by his first marriage had joined my sister to himself), marries another, he becomes my relative by affinity in the third kind.

Proof b. One relative by affinity does not descend from another: Therefore, in affinity, properly speaking, there are no degrees.

Proof c. Husband and wife become one flesh through marriage: Therefore, those who are blood relatives of the husband become also, as it were, blood relatives of the wife herself, i.e., relatives by affinity: and those who are blood relatives of the wife, they also become relatives by affinity, or quasi-blood relatives, to the husband. Wherefore, the computation of degrees in the tree of affinity is no different than that of consanguinity. He who is joined to the husband in the first degree of consanguinity is the wife’s relative by affinity in the first degree of affinity, and vice versa.

Latin:

Affinitas est coniunctio diversarum cognationum proveniens ex nuptiis, per quas consanguinei mariti fiunt affines uxoris, & consanguinei uxoris fiunt affines mariti. Genera affinitatis sunt tria: Primi generis affinitas est, quae mediante una persona per copulam carnalem iuncta contrahitur; secundi generis, quae mediantibus duabus personis, per totidem nuptias; tertii generis, quae mediantibus tribus personis, totidemque nuptiis contrahitur . Gradus in affinitate, per se & proprie, nulli sunt ; sed tantum quasi gradus, de quibus est regula: Quoto gradu cognationis consanguinei iunguntur marito, toto gradu iunguntur ipsius uxori, & vice versa .

Prob. a. Sororius meus, i. e. sororis meae maritus, est mihi affinis in primo genere. At si sororius meus, post sororem meam defunctam, aliam ducat uxorem, ea mihi fit affinis in secundo genere. Quod si altera uxor sororii mei, defuncto hoc marito (qui primis nuptiis sibi copulaverat sororem meam), alteri nubat, is mihi evadet affinis in tertio genere.

Prob. b. Affinium unus ab altero non descendit: Ergo in affinitate proprie loquendo non dantur gradus.

Prob. c. Maritus & uxor per nuptias fiunt una caro: Ergo qui mariti sunt consanguinei, ipsius etiam uxoris fiunt quasi consanguinei, i. e. affines: & qui consanguinei sunt uxoris, illi etiam marito fiunt affines, seu quasi consanguinei. Quare non alia est computatio graduum in arbore affinitatis, quam consanguinitatis. Qui iunctus est marito in primo gradu consanguinitatis, is est uxoris affinis in primo gradu affinitatis, & contra.


### Q. XIV. Which degrees of consanguinity are prohibited and impede marriages?

Among blood relatives in the direct line, marriages are prohibited to infinity by divine and natural law. In the equal collateral line, marriages are prohibited in the first degree by both divine and natural law. By positive ecclesiastical law, they are prohibited also in the second degree. In the unequal collateral line, marriages are prohibited in the second degree by divine and natural law. But by ecclesiastical law, they are prohibited also in the third degree: indeed, even in the fourth degree, if one person is distant from the common stock by only one degree.

Proof a. In the direct line, blood relatives stand as parents and children, although not all are parents from whom children immediately descend. That marriage cannot exist between parents and children is taught both by divine law, Levit. XVIII, 7, and by the law of nature, which dictates that children owe filial reverence to their parents, which expires between children and parents if a marriage is contracted between them. Indeed, the very instinct of nature also abhors such a conjunction. Whence, among all Gentiles, such marriages have always been held as illicit. From which we conclude that Adam, if he were recalled to this life, could marry no woman from his descendants.

Prob. b. That marriage between brothers and sisters is prohibited by divine law is clear from Leviticus 18:9. This very degree is also prohibited by the law of nature. For children are something of their parents and a part of their flesh, and therefore just as they are one flesh with their parents adequately; so they themselves are one flesh with each other, although not immediately, but mediately. Hence the nations, by the guidance of the light of nature, abstained from such a marriage.

Prob. c. Marriage between first cousins is not prohibited by divine law; because unity of flesh in one progenitor is not found between them; except remotely. However, the church prohibits this degree, so that men may be kept further away from marriages prohibited by divine and natural law.

Prob. d. The second degree of consanguinity is prohibited by divine law, Lev. 18:12, ch. 20:19, and by natural law: because such persons are flesh with a common stock, although inadequately. Moreover, that prohibition is valid not only regarding the persons expressly named, but also others equally distant.

Prob. e. When one of the persons to be joined is immediately under the stock, a paternal respect impedes the marriage. For that person, just as he is one flesh with a brother or sister on account of one parent; so he is in the place of a father or mother to those descending from the brother or sister.

Question XV.

Which degrees of affinity are prohibited and impede marriages?

In whatever degree of consanguinity marriages are prohibited, in that same degree of affinity they are considered prohibited. Therefore, in the direct line of affinity, they are prohibited simply and to infinity, a) in the equal collateral line, those related by affinity in the first degree are kept from marriage. b) In the unequal collateral line, marriages of those related by affinity in the second degree are prohibited.

Prob. a. God, through Moses in Leviticus 18:18, seriously prohibited marriage with a stepmother, v. 15 with a daughter-in-law, v. 17 with a stepdaughter. In the remaining degrees of the direct line, the same interdict holds, on account of the respect of parentage.

Prob. b. Leviticus 18:16, marriage with the widow of a deceased brother is prohibited. Therefore, marriage with the husband of a deceased sister is also prohibited on account of the identity of the foundation, so that no one may approach any person near in flesh.

There is an antithesis of the Papists, who deny that the degrees of consanguinity are prohibited by natural law. Their chief argument is: Natural law is indispensable: The law concerning the degrees of consanguinity impeding matrimony is not indispensable: Therefore, it is not natural law. The minor is proved because God in the beginning of the world dispensed regarding the marriage of the sons and daughters of Adam, who were brothers and sisters.

Resp. 1) Just as Adam, and not only he, but also his sons, had received the divine command to multiply the human race: so, in order to obey this command, they could not take other women as wives than their own sisters, on account of the extreme case of necessity, upon the ceasing of which, the dispensation or divine permission also ceased. 2) The degrees of consanguinity are unequal, and unequally against the law of nature.

Those that are in the ascending and descending line pertain closely to the law of nature, but the others do so remotely.

3) The law of nature is indispensable regarding first principles and conclusions closer to first principles: but in more remote conclusions, on account of certain circumstances, there is no doubt that God can dispense [*].

Latin:

Inter consanguineos in linea recta matrimonia in infinitum prohibita sunt iure divino & naturali . In linea collaterali aequali tam iure divino, quam naturali, prohibita sunt matrimonia in primo gradu . Iure ecclesiastico positivo prohibentur etiam in secundo gradu . In linea collaterali inaequali prohibita sunt matrimonia in gradu secundo, iure divino & naturali . Sed iure ecclesiastico prohibentur etiam tertio gradu: quin etiam in quarto gradu, si persona altera uno tantum gradu a communi stipite distet.

Prob. a. In linea recta consanguinei se habent, ut parentes & liberi, licet non omnes sint parentes, a quibus immediate liberi descendunt. Inter parentes autem & liberos matrimonium consistere non posse, docet tum ius divinum, Levit. XVIII, 7. tum ius naturae, quod dictat, liberos parentibus debere reverentiam filialem, quae inter liberos & parentes exspirat, si inter eos matrimonium contrahatur. Quin ipse instinctus naturae etiam a tali coniunctione abhorret. Unde apud omnes gentiles tales nuptiae pro illicitis semper habitae fuerunt. E quibus colligimus, Adamum, si in hanc vitam revocetur, nullam foeminam e posteris suis ducere posse.

Prob. b. Coniugium inter fratres & sorores iure diuino prohibitum esse, liquet ex Leuit. XVIII, 9. Hic ipse gradus etiam iure naturæ prohibitus est. Sunt enim liberi aliquid parentum & pars carnis eorum, adeoque sicut cum parentibus sunt vna caro adæquate; ita ipsi inter se sunt vna caro, licet non immediate, sed mediate. Hinc gentes ductu luminis naturæ a tali coniugio abstinuerunt.

Prob. c. Coniugium inter consobrinos non prohibetur iure diuino; quia inter illos vnitas carnis in vno generante non inuenitur; nisi remote. Prohibet tamen ecclesia hunc gradum, vt homines a coniugiis, iure diuino & naturali prohibitis, magis arceantur.

Prob. d. Gradus secundus consanguinitatis prohibetur iure diuino, Leu. XIIX, 12. cap. XX, 19. & naturali: quia eiusmodi personæ cum communi stipite sunt caro, licet inadæquate. Valet autem prohibitio illa non tantum quoad personas nominatim expressas, sed etiam alias æque distantes.

Prob. e. Quando vna ex personis iungendis immediate stipiti subest, respectus paternus coniugium impedit. Nam persona illa, sicut cum fratre, aut sorore vna caro est propter vnum parentem; ita descendentibus ex fratre, vel sorore patris, aut matris loco est.

Quæst. XV. Quinam gradus affinitatis prohibiti sunt, nuptiasque impediunt?

Quo gradu consanguinitatis prohibitæ sunt nuptiæ, eo etiam gradu affinitatis prohibite censentur.

Prohibentur itaque in linea recta affinitatis simpliciter & gradus pro in infinitum, a) in linea collaterali æquali affines in primo gradu a nuptiis arcentur. b) In linea collaterali inæquali coniugia affinium in secundo gradu prohibita sunt.

Prob. a. Deus per Mosen Leuit. XIIX, 18. coniugium cum nouerca v. 15. cum nuru v. 17. cum priuigna filia serio prohibuit. In reliquis gradibus lineæ rectæ idem valet interdictum, ob respectum parentelæ.

Prob. b. Leuit. XIIX, 16. coniugium cum defuncti fratris vidua prohibetur. Ergo etiam coniugium cum defunctæ sororis marito ob identitatem fundamenti, ne quis ad vllam personam carne propinquam accedat, interdictum est.

Antithesis est Pontificiorum, negantium, gradus consanguinitatis iure naturali esse prohibitos. Quorum palmarium argumentum est: Lex naturalis est indispensabilis: Lex de gradibus consanguinitatis matrimonium impedientibus non est indispensabilis: E. non est lex naturalis. Minor prob. quia Deus in primordio mundi dispensauit circa matrimonium filiorum & filiarum Adami, qui fuerunt fratres & sorores.

Resp. 1) Sicut Adam non solum, sed etiam filii eius mandatum diuinum acceperant de multiplicando genere humano: ita mandato huic obtemperaturi non poterant alias fœminas, quam proprias sorores ducere vxores, ob extremum necessitatis casum, quo cessante, cessauit etiam dispensatio, aut permissio diuina.

2) Gradus consanguinitatis sunt inæquales, & inæqualiter contra ius naturæ. Quot sunt in linea ascendente & descendente, illi proxime spectant ad ius naturæ, ceteri autem remote.

3) Indispensabilis est lex naturæ, quod prima principia & conclusiones primis principiis propiores: in conclusionibus autem remotioribus, ob certas quasdam circumstantias, Deum dispensare posse, nullum est dubium [*].


### Q. XVI. In what does the formal notion of marriage consist?

The form or formal notion of marriage consists in the conjugal bond, which is the mutual obligation of husband and wife to fidelity and conjugal duties .

Proof. The form of any thing is that by which, when it is posited, the thing itself is posited, and when it is removed, the thing itself is removed: But now, the mutual obligation of husband and wife to fidelity and conjugal duties being posited, marriage is posited, and that being removed, marriage is removed: Therefore that mutual obligation is the form of marriage.

Objection 1) Consent makes marriage: Therefore consent is its form. Response. When the form ceases, the thing of which it is the form ceases: But when consent ceases, marriage does not cease. For it often happens in practice that spouses no longer consent to mutual cohabitation, and desire to be separated, yet marriage is not dissolved.

Dic. 2) Carnal copulation consummates matrimony: Therefore it is its form. Response. Carnal copulation is a consequence of matrimony. But the conjugal bond is the form, since it endures, even when carnal copulation ceases.

Latin:

Forma seu ratio formalis coniugii consistit in vinculo coniugali, quod est mutua mariti & uxoris obligatio ad fidem & officia coniugalia .

Prob. Forma alicuius rei est, qua posita ponitur res ipsa, & sublata, tollitur res ipsa: Iam vero posita obligatione mutua mariti & uxoris ad fidem & officia coniugalia, ponitur coniugium, & ea sublata, tollitur coniugium: Ergo mutua illa obligatio est forma coniugii.

Dic. 1) Consensus facit coniugium: E. consensus est illius forma. Resp. Cessante forma, cessat res, cuius est forma: At cessante consensu, non cessat coniugium. Saepe enim usu venit, ut coniuges non amplius consentiant in mutuam cohabitationem, & segregari optent, nec tamen coniugium dissoluatur. Pertinet itaque consensus ad caussam efficientem matrimonii, cuius caussalitas est.

Dic. 2) Copula carnalis consummat matrimonium: E. est eius forma. Resp. Copula carnalis est consequens matrimonii. Vinculum autem coniugale est forma, cum illud perduret, cessante etiam copula carnali.


### Q. XVII. Is the conjugal bond indissoluble?

The conjugal bond of husband and wife, as long as they are survivors , is in itself indissoluble, both on account of mutual consent , and especially on account of divine institution . But per accidens, and on account of a supervening vice, sometimes divorce occurs, which is the separation of living spouses, arising from the dissolution of a legitimate and valid marriage, as regards the conjugal bond. The just causes of divorce are adultery and malicious desertion .

Obs. I. Divorce is so called from 'diverting' [diuertendo], because through divorce spouses 'divert' [diuertunt], that is, they go into different directions.

Obs. II. A distinction must be made between repudiation and divorce. Repudiation is a general term, and denotes the dismissal of both a betrothed woman and a wife: but divorce is a special term, and signifies only the dismissal of a wife.

Obs. III. God has never released anyone from the law. But those things which pertain to more abundant utility, to the distinguished excellence of men, and to the well-constituted order of the whole society of men, these have been determined by revealed laws (which they commonly call positive), but [they are] moral and common, or universal, by which all men are always bound, and the knowledge of which, from the age of Noah, has been carried to all nations by ancient and continuous tradition. As regards laws of this kind, there can be a certain singular reason why the Legislator might use his power of dispensing, as it is said, which is to be attributed to no one besides him.

Obs. III. Distinction between divorce properly and improperly so-called. Divorce, speaking properly, is the separation of living spouses, arising from the dissolution of a legitimate and valid marriage, which pertains to the matrimonial bond. For this reason, a) TERTULLIAN improperly calls death the divorce of soul and body. Death causes the dissolution of marriage, but not divorce. b) The separation of spouses regarding bed and board, on account of grave enmities, is improperly called divorce, since it is only a suspension of the acts of cohabitation and conjugal duty, with the bond of marriage remaining intact, so that neither spouse may enter into another marriage. c) The separation of persons whose nuptials are prohibited due to close degrees of consanguinity, or where there has been an error of person, or the impotence of one of the spouses, is not properly divorce, but only a declaration of nullity, because the marriage was not correctly contracted, nor ratified, valid, and legitimate.

Obs. IV. Distinction between active and passive divorce. The former is when the injured and innocent person initiates the divorce, or departs from the living spouse by voluntary separation. The latter is when the injured and innocent person suffers the divorce, against their will, and is abandoned by the spouse with whom they wished to cohabit longer. The sole cause of active divorce is adultery; the cause of passive divorce is malicious desertion.

Prob. a. That the matrimonial bond is dissolved by death is evident from Rom. VII, 2. 3. The law has dominion over a man for as long as he lives: for the woman who is under a husband is bound by the law to her living husband; but if the husband dies, she is released from the law of the husband. Wherefore, while the husband lives, she is called an adulteress if she becomes the wife of another man: but if the husband has died, she is free from the law, so that she is not an adulteress, even if she has become the wife of another man. From this apostolic pronouncement we learn that successive polygamy, by which one passes to second nuptials, is lawful.

Prob. b. Marriage is a contract by mutual consent for a partnership of life to be continued perpetually and throughout the whole of life: which contract, on account of the procreation of offspring and mutual aid in life, must be kept holy and inviolate.

Prob. c. Marriage is indissoluble, not only because of the mutual consent of the spouses; for if it had been contracted by consent alone, it could be dissolved by the mutual dissent of both: but chiefly because of the authority and institution of God, who said: A man shall leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and they shall be one flesh, Gen. II, 24. Therefore, what God has joined, let no man separate, Matth. XIX, 6.

Prob. d. 1) From the sentence of Christ, which is found in Matth. V, 32. Whoever shall put away his wife, except for the cause of fornication, makes her commit adultery, and whoever shall marry her that is put away, commits adultery. And Matth. XIX, 9. Whoever shall put away his wife, except for fornication, and shall marry another, commits adultery: and whoever marries her who is put away, commits adultery. Where, by the force of the exceptive proposition, two things are said: 1) He who repudiates a non-adulterous wife and marries another, commits adultery. 2) He who repudiates an adulterous wife and marries another, does not commit adultery. Therefore, according to the sentence of Christ, the bond of marriage between the living is dissolved by adultery, so that the injured party may justly repudiate the one who caused the injury.

2) From the nature of marriage, adultery in itself and directly is repugnant to the unity of flesh, and thus also to the substance of marriage, through which two become one flesh (not many into many fleshes): Gen. II, 24. For he who cleaves to a harlot becomes one flesh with the harlot, 1 Cor. VI, 16, and thus is no longer one flesh with the spouse. Where, however, one must distinguish between the cause just and necessary, or obligatory. For why, by the example of the Divine, might not the injured party be reconciled to the injurer, and the latter be received into the bosom of grace? says Dannhaver in his Theol. conscient., p. 808.

Prob. e. That malicious desertion releases the innocent party from the bond is proved 1) by the testimony of the Apostle, 1 Cor. VII, 15. But if the unbeliever depart, let him depart. A brother or a sister is not under bondage in such cases, so that it is not lawful for him to take another, or to marry another; but he or she becomes free from the bond and obligation to conjugal fellowship with the deserter, or desertress.

2) From the nature of divorce. Whatever immediately injures the conjugal faith itself and the use of the marriage bed, dissolves the conjugal bond, and thus opens the doors of a second marriage to the innocent party by the law itself: But malicious and incorrigible desertion does so, etc. Therefore.

3) From the absurd. Unless the deserted person is granted the power of a new marriage, they will be deprived of their right without any fault of their own, and will be exposed to perpetual burnings and the danger of fornication and pollution, which is repugnant to equity and divine law. For to avoid fornication, let every man have his own wife, 1 Cor. VII, 2.

Antithesis of the Papists, who maintain: 1) That true and properly so-called divorce has no place among the faithful of the New Testament: 2) That there are very many causes for divorce improperly so-called, or separation from bed and board.

Their chief arguments are: I. Whatever is a union of one male and one female that is indissoluble, its bond cannot be divided: But marriage is such, etc. Therefore. Resp. Marriage is a union, in itself indissoluble, by virtue of divine institution; but it is accidentally dissoluble, through adultery and malicious desertion.

Instantia I. Only adultery is a cause of divorce, as Christ teaches, Matth. XIX, 9. Resp. Only adultery is a cause of active divorce; malicious desertion is a cause of passive divorce.

Instantia II. Persistent denial of the conjugal debt is also a cause of divorce. Therefore there are more causes than adultery and malicious desertion. Resp. Persistent denial of the conjugal debt is equivalent to malicious desertion; because the spouse immediately injures the conjugal faith, and exposes the use of the bed and the injured person to the danger of fornication.

II. Whatever marriage is duly contracted and consummated, it cannot be dissolved without the mark of adultery: But the marriage of the faithful is such, etc. Therefore. The minor is proved from Mark X, 11. Whosoever shall put away his wife, and marry another, committeth adultery. Resp. The words of Christ are not to be understood absolutely, but restrictively; therefore, because the restriction or limitation is most clearly expressed, Matth. XIX, 9. Whosoever shall put away his wife, who has not broken the covenant of marriage by fornication, he committeth adultery.

Latin:

Vinculum coniugale mariti & uxoris, quamdiu superstites sunt , in se est indissolubile, cum ob mutuum consensum , tum inprimis ob institutionem diuinam . Per accidens autem, & ob superueniens vitium, quandoque fit diuortium, quod est separatio coniugum viuentium, ex dissolutione coniugii legitimi & validi, quoad vinculum coniugale, proueniens. Caussae iustae diuortii sunt adulterium & malitiosa desertio .

Obs. I. Diuortium dicitur a diuertendo, quia per diuortium coniuges diuertunt, hoc est in diuersas partes eunt.

Obs. II. Distinguendum est inter repudium, & diuortium. Repudium est nomen generale, & notat dimissionem cum sponsae, tum uxoris: diuortium vero est nomen speciale, significat tantum dimissionem uxoris.

Obs. III. Deus neminem unquam lege soluit. Quae autem ad uberiorem utilitatem, ad insignem hominum praestantiam, ad bene constitutum ordinem universae hominum societatis spectant, ea determinata sunt legibus reuelatis (quas vulgo positiuas nominant) sed, moralibus & communibus, siue uniuersalibus, quibus omnes homines semper obligati sunt, & quarum notitia, inde a Noachi aetate, antiqua & continua traditione ad omnes gentes perlata est. Ad eiusmodi leges quod attinet, singularis quaedam ratio esse potest, quam ob rem Legislator sua potestate dispensandi, ut dicitur, praeter eum nemini adferenda, vtatur.

Obs. III. Dist. inter divortium proprie, & improprie dictum. Divortium proprie loquendo est separatio coniugum viventium, ex dissolutione coniugii legitimi & validi, quod ad vinculum coniugale proveniens. Quam ob rem a) TERTULLIANUS mortem improprie vocat animae & corporis divortium. Mors dissolutionem matrimonii, non autem divortium facit. b) Separatio coniugum quoad torum & mensam, ob inimicitias graviores, improprie vocatur divortium, cum sit tantum suspensio actuum cohabitationis & officii coniugalis, vinculo coniugii salvo manente, ut neuter coniux aliud matrimonium inire queat. c) Non est proprie divortium separatio personarum, quarum nuptiae ob gradus propinquos consanguinitatis prohibitae sunt, aut ubi error personae, aut alterius coniugis impotentia intercessit, sed tantum declaratio nullitatis, quod non recte contractum sit coniugium, non ratum, validum & legitimum.

Obs. IV. Dist. inter divortium activum, & passivum. Illud est, quando persona laesa & innocens facit divortium, sive voluntaria separatione a coniuge vivente discedit. Hoc est, quando persona laesa & innocens patitur divortium, invita, & derinquitur a coniuge, cui cohabitare diutius volebat. Divortii activi unica causa est adulterium, passivi causa est malitiosa desertio.

Prob. a. Morte dissolvi vinculum coniugale, constat ex Rom. VII, 2. 3. Lex dominatur homini, per quantum tempus vivit: quae namque sub viro mulier est, viventi viro obligata est lege; quod si moriatur vir, absoluta est a lege viri. Quare vivente viro, moecha appellatur, si fiat uxor alterius viri: quod si mortuus fuerit vir, libera est a lege, ita ut non sit moecha. etiam si facta fuerit alterius viro (uxor.) Ex hoc effato apostolico discimus, polygamiam successivam, qua ad secundas nuptias transitur, esse licitam.

Prob. b. Contractum est coniugium per mutuum consensum de perpetuo & per omnem vitam continuando vitae consortio: qui contractus ob procreationem sobolis, & mutuum vitae adiutorium sancte & inviolate servandus est.

Prob. c. Indissolubile est matrimonium, non tantum ob mutuum coniugum consensum; si namque solo consensu contractum fuisset, mutuo utriusque dissensu solui posset: sed praecipue ob auctoritatem & institutionem Dei, qui dixit: Derelinquet vir patrem suum, & matrem suam, & adhaerebit uxori suae, & erunt in carnem unam, Gen. II, 24. Quidquid igitur Deus copulavit, homo ne separet, Matth. XIX, 6.

Prob. d. 1) Ex sententia Christi, quae habetur Matth. V, 32. Quisquis dimiserit uxorem suam extra causam scortationis, facit eam moechari, & quisquis repudiatam duxerit, moechatur. Et Matth. XIX, 9. Quicunque dimiserit uxorem suam, nisi ob fornicationem, & aliam duxerit, adulterium committit: & quicunque dimissam duxerit, adulterium committit. Vbi, vi propositionis exceptivae, duo dicuntur: 1) Qui repudiat uxorem non adulterantem, & ducit aliam, moechatur. 2) Qui repudiat uxorem adulterantem, & ducit aliam, non moechatur. E. ex sententia Christi vinculum matrimonii inter viventes, ut pars laesa laedentem iuste repudiare queat, adulterio solvitur.

2) Ex natura coniugii adulterium per se & directe repugnat unitati carnis, adeoque etiam substantiae coniugii, per quod duo in unam carnem fiunt (non plures in plures carnes): Gen. II, 24. Qui enim adhaeret scorto, etiam cum scorto una caro fit, 1 Cor. VI, 16. adeo que non amplius est una caro cum coniuge. Vbi tamen distinguendum est inter causam diuortii iustam, & necessariam, siue obligatricem. Quidni enim, exemplo Numinis, pars læsa possit lædenti conciliari, & hæc in gratiæ sinum receptari? inquit Dannhaver. in theol. conscient. p. 808.

Prob. e. Quod malitiosa desertio partem innocentem a vinculo soluat, probatur 1) ex testimonio Apostoli, 1 Cor. VII, 15. Quod si infidelis, separet se. Non seruituti addictus est frater, aut soror in talibus, vt non liceat ei aliam ducere, aut alteri nubere; sed liber, aut libera fit a vinculo atque obligatione ad consortium coniugale cum desertore, aut desertrice.

2) Ex natura diuortii. Quidquid fidem coniugalem ipsam, & vsum tori immediate lædit, soluit vinculum coniugale, adeoque parti innocenti fores secundi matrimonii iure ipso aperit: Atqui malitiosa & incorrigibilis desertio &c. Ergo.

3) Ex absurdo. Nisi desertæ personæ concedatur potestas noui matrimonii, iure suo absque omni culpa sua priuabitur, & perpetuis vstionibus, scortationis ac pollutionis periculo exponetur, quod æquitati & iuri diuino repugnat. Nam propter scortationes vitandas quilibet vxorem suam habeto, 1 Cor. VII, 2.

Antithesis Pontificiorum, statuentium: 1) Verum & proprie dictum diuortium inter fideles noui testamenti locum non habere: 2) Diuortii improprie dicti, siue separationis qua torum & mensam, plurimas dari caussas. Quorum potiora argumenta sunt:

I. Quidquid est vnius maris & vnius fœminæ coniunctio indissolubilis, illius vinculum diuidi non potest: Atqui coniugium &c. Ergo. Resp. Coniugium est coniunctio, in se indissolubilis, vi institutionis diuinæ; est autem per accidens dissolubilis, per adulterium & malitiosam desertionem.

Instantia I. Solum adulterium est caussa diuortii, docente Christo, Matth. XIX, 9. Resp. Solum adulterium est caussa diuortii actiui, malitiosa desertio est caussa diuortii passiui.

Instantia II. Pertinax debiti coniugalis abnegatio est etiam caussa diuortii. Ergo plures sunt caussæ, quam adulterium & malitiosa desertio. Resp. Pertinax debiti coniugalis abnegatio æquipollet malitiosæ desertioni; quia coniux immediate lædit fidem coniugalem, vsumque tori & personam læsam exponit periculo scortationis.

II. Quodcunque matrimonium rite contrahitur & consummatur, illud citra notam adulterii dissolui nequit: Atqui matrimonium fidelium &c. Ergo. Minor probatur ex Marc. X, 11. Qui dimittit vxorem, & aliam ducit, adulterium committit. Resp. Verba Christi non intelligenda sunt absolute, sed restricte; ideo, quod restrictio vel limitatio apertissime exprimitur, Matth. XIX, 9. Qui dimittit vxorem, quæ fornicatione fœdus, coniugii non fregit, is adulterium committit.


### Quæst. XVIII. What is the end of marriage?

The ultimate end of marriage is the glory of God . The intermediate end is either proper or accessory. The proper end is that which began immediately with the marriage itself, and is then the procreation of offspring, from which arises the propagation of the family, and the preservation of the church and the republic b), then mutual aid in life c). The accessory [end] is a remedy against wandering lusts d).

Prob. a. Just as the ultimate end of all of God's ordinances is the glory of God, so too is it for the ordinance of marriage. The general admonition of the Apostle looks to this, 1 Cor. X, 31. Do all things for the glory of God.

Prob. b. That the proper end of matrimony is the procreation of offspring, the author of marriage himself indicates, Gen. I, 28. Increase and multiply. By reason of this end, marriage is the seedbed of the church and the republic.

Prob. c. That the end of marriage is also mutual aid in life is clear from Gen. II, 18. It is not good for man to be alone: I will make him a helper.

Prob. d. A remedy against wandering lusts is an accessory end, which only by accident was added to marriage, namely in the state after the fall, concerning which the Apostle says, 1 Cor. VII, 2. Because of (avoiding) fornications, let every man have his own wife: and let every woman have her own husband.

Latin:

Finis coniugii vltimus est gloria Dei . Finis intermedius est vel proprius, vel accessorius. Proprius est, qui cum ipso statim coniugio cœpit, estque tum sobolis procreatio, e qua oritur familiae propagatio, & ecclesiae atque reipublicae conservatio b), tum mutuum vitae adiutorium c). Accessorius est remedium aduersus vagas libidines d).

Prob. a. Sicut omnium ordinationum Dei, ita quoque coniugalis ordinationis finis ultimus est gloria Dei. Huc spectat generalis admonitio Apostoli, 1 Cor. X, 31. Omnia in gloriam Dei facite.

Prob. b. Finem matrimonii proprium esse procreationem sobolis, ipse auctor coniugii indicat, Gen. I, 28. Crescite & multiplicamini. Ratione huius finis est coniugium seminarium ecclesiae & reipublicae.

Prob. c. Finem coniugii etiam esse mutuum vitae adiutorium, liquet ex Gen. II, 18. Non est bonum homini, esse solum: Faciam ei adiutorium.

Prob. d. Remedium aduersus vagas libidines est finis accessorius, qui per accidens tantum coniugio accessit, scilicet in statu post lapsum, de quo Apostolus inquit, 1 Cor. VIII, 2. Propter scortationes (vitandas) quilibet suam ipsius uxorem habeto: & quaelibet proprium virum habeto.


### Quaest. XIX. What are the duties of spouses?

The common duties of spouses are: to join together their minds, bodies, and resources a).

The duties of the husband are: to love his wife b), to govern c), to nourish d), and to protect e).

The proper duties of the wife are: to revere her husband, to obey him, and to do him good f).

Prob. a. By divine ordinance, there exists between spouses a communion of minds, bodies, and resources, concerning which see 1 Cor. VII, 3. Eph. V, 28. et seqq.

Prob. b. Wives are one flesh with their husbands, and therefore are to be loved. Prob.

c. Because the husband is the head of the wife, he should govern her in spiritual and temporal matters. Eph. V, 23. Prob. d. Let the husband nourish and cherish his wife, as his own flesh, Eph. V, 29. Prob.

e. A woman is a weaker vessel both in body and in mind, 1 Petr. III, 7. and therefore relies on the protection of her husband.

Prob. f. For the duties of wives, see Eph. V, 22. 1 Petr. III, 1.

Latin:

Officia coniugum communia sunt: animos, corpora & facultates coniungere a).

Officia mariti sunt: uxorem amare b), gubernare c), alere d), & protegere e).

Officia uxoris propria sunt: virum reuereri, ipsi obedire & benefacere f).

Prob. a. Ex ordinatione diuina intercedit inter coniuges communio animorum, corporum & facultatum, de qua vide 1 Cor. VII, 3. Eph. V, 28. seqq.

Prob. b. Vxores sunt cum viris una caro, adeoque sinere amandae. Eph. V, 28.

Prob. c. Quia maritus est caput uxoris, eandem gubernet in spiritualibus & temporalibus. Eph. V, 23. Prob. d. Maritus uxorem, tanquam carnem suam, nutriat & foueat, Eph. V, 29.

Prob. e. Mulier est vas infirmum & corpore & animo, 1 Petr. III, 7. ideoque nititur praesidio viri.

Prob. f. Officia uxorum descripta vide Eph. V, 22. 1 Petr. III, 1.


### Quaest. XX. What is paternal society?

Paternal society is the natural union of parents with children, divinely instituted for the education of offspring and the welfare of the whole family.

Latin:

Societas paterna est naturalis parentum cum liberis coniunctio, diuinitus instituta ad sobolis educationem & totius familiae salutem.


### Quaest. XXI. What are the duties of parents and children?

The duties of parents consist in the provision of food and clothing a) accordingly, and in honest education b). The duties of children consist in love, honor, and obedience c).

Prob. a.

It is the duty of parents to take care of their children, and to give them good gifts. Prob. b.

Children are to be brought up in the discipline and admonition of the Lord, Prob. c.

The duties of children are made known from the IV. commandment of the decalogue.

Question XXII.

What is the master-servant society?

The master-servant society is a legitimate union of masters and servants, divinely instituted, for mutual utility.

Question XXIII.

What are the duties of masters and servants?

It is the duty of masters to rule their servants, to provide them with necessary food, and to pay the promised wage: It is the duty of servants to honor their masters, to obey them, and to serve them faithfully.

Prob.

Paul has graphically described the duties of masters and servants, Cf.

Eph.

VI, 5.

SIGH To God the Father unbegotten, to God the Son only-begotten, to God the Holy Spirit proceeding from both, be praise and eternal glory for safety, for the strength of the body, for the gifts of the mind, and for the happy success of my labors!

Latin:

Officia parentum consistunt in suppeditatione victus & amictus a) iuxta, atque in honesta educatione b). Liberorum officia consistunt in amore, honore & obsequio c).

Prob. a.

Parentum est, curam gerere liberorum, iisque bona dare dona. Prob. b.

Educandi sunt liberi in disciplina et admonitione Domini, Prob. c.

Officia liberorum e praecepto IV. decalogi innotescunt.

Quaestio XXII.

Quae est societas herilis?

Societas herilis est legitima dominorum et servorum coniunctio, divinitus instituta, ob mutuam utilitatem.

Quaestio XXIII.

Quae sunt officia dominorum et servorum?

Dominorum est, servos regere, ipsis alimenta necessaria suppeditare, et promissam mercedem solvere: Servorum est, dominos honorare, ipsis obedire, atque fideliter servire.

Prob.

Officia dominorum et servorum graphice descripsit Paullus, Conf.

Eph.

VI, 5.

SUSPIRIUM Deo Patri ingenito, Deo Filio unigenito, Deo Spiritui S. ab utroque procedenti, fit pro incolumitate, pro viribus corporis, pro donis animi, pro felici laborum meorum successu, laus et gloria
